members.legal_issue: A cooperative forum may adjudicate a member's claim to recover premises from a former licensee when the dispute concerns the society's housing business and the parties do not stand in a landlord-tenant relationship.
material_facts: A housing society formed to provide accommodation to its members permitted an occupant to use a member's flat as a nominal member under a licence.
The member terminated the licence and sought eviction through a claim under the cooperative societies legislation.
The occupant resisted the claim by asserting that the arrangement was a lease and that the rent-control court had exclusive jurisdiction.
The cooperative courts found that the relationship was one of licensor and licensee and that the dispute touched the society's business.
members.legal_principle: Under section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, a dispute concerning the business of a housing society includes a claim by the society and a member to recover premises from a person permitted to occupy them as a nominal member after revocation of a licence. The provisions of the Bombay Rent Act, including section 28, govern matters involving the landlord-tenant relationship; they do not bar cooperative proceedings where the parties do not stand in that relationship. The Court applied O.P. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, [1982] 3 SCR 681.
members.conclusion: The cooperative courts had jurisdiction under section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, and section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act did not bar the proceedings.

rule.if: appeal_from_cooperative_eviction_award and housing_society_provides_member_accommodation and occupant_was_permitted_as_nominal_member_under_license and license_was_terminated and not landlord_tenant_relationship

predicates.appeal_from_cooperative_eviction_award: A party appealed an award directing an occupant to vacate premises after permission to occupy had ended.
predicates.housing_society_provides_member_accommod: The society was formed to provide residential accommodation to its members.
predicates.occupant_was_permitted_as_nominal_member: The society permitted the occupant to use a member's premises as a nominal member under a licence.
predicates.license_was_terminated: The member ended the occupant's permission to use the premises.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship: The parties stood in the legal relationship of landlord and tenant.

members.legal_issue: A cooperative court may hear a cooperative housing society’s possession dispute against a nominal member where the dispute touches the society’s business and the occupant has no landlord-tenant relationship protected by rent legislation.
material_facts: A tenant co-partner member and the cooperative housing society brought a proceeding to recover possession from an occupant who had been admitted as a nominal member.
The occupant’s licence had been terminated before the statutory eligibility date, so the occupant did not qualify for deemed-tenant protection under the rent legislation.
The dispute concerned the occupant’s continued possession of premises in a tenant co-partnership cooperative housing society.
members.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, covers qualifying disputes touching the business of a society between the parties described in that section. Section 28(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, does not bar such a proceeding where the parties do not stand in a landlord-tenant relationship protected by that Act. The Court relied on O.N. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas and Smt. Krishna Rajpal Bhatia v. Miss Leela H. Advani, and considered Deccan Merchants Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. M/s Dalichand Jugraj Jain. It distinguished Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Shyam Cooperative Housing Society because the occupant there was protected under the rent legislation.
members.conclusion: The possession dispute touched the business of the society, and the cooperative courts had jurisdiction; the rent legislation did not bar the proceeding.

rule.if: cooperative_housing_possession_dispute and occupant_was_a_nominal_member and licence_ended_before_eligibility_date and dispute_concerned_society_business

predicates.cooperative_housing_possession_dispute: A cooperative housing society and a member brought a proceeding to recover premises from an occupant.
predicates.occupant_was_a_nominal_member: The occupant had been admitted as a nominal member of the cooperative society.
predicates.licence_ended_before_eligibility_date: The permission to occupy had been terminated before the date on which the occupant had to be occupying under a subsisting licence to obtain rent-law protection.
predicates.dispute_concerned_society_business: The dispute concerned possession of premises in the cooperative housing society and the society’s relationship with its member and occupant.

members.legal_issue: A cooperative court has exclusive jurisdiction over a housing society’s possession dispute against occupants who claim through a member and whose occupation violates the society’s rules, when the dispute concerns the society’s business and the occupants are not statutory tenants.
material_facts: A housing society owned the flat and had allotted it to a member for residence.
The member permitted outsiders to occupy the flat as licensees without the society’s consent and contrary to its rules, bye-laws, and regulations.
The society sought possession from the member and the occupants, who claimed through the member.
The occupants were licensees, not statutory tenants, and the dispute concerned the society’s interest in having its flats occupied in accordance with its rules.
members.legal_principle: Section 91(1), including clause (b), covers disputes touching a society’s business where a party is a member or claims through a member; section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act gives the specified courts jurisdiction over landlord–tenant disputes concerning rent or possession. O.P. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, [1982] 3 SCR 681, supports treating proceedings by a housing society to remove an unauthorised occupant from a member’s flat as part of the society’s business, and harmonising the statutes by applying the Rent Act where the parties stand in a landlord–tenant relationship and section 91 where they do not. Deccan Merchants Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Dalichand Jugraj Jain, [1969] 1 SCR 887; Sabharwal Brothers v. Guna Amrit Thandani, [1973] 1 SCR 53; and I.R. Hingorani v. P.K. Shah, AIR 1972 SC 2161, were distinguished on their facts.
members.conclusion: The dispute fell within section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, and the cooperative court had exclusive jurisdiction; the Rent Act court did not.

rule.if: cooperative_society_possession_dispute and occupants_claim_through_member and dispute_touches_society_business and occupation_breaches_society_rules and occupants_are_not_statutory_tenants

predicates.cooperative_society_possession_dispute: A cooperative society brings a proceeding seeking possession of premises it owns or administers.
predicates.occupants_claim_through_member: The occupants derive their asserted right to occupy from a member of the society.
predicates.dispute_touches_society_business: The dispute concerns the society’s ordinary business or management, including ensuring that premises are occupied consistently with its rules.
predicates.occupation_breaches_society_rules: The member permitted the occupants to take possession contrary to the society’s rules or without required consent.
predicates.occupants_are_not_statutory_tenants: The occupants have not established statutory tenant status and do not stand in the relevant landlord–tenant relationship.

members.legal_issue: A claim to recover a housing-society flat from an occupant whose asserted status is that of a licensee, rather than a tenant, is not excluded from the cooperative forum merely because rent legislation gives certain courts exclusive jurisdiction over landlord–tenant disputes.
material_facts: The flat was held by a member of a tenant co-partnership housing society, which retained ownership and let flats to its members.
The member permitted the occupant to use the flat under a leave-and-licence agreement, and the society accepted the occupant as a nominal member.
The member alleged that the parties were licensor and licensee, and the agreement supported that characterization.
The licence was terminated and the occupant remained in possession.
In an earlier suit, the occupant’s claim to be a tenant was rejected, and that determination was not open to relitigation.
members.legal_principle: The exclusive jurisdiction conferred by section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 concerns claims arising between parties who have or had a landlord–tenant relationship; it does not confer exclusive jurisdiction over title or possession disputes involving a licensee or trespasser. The two enactments operate in distinct fields and should be harmonised by applying rent legislation to matters it covers. Jurisdiction is assessed on the claimant’s pleaded allegations, taken as true when the objection is in the nature of a demurrer, and the occupant bears the burden of establishing tenant status under section 5(11). The Court applied section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 and distinguished Deccan Merchants Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. M/s. Dalichand Jugraj Jain & Ors.; the earlier determination of the occupant’s status was also treated as res judicata under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
members.conclusion: The rent legislation did not bar the proceedings before the cooperative forum; because the parties did not stand in the relationship of landlord and tenant, the dispute was governed by the cooperative-society legislation.

predicates.cooperative_ejectment_proceeding: A housing society or its member brings a proceeding to recover a flat from an occupant.
predicates.claimant_pleads_license_relationship: The claimant alleges that the occupant entered under a licence rather than as a tenant.
predicates.occupant_fails_to_establish_tenant_statu: The occupant does not establish a landlord–tenant relationship that brings the dispute within rent legislation.

members.legal_issue: A housing society’s claim, joined with that of its member, to recover a flat from a former licensee whose permission to occupy has ended is a dispute touching the society’s business when providing member housing is its business and the society retains the relevant housing interest.
material_facts: The society was a tenant co-partnership housing society formed to provide residential accommodation to its members and retained ownership of the flat.
The member held the flat as a tenant-member under the society’s governing arrangements and could permit temporary occupation only in accordance with the society’s rules.
The occupant was admitted as a nominal member for the purpose of occupying the flat under a licence.
After the licence ended, the occupant remained in the flat without authorization, and the society joined the member’s claim for possession.
members.legal_principle: The expression “business of a society” in section 91(1) refers to the society’s actual trading, commercial, or similar activity authorized by its governing framework, as explained in Deccan Merchants Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. M/s. Dalichand Jugraj Jain & Ors. The society’s business must be identified by its objects and ordinary activities. For a tenant co-partnership housing society formed to provide homes to members, ensuring that a society-owned flat remains occupied in accordance with the society’s rules, including removing an unauthorized occupant after a licence ends, touches that business. Deccan Merchants was distinguishable because it concerned a cooperative bank and a dispute not between the society and a member or a person claiming through a member. Sabharwal Brothers v. Smt. Guna Amrit Thandani was also distinguished because the society there had sold the flat rather than letting it to the member under the applicable housing arrangements. Where a landlord–tenant relationship brings the matter within rent legislation, that legislation governs instead.
members.conclusion: The joint claim for ejectment was a dispute touching the business of the society within section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960.

rule.if: cooperative_dispute_proceeding and housing_society_business_is_member_accommodation and society_retains_interest_in_flat and occupant_entered_as_nominal_member_under_licence and licence_ended_and_occupant_remained

predicates.cooperative_dispute_proceeding: A claim is brought through the cooperative dispute-resolution process for possession of a housing unit.
predicates.housing_society_business_is_member_accom: The society’s object and ordinary activity include providing housing accommodation to its members.
predicates.society_retains_interest_in_flat: The society retains ownership or a comparable housing interest in the flat rather than having sold it outright.
predicates.occupant_entered_as_nominal_member_under: The society admitted the occupant as a nominal member so the occupant could use the member’s flat under a licence.
predicates.licence_ended_and_occupant_remained: The permission to occupy ended, but the occupant continued to remain in the flat.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should permit additional evidence that directly challenges the factual basis of the judgment when the application is relevant and the evidence is properly supported.
material_facts: The State applied during the appeal to introduce evidence that the sale transactions relied on below were collusive and that the claimants knew of the impending acquisition.
The proposed evidence directly challenged the foundation of the judgment under appeal.
The application was rejected without adequate reasons, and the relevant evidence was also before the Supreme Court in a companion appeal.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 governs additional evidence in appeals. In the circumstances described, evidence directly challenging the basis of the judgment should have been admitted; the Court considered the evidence because it was already part of the judicial record in the companion appeal.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have allowed the application to adduce the additional evidence.

predicates.civil_appeal_with_additional_evidence_ap: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which a party has applied to adduce additional evidence.
predicates.proposed_evidence_directly_challenges_ju: The proposed evidence challenges the factual foundation on which the judgment under appeal rests.
predicates.application_supported_by_relevant_materi: The application identifies relevant material supporting the proposed evidence.
predicates.application_rejected_without_adequate_re: The application was rejected without adequate reasons.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence when it requires that evidence to pronounce judgment, but a party has no right to produce additional evidence merely by seeking to do so.
material_facts: In an appeal, the High Court allowed registered sale deeds to be produced although they had not been produced at trial.
The High Court gave reasons for finding the deeds necessary to enable it to pronounce judgment.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had properly exercised its discretion.
members.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not confer a right on a party to introduce additional evidence. An appellate court may permit additional evidence when it requires a document to enable it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause; a properly exercised discretionary decision may be left undisturbed.
members.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to admit the sale deeds, and its decision to do so was not disturbed.

predicates.appeal_in_appellate_court: The proceeding is an appeal being heard by an appellate court.
predicates.party_seeks_additional_evidence: A party asks to introduce evidence that was not produced earlier.
predicates.appellate_court_requires_evidence_to_pro: The appellate court considers the evidence necessary to enable it to decide the appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_properly_exercises_discr: The appellate court gives a proper basis for exercising its discretion to admit the evidence.

members.legal_issue: Additional documentary evidence may be admitted at the first appellate stage when it is material to deciding the suit and the reason it was unavailable during trial is accepted.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to file additional documents during the first appeal, asserting that they had not been available during trial.
The first appellate court found the documents material and necessary for proper adjudication and accepted the explanation for their non-production at trial.
members.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits additional evidence in appeal when its requirements are met. Here, the evidence was found material and necessary, and the reason it could not be produced at trial was accepted; admitting it enabled a fair trial and substantial justice.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court was justified in admitting the additional documents to enable a fair trial and substantial justice.

rule.if: civil_first_appeal and additional_documents_material and documents_unavailable_at_trial and reason_for_unavailability_accepted

predicates.civil_first_appeal: A party sought to introduce further evidence in an appeal from a civil suit.
predicates.additional_documents_material: The appellate court found the further documents material and necessary to decide the suit properly.
predicates.documents_unavailable_at_trial: The party said the documents could not be filed during trial because they were unavailable.
predicates.reason_for_unavailability_accepted: The appellate court accepted the party's explanation for not filing the documents during trial.

members.legal_issue: Additional evidence may be received in an appeal when it is materially relevant to the issues and is needed for a complete and effective adjudication.
material_facts: In a civil appeal, the respondent sought to produce official records and public documents concerning the extent of the land and the parties’ competing claims to ownership or possession.
If proved, the documents could materially affect the issues and assist the appellate court in pronouncing judgment.
The documents were not in the respondent’s control or possession, and the High Court considered them necessary to determine the parties’ rights.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, additional evidence is not available as of right and may be admitted only within the statutory conditions, including where it is required by the appellate court to pronounce judgment or where the interests of justice make its admission imperative. The court must consider the evidence’s relevance, why it was not previously produced, the applicant’s diligence, and the need for it, and must give reasons. The Court applied Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin, (2012) 8 SCC 148.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in allowing the applications for additional evidence; the proposed evidence could be received subject to proof.

predicates.civil_appeal_with_additional_evidence_re: A party in a civil appeal asks the appellate court to receive evidence that was not produced earlier.
predicates.evidence_material_to_main_issues: The proposed evidence, if established, could materially affect the central issues in the case.
predicates.evidence_needed_for_appellate_judgment: The appellate court needs the proposed evidence to decide the issues and pronounce judgment effectively.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should not use its power to receive additional evidence to fill gaps in the prosecution’s case.
material_facts: At trial, the prosecution did not call a witness from the relevant office to establish when the first information report was received there, despite the disputed timing being material.
The High Court examined an office employee in the appeal to support the prosecution’s account of the report’s receipt.
The Supreme Court found that the prosecution had not attempted to produce that evidence at trial and that the appellate witness was unreliable.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court may have power to take additional evidence in a suitable case, but that discretion should not be exercised to fill gaps or lacunae in the prosecution evidence.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not correct to exercise its appellate discretion to examine the witness in these circumstances.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a criminal case.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_gap_at_trial: The prosecution did not present evidence at trial on a material point that it had an opportunity to prove.
predicates.appellate_court_takes_additional_evidenc: The appellate court receives evidence to supply the prosecution evidence missing from the trial record.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence establishing a material event that occurred after the decision below when considering it is necessary to determine the appeal justly.
material_facts: The probate was granted after the High Court had decided the appeal, so it could not have been produced there.
The appellants applied in the Supreme Court appeal to place the probate on the record.
The probate was a judgment in rem and concerned the appellants’ authority to pursue the mortgage claim.
The respondents objected that there was no specific provision for admitting additional evidence, that they had not been parties to the probate proceeding, and that the application was late.
members.legal_principle: Order 45, rule 5 of the Supreme Court Rules recognises the Court’s inherent power to make orders necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process. The Court relied on Indrajit Pratap Sahi v. Amar Singh for the power to admit evidence where sufficient grounds explain its earlier non-production, and on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, which approved the principle in Patterson v. State of Alabama that an appellate court may consider supervening changes in fact or law when determining what justice requires. A judgment in rem is not ineffective merely because the objecting respondents were not parties to it.
members.conclusion: The probate was admitted as additional evidence; the objections did not prevent its admission.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and additional_evidence_unavailable_below and material_event_occurred_after_lower_decision and evidence_is_judgment_in_rem and evidence_relevant_to_justice

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court from a lower court decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_unavailable_below: The party seeking admission could not produce the evidence in the court below.
predicates.material_event_occurred_after_lower_deci: The event established by the evidence occurred after the lower court decision.
predicates.evidence_is_judgment_in_rem: The evidence is a judgment that determines a matter with effect beyond the parties to the proceeding in which it was made.
predicates.evidence_relevant_to_justice: The evidence bears materially on the appellate court’s determination of what justice requires.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence only under a judicial, limited discretion, and should refuse it when it can decide the appeal on the existing material.
material_facts: The appellants applied to introduce additional documents and testimony in the appeal.
The Court was able to decide the appeal on the material already before it and found no inherent lacuna or obscurity requiring further evidence.
The Court considered that the application sought to fill gaps using revenue records that lower authorities had found spurious.
members.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines the appellate court’s discretion to admit additional evidence; the test is whether the court can pronounce judgment on the existing materials without the proposed evidence. The Court relied on Arjun Singh alias Puran v. Kartar Singh.
members.conclusion: The application to adduce additional evidence was rejected.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court is considering a matter in its appellate capacity.
predicates.additional_evidence_application: A party applies to introduce evidence that was not part of the existing record.
predicates.existing_record_sufficient: The court can decide the matter on the materials already before it without the proposed evidence.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot rely on additional evidence unless the governing conditions for admitting it are met and the reasons for its admission are recorded.
material_facts: During the hearing of the second appeal, the High Court directed a party to produce a grant document and relied on it.
The document had not been admitted as additional evidence through the prescribed procedure.
The High Court neither applied the conditions governing additional evidence nor recorded reasons for admitting it.
The finding that the property was family property and partible rested on the document and the resulting conclusion.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 27 CPC does not permit parties to produce additional evidence in an appellate court as a matter of course. Additional evidence may be allowed on the stated grounds, and Rule 27(2) requires the court to record reasons for its admission. The Court also held that a conclusion treating property as family property and partible cannot be reached without acceptable material considered through lawful procedure. No earlier case was cited for this issue.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s reliance on the document and its resulting finding that the property was partible family property could not be sustained.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and additional_evidence_relied_on and (admission_conditions_not_met or admission_reasons_not_recorded)

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court was deciding an appeal from a lower court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_relied_on: The appellate court relied on evidence that had not been part of the record before the lower court.
predicates.admission_conditions_not_met: The party or court did not satisfy the grounds required for admitting the additional evidence.
predicates.admission_reasons_not_recorded: The appellate court did not record reasons for admitting the additional evidence.

members.legal_issue: Additional evidence may be admitted in an appeal only when the requirements for doing so are established.
material_facts: The Wakf Board asked the courts to allow it to produce further documents, but had opportunities to produce them before both the trial court and the High Court.
The Board did not explain what the documents were or show that, despite due diligence, it could not produce them earlier.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a party to an appeal from producing additional evidence unless it shows that, despite due diligence, the evidence could not have been produced earlier and that the evidence is required to enable the court to pronounce a proper judgment.
members.conclusion: The Board was not entitled to adduce additional evidence, and the refusal to remand the matter was upheld.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and (earlier_opportunity_to_produce_evidence and not_due_diligence_shown) and (evidence_not_described or need_for_proper_judgment_not_shown)

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is before a court hearing an appeal.
predicates.earlier_opportunity_to_produce_evidence: The party had an opportunity to produce the evidence in the proceedings before the appeal.
predicates.not_due_diligence_shown: The party did not show that it could not have produced the evidence earlier despite due diligence.
predicates.evidence_not_described: The party did not identify the evidence it sought to produce.
predicates.need_for_proper_judgment_not_shown: The party did not show that the evidence was needed for the court to pronounce a proper judgment.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence when it requires the evidence to pronounce judgment or another substantial cause exists, and a proper exercise of that discretion will not be disturbed merely because the evidence was not produced at trial.
material_facts: The trial court awarded possession of certain lands because sale deeds had not been produced.
The appellate court admitted registered sale deeds under Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, giving reasons for considering them necessary to decide the appeal.
The appellate court relied on the deeds in allowing the appeal of the affected defendants.
members.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not give a party a right to produce additional evidence. It does, however, empower the appellate court to admit evidence where it requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. A properly exercised discretionary decision in the interest of justice is not to be interfered with.
members.conclusion: The appellate court properly admitted the sale deeds as additional evidence, and its decision to do so was not to be disturbed; once considered, the deeds defeated the possession decree that had rested only on their non-production.

predicates.appeal_before_appellate_court: The matter was an appeal before an appellate court.
predicates.appellate_court_requires_additional_evid: The appellate court considered additional evidence necessary to pronounce judgment or necessary for another substantial cause.
predicates.additional_evidence_is_material: The additional evidence was material to deciding the dispute.

members.legal_issue: An appellate authority in a rent-control appeal may admit additional evidence when further inquiry is warranted for fair disposal and the opposing party has a fair opportunity to address it.
material_facts: The landlord sought to introduce additional evidence in an appeal from the Rent Controller’s rejection of the eviction petition.
The pleadings did not clearly set out the allegation concerning the landlord’s sale of another house.
The parties had an opportunity to test and address the additional evidence, and the Court found no prejudice to the tenant.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(4) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 empowers the appellate authority to make further inquiry as it thinks fit, including by admitting additional evidence when the facts and pleadings warrant it. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K.M. Charia Abdullah & Co. for the principle that statutory power to make further inquiry supports such evidence-gathering for fair disposal of an appeal.
members.conclusion: The appellate authority had jurisdiction to admit the additional evidence, and its admission of that evidence was justified in the circumstances.

rule.if: rent_control_appeal and further_inquiry_authorized and evidence_warranted_for_fair_disposal and opposing_party_could_address_evidence and not unfair_prejudice

predicates.rent_control_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a rent-control authority’s decision in an eviction matter.
predicates.further_inquiry_authorized: The governing appeal process authorizes the appellate authority to make further inquiry.
predicates.evidence_warranted_for_fair_disposal: The facts and pleadings make the additional evidence relevant to fair disposal of the appeal.
predicates.opposing_party_could_address_evidence: The opposing party had an opportunity to test and make submissions about the additional evidence.
predicates.unfair_prejudice: The additional evidence caused unfair prejudice to the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court must permit additional evidence in an appeal against conviction when the evidence is necessary to decide the appeal and its exclusion risks a failure of justice.
material_facts: The accused appealed a conviction for cheating in connection with proposed sales of land held by a trust.

The trial record contained a photocopy of a trust deed, but the trial court did not consider it because it had not been proved; a related resolution authorising steps toward sale also had not been proved.
The trust deed and resolution were relevant to the basis for initiating the sale process and to assessing the accused’s intent.
The accused sought to place certified copies of the documents on the appellate record and to call a witness to prove them.
In a related prosecution arising from the same allegations and transaction, the trust deed and resolution were proved and the accused was acquitted.
members.legal_principle: Section 391(1) Cr.P.C. empowers an appellate court to take or direct additional evidence when it is necessary for deciding the appeal. Read with the appellate court’s powers under Section 386(b) Cr.P.C., the power is broad and must be exercised to secure justice; necessity is not confined to cases where judgment would otherwise be impossible, but includes cases where exclusion would risk a failure of justice. There is no fixed formula for necessity, and the power must be exercised sparingly and not as a disguise for retrial or to cause prejudice. Rajeswar Prasad Misra v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1965 SC 1887, and Rambhau v. State of Maharashtra, (2001) 4 SCC 759, apply these principles.
members.conclusion: The appellate court erred in rejecting the applications under Section 391 Cr.P.C. It must receive the trust deed and resolution and permit the accused to lead oral evidence, including at least one witness, to prove the contents of the deed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The person seeking to adduce evidence is pursuing an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.proposed_evidence_material_to_deciding_a: The proposed evidence bears on an issue the appellate court must decide.
predicates.existing_record_contains_only_unproved_c: The existing record contains only an unproved copy of a document relevant to the appeal.
predicates.proposed_documents_explain_basis_of_tran: The proposed documents explain the basis on which the transaction at the centre of the prosecution was initiated.
predicates.exclusion_would_leave_material_issue_une: Without the proposed evidence, a material issue in assessing the accused’s conduct or intent would remain unexamined.

members.legal_issue: A judgment from another land valuation proceeding may be considered as additional evidence only if its relevance is established and the appellate court follows the required reasoned procedure, including allowing an opportunity to rebut it.
material_facts: The High Court admitted as additional evidence a judgment concerning other land said to be adjacent to the lands in the appeals and acquired as part of the same layout scheme.
The judgment was not between the same parties and was not a judgment in rem; an appeal against it was pending.

The acquiring authority had no opportunity to show that the other land differed in location or value, and the High Court gave no reasons demonstrating that it had considered whether admission was necessary.
members.legal_principle: Under section 43 of the Evidence Act, judgments outside sections 40 to 42 are irrelevant unless relevant under another provision of the Act. A judgment from another proceeding is not res judicata between different parties and is not a judgment in rem, but Khaja Fizuddin v. State of Andhra Pradesh recognizes possible relevance where it concerns similarly situated properties and valuations made on dates fairly proximate to the relevant date. Under Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court admitting additional evidence must be satisfied that it is required to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause, record its reasons, and afford the opposing party an opportunity to rebut any inference from it. The Court declined to adopt an absolute exclusion of such judgments suggested in Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bombay v. Lakhamsi Ghelabhai.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside and the matters remanded. The High Court must decide, after giving the parties an opportunity to present necessary evidence, whether the other judgment may be admitted as additional evidence.

rule.if: compensation_appeal and other_judgment_offered_as_additional_evidence and other_judgment_concerns_similar_property and valuation_dates_are_proximate

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.other_judgment_offered_as_additional_evi: A party offers a judgment from a separate proceeding as additional evidence in the appeal.
predicates.other_judgment_concerns_similar_property: The separate judgment concerns property shown to be similarly situated to the property being valued.
predicates.valuation_dates_are_proximate: The valuation date addressed in the separate judgment is fairly close to the relevant valuation date in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence when it requires that evidence to clarify an issue and reach a proper decision.
material_facts: During the appeal, the appellate court considered the reasonableness of the lessor’s refusal of consent.
The appellate court directed that the lessor’s evidence be taken so that the relevant facts could be clarified and a proper decision reached.
The evidence was received at the appellate court’s direction.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure covers additional evidence required by the appellate court to clarify a matter and enable a proper decision; the court’s discretion to receive it may be exercised in those circumstances.
members.conclusion: The appellate court acted within its authority in receiving the additional evidence, and there was no ground to interfere with its exercise of discretion.

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil case.
predicates.appellate_court_requires_evidence_to_cla: The appellate court considers additional evidence necessary to clarify an issue and reach a proper decision.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may consider material subsequent events supported by documentary evidence and may require additional evidence when the court itself needs it to decide the appeal.
material_facts: After the trial court’s decree, the competent authority issued an order concerning whether the property exceeded the applicable land ceiling.
The respondent company was later declared sick by the relevant board.
The events were supported by documents, were substantially admitted, and the documents were public documents that could be placed before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an appellate court to require a document to be produced or a witness to be examined when the court needs that evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. The power is exercised to meet the court’s own need for evidence, not merely a party’s request; public documents may be placed before the court without formal proof where appropriate.
members.conclusion: The High Court could take the subsequent events into account, consider their effect on the judgment or relief, and use its power to require evidence if necessary for deciding the appeal.

rule.if: appellate_court_hearing_civil_appeal and material_subsequent_events_arose and events_supported_by_documentary_evidence and evidence_needed_for_satisfactory_decision

predicates.appellate_court_hearing_civil_appeal: An appellate court is hearing a civil appeal.
predicates.material_subsequent_events_arose: Events material to the dispute occurred after the decision under appeal.
predicates.events_supported_by_documentary_evidence: The subsequent events are supported by documentary evidence.
predicates.evidence_needed_for_satisfactory_decisio: The appellate court needs additional evidence to decide the appeal satisfactorily or for another substantial cause.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court must consider a pending application to adduce additional evidence before deciding the appeal, and may admit evidence only when a prescribed ground for doing so is established.
material_facts: In a second appeal, the appellant sought to place official records before the High Court as additional evidence.

The High Court had directed the Collector to produce an acquisition notification, and the Collector reported that no such notification existed because the land belonged to the government; the report also referred to compensation paid to the former holder.

The High Court dismissed the second appeal without considering the pending additional-evidence application or referring to the Collector’s report, although the records appeared capable of affecting the dispute about whether the decree had been obtained by concealment or fraud.
members.legal_principle: Section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and Order 41 Rule 27 create an exception to the general rule against introducing new evidence on appeal. Under Order 41 Rule 27(1), additional evidence may be admitted if the lower court wrongly refused evidence that ought to have been admitted; if, despite due diligence, the evidence was not known or could not have been produced earlier; or if the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. Under clause (b), the court must itself find the evidence needful; it may be needed to enable judgment or to clarify an obscurity so that judgment can be given more satisfactorily. The court must consider the application before deciding the appeal. These principles are drawn from Parsotim Thakur v. Lal Mohar Thakur and K. Venkataramiah v. A. Seetharama Reddy.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred by failing to consider the application before deciding the appeal. Its orders were set aside and the matter remitted for the application to be decided on its merits; the Supreme Court expressed no final view on whether the evidence should be admitted.

predicates.second_appeal_pending: A party’s appeal is pending before an appellate court as a second appeal.
predicates.additional_evidence_application_filed: A party has asked the appellate court to admit or obtain evidence not included in the record below.

members.legal_issue: When a first appellate court admits additional evidence and needs further fact-finding to decide the merits, it must use a remand or limited-issue procedure rather than decide the merits without that procedure.
material_facts: The first appellate court admitted additional evidence and relied on it to decide the appeals on their merits.
It neither set aside the trial court’s decision and remanded the suits for retrial nor retained the appeals while referring particular issues for findings by the trial court.
The Supreme Court found that the omission, together with the lack of an opportunity to adduce rebuttal evidence, caused prejudice and constituted jurisdictional error.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 23-A of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court may set aside the trial court’s judgment and remand the case for retrial; under Order 41 Rule 25, it may retain the appeal and refer particular issues to the trial court for findings. Where additional evidence is admitted and further trial-level proceedings are needed, the appellate court must use an appropriate procedure rather than decide the merits without them.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court should have used either a full retrial remand or a limited-issue reference for findings; its failure to do so rendered its merits decision unsustainable. The Supreme Court set aside the appellate merits decision and remanded the suits for retrial.

rule.if: first_appeal and additional_evidence_admitted and further_fact_finding_needed and appellate_court_decides_merits_without_trial_procedure

predicates.first_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a trial court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_admitted: The appellate court admits additional evidence for consideration in the appeal.
predicates.further_fact_finding_needed: The additional evidence requires trial-level proof or findings before the merits can fairly be decided.
predicates.appellate_court_decides_merits_without_t: The appellate court decides the merits without remanding for retrial or referring issues for trial-court findings.

members.legal_issue: Additional evidence in an appeal may be admitted only on a prescribed ground, and the appellate court must assess whether it needs the evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause rather than use it to fill a party’s evidentiary gaps.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought expert examination of the signature on a will during the first appeal, although no such application had been made at trial.
The plaintiff had not established that due diligence prevented him from seeking the examination before the trial court.
The first appellate court had allowed the application, but the Supreme Court did not decide whether the expert evidence should ultimately be admitted.
members.legal_principle: Section 107(1)(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order XLI Rule 27, makes additional evidence exceptional: it may be allowed where evidence that ought to have been admitted was refused, where despite due diligence it was unavailable or could not be produced at trial, or where the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. It cannot be used merely to patch weaknesses or fill gaps in a party’s case, and the court must record reasons for admitting it. The Court relied on K.R. Mohan Reddy v. Net Work Inc. (2007) 14 SCC 257, North Eastern Railway Admn. v. Bhagwan Das (2008) 8 SCC 511, N. Kamalam v. Ayyasamy (2001) 7 SCC 503, and Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin (2012) 8 SCC 148.
members.conclusion: The application was remanded for the first appellate court to decide afresh under the applicable principles; the Supreme Court expressed no view on its merits.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal was pending before an appellate court.
predicates.party_requests_additional_evidence: A party asked the appellate court to receive or obtain evidence not presented at trial.
predicates.appellate_court_must_reconsider_request_: The appellate court must decide the request by applying the exceptional grounds for additional evidence and whether the evidence is needed to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence when the existing record is insufficient to determine fair compensation and the proposed evidence bears directly on that determination.
material_facts: The appeal concerned a claim for enhanced compensation for acquired land.
The only evidence before the Reference Court and High Court was a sale deed that had been rejected, leaving no other material to determine fair market value.
The claimant sought to introduce sale deeds and certified copies of awards in other land acquisition cases, which could bear directly on the acquired land’s fair market value.
The High Court rejected the application without addressing whether the additional evidence was needed to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC, additional evidence is not admitted as of right. The controlling consideration is whether the appellate court can pronounce judgment on the existing materials without the proposed evidence, or whether the evidence is required for another substantial cause. Its relevance to the issue and whether the applicant had an earlier opportunity to produce it are not, by themselves, decisive. The Court relied on A. Andisamy Chettiar v. A. Subburaj, (2015) 17 SCC 713.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s rejection of the application was set aside, and the application to adduce the additional evidence was allowed.

predicates.compensation_appeal: A party appeals a decision determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.valuation_record_insufficient: The evidence in the existing record is insufficient to determine the fair value of the acquired land.
predicates.proposed_evidence_directly_bears_on_valu: The party seeks to introduce evidence that bears directly on determining the fair value of the acquired land.
predicates.appellate_court_cannot_pronounce_judgmen: The appellate court cannot adequately pronounce judgment on the existing record without the proposed evidence.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence only when a permitted ground exists, including when the evidence is necessary to enable it to pronounce judgment, and may not use that power to order a virtual retrial when the existing record permits decision.
material_facts: The High Court relied on documents already in the record that it considered supportive of the tenants’ allegations if unexplained.
The High Court did not identify a lacuna in the evidence or state that it needed additional evidence to pronounce judgment.
The High Court remitted the matter for additional evidence and a virtual retrial.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits additional evidence only on the grounds specified in the rule, including where the appellate court needs it to pronounce judgment. It does not permit evidence to be added merely to reach a particular result; its use is limited to a proper need such as removing a lacuna. A general retrial cannot be ordered under that rule, and the requirements for remand under Order XLI, rules 23 and 25 were not met.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to admit additional evidence or remit the case for a virtual retrial in those circumstances.

rule.if: civil_appeal_reviewing_evidence and existing_record_permits_judgment and additional_evidence_not_needed_to_enable_judgment and appellate_court_orders_virtual_retrial

predicates.civil_appeal_reviewing_evidence: An appellate court was considering whether to receive further evidence in a civil appeal.
predicates.existing_record_permits_judgment: The evidence already on the record could be considered and a judgment could be pronounced on that record.
predicates.additional_evidence_not_needed_to_enable: The appellate court did not need further evidence in order to pronounce judgment.
predicates.appellate_court_orders_virtual_retrial: The appellate court directed a new evidentiary hearing that amounted in substance to a retrial.

members.legal_issue: A first appellate court may allow additional evidence that is material to the disputed ground of eviction when it was unavailable despite due diligence or came into existence after the trial decree.
material_facts: The tenant appealed an eviction decree based on the landlord’s alleged bona fide requirement.

During the appeal, the tenant sought to produce correspondence concerning negotiations to sell or allow a third party to use the premises, a modified construction plan, and a public brochure concerning construction funds.
The correspondence was not available to the tenant despite due diligence, and the other documents came into existence after the trial decree.
The documents, if substantiated, could materially undermine the landlord’s asserted need for the premises.
The first appellate court found the documents necessary for a just decision and allowed their production.
members.legal_principle: Section 107(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers an appellate court to take additional evidence, while Order 41 Rule 27 permits parties to produce it only on the specified grounds, including where evidence was not available despite due diligence. Evidence bearing materially on whether a landlord’s asserted need is genuine may be relevant to the appeal. Under Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta (1999) 6 SCC 222, bona fide requirement must reflect a sincere and honest desire rather than a pretext; under Deena Nath v. Pooran Lal (2001) 5 SCC 705, it must be an actual, present need rather than a whim or fanciful desire.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court was justified in allowing the tenant to produce the documents as additional evidence.

rule.if: appeal_from_eviction_decree and evidence_material_to_landlord_need and (evidence_unavailable_despite_diligence or evidence_created_after_trial_decree)

predicates.appeal_from_eviction_decree: A tenant has pursued a first appeal from a decree ordering eviction on the ground of the landlord’s asserted need for the premises.
predicates.evidence_material_to_landlord_need: The evidence could materially affect whether the landlord’s asserted need for the premises is genuine.
predicates.evidence_unavailable_despite_diligence: The evidence was not available to the party despite the exercise of due diligence before the trial decree.
predicates.evidence_created_after_trial_decree: The evidence came into existence after the trial decree.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may admit material additional evidence in an appeal under its inherent power when the evidence could not have been produced before the decision under appeal and its consideration is necessary for justice.
material_facts: The plaintiffs appealed after the High Court dismissed their mortgage suit for failure to prove due attestation of the will under which they claimed the mortgage rights.
Probate of the will was granted after the High Court’s decision, so it could not have been produced there.
The plaintiffs applied in the Supreme Court appeal to place the probate on the record as additional evidence.
members.legal_principle: Rule 5 of Order 45 of the Supreme Court Rules recognises the Court’s inherent power to make orders necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process. The Court’s power to admit additional evidence is no less than that of the Privy Council, as stated in Inderjit Pratap Sahi v. Amar Singh. In Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, the Federal Court affirmed that an appellate court may consider changes in fact or law occurring after the decision under appeal when justice requires.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court had power to admit additional evidence and admitted the probate for consideration in deciding the appeal.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is being considered in an appeal.
predicates.material_evidence_arose_after_lower_deci: Material evidence came into existence after the decision under appeal and therefore could not have been produced before that decision.
predicates.evidence_is_necessary_for_justice: Considering the evidence is necessary to determine the appeal justly.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence only on the grounds permitted for doing so, and not merely to repair omissions or fill gaps in a party’s case.
material_facts: The party sought, about ten years after filing the appeal, to examine one of the will’s attesting witnesses as additional evidence.
The two attesting witnesses had been identified, but neither had been summoned or examined at trial.
The record did not establish that the witnesses were unavailable despite a diligent effort to obtain their evidence.
The proposed evidence was sought to cure the failure to prove the will at trial.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, additional evidence may be admitted in the specified circumstances, including where the appellate court needs it to pronounce judgment or there is another substantial cause. The provision does not permit evidence to be added merely to fill gaps. The Court relied on The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Lala Pancham (AIR 1965 SC 1008) and Smt. Pramod Kumari Bhatia v. Om Parkash Bhatia (AIR 1980 SC 446), and emphasized caution in admitting belated oral evidence at the appellate stage.
members.conclusion: The refusal to admit the additional evidence was not an erroneous or illegal exercise of discretion; the request was rejected.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and additional_evidence_sought and attestors_known_at_trial and attestors_not_summoned and evidence_unavailability_not_shown and application_substantially_delayed and evidence_would_fill_gap

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter was an appeal in which a party asked the appellate court to receive further evidence.
predicates.additional_evidence_sought: A party asked to introduce evidence that had not been presented at trial.
predicates.attestors_known_at_trial: The proposed witnesses were identified as witnesses to the document before the trial concluded.
predicates.attestors_not_summoned: The party did not summon the identified witnesses to give evidence at trial.
predicates.evidence_unavailability_not_shown: The party did not establish that the witnesses could not be produced despite a diligent effort.
predicates.application_substantially_delayed: The request to introduce the evidence was made long after the appeal had been filed.
predicates.evidence_would_fill_gap: The proposed evidence was intended to make up for a failure to prove an essential part of the party’s case at trial.

members.legal_issue: Additional evidence may be admitted at the appellate stage when the party gives a justifiable reason for not producing it earlier and the evidence is relevant and material to the dispute.
material_facts: The appellant sought to introduce documents from the State Land Revenue Department concerning the disputed land.
The appellant said the old public documents had been discovered only after the trial judgment and had been traced with difficulty.
The application explained why the documents had not been filed at trial, was supported by an affidavit that remained unrebutted, and stated why the documents were needed to decide ownership.
The respondents had not been served with notice of the appeal or the application, and the documents related to the disputed land.
members.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure enables a party to seek additional evidence at the appellate stage. Where the party shows a justifiable reason for not producing the evidence at trial and the evidence is relevant and material to deciding the parties’ rights, the court should allow it in order to do substantial justice. Admission of evidence does not amount to acceptance of it on the merits.
members.conclusion: The application to adduce additional evidence was allowed, and the documents were taken on record; their admission did not decide the merits of the parties’ claims.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party seeks to introduce evidence while an appeal is pending.
predicates.justifiable_failure_to_submit_earlier: The party gives a justifiable reason for not producing the evidence at the earlier hearing.
predicates.evidence_relevant_and_material: The evidence is relevant and material to deciding the rights in dispute.

members.legal_issue: When additional evidence is admitted in an appeal, the opposing party must have an opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.
material_facts: The Court admitted the appellant’s additional documents in the appellate proceeding.
The respondents had not been served with the application before it was decided.
The Court expressly afforded the respondents an opportunity to file additional evidence in rebuttal.
members.legal_principle: Once additional evidence is admitted, the appellate court is obliged to give the other side an opportunity to adduce evidence by way of rebuttal.
members.conclusion: The respondents were entitled to an opportunity to file additional evidence in rebuttal.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A dispute is being considered in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.additional_evidence_admitted: The appellate court permits a party to place additional evidence on the record.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence where a permitted ground under the procedural rule is met, including where the evidence has a direct and important bearing on the main issue and justice requires its admission.
material_facts: The appellants sought to introduce three revenue-authority orders in the Supreme Court.

An order already in evidence expressly referred to the Tahsildar’s 1971 order, and that order addressed whether revenue entries showing the plaintiffs’ possession had been made later and whether the entries should be corrected.
The Tahsildar’s order had a direct bearing on the main issue, while the other two proposed documents were not admitted.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits additional evidence only in specified circumstances, including where the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. Admission is discretionary and should be used sparingly; evidence with a direct and important bearing may be admitted where the interests of justice make it imperative. The Court relied on Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin (2012) 8 SCC 148, which discusses the rule and earlier authorities.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court admitted the Tahsildar’s 1971 order as additional evidence but declined to admit the other two proposed documents.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and proposed_evidence_is_referred_to_in_record and evidence_has_direct_important_bearing and interests_of_justice_require_admission

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court is deciding an appeal in which a party seeks to introduce evidence not produced below.
predicates.proposed_evidence_is_referred_to_in_reco: Evidence already properly before the appellate court refers to the proposed additional evidence.
predicates.evidence_has_direct_important_bearing: The proposed evidence directly and materially concerns the main issue in the proceeding.
predicates.interests_of_justice_require_admission: The appellate court determines that admitting the evidence is necessary in the interests of justice to address the matter fairly or pronounce judgment.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence only within the conditions governing that power, and an application decided before the appeal is heard on its merits cannot be used to establish that the evidence is required for judgment.
material_facts: The plaintiff applied during the first appeal to add a Will as evidence.
The first appellate court allowed the application before hearing the appeal on its merits.
The order allowing the application did not assess at the merits hearing whether the appellate court required the evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.
The Will was central to a claim not pleaded in the plaint and was not proved in the required manner.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 27 CPC permits additional evidence only in the specified circumstances, including where the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. The power is judicial, exceptional, and not a right to repair a party’s case; the application is considered at the hearing on the merits after assessing the existing record, and reasons should be recorded. The Court relied on K. Venkataramiah v. A. Seetharama Reddy, The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Lala Pancham, Haji Mohammed Ishaq v. Mohamed Iqbal, Arjan Singh v. Kartar Singh, and Parsotim Thakur v. Lal Mohar Thakur.
members.conclusion: The order admitting the Will, made before the hearing on the merits, was to be ignored; the Will could not be relied on to decide the appeal.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and additional_evidence_is_requested and (application_is_decided_before_merits_hearing or evidence_was_available_below_without_satisfactory_cause or appellate_court_does_not_require_evidence_to_decide_the_case)

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court is hearing an appeal from a lower court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_is_requested: A party asks the appellate court to add evidence that was not part of the lower court’s record.
predicates.application_is_decided_before_merits_hea: The appellate court decides whether to admit the evidence before hearing the appeal on its merits.
predicates.evidence_was_available_below_without_sat: The party had a fair opportunity to present the evidence below and has not shown a satisfactory reason for failing to do so.
predicates.appellate_court_does_not_require_evidenc: The appellate court can decide the appeal on the existing record and does not require the proposed evidence for judgment or another substantial cause.

members.legal_issue: An affidavit cannot be used to repair an evidentiary omission on appeal unless the court has ordered that it may be used as evidence.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied in the Supreme Court on an affidavit to establish the relationship of her sole witness to her and his connection to the property.
The affidavit was tendered belatedly to address a deficiency in the evidence given at trial.
The record did not show an order allowing the affidavit to be used as evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 does not include affidavits in the definition of evidence. An affidavit may be used as evidence only where the court, for sufficient reason, orders so under Order XIX, Rules 1 or 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. A party cannot belatedly fill a gap in its evidence at the Supreme Court stage. No earlier cases are relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The affidavit could not be relied on to fill the lacuna in the trial evidence at the Supreme Court stage.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and affidavit_offered_as_evidence and not court_order_allows_affidavit_as_evidence and affidavit_addresses_trial_evidence_gap

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal.
predicates.affidavit_offered_as_evidence: A party offers an affidavit to establish a fact relevant to its case.
predicates.court_order_allows_affidavit_as_evidence: The court has ordered that the affidavit may be used as evidence.
predicates.affidavit_addresses_trial_evidence_gap: The affidavit is offered to supply information missing from the evidence presented at trial.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence only when the evidence already on record reveals a lacuna or defect that prevents it from pronouncing judgment.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to introduce settlement-register entries for the first time in the appeal to show that a third son had relinquished his share in the disputed property.
The appellate judge allowed the evidence before hearing the appeal and without first finding that the existing evidence disclosed a gap that prevented a judgment.
The existing record was sufficient for the appellate court to decide the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code gives the appellate court judicial discretion, limited to the circumstances specified in the rule. The legitimate occasion for additional evidence is an inherent lacuna or defect apparent on examining the existing evidence, not discovery of fresh evidence outside court. The test is whether the appellate court can pronounce judgment on the existing materials without the proposed evidence. The Court relied on Kessowji Issur v. G. I. P. Railway (34 I.A. 115) and Parsotim v. Lal Mohan (58 I.A. 254).
members.conclusion: The additional evidence was improperly admitted and had to be ignored when deciding the case.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal in which a party seeks to introduce evidence not on the trial record.
predicates.existing_record_permits_judgment: The appellate court can decide the appeal on the evidence already before it.
predicates.additional_evidence_is_newly_sought: A party seeks to introduce fresh evidence discovered outside court rather than evidence needed to fill a gap apparent in the existing record.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court must decide on its merits an application to produce additional evidence, applying the statutory conditions for admission and giving reasons when evidence is admitted.
material_facts: Both sides filed applications in the High Court appeal seeking to produce additional materials.
The High Court referred to the applications but did not decide them.
The Supreme Court declined to assess the materials itself and directed the High Court to decide the applications and then dispose of the appeal.

The Supreme Court stated that additional evidence may be received where evidence was wrongly refused below, could not despite due diligence have been produced earlier, or is required to enable judgment or for another substantial cause; it may not be used to fill gaps or patch weak points.
members.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure limits the production of additional evidence in an appeal to specified circumstances and requires the appellate court to record reasons when it allows such evidence. Additional evidence cannot be used to fill lacunae or patch weak points. The Court relied on Jatinder Singh v. Mehar Singh, AIR 2009 SC 354, and Shyam Gopal Bindal v. Land Acquisition Officer, (2010) 2 SCC 316.
members.conclusion: The High Court was required to decide the additional-evidence applications on their merits; the applications were left for the High Court to determine under the applicable legal standard.

predicates.appeal_from_original_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from an original decree.
predicates.additional_evidence_application_filed: A party has applied in the appeal to produce additional evidence.

members.legal_issue: Setting aside a remand does not deprive the appellate court of power to require additional evidence when the court itself needs it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.
material_facts: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's remand and noted that the parties were not seeking to adduce further evidence apart from documents concerning subsequent events.
The Supreme Court clarified that the High Court retained authority to require documents or witnesses if the court itself needed them to decide the appeal satisfactorily.
members.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an appellate court to require additional evidence when it needs that evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. The power is exercised to meet the court's requirement, not merely a party's request.
members.conclusion: The High Court retained its power to require additional evidence on its own need, notwithstanding that the remand had been set aside.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal remains pending before the appellate court.
predicates.appellate_court_itself_needs_additional_: The appellate court itself considers additional evidence necessary to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on taking cognizance of certain document-related offences for want of a court complaint does not apply when only a copy of the allegedly forged document, and not the document itself, was produced in a court proceeding.
material_facts: A criminal prosecution alleged that a partnership deed had been forged and that offences involving the deed had been committed.
A copy of the deed was relied on in a civil proceeding to obtain a temporary injunction.
The original deed was not produced in the civil proceeding.
The magistrate declined to frame charges for certain offences without a complaint from the civil court, and the High Court directed that fresh charges be framed.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 bars cognizance of specified offences alleged in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding unless there is a complaint by that court. Production of a copy does not amount to production of the document itself, applying the plain grammatical meaning and practical sense of the provision. The Court relied on Sanmukhsingh v. The King, [1949] L.R. 77 I.A. 7, and Budhu Ram v. State of Rajasthan, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 376.
members.conclusion: The statutory restriction did not apply because the allegedly forged document itself was not produced in court. The direction to frame fresh charges was confirmed on that ground, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.forgery_prosecution_related_to_court_pro: A criminal prosecution alleges an offence involving a document connected with a court proceeding.
predicates.only_copy_produced: A party produced or relied on a copy of the allegedly forged document in the court proceeding.
predicates.original_document_not_produced: The allegedly forged original document was not produced or given in evidence in the court proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A court complaint is not required for prosecution concerning a forged document when only a copy, and not the forged original, was produced in the proceeding.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that a party to proceedings before an officer had used a forged verified claim.
The original claim was not produced before the officer; only an attested copy was submitted.
The Court assumed, without deciding, that the officer was a court for this purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a court complaint is required when the forged document itself is produced or given in evidence, not when only a copy is produced. The Court applied Sanmukh Singh v. The King, (1949) L.R. 77 I.A. 7, which relied on the practical distinction between an original and a copy; it also referred to Girdharilal v. The Emperor, A.I.R. (1925) Oudh 413.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the officer was a court, no complaint by the officer was required because the forged original was not produced before him.

rule.if: document_offense_prosecution and proceeding_party_accused and only_copy_produced and original_forged_document_not_produced

predicates.document_offense_prosecution: A person is prosecuted for an offense concerning a forged document.
predicates.proceeding_party_accused: The person accused is alleged to have committed the offense as a party to a proceeding before a court.
predicates.only_copy_produced: A copy of the alleged forged document, rather than its original, was produced in the proceeding.
predicates.original_forged_document_not_produced: The alleged forged original was not produced in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on cognizance for offenses involving a forged document does not apply when the alleged forgery was committed before the accused became a party to the proceeding in which the document was later produced.
material_facts: A private criminal complaint alleged that the accused forged a will before mutation proceedings began.
The complaint alleged that the accused later produced the will in connection with those proceedings.
The accused objected that the court could not take cognizance without a written complaint from a court.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to an offense alleged to have been committed by a party to a proceeding in that capacity—that is, after the person became a party. The Court relied on Patel Laljibhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat and Raghunath v. State of U.P. The restriction therefore did not apply to the alleged offenses under Sections 464, 467 and 468 of the Penal Code, which were alleged to have preceded the proceeding. Whether it applied to the alleged Section 471 offense was left undecided.
members.conclusion: The restriction did not prevent the Magistrate from taking cognizance of the alleged forgery offenses under Sections 464, 467 and 468 of the Penal Code because the alleged forgery occurred before the accused became parties to the mutation proceedings. The Court did not finally decide whether the restriction applied to the separate offense of using the forged document as genuine under Section 471; it left that question open.

rule.if: private_complaint_cognizance_challenge and forgery_predated_proceeding and accused_became_party_after_forgery and forged_document_later_produced_in_proceeding

predicates.private_complaint_cognizance_challenge: A person filed a private criminal complaint, and the accused challenged the court's authority to take cognizance of the alleged offenses.
predicates.forgery_predated_proceeding: The complaint alleged that the accused forged the document before the relevant proceeding began.
predicates.accused_became_party_after_forgery: The accused became parties to the relevant proceeding only after the alleged forgery.
predicates.forged_document_later_produced_in_procee: The complaint alleged that the accused later produced the document in the relevant proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The requirement for a court complaint does not bar a private prosecution for forgery and abetment when the forged document was never introduced in the related court proceeding.
material_facts: A forged sale deed was registered before the redemption suit was filed.
The private complainant initiated the criminal complaint after learning of the deed.
The forged deed was never produced in evidence at any stage of the redemption suit.
The prosecution alleged both forgery-related offences and an offence of fabricating false evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires a written complaint by a court for specified offences, including offences under Sections 193 to 196 of the Indian Penal Code, when alleged to have been committed in or in relation to a court proceeding. The Court approved the principle in In re V. V. L. Narasimhamurthy that, when a single transaction includes both an offence requiring a court complaint and an offence not requiring one, prosecution cannot be split to proceed on only the latter. But that principle did not bar prosecution here because the deed was never put in evidence and the alleged Section 193 offence was not within the restriction. The Court also relied on Patel Laljibhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat and Raghunath v. State of U.P. concerning the scope of the court-complaint restriction.
members.conclusion: The restriction in Section 195(1)(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply to the alleged offence under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code because the deed was never produced in the suit. The private complaint could therefore proceed for forgery and abetment, and the first accused could be convicted of abetment of forgery. The Magistrate could not take cognizance of the Section 193 offence in the circumstances.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_based_on_private_co: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution initiated on a private complaint.
predicates.alleged_false_evidence_involves_a_court_: The prosecution alleges that false evidence was fabricated for use in, or in relation to, a court proceeding.
predicates.forged_document_never_introduced_in_that: The forged document was not produced or given in evidence at any stage of the related court proceeding.
