members.legal_issue: The court-complaint restriction for offences involving forged documents applies when the forgery occurs after the document has been produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.
material_facts: The criminal complaint alleged that the receipt was fabricated before it was relied on in the civil suit.
The receipt was subsequently filed in the civil proceeding, and the trial court considered whether it was forged.
The High Court stayed the investigation into the alleged fabrication.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies only when an enumerated offence concerning a document is committed after the document has been produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding, while it is in custodia legis. The Court relied on the Constitution Bench decision in Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, which approved Sachida Nand Singh and rejected an interpretation that would shield a person who forged a document before arranging for it to be filed in court.
members.conclusion: The restriction did not prevent the criminal investigation because the alleged forgery was of a document later produced in court, rather than an offence committed after the document entered court custody.

predicates.criminal_case_concerns_document_forgery: The criminal proceeding concerns an allegation that a document was forged.
predicates.document_was_allegedly_forged_before_cou: The alleged forgery occurred before the document was produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The court-complaint requirement for forgery applies only when the offence is committed by a person in the capacity of a party to the proceeding, not when the forgery predates that person becoming a party.
material_facts: A sale deed was forged through the use of an impersonator before the revenue proceeding began.
The accused later relied on the deed in seeking a change to revenue entries.
The complainant initiated the criminal prosecution.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, read with Sections 190, 476, 476A and 476B, the restriction applies to specified offences committed by a party in that capacity. The court applied Patel Laljibhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat, which approved the approach in Emperor v. Kushal Pal Singh: a forgery committed before the offender became a party is not brought within the restriction merely because the document is later used in a proceeding.
members.conclusion: The prosecution for forgery was not barred for want of a complaint by the court in which the deed was later used; the time between the forgery and the deed’s later use was not controlling.

rule.if: prosecution_for_forgery and document_forged_before_proceeding and accused_not_yet_party_when_forgery_occurred and document_later_used_in_proceeding

predicates.prosecution_for_forgery: A criminal prosecution is brought for forgery.
predicates.document_forged_before_proceeding: The document was forged before the proceeding in which it was later used began.
predicates.accused_not_yet_party_when_forgery_occur: The accused had not yet become a party to the proceeding when the forgery occurred.
predicates.document_later_used_in_proceeding: The accused later used or produced the forged document in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A private criminal complaint alleging forgery or use of a forged document is not barred merely because the original document is produced in a court proceeding after the criminal court has taken cognizance.
material_facts: A private complaint alleged offences involving a fabricated agreement and its use.
The Magistrate took cognizance before the original agreement was produced in the civil proceeding.
The original agreement was produced in the civil proceeding after cognizance had been taken.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure bars cognizance of the specified forgery and use-of-forged-document offences when the original document in question has been produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding; production of only a copy does not attract the bar. Later production of the original does not set aside cognizance already taken. The court relied on Sections 195 and 340 of the Code, and on Budhu Ram v. State of Rajasthan, Patel Laljibhai and Somabhai v. State of Gujarat, Sushil Kumar v. State of Haryana, Sanmukhsingh v. The King, and Gopal Krishna Menon v. D. Raja Reddy, distinguishing the last where the original documents had been produced before cognizance.
members.conclusion: The later production of the original agreement did not invalidate the cognizance already taken, and the Magistrate could proceed with the criminal trial.

predicates.private_complaint_for_document_forgery_o: A private complainant initiates a criminal case alleging forgery of a document or use of a forged document.
predicates.cognizance_taken_before_original_produce: The criminal court takes cognizance before the original document is produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.
predicates.original_later_produced_in_court: The original document is produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding after the criminal court has taken cognizance.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on taking cognizance of document-related offences applies only when the offence was committed after the document was produced or given in evidence in court.
material_facts: The alleged will was said to have been forged before it was filed in probate proceedings.
The complainants initiated a private criminal complaint alleging forgery and related offences.
There was no allegation that an offence concerning the will was committed after it had been filed in court.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) CrPC requires a complaint by the court for the specified document-related offences only when they are committed after the document has been produced or given in evidence in court. Section 190 provides the general routes to cognizance, while Sections 340–343 prescribe the court-complaint procedure. The Court approved Sachida Nand Singh v. State of Bihar and explained that Surjit Singh v. Balbir Singh did not lay down a contrary rule; it also relied on Patel Lalji Bhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat, Raghunath v. State of U.P., and related earlier decisions concerning the corresponding provision in the former Code.
members.conclusion: The restriction did not prevent cognizance on the private complaint because the alleged forgery preceded the will’s production in court. The court’s complaint is required only when the specified document-related offence is committed after the document has been produced or given in evidence.

predicates.document_offence_prosecution: A criminal proceeding concerns an alleged offence involving a document produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.
predicates.document_offence_after_production: The alleged document-related offence was committed after the document had been produced or given in evidence in court.

members.legal_issue: The bar on prosecution for specified offences involving documents produced in court does not apply when the alleged forgery occurred before the document was produced in court.
material_facts: The alleged forged sale deeds were relied on in a civil suit to support a claim of title.
The alleged forgery was said to have occurred before the documents were produced in court; the documents were not alleged to have been forged while in court custody.
members.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to the specified offences only when they are committed in respect of a document after it has been produced or given in evidence in court and while it is in the custody of the court. The Court relied on the Constitution Bench decision in Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, which approved Sachida Nand Singh v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The bar in Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply, and it did not prevent the FIR or investigation in this case.

predicates.forgery_allegation_case: The criminal case concerns an allegation that a document was forged.
predicates.alleged_forgery_preceded_court_productio: The alleged forgery occurred before the document was produced or given in evidence in court.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for abetting suicide cannot be sustained when the prosecution has not proved instigation or intentional aid and guilty intent, and the conviction rests on conjecture rather than evidence.
material_facts: The deceased died by suicide after consuming pesticide.

The prosecution alleged that the deceased had been harassed over a cash demand shortly before her death, but the trial court found insufficient material to connect the death to a dowry demand and acquitted the accused of the charged dowry-related offences.
The evidence did not establish persistent harassment, direct cruelty, wilful neglect, or a positive act by the husband that instigated or aided the suicide.
Evidence showed that the deceased had received care and medical treatment from her husband and father-in-law, and the prosecution witnesses did not describe maltreatment during the marriage.

The trial court inferred that the deceased had been driven to suicide by circumstances in the matrimonial home, without identifying evidence of the husband's conduct or state of mind; the High Court upheld that inference.
members.legal_principle: Sections 107 and 306 IPC require proof that the accused instigated the suicide or intentionally aided it by an act or illegal omission, together with the necessary mens rea. There must be a positive act or direct or indirect incitement, and the prosecution must prove the accused's active role; harassment allegations alone, without a positive action proximate to the suicide, are insufficient. A court cannot infer abetment merely because a person died by suicide or speculate that the circumstances of the home drove the person to it. The Court relied on SS Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan, (2010) 12 SCC 190; Amalendu Pal alias Jhantu v. State of West Bengal, (2010) 1 SCC 707; and Mangat Ram v. State of Haryana, (2014) 12 SCC 595.
members.conclusion: The conviction under Section 306 IPC was set aside and quashed, and the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_suicide_abetment_conviction and suicide_established and prosecution_lacks_evidence_of_instigation_or_intentional_aid and guilty_intent_not_proved and conviction_based_on_speculation

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_suicide_abetment_co: The accused brings a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for abetting another person's suicide.
predicates.suicide_established: The evidence establishes that the deceased died by suicide.
predicates.prosecution_lacks_evidence_of_instigatio: The prosecution evidence does not establish that the accused instigated the suicide or intentionally aided it by an act or illegal omission.
predicates.guilty_intent_not_proved: The prosecution does not prove that the accused had the guilty state of mind required for abetting the suicide.
predicates.conviction_based_on_speculation: The conviction rests on conjecture about the circumstances of the deceased's life rather than evidence supporting the accused's role in the suicide.

members.legal_issue: A cruelty conviction and a married woman's suicide within seven years of marriage do not, without proof linking the accused's conduct to the suicide, establish abetment of suicide; recording that conviction on a charge that did not allege such a link was unsustainable in this case.
material_facts: The deceased died by consuming poison within seven years of her marriage, and cruelty involving an unlawful property demand was proved.
The prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that an act or illegal omission by the accused instigated the deceased to commit suicide.

There was no evidence of cruelty immediately before the suicide or of a proximate causal connection between the demand and the suicide; the deceased's last visit to her parents concerning the demand was about two months before her death.
The charge alleged dowry-related cruelty and an unnatural death but did not allege that the deceased had been driven to suicide or that the accused had abetted it.
members.legal_principle: Sections 107 and 306 of the Indian Penal Code require proof of abetment, including instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid. Under Section 113-A of the Indian Evidence Act, the court may presume abetment when a married woman commits suicide within seven years of marriage and was subjected to cruelty, but the presumption is discretionary, not automatic, and must be assessed in light of all the circumstances, including a cause-and-effect relationship between the cruelty and suicide. Sections 498-A and 306 create distinct offences, so proof of cruelty does not itself prove abetment. The Court applied Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh, State of West Bengal v. Orilal Jaiswal, K. Prema S. Rao v. Yadla Srinivasa Rao, Hans Raj v. State of Haryana, Pinakin Mahipatray Rawal v. State of Gujarat, and Mangat Ram v. State of Haryana.
members.conclusion: The conviction for abetment of suicide was set aside, and the accused was acquitted of that charge.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_suicide_abetment_conviction and married_woman_suicide_within_seven_years and cruelty_proven and absence_of_proven_instigating_act_or_omission and absence_of_proximate_causal_nexus and charge_omits_suicide_abetment_allegation

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_suicide_abetment_co: The accused appealed a conviction for abetting a woman's suicide, including a conviction entered although the charge alleged a different offence.
predicates.married_woman_suicide_within_seven_years: A married woman committed suicide within seven years of her marriage.
predicates.cruelty_proven: The prosecution proved that the accused subjected the woman to cruelty.
predicates.absence_of_proven_instigating_act_or_omi: The prosecution did not prove an act or illegal omission by the accused that instigated, aided, or otherwise abetted the suicide.
predicates.absence_of_proximate_causal_nexus: The evidence did not establish a proximate causal connection between the accused's conduct and the suicide.
predicates.charge_omits_suicide_abetment_allegation: The charge did not allege that the accused's conduct drove the woman to suicide or abetted her suicide.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for abetment of suicide cannot stand where the evidence does not establish intentional, continuous, and proximate conduct by the accused that instigated or aided the suicide.
material_facts: A woman and her two daughters died by suicide after consuming pesticide, following the disappearance of the woman’s husband about two years earlier.

The prosecution alleged that the husband’s relatives had deprived the family of property and had ill-treated and harassed them. The woman’s brothers acknowledged that she had received property, including a house and land, and that no complaint or civil suit had been brought alleging denial of entitlements or ill-treatment.

The suicide note blamed the husband’s relatives generally but identified no specific incident. It also referred to the woman’s ownership of land and a house; its handwriting was not proved through an expert.
The evidence did not establish threats, cruelty, harassment, or other continuous and proximate conduct by the accused that induced or compelled the deaths.
members.legal_principle: Sections 306 and 107 of the Indian Penal Code require proof of suicide and intentional abetment through instigation, conspiracy accompanied by an act or illegal omission, or intentional aid. Abetment requires a live link between culpable conduct and the suicide; intentional involvement and conduct that is continuous and proximate are necessary, while remote conduct or a general allegation is insufficient. Under Section 113A of the Indian Evidence Act, the court may presume abetment by a husband or his relative only if the prosecution proves the statutory preconditions, including suicide within seven years of marriage and cruelty; cruelty has the meaning assigned by Section 498A IPC. The court relied on Randhir Singh v. State of Punjab, State of W.B. v. Orilal Jaiswal, Amalendu Pal v. State of West Bengal, S.S. Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan, and Pinakin Mahipatray Rawal v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The ingredients of abetment of suicide were not proved. The conviction could not be sustained, the appeal was allowed, and the accused was acquitted.

predicates.appeal_from_suicide_abetment_conviction: The accused appeals a conviction for abetting another person’s suicide.
predicates.suicide_death: The person whose death is at issue died by suicide.
predicates.no_proven_continuous_proximate_intention: The evidence does not establish continuous and proximate conduct by the accused, undertaken with intent to instigate or aid the suicide.

members.legal_issue: Convictions for cruelty and abetment of suicide cannot stand when the prosecution fails to prove statutory cruelty or harassment and the evidence does not connect such conduct to the suicide.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged unlawful demands for household goods and property, harassment, and neglect after childbirth, but key witnesses relied on information from others, gave inconsistent accounts, or made improvements contradicted by their prior statements.
Letters written before the death contradicted the allegation that the deceased had been kept away from her matrimonial home for months and did not mention the alleged demands.
The deceased's letter reflected strained relations with her mother-in-law but did not mention an unlawful demand or harassment arising from one.
The evidence did not establish that the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment that drove her to suicide.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove that the victim was subjected to cruelty or harassment falling within the Explanation to Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code. Evidence based on hearsay or lacking personal knowledge cannot establish the charge, and the evidence must support the alleged cruelty and its connection to the suicide to sustain the convictions. The court relied on Section 498A and considered the charge under Section 306, both read with Section 34; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove the charges under Sections 498A and 306 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code; the convictions and sentences were set aside.

rule.if: appeal_was_from_conviction and (witnesses_lacked_personal_knowledge or accounts_were_materially_contradictory) and allegations_were_contradicted_by_documents and statutory_cruelty_was_not_proved and conduct_causing_suicide_was_not_proved

predicates.appeal_was_from_conviction: The accused brought an appeal challenging convictions entered after trial.
predicates.witnesses_lacked_personal_knowledge: Witnesses attributed alleged demands or harassment to information they had received from other people rather than to events they personally knew.
predicates.accounts_were_materially_contradictory: Prosecution witnesses gave materially inconsistent accounts about when the alleged demands began and why they were made.
predicates.allegations_were_contradicted_by_documen: Letters written before the death contradicted allegations of prolonged neglect and did not record the alleged demands.
predicates.statutory_cruelty_was_not_proved: The prosecution evidence did not establish conduct amounting to cruelty or harassment as legally defined.
predicates.conduct_causing_suicide_was_not_proved: The prosecution evidence did not establish conduct by the accused that drove the deceased to commit suicide.

members.legal_issue: Filing an appeal does not excuse a pre-emptor from complying with an unaltered decree requiring payment within a specified time, and failure to pay by that time results in dismissal of the suit.
material_facts: A decree in a pre-emption suit required the plaintiff to deposit the sale price within two months.
An appeal was filed against the decree and later withdrawn, but the decree was not altered.
The plaintiff did not deposit the price within the time fixed by the decree.
members.legal_principle: An appeal does not by itself suspend a decree. Unless the appellate court alters it, the decree must be obeyed. Under Order XX, Rule 14 of the Civil Procedure Code, failure to make the required deposit within the time fixed results in dismissal of the pre-emption suit.
members.conclusion: The suit stood dismissed because the required deposit was not made within the time fixed by the decree; filing an appeal did not suspend the decree.

rule.if: is_preemption_decree_proceeding and appeal_filed_against_decree and decree_not_altered_on_appeal and required_deposit_not_made_by_deadline

predicates.is_preemption_decree_proceeding: A court has issued a decree in a pre-emption proceeding requiring the claimant to make a deposit.
predicates.appeal_filed_against_decree: A party filed an appeal against the decree.
predicates.decree_not_altered_on_appeal: The appellate court did not alter the decree's relevant requirement.
predicates.required_deposit_not_made_by_deadline: The claimant did not make the required deposit by the deadline fixed in the decree.

members.legal_issue: Omitting an express direction in the decree that the suit will be dismissed for failure to make the required deposit does not prevent dismissal under the mandatory rule governing pre-emption decrees.
material_facts: The decree required the plaintiff to deposit the sale price within a specified time but did not expressly state that the suit would stand dismissed if the deposit was not made.
The plaintiff failed to deposit the price within the specified time.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XX, Rule 14 of the Civil Procedure Code, dismissal for failure to make the required deposit follows from the mandatory provision, not from a separate decision stated in the decree. Omitting an express direction to that effect does not affect the parties' rights.
members.conclusion: The omission of an express dismissal direction from the decree did not affect the parties' rights; the suit stood dismissed under the mandatory rule.

predicates.is_preemption_decree_proceeding: A court has issued a decree in a pre-emption proceeding requiring the claimant to make a deposit.
predicates.decree_omits_automatic_dismissal_directi: The decree does not expressly state that the suit will be dismissed if the required deposit is not made.
predicates.required_deposit_not_made_by_deadline: The claimant did not make the required deposit by the deadline fixed in the decree.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emptor’s failure to deposit the required price by the trial court’s deadline results in dismissal of the suit when no appellate stay relieves the pre-emptor of that obligation, and an appellate court cannot extend the deadline merely because it later changes the decree.
material_facts: The trial court decreed pre-emption for part of the land and directed the pre-emptors to deposit the required amounts by a specified deadline.
The pre-emptors did not make the deposits by that deadline.
On appeal, the lower appellate court extended the payment time while granting one pre-emptor pre-emption over an additional part of the land.
The lower appellate court had not granted a stay, and the pre-emptors had not deposited the amounts even within the extended time.
members.legal_principle: Order 20 Rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes the trial court’s directions for payment mandatory. A decree under that rule imposes reciprocal obligations, so a stay relieving the defendants of their obligation to deliver possession may also relieve the pre-emptor of depositing the price while the stay operates. Merely filing an appeal does not suspend the decree, and, absent a stay, failure to deposit within the time fixed results in dismissal; an appellate court cannot extend that time merely by altering the decree. The Court relied on Naguba Appa v. Namdev, AIR 1954 SC 50, and Dattaraya s/o Keshav Tawalay v. Shaikh Mahboob Shaikh Ali, [1969] 2 SCR 514.
members.conclusion: The appellate court was required to dismiss the pre-emption suit for failure to comply with the trial court’s payment directions; it could not extend the time for payment in the circumstances. The appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: preemption_proceeding and payment_required_by_trial_decree and payment_deadline_missed and no_appellate_stay

predicates.preemption_proceeding: The proceeding is a suit seeking possession by pre-emption.
predicates.payment_required_by_trial_decree: The trial court’s decree requires the pre-emptor to deposit the required price by a specified deadline.
predicates.payment_deadline_missed: The pre-emptor does not deposit the required price by the deadline fixed in the trial court’s decree.
predicates.no_appellate_stay: The appellate court has not stayed the decree in a way that relieves the pre-emptor of the deposit obligation.

members.legal_issue: Failure to comply with a peremptory specific-performance decree by the prescribed deadline and payment method causes the suit to stand dismissed.
material_facts: The decree required the buyer to deposit the balance consideration within the time it specified and by demand draft, and stated that non-deposit would result in dismissal of the suit.
The extended deadline fell on a court reopening day, but there was no evidence that the buyer attempted to deposit the money that day.
The buyer obtained a receipt order and deposited the money the next day, in cash rather than by demand draft.
members.legal_principle: A peremptory decree that makes dismissal the consequence of non-compliance operates according to its terms when the required payment is not made by the deadline and in the prescribed mode. The Court did not rely on a particular statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The buyer failed to comply with the decree, so the suit stood dismissed automatically and could not be executed.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and peremptory_decree_makes_noncompliance_self_executing and payment_deadline_missed and required_payment_method_not_used

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: A claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.peremptory_decree_makes_noncompliance_se: The court issued a decree stating that failure to comply with its payment direction would result in dismissal of the suit.
predicates.payment_deadline_missed: The claimant did not make the required payment by the deadline, including the applicable court reopening day.
predicates.required_payment_method_not_used: The claimant made the payment by a method different from the one required by the decree.

members.legal_issue: A short delay in filing an appeal should be condoned when a justice-oriented assessment establishes sufficient cause and refusing condonation would prevent a potentially meritorious matter from being decided on its merits.
material_facts: The appeal challenged an enhancement of compensation for acquired land that raised important questions about valuation.
The appeal was filed four days beyond the prescribed period.
The Court was satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay and that the appeal should be considered on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits a late appeal to be admitted where sufficient cause is shown. The phrase “sufficient cause” is elastic and should be applied rationally and pragmatically to advance substantial justice. Courts should not presume that delay was deliberate, caused by culpable negligence, or mala fide; a demand to explain every day is not a call for a pedantic approach. Where substantial justice conflicts with technical considerations, a non-deliberate delay should not ordinarily defeat a merits decision. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The delay was condoned, the order dismissing the appeal as time-barred was set aside, and the matter was remitted for decision on the merits.

rule.if: appeal_dismissed_as_time_barred and short_delay and important_merits_questions and sufficient_cause_for_delay

predicates.appeal_dismissed_as_time_barred: An appeal was rejected because it was filed after the prescribed period.
predicates.short_delay: The appeal was filed only a short time after the prescribed period expired.
predicates.important_merits_questions: The appeal raised important questions that warranted determination on their merits.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay: The circumstances of the delay were found to provide sufficient cause for filing late.

members.legal_issue: Conflicting judicial decisions on the appeal procedure constitute sufficient cause to grant relief from a filing delay.
material_facts: The appellant filed a separate appeal twenty-nine days after the limitation period had expired.
There was a conflict of decisions on whether separate appeals were required, both within the relevant High Court and among different High Courts in India.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 permits time to be extended where sufficient cause is shown. In the circumstances, conflicting judicial rulings on the procedural question justified giving the appellant that benefit; Mst. Lachmi v. Mst. Bhuli was applied, and Appa v. Kachai Bayyan Kutti was cited in support.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong not to give the appellant the benefit of an extension of time under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

predicates.appeal_seeking_extension_of_time: The proceeding is an appeal in which the appellant seeks relief from a filing delay.
predicates.appeal_filed_late: The appellant filed the appeal after the applicable limitation period.
predicates.conflicting_decisions_on_procedure: Different courts had issued conflicting decisions on the procedural requirement relevant to filing the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A delay in filing a first appeal should be condoned when the appellant bona fide prosecuted the appeal in a court lacking jurisdiction because of a mistaken belief, and the circumstances establish sufficient cause.
material_facts: The appellant pursued the appeal before a district court that lacked jurisdiction, believing that it was the proper court.
The jurisdictional error escaped notice both when the appeal was instituted and during its hearing.
The appellant then filed the appeal in the High Court late, and the respondent conceded that excluding the time spent in the district court would make it timely.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, delay may be condoned where sufficient cause is established. Bona fide prosecution of an appeal before a court lacking jurisdiction, in circumstances where the mistake escaped scrutiny, can constitute sufficient cause; the period so spent may be excluded when assessing whether the appeal was timely. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have condoned the delay. The Supreme Court set aside its refusal, condoned the delay, and remanded the first appeal for disposal in accordance with law.

rule.if: first_appeal_delay_case and bona_fide_wrong_forum_prosecution and jurisdiction_error_escaped_review and excluded_period_restores_timeliness

predicates.first_appeal_delay_case: The matter concerns an application to excuse delay in filing a first appeal.
predicates.bona_fide_wrong_forum_prosecution: The appellant pursued the appeal in a court that lacked jurisdiction because the appellant bona fide believed it was the proper court.
predicates.jurisdiction_error_escaped_review: The jurisdictional mistake was not noticed when the appeal was instituted or while it was heard.
predicates.excluded_period_restores_timeliness: Excluding the time spent pursuing the appeal in the court lacking jurisdiction makes the appeal timely.

members.legal_issue: A delay in filing a challenge may be condoned when the public agency takes steps to obtain the acquisition records and legal advice after learning of the decision and then files its challenge.
material_facts: The agency learned of the High Court’s judgment after receiving a communication seeking release of compensation funds.
After learning of the judgment, its officials collected the acquisition records and sought legal opinions before filing the special leave petitions.
The petitions were filed late, and the agency sought condonation of the delay.
members.legal_principle: Applying the approach to condonation of delay in Collector, Land Acquisition v. Katiji, (1987) 2 SCC 107, and State of Haryana v. Chandra Mani, (1996) 3 SCC 132, the Court condoned the delay in the circumstances of the case.
members.conclusion: The delay was condoned.

predicates.delayed_challenge_to_compensation_decisi: A challenge to a compensation decision is filed after the applicable filing period.
predicates.public_agency_challenger: The party seeking to file the delayed challenge is a public agency.
predicates.steps_taken_to_collect_records_and_obtai: After learning of the decision, the agency collected relevant records and obtained legal advice before filing.

members.legal_issue: A delay in appealing an administrative recovery order may be condoned where the appeal is filed within the transitional period after a new appeal right takes effect, if the appeal is otherwise maintainable and justice supports entertaining it.
material_facts: An amendment newly provided an appeal against an administrative recovery order.
The amendment prescribed a period for filing an appeal from the order, although the appeal right had not existed when earlier orders were made.

The Court stated that the appellate authority could consider condoning delay where an appeal was filed within three months after the new appeal right came into force, subject to maintainability and the interests of justice.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the condonation power under section 5 of the Limitation Act, as made available to the appellate authority under section 5A of the amended recovery law. It indicated that the newly created appeal right and the prescribed filing period could justify condoning delay for an appeal filed within the stated transitional period, provided the authority was satisfied that the appeal was otherwise maintainable and justice required its admission.
members.conclusion: The appellate authority may condone the delay in such a transitional appeal if it is otherwise maintainable and the interests of justice require that it be heard.

rule.if: appeal_from_administrative_recovery_order and appeal_right_newly_created and appeal_filed_within_transition_period and appeal_otherwise_maintainable and interests_of_justice_favor_hearing

predicates.appeal_from_administrative_recovery_orde: The proceeding is an appeal from an administrative order recovering granted land.
predicates.appeal_right_newly_created: The right of appeal became available only after the administrative order was made.
predicates.appeal_filed_within_transition_period: The appeal was filed within the transitional period following the new appeal right’s commencement.
predicates.appeal_otherwise_maintainable: The appeal satisfies the requirements for being entertained apart from the question of delay.
predicates.interests_of_justice_favor_hearing: The appellate authority considers that the interests of justice favor hearing the appeal.

members.legal_issue: Delay in seeking appellate review may be condoned when resolving the appeal on its merits is just because the litigation affects the rights of the public and final resolution is appropriate.
material_facts: The State’s application for leave to appeal was substantially out of time.
The State had not appealed earlier and had opposed the other party’s request for leave, but the outcome of the litigation affected members of the public.
The Court considered it just to determine the controversy on its merits so that it could be finally settled.
members.legal_principle: Although acquiescing in a judgment and allowing the appeal period to lapse ordinarily does not justify condonation merely because the party later changes its mind, the Court may condone delay where the litigation affects public rights and a decision on the merits is just to settle the controversy finally.
members.conclusion: The Court condoned the delay and heard the application on its merits.

predicates.late_appellate_application: A party makes an appellate application after the applicable time for filing has expired.
predicates.application_affects_public_rights: The outcome of the appellate proceeding affects rights of members of the public.
predicates.merits_review_needed_for_final_resolutio: Determining the merits is considered just to settle the controversy finally.

members.legal_issue: Delay in refiling an appeal with a certified copy may be condoned where sufficient cause is established and the delay is not attributable to the appellant's bad faith, inaction, or negligence.
material_facts: The appellant repeatedly applied for a certified copy of the order but the copying department supplied a copy of a different order and later failed to supply the requested copy despite further applications.
A family member obtained a certified copy but did not give it to the appellant.
The appellant was under the bona fide impression that the requested certified copy had not yet been supplied or was not ready.
After receiving a certified copy, the appellant filed it in court on the same day.
The Court found no bad faith or such inaction or negligence by the appellant as would deprive her of the protection of Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act gives the court discretion to condone delay where sufficient cause is shown. As stated in Krishna v. Chathappan, “sufficient cause” is construed liberally to advance substantial justice where negligence, inaction, or want of bona fides is not imputable to the appellant.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act and condoned the delay in refiling the appeal with the certified copy.

rule.if: application_to_condone_refiling_delay and repeated_copy_applications_made and copying_office_failed_to_supply_correct_copy and (copy_obtained_by_family_member_not_delivered or appellant_believed_copy_not_ready) and copy_filed_promptly_when_received and no_bad_faith_or_inexcusable_inaction

predicates.application_to_condone_refiling_delay: The appellant seeks condonation of delay in refiling an appeal with a required certified copy.
predicates.repeated_copy_applications_made: The appellant made repeated applications to obtain the certified copy.
predicates.copying_office_failed_to_supply_correct_: The copying office supplied an incorrect copy or failed to supply the requested copy despite the applications.
predicates.copy_obtained_by_family_member_not_deliv: A family member obtained the required copy but did not deliver it to the appellant.
predicates.appellant_believed_copy_not_ready: The appellant bona fide believed that the required copy had not been supplied or was not ready.
predicates.copy_filed_promptly_when_received: The appellant filed the certified copy promptly after receiving it.
predicates.no_bad_faith_or_inexcusable_inaction: The appellant's conduct showed no bad faith or inexcusable inaction or negligence.

members.legal_issue: Delay in appealing a rent-deposit order should be condoned when the circumstances explain the delay and refusing condonation would cause a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeal challenged an order directing future rent deposits and was accompanied by an application to condone delay.
The tenant stated that the orders were made in the tenant’s absence and were not communicated to the tenant.
The landlord’s suit was dismissed for default and later restored; the tenant appealed within three days of restoration.
The order appealed from was found to be interpolated, and refusal to condone delay left the tenant subject to the striking of a defence for noncompliance with a legally non-existent order.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, delay may be condoned for sufficient cause. Although a court ordinarily does not interfere with a factual decision on such an application, it may do so where the failure to exercise jurisdiction would cause a miscarriage of justice. The Court found the combination of lack of communication, the suit’s dismissal and restoration, the prompt appeal after restoration, and the interpolated nature of the order sufficient to justify condonation.
members.conclusion: The tenant had shown sufficient cause for the delay; the refusal to condone it was set aside and the delay was condoned.

predicates.appeal_against_rent_deposit_order: A party appealed an order requiring rent deposits during a pending rent dispute.
predicates.order_not_communicated_to_appellant: The order was made in the appellant’s absence and was not communicated to the appellant.
predicates.appeal_filed_promptly_after_obstacle_end: The appellant filed the appeal promptly after the circumstance preventing an earlier appeal ended.
predicates.refusal_to_condone_would_cause_miscarria: Refusing to excuse the delay would leave the appellant suffering a serious consequence based on an order later found to be legally non-existent.

members.legal_issue: Delay in a government appeal may be condoned where the circumstances, including serious failures by government law officers and the government’s reliance on them, support substantial justice and do not establish gross negligence, deliberate inaction, or bad faith by the government.
material_facts: The State sought condonation of substantial delays in filing appeals against enhanced land acquisition compensation awards.
The High Court found that government law officers had failed to perform basic duties, mishandled certified-copy applications, and impeded the government’s ability to ascertain the state of the cases.
The government relied on its law officers and took time to discover that they had failed that trust.
The Court considered the government’s delay after it had notice of the awards unjustifiably prolonged and its conduct perilously close to inaction.
The High Court had condoned the delays, and the Court concluded that the awards should not become final without merits review in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, “sufficient cause” is construed liberally to advance substantial justice, and delay is generally condoned where gross negligence, deliberate inaction, or lack of bona fides is not imputable to the applicant. There is no general rule excusing every mistake of counsel, and each case depends on its facts. Government remains responsible for its officers’ acts and omissions, but reasonable recognition may be given to governmental decision-making and procedural limitations, particularly where public interest is affected by officers’ fraud, bad faith, or conduct at cross-purposes with the government. The Court relied on Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal v. Rewa Coalfield Ltd.; Shakuntala Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumari; Concord of India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Nirmala Devi; Lala Mata Din v. A. Narayanan; Collector, Land Acquisition v. Katiji; Re: National Bank of Wales Ltd.; and Special Land Acquisition Officer v. B.M. Krishnamurthy.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s exercise of discretion and dismissed the appeals challenging condonation of delay.

rule.if: government_appeal_seeks_delay_condonation and law_officers_seriously_failed_duties and government_relied_on_law_officers and officer_conduct_delayed_discovery and public_interest_would_be_affected and not gross_negligence_or_bad_faith_attributable_to_government

predicates.government_appeal_seeks_delay_condonatio: The government seeks to excuse delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.law_officers_seriously_failed_duties: The government’s law officers failed to perform important duties involved in preparing or pursuing the appeal.
predicates.government_relied_on_law_officers: The government entrusted the conduct of the matter to its law officers and relied on them.
predicates.officer_conduct_delayed_discovery: The law officers’ conduct hindered the government from learning the true state of the matter promptly.
predicates.public_interest_would_be_affected: The loss of the government’s appeal would affect public interest rather than only an individual litigant.
predicates.gross_negligence_or_bad_faith_attributab: The government itself acted with gross negligence or deliberate inaction, or lacked bona fides, in seeking condonation.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide mistake of counsel that causes an appeal to be filed in the wrong forum can justify extending the time for filing it in the proper forum.
material_facts: The suit’s original valuation placed the appeal in the High Court, but counsel valued the appeal below the threshold and filed it in the District Court.
Counsel’s error was attributed to a genuine misunderstanding of a court rule concerning the forum for appeals in suits for accounts.
The memorandum disclosed both the original suit valuation and the appeal valuation, and the appellant paid the court fee that would have been payable in the High Court.
The appeal was filed in the High Court on the day it was returned by the District Court, and the record disclosed no underhand motive or attempt to evade limitation.
Counsel continued to act on the same understanding in seeking revision of the District Court’s order.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a mistake by counsel may justify condoning delay in appropriate circumstances, but counsel’s mistake is not by itself sufficient. The court must assess whether it was bona fide or a device to conceal an ulterior purpose, such as a litigant’s laches or an attempt to evade limitation. The court relied on section 39(1) of the Punjab Courts Act and Rule 4 in Chapter 3-B of Volume I of the High Court Rules and Orders to assess the asserted mistake. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have extended time under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908; its order was set aside and the appeal was remitted for hearing and disposal according to law.

rule.if: appeal_requires_delay_extension and appeal_filed_in_wrong_forum_on_counsel_advice and counsel_mistake_was_bona_fide and no_ulterior_motive and appeal_valuation_was_disclosed

predicates.appeal_requires_delay_extension: The litigant sought additional time because the appeal was not filed in the proper forum within the applicable period.
predicates.appeal_filed_in_wrong_forum_on_counsel_a: Counsel filed the appeal in a forum that lacked jurisdiction, acting on counsel’s understanding of the applicable forum rules.
predicates.counsel_mistake_was_bona_fide: Counsel’s error arose from a genuine misunderstanding rather than a deliberate attempt to mislead or evade the law.
predicates.no_ulterior_motive: The litigant did not use the mistaken filing to conceal personal inaction or to gain an improper advantage.
predicates.appeal_valuation_was_disclosed: The appeal papers disclosed the original suit valuation as well as the valuation asserted for the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A party's bona fide reliance on a plausible limitation period amid genuine uncertainty about the applicable limitation law can justify condoning delay in filing an appeal.
material_facts: The applicable limitation law was a complex and unsettled question, with two views regarded by the Court as equally plausible.
The appellants stated that they bona fide believed, apparently on legal advice, that the limitation period under the later limitation law applied.
They filed the appeal within the period they believed applied, but the appeal was beyond the shorter period prescribed by the former code.
The appellants applied for condonation of delay.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 145 of the Portuguese Code, a just impediment could justify delay. The Court held that, where the applicable limitation law presents a complex question with two equally plausible views, a party's bona fide choice to act consistently with one view can amount to sufficient cause and a just impediment. Article 116 of the Limitation Act, 1963, was the limitation provision the appellants believed applied; the Court did not decide whether it in fact governed.
members.conclusion: The Court granted the application for condonation of delay and directed that the appeal be taken on file for decision on its merits, without deciding which limitation law governed.

rule.if: appeal_against_civil_decree and limitation_law_genuinely_uncertain and appellant_bona_fide_followed_plausible_view and appeal_filed_within_believed_period

predicates.appeal_against_civil_decree: A party has brought an appeal against a civil decree.
predicates.limitation_law_genuinely_uncertain: The applicable limitation law presents a complex question on which more than one view is reasonably plausible.
predicates.appellant_bona_fide_followed_plausible_v: The appellant genuinely acted in accordance with one of the reasonably plausible views of the applicable limitation law.
predicates.appeal_filed_within_believed_period: The appellant filed the appeal within the period that the appellant believed applied.

members.legal_issue: A reasonable doubt that a tenant was pressured by police into an eviction compromise can justify condoning delay in appealing the compromise decree.
material_facts: The tenants alleged that police pressure led them to enter into a compromise concerning the eviction proceedings.
A compromise had earlier been made at a police station and was addressed to a police officer before the eviction petition was filed.
The landlord’s complaint alleged that the lease document was forged and denied the landlord-tenant relationship, yet the landlord later sought eviction on that relationship.
The appellate court found the complaint and police-station compromise unrebutted and considered the allegation of coercion prima facie acceptable.
The tenants filed their appeal against the compromise decree 604 days late, and the appellate court accepted their explanation for the delay.
members.legal_principle: Where there is reasonable doubt that police forced a party to enter into a compromise, the court process should weigh in favour of the party alleging that pressure. The Court relied on Ajad Singh v. Chatra (2005) 2 SCC 567, which treated a compromise recorded in a police station during pending litigation as a relevant circumstance warranting judicial scrutiny.
members.conclusion: The delay in filing the appeal was properly condoned; the High Court’s order setting aside condonation was reversed, and the appellate court’s order was restored.

rule.if: appeal_from_rent_compromise_decree and delayed_appeal and coercion_alleged and reasonable_doubt_of_police_pressure

predicates.appeal_from_rent_compromise_decree: The proceeding is an appeal filed late against a compromise decree concerning eviction from rented premises.
predicates.delayed_appeal: The party filed the appeal after the applicable filing time had passed.
predicates.coercion_alleged: The appealing party said that police pressure caused it to enter into the compromise.
predicates.reasonable_doubt_of_police_pressure: Circumstances such as a compromise made at a police station, unrebutted evidence, or inconsistent positions by the other party raised reasonable doubt that police pressure caused the compromise.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide filing-deadline miscalculation by counsel can constitute sufficient cause to condone an appeal’s delay, including for a co-appellant that entrusted the appeal to the primary beneficiary.
material_facts: The appellants filed their appeal two days after the deadline and sought condonation of the delay.
Counsel had mistakenly recorded a later filing deadline, and his affidavit stated that the mistake caused the delay.
The court accepted counsel’s account as probable and found the calculation error bona fide rather than negligent.
The university was the party primarily interested in the appeal because it had to pay the compensation, and the government had left the matter in the university’s hands.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, a lawyer’s mistake may, in the circumstances of a particular case, amount to sufficient cause for delay; there is no general rule that parties are protected from every consequence of wrong legal advice. The Court relied on Kunwar Rajendra Singh v. Rai Rajeshwar Bili and Others and its observations in Civil Appeals Nos. 821–823 of 1968. A bona fide mistake in calculation is not necessarily negligence. Where the government left the conduct of the matter to the party primarily interested in the appeal, it could rely on that party’s explanation for the delay.
members.conclusion: The counsel’s bona fide calculation error constituted sufficient cause for the delay, and the government could rely on the explanation given by the university. The refusal to condone the delay was set aside, and the appeals were to be admitted.

rule.if: appeal_delay_condonation_request and counsel_miscalculated_filing_deadline and counsel_error_was_bona_fide and counsel_error_caused_delay and co_appellant_entrusted_filing_to_primary_beneficiary

predicates.appeal_delay_condonation_request: An appellant sought condonation of delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.counsel_miscalculated_filing_deadline: Counsel recorded an incorrect filing deadline because of a calculation error.
predicates.counsel_error_was_bona_fide: The court accepted that counsel’s calculation error was genuine and not negligence.
predicates.counsel_error_caused_delay: Counsel’s calculation error caused the appeal to be filed late.
predicates.co_appellant_entrusted_filing_to_primary: A co-appellant left the conduct of the appeal to the party primarily interested in its outcome.

members.legal_issue: A substantial delay in filing an appeal should be condoned when the government acted promptly to initiate the appeal but delayed because it relied on an adverse legal opinion before later reconsidering the matter.
material_facts: The government received the single judge’s decision and instructed its government pleader to file an appeal within a short time.
The government pleader later advised against filing the appeal, and the government took no further action in reliance on that advice.
After the matter was re-examined in light of numerous similar pending cases, a new government pleader advised that an appeal should be filed, and the government filed it.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the delay was explained by the sequence of steps taken and the circumstances leading to the late filing. It relied on no cited statutory provision or earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The delay in filing the appeal was condoned, and the appellate court had been wrong to refuse condonation.

rule.if: government_appeal_from_writ_decision and prompt_instruction_to_appeal and delay_caused_by_reliance_on_legal_opinion and later_reconsideration_of_appeal

predicates.government_appeal_from_writ_decision: The government appealed a decision made in writ proceedings.
predicates.prompt_instruction_to_appeal: The government promptly instructed its representative to file an appeal after receiving the decision.
predicates.delay_caused_by_reliance_on_legal_opinio: The appeal was delayed because the government relied on its representative’s advice not to appeal.
predicates.later_reconsideration_of_appeal: The government later reconsidered the matter and decided that an appeal should be filed.
predicates.appeal_delay_condoned: The delay in filing the appeal is excused.

members.legal_issue: A delay in appealing the dismissal of execution-sale objections should be condoned when the delay is not substantial, the party acted after learning of the dismissal, and the circumstances do not show callous or mala fide conduct.
material_facts: The appellant’s objections to the execution sale were dismissed after it failed to appear to lead evidence, and the sale was confirmed.
The appellant’s first appeal was delayed by about two months and a few days; it sought condonation under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
The appellant relied on its former advocate’s failure to inform it of the dismissal and said it acted to file an appeal after learning of it.
The Court found that the appellant had taken steps to prosecute the matter, had not been absolutely callous or negligent, and would not have gained from delaying the appeal.
The Court considered that the delay was not so substantial as to warrant dismissal on a technical ground and that the respondent’s inconvenience could be addressed by costs.
The Executing Court had closed the appellant’s evidence, leaving the objections without a determination on their merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not prescribe a straight-jacket formula for deciding whether sufficient cause exists; each case must be assessed in light of its facts and the party’s conduct. As a general rule, delay should be condoned unless mala fides are writ large, and courts should endeavour to have matters contested on their merits rather than dismiss them on technicalities. The Court stated that it was unnecessary to address the cited decisions on Section 5. The objections were remitted for consideration under Order 21 Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, without any opinion on their merits.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the orders rejecting the appeal as time-barred, condoned the delay, and remitted the objections to the Executing Court for decision on the merits. The appellant was required to pay costs to the respondent as a condition of prosecuting its objections.

rule.if: appeal_seeks_review_of_rejection_as_time_barred and delay_not_substantial and party_acted_after_learning_of_dismissal and party_took_steps_to_prosecute and not callous_or_mala_fide_conduct

predicates.appeal_seeks_review_of_rejection_as_time: A party brings an appeal challenging the rejection of its appeal as filed out of time.
predicates.delay_not_substantial: The delay in filing the appeal is not so substantial that it warrants dismissal on that ground alone.
predicates.party_acted_after_learning_of_dismissal: The party took steps to appeal after it learned that its objections had been dismissed.
predicates.party_took_steps_to_prosecute: The party had taken steps to pursue the matter before the appeal was filed.
predicates.callous_or_mala_fide_conduct: The party’s conduct in pursuing the matter was callous or showed mala fides.

members.legal_issue: A court should take a justice-oriented and lenient approach to condonation of delay in a public authority’s appeal when deliberate lapses by public officials caused the delay and corrective steps were taken after the proceedings came to light.
material_facts: A town panchayat sought condonation of a 1373-day delay in filing a second appeal.
The Executive Officer took no steps at the relevant time, and the Supreme Court found that the delay was caused by deliberate lapses on the part of the officer then in charge.

The later Executive Officer learned of the proceedings when eviction steps were taken in execution, then sought certified copies and filed the appeal after obtaining sanction and completing procedural formalities.
The High Court had refused to condone the delay.
members.legal_principle: Under State of Nagaland v. Lipok Ao and others, (2005) 3 SCC 752, a court considering condonation of delay must adopt a justice-oriented approach. Where it is convinced that government officials or public servants attempted to defeat justice by causing delay, it should, in the larger public interest, take a lenient view, condone the delay however large, and allow the matter to be decided on its merits.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the refusal, condoned the delay, and remitted the matter to the High Court for consideration of the second appeal in accordance with law.

predicates.public_authority_appeal_delay_applicatio: A public authority sought condonation of delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.deliberate_official_lapses_caused_delay: Deliberate lapses by public officials caused the delay in taking the appeal forward.
predicates.corrective_steps_followed_discovery: After a responsible official learned of the proceedings, steps were taken to obtain the necessary documents and file the appeal.

members.legal_issue: Delay in appealing the rejection of a suit may be condoned when the litigant was unaware of the rejection and acted after learning of it, with an acceptable explanation for the delay.
material_facts: The litigant appealed the rejection of his suit and sought condonation of delay.
He said he did not know that the trial court had rejected the suit and believed his request for more time to pay court fees would be allowed.
After learning from his advocate that the suit had been rejected, he applied for a certified copy that same day.
The High Court rejected the condonation application for lack of sufficient grounds, but the Supreme Court found that decision unsustainable.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits condonation where sufficient cause is shown. The Court applied the substantial-justice and pragmatic approach in State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad Singh, Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy, and relied on Muneesh Devi v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. Length of delay is not by itself decisive; the acceptability of the explanation is the criterion.
members.conclusion: The delay in filing the appeal before the High Court was condoned.

rule.if: appeal_from_suit_rejection and litigant_unaware_of_rejection and prompt_action_after_learning and acceptable_explanation

predicates.appeal_from_suit_rejection: The litigant sought to appeal the rejection of a suit.
predicates.litigant_unaware_of_rejection: The litigant did not know that the trial court had rejected the suit.
predicates.prompt_action_after_learning: After learning of the rejection, the litigant promptly took steps to obtain the decision and pursue an appeal.
predicates.acceptable_explanation: The litigant gave an explanation for the delay that the court accepted.

members.legal_issue: An award that requires registration may nevertheless be filed in court before registration, but it cannot then be used as evidence to affect covered immovable property.
material_facts: The award was unregistered when the arbitrators first filed it in court.
The parties accepted that the award required registration.
The award was later registered and refiled.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, require registration for the relevant award to affect immovable property, but section 49 does not prohibit filing the unregistered award in court; it restricts its evidentiary use to affect such property.
members.conclusion: Filing an unregistered award was not prohibited by section 49 of the Registration Act, although the award could not be taken into evidence so as to affect immovable property covered by section 17.

predicates.arbitration_award_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an award made in an arbitration.
predicates.award_requires_registration: The award requires registration to affect the relevant immovable property.
predicates.award_filed_before_registration: The award was filed in court before it was registered.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot pronounce judgment under the arbitration procedure on an unregistered award that requires registration and is therefore inadmissible.
material_facts: The award created rights in immovable property and was unregistered.
The respondent’s application to set aside the award was dismissed as time-barred, after which the appellant asked the court to pronounce judgment in accordance with the award.
members.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 presupposes an award that the court may validly look into. An award inadmissible for want of registration cannot support judgment under that section. The registration requirement follows from section 17 of the Registration Act and the rule applied in Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar.
members.conclusion: The court could not look into the unregistered award and could not pronounce judgment in accordance with it; dismissal of the challenge as time-barred did not make the award admissible.

predicates.court_asked_to_enter_judgment: A party asked a court to pronounce judgment in accordance with an arbitral award.
predicates.award_requires_registration: The award created rights in immovable property of a kind and value that require registration.
predicates.award_is_unregistered: The award had not been registered.

members.legal_issue: An inseparable unregistered arbitral award cannot be enforced in part by severing provisions that do not themselves deal with immovable property.
material_facts: The award combined the allotment of the factory and other assets with payment obligations, allocation of debts, waivers, assistance with recovery and transfer of tenancy rights, and delivery of business documents.
The award conditioned running the factory on payment of the consideration to the other partner.
The award was unregistered and its provisions formed an integrated arrangement in which the other clauses constituted consideration for the property allotment.
members.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 applies only to an award that may validly be looked into by the court. Because this award was unregistered and its clauses were interdependent, the court could not enforce selected portions while excluding the provisions creating rights in immovable property.
members.conclusion: The award was an inseparable tangle of clauses and could not be enforced as to the parts that did not deal with immovable property.

predicates.court_asked_to_enforce_part_of_award: A party asked the court to give effect to only part of an arbitral award.
predicates.award_is_unregistered: The award had not been registered.
predicates.award_clauses_are_interdependent: The award linked its property allotment to other obligations, and those obligations formed consideration for the allotment.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered award affecting immovable property cannot be admitted in evidence to affect that property, although filing the award is not itself prohibited.
material_facts: The arbitrator applied to have the award filed and made a rule of the court.
An objection asserted that the unregistered award was inadmissible in evidence.
The award purported to effect a partition of immovable property.
members.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 does not prohibit filing an unregistered award; it prohibits using such an instrument as evidence to affect immovable property within section 17. The Court relied on Champalal v. Mst. Samarath Bai and Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Baskarsa Kabadi.
members.conclusion: Filing an unregistered award is not prohibited, but the award cannot be taken into evidence so as to affect immovable property for which registration is required.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator cannot enforce the terms of an unregistered lease that is compulsorily registrable, and a claim outside the scope of the arbitration clause cannot be decided under that clause.
material_facts: The lease was for a term exceeding one year, was compulsorily registrable, and had not been registered.
The arbitration clause was limited to disputes relating to or touching upon the lease deed.
The applicant sought enforcement of the lease and recovery of expenditure, either as damages for failure to grant the lease or as a claim independent of the lease.
The sale-agreement dispute was not covered by the lease deed’s arbitration clause.
members.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, sections 17 and 49, and Transfer of Property Act, 1882, sections 106 and 107, govern registration and the effect of non-registration of the lease. An unregistered instrument cannot affect the immovable property or be received as evidence of a transaction affecting it, subject to the limited uses in section 49. An arbitrator may not rely on the instrument to enforce its lease terms. A claim must also fall within the scope of the arbitration agreement, as reflected in the principle stated in Yogi Agarwal v. Inspiration Clothes & U, (2009) 1 SCC 372.
members.conclusion: The arbitrator could not rely on the unregistered lease to enforce its terms. If the expenditure claim was treated as damages for breach of the lease, it sought enforcement of terms that could not be relied upon; if treated as independent of the lease, it fell outside the limited arbitration clause.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered arbitration award that creates or declares rights in immovable property outside the subject matter of the arbitration cannot be relied on to support a decree.
material_facts: The arbitration references concerned alleged unpaid loans, not a dispute about the land or its transfer.
The awards declared that the respondents had become owners of the land, creating or declaring rights in immovable property that was not the subject matter of the arbitration.
The awards were not registered.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17(1)(b) and 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, 1908, require registration of non-testamentary instruments creating or declaring rights in immovable property, while providing an exception for court decrees subject to the stated compromise-decree qualification. Arbitration awards are not included in that decree exception. Section 49 limits the effect of an unregistered document that was compulsorily registrable. In Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit, AIR 1974 SC 1066, and Lachhman Dass v. Ram Lal, (1989) 3 SCC 99, the Court held that an award creating rights in immovable property requiring registration cannot be relied on for a decree when unregistered.
members.conclusion: The awards were compulsorily registrable; because they were unregistered, they could not be acted upon or admitted as a basis for passing decrees in their terms.

rule.if: arbitration_award_proceeding and award_creates_property_rights and property_outside_arbitration_subject and award_unregistered

members.legal_issue: A court cannot pronounce judgment on or make an award the rule of the court when the award requires registration but remains unregistered, and the registration objection may be raised in the proceeding seeking enforcement of the award.
material_facts: The award was unregistered when the court was asked to pronounce judgment upon it and make it the rule of the court.
The objection that the award was unregistered had not been raised before the trial court.
The award affected an ownership right in immovable property above the statutory value threshold.
members.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 requires the court to pronounce judgment upon a filed award and make it a rule of the court, but the court must be legally able to look into the award to do so. Under section 49 of the Registration Act, a document requiring registration cannot be received as evidence of a transaction affecting immovable property unless registered. Sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act concern challenges to an award, whereas the objection in a section 14 proceeding may be raised when the court is asked to enforce the award. Satish Kumar & Ors. v. Surinder Kumar & Ors. and Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit were relied upon.
members.conclusion: The court could not look into the unregistered award or pronounce judgment upon it in the proceeding to make it the rule of the court; the registration objection could be raised in that proceeding despite not having been raised earlier.

predicates.arbitration_award_enforcement_proceeding: A party asks a court to pronounce judgment upon an arbitration award and make it enforceable as the rule of the court.

predicates.award_unregistered_when_court_considers_: The award has not been registered when the court is asked to act upon it.

members.legal_issue: An objection that an arbitral award is unstamped or unregistered is not to be decided in proceedings to set aside the award, but may be raised when enforcement is sought.
material_facts: The parties referred a dispute over joint family property to arbitration, and the arbitral tribunal made an award.
Parties applied to set aside the award and objected that it was inadmissible and unenforceable because it was not stamped or registered.
The High Court set aside the order rejecting those applications on the ground that the award was unstamped and unregistered; no enforcement proceeding was before the courts.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 permits an award to be set aside only on the grounds enumerated there, so an objection concerning stamping or registration is not a ground to be decided in that proceeding. The question is relevant when the award is presented for enforcement under Section 36, where admissibility objections may be raised under Section 17 of the Registration Act. The question falls within Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure rather than Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The stamping and registration objection was premature in the proceedings to set aside the award. The High Court's judgment was set aside, the remaining objections under Section 34 were remitted to it, and the parties remained free to raise stamping and registration objections at the enforcement stage.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly cannot be held liable for murder through the assembly’s common object when that object was to cause grievous hurt and the fatal injury was neither shown to be within that object nor known to be likely in its prosecution.
material_facts: The deceased suffered several injuries, including one injury that was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The evidence did not establish which appellant inflicted the fatal injury, and none of the appellants had been specifically charged with causing that injury as murder.
The circumstances showed that the assembly’s common object was to cause grievous hurt with dangerous weapons.
The Court was not satisfied that the fatal injury was inflicted in prosecution of that common object or that the members knew it was likely to be inflicted in its prosecution.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code attributes an offence to members of an unlawful assembly when it is committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object or is an offence the members knew to be likely in prosecution of that object. On the facts, the common object was to cause grievous hurt with dangerous weapons, an offence under section 326; the conditions for murder liability under sections 302 and 149 were not established. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The convictions for murder with the aid of the unlawful-assembly rule were set aside, and the appellants were instead convicted of causing grievous hurt with dangerous weapons with the aid of that rule.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_case and fatal_injury_sufficient_to_cause_death and common_object_limited_to_grievous_hurt and fatal_injury_not_within_object and members_lacked_likelihood_knowledge

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The prosecution alleges that the accused acted as members of an unlawful assembly.

predicates.members_lacked_likelihood_knowledge: The evidence did not establish that the members knew the fatal injury was likely to be inflicted in prosecution of the common object.

members.legal_issue: Mere presence in an armed group does not establish shared responsibility for murder where the evidence does not prove that murder was the group’s common object or that its members knew murder was likely.
material_facts: After an argument, the lead assailant returned within minutes with armed companions and immediately shot the deceased.
The other armed companions did not fire at the deceased or at the people standing near him, and no other act by them showed an intention to kill or injure those people.
The companions later fired indiscriminately, causing simple injuries to villagers, but the evidence did not show that they shared a plan to kill the deceased.
The court found that the circumstances did not establish that the armed companions had formed an unlawful assembly with the common object of murder.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, constructive liability requires proof that an offence was committed by a member of an unlawful assembly and that it was committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object or was an offence the members knew was likely to be committed. Mere membership or presence with weapons is insufficient. The court relied on no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The convictions for murder on the basis of shared liability were set aside because the evidence did not establish the required common object or knowledge; the convictions for unlawful assembly were also set aside.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.

predicates.companions_do_not_attack_the_deceased_or: The evidence does not show the companions attacking the deceased or the people standing near the deceased.

members.legal_issue: A person charged with murder in furtherance of a common intention is not shown to share that intention where the evidence does not establish that person’s participation in the fatal attack.
material_facts: The fatal shot was attributed to one accused.
The other accused was not shown to have performed an overt act toward committing the murder.
The Court applied the same reasoning by which the acquittal of the other co-accused had been maintained.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the common-intention charge under Section 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code and concluded, on the evidence in this case, that the accused who had done no overt act toward the murder could not be held liable for it. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this issue.
members.conclusion: The accused who was not shown to have participated in the fatal attack was acquitted of the murder charge under Section 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code.
