predicates.fatal_act_attributed_to_another: The evidence attributes the act causing death to another accused.
predicates.no_overt_participation_in_fatal_attack: The accused is not shown to have performed an overt act toward the fatal attack.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on common intention is not justified where the appellate court finds that the accused were individually responsible for their acts and that there was no preconcert to commit an offence.
material_facts: The High Court found that the accused did not arrive together, that there was nothing to show a preconcert to commit an offence, and that the incident took an unexpected turn.
The High Court also found that the accused and another person were individually responsible for their acts, but nevertheless convicted the accused of murder with common intention.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, which provides for joint responsibility for an act done in furtherance of a common intention. On the High Court’s findings of individual responsibility and no preconcert, the conviction under Sections 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code could not stand. No earlier case is cited for this application.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in convicting the accused of murder with common intention on the findings it had made.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_common_inten: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction based on shared responsibility for an offence.
predicates.individual_responsibility_found: The court found that the accused were individually responsible for their respective acts.
predicates.preconcert_absent: The court found no evidence that the accused had concerted beforehand to commit an offence.

members.legal_issue: Members of an assembly are not constructively liable for murder when the assembly’s common object is lawful defence of property and the killings are neither in prosecution of that object nor known to be likely in its prosecution.
material_facts: The group’s common object was to prevent theft of fruit from land it possessed, not to kill the two victims.
The persons who caused the deaths exceeded the right of private defence.
The evidence did not establish which respondents were armed with the weapons that caused the fatal wounds or who inflicted those wounds.
The deaths were not committed in prosecution of the group’s common object, and the members were not shown to know that the deaths were likely to be committed in prosecution of that object.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code requires proof of an unlawful assembly and that the offence was committed in prosecution of its common object, or was one the members knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Read with sections 96 to 106, a lawful object of private defence does not establish an unlawful assembly merely because individuals exceed that defence. The Court relied on Kapildeo Singh v. The King and Kishori Prasad v. State of Bihar. It distinguished Gurudittamal v. State of U.P., where the individual appellants’ killings and their common intention had been established.
members.conclusion: The respondents could not be convicted of murder through constructive liability based on membership of the assembly; any person who exceeded the right of private defence could be individually responsible if the evidence established that person’s responsibility.

members.legal_issue: Joint murder liability based on common intention cannot be imposed when a shared intention to murder has not been established.
material_facts: The respondents wanted to prevent the collection of fruit from land in their possession.
A common intention among the respondents to murder either victim was not established.
The evidence did not establish which respondents caused the fatal wounds.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires a common intention to commit the offence for joint liability. The Court relied on Kishori Prasad v. State of Bihar and distinguished Gurudittamal v. State of U.P., where a common intention to kill had been found.
members.conclusion: The respondents could not be convicted of murder on the basis of common intention.

predicates.joint_homicide_liability_case: The prosecution seeks to hold multiple people jointly liable for murder based on their shared intention.
predicates.shared_intention_to_murder: The people charged shared an intention to kill the victim or victims.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly is not liable for a murder committed by another member unless the murder was committed to advance the assembly’s common object or the member knew it was likely to be committed in advancing that object.
material_facts: The group came to prevent the erection of a fence, not to kill the deceased.
The appellant was unarmed and used only his hands to push, slap, and box people at the scene.
The fatal stabbing was carried out by another group member, and the evidence did not establish that the appellant knew that member carried a knife.
Other alleged weapons were not used, and the deceased was being helped away after receiving a blow when he was stabbed.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 IPC applies if an offence is committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object, or if members knew that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Whether such knowledge existed is inferred from the totality of the circumstances, including the assembly’s nature, weapons, and conduct. The Court relied on Lalji v. State of U.P.; Dharam Pal v. State of U.P.; Chikkarange Gowda v. State of Mysore; Gajanand v. State of U.P., approving Ram Charan Rai v. Emperor; Mizaji v. State of U.P.; Shambhu Nath Singh v. State of Bihar; Gangadhar Behera v. State of Orissa; and Bishna alias Bhiswadeb Mahato v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s conviction for murder with the aid of Section 149 IPC was unsustainable, and he was acquitted of that charge.

members.legal_issue: Mere membership in an unlawful assembly formed to commit cattle trespass and forcibly prevent the watchmen from impounding cattle does not establish shared liability for murder when the other members’ knowledge of the fatal weapon’s use is unproved.
material_facts: The accused shepherds formed an unlawful assembly to graze cattle in a field and prevent the watchmen from carrying out their duties by force.
One accused took a sharp weapon from a watchman and used it to strike the victim’s head.
The sequence of the assault was uncertain, and the evidence did not establish that the other accused knew the weapon would be used in that manner.
The stick blows inflicted by the other accused were not aimed at the victim’s head.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 149 and 302 of the Indian Penal Code, murder liability through membership in an unlawful assembly requires a basis for attributing the murder to the assembly’s common object or to an offence its members knew was likely to be committed in pursuing that object. The assembly’s non-lethal object, the uncertainty about the sequence of events, the absence of proof that the other members knew how the sharp weapon would be used, and the direction of their blows did not establish that basis. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The acquittal of the other accused of murder liability through the unlawful assembly was correctly affirmed.

members.legal_issue: Persons present during a killing are not constructively liable for murder unless evidence connects the killer’s act to their shared intention or the assembly’s common object.
material_facts: The accused were present when one person stabbed the deceased, but the evidence did not establish that they shared an intention to kill or that killing was the assembly’s common object.
The earlier dispute could have prompted a confrontation or quarrel, but did not establish a plan to commit murder.
There was no evidence that the other accused knew the assailant was carrying a knife; they had no weapons, and the assailant inflicted a single stab without a further attack.
Witnesses described other accused restraining the deceased and witnesses, but those details were absent from the initial report, and the witnesses differed about who had restrained whom.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 34 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code, proof that every accused personally committed an overt act is not necessary for constructive liability. However, there must be material showing that the act of one or more accused was done in furtherance of the common intention of all, or in prosecution of the common object of the unlawful assembly. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish that the assailant’s act was in furtherance of a common intention or in prosecution of a common object. The convictions for constructive liability for murder were set aside, and the appellants were acquitted.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly are not liable for murder when the evidence establishes that their common object extended only to causing grievous hurt, rather than committing murder.
material_facts: The appellants were members of an armed assembly that went to a disputed field to dispossess the opposing party by force.
The evidence showed that the assembly intended to cause such injury as was necessary to achieve that object.
Apart from the shooter and the person who supplied him a cartridge, no member of the assembly took part in assaulting the deceased, and the other weapons were not used.
The court found that the evidence supported, at most, an intention among the other appellants to commit an offence under Section 325 IPC.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 IPC, the absence of an overt act by a member does not by itself disprove liability; the question depends on the facts of the case and whether the offence was within the unlawful assembly’s common object. The court found the common object here supported liability for grievous hurt under Section 325/149, but not murder under Section 302/149. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: For the appellants other than the shooter and the person who supplied him a cartridge, the court altered the conviction from Section 302/149 IPC to Section 325/149 IPC.

predicates.evidence_supported_only_grievous_harm_ob: The evidence supported an assembly object of causing grievous hurt, but not an object of committing murder.

members.legal_issue: Presence during a fatal attack, including restraining the victim, does not by itself establish common intention to commit murder with later-arriving attackers.
material_facts: Two accused caught hold of the victim.
Other accused then arrived with bladed weapons and struck the victim on the head, causing his death.
The evidence did not establish that the two who restrained the victim had shared a prior plan or common intention with the assailants who delivered the fatal blows.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires participation in a criminal act in furtherance of a common intention. A prior concert or meeting of minds must be proved, though it may be inferred from conduct or circumstances and may develop during the events. The mere fact that persons caught hold of the victim before others arrived and attacked him did not establish that common intention. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The two accused who caught hold of the victim could not be held guilty of murder on the basis of joint liability and were acquitted of that charge.

predicates.common_intention_not_proved: The evidence did not establish a prior concert or shared intention between the accused and the fatal assailants.

members.legal_issue: Participation in an assault does not establish a shared intention to murder when the participants caused only minor, non-vital injuries and the fatal injuries were attributable to other weapons.
material_facts: A group of accused persons was convicted of murder with shared intention for the death of one victim.
The accused whose murder convictions were reduced had used blunt weapons and caused injuries that were not vital.
The victim’s fatal injuries were caused by pointed weapons, and the medical evidence associated the minor injuries with blunt weapons.
The Court found that the evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that those accused shared an intention to murder.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 34 and 325 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention may form before or during an offence, but it must be inferred from proved circumstances and not merely from similar intentions, presence, weapons, or participation in an assault. The Court relied on Kripal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Pandurang, Tukia and Bhillia v. State of Hyderabad, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Hardev Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions of the accused who caused only minor, non-vital injuries were set aside and replaced with convictions for causing grievous hurt with shared intention.

predicates.shared_intention_to_murder_not_establish: The proved circumstances did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that those accused shared an intention to murder.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly are not liable for murder when the common object was to cause injuries likely to cause death, but the common object was not to cause death or commit murder and no individually attributable injury establishes murder liability.
material_facts: The accused attacked the deceased, a close family member, during an unexpected quarrel arising from a dispute over water rights.

The deceased suffered 27 injuries, mostly simple injuries to non-vital areas; two injuries involved a finger fracture, and the court found that no attacker intended to cause death or an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
Although the doctor stated that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the court was not satisfied that the injuries were cumulatively sufficient on that basis.
The court found that the assembly's common object was to cause bodily injuries likely to cause death, rather than to cause death or commit murder.
members.legal_principle: Under section 300(iii) of the Indian Penal Code, intentionally inflicting bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death constitutes murder. For liability under section 302 read with section 149, the prosecution must establish that the murder was committed in prosecution of the unlawful assembly's common object, or that the members knew murder was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Where a fatal injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature is attributable to an individual accused, that accused may be liable under section 302 without section 149; where the alleged sufficiency rests on the cumulative effect of injuries, the common object or the members' knowledge must support murder liability. On these facts, the common object was to cause injuries likely to cause death, an offence punishable under section 304(1). No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction was set aside and the accused were found guilty of culpable homicide punishable under section 304(1) read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and unlawful_assembly_caused_death and common_object_injuries_likely_to_cause_death and not common_object_to_cause_death_or_commit_murder and fatal_injury_not_individually_attributed

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_caused_death: Members of an unlawful assembly attacked a person, and the person died from the resulting injuries.
predicates.common_object_injuries_likely_to_cause_d: The assembly's common object was to cause bodily injuries likely to cause death.
predicates.common_object_to_cause_death_or_commit_m: The assembly's common object was to cause death or commit murder, or its members knew murder was likely in pursuing that object.
predicates.fatal_injury_not_individually_attributed: No accused was shown to have intentionally inflicted an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A person is not liable for a co-accused's fatal act through common intention unless the evidence establishes that the person shared that intention.
material_facts: The evidence attributed the fatal chest injury to one accused.

The evidence about the other accused's acts was inconsistent: witnesses attributed blows to different persons or parts of the deceased's body, and the evidence most specifically described a blow to the deceased's leg.
The trial court had found that no unlawful assembly or common object to assault or murder had been established.
The circumstances did not establish that the other accused shared the fatal assailant's intention.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires a shared common intention; similar intention or participation in an incident is not enough. Whether common intention existed is a question of fact inferred from the circumstances. Dukhmochan Pandey v. State of Bihar explains the distinction between common intention and similar intention. The court held that the evidence did not establish that the accused shared the intention behind the fatal blow.
members.conclusion: The conviction of the accused whose common intention was not established for the fatal offence through Section 34 could not stand; his conviction was instead entered for the injury offence supported by the evidence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and fatal_act_attributed_to_another_person and accused_evidence_shows_only_nonfatal_assault and shared_fatal_intention_not_established

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by a convicted person challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.fatal_act_attributed_to_another_person: The evidence attributes the act causing death to another person.
predicates.accused_evidence_shows_only_nonfatal_ass: The evidence concerning the accused establishes, at most, a nonfatal assault by that accused.
predicates.shared_fatal_intention_not_established: The evidence and surrounding circumstances do not establish that the accused shared the intention behind the fatal act.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot be held liable for another person’s murder on the basis of shared intention without evidence establishing a shared intention to commit that offence.
material_facts: One accused inflicted all the injuries on the deceased, including the fatal injuries.
The other accused persons were not shown to be armed or to have assaulted the deceased or exhorted the assailant.
The prosecution alleged generally that all the accused dragged the deceased from the train, but the evidence and circumstances did not establish prior concert or a meeting of minds.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires proof of a shared intention. The court found no evidence of prior concert or a meeting of minds, and cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The court held that the other accused persons could not be convicted of murder on the basis of shared intention and set aside their convictions for that offence.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and one_accused_inflicted_fatal_injuries and other_accused_unarmed and other_accused_did_not_assault_victim and no_exhortation_or_prior_concert_evidence and only_general_participation_alleged

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed from convictions entered by the lower courts.
predicates.one_accused_inflicted_fatal_injuries: The evidence attributed all injuries on the deceased, including the fatal injuries, to one accused.
predicates.other_accused_unarmed: The other accused persons were not shown to have been armed.
predicates.other_accused_did_not_assault_victim: The other accused persons were not shown to have assaulted the deceased.
predicates.no_exhortation_or_prior_concert_evidence: There was no evidence that the other accused persons exhorted the assailant or had agreed in advance to commit the attack.
predicates.only_general_participation_alleged: The allegation against the other accused persons was limited to a general act of participation without further evidence of a shared intention.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot sustain a murder conviction based on common intention merely because the accused were charged jointly when it leaves undisturbed a finding that they did not share the relevant common intention.
material_facts: The trial court found that the accused did not act in furtherance of a common intention and convicted two of them only of lesser offences.
The High Court convicted those two accused of murder read with common intention because they had been charged under that provision.
The High Court did not reverse the trial court’s finding that the accused had not shared a common intention to cause the relevant grievous injuries.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC requires criminal liability for a joint act to rest on a common intention shared by the participants; the existence of a charge alone does not establish that element. The Supreme Court applied this principle to the High Court’s appellate decision, which had not displaced the trial court’s finding on common intention.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s conclusion that the two accused were guilty of murder read with common intention was not justified because it left undisturbed the finding that they had not acted in furtherance of a common intention.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_reviewing_joint_murder_conviction and lower_court_found_no_common_intention and appellate_court_left_finding_undisturbed and charge_alone_used_to_convict

predicates.criminal_appeal_reviewing_joint_murder_c: An appellate court is reviewing a murder conviction imposed on multiple accused through a joint-liability theory.
predicates.lower_court_found_no_common_intention: The lower court found that the accused did not share the common intention required for joint liability.
predicates.appellate_court_left_finding_undisturbed: The appellate court did not reverse or displace the lower court’s finding that common intention was absent.
predicates.charge_alone_used_to_convict: The appellate court relied on the fact that the accused had been charged jointly, without establishing the required common intention.

members.legal_issue: A participant who did not share an intention to kill cannot be held liable for murder with common intention merely because another participant inflicted the fatal injuries.
material_facts: One accused inflicted the fatal blows on both deceased persons.
The other accused helped pull one deceased person down and inflicted only simple injuries with a stick.
The evidence did not establish that the latter accused shared an intention to kill.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, murder liability with common intention required proof that the accused shared the intention to kill. The Court found that the limited acts attributed to this accused did not establish that common intention. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions of the accused who did not share the intention to kill, under Sections 302 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code, were set aside.

rule.if: appeal_from_murder_conviction_with_common_intention and another_participant_inflicted_fatal_blow and accused_inflicted_only_simple_injuries and shared_intention_to_kill_not_established

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction_with_commo: The proceeding is an appeal from a murder conviction based on common intention.
predicates.another_participant_inflicted_fatal_blow: A different participant inflicted the fatal injury or injuries.
predicates.accused_inflicted_only_simple_injuries: The accused's own acts caused only simple injuries and did not include a fatal blow.
predicates.shared_intention_to_kill_not_established: The evidence did not establish that the accused shared an intention to kill.

members.legal_issue: A participant who inflicts a life-endangering injury during a sudden incident is not liable for murder through common intention when the circumstances do not establish that shared intention.
material_facts: The second accused participated in the same sudden incident as the first accused.
The second accused inflicted a nonfatal injury that the Court described as endangering life.
The fatal wound was inflicted by the first accused, and the circumstances did not establish that the second accused shared the first accused's intention to commit murder.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC requires common intention for joint liability. The circumstances of a sudden incident and the nature of the second accused's own injury did not establish a common intention to commit murder. An injury endangering life was punishable under Section 326 IPC. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The second accused's conviction and sentence for murder under Sections 302/34 were set aside, and he was instead convicted under Section 326 IPC and sentenced to five years' rigorous imprisonment.

rule.if: appeal_from_joint_murder_conviction and sudden_incident and accused_inflicted_nonfatal_injury and injury_endangered_life and common_intention_to_murder_not_established

predicates.appeal_from_joint_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a murder conviction imposed on the accused jointly with another person.
predicates.sudden_incident: The incident arose suddenly rather than through a planned attack.
predicates.accused_inflicted_nonfatal_injury: The accused inflicted an injury that did not cause the victim's death.
predicates.injury_endangered_life: The injury inflicted by the accused endangered the victim's life.
predicates.common_intention_to_murder_not_establish: The evidence and circumstances did not establish that the accused shared another participant's intention to commit murder.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot be convicted of murder on the basis of another person's fatal acts where the evidence establishes neither that the person participated in those acts nor that the persons shared an intention to kill.
material_facts: The eyewitness testified that the accused assaulted her, while identifying other accused as the persons who assaulted the two deceased people.
The eyewitness did not attribute to the accused any assault on the deceased people or any instigation of the assaults on them.
The acts attributed to the accused were distinct and separately described.
The acquittals of the persons identified as having assaulted the deceased people were confirmed, and the courts found no common intention to commit the murders.
members.legal_principle: The Court found no evidence connecting the accused to the deaths and no evidence establishing common intention to commit the murders. On that record, the murder conviction could not stand.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction was set aside, and the accused was acquitted of the murder offence.

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a murder conviction.
predicates.no_fatal_act_attributed_to_accused: The evidence does not attribute to the accused an act causing either death or instigation of the fatal assaults.
predicates.no_common_intention_evidence: The evidence does not establish that the accused shared an intention with others to cause the deaths.

members.legal_issue: An unlawful assembly's common object to cause death, and murder liability based on that object, are not established where the attack and medical evidence do not show an intention to kill or objectively establish injuries sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
material_facts: The appellants were convicted of murder with liability based on membership in an unlawful assembly.
The assailants used sharp-edged weapons and sticks, but the injuries to the deceased were principally on the arms and other non-vital parts.
The deceased's injuries included fractured ribs, but the medical evidence disclosed no damage to the heart or lungs and no corresponding external injuries for the rib fractures.
The medical evidence did not objectively establish that any injury was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature; most injuries were described as simple.
The deceased died from shock and haemorrhage, and the injuries to the other victims were also principally on their arms and legs.
members.legal_principle: The common object of an unlawful assembly must be inferred from circumstances including the nature of the weapons, the force used, and the injuries caused. Under Section 300, clauses 1 and III, IPC, the murder classification was not made out on these facts: there was no demonstrated intention to cause death, and the prosecution had not objectively proved that an injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The common object to cause death was not established, and the convictions for murder with liability based on the unlawful assembly were set aside. The appellants were instead convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304, Part II read with Section 149, IPC.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal_in_assembly_case and unlawful_assembly_attack and injuries_largely_non_vital and not objective_proof_of_fatal_sufficiency and not evidence_of_intent_to_kill

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal_in_assembly_cas: The case is an appeal from a murder conviction based on an accused's membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_attack: Members of the assembly attacked the victim together.
predicates.injuries_largely_non_vital: The injuries were principally inflicted on non-vital parts of the victim's body.
predicates.objective_proof_of_fatal_sufficiency: The medical evidence objectively establishes that an injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
predicates.evidence_of_intent_to_kill: The circumstances of the attack indicate that the assailants intended to cause death.

members.legal_issue: Sudden participation in an assault does not establish an unlawful assembly’s common object without evidence of that shared object, though a common intention may arise during the occurrence.
material_facts: The incident began when one accused was caught uprooting crops; the other accused arrived after a commotion and initially sought his release.
The assault began suddenly after the victim refused to release that accused before a village meeting.
The evidence did not establish a shared common object among the accused, but it showed that four accused formed a common intention during the occurrence and joined in acts resulting in the death.
The evidence did not establish that two other accused shared that intention, and the injuries attributed to them were not supported by the medical evidence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 141, 147, 148 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code require proof of an unlawful assembly and its common object; absent that proof, liability under those provisions cannot stand. Section 34 may apply where a common intention is formed during the transaction and the accused join in the act in furtherance of it. A person cannot be held liable for the resulting homicide merely by association where neither common object nor common intention, nor a causative act, is proved against that person.
members.conclusion: The unlawful-assembly and related rioting convictions were set aside. The surviving accused whose common intention and participation were established were convicted of culpable homicide with common intention; the other two accused were not liable for that homicide.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and sudden_group_occurrence and no_proof_of_shared_common_object and (common_intention_forms_during_occurrence and accused_join_in_fatal_act or no_proof_of_individual_causative_participation)

predicates.criminal_appeal: The accused appealed against criminal convictions arising from a group occurrence.
predicates.sudden_group_occurrence: Other participants arrived after a sudden dispute and the assault developed at the scene.
predicates.no_proof_of_shared_common_object: The evidence did not prove that the group shared an unlawful common object.
predicates.common_intention_forms_during_occurrence: The evidence showed that some participants formed a common intention during the occurrence.
predicates.accused_join_in_fatal_act: Those participants joined in acts in furtherance of the common intention that resulted in the victim’s death.
predicates.no_proof_of_individual_causative_partici: For other participants, the evidence did not establish a shared intention or a supported act contributing to the death.

members.legal_issue: A finding that culpable homicide was committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly's common object does not warrant substituting a murder conviction when the evidence does not establish murder.
material_facts: Two people died in the attack by members of the assembly.
The courts below found offences under the lesser culpable-homicide provision proved in prosecution of the assembly's common object.
The State appealed seeking convictions for murder, but the Court was not persuaded that murder had been proved.
members.legal_principle: Sections 302, 304 Part II, and 149 of the Indian Penal Code governed the State's request to replace the culpable-homicide findings with murder convictions and the basis for liability through the assembly. The Court concluded on the evidence that the lesser offence was proved but the murder charge was not; it cited no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The State's request for convictions for murder was rejected, and the convictions for culpable homicide not amounting to murder were upheld.

predicates.state_appeal_seeking_murder_conviction: The State appeals seeking a murder conviction in place of a lesser culpable-homicide conviction.
predicates.deaths_occurred_in_assembly_attack: People died during an attack carried out by members of an assembly.
predicates.evidence_supports_culpable_homicide_but_: The evidence establishes culpable homicide but does not establish the more serious offence of murder.

members.legal_issue: Reconsideration of an established Supreme Court decision requires compelling and substantial reasons, and a merely preferable alternative interpretation is insufficient.
material_facts: The petitioner sought reconsideration of the earlier Supreme Court decision that directly construed the provision.
That decision had governed annual-value assessments in the State for a long time and was based on the overriding clause in the provision.
The Court regarded the earlier interpretation as reasonably permissible and found no compelling reason to reconsider it.
members.legal_principle: Under The Keshav Mills Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, the Court is reluctant to revise an earlier decision unless compelling and substantial reasons make revision necessary in the public interest or for another valid and compelling reason; a view that an alternative interpretation is more reasonable is not, by itself, adequate.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reconsider the earlier decision because the test for reconsideration was not satisfied.

predicates.supreme_court_review_of_its_earlier_deci: A party asked the Supreme Court to reconsider its earlier decision.
predicates.earlier_decision_long_applied: The earlier decision had governed assessments for a long period.
predicates.earlier_view_reasonably_permissible: The Court considered the earlier interpretation a reasonably permissible view of the law.
predicates.no_compelling_substantial_reason_for_rev: The Court found no compelling and substantial reason requiring revision of the earlier decision.

members.legal_issue: An earlier constitutional ruling should not be reconsidered without substantial and compelling grounds showing that reopening it is necessary.
material_facts: The challenge relied substantially on grounds that had already been raised and rejected in an earlier decision concerning constitutional amendments.
The earlier decision had been followed in later decisions concerning laws placed in the protected schedule.
Accepting the challenge could place earlier constitutional amendments and numerous decisions concerning those laws in serious jeopardy.
members.legal_principle: A court should be reluctant to depart from an earlier decision unless it is absolutely necessary and essential to reopen the question. The inquiry includes the alleged infirmity in the earlier decision, its effect on the public good, the compelling character of the contrary arguments, and the consequences of disturbing settled decisions. The Court applied this approach to Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: There was no justification for reconsidering the earlier decision.

rule.if: constitutional_amendment_challenge and earlier_constitutional_ruling_on_same_issue and (earlier_ruling_followed_in_later_cases or reopening_would_jeopardize_settled_decisions) and not compelling_grounds_to_reopen

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a constitutional amendment.
predicates.earlier_constitutional_ruling_on_same_is: An earlier court ruling has decided the same constitutional issue.
predicates.earlier_ruling_followed_in_later_cases: Later cases have followed the earlier ruling.
predicates.reopening_would_jeopardize_settled_decis: Reversing the earlier ruling could put prior amendments or decisions based on it in serious jeopardy.
predicates.compelling_grounds_to_reopen: The challenge presents substantial and compelling reasons making it necessary to reopen the issue.

members.legal_issue: A recent Constitution Bench precedent governing the issue should not be reconsidered without extraordinary or special reasons.
material_facts: The appellant asked the Court to refer the matter to a larger bench to reconsider a recent Constitution Bench decision.
That decision governed whether a sale to an intermediary occasions export.
The Court found no extraordinary or special reason to reconsider the precedent.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of stare decisis is a valuable principle of precedent. A recent constitutional decision should not be reconsidered absent extraordinary or special reasons. The Court applied Md. Serajuddin v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to refer the matter for reconsideration and applied the existing precedent.

predicates.request_to_reconsider_recent_constitutio: A party asked the Court to have a recent constitutional decision reconsidered by a larger bench.
predicates.precedent_governs_issue: The recent decision addressed the legal issue raised in the proceeding.
predicates.extraordinary_reasons_shown: The party seeking reconsideration demonstrated extraordinary or special reasons for departing from the recent decision.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s view rests on ignoring admissible evidence or on erroneous considerations.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting the accounts of three eyewitnesses on considerations the High Court found extraneous.
The eyewitness accounts were found to be trustworthy, mutually corroborative, and supported by the first information report and medical evidence.
The High Court reappraised the evidence, identified errors in the trial court’s reasoning, and convicted the accused.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court has full power to review the evidence, although it ordinarily exercises caution because acquittal reinforces the presumption of innocence. The preference for an accused where two views are reasonably possible is a guideline for circumspection, not a jurisdictional limitation. A miscarriage of justice may arise from acquitting the guilty as well as from convicting the innocent. Where the trial court ignores legal and admissible evidence or adopts an erroneous view, the High Court must reappraise the evidence. The judgment refers generally to this Court’s prior pronouncements but identifies no earlier case by name; it discusses the High Court’s powers under Section 378 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reappraise the evidence and disturb the acquittal, and its decision disclosed no error on this ground.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The matter is an appellate proceeding challenging an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_ignored_admissible_evidence: The trial court failed to rely on evidence that was legally admissible.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_were_reliable: The eyewitness accounts were found trustworthy and supported by other evidence.
predicates.trial_court_used_extraneous_consideratio: The trial court rejected evidence on considerations not properly bearing on its assessment.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reach a different assessment of prosecution witnesses from the trial court when it reconsiders the evidence, particularly where the disagreement is not based on witness demeanour.
material_facts: The trial court rejected some evidence concerning certain accused but accepted the major part of the prosecution evidence about the occurrence.
The appellate court considered individual cases after rejecting the trial court's reliance on joint liability and reached different conclusions about the accused.
The criticism of the witnesses related mainly to their partisan character and overstatements, rather than their demeanour.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court is normally reluctant to differ from a trial court's assessment of oral evidence because the trial court can observe witnesses' demeanour, but it may do so in a proper case after reconsidering the evidence. The court noted that the trial court had substantially believed the prosecution account of the occurrence and that the disputed criticism was not principally about demeanour.
members.conclusion: The appellate court was entitled to reconsider the evidence and its findings about the victims and the accused were not invalid merely because they differed from the trial court's assessment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a conviction.
predicates.appellate_court_reassesses_witness_evide: The appellate court independently reconsiders the witness evidence.
predicates.trial_court_assessment_not_based_on_deme: The trial court's disputed assessment was not principally based on observing witness demeanour.

members.legal_issue: A higher court may set aside an acquittal where careful appraisal shows that the acquittal rested on conjecture and disregarded reliable evidence establishing guilt.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused persons, treating the death as suicide and rejecting prosecution evidence, including the dying declarations.
The High Court reappraised the evidence, found the witnesses and dying declarations reliable, and concluded that the circumstances formed a complete chain proving guilt.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s reasoning unsatisfactory, based on surmises and conjectures, and found that it had disregarded vital evidence.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the circumstantial-evidence standard requiring a complete chain of proved circumstances consistent only with guilt. It held on the facts that the trial court’s acquittal rested on surmises and conjectures and that the High Court’s appraisal justified reversal. The judgment cites Section 2(a) of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, as the basis of the appeal, and Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code for the conviction; it does not state a separate general test for appellate interference with an acquittal.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside the acquittal, and the Supreme Court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal brought under Section 2(a) of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and trial_court_rejected_reliable_evidence_on_conjecture and higher_court_reappraised_evidence and circumstances_proved_complete_chain

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal following an acquittal at trial.
predicates.trial_court_rejected_reliable_evidence_o: The trial court rejected evidence later found reliable on grounds the Supreme Court regarded as conjectural or insufficient.
predicates.higher_court_reappraised_evidence: The higher court carefully reconsidered the evidence before setting aside the acquittal.
predicates.circumstances_proved_complete_chain: The evidence established a complete chain of circumstances pointing only to guilt.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal where it rests on a material misreading of clear evidence rather than a reasonably available view of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted two accused on the ground that the witnesses had not specifically attributed participation in the assault to them.
Three witnesses had clearly testified that those accused participated in assaulting the deceased.
The appellate court reversed the acquittals, and the Supreme Court found the trial court's reasoning factually and legally erroneous.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a permissible choice between two reasonably possible views from correction of an acquittal founded on factual and legal error. It relied on no earlier cases or cited statutory provisions for this point.
members.conclusion: The reversal of the acquittals was upheld because the trial court had misread clear evidence of participation; this was not a case in which the appellate court merely preferred another reasonable view.

predicates.appeal_includes_reversal_of_acquittal: The criminal appeal challenges an appellate court's reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.clear_witness_evidence_shows_participati: Witnesses clearly testified that the acquitted accused participated in the conduct charged.
predicates.trial_court_misread_that_evidence: The trial court's stated basis for acquittal conflicts with the clear evidence of participation.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside an acquittal when a proper assessment of the evidence supports guilt and the trial court’s rejection of the evidence overlooked material features.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted all accused after treating the evidence concerning two incidents as generally unreliable.
The injured victim gave an account identifying the six appellants, and an earlier recorded statement substantially corroborated his testimony.
A co-sharer who accompanied the victim to the garden also supported the account of the assault.
The High Court separated the unreliable evidence concerning the later incident from the evidence concerning the first incident and considered the victim’s injuries and corroborated account.
members.legal_principle: An acquittal may be reversed where the evidence, properly sifted, supports the finding of guilt; here, the victim’s testimony was supported by the corroborating recorded statement and an eyewitness, and the trial court had overlooked material features. The judgment cites no earlier case or particular provision for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering with the acquittal of the six appellants in relation to the assault on the victim.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and victim_identifies_assailants and victim_account_is_corroborated and trial_court_overlooks_material_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The case is an appeal seeking to overturn an acquittal.
predicates.victim_identifies_assailants: The injured victim identifies the persons who committed the assault.
predicates.victim_account_is_corroborated: Other evidence, such as a prior recorded statement or an eyewitness, supports the victim’s account.
predicates.trial_court_overlooks_material_evidence: The trial court rejects the evidence without properly considering material evidence bearing on the incident.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s reasons for rejecting the core prosecution evidence are unsound and that evidence is reliable.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding problems in the witnesses’ accounts, including their implication of another accused who was later acquitted.
Three eyewitnesses consistently attributed the fatal stabbing to the accused, and their account of that act was corroborated by medical evidence.
The trial court’s reasons for rejecting this core evidence were found to be unsound and its evaluation of the evidence manifestly erroneous.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal has the same power to reappraise the evidence as in an appeal against conviction, but should not interfere merely because another plausible view is available. Interference is justified where the trial court’s reasons are unsound, perverse, legally erroneous, or based on wrongly assessed testimony. No earlier case or statutory provision is cited for this principle in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reappraise the evidence and reverse the acquittal; it did not exceed the limits on appellate interference with an acquittal.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and trial_reasons_unsound and core_witness_accounts_consistent and core_account_medically_corroborated

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution brought an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.trial_reasons_unsound: The trial court rejected the central evidence for reasons that were unsound or manifestly erroneous.
predicates.core_witness_accounts_consistent: The eyewitnesses consistently described the accused committing the central act, despite discrepancies or exaggeration about other events.
predicates.core_account_medically_corroborated: Medical evidence corroborated the eyewitnesses’ account of the central act.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside an acquittal when the trial court's assessment is perverse or unreasonable because it disregards material evidence or relies on irrelevant considerations, and no reasonable view of the evidence supports the acquittal.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting the eyewitnesses and injured witness on grounds that included missing documentary proof, doubts about their reasons for travel, and the absence of a produced general-diary entry.

The appellate court reassessed the record and found material support for the prosecution account, including the injured witness's evidence, corroborating circumstances, and evidence concerning the occurrence and injuries.
The Supreme Court identified serious errors in the trial court's legal approach and appreciation of the evidence, including non-consideration of material facts and consideration of irrelevant facts.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court ordinarily should not interfere with an acquittal where two reasonable views of the evidence are possible, since acquittal strengthens the presumption of innocence. However, interference is permissible where the acquittal is perverse or highly unreasonable, rests on irrelevant or inadmissible evidence, or material evidence has been ignored and the evidence does not reasonably support the acquittal. The Court relied on Mahadeo Laxman Sarane v. State of Maharashtra, Swami Prasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka.
members.conclusion: The appellate court was justified in setting aside the acquittal, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal against the resulting convictions.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The appellate proceeding challenges a judgment acquitting the accused.
predicates.trial_court_ignored_material_evidence: The trial court failed to consider evidence material to whether the accused committed the offence.
predicates.trial_court_relied_on_irrelevant_conside: The trial court relied on considerations that did not rationally bear on the reliability or sufficiency of the evidence.
predicates.acquittal_not_reasonably_supported_by_re: The evidence on the record does not reasonably support the acquittal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal only in exceptional circumstances where there are compelling reasons and the acquittal judgment is perverse, and it should not interfere merely because another view is possible.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, and the High Court reversed that acquittal after considering the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court’s judgment was based on the evidence and that the evidence had been properly reappreciated.
The Supreme Court found no perversity in the High Court’s judgment warranting further interference.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court must bear in mind the presumption of innocence, which is strengthened by an acquittal, and should avoid routine interference when another view is possible. In exceptional cases, compelling circumstances and perversity in the judgment under appeal permit appellate interference.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s reversal of the acquittal did not warrant interference, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.compelling_circumstances_exist: The circumstances of the case provide compelling reasons for appellate intervention.

members.legal_issue: A conviction imposed after reversal of an acquittal must be set aside where the appellate court’s view of the evidence is plainly unreasonable and the evidence does not reliably establish the accused’s involvement.
material_facts: The High Court reversed the trial court’s acquittal and convicted the accused after a State appeal.
The Supreme Court found substantial contradictions in the identification evidence, discrepancies in the numbers of assailants identified, and reasons to doubt the witnesses’ presence and credibility.
Several witnesses were related to or otherwise interested in the prosecution, and a witness said to have escaped the attack did not report the assailants’ names to people he encountered.
Public servants who arrived near the scene soon after the event were not told the assailants’ identities, and the first information report was lodged several hours after the occurrence.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had overlooked important evidence and that the trial court’s acquittal was justified.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not normally reappraise evidence assessed by the High Court, but may intervene where grave injustice has resulted from interference with an acquittal on plainly untenable grounds and the High Court’s view is clearly unreasonable on the evidence. The principles in Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor, Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Samman Dass require caution in overturning an acquittal and attention to the evidence, the trial court’s reasons, the presumption of innocence and reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the convictions and sentences, and acquitted the accused.

predicates.article_136_appeal_from_conviction_after: The proceeding is an appeal invoking the Supreme Court’s special appellate jurisdiction against a conviction imposed after an appellate court reversed an acquittal.
predicates.high_court_view_plainly_unreasonable_on_: The appellate court’s assessment of the evidence is plainly unreasonable, including because it overlooked material evidentiary problems.
predicates.prosecution_identification_evidence_unre: Prosecution witnesses gave materially inconsistent identification accounts or were otherwise not reliable on the accused’s involvement.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal after independently reappraising the evidence when it gives reasoned grounds for rejecting the trial court’s conclusions.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting the testimony of two eyewitnesses because they were close relatives of the deceased and had enmity with the accused.
The High Court reappraised the evidence, addressed the trial court’s reasons, and found the eyewitnesses’ testimony credible and supported by other evidence.
The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court’s decision to reverse the acquittal.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court may review the entire evidence and reach its own conclusions, but should address the reasons for acquittal and bear in mind the presumption of innocence, the benefit of doubt, and the trial court’s opportunity to observe witness demeanour. The Court relied on Sher Singh v. State of U.P. (AIR 1967 SC 1412), Dargahs v. State of U.P. (AIR 1973 SC 2695), Ravinder Singh v. State of Haryana (AIR 1975 SC 856), and Labh Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1976 SC 83).
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reverse the acquittal because it gave clear reasons for rejecting the trial court’s grounds and independently assessed the evidence.

members.legal_issue: In an appeal available as of right after an acquittal is reversed and a conviction is entered, the Supreme Court must decide the case on its merits rather than limit review to whether the High Court had sufficient grounds to interfere with the acquittal.
material_facts: The accused were acquitted at trial and convicted by the High Court in the State’s appeal against acquittal.
The accused brought an appeal under the provision granting an appeal as of right in the specified circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(a) of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 provides the specified accused with an appeal as of right. In such an appeal the Supreme Court acts as an appellate court and decides questions of fact and law on the merits. The limits relevant to the Court’s discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, including principles governing a High Court’s interference with an acquittal, do not govern this statutory appeal. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court had to consider all questions of fact and law and decide the appeal on its merits; whether the High Court had sufficient grounds to reverse the acquittal was not material to that review.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal on facts may reverse a trial court’s credibility finding when important considerations bearing on credibility or probability were not properly weighed and the record clearly shows the finding is wrong.
material_facts: The case was a civil appeal on facts from a decree in a suit for pre-emption.
The trial judge accepted the plaintiff’s and his witness’s account that the plaintiff first learned of the sale on a particular day and then performed the required demands.
The trial judge’s acceptance did not appear to rest on an impression formed from observing the witnesses’ demeanour.

The trial judge did not properly consider significant probabilities and inconsistencies in the account, including the witness’s reason for conveying the information, the plaintiff’s conduct after hearing it, and differences in the evidence about what information was conveyed.
The High Court considered those matters, rejected the account, and reversed the trial court’s decree.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court deciding an appeal on facts must reach its own decision while carefully considering the trial judge’s finding and recognising the advantage of having seen and heard the witnesses. It should not lightly displace a finding that depends on demeanour, but may reverse where important credibility considerations or probabilities were overlooked and clearly indicate that the finding is wrong. Where the issue is an inference from proved facts rather than demeanour-based credibility, the appellate court is in as good a position as the trial court. The Court relied on Shunmugaroya Mudaliar v. Manikka Mudaliar, Coghlan v. Cumberland, Watt (or Thomas) v. Thomas, Bonmax v. Austin Motor Co. Ltd., Sarju Pershad v. Raja Jwaleshwari Pratap Narain Singh, and Laljee Mahomed v. Girlder.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the trial court’s factual finding; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_on_facts: The proceeding is an appeal in which the appellate court may decide factual issues.

predicates.important_probability_considerations_ove: The trial court did not take into account or properly weigh significant matters bearing on credibility or the probability of the account.
predicates.record_clearly_displaces_trial_finding: The evidence and circumstances on the record clearly indicate that the trial court’s finding is wrong.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside an acquittal when its review of the evidence and the reasons for acquittal shows that the acquittal was not justified.
material_facts: The trial court found that the deceased party had deadly weapons and relied on that finding to uphold the accused persons’ claim of private defence.
The High Court found that the trial court’s finding about those weapons rested on conjecture and was contrary to the evidence, and explained why it reversed the acquittal.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal may review the entire evidence and reach its own conclusion, but must consider the evidence and the reasons supporting the acquittal and state why the acquittal was unjustified. The Court relied on Sheo Swarup v. Emperor, Sanwant Singh v. State of Rajasthan, and Harbans Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering with the acquittal because the trial court’s conclusion rested on an unsupported finding and the High Court gave reasons for holding the acquittal unjustified.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.trial_finding_based_on_conjecture: The trial court relied on a factual finding that was based on conjecture and contrary to the evidence.
predicates.reviewing_court_explains_why_acquittal_u: The reviewing court considers the evidence and gives reasons why the acquittal was unjustified.

members.legal_issue: A High Court may reverse an acquittal only when strong reasons grounded in the evidence dislodge the trial court’s findings, and not merely because it prefers another view of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding material contradictions in the family witnesses’ accounts, gaps in the prosecution evidence, and insufficient proof of the accused’s participation.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted accused 2 to 6, relying principally on the testimony of the deceased’s parents and brother.
The Supreme Court found no justification for the High Court to interfere with the trial court’s assessment.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the High Court may review the evidence and reach its own conclusions, but should interfere only where strong reasons based on the evidence dislodge the trial court’s findings, such as where the trial court made wrong assumptions about material facts or failed properly to appreciate the evidence. If two views are reasonably possible, the acquittal should not be reversed merely because the High Court would have preferred the view against the accused; the possibility of two views indicates that guilt has not been proved beyond reasonable doubt and the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt. The Court relied on G. B. Patel v. State of Maharashtra, Babu v. State of U.P., Awadhesh v. State of M.P., Thanedar Singh v. State of M.P., and State of Rajasthan v. Rajaram.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the acquittal; the appeal was allowed and the acquittal restored.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal in which a higher court is asked to reverse an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_properly_appreciated_evidenc: The trial court assessed the evidence and based its acquittal on its findings about that evidence.
predicates.two_reasonable_views_possible: The evidence reasonably permits both a view consistent with guilt and a view consistent with innocence.
predicates.high_court_lacks_strong_evidentiary_basi: The higher court has no strong evidentiary reason to dislodge the trial court’s findings.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal only when the trial court’s view is clearly unreasonable or perverse and substantial and compelling reasons justify intervention.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the appellant, but the High Court convicted him on the State’s appeal against acquittal.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s assessment perverse and unreasonable, including its rejection of credible eyewitness evidence and its reliance on extraneous matters.
The Supreme Court found reliable evidence implicating the appellant and held that there were compelling and substantial reasons for the High Court to interfere.
members.legal_principle: An acquittal strengthens the presumption of innocence. An appellate court should not disturb a reasonably possible view merely because another view is possible; it may intervene where the acquittal is clearly unreasonable or perverse and substantial and compelling reasons require intervention to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to reverse the acquittal, and the Supreme Court confirmed the conviction.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s assessment of credible evidence is perverse and no other reasonable view is available.
material_facts: The prosecution presented two eyewitnesses whose accounts described the origin and manner of the assault, and other witnesses substantially corroborated their account.
The trial court rejected evidence on trivial discrepancies, speculative grounds, and a misreading of the testimony.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s conclusions unsustainable and noted that the High Court considered whether any other view was reasonably possible.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court can reverse an acquittal where the trial court’s findings are perverse, based on a misreading of evidence or speculation, and the evidence supports no other reasonably possible view. The Court referred generally to principles previously laid down by it concerning reversal of acquittals but identified no earlier case by name. The convictions affirmed were under Sections 302/34 and 302/114 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The reversal of the acquittal and the resulting convictions were upheld; the appeals and special leave petition were dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court may reverse an acquittal after reviewing the evidence, while giving proper weight to the trial court’s assessment and the accused’s presumption of innocence; a reversal is supported where the evidence establishes guilt despite the grounds on which the trial court rejected it.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, relying on concerns including the reliability of the witnesses, the absence of independent witnesses, discrepancies about the shooting distance, and the prosecution’s inclusion of persons who were not present.

The High Court, in the prosecution’s appeal from the acquittal, relied on the testimony of eyewitnesses, including witnesses whose injuries were consistent in timing with the assault, and on supporting medical and other witness evidence.
The High Court did not rely on the testimony of the informant whose naming of absent persons had been criticized.
The trial judge’s conclusion was not founded on witness demeanour, apart from possibly the informant, and the injuries of the four witnesses supported their presence at the scene.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 417, 418, and 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal has power to review the evidence and reverse the acquittal. Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor requires the appellate court to give proper weight to the trial judge’s views on credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of doubt, and the advantage of the trial judge having seen the witnesses.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no substantial infirmity in the High Court’s assessment and declined to disturb its decision to set aside the acquittal and convict the accused.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The reviewing court considered an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.injured_witnesses_corrobated_by_medical_: Witnesses who testified to the incident had injuries whose medical evidence supported their presence at the time and place of the incident.
predicates.trial_court_rejection_not_based_on_demea: The trial court’s rejection of the relevant testimony rested on its assessment of the evidence rather than its observation of witness demeanour.
predicates.appellate_assessment_has_no_substantial_: The appellate court’s evaluation of the evidence disclosed no substantial flaw in its reasoning.
predicates.appellate_conviction_may_be_upheld: The reviewing court may leave in place the appellate court’s decision to reverse the acquittal and convict.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal may be reversed when the trial court’s rejection of reliable eyewitness evidence rests on unreasonable inferences that overlook corroborating evidence.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses said the assault occurred after sunrise, and their testimony was not shaken in cross-examination.
A third witness supported the account of when the victims left for the field, and medical evidence was consistent with injuries being sustained in the morning.
The trial court inferred that the incident occurred in darkness from the victims’ full intestines, without adequately considering the witness testimony and medical evidence.
The eyewitnesses had reasons to be at nearby fields, and the record did not show that they were inimical to the accused.
The High Court found the eyewitnesses truthful and reversed the acquittal; the Supreme Court held that the trial court’s rejection of their evidence was unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: The standard governing appeals against acquittal permits reversal where the trial court’s findings are unreasonable. In applying that standard, the Court assessed the eyewitness testimony, its corroboration by medical evidence, and the trial court’s reasons for rejecting it.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and recording a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code; the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: An accused may appeal to the Supreme Court as of right when an acquittal has been converted into a conviction carrying a life sentence, without obtaining a certificate from the High Court.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused of the charge concerning the death.
The High Court reversed that acquittal, convicted the accused of murder with common intention, and imposed a life sentence.
The appeal came to the Supreme Court with a High Court certificate, but the Court held that such a certificate was unnecessary.
members.legal_principle: Under the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, an appeal lies as of right when an acquittal is converted into a conviction and a life sentence is imposed; a High Court certificate is not necessary.
members.conclusion: The accused’s appeal lay to the Supreme Court as a matter of right, and no High Court certificate was required.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal may review the evidence and reverse the acquittal, while giving proper consideration to the trial judge’s credibility findings, the presumption of innocence, reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to see the witnesses.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after accepting his account that he had fired in private defence, although it considered the prosecution account to be true.
The High Court reviewed the evidence, rejected the accused’s account, and relied on prosecution witnesses whose account the trial court itself regarded as truthful.
The evidence supported the finding that the accused fired at the deceased without justifiable provocation, and the asserted private-defence account was not established.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had not overlooked the principles governing appeals against acquittal and was justified in reversing an acquittal based on surmises and conjectures.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the appellate court has full power to review the evidence and reach its own conclusion. Expressions such as “substantial and compelling reasons” do not limit that power, but the appellate court must properly consider the trial judge’s view of witness credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of any real and reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s advantage in seeing witnesses. The Court relied on Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor, 61 I.A. 398; Nur Mohammad v. Emperor, AIR 1945 PC 151; Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1961] 3 SCR 120; Ramaphupala Reddy & Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1970] 3 SCC 474; Gopi Nath Ganga Ram Surve & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra, [1970] 3 SCC 627; Dharam Das & Ors. v. State of U.P., [1973] 2 SCC 216; Lekha Yadav v. State of Bihar, [1973] 2 SCC 424; Samson Hyam Kemkar v. State of Maharashtra, [1974] 3 SCC 494; and Barati v. State of U.P., [1974] 4 SCC 258.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and convicting the accused; the Supreme Court upheld that reversal and dismissed the appeals.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside an acquittal when the acquittal rests on an erroneous or perverse assessment of the evidence, but must not disturb it when two reasonable views are possible.
material_facts: The High Court acquitted the accused after reversing the trial court’s convictions.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had ignored material evidence and relied on flimsy and untenable reasons, while the eyewitness and corroborative evidence supported the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: Under Sambasivan v. State of Kerala and Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, an appellate court may fully review and reassess the evidence in an appeal against acquittal. The accused retain a double presumption of innocence, and an acquittal should not be disturbed if two reasonable conclusions are possible; interference is warranted where the acquittal reflects an erroneous approach to the evidence or conclusions that are perverse. The Supreme Court exercised its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The acquittal was set aside and the trial court’s convictions were restored, with the sentences modified as to the death penalty and default imprisonment.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The challenged appellate judgment acquitted persons who had been convicted at trial.

predicates.acquittal_based_on_perverse_or_erroneous: The acquitting court disregarded relevant evidence or reached conclusions unsupported by a proper assessment of the record.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal may be reversed in an appeal when the reviewing court perversely rejects satisfactory incriminating evidence on grounds that do not undermine its value.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused on the evidence of an injured eyewitness and corroborating circumstances.

The High Court acquitted the accused after rejecting the eyewitness’s evidence and discounting corroborating evidence for reasons the Supreme Court found flimsy, irrelevant, or inconsistent with the record.
The eyewitness’s account was supported by evidence of his serious injuries, medical evidence, and other witnesses; the evidence, viewed as a whole, supported only the conclusion of guilt.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court ordinarily does not interfere unless the acquittal is perverse. State of U.P. v. Gokaran holds that interference is warranted when satisfactory incriminating evidence is brushed aside on the basis of circumstances that do not detract from its value. The Court also relied on Allarakha K. Mansuri v. State of Gujarat for the principle that defective investigation by itself is not a ground for acquittal. The benefit-of-doubt principles referred to in Harijana Thirupala v. Public Prosecutor and Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh did not apply because the evidence was neither ambivalent nor reasonably consistent with innocence.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s acquittal was perverse. The Court set it aside and restored the convictions entered by the trial court.
