material_facts: The prescribed authority considered evidence about the comparative hardship of the landlord and tenant and found the landlord’s need greater.
The District Judge affirmed that finding on appeal.
The High Court treated the comparative-need finding as one of fact and declined to disturb it in writ proceedings.
The challenge before the Supreme Court was that the High Court had not itself examined comparative hardship.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court does not reappraise evidence to reach a conclusion different from that of the Prescribed Authority or the District Judge on a factual question such as comparative hardship. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right not to reappraise the evidence or substitute its own conclusion for the factual finding affirmed by the District Judge; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenges_factual_findi: A party challenges a factual finding in proceedings seeking writ review of a lower authority’s decision.
predicates.comparative_hardship_assessed_on_evidenc: The lower authority assesses the parties’ comparative hardship on the evidence and makes a finding.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_affirmed_finding: A lower appellate court affirms the factual finding.

members.legal_issue: The revisional court may examine the evidence when the governing rent-control review power extends to the legality or correctness of the challenged order.
material_facts: The tenants challenged the eviction order in revision under a provision authorizing review of the legality or correctness of the order or proceeding.
The High Court considered the evidence in deciding whether the landlord had a reasonable bona fide requirement.
members.legal_principle: Section 50 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act authorizes examination of an order or proceeding for its legality or correctness. Under Bhoolchand & Anr. v. Kay Pee Cee Investments & Anr. [1991 (1) SCC 343], this revisional power is wider than the power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and does not preclude the High Court from appreciating evidence concerning reasonable bona fide requirement.
members.conclusion: The High Court acted within the scope of its revisional powers, and the Supreme Court found no fault in its understanding of that scope.

predicates.rent_control_revision_case: The proceeding is a revision concerning an order made in a rent-control matter.
predicates.review_authority_covers_correctness: The governing review authority permits examination of whether the challenged order or proceeding is correct.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising statutory revisional jurisdiction may not replace lower courts’ findings by reappraising evidence when those findings are not perverse or erroneous.
material_facts: The courts below found that the tenant was not in actual possession and that the occupier used the premises as a godown while having a separate shop.
The High Court reached a different comparative-hardship conclusion after considering the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had applied their minds and that their finding was not manifestly perverse or erroneous.
members.legal_principle: Under section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as substituted by Gujarat Act 18 of 1965, the High Court’s revisional jurisdiction is wider than its jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but is limited to satisfying itself that the decision is according to law. It cannot replace a lower court’s finding on reappraisal when that finding is not perverse or erroneous.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not substitute its finding for that of the courts below by reappraising the evidence.

predicates.statutory_rent_revision: The matter is before a High Court in revision under a rent-control statute.
predicates.lower_court_finding_is_not_perverse_or_e: The lower court’s finding is neither perverse nor erroneous.
predicates.proposed_interference_reappraises_eviden: The proposed intervention would replace the lower court’s finding through a fresh assessment of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising statutory revision cannot re-determine the factual sufficiency of compensation fixed by a District Court.
material_facts: The municipality challenged the amount of compensation fixed by the District Court in a revision before the High Court.
The District Court had heard the parties and received evidence before fixing compensation.
The High Court declined to reassess the amount, and the Supreme Court held that it could not determine factual questions about compensation in revision.
members.legal_principle: Section 392 of the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 makes District Court decisions subject to High Court revision unless the Act provides otherwise. Even assuming that this revisional power is wider than the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it does not extend to deciding questions of fact or fixing the amount of compensation.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to decline to consider whether the compensation was sufficient, because its revisional jurisdiction did not extend to determining questions of fact.

predicates.high_court_revision_from_compensation_or: A party brought a revision before a High Court challenging a District Court order fixing compensation.
predicates.challenge_requires_factual_reassessment: Deciding whether the compensation is sufficient would require the court to reassess factual matters.

members.legal_issue: A rent-control revisional court cannot reappreciate evidence and replace concurrent findings of the lower courts with its own conclusion, even when the findings concern the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship.
material_facts: The predecessor of the respondents had earlier claimed that he was a tenant, but the Land Tribunal rejected that claim and found from the owner’s accounts that he was only a manager of the theatre.
The Rent Control Court found that the respondents’ predecessor had accepted the appellants’ predecessor as landlord and ordered eviction; the Rent Control Appellate Authority affirmed that decision.
The High Court reversed the concurrent decisions after reassessing the evidence and concluding that a landlord-tenant relationship had not been established.
The Supreme Court found that the lower courts’ findings were supported by evidence and were not perverse.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, revisional jurisdiction, though wider than the jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, does not permit the High Court to act as a first or second appellate court or to reappreciate evidence and substitute its conclusion for that of the appellate authority. The revisional court’s consideration is confined to the legality, regularity and propriety of the impugned order. This applies even when the issue is a jurisdictional fact, such as whether a landlord-tenant relationship exists. The Court relied on Rukmini Amma Saradamma v. Kallyani Sulochana, Ubaiba v. Damodaran, and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited v. Dilbahar Singh.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by reappreciating the evidence. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the eviction decree affirmed by the Rent Control Appellate Authority was restored.

rule.if: rent_control_revision_case and concurrent_lower_court_findings and findings_supported_and_not_perverse and revisional_court_reappreciated_evidence

predicates.rent_control_revision_case: The proceeding before the High Court was a revision concerning a rent-control decision.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_findings: The trial-level court and the appellate authority reached the same findings.
predicates.findings_supported_and_not_perverse: The findings of the lower courts were supported by evidence and were not perverse.
predicates.revisional_court_reappreciated_evidence: The revisional court reassessed the evidence and substituted its conclusion for the concurrent findings below.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_decision_restored: The concurrent decision of the lower courts is restored.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may not overturn concurrent factual findings by reappraising evidence when it identifies no error of law or material irregularity requiring correction.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court both found that the tenant had sublet the premises and parted with possession without the landlord’s consent.
In a revision under the rent-control law, the High Court reappraised the evidence and set aside those concurrent findings without identifying an error of law or material irregularity.
The landlord challenged the High Court’s decision by appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, as amended in Gujarat, gives the High Court revisional power to correct errors that make a decision contrary to law and go to its root, but does not authorize rehearing or reappreciation of evidence. A different view on the evidence is not by itself a basis for revision. The Court applied Helper Girdharbhai v. Saiyed Mohmad Mirasaheb Kadri, which distinguishes appellate rehearing on law and fact from the limited purpose of revision: satisfying the court that the decision under challenge is according to law.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction; its judgment was set aside and the concurrent decisions of the lower courts were restored.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and concurrent_factual_findings and revisional_court_reappraised_evidence and not revisional_court_identified_root_error

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision arising from a decision in a rent-control case.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual conclusion.
predicates.revisional_court_reappraised_evidence: The revisional court reconsidered the evidence and substituted its own factual conclusion.
predicates.revisional_court_identified_root_error: The revisional court identified an error of law or material irregularity going to the root of the decision.
predicates.revisional_interference_is_unwarranted: The revisional court’s interference with the concurrent factual findings is not justified.

members.legal_issue: The High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts is exceptional and cannot be used as an appellate power to correct ordinary errors of fact or law.
material_facts: The challenge concerned decisions of subordinate civil courts in a private landlord-tenant proceeding.
The lower courts had made concurrent findings of fact, and the High Court declined to interfere with them.
The Supreme Court stated that supervisory intervention is confined to keeping subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority and to exceptional failures of justice.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 confers discretionary supervisory jurisdiction, not appellate jurisdiction. The High Court may intervene to keep subordinate courts within the bounds of their authority, including where they assume jurisdiction they lack, fail to exercise jurisdiction they possess, or exercise jurisdiction in a manner not permitted by law resulting in failure of justice. The Court relied on Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, AIR 1954 SC 215; Dalmia Jain Airways Ltd. v. Sukumar Mukherjee, AIR 1951 Calcutta 193; Manmatha Nath Biswas v. Emperor, AIR 1933 Calcutta 132; Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, AIR 1958 SC 398; State of Gujarat v. Vakhatsinghji Vajesinghji Vaghela, AIR 1968 SC 1481; Mani Nariman Daruwala v. Phiroz N. Bhatena, (1991) 3 SCC 141; Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram, (1986) 4 SCC 447; Laxmikant Revchand Bhojwani v. Pratapsingh Mohansingh Pardeshi, (1995) 6 SCC 576; and Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai, (2003) 6 SCC 675. The Court also held that curtailment of the revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not expand supervisory jurisdiction, and cited L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, (1997) 3 SCC 261, on Article 227’s constitutional status.
members.conclusion: Supervisory interference is warranted only in exceptional circumstances, including jurisdictional excess or refusal, a patent perversion, gross or manifest failure of justice, or violation of basic principles of natural justice; it is not available merely to correct an ordinary factual or legal error or to substitute another possible view.

rule.if: supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_court and (jurisdictional_overreach or jurisdictional_refusal or unlawful_jurisdictional_exercise_causing_injustice or patent_perversity or gross_failure_of_justice or basic_natural_justice_breach)

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_cou: A party challenges a subordinate court’s decision by seeking supervisory review.
predicates.jurisdictional_overreach: The subordinate court assumes authority it does not possess.
predicates.jurisdictional_refusal: The subordinate court refuses to exercise authority it possesses.
predicates.unlawful_jurisdictional_exercise_causing: The subordinate court exercises its authority in a manner not permitted by law and that causes failure of justice or grave injustice.
predicates.patent_perversity: The subordinate court’s decision is patently perverse.
predicates.gross_failure_of_justice: The subordinate court’s decision results in a gross or manifest failure of justice.
predicates.basic_natural_justice_breach: The subordinate court’s process violates basic principles of natural justice.

members.legal_issue: The provision barring a further appeal from an appellate decision does not, by itself, confer revisional jurisdiction on the High Court.
material_facts: A landlord appealed the dismissal of a possession suit, and the appellate court dismissed that appeal.
The landlord then applied to the High Court for revision, which treated the application as one under the then-applicable rent-control provision.
The applicable version of that provision barred a further appeal but did not grant the High Court power to revise the appellate decision.
members.legal_principle: Appeal and revision rights are created by statute; courts have no inherent right of appeal or revision. The Court relied on Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act as it stood before amendment, which barred a further appeal but did not provide for High Court revision, and on Keshavalal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas, which held that the later amendment expressly granting revisional power was not retrospective.
members.conclusion: The High Court had no revisional jurisdiction under that provision, so the revision was not competent on that basis.

predicates.rent_control_appellate_decision_followed: A party to a rent-control proceeding sought High Court revision after an appellate court had decided the matter.
predicates.applicable_text_barred_further_appeal: The governing enactment barred a further appeal from the appellate decision.
predicates.applicable_text_granted_no_high_court_re: The governing enactment did not authorize the High Court to revise the appellate decision.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court should not set aside a supported factual finding solely because the appellate authority did not describe each exhibit in detail when the record is available for review.
material_facts: After remand, the appellate authority referred to business records, including tax assessment materials, and found that the pawn-broking partnership business had been gradually expanding.
The High Court set aside that finding in part because the appellate authority had not identified and explained each exhibit in detail.
The exhibits were available to the High Court, and the Supreme Court considered the finding of expansion justified by the record.
members.legal_principle: Where the record is available and an appellate authority has identified evidence supporting its factual finding, a revisional court should assess the evidence rather than reject the finding solely for lack of detailed exhibit descriptions. The Court did not invoke a statutory provision or earlier case for this holding.
members.conclusion: The High Court acted with hyper-technicality by discarding the appellate authority's supported finding without examining the available record.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and appellate_finding_supported_by_record and record_available_to_reviewing_court and finding_rejected_only_for_lack_of_exhibit_detail

predicates.rent_control_revision: A reviewing court is considering a revision arising from a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.appellate_finding_supported_by_record: The appellate authority's factual finding is supported by evidence in the case record.
predicates.record_available_to_reviewing_court: The evidence relied on for the finding is available to the reviewing court.
predicates.finding_rejected_only_for_lack_of_exhibi: The reviewing court rejects the finding because the appellate authority did not describe the exhibits in sufficient detail.

members.legal_issue: Certiorari jurisdiction cannot be exercised merely because a question of law could be raised; the challenged order must suffer from an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The single Judge remanded the matter because questions of law could be urged on the material before the court.
The single Judge did not find that the Board of Revenue’s order was vitiated by an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
The Letters Patent Bench reversed the single Judge, and the Supreme Court held that the single Judge’s approach was untenable.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, the High Court may use certiorari to quash an order for an error of law only when the order suffers from an error of law apparent on the face of the record; the mere possibility of raising a question of law is insufficient. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the Board of Revenue’s order on the basis of the mere possibility of raising questions of law.

predicates.certiorari_writ: A party sought certiorari review of a tribunal’s order.
predicates.challenged_order_lacks_apparent_error_of: The reviewing court did not find an error of law apparent on the face of the challenged order.
predicates.only_possible_legal_question_identified: The reviewing court identified only a question of law that might be argued, without finding an apparent legal error in the order.

members.legal_issue: A rent-control revisional court whose authority extends to legality, regularity, and propriety may examine whether a lower court’s factual finding is proper, rather than being confined to jurisdictional errors.
material_facts: The parties sought revision before the District Court under the rent-control enactment after the Subordinate Judge ruled on the eviction application.
The District Judge reconsidered the evidence concerning subletting and reversed the Subordinate Judge’s finding.
The High Court later confirmed the District Judge’s order.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(1) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, empowered the District Court to examine records to satisfy itself as to the legality, regularity, or propriety of an order or proceeding and to pass an appropriate order. Its wording was wider than section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and did not confine revision to jurisdictional questions.
members.conclusion: The revisional authority under section 20 was not limited to jurisdictional questions and empowered the District Court to consider whether the finding on the evidence was proper. Because the High Court had confirmed the order, the Supreme Court did not examine whether the District Court had properly exercised that revisional power in this case.

predicates.rent_control_revision: A party brought a revision from an order or proceeding under a rent-control enactment.
predicates.revisional_power_includes_propriety: The revisional authority was empowered to examine the propriety of the challenged order or proceeding and make an appropriate order.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may not interfere with lower courts’ decision merely because of an error of law when those courts had jurisdiction to decide the dispute and committed no procedural error.
material_facts: The Rent Controller, the appellate authority, and the District Court found that the building had been leased for both trade and residence.
The landlord did not establish that any part of the building was being used for a purpose different from the purpose for which it was leased.
The High Court interfered with the lower courts’ decision in revision, although they had jurisdiction to decide the dispute and had committed no procedural error.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an error of law, however gross, does not by itself permit revisional interference where the lower courts had jurisdiction to decide the dispute and committed no procedural error. The Court applied the principles in Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria and Others and Pandurang Dhoni Chougule v. Maruti Hari Jadhav.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to interfere in revision, and the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_revisional_interference and lower_courts_had_authority_to_decide and no_procedural_error_occurred and lower_courts_concurred_on_lease_purpose and different_use_not_shown

predicates.appeal_challenges_revisional_interferenc: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a revisional court’s interference with a lower-court decision.
predicates.lower_courts_had_authority_to_decide: The lower courts had authority to decide the dispute before them.
predicates.no_procedural_error_occurred: The lower courts committed no procedural error in deciding the dispute.
predicates.lower_courts_concurred_on_lease_purpose: The lower courts agreed on the purpose for which the property had been leased.
predicates.different_use_not_shown: The party alleging a use different from the leased purpose did not establish that such a different use occurred.

members.legal_issue: Constitutional superintendence cannot be used as appellate review to correct factual errors when the subordinate tribunal has acted within its authority.
material_facts: The civil court considered the parties’ affidavits and gave them no weight because the deponents were interested persons.
The magistrate’s order conformed to the civil court’s possession finding.
The High Court set aside the orders on the ground that the civil court had failed to consider the affidavits, and that ground treated the civil court’s factual assessment as open to re-examination.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution remains available notwithstanding restrictions in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, but its supervisory scope is limited to keeping subordinate courts and tribunals within the bounds of their authority. It does not permit correction of factual errors or conversion of the High Court into a court of appeal. Waryam Singh v. Amar Nath, Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam, and Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarts were reiterated.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s superintendence power was not curtailed by the procedural bar, but it could not be used to correct a factual error or act as an appellate court; the circumstances did not justify intervention.

predicates.supervisory_review_proceeding: A party invoked the High Court’s supervisory power to challenge an order made in a subordinate proceeding.
predicates.subordinate_court_within_authority: The subordinate court acted within the limits of its authority.
predicates.challenge_seeks_correction_of_factual_er: The challenge asks the High Court to re-examine or correct the subordinate court’s factual assessment.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a statutory appeal does not enlarge the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction or permit it to reappreciate evidence as an appellate court.
material_facts: The challenged order was made by an inferior authority in a compulsory-purchase proceeding, and the statute provided no appeal against that order.
The High Court set the order aside after reassessing the valuation evidence and substituting its own conclusion for that of the authority.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, supervisory review may interfere with a tribunal’s finding if it failed to consider relevant material, considered irrelevant or extraneous material, relied on no evidence, or reached a conclusion no reasonable person could reach on the evidence. The availability of a statutory appeal does not alter those limits. The Court relied on C.B. Gautam v. Union of India, which addressed the safeguards and conditions for compulsory purchase under Chapter XX-C, and discussed Kailash Suneja v. Appropriate Authority as confirming that sufficiency or adequacy of material is not open to judicial review and that relevant and extraneous material may be examined.
members.conclusion: The absence of an appeal did not enlarge the High Court’s supervisory power, and the High Court could not act as an appellate court by reappreciating the evidence.

predicates.judicial_review_of_tribunal: A party asks a court exercising supervisory jurisdiction to review a decision made by an inferior tribunal.
predicates.no_statutory_appeal: The governing statutory scheme provides no appeal from the tribunal’s decision.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court was not justified in disturbing concurrent factual findings that no rent arrears were due.
material_facts: The trial court found that no rent arrears were due.
The appellate court also found that no rent arrears were due.
The High Court, in revision, held that rent was in arrears and relied on that conclusion in upholding eviction.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the question of arrears as a factual matter on which the lower courts had made concurrent findings and held that the High Court should not have interfered with that finding in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Although the parties relied on Vora Abbas Bhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi, the Court found it unnecessary to decide the broader question of the High Court’s revisional jurisdiction in the circumstances.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent finding that no rent arrears were due.

predicates.revision_from_rent_control_eviction_case: A party sought revision of a decision in a rent-control eviction case.
predicates.lower_courts_concurrently_found_no_arrea: Both the trial court and the appellate court found that the tenant owed no rent arrears.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction should not disturb concurrent factual findings of rent tribunals where the evidence supports those findings and the High Court’s intervention would cause injustice.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the Collector both found that the tenant was not a habitual defaulter.
The evidence accepted by those tribunals showed that the landlord had willingly accepted rent paid every three or four months without complaint.
The High Court accepted the landlord’s contention and interfered with the concurrent finding.
The Supreme Court considered that intervention an excess of the High Court’s narrow jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 confers narrow supervisory jurisdiction, which did not permit the High Court to interfere with the concurrent factual findings in these circumstances. The judgment refers generally to several earlier decisions of the Supreme Court but names none.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its narrow supervisory jurisdiction and ought not to have interfered with the concurrent finding; its judgment was set aside.

rule.if: high_court_supervisory_review and concurrent_factual_findings and evidence_supports_concurrent_findings and high_court_disturbs_findings

predicates.high_court_supervisory_review: The High Court is reviewing a lower tribunal’s decision in the exercise of supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: Two lower tribunals have made the same factual finding.
predicates.evidence_supports_concurrent_findings: Evidence accepted by the lower tribunals supports their shared factual finding.
predicates.high_court_disturbs_findings: The High Court sets aside or alters the shared factual finding.

members.legal_issue: The High Court may not use revisional jurisdiction to set aside a subordinate court’s decision merely because it considers the decision wrong on fact or law when the subordinate court acted within its jurisdiction.
material_facts: The District Court decided whether the tenant had established readiness and willingness to pay rent and permitted increases and dismissed the possession claim.
The High Court reversed that decision in revision based on its view of the tenant’s payment obligations and entitlement to protection.
The District Court had jurisdiction to decide the possession suit and the tenant’s claim to statutory protection.
members.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, permits revision where a subordinate court has exercised jurisdiction not vested in it, failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it, or acted illegally or with material irregularity in exercising jurisdiction. An error on a question within the subordinate court’s jurisdiction does not by itself permit revision. The Court relied on Balakrishna Udayar v. Vasudeva Aiyar, L.R. 44 I.A. 261; Rajah Amir Hassan Khan v. Sheo Baksh Singh, L.R. 11 I.A. 237; Joy Chand Lal Babu v. Laksha Chaudhury, L.R. 76 I.A. 131; and Manindra Land and Building Corporation v. Bhutnath Bannerjee, [1964] 3 S.C.R. 495.
members.conclusion: The High Court lacked authority under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to reverse the District Court merely for an alleged error of fact or law. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and restored the District Court’s order.

rule.if: revision_from_subordinate_court_decision and no_further_appeal_lies and subordinate_court_had_jurisdiction and alleged_error_is_only_merits_error

predicates.revision_from_subordinate_court_decision: A party asked the High Court to revise a decision made by a subordinate court.
predicates.no_further_appeal_lies: No further appeal lies from the subordinate court decision at issue.
predicates.subordinate_court_had_jurisdiction: The subordinate court had jurisdiction to decide the dispute and the question raised before it.
predicates.alleged_error_is_only_merits_error: The asserted error concerns the court’s factual or legal conclusion on a matter within its jurisdiction, rather than an excess, failure, or materially irregular exercise of jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A supervisory court is not justified in reappreciating evidence and reversing a concurrent factual finding when the finding is supported by evidence and the lower courts’ proceedings disclose no irrational reasoning, bias, or partiality warranting such intervention.
material_facts: The trial court found that the occupant used the cabin because of his attachment to the hospital as an honorary surgeon, relying on oral and documentary evidence and surrounding circumstances; the appellate court affirmed that finding.

The trial court gave several reasons for refusing a late request to recall a witness and obtain his income-tax returns, including the applicant’s failure to explain the source of newly acquired information and the availability of a prescribed process to seek the information.
The appellate court’s alternative conclusion about whether an assumed licence continued on the relevant date was not necessary to its decision on the actual arrangement between the parties.
The High Court treated those matters as grounds to reappreciate the entire record, although the concurrent factual finding was supported by evidence.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 confers supervisory power, not the role of a first appellate court. A concurrent finding of fact supported by evidence cannot be displaced merely because a procedural or evidentiary ruling may be wrong or because an appellate court made an arguably incorrect alternative observation. Unless the reasons given are unreal, flimsy, or irrational so as to disclose a non-judicial approach, bias, or partiality, those matters do not justify a full rehearing of the evidence.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reappreciating the evidence or reversing the concurrent factual finding, and its judgment could not be sustained.

rule.if: supervisory_review_proceeding and concurrent_factual_finding and finding_supported_by_evidence and reasoned_evidence_request_rejection and alternative_observation_inconsequential

predicates.supervisory_review_proceeding: A party asked a supervisory court to review decisions made by lower courts.
predicates.concurrent_factual_finding: Both lower courts reached the same finding on a disputed fact.
predicates.finding_supported_by_evidence: The lower courts’ factual finding had evidence in the record supporting it.
predicates.reasoned_evidence_request_rejection: The trial court rejected a request to obtain further evidence after giving reasons for its decision.
predicates.alternative_observation_inconsequential: The appellate court made an alternative observation that did not affect its decision on the central factual issue.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court is not justified in setting aside concurrent factual findings against eviction when its decision rests on mistaken assumptions and the evidence does not establish the required condition of the building.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found against the landlord on the building-condition ground, and the Appellate Authority concurred.
The High Court reversed those findings in revision and ordered eviction.
The High Court treated the roof collapse in one room as sufficient by itself and also mistakenly assumed that a wall had crumbled.
The expert evidence described the condition of three outer walls; the fourth wall was common to the room and an adjoining room.
The record showed no damage beyond the roof collapse in one room and did not establish that a substantial part of the building was unsafe or unfit for habitation.
members.legal_principle: The court held that the High Court’s revisional intervention was unjustified because it proceeded on mistaken factual assumptions and treated an isolated roof collapse as sufficient without evidence supporting a finding that the building or a substantial part of it was unsafe and unfit for habitation under Section 13(3)(a)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949. The court distinguished Balbir Singh v. Hari Ram, Chander Mohini v. Jiva Singh, and Sardarni Sampurna Kaur v. Sant Singh because their facts did not support the High Court’s conclusion in this case.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent findings and directing eviction on the evidence and assumptions before it.

predicates.tenant_eviction_revision: A landlord challenged an adverse eviction decision in revision, and the matter came before the Supreme Court on appeal.
predicates.concurrent_findings_against_unsafe_build: The first-instance and appellate decision-makers both found against eviction on the asserted building-condition ground.
predicates.revisional_court_relied_on_mistaken_assu: The revisional court relied on a factual assumption about damage that the evidence did not support.
predicates.evidence_not_supporting_substantial_buil: The evidence did not establish that the building or a substantial part of it was unsafe or unfit for habitation.

members.legal_issue: The High Court's supervisory jurisdiction does not permit it to set aside a subordinate court's order merely to correct an ordinary error when the subordinate court acted within its authority and no grave injustice or fundamental legal failure is shown.
material_facts: A District Judge, exercising revisional jurisdiction, allowed the defendant's application to amend its written statement.
The High Court set aside that order under its supervisory jurisdiction, reasoning that the amendment withdrew an admission and was sought after delay.

The Supreme Court found no admission being withdrawn, no demonstrated prejudice or loss of an accrued right, and no basis to treat the District Judge's order as a jurisdictional failure or a perverse finding.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court had acted as an appellate or revisional court rather than within the limits of supervisory jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution imposes a supervisory duty to keep subordinate courts and tribunals within the bounds of their authority, but does not confer an unlimited power to correct ordinary errors or substitute the High Court's judgment for that of a subordinate court. Interference is restricted to serious dereliction of duty, flagrant violation of fundamental principles of law or justice, or findings unsupported by evidence or so perverse that no reasonable person could reach them. The Court relied on Ahmedabad Mfg. & Calico Ptg. Co. Ltd. v. Ramtahel Ramanand, Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, and Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction; its order was set aside and the District Judge's order allowing amendment was restored.

rule.if: supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_order and subordinate_court_acted_within_authority and no_serious_dereliction and no_fundamental_violation and no_unsupported_or_perverse_finding

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_subordinate_ord: A party asked a High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction to set aside an order made by a subordinate court.
predicates.subordinate_court_acted_within_authority: The subordinate court made the challenged order while acting within its legal authority.
predicates.no_serious_dereliction: The subordinate court did not seriously fail to perform its judicial duty.
predicates.no_fundamental_violation: The subordinate court's order did not flagrantly violate a fundamental principle of law or justice.
predicates.no_unsupported_or_perverse_finding: The subordinate court's findings were supported by material and were not so unreasonable that no reasonable court could reach them.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising constitutional writ jurisdiction may correct jurisdictional errors and errors apparent on the face of the record, but does not act as an appellate court to reappraise facts.
material_facts: The High Court found that the rehabilitation authorities had cancelled an auction sale without complying with the required notice procedure.
The Supreme Court examined the official record and concluded that the finding of non-compliance was not erroneous.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court does not sit as a court of appeal to substitute its judgment for that of the empowered authorities, but may correct jurisdictional errors and errors apparent on the face of the record. Under S.L. Hegde & Ors. v. M.B. Tirumale, an error is apparent if it can be brought to the surface without prolonged argument.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to correct the apparent legal error and did not impermissibly substitute its factual judgment for that of the authorities.

predicates.high_court_writ_review: The matter is a proceeding in which a High Court reviews an administrative decision through constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.jurisdictional_error: The authority acted outside the jurisdiction conferred on it.
predicates.apparent_error_without_prolonged_argumen: The record discloses an error that can be identified without prolonged argument.
predicates.high_court_may_correct_the_error_without: The High Court may correct the jurisdictional or apparent error without acting as an appellate court on the facts.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may not disturb a subordinate court’s factual finding unless it is clearly perverse or patently unreasonable.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the appellate court’s eviction judgment through a petition invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
The appellate court had found that the Trial Court’s exercise of discretion was proper, even on the view that discretion existed.
The High Court allowed the petition without considering or setting aside that finding.
The relevant finding about the circumstances was a finding of fact and was not shown to be clearly perverse or patently unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution do not authorize the High Court to reweigh or interfere with subordinate-court findings of fact merely because it might reach a different view. Interference is unavailable unless the finding is clearly perverse or patently unreasonable; supervisory jurisdiction is limited to ensuring that the subordinate court acts within its authority. The Court relied on Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s interference was unwarranted, and its judgment was set aside in favour of the appellate court’s judgment.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_subordinate_court_: A party asks a High Court to review a subordinate court’s decision through supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.subordinate_court_made_factual_finding: The subordinate court made a finding based on the facts or circumstances of the case.
predicates.finding_not_clearly_perverse_or_patently: The factual finding is not clearly perverse or patently unreasonable.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional restriction requiring reservation of a Bill that endangers the High Court’s constitutional position is not engaged merely because a statute provides no appeal to the High Court.
material_facts: The state law provided for a tribunal appeal and a direct statutory appeal to the Supreme Court, but did not remove the High Court’s powers of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227.
The appellant argued that presidential assent under the second proviso to Article 200 could support the statutory appeal provision.
The Court found that the provision did not derogate from a power of the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The second proviso to Article 200 requires the Governor to reserve a Bill if, in the Governor’s opinion, it would so derogate from the High Court’s powers as to endanger the position the Constitution gives that Court. A statutory right of appeal is not inherent, and a statute is not invalid merely because it provides no appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s powers under Articles 226 and 227 remain protected as an inviolable basic feature under L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, but that protection does not turn those powers into ordinary appellate jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The second proviso to Article 200 was not attracted because the provision did not derogate from the High Court’s powers; the absence of a statutory appeal to the High Court did not itself trigger the proviso.

predicates.state_law_provides_no_high_court_statuto: A state law does not provide a statutory appeal to the High Court from the relevant tribunal decision.
predicates.high_court_constitutional_review_powers_: The law leaves the High Court’s constitutional judicial-review powers in place.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may determine whether a subordinate court correctly decided the facts on which its jurisdiction depends and may obtain additional evidence needed to decide those facts.
material_facts: The District Court considered an application seeking permission to sell property held under a trust.
The parties disputed whether the trust deed dedicated the property itself or only charged its income, and whether the property was a specific endowment subject to a different permission process.
The trust deed was the central document bearing on the character of the property and the District Court had proceeded on the basis that it had jurisdiction.
The Commissioner had raised the jurisdictional objections in the record, and the parties might seek to adduce further evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a High Court may examine whether a subordinate court correctly determined facts on which its jurisdiction depends. The Court relied on Chaube Jagdish Prasad v. Ganga Prasad, applying the principles stated in Queen v. Commissioner of Income Tax. The nature of the property determined whether the District Court could act under Section 34 of the Indian Trusts Act and whether permission under Section 34(1) of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act was implicated.
members.conclusion: The High Court could examine the jurisdictional facts in revision and, if necessary, receive further evidence itself or direct the District Court to record it.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A party brought a revision challenging an order made by a subordinate court.
predicates.subordinate_court_jurisdiction_depends_o: Whether the subordinate court had authority to deal with the matter depends on disputed facts about the subject matter.
predicates.central_document_available: A document central to determining the subject matter's character is available for consideration.
predicates.additional_evidence_needed: The parties may need to provide further evidence to resolve the disputed jurisdictional facts.

members.legal_issue: A High Court may exercise revisional jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure over a District Judge’s revisional order under the rent-control statute, even though that statute describes the District Judge’s order as final.
material_facts: A District Judge made an order while exercising revisional jurisdiction under the rent-control statute.
The High Court dismissed a further revision as not maintainable, relying on a later Full Bench decision that had treated the earlier Full Bench decision as no longer good law.
The statutory provision made the District Judge’s order final but contained no express words removing the High Court’s revisional jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure.
The Supreme Court had previously decided that a revision under the Code of Civil Procedure was available against an order under the same statutory provision.
members.legal_principle: Under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court may revise orders of subordinate courts, subject to that section’s limitations. The description of an order as final does not, without express statutory words excluding the jurisdiction, remove that power. Chhagan Lal v. Municipal Corporation, Indore and Krishnadas Bhatija v. A.S. Venkatachala Shetty support the availability of revision; Krishnaji Venkatesh Shirodkar v. Gurupad Shivaram Kavalekar was approved. Vishesh Kumar v. Shanti Prasad and Aundal Ammal v. Sadasivan Pillai were distinguished because they concerned different statutory schemes.
members.conclusion: A revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 50(1) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act is maintainable against a District Judge’s revisional order under section 50(2).

rule.if: rent_control_revision_case and district_judge_made_revisional_order and district_judge_order_called_final and no_express_exclusion_of_high_court_revision

predicates.rent_control_revision_case: The proceeding concerns a revision under a rent-control scheme.
predicates.district_judge_made_revisional_order: A District Judge made the challenged order while exercising revisional jurisdiction.
predicates.district_judge_order_called_final: The governing scheme describes the District Judge’s order as final.
predicates.no_express_exclusion_of_high_court_revis: The governing scheme contains no express words removing the High Court’s power to revise the District Judge’s order.

members.legal_issue: A High Court should not quash a revisional decision on the ground that an application was invalid for a deficient fee when the record discloses no patent error in the revisional authority's decision.
material_facts: The Central Government, exercising revisional powers, held that the original application remained valid because the State Government had accepted the fee deficiency and treated the application as pending.
The competing applicant challenged the Central Government's decision under Article 226 of the Constitution.
The High Court quashed the decision on the ground that the original application was no application in law because the full fee had not accompanied it.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 permits extraordinary judicial review, but the High Court had no patent error on the record to correct in the revisional authority's decision. The court held that the application and its accompanying fee were legally separable absent a rule making a deficient-fee application void, and that the authority could rely on the State Government's acceptance and treatment of the application. The court cited no earlier case by name.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in quashing the Central Government's order; the Central Government's decision was restored.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_revisional_order: A party challenged a revisional authority's decision by petition for judicial review.
predicates.authority_treated_application_as_valid: The revisional authority treated the application as valid after the licensing authority accepted the fee deficiency and considered the application.
predicates.no_patent_error_in_revisional_decision: The record disclosed no apparent error in the revisional authority's decision that warranted correction by the reviewing court.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may not reassess evidence and overturn concurrent factual findings when no legal infirmity in those findings is shown.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the first appellate authority both found that the landlord's need for the premises was bona fide.
The High Court reassessed the evidence in revision and reversed the concurrent findings.
No legal infirmity in the concurrent findings was shown.
members.legal_principle: In exercising revisional jurisdiction, the High Court may not reassess evidence to displace concurrent factual findings when no legal infirmity in those findings has been shown. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to reassess the evidence and reverse the concurrent findings in revision.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and concurrent_factual_findings and revisional_court_reassessed_evidence and no_legal_infirmity_shown

predicates.rent_control_revision: A tenant challenged an eviction decision through revision in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The initial decision-maker and the first appellate authority reached the same factual finding.
predicates.revisional_court_reassessed_evidence: The revisional court reconsidered the evidence and reached a different factual finding.
predicates.no_legal_infirmity_shown: No legal defect in the concurrent findings was identified.

members.legal_issue: A statutory declaration that a district court's decision is final does not prevent a High Court from exercising its revisional jurisdiction over that subordinate court's order where the applicable revision power extends to such orders.
material_facts: A district court decided an appeal concerning liability to municipal property tax and held that liability began only from a later period.
The municipality challenged that decision before the High Court in revision.
The High Court treated the district court as subordinate to it and exercised revisional jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Section 149(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, provided that the District Court's decision in the relevant assessment dispute was final. The Court held that section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowered the High Court to revise orders of subordinate courts, and the District Court was subordinate to the High Court.
members.conclusion: The district court's decision being described as final did not bar the High Court from exercising its revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: municipal_tax_appeal and district_decision_declared_final and district_court_subordinate_to_high_court and revision_power_covers_subordinate_court_orders

predicates.municipal_tax_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning liability to municipal tax.
predicates.district_decision_declared_final: The governing law describes the district court's decision in the dispute as final.
predicates.district_court_subordinate_to_high_court: The district court that made the decision is subordinate to the High Court.
predicates.revision_power_covers_subordinate_court_: The applicable procedural law empowers the High Court to revise orders of subordinate courts.
predicates.high_court_revision_jurisdiction_exists: The High Court may exercise revisional jurisdiction over the district court's decision.

members.legal_issue: Whether a revisional court may replace a concurrent factual finding that is supported by the record with its own assessment of the evidence.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the appellate authority both found that the ice-cream business had exclusive possession of part of the premises.
The High Court, exercising revision jurisdiction, reappraised the evidence and reversed that concurrent finding.
The High Court relied on plans produced in connection with a separate dispute about structural alterations, although that evidence had not been relied on to rebut exclusive possession.
members.legal_principle: The scope of revision depends on the language of the statute conferring it. Even where the revisional power permits examination of the legality or propriety of an order and is wider than the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, revision is not a first or second appeal. A revisional court should be reluctant to reassess evidence and supplant a factual finding where the record supports the finding reached below. Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, governed the revisional jurisdiction in this case.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in replacing the concurrent finding, which was supported by the evidence, with its own conclusion on an independent reassessment.

predicates.rent_revision_proceeding: A court is exercising revisional jurisdiction in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_finding_supported_by_record: The courts below reached the same factual finding and evidence in the record supports it.
predicates.revisional_court_reassesses_evidence_ind: The revisional court reassesses the evidence and substitutes a different factual conclusion.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may not overturn concurrent factual findings of revenue tribunals merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The Settlement Officer and the appellate District Judge both found that the respondent was a temporary lessee.

The respondent’s possession was undisputed, and evidence included the appellant’s failure to produce accounts, an admitted payment described as an advance, and a compromise concerning the respondent’s possession and departure.
The High Court reappraised the evidence and set aside the finding of a temporary lease.
The Supreme Court found that the revenue authorities’ conclusion had evidentiary material supporting it and was not shown to be perverse or beyond their jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution confers supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction. Under Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner, Hills Division, Assam, [1958] S.C.R. 1240, the High Court may intervene to keep subordinate tribunals within their authority, including where findings are based on no material or are perverse, but may not correct ordinary errors in appreciating evidence. Here, the evidence provided material supporting the revenue tribunals’ finding.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent finding that the respondent was a temporary lessee; the appeal challenging that interference was allowed.

rule.if: supervisory_jurisdiction_proceeding and concurrent_tribunal_findings and supporting_material_exists and not jurisdictional_overreach and not perverse_finding

predicates.supervisory_jurisdiction_proceeding: A party brought the tribunal’s decision before a High Court in a proceeding exercising supervisory rather than appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_tribunal_findings: The first-instance tribunal and the tribunal hearing the appeal reached the same factual finding.
predicates.supporting_material_exists: Evidence before the tribunals provided a basis for the factual finding.
predicates.jurisdictional_overreach: The tribunals exceeded the limits of their authority in reaching the finding.
predicates.perverse_finding: The finding was perverse, including because it was based on no material.

members.legal_issue: A supervisory court may not set aside factual findings of a subordinate tribunal merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The appellate rent court granted eviction on the basis of factual findings drawn from the evidence before it.
The reviewing court relied on material that had not been before the rent court and disturbed its findings.
The Supreme Court found no basis to treat the rent court’s findings as perverse or so unreasonable that no court could have reached them.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 confers judicial superintendence, not appellate jurisdiction to re-examine evidence or correct mere factual errors. Intervention is confined to keeping subordinate courts within their authority and is justified where findings are perverse or so unreasonable that no court could have reached them. The Court relied on Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte, M/s. India Pipe Fitting Co. v. Fakruddin M.A. Baker, and Sukhbir Narain v. Deputy Director of Consolidation.
members.conclusion: The reviewing court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by disturbing the eviction decree on those grounds.

rule.if: supervisory_review and findings_based_on_evidence and not findings_perverse_or_unreasonable

predicates.supervisory_review: A court reviews a subordinate court or tribunal in the exercise of supervisory rather than appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.findings_based_on_evidence: The subordinate court or tribunal reached its factual findings on the evidence before it.
predicates.findings_perverse_or_unreasonable: The subordinate court or tribunal’s factual findings are so perverse or unreasonable that no court could have reached them.
predicates.supervisory_court_must_not_disturb_factu: The supervisory court does not disturb the subordinate court or tribunal’s factual findings.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court exercising certiorari jurisdiction cannot reweigh a tribunal’s factual finding unless the finding involves a reviewable error of law or jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Collector found, after considering oral and documentary evidence, that the land had been cultivated by the tenant’s father and that the recorded difference in his parentage was a clerical error.
The reviewing courts found that the Collector’s finding was supported by evidence and was not based on legally inadmissible evidence or a refusal to admit admissible evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, certiorari is supervisory, not appellate: factual findings reached on appreciation of evidence cannot be reopened merely because they may be erroneous. Interference is available where a tribunal acts on legally inadmissible evidence, refuses admissible evidence, makes a finding unsupported by any evidence, exceeds or refuses jurisdiction, or acts illegally or improperly in a way that causes grave miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right not to interfere with the finding in certiorari jurisdiction, and there was no justification for setting aside the administrative orders on that ground.

rule.if: certiorari_review_of_tribunal_finding and finding_based_on_some_evidence and not finding_based_on_legally_inadmissible_evidence and not admissible_evidence_refused and not jurisdictional_or_procedural_illegality_causing_grave_injustice

predicates.certiorari_review_of_tribunal_finding: A party asks a reviewing court to use certiorari to examine a factual finding made by an inferior tribunal.
predicates.finding_based_on_some_evidence: The tribunal’s factual finding is supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.finding_based_on_legally_inadmissible_ev: The tribunal relied on evidence that the law did not permit it to consider.
predicates.admissible_evidence_refused: The tribunal refused to admit evidence that it was legally required to consider.
predicates.jurisdictional_or_procedural_illegality_: The tribunal exceeded or refused its jurisdiction, or acted illegally or improperly in a way that caused grave injustice.

members.legal_issue: A rent-control revisional court may interfere with a finding of fact based on no evidence, but may not act as an appellate court by reappraising evidence merely because it disagrees with the lower courts.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the appellate authority ordered eviction despite the absence of evidence establishing the landlord’s bona fide need.
The High Court exercised revisional jurisdiction and set aside those eviction orders.
The Supreme Court found that the lower authorities’ findings lacked evidentiary support on the landlord’s need.
members.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 empowers the High Court to examine the record for the regularity of proceedings and the correctness, legality, or propriety of a decision. This is supervisory rather than appellate jurisdiction: the High Court cannot interfere merely because it disagrees with a factual finding or reappraise evidence to substitute another finding, but it may intervene where the finding is based on no evidence.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering because the lower authorities’ eviction decision was unsupported by evidence; revisional jurisdiction does not otherwise permit mere reappraisal of evidence to reach a different factual finding.

predicates.rent_control_revision: A High Court considered a challenge to a rent-control decision in its revisional jurisdiction.
predicates.lower_eviction_finding_based_on_no_evide: The lower authorities ordered eviction without evidence supporting the landlord’s claimed bona fide need.

members.legal_issue: The High Court’s power to determine whether a District Court’s appellate order was made according to law does not include a general power to reappreciate evidence or retry factual findings.
material_facts: The District Court reversed the Insolvency Court after finding that the challenged mortgages were genuine and supported by consideration.
The High Court, exercising its supervisory power over the District Court’s appellate decision, reassessed the evidence and restored the Insolvency Court’s order.
members.legal_principle: Under the first proviso to section 75(1) of the Provincial Insolvency Act, the High Court may satisfy itself that the District Court’s appellate order was according to law, but has neither appellate power nor general jurisdiction to reappreciate evidence. A wrong factual decision by a competent court is still a decision according to law. The expression “according to law” is wider than “contrary to law” in section 100(1)(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the power resembles that under section 25 of the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act. The Court relied on Bell & Co. Ltd. v. Waman Hemraj and Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Chowdhury, and explained Official Receiver, Kanpur v. Abdul Shakur as confirming that factual findings, including findings about rebuttal of a statutory presumption, cannot be disturbed in that jurisdiction. Intervention may be warranted for matters such as lack of jurisdiction, reliance on inadmissible evidence, denial of a proper hearing, or placing the burden of proof on the wrong party.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to interfere merely because it would have assessed the evidence differently; it was generally bound by the District Court’s findings of fact. Its supervisory power is wider than the power under section 100(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and permits intervention where the decision was not according to law, but not a de novo examination of facts.

predicates.insolvency_appellate_revision: The proceeding involved supervisory review of a District Court’s appellate decision in an insolvency matter.
predicates.district_court_found_facts: The District Court decided the appeal on findings of fact.

members.legal_issue: Statutory finality of an order does not exclude the constitutional supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 227.
material_facts: The Sessions Judge's order in an appeal under the forest statute was declared final and not open to challenge in any court.
The State challenged the High Court's refusal to consider supervisory relief, while not contesting the conclusion that a statutory revision was unavailable.
members.legal_principle: A statutory declaration of finality cannot take away the constitutional jurisdiction preserved by Articles 32, 226 and 227. The Court relied on Lila Vati v. State of Bombay and Union of India v. A.V. Narasimhalu for the principle that statutory finality or exclusion of ordinary court jurisdiction does not exclude constitutional writ jurisdiction. It observed that, given the express finality language in Section 59(3) of the Indian Forest Act as amended, invocation of Section 482 of the Code might not be permissible, but that language could not bar Article 227 jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The statutory finality clause did not prevent the High Court from considering the matter under Article 227. The Court left open whether Section 482 of the Code could be invoked, set aside the High Court's refusal to exercise Article 227 jurisdiction, and directed it to consider the matter under that provision.

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: The challenged order was made in an appeal provided by a statute.
predicates.reviewed_order_declared_final: The statute declared the challenged appellate order final or not open to challenge in court.
predicates.constitutional_supervisory_challenge: A litigant asked the High Court to examine the challenged order through its constitutional supervisory jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A High Court cannot reject a request for supervisory review without properly considering a material statutory presumption that the lower appellate decision overlooked.
material_facts: Goods being transported in a truck were seized after the person accompanying them failed to produce a required permit.
The forest authority ordered confiscation of the truck.

The Sessions Judge held the confiscation order to be without jurisdiction on the basis that there had been no claim that the goods belonged to the State, without addressing the statutory presumption of State ownership.
The State relied on that presumption in seeking further review, but the High Court rejected supervisory intervention without examining the issue on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 69 of the Indian Forest Act provided the statutory presumption concerning State ownership of forest produce. The Court held that the issue whether the presumption applied was material and required examination; the department's reliance on the presumption meant a separate ownership claim was not necessary. The High Court was required to consider the issue under Article 227, even though the order was declared final under Section 59(3).
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in concluding that no case for examination had been made out. It was directed to consider the State's position concerning the statutory presumption, hear both parties, and decide the matter objectively on its merits and in accordance with law.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_proceeding and state_relied_on_ownership_presumption and appellate_decision_ignored_presumption and higher_court_declined_review_without_examining_it

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: The challenged order was made in an appeal provided by a statute.
predicates.state_relied_on_ownership_presumption: The State relied on a statutory presumption of its ownership of the relevant property.
predicates.appellate_decision_ignored_presumption: The appellate decision did not address the statutory ownership presumption when deciding the dispute.
predicates.higher_court_declined_review_without_exa: The High Court declined supervisory intervention without examining the material presumption issue on its merits.

members.legal_issue: A High Court exercising general civil revisional jurisdiction cannot correct a subordinate court’s error in construing a decree when that error has no relation to the subordinate court’s jurisdiction.
material_facts: In debt-adjustment proceedings, the District Court decided that a prior decree had extinguished the applicants’ right to redeem the mortgaged property.
The High Court, exercising general revisional jurisdiction, construed the decree differently and set aside the District Court’s decision.
The challenged construction concerned whether the debt and right of redemption remained subsisting, a matter the courts administering the debt-adjustment proceedings were authorized to determine.
The error alleged against the District Court’s construction did not concern its assumption, failure to exercise, or manner of exercising jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Under section 115(a), (b) and (c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, revisional intervention is confined to cases where a subordinate court has exercised jurisdiction not vested in it, failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it, or acted illegally or with material irregularity in exercising jurisdiction. An error of law, including an error in construing a decree or document of title, is not by itself enough if it has no relation to jurisdiction. The Court relied on Manindra Land and Building Corporation Ltd. v. Bhutnath Banerjee, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1336, and Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Safibhai, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1341. It noted that limitation and res judicata may raise jurisdictional questions, but did not treat the construction issue in this case as jurisdictional.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by interfering with the District Court’s construction of the decree; its order was set aside and the District Court’s order restored.

predicates.revision_under_limited_civil_revisional_: A party asks a higher court to review a subordinate court’s decision under a limited general civil revisional power.
predicates.subordinate_court_was_authorized_to_deci: The subordinate court was empowered to determine the substantive dispute before it.
predicates.challenged_error_concerned_construction_: The alleged legal error concerned how the subordinate court interpreted a decree.
predicates.challenged_error_had_no_relation_to_juri: The alleged error did not involve the subordinate court’s assumption, refusal to exercise, or exercise of jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising certiorari jurisdiction may not reappraise evidence and substitute its factual findings for supported findings of lower authorities unless a recognized ground for certiorari is established.
material_facts: Both lower authorities found on the evidence that a person who was not a member of the tenant’s family sat in the shop and conducted the tenant’s business on the tenant’s behalf.
The reviewing court rejected that finding after reassessing the evidence, including a commissioner’s report to which an objection remained undecided.
The lower authorities’ findings rested on evidence, and no jurisdictional error, breach of natural justice, or manifest or apparent error of law justified disturbing them.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, certiorari may issue where an inferior tribunal or subordinate court has committed an error of jurisdiction, breached natural justice, or made a manifest or apparent error of law. It does not authorize reappraisal of evidence without sufficient legal reason or substitution of contrary factual findings. The commissioner’s report, because an objection to it remained undecided, was not a final document and could not be relied upon as it stood. No earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The reviewing court exceeded its jurisdiction by reappraising the evidence; its order was set aside and the lower authorities’ orders were restored.

rule.if: certiorari_proceeding and supported_lower_fact_findings and no_recognized_certiorari_error and reviewing_court_reappraised_evidence

predicates.certiorari_proceeding: A party sought judicial review of a lower authority’s decision by a writ in the nature of certiorari.
predicates.supported_lower_fact_findings: The lower authorities made factual findings that rested on evidence.
predicates.no_recognized_certiorari_error: The lower authorities’ decision did not suffer from a jurisdictional error, a breach of natural justice, or a manifest or apparent error of law.
predicates.reviewing_court_reappraised_evidence: The reviewing court reassessed the evidence and reached factual findings contrary to those of the lower authorities.
predicates.reappraisal_exceeds_jurisdiction: The reviewing court’s reappraisal of the evidence exceeded its jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A High Court should not use supervisory jurisdiction to entertain a challenge to a civil court’s ex parte decree when the civil procedure provides a statutory appeal.
material_facts: The trial court passed an ex parte decree in a civil suit.
The defendants had a remedy of appeal to the First Appellate Court against the decree.
One defendant directly challenged the decree under Article 227, and the High Court set it aside.
members.legal_principle: Where proceedings are before a civil court and the Code of Civil Procedure provides an appellate remedy, that remedy ordinarily operates as a near-total bar to supervisory intervention under Article 227. The Court relied on Virudhunagar Hindu Nadargal Dharma Paribalana Sabai v. Tuticorin Educational Society, which applied the principles in Radhey Shyam v. Chhabi Nath and referred to A. Venkatasubbiah Naidu v. S. Chellappan. The defendants could also seek to set aside an ex parte decree under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in entertaining a supervisory revision against the ex parte decree because a statutory appeal was available.

predicates.civil_court_proceeding: The proceeding was conducted before a civil court.
predicates.ex_parte_decree_challenged: A party challenged a decree entered in that party’s absence.
predicates.statutory_appeal_available: The procedural law provided an appeal to a higher court against the decree.
predicates.supervisory_revision_should_not_be_enter: The High Court should not entertain supervisory review of the decree when the stated conditions apply.

members.legal_issue: The supervisory jurisdiction of a High Court cannot be used to correct an inferior court’s ordinary error when the court acted within its authority and the complaint does not disclose a jurisdictional or procedural failure.
material_facts: The petitioner challenged orders made in execution proceedings by petitioning the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.

An appeal was available against an order under Order XXI, Rule 92, and the dispute also raised a question under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure for which an appeal was available under the law then in force; even if no appeal lay, a revision under Section 115 was available.

The subordinate court had not failed to exercise jurisdiction, disregarded natural justice, or adopted a procedure contrary to law; the petitioner’s complaint did not establish an error of law or an error apparent on the face of the record.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 gives the High Court limited supervisory jurisdiction to ensure that an inferior court or tribunal functions within the limits of its authority; it does not make the High Court an appellate tribunal for reviewing evidence or correcting ordinary errors of fact or law. A mere wrong decision is insufficient. The Court also noted the available appeal under Order XLIII, Rule 1(j), the appealability under Sections 47 and 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure as they then stood, and the alternative remedy of revision under Section 115.
members.conclusion: The petition under Article 227 was misconceived, and the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the subordinate court’s orders on the grounds advanced.

predicates.supervisory_petition_against_lower_court: A party asks a higher court to use supervisory jurisdiction to interfere with an order of a lower court.
predicates.lower_court_acted_within_authority: The lower court acted within the authority given to it.
predicates.no_jurisdictional_or_procedural_failure: The lower court did not fail to exercise jurisdiction, violate natural justice, or use a procedure contrary to law.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising certiorari jurisdiction cannot act as an appellate court or interfere with a factual finding unless a recognized legal or jurisdictional error warrants intervention.
material_facts: The landlord challenged the revisional court’s decision in a proceeding under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.
The revisional court had corrected the trial court’s legal error and found that the landlord had not proved subletting.
The High Court interfered with that decision by treating the revisional court’s consideration of the evidence as an impermissible reappraisal.
The Supreme Court found no basis for the High Court to disturb the revisional court’s decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, certiorari is supervisory and does not permit the High Court to sit as a court of appeal over findings of fact. Under Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan & Ors., (1964) 5 SCR 64, an error of law apparent on the record may be corrected, but an error of fact, however grave, is not by itself a ground for certiorari interference.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by interfering with the revisional court’s decision; its order was vacated and the revisional court’s order restored.
