In the later proceedings concerning mesne profits, the tenant disputed the area included in the tenancy.
The court relied on the earlier affidavit in treating the tenant as estopped from taking the inconsistent position.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle of estoppel against taking a position inconsistent with an admission made in an affidavit in prior proceedings between the same parties. It upheld the factual finding because it was based on the record and was neither perverse nor illegal.
members.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from disputing the area previously admitted, and the finding on the area did not warrant interference.

predicates.appeal_challenges_mesne_profit_order: A party appeals an order fixing mesne profits for premises held after an eviction decree.
predicates.prior_affidavit_admits_tenanted_area: The tenant previously filed an affidavit in proceedings between the same parties admitting the area of the tenancy.
predicates.later_position_disputes_same_area: The tenant later disputed that same area when mesne profits were determined.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot introduce on appeal a new limitation theory that depends on factual matters not pleaded or tried below and would have required an issue and evidence.
material_facts: The appellant argued before the Supreme Court that limitation should run from the date the company’s title was perfected.
That theory had not been raised before the courts below, and the parties had adduced evidence on a different basis.
The Court observed that the proposed theory could have required an issue to be framed and evidence to be adduced.
members.legal_principle: Limitation is a mixed question of law and fact, and its application depends on the agreement and the parties’ conduct and understanding. A new factual theory that was not raised below and would have required an issue and evidence cannot be introduced for the first time in the Supreme Court. The Court applied Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and considered the approach described in Gunwantbhai Mulchand Shah v. Anton Elis Farel.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not raise the title-perfection limitation theory for the first time before the Supreme Court.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party challenged a civil judgment in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.limitation_theory_not_raised_below: The party did not advance the particular limitation theory before the lower courts.
predicates.theory_requires_factual_issue_or_evidenc: Deciding the new theory would require factual findings, an issue for trial, or evidence not addressed below.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot raise on appeal a statutory bar that was not founded in the pleadings or made the subject of an issue at trial.
material_facts: The defendants relied on a statutory bar to the suit based on the effect of consolidation proceedings.
Their written statement did not lay a foundation for that contention, and no issue on it was raised at trial.
members.legal_principle: Pleadings must provide a foundation for a contention, and a party cannot introduce a new contention on appeal when it was neither pleaded nor made an issue at trial. The court considered the contention under Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, but rejected it for lack of a pleading foundation; the judgment does not identify a specific provision of the Code of Civil Procedure as the basis for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The defendants could not raise the statutory-bar contention for the first time on appeal.

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.not_pleaded_in_written_statement: The party raising the contention did not set it out in its written statement.
predicates.no_trial_issue_on_contention: The trial court did not frame or decide an issue on the contention.

members.legal_issue: A belated challenge to a recovery sale is not a basis for disturbing the sale where the challenger’s asserted ownership is unsupported, the challenger abandoned the recovery objection, an appeal was available, and third-party rights arose before the challenge was brought.
material_facts: The challenger relied on an unregistered agreement to sell made with his brother, who was one of the judgment-debtors; the Court held that the agreement did not vest a legal right in the challenger.
Although the challenger filed an objection before the Recovery Officer, he stopped appearing or being represented after October 2005, and the sale order was made more than two years later.
The challenger did not object to the attachment or the auction notices and did not object in the purchaser’s mutation proceedings.

A statutory appeal to the Tribunal was available against the Recovery Officer’s order, but the challenger instead brought a writ petition after the auction had been confirmed, possession delivered, and mutation completed.
The challenger’s writ petition was brought after third-party rights had arisen in the property.
members.legal_principle: An unregistered agreement to sell does not vest the asserted legal right in the property. Under Section 30 of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, a person aggrieved by a Recovery Officer’s order may appeal to the Tribunal; the availability of that remedy weighed against intervention in writ jurisdiction. A claimant who abandons an objection, does not challenge the attachment or sale notices, and waits until third-party rights have arisen may have the challenge rejected for delay and laches. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The challenger’s objections and belated challenge should have been rejected for lack of a legal right, abandonment, and delay and laches; the High Court should not have disturbed the auction sale.

rule.if: challenge_to_recovery_sale and unregistered_agreement_claim and abandoned_recovery_objection and available_appeal_bypassed and delayed_challenge_after_third_party_rights

predicates.challenge_to_recovery_sale: A person challenges a property sale conducted to recover a debt in a recovery proceeding.
predicates.unregistered_agreement_claim: The challenger relies on an unregistered agreement to sell as the basis for claiming ownership of the property.
predicates.abandoned_recovery_objection: The challenger filed an objection in the recovery proceeding but stopped pursuing it before the sale was ordered.
predicates.available_appeal_bypassed: A statutory appeal against the Recovery Officer’s order was available, but the challenger did not use it.
predicates.delayed_challenge_after_third_party_righ: The challenger brought the challenge only after the sale had been completed and rights in the property had arisen in a third party.

members.legal_issue: A claim for compensation for change of residence cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when it was not urged before the High Court and no specific ground was taken.
material_facts: The claimant sought compensation for change of residence under the relevant compensation clause.
The point had not been raised or urged before the High Court.
No specific ground concerning that claim was included in the appeal to the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to permit a party to re-agitate an issue that had not been raised and urged before the High Court and for which no specific ground was taken in the appeal. The claim concerned Section 23(1), clause fifthly, of the Land Acquisition Act.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not permitted to raise the change-of-residence compensation claim in the Supreme Court appeal.

predicates.supreme_court_compensation_appeal: A party pursued an appeal to the Supreme Court concerning acquisition compensation.
predicates.compensation_claim_not_raised_below: The party had not raised or argued the compensation claim before the High Court.
predicates.no_specific_appeal_ground: The party had not included a specific ground for the claim in the Supreme Court appeal.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a court sale cannot be sustained on a ground that was not raised in the initial application to recall the sale and was added only at a later stage.
material_facts: The unsuccessful bidder initially sought recall of the accepted sale on grounds concerning the increased development potential and value of the land.
It later relied on a change in the successful bidder’s shareholding as an alleged breach of the tender condition against nomination.
The shareholding ground was not the basis on which the initial recall application had been made.
members.legal_principle: The Court rejected the successive addition of new grounds to attack an accepted court sale, reasoning that permitting such an attempt would undermine the sanctity of court sales. It did not decide the substantive merits of the alleged shareholding breach.
members.conclusion: The later-added shareholding ground did not warrant consideration as a basis for recalling the sale.

predicates.company_liquidation_sale_recall_challeng: A party challenges an order accepting a sale of assets in a company liquidation by seeking recall of that order.
predicates.ground_not_in_initial_recall_application: The asserted ground was absent from the party’s initial application to recall the sale.
predicates.ground_added_later: The party relies on that ground for the first time at a later stage of the challenge.
predicates.late_raised_ground_not_considered: The later-added ground is not considered as a basis for recalling the sale.

members.legal_issue: Evidence on title is inadmissible when title has not been pleaded or made an issue in the case.
material_facts: The respondent’s claim rested on possession, not title.
The pleadings and framed issues did not raise title, and the remand expressly limited the scope of the further proceedings.
The single judge permitted additional evidence concerning the appellant’s alleged title and relied on title-related findings.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule that evidence is not admissible in the absence of a plea, and noted that the single judge had also overlooked the limits on additional evidence in Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the restricted scope of the remand.
members.conclusion: The additional title evidence was inadmissible, and the single judge acted beyond the permissible scope of the appeal by admitting and relying on it.

rule.if: civil_appeal_proceeding and title_not_pleaded and title_not_in_issue and additional_title_evidence_admitted

predicates.civil_appeal_proceeding: The matter is a civil appeal in which the court is considering evidence beyond the original trial record.
predicates.title_not_pleaded: Neither party pleaded a claim or defence putting ownership in issue.
predicates.title_not_in_issue: The court did not frame ownership as an issue for decision.
predicates.additional_title_evidence_admitted: The appellate court admitted additional evidence concerning ownership.
predicates.title_evidence_inadmissible: Evidence concerning ownership cannot be admitted to decide an issue that was not pleaded or put in issue.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot raise an unpleaded waiver contention for the first time at the appellate stage.
material_facts: The party opposing the challenge to the award had not pleaded that the challenger waived the right to contest the award.
That party nevertheless argued waiver before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain the waiver contention because it had not been pleaded below and was raised at the appellate stage; no provision or earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The waiver contention was not competent to be raised at that stage because waiver had not been pleaded.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party is advancing a contention in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.waiver_not_pleaded_below: The party relying on waiver did not plead it in the proceedings below.
predicates.waiver_raised_at_appellate_stage: The party first advances the waiver contention at the appellate stage.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot decide a case on a ground outside the parties’ pleadings or make out a new case that was not raised by them.
material_facts: The State’s appeal did not raise the question whether the equitable interest directed by the earlier writ order could be granted.
The High Court relied on a decision concerning the availability of equitable interest and used that issue to set aside the additional interest.
The issue on which the High Court ruled had not been raised by the State.
members.legal_principle: Although Section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives an appellate court broad powers, a decision must remain within the case pleaded by the parties. The Court relied on Siddu Venkappa Devadiga v. Rangu S. Devadiga, which cites Trojan and Co. Ltd. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar and Raruha Singh v. Achal Singh for the rule that a decision cannot rest on grounds outside the parties’ pleas.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not go outside the pleadings and make out a new case; its decision on the unraised issue was erroneous.

predicates.statutory_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision made in a statutory proceeding.
predicates.issue_not_raised_in_pleadings: The parties did not raise the issue in their pleadings or submissions.
predicates.appellate_court_decides_unpleaded_issue: The appellate court decides the appeal on that unraised issue.

members.legal_issue: A new challenge to the validity of a transfer cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when it was not raised earlier in the litigation.
material_facts: The appellants argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that the transfer was invalid because it had not been effected by a registered document.
The appellants had not raised that ground at any earlier stage of the litigation.
A registered partition deed was part of the record.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a plea that had not been raised at any stage of the litigation before being advanced in the Supreme Court. It cited no provision or earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court did not permit the appellants to raise the registration challenge for the first time before it.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brought an appeal before a higher court.
predicates.challenge_first_raised_on_appeal: A party advanced a challenge for the first time in the appeal.
predicates.challenge_not_raised_at_earlier_stages: The party had not raised that challenge at any earlier stage of the litigation.

members.legal_issue: A claim that a widow’s title was extinguished by adverse possession cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when it was not pleaded or tried, and possession without effective exclusion does not establish adverse possession.
material_facts: The claim that the widow’s title had been extinguished by adverse possession was not raised at trial and was not included in the pleadings.
The estate was managed by the Court of Wards and later by the adopted son, but the widow lived with him and the evidence did not show that she was excluded from the estate or any part of it.
The widow received maintenance rather than managing the estate herself.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession presents mixed questions of law and fact and is effectively decided after the relevant facts are proved. Mere erroneous admission of another person’s title, without effective deprivation of possession, does not extinguish title by adverse possession.
members.conclusion: The appellate court properly refused to entertain the newly raised adverse-possession claim, and the circumstances described did not show effective deprivation of the widow’s possession sufficient to extinguish her title.

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning competing claims to property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_not_pleaded_or_: The party asserting adverse possession did not plead or litigate that claim at trial.
predicates.widow_not_effectively_excluded_from_prop: The widow was not effectively deprived of possession of the estate or any part of it.
predicates.possession_based_only_on_admission_of_an: The other person’s possession was accompanied only by an erroneous admission of that person’s title, without effective deprivation of the widow’s possession.

members.legal_issue: The appropriate development deduction from the assessed market value of acquired land depends on the land’s situation, existing development, and need for development.
material_facts: The acquired land was within municipal limits and adjoined an established township.
Before the acquisition, the surrounding area had roads and nearby educational, commercial, industrial, and medical establishments.
The court considered the sizes of the plots used for comparison with the acquired land.
The Reference Court had applied a lower deduction than the High Court, which imposed a larger deduction.
members.legal_principle: A development deduction must be based on the situation of the land and the development it requires. Where acquired land is amid already developed land with amenities such as roads, drainage, and electricity, a substantial deduction may not be justified. In Charan Dass v. H.P. Housing and Urban Development Authority (2010) 13 SCC 398, the Court held that a 40% deduction was not justified for land amid developed land with amenities. In Kasturi v. State of Haryana (2003) 1 SCC 354, a 20% deduction, below the normal one-third deduction, was held understandable and capable of justification. The size of comparable plots relative to the acquired land may also be considered.
members.conclusion: The larger deduction imposed by the High Court was not justified; the lower deduction applied by the Reference Court was appropriate and its award was restored.

rule.if: compensation_appeal_for_acquired_land and land_within_developed_municipal_area and surrounding_amenities_pre_existed_acquisition and comparative_plot_sizes_considered

predicates.compensation_appeal_for_acquired_land: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_within_developed_municipal_area: The acquired land was within municipal limits and amid an already developed area.
predicates.surrounding_amenities_pre_existed_acquis: Amenities and established institutions or businesses were present around the land before it was acquired.
predicates.comparative_plot_sizes_considered: The court considered the sizes of the plots used for comparison relative to the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land may be assessed by reference to the value on the date of the acquisition notification, and phased acquisition does not by itself invalidate that basis.
material_facts: The challenge concerned compensation assessed by reference to the value of the land when the acquisition notification was published, rather than when possession was taken.
The acquisition was for a public purpose.
The statutory scheme provided for interest on market value after a period of delay in payment and allowed sanctioned post-notification improvements to be considered in awarding compensation.
The challenge to phased acquisition was treated as, in substance, a challenge to the adequacy of compensation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(5) precluded the asserted challenge to the compensation basis for an acquisition for public purpose. Sections 4(3) of the Land Acquisition Amendment and Validation Act, 1957 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act provided for interest in the specified circumstances and consideration of sanctioned improvements. Section 23 concerned compensation, not procedure. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, which had upheld the notification and the compensation basis; the validation of phased acquisition under the 1957 Act had been upheld in Udai Ram Sharma v. Union of India, following the issue considered in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma.
members.conclusion: The challenge to assessing compensation by reference to the notification date was rejected; the phased-acquisition objection did not invalidate the acquisition.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the basis on which compensation is assessed in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.acquisition_for_public_purpose: The land is acquired to serve a public purpose.
predicates.compensation_based_on_notification_date: The compensation assessment uses the land's value when the acquisition notification is published.

members.legal_issue: The compensation for acquired land must reflect its market value when the land’s development potential, location, and nearby sale evidence support a higher valuation than the valuation adopted on appeal.
material_facts: A substantial portion of the owner’s agricultural holding was acquired for housing, leaving a smaller remainder that the owner said was uneconomical to farm.
The acquired land was suitable for housing and was located near a national highway and developed areas, between the highway and a railway track.
The acquiring authority based its valuation on a sale of land separated from the acquired land by a railway track.
Other nearby land had been sold at substantially higher rates shortly before the acquisition, although some of those parcels were closer to the highway.
The Reference Court awarded compensation above the acquiring authority’s valuation, and the High Court reduced that award.
members.legal_principle: In determining market value under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including on a reference under Section 18, the assessment must account for the land’s nature and present use, its capacity for higher potential, its precise location and relationship to adjoining land, and the use of neighbouring land. Relevant nearby sale transactions close to the acquisition may evidence value, but differences in location and characteristics must be considered. Compensation represents the value to the owner who parts with the property and should reflect the price between a willing buyer and a willing seller. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s reduction and restored the compensation awarded by the Reference Court.

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the amount of compensation determined for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_has_higher_development_pot: The acquired land is suitable for a more valuable use than its current use or has other characteristics supporting higher value.
predicates.nearby_sales_support_higher_value: Sales of nearby land close to the acquisition support a higher market value than the valuation challenged on appeal.
predicates.sale_comparisons_account_for_location_di: The valuation evidence and assessment take account of relevant differences in location and characteristics between the acquired land and the comparison parcels.

members.legal_issue: A deduction may be made to account for the time difference when the exemplar sale occurred after the relevant acquisition notification and land prices were rising.
material_facts: The exemplar sale occurred one year and more than seven months after publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.
The High Court deducted 10 percent for de-escalation in valuing the acquired land.
Earlier decisions had approved annual escalation rates ranging from 7.5 percent to 10 percent, and the Court took notice of the general rise in land prices.
members.legal_principle: Although escalation in land prices is ordinarily a question of fact to be proved by cogent evidence, the Court may take judicial notice of rising land prices in light of ground realities. The decisions in Delhi Development Authority v. Bali Ram Sharma, ONGC Ltd. v. Rameshbhai Jeewanbhai Patel, and Valliyammal v. Special Tehsildar support annual escalation rates within the range of 7.5 to 10 percent. A time-based adjustment was justified where the exemplar sale occurred more than a year after the preliminary notification.
members.conclusion: The High Court's 10 percent deduction for de-escalation was upheld.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and exemplar_sale_after_notification and sale_more_than_a_year_later and rising_land_prices

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by a public authority.
predicates.exemplar_sale_after_notification: The exemplar transaction took place after publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.
predicates.sale_more_than_a_year_later: More than a year elapsed between publication of the notification and the exemplar transaction.
predicates.rising_land_prices: The court found that land prices were generally rising during the relevant period.

members.legal_issue: The deduction from the assessed market value of acquired land must reflect the land’s developed status and location.
material_facts: The land was acquired for construction of a road, and the landowners appealed the compensation determination.

The High Court assessed the market value of irrigated and waste land at the same rate because of its residential and commercial potential, then deducted one-third because the land was somewhat away from the main road.
The land was within a well-developed area developed by the HUDA.
The Supreme Court found the one-third deduction harsh in light of the land’s developed status and considered a ten per cent deduction just.
members.legal_principle: In determining compensation for acquired land, a deduction from assessed market value may account for the land’s location and development, but its extent must be justified by the circumstances. The Court held that a one-third deduction was not justified for land forming part of a well-developed area and that a ten per cent deduction was appropriate. The acquisition arose under Sections 4 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the landowners had sought a reference under Section 18. No earlier cases were cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court modified the compensation determination by replacing the one-third deduction from the assessed market value with a ten per cent deduction, while preserving the claimants’ entitlement to statutory benefits on the enhanced compensation.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and land_in_well_developed_area and land_is_some_distance_from_main_road and market_value_assessed_before_deduction

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the compensation determined for acquired land.
predicates.land_in_well_developed_area: The acquired land forms part of a well-developed area.
predicates.land_is_some_distance_from_main_road: The acquired land is somewhat away from a main road.
predicates.market_value_assessed_before_deduction: The market value of the acquired land was assessed before a deduction was applied.

members.legal_issue: A claim to exclude land from a surplus-area determination as tenants’ permissible area or as uncultivated land requires supporting evidence of the relevant tenancy or land-use facts.
material_facts: The sons claimed that they had cultivated certain land as tenants before the relevant law commenced, but the authorities found the cultivation entries relied on for that claim to have been tampered with.
The record did not show that the sons paid rent or that an agreement relieved them of the obligation to pay rent.

The landowner claimed that certain land was uncultivated land to be excluded, but the authorities found no proof that it was not being used for an agricultural or agriculture-related purpose or for pasture at the relevant time.
members.legal_principle: Under the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, the Court considered the absence of rent or evidence of an agreement relieving the alleged tenants from rent in assessing the tenancy claim. Under section 2(8) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, a landowner claiming exclusion of banjar qadim or banjar jadid land had to prove that, at the relevant time, it was not used for an agricultural purpose, a purpose subservient to agriculture, or pasture.
members.conclusion: The claimed tenancy and uncultivated-land exclusions were not established and did not warrant disturbing the surplus-area determination.

rule.if: surplus_area_determination and tenancy_exclusion_claim and unreliable_cultivation_records and no_rent_or_rent_exemption_evidence and uncultivated_land_exclusion_claim and no_proof_of_nonagricultural_use

predicates.surplus_area_determination: An authority is determining which land is surplus for the purposes of a land-tenure regime.
predicates.tenancy_exclusion_claim: A party claims that land should be excluded because it was held or cultivated as tenants’ permissible area.
predicates.unreliable_cultivation_records: The records relied on to establish cultivation are found unreliable or tampered with.
predicates.no_rent_or_rent_exemption_evidence: There is no evidence of rent paid or of an agreement relieving the alleged tenants from rent.
predicates.uncultivated_land_exclusion_claim: A landowner claims that land should be excluded as uncultivated land.
predicates.no_proof_of_nonagricultural_use: There is no proof that the land was not used for agriculture, a purpose subservient to agriculture, or pasture at the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: Market value in a land acquisition proceeding must be determined objectively from reliable evidence of the land’s condition, use, potential, and comparable transactions, rather than from speculative potential or an unsuitable small-plot sale.
material_facts: The acquired lands were predominantly agricultural wet paddy fields, were relatively inaccessible, and required substantial levelling to become suitable for construction.
The Land Acquisition Officer’s material described the lands’ physical characteristics and levelling requirements.
The High Court rejected the claimants’ other evidence but relied on a sale of a small plot with a house, applied a deduction, and treated the acquired lands as fit for building purposes.
The Supreme Court found that the lands’ building-site potential was not established and that the small-plot sale was not a sound basis for valuing the large agricultural tract.
No other evidence was available to support the claimants’ requested higher valuation.
members.legal_principle: The claimants bear the burden of proving that the Collector’s offer is inadequate. Under Sections 4(1), 11, 18, and 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is assessed as of the notification date by objectively considering the land’s location, nature, use, income, potential, and comparable transactions. The court must assess what a prudent willing purchaser would pay in the open market, avoid speculative assumptions, and account for differences between the acquired land and a small plot or other comparator. The Court relied on Periyar and Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala, Basant Kumar v. Union of India, Special Land Acquisition Officer, Dharwad v. Tajar Hanifabi, and Agricultural Produce Market Committee v. Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s valuation was set aside, and the Supreme Court reassessed compensation on the record at a lower rate than the reference court had awarded.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: A court is determining compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.claimants_bear_burden_to_prove_higher_va: The claimants seek more than the Collector offered and therefore must establish that the offer is inadequate.
predicates.land_is_predominantly_agricultural_and_r: The acquired land is predominantly agricultural and requires substantial work before it can be used for the claimed developed purpose.
predicates.relied_on_small_plot_sale_is_not_compara: The principal relied-on sale concerns a small plot or otherwise differs materially from the acquired land.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_establishes_higher_: The evidence does not reliably establish that the acquired land would fetch a higher price in the open market.
predicates.market_value_redetermined_on_objective_r: Compensation is reassessed using an objective evaluation of the reliable evidence and relevant land characteristics.

members.legal_issue: Market value in a land acquisition must be assessed using relevant comparable sales and the circumstances affecting the acquired land.
material_facts: The acquired land was situated near a growing urban locality and was needed amid a serious housing shortage.
A nearby sale of a substantial parcel in the locality, shortly before the acquisition notification, indicated a substantially higher value than the amount fixed by the lower courts.
The lower courts rejected that sale based on the parcel’s proximity to a railway crossing, a mango grove, and its smaller area, but the Supreme Court found those reasons insufficient to disregard it.
The acquired land was lower than the adjoining road and had pits and water accumulation during the rainy season, which affected its value.
A much lower price accepted for other land years later was accepted as a nominal compromise connected with the owner’s interest in establishing a college, rather than as evidence of market value.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is assessed as of the date of the Section 4 notification. Relevant nearby sale transactions may illuminate that value; their location, size, timing, and other circumstances must be considered, along with disadvantages affecting the acquired land. The judgment cites no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court fixed the market value at a higher rate than the lower courts and partly allowed the appeal.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the State.
predicates.nearby_comparable_sale_indicates_higher_: A sale of nearby land around the relevant time indicates a higher market value than the value fixed below.
predicates.comparable_sale_is_substantial: The nearby sale concerns a parcel substantial enough to provide meaningful evidence of local market value.
predicates.acquired_land_has_value_affecting_disadv: The acquired land has physical or locational disadvantages that must be taken into account when assessing its value.

members.legal_issue: A compensation award must reflect the market value the deciding court itself has found on the evidence and applicable valuation factors.
material_facts: The land was a large tract of undeveloped agricultural land acquired for residential development.
The landowners presented oral evidence about the land’s location, access, surroundings, and development potential, but no sale deeds.
The High Court considered the land’s potential and the rate fixed by courts for adjacent land acquired at the same time, and stated that the market value was sixty-three rupees per square yard.
Despite that finding, the High Court awarded compensation at fifty rupees per square yard.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires assessment of fair market value as of the acquisition date. The Court considered the land’s location, potential, surroundings, nearby land values, undeveloped condition, and development costs, while recognizing that valuation requires assessment of the evidence rather than an exact formula. It applied the principles on development deductions in Brig. Sahib Singh Kalha v. Amritsar Improvement Trust, Chimanlal Hargovinddas v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Kasturi v. State of Haryana, Lal Chand v. Union of India, A.P. Housing Board v. K. Manohar Reddy, Special Land Acquisition Officer v. M.K. Rafiq Saheb, and Chandrashekar v. Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: The High Court had no justification for awarding less than the market value it had found; the Supreme Court fixed compensation at sixty-three rupees per square yard, with the statutory benefits payable under the Act.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.acquired_land_is_large_and_undeveloped: The acquired property is a large tract that has not been developed.
predicates.market_value_supported_by_location_and_p: Evidence about the land’s location, surroundings, access, or development potential supports a market-value assessment.
predicates.court_finds_a_market_value_higher_than_t: The deciding court finds a market value greater than the amount it has awarded.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must reflect its building-site potential when the overall evidence shows that the potential could be realised in the reasonably near future.
material_facts: Before the acquisition, the landowners obtained permission to convert adjoining agricultural land, which formed part of the same larger parcel, for construction of houses and voluntarily paid conversion charges for that purpose.
The acquired land was within municipal limits, on the edge of an inhabited locality, and near existing buildings and a road.
Evidence also included nearby land sales and negotiations to sell plots as building sites.

The Supreme Court found that these circumstances established building-site potential and, considering the overall evidence, increased the compensation above the amount awarded by the Collector and High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires assessment of market value. Applying the guidance in N.B. Jeejabhoy v. The District Collector, Thana, quoted in R.N. Singh v. U.P. Government, the Court treated potential use as relevant when it could be turned to account within a reasonably near future. The listed considerations are broad guidelines, not immutable rules; whether land has building-site potential is primarily a question of fact determined from the overall circumstances.
members.conclusion: The land had building-site potential that had to be reflected in its market value, and the Court increased the compensation accordingly.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_valuation and conversion_charges_paid_for_nearby_land and (land_within_municipal_limits and near_inhabited_locality and nearby_buildings_present) and evidence_supports_near_term_building_use

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_valuation: The proceeding concerns valuation of land acquired by the State for compensation.
predicates.conversion_charges_paid_for_nearby_land: The owner voluntarily paid charges to obtain permission to convert nearby land for building use.
predicates.land_within_municipal_limits: The acquired land lies within municipal limits.
predicates.near_inhabited_locality: The acquired land is on or near the edge of an inhabited locality.
predicates.nearby_buildings_present: Buildings are located in the immediate vicinity of the acquired land.
predicates.evidence_supports_near_term_building_use: The evidence, considered as a whole, shows that building use could reasonably be realised in the near future.

members.legal_issue: Market value must be assessed from evidence that reliably reflects the value of the acquired land and its relevant characteristics.
material_facts: The acquired land covered a large area and was mostly agricultural, although it had potential for building use.
A sale deed concerned only a small parcel and was not considered a suitable basis for valuing the much larger acquired area.
Other relied-on sales concerned developed areas or land far from the acquired land.

Government values used for stamp duty and registration and the Commissioner's valuation assessment were also relied on, but no evidence showed that the circular values reflected the prevailing market value of comparable land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed by reference to the land's relevant characteristics at the date of the Section 4(1) notification. Government circulars under Section 47A of the Stamp Act do not establish market value without evidence of prevailing local prices for land with similar advantages. A Commissioner's valuation based on best judgment is not a sufficient basis by itself. The judgment identifies no named precedent for these evidentiary propositions.
members.conclusion: The small-parcel sale, sales of dissimilar or distant land, stamp-duty circulars, and the Commissioner's assessment could not, on their own, form the basis for determining the acquired land's market value.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.comparable_is_small_or_dissimilar: A party relies on a sale of a small parcel or land whose development or location makes it materially unlike the acquired land.
predicates.stamp_value_lacks_comparable_market_evid: A party relies on government stamp-duty values without evidence that they reflect local prices for similarly advantageous land.
predicates.commissioner_value_is_best_judgment: A party relies on a Commissioner's valuation that is an assessment based on the Commissioner's best judgment.

members.legal_issue: The just market value must reflect the land's potential, its undeveloped condition, and the limitations of the available comparable evidence.
material_facts: The land was in a developing industrial area and had potential for building use, although most of it remained agricultural.
A small part had been converted to non-agricultural use, but the owners had not developed it into plotted land or provided amenities.
The comparable sales relied on by the claimants were not a reliable basis for valuing the large acquired area.
The High Court had fixed compensation at Rs. 18 per square yard, and the Supreme Court concluded that Rs. 20 per square yard was just compensation.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires assessment of market value at the date of the Section 4(1) notification. The land's location, potential use, existing use, state of development, and the reliability of comparable evidence inform that assessment. No named earlier case is relied on for the Court's final valuation on these facts.
members.conclusion: The Court fixed compensation at Rs. 20 per square yard and allowed the appeals to that extent.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and land_has_building_potential and development_is_incomplete and available_comparables_do_not_reliably_value_the_acquired_extent

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: A claimant appeals a court's determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_has_building_potential: The land could potentially be used for building purposes.
predicates.development_is_incomplete: The land has not been developed to the stage at which it can be used as building plots.
predicates.available_comparables_do_not_reliably_va: The available sale evidence does not reliably establish the value of the size and kind of land acquired.

members.legal_issue: Market value in a land acquisition must be determined by adjusting comparable sale evidence for the relevant differences between the sale property and the acquired land, and deductions may separately account for land size and development needs.
material_facts: The acquisition included 16 plots, including two very large plots and 14 smaller plots.
The principal comparable sale concerned a 46.30-square-metre property sold for Rs. 270 per square metre in a different locality.

Evidence showed that the acquired land had roads, electricity, water, non-agricultural use and nearby residential and commercial uses, but the area was not fully urbanized and its development had practically stopped because of the dam and expected submergence.
Development had shifted to an area across a river, and the acquired land was to be submerged.
The Reference Court deducted development costs from its valuation; the High Court made deductions that varied according to the size of the acquired plots.
The State challenged the deductions as insufficient, while the claimants argued that separate deductions for size and development were impermissible.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is assessed as of the date of the Section 4(1) notification, ordinarily by reference to what an informed willing buyer would pay a willing seller. Comparable sale evidence must be assessed for proximity in time and situation, with adjustments for positive and negative features of the sale property and acquired land; the valuation is not mathematically exact. A small-plot sale may be used for a larger acquisition if appropriate adjustments are made. Deductions for size and development depend on the facts and may be distinct; they are not automatic, and an already developed smaller portion of a larger tract may not warrant a deduction merely because the overall tract is large. The Court relied on Bhagwathula Samanna v. Special Tahsildar, L. Kamalamma v. Land Acquisition Officer, Basavva v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, K.S. Shivadevamma v. Assistant Commissioner, Hasanali Khanbhai & Sons v. State of Gujarat, Land Acquisition Officer v. Nookala Rajamallu, and the cases applying ordinary development deductions; it distinguished The Registrar, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad, on its agricultural-land facts.
members.conclusion: The Court determined compensation at Rs. 160 per square metre for the large plots and Rs. 175 per square metre for the small plots. It held that relevant deductions depend on the circumstances of the land and that deductions for the size of the land and for development are not necessarily impermissible when made separately.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_small_plot_sale and acquired_plots_differed_in_size and acquired_area_was_to_be_submerged and development_had_shifted_away

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_small_plot_sale: The court considered a sale of a small plot in a different locality as a comparable transaction.
predicates.acquired_plots_differed_in_size: The acquired land included both very large plots and smaller plots.
predicates.acquired_area_was_to_be_submerged: The acquired land was to be submerged as a result of the public project.
predicates.development_had_shifted_away: Development in the acquired locality had practically stopped and had shifted to another area.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land may reflect its potential use, but the valuation of a large tract must account for development costs.
material_facts: The acquired land was waste land that was fit for cultivation and possessed potential value for building purposes.
The land was on the outskirts of an industrial city and was acquired for industrial development.
The acquisition covered a large area.
The Court determined compensation at a net rate after deducting one-third for development charges and allowed statutory benefits on the enhanced compensation.
members.legal_principle: For compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed by applying the test of what a prudent willing purchaser would offer. The land's potential value may be considered, and the Court deducted an amount for development charges in assessing the net value of the large tract. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The land's potential value was properly taken into account, but compensation was fixed at a net rate of Rs. 22 per square metre after a one-third deduction for development charges; the claimants were also entitled to statutory benefits on the enhanced compensation.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the determination of compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.land_has_potential_value: The acquired land had potential for a more valuable use than its existing condition or use.
predicates.large_area_acquired: A large tract of land was acquired.

members.legal_issue: Comparable sales and other valuation evidence must establish market value through objective assessment of sufficiently similar land and reliable evidence.
material_facts: The acquired land formed part of a large estate and was not irrigated.
The claimant relied on sales of irrigated paddy land about four miles away and on a valuation from another acquisition.
The High Court found those properties unsuitable comparisons, and the Supreme Court agreed.
The High Court also found the claimant’s valuation evidence untrustworthy; the State’s valuation evidence had also been rejected.
members.legal_principle: Market value is assessed as the price a willing seller could reasonably obtain from a willing buyer acting at arm’s length, using recent bona fide sales of the acquired land or comparable neighbouring land with similar advantages. Differences in size, location, fertility, irrigation, development or potentiality may make sales incomparable and require adjustment. Courts may use other material or make a pragmatic estimate where precise comparable evidence is unavailable, but must avoid mechanical assessment and speculation. In a reference seeking increased compensation, the claimant must prove that the Collector’s offer is inadequate; the State may adduce rebuttal evidence. The Court relied on Gajapati Raju v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Adinarayana Setty, Tribeni Devi v. Collector of Ranchi, Dollar Co. v. Collector of Madras, Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, Chimanlal Hargovinddas v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, and Ezra v. Secretary of State for India, Raja Harish Chandra v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, Khorshed Shapoor Chenai v. Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, Dr. G.H. Grant v. State of Bihar, and Chaturbhuj Panda v. Collector, Raigarh.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s documents did not establish a higher market value, and the High Court was justified in rejecting the trial court’s valuation based on them.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_appe: The proceeding concerns an appeal about compensation for land taken by compulsory acquisition.
predicates.comparables_lacked_similarity: The claimant relied on sales or valuations of land materially different in location, quality, irrigation, size, or other relevant advantages from the acquired land.
predicates.claimant_valuation_evidence_untrustworth: The fact-finder found the claimant’s evidence offered to establish a higher value unreliable.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must reflect its comparable sale value, location, character, and building potential, subject to a deduction for the cost of developing a partly undeveloped area.
material_facts: The acquired land was in a developing town, near a grain market, municipal plots that had been sold, and shops and other constructions.
Nearby plots had substantial building potential, and evidence put the average sale value of comparable land at Rs. 15 per square yard; the State did not challenge that evidence.
The locality was not fully developed, and the High Court had upheld compensation of Rs. 2 per square yard.
The Supreme Court treated the comparable value as Rs. 15 per square yard and deducted one-third for the locality's incomplete development, resulting in compensation of Rs. 10 per square yard.
members.legal_principle: Compensation must be assessed with regard to the land's location, character, building potential, surrounding development, and comparable sale evidence. Where an area is not fully developed, a deduction of one-third may be made to account for land needed for roads, drainage, and other amenities, as stated in Tribeni Devi v. Collector of Ranchi. The judgment cites no statutory provision for this valuation principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court's valuation was wrong. Compensation was enhanced from Rs. 2 to Rs. 10 per square yard, with a proportionate increase in interest and solatium.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and nearby_comparable_sales_evidence and comparable_value_evidence_unchallenged and land_has_building_potential and locality_partly_undeveloped

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.nearby_comparable_sales_evidence: Evidence shows sale values for nearby land comparable to the acquired land.
predicates.comparable_value_evidence_unchallenged: The opposing party does not challenge the evidence of comparable sale values.
predicates.land_has_building_potential: The acquired land's location and surroundings give it building potential.
predicates.locality_partly_undeveloped: The locality is not fully developed and would require land or expenditure for development amenities.
predicates.compensation_enhanced_with_proportionate: Compensation is increased, with a corresponding increase in interest and solatium.

members.legal_issue: An enhanced land acquisition compensation award is not speculative when evidence supports it through land values, the acquired land's attributes, and changes in market prices.
material_facts: The acquired land had been purchased several years before acquisition at a lower per-acre rate than the compensation later determined.
The evidence included sale deeds for land in the same village and nearby villages, as well as Collector's awards concerning nearby land.
The evidence also addressed the acquired land's location, advantages, facilities, and the rise in land prices between purchase and acquisition.
The High Court increased the compensation rate, and the Supreme Court found that its decision had an evidentiary basis and did not depart from recognised principles.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires compensation to be determined on the relevant evidence of value. Oral and documentary evidence, comparable transactions or awards, the land's location, advantages and facilities, and an established rise in land prices may support an enhanced assessment; an assessment supported by such material is not speculative merely because some estimation is involved.
members.conclusion: The High Court's enhancement of compensation was supported by the evidence and was not based merely on speculation or conjecture; the State's appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_against_land_acquisition_compensation and compensation_enhanced and value_evidence_supports_assessment and land_attributes_considered and market_price_rise_supported

predicates.appeal_against_land_acquisition_compensa: An appeal challenges the amount of compensation determined for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_enhanced: The challenged decision increased the compensation previously determined for the acquired land.
predicates.value_evidence_supports_assessment: Oral or documentary evidence, including comparable sales or awards, supports the assessed value.
predicates.land_attributes_considered: The assessment takes account of the acquired land's location, advantages, or facilities.
predicates.market_price_rise_supported: The evidence supports a rise in land prices relevant to the valuation.

members.legal_issue: The fair market value of acquired land must reflect its value on the acquisition-notification date, including any supported increase in its potentiality.
material_facts: The acquired land was agricultural and had been shown in a green belt, but a planning change before acquisition allowed commercial warehousing and storage use.
The claimants argued that the planning change increased the land’s commercial potential, but produced no evidence establishing the value of the land for commercial use.
A prior judicial valuation of comparable agricultural land was used as a benchmark, with annual escalation applied to estimate value at acquisition.
The High Court considered different escalation methods and the land’s increased potentiality in fixing a value above the agricultural-land estimate.
The Supreme Court found the High Court’s assessment justified and saw no basis to interfere with it.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4, 18 and 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as of the date of the Section 4 notification. The land’s potentiality is relevant, but a claim for commercial value must be supported by material; where direct evidence is absent, a prior valuation of comparable agricultural land and reasonable escalation may inform the assessment. The Court referred to Dharambir & Ors. v. Union of India and Union of India v. Dharambir, and held that the valuation did not warrant interference under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the High Court’s market-value assessment and dismissed all appeals.

rule.if: compensation_appeal and comparable_prior_valuation and annual_escalation_applied and planning_change_increased_potential and commercial_value_evidence_absent and valuation_methods_considered

predicates.compensation_appeal: A party appealed a judicial assessment of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_prior_valuation: A prior valuation of comparable agricultural land was available as a benchmark.
predicates.annual_escalation_applied: The benchmark valuation was adjusted by applying annual increases to estimate value at acquisition.
predicates.planning_change_increased_potential: A planning change gave the land some additional commercial potential before acquisition.
predicates.commercial_value_evidence_absent: The claimants produced no material establishing the land’s market value for the proposed commercial use.
predicates.valuation_methods_considered: The reviewing court considered different valuation methods and weighed them against the land’s potentiality and the available evidence.
predicates.appellate_market_valuation_upheld: The appellate court leaves the market-value assessment in place.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must reflect its reasonably foreseeable potential and special advantages, while allowing a reasonable deduction for development and land needed for public amenities.
material_facts: The acquired land was within municipal limits and near developed urban areas.
The land was bounded by roads, part of it had been diverted from agricultural use, and it had a house and utility connections.
Agreements concerning nearby parcels contemplated their development and sale as plots, with the purchaser paying development charges.
The evidence indicated that part of the land would need to be set aside for roads and other amenities.
The High Court considered the land’s development potential but deducted development costs and land for amenities in calculating its value.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 23, 24 and 25 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed by reference to what a willing vendor and willing purchaser would reasonably agree, considering the land’s legitimate uses, reasonably foreseeable potential and special advantages, but not speculative or imaginary possibilities. Potential value must be determined from available evidence. The Court relied on Gajapatiraju v. Rev. Divisional Officer, A.I.R. 1939 P.C. 98; Mahabir Prasad Santuka v. Collector, Cuttack, [1987] 1 S.C.C. 587; and U.P. Government v. H.S. Gupta, A.I.R. 1957 S.C. 202.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the land’s potential value had not been adequately reflected and that the development deduction was excessive. It enhanced compensation for the land by one-sixth, setting the rate at Rs. 14,000 per acre, maintained solatium, and increased interest on the enhanced compensation to 9% until payment.

rule.if: acquired_land_compensation_case and land_near_developed_urban_area and (land_had_development_indicators or comparable_plot_transactions_supported_development_potential) and development_potential_underreflected and development_deduction_exceeded_reasonable_allowance

predicates.acquired_land_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.land_near_developed_urban_area: The acquired land was within or near a developed urban area.
predicates.land_had_development_indicators: The land had features such as road access, partial diversion, buildings or utility connections that supported its suitability for development.
predicates.comparable_plot_transactions_supported_d: Transactions involving comparable parcels supported the prospect of developing and selling land in plots.
predicates.development_potential_underreflected: The lower valuation did not adequately account for the land’s reasonably foreseeable development potential and special advantages.
predicates.development_deduction_exceeded_reasonabl: The lower valuation deducted more for development costs or land needed for amenities than the evidence reasonably supported.

members.legal_issue: The compensation for restricted land must reflect the relevant valuation date and the difference between that land and unrestricted land with development potential.
material_facts: For the acquisition under the later notification, the Court relied on its valuation of adjoining unrestricted land at Rs.110 per square metre as of the relevant valuation date and applied a 50% deduction for the agricultural-use restriction, resulting in Rs.55 per square metre.

For the acquisition under the earlier notification, the Court derived a value of Rs.90 per square metre for unrestricted land with development potential as of the relevant valuation date and applied a 50% deduction, resulting in Rs.45 per square metre.

The Court allowed the Board's appeal on compensation in the first two matters and rejected the landowner's appeal for an increase; it partly allowed the appeal concerning the other acquired portion. Statutory benefits were preserved.
members.legal_principle: Market value is assessed as of the relevant valuation date, using comparable land values and accounting for differences in use and development potential. The Court applied its valuation of adjoining unrestricted land, adjusted the value for the relevant valuation date where necessary, and deducted 50% to account for the restriction limiting the acquired land to agricultural use. The statutory benefits under sections 23(1A), 23(2), and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, were preserved as applicable.
members.conclusion: The compensation was reduced to Rs.55 per square metre for the land acquired under the later notification and to Rs.45 per square metre for the land acquired under the earlier notification, with the statutory benefits specified by the Court.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining compensation for land acquired through a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.restricted_agricultural_land: The acquired land is legally limited to agricultural use.
predicates.unrestricted_comparable_value_is_availab: A market value is available for comparable land that is not subject to the same use restriction.
predicates.comparable_value_is_adjusted_to_relevant: The value of the comparable land is adjusted to reflect the date relevant to assessing the acquired land's market value.

members.legal_issue: Fair market value for acquired land must be assessed from the evidence and circumstances as a whole, accounting for comparable sales, land characteristics, potential, and development costs.
material_facts: The acquisition comprised a large tract taken for residential and commercial development, with land abutting a road and land farther inside the tract.
The land had potential for development and nearby activity, but the sale evidence chiefly concerned very small plots and included varied prices.
The Collector and High Court had assessed separate values for roadside and interior categories of land; the High Court had enhanced the interior-land value but left the roadside-land value unchanged.
The Supreme Court considered location, surroundings, nature and potential of the land, small-plot rates, the acquisition purpose, development costs, and the absence of sales of large areas.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is determined as of the acquisition notification by assessing the evidence and circumstances, including what a hypothetical willing seller and prudent willing buyer would accept in normal market conditions. Recent bona fide sales of the acquired or nearby land with similar advantages are relevant, while small-plot values may require deductions for development. The landowner must produce relevant material to show that the Collector's offer is inadequate. The Court relied on Periyar and Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala (1991) 4 SCC 195 for the landowner's evidentiary burden and Atma Singh (Dead) through LRs v. State of Haryana (2008) 2 SCC 568 for development deductions.
members.conclusion: The Court fixed higher fair market values for both categories of land, determining compensation at Rs.45,00,000 per acre for the roadside category and Rs.35,00,000 per acre for the Nehri, Chahi category, while upholding the statutory compensation already awarded.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and market_value_requires_assessment and evidence_shows_distinct_land_categories and court_considers_location_potential_and_development_costs

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.market_value_requires_assessment: The court must determine the land's fair market value from the available evidence.
predicates.evidence_shows_distinct_land_categories: The evidence supports distinguishing land categories with materially different locations or characteristics.
predicates.court_considers_location_potential_and_d: The court assesses location, surroundings, development potential, and development costs in evaluating the evidence.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land with development potential must be assessed from relevant market evidence while accounting for development costs and the land’s location and potential.
material_facts: The acquired land was mostly vacant and agricultural, but lay within municipal limits near commercial and residential establishments and had potential for residential and commercial use.
The landowners’ nearby small-plot sale deeds indicated an average market value of Rs. 32,65,351 per acre; the Court considered a 60% deduction for development expenses.
The exact locations of the plots covered by the sale deeds were not established, and the sale considerations varied significantly.
The Collector had assessed compensation at Rs. 6,00,000 per acre, the Reference Court at Rs. 6,60,000 per acre, and the High Court at Rs. 9,00,000 per acre.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 23 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed by reference to the price a willing purchaser would pay, taking account of potential value and relevant comparable evidence. The Court relied on Smt. Tribeni Devi v. Collector of Ranchi and Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore v. T. Adinarayan Setty for valuation methods, and on the principles concerning deductions and development costs in Smt. Basavva, Bhagwathula Samanna, and Viluben Jhalejar Contractor. The amount of deduction depends on the circumstances, including the land’s size, situation, and development requirements.
members.conclusion: The Court awarded compensation of Rs. 12,00,000 per acre, together with the applicable statutory benefits and interest, and allowed the appeals.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and acquired_land_has_nonagricultural_potential and acquired_land_is_near_developed_area and nearby_sale_evidence_is_relevant and sale_values_vary_significantly and exact_sale_plot_locations_are_uncertain

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking a decision on compensation for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_has_nonagricultural_potent: The acquired land has potential for use beyond agriculture.
predicates.acquired_land_is_near_developed_area: The acquired land is situated near developed commercial or residential areas.
predicates.nearby_sale_evidence_is_relevant: Nearby sale transactions provide relevant evidence of market value for the acquired land.
predicates.sale_values_vary_significantly: The relevant sale transactions show substantial variation in consideration.
predicates.exact_sale_plot_locations_are_uncertain: The precise locations of the plots covered by the sale transactions are not established.

members.legal_issue: A deduction for development costs must reflect the land’s circumstances, and a deduction of one-third was appropriate for the acquired land in Talwandi Bhai.
material_facts: The land was within municipal limits and had been acquired for a new grain market.
The High Court had deducted 40 percent from the market value.
The Court considered the average sale price and an annual increase in value, and held that the 40 percent deduction was unjustified in the circumstances.
The Court assessed compensation after applying a one-third deduction.
members.legal_principle: A development-cost deduction is fact-specific; the Court considered the land’s location and the development needed, rather than applying a fixed percentage. It relied on Saibanna (Dead) by LRs. v. Assistant Commissioner and Land Acquisition Officer, which held that no rigid rule governs deductions and that a one-third deduction may be justified, as well as the principles discussed in Kasturi v. State of Haryana.
members.conclusion: The Court assessed compensation for the land at Rs. 7,25,000 per acre after applying a one-third deduction.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_is_within_municipal_limits: The acquired land is within municipal limits.
predicates.existing_deduction_exceeds_development_n: The deduction applied to the market value is greater than the development needs and circumstances justify.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsorily acquired surplus land is calculated using the rate applicable when the land vested under the law that remained in force after retrospective amendments were given effect.
material_facts: The applicable vesting date was the publication date of the surplus-land notification, rather than an earlier date attributed to the land by an intervening amendment.
The compensation rate had been reduced before the notification was published.
The respondent sought compensation calculated using the higher rate that had applied before the reduction.
members.legal_principle: Under section 18(3) of the principal Act, vesting occurred on publication of the notification, and section 50 and Schedule III governed compensation. The Court applied the amendment to Schedule III made by Act 39 of 1972, which changed the applicable compensation rate before the land vested.
members.conclusion: The compensation had to be calculated using the reduced rate applicable when the land vested, not the earlier, higher rate.

predicates.claim_for_compensation_after_surplus_lan: A claimant sought compensation for land taken as surplus under a land-reform process.
predicates.land_vested_on_notification_publication: The land vested in the government when the authority published the notification declaring it surplus.
predicates.compensation_rate_changed_before_vesting: The legally applicable compensation rate changed before the land vested.

members.legal_issue: The value of undeveloped acquired land must be reduced to account for the cost of providing development and civic amenities.
material_facts: The acquired area was undeveloped and required roads, parks, drainage, lighting, and other civic amenities.
The Supreme Court distinguished a prior case in which the acquired land was in a fully developed area.
The lower court had deducted one-third for development, and the Supreme Court upheld the need for that deduction.
members.legal_principle: Where acquired land is undeveloped and requires development, at least one-third must be deducted toward development charges. The Court relied on Brig. Sahib Singh Kalha v. Amritsar Improvement Trust, [1982] 1 SCC 419; Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, AIR 1988 SC 943; Special Tehsildar, Land Acquisition v. A. Mangal Gowri, [1991] 4 SCC 218; and Bhagwathula Samanna v. Special Tehsildar, Land Acquisition, [1991] 4 SCC 506, distinguishing the latter because the land there was fully developed.
members.conclusion: A deduction of at least one-third for development charges was necessary for the undeveloped land, and the Court applied that deduction to the market value.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.acquired_land_is_undeveloped: The acquired land has not been developed for its intended use.
predicates.development_and_civic_amenities_are_requ: The land requires development work and civic amenities before it can be used as intended.

members.legal_issue: The deduction for development costs must reflect the development required in the particular acquisition rather than a fixed general rate.
material_facts: The acquiring authority challenged the deduction made for development costs.
The acquired tract comprised about 27 acres.
The Court considered that development costs varied according to the location, area and work required.
members.legal_principle: There is no fixed deduction for development costs: the appropriate deduction varies from place to place and according to the area and the development work required. The Court relied on that principle and considered the size of the acquired tract in fixing the deduction.
members.conclusion: The Court increased the development-cost deduction from 10% to 25%.

predicates.acquiring_authority_appeals_development_: The acquiring authority appealed the deduction applied to account for development costs.
predicates.development_costs_required: Development work was required for the acquired land.
predicates.existing_deduction_inadequate: The Court found that the deduction already applied did not adequately account for development costs.

members.legal_issue: The deduction for development costs must reflect the circumstances of the acquired land and the comparable transaction, and a deduction of one-third was appropriate on these facts.
material_facts: The High Court valued the acquired land by relying on a sale of a small plot of 9 marlas that had occurred about 56 months before the acquisition notification.
The High Court applied an annual escalation of 10% to that sale price and then deducted 67.5% for development.
The acquired land required development for construction of a warehouse.
The Supreme Court considered the 67.5% deduction too high in these circumstances and applied a one-third deduction.
members.legal_principle: Deductions from the price of a small developed plot to value undeveloped or underdeveloped land depend on the land’s nature and location, the area needed for roads and other facilities, and development expenses. Lal Chand v. Union of India (2009) 15 SCC 769 and Haryana State Agricultural Market Board v. Krishan Kumar (2011) 15 SCC 297 address those factors. Major General Kapil Mehra v. Union of India (2015) 2 SCC 262 discusses the usual one-third deduction and the circumstances that can justify a different deduction; Subh Ram v. State of Haryana (2010) 1 SCC 444 held that a 67% deduction was not improper on its facts. The Court applied a one-third deduction to this case.
members.conclusion: The 67.5% deduction was reduced to one-third, resulting in compensation of Rs.4,43,258 per acre, with statutory benefits.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining compensation for land acquired through a compulsory acquisition process.
predicates.small_plot_sale_used_as_comparable: The valuation relies on a sale of a small plot as a comparable transaction.
predicates.acquired_land_requires_development: The acquired land requires development for the purpose for which it was acquired.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must reflect whether it is similarly situated to land already valued and the distinct characteristics of other portions.
material_facts: The land was divided into six belts according to its quality and situation.
Land in the first four belts was found to be similarly circumstanced to other land acquired under the same notification for which compensation had been fixed at a higher rate.
The fifth-belt land was assessed separately, while the sixth-belt land was proved to consist of hillocks.
members.legal_principle: The Court compared the circumstances and characteristics of the acquired land with comparable land and assessed compensation accordingly. It relied on the prior appellate determination concerning the comparable land, which had been affirmed by the Supreme Court, and found no basis to disturb the assessment for land proved to consist of hillocks.
members.conclusion: Compensation for the first four belts was fixed uniformly at the rate used for the comparable land; compensation for the fifth belt was increased to a reasonable rate; and the existing lower rate for the hillock land was upheld.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and (first_four_belts_similarly_situated_to_comparable_land or fifth_belt_requires_separate_assessment or sixth_belt_proved_to_be_hillocks)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The case is an appeal seeking increased compensation for acquired land.
predicates.first_four_belts_similarly_situated_to_c: The claimant's land in the first four belts is similarly situated to other land whose compensation was fixed at a higher rate.
predicates.fifth_belt_requires_separate_assessment: The land in the fifth belt has circumstances warranting a separate compensation assessment.
predicates.sixth_belt_proved_to_be_hillocks: The evidence establishes that the land in the sixth belt consists of hillocks.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must reflect its reasonably foreseeable building potential, and that potential must be assessed from evidence rather than conjecture.
material_facts: The land was being used as dry agricultural land when it was notified for acquisition.
The land was situated near roads, a railway station, an industrial estate, and residential developments; the area was developing rapidly and there was demand for residential plots.
The Land Acquisition Officer described the land as having high potential for development into housing colonies.

The Court explained that, where nearby plot-sale evidence is used, the acquired land may be assessed through a hypothetical layout with appropriate deductions for land used for roads and other facilities, development expenses, and other relevant factors.
