members.legal_principle: Under Sections 23(1) and 24(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as of the relevant notification date and may include value attributable to a reasonably foreseeable better use, but not an increase attributable merely to the use for which the land is acquired. The Court described the hypothetical-layout approach and referred to Bombay Improvement Trust v. Marwanji Manekji Mistry, AIR 1926 Bombay 420, for deductions from retail plot prices to estimate the wholesale value of undeveloped land.
members.conclusion: Building potential must be included in the market value if reliable evidence establishes that the land could be used for buildings in the immediate or near future. Its extent must be assessed from relevant evidence, including comparable sales and the costs or losses involved in development, rather than conjecture.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding determines compensation for land acquired by compulsory acquisition.
predicates.immediate_building_use_supported_by_reli: Evidence supports the inference that the land could be used for buildings in the immediate or near future.

members.legal_issue: Potential building-site value may be included in market value only when objective evidence shows that the potential can be realized within a reasonably near future.
material_facts: The acquired grove land was outside a town, abutted a main road, and was next to a school.
There was evidence of a few houses on nearby grove land, but no substantial building activity near the acquired land and no ascertainable trend of town development toward it.
members.legal_principle: Under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value reflects the land’s existing advantages and potential possibilities, but potential must be objective and capable of being turned to account within a reasonably near future. Whether building potential exists depends on the overall evidence, including building pressure, suitability, direction and pace of development, and nearby construction. The Court relied on South Eastern Rail Co. v. L.C.C. and N. B. Jeejabhoy v. The District Collector, Thana.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish building-site potential that could be used as a basis for valuing the land.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.no_substantial_nearby_building_activity: There was no substantial building activity in the neighbourhood of the acquired land.
predicates.no_ascertainable_development_toward_land: There was no ascertainable trend of development toward the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Comparable land sales must be assessed for their proximity, similarity and local conditions, and neither distant sales nor a general assumption of rising prices automatically establishes market value.
material_facts: Sales of nearby land showed lower prices than sales of land farther away.
The more distant sale relied on concerned land about a mile and a half away, while local industrial, social and geographic conditions could affect prices.
The evidence did not establish an inevitable rise in prices throughout the relevant period, and some evidence showed prices in the area had remained stationary.
members.legal_principle: Comparable sales may assist valuation, particularly when the sale of the acquired land is old, but their value as evidence depends on temporal proximity, comparable advantages and relevant local conditions. A distant sale is not automatically a guide, and a rise in land prices is not an axiomatic proposition. The Court applied the market-value principles in section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act and referred to S.L.A. Officer v. T.A. Setty concerning valuation by bona fide sales of acquired or comparable land.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court found that the High Court could reasonably assess the totality of the evidence and was not shown to have erred by relying on nearby sales and the circumstances of the area.

predicates.land_acquisition_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns the assessment of compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.comparable_sales_differ_in_proximity_or_: The sales offered as comparisons concern land that differs in distance, timing, advantages or other relevant characteristics.
predicates.local_conditions_affect_value: Geographic, economic, industrial or social conditions in the area affect land values.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must reflect just and reasonable value when the land is materially comparable to nearby land for which a higher compensation has been determined.
material_facts: The acquired lands were in the same village as lands acquired for another project and lay directly across a road from them.
Some land in the same survey number was acquired for both projects.
The Supreme Court had previously determined higher compensation for the lands across the road, while the High Court had reduced compensation for the lands in these appeals to the Collector’s amount.
The notifications for the two acquisitions were issued at different times, but the Court found the lands similarly situated despite the time gap.
The Court considered the evidence on record and the sale instances relied on by the landowners.
members.legal_principle: Under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, compensation must be just and reasonable. The Court considered the similarity in location and the earlier determination in Arawali Power Company Private Limited (Civil Appeal No. 8757 of 2016 and connected appeals, decided 5 September 2017), while also considering the evidence and sale instances in the present case. Sections 4, 6 and 11 of the Act concerned the acquisition notifications, declaration and Collector’s award in this case.
members.conclusion: The Court modified the High Court’s judgment and increased the compensation for the acquired lands to a just and reasonable level.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and (comparable_location or shared_survey_land) and prior_comparable_award_higher and significant_compensation_difference

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_location: The acquired land is located comparably to other acquired land for which compensation has been determined.
predicates.shared_survey_land: Some land in the same survey number was acquired for the different projects being compared.
predicates.prior_comparable_award_higher: A prior determination set higher compensation for land found comparable to the land in the appeal.
predicates.significant_compensation_difference: The compensation determinations for the comparable lands differ substantially.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for comparable acquired land should be adjusted to reflect changes in market value between the earlier benchmark acquisition and later acquisitions.
material_facts: The appeals concerned land acquired on four different dates after comparable land in the same village had been acquired in 1974.
In an earlier decision concerning the comparable land, the Court had fixed compensation at Rs. 17.50 per square yard after considering the relevant facts and lower court judgments.
The Court considered that market prices had risen between 1974 and 1978 and fixed compensation rates of Rs. 20, Rs. 25, Rs. 26 and Rs. 30 per square yard for the respective acquisition dates.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on its earlier decision in Paltoo Singh v. State of Haryana, which fixed the value of comparable land acquired in 1974 at Rs. 17.50 per square yard. Having regard to the rise in market prices through 1978, it considered it fair and reasonable to adjust the compensation for the different acquisition dates. The relevant acquisition dates were those stated in the Section 4 notifications.
members.conclusion: The market value was directed to be calculated at the rates fixed for each acquisition date: Rs. 20, Rs. 25, Rs. 26 and Rs. 30 per square yard, respectively.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and prior_comparable_land_award and later_acquisition_dates and intervening_market_price_rise

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.prior_comparable_land_award: A court has fixed compensation for comparable land acquired earlier.
predicates.later_acquisition_dates: The land in the proceeding was acquired after the comparable land.
predicates.intervening_market_price_rise: Market prices rose between the earlier comparable acquisition and the later acquisitions.
predicates.compensation_adjusted_for_acquisition_ti: Compensation is adjusted to reflect the difference in acquisition timing.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired agricultural land may reflect its potential value as a building site when the land’s situation and surrounding development support that potential and the valuation is supported by reliable comparable-sale evidence.
material_facts: The acquired land was agricultural and lay adjoining a railway track near a growing town.
The land had buildings on three sides and a metalled road on the fourth; railway staff quarters had been built on the land, and there was nearby construction.
The acquiring authority relied on a sale statement consisting mostly of older sales and produced no adequate evidence of comparable-site prices.
A sale of nearby, contiguous land shortly before the relevant valuation date was available as a guide to value.
members.legal_principle: In determining compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the land’s potential as a building site is a question of fact assessed from its condition and situation, present or reasonably possible use, suitability for building, proximity to developed areas and institutions, available or extendable amenities, the town’s prospects, and pressure of building activity. In the section 18 reference and appeals concerning compensation under section 23, the majority accepted a nearby sale of contiguous land as a safe guide in light of the surrounding circumstances; an unsupported sale statement based mostly on old transactions was not adequate evidence. The majority did not rely on an earlier case.
members.conclusion: The Court’s majority dismissed both appeals and upheld the enhanced compensation, finding no error in the valuation basis and no basis to regard the award as excessive or exorbitant.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and land_near_growing_town and (substantial_surrounding_development or nearby_building_activity) and reliable_comparable_sale_available

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.land_near_growing_town: The acquired land is situated near a town that is growing or developing.
predicates.substantial_surrounding_development: Buildings, roads, or other development are present around the acquired land.
predicates.nearby_building_activity: Building activity has occurred on or near the acquired land.
predicates.reliable_comparable_sale_available: A genuine sale of nearby or contiguous land with similar advantages provides a reliable guide to value.

members.legal_issue: A claim that acquired land was semi-developed or had substantial development potential must be supported by evidence.
material_facts: The claimants asserted that the area was semi-developed and had substantial potentiality.
The claimants did not examine witnesses to support those assertions.
members.legal_principle: The claimant bears the burden of adducing sufficient and cogent material to establish market value and relevant land characteristics. The court applied the valuation principles in Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat and Basavva v. Special Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: The court could not accept that the area was semi-developed or had substantial potentiality on the evidence presented.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.claimant_asserts_development_or_potentia: The claimant asserts that the acquired land was developed, semi-developed, or had substantial development potential.
predicates.supporting_evidence_absent: The claimant adduces no evidence supporting the asserted development or potentiality.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for extinguished property rights assessed at market value includes the additional amount payable for compulsory acquisition, subject to applicable statutory limits and exceptions.
material_facts: The holders sought an additional 15% on market-value compensation for rights extinguished under the provision concerning property vesting in the Government.
The compensation provision required the Collector to make an award in the manner prescribed by the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The High Court had allowed the additional amount for some categories of market-value compensation, and the State and the holders challenged aspects of that ruling.
members.legal_principle: Under section 7(1)(b) of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, the Collector makes an award in the manner prescribed by section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and is guided by sections 23 and 24 of that Act. Section 23(2) provides an additional 15% on market value for compulsory acquisition. The additional amount applies where the award is based on market value, subject to the limits and exceptions in section 7(1)(b)(i)–(iii); section 14(2), by contrast, refers to section 23(1) and excludes section 23(2).
members.conclusion: The holders were entitled to the 15% additional amount where compensation was based on market value, subject to the statutory conditions and exceptions; the High Court's direction was modified accordingly.

predicates.appeal_concerning_compensation_for_extin: An appeal concerns an award of compensation for property rights extinguished by a compulsory change in ownership or control.
predicates.compensation_based_on_market_value: The compensation award is assessed on the basis of the property's market value.
predicates.no_applicable_statutory_exception: No applicable limit or exception excludes the additional amount from the market-value award.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must be determined when final awards exist for comparable land acquired earlier and later.
material_facts: The land in the acquisitions under appeal came from the same block as land acquired under an earlier and a later notification.
The earlier acquisition's compensation award was finally determined, as was the later acquisition's award.
The court found the land to be of the same quality and in the same area as the land covered by those comparator awards.
The court considered the market value to have changed little between the two acquisitions under appeal.
The lower courts had awarded compensation below the amount the Supreme Court considered appropriate.
members.legal_principle: In a Land Acquisition Act, 1894 compensation appeal, final awards for land of the same quality in the same area can provide evidence of market value; where the land's value at the relevant time lies between the values established by earlier and later acquisitions, the court may estimate an intermediate value. The court recognized that valuation may involve conjecture because it depends on imponderables. The judgment refers to Sections 4 and 6 for the acquisition notifications and Section 18 for the compensation references, but cites no earlier cases or specific substantive valuation provision.
members.conclusion: The court fixed the market value for the acquisitions under appeal by taking the mean of the final comparator values and enhanced the compensation accordingly.

rule.if: acquisition_compensation_appeal and same_area_comparator_awards and comparator_awards_final and same_land_quality and relevant_value_between_comparators

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.same_area_comparator_awards: Awards exist for other land acquired from the same area as the land under appeal.
predicates.comparator_awards_final: The comparator awards have become final.
predicates.same_land_quality: The court finds the comparator land to be of the same quality as the land under appeal.
predicates.relevant_value_between_comparators: The court finds that the land's value at the relevant time lies between the values established by the comparator awards.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must account for its reasonably foreseeable potential for more valuable use, not only its actual agricultural use on the valuation date.
material_facts: The land was agricultural when acquired, but the evidence showed buildings and residential quarters on parts of it, and the acquisition itself was for quarters for company workers.
The land abutted roads, was near existing residential colonies and a factory, and evidence showed that nearby lands had been sold as house sites.
The Reference Court considered the evidence and fixed compensation at a higher rate than the Land Acquisition Officer; the High Court treated the land as agricultural and reduced the valuation.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as of the relevant notification date and includes the value of a better use for which the land is reasonably capable of being used in the immediate or near future. Potentiality is assessed from the land’s condition, situation, use, access, amenities, proximity to developed areas, and prospects of development. The acquisition’s purpose is also relevant, while advantages arising solely from carrying out the acquisition scheme are excluded. The Court relied on P. Ram Reddy v. Land Acquisition Officer, Hyderabad Urban Development Authority; State of Orissa v. Brij Lal Misra; Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat; Attar Singh v. Union of India; Avinash Dhavaji Naik v. State of Maharashtra; Atma Singh v. State of Haryana; and Nelson Fernandes v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, South Goa.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in disregarding the evidence of the land’s advantages and building potential. The Reference Court’s valuation was upheld.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and (evidence_of_existing_buildings or evidence_of_nearby_house_site_sales) and land_is_near_residential_development and land_has_road_access and acquisition_purpose_supports_development_use

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The case concerns compensation for land taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.evidence_of_existing_buildings: Evidence shows that buildings or residential quarters existed on the acquired land.
predicates.evidence_of_nearby_house_site_sales: Evidence shows that nearby land was sold or used as house sites.
predicates.land_is_near_residential_development: The acquired land is near existing residential development.
predicates.land_has_road_access: The acquired land abuts or is accessible from a road.
predicates.acquisition_purpose_supports_development: The purpose for which the land was acquired supports the conclusion that it was suitable for a more developed use.
predicates.reference_court_market_valuation_upheld: The valuation fixed by the court determining compensation is upheld.

members.legal_issue: Market value of acquired land must be estimated objectively using reliable evidence that reflects the land’s condition and potential value at the relevant time.
material_facts: The acquired land was in a developed area, and the evidence included a lease of nearby land and a sale of adjoining land.
The sale relied on by the High Court concerned land farther away and involved leasehold rights; the Court considered it an unsuitable comparator.
The rent under the acquired land’s earlier lease had been fixed years before the valuation date at a concessionary rate for the use made of the land.
The nearby lease and sale provided usable valuation evidence, but required adjustments for the difference in parcel size and other relevant features.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 23 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is the price a willing seller could reasonably expect from a willing buyer, assessed objectively as of the relevant valuation date and taking account of potential value. The Court may consider expert opinion, bona fide sale prices for the acquired or suitably comparable nearby land, and capitalised actual or immediately prospective profits; these methods are not exhaustive, and more than one may be used where necessary. The Court relied on Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore v. T. Adinarayan Setty, which identified the principal valuation methods.
members.conclusion: The Court set the market value at a reasonable estimate based on the nearby lease and sale, with appropriate adjustments, rather than the High Court’s more distant sale or the outdated rent. Compensation was fixed at the resulting rate, with statutory solatium and interest as specified in the decree.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and (nearby_comparable_sale_evidence and nearby_comparable_rental_evidence) and (distant_sale_is_unreliable or earlier_rent_does_not_reflect_current_value)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.nearby_comparable_sale_evidence: The parties presented evidence of a sale of nearby land that could be compared with the acquired land, subject to adjustments.
predicates.nearby_comparable_rental_evidence: The parties presented rental evidence for nearby land that could assist in estimating the acquired land’s value.
predicates.distant_sale_is_unreliable: The sale used as a valuation comparator concerned land materially farther away or otherwise insufficiently comparable.
predicates.earlier_rent_does_not_reflect_current_va: The rent for the acquired land was fixed earlier and did not reflect its value at the relevant valuation time.

members.legal_issue: A comparable sale price may be adjusted for the period before acquisition when evidence supports an increase in value due to the land’s potentiality.
material_facts: A comparable sale deed recorded a price of Rs. 15.40 per square yard before the acquisition proceedings.
There was a four-year interval between that sale and the acquisition proceedings.
Evidence showed high potential for building construction, including nearby development and facilities.
The High Court’s annual increase of 15% was not unreasonable, but it had to be applied to the comparable sale price and for the full interval.
members.legal_principle: In determining market value under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a comparable sale price may be increased to account for the passage of time where the evidence supports an increase based on the land’s potentiality. The increase must be calculated from the comparable sale price and for the full period between the sale and acquisition.
members.conclusion: The Court applied a 15% annual increase to the comparable sale price for four years and fixed the land value at Rs. 24.64 per square yard.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and comparable_sale_predates_acquisition and material_gap_between_sale_and_acquisition and evidence_of_high_development_potential

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.comparable_sale_predates_acquisition: A sale of comparable land occurred before the acquisition being valued.
predicates.material_gap_between_sale_and_acquisitio: A material period elapsed between the comparable sale and the acquisition.
predicates.evidence_of_high_development_potential: Evidence showed that the land had strong potential for development.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must reflect its market value on the relevant notification date, assessed using comparable evidence while accounting for differences in size, access, location, and development potential.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a tract of a little over fifty acres, used for agricultural purposes and lacking access to the main road.
The land had potential for urbanisation but was separated from the town’s expansion by a railway line and was in a less advantageous position than nearby land acquired for a grain market.

The sale instances relied on by the courts below concerned very small plots on the main road and occurred after the notification; the sale made about three and a half years after the notification was too distant in time to be used.

A nearby sale made about a year after the notification indicated a lower rate for a small, favourably situated plot, while an award for the grain-market land reflected land with better access and potential.
The Supreme Court reduced the compensation to a rate it considered just and fair in light of the acquired land’s disadvantages and the available valuation evidence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15, 23 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 guide the determination of compensation, with market value assessed as of the date of publication of the notification under Section 4. Comparable sales may inform that value, but land with special frontage or access is not to be treated as equivalent to interior or undeveloped land, and small plots fetching higher prices should not be compared without adjustment to a large tract. Periyar and Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala, AIR 1990 SC 2192, was relied on for those comparison principles. The compensation must be just both to the owner and to the public that pays it, and the Act is neither a means to deprive an owner of market value nor a source of fancifully inflated compensation.
members.conclusion: The compensation was reduced to Rs. 80,000 per acre; the existing conditions for solatium and interest remained unchanged.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_determinat: The proceeding requires determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_is_large_tract: The acquired property is a large tract rather than a small individual plot.
predicates.comparable_sales_are_small_advantaged_pl: The proposed sale comparisons concern small plots with better access or another locational advantage than the acquired land.
predicates.nearby_award_land_has_better_access_or_p: A nearby property used as a valuation reference had better access or development potential than the acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_has_less_access_or_potenti: The acquired land has poorer access or development potential than the properties used as valuation references.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land with non-agricultural potential must reflect comparable land values and its reasonably prospective use, with deductions tailored to actual development needs rather than applied mechanically.
material_facts: The land was acquired for industrial development and had non-agricultural and commercial potential; mineral deposits in the land were used as raw material for cement manufacture.

The Reference Court relied on a valuation adopted for comparable land in the same village, but deducted development charges, waiting-period charges and conversion expenses, and also reduced the value to account for the earlier acquisition notification.
The comparable land had been acquired for industrial development and was used for a similar industrial purpose, although its acquisition notification was later and the land was some distance away.

The acquired land was used for mineral extraction and factory infrastructure, and the Court found that development activities of the kind that would justify development-charge deductions were not involved.
The landowners appealed against the compensation fixed by the Reference Court and affirmed by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires market value to be assessed by reference to what a willing purchaser would pay a willing seller, considering both comparable land values and uses to which the land is reasonably capable of being put in the future. The Court relied on Raja Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Vizagapatam, whose principle that potential future uses may inform value was reiterated by this Court. It distinguished Chandrashekar v. Land Acquisition Officer and Another, which concerned cumulative deductions for development, de-escalation and waiting periods on different facts. Statutory benefits were awarded under Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), 28 and 27 of the Land Acquisition Act.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the landowners' appeal and re-determined the compensation at a higher market value, using the comparable land value with incidental and de-escalation deductions but without a development-charge deduction. It also awarded the applicable statutory solatium, additional amount, interest and costs.

predicates.appeal_seeks_review_of_compensation_for_: A landowner appealed a court determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_land_has_similar_potential_an: The evidence showed land with similar potential and a similar intended or actual use, suitable to inform the acquired land's market value.
predicates.acquired_land_has_no_comparable_developm: The acquired land was used for a purpose that did not require the development works that would justify a development-charge deduction.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired market land must reflect relevant comparable sales and evidence of the land’s location, development, and rising prices.
material_facts: The acquired property was market land that had been leased out.
Two nearby sales of leasehold rights were considered relevant; the High Court had averaged their prices when fixing compensation.
Witnesses described increasing land prices, nearby shops and houses, new roads, and growth in the locality.
The Supreme Court found the acquired land similar to land in connected appeals for which it upheld a higher compensation rate.
members.legal_principle: Market value is assessed from relevant comparable transactions together with evidence bearing on the land’s location, development, and price trends; the nature of the interests sold is relevant when comparing sale prices. The Court also relied on its valuation of similar land in connected appeals. The acquisition was notified under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; the judgment does not cite a separate valuation provision or an earlier reported case.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s appeal was allowed and compensation was fixed at Rs. 15,000 per Bigha, with an additional 15% for compulsory acquisition and 6% annual interest on the additional amount from possession until payment. The Collector’s appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: acquisition_compensation_appeal and market_land and comparable_leasehold_sales and locality_developing_and_prices_rising and similar_to_land_with_higher_approved_valuation

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: A party appealed the compensation fixed for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.market_land: The acquired land was used as market land and was being leased out.
predicates.comparable_leasehold_sales: Evidence included nearby sales of leasehold interests considered relevant to valuing the acquired land.
predicates.locality_developing_and_prices_rising: Evidence showed that the locality was developing and that land prices there were increasing.
predicates.similar_to_land_with_higher_approved_val: The court found the acquired land similar to other acquired land for which it had upheld a higher valuation.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for surplus land is determined by the rate in force on the date the land vests under the applicable notification.
material_facts: The notification declaring the respondent’s land surplus was published after an amendment had reduced the compensation multiple.
The later enactment was held to preserve vesting from the date of that notification, rather than from the earlier date attributed to vesting by the intervening amendment.
The Court therefore treated the land as having vested after the reduced compensation rate had come into force.
members.legal_principle: Under section 18(3) of the principal Act, as restored by the later enactment, vesting occurred on publication of the section 18(1) notification. Section 50 and Schedule III governed compensation, and the amendment to Schedule III reduced the applicable multiple from nine times to two times of net annual income with effect from its commencement. Because vesting occurred after that change, the reduced rate applied.
members.conclusion: Compensation was to be calculated using the reduced rate in force on the notification date, rather than the earlier rate.

predicates.surplus_land_compensation_dispute: The dispute concerns the amount payable for land acquired as surplus under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.vesting_occurs_on_notification_date: The land vests in the government on the date its surplus notification is published.
predicates.notification_date_follows_compensation_r: The notification is published after the compensation rate applicable to surplus land has been reduced.

members.legal_issue: Comparable acquisition evidence, rising prices, road access, and development potential justify enhancing the assessed market value, subject to a deduction for development costs.
material_facts: The claimants’ land was near a main road and had access to roads laid between the date of an earlier comparable acquisition and the later acquisition.
An earlier award for nearby land acquired for road widening assessed its value at six rupees per square yard.
The courts below had found that land prices were steadily rising, but had rejected further enhancement because the land lay inside the main road.
The land was found to have potential for housing development, and the Court applied a one-third deduction for development charges.
members.legal_principle: Market value may be assessed by reference to a comparable earlier acquisition, adjusted for the rise in prices and the acquired land’s access and development potential. Where development is needed, a deduction may be made for development charges. The Court relied on the earlier award, Exhibit P-7, but cited no statutory provision or earlier judicial decision for this valuation method.
members.conclusion: The Court enhanced the gross market value to eight rupees per square yard and applied a one-third deduction for development charges, holding the claimants entitled to the resulting amount.

rule.if: compensation_valuation_appeal and comparable_nearby_acquisition and rising_land_prices and (road_access or development_potential)

predicates.compensation_valuation_appeal: The case is an appeal concerning the valuation of land acquired for compensation.
predicates.comparable_nearby_acquisition: An earlier acquisition of nearby land provides a comparable valuation reference.
predicates.rising_land_prices: The evidence or findings show that land prices rose over the relevant period.
predicates.road_access: The acquired land had access to roads or comparable transport facilities.
predicates.development_potential: The acquired land had potential for development that could affect its market value.

members.legal_issue: Market compensation for acquired land must reflect its future development potential while accounting for differences between land categories and the comparability of other transactions.
material_facts: The acquired land was close to a developed planned city, a lake, and a railway track, and was within a zone frozen for future development.
Although acquired for brick kilns and not immediately usable for residential or commercial purposes, the land had potential for such future development.
The acquired land included cultivated, rainfed, and waste categories, which did not all warrant the same valuation.
The motor-market and housing-complex lands relied on by the claimants differed in location or advantages and did not provide directly comparable prices.
The Reference Court had awarded an increased value for cultivated land, and the Court considered evidence of rising land prices and the circumstances as a whole.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires just and reasonable compensation based on market value. Comparable sales may assist where the properties share similar advantages, but dissimilar properties do not furnish directly comparable prices. Potential for future development may inform a pragmatic assessment of market value even where the land cannot immediately be used for the potential purpose; the assessment must account for the land’s situation and category and need not rest on speculation. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The Court partly enhanced compensation, fixing different market values for the cultivated and rainfed categories while leaving the waste-land valuation undisturbed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and future_development_potential and distinct_land_categories and (reliable_comparable_sales_unavailable or comparator_lands_dissimilar)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.future_development_potential: The acquired land’s location and surrounding development give it potential for future use beyond its immediate use at acquisition.
predicates.distinct_land_categories: The acquired land consists of categories with different characteristics or advantages.
predicates.reliable_comparable_sales_unavailable: The record contains no reliable proved sales of sufficiently similar land from which market value can be directly assessed.
predicates.comparator_lands_dissimilar: The other lands relied on for comparison differ materially in location or advantages from the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Compensation must reflect the land's market value at the acquisition-notice date and account for its condition and the scale of the acquisition, rather than later development or an unsupported square-foot rate.
material_facts: The land was acquired to drain flood water from a low-lying area and was not developed at the relevant time.
The Collector's assessment used a later valuation and a rate per square foot, which the Court found unsupported as a basis for compensation.
The acquisition covered a large area, for which valuation by yardage and a deduction for development requirements were relevant.
A later purchase price for the property was placed before the Court, and subsequent development of the area was also discussed.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires market value to be determined as at publication of the Section 4(1) notification. Under Section 24, subsequent development is irrelevant to that determination. For a large acquisition, valuation should be on a yardage basis rather than a square-foot basis, with a deduction for land required for development. A sale may provide a basis for valuation if it is a bona fide transaction between willing parties in normal market conditions and was not intended to inflate the value of the acquired land.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the Collector's valuation and fixed total compensation at Rs. 25,000, with 15% solatium and 6% interest from possession until deposit, rather than remitting the matter for fresh valuation.

rule.if: compensation_appeal and acquired_land_was_undeveloped_at_notice_date and large_area_acquired and later_development_relied_on

predicates.compensation_appeal: An appeal concerns the amount of compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_was_undeveloped_at_notice_: The land had not been developed when the acquisition notice was published.
predicates.large_area_acquired: The acquisition covered a large tract of land.
predicates.later_development_relied_on: A party relies on development occurring after the acquisition notice to support the land's market value.

members.legal_issue: The deduction from the value of undeveloped or agricultural land for development costs must reflect the circumstances of the land and cannot be fixed by a universal formula.
material_facts: The acquired land formed part of a large tract intended for development as a housing scheme.
The claimants relied in part on development in the surrounding area, but the record did not establish that the acquired land itself was fully developed or required no further work.
The land required development works such as internal roads and civic infrastructure, while nearby development could reduce the extent of necessary work.
The appellate court had applied a deduction of 25 percent, and the Supreme Court substituted a one-third deduction while sustaining the assessed market value.
members.legal_principle: For agricultural or undeveloped land with potential for housing or commercial use, a deduction is normally made for development costs, commonly one-third, but the appropriate deduction varies with the land’s nature, location, extent, development expenditure, and land needed for roads and amenities. Adjoining a developed area does not by itself make the acquired land developed; a claimant asserting that no development is needed must establish that by evidence. The Court relied on Kasturi v. State of Haryana and also referred to Kiran Tandon v. Allahabad Development Authority, State of West Bengal v. Kedarnath Rajgarhia Charitable Trust Estate, and V. Hanumantha Reddy v. Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: The deduction of 25 percent was replaced with a one-third deduction, and the compensation entitlements were to be recalculated accordingly.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and undeveloped_land_with_development_potential and large_area_requires_infrastructure and fully_developed_status_not_proved

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.undeveloped_land_with_development_potent: The acquired land is agricultural or undeveloped land with potential for residential or commercial use.
predicates.large_area_requires_infrastructure: The size and condition of the acquired area require development works or provision of roads and civic infrastructure.
predicates.fully_developed_status_not_proved: The party claiming that the land is already fully developed has not established that claim with evidence.

members.legal_issue: The appropriate deduction for development expenses must reflect the characteristics of the acquired land and the comparable sale evidence.
material_facts: About 101 acres of land were acquired, and the acquired land was not fully developed.
The landowners relied on a sale of a small parcel of 19 guntas; it had two-road access and was developed, features absent from the acquired land.
The landowners produced no comparable sales of large parcels sold by the acre.
The Reference Court deducted 50% for development expenses. The High Court reduced the deduction to 25% without giving a sufficient reason for doing so.
The market value found by the Reference Court and upheld by the High Court was not challenged before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed on the relevant statutory parameters. Chimanlal Hargovinddas v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Poona & Anr. (1988) 3 SCC 751 sets out that comparable sale prices must be adjusted for relevant plus and minus factors, including the size and development of the land, using a common-sense assessment rather than a rigid rule. Union of India v. Raj Kumar Baghal Singh (Dead) Through Legal Representatives & Ors. (2014) 10 SCC 422 reiterates those principles. Trishala Jain & Anr. v. State of Uttaranchal & Anr. (2011) 6 SCC 47 and Vithal Rao & Anr. v. Special Land Acquisition Officer (2017) 8 SCC 558 support making a fact-dependent deduction for development expenses, including when small-parcel sales are used to value a large tract, and using reasonable guesswork where appropriate. The deduction depends on the nature and area of the land, its state of development, and the purpose of acquisition.
members.conclusion: The Reference Court was justified in deducting 50% for development expenses. The High Court's reduction to 25% was set aside, and the Reference Court's award was restored.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and large_acquired_tract and acquired_land_not_fully_developed and no_comparable_large_parcel_sales and benchmark_is_small_parcel and benchmark_has_advantages_absent_from_acquired_land and appellate_reduction_unreasoned

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.large_acquired_tract: The acquiring authority acquired a large tract of land.
predicates.acquired_land_not_fully_developed: The acquired land was not fully developed.
predicates.no_comparable_large_parcel_sales: The parties seeking compensation did not produce comparable sales of large parcels.
predicates.benchmark_is_small_parcel: The sale used as the valuation benchmark concerned a small parcel of land.
predicates.benchmark_has_advantages_absent_from_acq: The benchmark parcel was developed and had road-access advantages that the acquired land did not have.
predicates.appellate_reduction_unreasoned: The appellate court reduced the development deduction made by the lower court without giving a sufficient reason for the reduction.

members.legal_issue: Potential value for building use requires evidence of a contemporaneous market and reasonable possibility of that use, not merely municipal location or the purpose of acquisition.
material_facts: The lands were near a municipality and within its master plan, but were found to be interior agricultural lands with no neighbourhood development activity or upward price trend at the relevant time.
There was no reliable evidence of building activity, demand for building land, or a market for the lands’ immediate use as house sites.
The acquisition was intended to provide house sites, but that intended use did not establish existing potential value.
members.legal_principle: Potential value must be supported by evidence that, under market conditions prevailing on the notification date, there was demand and a market for the proposed use. Relevant evidence may include construction or development activity, nearby uses, amenities, and prospects of development. The land is not valued as if already developed; only a reasonable possibility of use existing at the relevant time may be considered. The Court distinguished Gulzara Singh v. State of Punjab, (1993) 4 SCC 245, and Inder Singh v. Union of India, (1993) 3 SCC 240, where evidence supported potential value.
members.conclusion: The lands were properly valued as agricultural land; the record did not establish potential value for building purposes.

rule.if: land_compensation_proceeding and land_is_agricultural and not contemporaneous_building_demand_evidence

predicates.land_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.land_is_agricultural: The land was being used and was found to be agricultural at the relevant time.
predicates.contemporaneous_building_demand_evidence: Evidence shows contemporaneous demand and a market for building use, such as nearby construction or development activity.

members.legal_issue: Compensation and statutory additions must be fixed by reference to the supported market value on the acquisition-notification date and the applicable statutory entitlements.
material_facts: The Court rejected the valuation methods relied on by the lower courts and found no other evidence establishing building potential.
The lands were treated as agricultural, and the record included the respective acquisition notifications and dates of possession.
The Court determined separate market values for the two acquisitions and awarded additional compensation, solatium, and interest.
members.legal_principle: Market value is determined as of the date of the Section 4(1) notification, applying Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and excluding considerations barred by Section 24. The Court applied Section 23(1-A) for additional compensation, Section 23(2) for solatium, and Section 28 for interest. The assessment must reflect the evidence of the land’s existing use and any proven potential value as of the notification date.
members.conclusion: The Court set the market value at Rs 65,000 per acre in the first acquisition and Rs 80,000 per acre in the second, awarded the applicable additional compensation, solatium, and interest, and set aside the lower courts’ decrees.

predicates.land_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.market_value_evidence_assessed_as_of_not: The evidence is assessed to determine the land’s market value as of the acquisition notification.
predicates.land_character_established: The evidence establishes the land’s existing character and any supported potential use.

members.legal_issue: The market value of compulsorily acquired land must be assessed by considering the land’s nature, present use, potential, location, and relationship to surrounding land and its uses.
material_facts: Land was compulsorily acquired for a railway project, and the appeal challenged the compensation awarded for it.
The Land Acquisition Officer treated the land as agricultural and awarded compensation at a lower rate than the District Court and High Court later assessed.
The record included a nearby award for other land, rental evidence for land used for timber depots, and a valuation of that land by capitalisation.
The Court considered the nature and present use of the acquired land, its potential, its location in relation to adjoining land, and the use of neighbouring land and its impact on the acquired land.
members.legal_principle: In assessing compensation for acquired land under the Land Acquisition Act, the court must take account of relevant circumstances, including the land’s nature, present use, capacity for higher potential, precise location in relation to adjoining land, and the use of neighbouring land and its impact on the acquired land. The judgment identifies no earlier case or specific provision as the basis for this valuation principle; it refers to the Act’s acquisition and reference proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Court increased the compensation for the acquired land above the amount awarded by the High Court, while maintaining the severance damages, solatium, and interest that the High Court had awarded.

predicates.compensation_appeal: An appellant challenges the amount of compensation awarded for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_valuation_depends_on_land_: The court assesses acquired land by considering its characteristics, use, potential, location, and the uses of neighbouring land and their impact.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsory requisition must account for the property's potential value when that value is supported by the available material.
material_facts: The premises were requisitioned for an indefinite period.
The intended user already had an office in a neighbouring building, making the requisitioned premises specially advantageous to that user and giving the owner greater bargaining power.
The arbitrator assessed an additional 10% for potential value and related factors, but the High Court rejected that addition without giving a reason.
members.legal_principle: The compensation principles under section 19 of the Defence of India Act are the same as those under section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Potentialities must be evaluated according to the circumstances and assessed as best as possible from the material available, without speculation. Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. The Revenue Divisional Officer (1939) L.R. 66 I.A. 104 was followed.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in disregarding the potential value; the principles for compensation under section 19 of the Defence of India Act are the same as those under section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, and potential value must be evaluated on the available material.

rule.if: requisition_compensation_proceeding and (special_advantage_to_intended_user or indefinite_requisition) and potential_value_supported_by_material and potential_value_excluded_without_reason

predicates.requisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for property taken by compulsory requisition.
predicates.special_advantage_to_intended_user: The intended user would gain a special advantage from using the property.
predicates.indefinite_requisition: The property was requisitioned for an indefinite period.
predicates.potential_value_supported_by_material: Material before the decision-maker supports a finding that the property's circumstances give it additional potential value.
predicates.potential_value_excluded_without_reason: A reviewing court excluded the property's potential value without giving a reason.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for land authorized for non-agricultural use may be assessed by reference to a supported agricultural-land value, conversion costs, and evidenced price movement rather than unadjusted small-plot prices.
material_facts: The acquired land had been authorized for non-agricultural use, while most surrounding acquired land was agricultural.
The High Court assessed agricultural land by reference to the evidence of a knowledgeable landowner who had sold plots in the area but claimed a lower value for his acquired land.
The High Court added the required conversion fine and an increase supported by documentary evidence when assessing land authorized for non-agricultural use.

The owners relied on evidence about higher prices for small plots and an alleged steep rise in prices, but the small plots were not comparable to large tracts and the evidence of the alleged rise was vague.
The Supreme Court found the High Court’s assessment reasonable and affirmed it, including the deduction for any unpaid conversion fine.
members.legal_principle: In assessing compensation under Sections 4(1) and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, the court may evaluate the land’s permitted use, the supported value of comparable agricultural land, required conversion costs, and price movements established by evidence. Prices for small plots and vague claims of price increases need not establish the value of larger tracts. No earlier case is cited.
members.conclusion: The compensation assessment for the land authorized for non-agricultural use was affirmed, as was the agricultural-land valuation used as its benchmark.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and conversion_authorized and agricultural_value_supported and conversion_cost_required and (small_plot_prices_not_comparable or price_rise_evidence_vague)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation assessed for acquired land.
predicates.conversion_authorized: The relevant land had been authorized for use beyond agricultural purposes.
predicates.agricultural_value_supported: Evidence from a knowledgeable person with experience selling land in the area supported the agricultural-land value used as a benchmark.
predicates.conversion_cost_required: A required cost was payable to convert the land to its authorized non-agricultural use.
predicates.small_plot_prices_not_comparable: The cited sale prices concerned small plots rather than comparable large tracts.
predicates.price_rise_evidence_vague: The evidence of a substantial rise in land prices did not reliably establish the relevant increase.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must reflect market value on the effective notice date, assessed using comparable transactions and acquisitions with appropriate regard to differences in size, location, and market movement.
material_facts: The High Court relied principally on two nearby acquisition awards, while also considering the differences in plot size, location, and timing.
The evidence showed that land prices were rising during the relevant period.
The company's land was closer to the main road, while the other claimant's land was farther from it.
members.legal_principle: Market value is determined as of the effective notice date. Comparable sale evidence and prior acquisition awards may guide valuation, with adjustments for differences such as size, location, and timing. The court considered the evidence of rising prices and the relative locations of the lands; no earlier case was cited for this valuation issue.
members.conclusion: The compensation was fixed at Rs. 9 per square yard for the company's land and Rs. 8 per square yard for the other claimant's land.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_market_evidence_available and land_prices_rising and acquired_parcels_differ_in_location

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.comparable_market_evidence_available: The record contains comparable sale transactions or acquisition awards that can inform the value of the acquired land.
predicates.land_prices_rising: Evidence in the record shows that land prices were increasing during the relevant period.
predicates.acquired_parcels_differ_in_location: The parcels being valued differ in location in a way that affects their relative market value.

members.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land must be assessed using relevant comparable sales while accounting for the land’s existing advantages and potential, but not advantages arising from the acquisition scheme.
material_facts: The dispute concerned compensation for acquired land in a land-acquisition proceeding.
The High Court considered sale transactions relied on by both sides, including transactions involving plots some distance from the acquired land.

The claimant’s other transactions involved small roadside plots sold after acquisition notification; the acquired land did not abut the road, and the High Court did not use those transactions as a safe criterion.
The High Court’s assessment included the acquired land’s potential value.
members.legal_principle: Under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is the price a willing purchaser would pay a willing seller, having regard to the land’s condition, existing advantages and potential possibilities when laid out advantageously, but excluding advantages due to the acquisition scheme. The vendor’s disinclination to sell and the purchaser’s urgent need to buy are disregarded. Sale transactions must be assessed for their relevance to the acquired land; small roadside plots sold by the claimant after notification were not a safe criterion in the circumstances, while transactions involving plots some distance away could not be excluded altogether merely for that reason. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s assessment of market value at Rs. 475 per katha was upheld; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and comparable_sale_transactions_available and (some_comparable_plots_are_distant or claimant_sold_small_roadside_plots_after_notice) and potential_use_considered

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining compensation for land acquired through a compulsory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.comparable_sale_transactions_available: The parties presented sale transactions as evidence of the acquired land’s market value.
predicates.some_comparable_plots_are_distant: Some plots involved in the sale transactions were situated at a distance from the acquired land.
predicates.claimant_sold_small_roadside_plots_after: The claimant sold small roadside plots after the land had been notified for acquisition, and those plots differed from the acquired land in location or suitability.
predicates.potential_use_considered: The court assessing value took account of the acquired land’s potential possibilities.
predicates.market_value_assessment_is_upheld: The market-value assessment is left undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: Potential building-site value must be established as existing at the notification date through evidence of the land's suitability and relevant market and development conditions, rather than inferred merely from its location within municipal limits or a later layout approval.
material_facts: The acquired land was within municipal limits, and the claimant argued that it had potential value as building sites.
The layout approval was obtained three years after publication of the acquisition notification.
There was no development in the neighbourhood at the relevant time.
The High Court found that the land did not have established potential value at the notification date and declined to determine compensation on a yardage basis.
members.legal_principle: Applying Acquisition Officer, Eluru v. Smt. Jasti Rohini and P. Ram Reddy v. Land Acquisition Officer, the court must assess potential value as a prudent willing purchaser would, in light of conditions at the notification date. Relevant matters include existing construction activity and comparable land conditions in the neighbourhood, suitability for building, access to amenities, and the possibility of obtaining layout approval; the assessment must account for prevailing market conditions.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to find that potential building-site value had not been established at the relevant date.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and building_site_potential_claimed and (potential_conditions_not_established_at_notification or no_neighbourhood_development and layout_approved_only_later)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.building_site_potential_claimed: A claimant seeks compensation on the basis that the acquired land had potential for use as building sites.
predicates.potential_conditions_not_established_at_: The evidence does not establish that the relevant potential conditions existed when the acquisition notification was published.
predicates.no_neighbourhood_development: There was no development in the neighbourhood at the relevant time.
predicates.layout_approved_only_later: Approval for a layout was obtained only after the acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: A compensation amount agreed between a claimant and an acquiring authority and accepted by the Collector may be evidence of the market value of land.
material_facts: The Collector’s order for other land recorded an agreed compensation figure reached by the claimant and the acquiring authority.
The Collector assessed other components of the property and accepted the agreed land value, although the Collector was not bound to accept the agreement.
The tribunal relied on that order in valuing adjacent land acquired at the same time.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Collector performs a statutory duty and must exercise judgment in assessing compensation; the Collector is not controlled by an agreement between interested parties. As explained in Samiullah v. Collector of Aligarh, that duty remains the Collector’s. Nevertheless, a compensation agreement accepted by the Collector may be good evidence of market value, and an order based on such an agreement is not rendered devoid of evidentiary value merely because it was consensual. The tribunal’s reliance on such evidence did not furnish a ground for interference under Section 77A of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911.
members.conclusion: The consent-based order had evidentiary value as evidence of market value, and the tribunal did not commit an error of law by relying on it.

rule.if: land_compensation_valuation and collector_considered_the_property and formal_compensation_agreement_reached and collector_accepted_agreement

predicates.land_compensation_valuation: The proceeding requires the market value of land acquired for public purposes to be assessed.
predicates.collector_considered_the_property: The Collector considered the property or its relevant components when making the compensation order.
predicates.formal_compensation_agreement_reached: The claimant and acquiring authority formally agreed on compensation for the land.
predicates.collector_accepted_agreement: The Collector accepted the agreement and made an order on its basis, while remaining free not to accept it.

members.legal_issue: Market value for acquired land must be determined from relevant comparable-sale evidence and appropriate adjustments, and a higher value for a later acquisition requires evidence supporting a substantial price increase.
material_facts: The Court considered sale instances relied on by both the acquiring authority and the landowners.
The High Court had accounted for the area that could actually be plotted, development costs, and other expenses.
The evidence did not show a fluctuation in prices of sufficiently high magnitude to justify a higher value for the later notification.
The Court adopted the average indicated by the sale instances and the plotted-area approach, and fixed compensation at Rs. 40 per square yard for both acquisitions.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as of the publication of the notification under Section 4(1), by reference to the price a willing seller might reasonably receive from a willing purchaser, without treating either as acting under compulsion. Potentiality must be assessed on available material rather than speculation. Comparable-sale evidence is most reliable when the transaction is within a reasonable time of the notification, bona fide, concerns the acquired or adjacent land, and relates to land with similar advantages: The Special Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore v. T. Adinarayan Setty. Sections 24 and 25 also govern matters excluded from consideration and the minimum compensation payable.
members.conclusion: The Court fixed compensation at Rs. 40 per square yard for both acquisitions and declined to award a higher rate for the later acquisition because the evidence did not establish a substantial price fluctuation.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and comparable_sale_evidence_considered and plotted_area_adjustment_supported and no_evidence_of_substantial_price_fluctuation

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_sale_evidence_considered: The court assesses sale transactions as evidence of the land's market value.
predicates.plotted_area_adjustment_supported: The evidence supports adjusting the valuation to account for the area that can actually be plotted and related costs.
predicates.no_evidence_of_substantial_price_fluctua: The evidence does not establish a substantial increase in prices that would justify a higher valuation for a later acquisition.

members.legal_issue: The first information report need not name every witness, and a witness’s testimony is not discredited merely because the witness was not named in that report.
material_facts: One eyewitness was not named in the first information report.
That eyewitness was injured and was related to a deceased person, and the High Court found the witness to be a natural witness of the occurrence.
The Court stated that the report’s purpose is to set the criminal law in motion and that the law does not require all witnesses to be named in it.
members.legal_principle: There is no requirement that the first information report name all witnesses; its object is to set the criminal law in motion. The Court cited no earlier case by name in stating this principle.
members.conclusion: The omission of the eyewitness’s name from the first information report did not justify rejecting the testimony.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_witness_testimo: The criminal proceeding relies on testimony from a witness to the occurrence.
predicates.witness_was_not_named_in_initial_report: The witness’s name was omitted from the initial report of the occurrence.
predicates.witness_was_a_natural_witness: The circumstances showed that the witness was naturally present at or able to observe the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: Minor, normal, or explainable discrepancies in testimony are not material discrepancies warranting rejection of the testimony.
material_facts: The witness’s evidence differed on details including who pressed the deceased to the ground, where the deceased was pressed, whether the fatal blow was delivered while he was standing or lying down, and the direction from which the blow was given.
The court regarded these differences as minor and natural, consistent with ordinary errors of observation or memory and the effects of shock and horror.
The medical evidence supported the witness’s account of an axe blow to the neck.
members.legal_principle: Witnesses may have normal discrepancies arising from errors of observation, memory, lapse of time, or mental disposition such as shock and horror. Material discrepancies are those that are not normal or expected of a normal person. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The discrepancies were not material and did not justify rejecting the witness’s evidence in its entirety.

predicates.criminal_evidence_assessment: The court is assessing testimony in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.testimony_contains_discrepancies: The witness’s account differs on some details of the occurrence.
predicates.discrepancies_are_minor_normal_or_explai: The differences concern details and are ordinary or explainable by observation, memory, lapse of time, or the witness’s mental state.

members.legal_issue: Credible eyewitness testimony may be accepted despite conflicting medical evidence when the medical opinion does not conclusively exclude the account and is unreliable or inadequately reasoned.
material_facts: The post-mortem report recorded no external or internal injuries and did not determine the cause of death.
The eyewitnesses consistently described a fatal assault, and the investigating officer and persons present at the inquest recorded injuries on the deceased’s body.
The Court found the eyewitness accounts reliable and the medical report deficient and in conflict with the other evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Kamaljit Singh v. State of Punjab, 2004 Cri LJ 28, minor variations between medical and ocular evidence do not displace the latter unless the medical evidence completely rules out the manner of injury described by eyewitnesses. Madan Gopal Kakad v. Naval Dubey (1992) 3 SCC 204 establishes that expert opinion assists the court but does not bind it; the court must assess the expert’s reasons and the other evidence. A serious contradiction may undermine the prosecution case, but an unreliable or perfunctory opinion does not automatically outweigh trustworthy eyewitness evidence.
members.conclusion: The medical report did not displace the credible eyewitness evidence, and the Court was entitled to rely on the eyewitness account.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and eyewitness_account_credible and medical_opinion_conflicts and medical_opinion_does_not_exclude_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_credible: The court finds the eyewitness account reliable and trustworthy.
predicates.medical_opinion_conflicts: The medical opinion differs from the eyewitness account.
predicates.medical_opinion_does_not_exclude_account: The medical opinion does not conclusively rule out the events described by the eyewitnesses.

members.legal_issue: Credible and corroborated eyewitness testimony is not rendered unreliable merely by the witnesses’ relationship or association with the deceased, explained injury discrepancies, or circumstances that do not establish that the first information report was lodged late.
material_facts: Three witnesses testified to the attack near the gate, and the Supreme Court found no cogent reason to disbelieve them; their accounts were mutually corroborative.
One witness was the father of a deceased person, and another jointly owned a car with a deceased person; the Court found these connections insufficient to discredit their testimony.

Some injuries were consistent with blunt force, although the accused were not shown to have blunt weapons; the testimony referred to brickbats at the scene and a blunt portion of a weapon that could have caused some injuries.
The delayed arrival of the report copy at the magistrate was explained by the difficulty in obtaining transport, and did not establish that the report had been lodged later than claimed.
The Court found the criticisms of a witness’s conduct, including changing clothes and not accompanying the injured person to hospital, insufficient to discredit his account.
members.legal_principle: A close relationship to a deceased person does not by itself discredit a witness; the Court observed that a close relative would normally be reluctant to spare the real assailants and falsely implicate others. Differences between the injuries and the weapons attributed to the accused do not necessarily make eyewitness testimony unreliable where the circumstances can explain those injuries. Delay in the magistrate’s receipt of a report copy does not necessarily prove that the report was lodged late. The Court applied the appellate-review principles stated in Section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and relied on Sheo Swarup v. The King Emperor, 61 I.A. 398; Satwant Singh v. State of Rajasthan; and Sohrab v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1972 (3) SCR 751.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness evidence was reliable, the High Court’s assessment of it disclosed no material infirmity, and the appeal was dismissed, leaving the convictions and sentences undisturbed.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction_after_acquittal_reversed and credible_corroborated_eyewitnesses and witness_connections_do_not_show_false_implication and injury_discrepancies_are_explained and report_delay_does_not_establish_late_lodging

predicates.appeal_from_conviction_after_acquittal_r: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction entered after a lower court acquitted the accused.
predicates.credible_corroborated_eyewitnesses: Eyewitnesses give accounts of the occurrence that corroborate one another and are found credible.
predicates.witness_connections_do_not_show_false_im: A witness’s relationship or association with a deceased person does not provide a cogent reason to infer false implication.
predicates.injury_discrepancies_are_explained: Differences between the injuries and the weapons attributed to the accused have an explanation consistent with the evidence.
predicates.report_delay_does_not_establish_late_lod: A delay in a report reaching an official does not, in the circumstances, establish that the report was lodged late.

members.legal_issue: Limited injuries consistent with an eyewitness account do not require rejection of that account unless the medical evidence is totally inconsistent with it.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses said one victim was dragged, but the medical evidence showed only two abrasions in the relevant area.
The Supreme Court held that the limited abrasions did not discredit the eyewitnesses’ account and that the prosecution evidence was not totally inconsistent with the medical evidence.
The Court distinguished Ram Narain v. State of Punjab on that basis.
members.legal_principle: Medical evidence may undermine eyewitness testimony where the two are totally inconsistent; the Court distinguished Ram Narain v. State of Punjab because the evidence in this case was not totally inconsistent with the medical findings.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness evidence could not be rejected merely because the medical evidence showed only two abrasions and did not establish the alleged manner of dragging.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and eyewitnesses_described_dragging and medical_findings_show_limited_injuries and medical_evidence_not_totally_inconsistent_with_eyewitness_account

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.eyewitnesses_described_dragging: Eyewitnesses described a victim being dragged during the incident.
predicates.medical_findings_show_limited_injuries: The medical findings showed only limited injuries relevant to the alleged dragging.
predicates.medical_evidence_not_totally_inconsisten: The medical findings did not make the eyewitness account impossible or wholly incompatible with the medical evidence.

members.legal_issue: Omission of details from an initial report does not by itself discredit eyewitness testimony when the omissions concern details and the report was made by an eyewitness.
material_facts: The initial report did not mention the alleged dragging of a victim or the victim’s alleged dying declaration.
The report was made by an eyewitness, and the omitted matters were details of the incident.
The Supreme Court held that the omissions did not discredit the eyewitness evidence.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the omitted matters as details and noted that the report was made by an eyewitness, making it unnecessary for the report to recount every part of the incident or a separate alleged dying declaration.
members.conclusion: The omissions from the initial report were of no consequence and did not require rejection of the eyewitness testimony.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.initial_report_made_by_eyewitness: The person who gave the initial report had witnessed the incident.
predicates.omitted_matters_are_details: The matters omitted from the initial report were details rather than facts that materially contradicted the reported account.

members.legal_issue: Discrepancies about collateral details do not justify rejecting eyewitness testimony when the core account is consistent.
material_facts: The witnesses differed about whether they and the deceased had left their hamlet on the day of the occurrence or a day earlier.
The witnesses testified about the events approximately seventeen months after the occurrence.
Their evidence was consistent on the substance of the prosecution account, and the defence had not cross-examined one witness about his whereabouts on the previous night.
members.legal_principle: Discrepancies about subsidiary facts or matters of detail may occur even in truthful testimony, particularly after a substantial passage of time. They are not ordinarily a ground for rejecting evidence when the witnesses generally agree about the substratum of the case.
