members.conclusion: The applications for impleadment were rejected.

predicates.appellate_impleadment_application: A person applies to be added as a party in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.predecessor_not_party_below: The applicant’s predecessor was not a party in the proceedings before the lower courts.
predicates.application_made_after_hearing_reserved: The application is made after the hearing is complete and the court has reserved its decision.

members.legal_issue: An objection to the competence of a statutory arbitration reference cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal against the decision on objections to the award when it was not raised at the reference stage.
material_facts: The parties appeared before the statutory arbitrator after the consolidation officer referred the title dispute.
The appellants did not object to the competence of the reference before the arbitrator.
They first challenged the reference because certain persons had not been joined when appealing the decision dismissing their objections to the award.
members.legal_principle: The court held that the proper stage for challenging the competence of a reference under section 12 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, is when the reference is made. An appellate court should not entertain that objection when it is raised for the first time later.
members.conclusion: The objection was raised too late and was properly rejected; it should have been raised when the reference was made.

predicates.award_objection_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning a decision on objections to a statutory arbitration award.
predicates.reference_competence_challenged: A party challenges whether the statutory arbitration reference was competent.
predicates.no_objection_at_reference: The challenging party did not raise that objection when the reference was made.
predicates.late_reference_objection_rejected: The objection to the reference is rejected as having been raised too late.

members.legal_issue: A legal question based on the pleadings and evidence may be raised for the first time in a second appeal, but a party cannot claim prejudice from a plea that was rejected and not appealed.
material_facts: In the second appeal, the opposing side raised a new contention about how the firm’s assets should be dealt with on dissolution.
The High Court rejected that contention, and the party that raised it did not appeal against that rejection.
members.legal_principle: A question of law arising from the pleadings and evidence may be raised for the first time before the High Court. Unlike Hardayal Gir v. Sohna Ram, where a new plea was accepted and prejudiced the opposing party, the plea here was rejected. Under Article 136, as discussed in Santakumari v. Lakshmi Amma Janaki Amma and Chandra Singh v. State of Rajasthan, the Court does not interfere absent grave injustice.
members.conclusion: The objection to the High Court considering the new contention failed; the contention had been rejected, and no appeal had been brought against that finding. A legal question grounded in the pleadings and evidence may be raised for the first time in a second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The challenged decision was made in a proceeding that was a second appeal.
predicates.record_based_legal_question: A party raised a legal question grounded in the pleadings and evidence already on the record.
predicates.plea_rejected_without_appeal: The court rejected the newly raised contention, and the party that raised it did not appeal that rejection.

members.legal_issue: A party may not raise in a further appeal an abatement objection that the party or its legal representatives knowingly and wilfully abandoned at the relevant stage of the earlier proceedings.
material_facts: The deceased claimant’s legal representatives knew of the death and knew they had been brought on record in the claimants’ appeal but not in the government appeal.
For about five years they did not seek dismissal of the government appeal on abatement grounds.
When the High Court heard both appeals, their counsel argued the merits without raising abatement.
After the High Court ruled against them, they raised abatement in seeking a certificate to appeal but did not seek review of the High Court’s judgment on that ground.
members.legal_principle: A plea of abatement is a defence that a legal representative may choose to raise or abandon. Abandonment cannot be inferred without clear, sufficient, and satisfactory evidence that the legal representative knew of the plea and wilfully abandoned it. A point of defence wilfully abandoned at the stage when it was material cannot later be revived at the party’s will. The Court distinguished Gaekwar Baroda State Railway v. Hafiz Habib-ul-Haq, Thakore Saheb Khanji Kashari Khanji v. Gulam Rosul Chandbhai, Punjab State v. Sardar Atma Singh, and State of Rajasthan v. Raghuraj Singh, which did not involve the same circumstances of wilful abandonment.
members.conclusion: The legal representatives wilfully abandoned the abatement objection in the High Court and could not revive it as a later, afterthought defence in the further appeal.

rule.if: further_appeal and abatement_objection_available and representatives_knew_of_objection and representatives_wilfully_abandoned_objection

predicates.further_appeal: A party seeks to raise an objection in an appeal following the proceeding in which the objection was available.
predicates.abatement_objection_available: The death of a party and failure to substitute that party’s legal representatives supplied a possible ground to seek dismissal for abatement.
predicates.representatives_knew_of_objection: The legal representatives knew the relevant circumstances and were aware, or were shown to be aware, that the abatement objection could be raised.
predicates.representatives_wilfully_abandoned_objec: The legal representatives deliberately proceeded on the merits without raising the objection at the relevant stage.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court need not entertain factual grounds that were not raised before the High Court and that would require a factual response or record not available on appeal.
material_facts: The challengers argued in the Supreme Court that the notification had not been issued by the Collector and that the required satisfaction of the Collector was absent.
Those grounds had not been argued before the High Court.
The Government would have had an opportunity to answer those factual claims below, and the Supreme Court lacked the resulting factual record.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain new grounds requiring factual answers where they had not been raised before the High Court and the appellate record lacked the facts needed to decide them. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this determination.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to allow the challengers to raise those grounds for the first time on appeal.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and grounds_not_raised_below and grounds_require_factual_response and appellate_record_lacks_relevant_facts

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal from a lower court decision.
predicates.grounds_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the grounds before the lower court.
predicates.grounds_require_factual_response: The grounds would require the opposing side to provide a factual answer.
predicates.appellate_record_lacks_relevant_facts: The appellate record does not contain the facts needed to decide the grounds.

members.legal_issue: A contention against civil court jurisdiction cannot be raised in a later appeal when the lower courts decided it and it was not challenged in the intervening High Court appeal.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court decided the jurisdiction issue against the respondent.
The respondent did not challenge that decision in the High Court.
The respondent attempted to raise the jurisdiction issue in the Supreme Court appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule of appellate procedure that a party may not raise at a later appellate stage a lower-court ruling that the party did not challenge in the intervening appeal.
members.conclusion: The respondent could not raise the jurisdiction contention at that stage.

predicates.later_appeal_proceeding: A party sought to raise an issue in an appeal following an intervening appellate decision.
predicates.lower_courts_decided_jurisdiction_issue: The lower courts had decided the jurisdiction issue against the party seeking to raise it later.
predicates.jurisdiction_issue_not_challenged_in_int: The party did not challenge that decision in the intervening appeal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court will not entertain a contention that was not raised before the court below.
material_facts: On appeal, counsel for the transferees sought to challenge the order restoring the property on the ground that they had not been heard before it was made.
That contention had not been raised in the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The court declined to consider a contention raised for the first time on appeal when it had not been taken in the High Court.
members.conclusion: The court did not permit the contention to be raised at the appellate stage.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is before a court deciding an appeal from a lower court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_before_lower_court: A party advances a contention on appeal that was not raised before the lower court.

members.legal_issue: Persons who were not parties to the lower-court appeal cannot be added as respondents to a further appeal without permission, and their names may be struck from the record.
material_facts: Several relatives were added as respondents to the petition of appeal in the Supreme Court.
Those persons had not been parties to the appeal in the High Court.
No order permitting their joinder in the Supreme Court appeal had been obtained, and the appellant did not object to striking their names.
members.legal_principle: A person who was not a party to the appeal below cannot be joined as a respondent in the further appeal without an order permitting joinder.
members.conclusion: The names of those respondents were struck from the record.

predicates.further_appeal: A party filed a further appeal from a lower-court appellate decision.
predicates.person_not_party_to_lower_appeal: A person named as a respondent in the further appeal had not been a party to the appeal in the lower court.
predicates.no_permission_for_joinder: No court order permitting that person's joinder in the further appeal had been obtained.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider new pleas that were not raised in the lower courts and do not present pure questions of law.
material_facts: During the appeal, the judgment debtor sought to advance pleas that had not been raised before either the executing court or the High Court.
The proposed pleas did not raise pure questions of law.
members.legal_principle: The court declined to consider pleas not raised in the lower courts where those pleas did not raise pure questions of law. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The court declined to allow the judgment debtor to advance the new pleas.

predicates.appeal_from_execution_proceeding: The matter before the court was an appeal arising from an execution proceeding.
predicates.plea_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The party had not advanced the plea before the lower courts.
predicates.plea_not_pure_question_of_law: The plea required consideration beyond a pure question of law.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to entertain a statutory-amendment argument that was not raised in the court below or preserved in the appeal materials.
material_facts: The manager argued in the Supreme Court that an amendment restricting post-decree interest prevented interest being awarded on an aggregate that included interest.
The argument had not been made before the High Court and was not raised in the grounds seeking the appeal or in the statement of case.
The Supreme Court noted that the amendment's applicability and potential effect on substantive rights would require consideration, but declined to permit the new argument.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural principle that an appellate court may refuse to consider a point not raised below or preserved for appeal. It did not decide the amendment's applicability or whether it operated retrospectively.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the amendment argument because it had not been raised earlier or properly preserved.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.amendment_argument_not_raised_below: The party did not present the statutory-amendment argument to the court below.
predicates.amendment_argument_not_preserved: The party did not include the argument in the appeal grounds or other appeal materials identified by the court.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider a mixed question of fact and law raised for the first time on appeal when it was not properly pleaded or raised below and consideration would prejudice the opposing party.
material_facts: The tenant sought to argue that the ejectment proceeding was not available because of an asserted defect concerning the tenant’s title and the type of proceeding used.
The written statement contained only a general assertion that the proceeding was not maintainable, without setting out the point in detail.
The point was not raised in the earlier writ proceedings, the grounds of appeal, or the stated points for decision.
The court considered the point to involve both fact and law and found that considering it at that stage could prejudice the opposing party.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law that is not dependent on disputed facts and goes to the root of jurisdiction may be raised for the first time on appeal, but a mixed question of fact and law that was not properly raised below need not be entertained, particularly where doing so would prejudice the other party. The appeal was considered under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The court declined to consider the contention for the first time on appeal.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and contention_not_properly_raised_below and contention_depends_on_facts_and_law and considering_contention_would_prejudice_opponent

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party asks an appellate court to consider a contention in an appeal.
predicates.contention_not_properly_raised_below: The party did not plead or argue the contention adequately in the proceedings below.
predicates.contention_depends_on_facts_and_law: Deciding the contention requires consideration of both factual matters and legal rules.
predicates.considering_contention_would_prejudice_o: Considering the contention for the first time on appeal would prejudice the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to entertain new grounds that a party failed to raise despite repeated opportunities to disclose its position in the proceedings below.
material_facts: The authority had repeated opportunities in the High Court to disclose the policies governing its demands and to clarify its position.
The authority did not adequately comply with those directions and did not distinguish the examples relied on by the High Court.
It sought to distinguish those examples and raise related grounds for the first time on appeal.
members.legal_principle: A party that failed to disclose its policy or raise relevant distinctions despite repeated opportunities in the court below should not be permitted to introduce those grounds for the first time on appeal. The Court relied on the procedural history of the case and the authority’s failure to comply with the High Court’s opportunities and directions.
members.conclusion: The authority should not be given an opportunity to raise those new grounds on appeal.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and party_had_repeated_opportunities_below and party_failed_to_disclose_relevant_position and new_ground_raised_first_on_appeal

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision made after litigation in a lower court.
predicates.party_had_repeated_opportunities_below: The party received repeated opportunities in the lower court to state its position or provide relevant information.
predicates.party_failed_to_disclose_relevant_positi: The party did not adequately disclose its relevant policy or factual position despite those opportunities.
predicates.new_ground_raised_first_on_appeal: The party sought to rely on a ground or distinction that it had not raised in the lower court.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should not finally decide issues that the trial court did not reach without addressing whether a party was denied an opportunity to present evidence and thereby prejudiced.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the pre-emption application solely because it considered the land agricultural and the civil court therefore without jurisdiction.
The first appellate court found the land non-agricultural but decided the pre-emption application on its merits instead of remanding the untried issues.
The Supreme Court considered it possible that the appellant had sought to lead evidence on other contentions and had been denied that opportunity, causing prejudice.
members.legal_principle: In the interests of justice, where the trial court has decided only a preliminary jurisdiction question and the appellate court has decided untried merits issues, the higher court should examine whether a party was denied an opportunity to present evidence and suffered prejudice. The appropriate course may be to remand the issues or call for findings. No procedural provision or earlier case is cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside and the matter remanded to it to determine whether other issues had been raised, whether an opportunity to lead evidence on them had been sought and denied, and whether that denial caused prejudice. If so, the High Court could order a trial-court decision on those issues or obtain findings from the trial court while retaining the matter.

rule.if: appeal_from_preemption_proceeding and trial_court_decided_only_jurisdiction and appellate_court_decided_untried_merits and possible_denial_of_evidence_opportunity

predicates.appeal_from_preemption_proceeding: The matter is an appeal arising from a proceeding seeking pre-emption of a property sale.
predicates.trial_court_decided_only_jurisdiction: The trial court dismissed the proceeding after deciding only whether it had jurisdiction.
predicates.appellate_court_decided_untried_merits: The appellate court decided the merits of issues that the trial court had not considered, rather than remanding them.
predicates.possible_denial_of_evidence_opportunity: A party may have sought to present evidence on the untried issues and may have been denied that opportunity.

members.legal_issue: A damages objection not pursued in the intermediate appeals and not raised in the appellant's statement of case need not be entertained at the final appellate stage.
material_facts: The trial court awarded damages despite noting that no witness had testified about damages and that the claimant's counsel had not argued the point.
The appellants did not challenge the damages award in either intermediate appeal, and their statement of case in the Supreme Court disclosed no grievance about it.
members.legal_principle: The Court did not consider it justified to permit the objection to be raised at the final appellate stage after it had not been pursued in the intermediate appeals or stated as a grievance in the case presented to the Court.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the damages objection at that stage.

predicates.final_appeal_challenges_damages: A party raised an objection to a damages award in a final appeal.
predicates.damages_objection_not_raised_in_intermed: The party did not challenge the damages award in the intermediate appellate proceedings.
predicates.no_damages_grievance_in_appellate_case: The party's statement of case in the final appeal did not identify the damages award as a grievance.

members.legal_issue: The government may not raise for the first time on appeal that an urgent acquisition was unauthorized because the land was not waste or arable when it did not raise that ground before the court below.
material_facts: The government issued a notification invoking the urgent acquisition power, which could be exercised only for waste or arable land.
The notification did not state that the land was waste or arable.
The government had not contended before the Judicial Commissioner that the land was not waste or arable or that the notification was unauthorized, but raised that contention on appeal.
members.legal_principle: The court stated that the powers under sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, may be exercised only when the land is waste or arable. Because the government had not challenged the notification on that ground before the Judicial Commissioner, it could not raise the contention for the first time on appeal. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: It was not open to the government to contend for the first time on appeal that the land was not waste or arable and that the urgent-acquisition notification was unauthorized.

predicates.appeal_from_acquisition_writ_order: The proceeding is an appeal from an order on a writ petition concerning a land acquisition.
predicates.urgent_acquisition_power_invoked: The government invoked an urgent acquisition power that is available only for land meeting a specified eligibility condition.
predicates.eligibility_ground_not_raised_below: The government did not argue before the court below that the land failed the eligibility condition.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider a quasi-contract ground that was not pleaded or raised in the proceedings below or preserved in the appeal materials.
material_facts: The State sought to rely on a statutory quasi-contract claim for the benefit conferred by operations on the land.
The claim had not been pleaded as a defence in the proceedings below, argued there, or included in the grounds of appeal or the statement of case.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain the argument based on section 70 of the Indian Contract Act because it had not been pleaded or raised in the proceedings below and had not been included in the appeal grounds or statement of case. The Court made no ruling on the substantive availability of a quasi-contract claim and relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the State to raise the quasi-contract ground at that stage and did not decide whether the claim could otherwise succeed.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The court is hearing an appeal from an earlier proceeding.
predicates.new_quasi_contract_ground_not_pleaded_be: A party advances a quasi-contract ground that was not pleaded or argued in the proceeding below.
predicates.ground_not_preserved_in_appeal_materials: The ground was omitted from the appeal grounds and the party's written case on appeal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider contentions that were not raised before the court below or included in the relevant applications for leave to appeal.
material_facts: The appellant sought to raise several contentions before the Supreme Court.
Those contentions had not been raised before the High Court Division Bench and were not included in the petition for special leave or the petition seeking leave to appeal from the High Court.
The Supreme Court declined to allow the appellant to agitate those contentions.
members.legal_principle: The Court confined consideration to the issue that had been presented before the High Court Division Bench and reflected in the applications for leave to appeal; it did not consider the newly raised contentions.
members.conclusion: The Court did not permit the appellant to raise the new contentions.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party presented contentions in an appeal to a higher court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_below: The party had not raised the contention before the relevant court below.
predicates.contention_omitted_from_leave_applicatio: The party had not included the contention in the applications seeking leave to appeal.
predicates.new_contention_not_considered: The higher court declined to consider the new contention.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot obtain appellate consideration of a procedural bar based on an earlier dismissed proceeding when the record needed to determine the bar was not developed and no issue was secured for trial.
material_facts: The defendants argued that an earlier possession proceeding dismissed for default barred the later suit.
No trial issue was framed on whether the earlier proceeding and the later suit had the same cause of action.
The parties did not lead evidence on that question or provide a copy of the earlier plaint.
The defendants had failed to obtain a trial issue on the point.
members.legal_principle: Order IX, Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure concerns the bar arising from dismissal of a prior suit for default. The Court declined to consider that bar because no issue had been framed and the record lacked evidence and the earlier plaint needed to determine whether the cause of action was the same.
members.conclusion: The defendants could not raise the asserted bar under Order IX, Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the Court.

predicates.possession_suit_with_prior_default_dismi: A party in a possession suit argues that an earlier suit dismissed for default bars the current suit.
predicates.no_trial_issue_on_identity_of_cause: The trial court did not frame an issue asking whether the earlier and current suits involved the same cause of action.
predicates.no_evidence_or_prior_pleading_to_establi: The parties did not provide evidence or the earlier pleading needed to determine whether the causes of action were the same.
predicates.appellant_failed_to_secure_trial_issue: The party raising the bar did not obtain a trial issue on that point.
predicates.prior_dismissal_bar_cannot_be_considered: The appellate court cannot consider the asserted bar on an undeveloped record where the party failed to secure a trial issue.

members.legal_issue: A respondent who contests special leave on the ground that an intermediate appeal was not pursued cannot raise that same objection again at the final hearing if the court rejected it when granting leave.
material_facts: The respondents objected at the final hearing that the appellants had not sought leave to appeal to a division bench under the Letters Patent.
The court explained that the record and circumstances at the time special leave was granted determine whether that objection may be raised at the final hearing.
members.legal_principle: A point argued and decided against a respondent at the special-leave stage cannot be reopened at the final hearing. If the respondent did not appear, did not raise the point, or the court did not decide it before granting leave, there is no technical bar of res judicata and the point may be considered at the final hearing.
members.conclusion: The objection may not be raised again if it was argued and rejected on its merits when special leave was granted; if it was not decided at that stage, it may be raised at the final hearing.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.respondent_objected_to_unpursued_interme: The respondent argued that the appellant had failed to pursue an available intermediate appeal.
predicates.objection_rejected_when_leave_granted: The court rejected that objection on its merits when granting special leave.

members.legal_issue: A procedural objection to a Collector’s order will not be considered for the first time on appeal when it was not specifically alleged below or raised in argument below.
material_facts: The respondent’s supporting affidavit in the High Court did not specifically allege that the Collector had failed to conduct the required inquiry or obtain the required prior sanction.
The parties did not raise those matters in argument before the High Court.
The respondent sought to raise the matters for the first time in the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances, it was not justified in allowing a party to raise for the first time on appeal an objection that had not been specifically alleged in the supporting affidavit or raised in argument before the lower court.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the procedural objections because they were raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court: A party seeks to raise an objection in an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.procedural_objection_not_specifically_pl: The party did not specifically allege the procedural objection in the material filed before the lower court.
predicates.procedural_objection_not_raised_in_lower: The party did not raise the objection in argument before the lower court.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the market value awarded in a land acquisition appeal is not considered when it was not raised before the lower appellate court and is unsupported by material in the appeal.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the market value awarded by the acquisition court, asserting that the amount claimed by the landholders was less than the amount awarded.
The appellant had not raised that contention before the High Court.
No material was placed before the Supreme Court to substantiate the contention.
A review petition concerning the High Court's decision had been dismissed, and no appeal was filed against that dismissal.
members.legal_principle: The Court did not identify a statutory provision or earlier case for this point; it declined to address an appellate contention that had not been raised before the High Court and was unsupported by material before it, also noting that no appeal had been filed against the dismissal of the review petition.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the market-value challenge and left the award undisturbed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and market_value_challenge_not_raised_below and no_supporting_material_on_appeal and review_dismissal_not_appealed

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a land acquisition award.
predicates.market_value_challenge_not_raised_below: The appellant did not raise the market-value challenge before the lower appellate court.
predicates.no_supporting_material_on_appeal: The appellant placed no material before the reviewing court to substantiate the market-value challenge.
predicates.review_dismissal_not_appealed: A review petition concerning the lower appellate decision was dismissed, and no appeal was filed against that dismissal.

members.legal_issue: An objection to the admissibility of evidence cannot be raised for the first time at a later appellate stage when it was not raised before the earlier decision-makers.
material_facts: The owner challenged the admissibility of a document relied on in connection with rental evidence.
No objection to the document's admissibility had been made before either the arbitrator or the High Court.
The document was not printed in the record before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a belated objection to admissibility where no objection had been made before the arbitrator or the High Court. No statute or earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The admissibility objection could not be raised at that stage.

predicates.requisition_compensation_appeal: The case is an appeal concerning the valuation of compensation for requisitioned property.
predicates.evidentiary_admissibility_objection: A party challenges the admissibility of evidence relied on in the proceedings.
predicates.no_objection_before_lower_decision_maker: The party did not raise the admissibility objection before the earlier decision-makers.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court deciding whether to entertain a pure legal objection first raised after prolonged delay and abandoned before the lower appellate tribunal must consider the parties’ conduct and any resulting prejudice.
material_facts: In an eviction proceeding, the tenant initially denied the landlord-tenant relationship but did not plead that the notice terminating the tenancy was absent or invalid.
The tenant sought to add that technical objection by amendment about eight years after the eviction proceeding began.
The tenant did not press the notice objection before the appellate tribunal, which recorded that no other point had been urged.
Had the objection been raised earlier, the landlord could have withdrawn the eviction petition and brought a fresh one after serving the required notice; the delay caused prejudice to the landlord.
members.legal_principle: Although a pure question of law not raised, or expressly abandoned, before the lower appellate court may sometimes be raised later, whether to permit it is a matter of judicial discretion. The court must consider all the circumstances, particularly the conduct of the party raising it and prejudice to the other party. The Court applied this principle in the context of an eviction appeal under Section 39(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and referred to the amendment of the written statement under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have permitted the tenant to argue the notice objection. Its judgment was set aside, and the eviction orders of the Rent Controller and Rent Control Tribunal were restored.

rule.if: eviction_appeal and technical_notice_defense and defense_raised_after_long_delay and defense_abandoned_below and delay_prejudiced_landlord

predicates.eviction_appeal: A party appeals in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.technical_notice_defense: The tenant relies on a technical objection that a required notice terminating the tenancy was absent or invalid.
predicates.defense_raised_after_long_delay: The tenant raises the objection only after a prolonged period in the proceeding.
predicates.defense_abandoned_below: The tenant does not press the objection before the lower appellate tribunal.
predicates.delay_prejudiced_landlord: The delay prevents the landlord from pursuing a timely alternative course, such as withdrawing and refiling after giving notice.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court need not consider a contention based on the legal effect of a land-tenure classification when that contention was not raised before the courts below.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the land’s tenure classification meant that the grant could be held only in a personal capacity.
The Supreme Court noted that this contention had not been raised before the High Court or any court below.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied no separately stated statutory provision or cited precedent to this point; it declined to entertain the contention because it had not been raised in the courts below.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the contention to be raised or to discuss its merits.

predicates.appeal_in_civil_case: A party raises a contention in an appeal in a civil case.
predicates.tenure_based_argument_not_raised_below: The contention based on the legal effect of a land-tenure classification was not raised before the courts below.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot establish a res judicata bar in an appeal on the basis of an earlier proceeding when that ground was not raised in the proceedings below.
material_facts: The appellant relied on an earlier proceeding from 1965 as a basis for res judicata in the appeal.
The appellant had not raised a res judicata plea based on that proceeding in the lower courts.
members.legal_principle: The court declined to decide the appeal on a res judicata ground that had not been raised in the lower courts. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The court rejected the res judicata contention based on the 1965 proceeding because the plea had not been raised in the lower courts.

predicates.appeal_challenges_rejection_of_res_judic: A party appeals after a lower court has rejected a res judicata objection.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_is_relied_on: The party relies on an earlier proceeding as the basis for the asserted bar.
predicates.res_judicata_ground_not_raised_below: The party did not raise that basis for res judicata in the lower courts.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider factual objections raised for the first time when they were not pleaded or investigated below.
material_facts: Several objections concerning the sale procedure and payment of the bid were raised for the first time in the appeal.
Those objections involved factual questions that had not been pleaded or investigated in the lower courts.
members.legal_principle: The Court did not decide the merits of the newly raised objections because they involved factual questions that were not pleaded or investigated in the courts below.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain those objections.

rule.if: civil_appeal and new_factual_objections and not pleaded_or_investigated_below

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal.
predicates.new_factual_objections: A party raises objections involving factual questions for the first time on appeal.
predicates.pleaded_or_investigated_below: The factual objections were pleaded and investigated in the lower courts.
predicates.appellate_court_declines_to_consider_new: The appellate court declines to consider the newly raised factual objections.

members.legal_issue: An objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction based on a different valuation cannot be raised for the first time at the final appellate stage when the suit was properly instituted according to its valuation.
material_facts: The suit was valued by reference to the redemption amount and was properly instituted on that valuation.
The respondent alternatively argued that a higher valuation would have deprived the trial court of jurisdiction, but the objection was raised at the final appellate stage.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the suit was properly laid according to its valuation and that an objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction could not in any event be entertained for the first time in the Supreme Court.
members.conclusion: The objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction was rejected; in any event, it could not be entertained for the first time at that stage.

predicates.final_appeal: The proceeding is at the final appellate stage.
predicates.jurisdiction_objection_raised_for_first_: A party raises an objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction for the first time at that appellate stage.

members.legal_issue: An objection to the competence of an appellate certificate based on valuation cannot be raised for the first time at a late stage.
material_facts: The respondent contended that the certificate was incompetent because the value had not exceeded the relevant threshold.
The respondent had not raised the objection when the matter was heard in the High Court or in the statement of case.
members.legal_principle: An objection to valuation cannot be raised at a late stage; the Court followed State of Assam and Anr. v. Basanta Kumar Dass and Ors. The Court also relied on the unfairness of allowing a late objection when the other party could have addressed it in the High Court.
members.conclusion: The valuation objection to the certificate could not be raised at that late stage.

predicates.appeal_on_certificate: The proceeding is an appeal brought under an appellate certificate.
predicates.respondent_raises_valuation_objection_la: The respondent raises a valuation objection to the certificate at a late stage.
predicates.respondent_raised_no_earlier_objection: The respondent did not raise the objection in the earlier proceedings or in the statement of case.
predicates.late_valuation_objection_not_permitted: The valuation objection cannot be considered at that late stage.

members.legal_issue: An objection to the sequence of acquisition notifications will not be entertained on appeal when it was not raised before the High Court.
material_facts: In the Supreme Court, the landowners argued that a later notification was void because it had been issued while an earlier notification remained in force.
The landowners had not raised that objection before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural principle that it need not entertain an objection raised for the first time on appeal when it was not raised at an earlier stage.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the objection because it had not been raised before the High Court.

predicates.appellate_case: The matter is being considered in an appeal.
predicates.party_raises_notification_sequence_objec: A party argues that the sequence in which acquisition notifications were issued made a notification invalid.
predicates.objection_not_raised_below: The party did not raise that objection before the court below.

members.legal_issue: An appellant may not obtain consideration of an alleged omission by the High Court merely by asserting that an argument was raised but not considered.
material_facts: In the appeal, the appellant alleged that the High Court had not considered a number of arguments.
The High Court's judgment addressed the factual and legal issues, and the appellant had not established that the alleged omissions were admitted or demonstrable.
The appellant had not obtained an order from the High Court on any material point said to have escaped scrutiny before its judgment was signed.
members.legal_principle: The High Court is a Court of Record. Unless an omission is admitted or demonstrably proved, the Supreme Court will not investigate an allegation that the High Court failed to consider an argument. A material point said to have escaped scrutiny should be brought to the High Court's attention before judgment is signed, and an order on that submission should be obtained before raising it on appeal.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to entertain the alleged omissions and deprecated the practice of making such allegations without first raising the omission before the High Court and obtaining its order.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and appellant_alleges_omitted_argument and (omission_not_admitted and omission_not_demonstrated)

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court from a High Court decision.
predicates.appellant_alleges_omitted_argument: The appellant claims that the High Court did not consider an argument raised before it.
predicates.omission_not_admitted: The High Court has not admitted that it omitted to consider the argument.
predicates.omission_not_demonstrated: The appellant has not demonstrably established that the High Court omitted to consider the argument.

members.legal_issue: A non-joinder objection cannot be raised for the first time at the appellate stage when it was not taken in the courts below.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the suit was defective because the other partners of the firm had not been joined.
The appellant had not raised the objection in the courts below.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural principle that a point not taken in the courts below cannot be raised for the first time at a late stage of the appeal.
members.conclusion: The non-joinder point could not be raised at that late stage.

predicates.appeal_raises_nonjoinder_objection: A party raises an objection in an appeal that necessary parties were not joined.
predicates.objection_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the non-joinder objection in the courts below.

members.legal_issue: A new legal plea that was not raised in the proceedings below may be declined when it is advanced for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The allottees relied on a statute-based plea that had not been included in their writ petitions or urged before the High Court.
They raised that plea for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal after having enjoyed the benefit of the excess allotment for many years.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a plea based on the Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Act, 1976, because it had not been raised in the writ petition or before the High Court and was advanced for the first time in the Supreme Court; the Court also noted the allottees’ long enjoyment of an undeserved benefit. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the allottees to raise the new plea for the first time in the Supreme Court.

rule.if: appeal_before_supreme_court and new_legal_plea_not_raised_in_lower_courts and plea_raised_for_first_time_on_appeal and party_long_enjoyed_undue_benefit

predicates.appeal_before_supreme_court: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.new_legal_plea_not_raised_in_lower_court: The party did not raise the legal plea in the proceedings before the lower courts.
predicates.plea_raised_for_first_time_on_appeal: The party advances the legal plea for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal.
predicates.party_long_enjoyed_undue_benefit: The party had enjoyed an undue benefit for a substantial period before raising the plea.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider a challenge to rights under a distinct part of a composite agreement when that challenge was not raised in the proceedings below.
material_facts: The agreement included an arrangement for a possible sale of the properties, distinct from the lease.
The notice challenged in the underlying proceeding referred to the lease and to directions concerning movables, not to cancellation of the sale arrangement.
The appellants did not raise their claim concerning the sale arrangement in their petition or at earlier stages of the proceedings and first argued it before the Supreme Court.
The Court left any rights apart from those arising from the lease open for determination by the appropriate authorities.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a contention first advanced before it where the claim concerning the distinct sale arrangement had not been raised in the petition or at any earlier stage. It left any rights apart from those arising from the lease for determination by the appropriate authorities.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the challenge concerning the sale arrangement and made no pronouncement on the appellants' rights under it.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and claim_first_raised_on_appeal and claim_concerns_distinct_agreement_rights and claim_not_within_matters_challenged_below

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal.
predicates.claim_first_raised_on_appeal: A party first advances the claim during the appeal.
predicates.claim_concerns_distinct_agreement_rights: The claim concerns rights arising from an agreement distinct from the rights directly challenged below.
predicates.claim_not_within_matters_challenged_belo: The claim was not among the matters challenged in the proceedings below.
predicates.appellate_court_declines_to_consider_new: The appellate court declines to consider the new claim.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings in an appeal are not reassessed when the appellant identifies no misreading of evidence or other error warranting reassessment.
material_facts: The courts below concurrently found that the parents had married and that the child was born of that marriage.
In the appeal, the appellant challenged those findings as based on misreading of evidence.
The appellant did not identify any such misreading or other error that would justify reassessing the evidence.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to reassess concurrent factual findings where the appellant could point to no misreading of important evidence or other error justifying reassessment. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings concerning the marriage and the child's parentage were left undisturbed.

predicates.appeal_challenging_concurrent_factual_fi: An appellant challenged factual findings reached by both lower courts.
predicates.no_misreading_or_other_reassessment_erro: The appellant identified no misreading of evidence or other error that would justify reassessing the facts.

members.legal_issue: An appellate challenge to a document's admissibility cannot be entertained while an unchallenged factual finding independently establishes that the alleged agreement was not proved.
material_facts: The High Court found that the alleged agreement to reduce the royalty had not been proved.
The appellant did not ask the Supreme Court to reverse that finding.
The appellant nevertheless sought to challenge the admissibility of the document recording the alleged agreement.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the unchallenged factual finding as standing in the appeal and stated that the admissibility contention could not be entertained so long as that finding was not set aside.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not entertain the admissibility contention while the High Court's finding that the agreement had not been proved remained undisturbed.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party has brought a civil appeal from a lower court's decision.
predicates.lower_court_found_agreement_unproved: The lower court found that the agreement relied on by a party had not been proved.
predicates.finding_not_challenged: The appellant has not sought to have the finding that the agreement was unproved reversed.
predicates.appellate_admissibility_challenge_not_en: The appellate court does not entertain the admissibility challenge while the unchallenged finding remains in place.

members.legal_issue: A concurrent factual finding is not disturbed on appeal when no special ground for interference is established.
material_facts: The lower courts concurrently found that the inams were pre-settlement grants excluded from the assets of the zamindari.
The appellants challenged that finding but did not establish a manifest error of law, disregard of judicial process, denial of fair hearing, or another special reason for revisiting it.
members.legal_principle: A concurrent finding of fact is not reopened on appeal without special grounds, such as a manifest error of law or disregard of judicial process or principles of fair hearing.
members.conclusion: The Court left the concurrent finding undisturbed and proceeded on the basis that the inams were pre-settlement grants excluded from the zamindari assets.

predicates.appeal_against_concurrent_factual_findin: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a factual finding reached concurrently by lower courts.
predicates.special_ground_for_interference: The appellant establishes a special reason to revisit the finding, such as a manifest error of law or disregard of judicial process or fair hearing.
predicates.concurrent_finding_left_undisturbed: The concurrent factual finding is not disturbed on appeal.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of fact supported by proper appreciation of the evidence are not reopened in an appeal under Article 136 absent legal infirmity.
material_facts: The trial court, first appellate court, and High Court made concurrent findings supporting the buyer’s account of the agreement and the parties’ performance.
The Supreme Court found those factual findings to be based on proper appreciation of the evidence and identified no legal infirmity in them.
The matter reached the Supreme Court by an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: In exercising jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court did not consider it appropriate to reopen questions of fact alone where the concurrent findings were based on proper appreciation of the evidence and disclosed no legal infirmity.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to revisit the concurrent factual findings.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court under its discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings_are_evidence_ba: The courts below reached the same factual conclusions after considering the evidence.
predicates.no_legal_infirmity_is_shown: The appellant identifies no legal defect undermining those factual conclusions.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for simple hurt need not be modified where the evidence supports the offence and no basis for changing the conviction or sentence is established.
material_facts: The appellant was convicted of simple hurt and sentenced to one year of rigorous imprisonment.
The Supreme Court found no reason to modify that conviction or sentence.
members.legal_principle: Section 323 of the Indian Penal Code provides for punishment for voluntarily causing hurt. The court found no ground to alter the conviction or sentence under that provision and cited no earlier case.
members.conclusion: The conviction for simple hurt and the one-year sentence were left unchanged.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_simple_hurt_: The case is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for simple hurt.
predicates.evidence_supports_simple_hurt: The evidence supports that the accused voluntarily caused hurt.
predicates.no_basis_to_modify_conviction_or_sentenc: The court finds no reason to change the conviction or sentence.

members.legal_issue: A maintenance award based on concurrent factual findings and supported by the evidence should not be disturbed when no sufficient basis to challenge those findings is established.
material_facts: The Magistrate assessed the respondent's salary and property and awarded maintenance to the wife and minor child.
The Additional Sessions Judge reconsidered the evidence and affirmed the Magistrate's findings and award.
The findings were concurrent, and the jurisdiction question was the only question argued before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the Magistrate's findings on maintenance as concurrent findings of fact, which ordinarily cannot be questioned in revision, and noted that the Additional Sessions Judge had accepted them after reconsidering the evidence. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: The Court restored the Magistrate's maintenance award along with the order, after holding that the Magistrate had jurisdiction.

rule.if: maintenance_proceeding and concurrent_maintenance_findings and award_based_on_evidence and no_sufficient_challenge_to_findings

predicates.maintenance_proceeding: A claimant initiated a summary proceeding seeking maintenance from a spouse or parent.
predicates.concurrent_maintenance_findings: Two lower courts reached the same factual findings on entitlement to maintenance and its amount.
predicates.award_based_on_evidence: The maintenance award was made after considering evidence relevant to the respondent's means and the claimants' needs.
predicates.no_sufficient_challenge_to_findings: No sufficient basis was established to disturb the concurrent factual findings.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings in an appeal by special leave are not open to further scrutiny unless they suffer from an error of law.
material_facts: Both the trial court and the High Court found that the temple was public and that the claimant had not established hereditary trusteeship.
The Supreme Court considered the claimant’s challenges to those findings and found no error of law warranting interference.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, a concurrent finding of fact is not open to further scrutiny by the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave unless it suffers from an error of law (Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayah Gosavi).
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings were upheld and were not reopened on the facts.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter came before the Supreme Court as an appeal by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same findings on the material facts.
predicates.no_error_of_law_found: The Supreme Court found no error of law in those concurrent findings.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings supported by the evidence should not be disturbed on special-leave appeal when no infirmity in those findings is established.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both found that the disputed property was funded by the waqf estate and that the beneficiary did not establish personal ownership.
The documentary and oral evidence supported those findings, particularly the evidence tracing the acquisition and construction expenses to waqf funds.
The appellant did not successfully challenge the primary factual findings and relied on a new theory that the Court rejected.
members.legal_principle: In reviewing concurrent factual findings on special leave, the Court does not ordinarily reappraise findings that are supported by the evidence and disclose no infirmity. The Court referred to Meenakshi Mills v. Commissioner of Income-tax and the principles concerning findings based on evidence discussed in Gangadara Ayyar v. Subramania Sastrigal; it did not need to decide which side of the general line of review the case occupied because the primary findings were clearly supported.
members.conclusion: The Court found no basis to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: special_leave_civil_appeal and lower_courts_made_concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and no_material_infirmity_shown

predicates.special_leave_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.lower_courts_made_concurrent_factual_fin: The trial court and the appellate court below reached the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The findings are supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.no_material_infirmity_shown: The appellant has not established a material flaw in the concurrent findings.

members.legal_issue: Discretionary appellate review does not warrant disturbing concurrent factual findings on execution and readiness where the findings were not challenged in the lower appellate proceedings and the contrary allegation is unsupported by evidence.
material_facts: The trial court found that the agreement had been executed and that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform.
The seller did not appeal or cross-object against those findings.
The seller’s principal factual defence was that the agreement was fabricated, but the courts found that defence unsupported by evidence.
The Supreme Court considered the matter in appeals invoking its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary appellate jurisdiction. On the facts here, the Court found no justification to exercise that jurisdiction against concurrent findings supported by the record, particularly where the relevant findings had not been challenged in the lower appellate proceedings and the allegation of fabrication was unproved.
members.conclusion: There was no valid ground to exercise Article 136 jurisdiction to interfere with the concurrent findings or the decree for specific performance.

predicates.appeal_under_discretionary_appellate_jur: A party sought discretionary appellate review of a decree enforcing a sale agreement.
predicates.concurrent_findings_on_execution_and_rea: The courts below made concurrent findings that the agreement was executed and the purchaser was ready and willing to perform.
predicates.findings_not_challenged_below: The party seeking review did not challenge those findings by appeal or cross-objection in the lower appellate proceedings.
predicates.fabrication_allegation_unsupported: The party alleged that the agreement was fabricated but produced no evidence substantiating that allegation.

members.legal_issue: A higher court should not interfere with a considered rejection of an objection to the competence of an appeal filed by the acquiring authority.
material_facts: The Collector appealed against the District Judge’s enhanced compensation award, and the landowners argued that the Collector was not competent to appeal because the State had not filed it.
The High Court considered and rejected the objection, and the Supreme Court declined to interfere with that finding in the interests of justice.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that the High Court had fully considered the objection and that, in the interests of justice, it was not disposed to interfere with the High Court’s finding; it stated no broader rule on the Collector’s authority to appeal.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s rejection of the competence objection.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a court’s determination of compensation on reference in a land acquisition matter.
predicates.competence_objection_fully_considered_be: A party challenges the competence of the acquiring authority’s appeal, and the court below fully considers and rejects that objection.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of guilt should not be disturbed on appeal when the courts below have assessed the evidence and no cogent basis is shown for finding their conclusions improbable or unsustainable.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the appellants, and the High Court affirmed the convictions.
The lower courts had considered the eyewitness evidence, the prompt report, the medical evidence, and the recovery of blood-stained clothes and swords after the appellants were arrested.
The Supreme Court found no ground to regard the lower courts’ findings as improbable or requiring reversal.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to re-examine the lower courts’ factual conclusions where they had addressed the factual and legal aspects of the case and no cogent reason for interference was shown. The judgment cites no separate provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: There was no cogent reason to interfere with the concurrent findings, and the appeals were dismissed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the first appellate court have both found the accused guilty.
predicates.no_cogent_basis_to_find_them_improbable_: The record supplies no cogent reason to conclude that the lower courts’ findings are improbable or unsustainable.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings supporting convictions for trespass, unlawful entry under local law, and causing hurt should not be disturbed when the appellate court finds no reason to differ from them.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court found that the accused grazed cattle in a field and damaged its crop.
Both courts rejected the defence that the field’s owner had permitted the grazing.
The High Court accepted eyewitness evidence and found that the accused were the aggressors.
The Supreme Court found no reason to differ from the concurrent findings supporting the convictions and dismissed the accused’s appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted the concurrent factual findings of the trial court and High Court on the evidence and stated that it found no reason to differ from them. It therefore left undisturbed the convictions under Sections 323 and 447 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 162(2) of the Gujarat Panchayats Act. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences challenged by the accused were affirmed, subject to the separate alteration of one accused’s homicide conviction in the State’s appeal.

rule.if: accused_appeal_from_conviction and concurrent_courts_found_unauthorized_grazing_and_crop_damage and permission_defence_rejected and eyewitness_evidence_supported_findings and supreme_court_found_no_reason_to_differ

predicates.accused_appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed convictions entered by the lower courts.
predicates.concurrent_courts_found_unauthorized_gra: The trial and appellate courts found that the accused grazed animals without permission and damaged a crop.
predicates.permission_defence_rejected: The lower courts rejected the claim that the property owner had permitted the conduct.
predicates.eyewitness_evidence_supported_findings: The lower courts relied on eyewitness testimony supporting their findings about the incident.
predicates.supreme_court_found_no_reason_to_differ: The Supreme Court found no reason to depart from the lower courts’ concurrent factual findings.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of guilt based on evidence are not disturbed on appeal unless their appreciation is unreasonable or unjustified.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court both convicted the appellants after assessing the evidence.
The Supreme Court found no basis to regard the lower courts’ appreciation of the evidence as unreasonable or unjustified.
members.legal_principle: On appeal, concurrent findings based on appreciation of evidence are not interfered with unless that appreciation is shown to be unreasonable or unjustified.
members.conclusion: There was no ground to interfere with the concurrent findings, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and concurrent_evidence_findings and not findings_unreasonable

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal against a conviction.
predicates.concurrent_evidence_findings: The trial court and the appellate court reached the same findings after assessing the evidence.
predicates.findings_unreasonable: The appellant showed that the courts’ appreciation of the evidence was unreasonable or unjustified.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings are not ordinarily disturbed in a special-leave appeal unless exceptional grounds for interference are shown.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that the claimant provided the purchase consideration and that the property was held in another person's name benami, rather than having been gifted to that person.
Those findings rested on a reasonable appreciation of the evidence, including bank records and testimony, and were affirmed by the High Court.
The appeal challenged those concurrent findings, but no perversity, lack of evidence, or material irregularity affecting them was established.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court ordinarily does not interfere with a finding of fact that is not perverse or based on no evidence. It may intervene where material circumstances or irregularities affect the finding, justice has failed, or the finding is likely to cause unduly excessive hardship. The Court relied on Babu v. Dy. Director, Prasad v. Govindaswamy, Dhanjibhai v. State of Gujarat, Ganga Bishan v. Jay Narayan, Uday Chand Dutt v. Saibal Sen, and Ram Singh v. Ajay Chawla.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent finding that the property was held benami and not gifted.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_fact_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and not material_irregularity_affecting_findings

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The trial court and the appellate courts reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The courts based their finding on a reasonable appreciation of evidence in the record.
predicates.material_irregularity_affecting_findings: A material irregularity affected the factual findings.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings are not disturbed in a special-leave appeal absent exceptional error.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court both found the appellants guilty on the evidence.
The Supreme Court found no manifest error, clear unreasonableness, injustice, illegality, or fundamental procedural or natural-justice violation warranting interference.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that, as a rule of practice, it is loath to disturb concurrent findings of fact unless the findings are manifestly erroneous, clearly unreasonable, unjust or illegal, or violate a fundamental rule of procedure or natural justice. The appeal was brought by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings were left undisturbed and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_fact_findings and not exceptional_error

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The case is an appeal brought by special leave from a judgment based on a criminal trial.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The trial court and the appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.exceptional_error: The concurrent finding is manifestly erroneous, clearly unreasonable, unjust or illegal, or violates a fundamental rule of procedure or natural justice.

members.legal_issue: Interference under Article 136 is not justified when the challenged appellate conviction reflects a proper appraisal of the evidence and the conclusions are not shown to be so erroneous as to warrant intervention.
material_facts: The accused sought special leave to appeal against convictions imposed by the High Court after it allowed the State's appeal against acquittal.

The Supreme Court considered the High Court's appraisal of the evidence and the criticism of the investigation, including the site-plan allegation, and found no error or sufficiently grave suspicion warranting a different conclusion.

The Supreme Court was not persuaded that the High Court had departed from the principles governing appeals against acquittal or that its conclusions were otherwise sufficiently erroneous to justify intervention.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, interference was not warranted on the arguments raised because the High Court had properly appraised the evidence, had not failed to follow the principles governing appeals against acquittal, and had not reached conclusions shown to be sufficiently erroneous. The Court considered and applied Sanwant Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1961] 3 S.C.R. 120, Rambhapala Reddy v. State of A.P., A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460, and Bansidhar Mohanty v. State of Orissa, A.I.R. 1955 S.C. 585.
members.conclusion: There was no ground for interference under Article 136, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_conviction_on_: The proceeding was a special-leave appeal against a conviction entered after a State appeal against acquittal.
predicates.high_court_properly_appraised_evidence: The High Court properly assessed the evidence and relevant circumstances.
predicates.no_failure_to_follow_acquittal_appeal_pr: The High Court did not fail to follow the principles governing appellate review of an acquittal.
predicates.no_sufficiently_erroneous_conclusion_sho: The appellant did not show that the High Court's conclusions were so erroneous as to warrant intervention.
predicates.supreme_court_does_not_interfere: The Supreme Court does not interfere with the challenged decision.

members.legal_issue: A Division Bench hearing an intra-court appeal should ordinarily avoid disturbing concurrent factual findings without cogent reasons.
material_facts: The trial court found that the claimant was not ready and willing to perform the agreement and that the property was not undervalued.
The High Court Single Judge affirmed the trial court’s findings.
The Division Bench reversed those findings, and the Supreme Court found that it had failed to consider material pleadings and testimony properly.
members.legal_principle: An intra-court appeal is not confined to the limits of Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but its entertainment is discretionary; ordinarily, a Division Bench should not differ from a Single Judge’s factual findings without cogent reasons. An appellate court should also exercise restraint when findings depend on the evidence. The Court relied on Smt. Asha Devi v. Dukhi Sao, Collector of Customs, Bombay v. Swastic Woollens (P) Ltd., West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission v. CESC Ltd., Commissioner of Customs, Chennai v. Adani Exports Ltd., and Manjunath Anandappa v. Tammanasa.
members.conclusion: The Division Bench should not have displaced the concurrent findings without cogent reasons, and its judgment could not stand.

predicates.intra_court_appeal: A party appealed within the same court system from a judgment of a single judge to a division bench.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the single judge reached the same factual findings.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_for_departure: The appellate court departed from those findings without a cogent reason for doing so.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that an accused was present and participated in an offence should not be disturbed when witness identification is corroborated and no strong ground for interference is shown.
material_facts: Several eyewitnesses identified the accused as present with the armed group, and some also identified him in a jail identification procedure.
The accused's firearm was his, and a ballistic examination detected combustion products in its barrel washing.
The accused was absent from his workplace around the time of the incident and did not provide evidence that he was elsewhere.
The accused's name was not specified in some contemporaneous accounts, but those accounts referred to several members of the same group without naming them individually.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the corroboration of eyewitness identification and the absence of a strong ground to disturb concurrent factual findings. It cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the concurrent finding that the accused was present and participated, finding no strong ground to interfere.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and concurrent_presence_findings and eyewitness_identification and corroborating_circumstances and no_strong_ground_to_interfere

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction based in part on the accused's presence at the offence.
predicates.concurrent_presence_findings: The trial court and appellate court both found that the accused was present and participated.
predicates.eyewitness_identification: Witnesses identified the accused as present with the group involved in the incident.
predicates.corroborating_circumstances: Independent evidence or circumstances support the eyewitness identification.
predicates.no_strong_ground_to_interfere: The appellant has not shown a strong reason to disturb the concurrent factual findings.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court generally should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact when a party has failed to prove the factual basis for its claim.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that money remained due under a usufructuary mortgage and sought compensation on that basis.
The Tribunal and the High Court both found that the appellants had failed to prove by proper evidence that any mortgage debt remained unpaid.
The Court considered the appellants’ arguments and found no reason to depart from the rule against interfering with concurrent findings on a pure question of fact.
members.legal_principle: The Court has repeatedly held that it will not generally interfere with concurrent findings on a pure question of fact. The judgment identifies no particular earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent finding that the appellants had not proved an outstanding mortgage debt and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_concurrent_factual_fin: A party brought a civil appeal against factual findings reached concurrently by the lower tribunal and court.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_outstanding_mor: A claimant failed to provide proper evidence that money remained due under a mortgage.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings supporting a necessary access right did not warrant interference by the Supreme Court in the appeal.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the access suit, but the first appellate court found that the adjoining land had no other approach and decreed relief.
The High Court declined to disturb the first appellate court’s factual findings in the second appeal.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s judgment in its special-leave jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: The High Court considered whether the concurrent factual findings warranted interference in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Supreme Court held that the judgment did not call for interference in its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, and dismissed the appeal.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s judgment and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave against a judgment dismissing a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_findings_support_access: The lower appellate courts concurrently found facts supporting the claimed access right.
predicates.findings_do_not_warrant_interference: The findings and judgment provide no sufficient basis for the Supreme Court to intervene.
predicates.supreme_court_does_not_interfere: The Supreme Court leaves the challenged judgment undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: A factual finding that a contracting party acted as a benamidar cannot be disturbed in a special appeal when evidence supports it.
material_facts: The agreement was in the name of one person, while the Election Tribunal found that the appellant’s father was the real contracting party and the named contractor was his benamidar.
The appellant accepted that there was evidence supporting the Tribunal’s benami finding, although he challenged its weight.
members.legal_principle: Whether a person is a benamidar is a question of fact; a finding supported by evidence is not open to interference in a special appeal. The Court relied on no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the Tribunal’s finding that the father was the real contracting party and declined to interfere with the benami finding.

predicates.special_appeal: The matter is a special appeal challenging a factual finding made by an Election Tribunal.
predicates.evidence_supports_benami_finding: Evidence supports the finding that the person named in the agreement acted as a benamidar for the real contracting party.
