He also argued that the assessment should be limited to villages listed in an inventory, although that claim had not been raised in the High Court and no evidence or finding on it was before the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court was hearing appeals from the High Court's decisions on the assessments.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court will not enter into a factual inquiry on a claim that was not raised before the High Court, particularly where the opposing party had no opportunity to meet it and the High Court made no finding on it.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected both grounds because they had not been raised in the High Court and could not be examined for the first time in those appeals.

predicates.appeal_from_tax_assessment_decision: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision concerning a tax assessment.
predicates.factual_ground_not_raised_before_high_co: The appellant did not raise the factual ground in the High Court.
predicates.no_high_court_finding_on_ground: The High Court made no finding on the factual ground.

members.legal_issue: A factual contention not raised in the courts below cannot be introduced for the first time in an appeal where its determination requires deciding a question of fact.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the land in its possession did not exceed its share of the joint property.
That contention had not been raised in either the trial court or the High Court.
The Court considered the contention to raise a question of fact.
members.legal_principle: A factual plea not raised in the courts below cannot be considered for the first time on appeal when it raises a question of fact. No provision or earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the contention in the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_lower_court_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment of lower courts.
predicates.factual_contention_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the factual contention in the courts below.
predicates.contention_requires_fact_finding: Resolving the contention requires deciding a question of fact.
predicates.new_factual_contention_not_considered: The new factual contention is not considered on appeal.

members.legal_issue: A factual contention not raised in the writ proceeding or before the High Court cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The appellant contended on appeal that no notice of demand had been served on the lessors before the garnishee notice was issued.
That factual contention had not been raised in the writ petition or argued before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: A question of fact that was not raised in the writ petition or argued before the High Court cannot be agitated for the first time on appeal.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not raise the factual contention for the first time in the Supreme Court.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_proceeding: The matter is an appeal following a writ proceeding in a lower court.
predicates.factual_ground_not_raised_below: The party first raises a factual contention on appeal that was not pleaded in the writ proceeding or argued in the lower court.

members.legal_issue: An alternative contention that a grant ceased to be enforceable after resumption or a change of sovereignty cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when it has no foundation in the pleadings or issues.
material_facts: The respondent argued in the Supreme Court that the grant had ended through resumption and was not recognised after the former state’s merger.
The contention had no foundation in the pleadings or in the issues framed in the lower courts.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to consider a contention raised for the first time on appeal when it had no foundation in the pleadings or the issues; no earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Court did not allow the alternative contention to be raised for the first time on appeal.

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal.
predicates.alternative_contention_not_raised_in_ple: The alternative contention was not set out in the pleadings below.
predicates.alternative_contention_not_in_issues: The alternative contention was not included in the issues framed below.
predicates.alternative_contention_is_not_considered: The court does not consider the alternative contention when it is raised for the first time on appeal.

members.legal_issue: A new contention dependent on facts not raised earlier and absent from the record will not be entertained for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The tenants argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that a particular area had been wrongly excluded because it was occupied by old tenants.
The point had not been raised at any earlier stage.
The record contained no facts about that area.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the contention as a factual issue that had not been raised below and for which the record contained no supporting facts, and therefore declined to consider it for the first time on appeal.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the tenants to raise the contention for the first time on appeal.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party presented a contention to an appellate court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_below: The party had not raised that contention before the lower decision-makers.
predicates.necessary_facts_absent_from_record: The record did not contain facts needed to decide the contention.

members.legal_issue: A contention based on a statutory restriction cannot be introduced for the first time at a later stage of review when no foundation for it was laid in the pleadings or earlier proceedings.
material_facts: The landowner relied on a statutory limit on the tenant’s purchase rights for the first time before the High Court.
The landowner had not pleaded facts relevant to that limit or raised the contention before the revenue authorities.
The landowner had also pursued claims concerning other tenants but did not continue those claims after the tribunal’s decisions.
members.legal_principle: A party cannot raise a contention at a later stage when the pleadings and earlier proceedings contain no factual foundation for it. The Court did not decide the scope or meaning of section 42(c) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, and relied on no earlier cases for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The landowner was not entitled to raise the contention because no foundation for it had been laid in the pleadings or at any earlier stage.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The dispute was before a court reviewing decisions made in earlier proceedings.
predicates.contention_omitted_from_pleadings: The party had not pleaded facts supporting the contention.
predicates.contention_not_raised_earlier: The party had not raised the contention before the earlier decision-makers.
predicates.late_raised_contention_barred: The party cannot raise the contention at the later stage.

members.legal_issue: A contention that was not raised before the revenue tribunal cannot be considered for the first time in a writ challenge to its decision.
material_facts: In the writ petition, the appellants argued that the principal had subsequently ratified the lease granted by the agent.
The Letters Patent Bench found that the ratification contention had not been urged before the Board of Revenue.
The Supreme Court held that the single Judge should not have considered that contention.
members.legal_principle: In reviewing a tribunal’s decision under Article 226, the High Court should not consider a contention that was not advanced before that tribunal. No earlier case was relied on for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to consider the ratification contention because it had not been raised before the Board of Revenue.

predicates.certiorari_writ: A party sought a writ challenging a tribunal’s decision.
predicates.plea_not_raised_before_tribunal: The party did not advance the contention before the tribunal whose decision was challenged.

members.legal_issue: A contention that an occupier was evicted without notice cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when it was not clearly pleaded or made an issue in the courts below.
material_facts: The claimant argued before the Supreme Court that no notice to quit had been given and that this prevented removal of the trees.
The plaint did not clearly allege eviction without notice, and its allegations about lacking an opportunity to remove improvements referred to other items.
No issue about lack of eviction notice was framed at trial, and no application to frame such an issue was made in the trial court, the High Court, or the Supreme Court.
The courts found that the claimant had deliberately occupied the land knowing that they had no right to enter it and had been rightly evicted.
members.legal_principle: The court declined to entertain a new appellate contention that was not clearly pleaded and was not made an issue in the courts below. The claimant’s testimony about not receiving notice did not overcome the failure to plead or seek an issue on that point, particularly in light of the findings that the occupation was deliberate and the eviction was rightful.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not permitted to raise the contention about lack of eviction notice for the first time before the Supreme Court.

rule.if: appeal_to_supreme_court and eviction_without_notice_contention_new_on_appeal and contention_not_clearly_pleaded and no_lower_court_issue_framed and deliberate_unauthorised_occupation

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court: A party appeals to the Supreme Court from a decision concerning eviction and a claim for improvements.
predicates.eviction_without_notice_contention_new_o: The appellant first argues in the Supreme Court that eviction occurred without notice.
predicates.contention_not_clearly_pleaded: The pleadings do not clearly allege that the appellant was evicted without notice.
predicates.no_lower_court_issue_framed: No issue about lack of eviction notice was framed in the lower courts, and no application to frame one was made there.
predicates.deliberate_unauthorised_occupation: The courts found that the appellant deliberately occupied land knowing they had no right to do so.

members.legal_issue: An alternative statutory ground that depends on proof of facts and is raised for the first time on appeal need not be considered.
material_facts: The State argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that villages not covered by the definition in the Madras Estates Land Act could nevertheless qualify as estates under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act.
The alternative argument depended on proof of the conditions specified in that Act.
The argument raised a mixed question of fact and law, and the State had not raised it in the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a new contention involving a mixed question of fact and law where its determination depended on proof of statutory conditions and it had not been raised in the High Court. The contention invoked section 2(g) of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1952; the Court left its merits open.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the alternative contention because it was raised for the first time and depended on proof of facts; it expressed no opinion on the contention’s merits.

predicates.appeal_in_supreme_court: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.alternative_statutory_ground_first_raise: A party raises an alternative statutory basis for the first time in the Supreme Court.
predicates.ground_requires_proof_of_facts: Determining the alternative ground requires proof of facts.

members.legal_issue: A fact-dependent challenge to a person’s authority to grant a lease cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court when it was not argued below and requires factual investigation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs challenged the lessor’s authority to grant the lease for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The challenge had not been argued before either the district court or the Judicial Commissioner.
Resolving the challenge would require investigation of facts.
members.legal_principle: Under the Court’s settled practice, a question not raised before the High Court is not considered for the first time in the Supreme Court when its resolution requires investigation of facts.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the challenge to the lessor’s authority.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal.
predicates.issue_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the issue before the lower appellate courts.
predicates.issue_requires_factual_investigation: Resolving the issue would require investigation of facts.

members.legal_issue: A new challenge to the validity of a notification, not raised in the courts below and requiring factual and interpretive determinations, need not be considered for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The tenants argued before the Supreme Court that most tenants had paid rent and the remaining tenants were willing to pay but disputed the amount demanded.
The contention had not been raised in the High Court.
Deciding the contention would have required determining disputed facts about tenants’ conduct and interpreting the meaning of a general refusal to pay.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a contention first raised on appeal where it depended on unresolved factual questions and an interpretation that had not been argued or considered at an earlier stage. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the tenants to raise the contention for the first time on appeal and did not decide the notification’s validity on that ground.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court: The matter was an appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_in_courts_below: The party had not raised the contention before the courts below.
predicates.contention_requires_unresolved_facts_and: Deciding the contention required resolving factual matters and interpreting a disputed legal expression.

members.legal_issue: A contention not pleaded in the written statement and not made the subject of an issue cannot be raised for the first time in the final appeal.
material_facts: The appellants contended that the shops had been bought with partnership funds and that the partners each had an equal share.
That contention had not been raised in the written statement, and no issue had been framed on it.
The contention was advanced for the first time before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: A contention that was not pleaded and on which no issue was framed cannot be introduced for the first time in the Supreme Court. No specific statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The court would not permit the contention to be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

rule.if: final_civil_appeal and contention_not_pleaded and no_issue_framed_on_contention and contention_raised_first_time_on_final_appeal

predicates.final_civil_appeal: The matter is a final appeal in a civil case.
predicates.contention_not_pleaded: The party did not raise the contention in its written pleading.
predicates.no_issue_framed_on_contention: The trial court did not frame an issue for decision on the contention.
predicates.contention_raised_first_time_on_final_ap: The party first advanced the contention in the final appellate court.
predicates.new_contention_not_considered: The court does not permit the contention to be raised for the first time in the final appeal.

members.legal_issue: A limitation bar cannot be decided as a pure question of law on appeal when its determination depends on unresolved facts and the affected parties had no fair opportunity to address it.
material_facts: The trial court decreed relief in the suit, but a defendant who had not filed a written statement raised limitation for the first time before the High Court.
Determining the relevant dissolution date could require evidence about when the last partner was served with the summons and plaint.
The record did not establish that service date, and the parties supporting the trial decree had no opportunity to amend their pleadings or present evidence on limitation.
The High Court treated the suit as time-barred and dismissed it.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 requires a court to take notice of limitation, and Article 106 was invoked in relation to the claim for accounts and profits. But where limitation is a mixed question of fact and law, the court should not decide a newly raised plea without allowing the affected parties to answer it and establishing the necessary facts. The court could have allowed amendment of pleadings, framed an issue, and obtained a finding from the trial court. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating limitation as a pure question of law and deciding it on appeal without factual inquiry or a fair opportunity for the affected parties to meet the plea. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s decision and restored the trial court’s decree.

rule.if: appeal_from_limitation_bar_ruling and limitation_plea_first_raised_on_appeal and limitation_depends_on_unproved_facts and affected_party_denied_opportunity_to_answer

predicates.appeal_from_limitation_bar_ruling: The proceeding is an appeal in which a court has dismissed a claim as time-barred.
predicates.limitation_plea_first_raised_on_appeal: A party first raised the limitation plea at the appellate hearing rather than in the trial pleadings.
predicates.limitation_depends_on_unproved_facts: Deciding whether the claim is late depends on facts that were not established in the record.
predicates.affected_party_denied_opportunity_to_ans: The parties opposing the limitation plea were not given a fair opportunity to amend their pleadings or present evidence in response.

members.legal_issue: A new objection to partition documents cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when deciding it would require further factual investigation.
material_facts: At trial, the case proceeded on the basis that the partition was oral and that the written partition lists were evidence of that oral partition.
No objection to the admissibility of the partition lists was raised at trial.
The objection that the lists required registration was raised for the first time in the High Court appeal.
Resolving that objection would have required further investigation of factual questions.
members.legal_principle: An oral partition is possible, and written lists may serve as evidence of an oral partition and an associated oral agreement. A new objection raised for the first time on appeal need not be entertained where its determination requires further factual investigation.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly declined to entertain the new registration objection for the first time on appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_decision: The matter is an appeal from a trial decision.
predicates.objection_first_raised_on_appeal: A party raises the objection for the first time in the appellate court.
predicates.deciding_objection_requires_further_fact: Resolving the objection would require further investigation of factual questions.

members.legal_issue: A new statutory ground that was not pleaded or supported by necessary facts in the writ proceedings cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: A party argued in the Supreme Court that the distillery operators needed a central industrial licence.
The writ petitions had not raised that ground or pleaded the facts necessary to establish its application.
The record did not show that the new distilleries would employ the number of workers that triggered the asserted licensing requirement.
members.legal_principle: A party cannot raise for the first time in an appeal under Article 136 a factual and statutory ground that was not pleaded below and for which the necessary supporting facts are absent. Sections 3(c), 3(d), and 11 of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 made the asserted licensing requirement dependent on the relevant undertaking and workforce threshold.
members.conclusion: The Court would not permit the new ground to be raised in the appeal.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_case: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.new_statutory_ground_not_pleaded_below: A party raises a statutory ground on appeal that was not raised in the proceedings below.
predicates.supporting_facts_absent: The pleadings and record do not contain the facts necessary to establish the new ground.

members.legal_issue: A legal ground that was neither raised before nor considered by the tax tribunal cannot be introduced in an appeal confined to a certified question merely because it might arise from the facts found.
material_facts: The assessee argued in the Supreme Court that the land had been acquired as a gift and that capital gains provisions could not apply without a cost of acquisition.

The cost-of-acquisition argument had not been raised before the income-tax authorities, the tribunal, or the High Court, and there was no finding that the land had been received without consideration.
The appeal certificate covered only whether granting long leases amounted to a transfer, not whether the provisions applied to property acquired without cost.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle in Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay v. Scindia Steam Navigation Co. Ltd., [1961] 42 ITR 589, a question of law that was neither raised before the tribunal nor considered by it does not arise out of its order, even if it might arise on the facts found. The appeal proceeded from a reference under Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and was limited by the certificate of fitness.
members.conclusion: The assessee could not raise the cost-of-acquisition argument in the appeal because it did not arise out of the tribunal’s decision.

predicates.tax_reference_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a tax tribunal’s decision through a reference to a court.
predicates.legal_ground_not_raised_before_tribunal: The party did not present the legal ground to the tax tribunal.
predicates.legal_ground_not_considered_by_tribunal: The tax tribunal did not consider or decide the legal ground.

members.legal_issue: A statutory rent-protection defence that was not raised in the lower courts cannot be introduced for the first time in a special-leave appeal when it depends on disputed facts, particularly where the suit seeks possession on the basis of title.
material_facts: The occupants denied that they were tenants and asserted that they owned the property by adverse possession.
The purchasers brought the suit for declaration of title and possession, rather than as an eviction suit under the Rent Act.
The occupants did not plead rent-protection entitlement in their written statement, and no such issue was framed or raised in the courts below.
The occupants sought to rely in the special-leave appeal on rent-protection provisions, including a provision introduced during the proceedings.
The occupants had denied the purchasers’ title, and that denial was found proved.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the reliance on Gyan Chand v. K.B. Lal and Ors. because this was a suit for possession based on title, not an eviction suit under the Rent Act. It considered Sections 13 and 13A of the Rent Act but held that the protection plea, never raised below and involving disputed facts, could not be entertained for the first time in the appeal. The Court also noted that the denial of the claimant’s title had been found proved.
members.conclusion: The rent-protection contention could not be considered at that stage because it had not been raised in the courts below and involved disputed questions of fact; it did not prevent the decree for possession in this title-based suit.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and title_based_possession_suit and rent_protection_not_pleaded_below and rent_protection_depends_on_disputed_facts

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The underlying suit sought possession on the basis of the claimant’s title rather than as an eviction proceeding under rent-control law.
predicates.rent_protection_not_pleaded_below: The occupants did not raise a claim to statutory rent protection in the lower courts.
predicates.rent_protection_depends_on_disputed_fact: Determining whether the occupants qualify for statutory rent protection requires resolution of disputed facts.

members.legal_issue: A newly raised statutory ownership claim that depends on unresolved possession facts should not be determined in an appeal on a record lacking evidence of those facts.
material_facts: A claim under the statutory provision concerning a female Hindu's full ownership was raised for the first time in the appeal after the lower courts had decided the suit.
The parties had not adduced evidence directed to the statutory claim.
The record did not establish whether the widow was in actual or constructive possession, or whether the daughters possessed the property permissively or independently.
The appellants did not clarify the relevant possession circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act was invoked, but the Court expressed no view on the claim's merits. It held that the claim should not be considered on an incomplete record when the possession facts material to its application had not been tried or established; those factual and legal questions could be considered in a future suit.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to determine the statutory ownership claim in the appeal and left the parties to raise it in a future suit if so advised.

rule.if: appeal_from_final_decree and new_statutory_ownership_claim and claim_not_raised_in_lower_courts and material_possession_facts_not_in_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_final_decree: The proceeding was an appeal from a final decree in a suit.
predicates.new_statutory_ownership_claim: A party advanced a statutory claim to full ownership for the first time in the appeal.
predicates.claim_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The statutory claim had not been raised before the lower courts disposed of the suit.
predicates.material_possession_facts_not_in_evidenc: The record lacked evidence establishing possession circumstances material to the statutory claim.

members.legal_issue: A valuation challenge dependent on the classification of land cannot be considered for the first time on appeal when its factual foundation was neither put in issue nor considered below.
material_facts: The appeals concerned compensation payable to landholders for land that had vested in tenants.
The appellants sought to contest whether the land was irrigated or non-irrigated for valuation purposes and raised the meaning of similar land in the valuation scheme.
The land’s nature had not been put in issue or considered in the High Court, and deciding the challenge would require an inquiry into facts not raised at the prior level.
members.legal_principle: A court will not decide on appeal a new issue requiring factual inquiry when the relevant factual foundation was not raised or considered in the court below. The Court therefore did not decide the substantive meaning of similar land under section 18(2) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the newly raised valuation issue because it required factual inquiry without a factual foundation below. The appeals were dismissed without costs.

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land transferred under a statutory purchase scheme.
predicates.land_classification_not_put_in_issue_bel: The appellant did not place the land’s relevant classification in issue before the lower court.
predicates.land_classification_not_considered_below: The lower court did not consider the land’s relevant classification.
predicates.valuation_challenge_requires_new_factual: Resolving the appellant’s valuation challenge would require a factual inquiry not undertaken below.
predicates.new_factual_valuation_challenge_not_ente: The appellate court does not entertain a valuation challenge that depends on facts not raised and considered below.

members.legal_issue: An appellant may not raise for the first time at the final appellate stage a factual objection that was not pleaded in the initial objection and was not urged in the intermediate appeal, particularly when deciding it requires factual investigation.
material_facts: The decree-holders' initial objection did not dispute that the mortgagees under the earlier and later mortgages were the same for purposes of the judgment debtors' accounts.
The trial court found that the mortgagees were the same as regards the judgment debtors.
Although the decree-holders alleged in their intermediate appeal that the mortgagees differed, they did not specifically urge that contention there.
The contention would have required investigation into the facts and was raised at the final appellate stage.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances, it was not right to allow a factual question requiring investigation to be raised at the final appellate stage when it had not been pleaded in the objection and had not been urged before the intermediate appellate court.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the decree-holders to raise the factual contention at that stage.

rule.if: final_appeal and factual_objection_requires_investigation and not pleaded_in_initial_objection and not urged_in_intermediate_appeal

predicates.final_appeal: The matter is before a court hearing the final appeal.
predicates.factual_objection_requires_investigation: The objection depends on disputed facts that require investigation.
predicates.pleaded_in_initial_objection: The appellant included the factual objection in its initial objection to the relief application.
predicates.urged_in_intermediate_appeal: The appellant specifically argued the factual objection before the intermediate appellate court.
predicates.final_appellate_court_refuses_new_factua: The final appellate court does not allow the appellant to raise the factual objection at that stage.

members.legal_issue: A budget objection that was not raised below and requires factual investigation cannot be entertained for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The contention that the local body could not impose taxes without a proper budget was not raised in the High Court.
Determining whether a budget had been prepared would require investigation of facts.
members.legal_principle: The Court would not consider on appeal an objection that was not made in the High Court and that required factual investigation.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the budget objection.

predicates.civil_tax_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning a local body’s tax levy.
predicates.budget_objection_not_raised_below: The party did not raise its objection about the local body’s budget in the court below.
predicates.budget_objection_requires_fact_inquiry: Resolving the budget objection requires investigation of facts.

members.legal_issue: A new factual contention about the character of land is not entertained on appeal when it was not raised in the pleadings or at trial.
material_facts: The claim that some of the land consisted of tank beds was not made in the pleadings or at any stage in the trial court.
Some records described land as “puramboke,” but the contention depended on a factual issue raised for the first time on appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered it unfair to permit a fresh contention concerning a question of fact to be raised at that stage. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the new factual contention that some of the land consisted of tank beds.

predicates.appeal_involving_land_classification: The appeal involves classification of land.
predicates.factual_contention_not_raised_in_pleadin: A party raises a factual contention on appeal that was not raised in the pleadings or at trial.

members.legal_issue: A contention not raised in the court below and not investigated there cannot be advanced for the first time on appeal in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The appellants argued on appeal that the replacement declaration was invalid because it followed the earlier notification under section 4 after unreasonable delay.
The appellants had not raised that contention in the High Court, and the question had not been put in issue or investigated there.
An injunction had restrained further acquisition steps for some time, but the appellate court did not decide whether the delay was unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a contention raised for the first time on appeal where it had not been put in issue or investigated in the court below. It expressly left undecided whether a declaration under section 6 must be issued without unreasonable delay after a notification under section 4.
members.conclusion: The appellants could not raise the unreasonable-delay contention for the first time on appeal; the Court expressed no opinion on whether the Government was required to act without unreasonable delay.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_appeal: An appeal challenges steps taken to acquire land.
predicates.delay_ground_not_raised_below: The appellant did not raise the claim of unreasonable delay in the court below.
predicates.delay_ground_not_investigated_below: The court below did not investigate the claim of unreasonable delay.

members.legal_issue: A limitation objection raised for the first time on appeal cannot be determined without the relevant factual materials and where the lower court has not considered it.
material_facts: The appellant argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that the cause of action had arisen long before the suit and that the suit and counterclaim were time-barred.
The limitation issue had not been raised before the lower court and had not been examined there.
The Court stated that limitation, if raised, should be decided after the date of accrual of the cause of action is determined from relevant materials.
members.legal_principle: Whether a claim is barred by limitation depends on determining the accrual date of the cause of action from relevant materials; the Court did not decide the limitation contention raised for the first time on appeal.
members.conclusion: The Court expressed no opinion on the limitation contention and left it to be decided on relevant materials.

predicates.limitation_objection_first_raised_on_app: A party raises a limitation objection for the first time before the appellate court.
predicates.lower_court_did_not_consider_limitation: The lower court did not examine the limitation objection.
predicates.accrual_date_requires_relevant_materials: Determining when the cause of action accrued requires consideration of relevant factual materials.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the contents of an eviction notice raised for the first time on appeal cannot be entertained when it is not a pure question of law and the notice is absent from the record.
material_facts: The occupant argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that the notice did not specify the required grounds for eviction.
The issue had not been raised before the authority or the courts below and depended on the notice's contents rather than on a pure question of law.
The occupant did not produce a copy of the notice.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the U.P. Land (Eviction and Recovery of Rent and Damages) Act, 1959 requires the notice to specify the grounds for proposed eviction. A challenge dependent on the notice's contents, not raised below and not a pure question of law, need not be considered for the first time on appeal where the notice is not in the record. In those circumstances, the maxim omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta applies, and regularity of the notice may be presumed.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the challenge and presumed that the notice specified the public purpose for the proposed eviction.

rule.if: appeal_from_eviction_order and notice_challenge_raised_first_on_appeal and challenge_not_pure_question_of_law and notice_copy_absent

predicates.appeal_from_eviction_order: The case is an appeal arising from an eviction proceeding.
predicates.notice_challenge_raised_first_on_appeal: The occupant challenges the notice's contents for the first time on appeal.
predicates.challenge_not_pure_question_of_law: Deciding the challenge requires examining facts or material beyond a pure question of law.
predicates.notice_copy_absent: The notice whose contents are challenged is not produced in the record.

members.legal_issue: A mixed question of fact and law that was not argued before the High Court cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal.
material_facts: The appellants argued that delay in making the award caused the acquisition proceedings to lapse.
The High Court's order did not address that contention, and the Supreme Court treated it as not having been argued there.
members.legal_principle: The Court considers matters dealt with or stated in the High Court's order and will not permit a party to raise a mixed question of fact and law or a disputed question for the first time in an appeal. The Court also stated that it could not look to affidavits filed before it to establish that the issue had been raised below.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not permit the appellants to raise the contention for the first time in the appeal.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal from a lower court's decision.
predicates.issue_not_decided_below: The lower court's order does not deal with the issue.
predicates.mixed_or_disputed_issue: The issue depends on mixed facts and law or on disputed facts.

members.legal_issue: A contention not raised in the pleadings or in the appeals before the lower courts cannot be advanced for the first time in the further appeal in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the tenant’s failure to sue for recovery of possession within the prescribed period had extinguished his right and title.
That contention had not been raised in the appellants’ written statement or in the grounds of their appeals before the lower courts.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain the contention because it had not been raised in the pleadings or in the grounds of appeal before the lower courts.
members.conclusion: The appellants could not canvass that contention for the first time in the further appeal.

predicates.further_appeal: The proceeding is a further appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.contention_not_raised_in_pleadings_or_lo: The party did not raise the contention in its pleadings or in its appeals before the lower courts.
predicates.new_contention_not_entertained: The party is not permitted to advance the contention for the first time in the further appeal.

members.legal_issue: A limitation plea that was not raised in the trial court or first appellate court and presents a mixed question of law and fact cannot be examined for the first time in a second appeal.
material_facts: The limitation plea had not been raised before either the trial court or the first appellate court.
The plea involved a mixed question of law and fact.
members.legal_principle: A mixed question of law and fact that was not raised in the lower courts cannot be examined for the first time in a second appeal. The High Court referred to the Limitation Act, 1963, but the Supreme Court did not decide the limitation issue on its merits. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The limitation plea could not be examined for the first time in the second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.limitation_issue_not_raised_in_lower_cou: The party did not raise the limitation issue before the trial court or the first appellate court.
predicates.limitation_issue_is_mixed_question_of_la: Deciding the limitation issue requires consideration of both law and facts.

members.legal_issue: A mixed question of law and fact that was not pleaded or raised in the lower courts cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal under special leave.
material_facts: The party invoked a statutory restriction on transfers for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal.
The party had not raised that plea before the trial court, the first appellate court, or the High Court, and had not laid a foundation for it in the pleadings.
The plea was a mixed question of law and fact.
members.legal_principle: A party must lay a foundation in the pleadings for a plea, particularly when it is a mixed question of law and fact. The Supreme Court, as the last appellate court, declined to permit such a plea to be raised for the first time under Article 136 of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The party could not raise the statutory-restriction plea for the first time in the appeal under Article 136.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and issue_not_raised_in_lower_courts and no_pleading_foundation_for_issue and issue_is_mixed_question_of_law_and_fact

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought under special leave to the Supreme Court.
predicates.issue_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The party did not raise the issue before the trial court, the first appellate court, or the High Court.
predicates.no_pleading_foundation_for_issue: The party did not set out a factual foundation for the issue in the pleadings.
predicates.issue_is_mixed_question_of_law_and_fact: Deciding the issue requires consideration of both law and facts.

members.legal_issue: A factual contention that was neither pleaded nor raised in the first appeal cannot properly be introduced for the first time in a second appeal.
material_facts: In the second appeal, the tenant contended that the landlord had rented out several ground-floor rooms shortly before filing the eviction petition.
That contention had not been specifically pleaded or raised in the first appeal.
members.legal_principle: The court upheld the conclusion that it was not proper to introduce in a second appeal a factual contention that had not been specifically pleaded or raised in the first appeal.
members.conclusion: The High Court rightly declined to entertain the contention in the second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter is before a court in a second appeal.
predicates.contention_not_specifically_pleaded: The factual contention was not specifically included in the pleadings.
predicates.contention_not_raised_in_first_appeal: The factual contention was not raised in the first appeal.

members.legal_issue: A new factual theory inconsistent with the pleaded case need not be entertained for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The written defence asserted that the properties were the religious head’s personal property and denied that any dedication or trust existed.
In the Supreme Court, the appellant advanced a different factual theory that some properties had been dedicated to a private trust.
The new theory depended on factual matters about dedication and the accounts, rather than being a purely legal contention.
members.legal_principle: A party cannot replace its pleaded factual case with a materially inconsistent factual theory at a later stage when that theory depends on facts the party knew or should have addressed. The Court rejected the argument that the new theory was purely legal because it essentially raised questions of fact.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the new factual plea.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The court is considering a party’s appeal from a lower-court decision.
predicates.new_factual_theory_is_inconsistent_with_: The party advances a factual case on appeal that materially differs from the case set out in its pleadings.
predicates.theory_depends_on_untried_facts: The new theory requires factual determinations that were not presented and tried as part of the pleaded case.

members.legal_issue: Falsehood or discrepancy in a witness’s evidence does not automatically require rejection of the whole testimony, but inseparable material discrepancies that destroy credibility may make the evidence unusable.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses gave materially conflicting accounts about the occurrence, the pathway and wall, the injuries to the accused, and the circumstances surrounding the first report.
The Court found that the prosecution evidence did not inspire confidence and that its material parts could not reliably be separated into credible and incredible portions.
The Court also found that the evidence as a whole was insufficient to establish the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a strict rule of Indian criminal law; courts generally sift reliable evidence from unreliable evidence, treating the principle as a rule of caution. Where material discrepancies undermine the witness’s credibility and the evidence cannot be separated without making it unacceptable, the court may reject it. The Court relied on Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, (2019) 8 SCC 50, and referred to Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand, (2013) 4 SCC 422.
members.conclusion: The evidence could not be salvaged by separating reliable portions from unreliable ones because the material discrepancies and suppression affected its credibility as a whole.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_witness_testimo: The prosecution relies on witness testimony to prove the accused’s guilt.
predicates.material_discrepancies_destroy_witness_c: The witnesses’ important contradictions or falsehoods undermine confidence in their accounts.
predicates.testimony_cannot_be_separated_into_relia: The credible parts of the testimony cannot be distinguished from the unreliable parts without making the evidence unacceptable.
predicates.inseparable_testimony_cannot_support_con: The inseparable testimony cannot provide a reliable basis for conviction.

members.legal_issue: An accused’s examination answers may be considered with the prosecution evidence, but they cannot alone supply the basis for conviction.
material_facts: The accused argued that answers given during examination under the criminal procedure code could not form the basis for conviction.
The prosecution had produced independent oral and documentary evidence establishing the chain of events.
The Court considered the accused’s answers alongside that prosecution evidence.
members.legal_principle: Answers given by an accused during examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, may be relevant for the court’s consideration, particularly where the prosecution has established the chain of events; they are not the sole basis for conviction in this case.
members.conclusion: The accused’s answers were a relevant consideration because the prosecution had independently established the chain of events.

predicates.criminal_case_under_review: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the evidential value of the accused’s examination answers is disputed.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_establishes_chain_o: Evidence independent of the accused’s answers establishes the sequence of events supporting the prosecution case.
predicates.accused_examination_answers_are_consider: The court assesses the accused’s answers alongside, rather than instead of, the prosecution evidence.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for forgery cannot be sustained on an unacceptable accomplice account that lacks material corroboration connecting the accused to the alleged forgery.
material_facts: The conviction concerned pattas alleged to have been forged as valuable securities.
The approver was the principal witness linking the appellant to the alleged forgery, but the Court found his account unimpressive and not trustworthy.
The pattas bore the appellant’s own signatures, and the evidence did not reliably establish that the other purported signatures were forged.
The Court found no corroboration of the approver’s account in material particulars connecting the appellant with the forgery.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act, an accomplice is competent to testify and a conviction on uncorroborated accomplice evidence is not legally invalid; however, the rule of prudence ordinarily requires corroboration in material particulars connecting the accused with the crime. The court must first assess the accomplice’s testimony on its own, and corroboration is unnecessary only where it is safe to dispense with it. For the forgery charge, Sections 463 and 467 of the Penal Code concern making a false document with the specified intent and punishment for forgery of a valuable security; Section 30 defines valuable security. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The conviction for forgery was unsustainable on the evidence and was quashed.

rule.if: appeal_from_forgery_conviction and conviction_depends_on_accomplice and approver_testimony_unacceptable and no_material_corroboration_connects_accused

predicates.appeal_from_forgery_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a conviction for forgery.
predicates.conviction_depends_on_accomplice: The conviction linking the accused to the forgery depends on testimony from an accomplice.
predicates.approver_testimony_unacceptable: The court finds the accomplice’s account intrinsically unconvincing or untrustworthy.
predicates.no_material_corroboration_connects_accus: There is no reliable supporting evidence in material particulars connecting the accused to the alleged forgery.

members.legal_issue: A conspiracy conviction cannot be sustained when the sole supporting accomplice account is unconvincing and uncorroborated, and the alleged acts in furtherance of the common criminal purpose have not been established.
material_facts: The only direct evidence of conspiracy was the approver’s testimony.
The Court had found the approver’s account concerning the alleged forgery unconvincing and did not accept it as reliable proof of the conspiracy.
The alleged acts said to have been done in furtherance of the conspiracy were not accepted by the Court as established criminal acts.
The approver’s account of the conspiracy was uncorroborated.
members.legal_principle: Conspiracy is generally proved by inference because direct independent evidence is seldom available, but the inference is ordinarily drawn from acts of the parties in pursuance of an apparent criminal purpose shared between them. An accomplice is competent to prove conspiracy, but the court applies the same caution concerning the reliability and corroboration of accomplice evidence. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The conspiracy charge could not be sustained, and the appellant’s conviction was quashed.

rule.if: appeal_from_conspiracy_conviction and only_approver_evidence and approver_account_unconvincing and no_accepted_common_purpose_acts

predicates.appeal_from_conspiracy_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a conviction for conspiracy.
predicates.only_approver_evidence: The accomplice’s testimony is the only direct evidence offered to prove the alleged conspiracy.
predicates.approver_account_unconvincing: The court finds the accomplice’s account of the alleged conspiracy unconvincing.
predicates.no_accepted_common_purpose_acts: The court does not accept as established acts showing pursuit of an apparent criminal purpose shared by the alleged conspirators.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand where the evidence against the accused is materially undermined by contradictions in key witnesses’ accounts and does not establish the prosecution’s essential case.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses who were the deceased’s brother and father said in court that they had received no information about the death and had not made the police statements attributed to them.
A police officer testified that he had recorded those statements, in which the witnesses had said they were present at the cremation.
The court considered that, even if no police statements had been recorded, the witnesses’ accounts first given in court had limited evidentiary value.
The evidence against the appellant was almost identical to that against relatives who had been acquitted, and the court found the essential elements of the prosecution case unproved.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the evidence cumulatively. It treated the police officer’s evidence as contradicting the witnesses’ denial of their statements under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and observed that, if their accounts had first been given in court, they would have had much reduced evidentiary value. The court also considered the similarity between the evidence against the appellant and the evidence against relatives acquitted of the same charge.
members.conclusion: On the cumulative evidence, the appellant’s conviction was set aside and he was acquitted.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_dowry_death_convict: The case is a criminal appeal from a conviction for a dowry-related death offence.
predicates.key_witness_accounts_contradicted_by_pol: Key witnesses gave accounts in court that conflicted with police statements, and a police officer testified about recording those statements.
predicates.essential_prosecution_elements_unproved: The evidence did not establish essential elements of the prosecution’s case.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for demanding dowry cannot safely rest on unreliable, materially improved testimony and inconclusive handwriting evidence that lacks substantial independent corroboration.
material_facts: The complainant was the sole witness to the alleged demands made directly by the accused and had made no mention of important alleged demands in earlier complaints or the first information report.
The complainant's account included material improvements and inconsistencies, and the other persons said to have witnessed the demands were not examined.
The handwriting expert could not give a definite opinion linking the accused to the disputed letters, and the complainant did not establish a basis for being familiar with the accused's handwriting.
The evidence did not reliably establish that the accused himself made a dowry demand, although a demand by his brother was established.
members.legal_principle: An accused is presumed innocent, and guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A handwriting expert's opinion is opinion evidence and ordinarily cannot safely support conviction without substantial corroboration: Magan Bihari Lal v. State of Punjab, Ram Chandra v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Ishwari Prasad v. Md. Isa, Shashi Kumar v. Subodh Kumar, and Fakhruddin v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Under Sections 67, 47, 45, and 73 of the Evidence Act, a document may be proved through a qualified witness familiar with the handwriting, expert opinion, comparison, or other recognized modes, but the evidence must be sufficiently persuasive. A witness's unsupported assertion of familiarity does not establish competence to identify handwriting, and inconclusive expert evidence requires reliable corroboration.
members.conclusion: The prosecution did not prove the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt, and the conviction and sentence were set aside.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_dowry_demand_conviction and sole_material_witness_materially_improved_or_unreliable and (material_witnesses_not_examined or no_independent_corroboration) and handwriting_opinion_inconclusive and witness_handwriting_familiarity_unestablished and direct_demand_by_accused_unproved

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_dowry_demand_convic: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for demanding dowry.
predicates.sole_material_witness_materially_improve: The prosecution relies on one material witness whose account contains material improvements or inconsistencies that undermine reliability.
predicates.material_witnesses_not_examined: People said to have witnessed the alleged demand are not examined at trial.
predicates.no_independent_corroboration: The material evidence is not supported by substantial independent corroboration.
predicates.handwriting_opinion_inconclusive: A handwriting expert cannot give a definite opinion identifying the accused as the author of disputed documents.
predicates.witness_handwriting_familiarity_unestabl: A witness asserting familiarity with the accused's handwriting does not establish a reliable basis for that familiarity.
predicates.direct_demand_by_accused_unproved: The evidence does not reliably establish that the accused personally made the alleged demand.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot safely stand when the prosecution evidence is unreliable and the courts below have overlooked material infirmities in assessing it.
material_facts: The earliest written report did not specify the place of occurrence, and the police record and witness evidence gave inconsistent indications about its location.
The report was lodged several hours after the occurrence, despite the witnesses being at a hospital close to the police station; the Court rejected the explanation for the delay.

The medical officer had sent an earlier intimation to the police, but the investigating officer denied knowing about it and gave an account of his actions that conflicted with other witnesses’ evidence.

The witnesses had a history of hostility and criminal cases involving the opposing side; their accounts were inconsistent, one witness did not implicate all the accused, and the evidence of the injured witness was also found unreliable.
The lower courts accepted the prosecution witnesses’ accounts without adequately addressing the significant inconsistencies and infirmities.
members.legal_principle: A conviction must rest on cogent, reliable, and trustworthy evidence; evidence that falls short of reliability and acceptability is unsafe to act upon. In this criminal appeal under Article 136, the Court could set aside the convictions where the lower courts’ assessment overlooked manifest errors and glaring infirmities.
members.conclusion: The prosecution evidence fell short of reliability and acceptability, making it unsafe to act upon; the charges were not established by cogent, reliable, and trustworthy evidence. The Court set aside the convictions and sentences and acquitted the appellants.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_unreliable: The prosecution evidence contains serious credibility problems, including material inconsistencies, unexplained delay, or unreliable witness testimony.
predicates.material_infirmities_overlooked: The courts below failed to address material errors or glaring weaknesses in the evidence.

members.legal_issue: Contradictions on central events can render eyewitness testimony unreliable and prevent proof of guilt through the last-seen theory and circumstantial evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on three witnesses to establish that the child was taken towards a field and that the accused was later seen leaving it.
The witnesses gave conflicting accounts of how the first report was made and written, where the body was found and taken, and when and where the inquest occurred.
The witnesses also gave inconsistent accounts of the victim’s clothing and whether it bore blood.
The prosecution relied on these witnesses to establish the last-seen circumstance, while the accused raised a defence of false implication arising from a property dispute.
members.legal_principle: Under the five principles in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, circumstances relied on for a circumstantial conviction must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive, exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence, and form a complete chain. The prosecution must first establish that the victim was last seen with the accused before invoking the rule concerning facts especially within the accused’s knowledge under Section 106 of the Evidence Act. Evidence must be assessed for its quality, with careful scrutiny of material contradictions.
members.conclusion: The contradictions on important matters made the testimony of the principal witnesses untrustworthy; the prosecution did not establish the last-seen circumstance or an unbroken chain of circumstances, and could not rely on the accused’s burden to explain facts especially within his knowledge.

predicates.circumstantial_evidence_conviction_appea: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction based on circumstantial evidence.
predicates.prosecution_relies_on_last_seen_evidence: The prosecution relies on evidence that the victim was last seen with the accused to connect the accused to the offence.
predicates.witnesses_give_materially_conflicting_ac: Prosecution witnesses give materially conflicting accounts about events central to the alleged offence or investigation.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot be sustained when the prosecution presents mutually contradictory sets of evidence that undermine each other’s reliability and leave no reliable evidence on which to base the conviction.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the testimony of the deceased’s sons and brother and his dying declaration, but relied on the testimony of another alleged eyewitness to convict two accused.
The High Court relied on both sets of eyewitness evidence to convict those accused of murder.

The sons’ and brother’s account of where they were when the assault began differed from the deceased’s account in his dying declaration, and the other eyewitness’s testimony indicated that they had not seen the occurrence.
The deceased’s dying declaration did not mention the other eyewitness, and the testimony of the sons and brother indicated that he had not witnessed the occurrence.
The prosecution’s own evidence thus cast doubt on the reliability of each set of eyewitness evidence, leaving no reliable and trustworthy evidence on which to sustain the convictions.
members.legal_principle: A criminal conviction must rest on reliable and trustworthy evidence. Although a conviction may be based on the testimony of a single witness if that testimony is convincing and reliable, that principle does not support a conviction when other prosecution evidence itself undermines the witness’s reliability. The Court referred to and distinguished Vadivalu Thevar v. The State of Madras, [1957] S.C.R. 981.
members.conclusion: The convictions could not be sustained. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the appellants were acquitted.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and prosecution_presented_two_sets_of_evidence and each_set_contradicted_the_other and each_set_undermined_the_other_reliability and no_reliable_evidence_remained_to_support_conviction

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by a person challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.prosecution_presented_two_sets_of_eviden: The prosecution relied on two distinct sets of evidence to establish the accused’s guilt.
predicates.each_set_contradicted_the_other: Each set of prosecution evidence conflicted with the account or implications of the other set.
predicates.each_set_undermined_the_other_reliabilit: The conflicts in the prosecution evidence cast doubt on the reliability of each set.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_remained_to_support: After considering the conflicts, no reliable and trustworthy evidence remained on which to base the conviction.

members.legal_issue: The conviction could not stand where the prosecution evidence had substantial credibility defects that the appellate court did not adequately address.
material_facts: The trial court found conflicting accounts about whether an earlier report had been made and when the formal report was recorded; the record did not establish when the report was sent to or received by the Magistrate.

Witnesses gave materially discrepant accounts of the alleged oral dying declarations, and the doctor said the deceased would likely have become unconscious within 10 to 15 minutes of sustaining their injuries.
The alleged recipients of the dying declarations had serious enmity with the accused.
The sole eyewitness did not tell family members about the incident after returning to the village and then hid for a period, conduct the trial court considered unnatural.
The High Court relied on the declarations and eyewitness account without adequately meeting the trial court’s reasons for doubting them.
members.legal_principle: A dying declaration must be assessed cautiously, including whether its maker was physically capable of making it and whether it represented the true state of affairs. An oral declaration to a person with serious enmity against the accused warrants hesitation and reservation. Material inconsistencies, medical evidence bearing on consciousness, and unnatural witness conduct are relevant to credibility. The absence of evidence about dispatch or receipt of the report by the Magistrate was also relevant under Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. No earlier cases are cited for these principles.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was erroneous; the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and restored the acquittal.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction_after_reversal_of_acquittal and (report_timing_conflicted and magistrate_report_transmission_unproved) and (declaration_accounts_inconsistent and medical_evidence_limits_consciousness) and declaration_recipient_hostile and sole_witness_conduct_unnatural and trial_reasons_unaddressed

predicates.appeal_from_conviction_after_reversal_of: The proceeding challenges a conviction entered after an appellate court reversed an acquittal.
predicates.report_timing_conflicted: The prosecution accounts or records materially conflict about whether or when the first report was made.
predicates.magistrate_report_transmission_unproved: The evidence does not establish when the report was sent to or received by the Magistrate.
predicates.declaration_accounts_inconsistent: Witnesses give materially different accounts of the alleged oral dying declaration.
predicates.medical_evidence_limits_consciousness: Medical evidence indicates that the injuries could have rendered the declarant unconscious before the alleged statement was made.
predicates.declaration_recipient_hostile: A recipient of the alleged declaration has serious enmity with the accused.
predicates.sole_witness_conduct_unnatural: The sole eyewitness behaves in a way the fact-finder considers inconsistent with the claimed presence or account of the incident.
predicates.trial_reasons_unaddressed: The appellate court does not adequately address material reasons given by the trial court for doubting the prosecution evidence.

members.legal_issue: Convictions cannot stand where the evidence against the accused is not safely reliable, lacks independent corroboration, and leaves a reasonable doubt about their participation.
material_facts: The evidence against the four persons attributed only that they surrounded the injured persons and thereby assisted the assault.
The trial court had identified reasons to doubt the independence of the eyewitnesses, and the appellate court did not address all those reasons.
The witnesses did not mention the injuries found on an accused, making it unsafe to rely on their testimony about the four persons without corroboration.
No circumstantial or other reliable evidence independently corroborated the witnesses’ account of those persons’ participation.
Evidence of local factional divisions supported a doubt about whether those persons had been falsely implicated.
members.legal_principle: The convictions under Sections 325/149, 323/149 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code required reliable evidence connecting the accused to the unlawful assembly and the assault. Where the witnesses were not fully independent, their account omitted injuries to an accused, and no independent reliable evidence corroborated the alleged participation, it was unsafe to sustain the convictions in the face of a subsisting doubt. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The convictions of the four persons whose participation was supported only by the unsafe and uncorroborated evidence were set aside, and they were acquitted.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and participation_based_on_witnesses and witnesses_not_fully_independent and witnesses_omitted_accused_injuries and not independent_corroboration_available and factional_doubt_present

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The convicted persons brought an appeal challenging their convictions.
predicates.participation_based_on_witnesses: The alleged participation of the accused was based on witnesses’ accounts.
predicates.witnesses_not_fully_independent: The evidence disclosed reasons to doubt that the witnesses were fully independent.
predicates.witnesses_omitted_accused_injuries: The witnesses did not mention injuries found on an accused.
predicates.independent_corroboration_available: Reliable circumstantial or other evidence independently supported the account of the accused’s participation.
predicates.factional_doubt_present: Evidence of factional divisions supported a doubt about whether the accused had been falsely implicated.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot safely rest on the uncorroborated testimony of an interested and partisan eyewitness when that testimony is materially unreliable and available material corroboration is withheld.
material_facts: The prosecution case rested on the sole eyewitness, who was related to the deceased and involved in civil litigation with the accused.
The eyewitness gave materially inaccurate or inconsistent evidence about the land dispute, possession of the land, and events surrounding the occurrence.
Another person identified as an eyewitness was not examined, and other available witnesses who could have corroborated the eyewitness were also not called.
The eyewitness said that his clothes became bloodstained while moving the deceased, but those clothes were neither produced nor seized.
The High Court disbelieved the recoveries of the weapons and clothes, leaving the eyewitness without that corroboration.
The circumstances, including the absence of an immediate provocation, cast further doubt on the prosecution account.
members.legal_principle: An accused is presumed innocent, and the prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence of a sole witness who is interested or partisan must be scrutinized with great care and caution; where material witnesses capable of corroboration are available but not examined, and the remaining evidence does not inspire confidence, a conviction is unsafe. The convictions had been entered under Sections 148 and 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, but the Court's decision rested on the failure of proof. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness's evidence did not inspire confidence and was unsafe to rely on without corroboration. The prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, so the convictions were set aside and the accused were acquitted.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and sole_witness_is_interested_or_partisan and (sole_witness_has_material_credibility_problems or available_material_witnesses_are_not_examined) and corroboration_is_absent_or_unreliable

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.sole_witness_is_interested_or_partisan: The prosecution relies on a sole eyewitness who has a relationship or enmity that may affect impartiality.
predicates.sole_witness_has_material_credibility_pr: The sole eyewitness gives materially inaccurate or inconsistent evidence about relevant circumstances.
predicates.available_material_witnesses_are_not_exa: The prosecution does not examine available witnesses who could materially corroborate its account.
predicates.corroboration_is_absent_or_unreliable: Other evidence that might corroborate the sole eyewitness is absent or has been disbelieved.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot be sustained where the prosecution’s eyewitness account, dependent on closely connected witnesses, is materially inconsistent and unsupported by independent evidence.
material_facts: The principal eyewitnesses were related to one another and to the deceased, and the two groups had a longstanding property dispute.

The witness who said he arrived first initially told police that he saw the accused fleeing, but testified at trial that he had witnessed the assault; the other witnesses said they arrived later and saw the assault in progress.
No independent villager who had gone to the scene was examined as an eyewitness.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Evidence from related witnesses is not thereby inadmissible, but where the circumstances warrant it, their testimony must be scrutinized with due care; material inconsistencies and the absence of independent support may leave the prosecution case unproved. No earlier case or specific provision is relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness testimony was not sufficiently credible to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the courts below erred by failing to scrutinize it with due care and caution.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and (key_eyewitnesses_are_close_relatives or witnesses_have_prior_family_hostility) and eyewitness_accounts_materially_conflict and no_independent_eyewitness_supports_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.key_eyewitnesses_are_close_relatives: The principal eyewitnesses who support the prosecution account are closely related to one another or to the person harmed.
predicates.witnesses_have_prior_family_hostility: The witnesses and the accused group had a longstanding dispute that could bear on the reliability of the account.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_materially_conflict: The witnesses give materially inconsistent accounts about what they saw or when they arrived.
predicates.no_independent_eyewitness_supports_accou: No independent person who was present at or went to the scene supports the prosecution’s eyewitness account.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot safely rest on the uncorroborated testimony of a very young child witness when the circumstances materially undermine the reliability of that testimony.
material_facts: The prosecution relied principally on the testimony of a child who was about six years old at the time of the incident and said he had witnessed the assault.
The child’s testimony was recorded long after the incident, leaving an opportunity for tutoring; the trial judge observed that he vacillated and sometimes failed to understand questions.

The prosecution did not call the child’s maternal uncle, the first person said to have met him after the incident, and there was no clear evidence that the child had disclosed the assailants’ names to his father.

The child said that after seeing his mother assaulted he went back to sleep, and the prosecution’s account of his presence and conduct was not independently confirmed in a way that established he had witnessed and recognized the assailants.
members.legal_principle: A child is competent to testify, but the court must evaluate a child’s evidence carefully because the child may be susceptible to tutoring. Where the testimony is doubtful or there is a possibility of tutoring, adequate corroboration should be sought before relying on it for conviction. The Court relied on Panchhi v. State of U.P. (1998) 7 SCC 177 and State of Assam v. Mafizuddin Ahmed (1983) 2 SCC 14.
members.conclusion: The child’s testimony was too unreliable, without adequate corroboration, to support the conviction.

rule.if: criminal_case and child_is_sole_material_eyewitness and child_is_very_young and (opportunity_for_tutoring_exists or testimony_has_material_reliability_concerns) and not adequate_corroboration_exists

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the reliability of a witness’s testimony bears on guilt.
predicates.child_is_sole_material_eyewitness: The prosecution relies on a child as its only material eyewitness to the alleged crime.
predicates.child_is_very_young: The eyewitness was of an age at which limited maturity of understanding may affect the reliability of the account.
predicates.opportunity_for_tutoring_exists: A substantial interval or other circumstances allowed the child to be coached before giving evidence.
predicates.testimony_has_material_reliability_conce: The child’s account or the surrounding evidence contains material omissions, unexplained conduct, or signs of uncertainty that cast doubt on reliability.
predicates.adequate_corroboration_exists: Independent evidence materially supports the child’s account of the crime and the identity of the perpetrator.

members.legal_issue: Weak recoveries, rejected conspiracy evidence, and an insufficient motive do not establish guilt when they do not reliably connect the accused to the crime.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the alleged evidence that witnesses had overheard the accused discussing a plan before and after the crime, and the higher court also did not rely on that evidence.
The alleged recoveries included ordinary, low-value household or religious articles, which the trial court considered unlikely to have been taken by the perpetrators.

The prosecution relied on a civil dispute concerning access to a shared area as a motive, but the Court considered it insufficient to explain the alleged crime and capable at most of raising suspicion.
The crime occurred in an area affected by dacoity, and the possibility that unknown criminals committed it was not excluded.
members.legal_principle: Suspicion or motive alone does not establish guilt, and weak recovery evidence cannot sustain conviction when it does not reliably connect the accused with the crime. The Court assessed these matters alongside the rejected conspiracy evidence and the possibility of unknown offenders; it cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this determination.
members.conclusion: The recoveries and motive were too weak to sustain conviction, particularly in the absence of reliable evidence connecting the accused to the crime.
