predicates.unlawful_assembly_prosecution: The prosecution alleges that the accused was a member of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_intentionally_joins_or_continues: The accused intentionally joins or remains in the assembly while aware of facts that make it unlawful.
predicates.accused_shares_common_object: The accused shares the assembly’s common object.
predicates.offence_committed_in_prosecution_of_obje: A member commits the offence in prosecution of the common object, or the offence is one the members know is likely to be committed in prosecution of it.
predicates.member_may_be_liable_without_personal_ov: The accused may be liable for the offence without proof of a personal overt act.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence for murder committed in furtherance of an unlawful assembly’s common object is not categorically barred merely because the accused did not personally commit the killing.
material_facts: The accused were convicted of murder with the aid of section 149 because members of their armed assembly committed five murders in furtherance of its common object.
Several accused carried firearms, and the courts relied on the circumstances and conduct of the assembly in imposing and confirming death sentences for those carrying firearms.
The Supreme Court held that the sentencing discretion had not been improperly exercised for the accused whose death sentences it confirmed.
members.legal_principle: Section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code permits conviction for murder based on membership in an unlawful assembly where the statutory conditions are met. There is no absolute rule that a death sentence may be imposed only on the accused who personally committed the killing; the sentence depends on the circumstances and the proper exercise of judicial discretion. Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, [1954] SCR 145, concerned appellate enhancement of a sentence and was distinguished.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected a categorical rule limiting the death sentence to the person who personally committed the murder; whether death is justified depends on the facts and circumstances of the case. It upheld the distinction made for firearm-carrying members in this case, subject to the separate modification for three young accused.

predicates.murder_conviction_under_common_object_li: The accused is convicted of murder through liability based on membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.murder_committed_by_assembly_member_in_f: An assembly member committed the murder in furtherance of the assembly’s common object.
predicates.sentencing_court_considers_case_circumst: The sentencing court considers the circumstances of the case when deciding the appropriate sentence.
predicates.death_sentence_not_categorically_limited: A death sentence is not categorically barred merely because the accused did not personally kill the victim.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons are liable for rioting while armed when the evidence establishes their participation in the assembly and assault.
material_facts: The six appellants were found to have participated in an unlawful assembly formed to assault the victim.
They were armed with deadly weapons when the assault occurred.
members.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code applies to rioting while armed with a deadly weapon or an object which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The court upheld the convictions under that provision; it noted that liability under Section 149 could have been applied to the assault offence, but that the High Court had not done so.
members.conclusion: The convictions of the six appellants for rioting while armed with deadly weapons were justified.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_proceeding: The case concerns alleged participation in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_participated_in_unlawful_assembl: The accused participated in an assembly with an unlawful common object.
predicates.accused_was_armed_with_deadly_weapon: The accused was armed with a deadly weapon or an object likely to cause death when used as a weapon of offence.

members.legal_issue: Membership in an armed unlawful assembly with the common object of killing the victim may be established by the overall, corroborated evidence, without proof of a specific overt act by every member.
material_facts: Several eyewitnesses consistently described a large armed assembly attacking the victim and dragging him while members continued beating him.

One eyewitness specifically identified the appellants whose convictions were upheld, and other witnesses corroborated material parts of his account, including threats to intervening witnesses and the manner of the assault.
The eyewitness evidence was supported by the extensive injuries and medical evidence, and, for some appellants, by recovery of blood-stained weapons or clothing.

The appellants whose convictions were upheld had additional identifying evidence connecting them to the assembly, including participation in an earlier assault arising from the same dispute or corroboration by another witness.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 141 and 149 IPC, formation of an unlawful assembly with the relevant common object permits liability to attach to its members for an offence committed in furtherance of that object; a specific overt act by each member need not be proved (Lalji v. State of U.P.). For a large assembly, evidence must be assessed for its quality and overall consistency: a wholly reliable single witness can suffice, though it is prudent to seek consistent support from more than one witness where many people witnessed the incident (Masalti v. State of U.P.; Chandra Shekhar Bind v. State of Bihar; Binay Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar). Consistency does not require every witness to repeat every accused’s name. A hostile witness’s testimony may be accepted to the extent it inspires confidence and is corroborated (Paulmeli v. State of Tamil Nadu), and relevant recovery evidence may be considered with the other evidence.
members.conclusion: The convictions of the five appellants whose participation was established beyond reasonable doubt were upheld. Once their membership in the unlawful assembly and its common object were established, proof of a particular overt act by each was unnecessary.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be held vicariously liable for a killing committed by one member when the killing furthered the assembly’s common object or was an offence the members knew was likely to be committed in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence accepted by the courts showed that more than five persons assembled with the principal assailant and came armed with lethal weapons.
The principal assailant shot and killed the deceased and also shot at the deceased’s brother.
The weapons carried and the group’s conduct supported the finding that the assembly shared an object of attacking the deceased and his brother and knew that the fatal attack was likely.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 IPC imposes vicarious liability where an offence is committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly’s common object or is an offence its members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. A prior meeting of minds or an overt act by every member is not necessary; the common object and members’ knowledge may be inferred from the assembly’s conduct, weapons, and surrounding circumstances. The Court relied on Mizaji v. State of U.P., Masalti v. State of U.P., and Pandurang Chandrakant Mhatre v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The appellants were rightly convicted for the killing with the aid of Section 149 IPC.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be convicted for grievous injuries inflicted on an injured victim when the evidence establishes their participation in the group assault.
material_facts: The injured eyewitness sustained ten injuries, including a fracture and other injuries caused by blunt weapons.
The Court found that she was present during the assault and accepted the eyewitness evidence against the appellants.
The High Court had convicted the appellants for the injuries caused to her with the aid of the unlawful-assembly rule.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code provides for liability of members of an unlawful assembly for offences committed in prosecution of its common object or known to be likely in its prosecution. The Court confirmed the convictions for grievous hurt to the injured eyewitness on the accepted evidence of the group assault and her injuries. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences for causing grievous hurt to the injured eyewitness with the aid of the unlawful-assembly rule were confirmed.

predicates.accused_participated_in_group_assault: The evidence establishes that the accused participated in the group assault.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for rioting is sustainable when the evidence establishes that the accused participated in a violent group attack while armed.
material_facts: The accepted evidence established that the appellants participated in the group attack.
The prosecution evidence described the appellants as carrying weapons during the occurrence.
members.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code concerns rioting while armed with a deadly weapon or with an instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The Court confirmed the conviction on the accepted evidence of the armed group attack. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appellants’ convictions for rioting while armed were confirmed.

predicates.accused_participated_in_violent_group_at: The evidence establishes that the accused took part in a violent group attack.
predicates.accused_were_armed: The accused carried weapons during the group attack.

members.legal_issue: Specific testimony from injured witnesses can support convictions for the assaults they describe, and group-offence convictions may be sustained where the evidence justifies applying the rules of unlawful assembly liability.
material_facts: Several witnesses had themselves been injured and gave specific accounts identifying the accused who struck them.
The Court found no shown motive for an injured witness to substitute a wrong person for the actual assailant.
The evidence supported the application of Sections 147 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code to the accused whose convictions were before the Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered an injured witness reliable as to the identity of the person who inflicted that witness's injuries, particularly where no motive to falsely substitute an assailant was shown. It held that Sections 147 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code were properly applied on the evidence in this case. No earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the convictions supported by the injured witnesses' specific accounts and held that applying Sections 147 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code to the accused was justified.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly may incur liability for an offence committed in pursuit of its shared object, or known to be likely in pursuit of that object, without proof of a separate overt act by that member.
material_facts: The accused went together to the disputed land armed with weapons while labourers harvested the complainant side’s crop.
After the complainant side objected, the accused shouted, pursued those who retreated, and carried out assaults resulting in death and injuries.
Witnesses described exhortations and acts by members of the group, and the court found the conduct established a shared object and action in concert.
members.legal_principle: Sections 141, 142, and 149 of the Indian Penal Code make membership of an unlawful assembly with a shared common object material; Section 149 does not require prior concert or a prior meeting of minds, and makes members liable for offences committed in prosecution of the common object or known to be likely in its prosecution. The court relied on Mizaji v. State of U.P., Masalti v. State of U.P., Bhajan Singh v. State of U.P., and Shri Gopal v. Subhash. It also noted, relying on Ram Tahal v. State of U.P., that Section 34 rests on common intention and is distinct from the common object required under Section 149.
members.conclusion: The evidence established collective criminal responsibility; a specific overt act by every accused was not required for liability based on membership and the shared object.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly are vicariously liable for murders committed in pursuit of its common object or which they knew were likely to be committed in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: An armed group of more than twenty people went to enforce control over the distribution of water by criminal force.
The group opened fire after members of the opposing party objected, killing four people and injuring another, who was later killed.
The victims’ bodies were dragged, dismembered and burned, and some members carried away severed heads.

The High Court found that the accused party had gone to the field armed to enforce its object by force and that those who took part in the incident also took part in moving the bodies and attempting to destroy evidence.
Five respondents whose participation in the assembly and the incident was established had been convicted of destroying evidence, but their murder convictions had been set aside.
members.legal_principle: Under section 141, fourth paragraph, of the Indian Penal Code, an assembly of five or more persons is unlawful when its common object is to deprive a person of the use of water or to enforce a right or supposed right by criminal force; under the Explanation to section 141, an assembly may become unlawful after it assembles. Under section 149, every member is liable for an offence committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object, and liability also extends to an offence the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The assembly was unlawful, and the five respondents were liable under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code for the five murders; their murder convictions were restored.

members.legal_issue: The sentence for a participant’s murder liability may reflect the participant’s prominence and active role in achieving the assembly’s common object.
material_facts: Three respondents were shown to have been armed with chopping weapons and to have decapitated the victims, severed their limbs and thrown the dismembered bodies into a fire.
The Court considered these respondents prominent members whose active participation was necessary for the assembly to achieve its common object.
The trial court had imposed death sentences, which the High Court had displaced when it set aside their murder convictions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and distinguished sentence according to the respondents’ proved roles: the three participants’ prominent and active involvement in achieving the assembly’s common object warranted restoration of the trial court’s death sentences. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The death sentences imposed on the three prominent participants were restored, along with their concurrent sentences for other offences.

members.legal_issue: Vicarious liability for an offence committed by an unlawful assembly requires the accused to be a member of the assembly when the offence is committed.
material_facts: The accused was inside the house where the victim was taken for only a short time and then left; he was not present when police entered the house.
The victim died from strangulation, but the evidence did not establish that the strangulation occurred before the accused left.
The evidence did not rule out that the strangulation occurred after the accused had left and ceased to be a member of the assembly.
members.legal_principle: Under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, the prosecution must establish that the accused was a member of the unlawful assembly when the offence was committed. The section imposes liability where an offence is committed by a member in prosecution of the assembly’s common object, or is one the members knew was likely in prosecution of that object. A person who has left and ceased to be a member before the offence is committed is not vicariously liable for a later act of the remaining members. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The accused’s conviction for murder with the aid of unlawful-assembly liability was set aside, and he was acquitted of that charge.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be held liable for offences committed in prosecution of its common object, including where the common object forms during the occurrence.
material_facts: A group of five or more persons chased and attacked the victims, killing four people and grievously injuring another.
The group’s conduct during the occurrence demonstrated a common object to commit serious offences.
The accused were found to have been members of the assembly when the offences were committed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 141 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code require an unlawful assembly of five or more persons and liability for an offence committed in prosecution of its common object, or an offence the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. The incriminating act must serve the common object or be within the members’ knowledge as a likely act: Kuldip Yadav v. State of Bihar (2011) 5 SCC 324. Common object is assessed from the circumstances, conduct and weapons of the assembly: Roy Fernandes v. State of Goa (2012) 3 SCC 221. It may form on the spur of the moment without prior concert: Ramchandran v. State of Kerala (2011) 9 SCC 257.
members.conclusion: The courts below correctly applied the law of unlawful assembly to uphold convictions for murder and attempted murder with the aid of the rule of collective liability.

members.legal_issue: Constructive liability for an offence committed by a member of an unlawful assembly depends on proof of a shared common object or the member’s positive knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence described a group of more than five armed persons arriving together, dragging the deceased from the temple and attacking him; one person also fired to prevent others from intervening.
The Court accepted the eyewitness evidence and found that the circumstances established the common object and the appellants’ membership of the assembly.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 141 and 149 IPC, mere presence in an assembly is insufficient: the accused must understand the assembly’s unlawful nature and share its common object, or have positive knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. A common object need not arise from prior concert, may develop during the incident, and may be inferred from the assembly’s conduct, weapons, and surrounding circumstances; an overt act by each member is not essential. The two branches of Section 149 must be distinguished. The Court relied on Chikkarange Gowda and others v. State of Mysore (AIR 1956 SC 731).
members.conclusion: Section 149 IPC was rightly applied to the appellants.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly may be held liable for an offence committed in prosecution of its common object even if no weapon is recovered personally from that member, where the evidence establishes participation and the required common object and knowledge.
material_facts: The accused was charged as a member of an unlawful assembly and was identified by eyewitnesses as participating in the group attack, including by striking a victim with an iron pipe.
The attack involved multiple blows with weapons, caused fatal injuries, and the evidence supported the finding that the assembly’s common object was to cause the victims’ deaths.
A weapon was not recovered personally from that accused, but the iron pipe was recovered from another accused’s house and weapons were recovered from other members of the group.
The trial court found the accused guilty as a member of the unlawful assembly, and the Supreme Court accepted the eyewitness and medical evidence implicating him.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, a court must make a clear finding about the nature and unlawful character of the assembly’s common object. The evidence must show that the offence was committed in prosecution of that object and that the other members knew or were aware that the offence was likely to be committed in its prosecution. Individual weapon recovery is not essential where the evidence otherwise establishes participation and the requirements for liability as a member of the assembly.
members.conclusion: The absence of a weapon recovery from the accused did not prevent his conviction; the evidence supported his liability as a member of the unlawful assembly.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be liable for murder when they pursue a common object by force, are prepared to use weapons if thwarted, and know that death is a likely consequence of that violence.
material_facts: The group took a longer route through several fields despite a shorter available route, causing damage to crops and making objections foreseeable.
The group’s common object was to take the carts through the fields to reach the public passage and to use force if obstructed.
Several members carried lathis and one carried a hatchet; the court concluded that the group was prepared to use those weapons if thwarted.
The victim suffered multiple injuries, including serious head wounds, and died from the injuries inflicted by the group’s concerted acts.
members.legal_principle: Under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, members of an unlawful assembly may be held liable for an offence committed in prosecution of its common object. The court concluded from the group’s weapons, readiness to use them if obstructed, and the circumstances of the chosen route that the members knew death was a likely consequence; it upheld liability for murder under section 302 read with section 149. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The group was prepared to use violence in prosecution of its common object and knew that death was a likely result of that violence. The victim’s death was caused in prosecution of the common object, making the offence murder, for which the members were liable under section 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly sharing an object to assault may be held liable for grievous hurt likely to be caused by the armed attack and for the associated rioting and assault proved against them.
material_facts: The courts found that the accused formed an unlawful assembly with a common object to assault the opposing party.
The armed group chased and assaulted members of that party, who were fleeing, and the evidence established grievous and other injuries.
The Supreme Court found the likelihood of grievous hurt and the evidence supporting the assault convictions sufficiently established.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 147 and 148 of the Indian Penal Code to rioting, and Sections 326/149 and 323 to grievous hurt and other assault. It held that where an armed unlawful assembly shares an object to assault, the likelihood of grievous hurt from the attack supports group liability for that offence. No earlier case was relied on.
members.conclusion: The convictions for rioting, grievous hurt with group liability, and the separately proved assaults were upheld.

members.legal_issue: Vicarious liability for an offence committed by an unlawful assembly requires established membership and either participation in the offence or knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed in pursuit of the assembly’s common object.
material_facts: The prosecution sought to impose liability for offences committed during a large group occurrence.
The Court distinguished those whose membership was established from people who were merely present.
The Court stated that a member’s overt act need not be proved if the member knew that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object and remained a member.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code attaches vicarious liability to a member of an unlawful assembly who participates by an overt act or knows that the offence is likely to be committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object and becomes or continues to remain a member. Mere presence does not establish membership.
members.conclusion: A member of an unlawful assembly is vicariously liable only where membership is established and the member either participates in the offence or has the requisite knowledge that it is likely to be committed in pursuit of the common object.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly is not liable for every separate assault committed during a group occurrence unless the assault was in prosecution of the common object or the member knew it was likely to occur in prosecution of that object.
material_facts: The occurrence involved a large crowd and assaults on different people at different points.
The Court found that the assembly formed to attack and beat the deceased, but that did not establish that all members shared a common object encompassing every separate assault on other people.

Some convictions for specific assaults had been imposed on other members with the aid of Section 149 despite no adequate basis to attribute those assaults to the assembly’s common object or the members’ knowledge.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, liability for an offence committed by one member extends to other members only when the offence is committed in prosecution of the common object or the other members knew it was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. A stray or separate assault in a large crowd does not, without that connection, establish such liability.
members.conclusion: The convictions for the separate assaults could not be sustained against the other accused through vicarious liability merely because they were members of the assembly.

members.legal_issue: Liability for an offence committed by members of an assembly requires proof that the assembly had a specified common object.
material_facts: The accused were among a group of at least five who were ploughing disputed land when the opposing party arrived and an altercation followed.
The prosecution evidence did not establish that the group had any of the specified common objects, either when it assembled or later.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code requires an assembly of five or more persons with a common object of a kind specified in Section 141, and the commission of an offence in prosecution of that object or one the members knew was likely. Under the explanation to Section 141, an assembly that was lawful when formed may later become unlawful, but the evidence must establish the required common object. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The convictions based on membership of an unlawful assembly could not stand because the prosecution had not proved a specified common object.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly may be liable for a killing committed in pursuit of the assembly's common object even without personally inflicting the fatal injury.
material_facts: The appellants were members of a group that came to the scene together carrying deadly weapons, including firearms carried by two members.
A member of the group began firing immediately, and the group attacked people at the scene and people who arrived to intervene.
Nine people sustained numerous injuries, and the deceased was killed during the attack.

The court found that the group's common object included causing the deceased's death, and that the appellants were members of the assembly, although they had not themselves inflicted the fatal injury.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes vicarious liability where an offence is committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly's common object, or is an offence that the members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Common object need not arise from prior concert and may form at the scene; mere presence in an assembly is insufficient unless the common object is shared. The principles are stated in Sukhbir Singh v. State of Haryana (2002) 3 SCC 327, Rajendra Shantaram Todankar v. State of Maharashtra (2003) 2 SCC 257, State of Rajasthan v. Nathu (2003) 5 SCC 537, Parsuram Pandey v. State of Bihar (2004) 13 SCC 189, and Rabindra Mahto v. State of Jharkhand, JT 2006 (1) SC 137.
members.conclusion: The appellants were properly convicted of murder with the aid of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code despite not personally causing the deceased's fatal injury.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for rioting may be affirmed when credible eyewitness testimony establishes the accused persons’ participation in an assembly that used force or violence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged convictions for rioting.
The evidence described a large armed group that used force and attacked people at the scene.
Several witnesses, including injured witnesses, identified the participants, and the trial court and High Court accepted their testimony.
The Supreme Court also accepted that testimony when assessing the related appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 147 of the Indian Penal Code concerns rioting. The Court relied on the credible eyewitness evidence, including evidence from injured witnesses, and found no infirmity in the concurrent findings of the trial court and High Court. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The convictions for rioting and the sentences imposed on the appellants in that appeal were affirmed, and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be liable for murder when a member commits the killing in pursuit of the assembly’s object or the members knew such an offence was likely in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: The accused approached the deceased together while armed with a spear, a gandasa, and lathis.

One accused restrained the deceased and urged the others to attack; another rejected the proposal to settle the dispute elsewhere, and the group then carried out a coordinated attack that caused fatal injuries.
The Court found that the accused acted together and knew the fatal consequence of their attack, even if the assembly’s original object had been only to beat the deceased.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes liability where an offence is committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly’s common object or is one the members knew to be likely in prosecution of that object. The Court relied on K.C. Mathew and Others v. State of Travancore-Cochin, [1955] 3 S.C.R. 1057, and explained that an assembly’s original object of beating may encompass a connected fatal attack when the members knew the weapons’ use was likely to cause death. It distinguished the authorities cited by the appellants, Shambhu Nath Singh v. State of Bihar, AIR 1960 SC 725, and The Queen v. Sabid Ali, 1873 Weekly Reporter (20), 5.
members.conclusion: The accused were guilty of murder read with the unlawful-assembly liability rule; the Court found no basis to reduce the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be convicted vicariously of grievous hurt even when a member’s act caused death and no person was convicted of the standalone grievous-hurt offence.
material_facts: The courts below found that the convicted accused formed an unlawful assembly whose common object was to cause grievous hurt, and that its members knew grievous hurt was likely in pursuit of that object.
One member caused the deaths of two people; the other members were found not responsible for the deaths.
The principal offender was convicted of murder, while the other convicted members were convicted of grievous hurt with the aid of the rule of unlawful-assembly liability.
No person was convicted of the standalone grievous-hurt offence.
The Supreme Court accepted the factual findings because no procedural illegality, unfair trial, or gross miscarriage of justice was shown.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes vicarious liability for an offence committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly’s common object, or for an offence members knew was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. Members’ knowledge and liability may differ. Grievous hurt is a minor offence in relation to murder, so the fact that a member committed murder does not prevent other members from being convicted of grievous hurt on the basis of the assembly’s object and their knowledge. The Court relied on Jahiruddin v. Queen Empress, ILR 22 Cal 306, and the approach in Bhagwat Singh v. Emperor, AIR 1936 Pat 481, and Sidhu Gope v. Emperor, AIR 1946 Pat 84; it rejected the contrary view in Ram Prasad Singh v. King Emperor, ILR 1 Pat 753 (AIR 1923 Pat 50), and distinguished Queen v. Sabid Ali, 20 Suth WR Cr 5 (FB).
members.conclusion: The convictions of the other members for grievous hurt through unlawful-assembly liability were legally sustainable, despite the murder conviction of the principal offender and the absence of a standalone grievous-hurt conviction; the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Participants may be convicted for offenses committed in furtherance of their common intention when a prior concerted plan is established from the circumstances, even if unlawful-assembly liability cannot be sustained.
material_facts: The remaining accused arrived together, armed, to pull down the thatch after a dispute and a threat that it should be removed.
When people resisted, the accused attacked them with weapons, causing severe injuries and the deaths of two people.
The evidence showed coordinated conduct during the attack, and the accused left the scene together.
The Court inferred a preconcerted plan to remove the thatch and to attack anyone who resisted.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies where a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. Common intention is distinct from the common object of an unlawful assembly and requires action in concert and a plan that precedes the act constituting the offense. The plan may develop at the scene, but it must exist before the relevant act. Common intention may be inferred from the totality of circumstances, including how the accused arrived and attacked, the coordinated nature of the injuries, assistance by other participants, and their conduct after the offense. The Court relied on Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Krishna Govind Patil v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The remaining accused were guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder and attempted murder under common-intention liability; those convictions replaced the convictions based on unlawful-assembly liability.

predicates.criminal_case_involving_joint_participat: The proceeding concerns offenses allegedly committed through the joint participation of multiple accused.
predicates.group_arrived_together_armed_to_carry_ou: The accused arrived together, armed, to carry out a shared objective.
predicates.participants_attacked_people_who_resiste: The accused attacked people who resisted their shared objective.
predicates.coordinated_conduct_supports_a_prior_pla: The manner of arrival, conduct during the attack, assistance among participants, or conduct afterward supports an inference that a common plan existed before the relevant criminal acts.
predicates.remaining_participants_are_convictable_f: The remaining participants may be convicted for offenses committed in furtherance of their common intention.

members.legal_issue: An assembly that begins lawfully may become an unlawful assembly when its members respond to a call to assault a person, even without prior concert.
material_facts: The courts found that the accused arrived with a large group of labourers and armed men while paddy was being cut.
When the complainant came to protest, one accused called for an assault and the others chased him in response.
The complainant was then assaulted.
The courts below had not established which side possessed the disputed land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 141 of the Indian Penal Code, including its Explanation, an assembly lawful at its inception may subsequently become unlawful, and previous concert is unnecessary. The common object under Section 141 differs from the common intention under Section 34. An unlawful act by one or two members does not change the character of an assembly if the others do not acquiesce. The Court relied on the statement of the principle in Ratanlal's Law of Crimes.
members.conclusion: The assembly became unlawful when the members responded to the call and chased the complainant; prior concert was not required.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and assembly_gathered_for_another_purpose and member_called_for_assault and members_chased_in_response and victim_was_assaulted

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a criminal conviction.

predicates.member_called_for_assault: A member of the group called for the victim to be assaulted.
predicates.members_chased_in_response: Other members chased the victim in response to that call.
predicates.victim_was_assaulted: The victim was assaulted by members of the group.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly who is armed with and uses a spear may be convicted under the provision governing rioting while armed with a deadly weapon.
material_facts: The assembly became unlawful when members chased the complainant in response to a call for assault.
One accused was armed with a spear and used it to injure the complainant.
members.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code applies to rioting by a person armed with a deadly weapon. Once the assembly was unlawful, the accused's being armed with and using a spear brought his case within that section.
members.conclusion: The conviction under Section 148 of the Indian Penal Code was upheld.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.person_was_member_of_unlawful_assembly: The person was a member of an unlawful assembly that engaged in rioting.
predicates.person_was_armed_with_deadly_weapon: The person was armed with a deadly weapon while participating in the rioting.

members.legal_issue: A common object under the unlawful-assembly provision may arise after people have assembled for a lawful purpose, without prior concert, if five or more people come to share an unlawful object and act together to achieve it.
material_facts: People gathered in response to cries and the noise of a fight, so the gathering did not initially establish an unlawful purpose.
The accepted evidence showed that the accused joined in beating the injured people and those who came to assist them.
The fact-finding courts concluded that five or more of the accused shared an unlawful object to beat the victims and acted together.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 149 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, common object and common intention are distinct concepts. Section 149 requires an assembly of five or more sharing an unlawful object, but does not require prior concert or a prior meeting of minds. An initially lawful object may develop into an unlawful one; mere presence at the gathering is not enough, and the court must determine who shared and acted on the unlawful object. No earlier case is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The findings supported convictions for rioting and causing hurt as members of an unlawful assembly; prior consultation or a prior meeting of minds was not necessary.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_conviction_challenge: The proceeding challenges a conviction based on participation in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.five_or_more_shared_unlawful_object: Five or more people came to share the same unlawful purpose, whether before or after assembling.
predicates.acted_together_to_achieve_object: The people sharing that purpose acted together to carry it out.

members.legal_issue: A participant in an unlawful assembly may be liable for a killing committed in pursuit of its common object when the killing was a likely consequence of the assault and the participant knew that it was likely.
material_facts: The assault involved firearms and other weapons, and people joined in beating victims who had already been shot or knocked to the ground.
Several people participated in the beating, and four victims died.
The court concluded that a person of reasonable intelligence would have known that death was likely in a melee of this kind.
members.legal_principle: For liability under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code for a killing beyond the common object to beat, the court required both that a killing was likely to result from the beating forming the common object and that each person convicted knew it might be a likely result. No earlier case is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The convictions for murder through the unlawful-assembly provision could be upheld because the killing was a likely consequence of the assault and the participants knew that it was likely.

rule.if: common_object_homicide_appeal and assault_resulted_in_death and death_was_likely_from_assault and participant_knew_death_was_likely

predicates.common_object_homicide_appeal: The proceeding challenges liability for a homicide attributed to members of a group sharing a common object.
predicates.assault_resulted_in_death: The collective assault resulted in one or more deaths.
predicates.death_was_likely_from_assault: The nature and circumstances of the assault made a death a likely consequence.
predicates.participant_knew_death_was_likely: The participant knew that a death was likely to result from the assault.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be held responsible for murders committed in prosecution of its common object when the evidence establishes that the assembly’s object included those murders.
material_facts: The accused acted together as an armed group against members of a family whom they believed were sheltering persons suspected of killing one of the accused’s relatives.
After the suspected persons were not found, the group continued the attack, fired on victims, restrained them, severed the heads of three victims, and threw a child into a fire.
The attack was sustained and coordinated, and the manner of the killings supported the finding that the group intended mass murder as well as revenge.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, members of an unlawful assembly may be liable for offences committed in prosecution of its common object. The object may be inferred from the assembly’s conduct and may develop during the occurrence. The Court considered Shambhu Nath Singh v. State of Bihar, Bhudeo Mandal v. State of Bihar, and Raghubir Singh v. State of Punjab, but held their ratios inapplicable on these facts.
members.conclusion: The common object of the unlawful assembly included committing mass murders, and the convictions for murder with the aid of the rule of common-object liability were upheld.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed convictions arising from an alleged group offence.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_proved: The evidence established that the accused acted together as an unlawful assembly.
predicates.coordinated_attack_continued_after_initi: The group continued its coordinated attack even after the persons it initially sought were not found.
predicates.attack_evidence_shows_common_object_incl: The group’s conduct, including coordinated killings and extreme violence, showed that its common object included murder.

members.legal_issue: An accused may be convicted for murder and related offences where the evidence establishes participation in an unlawful assembly with the relevant common object and proves the assaults and resulting injuries.
material_facts: The prosecution eyewitnesses identified the accused and described their assaults on the deceased and other people, the abduction of another person, and the removal of the bodies.
The Supreme Court found that the testimony of the eyewitnesses was credible and was corroborated by medical evidence concerning the injuries.
The evidence established motive arising from prior hostility, the presence of light at the scene, and circumstances connecting an accused’s recovered firearm with cartridges found there.
The Supreme Court found that the accused shared the relevant common object and upheld their convictions under Sections 302/149 and the other offences for which they had been convicted.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code supports liability for an offence committed by a member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of its common object. Applying that provision, the Court upheld the convictions under Sections 302/149, 147, 148, 323/149, 324/149, 307/149, 364/149 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code on the evidence of the assaults, the eyewitnesses, and the medical corroboration. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences were upheld, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_convictions: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging convictions and sentences.
predicates.eyewitnesses_identified_accused_and_desc: Witnesses who observed the occurrence identified the accused and described their participation in the assaults and related acts.
predicates.medical_evidence_corrobated_injuries: Medical evidence was consistent with the injuries described by the witnesses.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_shared_relevant_common: The accused acted as members of an unlawful assembly sharing a common object relevant to the offences committed.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly who shares its common object may be liable for the assembly’s killings even without proof that the member personally committed an assault.
material_facts: The State appealed the acquittal of two accused who had been convicted at trial.

The High Court accepted that the two accused were present with the other accused during the incident but acquitted them because the evidence did not show that they personally took part in the assault.
The trial court had found that the accused were members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of killing one of the deceased, and the High Court did not reject that finding.
The evidence accepted by the courts showed that the two accused had a motive, were present throughout with the group, and left with the others.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 IPC, a member of an unlawful assembly who shares its common object is liable for the offence committed in pursuit of that object even if no overt act is attributed to that member. The Court relied on Yunis alias Kariya v. State of M.P. (2003) 1 SCC 425, which holds that membership in the unlawful assembly is sufficient for liability when the charge is under Section 149 IPC.
members.conclusion: The State’s appeals were allowed, the acquittals were set aside, and the trial court’s convictions were restored.

rule.if: state_appeal_against_acquittal and accused_present_as_group and shared_common_object and unlawful_assembly_committed_killing and no_individual_assault_proved

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed an acquittal entered by an appellate court.

predicates.shared_common_object: The accused were found to share the unlawful assembly’s common object.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_committed_killing: The unlawful assembly committed a killing in pursuit of its common object.
predicates.no_individual_assault_proved: The evidence did not establish that the accused personally carried out an assault.

members.legal_issue: A killing committed to secure an unlawful assembly’s common object of forcibly taking possession is attributable to its members when it is immediately connected with that object.
material_facts: The group went armed to take forcible possession of land in another group’s cultivating possession.
When the occupants arrived and objected, the group gathered, threatened to finish them if they did not leave, and one member shot an occupant after he refused to go.
members.legal_principle: Under the first part of section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, the offence must be committed with a view to accomplishing the common object and must be immediately connected with it. The common object need not have been agreed at a prior meeting if it was adopted and shared by the members. The Court discussed Queen v. Sabid Ali (1873) 20 W.R. 5 Cr. in explaining the connection required between the offence and the common object.
members.conclusion: The killing was immediately connected with the common object of forcibly taking possession and was committed in prosecution of that object, bringing the members within the first part of section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_prosecution and shared_forcible_possession_object and (armed_resistance_expected or threats_used_to_enforce_object) and killing_immediately_connected_to_object

predicates.unlawful_assembly_prosecution: The proceeding concerns members of an unlawful assembly prosecuted for a killing committed by one of its members.
predicates.shared_forcible_possession_object: The members shared the object of forcibly taking possession of property held by others.
predicates.armed_resistance_expected: The members went armed to take possession in circumstances in which they expected resistance.
predicates.threats_used_to_enforce_object: The members threatened those resisting their action to make them leave.
predicates.killing_immediately_connected_to_object: A member killed a person who resisted the assembly while it was carrying out its common object.

members.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly are liable for an offence not directly committed to advance its common object when they knew that the offence was likely to be committed in its prosecution, rather than merely that it was possible.
material_facts: The members went to take forcible possession of land occupied by others while armed with a spear, a pistol and lathis.
The members gathered when the occupants objected, threatened them, and a member fired the pistol when the occupants refused to leave.
The Court accepted the finding that the weapons and the members’ conduct showed that they knew murder was likely in accomplishing their object.
members.legal_principle: The second part of section 149 of the Indian Penal Code applies where members knew that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object; “know” does not mean awareness of a mere possibility. The Court referred to Queen v. Sabid Ali (1873) 20 W.R. 5 Cr. and Chikkarange Gowde v. State of Mysore, A.I.R. 1956 S.C. 731, distinguishing the latter on its findings and the defects in its charge.
members.conclusion: The facts also established liability under the second part of section 149 because the members knew murder was likely to be committed in prosecution of their common object.

predicates.killing_not_directly_required_for_object: The killing was not itself shown to be a direct requirement of the assembly’s object.
predicates.lethal_weapons_carried: Members carried weapons capable of causing death while pursuing the common object.
predicates.threatening_conduct_used: The members used threats or other conduct showing their readiness to use force to accomplish the common object.
predicates.circumstances_show_members_knew_killing_: The weapons and conduct, considered in the circumstances, showed that the members knew a killing was likely in pursuing the common object.

members.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly whose common object develops at the scene and who remains a member of the assembly may be held liable for an offence committed in pursuit of that object without proof of that member's individual overt act.
material_facts: The common object developed at the scene when persons came to protest against the harvesting of paddy.
The appellants remained members of the assembly after its common object developed.
The High Court found that most appellants committed overt acts and assaulted the victims, and that the appellants were not merely passive or innocent spectators.
The appellants challenged their convictions on the ground that no individual overt act had been proved against some of them.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, a member of an unlawful assembly may be liable for an offence committed in prosecution of the assembly's common object where the member was part of the assembly sharing that object. Proof of a separate overt act by every member is not required in the circumstances found here. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The convictions under Section 326 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code were sustainable despite the absence of proof of an individual overt act by every appellant.

predicates.accused_remained_member_of_assembly: The accused continued as a member of the assembly after its common object developed.
predicates.assembly_members_committed_assault: Members of the assembly committed an assault in pursuit of its common object.
predicates.accused_was_not_passive_spectator: The accused was not merely a passive or innocent spectator at the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot decide a claim to emoluments attached to a village office where the governing law assigns that matter to revenue authorities.
material_facts: The claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession and related relief on the basis that he had a share in lands treated as emoluments of a village office.
The governing provisions assigned decisions about office emoluments and related claims to revenue authorities.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900, bars civil-court jurisdiction over claims to emoluments appertaining to the office of patel. Section 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, bars suits seeking decisions on matters that revenue authorities are empowered to determine, including claims against the State concerning property or emoluments of hereditary officers or servants.
members.conclusion: The civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain a claim to a share in the office emoluments.

predicates.civil_suit_claiming_share_in_office_emol: A person brought a civil suit claiming a share in emoluments attached to an office.
predicates.governing_law_assigns_emolument_claims_t: The applicable law assigns decisions about the office’s emoluments to revenue authorities.

members.legal_issue: Civil courts lack jurisdiction over a possession suit when deciding it requires determining who is the lawful ryot and that determination is exclusively assigned to a settlement authority whose decision is final.
material_facts: The respondents brought civil suits seeking possession and mesne profits from the appellants, who were in possession as sub-tenants.
After the estate vested in the State, deciding the suits required determining who was the lawful ryot of the land.
The governing law assigned that determination to the Settlement Officer and made the officer’s decision final and not open to challenge in court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 56(1) and (2) of the Madras Estates Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari Act, 1948, questions assigned to the Settlement Officer, including who is the lawful ryot, are for that officer to decide, and the finality of the officer’s decision ousts civil court jurisdiction over those questions. The Court applied Muddada Chayana v. Karnam Narayana and Oduru Chenchulakshamamma v. Duvvuru Reddy, which approved the view in Munuswami Naidu (dead) v. R. Venkata Reddy and rejected the earlier view in Cherukhuru Muthayya v. Gadde Gopalakrishnayya.
members.conclusion: The civil courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suits because determining the lawful ryot was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Settlement Officer. The appeals were allowed, and the order returning the plaints for presentation to the proper court was restored.

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A party brought a civil suit seeking possession of land from another party.
predicates.ryot_status_determination_required: Resolving the suit required determining who was the lawful ryot of the land.
predicates.settlement_authority_has_exclusive_final: The governing law assigned the ryot-status determination to a settlement authority and made its decision final and not challengeable in court.

members.legal_issue: Civil and revenue courts cannot decide evacuee-property status questions or review matters assigned to the Custodian authorities.
material_facts: The heirs brought a civil suit seeking possession and damages, arguing that the property was not evacuee property and challenging actions and orders of the Custodian authorities.
The suit also challenged the refusal to grant a certificate required for seeking restoration, and the relevant administrative orders had not been challenged through constitutional proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 28 and 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, make specified Custodian orders final against challenge in ordinary courts and bar civil or revenue courts from deciding whether property is evacuee property, questioning the legality of Custodian action, or deciding matters entrusted to the Custodian authorities. The Court relied on Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab v. Jafran Begum. The statutory bars do not displace the constitutional jurisdictions identified by the Court under Articles 226, 32 and 136.
members.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to decide whether the properties were evacuee property, to review the legality or correctness of the Custodian authorities’ actions and orders, or to decide the certificate question; the unchallenged orders had become final.

rule.if: civil_suit_or_revenue_proceeding and (evacuee_status_question_raised or custodian_action_legality_challenged or matter_assigned_to_custodian_authority)

predicates.civil_suit_or_revenue_proceeding: A party brings a civil or revenue proceeding concerning property dealt with as evacuee property.
predicates.evacuee_status_question_raised: The proceeding asks the court to decide whether property is or is not evacuee property.
predicates.custodian_action_legality_challenged: The proceeding challenges the legality or correctness of action taken by a Custodian authority.
predicates.matter_assigned_to_custodian_authority: The proceeding asks the court to decide a matter that the governing law assigns to a Custodian authority.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot adjudicate a claim for a declaration of bhumidhari rights when the governing Act assigns that claim exclusively to a Revenue Court.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of bhumidhari rights under section 11 in a civil suit.
The governing Act, read with its schedule, assigned adjudication of such claims to the appropriate Revenue Court.
The parties did not dispute that the civil court lacked jurisdiction over the bhumidhari-rights claim.
members.legal_principle: Under section 185 read with Schedule I of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, jurisdiction over claims for bhumidhari rights under section 11 lies exclusively with the appropriate Revenue Court, not the civil court. The Court applied Hatti v. Sunder Singh, which settled that such a claim is not maintainable in a civil court.
members.conclusion: The civil suit was not maintainable insofar as it sought a declaration of bhumidhari rights.

predicates.civil_suit_seeking_bhumidhari_declaratio: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking a declaration of bhumidhari rights.
predicates.statute_assigns_claim_to_revenue_court: The governing law assigns adjudication of the claimed rights exclusively to a Revenue Court.

members.legal_issue: The civil-court bar applies to claims against the Crown relating to land held as a Saranjam, including claims challenging governmental action concerning that land.
material_facts: The suit sought declarations that the government could not alter an earlier order concerning the Saranjam estate and that the plaintiff was entitled to the rights of its sole holder.
The challenged government orders concerned the resumption, regrant, possession, and recording of the Saranjam villages.
The plaintiff retained the government as a defendant and sought relief that would affect rights in the Saranjam estate.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876 bars civil-court jurisdiction over claims against the Crown relating to lands held as a Saranjam. Its language covers such claims even where the government action is alleged to be ultra vires. The court distinguished Province of Bombay v. Hormusji Manekji, 74 I.A. 103, which concerned section 4(b): its reference to an assessment being “authorised” required the court to consider whether the assessment was duly authorised before applying that bar.
members.conclusion: The suit was a claim against the Crown relating to land held as a Saranjam and was barred by section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876.

predicates.civil_suit: A person brought a claim for determination in a civil court.
predicates.claim_against_government: The claimant sought relief that would operate against the government.
predicates.concerns_saranjam_land: The claim concerned land held as part of a Saranjam estate.
predicates.civil_court_lacks_jurisdiction: The civil court cannot exercise jurisdiction over the claim.

members.legal_issue: An allegation that governmental action was ultra vires does not avoid the civil-court bar for claims against the Crown relating to Saranjam land.
material_facts: The plaintiff challenged the government’s authority to alter the resolution governing the Saranjam estate.
The challenged resolution dealt with the estate and the villages comprising it.
The suit sought relief against the government concerning that land.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(a) generally bars claims against the Crown relating to land held as a Saranjam, including claims that challenge the validity of governmental action. Province of Bombay v. Hormusji Manekji, 74 I.A. 103, did not govern because it concerned section 4(b), which bars objections to assessments “authorised” by the government; that wording required the court to determine whether the assessment was duly authorised. Section 4(a) contains no equivalent qualification.
members.conclusion: The allegation that the government acted beyond its powers did not remove the suit from the bar in section 4(a).

rule.if: civil_suit and claim_against_government and concerns_saranjam_land and government_action_alleged_ultra_vires

predicates.civil_suit: A person brought a claim for determination in a civil court.

predicates.concerns_saranjam_land: The claim concerned land held as part of a Saranjam estate.

predicates.civil_court_bar_applies_despite_ultra_vi: The allegation that the government acted beyond its authority does not prevent the jurisdictional bar from applying.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot grant relief concerning agricultural land where the claimant’s entitlement depends on landholding rights that remain to be determined exclusively by a revenue court.
material_facts: The dispute concerned agricultural land, and the claimant’s asserted share and landholding rights had not been determined by a revenue court.
The claimant had filed a revenue-court suit seeking determination of those rights.

The civil suit sought to invalidate a gift deed to the extent of the claimed share and to restrain dealings with the land; granting that relief required first determining the claimant’s landholding rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives civil courts jurisdiction over civil suits unless jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred. Under Sections 207 and 256 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, read with Section 88 and item 5 of the Third Schedule, a revenue court has exclusive jurisdiction over a suit to declare the specified landholding rights, and the civil-court bar also applies where the cause of action is one for which relief could be obtained in the revenue court, even if the civil suit seeks different or additional relief. Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code, a plaint is rejected when the suit appears from its statements to be barred by law. Bank of Baroda v Moti Bhai (1985) 1 SCC 475 requires attention to the substance of the matter rather than the form of the suit. Shri Ram v A.D.J. (2001) 3 SCC 24 distinguishes a recorded tenure-holder whose title is not under cloud from a claimant who first needs a revenue-court declaration; the latter must obtain that declaration before seeking civil relief that depends on it.
members.conclusion: The civil suit was barred while the claimant’s landholding rights remained pending before the revenue court. The High Court’s decision was upheld and the appeals were dismissed.

predicates.civil_relief_requires_prior_landholding_: The civil relief sought depends on first establishing that the claimant holds the asserted landholding rights.
predicates.revenue_court_has_exclusive_authority_to: The law assigns exclusive authority to a revenue court to determine the asserted landholding rights.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot entertain a suit challenging the validity or legality of an acquisition governed by a complete statutory acquisition code.
material_facts: Tenants filed a civil suit challenging the acquisition and award after acquisition proceedings had advanced to the award stage.
The landowner later joined that suit as a plaintiff.
The acquisition statute provided the remedies available to persons aggrieved by the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: The Land Acquisition Act provides a complete code for acquisition and remedies, excluding civil-court jurisdiction by necessary implication over challenges to the validity or legality of acquisition notifications and declarations; such a challenge may be brought before the High Court under Article 226. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Dhirendra Kumar.
members.conclusion: The civil suit challenging the acquisition was not maintainable because the civil court lacked jurisdiction.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_acquisition: A civil suit asks a court to invalidate or set aside an acquisition.
predicates.statutory_acquisition_remedies_exist: The governing acquisition scheme provides statutory procedures and remedies for challenging the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot determine a claim that in substance seeks recognition of tenure-holder rights over agricultural land, and a decree made without jurisdiction cannot create res judicata.
material_facts: A civil suit sought a declaration that an order vesting the land in the Gaon Sabha was illegal and asserted rights in the land as proprietors or through a claim to tenure-holder status.
The governing statute assigned claims for declaration of tenure-holder rights to the designated revenue forum and excluded civil-court jurisdiction.
The decision in the earlier suit set aside the vesting order but directed the Deputy Commissioner to reconsider the matter; the rights of the individual claimants were never finally determined.
members.legal_principle: Section 185 and the First Schedule to the Delhi Land Reforms Act assign claims for declaration of Bhumidhari rights to the designated revenue forum and bar civil-court jurisdiction. Hatti v. Sunder Singh, [1970] 2 SCC 841, and Gaon Sabha of Lado Sarai v. Jage Ram, ILR (1973) 1 Delhi 984, establish that a suit challenging vesting is outside civil jurisdiction when its substance is a claim to tenure-holder rights. Under Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, AIR 1954 SC 340, a decree passed without jurisdiction is a nullity and may be challenged whenever relied upon. Because the earlier proceedings remanded the matter for reconsideration and did not finally determine individual rights, there was no res judicata.
members.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction, so the decree in the earlier suit was a nullity and did not operate as res judicata.

predicates.civil_suit_challenged_land_vesting: A party brought a civil suit seeking to invalidate an order vesting agricultural land in a village body.
predicates.relief_required_recognition_of_tenure_ho: The substance of the requested relief was recognition of the claimant’s tenure-holder rights in the land.
predicates.statute_assigned_claim_to_revenue_forum: The governing legal scheme assigned that kind of rights claim to a designated revenue forum rather than a civil court.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_did_not_finally_deter: The earlier proceeding directed a fresh determination and left the parties’ individual rights unresolved.
predicates.civil_decree_is_nullity_and_does_not_cre: A civil-court decree made without jurisdiction is a nullity and does not bar later determination of rights as res judicata.

members.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a suit concerning agricultural land where the plaintiff’s own case requires determination of joint rights in the land or the plaintiff is no longer recorded as its tenure holder after mutation in favour of the purchasers.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought cancellation of sale instruments affecting both agricultural and abadi land, alleging that other persons also had rights in the agricultural land and that he was not its sole owner.
The revenue records had removed the plaintiff’s name and entered the purchasers’ names.
The trial court held that the civil court had jurisdiction over the abadi land but not the agricultural land; that determination concerning the abadi land became final.
The High Court held that the civil court could hear the cancellation suit, but the Supreme Court concluded that the agricultural-land dispute belonged before the revenue court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 229B of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, a claim to bhumidhari rights, including jointly held rights, is for the revenue court. Under Shri Ram v. Ist Addl. Distt. Judge, a recorded tenure holder in possession whose title is not under cloud may sue in civil court to cancel a sale deed obtained by fraud or impersonation; by contrast, a person who is not a recorded tenure holder and must establish title must seek relief in the revenue court. The legality of changes to the revenue records at issue here was also for the revenue court to determine.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the lower courts’ orders were restored. The civil court had no jurisdiction over the agricultural-land claim; the ruling concerning abadi land remained undisturbed.

predicates.agricultural_land_civil_suit: The plaintiff brought a civil suit challenging sale instruments affecting agricultural land.
predicates.joint_rights_claim: The plaintiff alleged that other persons also held rights in the land and that the plaintiff was not its sole owner.
predicates.plaintiff_removed_from_records: The revenue records removed the plaintiff’s name and entered the purchasers’ names.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot entertain an injunction suit concerning land acquired through completed acquisition proceedings where possession has vested in the acquiring authority, and a remand for evidence on the merits is therefore improper.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition, an award was made, and possession was taken and handed over to the acquiring authority.

The authority pleaded the acquisition, taking of possession, and subsequent development of the land, and produced the acquisition notification and award; the plaintiffs did not dispute those documents.
The plaintiffs purchased the land after the acquisition proceedings and sought a permanent injunction against interference with their possession.
The trial court dismissed the suit as not maintainable, but the High Court remanded it for evidence concerning possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, gives civil courts jurisdiction over civil suits unless their cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is a complete statutory scheme: it provides procedures for acquisition, compensation, and references or appeals, and, under Section 16, land vests absolutely in the State once possession is taken. Civil courts therefore cannot adjudicate the validity or legality of acquisition proceedings or grant even a bare injunction founded on their invalidity; an aggrieved person may seek constitutional relief under Articles 226 or 136. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Dhirendra Kumar (1995) 4 SCC 229, Laxmi Chand v. Gram Panchayat, Kararia (1996) 7 SCC 218, and Commissioner, Bangalore Development Authority v. K.S. Narayan (2006) 8 SCC 336. Even though the plaintiffs did not directly challenge the acquisition, the suit was not maintainable in light of the completed acquisition, the authority's asserted possession, and the undisputed acquisition documents.
members.conclusion: The civil suit was not maintainable, and the High Court erred in remanding it for evidence on the merits. The appeal was allowed and the trial court's dismissal was restored.

rule.if: civil_injunction_suit and acquisition_completed and authority_possession_established and acquisition_record_undisputed

predicates.civil_injunction_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking an injunction against an acquiring authority concerning land.
predicates.acquisition_completed: The acquisition process had reached an award and had otherwise been completed.
predicates.authority_possession_established: The acquiring authority had taken possession of the land and the record supported that possession.
predicates.acquisition_record_undisputed: The parties did not dispute the acquisition documents produced in support of the authority's case.

members.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a claim against the government relating to Saranjam lands when the claimant must invalidate or overcome a government order concerning those lands to obtain the relief sought.
material_facts: The claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession of lands held as a Saranjam maintenance grant.
The claimant expressly sought a finding that the government’s order granting the lands to another family member was null and ineffective.
Recovery of possession from that family member depended on removing the government order as an obstacle.
The government was a defendant to the claim concerning its order and the Saranjam lands.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(a), including its fourth sub-clause, bars civil-court jurisdiction over claims against the government relating to lands granted or held as Saranjam. The Court relied on Mallappa alias Annasaheb Basvantrao Desai Nadgouda v. Tukko Narshimha Mutalik Desai and Others, I.L.R. [1937] Bom. 464, concerning the distinction between claims and suits. A claim that requires the government’s order to be set aside or treated as ineffective is a claim against the government relating to Saranjam lands.
members.conclusion: The claim against the government fell within section 4 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, and the civil suit was barred.

predicates.civil_suit_over_saranjam_lands: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking relief concerning lands held as a Saranjam.
predicates.claim_against_government_concerning_gran: The claimant asks for relief that challenges the government’s decision concerning the grant of those lands.
predicates.relief_depends_on_displacing_government_: The claimant cannot obtain the relief sought unless the government order is set aside or treated as ineffective.

members.legal_issue: The civil-court exception for property-title questions does not confer jurisdiction to decide whether a sub-tenancy was lawful for purposes of a statutory direct-tenancy claim.
material_facts: The claimants relied on a statutory right to be treated as direct tenants because the accommodation had been lawfully sublet to them.
Their claim required a decision on the lawfulness of the subletting.
They invoked the civil-court exception for questions of title to accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Section 45(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, preserved civil-court jurisdiction over questions of title or interests in property existing apart from the Act, including matters incidentally addressed by the rent authority. It did not extend to a statutory right to direct tenancy under section 16(2) or to the lawfulness of subletting that had to be decided under section 15(3). No earlier cases were relied upon.
members.conclusion: The title exception did not authorize the civil court to decide the lawfulness of the subletting or make it competent to entertain the suit.

predicates.civil_suit_claims_direct_tenancy: The sub-tenants brought a civil suit seeking recognition as direct tenants of the landlord.
predicates.claim_depends_on_subletting_lawfulness: The claimed direct-tenancy right depended on whether the premises had been lawfully sublet.
predicates.claimant_invokes_property_title_exceptio: The claimant relied on an exception allowing civil courts to decide questions of title to accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a suit challenging surplus-land determination and allotment where those matters are assigned to statutory authorities and an available statutory remedy was not used.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed the disputed land under a 1970 civil court decree and alleged that they had not been notified or heard in the proceedings concerning the land.
In 1980, the prescribed authority considered a declaration filed by the plaintiffs’ father, which included the plaintiffs and the disputed land, and declared the land surplus.

The land was allotted in 1981. The plaintiffs did not pursue the remedies available under the statutory scheme and instead filed a civil suit in 1991 seeking to invalidate the surplus determination and allotment.
The civil suit was dismissed as not maintainable, and the plaintiffs challenged that result in the appeal before the Supreme Court.
