predicates.supervisory_review_was_available: The High Court could have considered the challenged order through its supervisory jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A plea of res judicata cannot be raised for the first time at the hearing before the Supreme Court when it was not pleaded or tried in the courts below.
material_facts: The claimant did not plead res judicata in the suit.
The pleadings and issues from the earlier suit were not tendered in evidence, and no res judicata issue was framed and tried.
The plea was not raised before the courts below or the High Court and was advanced before the Supreme Court only at the hearing.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law. In this case, the absence of a plea and of an issue tried below meant that the plea could not be raised for the first time at the hearing before the Supreme Court.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the res judicata plea to be raised for the first time before it and did not decide whether the earlier judgment was conclusive between the parties.

rule.if: appeal_heard_by_supreme_court and res_judicata_not_pleaded_below and res_judicata_not_tried_below and plea_first_raised_at_supreme_court_hearing

predicates.appeal_heard_by_supreme_court: The proceeding is an appeal heard by the Supreme Court.
predicates.res_judicata_not_pleaded_below: The party did not plead res judicata in the proceedings before the lower courts.
predicates.res_judicata_not_tried_below: The lower courts did not frame and try an issue of res judicata.
predicates.plea_first_raised_at_supreme_court_heari: The party first advances the res judicata plea at the hearing before the Supreme Court.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot raise in the Supreme Court a good-faith challenge that it abandoned before the intermediate appellate court.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors challenged the decree-holder’s good faith before a single judge.
They did not advance that challenge before the division bench, but raised it again in the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: A party may not raise before the Supreme Court a contention that it abandoned before the intermediate appellate court. The Court also agreed with the lower court’s finding that the decree-holder prosecuted the earlier execution proceeding in good faith and with due diligence.
members.conclusion: The good-faith challenge was not open to the judgment-debtors in the Supreme Court because they had abandoned it before the division bench; the Court also considered the single judge’s finding of good faith and due diligence correct.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.good_faith_challenge_omitted_before_inte: A party raised a good-faith challenge at an earlier stage but did not pursue it before the intermediate appellate court.

members.legal_issue: A new challenge to an administrative order that was not raised before the High Court will not be considered for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: During the appeal, counsel challenged the validity of the order releasing the property to its rightful owner on the ground that the occupants had not been heard.
That challenge had not been raised in the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court would not entertain at the appellate stage a challenge that had not been raised before the High Court.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the challenge to be raised at that stage.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal from a High Court decision.
predicates.challenge_not_raised_before_high_court: A party advances a challenge in the Supreme Court that was not raised before the High Court.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline to entertain an argument raised for the first time before it when the party did not raise the point in either court below.
material_facts: The appellant sought to argue that a respondent should not have been permitted to raise an objection to the suit.
The appellant had not raised that point in either of the two lower courts.
The Supreme Court declined to permit the argument to be raised for the first time before it.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural approach that it may refuse to permit a point to be raised for the first time before it when that point was not raised in the courts below.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the point because it had not been raised in either court below.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party brought an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.argument_raised_for_first_time: A party presented an argument to the Supreme Court that had not previously been presented in the case.
predicates.argument_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The argument was not raised in the courts below.

members.legal_issue: An objection that a referred question should not have been answered cannot be raised for the first time at the Supreme Court stage when it was not raised before the High Court or in the statement of the case.
material_facts: The Revenue argued that a question referred to the High Court did not arise from the Tribunal’s order.
The Revenue had not raised that objection before the High Court or in the statement of the case before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The court declined to entertain an objection not raised before the High Court or in the statement of the case. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this procedural ruling.
members.conclusion: The court did not allow the Revenue to raise the objection at that stage.

predicates.appeal_or_reference_case: The matter reaches the Supreme Court through an appeal or a reference arising from an earlier court or tribunal proceeding.
predicates.objection_not_raised_before_high_court: The party did not raise the objection before the High Court.
predicates.objection_not_in_statement_of_case: The objection was not included in the statement of the case presented to the Supreme Court.

members.legal_issue: A new challenge to the authenticity or admissibility of public documents cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal under the special appellate jurisdiction when no such objection was made in the courts below and the documents were received and relied upon there.
material_facts: Copies of old official letters setting out the terms on which government land had been placed in the zoo committee's charge were produced from official records.
The documents were received and relied upon by both courts below.
No objection to their authenticity or admissibility was made in either court below.
members.legal_principle: The letters were public documents within the meaning of the Evidence Act. The Court held that a new plea concerning authenticity or admissibility could not be accepted in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution where no such objection had been taken below.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the new challenge to the documents' authenticity and admissibility in the appeal.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_proceeding and public_documents_relied_on_below and no_objection_below and new_authenticity_or_admissibility_challenge

predicates.special_leave_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an appeal brought under the Supreme Court's special appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.public_documents_relied_on_below: Public documents were received and relied upon by the courts below.
predicates.no_objection_below: No objection to the documents' authenticity or admissibility was made in the courts below.
predicates.new_authenticity_or_admissibility_challe: A party raises an authenticity or admissibility objection to the documents for the first time in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A request for further inquiry cannot be raised for the first time before the High Court when it was not sought from the Tribunal.
material_facts: In a reference from the Tribunal, the appellant argued that the distinction between movable and immovable properties required further evidence and sought a remand.
The appellant had not applied to the Tribunal for an inquiry on that distinction.
The High Court declined to order a remand.
members.legal_principle: In a reference under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, a party that considers further inquiry necessary must seek it from the Tribunal; having failed to do so, it cannot call on the High Court to remand the matter for that purpose.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in declining to entertain the request for a remand.

predicates.high_court_tax_reference: The matter is before the High Court on a reference from a tax tribunal.
predicates.further_inquiry_not_requested_from_tribu: The party seeking further evidence did not ask the tribunal to order an inquiry.
predicates.remand_request_first_raised_before_high_: The party first asked for a remand before the High Court.

members.legal_issue: A claim for exclusion of time that depends on mixed questions of law and fact will not be considered when first raised in the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The plaintiffs argued for the first time in the Supreme Court that time spent in a pending summary proceeding should be excluded under section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
The argument raised mixed questions of law and fact and had not been raised in the courts below or in the stated appeal materials.
members.legal_principle: A contention raising mixed questions of law and fact, not raised in the courts below, need not be entertained when advanced for the first time in the Supreme Court. The contention invoked section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
members.conclusion: The Court did not allow the plaintiffs to raise the section 14 contention for the first time in the Supreme Court.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.exclusion_claim_raised_first_on_appeal: A claim to exclude time was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
predicates.claim_involves_mixed_law_and_fact: The exclusion claim raises mixed questions of law and fact.

members.legal_issue: A legal ground first raised before the Supreme Court, after not being raised before the earlier authorities or the High Court, may be declined for consideration.
material_facts: The appellants relied before the Supreme Court on provisions concerning declarations for unrecorded co-tenants and argued that the respondents could not claim shares without obtaining such a declaration.
The appellants had not raised those statutory arguments before the consolidation authorities or the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the procedural posture of the case: the arguments under the cited tenancy-acquisition provisions had not been urged before any earlier authority or the High Court, and the Court was therefore not inclined to deal with them. No earlier case was cited for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the newly raised statutory arguments.

predicates.final_appeal_proceeding: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal after decisions by lower authorities and a reviewing court.
predicates.legal_ground_not_raised_before_lower_aut: A party raises a legal ground in the final appeal that it did not raise before the earlier authorities or the reviewing court.

members.legal_issue: An authenticated government sanction order may be proved as a public document, and its admissibility cannot ordinarily be challenged for the first time on appeal after it was admitted without objection at trial.
material_facts: The prosecution produced the original government order authorizing prosecution, issued in the name of the Governor and authenticated by a government secretary.
The order stated that the competent authority had examined the material and considered prosecution appropriate.
A witness identified the secretary’s signature, and cross-examination did not undermine his ability to identify it.
The order’s authenticity was not disputed, and the defence did not object to its admission at trial.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, prosecution requires sanction from the competent authority. An authenticated executive order issued in the Governor’s name is a public document under Section 74 of the Indian Evidence Act and may be proved under Sections 76 to 78; proof is not confined to the opinion evidence contemplated by Section 47. Under Section 67, handwriting may be proved by any lawful mode. Gulzar Ali v. State of H.P. explains that handwriting may be established by modes other than Sections 45 and 47. A valid sanction may be proved by producing the original order containing the offence facts and grounds for satisfaction, or by other evidence showing that those facts were placed before the authority and satisfaction was reached, as held in Mohd. Iqbal Ahmed v. State of Andhra Pradesh. R.J. Singh Ahuluwalia v. State of Delhi concerned the absence of sanction by the competent authority. An objection to admissibility not raised when the document was admitted cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, as supported by Ranvir Singh v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The sanction order was admissible and sufficiently proved; the High Court erred in holding that it had not been proved in accordance with law.

rule.if: corruption_prosecution and (authenticated_original_sanction_order and competent_authority_considered_material and signature_identified and order_authenticity_unchallenged and no_trial_objection)

predicates.corruption_prosecution: The prosecution was brought for alleged corruption offences for which prior government approval was required.
predicates.authenticated_original_sanction_order: The prosecution produced an original government approval order authenticated as an official executive act.
predicates.competent_authority_considered_material: The order recorded that the authority empowered to remove the accused had examined the material and considered prosecution appropriate.
predicates.signature_identified: A witness identified the signature of the official who authenticated the order, and cross-examination did not undermine that identification.
predicates.order_authenticity_unchallenged: The opposing party did not dispute the authenticity of the official order.
predicates.no_trial_objection: The opposing party allowed the order to be admitted at trial without objection and challenged its admissibility only on appeal.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the validity of a statutory rent-demand notice cannot be raised for the first time in revision when it was not raised in the courts below.
material_facts: At trial, the tenant disputed the validity of the notice to quit but did not challenge the validity of the statutory notice under section 12(2).
The tenant did not raise the statutory-notice challenge before the appellate court and first raised it in revision.
members.legal_principle: A ground not raised before the courts below may be refused when raised for the first time in revision. The Court applied this principle to the challenge concerning notice under section 12(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947.
members.conclusion: The High Court properly refused to allow the tenant to raise the statutory-notice challenge for the first time in revision, and the point was not open in the appeal.

predicates.revision_proceeding: The proceeding is a revision before the High Court.
predicates.notice_validity_ground_not_raised_below: The party did not raise the notice-validity ground before the courts below.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not adjudicate a specific-performance issue that was not challenged before the High Court.
material_facts: The tribunal refused a direction requiring the concessionaire to perform its operating obligations.
The High Court recorded that the tribunal's refusal had not been challenged before it.
The Supreme Court therefore declined to decide the specific-performance issue.
members.legal_principle: The Court confined its consideration to issues properly raised and challenged before the High Court; it gave no separate substantive ruling on specific performance.
members.conclusion: The Court did not adjudicate the issue of specific performance.

predicates.appeal_before_supreme_court: A party brings an appeal before the Supreme Court concerning a dispute decided in lower courts.
predicates.issue_not_challenged_before_high_court: The party did not challenge the relevant ruling before the High Court.

members.legal_issue: A new factual plea that was not argued before the courts below cannot be raised for the first time in the final appellate court.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the mortgagors had remained members of an undivided family, or alternatively that the branches held the properties as co-owners, so that the redeeming co-mortgagor’s possession should also be treated as possession on behalf of the non-redeeming branch.
Neither plea had been argued before the High Court, and the record was too meagre to provide an adequate factual foundation for them.
members.legal_principle: The Court will not permit an appellant to take up a plea that was not agitated before the courts below; the lack of an adequate factual foundation further supported refusing the request to reopen the matter.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not raise either plea for the first time in the Supreme Court.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and new_factual_plea and not plea_agitated_below

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.new_factual_plea: An appellant advances a factual plea that was not the basis on which the matter was argued below.
predicates.plea_agitated_below: The appellant argued the plea before a court below.

members.legal_issue: A limitation objection that presents a mixed question of fact and law and was not raised in the High Court cannot be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The appellant did not raise a sufficiently clear limitation plea in the trial court or the High Court.
The appellant did not raise the limitation point in the High Court in support of the trial court's decree.
The point raised in the Supreme Court depended on both facts and law, including when the suit was first instituted and how the limitation period should be computed.
members.legal_principle: A mixed question of fact and law that was not raised in the High Court is not to be introduced for the first time in the Supreme Court, particularly where the omitted factual plea could have led to evidence or a record inquiry in the courts below.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to allow the appellant to raise the limitation point for the first time before it.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The case is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.limitation_issue_mixed_fact_law: Deciding the limitation issue requires both factual findings and application of law.
predicates.limitation_issue_not_raised_in_high_cour: The party did not raise the limitation issue in the High Court.

members.legal_issue: A contention first raised in the Supreme Court may be declined when it was not raised in the courts below.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the proceeding was not maintainable because the lease term had not expired.
The contention had not been raised in the courts below.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural principle that it may decline to entertain a contention raised for the first time on appeal when that contention was not presented to the courts below.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to allow the appellant to raise the contention for the first time on appeal.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party presented a contention to a higher court in an appeal.
predicates.contention_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The party had not presented that contention to the courts below.

members.legal_issue: A court should not decide the constitutional validity of a statutory provision on its own initiative when the challenge was not pleaded or properly raised in the proceeding.
material_facts: The dispute reached the High Court in a second appeal concerning a bank’s claim for repayment of an agricultural loan.
The borrower had not challenged the constitutional validity of the statutory exemption in the courts below or before the High Court.
The High Court, on its own initiative, held the exemption unconstitutional under Article 14.

The Supreme Court held that the challenge required specific, clear and unambiguous allegations and that it was inappropriate to decide it in this proceeding. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s finding.
members.legal_principle: A statutory provision is presumed constitutional, and the person challenging it must make specific, clear and unambiguous allegations sufficient to show that its classification lacks a rational basis. A court should not decide constitutionality on hypothetical or undeveloped grounds in a proceeding where the challenge was not raised. The Court relied on Harman Singh v. Regional Transport Authority, Sri Venkata Seetaramanjaneya Rice & Oil Mills v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Rajpur Ruda Meha v. State of Gujarat, and Somavanti v. State of Punjab; it also noted the prior decision in Bank of India v. Vijay Transport.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s finding that the exemption was unconstitutional was set aside because the issue had not been properly raised by a party in the proceeding.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal concerning a civil dispute.
predicates.constitutional_validity_not_pleaded: No party pleaded a challenge to the constitutional validity of the provision in the proceeding.
predicates.high_court_considers_validity_on_its_own: The High Court considered and decided the provision’s validity on its own initiative.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to rent-control provisions cannot be considered in appellate or revisional proceedings arising from rent-fixation orders when the original statutory authority lacked jurisdiction to decide that challenge.
material_facts: Rent-fixation proceedings had begun under an earlier rent-control statute and were continued under that statute after it was repealed, pursuant to transitional provisions.
The landlord argued that the transitional provisions requiring pending cases to be decided under the earlier statute violated the constitutional guarantee of equality.
The challenge was raised in proceedings reviewing rent-fixation orders made by the Rent Controller, an authority that could not determine the constitutional validity of the provisions it applied.
members.legal_principle: A reviewing court cannot consider a constitutional challenge in proceedings arising from an order of a statutory authority when deciding the validity of the legislation was outside that authority’s jurisdiction. The Court applied the principle in K.S. Venkataraman & Co. v. State of Madras, Commissioner of Income-tax, Madhya Pradesh v. Straw Products Ltd., Bhopal, and C.T. Senthilnathan Chettiar v. State of Madras, extending it from proceedings under taxing statutes to rent-fixation proceedings.
members.conclusion: The constitutional challenge could not be considered in proceedings arising from the Rent Controller’s orders; the appeals were dismissed.

predicates.rent_fixation_review: The proceeding is an appeal or revision arising from an order fixing rent under a statute.
predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party asks the reviewing court to hold a statutory provision constitutionally invalid.
predicates.original_authority_lacks_power_to_decide: The authority that made the order had no jurisdiction to determine the constitutional validity of the provision it applied.
predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge_not_co: The reviewing court does not consider the constitutional validity challenge in that proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A criminal conviction cannot stand where the prosecution evidence leaves reasonable doubt after material suppression, unreliable testimony, and a plausible defence are considered together.
material_facts: The prosecution’s account was affected by the deliberate suppression of the accused persons’ injuries and other facts relating to the prior dispute and the occurrence.
The prosecution witnesses’ accounts had material contradictions, and the Court found the evidence did not inspire confidence or permit reliable separation of credible from unreliable parts.
The accused had a plausible private-defence account supported by their injuries, and the Court found no adequate evidence of excessive force.
The Court found no reliable evidence that could support a different conclusion and held that the accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and must stand on its own evidence, not on weaknesses in the defence. The accused need only raise a plausible defence that creates doubt; the benefit of reasonable doubt follows if the prosecution fails to establish guilt. The Court relied on Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, (2019) 8 SCC 50, and Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand, (2013) 4 SCC 422, and applied the principles concerning fair investigation, private defence, and assessment of witness evidence.
members.conclusion: The convictions could not stand; the accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt, and the appeals against conviction were allowed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: An appeal before the Supreme Court challenges a criminal conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_is_materially_unrel: Material suppression, contradictions, or other deficiencies undermine the reliability of the prosecution evidence.
predicates.accused_has_plausible_defence: The evidence supports a reasonably probable account in the accused’s favour.
predicates.prosecution_has_not_proved_guilt_beyond_: The evidence does not establish the accused’s guilt to the required criminal standard.
predicates.conviction_cannot_stand_and_accused_get_: The conviction must be set aside and the accused receive the benefit of doubt.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for bribery and conspiracy cannot be sustained on circumstantial evidence when the circumstances relied on are materially contradicted or not firmly established as pointing to guilt.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on the accused referring the complainant to a colleague, but that conduct was also compatible with an innocent explanation.
The complainant’s testimony about a later conversation with the accused was materially contradicted in cross-examination.
The alleged presence of the accused during a colleague’s reduced bribe demand was contradicted by the complainant’s own testimony and was inconsistent with the official charge-transfer record.
The accused was absent when the colleague accepted the tainted money, and the evidence did not reliably establish the accused’s participation in the demand or an agreement to share the money.
members.legal_principle: Where a prosecution rests on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must first be firmly established and must be a definite pointer towards the accused’s guilt. Material contradictions and unproved circumstances make it unsafe to convict. The charges involved Section 5(1)(d) and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and Sections 161 and 120B read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence was too infirm to safely support the convictions; the appeal was allowed and the convictions and sentences were set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed against a criminal conviction.
predicates.circumstantial_evidence_case: The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence to establish the accused’s guilt.
predicates.essential_circumstances_materially_contr: Material circumstances relied on by the prosecution were contradicted or were not firmly established.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand where the prosecution evidence does not identify the accused as participants and the accused’s statement, standing alone, does not establish guilt.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses identified certain participants but did not identify the two accused whose convictions were challenged.
The accused’s statement that he had removed crops from his own field, considered by itself, was not an admission of guilt.
No other evidence supported those two convictions.
members.legal_principle: A conviction must have an evidentiary basis implicating the accused; an accused’s statement that, standing alone, is not an admission of guilt cannot supply that basis. The Court exercised its supervisory power under Article 227 in the appeal to set aside convictions that were manifestly erroneous on the face of the record.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the two accused were set aside, and they were discharged from bail.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and prosecution_witnesses_do_not_identify_accused and no_other_evidence_implicates_accused and accused_statement_alone_is_not_admission

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.

predicates.no_other_evidence_implicates_accused: No other evidence in the record connected the accused to the offence.
predicates.accused_statement_alone_is_not_admission: The accused made a statement which, considered by itself, did not amount to an admission of guilt.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for a fatal injury cannot stand where the evidence leaves reasonable doubt that the accused caused that injury.
material_facts: Only three witnesses attributed the fatal blow to the accused, while many other witnesses with an equally good opportunity to observe did not implicate him or mention the attack on the deceased.
The accounts did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the fatal injury was caused by the accused rather than another person, and the circumstances of the injury remained uncertain.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove the accused's responsibility for the fatal injury beyond reasonable doubt. Material omissions by witnesses who had an equally good opportunity to observe, together with uncertainty about who inflicted the injury, may create reasonable doubt. The Court applied the benefit-of-doubt principle to the charge under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code; no earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt on the fatal injury and was acquitted of the offence under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is a criminal appeal against a conviction.
predicates.fatal_injury_attributed_to_accused: The prosecution alleged that the accused caused an injury that resulted in death.
predicates.equally_well_placed_witnesses_do_not_imp: Witnesses with an equally good opportunity to observe did not implicate the accused in causing the fatal injury.
predicates.evidence_leaves_identity_of_assailant_un: The evidence does not establish beyond reasonable doubt who caused the fatal injury.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for a fatal offence cannot stand where the prosecution fails to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused’s injury caused the eventual death, even if the accused intended a grievous injury with a dangerous weapon.
material_facts: The assailant intentionally struck the victim’s head once with a sharp, dangerous weapon, causing a severe injury that was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The victim survived for 38 days after the injury, underwent surgery 23 days after it, and died after prolonged hospital treatment.
The prosecution did not provide evidence of the victim’s condition after surgery or establish whether an intervening condition contributed to death.
No post-mortem examination was conducted.
members.legal_principle: Section 300, clause thirdly, concerns an intended bodily injury that is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. However, the prosecution must also establish beyond reasonable doubt that the injury caused the death. Where that causal connection is not proved, an intentional grievous injury inflicted with a dangerous weapon may support conviction under Section 326 IPC, but not conviction for murder or culpable homicide on the evidence described.
members.conclusion: The court set aside convictions for murder and culpable homicide and substituted a conviction for voluntarily causing grievous hurt with a dangerous weapon, because the prosecution had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the injury was the eventual cause of death.

predicates.appeal_from_fatal_assault_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal from a conviction arising from an assault followed by the victim’s death.
predicates.intentional_grievous_injury_with_dangero: The accused intentionally inflicted a grievous injury on the victim using a dangerous weapon.
predicates.victim_survived_prolonged_treatment: The victim survived for a substantial period after the injury and received treatment before dying.
predicates.death_causation_not_proved_beyond_reason: The prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the injury was the cause of death, including because relevant evidence about the victim’s later condition was absent.
predicates.fatal_offence_conviction_reduced_to_grie: The fatal-offence conviction is reduced to a conviction for grievous injury.

members.legal_issue: Circumstantial evidence that raises suspicion but does not establish instigation beyond reasonable doubt is insufficient to convict a person of abetting a crime.
material_facts: The alleged abettor had a dispute with the victim concerning land and had an interest in the property.
The shooters were associated with the alleged abettor, and the prosecution suggested they had no independent motive to commit the crime.
The alleged instruction to the shooters on the day before the occurrence was unclear, and the witness had not mentioned it in her statement to the police.
The alleged abettor’s later request that the victim not involve him in the case did not establish guilt.
The prosecution’s case against the alleged abettor was circumstantial and did not provide clinching evidence of instigation.
members.legal_principle: A strong suspicion cannot substitute for proof beyond reasonable doubt; circumstantial evidence must lead unerringly to guilt. The court applied that standard to the charge of abetment under Section 302 read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. It cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The State’s appeal against the acquittal of the alleged abettor was dismissed, and the acquittal was confirmed because the circumstances, though suspicious, did not prove abetment beyond reasonable doubt.

predicates.property_dispute_and_assailant_associati: The accused had a dispute with the victim over property, and the assailants were associated with the accused.

predicates.later_request_not_to_involve_accused: After the occurrence, the accused asked the victim not to involve him in the case.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand when the prosecution evidence, assessed cumulatively, is insufficiently reliable to prove guilt.
material_facts: The recovered weapons were not forensically linked to the offence, and vital forensic evidence was withheld.
The identification parade had significant defects and the identified garment was not distinctively linked to the accused.

The sole eyewitness had severe perceptual limitations, faced adverse observation conditions, gave an implausible account of hearing the victim, and did not report the event despite knowing the victim.
The alleged motive was remote and unsupported by further material showing a proximate motive.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the rules that identification-parade evidence is not substantive evidence, that vital withheld evidence may warrant an adverse inference, that unreliable sole-eyewitness testimony cannot safely sustain a conviction, and that an accused receives the benefit where the evidence permits two views.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the judgments upholding the conviction were set aside.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and identification_evidence_unreliable and sole_eyewitness_testimony_unreliable and forensic_link_missing and alleged_motive_remote

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.identification_evidence_unreliable: The identification evidence has material defects that leave it unworthy of reliance.
predicates.sole_eyewitness_testimony_unreliable: The sole eyewitness’s testimony is unreliable because of deficiencies in perception, opportunity to observe, account, or conduct.
predicates.forensic_link_missing: The prosecution does not establish a forensic link between material recovered evidence and the offence.
predicates.alleged_motive_remote: The alleged motive is remote and lacks further material showing a proximate connection to the offence.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for causing a death cannot stand where the evidence that an accused used a weapon in the occurrence is doubtful and conflicts with the medical evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused took another person's gun and shot the victim's arm.
Ballistic examination did not link cartridges from the occurrence to that gun.
The alleged gun's owner was reportedly ill and confined to bed, making his presence at the scene doubtful.
The prosecution's account of the shot conflicted with the location of the entry wound on the victim's arm.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the doubtful prosecution account and conflict with the medical evidence made the conviction unjustified. Because the trial court had acquitted the accused, the High Court was not justified in reversing that acquittal on this evidence. The relevant conviction was under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code; no earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The conviction relating to the victim's death was set aside and the trial court's acquittal was maintained.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction_after_acquittal: The accused appealed a conviction entered after a trial court had acquitted the accused.
predicates.alleged_weapon_link_doubtful: The evidence that the accused used the alleged weapon was doubtful, including because forensic examination did not connect that weapon to the occurrence.
predicates.wound_evidence_conflicts_with_account: The physical location of the wound was inconsistent with the prosecution's account of how the shot was fired.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for causing a death cannot stand where the prosecution case against the accused is doubtful and the alleged weapon caused no injury.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused carried a spear during the occurrence.
No person on the prosecution side had a spear injury.
The Court found the case against the accused sufficiently doubtful, although the High Court had reversed the trial court's acquittal.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the doubtful case and absence of any spear injury did not justify the High Court's interference with the trial court's acquittal. The convictions included one under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code; no earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The convictions were set aside and the trial court's acquittal was maintained.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction_after_acquittal: The accused appealed a conviction entered after a trial court had acquitted the accused.
predicates.alleged_weapon_caused_no_injury: The prosecution alleged that the accused carried a weapon, but no person on the prosecution side had an injury caused by that weapon.
predicates.prosecution_case_doubtful: The evidence against the accused left the prosecution case sufficiently doubtful.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for dowry-related offences cannot stand where the evidence does not reliably establish the alleged demand and the surrounding evidence leaves a plausible basis for doubt.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the husband demanded money, but the principal witness’s earlier statement to the investigating officer did not mention that demand.
The evidence about the complainant selling his house to meet the demand was not supported by a sale document, and the land belonged to a public religious endowment.
A further alleged demand for money was attributed to the deceased’s in-laws rather than the husband.

The forensic report found no common metallic poison in the examined remains, which the Court considered inconsistent with the prosecution’s account that the deceased died after taking poisonous tablets.
The husband stated that the deceased had suffered from fits and that she had not been ill-treated for dowry; the Court considered this explanation plausible in the circumstances.
The trial court had acquitted the accused, and the High Court reversed that acquittal and convicted the husband.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the charges under Sections 304-B and 498-A of the Indian Penal Code against the evidence and gave the accused the benefit of doubt where the prosecution case contained material improvements, the forensic findings undermined its account, and the defence explanation was plausible.
members.conclusion: The prosecution evidence contained major improvements and did not reliably establish the alleged dowry demand or the prosecution’s account of death. The defence explanation was plausible, so the husband was entitled to the benefit of doubt and was acquitted of the charges under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC.

rule.if: dowry_death_or_cruelty_prosecution and alleged_demand_omitted_from_earlier_witness_statement and (supporting_transaction_evidence_unsubstantiated or forensic_findings_undermine_prosecution_account) and defence_explanation_plausible

predicates.dowry_death_or_cruelty_prosecution: The prosecution seeks a conviction for a death or cruelty alleged to be connected with dowry.

predicates.supporting_transaction_evidence_unsubsta: Evidence offered to support the alleged demand or payment lacks reliable corroboration.
predicates.forensic_findings_undermine_prosecution_: Forensic findings do not support, or are inconsistent with, the prosecution’s account of how the death occurred.
predicates.defence_explanation_plausible: The accused gives an explanation that remains plausible in light of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: Suspicion arising from circumstantial evidence does not establish guilt when proof is lacking or the identity of the perpetrators cannot be fixed.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness, and the prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence that included an alleged motive, the recovery of bodies, alleged confessions, and evidence of an accused’s association with a child.
The circumstances created suspicion, but the evidence did not establish who committed the alleged crime or whether one or more perpetrators were involved.
Even if the recovered bodies were those of the alleged victims and their deaths were homicidal, the identity of the perpetrators remained uncertain.
members.legal_principle: In a criminal case, suspicion alone is not proof and cannot warrant a finding of guilt. Circumstantial evidence must establish guilt; uncertainty about the identity of the perpetrators prevents that conclusion. No earlier case or statutory provision is cited for these principles.
members.conclusion: Suspicion, however strong, could not substitute for proof, and the evidence did not establish the accused’s guilt.

predicates.suspicion_without_proof: The circumstances create suspicion but do not provide proof sufficient to establish guilt.
predicates.perpetrator_identity_unfixed: The evidence does not establish who committed the alleged crime.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for a death cannot stand when the declarations identifying the accused are not relied upon and the remaining evidence does not establish responsibility beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The deceased persons were attacked at a place some distance from the house where the eyewitnesses saw the earlier attacks.
No witness directly saw the appellants attack those deceased persons.
The court found that the statement attributing those deaths to the appellants went beyond what its maker could have known or seen, and the other dying declarations were not relied upon.
After those declarations were left out of consideration, the court found no direct evidence or conclusive chain of circumstantial evidence connecting the appellants to those deaths.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the requirement that criminal responsibility be established by legally sufficient evidence. In the absence of direct evidence or a conclusive chain of circumstantial evidence, the appellants could not be held responsible for these deaths.
members.conclusion: The appellants could not legally be held responsible for the two deaths on the evidence available, and their convictions for those murders could not be maintained.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_convicted_of_death and identifying_declarations_not_reliable and no_direct_evidence and circumstantial_chain_not_conclusive

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.accused_convicted_of_death: The accused was convicted of causing a particular person's death.
predicates.identifying_declarations_not_reliable: The statements identifying the accused as responsible for the death are not relied upon as reliable evidence.
predicates.no_direct_evidence: No witness directly saw the accused commit the fatal attack.
predicates.circumstantial_chain_not_conclusive: The remaining circumstances do not form a conclusive chain establishing the accused's responsibility for the death.

members.legal_issue: A co-accused’s retracted confession cannot by itself sustain the conviction of another accused when no substantive independent evidence establishes that person’s guilt.
material_facts: The only evidence assigning roles in the killing to two of the accused was another accused’s judicial confession.
That confession was retracted and its voluntariness and reliability were not established to the required standard.
The extra-judicial confession of the principal accused implicated only himself, and the other evidence did not independently establish the two accused persons’ participation in the murder.
The two accused were tried jointly with the maker of the confession.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 30 of the Evidence Act, a confession by one person jointly tried with others may be taken into consideration against a co-accused, but it is not substantive evidence sufficient by itself to found a conviction. A co-accused’s confession is at most corroborative, and a retracted confession is especially unsafe as the sole basis for conviction. The Court relied on Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Ram Parkash v. State of Punjab, State of M.P. v. Paltan Mallah, State v. Sidharth, Navjot Sandhu v. State (N.C.T. of Delhi), and Bhuboni Sahu v. R.
members.conclusion: The confession could not, without independent substantive evidence and adequate corroboration, sustain the convictions of the co-accused; those convictions were set aside.

predicates.joint_criminal_trial: More than one accused is being tried jointly for the same offence.
predicates.conviction_of_coaccused_relies_on_anothe: The prosecution relies on one accused’s confession to establish the guilt of another accused.
predicates.confession_retracted: The maker later withdrew the confession.
predicates.no_independent_substantive_evidence: No independent substantive evidence establishes the co-accused’s guilt apart from the confession.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for an individual assault cannot be sustained by reconstructing a prosecution case when the prosecution has not established the true genesis and manner of the occurrence and the evidence leaves a probability of self-defence.
material_facts: The High Court found that the prosecution witnesses’ accounts were inconsistent and that the prosecution had not presented the true version of the occurrence.
People on both sides were injured, including grievous injuries, and the accused had multiple injuries, one of them grievous.
The High Court could not determine how the occurrence began or who was the aggressor, and found that it was not a free fight.
Although the High Court did not accept the defence account, the accused’s injuries made it difficult to exclude the probability that he acted in self-defence.
The High Court nevertheless upheld the accused’s conviction for an individual assault.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Where the true version and genesis of an occurrence are not established, a court cannot reconstruct a new case to sustain an individual assault; a probability that the accused acted in self-defence is sufficient to entitle the accused to acquittal. The judgment cites no earlier cases or statutory provision as the basis for this principle; Section 304, Part I, IPC is identified only as the provision under which the conviction had been entered.
members.conclusion: The conviction and sentence were set aside and the accused was acquitted because the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the court could not sustain the conviction by reconstructing a new case of individual assault.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: An accused appealed a criminal conviction for an individual assault.
predicates.prosecution_version_rejected: The court found that the prosecution had not established the true version, genesis, or manner of the occurrence.
predicates.injuries_on_both_sides: People on both sides of the dispute were injured, including people with grievous injuries.
predicates.aggressor_unknown: The court could not determine how the occurrence began or who was the aggressor.
predicates.not_free_fight: The court found that the occurrence was not a free fight.
predicates.self_defence_probable: The accused’s injuries and the circumstances left a probability that the accused acted in self-defence.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence cannot stand when the evidence does not form a complete chain pointing to guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on a disbelieved extra-judicial confession, kerosene residues on a child’s clothing, a kerosene can whose recovery was disbelieved, the appellant’s lack of burn injuries, and alleged motive.
The evidence did not connect the appellant to the kerosene on the clothing; kerosene was also used in the household, and the deceased did not accuse or suspect anyone in her declaration.
Other occupants of the house were also uninjured, and circumstances in the record left room for an explanation consistent with innocence.
The lower courts convicted the appellant, but the Supreme Court found the circumstantial chain incomplete and gave the appellant the benefit of doubt.
members.legal_principle: Under Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, the circumstances relied on must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive, exclude every reasonable hypothesis except guilt, and form a complete chain. The distinction between what may be true and what must be true is explained in Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra. Devilal v. State of Rajasthan, relying also on Sujit Biswas v. State of Assam and Raja v. State of Haryana, reiterates that suspicion cannot substitute for proof and that a reasonable view consistent with innocence entitles the accused to the benefit of doubt. A false defence cannot replace proof of the facts the prosecution must establish, as stated in Shankarlal. Motive, suspicion, and circumstances that do not connect the accused to the act do not establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: The conviction and sentence could not be sustained; the appeal was allowed, the conviction was set aside, and the appellant was acquitted on the benefit of doubt.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and circumstantial_case and (prosecution_links_incomplete or reasonable_innocent_hypothesis_remains)

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.circumstantial_case: The prosecution seeks to establish guilt through circumstances rather than direct evidence of the act.
predicates.prosecution_links_incomplete: The prosecution evidence does not establish a complete chain connecting the accused to the crime.
predicates.reasonable_innocent_hypothesis_remains: The established circumstances permit a reasonable explanation consistent with the accused’s innocence.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction resting on circumstantial evidence cannot stand when the circumstances relied on do not prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The conviction rested on alleged motive, an earlier sighting of the accused with the deceased, an extrajudicial confession, recovery of the bodies, and recovery of the deceased's belongings.

The alleged motive was speculative, the earlier sighting did not establish a last-seen circumstance, the confession lacked corroboration, the open-field recovery did not show exclusive knowledge, and the belongings were found where the deceased had lived.
The bodies were recovered months after death in a disintegrated condition, and the prosecution did not call a relative to identify them.
members.legal_principle: The Court required the prosecution's circumstantial case to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and concluded that the circumstances relied on did not do so. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The charge was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; the conviction and sentences were set aside and the appeal was allowed.

predicates.appeal_against_murder_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction for murder.
predicates.conviction_rests_on_circumstantial_evide: The conviction rested on a set of circumstantial evidence.
predicates.relied_on_circumstances_do_not_prove_cha: The circumstances relied on, considered together, did not prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction based on eyewitness identification of the assailant cannot stand where the medical evidence does not identify which of two similar seized weapons caused the fatal injury and the weapons were not shown to the medical witness.
material_facts: The deceased died from a sharp punctured wound to the chest, which the medical witness said might have been caused by a spear-like weapon.
The prosecution alleged that one accused used a spear and another used a similar weapon; both types of weapon were seized from their respective houses.
The medical witness had not seen the seized weapons and acknowledged that he could not distinguish between the two types as relevant to the injury.
The eyewitnesses attributed the fatal blow to one accused, but the Court found their evidence could not be accepted without independent corroboration in the circumstances of the case.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution, and the Court, should ensure that an alleged weapon of the offence, if available, is shown to the medical witness so that the witness can state whether it could have caused the injuries. Failure to do so may cause a miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on Kartarey v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: It could not be determined with certainty whether the fatal injury was caused by the weapon attributed to the convicted accused or by the similar weapon attributed to the other accused; the murder conviction could not be sustained.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.fatal_injury_could_be_caused_by_similar_: The medical evidence permits the fatal injury to have been caused by either of two similar weapons associated with different people.
predicates.seized_weapons_not_shown_to_medical_witn: The available weapons were not shown to the medical witness for an opinion about which could have caused the injury.
predicates.assailant_attribution_lacks_independent_: The evidence attributing the fatal act to the convicted person lacks independent corroboration sufficient to resolve the uncertainty.

members.legal_issue: Substantive convictions cannot stand when the proved criminal arrangement supports conspiracy but the substantive offences themselves have not been established.
material_facts: The Court accepted the conspiracy finding only in relation to the fraudulent claim for damage to stored goods.
The Court concluded that the substantive convictions for cheating and criminal misconduct could not be maintained.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the conspiracy proved in relation to the stored-goods claim from the substantive offences charged and held that the substantive convictions could not be maintained when those offences themselves had not been committed.
members.conclusion: The conviction for cheating and the conviction for criminal misconduct were set aside, while the conspiracy conviction was maintained.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal brought with special leave.
predicates.conspiracy_proven_for_compensation_claim: The evidence establishes a criminal agreement relating to a fraudulent compensation claim.
predicates.substantive_offences_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the separately charged substantive offences were committed.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based solely on circumstantial evidence cannot stand when the prosecution has not proved essential links that complete a chain excluding reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended entirely on circumstantial evidence.

The court was not satisfied that the accused had exclusive possession of the rooms where the body was found; the evidence supporting that claim came from witnesses whose testimony the court found unreliable or improbable.
The court rejected the evidence that the accused had been seen with the deceased shortly before the death and the evidence of an alleged extra-judicial confession.
The recovery of articles associated with the accused from the premises and of bloodstained clothing from his residence did not, in the circumstances, conclusively connect him to the murder.
The prosecution had not suggested or established a motive.
members.legal_principle: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances relied upon must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive in nature, and form a chain leaving no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with innocence. In such a case motive assumes greater importance, although a conviction may still be sustained without proof of motive if the established circumstances otherwise prove guilt. Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, a disclosure-based recovery may be considered with other circumstances if proved beyond reasonable doubt, but recovery alone does not necessarily complete the chain. No specific earlier case is named in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The chain of circumstances was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt, and the conviction and sentence were set aside on appeal.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and circumstantial_evidence_case and essential_links_unproved and remaining_evidence_inconclusive

predicates.remaining_evidence_inconclusive: The evidence left after the material circumstances were rejected did not conclusively establish guilt or complete the chain of circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A conviction must be set aside when the evidence leaves reasonable doubt about whether an accused participated in the attacks or instigated them.
material_facts: The accused was about 70 years old at the time of the occurrence.
The court found reasonable doubt about whether he had caught hold of the injured man and whether he had directed his sons to attack and kill the deceased persons.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that an accused is entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt. It found the evidence did not establish the accused's participation or instigation beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted him of the offences charged under sections 302/34 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The court gave the accused the benefit of reasonable doubt, set aside his convictions under sections 302/34 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code, and acquitted him.

predicates.accused_was_elderly: The accused was elderly at the time of the occurrence.
predicates.reasonable_doubt_about_participation: The evidence left reasonable doubt about whether the accused participated in or instigated the attacks.

members.legal_issue: Convictions for conspiracy and related offenses cannot stand when the prosecution fails to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged victim was defrauded.
material_facts: The alleged victim said she learned of the alleged deception shortly after the document was executed, but her early complaint did not identify the accused or state that she had not received the stated consideration.

The approver was the alleged victim’s trusted representative, admitted participating in the fraud for a share of the proceeds, and sought to become an approver about twenty months after the alleged offense.
The approver’s earlier statements to police were withheld from the defense, and his testimony lacked reliable corroboration on material aspects.
Despite knowing that the document purported to transfer her land, the alleged victim did not seek a civil declaration that it was obtained by fraud, and no explanation for that omission was given.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. An approver’s evidence requires careful scrutiny and corroboration, particularly where the witness admits betrayal for personal gain. The Court also treated the unexplained withholding of earlier police statements as supporting an adverse inference. The supplied judgment identifies no specific statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for these principles.
members.conclusion: The prosecution did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged victim had been defrauded. The accused were entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt, and their convictions and sentences were set aside.

predicates.accused_convictions_are_set_aside: The accused’s convictions are set aside.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence cannot stand when the circumstances relied on do not establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended on circumstantial evidence.
The prosecution did not establish that the house where blood was found was exclusively owned or possessed by the appellant, or that the recovered clothes belonged to him.
The alleged recovery of the weapon and clothes was disbelieved, and the evidence that the appellant took the deceased away was not supported by other conclusive circumstances.
The alleged motive did not connect the appellant to the crime, and the reporting of the discovery of the body was delayed.
The courts below had convicted the appellant of murder and related offences, and he appealed.
members.legal_principle: In a case resting on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must connect the accused to the crime sufficiently to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Here, the alleged blood evidence did not connect the appellant to the crime, and the circumstances relied on did not establish guilt. The Court referred to the charges under Sections 302 read with 34 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The prosecution had not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the conviction was set aside and the appeal allowed, with the appellant given the benefit of doubt.

predicates.appeal_from_circumstantial_conviction: The accused appeals against a conviction resting on circumstantial evidence.
predicates.key_circumstances_unproved: One or more circumstances essential to the prosecution case are not established by reliable evidence.
predicates.evidence_does_not_connect_accused: The evidence, even if accepted in part, does not reliably connect the accused to the crime.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for exceeding a right of private defence cannot rest solely on an accused’s statement when the prosecution evidence is unreliable and the accused’s account has not been disproved.
material_facts: The accused said that the deceased and another person attacked him and that villagers injured the deceased while coming to his aid.
The prosecution evidence was found untrustworthy, and the accused’s account could not be rejected as false.
The complainant sought conviction for culpable homicide on the basis that the accused had exceeded a right of private defence.
members.legal_principle: The accused’s statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not a substitute for prosecution evidence. Because the exculpatory account could not be rejected and the prosecution evidence was unreliable, the statement did not provide a basis for conviction under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code on the theory that the accused exceeded a right of private defence.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the request to convict the accused for exceeding a right of private defence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_seeking_conviction and accused_claims_defensive_response and prosecution_evidence_unreliable and defensive_account_not_disproved

predicates.criminal_appeal_seeking_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal asking the court to convict an accused who was acquitted.
predicates.accused_claims_defensive_response: The accused’s account is that the accused responded to an attack or acted to defend against it.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_unreliable: The evidence led by the prosecution is not sufficiently trustworthy to establish guilt.
predicates.defensive_account_not_disproved: The evidence does not establish that the accused’s account of a defensive response is false.

members.legal_issue: An accused cannot be convicted when the prosecution evidence and surrounding circumstances leave reasonable doubt about whether the accused committed the offence.
material_facts: The witnesses who were presented as independent arrived after the incident had begun and did not see how it started.
The prosecution witnesses did not explain the injuries on the accused, and some testimony omitted those injuries despite an earlier statement mentioning an injury to one accused.
The trial court’s account of a possible confrontation and the defence version of the incident could not be excluded by the evidence.
The Supreme Court considered the prosecution’s evidence insufficient to establish the offence beyond reasonable doubt, even though the accused’s right of private defence was not established.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. A defence account need not itself be established for the evidence and circumstances to leave reasonable doubt. The Court relied on the burden of proof and its assessment of the record; it cited no earlier cases or statutory provisions for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The prosecution had not proved the offence against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt, so the conviction was set aside and the appellant was acquitted.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_leaves_reasonable_d: The prosecution evidence and surrounding circumstances do not exclude a reasonable possibility inconsistent with the accused’s guilt.
predicates.witnesses_did_not_see_incident_begin: The witnesses whose testimony is relied on did not see how the incident began.
predicates.accused_injuries_were_unexplained: The prosecution evidence did not explain injuries found on the accused.

members.legal_issue: An accused cannot be convicted on the basis of an inadmissible repeated disclosure when no other circumstance connects that accused with the crime.
material_facts: The accused's only alleged link to the crime was a disclosure statement made after another accused had already disclosed the location of the concealed body.
The later statement was inadmissible because it repeated information already disclosed and capable of discovery.
The prosecution relied on no other circumstance connecting this accused with the crime.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, admits only the portion of a statement that distinctly leads to discovery; a repeated disclosure after the fact is already discovered is inadmissible. Without admissible evidence connecting the accused to the offence, the prosecution has not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The prosecution had not proved the case beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused's conviction and sentence were set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_criminal_conviction: The case is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.only_link_is_inadmissible_repeated_discl: The sole circumstance connecting the accused to the crime is a statement that repeats a fact already disclosed and discovered.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand when the prosecution has not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the evidence raises reasonable doubt about whether the accused was the aggressor.
material_facts: The High Court treated one witness as a false witness who had not seen the occurrence, leaving no accepted eyewitness account of the first shot at the first deceased.

The injured witness testified for the defence that the accused fired after being challenged and attacked, and evidence from the witness and his family supported allegations that police had pressured them to support the prosecution.
The doctor’s evidence about tattooing on the wounds was not properly displaced by the High Court’s unsupported hypothesis of mistake.

The Court found an important lacuna in the prosecution case and concluded that the defence evidence, considered with the accused’s statement, appeared to negate the prosecution claim that the accused was the aggressor.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Where the evidence leaves an important lacuna and the defence evidence raises reasonable doubt about the prosecution account, the accused is entitled to the benefit of that doubt. The Court applied Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, Section 27 of the Indian Arms Act, and Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in considering the charges and the accused’s account; it cited no earlier case for the benefit-of-doubt ruling.
members.conclusion: The prosecution had not proved the murder beyond reasonable doubt. The accused was acquitted, and the conviction under the Arms Act was also set aside on that basis.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.prosecution_case_has_material_lacuna: The prosecution evidence leaves an important gap in proving the accused’s guilt.
predicates.defence_evidence_raises_reasonable_doubt: The defence evidence, considered with the other evidence, raises reasonable doubt about whether the accused was the aggressor.

members.legal_issue: A forgery conviction cannot stand where the prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the case rests on suspicion or the accused’s benefit from the transaction.
material_facts: The impersonator who executed the power of attorney was not found or investigated.

Forensic evidence showed that the signature and fingerprints on the power of attorney did not match those of the property owner, but the prosecution did not prove that either accused made the document.
The trial and appellate courts relied on the accused’s benefit from, or involvement in, the mortgage transaction, without proof that they made the false power of attorney.
The High Court acquitted the accused, and the complainant appealed that acquittal.
members.legal_principle: In a criminal trial, guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; strong suspicion, coincidence, or grave doubt cannot replace proof. A reasonable doubt must be practical rather than an abstract theoretical hypothesis. The Court relied on Latesh @ Dadu Baburao Karlekar v. State of Maharashtra, (2018) 3 SCC 66, and applied the principle that penal liability cannot be established by inference from benefit or suspicion alone.
members.conclusion: The prosecution did not prove the forgery charge beyond reasonable doubt, and the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_acquittal and prosecution_did_not_prove_accused_made_false_document and imposter_not_investigated and conviction_rested_on_suspicion_or_benefit

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_did_not_prove_accused_made_f: The prosecution did not prove that the accused made the false document.
predicates.imposter_not_investigated: The person who impersonated the true document-maker was not located or investigated.
predicates.conviction_rested_on_suspicion_or_benefi: The conviction relied on suspicion or the accused’s benefit from the transaction rather than proof of the charged conduct.

members.legal_issue: A conviction cannot stand when no prosecution evidence identifies the accused as participating in the offence and the accused’s statement, by itself, does not admit guilt.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses identified one accused and two other persons as having cut and removed the crops, but did not identify the two appellants whose convictions were challenged.
One of those appellants stated that he had removed crops from his own field, but the Court held that this statement, standing alone, was not an admission of guilt.
The convictions of the two appellants were manifestly erroneous on the face of the record.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a conviction requires a legal evidentiary basis and that the statement about removing crops from one’s own field was not, standing alone, an admission of guilt. It exercised supervisory power under Article 227 in the appeal. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the two appellants were set aside, and they were discharged from bail.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: An accused appeals a conviction entered by a local adjudicatory body.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_do_not_identify_ac: The prosecution witnesses do not identify the accused as participating in the alleged offence.
predicates.accused_statement_alone_is_not_an_admiss: The accused makes a statement that, considered by itself, does not admit guilt of the offence.

members.legal_issue: A criminal conviction for forgery cannot be sustained where conflicting fingerprint-expert evidence and suspicious circumstances do not prove that the disputed impression was forged.
material_facts: The forgery charges concerned a will bearing the deceased's disputed thumb impression.
There was no direct evidence of forgery.
The prosecution expert examined the impressions briefly and identified differences, but acknowledged that some differences could result from pressure of ink or other factors.
Three defence experts opined that the disputed impression matched the admitted impression, and the Court found no positive dissimilarity between them.
The impressions had been taken with different inks and differed in angle and size, which could explain superficial differences.
members.legal_principle: For the charges under Sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, suspicion, even if relevant to the genuineness of a will in civil proceedings, cannot take the place of proof in a criminal case. The conflicting expert evidence did not establish forgery beyond the required criminal standard. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove that the thumb impression was forged, and the conflicting evidence and suspicious circumstances did not safely support a criminal conviction; the appellants were acquitted.

rule.if: criminal_forgery_prosecution and conflicting_expert_opinions and no_positive_impression_difference and suspicious_circumstances_only

predicates.criminal_forgery_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution alleging forgery of a document.
