predicates.trial_discretion_not_arbitrary: The trial court’s exercise of discretion was not capricious or arbitrary.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not re-examine a concurrent factual finding in a civil appeal when the finding is not shown to be legally vitiated.
material_facts: Both lower courts found that the business was separate and was neither a joint family business nor treated as one.
The appellant argued that the finding was legally defective because certain documents had not been considered.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had examined the documents and that the appellant had not shown the concurrent factual finding to be legally vitiated.
members.legal_principle: Following the usual practice under Article 133 of the Constitution, the Court does not further scrutinize a concurrent finding of fact in a civil appeal where no legal defect has been established.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the business was separate was not open to further scrutiny in the appeal and was left undisturbed.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_concurrent_factual_fin: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which both lower courts reached the same factual finding.
predicates.finding_not_legally_vitiated: The appellant has not established that the concurrent factual finding is legally defective.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court would not use its discretionary jurisdiction to disturb concurrent convictions supported by acceptable oral and documentary evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court had both convicted the accused on the charges upheld in the appeals.
The concurrent findings rested on oral and documentary evidence that the Supreme Court found acceptable.
The accused challenged those findings in appeals brought by special leave.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, the Court declined to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction where concurrent findings of conviction were based on acceptable evidence.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136 of the Constitution and dismissed both appeals.

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal before the Supreme Court brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_convictions_are_supported_by_: The lower courts made concurrent findings of guilt supported by acceptable oral or documentary evidence.

members.legal_issue: An appeal by special leave does not ordinarily warrant reappraisal of factual or legal conclusions unless a serious error causing injustice is shown.
material_facts: The courts below found that the claimants had not proved the asserted tenancy or personal cultivation and that the possession decree was not a nullity.
The Supreme Court found no misreading of evidence, serious misunderstanding of its effect, or disregard of important evidence that would fundamentally affect the result.
The challenged judgments were not shown to contain a serious legal infirmity resulting in grave injustice.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its settled practice in appeals by special leave: it does not ordinarily reconsider all factual or legal conclusions reached below, but may examine the evidence in rare cases involving misreading, serious misunderstanding, or complete disregard of important evidence that causes injustice. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reappraise the evidence or disturb the conclusions below and dismissed both appeals.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and lower_court_findings_challenged and not serious_error_causing_injustice_shown

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.lower_court_findings_challenged: The appellant asks the reviewing court to reconsider factual or legal conclusions reached by the courts below.
predicates.serious_error_causing_injustice_shown: The appellant establishes a serious evidentiary or legal error that caused injustice.

members.legal_issue: In an appeal by special leave, factual challenges are not entertained unless material evidence was ignored or the finding under challenge was perverse.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the adequacy of the sale consideration and alleged that some discharged debts were owed to company directors.
The High Court had made no finding supporting those allegations.
The Supreme Court found no basis to conclude that material evidence had been ignored or that the High Court’s finding was perverse.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court will not permit questions of fact to be raised unless material evidence has been ignored by the High Court or its finding is perverse.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not permit the factual challenges to be raised because the required basis for disturbing the High Court’s findings was absent.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and factual_challenge and (material_evidence_ignored or finding_perverse)

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.factual_challenge: A party asks the Supreme Court to revisit a factual issue decided below.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The court below failed to consider material evidence relevant to the factual finding.
predicates.finding_perverse: The factual finding of the court below is perverse.
predicates.factual_challenge_may_be_considered: The Supreme Court may consider the factual challenge.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court ordinarily does not reassess concurrent criminal findings in an appeal admitted by special leave unless a substantial error affecting the trial or the result is shown.
material_facts: The convictions and sentences had been confirmed by the High Court, and the appellants challenged the concurrent assessment of the evidence.
The Supreme Court found no error of the kind that warranted intervention.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 134 and 136 of the Constitution, an appeal admitted by special leave is distinct from an appeal available as of right or on a certificate. The Court ordinarily accepts concurrent findings and does not reassess the evidence at large; it may interfere where, for example, there is a violation of natural justice or the accused's rights, a misreading of vital evidence, an improper reception or rejection of evidence that leaves the conviction unsupported, or an error of law or procedure causing a failure of justice. No specific earlier case is cited for this principle in the majority opinion.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to disturb the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: special_leave_criminal_appeal and concurrent_lower_court_findings and not fundamental_error_shown

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The matter is a criminal appeal that the Supreme Court is hearing after granting special leave.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_findings: The lower criminal courts reached the same material findings.
predicates.fundamental_error_shown: The record establishes a serious legal, evidentiary, procedural, or fairness error that warrants intervention.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not disturb concurrent factual findings supported by proved facts merely by re-evaluating the evidence in an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found that the tenant had constructed the wall and installed the door and that the construction materially affected the building’s value or utility.
The Appellate Authority and High Court confirmed those findings.
The Supreme Court considered the challenge in an appeal by special leave.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not re-evaluate evidence to upset a concurrent finding of fact supported by proved facts.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding was a finding of fact supported by the evidence, and the Court would not re-evaluate the evidence and set it aside.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_supported_by_proved_facts: The factual finding rests on facts proved in the proceeding.
predicates.supreme_court_does_not_reweigh_evidence_: The Supreme Court does not re-evaluate evidence to set aside the supported concurrent factual findings.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not interfere with a tribunal’s decision affirmed by the High Court merely because another view of the facts is possible, absent a fundamental failure of justice or a patent procedural or legal error causing manifest injustice.
material_facts: The appeals challenged the High Court’s dismissal of applications seeking supervisory review of tribunal decisions.
The High Court had affirmed the tribunal’s findings.
The Supreme Court found no fundamental failure of justice, patent or flagrant procedural or legal error, or resulting manifest injustice.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, the Court will not interfere with the exercise of supervisory discretion merely because two views are possible on the facts. Intervention is justified where an order violates fundamental principles of justice and fair play, contains a patent or flagrant procedural or legal error, or results in manifest injustice. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s judgment, dismissed the appeals, and made no order as to costs.

rule.if: appeal_from_supervisory_review_dismissal and tribunal_decision_affirmed_by_high_court and no_fundamental_justice_violation and no_patent_procedural_or_legal_error and no_manifest_injustice

predicates.appeal_from_supervisory_review_dismissal: The appeal challenges a High Court decision dismissing an application for supervisory review of a tribunal decision.
predicates.tribunal_decision_affirmed_by_high_court: The High Court affirmed the tribunal’s decision.
predicates.no_fundamental_justice_violation: The reviewing court found no violation of fundamental principles of justice and fair play.
predicates.no_patent_procedural_or_legal_error: The reviewing court found no patent or flagrant procedural or legal error in the tribunal’s order.
predicates.no_manifest_injustice: The reviewing court found that the order did not result in manifest injustice.
predicates.appeal_dismissed_without_interference: The appeal is dismissed without the reviewing court interfering with the challenged decision.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not interfere in an appeal under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings that are supported by evidence and are not perverse, illegal, or arbitrary.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both found that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform and that the defendant had avoided the agreement.
The Supreme Court examined the evidence after leave had been granted and found that the concurrent findings were supported by the record and disclosed no perversity or illegality.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court is loath to reappreciate evidence in an appeal involving concurrent factual findings, particularly where the findings are not perverse, illegal, or arbitrary. No earlier case was cited for this proposition in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_under_article_136_from_concurrent: The proceeding is an appeal under Article 136 challenging factual findings reached by both lower courts.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent factual findings have support in the evidence on the record.
predicates.no_perversity_illegality_or_arbitrarines: The challenged findings are not perverse, illegal, or arbitrary.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise factual conclusions concurrently reached by the lower courts in an appeal by special leave.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court considered the evidence and circumstances and reached conclusions against the appellant.
The appellant's challenges to the reporting sequence, the injuries, and the location of blood principally sought different factual inferences.
The appeal was brought by special leave.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court will not ordinarily reopen factual conclusions reached by the High Court after consideration of the evidence where doing so would require reappraisal of factual inferences.
members.conclusion: The Court would not upset the High Court's conclusions by reappraising those factual matters.

predicates.appeal_by_special_leave: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the High Court have reached the same factual conclusion after considering the evidence.
predicates.challenge_requires_reappraisal: The challenge asks the Supreme Court to reconsider evidence or draw different factual inferences.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not interfere with an acquittal unless the appellate court’s appraisal of the evidence is vitiated by a glaring infirmity.
material_facts: The High Court acquitted the accused after finding the prosecution evidence insufficient and unreliable.
The State appealed against the acquittal, and the Supreme Court found no glaring infirmity in the High Court’s appraisal of the evidence.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal against an acquittal, the Court does not interfere with the High Court’s appraisal of evidence unless that appraisal is vitiated by a glaring infirmity. No earlier case or statutory provision is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the acquittal and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a judgment that acquitted the accused.
predicates.no_glaring_infirmity_in_evidence_apprais: The reviewing court finds no glaring infirmity in the acquitting court’s appraisal of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not interfere under its special-leave jurisdiction with the reduction of compensation rates where the overall factual result does not warrant interference.
material_facts: The State had no right of appeal to the Revenue Tribunal under the Act but persuaded the Tribunal, in the jagirdars’ appeal, to reduce some village-site land compensation rates.
The Tribunal also increased the area of village-site land eligible for compensation, and the net compensation payable to the jagirdars increased.
The Tribunal’s factual decision was not found to be erroneous.
members.legal_principle: Sections 16 and 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act did not give the State a right of appeal to the Tribunal. The Court considered that there might be substance in the argument that the State could not challenge the rates under Order 41 Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, referring to The Management of Itakhoolie Tea Estate v. Its Workmen. Nevertheless, taking the totality of the circumstances and the factual result, the Court declined to interfere under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the Tribunal’s decision on the compensation rates.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_compensation_decision and state_lacked_appeal_right and tribunal_reduced_rates_in_opponent_appeal and tribunal_increased_compensable_area and net_compensation_increased and factual_decision_not_erroneous

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_compensation_d: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging a compensation decision.
predicates.state_lacked_appeal_right: The State had no right of appeal to the tribunal from the original compensation decision.
predicates.tribunal_reduced_rates_in_opponent_appea: The tribunal reduced some compensation rates while deciding an appeal brought by the opposing claimant.
predicates.tribunal_increased_compensable_area: The tribunal increased the area for which compensation was payable.
predicates.net_compensation_increased: The overall amount payable after the tribunal’s decision increased despite the reduced rates.
predicates.factual_decision_not_erroneous: The tribunal’s factual decision was not found to be erroneous.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not normally reappraise evidence or interfere under its special appellate jurisdiction with concurrent findings of fact.
material_facts: The Assistant District Judge, Additional District Judge, and High Court all found that the society had been allotted only a plot of land.
The appeal challenged those concurrent findings.
The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and found no basis to reach a contrary conclusion.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not normally reappraise evidence or interfere with concurrent findings of fact, even where another conclusion might be possible on the evidence.
members.conclusion: The Court did not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_fact_findings: An appeal asks the Supreme Court to disturb factual findings that the lower courts reached concurrently.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent findings have evidentiary support in the record.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise concurrent factual findings in a criminal appeal absent perversity, legal or procedural error, or exceptional illegality or irregularity causing a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both found the appellants guilty after examining the eyewitness evidence.
The Supreme Court found no reason to disbelieve the eyewitnesses and no basis to characterize the concurrent findings as perverse or legally defective.
The evidence included natural witnesses to the occurrence, including a witness unrelated to the deceased, and the courts below had critically examined the testimony.
members.legal_principle: The Supreme Court is not a regular court of appeal for routine scrutiny of factual findings. It ordinarily will not reappraise evidence supporting concurrent findings unless there is an error of law or procedure, perversity, manifest illegality, or grave or serious irregularity resulting in a miscarriage of justice; it may intervene where a wrong inference of law has been drawn from proved facts. The Court relied on Duli Chand v. Delhi Administration (1975 (4) SCC 469), Ramnik Lal Gokaldas and Ors. v. The State of Gujarat (1976 (1) SCC 6), Mst. Dalbir Kaur and Ors. v. State of Punjab (1976 (4) SCC 158), Ramanbhai Naranbhai Patel and Ors. v. State of Gujarat (2000 (1) SCC 358), and Chandra Bihari Gautam and Ors. v. State of Bihar (JT 2002 (4) SC 62).
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to reappraise the evidence or interfere with the concurrent findings, and dismissed the appeals.

rule.if: supreme_court_criminal_appeal_against_conviction and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_not_perverse and no_serious_error_causing_miscarriage

predicates.supreme_court_criminal_appeal_against_co: The proceeding is a criminal appeal before the Supreme Court challenging a conviction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the High Court reached the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_not_perverse: The concurrent findings are not shown to be perverse.
predicates.no_serious_error_causing_miscarriage: No legal or procedural error, manifest illegality, or grave or serious irregularity causing a miscarriage of justice is established.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not reappreciate concurrent factual findings in an appeal under Article 136 when they are supported by the evidence and are not materially perverse or illegal.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court made concurrent findings on the material issues after considering the pleadings and evidence.
The findings were capable of being reached on the evidence and were not contrary to the pleadings, evidence or a principle of law.
The appellant did not establish material perversity or illegality in those findings.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, concurrent findings of fact are binding where they are supportable on the evidence and no material perversity or illegality is shown; the Court will not reappreciate the entire evidence in those circumstances.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to reappreciate the evidence or interfere with the concurrent findings, and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal invoking the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 136.
predicates.concurrent_findings_supported_by_evidenc: The lower courts reached the same factual findings, and those findings could be reached on the evidence.
predicates.no_material_perversity_or_illegality: No material perversity or illegality in the findings was established.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court ordinarily does not interfere with findings of fact reached by a High Court unless intervention is needed to prevent a gross miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The High Court found that the business was ancestral, that the partition was not vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation, and that the allocation of shares in the business was unfair and prejudicial to the minor sons' interests.
The Supreme Court found no justifiable ground to go behind those findings.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it is not its practice to interfere with findings of fact reached by a High Court except to prevent a gross miscarriage of justice.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to disturb the High Court's findings of fact.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal_from_high_court and high_court_found_facts and not gross_miscarriage_of_justice

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_from_high_court: A party brought an appeal to the Supreme Court from a High Court decision.
predicates.high_court_found_facts: The High Court reached findings of fact in the case.
predicates.gross_miscarriage_of_justice: Leaving the High Court's factual findings undisturbed would cause a gross miscarriage of justice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court ordinarily does not disturb a High Court’s factual finding in a special-leave appeal when the High Court was competent to decide the facts and the finding has support in the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court found that the daughter had died before the limited owner, relying on witness evidence and a revenue record that supported its conclusion.
The first appellate court reached the opposite conclusion without discussing the parties’ evidence in detail, relying in part on the absence of a statement that the daughter had inherited the land.
The High Court preferred the trial court’s view of the evidence and found that the daughter had died first.
The appeal to the Supreme Court was brought by special leave, and the High Court had jurisdiction to decide factual questions in the second appeal.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court will not ordinarily discard a High Court’s finding on a question of fact when the High Court was competent under the law governing the appeal to reach that finding. The Court also rejected the inference drawn by the first appellate court from the witnesses’ failure to say that the daughter inherited the property.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to disturb the High Court’s finding that the daughter had predeceased the limited owner and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and challenged_finding_is_factual and high_court_was_competent_to_decide_facts and evidence_supports_high_court_finding

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding before the Supreme Court is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.challenged_finding_is_factual: The finding challenged in the appeal concerns a question of fact.
predicates.high_court_was_competent_to_decide_facts: The High Court had authority under the law governing the appeal to decide the factual question.
predicates.evidence_supports_high_court_finding: The evidence in the record provides support for the High Court’s factual finding.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court’s review of concurrent factual findings in a criminal appeal by special leave is limited to exceptional defects causing grave injustice.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused, and the High Court affirmed the convictions after considering the evidence.
The Supreme Court found no qualifying defect in the concurrent findings concerning the appellants whose convictions it upheld.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 gives the Supreme Court a discretionary power exercised sparingly in exceptional criminal cases. Concurrent findings based on appreciation of evidence are ordinarily not reopened, though intervention may be justified by errors of law or procedure, violation of natural justice or fair hearing, material errors of record or misreading of evidence, disregard of vital inconsistencies, wrong legal inferences, or conclusions unsupported by evidence. The Court relied on Pritam Singh v. The State; Mohinder Singh v. The State; Hem Raj v. The State of Ajmer; Khachera Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh; Saravanabhavan v. State of Madras; Piara Singh v. State of Punjab; Nargun Sunder Das Godeia v. State of Rajasthan; Guli Chand v. State of Rajasthan; Kaur Sain v. State of Punjab; Abdul Gani v. State of Madhya Pradesh; Kanbi Nanji Virji v. State of Gujarat; and Dharam Das v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The Court would not undertake a fresh appraisal of evidence or reconsider witness credibility merely because special leave had been granted; arguments were confined to points that could justify special leave, and interference was warranted only in exceptional circumstances such as legal or procedural error, misreading of material evidence, or a manifestly perverse finding causing grave injustice.

rule.if: criminal_special_leave_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and not exceptional_review_defect

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The case is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the appellate court reached the same factual findings after assessing the evidence.
predicates.exceptional_review_defect: The appellate findings contain an exceptional legal or procedural defect, material misreading or omission of evidence, or manifest perversity that causes grave injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not disturb concurrent findings on witness evidence in a special-leave criminal appeal without an extraordinary showing of gross and palpable injustice.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both accepted the eyewitness evidence, which was corroborated by the dying declaration and medical evidence.

The appellants repeated challenges to the witnesses’ relationships, the medical evidence, and the injuries to the accused, but the Court found no serious infirmity in the evidence or extraordinary injustice.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court is very slow to interfere with concurrent conclusions on appreciation of witness evidence; an appellant must make out an extraordinary case of gross and palpable injustice. The Court applied this principle to the findings affirmed by the High Court.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings of the courts below.

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_evidence_findings: The trial court and appellate court reached the same findings on the evidence.
predicates.no_extraordinary_gross_injustice_shown: The appellant did not establish an extraordinary case of gross and palpable injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline to re-examine a factual question that the High Court has considered in detail and resolved on the evidence.
material_facts: The High Court considered whether notice had been affixed on the land, whether the appellant was available or resident in the area, and whether the notice sufficiently identified her.
The High Court found that notice had been affixed and that the circumstances did not undermine the award.
The appellate court affirmed those factual findings.
members.legal_principle: Where the High Court has considered a matter in detail and recorded findings on a factual question, the Supreme Court may decline to examine that question in a further appeal. The Court relied on Tika Ram v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to re-examine the factual question decided by the High Court.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court from a High Court decision.
predicates.high_court_made_detailed_factual_finding: The High Court considered the matter in detail and recorded findings on the factual question.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reassess evidence in a criminal appeal from a High Court unless the High Court overlooked material evidence or approached the case from a wholly wrong point of view.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the High Court’s confirmation of convictions after it had assessed the evidence and acquitted some accused persons.
The Supreme Court found no material evidence that the High Court had failed to consider and no wholly wrong approach to the case.
The Court found the criticisms of the High Court’s judgment invalid.
members.legal_principle: In a criminal case, the Supreme Court does not review the evidence merely because a party challenges the High Court’s assessment; review is warranted if material evidence was not considered or the High Court approached the case from a wholly wrong point of view.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not disturb the High Court’s assessment of the evidence, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_high_court and not material_evidence_overlooked and not wholly_wrong_approach

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_high_court: A party brought a criminal appeal to the Supreme Court challenging a High Court’s assessment of evidence.
predicates.material_evidence_overlooked: The High Court failed to take material evidence into consideration.
predicates.wholly_wrong_approach: The High Court approached the case from a wholly wrong point of view.

members.legal_issue: In an appeal challenging compensation for compulsory land acquisition, the Supreme Court does not reappraise evidence unless a legal principle has been violated or gross injustice has occurred.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the compensation assessed for acquired land and property, alleging gross overvaluation.
The Court found no violation of principle or gross injustice that would justify its intervention.
members.legal_principle: The Court's review of an evidentiary valuation is not an opportunity to reappraise the evidence; intervention is warranted only in special cases involving a violation of principle or gross injustice. The appeal was brought by certificate under Article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution as it then stood.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reappraise the evidence because no special ground for intervention was established.

rule.if: compensation_valuation_appeal and not legal_principle_violation and not gross_injustice

predicates.compensation_valuation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a court's valuation of compensation for acquired property.
predicates.legal_principle_violation: A legal principle was violated in reaching the valuation.
predicates.gross_injustice: The valuation resulted in gross injustice.

members.legal_issue: A request for detailed reappraisal of evidence does not require the Supreme Court to undertake that exercise in an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: The appellants asked the Supreme Court to undertake a detailed scrutiny and reappraisal of the evidence.
The matter was before the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave under Article 136.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it was not called upon to undertake detailed scrutiny and reappraisal of the evidence in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to undertake the requested detailed reappraisal of the evidence.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal under the Supreme Court’s special-leave jurisdiction.
predicates.detailed_evidence_reappraisal_requested: A party asks the Court to conduct detailed scrutiny and reappraisal of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily disturb concurrent factual findings in a discretionary appeal when no basis for interference is shown.
material_facts: The trial court found the will and gift deed proved, but the first appellate court and the High Court found them unproved and found suspicious circumstances surrounding their execution.
The findings that other properties were unavailable for division because of separate assignment documents had become final and were not in dispute.
The Supreme Court found no reason to depart from the concurrent appellate findings on the will and gift deed.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that concurrent findings of fact should not normally be interfered with in the exercise of its power under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, and found no reason to interfere in this case.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.supreme_court_discretionary_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court invoking its discretionary appellate power.
predicates.concurrent_appellate_factual_findings: The appellate court and the High Court have reached the same factual findings on the issue under appeal.
predicates.no_basis_for_interference: The Supreme Court finds no reason to depart from those concurrent factual findings.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court’s discretionary jurisdiction over appeals involving factual findings is exercised only exceptionally, including where a finding shocks the Court’s conscience or substantial and grave injustice has resulted from a disregard of legal process or a violation of natural justice.
material_facts: The accused appealed by special leave against their convictions and sentences entered by the appellate court after it reversed their acquittals.
The Supreme Court found that the appellate court had followed the principles governing appeals against acquittal and had given reasons for its decision.
The Supreme Court found no basis for treating the appellate court’s factual findings as exceptional or as causing substantial and grave injustice, and dismissed the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers a wide discretionary power, but the Court’s practice is not to interfere with findings of fact except in exceptional cases where the finding shocks its conscience. Interference is not permitted unless disregard of legal process, violation of natural justice, or otherwise results in substantial and grave injustice.
members.conclusion: No basis existed for the Supreme Court to interfere with the appellate court’s findings or judgment, so the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and factual_findings_challenged and acquittal_appeal_principles_followed and reasons_for_appellate_findings_given and findings_do_not_shock_conscience and no_substantial_grave_injustice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.factual_findings_challenged: The appellant asks the Supreme Court to disturb factual findings made by the appellate court.
predicates.acquittal_appeal_principles_followed: The appellate court followed the proper approach in reviewing and reversing the trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.reasons_for_appellate_findings_given: The appellate court stated reasons supporting its factual findings.
predicates.findings_do_not_shock_conscience: The appellate court’s factual findings are not of the exceptional kind that shocks the Supreme Court’s conscience.
predicates.no_substantial_grave_injustice: The record does not show substantial and grave injustice resulting from disregard of legal process or a violation of natural justice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not reopen factual findings in a special-leave appeal absent grave error in reaching those findings.
material_facts: The appeal included challenges to factual findings made by the High Court.
The Court described it as settled practice not to interfere with High Court factual findings unless grave errors had occurred.
The appellant was unable to identify any grave error in the findings.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136, the Court retains power to entertain an appeal, but its settled practice is not to interfere with a High Court’s factual findings unless it is satisfied that grave errors occurred in reaching them.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to permit argument on the factual findings.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.challenged_findings_are_factual: The challenged findings concern facts determined by the High Court.
predicates.no_grave_error_in_reaching_findings: The appellant did not establish a grave error in the process by which the High Court reached its factual findings.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings supported by the evidence when the parties understood and litigated the factual issue.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court concurrently found that the pathway had been used for access to the residential property.
The parties had understood and presented evidence on the implied-grant issue.
The High Court affirmed the concurrent findings, and the Supreme Court found no basis to disturb them.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to upset the concurrent findings of fact in the exercise of its powers under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, particularly where the parties had understood and adduced evidence on the issue.
members.conclusion: The concurrent factual findings were left undisturbed, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_findings and findings_are_factual and findings_are_supported_by_evidence and issue_was_understood_and_litigated

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging factual findings affirmed by successive courts.
predicates.findings_are_factual: The challenged findings concern what happened or what the evidence established.
predicates.findings_are_supported_by_evidence: The courts’ findings are supported by evidence presented in the case.
predicates.issue_was_understood_and_litigated: The parties understood the issue and presented their respective cases and evidence on it.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not interfere with a High Court’s factual finding based on its assessment of the evidence concerning whether an alienation was made for legal necessity.
material_facts: The High Court assessed the evidence and found that two transfers were not made for legal and pressing necessity.
The appellants challenged that finding in the appeal to the Supreme Court.
The challenge depended on the weight and sufficiency of the evidence considered by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The quantum of evidence sufficient to satisfy a court on a factual issue is within that court’s discretion; the Supreme Court therefore would not disturb the High Court’s finding on the evidence in this case.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not interfere with the High Court’s finding concerning the absence of legal necessity.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_high_court: The proceeding is a civil appeal from a High Court judgment.
predicates.high_court_finding_based_on_evidence_ass: The High Court made the challenged finding after assessing the evidence.
predicates.challenge_depends_on_weight_of_evidence: The challenge asks the appellate court to reassess the weight or sufficiency of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise evidence in a special-leave criminal appeal to displace concurrent factual findings merely because fact-finders accepted part of a witness’s testimony and rejected another part.
material_facts: The fact-finding courts made concurrent findings based on the portions of witness testimony they accepted.
The appellants argued that testimony was unsafe to rely on because other portions of the same witnesses’ evidence had been rejected.
The challenge asked the Supreme Court to review the evidence in a special-leave appeal.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court followed its practice of not reviewing concurrent factual findings merely because a fact-finder accepted one part of a witness’s evidence and rejected another. No earlier case is named in the judgment for this point.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to review the concurrent findings or reappraise the evidence.

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The lower fact-finding courts reached the same factual findings.
predicates.challenge_seeks_evidentiary_reappraisal: The appellant asks the Supreme Court to revisit the evidence underlying those findings.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings of guilt when consideration of the evidence as a whole does not show those findings to be erroneous.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused, and the High Court upheld the convictions and sentences.
The Supreme Court considered the evidence as a whole, including its weaknesses and corroborating circumstances, and did not find the concurrent findings of guilt to be erroneous.
The accused did not substantiate their pleas of alibi.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court assessed whether the concurrent findings of fact were really erroneous and whether the case warranted appellate interference; disagreement with the assessment of individual witnesses did not, on the totality of the evidence, make this a fit case for intervention.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136, upheld the convictions and sentences, and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal_from_convi: The accused brought a special-leave appeal challenging criminal convictions.
predicates.trial_and_appellate_courts_made_concurre: The trial court and the appellate court both found the accused guilty on the evidence.
predicates.totality_of_evidence_did_not_show_those_: On considering the evidence as a whole, the Supreme Court did not find the concurrent findings of guilt to be erroneous.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not normally disturb concurrent factual findings in a special-leave appeal unless grave and exceptional circumstances disclose a failure of justice.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The lower courts had concurrently convicted the appellants for the murders of three victims.
The Supreme Court found no circumstances of sufficient gravity to warrant interference with those convictions.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its special jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court does not normally reappraise evidence or disturb concurrent findings of fact unless grave and exceptional circumstances exist and there has been a failure of justice.
members.conclusion: The convictions for those three murders were left undisturbed.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and not grave_exceptional_failure_of_justice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The lower courts reached the same factual findings on the convictions under review.
predicates.grave_exceptional_failure_of_justice: The concurrent findings are affected by grave and exceptional circumstances resulting in a failure of justice.

members.legal_issue: A concurrent finding of fact is not interfered with in a special-leave appeal when the Supreme Court is asked to revisit that finding.
material_facts: In a special-leave appeal, the appellant disputed the lower courts’ concurrent finding that a vacancy had occurred and a tenancy had been created.
The trial court and the High Court had reached the same factual finding.
members.legal_principle: The Supreme Court declined to disturb the concurrent finding of fact in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not interfere with the concurrent factual finding.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter came before the Supreme Court as an appeal by special leave.
predicates.lower_courts_made_concurrent_factual_fin: The trial court and the High Court reached the same finding on a disputed fact.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not interfere under Article 136 where the High Court has examined the record and the challenged administrative decision caused no injustice warranting intervention.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a High Court judgment refusing relief against the Additional Director’s order.
The High Court had examined the records and concluded that the appellant’s asserted entitlement based on a report did not displace the effect of the revenue entries.
The High Court found that no injustice had been caused to the appellant.
The Supreme Court considered the case unsuitable for interference under Article 136.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 permits the Supreme Court to decline appellate interference where, on the facts and circumstances, the challenged decision presents no sufficient ground for intervention. The Court relied on the High Court’s examination of the record and its finding that no injustice had been caused.
members.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed, with each side bearing its own costs.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The matter before the Supreme Court is an appeal invoking its discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.high_court_examined_record: The High Court examined the relevant record in reviewing the challenged decision.
predicates.no_injustice_found: The courts found that the challenged decision caused no injustice requiring appellate intervention.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily re-examine evidence for a third time when the lower courts have reached the same factual conclusion and no legal reason warrants reconsideration.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court reached the same conclusion on whether authority to adopt had been given.
The appellant asked the Supreme Court to reconsider the evidence on that factual question.
The Court found no legal reason to depart from the concurrent findings and declined to review the evidence at large.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its settled practice not to examine evidence at large, particularly where the trial court and the High Court have reached identical conclusions, absent a legal reason warranting a different conclusion. No earlier case is cited for this practice in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reconsider the evidence on the disputed factual question.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not interfere under Article 136 with an equitable specific-performance decree where the record shows no grave injustice warranting intervention.
material_facts: The matter came before the Court in appeals under Article 136 against a decree granting specific performance to the extent of the contracting co-owners’ shares.
The purchaser had throughout been ready and willing to perform its obligations.
The property was not readily capable of valuation, and the parties could not state its present market value.
The purchaser paid a substantial amount to discharge the mortgage and avert the bank’s sale of the property.
The Court found that no substantial or grave injustice had been caused to the appellants.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 confers discretionary jurisdiction, and the Court may decline to interfere where the justice of the case does not require intervention. The Court relied on Taherakhatoon (D) by Lrs. v. Salambin Mohammad and considered the purchaser’s readiness and willingness, the difficulty of valuing the property, the discharge of the mortgage, and the absence of grave injustice.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s decree and dismissed the appeals, including the purchaser’s appeal seeking the entire property.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not interfere under its discretionary appellate jurisdiction with concurrent factual findings that follow a critical assessment of the evidence and are not shown to warrant intervention.
material_facts: The matter came before the Supreme Court as an appeal from concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court rejecting the property claim.
Both courts had examined the pleadings and oral and documentary evidence, including the claimant’s inconsistent testimony and the evidence concerning title, construction, and possession.
The Supreme Court found no material warranting interference with those findings.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary appellate jurisdiction; factual findings reached by the courts below after examining the evidence do not call for interference where no adequate basis for intervention is shown. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_factual_findings: A party appealed from factual findings made in the same way by the courts below.
predicates.findings_follow_critical_evidence_review: The courts below critically examined the relevant pleadings and oral and documentary evidence before making their findings.
predicates.adequate_basis_for_interference: The record disclosed a sufficient basis for the appellate court to interfere with the concurrent findings.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s active participation in executing a will does not, by itself, make the will suspicious or invalidate it when the evidence establishes due execution and attestation and supports the testator’s deliberate disposition.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that the will was duly executed and attested and that no circumstances cast doubt on the testatrix’s capacity or free will.
The beneficiaries had actively participated in the execution of the will.

Shortly before execution, the daughter reported that her mother was being abducted and filed a suit claiming title against her, supporting the finding that she knew her mother intended to dispose of the property.

The testatrix executed the will despite the daughter’s efforts to prevent the disposition, later lived with the daughter until her death, and neither complained about the will nor executed another will.
The daughter’s allegation that the beneficiaries procured the will by fraud was not substantiated, and the High Court dismissed the second appeal because it raised no question of law.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur, and Smt. Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, the propounder must establish the will and remove genuine suspicious circumstances; active participation by a beneficiary may be relevant but does not alone establish such suspicion. The Court also noted that the High Court had dismissed the second appeal because there was no question of law attracting Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
members.conclusion: The active participation of the beneficiaries was not sufficient, in the circumstances, to cast doubt on the will. The concurrent findings that the will was genuine and intended to be acted upon were upheld, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.no_other_circumstances_doubting_capacity: No other evidence casts doubt on the testator’s testamentary capacity or freedom of choice.

members.legal_issue: A will may be upheld when its execution is supported and the circumstances relied on as suspicious lack a factual foundation.
material_facts: A son propounded his mother’s registered will, which was executed about eight years before her death.
The will left the estate to the son, which the courts below treated as a suspicious circumstance because it deprived the daughters of inheritance.
The challengers did not plead the will’s invalidity, and the evidence did not establish the alleged pressure to execute it; cross-examination did not challenge the will’s correctness.
The subordinate appellate court considered the circumstances and upheld the will, while the High Court reversed without examining the evidence.
members.legal_principle: The propounder of a will must prove it and remove genuine suspicious features. Suspicion must be real, germane, and valid, not fanciful. The absence of a pleading challenging the will under Order 8 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the absence of evidence or cross-examination supporting the alleged pressure, were relevant to whether the asserted suspicion had a factual basis. No earlier case is identified by name in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The suspicions identified by the trial court had no factual foundation; the subordinate appellate court’s finding upholding the will was restored, and the properties covered by it were excluded from partition.

predicates.lower_appellate_court_upheld_will_on_evi: The lower appellate court considered the evidence and found the will valid.

members.legal_issue: An unprivileged will is proved when the evidence satisfies the statutory requirements for execution and attestation and persuades a prudent mind that it was duly executed.
material_facts: The dispute concerned an unprivileged will propounded to establish that the deceased testator’s property would pass to one beneficiary.
One of the two attesting witnesses was called and testified that the testator signed the will in his presence and that the other attesting witness was also present when the testator signed it.

The witness’s evidence established that both attesting witnesses signed in the testator’s presence; the statement that the other witness was present when the testator signed was not challenged in cross-examination.
The testator’s signature was placed at the bottom of the will in a manner indicating that the document was intended to operate as a will.
The will was registered, and the Court found no suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be signed by the testator, or by another person in the testator’s presence and at the testator’s direction; the signature must indicate an intention to give effect to the document as a will; and at least two witnesses must attest it in the prescribed manner, including signing in the testator’s presence. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one attesting witness must be called to prove execution when such a witness is available and capable of giving evidence. Registration does not dispense with proof of execution. The Court relied on Bhagwan Kaur v. Kartar Kaur (1994) 5 SCC 135, Seth Beni Chand v. Smt. Kamla Kunwar (1976) 4 SCC 554, Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam (2003) 2 SCC 91, Gurdev Kaur v. Kaki (2007) 1 SCC 546, Yumnam Ongbi Tampha Ibema Devi v. Yumnam Joykumar Singh (2009) 4 SCC 780, Rur Singh v. Bachan Kaur (2009) 11 SCC 1, Anil Kak v. Kumari Sharada Raje (2008) 7 SCC 695, and H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443. Proof need not reach mathematical certainty; it must satisfy the test of a prudent mind.
members.conclusion: The will’s execution was satisfactorily proved. The Division Bench erred in finding that the statutory requirements had not been met, and the Supreme Court restored the Single Judge’s decision.

predicates.two_attesting_witnesses_proved: The evidence proves that at least two witnesses attested the will in a legally sufficient manner.
predicates.witnesses_signed_in_testator_presence: Each attesting witness signed the will in the testator’s presence.
predicates.prudent_mind_satisfied: The evidence, considered as a whole, satisfies a prudent mind that the will was duly executed.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument must be proved through evidence establishing the testator’s execution and the attestation required by law.
material_facts: The propounder sought administration of an instrument said to be a will and produced two attesting witnesses and a registering officer.

One attesting witness could not recall whether the testator signed in his presence or whether he signed as an attesting witness, and said his signatures at registration were as an identifying witness.
The other attesting witness said he had not seen the testator sign, did not know the document’s contents, and had not been asked to attest it as a will.
The registering officer testified about the testator’s acknowledgment at registration but did not establish that the witnesses saw the testator sign or signed in the testator’s presence.
The evidence, considered together or separately, did not establish the required attestation or an intention to attest.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be attested by at least two witnesses in the specified manner. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one available attesting witness must prove execution; the registration exception for other documents does not apply to wills. Proof of the testator’s signature alone is insufficient. The Court relied on Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, which explains that the witness must prove the attestation required by Section 63(c), and on Bhaiya Guruji Dutt Singh v. Gangotri Dutt Singh concerning the need for an intention to attest.
members.conclusion: The instrument was not proved as a validly executed and attested will, so administration could not be granted on its basis.

predicates.testamentary_proceeding: A person seeks a grant of administration or other testamentary relief on the basis of an instrument said to be a will.
predicates.attesting_evidence_does_not_establish_re: The evidence of the available attesting witnesses does not establish that the testator signed or acknowledged the instrument and that the witnesses attested it in the required manner.
predicates.witness_signatures_lack_attesting_intent: The evidence shows that the witnesses signed only in another capacity or does not show that they intended their signatures to attest the will.

members.legal_issue: A disputed will was genuinely executed by the testator and attested in his presence.
material_facts: The testator signed every page of the will and a note listing corrections.
He personally presented the will for registration, admitted its execution before the registrar, and signed again in the registrar’s presence.
Two attesting witnesses testified that the testator signed in their presence and that they then attested in his presence.
The court accepted the signatures attributed to the testator’s wife and daughter-in-law as genuine, having considered the family letters and evidence about their relationship with the beneficiary.
A handwriting expert gave a contrary opinion, but the court considered handwriting comparison uncertain and not conclusive.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed execution and attestation from the document, registration endorsements, witness testimony, and surrounding evidence. It treated handwriting comparison as an imperfect science and the expert opinion as non-conclusive. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this determination.
members.conclusion: The evidence established that the testator executed the will and that the disputed signatures of the two family members were genuine; the accepted witness evidence supported due attestation.

predicates.testator_acknowledged_execution_during_r: The testator personally presented the will for registration and acknowledged its execution before the registrar.

predicates.surrounding_evidence_supported_disputed_: Evidence about the document and the parties’ circumstances supported the authenticity of signatures challenged as forged.

members.legal_issue: Suspicious circumstances surrounding a will do not prevent probate when the evidence as a whole dispels the suspicion.
material_facts: The testator lived for nearly four years after executing and registering the will and did not revoke or cancel it.
The testator personally arranged for registration at his residence, and the registration endorsements confirmed his presentation and acknowledgment of the will.
The will left the estate to a child who had been raised and genuinely loved as a member of the family.

The wife and daughter-in-law were not separately provided for, but the evidence showed that the family treated the beneficiary as their own child and that the daughter-in-law and the beneficiary’s mother managed the family estate without conflict.

The trial court granted probate, but the High Court set that grant aside on the basis of suspicious circumstances, including disputed signatures and the absence of separate provision for the wife and daughter-in-law.
members.legal_principle: The court considered suspicious circumstances in light of the whole evidentiary record, including the testator’s personal execution and registration of the will, his failure to revoke it during his lifetime, and the family circumstances explaining the disposition. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this determination.
members.conclusion: The circumstances identified as suspicious were dispelled by the evidence; the appeal was allowed, the High Court judgment was set aside, and the trial court’s grant of probate was restored.

rule.if: probate_appeal and testator_personally_registered_will and no_revocation_during_extended_survival and family_evidence_explained_omitted_provisions and evidence_as_a_whole_dispelled_suspicion

predicates.probate_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether a will should be admitted to probate.

predicates.no_revocation_during_extended_survival: The testator lived for a substantial period after making the will and took no step to revoke or cancel it.
predicates.family_evidence_explained_omitted_provis: Evidence of the family relationships and arrangements gave context for the will’s failure to make separate provision for certain family members.
predicates.evidence_as_a_whole_dispelled_suspicion: The evidence considered together answered the concerns raised about the will’s genuineness or circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A will may be proved despite suspicious circumstances when the propounder satisfactorily explains them and establishes the testator’s sound and disposing state of mind.
material_facts: The testatrix was over eighty and died five days after executing the will, which disinherited her only son.
The testatrix and her son had a long history of serious estrangement and litigation, and she had previously excluded him from gifts and testamentary dispositions.

The will benefited other members of the family, while the advocate who prepared or witnessed it had no interest in its outcome; another person accused of participating in a forgery stood to lose by the will.
Evidence supported that the will was read to the testatrix, that she was in a sound state of mind, and that the signatories witnessed its execution.
The son did not testify to support his accusation of forgery.
members.legal_principle: The burden of proof rests on the party propounding a will, who must satisfy the court that it is the last will of a free and capable testator. Ordinarily, proof of the testator’s signature or mark and due attestation discharges the burden, subject to the requirement in section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act to call an available attesting witness. Where suspicious circumstances surround execution, the propounder must remove the suspicion with satisfactory evidence and an explanation sufficient to satisfy a prudent mind; mathematical proof is not required. The Court applied the approach in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, and referred to Jarman on Wills and Harmes v. Hinkson on the assessment of testamentary proof.
members.conclusion: The propounder discharged the burden of proving the will and satisfactorily explained the suspicious circumstances; the will was established as the testatrix’s last will, made while she was of sound and disposing mind and memory.

rule.if: will_probate_proceeding and suspicious_execution_circumstances and propounder_satisfactorily_explains_suspicion and testator_sound_and_disposing_mind

predicates.propounder_satisfactorily_explains_suspi: The person propounding the will presented evidence and explanations that satisfactorily addressed the suspicious circumstances.
predicates.testator_sound_and_disposing_mind: The evidence established that the testator had a sound and disposing state of mind and memory when making the will.

members.legal_issue: A will is valid when the propounder proves its execution and the testator’s capacity, and the evidence satisfactorily dispels the suspicious circumstances surrounding it.
material_facts: The deceased had testamentary capacity and was in good health when the will was said to have been made.
The scribe and two attesting witnesses testified that the deceased dictated the will, read it, signed it in their presence, and that they then attested it.
The court found the scribe and attesting witnesses reliable and found no adequate basis to conclude that they had colluded to fabricate the will.
The beneficiaries had close connections with the deceased, and the dispositions were found neither unnatural nor unjust in light of their relationships and circumstances.
The will’s signature had been challenged, but the High Court preferred the defendants’ handwriting expert, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disagree with that assessment.
members.legal_principle: The propounder bears the burden of proving a will. If there are no suspicious circumstances, proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature as required by law is sufficient; if suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction. Once they are removed, the will must be given effect even if it cuts off near relatives. The Court relied on Shashi Kumar v. Subodh Kumar.
members.conclusion: The propounder proved the will; the High Court was correct to find it genuine and valid, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: will_validity_appeal and testator_capacity_established and execution_supported_by_scribe_and_attesting_witnesses and witnesses_found_reliable and signature_supported_by_expert_and_court_assessment and dispositions_reasonable_in_context

predicates.execution_supported_by_scribe_and_attest: The scribe and attesting witnesses testify to the testator’s execution of the will and its attestation.

predicates.dispositions_reasonable_in_context: The dispositions are consistent with the testator’s relationships and circumstances and are not found unnatural or unjust.

members.legal_issue: A will may be admitted to probate when its valid execution and the testator’s testamentary capacity are established, the challenger does not prove fraud, coercion or undue influence, and any suspicious circumstances are satisfactorily explained.
material_facts: The will left the testator’s entire estate to his second wife and made no provision for his mother or youngest daughter, circumstances the challengers relied on as suspicious and unnatural.
The courts accepted evidence that the testator signed the will in the presence of two witnesses, who attested it in his presence and in each other’s presence.
There was no effective challenge to the testator’s testamentary capacity and no evidence that he lacked a sound disposing mind or failed to understand the will’s effect.
The courts found that the second wife was present but had no part in preparing or executing the will.

The testator’s relations with his son and two daughters were hostile; he had already made arrangements for his daughters’ maintenance and considered that he could provide for his mother and youngest daughter during his lifetime.
The evidence accepted by the courts showed that the will was executed and attested on the same occasion and that the alleged later addition of the attestation clause was not established.
members.legal_principle: The propounder must establish the testator’s signature, sound disposing mind, understanding of the nature and effect of the dispositions, free volition, and execution in the presence of two attesting witnesses who attest in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence. Once established, that burden is discharged, but legitimate suspicious circumstances must be satisfactorily explained by the propounder. If the propounder takes a prominent part in execution and receives a substantial benefit, that is itself suspicious. The challenger bears the burden of proving allegations of fraud, coercion or undue influence. A testator’s choice is not displaced merely because it appears foolish or heartless if made with full comprehension. These principles were drawn from H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and Motibai Hormusjee Kanga v. Jamsetjee Hormusjee Kanga.
members.conclusion: The will was genuine, validly executed and duly attested by a testator in a sound disposing state of mind; the grant of probate was upheld.

predicates.testamentary_capacity_and_understanding_: The evidence establishes that the testator had a sound disposing mind and understood the nature and effect of the will’s dispositions.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_satisfactorily_: The propounder gives a satisfactory explanation for legitimate circumstances surrounding the will that could cast doubt on its genuineness or free execution.
predicates.no_legitimate_suspicious_circumstances_r: The evidence does not leave any legitimate circumstance that reasonably casts doubt on the will’s genuineness or the testator’s free will and mind.
predicates.challenger_fails_to_prove_fraud_coercion: The person challenging the will does not establish that it was procured by fraud, coercion or undue influence.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument duly proved and acknowledged by the opposing party is not rendered suspicious merely because it excludes close relatives when the surrounding circumstances support its execution.
material_facts: The beneficiary proved the registered testamentary instrument through witnesses in accordance with the formal requirements for proving a will.
A sibling of the beneficiary attested the instrument, and another sibling accompanied the testatrix when it was executed; neither raised an objection.
The opposing parties acknowledged the earlier instrument’s execution and relied on a later instrument said to replace it.
Both lower courts found the later instrument fabricated, and the alleged mortgage was not proved.
The first appellate court questioned the earlier instrument based on the exclusion of the beneficiary’s siblings, despite their participation and the opposing parties’ acknowledgment.
members.legal_principle: Sections 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 require proof of a will through the prescribed attestation process and at least one attesting witness. Under Evidence Act Sections 17 and 58, a clear admission is relevant and an admitted fact ordinarily need not be proved; Sections 8, 114(e) and 115 address conduct, the rebuttable presumption of regularity of official acts, and estoppel. Registration is optional for a will under Sections 17, 18 and 27 of the Registration Act, 1908, and is only an additional circumstance supporting proof. A testamentary court is a court of conscience, not suspicion; exclusion of a sibling alone does not create suspicion, particularly where the siblings participated and did not object.
members.conclusion: The earlier will was duly proved and the circumstances relied on by the first appellate court did not create suspicion requiring further dispelling; the trial court’s decree was restored.
