predicates.opponent_admitted_earlier_will: The opposing party acknowledged the earlier instrument’s execution, including by relying on a later instrument said to replace it.
predicates.close_relatives_participated_without_obj: Close relatives who were involved in the circumstances of execution did not object to the instrument.
predicates.surrounding_conduct_supports_execution: The conduct of the participants and other circumstances support the instrument’s proper execution.
predicates.later_replacement_document_found_fabrica: The document alleged to replace the earlier instrument was found to be fabricated.

members.legal_issue: A will is proved when its execution, attestation, the testator’s testamentary capacity, and the testator’s free and informed choice are established by the required evidence.
material_facts: The will’s execution was not disputed, and an attesting witness testified about the will being read and signed and about the witnesses’ attestation.
The court found that the testator understood the will’s contents and acted of his free will.
The testator was unwell, but the court proceeded on the basis that illness did not itself establish a lack of mental capacity.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be executed and attested in the prescribed manner; under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, its execution must be proved by at least one available and capable attesting witness. The propounder must establish execution, testamentary capacity, and the testator’s free and informed choice. The court relied on Apoline D’Souza v. John D’Souza, B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, and H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma.
members.conclusion: The court held that the will had been proved as a genuine, freely made testamentary disposition.

rule.if: will_validity_contested and testator_signature_proved and attesting_witness_examined and testator_understood_disposition and testator_had_testamentary_capacity and free_volition_established

predicates.will_validity_contested: A party challenged whether a will was validly made.
predicates.testator_signature_proved: Evidence established that the testator signed the will.
predicates.attesting_witness_examined: At least one attesting witness gave evidence about the will’s execution and attestation.
predicates.testator_understood_disposition: The evidence established that the testator understood the nature and effect of the disposition.
predicates.testator_had_testamentary_capacity: The evidence established that the testator had the mental capacity to make the disposition.
predicates.free_volition_established: The evidence established that the testator acted freely in making the will.

members.legal_issue: A codicil must satisfy the same execution and proof requirements as the will to which it relates.
material_facts: The disputed instrument was a statement made in connection with registration of an already executed will and was conceded to be capable of amounting to a codicil.
The statement purported to alter the will by limiting the beneficiary’s interest and providing for the property to pass to others after her death.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(b), 63, 64 and 70 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, read with Section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, support applying the same execution and proof rules to a codicil as to a will. A codicil forms part of the related will and alters its dispositions; it would be anomalous to require formal execution and proof of a will but not of an instrument that changes it.
members.conclusion: A codicil must be executed and proved in the same manner as a will; the disputed codicil was not proved and could not alter the will.

predicates.codicil_execution_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a purported codicil was validly executed and proved.
predicates.codicil_relates_to_will: The instrument explains, alters, or adds to dispositions made in a will.

members.legal_issue: The propounder of a will bears the burden of proving it and must remove legitimate suspicions surrounding its execution before the court accepts it as genuine.
material_facts: Executors sought probate of a will, and the testator’s relatives contested it on grounds including impaired mental capacity, undue influence, and allegedly inauthentic signatures.
The trial court found the testator’s and attesting witnesses’ signatures genuine, but refused probate because of doubts about the testator’s mental condition.
On appeal, the challenge to the genuineness of the signatures and the execution and attestation of the will was not pursued.
members.legal_principle: The mode of proving a will ordinarily follows the mode of proving other documents, subject to the special attestation requirement in section 63 of the Succession Act. The propounder bears the onus, and suspicious circumstances—including concerns about signature, mental capacity, unnatural or unfair dispositions, or whether the testator’s mind was free—must be satisfactorily removed. A prominent role by a propounder who receives substantial benefit is also relevant. The Court followed Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, and Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev.
members.conclusion: The propounder bears the onus of proving the will; proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature, together with legally required attestation, ordinarily suffices where there are no suspicious circumstances. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction and satisfy the court’s conscience.

predicates.probate_proceeding: A party seeks a court grant recognizing a purported will.
predicates.will_propounded: A party relies on a purported will as the basis for obtaining that grant.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances: Circumstances surrounding execution raise a legitimate doubt about the will’s authenticity, the testator’s capacity or freedom, or the fairness or naturalness of its dispositions.

members.legal_issue: The circumstances relied on in this case did not create unresolved suspicion about the will’s genuine execution or the testator’s capacity.
material_facts: The testator’s and attesting witnesses’ signatures were found genuine, and the will’s dispositions were found neither unfair nor unnatural.
The witnesses testified many years after execution, and the court considered their inability to recall particular dates understandable.

There was no evidence of an established practice requiring preservation of the draft or lawyer’s diary, and the relevant witnesses were not shown to have been withheld despite a demonstrated need to call them.
The use of known employees, a friend, and a relative as scribe or witnesses was considered normal; the medical evidence did not establish that the testator was comatose or had lost mental capacity.
A brother who received nothing under the will did not object to probate, the disposition was fair, and existing family litigation made a will intended to avoid future disputes plausible.
members.legal_principle: A circumstance is suspicious when it is abnormal, not normally expected in the situation, or not expected of a normal person. Suspicion does not require a court to persist in disbelief; the court must assess whether the circumstances are genuinely abnormal and whether any legitimate doubts have been removed. The Court applied the principles in Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, and Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and referred to Harmes v. Hinkson.
members.conclusion: The alleged suspicious circumstances were either explained or were normal circumstances, and the evidence supported the will’s genuineness and valid execution; probate was properly granted.

rule.if: probate_proceeding and testator_and_attesting_signatures_proved and no_evidence_of_lost_mental_capacity and disposition_fair_and_natural and alleged_irregularities_explained_or_normal and nonbeneficiary_relative_accepted_validity and family_dispute_made_will_plausible

predicates.probate_proceeding: A party seeks a court grant recognizing a purported will.
predicates.testator_and_attesting_signatures_proved: The evidence establishes the testator’s signature and the signatures of the witnesses who attested the will.
predicates.no_evidence_of_lost_mental_capacity: The evidence does not show that the testator lacked mental capacity when the will was executed.
predicates.disposition_fair_and_natural: The distribution in the will is fair and does not appear unnatural in the relevant circumstances.
predicates.alleged_irregularities_explained_or_norm: The claimed procedural or evidentiary irregularities are explained by the circumstances or reflect normal practice rather than abnormal conduct.
predicates.nonbeneficiary_relative_accepted_validit: A relative who received no benefit under the will accepted that it had been validly executed and attested.
predicates.family_dispute_made_will_plausible: Existing disputes among relatives made a will intended to prevent further disputes a plausible act.

members.legal_issue: A challenged will is valid where the evidence establishes its execution by a testator of sound disposing mind and the circumstances relied on to question it do not undermine that proof.
material_facts: The testatrix was elderly, chronically ill, physically weak, and had difficulty writing; evidence showed her hand was trembling and she was unable to sign her name when the will was executed.
The attesting witness and the beneficiary gave evidence that the testatrix was of sound mind and understood what she was doing when she executed the will; the court found their evidence trustworthy.
The court found that the testatrix’s letters showed distress about the challengers’ lack of attention, rather than that the beneficiary had confined or controlled her.
The beneficiary had cared for the testatrix for several years and handled her financial affairs; she had also held a joint bank account and locker with him.
The testatrix died on the day the will was executed, and the will bore her thumb-mark; it was registered after her death and made a general bequest without describing particular property.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the alleged suspicious circumstances against the evidence of execution and testamentary capacity. It treated the testatrix’s physical inability to sign as consistent with her thumb-mark, while finding that she had a sound disposing mind. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case.
members.conclusion: The will was duly executed and valid, and the appeals challenging it were dismissed.

rule.if: will_validity_appeal and testator_sound_mind and physically_unable_to_sign and execution_witnesses_credible and (alleged_control_unsupported or beneficiary_had_prior_trust_and_care)

predicates.will_validity_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the validity or due execution of a will.
predicates.testator_sound_mind: The testator understood what they were doing when the will was executed.
predicates.physically_unable_to_sign: The testator was physically unable to sign their name when the will was executed.
predicates.execution_witnesses_credible: The court found credible the evidence of witnesses to the will’s execution.
predicates.alleged_control_unsupported: The evidence did not support the allegation that the beneficiary controlled or confined the testator.
predicates.beneficiary_had_prior_trust_and_care: The testator had previously trusted the beneficiary with personal care or financial affairs.

members.legal_issue: A person propounding a will must remove legitimate suspicions about its genuineness before the court accepts it as the testator’s will.
material_facts: The purported will gave almost the entire estate to a distant relative and made limited provision for the testator’s widow and daughters.
The beneficiary had an active role in procuring the document, which was prepared at his home with a scribe and witnesses connected to him.
The court identified several circumstances raising suspicion about the document and its execution, and found no evidence that satisfactorily removed those suspicions.
members.legal_principle: Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, the special requirement of attestation applies to proof of a will. The propounder bears the onus of proving the will; absent suspicious circumstances, proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s legally required signature, together with due attestation, may discharge that onus. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction; a benefit to a propounder who actively participated in execution is a relevant suspicion. Where fraud, coercion, or undue influence is alleged, the person alleging it bears the burden of proving it. The court relied on Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, and Tyrrell v. Painton.
members.conclusion: The court held that the propounder had to satisfy the court about the will’s genuineness by removing the suspicions naturally arising from the circumstances, and that this burden had not been met.

predicates.will_propounded: A person asks a court to accept a document as a testator’s will.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: Circumstances surrounding the document, its execution, or its dispositions give the court legitimate reason to doubt that it represents the testator’s free and genuine act.

members.legal_issue: The propounder of a will must establish its execution and testamentary capacity, and must dispel legitimate suspicion arising from the circumstances of execution before the will can be accepted as genuine.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on a will that left the testator’s property to him and disputed the appellant’s status as the testator’s niece and natural heir.
The will’s genuineness was challenged, and the circumstances surrounding its execution included indications of the testator’s serious illness and other features casting doubt on its execution.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, the mode of proving a will is generally like that for other documents, subject to the statutory requirements for wills. In the absence of suspicious circumstances, proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature as required by law is sufficient; when suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder’s initial onus becomes heavier and those circumstances must be satisfactorily explained. The Court followed H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.
members.conclusion: The onus of proving a will rests on its propounder. Where suspicious circumstances surround execution, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction and remove legitimate suspicion before the will can be accepted as genuine.

predicates.will_proof_case: A party seeks to establish a testamentary document as the deceased person’s will.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: Circumstances surrounding the document’s execution raise legitimate doubt about whether it was genuinely executed as the deceased person’s will.

members.legal_issue: A will required to be attested must be proved through the prescribed execution and attestation evidence.
material_facts: The appellants relied on two later wills, whose execution the respondent disputed.
No attesting witness to either later will was examined, although attesting witnesses were alive and capable of being called.
The courts found that the later wills had not been proved.
members.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires a will to be signed or marked by the testator, or signed by another person in the testator’s presence and at the testator’s direction, and attested by at least two witnesses in the prescribed manner. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires at least one available and capable attesting witness to be called to prove execution. H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, explains these requirements; the Court also referred to Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, (2002) 2 SCC 85, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, (2006) 13 SCC 433, and Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma, (2007) 11 SCC 621, as following that law.
members.conclusion: The later wills were not proved because the required statutory proof of execution and attestation was not supplied.

rule.if: will_based_claim and execution_contested and attesting_witness_available and no_attesting_witness_examined

predicates.will_based_claim: A party relies on a will to establish testamentary rights or to establish that another will was revoked.
predicates.execution_contested: The opposing party disputes that the will was executed.
predicates.attesting_witness_available: At least one attesting witness is alive and capable of giving evidence.
predicates.no_attesting_witness_examined: The party relying on the will does not call an available attesting witness to prove its execution.

members.legal_issue: A will’s genuineness is established when its execution is proved by reliable evidence and suspicious circumstances surrounding it are satisfactorily explained.
material_facts: The probate proceeding concerned a will whose signature was admitted to be the testator’s, but the objectors alleged that it had been written on a blank paper bearing a signature obtained earlier.
Six people attested the will, and four attesters testified; the court found the attesting and other execution witnesses reliable and found no good reason to reject their evidence.
The testator had been found to be in a sound disposing state of mind, and that finding was not challenged in the appeal before the High Court.

The will made no bequest to one daughter and made substantial bequests to other relatives, but evidence showed that the testator had long intended to benefit his grandson and had discussed not leaving immovable property to that daughter.
Evidence also showed that the testator had asked a lawyer to prepare an earlier draft reflecting that intention, and that he had given or intended to give his daughter money.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, a will must satisfy the special requirements of attestation; proof is assessed by the satisfaction of a prudent mind rather than mathematical certainty. As stated in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, the propounder bears the onus of proving the will, and proof of testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature may suffice when suspicious circumstances are absent. If suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction. An apparently unnatural bequest calls for closer scrutiny, but does not itself invalidate a will; a court must not impose its own standard of conduct on a testator.
members.conclusion: The will was proved to be genuine, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: probate_proceeding_appeals_will_genuineness and testator_capacity_proven and will_signature_proven and will_execution_attested_as_required and execution_witnesses_reliable and (suspicious_circumstances_absent or suspicious_circumstances_explained)

predicates.probate_proceeding_appeals_will_genuinen: The proceeding is an appeal in a probate matter in which the genuineness of a will is contested.
predicates.testator_capacity_proven: Evidence establishes that the testator had testamentary capacity when the will was executed.
predicates.will_signature_proven: The testator’s signature on the will is established.
predicates.will_execution_attested_as_required: Evidence establishes that the will was executed with the required attestation.
predicates.execution_witnesses_reliable: The court finds the witnesses who testify about the will’s execution reliable.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_absent: No circumstances surrounding the will’s execution raise suspicion about its genuineness.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_explained: The propounder provides a satisfactory explanation for circumstances that raise suspicion about the will’s genuineness.
predicates.will_proved_genuine: The will is established as genuine.

members.legal_issue: A will is validly proved when its execution, attestation, the testator’s capacity and voluntary understanding are established, and the propounder adequately addresses any suspicious circumstances.
material_facts: The later will was signed by the testator with a thumb mark and was attested by two witnesses.

Both attesting witnesses testified that the testator was of sound disposing mind, that the will was read over to him, and that he voluntarily thumb-marked it; they signed in his presence and in the presence of each other.
The scribe testified that he prepared the will at the testator’s instance and that the testator acted voluntarily and was of sound mind.
Although the testator had previously signed another will, the evidence showed that he was illiterate, had learned to sign, and usually used his thumb mark.
The claim that the testator was unconscious when the later will was executed was not supported by other witnesses, and the court found the testimony of the attesting witnesses and scribe trustworthy.
members.legal_principle: A will must be proved by primary evidence unless secondary evidence is permitted. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one available, capable attesting witness must be called to prove execution. The requirements of Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, must also be satisfied: the testator must sign or mark the will voluntarily while of sound disposing mind and understanding its nature and effect, and two witnesses must attest it in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence. The propounder must remove any genuine suspicion surrounding the will. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The later will was genuine and validly executed; the propounder discharged the burden of proving it.

rule.if: will_validity_appeal and attesting_witnesses_proved_execution and testator_capacity_and_volition_proved and attestation_requirements_met and thumb_mark_explained and no_reliable_evidence_of_unconsciousness

predicates.will_validity_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which the validity of a will is contested.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_proved_execution: The attesting witnesses testified to the testator’s execution of the will and to their attestation of it.
predicates.testator_capacity_and_volition_proved: Evidence showed that the testator understood the will and acted voluntarily while of sound disposing mind.
predicates.attestation_requirements_met: Evidence showed that the required witnesses attested the will in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence.
predicates.thumb_mark_explained: Evidence showed why the testator used a thumb mark despite having signed an earlier document.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_unconsciousness: The claim that the testator was unconscious at execution was not supported by reliable evidence.

members.legal_issue: A will is proved where the evidence establishes its execution and attestation and the circumstances relied on to question it do not give rise to a sufficient suspicion about its genuineness.
material_facts: Two attesting witnesses testified that the testatrix signed the will in their presence and that they signed it in the presence of the testatrix and each other; the first appellate court accepted their evidence.
The will benefited a relative who had maintained good relations with and looked after the testatrix; the beneficiary and her husband were not present at the will’s execution.
The claimant did not specifically challenge the testatrix’s signature, allege forgery or undue influence, or otherwise plead that the will was invalid.
The beneficiary produced the will when she relied on it in her written statement; her earlier silence had occurred during proceedings focused on possession rather than title.
The first appellate court compared the testatrix’s signature on the will with undisputed signatures on rent receipts and found the signature genuine.
The testatrix was about fifty when she made the will, and the will itself referred to her physical weakness.
members.legal_principle: A will must be proved like any other document, with proof of the testator’s testamentary capacity and signature required in the absence of suspicious circumstances. Where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction. Circumstances identified as potentially suspicious include the propounder’s prominent role in execution coupled with substantial benefit, a shaky signature, a testator of feeble mind likely to be influenced, and an unfair or unjust disposition. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, and Guro v. Atma Singh. It also relied on Choteynarain Singh v. Mussamat Ratan Koer and Kristo Gopal Nath v. Baidya Nath for the principle that an asserted improbability must be clear and cogent, approaching impossibility, to prevail against a large and consistent body of evidence of execution and attestation. The testator’s age and the absence of an apparent motive, by themselves, did not make the will suspicious.
members.conclusion: The alleged circumstances did not make the will suspicious; the will was proved, and the beneficiary’s title under it was established.

rule.if: will_dispute and attesting_witnesses_support_execution and signature_supported and natural_beneficiary_relationship and no_material_suspicious_circumstances

predicates.will_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim of title based on a will.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_support_execution: Attesting witnesses testified to the testator’s signing and the required attestation, and their evidence was accepted by the fact-finding court.
predicates.signature_supported: Evidence supported the genuineness of the testator’s signature on the will.
predicates.natural_beneficiary_relationship: The will benefited a person whose relationship and conduct toward the testator made the disposition natural in the circumstances.
predicates.no_material_suspicious_circumstances: The alleged concerns, including delayed disclosure or the testator’s age, did not establish a material suspicious circumstance, and no other material circumstance undermined the will.

members.legal_issue: A will must be proved by its propounder, including removal of suspicious circumstances and proof of testamentary capacity and signature, even when secondary evidence is required because attesting witnesses cannot testify.
material_facts: A beneficiary relied on a will to exclude several properties from division in a family property dispute.
One attesting witness and the scribe had died before the evidence was taken; the other attesting witness was alive but unable to speak or move.
The beneficiary did not produce evidence establishing that the deceased attesting witness had attested the will, and the identifying witness did not testify to witnessing its execution.
There was no evidence establishing the testator’s mental and physical condition when the will was allegedly executed; evidence showed advanced age and serious physical and mental difficulties.
The courts found substantial differences among the testator’s signatures on the will, and the suspicious circumstances were not satisfactorily explained.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a will required by law to be attested cannot be used in evidence unless an attesting witness is called, if one is alive, subject to process, and capable of giving evidence. The propounder bears the burden of proving due execution, the testator’s signature and testamentary capacity, and of dispelling suspicious circumstances. If primary evidence through an attesting witness cannot be given, secondary evidence may be led, as recognized in Daulat Ram v. Sodha, but the burden of proof remains. The approach to suspicious circumstances is consistent with Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee and Pushpavathi v. Chandraraja Kadamba.
members.conclusion: The will was not proved and could not establish that the properties it described were unavailable for division.

predicates.will_dispute: The proceeding concerns a property claim in which a beneficiary relies on a will to establish that property is not available for division.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_unavailable_or_incap: The attesting witnesses cannot provide testimony because they are dead or incapable of giving evidence.
predicates.secondary_evidence_does_not_establish_ex: The evidence offered in place of testimony from an attesting witness does not establish that the witness attested the document or that the testator executed it.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_unresolved: Circumstances casting doubt on the testator’s signature, capacity, or freedom of choice remain unexplained.

members.legal_issue: A will is proved when the propounder establishes prima facie the testator’s capacity and execution in the required manner, and the evidence as a whole satisfies the civil standard of proof without a finding based merely on unsupported suspicion.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a registered will executed by the original owner in favour of her niece, followed by a registered sale from the niece to the claimant.
Two attesting witnesses testified, and the niece’s son testified because the niece was indisposed.
The evidence described the niece’s long-term care of the testator and a natural familial reason for the bequest.
The opposing party was a stranger to the family and alleged no specific facts challenging the testator’s disposing capacity; no other relative came forward to contest the will.

The courts below relied on the testator’s age, her death shortly after execution, the registrar’s visit to her home, the niece’s absence from the witness box, the attesting witnesses’ acquaintance with the niece’s son, and the absence of medical evidence.
An earlier judgment between the same parties had considered the same will and upheld its execution, but the courts below overlooked that judgment.
members.legal_principle: Proof of a will requires proof as for any other document, together with compliance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The propounder must establish the testator’s competence and execution in the prescribed manner. Prima facie proof shifts the onus to a contestant who adduces material against it; the propounder must then satisfy the court affirmatively that the testator understood the will and executed it with a sound disposing mind. Suspicion warrants closer scrutiny only when it is well founded; suspicion or conjecture alone cannot replace or demolish legal proof. The court referred to R v. Hodge (1838), 2 Lewis CC 227, in cautioning against reasoning that fills evidentiary gaps by supposition.
members.conclusion: The will was proved. The courts below allowed conjecture and unsupported suspicion to displace relevant evidence, so their findings were vitiated. The claimant was declared owner and entitled to recover possession.

predicates.civil_case_disputes_will: The proceeding is a civil case in which a party’s claim depends on a disputed will.
predicates.propounder_presents_prima_facie_executio: The person relying on the will presents evidence of its execution, including evidence addressing the applicable formal requirements.
predicates.testamentary_capacity_is_supported_by_ev: Evidence supports that the testator had the capacity to make the will when it was executed.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_lack_evidentiar: Circumstances treated as suspicious are not supported by evidence establishing a genuine basis to doubt the will.

members.legal_issue: When circumstances surrounding a will raise legitimate suspicion, the propounder must remove that suspicion with cogent evidence, and the circumstances must be assessed in light of the situation when the will was made.
material_facts: The beneficiary was a mortgagee and tenant of the testatrix, and the record did not establish that she was educated; she had made a thumb impression on the will.
The will excluded the testatrix’s surviving daughters, and the beneficiary was said to have participated in its execution.
The courts below relied in part on evidence that the daughters learned of their mother’s death several days later, although that event occurred long after the will was executed.
The Supreme Court considered whether the testatrix could have received independent advice and found that the lower courts had not addressed the relevant suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, the propounder must prove the testator’s sound and disposing mind, understanding of the disposition, and free execution, and must dispel legitimate doubts. Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, (2006) 14 SCALE 186, identifies circumstances including doubtful mental capacity, unnatural or unfair dispositions, and prominent participation by a beneficiary. Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, (1977) 1 SCC 369, requires a cogent and convincing explanation of suspicious circumstances. Anil Kak v. Kumari Sharada Raje, (2008) 7 SCC 695, requires the court to satisfy its conscience; exclusion of a natural heir is a relevant factor but is not, by itself, necessarily suspicious. The listed circumstances are not exhaustive.
members.conclusion: The propounder must remove legitimate suspicions surrounding a will with cogent, satisfactory and sufficient evidence. The circumstances are not exhaustive and must be assessed with reasonable explanations in mind, by reference to the facts prevailing when the will was executed. The daughters’ later learning of their mother’s death was of little significance to that assessment. The matter required fresh consideration.

predicates.will_dispute: The parties dispute whether a document is a valid will that establishes a claimed testamentary entitlement.
predicates.will_is_propounded: A person relies on the document as the testator’s will.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: Facts surrounding the making or contents of the will raise a legitimate doubt about the testator’s capacity, free choice, or due execution.

members.legal_issue: A will is proved genuine when the evidence of execution is supported by reliable witnesses and the surrounding circumstances are consistent with the testator’s intentions and competence.
material_facts: The will was supported by the evidence of an attesting witness whose testimony was not affected by the inconsistency in another attesting witness’s statements, as well as by the scribe and the beneficiary, who was present at execution.
The testator was about seventy when he executed the will, but lived for nearly seven more years and was not shown to have been mentally or physically incompetent.
The will was registered, and its disposition was consistent with the testator’s stated dissatisfaction with one son and appreciation of the beneficiary’s care and conduct.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed proof of due execution together with the circumstances bearing on genuineness, including the testimony of witnesses, the testator’s competence, the naturalness of the disposition, registration, and the testator’s survival for years after execution. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this determination in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The will was duly executed and genuine; the beneficiary’s participation in its execution did not undermine it in the circumstances.

rule.if: will_validity_challenged and execution_supported_by_reliable_evidence and testator_competent_at_execution and surrounding_circumstances_support_will

predicates.will_validity_challenged: A party to the proceeding challenges the genuineness of a will.
predicates.execution_supported_by_reliable_evidence: Reliable evidence from witnesses or other persons with knowledge supports that the testator executed the will.
predicates.testator_competent_at_execution: The testator was mentally and physically competent when the will was made.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_support_will: The surrounding circumstances, including the disposition and the testator’s subsequent conduct or circumstances, support the will’s genuineness.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is proved when the propounder establishes its execution and the testator’s testamentary capacity, and the opposing party does not substantiate alleged fraud, coercion, or suspicious circumstances.
material_facts: The testator’s written statement, filed before his death, expressly stated that he had executed the disputed will.
The will was registered, and its registration endorsement recorded the testator’s acknowledgment of execution and signatures of identifying witnesses.
An attesting witness and the scribe testified about the will’s execution; the evidence also supported that the testator was of sound mind.
The opposing parties produced no evidence of fraud, coercion, undue influence, or lack of testamentary capacity.

The lower courts relied on matters including the exclusion of an alleged adopted son, the distribution of most property to the beneficiaries, and the beneficiaries’ presence, which the Supreme Court found insufficient to invalidate the will.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Evidence Act, a document required by law to be attested must be proved through an attesting witness capable of giving evidence. Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act requires the testator’s signature or mark and attestation by two or more witnesses in the manner stated there. Registration does not dispense with proof of execution and attestation, but Section 114 of the Evidence Act permits a presumption that the Registrar’s recorded particulars were regularly and correctly made. The propounder must establish execution and testamentary capacity; the burden then shifts to the contestant to support allegations such as fraud, coercion, or undue influence, and may shift back to the propounder to dispel substantiated suspicious circumstances. The exclusion of natural heirs or a beneficiary’s mere presence does not, by itself, establish suspicion: Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty and Uma Devi Nambiar v. T.C. Sidhan.
members.conclusion: The propounders proved that the will was duly executed and was the testator’s last will; the beneficiaries and the widow were entitled to the properties allotted to them under it.

rule.if: will_property_dispute_appeal and testator_admitted_execution and attesting_witness_and_scribe_supported_execution and testator_was_of_sound_mind and opposing_party_produced_no_evidence_of_fraud_or_coercion

predicates.will_property_dispute_appeal: An appeal in a property dispute challenged a will offered to determine the parties’ property rights.
predicates.testator_admitted_execution: The person who made the will stated before death that they had executed it.
predicates.attesting_witness_and_scribe_supported_e: An attesting witness and the person who prepared the will gave evidence supporting its execution.
predicates.testator_was_of_sound_mind: The evidence showed that the person who made the will was of sound mind when it was executed.
predicates.opposing_party_produced_no_evidence_of_f: The party opposing the will produced no evidence that it resulted from fraud, coercion, or undue influence.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is valid where the propounder proves its due execution and the testator’s capacity, and satisfactorily explains any suspicious circumstances surrounding it.
material_facts: The dispute arose in a partition suit in which the appellants challenged a will that excluded certain properties from partition.

The scribe testified that the testator dictated the will. Two attesting witnesses testified that the testator signed it in their presence while of sound mind, understood its dispositions, and that they attested it in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence.
A handwriting expert testified that the signatures on all six pages of the will were the testator’s signatures.
The testator was 80 years old and died 15 days after executing the will, but the scribe and attesting witnesses testified that he was in sound physical and mental condition.

The properties allotted to two sons in an earlier partition had been held by tenants and later vested in the government, while the properties given to those sons by the will had been in the testator’s personal cultivation; the will also provided other heirs with rights to compensation for the vested lands.

The evidence showed that the daughters were present when the will was executed and that its contents had been disclosed at the testator’s final obeisance ceremony and during proceedings before forest authorities.

The will was registered four years after execution; the respondents explained that they did so on legal advice, and the scribe and attesting witnesses gave consistent accounts before the registrar and in court.
The evidence did not establish that a respondent’s presence in the house amounted to a prominent role in execution of the will.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will requires the prescribed attestation. The propounder bears the burden of proving due execution, testamentary capacity and the testator’s signature; where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must explain them to the court’s satisfaction. If undue influence, fraud or coercion is alleged, the person making that allegation bears the burden of proving it. Proof is assessed by the satisfaction of a prudent mind, and suspicious circumstances depend on the facts of the particular case. The court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma; Ramachandra Rambux v. Champabai; Surendra Pal v. Dr. (Mrs.) Saraswati Arora; Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur; and Meenakshiammal v. Chandrasekaran.
members.conclusion: The propounders proved that the will was duly executed by a testator of sound disposing mind, and the circumstances relied on to challenge it did not prevent its acceptance as genuine and valid. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: partition_suit_appeal_challenging_will and testamentary_execution_proved and testamentary_capacity_proved and (not suspicious_circumstances_present or suspicious_circumstances_explained)

predicates.partition_suit_appeal_challenging_will: A party in an appeal arising from a partition suit challenges the validity of a will affecting which property is available for partition.
predicates.testamentary_execution_proved: The propounder establishes that the testator signed the will and that the required witnesses attested it in the testator’s presence and in each other’s presence.
predicates.testamentary_capacity_proved: Evidence establishes that, when signing the will, the testator was of sound disposing mind and understood the nature and effect of its dispositions.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: Facts surrounding the will raise circumstances that could reasonably cast doubt on its genuine execution.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_explained: The propounder gives evidence that satisfactorily accounts for the circumstances capable of casting doubt on the will.

members.legal_issue: A will is proved when its execution is established and genuine, material suspicions are dispelled; excluding natural heirs, without more, does not make it suspicious.
material_facts: The testatrix executed and registered a will leaving the disputed property to one daughter, who had been widowed young, had lived with her mother for more than twenty years, and had cared for her.
The other daughters lived with their husbands elsewhere, and there was no evidence that the beneficiary received support from her late husband's family.
One attesting witness testified to the will, and the court found no defect in his testimony.
The testatrix personally attended the registration office and died several years after executing the will.
There was no evidence that the testatrix suffered from an ailment impairing her mental faculties when she executed the will.
The lower courts treated the exclusion of the other daughters, the testatrix's physical limitations, and the non-examination of the typist and an advocate as grounds for rejecting the will.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be signed or marked by the testator and attested by at least two witnesses in the prescribed manner; Section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, requires examination of an attesting witness, and its proviso permits proof by one attesting witness where applicable. The propounder bears the burden of proving the will and, where real suspicious circumstances arise, explaining them to the court's satisfaction; allegations of fraud, coercion, or undue influence must be proved by the person making them. Exclusion or reduced provision for natural heirs alone is not a suspicious circumstance, since a will alters the normal course of succession. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, PPK Gopalan Nambiar v. PPK Balakrishan Manbiar, Pushpavati v. Chandraja Kadamba, and Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee.
members.conclusion: The will was genuine. The exclusion of the other daughters was not, in these circumstances, a sufficient ground to doubt its authenticity, and the beneficiary's testimony from one attesting witness satisfied the applicable proof requirement.

rule.if: will_based_property_suit and attesting_witness_examined and (beneficiary_was_dependent_caregiver or exclusion_was_only_suspicion) and no_evidence_of_testator_mental_incapacity

predicates.will_based_property_suit: A civil property proceeding depends on whether a will is genuine.
predicates.attesting_witness_examined: The party propounding the will examined an attesting witness who testified to its execution, and the testimony was not found defective.
predicates.beneficiary_was_dependent_caregiver: The will benefited a person who depended on the testator and had cared for the testator over a substantial period.
predicates.exclusion_was_only_suspicion: The exclusion or reduced provision for natural heirs was the sole substantive ground for treating the will as suspicious.
predicates.no_evidence_of_testator_mental_incapacit: The opposing party produced no evidence that the testator's mental faculties were impaired when the will was executed.

members.legal_issue: The evidence, considered as a whole, sufficiently established the genuineness and voluntary character of a will despite the circumstances treated by the lower courts as suspicious.
material_facts: The testatrix left natural heirs out of the will, although some descendants of one branch of the family were beneficiaries.
The objection did not assert that the lawyer who identified the testatrix before the registrar had identified the wrong person.
The will and two later codicils were registered, and the registrar explained or read their contents to the testatrix.
Some attesting witnesses were interested in the executors.
A close relation of one executor played an active role in arranging execution of the will.
The testatrix made two codicils, the later one about three years after the will, because she had used some of the property listed in it.
The testatrix also sold property and received the price, and executed a fixed deposit receipt, demonstrating that she could deal with her property.
members.legal_principle: A will expresses the testator’s last wishes, but the propounder must remove suspicious circumstances before probate may be granted. Disinheriting natural heirs is not, by itself, suspicious because testamentary disposition departs from the ordinary line of succession. Identification before a registrar is not suspicious where the identity is not disputed. Where a registered will has been read or explained to the testator and its contents admitted, interest on the part of attesting witnesses loses significance. An active role by a person close to an executor may raise concern, but that concern must be assessed against the other evidence. The circumstances must be considered as a whole. The judgment cites no statutory provisions or earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances relied on by the lower courts did not outweigh the evidence supporting the testatrix’s voluntary and informed execution of the documents. The appeal was allowed, the lower courts’ judgments were set aside, and the will as modified by the two codicils was probated.

predicates.independent_property_dealings: The testator independently sold property, received its price, or otherwise dealt with property in a manner showing awareness and capacity.
predicates.ordinary_heirs_disinherited: The testator excluded natural heirs from some or all of the testamentary benefit.
predicates.interested_attesting_witnesses: One or more attesting witnesses had an interest connected with the beneficiaries or executors.

predicates.will_as_modified_probated: The will, as modified by its codicils, is granted probate.

members.legal_issue: A will must be proved through evidence satisfying the statutory requirements for execution and attestation.
material_facts: The original will was not produced, and proof was offered through a certified copy and a purported photocopy.

The scribe, who was also claimed to be an attesting witness, testified that the testatrix put her thumb impression only after he had signed and that he did not know whether anyone else attested the will.
The accounts of the other witnesses conflicted about the preparation, execution, and attestation of the will.
The evidence did not reliably establish that the testatrix understood and acknowledged the will’s contents or that two witnesses attested it in the required manner.
members.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires at least two attesting witnesses, each of whom has seen the testator sign or affix a mark, or has received the testator’s personal acknowledgment, and each of whom signs in the testator’s presence. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one attesting witness must be examined to prove execution and attestation. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, and Bhagatram v. Suresh.
members.conclusion: The will’s execution and attestation were not proved in accordance with law.

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought recognition of a will in a proceeding concerning the will.
predicates.attesting_witness_did_not_prove_required: The witness relied on to attest the will did not establish that the testator signed or acknowledged it and that the required attestation occurred.
predicates.attestation_accounts_were_contradictory: The witnesses gave conflicting accounts about how the will was prepared, signed, or attested.
predicates.will_execution_not_proved: The will’s execution is not established by legally sufficient proof.

members.legal_issue: Due execution, attestation, and the testator’s sound disposing state of mind may be established by evidence independent of the presumption for an ancient original document.
material_facts: The original will was filed in an earlier suit soon after its execution, and the testator’s mother relied on it in claiming the property.
The mother dealt with the property as its absolute owner and executed settlement deeds in favour of her daughters.
An attesting witness testified that the testator executed the will, that he attested it, and that the testator was in a sound disposing state of mind.
The courts below accepted the witness’s identification and testimony, and the terms of the will were found to be natural and rational.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the lack of a section 90 presumption did not prevent proof of execution and attestation through other evidence. It relied on the attesting witness’s testimony, the circumstances and conduct surrounding the will, and the rationality of its terms. Setthaya v. Somayajulu was applied in holding that, once a copy is properly admitted as secondary evidence of a document’s terms, the court may construe those terms.
members.conclusion: The evidence apart from any presumption under section 90 justified finding that the will was executed and attested and that the testator was in a sound disposing state of mind.

rule.if: testamentary_validity_dispute and execution_contested and attesting_witness_testified and witness_identification_accepted and conduct_supported_will and terms_were_natural_and_rational

predicates.testamentary_validity_dispute: The proceeding disputes the validity of a will.
predicates.execution_contested: A party disputes whether the testator executed the will.
predicates.attesting_witness_testified: A person who attested the will testified about its execution and the testator’s condition.
predicates.witness_identification_accepted: The court accepted that the witness was an attesting witness to the will.
predicates.conduct_supported_will: The testator’s family members acted in ways consistent with treating the will as valid.
predicates.terms_were_natural_and_rational: The court found the will’s terms natural and rational in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A will made by a competent and apparently free testator is not invalid for undue influence unless the challenger proves pressure that overbore the testator’s free agency.
material_facts: The testator’s execution of the will and testamentary capacity were undisputed.
The testator had a longstanding grievance about his younger son’s marriage, and the will’s recitals reflected that grievance.
The beneficiary had no part in preparing, executing, or registering the will; the testator made the arrangements himself and kept the will.
The evidence showed that the beneficiary had expressed views to the testator, but did not show that he impaired the testator’s free exercise of volition.
The testator lived for nearly a year after making the will and continued to say that it should stand.
members.legal_principle: Under Boyse v. Rossborough and Craig v. Lamoureux, once due execution by a competent person who was apparently a free agent is proved, the burden of proving undue influence rests on the person alleging it. Section 61 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 makes a will void when its making is caused by fraud, coercion, or importunity that takes away the testator’s free agency; Illustration (vii) confirms that persuasion does not invalidate a will where the testator acts in the free exercise of judgment and volition. As explained in Hall v. Hall, persuasion and appeals to affection or other sentiments are legitimate, but pressure that overbears the testator’s volition without convincing the judgment is undue influence.
members.conclusion: The challenger did not prove undue influence, and the will was not invalid on that ground.

predicates.will_executed_with_due_formalities: The will was executed with the required formalities.
predicates.testator_competent_and_apparently_free_a: The testator had the capacity to make the will and appeared to act freely.
predicates.evidence_of_fraud_coercion_or_overbearin: Evidence shows that fraud, coercion, or pressure overbore the testator’s free agency.
predicates.will_not_invalid_for_undue_influence: The will is not invalid on the ground of undue influence.

members.legal_issue: A will is proved when its execution and the testator’s capacity are established and any suspicious circumstances are satisfactorily explained.
material_facts: The beneficiaries relied on a will to defeat the deceased’s relatives’ claim to his separate properties.
The scribe testified that the testator instructed him, read the will before signing it, and signed it in the presence of the attesting witnesses, who attested in his presence.

The testator was elderly and had suffered a fracture, but the evidence showed that he was mentally alert; there was no evidence that he had become senile, and he had recently dealt with another property.

The testator’s relationship with his real sister was not cordial, he lived with and was cared for by his stepsister and the beneficiaries, and the claimants were absent during his hospitalization and treatment.

The scribe and witnesses supported execution of the will, and the evidence indicated that the beneficiary who brought them did so at the testator’s request. The testator had declined advice to register the will because he expected to live longer.
members.legal_principle: The propounder bears the burden of proving a will. Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the will must be proved through the legally required execution and attestation, together with proof of the testator’s capacity. If suspicious circumstances arise, the propounder must explain them to the Court’s satisfaction. Suspicion must be assessed in the circumstances of the particular case and cannot replace proof. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, Ryali Kameswara Rao v. Bendapudi Suryaprakasarao, and Sm. Chinmoyee Saha v. Debendra Lal Saha.
members.conclusion: The beneficiaries proved the execution, attestation, capacity, and genuineness of the will; the unexplained-suspicion challenge did not justify rejecting it.

rule.if: will_validity_dispute and testator_signed_will and execution_and_attestation_proved and testator_had_capacity and suspicious_circumstances_explained

predicates.will_validity_dispute: A party relied on a will in a dispute over who was entitled to the deceased’s property.
predicates.testator_signed_will: The evidence showed that the testator signed the will.
predicates.execution_and_attestation_proved: The evidence showed that the will was prepared on the testator’s instructions and signed and attested in the legally required presence of the testator and witnesses.
predicates.testator_had_capacity: The evidence showed that the testator understood the will and was mentally capable when it was made.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_explained: The evidence explained circumstances raised against the will, including the testator’s reasons for excluding relatives and the beneficiary’s role in bringing the scribe and witnesses.

members.legal_issue: A later will is valid when its propounder proves due execution and the testator’s capacity and free will, and removes legitimate suspicion; the beneficiary’s participation or the exclusion of natural heirs does not alone invalidate it.
material_facts: The testator read and signed the later will in the presence of the attesting witnesses, who then signed in the testator’s presence.
The evidence supported that the testator was mentally and physically sound when the will was made.
The beneficiary and his family had cared for the testator and his wife, while the other sons had received property in earlier partitions and had not cared for their parents in their old age.
The challenge to the will relied on circumstances that the Court found unsupported by evidence or not sufficient, by themselves, to establish suspicion.
The beneficiary succeeded before the revenue authority on the basis of the later will, and the opposing son had not challenged that final order.
members.legal_principle: Sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 govern proof of a will and its attestation. The propounder must prove execution, the testator’s sound and disposing mind, and that the testator acted freely. Where legitimate suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them; the usual standard is the satisfaction of a prudent mind, not mathematical certainty. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma; Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur; Uma Devi Nambiar v. T. C. Sidhan; and Pentakota Satyanarayana v. Pentakota Seetharatnam. Excluding natural heirs, a beneficiary’s participation, and non-registration of a will do not, without more, establish invalidity.
members.conclusion: The propounder discharged the burden of proving the later will and dispelling legitimate suspicion. The High Court erred in rejecting it; the appeals were allowed and the trial court’s judgment was restored.

predicates.civil_will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the validity of a will in a civil dispute.
predicates.will_execution_proved: The propounder proved that the testator signed the will and that the attesting witnesses attested it as required.
predicates.testator_had_capacity: The evidence showed that the testator had a sound and disposing mind when making the will.
predicates.testator_acted_freely: The evidence showed that the testator made the will of the testator’s own free will.
predicates.legitimate_suspicions_removed: The propounder answered the circumstances that could reasonably cast doubt on the will, and the remaining objections were unsupported or insufficient to establish such doubt.

members.legal_issue: A Will's execution is proved by examining an attesting witness whose evidence establishes the testator's and both attesting witnesses' signatures in the required circumstances.
material_facts: One attesting witness testified that the testator executed the Will and that the witness and the other attesting witness signed it.
The witness stated that the testator also signed the Will at the Tehsil office and that both witnesses witnessed it before the Sub-Registrar.
The witness's evidence that the testator and the other attesting witness were present and signed was not disputed in cross-examination; the scribe and a registration official also gave evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 prescribes the formalities for execution and attestation of a Will, and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires at least one attesting witness to be called to prove execution when available. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Seth Beni Chand v. Smt. Kamla Kunwar, and Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam. It distinguished M.L. Abdul Jabbar Sahib v. M.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons and N. Kamalam v. Ayyasamy because the witness examined here was an attesting witness, not merely a scribe.
members.conclusion: The attesting witness's testimony proved due execution of the Will, satisfying the applicable requirements for execution and proof.

predicates.will_execution_proof_proceeding: A party seeks to prove the execution of a Will in a court proceeding.
predicates.one_attesting_witness_examined: At least one person who attested the Will gives evidence in the proceeding.
predicates.witness_testifies_testator_and_both_witn: The attesting witness testifies that the testator and both attesting witnesses signed the Will in the required circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is genuine and freely executed when the evidence supporting its execution is credible and the circumstances raised against it do not undermine that evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court found the will genuine and freely executed.
An advocate testified that he advised on preparation of the will and saw the testator sign it; the scribe testified that he prepared and explained it to the testator.
The scribe had recorded the gist of the will in a regularly kept register on the date it was said to have been executed, and that entry was not challenged.
The testator’s son did not deny that the signature on the will was his father’s.
The Court found no substance in the claims that the will was antedated, unnatural, or inconsistent with an undertaking in earlier proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the evidence of the advocate and scribe, the contemporaneous record of the will, the absence of a denial of the signature by the testator’s son, and the lack of substance in the circumstances said to discredit the will. It found no basis to disturb the concurrent factual findings of the courts below.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings that the will was genuine and executed by the testator of his own free will were upheld.

predicates.appeal_challenges_concurrent_will_findin: An appeal challenges concurrent findings by lower courts that a will was genuine and freely executed.
predicates.credible_execution_witnesses: A credible witness saw the testator sign the will, and a credible scribe testified that the will was prepared and explained to the testator.
predicates.contemporaneous_will_record: The scribe made a contemporaneous record of the substance of the will in a regularly kept register.
predicates.signature_not_denied_by_close_relative: A close relative who could address the testator’s signature did not deny that the signature on the will was the testator’s.

members.legal_issue: Common intention to cause bodily injuries likely to cause death, formed during an attack, supports culpable homicide liability but does not establish murder where an intention to kill or inflict ordinarily fatal injuries is not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: Three accused acted together in attacking the deceased, who had intervened in the confrontation.
The deceased suffered multiple head injuries, including two fatal injuries, but the evidence did not establish which accused inflicted which injuries.

The court found that the common intention to cause bodily injuries developed at the scene, but that the accused had not formed a common intention to kill the deceased or inflict injuries ordinarily sufficient to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC requires a common intention and participation in the criminal act. A pre-arranged plan and meeting of minds are required, although the plan may develop at the scene; the common intention must precede the act constituting the offence. It may be inferred from conduct showing unity of purpose, the part played by the accused, the injuries inflicted, and other relevant circumstances. The Court relied on Krishna v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1963 SC 1413, and Ramashish Yadav v. State of Bihar, [1999] 8 SCC 555. Applying Sections 302 and 304 Part I IPC, the Court found a common intention to cause injuries likely to cause death, but reasonable doubt as to a common intention to kill or inflict injuries ordinarily sufficient to cause death.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions of the three accused under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC were set aside and replaced with convictions for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 IPC.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_murder_conviction and accused_acted_in_concert and common_intention_to_cause_likely_fatal_injuries_developed_before_attack and reasonable_doubt_about_intention_to_kill

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_murder_convictio: The proceeding is an accused’s appeal against a murder conviction.
predicates.accused_acted_in_concert: The accused participated together in the attack on the victim.
predicates.common_intention_to_cause_likely_fatal_i: Before inflicting the relevant injuries, the accused formed a common intention to cause bodily injuries likely to cause death, even if that intention arose during the incident.
predicates.reasonable_doubt_about_intention_to_kill: The evidence leaves reasonable doubt that the accused shared an intention to kill or to inflict injuries ordinarily sufficient to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A joint assault with the common intention to cause bodily injuries likely to result in death supports culpable-homicide liability with common intention when murder liability is excluded for excessive private defence.
material_facts: The accused made a combined assault on the deceased, inflicting numerous injuries, including fractures to vital parts of the body.
The Court found that the accused shared an intention to cause bodily injuries likely to result in death, and that this intention developed at the scene.
The Court also found that the accused had exceeded their right of private defence, taking the case out of murder.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Part I of Section 304 and Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, reasoning that a common intention to inflict bodily injuries likely to result in death developed at the scene during the combined assault. It read that liability alongside its conclusion that the excessive exercise of private defence brought the case within Exception 2 to Section 300. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions were altered to convictions for culpable homicide under Part I of Section 304 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, with a sentence of seven years' rigorous imprisonment.

predicates.criminal_homicide_case: The proceeding concerns criminal liability for a death caused by an assault.
predicates.murder_liability_excluded_by_excessive_p: The accused exceeded a right of private defence, excluding liability for murder.
predicates.group_made_combined_assault: The accused acted together in assaulting the deceased.
predicates.shared_intention_to_inflict_likely_fatal: The accused shared an intention to cause bodily injuries likely to result in death, and that intention arose during the incident.

members.legal_issue: A co-accused who does not physically assault the victim may share the intention to commit murder when the circumstances show purposeful assistance in carrying out the attack.
material_facts: The accused went together at night to the victim's home, where the victim was sleeping.
The assailant carried a cutting weapon and the co-accused carried a spear.
The victim appeared to have been purposefully sought rather than encountered by chance.
The co-accused did not strike the victim but used the spear to deter outside interference with the attack.
The accused fled together immediately after the killing.
members.legal_principle: For shared intention under Section 34 of the Penal Code, common intention may be inferred from the circumstances, including the time and place of the offence, the weapons carried, the accused persons' conduct and their concerted actions. A co-accused need not personally inflict the fatal injuries if his conduct shows intentional assistance toward the common object. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The circumstances supported the inference that the co-accused shared the intention to commit murder despite not participating in the physical assault, and the Court upheld his conviction under Sections 302 read with 34 of the Penal Code.

members.legal_issue: An accused who knowingly participates in restraining a victim so that an armed participant can shoot the victim may be held liable for murder as part of the common object or common intention.
material_facts: Two accused held the deceased’s arms to immobilize him while another accused fired a countrymade firearm at him.
The court found that the accused knew that the shooter was carrying a firearm and that the restraint facilitated the shooting.
One of the accused who restrained the deceased exhorted the shooter to kill him.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principles of common object under Section 149 and common intention under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, finding that the accused knew of the firearm and actively facilitated the killing; the exhortation further supported the finding against the accused who gave it. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The participation of the accused who restrained the deceased supported their convictions for murder with the shooter under the principles of common object and common intention.

members.legal_issue: Participants acting with a common intention to kill are liable for murder unless the killing is excused by a right of private defence that extends to causing death.
material_facts: The accused were found to be in possession of the field and entitled to cut the crop, but the deceased had a serious claim to possession supported by a civil decree and an order of relinquishment.

The deceased party went to harvest the crop under police protection, after lodging reports expressing apprehension of trouble; the evidence showed peaceful intentions and no dangerous weapons among the deceased party.
The accused attempted to send away the constables, then entered the field armed with guns and a spear and attacked the deceased at close range, killing three people; the accused were not injured.
The evidence established that the accused shared an intention to kill and participated in the attack.
The accused had an opportunity to seek assistance from public authorities but instead diverted a constable on a false pretext and used force that was more than necessary for defence.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code creates joint criminal liability where persons share a common intention and participate in acts in furtherance of it; it does not create a separate offence. Sections 96 and 98 provide that an act done in lawful private defence is not an offence. Under Section 103, private defence of property extends to causing death only for specified offences and subject to Section 99. Section 99 excludes the right where there is time to seek protection from public authorities and limits the right to harm necessary for defence. The Court held that the property-taking shown did not justify causing death, that there was no reasonable apprehension of death or hurt, and that the armed attack was unnecessary and excessive.
members.conclusion: The accused had no right of private defence extending to causing death, and their common intention and participation made them liable for murder.

members.legal_issue: Members of a group may be held liable for grievous injuries inflicted in pursuit of their common object even if the evidence does not establish which particular member caused each injury.
material_facts: The accused appellants attacked the complainant group together, carrying different weapons.
Several grievous injuries were inflicted, including injuries caused by sharp-pointed weapons.
The Supreme Court found that the circumstances showed the grievous injuries were inflicted in pursuit of the group's common object, even if one appellant did not personally cause an injury.
members.legal_principle: Section 326 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes liability for grievous injuries caused in prosecution of an unlawful assembly's common object; individual proof that every member personally inflicted an injury is not required where the common object and the injuries' connection to it are established. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The uncertainty about which appellant inflicted particular injuries did not exculpate any appellant, because the grievous injuries were caused in prosecution of the group's common object.

members.legal_issue: Common intention may be inferred in a group assault even when the prosecution cannot attribute a specific overt act to each participant.
material_facts: The accused arrived and acted as a group, forcibly taking two people onto a boat.
The group assaulted one of them with weapons, causing his death.
The eyewitness who escaped could not realistically pinpoint each participant’s individual act during the group attack.
The medical evidence was consistent with injuries inflicted by sharp weapons, and the accused had arrived armed.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies where the participants’ conduct establishes a shared common intention; a specific overt act by each participant is not necessary. The Court relied on Bishna alias Bhiswadeb Mahato v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The circumstances attracted common-intention liability despite the absence of proof of each accused’s individual overt act.

members.legal_issue: Common intention to cause death is not established for every participant in a group assault merely because the participants acted together, but may be established for participants who jointly inflict fatal injuries in circumstances showing a shared intention to cause those injuries.
material_facts: Two accused, each armed with a stick, each struck the deceased forcefully on the head, causing one injury apiece; the resulting head injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The other two accused assaulted the deceased and his brother with kicks and fists.

The court found no evidence that all four had arrived with a preplanned intention to cause the deceased’s death, and held that the other two’s participation and the armed assailants’ use of sticks did not establish their shared intention to cause death.
The appeal challenged convictions for murder with the aid of the common-intention provision.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Penal Code, common intention to cause the relevant fatal injury must be established; knowledge that weapons would be used in an assault is not, by itself, enough to establish a common intention to commit murder. Common intention may arise at the time of the occurrence, and the court inferred it for the two assailants who each delivered a forceful head blow sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions of the two accused who each delivered a forceful blow to the deceased’s head were maintained because they developed and shared the intention to cause the fatal injuries when delivering the blows. The murder convictions of the other two accused were set aside because the evidence did not establish their common intention to cause death.

members.legal_issue: Common intention to kill may be inferred from the circumstances and course of an assault even without direct evidence of a prior meeting of minds or attribution of the fatal injuries to particular assailants.
material_facts: The accused arrived together and assaulted the deceased with weapons.

The fatal injuries were not attributed to any particular accused, and there was no direct evidence of a prior meeting of minds.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention may form at the scene and may be inferred from the circumstances and manner in which the assault is carried out; direct evidence of prior concert is not essential. The Court treated continued assault despite intervention and the refusal to give water coupled with the threat to kill as evidence of the shared intention.
members.conclusion: The circumstances and sequence of events established the accused's common intention to kill the deceased, and the convictions were upheld.

members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the other appellants under sections 326/34 of the Indian Penal Code were set aside.
