members.legal_issue: A shared intention to kill may be inferred where identified assailants jointly attack a victim with deadly weapons on vital parts and cause death.
material_facts: The eyewitness evidence accepted by both lower courts identified three assailants as striking the deceased with spears on vital parts of the body.

The Supreme Court found no adequate basis to displace the lower courts’ conclusion about the assailants’ intention.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, inferring common intention to kill from the assailants’ coordinated use of deadly weapons against vital parts of the victim and the resulting death. No earlier case was relied on.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions of the three assailants on the basis of common intention were upheld.

Where the fatal injuries are inflicted in prosecution of the participants' common object, the accused cannot obtain an advantage merely because the evidence does not assign each injury to a particular participant. No earlier case is cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The inability of the witnesses to identify which accused inflicted each particular injury did not entitle the accused to relief.

The shooter fired the gun and killed the deceased.

members.legal_issue: Common intention to commit a homicide may be inferred from the participants’ coordinated conduct, and an independently proved overt act by each participant is not a legal requirement for shared liability for the homicide.
material_facts: The accused went together, armed with knives, concealed themselves, and waited for the deceased.
When the deceased arrived, the accused emerged and announced that they had been waiting for him.
One accused began the attack and was prevented by a witness from continuing; the other pursued and inflicted the fatal injuries.
The accused whose attack was interrupted was convicted of the homicide together with the other participant.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention; proof of an overt act by every participant is not a requirement. Common intention may be inferred from the proved circumstances. The Court relied on Chinta Pulla Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1993] Supp. (3) SCC 134, where a participant’s conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 was upheld although another accused alone inflicted the fatal injuries.
members.conclusion: The evidence permitted the inference that the accused shared the intention to kill, and the conviction for the homicide with the aid of common intention was justified even if he had not caused the head injury.

members.legal_issue: A participant is constructively liable for a fatal act committed by another when the participants act pursuant to a shared prearranged plan and the fatal act advances their common intention.
material_facts: The appellants shared the motive of the person who delivered the fatal blow.
The appellants and that person concealed themselves behind trees while armed, after learning that the victim would pass that way.
They rushed at and chased the victims, surrounded them, and the appellants participated in the assault while the other participant delivered the fatal blow.
The participants fled together after an alarm was raised.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code provides constructive liability where a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. Common intention requires action in concert, a prearranged plan and prior meeting of minds, and participation in the action; it is distinct from merely having the same or similar intention. The inference of common intention must be necessary from the circumstances. The Court relied on Mahabub Shah v. King Emperor.
members.conclusion: Although the unlawful-assembly basis of the murder conviction could not stand, the appellants were guilty of murder on the basis of their common intention with the person who delivered the fatal blow; the conviction was altered accordingly.

Common intention requires concert and a prior meeting of minds, which may be inferred from conduct and circumstances and may develop during the events. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The two assailants were guilty of murder with joint liability, and their convictions and life sentences were upheld.

members.legal_issue: Different individual motives do not prevent a finding of common intention when an accused intentionally facilitates another's killing of the victim.
material_facts: One accused restrained the victim and directed the other accused to shoot him.

The Court relied on Ramaswamy Ayyangar v. State of Tamil Nadu, 1976 (3) SCC 779, at page 783.
members.conclusion: The accused who restrained the victim and directed the shooting was properly held liable for murder with common intention.

members.legal_issue: Common intention may be inferred from the accused's conduct and the surrounding circumstances, and a participant may be jointly liable for a fatal act inflicted by a companion even without personally inflicting an injury on the victim.
material_facts: The appellant and his brother had prior hostility with the deceased and had threatened him.
Despite an arrangement for mediation, the appellant and his brother went armed with lethal weapons to the deceased's home and dragged him out.
The brother inflicted the fatal blows, while the appellant participated from the beginning through the end of the attack and assaulted witnesses who intervened.
The appellant did not personally inflict a blow on the deceased.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code imposes joint liability where a criminal act is done in furtherance of a common intention. Ram Tahal v. State of U.P., AIR 1972 SC 254, permits that intention to be inferred from the totality of conduct and circumstances; Rajesh Govind Jagesha v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2000 SC 160, states that direct evidence is unnecessary and that personal participation in every part of the offence need not be proved; Bishna v. State of West Bengal, AIR 2006 SC 302, states that a specific overt act is unnecessary; and Manik Das v. State of Assam, AIR 2007 SC 2274, relying on Ch. Pulla Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1993 SC 1899, explains that Section 34 can apply even where the particular accused caused no injury.
members.conclusion: The appellant shared the common intention and was jointly liable for the fatal act despite not personally injuring the deceased; his appeal was dismissed.

The Court relied on the circumstances showing the shared intention and replaced the High Court’s reliance on Section 149 with Section 34.

It is not necessary that each participant inflict a fatal injury, and the individual injuries inflicted by a participant need not themselves be sufficient to cause death. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The appellant shared the common intention to murder and was liable for murder with the other participant under the joint-liability principle; the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A participant who acts with a shared intention to murder is liable for the murder even when the shot fired at the intended victim strikes another person.
material_facts: The appellant and the shooter were on inimical terms with the intended victim.
After others began dragging the intended victim, the appellant urged the shooter to fire at him.
The shooter fired, but the shot struck the intended victim’s daughter, who later died.
The appellant again urged the shooter to fire at the intended victim and then aimed his own weapon at an intervening witness when the gun was taken from the shooter.
The trial court and the High Court found that the appellant shared the shooter’s intention to murder the intended victim.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. It held on the facts found by the lower courts that the appellant’s conduct went beyond merely shouting an exhortation and demonstrated a shared intention to commit murder. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s acts established a common intention with the shooter to murder the intended victim, and the conviction for murder on that basis was upheld.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and participant_urged_shooter_to_attack_intended_victim and participant_reinforced_attack_after_first_shot and participant_used_weapon_against_intervenor and shared_intent_to_murder_found

predicates.shared_intent_to_murder_found: The fact-finder found that the participant and shooter shared an intention to murder the intended victim.

members.legal_issue: A participant who shares an intention with an initial group to cause injuries may be liable for the injuries that participant inflicts even if the group did not share an intention to commit murder.
material_facts: The accused arrived with the initial group, which came together armed with weapons other than firearms.
The group confronted the deceased over a disputed passage and caused injuries during the confrontation.
The accused inflicted a sharp-edged-weapon wound on the deceased and a similar wound on an injured witness.
Medical evidence identified the wound on the deceased's elbow and an incised wound on the witness as consistent with a sharp-edged weapon.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC permits shared liability where common intention is proved from the participants' conduct and circumstances. The court found common intention among the initial group to cause injuries, while distinguishing that intention from an intention to commit murder; it relied on Hira Lal Malik v. State for the individualized assessment of participants' roles and criminality.
members.conclusion: The accused's murder and attempted-murder convictions were set aside, but his convictions for causing grievous and simple injuries with the aid of common intention were maintained.

predicates.accused_inflicted_proved_injuries: Evidence established that the accused personally inflicted injuries during the incident.

members.legal_issue: A person who arrives with others after a confrontation has begun is not vicariously liable for their acts without proof of a shared intention, but remains liable for injuries attributable to that person's own acts.
material_facts: The accused arrived with a later group carrying firearms after the initial confrontation had already begun.
The prosecution's account that the accused fired at the deceased's head was inconsistent with medical evidence that the head wound was not caused by a firearm.
The injured eyewitness could not identify who fired at him, although medical evidence showed firearm injuries and other injuries.
The court found no evidence that a common intention developed among the later arrivals, who acted individually.
The medical evidence supported attributing grievous and simple injuries to the accused's own use of a firearm.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC requires proof of common intention, which may be inferred objectively from conduct and surrounding circumstances; mere participation is insufficient. The court relied on Hira Lal Malik v. State and held that a later arrival, joining after the altercation began, was not vicariously liable without evidence of a shared intention, though individual acts remained attributable to their perpetrator.
members.conclusion: The accused's convictions for murder and attempted murder with the aid of common intention were set aside; he was liable for the grievous and simple injuries attributable to his own acts, and his convictions for those injuries were maintained without common-intention liability.

predicates.own_injury_causing_act_proved: Evidence established that the accused's own act caused injuries.

members.legal_issue: A shared intention to kill supports joint murder liability even when the other participants inflicted only simple injuries with the blunt side of a weapon.
material_facts: The other appellants accompanied the principal appellant at midnight and were found to share the intention to kill the deceased.
The other appellants had assaulted the deceased with the blunt side of the gandasa and were said to have inflicted only simple injuries.
Their argument that they should instead be convicted only for causing simple hurt was rejected.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, participants who share the intention to cause death may be held jointly liable for murder; the court rejected reduction to Section 323 where that common intention was established. No earlier cases are cited in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The convictions and life sentences of the other appellants under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code were confirmed.

members.legal_issue: Participants who jointly facilitate a killing may be convicted of murder on the basis of shared intention inferred from their coordinated conduct.
material_facts: After a quarrel, several accused arrived together, some carrying sticks and another carrying a spear.
One accused directed the others to kill the victim.
The accused with sticks moved to prevent the victim from escaping, while the spear-wielding accused fatally stabbed him.
The group had acted together in a continuing dispute and their conduct enabled the killing.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, shared intention may be inferred from concerted conduct and the circumstances of the attack. Conduct that blocks a victim’s escape while another participant carries out a killing, together with an order to kill and coordinated arrival armed for the encounter, supported the finding of shared intention. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions with the aid of the shared-intention principle were affirmed.

members.legal_issue: A participant who did not personally assault the victim could be convicted for murder where his conduct furthered the group's common intention to kill.
material_facts: The accused arrived together with others, carrying firearms.
Some members of the group took the victim into the residence, where one of them shot him.
The accused prevented witnesses from intervening while the victim was taken and attacked.
The group left together after the shooting.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code provides for joint liability where persons commit a criminal act in furtherance of their common intention. Common intention may be formed before or during the occurrence, but must precede the act constituting the offence; it may be inferred from the circumstances. Each participant need not personally assault the victim if each plays a role furthering the common intention. The Court applied Suresh v. State of U.P., (2001) 3 SCC 673, and distinguished Parshuram Singh v. State of Bihar, JT 2002 (1) SC 407, as turning on its particular facts.
members.conclusion: The accused shared the group's common intention to commit murder and was rightly convicted even though he did not personally assault the victim.

members.legal_issue: A pre-planned attack carried out with common intention can sustain joint liability for murder even without proof of a distinct overt act by each accused or an unlawful assembly of five or more persons.
material_facts: The accused returned to the disputed location armed with lathis after an earlier exchange about earth being placed on the land.
They gave a call to kill the deceased and attacked him together, causing injuries that medical evidence found ordinarily sufficient to cause death.

The evidence supported the finding that the attack was planned and that the participants acted with a common intention; fewer than five accused remained for consideration after other accused were acquitted.
The court found the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and rejected the contention that the incident was a sudden fight warranting a lesser homicide conviction.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, participants who commit murder in furtherance of a common intention may be held jointly liable; the extent of each participant’s overt act does not determine liability where common intention and participation are established. Section 34 does not require an unlawful assembly of five or more persons. The Court relied on Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1961 SC 1787, and distinguished Marimuthu v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2008) 3 SCC 205, because the attack was not a fight arising at the spur of the moment.
members.conclusion: The conviction for murder with the aid of common intention was affirmed, and the request to reduce the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder was rejected.

members.legal_issue: A person who accompanies an armed offender, fires a weapon to facilitate the offender’s attack, and leaves with the offender may be convicted of murder with the offender on the basis of shared participation.
material_facts: The accused father and his son arrived together at the victims’ home, armed respectively with a pistol and a sword, and left together after the attack.
The son attacked the victims and wounded a person who had grappled with him; the father fired his pistol, causing that person to release the son.
A cartridge was found at the scene, and a pistol and cartridges of the same bore were later recovered following information given by the father.
Eyewitness testimony and evidence that the father and son left together supported the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. It relied on the combined evidence of the accused arriving and leaving together, being armed, the father firing to enable the son to escape a grapple, and the physical evidence corroborating the eyewitness accounts. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The evidence established the father’s participation with the son in the murders; the acquittal was set aside and the father was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

members.legal_issue: A participant who restrains a victim while others inflict a fatal attack may share their common intention and be liable for the killing with them.
material_facts: Reliable eyewitnesses saw the accused hold the victim’s legs while two others struck the victim’s neck with a sharp weapon.
The three assailants left together after the attack.
The Court found no reasonable doubt that the accused shared the other assailants’ common intention.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, participation in an offence in furtherance of a shared common intention supports joint liability; the Court assessed the accused’s active assistance as part of the occurrence as a whole. The conviction was under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The accused shared the common intention to commit the killing and his conviction for murder with the other assailants was restored under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

members.legal_issue: Common intention may be inferred from participants’ coordinated conduct during an assault without proof of a prearranged plan, and minor discrepancies do not by themselves discredit the prosecution case.
material_facts: After a dispute about cleaning a drain, several members of one family entered the complainant’s home and assaulted her, then dragged her outside and beat her repeatedly.
The complainant had four simple injuries recorded in a medical certificate made that night after referral by a police constable.
The complainant’s account was supported by witnesses, while a defence witness admitted signing and the contents of a complaint about the incident.
The High Court relied on discrepancies about the objects used, the alleged number of blows, and the absence of medical examination of a neighbour who intervened.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC does not require proof of a prearranged plot or prior concert in every case; common intention may be established from the participants’ conduct and the circumstances. Exaggeration or minor discrepancies do not necessarily falsify the occurrence or undermine the prosecution case.
members.conclusion: The conduct established common intention to commit house trespass and cause hurt; the discrepancies and omissions identified by the High Court did not justify rejecting the prosecution case.

members.legal_issue: Where the evidence does not establish an unlawful assembly of five or more, a conviction may still be sustained under section 34 if the accused shared a common intention to attack and cause injuries capable of resulting in death.
material_facts: The appellant and the other convicted persons went armed and determined to fight the opposing party.
The facts supported a common intention to attack and cause injuries that might result in death.
The appellant was not proved to have personally caused an injury to the deceased, and his lack of involvement in the land dispute did not prevent him from sharing that intention.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code imposes joint liability for a criminal act done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. The Court considered the accused’s armed and determined participation and the intended attack, and held that personal infliction of an injury was not necessary to sustain liability on that basis.
members.conclusion: Even if the finding that more than five persons were in the appellant’s party was wrong, the convictions under sections 302 and 307 could be converted to convictions under those sections read with section 34.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_group_offence_co: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for an offence attributed to joint action.
predicates.accused_went_armed_and_determined_to_fig: The accused went with companions while armed and determined to engage in a fight.
predicates.shared_intention_to_attack_and_cause_pot: The accused shared the intention to attack the opposing party and cause injuries capable of resulting in death.

members.legal_issue: Common intention to commit murder may arise during an encounter, and a person who initiates an assault may share that intention with an armed companion who follows up the attack.
material_facts: The court found that the meeting between the two groups was probably accidental and that the prosecution had not established a prearranged plan to attack the victims.
One accused initiated the violence by attempting to assault a victim and continued the attack despite knowing that his son was armed with a gun and was behind him.
The armed son fired at the victims and pursued and shot one of them.
The court found that the common intention to murder developed after the encounter began, between the person who initiated the assault and the armed companion who followed it up.
The accused argued that the armed son had acted in private defence, but the court found that the other side had not initiated the violence.
members.legal_principle: Under section 34 read with section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention may develop at the scene and need not exist as a preconcerted plan before the encounter. The court inferred common intention from the initiator’s deliberate assault, his knowledge that the armed companion was behind him, and the companion’s subsequent use of the gun. Because the initiator was the aggressor, the companion could not rely on private defence on the facts found.
members.conclusion: The absence of a prearranged plan did not prevent a finding that common intention developed during the occurrence; the court sustained the murder convictions of the initiator and the armed companion, and rejected the claim that the companion acted in private defence.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may intervene in a criminal appeal where factual findings underlying a conviction are not properly considered or are contrary to the evidence on record.
material_facts: The appeals challenged convictions arising from two trials concerning the same occurrence, as well as acquittals in the later trial.
The Court found that material evidence concerning the accused persons’ injuries, the prior dispute, the investigation, and the prosecution witnesses’ contradictions had not been properly considered.
The Court concluded that the findings supporting conviction were contrary to the evidence and that the material deficiencies could not be overcome.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court may intervene where the findings in a criminal case are not properly grounded in the evidence or are contrary to the record; concurrent findings do not prevent intervention in such circumstances. The Court invoked Article 136 in its assessment of the record.
members.conclusion: The Court could exercise its appellate power to interfere with the convictions because the material facts had not been properly considered and the findings were contrary to the evidence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: An appeal before the Supreme Court challenges a criminal conviction.
predicates.material_evidence_not_properly_considere: The courts below failed to give proper consideration to material evidence bearing on guilt or the defence.
predicates.findings_contrary_to_record: The factual findings supporting conviction conflict with the evidence on record.
predicates.supreme_court_intervention_is_warranted: The Supreme Court may interfere with the conviction in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings when the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case, the evidence is wholly insufficient, and the lower courts grossly misappreciated it to the point of perversity, particularly where liberty is at stake.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the appellant, and the High Court affirmed the conviction.
The findings of guilt rested on evidence that did not establish conscious possession and on assumptions unsupported by the record.
The investigation left important evidence unexamined, and the evidence as a whole was insufficient to establish the prosecution’s case beyond reasonable doubt.
The appellant had suffered incarceration under the conviction.
members.legal_principle: Although the Court normally does not use Article 136 of the Constitution to reappreciate evidence or interfere with concurrent factual findings, it may intervene to protect individual liberty where the prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case, the evidence is wholly insufficient, and the lower courts’ gross misappreciation of evidence borders on perversity.
members.conclusion: The Court was not inhibited from reviewing the concurrent findings; it set aside the conviction, acquitted the appellant, and directed his release unless required in another case.

predicates.evidence_wholly_insufficient: The evidence was wholly insufficient to support the conviction.
predicates.lower_courts_grossly_misappreciated_evid: The lower courts grossly misappreciated the evidence, with their conclusions bordering on perversity.
predicates.liberty_at_stake: The challenged findings place the accused’s liberty at stake.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under its special-leave jurisdiction with factual findings that border on perversity and result in a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The matter was a special-leave appeal against an acquittal.
The High Court rejected the eyewitness’s evidence on grounds the Supreme Court found invalid, treating relationship as proof of interest and minor discrepancies as material.
The Supreme Court found that the acquittal resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with findings of fact made by the High Court. It may do so when those findings border on perversity and result in a miscarriage of justice. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court interfered with the factual findings, set aside the acquittal, and restored criminal liability.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging an acquittal.

predicates.findings_border_on_perversity: The factual findings are so unreasonable that they border on perversity.
predicates.findings_result_in_miscarriage_of_justic: The factual findings produce a miscarriage of justice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings in a criminal matter when the High Court has acted perversely or otherwise improperly.
material_facts: The appeals arose from convictions affirmed by the High Court as to the appellants’ participation, although the High Court reduced the principal offence and altered the related conviction.
The appellants argued that both courts had overlooked material evidence and serious infirmities in the prosecution case.
The Supreme Court found that the courts below had summarily dealt with the evidence and had overlooked manifest errors and glaring infirmities.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court ordinarily does not disturb concurrent findings of fact in criminal matters, but may do so in exceptional circumstances, including where the High Court has acted perversely or otherwise improperly. The Court relied on The State of Madras v. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer, Himachal Pradesh Administration v. Shri Om Prakash, Balak Ram v. State of U.P., Arunachalam v. P.S.R. Sadhananthan, State of U.P. v. Hamit Singh, and State of U.P. v. Pheru Singh.
members.conclusion: Article 136 permits interference with factual findings, including concurrent findings, where the High Court acted perversely or otherwise improperly; the Court found that threshold met in this case.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The matter is a criminal appeal brought before the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The courts below reached concurrent findings of fact relevant to the appeal.
predicates.high_court_acted_perversely_or_improperl: The High Court reached its findings through perverse or otherwise improper treatment of the case.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with a lower court’s finding of fact when it results from an erroneous application of law and is apt to cause a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave against the lower courts’ findings that the will was genuine.

The lower courts treated proof of execution as sufficient and did not properly assess the suspicious circumstances or the applicable standard of scrutiny where a daughter was disinherited in favour of grandchildren through another daughter.
The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had misapplied the legal principles governing proof of a will and that their approach could result in a miscarriage of justice.
members.legal_principle: Although the Court does not normally interfere with findings of fact, it may do so under Article 136 when a finding rests on an erroneous application of legal principle and is apt to result in a miscarriage of justice. Malkani v. Jamadar, AIR 1987 SC 767, was distinguished because the circumstances and the relationship between the competing beneficiaries differed.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court was justified in interfering under Article 136, set aside the judgments below, and allowed the appeal.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and lower_court_fact_finding and erroneous_application_of_law and likely_miscarriage_of_justice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court by special leave.

predicates.erroneous_application_of_law: The challenged finding was reached by applying a legal principle incorrectly.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may re-examine evidence despite concurrent judgments when the High Court’s approach to the evidence and the burden of proof is erroneous.
material_facts: Both courts below had convicted the appellants.
The High Court relied on the appellants’ failure to inform the deceased’s father and treated the accused as bearing the burden of explaining the death.
The Supreme Court considered that the High Court had overemphasized those circumstances and had misread the letters and other evidence.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it ordinarily does not go into questions of fact or examine evidence minutely when both courts below have given concurrent judgments, but may do so when circumstances such as an erroneous approach by the High Court warrant it. No provision or earlier case is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not examine facts minutely when the courts below have reached concurrent conclusions, the High Court’s erroneous approach justified re-examination of the evidence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_with_concurrent_findings: The case is a criminal appeal in which the courts below reached concurrent findings.
predicates.high_court_used_erroneous_approach: The High Court’s assessment relied on an erroneous approach to the evidence or the burden of proof.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may reappraise evidence in a special leave appeal when the High Court has missed the decisive issue, discredited evidence on erroneous grounds, and thereby risked grave injustice.
material_facts: The complainant brought a special leave appeal after the High Court altered the respondents’ murder convictions and reduced their sentences; the State did not appeal.
The High Court gave no cogent analysis of the evidence and relied on a statement made during investigation by a person who was not examined at trial.
The Supreme Court considered the record because it concluded that the High Court had missed the real point and had reached its conclusion on erroneous grounds.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise evidence to decide whether the High Court reached the correct factual conclusion. It may do so where the High Court has missed the real point requiring determination, discredited evidence on erroneous grounds, and failed to consider circumstances indicating a risk of grave injustice. The High Court’s powers in an appeal from conviction under section 386 of the Code of Criminal Procedure include reappraising the evidence and reaching its own conclusion on the record.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court was justified in examining the evidence to determine whether grave injustice had resulted.

rule.if: special_leave_criminal_appeal and high_court_missed_decisive_issue and high_court_discredited_evidence_on_erroneous_grounds and record_indicated_risk_of_grave_injustice

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: A complainant brought a special leave appeal in a criminal case after the High Court altered the accused persons’ convictions or sentences.
predicates.high_court_missed_decisive_issue: The High Court did not address the decisive issue raised by the evidence in the case.
predicates.high_court_discredited_evidence_on_erron: The High Court rejected or discounted evidence on grounds that were not supported by a proper assessment of the record.
predicates.record_indicated_risk_of_grave_injustice: The record contained circumstances suggesting that the High Court’s approach could have resulted in grave injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with factual findings in a special leave appeal when serious misconstruction of the record and unreasonable inferences cause grave injustice.
material_facts: The statutory authorities rejected the possession application after misconstruing the circumstances and disregarding material evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the resulting inferences were unreasonable and contrary to law, causing grave injustice.
members.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not interfere with findings of fact in special leave proceedings under Article 136 of the Constitution, it may do so where a statutory authority's decision rests on gross misconstruction of the facts and circumstances, ignores material evidence, and produces unreasonable inferences resulting in grave injustice. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The circumstances justified interference with the findings of the statutory authorities under Article 136.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and statutory_fact_findings_under_challenge and (material_evidence_ignored or facts_grossly_misconstrued) and unreasonable_inferences_caused_grave_injustice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party brings a special leave appeal challenging a decision made in a statutory proceeding.
predicates.statutory_fact_findings_under_challenge: The challenged decision includes factual findings by statutory authorities.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The authorities fail to consider material evidence in the record.
predicates.facts_grossly_misconstrued: The authorities materially misunderstand the facts or circumstances shown by the record.
predicates.unreasonable_inferences_caused_grave_inj: The authorities draw unreasonable inferences that result in grave injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent findings when the courts below have palpably misappreciated or ignored material evidence and their findings are inconsistent with the record.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court had both rejected the alleged relinquishment of interests in two properties.
The Supreme Court found that those courts had brushed aside oral and documentary evidence supporting the settlement and had ignored material facts and the parties’ conduct.
members.legal_principle: The Court’s power under Article 136 of the Constitution is exercised sparingly and in furtherance of justice, but permits review where findings are perverse or grossly or palpably erroneous, inconsistent with the material on record, or reached through perfunctory treatment of evidence. The Court relied on Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation v. P.H. Brahmbhatt, (1974) 3 SCC 601; (1974) 2 SCR 128.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings concerning the two properties were palpably erroneous and were set aside.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_findings and material_evidence_ignored and findings_palpably_inconsistent_with_record

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal invoking its special appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_findings: The courts below reached the same findings on the disputed issue.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The courts below failed to consider or properly weigh material oral or documentary evidence.
predicates.findings_palpably_inconsistent_with_reco: The findings cannot reasonably be reconciled with the evidence and material facts on the record.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with an appellate court’s altered offence classification when that classification rests on an erroneous appreciation of the evidence or law.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused of murder after finding that he caused the fatal injury.
The High Court changed the conviction to a lesser homicide offence, relying on the single blow and on its view that the doctor had not established the injury’s fatal character.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had misread the medical evidence and had treated the number of injuries as decisive.
The finding that the accused caused the fatal incident was not challenged.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution permits interference where findings of the court or courts below are contrary to the evidence on record. Toran Singh v. State of M.P. recognizes that limitation on the general reluctance to disturb findings based on appreciation of evidence; the Court also observed that the offence classification in this case was not a concurrent finding.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s altered conviction and restored the trial court’s judgment.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_from_appellate_clas: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court against an appellate court’s classification of the offence.
predicates.material_findings_below_are_contrary_to_: The material findings supporting the appellate court’s classification conflict with the evidence in the record.

members.legal_issue: A supervisory court may interfere with concurrent factual findings when the finding under review has no evidentiary support and rests on a manifest error.
material_facts: The tenancy authorities concurrently found that the occupant was the landowner’s tenant, but he had himself claimed to occupy as a subtenant of the original tenant.
The occupant did not testify, produced no rent receipts, and relied on a son who lacked knowledge of the relevant facts.
The effective revenue-record entries showed that the occupant was not in possession as the landowner’s tenant.
The High Court set aside the authorities’ finding, and the Supreme Court held that the finding lacked evidentiary support.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, a High Court cannot act as an appellate court and is generally bound by a tribunal’s findings of fact; however, the concurrent finding here was unsupported by evidence, so interference was justified. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court acted within its supervisory jurisdiction in setting aside the concurrent finding, and its judgment was affirmed.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_concurrent_factual: A supervisory court is reviewing a factual finding made concurrently by lower authorities.
predicates.finding_lacks_evidentiary_support: The finding is unsupported by evidence, including where the claimant supplies no competent supporting evidence and the relevant records contradict the finding.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of fact may be disturbed in a criminal appeal by special leave when exceptional features indicate a serious miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court had concurrently found the accused guilty.
The appellate record disclosed significant defects in the prosecution case that the lower courts had ignored or misread.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it does not ordinarily disturb concurrent findings of fact in an appeal by special leave, but may do so where exceptional features indicate a serious miscarriage of justice.
members.conclusion: The Court reassessed the evidence because the case disclosed exceptional features indicating a serious miscarriage of justice.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The lower courts reached the same factual findings.
predicates.exceptional_features_indicate_serious_mi: The record contains exceptional features indicating that the lower courts' findings may have caused a serious miscarriage of justice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may exercise its discretionary appellate jurisdiction to correct a legally deficient judgment involving an important question of law despite the parties’ procedural misconduct.
material_facts: The defendants had delayed filing their written statement and their appeal to the High Court was also late.
A sale deed had been executed in the plaintiff’s favour through a court-appointed commissioner.
The case raised an important legal question about what a court must do when a written statement is not filed, and the judgments below were deficient.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary jurisdiction; the Court stated that it is not bound to interfere merely because a judgment is incorrect, but exercised that jurisdiction because an important legal question required determination and the judgments could not be sustained.
members.conclusion: The Court exercised its discretion to allow the appeal, set aside the judgments below, and remand the case for a fresh decision.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party brings an appeal invoking the Supreme Court’s discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.important_legal_question: The appeal presents an important legal question requiring determination.
predicates.material_legal_deficiency: The judgment under appeal has a material legal deficiency.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere in a criminal matter on special leave when a violation of fundamental principles of justice or a grave and substantial miscarriage of justice has occurred, but not merely because of an error that caused no such injustice.
material_facts: The matter was a criminal appeal admitted by special leave.
The appellate court had left undecided a vital possession issue that affected assessment of the alleged common object and who was the aggressor.
The Supreme Court found that this omission was capable of causing serious and substantial injustice and interfered on that basis.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it was not bound by Privy Council practice and precedents but saw no reason to depart from their principles governing criminal appeals. It relied on Riel v. The Queen; In re Abraham Mallory Dillet; Ibrahim v. The King; Dal Singh v. King Emperor; Ex Parte Macrea; Taba Singh v. King Emperor; Easwaramurthi v. Emperor; George G. Feller v. The King; Md. Afdal Khan v. Abdul Hahman; and Louis Edouard Lanier v. The King. Those authorities establish that special-leave interference requires a clear departure from justice, a violation of natural justice, or serious and substantial injustice; an error or irregularity alone is insufficient where it has not caused a grave miscarriage of justice.
members.conclusion: The Court applied the established limits on interference in criminal cases and held that the failure to decide the vital possession issue justified its intervention.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.serious_substantial_injustice: A failure by a lower court to decide a material issue causes or threatens grave and substantial injustice to the accused.
predicates.fundamental_fairness_violation: The proceedings violate fundamental principles of natural justice or deprive the accused of the substance of a fair trial and the protection of the law.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may set aside concurrent factual findings in a special-leave appeal when they are manifestly unjust and cause grave injustice.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave after the trial court, the lower appellate court, and the High Court had all rejected the claim.

The lower courts' finding on readiness and willingness rested on an adverse inference from the absence of a bank passbook even though no one had asked for it to be produced, and overlooked evidence concerning the defendant's failure to attend the Sub-Registrar's office.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution gives the Supreme Court discretionary special-leave jurisdiction and does not require it to leave manifest injustice uncorrected merely because findings are concurrent. The Court relied on Variety Emporium v. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina, which states that once the burden of showing a concurrent decision is manifestly unjust is discharged, the Court has a duty to remedy the injustice.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court could re-examine and set aside the concurrent findings because they were manifestly unreasonable and perpetuated grave injustice.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and concurrent_findings and finding_manifestly_unjust and grave_injustice

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party brings an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_findings: Two or more lower courts reach the same finding on an issue.
predicates.finding_manifestly_unjust: The concurrent finding is manifestly unreasonable in light of the evidence and applicable law.
predicates.grave_injustice: Leaving the finding undisturbed would perpetuate grave injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings when exceptional circumstances show that material evidence was ignored and the resulting decision caused manifest injustice or grave miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeal challenged concurrent appellate findings that the transferees were bona fide purchasers.
The appellate courts had overlooked or excluded material evidence, including relationships among the parties and the lack of reliable support for recitals of consideration.
The High Court did not address a substantial question concerning a relevant family relationship and disposed of the appeal on a short ground.
members.legal_principle: Interference under Article 136 of the Constitution is sparing, but it is justified where exceptional circumstances show manifest injustice or grave miscarriage of justice caused by overlooking, ignoring or excluding material evidence. Once the burden of showing a manifestly unjust concurrent decision is discharged, the Court has a duty to remedy the injustice. The Court relied on Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakraborty, Basudev Hazra v. Meutiar Rahaman Mandal, and Bhanu Kumar Shastri v. Mohan Lal Sukhadia.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court was justified in exercising its discretionary jurisdiction to interfere with the concurrent findings and remedy the resulting injustice.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court challenging concurrent factual findings by lower courts.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The lower courts overlooked, ignored or excluded evidence material to resolving the dispute.
predicates.resulting_manifest_injustice: The treatment of the evidence resulted in manifest injustice or a grave miscarriage of justice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may reappraise evidence in a criminal appeal when the interests of justice require examination of a possible miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeals concerned convictions of many accused persons, largely based on eyewitness testimony.
The appellants alleged that the evidence had been incorrectly appreciated, raising a concern that the convictions might reflect a miscarriage of justice.
The Supreme Court examined the evidence itself.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, factual conclusions of the High Court are ordinarily treated as final, but that does not bar the Supreme Court from reappraising evidence when the interests of justice demand it.
members.conclusion: Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not reappraise evidence in its extraordinary appellate jurisdiction, it may do so when the interests of justice require it; it reappraised the evidence in this case.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case was an appeal in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.many_convictions_based_on_eyewitness_evi: Many accused persons had been convicted on the basis of eyewitness accounts.
predicates.possible_misappreciation_raised: The appellants challenged the appreciation of the evidence in a way that raised a concern about a possible miscarriage of justice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may intervene under Article 136 against an interim order in special circumstances to prevent manifest injustice or abuse of the court’s process.
material_facts: The appeal challenged an interim order in a pending writ proceeding and the appellate order declining to interfere with it.
The interim order departed from settled law on the availability of a statutory remedy, was made without hearing the creditor, and stayed recovery without special reasons.
The High Court’s approach was contrary to settled decisions of the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Supreme Court is ordinarily reluctant to interfere under Article 136 with an interim order in a pending proceeding, but may do so in special circumstances to prevent manifest injustice or abuse of the court’s process. The Court also relied on Dwarikesh Sugar Industries Ltd. v. Prem Heavy Engineering Works (P) Ltd. for the principle that subordinate courts should not disregard settled law or grant relief contrary to it.
members.conclusion: Special circumstances justified interference, and the challenged orders were set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_interim_order: The appeal asks the Supreme Court to review an interim order made in a pending proceeding.
predicates.order_contrary_to_settled_law: The challenged order departs from settled legal principles applicable to the dispute.
predicates.manifest_injustice_or_abuse_risk: The circumstances show a risk of manifest injustice or abuse of the court’s process if the order is left undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings in a rent-control appeal when the lower courts' legally erroneous approach produces a manifestly unjust result.
material_facts: The trial court and appellate court both rejected the claimed need after treating dire necessity, permanent job loss, and business preparations as necessary proof.
The High Court declined to interfere because the findings were concurrent findings of fact.
The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had used the wrong legal test and relied on irrelevant considerations.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court ordinarily does not disturb findings of fact, but may do so in exceptional cases where concurrent decisions are manifestly unjust or rest on a substantial and patent error of law. The Court relied on Variety Emporium v. V.R.M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina and Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan.
members.conclusion: This was an exceptional case for interference under Article 136, and the concurrent decisions could not stand.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: A party brought a special-leave appeal challenging factual findings reached by more than one lower court.
predicates.lower_courts_used_wrong_legal_test: The lower courts assessed the claim using a legal test that did not govern the issue.
predicates.resulting_decision_manifestly_unjust: Applying the wrong test led to a manifestly unjust decision.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of guilt may be set aside in a special-leave appeal when serious errors in assessing vital evidence leave the conviction resting on substantially discredited evidence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged convictions affirmed by the High Court after the trial court had also convicted the appellants.
The trial court found that the principal witnesses had falsely implicated the acquitted accused, and the High Court treated those accused as having received only the benefit of doubt.

The High Court rejected the evidence of two court witnesses but did not properly consider the effect of that rejection on the credibility of the principal witnesses, whose evidence those court witnesses had corroborated at trial.
The lower courts relied on a report to infer motive even though the prosecution's account contradicted it.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence against the appellants was considerably discredited and that the courts had reconstructed a story after substantially disbelieving the prosecution's case.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court does not normally reappraise evidence merely because it might take a different view of concurrent findings, but it may intervene where there is a glaring mistake or an omission to consider vital evidence. The Court found serious errors of that kind and concluded that the remaining evidence could not support conviction.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the convictions and sentences, acquitted the appellants, and allowed the appeal.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_against_conviction and concurrent_findings_of_guilt and vital_evidence_mishandled and prosecution_evidence_substantially_discredited

predicates.special_leave_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a special-leave appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the appellate court both found the accused guilty.
predicates.vital_evidence_mishandled: The lower courts seriously misassessed or failed to consider evidence material to the credibility or completeness of the prosecution case.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_substantially_discr: The evidence relied on for conviction is materially weakened by the rejection of its corroboration or by findings that the prosecution's account is false in significant respects.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may reappraise evidence in a special-leave appeal when the High Court has missed the real issue, discredited medical evidence on erroneous grounds, and failed to consider the risk of false implication arising from enmity.
material_facts: The High Court reversed a trial court acquittal and convicted the appellants.

The Supreme Court found that the High Court had missed the central question of whether the eyewitness account was safe to rely on, had discredited the medical testimony on erroneous grounds, and had failed to consider the implications of the long-standing enmity between the families.
members.legal_principle: A High Court hearing an appeal against acquittal may reappraise the evidence as it would in an appeal against conviction, while bearing the acquittal in mind. The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise evidence under Article 136, but may do so where the High Court has missed the real point, relied on erroneous grounds to discredit medical testimony, and failed to consider circumstances that may lead to false implication, in order to ensure that grave injustice has not occurred. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court was justified in examining the evidence to satisfy itself that grave injustice had not resulted, and it allowed the appeal and acquitted the appellants.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and high_court_reversed_acquittal and high_court_missed_real_issue and high_court_discredited_medical_evidence_on_erroneous_grounds and high_court_ignored_false_implication_risk

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The case came before the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.high_court_reversed_acquittal: The High Court reversed a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.high_court_missed_real_issue: The High Court failed to address the central question necessary to assess whether the prosecution account was safe to rely on.
predicates.high_court_discredited_medical_evidence_: The High Court rejected or criticised medical testimony on grounds the Supreme Court found erroneous.
predicates.high_court_ignored_false_implication_ris: The High Court failed to consider that enmity could lead witnesses to exaggerate or falsely implicate people.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings when those findings are perverse.
material_facts: The first appellate court reversed the trial court’s dismissal of the title suit, and the High Court affirmed that reversal.

The courts below treated the defendants’ patta as invalid without properly considering evidence that it had been issued in 1929 by an authorised officer, along with revenue records and revenue-authority findings supporting the defendants’ possession.
The first appellate court inferred that the patta was issued in 1954 from a witness’s age, although the documentary evidence showed that it was issued in 1929.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, concurrent findings are not ordinarily disturbed absent compelling reasons, but the Supreme Court may interfere when the findings are perverse. The Court relied on Mahesh Dattatray Thirthkar v. State of Maharashtra (2009) 11 SCC 141.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings of the first appellate court and the High Court were perverse and could be interfered with; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the trial court’s judgment.

rule.if: appeal_under_article_136 and concurrent_factual_findings and (findings_are_perverse or compelling_reasons_to_interfere)

predicates.appeal_under_article_136: A party brings an appeal to the Supreme Court under its special appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The lower appellate court and the High Court have reached the same factual conclusions.
predicates.findings_are_perverse: The lower courts’ factual conclusions disregard or misapprehend material evidence, or rest on an unsustainable inference.
predicates.compelling_reasons_to_interfere: The record presents reasons sufficiently strong to justify disturbing the concurrent findings.

members.legal_issue: The extraordinary criminal appellate jurisdiction permits interference when a judgment has caused grave injustice through material procedural unfairness or the misreading or unjustified disregard of important evidence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a conviction affirmed by the High Court.
The High Court’s treatment of the defence witness and medical evidence contained errors that prejudiced the accused and contributed to a miscarriage of justice.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court does not act as a general court of review or correct every error in a criminal case. It may intervene where the trial involved material illegality, procedural unfairness, or the judgment caused a miscarriage of justice by misreading or unjustifiably ignoring important evidence or relevant circumstances; the power is intended to be exercised where grave injustice is shown. No earlier case is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The case warranted interference under the extraordinary appellate jurisdiction because grave injustice had occurred.

rule.if: criminal_special_leave_appeal and (material_evidence_misread or important_evidence_ignored or procedural_unfairness) and grave_injustice

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The case is a criminal appeal seeking special leave to challenge a lower court judgment.
predicates.material_evidence_misread: The challenged judgment materially misreads important evidence.
predicates.important_evidence_ignored: The challenged judgment unjustifiably disregards important evidence or relevant circumstances.
predicates.procedural_unfairness: The proceedings involve material procedural illegality or unfairness to the accused.
predicates.grave_injustice: The errors or unfairness result in grave injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may examine the record closely in a death-sentence appeal when a serious claim of miscarriage of justice based on medical evidence is raised.
material_facts: The appeal challenged convictions that included death sentences and alleged a grave miscarriage of justice because the medical evidence supposedly conflicted with the eyewitness testimony.
The Supreme Court examined the record and found no support for that alleged conflict.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court does not ordinarily review the record in this manner, but it may examine it with anxious care in a criminal appeal involving a death sentence when a serious claim of miscarriage of justice is raised. No earlier case is cited for this statement.
members.conclusion: The Court examined the record with anxious care and found no ground to interfere on the asserted basis.

predicates.appeal_under_special_leave: The matter is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.death_sentence_at_issue: A death sentence is under challenge in the appeal.
predicates.serious_miscarriage_claim_based_on_evide: The appellant alleges a grave miscarriage of justice based on an asserted evidentiary conflict.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent convictions when material evidence has been misread or overlooked and the resulting findings are perverse or cause a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeal challenged convictions affirmed by the High Court.

The prosecution witnesses gave materially inconsistent accounts of who inflicted the fatal injury, and the courts below had treated their accounts as corroborative without addressing those inconsistencies.
The Supreme Court reappreciated the evidence and found that the convictions had been recorded while overlooking material contradictions.
members.legal_principle: Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure concerns appeals from convictions. Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not reassess evidence merely to reach a fresh view on guilt, it may interfere where evidence has been improperly received or rejected, vital evidence has been misread, or important points favouring the accused have been overlooked; see Saravanabhavan v. State of Madras. Where a High Court's factual finding is perverse and has caused a miscarriage of justice, the Supreme Court may hear the appeal on the evidence; see Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Under Article 136 of the Constitution, concurrent findings may be disturbed when perverse, and the Supreme Court may reappreciate evidence where the courts below have failed to assess it properly; see Ashoksinh Jayendrasinh v. State of Gujarat and Mahesh Dattatray Thirthkar v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court was entitled to reappraise the evidence, set aside the concurrent convictions, and acquit the appellants.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and concurrent_conviction_findings and material_evidence_overlooked and resulting_findings_perverse

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.concurrent_conviction_findings: The trial court convicted the accused and the appellate court affirmed that conviction.
predicates.material_evidence_overlooked: The courts below failed to take account of significant evidence or contradictions bearing on the accused's guilt.
predicates.resulting_findings_perverse: The findings of guilt are unreasonable in light of the evidence that was overlooked or misread.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may examine the merits despite concurrent factual findings when the lower courts have committed a substantial legal error that misapplies the governing law and risks grave injustice.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court both dismissed the owners’ eviction claim.
The lower courts misinterpreted the meaning of reasonable requirement and own occupation and failed to consider material evidence supporting the owners’ need.
The owners appealed by special leave, and the Supreme Court found that the legal misdirection had led to substantial injustice.
members.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact, it may do so in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 where the lower courts have made a substantial and patent error of law, misapplied the law, overlooked essential evidence, and thereby risked grave and substantial injustice.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court examined the merits and set aside the lower courts’ decisions because their substantial legal error warranted interference despite concurrent findings.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_findings and substantial_legal_error and material_evidence_overlooked and grave_injustice_risked

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: A party brought a special leave appeal challenging concurrent decisions of lower courts.
predicates.substantial_legal_error: The lower courts made a substantial legal error in interpreting or applying the governing law.
predicates.material_evidence_overlooked: The lower courts failed to consider evidence essential to deciding the dispute.
predicates.grave_injustice_risked: The legal error and omission of evidence risked causing grave and substantial injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere in a criminal appeal under its exceptional appellate jurisdiction when concurrent findings of guilt result in a grave miscarriage of justice through misreading or disregard of material evidence.
material_facts: The appellant appealed by special leave from a conviction affirmed by the High Court.
The courts below convicted the appellant despite evidence that the Supreme Court found insufficient and despite material evidence undermining the prosecution case.
The prosecution case against the appellant depended on circumstantial evidence, including testimony the Supreme Court found too infirm to safely rely on.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers a wide, overriding power that is ordinarily exercised sparingly in criminal appeals. The Court may intervene to further justice when a judgment has caused a grave miscarriage of justice through a misapprehension or mistake in reading the evidence, or by ignoring material evidence.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that it should not interfere with the concurrent findings, set aside the conviction, and acquitted the appellant.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the appellate court both found the accused guilty.
predicates.grave_miscarriage_from_misreading_or_ign: The findings resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice because material evidence was misread or ignored.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere in an appeal by special leave with concurrent factual findings when the findings are manifestly perverse and fail to address important circumstances that undermine the prosecution case.
material_facts: The Sessions Court and High Court had both found the appellants guilty.
The High Court largely affirmed the trial court’s findings without adequately analysing important evidence and circumstances.
The High Court failed properly to consider the serious unexplained injuries to an accused and misapplied the principles governing that omission.
The Supreme Court found that the overlooked circumstances materially undermined the prosecution case and made the High Court’s judgment manifestly perverse.
members.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court does not normally interfere in an appeal by special leave with concurrent findings of fact, it may do so in special circumstances where the judgment under appeal is manifestly perverse, important circumstances have not been considered, or the court below has committed an error of law in appreciating material evidence.
members.conclusion: The exceptional circumstances justified interference with the concurrent findings; the appeals were allowed, the convictions and sentences were set aside, and the appellants were acquitted.

predicates.appeal_by_special_leave_against_concurre: The appeal by special leave challenges factual findings made concurrently by the trial court and the appellate court.
predicates.findings_were_manifestly_perverse: The findings under challenge were manifestly perverse in light of the evidence and circumstances.
predicates.important_material_circumstances_were_ov: The court below failed to consider important circumstances bearing on the reliability of the prosecution case.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings in an appeal when those findings are perverse or result from erroneous appreciation of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court had both convicted the appellant.
The High Court had not properly appreciated the oral evidence, other evidence, and the appellant’s challenges to the prosecution case.
The Supreme Court found the lower courts’ findings perverse and their appreciation of the evidence improper.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court ordinarily does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact unless they are shown to be perverse. It may review the evidence where its appreciation is erroneous. The Court relied on Mahesh Dattatray Thirthkar v. State of Maharashtra, (2009) 11 SCC 141.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court interfered with the concurrent findings and set aside the conviction.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_from_concurrent_: A party brought an appeal to the Supreme Court challenging factual findings reached by both lower courts.
predicates.findings_are_perverse_or_based_on_errone: The Supreme Court found that the concurrent findings were perverse or resulted from erroneous appreciation of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent civil findings that rest on unsupported assumptions and inferences rather than evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court found fraud, collusion, and lack of bona fide purchase based on inferences from the speed and circumstances of the transaction.

The courts did not adequately consider material evidence, including the payment made directly to the testator, the grounds on which probate was revoked, and evidence concerning the heirs’ knowledge and conduct.
The findings of fraud or collusion against the purchaser lacked supporting pleadings and particulars.
members.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent civil findings in special-leave appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, it may review an inferential process where the conclusions rest on assumptions or circumstances offering no direct or positive support, or where relevant evidence has been ignored. Inferences must reflect the realistic diversity of the facts rather than dead uniformity. The Court applied this principle in reviewing the lower courts’ findings.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court reviewed and set aside the concurrent findings because their inferential basis was unsupported and material circumstances had been overlooked.

predicates.special_leave_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_findings_rest_on_unsupported_: The lower courts reached concurrent findings through assumptions or inferences that lack evidentiary support.
predicates.material_evidence_was_ignored: The lower courts failed to consider material evidence relevant to their findings.
predicates.supreme_court_may_interfere_with_concurr: The Supreme Court may review and set aside the concurrent findings.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may intervene under Article 136 despite concurrent findings of fact when essential facts required to support those findings were not found and manifest injustice is shown.
material_facts: The trial court, first appellate court and High Court concurrently found that sub-tenancy had been proved.
No court found that the alleged sub-tenant had exclusive possession of any part of the premises or that the tenant had relinquished control.
The appellant challenged the concurrent findings in an appeal by special leave and demonstrated that essential ingredients of sub-tenancy had not been established.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution of India confers a jurisdiction normally exercised sparingly in relation to concurrent findings of fact. However, where essential ingredients necessary to support a finding have not been found and the appellant discharges the burden of showing manifest injustice, the Court may—and has a duty to—remedy the injustice. The Court relied on M/s Variety Emporium v. V.R.M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina and also referred to Smt. Krishnawati v. Shri Hans Raj on the ordinary restraint concerning concurrent findings.
members.conclusion: The Court was entitled and required to examine and remedy the injustice despite the concurrent findings, and it set aside those findings.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_against_concurrent_: The proceeding is an appeal by special leave challenging concurrent factual findings of lower courts or tribunals.
predicates.essential_facts_not_found: The lower courts or tribunals did not find facts that are essential to support the conclusion they reached.
predicates.manifest_injustice_shown: The appellant demonstrates that the concurrent decision is manifestly unjust.
predicates.supreme_court_must_review_and_remedy_inj: The Supreme Court must examine the decision and remedy the injustice.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings that are manifestly perverse or unsupported by the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that an earlier oral gift had been made, although the written instrument described the alleged donor as remaining owner in possession and the record did not support the finding.

The lower courts inferred that the alleged donee had possession, but the evidence, including residence records, rent receipts, mutation records and title documents, did not support actual or constructive possession.
The Supreme Court scrutinized the evidence and rejected the concurrent findings as contrary to the record.
members.legal_principle: In exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court can interfere with concurrent findings of fact when the conclusions are manifestly perverse or unsupported by the evidence. The Court relied on Alamelu v. State, Heinz India (P) Ltd. v. State of U.P., and Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sarla Vishwanath Agrawal.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court was entitled to reassess and interfere with the concurrent factual findings because they were manifestly unsupported by the evidence.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_challenges_concurre: A special leave appeal challenges factual findings made by both lower courts.
predicates.findings_are_manifestly_perverse_or_unsu: The concurrent findings are manifestly perverse or lack support in the evidence.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to a deceased person is not, by itself, a reason to discard the witness’s testimony.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses were related to the deceased, and one eyewitness was injured in the occurrence.
The High Court found the witnesses’ presence at the scene established and their accounts trustworthy and corroborative.
The Court held that their relationships to the deceased did not justify rejecting their evidence.
members.legal_principle: A witness’s relationship to a deceased person, by itself, is not a sufficient ground for rejecting testimony. The Court considered the witnesses’ presence, the circumstances of the occurrence, and the reliability of their accounts; it cited no earlier case by name for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationships to the deceased were not a ground to discard their testimony.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_eyewitnesses: The criminal proceeding relies on eyewitness testimony to establish the occurrence.
predicates.witnesses_were_related_to_deceased: The eyewitnesses were related to a person who died in the occurrence.
