predicates.witnesses_were_natural_and_credible: The witnesses’ presence was natural in the circumstances and their testimony was found credible.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the victim does not, by itself, make the witness an interested witness.
material_facts: The witness was the deceased’s wife and was present with him when the attack occurred.
She was the only eyewitness and a natural witness in the circumstances.
A land dispute existed between the deceased’s family and the accused, but the court found no interest on the witness’s part in protecting the real culprit or falsely implicating the accused.
members.legal_principle: A witness is not interested simply because the witness is related to a party or victim. A witness is interested when the witness derives some benefit from the outcome, such as a civil decree or seeing an accused punished. A natural witness who is the only possible eyewitness is not, for that reason, interested. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The witness could not be treated as interested merely because she was related to the deceased.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and witness_is_related_to_victim and witness_is_natural_sole_eyewitness and not witness_derives_benefit_from_conviction

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which witness evidence is assessed.
predicates.witness_is_related_to_victim: The witness is related to the person who was harmed or killed.
predicates.witness_is_natural_sole_eyewitness: The witness was naturally present in the circumstances and was the only eyewitness.
predicates.witness_derives_benefit_from_conviction: The witness would derive a benefit from the outcome, such as a civil decree or the punishment of the accused.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s close relationship to the victim does not, without more, make the witness interested or justify rejecting the testimony.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were the deceased’s son and wife, and both were injured during the occurrence.
Their presence at the scene was natural, and the Court found their statements consistent, reliable, and supported by the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Dharnidhar v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2010) 7 SCC 759, Jayabalan v. Union Territory of Pondicherry (2010) 1 SCC 199, Ram Bharosey v. State of U.P., AIR 1954 SC 704, Mano Dutt v. State of U.P. (2012) 3 SCALE 219, and Satbir Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2009) 13 SCC 790, related or interested testimony must be assessed carefully but cannot be discarded merely because of the witness’s relationship. The relevant concern is whether the witness is unfairly motivated to falsely implicate the accused and whether the testimony is credible.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the witnesses’ relationship to the deceased made their testimony unworthy of belief.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and witness_related_to_victim and witness_presence_natural and witness_testimony_credible

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.witness_related_to_victim: A witness is closely related to the victim.
predicates.witness_presence_natural: The witness’s presence at the occurrence is natural in the circumstances.
predicates.witness_testimony_credible: The court finds the witness’s testimony credible.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s status as a next-door neighbour does not, by itself, justify rejecting the witness’s testimony.
material_facts: Witnesses gave oral evidence that the accused and his brother cultivated the land from which the stored foodgrains came.
The trial and appellate courts rejected the oral evidence as unreliable because the witnesses were next-door neighbours and were considered interested in the accused.
The Supreme Court found no adequate reason for rejection and stated that such testimony could be rejected only if something was intrinsically wrong with it.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the evidentiary principle that a witness’s proximity to a party does not alone make the witness’s testimony unreliable; the testimony may be rejected on that basis only where it is intrinsically flawed. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ testimony could not properly be rejected merely because they were next-door neighbours; there had to be something intrinsically wrong with the evidence.

predicates.criminal_case_evaluating_defence_testimo: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the court evaluates testimony offered in support of the defence.
predicates.witness_is_next_door_neighbour: The witness lives next door to the person whose defence the testimony supports.
predicates.testimony_has_no_intrinsic_flaw: The testimony has no intrinsic defect identified by the court.
predicates.testimony_not_rejected_solely_for_neighb: The testimony is not rejected solely because the witness is a neighbour.

members.legal_issue: Evidence from an interested witness is not inherently unreliable, and corroboration is not invariably required if the testimony remains convincing after careful scrutiny.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses were related to the deceased or otherwise said to be interested, and there was enmity between the families.
The Supreme Court scrutinized their evidence and found the testimony of the eyewitness and the supporting witnesses acceptable.
The eyewitness account was also supported by the evidence of witnesses who saw the accused leave with weapons and by other circumstances.
members.legal_principle: As stated in Raju @ Balachandran & Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2012) 12 SCC 701, interested-witness evidence must be carefully scrutinized. Such evidence is not infirm merely because of the witness’s interest, and corroboration is a matter of prudence rather than an absolute requirement where the testimony is intrinsically good.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship or interest did not make their evidence inadmissible or unusable; the evidence could be relied upon after careful scrutiny, with corroboration available in this case.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding and witness_has_interest_in_outcome and testimony_survives_careful_scrutiny and testimony_is_intrinsically_reliable

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which witness testimony is being assessed.
predicates.witness_has_interest_in_outcome: The witness has a relationship, stake, or enmity that may give the witness an interest in the outcome.
predicates.testimony_survives_careful_scrutiny: The court has closely examined the witness’s testimony and found it credible despite the claimed interest.
predicates.testimony_is_intrinsically_reliable: The testimony is convincing in itself and is not rendered unreliable by its content or circumstances.

members.legal_issue: The relationship of eyewitnesses to the deceased and their questionable antecedents do not justify rejecting their testimony wholesale.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses were related to the deceased and had questionable antecedents.
They lived with the deceased in the same hamlet, and their presence with him at the time and place of the occurrence was probable.
The appellate court rejected their evidence wholesale instead of assessing the role attributed to each accused.
members.legal_principle: Related or interested witnesses and witnesses with questionable antecedents are not necessarily untruthful. Their evidence must be examined with more than ordinary care and circumspection, including by considering the role attributed to each accused and whether surrounding circumstances provide assurance. No earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship to the deceased and their antecedents were not valid grounds, by themselves, for rejecting their evidence; their testimony required careful scrutiny, with credible parts accepted and unreliable parts rejected.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution relies on eyewitness testimony.
predicates.eyewitnesses_related: The eyewitnesses are related to the deceased.
predicates.witnesses_have_questionable_antecedents: The eyewitnesses have antecedents of a questionable nature.

members.legal_issue: The fact that prosecution witnesses are close relatives of the deceased does not, by itself, justify rejecting their testimony.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the testimony of witnesses who were related to the deceased because of that relationship.
The witnesses described the events at the scene and the deceased’s immediate identification of the person who poured acid on him.
The Supreme Court found no cogent reason to disbelieve the witnesses’ accounts.
members.legal_principle: Close relatives of a deceased person would normally be reluctant to spare the real assailant and falsely identify another person; relationship alone is therefore not a sufficient reason to disbelieve their testimony. The judgment does not rely on a cited statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The trial court was wrong to reject the witnesses’ evidence merely because they were related to the deceased.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which witness testimony is relied on to establish responsibility for an offence.
predicates.close_relative_witnesses: One or more witnesses whose testimony is relied on are close relatives of the deceased person.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_to_disbelieve: The evidence discloses no cogent reason, apart from the witnesses’ relationship, to disbelieve their testimony.

members.legal_issue: Evidence from a relative who witnessed the incident cannot be rejected merely because of the witness’s relationship to the deceased.
material_facts: The principal eyewitnesses were the deceased’s brother and widow, who were present near the incident.
Their accounts described the accused brothers attacking the deceased with spades.
The High Court accepted their evidence, and the Supreme Court found no basis to reject it solely because they were related to the deceased.
members.legal_principle: Once the prosecution proves its case through admissible and cogent evidence, the evidence is not to be brushed aside merely because the witnesses are relatives. A close relative who is a natural witness is not necessarily an interested witness; “interested” requires a direct interest in securing conviction because of animus or another reason. The Court relied on Anwar Ali v. State of U.P. (2011) 15 SCC 360, Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar (1996) 1 SCC 614, and Ashok Rai v. State of U.P. (2014) 5 SCC 713.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness accounts could not be discarded merely because the witnesses were close relatives of the deceased.

predicates.criminal_case_with_eyewitness_testimony: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution relies on eyewitness testimony.
predicates.witness_is_relative_of_deceased: A person who witnessed the incident is related to the deceased.
predicates.eyewitness_account_is_cogent: The eyewitness gives admissible and credible evidence describing the incident.

members.legal_issue: Eyewitness testimony cannot be rejected solely because the witnesses are related to the deceased, and their failure to intervene does not by itself make their evidence unnatural when they were unarmed and threatened.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were close relatives of the deceased and were also related to the accused.
There was no evidence that the witnesses were hostile to the accused or had a reason to falsely implicate them.
The witnesses were unarmed while the assailants had weapons, and the witnesses were threatened with death if they raised an alarm or intervened.
One witness was in an advanced stage of pregnancy, and the court found her presence at the scene plausible in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Related witnesses' evidence cannot be rejected solely because of their relationship to the deceased. The court must assess the evidence in its circumstances; a threat and the instinct of self-preservation can explain why unarmed witnesses do not intervene. No earlier case was relied on for these principles.
members.conclusion: The witnesses' relationship to the deceased, the pregnant witness's presence, and the witnesses' failure to intervene did not justify rejecting their evidence.

rule.if: murder_trial and eyewitnesses_related_to_deceased and no_evidence_of_false_implication and witnesses_unarmed_and_threatened

predicates.murder_trial: The proceeding is a trial for murder.
predicates.eyewitnesses_related_to_deceased: The eyewitnesses are related to the deceased.
predicates.no_evidence_of_false_implication: There is no evidence that the eyewitnesses were hostile to the accused or had a reason to falsely implicate them.
predicates.witnesses_unarmed_and_threatened: The witnesses were unarmed and were threatened if they intervened or raised an alarm.

members.legal_issue: Relationship to the deceased or an alleged motive to support the prosecution does not by itself justify rejecting eyewitness testimony that inspires confidence after cautious assessment.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were relatives of the deceased, and one was also related to a person with whom the accused had a civil dispute.
The witnesses gave categorical accounts of the shooting and were subjected to lengthy cross-examination, which did not elicit anything that undermined their creditworthiness.

Their presence with the deceased was natural in the circumstances, and another witness who was independent of both sides also gave evidence about seeing the accused with a gun and fleeing after the shot.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled principle that a witness’s relationship to a party is not, by itself, a ground for disbelieving the witness. The testimony must instead be examined with caution to determine whether it inspires confidence. No earlier case was named in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the related eyewitnesses at the threshold because of their relationship and alleged interest; their testimony had to be assessed with caution and could be relied upon because it inspired confidence.

rule.if: criminal_trial_testimony and eyewitness_related_to_deceased and testimony_survives_cross_examination and testimony_inspires_confidence

predicates.criminal_trial_testimony: The evidence is testimony given by an eyewitness in a criminal trial.
predicates.eyewitness_related_to_deceased: The eyewitness is related to the deceased or has a relationship that may create an interest in the prosecution outcome.
predicates.testimony_survives_cross_examination: Cross-examination does not elicit material that undermines the eyewitness’s creditworthiness.
predicates.testimony_inspires_confidence: After cautious assessment, the eyewitness’s testimony is found credible.

members.legal_issue: Testimony from a witness related to the victim is not inherently unreliable or liable to be rejected solely because of that relationship.
material_facts: The two eyewitnesses whose testimony the court accepted were the victim’s son and wife, and their presence at the scene was natural because the incident occurred outside their home in the morning.
Their accounts were consistent, cogent, and reliable, and the defence did not establish a motive to falsely implicate the accused.
members.legal_principle: A related witness is not necessarily an interested witness. A witness is interested when the witness has a benefit or direct or indirect interest in the outcome, such as a motive arising from enmity to secure punishment by false implication. The court should cautiously assess a related witness’s testimony for reliability, probability, cogency, and consistency, but should not treat it as inherently tainted. The court relied on State of Rajasthan v. Kalki, (1981) 2 SCC 752; Amit v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2012) 4 SCC 107; Gangabhavani v. Rayapati Venkat Reddy, (2013) 15 SCC 298; Ganapathi v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2018) 5 SCC 549; Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, 1954 SCR 145; and Jayabalan v. Union Territory of Pondicherry, (2010) 1 SCC 199.
members.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ testimony could not be disbelieved merely because they were close relatives of the victim.

rule.if: criminal_case and witness_is_related and witness_presence_is_natural and testimony_is_reliable and not evidence_of_motive_to_falsely_implicate

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the determination of criminal liability.
predicates.witness_is_related: The witness is related to the victim.
predicates.witness_presence_is_natural: The circumstances explain why the witness was naturally present at the scene.
predicates.testimony_is_reliable: The witness’s testimony is consistent, cogent, and reliable on the material events.
predicates.evidence_of_motive_to_falsely_implicate: Evidence shows that the witness had a motive to falsely implicate the accused.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the party who called the witness, or possible prejudice against the opposing party, does not by itself justify rejecting the witness’s evidence.
material_facts: The High Court substantially rejected witnesses supporting the adoption because they were related to the appellant or were said to be out of favour with the opposing side.
The trial court had assessed their testimony in the context of the evidence as a whole and had the opportunity to observe their demeanour.
members.legal_principle: A court must exercise appropriate caution when assessing a witness who is related to the party calling the witness or may be prejudiced against the opposing party, and must evaluate the evidence against the entire mosaic of facts. It is not open to reject the evidence on relationship, favour, or possible prejudice alone. The Court also said due consideration was owed to the trial court’s opportunity to observe the witnesses.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s relationship-based approach to credibility was erroneous; the evidence had to be assessed cautiously against the entire record rather than rejected on relationship or possible prejudice alone.

predicates.witness_credibility_assessment: The court is assessing the credibility and probative value of a witness’s testimony.
predicates.witness_related_to_calling_party_or_poss: The witness is related to the party calling the witness or may be prejudiced against the opposing party.
predicates.no_independent_reason_for_rejection: There is no reason for rejecting the testimony beyond the witness’s relationship, favour, or possible prejudice.

members.legal_issue: The testimony of eyewitnesses who are related to the deceased is not to be rejected solely because of that relationship or because independent eyewitnesses were not examined.
material_facts: Several eyewitnesses were close relatives of the deceased.
Their presence at the scene was natural in light of the time and place of the incident.
Their accounts corroborated one another in material particulars, and cross-examination disclosed no material infirmity in the principal account.
The defence argued that the witnesses should not be believed because they were related to the deceased and independent eyewitnesses had not been examined.
members.legal_principle: Related eyewitness testimony cannot be discarded merely because of the witnesses’ relationship to the deceased. The court must be on guard and scrutinize such testimony closely. The judgment invokes this as a settled principle but names no earlier case or statutory provision for it.
members.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ evidence could safely be relied upon despite their relationship to the deceased.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_after_acquittal_reversal and eyewitnesses_are_related_to_deceased and eyewitnesses_were_naturally_present and accounts_are_materially_corroborated and cross_examination_revealed_no_material_infirmity

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal_reversal: The accused brought a criminal appeal after an appellate court reversed their acquittal.
predicates.eyewitnesses_are_related_to_deceased: The eyewitnesses were close relatives of the deceased.
predicates.eyewitnesses_were_naturally_present: The circumstances of the time and place made the eyewitnesses’ presence at the scene natural.
predicates.accounts_are_materially_corroborated: The eyewitnesses’ accounts supported one another on material particulars.
predicates.cross_examination_revealed_no_material_i: Cross-examination did not reveal a material infirmity in the eyewitnesses’ account.

members.legal_issue: A witness's interest in the case does not, by itself, make the witness's testimony unsafe to accept when the testimony is consistent and corroborated.
material_facts: The principal eyewitness was cultivating the injured person's land as a tenant and was regarded by the High Court as having an interest in the outcome.
His account of seeing the assault was consistent and was corroborated by other witnesses and the injured person's statement.
His conduct in taking the injured person to the police station supported his stated concern for her.
members.legal_principle: A witness's interest in the outcome is a factor in assessing credibility, but it does not alone justify rejecting testimony that is consistent and corroborated. The Court applied this principle in assessing the evidence; no earlier case was cited for it.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that there was no adequate basis to reject the eyewitness's testimony merely because he was the injured person's tenant.

predicates.criminal_case_relies_on_interested_witne: The prosecution relied on testimony from a witness who had an interest in the outcome of the case.
predicates.testimony_is_consistent: The witness's account remained consistent on material aspects.
predicates.testimony_is_corroborated: Other evidence supported material parts of the witness's account.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the victim does not, by itself, make the witness’s testimony unreliable, particularly where the witness was naturally present or injured and the testimony is supported by other evidence.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses were members of the deceased’s family and were present in the house at the time of the nighttime attack.
Two of the principal witnesses had been injured, and witnesses identified the appellant during the incident.
Medical and other evidence supported the account of the attack and the injuries.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the credibility of the witnesses in light of their natural presence, the injuries suffered by two of them, the consistency of their accounts under cross-examination, and corroboration from medical and other evidence. It stated that relationship alone is not a sufficient ground to discard testimony; no specific earlier case was cited for this proposition in the Court’s discussion.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ close relationship to the deceased did not justify rejecting their testimony; their presence and accounts were credible in light of their injuries and the corroborating evidence.

rule.if: criminal_trial and eyewitness_related_to_victim and (eyewitness_injured or presence_at_scene_natural) and testimony_corroborated

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.eyewitness_related_to_victim: An eyewitness is related to the victim.
predicates.eyewitness_injured: The eyewitness sustained injuries during the incident.
predicates.presence_at_scene_natural: The eyewitness’s presence at the scene is natural in the circumstances.
predicates.testimony_corroborated: Other evidence supports the eyewitness’s testimony.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot reject a witness’s testimony solely because the witness is related to the party who called the witness or may be prejudiced against the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellate court substantially rejected the testimony of witnesses because they were related to the claimant or were said to be out of favour with the opposing side.
The trial court had considered the witnesses’ testimony in light of the surrounding circumstances and the full body of evidence.
The appellate court did not give adequate weight to the nature and probability of the evidence in the context of the record as a whole.
members.legal_principle: A witness’s relationship to the party producing the witness, or possible prejudice against the opposing party, calls for appropriate caution in assessing probative value. It does not, by itself, justify rejecting the testimony; the evidence must be considered in the context of the entire mosaic of facts on the record.
members.conclusion: Relationship or possible prejudice alone did not justify rejecting the witnesses’ testimony; it had to be assessed cautiously against the entire record.

predicates.witness_relationship_or_possible_prejudi: A witness was related to the party who called the witness or could be prejudiced against the opposing party.
predicates.evidence_assessable_in_record_context: The witness’s testimony could be assessed alongside the other evidence and surrounding circumstances in the case.

members.legal_issue: A witness's relationship to the deceased does not by itself make the witness unreliable when the witness was naturally present, was injured in the incident, and is corroborated by other eyewitnesses.
material_facts: The deceased's wife testified that she saw the accused assault him near their home after she heard her daughter shout.
She had injuries from the same occurrence, which were supported by medical evidence.
Two other witnesses whose presence was found natural supported her account on material particulars.
The Court found no cogent reason for the witnesses to falsely implicate the accused while leaving the real culprits unnamed.
members.legal_principle: A witness is not to be rejected merely because the witness is related to the deceased or may be interested. Natural presence, injury corroboration, support from other witnesses, and the absence of a reason to falsely implicate the accused may support reliance on the testimony. No earlier case was cited for this assessment in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court accepted the wife's testimony and found the account of the three eyewitnesses reliable.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and related_witness_naturally_present and witness_injured_in_occurrence and corroborated_by_other_eyewitnesses and no_cogent_reason_for_false_implication

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.related_witness_naturally_present: A witness related to the deceased was at a nearby home and came to the scene after hearing a commotion.
predicates.witness_injured_in_occurrence: The witness sustained injuries in the same incident, supported by medical evidence.
predicates.corroborated_by_other_eyewitnesses: Other eyewitnesses supported the witness's account on material details.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_for_false_implication: The evidence disclosed no cogent reason for the witnesses to implicate the accused falsely instead of the real culprits.

members.legal_issue: A complainant's personal grievance against an accused does not, by itself, justify rejecting the complainant's testimony.
material_facts: The complainant sought regularisation of land occupancy and alleged that the public servant demanded a bribe to assist with that process.
The complainant had a grievance because eviction proceedings concerning the occupancy were imminent.
Before paying the money, the complainant approached anti-corruption officials, who arranged a trap.
members.legal_principle: A complainant's adverse interest may call for closer scrutiny, but the testimony cannot be rejected at the threshold merely because the complainant is aggrieved by the accused. A contrary approach would risk insulating corrupt public servants from legal consequences.
members.conclusion: The complainant's grievance required careful scrutiny of the testimony but did not justify rejecting it outright; the grievance did not establish that the complaint was made only because of the eviction proceedings.

predicates.graft_complaint_case: A person alleges that a public servant sought a benefit in connection with official action.
predicates.complainant_personally_aggrieved: The complainant has a grievance arising from the public servant's conduct or the matter connected with the alleged demand.
predicates.complaint_made_before_trap_payment: The complainant reports the alleged demand to enforcement officials before making the arranged payment.

members.legal_issue: Testimony cannot be rejected solely because witnesses are relatives of the deceased.
material_facts: The two eyewitnesses were relatives of the deceased and inmates of the house, making their presence at the scene natural.
They were injured eyewitnesses, and their testimony remained unshaken in cross-examination.
The defence relied on family hostility to argue that the witnesses had falsely implicated the accused.
members.legal_principle: A witness is ordinarily treated as independent unless there is a basis to find that the witness is likely to be tainted. Relationship alone does not require rejection or corroboration of testimony, though the court must assess it carefully and examine whether a foundation exists for alleged false implication. The Court relied on Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, Guli Chand v. State of Rajasthan, Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras, Masalti v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ testimony was not liable to be discarded merely because they were relatives; the challenge to its credibility was rejected.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and witnesses_are_relatives and witnesses_were_naturally_present and testimony_is_cogent_and_credible

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.witnesses_are_relatives: The witnesses who gave the relevant testimony are related to the deceased or other persons involved.
predicates.witnesses_were_naturally_present: The witnesses were present at the scene for a reason consistent with their ordinary circumstances.
predicates.testimony_is_cogent_and_credible: The witnesses’ testimony is coherent and credible after the court assesses it, including in light of cross-examination.

members.legal_issue: Interested eyewitness testimony and the non-examination of other named witnesses do not by themselves require rejection of the eyewitness account when it withstands careful scrutiny and the other witnesses were not pursued by the defence.
material_facts: The three eyewitnesses included the deceased’s brother and witnesses connected with the deceased’s side in prior disputes.
The Supreme Court found that factional divisions made it difficult to obtain testimony from independent witnesses.
Other persons named as witnesses were tendered for cross-examination, but the defence allowed them to be discharged and did not seek their examination as court witnesses.
The defence did not seek additional evidence in the High Court, and the courts below found the eyewitness testimony truthful and trustworthy after scrutiny.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that interested or partisan testimony is not to be rejected merely on that account; the testimony must be scrutinized, and in this case it was found trustworthy. The Court also relied on the circumstances that the other witnesses were tendered for cross-examination, the defence did not pursue them or seek their examination as court witnesses, and no request for additional evidence was made.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness testimony was not unfit to be relied on merely because the witnesses were interested or partisan, and the Supreme Court found no sufficient reason to disturb the concurrent findings.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and partisan_witnesses_carefully_scrutinized and partisan_witnesses_found_trustworthy and named_witnesses_not_pursued_by_defense

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.partisan_witnesses_carefully_scrutinized: The court carefully examined the testimony of witnesses connected with one side of the dispute.
predicates.partisan_witnesses_found_trustworthy: The court found those witnesses’ account truthful and trustworthy after scrutiny.
predicates.named_witnesses_not_pursued_by_defense: Other named witnesses were made available for cross-examination, but the defence did not pursue their testimony or ask that they be examined by the court.

members.legal_issue: A witness is not disqualified as interested merely because the witness is related to the deceased when the witness was a natural observer and has no demonstrated animus against the accused.
material_facts: The assault occurred at night inside the family home, where the deceased’s wife and her mother were naturally present.
The witnesses observed the attack from close range in the light of a burning electric bulb.
There was no evidence that either witness bore animus against the accused.
The witnesses’ account was supported by evidence concerning the recent birth in the home, the electric lighting, and other circumstances.
members.legal_principle: A close relative who is a natural witness is not, for that reason alone, an interested witness; interest entails a direct motive to secure the accused’s conviction, such as animus. Partisan or related testimony is not mechanically rejected and is assessed on its reliability and circumstances. The Court relied on Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, Masalti v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Guli Chand v. State of Rajasthan, and referred to Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ testimony could not be rejected merely because they were relatives of the deceased, and the Court accepted the lower courts’ assessment of their evidence.

rule.if: criminal_evidence_case and relatives_were_natural_observers and no_proven_animus and corroborating_circumstances

predicates.criminal_evidence_case: The court is assessing witness testimony in a criminal case.
predicates.relatives_were_natural_observers: The witnesses were relatives who were naturally present and able to observe the event.
predicates.no_proven_animus: No evidence showed that the witnesses had animus or another direct motive to falsely implicate the accused.
predicates.corroborating_circumstances: Other evidence or circumstances supported material parts of the witnesses’ account.

members.legal_issue: The relationship of an eyewitness to an accused, without more, does not make the eyewitness’s testimony unreliable.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses included close relatives of the injured persons and were said to be on inimical terms with the accused because of a property dispute.
The courts below found the evidence against the appellants cogent and credible.
No adequate foundation was laid for the claim that the witnesses had falsely implicated the appellants.
members.legal_principle: A relative is not to be treated as an unreliable or partisan witness merely because of the relationship; the court must assess the evidence carefully and determine whether it is cogent and credible, and a claim of false implication requires a factual foundation. The Court relied on Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1953 SC 364; Guli Chand v. State of Rajasthan, (1974) 3 SCC 698; Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras, AIR 1957 SC 614; Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1957 SC 54; Masalti v. State of U.P., AIR 1965 SC 202; State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2407; and Lebna v. State of Haryana, (2002) 3 SCC 76.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationship to the injured persons and alleged hostility did not, by themselves, justify rejecting their testimony.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and related_eyewitnesses and credible_testimony and not substantiated_false_implication

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed against criminal convictions.
predicates.related_eyewitnesses: The prosecution relied on eyewitnesses who were related to the injured persons.
predicates.credible_testimony: The courts found the eyewitness testimony against the accused cogent and credible.
predicates.substantiated_false_implication: The accused provided a factual foundation for the claim that the witnesses falsely implicated them.
predicates.relationship_alone_does_not_discredit_te: The eyewitness testimony is not rejected solely because the eyewitnesses are related to the injured persons.

members.legal_issue: Eyewitness testimony should not be rejected merely because the witnesses are related to the victims, independent witnesses were not called, or witnesses differ about which nearby exit the assailants used.
material_facts: Several witnesses living nearby heard cries during the night, rushed to the scene, and testified that they saw the assailants fleeing, including some carrying axes.
The witnesses were relatives of the victims, and no independent witness was called.
Some witnesses differed about whether the assailants left through the eastern or western gate of the same house.
The record did not establish that an independent person who had witnessed a relevant event was left uncalled.
members.legal_principle: The natural witnesses to an incident at a dwelling may be its inmates or nearby residents, and courts should not insist on unrelated witnesses who may not have seen the event. Non-examination of an independent witness warrants adverse comment where the evidence or investigation records disclose that such a person witnessed a relevant event. Discrepancies should be assessed in light of the core evidence and broad probabilities, including the circumstances in which witnesses observed events.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the eyewitness evidence on these grounds; the discrepancy about the gate was not a material contradiction, and the witnesses’ relationship to the victims did not by itself justify rejecting their testimony.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and witnesses_rushed_to_scene_after_cries and witnesses_saw_assailants_flee and related_witnesses and no_independent_witness_shown_to_have_seen_event and discrepancy_concerned_nearby_exits

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed after the trial court convicted the defendants and the appellate court acquitted them.
predicates.witnesses_rushed_to_scene_after_cries: Nearby witnesses heard cries and went to the place from which the cries came.
predicates.witnesses_saw_assailants_flee: The witnesses testified that they saw the assailants leaving the scene.
predicates.related_witnesses: The witnesses who testified were related to the victims.
predicates.no_independent_witness_shown_to_have_see: The evidence and investigation records did not identify an independent person as having witnessed a relevant event.
predicates.discrepancy_concerned_nearby_exits: Witnesses differed about which of two nearby exits the assailants used.

members.legal_issue: The testimony of related witnesses is not rendered unreliable solely because disinterested neighbours who may have seen the occurrence were not examined.
material_facts: The witnesses who testified to the occurrence were related to, or interested in, the complainant.
The trial court and the High Court believed those witnesses.
The record did not show that anyone other than those witnesses had seen the occurrence.
The court noted that a co-accused’s petition for leave to appeal had been dismissed.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the assessment of the evidence on the facts of the case: the witnesses’ relationship or interest and the non-examination of neighbours did not, in these circumstances, make their accepted testimony unreliable. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The non-examination of neighbours did not provide a reason to reject the testimony accepted by the trial court and the High Court.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and related_witnesses_testified and lower_courts_credited_witnesses and no_other_eyewitnesses_identified and neighbours_not_examined

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.related_witnesses_testified: Witnesses who were related to or interested in the complainant testified about the occurrence.
predicates.lower_courts_credited_witnesses: The trial court and the appellate court accepted the testimony of those witnesses.
predicates.no_other_eyewitnesses_identified: The record did not identify other people who had seen the occurrence.
predicates.neighbours_not_examined: Neighbours who may have seen the occurrence were not examined as witnesses.

members.legal_issue: Witnesses’ alignment with a complainant’s group and existing enmity do not, by themselves, require rejection of their evidence when it is credible and corroborated by other evidence.
material_facts: There was longstanding factional enmity between the groups, and some eyewitnesses belonged to the complainant’s group.
The court found no intrinsic discrepancies in the eyewitness evidence and considered it supported by other evidence, including the nature of the injuries.
One eyewitness was treated as an independent and reliable witness, and another witness who appeared partisan was closely scrutinised rather than rejected solely for that reason.
The trial court’s concerns about the report’s timing and the nature and location of the injuries were rejected by the High Court after it assessed the evidence.
members.legal_principle: In assessing evidence in a criminal prosecution, enmity alone does not establish false implication. A witness’s partisan association is a reason for close scrutiny, not automatic rejection; the evidence may be relied on when it inspires confidence and is corroborated by other evidence, including the nature of the injuries. The Court applied Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code to the conviction but cited no earlier case for this evidentiary principle.
members.conclusion: The eyewitness evidence was not liable to be rejected merely because of enmity or the witnesses’ partisan association, and the evidence supported maintaining the conviction.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and prior_enmity and partisan_witnesses and testimony_confident and corroborated_evidence

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The evidence was assessed in a criminal prosecution relying on eyewitness testimony.
predicates.prior_enmity: The accused’s group and the complainant’s group had existing enmity.
predicates.partisan_witnesses: Some eyewitnesses belonged to the complainant’s group or otherwise appeared partisan.
predicates.testimony_confident: The eyewitness testimony inspired confidence and had no intrinsic discrepancies.
predicates.corroborated_evidence: Other evidence, including the nature of the injuries, supported the eyewitness account.
predicates.partisan_testimony_not_rejected_solely_f: The eyewitness testimony is not rejected solely because the witnesses were aligned with one side.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the victim or interest in the prosecution does not, by itself, justify rejecting the witness’s testimony.
material_facts: Two principal eyewitnesses were members of the victims’ families, and one of them was seriously injured during the incident.
The eyewitness accounts were consistent with one another.
The High Court rejected the eyewitnesses’ evidence because it considered them interested witnesses, without properly assessing their testimony.
members.legal_principle: An interested eyewitness’s testimony is not to be rejected solely because of the witness’s interest; the court may exercise caution and make a reasonable discount when assessing it. The circumstances of an injured eyewitness’s presence and the consistency of the accounts are relevant to evaluating reliability. The Court relied on no named earlier cases or specific statutory provisions for this principle.
members.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ evidence could not be rejected merely because they were interested; the court could assess it cautiously and allow a reasonable discount if required. The consistent evidence, particularly that of the injured eyewitness, was reliable and sufficient to implicate the accused.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and (eyewitnesses_are_interested or eyewitness_is_related_to_victim) and eyewitness_accounts_are_consistent and injured_eyewitness_supports_account

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed after an appellate court acquitted the accused.
predicates.eyewitnesses_are_interested: One or more eyewitnesses had an interest in the prosecution because of their connection to the victims.
predicates.eyewitness_is_related_to_victim: One or more eyewitnesses were members of the victims’ families.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_are_consistent: The eyewitnesses gave accounts that were consistent with one another.
predicates.injured_eyewitness_supports_account: An eyewitness was injured in the incident and supported the account of the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s interest in the case does not by itself make the witness’s testimony unreliable or require the court to reject it.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses challenged on the ground of interest were the deceased children’s mother and the injured man’s wife.
The prosecution relied on their accounts of the incident, and the defence argued that their relationship to the deceased made their testimony unworthy of consideration.
members.legal_principle: Interested witnesses’ testimony is not automatically disqualified, and a witness’s interest alone does not establish a willingness to spare the real culprit and frame an innocent person. The Court relied on Mohd. Ishaque v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The argument that the testimony should not be considered because the witnesses were interested had no merit; such testimony can carry substantial importance and weight.

predicates.criminal_case: The testimony is being assessed in a criminal case.
predicates.witness_is_interested: The witness has a personal or relational interest in the case.

members.legal_issue: Testimony of a related witness is not unreliable merely because of the witness’s relationship to the deceased.
material_facts: Two witnesses returning from a village gathering said they saw the accused attack the deceased in the courtyard, using the light of their torches.
The witnesses’ presence on the route was consistent with their attendance at the gathering, and their accounts were found credible, reliable, and corroborated.
Some witnesses were related to the deceased or to the person who reported the incident, but the court found no material contradictions in their testimony.
members.legal_principle: Under Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, a witness is ordinarily considered independent unless there is reason to believe the witness is tainted; relationship alone is not a basis to reject testimony. State of A.P. v. S. Rayappa, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Kishanpal, and Darya Singh v. State of Punjab affirm that a related witness is not necessarily an interested witness, and credible testimony from such a witness need not invariably be corroborated. The court must assess the evidence on the facts of the case.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ testimony could be relied on; their relationships to the deceased did not, by themselves, justify rejecting it.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and related_witnesses_testified and witnesses_had_natural_presence and testimony_was_credible and not material_contradictions

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding was a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.related_witnesses_testified: Witnesses who were related to the deceased or another person connected with the case gave evidence.
predicates.witnesses_had_natural_presence: The circumstances gave the witnesses a natural reason to be at the place where they observed the occurrence.
predicates.testimony_was_credible: The court found the witnesses’ accounts reliable and supported by other evidence.
predicates.material_contradictions: The witnesses’ accounts contained contradictions that materially undermined the prosecution’s case.

members.legal_issue: Natural witnesses should not be rejected merely because they are related to the victims, and minor discrepancies about events in a confused escape do not justify rejecting otherwise reliable testimony.
material_facts: The witnesses lived in or near the dwelling and said they rushed to the scene after hearing cries in the night.
They testified that they saw the accused fleeing, with two carrying axes and others carrying lathis.
Some witnesses differed about whether the assailants left through the western or eastern gate of the same house.
The prosecution did not examine other local residents, but no evidence showed that an unexamined independent person had witnessed the events.
members.legal_principle: Courts should assess testimony by its substance and broad probabilities. In an incident at a dwelling, its inmates and nearby residents may be the natural witnesses; courts should not insist on outsiders who may not have seen anything. Non-examination of another person warrants criticism when the evidence or investigation records indicate that person witnessed a relevant event. A discrepancy about the precise exit gate amid a nighttime commotion is not, by itself, a material contradiction.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to reject the witnesses’ testimony because they were related to the deceased, because other local residents were not called, or because of the discrepancy about the gate used.

rule.if: witnesses_were_natural_observers and witnesses_arrived_after_hearing_distress and discrepancy_concerned_precise_exit_route and no_evidence_unexamined_person_witnessed_event

predicates.witnesses_were_natural_observers: The witnesses were inmates of the dwelling or people living nearby who were naturally positioned to observe the event.
predicates.witnesses_arrived_after_hearing_distress: The witnesses went to the scene after hearing cries or other signs of distress.
predicates.discrepancy_concerned_precise_exit_route: The witnesses differed only about the precise route by which fleeing assailants left the scene.
predicates.no_evidence_unexamined_person_witnessed_: The evidence and investigation records did not show that another unexamined person had witnessed a relevant event.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s inimical relationship with the accused does not by itself prevent reliance on that witness’s testimony if the testimony withstands close scrutiny.
material_facts: A witness who was the deceased’s brother admitted that he was inimical to the accused.
The Supreme Court considered that witness’s testimony alongside the testimony of other eyewitnesses.
members.legal_principle: The judgment applies the principle that enmity calls for closer scrutiny of a witness’s evidence but does not, by itself, make the evidence unusable; no provision or earlier case is cited for this principle in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The witness’s admitted enmity required close scrutiny, but his testimony could be acted upon if it withstood that scrutiny.

predicates.witness_is_inimical: A witness has an inimical relationship with the accused.
predicates.testimony_survives_close_scrutiny: The court closely examines the witness’s testimony and finds that it withstands that examination.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to a victim does not, by itself, justify rejecting the witness’s testimony when the witness’s presence is natural and the testimony is credible and corroborated.
material_facts: The principal eyewitness was the son of one deceased person and the nephew of another; the injured eyewitness was the brother of two deceased persons; and another eyewitness shared land interests with the victims.
The eyewitnesses corroborated one another on material aspects, and lengthy cross-examination did not impair their credibility.
One eyewitness was injured in the incident, and the Supreme Court found no reason to doubt his presence or testimony.
members.legal_principle: There is no legal bar to examining family members or other persons known to the affected party. Related or friendly witnesses’ testimony cannot be discarded merely because of their relationship if their presence is natural and their credible, reliable testimony is corroborated. An injured witness’s evidence stands on a higher pedestal. The Court relied on Mano Dutt and Another v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2012) 4 SCC 79, and Dayal Singh and Others v. State of Uttaranchal, 2012 (7) Scale 165.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ relationships to the deceased did not justify rejecting their testimony; the High Court was justified in relying on it.

rule.if: criminal_case and witness_is_related and witness_presence_natural and testimony_credible and testimony_corroborated

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the prosecution of a person for a criminal offence.
predicates.witness_is_related: A witness is related to a victim or is otherwise known to the affected party.
predicates.witness_presence_natural: The witness’s presence at the place of the incident is natural in the circumstances.
predicates.testimony_credible: The witness’s testimony is credible and remains unimpaired after cross-examination.
predicates.testimony_corroborated: Other evidence or witnesses corroborate the witness’s testimony.

members.legal_issue: Interim protection of a claimant’s possession may be granted while a dispute over possession and title remains pending adjudication.
material_facts: The applicants sought an interim injunction to prevent interference with their claimed possession of part of the land.
The parties disputed the applicants’ claim to the land, and the underlying suit remained to be tried.
The Court declined to assess the evidence finally because doing so could prejudice a fair trial, but held that this was not a case in which interim protection should be refused.
members.legal_principle: When considering an interim injunction, a court may examine whether the applicant was at any time in lawful possession; if that is established prima facie, the opposing party may be asked to explain how the applicant was dispossessed. The court should avoid final findings on disputed evidence before trial where those findings could prejudice a fair decision. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The respondents were restrained from interfering with the applicants’ possession of the suit land pending adjudication.

predicates.interim_possession_injunction_case: The proceeding seeks an interim injunction against interference with possession while a land dispute is pending.
predicates.claimant_seeks_protection_of_possession: The claimant asks the court to protect the claimant’s possession of disputed land.
predicates.possession_dispute_remains_for_trial: The parties’ dispute about possession remains unresolved and is to be examined at trial.
predicates.interim_possession_protection_should_be_: The claimant’s possession should be protected by an interim injunction pending adjudication.

members.legal_issue: A person in established possession may obtain protection against interference by someone not shown to have a better title, even if the person's own title is not satisfactorily proved.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a permanent injunction against interference with the site.
The trial court and first appellate court found, on the evidence, that the plaintiff had possessed the site since purchasing it.
The defendant's better title to the site had not been established.
members.legal_principle: Possession is an important circumstance and may be protected against interference by a person who is not proved to have a better title. No provision or earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to the injunction protecting his possession, notwithstanding the failure to satisfactorily prove title.

predicates.injunction_suit: The proceeding seeks an injunction to prevent interference with possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_in_possession: The person seeking the injunction is found to have possessed the property.
predicates.defendant_better_title_unproved: The person accused of interference is not proved to have a better title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A claimant with a sufficiently supported prima facie claim to possession may receive temporary protection against interference even when the validity of the competing agreements and the parties’ ultimate rights remain undecided.
material_facts: The claimant relied on agreements and payments and claimed possession of the land.
The owners supported the claimant’s account of possession, and several owners filed affidavits stating that the claimant was in possession.
A court commissioner’s report following physical verification recorded that the claimant was in possession.
The competing claimants produced copies of bills and receipts for construction materials, which the trial court found did not establish their possession.
The trial court treated the claimant’s possession as permissive and granted a temporary injunction without finally resolving the validity of the competing agreements or title.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 39 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a prima facie possessory claim supported by the available material may justify temporary injunctive protection. A possessory right may suffice for that interim relief without deciding the validity of agreements or the parties’ title. No earlier cases are cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The claimant had made out a prima facie case for temporary protection of possession. The temporary injunction was restored, with directions to maintain the status quo and not create third-party rights, construct on the land, or alter its nature pending the suit.

predicates.temporary_injunction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks temporary protection against interference with a claimant’s possession.
predicates.claimant_possession_supported: The claimant’s possession is supported by material such as the opposing owners’ acknowledgments, affidavits, or a physical inspection report.
predicates.opposing_possession_not_established: The opposing claimants’ evidence does not establish that they possess the property.

members.legal_issue: Findings about rights, title, or possession made when deciding temporary injunctive relief are tentative and do not determine the merits of the pending suit.
material_facts: The underlying suit remained pending and the parties had yet to lead evidence.
The Court restored temporary relief while expressly stating that findings about rights, title, and possession were tentative and subject to the trial court’s findings after evidence was led.
members.legal_principle: Findings made at the interlocutory stage to decide temporary relief are provisional where the merits remain pending; they do not finally determine the parties’ rights, title, or possession. No provision or earlier case is cited for this express direction.
members.conclusion: The findings supporting temporary relief remain tentative and are subject to determination at trial.

predicates.temporary_injunction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns temporary injunctive relief before final determination of the dispute.
predicates.merits_suit_pending: The underlying suit remains pending and the merits have not been finally determined.

members.legal_issue: A person in possession cannot be forcibly dispossessed, even if the person is a trespasser, except through due process of law.
material_facts: The appellant’s predecessor received possession of the land under a registered sale deed.
The respondents forcibly occupied the land and raised construction without authorization.
The Special Court ordered their eviction, and the appellant’s predecessor regained possession through execution of that order.
members.legal_principle: Even a trespasser cannot be evicted by force and must be dispossessed through due process. Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, protects a person in possession from dispossession except in due course of law. The Court relied on Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, Ram Ratan v. State of U.P., Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Vankat Rao, and Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, among other authorities.
members.conclusion: The respondents’ forcible dispossession of the appellant’s predecessor was unlawful; possession could be recovered only through the procedure prescribed by law.

rule.if: possession_dispute and person_is_in_possession and dispossession_is_attempted_by_force and no_due_process_is_followed

predicates.possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns who is entitled to possess property.
predicates.person_is_in_possession: A person occupies or possesses the property before the attempted dispossession.
predicates.dispossession_is_attempted_by_force: Another person attempts to remove the occupant without that occupant’s consent.
predicates.no_due_process_is_followed: The occupant is not dispossessed through a legally recognized procedure.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff with clear, document-supported title may sue for possession without seeking a declaration of title when the defendant has not raised a serious cloud over that title.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession on the strength of a registered sale deed from the person found to have inherited the property as the surviving heir.
The defendant claimed to have inherited the property as an adopted daughter, but the adoption was not proved in any court.
The parties litigated title and adoption, and the courts found no serious cloud on the plaintiff’s title.
members.legal_principle: Under Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594 and Kurella Naga Druva Yudaya Bhaskara Rao v. Galla Jani Kamma (2008) 15 SCC 150, a declaration is necessary only when denial of title or a third party’s apparent right raises a serious cloud over the plaintiff’s title; a suit for possession based on clear title is maintainable without it. The Court distinguished a summary suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
members.conclusion: The suit for possession was maintainable without a separate prayer for declaration of title.

rule.if: title_based_possession_suit and plaintiff_has_document_supported_title and not serious_cloud_over_title

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit to recover possession on the basis of claimed title, rather than a summary suit based only on prior possession.
predicates.plaintiff_has_document_supported_title: The plaintiff relied on documents supporting the claimed title to the property.
predicates.serious_cloud_over_title: The defendant showed an apparent defect in the plaintiff’s title or a prima facie right of a third party over the property.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may not forcibly dispossess a tenant who is in possession, even when the tenant’s rights are alleged to have ended because of unpaid land revenue.
material_facts: The tenants were cultivators in possession of the agricultural land.
The landlord allegedly prevented them from cultivating the land and caused others to cultivate it.
The landlord claimed that the tenants’ rights had been extinguished because land revenue was unpaid.
The statutory scheme allowed the revenue authority, in specified circumstances, to accept arrears and provided procedures for recovering arrears and ejecting a defaulter.
The landlord took possession without using the prescribed legal process.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 82(3) and 137 of the Qanoon Ryotwari, arrears could lead to extinguishment of a khatedar’s right, but the provision permitting acceptance of arrears in specified circumstances meant the right was not automatically extinguished in every case of arrears. The statutory recovery process could not be bypassed by forcible dispossession. Indian law does not permit a person to take forcible possession and requires possession to be obtained through a court or other lawful process: Midnapur Zamindary Company Limited v. Naresh Narayan Roy; K.K. Verma v. Naraindas C. Malkani; Yar Mohammad v. Lakshmi Das; and Wali Ahmad Khan v. Ayodhya Kundu.
members.conclusion: The tenants’ alleged default did not entitle the landlord to take possession by force. The landlord had to proceed through the legally prescribed process, and the Board of Revenue’s decision was restored.

rule.if: tenant_restoration_proceeding and tenant_in_possession and landlord_used_force_to_eject and recovery_process_not_used and (arrears_claimed or tenancy_rights_alleged_to_have_ended)

predicates.tenant_restoration_proceeding: A tenant brought a proceeding seeking restoration after being dispossessed.
predicates.tenant_in_possession: The tenant was in possession of the land before the disputed dispossession.
predicates.landlord_used_force_to_eject: The landlord used force or self-help to remove the tenant from possession.
predicates.recovery_process_not_used: The landlord took possession without first using the legally prescribed recovery process.
predicates.arrears_claimed: The landlord relied on the tenant’s failure to pay land revenue as a basis for taking possession.
predicates.tenancy_rights_alleged_to_have_ended: The landlord alleged that the tenant’s rights had ended.

members.legal_issue: A summary possessory suit for unlawful dispossession concerns prior possession rather than title, and forcible entry by a landlord may constitute trespass for that purpose.
material_facts: The cultivators sought restoration of agricultural land under the summary procedure for unlawful disturbance of possession.
They alleged that they had been in possession and were forcibly prevented from cultivating the land.
The landlord argued that entry onto the land was not trespass because the cultivators’ tenancy had ended.
The statutory scheme provided a summary procedure for restoration after unlawful disturbance and a separate, longer procedure for other possession claims.
members.legal_principle: Sections 163 of the Qanoon Ryotwari and 326 of the Qanoon Mal provide for suits concerning trespass and obstruction, including summary restoration where possession has been unlawfully disturbed. Section 326 is similar in structure to section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877; “disturbed unlawfully” means disturbed otherwise than in due course of law, and “trespass” includes forcible entry and dispossession by a landlord. Title is irrelevant in such a possessory proceeding. The Court relied on the principles in Midnapur Zamindary Company Limited v. Naresh Narayan Roy, K.K. Verma v. Naraindas C. Malkani, Yar Mohammad v. Lakshmi Das, and Wali Ahmad Khan v. Ayodhya Kundu.
members.conclusion: The summary possessory provision applied to forcible dispossession by a landlord. The alleged title or termination of the tenants’ rights was irrelevant to that proceeding, which turns on possession and dispossession otherwise than in due course of law.

predicates.summary_possessory_proceeding: A person sought summary restoration of possession under a procedure for unlawful disturbance of possession.
predicates.prior_possession: The claimant was in possession before the disputed dispossession.
predicates.dispossession_not_in_due_course_of_law: The claimant was removed from possession otherwise than through lawful process.

members.legal_issue: The State cannot dispossess a person in bona fide possession by executive action without authority of law, even where the person’s precise rights or trustee status are disputed.
material_facts: The family members continued managing and possessing the buildings after the original manager died.
The State’s officials used force to dispossess them from part of the dharmasala and handed its management and possession to the municipality.
The State did not establish legal authority for the executive dispossession.
The State argued that the family members were trespassers or trustees, but the Court found that neither characterization permitted removal by executive fiat.
members.legal_principle: The State and its executive officers may not interfere with another’s rights without a specific rule of law authorising their acts. Even a trustee of a public trust can be removed only through procedure known to law; section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides a route for proceedings concerning a public trust. The Court relied on Wazir Chand v. The State of Himachal Pradesh and Ram Prasad Narayan Sahi v. The State of Bihar, and referred to Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution. It did not decide the precise rights arising from the original permission or whether it created a lease or licence under section 60(b) of the Easements Act, 1882.
members.conclusion: The executive dispossession violated the petitioners’ fundamental rights; the orders were quashed and the respondents were restrained from interfering with their management of the properties.
