predicates.executive_dispossession: Government officials dispossessed the claimant by executive action.
predicates.lawful_authority_for_dispossession: A law or lawful process authorised the dispossession.

members.legal_issue: A claimant’s possession of property claimed independently must be protected while the executing court adjudicates the obstruction claim.
material_facts: The appellant asserted possession of the disputed parcel under an independent claim.
The executing court had not yet determined whether that parcel formed part of the property covered by the decree.
members.legal_principle: The scheme of Order 21 Rules 97, 98 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires adjudication of the obstruction claim before its final resolution. The court should preserve possession in the interregnum on the factual circumstances so that execution does not cause injustice before the claimant’s right is determined.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s possession was to be protected by interim orders pending adjudication of the claim.

rule.if: execution_obstruction_proceeding and claimant_in_possession and independent_property_claim and claim_pending_adjudication

predicates.execution_obstruction_proceeding: A person resists delivery of immovable property during execution of a possession decree.
predicates.claimant_in_possession: The person asserting the claim is in possession of the disputed property.
predicates.independent_property_claim: The person asserts a right, title, or interest in the property independently of the judgment-debtor.
predicates.claim_pending_adjudication: The executing court has not yet determined the person’s claim.

members.legal_issue: Interim directions in a liquidation proceeding should not dispossess a claimant or recast the claimant’s possession before the claimant’s asserted tenancy rights have been adjudicated when those rights have prima facie support.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a sub-tenancy agreement with the company, and the company’s board had passed a special resolution affirming that agreement.
The landlord’s counsel stated that the landlord had orally consented to the sub-tenancy; this information had not been before the appellate court that imposed the challenged directions.
The claimant was in possession of a major portion of the premises when the liquidator was appointed.
The claimant’s suit to establish her tenancy rights remained pending, and those rights had not been determined.
The challenged directions placed the premises in the liquidator’s possession, recast the claimant as the liquidator’s agent, and required increased monthly compensation and a security deposit.
members.legal_principle: The Bombay Rent Control Act may protect a sub-tenant, and a company’s liquidation and appointment of a liquidator do not by themselves alter the company’s rights in relation to its landlord or tenants. Tenancy rights may not be assets for liquidation purposes. Where the asserted tenancy has prima facie support and remains to be adjudicated, interim arrangements should not determine the claim by dispossession or by changing the claimant’s status; the Court may protect the company’s interests pending adjudication through security. The Court did not decide whether the sub-tenancy was genuine or legally valid.
members.conclusion: The directions dispossessing the claimant and changing the character of her possession were not warranted at the interlocutory stage. The Court substituted an interim arrangement under which she could remain pending the suit, subject to furnishing security; if she failed to do so, the challenged directions would revive. The merits of the suit remained undecided.

rule.if: interlocutory_appeal_in_liquidation_proceeding and claimant_in_possession_before_liquidator and tenancy_claim_has_prima_facie_support and tenancy_rights_unadjudicated and liquidator_directed_to_dispossess_or_recast_claimant_possession

predicates.interlocutory_appeal_in_liquidation_proc: The dispute arises in an interlocutory appeal in a proceeding to wind up a company.
predicates.claimant_in_possession_before_liquidator: The claimant was occupying the disputed premises before the liquidator took control of them.
predicates.tenancy_claim_has_prima_facie_support: Evidence such as the company’s formal affirmation of the tenancy and the landlord’s consent supported the claimant’s tenancy claim at a preliminary level.
predicates.tenancy_rights_unadjudicated: The claimant’s suit to establish the tenancy rights remained pending and no final decision had been made on those rights.
predicates.liquidator_directed_to_dispossess_or_rec: An interim order directed the liquidator to take possession or changed the claimant’s occupancy into possession on the liquidator’s behalf.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may use a summary possessory suit to recover property from a trespasser who forcibly dispossessed a tenant in exclusive occupation.
material_facts: The landlord had let the property to a tenant who occupied it and was forcibly dispossessed by third parties.
The landlord brought a suit for recovery of possession against those who had taken possession.
The trial court found that the tenant had been forcibly dispossessed and ordered the defendants to return possession to the landlord.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits a person dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law, or a person claiming through that person, to sue for possession. Possession includes legal or constructive possession as well as actual physical possession; a landlord retains possession through a tenant, and the tenant's forcible dispossession by a third party also dispossesses the landlord. The Court agreed with Nobin Das v. Kailash Chandra Dey, Ratanlal Ghelabhai v. Amarsing Rupsing, Sailesh Kumar v. Rama Devi, Gobind Ram Jamna Dass v. Mst. Mewa, and Raghuvar Dayal v. Hargovind, and held that Veeraswami Mudali v. P.R. Venkatachala Mudali, (Kanneganti) Ramamanemma v. (Kanneganti) Basavayya, and Ramchandra v. Sambashiv did not state the correct law. The Court's explanation of possession was also informed by Halsbury's Laws of England and Pollock and Wright's An Essay on Possession in the Common Law.
members.conclusion: A landlord who retains legal or constructive possession through a tenant may maintain a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 against a trespasser who forcibly dispossesses the tenant, even though the tenant had actual occupation when dispossessed.

predicates.landlord_bringing_summary_possessory_sui: A landlord brought a summary suit seeking recovery of possession from a person alleged to have taken the property unlawfully.
predicates.landlord_possession_through_tenant: The landlord had let the property to a tenant and retained legal or constructive possession through that tenant.
predicates.tenant_forcibly_dispossessed_by_third_pa: A person other than the landlord forcibly deprived the tenant of occupation without the tenant's consent and otherwise than through legal process.
predicates.landlord_may_recover_possession: The landlord may maintain the summary suit to recover possession from the person who forcibly dispossessed the tenant.

members.legal_issue: A person in settled possession of property cannot be forcibly dispossessed by its owner without recourse to law, even if the person's right to remain in possession is disputed or has allegedly expired.
material_facts: The plaintiff entered possession of the restaurant business and its premises lawfully under an agreement permitting her to conduct the business.

The owner obtained possession behind the plaintiff's back, through collusion with others, and without establishing that the plaintiff had consented or that possession was recovered through legal process.
The trial court and High Court found that the plaintiff had been unlawfully dispossessed and decreed restoration of possession.
The owner argued that the agreement period had expired, but the Court found it unnecessary to decide whether the agreement created a licence or a sub-lease.
members.legal_principle: A person in settled possession may not be forcibly dispossessed, even by the true owner, and the owner must obtain possession through a court. The Court relied on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, which approved the statement in Midnapur Zamindary Company Limited v. Naresh Narayan Roy that possession in India must be obtained through a court, and on Ram Rattan v. State of Uttar Pradesh. The Court held that the principle applied even though the authorities discussed suits under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 or analogous earlier provisions, because this suit was brought within six months of the dispossession.
members.conclusion: The owner was not entitled to dispossess the plaintiff unlawfully, and the decree restoring possession was upheld.

predicates.settled_possession_restoration_case: The proceeding seeks restoration of possession after a person has been dispossessed.
predicates.settled_possession: The claimant had established possession of the property before the disputed dispossession.
predicates.owner_used_self_help: The owner took possession without the claimant's consent and without using legal process.

members.legal_issue: A trespasser whose possession has become settled may defend that possession against forcible dispossession, even by the true owner.
material_facts: A complainant had encroached on part of a public road, cultivated the land, and grown a paddy crop there.
The complainant had been in peaceful possession for two to three weeks before the incident, and the appellants knew of that possession.
The appellants entered the cultivated field with their cattle and tried to pass through it, damaging the crop; a complaint about the encroachment was already pending before the Panchayat.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle applied in Puran Singh & Ors. v. State of Punjab, settled possession sufficient to support a right of private defence requires effective, actual possession over a sufficient period, known to the owner or not concealed, with the process of dispossession complete; cultivation and a grown crop are relevant indicia. A true owner may remove a trespasser while the trespass is still in progress, but must use legal remedies once the trespasser has accomplished possession to the owner's knowledge.
members.conclusion: The complainant had settled possession and was entitled to defend it. The appellants could not forcibly dispossess him and had to pursue remedies under the law.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and trespasser_in_actual_possession and possession_known_to_owner and possession_accomplished and crop_grown

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.trespasser_in_actual_possession: A trespasser was in actual physical possession of the disputed property.
predicates.possession_known_to_owner: The owner knew, or the possession was not concealed from the owner, that the trespasser possessed the property.
predicates.possession_accomplished: The trespasser had completed the process of taking possession rather than merely beginning to trespass.
predicates.crop_grown: The trespasser had cultivated the land and grown a crop on it.

members.legal_issue: A lessor cannot forcibly recover possession from a lessee outside due process, even after the lease has expired or been terminated.
material_facts: The government declared the lease terminated and required the lessees to hand over the land and buildings.
The lessees remained in possession, and the government’s notice contemplated action to evict them if possession was not handed over.
members.legal_principle: A lessee's possession remains juridical possession after expiry or earlier termination of the lease, and the lessee cannot be dispossessed except in due course of law. The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, including sections 108, 111 and 114A, is relevant to the lessor-lessee relationship. The Court relied on Bishandas v. State of Punjab, [1962] 2 SCR 69, and held that the State has no superior right to use extra-judicial force.
members.conclusion: The government could resume possession only in a manner recognised by law and could not dispossess the lessees by force or other extra-judicial means.

predicates.lease_possession_recovery_dispute: A lessor seeks to recover possession from a lessee after the lease has expired or been terminated.
predicates.lessee_remains_in_possession_after_termi: The lessee continues to possess the property after the lease has expired or been terminated.

members.legal_issue: A trespasser in settled possession may exercise the criminal-law right of private defence of property against an attempt by the true owner to dispossess them by force.
material_facts: The appellants took actual possession of the land about a month before the occurrence, and the complainant knew that they had been dispossessed.
The appellants had grown a wheat crop on the land.
The complainant party went to the land armed and attempted to retake possession and destroy the crop.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 96 to 105 of the Indian Penal Code, as applied in Munshi Ram and Others v. Delhi Administration, a trespasser whose possession is settled may defend it against the true owner. Settled possession is not determined by a rigid time period: it requires actual physical possession over a sufficiently long period, possession known to the owner or not concealed and held with an intention to possess, completed and final dispossession acquiesced in by the owner, and, for cultivable land, may be shown by the trespasser having grown a crop. The Court explained Munshi Ram and relied on Horam v. Rex, Sangappa v. State, In re Mooka Nadar, Hazara Singh v. State, Bhartu v. State and Phula Singh v. Emperor.
members.conclusion: The appellants were in settled possession and could defend their possession against the complainant party, even though they were trespassers.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_private_defence_claim and actual_physical_possession_over_sufficient_period and possession_known_to_owner_or_not_concealed and completed_dispossession_acquiesced_in_by_owner and crop_grown_on_cultivable_land

predicates.actual_physical_possession_over_sufficie: The accused had actual physical possession of the property for a period sufficient, in the circumstances, to distinguish it from a stray or casual act of possession.
predicates.possession_known_to_owner_or_not_conceal: The owner knew, expressly or impliedly, of the accused's possession, or the accused did not try to conceal it and possessed the property with an intention to possess it.
predicates.completed_dispossession_acquiesced_in_by: The accused had completed the dispossession of the owner, and the owner acquiesced in that dispossession before attempting to retake the property.
predicates.crop_grown_on_cultivable_land: The accused had grown a crop on the cultivable land after taking possession.

members.legal_issue: A lessor seeking possession by enforcing forfeiture of a lease cannot use the summary eviction process against a lessee who acted under the lessor’s permission and is not an unauthorized occupant of public premises.
material_facts: The lessee constructed the building after receiving permission from the Union ministry responsible for the property.
The lessor’s notice sought re-entry and possession under the lease following alleged breaches.
The building and occupation were not, in the Court’s view, unauthorized occupation of public premises within the meaning of the Public Premises Act.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(e), 2(g) and 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorized Occupants) Act, 1971 govern public premises and unauthorized occupation. A lessee who occupies under authority and whose construction was permitted is not an unauthorized occupant on the facts found. The Court relied on Bishan Das v. State of Punjab, Wazir Chand v. State of Himachal Pradesh, and Ram Prasad Narayan Sahi v. State of Bihar, and criticized the contrary approach in State of Orissa v. Ram Chandra Dev. The Government may use the summary process where there is unauthorized construction or occupation on public premises.
members.conclusion: Enforcement of the alleged right of re-entry following forfeiture required a properly constituted suit; the summary eviction process was unavailable on these facts.

predicates.lease_forfeiture_dispute: A lessor seeks possession on the basis of alleged forfeiture of a lease.
predicates.lessee_acted_under_lessors_permission: The lessee’s occupation or construction was undertaken under permission given by the lessor.
predicates.unauthorized_occupation_of_public_premis: The occupant possesses public premises without authority or continues after the authority to occupy has ended.

members.legal_issue: A person in admitted possession cannot be dispossessed in execution of a decree that does not bind that person or order their eviction without due process of law.
material_facts: The appellant had been placed in possession of the premises by the tenant company, and his possession was admitted.
The purchaser knew of the appellant’s possession, but did not make him a party to the specific-performance suit or obtain a decree for his eviction in a proceeding against him.
The appellant was dispossessed in connection with execution of the decree while his application seeking adjudication of his right to remain in possession was pending.
There was no decree or order for eviction of the appellant.
members.legal_principle: A person in possession cannot be removed without due process of law. The executing court must adjudicate a claim to possession under Order 21, Rules 98 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the Court did not decide at this stage what rights arose from the appellant’s arrangement with his employer.
members.conclusion: The appellant was unlawfully dispossessed and had to be restored to possession pending adjudication of his application under Order 21, Rules 98 and 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.eviction_decree_against_occupant: A decree or order directs the eviction of that person from the property.
predicates.dispossessed_without_due_process: The person was removed from possession without a lawful process determining the right to remove them.
predicates.possession_claim_pending: The person has an unresolved application seeking adjudication of their right to remain in possession.

members.legal_issue: A person in possession of property has a protectable property interest against state interference unless that interference is authorized by law, even if final title to the property has not been determined.
material_facts: The petitioner purchased the property and claimed that the disputed wall was included in the sale.
The State admitted that the petitioner was in physical possession of the disputed wall.
The Court did not finally determine whether the disputed wall formed part of the historic fort wall.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and treated admitted possession as a protectable property interest; it did not rely on any earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The petitioner had possessory title in the wall and was entitled to protection against interference with that right without legal authority, although the Court did not decide final title or the wall’s identity as part of the fort wall.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_state_in: The proceeding challenges state interference with a claimed property interest.
predicates.possession_admitted: The State accepts that the claimant is in physical possession of the property in dispute.
predicates.final_title_unresolved: The court has not finally determined the claimant’s title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A title holder may rely on permissive occupants’ possession as the title holder’s possession until the occupants assert possession adverse to that title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs purchased the disputed lands from the defendants who held title and sought confirmation of possession and recovery of possession.
The defendants in possession cultivated the lands as kinsmen of the title holders under a permissive arrangement, rather than as tenants.
The rent receipts supported acknowledgment of the title holders’ rights, and any assertion of adverse possession occurred only shortly before the sale to the plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs were challenged on the ground that they had not themselves been in possession within the relevant twelve-year period.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that a person in permissive possession is treated as holding possession for the person whose title is acknowledged, until the possessor asserts an adverse right. It relied on the finding that the occupants’ rent payments acknowledged the title holders’ rights. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The defendants’ permissive possession was treated as possession through the title holders until an adverse claim was asserted, so the plaintiffs’ possession claim was not defeated merely because they had not personally possessed the lands during the relevant period.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_possession_decree: A party appealed a civil decree concerning recovery of possession.
predicates.claimant_acquired_title_from_title_holde: The claimant acquired title from a person who held title to the property.
predicates.occupant_possession_was_permissive: The occupant held and used the property with permission rather than under an adverse claim.
predicates.occupant_acknowledged_title: The occupant’s conduct, including rent payments, recognized the title holder’s rights.
predicates.adverse_claim_was_asserted_only_shortly_: The occupant asserted a claim adverse to the title holder only shortly before the property was transferred to the claimant.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking restoration of possession after unlawful dispossession is confined to determining prior possession and does not determine title or a better right to possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a summary suit seeking restoration of possession of a flat and an office after alleging that they had been dispossessed.
The parties disputed whether the plaintiffs had been in possession of the properties before the alleged dispossession.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a summary remedy for a person unlawfully dispossessed and is intended to discourage extra-legal self-help. The Court noted that Section 6(3) bars an appeal or review from a decree in such a suit, referring to P.S. Sathappan (Dead) by Lrs. v. Andhra Bank Ltd. & Ors. (2004) 11 SCC 672 in discussing the procedural context.
members.conclusion: In a suit of this kind, title and better rights to possession are not for adjudication; the relevant issue is whether the plaintiff was in possession at some time within six months before filing the suit.

predicates.summary_dispossession_proceeding: The plaintiff brought a summary proceeding seeking restoration after alleged unlawful dispossession.
predicates.dispute_concerns_prior_possession: The parties dispute whether the plaintiff possessed the property before the alleged dispossession.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may not recover possession from a tenant by force, even when the landlord claims a right to possession, and a person forcibly dispossessed may obtain restoration through a summary possessory proceeding.
material_facts: The occupant had carried on business in the premises as a tenant for many years and paid rent to the landlord.
The landlord had filed a pending suit to evict the tenant but, while that suit was pending, its workers forcibly took possession of the premises with police present.
The tenant promptly complained to the police and other authorities and filed a suit for restoration within six months of the dispossession.
The record contained no document showing that the tenant had voluntarily surrendered possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a summary remedy to restore possession to a person dispossessed otherwise than in due course of law, preventing self-help and discouraging forcible dispossession. In State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh (1989) 2 SCC 505, the Court held that even a lessor with the best title cannot resume possession extra-judicially by force; possession must be recovered in a manner recognized by law. The Court also emphasized that legal and constitutional rights cannot be overridden by powerful persons taking the law into their own hands.
members.conclusion: The forcible dispossession was unlawful, and the tenant was entitled to restoration of possession.

predicates.summary_possession_restoration_suit: A person brought a summary proceeding seeking restoration after being dispossessed of property.

predicates.landlord_forcibly_repossessed: The landlord took possession from the tenant by force rather than through a lawful process.
predicates.voluntary_surrender_evidence: The record contains evidence that the tenant willingly surrendered possession.

members.legal_issue: A person in possession cannot be forcibly dispossessed without due process, even if that person's possession is unlawful and does not qualify as lawful possession for licensing purposes.
material_facts: The lessee remained in possession after the lease expired.
The lessor sought eviction through a court proceeding rather than having already evicted the lessee through lawful process.
The lessee's continued possession did not qualify as lawful possession for renewal of the cinema licence.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 protects possession against dispossession otherwise than in due course of law. Lalu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and East India Hotels Ltd. v. Syndicate Bank affirm that a person in possession may not be removed by self-help, even where the person's title or right to remain is deficient. This protection against forcible dispossession is distinct from lawful possession for the purpose of obtaining or renewing a licence.
members.conclusion: The lessee could remain in possession until evicted in due course of law, but that protection did not make his possession lawful for renewal of the licence.

predicates.possession_recovery_or_eviction_dispute: The dispute concerns recovering premises from an occupant or evicting that occupant.
predicates.person_is_in_actual_possession: The person whose removal is sought is in actual possession of the premises.
predicates.person_has_not_been_ejected_through_due_: The person has not been removed from possession through lawful process.

members.legal_issue: A suit for a bare injunction is sufficient when the plaintiff is in lawful possession and faces interference or a threat, without a cloud over the plaintiff’s title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a permanent injunction on the basis that they were in possession of vacant sites and the defendant had interfered with that possession.
The defendant disputed both their possession and their title.
members.legal_principle: A person in lawful or peaceful possession may protect that possession against interference by seeking a prohibitory injunction, but a person in wrongful possession cannot obtain an injunction against the rightful owner. The court decides a bare-injunction claim by reference to possession, although title may arise incidentally or collaterally.
members.conclusion: A plaintiff in lawful or peaceful possession whose possession is interfered with or threatened may sue for an injunction simpliciter if the title is not disputed or under a cloud.

predicates.injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning immovable property.
predicates.plaintiff_lawfully_possessed: The claimant was in lawful or peaceful possession of the property.
predicates.interference_or_threat: The opposing party interfered with or threatened the claimant’s possession.
predicates.title_not_clouded: The opposing party’s claim did not raise a cloud over the claimant’s title.

members.legal_issue: A temporary injunction may be maintained where the claimant presents a prima facie claim supported by a legally effective sale certificate and official records indicating possession, without finally resolving disputed title at the interlocutory stage.
material_facts: The claimant sought a declaration of ownership and possession, and an injunction against interference, in a suit concerning disputed land.
The claimant relied on a sale certificate issued after an auction in a recovery proceeding; the certificate was later amended to include the disputed land.
Official records of rights indicated that the claimant was in possession.
The sale certificate had not been set aside or declared a nullity, and the competing claims raised serious issues for determination in the suit.
members.legal_principle: A court should not conduct a mini trial when deciding whether to grant a temporary injunction. A sale certificate retains legal validity and force unless set aside or declared a nullity, and rights may be derived from it. Possession indicated by records of rights cannot, at this stage, simply be treated as that of a trespasser where the claimant asserts possession in their own right. The judgment identifies no earlier case as authority for these propositions. The reference to Section 31 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, concerns the recovery proceeding in which the auction took place, rather than the injunction principle applied.
members.conclusion: The appellate court correctly maintained the temporary injunction, and the appeals challenging that order were dismissed.

rule.if: interlocutory_injunction_appeal and prima_facie_sale_certificate_supports_claim and possession_records_support_claim and sale_certificate_not_invalidated

predicates.interlocutory_injunction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order on an application for temporary injunction in a pending suit.
predicates.prima_facie_sale_certificate_supports_cl: The claimant relies on a sale certificate issued after an auction that, on its face, supports a claim to the disputed property.
predicates.possession_records_support_claim: Official records indicate that the claimant is in possession of the disputed property.
predicates.sale_certificate_not_invalidated: The sale certificate has not been set aside or declared a nullity.

members.legal_issue: A person in settled possession may obtain protection against interference even when that person has not proved title and the alleged owner has not established a better title.
material_facts: The plaintiff failed to prove title to the disputed land but was found to be in settled possession of it.
The defendant also failed to prove title to the disputed land.
The defendant obstructed the plaintiff’s use of the land, and the courts below restrained interference with the plaintiff’s possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Indian law, peaceful and settled possession is protected against forcible interference, even by the true owner; a person claiming a better right must obtain possession through due process. Settled possession must be effective and undisturbed, known to the owner or not concealed, and the dispossession of the owner must be complete and acquiesced in; casual or stray trespass does not suffice. The Court relied on Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Kumar Naresh Narayan Roy, Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, M.C. Chockalingam v. V. Manickavasagam, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao, Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, Ram Rattan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya v. Anil Panjwani. No statutory provision was relied on.
members.conclusion: The injunction protecting the plaintiff’s possession was properly granted, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_possessory_injunction_appeal and plaintiff_in_settled_possession and plaintiff_title_unproved and defendant_interference_threatened and defendant_better_title_unproved

predicates.civil_possessory_injunction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an injunction sought to protect possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_in_settled_possession: The plaintiff had effective, undisturbed possession of the property that was not concealed from the owner.
predicates.plaintiff_title_unproved: The plaintiff did not establish title to the property.
predicates.defendant_interference_threatened: The defendant threatened or attempted to interfere with the plaintiff’s possession.
predicates.defendant_better_title_unproved: The defendant did not establish a better title entitling the defendant to possession.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking only an injunction may be maintained when the plaintiff proves possession and faces invasion by a person who has not established title, even though title is disputed.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought relief based on both alleged title and possession but did not prove title.
The trial court found that the plaintiff had proved possession and that the defendant had not proved title to the disputed land.
The trial court left title undecided and granted an injunction against interference with possession.
members.legal_principle: A person seeking an injunction need not prove title if that person proves lawful possession and that possession is invaded or threatened by a person who has no established title. Where title is unclear but possession is established and was not obtained by unfair means shortly before suit, title may be left open while possessory relief is granted. The Court agreed with Fakirbhai Bhagwandas v. Maganlal Haribhai and the stated position in Kallappa Rama Londa v. Shivappa Nagappa Aparaj; it distinguished Sri Dasnam Naga Sanyasi v. Allahabad Development Authority. No statutory provision was relied on.
members.conclusion: The absence of a claim for declaration of title did not make the suit for injunction unmaintainable.

rule.if: injunction_only_suit and plaintiff_possession_proved and title_disputed and interference_by_unproven_claimant

predicates.injunction_only_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking an injunction without seeking a declaration of title.
predicates.plaintiff_possession_proved: The plaintiff proved possession of the property.
predicates.title_disputed: The parties disputed who held title to the property.
predicates.interference_by_unproven_claimant: A person who had not established title threatened or attempted to invade the plaintiff’s possession.

members.legal_issue: A judgment granting an injunction on the basis of possession without deciding title leaves the parties’ title claims open for later adjudication.
material_facts: The trial court decided the suit on possession after finding that neither party had established title.
The High Court upheld the injunction, and the Supreme Court clarified that the judgment did not decide title for or against either party.
members.legal_principle: A possessory injunction may be granted while the question of title is expressly left open; such a judgment is not an adjudication of title. The Court distinguished the title question from the possessory relief and confirmed that the parties could pursue their respective title claims in separate legal proceedings. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this clarification.
members.conclusion: The judgment did not determine title, and either party remained free to establish title in properly constituted proceedings.

predicates.possession_based_injunction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an injunction granted on the basis of possession.
predicates.title_issue_left_open: The court granting the injunction did not decide which party held title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A person who remains in actual possession of land may have a right to defend that property even when revenue records show the land as belonging to another entity.
material_facts: The disputed parcel had originally been in the accused’s possession as a tenant.
Consolidation proceedings affecting the land had been stayed.
The accused possessed adjoining land, tractor marks were found on the disputed parcel, and the prosecution did not explain the tractor’s presence there.
The revenue official’s evidence about cultivation and possession of the parcel was vague, despite his knowledge of the surrounding land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 97 of the Indian Penal Code, a person has a right of private defence of property. The court assessed actual possession from the prior possession, the stayed consolidation proceedings, the surrounding circumstances and the site evidence, rather than treating the recorded ownership as decisive. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The court found that the accused had remained in actual possession of the disputed parcel and had a right to defend the property, notwithstanding its recorded ownership by the village Panchayat.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_previously_possessed_land_as_tenant and consolidation_proceedings_were_stayed and vehicle_tracks_were_found_on_disputed_land and prosecution_did_not_explain_vehicle_presence

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.accused_previously_possessed_land_as_ten: The accused had previously possessed the land as a tenant.
predicates.consolidation_proceedings_were_stayed: Proceedings affecting the land’s consolidation or allocation had been stayed.
predicates.vehicle_tracks_were_found_on_disputed_la: Tracks of a vehicle were found on the disputed parcel.
predicates.prosecution_did_not_explain_vehicle_pres: The prosecution did not explain why the vehicle had been on the disputed parcel.
predicates.accused_had_right_to_defend_property: The court recognizes that the accused had a right to defend the property.

members.legal_issue: A person in long, continuous possession may obtain protection against dispossession without due process even when another person claims ownership.
material_facts: The respondent’s suit sought an injunction based on possession and did not claim title.
The trial court granted relief for part of the property on the basis of possession and the threat of dispossession otherwise than by due process, leaving title open.
The appellant claimed ownership, but title was not an issue in the proceedings.
The Supreme Court stated that long, continuous possession can be protected against persons other than the true owner and that even an owner must recover possession through due process.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles of possessory title and protection of long, continuous possession. It stated that a person in such possession may seek an injunction against anyone other than the true owner, and that even the owner may regain possession only through due process of law. The question of title remained open.
members.conclusion: The possession-based claim was not defeated by the appellant’s asserted title; possession could be protected against dispossession except through due process, while the parties’ title remained undecided.

predicates.possessory_injunction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks an injunction to protect possession rather than a decision establishing title.
predicates.claimant_in_long_continuous_possession: The claimant has been in long, continuous possession of the property.
predicates.threatened_dispossession_without_due_pro: Another person threatens to remove the claimant from possession without using due process of law.
predicates.possession_protected_until_due_process: The claimant’s possession may not be displaced except through due process of law.

members.legal_issue: A court may grant an injunction to protect established possession even when the parties’ title to the property remains unresolved.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a permanent injunction to preserve possession of the disputed leased properties.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the plaintiff was in sole possession.
The defendant’s claims under a will and an alleged allotment failed, while the question of title was left open for determination in appropriate proceedings.
members.legal_principle: On the facts of this case, established possession supported an injunction for its protection even though title was left open. The judgment cites no provision or earlier case for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The injunction was properly granted to protect the plaintiff’s possession, without deciding the parties’ title.

rule.if: permanent_injunction_suit and plaintiff_possession_established and defendant_claimed_basis_failed and title_question_left_open

predicates.permanent_injunction_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking a permanent injunction.
predicates.plaintiff_possession_established: The courts found that the plaintiff was in possession of the disputed property.
predicates.defendant_claimed_basis_failed: The defendant’s asserted basis for claiming the property was not proved.
predicates.title_question_left_open: The court left the parties’ title to be decided in another appropriate proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A legislature can retrospectively validate a tax held invalid only when it has authority to impose the tax and removes the defect that made the earlier levy invalid.
material_facts: The municipality assessed a tax on lands and buildings using a percentage of capital value under a provision authorizing a rate.
An earlier decision had held that the authorized rate was based on annual letting value and did not permit a levy based on capital value.
The legislature enacted a validation measure deeming the capital-value levy valid despite that decision and authorizing its collection for past periods.
A separate provision authorized municipalities to impose a tax on lands and buildings based on capital value or a percentage of capital value.
members.legal_principle: A legislature cannot validate a tax merely by declaring that a court decision does not bind. It must have legislative competence over the subject and must actually remove the defect found by the court through a legally adequate measure, which may include a retrospective taxing provision or a changed legislative meaning. A court decision remains binding unless the legal conditions on which it rested are fundamentally altered. The Court relied on Patel Gordhandas Hargovindas v. Municipal Commissioner, Ahmedabad for the meaning of “rate,” and Sudhir Chandra Nawn v. Wealth-Tax Officer, Calcutta for the scope of the State’s power to tax lands and buildings.
members.conclusion: The validation measure was effective, and the tax could not be challenged merely because the earlier provision used the term “rate”; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: validation_challenge_proceeding and legislature_has_taxing_power and prior_levy_defect_removed and retrospective_tax_authorization

predicates.validation_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a measure that retrospectively validates a previously imposed tax.
predicates.legislature_has_taxing_power: The legislature had authority over the subject of the tax.
predicates.prior_levy_defect_removed: The legislature changed the legal basis or conditions that had made the earlier levy invalid.
predicates.retrospective_tax_authorization: The legislature provided for the tax to be imposed or treated as authorized for past periods.
predicates.validation_effective: The retrospective validation stands and the tax is not invalid on the ground that the earlier levy had the identified defect.

members.legal_issue: A legislature cannot make prior civil court judgments ineffective merely by directing an administrator to disregard them, but may do so by changing the legal basis on which they rest.
material_facts: Civil court decrees had recognised private rights in lands and held that those lands fell outside the village common lands regulated by the principal law.
The later amendment empowered an Assistant Collector to decide claims concerning those lands notwithstanding the earlier decrees and orders.
The amendment did not alter the legal basis on which the decrees had been made or bring the lands covered by them within the regulated village common lands.
members.legal_principle: Under the constitutional separation of legislative and judicial functions, a legislature may not reverse a judicial decision by a bare declaration that it is invalid or not binding. It may render a decision ineffective by fundamentally changing the law on which the decision rests, including retrospectively. The Court followed Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Shri Raj Narain, and I.N. Saksena v. State of Madhya Pradesh; referred to Misrilal Jain v. State of Orissa; approved Bajinder Singh v. Assistant Collector; and distinguished Sunder Dass v. Ram Prakash.
members.conclusion: The provisions directing the Assistant Collector to disregard the earlier decrees and orders were unconstitutional; legislative action can affect such judgments only by altering, removing or neutralising their legal basis.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legislative_: A party challenged legislation that authorised an administrator to decide claims despite earlier court judgments.
predicates.prior_civil_judgment_recognises_private_: A civil court had recognised a private party's rights in property and determined that the property fell outside the regulated common lands.
predicates.legislation_directs_administrator_to_dis: The legislature empowered an administrator to decide the property claim notwithstanding the earlier judgment.
predicates.legislation_changes_legal_basis: The legislature altered the legal rule on which the earlier judgment rested.

members.legal_issue: A law that operates retrospectively to nullify earlier civil court adjudications is invalid to that extent, while its prospective operation may continue if it leaves those adjudications undisturbed.
material_facts: The amendment retrospectively barred civil courts from deciding specified questions about whether land was village common land or vested in a Panchayat.
It empowered revenue authorities to decide those questions, gave their decisions finality, and purported to give those powers effect from the commencement of the principal law.
The amendment was intended to allow those authorities to decide claims despite earlier civil court decrees and orders recognising private rights.
The amendment did not alter the legal basis of those earlier adjudications.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may legislate retrospectively within its field, but cannot use retrospective provisions merely to nullify prior judicial adjudications; it must alter, remove or neutralise the legal basis of those decisions. Prospective adjudication of later claims is permissible if it does not disturb earlier final adjudications. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Shri Raj Narain, and I.N. Saksena v. State of Madhya Pradesh; referred to Misrilal Jain v. State of Orissa; approved Bajinder Singh v. Assistant Collector; and distinguished Sunder Dass v. Ram Prakash.
members.conclusion: The amendment was invalid, inoperative and unconstitutional insofar as it operated retrospectively to nullify earlier civil court adjudications. It could operate prospectively in proceedings commenced after the amendment, provided it did not disturb the finality of earlier adjudications.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_retroactive_claim_law and prior_civil_adjudication_exists and law_operates_retrospectively_to_nullify_adjudication and not law_changes_legal_basis

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_retroactive_: A party challenged a law that assigned property claims to an administrative decision-maker and purported to apply retrospectively.
predicates.prior_civil_adjudication_exists: A civil court had already finally adjudicated a claim concerning the property.
predicates.law_operates_retrospectively_to_nullify_: The law purports to apply to earlier periods and allows the administrative decision-maker to undo the effect of the earlier adjudication.
predicates.law_changes_legal_basis: The law changes the legal rule on which the earlier adjudication rested.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective validating law is constitutionally valid when the legislature has competence over the subject, removes the legal basis of the earlier judgment, and complies with constitutional limitations.
material_facts: The earlier judgment held that the building permission conflicted with a zoning restriction limiting new buildings to 55 feet.
The legislature retrospectively raised the permitted building height to above 165 feet and provided for regularisation of certain deviations.
The challenged law applied the changed zoning rule retrospectively to the period during which the earlier restriction had been in force.
members.legal_principle: A legislature with competence over the subject may enact retrospective legislation and validate past acts if it removes the defect or legal basis that led to the earlier decision; it cannot merely declare that the decision is not binding. The law must also comply with constitutional limitations, including Part III. The Court applied Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills v. Broach Borough Municipality (1970) 2 SCC 388; Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd. (1975 Supp SCR 394); Hindustan Gum and Chemicals Ltd. v. State of Haryana (1985) 4 SCC 124; Vijay Mills Company Ltd. v. State of Gujarat (1993) 1 SCC 345; and Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala (1996) 7 SCC 637, among other decisions.
members.conclusion: The law was constitutionally valid because it materially changed the zoning rule on which the earlier judgment rested and thereby removed the basis of that judgment before validating the relevant construction.

rule.if: challenge_to_retrospective_validating_law and legislature_has_subject_matter_competence and earlier_decision_rest_on_prior_legal_restriction and legislature_retroactively_removed_that_restriction and law_complies_with_constitutional_limits

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_validating_la: A party challenged a law that retrospectively validates earlier acts.
predicates.legislature_has_subject_matter_competenc: The legislature had authority to make laws on the subject addressed by the challenged law.
predicates.earlier_decision_rest_on_prior_legal_res: An earlier court decision relied on a legal restriction that governed the conduct in dispute.
predicates.legislature_retroactively_removed_that_r: The legislature changed that restriction retrospectively so that the earlier decision would not follow under the changed law.
predicates.law_complies_with_constitutional_limits: The challenged law does not violate applicable constitutional limitations.
predicates.validating_law_is_constitutionally_valid: The retrospective validating law is constitutionally valid.

members.legal_issue: A legislature's alleged purpose of defeating an earlier judicial decision does not by itself invalidate a law that changes the governing legal rule.
material_facts: The respondents argued that the law was intended to nullify the earlier judgment and relied on its Statement of Objects and Reasons.
The law retrospectively changed the applicable building-height rule rather than merely declaring the earlier judgment non-binding.
members.legal_principle: The validity of legislation is determined by its constitutionality, not by an asserted legislative motive. A Statement of Objects and Reasons may be referred to for limited purposes, such as understanding factual background and the circumstances addressed, but cannot alone be the basis for invalidating a statute. The Court relied on T. Venkata Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1985) 3 SCC 198 and Gurudevdatta VKSS Maryadit v. State of Maharashtra (2001) 4 SCC 534.
members.conclusion: The alleged legislative intention to defeat the earlier judgment did not invalidate the law; legislative motive was not open to judicial scrutiny as a ground of invalidity.

predicates.challenge_to_legislation: A party challenged the constitutionality of a legislative enactment.
predicates.alleged_legislative_motive_is_to_defeat_: The challenger asserted that the legislature enacted the law to defeat an earlier judicial decision.
predicates.law_changes_the_governing_legal_rule: The enactment changes the legal rule governing the conduct addressed by the earlier decision.
predicates.alleged_motive_alone_does_not_invalidate: The asserted purpose of defeating an earlier judgment, by itself, does not make the law invalid.

members.legal_issue: Parliament may use its constitutional amendment power retrospectively to validate laws that courts have declared invalid.
material_facts: Some state agrarian laws had been declared invalid by courts.
The challenged constitutional amendment added laws to a protected schedule to secure their validity notwithstanding prior court decisions.
The amendment operated retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: The constitutional amendment power under Article 368 may be exercised prospectively or retrospectively. A legislature may enact a validating measure that operates notwithstanding a prior court judgment, and the Court held that the constitutional amendment power likewise permits retrospective validation.
members.conclusion: The retrospective operation of the amendment did not make it unconstitutional; Parliament could validate laws previously declared invalid by courts.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a constitutional amendment.
predicates.prior_court_decision_invalidated_law: A court had declared the law invalid before the validating measure was enacted.
predicates.amendment_retrospectively_validates_law: The constitutional amendment operates retrospectively to validate the law.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective validating amendment may impose a levy for a prior period when it remedies the defect that invalidated the earlier levy.
material_facts: An earlier levy had been invalidated because its substance was a levy on tea despatches rather than a levy on land.

The later amendment changed the basis of the levy to the production of green leaves on a tea estate treated as a land unit and gave the amended provisions retrospective effect for the period covered by the earlier levy.
The Court held that the defect identified in the earlier decision had been remedied.
members.legal_principle: Where an amendment remedies the defect identified in an earlier decision, the legislature may give the corrected law retrospective effect to cover the period governed by the earlier enactment. The Court stated that a law valid in its substance may be valid prospectively and retrospectively, and relied on the established legislative practice of giving corrective amendments retrospective effect.
members.conclusion: The retrospective effect of the amended levy was valid.

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_tax: A constitutional challenge concerns a tax provision given effect for a period before its enactment.
predicates.amended_levy_cures_prior_defect: The amendment changes the levy so that it remedies the defect that invalidated the earlier version.
predicates.retroactivity_covers_period_of_prior_lev: The amendment applies the corrected levy to the period previously governed by the earlier levy.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may give a law retrospective effect from the date on which the State Legislature acquired authority to legislate.
material_facts: The challenged law expressly operated from the date the State was formed, although it was enacted later.
The law retrospectively affected rights previously claimed under grants, agreements, or judicial decisions.
members.legal_principle: Unless constitutionally prohibited, legislative power includes the power to legislate retrospectively. The Court relied on Tata Iron and Steel Co. v. State of Bihar and Rama Krishna v. State of Bihar. It held that the express retrospective effect was tied to the date on which the State came into existence and its legislature became competent to enact the law.
members.conclusion: The retrospective operation was valid and did not make the law ultra vires.

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_state_law: A litigant challenged the retrospective operation of a state law.
predicates.law_expressly_operates_from_state_legisl: The law expressly states that it operates from the point at which the State Legislature acquired authority to enact it.
predicates.state_legislature_had_authority_from_tha: The State Legislature had legislative authority from the point selected for the law’s retrospective operation.

members.legal_issue: An earlier ruling that a decree is a nullity does not bar a later execution proceeding when the ruling rested on a jurisdictional defect that subsequent legislation removes and validates.
material_facts: An executing court previously refused to execute a decree, holding it a nullity because state rent-control legislation did not apply to buildings in the cantonment.
Subsequent legislation removed that defect and validated decrees made by applying the state rent-control law to the cantonment.
The landlords later sought execution, and the tenant argued that the earlier ruling barred it as res judicata.
members.legal_principle: Under Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dessibai N. B. Jeejeebhoy, an erroneous determination of a question concerning the court's jurisdiction does not operate as res judicata when later proceedings are affected by a change in the law. Treating the earlier ruling as binding after legislation removes the jurisdictional defect and validates the decree would create a special rule of jurisdiction for the parties contrary to the law declared by the legislature. Section 3(4) of the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, as amended by the 1972 Act, supplied the relevant validation.
members.conclusion: The earlier decision did not operate as res judicata and did not bar execution of the decree.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party seeks to execute a decree in a later execution proceeding.
predicates.prior_ruling_decree_was_nullity_for_lack: A court previously held the decree a nullity because it considered the governing law inapplicable and therefore refused to exercise jurisdiction.
predicates.later_law_removes_defect_and_validates_d: A later change in law removes the defect underlying the prior ruling and validates the decree.

members.legal_issue: A legislature with authority over a subject may enact provisions by incorporating provisions from an earlier enactment, including provisions that were invalid as legislation of another legislature.
material_facts: A prior decision held the state legislature lacked authority to enact a provision altering the terms of existing mineral leases because the relevant field had been placed under central legislative control.
The validating legislation was enacted by Parliament, which had legislative authority over the subject, and listed the state provision for treatment as if enacted by Parliament.
The challenge concerned whether Parliament could give the provision effect as its own legislation rather than merely declare the state enactment valid.
members.legal_principle: Legislative competence to enact on a subject includes the ability to legislate by incorporation or reference, absent a disabling constitutional factor. A legislature cannot validate another legislature's enactment merely by conferring competence it did not possess; however, Parliament may itself enact the substance of a provision within its own field. The Court relied on the distinction in Jaora Sugar Mills v. State and considered Jawaharmal v. State of Rajasthan, Shama Rao v. Pandicherry, and Gwalior Rayon Mills v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax.
members.conclusion: Parliament could not revive the provision as an enactment of the state legislature, but it could adopt the provision as its own law by incorporation because the subject was within Parliament's legislative authority.

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_validating_law: A proceeding challenges legislation that purports to give retrospective effect to an earlier provision.
predicates.prior_state_provision_lacked_state_legis: A state legislature enacted a provision on a subject it lacked authority to regulate.
predicates.subject_within_parliamentary_authority: The subject regulated by the provision fell within the national legislature's legislative authority.
predicates.parliament_adopted_provision_as_its_own_: The national legislature adopted the substance of the earlier provision as its own law rather than merely declaring the state legislature competent to enact it.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may retrospectively validate a rule made by its delegate even when the delegate originally exceeded the authority conferred on it.
material_facts: The state government made a rule under authority delegated by Parliament to regulate mineral leases.
The rule was held beyond the scope of the delegated rule-making power insofar as it altered the terms of leases already in existence.
Parliament's validating legislation listed the rule and provided for validation of laws and connected actions.
members.legal_principle: A legislature's power to legislate includes the power to legislate retrospectively. A rule made by a delegate of Parliament, although originally beyond the delegation, may be validated by Parliament. The Court relied on section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, the validating legislation and its Schedule, and the principles in West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. v. State of Madras and Jadao Bahuji v. Municipal Committee, Nagpur.
members.conclusion: Parliament could retrospectively validate the rule because it had been made by the state government as Parliament's delegate, and Parliament did so.

rule.if: challenge_to_retroactive_validating_law and rule_made_by_parliamentary_delegate and rule_exceeded_delegated_authority and parliament_retrospectively_validated_rule

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_validating_law: A proceeding challenges legislation that purports to give retrospective effect to an earlier provision.
predicates.rule_made_by_parliamentary_delegate: A state authority made a rule while acting as a delegate of the national legislature.
predicates.rule_exceeded_delegated_authority: The rule went beyond the authority originally granted to the delegate.
predicates.parliament_retrospectively_validated_rul: The national legislature enacted legislation purporting to validate the rule with retrospective effect.

members.legal_issue: A competent legislature may change the legal basis of occupation after a court ruling without impermissibly overruling that ruling or engaging in colourable legislation.
material_facts: Earlier decisions had invalidated the prolonged continuation of requisitions and directed that affected premises be returned to their owners after a period allowed for occupants to vacate.
The amendment ended requisitioning and changed the occupants' legal status from state allottees to tenants of the owners, with the owners becoming landlords.
The amendment left owners able to seek eviction on grounds available under the existing rent-control law and did not displace court eviction orders made before the stated cut-off date.

The stated objects included protecting occupants from imminent eviction and responding to the shortage of accommodation; the State had begun the derequisitioning process and had decided not to continue ordinary requisitioning.
members.legal_principle: A legislature cannot reverse a judicial decision merely by declaring it nonbinding, but, if competent over the subject, it may make a decision ineffective by changing the legal basis on which it rested so that the decision would not have been made under the changed conditions. Colourable legislation concerns legislative competence and is assessed by examining the law's substance, effect, object, purpose, or design, not legislative motive. The Court relied on K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills Ltd., Naga People's Movement of Human Rights v. Union of India, Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala, State of Tamil Nadu v. Arroran Sugars Ltd., and Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal.
members.conclusion: The amendment neither overruled the earlier judgments nor amounted to colourable legislation or an encroachment on judicial power.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and prior_court_ruling_invalidated_prolonged_requisition and legislature_competent_over_subject and law_changes_legal_basis_of_occupation and law_does_not_merely_declare_prior_ruling_nonbinding

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a law said to conflict with an earlier court ruling.
predicates.prior_court_ruling_invalidated_prolonged: A court invalidated the prolonged continuation of state requisition and addressed the resulting return of premises to their owners.
predicates.legislature_competent_over_subject: The enacting legislature has constitutional competence over the subject regulated by the law.
predicates.law_changes_legal_basis_of_occupation: The law changes the legal relationship under which occupants hold the premises rather than leaving their former basis of occupation unchanged.
predicates.law_does_not_merely_declare_prior_ruling: The law does more than announce that an earlier court ruling is not binding.

members.legal_issue: A prior judgment invalidating legislation for vagueness does not create res judicata preventing enforcement after the asserted defect is remedied by amendment.
material_facts: An earlier judgment had treated the original legislation as invalid because it did not define “cattle fair”.
The legislature later amended the statute to define a cattle fair as a gathering of more than twenty-five persons for the purpose of general sale or purchase of cattle.
The later challenge was brought after that amendment.
members.legal_principle: The earlier judgment did not render the statute permanently nonexistent or bar a later challenge after the legislature amended it. Its stated effect was confined to the statute as it stood without a definition of “cattle fair”; that defect was remedied by the amending legislation.
members.conclusion: The earlier judgment did not operate as res judicata against enforcement of the amended legislation; the amendment remedied the defect identified in that judgment.

predicates.later_challenge_to_amended_statute: A party challenged the enforcement of a statute after it had been amended.
predicates.earlier_judgment_resting_on_uncured_defe: An earlier judgment had invalidated the original enactment on the basis of a defect in its then-existing text.
predicates.legislature_amended_statute_to_address_d: The legislature later changed the statute to address the defect identified in the earlier judgment.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may retrospectively alter the legal basis of an earlier judgment and thereby render that judgment ineffective when it acts within its legislative competence, complies with the Constitution, and removes the defect or basis on which the judgment rested.
material_facts: An earlier judgment directed that the value of coal stock on the eve of nationalisation be taken into account in settling the mine owner's claim.

A later amendment retrospectively declared that the scheduled compensation had always included the value of coal stock and enacted a provision validating payments and accounts notwithstanding contrary court judgments.
The amendment changed the legal basis on which the earlier judgment had directed that the stock value be included.
members.legal_principle: Legislatures have plenary power to legislate prospectively and retrospectively within their assigned fields, subject to legislative competence and constitutional limits. A validating law can neutralise a judicial decision only by removing the defect or changing the legal basis on which that decision rested; merely declaring that a judgment is not binding is insufficient. The Court applied Shri P.C. Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality and relied also on West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras, Udai Ram Sharma v. Union of India, Tirath Ram Rajindra Nath v. State of U.P., Krishna Chandra Gangopadhyaya v. Union of India, Hindustan Gum & Chemicals Ltd. v. State of Haryana, and Utkal Contractors and Joinery (P) Ltd. v. State of Orissa. It distinguished D. Cawasji & Co. v. State of Mysore because the amendment there had not removed the defect. The relevant provisions were the retrospective amendment to Section 10 of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972 and the validating provision in Section 19 of the 1986 Amendment Act.
members.conclusion: The retrospective amendment was effective to alter the legal basis of the earlier judgment and render its direction ineffective; this did not amount to an impermissible exercise of judicial power.

rule.if: validating_legislation_challenged and prior_judgment_exists and retrospective_legislation_enacted and legislative_competence and constitutional_compliance and legal_basis_changed

predicates.validating_legislation_challenged: A party brought a proceeding challenging legislation that was intended to affect the legal effect of an earlier judgment.
predicates.prior_judgment_exists: A court had previously decided the relevant legal issue and issued a direction based on the law then in force.
predicates.retrospective_legislation_enacted: The legislature enacted a law that applies from a time before its enactment.
predicates.legislative_competence: The legislature acted within the subject matter on which it had power to legislate.
predicates.constitutional_compliance: The retrospective law did not violate a constitutional restriction.
predicates.legal_basis_changed: The later law altered or removed the legal basis on which the earlier judgment rested.

members.legal_issue: A competent legislature may enact a retrospective law that changes the legal basis of a levy invalidated by a court without impermissibly overruling the court’s judgment.
material_facts: Earlier decisions held that the State legislatures lacked competence to levy the disputed cesses and taxes on minerals.
Parliament enacted provisions creating those levies retrospectively, relying on its own legislative competence over the subject.
The earlier judgments did not hold that Parliament lacked power to impose the levies.
members.legal_principle: Under the separation of powers, a legislature cannot exercise judicial power by merely declaring a court’s decision ineffective. It may, however, alter the law or the basis of the decision, consistently with constitutional limits, so that the decision could not have been given in the altered circumstances. The Court applied Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills v. Broach Borough Municipality and distinguished Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India and A.V. Nachane v. Union of India, which it considered factually inapposite.
members.conclusion: The validation law did not annul or overrule the earlier judgments; Parliament validly changed the basis on which the levies were imposed.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.enacting_legislature_competent: The legislature enacting the new law has authority to legislate on the subject of the levy.
predicates.legal_basis_changed: The new law itself changes the legal basis of the levy rather than merely declaring the earlier court decision ineffective.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective validation of a levy permits collection of amounts due but not collected during the validated period.
material_facts: The law deemed the relevant levy provisions to have been enacted by Parliament for the validated period.
Some amounts due under those provisions had not been collected by the end of that period.
The law validated the levy and related actions, and did not limit its effect to amounts already collected.
members.legal_principle: Once the levy is validly created retrospectively, there is no principled distinction between amounts already collected and amounts that remain unpaid. The Court read the validation and collection provisions as validating the imposition as well as collection, and rejected the argument that the absence of an express recovery clause confined the law to preserving past collections.
members.conclusion: Amounts due but not collected during the validated period could be collected after that period.

predicates.validation_statute_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate a levy previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.retrospective_levy_created: The law creates the levy for a past period by giving legal effect to the levy terms for that period.
predicates.amount_remained_unpaid: An amount due under the levy for the validated period had not been collected.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may validate past actions that a court has held invalid without thereby exercising judicial power, provided the validating law is within its legislative competence and complies with constitutional limitations.
material_facts: A prior Supreme Court decision had held that a single acquisition notification could not support successive declarations covering different parcels of land.

Parliament enacted a law declaring that past acquisitions and related actions would not be invalid merely because more than one report or declaration had been made under the same notification, notwithstanding contrary court orders.
The law concerned land acquisition, a subject within Parliament's legislative competence.
members.legal_principle: The Indian Constitution does not apply the American doctrine of a strict separation of legislative and judicial powers. Legislative power to validate actions is ancillary to the power to legislate on the relevant subject, but remains subject to the constitutional distribution of legislative authority and fundamental rights. The Court relied on A.K. Gopalan v. State, The Queen v. Burah, United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum, Piare Dusadh v. The King Emperor, Basanta Chandra Ghose v. King Emperor, and West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The validating law did not encroach on judicial power and was not invalid merely because it affected actions previously held invalid by a court.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validating_l: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law that validates past actions.
predicates.prior_court_ruling_invalidated_the_actio: A court had previously held the relevant actions invalid.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_the_subje: The legislature that enacted the validating law had authority to legislate on the subject of those actions.

members.legal_issue: A municipality may retain property tax collected under an invalid assessment only to the extent that the tax has been assessed according to law.
material_facts: Property taxes were collected under assessments made using a valuation method that the Court had held invalid.
The governing amendment permitted reassessment under the amended rules and required previously collected amounts to be taken into account, with any excess refunded.
No assessment or reassessment in accordance with the amended provisions had been made when the appeals were heard.
members.legal_principle: Under section 152A(1) and (2) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, as amended, the municipality could reassess property tax under the amended provisions, take amounts already collected into account, and refund any excess. It could retain only tax assessed according to law; the section did not authorize retention of illegally collected amounts without such an assessment. The Court therefore found it unnecessary to examine the constitutional validity of section 152A itself.
members.conclusion: The relevant provision did not authorize the municipality to retain amounts collected illegally before a lawful assessment or reassessment had been made.

rule.if: property_tax_refund_proceeding and tax_collected_under_invalid_assessment and not lawful_reassessment_completed

predicates.property_tax_refund_proceeding: A proceeding seeks the return of property tax collected by a municipality.
predicates.tax_collected_under_invalid_assessment: The municipality collected tax under an assessment made using a method that was held invalid.
predicates.lawful_reassessment_completed: The municipality completed an assessment or reassessment of the tax in accordance with the governing legal requirements.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may retrospectively validate municipal property-tax assessments made under a doubtful or defective authority where the validation is constitutionally permissible and the taxing measure has not already been declared invalid.
material_facts: The municipality continued property-tax assessments using the method prescribed by a government order after the earlier municipal statute had been repealed.
A later amendment expressly validated municipal actions taken to continue the levy and collection of property tax using that method, notwithstanding the governing statute or transitional orders.
The amendment also amended the provisions governing the basis for property-tax assessment.
The validity of the validating provision was not challenged, and no court had declared the tax measure invalid before the amendment.
members.legal_principle: The legislative power to tax is sovereign and must be exercised within constitutional limits. Within those limits, a legislature may retrospectively regularise an irregular assessment and validate a taxing measure of doubtful validity where a court has not already declared it invalid. A statute is not declared unconstitutional unless specifically challenged. The Court distinguished Janapada Sabha Chhindwara v. The Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd., [1970] 3 SCR 745, where the validating enactment did not sufficiently amend the law and attempted to affect a court decision, and applied the rule in Shamarao V. Parulekar v. The District Magistrate, Thana, [1952] 3 SCR 683, that an amendment is read into the amended Act unless that produces inconsistency.
members.conclusion: The amendment validly validated the municipal actions and the resulting levy and collection; the challenge to them therefore failed.

rule.if: municipal_tax_appeal and legislature_enacted_clear_retroactive_validation and not prior_judgment_invalidated_tax_measure and not validation_law_challenged

predicates.municipal_tax_appeal: The proceeding challenges municipal property-tax assessments or their levy and collection.
predicates.legislature_enacted_clear_retroactive_va: The legislature enacted a measure that clearly validates the relevant municipal tax actions retrospectively.
