predicates.prior_judgment_invalidated_tax_measure: A court had already declared the relevant taxing measure invalid before the validating measure was enacted.
predicates.validation_law_challenged: The challenger specifically contested the validity of the validating law.

members.legal_issue: A legislature cannot, by a law directed at a final judicial finding on disputed facts, reverse that finding without changing the legal basis on which the judgment rested.
material_facts: The Court had heard the two States and determined on evidence that the dam was safe at the approved water level.
Soon after that judgment, the defendant State amended its legislation to designate the dam as endangered, limit its water level, and authorize a state authority to regulate or restrict its operation.
The amendment directly contradicted the earlier factual determination and sought to prevent implementation of the judgment.
The amendment did not validate a defective law or remove a defect identified by the Court.
members.legal_principle: The separation of powers is an entrenched constitutional principle and a component of the rule of law and Article 14. Under Articles 245 and 246, a legislature may enact a valid law that changes the basis of a judgment within its competence, but it cannot simply reverse a judicial finding or direct the disregard of a final decision. A validating law must be within legislative competence and remove the defect identified by the court; it must also comply with Part III. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, Janapada Sabha Chhindwara v. Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd., Mahal Chand Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India, P. Sambamurthy v. State of A.P., Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, Re, People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India, I.N. Saksena v. State of Madhya Pradesh, P. Kannadasan v. State of T.N., Indian Aluminium Company v. State of Kerala, Arooran Sugars Ltd. v. State of T.N., and I.R. Coelho v. State of T.N. The relevant amendment provisions included Sections 62 and 62A of the amended Kerala Act.
members.conclusion: The amendment was unconstitutional and ultra vires in its application to the dam, and the rights crystallized by the earlier judgment could not be nullified by legislation.

rule.if: state_to_state_dispute and final_judicial_finding_on_contested_facts and later_unilateral_law_contradicts_finding and no_fundamental_change_to_judgment_basis

predicates.state_to_state_dispute: The dispute is between governments of different States.
predicates.final_judicial_finding_on_contested_fact: A court reached a final finding on disputed facts after hearing the parties and considering evidence.
predicates.later_unilateral_law_contradicts_finding: One party later enacted a law that contradicts the final finding and impedes its implementation.
predicates.no_fundamental_change_to_judgment_basis: The later law does not fundamentally alter the legal basis on which the earlier judgment was decided.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may retrospectively amend the definition underlying a house-tax levy to remove the basis of a prior judgment, and a tax confined to buildings occupied by a factory falls within the State’s taxing competence over lands and buildings.
material_facts: The local body levied house tax on factory and other buildings under a law authorizing house tax.
The earlier definition excluded the buildings because of their entrances and did not expressly include factories.
A later amendment retrospectively removed the entrance condition and expressly included factories, and the buildings fell within the amended definition.
The tax was imposed on the buildings, excluding machinery and furniture.
members.legal_principle: Within its legislative competence and subject to constitutional limitations, a legislature may legislate retrospectively and may validate a levy by changing the law and removing the basis of a judicial decision. Article 246(3) read with Entry 49 of List II gives the State Legislature exclusive competence over taxes on lands and buildings; section 69(1)(a) authorized the local body to levy house tax, and Rule 6 excluded machinery and furniture from assessment. The Court applied United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum and Tirath Ram Rajindra Nath v. State of U.P.; it distinguished Municipal Corporation of the City of Allahabad v. New Shrock Spg. & Wvg. Co. Ltd., Janpada Sabha Chhindwara v. Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd., and State of Tamil Nadu v. M. Rayappa Gounder, where the legislative measures did not remove the basis of the judicial decisions or otherwise attempted to override them.
members.conclusion: The retrospective amendment was valid because it changed the law and removed the basis of the earlier judgment rather than directing the State’s instrumentalities to disregard that judgment. The house tax was lawful, including as applied to the buildings occupied by the factory.

rule.if: civil_tax_appeal and retrospective_definition_amended and amended_definition_covers_assessed_buildings and local_law_authorizes_house_tax and tax_confined_to_buildings

predicates.civil_tax_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning the validity of a local body’s tax levy.
predicates.retrospective_definition_amended: The legislature changed the definition relevant to the tax and made that change apply to an earlier period.
predicates.amended_definition_covers_assessed_build: The buildings assessed fall within the changed definition.
predicates.local_law_authorizes_house_tax: The governing law authorizes the local body to impose house tax.
predicates.tax_confined_to_buildings: The tax is imposed on buildings and does not include machinery or furniture.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may retrospectively validate conduct affected by a prior judgment by changing the legal basis on which the judgment rested, rather than merely declaring the judgment ineffective.
material_facts: An earlier judgment held construction on acquired land unlawful because the agreement governing the acquisition prohibited construction there.
The legislature amended the governing law retrospectively to remove that prohibition and validate specified development and construction carried out under statutory permissions.
The relevant legislative field included acquisition and requisition of property.
members.legal_principle: A legislature with competence over the subject may enact retrospective validating legislation if it removes the defect or legal basis on which a court decision rested and remains consistent with constitutional limitations. It cannot simply declare a judicial decision nonbinding. Bhaktwar Trust v. M.D. Narayan states the test of legislative competence, removal of the defect, and consistency with Part III. Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India cautions against retrospectively depriving accrued rights arising from a judgment. The Court also relied on Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule.
members.conclusion: The legislature was competent to enact the amendment retrospectively because it removed the basis of the earlier judgment; the amendment did not merely overrule that judgment.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validating_l: A party brings a constitutional challenge to legislation intended to validate conduct affected by a prior judicial decision.
predicates.legislature_acts_within_assigned_field: The legislature enacts the measure in a subject area assigned to it.
predicates.amendment_removes_basis_of_prior_judgmen: The legislature changes the underlying legal rule on which the prior judgment depended.
predicates.amendment_does_not_merely_nullify_judgme: The legislation changes the governing law rather than only declaring that the prior judgment has no effect.

members.legal_issue: Legislative provisions preventing enforcement of judicial orders concerning conduct validated by an amendment do not unlawfully displace judicial power when they are incidental and consequential to a valid change in the underlying law.
material_facts: The amendment changed the legal basis for the earlier judicial determination by removing the agreement’s prohibition on construction and validating specified conduct.
The amendment also restricted proceedings seeking cancellation or demolition of construction validated under the amended law.
The Court treated those restrictions concerning court orders as incidental and consequential to the validation measure.
members.legal_principle: A legislature cannot simply set aside a court’s decision, but it may change the underlying law and enact provisions consequential to validating conduct under that changed law. The Court applied the validation principles discussed in Bhaktwar Trust v. M.D. Narayan.
members.conclusion: The challenge based on the rule of law and judicial review did not succeed because the provisions concerning court orders were incidental and consequential to the validating amendment.

predicates.challenge_alleges_interference_with_judi: A party argues that legislation concerning the effect or enforcement of judicial orders interferes with judicial power.
predicates.amendment_changes_underlying_legal_basis: The legislature changes the legal rule on which the prior judicial determination depended.
predicates.order_related_bar_is_incidental_to_valid: The restriction on proceedings or enforcement operates as a consequence of validating conduct under the changed legal rule.

members.legal_issue: A legislature cannot retrospectively acquire property by a provision that directly nullifies a final judgment without changing the legal basis on which that judgment rests.
material_facts: A final judgment had declared the acquisition notices invalid and directed that the factories be returned to their owners.
A later amendment declared that the ten factories listed in its schedule stood transferred to the government, notwithstanding any judgment, and validated actions taken in relation to those factories.
The amendment did not alter the legal basis on which the earlier judgment had found the acquisition process invalid.
The factories were not acquired under the ordinary statutory acquisition provisions, and the scheduled acquisition provision did not provide notice, a hearing, or comparable safeguards.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 245 and 141 of the Constitution, the legislature makes law while courts declare the law. A legislature may retrospectively change the law and remove or alter the legal basis of a judicial decision, but it cannot simply declare a final decision between parties invalid or displace it without curing the defect on which it rests. Acquisition must also observe the rules of natural justice. The Court relied on State of T.N. v. M. Rayappa Gounder (1971) 3 SCC 1; D. Cawasji and Co. Mysore v. State of Mysore (1985) 1 SCR 825; State of Haryana v. Karnal Coop. Farmers’ Society Ltd. (1993) 2 SCC 363; Re Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 96; S.R. Bhagwat v. State of Mysore (1995) 6 SCC 16; and Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1996) 2 SCC 449.
members.conclusion: The scheduled acquisition provision was unconstitutional because it directly displaced a final judgment without curing the defect underlying that judgment; acquisition could not be effected through that provision without the required procedural safeguards.

rule.if: legislative_override_challenge and final_judgment_directed_return and later_law_expressly_overrides_judgment and underlying_defect_uncured

predicates.legislative_override_challenge: The case challenges a law that purports to validate a prior acquisition after a final adjudication concerning that acquisition.
predicates.final_judgment_directed_return: A final judgment between the affected parties directed return of the property after finding a defect in the acquisition process.
predicates.later_law_expressly_overrides_judgment: A later law purports to vest the same property despite the final judgment.
predicates.underlying_defect_uncured: The later law does not change or cure the legal defect on which the final judgment rested.

members.legal_issue: A legislature with authority over the subject may enact a retrospective validating law if it removes the defect that caused the earlier law to be invalid.
material_facts: The State legislature had authority over land acquisition, and its competence on the subject was not disputed.
An earlier judgment had held the State acquisition laws inoperative because they conflicted with a later parliamentary law and because the earlier method used to revive them was impermissible.
The later State enactment expressly operated retrospectively, revived the State laws, changed their operation and validated actions taken under them.
The later enactment applied provisions concerning compensation, rehabilitation, resettlement and infrastructure amenities from the parliamentary law.
members.legal_principle: Articles 245 and 246, read with Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule, confer legislative authority over acquisition of property. A legislature may legislate retrospectively and validate an invalid law by removing the defect, subject to limits including clear retrospective operation, reasonable retrospectivity and the prohibition on merely declaring a judicial decision wrong. The Court relied on National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Ltd. v. Union of India, Ujagar Prints (II) v. Union of India, Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala, State of Tamil Nadu v. State of Kerala, and Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality.
members.conclusion: The State legislature had competence to enact the retrospective validating law, and the law was a legitimate exercise of that competence.

rule.if: retrospective_validating_law_case and subject_matter_legislative_authority and retrospective_operation_is_clear and substantive_change_removes_invalidating_defect

predicates.retrospective_validating_law_case: The proceeding concerns a legislature's retrospective law intended to validate a law or actions previously held invalid by a court.
predicates.subject_matter_legislative_authority: The legislature has authority to make laws on the subject addressed by the validating law.
predicates.retrospective_operation_is_clear: The validating law clearly states or necessarily implies that it operates retrospectively.
predicates.substantive_change_removes_invalidating_: The validating law makes a substantive change that removes the defect on which the earlier invalidation rested.

members.legal_issue: A legislature does not impermissibly overrule a court judgment by enacting a valid law that removes the judgment's material basis rather than declaring the judgment ineffective.
material_facts: The earlier judgment concluded that a particular method of reviving the State acquisition laws did not satisfy the constitutional requirements for resolving the conflict with parliamentary legislation.
The later enactment used a different legislative method, was passed by the State legislature and received presidential assent.
The later enactment revived and amended the State laws and validated specified past actions; it did not simply repeat the method rejected by the earlier judgment.
The earlier judgment had not prohibited revival or validation by a constitutionally compliant method.
members.legal_principle: A legislature cannot directly overrule a judicial decision by declaration, but it may make the decision ineffective by changing the law within its competence and removing the material basis of the decision. The Court applied the principles in National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Ltd. v. Union of India, Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala, State of Tamil Nadu v. State of Kerala, and Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality. It also distinguished State of Karnataka v. Karnataka Pawn Brokers Association because that case concerned an impermissible overruling of a court's direction.
members.conclusion: The later enactment changed the law and removed the basis of the earlier judgment; it did not impermissibly overrule or nullify that judgment.

predicates.legislative_validation_after_judgment_ca: The proceeding concerns a legislature's later law intended to validate or revive a law after a court has ruled on it.
predicates.earlier_judgment_identified_a_defect: The earlier judgment identified a legal defect that made the relevant law or method of revival ineffective.
predicates.later_law_removes_material_basis: The later law changes the legal position that formed the basis of the earlier judgment.
predicates.later_law_does_not_merely_declare_judgme: The later law changes the law rather than simply declaring that the earlier judgment is invalid or not binding.

members.legal_issue: The legislature may retrospectively change the legal basis of a judicial decision and thereby make it ineffective, but may not set it aside by a bare declaration.
material_facts: An earlier judgment held that the former statutory provisions did not cover forest produce grown in Government forests.
The later ordinance enlarged the definition of forest produce and amended the provision rescinding contracts to cover produce grown or found on Government land and in Government forests.
The amendments were given retrospective effect, and the challengers argued that the ordinance encroached on judicial power by nullifying the earlier judgment.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 245 and 246, the legislature may enact valid retrospective legislation and render a judicial decision ineffective by changing the legal basis on which it rested. Validating legislation that removes the cause of invalidity or ineffectiveness is not an encroachment on judicial power, but a bare legislative declaration cannot directly overrule or set aside a judicial decision. The Court relied on Hari Singh v. The Military Estate Officer, [1973] 1 SCR 515; Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Tools Ltd., [1975] Supp. SCR 394; V.N. Saxena v. State of M.P., [1976] 3 SCR 237; and Misri Lal Jain v. State of Orissa, [1977] 3 SCR 714.
members.conclusion: The ordinance validly removed the statutory basis for the earlier decision and did not encroach on judicial power; retrospective legislation was permissible subject to legislative competence and other constitutional limits.

rule.if: validating_legislation_challenge and earlier_judgment_rest_on_old_legal_basis and later_law_changes_that_basis and later_law_is_within_legislative_competence and later_law_does_more_than_declare_the_judgment_wrong

predicates.validating_legislation_challenge: The proceeding challenges legislation enacted to validate action affected by an earlier judicial decision.
predicates.earlier_judgment_rest_on_old_legal_basis: The earlier judgment rested on the scope or effect of the law as it stood before the later enactment.
predicates.later_law_changes_that_basis: The later enactment changes the legal provisions that formed the basis of the earlier judgment.
predicates.later_law_is_within_legislative_competen: The later enactment is within the legislature’s authority and is not barred by another constitutional limitation.
predicates.later_law_does_more_than_declare_the_jud: The later enactment changes the governing law rather than merely declaring the earlier judgment to be wrong.

members.legal_issue: A legislature with authority over the subject may retrospectively validate actions taken under an enactment that was void, including because it contravened fundamental rights.
material_facts: The earlier acquisition enactment had been held void for lack of legislative competence.
The legislature later enacted a law on the subject and included provisions intended to validate actions taken under the earlier enactment.
The challenge argued that retrospective validation could not cure action taken under a law that violated fundamental rights.
members.legal_principle: A legislative power to enact laws on a subject includes the power to enact them retrospectively, subject to constitutional limitations. The Court distinguished the question of automatic revival considered in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which did not decide whether a legislature could retrospectively validate actions taken under a void law. It relied on the principle that a legislature may validate executive actions through legislation ancillary to its subject-matter powers, discussed in United Provinces v. Mst. Atiqabegum and Piare Dusadh v. The King Emperor, and on the general retrospective-legislation principles in Union of India v. Madan Gopal Kabra, M.P.V. Sundararamier & Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, M/s. J.K. Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Mt. Jadao Bahuji v. Municipal Committee, Khandwa, Jadab Singh v. Himanchal Pradesh Administration, and Raghubar Dayal Jai Prakash v. Union of India. The Court held that invalidity for lack of legislative competence and invalidity for contravention of fundamental rights both render the enactment void, and that the asserted limitation on retrospective validation had no basis.
members.conclusion: The legislature was competent to enact a retrospective law validating actions taken under a void enactment, including an enactment void for contravening fundamental rights.

rule.if: retrospective_validation_proceeding and legislature_has_subject_matter_authority and later_validating_law_is_retrospective and prior_action_was_taken_under_void_law

predicates.retrospective_validation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a legislature's attempt to validate earlier executive action through a later law.
predicates.legislature_has_subject_matter_authority: The legislature has authority to enact laws on the subject addressed by the later law.
predicates.later_validating_law_is_retrospective: The legislature enacted a law that operates retrospectively to validate earlier action.
predicates.prior_action_was_taken_under_void_law: An authority took the challenged action under an earlier enactment that was void.

members.legal_issue: Retrospective validating legislation may neutralize an earlier court judgment when it removes the legal basis on which that judgment rested.
material_facts: An earlier judgment directed that the value of coal in stock before the appointed day be credited to the mine owner in the accounts for the period of government management.
A later amendment, made retrospective, deemed the prescribed compensation to include the value of coal in stock and provided that no further amount was payable for it.
The amendment also addressed the effect of contrary judgments and the legislature's authority to enact the retrospective change was not successfully challenged.
members.legal_principle: Legislatures may enact retrospective legislation within their competence, subject to the Constitution. A validating law may neutralize a court judgment by changing the law's basis, but merely declaring that a judgment does not bind is insufficient: the defect or basis identified by the court must actually be removed. The Court applied Shri P.C. Mills v. Broach Municipality and the related principles in West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras, Udai Ram v. Union of India, Tirath Ram v. State of U.P., Krishna Chandra v. Union of India, Hindustan Gum & Chemicals Ltd. v. State of Haryana, and Utkal C. & J. (P) Ltd. v. State of Orissa. It distinguished D. Cawasji & Co. v. State of Mysore because the amendment there had not cured the defect underlying the earlier judgment. The Court also noted that the validity of the nationalisation legislation had been upheld in Tara Prasad Singh v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The retrospective amendment removed the basis of the earlier judgment and made its direction ineffective; the amendment could validly do so.

rule.if: challenge_to_retrospective_validating_legislation and prior_judgment_granted_claim and amendment_retroactively_changes_legal_basis and amendment_removes_basis_of_prior_judgment and legislation_within_legislative_competence

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_validating_le: The proceeding challenges legislation that purports to change the legal position for an earlier period.
predicates.prior_judgment_granted_claim: A court had previously granted a claim under the legal position then in force.
predicates.amendment_retroactively_changes_legal_ba: The legislature made a change that applies to the period and circumstances covered by the earlier judgment.
predicates.amendment_removes_basis_of_prior_judgmen: The change alters the legal basis on which the earlier judgment granted relief.
predicates.legislation_within_legislative_competenc: The legislature had authority to enact the change and no applicable constitutional bar prevented it.

members.legal_issue: A validating law may permissibly distinguish between cases needing validation and cases not needing validation, and the legislature may validate procedural defects within its authority.
material_facts: The validating enactment applied to acquisitions and related steps that had been undertaken under one procedure without following a competing improvement procedure.
Other cases did not require that validation because the relevant procedure had been followed.
The legislature acted within its authority over acquisition.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that validating enactments necessarily produce a distinction between cases in which validation is needed and cases in which it is not. Such class legislation is permissible, and a legislature acting within its jurisdiction may validate procedural defects.
members.conclusion: The distinction between cases requiring validation and those not requiring it was permissible, and the legislature was competent to validate procedural defects.

predicates.validation_law_case: The proceeding challenges a law enacted to validate earlier governmental actions.
predicates.procedural_defect_requires_validation: Some earlier cases contain a procedural defect requiring the legislature's validating action, while other cases do not.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_the_subje: The legislature enacting the validation law has authority over the subject to which the validated actions relate.

members.legal_issue: A legislature cannot make a properly rendered judicial judgment ineffective merely by declaring that it is ineffective.
material_facts: A court had held that the enhanced levy was unlawful because prior governmental sanction had not been obtained.

The later enactment purported to operate notwithstanding a court judgment and to deem the specified levies valid, without disclosing a substantive amendment that removed the defect identified by the court.
The judgment had been rendered by a properly constituted court in a matter before it and declared the law governing the levy.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may, within constitutional limits, retrospectively amend the law and declare what the law is deemed to have been; it may not simply declare ineffective a judgment properly rendered by a court or displace the court's declaration of law. The earlier decision in The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. v. The Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara was binding between the parties and, under Article 141 of the Constitution, on all courts in India.
members.conclusion: The legislature could not render the earlier judgment ineffective, either as a precedent or between the parties, by the terms of the later enactment.

rule.if: legislative_override_challenge and properly_rendered_judgment_exists and enactment_declares_judgment_ineffective and underlying_legal_defect_not_removed

predicates.legislative_override_challenge: The proceeding challenges a legislative enactment that purports to overcome a judicial judgment.
predicates.properly_rendered_judgment_exists: A properly constituted court has rendered a judgment in a matter before it and declared the governing law.
predicates.enactment_declares_judgment_ineffective: The enactment purports to make the judgment ineffective.
predicates.underlying_legal_defect_not_removed: The enactment does not substantively change the law in a way that removes the defect identified in the judgment.

members.legal_issue: A plausible plea of private defence supported by substantial injuries sustained by the accused in the same occurrence must be assessed on the available evidence, and an unexplained failure to investigate those injuries may create reasonable doubt.
material_facts: Two accused had numerous injuries, were referred by police for treatment, and remained admitted as hospital in-patients after the occurrence.
The prosecution witnesses denied or failed to explain the injuries, and the investigating officers did not investigate their cause or the circumstances in which they were sustained.
The accused relied on the injuries, the prior dispute, and the events preceding the occurrence to raise private defence.
The Court found the plea plausible, found no adequate evidence that the accused had exceeded any right of defence, and considered the prosecution evidence unreliable.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 105 of the Evidence Act, 1872, an accused bears the burden of establishing circumstances supporting a defence on a preponderance of probabilities, a burden less onerous than the prosecution’s burden. A defence need not be pleaded in a particular manner and may arise from the evidence. Sections 96–102 of the Indian Penal Code define the right of private defence, including its limits and its duration while apprehension of danger continues. Substantial injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence, if unexplained and uninvestigated, may make the prosecution account doubtful; the exception is where injuries are minor or superficial, or reliable evidence otherwise outweighs the omission. The Court relied on Kashiram v. State of M.P., (2002) 1 SCC 71, Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar, (1976) 4 SCC 394, Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1964 SC 1563, State of Punjab v. Gurbux Singh, 1995 Supp (3) SCC 734, Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P., (1990) 3 SCC 190, and Dev Raj v. State of H.P., 1994 Supp (2) SCC 552.
members.conclusion: The accused had raised a plausible private-defence plea and discharged their burden; they were entitled to the benefit of doubt, with no sufficient basis to find that they had exceeded the right of private defence.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_private_defence and accused_sustained_substantial_injuries_in_same_occurrence and prosecution_failed_to_explain_or_investigate_injuries and defence_is_plausible_on_the_evidence and not reliable_evidence_establishes_excessive_force

predicates.criminal_case_with_private_defence: The accused in a criminal case relied on circumstances suggesting that their conduct was defensive.
predicates.accused_sustained_substantial_injuries_i: One or more accused suffered numerous or substantial injuries during the occurrence being prosecuted.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_explain_or_investi: The prosecution did not adequately account for the accused persons’ injuries, and investigators did not examine how they were sustained.
predicates.defence_is_plausible_on_the_evidence: The evidence makes the accused’s defensive account reasonably probable rather than merely fanciful.
predicates.reliable_evidence_establishes_excessive_: Reliable evidence establishes that the accused continued to use force after the apprehension of danger had ceased.
predicates.accused_entitled_to_benefit_of_doubt_on_: The accused cannot be convicted because the plausible private-defence account leaves reasonable doubt and excessive force is not established.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain an accused person’s injuries does not by itself invalidate its case when the injuries are not serious and the prosecution evidence is cogent and credible.
material_facts: One accused had swelling and a fracture of the underlying bone in his upper arm, along with a complaint of shoulder pain.
The Court characterized the injuries as simple and superficial and found the evidence against the appellants cogent and creditworthy.
The prosecution had not explained the accused person’s injuries.
members.legal_principle: There is no absolute rule that the prosecution must explain every injury sustained by an accused in the same occurrence or that failure to do so requires rejection of the prosecution case. Under Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing, non-explanation may affect the prosecution case when the accused’s injury was serious and was caused during the occurrence in question. The Court also held that cogent and creditworthy prosecution evidence may outweigh the omission to explain injuries.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not undermine the prosecution case or warrant setting aside the convictions.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenges_conviction: The accused appeal a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injury_in_: An accused person was injured in the incident and the prosecution did not explain that injury.
predicates.injury_is_not_serious: The accused person’s injury was simple or superficial rather than serious.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_is_cogent_and_credi: The evidence supporting the prosecution case was cogent and creditworthy.

members.legal_issue: The failure to explain injuries sustained by a person on the opposing side does not necessarily undermine the prosecution case.
material_facts: A woman related to the accused sustained small gunshot injuries during the incident.

The courts below found that pellets fired at the deceased could have passed by him and accidentally struck her, and that her injuries were concealed by her clothing and may not have been noticed by the eyewitnesses.
The defence alleged that a member of the prosecution party had shot her, but she was not called as a defence witness.
members.legal_principle: Under State of Gujarat v. Sai Fatima, the failure to explain injuries on an accused may, depending on the facts, support self-defence, make the prosecution case doubtful, or have no effect on it. The court applied the third possibility here, finding the injuries consistent with accidental pellet strikes and not necessarily visible to the eyewitnesses.
members.conclusion: The prosecution sufficiently explained the injuries; even if they had remained unexplained, the circumstances did not require rejection of the prosecution case.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The matter is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution alleges that the accused committed an offence.
predicates.injuries_explained_by_prosecution: The prosecution provides an explanation for injuries sustained by a person on the opposing side.
predicates.injuries_could_have_been_unnoticed_and_a: The injuries could have been caused accidentally during the incident and could have gone unnoticed by the eyewitnesses.

members.legal_issue: Failure to prove an alleged part of an attack beyond reasonable doubt does not necessarily discredit the remaining prosecution evidence when that part is not found false and other evidence supports the assault.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses described firing during the attack, but the High Court found that firing had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt.
The High Court did not affirmatively find that the firing account was false, and the evidence did not rule out the possibility that some assailants fired weapons.
The eyewitnesses consistently described firing, while the other alleged assailants’ weapons and the evidence of the attack provided support independent of whether firing occurred.
The appeal challenged the remaining convictions on the ground that the firing account was integral to the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: A failure to establish one part of the prosecution account beyond reasonable doubt is not equivalent to an affirmative finding that the account is false; the remaining evidence must be assessed on its own. No particular statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The failure to prove firing beyond reasonable doubt did not require rejection of the rest of the prosecution case, and the convictions challenged in the appeal were upheld.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and alleged_firing_not_proved_beyond_reasonable_doubt and alleged_firing_not_found_false and other_evidence_supports_assault

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging criminal convictions.
predicates.alleged_firing_not_proved_beyond_reasona: The prosecution’s allegation that firearms were used was not established beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.alleged_firing_not_found_false: The court did not affirmatively find that the allegation of firing was false.
predicates.other_evidence_supports_assault: Other evidence, including eyewitness accounts and evidence of injuries caused by other weapons, supported the alleged assault apart from whether firing occurred.

members.legal_issue: An unexplained injury to an accused does not by itself require rejection of otherwise reliable prosecution evidence.
material_facts: The accused Mathan sustained injuries during the incident, and the prosecution did not explain them at trial.
The first information report stated that someone from the complainant side might have struck an aggressor while trying to save a life, but the defence did not produce the counter-case report.
Several eyewitnesses were injured; their accounts were clear and consistent and were corroborated by medical evidence and independent witnesses.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar, Dashrath Singh v. State of U.P., Shriram v. State of M.P., Laxman Singh v. Poonam Singh, Amar Malla v. State of Tripura, and Chacko alias Aniyan Kunju v. State of Kerala. Non-explanation of an accused’s injuries is a circumstance to consider when assessing the evidence, but it does not automatically invalidate the prosecution case; its effect depends on the quality of the evidence and the circumstances, including whether the defence account is probable.
members.conclusion: The failure to explain Mathan’s injuries did not justify rejecting the prosecution case because the evidence was clear, cogent, and corroborated.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and accused_injured_in_incident and prosecution_did_not_explain_injury and prosecution_evidence_clear_and_corroborated

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_injured_in_incident: An accused person sustained an injury during the incident being tried.
predicates.prosecution_did_not_explain_injury: The prosecution did not explain how the accused person sustained that injury.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_clear_and_corrobora: The prosecution evidence was clear and was supported by other witnesses or medical evidence.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain injuries sustained by accused persons in the same occurrence does not automatically require rejection of its case.
material_facts: Several accused sustained injuries in the occurrence, including a fracture and head injuries.
The prosecution witnesses said that members of the prosecution side used nearby bamboo sticks to repel an attack.
The court accepted the account of an independent eyewitness and other reliable witnesses, supported by the victim’s dying declaration.
The defence account did not appear as probable as the prosecution account.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles stated in Bhaba Nanda v. State of Assam, AIR 1977 SC 2252, and Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansingh, (2001) 6 SCC 145, the prosecution is not invariably obliged to explain injuries sustained by accused persons. The court must consider whether the injuries were serious and were sustained in the occurrence, and assess the omission in light of the quality of the prosecution evidence and the probability of the defence account. Non-explanation is a relevant circumstance, not by itself a ground to reject otherwise clear, cogent and credible evidence.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not justify rejecting the prosecution case because the reliable evidence established that the accused initiated the attack and the defence account did not compete in probability.

rule.if: criminal_case_evidence_review and serious_same_occurrence_accused_injuries and prosecution_evidence_clear_reliable and defence_version_not_equally_probable

predicates.criminal_case_evidence_review: The court was evaluating prosecution evidence in a criminal case.
predicates.serious_same_occurrence_accused_injuries: One or more accused sustained serious injuries during the same occurrence.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_clear_reliable: The prosecution evidence was clear and reliable, including evidence from witnesses whose account was supported by other evidence.
predicates.defence_version_not_equally_probable: The defence account did not have probability equal to the prosecution account.
predicates.prosecution_case_not_rejected_solely_for: The prosecution case is not rejected solely because serious injuries to accused persons were left unexplained.

members.legal_issue: The absence from the initial report of an explanation for injuries sustained by an accused does not by itself undermine the prosecution case.
material_facts: The accused sustained several injuries in the incident.
The eyewitness did not mention or explain those injuries in the initial report, but explained them in his trial evidence.
members.legal_principle: In an assault case, the prosecution’s obligation to explain injuries sustained by an accused arises, if necessary, at the stage of trial. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The omission from the initial report did not by itself affect the prosecution case; any obligation to explain the accused’s injuries arose, if necessary, at trial.

predicates.criminal_assault_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution alleging an assault.
predicates.accused_injuries_omitted_from_initial_re: The accused sustained injuries in the incident, and the initial report did not explain them.
predicates.initial_report_omission_alone_does_not_u: The omission of the explanation from the initial report, by itself, does not undermine the prosecution.

members.legal_issue: Unexplained injuries to an accused do not require rejection of otherwise corroborated prosecution evidence or establish that the accused acted in self-defence.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses did not explain the injuries found on one accused, whose injuries were recorded soon after the incident.
The injured persons had come to protest the cutting of a tree, and the evidence supported that they were unarmed when the assault began.
Eyewitness testimony identifying the principal assailants was corroborated by medical evidence and the presence of blood at locations along the path of the assault.
The evidence supported that the beating continued as the injured persons tried to flee.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302/34, 325/34, 323/34 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code, the court assessed the evidence of common participation and the assault. An unexplained injury to an accused is an infirmity that must be considered, but it does not by itself defeat a prosecution account that is supported by credible eyewitness, medical and circumstantial evidence. The evidence did not establish that the victims’ injuries were inflicted in lawful self-defence. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the four persons found to have actively assaulted the victims were upheld, and their appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and identified_assailants and credible_eyewitness_account and corroborating_medical_or_scene_evidence and victims_arrived_to_protest and victims_unarmed and accused_sustained_injuries

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The convicted persons brought an appeal challenging their convictions.
predicates.identified_assailants: Witnesses identified the persons who actively inflicted the assault.
predicates.credible_eyewitness_account: The eyewitness account of the assault was accepted as credible.
predicates.corroborating_medical_or_scene_evidence: Medical findings or physical evidence at the scene supported the eyewitness account.
predicates.victims_arrived_to_protest: The injured persons came to object to an act being carried out by the accused.
predicates.victims_unarmed: The injured persons were not armed when the assault began.
predicates.accused_sustained_injuries: At least one accused had injuries that the prosecution witnesses did not explain.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain an accused person’s injuries does not require rejection of an otherwise credible prosecution case where the circumstances support the possibility that the injuries were self-inflicted.
material_facts: The accused’s father claimed to have been injured by the deceased during the incident, but sought medical attention several hours later.
He did not undergo the advised radiological examination and did not tell the doctor how or why he had been injured.
The weapon allegedly used by the deceased to inflict those injuries was never recovered.
The Supreme Court agreed that the injuries were likely self-inflicted and that their non-explanation did not undermine the prosecution evidence.
members.legal_principle: Non-explanation of injuries on an accused is insufficient to discard the prosecution case if that case otherwise inspires confidence and is worthy of credence. The circumstances surrounding the injuries—including delayed medical attention, refusal of radiological examination, failure to give the doctor their history, and lack of corroboration of the alleged weapon—may be considered in assessing the defence account.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not require the prosecution case to be rejected, particularly in light of the circumstances suggesting that the injuries were self-inflicted.

rule.if: criminal_case_based_on_eyewitness_evidence and prosecution_case_otherwise_credible and accused_injuries_unexplained and circumstances_support_self_infliction

predicates.criminal_case_based_on_eyewitness_eviden: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution relies on eyewitness evidence.
predicates.prosecution_case_otherwise_credible: The prosecution evidence apart from the accused’s injuries is credible and worthy of reliance.
predicates.accused_injuries_unexplained: The prosecution has not provided an explanation for injuries sustained by an accused person.
predicates.circumstances_support_self_infliction: The surrounding circumstances support the possibility that the accused’s injuries were self-inflicted.

members.legal_issue: Unexplained injuries to accused persons do not undermine the prosecution case when the defence has not established that the injuries arose in the same occurrence and at the same place.
material_facts: Some accused persons had injuries that the prosecution did not explain.
The defence offered no counter-version identifying where or how the injuries occurred and did not claim self-defence.
The injuries were not fatal and did not threaten life.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution’s obligation to explain injuries to an accused depends on establishing that the injuries were sustained in the same occurrence and at the same place. In the absence of that foundation or a plea of self-defence, and where the injuries are not serious, their non-explanation does not require rejection of the prosecution case. The court distinguished Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar (1976) 4 SCC 394 and Siri Kishan v. State of Haryana (2009) 12 SCC 757 on their facts.
members.conclusion: The prosecution case could not be disbelieved because of the accused persons’ unexplained injuries.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries and not same_occurrence_and_place_established and no_counter_version and no_self_defence_claim and injuries_not_serious

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries: One or more accused persons had injuries that the prosecution did not explain.
predicates.same_occurrence_and_place_established: The defence established that the accused persons sustained their injuries in the same occurrence and at the same place.
predicates.no_counter_version: The defence did not provide a counter-version explaining where or how the injuries occurred.
predicates.no_self_defence_claim: The defence did not claim that the injuries arose while acting in self-defence.
predicates.injuries_not_serious: The injuries were not fatal and did not threaten life.

members.legal_issue: An injury that eyewitnesses did not specifically explain does not discredit the prosecution case when the medical evidence and circumstances support a natural reaction that could have caused it.
material_facts: The medical witness stated that one injury could have been caused if the deceased raised his arm while walking.
The eyewitnesses said that the accused challenged the deceased and then fired, but did not specifically describe the deceased raising his arm.
The Court considered it natural that the deceased might raise his hands in reaction to the challenge or to defend himself.
members.legal_principle: Human reactions are unpredictable and need not follow a fixed pattern. A possible reaction may be assessed in the context of the circumstances and the medical evidence; the Court relied on no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The absence of a specific explanation from the eyewitnesses for the injury did not discredit the prosecution case.

predicates.criminal_trial_evidence: The issue arises in the assessment of evidence in a criminal trial.
predicates.medical_evidence_links_injury_to_possibl: Medical evidence indicates that the injury could have resulted from a particular bodily reaction.
predicates.challenge_or_threat_preceded_injury: A challenge or threat immediately preceded the injury.
predicates.eyewitnesses_did_not_describe_that_react: The eyewitnesses did not specifically state that the injured person made the reaction identified by the medical evidence.

members.legal_issue: Injuries to accused persons do not by themselves discredit the prosecution when the prosecution evidence sufficiently explains them as occurring during a mutual fight.
material_facts: Three accused persons sustained injuries during the occurrence.
Prosecution witnesses said that members of the complainant's party wielded weapons when the accused attacked them, acting in self-defence.
The deceased and several prosecution witnesses also sustained injuries, and the evidence showed that a mutual fight occurred.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the evidence as a whole and held that the injuries to the accused did not undermine the prosecution where the witnesses explained that they occurred in the course of the mutual fight and the prosecution side also suffered injuries. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this determination.
members.conclusion: The prosecution had sufficiently explained the accused persons' injuries, so the case could not be rejected on the ground that those injuries were unexplained.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and accused_sustained_injuries and prosecution_witnesses_explained_injuries and prosecution_side_also_injured

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.accused_sustained_injuries: One or more accused persons sustained injuries in the occurrence.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_explained_injuries: Prosecution witnesses explained that the accused persons' injuries occurred during the fight after the accused attacked.
predicates.prosecution_side_also_injured: The deceased or members of the prosecution party also sustained injuries in the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain injuries sustained by the accused does not, in the circumstances found, undermine the accepted prosecution case.
material_facts: The accused sustained injuries, some of them serious, which the prosecution did not explain.
The trial court and the High Court accepted the prosecution evidence and rejected the defence versions, which were inconsistent with one another.
The High Court found no material infirmity in the eyewitness evidence.
members.legal_principle: The principles stated in AIR 1976 SC 2263 treat unexplained injuries as especially significant where the prosecution has suppressed the occurrence’s true origin, witnesses denying the injuries are unreliable, or a probable defence account explains them. Here, the concurrent findings accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the inconsistent defence accounts, and identified no material infirmity in the eyewitness testimony; the cited principles therefore did not assist the accused. The convictions under Sections 302, 307 and 323 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code were upheld.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not require rejection of the prosecution case or invalidate the convictions.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries and (concurrent_courts_accepted_prosecution_evidence and defence_versions_were_inconsistent and no_material_infirmity_in_eyewitness_evidence)

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging criminal convictions.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries: The accused sustained injuries that the prosecution did not explain.
predicates.concurrent_courts_accepted_prosecution_e: The trial court and the appellate court accepted the prosecution evidence.
predicates.defence_versions_were_inconsistent: The accused advanced inconsistent accounts of how the occurrence happened.
predicates.no_material_infirmity_in_eyewitness_evid: The courts found no material defect in the eyewitness evidence.

members.legal_issue: An accused’s lack of injuries or failure to rescue others from a fire does not by itself establish guilt of causing the fire.
material_facts: The appellant escaped the fire without injury, and the lower courts treated her lack of injuries as evidence that she had left before the fire spread.
The appellant was faulted for not alerting or rescuing the deceased and children.
Other occupants of the house were also uninjured despite the fire destroying the house and adjoining structures.
The deceased, who survived for a day after the fire, did not accuse or suspect the appellant.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the requirement that circumstantial evidence must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt and exclude reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence, as set out in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra. It observed that a natural response to a fire may be to escape, and that failure to return to rescue another person may be morally wrong but is not proof of a serious crime unless the other circumstances form a complete chain pointing to guilt.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s lack of injuries and failure to rescue the other occupants could not establish guilt without other circumstances in the chain pointing irresistibly to her guilt.

rule.if: fire_related_criminal_case and accused_uninjured and (accused_did_not_rescue_others or accused_did_not_raise_alarm) and no_other_complete_guilt_chain

predicates.fire_related_criminal_case: The proceeding concerns an allegation that the accused caused a fire resulting in death or injury.
predicates.accused_uninjured: The accused escaped the fire without physical injury.
predicates.accused_did_not_rescue_others: The accused did not bring other occupants out of the fire or return to rescue them.
predicates.accused_did_not_raise_alarm: The accused did not alert other occupants before they were caught in the fire.
predicates.no_other_complete_guilt_chain: The remaining circumstances do not form a complete chain establishing the accused’s guilt.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution fails to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt where the accused's injuries are left unexplained and the prosecution suppresses material evidence about how the occurrence began, in circumstances supporting private defence or casting doubt on the prosecution account.
material_facts: Two persons on the appellants' side had injuries, including gunshot injuries, and the prosecution gave no explanation for them.
The prosecution deliberately suppressed a material part of the origin of the occurrence.
The evidence supported the appellants' account that the complainant party had come armed to retake the land and destroy the crop.
members.legal_principle: Under State of Gujarat v. Sai Fatima, unexplained injuries on an accused may, depending on the facts, support a finding that the accused acted in self-defence, make the prosecution version doubtful so that the charge is not proved beyond reasonable doubt, or have no effect on the prosecution case. Where the prosecution suppresses the material origin of the occurrence, the resulting uncertainty may also prevent the prosecution from proving its case beyond reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: The appellants were protected by private defence, and in any event the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; the convictions and sentences were set aside.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution_for_violent_offence and accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries and prosecution_suppressed_material_origin and evidence_supports_private_defence_or_doubt

predicates.criminal_prosecution_for_violent_offence: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution alleging that the accused committed a violent offence.
predicates.accused_sustained_unexplained_injuries: One or more accused persons sustained injuries during the occurrence, and the prosecution did not explain them.
predicates.prosecution_suppressed_material_origin: The prosecution withheld or suppressed material evidence about how the occurrence began.
predicates.evidence_supports_private_defence_or_dou: The evidence supports a claim of private defence or otherwise leaves reasonable doubt about the prosecution account.

members.legal_issue: An inquest report is concerned with the apparent cause of death, and omission from it of the manner of the assault or the assailants does not by itself undermine the prosecution case.
material_facts: The High Court treated the omission of details of the occurrence from the inquest report as suggesting that the investigating officer was unsure of the case.
The omitted details concerned how the incident occurred and who was responsible, rather than the apparent cause of death and the injuries observed.
members.legal_principle: Section 174 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires an inquiry and report on the apparent cause of death and descriptions of wounds or other marks of injury; it does not require details of how the assault occurred or the identity of the assailants. Podda Narayana v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1975 SC 1252; Khujji v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1991 SC 1853; and Shakila Khadar v. Nausher Gama, AIR 1975 SC 1324, explain the limited scope of an inquest.
members.conclusion: The omission of those details from the inquest report did not justify doubting the prosecution case.

predicates.inquest_report_is_at_issue: The proceeding concerns whether an inquest report's contents undermine the prosecution case.
predicates.inquest_report_omits_occurrence_details: The inquest report does not state how the incident occurred or who committed the assault.

members.legal_issue: Serious unexplained injuries to an accused do not by themselves require rejection of reliable prosecution evidence, though they may bear on sentencing.
material_facts: The accused had sustained injuries in the incident, and their presence was undisputed.
The injuries were serious and were not explained by the prosecution.
An injured eyewitness acknowledged that a prosecution witness had beaten the accused after the assaults.
The prosecution eyewitnesses’ testimony was otherwise reliable and had not been shaken.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that injuries to an accused do not per se affect the prosecution version when that version is reliable; serious injuries that are not explained assume importance. In this case, the evidence remained credible, while the injuries were considered in assessing sentence.
members.conclusion: The injuries did not warrant disbelieving the reliable prosecution evidence, but their seriousness was relevant to the sentencing assessment.

predicates.criminal_case: The matter is a criminal proceeding.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_is_reliable: The prosecution evidence is otherwise cogent and credible after assessment by the court.
predicates.accused_sustained_serious_unexplained_in: The accused sustained serious injuries in the incident and the prosecution did not explain them.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution need not explain injuries on an accused as having been inflicted by the deceased when the accused do not claim that the deceased caused them.
material_facts: The accused did not claim, including in their examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the deceased had inflicted their injuries.
Their account was that unidentified assailants caused their injuries while they tried to intervene.
They did not report those injuries to the police.
The High Court relied on the prosecution’s failure to explain the injuries.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the distinction between injuries alleged to have been caused by the deceased and injuries which the accused attributed to unidentified assailants; because the accused did not claim that the deceased caused their injuries, an explanation on that basis did not arise. The Court referred to the accused’s examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. No earlier case was relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s reliance on the non-explanation of the accused persons’ injuries was unsustainable.

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The prosecution appeals against an acquittal.
predicates.accused_do_not_attribute_injuries_to_dec: The accused do not claim that the deceased inflicted their injuries.
predicates.accused_attribute_injuries_to_unknown_as: The accused attribute their injuries to unidentified assailants.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution's failure to explain minor injuries sustained by accused persons does not, by itself, require rejection of otherwise credible prosecution evidence.
material_facts: The defence medical evidence showed that the injuries to the two accused were at most minor and superficial; the claimed grievous injuries were not substantiated by the supporting X-ray records.
Four injured eyewitnesses gave clear accounts of the incident and each accused's role, and their presence at the scene was not in doubt.
The eyewitness accounts were consistent with one another and corroborated by medical evidence concerning the deceased and the other injured persons.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles stated in Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar (1976) 4 SCC 394, Rizan v. State of Chhattisgarh (2003) 2 SCC 661, Sekar alias Raja Sekharan v. State (2002) 8 SCC 354, and Anil Kumar v. State of U.P. (2004) 13 SCC 257, failure to explain injuries on an accused can be important, particularly where the prosecution evidence is interested or the defence account is comparably probable. But the omission does not by itself defeat the prosecution where the injuries are minor or superficial, or where clear, cogent and credible evidence outweighs the omission.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not undermine the prosecution case, because the injuries were minor and the prosecution evidence was clear, cogent and credible.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_suffered_minor_superficial_injur: The accused sustained injuries that were minor or superficial.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_clear_cogent_credib: The prosecution presented clear, cogent and credible evidence supporting its account.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain injuries on an accused person does not require rejection of all prosecution evidence when evidence of separate attacks is independently corroborated.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses did not explain the minor injuries sustained by one accused person.
The courts below rejected the prosecution account of the initial attack, but accepted evidence of later attacks on two deceased persons at separate locations.
Blood found at the location of one attack corroborated the evidence about that attack, and an independent witness testified about the other attack.
The Supreme Court found no valid basis to reject that corroborated evidence.
members.legal_principle: An accused person’s unexplained injuries may require careful scrutiny of prosecution evidence, but do not automatically make the entire prosecution case untruthful or establish self-defence. The Court applied Mohar Rai v. State of Bihar and Ugar Ahir v. State of Bihar, including the principle that falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is neither a sound rule of law nor a rule of practice.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not require the Court to discard the prosecution evidence as a whole; the corroborated evidence about the separate attacks could be accepted.

predicates.criminal_case: The prosecution tried people for criminal offences arising from an alleged violent incident.
predicates.accused_injuries_unexplained: The prosecution witnesses did not explain injuries sustained by an accused person.
predicates.separate_attack_corroborated_by_physical: Physical evidence at the scene corroborated testimony about an attack separate from the initial encounter.
predicates.separate_attack_supported_by_independent: A witness with no shown connection of friendship or enmity to either side testified about an attack separate from the initial encounter.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution's failure to explain minor and superficial injuries on the accused does not by itself undermine otherwise clear and credible evidence.
material_facts: The investigating officer observed injuries on two accused when they were arrested, and they reportedly attributed the injuries to the deceased.
The injuries were superficial, the accused were not sent for medical examination, and no suggestion about the injuries was put to the witnesses.
The prosecution evidence was clear and credible and was supported by injured eyewitnesses and medical evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Sri Ram v. State of M.P. (2004) 9 SCC 292, non-explanation of injuries on an accused is not invariably fatal, particularly where the injuries are minor or superficial, or the prosecution evidence is otherwise clear, cogent, probable, consistent and creditworthy.
members.conclusion: The unexplained injuries did not require rejection of the prosecution case, and the accused's contention was rejected.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_injuries_were_minor: The accused had injuries that were superficial or minor in nature.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_was_clear_and_credi: The prosecution evidence was clear and credible, with support from eyewitness and medical evidence.

members.legal_issue: The failure to explain a grievous injury sustained by an accused in the same occurrence does not by itself require rejection of a clear and trustworthy prosecution case.
material_facts: An accused sustained several injuries in the occurrence, including one established as grievous, and the prosecution did not explain them.
The courts found the evidence of the four eyewitnesses trustworthy and creditworthy.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution is ordinarily not obliged to explain every injury on an accused. An unexplained grievous injury may cause the court to view the prosecution case with suspicion, particularly where the witnesses are interested or inimical or the defence account is comparably probable. But under Mohar Rai v. State of Bihar, Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar, Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P., Ram Sunder Yadav v. State of Bihar, and Bhaba Nanda Sarma v. State of Assam, non-explanation alone does not require rejection of otherwise clear, cogent, and creditworthy evidence. The court applied these principles in the criminal appeal challenging the convictions.
members.conclusion: The unexplained grievous injury did not make the prosecution case fatal because the eyewitness evidence was clear, cogent, and trustworthy.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by a convicted person challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.grievous_injury_on_accused_unexplained: An accused sustained a grievous injury in the same occurrence, and the prosecution did not explain it.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_clear_and_trustwort: The court found the prosecution evidence clear, cogent, and trustworthy.

members.legal_issue: Unexplained injuries on an accused can materially undermine the prosecution case when they are supported by medical evidence and arise in circumstances where a complaint was made against the accused’s side.
material_facts: An accused had injuries that were confirmed by a doctor.
A complaint had been made by a family member of an accused against the deceased’s family.
The prosecution did not adequately explain the accused’s injuries, and the investigation did not properly place the related complaint and its disposition before the court.
members.legal_principle: When an accused’s injuries are established and the surrounding circumstances make their explanation material, the prosecution’s failure to explain them may be a serious defect in its case. Here, the Supreme Court considered that failure together with other evidentiary and investigative defects; it did not rely on an earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The failure to explain the accused’s injuries and the related investigative omissions were significant defects that, in the circumstances of this case, proved fatal to the prosecution case.

rule.if: criminal_case and accused_injuries_medically_confirmed and injuries_unexplained and related_counter_complaint

predicates.criminal_case: A court is deciding a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.accused_injuries_medically_confirmed: A medical witness confirmed that an accused had injuries.
predicates.injuries_unexplained: The prosecution did not explain how the accused sustained those injuries.
predicates.related_counter_complaint: A complaint was made against the victim’s side concerning the same incident or its surrounding events.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution need not explain simple and minor injuries on the accused when those injuries do not outweigh substantial reliable evidence of the crime.
material_facts: The accused had one incised wound each, which the doctor described as simple and minor.
The prosecution presented multiple independent witnesses who consistently described the attack and the accused carrying the deceased’s severed head.
The deceased had suffered numerous injuries, and the record did not establish that he caused or could have caused the accused’s injuries.
members.legal_principle: Whether the prosecution must explain injuries on an accused depends on the facts and circumstances. Simple, minor injuries do not outweigh consistent evidence from numerous independent witnesses, particularly where the evidence does not establish that the deceased caused those injuries.
members.conclusion: The failure to explain the accused’s minor injuries did not make the prosecution case suspect.

predicates.criminal_trial_for_offence: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove an accused person’s guilt.
predicates.accused_have_only_simple_minor_injuries: The accused’s injuries are limited and medically described as simple and minor.
predicates.multiple_independent_witnesses_give_cons: Several independent witnesses consistently describe the accused’s commission of the crime.
predicates.deceased_not_shown_to_have_caused_injuri: The evidence does not establish that the deceased caused or could have caused the accused’s injuries.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence and unexplained injuries to an accused do not defeat a prosecution case when the accused fails to establish the circumstances requiring defensive force and the prosecution evidence is clear and credible.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the deceased and his relatives began the fight and that the accused acted in private defence.
The accused relied on a counter-report that was not proved at trial and called no defence witnesses to establish their account of the incident.
One accused had injuries, but the medical evidence described them as simple, and the prosecution account was supported by credible eyewitness testimony.
members.legal_principle: The accused who claims private defence must establish the basic circumstances and occasion for exercising that right, and defensive force must be proportionate to the aggression. Although the prosecution should ordinarily explain injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence, non-explanation does not automatically defeat the case; it materially affects the prosecution only where the injuries were serious and were sustained at the time of the occurrence. Clear, cogent and creditworthy prosecution evidence may be accepted despite unexplained injuries. The Court relied on Rajender Singh v. State of Bihar, (2000) 4 SCC 298; Ram Sunder Yadav v. State of Bihar, (1998) 7 SCC 365; and Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P., (1990) 3 SCC 190.
members.conclusion: The private-defence claim was not established, and the failure to explain the accused’s injuries did not create a reasonable doubt or undermine the prosecution case.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and private_defence_claimed and accused_failed_to_establish_aggression and accused_injuries_were_simple and prosecution_evidence_was_clear_and_credible

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.private_defence_claimed: The accused said that they used force to defend themselves against an attack by the deceased or the deceased’s companions.
predicates.accused_failed_to_establish_aggression: The accused did not establish facts showing that the deceased or the deceased’s companions were the aggressors or that defensive force was necessary.
predicates.accused_injuries_were_simple: The medical evidence described the accused’s injuries as simple rather than serious.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_was_clear_and_credi: The prosecution presented evidence that the court found clear, credible and sufficient to distinguish the true account of the incident.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain serious injuries sustained by an accused during the occurrence may undermine its account, particularly when its witnesses are interested or inimical and the defence account is plausible.
material_facts: An accused had a grievous fracture and other serious injuries which the court found were sustained during the occurrence.
The prosecution did not explain those injuries, and some eyewitnesses said they had not seen any injuries on the accused.
The prosecution witnesses were interested or inimical, and the defence account that the occurrence arose in the accused’s plantain orchard was supported by evidence of damaged plants.
The evidence also suggested that the accused’s injuries and the circumstances of the occurrence could support either a claim of private defence or reasonable doubt about the prosecution account.
members.legal_principle: Under Mohar Rai v. State of Bihar, failure to explain injuries sustained by an accused in the occurrence may show that the prosecution witnesses’ account is untrue or not wholly true and may lend probability to the defence. State of Gujarat v. Bai Fatima and Puran Singh v. State of Punjab explain that the effect depends on the facts: it may support a right of private defence, make the prosecution version doubtful, or have no effect. The omission is especially significant where the injuries are serious and the evidence is interested or inimical, or the defence account competes in probability; it may matter less where injuries are minor or the prosecution evidence is exceptionally clear, independent and cogent.
members.conclusion: In the circumstances, the failure to explain the serious injuries was a major infirmity that made the prosecution version doubtful and the testimony of the witnesses unreliable; the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

rule.if: murder_prosecution and serious_occurrence_injuries_to_accused and prosecution_failed_to_explain_injuries and (witnesses_were_inimical or witnesses_denied_injuries or defence_account_was_plausible)

predicates.murder_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution for murder.
predicates.serious_occurrence_injuries_to_accused: An accused sustained serious injuries during the occurrence being tried.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_explain_injuries: The prosecution did not give a reasonable explanation for those injuries.
predicates.witnesses_were_inimical: The witnesses supporting the prosecution were interested in or hostile toward the accused.
predicates.witnesses_denied_injuries: One or more prosecution witnesses said they had not seen injuries on the accused.
predicates.defence_account_was_plausible: The defence gave an account of the occurrence that was supported by circumstances or evidence.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution’s failure to explain material injuries on an accused and to preserve relevant firearm evidence promptly can affect the assessment of its account, and does not permit an adverse inference against the defence for not having the firearm tested.
material_facts: The accused had injuries attributed to both a gunshot and blunt force, but the prosecution did not explain the non-gunshot injuries.
The firearm, cartridges and harrow were not collected promptly, and the firearm was not examined by a ballistic expert.
The firearm remained with a prosecution witness for several days before it was taken into custody.
members.legal_principle: The court stressed that material evidence should be collected and examined where it may resolve competing accounts, and that unexplained injuries on an accused are relevant to evaluating the prosecution case. It also noted that Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is intended to secure early information before it can be embellished or forgotten, but prompt reporting does not by itself establish the truth of the account. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: In the circumstances, it was the prosecution’s duty to preserve and test the firearm and related evidence, and no adverse inference could be drawn from the defence’s failure to have the firearm tested.
