rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_sustained_non_firearm_injuries and prosecution_failed_to_explain_injuries and relevant_firearm_not_seized_promptly

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.accused_sustained_non_firearm_injuries: An accused had injuries that could not be attributed to the firearm said to have been used in the incident.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_explain_injuries: The prosecution did not provide a supported explanation for the accused’s material injuries.
predicates.relevant_firearm_not_seized_promptly: The prosecution did not promptly take custody of and examine a firearm material to competing accounts of the incident.
predicates.no_adverse_inference_from_defence_failur: The court does not draw an adverse inference against the defence because it did not arrange testing of the firearm.

members.legal_issue: An accused may establish a plea of private defence by raising a reasonable doubt on the probabilities of the case, including where the prosecution has no plausible explanation for the injuries sustained by the accused.
material_facts: The accused specifically raised private defence in their statements under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Several accused had multiple injuries, some on vital parts, and the prosecution offered no plausible explanation for them.
The court considered the private-defence plea probable in light of the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: An accused need not establish private defence beyond reasonable doubt; it is sufficient if examination of the probabilities raises a reasonable doubt. The court considered the plea raised under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt on their plea of private defence.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_convictions and accused_raised_private_defence and accused_sustained_multiple_unexplained_injuries and some_injuries_were_on_vital_parts

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_convictions: The matter is an appeal against criminal convictions.
predicates.accused_raised_private_defence: The accused asserted that they acted in private defence.
predicates.accused_sustained_multiple_unexplained_i: The accused sustained multiple injuries that the prosecution did not plausibly explain.
predicates.some_injuries_were_on_vital_parts: Some of the accused's injuries were on vital parts of their bodies.
predicates.accused_entitled_to_benefit_of_doubt_on_: The accused are entitled to the benefit of doubt on their plea of private defence.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to investigate an occurrence report made by the accused and its withholding of evidence of their injuries can create reasonable doubt and serious prejudice, rather than amounting merely to defective investigation.
material_facts: The accused had lodged a report concerning the same occurrence, but the police did not investigate it.
Police evidence established that two accused had been admitted to hospital for injuries sustained in the occurrence and were discharged several days later.
The prosecution did not produce the accused persons’ injury report or explain its absence.
The courts had concurrently found that a verbal dispute and scuffle occurred and that both sides sustained injuries.
members.legal_principle: A fair criminal trial requires a fair investigation and the prosecution’s impartial disclosure of relevant material so the court can reach a just decision. Suppression of material relating to the accused, together with failure to investigate their report about the same occurrence, is distinguishable from a merely faulty investigation. The Court relied on Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal (2012) 8 SCC 263 and distinguished Gajoo v. State of Uttarakhand (2012) 9 SCC 532, which concerned failure to obtain a serologist report.
members.conclusion: The omissions were not merely defective investigation; withholding the relevant material caused serious prejudice and created doubts the prosecution could not answer. The Court declined to interfere with the High Court’s order.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_filed_report_about_same_occurrence and police_did_not_investigate_report and accused_received_treatment_for_occurrence_injuries and prosecution_withheld_injury_records and prosecution_could_not_explain_omissions

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_filed_report_about_same_occurren: The accused made a report concerning the same occurrence as the one prosecuted.
predicates.police_did_not_investigate_report: The police did not investigate the accused persons’ report about the occurrence.
predicates.accused_received_treatment_for_occurrenc: The accused received medical treatment for injuries sustained in the occurrence.
predicates.prosecution_withheld_injury_records: The prosecution did not place relevant records of the accused persons’ injuries before the court.
predicates.prosecution_could_not_explain_omissions: The prosecution could not explain why it failed to investigate the report or produce the injury records.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to explain injuries sustained by the accused in the same occurrence does not, by itself, require the prosecution case to be disbelieved.
material_facts: The accused sustained injuries during the same incident in which the deceased was attacked.
The prosecution did not explain those injuries apart from a statement in the complaint.
The eyewitness accounts were corroborated by medical evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Takhaji Hiraji v. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing (2001) 6 SCC 145, relying on Rajender Singh v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 298, Ram Sunder Yadav v. State of Bihar (1998) 7 SCC 365, and Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P. (1990) 3 SCC 190, the prosecution is not invariably obliged to explain injuries sustained by the accused in the same occurrence. Before non-explanation may affect the prosecution case, the injuries must have been serious and sustained during the occurrence. Even then, clear, cogent and credible evidence may prevent non-explanation from being a basis to reject the prosecution case.
members.conclusion: The accused’s unexplained injuries made it important to investigate the genesis of the occurrence, but they did not by themselves require rejection of the prosecution case.

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal from a conviction for causing a death.
predicates.accused_injuries_in_same_occurrence: The accused sustained injuries in the occurrence in which the deceased was injured.
predicates.accused_injuries_serious: The accused’s injuries were serious in nature.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_clear_cogent_and_cr: The prosecution evidence was clear, cogent and credible.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution’s suppression of the occurrence’s origin and failure to explain serious injuries, including a death, on the accused side may require acquittal rather than conviction on the basis of a free fight.
material_facts: The High Court noted that the parties disputed possession of the land where the occurrence took place and that the case arose from a cross-version.
The accused side had injuries, including serious head injuries to the appellants’ father, who later died, but the prosecution offered no explanation for those injuries.
The trial court did not discuss the defence evidence or exhibits concerning the accused side’s injuries.

The Supreme Court found that the prosecution had suppressed the origin and genesis of the occurrence and that the circumstances were not those of a free fight in which witnesses could not reasonably be expected to see and explain the defence injuries.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle applied in Lakshmi Singh and others v. State of Bihar, unexplained injuries on the accused side may support an adverse inference against the prosecution, particularly where the prosecution has suppressed the origin and genesis of the occurrence. The exception associated with a free fight applies where the occurrence may take place at different spots or in circumstances in which witnesses could not reasonably be expected to see and explain the defence injuries. The Court relied on no specific statutory provision as the basis for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not sustain the convictions by treating the case as a free fight; the appellants were entitled to the benefit of doubt and were acquitted of all charges.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and prosecution_suppressed_occurrence_genesis and prosecution_failed_to_explain_defence_injuries and serious_or_fatal_defence_injury and not free_fight_observation_exception

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by an accused challenging a criminal conviction.

predicates.prosecution_failed_to_explain_defence_in: The prosecution did not explain injuries sustained by people on the accused side.

predicates.free_fight_observation_exception: The occurrence took place in circumstances, such as at different spots, in which a witness could not reasonably be expected to see and explain the injuries on the accused side.

members.legal_issue: Permissive possession does not mature into adverse possession unless a hostile claim is asserted to the knowledge of the true owners for the requisite period.
material_facts: The property remained in the possession of the family's tenants.
The person who advanced the recovery amount and the later claimants could at most collect rent; their possession was, at most, symbolic and permissive because the initial possessor held a lien.
There was no evidence that any of those possessors asserted hostile title to the property to the knowledge of the true owners.
members.legal_principle: Permissive possession cannot become adverse possession without proof that the possessor asserted a hostile title to the knowledge of the true owners for twelve years or more. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.
members.conclusion: The possessors did not acquire title by adverse possession.

rule.if: property_recovery_suit and permissive_possession and not hostile_claim_known_for_limitation_period

predicates.property_recovery_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of property from persons claiming rights through possession.
predicates.permissive_possession: The possession began or continued with permission, including possession held only to secure reimbursement of an advance.
predicates.hostile_claim_known_for_limitation_perio: The possessor asserted a hostile title to the knowledge of the true owners for the requisite limitation period.

members.legal_issue: A claimant cannot establish title by adverse possession against a true owner without admitting that owner's title and proving the required hostile possession.
material_facts: The defendant denied the plaintiff's ownership and claimed the land both through inheritance as an adopted son and by adverse possession.
The plaintiff, whose ownership the lower courts upheld, was a party to the suit.
The defendant did not admit the plaintiff's ownership and failed to prove adverse possession; the lower courts' finding on that failure was concurrent.
members.legal_principle: A party claiming title by adverse possession bears the burden of proving the plea through proper pleadings and evidence. The claimant must proceed against the true owner, admit the owner's title to the owner's knowledge, and prove actual, peaceful, uninterrupted, hostile possession to the exclusion of the owner for the required period. A person who denies the true owner's title cannot successfully establish adverse possession against that owner.
members.conclusion: The defendant's adverse-possession plea could not succeed because he denied the true owner's title and did not prove the required possession; the concurrent finding against the plea was binding.

rule.if: adverse_possession_title_claim and (not true_owner_title_admitted or not true_owner_party or not hostile_continuous_possession_proved)

predicates.adverse_possession_title_claim: A person claims ownership of property on the basis of adverse possession.
predicates.true_owner_title_admitted: The claimant admits the true owner's title to the property to that owner's knowledge.
predicates.true_owner_party: The true owner is a party to the proceeding in which adverse possession is claimed.
predicates.hostile_continuous_possession_proved: The claimant proves actual, peaceful, uninterrupted, hostile possession to the exclusion of the true owner for the required period.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who denies the true owner’s title and asserts only long possession cannot establish title by adverse possession without pleading and proving possession hostile to the true owner.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s ownership based on an auction purchase was found established, and that finding was not disturbed.
The defendants asserted ancestral and continuous possession and denied that the property had vested in the authority that auctioned it or that the plaintiff owned it.
Some documents showed possession dating from 1963, but the defendants did not plead that their possession was hostile to the true owner.
The plaintiff filed a suit for possession on the basis of title in 1979.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, the person claiming title by adverse possession bears the burden of pleading and proving clear and unequivocal facts showing actual, open, peaceful, continuous and hostile possession, with the requisite animus possidendi and knowledge attributable to the true owner. Mere long possession or tax receipts are insufficient. A plea of adverse possession rests on acknowledging that ownership is in another; denying the true owner’s title without pleading possession hostile to that owner does not establish the plea. The Court relied on T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, Kurella Naga Druva Vudaya Bhaskara Rao v. Galla Jani Kamma, Brijesh Kumar v. Shardabai, Chatti Konati Rao v. Palle Venkata Subba Rao, Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur, M Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das, and the principles in P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy and Annakili v. A. Vedanayagam.
members.conclusion: The defendants had not established adverse possession; the High Court’s finding that their title had matured by adverse possession was legally unsustainable. The High Court’s judgment was set aside and the suit was decreed.

rule.if: suit_for_possession_on_title and adverse_possession_claimed and claimant_denied_true_owner_title and not hostile_possession_pleaded

predicates.suit_for_possession_on_title: A claimant brought a suit seeking possession on the basis of title.
predicates.adverse_possession_claimed: The opposing party claimed to have acquired title through adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_denied_true_owner_title: The party claiming adverse possession denied that the identified true owner held title to the property.
predicates.hostile_possession_pleaded: The party claiming adverse possession pleaded that its possession was hostile to the true owner.

members.legal_issue: A party claiming title by adverse possession must prove possession that clearly and unequivocally denies the true owner’s title; long possession or a belief that someone else owns the property is insufficient.
material_facts: The defendants claimed to have occupied the disputed property since 1969, put up a hutment, and paid municipal taxes.
They also claimed that the property belonged to the government and that they had acquired it by adverse possession.

The High Court treated their physical possession and the passage of time as sufficient, but the Supreme Court found that the evidence did not establish hostile possession denying the true owner’s title.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the party asserting adverse possession bears the burden of proving it affirmatively by clear and unequivocal evidence. Possession must be hostile to the true owner and amount to a denial of that owner’s title; its animus must be assessed from the facts and circumstances. Mere long possession is insufficient, and possession referable to a lawful title is not adverse. The Court relied on Annasaheb v. B.B. Patil and Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash, and referred to Ward v. Carttar in explaining hostile possession.
members.conclusion: The defendants had not established adverse possession, and the High Court’s decision concerning O.S. No. 168/85 was set aside.

rule.if: adverse_possession_defense_case and possession_longstanding and (true_owner_uncertain or hostile_denial_not_proved)

predicates.adverse_possession_defense_case: The proceeding includes a defendant's claim to have acquired title by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_longstanding: The claimant says that they have occupied the property for a substantial period.
predicates.true_owner_uncertain: The claimant's account shows that they were unsure who held the true title to the property.
predicates.hostile_denial_not_proved: The evidence does not clearly and unequivocally show possession hostile to, and denying the title of, the true owner.

members.legal_issue: Long possession does not establish title by adverse possession unless it is hostile to the true owner and continues with the necessary character for the limitation period.
material_facts: The claimant and her husband claimed the land under an allotment from the Slum Clearance Board and had paid instalments under that arrangement.
The claimant did not assert an independent claim by adverse possession before the writ appeal and did not claim adverse title from the commencement of possession.
The claimant relied on long possession, but the Board had no title to transfer the property.
The claimant did not establish the required hostile possession against the owners for the limitation period.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession requires possession adverse to the true owner, with animus possidendi existing from the commencement of possession and continuing for the prescribed period. Possession must be open, hostile, continuous, and adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent; mere long possession is insufficient. The Court relied on Saroop Singh v. Banto & Ors., T. Anjanappa & Ors. v. Somalingappa & Anr., and P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy & Ors. v. Revamma & Ors.
members.conclusion: The claimant had not acquired title by adverse possession; long possession and a claim derived from the Board did not establish the required hostile intent.

rule.if: possession_recovery_suit and adverse_possession_claim and (not hostile_intent_at_possession_start or not open_continuous_hostile_possession)

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: The plaintiff brings a proceeding seeking recovery of possession of property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The defendant claims to have acquired title through adverse possession.
predicates.hostile_intent_at_possession_start: The defendant’s possession was hostile to the true owner from its commencement.
predicates.open_continuous_hostile_possession: The defendant possessed the property openly, continuously, and in a manner hostile to the true owner for the required period.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who relies on title and adverse possession must establish the elements of adverse possession, including possession hostile to the true owner, and cannot rely on the two inconsistent claims without renouncing the title on which possession began.
material_facts: The government’s title was established through acquisition under the ancient-monuments legislation.
The government’s possession was not shown to have been to the exclusion of the Board with an intention to possess against it.
The government did not specifically plead and prove the Board’s earlier title or the point when the Board was dispossessed.
The government advanced both its own title and, alternatively, a claim of adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be peaceful, open, continuous, actual, visible, exclusive, and hostile to the true owner, and must be proved with adequate continuity, publicity, and extent. A claimant must plead and establish the nature and commencement of possession, the owner’s knowledge, its duration, and that it was open and undisturbed. Physical exclusive possession and animus possidendi are central. The Court relied on S. M. Karim v. Bibi Sakinal, AIR 1964 SC 1254; Parsinni v. Sukhi, (1993) 4 SCC 375; D. N. Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka, (1997) 7 SCC 567; Dr. Mahesh Chand Sharma v. Raj Kumari Sharma, (1996) 8 SCC 128; P. Periasami v. P. Periathambi, (1995) 6 SCC 523; and Mohan Lal v. Mirza Abdul Gaffar, (1996) 1 SCC 639. A claim based on title and a claim of adverse possession are mutually inconsistent unless the claimant disclaims the title under which possession began and proves hostile possession to the true owner’s knowledge.
members.conclusion: The alternative claim of adverse possession was unsustainable, and the High Court should not have granted relief on that ground.

rule.if: title_suit and (claimant_relies_on_own_title and adverse_possession_also_claimed) and (hostile_exclusive_possession_not_proved or prior_owner_or_dispossession_not_proved)

predicates.title_suit: The proceeding seeks a determination of title to property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_own_title: The claimant asserts that it owns the property under an independent source of title.
predicates.adverse_possession_also_claimed: The claimant also asserts that it acquired title through adverse possession.
predicates.hostile_exclusive_possession_not_proved: The claimant has not proved actual, exclusive possession with an intention to possess against the true owner.
predicates.prior_owner_or_dispossession_not_proved: The claimant has not established the other party’s prior title or when that party was dispossessed.

members.legal_issue: Longstanding permissive possession does not, by itself, become hostile possession sufficient to establish adverse title, particularly where the property has a unique impersonal character.
material_facts: The State's possession began permissively, and it continued for a long period.
The property was part of a special estate with a unique and impersonal character.
No issue of adverse possession had been claimed in the courts below.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a claim based on adverse possession requires possession that is adverse, not merely permissive. Permissive possession does not become hostile by the mere passage of time; the Court also relied on the property's unique and impersonal character and the absence of an adverse-possession issue in the courts below. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The State's long permissive possession did not establish adverse title to the property.

rule.if: title_dispute and adverse_possession_claim and possession_began_permissively and possession_was_longstanding and property_has_unique_impersonal_character

predicates.title_dispute: A civil dispute concerns title to property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: An occupant relies on possession as a basis for claiming title against another titleholder.
predicates.possession_began_permissively: The occupant began possessing the property with permission rather than hostile to the titleholder.
predicates.possession_was_longstanding: The occupant remained in possession for a long period.
predicates.property_has_unique_impersonal_character: The property has a distinctive character as an impersonal estate rather than ordinary personal property.

members.legal_issue: Possession held in the capacity of a pujari or agent, without a clear hostile assertion of shebaitship, does not bar a claim to the shebaitship by limitation.
material_facts: The widow performed worship and managed temple affairs in a role consistent with that of a pujari acting for the shebait.
The evidence did not establish that she had clearly asserted a right to shebaitship before making a will claiming an interest in the property.
The suit sought possession of temple property and recognition of the claimant’s shebaitship.
members.legal_principle: Possession in a subordinate or representative capacity, without a clear hostile assertion of the claimed right, does not establish adverse possession that bars the claim. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case in rejecting the limitation defence.
members.conclusion: The claim was not barred by limitation, and the defence that the widow had acquired shebaitship by adverse possession was rejected.

predicates.suit_concerns_recovery_of_temple_propert: The proceeding seeks recovery of temple property or recognition of the right to shebaitship.
predicates.possession_was_as_pujari_or_agent: The person in possession performed temple duties as a pujari or agent for the shebait.
predicates.clear_hostile_claim_of_shebaitship: The person in possession clearly asserted a claim to shebaitship hostile to the claimant’s right.
predicates.claim_not_barred_by_limitation: The claim is not barred by limitation.

members.legal_issue: A claimant establishes title by adverse possession only by proving possession hostile to the true owner and satisfying the required elements of that possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of land on the basis of their predecessor’s ownership.
The defendants claimed that they had purchased the land or entered possession under an agreement of sale, but neither the purported sale deed nor the agreement was produced.
The defendants relied on a tenant’s relinquishment of possession, but that relinquishment did not establish possession adverse to the true owner.
The defendants relied on a settlement proceeding, but the plaintiffs were not parties to it, no patta was issued to the defendants, and a rough patta was issued in the second plaintiff’s name.
The defendants did not establish the necessary facts showing that their possession was hostile to the true owner and continued openly and undisturbed for the required period.
members.legal_principle: Mere possession, however long, does not establish adverse possession. Possession must be actual, open, continuous, and hostile to the true owner’s title, and the claimant must prove the nature and commencement of possession, the owner’s knowledge, its duration, and that it was open and undisturbed. Once a plaintiff proves title, the burden shifts to the defendant claiming adverse possession to establish the necessary facts; the claimant has no equities in their favour. The Court relied on T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, (2006) 7 SCC 570; Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, (2004) 10 SCC 779; S.M. Karim v. Bibi Sakina, AIR 1964 SC 1254; Parsinni v. Sukhi, (1993) 4 SCC 375; D.N. Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka, (1997) 7 SCC 567; and Mahesh Chand Sharma v. Raj Kumari Sharma, (1996) 8 SCC 128. The judgment states that the plaintiff must prove title and possession within twelve years and that the defendant’s adverse possession must continue for twelve years thereafter.
members.conclusion: The defendants failed to prove title by adverse possession, so the Division Bench was right to reject that plea and decree the possession suit.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_in_possession_r: A defendant in a possession-recovery proceeding claims to have acquired title by adverse possession.
predicates.hostile_possession_not_established: The claimant has not established possession hostile to the true owner’s title.
predicates.required_adverse_possession_facts_not_es: The claimant has not established the required facts about the possession, including its nature, commencement, duration, openness, continuity, and the owner’s knowledge.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_fails: The claim to title by adverse possession fails.

members.legal_issue: A claimant relying on adverse possession must plead and prove the facts establishing actual, hostile, continuous, exclusive, and undisturbed possession to the knowledge of the true owner.
material_facts: The claimant sought ownership on the basis of alleged possession extending over time.

The Supreme Court stated that the claim required pleading and proof of actual possession, the period and date from which possession was claimed, continuity, exclusivity, lack of disturbance, and a hostile claim communicated to the true owner.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether those requirements were satisfied on the evidence and expressly left the merits for the High Court on remand.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides for extinguishment of the lawful owner's right to property when the owner does not sue for possession within the time allowed by law. A claimant relying on adverse possession must plead and prove the date and period of actual possession, that it was continuous, exclusive and undisturbed to the knowledge of the true owner, and that the claimant asserted and communicated a hostile title. The Court identified the application of Article 64, including whether a tenant's possession could be counted as the claimant's possession, as a question left for determination on remand.
members.conclusion: A claim to ownership by adverse possession requires the claimant to plead and prove the specified elements; the Supreme Court made no determination that the claimant in this case had done so.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The claimant asserted a right to property on the basis of adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_seeks_ownership_by_prescriptive: The claimant relied on possession over time as the basis for claiming ownership.

members.legal_issue: A claimant cannot acquire title to acquired land by adverse possession without pleading and proving the required hostile, known, acquiesced-in, and uninterrupted possession after possession has been taken and delivered.
material_facts: The claimants relied on adverse possession to assert title to land that had been acquired and delivered to the beneficiary.

They did not plead and prove that, after delivery of possession, they asserted their own right to the beneficiary's knowledge, that the beneficiary acquiesced, and that their possession was uninterrupted and nec vi, nec clam, nec precario.
members.legal_principle: A claim of adverse possession requires pleading and proof that, after possession has been taken and handed over, the claimant asserted a right hostile to the owner to the owner's knowledge, the owner acquiesced, and possession remained uninterrupted, nec vi, nec clam, nec precario. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The claimants acquired no title by adverse possession.

rule.if: acquisition_title_dispute and adverse_possession_claim and not (post_delivery_hostile_assertion_proved and owner's_knowledge_and_acquiescence_proved and uninterrupted_nec_vi_nec_clam_nec_precario_possession_proved)

predicates.acquisition_title_dispute: The dispute concerns a claim to land after possession has been taken in an acquisition proceeding and delivered to its beneficiary.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A claimant asserts that possession of the land has given them title by adverse possession.
predicates.post_delivery_hostile_assertion_proved: The claimant pleaded and proved that, after delivery of possession, they asserted their own right hostile to the owner.
predicates.owner's_knowledge_and_acquiescence_prove: The claimant pleaded and proved that the owner knew of the hostile assertion and acquiesced in it.
predicates.uninterrupted_nec_vi_nec_clam_nec_precar: The claimant pleaded and proved uninterrupted possession that was not by force, in secrecy, or by permission.

members.legal_issue: A claim to acquire title to public property by adverse possession fails unless the claimant proves open, hostile, continuous possession with the required animus for the required period by clear and reliable evidence.
material_facts: The property was owned by the State, and the claimant relied on adverse possession to establish title against that ownership.
The claimant's pleaded account of possession did not cover the required period, and the assertion of earlier possession by a predecessor was first raised during trial.
The claimed construction was supported only by oral assertion, and the electricity and water records were not reliably connected to the property through supporting evidence.
The evidence did not establish the nature, openness, hostility, continuity, or animus of possession for the required period.
members.legal_principle: Possession must be nec vi, nec clam, nec precario: adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent to be adverse to the true owner, and it cannot become adverse before actual possession with the required animus. The claimant bears the burden of proving hostile possession by clear and unequivocal evidence. In a claim against public property, the required ingredients must be established for the required period. The Court relied on P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, Secretary of State for India in Council v. Debendra Lal Khan, and Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil v. Balwant.
members.conclusion: The claimant had not proved acquisition of title by adverse possession, and the lower courts' judgments and decree were set aside and the suit dismissed.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_against_public_: The claimant seeks title by adverse possession against property owned by a public body.
predicates.required_period_of_hostile_possession_no: The claimant's evidence does not establish open, hostile, continuous possession with the required animus for the required period.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who claims adverse possession against the State through possession derived from an assignee must plead and establish a hostile claim brought to the State's knowledge and the State's failure to act within the prescribed period.
material_facts: The purchaser entered possession through a transfer from the original grantee, who had no right to alienate the assigned land.
The purchaser claimed to have possessed the land for more than twelve years but did not disclaim the derivative title or plead and prove a hostile claim brought to the State's knowledge.
No evidence established that the State knew of a hostile claim and failed to act within the prescribed period.
members.legal_principle: A person who enters possession under a derivative title from a grantee who could not alienate the land must disclaim that title and plead a hostile claim to the State's knowledge; the claimant must also establish that the State did not act within the prescribed period. Mere possession for a period of time does not establish adverse possession against the State. The Court distinguished K.T. Huchegowda v. Deputy Commissioner on the circumstances before it.
members.conclusion: The purchaser had not established title by adverse possession, and there was no need to remit the matter for reconsideration.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_in_assigned_lan: The proceeding concerns a claim of adverse possession against the State relating to assigned land.
predicates.possession_derived_from_assignee: The claimant's possession began through a transfer from the assignee rather than through an independent entry.
predicates.hostile_claim_to_state_not_pleaded_and_p: The claimant did not plead and establish a disclaimer of the derivative title and a hostile claim known to the State, together with the State's failure to act within the prescribed period.

members.legal_issue: Long possession does not establish title by adverse possession without possession that is sufficiently continuous, open, and extensive and an intention to possess adversely for the required period.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that his possession began under a lease and that he could add his predecessor’s possession to his own.

The lease agreement relied on for the earlier start date was altered, and the later registered lease was a separate document; the claimant did not establish possession for the required period before the State’s suit.
The claimant claimed under a lease rather than asserting hostile title, and he pleaded adverse possession only in the later suit.
He applied for occupancy rights and paid an assessment, conduct inconsistent with an intention to hold the land against the State’s title.
The Special Court and High Court found that the claimant had not established the required period of possession or the necessary intention.
members.legal_principle: A person claiming title by adverse possession must establish possession that is adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent, together with animus possidendi against the true owner for the required statutory period. The Court relied on S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina and Balkrishan v. Satyaprakash. Where the claimant initially possesses under a lease, the period of adverse possession starts only when both actual possession and an assertion of hostile title are established. Applying Section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908, the later registered lease related back only to its own execution, not to the earlier unregistered agreement; the Court distinguished Thakur Kishan Singh v. Arvind Kumar. An application for occupancy rights did not interrupt physical possession, but it contradicted the required hostile intention. Possession under a continuing lease could not be tacked as adverse possession against the State or the lessor.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not acquire title by adverse possession.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A party claims ownership of land on the basis of adverse possession.
predicates.possession_period_insufficient: The party fails to prove possession for the required statutory period, including by a valid basis for adding a predecessor’s possession.
predicates.hostile_intention_not_continuous: The party fails to prove a continuous intention to possess the land against the true owner, including because the party claims under a lease or seeks recognition of an occupancy right.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who asserts title solely through adverse possession must prove that claim with satisfactory evidence.
material_facts: The claimants asserted title against the State through alleged continuous possession by their predecessors and themselves for about a century.
They did not rely on a grant, lease deed, or patta from the State.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the evidence was inadequate to establish adverse possession, and no error of law in that finding was shown.
members.legal_principle: The burden of proving a pleaded claim of adverse possession lies on the claimant, who must support it with satisfactory evidence. A finding on that factual question, when concurrently made and not shown to contain an error of law, is binding in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC.
members.conclusion: The claimants failed to prove title by adverse possession, and the concurrent finding against their claim stood.

rule.if: civil_title_claim and title_claimed_only_by_adverse_possession and claimant_bears_burden and evidence_is_insufficient and concurrent_finding_against_claim

predicates.civil_title_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to title to property.
predicates.title_claimed_only_by_adverse_possession: The claimant relies solely on possession said to have been adverse to the asserted owner.
predicates.claimant_bears_burden: The party asserting adverse possession is responsible for proving it.
predicates.evidence_is_insufficient: The evidence does not satisfactorily establish the asserted adverse possession.
predicates.concurrent_finding_against_claim: The lower courts have both found that the claimant failed to prove adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: A plea of adverse possession between co-holders raises a title issue for referral only when the pleadings set out the essential facts constituting ouster and adverse possession.
material_facts: The opposing co-holder claimed exclusive title by adverse possession in resisting the partition suit.

The written statement did not specifically plead all essential ingredients of ouster, including hostile animus, uninterrupted possession for the required period, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to the knowledge of the other co-holders.
The defence also relied on alleged events predating the creation of the statutory co-holder rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 186(1) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act requires referral when a question of title is directly and substantially in issue; its explanation excludes a clearly untenable plea intended solely to oust the revenue court's jurisdiction. Section 332 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act was identified as in pari materia. For co-holders, possession is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all; adverse possession requires ouster or its equivalent, including hostile animus, long and uninterrupted possession, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to the knowledge of the other co-holder. The concurring judgment relied on Gaya Parshad Dikshit v. Nirmal Chander, Ezaz Ali v. Special Manager, Court of Wards, Maharajadhiraj of Burdhwan v. Subodh Gopal Bose, P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, Karbali Begum v. Mohd Sayeed, Coera v. Appuhamy, and Mohd. Zain-ul-Abdin v. Syed Ahmad Mohiuddin. It also relied on Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank for the proposition that statutory landholding rights are newly created rights.
members.conclusion: The written statement did not adequately raise a title issue, so there was no occasion to frame an issue or refer it to the civil court. The concurring judgment agreed that the appeal should be allowed on this ground, while disagreeing that the absence of a limitation period itself made an adverse-possession plea untenable.

predicates.statutory_partition_suit_by_coholder: A co-holder brought a statutory proceeding seeking partition of a common holding.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_against_coholde: Another co-holder claimed exclusive title against the claimant through adverse possession.
predicates.pleading_omits_essential_ouster_facts: The written defence did not set out the essential facts of hostile, uninterrupted, open, and known-to-the-other co-holder exclusive possession.

members.legal_issue: Permissive possession becomes adverse only when cogent and convincing evidence establishes hostile possession to the knowledge of the true owner.
material_facts: The person claiming adverse possession initially entered the land under a licence to operate a brick-kiln.
The appellate court considered the evidence and found that the possession was not adverse.
No cogent evidence established hostile animus and possession adverse to the knowledge of the true owner.
members.legal_principle: A licensee's, agent's, co-owner's, or other permissive possession must be shown by cogent and convincing evidence to involve hostile animus and possession adverse to the knowledge of the real owner. Mere possession for any length of time does not convert permissive possession into adverse possession.
members.conclusion: The person in possession did not acquire rights by adverse possession; the permissive possession did not become adverse merely through its duration.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_in_possession_s: A person resisting a claim for possession asserts that they acquired rights by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_began_with_permission: The person asserting adverse possession initially entered or remained in possession with the owner's permission.
predicates.cogent_evidence_of_hostility_known_to_ow: Cogent and convincing evidence shows hostile possession adverse to the true owner and brought to that owner's knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A claimant relying on adverse possession must disclose and prove when the adverse possession began and when it became complete.
material_facts: The plaintiffs amended their plaint to plead adverse possession after losing in the trial court in the first round of proceedings.
They did not establish when their alleged adverse possession began or when it became complete.
The Tehsildar had declared the plaintiffs encroachers in 1978.
members.legal_principle: A party pleading adverse possession must disclose and prove when the possession became adverse and when the required period of possession was completed. The court particularly noted the prior declaration that the plaintiffs were encroachers. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to prove their adverse-possession claim.

rule.if: civil_land_title_suit and claimant_relies_on_adverse_possession and claimant_did_not_prove_start_of_adverse_possession and claimant_did_not_prove_completion_of_adverse_possession and claimant_was_declared_an_encroacher

predicates.civil_land_title_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit in which a plaintiff claims rights to land.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_adverse_possession: The claimant relies on adverse possession as a basis for acquiring rights to land.
predicates.claimant_did_not_prove_start_of_adverse_: The claimant did not prove when the possession became adverse.
predicates.claimant_did_not_prove_completion_of_adv: The claimant did not prove when the adverse possession became complete.
predicates.claimant_was_declared_an_encroacher: An authority had declared the claimant an encroacher over the land.

members.legal_issue: A claim to ownership by adverse possession requires clear pleading and proof of possession that is open, continuous, and hostile, including when it became adverse; long possession alone is insufficient.
material_facts: The state authority alleged possession over an extended period but did not establish it with documentary evidence.
The authority did not plead when its possession became adverse or clearly plead denial of the private owners’ title.
Revenue records showed the property in the private owners’ names, and the authority’s alleged long possession was found unproved.
members.legal_principle: A person claiming adverse possession must clearly plead and establish the facts necessary to make the possession adverse; it must be adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent, and long possession by itself is not adverse possession. The Court relied on S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina and on P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, as discussed in Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan.
members.conclusion: The state authority failed to establish adverse possession, and the courts below properly rejected its claim; the Supreme Court dismissed its special leave petition.

predicates.adverse_possession_ownership_claim: A claimant in a property ownership proceeding asserts that possession has given the claimant title by adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_plead_when_possession_: The claimant does not clearly state when possession became adverse to the owner’s title.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_prove_open_continuous_: The claimant does not establish possession that was open, continuous, and hostile to the owner.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who enters possession under a derivative title from a grantee must establish the elements of adverse possession against the State, including a hostile claim disclaimed from the derivative title and brought to the State’s knowledge.
material_facts: The purchasers acquired the land through sale deeds from the original grantees, whose grants restricted alienation.
Their pleadings stated that they remained in possession and enjoyment after purchase but did not plead that they had disclaimed their derivative title or asserted a hostile title against the State.
There was no evidence that they had continuously possessed the land while asserting a hostile claim against the State to its knowledge.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be nec vi, clam, nec precario, with possession adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent to show hostility to the true owner. A purchaser who entered under a derivative title must plead and prove when and how that title was disclaimed, and that a hostile claim was asserted to the State’s knowledge without action by the State within the prescribed period. This follows R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka, applying the principles in Lakshmi Reddy, State for India v. Debendra Lal Khan, Kshitish Chandra, and Danappa Revappa Kolli v. Gurupadappa Kallappa Patana Shetti.
members.conclusion: The purchasers did not establish adverse possession against the State, and their claim could not defeat the proceedings to recover the granted land.

rule.if: appeal_from_granted_land_recovery_proceeding and purchaser_entered_under_grantee_title and no_hostile_disclaimer_pleaded and no_hostile_claim_to_state_proved

predicates.appeal_from_granted_land_recovery_procee: The case is an appeal arising from proceedings to recover land granted subject to restrictions on transfer.
predicates.purchaser_entered_under_grantee_title: The claimant entered possession through a transfer from the original grantee.
predicates.no_hostile_disclaimer_pleaded: The claimant did not plead that they disclaimed the title under which they entered and asserted a hostile title.
predicates.no_hostile_claim_to_state_proved: The claimant did not prove that a hostile claim was asserted to the State’s knowledge.

members.legal_issue: Long possession does not establish title by adverse possession unless it is accompanied by an open, continuous, hostile possession and a positive intention to dispossess the owner.
material_facts: The claimants asserted that they had possessed the land for more than fifty years and had exercised ownership rights over it.
Their possession followed purchases of land, including land previously conveyed to another claimant.
The claimants’ own evidence indicated that they learned of the other claimant’s rights only when their possession was challenged.
The Court found that the circumstances showed possession and an intention to possess, but did not establish the required positive intention to dispossess.
members.legal_principle: A claim of adverse possession requires a two-pronged inquiry: the limitation period must have run against the owner, and the possessor must have a positive intention to dispossess the owner. Intention to possess is not a substitute for intention to dispossess. Possession must be peaceful, open, continuous, exclusive, and hostile, in the sense of being sufficiently evident to give the owner reasonable notice. The Court relied on Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and on Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, Saroop Singh v. Banto, Thakur Kishan Singh v. Arvind Kumar, and Powell v. Macfarlane.
members.conclusion: Long possession alone was insufficient; the claimant must establish an intention to dispossess that is openly manifested and gives the owner reasonable notice and an opportunity to object.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and possession_is_long and (intent_to_possess_only or hostile_intent_not_openly_manifested)

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A possessor claims that possession has extinguished another person’s title and vested title in the possessor.
predicates.possession_is_long: The possessor has occupied or used the property for a lengthy period.
predicates.intent_to_possess_only: The possessor’s conduct shows an intention to occupy or use the property but does not show an intention to exclude the owner.
predicates.hostile_intent_not_openly_manifested: The possessor has not made an intention to exclude the owner sufficiently open and evident to give the owner reasonable notice.

members.legal_issue: A claimant asserting title by adverse possession must plead and prove when possession became adverse, the nature and extent of that possession, and facts showing that it was hostile to the identified owner.
material_facts: The claimants asserted that their possession had been open, continuous, uninterrupted, and hostile for more than fifty years.
Their pleadings and evidence did not disclose when their possession became adverse or adequately set out how it became open, continuous, and hostile.
The claimants’ asserted possession followed conveyances, one of which concerned land previously conveyed to another claimant.
The claimants had established no evidentiary basis for identifying a starting point from which adverse possession could be measured.
members.legal_principle: A plea of adverse possession is a mixed question of fact and law. The claimant must clearly plead and prove the starting point of adverse possession, the nature of possession, whether it was known to the owner, its duration, and whether it was open and undisturbed; the true owner must also be identified. Under Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, once the opposing party establishes title, the burden of proving adverse possession lies on the claimant. The Court relied on S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, Saroop Singh v. Banto, T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, and Narne Rama Murthy v. Ravula Somasundaram. It contrasted this allocation of the burden with Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
members.conclusion: The claimants had not pleaded and proved the facts necessary to establish adverse possession.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and (adverse_start_not_pleaded or possession_characteristics_not_proved or true_owner_not_identified)

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A claimant seeks to defeat another person’s title by asserting ownership through possession.
predicates.adverse_start_not_pleaded: The claimant has not pleaded when the possession became hostile to the owner.
predicates.possession_characteristics_not_proved: The claimant has not proved the nature, openness, continuity, extent, or notice of the claimed adverse possession.
predicates.true_owner_not_identified: The claimant has not specifically identified the person whose title the possession is said to have displaced.

members.legal_issue: Possession held as a servant or servitor is permissive, and a possession claim is not time-barred by adverse possession unless hostile possession is established for the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The defendants possessed the property as servants or servitors, and their possession was permissive.
In the earlier tribunal proceedings, the defendants claimed the status of servitors rather than setting up a hostile title against the claimant.
The suit for possession was filed after those proceedings, but the record did not establish hostile possession for the applicable limitation period.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, permissive possession does not itself establish adverse possession. Where possession began permissively, the claimant relying on limitation must establish possession hostile to the person entitled to the property for the applicable limitation period; Article 142 did not apply on these facts. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation under either Article 142 or Article 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

rule.if: possession_ejectment_suit and possession_began_as_servitor_or_servant and possession_was_permissive and hostile_title_not_established_for_limitation_period

predicates.possession_ejectment_suit: A party brought a suit seeking possession by ejecting persons in occupation.
predicates.possession_began_as_servitor_or_servant: The occupants entered or remained in possession in the capacity of servants or servitors.
predicates.possession_was_permissive: The occupants’ possession was initially allowed by the person or institution for whom they served.
predicates.hostile_title_not_established_for_limita: The evidence did not establish possession asserted adversely to the person entitled to the property for the applicable limitation period.
predicates.suit_not_barred_by_adverse_possession: The suit is not barred on the ground that the occupants acquired title by adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming ownership by adverse possession must prove possession that is open, continuous, peaceful, and hostile to the true owner, together with the intention to possess adversely and facts establishing when the possession became adverse.
material_facts: The claimant asserted ownership of the land, while the trial court described possession extending over many years and also found that the claimant had forcibly taken possession in 1960 and remained in possession until 1986.
The claimant did not plead adverse possession, and no issue on that basis was framed.

The first appellate court and the High Court found that the claimant had failed to establish title; the Supreme Court endorsed their findings and held that he had not established title by adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be nec vi, nec clam, nec precario and adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent; it must be actual, visible, exclusive, hostile, and continued for the applicable statutory period. The claimant must establish the nature and duration of possession, that it was open and known or capable of being known to the owner, the hostile claim and animus possidendi, and when the possession became adverse. The Court relied on Secretary of State for India v. Debendra Lal Khan, P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, S.M. Karim v. Bibi Sakina, R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka, D.N. Venkatarayappa v. State of Karnataka, Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagadish Kalita, Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, Saroop Singh v. Banto, M. Durai v. Muthu, T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, and P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma. The Court discussed Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and Articles 142 and 144 of the former Limitation Act.
members.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish that he had perfected title by adverse possession.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_title_suit and adverse_possession_claim and (not hostile_possession_proven or not open_continuous_possession_proven or not animus_possidendi_proven or not adverse_starting_point_identified)

predicates.civil_appeal_from_title_suit: A party brought a civil appeal arising from a suit seeking a declaration of ownership over property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A claimant relies on possession as the basis for acquiring ownership against the true owner.
predicates.hostile_possession_proven: The claimant proved possession asserting a hostile title in denial of the true owner’s title.
predicates.open_continuous_possession_proven: The claimant proved possession that was open and continuous for the required period.
predicates.animus_possidendi_proven: The claimant proved an intention to possess the property adversely to the true owner.
predicates.adverse_starting_point_identified: The claimant identified when possession became adverse so that the start of the applicable limitation period could be determined.

members.legal_issue: Permissive possession does not become adverse possession through duration alone; the possessor must establish hostile possession and hostile animus to the knowledge of the owner.
material_facts: The land was delivered to the defendant for cultivation on a share-cropping basis for a limited period.
The defendant remained in possession, but the lower courts found no evidence that he asserted a hostile title against the owner.
Revenue records supported the finding that the possession was permissive and that the plaintiff remained the owner.
The defendant relied on the alleged sale as the basis of entry, but the alleged sale was not proved.
members.legal_principle: A person whose possession began permissively must prove, by cogent and convincing evidence, hostile animus and possession adverse to the knowledge of the real owner; mere long possession does not convert permissive possession into adverse possession. The Court relied on Thakur Kishan Singh (Dead) v. Arvind Kumar, (1994) 6 SCC 591.
members.conclusion: The defendant did not acquire title by adverse possession because he failed to establish when or how his permissive possession became hostile to the owner.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim and permissive_entry and not hostile_animus_proved

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A person claims title to property by adverse possession.
predicates.permissive_entry: The person entered or remained in possession with the owner's permission or under an arrangement that did not assert ownership against the owner.
predicates.hostile_animus_proved: The person proves an assertion of hostile title and possession adverse to the owner's knowledge.

members.legal_issue: Long possession does not establish title by adverse possession against public land unless the claimant proves actual possession that was open, continuous and hostile to the true owner, with the necessary hostile intent.
material_facts: The occupants claimed that they and their predecessor had possessed and cultivated the public land for many decades.
They produced mainly disputed or illegible photocopies of notices and did not establish when possession began or provide credible proof of hostile possession for the required period.
They paid land revenue and sought assignment or regularisation of the land from the government.
The special forums rejected their adverse-possession claim, but the High Court accepted it.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession requires possession that is adequate in continuity, publicity and extent, hostile to the true owner, and accompanied by animus possidendi; long possession alone is insufficient. Actual possession with the necessary hostile intent must be shown from the commencement of the adverse possession. The Court relied on P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, State of Rajasthan v. Harphool Singh, Annakili v. A. Vedanayagam and P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma. A claim against public property calls for particular seriousness and circumspection because it may destroy the State’s title.
members.conclusion: The occupants failed to prove title by adverse possession, and the High Court was not justified in finding otherwise.

predicates.public_land_adverse_possession_claim: An occupant claimed title by adverse possession over land owned by the public.
predicates.no_credible_proof_of_hostile_possession: The claimant did not provide credible evidence establishing when possession began and that it was open, continuous and hostile to the owner.
predicates.claimant_acknowledged_owner_control: The claimant acted in a manner recognizing the public owner’s control, such as seeking assignment or regularisation or paying land revenue.
predicates.adverse_possession_title_not_established: The claimant did not establish title by adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: Title by adverse possession requires open, continuous, hostile possession, but not possession shown to have come to the owner's specific knowledge.
material_facts: The claimant and his predecessor asserted hostile title and possessed the land continuously for more than thirty years.
They used the land themselves and let it for cultivation, and their conduct was alleged and found to be open rather than concealed.
The municipality knew of the hostile claim, made some attempts to prevent use of the land, but made no serious effort to evict the claimant during the period of possession.
The claimant was dispossessed after a magistrate's order in proceedings concerning possession.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be continuous, open, and without concealment. It need not be so effective as to establish the owner's specific knowledge, except where ouster of title is pleaded. The judgment cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this principle.
members.conclusion: The claimant acquired title by prescription; the High Court applied an incorrect test by requiring possession to be effective enough to bring it to the owner's specific knowledge.

predicates.claim_for_title_by_adverse_possession: The proceeding includes a claim to acquire title through adverse possession.
predicates.possession_was_open_continuous_and_hosti: The claimant possessed the property continuously, openly and in assertion of a title hostile to the owner's title.
predicates.possession_exceeded_the_applicable_limit: The hostile possession continued for longer than the period required for title by prescription.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot claim title under a transaction and simultaneously claim adverse possession from the same commencement of possession without renouncing the title-based claim and establishing when possession became hostile.
material_facts: The defendant’s wife was said to have entered possession under an alleged sale agreement in 1976, and the defense claimed both ownership under documents relating to that transaction and adverse possession from the same period.
The alleged sale agreement and related documents were not proved, and the defense did not establish when possession became hostile to the owner.
members.legal_principle: Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India states that title and adverse possession are mutually inconsistent and that adverse possession does not begin until the title-based claim is renounced. Mohan Lal v. Mirza Abdul Gaffar likewise requires a person who entered under an agreement to disclaim that right and prove an independent hostile assertion to the knowledge of the owner or successor. P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma and Ram Nagina Rai v. Deo Kumar Rai support the need to identify when the owner was dispossessed and when possession became adverse.
members.conclusion: The claims of title under the alleged transaction and adverse possession from the same date were incompatible; adverse possession could not be recognized from that date without proof of when possession became hostile.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_possession_decree and claimant_asserts_transaction_based_title and claimant_asserts_adverse_possession_from_same_entry and hostile_possession_start_not_established

predicates.civil_appeal_from_possession_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree concerning possession of property.
predicates.claimant_asserts_transaction_based_title: The claimant relies on a transaction as the basis for title to the property.
predicates.claimant_asserts_adverse_possession_from: The claimant also alleges that adverse possession began when possession was taken under that transaction.
predicates.hostile_possession_start_not_established: The claimant has not established when possession became hostile to the true owner.

members.legal_issue: Adverse possession is not established unless the claimant proves possession that is open, peaceful, continuous and hostile to the true owner, identifies when it became hostile, and supports the claim with cogent evidence.
material_facts: The alleged adverse possessor was not examined at trial.
The alleged possession was said to have arisen from consideration paid under a sale agreement, but that agreement and related documents were found unreliable and were not proved.
The defense did not establish the date on which possession became hostile to the true owner.
The courts found serious discrepancies and alterations in the documents relied on to support the defense.
members.legal_principle: Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India requires possession to be nec vi, nec clam, nec precario: adequate in continuity, publicity and extent, and adverse to the true owner. P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma and M. Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das emphasize the need to establish the starting point of adverse possession. Ram Nagina Rai v. Deo Kumar Rai requires a party to plead and prove when permissive possession became adverse. The claim must have a clear and cogent basis because it defeats the true owner’s rights.
members.conclusion: The claim of adverse possession was not proved, and the appellants failed to establish that the defendant’s wife had perfected title by adverse possession.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_possession_decree and claimant_relies_on_adverse_possession and alleged_adverse_possessor_not_examined and hostile_possession_start_not_established and supporting_documents_unproved

predicates.civil_appeal_from_possession_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree concerning possession of property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_adverse_possession: The defending party relies on adverse possession to resist the owner’s claim to possession.
predicates.alleged_adverse_possessor_not_examined: The person alleged to have acquired title by adverse possession is not examined in support of that claim.
predicates.hostile_possession_start_not_established: The claimant has not established when possession became hostile to the true owner.
predicates.supporting_documents_unproved: Documents relied on to support the claimed basis of possession have not been proved.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee’s continued possession does not become adverse possession without proof that a hostile title was asserted to the owner’s knowledge.
material_facts: The mortgagee’s successors remained in possession after the debt was discharged.
There was no evidence showing when they asserted a title hostile to the mortgagor’s successors or that the latter knew of and acquiesced in such an assertion.
The mortgagor’s successors applied to recover possession under the special scheme.
members.legal_principle: A possession-based claim to ownership requires proof that the possessor asserted a hostile title to the owner’s knowledge. Mere continued possession, including possession that began as mortgagee possession, does not establish adverse possession without that proof. The court also held that no limitation period was prescribed under the scheme for an application to recover possession.
members.conclusion: The mortgagee’s successors did not establish title by adverse possession.

predicates.application_for_possession_under_special: The person entitled to possession applied to recover it through a special statutory scheme.
predicates.possession_began_as_mortgagee: The possessor entered or continued in possession in the capacity of a mortgagee.
predicates.no_hostile_title_known_to_owner_proved: The claimant did not prove that a hostile title was asserted and brought to the owner’s knowledge.

members.legal_issue: Possession that was held in a permissive or non-owner capacity does not establish adverse possession unless the claimant pleads and proves when and how it became open, hostile, and adverse.
material_facts: The earlier final judgment established that the respondents and their predecessor possessed the property as Pujaris and that their claim of ownership had been rejected.
The respondents claimed adverse possession based on the predecessor's alleged ownership and long possession.
The respondents neither pleaded nor proved that their possession became adverse after the earlier judgment, or the time and manner of any such change.
members.legal_principle: Where possession was initially held in a non-owner capacity and a competent court has rejected the possessor's claim of title, the claimant must allege and prove that the possession later became open, hostile, and adverse, including the time and manner of the change. Possession alone, without proof of that change, does not establish adverse title.
members.conclusion: The respondents did not establish title by adverse possession.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim: A party claims title to property through adverse possession.
predicates.prior_judgment_established_nonowner_poss: A prior final judgment established that the claimant or predecessor possessed the property in a non-owner capacity.
predicates.no_pleaded_or_proved_hostile_conversion: The claimant neither pleads nor proves when and how that possession became open, hostile, and adverse.

members.legal_issue: A former owner need not be given a further opportunity to ask the government to use other land or leave the acquired land out of the acquisition after the acquisition process is complete.
material_facts: The appellant asked for an opportunity to make a representation to the State Government.
The acquisition process had already been completed by the taking of possession.
The appellant owned substantial other land and was not thereby prevented from continuing its proposed educational activity.
members.legal_principle: Where the acquisition process has already been completed, the Court need not give the former owner liberty to seek a discretionary change from the government; the appellant's ownership of other land also meant the acquisition did not disable its proposed educational activity.
members.conclusion: No further opportunity to make a representation was required.

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition: A party challenged a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_process_completed: The acquisition process had been completed, including the taking of possession.
predicates.former_owner_has_other_suitable_land: The former owner has other land and is not thereby prevented from pursuing the activity for which it sought the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption decree based on an intermediary’s proprietary interest cannot be executed for possession after that interest has vested in the State and ceased to exist.
material_facts: A co-sharer obtained a pre-emption decree concerning a share in land and deposited the sale consideration before the land reform law took effect in the area.
The vendees remained in possession, so the decree-holder later sought execution to obtain possession.
Before execution was sought, the proprietary interests in the land had vested in the State, leaving the former proprietors with no surviving interest on which to base execution.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 6(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, intermediary rights, title and interest in the land vest in the State and cease to exist. A decree based on those former rights cannot be executed after they have lapsed, even without an express provision invalidating the decree. Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank Ltd. held that, absent the special remedy under section 6(h), a mortgage decree had nothing to proceed against once the former proprietary rights were extinguished; section 6(h), read with section 73 of the Transfer of Property Act, provided a remedy against compensation money. That reasoning answers the claim that the pre-emption decree survived. Shivashankar Prasad Shah v. Baikunth Nath Singh followed Rana Sheo Ambar Singh. The court expressed no opinion on any rights that might arise under section 18, and noted that Kailash Rai v. Jai Jai Ram concerned the meaning of possession under that section.
members.conclusion: The pre-emption decree was incapable of execution because the proprietary interests on which it was based had ceased to exist upon vesting in the State.

rule.if: preemption_decree_execution and decree_based_on_former_proprietary_right and land_proprietary_rights_vested_in_state and former_proprietary_rights_ceased and possession_still_required

predicates.preemption_decree_execution: The proceeding seeks to execute a decree granting pre-emption of an interest in land.
predicates.decree_based_on_former_proprietary_right: The decree rests on a claimant’s former proprietary interest in the land.
predicates.land_proprietary_rights_vested_in_state: The land’s proprietary rights vested in the State before execution was sought.
predicates.former_proprietary_rights_ceased: The former proprietary rights on which the decree depended ceased to exist, with no such rights surviving in the decree-holder.
predicates.possession_still_required: The decree-holder still needed execution to obtain possession of the land.

members.legal_issue: A former owner has no right to recover acquired land merely because it was not used for the purpose for which it was acquired after the award and possession vested the land in the State.
material_facts: An award had been made and possession of the acquired land had been taken, vesting the land in the State free from encumbrances.
Compensation had been paid to the former owners.
The land was not used for the purpose for which it had been acquired.
The State had initiated proceedings for resumption of the land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, after an award is made and possession is taken, the land vests in the Government free from encumbrances. Non-use or a later change in the purpose of use does not give the former owner a right to restitution. The Court relied on Gulam Mustafa v. State of Maharashtra, [1976] 1 SCC 800; Chandraguda Ramgonda Patil v. State of Maharashtra, [1996] 6 SCC 405; and C. Padma v. Dy. Secretary to the Government of T.N., [1997] 2 SCC 627.
members.conclusion: Non-use of the acquired land did not entitle the former owners to restitution or revesting of the land; any action concerning non-use was for the State to take.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The dispute concerns land acquired through compulsory acquisition proceedings.
predicates.award_made_and_possession_taken: An award was made and the acquiring authority took possession, causing the land to vest in the State.
predicates.acquired_land_unused: The acquired land was not used for the purpose for which it was acquired.

members.legal_issue: A person whose interest in land has been divested by acquisition cannot obtain an injunction restraining the public authority that holds the land as owner.
material_facts: The claimant brought a suit for perpetual injunction, asserting title to and possession of the disputed land.
The land had been acquired, possession had been taken and delivered to the public housing body, and the land was held for a public scheme and park.
The claimant’s claim of continuing title was inconsistent with his acknowledgment of the public body’s title and request for an alternative site.
members.legal_principle: Once possession of acquired land has been taken, Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for vesting free from encumbrances. A trespasser cannot claim an injunction against the true owner, and a claimant whose title has been divested cannot obtain an injunction against the public authority in which the land is vested.
members.conclusion: The injunction could not be granted against the public body as the true owner; the judgments granting it were set aside.

predicates.suit_for_perpetual_injunction: The claimant brought a suit seeking a perpetual injunction against interference with land.
predicates.land_taken_and_delivered_for_public_sche: The acquisition officer took possession of the land and delivered it to a public body for a public scheme.
predicates.claimant_has_no_remaining_title: The claimant’s interest in the land had been divested and the claimant had no remaining title to it.
predicates.injunction_unavailable_against_true_owne: An injunction cannot be granted against the public body that holds the land as true owner.
