members.legal_issue: A claimant’s title to land forming part of an acquired coal mine is extinguished when the rights in that mine vest absolutely in the government free from encumbrances.
material_facts: The claimants asserted title to leasehold land under a registered lease and sought a declaration of their rights and confirmation of possession.
The disputed land was found to form part of a mine within the meaning of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973.
The rights in the coal mine vested in the Central Government free from encumbrances, and the Act provided for vesting those rights in a government company.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 transfers and vests absolutely in the Central Government the owners’ rights, title and interest in the specified coal mines, free from encumbrances. Sections 5 and 6 address vesting in a government company and the discharge of encumbrances upon vesting. State of West Bengal v. Union of India, [1964] 1 SCR 371, was relied on for Parliament’s competence to legislate for acquisition of property owned by a State.
members.conclusion: The claimants’ title, if any, to the disputed land stood extinguished upon vesting of the mine’s rights under the Act; it was immaterial whether the mine had belonged to the State or to private parties.

predicates.civil_title_claim: A claimant seeks recognition of title to land in a civil proceeding.
predicates.land_fell_within_acquired_coal_mine: The land was found to form part of a coal mine covered by the acquisition.
predicates.mine_rights_vested_in_government_free_of: The rights in the coal mine vested in the government without being subject to encumbrances.

members.legal_issue: The end of the original purpose for which land was acquired does not entitle the former owners to restitution where the land was surrendered to the Government and assigned for another public purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act had become final, compensation had been paid to the appellants’ predecessor-in-title, and the land had vested in the State.
Under the agreement made for the acquisition, the company was required to surrender the land to the Government when the original purpose ceased.
The land was surrendered to the Government and assigned to another company for another public purpose.
members.legal_principle: The appellants relied on Sections 44-B and 40 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing that cessation of the public purpose invalidated the acquisition. The Court rejected that argument in light of the final acquisition, payment of compensation, vesting of the land in the State, and the agreement under Chapter VII requiring surrender to the Government when the purpose ceased. The land’s subsequent assignment for another public purpose did not give the former owners a right to restitution. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The appellants were not entitled to invalidate the acquisition or obtain restitution merely because the original purpose had ceased; the land had been resumed by the Government and assigned for another public purpose.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition and acquisition_proceedings_final and compensation_paid_to_former_owner and land_vested_in_state and beneficiary_surrendered_land_when_original_purpose_ended and land_assigned_for_another_public_purpose

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: The former owners brought a writ proceeding challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_final: The acquisition proceedings had become final.
predicates.compensation_paid_to_former_owner: Compensation for the acquired land was paid to the former owner or that owner's predecessor.
predicates.land_vested_in_state: The acquired land vested in the State.
predicates.beneficiary_surrendered_land_when_origin: The beneficiary surrendered the land to the Government when the original purpose ended, as required by the acquisition arrangement.
predicates.land_assigned_for_another_public_purpose: The Government assigned the surrendered land for another public purpose.
predicates.former_owners_not_entitled_to_restitutio: The former owners are not entitled to restitution of the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: When an estate vests in the State, a former proprietor cannot recover land from its occupants unless the land is within an interest saved from vesting, and a subsisting title to possession alone does not make land the proprietor’s khas possession.
material_facts: The estate vested in the State while the appeal was pending.
The mortgages had been redeemed in 1943, so no mortgage subsisted on the vesting date.
On the vesting date, the respondents were not in possession by cultivating the land themselves, through servants or hired labour, or with hired stock.
The land did not fall within any applicable category of land saved under section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
The respondents’ claim rested on their asserted right to recover possession, rather than on actual khas possession at vesting.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(1) and 4(a) and (f) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the estate and the proprietor’s interests vested in the State, except interests expressly saved by the Act, and the Collector took charge of the vested interests. Section 2(k) defined khas possession by reference to actual possession through specified forms of cultivation or horticultural operations. Section 6(1), including clause (c) as substituted by the Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1959, saved qualifying lands, including land forming the subject of a subsisting mortgage on redemption of which the intermediary was entitled to recover khas possession. Because no mortgage subsisted at vesting and the land was not in khas possession or otherwise saved, section 6 did not preserve the respondents’ interest. The Court followed the approach to vesting in Haji Sk. Subhan v. Madhorao, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 123, and rejected the broader reading of khas possession in Brijnandan Singh v. Jamuna Prasad, A.I.R. 1958 Pat. 589.
members.conclusion: The respondents’ interests, including the right to recover possession, vested in the State; they could not recover possession from the appellants after vesting.

rule.if: possession_recovery_suit and estate_vested_in_state and not land_in_khas_possession_at_vesting and not subsisting_qualifying_mortgage and not land_in_other_saved_category

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: A former proprietor brought a suit to recover possession of land from its occupants.
predicates.estate_vested_in_state: The estate containing the land vested in the State.
predicates.land_in_khas_possession_at_vesting: At vesting, the proprietor possessed the land through cultivation or horticultural operations by the proprietor, servants, hired labour, or hired stock.
predicates.subsisting_qualifying_mortgage: At vesting, a mortgage subsisted over the land and its redemption would entitle the intermediary to recover khas possession.
predicates.land_in_other_saved_category: The land fell within another category of land expressly saved from vesting.

members.legal_issue: A claim for restoration of land must be rejected when the claimant’s intermediary interest has validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
material_facts: The appellant sought restoration of possession of the acquired land.
In a separate judgment delivered the same day, the court held that the appellant’s intermediary interest in the estate had validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
members.legal_principle: The court applied its holding in the companion matter, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raja Anand Brahma Shah, that the intermediary interest had validly vested in the state under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, as amended.
members.conclusion: The claim for restoration of possession was rejected.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_restoration_of_land: A claimant seeks restoration of possession of land in a court proceeding.
predicates.claimant_intermediary_interest_validly_v: The claimant’s intermediary interest in the land has validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.

members.legal_issue: Taking possession after an award completes the acquisition and vests the land free of encumbrances, and delivery to the beneficiary gives it ownership.
material_facts: An award was made following notices to the interested persons.
An officer took possession, recording it in a panchanama signed by a witness.
The acquired land was handed over to the beneficiary society.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, after possession is taken following the award, the land vests in the State free from all encumbrances. The Court stated that possession may be taken through the usual mode of an officer preparing a panchanama signed by a witness, and that such possession is complete and conclusive. On handover, the beneficiary became absolute owner. No earlier cases were relied upon.
members.conclusion: Possession was validly taken and handed over; the State acquired the land free of encumbrances, and the beneficiary society became its absolute owner.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and award_made and possession_recorded_by_officer_in_witnessed_panchanama and acquired_land_delivered_to_beneficiary

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The land is the subject of a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.award_made: An award was made in the acquisition proceeding.
predicates.possession_recorded_by_officer_in_witnes: An officer took possession and recorded it in a panchanama signed by a witness.
predicates.acquired_land_delivered_to_beneficiary: The acquired land was handed over to the person or entity for whose benefit it was acquired.

members.legal_issue: The statutory vesting of land in the State free from all encumbrances extinguishes and transfers easementary rights over that land.
material_facts: The land had vested in a local public body and was used by the village community as pasture land, including for grazing.
The village community claimed an easementary right to use the land for grazing and other common purposes.
A later law provided that rights in the land would vest in the State free from all encumbrances, notwithstanding other laws, customs, agreements, or court orders.
The courts below held that the community’s easementary rights had not vested in the State.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Section 3 of the Himachal Pradesh Village Common Lands Vesting and Utilization Act, which extinguished rights in specified land and vested them in the State free from all encumbrances, notwithstanding other legal sources. An easement is a burden or charge on land and is included within the meaning of an encumbrance; the court relied on Abdul Karim Khan v. Managing Committee, George High School, Rashid Allidina v. Jiwandas Khemji, and Ganga Vishnu Swaika v. Machine Manufacturing Co. Ltd. It also relied on Fruit and Vegetable Merchants Union v. Delhi Improvement Trust concerning vesting free from encumbrances. Megh Raj v. Allah Rakhia and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab were distinguished because they addressed legislative competence, not whether easements are included in statutory vesting free from encumbrances.
members.conclusion: The easementary rights were extinguished and vested in the State along with the other rights in the land. The judgments below were set aside and the appeal was allowed. The question of whether the land should be used as pasture land was left open for the State Government to decide.

predicates.appeal_concerns_easement_surviving_statu: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether an easement survives a statutory transfer of land to the State.
predicates.land_transfers_to_state_free_of_encumbra: A law provides that land and rights in it transfer to the State free from all encumbrances, notwithstanding other legal sources.
predicates.community_easement_burdens_land: A community claims an easementary right to use the land, and that right burdens the land.
predicates.easementary_rights_extinguished_and_vest: The easementary rights are extinguished and vest in the State.

members.legal_issue: A landowner cannot use a statutory right to evict a tenant and resume possession of land after the land has been declared surplus under a scheme that reserves its use to the state.
material_facts: The land had been declared surplus under the applicable land-tenure scheme.
The landowner had acquired the land before the surplus declaration and was a small landowner in relation to the tenants.
The landowner later sought to evict the tenants and recover possession under the statutory provision allowing eviction by a small landowner.
The scheme empowered the state to use surplus land to resettle tenants and left the landowner with a right to receive rent from tenants settled there.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(5a), 9(1)(i), and 10-A(a) and (b) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, once land is declared surplus, the state controls its utilization for tenant resettlement and the landowner retains only the right to receive rent from tenants settled on it. The resumption contemplated by Section 9(1)(i) is unavailable where the landowner has no right to utilize or possess the surplus land. The Court noted Section 8 and Section 12(3) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, and the Full Bench decision in Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. State of Haryana, but held that even if the earlier transfer was protected from vesting under that Act, the landowner still could not resume possession under the 1953 Act.
members.conclusion: The landowner could not evict the tenants and resume possession of the land, so the application for possession was properly dismissed.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and land_declared_surplus and state_controls_surplus_land_use and owner_seeks_tenant_eviction

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landowner initiated a proceeding seeking to remove a tenant and recover possession of land.
predicates.land_declared_surplus: The land had been declared surplus under the applicable land-tenure scheme.
predicates.state_controls_surplus_land_use: The governing scheme assigned use of declared surplus land to the state and left the landowner with a right to receive rent from tenants settled on it.
predicates.owner_seeks_tenant_eviction: The landowner sought to evict a tenant and resume possession of the land.

members.legal_issue: Land acquired for a public purpose and vested in the acquiring body after possession and payment of compensation need not be returned to its former owners merely because it is surplus or remains unused for the original purpose.
material_facts: Land was notified for acquisition under Section 126(4) of the Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act after approval of a scheme by the State Government.

Possession was taken and the Land Acquisition Officer later made an award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; the Court stated that the land vested in the Municipality free from encumbrances.
The land was used for the stated purpose, and the remaining surplus was proposed for allotment to municipal councillors and employees.
A State Government resolution provided that surplus land should first be used for another public purpose and, alternatively, returned to the former owners.
The Court stated that adequate compensation had been paid according to the market value at the time of notification.
The petitioners sought restitution of the land, and the Court declined to direct its return.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that land acquired for a public purpose may be used for another public purpose and that land remaining unused need not be restituted to its former owner when adequate compensation has been paid. The acquisition notification was issued under Section 126(4) of the Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, and the award was made under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The former owners were not entitled to restitution of the acquired land; it could be used for another public purpose, and the Court would not direct its return merely because it was surplus or unused for the original purpose.

rule.if: writ_seeks_restitution_of_acquired_land and land_acquired_for_public_purpose and possession_taken_and_land_vested and adequate_compensation_paid

predicates.writ_seeks_restitution_of_acquired_land: The claimant asks in a writ proceeding for acquired land to be returned to its former owner.
predicates.land_acquired_for_public_purpose: The land was acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.possession_taken_and_land_vested: The acquiring body took possession of the land, which then vested in that body free from encumbrances.
predicates.adequate_compensation_paid: The former owner received adequate compensation for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: An owner cannot obtain a decree for possession of land after the land has vested in the State under land reform legislation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of land as owners.
The land vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act on January 26, 1955.
The plaintiffs conceded that they could not obtain a decree for possession after the vesting.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3, 4 and 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, land vests in the State, and an owner or landlord cannot obtain a decree for possession after that vesting. The Court relied on Ram Ran Bijai Singh v. Behari Singh and Gurucharan Singh v. Kamla Singh.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs could not obtain a decree for possession from the defendants after the land vested in the State.

predicates.land_possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking possession of land.
predicates.land_vested_in_state: The land vested in the State under land reform legislation.

members.legal_issue: A non-statutory land-disposal instruction does not entitle a former owner to reassignment of acquired land where the competent authority has not relinquished the land in accordance with the instruction.
material_facts: The former owner relied on a Board of Revenue standing order to seek reassignment of the unused land.
The record did not establish that the competent authority had relinquished the unused land.
The only cited communication was an engineer’s letter stating that the unused land was difficult to protect from encroachment.

The standing order provided procedures for disposal of relinquished land, including public auction in the circumstances specified in it; a later amendment directed that acquired land not needed for its original purpose be used for another public purpose as deemed fit.
members.legal_principle: The Court found no statutory basis for the Board’s Standing Order No. 90(32), and held that it could not override the Land Acquisition Act. Under the order, a claim concerning land no longer required for its acquired purpose depended first on relinquishment by the competent authority and then on the prescribed disposal process; the engineer’s letter alone did not amount to relinquishment. The 1998 amendment provided for use of acquired land for another public purpose where it was not needed for the purpose for which it had been acquired.
members.conclusion: The standing order did not support a direction to reassign the land to the former owner; the engineer’s letter did not establish relinquishment, and the amended instruction contemplated use for another public purpose.

rule.if: claim_for_return_under_local_land_disposal_instruction and acquired_land_vested_in_government and no_competent_relinquishment and only_staff_letter_reports_nonuse

predicates.claim_for_return_under_local_land_dispos: A former owner sought acquired land back by relying on a local instruction governing disposal of land no longer needed for its original purpose.
predicates.acquired_land_vested_in_government: The acquired land had vested in the government after possession was taken.
predicates.no_competent_relinquishment: The competent authority had not formally relinquished the land under the applicable disposal process.
predicates.only_staff_letter_reports_nonuse: The only evidence that the land was no longer needed was a staff member’s communication reporting non-use or difficulty protecting the land.
predicates.local_instruction_does_not_authorize_rea: The local instruction does not entitle the former owner to reassignment in those circumstances.

members.legal_issue: The statutory procedure for land acquired for public benefit applies only when qualifying agricultural or pasturage land is determined by the competent authority to be no longer required, and it does not itself justify returning land that has vested in the State.
material_facts: The land had been acquired for a public purpose and possession had been taken.
The former owner offered to refund the compensation received.
A resident engineer reported that the unused land was no longer required, but the Court held that this was not a decision by the competent authority that the land was no longer required.
The record did not establish a competent-authority determination that the land was no longer required.
members.legal_principle: Section 54-A of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Land Revenue Act concerns agricultural or pasturage land acquired for public benefit that is no longer required; it provides for a patta to the former owner or successor if that person consents to refund the compensation. The Court construed “no longer required” as not necessarily meaning no longer required for the specific purpose for which the land was acquired, but held that the determination must be made by the competent authority. The provision did not displace the consequences of vesting under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act as explained in State of Kerala v. M. Bhaskaran Pillai and the other authorities cited by the Court.
members.conclusion: The engineer’s letter alone did not satisfy the statutory condition that the land be determined by the competent authority to be no longer required, and the claim for reconveyance could not succeed on that basis.

predicates.claim_for_return_under_unused_public_ben: A former owner sought return of land under a procedure concerning land acquired for public benefit that is no longer required.
predicates.land_is_agricultural_or_pasturage: The acquired land is agricultural or pasturage land.
predicates.no_competent_determination_land_unneeded: The competent authority has not determined that the land is no longer required, even if a staff member has reported that it is unused or unnecessary.
predicates.statutory_return_procedure_not_triggered: The statutory procedure for return of qualifying land has not been triggered.

members.legal_issue: Land vests in the State free from encumbrances after an award is made and possession is taken.
material_facts: An award was made for the acquired land.
Symbolic possession was taken on the date of the award.
The writ petition challenging the acquisition was filed afterward.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the making of the award and taking of possession as resulting in vesting of the land in the State free from encumbrances. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The land had vested in the State free from all encumbrances before the writ petition was filed.

predicates.acquisition_writ_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a judgment reviewing land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.award_made: The acquiring authority made an award for the land.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land.

members.legal_issue: A former landholder is not entitled to restoration of possession when the relevant intermediary interest has validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
material_facts: The appellant sought restoration of possession of the acquired land.
In a companion decision, the Court held that the appellant’s intermediary interest in the estate had validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, as amended, and its conclusion in the companion decision, The State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raja Anand Brahma Shah, that the intermediary interest had validly vested in the state.
members.conclusion: The claim for restoration of possession was rejected because the intermediary interest had validly vested in the state.

predicates.writ_proceeding_seeking_restoration: A former holder sought restoration of possession in a writ proceeding.
predicates.intermediary_interest_validly_vested_in_: The holder’s intermediary interest in the estate had validly vested in the state under land-reform law.

members.legal_issue: After land validly vests in the State free from encumbrances, the former owner cannot object to the State changing its use.
material_facts: The State acquired the land and took possession of it.
The State handed the land to a public corporation for a stated public purpose.
The public corporation used part of the land for a bus depot although the land had been earmarked for residential purposes.
members.legal_principle: Once land validly vests in the State free from encumbrances, its subsequent use is not a concern of the former owner, and a later diversion to another public purpose does not invalidate the acquisition. The Court relied on Gulam Mustafa v. State of Maharashtra; C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu; Bhagat Singh v. State of U.P.; Niladri Narayan Chandradhurja v. State of West Bengal; and Northern Indian Glass Industries v. Jaswant Singh.
members.conclusion: The State could change the use of land after it vested in it, and the former owner could not challenge that change.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and valid_acquisition and possession_taken and state_changed_land_use

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns the acquisition of land by the State.
predicates.possession_taken: The State took possession of the land under the acquisition.
predicates.state_changed_land_use: After taking possession, the State or its transferee used the land for a purpose different from the one originally stated.

members.legal_issue: Repeal of the ceiling regime does not entitle a former owner to recover land where the State had already taken possession.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the ceiling regime and possession was taken before the regime was repealed.
The former owner sought relief after the repeal.
members.legal_principle: Under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, pending proceedings abate where the tenure-holder remained in possession; repeal does not benefit the owner where possession was already taken. The Court relied on Pt. Madan Swaroop Shrotiya Public Charitable Trust v. State of U.P.; Ghasitey Lal Sahu v. Competent Authority; and Mukarram Ali Khan v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The repeal did not confer any benefit on the former owner because possession had already been taken.

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_proceeding: The case concerns proceedings under an urban land ceiling regime.
predicates.repeal_after_acquisition: The regime was repealed after the land had been acquired under it.
predicates.possession_taken_before_repeal: The State had taken possession before the repeal took effect.

members.legal_issue: A decree-holder loses the right to execute a possession decree founded on proprietary rights when those rights vest in the State and no applicable provision preserves a right to recover possession.
material_facts: The decree-holder’s claim to possession rested on proprietary rights in the land.
The land was not protected home-farm land, and the governing law vested the proprietor’s rights in the State.
The law preserved the proprietor’s possession of qualifying home-farm land and recovery of sums already due, but did not preserve recovery of possession under a decree.
The decree was treated as a document affected by the statutory consequences of vesting.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4(1)(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, vest proprietary rights in the State and provide that the consequences apply notwithstanding a contract, grant, document, or other law. A court decree affecting proprietary rights is a document for this purpose. Sections 4(2) and 4(3) preserve specified rights but do not provide for recovery of possession under a decree; section 7 addresses the State taking charge of land. The statutory scheme therefore removes a proprietor’s decree-based right to possession when that right is not saved.
members.conclusion: The decree-holder’s proprietary right and consequent right to obtain possession ceased, so the possession decree became inexecutable.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and possession_decree_based_on_proprietary_right and proprietary_rights_vest_in_state and not land_is_protected_home_farm and no_preserved_right_to_recover_possession

predicates.execution_proceeding: The parties are before a court to enforce a decree.
predicates.possession_decree_based_on_proprietary_r: The decree awards possession because the decree-holder had proprietary rights in the land.
predicates.proprietary_rights_vest_in_state: A law transfers the proprietor’s rights in the land to the State.
predicates.land_is_protected_home_farm: The land falls within a category for which the proprietor’s possession is preserved after vesting.
predicates.no_preserved_right_to_recover_possession: The governing law does not preserve a right to recover possession under the decree after vesting.

members.legal_issue: A claimant cannot obtain a decree for possession of property after it has vested in the state under the applicable land reform law.
material_facts: The suit sought possession of properties that had vested in the state before the court decided the appeal.
The applicable land reform provision governed the effect of that vesting.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, precluded a decree for possession once the suit properties had vested in the State Government.
members.conclusion: The claim for a decree for possession could not succeed, and the dismissal of that claim was confirmed.

predicates.possession_suit: The proceeding includes a claim seeking possession of property.
predicates.property_vested_in_state: The property became vested in the state under the applicable land reform law.
predicates.possession_decree_unavailable: A decree granting possession of the property cannot be obtained.

members.legal_issue: A former proprietor cannot maintain a possession suit in that capacity for agricultural land after the statutory land reform scheme has ended proprietary rights as such.
material_facts: The respondent sued for possession of agricultural land claiming to be its proprietor.
The respondent's claimed entitlement to possession rested on his former proprietary status.
The Act provided that land outside a proprietor's holding vested in the Gaon Sabha and recognized Bhumidars, Asamis and the Gaon Sabha as the classes entitled to rights in agricultural land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6, 11, 13 and 154 of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, read together, extinguished proprietary rights as such and left rights in agricultural land with Bhumidars, Asamis and the Gaon Sabha. Section 84, read with item 19 of the First Schedule, provided the possession remedy for those recognized classes.
members.conclusion: A proprietor as such could not institute a suit for possession; the statutory right to sue for possession belonged to a Bhumidar, an Asami or the Gaon Sabha.

predicates.agricultural_land_possession_proceeding: The proceeding seeks possession of agricultural land governed by a statutory land reform scheme.
predicates.claimant_sues_as_former_proprietor: The claimant seeks possession on the basis of former proprietary status rather than a continuing recognized landholding status.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot obtain restitution of possession from a former possessor when the estate and the right to recover possession have vested in the State, which is deemed to have taken charge.
material_facts: The plaintiffs took possession under a High Court decree that was later reversed.
Before the restitution claim, the estate containing the lands had vested in the State, and the Collector was deemed to have taken charge of it from the date of vesting.

The earlier title proceedings had held that the plaintiffs had no subsisting right to recover possession and that the right to possession and to recover possession from a trespasser had vested in the State.
The State was not a party to the earlier title proceedings, but later asserted that the plaintiffs had surrendered possession to it; the plaintiffs also said they had surrendered possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 144 CPC ordinarily provides restitution when a decree under which a party obtained a benefit is reversed, but that ordinary rule did not apply where Sections 3 and 4(a) of the Bihar Lands Reforms Act vested the estate and unsaved interests in the State, and Section 4(f) deemed the Collector to have taken charge from the date of vesting. The Court relied on its earlier decision in Surajnath Ahir v. Prithinath Singh, which held that the former proprietors had no subsisting right to recover possession after vesting and that the right to possession and recovery from a trespasser vested in the State.
members.conclusion: The defendants were not entitled to restitution of possession from the plaintiffs because the State, rather than either litigating party, held the right to possession after vesting.

rule.if: restitution_proceeding_after_reversal and estate_rights_vested_in_state and state_deemed_in_charge and claimant_has_no_surviving_right_to_possession

predicates.restitution_proceeding_after_reversal: A party seeks restitution of possession after a decree under which another party took possession has been reversed.
predicates.estate_rights_vested_in_state: The estate containing the disputed property and the relevant rights have vested in the State.
predicates.state_deemed_in_charge: The governing law deems the State's officer to have taken charge of the vested estate from the date of vesting.
predicates.claimant_has_no_surviving_right_to_posse: The party seeking restitution has no surviving right to possess the property or recover it from its possessor.

members.legal_issue: A party who is not entitled to restitution of possession because the right to possession belongs to the State is also not entitled to mesne profits for the period of exclusion.
material_facts: The defendants sought mesne profits for the period after the plaintiffs took possession under the subsequently reversed decree.
The estate had vested in the State before that period, and the Collector was deemed to have taken charge of it from the date of vesting.
The defendants were not entitled to restitution of possession from the plaintiffs.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 144 CPC in light of the vesting provisions in Sections 3 and 4 of the Bihar Lands Reforms Act. Because the defendants had no right to restitution of possession after the estate and the relevant rights vested in the State, they could not recover mesne profits on the same basis.
members.conclusion: The defendants were not entitled to mesne profits.

predicates.mesne_profits_claim_in_restitution_proce: A party claims mesne profits in a proceeding seeking restitution after reversal of a decree.
predicates.claimant_not_entitled_to_restitution: The party claiming mesne profits is not entitled to restitution of possession.

members.legal_issue: A villagers’ right to graze cattle on estate land is an encumbrance within the statutory definition and is extinguished when the estate vests in the State free from encumbrances.
material_facts: An estate containing grassland used by villagers for cattle grazing vested in the State under a notification.
The villagers claimed that their pasturage right continued after vesting and sought an injunction against interference with its exercise.

The governing law defined encumbrances broadly to include rights or interests of whatever nature relating to estate land or its produce, subject to specified exceptions, and provided for vesting free from encumbrances.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(h) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, an encumbrance includes all rights or interests of whatever nature relating to land comprised in an estate or its produce, apart from the stated exclusions. Sections 4 and 5 provide for vesting free from all encumbrances. The Court applied the statutory language in light of the Act’s land-reform objective and held that the definition’s broad reach could not be cut down. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The grazing right is an encumbrance within the definition and was extinguished upon vesting; the appeal was allowed and the suit dismissed.

rule.if: estate_vesting_dispute and grazing_right_relates_to_estate_land and definition_covers_all_related_interests and estate_vests_free_of_encumbrances

predicates.estate_vesting_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a right survives the vesting of an estate in the State under a land-reform scheme.
predicates.grazing_right_relates_to_estate_land: Villagers claim a right to graze cattle on land comprised in the estate.
predicates.definition_covers_all_related_interests: The governing law includes rights or interests of whatever nature relating to estate land or its produce within its definition of encumbrances, subject to stated exclusions.
predicates.estate_vests_free_of_encumbrances: The governing law provides that the estate vests in the State free from encumbrances.

members.legal_issue: A landowner cannot recover land declared surplus merely because the government has not yet used it to resettle tenants.
material_facts: A competent authority declared part of the landowner’s holding surplus, and the declaration became final after appeal and revision proceedings.
The surplus land had not been used by the government to resettle tenants when the landowner sought to prevent its use.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 9(1)(i) and 10A(a) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, the government may use surplus land to resettle tenants ejected or liable to be ejected, and a final surplus declaration gives the government an indefeasible right to do so. The Act sets no time limit for that use and gives the owner no right to restoration merely because use has been delayed. Sections 10A(b) and 10B provide limited exceptions concerning acquisition and inheritance; those exceptions do not create a general right to recover land because of non-use.
members.conclusion: The landowner could not reclaim the surplus land on the ground that it had not been utilised; the government retained the right to use it for tenant resettlement without a time limit.

predicates.surplus_area_proceeding: The proceeding determines land surplus to a landowner’s permissible area for potential use in resettling tenants.
predicates.final_surplus_order: The competent authority made a surplus-land declaration that became final.
predicates.surplus_land_not_yet_utilized: The government had not yet used the declared surplus land to resettle tenants.

members.legal_issue: A successor who was not in physical possession of claimed home-farm land when proprietary rights vested in the State cannot rely on the statutory preservation of possession to recover the land.
material_facts: A limited proprietor had created occupancy tenancy rights over some land before her death, and other land remained with her.
After the limited proprietor died, her husband took possession of the remaining land; the estate’s proprietary rights later vested in the State under the abolition legislation.
The plaintiffs succeeded to the estate but were not in physical possession of the disputed land on the date of vesting.
The plaintiffs sought possession of the disputed land as home-farm land.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3 and 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, proprietary rights vested in the State. Section 4(2), read with the definition of home-farm land in Section 2(g), preserved a proprietor’s ability to continue in possession of qualifying land only if already physically in possession; it did not confer a right to recover possession from another. The Court applied Haji Sk. Subhan v. Madhorao, which held that a person not in possession at vesting could not rely on Section 4(2) to continue to retain possession, and identified personal cultivation at the relevant times as central to the statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs could not recover possession because they were not in physical possession of the land on the date of vesting; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.home_farm_possession_claim: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking possession of land claimed as home-farm land after proprietary rights in the estate vested in the State.
predicates.claimant_not_in_possession_at_vesting: The claimant was not in physical possession of the disputed land when the estate’s proprietary rights vested in the State.

members.legal_issue: The power to reconvey acquired land is limited to land that remains vested in the government and is no longer required for the acquisition purpose or any other public purpose, and reconveyance cannot be compelled when those conditions are not met.
material_facts: After compensation was paid, the acquired land was transferred to the housing board.
The board had used a substantial portion of the acquired land for housing, roads, residential plots, a school, and other purposes.
The board reported that the housing scheme remained in progress and that portions of the disputed land were allocated or intended for public uses.
The government rejected the owners’ requests for reconveyance after considering the board’s report.
members.legal_principle: Section 48-B of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as applicable in the State, permits the government to transfer acquired land to the original owner only when the land remains vested in the government and the government is satisfied that it is not required for the purpose of acquisition or any other public purpose; the owner must be willing to repay the compensation and applicable statutory amounts. The provision is an exception to the general rule and must be strictly construed. The housing board, as the receiving agency, was not competent to transfer the land under that provision. The Court also referred to Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. Keeravani Ammal and State of Kerala v. M. Bhaskaran Pillai (1997) 5 SCC 432.
members.conclusion: The government could not reconvey land that had already been transferred to the housing board, and the owners could not compel reconveyance where the land remained usable for a public purpose.

predicates.reconveyance_request_after_acquisition: An original owner sought reconveyance of land after it had been acquired and compensation had been paid.
predicates.land_transferred_to_another_agency: The government had transferred the acquired land to another agency.
predicates.public_purpose_remains_available: The land continued to be used, or remained available for use, for a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A former intermediary whose interest in requisitioned property has vested in the State cannot receive recurring compensation for periods after vesting.
material_facts: The claimants’ predecessor held patni rights in the property and was an intermediary under the applicable estates acquisition law.
The property’s requisition continued after the predecessor’s interest vested in the State.
The High Court awarded recurring compensation on the assumption that the claimants continued to hold rights in the property after vesting.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(1), 4(1)–(2), and 5 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 provide for acquisition of an intermediary’s interest and required the State to notify the entire area covered by the Act for vesting by the specified statutory deadline. Once the interest vested, the former intermediary and heirs had no continuing interest in the property, apart from the right to compensation under that Act.
members.conclusion: The claimants could not receive recurring compensation for periods after their interest vested in the State; the award had to be limited to the period before vesting.

predicates.requisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for property that was requisitioned.
predicates.intermediary_interest: The claimant or the claimant’s predecessor held an intermediary interest in the property.
predicates.estate_interest_vested: The intermediary’s interest in the property vested in the State.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence requires fully proved circumstances that form a complete chain consistent only with guilt and inconsistent with innocence.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including evidence of a dowry-related motive, two oral dying declarations, medical evidence, the accused persons’ conduct during and after the incident, and their absence from the village during the investigation.
The deceased’s parents resisted registering land in the husband’s name, and evidence showed that the deceased had been harassed over dowry and the land.
Witnesses testified that the deceased identified her mother-in-law as the person who poured kerosene on her and her husband as the person who set her on fire.
Medical evidence established extensive burns and supported the prosecution account of how the deceased was set on fire.
The accused persons did not try to extinguish the fire, provide first aid, or arrange or accompany the deceased to hospital; they were not found in the village when the police searched for them.
The Court found the established circumstances reliable, mutually consistent, and complete, with no gap in the chain.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3 of the Evidence Act, circumstantial evidence can establish guilt only where each relied-on circumstance is fully proved, the circumstances form a complete chain without gaps, and the chain is consistent only with the accused persons’ guilt and inconsistent with their innocence. Motive has particular significance in such a case. Absconding alone is not conclusive of guilt, but may assume significance when considered with the other established circumstances. No earlier case was cited for these evidentiary principles.
members.conclusion: The circumstances proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused persons committed the murder, and the conviction and sentence were upheld.

members.legal_issue: A conviction in a case based on circumstantial evidence may be sustained only when the proved circumstances form a complete chain that excludes every reasonable hypothesis consistent with innocence.
material_facts: There were no eyewitnesses to the assault, and the prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence.
The accused and deceased were related, and a dispute over partition of family land provided a possible motive.
The deceased’s gold ornaments, a weapon, and bloodstained clothing were recovered from the accused or at his instance on the day after the body was found.
Forensic examination established that the seized clothing bore bloodstains, and the accused gave no explanation for possession of the deceased’s articles.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove each incriminating circumstance beyond reasonable doubt, and the circumstances must be conclusive, consistent only with guilt, and form a complete chain excluding reasonable hypotheses of innocence. A false or absent defence cannot cure gaps in the prosecution case. The Court relied on Hukam Singh v. State of Rajasthan, Eradu v. State of Hyderabad, Earabhadrappa v. State of Karnataka, State of U.P. v. Sukhbasi, Balwinder Singh v. State of Punjab, Ashok Kumar Chatterjee v. State of M.P., Bhagat Ram v. State of Punjab, C. Chenga Reddy v. State of A.P., Padala Veera Reddy v. State of A.P., State of U.P. v. Ashok Kumar Srivastava, Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of M.P., and Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The circumstances, considered cumulatively, were sufficient to sustain the conviction, and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for murder may be upheld on circumstantial evidence when the established circumstances form a complete chain pointing to guilt and excluding reasonable possibilities consistent with innocence.
material_facts: The prosecution case rested on circumstantial evidence, with no eyewitness to the three killings.
The victims’ bodies were buried in a locked inner room of the premises where the accused and victims had lived; the room’s key was with one accused, and the room was accessible only to the accused.
Medical evidence established that the deaths were homicidal and that injuries had been inflicted with a sharp object found in the room.
The accused continued operating the business at the premises and did not seek to discover the whereabouts of the missing victims.
The courts found the established circumstances formed an unbroken chain consistent with the accused’s guilt.
members.legal_principle: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances forming the chain must be established and must be so complete as to rule out every reasonable possibility consistent with the accused’s innocence. Applying that principle, the Court relied on the proved circumstances as a whole to uphold the convictions under Sections 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence established the accused’s guilt, and their convictions for murder with common intention were upheld.

members.legal_issue: The proved circumstantial evidence, considered together with a co-accused’s confession used to lend assurance, was sufficient to sustain the conviction for murder and the firearms offence.
material_facts: There was evidence of a longstanding dispute over division of agricultural land and threats between the accused and the deceased.
Blood matching a deceased person was found on the accused’s shoes, and blood matching the accused was found in his toenail clippings.
Blood-stained clothes were recovered after the accused indicated where they had been kept.
The accused had an unexplained shoulder injury in a location consistent with repeated firing of a gun.
Witness evidence placed the accused leaving the area shortly after the murders.
The co-accused’s confession described the accused committing the murders and was used to lend assurance to the other proved circumstances, not as substantive evidence.
members.legal_principle: A conviction may rest on circumstantial evidence where the proved circumstances, considered together, sufficiently connect the accused with the crime. A co-accused’s confession is not substantive evidence against another accused, but may lend assurance to other evidence. The Court applied the principles in Kashmira Singh v. State of M.P. and Bhuboni Sahu v. R., as discussed in State v. Nalini.
members.conclusion: The conviction for murder and the firearms offence was affirmed because the proved circumstances, considered cumulatively and with the confession lending assurance, sufficiently connected the accused to the offences.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence cannot stand unless the established circumstances form a complete chain that excludes every reasonable hypothesis consistent with innocence.
material_facts: The case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence.
The evidence that the deceased was owed the sale price was doubtful, and the Court found that the alleged motive was not established.
The principal witnesses' accounts of the accused serving the deceased a cup of tea were unreliable and materially inconsistent.
The alleged poison was not detected in the water remaining in the tumbler or in the vomit, and the amount of the compound found in the viscera was not measured.

The accused promptly contacted the police after the deceased collapsed; the Court found that his account of events could not be treated as incriminating in light of the deficiencies in the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: Under Hanumant v. State of Madhya Pradesh, circumstances relied on for guilt must first be fully established, be consistent only with guilt, be conclusive in nature and tendency, and exclude every reasonable hypothesis other than guilt. The Court recalled the caution in Reg. v. Hodge against allowing conjecture or suspicion to substitute for proof.
members.conclusion: The circumstances did not form a complete chain excluding reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence, so the conviction and sentence were set aside and the accused was acquitted.

members.legal_issue: Whether the circumstantial evidence was sufficient to sustain the convictions for the alleged offences.
material_facts: The convictions rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, including an alleged motive involving a sale deed, evidence that the deceased was last seen with an appellant, recovery of a body, and identification of clothing found with it.

The evidence did not satisfactorily establish that someone had impersonated the deceased to execute the sale deed; the alleged impersonator’s thumb impression was not compared by an expert with the impression on the deed, and the witness who could have corroborated the account was not questioned about the deed or the people involved.

The body was recovered more than three months after the deceased allegedly disappeared. The doctor could not determine the cause or time of death, and the panch witnesses could not identify the clothing as belonging to the deceased.

The clothing identification was unreliable: the clothes had been removed and sealed before the identifying witness saw the body, and he identified them by a paper chit and a knot. The alleged last-seen account was also not credible in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: A conviction resting entirely on circumstantial evidence cannot be sustained when that evidence falls short of the required standard on material particulars. The Court applied this principle in reviewing convictions associated with Indian Penal Code Sections 302, 364 and 201; the judgment’s introductory account also refers to Section 210. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence fell short of the required standard on material particulars. The convictions and sentences were set aside, and the appellants were acquitted.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction may be sustained on circumstantial evidence when the circumstances are firmly established and form a complete chain excluding a reasonable hypothesis of innocence.
material_facts: A witness saw the accused in a perplexed state on the day the child disappeared, and that evidence was not challenged in cross-examination.
The accused voluntarily made the first disclosure identifying where the concealed body could be recovered.
The accused led the police to the indicated room and pointed out the place where the body was recovered from beneath a heap of chaff.
The testimony about the disclosure and recovery was cogent, trustworthy, and not undermined in cross-examination.
The medical evidence supported the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the rule for circumstantial evidence that the established circumstances must form a complete chain, point unerringly to guilt, and exclude hypotheses consistent with innocence. Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the portion of the accused's voluntary disclosure that led to discovery of the concealed body was admissible. The murder conviction was maintained under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The circumstantial chain established the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt; his conviction for murder and life sentence were maintained, while his separate conspiracy conviction was set aside.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence is sustainable when the established circumstances form a complete chain that points to guilt and excludes reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness, and the prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence.
The deceased was last seen alive in the accused’s company at their shared home and was not seen alive thereafter.
The accused gave changing explanations to the deceased’s daughter about her whereabouts, including claims that she had travelled abroad that were disproved by inquiries and her passport.
The accused identified the place where a box containing a skeleton and articles was buried in the backyard of the shared home.
DNA testing and skull superimposition identified the remains as those of the deceased, and witnesses identified articles recovered with them as hers.
The circumstances, considered cumulatively, established the accused’s guilt.
members.legal_principle: Under Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, circumstances relied on for conviction must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive, exclude every reasonable hypothesis except guilt, and form a complete chain. The Court also referred to Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra on the distinction between a conclusion that an accused may be guilty and one that the accused must be guilty. It cautioned, with reference to Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, that circumstantial evidence must be assessed with particular care. Where a wife dies unnaturally in a home occupied with her husband, the absence of an explanation may be a circumstance against him depending on the case’s facts; the Court referred to Nika Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh, Raj Kumar Prasad Tamarkar v. State of Bihar, and Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the conviction, finding that the established circumstances completed the chain of evidence and established guilt.

members.legal_principle: For a conviction resting on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must prove each circumstance, and the cumulative effect of the proved circumstances must exclude every other hypothesis and point unequivocally to guilt. members.conclusion: The circumstances did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the convictions and sentences were set aside and the accused was acquitted.

members.legal_issue: Circumstantial evidence, including reliable and corroborated evidence placing the accused at the scene and evidence of motive and subsequent conduct, can support affirmance of a murder conviction.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence showed longstanding and serious disputes between the accused and the deceased over their father's property.
A witness testified that he saw the accused enter the house at about midnight and later heard groaning; a report recording the witness's account was made before the murder was discovered.
The deceased was alone in the house before the incident, and the evidence placed only the accused and the deceased inside it at the relevant time.
The accused left the area after the incident and, despite learning that something serious had happened to his brother, made no inquiry to establish what had occurred.
The trial court convicted the accused of murder and imposed a death sentence, and the High Court upheld the conviction and sentence.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the cumulative force of the circumstances proved in the case, particularly the witness's evidence of the accused's presence at the house, corroboration by the report made before discovery of the murder, the fact that no one else was in the house, the property dispute, and the accused's conduct after the event. It found no reason to differ from the trial court and High Court on the witness's evidence. No earlier case was cited for this merits determination.
members.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence established the accused's guilt; the appeal was dismissed and the conviction and death sentence were confirmed.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence cannot stand unless the established circumstances point to guilt and exclude every reasonable possibility of innocence.
material_facts: The appellant was convicted of abetting a dacoity and murder, although the courts below did not find that he was one of the dacoits.

The prosecution relied on alleged enmity, the supposed purpose of the crime, an alleged sighting of the appellant with armed men before the crime, an alleged false alarm, and the appellant’s report to the police after the crime.
The Supreme Court found that the alleged circumstances were not established or were not sufficiently cogent; it also found the testimony supporting the alleged sighting unreliable.
Even assuming the appellant had been seen near the grove, that fact did not establish that he abetted the crime or exclude a reasonable possibility of innocence.
members.legal_principle: Under Hanumant v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1952] S.C.R. 1091, the circumstances from which guilt is inferred must first be fully established, must be conclusive and consistent only with guilt, and must form a complete chain that leaves no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with innocence. This standard applied to the charge under sections 396 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code. Suspicion or conjecture cannot replace proof.
members.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence did not satisfy the required standard; the conviction was set aside and the appellant was acquitted.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence requires a complete chain of firmly established circumstances that excludes reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness to the deaths.
The medical evidence did not conclusively establish whether the deaths resulted from an assault with an iron rod or from a collision and subsequent impact or run-over.
The prosecution did not conclusively connect the lorry to the deaths or establish that the accused were in it.
The evidence did not rule out the possibility that an unknown vehicle caused a fatal hit-and-run collision.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. In a case based on circumstantial evidence, each circumstance must be firmly established, the circumstances must cumulatively form a complete chain pointing to guilt, and the chain must exclude reasonable explanations consistent with innocence. Where two views are possible, the view consistent with innocence must be preferred. The Court relied on Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra (1973) 2 SCC 793; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Bablu v. State of Rajasthan (2006) 13 SCC 116; Vijay Shankar v. State of Haryana (2015) 12 SCC 644; Satish Nirankari v. State of Rajasthan (2017) 8 SCC 497; and Shanti Devi v. State of Rajasthan (2012) 12 SCC 158.
members.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the convictions could not stand.

members.legal_issue: A conviction may be sustained where the proved confession, disclosures, recoveries, and forensic circumstances collectively connect the accused to the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The death was found to be homicidal, and the injuries supported the finding of murder.
Reliable witnesses testified to a voluntary confession, and the accused’s disclosure statements led to recovery of the weapon and a concealed sheet bearing human blood.
An item recovered with the weapon bore a human hair, and the hair was found on examination to be human; the other proved circumstances were also considered by the courts.
The trial court convicted the accused and the High Court affirmed the conviction.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the circumstantial evidence cumulatively and found the confession, disclosure-led recoveries, and forensic findings sufficient. Applying State of Rajasthan v. Teja Ram on the blood evidence and the principles governing voluntary extra-judicial confessions and credible witness testimony, it held that the evidence proved the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: The combined circumstances sufficiently connected the accused with the murder; the conviction was affirmed and the appeal dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for a serious offence may rest on circumstantial evidence only when the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt through a complete chain that excludes reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence.
material_facts: All seven witnesses presented as eyewitnesses turned hostile in court, and the case was treated as one resting on circumstantial evidence.
The complainant lodged a prompt report naming the accused; he and another injured witness admitted their presence and injuries, and their medical evidence was consistent with the occurrence.

The witnesses had named the accused in their statements to the investigating officer, and the investigating officer testified to those statements and to recovery of the accused’s licensed gun at his instance.
The medical evidence recorded multiple firearm injuries to the deceased and injured persons.
The trial and High Courts had convicted the accused, and the Supreme Court considered the evidence as a whole.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and the burden never shifts. A serious or brutal offence calls for greater assurance and careful scrutiny, not conviction on suspicion or moral reaction. Under Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1984 SC 1622, the circumstances must be fully established, consistent only with guilt, conclusive, exclude every possible hypothesis except guilt, and form a complete chain leaving no reasonable ground consistent with innocence. The Court also relied on Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1952 SC 159; State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2407; Shankarlal Gyarasilal Dixit v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1981 SC 765; Mousam Singha Roy v. State of West Bengal, (2003) 12 SCC 377; Aloke Nath Dutta v. State of West Bengal, (2007) 12 SCC 230; Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1957 SC 637; State of Uttar Pradesh v. Satish, (2005) 3 SCC 114; Krishnan v. State, (2008) 15 SCC 430; Ramesh Bhai v. State of Rajasthan, (2009) 12 SCC 603; Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2009) 14 SCC 415; and Babu v. State of Kerala, JT 2010 (8) SC 560.
members.conclusion: The Court found no cogent reason to disturb the concurrent findings of guilt and dismissed the appeal; the conviction was sustained on the totality of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: An appeal that abates for failure to substitute a deceased respondent is not disposed of by a decree on the merits, and a second appeal cannot be brought against the abatement as though such a decree existed.
material_facts: A respondent died while a first appeal was pending, and no substitution was made within the prescribed time.
The first appellate court held that the appeal had abated but also stated that it was dismissed on contest and a decree was drawn up in those terms.
The first appellate court had not adjudicated the parties’ rights on the merits.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a decree requires a formal adjudication conclusively determining rights. Order 22 Rules 4, 9 and 11 govern substitution and abatement; abatement occurs by operation of law and is not an adjudication on the merits. Section 100 permits a second appeal from a decree passed in appeal, not from an order refusing to set aside abatement. The provision barring a fresh suit after abatement also reflects that abatement is not an adjudication attracting res judicata under Section 11.
members.conclusion: The first appeal stood disposed of by abatement, not by a decree; the purported decree dismissing it on contest was contrary to law and non-existent, so no second appeal lay against it.

members.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate as a whole when the heirs of a deceased defendant connected with one property are not substituted in time if the interests in the other properties are independent, though the appeal abates as to the deceased defendant's inseparable property interest.
material_facts: One defendant died after the High Court decree, and the application to substitute that defendant's heirs was not made within the prescribed time.
The deceased defendant and another purchaser held one property jointly, and the record did not establish that their interests were separate and distinct.
The interests of the defendants possessing the other properties were independent.
members.legal_principle: Where defendants' interests in different properties are independent, the failure to bring the heirs of a deceased defendant on the record within time does not cause the entire appeal to abate. If the deceased defendant's interest in a particular property is joint and not shown to be separate and severable from a co-owner's interest, abatement applies to that property. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this procedural ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal abated as to the jointly held property connected with the deceased defendant, but it did not abate as a whole and could proceed concerning the other properties.

members.legal_issue: When a defendant dies during an appeal and the defendant’s legal representatives are not brought on record, the appeal abates as to that defendant and the trial finding in that defendant’s favour becomes final and binding.
material_facts: A first defendant died while the first appeal was pending.
The first defendant’s legal representatives were not brought on record, and the defendant’s name was deleted from the array of parties.
The trial court had found that the suit property was allotted to that defendant in a partition.
The High Court treated the cause of action as surviving against the other defendant and granted partition, despite the abatement.
members.legal_principle: The judgment holds that failure to bring a deceased defendant’s legal representatives on record during the appeal results in abatement as to that defendant; the trial finding in that defendant’s favour then remains final and binding between the parties. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this point.
members.conclusion: The suit had abated as against the deceased first defendant; the trial finding in that defendant’s favour had become final and binding, and it was incorrect to hold that the cause of action survived against the other defendant.

predicates.legal_representatives_not_substituted: The deceased defendant’s legal representatives were not brought on record.
predicates.deceased_defendant_removed_from_case: The deceased defendant’s name was deleted from the case.
predicates.trial_finding_favored_deceased_defendant: The trial court made a finding in favour of the deceased defendant.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased_defendant_a: The appeal abates as to the deceased defendant and the trial finding in that defendant’s favour remains final and binding.

members.legal_issue: A pending criminal appeal against an accused abates when that accused dies after the appeal has been argued.
material_facts: The first accused died after the arguments in the appeals had concluded.
The appeals challenged the acquittals of the accused in a criminal prosecution.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that, in law, the criminal appeals against an accused who died while they were pending abated. The supplied text does not cite a statutory provision or earlier case for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The appeals against the deceased accused abated, although her role and involvement were still examined in light of the charges and evidence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.accused_dies_while_appeal_pending: An accused dies while the criminal appeal against that accused remains pending.

members.legal_issue: Adding a deceased party’s legal representatives in later proceedings in a suit does not preserve an appeal that had already been filed and in which the representatives were not added in time.
material_facts: A respondent died after an appeal against a preliminary decree had been filed.
The deceased respondent’s legal representatives were not brought on record in that appeal within the prescribed time.
The representatives were brought on record within time in later final decree proceedings in the suit.
The applicant argued that the final decree proceedings and the appeal were stages of the same suit, so the later substitution should prevent abatement of the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII, rules 3, 4 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order XVI, rules 14 and 14-A of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, treats a suit and an appeal as separate proceedings for abatement. An order adding legal representatives at one stage enures to subsequent stages, because an appeal is a continuation of the suit, but an order made in the suit after an appeal has already been filed cannot be projected backwards into that appeal. Brij Inder Singh v. Kanshi Ram, 44 I.A. 218, was distinguished; Shankarnaraina Saralaya v. Laxmi Hengsu, A.I.R. 1931 Mad. 277, was referred to.
members.conclusion: The order adding the legal representatives in the final decree proceedings did not benefit the previously filed appeal, which abated as against the deceased respondent.

predicates.appeal_pending_when_party_died: An appeal had already been filed and was pending when a party to it died.
predicates.representatives_not_added_to_appeal_in_t: The deceased party’s legal representatives were not brought on record in the appeal within the prescribed time.
predicates.representatives_added_in_later_suit_proc: The deceased party’s legal representatives were added in proceedings in the suit that occurred after the appeal had already been filed.

members.legal_issue: An appeal abates automatically when the appellant dies and no timely application is made to substitute the appellant’s legal representatives.
material_facts: The plaintiff died while her second appeal was pending.
No legal representatives applied to be substituted within the prescribed period, and the appeal proceeded without them.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rules 3(2) and 4(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure provide for abatement when no substitution application is made within the time allowed by law. The Court held that, on expiry of 90 days after the appellant’s death without such an application, the appeal stood dismissed as abated.
members.conclusion: The second appeal abated automatically upon expiry of the substitution period, leaving no appeal pending before the High Court.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party has brought an appeal before a court for decision.
predicates.appellant_dies: The appellant dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.substitution_not_sought_in_time: No one entitled to continue the appeal applies within the applicable time to replace the deceased appellant with the appellant’s legal representatives.
predicates.appeal_abates_automatically: The appeal ends by abatement without a further order dismissing it.

members.legal_issue: A judgment or decree made in an appeal after abatement, in favour of or against a deceased party who has not been replaced, is a nullity.
material_facts: The plaintiff-appellant and two defendant-respondents died during the second appeal.
No legal representatives were brought on record, and the High Court decided the second appeal after it had abated.
The High Court decreed specific performance in favour of the deceased plaintiff and against the deceased defendants.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rules 3(2) and 4(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure resulted in abatement when substitution applications were not made. Under Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, a decree passed without jurisdiction is a nullity. The Court also relied on N. Jayaram Reddy v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Ashok Transport Agency v. Awadhesh Kumar, and Amba Bai v. Gopal for the principle that a decree for or against a dead person is a nullity.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment and decree were a nullity because they were made after the appeal had abated and in favour of and against deceased persons.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and appellant_dies and substitution_not_sought_in_time and court_decides_after_abatement

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party has brought an appeal before a court for decision.
predicates.appellant_dies: The appellant dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.substitution_not_sought_in_time: No one entitled to continue the appeal applies within the applicable time to replace the deceased appellant with the appellant’s legal representatives.
predicates.court_decides_after_abatement: The court issues its decision after the proceeding has abated and without the deceased party’s legal representatives being substituted.
predicates.decree_is_nullity: The resulting judgment or decree has no legal validity.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s comparative-hardship claim does not remain for decision after the tenant dies during the appeal.
material_facts: The tenant died while the appeal was pending.
The dispute included whether eviction would cause greater hardship to the tenant.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the tenant’s death during the appeal meant that the question of greater hardship to that tenant under section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, no longer arose.
members.conclusion: After the tenant’s death during the appeal, the question of greater hardship to that tenant did not arise.

predicates.rent_eviction_appeal_with_tenant_compara: An appeal in a rent eviction proceeding includes an issue about hardship to the tenant.
predicates.tenant_dies_during_appeal: The tenant dies while the appeal is pending.

members.legal_issue: A deceased appellant’s right of appeal does not survive to the remaining appellants under the rule for survivorship when they have not established that they and the deceased formed a joint Hindu family.
material_facts: Nine plaintiffs jointly filed a second appeal; one appellant died while it was pending, and no timely application was made to bring his legal representatives on the record.
Although the surviving appellants were given time to provide evidence that they formed a joint Hindu family with the deceased, their affidavits did not make that assertion.
The application to substitute the deceased appellant’s sons described them as his heirs and legal representatives.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXII, rules 2, 3 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, survivorship applies only where the right to sue or appeal survives to the remaining parties.
