The evidence did not establish that the appellants formed a joint Hindu family or that the deceased appellant’s right to appeal survived to them.
members.conclusion: The surviving appellants could not continue the appeal on the basis that the right to appeal survived to them alone; the appeal abated as against the deceased appellant.

rule.if: joint_plaintiff_appeal and appellant_dies_during_appeal and no_timely_substitution and no_proof_of_joint_family

predicates.joint_plaintiff_appeal: Multiple plaintiffs jointly filed an appeal.
predicates.appellant_dies_during_appeal: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.no_timely_substitution: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not brought on the record within the required time.
predicates.no_proof_of_joint_family: The remaining appellants did not establish that they and the deceased appellant formed a joint family through which the right of appeal survived to them.

members.legal_issue: The power to appeal against an entire decree on a ground common to multiple plaintiffs does not permit surviving appellants to continue an appeal jointly filed by all plaintiffs after one appellant’s appeal has abated.
material_facts: All nine plaintiffs jointly filed the second appeal while the deceased appellant was alive and was himself an appellant.
The decree concerned a common, joint right to obtain ejectment, and the appeal abated as against the deceased appellant when his legal representatives were not substituted in time.
The respondents’ position was that allowing the survivors to proceed could result in inconsistent decrees concerning the joint right.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure allows one plaintiff or defendant to appeal from the whole decree where it proceeds on a ground common to all, but it did not apply because all plaintiffs had jointly filed this appeal and the survivors had not filed it as representatives of the deceased. Order XXII operates during the appeal and requires timely substitution; its abatement provisions are not overridden by rule 4. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram for the principle that abatement makes the decree final against the deceased party’s legal representatives and prevents direct or indirect modification affecting their rights. It approved Ramphal Sahu v. Babu Satdeo Jha, Amin Chand v. Baldeo Sahai Ganga Sahai, Baij Nath v. Ram Bharose, Nanak v. Ahmad Ali, Pyarelal v. Sikhar Chand, Raghu Sutar v. Narusingha Nath, Venkata Ram Rao v. Narayana, and Sonahar Ali v. Mukbul Ali, and disapproved the contrary approaches in Shripad Balwant v. Nagu Kusheba, Satulal Bhattachariya v. Asiruddin Shaikh, and Somasundaram Chettiar v. Vaithilinga Mudaliar.
members.conclusion: Order XLI, rule 4 did not apply, and the appeal could not proceed in favour of the surviving appellants after the deceased appellant’s appeal had abated.

rule.if: joint_plaintiff_appeal and all_plaintiffs_joined_in_filing and common_ground_for_all and joint_indivisible_right and appellant_dies_during_appeal and appeal_abates_as_to_deceased

predicates.joint_plaintiff_appeal: Multiple plaintiffs brought an appeal from a decree.
predicates.all_plaintiffs_joined_in_filing: All plaintiffs, including the later-deceased appellant, jointly filed the appeal while that appellant was alive.
predicates.common_ground_for_all: The decree under appeal rested on a ground common to all the plaintiffs.
predicates.joint_indivisible_right: The plaintiffs’ claimed right was joint and could not be divided without affecting the parties’ rights against one another.
predicates.appellant_dies_during_appeal: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased: The appeal abated as against the deceased appellant because the required substitution was not made in time.

members.legal_issue: The appellate court’s broad power to make further orders cannot be used to continue an appeal that is not competent after abatement or to defeat the finality of the decree as to the deceased appellant.
material_facts: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not substituted in time, so the decree became final against them.
The surviving appellants sought to rely on the appellate court’s broad powers even though the appeal could not competently proceed after the abatement.
The failure to take steps for substitution was attributable to the deceased appellant’s legal representatives and the surviving appellants.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the appellate court a wide discretion, including in exceptional cases where its non-exercise would make adjustment of parties’ rights difficult, but does not make an incompetent appeal competent or override abatement under Order XXII. The Court relied on Mahomed Khaleel Shirazi & Sons v. Los Panneries Lyonnaises, which held that rule 33 was not intended to apply to an appeal that was not competent against a party. The Court also explained that exercising the power to grant relief for the deceased appellant would create contradictory decrees and improperly defeat the finality resulting from abatement.
members.conclusion: Order XLI, rule 33 did not apply because the surviving appellants’ appeal was not competent in the circumstances; that rule could not be used to grant relief affecting the deceased appellant’s rights or nullify abatement.

rule.if: plaintiff_appeal_after_decree and appellant_dies_during_appeal and appeal_abates_as_to_deceased and surviving_appeal_is_incompetent

predicates.plaintiff_appeal_after_decree: A plaintiff brought an appeal from a decree.
predicates.appellant_dies_during_appeal: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased: The appeal abated as against the deceased appellant because the required substitution was not made in time.
predicates.surviving_appeal_is_incompetent: After the abatement, the surviving appellants’ appeal could not competently proceed in a way that affected the deceased appellant’s rights.

members.legal_issue: A co-appellant's death during the pendency of an appeal results in the appeal abating as against that co-appellant.
material_facts: One of the two appellants died while the appeal was pending.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the death of an appellant during the pending appeal as resulting in abatement of the appeal against that appellant; it cited no provision or earlier case for this disposition.
members.conclusion: The appeal abated as against the deceased appellant.

predicates.pending_appeal: A criminal appeal was pending before the Court.
predicates.appellant_died_during_appeal: An appellant died while the appeal was pending.

members.legal_issue: An appeal cannot proceed as a whole after it abates against a deceased respondent when deciding the remaining appeal would require inconsistent decrees or leave necessary relief unavailable, and the general appellate power to vary a decree for the benefit of parties does not cure that problem.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by subsequent purchasers against a decree for specific performance that required payment jointly to the vendor and the subsequent purchasers.
The plaintiffs had also sought substantial alternative monetary relief against the vendor.
The vendor died while the appeal was pending, and the application to substitute the vendor's legal representatives was dismissed.
Setting aside the specific-performance decree would affect the joint decree, and the alternative monetary relief could not be granted without the vendor or the vendor's legal representatives.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal abates as against a deceased party when the required legal representatives are not brought on record. Under State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 636, abatement makes the decree between the appellant and the deceased respondent final and prevents its direct or indirect modification. Rameshwar Prasad v. M/s Shyam Beharilal Jagannath, [1964] 3 S.C.R. 549, and Pandit Siri Chand v. M/s Jagdish Parshad Kishin Chand, [1966] 3 S.C.R. 451, support the rule that an appeal cannot continue where it is not properly constituted or its success would produce inconsistent decrees. Order 41, Rule 4 cannot overcome those problems where reversing the decree would affect a joint decree or required relief against the deceased party cannot be granted.
members.conclusion: The abatement concerning the vendor was fatal to the entire appeal; Order 41, Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not allow the appeal to proceed, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_case and respondent_dies_during_appeal and legal_representatives_not_substituted_in_time and (relief_would_modify_joint_decree or success_would_create_inconsistent_decrees or necessary_relief_unavailable_without_deceased_party)

predicates.appeal_case: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.respondent_dies_during_appeal: A respondent dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_substituted_in: The deceased respondent's legal representatives are not brought on record within the required time.
predicates.relief_would_modify_joint_decree: The relief sought on appeal would require changing a decree made jointly in favour of the deceased party and other parties.
predicates.success_would_create_inconsistent_decree: Allowing the appeal while the deceased party's decree remains final would result in inconsistent decrees concerning the same subject matter.
predicates.necessary_relief_unavailable_without_dec: The court cannot grant relief required to resolve the dispute without the deceased party or their legal representatives.

members.legal_issue: An appeal abates against a deceased appellant and the remaining appellants when legal representatives are not substituted and the cause of action is common to them.
material_facts: One appellant died while the appeal was pending.
The deceased appellant's legal representatives were not brought on record.
The cause of action underlying the appeal was common to the deceased appellant and the other appellants.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the procedural consequence of a deceased appellant's legal representatives not being substituted and held that abatement extended to the other appellants where the common cause of action operated against them as well. The judgment cites no provision or earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal abated against the deceased appellant and, because the cause of action was common, against the other appellants as well.

rule.if: civil_appeal_with_multiple_appellants and appellant_died and legal_representatives_not_substituted and cause_of_action_common_and_inseverable

predicates.civil_appeal_with_multiple_appellants: The proceeding is a civil appeal brought by more than one appellant.
predicates.appellant_died: One of the appellants died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_substituted: The deceased appellant's legal representatives were not substituted in the appeal.
predicates.cause_of_action_common_and_inseverable: The cause of action is common to the deceased appellant and the other appellants, such that the appeal cannot proceed separately against them.

members.legal_issue: A second appeal abates when the appellant dies during its pendency and the appellant’s legal representatives are not brought on record within the prescribed time, leaving the decree under appeal final.
material_facts: The defendant filed a second appeal against a first appellate decree granting specific performance.
The defendant died while the second appeal was pending.
The defendant’s legal representatives were not brought on record or otherwise took steps to continue the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rules 3 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure apply the procedure for substitution of a deceased plaintiff to an appellant in an appeal; under Order 22 Rule 3(2), failure to apply within the time limited by law results in abatement. Order 22 Rule 9 governs the consequences of abatement. In Rahmani Khatoon v. Harkoo Gope, the Court held that when an appeal abates, the judgment or decree challenged in it becomes final. Rajendra Prasad v. Khirodhar Mahto likewise supports the consequence that abatement of an appeal leaves the decree under challenge final.
members.conclusion: The second appeal abated, and the first appellate decree acquired finality.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding was a second appeal against a decree of a lower court.
predicates.appellant_died_during_appeal: The appellant died while the second appeal was pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_brought_on_rec: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not brought on record to continue the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A judgment disposing of an appeal against a person who had died before the judgment was delivered is a nullity.
material_facts: The appellant died while the second appeal was pending, before the court disposed of it.
The death was not brought to the court’s attention, and the court dismissed the appeal without the appellant’s legal representatives having been brought on record.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rules 3 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provide for bringing a deceased appellant’s legal representatives on record. The Court relied on Rajendra Prasad v. Khirodhar Mahto for the principle that a decree against a dead person is a nullity.
members.conclusion: The judgment dismissing the second appeal was a nullity because it was passed against a deceased person.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The proceeding was an appeal before a court.
predicates.party_died_before_decision: A party to the appeal died before the court delivered its decision.
predicates.deceased_party_not_substituted: The deceased party’s legal representatives were not substituted in the appeal before the decision.

members.legal_issue: An appeal cannot proceed against surviving respondents when success against them would contradict a decree that has become final following abatement of the appeal against a deceased respondent.
material_facts: The plaintiff respondent died while the appeal was pending, and the plaintiff’s legal representatives were not impleaded.
The appellant conceded that the appeal had abated against the deceased respondent.
The appellant sought to continue the appeal against the surviving respondents by arguing that the plaintiff’s mortgagor was a different defendant from the one identified in the decree below.
That argument, if accepted, would directly conflict with the decree affecting the deceased respondent, which had become final.
members.legal_principle: Although the Code of Civil Procedure does not provide for abatement of an appeal against the deceased respondent’s co-respondents, an appeal cannot proceed against surviving respondents if a decree in their favour would contradict the decree that became final upon abatement against the deceased respondent. This rule preserves consistency in judicial decisions and accords with the principle approved in State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram.
members.conclusion: The appeal abated in its entirety and was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_pending and respondent_deceased and legal_representatives_not_impleaded and appeal_abated_as_to_deceased and success_against_survivors_would_conflict_with_final_decree

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal is pending against multiple respondents.
predicates.respondent_deceased: One respondent dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_impleaded: The deceased respondent’s legal representatives are not brought into the appeal.
predicates.appeal_abated_as_to_deceased: The appeal abates as against the deceased respondent.
predicates.success_against_survivors_would_conflict: A decision in favour of the appellant against the surviving respondents would contradict the decree that became final as against the deceased respondent.

members.legal_issue: An appeal is defective as to property when a necessary party’s death causes the appeal to abate against that party.
material_facts: During the appeal, an heir of a co-lessee in respect of one plot died.
The appeal abated against that heir.
The Court found the appeal defective for non-joinder as to that plot, but not as to the remaining property.
members.legal_principle: The death and resulting abatement of a necessary party makes the appeal defective for non-joinder with respect to the property affected by that party’s interest; it does not necessarily defeat the appeal concerning other property.
members.conclusion: The appeal was defective for non-joinder as to the affected plot, but the defect did not extend to the rest of the appeal.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and necessary_party_died and appeal_abated_against_party and party_interest_limited_to_part_of_property

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brings an appeal concerning property.
predicates.necessary_party_died: A person whose presence is necessary to determine the appeal dies while it is pending.
predicates.appeal_abated_against_party: The appeal abates against the deceased person.
predicates.party_interest_limited_to_part_of_proper: The deceased person’s relevant interest concerns only part of the property in dispute.
predicates.appeal_defective_for_affected_property_o: The appeal is defective for non-joinder only as to the property affected by the deceased person’s interest.

members.legal_issue: A pending proceeding abates when the right to continue survives but the legal representatives of a deceased sole appellant are not brought on record within the prescribed period, unless the abatement is set aside.
material_facts: The sole appellant died while the appeal was pending.
The legal representatives were not brought on record within the prescribed period.
The Court dismissed the application to excuse the delay and the related substitution application.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that death does not cause abatement where the right to sue survives; Order 22 Rule 3 provides for bringing the deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives on record within the prescribed time; and Order 22 Rule 9 provides for setting aside abatement. Abatement for failure to apply within time occurs automatically, without a separate order declaring it. The Court relied on Mithailal Dalsangar Singh v. Annabai Devram Kini and Union of India v. Ram Charan.
members.conclusion: The appeal had abated and, as a result, stood dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_after_sole_appellant_death and right_to_continue_survived and no_substitution_within_limitation and abatement_not_set_aside

predicates.appeal_after_sole_appellant_death: An appeal was pending when its sole appellant died.
predicates.right_to_continue_survived: The deceased appellant’s claim could continue through legal representatives.
predicates.no_substitution_within_limitation: The legal representatives were not brought on record within the prescribed period.
predicates.abatement_not_set_aside: The court did not set aside the abatement.

members.legal_issue: An appeal abates in its entirety when proceeding without the deceased respondent’s legal representatives could produce a decree contradictory to the decree that became final in that respondent’s favour.
material_facts: The trial court declared the plaintiffs and the deceased respondent to be co-owners entitled to joint possession, although their respective shares were specified.
The deceased respondent was a beneficiary of the trial court decree and had a vested right under it; the property had not been partitioned.
The appellants appealed the decree, but did not bring the deceased respondent’s legal representatives on record within the prescribed time.

The application to condone the delay in seeking substitution was rejected, and the appellate court found that allowing the appeal could result in a decree inconsistent with the decree in favour of the deceased respondent.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXII Rules 4(3) and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal abates against a deceased respondent if legal representatives are not brought on record within the time allowed by law. Whether that abatement extends to the whole appeal depends on the circumstances, particularly whether deciding the appeal against the remaining parties could produce contradictory or inconsistent decrees concerning the same subject matter. The tests stated in State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, Sri Chand v. M/s Jagdish Pershad Kishan Chand, Ramagya Prasad Gupta v. Brahmadeo Prasad Gupta, Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta, and Shahazada Bi v. Halimabi include whether a successful appeal could conflict with the decree that became final against the deceased, whether effective relief remains possible, and whether the decree is joint and inseverable. A co-owner has a right to possession and enjoyment of every part of unpartitioned property jointly with the other co-owners; a stated share does not by itself make the decree severable. The relevant test is whether the decree concerning the remaining parties would be contradictory or inconsistent with the decree that became final for the deceased party.
members.conclusion: The appeal abated in its entirety, not merely as to the deceased respondent’s share.

rule.if: appeal_from_civil_decree and deceased_respondent_benefited_from_decree and deceased_respondent_not_substituted_in_time and (unpartitioned_property_held_in_joint_possession or appeal_success_could_conflict_with_final_decree)

predicates.appeal_from_civil_decree: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a civil court decree.
predicates.deceased_respondent_benefited_from_decre: The deceased respondent held a right under the decree being appealed.
predicates.deceased_respondent_not_substituted_in_t: The appellant did not bring the deceased respondent’s legal representatives on record within the time allowed.
predicates.unpartitioned_property_held_in_joint_pos: The decree concerns unpartitioned property in which the parties were declared co-owners entitled to joint possession.
predicates.appeal_success_could_conflict_with_final: Allowing the appeal against the remaining parties could produce a decree inconsistent with the decree that became final in favour of the deceased respondent.

members.legal_issue: An appeal against a decree concerning multiple co-sharers cannot proceed against surviving respondents when it has abated as to a deceased co-sharer and success could produce inconsistent decrees.
material_facts: A suit for partition resulted in a decree recognising the interests of several co-sharers and rejecting the alleged sale agreement.
The legal representatives of one respondent co-sharer were not substituted in the opposing parties’ appeal before the High Court, and the appeal abated as to that co-sharer.
The High Court nevertheless proceeded with the appeal and upheld the agreement against the surviving co-sharers, while the decree rejecting the agreement became final as to the deceased co-sharer.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII Rules 1, 2, 4(1)–(3) and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, govern abatement and apply to appeals. Where substitution is not made within the prescribed time, an appeal abates against the deceased respondent. Under State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, an appeal cannot proceed against remaining respondents when doing so would result in a decree inconsistent with the decree that has become final as to the deceased respondent. The Court also relied on Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta and Hemareddi v. Ramachandra Yallappa Hosmani, which address whether decrees are separable and whether inconsistent decrees would result.
members.conclusion: The appeal had abated as to the deceased co-sharer and could not proceed against the surviving respondents; the High Court appeal was incompetent and had to be dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_partition_decree and respondent_co_sharer_dies and legal_representatives_not_substituted and appeal_abates_as_to_deceased and success_against_survivors_would_create_inconsistent_decrees

predicates.appeal_from_partition_decree: The proceeding is an appeal against a decree concerning the division of property among co-sharers.
predicates.respondent_co_sharer_dies: A respondent co-sharer dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_substituted: The deceased respondent’s legal representatives are not brought into the appeal within the required time.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased: The appeal consequently abates as to the deceased respondent.
predicates.success_against_survivors_would_create_i: A decision for the appellant against the remaining respondents would conflict with the decree that has become final as to the deceased respondent.

members.legal_issue: Surviving appellants cannot use the provision permitting one plaintiff to appeal from the whole decree to overcome abatement when all plaintiffs originally appealed jointly.
material_facts: All the plaintiffs filed the second appeal jointly against the decree.
One appellant died during the appeal, and the appeal abated as to him because his legal representatives were not substituted in time.
The surviving appellants sought to continue the appeal and obtain relief affecting the deceased appellant's interests.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, Rule 4 permits one plaintiff or defendant to appeal from the whole decree where it proceeds on a ground common to that group. It applies at the institution of the appeal; Order XXII, Rules 3 and 9 apply during its pendency when a party dies and the appeal abates. The provisions address different stages and contingencies. The Court also relied on State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram for the principle that abatement makes the decree final as between the deceased party and the opposing party and prevents its direct or indirect modification in that party's absence.
members.conclusion: Order XLI, Rule 4 did not permit the surviving appellants to continue the appeal or obtain relief for the deceased appellant after abatement.

rule.if: appeal_from_decree and all_plaintiffs_filed_jointly and appellant_died and substitution_not_timely

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.all_plaintiffs_filed_jointly: All plaintiffs originally joined in filing the appeal.
predicates.appellant_died: A party to the appeal died during its pendency.
predicates.substitution_not_timely: The deceased party's legal representatives were not brought on the record within the prescribed time.
predicates.survivors_cannot_use_single_party_appeal: The surviving appellants cannot use the rule allowing one party to appeal from the whole decree to obtain relief for the deceased appellant.

members.legal_issue: The appellate court's broad power to make further or other orders cannot be used to nullify abatement or revive an incompetent appeal.
material_facts: The deceased appellant's legal representatives and the surviving appellants did not take timely steps to secure substitution.
The appeal had abated as to the deceased appellant, leaving the decree against his legal representatives final.
Relief for the deceased appellant's interests would conflict with that final decree, and the appeal by the surviving appellants was not competent in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, Rule 33 gives the appellate court a broad discretion to make decrees and orders required by the case, including in exceptional situations where necessary to adjust the rights of parties, but it does not authorize nullification of abatement. The Court relied on Mahomed Khaleel Shirazi & Sons v. Les Tanneries Lyonnaises for the principle that Rule 33 does not apply to an appeal that is not competent under the Code or applicable court rules, and on State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram concerning the finality resulting from abatement.
members.conclusion: Order XLI, Rule 33 did not permit the appellate court to continue the appeal or grant relief affecting the deceased appellant's interests; its discretionary power was not to be exercised to nullify abatement.

rule.if: appeal_from_decree and appeal_abated_as_to_party and relief_would_affect_deceased_party_rights and appeal_incompetent

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.appeal_abated_as_to_party: The appeal abated as to a party who died during its pendency.
predicates.relief_would_affect_deceased_party_right: The requested appellate relief would affect the rights of the deceased party or that party's legal representatives under the decree.
predicates.appeal_incompetent: The appeal that remains is not competent to provide the requested relief.
predicates.appellate_discretion_cannot_nullify_abat: The appellate court cannot use its broad discretionary power to nullify the abatement or grant relief affecting the deceased party's rights.

members.legal_issue: An appeal cannot proceed for surviving parties alone when their common and indivisible right would require inconsistent decrees in relation to the deceased party's final decree.
material_facts: The appellants had a common, indivisible interest in seeking ejectment of the defendant from the premises.
The appeal abated as to one appellant, and the decree in the defendant's favour became final against that appellant's legal representatives.
Allowing the surviving appellants to obtain ejectment would be inconsistent with the final decree under which the defendant could remain in occupation as against the deceased appellant's interest.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXII, Rules 3 and 9, abatement makes the decree final as between the deceased party and the opposing party. As stated in State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, the appellate court cannot directly or indirectly modify that decree in the absence of the deceased party's legal representatives. Where parties have a joint, indivisible right, proceeding with the appeal for some of them would risk contradictory decrees; the court therefore cannot continue the appeal in those circumstances.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not hear the surviving appellants' appeal, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_decree and common_indivisible_right and appeal_abated_as_to_party and continued_appeal_would_create_inconsistent_decrees

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.common_indivisible_right: The parties share a common right that cannot be divided for purposes of the requested relief.
predicates.appeal_abated_as_to_party: The appeal abated as to a party who died during its pendency.
predicates.continued_appeal_would_create_inconsiste: Granting relief in the continuing appeal would conflict with the final decree as it stands against the deceased party or that party's legal representatives.
predicates.appeal_cannot_proceed_for_survivors_alon: The appeal cannot proceed for the surviving parties alone.

members.legal_issue: An appeal cannot be heard and decided after a respondent whose estate must be represented has died until the court determines and brings the legal representative or representatives on record.
material_facts: A successful plaintiff died while the defendant's appeal from the decree was pending, and the right to continue the case survived against her estate.
Her husband and her nieces and nephews each sought to represent her estate, and the dispute between them remained undecided when the High Court heard and allowed the appeal.
The husband was added as legal representative only after the High Court had delivered its judgment.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(11) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines a legal representative to include a person who represents the estate or intermeddles with it. Order 22 Rules 4 and 5, read with Rule 11, require determination of a disputed representative and the bringing of the representative on record before an appeal can proceed. Section 33, Order 20 Rule 1, and Order 41 Rule 30 support the principle that judgment follows a hearing; an appeal is not heard in the eye of law when the deceased respondent's estate is unrepresented.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not proceed to hear the appeal on the merits before determining who represented the deceased respondent's estate and bringing that person or those persons on record. Because the estate remained unrepresented when the appeal was decided, the High Court's judgment was a nullity and inoperative; the appeal was restored for the High Court to determine representation first and then hear it on the merits.

rule.if: appeal_from_a_decree and respondent_dies_during_appeal and right_to_continue_survives_against_estate and estate_unrepresented_when_appeal_decided

predicates.appeal_from_a_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.respondent_dies_during_appeal: A respondent dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.right_to_continue_survives_against_estat: The right to continue the proceeding survives against the deceased respondent's estate.
predicates.estate_unrepresented_when_appeal_decided: The appeal is decided before a legal representative has been determined and brought on record to represent the deceased respondent's estate.

members.legal_issue: A pending appeal from a joint decree for pre-emption abates in its entirety when one appellant dies and the deceased appellant’s legal representatives are not brought on record, if the decree cannot be varied for the surviving appellants without creating conflicting decrees.
material_facts: The property was conveyed to multiple purchasers in a single transaction, with the purchasers to enjoy it in equal shares rather than as separate items of property.
A decree for pre-emption was passed against the purchasers, who appealed jointly.
One appellant died while the appeal was pending, and no application was made to bring that appellant’s legal representatives on record.
The decree for pre-emption as to the deceased appellant’s interest had become final by reason of the abatement.
members.legal_principle: Pre-emption substitutes the pre-emptor for the purchaser, and a partial pre-emption decree is not possible. Where a decree is joint and part of it becomes final through abatement, the entire appeal abates if allowing the remaining appeal would produce conflicting decrees. The Court relied on Jhanda Singh v. Gurmukh Singh.
members.conclusion: The entire appeal abated and was dismissed with costs.

predicates.appeal_from_joint_preemption_decree: The proceeding is an appeal by purchasers against a decree granting pre-emption.
predicates.appellant_died_without_representatives_a: One appellant died during the appeal and the appellant’s legal representatives were not added to the proceeding.
predicates.purchasers_acquired_property_jointly: The purchasers acquired the property together rather than acquiring distinct, separately conveyed items.
predicates.partial_relief_would_create_conflicting_: Proceeding with the surviving appellants’ appeal would risk inconsistent decrees concerning the same pre-emption claim.

members.legal_issue: An appeal against a surviving respondent cannot proceed when the appeal against a deceased respondent has abated and the decree under challenge is joint and indivisible, making adjudication without the deceased respondent’s legal representatives improper.
material_facts: Two landowners made a joint claim for compensation for the same acquired land and received a joint award and decree.

One respondent died while the State’s appeal was pending, and no application to substitute that respondent’s legal representatives was made in time, so the appeal against the deceased respondent abated.

The compensation concerned the same subject matter, and resolving the appeal against the surviving respondent would require the appellate court to determine the deceased respondent’s rights without that respondent’s legal representatives.
Although records showed specified shares, their correctness was not guaranteed, and determining the surviving respondent’s share would also require determining the deceased respondent’s share.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for abatement against the deceased respondent when the legal representatives are not brought on record in time, but does not itself provide for abatement against co-respondents. Under Order I Rule 9, the court should proceed so far as it can decide the controversy concerning parties before it; it must dismiss the appeal if it cannot do so. Relevant considerations include whether the surviving appeal is properly constituted, whether success could produce a decision conflicting with the final decree concerning the deceased respondent, whether the necessary relief could have been sought against the surviving respondents alone, and whether a resulting decree would be effective. Abatement makes the decree between the appellant and deceased respondent final and prevents its direct or indirect modification. A joint indivisible decree cannot be challenged against only one joint decree-holder, and recording specific shares does not by itself make the decree severable. The Court did not rely on earlier cases; it stated that reviewing them would serve no useful purpose.
members.conclusion: The appeal against the deceased respondent had abated, and because the joint decree could not be modified or effectively challenged without determining the absent legal representatives’ rights, the appeal against the surviving respondent could not proceed and was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_appeal and respondent_died_pending_appeal and legal_representative_not_substituted and joint_indivisible_decree and absent_party_rights_required_for_surviving_appeal

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil case.
predicates.respondent_died_pending_appeal: A respondent died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.legal_representative_not_substituted: The appellant did not bring the deceased respondent’s legal representative into the proceeding in time.
predicates.joint_indivisible_decree: The decree under appeal granted relief jointly and could not be treated as separate relief for the surviving respondent alone.
predicates.absent_party_rights_required_for_survivi: Deciding the appeal against the surviving respondent would require determining or affecting the rights of the deceased respondent or that respondent’s legal representatives.

members.legal_issue: An appeal concerning a deceased appellant’s property claim abates when the appellant dies during the appeal and no legal representatives are brought on record.
material_facts: The appeal concerned a field for which possession was claimed from one appellant.
That appellant died while the appeal was pending.
His legal representatives were not brought on record.
members.legal_principle: The judgment applies the procedural consequence of abatement where an appellant dies during the appeal and the appellant’s legal representatives are not brought on record. No specific provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal concerning that field had abated.

predicates.execution_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning execution of a decree.
predicates.appellant_died_during_appeal: An appellant died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_brought_on_rec: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not substituted in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: Enforcement after a constitutional judgment of a law protected from fundamental-rights challenge by its inclusion in a constitutional schedule remains immune from challenge on the ground that the enforcement infringes fundamental rights.
material_facts: The petitioner was directed to show cause why land held in excess of the ceiling should not be treated as surplus and vest in the State under an agricultural land-ceiling law.
The law had been included in the constitutional schedule before the earlier judgment relied on by the petitioner.
The petitioner argued that enforcement after that judgment could be challenged for infringing fundamental rights.
The challenged enforcement occurred after the earlier judgment.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the majority in I. C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) treated laws included in the Ninth Schedule as protected by Article 31B from challenge for infringing Part III rights. The prospective operation of that judgment did not make action taken after its delivery under amendments made before then invalid on fundamental-rights grounds. The Court also relied on State of Maharashtra v. Madhavrao Damodar Patilchand (1968), which had upheld the validity of the agricultural land-ceiling law as amended.
members.conclusion: The petitioner could not challenge the action on the ground that it was taken after the earlier judgment, and the petition was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_enforcem: A person brought a constitutional writ proceeding to challenge enforcement of a law against them.
predicates.schedule_protection_preceded_prior_judgm: The law had been placed within a constitutional schedule that protects it from fundamental-rights challenges before the earlier judgment relied on by the person.
predicates.fundamental_rights_infringement_alleged: The person alleged that enforcement of the law infringed fundamental rights.
predicates.enforcement_followed_prior_judgment: The challenged enforcement occurred after the earlier judgment relied on by the person.
predicates.challenge_to_enforcement_rejected: The challenge to enforcement on the asserted fundamental-rights ground is rejected.

members.legal_issue: Inclusion of legislation in the constitutional protection schedule prevents it from being invalidated for inconsistency with fundamental rights, with the protection operating from the legislation’s enactment.
material_facts: The estate-rights abolition regulation was challenged as violating the estate holder’s property right under Article 19(1)(f).
While the appeal was pending, the regulation was added to the Ninth Schedule.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that legislation included in the Ninth Schedule is not void, or ever deemed void, on the ground that it is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges rights conferred by Part III. The Court held that this cures any such defect retrospectively from enactment, relying on Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, Land Reforms, [1972] 1 SCR 1056 at 1070.
members.conclusion: The regulation was protected from the fundamental-rights challenge and was constitutionally valid; the protection operated retrospectively from the date of its enactment.

predicates.challenge_to_legislation: A party brought a proceeding challenging the constitutional validity of legislation.
predicates.alleged_fundamental_rights_violation: The challenger alleged that the legislation infringed a fundamental right.
predicates.legislation_added_to_constitutional_prot: The legislation was added to the constitutional list that protects included laws from fundamental-rights challenges.

members.legal_issue: A pre-constitutional law placed in the protected constitutional schedule is immune from a challenge based on the property guarantee carried over from the former constitutional order.
material_facts: The challenged acquisition law was enacted before the Constitution and was later placed in the protected constitutional schedule.
The challenge alleged that the law’s compensation provisions violated the property protection in the former constitutional order.
The appellants argued that the law was void when enacted and therefore could not receive constitutional protection.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule against challenges based on rights in Part III, including where the asserted right derives from Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was carried into Article 31(2). Article 366(10) did not exclude the pre-constitutional law from that protection. The Court applied Dhirubha Devisingh Gohil v. State of Bombay and State of Uttar Pradesh v. H.H. Maharaja Brijendra Singh. It distinguished N.B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector because the law there did not have Ninth Schedule protection.
members.conclusion: The law and its challenged provisions were protected from the challenge. The fact that the law predated the Constitution, or was alleged to have violated the former property guarantee, did not prevent that protection from applying.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_appeal and preconstitutional_law and law_in_protected_schedule and challenge_based_on_former_property_guarantee

predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the constitutional validity of a law or its provisions.
predicates.preconstitutional_law: The challenged law was enacted before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.law_in_protected_schedule: The challenged law was placed in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from specified rights-based challenges.
predicates.challenge_based_on_former_property_guara: The challenge relies on a property guarantee from the former constitutional order that was carried into the later Constitution.

members.legal_issue: A law protected by constitutional placement in the Ninth Schedule cannot be invalidated on the ground that it is inconsistent with or abridges the fundamental rights specified in Article 31B.
material_facts: The challenged enactment had been placed in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution.
The challengers argued that its provisions violated Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects laws included in the Ninth Schedule from invalidation on the ground that they are inconsistent with, take away, or abridge rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The fundamental-rights challenge had to be rejected because Article 31B protected the enactment from that challenge.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The case challenges the constitutional validity of an enactment.
predicates.enactment_has_ninth_schedule_protection: The enactment has the constitutional protection associated with inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_protected_fundamenta: The challenge asserts inconsistency with or abridgment of fundamental rights covered by the constitutional protection.

members.legal_issue: Constitutional amendments made before the Court’s prospective ruling remain effective, so laws protected by those amendments cannot be challenged on the ground that they violate fundamental rights.
material_facts: The challenged land-reform laws had been placed in a constitutional schedule by an amendment that had been upheld under earlier decisions.
The Court limited the effect of its new constitutional rule to the future and expressly preserved the validity of existing amendments.
The petitions sought to challenge the land-reform laws on fundamental-rights grounds.
members.legal_principle: Under the prospective-overruling ruling, the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act and other existing amendments affecting fundamental rights remained valid. As a result, the challenged laws could not be questioned on the stated grounds under Articles 13, 14 or 31. The judgment also discussed the protection afforded by Articles 31A and 31B; Hidayatullah, J. separately considered the challenged laws protected by Article 31A and the President’s assent.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the challenged laws could not be questioned on the stated fundamental-rights grounds because the existing amendment continued to protect them.

predicates.challenge_to_land_reform_laws: A party challenged land-reform legislation in a proceeding seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.existing_constitutional_protection_cover: An existing constitutional amendment placed the challenged laws within a form of constitutional protection from rights-based challenge.
predicates.prospective_ruling_preserves_existing_am: The Court limited its new rule to future amendments and left earlier amendments in force.

members.legal_issue: A law placed in the constitutional schedule before the relevant cutoff is protected from challenge for violating fundamental rights.
material_facts: The challenged 1955 land-reform law and the 1972 amendments had been placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973.
The petitioners conceded that the constitutional challenge to those laws was concluded by the Court's decision in Waman Rao.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects laws included in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973, from challenges based on inconsistency with or abridgment of Part III rights. The Court applied Waman Rao v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The 1955 Act and the 1972 amendments were immune from challenge on the ground that they violated Part III of the Constitution.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_fundamental_rights_val: A person brought a constitutional proceeding challenging a law on the ground that it violates fundamental rights.
predicates.law_was_scheduled_before_cutoff: The challenged law had been included in the protected constitutional schedule before the relevant cutoff.

members.legal_issue: A law included in the constitutional schedule with the specified protection cannot be challenged under the constitutional property-right provisions identified by the Court.
material_facts: The original land-reform Act had been included in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.
The amending Act was not included in that Schedule and could claim protection only under Article 31A.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protected the original Act after its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule. The Court distinguished that Act from the later amending Act, which was not included there and therefore had to rely on Article 31A for protection.
members.conclusion: The original Act could not be challenged under Article 31 because of its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant brought a constitutional challenge to a land-reform law.
predicates.challenged_law_was_included_in_protected: The challenged law had been included in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from the specified constitutional challenge.

members.legal_issue: A law included in the Ninth Schedule is protected against a challenge based on alleged violation of Part III rights, including rights under the second proviso to Article 31A(1).
material_facts: The challenged land-ceiling law had been included in the Ninth Schedule.
The challenge alleged that grouping family members’ holdings circumvented the second proviso to Article 31A(1) and exceeded legislative power.

The Court held that the proviso protects and confers rights to compensation, and found no issue of legislative competence of the kind that would arise from legislation trespassing on an exclusive legislative domain.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that laws and provisions specified in the Ninth Schedule are not void on the ground that they are inconsistent with, or take away or abridge, rights conferred by Part III. The protection can apply even where the alleged infringement concerns rights protected by the second proviso to Article 31A(1), because that proviso protects and confers individual rights to compensation. The Court relied on H.H. Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru v. State of Kerala concerning the effect of Article 31B and held that Article 31A and Article 31B may provide dual protection.
members.conclusion: Article 31B protected the challenged provisions from the asserted Part III-based attack. The second proviso to Article 31A(1) confers rights concerning compensation and did not impose the asserted limit on legislative competence.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A person challenges the validity of a law concerning land reform.
predicates.law_included_in_protected_schedule: The challenged law has been included in the constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from Part III-based invalidity.
predicates.challenge_alleges_part_three_rights_viol: The challenge alleges that the law violates rights protected by Part III of the Constitution.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional validity of a land-ceiling provision protected by Article 31-B cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates Article 31-A.
material_facts: The holder challenged the provision governing post-cutoff transfers as inconsistent with Article 31-A.
The Act and its relevant amendments had been included in the Ninth Schedule.
members.legal_principle: Articles 31-A and 31-B of the Constitution apply; Article 31-B protects a law included in the Ninth Schedule from the asserted constitutional challenge. The Court relied on D.G. Mahajan v. Maharashtra, [1977] 2 SCR 790, and Ambika Prasad v. U.P. State, [1980] 3 SCR 1159.
members.conclusion: The constitutional challenge could not succeed because Article 31-B immunised the provision from that challenge.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a land-ceiling law.
predicates.challenged_law_in_ninth_schedule: The challenged law has been included in the constitutional schedule that gives it immunity from the asserted challenge.

members.legal_issue: A challenge that a rule concerning prohibited transfers violates the agrarian-reform protection is barred where the governing legislation and that rule are protected by inclusion in the constitutional schedule.
material_facts: The challenged transfer provision formed part of the land-ceiling legislation.
The legislation was included in the protected constitutional schedule.
The appellants argued that the provision violated a limitation associated with the constitutional protection for agrarian-reform laws.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects legislation included in the Ninth Schedule. The Court treated that protection as sufficient to dispose of this challenge, without separately deciding the asserted limitation on the agrarian-reform protection.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the provision received the schedule's protection and did not decide the challenge on its merits under the agrarian-reform limitation.

predicates.scheduled_land_ceiling_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges a provision of a land-ceiling law that is included in a constitutionally protected schedule.
predicates.challenged_transfer_rule_is_part_of_sche: The challenged rule concerning transfers forms part of the scheduled land-ceiling law.

members.legal_issue: Protection for a pre-constitutional law placed in the constitutional schedule extends to a challenge based on a property right under the repealed constitutional statute that was carried into the fundamental-rights chapter.
material_facts: The challenged acquisition law was enacted before the Constitution and was later placed in the constitutional schedule.
The challenge alleged that the law’s compensation provisions violated the property guarantee in the repealed Government of India Act, 1935.
That guarantee was substantially carried into the fundamental-rights chapter of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-B protects a scheduled enactment or its provisions from being held void for inconsistency with, or taking away or abridging, rights in Part III. Section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935 was in substance a fundamental right carried into Part III, so Article 31-B protection extends to a challenge based on that repealed provision. The Court relied on Dhirubha Devisingh Gohil v. State of Bombay and State of Uttar Pradesh v. H.H. Maharaja Brijendra Singh, and distinguished N.B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector because the law there lacked Article 31-B protection.
members.conclusion: The protection attached to the scheduled law barred a challenge based on the repealed property guarantee, as well as a challenge based on the corresponding fundamental right.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preconstitut: A party in a constitutional challenge asks a court to invalidate a law enacted before the Constitution.
predicates.law_is_in_protected_schedule: The challenged law has been placed in the constitutional schedule that confers immunity from fundamental-rights challenges.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_transferred_property: The party relies on a property guarantee from a repealed constitutional enactment that was substantially carried into the Constitution’s fundamental-rights chapter.

members.legal_issue: Laws placed in the protected constitutional schedule are immune from challenges based on infringement of fundamental rights, including amendments enacted before the parent law was placed there.
material_facts: The landowners challenged legislation that transferred ownership of certain lands to protected tenants, alleging inconsistency with constitutional property rights.
The parent tenancy law and a later re-enactment were placed in the Ninth Schedule by a constitutional amendment.
The amendment that inserted the provision authorising the transfer of ownership had been enacted before the parent law was placed in the Ninth Schedule.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects an Act and its provisions included in the Ninth Schedule from challenges based on inconsistency with or abridgment of rights in Part III, notwithstanding contrary court orders. That protection also covers amending laws enacted before the parent Act was included in the Schedule. The Supreme Court's holding rested on Article 31B and the relevant Ninth Schedule entries; although the High Court had cited Sri Ram Narain v. State of Bombay concerning similar tenancy provisions, the Supreme Court did not rely on that case as the basis for this holding.
members.conclusion: The parent law, its amending laws, and the re-enactment were immune from challenge under Articles 19 and 31; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_constitutional_challenge and parent_law_in_protected_schedule and amendment_enacted_before_parent_schedule_entry and challenge_based_on_fundamental_rights

predicates.appeal_from_constitutional_challenge: A party appeals from the dismissal of a proceeding challenging the constitutionality of a law.
predicates.parent_law_in_protected_schedule: The legislature places the parent law in the constitutionally protected schedule.
predicates.amendment_enacted_before_parent_schedule: The legislature enacts an amendment to the parent law before the parent law is placed in the protected schedule.
predicates.challenge_based_on_fundamental_rights: A party alleges that the law or its provisions infringe constitutionally protected fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: An enactment included in the protective schedule is immune from invalidation under Part III whether it is inconsistent with a Part III provision or takes away or abridges a right conferred by Part III, and this immunity applies to post-constitutional as well as pre-constitutional laws.
material_facts: The challenged agricultural land ceiling legislation and its amendments were included in the protective schedule.
The challenge relied on the constitutional restriction concerning acquisition of land under personal cultivation within the applicable ceiling.
members.legal_principle: The broad text and purpose of Article 31B protect scheduled enactments from invalidation for inconsistency with, or taking away or abridging rights conferred by, any provision in Part III. Its wording applies to both pre-constitutional and post-constitutional legislation. The Court followed Hasmukhlal Dayabhai v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: Inclusion in the protective schedule protects an enactment from invalidation on either ground, including a challenge based on the second proviso concerning land under personal cultivation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party brings a constitutional challenge to legislation imposing limits on agricultural land holdings.
predicates.law_in_protective_schedule: The challenged enactment is included in a constitutional schedule that gives listed enactments protection from certain constitutional challenges.
predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three: The challenge alleges inconsistency with, or infringement of a right conferred by, the constitutional provisions concerning fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: A land-ceiling provision included in the protective schedule is valid against a challenge based on the constitutional restriction concerning acquisition of personally cultivated land.
material_facts: The challenged provision required certain transfers of land made after a specified date to be ignored when determining the ceiling and surplus area.
The High Court held that the provision violated the constitutional restriction concerning personally cultivated land within the applicable ceiling.
The enactment and its amendments were included in the protective schedule.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects a scheduled enactment from invalidation for inconsistency with, or infringement of a right under, Part III. The Court applied its holding in the connected constitutional challenge concerning Article 31B.
members.conclusion: The provision was valid because its inclusion in the protective schedule immunised it from invalidation on that ground, even if it contravened the constitutional restriction.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: A party challenges the constitutionality of a provision used to determine land ceilings or surplus land.
predicates.provision_in_protective_schedule: The challenged provision is part of an enactment included in a constitutional schedule that protects listed enactments from certain challenges.
predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three: The challenge alleges inconsistency with, or infringement of a right conferred by, the constitutional provisions concerning fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: A land-reform law added to the protective schedule after a judgment declaring provisions invalid is entitled to the schedule's immunity.
material_facts: A High Court had declared certain provisions of a land-reform enactment unconstitutional under the constitutional restriction concerning personally cultivated land.
The enactment was subsequently added to the protective schedule.
The later inclusion was relied on in an appeal from the High Court decision.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that scheduled enactments are not to be deemed void or ever to have become void on the specified Part III grounds, notwithstanding a contrary court judgment. The Court applied Hasmukhlal Dayabhai v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The later inclusion entitled the enactment to the immunity conferred by the protective schedule, and the challenged provisions did not suffer from the alleged constitutional infirmity.

predicates.appeal_from_judgment_invalidating_land_r: An appeal challenges a judgment that invalidated provisions of a land-reform law.
predicates.law_added_to_protective_schedule_after_j: The land-reform law is added to a constitutional schedule for protection after the judgment being appealed.
predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three: The invalidation rests on inconsistency with, or infringement of a right conferred by, the constitutional provisions concerning fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: An enactment listed in the constitutional schedule by its title is protected against fundamental-rights challenges together with amendments made before its listing.
material_facts: The land-ceiling enactment was amended before it was included in the constitutional schedule.
The schedule listed the principal enactment by title but did not separately identify the earlier amending enactment.
The challenge alleged that provisions of the amended enactment violated fundamental rights.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31B, the requirement is that the enactment be specified in the Ninth Schedule. Ordinarily, a reference to an Act by its title includes amendments made before the date of reference. The Court explained the observations in Shri Ram Narain v. The Simla Banking and Industrial Co. Ltd., [1956] S.C.R. 603, 614, as not requiring a different result.
members.conclusion: The protection extends to the enactment as amended up to the date it was included in the schedule, so it cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates fundamental rights.

predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge_to_amended_: A party in a constitutional validity proceeding challenges an enactment as violating fundamental rights.
predicates.principal_enactment_listed_by_title: The constitutional schedule identifies the principal enactment by its title.
predicates.amendments_preceded_listing: The enactment had been amended before it was included in the constitutional schedule.

members.legal_issue: A common-law rule concerning substantive rights that was adopted and applied before the Constitution remains law in force after the Constitution takes effect.
material_facts: The priority rule was based on common law and had been applied and upheld by courts in the relevant territory before the Constitution took effect.
The dispute concerned the continued operation of that rule after the Constitution took effect.
members.legal_principle: Article 372(1) continues laws in force immediately before the Constitution until they are altered, repealed, or amended by a competent authority. In Director of Rationing and Distribution v. The Corporation of Calcutta, the Court held that “laws in force” include common law adopted and applied in India. The Court applied that reasoning to substantive common-law rules recognized by Indian judicial decisions.
members.conclusion: The common-law priority rule, having been adopted and judicially applied in the relevant territory before the Constitution, continued as law in force after the Constitution took effect.

predicates.constitutional_continuity_case: A case concerns whether a rule applied before the Constitution continues to operate after it takes effect.
predicates.substantive_common_law_rule: The rule concerns a substantive right rather than merely a method of construing legislation.
predicates.rule_adopted_and_applied_before_constitu: Courts in the relevant territory adopted and applied the rule before the Constitution took effect.

members.legal_issue: A law enacted before the Constitution remains subject to review for inconsistency with fundamental rights and is not validated merely by its continued operation after the Constitution came into force.
material_facts: The challenged testamentary restriction was part of legislation enacted before the Constitution.
The legislation continued to operate after the Constitution came into force.
members.legal_principle: Article 13(1) makes pre-constitutional laws void to the extent that they are inconsistent with fundamental rights, while Article 372 continues existing laws subject to the Constitution. The Court relied on Keshavan Madhava Menon v. The State of Bombay and explained that an inconsistent provision is void prospectively from the commencement of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The law’s pre-constitutional enactment and continued operation did not prevent review of its consistency with fundamental rights.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preconstitut: The proceeding challenges the consistency of a law enacted before the Constitution with fundamental rights.
predicates.law_remained_in_force_after_constitution: The law continued to operate after the Constitution came into force.

members.legal_issue: A law listed in the protected schedule cannot be challenged for violating the protected right to property merely by relying on the corresponding property protection under the former constitutional regime.
material_facts: The challenged law abolished the relevant land tenures, vested specified property in the government, extinguished the former holders’ rights, and provided for compensation.
The law was specifically listed in the protected schedule after a constitutional amendment.
The appellants argued that the compensation was illusory and challenged the law under the former constitutional property protection; the law had not received a separate presidential certificate.
The appeals arose from proceedings challenging the law’s validity, and the court did not decide the adequacy of compensation on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-B protects laws listed in the Ninth Schedule from being treated as void on the ground that they are inconsistent with, or take away or abridge, rights protected by Part III. The property-acquisition protection at issue was in substance a fundamental right, although it had previously been secured as a restraint on legislative power by section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935. The form in which that earlier protection was expressed does not permit a challenge that Article 31-B otherwise bars. The court distinguished The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga (1952 SCR 889), which concerned legislative competence and an alleged fraud on legislative power rather than the property-right challenge presented here.
members.conclusion: The law’s validity could not be challenged on the asserted property-right ground, including by relying on the corresponding protection under the former constitutional regime; the appeals were dismissed with costs.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person brings a proceeding challenging the validity of a law.
predicates.challenged_law_is_listed_in_protected_sc: The challenged law is specifically included in a schedule that protects listed laws from specified rights-based challenges.
predicates.challenge_concerns_protected_property_ri: The challenger claims that the law violates a protected right governing the acquisition or deprivation of property.

members.legal_issue: A challenge under the fundamental-rights guarantees concerning property cannot invalidate a law protected by the constitutional provision shielding laws listed in the Ninth Schedule.
material_facts: The respondent challenged the acquisition law under the constitutional guarantees concerning property.
The challenged Act was listed in the Ninth Schedule.
The Court relied on the constitutional protection for listed laws rather than deciding the substantive merits of the asserted property-rights violations.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that Acts and provisions specified in the Ninth Schedule are not void on the ground that they are inconsistent with or abridge rights in Part III of the Constitution. The challenged Act was listed in the Ninth Schedule. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The challenge under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) was futile because Article 31B protected the Act as a law listed in the Ninth Schedule.

predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge_to_acquisit: A person challenges an acquisition law on the ground that it violates a fundamental right.
predicates.challenged_law_listed_in_protected_sched: The challenged law is listed in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from invalidation on fundamental-rights grounds.

members.legal_issue: Pre-Constitution legislation that had already extinguished rights does not revive those rights on the Constitution’s commencement, and legislation included in the Ninth Schedule is protected from a challenge based on inconsistency with Part III.
material_facts: The Abolition Regulation and the Commutation Regulation were enacted before the Constitution commenced.
The Abolition Regulation had extinguished the jagirdar’s rights in the jagir, and the Commutation Regulation had determined the commutation payable before the Constitution commenced.
Both regulations were later included in the Ninth Schedule by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act.
members.legal_principle: The Constitution does not operate retrospectively, and rights extinguished by legislation before its commencement are not thereby revived, as held in Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay, [1951] S.C.R. 228. Article 31B protects laws included in the Ninth Schedule from being deemed void on the ground that they are inconsistent with, take away, or abridge rights in Part III.
members.conclusion: The appellant had no rights in the jagirs at the commencement of the Constitution and could not obtain restoration of possession or commutation outside the regulation; the regulations were also exempt from challenge on the ground that they violated Part III rights.

predicates.appeal_challenges_preconstitution_regula: The proceeding is an appeal challenging regulations enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.regulations_were_preconstitution: The challenged regulations were enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.rights_extinguished_before_constitution: The challenged legislation had extinguished the claimant’s relevant rights before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.regulations_in_ninth_schedule: The challenged regulations were included in the Ninth Schedule.
predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge_and_revival: A challenge based on Part III rights and a claim to revive rights already extinguished are unavailable.

members.legal_issue: An enactment’s later inclusion in the protected schedule gives it retrospective protection against a fundamental-rights challenge, subject to the limitation that a post-cutoff constitutional amendment must not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure.
material_facts: The challenged Act was added to the Ninth Schedule after the date identified in the Court’s discussion of the basic-structure limitation.
The challenge alleged that the compensation provision violated Article 14.
The Court had concluded that the compensation provision did not violate Article 14.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B gives retrospective protection to Acts included in the Ninth Schedule against challenges based on Part III rights, notwithstanding prior judicial decisions. Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, Land Reforms states that inclusion can cure such a defect retrospectively. Under Waman Rao v. Union of India, additions made after April 24, 1973 are protected only if the constitutional amendment making the addition does not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure. Since the Court found no Article 14 violation, the basic-structure objection did not alter the result.
members.conclusion: The inclusion protects the Act retrospectively from the Article 14 challenge in these appeals because the provision was not discriminatory. The Court therefore applied the rule in Jagannath; the challenge based on damage to the basic structure did not succeed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheduled_la: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law that is included in a protected constitutional schedule.
predicates.law_added_to_protected_schedule: The law was added to the protected schedule by a constitutional amendment.
predicates.alleged_rights_violation_not_established: The court finds that the alleged fundamental-rights violation has not been established.

members.legal_issue: A law specifically included in the constitutional schedule is protected from being held invalid on the ground that it contravenes the earlier constitutional guarantee governing compulsory acquisition of property, including where the challenged provisions had previously been held invalid on that ground.
material_facts: Property was acquired under a law whose compensation provisions contained two provisos limiting how compensation was calculated.
The High Court dismissed the owner's petition but held that the two provisos contravened the earlier constitutional guarantee governing compulsory acquisition of property.
After the High Court's decision, the law was specifically included in the constitutional schedule by a constitutional amendment.
The appeal challenged the part of the High Court's judgment declaring the provisos invalid.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-B, read with the Ninth Schedule, provides that listed laws and their provisions are not to be deemed void, or ever to have been void, on the ground that they are inconsistent with or abridge rights in Part III. In Dhirubha Devisingh Gohil v. The State of Bombay, the Court held that the property-acquisition protection in section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, was in substance a fundamental right carried into Part III, so Article 31-B protection extends to it. Saghir Ahmad v. The State of U.P. did not apply because the law here was specifically saved by Article 31-B and its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule. Section 5 of the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, added the law to that Schedule.
members.conclusion: The inclusion of the law in the constitutional schedule protected it from being deemed void, or ever to have been void, on the ground that it contravened the earlier constitutional guarantee. The declaration that the provisos were invalid was set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_declaration_of_invalidity: An appeal challenges a judgment declaring provisions of a law invalid.
predicates.law_specifically_added_to_protected_sche: The law was specifically added to a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from invalidity on specified rights-based grounds.
predicates.challenge_based_on_protected_property_ac: The challenge asserts that the law contravenes a constitutional protection governing compulsory acquisition of property.

members.legal_issue: A valid scheme made before the Constitution does not become subject to a fundamental-rights challenge merely because its implementation continues after the Constitution takes effect.
material_facts: The scheme was framed under a law that was valid when the scheme was made, and a prior court challenge to it had failed.
The scheme had not been fully implemented before the Constitution came into force.
After the Constitution came into force, an executive officer gave notice seeking to take over the institution's administration and properties under the scheme.
The challenge argued that the later implementation deprived the office-holder of property in violation of the constitutional guarantee.
The court distinguished the earlier decision in Seth Shanti Sarup v. Union of India, where the impugned deprivation rested on orders that were invalid under the laws under which they were issued.
members.legal_principle: The fundamental rights conferred by the Constitution are not retrospective in operation. The court applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 13(1), and distinguished Seth Shanti Sarup v. Union of India because the orders there were invalid under the laws under which they purportedly had been made. A valid pre-Constitution scheme that had already effected the relevant deprivation was not made open to challenge merely by its continued operation after the Constitution came into force.
members.conclusion: The scheme could not be challenged under the constitutional guarantee merely because it had not been fully implemented before the Constitution and was sought to be implemented afterward; the appeal was dismissed.
