predicates.constitutional_rights_challenge_in_writ: A party brings writ proceedings claiming that implementation of a scheme violates a constitutional right.
predicates.scheme_validly_made_before_constitution: A scheme was validly made under the law in force before the Constitution took effect.
predicates.property_deprivation_effected_before_con: The scheme had already effected the relevant deprivation of property rights before the Constitution took effect.
predicates.implementation_continues_after_constitut: Implementation or enforcement of the scheme continues after the Constitution takes effect.

members.legal_issue: A law protected by its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule cannot be invalidated on the ground that it violates the right to equality.
material_facts: The challenged law was included in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.
The challenge alleged that the law discriminated between maintenance-holders and the principal landholder’s family members in distributing compensation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that an Act included in the Ninth Schedule, or its provisions, is not to be deemed void for taking away or abridging rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. Article 14 is in Part III. The law was listed in the Ninth Schedule. The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The challenge under Article 14 was unavailable because Article 31B protected the law from invalidation on that ground.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_law: A party challenges a law on the ground that it treats persons unequally.
predicates.law_in_ninth_schedule: The challenged law is included in the constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from certain fundamental-rights challenges.

members.legal_issue: A State enactment included in the Ninth Schedule is protected from review on the ground that it violates fundamental rights, and Parliament may provide that protection through its constituent power.
material_facts: The challenged State legislation was included in the Ninth Schedule by a constitutional amendment.
The challenge asserted that the legislation abridged fundamental rights.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B gives Ninth Schedule laws immunity from invalidation under Article 13(2). Parliament can confer that immunity by exercising its constituent power under Article 368, including for State enactments. The Court referred to Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in discussing the validity of a constitutional amendment that placed laws in the Ninth Schedule.
members.conclusion: The legislation was protected by Article 31B from challenge on fundamental-rights grounds, and the Court could not examine its constitutionality on those grounds; legislative competence remained open to review.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheduled_la: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law included in the constitutionally protected schedule.
predicates.state_enactment_is_in_ninth_schedule: A State legislature enacted the law and a constitutional amendment placed it in the Ninth Schedule.
predicates.challenge_is_based_on_fundamental_rights: The challenger alleges that the law violates or abridges fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: A provision including land held on a lease for erecting buildings within an agricultural area is limited to land used for agricultural purposes and, so construed, is protected from the asserted constitutional challenge.
material_facts: The law’s stated purpose was abolition of the zamindari system in agricultural areas and introduction of land reforms.
Other categories in the definition of agricultural area concerned land used for crops, groves, or pasture, and the definition excluded certain land occupied by buildings.
Related provisions conferred rights on lessees of land in an agricultural area and addressed its use for erecting buildings.
The provision was challenged as unrelated to agricultural reform and as violating constitutional protections.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed the provision in its statutory context and in light of the Act’s purpose, including the relationship between sections 2(1)(d), 17(1)(b), and 19(j), and the definition of land under the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939. It agreed with the result in Durga Prasad v. Board of Revenue, U.P., Allahabad, A.I.R. 1970 All. 159, although for different reasons. On this limited construction, the provision is connected with agricultural reform and receives the protection of Article 31A of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The provision applies only to land in an agricultural area used for agricultural purposes; on that construction it is connected with agricultural reform and is protected by Article 31A from the asserted challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law provision in a proceeding concerning land reform.
predicates.provision_limited_to_agricultural_use: The provision, properly construed, applies only to land used for agricultural purposes.

members.legal_issue: A court may decide a lis pendens issue that was not specifically pleaded when the parties knew it was in issue, had an opportunity to present evidence, and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The lis pendens issue was not expressly pleaded and no specific issue was framed on it.
The plaintiff raised the issue at the commencement of trial and introduced documents concerning the earlier proceedings and execution sale.
The defendants objected neither to the evidence nor to the issue being tried, cross-examined the plaintiff, presented their own evidence, and argued the issue on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Under Rani Chandra Kunwar v. Chaudhri Narpat Singh, an issue may be decided despite the absence of a specific pleading or framed issue when the parties went to trial knowing it was in issue and the opposing party was not taken by surprise. Siddik Mahomed Shah v. Mt. Saran does not bar consideration of evidence where the parties actually tried the issue and had an opportunity to adduce evidence on it.
members.conclusion: The omission of a specific pleading was a mere irregularity and did not prevent the court from deciding the lis pendens issue.

rule.if: title_suit_involving_lis_pendens and issue_raised_at_trial and opponent_knew_issue_was_contested and opponent_had_opportunity_to_present_evidence and no_trial_prejudice

predicates.title_suit_involving_lis_pendens: The proceeding seeks a determination of property title and the effect of a transfer made during earlier litigation.
predicates.issue_raised_at_trial: A party raised the lis pendens issue during the trial despite not specifically pleading it.
predicates.opponent_knew_issue_was_contested: The opposing party knew during the trial that the lis pendens issue was being contested.
predicates.opponent_had_opportunity_to_present_evid: The opposing party had an opportunity to cross-examine and present evidence on the issue.
predicates.no_trial_prejudice: The omission of a specific pleading did not take the opposing party by surprise or otherwise prejudice the trial.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s failure to disclose other accommodation does not by itself defeat a bona fide residential eviction claim when the parties litigate the accommodation’s suitability without prejudice.
material_facts: The landlord did not disclose two other properties in the eviction petition.
Material about those properties was placed before both the Rent Controller and the High Court, and both parties addressed whether the properties were suitable.
The tenant’s case was not prejudiced by the omission.
members.legal_principle: Ram Narain Arora v. Asha Rani holds that the existence of other reasonably suitable accommodation is a defence for the tenant and that suitability is intertwined with bona fide requirement. Non-disclosure is not fatal where both parties understand and address the issue and neither is prejudiced.
members.conclusion: The non-disclosure was not fatal to the eviction proceedings.

rule.if: bona_fide_residential_eviction_case and other_accommodation_not_disclosed and suitability_evidence_litigated and neither_party_prejudiced

predicates.bona_fide_residential_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide residential requirement.
predicates.other_accommodation_not_disclosed: The landlord did not initially disclose other accommodation that could be relevant to the residential requirement.
predicates.suitability_evidence_litigated: Both parties presented or addressed material concerning whether the other accommodation was suitable.
predicates.neither_party_prejudiced: The omission did not prevent either party from presenting its case on the suitability of the other accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A court may consider a statutory ground that was vaguely pleaded when the facts needed to decide it are before the court and the issue was fully argued without objection.
material_facts: The pleadings concerning the statutory exemption were vague.
The facts necessary to determine whether ancillary processes were carried on at the relevant premises were before the court.
The issue was fully argued before the High Court without objection, and the High Court decided it.
members.legal_principle: Where the necessary facts are before the court and an issue has been fully argued and decided without objection, vague pleadings do not prevent the court from considering that issue.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not prevent consideration of the statutory ground on the basis that it had not been specifically pleaded.

predicates.statutory_ground_vaguely_pleaded: A party's pleadings state a statutory ground without specificity.
predicates.necessary_facts_on_record: The facts needed to decide that statutory ground are before the court.
predicates.issue_fully_argued_without_objection: The parties fully argue the issue without an objection to its consideration.

members.legal_issue: A first appellate court should not remand a civil case for retrial when the parties had a full opportunity to present evidence and the record is sufficient to decide the appeal.
material_facts: The parties had adduced the evidence they wished to present at trial, and the appellants did not claim that they had been denied an opportunity to produce particular evidence or that the trial had been vitiated.
The High Court examined the existing evidence and circumstances, reversed the trial court’s conclusion, and had sufficient material to decide whether the purported will was genuine.
A retrial was not necessary to resolve the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rules 23 and 23A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, remand is appropriate where the relevant conditions are met and, under Rule 23A, a retrial is considered necessary after reversal of a decree. Rule 24 directs the appellate court to determine the case finally when the evidence on record is sufficient. Remand is not routine and should not be used merely to allow a party to fill a lacuna. The Court also considered Mohan Kumar v. State of Madhya Pradesh and distinguished cases in which an opportunity to adduce necessary evidence is required.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not required to remand the case; the Supreme Court rejected the remand argument and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: civil_first_appeal_from_a_trial_decree and appellate_record_sufficient_to_decide and parties_had_full_opportunity_to_present_evidence and not retrial_necessary

predicates.civil_first_appeal_from_a_trial_decree: A party brought a first civil appeal from a decree made after trial.
predicates.appellate_record_sufficient_to_decide: The evidence already on the record was sufficient for the appellate court to determine the dispute.
predicates.parties_had_full_opportunity_to_present_: The parties had an opportunity to present the evidence they wished to rely on at trial.
predicates.retrial_necessary: A new trial was required to enable a fair and complete determination of the dispute.

members.legal_issue: Ejectment may be granted on a permissive-occupation basis even when that basis was not expressly pleaded, if it was substantively tried and both parties had a fair opportunity to address it.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought ejectment on the basis of a tenancy, while the defendant admitted the plaintiff's ownership and claimed that his own possession rested on an agreement allowing him to remain until construction costs were repaid.
Both parties presented evidence about the basis on which the defendant occupied the premises.
The tenancy was not proved, and the defendant's asserted repayment condition was rejected, leaving the permissive character of his possession established.
The defendant did not identify any defence he could have raised had the plaintiff expressly pleaded permissive occupation in the alternative.
members.legal_principle: Relief generally must rest on the parties' pleadings and the issues framed for trial. However, a court may relax the formal requirement of an express pleading where the ground was in substance in issue, both parties knew it was being tried and had an opportunity to lead evidence, and reliance on it causes no prejudice. The Court distinguished Trojan & Co. Ltd. v. Rm. N. N. Nagappa Chettiar, which rejected a new and inconsistent claim, and referred to the same principle in Sheodhar Rai & Others v. Suraj Prasad Singh & Others. It also noted the Allahabad High Court decisions in Abdul Ghani v. Musammat Babni and Balmakund v. Dalu, which permitted ejectment where tenancy was unproved but permissive occupation was established.
members.conclusion: The decree for ejectment was properly confirmed on the basis that the defendant occupied the premises with the plaintiff's permission.

rule.if: ejectment_suit and alternative_ground_was_substantively_tried and both_parties_knew_ground_was_in_issue and both_parties_had_opportunity_to_lead_evidence and defendant_admitted_permissive_possession and asserted_possession_condition_was_rejected

predicates.ejectment_suit: The proceeding sought to recover possession from an occupant.
predicates.alternative_ground_was_substantively_tri: The basis for relief not expressly pleaded was nevertheless addressed in substance at trial.
predicates.both_parties_knew_ground_was_in_issue: Both parties understood that the alternative basis for relief was involved in the trial.
predicates.both_parties_had_opportunity_to_lead_evi: Each party had an opportunity to present evidence about that basis for relief.
predicates.defendant_admitted_permissive_possession: The occupant acknowledged that possession originated with the owner's permission.
predicates.asserted_possession_condition_was_reject: The occupant's claimed condition limiting the permission to remain was not established.

members.legal_issue: A court may grant ejectment on the basis of permissive possession even when the pleaded tenancy is not proved, if the licence issue was in substance tried and the parties had an opportunity to present evidence on it.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership and sought ejectment on the basis of a tenancy, while the defendant admitted the plaintiff’s title to the land and said he occupied the house with the plaintiff’s permission until construction costs were repaid.
The parties led evidence on the plaintiff’s tenancy claim and the defendant’s account of the terms on which he entered possession.
The trial court disbelieved the defendant’s account, and the High Court found the tenancy claim unproved but treated the defendant as a licensee.
The defendant did not identify any plea he could have raised or evidence he was prevented from presenting if licence had been expressly pleaded.
members.legal_principle: Relief ordinarily must rest on the pleadings and issues, and a party cannot sustain a claim on an entirely new ground that was neither raised nor tried. But the substance of the trial prevails over a formal defect in pleadings where the issue was in substance before the parties, both sides knew it was involved and had an opportunity to lead evidence, and allowing reliance on it causes no prejudice. The Court applied the principles in Trojan & Co. Ltd. v. Rm. N. N. Nagappa Chettiar, [1953] S.C.R. 789, and Sheodhar Rai v. Suraj Prasad Singh, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 758, distinguishing them because the alternative ground here was in substance covered by the parties’ cases and evidence. It also referred to Abdul Ghani v. Musammat Babni and Balmakund v. Dalu.
members.conclusion: The High Court could confirm the ejectment decree on the basis that the defendant was a licensee; the defendant’s appeal against ejectment was dismissed.

rule.if: ejectment_suit and owner_title_admitted and permissive_possession_admitted and tenancy_and_condition_claims_tried and both_parties_had_opportunity_to_present_evidence

predicates.ejectment_suit: The claimant brought a civil suit seeking to recover possession of property from its occupant.
predicates.owner_title_admitted: The occupant acknowledged the claimant’s ownership of the property or the underlying land.
predicates.permissive_possession_admitted: The occupant’s account of possession treated entry or continued occupation as permitted by the claimant, subject to a stated condition.
predicates.tenancy_and_condition_claims_tried: The parties presented competing accounts of whether occupation was a tenancy or permissive possession subject to a condition.
predicates.both_parties_had_opportunity_to_present_: Both parties knew the relevant possession issue was involved in the trial and had an opportunity to present evidence about it.

members.legal_issue: Omitting an issue from the trial court’s framed issues does not invalidate the trial when the parties understood the dispute and presented evidence on it.
material_facts: The trial court did not frame an issue on the karta’s authority to execute the agreement or on legal necessity.
The parties knew the opposing positions and led evidence supporting their respective contentions and refuting the other side’s contentions.
members.legal_principle: Order XIV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not require a trial to be vitiated for an omitted issue where the parties went to trial fully aware of the rival cases and led evidence on them. The Court relied on Kannan v. V.S. Pandurangam and Nedunuri Kameswaramma v. Sampati Subba Rao.
members.conclusion: The omission of an issue did not vitiate the trial.

rule.if: civil_trial_case and issue_not_framed and parties_understood_rival_cases and evidence_led_on_issue

predicates.civil_trial_case: The matter was tried in a civil court.
predicates.issue_not_framed: The trial court did not frame an issue on a matter later relied on in deciding the dispute.
predicates.parties_understood_rival_cases: Both sides understood the opposing positions on that matter.
predicates.evidence_led_on_issue: The parties presented evidence supporting or refuting those positions.

members.legal_issue: A party that understood the factual issue at trial and chose to adduce evidence on it cannot later prevent the court from considering that evidence merely because the issue was not properly pleaded or framed.
material_facts: The parties went to trial understanding that the location and use of the disputed land were in issue.
Both sides chose to adduce evidence concerning those matters.
The courts below considered that evidence.
On appeal, the claimants argued that the evidence should not be considered because there was no proper pleading or issue for determination.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle stated in Kunju Kesavan v. M.M. Philip & Others, [1964] 3 SCR 634: where the parties understood the central factual matter and tried the case on that basis, the absence of a formally framed issue does not prevent the evidence from being considered.
members.conclusion: The claimants could not retract from the evidence or prevent its consideration, and the Court rejected their contention.

rule.if: civil_appeal and parties_understood_factual_issue and parties_chose_to_adduce_evidence_on_it and lower_courts_considered_that_evidence

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil case.
predicates.parties_understood_factual_issue: The parties understood the factual matter they were required to prove at trial.
predicates.parties_chose_to_adduce_evidence_on_it: The parties voluntarily presented evidence concerning that factual matter.
predicates.lower_courts_considered_that_evidence: The lower courts considered the evidence presented on that factual matter.

members.legal_issue: A party may rely on a case supported by the evidence despite deficiencies in the form of its pleadings when the substance of the case was known and litigated without prejudice.
material_facts: The claimant described the school’s occupation as being under a licence.
The school’s managers pleaded that the premises had been permanently given for school use and that the school had made substantial additions and alterations at its own expense without objection.
The trial court framed issues concerning whether the licence was irrevocable, and both sides presented evidence on those issues.
The claimant called the former owner as a witness to support the contention that the licence was revocable.
members.legal_principle: Material facts must ordinarily be pleaded so the opposing party knows the case to meet, but pleadings receive a liberal construction and their substance, rather than their form, governs. Where the parties knew an issue was involved and led evidence on it without prejudice, a deficiency in the pleadings does not prevent the court from deciding it. The Court relied particularly on Bhagwati Prasad v. Shri Chandramaul, [1956] 1 SCR 286.
members.conclusion: The challenge based on the alleged absence of adequate pleadings failed because the pleadings, issues and evidence showed that the claimant knew and contested the case being advanced.

predicates.is_appeal_from_possession_suit: A claimant appealed after a court dismissed a suit seeking possession of property occupied by another party.
predicates.opponent_knew_the_case_to_meet: The opposing party’s pleadings or the course of trial made the substance of the other party’s case known.
predicates.issue_was_litigated_with_evidence: The parties proceeded to trial on the issue and presented evidence about it.

members.legal_issue: A party may obtain relief on a proven ground that was not expressly pleaded when the issue was understood and tried by both sides without surprise.
material_facts: The plaintiffs based their claim on title documents and tried to show that they had supplied the purchase money.
The defendant pleaded that the plaintiffs were benamidars and that the real ownership lay elsewhere.
The parties knew during the trial that the character of the transaction and the intention behind putting title in the plaintiffs’ names were in dispute, and they led evidence on those matters.
The defendant had not raised before the High Court an objection that the court could not consider whether the transaction was benami.
members.legal_principle: The general rule is that relief should rest on the pleadings, but a ground may be relied on if it is covered by an issue expressly or by implication, both sides knew it was involved in the trial, and evidence was led on it. The Court applied Bhagwati Prasad v. Shri Chandramaul, distinguished Trojan & Co. Ltd. v. R.M.N.N. Haggappa Chettiar, and referred to Ismail Mussajee Mookerdum v. Hafiz Boo.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not barred from claiming the house on the basis that the deceased purchaser intended the younger plaintiff to own it, despite their unsuccessful attempt to prove that they had supplied the purchase money.

rule.if: property_title_suit and alternative_title_ground_not_expressly_pleaded and both_sides_understood_ground_was_in_issue and both_sides_led_evidence_on_ground and no_trial_surprise

predicates.property_title_suit: The proceeding sought relief based on disputed property ownership.
predicates.alternative_title_ground_not_expressly_p: The party seeking relief did not expressly plead the ground on which the court ultimately relied.
predicates.both_sides_understood_ground_was_in_issu: Both sides understood during the proceeding that the ground was in dispute.
predicates.both_sides_led_evidence_on_ground: Both sides presented evidence bearing on the ground.
predicates.no_trial_surprise: Considering the ground did not take either side by surprise.

members.legal_issue: A party may rely on a basis for title that was not expressly pleaded when the issue was understood to be part of the trial and evidence was led on it without the other party being taken by surprise.
material_facts: The claim for possession was based on a title document in the plaintiffs’ names, and the defendant alleged that they held the property benami for its real owners.

The plaintiffs also sought to establish that they had paid the purchase price, but the parties knew during the trial that the nature and beneficial ownership of the transaction were in issue and led evidence on that question.
The defendant did not object before the High Court that the court could not consider whether the named transferees held the property for another person.
members.legal_principle: Relief is ordinarily founded on the pleadings, but a party may rely on a matter covered expressly or by implication in the issues where both parties knew it was involved and led evidence on it. The Court applied Bhagwati Prasad v. Shri Chandrainaul and distinguished Trojan and Co. Ltd. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar, where the alternative basis was not within the parties’ knowledge during trial.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not barred from relying on the contention that the purchase, though funded by the deceased relative, was intended to benefit the second plaintiff.

rule.if: suit_involves_a_title_dispute and issue_was_understood_by_both_sides and evidence_was_led_on_the_issue and other_side_was_not_taken_by_surprise

predicates.suit_involves_a_title_dispute: The parties disputed who held title to property that was the subject of a claim for possession.
predicates.issue_was_understood_by_both_sides: Both sides understood that the nature of the transaction and beneficial ownership were in issue.
predicates.evidence_was_led_on_the_issue: Both sides presented evidence concerning the nature of the transaction and beneficial ownership.
predicates.other_side_was_not_taken_by_surprise: The party opposing the claim was not taken by surprise by the issue during the trial.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff may obtain relief on an alternative factual case that was not pleaded when the defendant expressly admits and relies on that case and granting relief causes no injustice.
material_facts: The plaintiff pleaded that the money was paid toward the price under an alleged contract of sale and sought specific performance, but did not plead a loan as an alternative basis for recovery.
The defendants expressly pleaded that the money was received as a loan, and the courts found that this account was true.
The loan case was expressly raised in the defence, so the defendants had notice of it and no need arose for them to adduce evidence on facts they had admitted.
members.legal_principle: A court generally cannot grant relief on a case without a foundation in the pleadings if the opposing party was not called upon or given an opportunity to meet it. But relief may be granted on an alternative case expressly admitted and advanced by the defendant where the defendant cannot be prejudiced and no injustice can result. The Court relied on Babu Raja Mohan Manucha v. Babu Manzoor, in which restitution under section 65 of the Indian Contract Act was allowed despite the absence of an alternative claim in the plaint. The Court also stated that the Civil Procedure Code does not prevent a plaintiff from advancing inconsistent allegations and claiming relief in the alternative.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to a money decree for the loan even though that alternative case was absent from the plaint and inconsistent with the pleaded claim for specific performance.

predicates.civil_suit_with_alternative_money_relief: The proceeding is a civil suit in which the plaintiff seeks relief that can be granted on an alternative factual basis.
predicates.defendant_expressly_admitted_and_relied_: The defendant expressly admitted the alternative facts and put them forward as an answer to the plaintiff's claim.
predicates.no_prejudice_or_injustice_to_defendant: Granting relief on the admitted alternative facts does not surprise or otherwise prejudice the defendant and causes no injustice.
predicates.plaintiff_may_receive_relief_on_alternat: The plaintiff may obtain relief on the alternative factual case.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser may raise at trial an argument based on facts admitted or proved when the pleadings gave notice of the relevant factual basis and the opposing party is not taken by surprise.
material_facts: The purchaser argued that the proposed assignment was to a respectable and responsible person and that refusal of consent was unreasonable.
The pleading alleged that the purchaser was respectable and responsible and that refusal of consent would be unreasonable.
The argument relied on facts admitted or proved by the seller, and the courts found no element of surprise.
members.legal_principle: A party may rely at trial on a legal argument supported by admitted or proved facts where the pleading indicates its factual basis and the opposing party is not taken by surprise.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to raise the argument at trial; it was not an entirely new point that unfairly took the seller by surprise.

rule.if: civil_suit and pleading_indicates_argument_factual_basis and argument_relies_on_admitted_or_proved_facts and opposing_party_not_taken_by_surprise

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.pleading_indicates_argument_factual_basi: The pleading indicates the factual basis for the argument later advanced at trial.
predicates.argument_relies_on_admitted_or_proved_fa: The argument relies on facts admitted or proved in the proceeding.
predicates.opposing_party_not_taken_by_surprise: The opposing party is not unfairly surprised by the argument.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court need not remand a case merely because a material issue was not specifically framed or a pleading was deficient when the parties knew the issue was in dispute and had an opportunity to address it without prejudice.
material_facts: The trial court had not framed a specific issue on the plaintiff’s readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
The parties and the trial court were aware that readiness and willingness were in dispute, and the parties’ contentions on the matter were adjudicated.
No party claimed that evidence had been excluded or that the absence of a specific issue had caused prejudice.
The objection to the form of the pleadings had not been raised in the written statement, and the High Court could consider the relevant matters as the court of first appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 concerns the requirement that a plaintiff plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform. Under Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, AIR 1956 SC 593, evidence on an issue may be considered despite the absence of a specific pleading or framed issue when the parties went to trial knowing the issue was in dispute and had an opportunity to adduce evidence; the concern is whether the parties were taken by surprise or prejudiced.
members.conclusion: The absence of a specific issue or alleged deficiency in the pleadings did not require remand; the High Court could decide the matters on the existing record.

rule.if: civil_first_appeal and material_issue_not_specifically_framed and parties_knew_issue_was_disputed and parties_had_opportunity_to_present_evidence and no_prejudice_claimed

predicates.civil_first_appeal: The proceeding is a first appeal in a civil case.
predicates.material_issue_not_specifically_framed: A material issue was not specifically framed by the trial court or the pleadings did not expressly set it out.
predicates.parties_knew_issue_was_disputed: The parties proceeded with knowledge that the material issue was in dispute.
predicates.parties_had_opportunity_to_present_evide: The parties had an opportunity to present evidence relating to the issue.
predicates.no_prejudice_claimed: No party claimed that the omission prevented a fair opportunity to present its case or otherwise caused prejudice.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court need not remit a writ dispute for reconsideration when it has examined the record and a remand would serve no purpose because of the time already elapsed.
material_facts: The proceedings had been ongoing for a substantial period.
The Supreme Court examined the entire record and reappreciated the evidence while considering the appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered remittal but concluded that it would serve no purpose given the elapsed time and its own examination of the entire record; no earlier case was cited for this case-management conclusion.
members.conclusion: Rather than remit the matter to the High Court, the Supreme Court decided the appeal on the record before it.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: An appellate court considered an appeal from a judgment in a writ proceeding.
predicates.substantial_time_has_elapsed: A substantial period passed during the proceedings before the appeal was decided.
predicates.appellate_court_has_examined_entire_reco: The appellate court examined the complete record and reappreciated the evidence.

members.legal_issue: Omitting facts about other accommodation from pleadings does not by itself defeat an otherwise proved bona fide claim for personal occupation.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction for personal and family occupation and did not disclose in the plaint that her husband held a tenancy in another flat.
Her husband had left that flat years earlier, and his brother’s family had occupied it since then.

The trial court found that the landlord lacked suitable accommodation and bona fide required the premises; the Supreme Court held that the omission did not, by itself, show mala fides or disentitle her to relief.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that an omission to plead facts about other accommodation is not, by itself, enough to defeat a claim if the landlord otherwise proves a bona fide requirement. The Court relied on the general approach in Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, including that the landlord is the best judge of residential requirements, and referred to Dinshaw Billimoria v. Rustomji Master and the cited Calcutta decisions on the nature of a landlord’s requirement. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was identified as governing the omission issue itself.
members.conclusion: The omission was not sufficient to disentitle the landlord from eviction relief where she otherwise proved her reasonable and bona fide requirement.

rule.if: residential_eviction_for_owner_use and omitted_spouse_rental and other_dwelling_occupied_by_another_household and personal_need_proved

predicates.residential_eviction_for_owner_use: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding seeking premises for personal or family occupation.
predicates.omitted_spouse_rental: The landlord did not plead that the spouse held a tenancy in another dwelling.
predicates.other_dwelling_occupied_by_another_house: The spouse had left that dwelling and another household was occupying it.
predicates.personal_need_proved: Evidence established the landlord’s reasonable and bona fide need for the premises sought.

members.legal_issue: Evidence cannot be used to establish a materially different factual case that was not pleaded, except in the limited circumstances where the pleadings and issues substantially cover that case and the parties knowingly tried it.
material_facts: The specific-performance plaintiff pleaded that the workers’ union had refused consent to the sale because of collusion with the vendors.
The plaintiff later relied on letters said to show that the union had agreed to the sale on conditions, but the plaint was not amended to plead that alleged conditional agreement.

The letters were disputed; the person said to have supplied them was not called as a witness, and a witness’s identification of a signature did not establish the letters’ contents. The letters also contained contradictory statements.
members.legal_principle: Under the Code of Civil Procedure, pleadings and issues define the case the parties must meet, and evidence cannot ordinarily establish a new case outside them. A deficiency may be overlooked only in exceptional circumstances where the pleadings and issues substantially cover the matter, the parties knew it was in issue, and they led evidence on it. The Court relied on Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal, Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul and Ram Sarup Gupta v. Bishun Narain Inter College. It also applied the principles that admitting or marking a document does not by itself prove its contents or probative value, as discussed in Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd. v. Surendra Oil and Dal Mills, H. Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam and R.V.E. Venkatachala Gounder v. Arulmigu Viswesaraswami & V.P. Temple.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s Division Bench was justified in refusing to consider the letters as proof of a case that had not been pleaded; the letters did not establish the alleged conditional consent.

predicates.civil_specific_performance_case: A party brought a civil proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.material_factual_case_not_pleaded: A party relied on evidence to assert a material factual case different from the case set out in its pleadings.
predicates.no_amendment_to_pleadings: The party did not amend its pleadings to include that material factual case.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to remit a matter after substantial time has elapsed following dismissal of the underlying writ petition in limine.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine.
By the time of the appeal, seven years had passed since the relevant 1968 event.
The Court declined to send the case back and instead heard the substantive grievances.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that, after the passage of seven years, it could not consider sending the case back even if there might be justice in doing so. No provision or earlier case was cited for this decision.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to remit the matter to the High Court after the passage of time.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissed_in_limine: A party appeals after a court has dismissed its writ petition without a full hearing.
predicates.substantial_time_has_elapsed: A substantial period has passed since the event giving rise to the matter.

members.legal_issue: Vague or incomplete pleadings about the landlord's other accommodation do not prevent the court from deciding the bona fide requirement claim when both parties understood the issue, presented relevant material, and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The landlord's petition stated that he had no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation but did not disclose the other residence.
The tenant raised the other residence in the written statement, and the landlord denied having accommodation there in the reply.
Evidence about the other residence, its occupation, and its surrender was placed before the Rent Controller and considered in the proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Pleadings should not be analysed pedantically or dogmatically. If the pleadings are vague or incomplete but both parties understand the case on the relevant legal requirement and place material before the court, the court may decide the issue where neither party is prejudiced. The requirement concerning other reasonably suitable accommodation under Section 14(1)(e) may be raised and considered as a defence to a residential eviction claim.
members.conclusion: The omission or inadequacy of the pleadings was not fatal because the parties understood the issue and placed relevant material before the court without prejudice to either party.

rule.if: residential_eviction_claim and both_parties_understood_accommodation_issue and relevant_material_was_presented and neither_party_was_prejudiced

predicates.residential_eviction_claim: A landlord seeks recovery of residential premises on the ground of a bona fide residential requirement.
predicates.both_parties_understood_accommodation_is: Both parties understood that the landlord's other accommodation was at issue in deciding the residential requirement claim.
predicates.relevant_material_was_presented: The parties placed material before the court about the landlord's other accommodation.
predicates.neither_party_was_prejudiced: The way the accommodation issue was pleaded and addressed did not prejudice either party.
predicates.pleading_defect_is_not_fatal: An omission or vagueness in the pleadings does not prevent the court from deciding the accommodation issue.

members.legal_issue: Failure to frame a separate issue on res judicata does not invalidate a decision when the plea was sufficiently raised, the parties understood and litigated it, and the omission caused no prejudice.
material_facts: The plaintiff society’s pleading extensively referred to the earlier litigation and asserted that its findings barred the appellants’ claims.
The appellants responded to the earlier proceedings in their pleadings and acknowledged that the pending appeal concerned matters material to the later suit.
The parties placed the relevant pleadings, documents, and earlier judgments before the trial court and litigated the matters underlying the res judicata plea.
The appellants did not object to the plea at trial, and the Court found that they had adequate opportunity to meet it and had suffered no prejudice from the absence of a separately framed issue.
members.legal_principle: A res judicata plea should ordinarily be founded in the pleadings and addressed by an issue, as explained in V. Rajeshwari v. T.C. Saravanabava. However, the omission is not fatal where the relevant facts were before the parties and court, the parties went to trial knowing the real issue and had an opportunity to adduce evidence, and no prejudice resulted. The Court relied on the exception discussed in V. Rajeshwari and on Nedunuri Kameswaramma v. Sampati Subba Rao; it also referred to Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar on the effect of litigating an issue with full knowledge of it.
members.conclusion: The absence of a separately framed issue on res judicata did not prevent the court from applying the doctrine or invalidate its decision.

rule.if: civil_trial and res_judicata_pleaded_in_substance and parties_knew_issue_at_trial and relevant_evidence_adduced and no_prejudice_from_omission

predicates.civil_trial: The proceeding is a civil trial in which the court is asked to decide whether an earlier judgment bars a claim or issue.
predicates.res_judicata_pleaded_in_substance: A party’s pleadings set out the earlier proceeding and assert that its determination bars the matter in the current proceeding.
predicates.parties_knew_issue_at_trial: The parties understood that the effect of the earlier judgment was a matter to be determined at trial.
predicates.relevant_evidence_adduced: The parties put before the court the relevant earlier pleadings, judgments, or other evidence concerning the asserted bar.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_omission: The party opposing the bar had an adequate opportunity to meet it and was not disadvantaged by the failure to frame a separate issue.

members.legal_issue: A matter need not be remitted for reconsideration of a quashing order when the parties have fully argued the case and the appellate record contains sufficient material to decide it, particularly when remand would delay the trial.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the matter should be remitted because the High Court had not considered the charge-sheet and other material.
The parties had argued the matter fully before the Supreme Court and taken the Court through the criminal record.
The Supreme Court found sufficient material in that record to connect the respondent with the alleged crime and considered remand futile and likely to delay the trial.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its appellate discretion to avoid a futile remand where the matter had been fully argued and the record was sufficient to decide the challenge, taking account of the need not to delay the criminal trial. No earlier case was relied on for this specific remand decision.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to remit the matter to the High Court and decided the appeal on the record before it.

rule.if: appeal_from_quashing_order and parties_fully_argued and appellate_record_sufficient and remand_would_delay_trial

predicates.appeal_from_quashing_order: The proceeding is an appeal from an order quashing a criminal prosecution.
predicates.parties_fully_argued: The parties have fully presented their arguments to the appellate court.
predicates.appellate_record_sufficient: The record before the appellate court contains sufficient material to decide the challenge.
predicates.remand_would_delay_trial: Sending the matter back would cause avoidable delay to the criminal trial.
predicates.court_may_decide_without_remand: The appellate court may decide the challenge without remitting the matter for reconsideration.

members.legal_issue: A decree based on an implied grant of an easement may be supported even when implied grant was not specifically pleaded, if the parties understood and contested that issue and adduced evidence on it.
material_facts: The claimant pleaded an easement by grant, although the pleading did not specifically characterize the grant as implied.
Both sides understood and contested whether an implied grant existed and adduced evidence on that issue.
The trial court considered the pleadings and evidence and found an easement by grant.
members.legal_principle: A specific pleading of implied grant is not necessary when the parties understood the issue and adduced evidence to prove and contest it. The Court held that the concurrent factual findings did not warrant interference under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.
members.conclusion: The absence of a specific pleading of implied grant did not prevent the courts from granting relief on that basis.

rule.if: civil_easement_suit and implied_grant_not_specifically_pleaded and parties_understood_and_contested_implied_grant and evidence_adduced_on_implied_grant

predicates.civil_easement_suit: The proceeding seeks relief for an asserted easement.
predicates.implied_grant_not_specifically_pleaded: The pleading does not expressly identify implied grant as the basis of the easement claim.
predicates.parties_understood_and_contested_implied: Both sides understood that the existence of an implied grant was at issue and presented opposing positions on it.
predicates.evidence_adduced_on_implied_grant: The parties presented evidence relevant to whether an implied grant existed.

members.legal_issue: Failure to frame a formal issue does not invalidate a finding on a matter that was pleaded, contested, and addressed through evidence when the parties understood the rival cases and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The pleadings of both sides contained averments about possession.

The plaintiff and a witness gave evidence supporting the plaintiff’s possession, and the defendants did not cross-examine the plaintiff on that point or lead evidence to establish their own possession.
The parties understood the competing positions on possession, and the omission of a separately framed issue caused no prejudice.
members.legal_principle: A formal issue’s omission fades into insignificance when the parties understood the rival cases and extensive evidence was recorded without demur, provided the omission caused no prejudice. The Court applied Sri Gangai Vinayagar Temple v. Meenakshi Ammal.
members.conclusion: The absence of a separately framed issue on possession did not invalidate the finding or justify deleting it on review.

rule.if: civil_case and matter_pleaded_by_parties and evidence_recorded_on_matter and parties_understood_rival_cases and no_prejudice_from_omission

predicates.civil_case: The matter was decided in a civil proceeding.
predicates.matter_pleaded_by_parties: The parties included the matter in their pleadings.
predicates.evidence_recorded_on_matter: The parties presented evidence addressing the matter.
predicates.parties_understood_rival_cases: The parties knew and contested each other’s positions on the matter.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_omission: The omission of a separately framed issue did not prejudice either party or vitiate the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A court may decide an issue that was not specifically pleaded when the necessary facts are on the record and the issue was fully argued without objection.
material_facts: The written petition did not specifically plead the ground based on the second limb of section 4(4).
The facts necessary to decide that ground were before the court.
The ground was fully argued in the High Court without objection.
members.legal_principle: In proceedings under Article 226, the court could consider the issue on the record where the necessary facts were before it and the issue had been fully argued without objection. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The issue could be considered despite the absence of a specific pleading.

rule.if: writ_review and ground_not_specifically_pleaded and necessary_facts_on_record and ground_fully_argued_without_objection

predicates.writ_review: A court is reviewing a matter in a writ proceeding.
predicates.ground_not_specifically_pleaded: The party did not specifically plead the ground the court is asked to consider.
predicates.necessary_facts_on_record: The facts needed to decide the ground are before the court.
predicates.ground_fully_argued_without_objection: The ground was fully argued without an objection to the court considering it.

members.legal_issue: Failure to use the specific term ouster in a plaint does not defeat a claim where the pleadings, read as a whole, state the necessary facts and the parties understood the case they had to meet.
material_facts: The plaint alleged that the plaintiff had possessed the disputed land as owner and adversely to the defendants for twelve years.
The plaint did not specifically use the term ouster.
The parties went to trial knowing their respective cases, and the defendants were not misled or prevented from presenting evidence.
members.legal_principle: Pleadings must be construed reasonably and as a whole, and pleadings in mofussil courts are to be construed liberally. The Court relied on Devasahayam (D) by LRs. v. P. Savithramma and Ors. and held that omission of the appropriate terminology does not itself mean the statutory ingredients are absent.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the pleadings were sufficient despite the absence of a specific plea using the terminology of ouster.

rule.if: mofussil_proceeding and pleadings_state_hostile_exclusive_possession and parties_understood_the_case and no_trial_prejudice

predicates.mofussil_proceeding: The claim was brought in a mofussil court.
predicates.pleadings_state_hostile_exclusive_posses: The pleadings, read as a whole, allege possession as owner in denial of the other owners’ rights.
predicates.parties_understood_the_case: The parties understood the factual case each side was advancing.
predicates.no_trial_prejudice: The omission did not mislead a party or prevent that party from presenting evidence.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a formally pleaded exemption issue does not vitiate a trial when the parties understood that exemption was disputed and evidence on it was received without objection.
material_facts: The pleadings did not expressly raise the female’s exemption from Part IV of the Act, and no issue was framed on exemption.
The plaintiff’s replication asserted that the property was obtained under the Act.

The plaintiff was questioned about the female’s address, the defendant led evidence of an exemption notification, and the plaintiff neither objected to that evidence nor sought permission to rebut it.
The parties litigated whether the Act’s succession rules applied to the female.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a trial is not vitiated merely because no formal issue was framed when the parties understood the central disputed fact, evidence was received without objection, and the opposing party had an opportunity to seek to rebut it. The plaintiff’s replication also made the Act’s application to the property part of the dispute.
members.conclusion: The exemption question was properly raised and considered, and the absence of a separately framed issue did not vitiate the trial.

rule.if: succession_applicability_dispute and no_formal_exemption_issue and parties_understood_exemption_dispute and exemption_evidence_received_without_objection

predicates.succession_applicability_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether statutory succession rules govern the property.
predicates.no_formal_exemption_issue: The pleadings or framed issues do not expressly identify exemption as an issue for trial.
predicates.parties_understood_exemption_dispute: The parties’ conduct and claims show that they understood exemption to be part of the dispute.
predicates.exemption_evidence_received_without_obje: Evidence about exemption was received and the opposing party neither objected to it nor sought an opportunity to rebut it.

members.legal_issue: The omission of a specific pleading or framed issue does not require a remand when the parties knowingly litigated the matter, had an opportunity to present evidence, and suffered no prejudice; the first appellate court may decide it on the available record.
material_facts: The trial court did not frame a specific issue on readiness and willingness, but the parties and the trial court addressed whether the statutory requirement had been met.
The parties advanced contentions on that issue, and the trial court adjudicated them.
No party claimed prejudice from the absence of a specific issue or that evidence had been excluded or not allowed.
The High Court had also noted that the defendants had not pleaded the objection concerning compliance with the prescribed forms in their written statement.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, concerns pleading and proving readiness and willingness. Under Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, the rule against relying on evidence for an unpleaded issue does not apply where the parties went to trial knowing the matter was in issue and had an opportunity to adduce evidence; an omission causing no prejudice may be an irregularity. A first appellate court may decide questions of fact and law arising in the case.
members.conclusion: The High Court could assess the trial court's finding on the available material instead of remanding the case to frame additional issues and conduct a further trial.

rule.if: first_appeal and formal_pleading_or_issue_omitted and issue_knowingly_contested and evidence_opportunity_provided and not trial_prejudice

predicates.first_appeal: The court is hearing the first appeal in the case.
predicates.formal_pleading_or_issue_omitted: A material matter was not specifically pleaded or was not framed as a separate trial issue.
predicates.issue_knowingly_contested: The parties went to trial knowing that the matter was in dispute and addressed it.
predicates.evidence_opportunity_provided: The parties had an opportunity to present evidence on the matter.
predicates.trial_prejudice: A party was prejudiced at trial by the omission of a pleading or framed issue.

members.legal_issue: A will made while the testator lacks a sound disposing state of mind is not legally valid, and suspicious circumstances surrounding its preparation must be dispelled by its propounder.
material_facts: The testator was physically weak and suffering from typhoid, and the evidence supported that he was delirious when the will was executed; he died a week later.
The testator was young, below average in intelligence and understanding, and had lived with the beneficiary, who had considerable influence over him and his mother.
The beneficiary took a prominent part in arranging the scribe and attesting witnesses and procuring writing materials.
The will gave the beneficiary most of the property absolutely, while giving the testator’s mother only limited interests.
The evidence offered to show that the testator was of sound mind on the day of execution was not accepted.
members.legal_principle: The party propounding a will bears the burden of satisfying the court that it is the will of a free and capable testator. Where circumstances raise a well-grounded suspicion that the will does not express the testator’s mind, the propounder must remove that suspicion and affirmatively establish that the testator knew and approved of the document’s contents. A propounder’s prominent role in preparing or procuring execution of a will that confers substantial benefits on the propounder is itself a suspicious circumstance requiring vigilant and cautious scrutiny. The Court applied Barry v. Butlin, Fulton v. Andrew, Tyrrell v. Painton, and Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand.
members.conclusion: The will was not executed in a sound and disposing state of mind and was not legally valid or binding on the appellant.

rule.if: will_validity_appeal and testator_physically_weak_at_execution and evidence_of_delirium_at_execution and beneficiary_propounder_took_prominent_part and will_conferred_substantial_benefit_on_propounder and propounder_had_influence_over_testator

predicates.will_validity_appeal: The validity of a will is challenged in an appeal.
predicates.testator_physically_weak_at_execution: The testator was physically weak when the will was executed.
predicates.evidence_of_delirium_at_execution: Evidence indicated that the testator was delirious when the will was executed.
predicates.beneficiary_propounder_took_prominent_pa: The person propounding the will took a prominent part in arranging or procuring its execution.
predicates.will_conferred_substantial_benefit_on_pr: The will conferred a substantial benefit on the person propounding it.
predicates.propounder_had_influence_over_testator: The person propounding the will had considerable influence over the testator.
predicates.will_is_not_legally_valid: The will is not legally valid.

members.legal_issue: A will cannot be accepted as valid when suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution and attestation remain unexplained by the person relying on it.
material_facts: The will disinherited some natural heirs without stating a reason.
The initial written statement filed by the legatees did not mention the will; it was first mentioned in an additional written statement after another heir was added as a defendant.
The Sub-Registrar could not say whether the Lambardar who identified the executant was the person claimed by the District Judge to have done so.
The scribe testified that he did not know the executant.
The courts below found that the suspicious circumstances had not been dispelled to their satisfaction.
members.legal_principle: The person propounding a will must satisfy the court that it was executed and attested as required by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and that it was the product of the testator’s free volition, executed voluntarily with knowledge and understanding of its contents. When suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must dispel them. The Court relied on Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb (AIR 1962 SC 567), which relied on an earlier decision reported at AIR 1959 SC 443.
members.conclusion: The will was not accepted as valid, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, leaving the concurrent decisions below undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: Registration of a will alone does not dispel suspicious circumstances concerning its validity.
material_facts: The will was registered, and the Sub-Registrar recorded that the executant was introduced to him and admitted and signed the execution in his presence.
The courts below nevertheless identified suspicious circumstances concerning the will’s execution and found that they had not been dispelled.
members.legal_principle: Under Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb (AIR 1962 SC 567), registration by itself is insufficient to dispel suspicions where they exist; a general statement by a witness that the testator admitted execution is likewise insufficient to establish due execution and attestation. That decision relied on an earlier decision reported at AIR 1959 SC 443.
members.conclusion: The will’s registration did not remove the unresolved suspicions, and the decision rejecting it as valid was left undisturbed.

predicates.registration_alone_does_not_dispel_suspi: The will’s registration by itself does not remove the suspicions about its validity.

members.legal_issue: A propounded will surrounded by cumulative, material suspicious circumstances that remain unexplained cannot be accepted as genuine merely because its execution was formally supported by attesting-witness evidence.
material_facts: The document was typed on three differently coloured sheets, and the testator’s signatures were placed inconsistently, made with different pens, and absent from two pages that contained typed matter.
The document also contained blank spaces, incorrect or inconsistent property descriptions, mismatched calendar dates, and a recital describing a past event as future.
The explanation for the different pens was found implausible, and the account that the will had been kept in a sealed cover with an incomplete draft did not dispel the doubts.

Although attesting witnesses supported the alleged execution, the Supreme Court found that the combined abnormal features undermined the document’s genuineness and that the testator had not signed it as a genuine will.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be made by a person with testamentary capacity and executed as required, including placement of the signature so that it appears intended to give effect to the writing as a will. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires examination of at least one available and capable attesting witness to prove execution, but formal proof does not by itself establish genuineness. The propounder bears the initial burden; when real, germane suspicious circumstances arise, that burden becomes heavier and the propounder must remove them with cogent and satisfactory evidence before the will can be accepted. The Court applied H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Smt. Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, and K. Laxmanan v. Thekkayil Padmini.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to hold that the document was not the genuine will of the testator; the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A will is not proved where its execution is surrounded by serious unexplained suspicious circumstances and the evidence does not establish that the testator understood and accepted its contents.
material_facts: The attesting witnesses were no longer alive, and the will was supported by the testimony of the scribe, who was not an attesting witness.

The document contained suspicious features, including an incomplete typed date completed by hand, the scribe's signature inserted between the final lines, and evidence that the document had not in fact been prepared by the scribe as claimed.
The beneficiaries took the testatrix's thumb impression on the will, and she did not mention the will in a later written statement that discussed the property's history and administration.
The beneficiaries did not dispel these suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Proof of a will requires more than the mechanical act of signing: the evidence must establish that the testator intelligently appreciated and accepted its contents, and that the required attestation occurred. Under Section 68 of the Evidence Act or other applicable provisions, the evidence must establish due execution; serious suspicious circumstances must be satisfactorily explained before the will can be accepted. No earlier case is named by the Supreme Court in its discussion of this issue.
members.conclusion: The will was not proved, and the finding that it had been duly executed was correctly set aside.

members.legal_issue: A statement acknowledging that a will was made is not an admission of its genuine or duly executed character unless it clearly admits those matters.
material_facts: A pleading in a later suit referred to a will in favour of the beneficiary.
The witness said he learned about the will from the opposing party’s written statement and did not admit its genuineness.
The High Court treated the references as admissions that made independent proof unnecessary.
members.legal_principle: A clear and true admission can be decisive and may dispense with proof, but a reference to the making of a will is not an admission of its genuineness or due execution. The Court applied Section 58 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and relied on Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi, Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam, and Gautam Sarup v. Leela Jetly.
members.conclusion: The statements did not admit the genuineness or due execution of the will and did not dispense with the need to prove it.

members.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances cannot be accepted unless its propounder removes the legitimate doubts raised by those circumstances.
material_facts: The will gave the property to one beneficiary while excluding the testator’s other daughters without a convincing reason.
The will did not identify the specific property bequeathed.
The beneficiary participated in the preparation and registration of the will and was present when it was executed and presented for registration.
The will was presented for registration on separate occasions, and the witnesses did not satisfactorily explain the circumstances.
The evidence did not explain how the will came into the propounder’s possession or establish its proper custody.
The propounder did not satisfactorily explain the circumstances identified by the first appellate court.
members.legal_principle: The propounder bears the initial burden of proving the will and, where suspicious circumstances surround its execution, must remove all legitimate doubts with cogent and convincing evidence. The burden is heavier in such cases, and mere assertions or registration do not by themselves remove suspicion. The Court applied H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, and Ramachandra v. Champabia.
members.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances were not removed, so the will could not be accepted as genuine.

members.legal_issue: A will is not established as valid merely by proving its execution when suspicious circumstances surrounding its making remain unexplained.
material_facts: The testator was ill and died the day after the will was made; he had lived with the beneficiaries for the preceding six months.

The will gave all of the testator’s property to the sons of one daughter and excluded his other daughter, although no sour or estranged relationship between that daughter and the testator was found and no reason for excluding her was recorded.
The beneficiary’s father took an active part in arranging the will and fetched the professional scribe.
Although the testator could sign, he placed a thumb impression on the will. The scribe testified that he did not speak with the testator or ask about his health when he arrived.

The will’s recital listed various assets, including a house, factory, machinery and bank deposits, although there was no evidence that the testator owned a house other than one already sold, or owned a factory, machinery or bank deposits.
The lower courts treated proof of execution and the testator’s thumb impression as sufficient to establish the will’s genuineness.
members.legal_principle: A person may freely bequeath property, but the propounder must establish that the testator had a disposing mind and knew and understood the property and beneficiaries involved. The absence of a reason for excluding a person with a similar claim may cast suspicion on the disposition, and a propounder’s active participation raises a further strong suspicion. Proof of execution, including evidence from a scribe or attesting witness or proof of a thumb impression, does not by itself establish validity where suspicious circumstances remain; the court must be satisfied both as to execution and authenticity. The Court relied on H. Venkatachalliah v. N. Themmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, and Kalyan Singh v. Smt. Chhoti, [1989] JT 439. The judgment identifies the Indian Succession Act, 1925, but cites no specific provision.
members.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances were not dispelled, so the will was not established as authentic and valid. The appeal was allowed, the judgments below were set aside, and the suit seeking a declaration that the will was invalid was decreed.

members.legal_issue: A will cannot support a grant of letters of administration when the propounder fails to prove due execution and testamentary capacity or to dispel material suspicious circumstances with cogent evidence.
material_facts: The will was said to have been made shortly before the testator died, after he had suffered a paralytic stroke and been bedridden for months; the will itself described him as sick and getting weak.
No evidence from the doctor who treated the testator was produced to establish his mental and physical capacity when the will was made.

The attesting witness testified that the testator was paralysed and unable to write, and that the testator’s son, who was the sole beneficiary, did not know of the will during the eleven years he lived after its alleged execution.
The signature on the will appeared dissimilar to signatures in other documents, and the will’s text and signature did not appear to match.
The will was not produced for about fifteen years, until after the testator’s daughters sued for partition; the propounder gave no satisfactory explanation for its custody and delayed production.
The scribe was not identified or examined, the will did not state its date, and no evidence showed who had been instructed to prepare it.
The propounder and attesting witness gave discrepant accounts about whether she was present when the will was executed; other evidence supported the claim that the testator was gravely ill.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a testator must have testamentary capacity and the will must be signed and attested as prescribed; Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, govern proof of signature and attested documents. The propounder must prove due execution and a sound and disposing state of mind, and must dispel legitimate suspicious circumstances with cogent, satisfactory evidence. The court must assess suspicious circumstances cumulatively and satisfy its conscience. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, Bharpur Singh v. Shamsher Singh, Naranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Anil Kak v. Sharada Raje, and Leela Rajagopal v. Kamala Menon Cocharan.
members.conclusion: The propounders failed to prove the will in accordance with law or remove the suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution. The will was not validly proved, letters of administration could not be granted on its basis, and the trial court was right to dismiss the suit.

members.legal_issue: A will is not established as genuine merely by evidence of its execution when suspicious circumstances remain unexplained.
material_facts: The will made the claimant the sole legatee while making no provision for the testator’s wife, who was alive when it was executed.
The will was not produced for decades despite opportunities to rely on it in earlier litigation concerning the property.
The evidence concerning the will’s execution and witnesses was unsatisfactory, and the propounder did not satisfactorily explain the suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The propounder must establish a will’s genuineness with trustworthy and unimpeachable evidence. The court may assess not only testimony and demeanour but also circumstances appearing from the evidence or document, surrounding circumstances, and inherent improbabilities. Where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them to the court’s satisfaction. The court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. V. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, Smt. Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, and Mst. Biro v. Atma Ram.
members.conclusion: The will was not genuine and could not support the claimant’s title.

members.legal_issue: Formal proof of a will does not establish its genuineness when suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution remain unexplained.
material_facts: The proceeding sought probate or, alternatively, letters of administration for an unregistered will that left the testator’s Chittoor properties to one beneficiary alone.

The trial court and the High Court Single Judge identified numerous suspicious circumstances, including the testator’s occasional presence in the area, her unfamiliarity with the scribe, the interested relationships of witnesses, infirmities in their testimony, the unequal disposition, and apparent overlap with later settlement deeds.
The witnesses had not known the testator, gave evidence containing material inaccuracies, and did not adequately explain how the scribe came to prepare the will.
The Division Bench considered the formal requirements of execution and attestation satisfied but did not address the lower courts’ identified suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be executed and attested in the prescribed manner; under Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, its execution must be proved, including through at least one available and capable attesting witness where the document is required by law to be attested. The propounder must establish the testator’s signature, sound disposing state of mind, understanding of the dispositions, and free execution. Where legitimate suspicious circumstances attend execution, the propounder must remove them to the court’s satisfaction before the will is accepted; compliance with formal requirements alone is insufficient. The Court relied on Surendra Pal v. Dr. (Mrs.) Saraswati Arora, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Smt. Guro v. Atma Singh, Daulat Ram v. Sodha, Meenakshiammal v. Chandrasekaran, Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty, and Pentakota Satyanarayana v. Pentakota Seetharatnam. Allegations of fraud, coercion, or undue influence are for the caveator to prove, but legitimate doubts arising from the circumstances must be addressed by the propounder.
members.conclusion: The Division Bench applied the wrong legal test by treating formal proof as sufficient and disregarding the suspicious circumstances. Those circumstances were significant and were not shown to have been satisfactorily explained; the impugned judgment could not stand.

members.legal_issue: A will surrounded by multiple material and unexplained suspicious circumstances cannot be accepted as the testator’s duly executed last will merely upon proof of the testator’s signature and attestation.
material_facts: The beneficiary who sought probate was the major beneficiary and played an active role in arranging the will’s execution, while attempting to minimize or deny that role.

The other children were excluded from the execution process and the will gave no persuasive explanation for the unequal distribution; the provision for one daughter depended on uncertain construction work by the beneficiary.

The will’s central bequeathing terms were printed, while handwritten passages were copied from an unexplained note and used technical or legal language; there was no clear evidence that the testatrix understood the contents.

The beneficiary’s account conflicted with the attesting witnesses’ accounts on material aspects of the execution, and the beneficiary took inconsistent positions about an alleged additional page and claimed to have acted on its directions.
The trial court and High Court concurrently found that the suspicious circumstances had not been removed; the Supreme Court found no perversity warranting interference.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 59, 61, and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, the testator must have testamentary capacity and execute an unprivileged will with the prescribed signature and attestation; Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires examination of an attesting witness where available. The propounder must prove due execution and, when legitimate suspicious circumstances arise, remove them by cogent and satisfactory evidence. The assessment is holistic: no single factor, including unequal distribution or a beneficiary’s participation, necessarily invalidates a will by itself, but their cumulative effect may prevent the court from being satisfied. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb, Indu Bala Bose v. Manindra Chandra Bose, Smt. Jaswant Kaur v. Smt. Amrit Kaur, Uma Devi Nambiar v. T.C. Sidhan, Leela Rajagopal v. Kamala Menon Cocharan, and Shivakumar v. Sharanabasappa.
members.conclusion: The propounder failed to establish that the testatrix executed the document as her will after understanding its meaning and effect. Probate was rightly refused, and the appeal was dismissed.
