members.legal_issue: A purported will is not established as genuine where the circumstances of its execution and contents raise substantial suspicions and the propounder does not satisfactorily remove them.
material_facts: The purported will was said to have been executed at the beneficiary’s home, although the testator had been at a distant village until the previous afternoon and execution at the stated time was highly improbable.
The scribe and attesting witnesses were connected to the beneficiary rather than being shown to be the testator’s own friends; the beneficiary had actively participated in procuring the document.
The document was on flimsy paper, used high-flown Urdu although the testator could not read or write Urdu, and its layout suggested that the testator’s signature may have preceded the writing.
The document gave almost the entire substantial estate to a distant relative while providing little for the testator’s widow and daughters, despite the testator continuing to live with his wife.
The beneficiary did not establish that the will was brought to light promptly after the testator’s death, and the widow continued to possess the cash, valuables, and other movables.
The court found no satisfactory evidence removing the suspicions arising from these circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The propounder must prove execution and attestation and, where suspicious circumstances arise, remove them to the court’s satisfaction. The court may assess the credibility of execution witnesses against all attendant circumstances and the contents of the document. The court applied the principles in section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and relied on Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand, H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, Shashi Kumar Banerjee v. Subodh Kumar Banerjee, Kristo Gopal v. Baidya Nath, Chotey Narain Singh v. Mt. Ratan Koer, and Tyrrell v. Painton.
members.conclusion: The court upheld the finding that the purported will was not genuine, rejected the evidence offered to prove its execution, and dismissed the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a will was duly executed cannot be sustained where the evidence contradicts due execution and the assessment overlooks circumstances that cast suspicion on the will.
material_facts: The trial court found that due execution of the will was not proved, and the first appellate court affirmed that finding.
The High Court reversed those findings after reassessing the evidence, relying in part on the testator’s legal-clerk occupation and the interval between execution and death.
The legatee actively participated in the will’s execution, and the will made no provision for either of the testator’s two widows, including one unrelated to the legatee.
members.legal_principle: In assessing due execution, the court must consider the evidence and the totality of the circumstances, including circumstances creating suspicion. The court considered the legatee’s active participation and the omission of provision for both widows; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s decision was set aside, and the trial court’s decree as affirmed by the first appellate court was restored.

members.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances is not accepted as the testator’s last will unless the propounder satisfactorily removes those suspicions.
material_facts: The later wills were allegedly made while the testator was unwell and only a short time before his death.
They were allegedly made while the testator was staying at the residence of the person who benefited under them, although that person had received no provision under the earlier will.
The witnesses to the later wills were strangers to the family, and the wills surfaced only when a defence was filed in the suit.
The appellants did not remove the suspicious circumstances identified by the courts.
members.legal_principle: Under H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443, circumstances such as a weakened or debilitated testator, insufficient evidence of mental capacity, an unnatural or unfair disposition, or a bequest not shown to result from the testator’s free will may raise suspicion. The propounder bears a heavy burden to remove legitimate suspicions before the will can be accepted. The Court also cited Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, (2002) 2 SCC 85, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, (2006) 13 SCC 433, and Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma, (2007) 11 SCC 621, as following the governing law on proof of wills.
members.conclusion: The appellants failed to discharge the heavy burden of removing the suspicious circumstances, so the later wills could not be accepted as the testator’s last wills.

members.legal_issue: A will cannot be accepted as genuine unless its propounder proves its due execution and, when suspicious circumstances attend its execution, satisfactorily removes those suspicions.
material_facts: The propounder prepared the draft and dictated the will to the scribe, and his sons received substantial benefits under it.

The will contained elaborate recitals supporting the testatrix’s title and capacity to dispose of the properties, some of which were inconsistent with the evidence or had not been accepted by the courts below.
The evidence did not satisfactorily establish that the testatrix had approved the draft or understood the will’s contents and dispositions before signing it.
The testatrix’s signatures were proved, but the attesting evidence was inconclusive or inconsistent on whether the will had been read to her and understood by her.
The testatrix was ill and unable to leave her bed, although unconsciousness was not proved.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, the propounder must prove the testator’s signature, testamentary capacity, understanding and approval of the dispositions, and execution with the required attestation. Proof is assessed by the satisfaction of a prudent mind, not mathematical certainty. Where suspicious circumstances arise, the initial burden becomes heavier and the propounder must remove legitimate suspicions by cogent and satisfactory evidence; a prominent role in execution coupled with substantial benefit is itself generally suspicious. The Court applied Barry v. Butlin, Fulton v. Andrew, Vellasawmy Servai v. Sivaraman Servai, Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand, and Harmes v. Hinkson. Allegations of fraud, coercion, or undue influence must be proved by the person making them, but circumstances independently raising doubt must be addressed by the propounder.
members.conclusion: The propounder did not discharge the burden of proving the will in the face of the suspicious circumstances, and the High Court was right to find that due and valid execution had not been established.

rule.if: will_validity_proceeding and will_propounded and suspicious_execution_circumstances and propounder_took_prominent_role and propounders_close_beneficiaries_received_substantial_benefit and not satisfactory_explanation_of_suspicion

predicates.will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a document propounded as a will is the testator’s valid will.
predicates.will_propounded: A person relies on the document as the testator’s will and seeks to establish it.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: The circumstances of preparation or execution, or the document’s contents and dispositions, give the court legitimate reason to doubt that the document expresses the testator’s free and informed intentions.
predicates.propounder_took_prominent_role: The person relying on the will took a prominent part in preparing or procuring its execution.
predicates.propounders_close_beneficiaries_received: People closely connected to the propounder received substantial benefits under the will.
predicates.satisfactory_explanation_of_suspicion: The propounder presented cogent and satisfactory evidence that removed the legitimate doubts about the will’s execution and the testator’s understanding and approval.

members.legal_issue: Proof of a testator’s signature does not by itself establish the testator’s knowledge and approval of the contents of a will when suspicious circumstances call that approval into doubt.
material_facts: The testatrix’s signatures at five places on the will were proved.
The trial court treated proof of the signatures as raising a presumption that the testatrix knew the contents of the will.
The evidence did not satisfactorily show that the will was fully read to the testatrix or that she understood and approved its contents.
The circumstances surrounding preparation and execution of the will were suspicious.
members.legal_principle: Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, govern proof of signature and execution of an attested will, but proof of a signature alone does not establish knowledge and approval where suspicious circumstances remain. The Court explained and approved Surendra Nath Chatterji v. Jahnavi Charan Mukherji to the extent that any presumption from signature is liable to be rebutted by proof of suspicious circumstances.
members.conclusion: The trial court erred in treating proof of the testatrix’s signatures as a presumption that she knew the contents of the will; the signatures did not resolve the doubts about her understanding and approval.

predicates.will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a document propounded as a will is the testator’s valid will.
predicates.testator_signature_proved: Evidence establishes that the testator signed or marked the document.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: The circumstances of preparation or execution, or the document’s contents and dispositions, give the court legitimate reason to doubt that the document expresses the testator’s free and informed intentions.

members.legal_issue: Formal proof of a will is insufficient to establish its genuineness when suspicious circumstances exist and the propounder does not satisfactorily remove them.
material_facts: The testatrix was elderly, and the appellant took an active part in preparing and executing the will.
The will remained in the appellant’s custody, and the appellant did not disclose it to close relatives for a considerable time.
One attesting witness was not examined, and neither attesting witness signed the appendices on which the distributions depended.
The evidence showed that the appendices were not part of the will when it was executed, and the court found the will surrounded by suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act require proof of execution through an attesting witness where one is available and capable of giving evidence; attestation requires an intention to attest. The propounder bears the burden of proving valid execution, the testator’s free and informed act, and a sound disposing mind, and must remove any suspicious circumstances with sufficient evidence. Formal compliance alone is not enough, and the probate court must satisfy its conscience because its grant is a judgment in rem. The Court relied on B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, Adivekka v. Hanamavva, Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda, Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Shedage, Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty, and Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma; deprivation of an heir’s share alone is not necessarily suspicious, but the surrounding facts must be considered rationally.
members.conclusion: The propounder did not establish the will as genuine to the court’s satisfaction, and the refusal to grant probate was upheld.

predicates.probate_application: A party asks a court to grant probate or administration on the basis of a testamentary instrument.
predicates.will_surrounded_by_suspicious_circumstan: The circumstances surrounding preparation, custody, disclosure, execution, or supporting material give reason to doubt that the will is the testator’s genuine act.
predicates.propounder_fails_to_remove_suspicion: The person seeking probate does not provide sufficient and cogent evidence to satisfy the court that the suspicious circumstances are resolved.

members.legal_issue: A registered will is not proved by registration or other evidence when substantial suspicious circumstances remain unexplained by its propounder.
material_facts: The will was registered, but the testator was described as illiterate and the will contained unusual wording and a questionable description of the property and the transfer.
Before relying on the will in the suit, the beneficiary had claimed in response to a demand for partition that the property belonged to him absolutely, without referring to the will.
The evidence showed that the testator had received the allotment and that the beneficiary’s asserted ownership during her lifetime was at odds with the will’s stated bequest after her death.
The propounder did not remove the Court’s grave doubts about whether the testator and her family understood the nature of the document.
The propounder had not proved execution through an attesting witness, and the Court found the other evidence insufficient to prove execution.
members.legal_principle: The propounder must prove the will’s execution and, where circumstances raise legitimate suspicion, remove that suspicion before the will can be accepted. Registration is relevant but is not conclusive proof of due execution or a substitute for the statutory requirements of attestation and proof. Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act and 68 and 71 of the Evidence Act apply. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, M.B. Ramesh v. K.M. Veeraje Urs, and Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini.
members.conclusion: The will was not proved through other evidence because registration did not resolve the substantial suspicious circumstances, which the propounder failed to remove; the High Court’s judgment was set aside and the trial court’s partition decree restored.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party seeks to establish a will against a challenge to its execution or validity.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: The circumstances surrounding the will’s preparation or terms give reasonable grounds to doubt the testator’s understanding or free and informed execution.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_remove_suspicion: The party relying on the will does not adequately explain or dispel the reasonable doubts about its execution.

members.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances is not proved unless the propounder dispels those circumstances through satisfactory evidence of due execution and attestation.
material_facts: The will gave the testator’s entire property to the propounder, a distant relation, while providing only unspecified maintenance for the testator’s widow and sister and nothing for his daughter or nearer relations.
The propounder took part in the will’s execution and was its principal beneficiary.
The testator’s signature on the will differed from his usual signature, and the ink appeared different from that used for the body of the document.
The testator used to sign blank papers for court cases, which could have been available to people connected with the will’s preparation.
Only three attesting witnesses were produced from the sixteen who had signed the will; the witnesses produced were interested in the propounder, while independent witnesses were not called.
The witnesses gave contradictory accounts on material matters, and their evidence did not satisfactorily establish due execution and attestation.
members.legal_principle: Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must meet the special requirements for execution and attestation. As explained in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, the propounder bears the burden of proving the will; where suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them to the court’s satisfaction through clear and satisfactory evidence. The propounder’s benefit from the will and participation in its execution may themselves be suspicious circumstances.
members.conclusion: The propounder did not prove due execution and attestation or dispel the suspicious circumstances, so the will could not support a grant of letters of administration.

rule.if: probate_proceeding and suspicious_circumstances and propounder_benefits and interested_attestors_only and independent_attestors_not_called and witness_accounts_conflicted

predicates.probate_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking authority to administer an estate on the basis of a will.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances: The will contains an unnatural distribution, an unusual testator signature, or other circumstances raising doubt about whether it reflects the testator’s act and intention.
predicates.propounder_benefits: The person seeking to establish the will receives a substantial benefit under it and takes part in its execution.
predicates.interested_attestors_only: The witnesses produced to prove execution have connections or interests that make them not independent of the person seeking to establish the will.
predicates.independent_attestors_not_called: Other available witnesses who could provide independent evidence of execution are not produced.
predicates.witness_accounts_conflicted: The evidence of the witnesses produced contains material contradictions or otherwise fails to establish execution and attestation reliably.
predicates.will_execution_not_proved: The will’s due execution and attestation have not been established.

members.legal_issue: Registration of a will does not by itself dispel suspicions about its execution unless the evidence shows that the testator knew the document was a will and acknowledged its execution.
material_facts: The will was registered after an application for registration on commission was made by the testator’s representative, and a clerk rather than the registering officer went to the testator.

The evidence did not show that the will was read to the testator or that he read it, or otherwise establish that he knew the document whose execution he was admitting was a will disposing of his property.
The clerk gave only a general account that the testator admitted execution, and the identifying witness did not establish that the testator acknowledged the will to him or signed in his presence.
The evidence surrounding the original execution already contained substantial suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Applying the burden described in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma, registration may support a will’s genuineness but does not automatically remove suspicions. It can dispel doubt when the evidence shows that the testator understood that the document was a will, admitted its execution, and signed in token of that admission. Registration performed perfunctorily without establishing the testator’s awareness has little value. The Court referred to Vellasaway Sarvai v. L. Sivaraman Servai, Surendra Nath Lahiri v. Jnanendra Nath Lahiri, and Girji Datt Singh v. Gangotri Datt Singh in noting that registration does not invariably establish that a will is genuine.
members.conclusion: The registration evidence was insufficient to dispel the suspicions, and registration alone did not establish the will’s genuineness.

rule.if: probate_proceeding and suspicious_circumstances and will_registered and registration_process_perfunctory and testator_awareness_not_established

predicates.probate_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking authority to administer an estate on the basis of a will.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances: The circumstances surrounding the will raise a substantial doubt about its execution or genuineness.
predicates.will_registered: The document relied on as a will was registered.
predicates.registration_process_perfunctory: The registration evidence gives only a cursory account of acknowledgment and does not show meaningful verification of the testator’s understanding.
predicates.testator_awareness_not_established: The evidence does not show that the testator knew the document he acknowledged was a will disposing of his property.
predicates.registration_does_not_remove_suspicion: Registration is insufficient to dispel the suspicions surrounding the will.

members.legal_issue: The sufficiency of proof required to establish a will’s genuine execution when circumstances surrounding its making raise suspicion.
material_facts: The testator, who was suffering from cancer, made a will shortly before his death giving his only agricultural land to a niece and excluding his wife and children, including minor children; the reason for this disposition was not established.

The claimed close relationship and care between the testator and the beneficiary were disputed, and the beneficiary did not testify. Her husband, acting as her attorney, gave evidence of an earlier proposed purchase of the land and a substantial advance payment, but no document supported that payment and his evidence about the transaction was inconsistent.

The beneficiary’s husband said that he learned of the will after the testator’s death and obtained the original from the registration office, but how he obtained it was unexplained. The evidence about the will’s preparation and registration raised further doubts, including that registration was said to have occurred beyond office hours; the registering officer did not say that the contents were read over and explained to the testator.

The testator died shortly after the alleged execution of the will, and the land was sold within months of his death. The trial court decreed the suit, but the High Court reversed that decision on the basis that execution had been proved by the attesting witness and registering officer.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will must be executed in the prescribed manner; under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, its execution must be proved by at least one available and capable attesting witness. Formal compliance alone does not establish that a will is genuine when suspicious circumstances exist. The propounder bears the burden of proving valid execution, the testator’s understanding and sound disposing capacity, and—if suspicion exists—of removing it with sufficient and cogent evidence. The court must assess the circumstances as a whole rather than begin from suspicion or ignore well-founded suspicion. The Court relied on B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee, Venkatachala Iyengar, Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Shedage, Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty, and Joseph Antony Lazarus v. A.J. Francis. On the adverse inference from a party’s failure to testify, it relied on Sardar Gurbakhsh Singh v. Gurdial Singh, Martand Pandharinath v. Radhabai, Sri Sudhir Ranjan Paul v. Sri Chhatter Singh Baid, Tulsi v. Chandrika Prasad, and Binapani Paul v. Pratima Ghosh.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to reverse the trial court’s decision: the circumstances raising grave suspicion about the will were not satisfactorily dispelled, so the trial court’s decree was restored.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_reversal_in_will_: A civil appeal concerns a High Court reversal of a trial court decision in a suit where the genuineness of a will is disputed.
predicates.grave_suspicious_circumstances_surround_: The evidence shows serious unexplained circumstances about the will’s disposition, preparation, execution, or custody.
predicates.propounder_fails_to_remove_suspicion: The person relying on the will does not provide sufficient and cogent evidence to explain the suspicious circumstances and establish the testator’s informed and freely made execution.
predicates.high_court_relies_on_formal_execution_pr: The High Court reverses the trial court after relying on formal proof of execution without adequately addressing the suspicious circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A court should not uphold an alleged sale agreement when the evidence and surrounding circumstances leave its genuineness unproved, particularly where it is intertwined with a suspicious will.
material_facts: The opposing parties relied on an alleged sale agreement and a will that referred to the agreement and to the alleged seller’s debts; the courts below found the will suspicious and invalid.
The claimant denied that the agreement was genuine, leaving its proponents to prove it.
The alleged seller’s indebtedness was not supported by cogent evidence, and the evidence offered to show how the alleged purchaser raised the purchase money was unreliable.

The alleged purchaser did not obtain a registered sale deed despite the passage of time, and the explanation for the delay was inconsistent with other evidence of repayment of a loan and leasing of the property.
Neither the alleged purchaser nor the purchaser’s legal representatives sought specific performance of the agreement.
members.legal_principle: The party asserting an agreement bears the burden of proving it, and the evidence must be assessed in its full factual context. A document intertwined with a will found suspicious cannot be treated as an independent, established transaction without evaluating the relationship between the documents, the parties’ conduct, and the surrounding circumstances. The Court found the Trial Court’s assessment sound and the High Court’s contrary approach erroneous; it relied on no earlier case specifically for this evidentiary determination.
members.conclusion: The agreement was untrustworthy and unproved; the High Court erred in upholding it, and the Trial Court’s rejection of it was restored.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_sale_agreement_in_partition_suit and agreement_is_denied and agreement_is_intertwined_with_suspicious_will and alleged_seller_indebtedness_is_unproved and purchaser_funding_evidence_is_unreliable and delay_in_registered_transfer_is_unconvincingly_explained

predicates.appeal_concerning_sale_agreement_in_part: The proceeding is an appeal in a partition suit concerning an alleged sale agreement affecting the property claimed for partition.
predicates.agreement_is_denied: The party opposing the agreement denies that it was genuine.
predicates.agreement_is_intertwined_with_suspicious: The agreement is relied on together with a will that refers to it or to the circumstances said to explain the transaction, and the will is found suspicious.
predicates.alleged_seller_indebtedness_is_unproved: The evidence does not cogently establish the seller’s alleged debts said to explain the sale.
predicates.purchaser_funding_evidence_is_unreliable: The evidence offered to show how the purchaser obtained the purchase money is unsupported or unreliable.
predicates.delay_in_registered_transfer_is_unconvin: The purchaser did not obtain a registered transfer despite a substantial opportunity to do so, and the explanation is inconsistent with other evidence.

members.legal_issue: A will’s proponent must dispel material suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution before the will can be accepted as genuine.
material_facts: The beneficiary was a stranger to the testatrix’s family, and the will left valuable property to him without an adequately supported explanation of their relationship or the disposition.
The testatrix was elderly and ill, and the evidence did not show that she had independent advice about the will.
The original was not produced, the copies differed, and the witnesses gave inconsistent accounts of execution and attestation.
The beneficiary’s father took an active role in the process, and no independent witness explained the circumstances that brought the testatrix and beneficiary together.
The proponent did not provide sufficient evidence to remove the resulting suspicions.
members.legal_principle: The burden of proving valid execution and genuineness rests on the will’s proponent, who must remove well-founded suspicious circumstances with sufficient and cogent evidence. Compliance with formal proof requirements alone does not resolve such suspicions; the court must assess the circumstances as a whole. The Court relied on B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Niranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee, and Joseph Antony Lazarus v. A.J. Francis, and referred to Venkatachala Iyengar.
members.conclusion: The proponent failed to discharge the burden of proving the will’s genuineness and due execution in light of the suspicious circumstances.

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought recognition of a will in a proceeding concerning the will.
predicates.material_suspicious_circumstances: The circumstances surrounding the will’s preparation or execution give substantial reason to doubt whether it reflects the testator’s genuine act.
predicates.proponent_did_not_remove_suspicion: The party relying on the will did not provide sufficient evidence to explain or dispel the substantial doubts.
predicates.will_not_accepted_as_genuine: The will is not accepted as genuine and duly executed.

members.legal_issue: A will is not established merely by proof of the testator’s signature and attestation when the circumstances of its execution raise well-founded suspicions that the propounder has not dispelled with cogent evidence.
material_facts: The will was made while the testator was in an intensive-care unit, shortly after hospitalisation for serious ailments, and was said to have been drafted and executed there during non-visiting hours.

The appellant, who was the sole beneficiary and executor, took part in arranging the will and had a substantial benefit under it; the will excluded the testator’s wife and other children without giving a clear reason.

The will contained detailed asset and liability schedules, but there was no satisfactory evidence explaining how the information was obtained or showing that the testator had supplied it in the hospital.

The attesting witnesses were associated with the appellant, and the doctor treating the testator was not examined; the evidence concerning the testator’s condition and the circumstances of execution was found unsatisfactory.

The High Court accepted that the testator’s and attesting witnesses’ signatures could be genuine, but found the surrounding circumstances suspicious and the appellant had not removed those suspicions.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 63 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an unprivileged will must be proved in the prescribed manner, including through at least one available and capable attesting witness, and attestation requires animus attestandi. The propounder bears the burden of proving due execution, the testator’s signature, sound disposing mind, and free and informed execution; where well-founded suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them by sufficient and cogent evidence. A proved signature alone is not necessarily sufficient. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Shedage, (2002) 2 SCC 85; Sridevi v. Jayaraja Shetty, (2005) 8 SCC 784; H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, AIR 1959 SC 443; Management Committee, T.K. Ghosh’s Academy v. T.C. Palit, AIR 1974 SC 1495; and B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, 2006 (11) SCALE 148. A defence of fraud, coercion, or undue influence, if raised, places the burden on the caveator.
members.conclusion: The appellant did not establish entitlement to probate; proof of signatures and attestation did not overcome the unresolved suspicious circumstances, so the refusal of probate was upheld.

rule.if: probate_proceeding_for_a_will and propounder_receives_substantial_benefit and execution_surrounded_by_well_founded_suspicion and suspicion_not_removed_by_cogent_evidence

predicates.probate_proceeding_for_a_will: A person seeks probate of a will in a probate proceeding.
predicates.propounder_receives_substantial_benefit: The person seeking probate took a prominent part in the will’s execution and receives a substantial benefit under it.
predicates.execution_surrounded_by_well_founded_sus: The circumstances of the will’s preparation or execution, including its dispositions or the testator’s condition, give sound reason to doubt that it was freely and properly made.
predicates.suspicion_not_removed_by_cogent_evidence: The person seeking probate does not provide sufficient and persuasive evidence to explain or dispel the well-founded doubts.

members.legal_issue: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances is not proved unless the propounder satisfies the court that it was duly executed and removes the legitimate suspicions.
material_facts: A beneficiary propounded a will to defeat a claim to a share in the deceased testator’s estate.

The will, allegedly made years before the testator’s death, was not disclosed until after the estate claim was being litigated; the beneficiary said he had discovered it by chance but gave no details of that discovery.
The will favored the beneficiary and excluded the testator’s wife and several close relatives, including on the basis of alleged misconduct for which no evidence was led.
The attesting witnesses were strangers to the testator’s family, gave contradictory accounts of the execution, and could not adequately describe the circumstances surrounding it.
The persons named as executors were available but were not examined.
The beneficiary did not explain the suspicious circumstances, and the High Court accepted the will without addressing them or applying the governing burden of proof.
members.legal_principle: A will must be proved like any other document by evidence satisfying the prudent mind, without requiring mathematical certainty. Under section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a will must be attested; as stated in the judgment, section 63 of the Evidence Act requires at least one available and capable attesting witness to be called to prove execution. Because a will speaks from the testator’s death and the testator cannot testify about its execution, proof carries special solemnity. Where suspicious circumstances surround execution, the propounder’s initial burden is heavier and the propounder must remove all legitimate doubts with cogent and convincing evidence before the will can be accepted. These principles were drawn from and applied in R. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma & Others.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary failed to prove the will as the testator’s last will and testament. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the trial court’s judgment granting the estate claim was restored.

rule.if: will_propounded_in_estate_share_dispute and will_disclosed_only_after_testator_death_and_late_in_litigation and propounder_claimed_accidental_discovery_without_details and attesting_witnesses_were_strangers_and_gave_conflicting_accounts and available_named_executors_were_not_examined and will_favored_propounder_and_excluded_close_relatives and propounder_offered_no_explanation_for_suspicious_circumstances

predicates.will_propounded_in_estate_share_dispute: A person relied on a purported will to resist another person’s claim to a share in a deceased person’s estate.
predicates.will_disclosed_only_after_testator_death: The purported will was not disclosed until after the testator’s death and after litigation over the estate was underway.
predicates.propounder_claimed_accidental_discovery_: The person relying on the will said it was found by chance but gave no details explaining how it was found.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_were_strangers_and_g: The people who attested the purported will were strangers to the testator’s family and gave inconsistent accounts of its execution.
predicates.available_named_executors_were_not_exami: People named as executors in the purported will were available but were not called to give evidence.
predicates.will_favored_propounder_and_excluded_clo: The purported will substantially favored the person relying on it while excluding the testator’s wife and other close relatives.
predicates.propounder_offered_no_explanation_for_su: The person relying on the purported will gave no explanation for the circumstances that raised doubts about its execution.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a will was forged or procured through undue influence cannot rest on suspicion where the challenger did not plead and prove that allegation.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration and possession, while the beneficiaries relied on the will.
The High Court found that the claimants had not pleaded forgery or undue influence, although particulars of the will had been supplied to them.
The lower appellate court inferred forgery from circumstances including the beneficiaries’ involvement in bringing witnesses, the use of different ink, and the failure to register the will earlier.

The evidence showed that the beneficiary brought the scribe at the testator’s request; the testator read the will before signing it; and no suggestion was put to a witness that the signature was not the testator’s.

The Supreme Court found that the challenger bore the burden of proving forgery, undue influence, or collusion, and that the lower appellate court had no proper basis to find forgery in the absence of the required plea and proof.
members.legal_principle: A person alleging forgery, fraud, coercion, undue influence, or collusion must plead and prove the allegation; motive or opportunity, or suspicion alone, is insufficient. Once the propounder establishes prima facie proof of execution and capacity, the contestant may produce material to meet that case, after which the propounder may have to satisfy the Court that the testator understood and freely made the will. The Court relied on Madhukar D. Shende v. Tarabai Aba Shedage, Ryali Kameswara Rao v. Bendapudi Suryaprakasarao, and Sm. Chinmoyee Saha v. Debendra Lal Saha.
members.conclusion: The lower appellate court erred in holding that the will was forged; the challenge based on that finding failed.

predicates.will_challenge_proceeding: A proceeding challenged a will relied on to determine entitlement to property.
predicates.challenger_did_not_plead_forgery_or_undu: The person challenging the will did not plead that it was forged or procured by undue influence.
predicates.challenger_did_not_prove_forgery_or_undu: The person challenging the will did not produce proof establishing forgery or undue influence.
predicates.suspicion_is_the_basis_for_forgery_findi: The finding of forgery or undue influence rested on suspicious circumstances rather than proof of the alleged misconduct.

members.legal_issue: A transferee cannot acquire title under a subsequent sale from a seller who had no title to the property.
material_facts: The lender had acquired no title under the deed that was given only as security for a loan.
The lender later executed a registered sale deed in favour of the subsequent purchasers.
The lender’s name had been entered in the revenue records, but that entry did not establish title.
members.legal_principle: A transferor cannot convey a better title than the transferor possesses. Mutation or an entry in revenue records does not itself confer title in the absence of an underlying transfer of title. The Court cited no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this holding.
members.conclusion: The subsequent sale did not confer title on the purchasers because the seller had no title to convey; the revenue entry did not change that result.

predicates.subsequent_property_sale: A person later transferred the property to another purchaser.
predicates.seller_lacked_title: The person making the later transfer had not acquired title to the property.
predicates.revenue_entry_without_underlying_title: A revenue record showed the seller’s name, but no underlying transaction had given the seller title.

members.legal_issue: A transferee from a person who no longer owns the land acquires no title, and possession taken under a void order may be recovered by the statutory owner's successor.
material_facts: The tenant had become the statutory owner before the purported landlord sought possession.
A possession order was made on the mistaken basis that the tenant remained a tenant liable to pay rent.
The purported landlord then sold the land to transferees, who relied on that sale and order to claim ownership and retain possession.
The tenant's successor sought restoration of possession, and the authorities found that the transferees had acquired no title.
members.legal_principle: Sections 32, 14, 29, and 84 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, support the result: once the tenant became the statutory owner, no landlord-tenant relationship remained on which a landlord could base a possession proceeding for rent default. A sale by a person without title could convey no title, and possession taken under a wholly void order could be challenged and restored in the statutory recovery proceeding.
members.conclusion: The transferees acquired no title through the purported landlord, and the direction restoring possession to the statutory owner's successor was upheld.

predicates.statutory_owner_recovery_of_possession_c: A statutory owner's successor seeks recovery of possession of agricultural land.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires surplus land after it has vested in the State cannot challenge alleged State inaction in taking possession, and the transfer is void.
material_facts: The land vested in the State following publication of the vesting notification.
The claimant asserted that it purchased the land from the former holders after that notification.
The claimant objected to the possession notice and later claimed entitlement to relief based on alleged continuing possession.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Adarsh Seva Sahakari Ltd., Civil Appeal Nos. 369–370 of 2016, decided on 19 January 2016, for the principle that a transfer made after vesting is void ab initio and the transferee cannot challenge alleged State inaction in taking possession under Section 10(5) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The judgment identifies publication under Section 10(3) as the event upon which the surplus land vested in the State.
members.conclusion: The post-vesting transfer was void ab initio, and the transferee was not entitled to challenge alleged inaction by the State in taking possession.

predicates.transferee_challenge_proceeding: A transferee brings a proceeding challenging the State's alleged failure to take possession of surplus land.
predicates.transfer_after_state_vesting: The land was transferred to the claimant after it had vested in the State.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of land subject to acquisition proceedings is invalid where the required prior written permission was not granted by the authorized competent authority, and registration or mutation does not convey title.
material_facts: The land was subject to acquisition proceedings and had not been released from acquisition.
The appellants or their predecessors transferred the land after acquisition notices had been issued.
The documents relied on as permission or no-objection certificates were not shown to have been issued by the authorized competent authority.
The appellants did not establish that the prescribed applications had been made or that the required inquiry and permission had occurred.
Sale deeds were registered and mutations were granted in the appellants’ favour.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 of the Delhi Lands (Restrictions on Transfer) Act, 1972 require prior written permission from the competent authority for a covered transfer; Sections 5 and 8 govern the permission process and prohibit registration without that permission. The competent authority was the authority authorized under Section 2(b), not an unauthorized subordinate. Sections 4, 6, 16 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 govern the acquisition context and withdrawal from acquisition. The exception permitting transfer must be strictly applied. Under Babu Verghese v. Bar Council of Kerala, following Taylor v. Taylor, Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor, Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Deep Chand v. State of Rajasthan, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singhara Singh, where a law prescribes how an act must be done, it must be done in that manner or not at all.
members.conclusion: The transfers were illegal and without jurisdiction, conveyed no title to the appellants, and the consequential mutations were also without jurisdiction.

rule.if: land_subject_to_acquisition and transfer_after_acquisition_notice and prior_written_permission_required and not valid_permission_from_authorized_authority and mutation_granted_on_transfer

predicates.land_subject_to_acquisition: The land was subject to an acquisition proceeding that had not been withdrawn.
predicates.transfer_after_acquisition_notice: The owner or a later holder transferred the land after notice of acquisition had been issued.
predicates.prior_written_permission_required: The governing transfer rules required written permission from the authorized decision-maker before the transfer.
predicates.valid_permission_from_authorized_authori: The authorized decision-maker granted valid written permission before the transfer.
predicates.mutation_granted_on_transfer: An authority entered a mutation in the purchaser’s favour on the basis of the transfer.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to sell a publicly allotted residential site is unenforceable when its terms defeat the statutory scheme governing the allotment.
material_facts: A public authority allotted a site to a person under rules requiring the allottee to construct a residential building and restricting alienation.
The allottee agreed to sell the vacant site, deliver possession to the buyer, and convey title after obtaining the authority’s sale deed.
The agreement fixed consideration for the site alone and left no practical possibility for the allottee to fulfil the obligation to construct a residential building.
The buyer sought specific performance of that agreement.
members.legal_principle: Sections 10 and 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 require a lawful object and render void an agreement whose object is forbidden by law or would defeat the provisions of law. Statutory rules are law for this purpose. Under Rules 17 and 18 of the City of Bangalore Improvement (Allotment of Sites) Rules, 1972, an allottee was required to build a residential building, and a vacant site could not simply be sold to a third party in the circumstances presented. Section 29(3) of the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945 gave restrictions in a grant or transfer effect according to their terms. Applying Kedar Nath Motani v. Prahlad Rai, AIR 1960 SC 213, and Narayanamma v. Govindappa, (2019) 19 SCC 42, the Court considered whether the illegality went to the root of the claim and whether the claimant had to rely on it. Jambu Rao Satappa Kocheri v. Neminath Appayya Hanamannayar, AIR 1968 SC 1358, and the conditional-decree cases including Motilal v. Nanhelal, AIR 1930 PC 287, were distinguished: those cases concerned contracts capable of lawful completion after permission or fulfilment of a condition, unlike this agreement, which defeated the allotment scheme itself.
members.conclusion: The agreement was unlawful and unenforceable because enforcing it would defeat the statutory rules governing the public allotment.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and public_residential_allotment and allottee_required_to_build and agreement_requires_vacant_site_transfer and agreement_prevents_required_construction and claim_depends_on_agreement

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.public_residential_allotment: A public authority allotted the property under a scheme intended to provide sites for residential construction.
predicates.allottee_required_to_build: The allottee was required to construct a residential building on the allotted site.
predicates.agreement_requires_vacant_site_transfer: The agreement contemplated transfer of the vacant site rather than transfer of a site with the required building.
predicates.agreement_prevents_required_construction: The agreement’s terms prevented or made practically impossible the allottee’s required construction.
predicates.claim_depends_on_agreement: The claimant’s case for relief depended on enforcing that agreement.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may make transfers of granted land that breached a transfer restriction void and provide for recovery of the land when the transferee’s title remained defeasible at the law’s commencement.
material_facts: The lands had been granted to members of disadvantaged communities subject to restrictions on transfer.
The purchasers acquired the lands in breach of those restrictions and were presumed to know of them.
Before the challenged law, such transfers were voidable and the land could be recovered through legal process.
The challenged law provided for recovery through an administrative process that included an opportunity for the affected person to be heard.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978 could replace prolonged legal proceedings with a speedier process to protect the intended beneficiaries of the grants. A transferee who acquired land in breach of a known restriction acquired only a defeasible title, not a vested title immune from lawful avoidance. The measure furthered the State’s public policy of social and economic justice, consistent with Article 46 of the Constitution; the procedure must be consistent with natural justice.
members.conclusion: The legislature could make the still-defeasible transfers void and provide for their recovery; doing so did not unconstitutionally impair the transferees’ vested rights.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_recovery_law and transfer_breached_grant_restriction and transferee_knew_of_restriction and title_still_defeasible_at_law_start and affected_person_given_hearing_opportunity

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_recover: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law providing for recovery of land.
predicates.transfer_breached_grant_restriction: A transfer of granted land occurred in breach of a restriction governing that grant.
predicates.transferee_knew_of_restriction: The transferee knew, or was treated as knowing, of the restriction on transfer.
predicates.title_still_defeasible_at_law_start: The transferee’s title remained liable to be defeated when the recovery law commenced.
predicates.affected_person_given_hearing_opportunit: The recovery process gave the affected person an opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: A transferee cannot claim acquisition compensation on the basis of a transfer that is void because the landholder belongs to a protected community and the transferee does not.
material_facts: The original landholders belonged to a Scheduled Caste, and that fact was not disputed by the society.
The society relied on alleged agreements to purchase the land from the original landholders, but did not produce the agreements.
The society was a juristic person and did not itself belong to the Scheduled Caste; the civil decrees in its favour were based on the alleged agreements.
The society claimed compensation on the basis of its alleged interest in the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act declares void a transfer by a Scheduled Caste landholder to a person outside that community. Read with Article 341 of the Constitution, the statutory reference to a member of a Scheduled Caste means a natural person included in the relevant constitutional notification, not a juristic person. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act cannot protect a claimant under a void transaction. State of Rajasthan v. Aanjaney Organic Herbal Pvt. Ltd. holds that the bar applies to a juristic transferee; Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka supports legislative protection of land held for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Babu Lal and Lincal Gamango v. Dayanidhi Jena address the consequences of prohibited transfers. Ram Karan v. State of Rajasthan also recognises the unlawfulness of a prohibited transfer. The right to compensation rests on a right, title, or interest in the land, which the void transfer did not confer.
members.conclusion: The alleged transfers were void from their inception, the decrees founded on them were nullities, and the society acquired no right to claim compensation. The original landholders, or their legal representatives, were entitled to the compensation.

rule.if: compensation_entitlement_proceeding and protected_community_landholder and transferee_outside_protected_community and claim_depends_on_prohibited_transfer

predicates.compensation_entitlement_proceeding: A proceeding concerns who is entitled to compensation for acquired land.
predicates.protected_community_landholder: The landholder who transferred or purported to transfer the land belonged to a community protected by restrictions on transfer of the land.
predicates.transferee_outside_protected_community: The purported transferee did not belong to the protected community.
predicates.claim_depends_on_prohibited_transfer: The claimant's asserted interest in the land and claim to compensation depend on the prohibited transfer.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of assigned land made contrary to an absolute restriction on alienation is void even if the transfer occurs after the period asserted by the purchaser.
material_facts: The land was assigned for the original grantee's personal cultivation, and the grant terms prohibited alienation while permitting encumbrances only for specified purposes connected with improving or cultivating the land.
The grantee's successors sold the land to the purchaser, who relied on the passage of time since the assignment and argued that the restriction lasted only ten years.
The authorities set aside the transfer under a rule prohibiting alienation of assigned land.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the restriction as implementing the constitutional policy of economic empowerment of weaker sections, reflected in the Preamble and Articles 14, 21, 38, 39 and 46 of the Constitution, and the distribution of community resources contemplated by Article 39(b). A prohibited transfer is opposed to public policy and void under Section 23 of the Contract Act. The Court relied on Murlidhar Dayandeo Kesekar v. Vishwanath Pandu Barde for the constitutional purpose of protecting assigned land, and agreed with Smt. Ammanamma v. Venkataiah that an absolute statutory prohibition cannot be avoided by a contrary grant.
members.conclusion: The transfer was invalid and void because it contravened the absolute prohibition on alienation and was opposed to public policy.

predicates.assigned_land_transfer_appeal: The proceeding concerns a challenge to the validity of a transfer of land assigned for the beneficiary's cultivation.
predicates.grant_or_governing_rule_absolutely_prohi: The terms governing the assignment prohibit alienation without a time-limited permission to transfer.
predicates.transfer_contravenes_prohibition: The assigned land was transferred despite the governing prohibition.

members.legal_issue: A transfer prohibited by the agricultural ceiling regime does not convey title, and a final determination that the holding exceeds the ceiling leaves the land subject to the regime’s consequences for the State.
material_facts: The landholder transferred the land after the ceiling regime had come into force.
The ceiling tribunal determined that the landholder held land in excess of the prescribed ceiling and held the transfer void.
That tribunal determination had attained finality.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7(2) and 17 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 prohibited the relevant transfer after the Act came into force. Sections 10 and 11 and related provisions governed surrendered or deemed-surrendered land. A transferor cannot convey rights that the transferor does not have.
members.conclusion: The transfer was null and void and conveyed no right, title, or interest to the purchasers; the land was subject to the statutory surrender process and the State’s rights under the ceiling regime.

predicates.property_transfer_after_ceiling_restrict: A holder transferred property after a restriction on transfers under an agricultural ceiling regime had begun to apply.
predicates.ceiling_tribunal_finally_determined_exce: A ceiling tribunal finally determined that the holder’s land exceeded the prescribed ceiling.

members.legal_issue: A government permission to sell excess vacant land issued without authority under the governing transfer rules is void, and a sale deed made under that permission is invalid and inoperative.
material_facts: The State Government issued orders exempting excess vacant land and permitting its sale to a purchaser.
The landholder then executed a sale deed for the land in reliance on those orders.
The orders and the sale deed were challenged in proceedings concerning the legality of the exemption and transfer.
members.legal_principle: Because Sections 20(1)(a) and 20(1)(b) do not authorize exemption for the purpose of transferring excess vacant land, an order purporting to permit such a sale is without jurisdiction. A sale deed executed on the basis of that unauthorized permission cannot give effect to a transfer the landholder had no legal right to make. The Court relied on the statutory scheme governing exemptions and transfers in Sections 20 and 26 to 28 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976.
members.conclusion: The exemption and sale-permission orders were void ab initio, and the sale deed was invalid and inoperative because the landholder had no legal right to transfer the land to the purchaser.

predicates.appeal_challenges_exemption_and_sale: The proceeding challenges both a government exemption or sale permission and a transfer made under it.
predicates.government_order_purported_to_permit_sal: The government issued an order purporting to allow the sale of excess vacant land.
predicates.sale_deed_was_executed_under_that_permis: The landholder executed a sale deed in reliance on the government’s permission.

members.legal_issue: A land transfer made contrary to the statutory restriction is void and causes the transferred land to vest in the State.
material_facts: The company purchased land exceeding the statutory limit without obtaining the required permission.
The company did not establish that the transfer fell within an exception to the restriction.
The company acknowledged in its lease agreement that the transfers were contrary to the restriction and that the excess land had vested in the State.
members.legal_principle: Sections 154(1) and 154(2) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act impose the transfer restriction and provide specified exceptions. Section 166 makes a transfer contrary to the Act void. Section 167(1)(a) provides that the subject matter of a void transfer vests in the State free from encumbrances from the date of transfer, and section 167(2) authorizes the Collector to take possession and direct eviction. The Court also described the later-added section 154(3) as requiring prior approval for excess transfers while permitting post facto approval in the circumstances specified there.
members.conclusion: The transfers of land in excess of the permitted limit were void, and the excess land vested in the State from the date of transfer.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_land_transfer and land_transfer_exceeds_limit and required_permission_absent and no_applicable_exception

predicates.appeal_concerning_land_transfer: A party appeals a decision about the validity or consequences of a land transfer.
predicates.land_transfer_exceeds_limit: The transfer caused the transferee's relevant holding to exceed the statutory limit.
predicates.required_permission_absent: The required government permission or approval was not obtained.
predicates.no_applicable_exception: The transfer did not qualify for an applicable statutory exception.

members.legal_issue: The State must not renew a lease that gives temporary legitimacy to possession of land that vested in it following a void transfer.
material_facts: The company had acquired land in excess of the statutory limit, and the excess land had vested in the State.
The State subsequently leased the excess land to the company for a fixed term.
The Court considered that granting the lease frustrated the purpose of the land-reform legislation and the vesting order.
members.legal_principle: Sections 154, 166, and 167 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act restrict excess transfers, make contravening transfers void, and provide for vesting in the State. The Court reasoned that leasing the vested land back to the transferee frustrated the legislation's purpose and directed that the lease not be renewed.
members.conclusion: The State was directed not to renew the lease when its term ended and to deal with the excess land in accordance with the Act.

predicates.land_vested_in_state_after_void_transfer: The land vested in the State as a consequence of a void transfer.
predicates.state_leased_vested_land_to_transferee: The State granted the former transferee a lease of the vested land.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of land by a member of a Scheduled Caste to a person outside the protected communities is invalid when the required prior written permission was not obtained, and the land may be restored to the transferor.
material_facts: The transferors belonged to the Dhoba caste, which was a Scheduled Caste in the State.
The land was transferred to a person belonging to the Brahmin caste.
The Revenue Officer’s prior written permission for the transfers had not been obtained.
The restoration proceedings resulted in orders directing restoration of the land to the transferors.
members.legal_principle: Sections 22(1) and 22(5) of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 apply the restriction on transfers by members of Scheduled Tribes, mutatis mutandis, to transfers by members of Scheduled Castes. A transfer to a person outside the protected communities requires the Revenue Officer’s previous written permission. Section 23 provides for proceedings concerning a transfer in contravention of that restriction, and section 23-B places the burden of proving validity on the transferee when validity is in question.
members.conclusion: The transfers were invalid, and the transferees were required to restore the lands to the transferors’ possession.

rule.if: land_transfer_restoration_proceeding and transferor_belongs_to_protected_caste and transferee_outside_protected_communities and prior_written_permission_absent

predicates.land_transfer_restoration_proceeding: A proceeding seeks restoration of land following a transfer by a member of a protected community.
predicates.transferor_belongs_to_protected_caste: The transferor belongs to a community covered by the statutory restriction on land transfers.
predicates.transferee_outside_protected_communities: The transferee does not belong to a community within the protected categories for which the restriction permits a transfer without permission.
predicates.prior_written_permission_absent: The required written permission from the responsible revenue authority was not obtained before the transfer.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to transfer protected assigned land in breach of the protections governing its alienation is void as opposed to public policy.
material_facts: The State had allotted the land to a tribal beneficiary.
The beneficiary entered into an agreement to sell the land, subject to the Collector’s permission.
The authorities refused permission, and the proposed sale was inconsistent with the protection against alienation of the assigned land.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Contract Act renders an agreement void when its object or consideration is opposed to public policy. The Court relied on DTC v. DTC Mazdoor Congress and held that restrictions on alienation of assigned land give effect to the constitutional policy of economic empowerment and protection of weaker sections, including under Articles 14, 21, 38, 39 and 46.
members.conclusion: The agreement was void under section 23 of the Contract Act as opposed to public policy.

predicates.agreement_to_transfer_protected_assigned: A beneficiary and another person made an agreement to transfer land assigned for the beneficiary’s protection.
predicates.transfer_lacks_required_permission: The transfer was subject to official permission and that permission was not obtained.
predicates.transfer_defeats_protective_policy: The proposed transfer would defeat the protections intended to preserve the assigned land for the beneficiary or protected group.

members.legal_issue: Transfers of land made in breach of statutory restrictions on surplus land are void, and later transactions derived from a void transfer do not validate it.
material_facts: Final ex parte assessment orders had declared land held by the original tenure holders to be surplus, and those orders had not been challenged.

The original tenure holders transferred land to a housing society after the land-ceiling regime had commenced; the Court accepted the finding that the transfer was prohibited and void under the statutory restrictions.
The alleged sale deed to the housing society and the later deeds in the chain of transfers were not produced, and the appellants did not provide the relevant notification date or supporting details.
The appellants claimed through subsequent transfers and relied on later development of the land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5(1), 5(3), and 10(4) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 restrict transfers of excess vacant land and provide for nullity in the specified circumstances. An action unlawful at its inception cannot be validated by later events; the Court relied on Upen Chandra Gogoi v. State of Assam, Satchidananda Misra v. State of Orissa, Regional Manager, SBI v. Rakesh Kumar Tewari, C. Albert Morris v. K. Chandrasekaran, and Mangal Prasad Tamoli v. Narvadeshwar Mishra.
members.conclusion: The initial transfer was a void transaction, and the subsequent transactions derived from it had to be ignored.

predicates.land_was_finally_declared_surplus: The land had been finally declared surplus under the applicable land-ceiling process.
predicates.transfer_breached_restrictions_on_surplu: A transfer of the surplus land was made in circumstances in which transfer was prohibited by the applicable restrictions.
predicates.later_claim_derives_from_initial_transfe: A later claimant relies on a chain of transactions originating in the prohibited transfer.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of excess vacant land made without the required filing and notification is null and void, and permission concerning different land does not validate the transfer.
material_facts: The claimant’s title depended on a sale of land declared surplus in ceiling proceedings.
The transfer occurred after the original order declaring the land surplus had been set aside and the matter remanded, but before any fresh order or notification concerning the excess land was made.
The required statement had not been filed and no operative notification concerning the excess land had been published when the transfer was made.
The authority had refused permission to transfer the disputed land because a suit concerning it was pending; permission later granted concerned land retained by the transferor, not the disputed land.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(3) prohibits transfer of excess vacant land until the landowner has furnished the statement required by Section 6 and a notification concerning the excess land has been published under Section 10(1); a transfer contrary to that prohibition is null and void. Section 27 requires prior written permission for the specified transfers of urban or urbanisable land with a building, but permission for other land does not authorize the disputed transfer. The Court also applied Ritesh Tiwari v. State of U.P. in addressing the transferor’s inability to transfer land subject to ceiling proceedings.
members.conclusion: The transfer was null and void under Section 5(3) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The permission granted for different land did not authorize the transfer, so the claimant acquired no title on which to base the suit.

rule.if: civil_title_suit and transfer_claimed_as_source_of_title and excess_vacant_land_transferred and statement_not_filed and notification_not_published

predicates.civil_title_suit: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking title-based relief concerning property.
predicates.transfer_claimed_as_source_of_title: The claimant relied on a transfer from an earlier holder as the source of the claimant’s title.
predicates.excess_vacant_land_transferred: The transferred land was treated as excess vacant land in ceiling proceedings.
predicates.statement_not_filed: The landholder had not furnished the required statement concerning the land before the transfer.
predicates.notification_not_published: No notification concerning the excess land had been published before the transfer.

members.legal_issue: A transfer contrary to restrictive terms of a grant does not confer valid title on the purchaser.
material_facts: The land was granted subject to a prohibition on alienation, which applied permanently.
The original grantees sold the land in violation of the grant restrictions.
The purchasers relied on those sales as the source of their title.
members.legal_principle: The Act’s Section 4(1) treats transfers made in contravention of the terms of a grant as null and void and provides that no right, title, or interest is conveyed by them. The Court relied on R. Chandevarappa v. State of Karnataka and Papaiah v. State of Karnataka, and on the protective purpose reflected in Articles 39(b) and 46 of the Constitution; it also referred to Section 23 of the Contract Act. It distinguished K.T. Hutchegowda v. Deputy Commissioner, in which the relevant question had not been raised or considered.
members.conclusion: The purchasers acquired no valid title under the prohibited sales, and their possession under those sales did not establish title against the State.

predicates.granted_land_recovery_proceeding: The case concerns recovery of land that was granted subject to restrictions.
predicates.grant_prohibited_alienation: The terms of the grant prohibited alienation of the land.
predicates.sale_violated_grant_restriction: The grantee sold the land contrary to the restriction in the grant.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser does not acquire title through a sale deed when the vendor had no transferable title to the land.
material_facts: The Government had leased the land to the vendor, and the lease prohibited transfer of the land.
The vendor later executed a registered sale deed in favour of the respondent and delivered possession.
The respondent acknowledged in a letter that the vendor had no title and had misrepresented its authority to sell.
The evidence established that the vendor was only a Government lessee.
members.legal_principle: The maxim nemo dat quod non habet means that no person can give what that person does not have, and nemo plus juris tribuit quam ipse habet means that no person can confer a greater right or better title than that person possesses. A claimant relying on a sale must establish that the vendor had title capable of transfer; the purchaser cannot obtain a better title than the vendor had.
members.conclusion: The sale deed was invalid and inoperative because the vendor was merely a lessee and had no title that could be transferred to the respondent.

rule.if: civil_land_title_claim and claimant_derives_title_from_sale and vendor_was_only_a_lessee and vendor_had_no_transferable_title

predicates.civil_land_title_claim: A party brought a civil proceeding claiming ownership of land.
predicates.claimant_derives_title_from_sale: The claimant relied on a sale by another person as the source of the claimant’s title.
predicates.vendor_was_only_a_lessee: The person who made the sale held the land only as a lessee.
predicates.vendor_had_no_transferable_title: The person who made the sale lacked title capable of being transferred to the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: A land transfer made during the statutory period is void for ceiling computation when it reduces the surplus land otherwise available, regardless of whether the transfer was bona fide.
material_facts: The disputed land transfers occurred during the period specified by the statute for review of transfers.
The transfers reduced the surplus land that would otherwise have been available for acquisition under the ceiling scheme.
The transfers took different forms, including bona fide sales and other alienations.
The land authorities treated the transfers as void for ceiling purposes, while the High Court held that only sham, nominal, or mala fide transactions could be invalidated.
members.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961 permits the authorised officer to declare a transfer or partition made during the specified period void if it defeats any provision of the Act; it does not require proof that the transaction was sham, nominal, bogus, or mala fide. Read with section 7 and the Act's scheme for identifying and acquiring surplus land, a transaction that reduces the surplus defeats the Act even if bona fide. The Court applied literal and policy-oriented statutory interpretation, noting that the mischief rule from Heydon's Case and the grammatical or golden rule led to the same result, and emphasized the social-justice purpose of agrarian reform under Part IV of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court held that a transfer which reduces the surplus land available under the ceiling scheme defeats the Act and may be disregarded as void when calculating permissible and surplus land, whether or not it was bona fide. The appeals were allowed and the tribunal's decision was restored.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding to determine permissible and surplus land under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.covered_transfer: A landholder transferred or otherwise alienated land during the period specified for review of such transactions.
predicates.surplus_reduced: The transaction reduces or impairs the surplus land otherwise available beyond the ceiling.
predicates.transfer_disregarded_for_ceiling_computa: The transfer is disregarded as void when permissible and surplus land are calculated.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of granted land that contravenes the terms of the grant is void and conveys no right, title, or interest, and the land may be restored to the original allottee through the statutory process.
material_facts: The original allottees transferred granted lands to third parties without obtaining the required permission and contrary to the grant restrictions.

The original allottees or their successors sought restoration, and the Assistant Commissioner investigated the transfers, found them contrary to the grant conditions, and ordered restoration after proceedings in which affected parties could be heard.
The appellate authority dismissed challenges to those orders, and the High Court Single Judge upheld them.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978 makes a transfer of granted land, whether made before or after the Act commenced, null and void when it contravenes the terms of the grant or the law governing the grant, and provides that no right, title, or interest passes. Section 5 authorizes restoration following an inquiry and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, and Section 11 gives the Act overriding effect. The Court also relied on Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka concerning the protective purpose and validity of grant restrictions.
members.conclusion: The transfers contrary to the grant conditions were null and void, and the restoration orders were properly made; the Single Judge's decision was upheld.

predicates.land_restoration_proceeding: The proceeding concerns restoration of granted land after a disputed transfer.
predicates.transfer_breaches_grant_terms: The land was transferred contrary to a condition of its grant.
predicates.authority_finds_transfer_void: The competent authority, after inquiry, determined that the transfer was void.

members.legal_issue: A landholder who acquires land after commencement of a land-ceiling law and thereby exceeds the permissible area cannot reduce the surplus area by making later transfers or obtaining decrees diminishing the holding.
material_facts: In one appeal, a landholder who had held less than the permissible area inherited land and thereby came to hold more than that area; he later made a gift and possessory mortgages that reduced the land shown in his name.
In the other appeal, a landholder inherited additional land that took his holding above the permissible area and later transferred land to close relatives pursuant to a civil court decree.
The Collector disregarded the later transactions and declared surplus land; the High Court held that the transactions were not affected by the statutory scheme.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 19B(1) and 19B(4) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a person whose post-commencement acquisition takes the aggregate holding above the permissible area must declare the holding and the excess is available for the statutory surplus pool. Section 10A(c) requires relevant later judgments, decrees, or orders diminishing the area that could be declared surplus to be ignored. Section 10A(b)'s inheritance-related saving does not displace section 19B where the heir's aggregate holding itself exceeds the permissible area. The provisions should be interpreted to advance the Act's general purpose of building a surplus pool for redistribution, as held in Amar Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1974 SC 994, 996.
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed. The later transfers and decrees could not be used to diminish the surplus area, and the surplus determinations were restored.

predicates.surplus_area_determination_proceeding: An authority is determining the surplus land of a person under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.post_commencement_acquisition_exceeds_ce: A person acquires land after the scheme begins and, together with land already held, exceeds the permitted holding.
predicates.later_disposition_or_decree_reduces_hold: After acquiring the excess, the person transfers land or obtains a decree that reduces the holding shown in the person's name.
