predicates.later_dispositions_do_not_reduce_surplus: Later transfers or decrees are not counted to reduce the person's surplus area.

members.legal_issue: The period allowed to declare land acquired in excess of the permissible area does not authorize transfers intended to defeat the land-ceiling scheme.
material_facts: The landholders were required, after acquiring holdings above the permissible area, to provide a return and select the land they wished to retain within a prescribed period.
The landholders made transfers during the period in which they could provide that return and make that selection.
The High Court treated the time allowed for filing the return as permitting those transfers.
members.legal_principle: Section 19B(1) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, provides time for a person whose aggregate holding exceeds the permissible area to furnish a return and select land to retain. That procedural period does not suspend the substantive obligation to make excess land available under section 19B(4), or permit transfers to thwart the Act's purpose. The Court relied on the interpretive approach in Amar Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1974 SC 994, 996, and referred to the judicial role in giving effect to legislation as described in Corocraft Ltd. v. Pan American Airways Inc., [1968] 3 W.L.R. 714, 732.
members.conclusion: The time allowed is a procedural facility for identifying inherited assets, selecting the land to retain, and filing the return; it cannot be used as an opportunity to defeat the substantive ceiling and redistribution scheme.

rule.if: surplus_area_determination_proceeding and inheritance_creates_excess_holding and return_period_available and transfer_during_return_period

predicates.surplus_area_determination_proceeding: An authority is determining the surplus land of a person under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.inheritance_creates_excess_holding: A person inherits land that, together with land already held, exceeds the permitted holding.
predicates.return_period_available: The person is allowed a period to identify the acquired assets, select the land to retain, and file a return.
predicates.transfer_during_return_period: The person transfers land during the period allowed for filing the return and making the selection.

members.legal_issue: Land subject to a transfer must be excluded as far as possible when determining surplus land, even where the transfer is found not to be bona fide.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned determination of surplus land under land-ceiling law.
The land subject to the transfer was identifiable as a particular plot.
The Prescribed Authority found that the transfer was not bona fide, a finding the court assumed to be correct.
The Prescribed Authority did not exclude the transferred area when determining surplus land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 12A(d) of the applicable Act, the surplus-land determination must exclude the area subject to the transfer as far as possible, even on the assumption that the finding that the transfer was not bona fide is correct. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The court set aside the judgments of the High Court and the Prescribed Authority and remitted the matter for redetermination of surplus land, excluding the transferred area as far as possible.

rule.if: surplus_land_determination and identifiable_transferred_area and transfer_found_not_bona_fide and transferred_area_not_excluded

predicates.surplus_land_determination: The proceeding concerns determination of the area of land that is surplus.
predicates.identifiable_transferred_area: A particular area of land is identifiable as the subject of a transfer.
predicates.transfer_found_not_bona_fide: The authority determining surplus land found that the transfer was not bona fide.
predicates.transferred_area_not_excluded: The authority determining surplus land did not exclude the transferred area from its determination.
predicates.transferred_area_excluded_as_far_as_poss: The transferred area is excluded from the surplus-land determination as far as possible.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of land during the continuation of proceedings to determine surplus land is void even if it is involuntary and conducted under a court order.
material_facts: The auction sale took place while proceedings to determine the tenure-holder’s surplus land were pending.
The sale was conducted by an executing court to recover decretal sums.
The sale was confirmed and certificates were issued, but the transfer occurred during the pending ceiling proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(8) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, notwithstanding subsections (6) and (7), makes a transfer during the continuation of surplus land determination proceedings void. Its explanation identifies when those proceedings are deemed to commence and conclude. The Court held that the rule applies to involuntary as well as voluntary sales and that a civil court’s order cannot validate a sale that would defeat the ceiling law. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The sale was void because it took place during the continuation of the surplus land proceedings, and the court order did not validate it.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding to determine a landholder’s surplus land was underway.
predicates.land_transfer_during_proceeding: Land held by the person whose surplus was being determined was transferred before that proceeding had concluded.

members.legal_issue: A land transfer from a member of a protected caste to a person outside that group is void when the transfer occurs after the statutory prohibition on that transfer has taken effect.
material_facts: The landholder belonged to a Scheduled Caste, while the purchasers did not.
The land was transferred after a 1956 amendment had prohibited such transfers.
The purchasers relied on a decision concerning a transfer made before that amendment.
members.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, as amended by the Rajasthan Tenancy (Second) Amendment Act, 1956, prohibited the transfer. Under Sections 23 and 2 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement forbidden by law is unlawful and void. Triveni Shyam Sharma v. Board of Revenue concerned the retrospective application of the prohibition to a transfer made before the amendment, and therefore did not govern a transfer made after it took effect.
members.conclusion: The transfer was void because it contravened the prohibition in force when it was made. The earlier decision did not apply because it concerned a transfer made before the prohibition took effect.

rule.if: land_transfer_validity_is_contested and seller_belongs_to_protected_caste and buyer_is_outside_protected_group and transfer_followed_effective_prohibition

predicates.land_transfer_validity_is_contested: The parties disputed whether a land transfer was legally effective.
predicates.seller_belongs_to_protected_caste: The person transferring the land belonged to a caste protected by the applicable restriction.
predicates.buyer_is_outside_protected_group: The person receiving the land did not belong to the protected group.
predicates.transfer_followed_effective_prohibition: The transfer occurred after the restriction on that kind of transfer had taken effect.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot obtain title from a transferor who has no right in the property to convey.
material_facts: Purchasers claimed under sale deeds executed by a legatee who asserted title under the will.
The will did not confer an enforceable right to the disputed properties because severance before the testator’s death was not established.
The widow’s interest had become absolute and she had given up her rights in the disputed properties under the compromise.
The transferor therefore had no right in those properties to pass to the purchasers.
members.legal_principle: A transferor cannot convey a greater title than the transferor possesses. Because the asserted testamentary title failed and the widow’s rights had become absolute before she relinquished them under the compromise, the transferor had no title to convey.
members.conclusion: The purchasers acquired no enforceable title through the transferor, and their appeals were dismissed.

predicates.purchaser_claims_through_transferor: A purchaser bases title to property on a conveyance from another person.
predicates.transferor_has_no_title_to_property: The person who made the conveyance had no enforceable right in the property to transfer.
predicates.purchaser_acquires_no_title: The purchaser acquires no enforceable title through that conveyance.

members.legal_issue: A law whose dominant purpose is agrarian reform is protected from challenges under the specified equality, freedom, and property guarantees even if some provisions are ancillary to that reform.
material_facts: The challenged law transferred rights in certain agricultural lands to the State and provided for the tillers to become owners of land they cultivated.
It imposed limits on the land that any person could hold and included provisions on resumption, payment, use, and transfer of land.
The law followed a series of earlier land reforms and recommendations directed at addressing defects in those reforms.
members.legal_principle: Whether legislation is a measure of agrarian reform depends on its dominant purpose. A large and liberal meaning is given to the relevant expressions in Article 31A. Ancillary measures serving a general scheme of agrarian reform do not take the law outside that protection. The Court relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, which treated Kavalappara Rottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras as a special case not applicable where the general scheme is definitely agrarian reform and ancillary measures serve it. Article 31A applied in the State with the modification made by the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954. Article 31 had been repealed with effect from June 20, 1979.
members.conclusion: The law was a measure of agrarian reform because its dominant purpose was a just and equitable redistribution of land through tiller ownership and landholding ceilings; it was therefore protected from the stated constitutional challenges.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A person challenges the validity of a law that reorganizes rights in agricultural land.
predicates.dominant_purpose_is_agrarian_redistribut: The law's main purpose is to redistribute agricultural land justly and equitably.
predicates.cultivators_become_owners: The law makes cultivators owners of the land they cultivate.
predicates.landholding_ceiling_imposed: The law limits the amount of land a person may hold.

members.legal_issue: A law providing for State acquisition of estates, after receiving the President's assent, is protected from challenge based on rights in Part III of the Constitution.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized the State to acquire estates or tenures and provided for their transfer to the State free from encumbrances.
The law defined estates by reference to land entries in general registers maintained under the land-tenure law, and the properties of the parties were entered in those registers.
The law had been reserved for the President and received the President's assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects a law providing for acquisition by the State of an estate or rights in an estate from challenge for inconsistency with, or taking away or abridging, rights in Part III. Article 31-A(2)(a) gives “estate” the meaning assigned by the existing land-tenure law for the relevant area. The Court also explained that Article 31-A affords wider protection than Article 31(4), which concerns only Article 31(2), and that the President's assent meant the proviso to Article 31-A did not apply.
members.conclusion: The law provided for State acquisition of estates and was protected by Article 31-A, so its validity could not be challenged for contravening rights in Part III, including property rights and equality rights.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law by alleging that it infringed constitutional rights.
predicates.law_provides_state_acquisition_of_estate: The law provides for the State to acquire estates or rights in estates as understood under the applicable land-tenure law.
predicates.presidential_assent_given: The President assented to the law.

members.legal_issue: A law that broadly abolishes intermediaries and establishes a direct relationship between the state and cultivators is a measure of agrarian reform protected from specified fundamental-rights challenges when it has the required assent.
material_facts: The law transferred janmam estates to the government and provided for ryotwari pattas for qualifying cultivators and tenants.
Its general scheme was to abolish intermediaries and establish a direct relationship between the state and actual cultivators.
The law received the President’s assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects laws providing for acquisition or modification of rights in estates when connected with agrarian reform, subject to the required assent for a state law. The court relied on Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector for the requirement that the acquisition be connected with agrarian reform.
members.conclusion: The law, in its broad outlines, was a measure of agrarian reform protected by Article 31A from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31, subject to the separate ruling concerning forests.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law concerning the acquisition or reorganization of land rights.
predicates.law_abolishes_intermediaries_and_benefit: The law removes intermediaries between the state and cultivators and provides a direct state-cultivator relationship for qualifying cultivators.
predicates.law_received_required_assent: The state law received the assent required for the constitutional protection to apply.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot invalidate protected land-reform restrictions merely because they are harsh or burden a cultivator's rights when the restrictions are part of a law protected from fundamental-rights challenge.
material_facts: The challenged provisions prevented a tenant from resuming personal cultivation after a bargadar voluntarily surrendered or abandoned the land, and instead required cultivation by another person with official permission.
The Court considered the provisions harsh and said they bordered on arbitrariness and seriously curbed the cultivator's occupational rights.
The provisions were part of the 1972 amendment, which had been placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B protects qualifying Ninth Schedule laws from challenges based on Part III. Under Waman Rao v. Union of India, laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973, receive that protection. The Court also observed that legislative relief could address the provisions' harshness.
members.conclusion: The Court could not strike down the provisions because they were protected from fundamental-rights challenge; it left it to the legislature to soften their rigour.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_cultiva: A person brought a constitutional proceeding challenging restrictions on a landholder's ability to cultivate land personally.
predicates.restrictions_bar_personal_resumption_aft: The restrictions prevent a landholder from resuming personal cultivation after a sharecropper voluntarily gives up or abandons cultivation.
predicates.law_was_scheduled_before_cutoff: The law containing the restrictions had been included in the protected constitutional schedule before the relevant cutoff.

members.legal_issue: Legislation imposing ceilings on land holdings falls within the protection for agrarian reform legislation.
material_facts: The challenged legislation imposed ceilings on agricultural land holdings and sought to redistribute surplus land and promote rural development.
The Court described equitable land distribution, ending concentrated ownership through ceilings, and rural economic planning as features of agrarian reform.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A broadly protects agrarian reform, including land-ceiling measures; the Court relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab and State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing (Weaving) Co. Ltd. The Court also stated that it did not rest its ultimate decision on Article 31A.
members.conclusion: The Court held that Article 31A’s protection extends to land-ceiling legislation against challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law that limits land holdings.
predicates.law_redistributes_land: The challenged law is directed toward distributing land more equitably.
predicates.law_limits_concentrated_land_ownership: The challenged law limits concentrated ownership of land through ceilings.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge based on equality or property rights cannot be entertained against a protected land-reform enactment that has received presidential assent.
material_facts: The endowment argued that the provisions preventing it from claiming possession for personal cultivation violated equality and property rights.
The governing enactment had received the President’s assent.
The Court relied on earlier decisions upholding the enactment’s constitutional validity.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A of the Constitution protects qualifying land-reform legislation from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. The Court relied on Shri Mahadeo Paikaji Kolhe Yavatmal v. The State of Bombay and Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. The State of Bombay, which upheld the relevant legislation against constitutional challenge.
members.conclusion: The constitutional challenge under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) could not be entertained because Article 31A rendered the enactment immune from that challenge.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenges legislation governing agricultural land or tenancy as unconstitutional.
predicates.law_received_presidential_assent: The challenged land-reform law received the President’s assent.
predicates.challenge_invokes_equality_or_property_r: The constitutional challenge relies on equality or property-right protections.

members.legal_issue: Agrarian legislation acquiring estates and extinguishing intermediary rights is protected from challenges based on specified fundamental rights.
material_facts: The challenged laws acquired rights in inam estates and other covered lands, abolished intermediary holders, and established a direct relationship between the government and the occupants.
The laws formed part of an agrarian reform programme.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for the acquisition by the State of an estate or rights in an estate, or the extinguishment or modification of such rights, from invalidation under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The definition of estate in Article 31A(2) includes the relevant categories of land. The Court followed B. Shankara Rao Badami v. State of Mysore, [1969] 3 S.C.R. 1.
members.conclusion: The laws could not be challenged as violating Articles 14, 19 or 31 because Article 31A protected legislation of this kind.

rule.if: agrarian_acquisition_proceeding and (state_acquires_estate_rights or state_extinguishes_intermediary_rights) and agrarian_reform_purpose

predicates.agrarian_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to legislation acquiring land or rights in land as part of an agrarian reform.
predicates.state_acquires_estate_rights: The legislation provides for the State to acquire an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.state_extinguishes_intermediary_rights: The legislation provides for the extinguishment or modification of intermediary rights in land.
predicates.agrarian_reform_purpose: The legislation forms part of a programme of agrarian reform.

members.legal_issue: Legislation providing for acquisition of an estate or rights in agricultural land, or their extinguishment or modification, is protected from challenges based on specified fundamental rights, including when the affected interest is a right to obtain a patta.
material_facts: The challenged amendment brought the landholders’ lands within legislation providing for acquisition of landholders’ rights and ryotwari settlement.
The landholders argued that they had a right to obtain pattas and that the lands should be treated as ryotwari lands rather than estates subject to the legislation.
The challenged legislation formed part of agrarian reform, and the constitutional definition of an estate included ryotwari land and agricultural land.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for acquisition by the State of an estate or rights in it, or for extinguishment or modification of such rights, from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31. Article 31A(2), as amended by the Seventeenth Amendment, includes ryotwari land and land held or let for agriculture within the meaning of “estate.” A right to obtain a patta in respect of agricultural land is also a right that may be affected by such a law. The Court followed Khajamian Wakf Estates v. State of Madras and relied on B. Sankara Rao Badami v. State of Mysore.
members.conclusion: The legislation was protected by Article 31A and could not be challenged on the grounds that it violated Articles 14, 19, or 31, including on the basis that the affected interest was a right to obtain a patta.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging agrarian-reform legislation on constitutional grounds.
predicates.affected_land_is_agricultural_or_ryotwar: The affected land is used or held for agriculture, or is held under a ryotwari settlement.
predicates.affected_interest_is_right_to_pattta: The affected interest includes a claimed right to obtain formal recognition of entitlement to the land.
predicates.law_changes_estate_rights_for_agrarian_r: The law provides for State acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or for their extinguishment or modification, as part of agrarian reform.

members.legal_issue: A land-reform law protected by Article 31-A could not be invalidated on grounds concerning compensation, public purpose or equality, and the challenged law in any event did not fail on those grounds.
material_facts: The law acquired jagir interests and provided compensation based principally on income, with additional rehabilitation grants and other benefits.
The holders argued that compensation was inadequate, that there was no public purpose, and that the law discriminated by permitting resumption on different dates.
The law made all jagirs liable to resumption, conferred no discretionary power to exempt selected jagirs, and allowed different classes to be resumed on different dates for practical reasons.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A barred challenges to a protected acquisition law based on Part III, including Article 31(2) and Article 14. A protected law could still be attacked as a fraud on the Constitution if its true intention were to take property without payment and its compensation provisions were merely illusory. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh, Visveshwar Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjea, Raja Suriya Pal Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Biswambhar Singh v. State of Orissa. It held that the law served a public purpose and that different resumption dates for practical and administrative reasons were not discriminatory.
members.conclusion: The compensation, public-purpose and equality objections were barred by Article 31-A. The compensation provisions were not shown to be illusory or a device to take property without payment; the law served a public purpose, and the uniform liability of jagirs to resumption did not violate Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenges a law that acquires property on grounds concerning compensation, public purpose or equality.
predicates.land_reform_law_is_protected: The acquisition law concerns land tenures or grants within the relevant constitutional protection for land reform.
predicates.compensation_provisions_are_not_illusory: The law provides compensation or other meaningful benefits and the evidence does not show that these are merely a device to take property without payment.

members.legal_issue: A law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings and distributing surplus land is agrarian reform legislation protected from fundamental-rights challenges.
material_facts: The legislation imposed ceilings on agricultural holdings and provided for acquiring and distributing surplus land to landless and weaker sections of society.
The legislation was enacted to give effect to the principles concerning distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31A, legislation that in substance concerns agrarian reform is protected against challenges based on Articles 14, 19, and 31. The Court relied on Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India, Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, and State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh.
members.conclusion: The legislation, including its amendments, was in substance agrarian reform and fell within the constitutional protection for such legislation, making it immune from challenges based on fundamental rights concerning equality, property, and related freedoms.

predicates.agrarian_land_ceiling_case: The proceeding challenges legislation that imposes ceilings on agricultural landholdings.
predicates.surplus_land_is_acquired_for_redistribut: The legislation provides for acquiring surplus agricultural land and distributing it to landless or weaker sections.

members.legal_issue: A land-tenure law that substantially modifies a landowner’s rights to hold, use, lease, or transfer land is protected from challenge under the fundamental-rights provisions identified by the Court.
material_facts: The legislation restricted the land a landowner could retain for self-cultivation and permitted surplus land to be used for tenant resettlement.
It limited the landowner’s freedom to choose the terms and persons for leasing land.
It required specified land to be sold to eligible tenants at a price fixed under the legislation rather than at a price freely chosen by the landowner.
The petitions alleged violations of constitutional rights concerning equality and property.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for the extinguishment or modification of rights in an estate. The Court found substantial modification where legislation restricted a landowner’s choices about leasing, curtailed cultivation of surplus land, and constrained transfers to specified persons at a statutorily determined price. It distinguished Thakur Raghubir Singh v. Court of Wards, Ajmer, because that case concerned suspension of management rather than the substantial modification of proprietary rights at issue here, and applied Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay.
members.conclusion: The legislation substantially modified landowners’ rights in their estates or holdings and was protected by Article 31A from attack under Articles 14, 19, and 31; the petitions were dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party in a constitutional proceeding challenges a law that reforms land rights.
predicates.law_substantially_modifies_landowner_pro: The law substantially changes a landowner’s rights in the land.
predicates.law_restricts_land_use: The law limits the landowner’s use or cultivation of the land.
predicates.law_restricts_land_transfer: The law limits the persons to whom, or the terms on which, the landowner may transfer the land.
predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge_is_barred_b: The law is protected from the asserted fundamental-rights challenge by the constitutional protection for land reform.

members.legal_issue: A land-reform law transferring landowners' interests to tenants and providing for state acquisition of land is protected from challenge to its validity under the constitutional rights at issue when it has received the required presidential assent.
material_facts: The law entitled tenants, subject to conditions and payment of compensation, to acquire landowners' interests in land held by them.
The law also provided for the state to acquire landowners' interests and prescribed methods for determining compensation.
The state law had been reserved for the President's consideration and received presidential assent.
The landowners challenged the law under Articles 19 and 31.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(a), as substituted with retrospective effect by the Fourth Amendment, protects laws providing for acquisition by the State of an estate or rights in it, or their extinguishment or modification, from invalidity on the grounds specified in that Article, including infringement of Articles 19 and 31. For a state law to receive that protection, it must have been reserved for the President's consideration and receive assent. Article 31 also provided that a compulsory-acquisition law could not be challenged on the ground that its compensation was inadequate. Applying Sri Ram Narain v. State of Bombay, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 489, the Court treated a law effecting agrarian reform by transferring landowners' interests to tenants as within Article 31A(a).
members.conclusion: The law fell within Article 31A's protection and could not be challenged as infringing Articles 19 and 31; the petitions therefore failed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A constitutional challenge is brought against a law that changes ownership interests in land as part of land reform.
predicates.law_transfers_landowners_interests_to_te: The law enables tenants to acquire landowners' interests in land held by the tenants, subject to its conditions.
predicates.law_provides_for_state_acquisition_of_la: The law provides for the state to acquire landowners' interests in land.
predicates.state_law_received_required_presidential: The state law was reserved for presidential consideration and received the required assent.

members.legal_issue: Land-reform statutes protected by the earlier constitutional amendment remain immune from fundamental-rights challenges after the Court applies its new rule prospectively.
material_facts: The challenged land-reform statutes had been included in the Ninth Schedule by the Seventeenth Amendment.
The Court applied its new interpretation prospectively and declared that its decision would not affect the validity of that amendment.
The parties accepted that, while the amendment remained valid, the statutes could not be challenged on the stated fundamental-rights grounds.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied prospective overruling to preserve the Seventeenth Amendment and other earlier amendments. Article 31-B provides that statutes specified in the Ninth Schedule are not void on the ground that they conflict with or abridge rights in Part III. The Court did not decide whether the challenged statutes could be sustained on any other constitutional basis.
members.conclusion: Because the Seventeenth Amendment remained valid, the challenged statutes could not be questioned on the ground that they infringed fundamental rights.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenged land-reform statutes on constitutional grounds.
predicates.laws_were_listed_in_protected_schedule: The challenged statutes had been placed in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from specified rights-based challenges.
predicates.earlier_amendment_is_preserved: The constitutional amendment that provided the protection remains valid for the relevant laws.

members.legal_issue: Amendments to a protected agrarian-reform scheme remain shielded from fundamental-rights challenge when they preserve the scheme and satisfy the conditions for that protection.
material_facts: The underlying tenancy legislation had previously been held to implement agrarian reform and to be protected from challenges under the fundamental-rights provisions.

The challenged amendments changed the procedures for recovering the purchase price from tenant-purchasers, allowed additional time in specified circumstances, and postponed the ineffectiveness of a purchase until recovery efforts failed.
The amendments retained the scheme under which tenants could acquire the land and former landlords could recover the purchase price.
The petitioner argued that the changes made recovery of the price and repossession of the land illusory or unreasonably delayed.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31A, once legislation concerning agrarian reform is protected, an amendment changing details of its scheme is also protected if it does not take the legislation outside Article 31A or independently fall outside that protection, and the amending statute has received the President's assent. Changes to the transfer of tenure, payment by instalments, or postponement of payment do not alone remove that protection if the amendment continues to implement agrarian reform. Relying on Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, [1959] 1 Supp. S.C.R. 489, the Court treated the underlying legislation as protected; it held Maharana Shri Jayvantsinghji Ranmalsinghji v. State of Gujarat, [1966] Supp. S.C.R. 411, inapplicable. Once Article 31A applies, challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31 cannot be pursued against the protected scheme.
members.conclusion: The amendments did not take the legislation outside the constitutional protection for agrarian reform. The petitioner could not challenge them under the fundamental-rights provisions, and the petition was dismissed.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge and underlying_agrarian_scheme_protected and amendment_preserves_agrarian_reform and presidential_assent

predicates.constitutional_challenge: A claimant brings a constitutional proceeding challenging the validity of legislation.
predicates.underlying_agrarian_scheme_protected: A prior ruling has treated the underlying agrarian-reform scheme as constitutionally protected.
predicates.amendment_preserves_agrarian_reform: The legislature changes details of the scheme while retaining its agrarian-reform purpose and operation.
predicates.presidential_assent: The amending legislation receives the President's assent.

members.legal_issue: Land-ceiling provisions and implementing rules that form part of a land-reform scheme are protected from fundamental-rights challenge.
material_facts: A constitutional petition challenged a land-ceiling provision and an implementing rule on fundamental-rights grounds.
The disputed land was admitted to be a holding under the governing legislation.
The court held that the challenged provision and rule were part of a land-reform scheme.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects provisions that form part of a land-reform scheme from the asserted fundamental-rights challenge. The Court applied this principle to section 6(xvii) of the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, and rule 4(4) of the Rules made under it; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The provision and rule were protected from attack under Article 31A and were valid.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: A person challenged the validity of a land-ceiling measure on fundamental-rights grounds.
predicates.measure_part_of_land_reform_scheme: The challenged measure formed part of a land-reform scheme.

members.legal_issue: An amendment forming part of agrarian reform and clarifying the amended legislation is protected from the asserted constitutional challenge.
material_facts: The amendment was challenged as offending Articles 14, 19 and 31.
The High Court treated the amendment as part of a chain of agrarian reform and as clarificatory in nature.
The Supreme Court accepted the High Court’s reasons for upholding the amendment.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted the High Court’s conclusion that the amendment formed part of agrarian reform and was protected by Article 31A(1)(a); it also accepted the characterization of the amendment as clarificatory. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The amendment’s validity was upheld and the challenge was rejected.

predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: A party appealed from a decision on a challenge to the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.amendment_part_of_agrarian_reform: The challenged amendment formed part of a broader agrarian reform measure.
predicates.amendment_is_clarificatory: The challenged amendment clarified the existing law.
predicates.constitutional_challenge_rejected: The constitutional challenge to the amendment is rejected.

members.legal_issue: A law acquiring estate rights as part of agrarian reform and receiving the required presidential assent cannot be invalidated on the ground that its compensation is inadequate under the constitutional guarantee for property acquisition.
material_facts: The challenged law vested the inam estates and the inamdars’ rights in the State and was intended to abolish intermediate holders as part of agrarian reform.
The law had received the President’s assent.
The petitioners argued that the compensation provided by the law was not the market value or a just equivalent of the property acquired.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A, as introduced and amended, protects a state law providing for acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or their extinguishment or modification, from invalidation for inconsistency with the rights in Part III, provided the state law receives presidential assent. The Court distinguished State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, and P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector because those cases concerned laws not protected as agrarian-reform legislation under Article 31A.
members.conclusion: The law was protected from a challenge based on the compensation guarantee, so the petitioners could not invalidate it for providing inadequate or illusory compensation.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law_for_inadequate_compensation and law_acquires_estate_rights and law_is_part_of_agrarian_reform and state_law_received_presidential_assent

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: The challengers asked a court to invalidate a law acquiring property because the compensation it provided was inadequate.
predicates.law_acquires_estate_rights: The law transfers estate interests or rights in estates to the State, or extinguishes or modifies those rights.
predicates.law_is_part_of_agrarian_reform: The law forms part of a legislative program to reform agrarian relationships, including by abolishing intermediaries.
predicates.state_law_received_presidential_assent: The state law received the President’s assent.
predicates.estate_reform_law_not_invalidated_for_co: The estate-reform law cannot be invalidated on the ground that its compensation is inadequate.

members.legal_issue: An amendment extending an existing compulsory-acquisition law to additional categories of property is protected from fundamental-rights challenge when the amendment receives presidential assent.
material_facts: The original law provided for abolition and vesting of estates for a public purpose.
The amendment widened the definition of estate to cover additional property, including minor inams, and extended the existing abolition scheme to that property.
The amendment was reserved for presidential consideration and received the President’s assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1) protects laws providing for acquisition of estates or rights therein from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31, subject, for a State law, to presidential assent. Article 31A(2)(a) includes inams within the meaning of estate. The Court treated an amendment extending an existing acquisition law as an extension of that law, to which the President’s assent applies; it also considered the assent requirement under Article 31 and the effect of Article 31(4). No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The amendment was valid and protected by Article 31A; presidential assent to the amendment extended the protection to the newly covered categories of property.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: The affected property holders brought a constitutional challenge to a law providing for acquisition of property.
predicates.amendment_extends_existing_acquisition_l: The legislature amended an existing acquisition law to extend its operation to additional categories of property.
predicates.existing_law_provides_compulsory_acquisi: The existing law provides for compulsory acquisition of property for a public purpose.
predicates.amendment_received_presidential_assent: The amendment was reserved for presidential consideration and received the President’s assent.

members.legal_issue: A State law acquiring an estate that was pending when the Constitution commenced and received presidential assent is protected from a challenge based on Part III rights.
material_facts: The Bill was pending before the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
The enacted law received the President's assent.
The law provided for acquisition of estates.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(4) applied because the Bill was pending when the Constitution commenced. Article 31A, subject to its assent requirement for State laws, and article 31B also protected the law from attack based on Part III. The Court held that Part III was not repealed, but that the relevant protections prevented the appellants from challenging this law on those grounds.
members.conclusion: The Act could not be invalidated on the basis of rights in Part III of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_estate: A party challenges a State law that provides for acquisition of estates.
predicates.bill_pending_at_constitution_commencemen: The Bill that became the law was pending before the Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
predicates.presidential_assent_received: The State law received the President's assent.

members.legal_issue: A state agrarian-reform law that extinguishes landholder rights in land within an estate is protected from specified fundamental-rights challenges when the constitutional requirements for that protection are met.
material_facts: The appellants challenged a state law imposing a ceiling on landholdings and acquiring land above the ceiling.
The lands at issue were accepted to fall within an estate under the Constitution.
Under the existing tenure law, landholders had permanent, heritable and transferable rights of use and occupancy, subject to payment of revenue and other lawful charges.
The state law extinguished or abridged those rights, and the law and its amendment had received presidential assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a), subject to its requirement of presidential assent for a state law, protects laws providing for acquisition of an estate or rights therein, or extinguishment or modification of such rights, from specified fundamental-rights challenges. Under Article 31A(2)(b), the expression “rights in relation to an estate” has wide amplitude and is to be construed liberally. The Court applied sections 3(g), 8 and 9 of the Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, and relied on Thakur Raghubir Singh v. The State of Ajmer, Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. The State of Bombay, and Atma Ram v. The State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The extinguished rights were rights in relation to an estate, and the state law was protected from the challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_agrari: A person challenges the validity of a state law that reforms the distribution or holding of agricultural land.
predicates.presidential_assent_obtained: The state law has received the assent required for this constitutional protection to apply.
predicates.land_is_within_constitutional_estate: The land affected by the law falls within the constitutional meaning of an estate.
predicates.law_extinguishes_or_modifies_landholder_: The law acquires, extinguishes or modifies landholder rights connected with the affected land.

members.legal_issue: A land-ceiling law enacted within the legislature’s authority over land and protected as an agrarian-reform measure cannot be invalidated on the asserted grounds of legislative incompetence or violation of fundamental rights.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the validity of the provision authorizing reopening of agricultural ceiling cases.
The law concerned ceilings on agricultural land and was enacted to implement agrarian reform.
The Act was included in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: Entry 18 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule gives the State Legislature competence to legislate on land. The Court held that agrarian-reform legislation of this kind was protected under Articles 31-A and 31-C and, because the Act was placed in the Ninth Schedule, was immune from challenge on the ground of violation of fundamental rights. It also relied on Sukhdarshan Singh v. State of Rajasthan, in which Section 15 had been upheld.
members.conclusion: The State Legislature was competent to enact the land-ceiling law, and the Act was protected from challenge on the ground that it violated fundamental rights.

rule.if: land_ceiling_law_challenge and legislature_has_authority_over_land and law_implements_agrarian_reform and act_has_fundamental_rights_protection

predicates.land_ceiling_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law governing ceilings on agricultural land.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_land: The legislature enacting the law has authority to legislate on land.
predicates.law_implements_agrarian_reform: The law is directed to implementing agrarian reform.
predicates.act_has_fundamental_rights_protection: The law has constitutional protection against a challenge based on violation of fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: Agrarian legislation operating on land that constitutes an estate is protected from challenge on the grounds that it violates the specified fundamental rights.
material_facts: The Act provided for acquisition of agricultural land exceeding statutory maximum extents.
The petitioner’s Pandaravaka Verumpattom and Puravaka lands were held to constitute estates under Article 31A(2)(a) by the majority.
The petitioner challenged the Act as inconsistent with fundamental rights.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects a law providing for acquisition of an estate or rights in an estate from invalidation on the ground that it is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges the rights specified in that provision, provided the constitutional requirements for State legislation are met. Because the holdings were estates under Article 31A(2)(a), the majority did not decide the petitioner’s fundamental-rights challenge on its merits. Justice Ayyangar would have found the Pandaravaka lands outside the protection, but agreed that the Puravaka lands were covered.
members.conclusion: The Act, insofar as it operated against the petitioner’s holdings, was protected by Article 31A(1)(a) and could not be challenged on the asserted grounds under Articles 14, 19, and 31; the petition was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_leg: A party challenges agrarian legislation on the ground that it interferes with constitutional rights.
predicates.legislation_provides_for_acquisition_of_: The legislation provides for acquisition of land or rights in land.
predicates.affected_land_qualifies_as_estate: The land affected by the legislation qualifies as an estate or its local equivalent.
predicates.required_assent_obtained: The constitutionally required assent for the State legislation was obtained.

members.legal_issue: The agrarian reform law constitutes genuine agrarian reform protected from challenges under the constitutional guarantees concerning equality, freedom and property.
material_facts: The law vested in the State land that was not in the owner's personal cultivation and land held in personal cultivation above a ceiling.
It provided for State disposal of surplus land and its equitable distribution to tillers for personal cultivation, subject to a ceiling.
The petitioners challenged the law's validity, including the adequacy of compensation and its effects on landowners.
members.legal_principle: A law must disclose a genuine scheme of agrarian reform to receive Article 31A protection; its title alone is not decisive. When Article 31A applies, challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31 are unavailable. The Court relied on Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raja Anand Brahma Shah, Kannan Devan Hills Produce v. State of Kerala, and State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Mfg. (Wvg.) Co. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The law provides a definite programme of agrarian reform and is protected by Article 31A as applicable to the State; the challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31 therefore fail.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law presented as an agrarian reform measure.
predicates.law_takes_nonpersonally_cultivated_land: The law transfers to the State land that its owner does not personally cultivate.
predicates.law_limits_personally_cultivated_holding: The law transfers to the State personally cultivated land held above a specified ceiling.
predicates.law_provides_for_surplus_distribution_to: The law provides for surplus land to be distributed to tillers for personal cultivation, subject to a ceiling.

members.legal_issue: A law that transfers title in an estate to a tenant on a specified trigger, subject only to specified events that can defeat the transfer, modifies or extinguishes the landholder’s rights and is protected from challenges based on specified fundamental rights.
material_facts: The measure provided that tenants would be deemed to have purchased qualifying land on a specified day.
The tenant’s title passed on that day and remained effective unless the tenant declined to purchase or failed to pay the purchase price as required.
The provisions therefore transferred title rather than merely suspending the landholder’s title.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) separately covers acquisition by the State and extinguishment or modification of rights in an estate; extinguishment or modification need not occur in the course of State acquisition. The Court held that title passed on the statutory trigger and was defeasible only on specified events. It distinguished Thakur Raghubir Singh v. Court of Wards, Ajmer, which concerned suspension of a right of management rather than transfer of title.
members.conclusion: The measure provided for extinguishment or modification of rights in estates and was protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31; the asserted fundamental-rights challenges could not succeed.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_proceeding and holding_is_an_estate and transfer_to_tenant_occurs_at_trigger and title_passes_immediately and title_is_defeasible_only_on_specified_events

predicates.constitutional_validity_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding challenging the constitutional validity of legislation.
predicates.holding_is_an_estate: The affected landholding is an estate for the purpose of constitutional protection.
predicates.transfer_to_tenant_occurs_at_trigger: The law provides for the tenant to acquire the land on a specified legal trigger.
predicates.title_passes_immediately: The landholder’s title passes to the tenant when the legal trigger occurs.
predicates.title_is_defeasible_only_on_specified_ev: The transferred title can be defeated only if specified events, such as the tenant declining the purchase or defaulting on payment, occur.

members.legal_issue: An occupant who seeks to remain in property after another person establishes title must plead and document a sufficiently particularized basis for the claimed right to continue in possession.
material_facts: The title-holder's pleadings and documents established title to the property.
The occupant claimed a right to remain in possession but did not establish title or prove the alleged family arrangement.
The occupant's asserted basis for continuing in possession was not supported by sufficiently particularized pleadings and documents.
members.legal_principle: Where pleadings and documents establish title and continued possession is disputed, the person resisting recovery or claiming a right to remain must provide detailed pleadings, particulars and supporting documents. The Court must examine pleadings and documents before framing issues; vague pleadings do not raise an issue and may justify rejection of the claim or a decree on admission. The Court also emphasized discovery and production powers under Section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The occupant had not established a basis to continue in possession; the courts must require sufficient particulars and supporting documents before framing an issue for trial on such a claim.

rule.if: civil_possession_dispute and claimant_established_title and occupant_claims_right_to_remain and occupant_lacks_specific_pleadings_or_supporting_documents

predicates.civil_possession_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns recovery of property or a claimed right to remain in possession.
predicates.claimant_established_title: The person seeking recovery established title to the property through pleadings and documents.
predicates.occupant_claims_right_to_remain: The person in occupation asserts a right to continue in possession.
predicates.occupant_lacks_specific_pleadings_or_sup: The occupant does not provide sufficiently detailed particulars and documents supporting the asserted right to remain.

members.legal_issue: A person seeking a declaration that inam land is not an estate bears the burden of proving that it is not an estate and fails if the necessary facts are left unproved.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration that the lands covered by the principal title deed were not an estate.
The grant was of a named village, and minor inams covered some lands within the village.
The dates of the minor inam grants were not established, and the plaintiff did not prove that they postdated the grant of the rest of the village as a named village.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 101, 102 and 103 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a person seeking judgment on asserted facts must prove them; the burden lies on the person who would fail if neither side produced evidence, and the burden as to a particular fact lies on the person asking the court to believe it unless law provides otherwise. Because the legislature created no presumption either way, the plaintiff had to prove the lands were not an estate. District Board, Tanjore v. Noor Mohammad was distinguished because the burden point there rested on counsel's concession and was not decided after discussion.
members.conclusion: The burden rested on the plaintiff to prove that the lands were not an estate, including by showing that the minor inams were granted after the named-village grant. The plaintiff failed to discharge that burden, so the suit was rightly dismissed and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.declaratory_suit_claiming_inam_land_not_: A claimant brings a suit seeking a declaration that land held under an inam grant is not an estate.
predicates.named_village_grant: The grant described the subject of the inam as a village by name.
predicates.minor_inam_grant_dates_unproved: The evidence does not establish when the grants of excluded minor inams were made.
predicates.claimant_did_not_prove_minor_grants_post: The claimant did not establish that the minor inams were granted after the grant of the rest of the village as a named village.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking relief based on statutory protection for occupants of a notified slum area must prove that the disputed property is within the area covered by the notification.
material_facts: The tenants brought suits seeking relief based on the claim that their property lay in a notified slum area and that eviction proceedings required prior permission.
The landlady denied that the property was in the survey area said to have been notified and presented evidence identifying it with a different survey area.
The documents relied on by the tenants did not identify the disputed property, and the High Court found their oral evidence insufficient to prove that it was within the notified area.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3 and 29 of the Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, the claimed protection depended on the property being in an area declared a slum area. A plaintiff seeking affirmative relief on that basis bears the burden of proving the facts that entitle the plaintiff to relief, including the property's identity and its location within the notified area. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The burden was on the tenant-plaintiffs to establish the identity of the disputed property and prove that it lay in the notified slum area; because they failed to do so, they were not entitled to the injunction based on the statutory protection.

predicates.plaintiff_sought_relief_based_on_slum_ar: A plaintiff sought relief on the basis that statutory protection applied to occupants of a notified slum area.
predicates.plaintiff_claimed_property_was_in_notifi: The plaintiff claimed that the disputed property was within an area declared a slum area.
predicates.defendant_disputed_property_identity_or_: The defendant disputed that the property's identity or location placed it within the area covered by the notification.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking relief on the basis of title must establish the plaintiff’s own title and cannot succeed merely because the defendant has not proved title.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title and possession based on an alleged settlement of the disputed land.
The Supreme Court stated that the plaintiff had to prove title on the basis of that settlement and that the defendant was not obliged to prove title in the case.
members.legal_principle: A party seeking relief on title must establish its own title rather than rely on a failure by the opposing party to establish title. The Court cited no provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff bore the burden of proving the title on which the claim was based; the plaintiff had to succeed on the strength of that case.

predicates.title_and_possession_suit: The proceeding is a suit in which the plaintiff seeks relief concerning title and possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_claimed_title_from_own_source: The plaintiff bases the claimed title on a source of title asserted by the plaintiff.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession on the strength of title must prove that title, and failure by the opposing party to prove its own title does not by itself entitle the claimant to relief.
material_facts: The suit sought recovery of possession on the strength of a claimed title derived from a lease.
The opposing occupants denied the claimed title and asserted title of their own.
The courts below found that the claimant had not established title, while also finding that the occupants had not established the title they asserted.
members.legal_principle: In a suit for recovery of possession on the strength of title, the claimant must establish that title. A court may consider the rival title asserted by the defendants, but their failure to prove it does not discharge the claimant’s burden. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this proposition in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The burden remained on the claimant to establish title; weakness in the defence or failure to establish the defence title could not alone support a decree for possession.

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_title: The proceeding is a suit seeking possession on the basis of a claimed title.
predicates.claimant_seeks_possession: The claimant asks the court to recover possession from the opposing occupants.
predicates.opposing_title_is_unproved: The opposing occupants fail to establish the title they assert.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a declaration of title and possession must establish its own title, rather than relying on weaknesses in the opposing party’s title.
material_facts: The housing society sought a declaration of title and recovery of possession over the disputed land.
The society relied on its predecessors’ title and its own purchase, but the registered family settlement and partition deed did not mention the disputed land.
The society did not provide an acceptable explanation for the omission, and the lower courts focused substantially on the evidentiary value of the government’s land-register entries.
members.legal_principle: In a suit for declaration of title and possession, the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of its own title, irrespective of whether the defendant proves its competing claim. The Court relied on Maran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Thukalan Paulo Avira, AIR 1959 SC 31, and Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, (1995) 3 SCC 426.
members.conclusion: The society failed to establish its own title and possession, so the declaration and related relief could not stand; the appeal was allowed and the lower courts’ judgments were set aside.

predicates.title_declaration_possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of title and possession of property.
predicates.claimant_title_document_omits_disputed_p: The document relied on to establish the claimant’s title did not identify or include the disputed property.
predicates.no_acceptable_explanation_for_omission: The claimant did not provide an acceptable explanation for the omission of the disputed property from the title document.
predicates.claimant_does_not_independently_establis: The claimant failed to establish title through evidence independent of the evidence that was insufficient to prove title.

members.legal_issue: Once legal title to property is established, a person in occupation who claims a right to remain must specifically plead and prove the basis for that right.
material_facts: The society’s ownership of the property was established.
The occupant sought to remain in possession and relied on a claim of adverse possession and documents including ration cards and tax receipts.
The Court found that the adverse-possession claim lacked a factual basis and that the documents relied on did not establish it.
members.legal_principle: In a claim for recovery of possession, occupation by someone other than the legal title-holder is presumed to be under and subordinate to that title. The person resisting recovery must provide sufficiently detailed pleadings and supporting documents identifying the basis for remaining in possession, and must prove the pleaded facts. The Court relied on paragraphs 63–71 and 76 of Maria Margarida Sequeria Fernandes v. Erasmo Jack de Sequeria, (2012) 3 SCALE 550.
members.conclusion: The occupant failed to establish a right to continue in possession, and the owner’s claim for possession prevailed.

predicates.civil_property_possession_claim: The proceeding is a civil claim concerning recovery or protection of possession of property.
predicates.legal_title_established: A party has established legal title to the property in dispute.
predicates.another_person_claims_continuing_occupat: A person other than the title-holder occupies the property and claims a right to remain there.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking title to alluvial accretions must establish that the accretions attached to plots held by the claimant or the claimant’s predecessors and must identify the accretions attributable to those plots.
material_facts: The claimants relied on a statutory claim to lands said to have formed through river accretion.
The evidence did not establish that the claimants or their ancestors held the plots to which the disputed accretions were said to have attached when the accretions formed.
The evidence showed that different branches separately held and enjoyed frontier plots, and the claimants made no attempt in the courts below to apportion the accretions among the plots.
The claimants did not plead or prove joint ownership and possession with the other branch, and the evidence did not establish that the other branch had lost its title.
The claimants advanced a new theory of common ownership by a remote ancestor only at the Supreme Court, without supporting pleadings or proof.
members.legal_principle: Under clause (1) of section 4 of Bengal Alluvion and Deluvion Regulation XI of 1825, a claimant must prove gradual accession from the recess of the river and that the accretion attached to plots in the possession of the claimant or the claimant’s predecessors. The entitlement extends only to accretions before the relevant plots; where multiple plots are involved, their accretions must be apportioned by projecting perpendicular lines from their boundary points to the new river course. A claim to the whole area also requires pleading and proof of the asserted joint title and possession.
members.conclusion: The claimants failed to establish title to the disputed accretions or a right to recover the entire area. The Court stated that accretions must be apportioned by drawing perpendicular lines from the boundary points of each plot to the new river course, but declined to remand the case for the missing investigation. It did not express an opinion on whether the lands had been gained by gradual accession.

rule.if: alluvial_title_claim and claimant_plot_holding_at_accretion_unproved and separate_plot_holders_identified and accretions_not_apportioned

predicates.alluvial_title_claim: The proceeding includes a claim to title based on land formed by river accretion.
predicates.claimant_plot_holding_at_accretion_unpro: The claimant does not prove that the claimant or predecessors held the plots to which the claimed accretions attached when they formed.
predicates.separate_plot_holders_identified: The evidence indicates that different persons or branches separately held the relevant frontier plots.
predicates.accretions_not_apportioned: The claimant does not identify or establish which accretions belong to the plots held by the claimant’s predecessors.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession on title must establish that the title document covers the specific property claimed.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of three rooms based on a court-auction sale certificate issued to their predecessor.
The certificate described a house by division and serial number and gave boundaries, but did not identify the claimed rooms as part of that house.
The schedule said to describe the suit property was absent from the record, and the alleged municipal statement supporting the plaintiffs’ claim was not proved.
The trial and appellate courts found that the certificate did not connect the property it covered with the claimed rooms.
members.legal_principle: A claimant relying on a title document must prove that it relates to the specific property claimed; a factual finding based on relevant evidence is not displaced merely by assertion on second appeal. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish title to the suit rooms, and the concurrent factual finding was not shown to be illegal or liable to interference in second appeal.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiffs brought a suit seeking possession on the basis of claimed title.
predicates.only_title_document_is_sale_certificate: The plaintiffs relied on a sale certificate as their only evidence supporting title.
predicates.certificate_does_not_identify_claimed_pr: The sale certificate did not connect the property it described with the specific rooms for which possession was sought.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking relief for alleged encroachment must prove that the disputed land forms part of the property claimed by the plaintiff.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought injunctions and removal of structures on land they claimed had been encroached upon.
The plaintiffs relied on a document allocating different land identifiers to the respective plots, but the disputed land’s identity as part of their plots was not established by that document alone.
The courts below placed a burden on the defendants to establish their position concerning the land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, the party asserting a fact necessary to obtain judgment bears the burden of proving it. Section 83 did not assist in establishing the disputed land’s identity in this case. A record of rights is not a document of title. In Narain Prasad Aggarwal (D) by LRs. v. State of M.P. [2007 (8) SCALE 250], the Court held that entries in a record of rights are admissible and may carry a rebuttable presumption of correctness, but do not constitute title.
members.conclusion: The burden was on the plaintiffs to prove that the disputed land formed part of the properties they claimed; the suit could not be decreed on the document alone.

predicates.injunction_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking injunctive relief concerning land.
predicates.plaintiff_claims_encroachment: The plaintiff alleged that another party had encroached on land claimed by the plaintiff.
predicates.land_identity_disputed: The parties disputed whether the land at issue formed part of the property claimed by the plaintiff.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking ejectment must establish the plaintiff's own title and cannot succeed merely because the defendant in possession lacks title.
material_facts: The claimant brought a suit for possession of properties belonging to the Dera on the basis of his asserted title as successor to the Mahant.
The claimant failed to establish title to the headship and the properties.
The claimant argued that others in possession had no title, but the Court assumed that submission in considering the issue.
members.legal_principle: In an ejectment suit based on the plaintiff's title, the plaintiff must succeed or fail on the title established by the plaintiff; the defendant's lack of title does not supply the plaintiff's missing title. The Court referred to Mukherjea's Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts, Second Edition, page 317, which states that a claimant to the office of Mohunt must affirmatively prove the usage on which the claim rests and cannot succeed merely because the defendant is a trespasser.
members.conclusion: The suit for ejectment was properly dismissed because the claimant failed to establish his own title, notwithstanding the possibility that the defendant in possession lacked title.

predicates.ejectment_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking ejectment or possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_claims_possession_on_own_title: The plaintiff seeks possession on the basis of the plaintiff's own asserted title.
predicates.plaintiff_fails_to_establish_title: The plaintiff does not prove the title on which the claim for possession rests.
predicates.ejectment_claim_fails_even_if_defendant_: The plaintiff's claim for ejectment fails even if the defendant in possession has no title.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession in an ejectment suit must succeed on the strength of the claimant's own title, not on the weakness of the opposing party's case.
material_facts: The claimants sought possession of church properties on the basis that they had been validly elected trustees.
The opposing party's alleged separation from the church did not itself establish the claimants' title as trustees.
members.legal_principle: The established rule for an ejectment suit is that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of the plaintiff's own title and not on the weakness of the defendant's case.
members.conclusion: The claimants had to establish their own title as trustees; defeating the opposing party's claim alone would not entitle them to possession.

predicates.ejectment_suit: The proceeding sought recovery of possession from an opposing party.
predicates.claimant_seeks_possession: The claimant sought possession based on an asserted right or title.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession must establish the basis of the claimant's own right even if the opposing party has not established title to the office or property.
material_facts: The claimant sued for possession of the institution and its properties on the basis of his asserted status as the duly installed Mahant.
The claimant did not establish the claimed Chela relationship, the custom governing succession, or his installation as Mahant, and he never obtained possession of the office or properties.
The opposing party's entitlement was disputed, but the claimant's failure to establish the grounds of his own claim remained decisive.
members.legal_principle: A claimant seeking possession on a particular asserted right must prove the facts forming the basis of that right; failure by the opposing party to establish title does not itself prove the claimant's case.
members.conclusion: No decree for possession could be made for the claimant, even assuming the opposing party had not established a right or title to the office or properties.

rule.if: suit_for_possession_of_institutional_property and claimant_relies_on_succession_right and claimant_fails_to_prove_basis_of_right and opposing_title_not_established

predicates.suit_for_possession_of_institutional_pro: A claimant brought a suit seeking possession of property belonging to an institution.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_succession_right: The claimant based the request for possession on an asserted succession to the institution's managing office.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_prove_basis_of_right: The claimant did not prove the facts on which the asserted succession right depended.
predicates.opposing_title_not_established: The opposing party's right or title to the office or property was not established.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a declaration of ownership over disputed property must establish the claimed title before obtaining a decree.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership over a one-third share of the property.
The defendants disputed the plaintiff’s ownership and the registered ownership stood in the defendants’ favour.
The plaintiff produced no document of title in her name, and the Supreme Court upheld the finding that she had not established her title.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 101 and 102 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the initial burden of proving a claimed legal right rests on the party seeking relief and does not shift unless that party first makes out a case. The Court relied on Anil Rishi v. Gurbaksh Singh and the principle stated in R.V.E. Venkatachala Gounder v. Arulmigu Viswesaraswami & V.P. Temple, including the distinction between the burden of proof and the shifting onus of proof.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff had to prove her claimed ownership and, having failed to do so, was not entitled to the decree; the High Court’s decision on this issue was correct.

predicates.title_based_claim: The claimant sought relief on the basis that the claimant owned the disputed property or a share in it.
predicates.title_is_disputed: The opposing party disputed the claimant’s ownership of the property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_establish_title: The claimant did not establish the claimed ownership on the evidence presented.

members.legal_issue: The requirement that a plaintiff succeed on the strength of the plaintiff’s own title applies to suits seeking declaration of title and possession, not to a suit seeking only an injunction based on possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought an injunction and did not seek a declaration of title or possession.
The plaintiff’s possession was established on the evidence, including the defendant’s admission and the outcome of the defendant’s prior litigation concerning the property.
The plaintiff relied on a sale deed, but the High Court’s decision to grant an injunction did not depend on adjudicating the validity of the title documents.
members.legal_principle: In suits for declaration of title and possession, the plaintiff must establish the plaintiff’s own title irrespective of whether the defendant proves a competing case; the Court relied on Jagdish Prasad Patel v. Shivnath and Union of India v. Vasavi Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. That principle did not control a suit seeking only an injunction based on possession. The Court distinguished Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, Advocate, which involved a disputed title claim in an injunction suit and a missing title document.
members.conclusion: The rule requiring a plaintiff to establish title independently of the weakness of the defendant’s case did not govern this injunction suit.

predicates.proceeding_is_bare_possession_injunction: The plaintiff brought a proceeding seeking an injunction to protect possession and did not seek a declaration of title and possession.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking a declaration of rights to land must prove the basis of the claim, and the opposing party’s failure to prove its allegations does not shift that burden.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed rights based on an oral grant of a tenancy, but did not state when the grant was made or produce receipts for land revenue or crop payments.

The plaintiffs produced revenue entries for some plots from 1950 to 1952, when the land had admittedly been allotted to the plaintiff’s father for one year; later entries recorded the land as part of an industrial area in favour of the State’s Commercial Department.
The plaintiffs’ names appeared in the revenue record as encroachers, and the State had declared them encroachers in 1978.

The trial court and first appellate court dismissed the suit, but the High Court reversed those concurrent decisions, reasoning in part that the State had not produced original revenue entries and had not proved the plaintiffs’ possession was that of encroachers.
members.legal_principle: A plaintiff seeking relief must prove the plaintiff’s own case; the defendant’s failure to prove an allegation does not relieve the plaintiff of that burden. The Supreme Court cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred by placing the burden of proving the plaintiffs’ title and possession on the State. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the concurrent dismissal of the suit.

predicates.civil_land_title_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit in which a plaintiff claims rights to land.
