predicates.second_appeal_reverses_concurrent_dismis: A second appellate court reverses concurrent decisions dismissing the plaintiff’s suit.
predicates.plaintiff_claimed_title_without_identify: The plaintiff relied on an alleged oral grant but did not identify when it was made.
predicates.claimant_lacked_supporting_revenue_or_cr: The claimant did not produce receipts supporting the claimed landholding or payments to the alleged grantor.
predicates.appellate_court_shifted_burden_to_defend: The appellate court relied on the defendant’s failure to prove its allegations rather than requiring the plaintiff to prove the plaintiff’s claim.
predicates.second_appeal_reversal_is_set_aside: The reversal of the concurrent dismissals is set aside.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who bears the burden of proving an ownership share must establish that share through evidence of their own contribution, and an agent’s testimony cannot replace the claimant’s evidence about personal financial matters.
material_facts: The claimants sought to establish shares in property attached in connection with debt-recovery proceedings and bore the burden of proving their ownership.
The purchase consideration had been paid by a Hindu undivided family, a distinct legal entity.
The claimants did not testify personally about their independent income or contributions; the power-of-attorney holder testified instead and lacked personal knowledge of those matters.
The documentary evidence did not establish that the purchase funds came from the claimants’ independent income, and the material relied on included an alteration to a stated ownership share.
members.legal_principle: The burden of proving a claimed ownership share rested on the claimants. They had to establish an independent source of income and a contribution to the purchase from that income; names in a sale indenture alone were not conclusive proof of co-ownership. Under Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, failure by a party to testify and offer themselves for cross-examination may give rise to a presumption that their case is not correct. Evidence from a power-of-attorney holder could not establish matters within the claimants’ personal knowledge.
members.conclusion: The claimants failed to prove that they had contributed to the purchase from independent income or that they were co-owners. The tribunal’s finding that they had a share was set aside, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: claim_to_share_in_property_to_resist_execution and claimant_bears_burden_to_prove_share and claimant_did_not_testify_personally and agent_lacked_personal_knowledge and evidence_did_not_establish_claimant_independent_contribution

predicates.claim_to_share_in_property_to_resist_exe: A claimant asserts an ownership share in property to resist its sale in debt-recovery execution proceedings.
predicates.claimant_bears_burden_to_prove_share: The claimant is responsible for proving the asserted ownership share.
predicates.claimant_did_not_testify_personally: The claimant does not give evidence personally about the matters supporting the claimed share.
predicates.agent_lacked_personal_knowledge: The agent who gives evidence does not have personal knowledge of the claimant’s relevant financial matters or contribution.
predicates.evidence_did_not_establish_claimant_inde: The evidence does not establish that the claimant contributed to the property’s purchase from the claimant’s independent income.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_prove_ownership_share: The claimant does not establish the claimed ownership share.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a declaration of title must establish title through the claimant’s own evidence, and revenue entries alone do not prove or confer title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration of title and consequential possession but did not produce the patta on which they relied.
The plaintiffs relied on revenue entries in their favour for only two years, while entries for other years and the revenue-authority findings supported the defendants’ predecessor’s possession.
The evidence showed that the entries relied on by the plaintiffs had been made through misconduct, and the defendants produced a patta and evidence of continued possession.
members.legal_principle: In a suit for declaration of title, the burden lies on the plaintiff to establish a clear title through the plaintiff’s own case; weakness in the defendant’s case cannot supply that proof. Revenue entries are maintained for revenue purposes and do not, by themselves, prove or confer title. The Court relied on Union of India v. Vasavi Co-operative Housing Society Limited (2014) 2 SCC 269.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish their title, and their suit for declaration and possession was dismissed.

predicates.civil_title_suit: A claimant brings a civil proceeding seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.claimant_lacks_sufficient_title_evidence: The claimant does not produce or otherwise prove evidence sufficient to establish the claimed title.
predicates.claimant_relies_only_on_revenue_entries: The claimant relies on revenue-record entries without other sufficient proof of title.

members.legal_issue: In a title claim, the claimant bears the burden of proving the claimant’s own title, and a failure by the opposing party to prove its title does not discharge that burden.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership through an alleged historic grant, family succession, and partition.
The trial court found that the plaintiff had not proved the family pedigree, the alleged grant, or the alleged partition.
The appellate courts shifted the burden to the government because it had not proved its own title, although the plaintiff’s title was the issue to be determined.
The plaintiff’s other asserted evidence did not establish title.
members.legal_principle: The party making a factual averment bears the burden of proving it. A claimant seeking title must establish that title; failure to prove an opposing defence does not amount to an admission or reverse the claimant’s burden. The Court applied the principles in Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act and relied on L.I.C. of India v. Ram Pal Singh Bisen and authorities concerning burden of proof.
members.conclusion: The appellate courts erred in shifting the burden to the government; the plaintiff failed to prove title and could not succeed merely because the government’s title had not been proved.

predicates.civil_title_proceeding: A party brings a civil proceeding to establish ownership of property.
predicates.claimant_asserts_ownership: The claimant asserts a right of ownership in the disputed property.
predicates.claimant_does_not_prove_the_material_bas: The claimant fails to prove the facts or evidence on which the asserted title depends.
predicates.the_decision_maker_treats_opponent_failu: The decision-maker treats the opposing party’s failure to establish its own title as enough to find for the claimant.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking possession on the ground of a recent encroachment must prove the alleged encroachment in light of the material evidence concerning the disputed structures.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that the opposing party had recently raised a mud wall and extended a tiled roof onto the land.
The claimant’s vendor acknowledged that the tiled roof and adjoining mud walls had existed for about 28 years and had been affected by salt.
The opposing party testified that the wall and roof had existed for about 28 years, and the court-appointed Amin’s report described them as 25–30 years old.
The lower appellate court found the structures to be recent without considering the opposing party’s testimony and the Amin’s report.
members.legal_principle: A claimant seeking recovery of possession on the pleaded basis of trespass and encroachment must prove that case. The court must assess the material evidence on the alleged encroachment; the judgment relies on no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The alleged recent encroachment was not proved; the evidence established that the wall and tiled roof were longstanding structures, and the claimant was not entitled to possession on the pleaded encroachment theory.

rule.if: possession_recovery_proceeding and claim_alleges_recent_encroachment and (vendor_admitted_longstanding_structure or opposing_party_testified_to_longstanding_structure or inspection_report_indicated_old_structure)

predicates.possession_recovery_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking possession of land said to have been encroached upon.
predicates.claim_alleges_recent_encroachment: The claimant alleged that the opposing party recently placed or extended a structure onto the claimant’s land.
predicates.vendor_admitted_longstanding_structure: The claimant’s vendor testified that the disputed structure had existed at the site for a long time.
predicates.opposing_party_testified_to_longstanding: The opposing party testified that the disputed structure had existed at the site for a long time.
predicates.inspection_report_indicated_old_structur: A court-appointed inspection report described the disputed structure as old.

members.legal_issue: A declaration of title does not by itself entitle a claimant to recovery of possession from an actual possessor; the claimant must establish entitlement to possession and that the claim is not barred by limitation.
material_facts: The First Appellate Court found that the plaintiff owned one portion of the property and the defendant owned another, but the defendant was in possession of the whole property.
The defendant asserted in the written statement that he had possessed and occupied the property as owner for years, including continuous possession from the time of a release deed.
The plaintiff did not state in the plaint when the defendant or his predecessor took possession or facts showing that the claim for possession was within limitation.
The plaintiff did not establish the alleged landlord-and-tenant relationship, and the First Appellate Court had refused recovery of possession.
The High Court granted possession based on the defendant’s failure to plead adverse possession expressly.
members.legal_principle: A decree for possession does not automatically follow a declaration of title. The claimant must establish entitlement to possession and that the claim is not barred by limitation; the Court also stated that a claimant must show possession before the alleged trespasser took possession. Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires dismissal of a time-barred suit even if limitation is not pleaded in defence, and Articles 64 and 65 prescribe limitation rules for possession claims based respectively on prior possession and title. The presumption that possession follows title applies only where the property’s nature does not admit actual and exclusive occupation and there is no definite proof of another person’s possession. A claimant must succeed on the strength of the claimant’s own case, not the opponent’s weakness. The Court relied on Baba Kartar Singh v. Dayal Das and Peri v. Chrishold. It observed that the defendant’s pleaded claim of long possession as owner was, in substance, a defence of adverse possession, but did not decide whether the defendant had acquired title by adverse possession.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in granting possession. The First Appellate Court’s refusal of that relief was restored, while its declaration of the plaintiff’s title to a portion of the property remained in place.

predicates.possession_suit: The claimant seeks recovery of possession of immovable property in a civil proceeding.
predicates.defendant_in_actual_possession: The opposing party is in actual possession of the property claimed.
predicates.plaintiff_fails_to_establish_entitlement: The claimant does not establish both a right to obtain possession and that the claim for possession is within the applicable limitation period.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking declaration of title and recovery of possession must establish the pleaded basis for entitlement and cannot obtain relief on an unpleaded, unproved claim to be acting as a mutawalli or on the weakness of the defendant’s title.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declaration of title and possession on the basis of an agreement said to transfer mutawalliship to it.
The courts found that the agreement did not validly transfer mutawalliship to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff had not pleaded that it was independently entitled to relief because it was acting as a mutawalli, and no issue on that basis was tried.

The evidence was not sufficient to establish that the plaintiff was in fact acting as a mutawalli; the Wakf Board’s statements about the plaintiff’s accounts and contributions did not bind the defendant or substitute for proof.
The defendant’s own claim of title was rejected by the first appellate court.
members.legal_principle: In a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession, the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of its own case, not the weakness of the defendant’s case. Necessary facts must be pleaded and proved so the opposing party can meet them. Section 3(f) of the Wakf Act, 1954 includes a person acting as a mutawalli, but the principle discussed in Moideen Bibi Ammal v. Rathnavelu Mudali, AIR 1927 Madras 69, could not assist without the necessary pleading and proof. The court also referred to Syed Mustafa Peeran Sahib v. State Wakf Board, AIR 1969 Madras 66.
members.conclusion: Because the plaintiff could not establish its title on the pleaded basis and could not rely on the unpleaded and unproved mutawalli basis, the suit had to be dismissed notwithstanding the failure of the defendant’s title claim.

rule.if: title_and_possession_suit and transfer_basis_invalid and alternative_mutawalli_basis_unpleaded and alternative_mutawalli_basis_unproved

predicates.title_and_possession_suit: A plaintiff brings a suit seeking declaration of title and recovery of possession.
predicates.transfer_basis_invalid: The plaintiff’s pleaded claim depends on a transfer that is found not to have validly conveyed the asserted right.
predicates.alternative_mutawalli_basis_unpleaded: The plaintiff did not plead that its entitlement arose independently from acting as a mutawalli.
predicates.alternative_mutawalli_basis_unproved: The plaintiff did not establish with sufficient evidence that it was in fact acting as a mutawalli.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking title and possessory relief must establish that the land in dispute is the land described in the claimant’s title documents and that the claimant is lawfully entitled to possess it.
material_facts: The appellants produced sale deeds for specified parcels but did not establish the boundaries or location of those parcels with a site plan, demarcation report, or comparable evidence.
The evidence did not connect the site of the restaurant to the parcels described in the sale deeds.
The trial court found that the appellants had not proved lawful possession of the restaurant site, and the Supreme Court upheld that finding.
members.legal_principle: A claimant asserting title must prove the identity of the land claimed and connect it to the title documents; evidence that a different parcel was purchased does not establish title to the disputed site. The Court upheld the factual finding that the appellants had not made that connection and noted the High Court’s reliance on Rajinder Kakkar v. Delhi Development Authority. The trial court also treated revenue entries such as khasra girdawari as not being documents of title.
members.conclusion: The appellants failed to prove that the restaurant stood on the land they had purchased or that they were lawfully in possession of the disputed site, so their claimed title and possession relief could not succeed.

predicates.title_and_injunction_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking recognition of title and relief concerning possession of land.
predicates.property_identity_unproved: The claimant did not prove that the disputed site was the parcel identified in the claimant’s title documents.
predicates.lawful_possession_unproved: The claimant did not prove a lawful basis for possessing the disputed site.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract.
material_facts: The buyer pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform and testified to that effect.
He paid substantial advances, produced evidence of funds and financial capacity, and corresponded with the bank about settlement of the debt.
The sellers did not show that they had demanded further payment from the buyer or that he had failed to respond to such a demand.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the plaintiff to plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract. Readiness concerns financial capacity, while willingness is assessed from conduct. The court assesses the entirety of the facts and circumstances, including conduct before and after suit; no fixed formula applies. The plaintiff need not actually tender or deposit money unless directed by the court. The Court relied on N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, P. D'Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, and R.C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal.
members.conclusion: The buyer proved readiness and willingness, and the concurrent findings granting specific performance on this ground were upheld.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaintiff_claims_contract_performance and (plaintiff_shows_financial_capacity and plaintiff_shows_consistent_willing_conduct) and not credible_contrary_evidence

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_claims_contract_performance: The plaintiff asserts that they have performed or are ready and willing to perform their essential contractual obligations.
predicates.plaintiff_shows_financial_capacity: The plaintiff produces evidence that they had the financial means to perform the payment obligations.
predicates.plaintiff_shows_consistent_willing_condu: The plaintiff's pleadings, payments, testimony, and other conduct show a continuing willingness to complete the contract.
predicates.credible_contrary_evidence: The opposing party produces credible evidence that the plaintiff was unable or unwilling to perform.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish both readiness and willingness to perform the contract, and failure to establish willingness defeats the claim.
material_facts: The agreement required the defendant to evict the tenants and deliver vacant possession before executing the sale deed.
The plaintiff’s notice and plaint insisted on vacant possession and did not state that the plaintiff would purchase the property with the tenants.
The trial court found the plaintiff ready but not willing to purchase the property with the tenants; the plaintiff first claimed willingness to do so in an affidavit filed in the High Court.
The Supreme Court agreed that the plaintiff had not established willingness to purchase the property with the tenants.
members.legal_principle: A decree for specific performance requires proof of both readiness and willingness. Where the evidence and pleadings establish that the plaintiff was unwilling to perform on the terms available, the plaintiff is not entitled to the decree. The Court applied this principle in considering the requirement of readiness and willingness for specific performance.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to specific performance because he had not proved willingness to perform the contract.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_accept_performance_wit: The plaintiff insisted on vacant possession and did not establish willingness to purchase the property with the tenants remaining in occupation.
predicates.specific_performance_must_be_refused: The plaintiff is not entitled to a decree for specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract, and an unoverturned finding that this requirement was not met prevents a decree.
material_facts: The purchaser sought specific performance and pleaded that he had always been ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
The trial court found, based on the purchaser's evidence and conduct, that he was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
That finding was not challenged before the High Court, and the High Court did not hold it to be incorrect.
The Supreme Court accepted the trial court's finding and held that the High Court could not grant specific performance without setting it aside.
members.legal_principle: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform from the date of the contract until the hearing; failure to establish this requires dismissal of the claim. The court relied on Ardeshir Mamna v. Flora Sassoon. It also held that the trial court's adverse finding could not be disregarded without considering the evidence and setting the finding aside.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was not entitled to specific performance, and the trial court's dismissal of the suit was restored.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.claimant_not_continuously_ready: The claimant did not establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform the claimant's part of the contract.
predicates.adverse_readiness_finding_not_overturned: The trial court found against the claimant on readiness and willingness, and that finding was not set aside on appeal.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness, including the capacity to pay the balance of the sale consideration.
material_facts: The parties agreed to sell a shop, with part of the price paid as earnest money and the balance due when the sale deed was to be executed.
Although both parties attended the Sub-Registrar’s office on the agreed date, no sale deed was executed.
The plaintiff sued for specific performance but produced no documentary evidence that he had the balance amount available at the relevant time.
The plaintiff said that he had borrowed the money from friends but could not name them or establish that he had raised the money.
The trial court dismissed the suit for failure to prove readiness and willingness; the appellate court and High Court reversed that decision and granted specific performance.
members.legal_principle: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish readiness and willingness throughout, and must show the capacity to perform the contractual obligation to pay the balance consideration. The relief is discretionary, and the court should examine the plaintiff’s capacity to pay. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for these principles.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to prove readiness and willingness because he did not establish his capacity to pay the balance consideration. The appellate court and High Court had not properly assessed the evidence and were wrong to reverse the trial court; the decree for specific performance was set aside.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement for sale.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_prove_capacity_to_pay_: The plaintiff failed to establish that they could pay the balance consideration when required to perform the agreement.
predicates.plaintiff_provided_no_reliable_evidence_: The plaintiff produced no reliable evidence, such as financial records or a negotiable instrument, showing that the required funds were available.
predicates.plaintiff_could_not_substantiate_claimed: The plaintiff claimed to have borrowed the required funds but could not identify the lenders or otherwise establish that the funds had been raised.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance requires the claimant to plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the operative contract according to its true construction.
material_facts: The operative reconveyance agreement required payment of Rs.25,000.
The plaintiffs' pleadings and evidence maintained that they were ready and willing to purchase the property for Rs.10,000, and they did not plead or prove readiness and willingness to pay Rs.25,000.
The plaintiffs had paid Rs.5,000 in two instalments, but the record contained no specific statement that they were ready and willing to pay the full reconveyance price.
The plaintiffs sought specific performance of the reconveyance agreement.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and Explanation (ii) require an averment and proof of readiness and willingness to perform the contract according to its true construction, assessed from the pleadings and evidence as a whole and maintained from institution of the suit through decree. The court relied on Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, AIR 1999 SC 3029, for reading pleadings as a whole; Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi, (2000) 6 SCC 420, for assessing whether the plaint as a whole indicates readiness and willingness; and Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan, (2005) 6 SCC 243, for assessing conduct in light of all attending circumstances and the evidence. The court noted the discretion under Section 20 but did not decide whether its exercise would otherwise have been equitable.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs failed to establish readiness and willingness to perform the operative contract, so specific performance was unavailable and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brings a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.operative_contract_requires_full_perform: The contract found to govern the dispute requires the claimant to perform specified essential terms.
predicates.claimant_pleads_or_proves_readiness_only: The claimant's pleadings or evidence show readiness to perform less than the essential performance required by the operative contract.

members.legal_issue: A transferee relying on part performance to defend possession must specifically plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the agreement.
material_facts: The respondent, a subsequent purchaser and successor in interest, sued for possession of the property.
The appellant relied on part performance to retain possession.
The appellant’s written statement contained only a vague denial concerning readiness and willingness, rather than a specific plea.
The appellant had paid only part of the stated consideration and did not pay the balance before the sale to the respondent, deposit it when the suit was filed, or offer payment.
members.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, makes the protection of part performance conditional on the transferee’s continuing willingness to perform the contract. A transferee invoking that protection in a suit for possession must plead and prove readiness and willingness. Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, requires a plaintiff seeking enforcement of a contract to plead readiness and willingness; the same requirement applies when a transferee seeks to retain possession under Section 53-A. The principle that a person seeking equity must do equity supports this requirement.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not retain possession under Section 53-A because he had not specifically pleaded and proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the agreement.

rule.if: possession_suit and part_performance_defense and (readiness_not_specifically_pleaded or readiness_not_proved)

predicates.possession_suit: A person seeking possession brought a suit against the occupant.
predicates.part_performance_defense: The occupant relies on part performance of a transfer agreement to retain possession.
predicates.readiness_not_specifically_pleaded: The occupant did not specifically plead continuing readiness and willingness to perform the agreement.
predicates.readiness_not_proved: The occupant did not prove continuing readiness and willingness to perform the agreement, including by performing or offering to perform outstanding obligations.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract, and inconsistent claims that the debt was discharged cannot be reconciled with an unconditional willingness to pay the agreed consideration.
material_facts: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to reconvey property but principally asserted that the transaction was a mortgage and that the debt had already been discharged through rent or under debt-relief proceedings.
The claimant sought accounting and offered to pay any amount found due only if the claims of discharge and mortgage redemption were rejected.
In cross-examination, the claimant stated that he had no income, funds, bank account, or source from which to raise the money.
The trial court and the High Court Single Judge found that the claimant was not ready and willing to perform; the High Court Division Bench reversed that finding.
members.legal_principle: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c), requires a plaintiff to aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract according to its true construction. The court assesses the plaintiff’s conduct throughout the case and the attending circumstances; a bare pleading or examination-in-chief is insufficient, and the plaintiff must prove that the consideration could be arranged when required. A conditional offer and a claim that the debt was already discharged are inconsistent with an unconditional willingness to pay. The Court relied on N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, Mahabir Prasad Jain v. Ganga Singh, Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James, Manjunath Anandappa v. Tammanasa, Pukhraj D. Jain v. G. Gopalakrishna, and Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing & Construction Pvt. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not prove readiness and willingness to perform the agreement, and was not entitled to specific performance. The Division Bench erred in granting that relief.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and (claimant_asserts_debt_already_discharged or claimant_makes_only_conditional_offer) and claimant_lacks_evidence_of_ability_to_pay

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking an order that the other party carry out an agreement.
predicates.claimant_asserts_debt_already_discharged: The claimant asserted that the obligation to pay had already ended, including by repayment, set-off, or discharge.
predicates.claimant_makes_only_conditional_offer: The claimant offered to pay only if the claimant’s other claims were rejected or an accounting showed an amount remained due.
predicates.claimant_lacks_evidence_of_ability_to_pa: The claimant provided no evidence that the required money was available or could be arranged when payment was required.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must prove readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual obligations.
material_facts: The agreement required the purchaser to complete the purchase within a stipulated period that the lower courts found was essential.
The purchaser made no effective effort to complete the purchase during that period and brought the specific-performance suit years after it expired.
The purchaser falsely claimed to have made a payment under an alleged later agreement and relied on a document found to be fabricated.
The lower courts found that the purchaser had not been ready and willing to perform the contract.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to aver and prove performance, or continuous readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms required of that plaintiff. A false claim of payment supported by a fabricated document is inconsistent with readiness and willingness to perform the contractual payment obligation.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to establish readiness and willingness, so the decree for specific performance could not stand.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding was a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_failed_to_prove_readiness: The plaintiff did not establish readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual obligations.
predicates.false_payment_claim: The plaintiff falsely asserted that a payment had been made and relied on a fabricated document to support that assertion.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and prove performance, or continuous readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms required of the claimant.
material_facts: The claim sought specific performance of an alleged agreement to sell, under which part of the price had been paid and the balance was payable when the sale deed was executed and registered.

The plaint referred to the agreement, the payment, a later notice asking the seller to obtain permission and execute the sale deed, and the seller’s failure to do so, but did not suggest that the claimant had performed or was continuously ready and willing to perform his own obligations.

The claimant’s testimony principally addressed the existence and validity of the agreement and the parties’ dealings, and did not categorically assert performance or continuous readiness and willingness.

The opposing party’s written statement did not raise the absence of the required averment, but the claimant did not establish readiness and willingness through the pleadings and evidence considered as a whole.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as applicable to the suit, specific performance could not be enforced for a claimant who failed to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms required of that claimant, except terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the other party. The required averment did not demand a particular formula, but its substance had to appear in the plaint; the whole pleadings and evidence, and the claimant’s conduct, had to be assessed. The opposing party’s failure to object did not remove the claimant’s burden. The Court relied on Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan (2005) 6 SCC 243; A. Kanthamani v. Nasreen Ahmed (2017) 4 SCC 654; Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty (1999) 6 SCC 337; and Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha (2005) 7 SCC 534, including the requirements reflected in Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
members.conclusion: Specific performance was properly refused because the claimant failed to aver and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.readiness_not_pleaded: The claimant did not plead in substance that the claimant had performed or was continuously ready and willing to perform the essential obligations required of the claimant.
predicates.readiness_not_proven: The claimant’s evidence and conduct, considered with the whole record, did not establish performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential obligations required of the claimant.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish the statutory and equitable requirements for that relief, including readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of a contract concerning land.
The trial court and the High Court found, on the pleadings and evidence, that the plaintiff had not been ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
The Supreme Court found no material perversity or illegality in those concurrent findings.
members.legal_principle: Specific performance is a discretionary and equitable relief. The court must consider whether a valid and concluded contract exists; whether the plaintiff was and remains ready and willing to perform; whether the plaintiff performed in accordance with the contract; whether granting relief would be equitable or cause hardship; and whether alternative relief is available. These matters must be properly pleaded and proved. The requirements arise under Sections 16(c), 20, 21, 22 and 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to C of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to specific performance, and the concurrent findings denying that relief were upheld.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_not_ready_and_willing: The evidence established that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform the plaintiff's part of the contract.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, although no particular wording is required in the pleading.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of a sale agreement.

The trial court found that the plaintiff had not offered the balance of the price as alleged and had not established that he was ready and willing to perform; the first appellate court affirmed those findings.
The High Court considered the pleading sufficient but did not explain how the plaintiff had proved readiness and willingness.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with Explanation (ii), requires the claimant to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms that remain to be performed by the claimant, except terms whose performance the defendant prevented or waived. Under Explanation (i), actual tender or deposit of money is generally unnecessary unless the court directs it. The pleading is judged in substance and as a whole, not by a required formula: Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon; Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing and Construction (Private) Ltd.; Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal; Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty; Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi; and Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff’s pleading could be assessed by reading it as a whole, without requiring particular words, but the requirement of Section 16(c) was not met because readiness and willingness were not proved. The High Court’s judgment was therefore set aside.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and (not readiness_pleaded or not readiness_proved)

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.readiness_pleaded: The claimant’s pleading, read as a whole, conveyed readiness and willingness to perform the claimant’s essential contractual obligations.
predicates.readiness_proved: The claimant established by evidence that the claimant performed or remained ready and willing to perform the claimant’s essential contractual obligations.

members.legal_issue: Pleadings that sufficiently allege readiness and willingness satisfy the pleading requirement for a claim seeking specific performance.
material_facts: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to reconvey property.
The trial court found sufficient pleading concerning readiness and willingness.
The Supreme Court agreed that the pleadings sufficiently addressed readiness and willingness, while separately considering whether the claimant proved it.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a claimant seeking specific performance to plead and prove readiness and willingness. The Court treated the pleading requirement as sufficiently met, without treating that pleading alone as proof of readiness and willingness.
members.conclusion: The pleadings sufficiently complied with the requirement concerning readiness and willingness.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant sought a decree requiring performance of an agreement.
predicates.plaint_alleges_readiness_and_willingness: The claimant alleged in the pleadings that he was ready and willing to perform his contractual obligations.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness, including the means to arrange the required consideration, and a bare assertion of willingness is insufficient.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that he was ready to pay the consideration, but pleaded that he had no business, profession, source of income, or movable or immovable property.
Apart from a witness’s statement, there was no evidence that the claimant had the means to arrange the consideration.
Before filing suit, the claimant had sought relief to extinguish the debt and recover the property rather than to pay under the reconveyance agreement.
The reconveyance agreement provided for interest, but the claimant alleged that no interest was payable.
The property had been mortgaged to a bank, and the defendants paid the claimant’s debt after the bank obtained an award and the property was put up for auction.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, continuous readiness and willingness is a condition precedent to specific performance; a claimant must both aver and prove it. The court considers the claimant’s conduct before and after suit and all attending circumstances, and the required consideration must be shown to be available, though it need not be held as cash in hand if the claimant proves the means to generate it. The Court relied on N.P. Thirugnanam (Dead) by LRs. v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao and Others; Pushparani S. Sundaram and Others v. Pauline Manomani James (deceased) and Others; Manjunath Anandappa URF Shivappa Hanasi v. Tammanasa and Others; Pukhraj D. Jain and Others v. G. Gopalakrishna; and Umabai and Anr. v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan (Dead) by LRs. and Anr.
members.conclusion: The claimant failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his obligations, so specific performance was unavailable. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s decree was set aside, and the trial court’s dismissal of the suit was restored.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and (no_evidence_of_means_to_arrange_consideration or (sought_debt_extinguishment_instead_of_contractual_payment and denied_contractual_interest and defendants_paid_claimant_bank_debt))

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant sought a decree requiring performance of an agreement.
predicates.no_evidence_of_means_to_arrange_consider: The claimant offered no evidence, beyond a witness’s statement, that he had the means to arrange the required consideration.
predicates.sought_debt_extinguishment_instead_of_co: The claimant sought an order extinguishing the debt and returning the property rather than establishing that he would pay under the reconveyance agreement.
predicates.denied_contractual_interest: The claimant disputed that he was required to pay interest even though the agreement provided for it.
predicates.defendants_paid_claimant_bank_debt: The defendants paid the claimant’s bank debt after the property faced auction.

members.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance cannot be reversed on hardship grounds when hardship was not pleaded or supported by evidence, particularly where the agreement and the purchaser’s readiness and willingness were established.
material_facts: The purchaser proved the agreement for sale, payment of earnest money, and readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s obligations.
The seller did not plead hardship or adduce evidence in support of a hardship defence, and no hardship issue was framed.
The first appellate court accepted the findings on the agreement and readiness and willingness but denied specific performance on the ground that the seller would become landless.
The evidence showed that the seller retained cultivable and uncultivable land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, hardship may be a defence to specific performance, but it must be raised by the defendant and supported by evidence. Whether granting specific performance would cause hardship is a question of fact; an appellate court should not reverse a decree on that ground without a properly raised and evidenced issue. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the decisions denying specific performance, and restored the trial court’s decree for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and agreement_proved and buyer_ready_and_willing and not hardship_defense_pleaded and not hardship_evidence_present and not hardship_issue_framed

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether a decree for specific performance should be granted.
predicates.agreement_proved: The purchaser established that the parties made the agreement for sale.
predicates.buyer_ready_and_willing: The purchaser established readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.hardship_defense_pleaded: The seller pleaded that granting specific performance would cause hardship.
predicates.hardship_evidence_present: Evidence was presented to support the seller’s claim that granting specific performance would cause hardship.
predicates.hardship_issue_framed: The court framed an issue for determination on whether granting specific performance would cause hardship.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must plead the agreement relied on, a specific request that it be performed, and continuing readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s part.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an agreement to reconvey property.
The plaintiff alleged that the documents recording the transactions were sham and unsupported by consideration.

The trial court found that the documents were genuine and operative, that consideration had been paid, and that possession and title had passed; the plaintiff did not challenge those findings in the High Court.
The plaint did not plead that the plaintiff had specifically requested performance of the agreement or that the plaintiff had been and remained ready and willing to perform his part.
members.legal_principle: A suit for specific performance must conform to Forms 47 and 48 in the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure: the plaintiff must set out the agreement, plead a specific application to the defendant to perform it and the defendant’s failure to do so, and plead that the plaintiff has been and remains ready and willing to perform. The Court applied Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley and relied on its statement of the rule, including its reference to Pt. Prem Rai v. The D.L.F. Housing and Construction (Private) Ltd.
members.conclusion: The plaint did not contain the pleadings required for specific performance, so the plaintiff was not entitled to that relief.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brings a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.pleaded_specific_request_for_performance: The plaintiff pleads that the plaintiff specifically asked the defendant to perform the agreement and that the defendant did not do so.
predicates.pleaded_continuing_readiness_and_willing: The plaintiff pleads readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s part, both previously and at present.
predicates.specific_performance_decree_unavailable: The plaintiff cannot obtain a decree for specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, although the required substance may be conveyed without using exact formulaic words.
material_facts: The plaintiff did not expressly plead readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.

The plaint stated only that he had asked the agent to arrange execution of the sale deed, without identifying when the demand was made; no demand or tender was made to the owner within the contractual period.
The plaintiff served notice only on the agent after that period had expired and after learning that the property had been sold to another purchaser; the owner did not receive notice.
The plaintiff's testimony that he was then ready to pay the balance did not establish that he had been ready and willing throughout the relevant period.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires both an averment and proof that the plaintiff has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms required of him. Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to the Code of Civil Procedure indicate the required pleadings. Exact words are not indispensable where the pleadings as a whole and the evidence at trial show readiness and willingness in substance, but a bare plea is insufficient without proof. The Court relied on Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley, Abdul Khader Rowther v. P.K. Sara Bai, Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi, and Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff had not substantially complied with the requirements for specific performance, and could not obtain that relief.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.no_substantive_readiness_pleading: The plaintiff's pleadings, read as a whole, do not convey that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform the essential terms required of the plaintiff.
predicates.no_proof_of_continuous_readiness: The evidence does not establish that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform those terms throughout the relevant period.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking protection for possession in part performance must plead that the possession was taken in part performance of the contract.
material_facts: A party relied on an agreement and asserted that possession was protected because the agreement had been acted upon.
That party’s written statement did not plead that possession had been taken in part performance of the contract.
members.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires a party seeking its benefit to plead that possession was taken in part performance of the contract. Pleadings give notice of each side’s case and identify the matters for decision; relief cannot be granted without the necessary pleading.
members.conclusion: The party could not claim the benefit of protection for possession in part performance.

predicates.property_dispute_involving_part_performa: A property dispute involved a party relying on an agreement as a defense based on part performance.
predicates.party_seeks_part_performance_protection: A party asked the court to protect possession on the basis that the agreement had been acted upon.
predicates.possession_in_part_performance_not_plead: The party’s pleadings did not state that possession had been taken in part performance of the agreement.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish continuing readiness and willingness, including the financial capacity to pay the balance consideration.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement to sell land and was required to pay a substantial balance of the sale consideration.
The plaintiff had low income and a low bank balance, and the evidence did not show that he had sufficient funds or could arrange them to pay the balance consideration.
The plaintiff had taken a loan from a relative for his business, but the evidence did not show that he could repay that loan and also arrange the money required for the land.
members.legal_principle: Readiness concerns the plaintiff’s capacity to perform, including the financial position to pay the purchase price; willingness is assessed from the plaintiff’s conduct and surrounding circumstances. The plaintiff must prove readiness and willingness from the execution of the agreement through the decree. The Court relied on His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, (1996) 4 SCC 526, and I.S. Sikandar (Dead) by Lrs. v. K. Subramani, (2013) 15 SCC 27. No statutory provision was cited for this principle in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement, so he was not entitled to specific performance. The Supreme Court allowed the vendors’ appeal and set aside the High Court’s decree.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.plaintiff_lacked_financial_capacity: The plaintiff’s financial circumstances showed that the plaintiff could not pay the balance consideration.
predicates.no_evidence_of_funds_arrangement: The record did not show that the plaintiff could arrange the funds needed to pay the balance consideration.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform, and a later deposit of the balance consideration alone does not establish that requirement.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought specific performance of the alleged sale agreement.
The original plaint did not plead readiness and willingness to perform; the plaintiffs sought and obtained permission to add that plea after the defendants raised its absence.
The plaintiffs deposited the balance consideration after the High Court had decreed the suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with Explanation (ii), requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to aver and establish readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s part of the contract. The Court relied on Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha, which explains that the claimant’s conduct must entitle the claimant to the equitable relief, and on Surya Narain Upadhyaya v. Ram Roop Pandey.
members.conclusion: Readiness and willingness must be pleaded and proved, and cannot be inferred merely from depositing the balance consideration after the High Court’s order. The Court did not decide whether the plaintiffs could ultimately prove readiness and willingness at trial.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant sought specific performance of an alleged contract.
predicates.readiness_and_willingness_required: The claimant’s entitlement to the requested relief depended on readiness and willingness to perform the claimant’s contractual obligations.
predicates.balance_deposited_only_after_order: The claimant deposited the balance consideration only after the court had made the order granting relief.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and establish readiness and willingness to perform the contract, but an additional oral demand need not be separately proved where the required pleading and evidence establish that demand and ability to perform.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s plaint specifically averred readiness and willingness to perform the contract and stated that the plaintiff had demanded receipt of the balance consideration and execution of a registered sale deed.
The plaintiff had sufficient funds to pay the balance consideration and the evidence satisfied the Court that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform.
The High Court wrongly concluded that no evidence showed a demand for performance.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, and Forms 47 and 48 of Appendix A to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, governs the pleadings and proof for a specific-performance suit. The claimant must plead and prove readiness and willingness. The Court observed that an oral demand cannot itself be proved by evidence, and found the required averments and evidence of financial ability and readiness in this case.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff had fulfilled the formalities required for specific performance and was ready and willing to perform; the High Court was wrong to find otherwise for want of proof of demand.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.

predicates.evidence_shows_ability_to_pay_and_readin: The evidence establishes the claimant’s ability to pay the balance due and readiness to perform.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s contractual obligations.
material_facts: The purchaser knew of the mortgage when the later sale agreement was made.

The agreement required completion by a specified deadline, but the purchaser took no steps toward completion around that deadline and there was a substantial period before the next payment and communication.
The purchaser did not establish that he had performed the later proposed arrangement to pay the bank and the seller; the seller independently paid the bank.
The purchaser’s general assertion of readiness was not supported by evidence of continuous steps to complete the transaction.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual terms continuously from the contract through the hearing. The Court relied on Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Pallaniswami Nadar, which quoted Ardeshir Mama v. Flora Sassoon, and J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao, including its statement that the burden rests on the plaintiff.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness, so the specific-performance suit had to be dismissed.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit asking a court to compel completion of a sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_knew_of_encumbrance: The purchaser knew of an encumbrance affecting the property when entering the operative sale agreement.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must plead readiness and willingness in the manner required for that remedy.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s pleading stated that he was ready and willing to pay the balance and take the sale deed.
The pleading did not conform to the prescribed allegation that the plaintiff had been and continued to be ready and willing specifically to perform the agreement after the defendant had notice of it.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act requires the plaintiff to aver and prove performance, or continuous readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms of the contract. Order VI Rule 3 and Form 47 in Appendix A of the Code of Civil Procedure prescribe the relevant form of pleading. The Court relied on Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh, Ram Awadh v. Achhaibar Dubey, Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley, Abdul Khader Rowther v. P.K. Sara Bai, Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James, and Manju Nath Anandappa v. Tammanasa.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff did not satisfy the mandatory pleading requirement, and the finding granting specific performance was erroneous in law.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for the sale of property.
predicates.pleading_lacks_required_readiness_allega: The plaintiff’s pleading did not make the required allegation of having been and continuing to be ready and willing specifically to perform the agreement.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who relies on part performance must demonstrate readiness and willingness to perform the agreement and acts of part performance referable to that agreement.
material_facts: The parties agreed to a sale for a price of 17,000, and the transferee paid 12,000 and took possession under the agreement.
The transferee maintained that the agreed price was only 12,000 and did not pay the remaining 5,000 despite a demand for payment.
The transferee relied on part performance to resist the transferor’s claim for possession.
members.legal_principle: Under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a transferee must be ready and willing to perform the agreement. Acts relied on as part performance must be referable to the alleged agreement and not to another title, and must be unequivocally referable to an agreement of the kind alleged. Part performance operates as a shield to protect possession, not as a sword.
members.conclusion: The transferee was not entitled to protection based on part performance because he was not ready and willing to perform the agreement alleged by the transferor; possession alone did not establish part performance of that agreement.

members.legal_issue: After reducing a murder conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, the sentence may be limited to the period already undergone when substantial time has passed and the accused has already served a substantial period.
material_facts: More than thirteen years had elapsed since the incident.
The accused had already undergone about four years of imprisonment and was on bail.
The court retained the conviction for causing hurt but imposed no separate sentence for that offence.
members.legal_principle: The court imposed sentence based on the elapsed time and the period already served. The judgment does not identify a statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The sentence for culpable homicide was limited to the period already undergone, the hurt conviction remained unchanged, and no separate sentence was imposed for that conviction.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_offence_reclassifi: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which the offence of conviction has been reduced.

predicates.substantial_sentence_already_served: The accused has already served a substantial period of imprisonment.

members.legal_issue: The custodial sentences of offenders convicted of causing injuries may be reduced to the period already served in light of the circumstances of the offence and the time already spent in custody.
material_facts: The offenders inflicted injuries with a jaily and lathis during the incident.
Their convictions for causing injuries were confirmed on appeal.
The incident arose from a dispute over cutting reeds and a wordy altercation.
The occurrence had taken place many years before the appeal was decided, and the offenders had already served periods in custody.
members.legal_principle: Sentencing is discretionary and must account for the gravity and nature of the offence, the motive, the manner of its commission and other attendant circumstances. The Court relied on State of M.P. v. Bablu Natt, Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra and Soman v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The convictions were confirmed, but the custodial sentences were reduced to the periods already undergone by the respective offenders.

members.legal_issue: A sentence should be reduced when the sentencing courts have not meaningfully assessed proportionality and the circumstances of the offence and offender support mitigation.
material_facts: The incident arose from a pre-existing dispute between two families and began suddenly after a quarrel, without premeditation.
It was a free fight, and both sides suffered injuries.
The fatal injury was caused with a wooden log readily available at the scene.
The appellants reported the incident to the police, alleging that the complainant party was the aggressor.
No prior criminal antecedents or later untoward incidents involving the appellants were reported.

The trial court recorded the appellants’ requests for minimal sentences but did not meaningfully analyze the relevant circumstances; the High Court affirmed the sentences without considering their quantum.
members.legal_principle: Sentencing must reflect just punishment and proportionality and must be based on the circumstances of the offence and offender, including culpability, antecedents, prospects of reformation, and other mitigating factors. There is no rigid formula; judicial discretion must be rationally exercised. The Court relied on Gopal Singh v. State of Uttarakhand, (2013) 7 SCC 545, and noted the sentencing process under Section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal and reduced the sentences: the sentences of two appellants for their offences were reduced to the period already undergone, and the sentences of three appellants for their homicide-related offences were reduced to five years each, without disturbing the fines.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer's exclusive possession of jointly held property does not become adverse to the other co-sharers without a clear ouster, and mutation alone does not establish ouster unless it clearly denies their title.
material_facts: A successor to one co-sharer and, later, that successor's descendants possessed the land, including the share claimed by other collaterals, from 1930.
The descendants obtained mutation of their names after the claims of the claimant and other collaterals had been rejected.
The predecessor mortgaged part of the land and sold part of it while treating himself as owner.
The appellants' possession was continuous for more than the statutory period, public, and adverse to the other collaterals.
members.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all co-sharers. Adverse possession against the others requires a clear ouster through denial of their title; mutation in one co-sharer's name is insufficient unless accompanied by a clear declaration denying the others' title. The Court discussed Sardar Amar Singh v. Sardarni Shiv Datt Kaur and Bashir Ahmad & Ors. v. Parshottam & Ors., and stated the ouster rule as the correct legal position.
members.conclusion: The appellants established clear ouster and adverse possession, perfected title to the disputed land, and the appeal was allowed with the trial court's dismissal of the suit restored.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer who relies on ouster or adverse possession must prove possession hostile to the other co-sharers’ title; failure to do so does not defeat their title.
material_facts: The son asserted that the property belonged to him and pleaded ouster, while the daughters claimed shares as heirs of their mother.
The son objected when the daughters’ names were entered in the municipal records, but the mutation was allowed and he took no further step to challenge it.
The record did not establish possession that clearly denied the other co-sharers’ title.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession requires hostile possession that denies the true owner’s title; the person asserting it must prove that hostility by clear and unequivocal evidence. A claimant who is uncertain of the true owner cannot establish hostile possession against that owner. The Court relied on T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, (2006) 7 SCC 570, as well as Govindammal v. R. Perumal Chettiar, (2006) 11 SCC 600; P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, decided 24 April 2007; and Syed Abdul Khader v. Rami Reddy, (1979) 2 SCC 601.
members.conclusion: The plea of ouster was not established, and the son could not thereby defeat the other co-sharers’ title.

predicates.clear_hostile_denial_of_other_sharers_ti: The claimant clearly and unequivocally possessed the property in denial of the other co-sharers’ title.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer's possession does not become adverse to other co-sharers without a denial of their rights known to them and an ensuing ouster for the required period.
material_facts: The parties were co-sharers in the inherited estate.
The plaintiffs continued to receive income from the estate, and their receipts were of the same character as those of the defendants.
The defendants did not deny the plaintiffs' title until they executed a deed asserting control over the property.
members.legal_principle: As between co-sharers, possession by one is ordinarily possession by all. It becomes adverse only when the person in possession denies the others' rights to their knowledge and exclusion and ouster follow for the statutory period. Participation in profits, even to some degree, negates ouster. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs' claim was not barred by adverse possession because there had been no ouster before the denial of their title, and they had continued to participate in the income.
