members.legal_issue: A co-heir’s rights are not barred by ouster merely because another co-heir possesses and manages the property or the first co-heir does not demand a share; ouster requires an open hostile assertion coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment to the other co-heir’s knowledge.
material_facts: The claim was between co-heirs over rights to manage a religious institution and share its income and offerings.
The co-heirs in possession asserted that the claimant had no right, relying in part on an earlier decree that did not decide the claimant’s entitlement and in which the claimant was not a party.
The claimant had not demanded a share during her lifetime, but evidence showed that her brothers looked after her and paid her portions of the income.
There was no evidence that the possessing co-heirs openly denied the claimant’s rights in a manner that brought the denial to her knowledge.
members.legal_principle: As between co-heirs, possession by one is in law possession by all, and sole possession or receipt of profits does not by itself make that possession adverse. Ouster requires an open assertion of hostile title, coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment, to the knowledge of the other co-heir; secret hostile intent or a failure to demand a share is insufficient. The Court relied on P. Lakshmi v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, [1957] SCR 195. The judgment refers to the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, but cites no specific provision.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s rights were not shown to have been extinguished by ouster. The High Court erred in treating the earlier decree and the absence of a demand as sufficient proof of ouster; the decree below was restored with a modification to the rotation of management days.

rule.if: coheir_ouster_proceeding and not (hostile_title_openly_asserted and exclusive_possession_and_enjoyment and hostile_assertion_known_to_other_coheir)

predicates.coheir_ouster_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim that one co-heir’s rights were extinguished by another co-heir’s ouster.
predicates.hostile_title_openly_asserted: The co-heir in possession openly asserted a title hostile to the other co-heir.
predicates.exclusive_possession_and_enjoyment: The co-heir in possession exclusively possessed and enjoyed the property or its benefits against the other co-heir.
predicates.hostile_assertion_known_to_other_coheir: The hostile assertion was brought to the knowledge of the other co-heir.

members.legal_issue: A plea of adverse possession fails when the claimant previously asserted a right as a co-owner and does not plead and prove when possession became hostile to the owner.
material_facts: The defendant pleaded continuous, open and uninterrupted possession for longer than the prescriptive period and claimed to have perfected title by adverse possession.
In an earlier suit, the defendant claimed to be an adopted son and sought a share in the property, asserting a claim as a co-owner in possession.
The defendant did not plead how or when his possession became hostile to the title of the owners and did not substantiate the adverse-possession plea.
members.legal_principle: A party claiming title by adverse possession must plead and prove how and at what point the possession became hostile to the owner. A prior claim of possession as a co-owner makes it necessary to establish when and how that claim changed into hostile possession. The Court applied the requirements of pleading and proof for adverse possession; it cited no earlier case in deciding this issue.
members.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea was vague, unsubstantiated and without merit.

predicates.appeal_in_civil_property_title_suit: The matter is an appeal in a civil suit seeking a determination of title to property.
predicates.claimant_previously_asserted_coownership: The person claiming adverse possession previously asserted a right to possess the property as a co-owner.
predicates.hostile_possession_start_not_pleaded_or_: The person claiming adverse possession did not plead and prove when and how possession became hostile to the owner.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner’s long exclusive possession does not confer a permanent right against the other co-owners unless the possession is adverse to them.
material_facts: The appellant was found to be a co-owner of the disputed lands.
The appellant relied on long exclusive possession to claim permanent rights.
The appellant had not pleaded adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Once a person is found to be a co-owner, possession, however long, does not confer a right against the other co-owners unless it is adverse to them. The Court noted that no plea of adverse possession had been made. No provision or earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s long exclusive possession did not confer a permanent right in the lands.

predicates.coownership_established: The person in possession is established to be a co-owner of the property.
predicates.long_exclusive_possession: The co-owner has been in exclusive possession of the property for a long time.
predicates.possession_not_adverse_to_other_coowners: The possession has not been adverse to the other co-owners.
predicates.no_permanent_right_acquired_by_possessio: The possession does not confer a permanent right against the other co-owners.

members.legal_issue: Possession held under an arrangement between co-sharers does not establish adverse possession in the circumstances of the dispute.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed to have acquired title by adverse possession through long possession.
The possession was under an arrangement between the co-sharers.
No issue on adverse possession was framed, no trial-court finding was recorded, and the point was not included in the grounds of appeal to the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that possession under an arrangement between co-sharers, in the circumstances described, does not establish adverse possession. It cited no provision or earlier case for this point.
members.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea had no substance and was rightly rejected because possession under the arrangement between co-sharers did not give rise to adverse possession in these circumstances.

predicates.coownership_partition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns partition of property held by co-owners.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_made: A claimant asserts that possession has acquired title by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_under_coowner_arrangement: The possession was held under an arrangement between the co-owners.

members.legal_issue: A co-heir’s possession becomes adverse to another co-heir only when the required ouster is established.
material_facts: The parties were found to be agnatic relations of the same degree and co-heirs of the deceased owner.
One co-heir obtained possession after suing alone on a claim of exclusive title, and he alone enjoyed the properties and their profits.
The other co-heir did not participate in the earlier suit and remained silent about his asserted right.
The court considered that the circumstances might support an inference of ouster, but declined to decide the appeal on that ground.
members.legal_principle: Possession by one co-heir is presumed to rest on the joint title and does not become adverse merely because that co-heir has sole possession or a secret hostile intention. Ouster requires an open assertion of hostile title and exclusive possession and enjoyment to the knowledge of the excluded co-heir; the burden rests on the person claiming to displace the co-heir’s title. The court relied on Corea v. Appuhamy, N. Varada Pillai v. Jeevarathnammal, Culley v. Deod Taylerson, and Govindrao v. Rajabai.
members.conclusion: A co-heir’s possession is ordinarily treated as possession for all co-heirs. To establish adverse possession against another co-heir, the claimant must prove an open assertion of hostile title together with exclusive possession and enjoyment to the other co-heir’s knowledge. The court did not decide whether ouster was established on these facts.

rule.if: coheir_adverse_possession_claim and hostile_title_openly_asserted and exclusive_possession_and_enjoyment and other_coheir_knew

predicates.coheir_adverse_possession_claim: A person claiming adverse possession seeks to defeat another person’s title as a co-heir.
predicates.hostile_title_openly_asserted: The co-heir in possession openly asserted a title hostile to the other co-heir’s title.
predicates.exclusive_possession_and_enjoyment: The co-heir in possession held and enjoyed the property exclusively.
predicates.other_coheir_knew: The other co-heir knew of the hostile assertion and exclusive possession and enjoyment.

members.legal_issue: A co-heir’s title is not displaced by adverse possession when the period of the claimant’s actual adverse possession is insufficient, without counting the receiver’s earlier possession.
material_facts: The property was held by a receiver before the person asserting adverse possession obtained actual possession.
The later possessor obtained actual possession from the receiver and thereafter possessed the property.
The suit to recover the co-heir’s share was filed less than twelve years after the later possessor obtained actual possession.
The court assumed, without deciding, that the later possession was adverse and amounted to ouster.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent, and limitation cannot run before the claimant has actual possession under a hostile claim and the opposing party can bring an action to vindicate title. The court relied on Secretary of State for India v. Debendra Lal Khan, Radhamoni Debi v. Collector of Khulna, Agency Company v. Short, and Dwijendra Narain Roy v. Joges Chandra De. No particular provision of the Limitation Act was identified in the judgment as the basis for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The respondent did not lose his title by adverse possession and was entitled to the decree. Even assuming the later possession was adverse, it was insufficient in duration, and the receiver’s possession could not be counted toward it.

predicates.coheir_title_displacement_claim: A person seeks to defeat a co-heir’s title by adverse possession.
predicates.claimant_obtained_actual_possession_afte: The person claiming adverse possession obtained actual possession only after a receiver had held the property.
predicates.actual_adverse_possession_period_insuffi: The period of the claimant’s actual adverse possession before the action was insufficient to displace the other co-heir’s title.

members.legal_issue: A co-heir’s right to partition and a share in inherited property is not extinguished by adverse possession merely because another co-heir has possessed the property exclusively, profits were not shared, or a partition notice was left unpursued, without proof of a hostile denial of rights brought to the excluded co-heir’s knowledge for the statutory period.
material_facts: The claimant was established to be the deceased owner’s legally married second wife, and the owner died intestate, leaving her and two sons as heirs.
The courts found that the disputed B-schedule properties were the deceased owner’s self-acquired properties; the daughter had given up her share.
The claimant initially received income from the properties, but the sons later stopped paying her income and dealt with the properties.
The defendants relied on an alleged partition notice from 1955 that was not pursued; the claimant denied sending it, and the defendants did not produce the alleged advocate to prove it.
The claimant learned that properties were being sold and brought the partition suit in 1979.
The defendants did not establish a hostile, open denial of the claimant’s rights that had been brought home to her for the statutory period.
members.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is ordinarily possession for all co-sharers. Exclusive or long possession, or non-participation in profits, does not by itself establish ouster or adverse possession; there must be a hostile, open denial or repudiation of the other co-sharer’s rights brought to that co-sharer’s knowledge for the statutory period. A partition notice left unpursued is not, by itself, enough to extinguish the claimant’s rights. The Court relied on Hardit Singh v. Gurmukh Singh, AIR 1918 PC 1; Varada Pillai v. Jeevarathnammal; Mohaideen Abdul Kadir v. Mohammad Mahaideen Umma; Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash, (1995) 4 SCC 496; Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, AIR 1956 SC 548; Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagadish Kalita, (2004) 1 SCC 271; T.P.R. Palania Pillai v. Amjath Ibrahim Rowther, AIR 1942 Madras 622; and Nirmal Chandra Das v. Mohitosh Das, AIR 1936 Calcutta 106. No statutory provision was cited in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s share was not extinguished by adverse possession. She was entitled to a one-third share in the B-schedule properties and rendition of accounts, and she was also entitled to her share in the A-schedule properties.

rule.if: partition_and_separate_possession_suit and claimant_is_coheir and property_possessed_by_coheirs and partition_notice_left_unpursued and clear_hostile_ouster_not_proved

predicates.partition_and_separate_possession_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition and separate possession of inherited property.
predicates.claimant_is_coheir: The person claiming partition is an heir who holds a share in the property with the other heirs.
predicates.property_possessed_by_coheirs: The other heirs possess or deal with the property as co-heirs.
predicates.partition_notice_left_unpursued: The claimant sent or was alleged to have sent a partition notice but did not pursue it at that time.
predicates.clear_hostile_ouster_not_proved: The other heirs did not prove a hostile and open denial of the claimant’s rights brought to the claimant’s knowledge for the statutory period.

members.legal_issue: Possession by one co-owner is not adverse to another co-owner without an unequivocal, open denial of the other’s title and exclusion of that co-owner.
material_facts: One co-owner possessed the properties.
The other co-owners had been kept from knowing the properties’ true character, and the evidence did not show that they knew of an ouster.
There was no evidence that the possessor openly denied the other co-owners’ title or excluded them from the properties.
members.legal_principle: Possession by one co-owner is presumed to be possession for all co-owners unless it is shown to be hostile to them through denial of their title and exclusion of them. Ouster requires an unequivocal act asserting title and an open denial of the entitled parties’ rights.
members.conclusion: The plea of adverse possession failed.

rule.if: co_owner_adverse_possession_proceeding and one_co_owner_possesses_property and not open_unequivocal_ouster

predicates.co_owner_adverse_possession_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim that one co-owner acquired the property against another by adverse possession.
predicates.one_co_owner_possesses_property: A co-owner possesses property also claimed by other co-owners.
predicates.open_unequivocal_ouster: The possessor openly and unequivocally denies the other co-owners’ title and excludes them from the property.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s title is not extinguished by adverse possession where the alleged adverse possession is effectively interrupted by the co-sharer’s acts of possession during the claimed period.
material_facts: The dispute concerned alleged adverse possession by one co-sharer against another, whose possession in law was also the possession of the other co-sharer unless ouster was established.

The alleged adverse possessor openly asserted a claim to the whole house and enjoyed it, but the other co-sharer stayed in the house on different occasions and openly asserted his title in a municipal survey entry made after that claim.
The other co-sharer’s evidence of staying in the house was corroborated, and his assertion of title and acts of possession were accepted by the trial court and the High Court Single Judge.
The Supreme Court held that these acts interrupted the continuity and exclusiveness of the alleged adverse possession; the other co-sharer’s stays were not merely visits as a guest.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be adequate, continuous, and exclusive, and the burden of proving those characteristics rests on the adverse possessor: Kuthali Moothavar v. Paringati Kunharankutty, (1921) 48 I.A. 395 at 404. Between co-sharers, adverse possession requires ouster through an open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment to the other co-sharer’s knowledge: Lakshmi Reddy v. Lakshmi Reddy, [1957] S.C.R. 195 at 202, and Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, A.I.R. 1956 S.C. 548. Once possession has become adverse by ouster, a mere assertion of joint title does not interrupt it; effective re-entry or resumption of possession is required: Wuntakal Yalpi Chenabasavana Gowd v. Y. Mahabaleshwarappa, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 131 at 138. A mere stay as a guest is insufficient: Ammakannu Ammal v. Naravanaswami Mudaliar, A.I.R. 1923 Mad. 633. Acts of possession by the title holder may nevertheless interrupt the continuity or exclusiveness required for adverse possession.
members.conclusion: The alleged adverse possession did not extinguish the co-sharer’s title, and the Supreme Court restored the decree recognizing that title.

predicates.co_sharer_adverse_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns one co-sharer’s claim to have acquired another co-sharer’s title through adverse possession.
predicates.other_co_sharer_claimed_exclusive_hostil: One co-sharer claimed exclusive possession of the property and asserted a hostile claim against the other co-sharer.
predicates.title_holder_effectively_reentered_or_re: The co-sharer whose title was challenged effectively re-entered the property or resumed possession during the claimed period.
predicates.title_holder_stayed_and_openly_asserted_: The co-sharer whose title was challenged stayed in the property and openly asserted ownership during the claimed period.
predicates.co_sharer_title_not_extinguished_by_adve: The co-sharer’s title remains unextinguished by the other co-sharer’s adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer cannot obtain a perpetual injunction against another co-sharer, or a transferee from that co-sharer, merely by claiming possession of jointly owned property without proving exclusion and ouster.
material_facts: The suit property formed part of land inherited by several brothers.
The defendants had purchased the suit land from one co-sharer, while the plaintiffs were the sons of another co-sharer.
The plaintiffs sought a perpetual injunction and claimed possession, but the lower courts found that they had not proved exclusive possession to the exclusion of the other co-sharers.
The plaintiffs did not establish a denial of the other co-sharers’ rights to their knowledge followed by exclusion and ouster for the statutory period.
members.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is possession by all and is not adverse to the others unless the person in possession denies their rights to their knowledge and exclusion and ouster follow for the statutory period. A purchaser from a co-sharer steps into the vendor’s shoes and may defend the vendor’s title and possession. The Court relied on Mohammad Baqar & Ors. v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi & Ors. (AIR 1956 SC 548); it cited no specific statutory provision.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not entitled to an injunction against the purchasers, who had stepped into the shoes of their co-sharer vendor and could defend their title and possession.

rule.if: injunction_suit and claimant_is_cosharer and defendant_is_transferee_from_cosharer and not ouster_proved

predicates.injunction_suit: The proceeding seeks an injunction concerning possession of property.
predicates.claimant_is_cosharer: The claimant holds an interest in the property as a co-sharer.
predicates.defendant_is_transferee_from_cosharer: The defendant acquired the relevant interest from another co-sharer.
predicates.ouster_proved: The claimant establishes a denial of the other co-sharers’ rights to their knowledge followed by exclusion and ouster for the statutory period.
predicates.injunction_unavailable: The claimant is not entitled to the injunction against the defendant.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s possession becomes adverse to another co-sharer only upon a sufficiently clear ouster, and prolonged possession or municipal mutation alone does not establish ouster.
material_facts: The defendants claimed long and uninterrupted possession and asserted that one predecessor had possessed the property exclusively.
The parties’ predecessor interests may have remained co-sharers because it was unresolved whether the property had been partitioned by metes and bounds.
The defendants did not specifically plead when possession became adverse to the other co-sharers, and the High Court made no finding identifying when adverse possession began.
The High Court relied on municipal records, non-payment of rent or taxes, and an asserted open ouster, but did not explain how these established denial of the other co-sharers’ title.
The Supreme Court observed that possession by one co-sharer is ordinarily on behalf of all, and that possession might have been permissive or based on an arrangement.
members.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is presumed to be on behalf of the others. Ouster requires denial of the other co-sharers’ title, hostile animus, long and uninterrupted possession, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to their knowledge. Mere non-participation in rent or profits, long possession, or mutation in one co-sharer’s name is insufficient by itself. The Court relied on Karbalai Begum v. Mohd. Sayeed, Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil v. Balwant, Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash, P. Lakshmi Reddy, Mohd. Zainulabudeen v. Sayed Ahmed Mohideen, and Darshan Singh v. Gujjar Singh.
members.conclusion: The findings that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession could not stand: the record did not establish the clear ouster and hostile possession required against co-sharers. The judgment was set aside and the matter remitted for fresh consideration; the Supreme Court did not finally determine title.

rule.if: co_sharer_title_dispute and one_co_sharer_in_possession and not clear_hostile_ouster

predicates.co_sharer_title_dispute: The dispute concerns title to property claimed by people whose interests may be those of co-sharers.
predicates.one_co_sharer_in_possession: One co-sharer or that co-sharer’s predecessor possessed the commonly claimed property.
predicates.clear_hostile_ouster: The possessor clearly denied the other co-sharers’ title and openly exercised exclusive ownership to their knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A dispossessed co-owner’s later assertion of joint title does not interrupt established adverse possession unless possession changes or the possessing co-owner acknowledges the other’s title or ends the exclusive possession.
material_facts: The father’s earlier acts as guardian had placed the property in the lessee’s possession on behalf of the minor, excluding the father.
The father later executed a mortgage in his personal capacity, asserting his own interest as co-owner.
The property remained in the lessee’s possession, and the father did not re-enter or resume possession.
The minor did not acknowledge the father’s title or discontinue exclusive possession.
members.legal_principle: Once a co-sharer’s possession has become adverse by ouster, a mere assertion of joint title by the dispossessed co-sharer does not stop the running of adverse possession. Interruption requires effective re-entry or resumption of possession, acknowledgment of the dispossessed co-owner’s title by the possessor, or discontinuance of exclusive possession. A mental change or assertion unaccompanied by a change in possession is insufficient. No earlier cases were cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The father’s later assertion of joint title did not interrupt the minor’s adverse possession; the High Court’s contrary conclusion could not be sustained.

rule.if: coowner_adverse_possession_dispute and adverse_possession_already_established and dispossessed_coowner_makes_later_title_assertion and no_effective_reentry and possessor_does_not_acknowledge_title and exclusive_possession_continues

predicates.coowner_adverse_possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns adverse possession claimed by one co-owner against another.
predicates.adverse_possession_already_established: The possessing co-owner has already excluded the other co-owner and begun adverse possession.
predicates.dispossessed_coowner_makes_later_title_a: The dispossessed co-owner later asserts a right to joint ownership.
predicates.no_effective_reentry: The dispossessed co-owner does not re-enter or otherwise effectively resume possession.
predicates.possessor_does_not_acknowledge_title: The possessing co-owner does not acknowledge the dispossessed co-owner’s title.
predicates.exclusive_possession_continues: The possessing co-owner’s exclusive possession continues.

members.legal_issue: A claim of adverse possession against other heirs is not established when the claimant pleads the duration of exclusive possession but fails to plead acts showing when that possession became hostile and notorious to the exclusion of the other heirs.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a duration of exclusive possession of the house against the other heirs.
The written statement did not identify an overt act or a point in time from which possession became hostile and notorious to the other heirs' exclusion.
Municipal register entries were offered as evidence, but the court held that evidence could not substitute for the necessary pleadings.
The High Court reversed the lower courts' finding for the claimant, and the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with that reversal.
members.legal_principle: A claimant relying on adverse possession must plead facts showing that possession became hostile and notorious, openly and to the exclusion of the other heirs, from an identifiable point in time. Evidence, including municipal register entries, cannot substitute for pleadings, which form the foundation of a litigant's claim. The court cited no provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The adverse-possession claim failed because the pleadings did not state the hostile and notorious acts on which it depended, and the High Court's reversal was upheld.

rule.if: adverse_possession_title_dispute and claim_against_coheirs and exclusive_possession_duration_pleaded and pleading_omits_hostile_overt_acts

predicates.adverse_possession_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to establish title by adverse possession.
predicates.claim_against_coheirs: The claimant asserts adverse possession against other heirs to the property.
predicates.exclusive_possession_duration_pleaded: The claimant pleads how long the claimant remained in exclusive possession.
predicates.pleading_omits_hostile_overt_acts: The claimant's pleading does not identify acts showing when possession became hostile and notorious to the other heirs' exclusion.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s non-participation in the rents and profits of jointly held land does not by itself amount to ouster or give another co-sharer title by adverse possession.
material_facts: The parties were recorded as co-bhumidars and had held a joint khewat.
The defendants managed the land while the plaintiff lived elsewhere; she said they gave her shares from time to time and assured her that her interest would be protected.
The defendants claimed separate occupation, but the District Judge found no evidence that the plaintiff had not received a share of the produce and no clear ouster was established.
members.legal_principle: A co-sharer’s mere non-participation in rents and profits does not constitute ouster sufficient to establish the other co-sharer’s title by adverse possession. In that situation, the co-sharer in possession is treated as a constructive trustee for the other co-sharer, whose possession is protected through that relationship. No particular statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The defendants’ possession was in law also the plaintiff’s possession. Mere non-participation in rents and profits did not oust her or give the defendants title by adverse possession; the defendants’ position was also in the nature of constructive trustees for her.

rule.if: co_sharer_possession_dispute and joint_co_ownership and not clear_ouster

predicates.co_sharer_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns a co-owner’s claimed right to possession of jointly held land against another co-owner.
predicates.joint_co_ownership: The parties held the land jointly as co-owners.
predicates.clear_ouster: The co-owner in possession clearly excluded the other co-owner from possession.

members.legal_issue: A limitation defence based on adverse possession fails when it was abandoned at an earlier appellate stage or when the party asserting it has not adequately pleaded when and how adverse possession began.
material_facts: The trial court found the suit within time, and the parties did not contest that finding in the intermediate appeal.
The defendants pleaded that adverse possession began in 1954, but that position depended on their unsuccessful claim under a later will.
They did not plead that adverse possession began under the compromise or at a later point, and the sale deed did not state that possession was delivered.
The mother retained and exercised her right to the first floor; the claimant brought the partition suit within the relevant limitation period and challenged the purchasers’ claimed rights.
members.legal_principle: A party cannot re-agitate a plea abandoned at an appellate stage. Adverse possession is a mixed question of fact and law, and the party asserting it must plead with sufficient clarity when the possession became adverse and the nature of that possession. A party asserting adverse possession has no equities in its favour and bears the burden of establishing the necessary facts.
members.conclusion: The limitation defence was rejected. The defendants could not re-agitate the unchallenged finding that the suit was timely, and their adverse-possession plea was not sufficiently pleaded or established.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding seeks partition or possession of property held in common.
predicates.limitation_finding_not_contested_in_inte: A finding that the suit is within time was not contested at an intermediate appellate stage.
predicates.adverse_possession_start_not_adequately_: The party asserting adverse possession has not clearly pleaded when and how that possession became adverse.
predicates.claimant_sued_within_limitation_period: The claimant brought the relevant claim within the applicable limitation period.

members.legal_issue: A coparcener’s possession of joint family property does not become adverse to another coparcener without clear and unequivocal proof of an exclusive hostile claim, known to the other member, maintained for the required period.
material_facts: The claimant sought partition after regrant made the lands partible.
The opposing family member relied on mutation and possession as showing exclusive ownership.

Possession could be referred to the family’s lawful joint title, and there was no pleading and proof that the opposing member asserted exclusive hostile title to the claimant’s knowledge or that the claimant acquiesced in it for the statutory period.
members.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 places the burden on the person claiming adverse possession to prove clear and unequivocal hostile possession amounting to a denial of the true owner’s title. Possession referable to lawful title is not adverse. In a Hindu joint family, possession by one member is ordinarily treated as possession on behalf of all; mutation for collection of rent or revenue does not by itself prove a hostile act. The claimant must prove an exclusive hostile assertion to the other member’s knowledge, exclusion from enjoyment, and continuation for the statutory period.
members.conclusion: The opposing member did not acquire title by adverse possession.

predicates.adverse_title_claim_against_coparcener: A person in a family-property dispute claimed ownership by adverse possession against another coparcener.
predicates.possession_traceable_to_joint_title: The possessor’s occupation could be explained by the family’s lawful joint title or possession on behalf of the family.
predicates.no_known_exclusive_hostile_assertion_pro: The claimant did not prove that the possessor clearly asserted exclusive hostile ownership to the claimant’s knowledge and excluded the claimant from enjoyment.
predicates.statutory_period_of_hostile_possession_n: The claimant did not prove that the hostile possession continued for the legally required period.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner’s exclusive possession does not by itself establish ouster or adverse possession against another co-owner.
material_facts: The plaintiff asserted that she had been dispossessed from the property in 1957.
The defendant claimed exclusive possession from 1956, payment of property taxes, and a patta in his name.
The defendant also pleaded hostile animus and exclusive possession, while the plaintiff sought partition as a co-owner.
members.legal_principle: A co-owner’s possession is presumed to be possession for all co-owners. Under P. Lakshmi Reddy v. R. Lakshmi Reddy, the possession must be adverse in continuity, publicity, and extent, and ouster requires an open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment to the knowledge of the other co-owner. Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash identifies hostile animus, long and uninterrupted possession, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to the other co-owner’s knowledge as necessary elements. The court also relied on Syed Shah Ghulam Ghouse Mohiuddin v. Syed Shah Ahmed Mohiuddin Kamisul Quadri.
members.conclusion: Between co-owners, possession is presumed to be on behalf of all, and ouster requires more than sole possession and enjoyment; it requires an open hostile assertion, exclusive possession, and exercise of exclusive ownership to the other co-owner’s knowledge.

predicates.co_owner_partition_case: A co-owner seeks partition of property held in common.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: One co-owner claims that possession has become adverse to another co-owner.
predicates.exclusive_possession_alone: The asserted basis for adversity is exclusive possession without proof of open hostile assertion and exclusion to the other co-owner’s knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A co-heir’s possession defeats another co-heir’s partition and possession claim only when it establishes sustained possession to the other’s exclusion under a hostile claim of title.
material_facts: The claimant and the possessor were co-widows entitled to shares in their deceased husband’s property.
The possessor remained in possession of the property after her husband’s death, but continued paying maintenance to the claimant from the property until 1958.
The possessor sought mutation of her name as an heir and insured some of the properties; the court found no evidence that these acts asserted an absolute title excluding the claimant.
There was no evidence that the possessor asserted hostile, exclusive possession for the limitation period before the partition suit was filed.
members.legal_principle: A co-heir relying on adverse possession must establish possession to the exclusion of the other co-heir and a hostile claim of title for the required limitation period. Applying that principle, seeking mutation as an heir did not show an exclusive claim, insuring property was an act of management rather than proof of ouster, and paying maintenance from the property did not establish exclusion. The judgment cites no statutory provisions or earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The possessor did not establish adverse possession, so the partition and possession suit was not barred by limitation; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.partition_possession_claim_between_cohei: A person claiming a share in property seeks partition and possession against another person who also claims through the same predecessor.
predicates.no_sustained_hostile_exclusion: The possessor did not establish sustained possession excluding the claimant under a hostile claim of title.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner's possession does not establish ouster of another co-owner without a clear, open, hostile assertion of exclusive title brought to the other co-owner's knowledge.
material_facts: The appellant relied on his possession of part of a house and correspondence in which he rejected his sister's claim to a share.
The appellant sought a share for himself, thereby recognizing the interests of other co-owners, and his ouster plea targeted only his sister.
The evidence showed that the appellant possessed the ground floor while another plaintiff possessed the first floor.

The relied-on correspondence asserted that the sister had received benefits and was not entitled to a share, but did not assert that the appellant alone owned the property in a right independent of co-ownership.
members.legal_principle: A co-owner's possession is ordinarily presumed to be on behalf of all co-owners. Ouster requires the elements of adverse possession, including open assertion of hostile title, exclusive possession, and knowledge of the other co-owner. The Court relied on P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy; Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagadish Kalita; Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash; Darshan Singh v. Gujjar Singh; and Mohd. Zainulabudeen v. Sayed Ahmed Mohideen.
members.conclusion: The appellant did not establish ouster of the co-owner and could not defeat her partition claim on that basis.

predicates.partition_suit_between_coowners: The proceeding concerns a claim to partition property among persons who hold or claim co-ownership interests.
predicates.coowner_possession_referable_to_shared_t: The person relying on possession held the property in circumstances consistent with possession as a co-owner.
predicates.hostile_exclusive_title_asserted_to_othe: The possessor openly asserted an exclusive title hostile to the other co-owner and made that assertion known to that co-owner.
predicates.ouster_claim_limited_to_one_while_other_: The possessor claimed to exclude only one co-owner while recognizing or seeking to retain the shares of other co-owners.

members.legal_issue: A court may consider subsequent events only when they are promptly and procedurally brought before it, the opposing party has an opportunity to respond, and they materially affect a party’s right to relief.
material_facts: The tenant relied on events during the litigation, including the landlord’s frequent travel to and residence in Canada, his acquisition of Canadian status and citizenship, and his earlier negotiations to sell the property to the tenant.

The landlord had an opportunity to explain the sale negotiations and stated that he had considered selling because he thought it would be difficult to recover possession, but the negotiations failed and he later decided to live in the property.
There was no evidence that the landlord had tried to sell the property to anyone else, before or after those negotiations.
The Supreme Court found that the events did not undermine the established bona fide need and instead reinforced it.
members.legal_principle: A court may take account of subsequent events if they are brought promptly to its attention, presented through procedures that allow the court to consider them and the opposing party to answer them, and have a material bearing on the right to relief. On the facts, the events relied on did not dent the established need; the landlord’s explanation of the negotiations was reasonable and probable. The Court also relied on Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan for the principle that the landlord is the best judge of residential requirements and courts should not dictate how the landlord should live.
members.conclusion: The subsequent events did not defeat or weaken the landlord’s bona fide requirement for the property.

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking eviction from a residential property on the ground of the landlord’s personal need.
predicates.subsequent_events_presented_for_consider: Events occurring during the proceeding are brought before the court for consideration and the opposing party has an opportunity to address them.
predicates.landlord_explains_sale_negotiations_cred: The landlord gives a reasonable explanation for prior negotiations to sell the property that is consistent with a later genuine decision to occupy it.
predicates.no_evidence_of_other_sale_attempts: There is no evidence that the landlord attempted to sell the property to other prospective purchasers.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may consider a subsequent event that fundamentally affects the claimed right to relief when the event is diligently brought to its attention and procedural fairness is preserved.
material_facts: During the appeal, the tenant applied to submit a partition decree and asserted that the shop had been allotted to a person who was not a party to the eviction proceeding.
The application was supported by an affidavit and the appellate court considered the contention on its merits.
The High Court declined to consider the evidence on the technical ground that no proper application for additional evidence was on record, although such an application was on record.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders and Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhri for the principle that an appellate court may take account of subsequent facts that affect the relief, provided fairness is observed. It also applied Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the application for additional evidence.
members.conclusion: The appellate court could not disregard the application and evidence on that technical ground; the subsequent event had to be considered, subject to a fair opportunity for both sides to address it.

rule.if: appeal_in_pending_eviction_proceeding and subsequent_event_fundamentally_affects_relief and event_diligently_brought_to_court and both_sides_can_address_event

predicates.appeal_in_pending_eviction_proceeding: An appeal is pending in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.subsequent_event_fundamentally_affects_r: An event occurring after the proceeding began could fundamentally affect the claimant’s entitlement to relief.
predicates.event_diligently_brought_to_court: A party brought the subsequent event to the court’s attention with due diligence.
predicates.both_sides_can_address_event: The parties are given a fair opportunity to address the subsequent event and any related evidence.
predicates.appellate_court_must_consider_subsequent: The appellate court must consider the subsequent event when deciding the relief.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may take account of a material change in fact or law that occurs after the decision under appeal when shaping the relief required by justice.
material_facts: The probate was granted after the High Court’s decision but before the Supreme Court decided the appeal.
The grant addressed the defect on which the High Court had relied to find that the appellants lacked standing.
The Supreme Court considered the probate in deciding the appeal and remitted the case for determination of the remaining issues.
members.legal_principle: The Court adopted the principle stated in Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, drawing on Patterson v. State of Alabama, that an appellate court may consider changes in fact or law occurring after the decision under review when determining the disposition justice requires. It also referred to the appellate process as a rehearing in which later events may be considered when moulding relief.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court took the supervening grant of probate into account in deciding the appeal.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The court is reviewing a decision in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.material_change_after_decision_under_rev: A material change in fact or law occurred after the decision being reviewed.
predicates.change_relevant_to_relief: The change bears on the relief or disposition that justice requires.

members.legal_issue: A court deciding a pending case must apply the law as it exists at the time of decision and may hear arguments about the effect of an intervening amendment on an issue already before it.
material_facts: The central legislation had been amended while the appeals and petitions were pending.
The Court invited further argument about how the amended provisions affected the question already under consideration.
A party objected that considering those arguments would allow a new question to be raised.
members.legal_principle: Courts take judicial notice of the law as it exists and must apply current law rather than law as it once was. Allowing the parties to address the effect of an amendment on the same issue does not, for that reason alone, permit a new question to be raised.
members.conclusion: Considering the effect of the amended law on the existing issue did not amount to allowing a new question; the Court was required to apply the law as it then existed.

predicates.pending_case_involves_existing_issue: A case is pending before a court on an issue already placed before it.
predicates.governing_law_changed_before_decision: The law relevant to that issue changes before the court decides the case.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may permit and consider a local commissioner's report of a material subsequent change in premises, provided the change is relevant to the relief and the parties receive fair treatment.
material_facts: During the long-pending revision, the landlord alleged that the shop's roof had fallen and that the premises had further deteriorated, and sought a local commissioner.
The commissioner inspected the premises and reported a hole in the roof, decayed supports and damaged planks, and substantial cracks in two walls.
The tenant objected to the report and sought another commissioner, but did not ask the High Court for an opportunity to lead evidence to contradict the report.
The Supreme Court noted that a commissioner could report the premises' existing condition but could not establish who caused the damage.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, a revisional court may consider relevant subsequent facts that bear directly on the issue or relief. Courts should assess the material bearing of the event and act cautiously, ensuring fairness and refusing to admit later events where they are used to delay proceedings, harass another party, or pursue an ulterior motive. Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders and Ramesh Kumar v. Kesho Ram support taking cautious cognizance of material subsequent events, subject to fairness. A local commissioner may report the existing physical condition of premises, but not who caused that condition.
members.conclusion: The High Court did not exceed its revisional jurisdiction by permitting the commissioner's report to be placed on the record and relying on it to assess the shop's condition.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_revision and material_subsequent_change_alleged and change_bears_on_relief and commissioner_reports_existing_condition and party_had_fair_opportunity_to_object

predicates.rent_control_eviction_revision: The proceeding is a revision in an eviction dispute governed by rent-control law.
predicates.material_subsequent_change_alleged: A party alleges a change in the premises after the proceeding began that could materially affect the dispute.
predicates.change_bears_on_relief: The alleged change is relevant to the issue or relief the court must decide.
predicates.commissioner_reports_existing_condition: A local commissioner reports the premises' physical condition at the time of inspection, rather than who caused it.
predicates.party_had_fair_opportunity_to_object: The opposing party has an opportunity to challenge the commissioner's report.

members.legal_issue: A court may take material changes occurring after litigation began into account when deciding entitlement to relief or how relief should be moulded.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned an eviction claim based on the landlord’s alleged bona fide need.
After the eviction petition began, the landlord relied on changes in his family’s circumstances, including his son’s cardiac problems, the births of grandchildren and another son’s marriage.
The High Court considered those subsequent events while deciding the landlord’s revision petition.
members.legal_principle: Although rights and obligations are ordinarily assessed as at the commencement of litigation, a court may consider material subsequent events to promote substantial justice, subject to other legal or equitable circumstances. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhari, Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders, and Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad.
members.conclusion: A court may cautiously consider material subsequent changes of fact or law while litigation remains pending if they affect entitlement to relief or the manner in which relief should be moulded.

rule.if: appellate_or_revisional_proceeding and litigation_pending and subsequent_change_material_to_relief and change_brought_diligently

predicates.appellate_or_revisional_proceeding: The matter is being considered in an appeal or revision.
predicates.litigation_pending: The underlying litigation remains pending when the later event is raised.
predicates.subsequent_change_material_to_relief: A factual or legal change after the litigation began bears materially on entitlement to relief or the form of relief.
predicates.change_brought_diligently: A party brings the later change to the court’s attention diligently.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising appellate jurisdiction may take account of material events that occur after proceedings begin when shaping relief.
material_facts: During the pending rent-control eviction proceedings, the landlord came into possession of another non-residential accommodation in the same town.
The statutory condition for the claimed eviction ground required that the landlord not be occupying a non-residential building in the town.
The later-acquired accommodation was brought to the High Court’s attention and materially affected the landlord’s entitlement to eviction.
members.legal_principle: Although entitlement to relief is ordinarily assessed as of the institution of proceedings, a court may—and in appropriate cases must—cautiously consider subsequent events that materially affect the right to relief or the way relief should be moulded, provided fairness to both sides is preserved. Procedure is the handmaid of justice, and this power is not confined to the trial court. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, which referred to Patterson v. State of Alabama and Minnesota v. National Tea Co. The later accommodation was material under section 10(3)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to consider the subsequent event in deciding the eviction claim.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and material_post_filing_event and event_brought_to_court and fairness_preserved

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.material_post_filing_event: A fact arose after the proceeding began that materially affects entitlement to relief or the form of relief.
predicates.event_brought_to_court: A party brought the subsequent event to the court’s attention.
predicates.fairness_preserved: The parties are afforded fairness in the court’s consideration of the subsequent event.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal may take account of intervening facts and legislative changes when moulding the relief.
material_facts: The decree under appeal had been made before the relevant legislative change took effect.
The claimant's appeal remained pending before the Supreme Court when the change took effect.
The Supreme Court had seisin of the case on appeal and considered the effect of the intervening change on the relief.
members.legal_principle: An appeal is in the nature of a rehearing, and an appellate court may consider facts and events arising after the decree, including legislative changes, when moulding relief. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar v. Keshwar Lal, Shyabuddinsab v. The Gadag-Betgeri Municipal Borough, The King v. The General Commissioner of Income Tax, Mukharjee Official Receiver v. Ramratan Kaur, Dayawati v. Inderjit, Mohanlal Jain v. His Highness Maharaja Shri Man Singh, and Amerjit Kaur v. Pritam Singh. It distinguished Nand Kishore Marwah v. Samundri Devi.
members.conclusion: The Court was competent to apply the legislative change while deciding the pending appeal, rather than assessing the decree only under the law as it stood when the lower court decided the case.

predicates.appeal_pending_after_decree: A party appealed a decree, leaving the case pending before an appellate court.
predicates.intervening_law_changed_before_appeal_de: A legislative change took effect after the decree and before the appellate court decided the appeal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may permit amendment of pleadings to address a change in law affecting a pending proceeding, while giving the opposing party an opportunity to respond.
material_facts: While the Letters Patent appeal was pending, the law applicable to the eviction suit had changed retroactively.
The landlord sought and obtained leave to amend the plaint to address the change.
The tenant filed an additional written statement in response to the amended plaint.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the approach in B. Banerjee v. Anita Pan, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 774, for working out the mechanics of applying the retroactive amendment to pending litigation. It also referred to Order 6, Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, under which amendment may be permitted at a stage that can include an appeal or second appeal.
members.conclusion: The court hearing the Letters Patent appeal could permit amendment of the pleadings and give the opposing party an opportunity to answer the amended case.

predicates.pending_appeal_affected_by_change_in_law: An appeal was pending when a change in law affected the case.
predicates.pleadings_need_adjustment_to_address_tha: A party's existing pleadings did not address matters made relevant by the change in law.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may allow a pleading amendment based on a material event occurring after the suit began when the event gives rise to a fresh claim and allowing the amendment is just and can shorten the litigation.
material_facts: During the appeal, the person who had held a limited estate died.
The appellant claimed that he was the deceased person’s next reversioner and sought to amend his written statement to assert a right arising on her death.
The asserted claim could not have defeated the respondent’s claim during the deceased person’s lifetime, and the death gave rise to a fresh cause of action.
Allowing the amendment could shorten the litigation; the respondent was to be given reasonable time to reply and present any new plea.
members.legal_principle: A suit is ordinarily tried on the cause of action existing when it was instituted, but a court, including an appellate court, may take notice of subsequent events and grant relief in changed circumstances where the original relief has become inappropriate, where noticing the change will shorten litigation, or where it is necessary to do complete justice. The Court relied on Rai Charan Mandal v. Biswanath Mandal.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the amendment, directed that the case return to the trial court for evidence and findings on the new plea and any reply, and permitted the respondent to raise a plea based on later-acquired rights.

rule.if: appeal_pending and material_event_after_suit_filing and event_created_fresh_claim and amendment_facilitates_justice_or_shortens_litigation

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the suit is pending when the application to amend is made.
predicates.material_event_after_suit_filing: A material event affecting the parties’ rights occurs after the suit is filed.
predicates.event_created_fresh_claim: The later event gives the party seeking amendment a claim that was not available before the event.
predicates.amendment_facilitates_justice_or_shorten: Allowing the amendment is just or is likely to shorten the litigation.
predicates.appellate_court_may_allow_pleading_amend: The appellate court may permit the party to amend a pleading to raise the claim arising from the later event.

members.legal_issue: A court may take account of a subsequent event that materially affects relief while litigation is pending, provided fairness to both sides is preserved.
material_facts: The building reached the age threshold for rent-control protection after the eviction suit was filed but before the litigation concluded.
The tenant brought the building’s changed status and the resulting claim for protection to the court’s attention.
The case was remanded so the parties could address the amounts due and the tenant could meet the conditions for protection.
members.legal_principle: In Pasupati Venkateswarlu v. Motor and General Traders, the Court held that a court may, and in appropriate cases must, take cautious account of events after a proceeding begins when they fundamentally affect the right to relief or how relief should be moulded, provided fairness to both sides is observed. The Court applied that principle here.
members.conclusion: The court could and should take account of the building reaching the relevant age during the litigation, subject to scrupulous fairness to both sides.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_pending and subsequent_event_materially_affects_relief and subsequent_event_brought_to_court and fairness_to_both_sides_preserved

predicates.eviction_proceeding_pending: A court proceeding concerning eviction remains unresolved.
predicates.subsequent_event_materially_affects_reli: An event after the proceeding began changes the parties’ entitlement to relief or how that relief should be shaped.
predicates.subsequent_event_brought_to_court: A party brings the later event to the court’s attention while the proceeding is pending.
predicates.fairness_to_both_sides_preserved: The court gives both sides a fair opportunity to address the later event and its consequences.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may consider later developments that are genuine, relevant, and important to deciding the dispute or preventing injustice.
material_facts: In the appeals, competent authorities and courts had made findings that the claimant was not the asserted adopted heir and that the adoption document was forged or fabricated.
The findings went to the basis of the claimant’s asserted rights in the land, and the claimant did not effectively deny the existence of the orders recording them.
members.legal_principle: Relevant and genuine subsequent facts may be considered at the appellate stage when necessary to decide the issues effectively, achieve substantial justice, or prevent a miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on competent judicial and statutory authorities’ orders concerning the asserted adoption and entitlement; it cited no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The later developments could and should be considered at the appellate stage, and they were sufficient to disentitle the claimant from relief and to dismiss the appeals.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party appealed a decision concerning its claimed rights in property.
predicates.later_authoritative_findings_undermine_c: Competent adjudicative bodies later made findings that undermine the factual basis of the appealing party’s claimed entitlement.
predicates.findings_not_effectively_denied: The appealing party did not effectively deny the existence of the later findings or orders.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may permit a party to amend its pleadings to raise a new plea even when the material needed to decide that plea is not already before the court.
material_facts: The Government sought to amend its written statement during the appeal to plead res judicata based on a separate suit.
The Government explained that it had not sought amendment earlier because an appeal in the separate suit was pending, and it sought amendment soon after that decision was affirmed.
The High Court accepted the explanation and permitted the amendment.
members.legal_principle: There is no bar against an appellate court permitting an amendment to pleadings to raise a new plea. The court applies the usual principles governing amendments, including considering delay and the reason for seeking amendment at the appellate stage. The fact that material needed to decide the plea is not already before the court is relevant but is not, by itself, a prohibition against amendment.
members.conclusion: The appellate court acted within its discretion in permitting the amendment, and there was no ground to interfere with that decision.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and amendment_sought_to_raise_new_plea and delay_reasonably_explained and application_made_promptly

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is being considered by a court hearing an appeal.
predicates.amendment_sought_to_raise_new_plea: A party asks to amend its pleadings in order to raise a plea not previously pleaded.
predicates.delay_reasonably_explained: The party gives a reason accepted by the court for not seeking the amendment earlier.
predicates.application_made_promptly: The party seeks the amendment soon after the circumstance explaining the earlier delay ends.

members.legal_issue: A court may take account of a subsequent event affecting relief only when the event meets the requirements for changing the relief and is presented through fair and proper procedure.
material_facts: The tenant relied on proceedings by a public authority that began after the eviction suit was filed.
The authority’s resumption order was set aside, and the record did not establish that the proceedings had reached a final outcome preventing the landlord from defending the allotment.
The tenant mentioned the subsequent factual event in an affidavit but did not seek an amendment to the pleadings or ask the Court to mould or deny relief on that basis.
The event was not presented in a way that gave the landlord an opportunity to meet the case sought to be raised.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, parties’ rights are determined as they stood when the suit was instituted. A court may consider a subsequent event if the original relief has become inappropriate or unavailable, considering the event would shorten litigation and promote complete justice, and the event is promptly brought to the court in accordance with procedural rules without unfair surprise. Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders recognises this power subject to caution and fairness. When the event is a disputed fact, it should ordinarily be introduced by amendment under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Messrs. Trojan & Co. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar and Sri Mahant Govind Rao v. Sita Ram Kesho support the rule that relief must be founded on the pleadings. Chhote Khan v. Mohammad Obedulla Khan explains the exceptional nature of considering later events, particularly at the appellate stage.
members.conclusion: The Court would not take notice of the subsequent factual event to impair the eviction judgment, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_against_eviction_decree and subsequent_factual_event_relied_on and (not relief_made_inappropriate_or_unavailable or not event_would_shorten_litigation_and_promote_complete_justice or not event_presented_promptly_and_procedurally_fairly)

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree granting eviction.
predicates.subsequent_factual_event_relied_on: A party relies on a factual event that occurred after the suit began as a reason to change the relief.
predicates.relief_made_inappropriate_or_unavailable: The later event has made the relief originally claimed inappropriate or impossible to grant.
predicates.event_would_shorten_litigation_and_promo: Considering the later event would shorten the litigation and enable complete justice between the parties.
predicates.event_presented_promptly_and_procedurall: The party brought the event promptly through proper procedure and in a manner that gives the opposing party a fair chance to respond.

members.legal_issue: A court that allows an amendment to pleadings must give the opposing party a fair opportunity to answer and contest the amended plea before deciding it.
material_facts: The High Court allowed an amendment seeking a higher interest rate while disposing of the appeal on the same day.
No amended pleading was filed and the defendants were not given an opportunity to contest the amended claim.
The decree awarded interest at a rate exceeding even the rate sought in the permitted amendment.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings to determine the real questions in controversy, but the opposing party must be allowed to respond and the court must decide the contested issue. J. Jermons v. Aliammal held that a new plea cannot be raised without amendment, a reasonable opportunity for further pleadings, and an opportunity to adduce evidence.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s award of interest beyond the original claim was illegal and unsustainable because the amended plea had not been contested and was decided without a fair opportunity to respond.

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal in a civil suit.
predicates.amended_plea_allowed: The court permitted a party to amend a plea in its pleadings.
predicates.opposing_party_not_given_opportunity: The opposing party was not given a reasonable opportunity to answer the amended plea and contest it.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may account for material subsequent events when deciding whether the relief claimed has become inappropriate, and may mould relief to achieve complete justice while respecting procedural fairness.
material_facts: During the suits, an interim order permitted construction on the condition that five flats be kept reserved subject to the outcome of the litigation.
A later interim order continued the restriction against creating third-party rights in the reserved flats.
The appellants proceeded with construction knowing that the rights to the reserved flats remained subject to the litigation, and obtained benefits from other flats in the building.

By the time of the appeals, the tenancy transfer and the replacement lease on which the construction depended had been held invalid, and the municipal landlord had acquired the remaining portions of the property.
The respondents claimed a 6/15 share; the High Court allocated the reserved flats to them, and the Supreme Court found no specific contrary submission undermining that share determination.
members.legal_principle: Although rights are ordinarily assessed as at the institution of the suit, a court may take cautious cognizance of subsequent events that materially affect entitlement to relief or the way relief should be moulded, provided fairness to both sides is maintained. Relief may be moulded where subsequent events make the original relief inappropriate, taking account of the changes would shorten litigation or enable complete justice, and the events are brought to the court's attention promptly and in accordance with procedural rules. The Court relied on Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor and General Traders (1975), Ramesh Kumar v. Kesho Ram (1992), Om Prakash Gupta as discussed in Sheshambal v. Chelur Corporation (2010), and Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Choudhury (1941), among other authorities. Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 did not prevent the High Court from moulding relief on that basis.
members.conclusion: The High Court acted within its appellate powers in considering the subsequent events and moulding the relief; the allocation of the five reserved flats to the respondents as representing their share was upheld.

rule.if: first_appeal_in_civil_suit and subsequent_events_materially_changed_the_relief_context and subsequent_events_were_brought_to_the_court_attention and affected_parties_had_fair_opportunity and interim_construction_was_conditional_on_reserved_flats

predicates.first_appeal_in_civil_suit: The proceeding was a first appeal arising from civil suits.
predicates.subsequent_events_materially_changed_the: Events after the suits began materially changed what relief would be appropriate or effective.
predicates.subsequent_events_were_brought_to_the_co: The changed circumstances were placed before the court while the litigation was pending.
predicates.affected_parties_had_fair_opportunity: The parties affected by the proposed relief had a fair opportunity to address the relevant circumstances.
predicates.interim_construction_was_conditional_on_: Construction was allowed during the litigation on condition that specified flats remain reserved subject to its outcome.

members.legal_issue: A court hearing a pending appeal against an eviction order may consider material developments that occurred after the eviction proceeding began and may alter the relief accordingly, even though the order was affirmed below.
material_facts: The tenant’s appeal by special leave was pending when the original landlord died and the business was shifted to a different building.
The landlord’s heirs became co-owners of both the building where the business was being carried on and the building from which eviction had been ordered.
The subsequent ownership and business arrangements affected whether the landlords remained entitled to eviction, and the eviction order had not become final while the appeal was pending.
members.legal_principle: A mere right to take advantage of a statutory provision is not an accrued right, as stated in Abbott v. Minister for Lands and accepted in Kanaya Ram v. Rajender Kumar. Under Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders, a court may, subject to fairness and any contrary legal or equitable circumstances, take cautious notice of post-filing events that fundamentally affect entitlement to relief or how relief should be moulded. That power applies in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court could consider the subsequent developments in the pending appeal and set aside the eviction order; the order did not give the landlords an indefeasible vested right before becoming final and conclusive.

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_order_pending: A party has a pending appeal against an eviction order.

predicates.eviction_order_not_final: The eviction order remains under challenge and has not become final and conclusive.

members.legal_issue: Courts may consider relevant and material events occurring after the commencement of a rent-control proceeding when doing so is fair to both sides.
material_facts: During the eviction proceedings, the alternative floor became vacant on more than one occasion and was let to other occupants.
The later vacancies and lettings were brought to the Supreme Court's attention by affidavit, and both sides addressed the subsequent events.
members.legal_principle: Relying on Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders, Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, and Variety Emporium v. V.R.M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina, the Court held that, to make a remedy just and meaningful in light of current realities, courts may—and in many cases must—take cautious cognizance of later events, provided fairness to both sides is observed. Firm Ram Sewa Hari Ram v. Sain Datt Mal and Abdul Hamid v. Nur Mohammad were also approved.
members.conclusion: The Court may take subsequent events into account cautiously when they are relevant and material and the rules of fairness to both sides are observed.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court may take account of material events occurring after the decision under review when determining the relief to grant.
material_facts: The cultivator died while the writ petition was pending before the High Court.
The cultivator’s legal representatives continued in possession, although any permission granted to the cultivator was limited to his lifetime.
The death affected whether the continuing possession could be treated as authorised.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court may consider facts and events arising after the decision under review when moulding relief. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, 1940 FCR 84, Patterson v. State of Alabama, 294 US 600 (1934), and Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, (1974) 2 SCR 539.
members.conclusion: The Court took account of the death during the pending proceeding and determined the legal effect of the heirs’ continued possession on that basis.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may take account of changes in law occurring during an appeal and adjust the relief to reflect those changes.
material_facts: The appeal remained pending when the earlier rent-control enactment was repealed and a replacement enactment came into force.
The intervening change affected whether statutory protection continued to prevent recovery of possession.
The court could resolve the parties’ dispute in the appeal by considering the law in force when it decided the case.
members.legal_principle: An appeal is in the nature of a rehearing, and the appellate court may consider subsequent changes in fact or law when determining the relief justice requires. The court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, A.I.R. 1941 Federal Court 28, including the observations of Gwyer C.J. and Varadachariar J.
members.conclusion: The appellate court could consider the intervening legislative change and mould the relief accordingly.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may take account of material subsequent events established by admitted or public documentary evidence when reviewing the decision and may mould the relief accordingly.
material_facts: After the trial decree, the competent authority declared that the property was within the applicable land ceiling limits, and the order was later communicated to the vendors.
After the decree, the respondent company was declared sick by the industrial reconstruction body.
The Supreme Court considered both events material, documentary, and almost admitted between the parties.
members.legal_principle: A first appellate court may consider material subsequent events supported by relevant documents and may assess the decision in light of those events or mould the relief. Public documents of the kind identified by the Court need not be formally proved.
members.conclusion: The High Court could receive the relevant documents, take account of the subsequent events when testing the judgment under appeal, and mould the relief as necessary.

members.legal_issue: A limited estate held by a Hindu woman under a bequest for her maintenance is enlarged into absolute ownership when the applicable succession law so provides.
material_facts: The owner’s will gave the woman property for her maintenance and restricted her power to alienate it, with the property to revert to his daughter after the woman’s death.
The woman held the property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
She later sold and gifted property, and the appellant sought possession on the basis of the will’s reversionary provision.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a limited interest held by a Hindu woman in property acquired in recognition of her right to maintenance is enlarged into an absolute estate. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy, which held that a woman in a similar position became absolute owner of the property.
members.conclusion: Section 14(1) enlarged the woman’s limited interest into absolute ownership, so the will’s restriction and reversionary provision did not entitle the appellant to possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: A female Hindu who already held a property right and possessed the property when the succession reform law commenced became its full owner when a partition allotted her share, even where the partition award described her interest as a limited estate.
material_facts: The widow inherited an interest in her husband's property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, and had a pre-existing right to a share.
Before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 commenced, an arbitration award partitioned the property and allotted her specific properties; the award was made a decree.
The award described her interest in the allotted properties as a widow's estate and provided for her physical or constructive possession.
A suit sought to restrain her from alienating the properties on the ground that she remained a limited owner.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1), including its Explanation, gives the widest meaning to possession and acquisition: possession may be actual or constructive, and property may be acquired in any manner, including inheritance or partition. Section 14(2) is an exception to section 14(1), applying when an instrument, decree, order, or award creates an acquisition for the first time without a pre-existing right. The Court applied sections 3(1)–(3) of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, and followed Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veerayya, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 968; S.S. Munnalal v. S.S. Rajkumar, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 418; and Sukhram v. Gauri Shankar, [1968] 1 S.C.R. 476. It also referred to Rangaswami Naicker v. Chinnammal, A.I.R. 1964 Mad. 387, on the purpose of section 14.
members.conclusion: The widow became the full owner of the allotted properties under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Section 14(2) did not apply because the award separated property to which she already had a pre-existing right. The appeal was dismissed.
