members.legal_issue: A limited interest in property given to a Hindu woman in lieu of her pre-existing right to maintenance becomes full ownership when she possesses the property at the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
material_facts: The arbitration reference recognised the widow’s pre-existing right to maintenance and provided for both property and money in settlement of that right.
The award gave her the right to reside in and use the chosen property for life, make certain changes and repairs, and prohibited her from transferring or damaging it.
She chose the Bidasar property and took possession of it under a document confirming her right to reside there and use it.
She possessed the property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
She later executed sale deeds for parts of the property’s nohra.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and its Explanation broadly cover property possessed by a female Hindu and acquired in lieu of maintenance; Section 14(2) is confined to property acquired for the first time without a pre-existing right under an instrument prescribing a restricted estate. Under V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, property allotted in satisfaction of a widow’s pre-existing maintenance right is not a first-time grant. Smt. Gulwant Kaur v. Mohinder Singh, Badri Pershad v. Smt. Kanso Devi, and Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai support the requirement of a lawful vestige of title and the enlargement of a limited interest. Eramma v. Veerupana and Mangal Singh v. Smt. Rattno establish that mere possession without title is insufficient; they do not exclude an interest arising from a pre-existing maintenance right.
members.conclusion: The widow acquired limited ownership rights in the property in recognition of her pre-existing right to maintenance; those rights became full ownership under Section 14(1), and she was entitled to sell the nohra. Section 14(2) did not prevent that result because the property was provided in satisfaction of a pre-existing right, not acquired for the first time without such a right.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu woman who possesses property given in recognition of her right to maintenance acquires full ownership of it even if no separate restricted estate or right to alienate is shown.
material_facts: A husband entrusted land to his wife and stated that its produce would provide for her maintenance.
The correspondence between the spouses established that the land was given in lieu of maintenance.
The wife relied on the land and its produce, and the purchaser sought to restrain her from interfering with possession.
The High Court held that the wife had only been allowed to use the land’s proceeds for day-to-day expenses and had acquired no limited interest in the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with its Explanation, enlarges into full ownership a Hindu woman’s interest in property possessed by her where that possession has a lawful origin, including property acquired in lieu of maintenance. Her pre-existing right to maintenance is sufficient title; she need not establish a further title or prove a separately granted restricted estate. Section 14(2) is an exception and does not govern acquisitions traceable to an antecedent right. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, Badri Pershad v. Kanso Devi, Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, Sellammal v. Nellammal, Santhanam v. Subramanya, and Krishna Das v. Venkayya, and distinguished Eramma v. Verrupanna.
members.conclusion: The land was given to the wife in lieu of maintenance, and her maintenance right was sufficient title for her possession to mature into full ownership. The distinction between day-to-day expenses and maintenance was erroneous; the judgment recognizing her full ownership was restored.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s limited interest in property given to her in lieu of maintenance is enlarged into an absolute estate when she possessed the property as the relevant succession law took effect.
material_facts: The widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance from the joint family.
A family member placed her in possession of the suit property in lieu of maintenance, and the maintenance arrangement gave her a life interest.
She remained in possession of the property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.

The trial court found that the maintenance arrangement recognized her maintenance right and that her will was valid; the High Court reversed on the ground that Section 14(2), rather than Section 14(1), applied.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the issue was fully covered by V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy and followed that decision. Applying Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, it treated a limited interest given in recognition of a pre-existing right to maintenance as one that is enlarged under Section 14(1), rather than excluded from enlargement by Section 14(2).
members.conclusion: The limited interest was enlarged under Section 14(1) into an absolute estate; Section 14(2) did not prevent enlargement. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the trial court’s judgment and decree were restored.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s limited interest in property allotted in satisfaction of a pre-existing right to maintenance becomes an absolute interest when the statutory enlargement of her property rights takes effect.
material_facts: A widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance from her deceased husband’s estate.
Under a compromise decree, she retained a share of her husband’s land in lieu of maintenance, with possession to pass to his adopted son after her death.
The widow later bequeathed the land and died; the adopted son claimed that the decree had left her only a limited interest.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) enlarges a Hindu woman’s limited interest in property possessed by her when that property was acquired in recognition or satisfaction of a pre-existing right to maintenance. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi (1977), which held that property allotted under a compromise in lieu or satisfaction of a maintenance right became the woman’s absolute property when the Act came into force.
members.conclusion: The widow’s interest in the land allotted for maintenance became absolute under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and the adopted son could not recover it on the basis of the compromise decree.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s restricted interest in property she possesses under a recognized existing right is enlarged into absolute ownership when the property is held under that right, rather than acquired under an instrument creating a new and independent title.
material_facts: The widow remained in rightful possession of the disputed property after her husband’s death and continued to possess it after the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The will provided that the husband and his wife would retain ownership, control, and rights over the property during their lives, with the property passing to the named legatee after both had died.
A compromise decree recognized the widow’s ownership and possession under the will; it did not create a new title in her for the first time.
The widow executed sale deeds concerning the property, and the plaintiffs later sued as reversioners for possession, arguing that she had only a restricted interest.
The appeal challenged a decree granting the plaintiffs possession of part of the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, including its Explanation, enlarges property possessed by a female Hindu under a claim, right, or title into full ownership. Under Section 14(2), a restricted estate may remain where an instrument, decree, gift, or other disposition creates an independent and new title for the first time; that exception does not apply where the instrument recognizes or confirms a pre-existing right, including a right to maintenance. The court applied V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy and also referred to Ram Kali v. Choudhri Ajit Shankar and Bhoomireddy Chenna Reddy v. Bhoospalli Pedda Verrapa. It construed the will and compromise decree as recognizing the widow’s ownership and possession, and held that her pre-existing maintenance right also supported the result even if her interest were assumed to be limited.
members.conclusion: The widow’s interest was governed by Section 14(1), not Section 14(2), and any limited interest she had became absolute ownership. She was competent to transfer the property, so the plaintiffs could not recover it on the basis asserted.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired by a Hindu female in lieu of maintenance in recognition of a pre-existing right falls within the enlargement of limited ownership into full ownership, notwithstanding restrictions imposed by the instrument or decree granting it.
material_facts: A partition decree required the male holders to pay yearly maintenance to a widow and entitled her, upon default, to take possession of specified land in lieu of maintenance.
After default, the widow obtained possession of the land under the decree, which restricted her power to alienate it.
The widow later transferred part of the land, and the transfer was challenged as void.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with the Explanation to Section 14(1), require a broad construction of the main provision and a construction of the exception that does not defeat its social purpose. Property acquired in lieu of maintenance is expressly included in the Explanation, and where it recognizes a pre-existing right, Section 14(2) does not apply. The Court followed V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy and agreed with its overruling of Naraini Devi v. Smt. Ramo Devi; it also relied on the principle in Eramma v. Veerupanna and Mangal Singh v. Shrimati Rattno that enlargement requires some existing ownership interest.
members.conclusion: The property acquired in lieu of maintenance was within Section 14(1) and its Explanation; Section 14(2) did not exclude it from the enlargement of her limited interest into full ownership.

members.legal_issue: A restricted interest held by a Hindu woman under a will, decree, or other instrument becomes absolute when it rests on a pre-existing right in the property.
material_facts: In the cases before the Court, Hindu widows received restricted interests in property under wills, compromise decrees, or court orders, including rights connected with maintenance or residence.
The women were in possession or enjoyment of the relevant property when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The women or persons claiming through them later dealt with the property, and remaindermen disputed their authority to do so.
members.legal_principle: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(1), its Explanation, and Section 14(2) must be read as an integral scheme. Section 14(2) is an exception to Section 14(1) and applies to a first-time grant made without a pre-existing right. The Court followed Badri Prasad v. Smt. Kanso Devi, V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddy, and Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, among other consistent authorities. It distinguished Mst. Karmi v. Amru as not deciding the scope of Section 14(1) and (2).
members.conclusion: A restricted interest becomes full ownership under Section 14(1) if the woman’s interest rests on a pre-existing right; Section 14(2) applies only when the property is granted for the first time without such a right. The appeals and special leave petitions were dismissed.

members.legal_issue: The time at which an absolute interest in property vested under a family settlement providing for maintenance during a widow’s lifetime and enjoyment thereafter.
material_facts: A written settlement gave a widow and her daughter possession of land and the right to enjoy its income for maintenance.
The settlement provided that after the widow’s death the daughter and her children would enjoy the property with powers of gift, transfer, and sale.
The daughter died before the widow.
The courts below disagreed about whether the daughter had acquired an absolute interest immediately; the High Court’s Division Bench held that she had not.
members.legal_principle: A document must be construed from its own words; earlier decisions construing other documents do not bind the interpretation of the document at hand. Although the phrase “Pasupu Kumkuma” has been understood to convey an absolute estate (Jagannadha Rao v. Jatmal Madanlal, AIR 1958 Andhra Pradesh 662; Musiligadu v. Nannigadu, (1905) 15 Mad LJ 492; Venkata Rama v. Rajyalakshmi; and Yadeorao v. Vithal, AIR 1952 Nagpur 55), the full terms here deferred the daughter’s absolute enjoyment until the widow’s death. Until then, both women were entitled only to possession and income for maintenance.
members.conclusion: The daughter’s right was initially limited to maintenance and enjoyment of income, and her absolute interest would have arisen only on the widow’s death. Because the daughter died first, she never acquired that absolute interest. The appeal was dismissed and the High Court’s Division Bench decision was upheld.

members.legal_issue: Property allotted to a husband at partition and later possessed by his widow with a right to its income for her maintenance becomes her full property when she has a pre-existing right to maintenance.
material_facts: A family partition allotted the disputed property to the husband and allotted separate properties to the children.
The partition arrangement allowed the wife to reside in the property and, after her husband's death, to take its income.
After her husband's death, the widow exclusively possessed the property and used its income for her maintenance.
The widow's right to maintenance arose from her husband's personal obligation to maintain her.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) applies to property possessed by a female Hindu and includes property acquired in lieu of maintenance. A Hindu woman's right to maintenance is a tangible, pre-existing right against property, and a husband has a personal obligation to maintain his wife. When she is placed in exclusive possession of property with a right to its income for maintenance, the property is presumed to have been given in lieu of maintenance; no express statement to that effect is required. Section 14(1) is to be construed liberally. The Court relied on V. Tulsamma v. Sesha Reddi and Gulwant Kaur v. Mohinder Singh, and treated Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai as consistent with that principle.
members.conclusion: The widow's possession and maintenance rights brought the property within Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and she held it as full owner.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary life interest given to a Hindu wife for her maintenance enlarges into an absolute interest when it recognizes her pre-existing maintenance right and she possesses or enjoys the property.
material_facts: The owner’s will gave his wife lifetime enjoyment of specified property and provided for her use of related facilities.
The wife had a pre-existing right to maintenance from her husband’s property and continued to enjoy the property during her lifetime.
The will’s arrangement was not disputed, and the property was treated as having been given to the wife for her maintenance.
The trial court treated the wife’s interest as limited and recognized a vested remainder in another family member; the High Court held that the wife acquired absolute ownership.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is construed liberally to enlarge a Hindu woman’s limited interest where the property is held under a pre-existing right, including a right to maintenance. Section 14(2) applies to a grant creating a new and independent title for the first time, not to an instrument recognizing a pre-existing right. No express statement that a life interest is granted in lieu of maintenance is necessary where that purpose is established by the circumstances. This follows V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) 3 SCC 99, R.B. S.S. Munnalal v. S.S. Rajkumar, AIR 1962 SC 1493, Nirmal Chand v. Vidya Wanti (1969) 3 SCC 628, Thota Sesharathamma v. Thota Manikyamma (1991) 4 SCC 312, Shakuntala Devi v. Kamla (2005) 5 SCC 390, and Nazar Singh v. Jagjit Kaur (1996) 1 SCC 35. Mst. Karmi v. Amru (1972) 4 SCC 86 did not govern these facts; Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike (2006) 8 SCC 75 was distinguishable because it proceeded on the basis that no pre-existing right existed. Section 30’s recognition of testamentary disposition does not displace the operation of Section 14(1) in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The wife’s limited interest enlarged into an absolute interest; the remainder was extinguished, and she could bequeath the property. The High Court’s decision was correct and the appeal was dismissed.
