members.legal_issue: A female Hindu with a pre-existing interest in property that is partitioned and possessed by her becomes its full owner under the statutory conversion rule, even if the partition award describes her estate as restricted.
material_facts: Under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, the widow had an existing interest in her deceased husband's property and a right to seek partition, although her interest was limited.
An arbitration partition allocated specific properties to her and described her interest as a widow's estate; the award was made a court decree.
She possessed the allotted properties when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
A suit sought to restrain her from alienating the properties on the basis that she remained a limited owner.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) and its Explanation cover property possessed by a female Hindu, including property acquired at partition, and “possessed” includes actual or constructive possession. Section 14(2) is an exception to subsection (1) and applies where property is acquired for the first time under a gift, instrument, decree, order, or award prescribing a restricted estate, without a pre-existing right. Under Sections 3(1)–(3) of the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, the widow had an interest and a right to partition, though that interest was limited before the Hindu Succession Act. The Court relied on Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veerayya on the meaning of possession; S. S. Munna Lal v. S. S. Rajkumar on possession of a share declared by decree; Rangaswami Naicker v. Chinnammal on Section 14(2) preserving restrictions imposed on rights created for the first time; and Sukhram v. Gauri Shankar on conversion of a pre-existing limited interest into full ownership under Section 14(1).
members.conclusion: The widow became the full owner of the allotted properties under Section 14(1); the partition award and decree did not bring the case within Section 14(2) because the allotment gave effect to her pre-existing right.

rule.if: female_property_ownership_dispute and preexisting_interest_in_property and partitioned_to_realize_existing_interest and possessed_when_law_commenced

predicates.female_property_ownership_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a female Hindu's interest in property is full ownership or a restricted estate.
predicates.preexisting_interest_in_property: The female Hindu had an interest in the property before it was allotted to her at partition.
predicates.partitioned_to_realize_existing_interest: The property was allotted to the female Hindu through a partition that gave effect to her existing interest.
predicates.possessed_when_law_commenced: The female Hindu possessed the property, actually or constructively, when the law providing for conversion of her interest came into force.

members.legal_issue: A limited property interest given to a Hindu woman in recognition of a pre-existing right to maintenance becomes her absolute property when she retains a right to possession of that property.
material_facts: The compromise gave the mother a right to reside in the first floor of the house and maintenance, with a higher maintenance payment if she did not reside there.
The right of residence was given in recognition of her pre-existing right to maintenance.
She retained a right to possession of the first floor; the compromise had given the son rights over the rest of the house.
The mother did not give up her right to the first floor, and the evidence showed that she resided there before her death.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, enlarges a Hindu woman’s limited interest into absolute ownership where the property is held in recognition of a pre-existing right. A right to possession need not amount to actual physical occupation. Section 14(1), rather than Section 14(2), applied because the right of residence was in recognition of the pre-existing right to maintenance. The Court relied on V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, (1977) 3 SCC 99, and Mangat Mal v. Punni Devi, (1995) 6 SCC 88.
members.conclusion: The mother became absolute owner of the first floor under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, but did not become owner of the whole house.

predicates.female_hindu_has_limited_property_intere: A Hindu woman holds a limited interest in property.
predicates.interest_recognizes_preexisting_maintena: The interest was given in recognition of her pre-existing right to maintenance.
predicates.right_to_possession_is_retained: The woman retains a right to possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: Property given to a Hindu woman in lieu of maintenance under a post-Act compromise becomes her absolute property when she is placed in possession, despite restrictions in the compromise.
material_facts: A compromise made after the Hindu Succession Act came into force gave the woman land in lieu of maintenance and placed her in possession.
The compromise restricted her ability to sell or mortgage the land and described her interest as limited.
She remained in possession and enjoyment of the land and later sold part of it.
The plaintiffs sought possession on the basis that the woman had only a limited interest in the land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, read with its Explanation, property possessed by a female Hindu includes property acquired in lieu of maintenance and is held by her as full owner. Section 14(2) is confined to property acquired for the first time as a grant without a pre-existing right where the grant's terms prescribe a restricted estate; it does not apply to property acquired in lieu of a pre-existing right to maintenance. Under Section 14(1), a post-Act grant in lieu of maintenance becomes absolute when the woman is placed in possession despite restrictive terms. The Court applied V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, reiterated in later decisions, and referred to Jagannathan Pillai v. Kunjithapadam Pillai and Mangat Mal v. Punni Devi; it distinguished Gumpha v. Jaibai, which concerned property given under a will.
members.conclusion: The land became the woman's absolute property when she was placed in possession, notwithstanding the restrictions in the compromise; the appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed.

predicates.civil_appeal_challenging_limited_estate: A civil appeal challenges a decision treating property held by a woman as only a limited estate.
predicates.hindu_woman_received_property_for_mainte: A Hindu woman received the property in lieu of a right to maintenance.
predicates.woman_was_placed_in_possession: The woman was placed in possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: Property allotted to a Hindu female in satisfaction of her pre-existing right to maintenance is enlarged into full ownership despite restrictions imposed by the allotment instrument.
material_facts: A widow claimed maintenance from joint family property held by her deceased husband's brother, and her claim was decreed.
In execution of the decree, a court-certified compromise allotted property to her in lieu of maintenance, restricted her interest to her lifetime, and prohibited alienation.
She remained in possession of the property when the Hindu Succession Act came into force and later leased and sold portions of it.
The successor to the property sought a declaration that the alienations were not binding beyond her lifetime.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with its Explanation, broadly enlarges a Hindu female's limited interest in property possessed by her, including property acquired in lieu of maintenance. Section 14(2), as an exception to subsection (1), applies to a restricted grant creating a new title for the first time, not an instrument that merely recognises or gives effect to a pre-existing right. A widow's right to maintenance from joint family property is a pre-existing right against property. The Court relied on S.S. Munna Lal v. S.S. Raikumar and Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veeravva for the breadth of subsection (1) and the meaning of possession; Badri Pershad v. Smt. Kanso Devi and Nirmal Chand v. Vidya Wanti for the distinction between a new grant and recognition of a pre-existing right; and Rani Bai v. Shri Yadunandan Ram on the widow's maintenance right.
members.conclusion: The allotment recognised and satisfied the widow's pre-existing right to maintenance, so Section 14(1), read with its Explanation, applied rather than Section 14(2). She became full owner despite the restrictions in the compromise, and the challenge to her alienations failed.

rule.if: appeal_against_limited_estate_ruling and property_given_in_lieu_of_maintenance and maintenance_right_preexisted and female_possessed_property_when_law_changed

predicates.appeal_against_limited_estate_ruling: A party appeals a ruling that a female holds property only for a limited period or purpose.
predicates.property_given_in_lieu_of_maintenance: Property was allotted to a female to satisfy her claim for maintenance.
predicates.maintenance_right_preexisted: The female had a right to maintenance from the property before the instrument allotting it was made.
predicates.female_possessed_property_when_law_chang: The female possessed the property when the law enlarging limited interests came into force.

members.legal_issue: A surviving widow’s land rights became absolute under the later succession laws, requiring her to be recorded as the absolute owner and bhumidar.
material_facts: The widow of the last proprietor was recorded as his widow and had been mutated on the basis of a statement allegedly made before the later succession laws came into force.

When the consolidation authorities decided the dispute, the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act and the Hindu Succession Act had come into force and conferred absolute proprietary rights on the widow.
The widow was still alive when the Supreme Court decided the appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act and the Hindu Succession Act conferred absolute proprietary rights on the widow, so the earlier statement and the view that she held only a life interest could not govern the decision. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The widow was the absolute proprietor of the land and had to be recorded as its absolute owner and bhumidar; the consolidation decision and the High Court judgment were set aside.

predicates.consolidation_writ_appeal: The matter is an appeal from the dismissal of a writ challenging a consolidation decision.
predicates.widow_is_surviving_recorded_spouse: A surviving widow of the last proprietor was recorded in the land records as his widow.
predicates.later_succession_laws_granted_absolute_p: Later succession laws granted the surviving widow absolute proprietary rights in the land.
predicates.widow_must_be_recorded_as_absolute_lando: The surviving widow must be recorded as the absolute owner of the land.

members.legal_issue: A limited interest granted to a dependent widowed daughter in recognition of her pre-existing maintenance right against her father and his estate becomes full ownership under the rule enlarging a female Hindu’s limited interest, rather than remaining restricted under the exception for a grant without a pre-existing right.
material_facts: The daughter was widowed, destitute, dependent on her father, and maintained by him during his lifetime.
She had no property or other source of support, and the record did not show that she could obtain maintenance from her husband’s estate or other specified relatives.
The will gave her a life interest in part of the father’s property and reflected his concern for her maintenance after his death.
The father’s estate passed under the will to other beneficiaries, against whom her maintenance right could operate.
members.legal_principle: Sections 19(1)(a), 21(vi), and 22(2) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 support a widowed daughter’s maintenance rights against her father during his lifetime and against the estate taken by his heirs where she cannot maintain herself from the sources specified by the Act. Under Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a restricted grant in lieu of a pre-existing right is enlarged into full ownership; the exception applies to a grant made for the first time without such a right. V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi and Badri Pershad v. Smt. Kanso Devi are relied on for that interpretation.
members.conclusion: The daughter had a pre-existing right to maintenance against her father during his lifetime and against his estate after his death. The property given to her in lieu of that right became her full property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; Section 14(2) did not apply.

predicates.testamentary_property_dispute: The dispute concerns property given to a beneficiary under a will.
predicates.widowed_beneficiary_is_destitute: The beneficiary is a widowed daughter who is unable to maintain herself and depends on her father for support.
predicates.beneficiary_lacks_other_maintenance_sour: The beneficiary has no earnings or property and cannot obtain maintenance from the other sources relevant to her circumstances.
predicates.grant_recognizes_preexisting_maintenance: The property is given to the beneficiary in recognition of a maintenance right that existed before the will took effect.

members.legal_issue: A limited interest in property given to a woman in lieu of her pre-existing maintenance right becomes absolute when the statutory enlargement of women's property rights applies.
material_facts: A widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance from her husband's estate.
Under a compromise decree, she retained a share of the estate in lieu of maintenance, subject to the agreement that another person would receive possession after her death.
She possessed the share when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
She later bequeathed the share, and the petitioner conceded that the will was genuine and valid.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as applied in V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi, property allotted to a Hindu woman in recognition of her pre-existing right to maintenance became her absolute property despite a restriction in the instrument granting it.
members.conclusion: The widow's interest became absolute under Section 14(1), so the petitioner could not recover the property after her death on the basis of the compromise decree's restriction; the special leave petition was dismissed.

predicates.civil_claim_for_recovery_after_widow_dea: A civil proceeding seeks recovery of property after the death of a woman who had held it.
predicates.property_given_in_lieu_of_preexisting_ma: The woman received the property in recognition or satisfaction of a maintenance right she already had.
predicates.grant_restricted_the_woman_to_a_limited_: The instrument granting the property purported to limit her interest or provide for another person's possession after her death.
predicates.woman_held_property_when_rights_reform_t: The woman possessed the property when the legal reform enlarging women's property rights took effect.

members.legal_issue: Property allotted to a woman in lieu of maintenance and held by her when the succession law commenced became her absolute property under the general enlargement provision rather than remaining a restricted estate under the exception for newly created rights.
material_facts: The woman was allotted the disputed properties in a family settlement in lieu of her claim for maintenance and residence.
The lower courts found that she remained in possession of the properties when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The defendants’ claim that she had surrendered possession in exchange for annual maintenance payments was rejected by the lower courts.
The courts below held that the allotment recognized her pre-existing maintenance right and that she acquired an absolute interest.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) and its Explanation of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property possessed by a Hindu woman and received in lieu of maintenance in recognition of a pre-existing right becomes her absolute property. Section 14(2) does not apply to such an allotment. The Court agreed with the High Court for the reasons given in Civil Appeal No. 1360 of 1968, heard along with this appeal; the judgment also identifies the matter as an appeal concerning Chellammal v. Nellammal.
members.conclusion: The allotment fell under Section 14(1), not Section 14(2), of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; the woman acquired an absolute interest in the properties, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_challenges_womans_property_intere: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a ruling on a woman's interest in property allotted to her.
predicates.property_given_in_lieu_of_maintenance: The property was given to the woman in recognition of her claim to maintenance.
predicates.holder_possessed_property_when_successio: The woman held possession of the property when the succession law commenced.

members.legal_issue: A female Hindu’s limited interest is enlarged into absolute ownership when it rests on a pre-existing right, including a right to maintenance, rather than a new restricted interest created by an instrument.
material_facts: The widow had a pre-existing right to maintenance and, upon her husband’s death while the property remained joint, acquired an interest under the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937.
She asserted rights to the property and sought partition and possession in the earlier suit.
The will, if treated as operative, provided the widow with a life interest and directed that income from the properties be used for her expenses and for specified family purposes.
The widow later entered into a compromise under which she gave up her rights in the properties at issue in favour of the other branch.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 enlarges a female Hindu’s limited interest where the property is possessed under a pre-existing right, including maintenance; Section 14(2) applies to a new and independent restricted grant, not an instrument recognising such a right. Section 3(2) of the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937 gave a widow an interest in joint-family property, and the Court considered the meaning of possession under Section 14(1). It relied on V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, Mst. Karmi v. Amru, Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veeravva, Mangal Singh v. Smt. Rattno, Eramma v. Veerupana, and distinguished Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike.
members.conclusion: Section 14(1), rather than Section 14(2), applied; the widow’s limited interest became absolute, and the compromise by which she gave up her rights supported the other branch’s title.

rule.if: female_property_right_proceeding and pre_existing_maintenance_or_statutory_right and property_possessed_under_claim_of_right and interest_recognises_existing_right

predicates.female_property_right_proceeding: A court is determining the extent of a female Hindu’s interest in property.
predicates.pre_existing_maintenance_or_statutory_ri: The female Hindu had an existing right to maintenance or another legally recognised right in the property before the instrument or event said to limit her interest.
predicates.property_possessed_under_claim_of_right: She possessed or claimed the property under a legally recognisable right, rather than as a mere trespasser.
predicates.interest_recognises_existing_right: The limited interest recognises or provides for an existing right instead of creating an independent new interest subject to restriction.
predicates.limited_interest_enlarged_to_absolute_ow: The female Hindu’s limited interest becomes absolute ownership.

members.legal_issue: A party may amend a written statement to explain an earlier admission and advance an inconsistent plea, and allowing such an amendment is not a material irregularity where the agreement’s terms remain open for explanation in evidence.
material_facts: In a suit for a perpetual injunction, the defendants’ written statement admitted that they had entered into an agreement of sale, while also asserting that possession had not been delivered.
The defendants sought to amend the written statement to deny that the agreement was for sale and to plead instead that it was an agreement to develop the land for the parties’ mutual benefit.
The trial court rejected the amendment, but the High Court allowed it; the nature and terms of the agreement remained in issue in the suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a pleading may be amended even when the amendment explains an admission or introduces an inconsistent plea. An admission is material evidence, but it may be explained. Applying its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court found no material irregularity in allowing the amendment. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court committed no material irregularity in allowing the amendment. The appeal was dismissed, and the parties remained free to explain the agreement’s terms and the circumstances of its execution while adducing evidence.

predicates.challenge_to_order_allowing_written_stat: A party challenged a higher-court order allowing an amendment to a written statement.
predicates.earlier_pleading_admitted_transaction_ty: A party’s earlier written statement expressly described the parties’ agreement as one type of transaction.
predicates.proposed_amendment_changes_transaction_t: That party proposed to replace the earlier description with a different characterization of the agreement.
predicates.agreement_terms_remain_for_evidence: The agreement’s terms and the circumstances of its execution remained matters the parties could address in evidence.

members.legal_issue: A party may seek to amend a pleading to explain or clarify an admission without wholly withdrawing it.
material_facts: The defendants said their amendment was intended to explain the circumstances in which a letter referring to relinquishment had been written, rather than to resile from the letter or their earlier pleading about it.
The Court rejected the proposed amendment insofar as it withdrew the admissions, but permitted the defendants to apply to explain or clarify them.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings, and a categorical admission may be explained or clarified even though it cannot be wholly withdrawn. The Court relied on Gautam Sarup v. Leela Jetly and distinguished the principle concerning withdrawal in Panchdeo Narain Srivastava. An alternative plea may be available, but alternative pleas cannot be mutually destructive of one another.
members.conclusion: The defendants were permitted to file an application limited to explaining or clarifying the disputed admissions, to be considered on its merits in light of the Court's observations.

predicates.amendment_application_in_pending_suit: A party applied to amend its pleading in a pending suit.
predicates.pleading_contains_admission: The pleading contains an admission of fact by the party seeking amendment.
predicates.proposed_amendment_explains_or_clarifies: The proposed amendment supplies an explanation or clarification of the admission rather than wholly retracting it.

members.legal_issue: Delay alone does not determine whether an amendment to a written statement should be permitted.
material_facts: The defendants sought amendment about twenty-five years after filing their written statement.
Issues in the suit had been framed only in 2009, and the Court considered the nature and character of the proposed amendment and the surrounding circumstances as relevant to the delay.
members.legal_principle: In considering an application under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, delay is not by itself crucial. The court must consider the nature and character of the amendment and the circumstances of the case, along with the established amendment principles summarized in Revajeetu Builders and Developers v. Narayanaswamy and Sons, including bona fides, prejudice, injustice, and the effect on the nature of the case.
members.conclusion: Delay by itself was not decisive; the nature and character of the amendment and the other circumstances had to be considered, although the proposed wholesale withdrawal of the admissions was impermissible.

predicates.amendment_application_in_pending_suit: A party applied to amend a pleading in a pending suit.
predicates.amendment_is_delayed: The party applied to amend after a substantial period had passed since filing the pleading.

members.legal_issue: The length of delay alone does not determine whether delay should be condoned; the acceptability of the explanation is the controlling consideration.
material_facts: An application to restore a proceeding dismissed for default was filed 883 days after the dismissal.
The applicant said his advocate had not informed him of the dismissal and that he learned of it after receiving execution-related process.
The trial court accepted the explanation and condoned the delay.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, “sufficient cause” is construed liberally to advance substantial justice. The length of delay is not decisive; the acceptability of the explanation is. Delay should not be condoned where the explanation is mala fide or part of a dilatory strategy. The Court relied on Shakuntala Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumari, AIR 1969 SC 575, and State of West Bengal v. The Administrator, Howrah Municipality, AIR 1972 SC 749.
members.conclusion: The length of the delay did not itself prevent condonation; an acceptable explanation may justify condoning even a very long delay, while a short delay may be refused if its explanation is unacceptable.

rule.if: delay_condonation_application and explanation_is_acceptable and not explanation_is_mala_fide_or_dilatory

predicates.delay_condonation_application: A party applied to have a delayed proceeding or filing accepted.
predicates.explanation_is_acceptable: The court found the applicant’s account of the delay satisfactory.
predicates.explanation_is_mala_fide_or_dilatory: The explanation was shown to be dishonest or offered as a strategy to gain time.

members.legal_issue: Delay in seeking a pleading amendment, or the possibility that a fresh claim would be time-barred, does not remove the court’s power to allow amendment, though limitation and prejudice are relevant to its discretion.
material_facts: The application to amend the plaint was made during the appeals and was challenged as belated.
The respondent did not claim that the amendment made available relief that would otherwise have been barred by limitation.
The High Court set aside the amendment order based on the proviso, and the Supreme Court remitted the matter for fresh consideration with all contentions open.
members.legal_principle: Under L.J. Leach and Company Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co. and Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, amendments should be assessed by whether they are necessary to determine the real controversy and whether they cause injustice that cannot be compensated in costs. A claim that would be time-barred in a fresh suit is a relevant discretionary consideration, not a limit on the court’s power. The Court also referred to Rajesh Kumar Aggarwal v. K.K. Modi, Pankaja v. Yellappa, Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh, Gajanan Jaikishan Joshi v. Prabhakar Mohanlal Kalwar, and A.K. Gupta and Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation.
members.conclusion: Delay or laches is distinct from prejudice, and limitation is a relevant factor in deciding whether to allow an amendment but does not eliminate the court’s power to do so. The Supreme Court did not decide whether the amendment should ultimately be allowed; that question remained open on remand.

predicates.civil_pleading_amendment_request: A party in a civil proceeding requested permission to amend a pleading.
predicates.application_is_delayed: The amendment request was made after delay or laches.
predicates.fresh_claim_would_be_time_barred: A fresh suit on the claim in the proposed amendment would be barred by limitation.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to a tenant’s pleading that particularizes a material subsequent event should not be refused merely because it was sought after delay where the event is admitted and the issue was already raised.
material_facts: The tenant’s original defence asserted that the landlord had suitable alternative accommodation in the adjoining portion of the building.
While the appeal was pending, the tenant sought to amend the written statement to state that the landlord had obtained actual possession of that portion.
The landlord’s possession of the adjoining portion was admitted, but the High Court refused the amendment on grounds of delay and laches.
members.legal_principle: Order VI, Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings. The amendment was in substance superfluous because the alternative-accommodation issue was already pleaded, but it should be allowed to place the admitted subsequent event expressly before the court. The burden of establishing the absence of reasonably suitable alternative accommodation rested on the landlord, and the court relied on the rule that a pending appeal allows consideration of relevant subsequent events.
members.conclusion: The amendment should have been allowed; the Supreme Court granted it and held that the High Court had rejected it on an untenable ground.

rule.if: eviction_appeal_pending and alternative_accommodation_defence_already_raised and amendment_particularizes_subsequent_event and subsequent_event_is_admitted

predicates.eviction_appeal_pending: An appeal from an eviction decision is pending.
predicates.alternative_accommodation_defence_alread: The tenant’s existing pleading already asserts that the landlord has suitable alternative accommodation.
predicates.amendment_particularizes_subsequent_even: The proposed amendment specifies a later event relevant to the existing alternative-accommodation defence.
predicates.subsequent_event_is_admitted: The fact stated in the proposed amendment is admitted or undisputed.

members.legal_issue: A belated amendment that makes the dispute more precise and assists its adjudication may be allowed when the delay can be compensated by costs.
material_facts: The claimant sought a further amendment to make the disputed property more precisely identifiable.
The amendment was sought belatedly but would help the court determine the real dispute more satisfactorily.
The court considered that the delay could be compensated by awarding costs to the opposing occupants.
members.legal_principle: The court may allow a belated amendment that enables a more precise determination of the real dispute, where the prejudice from delay can be compensated by costs. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The amendment was allowed, with the claimant required to pay costs thrown away and the opposing occupants permitted to respond to the amended pleading.

rule.if: civil_property_suit and amendment_sought and amendment_clarifies_real_dispute and delay_compensable_by_costs

predicates.civil_property_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit concerning rights in property.
predicates.amendment_sought: A party asks to amend its pleading.
predicates.amendment_clarifies_real_dispute: The proposed amendment makes the dispute more precise and assists its adjudication.
predicates.delay_compensable_by_costs: The prejudice caused by the lateness of the amendment can be compensated by costs.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement may be allowed when it assists proper adjudication of the dispute and causes no serious prejudice or loss of an accrued right, even if it adds an alternative defence or is sought after delay.
material_facts: In an eviction suit, the defendant sought to amend its written defence to elaborate its position on the alleged landlord-tenant relationship and to rely on revenue records.

The proposed amendment added an alternative or additional defence; the court found no admission that it sought to withdraw and no accrued right or serious prejudice to the plaintiff that would result.
The plaintiff could respond to the amended written statement, and the proposed amendment was relevant to adjudicating the controversy and avoiding further proceedings.
The application was made after delay, but the court found that delay alone did not establish prejudice.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, pleadings may be amended when necessary for proper and effective adjudication and to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, subject to the amendment not causing injustice or serious prejudice. A defendant may raise an alternative or additional defence, and the principles governing amendments apply to written statements, with courts generally taking a more generous approach to them. A clear admission conferring a right on the plaintiff is ordinarily not to be withdrawn if doing so would prejudice that right. Delay alone is insufficient to refuse amendment where serious prejudice is not shown and may be compensated. The Court relied on B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai, A.K. Gupta and Sons Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation, Weldon v. Neal, Charan Das v. Amir Khan, and L.J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co.
members.conclusion: The amendment application should be allowed; the High Court's order setting aside the order allowing the amendment was unsustainable.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and (amendment_needed_for_adjudication or amendment_avoids_multiple_proceedings) and no_serious_prejudice and no_accrued_right_is_prejudiced

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A defendant in a civil proceeding applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.amendment_needed_for_adjudication: The proposed amendment supplied material relevant to properly deciding the controversy between the parties.
predicates.amendment_avoids_multiple_proceedings: The proposed amendment could help resolve the dispute without further judicial proceedings.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious or irretrievable prejudice from the amendment.
predicates.no_accrued_right_is_prejudiced: The proposed amendment was not shown to take away an accrued right of the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: A proposed amendment to a written statement that elaborates the defence and assists in determining the real controversy should be considered liberally where it causes no serious injustice or prejudice.
material_facts: The defendants sought to add facts about the source of the purchase money and the later mutation of the property, describing the changes as an elaboration of their defence.
The proposed amendments raised matters relevant to the dispute over ownership and possession.
The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice from the amendment.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court broad discretion to permit amendments needed to determine the real questions in controversy, on just terms. Courts should exercise that power liberally unless serious injustice or irreparable loss would result. Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Hnaung states that amendment powers serve the proper administration of justice but do not permit substitution of one distinct cause of action for another.
members.conclusion: The lower courts erred in rejecting the amendment application; the amendment was allowed.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and proposed_amendment_elaborates_defence and amendment_assists_real_dispute and no_serious_prejudice

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.proposed_amendment_elaborates_defence: The proposed changes added detail to or developed the defence already advanced.
predicates.amendment_assists_real_dispute: The proposed changes concerned matters relevant to deciding the dispute between the parties.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice or injustice from the proposed changes.

members.legal_issue: A limitation defence may be added to a written statement by amendment where its applicability is disputed and can be determined as an issue in the suit.
material_facts: The defendants sought to add a defence that the suit was barred by limitation.
Whether limitation barred the suit was disputed and could be determined after the amendment was allowed.
members.legal_principle: In Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan, the Court held that an amendment should not be refused merely because the proposed relief may be time-barred where limitation is arguable; the limitation plea can be made an issue after amendment. The dominant purpose of allowing amendment is to minimize litigation.
members.conclusion: The limitation defence could be added by amendment, and its merits could be decided as an issue in the suit.

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.additional_limitation_defence_proposed: The proposed amendment added a defence that the claim was brought too late.
predicates.limitation_applicability_disputed: The parties disputed whether the claim was barred by the applicable time limit.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement is not barred merely because it is said to withdraw an admission, particularly where no admission is in fact withdrawn and the amendment explains or develops the defence.
material_facts: The original written statement denied that the plaintiff had paid the purchase price and asserted that the parents had sufficient income to purchase the property.
The proposed amendment added that the plaintiff lacked funds and that the property had later been mutated in the names of the plaintiff and defendants in equal shares.
The Court found no admission in the written statement that the proposed amendment sought to withdraw.
members.legal_principle: The Court found no admission being withdrawn on the facts. In Estralla Rubber v. Dass Estate (P) Ltd., it was held that even admissions in evidence or in a written statement may be explained by an amendment application.
members.conclusion: The amendment could not be rejected on the ground that it withdrew an admission; the proposed changes did not withdraw an admission, and even an admission may be explained by amendment.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and (proposed_change_elaborates_existing_defence or proposed_change_explains_admission) and no_serious_prejudice

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.proposed_change_elaborates_existing_defe: The proposed change added detail to or developed a defence already stated.
predicates.proposed_change_explains_admission: The proposed change supplied an explanation for a statement previously made by the defending party.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice or injustice from the proposed change.

members.legal_issue: Delay alone does not justify rejecting an amendment to a written statement where no serious prejudice or loss of an accrued right is shown.
material_facts: The defendants applied to amend their written statement three years after filing it.
The opposing party was not shown to have suffered serious prejudice that would take away an accrued right.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that mere delay in applying to amend a written statement is not a ground for rejection when no serious prejudice is shown to have been caused to the opposing party so as to take away an accrued right.
members.conclusion: The three-year delay was not, by itself, a sufficient ground to reject the amendment application.

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A party defending a civil suit applied to amend its written statement.
predicates.amendment_delayed: The party applied to amend its written statement after a period of time had passed since filing it.
predicates.no_serious_prejudice_to_accrued_right: The opposing party was not shown to suffer serious prejudice that would deprive it of an accrued right.

members.legal_issue: An alternative defence may be added to a written statement when it is relevant to a live issue, does not contradict the existing defence or withdraw an admission, and any resulting prejudice or delay can be addressed by costs.
material_facts: The defendant had pleaded that he was a lessee, not a licensee.
During trial, he sought to add an alternative plea that, if found to be a licensee, he was entitled to an irrevocable licence because he had carried out permanent works and incurred expenses.

The court found that the proposed plea was neither inconsistent with nor repugnant to the existing defence, and that it responded to the issue of whether he could be dispossessed if found to be a licensee.
The court rejected the finding that the amendment withdrew an admission or would cause irretrievable prejudice.
The amendment application had been made after prolonged delay, but the plaintiff could be compensated by costs.
The plaintiff asserted that licence fees remained unpaid, and the court required payment of arrears as a condition of allowing the amendment.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendment of pleadings is discretionary and should generally be allowed when necessary to determine the real controversy, including an alternative defence in a written statement, unless it introduces a new cause of action or case, contradicts admitted facts, withdraws an admission, causes prejudice that cannot be compensated, or defeats a right accrued through lapse of time. Delay may be compensated by costs. The court relied on A.K. Gupta & Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation, Smt. Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, and M/s. Ganesh Trading Company v. Moji Ram. The proposed defence invoked Section 60(b) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882.
members.conclusion: The defendant could amend the written statement to add only the alternative plea of entitlement to the benefit of Section 60(b) of the Indian Easements Act, subject to paying the outstanding licence fees and costs.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_proceeding and alternative_defence_proposed and amendment_relevant_to_live_issue and amendment_not_inconsistent_with_existing_defence and no_admission_withdrawn and prejudice_compensable_by_costs and delay_compensable_by_costs and outstanding_fees_asserted

predicates.written_statement_amendment_proceeding: A defendant sought to amend a written statement during the proceeding.
predicates.alternative_defence_proposed: The defendant proposed a defence that would apply if the court rejected the defendant’s primary position.
predicates.amendment_relevant_to_live_issue: The proposed defence addressed an issue already arising for determination in the proceeding.
predicates.amendment_not_inconsistent_with_existing: The proposed defence could be advanced alongside the defence already pleaded without contradicting it.
predicates.no_admission_withdrawn: The proposed amendment did not withdraw an admission made in the existing pleading.
predicates.prejudice_compensable_by_costs: Any prejudice to the opposing party from the amendment could be compensated by costs.
predicates.delay_compensable_by_costs: The delay in seeking the amendment could be addressed by an award of costs.
predicates.outstanding_fees_asserted: The opposing party asserted that fees remained unpaid.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement may be allowed when it elaborates an existing defence rather than withdrawing an admission and causes no prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The original written statement already alleged that the property was joint-family property and described a joint-family arrangement.
The proposed amendment added detail about the property’s inheritance and asserted coparcenary rights.
After the plaint was amended, the defendant had filed a written statement responding to the amended plaint.
The Court found that the proposed amendment elaborated the existing defence, would not withdraw an admission, and would cause no prejudice to the plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs amendment of pleadings. Whether an amendment should be allowed does not depend on whether the proposed case will ultimately succeed at trial. An amendment elaborating an existing defence does not amount to withdrawal of an admission, and the Court noted that this amendment would cause no prejudice to the plaintiff.
members.conclusion: The amendment of the written statement was properly allowed, and the trial court’s order allowing it was affirmed.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_pleading_amendment: The proceeding is a civil suit in which a party seeks to amend a pleading.
predicates.proposed_written_statement_elaborates_ex: The proposed written-statement amendment adds detail to a defence already pleaded rather than replacing it with a new defence.
predicates.amendment_causes_no_prejudice: Allowing the amendment would not prejudice the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: A written statement may be amended to add an allegation about possession when the allegation does not withdraw an admission or prejudice the opposing party’s case.
material_facts: From the outset, the defendants denied that the plaintiff had an interest in the Schedule-B properties.
The proposed amendment added that those properties were in the possession of trespassers.
The amendment did not withdraw an admission in the plaintiff’s favour or otherwise displace the plaintiff’s case concerning those properties.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendment of a written statement may be permitted where it does not withdraw an admission in the plaintiff’s favour or cause prejudice by displacing the plaintiff’s case. Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co. establishes the restriction on amendments that withdraw prejudicial admissions; the circumstances here did not attract that restriction. The Court observed that the High Court had, strictly speaking, exceeded the limits of revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but declined to interfere with this part of its order in exercise of Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The amendment concerning the Schedule-B properties remained allowed; the Supreme Court declined to interfere with that part of the High Court’s order, while observing that the High Court should not have interfered under its revisional jurisdiction.

rule.if: civil_suit and original_defense_denied_claimant_interest and amendment_adds_possession_allegation and amendment_does_not_withdraw_admission and amendment_does_not_prejudice_claimant

predicates.civil_suit: A claimant brought a civil action against a defending party.
predicates.original_defense_denied_claimant_interes: The defending party’s original written statement denied that the claimant had an interest in the property.
predicates.amendment_adds_possession_allegation: The defending party sought to add an allegation that the property was in the possession of trespassers.
predicates.amendment_does_not_withdraw_admission: The proposed change did not retract an admission previously made in the claimant’s favour.
predicates.amendment_does_not_prejudice_claimant: The proposed change did not displace the claimant’s case or adversely affect a right arising from an admission.

members.legal_issue: A pleading amendment seeking declaratory relief may be allowed despite an alleged limitation bar when the limitation question is genuinely disputed and requires determination at trial.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a pending suit seeking injunction and possession and later sought to add a prayer declaring their ownership.
The defendants disputed the plaintiffs’ title in their written statement.
The defendants contended that the declaration claim was out of time, while the plaintiffs relied on different limitation periods; the applicable limitation period was therefore disputed.
The original plaint already contained factual averments concerning the plaintiffs’ title, and allowing the amendment would permit the limitation question to be tried.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court has discretion to allow amendments, including when an amended claim may be time-barred, and must exercise that discretion judiciously in the interests of justice. Limitation is a factor in that exercise, not an absolute bar to amendment. Where limitation is disputed and arguable, it may be decided as an issue after amendment. The Court relied on L.J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co. (AIR 1957 SC 357), T.N. Alloy Foundry Co. Ltd. v. T.N. Electricity Board (2004) 3 SCC 392, and Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan (2001) 2 SCC 472.
members.conclusion: The amendment should be allowed, and the trial court should frame and decide the limitation issue in accordance with law.

predicates.pending_suit_amendment: A plaintiff sought to amend pleadings in a pending civil suit.
predicates.limitation_disputed: The parties disputed whether the proposed claim was out of time and which limitation period applied.
predicates.amendment_serves_justice: Allowing the amendment would help resolve the dispute in the pending suit and avoid further litigation.

members.legal_issue: A court may allow a late amendment relying on a subsequent event when the amendment enables the dispute to be resolved in the existing proceeding and avoids further litigation without unfairly taking the opposing party by surprise.
material_facts: During the suit, the Society received a further lease over part of the disputed land.
The Society’s written statement did not plead that lease as a basis for its defence, and it sought amendment only at the end of the High Court appeal, after a lengthy delay.
The documents concerning the lease were already on the record, the proposed amendment remained within the subject matter of the suit, and the opposing party could answer the new plea.
Without the amendment, a separate suit concerning the later lease would be inevitable; allowing the amendment would permit the issue to be tried on remand and reduce litigation.
members.legal_principle: Amendment is discretionary, and delay does not invariably preclude it where the amendment allows complete justice, does not open an unrelated case or unfairly surprise the other party, and avoids circuity of action. Subsequent events may be considered when they reduce litigation. The Court relied on Ram Ratan Sahu v. Mohant Sahu, Raicharan Mandal v. Biswanath Mandal, Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chandhuri, Patterson v. State of Alabama, Surinder Kumar v. Gian Chand, and the amendment authorities L. J. Leach & Co. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., Pungonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, and A. K. Gupta & Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation; it distinguished the authorities relied on against amendment, including Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Huaung and Kanda v. Waghu.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the amendment concerning the later lease and remanded the dispute over the affected portion for trial of the issue raised by the amendment.

rule.if: civil_appeal and proposed_amendment_relies_on_subsequent_event and amendment_within_existing_dispute and opposing_party_can_answer_new_plea and amendment_avoids_separate_litigation and amendment_will_not_unfairly_surprise_opponent

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal in which the court can consider a proposed pleading amendment.
predicates.proposed_amendment_relies_on_subsequent_: The proposed amendment relies on an event that occurred after the original pleading.
predicates.amendment_within_existing_dispute: The amendment concerns the same underlying dispute rather than introducing an unrelated case.
predicates.opposing_party_can_answer_new_plea: The opposing party has an opportunity to contest the new plea.
predicates.amendment_avoids_separate_litigation: Allowing the amendment enables the issue to be determined in the existing proceeding instead of requiring a separate suit.
predicates.amendment_will_not_unfairly_surprise_opp: The amendment does not unfairly take the opposing party by surprise.

members.legal_issue: A pleading may be amended to correct the description of disputed property when the correction is needed to bring the real controversy before the court, notwithstanding that the applicant did not seek it promptly, with prejudice to the opposing party addressed by costs.
material_facts: The plaint described a substantially larger area than the area the plaintiff later said was actually in dispute, and the proposed amendment corrected the property description.

The defendants had challenged the description in their written statement and during related proceedings, but the plaintiff sought amendment later and had maintained the original description in the meantime.
The Supreme Court considered the case factually close to an earlier decision allowing correction of a property description despite the plaintiff’s lack of promptness.
The defendants said they had suffered an injunction concerning property they owned, and the Court considered that the resulting prejudice could be met by an order for costs.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended, restricts amendments after commencement of trial unless the party could not have raised the matter earlier despite due diligence. The Court did not decide the broader question of when trial commences; it followed Sajjan Kumar v. Ram Kishan, (2005) 13 SCC 89, which allowed correction of a property description despite the plaintiff’s lack of diligence where the amendment was needed to bring out the real controversy and refusal could create complications at execution. Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh, (2006) 6 SCC 498, and Ajendraprasadji N. Pandey v. Swami Keshavprakeshdasji, (2006) 12 SCC 1, were considered in relation to commencement of trial, but the Court made no ruling on that broader issue here.
members.conclusion: The proposed amendment to the plaint was allowed subject to payment of costs to the defendants.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_amendment_denial and property_description_correction_needed and amendment_clarifies_real_dispute and prejudice_can_be_addressed_by_costs

predicates.civil_appeal_from_amendment_denial: A party appeals in a civil proceeding after a court has refused an application to amend a pleading.
predicates.property_description_correction_needed: The applicant seeks to correct the description of property identified in the pleading as the subject of the dispute.
predicates.amendment_clarifies_real_dispute: The proposed correction brings the actual disputed property or controversy into clearer focus.
predicates.prejudice_can_be_addressed_by_costs: Any prejudice to the opposing party from allowing the correction can be addressed by requiring the applicant to pay costs.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement may add a conditional qualification to an admission and raise a defence about a claimant’s entitlement without impermissibly withdrawing the admission or displacing the claimant’s case.
material_facts: The defendants had admitted that the plaintiff and certain other defendants were entitled to a half share in the properties.
The proposed amendment retained that admission but added a qualification that entitlement depended on proving the relevant claimants’ legitimacy and right to inherit.
The amendment raised an issue for determination and did not replace the plaintiff’s case or cause irretrievable prejudice.
The trial had not commenced when the amendment was sought.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, pleadings may be amended where necessary to determine the real controversy; the post-commencement due-diligence proviso did not apply because the trial had not commenced. Courts generally take a more liberal approach to amendments of written statements than amendments of plaints: a defendant may add or alter a defence, take inconsistent pleas, and explain an admission, provided the amendment does not cause serious injustice or irreparable prejudice. The Court relied on Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Hnaung, B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai, Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh, L.J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co., Basavan Jaggu Dhobi v. Sukhnandan Ramdas Chaudhary, and Akshaya Restaurant v. P. Anjanappa. It distinguished Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co. and Heera Lal v. Kalyan Mal because the proposed amendment here preserved the admission and did not displace the claimant’s case or cause irretrievable prejudice.
members.conclusion: The amendment was permissible, and the application to amend the written statement was allowed.

rule.if: civil_written_statement_amendment_case and admission_preserved_with_qualification and amendment_raises_issue_for_decision and not irretrievable_prejudice

predicates.civil_written_statement_amendment_case: A party in a civil suit sought to amend its written statement.
predicates.admission_preserved_with_qualification: The proposed amendment retained an earlier admission while adding a qualification to it.
predicates.amendment_raises_issue_for_decision: The proposed amendment added facts or a defence relevant to resolving an issue in the dispute.
predicates.irretrievable_prejudice: The proposed amendment would cause the opposing party irretrievable prejudice.

members.legal_issue: A defendant may amend a written statement to add an alternative defence where it does not contradict the existing defence or withdraw an admission, and any prejudice to the plaintiff can be addressed by terms.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought the defendant’s eviction on the basis that the defendant was a licensee, while the defendant’s existing written statement claimed that he was a lessee.
The defendant sought to add an alternative plea that, if found to be a licensee, the licence was irrevocable because he had carried out permanent works and incurred expenses in reliance on it.
The proposed alternative plea was connected to the existing dispute and was not inconsistent with or repugnant to the defences already raised.
The application to amend was delayed, but the plaintiff could be compensated by costs.
The plaintiff asserted that licence fees were unpaid, and the court made permission to amend conditional on payment of the arrears and costs.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives courts a broad discretion to allow amendments in the interests of justice, while requiring judicial care. Under A.K. Gupta & Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation, an amendment that is only a different or additional approach to the same facts may be allowed even after limitation has expired, but a new claim based on new facts or a new set of ideas prejudicing an accrued right should not be introduced. Smt. Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar recognises the breadth of the discretion and the need for care; M/s. Ganesh Trading Company v. Moji Ram holds that amendments should promote justice, that written statements may be amended generously, and that alternative pleas may be taken unless they cause irremediable injustice or withdraw an admission. The proposed defence relied on Section 60(b) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, concerning when a licence is irrevocable.
members.conclusion: The refusal of the amendment was set aside, and the defendant was permitted to add the alternative defence, subject to payment of the licence-fee arrears and costs.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_application and alternative_defence_to_same_dispute and not contradictory_to_existing_defence and prejudice_compensable_by_terms and licence_fee_arrears_asserted

predicates.written_statement_amendment_application: A defendant in a suit applies to amend the written statement.
predicates.alternative_defence_to_same_dispute: The defendant seeks to add an alternative defence addressing the same dispute already raised in the suit.
predicates.not_contradictory_to_existing_defence: The proposed defence does not contradict the defendant’s existing position or withdraw an admission in the plaintiff’s favour.
predicates.prejudice_compensable_by_terms: Any prejudice to the opposing party from allowing the amendment can be addressed by costs or other conditions.
predicates.licence_fee_arrears_asserted: The opposing party asserts that licence fees remain unpaid.
predicates.amendment_permitted_subject_to_payment_o: The amendment is allowed on terms requiring payment of the asserted arrears and costs.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal cannot stand where the appellate court disregards compelling, corroborated evidence and the record permits only the conclusion that the prosecution proved guilt.
material_facts: Eleven eyewitnesses supported the prosecution account, including five who had sustained gunshot injuries.
Medical evidence corroborated the injuries and deaths described by the eyewitnesses.
The High Court relied on weak or inadmissible circumstances and failed to consider the material eyewitness evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence did not permit two reasonable views.
members.legal_principle: Although an acquittal should not be disturbed where the evidence reasonably permits two views, intervention is warranted when the acquittal results from disregarding material evidence or relying on legally impermissible grounds and the record supports only guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The respondents cited Ashok Kumar v. State of Rajasthan, Arun Kumar v. State of U.P., and Bharwad Jakshibhai Nagjibhai v. State of Gujarat in support of non-interference; the Court found this was not a case where two views were possible.
members.conclusion: The appeal against acquittal was allowed, the acquittal was set aside, and the trial court’s convictions and sentences were restored.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and compelling_evidence_supports_prosecution and material_evidence_was_ignored and only_guilt_view_is_reasonable

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal against an acquittal.
predicates.compelling_evidence_supports_prosecution: The record contains compelling evidence supporting the prosecution account.
predicates.material_evidence_was_ignored: The acquitting court failed to consider material evidence or relied on legally impermissible grounds.
predicates.only_guilt_view_is_reasonable: The evidence permits only the reasonable conclusion that guilt was proved.

members.legal_issue: A conviction entered after reversal of an acquittal is unsustainable when the trial court’s view remains at least as acceptable as the appellate court’s view on the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused only for injuring one person and acquitted him of the charge relating to the death of another person.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the accused of murder with common intention.

The first information report, made several hours after the occurrence by the deceased’s father, did not say that the accused had stabbed the deceased; the alleged eyewitnesses and the alleged dying declaration were also not mentioned as such in it.

The evidence about where the stabbing took place was uncertain, the site plans did not record where blood was found, and the medical evidence cast doubt on the account that the deceased had moved after being stabbed or made the alleged declaration.

The Court found the alleged eyewitness accounts not credible and the alleged dying declaration unreliable, and considered the trial court’s view that the deceased had been stabbed by another accused in the lane more likely.
members.legal_principle: On an appeal against acquittal, an appellate court should not interfere merely because it can adopt one of two reasonably possible views favouring conviction; it may interfere if the trial court’s view is not reasonably sustainable on the evidence. When the High Court reverses an acquittal and convicts, the Supreme Court may set aside that decision if, after considering the cases and crucial evidence, the trial court’s view is at least as acceptable as the High Court’s. No earlier case is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The trial court’s view was at least as acceptable as the High Court’s view, so the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s murder conviction and sentence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal_reversal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which an appellate court reversed a trial court’s acquittal and convicted the accused.
predicates.trial_view_at_least_as_acceptable: The evidence leaves the trial court’s view at least as acceptable as the view supporting the appellate conviction.

members.legal_issue: A conviction entered after an appellate court reverses an acquittal is sustainable where the trial court rejected credible eyewitness evidence on manifestly erroneous grounds and the evidence supports the conviction.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after doubting the daughter’s presence at the killing, rejecting other eyewitnesses because they did not intervene, and drawing an adverse inference from an initial report that omitted the victim’s and assailant’s names.
The daughter testified that the accused attacked her mother and that she was injured while trying to shield her mother; her injuries were medically examined and were consistent with her account.
Three independent eyewitnesses substantially corroborated the daughter’s account.
The initial report was a brief report of a murder, and its author explained why he omitted names and details.

The High Court reappraised the evidence, reversed the acquittal and convicted the accused; the Supreme Court found the trial court’s reasons for rejecting the eyewitnesses manifestly erroneous, dismissed the appeal, and maintained the conviction and sentence.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the witnesses and surrounding evidence on their merits: the daughter’s injuries supported her presence and account, independent eyewitnesses corroborated her, and the other witnesses’ failure to intervene did not by itself make their evidence unreliable. The omission of names and details from the initial report was not fatal in light of the explanation for that omission. The trial court’s manifestly erroneous reasons did not justify rejecting the eyewitness evidence. No earlier cases or statutory provisions were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal, and the conviction and sentence were maintained.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding challenged a conviction entered after an appellate court reversed an acquittal.
predicates.trial_rejection_based_on_erroneous_infer: The trial court rejected prosecution evidence on inferences that the reviewing court found manifestly erroneous.
predicates.injured_eye_witness_corrobated_by_indepe: An eyewitness sustained injuries consistent with the account of the event, and independent eyewitnesses substantially corroborated that account.
predicates.witness_nonintervention_used_to_reject_e: The trial court treated the fact that eyewitnesses did not intervene to rescue the victim as a reason to reject their evidence.

members.legal_issue: The appellants’ identities as assailants were established by the evidence, so the convictions entered after reversal of their acquittals could be upheld.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the appellants, but the High Court found that acquittal perverse and convicted them.
Several prosecution eyewitnesses identified the appellants as participants in the assault that caused the deceased’s death.
The deceased’s son promptly lodged a report naming the appellants as assailants.

The contractor, who was present at the scene, testified that the deceased was assaulted by the persons working there and identified the appellants in court; his testimony supported the prosecution account.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 304 Part II and 149 of the Indian Penal Code in affirming the convictions. It accepted the High Court’s assessment of the evidence, including eyewitness identification corroborated by the contractor’s testimony and the promptly lodged report, and found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s reversal of the acquittal. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court’s assessment that the appellants’ identities were established, upheld their convictions under Section 304 Part II read with Section 149 of the IPC and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction_reversing_acquitt: The prosecution appealed an acquittal, the appellate court reversed it and convicted the accused, and the accused challenged that conviction on appeal.
predicates.multiple_eyewitnesses_identified_accused: More than one witness to the assault identified the accused as participants.
predicates.prompt_report_named_accused: A report was lodged soon after the incident and named the accused as assailants.
predicates.contractor_witness_saw_assault_and_ident: A contractor present at the scene testified that the deceased was assaulted and identified the accused in court.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal may be set aside on a State appeal where eyewitness testimony against an accused receives sufficient assurance from prompt reporting and other evidence.
material_facts: The State appealed from an acquittal in a murder prosecution.
Two eyewitnesses consistently identified two accused as participating in the killing of one deceased.
The informant’s prompt report supported the eyewitness account.
Evidence of motive supported one accused, while motive and the recovery of a rifle linked by expert evidence to a cartridge at the scene provided further assurance against the other.
members.legal_principle: In assessing interested eyewitness testimony, the court required assurance from surrounding circumstances or other evidence as a matter of caution. It found that the prompt report, evidence of motive, and the firearm evidence sufficiently supported the testimony against these accused. The court applied Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code and cited no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The acquittal of the two accused was set aside, and they were convicted of the murder of the deceased under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The State appeals against the acquittal of persons accused of a criminal offence.
predicates.eyewitnesses_identify_accused: Eyewitnesses identify the accused as participating in the alleged homicide.
predicates.testimony_has_corroborative_assurance: The eyewitness testimony is supported by surrounding circumstances or other evidence, such as a prompt report, motive, or forensic evidence.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction may be restored in an appeal against acquittal when credible eyewitness testimony proves the accused inflicted the fatal injury and the reasons for rejecting that testimony are merely technical.
material_facts: A witness who was naturally present in the home testified that the accused fired at her husband, causing a fatal injury.

The witness’s account was challenged over her description of the firearms, the sequence of shots, and the injuries to another participant, but the Court found these discrepancies did not undermine the central account.
The medical evidence did not establish that the deceased was incapable of firing a weapon, and the Court found no fundamental conflict between that evidence and the eyewitness account.
The delayed transmission of the first information report and failures to seize firearms, spent cartridges, and bloodstained clothing did not displace the eyewitness testimony.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, a credible eyewitness account may establish murder. Ocular testimony is ordinarily preferred over medical evidence unless it contradicts fundamental facts. A witness’s account must be assessed in the circumstances of the event and with due regard to a rural witness’s background; technical discrepancies and investigative omissions do not by themselves make reliable testimony unacceptable. The Court accepted that appellate restraint in appeals against acquittal is an established principle, citing State of Haryana v. Sher Singh, State of U.P. v. Ram Bahadur Singh, Chanakya Dhibar v. State of West Bengal, and Vijaybhai Bhanabhai Patel v. Navnitbhai Nathubhai Patel, but found that principle did not preclude correction of the High Court’s error on these facts.
members.conclusion: The acquittal on the murder charge concerning the deceased husband was set aside, and the trial court’s conviction was restored.

rule.if: state_appeal_against_acquittal and eyewitness_directly_identifies_accused_as_fatal_shooter and eyewitness_account_is_credible and not fundamental_conflict_with_medical_evidence

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against an acquittal on the charge at issue.
predicates.eyewitness_directly_identifies_accused_a: An eyewitness testified that the accused fired the shot that caused the deceased’s fatal injury.
