predicates.claimant_parcel_acquired: The acquiring authority included the claimant’s parcel in the acquisition.
predicates.no_reason_for_different_treatment_provid: The State did not explain why it treated the claimant’s parcel differently from the comparable parcels.

members.legal_issue: A land-revenue assessment scheme violates equality when its classifications lack a rational connection to the basis and objectives of assessment.
material_facts: The earlier land-assessment systems classified soils by quality and productivity, with rates adjusted for relevant differences in water supply or location.
The challenged scheme imposed a minimum flat assessment on dry land without regard to soil quality or productivity.

For wet land, the scheme used the size of the irrigation area to determine categories and minimum assessments, but that measure did not reliably correspond to water-supply duration, soil quality, or productivity.
In many instances, the minimum assessment exceeded the stated percentage increase over the earlier assessment.
members.legal_principle: Equality permits legislative classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relation to the law’s objective. These requirements apply to fiscal laws, although legislatures receive wider latitude in tax classifications. The Court applied Article 14 and relied on Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer.
members.conclusion: The classifications and minimum assessments lacked a reasonable relationship to fair assessment and rationalisation of the revenue structure, so the scheme violated the constitutional guarantee of equality.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_assessm: A party challenged the constitutionality of a scheme imposing assessments on land.
predicates.dry_land_minimum_ignores_soil_productivi: The scheme imposed a minimum assessment on dry land without taking account of differences in soil quality or productivity.
predicates.wet_land_categories_do_not_track_water_s: The scheme classified wet land using a measure that did not reliably correspond to water-supply duration, soil quality, or productivity.

members.legal_issue: Applying a uniform floor-area valuation to dissimilar properties without rational classification violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The municipality applied floor-area rates to factories that differed in location, age and construction.
There was no rational classification of the factories that could justify applying the same rates to properties with materially different rental characteristics.
The municipality divided buildings into processing and non-processing categories without establishing a rational basis for that distinction.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unequal treatment resulting from an arbitrary or irrational classification. Lokmanya Mills v. Barsi Borough Municipality, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 306, was relied on concerning the arbitrary use of floor area to value dissimilar properties. Bhuvaneswariah v. State, A.I.R. 1965 Mys. 170, and N. Kunhali Haji v. State of Kerala, A.I.R. 1966 Ker. 14, were referred to in relation to the inequality that can result from taxation based on floor area without rational classification.
members.conclusion: The assessment method, as applied, violated Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a municipal assessment of property tax.
predicates.dissimilar_properties_given_uniform_floo: The assessing authority applied the same floor-area rates to properties that differed in characteristics relevant to their rental value.
predicates.no_rational_classification: The assessing authority did not classify the properties on a rational basis that justified the different or uniform treatment.

members.legal_issue: A statutory scheme defining covered land through unguided selection and irrational classifications, without safeguards for affected owners, violates equality and the former constitutional protection of property.
material_facts: The definition covered land that was genuinely unbuilt, land with unauthorised structures selected by an authority, and land placed in a schedule, including land later added by the government without stated criteria.
The authority could select some lands with unauthorised structures and leave similarly situated lands untouched.
The scheme did not distinguish owners who built unauthorised structures from owners whose land had been occupied or built upon by trespassers.

It treated wholly unbuilt plots as covered while excluding plots with even small lawful structures, and the schedule included varied lands without an evident rational connection to the stated purpose.
The statute prescribed no procedure requiring notice or a hearing before the relevant declarations or eviction decisions.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 requires classifications to rest on a rational basis and to serve the law’s purpose; arbitrary selection and treating materially different persons alike offend that guarantee. Article 19(1)(f), while it remained part of the Constitution, also constrained laws affecting property. Discretion affecting property cannot be left uncontrolled where the scheme lacks standards and safeguards appropriate to the decision. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for these propositions.
members.conclusion: The definition of covered land, in each of its parts, violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution as it then stood; the Act was unconstitutional, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and (unguided_land_selection or irrational_classification or no_hearing_before_adverse_decision)

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law governing occupation of land and eviction from it.
predicates.unguided_land_selection: The law permits authorities to select which similarly situated lands are covered without objective standards controlling that choice.
predicates.irrational_classification: The law treats materially different owners or plots alike, or distinguishes between plots without a rational connection to its purpose.
predicates.no_hearing_before_adverse_decision: The law provides no opportunity for affected people to be heard before an adverse declaration or eviction decision.

members.legal_issue: Different compensation treatment for land acquired for housing schemes and land acquired for other public purposes violates equality when the distinction has no rational relation to the legislative objective.
material_facts: Owners whose land was acquired for housing schemes received less than owners whose same or similar land was acquired for another public purpose under the principal law.
The challenged law extended to housing schemes with varied objectives, not only slum clearance, and allowed acquisition for housing prosperous sections as well as poorer sections.
The differences between the affected owners and lands, including extent, quality, suitability, and ownership, had no reasonable relation to the law's objective.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits legislative classification only where it is founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those included from those excluded and that differentia has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court applied these two tests to the distinction between acquisitions for housing schemes and acquisitions for other public purposes.
members.conclusion: The challenged law violated Article 14 because the different treatment of owners whose land was acquired for housing schemes was not supported by a reasonable classification, and the law was void.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorizing the State to acquire property.
predicates.housing_acquisition_receives_lower_compe: Owners whose property is acquired for housing receive less compensation than owners whose same or similar property is acquired for another public purpose.
predicates.housing_law_covers_varied_objectives: The law permits acquisitions for housing objectives extending beyond a narrowly identified social need.
predicates.no_rational_basis_for_different_treatmen: The differences between the affected owners or properties have no rational relation to the law's objective.

members.legal_issue: A building tax imposed solely on floor area, without rationally classifying materially dissimilar buildings, violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The tax applied to buildings meeting a minimum floor-area threshold and used floor area as its sole basis for determining liability and the amount of tax.
The same basis applied to buildings that differed in class, construction, use, location, capacity for profitable use, cost, and economic rental.
The legislation made no rational classification based on those or other relevant circumstances.
members.legal_principle: A taxing law must be within legislative competence and consistent with the Constitution; its validity may be challenged for violating fundamental rights. Under Articles 13(2), 14 and 265, a tax imposed by law cannot deny equality. Fiscal legislation allows the legislature broad discretion in classification, but imposing a uniform tax on essentially dissimilar persons, objects or transactions may deny equality when the legislature fails to make a rational classification. The Court relied on K.T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer, Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, and applied New Manek Chowk Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad. The Court left open whether taxing only buildings completed after the legislation took effect, while exempting earlier buildings, violated equality.
members.conclusion: The charging provision violated the equality clause of the Constitution, and the appeals challenging the High Court’s decision were dismissed.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_challenge and tax_based_only_on_floor_area and covers_materially_different_buildings and omits_relevant_taxation_characteristics

predicates.constitutional_tax_challenge: A person challenges the validity of a taxing law on constitutional equality grounds.
predicates.tax_based_only_on_floor_area: The legislature bases liability and the amount of a building tax solely on the building’s floor area.
predicates.covers_materially_different_buildings: The tax applies on the same basis to buildings that differ in relevant characteristics such as class, construction, use, location, or capacity for profitable use.
predicates.omits_relevant_taxation_characteristics: The legislature does not take relevant differences between buildings into account when classifying them for taxation.

members.legal_issue: A land-ceiling scheme that uses an artificial definition of family and different ceiling treatment for members of natural families violates equal protection when it discriminates between similarly situated persons.
material_facts: The law fixed the same ceiling for an individual and a defined family of up to five members, with a different ceiling for larger defined families.
Its definition of family excluded some members of natural families recognized under personal law, including major sons in the example considered by the Court.
Applying the definition and ceiling could leave members of the same natural family with materially different amounts of land, without justification for that difference.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits discrimination between persons equally circumstanced. Following Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala, an artificial family definition combined with different ceiling standards may produce unconstitutional discrimination. The Court noted that the law was not protected by Article 31-A.
members.conclusion: The ceiling provision violated Article 14, and because it was the basis of the chapter on fixation of ceiling, that entire chapter had to fall.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: Persons brought a constitutional challenge to a law that imposed limits on land holdings.
predicates.artificial_family_definition: The law defined a family in a way that did not correspond to natural families recognized under personal law.
predicates.unequal_burdens_within_natural_families: Applying the family definition and ceiling left members of the same natural family with different land burdens, without an identified justification.

members.legal_issue: A compensation scheme that progressively reduces effective compensation as the landholder's net income increases violates equal protection when it discriminates between similarly situated persons.
material_facts: The law calculated compensation for acquired land using successive slabs of net annual income and lower multipliers for later slabs.
The resulting effective reduction in compensation increased as total net annual income increased.

The Court found the scheme's effect comparable to the discriminatory progressive cuts considered in Karimbil Kunhikoman; the State's comparison to higher income-tax rates on higher income slabs had already been rejected in that case.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits discriminatory treatment of similarly situated persons. The Court followed Karimbil Kunhikoman v. State of Kerala, which rejected justification of progressive reductions in compensation by analogy to higher income-tax rates on higher income slabs. The law was not protected by Article 31-A.
members.conclusion: The compensation provisions violated Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: Persons brought a constitutional challenge to a scheme for compensating landholders for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_uses_progressively_lower_mu: The scheme applied lower multipliers to successive higher slabs of a landholder's net income.
predicates.effective_compensation_cut_increases_wit: The scheme's effective reduction in total compensation grew as a landholder's net income increased.

members.legal_issue: Excluding debts from a debt-reduction scheme according to the identity of the creditor violates equality when that classification has no rational relationship to the scheme’s objective.
material_facts: The law aimed to reduce debts secured on property that had been resumed, because resumption reduced the property holders’ capacity to pay.
The law excluded debts owed to specified public bodies and other categories of creditors, while leaving other private debts within the scheme.
The excluded categories had no discernible common principle, and creditor identity had no rational relationship to the objective of reducing debts secured on resumed property.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia distinguishing the included group from those left out and that differentia has a rational relationship to the statute’s objective. The Court relied on this test and distinguished Manna Lal v. Collector of Jhalwar, which concerned a special facility for recovery of government-owned bank debts; it disagreed with the reasoning in Nand Ram Chhotey Lal v. Kishore Raman Singh and found Jamnalal Ramlal Kimtee v. Kishendas and State of Hyderabad unpersuasive because it did not address the required rational relationship.
members.conclusion: The creditor-based exclusions were invalid because no reasonable classification justified them under the equality guarantee.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and debt_relief_targets_resumed_property_debts and exclusions_turn_on_creditor_identity and (exemptions_have_no_common_principle or creditor_status_unrelated_to_relief_objective)

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law in a proceeding concerning debt relief.
predicates.debt_relief_targets_resumed_property_deb: The law sought to reduce debts secured on property taken over by the state, where that taking reduced the debtor’s capacity to pay.
predicates.exclusions_turn_on_creditor_identity: The law excluded debts according to the identity or category of the creditor.
predicates.exemptions_have_no_common_principle: The excluded creditor categories did not share a discernible principle distinguishing them from creditors whose debts remained covered.
predicates.creditor_status_unrelated_to_relief_obje: The identity or status of the creditor had no rational connection to the law’s objective of reducing debts secured on resumed property.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition law violates equal protection when it gives differently compensated treatment to similarly situated landowners without a reasonable relation to the object of acquisition.
material_facts: The general land-acquisition law permitted acquisition for public purposes with compensation based on market value, while the special law permitted acquisition for flood-control and erosion-prevention works using a different and substantially lower compensation method.
Landowners could lose land to the State under either law, but the purpose of acquisition did not provide a reasonable basis for the different treatment.
The Court rejected the classification between land acquired for flood-control purposes and land acquired for other public purposes as unrelated to the object of acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification and differential treatment only where substantial differences bear a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court relied on P. V. Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector, [1965] 1 SCR 614, which held that differential acquisition and compensation treatment for land acquired under different laws could violate Article 14.
members.conclusion: The special acquisition law violated Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law governing the acquisition of land.
predicates.similarly_situated_landowners_face_diffe: Landowners in materially similar circumstances receive different compensation treatment because their land is acquired under different legal regimes.
predicates.classification_lacks_relation_to_acquisi: The difference in treatment has no reasonable relation to the object of acquiring the land for the State.

members.legal_issue: Different compensation and review rules for landowners whose land is compulsorily acquired for a local authority violate equal protection when the acquiring authority is the government and the distinctions do not rest on a relevant classification.
material_facts: Land was compulsorily acquired by the Collector for a municipal authority and then transferred to that authority.

The challenged modifications excluded potential value from compensation, restricted access to compensation review unless security for costs was deposited, and initially excluded solatium for certain acquisitions.
Under the unmodified acquisition law, similarly situated landowners could receive more compensation and seek review without the challenged security requirement.
The government could acquire land for the same public purpose under either the unmodified law or the modified rules, resulting in different treatment of landowners.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits legislative classification only when it is based on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus with the legislative object. Different compensation or review rules cannot ordinarily be justified merely because land is acquired for a particular public purpose or under a different acquisition regime when the acquiring authority is the government and affected owners are similarly situated. The Court followed Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, [1973] 1 SCC 500. The Court also relied on sections 16, 17-A and 376, Schedule II, and section 372(1) of the U.P. Nagar Mahapalika Adhiniyam, 1959, in determining the acquiring authority and the effect of the challenged rules.
members.conclusion: The challenged modifications discriminated between similarly situated landowners and violated Article 14; the modifications were quashed.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_rules and government_acquires_for_local_authority and landowners_are_similarly_situated and modified_rules_reduce_compensation_or_review_rights and treatment_differs_without_relevant_classification

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenges the constitutionality of rules governing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.government_acquires_for_local_authority: The government compulsorily acquires land for a local authority and transfers the land to that authority.
predicates.landowners_are_similarly_situated: The affected landowners are similarly situated in relation to the acquisition.
predicates.modified_rules_reduce_compensation_or_re: The rules applied to the acquisition reduce compensation or restrict the landowners' ability to obtain review of the award.
predicates.treatment_differs_without_relevant_class: Landowners receive different treatment despite no relevant distinction that justifies the difference.

members.legal_issue: A special acquisition regime cannot deny statutory solatium to landowners when that denial discriminates from the treatment of owners whose land is acquired under the ordinary acquisition regime without a rational basis.
material_facts: The lands were compulsorily acquired for a public improvement purpose under an improvement-trust law.
Owners whose lands were acquired under the ordinary acquisition law were entitled to a statutory addition to market value for compulsory acquisition.
The replacement improvement-trust law excluded that addition for acquisitions under its regime.
The lands were not within the earlier law’s exception that denied solatium for certain land in declared congested or slum areas.
The acquisition proceedings were treated as having been taken under the replacement law, but the exclusion in that law deprived the owners of the statutory addition.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unequal treatment of owners whose land is compulsorily acquired where no rational classification with an intelligible differentia and a reasonable relation to the statutory object supports the distinction. Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act ordinarily provided solatium in addition to market value. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasiva Mudaliar, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, and N. B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector, which invalidated discriminatory compensation provisions. It distinguished Dalchand v. Delhi Improvement Trust because the acquisition and vesting there occurred before the Constitution, so no equality claim arose.
members.conclusion: The provision excluding statutory solatium was invalid under the equality guarantee, and the owners were entitled to solatium under section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_case and special_regime_acquisition and ordinary_regime_solarium_entitlement and special_regime_denies_solarium and no_rational_basis_for_distinction

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_case: A proceeding concerns land compulsorily acquired by public authority.
predicates.special_regime_acquisition: The land was acquired under a special regime rather than the ordinary acquisition regime.
predicates.ordinary_regime_solarium_entitlement: Owners whose land is acquired under the ordinary regime receive a statutory addition to market value because the acquisition is compulsory.
predicates.special_regime_denies_solarium: The special regime denies owners that statutory addition.
predicates.no_rational_basis_for_distinction: No rational classification related to the subject matter or purpose justifies treating the special-regime owners differently.

members.legal_issue: A law that treats similarly situated acquired properties differently violates equality when the distinction has no rational relation to the law’s objective.
material_facts: The state had issued notices in identical terms to 46 factories, and the factories were similarly situated for the purpose of the stated objective of avoiding unemployment among cashew workers.
The amendment placed ten factories in its schedule for acquisition but did not do so for the other 36 factories.

The different management bodies operating the two groups did not distinguish them in relation to the objective of avoiding worker unemployment; both groups involved unemployment concerns and potential financial loss to the government and the managing bodies.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only where it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court found no such distinction between the two groups of factories. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The distinction between the ten scheduled factories and the other 36 factories had no intelligible differentia rationally related to the objective and violated Article 14; the acquisition provision was therefore unconstitutional on this ground as well.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_acquisition_classification and affected_groups_similarly_situated and only_one_group_selected and group_difference_unrelated_to_object

predicates.equality_challenge_to_acquisition_classi: The case challenges a law that selects some acquired properties for different treatment on equality grounds.
predicates.affected_groups_similarly_situated: The properties in the groups are similarly situated in relation to the objective the law seeks to achieve.
predicates.only_one_group_selected: The law selects one group for the challenged treatment but excludes the comparable group.
predicates.group_difference_unrelated_to_object: Any difference between the groups does not rationally relate to the law’s stated objective.

members.legal_issue: Refusing to withdraw land from acquisition while granting withdrawal to similarly situated owners in the same acquisition proceedings is discriminatory when the different treatment has no valid basis.
material_facts: The owners sought withdrawal of their land from acquisition after the State had released land belonging to numerous other owners under the same acquisition proceedings and for the same public purpose.
Some of the other owners had vacant plots, and some had not challenged the acquisition; others had challenged it but their requests for release had not been recommended by the inspection committee.

Before the relevant later policy was adopted, the State had no uniform policy governing withdrawal, and that later policy had not been applied to the owners whose land was released in the same acquisition proceedings.
The State rejected the owners’ representations by relying on the later policy and did not allege that the comparable releases were unlawful, mistaken, fraudulent, or contrary to public interest.
The Court directed that land forming part of roads, common sites, or public utility areas would not be considered for release.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 requires fairness, consistency, and non-arbitrariness in State action, including discretionary decisions concerning withdrawal from acquisition. Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 empowers the Government to withdraw from acquisition before possession is taken and prescribes no particular procedure for doing so. A person has no right to repeat an unlawful benefit granted to someone else, but where the State has lawfully exercised its withdrawal power for similarly situated owners in the same acquisition, it must treat other similarly situated owners consistently and may not create artificial distinctions without a valid basis. The Court applied International Trading Co. v. Union of India (2003) 5 SCC 437 on reasoned and non-arbitrary State action; Sube Singh v. State of Haryana (2001) 7 SCC 545 on unreasonable classification; and the principles against negative equality discussed in Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain (2003) 5 SCC 437, Jalandhar Improvement Trust v. Sampuran Singh (1999) 3 SCC 494, Anand Buttons Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2005) 9 SCC 164, and Vishal Properties (P) Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2007) 11 SCC 172. Ved Prakash v. Ministry of Industry (2005) 9 SCC 164 was also considered concerning the State’s consideration of representations for withdrawal.
members.conclusion: The State’s rejection of the representations was discriminatory and unlawful. The rejection order was set aside, and the State was directed to issue orders concerning the owners’ land on the same terms and in the same manner as the comparable releases, excluding portions forming part of roads, common sites, or public utility areas.

rule.if: appeal_from_rejection_of_withdrawal_representation and same_acquisition_and_public_purpose and comparable_owners_received_withdrawal and state_relied_on_standard_not_used_for_comparators and no_claim_comparator_releases_were_unlawful and requested_land_not_in_public_utility_area

predicates.appeal_from_rejection_of_withdrawal_repr: The proceeding challenges the State’s rejection of a landowner’s request to withdraw land from acquisition.
predicates.same_acquisition_and_public_purpose: The landowner’s land and the comparator owners’ land were acquired in the same proceedings for the same public purpose.
predicates.comparable_owners_received_withdrawal: The State withdrew comparable owners’ land from acquisition, including land with similar circumstances.
predicates.state_relied_on_standard_not_used_for_co: The State rejected the landowner’s request using a decision-making standard that it had not applied when releasing the comparator owners’ land.
predicates.no_claim_comparator_releases_were_unlawf: The State did not claim that the comparator owners’ releases were unlawful, mistaken, fraudulent, or contrary to public interest.
predicates.requested_land_not_in_public_utility_are: The land for which equal withdrawal treatment is sought does not form part of a road, common site, or public utility area.

members.legal_issue: A special law applicable only in one State violates equality when its geographical classification lacks a rational connection to its stated objective and its procedures frustrate that objective.
material_facts: The challenged law applied only in one State, while a different legal process applied elsewhere in the country.

The stated objective was to identify and remove illegal migrants, but the challenged law imposed procedures that the Court found substantially less effective for that purpose than the process applicable elsewhere.

The law’s operation produced very few physical removals relative to the number of inquiries initiated, and the Court found that its provisions tended to benefit the people it was intended to identify and remove.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only where it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational nexus with the law’s object. The Court applied the dual test stated in Kangshari Haldar v. State of West Bengal and referred to Budhan Choudhry v. State of Bihar. It distinguished the proposition in In re The Special Courts Bill, 1978 and A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak because the objection was not merely that the special law offered greater safeguards, but that its procedures defeated its stated purpose.
members.conclusion: The law’s application only in the State lacked a rational nexus with its objective and violated Article 14.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_law and law_applies_only_in_one_region and stated_objective_is_detection_and_removal and procedure_frustrates_objective and generally_applicable_procedure_is_more_effective

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law.
predicates.law_applies_only_in_one_region: The challenged law applies in one geographic region while a different legal regime applies elsewhere in the country.
predicates.stated_objective_is_detection_and_remova: The law states that its purpose is to identify and remove people who entered or remain unlawfully.
predicates.procedure_frustrates_objective: The law’s procedures materially impede achievement of its stated purpose.
predicates.generally_applicable_procedure_is_more_e: The legal process applicable more generally is materially more effective at achieving the same purpose.

members.legal_issue: Exempting certain plantation crops from land-acquisition and ceiling rules while excluding comparable plantation crops violated equal protection, and the discriminatory plantation provisions could not be severed from the law as applied to the affected ryotwari lands.
material_facts: The law exempted plantations of specified crops from provisions concerning acquisition of landowners' interests and land ceilings, while areca and pepper plantations received no equivalent exemption.

The evidence before the Court showed that areca and pepper plantations could involve substantial investment, delayed returns and plantation-scale cultivation, including large and organized operations.
The State gave no sufficient reason for treating those crops differently from the exempted plantation crops in light of the objects of the law.
The plantation exemptions affected the operation of the law's principal acquisition and ceiling schemes.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14 and the classification principles summarized in Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia related to the law's object; the presumption of constitutionality cannot supply an undisclosed basis where none appears in the law or surrounding circumstances. The Court considered the land-reform objectives and the plantation-exemption criteria discussed in the Second and Third Five Year Plans. Because the legislature would not have intended the central acquisition and ceiling schemes to operate by breaking up the exempted plantations, the discriminatory provisions were not severable.
members.conclusion: The plantation provisions violated Article 14; they could not be severed from the rest of the law, which was therefore invalid insofar as it applied to the relevant ryotwari lands.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a land-reform law.
predicates.some_plantation_crops_exempted_but_compa: The law exempts some plantation crops from its acquisition or ceiling rules while leaving comparable plantation crops subject to them.
predicates.no_relevant_basis_for_crop_distinction: The record shows no intelligible distinction related to the law's purposes that justifies the different treatment.
predicates.plantation_exemptions_integral_to_law: The exemptions are integral to the operation of the law's principal acquisition and ceiling schemes and cannot be severed without defeating legislative intent.
predicates.law_invalid_as_applied_to_covered_ryotwa: The law is unconstitutional insofar as it applies to the affected ryotwari land.

members.legal_issue: A land ceiling based on separate individual and artificially defined family standards violated equal protection when it caused similarly situated landholders to surrender unequal amounts of land without justification.
material_facts: The law set one ceiling for an adult unmarried person and a different ceiling for a family defined by reference to a husband, wife and unmarried minor children or such of them as existed.
That definition did not correspond to the family forms recognized under the personal laws relevant to the State.
The different standards could cause persons with equal landholdings, including an adult unmarried person and a minor orphan, to retain different amounts of land.
The State provided no justification for the resulting difference.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits classifications that produce unequal treatment without a rational basis connected to the law's purpose. The Court examined the actual consequences of the ceiling scheme rather than its facial application to each defined category, and held that the artificial family definition combined with separate standards produced unjustified discrimination.
members.conclusion: The ceiling provision violated Article 14, and because it formed the basis of the entire ceiling chapter, that chapter was invalid in its application to the affected ryotwari lands.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The proceeding challenges a statutory land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.ceiling_uses_distinct_individual_and_fam: The scheme applies different land limits to individuals and families.
predicates.family_category_artificially_defined: The statutory family category does not correspond to the family forms relevant under applicable personal law.
predicates.equal_landholdings_produce_unequal_retai: The scheme causes persons with equal landholdings to retain different amounts of land, without a justification for the difference.
predicates.ceiling_scheme_unconstitutional: The land-ceiling scheme violates equal protection.

members.legal_issue: Progressively reducing compensation rates for larger property valuations, without a relevant basis connected to the law's purposes, discriminated between persons whose property was acquired.
material_facts: The law calculated compensation by applying progressively lower rates to higher slabs of purchase price or market value.
The reduction depended on the total valuation of the property, rather than a difference in the nature of the property being acquired.
The State relied on an analogy to progressive taxation, but the Court found no relevant basis for applying that principle to compensation for acquired property.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 requires an intelligible differentia rationally related to the law's objects. The majority held that progressive taxation principles did not justify paying different compensation rates for property acquired by the State merely because one person's property had a higher valuation. It relied on the reasoning of the Special Bench in Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar, which rejected progressive compensation rates as discriminatory. Justice Sarkar's separate opinion considered ability to bear loss a relevant basis and would have upheld the rates.
members.conclusion: The majority held that the progressive compensation cuts violated Article 14 and, because compensation provisions were pervasive, the law was invalid insofar as it applied to the affected ryotwari lands. Justice Sarkar dissented on the validity of the progressive compensation rates.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: The proceeding challenges a statutory compensation scheme for acquired property.
predicates.compensation_rate_decreases_as_property_: The scheme applies lower compensation rates to higher valuation slabs.
predicates.property_differs_only_in_extent_or_value: The acquired properties are of the same relevant kind and differ only in their size or valuation.
predicates.no_relevant_basis_for_different_rates: No intelligible basis connected to the law's purposes justifies the different compensation rates.
predicates.progressive_compensation_scheme_unconsti: The progressive compensation scheme violates equal protection.

members.legal_issue: A government release of acquired land that selectively favors particular owners without legal or constitutional justification violates the equality guarantee.
material_facts: Land was notified for acquisition for a public housing purpose.
Several years after the notification, the government released a small portion of the acquired land belonging to a particular family.
The stated justification that substantial buildings stood on the land was contradicted by the evidence, and comparable structures on other acquired land had not resulted in its release.
The release was found to be favouritism without legal or constitutional justification.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary and unjustified State action. The government’s release under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was invalid because it bestowed favourable treatment without a reasonable justification.
members.conclusion: The release order was non est because it violated Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns government proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.government_released_acquired_land: The government released land that had already been included in an acquisition.
predicates.selective_favour_without_justification: The release specially benefited particular owners without a supported legal or public-interest justification.

members.legal_issue: Injuries on accused persons do not, without a sufficient evidentiary basis in the circumstances, establish that they acted in private defence.
material_facts: The trial court relied on injuries to some accused persons to find that they had acted in private defence and acquitted them.
The High Court considered the sequence of events, the injuries to the deceased, the minor nature of most injuries to the accused, and the evidence identifying the accused as aggressors.
The Supreme Court held that the trial court had relied on the injuries without legal and admissible evidence establishing the claimed justification.
members.legal_principle: The right of private defence under Sections 96 and 100 of the Indian Penal Code must be supported by evidence and assessed in light of the circumstances. The existence of injuries on an accused, by itself, does not establish that the accused were entitled to cause death in private defence.
members.conclusion: The trial court was wrong to treat the injuries on the accused as sufficient to justify the deaths in private defence; the High Court’s rejection of that basis was upheld.

predicates.criminal_case_involving_private_defence: The criminal proceeding concerns a claim that the accused acted in private defence.
predicates.accused_had_injuries: One or more accused persons had injuries.
predicates.circumstances_identified_accused_as_aggr: The surrounding circumstances showed that the accused initiated or carried out the attack.
predicates.no_evidence_established_justifying_defen: No legal and admissible evidence established that the accused were justified in using the force claimed.

members.legal_issue: An accused who initiates an armed attack cannot rely on private defence against the response to that attack when the alleged victim is found to have been unarmed.
material_facts: The accused came armed to the complainant party’s home, abused and challenged its occupants, and initiated the confrontation.
The deceased was attacked at the start of the ensuing fight; the courts rejected the claim that he had first attacked an accused and found him unarmed.
The injured son participated in the fight after his father had been attacked, but the accused who inflicted his grievous injury had been part of the aggressing group.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the law of private defence under the Indian Penal Code to the facts found by the courts below. Since the accused were the aggressors and the deceased’s alleged prior attack was disbelieved, neither private defence nor the question of exceeding that right arose. The Court relied on the factual reasons given by the High Court and cited no earlier case for this issue.
members.conclusion: The plea of private defence was unavailable to the accused who attacked the deceased and to the accused who inflicted the grievous injury on the deceased’s son.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by an accused challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_initiated_armed_confrontation: The accused arrived armed and initiated the confrontation that led to the violence.
predicates.alleged_victim_did_not_first_attack: The court found that the alleged victim did not first attack the accused.

members.legal_issue: The right of private defence does not justify a fatal attack where the accused were the aggressors and faced no imminent danger requiring defensive force.
material_facts: The deceased was cleaning disputed land and had only a broomstick; the evidence showed that he committed no overt act and posed no threat to the accused or their property.
The accused arrived with the principal assailant, carrying lethal weapons, and the principal assailant shot the deceased and his brother.
The courts found that the accused were the aggressors and that there was no necessity to use force to avert an imminent danger.
members.legal_principle: Sections 96 and 97 IPC recognize private defence of the body and property, subject to the restrictions in Section 99; Section 100 permits causing death only in specified circumstances, including an assault reasonably causing apprehension of grievous hurt. Under Sections 102 and 105, the right begins when a reasonable apprehension of danger arises and continues while it lasts. Private defence is defensive, not aggressive or retaliatory, and the force used must not be unduly disproportionate. The accused bear the burden of establishing the plea on a balance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. The Court relied on Jai Dev v. State of Punjab, Laxman Sahu v. State of Orissa, Dharam v. State of Haryana, Vidhya Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and the other authorities cited in its discussion.
members.conclusion: The appellants failed to establish a right of private defence, and their claim was rejected.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_raises_private_defence and accused_party_are_aggressors and no_imminent_danger_to_body_or_property and accused_use_fatal_force

predicates.criminal_appeal_raises_private_defence: The accused appeal a criminal conviction and rely on a claim that their conduct was defensive.
predicates.accused_party_are_aggressors: The accused initiated or escalated the violence rather than responding defensively to an attack.
predicates.no_imminent_danger_to_body_or_property: The accused faced no imminent threat of harm to a person or property that required immediate defensive action.
predicates.accused_use_fatal_force: The accused used force that caused a person’s death.

members.legal_issue: The use of potentially lethal force to protect disputed land was not justified as an exercise of the right of private defence on the evidence presented.
material_facts: Revenue records named the accused side, but the entries were contested and proceedings concerning them were pending.
The opposing group claimed possession, and evidence accepted by the High Court rebutted the presumption arising from the revenue entries.
The High Court found no evidence that the opposing group was armed with firearms or had fired first; the items said to be empty cartridges were found to be plastic pieces.
No member of the accused group had sustained an injury.
The accused used weapons capable of causing death, and the Supreme Court found no error in the High Court’s assessment of the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 117 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1939, a revenue entry gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of possession, which may be displaced by evidence. Even assuming a person is in possession of land, that fact does not justify using firearms or other weapons capable of causing death merely against persons attempting to trespass. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The appellants’ claim of private defence was rejected, and the convictions and sentences upheld by the High Court were affirmed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by convicted persons challenging their convictions.
predicates.deadly_force_used_to_protect_land: The accused used firearms or other weapons capable of causing death in an incident connected with protecting land.
predicates.opponents_not_proved_armed_or_to_have_fi: The evidence did not establish that the opposing group was armed with lethal weapons or fired first.

members.legal_issue: An accused cannot establish a right of private defence merely from an injury where the evidence does not support a reasonable apprehension of danger and instead shows that the accused attacked an unarmed person.
material_facts: The dying declaration described the accused fetching a spear from his house and attacking the unarmed deceased.
The accused had a sutured injury to his lip and chin, but the evidence did not establish that the deceased had caused it; the timing and cause of the missing or loose teeth were also uncertain.
The Court considered that the lip injury could have resulted when the accused fell during the deceased’s resistance.
The evidence did not show that the accused had a reasonable apprehension of danger to his life from the deceased.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the claim of private defence against the circumstances shown by the evidence, including who initiated the attack and whether there was a reasonable apprehension of danger. It relied on no cited provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not support an inference that the accused acted in private defence.

predicates.private_defence_issue_in_criminal_convic: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction in which the accused’s claim of private defence is considered.
predicates.accused_initiated_attack_on_unarmed_pers: The evidence shows that the accused initiated an attack on an unarmed person.
predicates.accused_fetched_dangerous_weapon: The accused obtained a dangerous weapon before carrying out the attack.
predicates.accused_injury_not_linked_to_victim_atta: The evidence does not establish that the victim caused the accused’s injury during an attack by the victim.
predicates.no_evidence_of_reasonable_apprehension_o: The evidence does not show that the accused reasonably apprehended danger from the victim.

members.legal_issue: The presence of injuries on an accused and a family member does not, without support from the surrounding circumstances, establish a claim of private defence.
material_facts: The accused and another family member had pellet injuries, and the family member also had simple injuries.
The family member’s injuries were superficial, and the accused were not shown to have surrendered themselves at the time those injuries were allegedly inflicted.
The accused were arrested and medically examined weeks after the occurrence, while the family member was examined several days after it.
The Court found that the injuries alone did not make the defence probable in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the nature, timing, and surrounding circumstances of the injuries, and held that the mere presence of injuries was insufficient to make the defence probable in this case. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The injuries on the accused and their family member, standing alone, did not establish or make probable the plea of private defence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_or_family_member_injured and injuries_only_support_for_private_defence and injury_circumstances_do_not_corrobate_defence

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_or_family_member_injured: The accused or a member of the accused’s family had injuries associated with the occurrence.
predicates.injuries_only_support_for_private_defenc: The injuries are the only material relied on to support the plea of private defence.
predicates.injury_circumstances_do_not_corrobate_de: The nature or timing of the injuries and the surrounding conduct do not support the claimed defensive account.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence is not established where the evidence shows that the accused were the aggressors and the accused's account of his injuries lacks supporting material.
material_facts: The accused claimed that one of them opened a water outlet and was assaulted by the deceased and an eyewitness, prompting him to act in private defence.
The eyewitness testified that the accused initiated the assault and that the deceased and the eyewitness retaliated.
The eyewitness’s account was found reliable, and there was no material supporting the accused’s account of how he sustained his injuries.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the private-defence claim against the reliable evidence of the incident and the absence of supporting material for the accused’s account of his injuries. The judgment cites no specific provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The accused were the aggressors, and the deceased and the eyewitness were justified in assaulting the injured accused in exercise of their right of private defence; the accused’s private-defence claim was rejected.

predicates.homicide_assault_case: The proceeding concerns an assault that resulted in a death.
predicates.reliable_evidence_shows_accused_initiate: Reliable evidence shows that the accused initiated the assault.
predicates.accused_account_of_injuries_lacks_suppor: The accused’s account of how he sustained his injuries has no supporting material.
predicates.accused_private_defence_claim_is_rejecte: The accused’s claim that the assault was in private defence is rejected.

members.legal_issue: A claim that the complainant side was the aggressor is not accepted when it is unsupported by evidence and the prosecution evidence shows that the accused side was armed while the complainant side was not.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the complainant side came to demolish a boundary wall and that a person in a crowd fired the fatal shot.
No person whose boundary wall was allegedly demolished, or person connected with the alleged place of worship, testified to support that account.
The evidence did not show that the complainant side was armed, while the accused side carried a firearm and other weapons; the complainant side sustained more serious injuries.
members.legal_principle: The court assesses a claim of aggression against the evidence supporting it, the weapons carried by each side, and the nature of the injuries; an unsupported defence account does not displace established prosecution evidence.
members.conclusion: The claim that the complainant side was the aggressor was baseless and was rejected.

predicates.accused_side_armed_with_weapons: The evidence shows that the accused side carried weapons during the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence is not established by a speculative account contradicted by eyewitness and physical evidence.
material_facts: The defence claimed that the deceased entered a home, attacked a woman and attempted to outrage her modesty, and that the fatal injuries were inflicted in self-defence.
Eyewitnesses described the deceased being taken into the home and assaulted by several people.
Blood was found in the courtyard and inside the room where the body was found, corroborating the account of an assault in those locations.
The appellant was found at the scene near the deceased and a bloodstained knife was seized from him.
The appellant's account that he arrived after the occurrence and was attacked by the witnesses was inconsistent with the proposed account of a defensive assault.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the defence account against the eyewitness evidence and corroborating circumstances. It found the suggested entry and assault by the deceased speculative and inherently improbable; it identified no earlier case or statutory provision as the basis for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The private-defence contention was rejected, and the conviction was upheld.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution for a criminal offence.

predicates.eyewitness_account_of_assault: Witnesses describe the accused or others assaulting the alleged victim rather than acting defensively.
predicates.physical_evidence_supports_assault: Physical circumstances at the scene corroborate the account that the alleged victim was assaulted.
predicates.defence_account_is_implausible: The accused's account is inconsistent with the evidence or is inherently improbable in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A claim of defence of person fails when the circumstances do not reasonably indicate an imminent danger to the accused.
material_facts: The accused arrived armed with firearms, while the prosecution evidence indicated that the opposing group was unarmed.
The opposing group was attempting to resolve the land dispute through intermediaries, and some of its members were leaving when shots were fired.

Shots were fired at close range in some instances, but the evidence did not establish that the groups were all at such close quarters as to create a reasonable belief that the accused's lives were in danger.
The accused's injuries were simple and not incised, and shots were fired and people chased even as the opposing group fled.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the circumstances gave the accused a reasonable apprehension of danger warranting defence of person. It cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The circumstances did not give the accused reasonable cause to fire in defence of their persons.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and accused_armed and opposing_group_fleeing_when_shots_fired and no_reasonable_apprehension_of_imminent_danger

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction in which defence of person is claimed.
predicates.accused_armed: The accused entered the incident armed with weapons.
predicates.opposing_group_fleeing_when_shots_fired: Members of the opposing group were fleeing when shots were fired at them.
predicates.no_reasonable_apprehension_of_imminent_d: The circumstances do not reasonably indicate that the accused faced imminent danger to their persons.

members.legal_issue: The right of private defence does not justify a deadly attack in a land dispute when the opposing party is unarmed and either has possession or entered without the intent required for criminal trespass.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence showed that the complainant party had cultivated the land and had sown crops on it; the trial court found that it was in possession.
The accused were already ploughing the land and were armed with firearms and lathis when the deceased and another person arrived unarmed and questioned them.
The accused shot the deceased and assaulted him and the other person with lathis.

Even on the alternative assumption that the accused were in possession, there was no evidence that the complainants entered with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the persons in possession.
members.legal_principle: Sections 97 and 99 IPC govern the right and restrictions on private defence of person and property. Under Section 441 IPC, entry on property is criminal trespass only if accompanied by the specified intent. Section 103 IPC does not permit causing death merely to resist ordinary criminal trespass; the judgment also refers to Section 104 IPC. Relying on Rajinder v. State of Haryana, (1995) 5 SCC 187, the Court held that the required intent for criminal trespass must be established from the facts and circumstances, and that an armed, premeditated murderous attack in these circumstances was not justified as private defence.
members.conclusion: The accused could not rely on the right of private defence to justify the attack.

rule.if: land_dispute_assault_case and accused_armed_and_prepared and complainants_unarmed and (complainants_in_possession or complainants_lacked_trespass_intent)

predicates.complainants_lacked_trespass_intent: The opposing persons entered or approached the land without intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy a person in possession.

members.legal_issue: The right to defend property does not justify using deadly force against an unarmed trespasser who poses no threat of death or grievous hurt.
material_facts: The deceased entered the shop during a dispute over construction of a partition wall, and the court considered it likely that he was committing criminal trespass.
The court found no justification for concluding that the deceased was armed or intended to injure the appellant or his brother-in-law.

The appellant used a knife to inflict two fatal wounds to the deceased’s chest, although the circumstances did not create an apprehension that death or grievous hurt would be caused to the appellant or his brother-in-law.
members.legal_principle: A person may use force to remove a trespasser from property, but the court held that deadly force exceeded that right in the circumstances found here, where the trespasser was unarmed and posed no threat of death or grievous hurt. The judgment refers to Sections 302 and 304(1) of the Indian Penal Code in setting out the conviction and its replacement; it relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The appellant had a right to remove the deceased from the shop, but exceeded his right of private defence of property by using the knife with deadly effect.

predicates.murder_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.

predicates.intruder_unarmed: The court found no basis to conclude that the deceased was armed.
predicates.no_threat_of_death_or_grievous_hurt: The court found no apprehension that the deceased would cause death or grievous hurt to the accused or another person being defended.
predicates.deadly_force_used: The accused used a dangerous weapon with deadly effect against the trespasser.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence may be rejected where the courts have assessed the circumstances and the manner of the assault, found the claimants to be the aggressors, and no basis is shown to disturb that finding on appeal.
material_facts: The accused claimed a right to defend their person and property, asserting that the opposing group had trespassed on land they possessed.
The trial court and the High Court considered the circumstances of the incident and the manner in which blows were inflicted when assessing the private-defence claim.
Both courts rejected the claim, and no justification was shown for disturbing their finding.
members.legal_principle: The legitimacy of private defence was assessed in light of the evidence about the setting of the incident, the manner in which the injuries were inflicted, and who was the aggressor. The Court found no justification to disturb the concurrent factual assessment. No provision or earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the plea of private defence was upheld.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and private_defence_claimed and courts_assessed_incident_circumstances and concurrent_finding_claimants_were_aggressors and no_basis_to_disturb_finding

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.private_defence_claimed: The accused claim that they acted to defend themselves or their property.
predicates.courts_assessed_incident_circumstances: The courts consider the circumstances of the incident and the manner in which the injuries were inflicted.
predicates.concurrent_finding_claimants_were_aggres: The trial court and the appellate court find that the persons claiming private defence were the aggressors.
predicates.no_basis_to_disturb_finding: No sufficient basis is shown for disturbing the courts’ factual assessment on appeal.

members.legal_issue: An unexplained injury to an accused, without circumstances establishing a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, does not establish a right of private defence permitting fatal force.
material_facts: The accused relied on an injury suffered by a co-accused, which the prosecution had not explained.

The evidence established a quarrel between the groups, but the circumstances did not establish that the accused faced a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt requiring the use of fatal force.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 96–100 and 102 of the Indian Penal Code, private defence is preventive, not punitive, and the right to cause death is limited to circumstances giving reasonable grounds to apprehend death or grievous hurt; Section 99 limits force to what is necessary. The court applied Deo Narain v. State of U.P., Bishna Alias Bhiswadeb Mahato v. State of W.B., Surendra v. State of Maharashtra, Surendra Singh @ Bittu v. State of Uttaranchal, Siva Kumar v. State by Inspector of Police, and Hafiz v. State of U.P. An accused may rely on the circumstances of the case without examining defence witnesses, but the facts must make the plea probable.
members.conclusion: The plea of private defence was not established.

predicates.criminal_appeal_with_private_defence_cla: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which the accused claims to have acted in private defence.
predicates.accused_or_associate_injured: The accused or an associate suffered an injury during the incident.
predicates.evidence_of_reasonable_apprehension_of_d: The circumstances provide evidence that the accused reasonably apprehended death or grievous hurt.

members.legal_issue: A plea of private defence is not established where the accused's account is not probable in light of the circumstances and the prosecution evidence.
material_facts: The accused said that members of the victim's party attacked him and damaged his tractor, but the Court found the account improbable.
The accused's injuries were simple and superficial, and the medical evidence did not establish that they were inflicted during the occurrence.
No lathi or spear was found at the scene, and the Court found no reason for the alleged attackers to have carried those weapons to the field.
The Court found that the accused had gone home to obtain a gun after a protest about damage to a newly sown crop, and then fired twice, the second time after reloading.
The courts below had rejected the defence account and accepted the prosecution case; the Supreme Court found no reason to differ.
members.legal_principle: An accused must make a private-defence plea probable by reference to the circumstances and evidence; a plea that does not preponderate against the prosecution case does not discharge that burden. The Court relied on the concurrent findings of the courts below and the evidence in the record. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this application.
members.conclusion: The accused failed to make the plea of private defence probable. The prosecution case stood proved, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and accused_raises_private_defence and injuries_do_not_support_attack_account and alleged_weapons_not_found and prosecution_evidence_supports_deliberate_shooting

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a criminal case against the appellant's conviction.

predicates.injuries_do_not_support_attack_account: The accused's injuries do not reliably establish that the alleged attack occurred as described.

predicates.private_defence_not_established_and_conv: The plea of private defence is not established and the conviction remains in force.

members.legal_issue: The accused did not establish that their use of force was justified by a right of private defence.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the opposing side had initiated the assault and that their own injuries showed they acted in private defence.
The occurrence took place in the opposing side's agricultural field, where the accused came armed with weapons.
The injured eyewitness's account and the deceased witness's statement described the accused initiating the attack and inflicting injuries on the deceased and others.
The deceased woman was unarmed and did not participate in the assault; she was fatally injured while intervening.
The accused's injuries did not establish that the opposing side had started the assault, and the Court considered the surrounding circumstances and medical evidence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code govern private defence. Under Sections 96, 97 and 100, force, including force causing death in the circumstances specified by Section 100, may be justified when there is an immediate necessity to avert an impending danger not created by the person claiming the right. The right is preventive, not retributive, and its existence is assessed from the occurrence and surrounding circumstances, including who began the assault. The accused bears the burden of establishing the plea but may rely on prosecution evidence. The Court relied on Laxman Sahu v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The accused failed to discharge their burden of showing that they killed the deceased in exercise of a right of private defence.

members.legal_issue: An accused’s claim of acting in defence of a person is not established when the court finds the asserted attack and the accused’s account of the incident unconvincing.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the deceased fired at him and struck him with the firearm, prompting him to use his weapon in self-defence.
The asserted firearm defect was unsupported by evidence, and the account of the incident given by the accused was not accepted as convincing.

The court found the prosecution and defence accounts of the incident’s origin and manner unsatisfactory, but was unable to find that the deceased’s injuries were inflicted in defence of the accused’s person.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed whether the evidence established the claimed defensive attack and concluded that it did not. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The court did not accept that the accused injured the deceased in exercise of the right of private defence of person.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence is not made out when the account that the complainant side attacked first is improbable and is inconsistent with the injuries and other circumstances.
material_facts: The defence claimed that several people from the complainant side, armed with weapons, attacked the accused at their house.
No injuries were found on the accused side.
The deceased and two people who went to his aid were injured, while the other alleged members of the attacking group were not injured.
The prosecution witnesses’ presence at the scene was admitted in part by the defence.
members.legal_principle: A plea of private defence must be assessed against the surrounding circumstances, including whether the claimed attack is plausible and whether the presence or absence of injuries supports that account.
members.conclusion: The defence account that the complainant side was the aggressor was rejected, and private defence was not established.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence does not succeed where the evidence shows that the injured persons had possession, were unarmed and peacefully working, and were attacked by armed persons, while the accused persons’ injuries were simple.
material_facts: The injured persons had been given possession of the disputed land before the incident and were carrying out agricultural work there.
The injured persons were unarmed and were peacefully working when the accused persons arrived armed and attacked them.
The attack caused grievous injuries, including the loss of the injured person’s hand from the wrist.
The accused persons’ injuries were simple.
members.legal_principle: A right of private defence may be inferred from surrounding facts and circumstances even if it was not specifically raised in the accused’s statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Whether the right is established depends on the evidence, including possession and the nature of the injuries sustained. The Court relied on Vidya Singh v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, Sikandar Singh v. State of Bihar, and State of Rajasthan v. Manoj Kumar.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish a right of private defence, and the conviction for the grievous injury offence was upheld.

members.legal_issue: A pending suit for injunction may be amended before trial to seek declaration of title and recovery of possession when the amendment changes the relief but does not alter the suit’s basic structure.
material_facts: The plaintiff had filed a suit seeking a permanent injunction concerning agricultural land, and the defendant disputed the plaintiff’s possession.
Before trial, the plaintiff sought to amend the plaint, alleging that the defendant had dispossessed him during the suit and seeking declaration of title and recovery of possession.
The court found that the amendment did not alter the basic structure of the suit, would help determine the real controversy, and could avoid a separate suit and multiplicity of proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 CPC empowers a court to permit amendments needed to determine the real questions in controversy. As stated in Mst. Rukhmabai v. Lala Laxminarayan, AIR 1960 335, a suit should not automatically be dismissed for omission of an appropriate relief where the plaintiff seeks to amend. Pre-trial amendments are generally allowed more liberally because the opposing party has an opportunity to meet the amended case; delay alone is not a ground for refusal. The court considers prejudice in the circumstances of the particular case.
members.conclusion: The amendment should be allowed, subject to payment of costs and protection against depriving the defendant of any prescriptive rights that may have accrued.

rule.if: pending_suit_amendment and amendment_before_trial and basic_structure_unchanged and relief_changes_only and amendment_resolves_real_controversy and amendment_avoids_separate_proceeding

predicates.pending_suit_amendment: A party sought to amend pleadings in a civil suit that was still pending.
predicates.amendment_before_trial: The amendment was sought before the trial commenced.
predicates.basic_structure_unchanged: The proposed amendment left the basic structure of the existing suit unchanged.
predicates.relief_changes_only: The proposed amendment changed the relief sought without changing the suit’s basic structure.
predicates.amendment_resolves_real_controversy: The proposed amendment would assist in determining the real questions in controversy between the parties.
predicates.amendment_avoids_separate_proceeding: Allowing the proposed amendment would avoid the need for a separate proceeding and reduce multiplicity of proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended before trial to add particulars supporting an existing claim, including by adding persons connected with the alleged payments, when the amendment does not change the cause of action or unfairly prejudice the opposing party.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an agreement concerning a share in property and alleged that consideration had been paid.
The original plaint asserted that the full consideration under the agreement had been paid but did not set out the details of how the money was paid.
The amendment sought to explain the mode of payment and to add proposed plaintiffs and defendants associated with the payments.
The amendment application was filed before trial commenced.

The courts below allowed only part of the requested amendment, and the Supreme Court found that the permitted changes supplied details supporting the existing payment contention without changing the cause of action or prejudicing the defendants.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rules 2 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 require pleadings to state material facts and authorize just amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy. Amendment is not a matter of right, but courts should generally adopt a liberal rather than hyper-technical approach to bona fide, legitimate and necessary amendments, particularly where prejudice can be compensated by costs. The court should consider whether the amendment changes the nature of the case, introduces a new cause of action, causes irremediable prejudice, or defeats limitation. These principles are drawn from Rajkumar Gurawara (Dead) Through L.Rs. v. S.K. Sarwagi & Company Private Limited and Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons. Order I Rule 1 concerns who may be joined as plaintiffs.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed to the extent permitted by the courts below; it supplied supporting details rather than changing the cause of action, and the objection that the proposed plaintiffs were not parties to the agreement did not warrant setting aside that order.

rule.if: civil_suit_amendment_application and filed_before_trial and original_pleading_laid_foundation and amendment_adds_supporting_payment_details and does_not_change_cause_of_action and does_not_cause_irremediable_prejudice

predicates.civil_suit_amendment_application: A party applied to amend pleadings in a civil suit.
predicates.filed_before_trial: The amendment application was filed before the trial commenced.
predicates.original_pleading_laid_foundation: The original pleading already stated the essential basis of the claim that the proposed amendment supported.
predicates.amendment_adds_supporting_payment_detail: The proposed amendment adds particulars about how payments relating to the existing claim were made.
predicates.does_not_change_cause_of_action: The proposed amendment does not introduce a different cause of action.
predicates.does_not_cause_irremediable_prejudice: Allowing the amendment does not cause the opposing party prejudice that cannot be adequately remedied.

members.legal_issue: An amendment that only supplies further particulars supporting an existing claim is not barred by limitation merely because those particulars are added after the original pleading.
material_facts: The original plaint alleged that the full consideration under the agreement had been paid but did not explain the mode of payment.
The proposed amendment supplied details of payments made before the agreement and alleged that the payments were made through nominees and treated as payments to the contracting defendant.
The Supreme Court concluded that the amendment explained the existing payment contention and did not alter the cause of action.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, limitation is a relevant consideration in deciding an amendment application; as stated in Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons, courts should generally decline an amendment if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation on the date of the application. Here, the amendment supplied particulars supporting the existing claim and did not introduce a new cause of action, so the limitation objection failed.
members.conclusion: The amendment was not barred by limitation.

predicates.civil_suit_amendment_application: A party applied to amend pleadings in a civil suit.
