predicates.amendment_adds_particulars_to_existing_c: The amendment supplies further particulars supporting a claim already made in the pleading.
predicates.does_not_introduce_new_cause_of_action: The amendment does not introduce a new cause of action.

members.legal_issue: A proposed plaint amendment should be permitted where the suit remains at the pre-trial stage, the amendment does not change the nature of the suit, and the procedural history explains why the application was made when it was.
material_facts: The suit had initially been dismissed as not maintainable before trial and was later remanded for decision on the merits.
After remand, the plaintiff applied to amend the plaint; the trial had not begun.
The proposed amendment did not change the nature of the suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court considered that the suit was still at its initial stage, the proposed amendment did not change the nature of the suit, and the procedural history meant the application could not be treated as belated. In those circumstances, the courts should have taken a liberal approach. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The application to amend the plaint should have been allowed, subject to payment of costs; the defendant was to have an opportunity to make consequential amendments to its written statement.

rule.if: application_to_amend_in_pending_suit and suit_at_pretrial_stage and amendment_preserves_suit_nature and application_follows_remand_after_earlier_maintainability_dismissal

predicates.application_to_amend_in_pending_suit: A party to a pending civil suit applied to amend its pleading.
predicates.suit_at_pretrial_stage: The suit had not yet reached trial.
predicates.amendment_preserves_suit_nature: The proposed amendment did not change the nature of the suit.
predicates.application_follows_remand_after_earlier: The suit had been dismissed as not maintainable before trial, remanded for trial, and the amendment application was made after remand.

members.legal_issue: A plaint in a specific-performance suit may be amended to add an omitted readiness-and-willingness averment when the amendment completes the existing claim without causing irremediable prejudice.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued to enforce an agreement to sell property, alleging part payment and possession, after the defendant failed to execute the sale deed following receipt of the required permission.
The original plaint did not specifically allege that the plaintiff was and had always been ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement.
The defendant objected that the suit was not maintainable, and that issue was set for preliminary determination.

The plaintiff sought to amend the plaint to add the readiness-and-willingness averment; the trial court rejected the request, and the High Court upheld that decision because the request was made after limitation and would disturb a vested right.
The proposed amendment added no new cause of action and was intended to complete the existing claim for specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy should generally be allowed if they do not work injustice to the other side. An amendment should be refused where the other party would suffer an injury that cannot be compensated in costs. The possibility that a fresh suit on an amended claim would be time-barred is a factor in exercising discretion, not a limit on the court's power to allow an amendment in the interests of justice. Here, the amendment merely completed the existing cause of action by adding the averment required by Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and introduced no fresh cause of action. The Court relied on Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil and L.J. Leach & Co. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., and distinguished Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley, where a decree had been granted on an agreement different from the one pleaded by the plaintiff.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the lower courts' orders were set aside, and the amendment was permitted.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and amendment_application_pending and amendment_needed_for_real_controversy and opponent_would_suffer_no_irremediable_injury and (not fresh_suit_on_amended_claim_time_barred or amendment_adds_no_new_cause_of_action)

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.amendment_application_pending: The plaintiff applied to amend the plaint while the suit was pending.
predicates.amendment_needed_for_real_controversy: The proposed amendment supplied an omitted averment needed to complete the plaintiff's existing claim.
predicates.opponent_would_suffer_no_irremediable_in: The amendment would not cause the opposing party an injury that could not be compensated or otherwise addressed.
predicates.fresh_suit_on_amended_claim_time_barred: A fresh suit asserting the claim in the proposed amended form would be barred by limitation when the amendment was sought.
predicates.amendment_adds_no_new_cause_of_action: The proposed amendment did not introduce a cause of action different from the one already pleaded.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended to add an alternative relief and inconsistent pleas when the amendment does not change the cause of action or materially affect the relief.
material_facts: The claimants sued for specific performance of an agreement of reconveyance and sought to amend the plaint to plead that the sale and reconveyance documents formed a single transaction in the nature of a mortgage by conditional sale.
The proposed amendment added an alternative prayer for redemption of the mortgage.
The trial court rejected the amendment, and the High Court upheld that decision on the ground that the amendment would change the nature of the suit and its cause of action.
The Supreme Court examined the original reconveyance document, whose recitals supported the claimants’ contention.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 16 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as identified in the judgment, a plaintiff may plead inconsistent pleas and seek alternative relief. An amendment may be allowed where it does not change the cause of action or materially affect the relief. The judgment cites no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The amendment was allowed because the claimants could plead inconsistent alternative pleas, and the amendment neither changed the cause of action nor materially affected the relief.

rule.if: amendment_appeal and alternative_relief_sought and amendment_leaves_cause_of_action_unchanged and amendment_does_not_materially_affect_relief and document_recitals_support_pleaded_transaction

predicates.amendment_appeal: The claimant appealed after a court refused an application to amend the pleading.
predicates.alternative_relief_sought: The claimant sought to add a remedy as an alternative to the remedy already claimed.
predicates.amendment_leaves_cause_of_action_unchang: The proposed amendment left the existing basis of the claim unchanged.
predicates.amendment_does_not_materially_affect_rel: The proposed amendment did not materially alter the relief sought.
predicates.document_recitals_support_pleaded_transa: The claimant produced a document whose recitals supported the pleaded account of the transaction.

members.legal_issue: A pleading may be amended after the limitation period has expired when the amendment corrects a defect without introducing a new case or changing the relief sought, and does not cause injustice that cannot be compensated.
material_facts: A suit seeking a declaration of entitlement to possession was brought after an obstruction-removal application was dismissed.
The original pleading relied on an earlier possession decree but did not state the particular facts supporting the plaintiff’s title against the obstructing defendant.
The proposed amendment supplied particulars of the asserted title and explained the relationship between the defendant and the property; it did not change the relief sought.
The defendant had objected to the lack of particulars before the amendment was requested, and the Court found that the amendment did not take him by surprise or require him to meet a new claim.
The amendment request was made after the limitation period for the suit had expired, and the appellate court allowed it subject to terms including costs.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court has discretion to allow amendments necessary to determine the real controversy, provided they do not work injustice to the other side. Expiry of limitation is a relevant factor, but does not remove the court’s power to allow an amendment. An amendment should generally be refused where it sets up a fresh time-barred claim that deprives the other party of a defence that cannot be compensated by costs. The Court applied Charan Das v. Amir Khan, followed L. J. Leach & Co. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., and approved Batchelor J.’s observations in Kisandas Rupchand v. Rachappa Vithoba. The suit arose under Order XXI, rule 103, following proceedings under rules 97 and 99 of the Code.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed notwithstanding that the limitation period had expired, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: pleading_amendment_request and limitation_period_expired and amendment_supplies_missing_particulars and amendment_preserves_claim and amendment_preserves_relief and opponent_not_surprised and prejudice_compensable_by_costs

predicates.pleading_amendment_request: A party requested amendment of a pleading in a civil suit.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The limitation period for bringing the relevant suit had expired before the amendment was requested.
predicates.amendment_supplies_missing_particulars: The proposed amendment supplied particulars missing from the original pleading about the factual basis of the claim.
predicates.amendment_preserves_claim: The proposed amendment did not introduce a new case or a fresh claim.
predicates.amendment_preserves_relief: The proposed amendment did not change the nature of the relief sought.
predicates.opponent_not_surprised: The opposing party was not taken by surprise by the proposed amendment and did not have to meet a new claim.
predicates.prejudice_compensable_by_costs: Any disadvantage caused to the opposing party could be addressed by costs rather than depriving that party of an uncompensable defence.

members.legal_issue: A remand is unnecessary when an amendment merely formalizes relief supported by facts already pleaded and any needed response can be obtained without restarting proceedings.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had pleaded the facts on which relief for the institution’s benefit could be granted, although they had not sought that relief in proper form.

The High Court permitted an amendment clarifying that the suit was brought for the institution by its de facto managers, then set aside the trial decree and remanded the suit to allow a supplementary written statement.
The Supreme Court considered the amendment purely formal and said the High Court could have called for a reply and determined whether further proceedings were needed.
members.legal_principle: Where an amendment is formal and the facts supporting the properly framed relief are already pleaded, a remand is not required merely to allow a response; the appellate court can call for the response and determine whether further proceedings are necessary. No earlier cases or statutory provisions were relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the remand because it was unnecessary; the High Court should have obtained any required reply itself and decided whether further proceedings were warranted.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_remand_in_civil_suit and amendment_is_formal and supporting_facts_are_already_pleaded and any_needed_reply_can_be_obtained_by_appellate_court

predicates.appeal_challenges_remand_in_civil_suit: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order that remanded a civil suit.
predicates.amendment_is_formal: The amendment changes the form or clarification of the claim rather than introducing a materially new factual basis.
predicates.supporting_facts_are_already_pleaded: The facts necessary to support the properly framed relief are already set out in the pleadings.
predicates.any_needed_reply_can_be_obtained_by_appe: The opposing party’s response to the amendment can be obtained and considered by the appellate court.

members.legal_issue: A pleading amendment adding a relief should be allowed when it does not change the suit’s nature, deprive the opposing party of an accrued limitation right, or cause serious injustice that cannot be compensated by costs.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to amend the plaint to add a relief for recovery of possession.
The District Judge found that the amendment would cause no grave or serious prejudice to the defendant.
The amendment did not alter the nature of the suit or take away a valuable limitation right accrued to the defendant.
Any prejudice to the defendant could be compensated by costs.
members.legal_principle: Under Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shilgonda Patil (1957 SCR 595), the test for allowing an amendment is whether it causes serious injustice to the other side. Courts should be extremely liberal in allowing pleading amendments unless serious injustice or irreparable loss would result; prejudice that can be compensated by costs does not require refusal.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed, subject to the plaintiff paying costs and filing the amended plaint as directed; the District Judge’s order was restored.

rule.if: civil_suit_amendment and proposed_change_adds_possession_relief and suit_nature_unchanged and no_limitation_right_lost and serious_prejudice_absent and prejudice_compensable_by_costs

predicates.civil_suit_amendment: A party in a civil suit requested an amendment to a pleading.
predicates.proposed_change_adds_possession_relief: The requested change added a claim for recovery of possession.
predicates.suit_nature_unchanged: The requested change did not alter the nature of the suit.
predicates.no_limitation_right_lost: The requested change did not remove a valuable limitation right already accrued to the opposing party.
predicates.serious_prejudice_absent: The amendment would not cause grave or serious prejudice to the opposing party.
predicates.prejudice_compensable_by_costs: Any prejudice to the opposing party could be compensated by an award of costs.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to correct the valuation of the subject matter of a suit should be allowed when it does not change the nature of the suit or cause irremediable prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a suit for specific performance and initially stated a value for the property that it later acknowledged was incorrect.
The plaintiff applied to amend the plaint to state the property's correct market value and offered to pay the additional court fee.
The defendant had itself alleged in its written statement that the plaintiff had undervalued the property.
The amendment would not change the nature of the suit, and no prejudice to the defendant that could not be compensated was identified.
The lower courts rejected the amendment in part because the increased valuation would result in the suit being transferred to the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendments are generally to be allowed unless they change the nature of the suit or cause prejudice to the opposing party. As stated in North Eastern Railway Administration, Gorakhpur v. Bhagwan Das (D) by LRs. (2008) 8 SCC 511, relying on Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil (1957) 1 SCR 595, amendments should be allowed when they do not work injustice and are necessary to determine the real questions in controversy; refusal is warranted where the opposing party cannot be restored to its original position and would suffer injury that cannot be compensated in costs. Transfer of the suit because of the amended valuation is not, by itself, a reason to refuse amendment.
members.conclusion: The amendment should have been allowed. The orders rejecting it were set aside, and the trial court was directed to permit the plaintiff to amend the plaint. The transfer of the suit resulting from the increased valuation was not a valid reason to refuse the amendment.

rule.if: pleading_amendment_application and seeks_correct_property_valuation and nature_of_suit_unchanged and no_irremediable_prejudice

predicates.pleading_amendment_application: A party to a civil suit applied to amend a pleading.
predicates.seeks_correct_property_valuation: The applying party sought to replace an incorrect valuation of the property with its correct market value.
predicates.nature_of_suit_unchanged: The proposed amendment would leave the nature of the suit unchanged.
predicates.no_irremediable_prejudice: The opposing party would not suffer prejudice that could not be remedied, including by an award of costs.

members.legal_issue: An amendment that adds facts supporting an existing basis for relief or defence, without introducing a new claim on a new factual basis, does not introduce a new cause of action.
material_facts: The tenant sought only the protection of the rent-control Act, which became applicable to the building during the litigation.
The Act contemplated necessary amendments to the pleadings and the taking of additional evidence where required.
The court held that seeking this protection did not change the cause of action.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied A.K. Gupta & Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation: an amendment that merely adds to facts already on the record, without making a new claim on a new factual basis, does not introduce a new cause of action and may be allowed even after the limitation period. Section 39 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, also contemplates necessary amendments and additional evidence.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s request for the Act’s protection did not create a new cause of action, and necessary amendments to the pleadings and additional evidence could be allowed.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_pending: A court proceeding concerning eviction remains unresolved.
predicates.amendment_adds_supporting_facts: A party seeks to add facts that support a claim or defence already raised in the proceeding.
predicates.amendment_introduces_no_new_claim_basis: The proposed amendment does not assert a new claim founded on a new factual basis.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended to include claims arising from events during the suit when the amendment serves the interests of justice and avoids multiplicity of litigation, even if limitation is disputed and can be decided later.
material_facts: The pending suit sought an injunction against demolition of a compound wall.
During the suit, the defendants were alleged to have demolished parts of the wall and damaged the entrance gate.
The plaintiff sought to amend the plaint to plead those subsequent events and seek relief concerning them.
The limitation objection was disputed and could be decided as an issue after the amendment was allowed.
members.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives courts broad power to allow amendments in the interests of justice. Under B.K.N. Pillai v. P. Pillai, courts should generally take a liberal rather than hypertechnical approach, particularly where the opposing party can be compensated by costs, and amendments may be allowed to avoid multiplicity of litigation. That decision referred to Charan Das v. Amir Khan, L.J. Leach & Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner & Company, Smt. Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, and M/s. Ganesh Trading Co. v. Moji Ram. A disputed, arguable limitation objection may be decided as an issue after allowing the amendment.
members.conclusion: The amendment should be allowed, subject to payment of costs, and the limitation question may be determined after the amendment.

rule.if: pending_civil_suit and amendment_concerns_events_during_suit and amendment_relates_to_existing_dispute and amendment_avoids_multiplicity and limitation_is_disputed

predicates.pending_civil_suit: A civil suit is pending when a party seeks to amend its pleading.
predicates.amendment_concerns_events_during_suit: The proposed amendment pleads events alleged to have occurred while the suit was pending.
predicates.amendment_relates_to_existing_dispute: The events pleaded in the amendment concern the subject matter already in dispute in the suit.
predicates.amendment_avoids_multiplicity: Allowing the amendment would enable connected claims to be addressed in the existing suit rather than in separate litigation.
predicates.limitation_is_disputed: The opposing party raises a limitation objection whose resolution is arguable and can be determined after the amendment.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended to add a formal prayer for relief when the relevant allegations and dispute were already pleaded and tried.
material_facts: The plaint contained allegations that the property was a specific endowment and that the defendants had failed to carry out its purpose, but did not include a formal prayer for a declaration.
The defendants raised the nature of the grant in their pleas, an issue was framed on that question, and both sides knew the points in controversy and led the necessary evidence.
The additional declaration was relief flowing from the existing allegations and did not require new facts or a fresh trial.
members.legal_principle: An amendment adding formal relief may be allowed when necessary allegations have already been made, the parties have addressed the issue and led evidence, and the amendment does not change the cause of action or require a fresh trial.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to allow the amendment adding the formal prayer for a declaration.

rule.if: civil_suit_involving_endowment_claim and necessary_allegations_already_pleaded and parties_aware_of_dispute and necessary_evidence_led and added_prayer_is_formal_relief

predicates.civil_suit_involving_endowment_claim: A civil suit concerns whether property is held for an endowment and whether its purpose has been carried out.
predicates.necessary_allegations_already_pleaded: The plaint already alleges the material facts supporting the relief later sought.
predicates.parties_aware_of_dispute: The parties know the issue on which the additional relief depends, and it has been put in dispute.
predicates.necessary_evidence_led: The parties have already presented the evidence needed to decide that issue.
predicates.added_prayer_is_formal_relief: The added prayer follows from the existing allegations and does not require a new cause of action or a fresh trial.

members.legal_issue: A plaint amendment that assists in determining the real controversy and does not change the nature of the suit may be allowed without deciding the merits of the amended claim at the amendment stage.
material_facts: The suit, which sought eviction and mesne profits or damages, had been restored after the ex parte decree was set aside.
The plaintiff sought to delete a separate claim for delivery of air tickets and include their value with the claim for mesne profits, together with a consequential amendment.
The proposed amendment concerned the amount of mesne profits or damages and relied on contractual rent and the value of a benefit received through letting the premises.
The courts below rejected the amendment, including on the view that contractual charges were not relevant to determining mesne profits.
The Supreme Court found the amendment necessary to determine the real controversy over the quantum of mesne profits or damages and found that it would not change the nature of the suit.
members.legal_principle: An amendment may be allowed when it is necessary to adjudicate the real controversy and does not change the nature of the suit. At the amendment stage, the court must not decide the merits of the claim, which are to be determined when the suit is decided. A plaintiff may plead and prove contractual rent and the equivalent benefit received from letting the property in support of a mesne-profits or damages claim; on the lease agreement in this case, such damages could not be less than the contractual rate of use and occupation charges. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for these principles.
members.conclusion: The orders refusing the amendment were set aside and the amendment was allowed. The plaintiff could plead and prove the contractual rent and the equivalent benefit received, while the merits of the claim remained for decision at trial.

rule.if: plaint_amendment_application and suit_restored_for_trial and amendment_addresses_mesne_profit_quantum and amendment_adds_contractual_use_value and amendment_does_not_change_suit_nature

predicates.plaint_amendment_application: A party applied to change the pleading in a pending civil suit.
predicates.suit_restored_for_trial: The suit was returned to the trial process after an earlier ex parte decree was set aside.
predicates.amendment_addresses_mesne_profit_quantum: The proposed change concerned the amount of mesne profits or damages in dispute.
predicates.amendment_adds_contractual_use_value: The proposed change included contractual rent or the value of a contractual benefit in the mesne-profits or damages claim.
predicates.amendment_does_not_change_suit_nature: The proposed change left the essential nature of the suit unchanged.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended to add a formal prayer for relief when the necessary allegations and evidence are already before the court and the amendment does not change the cause of action or require a new trial.
material_facts: The original plaint sought recovery of arrears and future payments for services and expenses associated with the deity.
The proposed amendment added a declaration that the properties and their income formed a specific endowment and that the defendants were liable to pay the entire income.
The necessary allegations had been made, an issue had been framed on the nature of the grant, the parties knew the dispute, and the relevant evidence had been adduced.
The High Court considered the added prayer formal and found it introduced neither a new cause of action nor a need for a fresh trial.
members.legal_principle: An amendment adding a formal relief may be allowed where the relevant allegations and evidence are already present, the parties have addressed the real controversy, and the amendment neither changes the cause of action nor requires a fresh trial. The Court relied on no earlier case or statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The High Court rightly allowed the amendment adding the declaratory prayer.

rule.if: civil_appeal_reviews_pleading_amendment and necessary_allegations_already_pleaded and parties_understood_real_dispute and relevant_evidence_already_led and amendment_adds_formal_relief and not amendment_changes_cause_of_action and not amendment_requires_fresh_trial

predicates.civil_appeal_reviews_pleading_amendment: The matter is a civil appeal in which the court reviews an order allowing an amendment to a pleading.
predicates.necessary_allegations_already_pleaded: The original pleading already contains the allegations needed to support the proposed relief.
predicates.parties_understood_real_dispute: The parties knew the real controversy and had addressed it in the proceedings.
predicates.relevant_evidence_already_led: The parties had already adduced the evidence relevant to the controversy.
predicates.amendment_adds_formal_relief: The amendment adds a prayer for relief flowing from the existing allegations.
predicates.amendment_changes_cause_of_action: The amendment changes the cause of action.
predicates.amendment_requires_fresh_trial: The amendment requires a fresh trial.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended to enhance an alternative damages claim where the amendment concerns relief based on facts already pleaded, the trial has not commenced, and the opposing party can meet the amended claim without irreparable prejudice.
material_facts: The pending suit sought specific performance and, in the alternative, damages; the original plaint already pleaded a claim for damages.
The plaintiffs sought to increase the damages claimed, relying on the increase in the value of the property and the delay in prosecuting the suit.
The trial had not commenced, and the defendant was permitted to file an additional written statement and contest the amended claim.
The courts below left the limitation issue open for determination at trial.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, amendments necessary to determine the real controversy should generally be allowed where they do not introduce an entirely new cause of action, cause injustice that cannot be compensated by costs, withdraw an admission conferring a right on the other side, or defeat an accrued legal right. Limitation is a relevant discretionary consideration, but an amendment is not automatically barred merely because a fresh claim might be time-barred; where limitation is a disputed issue, it may be left for trial. The Court relied on L.J. Leach & Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., Charan Das v. Amir Khan, Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, Ganesh Trading Co. v. Moji Ram, South Konkan Distilleries v. Prabhakar Gajanan Naik, A.K. Gupta & Sons Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation, Pankaja v. Yellappa, Ragu Thilak D. John v. S. Rayappan, Vishwambhar v. Laxminarayan, Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera, and B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameswaran Pillai.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed, and the order allowing it was upheld; the appeal was dismissed, with limitation left open for trial.

rule.if: pending_specific_performance_suit and damages_already_claimed and amendment_only_enhances_relief_on_pleaded_facts and trial_not_commenced and opposing_party_can_contest_amendment and not irreparable_prejudice

predicates.pending_specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff has a pending suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.damages_already_claimed: The plaintiff's existing pleading already seeks damages in the alternative.
predicates.amendment_only_enhances_relief_on_pleade: The proposed change increases or adjusts the relief sought on facts already set out in the pleading, rather than introducing an entirely new case.
predicates.trial_not_commenced: The trial has not begun when the amendment is sought.
predicates.opposing_party_can_contest_amendment: The opposing party can respond to the amendment and challenge the claim in the proceedings.
predicates.irreparable_prejudice: The amendment would cause the opposing party prejudice that cannot be remedied, including by costs or an opportunity to respond.

members.legal_issue: An amendment correcting inadvertent wording may be allowed where the pleading already advances the intended case and the amendment does not introduce a different case.
material_facts: The plaintiff applied to delete words in the plaint that he said had been included through inadvertence and mistake.
The plaint, even without the amendment, was properly construed as seeking partition by metes and bounds rather than severance of joint-family status.
The amendment did not introduce a new case, and refusing it could require the plaintiff to bring another suit.
The court considered the amendment under Order 6, Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure and relied on L. J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6, Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may allow an amendment where justice requires it; the rule’s purpose includes avoiding multiplicity of suits. L. J. Leach and Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner and Co. establishes that the possibility that a fresh suit on an amended claim would be barred by limitation is a factor in the court’s discretion, but does not remove the power to allow an amendment when justice requires it.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed, and the suit was properly remanded for retrial.

rule.if: civil_suit_amendment_proceeding and proposed_change_corrects_inadvertent_wording and original_pleading_already_advances_intended_case and amendment_does_not_introduce_different_case and refusal_may_require_another_suit

predicates.civil_suit_amendment_proceeding: A party applies to amend a pleading in a civil suit.
predicates.proposed_change_corrects_inadvertent_wor: The proposed change corrects wording included through mistake or inadvertence.
predicates.original_pleading_already_advances_inten: The original pleading, properly construed, already presents the case the party intends to pursue.
predicates.amendment_does_not_introduce_different_c: The proposed change does not substitute a different case for the one already pleaded.
predicates.refusal_may_require_another_suit: Refusing the amendment may require the party to bring another suit.
predicates.amendment_may_be_allowed: The court may permit the proposed amendment.

members.legal_issue: A pleading may be amended to add relief concerning disputed transfers when the existing pleading already contains the necessary factual basis, the amendment does not change the basic nature of the suit, and allowing it causes no prejudice or avoidable further litigation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had brought a civil suit seeking an injunction against being forcibly dispossessed from land.
The defendants asserted in their written statement that they had acquired interests in the land through sale deeds.
The original plaint already set out the factual basis for challenging the transferors’ authority to sell and disputing the sale deeds’ effect on the plaintiffs’ rights.
The amendment sought relief concerning the validity of the sale deeds and a declaration of title, matters already in dispute between the parties.
The proposed relief was not barred in law when the amendment application was filed and could otherwise have been sought in a separate suit.
Allowing the amendment would not prejudice the defendants, who could file an additional written statement, and would avoid multiplicity of litigation.
The amendment was also prompted by an earlier observation that interim injunctive relief without seeking cancellation of the sale deeds was not maintainable.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy. The power is wide and is generally exercised liberally in the interests of justice, provided the amendment does not cause injustice or prejudice or change the basic nature of the suit. Where an application is made after trial has commenced, the proviso requires the court to be satisfied that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier. The court reiterated the principles in J. Samuel and Others v. Gattu Mahesh and Others, (2012) 2 SCC 300, and Rameshkumar Agarwal v. Rajmala Exports Pvt. Ltd. and Others, (2012) 5 SCC 337. It relied on Pankaja v. Yellapa (Dead) by LRs. and Others, AIR 2004 SC 4102, (2004) 6 SCC 415, for the principles that an amendment serving justice and avoiding further litigation should be allowed and that a title-related relief does not introduce a different relief when its factual basis is already pleaded.
members.conclusion: The amendment application should be allowed; the orders refusing it were set aside.

rule.if: civil_suit_pleading_amendment and necessary_factual_basis_already_pleaded and proposed_relief_addresses_existing_dispute and not basic_nature_changed and not relief_barred and not opposing_party_prejudiced and further_litigation_avoided

predicates.civil_suit_pleading_amendment: A party in a civil suit applied to amend its pleading.
predicates.necessary_factual_basis_already_pleaded: The original pleading already stated the material facts supporting the proposed relief.
predicates.proposed_relief_addresses_existing_dispu: The proposed relief concerns a matter already placed in dispute by the parties’ pleadings.
predicates.basic_nature_changed: The proposed amendment changes the basic nature of the suit.
predicates.relief_barred: The proposed relief was barred in law when the amendment was sought.
predicates.opposing_party_prejudiced: Allowing the amendment would cause prejudice to the opposing party that could not be addressed through a fair opportunity to respond.
predicates.further_litigation_avoided: Allowing the amendment would avoid the need for further litigation over the same dispute.
predicates.pleading_amendment_allowed: The court allows the pleading to be amended.

members.legal_issue: A pleading may be amended to add related relief where the amendment does not substitute a distinct cause of action or change the suit’s subject matter, and does not cause irremediable prejudice.
material_facts: The original plaint referred to a partnership arrangement and the plaintiff’s share in it, although it initially sought partition of the theatre structure.
The amendment added claims for dissolution of the partnership and accounts of the cinema business, based on substantially the same facts.
Allowing the amendment could avoid multiple proceedings, and the opposing party had a full opportunity to meet the amended case.
The amendment was sought late, and the court imposed costs as a condition of allowing it.
members.legal_principle: Amendments should be liberally allowed to secure the proper administration of justice and avoid multiplicity of proceedings, provided they do not substitute one distinct cause of action for another or change the suit’s subject matter, and do not inflict irremediable prejudice. Delay or negligence may be addressed by imposing costs. The Court relied on Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Po Hnaung, AIR 1922 PC 249, and the general principles governing amendments under the CPC (1908).
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed because it did not totally transform the nature of the litigation or cause irremediable prejudice; the delay could be addressed by costs.

rule.if: pleading_amendment_motion and (added_claim_has_existing_factual_basis and amendment_preserves_action_character and multiplicity_of_proceedings_avoided) and opposing_party_can_meet_amended_case and not irremediable_prejudice

predicates.pleading_amendment_motion: A party asks a court in an existing suit to amend a pleading.
predicates.added_claim_has_existing_factual_basis: The original pleading already refers to the factual basis for the claim added by the amendment.
predicates.amendment_preserves_action_character: The amendment does not substitute a distinct cause of action or change the subject matter of the suit.
predicates.multiplicity_of_proceedings_avoided: Resolving the added claim in the existing suit can avoid separate proceedings.
predicates.opposing_party_can_meet_amended_case: The opposing party has an opportunity to answer the case presented by the amended pleading.
predicates.irremediable_prejudice: The amendment causes prejudice to the opposing party that cannot be remedied, including by appropriate conditions such as costs.

members.legal_issue: A revenue record identifying a person as an occupant does not, without more, establish that the person acquired title to the property.
material_facts: The property had substantial value, and no registered instrument transferring it to the claimant had been executed.
The revenue entry described the claimant and the prior holder as occupants; the claimant relied on it as proof of title.
members.legal_principle: A revenue entry may support a presumption concerning possession, but in the circumstances here it did not establish title. The Court distinguished the reliance on revenue entries in Gangabai v. Fakirgowda Somaypagowda Desai and Desai Navinkant Kesarlal v. Prabhat Kabhai.
members.conclusion: The entry could support a presumption of the claimant’s possession, but not of her title.

predicates.revenue_entry_offered_to_prove_title: A party relied on a revenue record as evidence that the party acquired title to property.
predicates.entry_identified_person_as_occupant: The revenue record described the person relying on it as an occupant rather than recording a transfer of title.
predicates.no_registered_transfer_was_executed: No registered instrument transferring the property to that person was executed.

members.legal_issue: Mutation of land in revenue records does not create or extinguish title to the land and has no presumptive value as to title.
material_facts: The dispute concerned entries in revenue records relating to land.
Civil suits concerning the land were pending between the parties.
members.legal_principle: As held in Sawarni (Smt.) v. Inder Kaur, (1996) 6 SCC 223; Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh, (1997) 7 SCC 137; and Narasamma v. State of Karnataka, (2009) 5 SCC 591, mutation entries do not determine ownership and serve only the purpose of enabling payment of land revenue.
members.conclusion: Mutation in revenue records does not create or extinguish title and has no presumptive value as to title; it only enables the person in whose favour it is ordered to pay the land revenue.

predicates.land_revenue_entry_made: An authority made an entry in the revenue records concerning land.
predicates.mutation_entry_does_not_create_or_exting: A revenue-record mutation does not create or extinguish title to the land.

members.legal_issue: An official statement describing land as private, or acknowledging an absence of acquisition records, does not by itself establish an individual’s title to that land.
material_facts: The petitioner claimed to act as a trustee for a trust said to own the land, but the trust was not the named petitioner.
The High Court had no finding that the trust held valid and subsisting title or that the petitioner was entitled to litigate on its behalf.
Government officers stated that they lacked documentary evidence of acquisition for most of the land, and the authority referred to a government letter describing it as private land.
The conveyance and confirmation deeds raised unresolved questions concerning ownership and the persons claiming as purchasers.
members.legal_principle: A court must evaluate the relevance and effect of official statements when deciding a dispute; a statement that land is private or that acquisition documents are unavailable does not itself establish or confer title. The court must examine the material bearing on title and entitlement. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The statements relied on by the High Court did not amount to a concession recognizing the petitioner’s title and could not themselves confer title to immovable property.

predicates.public_law_writ: A person brought a public-law proceeding seeking discretionary relief from a court.
predicates.title_is_disputed: The parties’ claims depend on a disputed right of ownership of land.
predicates.official_statements_are_the_only_basis_f: The court relies only on statements by public officials to recognize a claimant’s title.
predicates.official_statements_do_not_establish_tit: The official statements do not establish the claimant’s title.

members.legal_issue: A ryotwari patta granted in a revenue settlement does not, by itself, adjudicate civil title to the land.
material_facts: The settlement authority granted pattas following the abolition of minor inams.
The patta identified the tenant as entitled in respect of the building and the former inamdar as entitled in respect of the site.
The tenant relied on the patta to claim ownership of the site and to defeat the former inamdar's claim.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3, 8, 11 and 12 of the Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 establish a process for vesting minor inams in the Government, determining entitlement to ryotwari pattas, and collecting land revenue. Sections 43 and 46 make decisions binding or final only as to matters falling within the statutory process. The Court relied on State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam, AIR 1986 SC 794, concerning the limited revenue purpose of settlement decisions, and distinguished Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu, [1991] 2 SCR 531, which concerned a matter entrusted to revenue authorities for determination.
members.conclusion: The grant of a ryotwari patta was a revenue settlement and did not determine title to the land.

predicates.minor_inam_revenue_settlement_case: The proceeding concerns a revenue settlement arising from the conversion of minor inam land.
predicates.settlement_authority_granted_ryotwari_pa: A settlement authority issued a ryotwari patta in the course of that revenue settlement.

members.legal_issue: The non-production of land revenue records does not by itself defeat established title to property.
material_facts: The plaintiff did not produce certain land revenue records for earlier years.
The court concluded that the missing records did not affect title or ownership of the property.
members.legal_principle: The absence of land revenue records does not by itself determine or defeat ownership where it does not affect the title to the property.
members.conclusion: The non-production of the land revenue records made no difference to the determination of title.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns ownership or title to property.
predicates.land_revenue_records_not_produced: A party did not produce relevant land revenue records.
predicates.missing_records_do_not_affect_title: The missing records do not alter or undermine the title evidence in the case.

members.legal_issue: Entries in revenue records or a record of rights, and the conferment of patta, do not by themselves establish title to property.
material_facts: The society relied on settlement and revenue records showing its predecessors as pattadars of the relevant survey land.
The society also relied on survey and revenue entries as evidence of its predecessors’ ownership.
The Court found that those entries did not independently establish title and that the society had to prove its predecessors’ title and the identity of the property conveyed to it.
members.legal_principle: Revenue records are not documents of title, entries in jamabandi do not prove title, and entries in revenue papers cannot by themselves form the basis for a declaration of title. A patta also does not itself confer title. The Court relied on Corporation of the City of Bangalore v. M. Papaiah, (1989) 3 SCC 612; Guru Amarjit Singh v. Rattan Chand, (1993) 4 SCC 349; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Keshav Ram, (1996) 11 SCC 257; Syndicate Bank v. Estate Officer & Manager, APIIC Ltd., (2007) 8 SCC 361; and Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu, 1991 Supp (2) SCC 228.
members.conclusion: The revenue and settlement entries, even if they carry evidentiary value, did not by themselves confer or establish title to the disputed land.

predicates.title_declaration_possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of title and possession of property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_revenue_or_settlement: The claimant relied on entries in revenue, settlement, or record-of-rights documents to support its claim of ownership.

members.legal_issue: A revenue-record entry identifying a person as occupant does not, by itself, transfer title to immovable property.
material_facts: The property had been acquired and developed with joint-family funds.
A revenue entry first recorded the prior owner and was later changed to identify the claimant as occupant after statements were made to revenue officials.
No registered instrument of transfer was executed, and the entry described the claimant as an occupant.
members.legal_principle: A mutation or occupancy entry is not itself a conveyance of title. The Court distinguished the presumptive evidentiary value attributed to revenue entries in Gangabai v. Fakirgowda Somaypagowda Desai and Desai Navinkant Kesarlal v. Prabhat Kabhai, holding that this entry, which recorded the claimant as occupant and was unsupported by a registered transfer, could support possession but not title.
members.conclusion: The revenue entry did not establish that title had passed to the claimant; in the circumstances, it supported an inference about possession only.

predicates.title_dispute_over_immovable_property: The parties disputed who held title to immovable property.
predicates.revenue_entry_records_occupancy: A public revenue record identified a person as occupying the property.
predicates.no_registered_transfer: No registered instrument transferring the property to that person was executed.

members.legal_issue: Revenue records may support a rebuttable inference of possession but do not establish title to property.
material_facts: The courts below considered revenue-record entries and a document identifying land parcels in deciding the property dispute.
A revenue-record entry showed the Municipal Corporation’s name in respect of the land adjoining the disputed plots.
The trial court nevertheless proceeded on the basis that the adjoining property might belong to the defendants.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, entries in a record of rights are admissible as relevant evidence and may carry a rebuttable presumption of correctness, but they are not documents of title. A revenue record raises a presumption regarding possession, and Section 110 of the Act may support presumptions of possession and its continuity. The Court relied on Narain Prasad Aggarwal (D) by LRs. v. State of M.P. [2007 (8) SCALE 250] concerning the evidentiary status of record-of-rights entries.
members.conclusion: The courts were required to assess the records under the correct principles: revenue records are not documents of title, though they may be relevant to possession and carry a rebuttable presumption.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: The parties disputed rights in identified property.
predicates.revenue_records_relied_on: A party or court relied on entries in revenue records concerning the property.

members.legal_issue: Entries in revenue and mutation registers are not conclusive proof of proprietary title.
material_facts: The leaseholders relied on entries in Register D to show that their predecessor was proprietor of the estate and could grant the original mining lease.
The entries reflected changes recorded in the land registers, and the leaseholders did not produce clear, conclusive and unimpeachable documentary evidence establishing the predecessor's title.
members.legal_principle: Under the Land Registration Act, 1876, Register D records changes affecting entries in other registers. Nirman Singh v. Lal Rudra Partab Narain Singh, 53 IA 220, holds that mutation proceedings are fiscal enquiries and do not determine title. Sri Marudeswarar Temple v. Dhanalakshmi Ammal, Civil Appeal No. 236 of 1961, holds that a revenue entry is not conclusive of title. The Court also referred to Lodna Colliery Company (1920) Ltd. v. Bhola Nath Roy, AIR 1964 SC 918, concerning proprietary rights in sub-soil minerals.
members.conclusion: The Register D entries were strong prima facie evidence but were not conclusive evidence of title.

predicates.title_claim_rests_on_revenue_register_en: A party relies on entries in a revenue or mutation register to establish proprietary title.

members.legal_issue: Entries in municipal tax records do not establish title, although they may evidence tax liability or, depending on the governing scheme and surrounding circumstances, possession.
material_facts: The municipal records identified the plaintiff and his predecessors in the ownership column, and the plaintiff produced property-tax payment records.
The temple's name was not entered in the municipal records before the dispute arose.
The temple relied on its later collection of rent and payment of property tax, but those records arose after the dispute had developed.
The temple produced no other evidence establishing its title.
members.legal_principle: A municipal assessment or tax entry is not, by itself, evidence of ownership. Depending on the scope of the governing provision, it may show who was treated as liable for rates and taxes and may evidence possession. Entries over time and related tax payments may be considered with other evidence, but do not substitute for proof of title.
members.conclusion: The municipal entries did not themselves prove title, but the long-standing entries and tax payments were relevant to show who was treated by the municipality as liable for the taxes and could support an inference concerning possession. The temple's later entries and payments did not establish its title.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to determine ownership of property.
predicates.municipal_records_are_relied_on_as_owner: A party relies on municipal assessment or tax records to support a claim of ownership.

members.legal_issue: Mutation of property in revenue records does not transfer or extinguish ownership title.
material_facts: The property had been purchased in the name of the deceased owner and stood in her name in the revenue records.
After her death, her husband accepted a change of the revenue entry into the name of their son, and the entry was not challenged.
The husband had not relinquished or released his share, and the claim based on the mutation entry did not plead such a relinquishment.
members.legal_principle: A mutation entry neither creates nor extinguishes title and has no presumptive value on title; it enables collection of land revenue. The Court applied Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh (1997) 7 SCC 137, which quoted and applied Sawarni v. Inder Kaur (1996) 6 SCC 223.
members.conclusion: The mutation entry did not divest the husband of his share; it was relevant to revenue collection and did not convey or extinguish title.

predicates.civil_title_dispute: A civil proceeding concerns competing claims to ownership of property.
predicates.revenue_mutation_recorded: A revenue authority entered a person’s name in property records after a proposed change of ownership.

members.legal_issue: Mutation of names in revenue records does not establish title to land, and title to open land follows possession.
material_facts: The appellants relied on a partnership’s name having been entered in the revenue records to claim ownership.
The entry was found to have been procured fraudulently, and the land was treated as Government land.
The appellants transferred land despite an order requiring the status quo to be maintained.
members.legal_principle: Mutation entries are not evidence of title, though they may be relevant for other purposes; in respect of open land, title follows possession. The Court relied on Nirman Singh v. Rudra Patrab Narain Singh, Nageshar Baksh Singh v. Mt. Ganesha, Durga Prasad v. Ghansham Das, Ramana v. Sambamoorthy, Mohinder Singh v. State of Punjab, and Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu.
members.conclusion: The revenue-record mutation did not prove ownership, and the appellants could not establish that the land was their own on that basis.

predicates.land_title_dispute: The case concerns competing claims to ownership of land.
predicates.ownership_claim_based_on_revenue_mutatio: A party relies on a name entered in revenue records as evidence of ownership.
predicates.no_independent_title_basis_established: The party has not established ownership by an independent basis apart from the revenue entry.

members.legal_issue: Possession and revenue entries do not establish title when the evidence discloses a competing title, and revenue entries are evidence of possession rather than documents of title.
material_facts: The respondent relied on its possession and revenue entries, including an entry showing another person as pattadar, to support its claim of ownership.
The respondent did not explain the pattadar’s connection to it, and that person was not joined in the suit.
Documents showed that the Government had owned the land since at least 1920.
The respondent had also paid rent to the Government and had previously sought a lease from it.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 110 and 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872, possession may support a rebuttable presumption of title where possession is prima facie lawful and the competing party has no title, particularly where there is no or very little proof of ownership. The presumption does not arise where the facts disclose title. A revenue record is not a document of title and raises, at most, a presumption concerning possession. The Court relied on Gurunath Manohar Pavaskar v. Nagesh Siddappa Navalgund, AIR 2008 SC 901; Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, AIR 1968 SC 1165; and Chief Conservator of Forests, Govt. of A.P. v. Collector, AIR 2003 SC 1805. The possession principle also serves the public purpose reflected in Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Sections 154 and 158 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Acceptance of municipal or agricultural tax does not prevent the State from contesting ownership, and there can be no estoppel against a statute.
members.conclusion: The lower courts erred in treating the revenue entries and possession as establishing title or shifting the burden to the Government; the possession-based presumption did not overcome the evidence of the Government’s title.

predicates.civil_land_title_claim: A party brought a civil proceeding claiming ownership of land.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_possession_or_revenue: The claimant relied on possession or revenue entries as evidence of ownership.
predicates.competing_party_has_proof_of_title: The competing party produced evidence supporting its title to the land.

members.legal_issue: A revenue-record entry unsupported by a valid instrument does not establish title or a right to land covered by forest proceedings.
material_facts: The claimant's name appeared in a later land record as having possession of part of the land.
The earlier land records recorded the land as transferred to the forest department under the forest legislation.
No supporting written lease or other instrument creating the claimant's right was produced.
members.legal_principle: In Prahlad Pradhan v. Sonu Kumhar, (2019) 10 SCC 259, the Court held that revenue entries do not confer title and serve to identify the person liable to pay land revenue. The Court applied that principle here and held that an entry unsupported by the written instrument required to create the claimed right was insufficient.
members.conclusion: The claimant's revenue-record entry was inconsequential and created no right, title, or interest in the land.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: The proceeding is an appeal from a writ order concerning an entry in a land record.
predicates.land_record_names_claimant: A land record names the claimant as an occupant or holder of the land.
predicates.no_supporting_title_instrument: No valid instrument supporting the claimant's asserted title or right was produced.

members.legal_issue: A mutation in revenue records does not create or extinguish title to property.
material_facts: The property was mutated in the name of the appellant’s mother following an alleged oral gift.
The alleged oral gift was not proved, and the appellant relied on possession and the mutation in support of her ownership claim.
members.legal_principle: Mutation proceedings are fiscal in nature: they enable collection of land revenue and neither create nor extinguish title, nor carry presumptive value as to title.
members.conclusion: The mutation did not confer title or establish a right capable of supporting the appellant’s claim to absolute ownership.

predicates.property_title_claim_based_on_mutation: A party to a property-title dispute relies on a mutation entry as support for ownership.
predicates.mutation_is_only_revenue_record_entry: The mutation is an entry made for revenue administration rather than a determination of title.

members.legal_issue: Revenue mutation entries do not themselves establish title to property.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on revenue entries made after the claimed purchase and during the pendency of an earlier suit.
The sale deed said to support the plaintiff’s title was not produced.
The appellate court relied on the revenue entries without determining whether the plaintiff had proved title.
members.legal_principle: Mutation in revenue records is a fiscal inquiry for identifying the person from whom revenue may be collected; it is not a source of title. The court relied on Nirman Singh v. Lal Rudra Partab, 1926 PC 100. It also noted that entries made during the pendency of earlier litigation were of little consequence in the circumstances of this case.
members.conclusion: The revenue entries did not establish title and could not justify decreeing the suit without proof of title.

predicates.title_claim_in_property_suit: A party in a property suit claims ownership of the disputed property.
predicates.title_based_on_mutation_entries: A party relies on mutation entries in revenue records as proof of ownership.

members.legal_issue: A revenue mutation entry does not create or extinguish title to property and has no presumptive value as proof of title.
material_facts: The disputed land had been mutated in the revenue records in the name of a person who claimed to be an heir and later sold the land.
The lower appellate court treated the mutation as establishing the seller’s title.
members.legal_principle: Mutation in revenue records serves to enable collection of land revenue from the person recorded; it neither creates nor extinguishes title and has no presumptive value on title. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The mutation did not confer title on the person recorded or enable her to pass title to the purchasers.

predicates.land_title_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim to title in land.
predicates.revenue_mutation_recorded: A person’s name was entered in revenue records by mutation.
predicates.title_inferred_from_mutation: A decision-maker treated the mutation entry as establishing that person’s title.

members.legal_issue: A revenue-record entry made pursuant to an alleged correction order, without other evidence of title, is insufficient to establish ownership of land.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration of ownership and possession of the disputed land.
The original revenue record showed the land in the name of a former intermediary and later in the name of the State.
The alleged order directing correction of the record was not produced; the claimants relied on the resulting entry in the register.
The claimants identified no other document or evidence supporting their title.
members.legal_principle: An entry in revenue records does not create or extinguish title and cannot, by itself, support a declaration of ownership. No earlier cases or statutory provisions were relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The courts below erred in declaring the claimants’ title on the basis of the correction and resulting revenue entry. The appeal was allowed, the judgments and decrees were set aside, and the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: declaratory_title_suit and revenue_entry_is_only_title_evidence and correction_order_not_produced and no_other_title_evidence

predicates.declaratory_title_suit: The claimants brought a civil suit seeking a declaration that they owned land.
predicates.revenue_entry_is_only_title_evidence: The claimants relied on an entry in a revenue record as their evidence of ownership.
predicates.correction_order_not_produced: The claimants did not produce the order said to have directed the correction of the revenue record.
predicates.no_other_title_evidence: The claimants identified no other evidence supporting their asserted ownership.

members.legal_issue: Lands in different villages acquired for the same purpose should receive equivalent compensation when their nature and quality are similar.
material_facts: Land in multiple villages was acquired under a notification issued under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act for development around an airport.
The High Court fixed compensation by relying on a decision concerning land acquired for the same purpose in a nearby village.
The High Court found that the lands were broadly similar in nature and quality, and that paying different compensation would unfairly discriminate between landowners.
The Supreme Court considered that contiguity alone would not establish similarity, but upheld the High Court’s finding of similarity.
members.legal_principle: Contiguity of villages alone is insufficient to infer that lands are similar in character. But where lands acquired for the same purpose are found to be similar in nature and quality, there is no justification for distinguishing between them in compensation. The Court applied Kunwar Singh v. Union of India on the insufficiency of contiguity alone and followed Satpal v. Union of India as the basis for assessing compensation for comparable land.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s compensation determination was fair and reasonable, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.same_acquisition_purpose: The compared lands were acquired for the same purpose.
predicates.similar_land_nature_and_quality: The court found that the compared lands were similar in nature and quality.

members.legal_issue: Consistency in valuation supports maintaining a final compensation determination for comparable land acquired through the same acquisition process.
material_facts: The High Court had previously fixed compensation for land acquired in the same acquisition process at the same rate ultimately awarded to the appellants.
The earlier determination had attained finality, and the land in the earlier proceeding had not been shown to differ from the land in question.
The connected appeals concerned land from another revenue estate that the High Court regarded as having a lower market value because it was farther from the town centre.
The Supreme Court nevertheless considered the same compensation rate appropriate for the connected land in the circumstances of the case.
members.legal_principle: Consistency in judicial determination is important. Where land acquired through the same process has been assigned a final value in an earlier proceeding and the land is not shown to be materially different, maintaining a uniform valuation is justified. The Court also affirmed the value for the connected land in the particular circumstances before it.
members.conclusion: The compensation fixed by the High Court was affirmed for both sets of appeals, including the connected land considered to have a lower market value.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and land_acquired_in_same_process and prior_compensation_determination_is_final and court_finds_uniform_valuation_appropriate

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_acquired_in_same_process: The land was acquired through the same acquisition process as land addressed in another compensation determination.
predicates.prior_compensation_determination_is_fina: An earlier compensation determination concerning land acquired through that process has become final.
predicates.court_finds_uniform_valuation_appropriat: The court considered a uniform valuation appropriate in the circumstances, including any relevant differences between the lands.

members.legal_issue: Lands found to have equal value should be valued uniformly for compensation.
material_facts: The High Court found that the acquired lands were of equal value and that classification was unwarranted.
The State did not seriously dispute in the High Court that all the lands were of equal value.
members.legal_principle: Where the evidence supports a finding that acquired parcels have equal value, compensation may be determined uniformly. The Court accepted the High Court's finding on this record.
members.conclusion: The Court accepted the finding that compensation should be determined at a uniform rate for all the lands.

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.parcels_found_equal_in_value: The court found that the acquired parcels were equal in value.

members.legal_issue: A difference in the timing of acquisition, by itself, does not justify enhanced compensation when the lands have been awarded a uniform rate and no sufficient basis for distinguishing them is shown.
material_facts: A notification for acquisition of a large extent of land was published in 1961.
The High Court awarded a uniform rate of compensation for the lands and followed an earlier decision concerning land notified for acquisition in 1959.
The appellants argued that the time elapsed between the notifications entitled them to higher compensation.
The Supreme Court found no sufficient justification for distinguishing the appellants’ lands from those in the earlier decision.
members.legal_principle: In this land-acquisition compensation appeal, the Court relied on the earlier decision in Sanwalia & Ors. v. Union of India, which the High Court had followed, and found no sufficient justification to distinguish the appellants’ lands merely on the basis advanced. The judgment identifies Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act as the basis for the acquisition notification but states no further statutory valuation rule.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to enhance compensation and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and uniform_compensation_rate and earlier_notification_comparator and elapsed_time_relied_on and no_sufficient_basis_to_distinguish

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal seeking higher compensation for land acquired through a compulsory acquisition process.
predicates.uniform_compensation_rate: The lower court awarded the same rate of compensation for the lands at issue.
predicates.earlier_notification_comparator: The appellants relied on a comparison with land covered by an earlier acquisition notification.
predicates.elapsed_time_relied_on: The appellants argued that the interval between the acquisition notifications supported a higher award.
predicates.no_sufficient_basis_to_distinguish: The Court found no sufficient justification for treating the appellants’ lands differently from the comparator lands.

members.legal_issue: Awards made by a land acquisition authority for comparable land in reasonable proximity are admissible and may provide a reliable basis for determining compensation.
material_facts: The compensation proceedings included two awards made by the Collector for land in a nearby area, at rates that provided evidence of land values.
The High Court considered those awards along with sale deeds and other evidence concerning land in the surrounding localities.
The Supreme Court held that such awards were relevant material and could not be rejected as inadmissible for determining compensation.
members.legal_principle: In determining compensation under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Collector's awards are relevant material and may constitute admissions concerning land value on behalf of the State. If the lands are comparable and reasonably proximate, the rates in the awards can provide a reliable basis for determining compensation.
members.conclusion: Awards made by a Collector are admissible evidence and may be used as safe guides when they concern comparable land in reasonable proximity to the acquired land.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and collector_awards_used_as_value_evidence and (awarded_land_comparable and awarded_land_reasonably_nearby)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: A proceeding seeks determination of compensation for land acquired by the State.
predicates.collector_awards_used_as_value_evidence: A party relies on awards made by a land acquisition authority as evidence of land value.
predicates.awarded_land_comparable: The land covered by the awards is comparable to the acquired land.
predicates.awarded_land_reasonably_nearby: The land covered by the awards is in reasonable proximity to the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: A single compensation rate should be used for acquired lands that are materially similar when no significant differences in their nature or quality are proved.
material_facts: The reference court fixed different rates within a range for different landowners.
The Supreme Court found that the lands were more or less similar in nature and that the landowners had not proved significant improvements, additions, or differences in quality.
Taking the factual circumstances and the extent of each holding into account, the Court fixed one rate for all the landowners’ lands.
members.legal_principle: Where acquired lands are more or less similar and no evidence establishes a significant difference in their nature or quality, differing rates for individual owners are unwarranted; the compensation rate should be uniform. The Court applied this principle to the evidence and circumstances of the case.
members.conclusion: The reference court should have fixed one uniform rate, and the landowners were entitled to compensation at Rs.90 per square foot.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_lands_materially_similar: The acquired lands are more or less similar in nature.
predicates.no_significant_land_differences_proved: The landowners have not proved significant differences in the lands’ improvements, additions, or quality.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for similar nearby lands acquired at the same time for the same purpose must not differ without a strong basis for distinction.
material_facts: Land was acquired for resettlement of displaced families, and the appellants’ land was acquired at about the same time as land in nearby areas for the same purpose.
The acquired lands were adjacent or close to one another and were found to be similar.
Landowners in other references concerning comparable acquired land were awarded compensation of Rs.4,00,000 per Kanal, while the appellants were awarded Rs.2,50,000 per Kanal.
The appellants presented witness evidence and a sale deed relating to a small parcel in the vicinity to support their claim that the lower valuation was inadequate.
members.legal_principle: Where land is acquired at the same time for the same purpose and the lands are identical or similar and situated nearby, landowners should not be paid different compensation without strong reasons. Comparable lands may be used as a comparative unit for determining market value. The Court relied on Union of India v. Bal Ram, (2010) 5 SCC 747, and Union of India v. Harinder Pal Singh, (2005) 12 SCC 564. The acquisition in this case was made under Section 4(1) of the Jammu and Kashmir Land Acquisition Act.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court’s judgments and held that the appellants were entitled to compensation at Rs.4,00,000 per Kanal, with 15% solatium and other statutory benefits, on a par with the other landowners.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and acquisitions_same_period and acquisitions_same_purpose and lands_similar and lands_nearby and comparable_landowners_received_higher_compensation

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning the amount of compensation payable for acquired land.
predicates.acquisitions_same_period: The land in the proceeding and comparable land were acquired at about the same time.
predicates.acquisitions_same_purpose: The land in the proceeding and comparable land were acquired for the same purpose.
predicates.lands_similar: The acquired lands were found to be identical or similar in relevant respects.
predicates.lands_nearby: The acquired lands were situated near or adjacent to one another.
predicates.comparable_landowners_received_higher_co: Landowners whose land was considered comparable received higher compensation in other proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Land acquired later in a nearby locality may receive the same compensation rate as land in a less distant locality where the court has upheld a lower-value finding for the former but awards the common rate in light of its later acquisition.
material_facts: The land in the farther locality was notified for acquisition 18 months after land in the less distant locality.
The Reference Court found, and the High Court upheld, that the farther locality's land had a lower market value because it was farther away.
The claimants did not show that the land in the farther locality had the same market value as the other land.
The High Court nevertheless awarded the same compensation rate, and the Supreme Court upheld that result and applied the enhanced rate of Rs. 7,000 per bigha.
members.legal_principle: Market value is determined by the land's value at the relevant notification date and its location and advantages. The Court accepted the concurrent finding that the farther locality had a lower market value, but upheld the same compensation rate awarded for the locality notified earlier because the farther locality was notified later.
members.conclusion: The claimants whose land was in the farther locality were entitled to the same compensation rate of Rs. 7,000 per bigha as the land in the less distant locality.

rule.if: acquisition_compensation_appeal and later_notified_locality and locality_is_farther and lower_value_finding_upheld

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding challenges compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.later_notified_locality: The land in one locality was notified for acquisition after comparable land in another locality.
predicates.locality_is_farther: The court finds that the later-notified locality is farther from the relevant area or feature affecting value.
predicates.lower_value_finding_upheld: The finding that the later-notified locality's land had a lower market value is upheld.

members.legal_issue: A compensation award for land acquired under the same notification may support the valuation of other land acquired under that notification when the award has attained finality and there are no relevant sale instances.
material_facts: The reference court relied on an award for land in another village that was acquired under the same notification as the land in dispute.
That award had not been appealed by either the landowners or the State.
The courts found that the parties had produced no relevant sale instances for determining market value.
The High Court maintained the compensation assessed on the basis of the unchallenged award.
