members.legal_principle: In a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, where no relevant sale instance is available, an unchallenged determination of compensation for land acquired under the same notification may provide a basis for determining the market value. The court treated the award for the other village under the same notification as the relevant prior determination.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to rely on the compensation award for land acquired under the same notification, and there was no error warranting appellate interference.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and same_notification_award_exists and same_notification_award_unappealed and no_relevant_sale_instances

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the compensation payable for acquired land.
predicates.same_notification_award_exists: A compensation award exists for other land acquired under the same notification as the land being valued.
predicates.same_notification_award_unappealed: Neither side appealed the award for the other land, so that award attained finality.
predicates.no_relevant_sale_instances: The parties produced no sale instances that the courts found relevant to determining market value.
predicates.same_notification_award_accepted_as_valu: The award for land acquired under the same notification is accepted as a basis for determining market value.

members.legal_issue: Equal compensation cannot be awarded merely because acquired lands are in the same village or were covered by the same notification.
material_facts: The claimants relied on awards in other cases arising from the same notification and concerning land in the same village.
Those earlier awards treated the village lands as one unit, but the claimants did not establish that their lands had the same advantages, features, or value as the lands in those cases.
The acquired area was extensive, and land within the same village could differ in location and market value.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed from the standpoint of a willing and prudent purchaser in an open market, comparing land with similar advantages and features. The claimant bears the burden of proving market value. The Court rejected the approach in the cited Chet Ram and Raghubir Singh decisions of treating all lands in a village as one unit, and held that their finality did not require repeating an erroneous principle.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the compensation awarded in the earlier cases merely on grounds of parity; equal compensation is permissible when the lands are proved to possess the same advantages and features.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding seeks judicial determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.same_village_or_notification_is_basis_fo: The claimant relies on the land being in the same village or covered by the same acquisition notification as land awarded a particular compensation.
predicates.comparable_land_advantages_proved: The claimant establishes that the lands have comparable advantages, features, and value.

members.legal_issue: Comparable awards for nearby land acquired at different times support revising compensation to reflect the acquired land’s just market value.
material_facts: Land in Mewla, Maharajpur, was acquired for development, and the High Court assessed compensation in related matters at Rs. 280 per square yard.
Awards for comparable land in the same village and nearby areas included Rs. 328.50, Rs. 337, Rs. 392.50 and Rs. 435 per square yard, with some awards relating to acquisitions at different times.
The Court considered the passage of time between acquisitions and concluded that Rs. 325 per square yard was just compensation for the relevant Mewla lands.
members.legal_principle: Compensation must reflect the market value of the acquired land, assessed using relevant comparable transactions or awards and the timing of the acquisitions. The Court applied the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and relied on its comparison of awards for similar lands in the same area; it also referred to State of Haryana v. Gurbax Singh and Union of India v. Harinder Pal Singh concerning comparable development potential and increases in value.
members.conclusion: Compensation for the Mewla lands in the relevant cases was increased to Rs. 325 per square yard, with statutory benefits.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_land_awards_exist: Courts or authorities have assessed compensation for comparable land in the same or a nearby area.
predicates.acquisition_dates_differ: The comparable land was acquired at a different time from the land under consideration.

members.legal_issue: A reduction in compensation cannot be based solely on the aggregate size of an acquisition or the distance between the acquired lands when the lands are comparable and no evidence shows that the acquired lands are inferior.
material_facts: The compensation appeals concerned land acquired from multiple owners, whose holdings were small individually but amounted to about 20 hectares when combined.
The earlier award concerned about 2 hectares of land and had become final.
The two sets of lands were found similar in quality and development potential, and the State produced no evidence that the acquired lands were inferior.

The acquired lands were about 3 kilometres from the town, while the lands covered by the earlier award were about 2 kilometres from it; the distance between the two sets of lands was about 5 kilometres.
members.legal_principle: In determining market value under Sections 4 and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, a difference in area or distance does not by itself justify reducing the value indicated by a comparable prior award; distance matters where evidence shows a relevant difference in the land’s quality or potentiality. Here the lands were found similar and no evidence established inferiority.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reducing compensation on the grounds of the combined area of the acquisition and the distance between the lands. The reduction was set aside and the compensation determined by the Reference Court was upheld.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_prior_award and lands_similar_in_quality_and_potentiality and no_evidence_of_inferiority and (individual_holdings_are_small or distance_alone_is_relied_on)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal about compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_prior_award: A prior award concerns land used as a comparison for valuing the acquired land.
predicates.lands_similar_in_quality_and_potentialit: The lands being compared have similar quality and development potential.
predicates.no_evidence_of_inferiority: The party seeking a reduction presents no evidence that the acquired land is inferior to the comparable land.
predicates.individual_holdings_are_small: The acquisition appears large only when multiple owners’ individually small holdings are combined.
predicates.distance_alone_is_relied_on: The proposed reduction relies on distance without evidence that the difference makes the acquired land inferior.

members.legal_issue: A finalized prior award for comparable land may be relied on to determine compensation when evidence supports the comparability of the lands and other valuation evidence is available.
material_facts: The claimants relied on a prior award for land in the same village, acquired before the land at issue, which had become final and fixed compensation at Rs. 64 per square metre.
Evidence was presented that the lands covered by the prior award and the current acquisition were similar in their relevant characteristics and potentiality.
The State relied on another earlier acquisition award and proposed the yield method, but the Reference Court and the High Court rejected those approaches.
The courts had evidence describing the acquired lands and their similarity to the lands covered by the prior award.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act govern the determination and reference of compensation. Under Special Land Acquisition Officer v. P. Veerabhadrappa, the yield method may be used when other evidence, such as sale transactions or expert opinion, is unavailable. A prior award can provide a valuation basis where evidence establishes the relevant similarity of the lands; the Court upheld reliance on the prior award in this case.
members.conclusion: The prior award was properly used as the basis for determining compensation, and the State’s appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and finalized_prior_award and evidence_of_comparable_lands and other_valuation_evidence_available

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal about compensation for acquired land.
predicates.finalized_prior_award: An earlier award concerning other land has become final.
predicates.evidence_of_comparable_lands: Evidence supports that the land covered by the earlier award is comparable to the acquired land.
predicates.other_valuation_evidence_available: Valuation evidence other than the yield method is available to assess the land.

members.legal_issue: The market value for land acquired under the same notification must follow an earlier determination where the evidence is materially identical.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the same notification as land considered in an earlier appeal.
The reference court recorded that the evidence in these cases was identical or substantially similar to the evidence in the earlier case.
The earlier determination fixed the market value at Rs. 76,550 per bigha, and the claimants did not establish a material basis for distinguishing it.
The High Court had relied on later transactions and government schedule rates to award a higher market value.
members.legal_principle: Where land is acquired under the same notification and the evidence is materially identical to that considered in a prior decision, the court should not take a different view of market value without a basis for distinguishing that decision. The Court applied its decision in Karan Singh v. Union of India, which had fixed the value at Rs. 76,550 per bigha, and considered the acquisition under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed and the compensation was reduced to Rs. 76,550 per bigha, with statutory benefits calculated on that amount.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_enhanced_compensation and same_acquisition_notification and materially_similar_evidence and prior_market_value_determination

predicates.appeal_challenging_enhanced_compensation: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an award that enhanced compensation for acquired land.
predicates.same_acquisition_notification: The land was acquired under the same notification as land covered by an earlier market-value determination.
predicates.materially_similar_evidence: The evidence concerning the acquired land is materially similar to the evidence considered in the earlier determination.
predicates.prior_market_value_determination: A prior decision determined the market value of land acquired under that notification.

members.legal_issue: A finalized valuation for comparable land in a neighboring area may support the market-value determination when the land was acquired for the same purpose and no material distinction is shown.
material_facts: Land in a neighboring village had been acquired for the same purpose.
A prior valuation for that land had become final and provided different rates for different categories of agricultural land.
The acquiring authority could not identify a distinction between the relevant land and the neighboring land.
The court also referred to state sale instances and upheld the compensation determination, including treating the relevant Chahi and Nahri land alike.
members.legal_principle: In determining compensation for acquired land, a finalized valuation of land in a neighboring area acquired for the same purpose may be used as a judicial instance when no relevant distinction is shown, and may be considered with other sale instances. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in relying on the neighboring-area valuation together with the state sale instances, and the compensation determination was upheld.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and neighboring_land_acquired_for_same_purpose and neighboring_valuation_finalized and no_material_difference_shown and state_sale_instances_available

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.neighboring_land_acquired_for_same_purpo: Land in a neighboring area was acquired for the same purpose as the land under assessment.
predicates.neighboring_valuation_finalized: The valuation determined for the neighboring land had become final.
predicates.no_material_difference_shown: The acquiring authority did not establish a material difference between the lands being compared.
predicates.state_sale_instances_available: Sale instances produced by the acquiring authority were available for consideration.

members.legal_issue: Comparable lands acquired under the same notification for the same purpose should receive the same compensation rate when their areas and situations are comparable.
material_facts: The lands in question and the comparable lands were acquired under the same notification for a housing scheme.
The comparable lands, including adjoining land, were similar in area and situation to the lands in question.

In a separate proceeding concerning lands acquired under the same notification, the High Court had awarded a higher compensation rate, and that decision had become final without an appeal by the State.
The claimant challenged the High Court’s reduction of the compensation rate in an appeal concerning land acquisition compensation.
members.legal_principle: Where lands acquired under the same notification for the same purpose are comparable in area and situation, consistency requires the same compensation rate as that awarded for comparable lands in a final decision. The Court relied on the High Court’s final decision concerning comparable lands acquired under the same notification. No statutory provision or named earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to the same compensation rate as that awarded for the comparable lands; the compensation was enhanced accordingly, with consequential increases in solatium and interest.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_lands_same_notification and comparable_lands_same_purpose and comparable_lands_similar_area_and_situation and final_comparable_award_unappealed_by_acquiring_state

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: A claimant brought an appeal challenging the compensation rate fixed for land acquired by the government.
predicates.comparable_lands_same_notification: The lands used for comparison were acquired under the same notification as the claimant’s lands.
predicates.comparable_lands_same_purpose: The claimant’s lands and the comparison lands were acquired for the same purpose.
predicates.comparable_lands_similar_area_and_situat: The court found the comparison lands similar to the claimant’s lands in area and situation.
predicates.final_comparable_award_unappealed_by_acq: A compensation award for the comparison lands had become final, and the acquiring state had not appealed it.
predicates.claimant_receives_same_compensation_rate: The claimant is awarded the same compensation rate as was awarded for the comparable lands.

members.legal_issue: Compensation should not be reduced below that awarded for materially similar adjacent land when no material difference in the land is shown.
material_facts: The acquired land was adjacent to other land for which compensation had been fixed at a higher rate in decisions concerning the same acquisition area.
The respondents did not identify a material difference in situation, topography or layout between the acquired land and the adjacent land.
The evidence showed that the acquired land was near an industrial area, was suitable for non-agricultural use and had future potential as a factory or building site.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires compensation based on market value, including the land’s advantages, nearby development and potentiality. The Court considered the High Court’s awards for adjacent plots, including Collector, Cuttack v. Karunakar Mahanty, and found no material difference that justified a lower valuation.
members.conclusion: The landowners were entitled to compensation at the same rate as for the materially similar adjacent land, and the reduced award was set aside. The Court relied on the High Court’s decisions concerning adjacent plots, including Collector, Cuttack v. Karunakar Mahanty, First Appeals Nos. 173 and 174 of 1971, decided October 21, 1975.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: An owner appealed the compensation determined for land acquired by the government.
predicates.adjacent_comparable_land_received_higher: Adjacent land in the same acquisition area with similar characteristics received higher compensation.
predicates.no_material_difference_in_land_features: The opposing party did not show a material difference in situation, topography or layout between the acquired land and the adjacent land.

members.legal_issue: A final award for neighbouring land may furnish a proper price basis when the lands were similarly situated and the comparison supports the market value found for the acquired land.
material_facts: A related acquisition award had fixed compensation for neighbouring land at Rs.32,000 per acre and had become final.
The related land and the acquired land were both in undeveloped areas and were similarly situated in potentialities.
The related land was farther from developed localities than the acquired land.
The High Court accepted the related award as the price basis and fixed compensation at Rs.32,000 per acre.
members.legal_principle: In determining market value, the court may assess relevant material and comparable circumstances as a prudent willing purchaser would. The High Court treated a final award for similarly situated neighbouring land as a proper price basis after comparing the lands' locations and potentialities.
members.conclusion: The High Court properly used the final award for the neighbouring land as a price basis for the acquired land.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and neighbouring_land_award_final and lands_similarly_situated and comparison_supports_award_as_price_basis

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.neighbouring_land_award_final: An award determining compensation for neighbouring land has become final.
predicates.lands_similarly_situated: The acquired land and the land covered by the earlier award have similar relevant location and potential characteristics.
predicates.comparison_supports_award_as_price_basis: A comparison of the lands supports using the earlier award as the price basis for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: The death sentence is not warranted where the murder was committed without premeditation and the circumstances do not show brutality or a particularly cruel manner of killing.
material_facts: The appellant's conviction for murder was affirmed, and the evidence showed that he intended to kill the deceased.
The High Court had acquitted the appellant's father of the charge based on an alleged order to kill, so that alleged order did not establish premeditation by the appellant.
The Court found that the appellant acted in excitement at the scene and that the crime was not brutal or dastardly; he did not aim at the deceased's head or heart.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the appropriateness of the death sentence in light of the circumstances of the offence, including the absence of premeditation and of brutality or dastardliness. It relied on no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this sentencing conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Court affirmed the murder conviction but commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment.

predicates.murder_sentence_review: The proceeding reviews a sentence imposed following a murder conviction.
predicates.no_premeditation: The killing was not planned in advance by the offender.
predicates.no_brutal_or_dastardly_manner: The manner of killing was not brutal or dastardly.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is not justified when the circumstances do not establish that the case is among the rarest of rare cases.
material_facts: The trial court imposed death sentences on two accused persons.
The Supreme Court was not persuaded that the reasoning or circumstances established that the case warranted the death penalty.
members.legal_principle: The death penalty is reserved for the rarest of rare cases. The Court applied that principle in reviewing the trial court’s sentence and concluded that the case did not meet that threshold; no earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for this sentencing determination.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were replaced with sentences of life imprisonment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_involving_death_sentence: The matter is a criminal appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.lower_court_imposed_death_sentence: A lower court imposed the death penalty on the accused.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_meet_rarest_case_th: The circumstances and reasons on the record do not establish that the case warrants the most exceptional punishment.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is not justified when the circumstances of the offence do not make the case one of the rarest of rare cases.
material_facts: The trial court imposed the death penalty on the accused it regarded as the ringleader in a planned murder.
The Supreme Court maintained the convictions but found that the circumstances did not place the case among the rarest of rare cases.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rarest-of-rare standard for imposing the death penalty. It cited no earlier case for this sentencing determination.
members.conclusion: The Court reduced the death sentence to life imprisonment and maintained the other sentences imposed on that accused.

predicates.death_sentence_under_review: The proceeding included review of a sentence of death imposed after conviction for a serious offence.
predicates.circumstances_not_rarest_of_rare: The circumstances of the offence did not make the case one of the rarest of rare cases.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is unjustified when the circumstances do not establish a rarest-of-rare case warranting capital punishment.
material_facts: The convicted accused alone was found responsible for the killing, while the alleged participation of the other accused was not proved.
The case against the convicted accused was established through circumstantial evidence and his extra-judicial confession, rather than an eyewitness account.
The killing occurred while the deceased was asleep and was committed for financial gain arising from the offender’s circumstances and conduct.
The Court found no special reason requiring a death sentence and concluded that the case did not meet the rarest-of-rare threshold.
members.legal_principle: Under the rarest-of-rare framework, capital punishment is reserved for cases in which, after considering aggravating and mitigating circumstances, the death sentence is necessary and no lesser sentence is adequate. The assessment is case-specific; the nature of the crime alone does not dispense with that evaluation. The Court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, and the principles applied in Sahdeo v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Sheikh Ishaqe v. State of Bihar concerning capital punishment in cases proved by circumstantial evidence.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was commuted to imprisonment for life, while the remaining parts of the conviction and sentence were upheld.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_death_sentence and case_proved_by_circumstantial_evidence and rarest_of_rare_threshold_not_met and no_special_reason_for_capital_punishment

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_death_senten: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a death sentence.
predicates.case_proved_by_circumstantial_evidence: The conviction is based on circumstantial evidence rather than direct eyewitness evidence.
predicates.rarest_of_rare_threshold_not_met: The circumstances, including the aggravating and mitigating factors, do not make the case one in which capital punishment is necessary.
predicates.no_special_reason_for_capital_punishment: The record does not establish a special reason requiring a death sentence rather than a lesser sentence.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is inappropriate when the circumstances, assessed with full weight given to mitigation, do not make life imprisonment an inadequate alternative.
material_facts: The accused was convicted of murdering three members of his family and was sentenced to death.
The dispute arose after the accused’s father took back land that had been given to the accused for cultivation, and the accused viewed his brother and sister-in-law as responsible.
There had been frequent family quarrels, including a bitter quarrel shortly before the killings.
The evidence indicated an impulsive act rather than planned assaults, with no evidence of diabolic planning.
The accused had been deprived of his livelihood through the loss of the land and sustained serious injuries during the incident.
The Court considered the killings cruel but found the surrounding circumstances relevant to sentence.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 354(3) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Sections 360 and 361 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, life imprisonment is the ordinary sentence for murder and death requires special reasons. The Court applied the requirement to weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances, giving full weight to mitigation and imposing death only when life imprisonment is an inadequate alternative and that alternative is foreclosed. It relied on Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions were confirmed, but the death sentence was replaced with imprisonment for life because death was not appropriate in the circumstances.

rule.if: appeal_from_death_sentence and multiple_deaths_occurred and crime_arose_from_family_dispute and repeated_quarrels_indicated_no_planning and offender_sustained_serious_injuries and mitigating_circumstances_remain_significant

predicates.appeal_from_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.multiple_deaths_occurred: The crime resulted in the deaths of multiple victims.
predicates.crime_arose_from_family_dispute: The crime arose from a dispute among family members.
predicates.repeated_quarrels_indicated_no_planning: The history of recurring quarrels supported the view that the crime was impulsive rather than planned.
predicates.offender_sustained_serious_injuries: The offender sustained serious injuries during the incident.
predicates.mitigating_circumstances_remain_signific: After the aggravating circumstances are considered, substantial circumstances in the offender’s favour remain relevant to sentence.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is not warranted where the sentencing courts treated rape as a basis for the sentence but the evidence does not establish rape.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court imposed and maintained a death sentence for the murder after being appalled by the allegations and findings of rape and murder.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence did not establish rape, set aside that conviction, and maintained the conviction for murder.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances of this case, the death sentence was not called for once the rape charge was found not proved. It relied on no separate provision or earlier case for this sentencing conclusion.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

predicates.appeal_from_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal against a death sentence.
predicates.murder_conviction_sustained: The conviction for murder is maintained on appeal.
predicates.rape_basis_for_sentence_not_proved: The sentencing courts relied on rape as part of the basis for the death sentence, but the evidence on appeal does not establish rape.

members.legal_issue: The death sentence for murder was not justified where the crime arose from a dispute, the offender was not a habitual criminal, the circumstances were unlikely to recur, and the crime was not committed for personal gain.
material_facts: The appellant was convicted of murdering a young boy.
The murder arose from a land dispute involving the boy’s father and other persons.
The appellant was not a habitual criminal.
The circumstances leading to the crime were unlikely to recur.
The crime was not committed for personal gain.
The lower courts imposed the death sentence and gave special reasons for doing so.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 302 of the Indian Penal Code and 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the normal sentence for murder is life imprisonment, and the death sentence is reserved for very extreme and rare cases. The Court applied Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, which requires the normal-sentence rule to be observed in letter and spirit.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was set aside and life imprisonment was imposed instead.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_death_sentence_for_murder and dispute_triggered_the_crime and offender_not_habitual and triggering_circumstances_unlikely_to_recur and crime_not_for_personal_gain

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_death_senten: An accused appealed a death sentence imposed for murder.
predicates.dispute_triggered_the_crime: The crime arose from a dispute involving persons connected to the victim.
predicates.offender_not_habitual: The offender was not a habitual criminal.
predicates.triggering_circumstances_unlikely_to_rec: The circumstances that led to the crime were unlikely to recur.
predicates.crime_not_for_personal_gain: The offender did not commit the crime for personal gain.

members.legal_issue: Death sentences are not warranted where the circumstances include provocation by the deceased’s side, intoxication, an antecedent dispute, and no well-planned attack aimed at eliminating the opposing group.
material_facts: An irrigation-water dispute between the groups had been addressed by mediation but remained a source of friction.
Members of the prosecution group were drinking when one appellant arrived and was beaten by them.
The appellant later returned with armed companions and the attack resulted in three deaths.

The Supreme Court found that the deceased’s side had supplied the earlier provocation, that the parties were tipsy, that the dispute predated the incident, and that there had been no pre-planned, well-laid attack to eliminate the opposing group.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 IPC and 354(3) CrPC, death is the graver alternative and requires special reasons. Applying the offender-focused sentencing principles in Ediga Annamma, Rajendra Prasad, and Bishnu Deo Shaw, the majority held that the circumstances of provocation, intoxication, antecedent dispute, and absence of a planned attack did not warrant death.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were reduced to life imprisonment.

rule.if: appeal_against_death_sentence and provocation_by_deceased_side and participants_tipsy and antecedent_dispute and no_well_planned_attack

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: A convicted person appeals against a death sentence for murder.
predicates.provocation_by_deceased_side: Members of the deceased’s side first provoked the confrontation by beating the accused.
predicates.participants_tipsy: The people involved in the confrontation, including members of the prosecution group, had been drinking.
predicates.antecedent_dispute: The groups had a pre-existing dispute that remained unresolved despite mediation.
predicates.no_well_planned_attack: The attack was not a pre-planned, well-laid effort to eliminate the opposing group.
predicates.death_sentence_reduced_to_life_imprisonm: The death sentence is replaced with a sentence of life imprisonment.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is not warranted where the evidence does not establish that the murder falls within the rarest of rare cases calling for the extreme penalty.
material_facts: The appeal challenged death sentences imposed for the murders of three victims, including a young child.
The courts below relied on the cruelty of the killings, the fact that the child was not spared, and an asserted property motive as special reasons for imposing death.
The prosecution did not establish that the murders were cold-blooded, and the record did not show how they had occurred.
The Supreme Court concluded that the case did not fall within the rarest of rare category.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, life imprisonment is the rule for murder and death is an exception requiring special reasons. Under Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, death may be imposed only in rarest of rare cases; murders committed in an extremely brutal, grotesque, diabolical, revolting, or dastardly manner that arouse intense and extreme community indignation may fall within that category. The evidence here did not establish such a case.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were set aside and replaced with imprisonment for life, while the murder convictions were upheld.

predicates.death_sentence_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal reviewing a death sentence imposed for murder.
predicates.no_evidence_of_manner: The record does not establish how the murder was carried out.
predicates.no_proof_of_extreme_brutality: The prosecution has not proved circumstances establishing the extreme brutality required to place the murder in the rarest of rare category.

members.legal_issue: The circumstances did not meet the threshold for a death sentence where the crime arose from a property dispute and the offender’s circumstances did not show that he was beyond reform or posed a continuing threat to society.
material_facts: The accused was sentenced to death for multiple murders arising from frustration over a property-partition dispute.
He had no criminal tendency and was employed as a scientific assistant.
The Court found no reason to believe that he could not be reformed or rehabilitated or that he would continue violent criminal acts as a threat to society.
The Court considered that the offender should serve a minimum period of imprisonment before release could be considered.
members.legal_principle: The death penalty is reserved for the rarest of rare cases; the gravity and brutality of a crime must be considered alongside the offender’s circumstances, prospects of reform and continuing danger to society. The Court relied on Om Prakash v. State of Haryana and Shri Bhagwan v. State of Rajasthan, and referred to Section 57 of the Indian Penal Code and Dalbir Singh v. State of Punjab concerning life imprisonment and release.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was set aside and replaced with imprisonment for life, with release barred until the accused had served the minimum period fixed by the Court.

rule.if: appeal_from_death_sentence and crime_arose_from_situational_dispute and offender_has_reform_prospects and no_continuing_societal_threat

predicates.appeal_from_death_sentence: The offender appealed a sentence of death.
predicates.crime_arose_from_situational_dispute: The crime arose from a specific dispute or situational frustration rather than an established pattern of criminal conduct.
predicates.offender_has_reform_prospects: The offender’s circumstances did not show that reform or rehabilitation was impossible.
predicates.no_continuing_societal_threat: The evidence did not show that the offender was likely to continue violent criminal acts and pose a continuing threat to society.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is not warranted where the killing was unpremeditated and the accused drew the weapon only after a slap and the ensuing quarrel.
material_facts: The accused was slapped during a quarrel and then drew a penknife from his waist before stabbing the deceased.
The killing was not premeditated.
The slap evidently caused the accused, described by the court as hot-blooded, to lose control, but the deceased was an innocent bystander who had mildly intervened.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the appropriate sentence in light of the lack of premeditation and the circumstances in which the weapon was drawn, while noting that those circumstances did not justify killing an innocent bystander. No specific provision or earlier case was relied on for this sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was reduced to transportation for life.

rule.if: appeal_against_death_sentence and killing_was_unpremeditated and weapon_drawn_after_quarrel_began and provocation_preceded_killing

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.killing_was_unpremeditated: The killing was not planned in advance.
predicates.weapon_drawn_after_quarrel_began: The accused drew the weapon after the quarrel had begun.
predicates.provocation_preceded_killing: A provocation occurred before the accused killed the victim.

members.legal_issue: The appropriate punishment for murder must be assessed in light of the circumstances of the offense, and death was not warranted in this case.
material_facts: The appellant committed the murder within about a month after release on parole, a circumstance the State relied on in seeking the death penalty.
The assault was immediately connected to a dispute over a power of attorney executed by the appellant’s father and challenged by the father’s two brothers.
The appellant assaulted the deceased with the blunt side of a gandasa.
members.legal_principle: In imposing punishment for murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, the court considered the circumstances that immediately led to the assault and the use of the blunt side of the weapon. No earlier cases are cited in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The extreme penalty of death was not warranted; the appellant was sentenced to imprisonment for life under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_sentence and murder_conviction and immediate_property_dispute_precipitated_assault and blunt_side_of_weapon_used

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_sentence: The matter is an appeal challenging the sentence for murder.
predicates.murder_conviction: The appellant stands convicted of murder.
predicates.immediate_property_dispute_precipitated_: A dispute concerning property or a related instrument was the immediate cause of the assault.
predicates.blunt_side_of_weapon_used: The assailant used the blunt side of a weapon in the assault.

members.legal_issue: The death sentence was not justified in light of the circumstances surrounding the killing, including the likely provocation by the victim.
material_facts: The accused had been sentenced to death for murdering his father, and the death sentence had been confirmed on appeal.
The shooting followed a dispute about access to irrigation water, during which the victim had sided with the accused's step-brother.
The court considered it most probable that the victim offered some provocation before the accused fired.
The accused fired the fatal shots, and the murder conviction was upheld.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed whether the circumstances warranted the death sentence and concluded that, despite the murder conviction, the circumstances it identified did not justify that sentence. The court cited no earlier cases or separate sentencing provision as the basis for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was replaced with imprisonment for life; the appeal was otherwise dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_against_death_sentence and murder_conviction_supported and some_provocation_preceded_shooting and killing_arose_from_family_dispute

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.murder_conviction_supported: The evidence establishes the accused's responsibility for a killing classified as murder.
predicates.some_provocation_preceded_shooting: The victim offered some provocation before the accused fired the shots.
predicates.killing_arose_from_family_dispute: The killing arose from a dispute between family members.
predicates.death_sentence_replaced_with_noncapital_: The death sentence is replaced with a non-capital sentence.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is not warranted where the case does not satisfy the rarest-of-rare standard after considering the crime, the offender, and the uncertainty associated with a conviction resting solely on circumstantial evidence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a death sentence for murder, and the conviction rested solely on circumstantial evidence.
The Court found that the murder was not shown to be a diabolical crime and that the evidence did not establish meticulous pre-planning.
The Court considered that the accused’s property-related motive did not by itself make the crime a statistically rarest-of-rare case.
At the sentencing hearing, the accused accepted responsibility for burying the body and offered an explanation for doing so.
The accused was more than 64 years old and had spent approximately 16 years in custody.
The Court concluded that imprisonment for the remainder of the accused’s life would serve the ends of justice and directed that the life sentence mean imprisonment for life.
members.legal_principle: Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure makes death the exception and requires special reasons for its imposition. Under Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, the rarest-of-rare standard requires an individualized assessment of the crime and the offender. A conviction based solely on circumstantial evidence is a factor weighing against the maximum punishment because of the greater risk of uncertainty, but it does not create an absolute bar to a death sentence. The Court relied on, among other authorities, Bishnu Prasad Sinha v. State of Assam, Raju v. State of Haryana, and Kashmir Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh. It also relied on Subhash Chander v. Krishan Lal and the decisions in Ram Anup Singh v. State of Bihar, Prakash Dhawal Khairnar (Patil) v. State of Maharashtra, Shri Bhagwan v. State of Rajasthan, and Mohd. Munna v. Union of India in recognizing a life sentence that requires imprisonment for the offender’s natural life.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the death sentence and substituted imprisonment for the remainder of the accused’s natural life, with the direction that the life sentence was to mean life imprisonment.

rule.if: appeal_against_death_sentence and conviction_based_solely_on_circumstantial_evidence and crime_not_exceptionally_extreme and premeditation_not_fully_established and offender_related_mitigating_facts_present

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a death sentence imposed for murder.
predicates.conviction_based_solely_on_circumstantia: The conviction rests solely on circumstantial evidence.
predicates.crime_not_exceptionally_extreme: The court finds that the crime does not display the exceptional brutality or depravity that would justify the maximum punishment.
predicates.premeditation_not_fully_established: The evidence does not establish that the crime was meticulously planned in advance.
predicates.offender_related_mitigating_facts_presen: The court finds mitigating facts about the offender, such as an acknowledgment of involvement, advanced age, or lengthy time in custody.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is not justified for an offender when the evidence about that offender’s individual role is not of sufficient quality to establish the exceptional culpability required for that sentence.
material_facts: The offender’s convictions for participating in the murders were supported by the accomplice’s testimony and corroborating evidence establishing common intention.
The evidence about the offender’s particular actions in two murders came from the accomplice, whose account contained a discrepancy about the offender’s role.
The other convicted participants’ retracted confessions implicated the offender but could not be used to assess the nature of his individual participation for sentencing.
The court distinguished this offender’s evidence and role from those of the two leading participants.
members.legal_principle: The choice of sentence requires an individualized assessment of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, including the offender’s role and the quality of the evidence establishing that role. The court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and, on the significance of evidence quality when considering death, Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Suresh v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The court upheld the offender’s convictions but reduced the death sentence to imprisonment for life.

predicates.capital_sentencing_appeal: The case is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.conviction_for_murder_supported: The court upheld the offender’s murder conviction on the evidence supporting participation and common intention.
predicates.evidence_of_individual_role_insufficient: The evidence establishing the offender’s particular role was not sufficiently reliable or strong to justify the extreme sentence.

members.legal_issue: The extreme penalty of death is not warranted where the circumstances of the case, including substantial delay in the proceedings, make that penalty inappropriate.
material_facts: The trial court had imposed a death sentence on the participant who personally shot three of the deceased.
More than eight years had elapsed since the occurrence, and the Supreme Court appeal had been pending for five years.
The Court described the killings as extremely gruesome but concluded that death was not called for in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the extreme penalty was called for in the circumstances, taking account of the nature of the killings and the passage of time during the proceedings. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this sentencing conclusion.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was not imposed; the accused were sentenced to imprisonment for life for the murder convictions.

rule.if: criminal_sentencing_appeal and death_sentence_was_imposed and substantial_proceeding_delay and court_finds_death_penalty_unwarranted_in_the_circumstances

predicates.criminal_sentencing_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which the sentence for a criminal conviction is under review.
predicates.death_sentence_was_imposed: The court below imposed a sentence of death on the convicted person.
predicates.substantial_proceeding_delay: A substantial period passed between the offence and the final appellate decision.
predicates.court_finds_death_penalty_unwarranted_in: The reviewing court finds that the circumstances do not warrant the extreme penalty.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence should not be imposed when the court is not satisfied that the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
material_facts: The appeal concerned a death sentence imposed for a planned, cold-blooded murder motivated by the desire to obtain the victim’s wealth.
The victim was apparently unaware of the betrayal and the manner of killing was not shown to have caused her mental or physical pain.
The offender had partially confessed, and the Court considered the irreversibility of execution and inconsistency in the administration of death sentences.
The Court regarded the crime as grave and its motive as highly depraved, but remained hesitant to affirm the death sentence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the principles in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, death is an exceptional punishment for the rarest of rare cases, and may be imposed only when the alternative option is unquestionably foreclosed. Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab provides useful but flexible guidelines and does not create inflexible categories. The Court also stressed that the gravity of the crime must be assessed alongside the circumstances of the offender, and that a court must be especially cautious because an executed death sentence cannot be undone.
members.conclusion: The Court commuted the death sentence rather than affirming it.

rule.if: death_sentence_appeal and planned_grave_murder and (victim_unaware_of_betrayal or killing_caused_no_shown_pain) and court_hesitant_to_affirm_execution

predicates.death_sentence_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a death sentence imposed by a lower court and affirmed on review.
predicates.planned_grave_murder: The offender deliberately planned and carried out a grave murder for a depraved motive.
predicates.victim_unaware_of_betrayal: The victim apparently did not know before death that a trusted person had betrayed her.
predicates.killing_caused_no_shown_pain: The evidence did not show that the manner of killing caused the victim mental or physical pain.
predicates.court_hesitant_to_affirm_execution: The court was reluctant to affirm execution after considering the case circumstances and the irreversible nature of death.

members.legal_issue: A concurrent finding that the landlord would suffer greater comparative hardship is not open to interference in a second appeal, particularly where the tenant provides no evidence that alternative accommodation is unavailable.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found, after comparing the parties’ circumstances, that the landlord would suffer greater hardship if eviction were refused.
The tenant presented no evidence that alternative accommodation could not be obtained in the town.
The High Court disturbed the concurrent hardship finding in the second appeal.
members.legal_principle: Comparative hardship is a factual question; a concurrent finding on it is not open to interference in a second appeal absent a proper basis for such interference. A tenant claiming greater hardship must show that alternative accommodation cannot be obtained in the relevant town. The court relied on Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan and the limits on second appeals under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the landlord would suffer greater hardship should have been accepted and was not open to challenge in the second appeal.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from a decree made in appeal by a subordinate court.
predicates.lower_courts_found_landlord_would_suffer: The lower courts compared the parties’ circumstances and found that refusing eviction would cause greater hardship to the landlord.
predicates.tenant_provided_no_evidence_alternative_: The tenant did not present evidence that alternative accommodation could not be obtained in the relevant town.

members.legal_issue: A supported factual finding establishing the historical rent and similar circumstances, with no legal infirmity, may be left undisturbed on appeal.
material_facts: The tenant applied for fair rent, and the Rent Controller found the evidence insufficient to determine basic rent and maintained the contractual rent with an addition for taxes.
The District Judge accepted evidence that the historical rent for the premises was established for similar circumstances and allowed an increase under the Act.
The High Court affirmed the District Judge’s determination, and the Supreme Court found no legal infirmity warranting interference.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(2)(a) and 4(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 governed the determination of basic rent and the permitted increase. The Court found no infirmity of law in the District Judge’s factual finding, as affirmed by the High Court, that the prevailing rent had been proved for similar circumstances.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not disturb the District Judge’s finding fixing fair rent on the historical rent established by the evidence and the applicable statutory increase.

predicates.appeal_from_fair_rent_determination: A party appeals from a determination of fair rent made in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.historical_rent_finding_has_evidentiary_: The lower court’s finding about the historical rent and the relevant circumstances is supported by evidence it accepted.
predicates.no_legal_infirmity_in_finding: The challenged finding contains no legal error warranting appellate interference.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not disturb supported factual findings on a landlord’s bona fide need and comparative hardship absent sufficient grounds for interference.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the landlord reasonably and bona fide required the premises for personal occupation and that eviction would not cause hardship to the tenant.
The High Court affirmed those findings in revision.
The Supreme Court considered that the record permitted competing views but found no sufficient ground to upset the findings.
members.legal_principle: The revisional power under section 50 of the Mysore Rent Control Act, 1961 is wider than the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but does not make the High Court a second court of first appeal. Supported findings of fact are not to be disturbed without sufficient grounds for interference.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the findings on bona fide requirement and comparative hardship and left them undisturbed.

rule.if: eviction_appeal and first_appellate_court_made_factual_findings and high_court_affirmed_findings and record_permitted_competing_views and no_sufficient_ground_to_interfere

predicates.eviction_appeal: The matter is an appeal in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.first_appellate_court_made_factual_findi: The first appellate court made findings about the landlord’s need for the premises and the comparative hardship of eviction.
predicates.high_court_affirmed_findings: The High Court affirmed the first appellate court’s findings in revision.
predicates.record_permitted_competing_views: The evidence in the record permitted more than one view on the disputed factual matters.
predicates.no_sufficient_ground_to_interfere: The record disclosed no sufficient ground for a further court to disturb the affirmed factual findings.

members.legal_issue: A concurrent finding rejecting a landlord-acquiescence defense to a tenant’s change of use is not disturbed when there is no reason to do so.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the landlord had acquiesced in the different use of the premises.
The trial court and appellate court rejected that plea, and the High Court accepted their finding.
The Supreme Court found no reason to disturb the lower courts’ finding.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied no separate statutory test or earlier case concerning acquiescence; it accepted the concurrent factual finding against the tenant and stated that there was no reason to disturb it.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s acquiescence plea did not prevent eviction, and the concurrent finding against that plea was left undisturbed.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The tenant appealed in proceedings concerning an eviction order.
predicates.lower_courts_rejected_the_acquiescence_p: The lower courts found against the tenant’s claim that the landlord acquiesced in the different use.
predicates.no_reason_to_disturb_the_concurrent_find: The Supreme Court found no reason to set aside the lower courts’ concurrent finding.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that premises are bona fide required for the landlord’s personal use are not disturbed in a special-leave appeal absent perversity or misinterpretation or misapplication of law.
material_facts: The eviction suit was based on the landlord’s bona fide need to provide business premises for her sons.
The sons lacked suitable business accommodation: one operated a tailoring business in a small passage, another had no shop for his repair business, and a third intended to start a laundry business.
The trial court, the appellate court, and the High Court all found the requirement genuine and bona fide.
The tenant did not establish that the concurrent finding was perverse or that relevant law had been misinterpreted or misapplied.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave, a concurrent finding of fact is not to be overturned unless it is shown to be perverse or the relevant law has been misinterpreted or misapplied. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to disturb the concurrent finding of bona fide requirement.

predicates.special_leave_eviction_appeal: A tenant pursued a special-leave appeal against an eviction decree.
predicates.concurrent_bona_fide_need_findings: The courts below consistently found that the landlord genuinely required the premises for personal use.
predicates.no_perversity_or_legal_error_shown: The appellant did not show that the concurrent finding was perverse or resulted from misinterpretation or misapplication of law.

members.legal_issue: A supported finding that the landlord would suffer greater comparative hardship should stand when the writ court has not specifically considered or categorically displaced it.
material_facts: The prescribed authority and appellate authority found that the landlord’s hardship would be greater than the tenant’s and allowed release.
The prescribed authority noted that the landlord had no shop for the intended business and that there was no evidence that the tenant had tried to find alternative accommodation.
The High Court did not specifically consider or categorically set aside the comparative-hardship finding.
members.legal_principle: In deciding an application for release under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the factual assessment of comparative hardship by the prescribed and appellate authorities should not be disturbed where the reviewing court has not specifically considered or categorically displaced that finding. No earlier case was cited for this point.
members.conclusion: The comparative-hardship finding did not warrant interference and remained effective.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_review_of_release_order: An appeal challenged a writ judgment reviewing an order on an application to release a tenanted building.
predicates.lower_authorities_found_landlord_hardshi: The first-instance and appellate authorities found that the landlord would suffer greater hardship than the tenant.
predicates.writ_court_did_not_categorically_displac: The writ court did not specifically consider or categorically overturn the comparative-hardship finding.

members.legal_issue: A partition's bona fides may be relevant to assessing a landlord's bona fide requirement, but a partition issue finally decided between the same parties in certificate proceedings cannot be reopened in later possession proceedings.
material_facts: The tenants contested the landlord's exemption-certificate proceedings, principally arguing that the family partition was contrived to secure the certificate.
The partition's bona fides were decided against the tenants at successive levels, and the certificate proceedings became final.
In the later possession proceedings, the tenants sought to challenge the partition again as bearing on the landlord's bona fide requirement.
members.legal_principle: Sections 88-C and 33-B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, govern the certificate proceedings and the subsequent possession claim. A court assessing bona fide requirement may consider how the landlord acquired the land, including the bona fides of a partition, as recognized in Arvind Lal Bhukanda v. Khandu; however, an issue already directly and substantially decided between the parties in final certificate proceedings cannot be relitigated in the later proceedings.
members.conclusion: The partition could not be reopened in the possession proceedings because its bona fides had already been directly and substantially decided between the parties in the final certificate proceedings.

predicates.excluded_tenant_possession_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a certified landlord's claim to recover exempted land from an excluded tenant.
predicates.partition_issue_finally_decided_between_: The same parties previously litigated the partition's bona fides in certificate proceedings, and that issue was finally decided.

members.legal_issue: A revisional authority cannot justify remanding a possession claim to admit evidence aimed at reopening a partition issue already finally decided, where the landlord's bona fide requirement was concurrently found by the fact-finding authorities.
material_facts: After remand, the Tehsildar found that the landlord bona fide required the land for personal cultivation, and the first appellate court affirmed that finding.
The tenants sought to introduce additional evidence bearing on the partition's bona fides.
The Revenue Tribunal relied on the exclusion of that evidence to set aside the concurrent findings and remand the matter.
The partition's bona fides had already been finally decided in the earlier certificate proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 88-C and 33-B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, frame the earlier certificate proceedings and the later possession proceedings. The final determination of the partition issue between the parties barred its relitigation; accordingly, additional evidence directed to that issue did not warrant a remand. The Court also treated the Tehsildar's finding, affirmed by the first appellate court as the last fact-finding court, as not open to reopening on that ground.
members.conclusion: The evidence directed to reopening the partition issue was no longer relevant, and the High Court was justified in setting aside the Tribunal's remand; the concurrent finding of bona fide requirement was not reopened on that basis.

predicates.tribunal_revision_of_possession_order: A revisional authority is reviewing an order in a certified landlord's possession claim against an excluded tenant.
predicates.concurrent_bona_fide_need_finding: The original fact-finding authority found bona fide need for personal cultivation and the first appellate authority affirmed that finding.
predicates.proposed_evidence_only_attacks_final_par: The proposed additional evidence is directed to challenging the partition's bona fides.
predicates.partition_issue_finally_decided_between_: The same parties previously litigated the partition's bona fides in certificate proceedings, and that issue was finally decided.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a landlord bona fide requires additional accommodation for the household is not perverse merely because the landlord understated the number of rooms, the household has managed to share rooms, or there is no evidence that adult family members will marry imminently, where the actual accommodation and household needs support the finding.
material_facts: The landlord lived in the house with his wife, a married son and the son's wife, three adult unmarried sons, and a daughter.
A court-appointed commissioner inspected the house and reported on the number, use, and small dimensions of the rooms available to the landlord.
The trial court found that the married couple occupied one room and the three adult sons shared another, leaving inadequate space for the household; the appellate court independently agreed.
The High Court reversed the concurrent findings, relying in part on the landlord's failure to state the full number of rooms and the absence of evidence of imminent marriages.
members.legal_principle: A second appellate court should not set aside concurrent factual findings as perverse when the evidence, including an inspection of the actual accommodation and the household's needs, supports them. The assessment of bona fide need must consider the size and use of the rooms, privacy and convenience, and the household as a whole; proof of imminent marriages is not required in these circumstances. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding of bona fide need for additional accommodation was supported by the evidence and was not perverse; the High Court was not justified in reversing it.

predicates.second_appeal_from_concurrent_eviction_f: The matter is a second appeal from concurrent findings in an eviction suit.
predicates.landlord_seeks_additional_family_space: The landlord seeks possession of leased space to provide additional accommodation for the household.
predicates.inspected_rooms_are_inadequate_for_house: An inspection shows that the rooms available to the household are too small or insufficient for its members and their reasonable living needs.
predicates.findings_are_supported_by_evidence: The courts' factual findings are supported by evidence about the accommodation and the household.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that a landlord failed to prove bona fide requirement should not be disturbed where no acceptable ground for interference is shown.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the appellate authority considered the relevant circumstances and found that the landlord had not proved bona fide requirement.
The High Court reconsidered the record and confirmed that finding.
No acceptable ground for interfering with the concurrent findings was shown in the appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court found no acceptable ground to interfere with the concurrent factual findings of the Rent Controller, the appellate authority and the High Court on the landlord’s failure to prove bona fide requirement.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings on bona fide requirement were left undisturbed, and the landlord’s appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_challenging_bona_fide_requirement: The appeal challenged a finding concerning whether the landlord had a bona fide requirement for eviction.
predicates.concurrent_finding_that_requirement_not_: The lower decision-makers consistently found that the landlord had not proved bona fide requirement after considering the relevant circumstances.
predicates.no_acceptable_ground_to_interfere: No acceptable basis for disturbing the concurrent findings was shown.
predicates.concurrent_finding_left_undisturbed: The concurrent finding that bona fide requirement was not proved remained in place.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings on the landlord’s need should not be reappraised when there is no reason to disregard them.
material_facts: The lower courts had made concurrent findings on the landlord’s need.
The appellant challenged those findings on the merits.
The Supreme Court found no reason to disregard the findings.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to reappraise concurrent factual findings when it found no reason to ignore them. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reappraise the evidence and left the concurrent findings undisturbed.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party brought a civil appeal challenging a lower-court decision.
predicates.concurrent_findings_challenged: The appellant challenged factual findings that the lower courts had made concurrently.
predicates.no_reason_to_disregard_findings: The Court found no reason to disregard the concurrent findings.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a landlord has a bona fide need for the premises is not disturbed on appeal when it is a factual finding and is not perverse.
material_facts: The landlord had retired and asserted that he had no other suitable house of his own in the city for himself and his family.
The High Court found that the landlord had established a bona fide need for residence.
The Supreme Court found no perversity or other good ground to interfere with the High Court’s factual finding.
members.legal_principle: Bona fide need under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 was treated as a question of fact. The Supreme Court held that the High Court’s factual finding did not call for interference because it was not perverse.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s finding of bona fide need was upheld and was not disturbed on appeal.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_appeal and landlord_needs_premises_for_self_or_family and landlord_lacks_other_suitable_home and lower_court_finding_not_perverse

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal concerning an eviction proceeding.
predicates.landlord_needs_premises_for_self_or_fami: The landlord asserted that the premises were needed for the landlord’s own residence or the residence of family members.
predicates.landlord_lacks_other_suitable_home: The landlord had no other suitable home available for that residential need.
predicates.lower_court_finding_not_perverse: The appellate court’s finding on the landlord’s need was not shown to be perverse.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that a landlord has a bona fide personal requirement should not be disturbed without an appropriate basis for doing so.
material_facts: The appellate authority found that the landlord had a bona fide requirement for the shop.
The High Court affirmed that finding after considering the matter from all aspects.
The Supreme Court found no appropriate basis to disturb the factual finding.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it should not disturb a factual finding of bona fide requirement reached by the appellate authority and affirmed by the High Court unless an appropriate case is made out.
members.conclusion: The finding of bona fide personal requirement was left undisturbed, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_from_eviction_finding: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a finding made in a tenant-eviction case.
predicates.lower_courts_concurrently_found_bona_fid: The appellate court and the High Court both found that the landlord genuinely required the premises for personal use.
predicates.appropriate_basis_to_disturb_finding: There is a proper basis for the reviewing court to set aside the concurrent factual finding.

members.legal_issue: A concurrent finding that a landlord’s personal need for occupation is proved cannot be reopened on a challenge that concerns appreciation of the evidence in these circumstances.
material_facts: The appellate authority found the landlord’s personal need proved, and the High Court affirmed that finding.
The landlord testified and proved the need of the other landlord, who did not testify.
The other landlord was practising at a distance from the premises because suitable accommodation was unavailable there.
The challenge based on the other landlord’s non-examination and place of practice was not seriously pursued in the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the challenge as one concerning appreciation of evidence, not a basis for reopening a concurrent factual finding, particularly where the testifying landlord had proved the need and the finding had not been seriously challenged in the High Court.
members.conclusion: The finding of personal need was unassailable and could not be reopened on the grounds advanced.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_eviction_order and concurrent_finding_of_personal_need and landlord_testified_to_prove_need and challenge_concerns_evidence_appreciation

predicates.appeal_challenges_eviction_order: A tenant appealed an order directing eviction.
predicates.concurrent_finding_of_personal_need: The appellate authority found the landlord’s personal need proved and a higher court affirmed that finding.
predicates.landlord_testified_to_prove_need: A landlord testified and supported the claimed need for occupation.
predicates.challenge_concerns_evidence_appreciation: The challenge relied on matters such as a person with the need not testifying or practising elsewhere, rather than establishing a basis to displace the concurrent finding.

members.legal_issue: Pure factual findings on a landlord’s bona fide requirement and comparative hardship are not disturbed on appeal when they are supported by the fact-finding authority’s assessment.
material_facts: The prescribed authority considered the parties’ pleadings and evidence and found that the landlords bona fide required the shop and would suffer greater hardship if it were not released to them.
The appellate court affirmed those findings, and the tenants challenged them before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the prescribed authority’s findings on bona fide requirement and comparative hardship as pure findings of fact and held that they could not be upset in this appeal. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to disturb the findings on bona fide requirement and comparative hardship because they were findings of fact.

predicates.eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an eviction order.
predicates.bona_fide_requirement_found_on_evidence: The fact-finding authority assessed the evidence and found that the landlord genuinely required the premises.
predicates.comparative_hardship_found_on_evidence: The fact-finding authority assessed the evidence and found that refusing eviction would cause the landlord greater hardship than granting it would cause the tenant.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a landlord has a bona fide need and no other suitable accommodation may be left undisturbed when the appellate finding is supported by the evidence and a local commission report.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement for himself and his family, which included three sons and five daughters.
The Rent Control Tribunal found the available accommodation insufficient and the requirement bona fide; it also found that the premises had been let for residential use.
During the second appeal, the High Court appointed a local commissioner to inspect rooms alleged to have become vacant.
The commissioner’s report corroborated the landlord’s position that the rooms were occupied by the legal heirs of tenants and were not suitable for residential use.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 provides the ground of eviction for bona fide requirement and absence of reasonably suitable accommodation. The court relied on Vinod Kumar Arora v. Surjit Kumar in concluding that further interference with the appellate court’s factual findings was unwarranted, and cited V. Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal in addressing the eviction proceeding.
members.conclusion: The landlord proved bona fide need and the absence of other suitable accommodation, and the High Court was justified in not interfering with the Tribunal’s findings.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and landlord_has_family_requirement and appellate_court_finds_no_suitable_accommodation and local_commission_report_supports_landlord

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.landlord_has_family_requirement: The landlord seeks the premises for a requirement that includes the needs of the landlord’s family.
predicates.appellate_court_finds_no_suitable_accomm: The appellate court finds that the landlord has no other reasonably suitable accommodation.
predicates.local_commission_report_supports_landlor: A court-appointed local commissioner reports facts that corroborate the landlord’s position about the availability or suitability of other rooms.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment removing rights to contest certain alienations does not defeat an appeal concerning an alienation protected by an unchanged saving provision.
material_facts: The appeals concerned an alienation made before the 1920 legislation came into force.
The 1973 amending legislation changed provisions governing the right to contest alienations but left the saving provision unchanged.
The saving provision preserved rights to contest alienations made before the original legislation came into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Punjab Customs (Power to Contest) Act, 1920 preserved rights to contest an alienation made before that Act came into force. The 1973 amendment did not amend that saving provision; the Court also noted that the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 had not been repealed.
members.conclusion: The 1973 amendment did not make the appeals untenable because the earlier alienation remained protected by the saving provision.

predicates.appeal_concerns_pre_existing_alienation: The appeal concerns an alienation made before the legislation that later regulated the right to contest alienations came into force.
predicates.saving_provision_preserves_pre_existing_: A saving provision preserves the right to contest an alienation made before that legislation came into force.
predicates.later_amendment_leaves_saving_provision_: A later amendment changes other provisions but does not alter the saving provision protecting the earlier right.

members.legal_issue: A statutory prohibition on passing decrees in pre-emption suits applies when an appeal from a trial-court decree remains pending after the prohibition takes effect, because the appeal reopens the subject matter and the appellate decree replaces the trial decree.
material_facts: A trial court had passed a decree enforcing a right of pre-emption.
After the statutory prohibition on passing decrees in pre-emption suits took effect, the decree was challenged in appellate proceedings and the dispute remained pending on further appeal.
The appellate hearing reopened the subject matter of the trial decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973 bars a court from passing a decree in a pre-emption suit from the Act's commencement. An appeal is a rehearing of the whole subject matter, and the trial decree merges into the appellate decree, so the statutory bar applies to a decree passed in appeal. The Court relied on Official Liquidator v. R. Desikachar.
members.conclusion: The prohibition applies to the appellate decree as well as to a decree at trial. The appeal was allowed and the pre-emption suit was dismissed.
