rule.if: preemption_suit_appeal and trial_decree_under_review and decree_bar_became_effective and appellate_hearing_reopens_subject_matter

predicates.preemption_suit_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a suit seeking enforcement of a right of pre-emption.
predicates.trial_decree_under_review: A trial court has passed a decree in the suit, and that decree is under review in the appeal.
predicates.decree_bar_became_effective: A statutory prohibition on passing decrees in such suits took effect before the appellate court passes its decree.
predicates.appellate_hearing_reopens_subject_matter: The appellate hearing reopens the whole subject matter of the trial decree.

members.legal_issue: An ejectment suit pending on appeal from a decree for the successful plaintiff abated when the amended law made the suit invalid, even if possession had been delivered during the appeal.
material_facts: The trial court decreed possession for the plaintiff, and the defendant appealed; that appeal remained pending when the amendment commenced.
The decree had not become final because the appeal was pending.
Possession was delivered to the plaintiff during the appeal before the amendment commenced.
Under the amended law, the tenure was protected from annulment, so the suit could not validly have been instituted under that law.
members.legal_principle: An appeal is a continuation of the original suit, so the pending case fell within section 7(1)(a), not section 7(1)(b), which concerned an appeal or other application by an unsuccessful plaintiff or applicant. Section 7(2) concerned decrees or orders that had become final; its proviso protected possession delivered in execution before commencement in respect of such a decree or order. Because the decree here was not final, the suit abated under section 7(1)(a). The Court relied on the settled principle that an appeal is a continuation of the suit and cited no earlier case by name.
members.conclusion: The suit abated under section 7(1)(a) when the amendment commenced. It was unnecessary to decide the effect of the delivery of possession during the pending appeal.

rule.if: pending_ejectment_suit_on_appeal and defendant_appeal_pending and decree_not_final and suit_barred_under_amended_rule

predicates.pending_ejectment_suit_on_appeal: An ejectment suit remained pending because an appeal from its decree was undecided.
predicates.defendant_appeal_pending: The pending appeal was brought by the defendant against the decree for ejectment.
predicates.decree_not_final: The ejectment decree had not become final when the new law took effect.
predicates.suit_barred_under_amended_rule: Under the amended rule, the purchaser could not validly have brought the ejectment suit.

members.legal_issue: A valid retrospective law containing clear deeming provisions can remove the legal basis of a court judgment, requiring the court to decide a pending appeal on the law as retrospectively changed.
material_facts: The earlier High Court judgment directed compensation to be calculated on the basis of an amendment that had shifted the deemed vesting date.
The later legislation expressly deemed that amendment never to have been made, addressed the effect of court judgments, and restored vesting on publication of the notification.
The State's appeals against the relevant High Court judgments were pending, and the earlier judgment rested on the amendment that the later legislation removed.
members.legal_principle: A statutory fiction must be given full effect and carried to its logical consequences, as stated in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and followed in State of Bombay v. Pandurang Vinayak, Chief Inspector of Mines v. Karam Chand Thapar, J.K. Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, M. Venugopal v. Divisional Manager, LIC, and Harish Tandon v. Additional District Magistrate. Under Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality and Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., the legislature may retrospectively alter the law and remove the basis of a judgment, but cannot simply exercise judicial power by declaring a judgment ineffective while leaving its legal basis unchanged.
members.conclusion: The Court had to proceed as if the removed amendment had never been made; the basis of the earlier High Court judgment was thereby removed, and that judgment could not stand.

predicates.appeal_against_court_judgment: A party brought an appeal against a court judgment that applied the law as it stood before later legislation.
predicates.later_law_expressly_erased_the_judgment_: The legislature expressly and retrospectively removed the legal provision on which the judgment depended.
predicates.later_law_is_constitutionally_valid: The later legislation survived the constitutional challenge made against it.

members.legal_issue: A later procedural restriction on second appeals does not remove a vested right of appeal in a pending suit unless the later law expressly or by necessary implication makes that restriction applicable.
material_facts: The suit was instituted when the procedural code then governing it allowed a second appeal on questions of fact as well as law.
After the suit was instituted, a different procedural code was extended to the territory and restricted the High Court’s second-appeal jurisdiction.
The later legislation contained no express provision, or necessary implication, applying that restriction retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: Procedural changes are generally retrospective, but a right of appeal is a substantive vested right governed by the law in force when the suit is commenced. That right includes successive appeals in the same proceeding and may be taken away only expressly or by necessary implication. The Court relied on Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. v. Irving, Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. Ltd. v. Income-tax Commissioner, and Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhury.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s jurisdiction in the second appeal continued to be governed by the earlier procedural code, and the later restriction applied only to suits instituted after it took effect.

rule.if: second_appeal_from_trial_decree and suit_began_under_broader_appeal_right and later_law_restricted_appeals and not later_law_made_restriction_retroactive

predicates.second_appeal_from_trial_decree: The proceeding is a second appeal from a decree made in a first appeal.
predicates.suit_began_under_broader_appeal_right: The suit began when the governing law allowed a second appeal on questions of fact as well as law.
predicates.later_law_restricted_appeals: A later law restricted the scope of second appeals.
predicates.not later_law_made_restriction_retroacti: The later law did not expressly or by necessary implication apply its restriction to suits already pending.

members.legal_issue: A pending application for relief under a provision that is omitted by a retrospectively applicable amendment cannot be decided under that omitted provision.
material_facts: A decree for possession had been made against a tenant, and execution proceedings were pending when the original protective legislation came into force.
While execution remained pending, the tenant applied for the decree to be rescinded or varied under a provision empowering courts to grant that relief.
The application remained undecided when an amendment omitted that provision and applied the amended legislation to proceedings pending at an earlier commencement point.
The application was still pending when the amendment became effective.
members.legal_principle: Under section 8 of the Bengal General Clauses Act, repeal ordinarily does not affect accrued rights or pending proceedings unless a contrary intention appears. Provisions creating or taking away substantive rights are ordinarily prospective, but may operate retrospectively by express words or necessary implication, and only to that extent. Legislative intention is gathered from the words’ plain, normal, grammatical meaning. Ambiguity in beneficent legislation should be resolved to preserve the benefit, and a grammatical reading producing absurdity or inconsistency may be rejected; neither principle applies where the language is unambiguous. Section 1(2) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Amendment Act, 1953 applied the amended Act to pending proceedings, and “amended” covered omissions as well as additions and alterations. Because section 28 of the 1949 Act was omitted, the court no longer had power to grant relief in applications still pending. The contrary view in Deorajan Debi v. Satyadhan Ghosal, (1953) 58 C.W.N. 64, was overruled.
members.conclusion: The application had to be dismissed because the retrospectively applicable amended legislation had removed the court’s power to grant relief under the omitted provision.

predicates.pending_execution_case: A proceeding to execute a possession decree against a tenant was pending.
predicates.relief_application_pending_when_amendmen: The tenant’s application for relief against the decree remained undecided when the amendment took effect.
predicates.amended_framework_applied_retroactively_: The legislature made the amended framework apply retrospectively to proceedings that were pending at an earlier point.
predicates.relief_granting_power_removed: The amendment removed the power that had enabled courts to grant the requested relief.

members.legal_issue: A later law that clearly applies to pending matters may be applied in an appeal even when it affects substantive rights obtained under the judgment being appealed.
material_facts: The trial court entered a judgment before the relevant legislation was extended to the territory.
The legislation expressly applied to suits pending when it commenced.
An appeal concerning the interest awarded by the trial court remained pending when the legislation became applicable.
The appellate court applied the amended interest provisions to reduce the interest awarded.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, appellate rights are determined under the law in force at the date of the suit, and procedural laws are generally retrospective. But there is no absolute rule that substantive rights are inviolable: where a later law expressly or by clear intendment covers pending matters, both the trial court and the appellate court must give effect to it, even after the first-instance judgment. The Court relied on sections 5 and 6 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act and section 3 of the Usurious Loans Act as amended, and referred to Quilter v. Mapleson, Stovin v. Fairbrass, and Mukerjee (K.C.) v. Mst. Ramratan.
members.conclusion: The appellate court could apply the later law because its clear retrospective language covered the pending suit, notwithstanding that it affected rights obtained under the trial court’s judgment.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_judgment_pending: An appeal from a trial judgment remains pending when the later law becomes applicable.
predicates.later_law_clearly_covers_pending_matters: The later law expressly or by clear intendment applies to matters that are pending when it takes effect.
predicates.later_law_changes_substantive_entitlemen: Applying the later law would alter a substantive entitlement obtained under the judgment being appealed.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment governing pre-emption suits requires a pending appeal to be decided under the amended law, so a decree based on a pre-emption right removed by the amendment cannot stand.
material_facts: The respondents’ pre-emption suits had been decreed under provisions that recognized their claimed right, and those decrees were under appeal.
While the appeals were pending, an amendment deleted the provisions on which the decrees rested and directed that no decree inconsistent with the amended law be passed.
members.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960, operates retrospectively and applies in pending appellate proceedings. Under Ram Sarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 858, its language requires an appellate court to give effect to the substantive provisions of the amendment, whether the appeal is against a decree granting or refusing pre-emption.
members.conclusion: The provision requiring decrees to conform to the amended law operated retrospectively. The decrees based on the deleted right could not be sustained and were set aside.

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: A pre-emption suit is pending before an appellate court.
predicates.prior_preemption_right_removed: An amendment removes the category of pre-emption right recognized when the claim was decided below.
predicates.decree_based_on_prior_right: The decree under appeal rests on the removed category of pre-emption right.

members.legal_issue: A later enactment that retrospectively deems an amendment never to have been made removes the basis of a judgment founded on that amendment, and the court must decide the pending appeal on the altered legal footing.
material_facts: The High Court directed compensation to be calculated by relying on a retrospective amendment that deemed vesting to have occurred earlier.
The later enactment expressly deemed that amendment never to have been made and addressed the effect of judgments and orders.
The appeals against the High Court judgments were still pending, and the judgments rested on the amendment that the later enactment effaced.
members.legal_principle: A statutory legal fiction must be given full effect and carried to its logical conclusion, including its inevitable consequences. The Court relied on East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and State of Bombay v. Pandurang Vinayak, among other cases. A legislature may alter the law retrospectively and remove the basis of a judgment, but may not simply exercise judicial power by reversing a judgment while leaving its legal basis unchanged. The Court relied on Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality and Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., and distinguished Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The Court had to proceed as if the effaced amendment had never been introduced, and the High Court judgment founded on it could not stand.

rule.if: appeal_against_judgment and judgment_depends_on_prior_amendment and later_law_retroactively_deems_amendment_never_made and later_law_changes_legal_basis

predicates.appeal_against_judgment: A party has appealed a judgment that remains under review.
predicates.judgment_depends_on_prior_amendment: The judgment rests on an earlier statutory amendment.
predicates.later_law_retroactively_deems_amendment_: The legislature later enacted a law that retrospectively treats the earlier amendment as never having been made.
predicates.later_law_changes_legal_basis: The later law changes the legal basis on which the judgment was reached, rather than merely directing that the judgment be disregarded.

members.legal_issue: A statutory procedure for review does not restrict an appellate court's power to decide a properly pending appeal under a retrospective amendment.
material_facts: The amending Act provided for review of certain decisions setting aside assessments made by additional collectors.
The State sought review of the High Court's judgment, but the High Court rejected the application as not maintainable under that review provision.

The State's appeal was properly before the Supreme Court, which considered the effect of the retrospective amendment without deciding whether the High Court was right to reject the review application.
members.legal_principle: A review provision such as section 11 of the United Provinces Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1956, does not displace or impair an appellate court's power to decide an appeal properly before it under the law as retrospectively amended. The Court expressed no opinion on the correctness of the High Court's ruling on the maintainability of the review application and cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The review provision did not affect the Supreme Court's power to decide the appeal in light of the retrospective amendment.

predicates.appeal_pending_before_appellate_court: An appeal is properly before an appellate court.
predicates.retrospective_amendment_applies: A retrospective amendment governs the dispute being considered on appeal.
predicates.review_procedure_is_provided: The legislature has provided a procedure to seek review of certain decisions affected by the amendment.

members.legal_issue: A statutory remedy omitted by an amendment is unavailable in proceedings to which the amendment applies, even if those proceedings began while the remedy was in force.
material_facts: The tenants applied under the original statute to have an ejectment decree rescinded, and that application remained pending when the relevant ordinance and amending statute took effect.
The amending statute omitted the provision that had authorized the application and provided that the amended statute applied to proceedings pending when the ordinance commenced.
The trial court rescinded the ejectment decree after the matter was remanded.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its decision in Mahadeolal Kanodia v. The Administrator-General of West Bengal, holding that section 28 of the original Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, after its omission by the amending Act, was unavailable in proceedings pending when the 1952 Ordinance commenced. The amended statute’s provision applying the amended law to those pending proceedings governed the matter.
members.conclusion: The omitted statutory remedy was unavailable in the pending proceeding, so the trial court acted without jurisdiction in rescinding the ejectment decree.

predicates.statutory_tenancy_decree_rescission_proc: A party sought to rescind an ejectment decree by invoking a statutory tenancy remedy.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_amendment_applie: The proceeding remained pending when the amended law was made applicable to it.
predicates.amendment_omitted_existing_rescission_re: The amendment applicable to the proceeding omitted the provision that had supplied the rescission remedy.

members.legal_issue: A non-retrospective statutory amendment removing a pre-emption right does not defeat a decree already granted in a pending appeal.
material_facts: A co-sharer brought a pre-emption suit under the then-applicable law, and the trial court decreed the suit.
The claimant deposited the purchase money as required after the decree, and the decree was affirmed on appeal.
While a further appeal was pending, an amendment substituted the provision governing pre-emption and limited the right to tenants; the amendment did not state that it applied retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: A substantive right is governed by the law in force when the suit is commenced or adjudicated unless the later enactment applies retrospectively expressly or by necessary intendment. An appeal may be a continuation of the suit, but that does not authorize applying a prospective enactment to impair an accrued or vested right. Order 20 Rule 14 CPC provides for transfer of title upon the pre-emption decree-holder’s deposit of the purchase money. The Court approved Didar Singh v. Ishar Singh and Shantidevi v. Hukum Chand, and held that Ramjilal v. Ghisa Ram did not state the correct law; it distinguished the retrospective enactments considered in Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, Ram Sarup v. Munshi and Amir Singh v. Ram Singh.
members.conclusion: The amendment did not affect the parties’ substantive rights fixed by the trial court decree. The appellate court was not required to apply the substituted provision, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: preemption_suit_appeal and first_instance_decree_for_claimant and purchase_money_deposited and amendment_has_no_retroactive_intent

predicates.preemption_suit_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking pre-emption of a sale.
predicates.first_instance_decree_for_claimant: The court of first instance granted the claimant a decree for pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited: The claimant deposited the purchase money after the decree.
predicates.amendment_has_no_retroactive_intent: The later amendment contains no express or necessarily implied intention to apply retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court must decide a pending case under the law in force when it gives judgment, including where an exclusion notification has been cancelled before judgment.
material_facts: The government issued an exclusion notification and later cancelled it while the possession dispute was still pending in appeal.
The landlords had not obtained a final effective decree resulting in the tenants' eviction.
When the appellate court decided the dispute, no exclusion notification was in force for the land.
members.legal_principle: A court deciding an appeal applies the law in force when it gives judgment. A change during the proceedings does not reopen an effective decree that has become final and resulted in eviction, but no such vested position existed here. Under section 88(1)(d) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the land was outside the statutory exclusion once the notification had been cancelled.
members.conclusion: The appellate court had to apply the law as it stood on the date of its judgment. The tenants could claim the protection of the tenancy law, and the cancellation of the earlier notification did not take away any vested right of the landlords.

predicates.possession_suit_pending_on_appeal: A suit seeking possession remains pending before an appellate court.
predicates.exclusion_notification_cancelled_before_: The government cancels an area-exclusion notification before the appellate court gives judgment.
predicates.no_final_effective_eviction_decree: No final effective decree has resulted in the tenant's eviction before the appellate judgment.

members.legal_issue: A special leave petition challenging a judgment is a pending appeal for the purpose of applying an intervening legal change when leave is granted after that change.
material_facts: The defendants filed a special leave petition challenging the judgment that had dismissed their appeal.
The special leave petition was pending when the intervening benami legislation came into force; special leave was granted later.
The defendants had sought permission to rely on the intervening legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the defendants could challenge the judgment by special leave, and the appeal could be heard after leave was granted. The court held that the challenge was pending before it once the judgment had been challenged, and that an appeal is a continuation of the suit. Applying Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare, the expressions “shall lie” and “shall allow” in Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, apply prospectively to future stages of pending proceedings and to future proceedings; “any property held benami” is not limited by time. A pending appeal therefore permits the appellate court to take account of the later legislative change.
members.conclusion: The challenge was pending when the legislation came into force, even though special leave had not yet been granted, and the appellate court could take account of the intervening legal change.

predicates.benami_property_recovery_suit: The proceeding is a suit to recover property on the basis that it was held benami.
predicates.judgment_challenged_by_leave_petition: The party challenging the judgment filed a petition seeking special leave to appeal from it.
predicates.leave_petition_pending_when_law_changed: The special leave petition remained pending when the intervening legal change took effect.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment barring decrees inconsistent with its substantive pre-emption provisions applies in a pending appeal, including an appeal from a decree that granted pre-emption under the former law.
material_facts: A claimant obtained a trial decree for pre-emption under a statutory category that gave a right to owners within an estate.

While the case was on appeal, an amendment removed that category and provided that no decree inconsistent with the amended enactment could be passed in suits instituted before or after its commencement.
The appeal remained pending when the amendment took effect.
members.legal_principle: The amendment’s language was comprehensive and retrospective, requiring appellate courts to apply its substantive provisions whether the appeal was from a decree granting or refusing pre-emption. An appeal is a rehearing, and the trial decree does not retain finality while the appeal is pending. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri and approved Ram Lal v. Raja Ram.
members.conclusion: The amended substantive law applied to the pending appeal; the pre-emption decree was set aside and the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: pending_preemption_appeal and amendment_covers_preexisting_suits and amendment_removed_basis_for_claim and decree_conflicts_with_amended_law

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: An appeal concerning a pre-emption claim remains pending when the governing law changes.
predicates.amendment_covers_preexisting_suits: The amendment expressly applies to suits instituted before as well as after it takes effect.
predicates.amendment_removed_basis_for_claim: The amendment removes the statutory category on which the claimant relied for pre-emption.
predicates.decree_conflicts_with_amended_law: The existing decree grants relief that the amended substantive law no longer permits.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court deciding an appeal in a pre-emption suit must take account of a legal bar that came into force after the decree under appeal when confirming that decree would itself amount to passing a decree in the suit.
material_facts: A suit sought to enforce a right of pre-emption, and the trial court decreed the suit; the lower appellate court affirmed that decree.
While a further appeal was pending, a new law came into force prohibiting courts from passing decrees in pre-emption suits.
The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit.
members.legal_principle: An appeal is in the nature of a rehearing, and an appellate court may take account of facts and events arising after the decree under appeal when moulding relief. When an appellate court confirms a decree, it passes a decree of its own. Under section 3 of the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973, no court could pass a decree in a pre-emption suit after the Act commenced. The Court relied on Lachweshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhury, [1940] F.C.R. 84, and Kristnama Chariviar v. Mangammal, [1902] I.L.R. 26 Mad. 91, at pp. 95–96.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to allow the appeal and dismiss the suit because confirming the decree would have amounted to passing its own decree in a pre-emption suit after the statutory bar had come into force.

rule.if: appeal_in_preemption_suit and lower_court_decreed_preemption and legal_bar_took_effect_during_appeal and law_prohibited_decreeing_preemption_suits and appellate_confirmation_would_be_its_own_decree

predicates.appeal_in_preemption_suit: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking to enforce a right of pre-emption.
predicates.lower_court_decreed_preemption: A court below granted a decree enforcing the claimed right of pre-emption.
predicates.legal_bar_took_effect_during_appeal: A legal bar to granting the requested decree took effect while the appeal was pending.
predicates.law_prohibited_decreeing_preemption_suit: The law in force prohibited courts from granting decrees in suits seeking pre-emption.
predicates.appellate_confirmation_would_be_its_own_: Confirming the decree below would constitute the appellate court passing a decree of its own.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment that removes a pre-emption right governs a pending appeal and prevents an appellate court from granting relief based on that right.
material_facts: The appellants claimed pre-emption on the basis of a status that a later amendment retrospectively ceased to recognize as a ground for pre-emption.
The amendment prohibited courts from passing decrees inconsistent with the amended law.
The appellants sought to appeal a decree concerning the amount payable for pre-emption.
members.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960, required courts to give effect to the amendment retrospectively, including in an appeal from a decree granting or refusing pre-emption. The Court applied Ram Swarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 SCR 858, which had construed section 31.
members.conclusion: The appellants could not obtain a decree of pre-emption after the amendment had removed their right, and the appellate court was required to apply the amendment.

predicates.appeal_from_preemption_decree: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a decree granting or refusing pre-emption.
predicates.claimant_right_removed_by_retroactive_ch: A legal change applied retrospectively removed the claimant's asserted basis for obtaining pre-emption.

members.legal_issue: A public interest petition challenging a land allotment may be dismissed for delay when it is brought substantially after the allotment and sale deed.
material_facts: The allotment was made and a sale deed was executed before the public interest petition was filed.
The petition was filed about three years after the allotment and execution of the sale deed.
members.legal_principle: A court should consider delay and laches in deciding whether to entertain a public interest petition; on these facts, the delay warranted dismissal.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have dismissed the petition on the ground of delay and laches.

predicates.public_interest_litigation: The proceeding was a public interest petition challenging a land allotment.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The challenge was brought substantially after the allotment and transfer had taken place.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging completed land acquisition proceedings must be dismissed when it is filed after an inordinate and unexplained delay.
material_facts: The former owners filed their writ petition about 17 years after the award and after possession had been taken.
They accepted the awarded compensation and pursued a reference and appeals seeking enhanced compensation without challenging the acquisition notifications.
They gave no adequate explanation for the delay; the fact that enhanced compensation had not been fully paid was not sufficient.
The acquisition proceedings had been completed before the writ petition was filed.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the court has discretion to quash acquisition notifications, but a challenge brought after an inordinate delay is liable to be dismissed, particularly when the acquisition steps have become final and an award has been made and possession taken. A claimant cannot wait while the State completes the acquisition and later challenge grounds that were available earlier. The Court relied on Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, [1998] 4 SCC 387, and Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., [1996] 2 SCC 501.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have dismissed the writ petition on the ground of delay and laches; its order granting relief was set aside.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_writ: A claimant filed a writ petition challenging land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.long_unexplained_delay: The claimant waited an inordinate period before filing the challenge and did not adequately explain the delay.
predicates.acquisition_steps_finalized: The award had been made and possession had been taken before the challenge was filed.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a completed state land-possession action may be denied when it is brought after a long, unexplained delay despite the petitioners’ prior knowledge of the action.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged a possession panchnama made in 1986 in a writ petition filed in 2001.

The State’s assertion that possession had been taken was recorded in proceedings in which the petitioners were involved by 1998, and compensation proceedings had also followed the taking of possession.
The petitioners did not explain the delay with a plausible reason; their explanation that they believed a deceased owner’s attorney was handling the matter did not justify the delay.
The petition sought to challenge the possession panchnama after the earlier proceedings had attained finality, without seeking broader relief concerning those proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and equitable; delay and laches may defeat a claim, because equity favours a vigilant litigant rather than an indolent one. The Court relied on Shivgonda Anna Patil v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1990 SC 2281, and Municipal Council, Ahmednagar v. Shah Hyder Beig, JT 1999 (10) SC 336.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was hopelessly delayed and barred by laches, so the appeal was dismissed without deciding the parties’ other contentions on the merits.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_state_possession and long_delay_after_possession_action and prior_knowledge_of_possession_action and no_plausible_explanation_for_delay

predicates.writ_challenge_to_state_possession: The petitioners brought a writ proceeding to challenge a state action taking possession of land.
predicates.long_delay_after_possession_action: The petitioners waited a long time after the possession action before bringing the challenge.
predicates.prior_knowledge_of_possession_action: The petitioners knew of the possession action before they brought the challenge.
predicates.no_plausible_explanation_for_delay: The petitioners did not provide a plausible explanation for waiting to bring the challenge.

members.legal_issue: A later writ petition challenging an award may be barred where the award challenge was omitted from earlier related proceedings and the later challenge is brought after substantial unexplained delay.
material_facts: The landowners had unsuccessfully challenged the acquisition and were given liberty to make a representation about release of the land.
An award had been made before the landowners brought their second set of writ petitions, but those petitions challenged only the rejection of their representation and did not challenge the award.
The second set of proceedings also failed, with the rejection of the representation upheld by the Supreme Court.
The landowners first challenged the award in a fresh writ petition filed in 2004, after the earlier proceedings had concluded.
members.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a later suit or proceeding where a claim that could have been raised in an earlier proceeding arising from the relevant cause was omitted; a challenge brought after substantial unexplained delay may also be barred by laches. The Court applied these principles because the award existed during the earlier proceedings in which the landowners challenged only the rejection of their representation.
members.conclusion: The fresh writ petition was not maintainable because the award challenge was barred by Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and by laches and delay.

rule.if: later_writ_petition and prior_acquisition_challenge_lost and representation_challenge_lost and award_claim_omitted_in_prior_petition and substantial_unexplained_delay

predicates.later_writ_petition: The claim is brought in a later writ petition challenging an award.
predicates.prior_acquisition_challenge_lost: The claimants previously challenged the acquisition and that challenge failed.
predicates.representation_challenge_lost: The claimants later challenged the rejection of a representation concerning the acquired land, and that challenge failed.
predicates.award_claim_omitted_in_prior_petition: The award existed during the earlier related petition, but the claimants did not challenge it in that petition.
predicates.substantial_unexplained_delay: The claimants waited a substantial period to bring the award challenge without explaining the delay.

members.legal_issue: An unexplained, substantial delay in filing a writ petition challenging a land acquisition is a sufficient ground to dismiss the petition.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the validity of a land acquisition by filing a writ petition.
The acquisition notifications had been issued years before the petition was filed; the petition was filed more than 17 months after the award and after the Collector had taken possession.
The petitioners did not satisfactorily explain the delay.
members.legal_principle: Whether delay warrants dismissal depends on the facts of each case. Unexplained delay in seeking writ relief may itself justify dismissal. The judgment notes that counsel referred to this Court's decisions on delay but does not identify them by name; it cites no statutory provision as the basis for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The unexplained delay was a sufficient ground to dismiss the writ petition, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.writ_challenges_land_acquisition: The petitioners filed a writ petition challenging the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.filing_was_substantially_delayed: The petitioners filed the writ petition substantially later than the acquisition notifications and more than 17 months after the award.
predicates.delay_lacked_explanation: The petitioners did not satisfactorily explain the delay in filing.

members.legal_issue: A later writ petition seeking restoration of a cancelled lease cannot succeed where the allottee accepted a refund, failed to meet a conditional opportunity to restore the lease, and had already unsuccessfully sought restoration in an earlier writ petition.
material_facts: The lease was cancelled after the allottee defaulted on an instalment and received notice and an opportunity to be heard.
After the forfeiture was reduced, the allottee accepted the refund of the deposited amount.
The Chief Commissioner later offered restoration if the entire required payment was made within a specified time, but the allottee did not pay within that time.
An earlier writ petition seeking restoration was dismissed, and review was also dismissed.
The allottee later brought another writ petition, relying on an alleged restoration policy and on the treatment of another allottee.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the allottee's acceptance of the refund and acquiescence in cancellation, failure to comply with the conditional restoration order, and the prior dismissal of a writ petition seeking restoration. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this application.
members.conclusion: The later writ petition should not have been allowed; the appeal was allowed and the High Court's judgment set aside.

rule.if: later_restoration_writ and lease_cancelled_after_hearing and refund_accepted and conditional_restoration_deadline_missed and prior_restoration_writ_dismissed

predicates.later_restoration_writ: The allottee brought a later writ petition seeking restoration of a cancelled lease.
predicates.lease_cancelled_after_hearing: The authority cancelled the lease after giving the allottee notice and an opportunity to be heard.
predicates.refund_accepted: The allottee accepted the return of the deposited money after deduction of the forfeited amount.
predicates.conditional_restoration_deadline_missed: The allottee did not make the required payment within the time allowed for conditional restoration.
predicates.prior_restoration_writ_dismissed: An earlier writ petition by the allottee seeking restoration was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a lease cancellation cannot be allowed by applying an earlier decision when the cases are materially different, particularly where the allottee accepted a refund, did not challenge the cancellation at the time, and delayed bringing the challenge without a substantiated explanation.
material_facts: The allottee defaulted on an instalment, and the lease was cancelled after she expressed inability to pay.
In her appeal, she challenged only the amount forfeited and did not challenge the cancellation.
After the forfeiture was reduced, she accepted the balance of her money and took no further action for many years.
She later challenged the cancellation, relying on an earlier High Court decision involving materially different facts.
Her claimed pending revision was denied by the Administration and was not substantiated; she also did not explain the lack of inquiry or action during the delay.
members.legal_principle: A claimant's entitlement must be assessed on the facts of that claimant's case, and a prior decision does not govern a case with materially different facts. Acceptance of a refund, failure to contest cancellation, and a long unexplained delay weighed against relief. The Court considered Jaswant Singh v. Chandigarh Administration (1992 PLJ 522) but held its facts different and expressly left its correctness undecided. No statutory provision was relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing the writ petition; the appeal was allowed and its judgment set aside. The Court expressed no opinion on whether the earlier decision was correct.

rule.if: cancellation_challenge_writ and cancellation_not_contested_earlier and refund_accepted and prolonged_unexplained_delay and cited_case_materially_different

predicates.cancellation_challenge_writ: The claimant brought a writ petition challenging the cancellation of a lease.
predicates.cancellation_not_contested_earlier: The claimant did not challenge the cancellation when pursuing the earlier appeal or remedy.
predicates.refund_accepted: The claimant accepted the return of the deposited money after deduction of the forfeited amount.
predicates.prolonged_unexplained_delay: The claimant waited a prolonged period to challenge the cancellation without substantiating an adequate explanation for the delay.
predicates.cited_case_materially_different: The earlier decision relied on by the claimant concerned facts materially different from the claimant's case.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a consolidation scheme may be dismissed in limine when the challenge is brought after years of inaction and omits landholders likely to be affected by disturbing the scheme.
material_facts: The appellants challenged a village consolidation scheme only after years without raising objections to it.
Other landholders were likely to be affected if the scheme were disturbed, but they were not joined in the writ petition.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine.
members.legal_principle: A delayed challenge to a consolidation scheme may be dismissed where the petitioners failed to object for years and did not join landholders likely to be affected by disturbing the scheme.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition in limine, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.writ_challenges_consolidation_scheme: The petitioners brought a writ petition challenging a consolidation scheme.
predicates.challenge_delayed_for_years: The petitioners let years pass without raising an objection to the scheme.
predicates.affected_landholders_not_joined: The petitioners did not join landholders likely to be affected if the scheme were disturbed.
predicates.writ_dismissal_justified: The writ petition may be dismissed in limine.

members.legal_issue: A defaulting allottee who accepted a refund, failed to comply with a later conditional opportunity for restoration, and had already failed in a restoration proceeding could not obtain restoration through a further writ petition on the asserted basis of another allottee’s treatment.
material_facts: The allottees defaulted on an instalment, and their lease was cancelled after notice and an opportunity to be heard.
After the forfeiture was reduced, the allottees took back the balance of their deposit.
A later administrative order offered restoration if the allottees paid the full amount within a specified time, but they did not comply.
A prior writ petition seeking restoration was dismissed, and a review of that dismissal was also rejected.

The later writ petition was allowed by the High Court on the basis of restoration granted to another allottee, without establishing that the cases were materially similar or that the other restoration order was lawful.
members.legal_principle: A writ claim must be decided on its own facts and applicable legal principles; the discretionary writ jurisdiction cannot require an authority to repeat an illegal or unwarranted action. The decision also notes that an earlier restoration opportunity was not taken and that a prior writ seeking restoration had been dismissed. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on to determine this claim.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside; the allottees were not entitled to restoration on the basis relied on by the High Court.

rule.if: writ_petition_seeks_plot_restoration and lease_cancelled_after_payment_default and allottee_accepted_refund and conditional_restoration_offer_not_met and prior_restoration_writ_dismissed

predicates.writ_petition_seeks_plot_restoration: An allottee seeks restoration of a plot through a writ petition.
predicates.lease_cancelled_after_payment_default: The allottee’s lease was cancelled after the allottee defaulted on a required payment.
predicates.allottee_accepted_refund: The allottee took back the deposited amount after deduction of the amount forfeited.
predicates.conditional_restoration_offer_not_met: The allottee did not satisfy the payment condition attached to a later opportunity to restore the plot.
predicates.prior_restoration_writ_dismissed: A prior writ petition by the allottee seeking restoration was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A writ challenging cancellation of a lease was not governed by an earlier decision involving materially different facts where the claimant had accepted the refund and waited seventeen years to challenge the cancellation without substantiating an explanation for the delay.
material_facts: The allottee defaulted on an instalment, and the lease was cancelled after a show-cause process.
In the appeal from cancellation, the allottee sought only a reduction in the forfeiture and did not challenge the cancellation.
After the forfeiture was reduced, the allottee took back the balance of the deposit and remained inactive for seventeen years before challenging the cancellation by writ.
The allottee’s explanation that a revision had been filed and remained pending was not substantiated; the allottee also did not explain the failure to inquire or seek a decision during that period.
The High Court allowed the writ petition on the basis of an earlier decision that concerned materially different facts and grounds.
members.legal_principle: The earlier decision in Jaswant Singh v. Chandigarh Administration did not govern because its facts and grounds were materially different. The Court expressed no opinion on whether that earlier decision was correct. The claimant’s own conduct and circumstances had to be considered; no statutory provision is cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing the writ petition; the appeal was allowed and its judgment set aside.

predicates.writ_petition_challenges_lease_cancellat: An allottee brings a writ petition challenging cancellation of a lease.
predicates.allottee_accepted_refund_without_challen: The allottee sought only a reduction in forfeiture, accepted the remaining refund, and did not challenge cancellation at that time.
predicates.challenge_delayed_for_long_period_withou: The allottee waited a long period before challenging cancellation and did not substantiate an explanation for the delay.
predicates.cited_precedent_materially_different: The earlier decision invoked to support the writ petition concerned materially different facts or grounds.

members.legal_issue: Relief under Article 226 may be refused when a claimant delays asserting a claimed right beyond a reasonable time.
material_facts: The governing enactment had been in force for many years before the claimant applied for a ryotwari patta.
The claimant sought relief in writ proceedings after that prolonged delay.
members.legal_principle: The extraordinary remedy under Article 226 may be refused where delay, laches, acquiescence or failure to assert a right within a reasonable time makes relief inappropriate. The Court also noted that the governing enactment contemplated an application soon after its commencement.
members.conclusion: Relief was also liable to be refused for delay, laches, acquiescence or omission to assert the claimed right within a reasonable time.

predicates.article_226_claim_for_ryotwari_patta: A claimant sought a ryotwari patta through writ proceedings.
predicates.claimant_delayed_asserting_right_beyond_: The claimant waited beyond a reasonable time after the relevant opportunity arose before asserting the claimed right.

members.legal_issue: A writ challenge to land acquisition proceedings may be refused for laches when it is brought only after substantial delay and after the award has been made and possession taken.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the acquisition declaration more than two years after it was made.
By the time they filed that challenge, an award had been made and possession had been taken; possession had also been handed over to the public-purpose corporation.
The challenge alleged that the declaration had been made beyond the statutory time limit, but the Court did not decide that issue on its merits.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, a court should be loath to quash land-acquisition proceedings when there is inordinate delay and the award has been made and possession taken; such challenges should ordinarily be brought at least before the award and taking of possession. The Court relied on Swaika Properties (P) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. (P) Ltd., State of Rajasthan v. D.R. Laxmi, Municipal Council, Ahmednagar v. Shah Hyder Beig, and C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu.
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s orders were set aside because the challenge was brought after gross delay. The Court did not decide whether the declaration complied with the statutory time limit.

rule.if: land_acquisition_writ_challenge and substantial_delay_after_declaration and award_before_challenge and possession_taken_before_challenge

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A writ petition seeks to invalidate land-acquisition proceedings.
predicates.substantial_delay_after_declaration: The landowners waited a substantial period after the acquisition declaration before challenging it.
predicates.award_before_challenge: The acquisition award was made before the landowners filed their challenge.
predicates.possession_taken_before_challenge: The authorities took possession of the land before the landowners filed their challenge.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional writ petition challenging an administrative determination may be dismissed for undue delay when the challengers participated in the proceedings, failed to pursue available remedies, and waited years to seek relief.
material_facts: The ryots participated in the inquiry through counsel until counsel stopped appearing.
The Assistant Settlement Officer made the determination in 1959, but the ryots did not seek restoration or appeal from it.
The State appealed, and the Tribunal affirmed the determination.
The ryots filed a writ petition about four and a half years after the Assistant Settlement Officer's order.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 may be refused for undue delay. Where challengers knew of the proceedings, participated through counsel, and did not pursue available remedies, a later writ challenge may be rejected as delayed. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was properly dismissed for delay, and the High Court Division Bench erred in setting that dismissal aside.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenging_administrative_determination and participated_in_underlying_proceedings and failed_to_pursue_available_remedies and substantial_delay_before_writ

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_administ: The proceeding is a constitutional writ challenging an administrative determination.
predicates.participated_in_underlying_proceedings: The challengers took part in the underlying proceedings, personally or through a representative.
predicates.failed_to_pursue_available_remedies: The challengers did not use available procedures to seek restoration or appeal the determination.
predicates.substantial_delay_before_writ: The challengers waited a substantial period after the determination before filing the writ petition.

members.legal_issue: A writ challenge to a land acquisition may be dismissed for delay and laches when it is brought after possession has been taken and the award has become final, particularly where the delay is unexplained.
material_facts: The landowners objected to the acquisition and initially challenged it in a court that lacked territorial jurisdiction; that challenge ended when the Supreme Court set aside the interim order for want of jurisdiction.
After that proceeding ended, the landowners did not challenge the acquisition for a period and gave no explanation for the delay; a later writ petition was withdrawn and then refiled.
The Supreme Court treated possession as having been taken and the award as having become final before the writ challenge was determined.
The landowners also sought enhancement of compensation through a reference proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The discretionary power under Article 226 should not ordinarily be exercised to quash acquisition proceedings where there is inordinate, unexplained delay and the acquisition has progressed to possession and a final award. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd. (1996) 11 SCC 501, State of Rajasthan v. D.R. Laxmi (1996) 6 SCC 445, Municipal Council, Ahmednagar v. Shah Hyder Beig (2000) 2 SCC 48, and C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu (1997) 2 SCC 627. It also referred to the vesting consequence described in Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
members.conclusion: The writ petition and appeal were dismissed for delay and laches, without deciding the merits of the acquisition; the High Court's dismissal was affirmed.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition and unexplained_delay and possession_preceded_writ and award_was_final

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: The landowner brought a writ proceeding challenging the land acquisition.
predicates.unexplained_delay: The landowner left a period without pursuing the acquisition challenge and gave no explanation for that delay.
predicates.possession_preceded_writ: The acquiring authority had taken possession of the acquired land before the writ challenge was brought.
predicates.award_was_final: The award for the acquired land had become final.

members.legal_issue: A claimant’s substantially delayed challenge to an administrative decision may be denied relief for delay and laches.
material_facts: The Collector rejected the land application in 1999, and the revision challenging that decision was filed more than five years later.
The revisional authority rejected the revision for delay in 2005, but the respondent challenged that decision in the High Court only in 2011.
The respondent said it had recently learned of the revisional decision, but the Supreme Court agreed that it had remained indolent in pursuing its remedy.
The Supreme Court was hearing an appeal from a Division Bench decision that had reversed the Single Judge’s dismissal of the delayed challenge.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a party who delays substantially in pursuing a remedy may be denied relief on grounds of delay and laches. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The Single Judge was right to deny indulgence because of the respondent’s delay and laches, and the Division Bench was not justified in reversing that decision.

rule.if: appeal_reviews_appellate_order_reversing_dismissal and writ_challenges_administrative_decision and challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay and no_adequate_explanation_for_delay

predicates.appeal_reviews_appellate_order_reversing: An appeal reviews an appellate order that reversed the dismissal of a claimant’s challenge.
predicates.writ_challenges_administrative_decision: A claimant brings a writ proceeding to challenge an administrative decision.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The claimant files the challenge after a substantial delay in pursuing the available remedy.
predicates.no_adequate_explanation_for_delay: The claimant does not provide an explanation that the court accepts as adequate for the delay.

members.legal_issue: A writ challenge to an acquisition notice or proceedings cannot be brought after the acquisition award has been made and possession has been taken.
material_facts: The award for the acquired land was made in 1976 and possession was taken that year.
The claimants filed their writ petition in 1992 and sought to quash the acquisition notification and obtain possession of the land.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu, [1997] 2 SCC 627, which held that after the acquisition proceedings have become final and possession has been taken, the former owners have no right to challenge the notification. It also relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., [1996] 11 SCC 501, which states that courts should be loath to quash acquisition notifications after the award and possession, while considering the relevant factors in exercising their discretion under Article 226 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The acquisition challenge could not succeed after the award had been made and possession had been taken.

predicates.acquisition_notice_writ_challenge: The claimant brought a writ challenge to an acquisition notice or proceedings.
predicates.award_made: An award for the acquired land had been made.
predicates.possession_taken: Possession of the acquired land had been taken.
predicates.post_award_acquisition_challenge_not_ent: A writ challenge to the acquisition notice or proceedings is not entertained after the award and taking of possession.

members.legal_issue: Failure to examine available independent eyewitnesses may justify an adverse inference against the prosecution when its interested witnesses have material infirmities and need corroboration.
material_facts: The prosecution eyewitnesses were interested, inimical to the accused, and associated with the deceased’s faction.
The prosecution evidence indicated that two independent eyewitnesses had seen the occurrence, but the prosecution did not examine them or give a reasonable explanation for their absence.
The trial court considered the independent evidence necessary to corroborate the infirm prosecution testimony.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution need not examine every witness merely to multiply testimony. However, that general rule does not apply in the same way where the eyewitness evidence has material infirmities and can be relied upon only if properly corroborated, and available independent witnesses are not examined without reasonable explanation.
members.conclusion: In these circumstances, the trial court was justified in drawing an adverse inference against the prosecution; its refusal to accept the eyewitness testimony was not unreasonable.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and eyewitnesses_interested_or_inimical and eyewitness_evidence_needs_corroboration and independent_eyewitnesses_available_but_not_examined_without_explanation

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on eyewitness testimony.
predicates.eyewitnesses_interested_or_inimical: The eyewitnesses who testified have an interest in the outcome or animus against the accused.
predicates.eyewitness_evidence_needs_corroboration: Material infirmities in the eyewitness testimony make corroboration necessary before it can safely be relied upon.
predicates.independent_eyewitnesses_available_but_n: Independent eyewitnesses were available to the prosecution but were not called, and no reasonable explanation was given for their absence.

members.legal_issue: An accused’s failure to explain incriminating circumstances in the examination following the prosecution evidence may support an adverse inference where those circumstances call for an explanation.
material_facts: The accused did not deny visiting the complainant’s home and staying there, and did not explain the visit.
Treated currency was recovered from the pocket of the accused’s trousers, and his hands and part of his trousers turned pink when washed.
When questioned about the incriminating circumstances, the accused gave no explanation for them.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an accused may remain silent or deny the allegations, but the court may draw an adverse inference permissible by law when the accused gives no explanation for incriminating material put to him. The court relied on Ramnaresh & Ors. v. State of Chhattisgarh, AIR 2012 SC 1357; Munish Mubar v. State of Haryana, AIR 2013 SC 912; and Raj Kumar Singh alias Raju @ Batya v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 2013 SC 3150.
members.conclusion: The court was entitled to draw an adverse inference from the accused’s failure to explain the incriminating circumstances.

predicates.criminal_trial_with_accused_examined_on_: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the accused is examined about incriminating evidence.
predicates.incriminating_circumstances_call_for_exp: The prosecution evidence presents circumstances against the accused that call for an explanation.
predicates.accused_offers_no_explanation: The accused gives no explanation for those circumstances when examined.

members.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference when a party who could testify does not enter the witness box and gives no explanation for not doing so.
material_facts: The original defendant did not appear to testify or submit to cross-examination.
His younger brother testified under a power of attorney and acknowledged that he and the original defendant had separated.
No explanation was given for the original defendant’s failure to testify.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 114, Illustration (g), of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the court may draw an adverse inference from a party’s failure to give evidence. The court relied on Iswar Bhai C. Patel v. Harihar Behera, (1999) 3 SCC 457, which states that an adverse presumption is to be drawn where a party does not enter the witness box and present himself for cross-examination.
members.conclusion: An adverse inference was properly drawn against the original defendant.

predicates.civil_property_suit: The proceeding was a civil suit concerning property.
predicates.party_with_relevant_knowledge_did_not_te: A party with relevant knowledge did not enter the witness box or submit to cross-examination.
predicates.failure_to_testify_unexplained: The party gave no explanation for not testifying.

members.legal_issue: A party’s failure to testify on their own behalf and submit to cross-examination may support an adverse inference against that party.
material_facts: The defendant who disputed the sale did not enter the witness box or testify under oath to the facts pleaded in his defence.
The disputed transaction and any payment under it had not occurred in that defendant’s presence, and he had no personal knowledge of its terms.
The defendant avoided cross-examination while the vendor admitted the plaintiff’s claim and testified to the sale.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, the court may draw an adverse inference when a party does not testify to their own case and submit to cross-examination. The Court relied on Sardar Gurbakhsh Singh v. Gurdial Singh, Kirpa Singh v. Ajaipal Singh, Martand Pandharinath Chaudhari v. Radhabai Krishnarao Deshmukh, Gulla Kharagjit Carpenter v. Narsingh Nandkishore Rawat, Arjun Singh v. Virender Nath, and Bhagwan Dass v. Bhishan Chand.
members.conclusion: An adverse presumption arose against the defendant who withheld his testimony, supporting rejection of his claim that the sale was fictitious.

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute was heard as a civil suit.
predicates.party_did_not_testify: A party did not enter the witness box to give their own evidence on the case they pleaded.
predicates.party_did_not_submit_to_cross_examinatio: The party did not make themselves available for cross-examination by the opposing side.

members.legal_issue: A party’s failure to produce relevant account books in its possession may support an adverse inference against its compensation claims.
material_facts: The claimant sought compensation for damage to a building and for water pipes.
The claimant had maintained accounts relating to construction and repairs but did not produce them.
The claimant did not produce accounts that could have shown the length of pipes used.
The High Court reduced the amounts awarded for the building damage and the pipes, and the Supreme Court upheld those reductions.
members.legal_principle: When a person fails to produce account books in that person’s possession, an adverse inference may be drawn. The Court relied on Seth Maganmal Since Deceased v. Darbarilal Chowdhry, AIR 1928 PC 39.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to disallow the major part of the claims for building damage and water pipes because the relevant account books were not produced.

predicates.compensation_award_appeal: The proceeding challenges an appellate court’s reduction of compensation amounts awarded by an arbitrator.
predicates.relevant_accounts_held: The claimant maintained or possessed accounts relevant to the claimed damage or materials.
predicates.relevant_accounts_not_produced: The claimant did not produce those relevant accounts as evidence.

members.legal_issue: Public authorities directed to produce relevant documents must place them before the court, and withholding a relevant document may justify an adverse inference or another appropriate order.
material_facts: The High Court directed the State and municipal authority to produce documents under multiple headings.
The directions had been made without hearing those authorities and without considering the practical hardship of producing a large volume of documents.
The Supreme Court required the authorities to place all relevant documents before the High Court while leaving the High Court free to respond appropriately if relevant documents were withheld.
members.legal_principle: The Court tailored the document-production direction to account for the authorities’ hardship while preserving the High Court’s ability to address the withholding of relevant material through an adverse inference or another appropriate order.
members.conclusion: The State and municipal authority were required to place all relevant documents before the High Court; if a relevant document was later found to have been withheld, the High Court could draw an adverse inference or make another appropriate order.

predicates.appeal_from_interim_order_in_public_inte: The matter is an appeal concerning an interim order in a public interest proceeding.
predicates.public_authorities_hold_documents_releva: Public authorities possess documents relevant to the case pending before the court.

members.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference when a party withholds important, relevant documents in that party’s possession, even if the burden of proof does not rest on that party and production was not expressly demanded.
material_facts: The dispute concerned ownership of land associated with a public religious trust.
The claimant, who managed the trust and admitted possessing separate accounts of its income, did not produce those accounts or his own accounts showing how income from the land was dealt with.
The accounts could have shed light on whether the land and its income belonged to the trust or to the claimant.
members.legal_principle: Under section 114, illustration (g), of the Evidence Act, a court may infer that withheld evidence would be unfavorable to the person withholding it. The court applied Murugesam Pillai v. Manickavasaka Pandara and Biltu Ram v. Jainandan Prasad, and explained that Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh does not bar such an inference merely because a demand for production was not made.
members.conclusion: The court may draw an adverse inference against a party who withholds important documents in that party’s possession, notwithstanding the allocation of the burden of proof or the absence of an express demand for production.

rule.if: civil_property_dispute and important_records_in_party_possession and records_relevant_to_dispute and party_withheld_records

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The proceeding involves a dispute over ownership or rights in property.
predicates.important_records_in_party_possession: A party possesses important records that could assist in deciding the dispute.
predicates.records_relevant_to_dispute: The records could shed light on a fact in issue.
predicates.party_withheld_records: The party did not produce the relevant records to the court.

members.legal_issue: Failure to examine a material prosecution witness may support an adverse inference against the prosecution when that witness could clarify a contested part of the prosecution’s own case.
material_facts: The prosecution’s case depended on what was decided at a meeting about whether the accused should visit the affected landowners and pursue payment of compensation.
The official who convened or participated in that meeting was not examined, although he could have clarified what directions were given.
An accountant who could have addressed the whereabouts of the money was also not examined.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish its own case and should examine material witnesses capable of clarifying its narrative; it cannot shift that task to the accused. The judgment applies the general criminal-trial burden of proof and the rule that the prosecution’s onus does not shift.
members.conclusion: The court was entitled to draw an adverse inference against the prosecution from its failure to examine the material accountant, and the non-examination of the official who could clarify the meeting left the prosecution’s account unsupported.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution must prove its case.
predicates.material_prosecution_witness_not_examine: The prosecution does not call a witness material to its case.
predicates.witness_could_clarify_prosecution_case: The uncalled witness could provide material evidence about a contested part of the prosecution’s account.

members.legal_issue: A court may infer that missing official records would support a party’s account when the responsible authority fails to produce those records after being directed to do so and warned of the consequence.
material_facts: The Court directed the State to produce the records containing the landholder’s objections and gave further time to comply.
The Court warned that failure to produce the records would result in an adverse inference.
The State did not produce the records and later stated that they could not be traced.
The State’s own pleadings acknowledged that the landholder’s return referred to the pending title suit.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the failure to produce records after a production direction and an express warning as warranting an adverse inference. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this inference.
members.conclusion: The Court inferred that the landholder had properly disclosed the pending suit in the return.

predicates.appellate_review_of_land_ceiling_action: A court is reviewing an appeal concerning action taken in a land-ceiling proceeding.
predicates.court_ordered_record_production: The court directed the responsible authority to produce records relevant to a disputed factual issue.
predicates.responsible_authority_failed_to_produce_: The authority did not produce the ordered records despite being warned that nonproduction could have an evidentiary consequence.

members.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference when a claimant fails to produce a material document in the claimant's possession that could establish the claimed continuing co-ownership.
material_facts: The claimants asserted that they had retained a small area in the relevant holdings after transferring their other co-ownership rights.
The sale deed recording the transfer was not produced, although it was in the claimants' power and possession and could have shown whether any relevant land had been retained.
The claimants did not establish by other evidence that the retained area was in the holdings containing the land subject to pre-emption.
members.legal_principle: A court may draw an adverse inference from a party's failure to produce a material document within that party's power and possession. The judgment applies this principle to the claimants' failure to produce the transfer deed; it cites no earlier cases for the principle.
members.conclusion: The omission justified an adverse inference that the sale deed would have shown that the claimants retained no land relevant to their pre-emption claim; oral evidence did not cure the failure to establish the claimed interest.

rule.if: preemption_suit and material_transfer_document_in_claimant_control and claimant_failed_to_produce_document and document_could_show_retained_interest

predicates.preemption_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking to pre-empt a sale of land.
predicates.material_transfer_document_in_claimant_c: A document recording the claimant's transfer of co-ownership rights was within the claimant's power and possession.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_produce_document: The claimant did not produce that transfer document.
predicates.document_could_show_retained_interest: The transfer document could establish whether the claimant retained an interest in the land subject to pre-emption.
predicates.adverse_inference_against_claimant_justi: The court is justified in inferring that the withheld document would not support the claimant's assertion of a retained interest.

members.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference when a party withholds the best evidence in its possession concerning disputed goods and their disposal.
material_facts: The appellant had taken possession of the goods and was in a position to provide evidence about them and their disposal.
The appellant sold goods and machinery, but did not produce the best evidence available to it concerning the goods despite prolonged litigation.
The appellant’s denials concerning the sale and the bank’s charge were vague, while the documentary and oral evidence supported the bank’s claim.
members.legal_principle: Where a party withholds the best evidence within its power and possession, the Court may draw an adverse inference against that party and doubt its bona fides.
members.conclusion: The Court drew an adverse inference against the appellant because it failed to produce the best evidence in its possession.

rule.if: court_proceeding and party_controlled_best_evidence and party_failed_to_produce_it and evidence_concerns_disputed_goods_or_their_disposal

predicates.court_proceeding: A dispute concerning goods or their disposal is before a court.
predicates.party_controlled_best_evidence: A party had the best evidence about the disputed goods or their disposal in its possession or control.
predicates.party_failed_to_produce_it: The party did not produce that evidence before the court.
predicates.evidence_concerns_disputed_goods_or_thei: The withheld evidence relates to the goods or their disposal that are in dispute.

members.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference from a party’s withholding of evidence only after assessing its relevance and the parties’ pleadings, burdens, and diligence, including whether the opposing party sought its production through the available procedure.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought inspection of government records from authorities controlled by the defendant but was not permitted to inspect them.
The plaintiff did not seek interrogatories, inspection, or production through the prescribed court procedure, and no court order directing production was made.
The appellate courts drew an adverse inference against the defendant for not producing the records.
members.legal_principle: Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act makes an adverse inference discretionary, not automatic. The court must consider the relevance of withheld evidence, the burden of proof, the other party’s diligence and available discovery procedures, and any explanation for non-production. The Court relied on Murugesam Pillai v. Gnana Sambandha Pandara Sannadhi, Gopal Krishnaji Ketkar v. Mohamed Haji Latif, Kamma Otukunta Ram Naidu v. Chereddy Pedda Subba Reddy, Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas, Mahant Shri Srinivas Ramanuj Das v. Surjanarayan Das, Ramrati Kuer v. Dwarika Prasad Singh, and the discovery and inspection procedures in Order XI CPC.
members.conclusion: The appellate courts were not entitled to draw an adverse inference against the defendant on these facts.

rule.if: civil_title_proceeding and evidence_is_held_by_opposing_party and opposing_party_did_not_seek_production_through_available_procedure and no_court_order_to_produce_was_disobeyed

predicates.civil_title_proceeding: A party brings a civil proceeding to establish title to property.
predicates.evidence_is_held_by_opposing_party: Material evidence relevant to the dispute is held by the opposing party.
predicates.opposing_party_did_not_seek_production_t: The party seeking the evidence does not use the available procedure to request its production or inspection.
predicates.no_court_order_to_produce_was_disobeyed: The court has not ordered the holder to produce the evidence, or the holder has complied with any such order.

members.legal_issue: The unexplained withholding of available witnesses who are essential to the prosecution account may support an adverse inference when the evidence already presented is not unimpeachable.
material_facts: The prosecution did not examine the deceased’s husband, who had been present from the beginning and could have clarified how the incident began.
