members.legal_issue: A rise in property value during litigation, by itself, does not justify refusing specific performance, though the court may impose reasonable conditions to balance the parties’ equities.
material_facts: A registered sale agreement was executed through an agent authorized to sell the owner’s share of the property.
The trial court found that the buyer had paid the consideration and had remained ready and willing to perform, while the defendants had not completed the sale.
The buyer filed suit relatively soon after the agreement, but the dispute remained in court for many years and the property’s value increased substantially.
The Supreme Court restored the decree for specific performance on condition that the buyer pay an additional amount to the owner.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the discretion to grant specific performance must be exercised judicially on fair and reasonable principles. A rise in price or passage of time alone is not a valid reason to deny relief, although the court may impose a reasonable condition, including additional payment, after considering the totality of the circumstances. The Court relied on Satya Jain v. Anis Ahmed Rushdie, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal and K. Prakash v. B.R. Sampath Kumar; it distinguished K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan and Vimaleshwar Nagappa Shetty v. Noor Ahmed Sheriff on their facts.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s refusal of specific performance was set aside. The trial court’s decree was affirmed subject to a reasonable additional payment condition to account for the circumstances, including the substantial increase in value during the prolonged litigation.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and valid_sale_agreement_proved and buyer_continuously_ready_willing and seller_failed_to_complete_sale and property_value_increased_during_litigation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.valid_sale_agreement_proved: The sale agreement is legally valid and proved.
predicates.buyer_continuously_ready_willing: The buyer remained ready and willing to perform the buyer’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.seller_failed_to_complete_sale: The seller failed to complete the sale as agreed.
predicates.property_value_increased_during_litigati: The property increased in value while the dispute was being litigated.

members.legal_issue: A substantial increase in property value during litigation does not, by itself, justify denying specific performance to a purchaser who was not in breach.
material_facts: The purchaser filed suit within a month of the agreed possession date and had already paid more than half of the purchase price.
The courts had found that the purchaser was always ready and willing to perform and that the sellers breached the agreement.

The purchaser had continued to pursue her claim while other purchasers settled, and was willing to accept the incomplete flat without a price reduction or holding the sellers responsible for its incomplete state.
The property’s value had increased substantially during the prolonged litigation.
members.legal_principle: Specific performance is discretionary and need not be granted merely because it is legally available. A court may consider a phenomenal increase in value among the circumstances relevant to its decision, but ordinarily should not deny specific performance on that ground alone. It must assess the totality of circumstances, including which party defaulted, whether either party seeks an undue advantage, and the hardship to the defendant. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this principle; it refers to the differing opinions of the two judges who heard the appeal earlier in the same matter.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance notwithstanding the increase in property value; that increase alone was not a reason to deny relief or deprive her of its benefit. The decree was conditional on payment of an additional reasonable amount.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_not_in_breach and seller_breached_agreement and (purchaser_sued_promptly or purchaser_paid_more_than_half or purchaser_willing_to_accept_incomplete_property) and property_value_increased_during_litigation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.purchaser_not_in_breach: The purchaser was found ready and willing to perform and had not breached the agreement.
predicates.seller_breached_agreement: The seller failed to carry out the agreement.
predicates.purchaser_sued_promptly: The purchaser filed suit soon after the agreed time for performance passed.
predicates.purchaser_paid_more_than_half: The purchaser had paid more than half of the agreed purchase price.
predicates.purchaser_willing_to_accept_incomplete_p: The purchaser agreed to accept the property in its incomplete condition without a price reduction or holding the seller responsible for the incompleteness.
predicates.property_value_increased_during_litigati: The property’s value increased while the litigation was pending.

members.legal_issue: A court granting specific performance may require a purchaser to pay a reasonable additional amount, assessed in light of the parties’ conduct and the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The sellers had been deprived for many years of the unpaid balance of the purchase price.
The purchaser was willing to pay interest on that unpaid balance and to accept the incomplete flat without seeking a reduction in the agreed price.
The sellers had breached the agreement, and the purchaser had not defaulted.
The purchaser had continued the litigation for more than three decades.
The court considered a payment of Rs.40,00,000 too onerous, but considered it reasonable to require an additional payment of Rs.6,25,000 instead of the original unpaid balance of Rs.25,000.
members.legal_principle: The court’s equitable discretion in granting or refusing specific performance includes the power to impose a reasonable condition, including an additional payment. The amount and whether such a condition is appropriate depend on the totality of the circumstances, including who defaulted, whether a party is seeking an undue advantage, and the hardship the order would cause. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this principle; it notes the differing opinions of the two judges who heard the appeal earlier in the same matter.
members.conclusion: The purchaser could obtain specific performance on condition that she pay the sellers Rs.6,25,000 in addition to the amount already paid, within six weeks; failure to comply would extinguish her entitlement to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_not_in_breach and seller_breached_agreement and seller_deprived_of_unpaid_price_for_years and (purchaser_willing_to_accept_incomplete_property or large_additional_payment_would_be_onerous)

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.purchaser_not_in_breach: The purchaser was found ready and willing to perform and had not breached the agreement.
predicates.seller_breached_agreement: The seller failed to carry out the agreement.
predicates.seller_deprived_of_unpaid_price_for_year: The seller remained without the unpaid part of the purchase price for a prolonged period.
predicates.purchaser_willing_to_accept_incomplete_p: The purchaser agreed to accept the property in its incomplete condition without a price reduction or holding the seller responsible for the incompleteness.
predicates.large_additional_payment_would_be_onerou: The court found that the proposed large additional payment would impose an excessive burden on the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: Specific-performance relief may be conditioned on further payment when the passage of time and appreciation in the property’s value warrant an adjustment that the plaintiff accepts.
material_facts: A substantial period had passed, and the value of the urban property had appreciated.
The court proposed that the plaintiff pay a further sum, and the plaintiff agreed.
The Supreme Court made specific performance conditional on depositing that further sum, in addition to the amount already deposited.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its discretion concerning specific-performance relief, the Court may account for the passage of time and appreciation in the property’s value and condition relief on an additional payment accepted by the plaintiff. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this adjustment.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to specific performance upon depositing the further sum directed by the Court.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and substantial_time_has_passed and property_value_has_appreciated and plaintiff_accepted_additional_payment

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning relief in a specific-performance suit.
predicates.substantial_time_has_passed: A substantial period elapsed before the court determined the relief.
predicates.property_value_has_appreciated: The property increased in value during the elapsed period.
predicates.plaintiff_accepted_additional_payment: The plaintiff agreed to make a further payment proposed by the court.

members.legal_issue: An increase in property value during the period before enforcement does not, by itself, justify refusing specific performance or requiring a higher payment.
material_facts: The seller accepted part-payments from the buyer over time and accepted a further substantial payment shortly before the suit was filed.
The seller redeemed the mortgage after receiving the required payment from the buyer.
The seller’s hardship argument based on increased property prices had not been raised before the High Court.
The buyer would also suffer hardship if the agreement were not performed.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary, and the court must consider the circumstances, including unfair advantage and hardship. Explanation I to Section 20 provides that inadequacy of consideration or an onerous or improvident bargain, by itself, does not constitute unfair advantage. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation does not establish an absolute rule that escalation in property prices requires refusal of specific performance or an increased payment; the result depends on the circumstances of each case.
members.conclusion: The increase in property prices did not justify denying the buyer the benefit of specific performance in the circumstances of the case.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and property_value_increased and seller_accepted_buyer_performance and buyer_would_suffer_from_nonperformance

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a claim by a buyer for specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.property_value_increased: The value of the property rose between the agreement and the court’s consideration of enforcement.
predicates.seller_accepted_buyer_performance: The seller accepted payments or other performance from the buyer while the agreement remained in issue.
predicates.buyer_would_suffer_from_nonperformance: The buyer would face hardship if the agreement were not performed.

members.legal_issue: Escalation in property prices and delay caused by court proceedings do not, without case-specific equitable grounds, justify requiring the purchaser to pay additional compensation as a condition of specific performance.
material_facts: The agreed price for the flat was Rs. 60,000, and the purchaser had consistently been ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement.
The purchaser had not caused the delay; the seller had sought to avoid the agreement.
The market value of the flat had risen substantially, but the purchaser had not offered to pay additional compensation.
The proposed additional payment of Rs. 40 lakhs might frustrate the agreement because the purchaser might not be able to pay it.
In the cited case of Gobind Ram, additional compensation had been directed on a concession by the purchaser; the court did not treat that result as a universal rule.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary, but the discretion must be exercised on sound judicial principles. Escalation in price is not by itself a universal ground to refuse specific performance or to require additional compensation; the result depends on the circumstances of the case. In Gobind Ram v. Gian Chand, additional compensation was ordered on the purchaser’s concession. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan concerned prolonged inaction by the purchaser coupled with a substantial rise in prices. V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal recognized that a rise in price may be relevant when the court is considering whether to grant specific performance for the first time.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance at the price stated in the agreement, without the additional Rs. 40 lakhs being imposed as a condition.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and purchaser_ready_willing and purchaser_not_responsible_for_delay and seller_attempted_to_avoid_agreement and property_prices_escalated and purchaser_did_not_offer_additional_compensation and additional_payment_may_frustrate_agreement

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.purchaser_ready_willing: The purchaser was ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.purchaser_not_responsible_for_delay: The purchaser did not cause the delay in the proceedings.
predicates.seller_attempted_to_avoid_agreement: The seller sought to escape performance of the agreement.
predicates.property_prices_escalated: The value of the property increased after the agreement was made.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_offer_additional_compe: The purchaser did not offer to pay compensation over and above the agreed price.
predicates.additional_payment_may_frustrate_agreeme: Requiring an additional payment might prevent the purchaser from completing the purchase and thereby defeat the agreement.

members.legal_issue: An increase in the value of the property does not, by itself, justify denying specific performance at the appellate stage after the lower courts have granted the decree.
material_facts: The property was in an urban area, and the sellers argued that its price had risen.
The trial court and the appellate court had both granted specific performance before the matter reached the Supreme Court.
The sellers had not entered the witness box or led evidence supporting their allegations.
members.legal_principle: A rise in the price of land may be relevant when a court is considering whether to grant specific performance for the first time, but it is not a relevant factor at the Supreme Court stage when the courts below have already granted the decree. The Court discussed V. Pechimuthu v. Gowrammal and distinguished K. S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan.
members.conclusion: The alleged rise in the property’s price did not justify denying specific performance at this stage, and the Court dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_concurrent_specific_performa: The proceeding is an appeal after the lower courts have both granted specific performance.
predicates.property_value_increased: The value of the property increased after the sale agreement.

members.legal_issue: An increase in the value of property, by itself, is not a sufficient reason to refuse specific performance of a lawful agreement for sale.
material_facts: The courts below found that the parties had entered into a genuine agreement for sale and decreed specific performance.
The seller had received further payment after entering into the agreement and had also entered into other agreements concerning the same property.
The seller argued that the rise in property prices meant the court should not exercise its discretion to order specific performance.
The courts below rejected the seller’s reliance on an alleged earlier agreement with a relative, which the court found had not been acted upon.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the court exercises discretion in deciding whether to grant specific performance, but an increase in the price of immovable property, by itself, is not a ground to refuse enforcement of a lawful agreement for sale. The court relied on P.D’ Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu and Jai Narain Parasrampuria v. Pushpa Devi Saraf.
members.conclusion: The increase in the property’s price did not justify refusing specific performance, and the decree was upheld.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: A party appealed a decree granting specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.lawful_sale_agreement: The courts found that the parties had made a genuine and lawful agreement for sale.
predicates.seller_relies_on_price_increase: The seller relied on an increase in the property’s value as a reason to refuse specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A rise in property value during litigation does not, by itself, justify refusing specific performance.
material_facts: The seller argued that the agreed price was low and that the property’s value had increased substantially during the litigation.
The Supreme Court regarded the increase in price as a normal change of circumstances and held that it was not, by itself, hardship requiring refusal of specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the court exercises equitable discretion by considering the totality of the circumstances. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., (2002) 8 SCC 146, holds that phenomenal appreciation during litigation ordinarily does not alone defeat specific performance, though it may be considered alongside other circumstances when balancing the equities.
members.conclusion: The increase in property value during the litigation did not justify reversing the specific-performance decree on its own.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.property_value_increased_during_litigati: The value of the property increased while the specific-performance dispute was being litigated.
predicates.increase_is_the_only_ground_for_refusal: The asserted ground for refusing specific performance is the increase in the property’s value, without an additional circumstance justifying refusal.

members.legal_issue: A court granting specific performance may require additional consideration to balance the equities when circumstances, including a substantial increase in property value, warrant that condition.
material_facts: The agreement had been made several years before the Supreme Court’s decision, and the property’s value had increased substantially in the meantime.
The seller relied on the increase in value as a hardship, while the Court concluded that the increase alone did not warrant refusing specific performance.
Considering the elapsed time, the scale of the increase, and the circumstances as a whole, the Court required a higher total consideration as a condition of completing the sale.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits the court to impose a reasonable condition when granting specific performance. Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., (2002) 8 SCC 146, recognizes that an additional payment may be required to balance the equities, having regard to the totality of the circumstances, including who defaulted, whether a party seeks an undue advantage, and the hardship caused.
members.conclusion: The specific-performance decree was restored on condition that the purchaser pay increased consideration, less the amount already paid, and the seller execute a registered sale deed.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.substantial_property_value_increase: The property’s value has increased substantially since the contract was made.
predicates.court_finds_equities_require_compensatio: The court finds, after considering the circumstances as a whole, that compensation is appropriate to balance the equities.

members.legal_issue: A substantially delayed challenge to a public-purpose land acquisition may be refused where entertaining it risks prejudice to the beneficiaries of the scheme and planned development.
material_facts: The declaration was published in the official gazette on 24 May 1994, while the landowners filed their writ petitions virtually two years later.
The acquisition was for a residential scheme intended to further planned development and benefit the scheme’s intended beneficiaries.
The Court considered that entertaining the delayed challenges could cause serious prejudice to those beneficiaries and to planned development.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the law of delay and laches in challenges to land acquisition and relied on Reliance Petroleum Ltd. v. Zaver Chand Popatlal Sumaria and Hari Singh v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The delayed writ challenges ought not to have been entertained, and the High Court should have dismissed them on the ground of delay and laches.

rule.if: land_acquisition_writ_challenge and challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay and acquisition_serves_public_scheme and entertaining_challenge_may_cause_prejudice

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A person has brought a writ challenge to a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The challenge was brought substantially after the acquisition step being challenged.
predicates.acquisition_serves_public_scheme: The land acquisition is for a public scheme, such as a scheme for planned development.
predicates.entertaining_challenge_may_cause_prejudi: Entertaining the challenge may seriously prejudice the scheme’s intended beneficiaries or planned development.

members.legal_issue: A court is not obliged to entertain a fresh legal ground raised after avoidable delay in a challenge to a public-purpose land acquisition.
material_facts: The landowners raised the time-limit ground for the first time during their appeals in the High Court, although it had been available for nearly seven years.
The challenge concerned an acquisition for a public purpose, and setting aside such an acquisition could cause public expense and delay a project for the general public good.
The Supreme Court examined the ground to address the scope and applicability of the statutory time limit, while clarifying that this did not impose an obligation to examine late grounds.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing delayed challenges in proceedings under Articles 226 and 136 of the Constitution. A fresh legal ground is not governed by a different rule merely because it raises a question of law. In public-purpose acquisition challenges, avoidable delay or laches weighs against entertaining the challenge because setting aside an acquisition may waste public money and delay projects for the public good. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The examination of the late ground did not establish an obligation to entertain such grounds; courts should be averse to entertaining acquisition challenges involving avoidable delay or laches.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenged a land acquisition.
predicates.public_purpose_acquisition: The acquisition was made for a public purpose and a project intended to benefit the public.
predicates.fresh_ground_raised_after_avoidable_dela: A ground that had been available earlier was first raised after avoidable delay.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a land acquisition cannot be entertained after a prolonged delay where the acquisition has long been final and the challenge concerns the purpose for which the land was acquired or its later use.
material_facts: The acquisition had become final and the land had vested in the State after compensation was paid.
The appellants challenged the acquisition approximately three decades after it was made, arguing that the original purpose had ceased and that the land could not be used for another purpose.
The High Court refused to entertain the challenge, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a challenge could not be entertained after the acquisition question had stood settled for approximately three decades. It cited no earlier cases or separate statutory limitation provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The writ challenge was too late to be entertained, whether it asserted that the original purpose was not a public purpose or that the land could not be used for another purpose.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: The former owners brought a writ proceeding challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_issue_settled_long_before_ch: The acquisition issue had been settled for a prolonged period before the challenge was brought.
predicates.challenge_concerns_original_purpose_or_l: The challenge asserts that the original purpose was not a public purpose or that the land cannot be used for another purpose.
predicates.delayed_acquisition_challenge_not_entert: The court does not entertain the delayed challenge to the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A delayed writ challenge should not be entertained where the delay has allowed third-party rights to arise and relief would prejudice those parties.
material_facts: The writ petition challenging the approvals was filed nearly seven years after they were made.
By then, 42 of the 52 plots had been sold to purchasers for consideration.
Some purchasers had completed construction and others had construction in advanced stages.
The purchasers faced adverse consequences despite not being heard before the challenged judgment.
members.legal_principle: Writ relief is discretionary. Under State of M.P. v. Nandlal Jaiswal (1986) 4 SCC 566, as discussed in Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. v. K. Thangappan (2006) 4 SCC 322 and later cited in Yunus (Baboobhai) A. Hamid Padvekar v. State of Maharashtra (2009) 3 SCC 281, substantial delay, particularly when third-party rights have arisen in the meantime, may justify refusing writ relief because intervention can cause hardship, inconvenience, and injustice.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition because the delay and laches had allowed third-party rights to arise; the application of promissory estoppel and lis pendens did not justify disturbing those rights in these circumstances.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_administrative_approva: A party sought writ relief against an administrative approval.
predicates.substantial_delay_before_challenge: The party waited a substantial period after the approval before bringing the challenge.
predicates.third_party_rights_created_before_challe: Rights of third parties arose before the challenge was brought.

members.legal_issue: A delayed writ challenge to land acquisition may be dismissed for laches where the delay is substantial and interference would cause public prejudice.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications were published in the official Gazette, and the challengers filed their writ petition nearly two and a half years later.

The challengers said they learned of the acquisition only when compensation notices were issued, but did not allege that the substance of the notification had not been publicly announced in the locality.
The challengers lived in the small locality where the lands were situated, and the Court considered it difficult to believe they remained unaware of the acquisition.
Interference at that stage was likely to cause serious public prejudice.
members.legal_principle: A writ challenge brought after substantial delay may be rejected for laches, particularly where interference would cause serious public prejudice. The Court also applied the presumption that official acts have been duly performed, in the absence of an allegation that the required local public notice was not given.
members.conclusion: The challenge was liable to be dismissed on the ground of laches alone.

rule.if: acquisition_writ_challenge and substantial_unexplained_delay and (local_residents_likely_aware or not_local_notice_failure_alleged) and interference_causes_public_prejudice

predicates.acquisition_writ_challenge: The proceeding is a writ challenge to a land acquisition.
predicates.substantial_unexplained_delay: The challenger waited a substantial period after publication before bringing the challenge without adequately explaining the delay.
predicates.local_residents_likely_aware: The challengers lived in a small locality where the acquisition was likely to become widely known.
predicates.not_local_notice_failure_alleged: The challengers did not allege that the substance of the acquisition notice had not been publicly announced in the locality.
predicates.interference_causes_public_prejudice: Interference with the acquisition at the time of the challenge would likely cause serious public prejudice.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a land acquisition may be refused where it is brought after inordinate and unexplained delay by landowners who knew of and participated in the acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the acquisition 16 years after the award was made.
They had been aware of the acquisition and had participated in proceedings before the Land Acquisition Collector.
They gave no explanation for the delay.
The High Court allowed the petition by relying on an earlier decision, without addressing the objection of delay and laches.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 is discretionary, and a court may refuse it where a petitioner has delayed without satisfactory explanation and the circumstances make relief inappropriate. The same principle concerning stale claims was recognized under Article 32 in Rabindranath Bose v. Union of India and applies to Article 226, as confirmed in Yunus (Baboobhai) A. Hamid Padvekar v. State of Maharashtra. The Court also relied on Durga Prashad v. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, including its reliance on Smt. Narayani Devi Khaitan v. State of Bihar; Tridip Kumar Dingal v. State of West Bengal; P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of Tamil Nadu; P. Chinnanna v. State of A.P.; Hari Singh v. State of U.P.; and Printers (Mysore) Ltd. v. M.A. Rasheed. In land-acquisition cases, courts should be particularly cautious about entertaining stale challenges because setting aside acquisitions may cause public loss and delay projects for the general good. The Court stated that the approach in Dayal Singh v. Union of India was not consonant with the Constitution Bench decision in Rabindranath Bose, which Dayal Singh had not noticed.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition; the appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the writ petition was dismissed on the ground of delay and laches.

rule.if: land_acquisition_writ_challenge and petition_filed_after_inordinate_delay and delay_unexplained and petitioners_knew_of_acquisition and petitioners_participated_in_acquisition

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: The petitioners brought a writ proceeding challenging the acquisition of land.
predicates.petition_filed_after_inordinate_delay: The petitioners waited an inordinate length of time after the acquisition award before bringing the petition.
predicates.delay_unexplained: The petitioners gave no satisfactory explanation for the time they waited to bring the petition.
predicates.petitioners_knew_of_acquisition: The petitioners knew that their land was being acquired.
predicates.petitioners_participated_in_acquisition: The petitioners took part in proceedings before the land-acquisition authority.

members.legal_issue: A delayed public-interest challenge to a developmental project may be barred by laches after the project has been cleared, construction has begun, and substantial public money has been spent, except insofar as it concerns implementation of rehabilitation obligations.
material_facts: The petitioner had opposed the project for years but challenged the environmental clearance and construction only after construction had begun and substantial public funds had been spent.
The Court entertained the petition to examine whether rehabilitation measures required for protecting affected people were being implemented, but treated the other challenges as belated.
members.legal_principle: Ordinary principles of laches apply to public-interest litigation. Under the Court’s approach to judicial review, a project decision cannot ordinarily be challenged after a lengthy delay during which execution and public expenditure have proceeded; the Court nevertheless may examine compliance with obligations protecting fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: Challenges concerning the project’s height, submergence, environmental studies and clearance, hydrology, and seismicity were not entertained because they were brought too late; implementation of relief and rehabilitation remained open to scrutiny.

rule.if: public_interest_project_challenge and decision_known_to_challenger and construction_started and substantial_public_funds_spent and challenge_delayed and not challenge_limited_to_rehabilitation_implementation

predicates.public_interest_project_challenge: A petitioner brings a public-interest proceeding challenging a developmental project.
predicates.decision_known_to_challenger: The petitioner knew of the decision to undertake the project while there was an opportunity to challenge it earlier.
predicates.construction_started: The project authorities began construction before the challenge was filed.
predicates.substantial_public_funds_spent: Substantial public money was spent on the project before the challenge was filed.
predicates.challenge_delayed: The petitioner waited a lengthy period after learning of the decision before approaching the court.
predicates.challenge_limited_to_rehabilitation_impl: The challenge is confined to whether rehabilitation obligations for affected people are being implemented.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to land acquisition brought long after possession has been taken and the land has vested in the State may be rejected as belated where the scale of the acquisition supports an inference that the challenger knew or should have known of it.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large area belonging to numerous persons for planned industrial development.
Possession had been taken and the land had vested in the State before the challenge was brought.
The appellant challenged the award and acquisition proceedings about a decade after possession was taken.
The Court considered it difficult to accept that the appellant had lacked knowledge of the proceedings and noted the High Court’s finding that she had remained silent despite being aware of them.
members.legal_principle: Acquisition proceedings cannot be challenged at a belated stage where the circumstances support knowledge of the acquisition, particularly after possession has been taken and the land has vested in the State. The Court relied on Swaran Lata v. State of Haryana, which held that a very large acquisition affecting numerous landholders could not be presumed to have remained unknown to them; it also applied the principle that land vested upon possession cannot be divested for an irregularity in the acquisition proceedings.
members.conclusion: The belated challenge to the acquisition could not succeed; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge and challenge_brought_long_after_possession and large_scale_public_acquisition and challenger_knew_or_should_have_known

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a public land acquisition.
predicates.challenge_brought_long_after_possession: The challenge was brought long after possession of the acquired land had been taken.
predicates.large_scale_public_acquisition: The acquisition covered a large area or affected numerous landholders.
predicates.challenger_knew_or_should_have_known: The circumstances support that the challenger knew or should have known of the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A delayed challenge to a land acquisition may be denied where the challengers knew of the acquisition, possession had been taken, and substantial development had occurred in reliance on it.
material_facts: Possession of the acquired land had been delivered to the Trust.
The Trust had spent substantial sums on roads and development materials.
The challengers knew of the development but did not take timely steps to challenge the acquisition.
The challenge was brought after the acquisition and development had proceeded, and the Court considered the risk of successive challenges by owners of separate plots.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the equitable discretion governing delayed challenges, considering possession, expenditure and development undertaken with the challengers' knowledge, and the prejudice that piecemeal challenges could cause. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this determination.
members.conclusion: The High Court properly exercised its discretion against the challengers on grounds of delay and laches, and the Supreme Court saw no reason to take a contrary view.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and possession_delivered and substantial_development_expenditure and challengers_knew_of_development and challengers_delayed

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a land acquisition.
predicates.possession_delivered: The acquiring authority or its transferee took possession of the acquired land.
predicates.substantial_development_expenditure: The acquiring authority or its transferee spent substantial resources developing the land.
predicates.challengers_knew_of_development: The challengers knew that development was taking place.
predicates.challengers_delayed: The challengers did not bring their challenge promptly despite that knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A public interest challenge to building construction may be denied when it is brought after substantial delay and construction has substantially progressed, particularly where interests of third parties have arisen.
material_facts: The construction began after permissions were granted and was stopped following an earlier High Court decision.
The Corporation later permitted construction to resume, and the public interest petition was filed after construction had resumed and was nearly complete.
Flat purchasers and occupants had acquired interests in the buildings before the petition was filed.
The Court found the delay fatal and held that third-party interests should not be disturbed in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 is discretionary, and delay and laches may make a petition unfit for relief even where a legal grievance is alleged. In State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai, the Court treated the limitation period for a comparable civil remedy as a guide to reasonable delay; Rabindra Nath Bose v. Union of India, Durga Prasad v. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, Ashok Kumar Mishra v. Collector, Raipur, and State of Maharashtra v. Digambar affirm that unexplained or blameworthy delay may justify refusal of discretionary relief, particularly where others have acted or acquired interests. The Court also reiterated from Balco Employees' Union v. Union of India and Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware v. State of Maharashtra that public interest litigation is an exceptional remedy to be used cautiously and by vigilant litigants for genuine public concerns.
members.conclusion: The delay was fatal, and the public interest challenge did not justify disturbing the construction and interests that had arisen.

rule.if: public_interest_challenge_case and challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay and construction_substantially_progressed and third_party_interests_arose

predicates.public_interest_challenge_case: A petitioner brought a proceeding in the public interest challenging the legality of a building or its construction.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The petitioner waited a substantial period after the challenged action before bringing the proceeding.
predicates.construction_substantially_progressed: The builder had substantially advanced or nearly completed construction before the challenge was brought.
predicates.third_party_interests_arose: People other than the builder acquired interests in or occupied the building before the challenge was brought.

members.legal_issue: A landowner who did not object during the statutory inquiry cannot later challenge the acquisition on personal grounds that could have been raised there, but may still challenge whether the acquisition serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The landowner had not filed objections during the inquiry into objections to the proposed acquisition.
The challenge relied on matters personal to the landowner or the land, including whether the land was necessary or should be excluded in light of particular circumstances.
The existence of a public purpose was not disputed in the case.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, objections may concern the existence of a public purpose or matters personal to the land or objector. A person who does not raise personal objections is deemed to have waived them and cannot later challenge the Section 5A inquiry or Section 6 declaration on those grounds. The court applied the principle stated in Abhey Ram v. Union of India, while recognizing that the public-purpose objection remains available even if no objections were filed.
members.conclusion: Personal grounds that could have been raised in the inquiry were deemed waived, and the landowner could not use them to challenge the inquiry or declaration. The failure to object does not prevent a challenge to whether the acquisition is for a public purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of land-acquisition proceedings.
predicates.no_objections_submitted: The affected landowner did not submit objections during the statutory inquiry into the proposed acquisition.
predicates.challenge_rests_on_personal_or_land_spec: The challenge concerns the landowner's individual circumstances or the suitability or necessity of acquiring that particular land.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a land-ceiling determination may be rejected where the determination became final without an appeal or revision, the land vested in the State, and the challenge was brought long afterwards.
material_facts: The competent authority declared land excess, and no appeal or revision was filed against that determination.
The land was subsequently notified and vested in the State.
The appellants brought a writ challenge about ten years after the determination.
The appellants sought to reopen the proceedings on the ground that their sister's share had not been considered.
The sister knew of the proceedings but filed no objection before vesting, and her later writ petition was dismissed.
The appeal arose from the summary dismissal of the appellants' writ petition.
members.legal_principle: An unappealed or unrevised determination becomes final and binding. Where the land has vested in the State and a writ challenge is brought many years later, the High Court may summarily dismiss the challenge; the Court also noted that the sister had not objected before vesting.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the competent authority's determination was without substance, and the High Court was justified in summarily dismissing the writ petition; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_summary_writ_dismissal and challenge_to_land_ceiling_determination and determination_unappealed_or_unrevised and land_vested_in_state and challenge_brought_long_after_determination

predicates.appeal_from_summary_writ_dismissal: The proceeding is an appeal from a summary dismissal of a writ petition challenging a land determination.
predicates.challenge_to_land_ceiling_determination: The party challenged a determination that land was excess under a land-ceiling process.
predicates.determination_unappealed_or_unrevised: No appeal or revision was filed against the determination, leaving it final and binding.
predicates.land_vested_in_state: The land was notified and vested in the State before the challenge was brought.
predicates.challenge_brought_long_after_determinati: The party brought the challenge many years after the determination.

members.legal_issue: Delay in challenging an emergency acquisition and completed development may disentitle a claimant to equitable relief that would undo the acquisition.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the acquisition more than two years after possession had been taken and did not satisfactorily explain the delay.
The acquired area had been developed and industrial plots had been allotted to third parties.
The award had been accepted by nearly all other affected owners, and substantial public and private resources had been invested in development.
members.legal_principle: Justice Kumar applied equitable principles concerning delay and laches and relied on Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. L. Chandrasekaran and A.S. Naidu v. State of Tamil Nadu concerning the consequences of disturbing completed development and third-party interests. Justice Ganguly considered the completed development and third-party interests relevant to choosing compensation rather than restoration as the remedy.
members.conclusion: Justice Swatanter Kumar held that the claimants were not entitled to equitable relief undoing the acquisition, given the unexplained delay, completed development, and reliance by others. Justice Ganguly also declined to restore the land in the circumstances, instead directing compensation to be assessed on a later valuation basis. The judges differed on the legal basis and remedy, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_case: The proceeding challenges a compulsory acquisition and seeks relief that would undo it.
predicates.unexplained_delay_in_challenge: The landowner brought the challenge after substantial delay that was not adequately explained.
predicates.development_completed_with_third_party_i: The acquired land was developed and third parties obtained interests in it.

members.legal_issue: A substantially delayed challenge to a completed land acquisition may be denied as equitable writ relief where the claimants’ conduct is inconsistent with continuing to challenge the acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was issued in 1971, the award was made and possession was taken in 1976, and the writ petition challenging the acquisition was filed in 1992.
The claimants later sought execution of the award, and the execution proceedings led to a civil revision in which the acquiring authority deposited the compensation amount.
Two of the owners claimed compensation before the acquiring authority, and another owner authorised one of them to act and receive compensation on his behalf.
The land had been reserved for public purposes in the development plan since 1952.
The claimants did not disclose the execution application in their amended writ petition.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and equitable; delay defeats equity, and equity favours a vigilant rather than an indolent litigant. Although no fixed limitation period governs the writ, the ordinary period for bringing a civil proceeding is a relevant guide. The Court considered N.L. Abhyankar v. Union of India, [1995] 1 MHLJ 503, and relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., [1996] 11 SCC 501. It distinguished Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Dolly Das, [1999] 4 SCC 450, which concerned a different legal context and different facts.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have granted relief. The writ petition was dismissed because the delay and the claimants’ conduct defeated their entitlement to equitable relief.

rule.if: acquisition_writ_challenge and substantial_delay and acquisition_completed and (claimant_pursued_award_execution or claimant_claimed_compensation)

predicates.acquisition_writ_challenge: The claimant brought a writ proceeding challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.substantial_delay: The claimant waited a substantial period after the acquisition steps before bringing the challenge.
predicates.acquisition_completed: An award had been made and possession of the acquired land had been taken.
predicates.claimant_pursued_award_execution: The claimant sought to have the acquisition award executed.
predicates.claimant_claimed_compensation: The claimant asserted a claim for compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.equitable_writ_relief_denied: The claimant is denied equitable relief in the writ proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a completed land acquisition may be refused for unreasonable and unexplained delay where the land has been used for its public purpose and rights of third parties have been created.
material_facts: The landowner filed the writ petition about nine years after publication of the acquisition declaration and about six years after the award, without a sufficient explanation for the delay.
An earlier civil suit sought fresh acquisition proceedings and payment of compensation after subdivision of the land; it did not seek to quash the acquisition notifications.
By the time the writ petition was filed, the acquired land had been developed for a residential scheme, plots and flats had been allotted, and third-party rights had been created.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 226 is discretionary, and unreasonable delay may justify refusal even where no limitation period applies to the writ petition. The limitation period for a comparable civil action is ordinarily a guide to whether delay is unreasonable. Delay in challenging a land acquisition is viewed seriously, especially where the land has been used for the public purpose or third-party rights have accrued. The Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai, Ajodhya Bhagat v. State of Bihar, State of Rajasthan v. D.R. Laxmi, Girdharan Prasad Missir v. State of Bihar, Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., Urban Improvement Trust, Udaipur v. Bheru Lal, Ganpatibai v. State of M.P. and Sawaran Lata v. State of Haryana; it distinguished Vyalikaval Housebuilding Cooperative Society v. V. Chandrappa, involving fraud and mala fides, and Babu Ram v. State of Haryana, where the circumstances did not show negligence or delay.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have refused relief because of laches, even though the acquiring authority had not raised that objection in its affidavits.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition and unreasonable_unexplained_delay and (acquired_land_used_for_public_purpose or third_party_rights_created)

predicates.writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: A person asks a court exercising writ jurisdiction to set aside a land acquisition.
predicates.unreasonable_unexplained_delay: The person waits an unreasonable time to bring the challenge and does not plausibly explain the delay.
predicates.acquired_land_used_for_public_purpose: The acquired land has been put to use for the public purpose for which it was acquired.
predicates.third_party_rights_created: Rights in the developed or allotted land have accrued to people other than the challenger.

members.legal_issue: The State Legislature had competence to enact a law transferring rights in property to the State.
material_facts: The State Legislature enacted amendments transferring the right to hold certain fairs from former proprietors and tenure-holders to the State.
The amendments concerned the acquisition of property.
members.legal_principle: Article 246, read with Entry 42 of the Concurrent List as amended by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, authorised legislation concerning the acquisition of property. The Court held that the amended legislative allocation permitted a State Legislature to enact an acquisition law even without a public purpose, subject to the separate restriction in Article 31(2).
members.conclusion: The amending legislation was within the State Legislature’s legislative competence under Article 246.

rule.if: legislative_competence_challenge and state_legislature_enacted_law and law_concerns_property_acquisition and constitutional_allocation_authorizes_state_acquisition_laws

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: A proceeding challenges whether a State Legislature had authority to enact the law.
predicates.state_legislature_enacted_law: A State Legislature enacted the law under challenge.
predicates.law_concerns_property_acquisition: The law provides for the transfer or acquisition of property rights by the State.
predicates.constitutional_allocation_authorizes_sta: The constitutional allocation of legislative powers authorises the State Legislature to enact laws concerning property acquisition.

members.legal_issue: The state legislature had competence to enact legislation concerning land and the prevention of unauthorised occupation and eviction.
material_facts: The legislation dealt with land in urban areas, unauthorised occupation, and eviction.
The challenge asserted that the state legislature lacked competence to enact the legislation.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the subject matter fell within the state legislature’s competence under Entries 18, 64 and 65 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the Act under Entries 18, 64 and 65 of List II.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a state legislature had authority to enact the law.
predicates.state_land_and_occupation_subject_matter: The law concerns land and the regulation of unauthorised occupation and eviction.

members.legal_issue: A State legislature may legislate to reduce tenants' liability for arrears of rent or, alternatively, debts owed by agriculturists.
material_facts: The challenged laws reduced tenants' liability to pay arrears of rent, whether or not the arrears had been decreed.
The arrears could be treated either as rent arrears or as debts due from agriculturists.
members.legal_principle: Under Entry 18 of List II of the Seventh Schedule, the State legislature may legislate concerning rent. Under Entry 30 of List II, it may legislate concerning debts due from agriculturists.
members.conclusion: The State legislature was competent to enact the provisions under either characterization of the arrears.

predicates.tenant_liability_legislation: The case concerns legislation altering tenants' liability to pay arrears.
predicates.arrears_are_rent_or_agriculturist_debts: The arrears are either rent arrears or debts owed by agriculturists.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature may enact land-tenure reforms that limit a landowner’s holding and alter landlord-tenant relations to make land available for cultivation by tenants.
material_facts: The challenged legislation limited the area a landowner could hold for self-cultivation and made surplus land available for resettling tenants.
The legislation also allowed specified tenants to purchase land from landowners and become landowners themselves.
The petitions challenged the legislation’s constitutional validity, including the state legislature’s competence to enact it.
members.legal_principle: Entry 18’s terms concerning rights in or over land, land tenures, and the landlord-tenant relation are broad enough to cover land-tenure reform limiting land held by landowners and changing tenants’ rights. Article 246(3) gives the state legislature exclusive power over matters in List II. The Court relied on The United Provinces v. Mst. Atiqa Begum, which read legislative-list entries broadly to include ancillary matters, and Megh Raj v. Allah Rakhi, which applied a wide construction to the land entry and the relations concerning agricultural land.
members.conclusion: The state legislature had exclusive competence to enact the legislation under Entry 18 of List II, read with Article 246(3) of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_tenure_: A party in a constitutional challenge to a law governing land tenure disputes the legislature’s authority to enact it.
predicates.law_limits_land_held_for_self_cultivatio: The law limits the land a landowner may hold for self-cultivation.
predicates.law_changes_landlord_tenant_relations: The law changes rights or relations between landlords and tenants.
predicates.state_legislature_has_competence_to_enac: The state legislature has authority to enact the land-tenure reform.

members.legal_issue: The State Legislature had competence to enact a law converting the occupancy of persons in requisitioned premises into protected tenancies and regulating the landlord-tenant relationship.
material_facts: The State had requisitioned premises, allotted some of them to occupants, and paid compensation to owners; the occupants paid compensation for their occupation.
The amendment ended the requisitioning of the premises and deemed the occupants to be tenants of the owners, who became their landlords, with the previous compensation treated as rent.

The amendment subjected eviction and rent fixation to the existing rent-control framework, while preserving landlords' rights to seek possession on the statutory grounds available under that framework.
The stated purpose was to address the risk of occupants being left without homes or necessary accommodation for public services amid an acute shortage of accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Legislative entries are fields of legislation, not independent sources of power; competence is determined by the pith and substance, object, scheme, and actual effect of the law, giving the entries a broad and effective interpretation while respecting their limits. House and building tenancies fall within the relevant fields concerning transfer of property, contracts, and civil procedure in the Concurrent List, rather than the State List entry concerning land. These fields encompass statutory regulation of landlord-tenant relations, including eviction. The Court relied on Accountant & Secretarial Services (P) Ltd. v. Union of India, Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, Indu Bhushan Bose v. Rama Sundari Debi, Chaturbhai M. Patel v. Union of India, Diamond Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Synthetics & Chemicals Ltd. v. State of U.P., United Provinces v. Mt. Atiqa Begum, Lingappa Pochanna Appealwar v. State of Maharashtra, and Maneklal Chhotalal v. M.G. Makwana. It also considered Articles 37, 38, and 39 as interpretive guides.
members.conclusion: The amendment was within the legislative competence of the State Legislature.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and state_enacts_occupancy_law and law_changes_requisitioned_occupants_into_tenants and law_regulates_landlord_tenant_relations

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state law.
predicates.state_enacts_occupancy_law: A state legislature enacts a law governing the occupancy of premises previously allocated by the state.
predicates.law_changes_requisitioned_occupants_into: The law converts occupants who held premises through state requisition into tenants of the owners.
predicates.law_regulates_landlord_tenant_relations: The law regulates rent, eviction, or other aspects of the relationship between owners and occupants.

members.legal_issue: A State Legislature has competence to impose ceilings on agricultural land, acquire surplus land, and distribute it to advance agrarian reform and reduce concentration of land ownership.
material_facts: The law imposed ceilings on agricultural land holdings and provided for acquisition of land held beyond the ceiling.
The acquired surplus land was to be distributed to landless and other persons to reduce disparities in land ownership and advance the stated common-good objectives.
Persons whose surplus land was acquired were entitled to compensation.
The challengers argued that the State Legislature lacked power to enact this scheme under the relevant legislative entries.
members.legal_principle: Legislative-list entries describing a subject are construed broadly, and the land entry encompasses a wide range of legislation concerning rights in or over land, including agrarian reform and measures to improve land use. Although acquisition is not directly covered by the land entry, the State may acquire surplus land under that entry read with the concurrent entry on acquisition and requisitioning of property, including to advance Article 39(b) and (c). The Court relied on Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, Atma Ram v. State of Punjab, Sonapur Tea Co. Ltd. v. Mst. Mazirunnessa, and State of Maharashtra v. Patilchand.
members.conclusion: The State Legislature was competent to enact the land-ceiling scheme: the legislation fell within the broad scope of the State's land-related legislative field, and acquisition of surplus land was supported by the concurrent power over acquisition and requisitioning of property.

predicates.challenge_to_state_legislative_competenc: A challenge claims that a State Legislature lacks power to enact a land-reform measure.
predicates.law_limits_agricultural_land_holdings: The law sets a maximum area of agricultural land that a person or family may hold.
predicates.surplus_land_is_acquired_for_redistribut: The law provides for acquiring land above the ceiling so it can be distributed to landless or other persons.
predicates.acquisition_is_compensated: The law provides compensation to persons whose surplus land is acquired.

members.legal_issue: A State Legislature is competent to enact legislation resuming jagirs where the legislation concerns rights in land or land revenue.
material_facts: The legislation provided for resumption of jagirs consisting of rights to land revenue.
The challengers argued that the State Legislature lacked competence to enact the legislation and to amend its definition of State Government.
The subject matter concerned land, land tenure, and land revenue.
members.legal_principle: Entries 18 and 45 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution confer legislative competence over land and land revenue, including land rights and the collection or alienation of revenue. The Court held that resumption of jagirs concerning land revenue falls within those subjects and that an amendment concerning the same subject matter is likewise within competence.
members.conclusion: The legislation, including the amendment, was within the State Legislature’s competence under entries 18 and 45 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

predicates.challenge_to_resumption_law: A proceeding challenges the validity of legislation providing for resumption of jagirs.
predicates.law_resumes_land_or_revenue_rights: The legislation concerns rights in land, land tenure, or land revenue.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature may provide agricultural debt relief for agriculturists whose property was sold to discharge their debts, even when the debt no longer subsists.
material_facts: The law provided relief to agriculturists whose immovable property had been sold in execution to recover a debt.
The challengers argued that the state legislature could not legislate about a debt that had already been discharged by the sale.
The relief addressed agriculturists who had lost property and the means of livelihood through distress sales.
members.legal_principle: Article 246(3) of the Constitution gives a state legislature exclusive power over matters in List II, and Entry 30 of List II includes money-lending and relief of agricultural indebtedness. That entry is not confined to subsisting debts and encompasses relief for agriculturists who lost property through execution sales. The Court relied on Fatehchand Himmatlal v. State of Maharashtra and the principle of liberal construction of constitutional legislative entries stated in Navinchandra Mafatlal v. Commissioner of Income-tax.
members.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the debt-relief provision, including relief for agriculturists whose debts had been discharged through sales of their property.

predicates.state_legislation_addresses_agricultural: A state legislature enacts a law providing relief to indebted agriculturists.
predicates.relief_covers_property_lost_to_discharge: The law provides relief to an agriculturist whose property was sold to discharge the debt, even though the debt no longer subsists.
predicates.challenge_to_state_legislative_competenc: The proceeding challenges the state legislature's authority to enact the relief measure.

members.legal_issue: The legislature was competent to enact a law acquiring proprietary land rights as part of land-tenure reform.
material_facts: The law acquired proprietary rights in estates, villages and lands and transferred them to the State.
The law aimed to eliminate intermediaries between the State and cultivators and to bring cultivators into direct contact with the State.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the legislation fell within the legislative subject of acquisition under entry 36 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The legislature had competence to enact the acquisition law.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of land rights.
predicates.law_transfers_proprietary_land_rights_to: The law transfers proprietary land rights to the State.

members.legal_issue: A State Legislature is competent to enact a land-ceiling law governing land vested in the State and its use for agricultural purposes.
material_facts: The enactment imposed ceilings on agricultural landholdings and provided for acquisition and distribution of surplus land.
The challenged provision concerned land that had vested in the State and addressed continued agricultural use and supply of raw material from that land.
The challenge asserted that the State Legislature lacked competence because the provision concerned a centrally controlled industry.
members.legal_principle: The enactment, apart from the challenged provision, fell within Entry 18 of List II and Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule. The challenged provision fell within Entry 35 of List II because it dealt with land vested in the State, including its agricultural use and management.
members.conclusion: The State Legislature was competent to enact the impugned law, including the challenged provision concerning land vested in the State.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: A party in a constitutional competence proceeding disputes a State Legislature's authority to enact a law.
predicates.state_law_regulates_land_and_acquisition: The State law regulates land, agricultural holdings, or acquisition and distribution of property.
predicates.challenged_provision_governs_state_veste: The challenged provision governs the use or management of land after it has vested in the State.

members.legal_issue: The central legislature had competence to enact a law whose dominant purpose was acquisition of property.
material_facts: The enactment transferred rights in the specified area to the Central Government following communal violence and the demolition of the disputed structure.
Uttar Pradesh was under President's rule when the enactment was made.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Entry 42 of List III, which covers acquisition and requisitioning of property. It relied on The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga and Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma for identifying the pith and substance of legislation, and noted the breadth of Entry 42 after the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act.
members.conclusion: The enactment was within Parliament's legislative competence because its pith and substance was acquisition of property, not public order.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: A party challenges whether the central legislature had authority to enact the law.
predicates.law_substantially_acquires_property: The law's dominant purpose and substance is the acquisition of property.

members.legal_issue: Parliament has legislative competence to authorize acquisition of property owned by a State under its acquisition power, including when the acquisition supports national regulation of an industry or resource.
material_facts: Parliament enacted legislation authorizing acquisition of coal-bearing land and rights for development of the coal industry.
The legislation pursued greater public control over coal mining and mineral development under national control.

The Constitution assigned acquisition and requisition of property to a concurrent legislative field and assigned Parliament powers concerning industries and the regulation of mines and mineral development under Union control.
The State contended that Parliament could not use its acquisition power to acquire State property.
members.legal_principle: Entry 42 of List III, read with Article 246, empowers Parliament to legislate concerning acquisition and requisition of property. That power is not restricted to privately owned property and may support the exercise of powers under Entries 52 and 54 of List I concerning industries and mines under Union control. Articles 294 and 298 do not bar acquisition of State property. The majority relied on the broad construction of legislative powers and discussed United States v. Darby, State of Oklahoma ex rel. Phillips v. Guy F. Atkinson Company, Kohl v. United States, Attorney-General for British Columbia v. Canadian Pacific Railway Company and Attorney-General for Quebec v. Nipissing Central Railway Company.
members.conclusion: Parliament is competent to enact a law providing for acquisition of State property; the challenged statute was not ultra vires on that ground.

predicates.challenge_to_parliamentary_acquisition_p: A proceeding challenges Parliament’s authority to legislate for compulsory acquisition of property owned by a State.
predicates.constitution_assigns_concurrent_acquisit: The constitution assigns legislative authority over acquisition of property to both national and regional legislatures.
predicates.national_legislation_pursues_control_of_: The national legislature has enacted a law to advance national control or regulation of an industry or resource.
predicates.target_property_is_state_owned: The property that the national law authorizes the government to acquire is owned by a regional government.

members.legal_issue: State legislative power extends to laws governing land reconstitution and orderly town planning.
material_facts: The challenged legislation established procedures for preparing and executing town planning schemes, including changing plot boundaries, reconstituting plots, transferring or extinguishing rights, and allocating land for public purposes.
The legislation sought to secure the healthy and orderly development of urban areas through planned amenities and improvements.
members.legal_principle: Constitutional legislative entries are construed broadly and liberally, unless their wording or another part of the Constitution requires a narrower construction. The Court relied on Entry 18 of List II, concerning land, and Entry 20 of List III, concerning economic and social planning. It applied Navinchandra Mafatlal v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay City, Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab; Atma Ram followed the Privy Council’s approach in Megh Rai v. Allah Rakhia to a broad construction of the land entry.
members.conclusion: The State Legislature was competent to enact the legislation under the constitutional subjects of land and economic and social planning.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law: A person challenges the constitutional validity of a law governing town planning.
predicates.law_regulates_land_development: The law governs land development, including reconstituting plots or adjusting rights in land.
predicates.law_organizes_orderly_urban_growth: The law establishes planning measures intended to promote the healthy and orderly development of urban areas.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition and retention of surplus agricultural land as part of a scheme to prevent concentration of holdings and promote efficient agriculture and rural welfare is a measure of agrarian reform.
material_facts: The enactment imposed ceilings on agricultural holdings, provided for acquisition of surplus land, and provided for distribution of surplus land.
For land held by industrial undertakings and used to produce raw material, the enactment provided for maintaining the land in compact blocks and cultivating it efficiently.
Efforts to establish joint farming societies did not succeed, and the legislature provided for the land to be cultivated on a continuing basis by a state-owned farming corporation.
The stated reasons included avoiding fragmentation, enabling improvement and efficient use of the land, and maintaining the supply of agricultural raw material.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects acquisition of land when it is for agrarian reform. Agrarian reform is wider than land redistribution and includes measures to improve the rural economy and welfare; a scheme may retain particular compact tracts with the State or a state-owned corporation where that retention serves the scheme's general agrarian purpose and is not an oblique deviation from it. The Court relied on Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, Balmadies Plantations Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu, Kanan Devan Hills Produce Co. Ltd. v. State of Kerala, State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing (Wvg.) Co. Ltd., and Kh. Fida Ali v. State of Jammu and Kashmir.
members.conclusion: The impugned provisions, including the provision for continued cultivation of the acquired industrial land by the state-owned farming corporation, were protected by Article 31A as measures of agrarian reform.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law or measure that acquires land.
predicates.agricultural_holdings_are_subject_to_a_c: The scheme limits the amount of agricultural land a person may hold.
predicates.surplus_land_is_acquired_for_the_scheme: Land exceeding the applicable holding limit is acquired as part of the scheme.
predicates.acquired_land_is_retained_compact_for_ef: Some acquired land is kept in compact blocks and cultivated by a public body rather than distributed in the same way as other surplus land.
predicates.retention_serves_agrarian_reform_and_rur: The retention is intended to support the scheme's agricultural and rural-welfare purposes, such as preventing fragmentation and improving efficient cultivation.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature may enact agrarian-reform legislation that regulates rights in agricultural land and the relationship between landholders and tenants.
material_facts: The challenged measure fixed limits on landholdings and provided for tenants in possession to purchase land, subject to provisions for landholders who required land for personal cultivation.
The measure was intended to distribute ownership and control of agricultural land and prevent its concentration.
members.legal_principle: Legislative entries in the constitutional lists are not to be construed narrowly or pedantically; they receive a large and liberal interpretation that includes ancillary or subsidiary matters fairly comprehended by their terms. The Court relied on British Coal Corporation v. The King, United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum, Navinchandra Mafatlal v. The Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay City, and Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan.
members.conclusion: The legislation fell within the state legislative field concerning land, including land tenures, landlord-tenant relations, and the transfer of agricultural land.

predicates.constitutional_validity_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding challenging the constitutional validity of legislation.
predicates.regulates_land_relations: The challenged measure regulates relations between agricultural landholders and cultivators.
predicates.concerns_agricultural_land_transfer: The challenged measure provides for the transfer or distribution of interests in agricultural land.

members.legal_issue: An oral family arrangement followed by a writing that merely records the completed arrangement for the information of a court or revenue authority does not require compulsory registration.
material_facts: The parties reached an oral family arrangement before filing a petition for mutation of the land records.
The petition stated that a compromise had already been made and asked the revenue authority to mutate the parties’ names according to their allotted properties.
The parties had sought an adjournment while the compromise was being made, and the petition did not itself create or declare rights in the properties.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, registration is required when a writing itself creates or declares rights in immovable property, not when the parties first settle orally and later prepare a memorandum solely to record the settlement or inform a court. Tek Bahadur Bhujil v. Devi Singh; Ram Gopal v. Tulshi Ram; and the court’s discussion of Sitala Baksh Singh, Mst. Kalawati, Bakhtawar, and Awadh Narain Singh support this distinction.
members.conclusion: The oral arrangement was not required to be registered, and the later petition was only a memorandum of it; the arrangement could therefore be relied upon.

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a settlement among family members resolving property disputes is effective.
predicates.arrangement_completed_orally: The parties completed their settlement orally before preparing the later writing.
predicates.later_writing_only_records_settlement: The later writing merely reports the completed settlement to a court or authority and does not itself create or declare property rights.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered writing that merely records a previously completed family arrangement does not require registration merely because it refers to rights in immovable property, but its admission does not prove the underlying property transaction.
