material_facts: The family properties had already been divided under an earlier partition, and the properties at issue had become separate properties of the family members.

The disputed family writing described adjustments said to have been made after that partition and stated that it was executed for record and remembrance; the Court found that it referred to alleged past arrangements rather than itself creating, declaring, assigning, limiting or extinguishing property rights.
The disputed receipt recorded an alleged payment connected with the respondent vacating a house portion.
The trial court allowed the writings to be marked, while the High Court held them inadmissible for want of registration and stamp duty.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act, 1908, an instrument that itself operates to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in immovable property, or acknowledges consideration on account of such a transaction, is generally compulsorily registrable. Section 49(a) and (c) bars an unregistered instrument from affecting the property or being used as evidence of a transaction affecting it, while its proviso permits evidence of a collateral transaction that does not itself require a registered instrument. A family arrangement may be oral; a writing that merely records a completed arrangement is distinguishable from one that itself effects the arrangement. The Court relied on Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, Subraya M.N. v. Vittala M.N., Thulasidhara v. Narayanappa, Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh, and Yellapu Uma Maheswari v. Buddha Jagadheeswararao. It also referred to Order 13 Rules 3 and 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and A.C. Lakshmipathy v. A.M. Chakrapani Reddiar on the stamp-duty treatment of a memorandum recording an existing family arrangement.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside. The family writing, as a record of alleged past transactions that did not itself affect property rights, could be admitted without registration; its admission did not permit the parties to prove through it a transaction affecting immovable property. On the Court’s characterization of that writing, it did not require stamp duty. The documents could be marked subject to these limitations.

predicates.civil_document_admissibility_proceeding: A court is deciding whether a writing may be admitted in a civil proceeding concerning property.
predicates.family_property_was_previously_divided: Family members had already divided the family property before the writing was made.
predicates.writing_records_a_completed_family_arran: The writing records an arrangement that the parties say was completed before the writing was made.
predicates.writing_does_not_itself_alter_property_r: The writing does not itself operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: A family settlement relinquishing interests in immovable property may be established by an oral arrangement, with an unregistered written record serving as evidence of an arrangement already made.
material_facts: Two claimants signed a village-panchayat resolution stating that they had relinquished their interests in two properties in exchange for consideration, and evidence supported that payments were made.
The resolution was unregistered, but the court found that it recorded a family settlement already reached between the family members.
The parties’ subsequent conduct, including living separately and not seeking partition for a period, supported the settlement.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, a writing that itself creates or extinguishes interests in immovable property generally requires registration and, if unregistered, cannot prove the transaction affecting the property. An oral family settlement is not required to be registered; an unregistered writing recording an earlier oral settlement may be used as corroborative evidence to explain the settlement and the parties’ conduct. Section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872, does not make such an unregistered writing proof of a transaction that required registration. No earlier case was cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: The claimants had relinquished their interests in the two properties, and the partition claim concerning those properties was dismissed.

rule.if: partition_appeal and oral_family_settlement and unregistered_record_memorializes_prior_settlement and settlement_record_signed_by_participants and consideration_paid and conduct_supports_settlement

predicates.partition_appeal: The dispute is before the court in an appeal arising from a partition proceeding.
predicates.oral_family_settlement: The family members had reached an oral arrangement concerning their interests in the property.
predicates.unregistered_record_memorializes_prior_s: A written record was unregistered and recorded an arrangement already reached, rather than itself being intended to create the arrangement.
predicates.settlement_record_signed_by_participants: The participants in the arrangement signed the written record.
predicates.consideration_paid: The person receiving the property paid consideration to the persons relinquishing their interests.
predicates.conduct_supports_settlement: The parties’ subsequent conduct was consistent with the arrangement having been made and acted upon.

members.legal_issue: A written family arrangement requires registration when it itself creates or transfers an interest in immovable property in the present, but not when it only sets terms for a possible future partition.
material_facts: The written agreement provided for the family to remain joint and for the parties to continue managing the property as before.
It set the shares to be taken if and when a partition occurred in the future.
It did not divide the property by metes and bounds, sever the parties’ status, or otherwise affect their interests in immovable property in the present.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act applies where an instrument itself creates, declares, assigns, limits, or extinguishes an interest in immovable property in the present. The Court distinguished Thakur Umrao Singh v. Thakur Lachman Singh, where the instrument was intended to effect an immediate partition, and considered Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar and, by analogy, Hari Sankar Paul v. Kedar Nath Saha.
members.conclusion: The agreement did not require registration.

rule.if: family_arrangement_registration_dispute and written_family_arrangement and partition_only_in_future and no_present_property_interest_created

predicates.family_arrangement_registration_dispute: A party disputes whether a written family arrangement must be registered.
predicates.written_family_arrangement: The family arrangement is recorded in a written instrument.
predicates.partition_only_in_future: The instrument provides for shares to apply only if a partition takes place later and does not itself effect a partition.
predicates.no_present_property_interest_created: The instrument does not itself create, transfer, or alter an interest in immovable property in the present.

members.legal_issue: A family arrangement that only records steps for dividing property in the future, without itself creating rights in specific immovable property, does not require registration.
material_facts: The document described as an award recorded a family arrangement and proposed steps for dividing the family properties in the future.
It did not allot specific items of immovable property or itself create rights in particular properties.
A prior court had held the document inadmissible because it was not registered.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 17(2)(v) of the Registration Act, 1908, a document that does not itself create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in specific immovable property, but merely creates a right to obtain a later document that will do so, is exempt from compulsory registration. The court applied Ranjangam Iyer v. Ranjangam Iyer and distinguished documents that themselves allot specific property, as discussed in Shiromani v. Hem Kumar, Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar, and Lachhman Dass v. Ram Lal. It also considered the family-arrangement principles in Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation.
members.conclusion: The document was a memorandum of understanding or family arrangement that did not require registration; the prior order holding it inadmissible for want of registration was incorrect.

predicates.family_partition_document_dispute: The dispute concerns a document recording an arrangement to divide family property.
predicates.document_only_records_future_division: The document records steps or an arrangement for dividing the property in the future rather than effecting the division itself.
predicates.document_creates_rights_in_specific_prop: The document itself creates, declares, assigns, limits or extinguishes a person's rights in a specific item of immovable property.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered written record of an oral family partition may be considered as a list corroborating the arrangement and the parties’ conduct when it records an arrangement already made orally rather than itself creating or extinguishing rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff admitted that an oral partition had taken place and that he received a share consistent with the written record.
The written record was signed by the plaintiff and other family members and by people associated with the village council.
Witnesses supported the execution of the record.
The lower courts treated the document as admissible, while the High Court excluded it solely because it was unregistered.
members.legal_principle: A writing that merely records a completed oral family arrangement does not require registration as an instrument creating or extinguishing rights, and an unregistered written family arrangement may be used as corroborative evidence explaining the arrangement and the parties’ conduct. A family settlement may also operate as an estoppel between its participants. The Court relied on Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai, and Subraya M.N. v. Vittala M.N. and Others.
members.conclusion: The document could be considered as a list of properties partitioned and as corroborative evidence of the oral arrangement and the parties’ conduct; the High Court erred in excluding it solely for want of registration.

rule.if: family_partition_proceeding and prior_oral_partition_admitted and writing_records_existing_arrangement and participants_signed_or_followed_arrangement

predicates.family_partition_proceeding: The dispute concerns an alleged partition or family arrangement among family members.
predicates.prior_oral_partition_admitted: A participant admitted that the family arrangement had already been made orally.
predicates.writing_records_existing_arrangement: The writing records or lists the terms or property allotments of the existing arrangement rather than itself creating or extinguishing rights.
predicates.participants_signed_or_followed_arrangem: The participants signed the writing or their conduct was consistent with the recorded arrangement.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered private arbitration award that declares a pre-existing interest in immovable property, rather than creating or extinguishing that interest, is not compulsorily registrable and may be relied on as evidence of the pre-existing interest.
material_facts: Two brothers jointly funded the purchase of a house, each contributing half of the purchase price, although the sale certificate was issued only in one brother’s name.
A private arbitration award declared that the brother named on the sale certificate had held the property as benamidar and that both brothers had owned equal shares from the date of purchase.
The award was made a rule of court years before the named brother entered into the sale agreement concerning the property.
The evidence showed joint mutation and joint possession and enjoyment of the property.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, a non-testamentary instrument that creates, declares, assigns, limits, or extinguishes an interest in immovable property of the prescribed value must be registered, and an unregistered instrument required to be registered cannot affect the property or be received as evidence of a transaction affecting it. Whether registration is required depends on what the instrument purports to do: an instrument creating or extinguishing an interest is registrable, but one that merely declares a pre-existing interest is not. An unregistered award is not inadmissible for every purpose and may be relied on to show resolution of a dispute and the parties’ acceptance or conduct. The Court relied on Lachhman Dass v. Ram Lall, Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar, Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit, Uttam Singh Duggal v. Union of India, Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Bhaskarsa Kabadi, Champalal v. Samarath Bai, Addanki Narayanappa v. Bhaskara Krishtappa, CIT v. Juggilal Kamalapat, and Kale v. Dy. Director of Consolidation.
members.conclusion: The award declared the appellant’s pre-existing half share and did not create a new interest in the property. It was therefore not compulsorily registrable, and the appellant could rely on it as evidence of his ownership.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and private_arbitration_award and award_declares_preexisting_interest and joint_contribution_to_purchase and named_titleholder_was_benamidar

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over a claimed interest in immovable property.
predicates.private_arbitration_award: The parties referred their dispute to private arbitration and an award was made.
predicates.award_declares_preexisting_interest: The award describes an interest in the property as already existing rather than as newly created or extinguished by the award.
predicates.joint_contribution_to_purchase: The person claiming an interest contributed to the purchase price together with the person named in the title document.
predicates.named_titleholder_was_benamidar: The person named in the title document held the property on behalf of the other contributor as well as himself.

members.legal_issue: A writing that records a previously completed partition and lists the properties allotted to each side is not an instrument of partition requiring registration.
material_facts: The agricultural properties had already been divided between the two family branches, and their respective shares had been entered separately in the revenue records, disrupting their joint status.
The writing described the residential properties and other remaining properties allotted to each branch and began by recording that the parties had discussed and mutually agreed on the arrangement.
The parties disputed their respective claims to the properties, and the writing recorded the arrangement rather than itself effecting a change in their legal relations.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, a document requires registration when it itself operates or purports to operate to create or declare rights in immovable property. A writing that merely records a completed partition, or is only a list of properties allotted, does not require registration. A document that itself effects division and embodies the terms of the bargain must be registered, and if it is not, Section 49 excludes it from evidence; secondary evidence of that partition is also barred by Section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872. The Court relied on Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar, Nani Bai v. Gita Bai, and the principles discussed in Narayan Sakharam Patil v. Cooperative Central Bank, Bageshwari Charan Singh v. Jagarnath Kuari, and Subramanian v. Lutchman.
members.conclusion: The writing was a memorandum recording a past arrangement, not an instrument that itself effected partition; it did not require registration and was admissible in evidence to prove the partition.

rule.if: civil_appeal and prior_severance_of_joint_status and writing_records_past_arrangement and writing_lists_property_allocations

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal.
predicates.prior_severance_of_joint_status: The family members had already divided some joint property and thereafter held their respective shares separately.
predicates.writing_records_past_arrangement: The parties made a writing that records an arrangement already reached rather than itself expressing a decision to change their legal relations.
predicates.writing_lists_property_allocations: The writing sets out the properties allotted to the respective parties.

members.legal_issue: A document that merely records a partition already completed by the parties does not require registration as an instrument creating rights in immovable property.
material_facts: The arbitrators’ records described property divisions that had already been made and accepted by the parties.
The parties’ acceptance and the completed divisions, rather than the records themselves, gave effect to the allotments.
Some records concerned immovable property.
members.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, requires registration of specified non-testamentary instruments that themselves create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish rights in immovable property. A record that merely acknowledges a division already completed and accepted does not itself create those rights and is not compulsorily registrable.
members.conclusion: The records were acknowledgments of completed partitions and were not required to be registered under section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The court is deciding a proceeding concerning the division of property.
predicates.document_records_completed_partition: The document describes a division of property that had already been completed by the parties.
predicates.document_does_not_itself_create_property: The parties’ completed acts, rather than the document itself, created or changed their property interests.

members.legal_issue: An arbitration award that preserves existing securities over land without creating or declaring an interest in immovable property does not require registration.
material_facts: The award stated that existing documents relating to debts secured on land would remain as before and continue as security until payment.
The award also stated that the debtor would have no right to transfer the land, but the Court treated this as stating an existing fact rather than creating or declaring an interest in the land.
The award was filed for the purpose of obtaining a decree.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, registration is required for an instrument within its scope that creates or declares an interest in immovable property. The award did not itself create or declare such an interest.
members.conclusion: The award was not within the category of instruments requiring registration, so its lack of registration did not prevent a decree from being passed in its terms.

predicates.arbitration_award_decree_proceeding: A party sought a court decree on an arbitration award.
predicates.award_preserves_existing_land_security: The award continued existing documents and securities relating to debts secured on land.
predicates.award_does_not_create_property_interest: The award stated the existing position concerning land rather than itself creating or declaring an interest in it.

members.legal_issue: An arbitration award that makes a party’s relinquishment of an interest in immovable property conditional on payment, without itself creating or extinguishing that interest, does not require compulsory registration.
material_facts: The award stated that one heir would give up her interest in the property only after receiving a specified payment.
Until payment, that heir could continue occupying the portion of the house in her possession.
The High Court declined to make the award a rule of the court because it was unregistered.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires registration of a non-testamentary instrument that itself creates, declares, assigns, limits or extinguishes a qualifying right in immovable property. An award that only quantifies the value of an existing entitlement and makes relinquishment conditional on payment does not itself create or extinguish that right. The Court relied on Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar, Upendra Nath Bose v. Lall, and Sheonarain Lal v. Rameshwari Devi, and distinguished Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar and Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit.
members.conclusion: The award did not create or extinguish a right in immovable property and therefore did not require compulsory registration; the award could be made a rule of the court.

predicates.arbitration_award_proceeding: The dispute was referred to arbitration and the court considered whether the resulting award could be made a rule of the court.
predicates.relinquishment_conditional_on_payment: The award made a party’s relinquishment of an interest in property conditional on that party first receiving payment.
predicates.award_does_not_itself_change_property_ri: The award described an existing property entitlement and the method for working it out, rather than itself creating or extinguishing a property right.

members.legal_issue: A family arrangement may be established by an oral agreement recorded in a writing, and the absence of a family member’s written statement does not invalidate the arrangement where that member consented to it.
material_facts: The parties asserted competing claims to the properties, with the appellant claiming that the properties were his self-acquired property and the plaintiff claiming a share.
A document recorded the brothers’ statements and their agreement about the properties and their enjoyment.
The plaintiff alleged and testified that their mother consented to the arrangement and was to retain and enjoy a house property, although her statement was not recorded in the document.
members.legal_principle: A family arrangement may be made orally, and a writing may simply record what has already been agreed. The Court also relied on Sahu Madho Das v. Mukhand Ram in explaining the treatment of antecedent claims in family arrangements.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding that the parties had made a family arrangement and that the document recorded it; the mother’s consent did not have to be recorded in the document.

rule.if: civil_property_partition_dispute and competing_property_claims and arrangement_resolves_claims and oral_family_agreement and family_member_consented

predicates.civil_property_partition_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to divide or obtain possession of property among persons asserting family-related rights.
predicates.competing_property_claims: The participants assert competing claims concerning rights in the property.
predicates.arrangement_resolves_claims: The participants agree how the disputed property or its enjoyment will be allocated among them.
predicates.oral_family_agreement: The arrangement was agreed orally, even if its terms were later recorded in writing.
predicates.family_member_consented: A family member whose interests were addressed by the arrangement consented to it, even though that member’s statement was not written into the record.

members.legal_issue: A writing recording a family arrangement does not require compulsory registration when it merely memorializes an arrangement already made and is not itself the instrument that creates or declares the parties’ rights.
material_facts: The document recorded the brothers’ statements and said that they had agreed to those statements and kept copies as proof.
The Court found that the document recorded what had already been decided and was evidence of the arrangement, not the basis of the parties’ rights in the property.
The document did not recognize any brother as sole owner transferring property to the others.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act, compulsory registration applies when the writing itself brings about the arrangement or declares rights in property for future use as a document of title. A writing that only records a prior oral arrangement as evidence does not require compulsory registration.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the document was a memorandum of the arrangement and did not require compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act.

rule.if: family_property_arrangement_dispute and writing_records_prior_agreement and writing_is_evidence_only and writing_does_not_create_or_declare_property_rights

predicates.family_property_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns an arrangement about rights in family property.
predicates.writing_records_prior_agreement: The participants made the arrangement before the writing was prepared, and the writing records what they had agreed.
predicates.writing_is_evidence_only: The writing serves as proof or a record of the prior arrangement rather than as the operative instrument of agreement.
predicates.writing_does_not_create_or_declare_prope: The writing itself does not create or declare the participants’ property rights for the future.

members.legal_issue: An arbitration award that directs the parties to execute later documents to create or transfer rights in immovable property is not compulsorily registrable when the award itself does not create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish those rights.
material_facts: The parties referred their disputes to a sole arbitrator, whose award concerned immovable property valued above the statutory threshold for compulsory registration.
The award directed the property-holding company to execute documents declaring the other parties’ shares and transferring the property and lease into joint names.
The High Court held that the award required registration and could not be made a rule of court because it was unregistered.
The Supreme Court concluded that the award itself did not create or alter rights in the property; it created a right to obtain later documents that would do so.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, a document is compulsorily registrable if it itself purports or operates to create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish the specified rights in immovable property. Under section 17(2)(v), a document that merely creates a right to obtain another document that will create or alter those rights is not compulsorily registrable. The Court applied Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar, Sheonarain Lal v. Rameshwari Devi, Satish Kumar v. Surinder Kumar, and Ratan Lal Sharma v. Purshottam Harit to distinguish an award that itself effects rights in property from one that requires a later instrument to do so.
members.conclusion: The award fell within section 17(2)(v) of the Registration Act and was not compulsorily registrable. The High Court’s ruling was reversed and the appeal was allowed.

predicates.appeal_from_registration_based_rejection: An appeal challenges a decision rejecting an arbitration award from admission or enforcement because it was not registered.
predicates.arbitration_award_orders_future_property: An arbitrator directs a party to execute later documents to declare or transfer rights in immovable property.
predicates.award_does_not_itself_alter_property_rig: The award itself does not create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish rights in the property, but only gives a right to obtain a later document that will do so.

members.legal_issue: An award that merely records a partition already completed does not, on that account, require registration as an instrument creating or declaring rights in immovable property.
material_facts: The family’s immovable properties had been partitioned before the award was made, and the parties had taken separate possession and enjoyment of their allotted properties.
A later arbitration agreement recorded that the partition had already occurred and that a party who had previously been a minor accepted it.
The award referred to the completed partition and the parties’ possession under it; it did not itself effect that partition.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, a non-testamentary instrument that creates or declares rights or interests in immovable property of the specified value requires registration. A recital of an existing partition does not itself create or declare those rights. The Court relied on Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Bhaskarsa Kabadi.
members.conclusion: The award’s reference to the prior partition did not make it compulsorily registrable as an instrument creating or declaring interests in immovable property.

predicates.award_enforcement_proceeding: A party sought to have an arbitration award filed and enforced, and the opposing party contested its admissibility.
predicates.partition_previously_completed: The parties had already divided the immovable property and taken possession of their respective shares before the award was made.
predicates.award_only_recites_partition: The award referred to the earlier division and possession but did not itself carry out the division.

members.legal_issue: A highest bidder at a public auction acquires no vested right to the property before the competent authority confirms the provisional bid.
material_facts: The bidder offered the highest bid at a public auction and deposited the required earnest money.
The auction terms made acceptance of the highest bid provisional and subject to confirmation by the competent authority.
The competent authority did not confirm the bid and cancelled it, citing inadequate publicity and the prospect of obtaining a better price through re-auction.
members.legal_principle: Rule 8(1)(h) of Chapter III of the Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Rules, 1976 makes acceptance of the highest bid provisional and subject to confirmation by the Sales Commissioner. The Court also applied the settled principle that the State is not bound to accept the highest bid and that the bidder's rights depend on the conditions governing the auction.
members.conclusion: The bidder acquired no vested right to have the sale completed because the provisional bid was never confirmed.

rule.if: public_property_auction and highest_bid_provisionally_accepted and not sale_confirmation_issued

predicates.public_property_auction: A public authority offered property for sale through a public auction.
predicates.highest_bid_provisionally_accepted: The auction authority provisionally accepted a bidder's bid as the highest bid.
predicates.sale_confirmation_issued: The competent authority issued confirmation of the auction sale.

members.legal_issue: A person who makes the highest bid at a public auction has no right to require completion of the sale when the auction terms reserve final acceptance of the bid and that acceptance has not occurred.
material_facts: The auction conditions reserved final authority to accept a bid to the board’s chairperson.
The respondent made the highest bid and deposited an initial amount, but the chairperson had not accepted the bid before the auction was cancelled.
members.legal_principle: The rights of a highest bidder depend on the auction conditions; where final acceptance is reserved to the public authority, no right to completion arises before acceptance. The Court relied on Laxmikant v. Satyawan, (1996) 4 SCC 208, and referred to Trilochan Mishra v. State of Orissa, (1971) 3 SCC 153, State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal, (1972) 2 SCC 36, Union of India v. M/s Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram, (1969) 3 SCC 146, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Vijay Bahadur Singh, (1982) 2 SCC 365.
members.conclusion: The highest bidder acquired no vested right to have the auction concluded in its favour, and the High Court could not direct issuance of a demand for the balance of the price.

predicates.public_auction_case: The proceeding concerns a bid made at a public auction conducted by a public authority.
predicates.final_bid_acceptance_reserved_to_authori: The auction terms reserve final acceptance or rejection of a bid to the public authority.
predicates.bid_not_finally_accepted: The public authority has not finally accepted the bidder’s offer.

members.legal_issue: An auction bid that is expressly subject to confirmation does not create a completed sale before confirmation.
material_facts: The highest bid was made subject to confirmation by the Chief Commissioner, who could reject it.
The Chief Commissioner did not confirm the bid.
members.legal_principle: Under clause 33 of the auction conditions, final bids were subject to the Chief Commissioner's confirmation; clause 16 of Rule 5.34 also made sales open to revision by the Chief Commissioner. A conditional acceptance does not conclude a contract, and the offer may be withdrawn before absolute acceptance. The Court relied on Hussey v. Horne Payne, [1878] 8 Ch. D. 670 at 676.
members.conclusion: The sale was not complete without confirmation, and the bidder could withdraw the bid before confirmation without incurring liability for breach of contract or a resale shortfall.

predicates.conditional_auction_contract_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an auction bid created a binding contract.
predicates.bid_subject_to_confirmation: The auction terms made the bid subject to confirmation by an authority.
predicates.confirmation_not_given: The authority did not confirm the bid.

members.legal_issue: A bidder is not liable for a resale price deficiency where the auction sale was subject to confirmation and no completed sale resulted.
material_facts: The bidder did not pay the required deposit after the auction.
The Chief Commissioner did not confirm the bid, and the licence was resold at a lower price.
The Collector sought to recover the difference between the bids from the original bidder.
members.legal_principle: Clause 21 of Rule 5.34 distinguishes a person to whom a shop has been sold from a bidder whose bid has only been provisionally accepted. Its first part concerns a completed sale; its later part expressly addresses an auction conducted by an officer lower in rank than the Collector and permits recovery of a deficiency from a defaulting bidder in that situation. Because the sale here required confirmation and was not confirmed, the essential prerequisites of a completed sale were absent. Clause 33 of the auction conditions made bids subject to confirmation.
members.conclusion: The original bidder was not liable for the resale deficiency because the sale had not been completed.

rule.if: resale_deficiency_recovery_dispute and auction_sale_subject_to_confirmation and confirmation_not_given and resale_deficiency_claimed

predicates.resale_deficiency_recovery_dispute: The proceeding concerns recovery from an auction bidder of a price deficiency following resale.
predicates.auction_sale_subject_to_confirmation: The auction terms required confirmation before the sale became complete.
predicates.confirmation_not_given: The authority did not confirm the bidder's bid.
predicates.resale_deficiency_claimed: A deficiency arose on resale and recovery of it was sought from the original bidder.

members.legal_issue: A highest bidder whose bid has not been accepted and who has not received an allotment letter has no vested right to the property and cannot obtain an order compelling allotment through a suit for declaration and mandatory injunction.
material_facts: The plaintiff submitted the highest bid and paid the required initial deposit at the auction.
The competent authority did not accept the bid, and no allotment letter was issued.
The plaintiff sought a declaration that rejection was illegal and a mandatory order requiring allotment.
The court could not itself accept the bid; a declaration that the rejection was unlawful would not establish a concluded contract.
members.legal_principle: Under Regulation 6(2) of the Haryana Urban Development (Disposal of Land and Buildings) Regulations, 1978, acceptance by the competent authority and issuance of the allotment letter precede the further payment obligation and formation of a concluded contract. A highest bidder acquires no vested right merely by making the highest bid or paying a deposit. The Court relied on Uttar Pradesh Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Om Prakash Sharma (2013) 5 SCC 182, including its discussion of Rajasthan Housing Board v. G.S. Investments (2007) 1 SCC 477 and State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal (1972) 2 SCC 36.
members.conclusion: The suit, in the form filed, was not maintainable for the relief sought, and mandatory allotment could not be ordered in the absence of an accepted bid and an allotment letter.

rule.if: civil_suit_seeking_allotment and bid_not_accepted and allotment_letter_not_issued and (highest_bid_submitted or initial_deposit_paid)

predicates.civil_suit_seeking_allotment: The bidder brought a civil suit seeking a declaration about rejection of the bid and an order requiring allotment.
predicates.bid_not_accepted: The competent authority did not accept the bidder’s offer.
predicates.allotment_letter_not_issued: The authority did not issue an allotment letter to the bidder.
predicates.highest_bid_submitted: The bidder submitted the highest offer at the auction.
predicates.initial_deposit_paid: The bidder paid the initial deposit required at the auction.

members.legal_issue: A person who makes the highest bid at a public auction has no enforceable right to transfer of the property before the bid is accepted in accordance with the auction requirements.
material_facts: The auction did not reach its final round because it was stayed, and the bidder’s offer was not confirmed by the Trust.
The auction conditions made acceptance by the Board of Trustees necessary and required a confirmation letter before the balance of the premium was payable.
The High Court directed transfer to the bidder despite finding that the auction had not culminated in a completed contract.
members.legal_principle: Rule 4(3) of the Nagpur Improvement Trust Land Disposal Rules, 1955 must be read with its proviso and the notified auction conditions. A highest bidder’s rights depend on the conditions of the auction and do not arise merely from making the highest offer where acceptance or confirmation is required. The Court relied on Trilochan Mishra v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal, Union of India v. M/s Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Vijay Bahadur Singh.
members.conclusion: The bidder acquired no enforceable right to transfer of the land; the appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_direction and public_land_auction and bidder_made_highest_offer and auction_terms_required_acceptance and not bid_accepted

predicates.appeal_from_writ_direction: An appeal concerns a direction in a writ proceeding requiring a public authority to transfer property to an auction bidder.
predicates.public_land_auction: A public authority offered land for disposal by auction.
predicates.bidder_made_highest_offer: A bidder made the highest offer received in the auction process.
predicates.auction_terms_required_acceptance: The announced auction terms required the authority to accept the bid before the bidder could obtain rights to the property.
predicates.bid_accepted: The authority accepted the bid in the manner required by the auction terms.

members.legal_issue: A provisional acceptance of an auction bid subject to government confirmation does not create a concluded contract unless the required confirmation is given.
material_facts: The highest bid was below the reserve price, and the auction officer accepted it subject to confirmation by the government.
The government did not confirm acceptance of that bid; it instead acted on the bidder’s later offer to take the settlement at the reserve price.
The bidder withdrew that later offer by asking for settlement at the original auction bid, and acceptance of the later offer was not put in transmission to the bidder.
members.legal_principle: A conditional or provisional acceptance does not itself create a binding contract; an offer may be withdrawn before acceptance. The Court applied Somasundaram Pillai v. Provincial Government of Madras, AIR 1947 Madras 366, and distinguished The Rajanagaram Village Cooperative Society v. Veeraswami Mudaly, [1950] 11 M.L.J. 486. It also referred to Williston on Contracts, section 77A, concerning an acceptance that is not effective until a future event.
members.conclusion: There was no concluded contract between the bidder and the government.

rule.if: auction_contract_dispute and bid_acceptance_subject_to_confirmation and government_did_not_confirm_bid and later_offer_withdrawn_before_effective_acceptance

predicates.auction_contract_dispute: The parties disputed whether an agreement resulted from an auction settlement.
predicates.bid_acceptance_subject_to_confirmation: The auction officer accepted a bid on the condition that a government authority confirm it.
predicates.government_did_not_confirm_bid: The government authority did not confirm the auction officer’s acceptance of that bid.
predicates.later_offer_withdrawn_before_effective_a: The bidder withdrew a later offer before its acceptance was communicated or put in transmission to the bidder.

members.legal_issue: A person who submits the highest bid at a public auction acquires no vested right in the property and no concluded contract arises before acceptance by the competent authority.
material_facts: A public auction was held for a property, and the plaintiff submitted the highest bid and deposited part of the bid amount and earnest money.
The auction officer did not accept the bid, and the competent authority rejected it and refunded the deposit.
No allotment letter was issued to the plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: A bidder has a right to equality and fair treatment in the evaluation of bids, but no vested right to have the auction concluded in their favour until the competent authority accepts the bid. The authority may reject even the highest bid for good and sufficient reasons, provided it acts without arbitrariness or favouritism. No concluded contract arises before acceptance. The Court relied on Meerut Development Authority v. Association of Management Studies, Rajasthan Housing Board v. G.S. Investments, State of U.P. v. Vijay Bahadur Singh, Laxmikant v. Satyawan, State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal, and Union of India v. Bhimsen Walaiti Ram.
members.conclusion: The highest bid and deposit did not give the plaintiff a vested right to the property or create a concluded contract.

rule.if: public_auction_proceeding and highest_bid_submitted and bid_deposit_made and bid_not_accepted_by_competent_authority

predicates.public_auction_proceeding: The dispute concerns a person’s participation in a public auction for property.
predicates.highest_bid_submitted: The claimant submitted the highest bid in the auction.
predicates.bid_deposit_made: The claimant deposited the required portion of the bid or earnest money.
predicates.bid_not_accepted_by_competent_authority: The authority empowered to accept the bid did not accept it.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff cannot obtain a declaration of a right to auctioned property when the bid was not accepted and no acceptance was communicated, because no legal right or concluded contract arose.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration that the auction was final and binding and that the plaintiff was the owner or allottee of the property.
The competent authority rejected the bid, and neither it nor the auction officer accepted the bid in writing or communicated acceptance to the plaintiff.
No allotment letter was issued.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, declaratory relief requires an existing legal character or right. Under Sections 3 and 4 of the Contract Act, 1872, an offer must be accepted and the acceptance communicated as required for a contract to arise. A highest bid alone does not create an enforceable right. The Court relied on Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd., Bhagwan Das Goverdhan Das Kedia v. Girdhari Lal & Co., and Haridwar Singh v. Begum Sumbrui.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff had acquired no legal right to the property, so the declaratory suit was not maintainable.

rule.if: declaratory_suit and claim_based_on_auction_bid and bid_not_accepted and acceptance_not_communicated

predicates.declaratory_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of a legal right in property.
predicates.claim_based_on_auction_bid: The claimant based the asserted property right on a bid made at an auction.
predicates.bid_not_accepted: No competent authority accepted the claimant’s bid.
predicates.acceptance_not_communicated: No acceptance of the bid was communicated to the claimant.

members.legal_issue: Substantial questions of law do not arise for determination in a second appeal when the claim depends on an unaccepted auction bid that created no legal right.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s second appeal challenged the judgment dismissing the suit and sought to establish a right to the property based on the auction bid.
The competent authority had not accepted the bid, and no concluded contract or legal right had arisen.
The High Court framed substantial questions of law and allowed the second appeal.
members.legal_principle: A second appellate court must address substantial questions of law that arise from the case. Where the claimant acquired no legal right because the bid was never accepted and no concluded contract existed, questions framed to support that claimed right do not arise for determination. The Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the dismissal of the suit.
members.conclusion: The substantial questions framed by the High Court did not arise for consideration, and its decision allowing the second appeal was erroneous.

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal to a higher court from an appellate judgment in a civil suit.
predicates.claim_based_on_unaccepted_auction_bid: The claimant’s case in the appeal depends on a bid made at an auction that was not accepted.
predicates.claimant_has_no_legal_right_from_the_bid: The facts establish that the claimant acquired no legal right through the bid.

members.legal_issue: An auction bid accepted internally but not communicated to the bidder does not complete the sale or create an enforceable right to the property.
material_facts: The competent authority recorded acceptance of the bid on its file after an interim court order had stayed the auction.
The authority did not communicate its acceptance to the bidders, although they later learned that it had been recorded.
The bidders had paid only 25 per cent of the bid amount.
members.legal_principle: Acceptance of a bid at a public auction must be communicated to be complete; recording acceptance on an authority’s file and receiving a partial deposit do not themselves transfer property. The Court relied on no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The acceptance was incomplete, and the bidders acquired no enforceable right to the plot through the auction.

predicates.public_land_auction_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claimed right arising from a public authority’s land auction.
predicates.bid_acceptance_uncommunicated: The public authority did not communicate its recorded acceptance of the bid to the bidder.
predicates.acceptance_recorded_after_stay: The authority recorded its acceptance after a court had stayed the auction.

members.legal_issue: A statutory sale of secured assets is not complete merely upon confirmation of the auction when the full sale consideration has not been paid.
material_facts: The secured assets were put to auction before the insolvency proceeding began, and the auction was confirmed after the purchasers paid 25% of the bid amount.
The purchasers paid the remaining 75% after the insolvency proceeding had commenced.
The sale was governed by the statutory sale procedure in Rules 8 and 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002.
members.legal_principle: Rules 8 and 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 govern the statutory sale, which is complete only when the purchaser makes the entire payment and the authorised officer issues the sale certificate. The Court distinguished Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, (1999) 3 SCC 573, B. Arvind Kumar v. Govt. of India, (2007) 5 SCC 745, and Kaliaperumal v. Rajagopal, (2009) 4 SCC 193, and relied on Shakeena v. Bank of India, 2019 SCC OnLine SC 1059, followed in S. Karthik v. N. Subhash Chand Jain, 2020 SCC OnLine SC 787, concerning completion of a sale under the SARFAESI statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The sale was not complete upon confirmation or part payment; under the statutory sale procedure, it could be completed only upon payment of the entire consideration and issuance of the sale certificate.

predicates.statutory_asset_sale: A creditor conducted a sale of secured assets under a statutory enforcement process.
predicates.full_consideration_unpaid: The purchaser had not paid the entire sale consideration to the creditor.

members.legal_issue: A bid made under a state-issued tender that reserves the state’s right to accept or reject offers does not become a concluded sale contract without the state’s approval.
material_facts: The state issued the advertisement inviting bids and reserved the right to accept or reject any offer.
The proposed purchaser submitted its bid in response to that advertisement.
The company’s board resolution stated that the decision would be sent to the state for its formal approval.
The state’s order concerning the company’s closure and sale proceeds did not grant approval for this particular sale.
members.legal_principle: The terms of the tender reserved acceptance to the state, so the company’s board decision alone did not complete the transaction. The resolution’s stated intention to seek formal approval and the absence of an approval for the particular sale meant that the necessary acceptance had not occurred.
members.conclusion: The state’s approval was necessary, and the record did not establish that it had been granted. There was therefore no concluded contract on which the proposed purchaser could obtain an order directing execution of a sale deed.

predicates.sale_offer_followed_state_tender: A proposed purchaser made its offer in response to a tender issued by a state authority.
predicates.tendering_authority_reserved_acceptance_: The tender terms reserve to the issuing authority the right to accept or reject the offer.
predicates.approval_not_granted: The issuing authority has not approved the particular proposed sale.
predicates.no_concluded_sale_contract: The offer and board decision do not amount to a concluded sale contract.

members.legal_issue: An auction declaration and approval of a bid do not transfer property where the sale terms require full payment and a sale certificate before ownership is transferred.
material_facts: Property in the compensation pool was put up for public auction, and bidders were declared, including a highest bidder.
The sale terms made the bid subject to approval and provided that ownership would be transferred and a sale certificate issued after the purchase price was paid in full.
The occupant claimed protection from eviction on the basis that the property had been transferred to the auction purchaser.
The occupant did not establish that the purchase price had been paid in full or that a sale certificate had been issued.
members.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, gives a qualifying person in lawful possession protection as a tenant of a transferee when notified property is transferred, including protection against eviction for the prescribed period except on specified grounds. Under section 20, a transfer may be made by sale, subject to the rules. Rule 90(3) provides for notice of sale terms; rule 90(8) requires an initial deposit; rule 90(10) makes a bid subject to approval; rule 90(11) requires payment of the balance after approval; and rule 90(15) provides for a sale certificate when the price has been realised in full. In this sale, the terms also expressly made full payment the condition for transfer of ownership. A highest bid or its approval may create a binding contract, but does not itself transfer the property in these circumstances. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: There had not yet been a transfer of the property to the auction purchaser, so the occupant could not claim the protection that depended on a transfer.

rule.if: claim_for_protection_after_property_transfer and auction_sale and (bid_not_approved or purchase_price_not_paid_in_full or sale_certificate_not_issued)

predicates.claim_for_protection_after_property_tran: An occupant claims protection against eviction on the basis that property has been transferred to another person.
predicates.auction_sale: The property was offered for sale by public auction under terms governing completion of the sale.
predicates.bid_not_approved: The competent authority had not approved the successful bid.
predicates.purchase_price_not_paid_in_full: The purchaser had not paid the full purchase price required by the sale terms.
predicates.sale_certificate_not_issued: The authority had not issued the sale certificate required by the sale terms to complete the transfer.
predicates.no_transfer_for_tenant_protection: The property has not been transferred for purposes of the occupant’s claimed protection.

members.legal_issue: Delegating to the executive the power to extend enactments to a territory without its own legislature does not amount to an unconstitutional abdication of legislative power when the delegation is guided and confined to selecting suitable laws enacted by competent legislatures.
material_facts: The territory had no local legislature, and Parliament had legislative responsibility for it.
The challenged provision empowered the executive to extend to the territory enactments in force in a State, subject to restrictions or modifications.
The territory was small and situated among areas with their own legislatures, while Parliament had limited time to address its detailed legislative needs.
The executive’s role was to select suitable enacted laws for the territory, rather than to make a new law or change an enactment’s substance.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 246(4) of the Constitution and section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, Parliament may delegate subordinate legislative tasks but must retain the essential legislative function of laying down policy and standards. The Court applied the policy-and-guidelines approach and the reasoning in In re Delhi Laws Act, [1951] SCR 747, and referred to Registrar of Cooperative Societies v. Kunhambu, [1980] 2 SCR 260, and Gwalior Rayon Silk Mfg. (Wvg.) Co. Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, [1974] 2 SCR 879. A broad indication of policy is sufficient in this context; the delegation is not abdication where the executive selects among laws already enacted by competent legislatures for their suitability to local conditions.
members.conclusion: The delegation was valid and did not constitute abdication or effacement of Parliament’s legislative power.

rule.if: challenge_to_executive_extension_power and territory_without_local_legislature and executive_selects_enacted_laws and selection_guided_by_local_suitability and executive_cannot_make_substantive_law_changes

predicates.challenge_to_executive_extension_power: A proceeding challenges the validity of giving the executive authority to extend laws to a territory.
predicates.territory_without_local_legislature: The territory for which the laws are to be extended has no local legislature.
predicates.executive_selects_enacted_laws: The executive is empowered to select laws that have already been enacted by competent legislatures.
predicates.selection_guided_by_local_suitability: The executive selects laws by assessing their suitability to the territory’s local conditions.
predicates.executive_cannot_make_substantive_law_ch: The executive’s authority does not permit it to make a new law or substantially alter the substance of an enacted law.

members.legal_issue: Delegating the identification of relatives whose transfers are disregarded does not amount to an abdication of legislative power when the legislature has stated the governing policy.
material_facts: The statute required transfers to prescribed relations to be disregarded when determining surplus land.
The statute left the enumeration of those relations to the government.
The statutory policy was to prevent transfers to relatives that could conceal the transferor’s land or indirectly benefit the transferor.
members.legal_principle: A delegation is not an abdication merely because the government is left to enumerate the relevant relations, where the legislature has laid down a policy that makes the enumeration workable. The Court treated the relevant relations as those commonly used for benami transfers or whose benefit would indirectly benefit the transferor, and found that the rule substantially reflected that policy.
members.conclusion: The delegation was valid because the legislature had laid down a policy that guided the enumeration of the relations.

predicates.land_ceiling_delegation_challenge: The proceeding challenges a delegation within a law setting a ceiling on land and identifying surplus land.
predicates.statute_states_anti_evasion_policy: The statute states a policy of preventing transfers to relations from being used to evade the land ceiling.
predicates.delegated_enumeration_is_guided_by_that_: The government’s task is to identify relations in whose favour transfers may conceal the transferor’s land or indirectly benefit the transferor.

members.legal_issue: Delegating the choice of collection category to an administrative body is not excessive when the enactment supplies a policy and the body is subject to meaningful safeguards and control.
material_facts: The law authorized the Board to collect the duty from either rubber-estate owners or manufacturers who used rubber, in accordance with rules made by the Central Government.
The statute stated the purpose of developing the rubber industry and provided for a Board representing producing interests, manufacturers, labour, and others.
The Board’s actions were subject to Central Government control.
The rules had to be placed before both Houses of Parliament, which could modify or annul them.

The Board was responsible for collecting the duty, and the legislative materials described difficulties in collecting it from numerous estate owners and the relative ease of collecting it from manufacturers.
members.legal_principle: Essential legislative functions, including determining legislative policy, cannot be delegated, but subordinate legislation needed to implement a sufficiently clear policy may be delegated where guidance and safeguards exist. Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Cotton, Spinning and Weaving Mills was followed. The Court also referred to M.M. Ipoh v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Raghubar Dayal Jai Prakash v. Union of India in considering guided administrative choice.
members.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive, and the statutory arrangement did not amount to an abdication of legislative functions.

rule.if: excessive_delegation_challenge and enactment_states_public_policy and choice_limited_to_defined_categories and delegated_body_is_subject_to_oversight and rules_are_subject_to_legislative_review

predicates.excessive_delegation_challenge: A party challenges a law on the ground that it delegates legislative power excessively.
predicates.enactment_states_public_policy: The enactment states the public purpose that the delegated power is meant to serve.
predicates.choice_limited_to_defined_categories: The enactment confines the delegate’s choice to specified categories of persons from whom collection may be made.
predicates.delegated_body_is_subject_to_oversight: The delegate’s actions are subject to control by a government authority.
predicates.rules_are_subject_to_legislative_review: Rules made under the enactment must be presented to the legislature, which may review and change them.
predicates.delegation_is_not_excessive: The delegation is not invalid as an excessive delegation of legislative power.

members.legal_issue: Allowing the executive to extend an existing law to different geographical areas at different times does not amount to excessive delegation of essential legislative functions.
material_facts: The legislature reserved power for the government to apply an existing land-reform law to areas where it had not initially applied.
The government later applied the law to the former State's territory.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may leave to the executive the application of an enacted law to different geographical areas at different times, having regard to relevant considerations. The Court considered section 2(1) of the Abolition Act.
members.conclusion: The delegation of power to extend the law geographically was not excessive.

predicates.challenge_to_geographical_extension_powe: A constitutional challenge contends that executive authority to extend a law to additional areas delegates essential legislative functions.
predicates.legislature_enacted_law_before_executive: The legislature enacted the law and left the executive to decide when it would apply in different geographical areas.

members.legal_issue: The authority to set different conservancy-tax rates for property classes does not amount to excessive delegation when the tax is guided by total service costs and a safeguarded budget process.
material_facts: The rate-setting process was connected to the total expense of conservancy services.
The Commissioner prepared budget estimates and tax proposals; the Standing Committee considered them; and the Corporation considered and determined the rates.
The statutory process provided for review and consideration of the estimates and proposals before rates were set.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to section 129(b) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, as amended, permits different conservancy-tax rates for different property classes. The Corporation's opinion is formed through the budget procedure in sections 95, 96, 99, and 100, with the related procedure under section 150 where applicable. The total conservancy-service expense and the procedural safeguards provide adequate guidance.
members.conclusion: The authority to determine different rates for different property classes did not suffer from excessive delegation of legislative power.

rule.if: challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting and tax_rates_were_guided_by_total_service_cost and commissioner_prepared_budget_proposals and standing_committee_reviewed_estimates and municipal_council_considered_estimates

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting: A party challenged the municipality's authority to determine tax rates for different property classes as an excessive delegation of legislative power.
predicates.tax_rates_were_guided_by_total_service_c: The rate-setting authority was guided by the total expense of providing the relevant services.
predicates.commissioner_prepared_budget_proposals: The municipal commissioner prepared budget estimates and proposals concerning taxation.
predicates.standing_committee_reviewed_estimates: A standing committee considered the budget estimates and taxation proposals.
predicates.municipal_council_considered_estimates: The municipal council considered the estimates before determining the rates.

members.legal_issue: Delegating authority to set a municipal property-tax rate without prescribing a maximum rate is not excessive when the governing statutory scheme provides sufficient policy, guidance, and control.
material_facts: The statutory scheme did not prescribe a maximum rate for the relevant property tax.
The tax could be levied only for purposes authorized by the governing law, and receipts and spending were restricted to municipal purposes and budgetary controls.
The rate was determined by an elected municipal body accountable to the people, after consideration and adoption of annual budget estimates.
The legislature retained power to alter the delegation, and the scheme provided controls over municipal rules and expenditure.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that fixing a tax rate may be delegated where the statute provides policy or guidance and the delegation is controlled by the statutory scheme. It relied on the purposes-of-the-Act principle in Western India Theatres Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Poona, the delegation principles in Pandit Banarsi Das Bhanot v. Madhya Pradesh, and Corporation of Calcutta v. Liberty Cinema. It considered Devi Das v. Punjab and followed the guidance analysis in Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Mills. The court examined ss. 127 and 129, the budget and municipal-fund controls in ss. 82, 86, 88, 89, and 95–100, and the rule-making controls in ss. 454–457 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act. It also noted the legislature’s power to impose a maximum rate, which it later exercised.
members.conclusion: The absence of a statutory maximum rate did not make the delegation of taxing power excessive or arbitrary.

rule.if: municipal_tax_rate_delegation_case and tax_restricted_to_authorized_purposes and elected_taxing_body_accountable and municipal_funds_and_budgets_controlled

predicates.municipal_tax_rate_delegation_case: The proceeding challenges the delegation of authority to set a rate of municipal tax.
predicates.tax_restricted_to_authorized_purposes: The law restricts the tax to purposes authorized for the municipality.
predicates.elected_taxing_body_accountable: An elected municipal body responsible to the people sets the tax rate.
predicates.municipal_funds_and_budgets_controlled: The law subjects municipal receipts and expenditure to fund and budget controls.

members.legal_issue: The legislature may authorize the executive to adjust the powers and duties of restored administrative commissioners without unlawfully delegating or abandoning its legislative function when the authority is guided and the substantive law remains unchanged.
material_facts: The legislation restored the offices of divisional commissioners and authorized the state government to impose restrictions on, or withdraw, powers assigned to commissioners, and to confer on them powers and duties under other enactments.

The legislation and its schedule indicated the kinds of powers that could be assigned, while the commissioners’ office and prior duties pointed to revenue and executive functions of the state government and officers of equivalent rank.
The challenged changes assigned functions under the land acquisition law to a commissioner; they changed the authority administering the law, not the substantive law itself.
members.legal_principle: The legislature must lay down the essential legislative policy, but may leave administrative implementation and the assignment of executive functions to an appropriate authority where the legislation supplies guidance. The Court relied on the Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1957, including sections 3(3), 3(4), 6 and 7, and applied the principle in Harishankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, which upheld delegation where the legislature selected the classes of authorities and supplied the governing framework. It also referred to the reasoning in Shannon’s case and noted decisions of the Bombay High Court upholding the Act.
members.conclusion: The challenged provisions did not amount to excessive delegation or abdication of legislative power and were valid.

rule.if: commissioner_reorganization_proceeding and legislative_guidance_exists and powers_are_administrative and substantive_law_remains_unchanged

predicates.commissioner_reorganization_proceeding: The proceeding challenges legislation that restores administrative commissioners and provides for assigning them governmental powers or duties.
predicates.legislative_guidance_exists: The legislature indicates the kinds of powers or duties that may be assigned and the administrative purpose of the assignment.
predicates.powers_are_administrative: The powers or duties assigned are executive or revenue functions appropriate to the commissioners’ administrative office.
predicates.substantive_law_remains_unchanged: The arrangement changes which authority administers the law without changing the substantive law being administered.

members.legal_issue: Delegating the setting of a tax rate within a statutory maximum is not excessive merely because the statute sets no minimum, when it provides sufficient guidance for fixing the rate.
material_facts: The statute set a maximum rate but did not set a minimum rate.
It authorized the government to specify the rate within that maximum.
The rate for a division was guided by the expenditure required for the drainage scheme in that division.
The government specified a rate at the statutory maximum.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may prescribe a maximum rate and authorize the designated authority to levy up to that limit. The absence of a statutory minimum does not by itself invalidate a taxing statute. Here, the Act provided guidance by tying the rate in each division to the expenditure for that division’s drainage scheme. The Court referred to section 3 and the statutory schedule, and to the discussion in Cooley’s Law of Taxation on legislative limits on taxation.
members.conclusion: There was no excessive delegation of legislative power, and the absence of a minimum rate did not invalidate the taxing law.

rule.if: challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting and statute_sets_a_maximum_rate and statute_sets_no_minimum_rate and rate_is_guided_by_scheme_expenditure and administering_authority_stays_within_maximum

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting: A person challenged the legislature’s delegation of authority to set a tax rate.
predicates.statute_sets_a_maximum_rate: The law fixed an upper limit on the rate that could be imposed.
predicates.statute_sets_no_minimum_rate: The law did not fix a lower limit on the rate.
predicates.rate_is_guided_by_scheme_expenditure: The law guided the rate by reference to expenditure required for the relevant scheme.
predicates.administering_authority_stays_within_max: The authority setting the rate imposed no rate above the statutory upper limit.

members.legal_issue: Delegating decisions about the size, boundaries, and number of local administrative areas to the executive is not excessive when the legislation states its policy and supplies guidance for those decisions.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the law gave the government unguided power to create and reorganize administrative areas.

The enactment stated its democratic and administrative objectives, described the purposes and duties of local bodies, and left choices about area size, territory, and number of bodies to the government.
The Court considered those choices appropriate for executive determination in light of local wishes, political exigencies, and administrative needs.
members.legal_principle: The legislative policy and objectives may be ascertained from the preamble and other provisions, and the legislature may leave implementation details to the executive when it has sufficiently expressed its policy and supplied guidance. The Court followed State of Bhopal v. Champalal, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 35.
members.conclusion: The enactment did not confer unfettered or uncanalized power, and the delegation was valid.

predicates.challenge_to_legislative_delegation: A person challenges legislation on the ground that it delegates legislative power to the executive.
predicates.legislation_states_policy_and_objectives: The legislation states its underlying policy and the objectives the executive is to implement.
predicates.executive_choices_are_implementation_det: The executive choices concern practical details of implementation, such as the size, territory, or number of local administrative areas.

members.legal_issue: Delegating authority to prescribe tribunal members’ qualifications and service conditions is not excessive where the governing legislative policy and binding constitutional principles sufficiently guide the delegate.
material_facts: The legislation authorised the Central Government to make rules on tribunal members’ qualifications, appointments, tenure, remuneration, resignation, removal and other service conditions.
The legislation set maximum tenure and age limits and prohibited disadvantageous changes to service conditions after appointment.
The governing tribunal statutes and this Court’s prior decisions supplied principles concerning tribunal independence and the necessary qualifications and protections of members.
members.legal_principle: The legislature must retain essential legislative functions, including determining policy, but may delegate ancillary details where the legislative policy and standards provide sufficient guidance. The Court relied on In re Delhi Laws Act; B. Shama Rao v. Union Territory of Pondicherry; Ramesh Birch v. Union of India; Devi Das Gopal Krishnan v. State of Punjab; Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Birla Cotton; M.K. Papiah & Sons v. Excise Commissioner; Registrar of Cooperative Societies v. K. Kunjabmu; Keshavlal Khemchand and Son Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India; and Gwalior Rayon Silk Mfg. Co. v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales. It held that the objectives of the parent enactments and the binding principles in R.K. Jain, L. Chandra Kumar, Union of India v. R. Gandhi, Madras Bar Association and Gujarat Urja Vikas Ltd. guide the rule-maker.
members.conclusion: The delegation did not suffer from excessive delegation of legislative functions.

predicates.tribunal_service_conditions_delegated: The legislature authorises the executive to prescribe details of tribunal members’ qualifications, appointments or service conditions.
predicates.governing_policy_and_binding_principles_: The legislation and binding judicial principles provide standards that guide the executive’s exercise of the delegated authority.

members.legal_issue: The statutory delegation of power to Commissioners of Divisions to exercise specified governmental functions is constitutionally valid where the legislature has laid down the policy and left administrative reorganisation to the executive.
material_facts: A state statute authorised the government to confer statutory powers and duties on Commissioners of Divisions by notification and to make corresponding adaptations to enactments.
The land acquisition proceedings relied on powers conferred on Commissioners under that statutory arrangement.
members.legal_principle: Following Arnold Rodricks & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors., [1966] 3 S.C.R. 885, the delegation was guided by the legislature's policy of reorganising administration consequent on the establishment of Commissioners of Divisions and did not amount to abdication of legislative power.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the validity of the Commissioners of Divisions Act on grounds of excessive delegation and legislative abdication failed.

predicates.delegation_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a law that delegates statutory functions to administrative officers.
predicates.legislature_set_policy: The legislature stated the policy guiding the delegation.
predicates.executive_role_limited_to_administrative: The executive was authorised to organise administration in accordance with that legislative policy.

members.legal_issue: Delegating the identification of affected areas to the executive is not an excessive delegation when the legislation states its policy and purpose and the identification depends on facts unsuitable for legislative definition.
material_facts: The legislation stated that its purpose was to reclaim and develop land by eradicating the weed from affected areas.
The executive was empowered to identify the affected areas based on the extent and distribution of the weed.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may delegate implementation of its stated policy where it supplies adequate guidance; determining which areas meet a factual criterion that is not readily capable of legislative definition may be left to the executive. The Court considered the preamble and long title of the Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Lands (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954, and section 4(1). It relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive because the legislation supplied policy and guidance, while identifying the affected areas was an executive determination of fact.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_delegation: The proceeding challenges whether legislation has impermissibly delegated legislative power.
predicates.legislation_states_policy: The legislation states the policy and purpose that the delegated power is intended to carry out.
predicates.affected_areas_require_factual_identific: The executive must identify affected areas by assessing facts such as the intensity and distribution of a condition.

members.legal_issue: Leaving the application of a law to an administering authority is not an excessive delegation of legislative power when the legislature has stated the law’s policy and purpose.
material_facts: The enactment left the competent authority to decide, after an inquiry, whether permission to execute an eviction decree should be granted.
The enactment’s preamble and operative provisions identified the purposes of slum improvement and clearance and tenant protection.
The challenge argued that the legislature had delegated power without prescribing detailed criteria for each eviction case.
members.legal_principle: The essential legislative function is to determine legislative policy and enact it as a binding rule. When the legislature states the policy and purpose of a law, it may leave its detailed application and the determination of relevant facts to designated authorities; the law need not specify every possible case. The Court relied on the delegation principles discussed in Harishankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh and the authorities considered in its Article 14 analysis, including Ramakrishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar.
members.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive because the legislature had indicated the policy and purpose that guided the authority, and it was not required to prescribe every detail of the law’s application.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_administrative_po: A proceeding contends that the legislature improperly delegated its lawmaking power to an administrator.
predicates.legislature_has_stated_policy_and_purpos: The legislature has identified the objectives and policy that the law is intended to advance.
