predicates.authority_applies_policy_to_individual_c: The authority applies the law’s policy when deciding how it applies to particular cases.

members.legal_issue: Delegating authority to adjust legislative limits is not excessive when the legislature has settled the policy and broad principles and the delegated discretion is bounded by relevant criteria.
material_facts: The legislature itself set the ordinary limits for landholdings and economic holdings and stated the agrarian-reform policy.

The delegated authority could vary those limits only on a public-interest basis, having regard to the land’s situation, productive capacity, location in a backward area, and other prescribed factors of the same kind.
The measure did not authorize variation for an individual’s private benefit or on an unrelated consideration.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may leave matters of detail to the executive after settling policy and broad principles. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga, Dr. N.B. Khare v. State of Delhi, State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, and Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India. It also applied the principle that a law is not invalid merely because delegated discretion might be abused; the abuse, if established, may be challenged separately.
members.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive, and the provision authorizing variations was valid.

predicates.delegation_is_limited_by_relevant_criter: The delegated authority must act with regard to criteria connected to the subject and in the public interest.
predicates.residual_criteria_are_similar_in_kind: Any additional criteria are limited to factors similar in kind to the criteria expressly stated.

members.legal_issue: Intentionally inflicting a bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death constitutes murder when the elements of the applicable murder clause are established.
material_facts: The accused inflicted three sharp-edged injuries on the victim.
After the first injury caused the victim to fall, the accused inflicted two further injuries while the victim was on the ground.
The third injury cut the victim’s neck and was found sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The court inferred that the accused intended to inflict the two injuries delivered after the victim had fallen.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 299 and 300 clause thirdly IPC, culpable homicide is murder where the accused intends to inflict the bodily injury actually found and that injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Applying Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1958 SC 465, the court treats the existence and nature of the injury, the intention to inflict that injury, and its objective sufficiency to cause death as distinct matters. The intention is inferred from all the circumstances, including the location and nature of the injury, the weapon, and the force used. Death need not be inevitable: a very high probability of death is sufficient; where the probability is lower, the offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Rajwant Singh v. State of Kerala, AIR 1966 SC 1844, was also relied on.
members.conclusion: The intentional infliction of the fatal injury, which was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, brought the offence within clause thirdly of Section 300 IPC and constituted murder.

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.

predicates.injury_sufficient_in_ordinary_course_to_: The bodily injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

members.legal_issue: An accused who deliberately inflicts the fatal injury on a helpless victim is individually liable for murder even when the other participants did not share an intention to kill.
material_facts: One accused stabbed the deceased in the jaw with a spear while the deceased was lying on the ground.
The wound penetrated the skull and injured the brain, and the medical evidence identified it as the cause of death.
The stabber placed his legs on the deceased’s chest and extracted the spear blade from the wound.
The Court found the act brutal and fatal and inferred a deliberate intention to finish the deceased, rather than an accidental act.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code to the accused’s own fatal act. It inferred intention from the nature and effect of the wound and the circumstances in which it was inflicted; no earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The accused who inflicted the fatal spear wound was guilty of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, and his murder conviction was maintained.

members.legal_issue: An intentional infliction of an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death constitutes murder even if the accused did not intend to cause death.
material_facts: An accused took a sharp weapon from a watchman and struck the victim on the head three times.
The victim sustained serious head injuries, including a fractured skull, and died that evening.
The medical evidence was consistent with the eyewitness account that the accused inflicted the weapon blows.
The injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the third clause of Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code: an intentional infliction of an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death falls within murder, even where the accused did not intend to cause death. The conviction and punishment were therefore under Section 302 rather than Section 304 Part II. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The accused’s offence fell under the murder provision, rather than culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and his conviction was altered accordingly.

members.legal_issue: A single fatal blow with a deadly weapon to a vital part of the body can constitute murder when the circumstances establish that the offender knew the act was so imminently dangerous that it would in all probability cause death, and the mere fact that the blow was single does not establish a sudden fight or exclude murder.
material_facts: Four eyewitnesses, including an injured witness, consistently testified that the respondent struck the deceased on the skull with an axe.
Medical evidence established that the sharp-edged weapon caused a fractured skull and that the injury caused the deceased’s death.
A blood-stained axe was recovered at the respondent’s instance.
The deceased was unarmed when he was seized and assaulted.
The record did not support the High Court’s inference that the incident arose without premeditation in a sudden fight.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 300 Fourthly of the Penal Code, an act is murder where the offender knows it to be so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death. Whether a single blow establishes the requisite intention or knowledge depends on the circumstances, including the weapon, the part of the body struck, the force and manner of the blow, and the surrounding events; a single blow does not by itself rule out murder (Mahesh Balmiki v State of M.P.; Hukam Chand v State of Haryana; Pulicherla Nagaraju v State of A.P.; Singapagu Anjaiah v State of A.P.; Som Raj v State of H.P.). Exception 4 to Section 300 requires all of the following: absence of premeditation, a sudden fight, the act occurring in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct. A sudden fight involves mutual provocation and blows, and the exception cannot be established merely by showing absence of premeditation (Dhirajbhai Gorakhbhai Nayak v State of Gujarat).
members.conclusion: The respondent’s act fell within Section 300 Fourthly of the Penal Code and constituted murder under Section 302. Exception 4 to Section 300 did not apply; the single-blow circumstance did not justify reducing the conviction to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

members.legal_issue: A fatal injury inflicted with a sharp-edged weapon on a vital part of the body can constitute murder even when it is caused by a single blow.
material_facts: The accused inflicted one incised wound on the deceased’s neck with a sharp-edged weapon.
The wound severed major blood vessels and other structures in the neck, causing excessive bleeding and heart failure.
The medical evidence identified the neck wound as the cause of death.
The trial court found the accused guilty of murder, while the High Court reduced the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, relying in part on the fact that there was only one blow.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 300 and 302 of the Indian Penal Code, culpable homicide is murder where the offender causes a bodily injury that the offender knows is likely to cause death and the victim dies from it. The number of injuries is not decisive; the nature of the injury, the body part struck, and the weapon used are relevant to intention and knowledge. A hypothetical possibility of survival with medical care does not displace the ordinary consequences contemplated by Section 300. The Court distinguished Ramchandra Ohdar v. State of Bihar, where the medical evidence did not establish the injury’s nature, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kalu Ram, which turned on different facts. It also held that Toran Singh v. State of M.P. did not preclude intervention where findings below were contrary to the evidence.
members.conclusion: The injury and the circumstances established the intention and knowledge required for murder; the single blow did not justify reducing the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

members.legal_issue: An accused who inflicts an injury sufficient to cause death and has no right of private defence is liable for murder.
material_facts: One appellant inflicted the fatal abdominal injury on the deceased with a pointed weapon.
The injury was sufficient to cause death.
The appellant had no right of private defence because the complainant was in settled possession and the appellants were the aggressors.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, reasoning that once the right of private defence was unavailable and the injury inflicted was sufficient to cause death, the assailant could not escape conviction for murder.
members.conclusion: The conviction of the appellant who inflicted the fatal injury under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code was affirmed.

members.legal_issue: A participant who personally inflicts a fatal wound remains individually liable for that act even when the other participants are not vicariously liable for it.
material_facts: One participant personally thrust a spear into the victim’s abdomen.
The wound was fatal, and the victim died from the resulting injuries.
The assault occurred during a sudden fight without premeditation.
members.legal_principle: Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code applied to the participant’s own fatal act. The absence of an unlawful common object precluded vicarious liability for others’ acts but did not displace liability for an act personally committed. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The conviction of the participant who inflicted the fatal wound under section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code was maintained, and the Court held that the sentence was not excessive.

predicates.accused_personally_inflicted_fatal_wound: The accused personally inflicted a wound that was fatal.
predicates.fatal_wound_caused_death: The fatal wound caused the victim’s death.

members.legal_issue: An accused who intentionally inflicts the injuries actually suffered by the victim is guilty of murder when those injuries are sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, even without an intention to cause death.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses gave trustworthy accounts that the accused attacked the victim and inflicted injuries on him.
One accused struck the victim on the head, causing fractures to both parietal bones.
The medical evidence established that the head injuries were grievous and sufficient to cause death.
The trial court found that the accused had intended the injuries inflicted, although it found no intention to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Under clause thirdly of Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, murder is established where the accused intended to inflict the particular injuries actually caused and those injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; an intention to cause death is not necessary. The court relied on Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab, 1958 SCR 1985, and State of Andhra Pradesh v. Royavarasu Punnayya, and held the offence punishable under Section 302 of the Code.
members.conclusion: The court held that the accused were guilty of murder, upheld the High Court’s alteration of their convictions to murder, and dismissed their appeal.

predicates.injuries_sufficient_to_cause_death: The injuries inflicted were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A person who directly inflicts an injury sufficient to cause death may be convicted for the homicide without relying on common-intention liability.
material_facts: The medical evidence established that the deceased's chest injury was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
The evidence attributed that fatal injury to the appellant whose conviction the court considered.
The lower courts had convicted that appellant of the homicide together with another person through common-intention liability.
members.legal_principle: Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code applies where the accused's own act constitutes the murder. The court relied on the medical evidence identifying the injury sufficient to cause death and the eyewitness evidence attributing that injury to the accused; it therefore did not need to sustain that accused's conviction through Section 34.
members.conclusion: The direct assailant's conviction was altered to a conviction for murder based on his own act, and the life sentence was affirmed.

predicates.injury_sufficient_to_cause_death: The medical evidence establishes that the injury was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction may stand against the person whose responsibility for inflicting the fatal injuries is established by reliable evidence, even when shared intention with others is not proved.
material_facts: The eyewitness evidence against one accused was found reliable and compelling.
The deceased had multiple incised wounds and abrasions, all attributed to that accused.
The other accused persons were not shown to share his intention.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code to the accused whose responsibility for the fatal assault was established. It cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The court upheld the individual assailant’s murder conviction, converting it from a conviction with shared-intention liability to a conviction for murder simpliciter, and retained the life sentence.

predicates.fatal_injuries_attributed_to_that_assail: The fatal injuries were attributed to that accused.

members.legal_issue: A fatal stab wound that caused death in the ordinary course of nature supports a murder conviction where the evidence does not establish that medical treatment negligently caused the death.
material_facts: The accused stabbed the deceased in the chest with a penknife, injuring the diaphragm and pleura and extending the wound into the abdominal cavity.
The deceased experienced difficulty breathing, and the stomach and omentum herniated through the wound.
The deceased died about twelve hours later. The doctor considered the injury fatal, and the post-mortem findings supported that assessment.
The court found no evidence of negligence by the doctor in performing the operation.
members.legal_principle: Whether a particular injury is fatal is a question of fact assessed on the evidence in the case. Medical literature does not establish that diaphragm injuries cannot be fatal. The court relied on the doctor's evidence and the post-mortem findings, applied the ordinary-course-of-nature test under Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, and upheld the conviction under Section 302. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The injury was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature, the doctor's treatment did not break the causal connection, and the conviction for murder was upheld.

members.legal_issue: A person who deliberately inflicts a bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death is guilty of murder even when the attack follows a sudden quarrel.
material_facts: During a sudden dispute, the first accused went directly to the deceased and inflicted a forceful knife wound to the spinal region.
The wound penetrated the liver and was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The first accused also inflicted injuries on two witnesses; the evidence did not describe the fatal injury as being inflicted during grappling or struggle.
members.legal_principle: Under Clause III of Section 300 IPC, the intention to inflict the particular injury is inferred from the facts and circumstances, including the weapon, force, location and manner of attack. If that injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the offence is murder; a sudden quarrel does not reduce liability to knowledge alone where the accused deliberately inflicted the injury. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The first accused was guilty of murder as the direct perpetrator. His conviction under Sections 302/34 was altered to a conviction under Section 302 simpliciter, and the life sentence was confirmed.

members.legal_issue: An individual murder conviction is sustainable when the injury personally caused by the accused is medically established to be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
material_facts: The appeal challenged individual convictions for murder, without reliance on joint-liability provisions.
Two appellants were each found to have caused a specific injury to the deceased.
The doctor testified that each of those injuries, with its corresponding internal injury, was fatal by itself and sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 302 of the Penal Code, an individual murder conviction was justified where the injury caused by that accused was medically established as sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The judgment relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions and sentences of the two appellants were upheld.

members.legal_issue: An intentionally inflicted bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death can constitute murder even when the assailant inflicted only one blow.
material_facts: The accused armed himself with a dagger and pursued the victim after ill feeling had developed between them over a dispute.
The accused inflicted one severe stab wound to a vital region of the victim’s body, perforating the lung and penetrating the heart.
The autopsy doctor testified that the wound was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and the victim died from bleeding and shock following the injury.
members.legal_principle: Under clause thirdly of section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, culpable homicide is murder where the act is done with the intention of causing the bodily injury inflicted and that injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The number of blows does not by itself reduce the offence where those requirements are met. The Court followed Gudar Dusadh v. State of Bihar, AIR 1972 SC 952.
members.conclusion: The circumstances established that the accused deliberately inflicted the fatal injury, and the murder conviction was maintained notwithstanding that there was only one stab wound.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be reduced when the circumstances of the offence, including continuing excitement after a threat has ended, provide an extenuating basis for a lesser sentence.
material_facts: The accused were convicted of murder and sentenced to death.

The court held that the threat had ended before the accused fired the fatal shots, but considered the background of the incident, the threat posed by the crowd, and the excitement that may have continued in the accused's minds.
The State did not press for the death sentence.
members.legal_principle: In assessing sentence, the court considered the background of the incident, the nature and extent of the threat, and the excitement that may have persisted even after the right of private defence had ended; in the special circumstances, that excitement was an extenuating circumstance warranting a lesser sentence.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were set aside and replaced with sentences of imprisonment for life, while the murder convictions were confirmed.

predicates.threat_had_ended_before_killing: The threat had ended before the accused committed the killing.
predicates.continuing_excitement_and_incident_conte: The circumstances of the incident support finding that excitement persisted and is extenuating.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence for murder should be commuted to imprisonment for life when the mitigating circumstances, considered together, outweigh the reasons for imposing capital punishment.
material_facts: The appeal concerned death sentences imposed on two murder convicts.

The fatal violence arose amid a longstanding land-possession dispute, and the court considered it probable that the deceased had helped precipitate the tragedy by insisting on retaining or retaking land allotted to the accused.
One appellant was found to have caused only one of the three fatal injuries to a deceased person; the other injuries were attributed to other accused who received lesser sentences.
The appellants were immature youths who appeared to have acted at the instigation of an elder.
The appellants had endured prolonged mental anguish while under sentence of death.
The court considered these circumstances collectively and maintained the convictions while commuting the death sentences.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 302 of the Penal Code, as applied after the 1955 amendment to Section 367(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure removed the former requirement to give reasons for imposing the lesser penalty, the court had discretion to impose either prescribed penalty. The court stated that death was exacted only where the murder was marked by brutality, and that mitigating circumstances—including a role in provoking the tragedy, the offender’s part in the fatal assault, youth and influence by an elder, and prolonged mental agony under a death sentence—could justify life imprisonment when considered together. It relied on Vivian Rodrick v. State of West Bengal, Gurdip Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Maharashtra v. Naglya Dhavu Kongil, State of Bihar v. Pashupati Singh, Gajanand v. State of U.P., and Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh; it distinguished Brij Bhukhan, Mizaji, and Jagmohan Singh on their facts. The forthcoming 1973 Code’s requirement to give reasons for a death sentence was noted as a legislative trend, not as the basis of decision.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were commuted to imprisonment for life on each count, with the sentences to run concurrently.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be replaced with life imprisonment where substantial time has passed in the proceedings before final consideration of the sentence.
material_facts: The trial court imposed a death sentence for murder.
The High Court subsequently acquitted the accused, and the Supreme Court later restored the conviction.
The trial court's conviction and sentence and the High Court's acquittal had both occurred several years before the Supreme Court considered the sentence.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the passage of time between the trial court's sentence, the appellate acquittal, and final consideration of the case, and held that the extreme penalty was not called for in the circumstances. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not impose the death penalty and sentenced all the accused to imprisonment for life.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be commuted to life imprisonment for an accused whose age and lesser established responsibility make that punishment appropriate, even when death sentences are maintained for co-accused.
material_facts: The accused whose sentence was commuted was in his twenties and was a grand-nephew of the deceased family members.
The court could not find, for lack of legal evidence, that he was responsible for two of the five deaths.
The court generally agreed with the reasons given below for imposing the death penalty but considered a more lenient sentence appropriate for this accused.
members.legal_principle: The court applied individualized sentencing, considering the accused's age and the extent of responsibility established by legally sufficient evidence. It found those considerations justified a more lenient sentence for this accused while leaving the sentences of the other two appellants undisturbed.
members.conclusion: The death sentence for this accused was commuted to life imprisonment, while the death sentences for the other two appellants were maintained.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be reduced to imprisonment for life when the circumstances of the case make that lesser sentence sufficient to meet the ends of justice.
material_facts: The trial court imposed a death sentence for murder, and the High Court confirmed it.
The Court held that the discretion between death and imprisonment for life had been widened by the amendment to Section 367(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure made by Act 26 of 1955.
Considering the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, the Court concluded that imprisonment for life would meet the ends of justice.
members.legal_principle: After the 1955 amendment to Section 367(5) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court’s discretion in choosing between death and imprisonment for life was wider. The Court applied that discretion in light of the particular circumstances and held that imprisonment for life would meet the ends of justice. No earlier case is cited for this sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was reduced to imprisonment for life.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is unwarranted where the circumstances of the murder do not make it brutal or ghastly and life imprisonment is sufficient to meet the ends of justice.
material_facts: Two appellants were sentenced to death for murder under the rule of constructive liability rather than convicted of murder simpliciter.
The medical evidence did not establish which of the two gunshot injuries was independently sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The victim died from the cumulative effect of all the injuries, after being first assaulted with lathis and then shot from a distance.
The Court considered that the murder was not shown to have been committed in a brutal manner or to be ghastly in nature, and that life imprisonment for the group of offenders was sufficient.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that death is to be imposed when a murder is committed in a brutal manner or when the nature of the crime is ghastly. Applying that principle to the evidence and circumstances, it held that life imprisonment would meet the ends of justice. The convictions and sentences were under Sections 302/149 and 148 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were commuted to imprisonment for life; the other convictions and sentences were maintained.

members.legal_issue: A prolonged delay between a murder and the hearing of a capital appeal may justify substituting life imprisonment for death even when the murder was gruesome and cold-blooded.
material_facts: The trial court had imposed death sentences for a gruesome and cold-blooded murder.
The occurrence had taken place over a decade before the Supreme Court decided the appeal.
members.legal_principle: The headnote identifies Order XXII read with Order XLVI of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, and Article 142(1) of the Constitution as the basis relevant to altering the sentence. The court held that the long delay justified substituting life imprisonment even though the murder was gruesome and cold-blooded. No earlier cases are cited for this holding.
members.conclusion: The court retained the convictions but altered the death sentences to life imprisonment because of the long delay before the appeal was heard.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence for a premeditated multiple murder must be reduced where, after balancing the aggravating circumstances against substantial mitigating circumstances concerning the offender and the background to the crime, life imprisonment is not shown to be inadequate.
material_facts: The appeal before the Court was limited to the sentence, and the death sentence had been imposed following a murder conviction.
The offender deliberately killed multiple victims, including women and children who were asleep and had given no provocation.

The killings followed a prolonged dispute and repeated incidents of harassment and violence against the offender’s family. The offender had made repeated written requests for protection and action, but the authorities had failed to provide effective relief.
The offender was 23 years old at the time of the crime, had no previous criminal record, and was serving in a disciplined armed force.

The Court considered that the offender had felt morally justified in taking revenge, that his mental state had been affected by the continuing circumstances, and that the record gave no reason to believe he could not be reformed or would remain a continuing threat to society.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, death is an exceptional sentence reserved for the rarest of rare cases in which life imprisonment is inadequate. The court must balance the aggravating and mitigating circumstances, considering both the crime and the offender, and give mitigating circumstances a liberal and expansive construction. Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1980] 2 SCC 684, identifies relevant mitigating circumstances including youth, the probability of reform and rehabilitation, the offender’s belief that the act was morally justified, and mental defect affecting appreciation of the act’s criminality; the State must prove that the offender does not satisfy the relevant reformability condition. Shankar v. State of Tamil Nadu, [1994] 4 SCC 478, reiterates that death is appropriate only where the circumstances show that life imprisonment is inadequate and the offender is a menace to society.
members.conclusion: The crime, though gruesome and premeditated, was not one of the rarest of rare cases in which life imprisonment would be inadequate. The death sentence was replaced with imprisonment for life.

members.legal_issue: The death sentence was not warranted where the offenders' age and the possibility of their reformation and rehabilitation were mitigating circumstances, despite the grave circumstances of the murders.
material_facts: The offenders were 34 and 22 years old at the time of the murders.
The Court considered the possibility that they could be reformed and rehabilitated.
They had caused the deaths of four people, including a family and two children, in the presence of the surviving eyewitness.
The murders arose from a family property dispute.
The Court found that the totality of the circumstances did not warrant capital punishment.
members.legal_principle: Applying the capital-sentencing principles in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) 3 SCC 470, and Sangeet v. State of Haryana (2012) 11 SCALE 140, the Court treated age and the probability of reformation and rehabilitation as relevant mitigating circumstances. It also relied on Sandeep v. State of U.P. (2012) 6 SCC 107 in fixing a minimum period of imprisonment as part of the life sentence.
members.conclusion: The Court substituted life imprisonment for the death sentences and directed that the offenders serve a minimum term without remission.

members.legal_issue: Life imprisonment rather than a death sentence is appropriate when the murder does not qualify as a rarest-of-the-rare case and the offenders were misled youths.
material_facts: The accused were convicted of murder and related offences based on their participation in the killing.
The court considered them misled youths and found that the case did not warrant the maximum penalty.
members.legal_principle: The death penalty is reserved for the rarest of the rare cases; the court concluded that this case did not meet that standard and that the offenders' status as misled youths weighed against the maximum penalty.
members.conclusion: The accused were sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder, without separate sentences for the other offences.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be commuted where a substantial delay has elapsed since the offence and the accused is not responsible for that delay.
material_facts: About six years had elapsed between the occurrence and the Supreme Court’s decision.
The accused was not responsible for the lapse of time.
members.legal_principle: The court treated the passage of six years, coupled with the accused’s lack of responsibility for the delay, as grounds to commute the death sentence to life imprisonment. The judgment cites no provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment because of the delay, and the appeal was otherwise dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be replaced with a life sentence in light of prolonged exposure to the death sentence and evidence suggesting the offender may have been instigated.
material_facts: The appellant's death sentence had remained in place for more than three years and seven months while the appeal was pending.
The evidence indicated that the appellant was probably instigated, directly or indirectly, by his father.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the prolonged period during which the appellant remained under the death sentence and the indication that he was probably instigated, and held that imprisonment for life was appropriate in the circumstances. No specific statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The Court confirmed the conviction but substituted imprisonment for life for the death sentence.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence for murders committed in a family quarrel may be replaced with life imprisonment and a fine directed to compensate the surviving dependants when the circumstances do not call for the extreme penalty.
material_facts: The murders were committed during a family quarrel, and the deceased were the accused’s father and brother.
The accused had been under sentence of death for six years.
The brother’s widow and minor children had suffered loss from his death.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the circumstances did not call for the extreme penalty and considered compensation for the deceased’s dependants appropriate. Relying on Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, it stated that payment of compensation to dependants is appropriate where the accused has the capacity to pay. No statutory provision was identified as the basis for this sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the death sentence and substituted life imprisonment and a fine to be paid to the widow and children if collected; default in payment carried rigorous imprisonment.

members.legal_issue: Landowners awarded compensation for compulsorily acquired land are entitled to the applicable statutory additions and interest.
material_facts: The landowners sought enhanced compensation for land compulsorily acquired.
The Court revised the compensation assessment and expressly held that the landowners were also entitled to statutory additions and interest.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(1-A) and 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act provide for the statutory amount and solatium, respectively, and Section 28 provides for interest. The Court applied those provisions to the compensation awarded for the acquired land.
members.conclusion: The landowners were entitled to the statutory amount, solatium, and interest provided for by the Land Acquisition Act.

members.legal_issue: Claimants receiving enhanced compensation are entitled to interest, solatium, and an additional amount calculated on the market value as directed by the Court.
material_facts: The claimants obtained enhanced compensation for the acquired land.
Possession had been taken, and the notification under Section 4(1) had been published before the Collector made the award.
The Court directed interest on enhanced compensation, solatium on enhanced compensation, and an additional amount on market value, each calculated over the periods specified in its order.
members.legal_principle: The Court ordered interest and solatium on the enhanced compensation and an additional amount on market value, using the possession date, notification date, Collector's award date, and deposit date specified in its order. Section 4(1) and Section 23(1-A) are mentioned in the judgment in connection with the notification and additional amount. No earlier case was cited for these directions; the judgment does not identify a statutory provision for the interest or solatium directions.
members.conclusion: The claimants were awarded interest on enhanced compensation at 9% for the first year from possession and 15% thereafter until deposit; solatium at 30% on enhanced compensation until deposit; and an additional amount at 12% on market value from publication of the notification until the Collector's award or taking of possession, whichever was earlier.

The Court also extended the statutory benefits to the enhanced compensation.

The claimants’ acquisition proceedings were pending in 1984.
The claimants challenged the compensation awarded for their land.

members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to solatium at 30%, interest and additional compensation under the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984.

The claimants’ acquisition fell within the relevant amendment’s application, and possession of the acquired land had been taken.
The respondent accepted that the claimants were entitled to enhanced solatium and interest under the applicable amendment.

members.legal_issue: A grantee whose land is taken through statutory acquisition is entitled to compensation for the grantee’s interest, valued subject to a restriction reserved to the government in the grant.
material_facts: The government granted land subject to a condition requiring the grantees to surrender it without compensation if the government required it.
The government acquired the land through the statutory process, took possession under its urgency power, and did not invoke the grant condition to obtain the land.
The acquisition officer awarded no compensation for the land, though compensation was awarded for improvements.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government may acquire land for a public purpose and, in an urgent case, take possession so that the land vests in it. As reflected in Attorney-General v. De Keyser’s Royal Hotel Ltd., the government cannot obtain possession under statutory authority and then rely on a different source of power to avoid the consequences of that statutory process. But the restriction in the grant remains relevant to valuation: compensation is the market value, at the date of notification, of the interest actually held by the grantee, subject to that restriction.
members.conclusion: After taking possession under statutory authority, the government could not resort to the grant condition to avoid compensation. The grantees were entitled to compensation for their interest, measured by the market value of that interest subject to the government’s reserved right.

members.legal_issue: A separate application for condonation of delay is not indispensable when the application to set aside an ex parte decree itself explains the delay and the court considers that explanation on the evidence.
material_facts: The defendants relied on an out-of-court compromise under which they understood that the plaintiff would withdraw or get the suit dismissed, and they therefore did not attend later proceedings.
They said they learned of the ex parte decree only when execution proceedings began and included that explanation in their application to set it aside.
The trial court considered the application on its merits and received evidence about the compromise and the defendants’ lack of knowledge; the appellate court found their explanation justified.
members.legal_principle: Under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act, an application’s substance may supply the explanation for delay; a separate application is not required where the court has considered that explanation. Procedure is the handmaid of justice. The Court distinguished Sneh Gupta v. Devi Sarup, where the applicant knew of the decree but had not sought condonation of delay.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating the absence of a separate application for condonation of delay as fatal. The application to set aside the decree contained the necessary explanation and could be considered on its merits.

predicates.delay_explanation_in_application: The application itself explained why it was not filed earlier.
predicates.court_considered_delay_evidence: The court considered evidence bearing on the explanation for the delay.

members.legal_issue: For an application to set aside an ex parte decree, limitation runs from the applicant’s knowledge of the decree when the applicant had no notice of the decree or proceedings, and delay may in any event be excused by a satisfactory explanation.
material_facts: The defendants did not know of the proceedings or decree because they believed, based on the compromise, that the plaintiff would discontinue the suit.
The order-sheet entries relied on to suggest their presence lacked their signatures, and the appellate court found they had not attended and did not know of the proceedings.

They learned of the decree through an execution notice and filed their application within thirty days of that knowledge; the courts had also considered evidence supporting their explanation for not applying sooner.
members.legal_principle: Article 123 of the Limitation Act provides for the limitation period for setting aside an ex parte decree and, where summons have not been served, reckons time from knowledge of the decree. The Court applied that principle to the absence of notice and the later discovery of the decree. It distinguished Sneh Gupta v. Devi Sarup, where the applicant knew of the decree, and held that the supported explanation would also justify the delay if time were counted from the decree’s date.
members.conclusion: The application was within time when limitation was reckoned from the defendants’ knowledge of the decree. Even if limitation were reckoned from the decree’s date, the delay was satisfactorily explained.
