predicates.no_notice_of_proceedings_or_decree: The party had no notice of the proceedings or the decree before learning of it later.
predicates.knowledge_of_decree_acquired_later: The party learned of the decree after it had been entered.
predicates.application_filed_within_applicable_peri: The party filed the application within the applicable limitation period after learning of the decree.

members.legal_issue: When summons was not duly served, the limitation period for an application to set aside an ex parte decree runs from the applicant’s knowledge of the decree.
material_facts: The applicant applied to set aside the ex parte decree after learning of it from a relative in the first week of November 1975.
The application was filed on December 2, 1975.
The suit record showed no direction for issuing summons to the applicant, and the process server’s return and testimony were found unreliable.
The applicant’s account that he had not been served and had learned of the decree only shortly before applying was not rebutted by testimony from the opposing parties.
members.legal_principle: Article 123 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides a thirty-day period to apply to set aside an ex parte decree, running from the decree when summons was duly served and from knowledge of the decree when summons was not duly served. Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for setting aside an ex parte decree in the relevant circumstances. Order V Rules 19 and 19A and the pre-amendment Order IX Rule 6(1) govern inquiry into service and proceeding ex parte. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The application was not barred by limitation, and the order setting aside the ex parte decree was confirmed as against the applicant.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_ex_parte_decree: A party applies to set aside a decree made in that party’s absence.
predicates.summons_not_duly_served: The party was not duly served with summons in the proceeding that resulted in the decree.
predicates.filed_within_limitation_from_knowledge: The application was filed within the applicable limitation period measured from the party’s knowledge of the decree.

members.legal_issue: A finding that sufficient cause existed to set aside an ex parte decree and condone delay may be upheld when it is a well-reasoned finding of fact.
material_facts: The purchaser said that the ex parte decree was not known to the purchaser, explaining the delay in applying.
The trial court condoned the delay and found sufficient cause to set aside the decree.
The Supreme Court considered that finding factual and well reasoned.
members.legal_principle: Order 9 Rule 13 CPC requires sufficient cause for setting aside an ex parte decree, and Section 5 of the Limitation Act governs condonation of delay. The Court treated whether sufficient cause existed on these facts as a factual determination and found the trial court’s reasoned finding sustainable.
members.conclusion: The finding in favour of the purchaser on sufficient cause and condonation of delay was upheld.

predicates.ex_parte_set_aside_application: A person applies to set aside an ex parte decree after time has passed.
predicates.applicant_unaware_of_decree: The applicant did not know that the ex parte decree had been entered.
predicates.lower_court_found_sufficient_cause: The lower court found sufficient cause for setting aside the decree and excusing the delay.

members.legal_issue: Delay in applying to set aside an ex parte decree should be condoned when the applicant satisfactorily explains it and the circumstances do not establish negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides.
material_facts: The applicants sought condonation of delays of 355 and 382 days in filing their applications to set aside ex parte decrees.
They stated that they learned of the decrees when they saw a public notice concerning attachment of the property.
The Supreme Court found that the applicants had satisfactorily explained the reasons for the delay.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act requires sufficient cause for condonation of delay. The expression ‘sufficient cause’ is to be construed liberally to advance substantial justice where negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides is not attributable to the applicant; the discretion must be exercised judicially, with vigilance and circumspection, and the applicant’s due diligence is the relevant test.
members.conclusion: The delay in filing the applications to set aside the ex parte decrees was condoned.

predicates.ex_parte_set_aside_proceeding: A defendant applied to set aside an ex parte decree and sought condonation of delay in making the application.
predicates.delay_satisfactorily_explained: The defendant satisfactorily explained the reasons for the delay in applying to set aside the decree.
predicates.applicant_negligent_or_inactive_or_not_b: The defendant was negligent or inactive, or acted without bona fides, in pursuing the application.

members.legal_issue: Knowledge that a suit is pending does not by itself prevent setting aside an ex parte decree when the defendant lacked notice of the hearing date and sufficient time to appear.
material_facts: The defendant had acknowledged in another proceeding that he knew the suit was pending.
The defendant's unchallenged testimony did not establish that he knew the date of hearing and had sufficient time to appear and answer the claim.
The court found that the summons had not been served.
members.legal_principle: The second proviso to Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure prevents setting aside a decree merely for an irregularity in service only where the defendant had notice of the date of hearing and sufficient time to appear and answer the claim. Knowledge of the pendency of the suit is not the required notice, and the proviso does not address non-service. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: Knowledge of the suit's pendency did not bar setting aside the decree; the second proviso to Order 9 Rule 13 did not apply to the established non-service.

rule.if: challenge_to_ex_parte_decree and suit_pendency_known and not hearing_date_and_time_notice and summons_not_served

predicates.challenge_to_ex_parte_decree: A defendant seeks to set aside a decree entered after the defendant did not appear.
predicates.suit_pendency_known: The defendant knew that the suit was pending.
predicates.hearing_date_and_time_notice: The defendant had notice of the hearing date and sufficient time to appear and answer the claim.
predicates.summons_not_served: The summons was not duly served on the defendant.

members.legal_issue: Time spent pursuing a remedy to set aside an ex parte decree may constitute sufficient cause to condone delay in a subsequent appeal against the decree when the remedies were pursued consecutively in good faith and without dilatory conduct or gross negligence.
material_facts: A partition suit resulted in an ex parte preliminary decree.
The defendants first applied to set aside the decree; that application was dismissed on its merits, and they appealed against the dismissal.
After that appeal had remained pending for about three years, they withdrew it and filed an appeal against the ex parte decree the following day, seeking condonation of delay.
The courts found no gross negligence in pursuing the matter, and the defendants would otherwise lose the opportunity to challenge the preliminary decree on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits a liberal construction of “sufficient cause” to advance substantial justice where inaction, negligence, or lack of bona fides is not attributable to the litigant. The right of appeal under Section 96(2) CPC is statutory, and Section 97 CPC makes an appeal against a preliminary decree important because its correctness may not later be disputed in an appeal from the final decree. Order IX Rule 13 and Section 96(2) provide distinct remedies; consecutive pursuit is not automatically barred, although delay may be refused where the litigant used dilatory tactics or lacked bona fides. The Court relied on B. Madhuri Goud v. B. Damodar Reddy and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy on sufficient cause and limitation, and Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar on the statutory appeal right.
members.conclusion: The time spent pursuing the set-aside remedy constituted sufficient cause on these facts. The delay in filing the appeal against the ex parte decree was condoned, and the appeal was restored.

rule.if: appeal_against_ex_parte_decree and prior_set_aside_proceeding and prior_proceeding_caused_delay and bona_fide_pursuit and no_dilatory_tactics and no_gross_negligence

predicates.appeal_against_ex_parte_decree: The litigant filed an appeal challenging a decree entered in the litigant’s absence.
predicates.prior_set_aside_proceeding: The litigant first pursued a proceeding seeking to set aside that decree.
predicates.prior_proceeding_caused_delay: The time spent pursuing the earlier proceeding contributed to the delay in filing the appeal against the decree.
predicates.bona_fide_pursuit: The litigant pursued the available remedies in good faith.
predicates.no_dilatory_tactics: The litigant did not use the proceedings to delay the opposing party’s case.
predicates.no_gross_negligence: The litigant was not grossly negligent in pursuing the matter.
predicates.delay_condoned: The delay in filing the appeal is excused.

members.legal_issue: An ex parte appellate judgment must be set aside and the appeal reheard when the absent respondent had sufficient cause for not appearing.
material_facts: The appellant was the principal respondent in a second appeal before the High Court.
The second appeal was allowed ex parte when the appellant did not appear at the hearing.
The appellant said he had not been served with notice of the second appeal, and the Supreme Court found that he had sufficient cause for not appearing.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that an ex parte appellate judgment should be set aside and the appeal remitted when the absent party had sufficient cause for nonappearance. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The ex parte judgment was set aside and the second appeal was remanded to the High Court for disposal according to law.

predicates.appeal_challenges_ex_parte_appellate_jud: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an appellate judgment made ex parte against a respondent.
predicates.respondent_had_sufficient_cause_for_abse: The respondent had sufficient cause for not appearing at the hearing.

members.legal_issue: A first appeal dismissed without a hearing on the merits should be restored when the application establishes sufficient cause for nonappearance, with terms available to address prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellant’s first appeal from a decree was dismissed in default because its counsel did not appear when the appeal was called for hearing.
The appellant applied for recall of the dismissal order and restoration of the appeal.
The Supreme Court found that the restoration application established sufficient cause under Order 41 Rule 19.
The dismissal was in default, not on the merits, and the appeal was a valuable right to be heard on its merits.
The Court conditioned restoration on payment of costs to the respondent.
members.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits readmission of an appeal dismissed for default where sufficient cause prevented the appellant from appearing. As explained in Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah, AIR 1955 SC 425, procedural rules should be applied to facilitate justice and consistently with natural justice, rather than used to deprive a litigant of participation when a fair remedy, such as costs, can address prejudice to the other side.
members.conclusion: The restoration application was allowed and the first appeal was restored for hearing on the merits, subject to payment of costs to the respondent.

predicates.first_appeal_dismissed_without_merits: A party’s first appeal was dismissed without the court hearing or deciding its merits.
predicates.appellant_failed_to_appear: The appellant or its representative did not appear when the first appeal was called for hearing.
predicates.restoration_application_shows_sufficient: The appellant’s application establishes a sufficient reason for the failure to appear.
predicates.appeal_restored_on_just_terms: The dismissed appeal is restored for a hearing on its merits, subject to appropriate terms addressing prejudice to the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: An ex-parte decree should be set aside when the defendant establishes a genuine and sufficient reason for absence on the hearing date and applies promptly, even if earlier negligence is alleged.
material_facts: A suit for rent, eviction and damages was decreed ex parte after neither the defendant nor his lawyer appeared on the hearing date.
The defendant said that illness while he was away for work prevented him from returning to court, and that his lawyer could not attend because the lawyer’s nephew died in an accident that day.
The defendant supported his application with an affidavit and medical certificate and applied within the statutory period.
The defendant had raised a substantive defence to the suit.
The lower courts rejected the application, including because the medical certificate was from a private doctor and because of the defendant’s previous conduct.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an ex-parte decree may be set aside if summons were not duly served or if sufficient cause prevented the defendant from appearing when the suit was called for hearing. Sufficient cause is an elastic expression to be construed liberally in light of the circumstances of each case, particularly where the absence was not negligent or intentional. The relevant cause concerns the date on which the ex-parte proceedings began; prior negligence that was overlooked or condoned does not defeat an application if sufficient cause for absence on that date is shown. A prompt application and absence that was not mala fide or intentional normally support exercising discretion in the defendant’s favour, and the other party may be compensated by costs. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The absence was supported by sufficient cause, and the application should have been allowed. The ex-parte decree and the lower courts’ orders were set aside on payment of costs, with the defendant given an opportunity to prove his case.

rule.if: ex_parte_decree_challenge and (defendant_absence_due_to_illness_or_work_emergency or counsel_absence_due_to_family_emergency) and prompt_application and absence_not_intentional

predicates.ex_parte_decree_challenge: The proceeding challenges a decree made after the defendant did not appear when the suit was called for hearing.
predicates.defendant_absence_due_to_illness_or_work: The defendant was unable to attend because illness or a work-related emergency prevented attendance.
predicates.counsel_absence_due_to_family_emergency: The defendant’s lawyer was unable to attend because of a family emergency.
predicates.prompt_application: The defendant applied to set aside the decree within the applicable statutory period.
predicates.absence_not_intentional: The defendant’s absence was not deliberate or mala fide.

members.legal_issue: A delay in applying to set aside an ex parte decree may be condoned when the explanation is acceptable and the circumstances support advancing substantial justice.
material_facts: The application to set aside the ex parte decree was filed 554 days late.

The appellant said he did not learn of the decree until receiving notice of execution proceedings and that the person who had appeared for the company had left after his son died, without informing him of later proceedings.
The Court considered the appellant insufficiently vigilant but not so irresponsible that he should be excluded from litigation over valuable property.
The inconvenience to the respondent from the delay could be compensated by exemplary costs.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, the court has discretion to admit an application after the prescribed period where sufficient cause is shown; that discretion should be exercised to advance substantial justice. The explanation’s acceptability, rather than the length of delay, is the principal criterion, and delay should generally be condoned absent gross negligence, deliberate inaction, or lack of bona fides. The Court relied on Ramlal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd., The State of West Bengal v. The Administrator, Howrah Municipality, G. Ramegowda v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy.
members.conclusion: The delay was condoned, subject to payment of exemplary costs to the respondent.

rule.if: application_to_set_aside_ex_parte_decree and delay_in_filing and (acceptable_explanation or valuable_property_stake) and not deliberate_or_grossly_negligent_delay and delay_prejudice_compensable_by_costs

predicates.application_to_set_aside_ex_parte_decree: The defendant applied to set aside a decree entered when the defendant did not appear at the hearing.
predicates.delay_in_filing: The defendant filed that application after the applicable filing period had expired.
predicates.acceptable_explanation: The defendant gave an explanation for not filing the application within the prescribed period that the court found acceptable.
predicates.valuable_property_stake: The litigation concerned property the court regarded as valuable and involving a significant stake for the parties.
predicates.deliberate_or_grossly_negligent_delay: The party’s delay resulted from deliberate inaction, gross negligence, or lack of bona fides.
predicates.delay_prejudice_compensable_by_costs: The inconvenience caused to the opposing party by the delay could be compensated by an award of costs.
predicates.delay_condoned_subject_to_costs: The court admits the late application on the condition that the applicant pay costs.

members.legal_issue: An ex parte decree should be set aside when sufficient cause prevented the defendant from appearing when the suit was heard.
material_facts: The appellant said he was unaware of the decree until he received notice of execution proceedings.
The person who had appeared for the company had left after his son died, and the appellant said nobody informed him of the later proceedings.
The appellant applied to set aside the decree after learning of it.
The Court examined the application on its merits and found sufficient grounds to set aside the decree.
members.legal_principle: The governing sufficient-cause standard for setting aside an ex parte decree is that the defendant must satisfy the court that sufficient cause prevented appearance when the suit was called for hearing. The Court applied that standard and found sufficient grounds on the facts presented.
members.conclusion: The application to set aside the ex parte decree was allowed, subject to payment of exemplary costs; otherwise the appeal would be deemed dismissed and the decree revived.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_ex_parte_decree: The defendant applied to set aside a decree entered when the defendant did not appear at the hearing.
predicates.defendant_prevented_from_appearing_by_su: Circumstances the court accepts as sufficient prevented the defendant from appearing when the suit was heard.
predicates.ex_parte_decree_set_aside: The court sets aside the decree entered in the defendant’s absence.

members.legal_issue: Delay in seeking to set aside an ex parte divorce decree may be condoned, and the decree set aside, where substituted service was used without proper resort to ordinary service and the respondent lacked knowledge of the proceedings.
material_facts: The respondent was an illiterate woman living in a different town from the court where the divorce proceeding was filed.
Notice of the divorce proceeding was served by newspaper publication as substituted service.
The record did not show proper attempts to serve her by ordinary means before resorting to substituted service.
The court found that she had not known about the proceeding or decree earlier and that sufficient cause existed for the delay in applying to set aside the decree.
members.legal_principle: Under Order V Rules 12, 15 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, ordinary service is to be attempted as applicable; Order V Rule 20 permits substituted service only as a last resort when ordinary service cannot be effected and the court is satisfied that the defendant is avoiding service or that another reason prevents ordinary service. Order IX Rule 13 permits an ex parte decree to be set aside on the requisite grounds, and sufficient cause may justify condoning delay. The Court also considered the appealability of the rejection under Order XLIII Rule 1(d) and the appealability of a divorce decree under Section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to condone the delay and set aside the ex parte decree, and its decision warranted no interference.

rule.if: ex_parte_divorce_challenge and substituted_service_without_ordinary_attempts and respondent_unaware_of_proceeding and sufficient_cause_for_delay

predicates.ex_parte_divorce_challenge: A respondent seeks to set aside an ex parte decree dissolving a marriage.
predicates.substituted_service_without_ordinary_att: The court used substituted service without first making proper efforts to serve the respondent by ordinary means.
predicates.respondent_unaware_of_proceeding: The respondent did not know of the proceeding when it was heard and the decree was made.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay: The circumstances explain the respondent's delay in applying to set aside the decree.

members.legal_issue: The general application of limitation-law provisions through the special-law saving provision does not extend to appeals or applications filed before statutory authorities that are not courts.
material_facts: The special enactment prescribed a period for filing an appeal before the commissioner, a statutory authority rather than a court.
The appellant argued that the general saving provision in the Limitation Act could not make Section 5 applicable to an appeal before that authority.
The Court considered authorities addressing whether the Limitation Act applies to proceedings before courts or non-court tribunals.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that suits, appeals and applications referred to in the Limitation Act and its Schedule are proceedings to be filed in court. Section 29(2) therefore applies where a special or local law prescribes a different limitation period for a suit, appeal or application in court, not one before a statutory authority or tribunal. The Court relied on Nityananda M. Joshi v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Town Municipal Council, Athani v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Sakuru v. Tanaji, Officer on Special Duty (Land Acquisition) v. Shah Manilal Chandulal, Consolidated Engineering Enterprises v. Principal Secretary, Irrigation Department, and M.P. Steel Corporation v. Commissioner of Central Excise. It followed Parson Tools and Plants over the contrary treatment of Section 12(2) in Commissioner of Sales Tax, U.P. v. Madan Lal Das & Sons, which had not considered the earlier equal-strength decision. Mukri Gopalan v. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker was treated as no longer good law to the extent it conflicted with the later binding decisions. The Court distinguished State of Madhya Pradesh v. Anshuman Shukla because the revision there was before the High Court, a court.
members.conclusion: The special-law saving provision did not apply to the statutory appeal before the commissioner, and could not make Section 5 applicable to it.

predicates.special_law_proceeding: A person pursued a suit, appeal, or application created or regulated by a special or local enactment.
predicates.special_law_prescribes_a_limitation_peri: The special or local enactment sets a limitation period for the proceeding.
predicates.filing_forum_is_statutory_authority_not_: The proceeding is filed before a statutory authority or tribunal that is not a court.

members.legal_issue: A statutory commissioner cannot condone a late appeal by applying the general power to extend time in the Limitation Act where that Act does not apply to the proceeding.
material_facts: A respondent filed a statutory appeal before the commissioner after the prescribed filing period had expired.
The respondent sought condonation of a 266-day delay, attributing it to illness that prevented travel to instruct counsel.
The commissioner condoned the delay, and the appellant challenged that order.
The appeal was before a statutory authority that the Court held was not a court.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 allows a court to admit a late appeal or application on sufficient cause, but it does not, by itself, apply to proceedings before non-court statutory authorities. Section 29(2) does not extend Section 5 to such proceedings. The Court relied on Nityananda M. Joshi, Athani, Parson Tools and Plants, Sakuru, Shah Manilal Chandulal, Consolidated Engineering Enterprises and M.P. Steel Corporation, and held that Mukri Gopalan did not govern in light of the later binding decisions.
members.conclusion: The commissioner was not entitled to condone the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act; the order condoning delay was set aside and the delayed appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_proceeding and appeal_is_late and appeal_forum_is_not_a_court and no_special_law_authorizes_extension

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: A party filed an appeal provided by a special or local enactment before the authority designated by that enactment.
predicates.appeal_is_late: The party filed the appeal after the filing period prescribed for it had expired.
predicates.appeal_forum_is_not_a_court: The authority hearing the appeal is not a court.
predicates.no_special_law_authorizes_extension: The governing enactment does not separately authorize the appeal-hearing authority to extend the filing period on sufficient cause.

members.legal_issue: An appellate authority that is not a court cannot condone delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act when the governing special enactment adopts limitation rules only for computing the filing period and gives no express power to extend it.
material_facts: A landholder filed an appeal to the Collector long after the order under appeal and sought condonation under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The Collector condoned the delay and allowed the appeal; the High Court, on revision, set that order aside.
At the relevant time, section 93 of the special enactment applied limitation provisions only for computation of the filing period.
members.legal_principle: The Limitation Act, 1963 applies to proceedings in courts, not ordinarily to proceedings before quasi-judicial tribunals or executive authorities. A special enactment may expressly make section 5 applicable to such proceedings. Section 93, as it then stood, adopted only provisions concerning computation of limitation, found in sections 12 to 24 of the Limitation Act; section 5 concerns extension after computation shows that a filing is late. The Court approved K. Venkaiah v. K. Venkateswara Rao and relied on Town Municipal Council, Athani v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Hubli; Nityananda M. Joshi v. Life Insurance Corporation of India; and Sushila Devi v. Ramanandan Prasad.
members.conclusion: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 did not apply to the appeal before the Collector, and the Collector had no jurisdiction to condone the delay under that section.

predicates.special_enactment_appeal_before_non_cour: The proceeding is an appeal under a special enactment before an authority that is not a court.
predicates.limitation_rules_adopted_only_for_comput: The special enactment adopts limitation rules only for computing the filing period.
predicates.no_express_power_to_extend_delay: The governing enactment contains no express provision empowering the authority to extend the filing period upon sufficient cause.

members.legal_issue: The Land Acquisition Collector cannot extend the time for an application seeking a reference, even when the applicant gives a genuine reason for delay.
material_facts: The Collector rejected the landowners’ applications as late.
The High Court later considered that they could have sought condonation of delay from the Collector.
members.legal_principle: In Officer on Special Duty (Land Acquisition) v. Shah Manilal Chandulal, the Court held that section 29(2) of the Limitation Act does not make sections 4 to 24 of that Act available for applications under section 18, and that section 5 cannot be invoked because the Collector is not a court. Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. S.U.T.N.I. Sangam reiterated that conclusion. The Land Acquisition Act provides no power for the Collector to extend the prescribed time, even for genuine and bona fide grounds.
members.conclusion: The Collector had no power to condone the delay or extend the time for seeking a reference.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_proceeding: A person applied to the Collector to refer a land-acquisition compensation claim to a court.
predicates.application_outside_prescribed_time: The application was made after the time allowed for seeking the reference had expired.

members.legal_issue: Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not permit condonation of delay in an application to enforce a statutory right of pre-emption when the special law prescribes a filing period but provides no extension mechanism for that application.
material_facts: In both appeals, applicants sought pre-emption under a land-reform statute as adjoining or contiguous landowners.
The statute prescribed a specific period for making a pre-emption application, but did not provide for extending that period or applying the principles of Section 5 to such applications.
The same statute expressly provided for extension or application of Section 5 in relation to certain appeals and revisions, but contained no corresponding provision for pre-emption applications.
The applications were filed years after the transfers, beyond the applicable statutory period; one applicant relied on lack of knowledge of the transfer and sought condonation.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3, 5 and 29(2) of the Limitation Act, Section 5 may apply to a period prescribed by special or local law unless its application is expressly excluded. Applying Hukumdev Narain Yadav v. Lalit Narain Mishra and Anwari Basavaraj Patil v. Siddaramaiah, exclusion may be gathered from the scheme and nature of the special law, even without express words. The court relied also on Commissioner of Sales Tax v. Parson Tools and Plants and approved Serish Maji v. Nishit Kumar Dolui. It treated an application under Section 8 of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act as in the nature of a suit for limitation purposes, noting the references to pre-emption suits in Section 8 and Article 97 of the Limitation Act; Article 137 therefore did not govern. The express provision for applying Section 5 to other proceedings under the special law, coupled with its omission for pre-emption applications and the statute's specific filing period, showed exclusion. The court distinguished Mangu Ram v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi and Mukri Gopalan v. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker, and referred to Mattoo Devi v. Damodar Lal for the weak nature of the pre-emption right and the need to exercise it strictly.
members.conclusion: Section 5 of the Limitation Act is unavailable to condone delay in an application under the special law for pre-emption. The specific period prescribed by that law governs, and a late application must be dismissed; Article 137 does not supply a different period.

predicates.preemption_application_under_self_contai: A person applied under a special law to enforce a statutory right of pre-emption.
predicates.special_law_sets_filing_period: The special law prescribed a period for making the pre-emption application.
predicates.special_law_allows_extension_for_other_p: The special law provided for extending time or applying sufficient-cause principles to some other proceedings, but made no such provision for pre-emption applications.
predicates.application_filed_after_filing_period: The pre-emption application was made after the filing period prescribed by the special law had expired.

members.legal_issue: The statutory officer receiving a land-acquisition reference application cannot use the general power to excuse delay to extend the application deadline, even where a local amendment gives orders on such applications a limited route of judicial revision.
material_facts: The applicants were present when the land acquisition officer announced the award.
They applied for a reference after the applicable six-week period had expired.
The officer rejected the applications as time-barred.
The High Court treated the officer as a court for this purpose under a local amendment and condoned the delay, relying on the applicants’ efforts to obtain a copy of the award and consult counsel.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 18(1) and the proviso to Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, a timely written application is a condition for a valid reference; where the applicant was present or represented when the award was made, the application must be made within six weeks. The Collector acts as a statutory authority, distinct from the court defined in Section 3(d), and a local provision treating the Collector as a subordinate court for the limited purpose of revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not make the Collector a court for Section 5 of the Limitation Act. Section 5 applies to a court, while Section 29(2) does not supply an extension power in this setting. The Court relied on Mohd. Hasnuddin v. State of Maharashtra, which treated compliance with Section 18’s conditions, including limitation, as necessary for a valid reference; State of Punjab v. Satinder Bir Singh, which applied the statutory reference deadline; Nityananda, M. Joshi v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Smt. Sushila Devi v. Ramanandan Prasad, and Mohd. Ashfaq v. State Transport Appellate Tribunal, concerning the limits of Section 5 when the decision-maker is not a court; and P.V. Gadgil v. P.Y. Deshpande, which rejected the same argument about the Collector’s status.
members.conclusion: The officer was not a court for the purpose of extending the deadline, and the applications were barred by limitation. The officer had no power to extend the time for making them, so the High Court’s orders were set aside.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_request and applicant_present_at_award and request_after_applicable_deadline and collector_acting_as_statutory_referrer

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_request: A person seeks a court’s determination of an objection to a land acquisition award by applying to the officer who received the objection.
predicates.applicant_present_at_award: The applicant was present or represented when the officer announced the award.
predicates.request_after_applicable_deadline: The applicant made the reference request after the deadline applicable to that applicant had expired.
predicates.collector_acting_as_statutory_referrer: The officer was performing the statutory function of deciding whether to refer the dispute to a court.

members.legal_issue: A Rent Controller acting as a statutory authority and persona designata cannot condone delay in an application for leave to contest a special eviction petition when the governing statute gives no power to extend the filing period.
material_facts: A landlord sought eviction under the special procedure for a non-resident Indian owner, and the tenant was summoned to apply for leave to contest within the prescribed 15-day period.
The tenant filed the leave application one day after that period expired and sought condonation of the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
The Rent Controller was appointed by the State Government, was a member of the State civil service, and had no statutory authority to extend the time for filing the leave application.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 13-B and 18-A(2) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, a tenant must apply for leave to contest within the period specified in the summons. The Act gives the Rent Controller no power to extend that period. Because the Rent Controller is a statutory authority and persona designata, rather than a court, Section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot confer that power; Section 29(2) does not make it available in these circumstances. The special procedure is a complete code to the extent stated in Prithipal Singh v. Satpal Singh. Mukri Gopalan v. Cheppilat Puthanpurajil Aboobacker was distinguishable because the appellate authority there was a court. Prakash H. Jain v. Marie Fernandes supports the conclusion that a statutory authority lacking power to condone delay must act within its statutory powers. Gaya Prasad Kar v. Subrata Kumar Banerjee did not assist the tenant insofar as the statute considered there specifically empowered the Rent Controller to extend time for rent deposits.
members.conclusion: The Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to condone the delay, and rejection of the late leave application was not an error of law.

rule.if: special_eviction_leave_proceeding and leave_application_filed_after_deadline and decision_maker_is_persona_designata and governing_law_grants_no_power_to_extend_deadline

predicates.special_eviction_leave_proceeding: The matter is a special eviction proceeding in which a tenant must obtain leave to contest.
predicates.leave_application_filed_after_deadline: The tenant filed the application for leave to contest after the period specified for filing it had expired.
predicates.decision_maker_is_persona_designata: The decision-maker is a statutory authority acting as a designated person rather than as a court.
predicates.governing_law_grants_no_power_to_extend_: The law governing the proceeding does not empower the decision-maker to extend the filing deadline.

members.legal_issue: A late initial application seeking a reference cannot be extended by applying the general statutory power to condone delay in proceedings before the land-acquisition authority.
material_facts: Some claimants made their initial applications for references after the period prescribed for seeking them had expired.
The State argued that Section 5 of the Limitation Act did not apply to those applications.
The Court held that an initial application for a reference must be made within the time fixed by the Karnataka amendment.
members.legal_principle: Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act as amended in Karnataka requires the initial application to be made within the prescribed 90-day period. Shah Manilal holds that Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply to proceedings before the land-acquisition authority; the application must therefore comply with the statutory time limit.
members.conclusion: Section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot be used to extend the time for an initial application seeking a reference before the land-acquisition authority.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim for compensation for acquired land and a request for a reference for determination of that claim.
predicates.initial_reference_request_filed_after_st: The claimant submitted the initial request for a reference after the applicable statutory filing period had expired.

members.legal_issue: A court or acquisition officer dealing with a reference application has no power to condone delay in filing it.
material_facts: The reference application was filed outside the applicable six-week period after the claimant received notice of the award.
The State challenged the reference as late, and the absence of a power to condone delay was not disputed before the Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the limitation requirements in Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act and noted that neither the acquisition officer making a reference nor the court considering one has power to condone delay in making the application. This absence of power was not disputed before the Court.
members.conclusion: The delay in making the reference application could not be condoned by the acquisition officer or the court considering the reference.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_proceeding: A person sought a court reference concerning compensation in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.reference_application_filed_after_applic: The person filed the reference application after the applicable time limit had expired.

members.legal_issue: The general limitation statute’s extension provisions do not apply to a compensation-redetermination application made to the Land Acquisition Collector under the statutory scheme.
material_facts: The application was made to the Land Acquisition Collector for redetermination based on a court award.
The Collector acts as a quasi-judicial authority, and the governing scheme specifies the period for making the application.
members.legal_principle: Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 prescribes the filing period for an application to the Collector. Union of India v. Mangatu Ram and Tota Ram v. State of U.P. hold that the Collector is not a court but a quasi-judicial authority and that the Limitation Act, 1963 does not apply to such an application.
members.conclusion: The Limitation Act, 1963, including its provision for extending time, did not apply; the application had to comply with the period prescribed by the governing land-acquisition provision.

predicates.application_is_made_to_quasi_judicial_co: A person makes the relevant application to an authority that acts in a quasi-judicial capacity rather than as a court.
predicates.governing_scheme_prescribes_filing_perio: The governing statutory scheme specifies a period within which the application must be made.

members.legal_issue: A statutory authority operating under a special summary eviction procedure cannot condone delay in filing the affidavit seeking leave to defend when the procedure fixes a filing deadline and grants no power to extend it.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought under a special summary procedure for recovery of possession from a tenant or licensee.
The summons was served, but the occupant did not file an affidavit seeking leave to defend within the prescribed period; an earlier application to summon a document did not seek leave to defend.
The Competent Authority condoned the delay and later granted leave to defend.
The special procedure prescribed the steps and consequences for seeking leave, and did not confer power on the Competent Authority to extend the filing period.
members.legal_principle: The special procedure in Chapter VIII of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, particularly Sections 39 and 43(4), governs the Competent Authority and overrides inconsistent provisions of other laws. The Authority is a statutory, quasi-judicial authority whose powers are confined to those conferred by the statute; deeming it a civil court for limited purposes does not make it a court for all purposes or attract the Limitation Act, 1963. A statutory authority has no inherent power to condone delay. The Court distinguished the treatment of courts in Mukri Gopalan v. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker and P. Sarathy v. State Bank of India, and considered Sakuru v. Tanaji, Birla Cement Works v. G.M. Western Railways, France B. Martins v. Mafaida Maria Teresa Rodrigues, Thakur Jugal Kishore Sinha v. Sitamarhi Central Co-operative Bank, and Gurditta Mal v. Bal Swarup; it rejected reliance on inherent powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for this statutory authority.
members.conclusion: The Competent Authority had no power to condone the delay or grant leave on the late application. The High Court correctly set aside those orders, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: summary_eviction_proceeding and summons_duly_served and defence_leave_affidavit_filed_after_deadline and procedure_fixes_filing_deadline and authority_has_no_power_to_extend_deadline

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a special summary procedure.
predicates.summons_duly_served: The person defending the eviction proceeding was duly served with summons.
predicates.defence_leave_affidavit_filed_after_dead: The person filed the affidavit seeking leave to defend after the applicable filing deadline.
predicates.procedure_fixes_filing_deadline: The governing procedure requires an affidavit seeking leave to defend to be filed within a specified period.
predicates.authority_has_no_power_to_extend_deadlin: The authority deciding the proceeding was not given power to extend the specified filing period.

members.legal_issue: The statutory power to condone delay in an appeal or application does not apply to an application made to a non-court authority where no time limit is prescribed for that application.
material_facts: The applicant asked an officer exercising Collector functions to extend the time for payment fixed by an earlier order.
The officer was not a court, and no time limit was prescribed for the type of application made.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, permits an appeal or application to be admitted after the prescribed period if sufficient cause is shown. It did not apply because the decision-maker was not a court and the application had no prescribed time limit capable of extension.
members.conclusion: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, could not be invoked to condone delay on that application.

predicates.delay_condonation_application: A party asked for more time to comply with an earlier order.
predicates.recipient_is_not_a_court: The application was made to an administrative officer rather than a court.
predicates.no_prescribed_time_limit_for_application: No time limit was prescribed for making that type of application.

members.legal_issue: A fixed statutory period for applying to be registered as an occupant cannot be extended by equitable interpretation when the statute provides no power to condone delay.
material_facts: The application for registration as an occupant was filed after the statutory application period had expired.
The earlier statutory provision allowing the Tribunal to admit a late application for sufficient cause had been deleted, and no other provision authorizing extension was identified.
members.legal_principle: Sections 45 and 48-A of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 fixed the period for applying and, after the amendment removed the power to condone delay, did not permit an extension. The Court relied on Virupaxappa v. Land Tribunal (1980 (2) Karnataka L.J. 428); Tirath Singh v. Bachiter Singh (AIR 1955 SC 830) and Sham Rai v. District Magistrate (AIR 1952 SC 624) on avoiding unjust or absurd constructions only where the language admits another interpretation; and Nagendranath Dev v. Suresh Chandra Dev (ILR 60 Cal 1 (PC)) on applying the strict grammatical meaning of limitation provisions despite possible hardship.
members.conclusion: The application was time-barred, and the fixed filing period could not be extended through a liberal or equitable interpretation.

predicates.occupancy_registration_application: A person applies to be registered as an occupant of land under a land-tenancy regime.
predicates.fixed_filing_period_expired: The filing period fixed by law for that application has expired before the application is filed.

members.legal_issue: A court should not decide an affected person's rights adversely in public-interest litigation without giving that person notice and an opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The High Court decided that the project proponent lacked permission without giving it notice or an opportunity to address that issue.
The project proponent later sought review based on the factual controversy over whether permission had been granted.
The High Court rejected review as involving a factual controversy, although the court identified that proceeding as an opportunity to correct the earlier error.
members.legal_principle: The requirement of notice and an opportunity to be heard applies when a court is asked to decide a matter adversely affecting a party that was not heard. The court relied on Iskcon v. Nanigopal Ghosh, where a decision in public-interest litigation was set aside and remitted for consideration after affected parties received an opportunity to be heard.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in deciding the permission issue without hearing the affected project proponent and also erred in rejecting review without correcting that error.

predicates.public_interest_case: The proceeding was brought in the public interest.
predicates.court_decides_against_affected_project_p: The court made a decision adverse to a person whose project was at issue.
predicates.proponent_received_no_notice_or_opportun: The affected project proponent was not given notice and a chance to present its position before the adverse decision.

members.legal_issue: A person must receive a fair hearing before an authority makes a prejudicial order in a revision proceeding.
material_facts: The Court distinguished the purported review from the separate revision power available under Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
The Court left it open to the Chief Settlement Commissioner to initiate revision proceedings.
The Court directed that no order prejudicial to the affected persons be made in any such proceedings without giving them a fair hearing.
The affected persons were left free to raise all pleas available to them under the law.
members.legal_principle: Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 permitted the Chief Settlement Commissioner to exercise revision powers directly or through a delegate. The Court did not determine the full scope of that power, but directed that any prejudicial order in proceedings taken under it must follow a fair hearing and that the affected persons may raise their available legal pleas. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: If revision proceedings are initiated, no prejudicial order may be made without first giving the affected persons a fair hearing.

predicates.administrative_revision_proceeding: The matter concerns a proceeding to revise an earlier administrative determination.
predicates.authority_initiates_revision: An authority initiates proceedings to reconsider the earlier determination through revision.
predicates.proposed_order_may_prejudice_affected_pe: The proposed order may adversely affect a person whose interests are involved.

members.legal_issue: A revisional order that adversely affects rights acquired through completed allotments and leases cannot be made without giving the affected allottees a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The allottees had received allotments, executed leases, paid the required amounts, and taken possession before the first orders directing cancellation were made.
The State Government made those orders without hearing the allottees and without considering their objections.
The High Court set aside those orders and directed fresh consideration after a hearing; the Supreme Court had also directed a fresh reasoned decision after a hearing.
members.legal_principle: Section 41(3) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, as applied to the Authority through section 12 of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, prohibits a prejudicial revisional order without a reasonable opportunity of hearing. Independently, principles of natural justice require a hearing before acquired valuable rights are adversely affected.
members.conclusion: The orders made without a hearing were rightly set aside, and the direction to reconsider the matter after hearing the allottees was proper.

predicates.prejudicial_revisional_order: A reviewing public authority makes an order that adversely affects a person's existing position.
predicates.affected_party_has_acquired_valuable_rig: The affected person has acquired valuable rights through completed administrative or contractual steps.
predicates.no_reasonable_hearing: The affected person was not given a reasonable opportunity to present objections before the adverse order was made.

members.legal_issue: A court must give a person notice and a proper opportunity to be heard before making a winding-up direction that would prejudicially affect that person’s rights.
material_facts: The Official Liquidator sought directions to sell leasehold rights and structures on land owned by a person outside the winding-up proceeding.
The Company Judge ordered the sale without issuing notice to or hearing the landowner.
The sale order directly affected the landowner’s asserted rights in the land and leasehold rights.
members.legal_principle: Rule 103 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 provides for summons seeking directions concerning, among other matters, the Official Liquidator’s exercise of powers under section 457(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1956, including the power to sell company property. Although the Rule expressly requires notice to the winding-up petitioner, it implicitly requires notice to any person who would be prejudicially affected by the directions. Natural justice requires notice and a proper opportunity to present that person’s case before an order affecting the person’s rights is made. Rule 139 did not justify denying the appeal because the affected person had not appeared before the Company Judge.
members.conclusion: The Official Liquidator and the Company Judge were required to notify and hear the person whose rights would be prejudicially affected before making the order.

predicates.winding_up_court_direction: A court considers a request for directions in a company winding-up proceeding.
predicates.direction_prejudicially_affects_nonparty: The proposed direction would prejudicially affect the rights of a person who is not a party to the proceeding.
predicates.nonparty_not_given_notice_or_hearing: The affected non-party has not been notified of the request or given an opportunity to present their case.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may not make an order prejudicial to a person without giving that person an opportunity to be heard, even when the person has not yet been summoned as an accused.
material_facts: A complainant filed a complaint and sought a police investigation; the Magistrate refused that request, found police investigation unnecessary, and directed the complainant to present evidence under the complaint procedure.
The complainant challenged the Magistrate’s order in revision but did not join the person whose interests were affected.
Without hearing that person, the High Court set aside the Magistrate’s order and directed a preliminary police inquiry.
The Supreme Court found that the Magistrate had applied his mind to the complaint and taken cognizance, and that the High Court’s order could prejudice the absent person.
members.legal_principle: The requirement of an opportunity to be heard applies to a revisional order prejudicial to an accused or any other person, including at the pre-summoning stage. The Court applied the audi alteram partem principle and the requirement reflected in Section 401(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, relying on Makkapati Nagaswara Sastri v. S.S. Satyanarayan and P. Sundarrajan v. R. Vidhya Sekar. It distinguished Chandra Deo Singh v. Prokash Chandra Bose and Mohd. Yousuf v. Afaq Jahan, and noted that the Magistrate had taken cognizance and proceeded under the complaint procedure.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order was set aside, and the revision was remitted for the affected person to be joined, heard, and for the matter to be decided afresh.

rule.if: criminal_revision_proceeding and magistrate_applied_mind_to_complaint and revision_order_prejudices_absent_person and absent_person_was_not_given_opportunity_to_be_heard

predicates.criminal_revision_proceeding: The matter is a revision of a Magistrate’s order in a criminal complaint proceeding.
predicates.magistrate_applied_mind_to_complaint: The Magistrate considered the complaint and chose to proceed by examining the complainant or witnesses rather than directing police investigation.
predicates.revision_order_prejudices_absent_person: The revisional court’s order adversely affects a person who was not heard.
predicates.absent_person_was_not_given_opportunity_: The affected person was neither joined nor given an opportunity to present their position before the revisional order was made.

members.legal_issue: Residents must be given a fair opportunity to be heard before an administrative decision exposes them to civil consequences, unless the law excludes natural justice.
material_facts: The notification removed the affected areas from the jurisdiction of existing Gram Panchayats, causing elected representatives to cease holding office in respect of those areas.
The change would subject residents to higher taxes and a change from an agricultural to a semi-urban way of life.
The residents were not given an opportunity to present their views before the notification was made.
The statute made no provision expressly excluding an opportunity to be heard.
members.legal_principle: Where administrative action entails civil consequences, natural justice applies unless the law excludes it. The Court relied on S.L. Kapoor v. Jagmohan and State of Orissa v. Sridhar Kumar Mallik. Although Section 256 of the Himachal Pradesh Municipal Act, 1968 did not expressly provide for a hearing, it did not exclude natural justice; the opportunity may be provided through written objections that are fairly considered.
members.conclusion: The residents had to be given an opportunity to be heard before the notified area was constituted; a fair process of inviting and considering objections was sufficient, and an oral hearing was not required.

predicates.challenge_to_notified_area_decision: A party challenged an administrative decision designating an area as a notified area.
predicates.designation_caused_civil_consequences: The designation affected residents' local representation, tax burden, or way of life.
predicates.law_did_not_exclude_natural_justice: The governing law did not expressly exclude a fair opportunity for affected residents to present their views.
predicates.residents_must_receive_a_fair_opportunit: Affected residents must be given a fair opportunity to present their views before the designation is made.

members.legal_issue: A court may not finally decide a public interest writ against an affected party without ensuring that the party, or appropriate successors where the party has died, had notice and an opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The public interest writ challenged government orchard grants, and an earlier remand directed that the nominees be given an opportunity to participate.
One grantee died before the High Court ordered that grantee’s impleadment.
The High Court’s judgment did not establish when or whether service was complete, and the deceased grantee could not appear; the grantee’s successors asserted that they had received no notice.
The High Court proceeded to final disposal without hearing the grantee or the successors.
members.legal_principle: A court must not finally determine a matter affecting a party without ensuring proper notice and an opportunity to be heard. Where the named party died before impleadment, the court must ensure that the appropriate successors can participate. This follows from the requirements of a fair hearing and the earlier remand direction to hear the nominees; the proceeding was under Article 226, and no separate statutory provision was applied to this ruling.
members.conclusion: The judgment was set aside insofar as it concerned the grants attributed to the deceased grantee, and the matter was remanded for fresh consideration.

predicates.public_interest_writ_challenges_public_a: A person brings a public interest writ challenging grants of public assets to private parties.
predicates.affected_grantee_dies_before_impleadment: A grantee affected by the writ dies before the court orders that grantee to be joined as a party.
predicates.court_finalizes_case_without_ensuring_no: The court finally decides the matter without establishing that the deceased grantee’s appropriate successors received notice and an opportunity to participate.

members.legal_issue: An administrative order that adversely affects a person’s rights and has civil consequences must not be made without giving that person an opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: An officer cancelled a subordinate authority’s approval of timber tallies and directed that the timber be treated as removed in a later season, causing the purchaser considerable loss.
The officer made the order without seeking the purchaser’s explanation or giving him a hearing.
The order affected the purchaser’s rights and involved civil consequences.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles of natural justice applied in State of Orissa v. Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei, a person prejudiced by an order involving civil consequences is entitled to a hearing, whether the order is administrative or quasi-judicial; the rule protects against arbitrary action by the State or its officers.
members.conclusion: The order was invalid because it was made contrary to the basic rules of natural justice without giving the affected person a hearing.

rule.if: writ_challenges_administrative_order and order_affects_persons_rights and order_has_civil_consequences and no_opportunity_to_be_heard

predicates.writ_challenges_administrative_order: A person challenges an administrative order in a writ proceeding.
predicates.order_affects_persons_rights: The order adversely affects a person’s rights.
predicates.order_has_civil_consequences: The order has consequences affecting the person’s civil interests.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_be_heard: The affected person was not given an opportunity to explain or respond before the order was made.

members.legal_issue: A court may not pass an order affecting a party to judicial proceedings without first hearing that party.
material_facts: The appellants were parties to a writ petition concerning alleged encroachment on land belonging to a village council.
The High Court issued mandatory directions concerning the subject matter of the writ petition without hearing the appellants.
The appellants challenged that order in appeals.
members.legal_principle: Natural justice requires a court to hear a party to judicial proceedings and consider that party’s position before making an order relating to the proceedings’ subject matter. The Court relied on the observations in Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal (AIR 1955 SC 425).
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the writ petition was restored for determination after hearing all parties.

rule.if: appeal_against_judicial_order and party_to_proceeding and order_affects_subject_matter and party_not_heard

predicates.appeal_against_judicial_order: A party has appealed against an order made in judicial proceedings.
predicates.party_to_proceeding: The person affected by the order was a party to the judicial proceedings.
predicates.order_affects_subject_matter: The order relates to the subject matter of the judicial proceedings and affects the party.
predicates.party_not_heard: The court made the order without hearing the affected party.

members.legal_issue: A court should not base adverse findings on crucial matters drawn from the record without giving the affected parties an opportunity to address those matters.
material_facts: The High Court examined official files and found irregularities in the land allotments.
The High Court did not ask the parties to clarify doubts about crucial matters that formed the foundation of its conclusions.
The Supreme Court remitted the matter for fresh consideration and directed that the parties be permitted to submit further material, without expressing an opinion on the merits.
members.legal_principle: The Court required an opportunity for the parties to address crucial matters on which adverse conclusions were based. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this procedural ruling and expressly left the merits undecided.
members.conclusion: The High Court's order was set aside and the matter was remitted for fresh consideration after the parties had an opportunity to provide relevant material and address the issues.

predicates.writ_proceeding: A court is deciding a writ proceeding.
predicates.court_bases_adverse_findings_on_unaddres: The court relies on material in the record to reach adverse findings on crucial matters without giving the affected parties an opportunity to address those matters.

members.legal_issue: Administrative decisions declaring areas to be slums or clearance areas, and related action affecting dwellings or property, require affected people to have an opportunity to make representations before the decision is taken.
material_facts: The authorities issued declarations concerning a slum area and a clearance area, as well as a notification providing for acquisition of land.
The affected people were not given an opportunity to make representations against the proposed actions.
The decisions could have serious consequences, including restrictions on buildings and demolition; some buildings in a proposed clearance area might not be unfit or dangerous.
The statute provided no appeal against the declarations concerning slum areas and clearance areas.
members.legal_principle: The audi alteram partem principle applies to administrative decisions with serious consequences for affected people even when the statute is silent, unless the statute indicates otherwise. The hearing must be suited to the function and circumstances; the Court held that hearing objections and conducting spot inspections where needed would suffice. It relied on Binapani Dei, Kraipak, Daud Ahmed, and Cooper.
members.conclusion: The three notifications were invalid because the affected people had not been given an opportunity to make representations. The required hearing could consist of hearing objections, with spot inspections where needed; a quasi-judicial trial was not required.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_notification: A party challenged administrative notifications that classify an area or provide for action affecting property.
predicates.proposed_action_has_serious_effects_on_i: The proposed action can materially affect people’s dwellings, property, or related rights.
predicates.affected_people_received_no_opportunity_: The people affected were not given an opportunity to present objections before the action was decided.

members.legal_issue: An authority must give affected inhabitants an opportunity to be heard before rescinding or altering prior slum-area declarations in a way that prejudicially affects them.
material_facts: The government had first declared a larger area to be a slum area and then declared it a slum clearance area after considering objections.
The government later cancelled the earlier notification and declared only a smaller area, excluding much of the previously covered area.
Inhabitants had been affected by the earlier action and the change affected the scope of the scheme concerning their area.
The affected slum dwellers were not given an opportunity to be heard before the change.
members.legal_principle: The audi alteram partem rule applies when the statutory duty and circumstances imply an obligation to hear, unless the statute prohibits a hearing. Where the exercise of power can prejudice a person, a duty to act judicially is implicit. Sections 3 and 11 of the Karnataka Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1973, including the proviso to section 11(1), and the Act’s purpose of improving public health informed the requirement to hear inhabitants affected by alteration of the scheme. The Court relied on Government of Mysore v. J. V. Bhat and applied the requirement that rescission under section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, be exercised subject to like conditions.
members.conclusion: Rescinding the earlier notifications without hearing the affected slum dwellers violated natural justice, so the later notification was quashed; the government could proceed after giving them an opportunity to be heard.

predicates.administrative_change_to_existing_slum_a: An authority rescinds or alters an earlier declaration or scheme concerning a slum area.
predicates.affected_inhabitants_prejudiced_by_chang: The change affects inhabitants who were affected by the authority’s earlier action concerning the area.
predicates.affected_inhabitants_heard: The authority gave the affected inhabitants an opportunity to be heard before making the change.

members.legal_issue: An administrative authority conducting a revision that may affect civil rights must disclose adverse material on which it relies and give the affected parties a fair opportunity to respond.
material_facts: The State Government revised the demand for seigniorage fee after proceedings in which the Department relied on reports and inspection notes concerning the material excavated.
Those reports and inspection notes were not supplied to the affected contractors, and the revisional order did not refer to the inspection notes later relied on by the High Court.
The High Court rejected the objection that the material had not been disclosed, finding no demonstrated prejudice.
members.legal_principle: The audi alteram partem rule requires fair notice of the case to be met and an adequate opportunity to respond before an adverse order affecting civil consequences is made. Natural justice applies to administrative as well as quasi-judicial action. The Court relied on A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works, Board of Education v. Rice, and Spackman v. Plumstead District Board of Works.
members.conclusion: The revisional process disregarded natural justice. The High Court order was set aside, and the matter was remitted for reconsideration after the reports and inspection notes relied on by the Department were supplied to the contractors.

predicates.administrative_revision_affecting_civil_: An administrative authority conducts a revision that may affect a person's civil rights or interests.
predicates.authority_relied_on_adverse_material: The authority relies on material that may support an adverse decision against an affected person.
predicates.affected_party_was_not_given_that_materi: The affected person was not given the material on which the authority relied.

members.legal_issue: A public authority may reject the highest tender to seek a better economic return on public property without acting arbitrarily where the rejection is bona fide.
material_facts: The appellants submitted the highest offers for specified plots in response to a public tender and met the deposit requirements.
The respondent rejected the offers without assigning reasons.
There was no allegation of mala fides, and the Court proceeded on the basis that the respondent sought better offers in its economic interest.
members.legal_principle: An entity that is State must comply with the rule of law and Article 14, but it may protect its economic interest by seeking a proper price for its property. The Court relied on R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India and referred to decisions concerning State action under excise laws.
members.conclusion: The State is entitled to seek the best deal for its property, and on the facts the rejection of the highest offers was not arbitrary.

rule.if: public_tender_dispute and state_entity_disposes_public_property and highest_offer_rejected and no_mala_fides_alleged and rejection_aimed_at_better_economic_return

predicates.public_tender_dispute: The case concerns offers submitted in response to a public tender.
predicates.state_entity_disposes_public_property: A State entity is disposing of property held for public purposes.
predicates.highest_offer_rejected: The public authority rejects the highest offer received.
predicates.no_mala_fides_alleged: No mala fides are alleged in the public authority's rejection of the offer.
predicates.rejection_aimed_at_better_economic_retur: The authority rejects the offer to seek a better economic return on the property.

members.legal_issue: A public authority rejecting the highest commercial tender offer should provide reasons sufficient to indicate its position and ordinarily communicate them to the offeror, absent specific justification.
material_facts: The appellants' highest commercial offers for plots were rejected without reasons being assigned or communicated.
The Court considered the need for public accountability and objective review of administrative action.
members.legal_principle: Recording reasons for executive action promotes credibility, accountability, public scrutiny, and objective administrative or judicial review. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Raj Narain and discussed the expanding scope of judicial review of administrative action.
members.conclusion: Reasons sufficient to indicate the authority's position should be made available and ordinarily communicated to the affected parties, unless there is specific justification not to do so. The Court expressly declined to apply this test to these appeals, which were dismissed.

predicates.specific_justification_for_noncommunicat: A specific justification exists for not making the reasons available or communicating them to the affected party.

members.legal_issue: The Government was not required to accept the highest tender and could prefer a lower tenderer on an overall assessment of suitability.
material_facts: In some units, persons whose tenders were lower were asked to raise their offers to the highest price before their tenders were accepted.
The Government preferred some tenderers on considerations including past experience and a clean record.
The Government rejected some high tenders because of default, failure to provide a required guarantee, or other unsuitability.
members.legal_principle: In considering a challenge under Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) to public contracting, the Government need not accept the highest tender and may prefer another tenderer on an overall assessment, including experience and past conduct. Rashbehari Panda v. State of Orissa condemned a scheme that restricted the opportunity to offer to a limited class; it did not require acceptance of the highest offer in every tender process.
members.conclusion: The Government was not bound to accept the highest tender and could accept a lower tender when, on an overall consideration, it preferred that tenderer; the preferences shown did not establish an unlawful choice.

members.legal_issue: A court should not interfere under its writ jurisdiction with cancellation of a public auction when the decision is supported by material indicating an unfairly low price and serves the public interest in protecting public revenue.
material_facts: The auction produced a highest bid substantially below prices previously obtained for plots in the same area.
The State Government had received a report concerning bungling in the auction and disapproved it, directing a fresh auction to protect the Board’s revenue.
The High Court directed the authority to consider the bidder’s representation and issue a demand for the balance, effectively confirming the auction.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, judicial review examines the decision-making process rather than substituting the court’s view on the merits. Review is subject to restraint, Article 14, and the need to avoid arbitrary, biased, or mala fide action; intervention in public contracts is warranted only where required by the larger public interest. The Court relied on Master Marine Services (P) Ltd. v. Metcalfe and Hodgkinson (P) Ltd., (2005) 6 SCC 138, Tata Cellular v. Union of India, (1994) 6 SCC 651, Sterling Computers Ltd. v. M/s M.N. Publications Ltd., (1993) 1 SCC 445, Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd., (1999) 1 SCC 492, and Air India Ltd. v. Cochin International Airport Ltd., (2000) 2 SCC 617.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have interfered with the cancellation or directed completion of the auction; its orders were set aside and the writ petition was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A public authority rejecting the highest tender must make sufficient reasons for its decision available and ordinarily communicate them to the affected tenderers.
material_facts: A government company acting as a development authority invited tenders for specified plots and rejected the appellants’ highest offers.
The tender scheme reserved a discretion to reject any or all offers without assigning reasons.
The authority stated that it had acted bona fide in seeking better offers; the Court did not apply its reasons requirement to the appeals, which failed.
members.legal_principle: The need for reasons in public decision-making supports transparency, accountability, administrative and judicial review, and the public’s interest in knowing about public transactions. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975) 4 SCC 428 and its discussion of expanding judicial review of administrative action.
members.conclusion: When a public authority rejects the highest offer of this kind, it must make available reasons sufficient to indicate its position and ordinarily communicate them to the affected parties, unless there is a specific justification for not doing so. The Court did not apply that test to these appeals.

members.legal_issue: A public authority disposing of property may seek a better economic return rather than accept the highest offer.
material_facts: The authority rejected the appellants’ highest offers for specified plots.
There was no allegation of mala fides in the authority’s refusal to accept those offers.
The Court proceeded on the basis that the authority sought better offers in the economic interests of the authority.
members.legal_principle: The State may seek the best return for its property; the Court noted that this approach had been accepted in decisions concerning state action under excise laws. This discretion remains subject to the requirements of non-arbitrary public action and giving reasons for rejection of the highest offer.
members.conclusion: The State is entitled to seek the best deal for its property, and the authority’s bona fide pursuit of better offers could justify not accepting the highest offers, subject to the requirement to make reasons available.
