members.legal_issue: An auction presiding officer who is authorized by the auction terms and the authority’s delegation may reject a bid, subject to the scope of that authorization.
material_facts: The auction terms reserved to the presiding officer the right to reject any bid.
The Administrator presided over the auction and later rejected the bids.
The authority had delegated auction-bid functions to the Administrator, and the bidder had not challenged the delegation order.
The delegation provided for the Administrator to accept specified bids when the stated conditions were met; the auction terms independently reserved a right to reject bids.
members.legal_principle: Section 51(1) of the Haryana Urban Development Authority Act, 1977, permitted delegation by the Authority. The Court relied on the delegation order and the auction term reserving the presiding officer’s power to reject a bid. It held that, absent a challenge to the delegation, the bidder could not invalidate it by asserting that delegation under section 51(4) was required.
members.conclusion: The Administrator had authority to reject the bids as presiding officer under the auction terms and under the delegation that had not been challenged.

members.legal_issue: Rejection of the highest bid is not arbitrary where the authorized decision-maker considers relevant reports and market information and gives a reasoned public-interest basis for rejecting the bids.
material_facts: The Administrator rejected seven bids rather than only the plaintiff’s bid.
The rejection communication recorded that relevant reports and aspects had been examined.
The auction committee’s recommendations and comparative price information indicated that the prices fetched were considered low in relation to market trends for similar property elsewhere.
The authority stated that the decision was taken to protect public revenue, and the Court found that the decision reflected application of mind.
members.legal_principle: A public authority is not obliged to accept the highest bid and may reject it for good and sufficient reasons, but its decision must be free from arbitrariness or favouritism and reasons should be available. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Vijay Bahadur Singh (1982) 2 SCC 365, Laxmikant v. Satyawan (1996) 4 SCC 208, Meerut Development Authority v. Association of Management Studies (2009) 6 SCC 171, and M/s. Star Enterprises v. City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra Ltd. (1990) 3 SCC 280. It also applied Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) 1 SCC 405, explaining that the reasons here were reflected in the rejection decision and the reports considered; a bid above the reserve price alone did not require acceptance.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the bids was justified and was not illegal or arbitrary; the rejection was not open to interference on the grounds advanced.

members.legal_issue: A government may reserve discretion to reject the highest tender or select another tender, and is not bound to accept the highest tender, provided its decision is not vitiated by mala fides or reviewable arbitrariness.
material_facts: The government invited sealed tenders for a lease and stated that the highest tender would ordinarily be accepted but that it could select any tender or reject all tenders without giving a reason.
One tender was higher than the leaseholder’s original tender.
The leaseholder was asked to raise its offer and did so, offering more than the highest original tender.
The lease was granted to the leaseholder, and the highest original tender was not accepted.
The challenging tenderer did not allege mala fides, and the grant was not shown to be vitiated by arbitrariness warranting judicial interference.
members.legal_principle: In government contracting, a condition reserving the right to select any tender or reject all tenders is not, by itself, contrary to Article 14, and the government need not accept the highest tender. The Court relied on C.K. Achuthan v. State of Kerala, Trilochan Mishra v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal, Cooverjee B. Bharucha’s case, and Union of India v. M/s Bhimsen Walaiti Ram. It distinguished Century Spinning & Manufacturing Co. v. Ulhasnagar Municipal Council, Rashbihar Panda v. State of Orissa, Dwarka Prasad Laxmi Narain v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Guruswamy v. State of Mysore. The general principles in the relied-on cases applied even though those cases involved statutory provisions.
members.conclusion: The reservation of discretion was not contrary to Article 14, and the government was not required to accept the highest tender; the grant was not shown to warrant judicial interference.

members.legal_issue: A public authority is not invariably required to transfer auctioned land to the highest bidder when the governing auction rule and auction conditions preserve discretion to reject that bid or take another permitted course.
material_facts: The governing rule provided for transfer to the highest bidder but also permitted acceptance of a lower bid or withdrawal of the land from auction in specified circumstances.
The notified auction conditions reserved the Board’s authority to accept or reject the highest bid and to reject any bid.
The Board resolved to reject the bidder’s offer and reinstate the former allotment.
members.legal_principle: Rule 4(3) of the Nagpur Improvement Trust Land Disposal Rules, 1955 must be read together with its proviso, which permits a lower bid to be accepted or the land to be withdrawn from auction in the stated circumstances. The notified conditions also made acceptance dependent on the Board and reserved the Trust’s right to reject the highest or any bid. The Court relied on Trilochan Mishra v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal, Union of India v. M/s Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Vijay Bahadur Singh for the principle that a public authority is not bound to accept the highest bid, subject to the governing auction conditions.
members.conclusion: The rule did not leave the Trust without discretion to reject the highest bid, and the Board’s resolution was not invalid merely because the bidder had made the highest offer.

members.legal_issue: A public authority may reject the highest bid above the reserve price, but its decision must be reasoned, non-arbitrary, and supported by the stated grounds.
material_facts: The successful bids were only marginally above the reserve prices.

The stated basis for re-auctioning the two properties was that the bids were marginally above the reserve prices, but no evidence supported the contention that they were too low compared with prevailing market prices.
Other bids only marginally above reserve prices had been accepted in the same auction.
The decision to re-auction only the two properties lacked a recorded sustainable justification.
members.legal_principle: An auctioneer's reserve price prevents acceptance of a bid below that price but does not guarantee acceptance of a bid above it: Anil Kumar Srivastava v. State of U.P. (2004) 8 SCC 671, approving B. Susila v. Saraswathi Ammal, AIR 1970 Mad 257, and Ram Kishun v. State of U.P. (2012) 11 SCC 511. A public authority nevertheless cannot act capriciously, arbitrarily, or prejudicially and must give an informed decision supported by reasons. The Court relied on Sterling Computers Ltd. v. M & N Publications Ltd. (1993) 1 SCC 445, Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) 6 SCC 651, Air India Ltd. v. Cochin International Airport Ltd. (2000) 2 SCC 617, B.S.N. Joshi & Sons Ltd. v. Nair Coal Services Ltd. (2006) 11 SCC 548, and Jagdish Mandal v. State of Orissa (2007) 14 SCC 517. Cartelization or pooling may justify cancellation; a bid shown to be too low against market value may also justify it if that approach is applied uniformly.
members.conclusion: The Government was not bound to accept every highest bid above the reserve price, but the selective re-auction in this case was unjustified and arbitrary because its stated basis lacked supporting evidence and comparable bids had been accepted.

members.legal_issue: A public authority’s cancellation of a tender process is not arbitrary or mala fide when the decision is supported by bona fide reasons and serves the public interest in obtaining a fair price for a public asset.
material_facts: The authority had issued letters of intent, but formal allotments were dependent on regulatory clearances that were not received for more than five years.
During the delay, the market value of the plots rose substantially above the value underlying the original tender process.
The successful bidder had paid only earnest money and had not paid the remaining premium.
Before cancelling the process and deciding to invite fresh tenders, the authority obtained legal advice that it could do so.
The challenge did not contain specific pleadings explaining how the cancellation was motivated by mala fides.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, judicial review of a tender decision examines the legality of the decision-making process, not the merits of the decision itself. A public authority may refuse a bid or discontinue a tender for good and sufficient reasons, including where the bid does not represent market value; disposal of public property must be fair and transparent. The Court relied on Meerut Development Authority v. Association of Management Studies (2009) 6 SCC 171, Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) 6 SCC 651, Tejas Constructions and Infrastructure (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Council, Sendhwa (2012) 6 SCC 464, Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd. (1999) 1 SCC 492, and the distinction between administrative and contractual issues explained in Kisan Sehkari Chini Mills v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500.
members.conclusion: The cancellation was based on valid considerations, was not arbitrary or mala fide, and was justified by the public interest in obtaining a realistic price for valuable public property.

members.legal_issue: An officer conducting a public-ferry auction may reject the highest bid only by exercising the statutory discretion on relevant material and considering the prescribed factors.
material_facts: A public ferry was auctioned, and the first respondent made the highest bid.
The officer awarded the ferry to a lower bidder, recording only that the two higher bidders appeared on a government-maintained special list.
The officer did not independently assess material about the highest bidder or consider the prescribed factors before rejecting his bid.
The highest bidder had previously been prosecuted for a prohibition offence but was discharged.
members.legal_principle: Under section 8 of the Northern India Ferries Act, 1878, and rule 19 framed under section 12, a ferry sale should generally go to the highest bidder, although the officer may reject that bid for sufficient reasons recorded in writing. The discretion is wide but not unrestricted: the officer must consider the factors specified in rule 19 and act on relevant material. A court will not reverse a properly exercised discretion, but rejection without material supporting it is non-compliance with the rule.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the highest bid was not in accordance with the governing Act and rule because the officer had no relevant material on which to exercise the discretion and rejected the bid solely because the bidder appeared on the special list.

members.legal_issue: A killing in a sudden, unpremeditated fight, without undue advantage or cruel conduct, falls within the sudden-fight exception to murder where the offender had knowledge of the fatal risk but no intention to cause death.
material_facts: A verbal objection during ongoing legal proceedings led to a sudden scuffle between opposing groups, and the attack was not premeditated or planned.
The offender used a small kirpan in the spur of the moment and inflicted stab wounds, one of which caused a death.
The Court found that the offender did not intend to cause death, take undue advantage, or act cruelly.
The Court treated the case as involving knowledge of the risk but no intention to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 300 Exception 4 of the Indian Penal Code, culpable homicide is not murder when it is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually; the fight must involve the person killed. All these requirements must be met. Under Sections 299, 300 and 304, culpable homicide committed with knowledge but without intention to cause death is punishable under Section 304 Part II. The Court relied on State of A.P. v. Rayavarapu Punnayya, which distinguishes murder from culpable homicide and explains the relevant stages of analysis; Budhi Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh, on evaluating provocation and temporary loss of self-control in context; and Kikar Singh v. State of Rajasthan, on the requirements of a sudden fight and the bar on undue advantage or cruel conduct.
members.conclusion: The killing was culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable as culpable homicide committed with knowledge but without intention to cause death. The murder conviction was altered accordingly, and a sentence of ten years’ imprisonment was imposed.

members.legal_issue: A killing committed in a sudden fight without premeditation, in the heat of passion, and without undue advantage or cruel conduct falls within the sudden-fight exception to murder, while injuries indicating intention and knowledge support conviction for culpable homicide with intention.
material_facts: A dispute over cutting a tree led to a verbal altercation, during which the accused attacked the deceased.
The evidence showed that the attack occurred during the sudden altercation and was not premeditated.
Although the accused had weapons, the sequence of events and the injuries did not show that they took undue advantage or acted cruelly.
The deceased sustained serious injuries to the head, including injuries to multiple regions of the head, which indicated intention and knowledge.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC requires a sudden fight, absence of premeditation, action in the heat of passion, and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct; the fight must be with the person killed. The number of wounds is not decisive, and ‘undue advantage’ means unfair advantage (Surinder Kumar v. Union Territory of Chandigarh; Arumugam v. State). Where there is intention and knowledge, the offence falls under Section 304 Part I IPC; where there is knowledge but no intention, it falls under Section 304 Part II IPC.
members.conclusion: The sudden-fight exception applied, so the murder conviction was modified to a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder with intention, rather than a conviction based only on knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A fatal assault committed without premeditation during a sudden fight, without cruel or unusual conduct, falls within the exception for culpable homicide that is not murder.
material_facts: The appellant arrived with cattle at a field where the deceased and other labourers were working, and an altercation followed an objection to the cattle grazing there.
There was no premeditation for the assault; during the sudden fight, the appellant delivered one blow with a pharsa to the deceased’s head.
The deceased died from the injury, but the appellant inflicted no further injuries, left after the blow, and did not assault the other people present.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC and Section 304 Part I IPC. It treated the absence of premeditation, the sudden fight, the single blow, and the absence of cruel or unusual conduct as establishing that the offence fell within Exception 4. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The exception to murder applied, and the appellant was guilty of culpable homicide punishable under Section 304 Part I IPC, rather than murder under Section 302 IPC.

members.legal_issue: A homicide committed during a sudden fight without premeditation, undue advantage, or cruel or unusual conduct falls within Exception 4 to the definition of murder.
material_facts: A dispute over a tree led to a verbal altercation and then a fight; the fatal injuries were inflicted in the heat of passion.
The accused had not come prepared for an attack, and the earlier land dispute had not involved physical combat.
The injuries were inflicted at random, and there was no evidence that the deceased was further injured after falling and becoming helpless.
One injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, but the manner of the assault was not cruel or unusual.
members.legal_principle: Under Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, homicide is excluded from murder when it is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. A sudden fight involves a combat between two or more persons; heat of passion allows no time for passions to cool. All ingredients must be established, and undue advantage means unfair advantage. The court relied on Sukhbir Singh v. State of Haryana (2002) 3 SCC 327.
members.conclusion: Exception 4 applied. The murder conviction was replaced with a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and the court imposed a custodial sentence of ten years and a fine.

members.legal_issue: A homicide committed without premeditation during a sudden fight in the heat of passion, without undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct, falls within the sudden-fight exception and is not murder.
material_facts: The incident arose when a bullock cart entered land whose occupants objected to its passage, followed by a verbal altercation and a sudden fight.
The occupants were proceeding to agricultural work, and the agricultural implements used in the assault were ordinary tools they could normally carry for that work.
The deceased sustained two incised injuries, and the evidence did not establish that the appellants took undue advantage or acted cruelly or unusually.
The Court found that the homicide occurred without premeditation in a sudden fight.
members.legal_principle: Under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, culpable homicide is not murder when it is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. All those conditions must be established; the fight must involve the person killed. The Court relied on Sridhar Bhuyan v. State of Orissa (2004) 11 SCC 395 for these principles and altered the conviction to Section 304 Part I IPC.
members.conclusion: The Court applied Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, altered the conviction from Section 302/34 IPC to Section 304 Part I IPC, and imposed a ten-year term of imprisonment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and no_premeditation and sudden_fight and heat_of_passion and fight_involved_person_killed and not undue_advantage and not cruel_or_unusual_conduct

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.no_premeditation: The killing was not planned or preceded by a determination to fight.
predicates.sudden_fight: A fight arose suddenly between the participants.
predicates.heat_of_passion: The participants acted while passion from the sudden quarrel clouded their reason, without time for it to cool.
predicates.fight_involved_person_killed: The person killed was involved in the fight.
predicates.undue_advantage: The offender took an unfair advantage during the fight.
predicates.cruel_or_unusual_conduct: The offender acted cruelly or in an unusual manner during the fight.

members.legal_issue: A killing committed without premeditation during a sudden fight and in the heat of passion, with knowledge that the act was likely to cause death but without an intention to cause death, is culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
material_facts: A quarrel between the accused and his wife arose suddenly during the night and escalated into an assault.
The child, who had been sleeping in another room, woke and cried after hearing the disturbance; the accused then assaulted the child, causing fatal injuries.
The child suffered two injuries and a fracture, and the evidence did not show that the accused used the sharp-edged weapon used against the adult victims to injure the child.

The evidence supported the conclusion that the accused acted in the heat of passion during the sudden events, without premeditation or an intention to cause the child's death, but with knowledge that the injuries were likely to cause death.
The Court found no evidence that the accused acted cruelly or took undue advantage in the assault on the child.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished an intention to cause death from knowledge that an act is likely to cause death. It treated the absence of premeditation, the sudden quarrel and heat of passion, the nature and number of the child's injuries, and the fact that the sharp-edged weapon was not used on the child as supporting culpable homicide without an intention to cause death, but with the requisite knowledge. The resulting conviction was under Section 304 Part II of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction was set aside and replaced with a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and sudden_unpremeditated_fight and fatal_act_in_heat_of_passion and no_intention_to_cause_death and knowledge_death_likely

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a murder conviction.
predicates.sudden_unpremeditated_fight: The fatal incident arose from a sudden fight or quarrel without premeditation.
predicates.fatal_act_in_heat_of_passion: The accused committed the fatal act in the heat of passion generated by the sudden incident.
predicates.no_intention_to_cause_death: The circumstances do not establish an intention to cause the victim's death.
predicates.knowledge_death_likely: The nature of the act and injuries establishes that the accused knew the act was likely to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A homicide committed without premeditation during a sudden fight in the heat of passion, without undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct, is culpable homicide rather than murder.
material_facts: The fatal assault followed a sudden quarrel arising from a long-running land dispute while a court-appointed commissioner was at the scene.
People on both sides sustained injuries, and one person on each side died a homicidal death.
The court found no clear evidence that either side took undue advantage or acted cruelly or unusually, and found no evidence of an intention to kill before the sudden confrontation.
The evidence established that the two appellants attacked the two deceased persons.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to section 300 of the Indian Penal Code provides that culpable homicide is not murder when it is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offenders taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. Applying those requirements to the sudden confrontation and the injuries and deaths on both sides, the majority applied section 304(1) read with section 34. No earlier cases are cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: By majority, the court held that Exception 4 to section 300 of the Indian Penal Code applied to the two appellants who attacked the deceased. It altered their convictions from murder with common intention under sections 302/34 to culpable homicide under section 304(1)/34 and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for seven years.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and sudden_quarrel and heat_of_passion and no_premeditation and fatalities_on_both_sides and no_undue_advantage and no_cruel_or_unusual_conduct

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.sudden_quarrel: The fatal violence began during a sudden quarrel between the sides.
predicates.heat_of_passion: The participants acted in the heat of passion during the confrontation.
predicates.fatalities_on_both_sides: The confrontation resulted in a homicidal death on each side.
predicates.no_undue_advantage: The offenders did not take undue advantage during the fight.
predicates.no_cruel_or_unusual_conduct: The offenders did not act cruelly or unusually.

members.legal_issue: A killing in a sudden fight is excluded from murder when it occurs without premeditation, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually.
material_facts: The fatal injury was inflicted during a sudden and free fight, without premeditation and in the heat of passion following a sudden quarrel.
Both contending parties were armed with dangerous sharp-edged weapons.
The deceased’s party was not unarmed or armed only with weapons that were not lethal or dangerous.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code applies when a death is caused without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel or unusual manner. Whether conduct was cruel or unusual depends on the circumstances; where both sides in a free fight are armed with dangerous weapons, the use of such weapons does not, in those circumstances, establish that either side acted cruelly or unusually. The court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The facts fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code, so the appellant could not be convicted of murder under Section 302; the offence was reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304.

rule.if: appeal_from_murder_conviction and sudden_fight and no_premeditation and heat_of_passion_after_sudden_quarrel and no_undue_advantage_or_cruel_or_unusual_conduct and both_sides_armed_with_dangerous_weapons

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The case is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.sudden_fight: The fatal injury was inflicted during a sudden fight.
predicates.no_premeditation: The fatal injury was inflicted without premeditation.
predicates.heat_of_passion_after_sudden_quarrel: The fatal injury was inflicted in the heat of passion following a sudden quarrel.
predicates.no_undue_advantage_or_cruel_or_unusual_c: The offender did not take undue advantage or act cruelly or unusually in inflicting the fatal injury.
predicates.both_sides_armed_with_dangerous_weapons: Both sides in the fight were armed with dangerous weapons.

members.legal_issue: A killing committed during a sudden fight without premeditation, in circumstances satisfying the requirements of the sudden-fight exception, is culpable homicide not amounting to murder where the offender had knowledge that the injuries were likely to cause death.
material_facts: The accused and the deceased became involved in a sudden quarrel after the deceased objected to the accused grazing buffaloes in the deceased’s field.
There was no prior deliberation or premeditation to fight.
During the altercation, the accused struck the deceased’s head with an axe, causing six head injuries and death.
The weapon and the injuries to the head supported attributing knowledge that the injuries were likely to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies where death is caused without premeditation, in a sudden fight, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually, and in a fight with the person killed. Where the exception applies but the offender had knowledge that the injuries were likely to cause death, the offence is punishable under Section 304 Part II IPC.
members.conclusion: The conviction for murder was modified to a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC because the killing fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and sudden_fight and no_premeditation and fight_with_deceased and no_undue_advantage_or_cruel_conduct and knowledge_injuries_likely_fatal

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.sudden_fight: The accused and the deceased became involved in a fight that arose suddenly.
predicates.no_premeditation: The accused had not deliberated or determined in advance to fight or kill the deceased.
predicates.fight_with_deceased: The sudden fight was between the accused and the person who died.
predicates.no_undue_advantage_or_cruel_conduct: The accused did not take undue advantage or act cruelly or unusually during the fight.
predicates.knowledge_injuries_likely_fatal: The accused inflicted injuries in circumstances showing knowledge that they were likely to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A homicide committed during a sudden, unpremeditated fight in the heat of passion, without undue advantage or cruel conduct, falls within the sudden-fight exception to murder even if several injuries were inflicted and one proved fatal.
material_facts: A dispute over the return of a kitchen led to a heated argument and sudden quarrel, with no evidence of prior ill-will or premeditation.
During the argument, one participant took out a penknife; the appellant went into the adjoining kitchen, picked up a knife, and inflicted a simple injury on that participant.
The deceased intervened in the scuffle and suffered three knife injuries, one of which proved fatal.
The court found that the number of injuries did not, in the circumstances, establish cruel or unusual conduct or the taking of undue advantage.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code applies when there is a sudden fight, no premeditation, action in the heat of passion, and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct. The cause of the quarrel and who provoked or started the assault are immaterial; the number of wounds is not decisive. A person who, in a sudden quarrel and heat of the moment, uses a handy weapon and causes a fatal injury may receive the exception’s benefit if the other requirements are met. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The appellant was entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code. The murder conviction was set aside and replaced with a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I.

rule.if: appeal_from_murder_conviction and sudden_fight and no_premeditation and heat_of_passion and absence_of_undue_advantage_and_cruel_conduct

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.sudden_fight: The fatal violence occurred during a sudden fight arising from a quarrel.
predicates.no_premeditation: The assailant had not planned the violence before the quarrel.
predicates.heat_of_passion: The assailant acted in the heat of passion during the quarrel.
predicates.absence_of_undue_advantage_and_cruel_con: The assailant did not take undue advantage or act cruelly or unusually.

members.legal_issue: A homicide committed without premeditation during a sudden fight in the heat of passion falls within the sudden-fight exception when the offender takes no undue advantage and acts neither cruelly nor unusually.
material_facts: The parties had assembled to discuss a dispute, and there was an exchange of words followed by a scuffle in which both sides sustained injuries.
There was no clear evidence of who started the attack, and the parties had initially been unarmed.
During the scuffle, one accused went inside a nearby room, brought an axe and struck the deceased on the head.
The deceased survived for about a month, and the Court found that the accused had not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies where the act is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel or unusual manner. All its ingredients must be established. Sridhar Bhuyan v. State of Orissa (2004) 11 SCC 395 explains that the fight involves mutual provocation and blows and that whether a quarrel was sudden depends on the proved facts.
members.conclusion: The acts fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.

rule.if: homicide_conviction_appeal and no_premeditation and sudden_fight_in_heat_of_passion and fight_with_deceased and not undue_advantage_taken and not cruel_or_unusual_conduct

predicates.homicide_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal from a conviction for causing a death.
predicates.no_premeditation: The act was not planned or deliberated beforehand.
predicates.sudden_fight_in_heat_of_passion: A sudden quarrel led to a fight while the participants were in the heat of passion.
predicates.fight_with_deceased: The fight was with the person who died.
predicates.undue_advantage_taken: The offender took an unfair advantage during the fight.
predicates.cruel_or_unusual_conduct: The offender acted in a cruel or unusual manner.

members.legal_issue: When the sudden-fight exception applies but the offender intended to inflict an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the offence is culpable homicide rather than murder, with the higher degree of culpable homicide applying.
material_facts: The deceased was struck on the head with an axe and sustained multiple fractures and brain injuries.
The Court found that the weapon and manner of the blow established an intention to inflict the injury that was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The Court found that the act fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
members.legal_principle: The third clause of Section 300 IPC requires proof both that the offender intended to inflict the injury and that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Nankaunoo v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2016) 3 SCC 317 explains that sufficiency means a high probability of death in the ordinary course of nature and is assessed with regard to such matters as the weapon and the part of the body injured. Where the sudden-fight exception applies, but the offender intended to inflict an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the conviction is for culpable homicide under Section 304 Part I IPC.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction was modified to a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC.

rule.if: homicide_conviction_appeal and sudden_fight_exception_applies and intended_injury_inflicted and injury_sufficient_in_ordinary_course_to_cause_death

predicates.homicide_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal from a conviction for causing a death.
predicates.sudden_fight_exception_applies: The act satisfies the requirements of the sudden-fight exception.
predicates.intended_injury_inflicted: The offender intended to inflict the injury that was caused.
predicates.injury_sufficient_in_ordinary_course_to_: The injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A homicide committed in a spontaneous fight without premeditation and without unfair advantage or cruel or unusual conduct falls within the sudden-fight exception to murder.
material_facts: A property dispute existed between the two groups, but the evidence did not establish a premeditated plan to attack the deceased.
A witness present at the incident testified that the deceased began verbally abusing the group, and the Court accepted that this could have instigated retaliation.
The Court found that a verbal quarrel suddenly escalated into a physical attack.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies where the homicide occurs without premeditation, in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and the offender neither takes undue advantage nor acts cruelly or unusually. All its ingredients must be established. The Court relied on Sridhar Bhuyan v. State of Orissa, (2004) 11 SCC 395, which explains that a sudden fight involves mutual provocation and that the application of the exception depends on the proved facts.
members.conclusion: The circumstances supported treating the incident as a sudden fight without premeditation, bringing the homicide within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.

rule.if: appeal_against_murder_conviction and no_premeditated_plan and sudden_fight_after_quarrel and heat_of_passion and not unfair_advantage and not cruel_or_unusual_conduct

predicates.appeal_against_murder_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction for murder arising from the death.
predicates.no_premeditated_plan: The evidence showed no prior plan or deliberation to attack the deceased.
predicates.sudden_fight_after_quarrel: A quarrel suddenly escalated into a fight between the deceased and the accused.
predicates.heat_of_passion: The fight occurred in the heat of passion before the parties had time to cool down.
predicates.unfair_advantage: The accused took an unfair advantage during the fight.
predicates.cruel_or_unusual_conduct: The accused acted cruelly or in an unusual manner during the fight.
predicates.homicide_is_not_murder_under_sudden_figh: The homicide is treated as not amounting to murder under the sudden-fight exception.

members.legal_issue: The requirement to give public notice in the locality of the substance of an acquisition notification is mandatory and is not displaced when the opportunity to object is dispensed with.
material_facts: An acquisition notification was published in the official gazette, but the Collector did not give public notice of its substance at convenient places in the locality where the land was situated.
The opportunity to object to the acquisition was dispensed with under the urgency procedure.
A later declaration was issued and the acquisition proceedings were challenged.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is an integrated provision requiring both publication in the official gazette and public notice of the substance of the notification in the locality. The local notice is mandatory, and its absence vitiates the acquisition proceedings. Under section 4(2), the notice is also a necessary condition for exercising the power of entry, and non-compliance makes entry unlawful. The notice serves to inform interested persons of the acquisition so they may exercise the valuable right to object under section 5-A. Dispensing with objections under section 17(4) does not alter the requirements of section 4(1). The Court relied on Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan and State of Mysore v. Abdul Razak Sahib.
members.conclusion: The local public-notice requirement was mandatory despite the dispensation of the opportunity to object; because the notice was not given, the acquisition proceedings were vitiated and were quashed.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and gazette_notification_published and not locality_notice_given

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.gazette_notification_published: The government published a notification stating that the land was needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose in the official gazette.
predicates.locality_notice_given: The Collector caused public notice of the substance of the notification to be given at convenient places in the locality where the land was situated.

members.legal_issue: Publication of both the acquisition notification in the official gazette and the substance of that notification in the affected locality is mandatory, and filing objections does not cure the failure to publish locally.
material_facts: A later acquisition notification was published in the official gazette but identified a different plot and area from the land actually intended for acquisition.
A corrigendum corrected the plot and area, but neither the notification as published nor the corrigendum was followed by publication of its substance in the locality.
The landowner filed detailed objections after receiving notice of the proposed acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires both gazette publication and local publication of the substance of the notification. Both requirements are mandatory, and the local notice must relate to the notification actually published in the gazette; it cannot precede that notification. The requirement is not reduced to a means of enabling objections under section 5A, nor is its breach cured because objections were in fact filed. The Court relied on Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan, Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay (distinguished on its facts), Somavanti v. State of Punjab, State of Mysore v. Abdul Razak Sahib, and Narendra Bahadur Singh v. State of U.P.; it also relied on Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of Uttar Pradesh regarding the legal effect of gazette publication. The Court did not decide the effect of the later 1974 amendment because it post-dated the notification at issue.
members.conclusion: The failure to publish the substance of the operative notification in the locality invalidated the acquisition proceedings; the landowner's filing of objections did not cure that failure.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government or an acquiring authority initiated proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.gazette_notification_published: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette.
predicates.operative_notice_not_published_locally: The acquiring authority did not publish the substance of the operative notification in the locality where the land was situated.

members.legal_issue: The statutory requirement to publish an estate-vesting notification in newspapers, as well as in the official gazette, is mandatory when that requirement applies.
material_facts: The notification declared that an estate would vest in the State and thereby affect the proprietor’s vested rights.
The applicable version of the statute required publication in the official gazette and in at least two issues of two newspapers.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(2) and 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the notification had to be published in the manner prescribed by section 3(2) before the vesting consequences under section 4(a) could take effect. The definition of the date of vesting in section 2(h), referring to publication in the Official Gazette, fixed the date from which vesting would operate once the required publication was complete; it did not dispense with the newspaper publications. The Court distinguished Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 970, and disapproved Rebati Ranjan v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1953 Patna 121.
members.conclusion: Publication in the required newspaper issues was mandatory and could not be treated as merely directory.

predicates.estate_vesting_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a notification caused an estate to vest in the State.
predicates.notification_transfers_proprietary_right: The notification would transfer the proprietor’s rights in the estate to the State.
predicates.notification_required_publication_beyond: The applicable legal requirements called for publication of the notification beyond its publication in the official gazette.
predicates.additional_publication_is_mandatory: The required publication beyond the official gazette must be completed before the notification can produce its vesting effect.

members.legal_issue: Failure to comply with every mandatory mode of publishing a preliminary land-acquisition notification invalidates the acquisition proceedings from the objection stage onward, notwithstanding individual notice or actual awareness.
material_facts: The acquisition notification appeared in two daily newspapers, but neither publication satisfied the requirement that at least one newspaper be in the regional language.
A corrigendum enlarging the area proposed for acquisition was not published in any newspaper.
The landowners had not filed objections within the prescribed period, and the authorities relied on individual notices and the landowners’ awareness of the acquisition proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1)(a)–(c) and 5-A of the Jammu and Kashmir Land Acquisition Act, the prescribed methods of publishing a preliminary notification must all be strictly followed; none may be omitted or waived, and individual notice or actual awareness does not replace statutory publication. Because the Act affects landowners’ rights, these requirements are strictly construed. The Court relied on Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan, which held that mandatory publication requirements must be obeyed and non-compliance invalidates the ensuing proceedings; Syed Hasan Rasul Numa v. Union of India, which reiterated that publication by only some required methods is insufficient; and Kunwar Pal Singh v. State of U.P., which held that all prescribed modes of publication must be used.
members.conclusion: The prescribed publication requirements were mandatory and had not been strictly complied with. Individual notice or awareness did not cure the defects. The acquisition proceedings were properly quashed from the objection stage onward, and the landowners were permitted to submit further objections.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The authorities initiated a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.required_publication_modes_not_all_compl: The authorities failed to use every legally prescribed mode of publishing the acquisition notification, including any required publication of a corrigendum.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition notification is invalid when public notice of its substance in the locality is not given alongside or immediately after its official publication.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette.
Public notice of the substance of the notification was not given in the locality until substantially later.
The affected landowner filed objections after the period for objections had expired.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires both publication of the notification in the Official Gazette and public notice of its substance at convenient places in the locality; the local notice must accompany or immediately follow the gazette publication. This local notice is mandatory because, without it, interested persons may be deprived of the valuable right to object under section 5A(1), which allows objections within thirty days after issue of the notification. The Court agreed with Gangadharaiah v. State of Mysore and Ors. (1961 Mys. L.J. 883).
members.conclusion: The notification did not comply with the mandatory requirements and was invalid. The High Court was justified in quashing the acquisition proceedings, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a notification issued for a land acquisition.
predicates.official_publication: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette.
predicates.locality_notice_accompanied_or_immediate: Public notice of the substance of the notification was given in the locality at the same time as, or immediately after, official publication.

members.legal_issue: The requirement to give public notice of the substance of a preliminary land-acquisition notification at convenient places in the locality is mandatory, and its breach invalidates the acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The acquisition authority did not give the required public notice of the substance of the preliminary notification at convenient places in the locality.
The later notification giving particulars of the land was issued after the stage at which the authority could enter and survey the land.
The landowners challenged the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the required public notice had not been given.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, requires the Collector to give public notice of the substance of the preliminary notification at convenient places in the locality. Under section 4(2), that notice is a condition precedent to an authorised officer’s entry onto the land. The later notice under section 5(2), which provides particulars of the land, serves a different purpose and does not replace the earlier notice. The Court distinguished Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, which concerned a formal defect in a notification rather than failure to give the required public notice, and said that Somavanti v. State of Punjab did not bear on this issue. The Court applied the principle that compulsory-acquisition powers must be strictly construed and that ‘shall’ is ordinarily mandatory where that construction accords with the statutory purpose and consequences of breach.
members.conclusion: The public-notice requirement was mandatory, and non-compliance made the acquisition proceedings void; the awards could not be given effect.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government pursued a proceeding to acquire land compulsorily.
predicates.collector_did_not_give_locality_notice: The Collector did not give public notice of the substance of the preliminary acquisition notification at convenient places in the locality.
predicates.later_particulars_notice_served_a_differ: A later notice provided particulars of the land after the earlier stage at which notice was intended to inform the owner before entry onto the land.

members.legal_issue: Failure to publish the substance of an acquisition notification in the locality within the required period invalidates the acquisition.
material_facts: A notification proposing to acquire land was published in the Government Gazette.
The substance of the notification was published in the locality more than forty days later.
The applicable amended requirement made publication within forty days mandatory.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by the Andhra Pradesh (Amendment) Act, 1983, made the forty-day period for publication of the substance of the notification in the locality mandatory. Non-compliance renders the acquisition bad in law. No earlier cases are identified by the Court as the basis for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was bad in law because the substance of the notification was not published in the locality within forty days of its Gazette publication; any possession taken had to be returned.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: An authority undertook proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.required_local_publication_deadline_exce: The acquiring authority published the substance of the acquisition notice in the locality after the required period had expired.

members.legal_issue: The initial notice in a land acquisition proceeding must specify the locality in which land is needed, and omission of that locality invalidates the proceeding despite details in a later notice.
material_facts: The initial notice stated that land described in a schedule was needed for a public purpose, but the schedule gave no locality particulars and only said that a plan could be inspected at the Collector’s office.
A later notice identified the land more specifically, including its locality and area.
The acquiring authority gave no valid reason why the particulars in the later notice could not have been included in the initial notice.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Government need not identify the precise land ultimately to be acquired, but must specify the locality in which the land is needed. A Section 4(1) notification is a condition precedent to further powers under the Act, must be strictly construed, and a serious defect cannot be cured by particulars in a Section 6(1) notification. The Court relied on Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay and Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The initial notice was seriously defective and invalid; the later notice could not cure the defect, so the acquisition proceedings could not stand.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: An authority initiated a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.initial_notice_omitted_locality: The authority’s initial public notice did not identify the locality in which the land was needed.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition notification is invalid when public notice of its substance is not given in the locality within the required time after publication in the official gazette.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette on 18 October 1979.
The Revenue Divisional Officer directed that public notice be given in the locality on 19 November 1979.
The Village Officer submitted a compliance report on 18 December 1979, and the court upheld the finding that public notice was given on that date.
The notice was therefore given more than forty days after publication.
members.legal_principle: Under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended and retrospectively validated by the Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983 with effect from 12 September 1975, public notice of the substance of a notification issued on or after that date must be given in the locality within forty days of its publication in the official gazette; otherwise the notification is invalid. The Court applied its decision delivered the same day in Civil Appeals Nos. 5839–42 of 1983.
members.conclusion: The notification was invalid, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification: The government issued a notification proposing to acquire land.
predicates.locality_notice_not_given_within_require: Public notice of the substance of the acquisition notification was not given in the locality within the required time after its official publication.

members.legal_issue: Publication of the substance of a land acquisition notification in the locality is a mandatory requirement.
material_facts: The substance of the acquisition notification was published in the locality by public announcement.

The court considered that owners, particularly in rural areas, might not learn of a proposed acquisition from publication in the Gazette or newspapers and needed notice to exercise their right to object.
members.legal_principle: Whether a statutory requirement is mandatory or directory depends on the statute’s purpose, the nature of the requirement, legislative intent, and the consequences of each construction. Applying that approach, the court held the local-publication requirement in Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, mandatory because it serves to inform landowners of their opportunity to object under Section 5-A. The court relied on Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board.
members.conclusion: Local publication of the substance of the acquisition notification is mandatory.

predicates.land_acquisition_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.section4_locality_notice_omitted: The authority did not publish the substance of the acquisition notification in the locality.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notice must identify the locality and land proposed for acquisition with sufficient clarity, and later particulars cannot cure a material deficiency in the initial notice.
material_facts: The initial notice identified the land only by the name of a large city and gave no khasra numbers or precise locality.
A later declaration included khasra numbers and stated that a plan could be inspected at the Collector’s office.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 4(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a notice must sufficiently identify the locality and land so affected persons can know whether their land is proposed for acquisition and take steps under the Act. A defect in the Section 4 notice is not cured by fuller particulars in a later declaration. The Court relied on Narendrajit Singh v. State of U.P. and Anr.
members.conclusion: The initial notice’s description of the land was insufficient, and the later declaration could not cure the defect; the acquisition proceedings were invalid.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition of land.
predicates.locality_not_precisely_identified: The initial acquisition notice identifies only a broad area and does not specify the locality with sufficient precision.
predicates.land_not_identifiable_from_initial_notic: A person affected by the proposed acquisition cannot determine from the initial notice whether their land is included.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition notification is invalid when local notice of its substance is given later than the maximum interval that applies between Gazette publication and local notice.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette on 4 August 1977.
Notice of the substance of the notification was given in the locality on 3 October 1977, more than forty days after gazette publication.
A later notification declared the remaining land needed for the acquisition, and the landowners challenged both notifications.
The amendment imposing the maximum interval was expressly retrospective and applied to the acquisition notification.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Sections 1(3) and 2 of the Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, required local notice within forty days of Gazette publication and applied retrospectively to covered notifications. A breach introduced a fatal infirmity. This is consistent with Deepak Pahwa v. Lt. Governor, Delhi, (1984) 4 SCC 308: the two steps need not be simultaneous, but a large gap may indicate a break in continuity; the amendment legislatively fixes the limit beyond which that break is presumed. The later notification could not stand once the foundational acquisition notification was invalidated.
members.conclusion: The acquisition notification was invalid because local notice was given outside the required interval; the later notification also failed, and the decision quashing both notifications was sustained.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and gazette_publication_made and local_notice_given and notification_covered_by_retroactive_requirement and notice_gap_exceeded_limit

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the validity of notifications issued as part of a land acquisition.
predicates.gazette_publication_made: The acquiring authority published the acquisition notification in the official gazette.
predicates.local_notice_given: The acquiring authority gave local notice of the substance of the acquisition notification.
predicates.notification_covered_by_retroactive_requ: The acquisition notification was issued within the period to which the retrospectively effective requirement applies.
predicates.notice_gap_exceeded_limit: The interval between gazette publication and local notice exceeded the maximum interval required by the applicable rule.

members.legal_issue: The requirement to notify the land-requiring department of objections and provide it an opportunity to answer is mandatory, and failure to comply invalidates the ensuing objection-inquiry decision but does not invalidate the preliminary acquisition notification.
material_facts: The applicable rule required notice of the objection hearing to the objector and the land-requiring department, and provided for the department to answer the objections.
The department requiring the land was not given the required notice.
The Collector conducted the inquiry and reported to the Government, which rejected the objections and issued a later acquisition notification.
members.legal_principle: Whether a provision is mandatory depends on legislative intent, assessed from its language, subject matter, importance, design, relation to the provision’s purpose, and the consequences of competing interpretations. The rule was intended to ensure that the Collector had relevant material for the report and that the Government could make a proper decision. The Court relied on section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act and the approach in Lonappan v. Sub-Collector of Palghat, AIR 1959 Kerala 343, and K. V. Krishna Iyer v. State of Madras, (1967) 2 Madras Law Journal 422. It upheld the preliminary notification while quashing the inquiry proceedings and subsequent decision.
members.conclusion: The rule was mandatory. The Collector’s inquiry proceedings and the Government’s decision based on the resulting report were quashed, and the later acquisition notification was quashed. The preliminary notification was not quashed; the Collector was directed to conduct a fresh inquiry on the objections already filed after notifying the department and allowing it to answer.

predicates.land_acquisition_objection_inquiry: An authority is conducting an inquiry into objections to a proposed land acquisition.
predicates.department_notice_required: The applicable rule requires the land-requiring department to receive notice of the objections and an opportunity to answer them.
predicates.department_not_notified: The authority conducted the inquiry without giving the land-requiring department the required notice.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should not reappreciate evidence already analyzed by the tribunal unless the appellant shows that the tribunal’s finding is perverse or suffers from an error apparent on the record.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the tribunal’s factual finding about the structure on the land.
The tribunal had analyzed documentary evidence, including survey reports and property records.
The Supreme Court reviewed the contemporaneous records and found no basis to take a different view.
members.legal_principle: In an appeal from a tribunal, the existence of appellate jurisdiction does not by itself require the appellate court to reappreciate all the evidence. Intervention is warranted where the appellant demonstrates an error apparent on the face of the record or perversity. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was relied on for this standard in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The tribunal’s factual finding was left undisturbed.

rule.if: appeal_from_tribunal_order and tribunal_analyzed_evidence and not demonstrated_perversity_or_apparent_error

predicates.appeal_from_tribunal_order: A party appealed from an order made by a tribunal.
predicates.tribunal_analyzed_evidence: The tribunal examined the evidence relevant to the disputed factual finding.
predicates.demonstrated_perversity_or_apparent_erro: The appellant showed that the tribunal’s finding was perverse or contained an error apparent on the record.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising writ jurisdiction does not sit as an appellate court over an administrative decision merely to reassess its merits.
material_facts: The society challenged the municipal commissioner’s rejection of its alternative demolition proposal through court proceedings.
The commissioner’s decision followed examination of the proposal by architects and engineers.
The court found no want of jurisdiction, violation of law or rules, or mala fides in the decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court is not an appellate court over administrative decisions. The court also considered its special leave jurisdiction under Article 136, but cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The court held that writ jurisdiction does not make the High Court an appellate court over administrative decisions and found no basis to interfere in this case.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_administrative_decisio: A party challenged an administrative decision in a proceeding invoking writ jurisdiction.
predicates.decision_examined_by_authority: The authority examined the relevant proposal before making its decision.
predicates.no_jurisdictional_or_legal_defect: The decision was not shown to exceed the authority’s jurisdiction or violate law or rules.

members.legal_issue: A review of an appealable judgment cannot be used to rehear the dispute or correct an alleged error that is not self-evident on the record.
material_facts: The High Court reviewed its judgment in a second appeal and reversed the result, relying on the view that a separate suit was barred because leave to sue later had not been obtained.
The earlier plaint referred to the agreement for sale and expressly reserved the right to bring a suit for specific performance.
Whether the separate specific-performance suit was barred was not relevant to the suit seeking cancellation of the later sale deed.
The asserted error required examination of the pleadings and reasoning; it was not an error apparent on the face of the record.
members.legal_principle: Section 114 CPC is read with Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC, which permits review on discovery of new and important matter or evidence unavailable despite due diligence, an error apparent on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason. Review is not an appeal in disguise and cannot be used to rehear a dispute or correct an error on the merits. An error is not apparent if establishing it requires a long or debatable process of reasoning. The Court relied on Thungabhadra Industries Ltd. v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, Meera Bhanja v. Nirmala Kumari Choudhary, Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aribam Pishak Sharma, Shivdeo Singh v. State of Punjab, Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Hegde v. Mallikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale, and Parsion Devi v. Sumiri Devi.
members.conclusion: The review was outside the permissible scope of review jurisdiction. The Supreme Court set aside the review order and restored the judgment in the second appeal.

predicates.review_application_after_appealable_judg: A party applied to the court that issued an appealable judgment to review it.
predicates.alleged_error_requires_reasoning_or_rehe: The alleged error could be established only by examining and reasoning through the dispute rather than by merely looking at the record.
predicates.new_material_unavailable_despite_due_dil: The review applicant relied on new and important material that could not have been obtained or produced earlier despite due diligence.
predicates.self_evident_record_error: The alleged error was immediately apparent from the record without a lengthy or debatable process of reasoning.

members.legal_issue: Review is unavailable to reargue the merits where the asserted new evidence does not satisfy the requirements for newly discovered material and the alleged error is not self-evident from the record.
material_facts: The applicant had not produced evidence before the Reference Court that the sale transaction relied on to determine compensation was not bona fide or that the price had been inflated for an extraneous reason.
The applicant did not explain why, despite having access to the other sale transactions in the proceedings, it failed to investigate or adduce evidence about the difference in prices earlier.

The additional records did not establish that the two companies had common management when the sale price was agreed, and the applicant did not controvert evidence of other nearby land sales at substantially higher prices.
Determining whether the transaction was invalid or artificially priced would require a factual inquiry and reassessment rather than correction of an evident error.
members.legal_principle: Article 137 of the Constitution and Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit review on limited grounds, including relevant new material that could not have been produced despite due diligence and an error apparent on the face of the record. Review cannot correct an alleged error requiring extended reasoning or a rehearing on the merits. The Court relied on S. Nagaraj v. State of Karnataka, Moran Mar Basselios Catholicos v. Most Rev. Mar Poulose Athanasius, Thungabhadra Industries Ltd. v. Govt. of A.P., Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aibam Pishak Sharma, Meera Bhanja v. Nirmala Kumari Choudhury, Parsion Devi v. Sumitri Devi, Lily Thomas v. Union of India, Haridas Das v. Usha Rani Banik, and State of West Bengal v. Kamal Sengupta.
members.conclusion: The Court held that no ground for review had been established and dismissed the review petitions.

rule.if: review_proceeding and (new_evidence_available_with_due_diligence or new_evidence_not_relevant_or_material) and alleged_error_requires_reassessment

predicates.review_proceeding: A party seeks review of a court's decision.
predicates.new_evidence_available_with_due_diligenc: The material offered as new could have been found or produced earlier through due diligence.
predicates.new_evidence_not_relevant_or_material: The material offered as new does not substantiate a fact that could affect the decision.
predicates.alleged_error_requires_reassessment: Establishing the alleged error requires factual reassessment or extended reasoning rather than revealing an evident error on the record.

members.legal_issue: A supervisory court exceeds its limited jurisdiction when it reassesses the merits of a proposed pleading amendment to overturn the trial court’s decision allowing it.
material_facts: The trial court allowed an application to amend a written statement.
The High Court set aside that order after considering whether the proposed defence was legally tenable on its merits.
The proposed defence elaborated on a joint-family-property defence already pleaded in the written statement.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 227 of the Constitution, supervisory jurisdiction is confined to determining whether the inferior court or tribunal acted within its jurisdiction; the High Court does not act as an appellate court or reassess the merits of the evidence or proposed case. The Court relied on Sadhna Lodh v National Insurance Company, (2003) 3 SCC 524.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order was unsustainable because it went beyond the limits of supervisory jurisdiction; the trial court’s order allowing the amendment was affirmed.

predicates.appeal_challenges_supervisory_interferen: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a supervisory court’s intervention in a trial court’s order.
predicates.trial_court_allowed_pleading_amendment: The trial court allowed a party to amend a pleading.
predicates.supervisory_court_assessed_amendment_mer: The supervisory court assessed the merits of the case proposed by the amendment when intervening.

members.legal_issue: A review court exceeds its limited jurisdiction when it reappraises the evidence to correct an alleged error that is not self-evident.
material_facts: A High Court division bench had allowed a second appeal and granted a decree for partition of disputed land.

In review, another division bench reconsidered the documentary and oral evidence, reached different conclusions about title, possession, and whether the land conveyed was demarcated, and set aside the partition decree.
The alleged error required reconsideration of the evidence and reasoning rather than being apparent on merely looking at the record.
The Supreme Court found that the review bench had effectively sat in appeal over the earlier decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 47, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, review is not an appeal and is confined to specified grounds, including an error apparent on the face of the record. Such an error must be self-evident; an alleged error requiring a long-drawn process of reasoning where more than one view is possible is not apparent. Review cannot be used to correct an allegedly erroneous decision on the merits by reappreciating evidence. The Court applied the principles in Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aribam Pishak Sharma, which referred to Shivdeo Singh v. State of Punjab, and Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Hegde v. Mallikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale. The Court noted the analogous review jurisdiction discussed under Article 226; the appeal before it was brought under Article 136.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed; the review judgment and the consequential order dismissing the second appeal were set aside, and the earlier judgment granting partition was restored.

predicates.review_proceeding: A court considered an application seeking review of an earlier judgment.
predicates.entire_evidence_reappraised: The reviewing court reconsidered the oral and documentary evidence and reached its own conclusions on the merits.
predicates.alleged_error_required_extended_reasonin: Establishing the alleged error required extended reasoning rather than the error being self-evident from the record.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising review jurisdiction over a writ judgment cannot use review to correct an alleged error on the merits or to reconsider procedural objections that do not disclose a proper ground for review.
material_facts: A writ petition challenging a settlement of part of a public road was allowed on the ground that the settlement was prohibited by the applicable land laws.

The respondents sought review, relying on two documents already in the record that had not been relied on in the parties’ affidavits, and arguing that separate writ petitions should have been filed to challenge settlements in favour of different respondents.
A successor judicial commissioner allowed the review and dismissed the writ petition.
members.legal_principle: A court exercising plenary jurisdiction under Article 226 has an inherent power of review to prevent a miscarriage of justice or correct grave and palpable errors, as recognized in Shivdev Singh v. State of Punjab. The power is limited: it may be exercised on discovery of new and important matter or evidence that, despite due diligence, was not within the applicant’s knowledge or could not have been produced earlier, on an error apparent on the face of the record, or on an analogous ground. It cannot be used to correct an alleged error on the merits, which is the province of an appellate court. The Court also held that the failure to consider documents already on the record but not relied on in the affidavits, and an objection that separate writ petitions should have been filed, did not justify review under Order 47, Rule 1 and Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The grounds given for allowing review were not proper grounds for review, so the judicial commissioner acted without jurisdiction. The review order was set aside and the original order allowing the writ petition was restored.

rule.if: review_of_writ_order and (overlooked_record_evidence_not_relied_on or objection_to_single_petition) and no_independent_valid_review_ground

predicates.review_of_writ_order: A party sought review of a court’s order deciding a writ petition.
predicates.overlooked_record_evidence_not_relied_on: The review applicant relied on documents already in the record that had not been relied on in the parties’ affidavits.
predicates.objection_to_single_petition: The review applicant argued that challenges concerning different respondents should have been brought in separate petitions.
predicates.no_independent_valid_review_ground: The review application rested on those grounds and did not establish another proper ground for review, such as qualifying new evidence or an apparent error.
predicates.review_order_set_aside: The court’s order allowing review is set aside.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court cannot recall an earlier order by reconsidering its merits when the record discloses no self-evident error.
material_facts: The High Court had dismissed revision petitions challenging the trial court’s decision to implead a neighbour in a suit concerning a municipal notice and construction.

On review, the High Court considered documents that had not been before the trial court and reconsidered whether the neighbour was a proper party, then recalled its earlier order and directed fresh consideration.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had reconsidered the merits and that no mistake apparent on the face of the record justified review.
members.legal_principle: Review jurisdiction is extremely limited: an order may be reviewed for a mistake apparent on the face of the record, meaning a self-evident mistake that requires no search to identify. Review is not an appeal in disguise and does not permit rehearing on the merits. Although the dispute concerned impleadment under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Supreme Court did not independently decide the merits of that question. No earlier case was relied on by the Supreme Court in stating the review principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its limited review jurisdiction. The Supreme Court set aside the order recalling the earlier order and allowed the appeals.

predicates.appeal_from_review_order: An affected party appealed from an order made while reviewing an earlier judicial order.
predicates.merits_reconsidered: The reviewing court reconsidered the merits of its earlier order rather than limiting itself to correcting an apparent record error.
predicates.no_self_evident_error: The earlier order contained no self-evident mistake apparent from the record that required no search to identify.

members.legal_issue: A writ court exceeds its jurisdiction by deciding disputed factual questions about private property possession and ordering restoration of possession on that basis.
material_facts: The writ court determined that the claimant had been in possession of the flat and ordered the other private individual to restore possession.
The parties disputed who possessed the flat and their respective ownership and possession rights.
Resolving those questions required assessment of evidence in an ordinary civil proceeding, and possession disputes could also be addressed through the applicable criminal proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The extraordinary jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution is not to be used to decide disputed property facts that require evidence or to convert a writ petition into a civil suit. A possession dispute between private individuals must be determined through an appropriate ordinary proceeding, including a civil suit or, where applicable, proceedings under Section 145 CrPC. The Court relied on Mohan Pande v. Usha Rani, (1992) 4 SCC 61, and Dwarka Prasad Agrawal v. B.D. Agrawal, (2003) 6 SCC 230, concerning the limits of writ jurisdiction and the availability of ordinary remedies.
members.conclusion: The writ court was not justified in making factual findings and ordering restoration of possession; its order was set aside.

predicates.constitutional_writ_for_property_possess: A claimant brought a constitutional writ petition seeking possession-related relief concerning property.
