predicates.private_parties_dispute_property_rights: Private individuals asserted competing rights to ownership or possession of the property.
predicates.writ_court_decided_disputed_possession_f: The writ court resolved disputed facts about who possessed the property or the circumstances of that possession.
predicates.evidence_needed_to_determine_property_cl: Determining the parties’ property claims required assessment of evidence in an ordinary proceeding.
predicates.writ_court_ordered_restoration_against_p: The writ court directed one private individual to restore possession to another.

members.legal_issue: A writ court exceeds its review limits by reappraising evidence and overturning concurrent, reasoned factual findings of special forums without a proper basis for intervention.
material_facts: The Special Tribunal and Special Court both found that the land was government land, that it had been illegally occupied, and that the occupants had not proved adverse possession.
The High Court reconsidered the evidence and reached a different conclusion about possession and title.
The High Court did not displace the concurrent finding that the land belonged to the government.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, certiorari review is not an opportunity to reappraise evidence merely because a different factual conclusion could be reached. The Court referred to Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan and held that the High Court had exceeded the limits of its review by disregarding the special forums’ reasoned findings.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by interfering with the concurrent findings of the Special Tribunal and Special Court.

predicates.writ_review_of_special_forum_decision: A party asked a writ court to review a decision of a special forum.
predicates.concurrent_reasoned_findings: Two special forums reached the same factual findings and gave reasons for them.
predicates.high_court_reappraised_evidence: The writ court reconsidered the evidence and reached a different factual conclusion.
predicates.writ_interference_exceeded_review_limits: The writ court went beyond its permissible review role by disturbing the special forums’ findings.

members.legal_issue: A review court cannot reconsider the merits as an appellate court absent an error apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The tenant sought review of the order fixing mesne profits, raising the new-law cap argument and disputing the area included in the tenancy.
The High Court concluded that the new law did not govern the pending suit and that the tenant’s objection to the area was not a basis for review.
The High Court dismissed the review, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
members.legal_principle: The High Court applied the principle that review is not an appeal in disguise and that the reviewing court does not reassess the merits unless an error apparent on the face of the record is shown. The Supreme Court upheld that approach in light of the savings provision in Section 32 of the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2001 and the record concerning the tenanted area.
members.conclusion: The review petition was properly dismissed because the tenant had not shown an apparent error warranting review.

predicates.review_challenges_mesne_profit_order: A party seeks review of an order fixing mesne profits.
predicates.no_error_apparent_on_record: The party does not establish an error apparent on the face of the record.

members.legal_issue: A writ court may set aside an appellate authority’s decision when it rests on a patent error of law, even though the writ court is not acting as an appellate court on the merits.
material_facts: The District Magistrate treated the company’s buildings as separate for water-tax purposes by relying on the definition of an appurtenant compound.
The District Magistrate did not consider the part of the statutory definition addressing several buildings in a common compound.
The single judge intervened, although the single judge’s own reasoning about appurtenance was not correct.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, the High Court does not act as a court of appeal, but may correct patent errors of law. The Court accepted that principle as supported by Shri Ambica Mills Co. Ltd. v. Shri S.B. Bhatt, Syed Yakoob v. K.S. Radhakrishnan, Bhutnath Chatterjee v. State of West Bengal, Mohd. Yunus v. Mohd. Mustaqim, and Harbans Lal v. Jagmohan Saran.
members.conclusion: The single judge was justified in intervening because the District Magistrate’s omission produced a patent error of law; the single judge reached the correct result despite using an inaccurate line of reasoning.

predicates.writ_review_of_appellate_tax_decision: A party sought writ review of an appellate authority’s decision concerning a tax assessment.
predicates.appellate_authority_omitted_relevant_sta: The appellate authority failed to consider a relevant part of the governing statutory definition.
predicates.omission_caused_patent_error_of_law: The failure to consider that definition materially affected the authority’s legal reasoning.

members.legal_issue: A special summary procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants of public property does not violate equality merely because an ordinary civil remedy may also be available or because the procedure applies to a distinct class of property.
material_facts: The challenged procedure applied to unauthorised occupants of premises belonging to a municipal corporation.
The law provided a special procedure for eviction, while eviction could also be pursued through an ordinary suit in some cases.
The special procedure was intended to provide a speedy method of recovering public property.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, legislation may establish a special procedure for a distinct class of cases when its purpose and policy provide guidance for applying that procedure. Applying Maganlal Chhagganlal Private Limited v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, the Court held that a special speedy procedure for recovering public property is not invalid merely because another procedure may be available; Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab no longer governed the issue.
members.conclusion: The special procedure did not violate Article 14 on the ground that the Commissioner had an unguided choice between that procedure and an ordinary suit.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_summary_evic: A person challenged the constitutionality of a summary procedure used to recover property.
predicates.unauthorised_occupation_of_public_proper: The proceeding concerned a person's unauthorised occupation of property belonging to a public body.
predicates.legislature_provided_special_speedy_proc: The legislature established a special process intended to recover the public body's property speedily.

members.legal_issue: Different allotment terms for rehabilitated stallholders and tender-selected licensees are consistent with equality when the groups are materially distinct and the difference rationally serves a public purpose.
material_facts: Stallholders had occupied stalls for decades, and the land they occupied was required for road widening.
The authority reserved shops for those stallholders to induce them to relocate and offered them a lower licence fee and relaxed zoning restrictions as part of their rehabilitation.

Other shops were allotted through tenders; the tender documents disclosed the reserved shops and the zoning restrictions, and the successful tenderers accepted those terms and offered licence fees above the reserved rates.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits different treatment of distinct classes where the classification has a reasonable basis and serves a rational purpose. Rehabilitation of long-standing stallholders displaced for a public project, supported by relocation concessions, was a proper basis for different terms.
members.conclusion: The rehabilitated stallholders formed a separate class, and the different licence fees and zoning terms were reasonable and rational; the differential treatment did not violate Article 14.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_differential_allot: A person challenging an authority’s allotment terms alleges unequal treatment in a proceeding reviewing the legality of that treatment.
predicates.displaced_occupants_needed_rehabilitatio: A group had occupied sites for a substantial period and had to leave because the sites were required for a public purpose.
predicates.concessions_induced_relocation_for_publi: The authority offered that group more favourable terms to induce relocation and facilitate the public purpose.
predicates.tender_allottees_accepted_disclosed_term: Other allottees obtained their interests through a tender process, knew the applicable terms, and accepted them.

members.legal_issue: Providing a special eviction procedure for occupants of government or municipal premises, distinct from the procedure applying to occupants of private premises, is consistent with the equality guarantee when the distinction serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The challenged laws provided a special process for recovering government or municipal premises from unauthorised occupants.
The legislation was directed at enabling speedy recovery of those premises for public purposes, including public development and housing-related objectives.
The ordinary civil process was considered costly and slow in comparison.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification founded on an intelligible differentia that bears a rational relation to the object of the legislation. The Court applied the classification principles discussed in Ramkrishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar and relied on decisions including Baburao Shantaram More v. Bombay Housing Board, Collector of Malabar v. Erimal Ebrahim Hajee, and Lachhman Das v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The distinction between occupants of government or municipal premises and occupants of private premises was a valid classification and did not violate Article 14.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns recovery of premises held for a government or public body.
predicates.public_and_private_occupants_are_treated: The law provides occupants of public premises a different process from occupants of private premises.
predicates.speedy_recovery_serves_public_use: The legislation seeks prompt recovery of public premises so they can be used for public purposes.

members.legal_issue: Making a special eviction process available alongside an ordinary civil suit does not violate the equality guarantee where legislation guides the choice between procedures and the special process is not substantially and qualitatively more prejudicial.
material_facts: The challenged laws allowed recovery of public premises through a special eviction process, while an ordinary civil suit was also available in the cases before the Court.
The legislative purpose was speedy recovery of public premises, and the nature and complexity of a dispute could inform whether the special or ordinary process should be used.

The special process provided notice of the grounds, an opportunity to respond and submit documents, representation by counsel, powers to summon witnesses and require documents, and an appeal to a senior judicial officer.
The affected person could also seek review under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, alternative procedures are discriminatory where similarly situated persons may face a substantially more drastic procedure without legislative guidance for choosing between them. Legislative policy may supply guidance for administrative selection, including the need for speedy recovery and the nature and complexity of the dispute. The procedures must be compared for substantial and qualitative disparity, not merely because one is administered by an executive officer and the other by a civil court. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra, Kedar Nath Bajoria v. State of West Bengal, A. Thangal Kunju Musaliar v. M. Venkitachalam Potti, Jyoti Pershad v. Administrator for the Union Territory of Delhi, Suraj Mall Mohta v. A. V. Visvanatha Sastri, Shree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. A. V. Visvanatha Sastri, and M. Ct. Muthiah v. Commissioner of Income-tax. The majority overruled Northern India Caterers Ltd. v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The special procedures were not substantially and qualitatively more drastic or prejudicial than the ordinary civil procedure, and the provisions did not violate Article 14. The majority overruled Northern India Caterers Ltd. v. State of Punjab; Justice Khanna agreed that the challenge failed but considered overruling that precedent unnecessary.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_proceeding and alternative_procedures_are_available and legislation_guides_procedure_selection and case_complexity_can_guide_forum_choice and special_process_provides_notice_and_hearing and affected_person_can_submit_evidence_and_use_counsel and decision_maker_can_compel_witnesses_and_documents and appeal_is_to_senior_judicial_officer and constitutional_review_is_available

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction from premises held for a government or public body.
predicates.alternative_procedures_are_available: The public body can seek recovery through a special process or an ordinary civil suit.
predicates.legislation_guides_procedure_selection: The legislation identifies speedy recovery of public premises for public purposes as the policy guiding use of the special process.
predicates.case_complexity_can_guide_forum_choice: The nature and complexity of the dispute may be considered in choosing between the special process and the ordinary process.
predicates.special_process_provides_notice_and_hear: The special process gives the affected person notice of the grounds and an opportunity to respond.
predicates.affected_person_can_submit_evidence_and_: The affected person may submit documents and appear through counsel in the special process.
predicates.decision_maker_can_compel_witnesses_and_: The decision-maker in the special process can summon witnesses and require the production of documents.
predicates.appeal_is_to_senior_judicial_officer: An affected person may appeal to a senior judicial officer.
predicates.constitutional_review_is_available: The affected person may seek constitutional review of the decision.

members.legal_issue: A special statutory procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants of government land does not violate the guarantee of equality merely because the government may also bring an ordinary civil suit.
material_facts: The petitioners received notices under the statutory procedure seeking their eviction from land claimed to belong to the government.
The statute applied to unauthorised occupation of government land and provided for eviction after notice and a reasonable time to vacate.
The statutory scheme provided for an appeal, revision by the government, and a right to bring a suit by a person aggrieved by proceedings under the Act.
The constitutional challenge rested on the contention that the availability of a special procedure alongside an ordinary civil suit permitted arbitrary choice and discrimination.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a special procedure merely because an ordinary civil remedy is also available. A special procedure is not invalid where its purpose and scope guide the authority's choice, the procedure is not so harsh or onerous as to create unconstitutional discrimination, and the risk of discriminatory selection is not real merely because it is imaginable. The Court applied Maganlal Chhagganlal Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which considered Anwar Ali Sarkar, Suraj Mall Mohta, Saurashtra, Jyoti Pershad, Haldar and Bajoria, and declined to follow the contrary majority view in Northern India Caterers v. Punjab.
members.conclusion: The special eviction procedure did not violate the equality guarantee, and the petitions challenging the statute were dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_evic: A person subject to a statutory eviction process challenges that process as inconsistent with the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.unauthorised_occupation_of_government_la: The eviction process concerns a person's unauthorised occupation of land belonging to the government.
predicates.special_procedure_has_defined_eviction_p: The statutory process is directed at the eviction of unauthorised occupants from government property through a procedure intended to address that purpose.
predicates.special_procedure_has_procedural_safegua: The statutory process provides notice and a reasonable opportunity to vacate, together with avenues to challenge or review the eviction proceedings.
predicates.ordinary_civil_suit_also_available: A person aggrieved by the statutory proceedings may also seek relief through an ordinary civil suit.

members.legal_issue: A statutory power to evict persons from municipal premises on grounds including unauthorised occupation does not violate equality guarantees when it concerns property belonging to government or a semi-government body and provides a hearing opportunity.
material_facts: The Chief Officer was empowered to order a person in unauthorised occupation of municipal premises to vacate.
Before making an eviction order, the Chief Officer had to give notice of the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to explain and produce evidence.
The person served with the eviction notice challenged the statutory eviction power as unconstitutional.
An appeal against an eviction order could be made to the Government, which could condone delay for sufficient cause.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, property belonging to government or semi-government bodies may constitute a reasonable class. Once that classification is reasonable, the absence of a civil remedy does not by itself make the eviction provision discriminatory. The Court relied on Chhaganlal Maganlal, which overruled Northern India Caterers’ contrary approach, and on Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram, which upheld a provision in pari materia. The availability of an administrative appeal was also noted.
members.conclusion: The statutory eviction power was not invalid under Article 14; the High Court’s contrary judgment was set aside and the Chief Officer’s order was affirmed.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person affected by an eviction scheme challenged its constitutional validity.
predicates.public_body_property: The property subject to eviction belonged to a government or semi-government body.
predicates.eviction_power_with_hearing: An authority could order eviction from the property after giving the affected person notice and an opportunity to explain and produce evidence.

members.legal_issue: A statutory summary-eviction procedure for municipal premises does not violate equal protection merely because the municipality may use it instead of an ordinary civil suit.
material_facts: The statute allowed the municipal authority to order eviction for specified breaches of occupancy terms or unauthorised occupation, while the municipality could also seek possession through an ordinary civil suit.
The occupants challenged the procedure as giving the municipality unguided discretion to choose between the two remedies.

The authority served a notice stating the grounds for proposed eviction and gave the occupant an opportunity to respond; after the occupant denied unauthorised occupation and did not vacate, the authority ordered him to do so.
The High Court had invalidated the provision, but the Supreme Court had already considered materially identical provisions in earlier decisions.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed Maganlal Chhaganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which overruled Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab, and Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram, which reversed the Gujarat High Court’s ruling on a provision in identical terms. It also relied on State of Gujarat v. Patel Beva Karsan. Those decisions established that the materially identical summary-eviction provision was intra vires; the challenge here therefore failed.
members.conclusion: The provision was not invalid under Article 14, and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.

predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: A party appealed from a judgment invalidating a statutory summary-eviction procedure.
predicates.summary_remedy_choice_challenged: An occupant argued that the authority could choose summary eviction instead of an ordinary civil suit without adequate guiding criteria.
predicates.comparable_supreme_court_decisions_consi: The Supreme Court considered its earlier decisions addressing materially identical statutory eviction procedures.

members.legal_issue: A special procedure for evicting unauthorized occupants from public property is not invalid under the equality guarantee merely because authorities might apply it discriminatorily or because ordinary civil proceedings are also available.
material_facts: The challenged law provided a procedure intended to enable speedy eviction of unauthorized occupants from government premises.
The High Court allowed the constitutional writ petition solely on the ground that the law was unconstitutional, following an earlier High Court ruling.
The appeal challenged that decision, and the Supreme Court considered the law’s constitutionality under Article 14.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a law providing a special procedure for speedy eviction of unauthorized occupants from public property is not invalid merely because it creates a possibility of discriminatory treatment or offers a procedure different from ordinary civil proceedings. A stated legislative purpose can provide sufficient guidance to authorities, and the procedure is not discriminatory merely because a special process is available; courts remain able to address discriminatory application. The Court applied Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which disapproved the majority view in Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab, and followed State of Uttar Pradesh v. Arshad Ali Khan. It held that Raja Ram Verma v. State of Uttar Pradesh could no longer be treated as good law. Article 226 was the basis of the writ petition before the High Court.
members.conclusion: The law could not be treated as constitutionally infirm on the ground decided by the High Court. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court’s judgment, and remanded the matter for decision on the other grounds raised in the writ petition.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_judgment and special_process_for_unauthorized_public_occupants and special_process_aims_at_speedy_eviction and process_has_legislative_guidance and process_is_not_harsh_or_onerous and challenge_rests_on_possible_differential_treatment

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: The matter is an appeal from a judgment on a constitutional writ petition.
predicates.special_process_for_unauthorized_public_: A law provides a special procedure for evicting unauthorized occupants from public property.
predicates.special_process_aims_at_speedy_eviction: The special procedure is intended to secure speedy eviction of unauthorized occupants.
predicates.process_has_legislative_guidance: The law’s stated purpose gives authorities guidance in deciding whether to use the special procedure.
predicates.process_is_not_harsh_or_onerous: The special procedure is not so harsh or onerous as to indicate discriminatory treatment.
predicates.challenge_rests_on_possible_differential: The challenge relies on the possibility that use of the special procedure could result in discriminatory treatment.

members.legal_issue: The availability of a separate tenancy-law procedure for ejectment does not make a public-premises eviction procedure discriminatory when the public-premises law itself provides only one procedure.
material_facts: The appellants relied on the availability of ejectment procedures under sections 42 and 43 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887.
The replacement public-premises law provided one procedure for ejecting unauthorised occupants of public premises and barred court proceedings in respect of that eviction.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 is not infringed on this ground where the public-premises law provides only one procedure for ejectment; the existence of a procedure under the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, does not create the choice between alternative procedures under the public-premises law that had produced the discrimination identified in Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab, [1967] 3 SCR 399. The Court relied on sections 15 and 20 of the 1971 Act and considered sections 42 and 43 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887.
members.conclusion: The availability of the tenancy-law procedure did not make the public-premises eviction procedure discriminatory under Article 14.

predicates.challenge_is_to_public_premises_eviction: A party challenges the procedure used to evict an unauthorised occupant from public premises.
predicates.public_premises_law_provides_one_evictio: The public-premises law provides only one procedure for ejectment of unauthorised occupants.
predicates.separate_tenancy_ejectment_procedure_is_: A separate law provides a procedure for ejectment in tenancy matters.

members.legal_issue: The enactment of a special eviction procedure does not impliedly remove the government’s right to seek eviction under the ordinary law when the two remedies can coexist without contradiction or absurdity.
material_facts: The government leased public premises to the occupants for a fixed term, and the lease expired.
The government called on the occupants to return the premises and initiated proceedings under a special statute providing a speedier eviction procedure.
The statute did not expressly bar an ordinary suit, and its stated purpose was to add a speedier remedy to the existing one.
members.legal_principle: Implied repeal is disfavoured and is justified only where the later enactment is incompatible with the earlier law, makes their coexistence absurd or inconvenient, or otherwise necessarily displaces the earlier law. The Court relied on Re Drummond, [1891] 1 Ch. 524; Re Chance, [1936] Ch. 266; and the statement in The India, as quoted in Craies on Statute Law, 6th ed., p. 371. The later enactment’s affirmative provision of a speedier remedy did not exclude the ordinary suit remedy.
members.conclusion: The special statute did not impliedly repeal or take away the government’s right to sue for eviction under the ordinary law.

predicates.challenge_to_eviction_law: A party challenging an eviction law argues that its enactment removed an existing ordinary-law remedy.
predicates.later_law_adds_a_remedy: The later law provides an additional procedure for obtaining eviction rather than expressly excluding the prior procedure.
predicates.remedies_can_coexist_without_absurdity: The ordinary and special procedures can operate together without contradiction, inconvenience, or absurd consequences.

members.legal_issue: Classifying occupants of publicly owned premises separately from occupants of privately owned premises is valid when the classification bears a rational relationship to the public interest in speedy recovery of public property.
material_facts: The challenged law applied a special procedure to occupants of public premises, distinguishing them from occupants of private premises.
The law’s object was to keep public premises free from encroachment and unauthorised occupation and to enable their speedy recovery.
The public has a vital interest in the recovery of public premises.
members.legal_principle: A classification is valid if it rests on an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons from others and that differentia has a rational relationship to the legislation’s object. Applying that test, the Court relied on Baburao Shantaram More v. The Bombay Housing Board, [1954] S.C.R. 572, which upheld differential treatment of tenants of public property where the classification was reasonably related to the legislative object.
members.conclusion: The classification between occupants of public premises and occupants of private premises was based on an intelligible differentia with a rational relationship to the law’s object and did not violate the equality guarantee.

predicates.challenge_to_public_property_classificat: A party challenges a law that treats occupants of public premises differently from occupants of private premises.
predicates.occupants_of_public_and_private_premises: The law places occupants of publicly owned premises in a distinct group from occupants of privately owned premises.
predicates.public_has_a_vital_interest_in_recovery: Members of the public have a vital interest in seeing the publicly owned premises freed from encroachment or unauthorised occupation.
predicates.speedy_recovery_is_the_legislative_objec: The law is intended to enable the prompt recovery of public premises.

members.legal_issue: A statutory summary procedure for eviction from public premises does not violate equality merely because it provides a different procedure and forum from ordinary proceedings.
material_facts: A constitutional challenge alleged that the law governing eviction from public land denied equality before the law.
The law provided a different procedure and forum for recovering possession of covered premises.
The High Court had invalidated the law, and the State appealed.
The Supreme Court had previously upheld analogous summary eviction provisions and had already applied that reasoning to reject a challenge to this law.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, providing a distinct summary procedure and forum for eviction from public premises is not, by itself, a denial of equality. The Court applied Maganlal Chhaganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which upheld analogous provisions, and Jai Dutta v. State of U.P., which held that the Article 14 challenge to this law was concluded by Maganlal Chhaganlal.
members.conclusion: The equality challenge fails; the law is constitutionally valid on that ground. The appeal is allowed, the High Court judgment is set aside, and the writ petition is dismissed.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_law and distinct_summary_eviction_procedure and constitutional_validity_appeal and analogous_procedure_previously_upheld

predicates.public_premises_eviction_law: The challenged law governs eviction from premises treated as public premises.
predicates.distinct_summary_eviction_procedure: The law provides a different procedure and forum for recovering possession than the ordinary process.
predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: An appeal concerns a judgment invalidating the law on constitutional grounds.
predicates.analogous_procedure_previously_upheld: A prior controlling decision upheld analogous summary eviction procedures against an equality challenge.

members.legal_issue: A final decision on an issue between the same parties in a proceeding binds them at a later stage of that proceeding, unless the issue concerns jurisdiction or conflicts with a statutory direction or prohibition.
material_facts: Earlier orders in the same proceedings between the parties permitted the principal’s existing power-of-attorney holder to appear only in that capacity, not as an advocate.
At a later stage, the opposing party again challenged the holder’s participation, including her examination of witnesses.
The earlier orders had been made by a competent court and had not been set aside or modified.
The Supreme Court found that the earlier orders did not conflict with a statutory prohibition or raise a jurisdictional issue.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 reflects the general doctrine of res judicata. The doctrine applies at a later stage of the same proceeding as well as in subsequent proceedings: Y.B. Patil v. Y.L. Patil. Even an erroneous decision between the same parties binds them when made by a competent court: Gorie Gouri Naidu v. Thandrothu Bodemma. A binding decision cannot be disregarded as per incuriam on principles applicable to precedent: S. Nagaraj v. B.R. Vasudeva Murthy. The doctrine does not apply where the issue concerns jurisdiction or giving effect to the decision would conflict with a statutory direction or prohibition: Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy and Allahabad Development Authority v. Nasiruzzaman. The doctrine is founded on finality and public policy: Daryao v. State of U.P.; Lal Chand v. Radha Krishan. A precedent binds in similar cases, whereas res judicata binds the parties to the proceedings: Makhija Construction & Engineering (P) Ltd. v. Indore Development Authority.
members.conclusion: The earlier orders operated as res judicata and barred reopening the issue of the holder’s capacity in the same proceedings. The High Court erred in deciding otherwise; its order was set aside and the trial court’s orders were restored.

rule.if: same_proceeding_stage and same_parties and same_issue_finally_decided_by_competent_court and not jurisdiction_or_statutory_conflict

predicates.same_proceeding_stage: The later dispute arose at a subsequent stage of the same proceeding in which the earlier decision was made.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later dispute were the same parties, or their privies, as those bound by the earlier decision.
predicates.same_issue_finally_decided_by_competent_: A competent court had finally decided the same issue between those parties.
predicates.jurisdiction_or_statutory_conflict: The issue concerns the court’s jurisdiction or giving effect to the earlier decision would conflict with a statutory direction or prohibition.

members.legal_issue: A Supreme Court determination of a legal question binds later challengers, including those who were not parties to the earlier proceeding, and prevents reopening that question in a later challenge.
material_facts: An earlier Supreme Court judgment had decided the interpretation and validity-related questions concerning the same acquisition, including whether the shares vested, whether there was a public purpose, and whether compensation was provided.
The petitioners sought to raise those questions again in a later constitutional writ petition.
The Court held that the earlier judgment bound the petitioners even if they had not been parties to it, and that the decided questions could not be collaterally reopened.
members.legal_principle: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India. In M/s. Shenoy and Co. v. Commercial Tax Officer, the Court explained that a Supreme Court judgment binds those concerned whether or not they were parties to it. T. Govindaraja Mudaliar v. State of Tamil Nadu, relying on Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab, states that a decision remains binding where the point was actually decided, even if a particular argument was not considered.
members.conclusion: The earlier Supreme Court judgment was binding under Article 141 of the Constitution, and the questions it had decided were no longer open for agitation in the later petition.

predicates.later_constitutional_challenge: A person brings a later constitutional proceeding to challenge a legal measure or its application.
predicates.earlier_supreme_court_judgment_decided_t: The Supreme Court had already decided the same legal question in an earlier judgment.

members.legal_issue: An issue directly and substantially decided in an earlier proceeding between the parties cannot be relitigated in a later proceeding.
material_facts: In an earlier proceeding, the High Court dismissed the appellant’s challenge after deciding that the other party had acquired occupant rights upon abolition and vesting.
That issue was directly and substantially in dispute in the earlier proceeding.
The appellant sought to contest the same occupant-rights issue again in the later proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The principles of res judicata prevent re-agitation of an issue that directly and substantially fell for determination and was decided against a party in an earlier proceeding. The Court applied those principles to the earlier High Court decision concerning acquisition of occupant rights.
members.conclusion: The question whether the other party had acquired occupant rights was barred by res judicata and could not be re-agitated.

predicates.later_proceeding_repeats_issue: A party raised in a later proceeding an issue that had been raised in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue_directly_and_substantially_de: The same issue directly and substantially arose in the earlier proceeding and was decided against that party.

members.legal_issue: A finding on a matter essential to an earlier final decision binds the parties in later proceedings even if no formal issue was framed on that matter.
material_facts: In the earlier civil suit, the Endowments Commissioner pleaded that the gift deed gave only a general power of attorney, making the nature and effect of the deed material to the dispute.
The first appellate court and the High Court found that the land had been gifted absolutely, that the Government had no interest in it, and that the private temple did not make the land an endowment.
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals from those decisions and stated that the findings had to be sustained.
The appellants later sought to reopen those findings, although they had become final and were necessary to resolve the earlier dispute.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC embodies res judicata. Under Sajjadanashin Sayed v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer, whether a matter was directly and substantially in issue depends on whether its decision was material and essential to the earlier judgment, assessed from the pleadings and decision rather than solely from the formal issues. The court also relied on Vithal Yeshwant Jathar v. Shikandarkhan Makhtumkhan Sardesai and Raj Laxmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen, and distinguished decisions concerning incidental findings or decisions made without jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The findings in the earlier litigation were binding and could not be reopened; the bar of res judicata applied despite the absence of a formally framed issue.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: A later proceeding concerns the same parties or persons claiming through them.
predicates.earlier_decision_final: An earlier court decision resolving the matter has become final.
predicates.disputed_finding_essential_to_earlier_de: The disputed finding was material and necessary to the earlier court’s decision, even if no formal issue was framed on it.

members.legal_issue: A final determination between the same parties on the Family Court’s jurisdiction to hear their property dispute binds those parties in a later challenge.
material_facts: A Division Bench of the Kerala High Court had previously decided, in a dispute between the same parties, that a dispute over property between parties to a marriage was not limited to parties whose marriage was still subsisting.
That decision had attained finality.
The appellant later challenged the Family Court’s jurisdiction in the property dispute.
members.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the prior Division Bench decision and held that, because it was between the same parties and had attained finality, it operated as res judicata.
members.conclusion: The prior final determination between the parties operated as res judicata on the jurisdiction issue.

predicates.later_jurisdiction_challenge: A party later challenged the tribunal’s authority to hear the dispute.
predicates.prior_final_interparty_determination_on_: A prior final decision between the same parties had determined the same jurisdiction issue.

members.legal_issue: A final order made at an earlier stage of a proceeding may bind the parties at a later stage of that same proceeding under the principles of res judicata.
material_facts: A court had earlier held that the tribunal could not reopen factual findings in revision and remanded the matter for decision consistently with that direction.
No appeal was filed against the earlier order, which became final.
At the later stage of the same proceeding, the tribunal followed the direction and the appellants sought to challenge the resulting decision.
members.legal_principle: The principles of res judicata apply not only between separate proceedings but also at a subsequent stage of the same proceeding: an order that becomes final during a proceeding binds at a later stage. The Court applied this principle to the earlier High Court order directing the tribunal not to reopen questions of fact in revision; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The earlier final order bound the parties and the tribunal at the later stage, and the factual questions it had settled could not be reopened.

predicates.same_proceeding: The later decision is made at a subsequent stage of the same proceeding in which the earlier order was made.
predicates.prior_order_final: An earlier order resolving the relevant issue became final and was not successfully challenged.
predicates.later_stage_revisits_same_issue: A party seeks at a later stage to reopen an issue resolved by the earlier order.

members.legal_issue: An issue finally decided in one of two separate suits between the same parties cannot be reopened in a second appeal arising from the other suit when the decision in the first suit was not appealed.
material_facts: The parties brought two separate suits that raised the same question of an easement for the flow of water for fishing purposes.
The issue was directly and substantially in issue in the suit brought by the respondents and was decided against them by the District Court.
The respondents did not appeal the District Court’s decision in their suit, so it became final.
The respondents’ second appeal concerned the decree in the appellant’s separate suit; the District Court had disposed of appeals from both suits in a common judgment.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation I, bars trial of an issue directly and substantially in issue between the same parties when it has been heard and finally decided in a former suit; a suit decided earlier is a former suit even if instituted later, provided its decision preceded the decision in the suit under consideration. Under Sheodan Singh v. Smt. Daryao Kunwar, decisions in separate suits on common issues can operate as res judicata in one another; Badri Narayan Singh v. Kamdeo Prasad Singh confirms that a common appellate judgment may embody separate decisions. Narhari v. Shanker was distinguished because it concerned one suit, not separate suits.
members.conclusion: The fishing-easement issue was barred by res judicata and could not be decided again in the second appeal arising from the other suit.

rule.if: separate_suits_between_same_parties and same_issue_directly_and_substantially_in_both and issue_finally_decided_in_one_suit and decision_not_appealed_in_that_suit and second_appeal_arises_from_other_suit

predicates.separate_suits_between_same_parties: The same parties litigated the matter in two separate suits.
predicates.same_issue_directly_and_substantially_in: The same issue was directly and substantially in dispute in each suit.
predicates.issue_finally_decided_in_one_suit: A court heard and finally decided the issue in one of the suits before the second appeal was decided.
predicates.decision_not_appealed_in_that_suit: The party against whom the decision was made did not appeal the decision in that suit.
predicates.second_appeal_arises_from_other_suit: The proceeding is a second appeal arising from the other of the two suits.

members.legal_issue: A court’s express determination of a matter at an earlier stage of the same proceeding binds the parties at later stages when it is not merely interlocutory and has not been successfully challenged.
material_facts: In the proceeding to set aside the ex parte eviction order, the court accepted the tenant’s unrebutted evidence that the landlord had agreed to withdraw the eviction petition and had received rent directly from the tenant.
The landlord had contested the tenant’s account but did not enter the witness box, and the court expressly found that the landlord had agreed to withdraw the petition and receive rent.
The eviction petition was later allowed to proceed on the ground of rent arrears, and the earlier finding was not set aside on appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle of res judicata between stages of the same litigation, a matter decided at an earlier stage cannot ordinarily be re-agitated at a later stage. As stated in Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, this principle applies where a court has already decided a matter in one way in the same proceeding. It does not prevent reconsideration of interlocutory orders that do not finally determine the parties’ rights, and an earlier decision may be reviewed by an appellate authority in an appeal against the final judgment. Here, the express finding in the proceeding to set aside the ex parte order was binding because it determined the disputed matter and was not successfully challenged.
members.conclusion: The earlier finding bound the landlord at the later stage of the same proceeding. The eviction petition should therefore be dismissed; the appeal was allowed and the judgments below were set aside.

predicates.same_proceeding: The parties are at a later stage of the same proceeding in which the earlier determination was made.
predicates.earlier_court_expressly_determined_dispu: A court expressly decided a disputed matter at an earlier stage of the proceeding.
predicates.determination_was_not_merely_interlocuto: The earlier determination finally resolved the disputed matter rather than addressing a matter that did not purport to decide the parties’ rights.
predicates.determination_was_not_successfully_chall: The earlier determination was not set aside or otherwise successfully challenged through an available appeal or review.
predicates.earlier_determination_binds_parties_at_l: The parties cannot re-agitate the matter decided by the earlier determination at a later stage of the same proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Findings in an earlier final judgment between the same parties remain binding in later proceedings when special leave to appeal from that judgment was not granted.
material_facts: An earlier High Court Division Bench had decided that the government grant was valid, that the claimants were entitled to the price of the land rather than its restoration, and that they had waived their right to occupy it.

The claimants sought special leave to appeal from that judgment, but the Supreme Court disposed of the petition without granting special leave, leaving them liberty to ask the government to consider modifying the grant.
In later proceedings, the High Court treated the earlier findings as non-binding, in part because it considered the earlier judgment per incuriam.
members.legal_principle: Under Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, refusal of special leave does not attract the doctrine of merger or substitute the challenged order. A prior judgment's findings between the parties remain binding in later proceedings. The doctrine of per incuriam concerns precedent and does not displace res judicata; as explained in Tarini Charan Bhattacharjee v. Kedar Nath Haldar, the correctness of a prior decision does not determine whether it operates as res judicata.
members.conclusion: The earlier findings remained final and binding between the parties; the Supreme Court's order refusing special leave did not replace or disturb the earlier judgment.

predicates.earlier_writ_appeal_decided_issues: An earlier appellate proceeding decided issues concerning the same underlying dispute.
predicates.same_parties_later_proceeding: The parties to the earlier proceeding or their successors raised the dispute again in a later proceeding.
predicates.special_leave_not_granted: The reviewing court disposed of the challenge without granting special leave to appeal.

members.legal_issue: A finding on an issue in an earlier proceeding is binding in a later proceeding only when it was directly and substantially in issue, rather than merely collateral or incidental.
material_facts: The appeal concerned whether findings in earlier proceedings barred a later inquiry into whether the religious endowments were public trusts.
The earlier proceedings included a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure and administrative inquiries under the public trusts law.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure distinguishes matters directly and substantially in issue from matters only collaterally or incidentally in issue. Applying the tests discussed in Mulla, the court said the pleadings, issues, and judgment must be examined to determine whether resolution of the issue was necessary and material to the decision. It relied on Ishwar Singh v. Sarwan Singh and Mohd. S. Labbai v. Mohd. Hanifa, and discussed Run Bahadur v. Lucho Koer, Asrar Ahmed v. Durgah Committee, Pragdasji v. Ishwarlal Bhai, Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, and Uthiva Somasundareswarar v. Rajanga as illustrations of the distinction.
members.conclusion: A finding on an issue that was only collateral or incidental in the earlier proceeding is not ordinarily res judicata; the court must determine whether the issue was necessary to the earlier decision and formed its substantive basis.

predicates.prior_and_later_proceedings: A party relies on a finding from an earlier proceeding in a later proceeding.
predicates.issue_was_necessary_to_prior_decision: The earlier court had to decide the issue to adjudicate the principal matter before it.
predicates.prior_decision_rest_on_issue: The earlier decision rested substantively on its determination of the issue, rather than treating it as an auxiliary step in its reasoning.

members.legal_issue: A difference in the right of appeal from two decisions does not prevent res judicata when the same issue has been finally decided and the earlier decision has not been challenged.
material_facts: The High Court heard and decided the appeals in the partition suit and the money suit together, issuing separate judgments and decrees.
The appellant could appeal to the Supreme Court as of right in the partition suit but had no equivalent right in the money suit.
The appellant did not challenge the High Court’s decision in the money suit, including by seeking special leave, and that decision became final.
The issue decided in the money suit was also material to the partition suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the relevant question is whether the same issue was heard and finally decided, not whether each decision carried the same right of appeal. Explanation I addresses a decision in a former suit that has become final. The Court relied on Lortankutty v. Thomman and Bhugwanbutti Chowdhrani v. A.H. Forbes.
members.conclusion: The different rights of appeal did not prevent the final decision in the money suit from operating as res judicata in the appeal concerning the partition suit.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_a_decision_on_a_shared_issue and same_issue_was_finally_decided in another suit and other_suit_decision_was_left_unchallenged and appeal_rights_differed

predicates.appeal_challenges_a_decision_on_a_shared: A party appeals from a decision that concerns an issue also decided in another suit.
predicates.same_issue_was_finally_decided in anothe: The issue was heard and finally decided in the other suit.
predicates.other_suit_decision_was_left_unchallenge: The party did not pursue an available procedure to challenge the decision in the other suit, and it became final.
predicates.appeal_rights_differed: The party had a different right or route of appeal against the two decisions.

members.legal_issue: A factual issue finally determined between parties remains binding on them in a later proceeding, even when that proceeding concerns different property and a different cause of action.
material_facts: The earlier proceeding between the parties determined as a matter of fact that the claimants were born to the deceased.
That factual determination became final.
The claimants accepted the earlier finding about their parentage in the later proceeding, which concerned different land.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished res judicata from issue estoppel. Where the later proceeding concerns different property and a different cause of action, res judicata does not bar the proceeding; however, factual issues finally determined between the parties remain binding through issue estoppel. The Court described estoppel as arising from principles of evidence, including Sections 115, 116 and 117 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and principles of equity, and referred to Ahsan Hussain Abdul Ali Bohari v. Maina W/o Nathu Telanga.
members.conclusion: The final factual determination remained binding on the parties under issue estoppel, although the legal question decided in the earlier proceeding could be reconsidered.

rule.if: subsequent_proceeding_different_property and same_parties and different_cause_of_action and prior_judgment_final and prior_factual_issue_determined

predicates.subsequent_proceeding_different_property: A party brought a later proceeding concerning property different from the property in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later proceeding were the same as the parties to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.different_cause_of_action: The later proceeding arose from a cause of action different from the one in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_judgment_final: The earlier judgment between the parties had become final.
predicates.prior_factual_issue_determined: The earlier proceeding finally determined a factual issue between the parties.

members.legal_issue: Equality does not entitle a person to receive a benefit granted to another person, including a benefit that is unlawful or irregular.
material_facts: The tender allottees sought the lower fees and relaxed zoning restrictions given to the stallholders, or argued that the differences made their treatment discriminatory.
The tender allottees had accepted their own allotment terms, including the applicable fee and trade-zone restrictions.
The court held that a person may challenge an unlawful benefit given to another but cannot demand that the same unlawful benefit be extended to them.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 guarantees equality as a positive right and does not require the State to repeat an illegality or irregularity. A claim under Article 14, including in proceedings under Article 226, must establish that a just and lawful entitlement was denied while being extended to others; Article 12 identifies the State authorities to which the equality guarantee applies.
members.conclusion: The allottees could not claim the concessions given to the stallholders merely on grounds of equality.

predicates.equality_claim_seeks_extension_of_anothe: A claimant in an equality review proceeding asks the authority to extend to them a benefit granted to another group.
predicates.claimant_accepted_different_allotment_te: The claimant knowingly accepted allotment terms different from those granted to the other group.

members.legal_issue: A claimant cannot obtain equal treatment by relying on benefits wrongly granted to other ineligible applicants.
material_facts: The claimant argued that other societies in a similar position had received the scheme’s benefits.
The Authority disputed that assertion, but the Court considered the argument on the assumption that benefits had been granted to ineligible societies.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require repetition of an unlawful action to achieve equal treatment; equal treatment presupposes a similar legal footing and does not recognize negative equality. The Court relied on Union of India v. International Trading Co. (2003) 5 SCC 437.
members.conclusion: Even if other ineligible societies received the benefits, that did not give the claimant a right to them or establish discrimination.

predicates.benefit_denial_appeal: A claimant appeals a decision upholding the denial of benefits under a scheme.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_other_grants: The claimant relies on benefits granted to other applicants as a basis for demanding the same treatment.
predicates.other_grants_were_to_ineligible_applican: The other applicants who received benefits did not qualify for them.

members.legal_issue: Article 14 does not entitle a person to an unlawful land allotment merely because comparable allotments have been made to others.
material_facts: The private respondents asserted that similarly situated persons had received land at concessional rates.
The Court found that no factual foundation had been laid for that assertion.
The allotments under challenge were themselves contrary to the governing statutory rules.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 embodies a positive concept of equality and cannot be invoked to perpetuate an illegality. The Court relied on Jalandhar Improvement Trust v. Sampuran Singh and State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Prasad Singh.
members.conclusion: The asserted treatment of other applicants could not sustain the challenged allotments or support an Article 14 claim to repeat an illegality.

predicates.land_allotment_equality_claim: A party claims equal treatment in a land-allotment matter by referring to other applicants.
predicates.challenged_allotment_is_illegal: The allotment at issue is contrary to the governing law or rules.
predicates.no_factual_basis_for_comparator_claim: The party has not established a factual basis showing that the asserted comparators were similarly situated.

members.legal_issue: Equal protection does not entitle a claimant to repeat a benefit given to others in a special case or to perpetuate an erroneous benefit.
material_facts: The appellant argued that denying her the benefit was discriminatory because other persons had received benefits under the Government Orders.
The benefit had been given to three co-owners as a special case because their strip of land remained outside the allotment and was unsuitable or inconvenient to use independently.
The general policy consistently excluded purchasers who acquired land after publication of the acquisition notice.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution does not require the repetition or perpetuation of a wrong. A claimant cannot demand equal treatment with beneficiaries whose benefits arose from a special, materially different circumstance, or obtain a benefit merely because it may have been wrongly granted to others.
members.conclusion: The denial of the benefit was not invidiously discriminatory, and any benefit wrongly given to others did not entitle the appellant to the same benefit.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge_to_denial: The proceeding includes a challenge that denying a claimed benefit while others received it violated equal protection.
predicates.other_benefit_confined_to_special_circum: The benefit given to others arose from a specific circumstance not shared by the claimant.
predicates.claim_seeks_repetition_of_that_benefit: The claimant seeks the same benefit on the ground that it was granted to others, including where that grant may have been erroneous.

members.legal_issue: A writ court cannot require an authority to extend a benefit merely because it granted that benefit to another person, without determining that the other grant was lawful and that the cases are materially similar.
material_facts: The High Court ordered restoration of a cancelled plot because another allottee had obtained restoration on different terms.
The High Court did not determine whether the other allottee’s restoration was lawful or whether the cases were materially similar.
The Administration said the other allottee had not received a refund of her deposited money, unlike the respondents, but the High Court did not resolve that distinction.
members.legal_principle: The discretionary and extraordinary writ jurisdiction cannot be used to compel an authority to repeat an illegal or unwarranted act. A prior administrative order is not a judicial precedent. A similar benefit may be extended only if the earlier order was lawful and justified and the claimant’s case is similar in material respects. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not grant relief on that basis; the appeal was allowed and its judgment set aside.

predicates.writ_petition_seeking_comparator_treatme: The claimant brought a writ petition seeking the same treatment that an authority had given to another person.
predicates.comparator_order_unlawful: The other person's benefit was contrary to law or unwarranted in the circumstances of that person's case.
predicates.materially_similar: The claimant's case is similar to the other person's case in material respects.

members.legal_issue: A writ cannot be granted solely because another person received similar relief unless the other person’s order was lawful and the claimant’s case was materially similar.
material_facts: The High Court directed restoration of a plot based on restoration granted to another allottee after a settlement before a Lok Adalat.
The High Court did not investigate the facts of the other allottee’s case or find that the restoration order was lawful and justified.
The Administration pointed out that the other allottee had not received a refund of the amount paid, unlike the claimants, but the High Court did not resolve that distinction.
members.legal_principle: The discretionary writ jurisdiction cannot compel an authority to repeat an illegal or unwarranted order. An order or action of an authority does not become a judicial precedent merely because it was made in another case. The claimant’s entitlement must be assessed on the facts and law applicable to that claimant. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not grant relief on the basis of discrimination without finding that the comparator’s order was lawful and that the cases were similar in material respects.

rule.if: writ_petition_claims_equal_treatment and relief_was_granted_to_comparator and (comparator_order_lawfulness_not_established or material_similarity_not_established)

predicates.writ_petition_claims_equal_treatment: A person seeks relief in a writ petition on the ground that another person received equal treatment.
predicates.relief_was_granted_to_comparator: An authority granted the assertedly comparable person the relief sought by the writ petitioner.
predicates.comparator_order_lawfulness_not_establis: The court has not established that the order granting relief to the comparable person was lawful and justified.
predicates.material_similarity_not_established: The court has not established that the claimant’s case is similar to the comparable person’s case in material respects.

members.legal_issue: An exemption wrongly granted to another landholder does not entitle a claimant to the same exemption under the principle of equality.
material_facts: An adjacent nursery had received an exemption from acquisition.
The appellant’s residential site was not exempted, and he sought the same benefit.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution does not require an authority to extend a benefit granted through wrongful action to another person; a wrongful exemption does not create a right to equal treatment in that wrong. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The exemption granted to the adjacent nursery did not entitle the appellant to an exemption, and the claim of discrimination under Article 14 failed.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity or effect of a land acquisition.
predicates.claimant_seeks_same_exemption: The claimant seeks an exemption because another landholder received one.
predicates.comparator_exemption_was_wrongful: The exemption received by the other landholder was granted through wrongful action by the authorities.
predicates.wrongful_exemption_does_not_require_equa: A wrongful exemption granted to another person does not require the same exemption to be granted to the claimant.

members.legal_issue: Article 14 does not entitle a person whose land is acquired to the same exemption as another person if that other person’s exemption was unlawful.
material_facts: The landowners challenged the acquisition as discriminatory because several other industrial units had been exempted.
The exempted units had constructed factory buildings and begun manufacturing; the appellants had taken no tangible steps to erect factory buildings or begin production.
One exempted unit’s construction, alleged to be unlawful, had been regularized.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require repetition of an unlawful act as a form of equal treatment; equal treatment presupposes a similar legal foothold. The Court applied Union of India v. International Trading Co. and Anr.
members.conclusion: Even if the exemptions granted to the other units were erroneous or illegal, the appellants had no right under Article 14 to receive the same relief; granting it would perpetuate a wrong.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the acquisition of their land.
predicates.exemption_claim_based_on_comparator: The person claims exemption by relying on another landholder who was exempted from acquisition.
predicates.comparator_exemption_was_illegal: The other landholder’s exemption was unlawful or unjustified.

members.legal_issue: Article 14 does not entitle a person to retain or obtain an unlawful benefit merely because others obtained similar benefits.
material_facts: Some beneficiaries of the impugned allotment arrangements had received plots or possession.
The applicants relied on the treatment of other persons and on later regularization measures to claim comparable relief.
The asserted benefits arose from allotments or transactions already held unlawful.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 protects persons who have a legal and valid right and does not require repetition or continuation of illegal or ultra vires acts. The Court relied on Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain (1997) 1 SCC 35, which rejected the use of equality to legitimize unlawful allotments.
members.conclusion: The applicants could not claim regularization or equal treatment by relying on unlawful benefits conferred on others.

predicates.equal_treatment_claim: A person seeks the same treatment or benefit given to other persons said to be similarly situated.
predicates.claimed_comparator_benefit_is_unlawful: The benefit relied on was conferred through an unlawful or ultra vires act.

members.legal_issue: Equal protection does not entitle an owner to an exemption merely because another owner received one, particularly where the owners have not been shown to be similarly situated in all material respects or the claimant does not meet the governing eligibility requirements.
material_facts: The owners alleged that other orchard lands had been exempted while their orchard land was not.
The record did not establish that the other landowner’s circumstances were similar in all essential particulars.
The owners’ land had not been found unnecessary for the scheme, and the asserted exemption of another owner did not establish that they met the statutory conditions.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution requires equal treatment of persons in substantially the same circumstances, including in the administration of law. It does not require repetition of an erroneous benefit, nor does it assist a claimant who fails to satisfy the applicable requirements of Section 56 of the Punjab Towns Improvement Act, 1922. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The owners had not established hostile discrimination, and an exemption allegedly granted to another person, even if granted erroneously, did not give them a right to exemption.

predicates.acquisition_exemption_challenge: A person challenges the administration of an acquisition scheme on the ground that another landowner received an exemption.
predicates.similarly_situated: The claimant and the person who received an exemption are alike in all material circumstances.
predicates.claimant_ineligible: The claimant does not satisfy the requirements governing the claimed exemption.

members.legal_issue: Equal treatment does not entitle a litigant to relief merely because similar litigants previously received relief through erroneous orders.
material_facts: The appellants relied on other similar matters in which delay had been condoned on the condition that interest would not be paid for the period of delay.
The Court considered those orders erroneous because they had been made without addressing the requirement of sufficient cause.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution does not provide negative equality or require the repetition of an illegality. The Court relied on Chandigarh Administration v. Jagjit Singh, M/s. Anand Button Ltd. v. State of Haryana, K.K. Bhalla v. State of M.P., and Fuljit Kaur v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The earlier orders did not entitle the appellants to the same relief; an erroneous or illegal order cannot be repeated on grounds of equality.

predicates.delayed_statutory_appeal: The matter concerns a statutory appeal filed after the prescribed period.
predicates.equal_treatment_claim: The applicant seeks the same relief as other litigants on the ground of equal treatment.
predicates.prior_similar_relief_granted_erroneously: Other litigants received similar relief through orders that failed to apply the governing legal requirements.

members.legal_issue: The equality guarantee does not entitle a person to repeat or retain an unlawful allotment granted to someone else.
material_facts: The respondents sought possession partly because other persons had obtained possession under allotments founded on the same invalid award and asserted policy.
The authority had cancelled some allotments, withheld possession in other cases, and consistently resisted enforcement of the unlawful allotments.
The High Court nevertheless directed allotment to the respondents on the ground that denying them the same benefit would be discriminatory.
members.legal_principle: The equality guarantee protects legal rights and similarly situated persons who have a valid legal claim; it does not require repetition or perpetuation of an illegal or ultra vires act. The Court relied on Yadu Nandan Garg v. State of Rajasthan, Coromandel Fertilizers Ltd. v. Union of India and Chandigarh Administration v. Jagjit Singh, which hold that a wrong benefit granted to one person does not entitle another to the same benefit.
members.conclusion: The respondents could not rely on equality to obtain an unlawful allotment, and the High Court erred in directing allotment on that basis.

predicates.equality_claim_case: The proceeding includes a claim that unequal treatment violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.claimant_seeks_same_benefit_as_another_p: The claimant seeks a benefit because another person received a similar benefit.
predicates.comparator_benefit_is_unlawful: The benefit received by the other person was contrary to law or unsupported by legal authority.

members.legal_issue: A final decision in an injunction suit can bar a later title suit when title was directly and substantially in issue and decided in the injunction suit.
material_facts: In an earlier injunction suit, the court considered the parties’ competing rights in the property and determined the nature of the interest created by a settlement deed.
The injunction decree became final, and the same title issue was raised in a later suit between the parties or their privies.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC applies when title is directly and substantially in issue in an injunction suit and is decided; the equitable nature of the injunction remedy does not prevent the decision from operating as res judicata in a later title suit between the same parties or their privies.
members.conclusion: The injunction decree operated as res judicata in the later suit based on title because the title issue had been directly and substantially in issue and decided in the earlier suit.

rule.if: injunction_suit and title_directly_in_issue and title_finally_decided and later_title_suit_between_parties_or_privies

predicates.injunction_suit: The earlier proceeding sought an injunction concerning rights in property.
predicates.title_directly_in_issue: The parties’ title or interest in the property was directly and substantially in issue in that proceeding.
predicates.title_finally_decided: The court decided the title or interest issue, and its decision became final.
predicates.later_title_suit_between_parties_or_priv: A later suit based on title was brought between the same parties or persons claiming through them.

members.legal_issue: A finding on title in an earlier proceeding bars a later title determination only when title was directly and substantially in issue and was heard and finally decided.
material_facts: A person claiming ownership brought a later suit seeking a determination of title after an eviction suit in a Small Causes Court.
The defendant in the eviction suit had filed a written statement claiming ownership, but the Small Causes Court’s decision did not refer to that pleading or address title.
The later suit directly raised the question of title.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle in Gangabai w/o Rambilas Gilda v. Chhabubai w/o Pukharajji Gandhi, a matter bars a later suit as res judicata only if it was directly and substantially in issue in the earlier suit and was heard and finally decided. A finding that is merely collateral or incidental does not suffice.
members.conclusion: Res judicata did not bar determination of title in the later suit because the earlier court had not addressed or decided title.

predicates.later_suit_seeks_title: A party brought a later suit seeking a determination of rights in property based on title.
predicates.earlier_case_was_small_causes_eviction: The earlier proceeding was an eviction suit before a Small Causes Court.
predicates.prior_title_issue_was_not_adjudicated: The earlier court did not address or decide the title issue, even though a party had raised a claim of ownership.

members.legal_issue: An earlier judgment in an injunction suit does not bind a later proceeding on title unless deciding title was necessary to grant or refuse the injunction and the relief was based on that title determination.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought an injunction and was not a suit on title.
The earlier decision did not decide title.
The later proceedings directly concerned title to the property.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11 CPC, an incidental finding on title in an earlier injunction suit is not binding in a later proceeding where title is directly in issue unless it was necessary to decide title to grant or refuse the injunction and the relief was founded on that title finding. The Court relied on Sajjadanashin Sayed v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer, (2000) 3 SCC 350.
members.conclusion: The earlier injunction decree could not bind the parties on title because title had not been decided in that suit. An incidental title finding would not bind a later proceeding in which title is directly in issue unless deciding title was necessary to the injunction and the relief was based on that finding.

rule.if: later_proceeding_directly_puts_title_in_issue and earlier_suit_sought_only_injunction and (not title_finding_necessary or not injunction_relief_based_on_title)

predicates.later_proceeding_directly_puts_title_in_: The later proceeding directly requires determination of title to the property.
predicates.earlier_suit_sought_only_injunction: The earlier suit sought an injunction rather than a determination of title.
predicates.title_finding_necessary: A finding on title was necessary to grant or refuse the injunction in the earlier suit.
predicates.injunction_relief_based_on_title: The relief granted or refused in the earlier suit was founded on the title finding.

members.legal_issue: A final determination of title in a land acquisition reference operates as res judicata in a later suit between the parties when title was necessarily and substantially in issue.
material_facts: Rival claimants sought compensation for acquired property on the basis of competing claims to the same share of an estate.
The apportionment dispute required the court to decide which claimant held title to that share.
The title question was contested through the lower courts and finally decided on appeal.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata rests on general principles of jurisprudence, not solely on section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A decision on title in a compensation reference is binding when title was necessarily and substantially determined. The Court applied Ramachandra Rao v. Ramachandra Rao and Bhagwati v. Ram Kali, and referred to the general principles discussed in Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Singh, Badar Bee v. Habib Merican Noordin, and Hook v. Administrator-General of Bengal.
members.conclusion: The final title determination in the land acquisition proceedings barred the rival claimant from relitigating title in the subsequent possession suit.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and rival_title_claims and title_necessary_to_apportionment and title_decided_finally and same_parties_or_privies

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A dispute over compensation for acquired property was referred to a court for determination.
predicates.rival_title_claims: Competing claimants asserted that they held title to the property or share relevant to the compensation.
predicates.title_necessary_to_apportionment: The entitlement to compensation depended on resolving the competing claims to title.
predicates.title_decided_finally: The court finally determined the title question after it was contested.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The later dispute over title involved the same parties or persons claiming through them.

members.legal_issue: Findings essential to judgment in an earlier injunction suit based on title may preclude the parties from relitigating those findings in later partition proceedings.
material_facts: The purchasers’ predecessors brought an injunction suit relying on the 1959 sale deed and claiming rights over the entire disputed property.
The courts in that suit found that the sale was affected by lis pendens, that the purchaser could claim only the vendor’s share, and that adverse possession had not been established.
The injunction suit’s findings were affirmed in the appellate proceedings and were not open to challenge in the later final-decree proceedings.
