members.legal_principle: Under the res judicata principles explained in Sajjadanashin Sayed Md. B.E. Edr. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer and Commissioner of Endowments v. Vittal Rao, a matter is directly and substantially in issue when its determination was necessary and material to the earlier judgment and formed its substantive basis. Whether a title finding in an injunction suit has that effect depends on the pleadings, issues, judgment, and whether title was essential to the relief, consistently with Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy.
members.conclusion: The findings that the purchase was made during the pending partition suit and that the purchaser could claim only the vendor’s share were final and operated as res judicata in the later proceedings; the court nevertheless examined the relevant matters afresh on their merits.

rule.if: injunction_suit_based_on_title and (title_or_transfer_finding_essential or purchase_during_pending_partition_found) and earlier_finding_final

predicates.injunction_suit_based_on_title: A claimant brought an injunction proceeding relying on a claimed interest in the disputed property.
predicates.title_or_transfer_finding_essential: The court had to determine title or the legal effect of a transfer to decide the requested injunction.
predicates.purchase_during_pending_partition_found: The earlier court determined that the property had been purchased while a partition proceeding was pending.
predicates.earlier_finding_final: The finding was affirmed or otherwise became final and was not set aside.

members.legal_issue: A later land-grabbing proceeding is barred by res judicata when a competent court has finally determined the same parties’ substantial dispute over the identity and title of the same property.
material_facts: An earlier specific-performance proceeding finally determined that the disputed land was part of one survey parcel and distinct from the other parcels later claimed by the opposing side.
Earlier land-grabbing proceedings concerning the same property were dismissed, and the determination of the property’s identity and ownership attained finality.
A later land-grabbing case again disputed the identity and title of the same property.
The Supreme Court found that the requirements of res judicata were satisfied.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata is a principle of public policy that promotes finality and prevents repeated litigation of the same matter. It is not confined to suits governed by Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and may apply to other proceedings. Its requirements include the same litigating parties, an identical subject matter, a final decision, and a decision by a competent court. A final determination of the same substantial issue cannot be relitigated in a later proceeding. The Court relied on Bombay Gas Co. v. Jagannath Pandurang; Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramanandan Prasad Narayan Singh; Sri Bhavanarayanaswamivari Temple v. Vadapalli Venkata Bhavanarayana Charyulu; Syed Mohd. Salie Labbai v. Mohd. Hanifa; Narayana Prabhu Venkateswara Prabhu v. Narayana Prabhu Krishna Prabhu; and Ramji Gupta v. Gopi Krishan Agrawal. The later proceeding was before the Special Court under Section 8(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, but the bar arose from res judicata.
members.conclusion: The later land-grabbing proceeding was barred by res judicata. The orders refusing to quash it, and the High Court judgment upholding those orders, were set aside.

rule.if: later_land_grabbing_proceeding and prior_competent_final_adjudication and same_litigating_parties and same_substantial_property_issue

predicates.later_land_grabbing_proceeding: A claimant brought a later proceeding under a special process for adjudicating alleged land grabbing.
predicates.prior_competent_final_adjudication: A court with authority had finally determined the identity or title of the disputed property in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_litigating_parties: The parties to the later dispute were the same as, or legally represented by, parties to the earlier adjudication.
predicates.same_substantial_property_issue: The later proceeding disputed the identity or title of the same property that had been substantially determined earlier.

members.legal_issue: A later title-and-possession suit is barred by res judicata, even though the earlier suit sought eviction on a tenancy basis, when the same tenancy-derived status was directly and substantially litigated and a finding of adverse possession became final against the relevant defendants.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought rent and possession, relying both on a rent note and on the alleged tenancy of the defendants’ father under the owner’s predecessor.
The trial court rejected the tenancy claims and found that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession.
The plaintiff’s appeal was dismissed as time-barred against two defendants, and the adverse-possession finding concerning them was not disturbed in the later appeals.
The later suit involved the same parties and property, sought title and possession, and again relied on the alleged tenancy of the defendants’ father.
members.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a matter directly and substantially in issue that has been finally adjudicated between the same parties concerning the same subject matter cannot be reopened in a subsequent suit. A difference in the form of relief or in the later suit’s emphasis on title does not avoid the bar where the tenancy-derived status was directly and substantially in issue and its rejection was necessary to the earlier adverse-possession finding. The Court relied on Krishna Behari Roy v. Banwari Lall Roy for the rule against retrying a finally determined issue concerning status.
members.conclusion: The later suit was barred by res judicata against the two defendants for whom the adverse-possession finding had become final, but not against the other defendants.

rule.if: prior_eviction_proceeding and later_title_and_possession_proceeding and same_parties_and_property and tenancy_derived_status_directly_litigated and adverse_possession_finding_left_final_for_those_parties

predicates.prior_eviction_proceeding: A claimant brought an earlier proceeding seeking possession by evicting occupants on a tenancy basis.
predicates.later_title_and_possession_proceeding: The claimant later brought a proceeding seeking a declaration of title and possession of the same property.
predicates.same_parties_and_property: The earlier and later proceedings involved the same opposing parties and the same property.
predicates.tenancy_derived_status_directly_litigate: The parties directly disputed whether the occupants’ status derived from an earlier tenancy of their predecessor.
predicates.adverse_possession_finding_left_final_fo: A court found that the occupants had acquired title by adverse possession, and that finding remained undisturbed and final as to those parties.

members.legal_issue: A finding on an heirship issue in an earlier suit between the same parties is res judicata in a later possession suit when the issue was directly and substantially in dispute and its determination was necessary to decide the earlier suit fully.
material_facts: In the earlier suit, the claimant sought a declaration of title and an injunction, relying both on an alleged oral will and on his lawful possession of the property.

The claimant disputed that the opposing parties were related to the deceased owner or had any title superior to his possessory claim; the opposing parties asserted that they were the deceased’s collaterals and heirs.
The relationship issue was pleaded, denied, framed as an issue, and tried with evidence.
The trial court found that the opposing parties had not proved the relationship, but the appellate court reversed that finding and held that they were collaterals of the deceased.
The later suit sought possession on the basis of the opposing parties’ title as heirs, and the same parties were involved.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation 3, a matter is directly and substantially in issue when it is raised by one party, denied by the other, and its decision would materially affect the suit. The question is assessed from the pleadings, issues, and decision. An issue may meet that test even if the suit was dismissed on another ground, where the issue was relevant to a claim based on possession and to whether the opposing parties had a superior title. The Court also held that the parties’ litigation was under the same title because the earlier claim included a right to remain in possession, not merely a claim under the alleged will.
members.conclusion: The appellate finding that the opposing parties were the deceased’s collaterals was res judicata and barred the claimant from disputing their heirship in the later suit.

rule.if: later_possession_suit and same_parties and prior_claim_included_possessory_right and relationship_disputed_in_prior_suit and relationship_issue_tried and prior_appellate_finding_on_relationship and relationship_material_to_relief

predicates.later_possession_suit: The later proceeding is a suit for possession in which a party relies on title derived from the deceased owner.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the earlier suit and the later suit are the same.
predicates.prior_claim_included_possessory_right: In the earlier suit, the claimant relied on a right to remain in possession as well as on any separate asserted source of title.
predicates.relationship_disputed_in_prior_suit: In the earlier suit, one party asserted and the other denied that the opposing parties were related to the deceased owner and entitled to succeed to the property.
predicates.relationship_issue_tried: The relationship dispute was framed as an issue and the parties led evidence on it in the earlier suit.
predicates.prior_appellate_finding_on_relationship: An appellate court in the earlier proceeding made a finding determining the relationship dispute.
predicates.relationship_material_to_relief: Determining the relationship dispute was relevant to whether the opposing parties had a title superior to the claimant’s asserted possessory right and was needed to resolve the claims for relief.

members.legal_issue: A final determination of ownership directly and substantially in issue between the parties bars a party from denying that ownership in a later suit.
material_facts: In an earlier suit involving the same parties, a competent court decided that the vendor owned the property and had validly transferred it to the purchaser.
The defendant had disputed the vendor’s ownership and the purchaser’s title in the earlier suit, but did not challenge the determination against him.
The later suit concerned the purchaser’s claim to possession of the same property.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 bars retrial of an issue directly and substantially in issue between the same parties that was heard and finally decided by a competent court. The Court relied on Pawan Kumar Gupta v. Rochiram Nagdeo, which explains that a decision on an issue may operate as res judicata even when the suit in which it was made was ultimately dismissed, and also referred to P.K. Vijayan v. Kamalakshi Amma, K. Ethirajan v. Lakshmi, Marwari Kumhar v. Bhagwanpuri Guru Ganeshpuri, Madhavkrishna v. Chandra Bhaga, Konda Lakshmana Bapuji v. Government of A.P., and Most Rev. P.M.A. Metropolitan v. Moran Mar Marthoma.
members.conclusion: The defendant was barred from denying the purchaser’s title, and the earlier determination of ownership operated as res judicata.

rule.if: later_possession_suit and same_parties_in_both_suits and prior_court_competent and ownership_issue_directly_decided and prior_decision_final

predicates.later_possession_suit: A party brought a later suit seeking possession of property from another party.
predicates.same_parties_in_both_suits: The parties to the later suit were parties to the earlier suit in which ownership was decided.
predicates.prior_court_competent: A court competent to decide the ownership issue heard the earlier suit.
predicates.ownership_issue_directly_decided: The earlier court directly and substantially considered and decided who owned the property.
predicates.prior_decision_final: The decision on ownership became final between the parties.

members.legal_issue: A final adjudication of a transferor’s rights in property binds later claimants who derive their title from that transferor when the governing law has not changed.
material_facts: In earlier litigation between the son and the wife, the courts held that the wife had only a limited interest and could not alienate the property.
That adjudication was affirmed through the appellate process, and the challenge to it was dismissed by the Supreme Court.
The later purchasers claimed through the wife, whose rights had already been adjudicated.
The High Court treated the earlier adjudication as non-binding on the basis that the law had changed, but the Supreme Court found that the relevant law had not changed between the proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The finality of an adjudication applies to later claims derived from a party whose rights were determined in the earlier litigation. The court rejected the High Court’s reliance on Shakuntla Devi v. Kamla and Mathura Prasad Bajoo v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejebhoy because there had been no intervening change in the law. The prior judgment binding the transferor could not be avoided by conveying property to third parties.
members.conclusion: The earlier adjudication remained binding on the wife and on those deriving title from her; she could not create rights for later claimants contrary to that adjudication.

rule.if: later_title_dispute and prior_final_adjudication_of_same_title and transferor_bound_by_prior_adjudication and claimant_derives_title_from_transferor and no_change_in_governing_law

predicates.later_title_dispute: The case involves a later dispute over rights in property previously litigated.
predicates.prior_final_adjudication_of_same_title: A final judgment in earlier litigation determined the relevant property rights.
predicates.transferor_bound_by_prior_adjudication: The person who later transferred the property was bound by the earlier judgment.
predicates.claimant_derives_title_from_transferor: The later claimant asserts rights obtained from the person bound by the earlier judgment.
predicates.no_change_in_governing_law: The legal rule governing the property rights did not change between the earlier and later proceedings.
predicates.prior_adjudication_binds_successors: The earlier judgment binds later claimants whose asserted rights derive from the party bound by it.

members.legal_issue: A title finding in an earlier injunction suit can bar a later title suit only when title was directly and substantially in issue and its determination was necessary to the earlier judgment.
material_facts: In this case, the plaint did not plead the alleged oral gift or the facts supporting the claimed ostensible ownership, and no issue on title was framed.
The High Court nevertheless made findings on title in the injunction suit; the Supreme Court held that those findings could not be made in the absence of the necessary pleadings and issue.
members.legal_principle: The court reconciled Vanagiri Sri Selliamman Ayyanar Uthirasomasundareswarar Temple v. Rajanga Asari with Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, as explained in Sajjadanashin Sayed Md. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer and reiterated in Annaimuthu Thevar v. Alagammal. A later suit is barred only where title was pleaded, an issue on title was raised, evidence was led, and the court decided title because that determination was necessary to its judgment.
members.conclusion: An incidental or collateral title finding does not operate as res judicata when title was not necessary to decide possession; a title finding may do so when title was directly and substantially in issue and necessary to the judgment.

rule.if: earlier_injunction_suit and title_pleaded_and_issued and title_finding_necessary and title_decision_final

predicates.earlier_injunction_suit: A party previously brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning the property.
predicates.title_pleaded_and_issued: The parties pleaded title and an express or implied issue on title was before the court.
predicates.title_finding_necessary: The court had to decide title to determine the claim for possession or injunction.
predicates.title_decision_final: The court’s decision on title attained finality.

members.legal_issue: A final judgment between the parties that determined title binds them in a later suit concerning the same title.
material_facts: In an earlier contested suit, the community's title to the property was affirmed by a competent court, and the judgment became final.
The earlier suit included the respondents, with the minor respondent represented by his mother, who was also a party in her individual capacity.
The earlier judgment determined that the respondents and their predecessor possessed the property as Pujaris, not as owners.
The respondents again claimed ownership through their predecessor in the later suit.
members.legal_principle: The principle of res judicata precludes parties from relitigating a matter of title that was finally decided between them by a competent court. The Court applied that principle to the final judgment in the earlier suit.
members.conclusion: The earlier judgment was binding on the respondents, who were precluded from denying the community's title.

predicates.later_suit_about_same_title: A party brings a later suit concerning title to property that was at issue in an earlier suit.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_between_parties: A competent court issued a final judgment between the parties, including any party properly represented in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_judgment_determined_title: The earlier judgment determined which party held title to the property.

members.legal_issue: An FIR alleging a cognizable offence cannot be quashed by assessing the reliability of its allegations or weighing evidence at the investigation stage.
material_facts: A complaint alleged that documents, including a power of attorney, a sale-and-possession receipt, and affidavits, had been forged or fabricated, and an FIR alleging cognizable offences was registered.
The High Court examined the documents, compared signatures, considered photographs and other material produced by the accused, and concluded that the complaint was false and vexatious.
The High Court did not find that the allegations, taken at face value, failed to disclose an offence or a cognizable offence.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 154, 156 and 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, information disclosing a cognizable offence must be registered and investigated as provided by law. Under Section 482 and Article 226, quashing is to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection; a court ordinarily may not test the reliability or genuineness of FIR allegations or anticipate whether they will be proved. The illustrative grounds in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal permit quashing in specified circumstances, including where allegations taken at face value disclose no offence or cognizable offence, but those circumstances were not established here.
members.conclusion: The High Court's order quashing the FIR was unsustainable; it was set aside and the investigation was permitted to proceed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_fir_quashing: The matter is an appeal from an order quashing an FIR.
predicates.fir_alleges_cognizable_offence: The FIR alleges conduct that, taken at face value, discloses a cognizable offence.
predicates.quashing_court_assessed_evidence: The court quashing the FIR assessed the reliability of allegations or weighed documents or other evidence.

members.legal_issue: A criminal proceeding should not be quashed at the threshold under the court’s inherent powers when the allegations, taken at face value, disclose an offence and their truth or reliability requires evidentiary assessment.
material_facts: The investigation alleged that a father and his son acted together to create and submit false documents and explanations to make cash recovered from the son’s home appear to belong to the father and to derive from property sales.

The investigation identified alleged inconsistencies in the sale explanations and supporting documents, including evidence that entries in a stamp vendor’s register had been made later than represented and that business records had been manipulated.

The High Court quashed the FIR and charge-sheet after assessing the prosecution’s reasons and the credibility of the alleged property transactions, even though the evidence had not been tested at trial.
The Supreme Court found that the allegations and material, accepted at face value, disclosed the alleged offences and that their truthfulness and veracity were matters for the trial court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court’s broad inherent power must be exercised sparingly and cautiously. It may be used to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, including where allegations taken at face value do not disclose an offence, but it must not be used to stifle a legitimate prosecution. Where the allegations disclose an offence and the relevant facts are incomplete or disputed, the High Court should not decide the truth or reliability of the allegations before evidence is led. The Court relied on R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab, State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, State of West Bengal v. Swapan Kumar Guha, Madhavrao Jiwajirao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, State of Bihar v. Murad Ali Khan, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, and Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal, among other authorities.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR and charge-sheet under its inherent powers; its judgment was set aside and the prosecution was permitted to proceed.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_at_thresh: An accused seeks to end a criminal investigation or prosecution before the allegations have been tested at trial.
predicates.face_value_allegations_disclose_offence: The prosecution alleges facts which, if accepted as stated, describe conduct amounting to an offence.
predicates.truth_or_reliability_requires_evidence: Determining whether the allegations are true or reliable requires evidence that has not yet been tested by the trial court.

members.legal_issue: A criminal FIR cannot be quashed at the threshold under the inherent jurisdiction when the investigation remains incomplete and material factual matters require investigation.
material_facts: A father lodged an FIR alleging that his son’s wife and her family members had harassed his son and abetted his suicide.
The police investigation was pending, and the record indicated that further inquiry remained to be done.
The suicide notes had been reported to match the deceased’s handwriting, and the FIR raised factual matters including whether the deceased had a prior mental condition.
The High Court assessed the parties’ factual assertions and quashed the FIR before the investigation was completed.
members.legal_principle: The inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be exercised cautiously. Consistent with the Court’s prior decisions, an FIR may be quashed when continuing the investigation would amount to an abuse of process; where unresolved factual assertions require investigation, the court should not prematurely determine them while quashing the FIR. The judgment refers to a catena of this Court’s decisions but does not identify them by name. It makes no determination on whether the ingredients of abetment of suicide are ultimately established.
members.conclusion: The High Court quashed the FIR prematurely. Its order was set aside, and the investigative authorities were directed to complete the investigation promptly and take it to its logical conclusion, without treating the Supreme Court’s observations as findings on the merits.

predicates.criminal_fir_quashing_proceeding: A person sought to have a criminal FIR quashed by a court.
predicates.investigation_pending: The investigation into the FIR had not been completed.
predicates.material_factual_questions_require_inves: Material factual matters raised by the allegations remained unresolved and required investigation.
predicates.quashing_order_set_aside_and_investigati: The quashing order is set aside and the investigative authorities are directed to complete the investigation.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings should not be quashed when the complaint and supporting material prima facie disclose the ingredients of offences and the accused’s defenses depend on disputed facts for trial.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that the accused inflicted injuries, attempted to strike the complainant on the head with an iron rod, and threatened to kill the complainant.
The Magistrate-recorded statements, together with the complaint, were found to disclose the ingredients of the offences charged.
The accused relied on pending civil disputes and a prior criminal complaint to argue that the complaint was a counterblast, and disputed whether one accused was present at the incident.
The High Court refused to quash the proceedings, and the accused appealed that refusal.
members.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure preserves a broad but sparingly exercised inherent power to give effect to orders under the Code, prevent abuse of process, and secure the ends of justice. A court considering quashing may assess whether the allegations, taken at face value, disclose the ingredients of an offence, but must not conduct a trial, assess the reliability of evidence, or decide disputed factual defenses. Proceedings may be quashed where the allegations disclose no offence or where a recognized ground for intervention applies. The Court relied on Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Mohd. Sharful Haque, S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar, M.A.A. Annamali v. State of Karnataka, Sharda Prasad Sinha v. State of Bihar, Smt. Nagawwa v. Veeranna Shivlingappa Konjalgi, Dharampal v. Smt. Ramshri, State of Haryana v. Bhajanlal, Dhanalakshmi v. R. Prasanna Kumar, and State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy.
members.conclusion: The proceedings were not fit to be quashed, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_from_refusal_to_quash: The accused appealed after a court refused to quash pending criminal proceedings.
predicates.complaint_alleges_conduct_matching_offen: The complainant alleged conduct that, taken at face value and with the supporting material, corresponds to the elements of the offences alleged.
predicates.defense_depends_on_disputed_facts: The accused relied on contested matters, such as presence at the incident or alleged false implication, that require evidence to resolve.

members.legal_issue: Alleged mala fides of an informant do not by themselves justify quashing a criminal proceeding when the allegations and investigative materials otherwise call for adjudication.
material_facts: The respondents argued that the prosecution was politically motivated and intended to harass them and another person.
The allegations concerned serious offences, and the investigating agency had collected documentary and oral materials while investigation was ongoing.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, alleged mala fides of the informant are of secondary importance and cannot alone provide a basis for quashing proceedings. The Court relied on Dhanalakshmi v. R. Prasanna Kumar, State of Bihar v. P. P. Sharma, Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill, State of Kerala v. O. C. Kuttan, State of U.P. v. O. P. Sharma, Rashmi Kumar v. Mahesh Kumar Bhada, Satvinder Kaur v. State, Rajesh Bajaj v. State, State of Karnataka v. M. Devendrappa, and State of M.P. v. Awadh Kishore Gupta. The separate category in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal for proceedings manifestly attended with mala fides does not make an allegation of bad motive, standing alone, sufficient.
members.conclusion: The allegations of mala fides could not, by themselves, justify quashing the proceedings; the High Court’s quashing orders were set aside.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_quashing_challenge: A person seeks to have a criminal investigation or prosecution terminated by a court exercising its inherent criminal jurisdiction.
predicates.mala_fides_alleged: The accused claims that the informant or prosecuting agency acted from an improper or vindictive motive.
predicates.allegations_or_materials_support_further: The allegations or materials collected provide a basis for the criminal matter to proceed for investigation or adjudication.
predicates.mala_fides_alone_do_not_justify_quashing: The proceeding should not be quashed solely because an improper motive is alleged.

members.legal_issue: An FIR should not be quashed where its allegations, taken at face value, attribute a specific role in an alleged conspiracy connected to extortion and prima facie disclose the alleged offence.
material_facts: The FIR alleged that certain persons entered into agreements with the property claimants to finance litigation concerning the disputed land and were involved in a conspiracy to obtain money from the complainant.
The FIR attributed specific conduct to two of those persons, including executing powers of attorney and memoranda of understanding connected with the disputed land.

The High Court found that the allegations disclosed extortion by two other accused but did not adequately examine whether the other accused were alleged to be privy to that extortion through a conspiracy.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the test for quashing an FIR is whether the allegations in the complaint, taken as they stand and without adding to or detracting from them, prima facie establish the ingredients of the alleged offence. The High Court cannot test the allegations’ veracity or proceed as if conducting a trial. Mahendra KC v. State of Karnataka states this test. Where a charge-sheet has been filed before the Magistrate, Kaptan Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh requires the High Court to consider the material collected during investigation. The allegations here included conspiracy under Section 120B and extortion under Section 385 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the FIR against persons to whom the allegations attributed a specific role in the alleged conspiracy and extortion; its quashing order was set aside as to the relevant appeals.

rule.if: fir_quashing_proceeding and allegations_taken_at_face_value and specific_role_in_alleged_conspiracy and alleged_conspiracy_connected_to_extortion

predicates.fir_quashing_proceeding: A person asked a High Court to quash an FIR using its inherent criminal jurisdiction.
predicates.allegations_taken_at_face_value: The allegations in the FIR are considered as stated, without deciding whether they are true.
predicates.specific_role_in_alleged_conspiracy: The FIR attributes particular conduct to the accused as part of an alleged agreement or plan involving other accused.
predicates.alleged_conspiracy_connected_to_extortio: The alleged plan is said to involve obtaining money from the complainant through extortion.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution should not be quashed at the threshold when the complaint attributes specific official acts to public officials and their asserted innocent explanation depends on disputed facts requiring evidence.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that officials recommended a land conversion and issued an endorsement stating that the land was not subject to acquisition.
The complaint alleged that the officials acted despite circumstances involving competing claims to the land and land that had already been acquired.
The appellants argued that they had merely acted on a court decree, but the court considered whether they had failed to account for the competing claims and acquisition as matters for evidence.
members.legal_principle: At the threshold, proceedings should not be quashed on the basis of an asserted defence when the complaint attributes official acts to the accused and alleges circumstances that could indicate abuse of office. Whether the officials acted innocently or culpably depends on the evidence. The court relied on the allegations in the complaint and treated the appellants' explanation as a matter for trial rather than accepting it as a basis for quashing.
members.conclusion: The allegations against the appellants were sufficient to prevent quashing at this stage; their explanation and culpability were matters to be assessed on evidence.

predicates.threshold_quashing_challenge: An accused person asks a court to terminate criminal proceedings before the allegations have been tested at trial.
predicates.complaint_attributes_official_acts_to_ac: The complaint identifies official acts performed by the accused and alleges that those acts assisted the alleged wrongdoing.
predicates.alleged_irregularities_require_evidence: The complaint alleges circumstances suggesting that the official acts may have disregarded material competing claims or other relevant facts.
predicates.asserted_defence_depends_on_disputed_fac: The accused's explanation depends on facts whose truth or significance must be assessed through evidence.

members.legal_issue: A criminal investigation should not be quashed when the first information report contains specific allegations that, taken at face value, disclose a prima facie cognizable offence and the case does not fall within the exceptional categories permitting quashing.
material_facts: The first information report alleged that government officers and private individuals colluded to forge documents used in assessing compensation relating to a vested estate and to commit fraud and misappropriate state funds.
It specifically alleged conspiracy involving the private respondents and a concerned officer.
The High Court quashed the entire investigation, although the allegations, taken at face value, disclosed offences and a cognizable offence.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution and Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court may quash proceedings to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, but must exercise that power sparingly and with circumspection. Under the categories identified in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, quashing may be appropriate where allegations taken at face value do not prima facie constitute an offence, or where the FIR and accompanying material do not disclose a cognizable offence justifying police investigation under Section 156(1), except pursuant to a Magistrate’s order under Section 155(2). Specific allegations of forgery, fraud, and conspiracy disclosed offences under Sections 419, 467, 420, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code, and this case was not one of the rare cases warranting quashing.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in quashing the investigation; its judgment was set aside and the police were permitted to complete the investigation.

rule.if: criminal_investigation_quashing_challenge and specific_offence_allegations and cognizable_offence_disclosed and not exceptional_quashing_case

predicates.criminal_investigation_quashing_challeng: A party challenged a court's decision quashing a criminal investigation.
predicates.specific_offence_allegations: The first information report made specific allegations of criminal conduct against the accused.
predicates.cognizable_offence_disclosed: The allegations and accompanying material, taken at face value, disclosed a cognizable offence warranting police investigation.
predicates.exceptional_quashing_case: The case fell within an exceptional category in which quashing was warranted, such as where the allegations disclosed no offence or no cognizable offence.

members.legal_issue: At the quashing stage, the court must assess the complaint, FIR, charge-sheet and supporting material on their face without deciding the truth of the allegations or accepting disputed defence material as conclusive.
material_facts: A charge-sheet had been filed and placed before the High Court, but the High Court's decision did not examine it and focused on the agreement, its termination and the pending arbitration.
The complaint, FIR and charge-sheet contained allegations which the Supreme Court considered capable of disclosing offences.

The respondent relied on documentary material and argued that the agreement had been terminated because of the complainant's breach; the Supreme Court held that this defence was not for the High Court to decide when considering quashing.
The Supreme Court held that the truth or falsity of the allegations was to be determined on evidence at trial.
members.legal_principle: The inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC requires examination of the complaint, FIR, charge-sheet and relevant material as presented, without a critical determination of their truth. The categories in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal guide, but do not exhaust, the circumstances for quashing. Arnab Manoranjan Goswami v. State of Maharashtra was cited on the contours of the jurisdiction, and Nagpur Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. P. Radhakrishna supports leaving the truth of allegations to trial where an offence is disclosed.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the proceedings by overlooking the charge-sheet or resolving disputed factual matters; the allegations and materials had to be considered on their face, with their truth left to trial.

predicates.criminal_quashing_proceeding: The court is considering whether to quash a criminal complaint, FIR or prosecution.
predicates.face_value_material_discloses_offence: The allegations and accompanying material, taken at face value, disclose a possible criminal offence.
predicates.disputed_truth_or_defence_requires_evide: The accused disputes the allegations or relies on a defence whose correctness depends on resolving facts or evidence.
predicates.court_must_leave_disputed_truth_for_tria: The court must not determine the disputed truth or defence at the quashing stage and must leave it for trial.

members.legal_issue: A court considering a challenge to registration of an FIR must allow the investigation to proceed when the FIR prima facie discloses cognizable offences, rather than evaluating disputed evidence or quashing parts of the FIR.
material_facts: Several complaints alleged that multiple persons had conspired to obtain bogus powers of attorney, fraudulently transfer valuable land, and commit related offences.
The complaints and documents led to registration of an FIR alleging several cognizable offences.
The accused sought to quash the FIR under the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction, relying on documents and an alleged settlement whose contents and correctness were disputed.
The High Court examined the factual details at length, quashed the FIR as to some alleged offences, and allowed investigation into the remaining allegations.
The Supreme Court found that the complaints and FIR, read with the material enclosed, prima facie disclosed various cognizable offences and refrained from deciding disputed matters on their merits.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 157 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the High Court’s jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution, the threshold question is whether the FIR prima facie discloses a cognizable offence. If it does, the police may investigate and the court should not stop the investigation. At the quashing stage, the court examines the FIR and prima facie material that requires no proof; it must not act as an investigating agency or appellate court by appreciating evidence or drawing its own inferences, particularly where the material is disputed. The Court applied State of West Bengal v. Swapan Kumar Guha, AIR 1982 SC 949, and distinguished the decisions reported at (2015) 11 SCC 730 and (2011) 3 SCC 351 because they concerned complaints brought before a court, not challenges to registration of an FIR.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside, the accused persons’ applications to quash the FIR were dismissed, and the entire FIR was left for investigation. The investigation was directed to proceed impartially, in accordance with law, and expeditiously.

predicates.fir_quashing_challenge: The accused challenged the registration of an FIR by invoking a court’s jurisdiction to quash it.
predicates.fir_prima_facie_discloses_cognizable_off: The contents of the FIR and accompanying material, considered at face value, disclosed allegations amounting to at least one cognizable offence.
predicates.whole_fir_left_for_investigation: The entire FIR remains for investigation rather than being quashed in part at the threshold.

members.legal_issue: An FIR under investigation should not be quashed when the complaint, taken at face value, alleges the basic facts of an offence and the accused persons’ culpability requires investigation.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that documents relied on to claim title to land were forged and used as genuine in a civil suit and in dealings with government authorities.
The complaint alleged that the accused had assisted in fabricating or using the documents.
The genuineness of the documents and the accused persons’ involvement had not been established and were matters for investigation.
A civil suit concerning title to the land and relying on the documents was pending.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 226 of the Constitution, quashing an FIR during investigation is an exceptional remedy. A High Court should not quash proceedings if the complaint lays the factual foundation for an offence, or decide disputed facts and culpability before evidence is collected. The Court applied State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, Rajesh Bajaj v. State, NCT of Delhi, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Awadh Kishore Gupta, V.Y. Jose v. State of Gujarat, and Harshendra Kumar D. v. Rebatilata Koley.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in quashing the FIR and the ongoing investigation. The appeal was allowed and the matter was left for investigation without any finding on its merits.

predicates.f_ir_quash_petition_during_investigation: A party sought to quash an FIR while the police investigation was ongoing.
predicates.complaint_alleges_basic_offense_facts: The complaint described facts which, if accepted as true, provide the basic foundation for a criminal offence.
predicates.accused_culpability_requires_investigati: Whether the accused committed an offence depends on facts that have not yet been established through investigation.

members.legal_issue: A criminal case should not be quashed under the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction when the allegations are prima facie and material facts or evidence needed to assess the accused’s involvement remain unresolved.
material_facts: The accused was a Deputy Registrar during a period in which more than 102 sale deeds connected with rehabilitation benefits were registered.
Inquiry reports and the charge-sheets alleged that numerous deeds were fraudulent, that fictitious persons were involved, and that the accused had conspired in or abetted the fraud.
The investigation and collection of evidence were incomplete, and the accused’s alleged involvement had not been finally established.
The High Court quashed the FIRs, charge-sheets, and criminal cases; the State appealed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court does not act as a court of appeal or revision and must exercise its inherent power sparingly, carefully, and with caution. It should not ordinarily assess the reliability of allegations or decide a case on incomplete and hazy facts before the evidence has been collected. The Court relied on M.M.T.C. v. Medchl Chemicals & Pharma (P) Ltd., State of Orissa v. Saroj Kumar Sahoo, and Eicher Tractors Ltd. v. Harihar Singh.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the FIRs and charge-sheets because the allegations and the accused’s involvement required consideration on evidence. The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s judgments were set aside.

predicates.appeal_challenges_quashing_of_criminal_p: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision to quash criminal proceedings.
predicates.prima_facie_allegations_of_involvement: The prosecution alleges facts which, if established, connect the accused to the alleged offence.
predicates.evidence_not_fully_collected: The investigation or collection of evidence concerning the alleged involvement remains incomplete.
predicates.involvement_requires_factual_assessment: Assessing the accused’s involvement depends on facts that cannot fairly be resolved without considering evidence.

members.legal_issue: The additional compensation introduced by the 1984 amendment is unavailable where the acquisition award was made before the applicable transitional threshold.
material_facts: The relevant awards were made before the transitional threshold specified for entitlement to the additional compensation.
The High Court had granted the additional compensation in some appeals despite those awards having been made before that threshold.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the five-judge decision in K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, which overruled Union of India v. Zora Singh and held that entitlement to the additional amount for earlier acquisition proceedings is restricted by the transitional provisions of the amending law.
members.conclusion: The claimants whose awards were made before the transitional threshold were not entitled to the additional compensation, and the contrary directions were set aside.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_claim: The proceeding seeks the additional compensation introduced by an amendment to the general acquisition law.
predicates.award_made_before_transitional_threshold: The acquisition award was made before the transitional threshold relevant to entitlement to the additional compensation.

members.legal_issue: Amended acquisition benefits cannot be added in a revision when the amendment does not apply to the compensation enhancement determined in that proceeding.
material_facts: The High Court awarded additional benefits and enhanced solatium and interest under an amending Act in a revision concerning acquisition compensation.
The compensation enhancement in the revision was determined when the amending Act did not apply to it.
The claimants sought execution of those additional benefits.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(1-A), 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for additional amount, solatium and interest in the circumstances prescribed by the Act. Union of India v. Raghubir Singh and K.S. Paripoornan (II) v. State of Kerala, along with the other cited decisions, were relied on for the inapplicability of the amendment to the enhancement made in revision. Sections 151 and 152 CPC did not provide a basis to amend the original order in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its power by awarding the amended benefits in the circumstances, and those benefits could not be enforced.

predicates.land_acquisition_revision: The proceeding is a revision concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.amended_benefits_are_awarded: The revisional determination adds benefits introduced by an amendment to the acquisition law.
predicates.amendment_does_not_apply_to_revision_enh: The amendment does not apply to the compensation enhancement determined in the revision.

members.legal_issue: The additional amount under Section 23(1-A) is unavailable when the Collector's award falls outside the applicable eligibility period.
material_facts: The Collector made the award on May 17, 1979.
The Court held that the claimants were not entitled to the additional amount under Section 23(1-A).
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 23(1-A) and treated the date of the Collector's award as excluding entitlement to the additional amount. The judgment does not state the applicable eligibility period or cite an earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the additional amount under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.collector_award_outside_additional_amoun: The Collector's award was made outside the period in which the additional acquisition amount is available.

members.legal_issue: The enhanced solatium introduced by the 1984 central amendments does not apply to an acquisition under the state acquisition law merely because an appeal remains pending when the amendments take effect.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeded under the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961, rather than the central Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The Collector made the award in 1969 and the civil court made its award in 1972, both before the relevant transitional period.
The appeal remained pending after the 1984 amendments took effect.
The claimant sought the enhanced solatium under the amended central law.
members.legal_principle: Section 30(1) of the Land Acquisition Amendment Act, 1984 applies its transitional provisions to proceedings under the principal central Act, not to this acquisition under the Kerala Act. Under Section 30(2), read with Section 23(2), enhanced solatium applies to qualifying awards made during the stated transitional period; the mere pendency of an appeal from an earlier award does not qualify it. The court relied on Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, referred to Kanthimathy Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Kerala, and distinguished Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to enhanced solatium; the applicable solatium remained 15 per cent.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and acquisition_under_state_law and collector_and_court_awards_precede_transitional_period and only_appeal_remains_pending

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for an acquired land interest.
predicates.acquisition_under_state_law: The acquisition was conducted under a state acquisition law rather than the central acquisition law.
predicates.collector_and_court_awards_precede_trans: Both the initial award and the award on reference were made before the relevant transitional period.
predicates.only_appeal_remains_pending: The matter pending during the later period is an appeal from the earlier awards.

members.legal_issue: A pending appeal does not make the additional compensation benefit available when both the Collector and the Reference Court made their awards before the benefit took effect.
material_facts: The Court distinguished a proceeding still awaiting a reference-court award from a case in which the Collector and the Reference Court had both already made awards and only an appeal remained pending.
It treated an appellate court’s decision as a decree rather than a new award for purposes of Section 23(1-A).
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) speaks of an “award,” which is distinct from a “decree.” Under Section 3(d), the relevant Court is the principal court of original jurisdiction, including the court deciding a Section 18 reference. When both awards predate the provision, an appellate court deciding an appeal makes a decree, not an award that brings Section 23(1-A) into operation. The Court’s construction is consistent with its discussion of Union of India v. Raghuvir Singh and its reliance on K. Kamala Jammannia-varu rather than the expanded reading in Bhag Singh.
members.conclusion: The additional benefit does not apply merely because an appeal remains pending after both the Collector and the Reference Court have made their awards.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: A party is pursuing an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.collector_award_before_benefit_takes_eff: The Collector made the initial compensation award before the additional-benefit provision took effect.
predicates.reference_court_award_before_benefit_tak: The court deciding the compensation reference also made its award before the additional-benefit provision took effect.

members.legal_issue: Statutory compensation benefits introduced by a later amendment are unavailable for an acquisition where possession and the original award predate the amendment’s extension to that acquisition regime.
material_facts: Land was acquired under a state urban improvement statute, and possession was taken before the central amendment was extended to acquisitions under that statute.
The original compensation award was made before that extension.
The state statute provided for interest at six per cent from the date possession was taken but did not itself provide for solatium or the other additional benefits at issue.
A court later awarded the additional benefits under the amended central land acquisition law.
members.legal_principle: Sections 52 and 60A of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, as amended by the Rajasthan Amendment Act 29 of 1987, governed the extension and transition of the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Act 68 of 1984. The court relied on Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, K.S. Paripoornan (II) v. State of Kerala, and Umed Industries and Land Development Co. v. State of Rajasthan in explaining the temporal limits on benefits under Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), and 28; the state statute’s applicable interest provision remained the basis for six per cent interest.
members.conclusion: The later award of solatium, additional amount, and enhanced statutory interest under the amended central law was not authorized; liability was to be recomputed under the governing state statute, including interest at six per cent from the date possession was taken.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired under a statutory acquisition regime.
predicates.possession_before_extension: Possession of the acquired land was taken before the later amendment was extended to that acquisition regime.
predicates.original_award_before_extension: The original compensation award was made before the later amendment was extended to that acquisition regime.

members.legal_issue: The additional amount under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act is unavailable where the acquisition notification and Collector’s award predate the provision’s applicable period.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published before the Collector made the award.
Both events occurred before the period in which the additional amount under Section 23(1-A) applied to the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the temporal scope of Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act and held that the additional amount was unavailable given the timing of the acquisition notification and the Collector’s award.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the additional amount under Section 23(1-A).

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for acquired land.
predicates.notification_precedes_collector_award: The acquisition notification was issued before the Collector made the award.
predicates.both_events_precede_applicability_of_add: Both the notification and the Collector’s award occurred before the additional amount became applicable to the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A substantive change to the compensation limit does not apply retrospectively to an earlier acquisition merely because an appeal remains pending when the change takes effect.
material_facts: The Collector made the award before the statutory amendment took effect.
The matter remained pending in appeal when the amendment took effect.
The amendment did not state that its revised compensation limit applied retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: A substantive provision is not retrospective unless the provision indicates that effect. The Court distinguished Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, which concerned the transitional provision in Section 30(2) relating to solatium under Section 23(2), and which did not extend the amended Section 25 to earlier awards.
members.conclusion: The amended limit did not apply to the earlier award or the pending appeal; the case remained governed by the unamended provision.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and award_preceded_change and appeal_pending_when_change_took_effect and substantive_limit_changed

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.award_preceded_change: The initial compensation award was made before a statutory change took effect.
predicates.appeal_pending_when_change_took_effect: The compensation dispute remained pending on appeal when the statutory change took effect.
predicates.substantive_limit_changed: A statutory change altered the substantive limit on compensation that a court could award.

members.legal_issue: The additional acquisition amount is not available merely because a reference court decides the compensation claim after an amendment takes effect when the acquisition and the collector’s award predate the amendment’s transitional trigger.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings began before the transitional trigger and the Collector made the award before that trigger.
The claimants sought a reference, and the Civil Court enhanced compensation after the amendment had taken effect.

The acquisition did not fall within either of the amendment’s specified transitional categories: an acquisition pending at the trigger with no Collector’s award yet made, or an acquisition commenced after the trigger.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) forms part of the substantive scheme for determining compensation, read with Sections 11 and 15 and the governing market-value date under Section 23(1). A substantive amendment operates prospectively unless retrospective effect is provided expressly or by necessary intendment. Section 30(1)(a) and (b) supplies limited retrospective operation for its specified transitional categories; the Court considered that those categories, rather than the date of a reference court’s decision alone, control. The Court regarded the reasoning in Union of India v. Fillip Tiago De Gama of Vedem Vasco De Gama as persuasive on this point, questioned the broader reading in Union of India v. Zora Singh, and distinguished the separate transitional issue addressed in Union of India v. Raghubir Singh.
members.conclusion: The Court considered the claimants not entitled to the additional amount on these facts. It held that the contrary interpretation in Zora Singh conferred a benefit beyond the amendment’s limited transitional provisions and required reconsideration, so it referred the matter to a larger Bench rather than finally resolving the conflict.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and acquisition_notification_preceded_amendment_effectiveness and collector_award_preceded_transition_trigger and reference_decision_followed_amendment_effectiveness and not (acquisition_pending_without_collector_award_at_trigger or acquisition_commenced_after_trigger)

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: The proceeding is a reference for determination of compensation in a land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_notification_preceded_amendm: The acquisition was initiated under a notification issued before the amendment became effective.
predicates.collector_award_preceded_transition_trig: The Collector made the acquisition award before the transitional trigger specified by the amendment.
predicates.reference_decision_followed_amendment_ef: The court deciding the compensation reference issued its decision after the amendment became effective.
predicates.acquisition_pending_without_collector_aw: The acquisition was pending at the amendment’s transitional trigger and the Collector had not yet made an award.
predicates.acquisition_commenced_after_trigger: The acquisition proceedings commenced after the amendment’s transitional trigger.

members.legal_issue: The increased solatium does not apply to an award made before the retrospective period merely because an appeal concerning that award remains pending.
material_facts: The land was acquired under notifications issued well before the retrospective period for the amendment.
The claimant and the State appealed the compensation determination, and those appeals remained pending when the amendment was introduced.
The claimant sought the increased solatium on the ground that the compensation proceedings had not become final.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(2) and 30(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by section 15(b) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, make the increased solatium applicable to awards made during the specified retrospective period and to appellate orders arising from those awards. They do not extend it to older awards solely because an appeal is pending. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to the increased solatium because the award predated the retrospective period; the pendency of appeals did not bring the award within that period.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.original_award_predates_retroactive_peri: The original compensation award was made before the period to which the increased solatium applies retrospectively.
predicates.appeal_pending_during_transition: An appeal concerning the award remained pending during the transition associated with the amendment.

members.legal_issue: An additional compensation amount is unavailable when the acquisition began before the transition date and the Collector had already made an award before that date.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings began before the transition date for the additional amount.
The Collector made the award before that date, so no proceeding remained pending before the Collector on that date.
The claimant sought the additional amount in the later compensation proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, provides an additional amount, but Section 30(1)(a) applies it to proceedings pending before the Collector on the transition date in which no award had yet been made, and Section 30(1)(b) applies it to proceedings commenced after that date. The amount therefore does not apply where the acquisition began earlier and the Collector had already made the award before the transition date. The Court rejected the contrary approach of the Karnataka and Bombay High Courts, which had relied on Bhag Singh, because Bhag Singh was overruled by Union of India v. Raghubir Singh.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to the additional amount, and the High Court’s award of it was deleted.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.acquisition_started_before_transition: The acquisition proceedings began before the statutory transition date for the additional amount.
predicates.collector_award_preceded_transition: The Collector made the initial award before that transition date, leaving no acquisition proceeding pending before the Collector on that date.

members.legal_issue: Claimants in this acquisition were not entitled to the additional amount under section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act.
material_facts: The claimants sought an additional amount under section 23(1-A) in the land-acquisition compensation proceeding.
The Court denied that additional amount while allowing other compensation relief.
members.legal_principle: The Court expressly denied the additional amount under section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, but gave no further explanation or identified earlier authority for that conclusion.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the additional amount under section 23(1-A).

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimants_sought_additional_statutory_am: The claimants sought an additional amount in the acquisition-compensation proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made during litigation remains effective between transferor and transferee, but is subject to rights established by the decree, and property already transferred does not become the insolvent transferor’s property merely because insolvency occurs later.
material_facts: The mortgagor conveyed the properties while a suit seeking maintenance and a charge over them was pending.
The conveyance preceded the mortgagor’s adjudication as insolvent.
The decree-holder later purchased the properties in execution of the charge decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act does not make a transfer pendente lite void; it makes the transfer subject to rights under the decree or order in the pending proceeding. Under section 28(2) of the Insolvency Act, only the insolvent’s property vests in the Official Receiver. The court also referred to Kala Chand Banerjee v. Jagannath Marwari.
members.conclusion: The transfer vested title in the transferee as between the parties to the transfer, subject to the rights established in the pending suit; the later insolvency did not vest the transferred properties in the Official Receiver.

predicates.property_title_proceeding_pending_at_tra: A proceeding directly concerning rights in property was pending when the property was transferred.
predicates.transfer_completed_before_transferor_ins: The transfer was completed before the transferor was adjudicated insolvent.

members.legal_issue: A purported transfer that creates new rights in property during pending litigation concerning that property is subject to the doctrine of lis pendens.
material_facts: The company had brought a suit for specific performance concerning an agreement to lease the theater.
While that suit and litigation concerning rights in the theater were pending, a compromise decree was followed by execution of a lease purporting to give the company new rights in the property.
The Court found that the lease purported to create entirely new rights rather than merely enforce an antecedent or pre-existing right.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. The doctrine applies where litigation relating to property is pending and a party purports to create new rights in that property during the litigation. The Court relied on Jayaram Mudaliar v. Ayyaswami and distinguished the argument based on Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh that the lease merely enforced a pre-existing right.
members.conclusion: The purported lease was invalid from the outset under the doctrine of lis pendens.

predicates.property_litigation_pending: A proceeding concerning rights in the property is pending.
predicates.transfer_during_litigation: A party purports to transfer or otherwise deal with the property while that proceeding is pending.
predicates.transfer_creates_new_property_rights: The transaction purports to create new rights in the property rather than merely enforce an existing right.
predicates.transfer_is_bound_by_lis_pendens: The transaction is subject to the rule that dealings during the pending litigation cannot defeat the rights determined in that litigation.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of property by a party while a non-collusive suit directly and specifically concerns rights in that property, made without the court’s authority, is subject to the rights determined by the decree and does not affect those rights.
material_facts: The suit directly and specifically concerned rights in the disputed property.
While the suit was pending, defendants transferred the property to the proposed parties by registered sale deeds.
The transfers were not made with the authority of the court.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that during the pendency of a non-collusive suit or proceeding in which rights to immovable property are directly and specifically in question, a party cannot transfer or otherwise deal with the property so as to affect another party’s rights under a decree or order, except with the court’s authority and on its terms.
members.conclusion: The transfers were hit by the doctrine of lis pendens and were subject to the rights determined in the suit; the purchasers’ transfers did not make them necessary or proper parties.

predicates.non_collusive_property_rights_suit_pendi: A non-collusive suit or proceeding directly and specifically concerning rights in property is pending.
predicates.party_transfers_property_in_dispute: A party to the proceeding transfers or otherwise deals with the property in dispute while the proceeding is pending.
predicates.transfer_without_court_authority: The party makes the transfer without obtaining the court’s authority.
predicates.transfer_subject_to_rights_under_decree: The transfer remains subject to the rights determined by the decree and does not affect those rights.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of disputed property made while litigation concerning its sale is pending remains subject to the outcome of that litigation.
material_facts: The property was transferred to a third person during the pendency of the appeal.
The Court restored the decree for specific performance and directed performance of the obligations under the agreement notwithstanding the later transfer.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of lis pendens makes a transfer of property during pending litigation subject to the result of that litigation. The Court applied that doctrine to the transfer made during the appeal.
members.conclusion: The later transfer was subject to the doctrine of lis pendens, and the respondents remained bound to perform the agreement notwithstanding that transfer.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: An appeal concerns a claim for specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.property_transferred_during_pending_liti: The disputed property was transferred to another person while the litigation was pending.

members.legal_issue: The doctrine of lis pendens applies to a transfer of property during litigation only when the transfer is made by a party to that litigation.
material_facts: A suit concerning the property was pending when the son of the original allottee transferred the property to a purchaser.
The son and the purchaser were not parties to the suit when the transfer took place and were impleaded later.
The allottee’s husband was already a party and had given a no-objection that enabled the son to obtain title.

The Court held that even if the husband’s conduct could be treated as dealing with the property, lis pendens would not invalidate the later sale; at most, a transfer by a party would remain subject to the final result of the litigation.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. Its indispensable requirement is that the transfer or other dealing with the property be made by a party to the litigation while the proceeding is pending. The doctrine is based on expediency and the finality of adjudication, not notice or good faith. A transfer to which the doctrine applies is not void; it is subject to the final decision. The Court relied on the principle expressed in pendente lite nihil innovetur and considered the treatment of the doctrine in Manjeshwara Krishnaya v. Vasudeva Mallya, AIR 1918 Mad 578, and distinguished Nallakumara Goundan v. Pappayi Ammal, AIR 1945 Mad 219.
members.conclusion: The sale by the son was not hit by lis pendens because he was not a party to the suit when he made the transfer. The High Court erred in holding otherwise.

predicates.property_in_litigation: The property being transferred was the subject matter of a pending proceeding.
predicates.transfer_during_pending_proceeding: The transfer took place while that proceeding was pending.
predicates.transferor_not_party: The person who made the transfer was not a party to the proceeding at the time of transfer.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of immovable property during a pending suit directly concerning rights in that property is not void but remains subject to the result of the suit.
material_facts: The pending suit directly placed rights in the property in issue.
The court considered the effect of a transfer made while the suit was pending.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. As explained in Bellamy v. Sabine, the doctrine prevents a party from defeating the outcome of litigation through a transfer during the proceedings. It does not make the transfer void; the transfer is instead subordinate to the rights of the other parties as determined in the litigation.
members.conclusion: A transfer during the suit is not annulled by the doctrine of lis pendens; it is subject to the rights ultimately established by the decree or order in the suit.

predicates.pending_suit_directly_concerns_property_: A suit is pending in which rights to immovable property are directly in issue.
predicates.property_transferred_during_suit: A party transfers or otherwise deals with the property while the suit is pending.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of property made by a party while a non-collusive suit directly concerning that property is pending remains valid but is subject to the rights determined by the decree.
material_facts: The suit directly concerned rights in immovable property and was pending when the vendors executed and registered the transfers to the later purchasers.
The courts rejected the later purchasers’ claim that they lacked knowledge of the earlier transaction and pending suit.
The High Court treated the transfers as illegal, but the Supreme Court held that this went beyond the effect of the doctrine of lis pendens.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that during the pendency of a non-collusive suit in which rights to immovable property are directly and specifically in question, a party cannot transfer or deal with the property so as to affect another party’s rights under the eventual decree. The effect is to make the transfer subservient to the decree, not to annul it. The Court relied on Guruswamy Nadar v. P. Lakshmi Ammal, (2008) 5 SCC 796, clarified the scope of Sarvinder Singh v. Dalip Singh, (1996) 5 SCC 539, and relied on A. Nawab John v. V.N. Subramaniyam, (2012) 7 SCC 738.
members.conclusion: The transfers were subject to the outcome of the suit and could not adversely affect the plaintiffs’ rights under the decree, but they were not illegal or void merely because they occurred during the suit.

rule.if: property_rights_suit_pending and suit_directly_concerns_immovable_property and suit_is_not_collusive and party_transfers_property_during_suit

predicates.property_rights_suit_pending: A suit concerning rights in property is pending before a competent court.
predicates.suit_directly_concerns_immovable_propert: The suit directly and specifically puts rights in immovable property in issue.
predicates.suit_is_not_collusive: The suit was not brought or pursued collusively.
predicates.party_transfers_property_during_suit: A party to the pending suit transfers or otherwise deals with the property while the suit is pending.

members.legal_issue: A voluntary transfer of disputed immovable property by a party during a pending partition suit is subject to the outcome of the suit when it may affect another litigant’s rights under the decree.
material_facts: A partition suit concerning joint-family properties was pending before the voluntary sale of some of those properties.
The sale was made by the managing family member and some of his sons, did not purport to bind the whole family, and was not shown to have been made on behalf of the family for legal necessity.
The sale was supported by consideration, but the purchaser’s claimed debts and the sale did not establish that the transfer bound the entire family.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to transfers or other dealings by a party during a non-collusive suit in which rights to immovable property are directly and specifically in question, where the dealing may affect another party’s rights under the decree. The doctrine preserves the court’s control over the subject matter. The court also relied on K.N. Lal v. Ganeshi Ram to reject the contention that an earlier attachment removed property from the operation of lis pendens, and distinguished Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh as concerning the particular nature of a pre-emption right.
members.conclusion: The voluntary sale was affected by lis pendens and could not prejudice the other family member’s rights under the partition decree.

predicates.partition_suit_pending: A partition proceeding is pending in court.
predicates.disputed_immovable_property_at_issue: The transferred immovable property is directly and specifically involved in the proceeding.
predicates.party_voluntarily_transfers_property_dur: A party to the proceeding voluntarily transfers or deals with the property while the proceeding is pending.
predicates.transfer_may_affect_another_litigants_de: The transfer may affect another litigant’s rights under the decree in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made during pending litigation is not void merely because it was made while the proceeding was pending, but remains subject to the rights determined in that proceeding.
material_facts: A party to the partition suit sold the disputed property while the suit was pending and without court authority.
The seller held only a 14/104 share in the property, while the sale purported to cover the whole property.
The preliminary and final decrees determined the parties’ shares and recognized the transfer only to the extent of the seller’s share.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act makes a pendente lite transfer subservient to the rights determined in the litigation rather than void. Thomson Press (India) Ltd. v. Nanak Builders and Investors, A. Nawab John v. V.N. Subramaniyam, Vinod Seth v. Devinder Bajaj, and Sanjay Verma v. Manik Roy apply that principle. The transferee takes the rights and obligations ultimately determined for the transferor.
members.conclusion: The sale was not void as a whole under the transfer-pendency rule; it remained valid only to the extent of the seller’s 14/104 share and was subject to the outcome of the suit.

predicates.property_transfer_dispute: The court considered the effect of a property transfer in litigation concerning that property.
predicates.transfer_during_pending_litigation: A party transferred the property before the litigation was finally disposed of.
predicates.transferor_had_limited_share: The transferor owned only a defined share of the property.
