predicates.deceased_claimant_had_independent_claim: The deceased party asserted a right or claim distinct from those of the other parties.
predicates.refusal_would_block_merits_for_surviving: Rejecting substitution would prevent surviving parties from obtaining a decision on their own claims.

members.legal_issue: Sufficient cause for delay in seeking to bring a deceased appellant’s legal representatives on record after abatement must be assessed in a manner that advances justice rather than by taking an unduly strict or pedantic approach.
material_facts: A party to a pending appeal died, and no application to bring his legal representatives on record was made within the applicable period, resulting in abatement.
The deceased appellant’s young son, who applied as a legal representative, stated that he did not know the appeal was pending.
The son learned of the appeal shortly before applying and acted promptly after learning of it.
The appellants were agriculturists living in villages, and the applicant had little knowledge of the steps required.
members.legal_principle: In considering an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the court should assess the circumstances without taking an unduly strict or pedantic view that would cause injustice, and should adopt an approach that advances justice. The Court relied on settled law and decisions cited before it, but the judgment does not identify those decisions by name.
members.conclusion: The Court found sufficient cause for the delay, allowed the application subject to payment of costs, set aside the High Court’s judgment, and remanded the matter for decision on the merits.

predicates.substitution_after_abatement_in_appeal: A party to a pending appeal died, and the legal representatives sought to be brought on record after the appeal had abated.
predicates.applicant_unaware_of_appeal: The deceased appellant’s legal representative who applied did not know that the appeal was pending.
predicates.applicant_learned_recently: The applicant learned of the pending appeal shortly before applying to be brought on record.
predicates.applicant_acted_promptly: The applicant applied promptly after learning of the pending appeal.
predicates.applicant_lacked_procedural_experience: The applicant was young and had little knowledge of the procedural steps required.

members.legal_issue: A delayed application to substitute the legal representatives of deceased respondents in a certified appeal may be allowed when sufficient cause for the delay is shown and the applicable time-extension power is exercised.
material_facts: The appeal was pending after a certificate had been granted and before the record was dispatched to the Supreme Court.
Two respondents died during that period, and applications to substitute their legal representatives were filed more than 90 days after their deaths.
The Court found sufficient cause for condoning the delay and considered that it could also enlarge the prescribed time.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XVI Rule 12 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, an application to substitute a deceased party before dispatch of the record was subject to a 90-day period, but delay could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act; Order XLV Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules also empowered the Court to enlarge a time fixed by those Rules.
members.conclusion: The Court enlarged the time for filing the applications and directed that the legal representatives of the deceased respondents be substituted.

predicates.certified_appeal_pending_before_record_d: A certified appeal was pending before the record was dispatched to the Supreme Court.
predicates.respondents_died_during_proceedings: One or more respondents died while the appeal proceedings were pending.
predicates.substitution_applications_filed_after_de: Applications to substitute the deceased respondents' legal representatives were filed after the prescribed filing period.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay: The Court found sufficient cause for the delay in applying to substitute the deceased respondents' legal representatives.
predicates.time_for_respondent_substitution_extende: The time for applying to substitute the deceased respondents' legal representatives is extended.

members.legal_issue: The time for an application to substitute a deceased appellant in a pending appeal may be enlarged even when the applicable procedural rule does not expressly provide for condoning delay.
material_facts: An appellant died after the appeal records had been dispatched to the Supreme Court but before a formal petition of appeal was lodged there.
The application to substitute the appellant's legal representative was filed more than 90 days after the death.
The Court found that its power to enlarge time applied and, in the circumstances, granted an extension.
members.legal_principle: Order XVI Rules 13 and 14 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950 required an application to substitute a deceased appellant to be filed within 90 days, and Order XVI Rule 14A made the abatement provisions of Order XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure applicable. Although the relevant rule did not provide for condonation under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, Order XLV Rule 13 of the Supreme Court Rules empowered the Court to enlarge the time fixed by the Rules.
members.conclusion: The Court enlarged the time for filing the substitution application and directed that the deceased appellant's legal representative be substituted.

rule.if: appeal_pending_before_formal_filing and appellant_died_during_proceedings and substitution_application_filed_after_deadline and case_circumstances_support_extension

predicates.appellant_died_during_proceedings: An appellant died while the appeal proceedings were pending.
predicates.substitution_application_filed_after_dea: The application to substitute the deceased appellant's legal representative was filed after the prescribed filing period.
predicates.case_circumstances_support_extension: The circumstances of the case supported enlarging the time for the substitution application.
predicates.time_for_appellant_substitution_extended: The time for applying to substitute the deceased appellant's legal representative is extended.

members.legal_issue: The phrase “sufficient cause” for condoning delay in filing an appeal must be applied through a fact-sensitive exercise of judicial discretion that advances substantial justice where negligence, inaction, or want of bona fides is not imputable to the appellant.
material_facts: The State sought condonation of delay in filing appeals from land-acquisition reference decisions.
The High Court rejected the applications without explaining why the stated reasons did not constitute sufficient cause.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the court has discretion to condone delay when sufficient cause is established. The expression should receive a liberal construction to advance substantial justice when negligence, inaction, or want of bona fides is not imputable, while also respecting the right acquired by the successful party when limitation expires. The same principles apply to government and private litigants. The Court relied on Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd. and Shakuntala Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumari, and referred to Ram Narain Joshi v. Parmeshwar Narain Mahta and Kunwar Rajendra Singh v. Rai Rajeshwar Bali.
members.conclusion: Sufficient cause cannot be defined by a fixed list of circumstances; it must be assessed liberally but judicially, having regard to whether the appellant failed to take necessary steps through negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides.

rule.if: appeal_delay_condonation_proceeding and not appellant_negligent and not appellant_inactive and not appellant_lacking_bona_fides

predicates.appeal_delay_condonation_proceeding: A party asks a court to excuse delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.appellant_negligent: The appellant failed through negligence to take necessary steps that it could or should have taken.
predicates.appellant_inactive: The appellant did not take necessary steps to pursue the appeal.
predicates.appellant_lacking_bona_fides: The appellant acted without bona fides in relation to the delay.

members.legal_issue: A court considering an application to condone delay must scrutinize the reasons given and decide them on their merits; acting on mistaken legal advice and then taking diligent steps can constitute sufficient cause when negligence or want of bona fides is not established.
material_facts: The State discovered on March 4, 1965, that appeals had not been filed against the land-acquisition reference decisions.
After that discovery, the State investigated how to challenge the decisions and acted on its lawyer’s advice to seek relief under Article 227 of the Constitution.
The State filed those applications and, after the High Court directed it to file regular appeals, filed the appeals with applications to condone delay.
The respondents did not specifically deny the State’s account of when it learned that no appeals had been filed or the advice it received.
The High Court rejected the condonation applications without giving reasons addressing the State’s explanations and did not find that the State had acted negligently or without bona fides.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires the court to examine the reasons advanced for delay on their merits rather than reject an application without addressing them. Mistaken advice from a legal adviser may, depending on the circumstances, amount to sufficient cause; it does not automatically establish negligence. The Court applied the principles in Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd. and Kunwar Rajendra Singh v. Rai Rajeshwar Bali, and distinguished Ram Narain Joshi v. Parmeshwar Narain Mahta because the lower court there had fully considered the reasons for delay.
members.conclusion: The State showed sufficient cause for the delay; the High Court was not justified in rejecting the applications without properly considering the explanations, and the delay was condoned.

rule.if: appeal_delay_condonation_proceeding and appellant_learned_late_that_appeals_were_not_filed and appellant_took_diligent_steps_after_learning and appellant_followed_legal_advice and lower_court_failed_to_assess_reasons and not appellant_negligent

predicates.appeal_delay_condonation_proceeding: A party asks a court to excuse delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.appellant_learned_late_that_appeals_were: The appellant learned only after a period of delay that the appeals had not been filed.
predicates.appellant_took_diligent_steps_after_lear: After learning that the appeals had not been filed, the appellant promptly investigated and took steps to challenge the decisions.
predicates.appellant_followed_legal_advice: The appellant acted on legal advice about the procedure for challenging the decisions, even though that advice was mistaken.
predicates.lower_court_failed_to_assess_reasons: The court that rejected condonation did not scrutinize and explain its assessment of the reasons offered for the delay.
predicates.appellant_negligent: The appellant failed through negligence to take necessary steps that it could or should have taken.

members.legal_issue: A liberal, justice-oriented assessment of sufficient cause is required when deciding whether to condone delay in seeking to set aside abatement and substitute a deceased party in a pending appeal.
material_facts: Several appellants in a pending partition appeal died, and applications to substitute some of their heirs were filed after delays ranging from months to years.

The appellants belonged to different families and villages; the affected appellants were rustic and illiterate villagers, and some deceased appellants were transferees living in different areas from the joint-family parties.
After learning of the deaths from counsel, an appellant obtained the heirs’ authorisations and the substitution application was filed promptly.

The respondents did not allege that the delay was mala fide, intentional, or part of a dilatory strategy, and did not deny that the appellants were rustic villagers and, with one exception, illiterate.
The High Court refused to condone the delay and set aside abatement for the affected appellants’ appeals.
members.legal_principle: The expression “sufficient cause” in Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, Order 22 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and similar provisions should be construed liberally to advance substantial justice where negligence, inaction, or want of bona fides is not imputable to the party. There is no fixed formula: the acceptability of the explanation, rather than the length of delay alone, is the criterion. Courts should ordinarily accept an adequate explanation, while considering any valuable right acquired by the opposing party and balancing the consequences of the decision. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Administrator, Howrah Municipality (1972) 1 SCC 366; Sital Prasad Saxena v. Union of India, AIR 1985 SC 1; Rama Ravalu Gavade v. Sataba Gavadu Gavade (1997) 1 SCC 261; N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy (1998) 7 SCC 123; and Shakuntala Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumari (1969) 1 SCR 1006.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in refusing relief. It condoned the delay, set aside abatement, allowed substitution, and remitted the appeal for decision on its merits.

rule.if: pending_appeal_affected_by_party_death and delayed_substitution_application and parties_are_rural_or_illiterate and prompt_action_after_learning and not intentional_or_mala_fide_delay

predicates.pending_appeal_affected_by_party_death: An appeal was pending when a party to it died, making substitution of that party’s legal representatives relevant to continuing the appeal.
predicates.delayed_substitution_application: The application to substitute the deceased party’s legal representatives was filed after the prescribed time.

members.legal_issue: A late application to substitute a deceased defendant’s legal representatives and set aside abatement requires sufficient cause both for the delay in seeking to set aside abatement and for failing to substitute the representatives within the prescribed time.
material_facts: The defendant died before the suit reached decree, and the suit abated when the plaintiff did not apply to substitute his legal representatives within the prescribed period.
The plaintiff later applied both to set aside the abatement and to substitute the representatives, and the application was substantially delayed.
The subordinate court found sufficient cause for the plaintiff’s delay in applying to set aside abatement and for failing to apply for substitution in time.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII rules 4 and 9(2) and (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with sections 3 and 5 and Articles 171 and 176 of the Limitation Act, require the applicant to establish sufficient cause for the delay in applying to set aside abatement and for not bringing the legal representatives on record within time. Section 5 permits the court to admit a covered application after the limitation period if sufficient cause is shown.
members.conclusion: Both forms of sufficient cause had to be established. The subordinate court found them established, and its order allowing the application was restored.

predicates.late_substitution_after_abatement: A party applies to substitute a deceased litigant’s legal representatives after the proceeding has abated and the prescribed time has elapsed.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_delay_in_seeking_to: The applicant establishes a sufficient reason for not applying to set aside abatement within the prescribed time.
predicates.sufficient_cause_for_failure_to_substitu: The applicant establishes a sufficient reason for not applying to substitute the legal representatives within the prescribed time.
predicates.late_substitution_application_may_be_all: The court may admit the delayed application and set aside the abatement.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is appropriate only in the rarest of rare cases after the aggravating and mitigating circumstances relating to both the crime and the offender have been balanced.
material_facts: The principal offender planned the killings to obtain control of family property before his father’s death.
He killed three members of the family, including young and helpless victims, after the victims were confined inside the house.
He inflicted numerous knife injuries on the victims, and the Court characterized the killings as exceptionally brutal and deliberate.
The offender was 25 years old and had no prior criminal history; the Court considered these and other mitigating submissions but found them outweighed by the circumstances of the crime.
The other convicted participant received life imprisonment, and that sentence was also confirmed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, life imprisonment is the rule and death is the exception. The court must consider circumstances of both the crime and the offender, give full weight to mitigating circumstances, and impose death only where life imprisonment is inadequate and no alternative can be conscientiously chosen. The Court applied Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and the categories and guidance in Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, including consideration of planning, brutality, motive, magnitude of the crime, victims’ vulnerability, and mitigating circumstances.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the principal offender’s crimes were of extreme culpability and fell within the rarest of rare category, so it confirmed the death sentence; it also confirmed the life sentence imposed on the other convicted participant.

members.legal_issue: The death sentence is appropriate for murders involving extreme brutality and grave criminality that fall within the rarest of rare cases.
material_facts: Two appellants were convicted of murdering two young women in a coordinated, cold-blooded attack and received death sentences.
The victims were attacked with sharp weapons; one victim’s neck was severed, and the other was fatally wounded after her hand was chopped off.
The court found that the murders were committed out of greed and personal vengeance arising from a property dispute.
The appeal was argued mainly on the question of sentence, and the court found no reason to interfere with the death sentences.
members.legal_principle: Punishment must fit the crime, and courts must impose proper punishment according to the degree of criminality and the desirability of that punishment. Under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, death may be imposed in cases meeting the rarest-of-rare test described in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and elaborated in Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab. The court considered extreme brutality and the need for social protection and deterrence.
members.conclusion: The murders fell within the rarest of rare cases, and the death sentences were confirmed as appropriate punishment and as a measure of social necessity and deterrence.

rule.if: capital_sentence_appeal and multiple_victims_killed and extreme_brutality and personal_vengeance_motive

predicates.capital_sentence_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which the appropriateness of a death sentence is considered.
predicates.multiple_victims_killed: The offenders killed more than one victim.
predicates.extreme_brutality: The killings were carried out with extreme brutality.
predicates.personal_vengeance_motive: The offenders committed the killings to exact personal vengeance.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty may be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases after considering the offender's circumstances, aggravating and mitigating factors, and whether life imprisonment is inadequate.
material_facts: The principal accused masterminded and participated in the killings of his wife and two young children after a planned course of conduct.
The killings were found to be exceptionally brutal and cruel, and the Court found no mitigating circumstances for that accused.
The appeal challenged the death sentence affirmed by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires special reasons for a death sentence. Life imprisonment is the rule and death is an exception for the rarest of rare cases, where the offender's circumstances and the aggravating and mitigating circumstances are assessed and life imprisonment is altogether inadequate. The Court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, and Dhananjoy Chatterjee v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the case fell within the rarest of rare category and affirmed the death sentence for the principal accused.

rule.if: capital_sentencing_review and extreme_culpability_proved and aggravating_factors_outweigh_mitigating_factors and life_imprisonment_inadequate

predicates.capital_sentencing_review: The proceeding is a review of a sentence of death imposed for a criminal offence.
predicates.extreme_culpability_proved: The offender's role and the circumstances of the crime establish exceptionally grave culpability.
predicates.aggravating_factors_outweigh_mitigating_: The court evaluates the aggravating and mitigating circumstances and finds the aggravating circumstances decisive.
predicates.life_imprisonment_inadequate: The court finds that life imprisonment would be altogether inadequate punishment in light of the relevant circumstances.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified only in a rarest-of-rare case in which the aggravating circumstances, considered with the offender’s circumstances and any mitigation, make a lesser sentence inadequate.
material_facts: The accused whose death sentences were upheld were found to have taken part in several planned, brutal killings and in concealing or disposing of the bodies.
The evidence showed organised criminal activity, repeated elimination of people regarded as obstructing that activity, and especially cruel and calculated conduct.

The Court considered the circumstances of the crimes and offenders, the roles and participation of the accused, and the proposed mitigating circumstances, including claimed distress and other explanations.
The Court found the relevant accused’s conduct exceptionally cruel and depraved and found the crimes and offenders presented a grave danger to society.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 354(3) and 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, life imprisonment is the rule and death the exception; the court must give special reasons and consider both the crime and the criminal, weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Death is reserved for the gravest cases of extreme culpability where the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. The Court relied on Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P., Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration), Mangal Singh v. State of U.P., Ediga Anamma v. State of A.P. and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The death sentences imposed on the two accused whose participation was established by their own corroborated confessions and other evidence were confirmed as warranted in rarest-of-rare cases.

rule.if: capital_sentence_appeal and multiple_planned_brutal_killings and exceptional_cruelty_or_depravity and offender_presents_serious_social_danger and mitigating_circumstances_do_not_make_lesser_sentence_adequate

predicates.capital_sentence_appeal: The court is reviewing a death sentence in a criminal appeal.
predicates.multiple_planned_brutal_killings: The offender participated in multiple planned and brutal killings.
predicates.exceptional_cruelty_or_depravity: The manner and circumstances of the crimes showed exceptional cruelty or depravity.
predicates.offender_presents_serious_social_danger: The court found that the offender’s conduct showed a serious continuing danger to society.
predicates.mitigating_circumstances_do_not_make_les: The court considered the offender’s mitigating circumstances and found that they did not make a lesser sentence adequate.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence must be assessed individually, and it should not be imposed when the evidence about the accused’s particular participation is not sufficiently safe or strong to justify that extreme penalty.
material_facts: One accused was convicted of murder on evidence supporting common intention, including the approver’s testimony and corroborating evidence.
The evidence of the approver about this accused’s precise participation in two killings contained a discrepancy about whether he held a victim’s legs.
The only evidence describing that accused’s particular role in those killings was the approver’s evidence; there was no other evidence of the precise nature of his participation.
The co-accused’s retracted confessions implicated him, but the Court declined to use those confessions to assess his individual participation for the death-sentence decision.
The Court distinguished his evidence and role from those of the two accused whose death sentences it upheld.
members.legal_principle: The sentencing court must consider the role of each offender and the quality of the evidence bearing on that role, while weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. A co-accused’s confession cannot be used to determine the nature of another accused’s individual participation for deciding whether to impose death. The Court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and, on the significance of evidentiary quality at sentencing, Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of U.P. and Suresh v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The accused’s murder convictions and other sentences were confirmed, but his death sentence was reduced to imprisonment for life because the evidence of his particular participation was not sufficiently safe to justify the extreme sentence.

predicates.capital_sentence_appeal: The court is reviewing a death sentence in a criminal appeal.
predicates.individual_role_evidence_uncertain_or_we: The evidence of the accused’s particular participation was uncertain or insufficiently strong, even though evidence supported the conviction.
predicates.death_sentence_assessment_depends_on_tha: The accused’s particular role and the quality of evidence about it are relevant to whether the extreme sentence is justified.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is appropriate only in a rarest-of-rare case in which, after considering the offender and the crime and giving full weight to mitigating circumstances, life imprisonment is inadequate.
material_facts: The victim was raped and then strangled to death, and the judgment described the murder as a brutal act committed to avoid detection.
The trial court imposed the death penalty, and the High Court confirmed it.
The Supreme Court applied the rarest-of-rare tests and held that the case met them.
members.legal_principle: Under Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, life imprisonment is the rule and death is an exception reserved for the gravest cases of extreme culpability. The court must consider the circumstances of both the offender and the crime, give full weight to mitigating circumstances, balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances, and impose death only where life imprisonment is inadequate and cannot conscientiously be imposed.
members.conclusion: The case fell within the rarest-of-rare category, and the death sentence was appropriate; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: capital_sentence_review and murder_extremely_brutal and murder_committed_to_avoid_detection and life_imprisonment_inadequate_after_full_balance

predicates.capital_sentence_review: The proceeding requires a court to review whether a death sentence is appropriate.
predicates.murder_extremely_brutal: The murder was committed with extreme brutality.
predicates.murder_committed_to_avoid_detection: The offender committed the murder to avoid detection of another serious crime.
predicates.life_imprisonment_inadequate_after_full_: After considering the offender and the crime and giving full weight to mitigating circumstances, life imprisonment is inadequate.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence requires special reasons that take account of the offender, and the gravity or number of deaths alone does not justify the extreme penalty.
material_facts: The High Court affirmed death sentences after emphasizing that the two accused had fired at and killed three unarmed people.
The Supreme Court considered that sentencing factors had been dealt with casually, as though the nature of the crime alone determined punishment.
members.legal_principle: Sections 302 of the Indian Penal Code and 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provide the choice between death and life imprisonment and require special reasons for death. Section 235(2) CrPC provides for a sentencing hearing. Applying Ediga Annamma, Rajendra Prasad, and Bishnu Deo Shaw, the Court held that sentencing must consider the criminal and the offender’s social and personal circumstances; the crime’s gravity or the number of deaths is not by itself the controlling criterion.
members.conclusion: The court imposing a death sentence must record special reasons, and sentencing must consider the offender and the offender’s circumstances rather than focus solely on the crime or the number of victims.

predicates.death_sentence_case: A court is deciding whether a person convicted of murder should receive a death sentence.
predicates.sentencing_based_only_on_crime: The sentencing court focuses on the nature or number of the crimes and does not adequately consider the offender and the offender’s circumstances.
predicates.death_sentence_not_justified_without_spe: A death sentence is not justified without special reasons that take account of the offender.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified only in the gravest cases where, after balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances, life imprisonment is inadequate.
material_facts: The accused deliberately brought fuel and weapons to a family home, poured fuel in a room where the family was eating, set it alight, and closed the door.
The accused attacked a victim who escaped the burning room with a sword, causing a fatal neck wound.
Five people died, several of them after suffering extensive burns, and the sole survivor sustained extensive burns.
The court found that the attack was planned, cold-blooded, extremely cruel, and committed without immediate provocation; the victims were helpless, and the offence effectively destroyed a family.
The court found no mitigating circumstance sufficient to outweigh the aggravating circumstances and rejected the argument that the passage of time justified reducing the sentence.
members.legal_principle: Under Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, the death penalty may be imposed only in the gravest cases and only when life imprisonment appears inadequate, after an overall balancing of aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab elaborated on that balance and identified circumstances such as extreme brutality, multiple murders, and the murder of helpless victims. The Court also considered Devender Pal Singh v. State of NCT of Delhi, Atbir v. Government of NCT of Delhi, C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu, Ravji alias Ram Chandra v. State of Rajasthan, Dhananjoy Chatterjee v. State of West Bengal, State of U.P. v. Dharmendra Singh, Triveniben v. State of Gujarat, Sushil Murmu v. State of Jharkhand, Gurdev Singh v. State of Punjab, Haru Ghosh v. State of West Bengal, Dilip Premnarayan Tiwari v. State of Maharashtra, and Swamy Shraddananda v. State of Karnataka.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the case was one of the rarest of the rare, upheld the death sentence, and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.life_imprisonment_inadequate: The court found that life imprisonment would be an inadequate punishment for the offence.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified only in an exceptional murder case after balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances concerning both the crime and the offender.
material_facts: The court found that two leading participants were responsible for multiple planned, brutal and gruesome murders committed as part of organized criminal activity.
The victims were helpless, and the perpetrators concealed or disposed of the bodies to screen the crimes.
The court considered the offenders’ roles and the arguments advanced as mitigating circumstances, but found the crimes exceptionally grave and the offenders a menace to society.
members.legal_principle: Sections 354(3) and 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure require death to be an exceptional sentence: the court must consider aggravating and mitigating circumstances, pay due regard to both the crime and the criminal, and impose death only when the alternative is unquestionably foreclosed. The court relied on Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P., Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration), Mangal Singh v. State of U.P., and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The court confirmed the death sentences for the two leading participants, finding the case to be among the rarest of rare cases and the alternative of life imprisonment inadequate.

predicates.capital_sentencing_appeal: The case is an appeal in which a death sentence is under review.

predicates.offender_led_or_actively_drove_crimes: The offender led or actively drove the criminal activity that resulted in the murders.

predicates.life_sentence_inadequate: The court found that a life sentence would be inadequate in light of the offender’s conduct and the gravity of the crimes.

members.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified in a rarest-of-rare case when the aggravating circumstances of the crime and the offenders outweigh the mitigating circumstances and leave no adequate alternative.
material_facts: Six accused appealed death sentences for their roles in a coordinated attack in which five people were killed.
The murders were pre-planned and exceptionally brutal: three victims were beheaded, and a child was thrown into a fire and burned alive.
The offenders carried the severed heads in a procession and proclaimed victory.
The Court considered the proposed mitigating circumstances but found that they were outweighed by the scale and brutality of the crime, its motive, and the offenders’ conduct.
members.legal_principle: Life imprisonment is the rule and death is an exception; death may be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases when the alternative option is unquestionably foreclosed. The court must balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances and consider both the crime and the criminal. The Court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the case fell within the rarest-of-rare category and upheld the death sentences of the six accused.

predicates.aggravating_circumstances_outweigh_mitig: After considering both sides, the court found the aggravating circumstances outweighed the mitigating circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A property-identity objection already determined in eviction proceedings cannot be reopened in execution proceedings to prevent enforcement of the eviction decree.
material_facts: The eviction proceedings included a specific issue about the correctness of the property plan, and that issue was decided against the tenants.
The tenant admitted in evidence that the plan correctly depicted the shop, and the tenants did not pursue the issue in their appeal, revision, or earlier petition for special leave.

In execution, the tenants repeatedly disputed the identity and boundaries of the property; the executing court rejected those objections, and an earlier revision challenging that rejection was also dismissed.
The High Court later treated the identity objection as unresolved, directed that it be considered before enforcement, and ordered restoration of possession.
members.legal_principle: An executing court cannot go behind the decree or reopen an issue determined in the proceedings that produced it. The Court applied this principle to execution of an eviction decree and referred to the execution proceedings under Order XXI Rule 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure; it relied on no earlier case.
members.conclusion: The High Court's order was erroneous and was set aside; the identity of the property could not be reopened in execution after it had been decided in the eviction proceedings.

predicates.execution_of_eviction_decree: The proceeding is execution of a decree ordering eviction of a tenant.
predicates.property_identity_decided_in_eviction_ca: The identity or description of the property was determined in the proceedings that produced the eviction decree.
predicates.same_identity_objection_repeated_in_exec: The judgment debtor raises the same property-identity objection again during execution.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot reopen matters that were determined in the proceedings resulting in the decree.
material_facts: The respondent objected during execution on grounds that had been considered in the eviction proceedings resulting in the decree.
The respondent also alleged fraud, which had not been raised during the trial leading to the decree.
The executing court rejected the objections, and the Supreme Court found no basis to accept the repeated objections.
members.legal_principle: Questions determined in the proceedings resulting in a decree cannot be reopened by an executing court. A fraud objection also cannot succeed without a pleaded and proved basis.
members.conclusion: The executing court was right to reject objections that sought to reopen matters settled before the decree, including the unsupported fraud allegation.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party raised an objection in a proceeding to enforce a decree.
predicates.objection_relates_to_matter_decided_in_d: The objection concerned a matter already determined in the proceedings that produced the decree.
predicates.execution_objection_rejected: The executing court rejects the objection.

members.legal_issue: A proceeding concerning delay in execution after final confirmation of a death sentence does not permit the Court to reopen the judicial conclusions that confirmed the sentence.
material_facts: The death sentence had been confirmed by the High Court and the Supreme Court before the proceeding seeking relief for delay was brought.
The relief sought concerned the subsequent delay in execution and the pending mercy process.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 32, the Court may examine undue delay in execution of a death sentence after the judicial process has finally confirmed it, but its review is confined to the delay and the circumstances that followed confirmation. Smt. Triveniben v. State of Gujarat states this limitation; the Court also relied on T.V. Vatheeswaran v. State of Tamil Nadu and Sher Singh v. State of Punjab in addressing delay in execution.
members.conclusion: The Court may examine the nature of the delay and the circumstances after final confirmation, but has no jurisdiction in that proceeding to reopen the conclusions reached when the death sentence was finally maintained.

predicates.article_32_death_sentence_delay_proceedi: A proceeding under the constitutional remedy is brought to seek relief for delay in executing a death sentence.
predicates.death_sentence_finally_confirmed: The death sentence was finally maintained through the judicial process before the delay proceeding was brought.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot reopen in the same proceedings a land-exemption issue already finally decided, or advance a ground that could have been raised before that final decision, merely because of new evidence or a later interpretation of the law.
material_facts: The landholder's original return claimed land as fuel area and rested tea area but did not claim exemption on the ground that cardamom plantation existed there.
The Supreme Court had earlier finally restored the land board's determination concerning the fuel area and rested tea area.
On remand, the landholder sought to recharacterize part of the same land as cardamom plantation and again claimed the rested tea area.
The landholder relied on later decisions and a subsequent report about the cardamom plantation, but had not amended its original return to make the cardamom claim.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata and estoppel, grounded in public policy and justice, apply to administrative proceedings as well as court proceedings. They prevent relitigation of an issue finally decided, including at a later stage of the same proceedings, and constructive res judicata prevents a party from raising a ground that should have been raised earlier. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not exhaust the general doctrine. The Court relied on Devilal Modi v. Sales Tax Officer, Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal, Y.B. Patil v. Y.L. Patil, and Gopal Prasad Sinha v. State of Bihar; it declined to apply the exception to issue estoppel discussed in Arnold v. National Westminster Bank. The available review powers under Section 85(9) and (9A) did not provide a basis to reopen these matters.
members.conclusion: The earlier final determination barred reopening the fuel-area and rested-tea issues in the same proceedings. The later cardamom claim could not be introduced on remand, and the High Court's determination on those matters was upheld.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding_on_remand: The matter concerns a land-ceiling proceeding being considered again after remand.
predicates.prior_final_decision_on_same_land_issue: A final decision in the same proceedings determined the exemption issue concerning the land in dispute.
predicates.party_seeks_to_reopen_decided_issue: A party seeks to litigate again an exemption issue already finally decided.
predicates.party_raises_ground_that_could_have_been: A party advances a ground that could have been raised before the earlier final decision.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot exclude an amount included in a decree by reconsidering the decree's entitlement to that amount.
material_facts: The compensation decrees included interest.
The successor state asked for interest to be disallowed, at least for the period before it received notice of the proceedings.
The dispute arose in execution proceedings.
members.legal_principle: An executing court cannot go behind the decree; it must enforce the decree as made. The Court cited no particular statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The executing court could not disallow the interest included in the decrees and was required to enforce the entire decretal amount.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce a court decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_includes_interest: The decree awarded interest as part of the amount payable.
predicates.judgment_debtor_seeks_to_exclude_interes: The judgment-debtor asked the executing court to disallow interest included in the decree.

members.legal_issue: Matters finally determined in earlier proceedings cannot be reopened through repeated administrative proceedings on the same grounds.
material_facts: Earlier proceedings involving the same land and parties had determined the validity of the transfer, the ownership recorded in the revenue entry, the applicability of the agricultural land ceiling law, and the relevant land-use scheme.
The authorities later issued notices and orders raising grounds that had already been raised and determined in those proceedings.
The earlier decisions had been upheld or left undisturbed in subsequent proceedings, including dismissal of a review petition.
members.legal_principle: The finality of judicial and administrative decisions precludes re-litigation of matters already determined. The Court held that its binding judgments could not be disregarded by authorities on the basis that facts had not been fully presented or that the prior decisions were only collateral. It relied on the prior proceedings in this dispute, including the High Court judgment in Special Civil Application No. 1032 of 1996, the Supreme Court’s decisions in the connected proceedings, and the dismissal of the review petition; it also referred to Article 142 of the Constitution in stating that authorities were bound by this Court’s judgments.
members.conclusion: The authorities could not reopen matters concluded by earlier decisions; pending appeals could be considered only on matters not covered by those decisions.

predicates.appeal_from_repeated_administrative_proc: A party appeals against administrative proceedings initiated again after earlier proceedings concerning the same dispute.
predicates.same_grounds_previously_decided: The authorities rely on grounds that were raised and determined in earlier proceedings involving the dispute.
predicates.prior_decisions_final: The earlier determinations were not displaced in subsequent proceedings and had become final.

members.legal_issue: Issues concerning execution proceedings that have been finally determined cannot be reopened through later objections in the same execution.
material_facts: The objections to the auction sale, its confirmation, the sale certificate, and the compromise were rejected by the executing court and the resulting decisions were upheld on appeal; a further challenge was dismissed.
A later order rejecting objections, including the contention that the compromise had adjusted the decree, was not appealed.
The judgment debtor raised previously decided matters again when resisting delivery of possession.
members.legal_principle: A judicial determination that has attained finality binds the parties, and repeating the same challenge in later proceedings is impermissible and may amount to abuse of process. The court applied this principle to the earlier determinations concerning the execution sale, the compromise, and the alleged adjustment of the decree, including the contention under Order XXI Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The previously determined issues had attained finality and could not be re-agitated in later execution proceedings.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is an objection or other proceeding arising during execution of a decree.
predicates.issue_previously_decided_finally: A court has already decided the issue and that decision has become final between the parties.
predicates.later_objection_repeats_issue: A party raises the same issue again in a later objection or proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A power to initiate fresh proceedings that was enacted after a land-ceiling proceeding had been finally determined cannot be used to reopen that proceeding.
material_facts: The land-ceiling proceeding had ended with a final order before the provision permitting fresh proceedings was enacted.
The final order was not challenged.
Fresh proceedings were initiated after the provision was enacted, relying on the fact that the consequential final statement had not been issued.
members.legal_principle: Section 32B, inserted by Bihar Act 55 of 1982, did not apply to a proceeding that had been concluded before its enactment. The absence of the final statement required by Section 11(1) did not permit the authorities to use Section 32B to reopen the concluded proceeding.
members.conclusion: The later-enacted power to initiate fresh proceedings could not be exercised because the proceeding had ended before that power was introduced.

rule.if: land_ceiling_proceeding and final_order_before_new_reopening_power and order_unchallenged and fresh_proceedings_rely_on_new_power

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter concerns a proceeding to determine whether a landholder possesses land beyond a ceiling.
predicates.final_order_before_new_reopening_power: The authority made its final order before a new power to initiate fresh proceedings was enacted.
predicates.order_unchallenged: No party challenged the final order.
predicates.fresh_proceedings_rely_on_new_power: The authority initiated fresh proceedings by relying on the subsequently enacted reopening power.

members.legal_issue: The government cannot use a later administrative decision to reopen issues conclusively decided in a prior judgment between the parties.
material_facts: The earlier High Court judgment had held that the grant was valid, that the claimants were entitled to the price rather than restoration of the land, and that they had waived their right to occupy it.
The Supreme Court later allowed the claimants to apply to the government for modification of the grant but did not direct the government to cancel it.

When considering the application, the government proceeded on the basis that confirmation of the claimants' occupancy rights made them owners and ordered cancellation of the grant and transfer of vacant sites or payment of compensation.
members.legal_principle: A new cause of action may permit a fresh proceeding, but issues already decided between the parties cannot be reopened. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. M.P. Mohla for that distinction and Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India for the principle that a final judgment must be obeyed while it stands and cannot be ignored by an executive decision. The Supreme Court's earlier order granted liberty to seek modification but did not mandate cancellation of the grant.
members.conclusion: The government could consider the application but could not disregard the earlier binding findings; the directions cancelling the grant and transferring vacant sites or awarding compensation were set aside.

predicates.administrative_reconsideration_after_fin: A government authority reconsidered a matter after a final judgment concerning it.
predicates.prior_judgment_decided_the_dispute: The final judgment decided the parties' rights concerning the disputed grant or property.
predicates.administrative_order_reopens_decided_iss: The authority issued an order based on a position inconsistent with an issue decided in that judgment.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot use fresh proceedings before subordinate authorities to reopen a matter finally decided by a higher court when those authorities lack power to set aside that decision.
material_facts: The High Court had finally resolved the dispute in the respondents’ favour by quashing the appellate and revisional orders and maintaining the Consolidation Officer’s order.
The appellants did not challenge that judgment by seeking further review in the Supreme Court but instead made a fresh application to the Settlement Officer (Consolidation).
The Settlement Officer rejected the fresh application, the revisional authority rejected the challenge, and the High Court dismissed a further writ petition.
The consolidation authorities had no jurisdiction to set aside the earlier High Court judgment.
members.legal_principle: A final higher-court decision cannot be set aside by subordinate administrative or consolidation authorities that lack jurisdiction to do so. Resort to such authorities to reopen the decided matter is not a valid remedy and, in the circumstances described, cannot constitute good-faith prosecution for purposes of excluding time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
members.conclusion: The fresh proceedings before the consolidation authorities were not legally valid as a means of reopening the matter, and pursuing them could not support exclusion of time on the basis of good faith.

predicates.collateral_proceeding_after_final_court_: A party starts a fresh proceeding before a lower authority to reopen a matter already finally decided by a higher court.
predicates.lower_authority_cannot_set_aside_decisio: The lower authority lacks power to set aside or alter the higher court’s final decision.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected at the threshold when a meaningful reading of its averments shows that it discloses no right to sue or that the suit is barred by law.
material_facts: The defendants applied during the suit for rejection of the plaint.
The plaintiff alleged that the disputed property was Wakf property and sought cancellation of a sale deed.
The courts below found that the property was not included in the published list of Wakf properties, and the Supreme Court assessed the plaint on that basis.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must read the plaint as a whole and consider its averments alone; the written statement and the defendant’s contentions are immaterial. Even if the plaint’s allegations are accepted as true, rejection is proper if they disclose no cause of action or show that the suit is barred by law. Because rejection terminates a civil action at the threshold, the statutory conditions must be strictly applied; clever drafting cannot create an illusion of a cause of action.
members.conclusion: The plaint was liable to be rejected because its averments disclosed no cause of action and the suit was barred by law.

predicates.plaint_rejection_application: A defendant applied to have the plaint rejected during the civil suit.
predicates.plaint_allegations_disclose_no_suable_ri: The plaint’s allegations, read as a whole and taken at face value, disclose no right to sue.
predicates.plaint_allegations_show_legal_bar: The plaint’s allegations, read as a whole and taken at face value, show that the suit is barred by law.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected as barred by law when the bar is apparent from its own statements, even if the proper ground is not failure to disclose a cause of action.
material_facts: The plaint alleged that the registered conveyance was only security for a loan and that the loan was repaid, with a promise to reconvey, on 25 March 1987.
The suit was filed on 26 August 1996, seeking a declaration of ownership and an injunction.
The High Court upheld rejection on the ground that the plaint disclosed no cause of action, while the Supreme Court found that the plaint itself showed the suit was barred by law.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaint may be rejected when the suit appears from its statements to be clearly barred by law. The plaint is read meaningfully as a whole, and the court may act on a bar apparent from the pleaded facts. The Court relied on T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, (1977) 4 SCC 467, concerning meaningful reading and screening of meritless pleadings.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to reject the plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action, but rejection was justified because the plaint's own allegations showed that the suit was barred by law.

rule.if: civil_plaint_rejection_case and (plaint_allegations_disclose_cause_of_action or not plaint_allegations_disclose_cause_of_action) and pleaded_facts_show_clear_legal_bar

predicates.civil_plaint_rejection_case: A court is deciding whether to reject a civil plaint.
predicates.plaint_allegations_disclose_cause_of_act: The plaint states facts that, if accepted, identify a basis for seeking relief.
predicates.not_plaint_allegations_disclose_cause_of: The plaint does not state facts that, if accepted, identify a basis for seeking relief.
predicates.pleaded_facts_show_clear_legal_bar: The facts stated in the plaint themselves show that the suit cannot proceed under an applicable legal rule.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected for limitation at the pleading stage only when the bar appears from the plaint read as a whole and its accompanying documents.
material_facts: The defendant sought rejection of the plaint on limitation grounds under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The plaint and documents attached to it described the agreement, the exercise of an option to renew, the denial of renewal, and the later injunction claim.
The courts considered the plaint and its annexures rather than relying on the defence to establish the limitation bar.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaint may be rejected where the suit appears from its statements to be barred by law, including limitation. The plaint must be read as a whole, its averments and annexures being taken as correct; it is not permissible to isolate a sentence or add to or subtract from the pleading. The Court relied on Liverpool & London S.P. & I Association Ltd. v. M.V. Sea Success I, Popat and Kotecha Property v. State Bank of India Staff Association, T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, and I.T.C. Limited v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal.
members.conclusion: The limitation question could be decided under Order VII Rule 11(d) because the bar appeared from the plaint and its annexures.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A party applies for rejection of a plaint on the ground that the suit is barred by law.
predicates.limitation_bar_apparent_from_plaint_as_a: The plaint, read as a whole with its annexures and with its averments taken as correct, shows that the suit is out of time.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected at the threshold when its own averments show that a suit for specific performance is barred by limitation.
material_facts: The defendants applied for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was time-barred.
The plaint stated the agreement’s fixed performance date, the requested extensions and their final expiry, and the later date on which the suit was filed.
The trial court rejected the plaint as barred by limitation, but the High Court reversed that order; the Supreme Court restored the trial court’s order.
members.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the court to consider whether the plaint discloses a cause of action and whether it appears to be barred by law. Read with Article 54 of the Limitation Act, the plaint’s own dates showed that the specific-performance suit was time-barred. The judgment does not rely on an earlier decision in its reasoning.
members.conclusion: The plaint was properly rejected because its averments showed that the suit was barred by limitation.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.plaint_rejection_sought: The opposing party applied for rejection of the plaint.
predicates.plaint_dates_show_limitation_bar: The dates and other averments stated in the plaint show that the applicable limitation period had elapsed before the suit was filed.

members.legal_issue: A plaint that is manifestly vexatious and meritless on a meaningful reading, and discloses no clear right to sue, is subject to rejection when a ground for rejection is met.
material_facts: An eviction order had been contested through trial, appeal, and revision and had been confirmed.
A later suit sought a declaration that the eviction order was obtained by fraud and collusion and sought to prevent its execution.
The Court found the pending suit to be a flagrant misuse of the process of receiving plaints and to have no survival value.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must read the plaint meaningfully rather than formally and reject it when it is manifestly vexatious and meritless, discloses no clear right to sue, and a specified ground for rejection is fulfilled. No earlier case is relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The trial court should reject the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 if a ground specified there is fulfilled.

rule.if: civil_suit and plaint_read_meaningfully and plaint_is_manifestly_vexatious_and_meritless and plaint_discloses_no_clear_right_to_sue and rejection_ground_is_satisfied

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.plaint_read_meaningfully: The court assesses the substance of the plaint rather than relying on its formal wording.
predicates.plaint_is_manifestly_vexatious_and_merit: The plaint's substance shows that the claim is plainly vexatious and without merit.
predicates.plaint_discloses_no_clear_right_to_sue: The plaint does not disclose a clear right to sue.
predicates.rejection_ground_is_satisfied: The facts satisfy a ground that permits rejection of the plaint.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected as barred by law only when its statements, read as a whole and without resolving disputed facts, unambiguously establish the legal bar.
material_facts: The defendant applied to reject the plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d) on limitation grounds.
The plaint sought several forms of relief, including specific performance, damages, recovery or accounting for amounts collected, and injunctions.
Whether the amounts collected related to a period beyond the agreed lease term required evidence.
The trial court had rejected the application, but the High Court reversed that decision on the view that the claims centered on non-execution of the lease.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court examines the plaint’s averments, not the defendant’s pleas, and may reject the plaint only if those averments, read as a whole and without doubt or dispute, show that the suit is barred by law. Disputed questions cannot be decided at this stage. Order VI Rule 2(1) requires pleadings to state material facts, and the plaint cannot be dissected or read out of context. This approach is supported by Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill, Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, and Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner. Limitation generally bars the remedy, not the underlying right; the Court referred in this connection to V. Subba Rao v. Secretary to Government, France B. Martins v. Mafalda Maria, and N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishna Murthy.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to hold that the plaint was barred on its face. The appeal was allowed, and the disputed limitation issues were left for the trial court to decide without any opinion on the merits.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A party applies for rejection of a plaint on the ground that the suit is barred by law.
predicates.plaint_alone_unambiguously_shows_legal_b: The plaint, read as a whole and without resolving disputed facts or relying on material outside it, clearly establishes that the suit is barred by law.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected as time-barred only when its own statements, accepted as true, show without addition or subtraction that the suit is barred.
material_facts: The suit sought declaration of title and an injunction, with recovery of possession as an alternative if the plaintiff was out of possession.

The plaintiff alleged that he learned of an error in the property boundaries at a particular time; the defendant contended that the plaintiff knew of the issue earlier, including from prior proceedings.
The trial court treated the timing of the plaintiff’s knowledge as a factual matter for trial, but the High Court rejected the plaint as barred by limitation.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court considers only the plaint’s averments, taken at face value and as a whole; the plaint must show on its own that the suit is barred by law. A limitation question that depends on disputed facts cannot be resolved at this stage. The Court relied on Popat and Kotecha Property v. State Bank of India Staff Association and Balasaria Construction (P) Ltd. v. Hanuman Seva Trust.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the plaint because the plaint did not itself establish that the suit was barred; the limitation-related disputes could not be decided on the application to reject the plaint.

rule.if: plaint_rejection_application and (plaint_seeks_alternative_possession or limitation_depends_on_disputed_facts) and not plaint_itself_shows_bar

predicates.plaint_rejection_application: A defendant applied for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was barred by law.
predicates.plaint_seeks_alternative_possession: The plaintiff sought recovery of possession as an alternative to other relief concerning the property.
predicates.limitation_depends_on_disputed_facts: The parties disputed facts relevant to when the plaintiff learned of the alleged problem or when the right was threatened.
predicates.plaint_itself_shows_bar: The plaint’s own statements, accepted as true and read without adding or subtracting anything, show that the suit is barred.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected at the threshold when a meaningful reading of its allegations, taken at face value, shows that none of the reliefs claimed is legally available.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought declarations concerning the partnership firm's assets and representation of the firm, injunctions, accounts, and dissolution.
The plaintiffs claimed through deceased partners but were not themselves partners; the pleaded facts also described the firm as continuing its business.
The court assessed whether the pleaded reliefs could be granted without considering the defendants’ defence and agreed that none could be granted in law.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must scrutinise the plaint’s averments, read meaningfully and as a whole, together with documents relied on, to determine whether it discloses a cause of action; the defence is not considered. If the reliefs claimed cannot be granted on the pleaded facts, the suit need not proceed to trial. The court relied on T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, Pearlite Liners (P) Ltd. v. Manorama Sirsi, and Dahiben v. Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali; Dahiben also referred to Azhar Hussain v. Rajiv Gandhi and Liverpool & London S.P. & I Assn. Ltd. v. M.V. Sea Success I. The power is drastic and the conditions for its exercise must be strictly followed.
members.conclusion: The plaint was properly rejected, and the appeals challenging that rejection were dismissed.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A party applied for rejection of a plaint in a civil suit.
predicates.plaint_assessed_on_its_averments: The court assessed the pleaded allegations at face value, without relying on the opposing party’s defence.
predicates.every_claimed_relief_unavailable: The pleaded facts leave none of the reliefs requested legally available to the claimant.

members.legal_issue: A court that rejects a plaint because the suit appears from its statements to be barred by law cannot grant the plaintiff time to amend the plaint after rejection.
material_facts: The trial court allowed an application to reject the plaint because the suit appeared to be barred by law.
After allowing the application, the trial court directed the plaintiff to seek proper relief and pay the required court fee within a fixed time.
The statutory provision allowing additional time for correcting valuation or supplying stamp paper concerns those specific grounds for rejection, not rejection because the suit appears barred by law.
members.legal_principle: Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires rejection where the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by law. The proviso to that rule concerns time fixed for correcting valuation or supplying requisite stamp paper in cases under clauses (b) and (c), and does not apply to rejection under clause (d). The Court relied on this distinction in holding that the trial court's further direction was not in accordance with law.
members.conclusion: The direction permitting amendment after rejection of the plaint was not in accordance with law.

predicates.plaint_rejected_as_barred_by_law: The court rejected the plaint because the suit appeared from its statements to be barred by law.
predicates.court_granted_post_rejection_amendment_t: After rejecting the plaint, the court gave the plaintiff time to amend it and pay the required court fee.

members.legal_issue: A plaint may be rejected for limitation only when, on reading the plaint as a whole, the limitation bar is apparent on its face.
material_facts: The defendants applied to reject the plaint on limitation grounds.

The plaint alleged that advertisements indicating an intended transfer appeared and that an attempt was made to dispossess the plaintiffs in 2010; it identified that attempted dispossession as the cause of action.
The High Court relied on an earlier paragraph of the plaint and did not consider the plaint as a whole.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaint can be rejected for limitation only if the bar is apparent on its face. The court must read the plaint as a whole, rather than isolating selected lines or passages. The Court applied Ram Prakash Gupta v. Rajiv Kumar Gupta, (2007) 10 SCC 59, which states that the whole plaint must be considered when deciding an application under that rule.
members.conclusion: The plaint could not be rejected as facially barred by limitation. The High Court’s order was set aside and the trial court’s refusal to reject the plaint was restored.

rule.if: plaint_rejection_application and limitation_is_basis and plaint_as_a_whole_alleges_a_later_cause_of_action and limitation_bar_not_apparent_on_face

predicates.plaint_rejection_application: A defendant applies to have a plaint rejected before trial.
predicates.limitation_is_basis: The defendant relies on limitation as a ground for rejecting the plaint.
predicates.plaint_as_a_whole_alleges_a_later_cause_: The plaintiffs’ allegations, read together, identify a later event as giving rise to the cause of action.
predicates.limitation_bar_not_apparent_on_face: The allegations in the plaint do not establish, on their face, that the claim is out of time.

members.legal_issue: A deed transferring possession and enjoyment of property is a lease rather than a mortgage when its terms and the parties’ treatment show a right to enjoy the property, not a transfer of the property as security for repayment of debt.
material_facts: The deed recited existing debts and money received, transferred possession of the land for a stated term, and allowed the transferee to enjoy it.
The transferee had to pay a fixed annual amount to the transferor in addition to government revenue.
The deed did not state that the land was transferred as security for the debt, provide a right to sell it if the debt was unpaid, or show that the usufruct would reduce the principal debt.
The transferors later assigned the ownership rights in the property, including the debt, for a sum that included the debt recited in the deed.
The dispute arose in a proceeding to apportion compensation for acquired property, and the classification affected the competing claims to compensation.
members.legal_principle: The court determines the nature of a mixed instrument from the whole document, the surrounding circumstances, and the parties’ treatment of it; its label is not conclusive. The essential feature of a mortgage is that the property is transferred as security for repayment of a debt, while a lease transfers a right to enjoy the property. The court applied the test approved in Velayudhan Vivekanandan v. Ayyappan Sadasivan, I.L.R. [1975] 1 Kerala 166. The compensation dispute arose under the Land Acquisition Act and the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, but no specific statutory provision was cited as governing the classification test.
members.conclusion: The deed was a lease, not a mortgage, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: instrument_classification_dispute and property_given_for_enjoyment and fixed_annual_payment_independent_of_principal and not property_transferred_as_debt_security and not creditor_right_to_sell_for_unpaid_debt and not usufruct_applied_to_reduce_principal and transferors_treated_transaction_as_lease

predicates.instrument_classification_dispute: The court is deciding whether an instrument is a mortgage or a lease.
predicates.property_given_for_enjoyment: The transferor gave the transferee possession of property and the right to enjoy it.
predicates.fixed_annual_payment_independent_of_prin: The transferee had to pay a fixed annual amount to the transferor that was not intended to reduce the principal debt.
predicates.property_transferred_as_debt_security: The instrument states that the property is transferred as security for repayment of a debt.
predicates.creditor_right_to_sell_for_unpaid_debt: The instrument gives the creditor a right to sell the property if the debt is not repaid.

members.legal_issue: A single instrument providing for repayment and retransference of property is a mortgage by conditional sale when its terms and the circumstances establish a secured loan rather than an outright sale with a right to repurchase.
material_facts: The landowner received money from the other party as a loan and executed one registered instrument concerning the land.
The instrument was styled as a deed of conditional sale and provided that the landowner could repay the stated amount within five years and obtain a sale deed retransferring the land.
The recipient was placed in possession and could enjoy the land during that period.
The landowner offered to repay the amount and sought redemption of the land.
The trial court and the High Court accepted the evidence supporting the loan and mortgage character of the transaction.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a transaction is a mortgage by conditional sale where, among the specified alternatives, payment by the seller requires the buyer to transfer the property back, provided the condition is embodied in the document effecting or purporting to effect the sale. Under Chunchun Jha v. Ebadat Ali, the parties’ intention is gathered first from the instrument; clear words control, while surrounding circumstances may be considered if the language is ambiguous. A single instrument containing the relevant condition may be a mortgage, and where the Section 58(c) requirements are met, the deed is construed as a mortgage. The Court preferred Chunchun Jha, a larger-Bench decision, and distinguished Vanchalabai Raghunath Ithape, where there was no debtor-creditor relationship.
members.conclusion: The instrument was a mortgage by conditional sale, not an outright sale with a condition to repurchase; the decree granting redemption was restored.

members.legal_issue: An ostensibly absolute conveyance with a condition of reconveyance is a mortgage by conditional sale when the deed and surrounding circumstances show that the transfer secures a debt and creates a debtor-creditor relationship.
material_facts: The transferors were indebted and used the consideration to discharge debts owed to a bank and to the transferees and their associates.

The deed provided for reconveyance at the stated prices and also allowed the transferees, after a specified period, to require the transferors to take back properties and repay the consideration, including where the properties had been adversely affected by circumstances beyond the transferees’ control.
A same-day agreement required the transferors to pay the difference between net rents and interest on the consideration until reconveyance.
The properties were worth substantially more than the prices stated in the deed.
The transferors brought a suit for redemption, contending that the conveyance was a mortgage.
members.legal_principle: Under section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, including its proviso added by Act XX of 1929, a mortgage by conditional sale requires the condition to be embodied in the instrument effecting or purporting to effect the sale. Incorporation of the condition does not by itself establish a mortgage: the parties’ intention must be determined from the deed read with surrounding circumstances. The distinction is whether the transfer creates a debtor-creditor relationship and provides security for a debt, or instead creates an outright sale subject to an obligation to retransfer. The form of the deed, and a strict time limit for repurchase, are not decisive. The Court relied on Narasingerji Gyanagerji v. Panuganti Parthasarathi and Others (1924) L.R. 51 I.A. 305.
members.conclusion: The transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale, not an absolute sale with a right of repurchase, and the transferors could redeem the properties. The appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A transfer subject to a repurchase condition in the same document is a mortgage by conditional sale when the parties intended the transfer as security, and refusal of a timely tender prevents the transaction from becoming an absolute sale for default.
material_facts: The document described the transaction as a mortgage by conditional sale and included in that same document a condition for repayment and reconveyance.
The contents of the document and the surrounding circumstances showed that the transfer was intended as security.
The mortgagor tendered repayment within the stipulated time, but the mortgagee refused to accept it.
The plaintiff held the property through a transfer from the mortgagor and sought redemption.
members.legal_principle: Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act requires the repurchase condition to be embodied in the document effecting or purporting to effect the sale. The controlling test is the parties’ intention, assessed from the document and surrounding circumstances; where the transfer is intended as security, it is a mortgage. The Court relied on Balkishen Das v. Legge, Bhaskar Woman Joshi v. Shrinarayan Rambilas Agarwal, and P.L. Bapuswami v. N. Pattay Gounder.
members.conclusion: The transaction remained a mortgage by conditional sale because the mortgagor had tendered repayment and was not in default; the plaintiff as assignee was entitled to seek redemption.
