members.legal_issue: A deed securing repayment of a debt by an interest in land creates a mortgage rather than a lease when the parties’ intention and the transaction’s terms establish a debtor-creditor relationship and the land is security for repayment.
material_facts: The executant was indebted to the other party, and the deed arranged for the debt to be repaid after a specified term.
The deed expressly made the land interest security for the amount payable and described the transaction in several places as a mortgage.
The other party was to receive income from the land and apply it towards interest, while the executant retained an obligation to repay the principal.
members.legal_principle: The parties’ intention, discerned from the deed as a whole, governs its construction. Where there is a debt and land is given as security for its repayment, the transaction is a mortgage whatever name the deed uses. The Court referred to Ghosh on Mortgages for this guiding rule.
members.conclusion: The transaction was a mortgage, not a lease.

predicates.redemption_suit_classifies_deed: A suit for redemption requires the court to determine whether a deed created a mortgage or a lease.
predicates.indebtedness_between_parties: One party owed money to the other party under the transaction or an existing debt arrangement.
predicates.property_secures_debt_repayment: The deed made an interest in land security for repayment of the debt.

members.legal_issue: Whether a conditional transfer of property is a mortgage by conditional sale or an outright sale reserving a right of repurchase is determined by the parties’ intention as shown by the document and the surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The transfer document described the transaction as a sale, referred to the recipients as vendees, and stated that the transferors could take back the property by repaying the stated amount within the agreed period.
The recipients were put in possession of the property.
The transferors stated that they needed money for several debts and expenses, not merely to discharge an earlier loan from the recipients.
About a year earlier, a larger area had secured a smaller loan from the recipients; the later transfer covered a smaller area for a higher amount.
The higher amount represented the actual value of the property transferred.
members.legal_principle: A mortgage by conditional sale preserves the debtor-creditor relationship and the debtor’s right to redeem, whereas a sale with a condition of repurchase transfers the owner’s rights and reserves a personal right to buy the property back. Classification depends on the parties’ intention, assessed from the document and relevant surrounding circumstances; tests from decided cases are illustrative, not exhaustive. The Court distinguished Pandit Chunchun Jha v. Sheikh Ebadat Ali, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 174, explaining that construing another document ordinarily provides no guidance unless its terms are exactly similar. No statutory provision is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The document was an outright sale with a condition of repurchase, not a mortgage by conditional sale, so the claim for redemption could not succeed.

rule.if: redemption_suit_based_on_conditional_transfer and document_uses_sale_and_vendee_language and document_reserves_repurchase_on_repayment and smaller_area_transferred_for_higher_amount_than_prior_loan and transfer_amount_matches_property_value

predicates.redemption_suit_based_on_conditional_tra: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking redemption on the basis that a conditional transfer of property was a mortgage.

members.legal_issue: Whether a transfer expressed as a sale with a condition for repayment is a mortgage by conditional sale or an outright sale with a right to repurchase.
material_facts: The owners executed one deed that used sale language, described the transferee as becoming proprietor, and provided for the owners to regain possession if they repaid within a specified time; if they did not, the transferee would remain in possession and take the produce.
The deed did not expressly provide for reconveyance of title, and its language was ambiguous when read as a whole.
Most of the stated consideration discharged an existing mortgage debt, and additional money was advanced to continue proceedings concerning the land, which benefited the owners if successful.

The transferee was to possess the property and retain its produce, and the deed contained provisions requiring the owners to repay the consideration with interest and damages if the transferee was dispossessed.
The plaintiff sought redemption on the basis that the deed created a mortgage, and the courts below had reached conflicting conclusions about the deed's character.
members.legal_principle: The parties' intention controls, but it is first determined from the document. Clear language governs without extrinsic inquiry; surrounding circumstances may be considered when the document is ambiguous. Under section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, as amended, a sale and repurchase agreement in separate documents cannot constitute a mortgage, while a single document does not automatically constitute either a mortgage or a sale. Where one document has the form of an ostensible sale and its conditions satisfy section 58(c), it is to be construed as a mortgage unless express words indicate otherwise or, in an ambiguous case, the surrounding circumstances necessarily point to the contrary. The Court relied on Balkishen Das v. Legge, Alderson v. White, Bhagwan Sahai v. Bhagwan Din, and Jhanda Singh v. Wahid-ud-din.
members.conclusion: The deed was a mortgage by conditional sale, so the appeal was allowed and the lower appellate court's decree was restored, apart from costs.

members.legal_issue: An ostensible sale with a condition for reconveyance constitutes a mortgage by conditional sale when the parties’ intention and the surrounding circumstances establish a debtor-creditor relationship and a transfer intended as security.
material_facts: The instrument was framed as a sale but required reconveyance to the original owner on repayment of the same amount after five years and within seven years.
The condition for reconveyance was included in the sale instrument.
The lower courts found that the property was worth substantially more than the stated consideration.
The land records remained in the original owner’s name, and the original owner and, after his death, his sons continued paying the land revenue.
The plaintiff acquired an assignment from the original owner’s sons and sought redemption.
members.legal_principle: Under section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as amended by Act 20 of 1929, the condition must be embodied in the instrument effecting or purporting to effect the sale for the transaction to be deemed a mortgage by conditional sale. That requirement alone does not establish a mortgage: intention is determined from the instrument’s language read with the surrounding circumstances. The essential distinction is whether the transfer creates a debtor-creditor relationship and operates as security for a debt, or is instead a sale subject to an obligation to reconvey. The form of the document is not decisive. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale, not an outright sale with a condition for retransfer, and the plaintiff was entitled to a preliminary decree for redemption.

members.legal_issue: A deed whose operative terms create a loan secured by property, provide for redemption, and allocate interest and possession is a mortgage rather than an outright sale.
material_facts: The registered deed described the transaction as a mortgage and stated that the property secured money advanced.
It provided for redemption and addressed interest, rent, possession, and repair costs.
A later unregistered document was relied on to argue that the transaction was actually an outright sale.
members.legal_principle: The nature of an instrument is determined from its terms. The Court found that the terms of the registered deed clearly created a mortgage; it cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this construction.
members.conclusion: The registered deed, considered on its own, was a mortgage deed and not a sale deed.

predicates.mortgage_or_sale_classification_dispute: The case involves a dispute over whether a deed creates a mortgage or an outright sale.
predicates.deed_secures_loan: The deed states that property is given as security for money advanced.
predicates.deed_provides_for_redemption: The deed gives the transferor a right to recover the property by paying the secured amount.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of land with fruit-bearing trees for their enjoyment and for planting further trees was a tenancy rather than a usufructuary mortgage where its terms and surrounding documents showed that the transfer enabled enjoyment of the land and did not secure repayment of a debt.
material_facts: The appeal arose from a suit seeking redemption of land on the claim that the transfer documents created usufructuary mortgages.
The documents transferred land with standing fruit-bearing trees for a fixed term, for enjoyment of the land and trees and for planting additional fruit-bearing trees.
The transferees paid specified consideration, could set off the land’s income against interest, and could retain possession until the consideration and the value of trees they planted were paid.
The documents were styled as kanam deeds, described the consideration as kanartham, and one expressly described the transfers as kanam-kuzhikanam.
Later documents also described the transactions as kanam-kuzhikanam.
The documents contained no recital that the transfers secured repayment of a debt and did not describe the transactions as mortgages.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(23) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, kanam-kuzhikanam includes a transfer of land, with fruit-bearing trees if any, for enjoyment of those trees and planting such trees, with the specified rights and liabilities concerning the kanartham and interest; a usufructuary mortgage as defined by section 58(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, is excluded. The essential distinction is that a lease transfers a right to enjoy property, whereas a mortgage transfers an interest in property to secure a debt. The transaction’s description by the parties is relevant but not decisive. Under section 12 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, parties may prove that a document purporting to be a mortgage is in substance a lease; that provision does not apply where the document, properly construed, purports to be a lease. Section 2(57) includes a kanam-kuzhikanamdar within the meaning of tenant, and section 13 gives tenants fixity of tenure. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The transactions were kanam-kuzhikanam leases, not usufructuary mortgages, and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A Collector cannot reopen a final revisional decision when the statute confers no power of review.
material_facts: The tenants sought revision of the Mamlatdar’s eviction order after the appeal period had expired.
The Collector called for the record, then rejected the revision applications before the record arrived, deciding that there was no ground to interfere.
After receiving the record and hearing the parties, the Collector later reversed the Mamlatdar’s order.
members.legal_principle: Section 76A of the Act permits the Collector to exercise revisional jurisdiction where no appeal has been filed. The Collector may refuse to interfere on the materials before him without first receiving the record, even if he has called for it; such a refusal is a final quasi-judicial order. Because the Act gives no power to review that order, the Collector cannot later reopen it and reverse the decision.
members.conclusion: The Collector’s earlier refusals were final quasi-judicial orders, and the later reversal was illegal, ultra vires and without jurisdiction because the Act did not authorize review.

predicates.statutory_revisional_proceeding: A proceeding asks an administrative authority to revise a lower tribunal’s order after the ordinary appeal period has expired.
predicates.collector_made_final_refusal_to_interfer: The Collector decided that the lower tribunal’s order did not warrant revision and refused to alter it.
predicates.collector_later_reopened_same_decision: The Collector later reconsidered the same matter and made a different revisional decision.
predicates.no_review_power_conferred: The governing law did not authorize the Collector to review a final revisional decision.

members.legal_issue: A statutory officer cannot review a final order when the governing law does not confer review power, and a final order cannot be reopened through a restoration application outside the prescribed remedies.
material_facts: The competent officer issued notices to the non-evacuee co-sharers, but no claim was filed, and an order vesting the evacuee interest in the Custodian was made.
The co-sharers did not appeal or seek revision of that order, which became final under the governing law.

The co-sharers later obtained orders setting aside the vesting order and transferring the evacuee interest to them through a restoration application; the officer subsequently reviewed those orders after applications by the Assistant Custodian.
The governing law provided for appeal and revision but contained no provision authorizing the competent officer to review his own orders.
members.legal_principle: The Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, sections 6, 7, 11, 14 and 15 provided for notices, claims, vesting, appeal and revision; section 18 made orders final subject to the Act’s express exceptions. The Court applied the principle that review is available only where statute provides for it, relying on Harbhajan Singh v. Karam Singh, which approved Baijnath Ram Goenka v. Nand Kumar Singh and Anantharaju Shetty v. Appu Hegde, and reiterated Patel Chunibhai Dajibhai v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar.
members.conclusion: Review is a creature of statute and cannot be exercised without statutory authority. The orders reopening the final vesting order and the later review orders were without jurisdiction.

predicates.statutory_officer_order_review_proceedin: A proceeding seeks reconsideration by a statutory officer of an order the officer previously made.
predicates.review_power_not_conferred: The governing legal scheme does not authorize that officer to review the order.

members.legal_issue: An administrative authority cannot use a power of review that the governing law does not confer to set aside an earlier order of a coordinate authority.
material_facts: An earlier administrative order verified a claim and compensation was later quantified on that basis.
A subsequent officer purported to review the earlier verification and rejected the claim in full.
The parties accepted that the subsequent order was made in exercise of review, rather than revision.
The Court found no review power in the governing statute.
members.legal_principle: The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 did not confer the review power exercised to vacate the earlier order. Section 24 of that Act provided a distinct power of revision, but the Court held that the order before it was one of review, not revision. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The purported review order was invalid and could not stand.

members.legal_issue: An administrative authority cannot review its final order rejecting a revision application when it has no express statutory power of review.
material_facts: A party applied to the State authority for revision of an order concerning land allotments.
The authority rejected the revision application, then later reconsidered the same application, heard the parties, and allowed it.
The governing Act contained no express power authorising review of an order made on a revision application.
members.legal_principle: Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 empowered the State Government to examine specified records and pass orders, but did not expressly confer a power to review an order made under that section. A final order cannot be set aside or reviewed by the authority that made it unless statute grants that power. The Court relied on Drew v. Willis, Hession v. Jones, Anantharaju Shetty v. Appu Hegada, and Baijnath Ram Goenka v. Nand Kumar Singh, and followed Patel Chunibhai Dajibhai v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar. The High Court could quash the jurisdictionally invalid order under Article 226 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The authority lacked jurisdiction to review its earlier rejection, so its later order allowing the revision was ultra vires and was rightly quashed by the High Court.

members.legal_issue: A government delegate cannot review and set aside the government’s earlier order unless the government has power to review that order, and an operative order cannot be ignored unless set aside or declared void by a competent authority.
material_facts: The government had set aside earlier administrative decisions and remanded the matters for reconsideration.
A later commissioner, acting as the government’s delegate, set aside the government’s earlier order on the ground that it had been made without legal authority.
No provision conferring review power on the government, either expressly or by necessary implication, was identified.
The government’s earlier order had not been set aside or declared void by a competent authority.
members.legal_principle: The power to review is not inherent and must be conferred by law, expressly or by necessary implication. A delegate cannot exercise a review power that the government itself does not possess. An order remains binding on subordinate tribunals unless it is set aside or declared void by a competent authority. The Court identified no provision of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act conferring review power; it did not decide whether Section 63(2) authorized the government to entertain the earlier revision application. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The commissioner lacked competence to review and set aside the government’s earlier order. The commissioner’s order was liable to be set aside, and the operative earlier order could not be ignored by subordinate tribunals.

members.legal_issue: An authority cannot rescind an instrument in a way that effectively reviews and nullifies its final quasi-judicial decision when no power of review has been conferred.
material_facts: The Lieutenant Governor had allowed the Society’s appeal against the Registrar’s refusal to register a membership amendment and had issued a final quasi-judicial decision directing the amendment.
A later notification purported to rescind the earlier notification that had given the amendment retrospective effect, without expressly rescinding the earlier quasi-judicial decision.

In practical effect, the later notification nullified that decision. The earlier decision and notification had also created substantive rights for affected members, and the Act conferred no power to review the quasi-judicial decision.
members.legal_principle: A final quasi-judicial order cannot be reviewed by the authority that made it unless a power of review has specifically been conferred. The order was made under Section 76 of the Delhi Cooperative Societies Act, 1972, which conferred no such review power. The Court relied on G.V. Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh for the rule that general powers to exercise a function from time to time do not authorise review of a quasi-judicial order, and on State of Kerala v. K.G. Madhavan Pillai for the principle that a general power to rescind cannot be used to take away rights already acquired under an earlier order. The rescission power was considered in relation to Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
members.conclusion: The later rescission notification was ultra vires and invalid because it effectively nullified a final quasi-judicial decision without a conferred power of review; it was also invalid insofar as it took away rights created by the earlier decision and notification.

rule.if: challenge_to_rescission_of_final_quasijudicial_decision and ((earlier_decision_was_final and later_action_effectively_nullified_it and no_review_power_was_conferred) or (earlier_action_created_enforceable_rights and later_action_took_them_away))

predicates.challenge_to_rescission_of_final_quasiju: The proceeding challenges a later rescission that affects an earlier quasi-judicial decision.
predicates.earlier_decision_was_final: The earlier quasi-judicial decision had become final.
predicates.later_action_effectively_nullified_it: The later action effectively nullified the earlier decision, even though it did not expressly rescind that decision.
predicates.no_review_power_was_conferred: The governing law did not confer power on the decision-maker to review the earlier decision.
predicates.earlier_action_created_enforceable_right: The earlier decision and related action created rights enforceable by the affected persons.
predicates.later_action_took_them_away: The later action took away rights created by the earlier decision and related action.

members.legal_issue: The Government cannot review or modify its final quasi-judicial order made in revision unless the governing law expressly confers a power of review.
material_facts: The Government investigated the competing claims, gave the parties an opportunity to present evidence, and made an order restoring the land to the applicant.
The order was made in the exercise of revisional authority, although it did not expressly cite the relevant statutory provisions.
On a later application by the occupants, the Government altered its earlier order to allow them to retain possession on payment of rent.
The governing law contained no express provision authorizing the Government to review its revisional order.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 79 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, empowered the relevant authorities to make or revise the land-related order, but did not confer a power on the Government to review its own final revisional order. A revisional authority acts judicially or quasi-judicially, and its order cannot be altered as though it were an administrative order subject to general control under section 74. The Court relied on the quasi-judicial principles in Gullapalli Nageswara Rao and Board of High School and Intermediate Education, U.P. v. Ghanshyam Das Gupta.
members.conclusion: The Government’s later modification was ultra vires and beyond its jurisdiction because the earlier revisional order was quasi-judicial and final, and there was no express power to review it.

predicates.review_of_revisional_adjudication: The proceeding concerns a later attempt by an authority to reconsider an order it previously made in revision.
predicates.prior_order_resolved_contested_rights: The earlier order resolved competing claims after an inquiry and determined rights affecting the parties.
predicates.no_express_review_power: The governing law does not expressly authorize the authority to review its own revisional order.

members.legal_issue: The inherent jurisdiction of a court cannot be used to review or alter a signed final judgment where no law expressly authorizes that review or alteration.
material_facts: The applicant invoked the High Court's inherent power to obtain clarification of its earlier signed criminal order.
The requested relief would have altered the effect or scope of the earlier order by deciding whether it affected the applicant's claimed property and possession rights.
No express authority to review or alter the order applied to the requested relief.
members.legal_principle: Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, prohibits alteration or review of a signed judgment or final order except to correct clerical or arithmetical errors, subject to express authorization in that Code or another law. The saving words apply only where a court is expressly authorized to alter or review its judgment; inherent power under section 482 is not such authorization and cannot be exercised to do what the Code specifically prohibits. The Court relied on Sankatha Singh v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The inherent power could not be used to grant the requested relief, and the High Court was right to decline the application.

rule.if: post_judgment_criminal_application and signed_final_order and inherent_power_invoked and substantive_alteration_sought and not express_review_authorization

predicates.post_judgment_criminal_application: A person filed an application after a criminal proceeding seeking clarification or change to a signed final order.
predicates.signed_final_order: The court had signed a final order disposing of the proceeding.
predicates.inherent_power_invoked: The applicant relied on the court's inherent authority to obtain the requested relief.
predicates.substantive_alteration_sought: The requested relief would change the substance, effect, or scope of the signed order.
predicates.express_review_authorization: A law expressly authorized the court to review or alter the signed order in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A statutory tribunal cannot substantively review an earlier order unless legislation specifically confers that power.
material_facts: A Competent Officer had ordered the disputed property transferred to the respondent on payment of an assessed amount.
The appellant, which had not been a party to the original proceedings, later applied to the Competent Officer for review and transfer of the property to itself.
The Competent Officer reviewed the earlier order, held it illegal, and directed that the property be sold in the open market; the Appellate Officer confirmed that order.

The Act provided for appeals and revision and allowed correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors arising from accidental slips or omissions, but the Court found no provision conferring the substantive review power exercised.
members.legal_principle: A tribunal has no inherent power to review its earlier order; that power must be specifically conferred by statute. Section 16 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 permitted correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors caused by accidental slips or omissions, not substantive review. Sections 14 and 15 dealt with appeals and revision. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Competent Officer lacked power to review the earlier order in the manner undertaken, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.challenge_to_tribunal_review_order: A party appealed against an order made by a statutory tribunal after it reconsidered an earlier order.
predicates.review_authority_not_conferred: The governing law did not confer on the tribunal authority to substantively review the earlier order.
predicates.correction_power_is_limited_to_accidenta: The tribunal's relevant correction authority was confined to clerical or arithmetical mistakes and errors arising from accidental slips or omissions.
predicates.substantive_review_power_absent: The tribunal had no authority to make the substantive review order.

members.legal_issue: A judicial or quasi-judicial authority cannot review its earlier order without a power of review granted by law, and a court cannot confer that power.
material_facts: The Corporation had earlier approved the hoarding after an administrative examination.
The High Court permitted the Corporation to withdraw its earlier approval and pass a fresh order, although no power of review had been identified.
The Corporation then passed a fresh order that did not approve the hoarding.
members.legal_principle: Review is not an inherent power and must be expressly or impliedly conferred by law; an order reviewing an earlier order without that power is without jurisdiction. The Court relied on Patel Chunibhai Dajibha v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar, AIR 1965 SC 1457; Harbhajan Singh v. Karam Singh, AIR 1966 SC 641; Patel Narshi Thakershi v. Shri Pradyuman Singhji Arjunsinghji, AIR 1970 SC 1273; Maj. Chandra Bhan Singh v. Latafat Ullah Khan, AIR 1978 SC 1814; Dr. Smt. Kuntesh Gupta v. Management of Hindu Kanya Mahavidhyalaya, AIR 1987 SC 2186; State of Orissa v. Commissioner of Land Records and Settlement, (1998) 7 SCC 162; and Sunita Jain v. Pawan Kumar Jain, (2008) 2 SCC 705.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not confer review jurisdiction on the Corporation. Its order permitting review was without jurisdiction and a nullity, and the consequential order passed by the Corporation was unenforceable.

predicates.review_of_quasi_judicial_order: An authority reconsidered and altered its own earlier judicial or quasi-judicial order.
predicates.no_review_power_granted_by_law: The law did not grant the authority power to review its earlier order.

members.legal_issue: A tenancy newly created by a receiver in breach of an injunction cannot confer statutory tenancy protection on the new occupant.
material_facts: The injunction restrained the receiver from transferring the property or creating a new tenancy.
After the original tenant surrendered two flats, the receiver let those flats to a new occupant.
The new occupant's tenancy was created in breach of the injunction.
members.legal_principle: A receiver is an officer of the court, holds no title to the property, and acts subject to the court's directions. The court relied on Order 40 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Kanhaiyalal v. Dr. D.R. Banaji concerning the receiver's role, and on Smt. Ashrafi Devi v. Satyapal Gupta and Arumugha Gounder v. Ardhanari Mudaliar concerning tenancies created contrary to court orders and the limits of statutory protection.
members.conclusion: The new occupant acquired no right to statutory protection under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act and was liable to be evicted.

predicates.receiver_tenancy_dispute: The proceeding concerns a tenancy created by a receiver appointed by a court.
predicates.receiver_created_new_tenancy: The receiver created a new tenancy in favour of an occupant.
predicates.court_order_prohibited_new_tenancy: A court order in force prohibited the receiver from creating a new tenancy over the property.

members.legal_issue: A tenancy created after a statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies has taken effect is invalid and cannot establish a right to remain in possession.
material_facts: The defendant claimed that an oral lease made him a tenant from 1971.
The alleged lease was created after the statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies had taken effect.
The plaintiff sought recovery of possession, and the defendant relied on the alleged tenancy to resist that claim.
members.legal_principle: Section 74 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act prohibits the creation of a tenancy after the Act’s commencement and makes a tenancy created in contravention of that prohibition invalid. In light of that absolute bar and the undisputed timing of the alleged lease, the Court held that remand would serve only to prolong the litigation.
members.conclusion: The alleged tenancy was invalid, and no court could find that it gave the defendant tenant status. A remand was unnecessary, and the decree for possession was properly upheld.

predicates.property_possession_suit_involves_tenant: A suit seeking possession of property is resisted on the basis of a claimed tenancy.
predicates.alleged_tenancy_created_after_prohibitio: The alleged tenancy was created after a statutory prohibition on creating new tenancies had taken effect.

members.legal_issue: A person must have lawful cultivatory possession to qualify for statutory rights based on possession during the specified agricultural year, and forcible or surreptitious occupation without a right does not qualify.
material_facts: The claimant had no established right to occupy the land and was not shown to have possessed it through the end of the preceding agricultural year.
The records did not establish actual cultivatory possession during the relevant year, and the claimant offered no direct evidence of such possession.
The claimant was recorded as a sub-tenant without settlement of rent, but did not claim or prove a tenancy agreement with the owners.
The owners denied that they had leased the land to the claimant or received rent from the claimant.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952, requires a claimant to establish cultivatory possession during the specified year and grants rights against tenure holders to persons who had been admitted to such possession. The Explanation excludes specified forms of participation in cultivation. The Court held that qualifying cultivatory possession must be lawful and for the whole year; a trespasser who forcibly or surreptitiously occupies land does not qualify. Ram Krishna v. Bhagwan Baksh Singh, [1961] A.L.J. 301, was approved, and Nanhoo Mal v. Muloo, I.L.R. [1963] All. 751, was disapproved.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not establish cultivatory possession qualifying for adhivasi rights under section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952; wrongful occupation could not confer those rights against the owners.

predicates.claim_under_possession_based_land_rights: A claimant seeks statutory land rights based on cultivatory possession during a specified period.
predicates.actual_cultivatory_possession_establishe: Evidence establishes that the claimant actually cultivated the land throughout the required period.
predicates.forcible_occupation_without_right: The claimant entered or remained on the land by force or surreptitiously without a lawful right to occupy it.

members.legal_issue: A person cultivating land as a subtenant under a tenancy regime that prohibits subletting cannot qualify as a deemed tenant where deemed tenancy requires lawful cultivation.
material_facts: The occupant claimed that he possessed the land as a subtenant of the original tenant.
The applicable tenancy law prohibited subletting, and the tenancy was liable to termination on the ground of subletting.
The statutory route to deemed tenancy required the claimant to cultivate the land lawfully.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, required lawful cultivation for deemed tenancy. Section 27 invalidated subletting, and Section 14(1)(a)(iii) made a tenancy liable to termination for subletting. Read together, those provisions meant that cultivation by a subtenant was not lawful for this purpose. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The occupant’s claimed status as a subtenant did not make him a deemed tenant.

rule.if: tenancy_status_determination and claimant_cultivated_as_subtenant and applicable_law_prohibits_subletting and deemed_tenancy_requires_lawful_cultivation

predicates.tenancy_status_determination: A proceeding determines whether a person occupying land qualifies as a tenant under the applicable tenancy regime.
predicates.claimant_cultivated_as_subtenant: The claimant cultivated the land under a tenant rather than directly under the landowner.
predicates.applicable_law_prohibits_subletting: The applicable tenancy regime does not permit a tenant to sublet the land.
predicates.deemed_tenancy_requires_lawful_cultivati: The applicable route to deemed tenancy requires the claimant’s cultivation to be lawful.

members.legal_issue: Cultivatory possession obtained under a landholder who had no right to induct the occupant does not qualify as lawful possession for acquiring statutory occupancy status.
material_facts: The thekadars had acquired hereditary-tenant rights and were in possession of the disputed land.
The landholders inducted the lessees after they no longer had the right to grant possession against the thekadars.
The lessees claimed occupancy status based on cultivatory possession during the relevant agricultural year, but their possession was unlawful against the thekadars.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952 requires lawful cultivatory possession for the relevant year to acquire the claimed status. Sonawati v. Shri Ram holds that a person must have a lawful right to possession and that forcible or wrongful occupation does not qualify; Ram Krishna v. Bhagwan Baksh Singh is consistent with that principle. The Court rejected the contrary view in Nanhoo Mai v. Muloo.
members.conclusion: The lessees did not acquire adhivasi rights because their cultivatory possession was not lawful; the hereditary tenants were entitled to a decree for possession.

rule.if: land_possession_recovery_proceeding and occupancy_status_claim_based_on_cultivation and cultivatory_possession_during_qualifying_year and prior_tenant_had_acquired_rights and landholder_inducted_claimant_after_losing_right and not possession_lawful

predicates.land_possession_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding concerns recovery of agricultural land from an occupant claiming a statutory occupancy status.
predicates.occupancy_status_claim_based_on_cultivat: The occupant claims statutory status on the basis of cultivatory possession.
predicates.cultivatory_possession_during_qualifying: The occupant was in cultivatory possession during the relevant agricultural year.
predicates.prior_tenant_had_acquired_rights: A prior cultivating tenant had acquired rights to the land before the occupant was inducted.
predicates.landholder_inducted_claimant_after_losin: The landholder inducted the occupant after losing the right to grant possession against the prior tenant.
predicates.possession_lawful: The occupant's possession was supported by a lawful right against the prior tenant.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who acquired no valid interest in land cannot claim the statutory right to retain it as an intermediary or other qualifying landholder.
material_facts: The appellants relied on a sale deed to claim the former owner's proprietary interest in the disputed land.
The arbitrator found that the transfer was unsupported by legal necessity and did not bind the owner's sons.
The appellants therefore had acquired no interest in the land under the sale deed and held no intermediary interest immediately before vesting.
members.legal_principle: Section 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, confers retention rights on intermediaries and specified cultivators. A person who acquired no interest under an invalid transfer and held no qualifying interest immediately before vesting cannot claim those rights.
members.conclusion: The appellants did not qualify for the statutory right to retain the land, and the arbitrator's failure to grant them that right was not an error of law warranting the award being set aside.

predicates.award_challenge_for_legal_error: The matter is a challenge to an award on the ground that it contains an error of law.
predicates.transfer_invalid: The asserted transfer of the land was found invalid and not binding on the persons claiming rights through the transferor.
predicates.no_qualifying_interest_at_vesting: The claimant held no qualifying intermediary or other statutory interest immediately before vesting.
predicates.no_statutory_retention_right: The claimant has no statutory right to retain the land on the asserted basis.

members.legal_issue: A trespasser without a lawful right in land is not in cultivatory possession for purposes of acquiring the statutory status available to qualifying cultivators.
material_facts: The appellants' sale deed was found not to have transferred a valid interest in the disputed land.
After the transferor's death, the appellants' possession became illegal and adverse to her sons.
The appellants claimed statutory status based on their asserted cultivatory possession during the relevant agricultural year.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952, does not protect a trespasser's possession. Its explanation indicates that a person without a lawful right in the land cannot claim to be in cultivatory possession. The court relied on Ram Krishna v. Bhagwan Baksh Singh, (1961) ALJ 301, and Badri v. Juthan Singh, (1969) ALJ 411, which held that a trespasser is not in cultivatory possession for this purpose.
members.conclusion: The appellants were not in cultivatory possession within the meaning of section 3(1) and were not entitled to the benefit of that provision.

predicates.statutory_cultivatory_status_claim: The matter is a claim to statutory status based on cultivatory possession of land during the relevant agricultural year.
predicates.possession_without_lawful_right: The claimant possessed the land without a lawful right to do so.
predicates.no_statutory_cultivatory_status: The claimant is not treated as being in cultivatory possession for the purpose of obtaining that statutory status.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot acquire adhivasi status on the basis of cultivatory possession when that possession is unlawful.
material_facts: The lessees claimed that they were in cultivatory possession during 1359 Fasli and had thereby acquired adhivasi rights.
The thekedars had acquired hereditary-tenant status and were entitled to the land; the zamindars therefore had no right to induct the lessees after depriving the thekedars of possession.
The lessees’ possession during 1359 Fasli was consequently unlawful against the thekedars.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952 confers adhivasi status on a qualifying person in cultivatory possession during 1359 Fasli, subject to the section’s conditions. Cultivatory possession for this purpose must be lawful; a person who enters or remains on land without a lawful right cannot acquire the status merely through such possession. The Court relied on Sonawati v. Sri Ram.
members.conclusion: The lessees did not acquire adhivasi rights and the hereditary tenants were entitled to a decree for possession.

predicates.adhivasi_status_claim_under_supplementar: A person claimed land status on the basis of cultivatory possession under a supplementary land-reform scheme.
predicates.cultivatory_possession_during_relevant_y: The claimant was in cultivatory possession of the land during the legally relevant year.
predicates.possession_unlawful: The claimant had no lawful right to possess the land, including because another person had the superior right to it and the claimant was inducted without authority.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot acquire landholder rights through a tenancy that was never validly created before the relevant statutory transition.
material_facts: The cultivator relied on a patta granted by a temple priest who lacked authority to lease the government-owned temple land.
The cultivator claimed landholder rights on the basis that he was a subtenant when the statutory land code came into force.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 185, 189 and 190 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, the asserted route to Bhumiswami rights depended on the person being an occupancy tenant and on the statutory conditions for conversion being met. Because the invalid patta created no tenancy rights, the cultivator was not a subtenant at the commencement of the Code and could not acquire those rights through that route.
members.conclusion: The cultivator did not acquire Bhumiswami rights because the invalid patta did not make him a subtenant at the relevant time.

predicates.landholder_rights_claimed_through_tenanc: An occupant claims landholder rights on the basis of a tenancy or subtenancy.
predicates.purported_lessor_lacked_authority: The person who purported to grant the tenancy had no authority to do so.
predicates.no_valid_tenancy_at_transition: The occupant had no valid tenancy when the relevant statutory transition occurred.

members.legal_issue: Persons inducted onto land by someone who has lost the right to possess it cannot obtain tenant protection merely by cultivating the land.
material_facts: A decree established an adopted son’s right to the land and to possession of it.
After the decree, the widow who had been dispossessed of the land leased it to the claimants, although she no longer had a right to possess or lease the land.
The claimants sought restoration of possession on the basis that they had cultivated the land as tenants.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 32(1), 2(v) and 5 of the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, a claim for possession as a tenant requires the relevant tenant status, and deemed tenancy under Section 5 requires lawful cultivation. The meaning of “asami shikmi” referred to in Section 2(13) of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act requires a lessee holding under a written instrument or oral agreement, but an agreement with someone who has no right to possess the land cannot confer the claimed protection. Dahya Lal v. Rasul Mohammed Abdul Hakim was distinguished because the tenant there had been lawfully inducted by a mortgagee in possession acting in the ordinary course of management. Mohima Chunder Saha v. Hazari Pramanik and Binad Lal Pakrashi v. Kalu Pramanik were distinguished because they applied the different protective scheme of the Bengal Tenancy Act.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to tenant protection because they had been inducted by a person who was a trespasser when she inducted them, and they could not be regarded as lawfully cultivating the land.

rule.if: tenant_possession_restoration_claim and claim_based_on_cultivation and induction_after_loss_of_possessory_right and inducer_lacked_authority_to_lease

predicates.tenant_possession_restoration_claim: The cultivators sought restoration of possession on a claim to tenant status.
predicates.claim_based_on_cultivation: The cultivators relied on their cultivation of the land as the basis for claiming tenant protection.
predicates.induction_after_loss_of_possessory_right: The person who placed the cultivators on the land did so after a decree had established another person's right to the land and possession.
predicates.inducer_lacked_authority_to_lease: When placing the cultivators on the land, the person who inducted them had no right to possess or lease it.

members.legal_issue: A coordinate bench that disagrees with a binding decision of another coordinate bench must follow it or refer the issue to a larger bench rather than decide the issue inconsistently.
material_facts: An earlier Full Bench had decided the same or similar legal issues as the later Full Bench.
The later Full Bench disagreed with the earlier decision and treated it as non-binding without establishing a valid basis for applying the doctrine of per incuriam.
The later Full Bench issued conclusions conflicting with the earlier Full Bench's conclusions.
members.legal_principle: Judicial discipline and certainty require a bench of coordinate jurisdiction that disagrees with an earlier decision to follow it or refer the matter to a larger bench, rather than leave conflicting decisions in force. A prior decision ceases to state correct law where a subsequent change in law is shown. The Court relied on Dr. Vijay Laxmi Sadho v. Jagdish and Pradip Chandra Parija v. Pramod Chandra Patnaik, which set out the proper course when benches disagree, and Govt. of Andhra Pradesh v. B. Satyanarayana Rao, concerning the effect of a subsequent change in law.
members.conclusion: The later Full Bench was not entitled to disregard the earlier decision; it had to follow that decision or seek resolution by a larger bench. The impugned judgment was set aside and the matter remanded for reconsideration in accordance with law.

rule.if: later_coordinate_bench and earlier_binding_decision and later_bench_disagrees and not subsequent_change_in_law

predicates.later_coordinate_bench: A later bench of coordinate jurisdiction considers an issue decided by an earlier bench of coordinate jurisdiction.
predicates.earlier_binding_decision: An earlier decision of coordinate jurisdiction addressed the same issue and was binding on the later bench.
predicates.later_bench_disagrees: The later bench considers the earlier decision incorrect on the issue.
predicates.subsequent_change_in_law: A change in law after the earlier decision has displaced its rule.

members.legal_issue: A High Court bench that disagrees with a decision of a coordinate bench of that court should refer the question to a larger bench rather than decline to follow the earlier decision.
material_facts: One division bench of the High Court held that the relevant statutory settlement was limited to buildings lawfully held.
A later division bench declined to follow that decision and reached the contrary interpretation.
The Supreme Court stated that the later bench should have referred the question to a larger bench.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule of judicial propriety that a bench of a High Court should not sit in judgment on the correctness of a decision of a coordinate bench; disagreement should be resolved by reference to a larger bench. The Court discussed Pheku Chamar v. Harish Chandra and Bharat v. Ch. Khazan Singh in applying that principle.
members.conclusion: Judicial propriety requires a coordinate bench unable to agree with an earlier coordinate-bench decision to refer the question to a larger bench.

predicates.coordinate_bench_case: The matter is before a bench of a court considering a question previously decided by a bench of that same court.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_bench_decision_exists: A coordinate bench of the same court has already decided the question.
predicates.later_bench_disagrees_with_earlier_decis: The later bench cannot agree with the earlier coordinate bench’s decision.

members.legal_issue: A later bench of a court should follow an earlier decision of a coordinate bench on the same issue unless a compelling basis, such as the earlier decision being per incuriam, justifies departure.
material_facts: A coordinate bench had dismissed a challenge by the tenant on grounds that were identical to those later advanced by the Municipal Corporation.
A later coordinate bench dismissed the Municipal Corporation’s appeal on those identical grounds.
The Municipal Corporation subsequently sought supervisory relief on the same underlying grounds.
members.legal_principle: Judicial discipline and the need to avoid conflicting decisions require a coordinate bench to follow an earlier coordinate-bench decision on the same issue, except in compelling circumstances, such as where the earlier decision is per incuriam because it overlooked a binding precedent or a statutory or constitutional provision.
members.conclusion: The later coordinate bench’s dismissal was consistent with judicial discipline, and the subsequent supervisory proceeding could not properly be used to avoid that result without a compelling basis for departing from the earlier decision.

rule.if: later_coordinate_bench_case and earlier_coordinate_decision_on_same_issue and not earlier_decision_per_incuriam

predicates.later_coordinate_bench_case: A matter is before a bench of the same court with the same level of authority as an earlier bench.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_decision_on_same_issu: An earlier coordinate bench decided the same issue.
predicates.earlier_decision_per_incuriam: The earlier decision was made in ignorance of a binding precedent or a governing statutory or constitutional provision.

members.legal_issue: A judge of a High Court must follow an earlier decision of that same court on the point, or refer the matter to a larger bench if the judge disagrees, unless a larger-bench ruling has displaced it.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the eviction order in a writ petition before the High Court.
An earlier decision of that High Court had held that the landlord-successor rule applied to partition.
The Court stated that the judge deciding the later matter should have followed that earlier decision unless a larger bench had ruled otherwise, or referred the disagreement to a Division Bench.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Ram Chandra Singh v. Ram Saran, AIR 1978 All 173, and the rule of precedent within the same High Court: a judge should follow the earlier decision unless a larger bench has ruled contrary to it; a judge who disagrees should have the matter considered by a Division Bench.
members.conclusion: The High Court judge should have followed the earlier decision of the same High Court or, if differing from it, referred the matter to a Division Bench.

predicates.single_judge_writ_review: A single judge reviews the matter in a writ proceeding.
predicates.earlier_same_high_court_decision_on_the_: The same High Court had already decided the legal point in an earlier case.
predicates.no_contrary_larger_bench_decision: No decision of a larger bench of that High Court had displaced the earlier ruling.

members.legal_issue: A court that disagrees with a decision of a coordinate bench must follow it or refer the matter to a larger bench rather than disregard it.
material_facts: A prior decision of a coordinate bench had held that the government’s power to form a corporation was legislative in character and that natural justice did not apply to its exercise.
The High Court was referred to that prior decision and recognized its stated legal principle.
The High Court neither followed the prior decision nor referred the matter to a larger bench, and instead directed the government to reconsider the proposal and hear parties.
members.legal_principle: Judicial propriety and the doctrine of binding precedent require a bench that disagrees with a decision of a coordinate bench to refer the issue to a larger bench rather than overrule or disregard that decision. The Court relied on Mahadeolal Kanodia v. Administrator General of West Bengal, Lala Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand, and Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, and discussed the prior decision in Village Panchayat Chikalthane v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The High Court acted contrary to judicial propriety by not following the coordinate-bench decision or referring the issue to a larger bench.

rule.if: judicial_proceeding_before_coequal_bench and coordinate_bench_decision_exists and later_bench_disagrees and later_bench_neither_follows_nor_refers

predicates.judicial_proceeding_before_coequal_bench: A judicial matter was heard by a bench of the same level as a bench that had previously decided the relevant legal issue.
predicates.coordinate_bench_decision_exists: A coordinate bench had already issued a decision on the relevant legal issue.
predicates.later_bench_disagrees: The later bench considered the earlier decision inconsistent with the result it proposed to reach.
predicates.later_bench_neither_follows_nor_refers: The later bench neither applied the earlier decision nor sent the issue to a larger bench.

members.legal_issue: A Division Bench must follow an earlier Division Bench’s decision on the same legal point, or refer the matter to a larger bench before departing from it, regardless of whether the earlier decision arose in an appeal or the later proceeding is a writ matter.
material_facts: An earlier Division Bench had decided the relevant legal point in an appeal.
A later Division Bench considered the same legal point in a writ proceeding and declined to follow the earlier decision because it arose in an appeal.
members.legal_principle: The rule of judicial precedent binds a Division Bench to the ratio of an earlier Division Bench on the same point, regardless of whether the earlier decision arose in an appeal or the later matter is a writ proceeding. A Bench wishing to differ must refer the matter to a larger bench. The Court rejected the later Bench’s treatment of Mst. Jaini v. Ram Prasad, A.I.R. 1952 All. 852, as distinguishable solely because it had been decided in an appeal.
members.conclusion: The earlier Division Bench’s ratio was binding despite the different procedural forms; the later Division Bench could not disregard it and should have referred the matter to a larger bench if it wished to differ.

predicates.later_division_bench_proceeding: A Division Bench later considered a legal point in a proceeding before it.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_bench_decided_same_le: An earlier Division Bench had decided the same legal point.
predicates.procedural_form_is_different: The earlier and later proceedings had different procedural forms.

members.legal_issue: A single judge who disagrees with a governing Full Bench decision must follow the prescribed procedure for obtaining reconsideration rather than refusing to follow or effectively overruling that decision.
material_facts: A Full Bench had previously decided the relevant question of Hindu law.
The single judge declined to follow that Full Bench decision and reached a contrary result.
The single judge did not refer the matter for consideration by a Full Bench or place it before the Chief Justice for a reference.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of judicial precedent supports certainty in the law. The Court stated that conventions and rules framed by several High Courts require a single judge or Division Bench that does not agree with a Full Bench decision to make a reference or place the matter before the Chief Justice for that purpose; a judge should not effectively overrule the Full Bench decision. The Court particularly noted the governing Full Bench decisions in Amirthammal v. Vallimayil Ammal, ILR 1942 Mad 807 (FB), and Kesava v. Govindan, ILR 1946 Mad 452 (FB).
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court deprecated the single judge’s approach and stated that disagreement with a Full Bench decision should be referred to a Full Bench or brought to the Chief Justice for a reference, as required by the applicable practice and rules.

rule.if: appeal_from_judgment_disregarding_full_bench_precedent and applicable_full_bench_precedent_exists and single_judge_disagreed_with_precedent and no_reference_procedure_followed

predicates.appeal_from_judgment_disregarding_full_b: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment in which a lower-court judge declined to follow a Full Bench decision.
predicates.applicable_full_bench_precedent_exists: A Full Bench decision governs the legal issue being decided.
predicates.single_judge_disagreed_with_precedent: A single judge reached a conclusion inconsistent with the governing Full Bench decision.
predicates.no_reference_procedure_followed: The judge neither referred the disagreement to a Full Bench nor placed the matter before the Chief Justice for a reference.

members.legal_issue: A Supreme Court Division Bench cannot disregard a binding pronouncement of an equal- or greater-strength Division Bench and must refer a conflicting view for resolution by a larger bench.
material_facts: A two-judge bench encountered two earlier decisions that expressed conflicting views on the legal issue.
The earlier decisions included one by a bench with more judges than the referring bench.
The two-judge bench referred the issue to a five-judge bench for reconsideration.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the doctrine of binding precedent and Article 141 of the Constitution. It relied on, among other authorities, John Martin v. State of West Bengal, Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, Ganapati Sitaram Balvalkar v. Waman Shripad Mage, Mattulal v. Radhe Lal, Acharya Maharajshri Narandraprasadji v. State of Gujarat, and Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India Ltd. A larger bench’s decision binds a smaller bench, and a bench of equal strength cannot resolve a conflict by deciding that the other bench was wrong; reference to a larger bench preserves consistency and certainty.
members.conclusion: A Division Bench’s statement of law binds a Division Bench of the same or a smaller number of judges. A bench that considers an earlier binding decision incorrect must not overrule it itself; the matter should be referred to a larger bench. The Court also stated that, for certainty and authority, future decisions should ordinarily be given by benches of at least three judges unless compelling reasons prevent that.

predicates.supreme_court_division_bench_case: The matter is before a Division Bench of the Supreme Court.
predicates.earlier_division_bench_law_on_point: An earlier Division Bench has stated the law on the same legal point.
predicates.earlier_bench_has_equal_or_greater_stren: The earlier Division Bench had the same number or more judges than the later bench.
predicates.later_bench_cannot_overrule_precedent_un: The later bench must follow the binding decision or refer the issue for determination by a larger bench.

members.legal_issue: A coordinate bench must follow an earlier coordinate-bench decision on the same issue or refer the matter to a larger bench before taking a different view.
material_facts: An earlier coordinate-bench decision had held that approval could not be deemed merely from the passage of time.
A later coordinate bench considered the same rule, took a contrary view, and extended the decision period without referring the issue to a larger bench.
members.legal_principle: Judicial discipline and the rule of precedent require a coordinate bench to follow an earlier decision on the same or a similar issue; if it proposes a different view, it must refer the matter to a larger bench. The Court relied on Tribhovandas Purshottamdas Thakkar v. Ratilal Motilal Patel; Sub-Committee of Judicial Accountability v. Union of India; State of Tripura v. Tripura Bar Association; and Rajasthan Public Service Commission v. Harish Kumar Purohit. The earlier decision on the relevant rule was B.B. Chibber v. Anand Lok Co-operative Group Housing Society.
members.conclusion: The later bench was not entitled to take a divergent view of the earlier coordinate-bench decision; its approach was impermissible.

predicates.same_court_coordinate_bench_case: A bench is deciding an issue within a court where another bench of equal strength has decided the same or a similar issue.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_decision_on_same_issu: An earlier bench of equal strength has decided the issue before the later bench.
predicates.later_bench_takes_conflicting_view_witho: The later bench adopts a different view without referring the issue to a larger bench.

members.legal_issue: When decisions of the Supreme Court conflict on the same point, a larger bench’s view is to be followed in preference to a smaller bench’s view.
material_facts: The parties relied on Supreme Court decisions expressing different views on the legal character of grants relating to forest produce.
The Court identified relevant decisions of larger benches and a contrary decision of a smaller bench.
members.legal_principle: The rule stated in Union of India v. K.S. Subramanian is that a court should identify and follow the view expressed by a larger bench in preference to a conflicting view expressed by a smaller bench; the practice has crystallized into a rule of law.
members.conclusion: The larger-bench decisions governed, and the contrary smaller-bench approach could not be preferred.

predicates.court_faces_conflicting_supreme_court_de: A court encounters Supreme Court decisions that express conflicting views on the same legal point.
predicates.conflicting_decisions_are_of_different_b: The conflicting decisions were delivered by benches of different sizes.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected at the threshold as time-barred where its allegations, read as a whole, leave material questions about when the right to sue accrued or depend on disputed facts.
material_facts: An administrator of a will brought a suit seeking partition of the estate and related relief, including accounts and declarations concerning a tenancy and mortgage claims.

The plaint alleged that a written undertaking recorded that the defendant would not claim tenancy rights or a charge over the property and would render accounts concerning rental income and redeemed mortgages.
The plaintiff alleged that the parties’ dispute arose after the defendant acted contrary to the undertaking, and that the suit was filed following that dispute.
The defendant disputed the undertaking, and the High Court held some of the claims time-barred on the basis of the plaint.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the plaint must be read in its entirety, without adding to or subtracting from it, to determine whether it shows that the suit is barred by law. As stated in Popat and Kotecha Property v. State Bank of India Staff Association, the bar must appear from the plaint itself. Where the limitation question depends on disputed facts or on when the right to sue accrued, it is a mixed question of fact and law and cannot be resolved on an application to reject the plaint. The parties’ arguments invoked Articles 58, 59 and 69 of the Limitation Act, 1963, but the Court did not finally determine the applicable limitation period or its merits.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing the plaint to be rejected in part as time-barred. The Supreme Court set aside that decision and rejected the application for rejection of the plaint, leaving the suit to proceed without deciding limitation on its merits.

rule.if: threshold_plaint_rejection_application and plaint_alleges_undertaking_before_dispute and defendant_disputes_undertaking and plaint_claims_connected_estate_relief

predicates.threshold_plaint_rejection_application: A defendant sought rejection of a plaint at the threshold on the ground that the suit was barred by law.
predicates.plaint_alleges_undertaking_before_disput: The plaintiff alleged that an undertaking addressed the disputed rights before a later dispute arose.
predicates.defendant_disputes_undertaking: The defendant disputed the undertaking on which the plaintiff relied.
predicates.plaint_claims_connected_estate_relief: The plaintiff sought partition of an estate together with related accounts or declarations.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected as time-barred at the threshold when the plaintiffs plead that they lacked notice of the relevant proceedings and learned the essential facts later, and the timing of their knowledge depends on evidence.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that they learned of the tenancy proceedings and related transactions only after inspecting records held by the Court Receiver.
They alleged that the proceedings were conducted without notice to them and were fraudulent or collusive.

The defendant sought rejection of the plaint on limitation grounds, relying in part on constructive notice; whether notice was issued or served and when the plaintiffs learned of the proceedings had not been tried.
members.legal_principle: Limitation is a mixed question of fact and law. Rejection under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a drastic power, and where a plaintiff pleads that the essential facts became known only later, that plea must be accepted at the threshold stage. The date of knowledge may be a triable issue. The Court relied on P.V. Guru Raj Reddy v. P. Neeradha Reddy and Chhotanben v. Kiritbhai Jalkrushnabhai Thakkar. Actual or constructive notice under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act is a matter to be established through evidence; possession by a Court Receiver did not permit reliance on Explanation II to that section in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The courts below were wrong to reject the plaint on limitation grounds at the threshold because the issue depended on evidence about notice and the plaintiffs’ knowledge.

predicates.civil_suit_plaint_rejection_motion: A defendant seeks rejection of a civil suit’s plaint at the threshold on limitation grounds.
predicates.plaintiffs_allege_later_discovery: The plaintiffs say they learned the essential facts giving rise to their claim only after an earlier event or investigation.
predicates.notice_or_knowledge_depends_on_evidence: Whether notice was given or when the plaintiffs learned of the relevant proceedings depends on evidence.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected at the threshold for limitation when, read as a whole and treated as true, its allegations do not show that the suit is time-barred.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that they learned of the relevant property transactions in 1999 and filed the suits in 2002.
The suits sought declarations of title and possession, along with related reliefs.
The defendants sought rejection of the plaints, relying in part on limitation.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, rejection of a plaint is a drastic threshold power subject to stringent conditions. The plaint must be read as a whole, and its averments must be accepted as true; the defendants’ written statement or assertions in their rejection application are immaterial at this stage. A plaint may be rejected only where it ex facie discloses no cause of action or shows that the suit is barred by law; otherwise, the claims must be adjudicated at trial. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The plaints did not disclose on their face that the suits were barred by limitation, so rejection under Order VII Rule 11 was not justified; the suits were to be decided on their merits.

rule.if: civil_suit_plaint_rejection_application and plaint_read_as_whole and pleaded_discovery_within_three_years_before_filing and no_bar_apparent_on_plaint

predicates.civil_suit_plaint_rejection_application: A party in a civil suit applied to have the plaint rejected at the threshold.
predicates.plaint_read_as_whole: The court assessed the plaint as a whole and treated its factual allegations as true for the application.
predicates.pleaded_discovery_within_three_years_bef: The plaintiffs alleged that they discovered the essential facts within three years before filing the suit.
predicates.no_bar_apparent_on_plaint: The allegations in the plaint did not themselves show that the suit was barred by law.
predicates.plaint_not_rejected_at_threshold: The plaint is not rejected at the threshold and the claims proceed for adjudication.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected at the threshold for being barred by law when that bar depends on disputed facts or material beyond the plaint.
material_facts: An earlier partition suit resulted in a preliminary decree defining the parties’ shares, but the final-decree proceedings were dismissed without a partition of the land by metes and bounds.

The present suit sought partition of properties described in the earlier suit, and the parties disputed whether the properties had been divided, were available for partition, or had been separately possessed or alienated.
The trial court rejected the plaint, and the High Court affirmed, relying on the earlier proceedings and the asserted bar arising from them.
The Supreme Court found that determining the effect of the earlier proceedings and the availability and identity of the properties required factual adjudication beyond the plaint.
members.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure applies where the suit appears from the statements in the plaint itself to be barred by law. For that inquiry, the plaint’s averments must be taken as true, without adding to or subtracting from them, and the court cannot consider evidence, the defence, or disputed questions of fact. Whether res judicata applies when it requires factual inquiry may be considered as a preliminary issue or at the final hearing, rather than under this rule. The Court relied on Liverpool & London S.P. & I Association Ltd. v. M.V. Sea Success I, C. Natrajan v. Ashim Bai, Popat and Kotecha Property v. State Bank of India Staff Association, Balasaria Construction (P) Ltd. v. Hanuman Seva Trust, and T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal; it also referred to Order XIV Rule 2 and to the earlier court’s invocation of Section 12 read with Order II Rule 2.
members.conclusion: The plaint could not be rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) on the basis of the disputed matters; the appeal was allowed and the parties were left free to raise their contentions at the appropriate stage.

predicates.threshold_plaint_rejection_application: A party seeks rejection of a plaint at the threshold on the ground that the suit is barred by law.
predicates.bar_not_apparent_from_plaint: The alleged legal bar does not follow from the plaint’s statements when those statements are taken as true.
predicates.deciding_bar_requires_disputed_facts: Determining whether the legal bar applies requires resolving disputed facts or considering material beyond the plaint.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) when its averments do not conclusively show that the suit is barred and determining whether the benami transaction falls within the fiduciary-capacity exception requires evidence.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that he paid the purchase consideration for the property, which was registered in his father's name, and relied on a written acknowledgment by his father of the plaintiff's payment and claimed rights.
The defendant applied for rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 on the ground that the suit was barred by Section 4 of the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, 1988.
Whether the pleaded transaction fell within the fiduciary-capacity exception under Section 4(3)(b) depended on the factual context and required consideration of evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaint may be rejected as barred by law only where its statements, accepted as true, show the bar without doubt or dispute; disputed questions cannot be decided at that stage. Section 4(1) and (2) of the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, 1988 bar certain claims and defences concerning benami property, but Section 4(3)(b) provides an exception for property held by a trustee or a person in a fiduciary capacity for another. Whether a relationship is fiduciary must be determined in its factual context and may require evidence: Marcel Martins v. M. Printer and others. Popat and Kotecha Property v. State Bank of India Staff Association supports the rule that disputed questions are not decided under Order VII Rule 11(d). Om Prakash and another v. Jai Prakash was distinguished because it concerned the Act’s application to actions initiated before the Ordinance, not the issue in this case.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the decisions of the courts below were set aside, and the application to reject the plaint was dismissed. Whether the suit is barred under Section 4, and the merits of the parties’ claims, were left for determination after evidence.

predicates.rejection_application_proceeding: A defendant sought rejection of the plaint at the threshold on the ground that the suit was barred by law.
predicates.plaint_averments_do_not_conclusively_sho: The plaintiff's pleaded facts, accepted as true, do not establish without doubt or dispute that the suit is barred.
predicates.fiduciary_exception_depends_on_evidence: Whether the pleaded property arrangement falls within an exception based on a fiduciary relationship depends on facts that require evidence.
predicates.plaint_must_not_be_rejected_at_threshold: The plaint is not rejected at the threshold and the disputed issue is left for determination after evidence.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected as time-barred when, read as a whole, it alleges facts about discovery of the challenged decision and subsequent steps that prevent the suit from appearing barred on the plaint alone.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that he first learned of the challenged decree when relatives claimed rights under it, but was not then given its particulars.
The plaintiff alleged that the decree’s details became available in a later proceeding, after which he inspected the relevant court file and brought the suit at the earliest possible opportunity.

The application to reject the plaint was made after the written statement, framing of issues and the plaintiff’s cross-examination; limitation was an issue, but no question or suggestion about limitation had been put to the plaintiff in cross-examination.
The trial court rejected the plaint on limitation without considering all its averments, and the High Court affirmed that decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court determines whether a suit appears barred by law from the plaint’s averments, not from the defendant’s written statement. The entire plaint must be read as a whole, rather than selecting isolated passages. The applicant must satisfy the court that the plaint does not disclose how the suit is in time. Order VII Rule 12 requires reasons to be recorded when a plaint is rejected. Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides a three-year period from knowledge for the relevant type of suit. The Court relied on Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, (2003) 1 SCC 557; I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, (1998) 2 SCC 70; T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, (1977) 4 SCC 467; Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill, (1982) 3 SCC 487; Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, (1998) 7 SCC 184; and Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, (2004) 3 SCC 137.
members.conclusion: The plaint was not shown by its statements, read as a whole, to be barred by limitation and should not have been rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d). The orders below were set aside, and the suit was restored for decision on its merits; the Court did not decide the parties’ underlying claims.

rule.if: time_bar_rejection_application and pleading_alleges_later_discovery and pleading_alleges_lack_of_details_at_first_notice and pleading_alleges_follow_up_after_details

predicates.time_bar_rejection_application: A defendant applies to have a plaint rejected on the ground that the suit is time-barred.
predicates.pleading_alleges_later_discovery: The plaintiff alleges that they learned of the challenged decision after it was made.
predicates.pleading_alleges_lack_of_details_at_firs: The plaintiff alleges that the particulars needed to identify or investigate the challenged decision were not provided when they first learned of it.
predicates.pleading_alleges_follow_up_after_details: The plaintiff alleges that, after obtaining the particulars, they took steps to investigate the decision and brought the suit.

members.legal_issue: A plaint containing independent claims cannot be rejected as time-barred when deciding whether the entire suit is barred requires resolving disputed facts.
material_facts: The plaint included claims concerning amounts allegedly collected by the defendant, as well as claims concerning execution of a lease and other relief.
The High Court treated non-execution of the lease as the focal point of all the claims.
The Supreme Court held that the other claims had independent existence and that determining the period to which the collections related required evidence.
The Supreme Court did not decide the merits of the claims or the limitation issues.
members.legal_principle: Order VII Rule 11(d) applies only where the plaint’s own statements show, without doubt or dispute, that the suit is barred.
