The whole plaint must be read together; claims must not be compartmentalized or reduced to a single asserted focal point when the plaint also advances independently existing claims. Disputed limitation questions requiring evidence are for later determination, not for decision on an application under that rule. The Court relied on Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, and Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner.
members.conclusion: The plaint could not be rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) on the basis that the entire suit was time-barred. The limitation issues were left for determination by the trial court in accordance with law.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A party applies for rejection of a plaint on the ground that the suit is barred by law.
predicates.plaint_contains_independent_claims: The plaint advances more than one claim, and at least one claim has an existence independent of the claim treated as the central claim.
predicates.limitation_depends_on_disputed_facts: Determining whether the claims are time-barred requires resolving disputed facts or receiving evidence.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected at the threshold on the ground of res judicata when determining the bar requires examination of the pleadings, issues, and decision in a previous suit rather than the statements in the plaint alone.
material_facts: The defendant sought rejection of a plaint in a subsequent suit, arguing that a previous suit between the parties had already adjudicated the dispute over the property and sale.
The plaintiff's plaint disclosed that the previous suit was pending when the subsequent suit was filed and that the plaintiff knew of it.
The previous suit was decided after the subsequent suit had been instituted.

Determining whether the issues in the two suits were directly and substantially the same, and had been finally decided, required examination of the pleadings, issues, and judgment in the previous suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, whether a suit appears barred by law must be determined from the plaint statements alone; the defendant's case and other material cannot be considered at that stage. Section 11 of the Code defines res judicata. Its application requires the previous suit to have been decided, the relevant issues to have been directly and substantially in issue in both suits, the parties to have litigated under the same title, and the issues to have been finally decided by a competent court. V. Rajeshwari v. T.C. Saravanabava, relying on Syed Mohd. Salie Labbai v. Mohd. Hanifa, Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, and Kali Krishna Tagore v. Secretary of State for India in Council, explains that the previous pleadings, issues, and judgment are ordinarily needed to establish res judicata. Kamala v. K.T. Eshwara Sa holds that a mixed question of law and fact requiring other evidence or the previous order cannot be decided under Order 7 Rule 11(d). Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, Church of Christ Charitable Trust & Educational Charitable Society v. Ponniamman Educational Trust, Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, Mayar (H.K.) Ltd. v. Vessel M.V. Fortune Express, and Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. v. Central Bank of India reaffirm that the plaint alone is considered at this stage. Soumitra Kumar Sen v. Shyamal Kumar Sen likewise states that recourse to Order 7 Rule 11 is inappropriate where the res judicata contention depends on matters outside the plaint, while allowing maintainability issues to be taken up after issues are framed.
members.conclusion: The plaint was not liable to be rejected on the ground of res judicata because that ground could not be determined from the plaint alone. The Court expressed no opinion on whether the subsequent suit was in fact barred, and permitted the defendant to raise maintainability before the trial court, which was to consider whether to frame a preliminary issue.

rule.if: threshold_plaint_rejection_application and res_judicata_is_ground and (plaint_alone_does_not_establish_prior_final_decision or deciding_bar_requires_prior_suit_record)

predicates.threshold_plaint_rejection_application: A defendant asked the court to reject a plaint before trial.
predicates.res_judicata_is_ground: The defendant argued that an earlier suit between parties litigating under the same title had already decided the dispute raised in the plaint.
predicates.plaint_alone_does_not_establish_prior_fi: The statements in the plaint alone do not establish that the relevant issues were finally decided in the earlier suit.
predicates.deciding_bar_requires_prior_suit_record: Determining whether the earlier suit finally decided the same issues requires examination of its pleadings, framed issues, or judgment.
predicates.plaint_not_rejected_on_res_judicata_grou: The plaint is not rejected at the threshold on the basis of res judicata.

members.legal_issue: A plaint that, read as a whole and taken at face value, discloses a real cause of action cannot be rejected for failure to disclose a cause of action.
material_facts: The plaint alleged that the plaintiff gave a cheque to an advocate as security under an agreement, subject to the defendant fulfilling an undertaking.
The plaint alleged that the defendant failed to fulfil that undertaking, the cheque was handed over contrary to the agreement, and the cheque was dishonoured after presentation.
The defendant sought rejection of the plaint, including on the ground that it disclosed no cause of action.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the plaint must be read as a whole, with its averments taken as true for this purpose. The Court relied on T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, Azhar Hussain v. Rajiv Gandhi, Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, Liverpool & London S.P. & I Assn. Ltd. v. M.V. Sea Success I, Madanuri Sri Rama Chandra Murthy v. Syed Jalal, Dahiben v. Arvindbhai Kalyanji Bhanusali, Rajendra Bajoria v. Hemant Kumar Jalan, Hardesh Ores (P.) Ltd. v. Hede & Co., D. Ramachandran v. R.V. Janakiraman, and Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The plaint disclosed a cause of action on its face and could not be rejected on the ground that it failed to disclose one.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A party applied for the plaint in a suit to be rejected at the threshold.
predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.plaint_read_as_whole_discloses_real_caus: The plaint's averments, taken as true and read together, set out a real basis for seeking relief.

members.legal_issue: A plaint cannot be rejected as barred by res judicata at the threshold when the plaint alleges fraud and collusion and deciding the bar requires inquiry beyond the plaint.
material_facts: A society that was not a party to an earlier suit for specific performance claimed ownership of the disputed land under gift deeds.
The society’s execution objections and its application to set aside the earlier decree were unsuccessful.
The society later filed a declaratory suit alleging that the earlier decree and related transactions were fraudulent and collusive.
The defendants sought rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of res judicata.

The trial court relied on the written statement as well as the plaint to reject the plaint; the High Court restored that rejection, although the Supreme Court found that the fraud and collusion allegations and the distinct grounds raised in the suit required a trial.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, whether a suit is barred by law must be determined from the plaint alone, without adding to or subtracting from its averments or considering evidence or the written statement. Res judicata may involve mixed questions of fact and law and must be established on the basis of the prior pleadings, issues, and judgment; where that requires factual inquiry, it cannot be determined at the plaint-rejection stage. The Court relied on V. Rajeshwari v. T.C. Saravanabava, Kamala v. K.T. Eshwara SA, and Balasaria Construction (P) Ltd. v. Hanuman Seva Trust.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the order restoring the suit was reinstated. On the plaint alone, the suit could not be held barred by res judicata; the framed issues required trial.

predicates.order_7_rule_11_d_application: A defendant applied to have the plaint rejected on the ground that the suit was barred by law.
predicates.plaint_alleges_fraud_or_collusion: The plaint alleges that the earlier judgment or proceeding was brought about by fraud or collusion.
predicates.res_judicata_requires_factual_inquiry: Deciding whether the earlier proceeding bars the suit requires inquiry into facts or matters beyond the plaint.

members.legal_issue: A court retains the power to extend a time limit it has fixed for taking a procedural step.
material_facts: The High Court fixed a time for taking steps to serve notice in an appeal and initially directed that the appeal would stand dismissed if the steps were not taken.
The High Court subsequently extended the time for taking the steps.
The appellant argued that the appeal had already stood dismissed under the initial order.
members.legal_principle: When a court fixes time for doing a procedural act, it retains the power to extend that time. The Court applied that principle to the successive procedural orders in the High Court appeal.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the High Court retained power to extend the time it had fixed, so the appeal had not stood dismissed under the initial order.

predicates.appellate_proceeding_with_court_fixed_co: An appellate court has fixed a time for a party to complete a procedural step.

members.legal_issue: A court retains authority over a decree for specific performance to extend the time for compliance, and a prompt, bona fide payment after appellate confirmation need not defeat execution.
material_facts: The decree-holder had paid most of the sale consideration before the decree was made.
The trial court directed execution of the sale deed upon payment of the balance, but did not separately state a period for the decree-holder to make that payment.
The appellate court affirmed the decree, and the decree-holder deposited the balance about a month later.
The court found that the decree-holder had acted bona fide and that the equities favoured execution.
members.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act allows the court, on an application, to rescind a contract when the purchaser fails to comply with the decree, and also permits the court to extend the time for compliance. The court does not become functus officio after granting specific performance; the decree is in the nature of a preliminary decree, and the court retains jurisdiction until the sale deed is executed. The Court relied on Sardar Mohar Singh v Mangilal and Bhupinder Kumar v Angrej Singh. It distinguished V S Palanichamy Chettiar Firm v C Alagappan, where the delay was substantially longer and unexplained, and emphasised the decree-holder’s conduct and the circumstances of the case.
members.conclusion: The delayed deposit did not render the decree inexecutable; the executing court was justified in rejecting the judgment debtor’s objections.

rule.if: specific_performance_execution and substantial_prior_payment and appeal_affirmed_decree and balance_paid_promptly_after_appeal

predicates.specific_performance_execution: A party is seeking execution of a decree for specific performance.
predicates.substantial_prior_payment: The decree-holder paid a substantial part of the agreed consideration before seeking execution.
predicates.appeal_affirmed_decree: An appellate court affirmed the specific-performance decree.
predicates.balance_paid_promptly_after_appeal: The decree-holder paid the remaining consideration soon after the appellate decision.

members.legal_issue: A court retaining control of a specific performance suit may extend the time for a purchaser to deposit the amount required to complete the contract, even after the original deadline has passed.
material_facts: The trial court decreed specific performance and directed the purchaser to deposit the outstanding mortgage amount by a specified deadline, but she did not deposit it in time.
The High Court vacated the clause that would automatically dismiss the suit for failure to deposit by the deadline, but later rescinded the contract.
The purchaser sought further time and credit for money she had paid to the mortgagee, and the Supreme Court granted an opportunity to deposit the amount required by the trial court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, a specific performance decree is, for practical purposes, a preliminary decree: the suit remains under the court’s control until a party applies for a final decree. The court may extend the time for deposit; the relief is equitable and may be granted on terms that do equity to the opposite party.
members.conclusion: The court could extend the time for deposit. It granted additional time, subject to equitable conditions, rather than allowing the contract to be rescinded outright.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks enforcement of an agreement by specific performance.
predicates.deposit_deadline_missed: The purchaser did not deposit the amount required by the decree within the time originally allowed.
predicates.suit_remained_under_court_control: The suit remained before the court for further steps toward a final decree.

members.legal_issue: The court that passed a decree for specific performance may consider an application to extend the time for payment when it is also the executing court.
material_facts: The decrees for specific performance required the purchasers to deposit the balance consideration within a specified period.
The purchasers sought extensions after the deposit deadline had passed, and the applications were sent to the executing court, which was the court where the original suits had been filed.
members.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, permits the court to extend the time for payment after a decree for specific performance and does not make the court functus officio. Under Ramankutty Guptan v. Avara, an application under Section 28 may be made in the executing court when it is the same court that passed the decree; Sardar Mohar Singh v. Mangilal likewise recognizes the court's continuing power to extend time.
members.conclusion: The court that passed the decree retains jurisdiction to extend the time for compliance, and where that court is also the executing court it may consider the application in the execution proceedings, treating it as an application in the original suit.

predicates.specific_performance_decree: The proceeding concerns execution of a decree requiring performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property.
predicates.extension_application_after_decree: The party required to make payment applies for more time after the decree has been made.
predicates.original_court_is_executing_court: The court handling execution is the same court in which the original suit was filed and the decree was passed.

members.legal_issue: A court may extend a court-fixed time for payment, and a purchaser's failure to pay during an appeal by the seller does not by itself defeat specific performance.
material_facts: The trial court directed the purchaser to pay a remaining amount by a stated deadline as a condition of the decree for specific performance.
The seller appealed the decree, leaving the purchaser without a final determination of the seller's challenge.
The purchaser had already paid a substantial part of the price and had litigated for years without receiving the property.
The appellate court exercised its discretion in the purchaser's favour and extended the time for payment.
members.legal_principle: A time limit fixed by a court in its discretion may be extended by the court. In the circumstances, the purchaser could not be expected to pay more while the seller's appeal against the decree remained pending; the court could decide whether to extend the time.
members.conclusion: The purchaser's failure to make the court-directed payment by the original deadline did not by itself disentitle the purchaser to specific performance, and the extension of time was proper.

rule.if: specific_performance_appeal and seller_appealed_decree and substantial_price_already_paid and court_fixed_payment_unpaid_pending_appeal

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: An appeal concerns a decree granting specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.seller_appealed_decree: The seller appealed the decree requiring performance.
predicates.substantial_price_already_paid: The purchaser had already paid a substantial part of the agreed price.
predicates.court_fixed_payment_unpaid_pending_appea: A court-fixed balance remained unpaid while the seller's appeal was pending.
predicates.court_may_extend_payment_time_without_di: The court may extend the payment time rather than dismiss the specific-performance claim solely for non-payment by the original deadline.

members.legal_issue: An application to extend the time for payment or rescind a contract after a decree for specific performance may be entertained by the court of first instance when the appellate decree arose in the same suit, but it must be dealt with on the original side rather than as an execution proceeding.
material_facts: The appellate court granted a decree for specific performance and fixed a time for payment of the balance consideration.
The judgment-debtor applied for rescission under Section 28 while execution was proceeding in the court where the original suit had been filed.
The High Court rejected the application as not maintainable on the execution side.
members.legal_principle: Section 28(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires an application for extension of time or rescission to be made in the same suit. Under Section 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court of first instance is included as the court that passed an appellate decree for execution purposes; an appeal is a continuation of the suit. The court retains control over a decree for specific performance after it is passed. Procedure should be moulded to serve substantial justice unless it concerns jurisdiction. The Court approved Maruti Vishnu Kshirsagar v. Bapu Keshav Jadhav, rejected Ibrahim Shariff v. Masthan Shariff, and relied on K. Kalpana Saraswathi v. P.S.S. Somasundaram Chettiar.
members.conclusion: The application was maintainable in the court of first instance because the appellate decree was part of the same suit, but it should have been treated as an interlocutory application on the original side and decided according to law, rather than dismissed merely because it was filed on the execution side.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and appellate_decree_in_same_suit and original_suit_and_execution_in_same_court and application_filed_on_execution_side

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a decree for specific performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property.
predicates.appellate_decree_in_same_suit: An appellate court granted the decree for specific performance in the same suit in which the original court had acted.
predicates.original_suit_and_execution_in_same_cour: The original suit and the execution proceeding are before the same court of first instance.
predicates.application_filed_on_execution_side: A party filed an application for extension of time or rescission as part of the execution proceeding rather than on the original side.

members.legal_issue: A court may extend a time limit fixed by its decree, even after expiry, but may refuse an extension when the applicant’s conduct and the circumstances do not justify it.
material_facts: The buyer applied for an extension after the deadline had passed.
There was no evidence that the buyer attempted to deposit the balance consideration by the deadline.
The buyer deposited the money late and by a method different from that required by the decree.
The buyer also filed the application for extension after a delay, and the courts found no sufficient basis to grant relief.
members.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers a court to extend time fixed by it, including after the original period has expired. The power is discretionary, and the court may consider the applicant’s conduct. The Court relied on Johri Singh v. Sukh Pal Singh, (1989) 4 SCC 403.
members.conclusion: The buyer did not establish a case for extension of time or condonation of delay, and the application was rejected on its merits.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and application_to_extend_decree_time and no_evidence_of_timely_payment_attempt and late_payment and required_payment_method_not_used

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: A claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.application_to_extend_decree_time: The claimant applied to the court to extend the time fixed for complying with the decree.
predicates.no_evidence_of_timely_payment_attempt: The claimant did not establish that they attempted to make the required payment by the deadline.
predicates.late_payment: The claimant made the required payment after the deadline.
predicates.required_payment_method_not_used: The claimant made the payment by a method different from the one required by the decree.

members.legal_issue: A payment deadline under a decree may be extended and delay in payment condoned when interim appellate orders stayed execution and the required deposits were made pursuant to those proceedings.
material_facts: The trial court set a deadline for the defendants to pay or deposit the money.
The High Court stayed execution and directed the defendants to make deposits while the appeals were pending.
The defendants made the deposits directed by the interim orders, and the deposited money remained in court investments.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its authority to give effect to the trial court’s decree in light of the interim orders that had stayed execution and required deposits; it held that delay attributable to that procedural history deserved to be condoned.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court condoned any delay in deposit and treated the time for deposit under the trial court’s decree as extended to the dates on which the deposits were actually made.

predicates.decree_compliance_in_appeal: A party must comply with a payment or deposit requirement imposed by a decree while an appeal concerning that decree is pending.
predicates.execution_was_stayed_by_interim_order: An appellate court stayed execution of the decree by an interim order.
predicates.required_deposit_was_made_under_interim_: The party made deposits in response to the appellate court’s interim directions.

members.legal_issue: A court may extend time to pay a court fee despite expiry of the time fixed by a peremptory procedural order stating that the appeal will stand dismissed for non-payment.
material_facts: The court directed the appellant to pay the deficit court fee within a fixed period and stated that the appeal would stand dismissed if payment was not made in time.

The appellant applied for an extension on the last day of the period, before it expired, but the application was heard after expiry and dismissed on the ground that the appeal had already stood dismissed.
The court later rejected further applications on the same ground without considering whether time could be extended.
members.legal_principle: Sections 148 and 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, permit enlargement of time even after the period fixed has expired, and section 151 preserves the court’s inherent power to do justice. A peremptory procedural order, unlike a conditional decree, is in essence in terrorem and does not completely estop the court from considering events and circumstances arising within the time fixed. The court relied on Lachmi Narain Marwari v. Balmakund Marwari and referred to Latham v. Johnson.
members.conclusion: The court retained power to extend the time notwithstanding the peremptory order and the expiry of the original period; the orders refusing to consider that power were erroneous.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and court_fixed_time_for_court_fee and order_was_peremptory_procedural_order and request_for_extension

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal in which the appellant must comply with a court-fixed requirement.
predicates.court_fixed_time_for_court_fee: The court set a period within which a party had to pay a court fee.
predicates.order_was_peremptory_procedural_order: The court stated that non-compliance within the period would result in dismissal, through a procedural order rather than a conditional decree.
predicates.request_for_extension: A party asked the court to enlarge the time for compliance.

members.legal_issue: A court retains jurisdiction to extend the time for compliance with a conditional decree for specific performance until the sale deed is executed.
material_facts: A decree for specific performance required the respondent to pay specified sums within three months and, in default, to execute the sale deed.
The sale deed had not been executed when the respondent applied for rescission and an extension of time.
members.legal_principle: Section 28(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits an application to rescind a specific-performance contract when the required payment is not made within the time allowed. That power shows the court does not become functus officio upon making the decree; until the sale deed is executed, it retains jurisdiction, including power to extend the time for compliance. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The court retained jurisdiction to deal with the decree and had discretion to extend the time for compliance.

predicates.specific_performance_decree_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a decree for specific performance of a contract involving immovable property.
predicates.conditional_payment_required: The decree requires a party to make a payment as a condition of compliance.
predicates.sale_deed_unexecuted: The sale deed required by the decree has not yet been executed.

members.legal_issue: An exemption for buildings owned by public religious and charitable trusts satisfies equal protection when the class is distinct and the exemption has a rational connection to the purpose of the exemption power.
material_facts: Tenants challenged a notification exempting buildings owned by public religious trusts and public charitable trusts from all provisions of the rent-control law.

Public religious and charitable trusts served public purposes, and the use of their income was governed by the purposes for which they were created, distinguishing their buildings from those of private landlords.

The government stated in affidavits that rents paid by tenants were very low, statutory fair-rent fixation would not meet the needs of the trusts, and tenants were exploiting the trusts’ situation and helplessness.
The tenants filed no rejoinder affidavits disputing the government’s account.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification based on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus with the relevant statutory purpose. The exemption power must be exercised consistently with the rent-control law’s policy, including relief from undue hardship or abuse of its protections. P.J. Irani v. State of Madras recognised that a class of buildings belonging to charitable or religious bodies could be rationally distinguished. State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal illustrates that the government must consider grounds germane to the law’s purpose; State of Rajasthan v. Mukanchand was inapplicable because the classification here had the required nexus.
members.conclusion: The classification was based on an intelligible differentia and had a rational connection to relieving hardship arising from the uniform application of the rent-control law; the exemption did not violate equal protection.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge_to_exemption_: The proceeding challenges on equal-protection grounds a government notification exempting a class of buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.public_endowment_owners: The exempted buildings are owned by public religious or charitable bodies whose income is applied according to their public purposes.
predicates.distinct_public_purpose_and_income_const: The owners’ public functions and constraints on use of their income distinguish them from ordinary private landlords.
predicates.unchallenged_evidence_of_inadequate_rent: The government presents evidence that protected rents are inadequate and uniform application of rent-control protections causes hardship to the owners, and the challengers do not dispute that evidence.

members.legal_issue: A temporary exemption for new buildings that encourages additional housing is consistent with the tenant-protection policy of rent-control legislation and is not discriminatory when the classification has a reasonable connection to that purpose.
material_facts: The notification exempted new buildings from rent-control protections for a limited period.
The administration stated that the exemption was intended to encourage investment in new construction and increase the supply of housing.
The Court found that additional housing could mitigate hardship for tenants and that the temporary exemption balanced landlords' and tenants' interests.
The distinction between exempt and non-exempt buildings was connected to the aim of creating additional housing.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a statute's object and policy are not always confined strictly to its preamble and express provisions. The broader policy of the rent-control legislation was to mitigate tenant hardship, and encouraging new construction could advance that policy by increasing housing supply. The temporary classification had a reasonable nexus to that objective and did not violate Article 14. The relevant provisions were section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, as modified for the territory, and Article 14 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The exemption was not outside the object and policy of the legislation and was not discriminatory, arbitrary, or unreasonable.

predicates.challenge_to_exemption_as_inconsistent_o: A challenge alleges that an exemption from rent-control protections is inconsistent with the law's purpose or discriminates between buildings.
predicates.rent_law_aims_to_mitigate_tenant_hardshi: The rent-control scheme is intended generally to mitigate hardship faced by tenants.
predicates.temporary_exemption_encourages_new_housi: The executive grants a limited-duration exemption to encourage investment in new housing construction.
predicates.exempted_class_has_reasonable_nexus_to_a: The buildings given the exemption form a class reasonably connected to increasing the supply of housing.

members.legal_issue: A category-based exemption from rent regulation for buildings belonging to public religious or charitable institutions is not an impermissible classification when it serves the institutions’ public purposes.
material_facts: The government issued notifications exempting buildings owned by religious institutions and related bodies from several provisions regulating leases, rent, and eviction.
The exempted owners were religious or charitable institutions whose income and its use were governed by their institutional objects.
The exemption was intended to allow those institutions to carry out their purposes.
The challenge relied on the fact that the exemption covered a broad category of buildings, including buildings used commercially.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 25 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, the government may grant an exemption in the public interest or for other sufficient cause, but may not exercise that power arbitrarily. Article 14 prohibits arbitrary discrimination. In P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, religious and charitable trusts were treated as a distinct class; S. Kandaswamy Chettiar v. State of Tamil Nadu upheld a total exemption for public religious or charitable trusts because they serve public purposes and their income is governed by their objects. The Court also relied on Jayakaran v. Kerala Health R&W Society, State of Kerala v. Vijayan, and Lakshmanan v. Mohamood in rejecting distinctions based on ownership or the breadth of the exempted category.
members.conclusion: The category is distinct from private landlords, and exempting its buildings was not arbitrary or contrary to Article 14; the notifications were valid.

predicates.rent_exemption_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges government notifications that exempt a category of buildings from rent regulation.
predicates.public_religious_charitable_owners: The buildings belong to public religious or charitable institutions whose income and its use are governed by their institutional objects.
predicates.exemption_serves_institutional_objects: The government granted the exemption to enable the institutions to carry out their public religious or charitable purposes.

members.legal_issue: Exempting newly constructed buildings from rent-control restrictions for a limited period is not contrary to the protective purpose of rent-control legislation or discriminatory merely because tenants of older buildings receive protection sooner.
material_facts: Rent-control restrictions had discouraged investment in new construction, contributing to a shortage of accommodation.

The exemption gave newly constructed buildings a limited period outside the restrictions, after which the buildings would be governed by the rent-control scheme, subject to the measure governing suits filed during the exemption.
The resulting classification distinguished buildings by their completion and exemption status, and the exemption was intended to encourage construction and increase accommodation.
members.legal_principle: An exemption intended to encourage construction may advance the ultimate purpose of rent-control legislation by increasing accommodation for tenants. A classification based on the date of completion is valid where it rests on an intelligible differentia rationally connected to the legislative objective. The Court relied on Punjab Tin Supply Company v. Central Government and followed Mohinder Kumar v. State of Haryana in applying the equality principle.
members.conclusion: The exemption advanced the ultimate purpose of the legislation and the classification of buildings by completion date had an intelligible basis and a rational connection to that purpose; it did not violate equality guarantees.

rule.if: rent_control_exemption and new_building_incentive and limited_exemption_period and completion_based_classification

predicates.rent_control_exemption: A proceeding challenges an exemption from restrictions governing rent or eviction of tenants.
predicates.new_building_incentive: The exemption is intended to encourage construction of new buildings and increase available accommodation.
predicates.limited_exemption_period: The exemption lasts for a limited period, after which the buildings generally become subject to the rent-control scheme.
predicates.completion_based_classification: The measure treats buildings differently according to when they were completed.

members.legal_issue: Different treatment of religious trusts associated with different religious communities is constitutionally permissible when the classification rests on relevant differences and is rationally related to the legislation’s purpose.
material_facts: The challenged legislation covered Hindu and Jain religious trusts but excluded Sikh religious trusts, and provided distinct arrangements for the two main Jain branches.
The religious communities differed in beliefs, practices, and the organization of their religious trusts; the needs of Hindu and Jain trusts in administration were not the same.
The legislation was intended to improve the administration of religious trusts and protect and preserve trust property.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification where it is based on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those included from those excluded and that differentia has a rational relation to the statute’s object. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, [1959] S.C.R. 279, and stated that constitutionality is presumed and the challenger bears the burden of showing a clear infringement.
members.conclusion: The classification did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_regulation: The litigants challenged a law governing the administration of religious trusts.
predicates.religious_groups_differ_in_trust_organiz: The religious communities whose trusts were treated differently had distinct practices or organizational arrangements for their trusts.
predicates.classification_tracks_relevant_differenc: The legislature grouped or separated trusts according to differences relevant to their administration.
predicates.classification_advances_regulatory_purpo: The classification related to the legislation’s aim of improving trust administration and protecting trust property.

members.legal_issue: Classifying tenants by net income for access to statutory rent protection is consistent with the constitutional guarantee of equality when the classification serves the protection of economically weaker tenants and the encouragement of building construction.
material_facts: A tenant sought protection under rent-control legislation, but the lower courts held that the tenant’s net income placed it outside the legislation’s protection.
The legislation applied its rent protection according to the tenant’s net income, including income earned inside or outside the state.
The challenge contended that the income distinction was arbitrary and unrelated to the legislation’s purpose.
The legislation aimed both to protect economically weaker tenants and to encourage construction of buildings.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a classification is permissible when it rests on an intelligible differentia and that differentia has a rational relation to the statute’s object, as stated in Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar. An income-based classification can rationally serve the twin aims of protecting economically weaker tenants and encouraging construction. The Court approved J & K Bank Ltd. v. State of J & K, distinguished Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu and Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and relied on Kerala Hotel & Restaurant Association v. State of Kerala. It also observed that legislative social and economic experimentation should not be displaced absent blatant disregard of constitutional provisions.
members.conclusion: The income-based classification is reasonable and does not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.appeal_challenges_income_based_rent_prot: A party in an appeal challenges a legal classification that determines access to rent protection by reference to a tenant’s income.
predicates.rent_protection_targets_economically_wea: The rent-protection scheme is intended to protect tenants with less economic capacity from unreasonable eviction or unfair rent.
predicates.classification_encourages_building_const: The classification is designed in part to encourage the construction of buildings.
predicates.tenant_income_indicates_financial_capaci: The classification uses a tenant’s income as an indicator of the tenant’s financial capacity.

members.legal_issue: A time-limited exemption from rent-control legislation for new buildings is constitutionally valid when it reasonably incentivizes construction to address housing scarcity.
material_facts: The amended provision exempted buildings completed on or after the Act’s commencement from rent-control legislation for ten years from completion.
The exemption was intended to encourage new construction, increase the supply of accommodation, and ultimately mitigate tenants’ hardship.
The exemption was for a definite period, which the Court considered neither too long nor unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not prohibit a reasonable, time-limited incentive for new construction where the incentive has a rational connection to easing accommodation scarcity and mitigating tenants’ hardship. The duration and effective date of such an exemption are ordinarily matters of legislative policy, subject to review if unreasonable or arbitrary. The Court relied on M/s Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government and distinguished Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, which concerned an exemption of indefinite duration.
members.conclusion: The exemption was constitutionally valid and was not arbitrary or unreasonable under Article 14.

predicates.a_constitutional_challenge_to_a_rent_con: A party challenged the constitutional validity of an exemption from rent-control protections.
predicates.the_exemption_encourages_new_constructio: The exemption was provided as an incentive to persons who construct new buildings.
predicates.the_exemption_has_a_rational_connection_: The exemption was intended to increase accommodation and thereby address housing scarcity and tenants’ hardship.
predicates.the_exemption_is_for_a_definite_reasonab: The exemption lasts for a defined period that is not unduly long.

members.legal_issue: Classifying buildings according to whether their construction was completed before or on or after the commencement of rent-control legislation is constitutionally permissible when the distinction is rationally related to encouraging new construction.
material_facts: The provision exempted buildings completed on or after the Act’s commencement, while buildings completed earlier remained subject to rent-control protections.
The distinction was based on when construction was completed and was intended to encourage construction after the Act commenced.
The Court found that the classification had an intelligible basis and a rational connection to the objective of increasing accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia and have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court applied this principle to the classification of buildings and their landlords and tenants by the time of construction, relying on M/s Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government and finding Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh inapplicable to the time-limited exemption at issue.
members.conclusion: The classification was not arbitrary or invidiously discriminatory and did not violate Article 14.

predicates.a_challenge_to_building_classification_i: A party challenged a classification of buildings made by a rent-control law.
predicates.buildings_are_classified_by_construction: The law distinguishes buildings according to when their construction was completed in relation to the law’s commencement.
predicates.the_classification_encourages_new_constr: The distinction is intended to encourage the construction of new buildings.
predicates.the_classification_has_a_rational_relati: The distinction is rationally connected to increasing the supply of accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A class-wide exemption of buildings owned by cooperative societies from rent-control protections is consistent with equality when the societies’ regulated structure and the circumstances supporting the exemption provide a rational connection to the purposes of rent control.
material_facts: The petitioners were tenants in buildings owned by a cooperative society and challenged a notification exempting buildings owned by all cooperative societies from the rent-control statute.
Cooperative societies were established to promote members’ economic interests through cooperative principles and to advance social and economic welfare.
The governing cooperative legislation restricted distributions of profits through limits on dividends and bonuses and required allocations to various funds.

The State asserted that cooperative societies did not ordinarily purchase buildings as a business for letting them out, that societies had faced hardship under the rent-control law, and that withdrawing tenant protections would not lead to rack-renting or unreasonable eviction.
The State’s factual assertions were unchallenged; the court also noted the hardship experienced by the society whose buildings the tenants occupied.
members.legal_principle: Under section 29 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, the exemption power must be exercised consistently with the guidance of that Act’s purpose and provisions. Article 14 permits a classification where the differentia has a rational nexus to the object of the law. Sections 4 and 62 of the Tamil Nadu Co-operative Societies Act, 1961, and rule 46 of the rules made under it reflect cooperative principles and restrict the distribution of profits, distinguishing cooperative societies from commercial landlords and supporting an inference that they would not engage in rack-renting or unreasonable eviction. The State’s unchallenged evidence of cooperative societies’ welfare activities, operational difficulties, and lack of a letting business further supported the nexus. Baburao Shantaram More v. Bombay Housing Board did not establish that exemptions for cooperative-owned buildings are invalid; it concerned a different exemption and did not decide that question.
members.conclusion: The exemption notification was a valid exercise of the statutory exemption power and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality; the petitions were dismissed.

rule.if: challenge_to_class_wide_rent_control_exemption and cooperative_society_owned_buildings and regulated_distribution_of_cooperative_profits and cooperative_welfare_purpose and no_building_letting_business and state_found_no_expected_rack_renting_or_unreasonable_eviction and unchallenged_evidence_of_operational_hardship

predicates.challenge_to_class_wide_rent_control_exe: A party brings a constitutional challenge to an exemption from rent-control protections that applies to a class of property owners.
predicates.cooperative_society_owned_buildings: The exempted buildings are owned by cooperative societies.
predicates.regulated_distribution_of_cooperative_pr: The legal framework governing the owners restricts distributions of profits and requires some profits to be allocated to designated funds.
predicates.cooperative_welfare_purpose: The owners operate on cooperative principles to promote members’ economic interests and broader social or economic welfare.
predicates.no_building_letting_business: The owners do not conduct the purchase of buildings for the purpose of letting them out as a business.
predicates.state_found_no_expected_rack_renting_or_: The government determined that removing rent-control protections for the class was not expected to result in rack-renting or unreasonable eviction.
predicates.unchallenged_evidence_of_operational_har: The government presented evidence that applying rent-control restrictions caused operational hardship to members of the class, and that evidence was not challenged.

members.legal_issue: Repeatedly raising objections already determined, in order to delay enforcement of an eviction decree and despite an undertaking to deliver possession, may warrant exemplary costs.
material_facts: The tenants repeatedly raised objections about the identity and boundaries of the property after those matters had been decided, and courts had rejected similar objections in execution.
The tenants did not deliver possession by the date promised in their undertaking, and enforcement required repeated steps, including execution of a warrant with police assistance.
The Court characterized the renewed objections as an abuse of the process intended to delay eviction and imposed exemplary costs.
members.legal_principle: Courts should prevent abuse of process that delays a decree-holder from obtaining the benefit of a decree and may impose exemplary costs in response. The judgment cited no specific provision or earlier case as the basis for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed with exemplary costs imposed on the tenants.

predicates.execution_of_eviction_decree: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a decree ordering eviction of a tenant.
predicates.repeated_objections_to_decided_property_: The judgment debtor repeatedly raises a property-identity objection that has already been decided.
predicates.possession_withheld_after_undertaking: The judgment debtor does not deliver possession by the time promised in an undertaking to the court.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may impose costs when a litigant takes inconsistent positions and dishonestly prolongs proceedings.
material_facts: The licensee abandoned its claim that the licence was irrevocable to revive its suit, later again asserted that claim, and pursued inconsistent positions in multiple proceedings.
The inconsistent positions allowed the licensee to retain possession after the licence expired and prolonged proceedings for more than a decade.
The Court found that the licensee had not pursued its proceedings honestly.
members.legal_principle: The rule against approbating and reprobating prevents a litigant from obtaining benefits through inconsistent positions. The Court treated the litigant’s inconsistent conduct and dishonest prolongation of proceedings as warranting an award of costs, relying on the doctrine of election and approbation and reprobation discussed in Benjamin Scarf, Tinkler, Clough, Harrison, Kok Hoong, Dwijendra Narain Roy, C. Beepathumma, and New Bihar Biri Leaves.
members.conclusion: The Court dismissed the licensee’s appeal with costs payable to the Supreme Court Mediation Center.

predicates.appellate_litigation_proceeding: The court is deciding an appeal arising from litigation in which a party has taken positions before courts or tribunals.
predicates.litigant_takes_inconsistent_positions: A litigant advances incompatible positions in the proceedings.
predicates.litigation_is_dishonestly_prolonged: The litigant’s conduct dishonestly causes the proceedings to continue for an extended period.

members.legal_issue: A litigant who misleads the court by making incorrect statements and submitting a wrong document may be ordered to pay costs.
material_facts: In the appeal, the builders made an incorrect statement about the contents of a letter and submitted a different version of that letter as an additional document.
The Court found that the builders had sought to mislead it.
members.legal_principle: The Court imposed costs in response to the litigants' conduct in making incorrect statements and submitting a wrong document; the judgment cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this sanction.
members.conclusion: The Court ordered the builders to pay costs to the National Legal Services Authority.

predicates.proceeding_is_an_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before a court.
predicates.litigant_makes_incorrect_statements: A litigant makes statements to the court that are incorrect.
predicates.litigant_submits_wrong_document_to_court: A litigant submits a document that does not accurately represent the document or facts relied on.
predicates.court_may_impose_costs_for_misleading_co: The court may impose costs on a litigant for conduct that misleads it.

members.legal_issue: Exemplary costs may be imposed when clever drafting disguises a hopelessly barred suit and prolongs meritless litigation.
material_facts: The Court found that the plaint had been cleverly drafted to get around limitation and court-fee requirements while omitting relief central to the pleaded transaction.
The suit was found to be hopelessly barred, and the appellants pursued the litigation through the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, (1977) 4 SCC 467, states that courts should meaningfully examine a plaint and stop meritless litigation created by clever drafting at an early stage. Relying on that principle, the Court imposed additional costs in this case.
members.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed with costs throughout, and additional exemplary costs were imposed for prosecuting and prolonging the hopelessly barred suit.

predicates.appeal_from_rejection_of_civil_plaint: An appeal challenges an order rejecting a civil plaint.
predicates.plaint_cleverly_disguises_hopelessly_bar: The plaint's drafting disguises a claim that is plainly barred on its pleaded facts.
predicates.litigation_prolonged_despite_clear_bar: The party continues the litigation through further proceedings despite the clear bar.

members.legal_issue: A party that prolongs litigation through abusive applications to evade a final judgment may be ordered to pay realistic litigation costs.
material_facts: After the final judgment and dismissal of review and curative petitions, the applicants filed further applications seeking to relitigate settled issues and delay payment.
The respondents were compelled to defend the applications, and court time was expended on the prolonged litigation.
The court found the applications devoid of merit and part of an effort to avoid compliance with its orders.
members.legal_principle: Courts have a duty to prevent abuse of their process and to neutralize undeserved advantages obtained through delay. Realistic costs may reflect the burden imposed on the opposing parties and may deter dishonest or obstructive litigation. The court relied on Sita Ram Bhandar Society v. Lieutenant Governor, Government of NCT, Delhi, Ramrameshwari Devi v. Nirmala Devi, and the restitution and costs principles discussed in Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer and South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P.
members.conclusion: The applicants were ordered to pay costs for the litigation, with the costs directed to be used for remedial measures in the affected area.

predicates.court_proceeding_to_enforce_final_judgme: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a final court judgment.
predicates.repeated_meritless_applications_to_delay: A party repeatedly filed applications lacking merit in order to delay compliance with the judgment.
predicates.opposing_parties_forced_to_defend: The repeated applications required the opposing parties to incur the burden of defending the litigation.

members.legal_issue: A court should prevent a litigant from gaining an unfair advantage through false or irrelevant claims and should impose appropriate costs where litigation abuses the judicial process.
material_facts: The Court found that the occupant had suppressed material facts and introduced false, untenable and irrelevant pleas and documents.
The litigation over the premises continued for many years, and the Court considered that the occupant had obtained an undue benefit from the prolonged proceedings.
The Court stated that it would ordinarily have imposed heavy costs and ordered restitution, but imposed nominal costs in light of the occupant’s financial circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Courts should adopt a realistic approach to costs and restitution so that wrongful or undeserved advantages gained through litigation are neutralized and dishonest or frivolous litigation is discouraged. The Court relied on Ramrameshwari Devi v. Nirmala Devi, (2011) 8 SCC 249; Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, (2011) 8 SCC 161; Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer, (1980) 2 SCC 191; Kavita Trehan v. Balsara Hygiene Products, (1994) 5 SCC 380; South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P., (2003) 8 SCC 648; and Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd., (1999) 2 SCC 325.
members.conclusion: The Court dismissed the appeals, imposed nominal costs, and directed the occupant to vacate and hand over possession. It reiterated that costs and, where appropriate, restitution should be used to neutralize unfair benefits obtained through abuse of process.

predicates.litigant_uses_false_or_irrelevant_claims: A litigant advances false, untenable or irrelevant claims or material.
predicates.conduct_causes_unfair_advantage_or_unnec: The litigant’s conduct produces an unfair benefit or unnecessarily prolongs the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Courts may impose realistic costs on litigants who use frivolous proceedings and obstructive tactics to delay civil litigation.
material_facts: The appellants pursued repeated applications and proceedings that obstructed progress in the suit.
They continued the litigation over several decades despite earlier adverse decisions.
The High Court found that their synopsis contained incorrect dates, and the Supreme Court agreed that their conduct had wasted judicial time and harassed the respondents.
The appeals challenged the High Court’s orders, including its imposition of costs.
members.legal_principle: Courts should impose actual, realistic costs to remove the incentive for frivolous litigation and obstruction, and should apply restitution pragmatically. The Court referred to Swaran Singh v. State of Punjab (2000) 5 SCC 668 and Mahila Vinod Kumari v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2008) 8 SCC 34 in discussing false evidence and perjury, and to the provisions in Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure concerning perjury.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s order and imposed additional costs, holding that wrongdoers should not benefit from frivolous litigation.

predicates.appeal_challenges_costs_in_civil_litigat: A party appeals an order imposing costs in connection with civil litigation.
predicates.repeated_frivolous_proceedings: A litigant repeatedly brings applications or proceedings that lack a proper basis.
predicates.conduct_obstructed_or_delayed_trial: The litigant’s conduct obstructs or delays the progress of the trial.

members.legal_issue: Courts should impose exemplary costs to deter frivolous proceedings that abuse judicial process and consume resources needed for genuine cases.
material_facts: The litigants obtained an initial period and a further extension to vacate, then sought review and a much longer extension while continuing to challenge the possession decree.
The Supreme Court found the proceedings frivolous and an abuse of process, and observed that they prolonged a stale dispute and consumed court time.
members.legal_principle: The court stated that it is the duty of courts to deal firmly with frivolous filings and abuse of process. Exemplary, real costs are a necessary instrument to deter litigation designed to benefit from delay, protect judicial resources, and preserve access to courts for genuine causes. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The court imposed exemplary costs on the litigants.

predicates.court_proceeding_involving_possession_di: A court proceeding concerned a dispute over possession of premises.
predicates.repeated_extensions_used: The litigant obtained more than one extension of time to vacate the premises.
predicates.frivolous_challenges_prolonged_dispute: The litigant pursued challenges that the court found frivolous and that prolonged the dispute.

members.legal_issue: Exemplary costs are warranted when litigation is used to obstruct enforcement of a final court order and prolongs the successful party's inability to obtain its benefit.
material_facts: An eviction order had become final, but execution to recover possession remained pending.
During execution, a relative of the person subject to eviction brought a suit asserting ownership and obtained an ex parte injunction.
The suit followed the failure of the person subject to eviction to establish the same essential claim in the eviction proceedings and delayed recovery of possession for many years.
The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and imposed costs payable to the party entitled to possession.
members.legal_principle: Courts should take serious note of attempts to circumvent court orders through dubious or obstructive litigation and may impose exemplary costs to curb that conduct. The Court relied on the circumstances and prolonged obstruction in this case; it cited no specific provision or earlier case for the costs ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court imposed exemplary costs on the appellant for litigation that delayed enforcement of the final eviction order.

predicates.execution_obstruction_suit: A litigant brought a separate suit while enforcement of a final court order was underway, seeking relief that obstructed that enforcement.
predicates.final_court_order_delayed_by_litigation: The separate litigation prolonged the successful party's inability to obtain the benefit of the final order.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking to amend pleadings in a civil suit after trial has commenced must establish that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised before trial commenced.
material_facts: The defendants applied to amend their written statement after the issues had been settled and the suit had been set down for recording evidence.
The proposed matters were known to the defendants and had been raised in earlier proceedings.
The amendment application did not set out facts or grounds showing that the matters could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence.
The proposed amendment introduced new and inconsistent pleas, and allowing it at that stage would prejudice the plaintiffs.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2002, restricts amendments after trial has commenced unless the court concludes that, despite due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before trial commenced. The proviso must be given full effect and was intended to prevent delay. Salem Advocate Bar Association, T.N. v. Union of India (2005) explains the proviso’s purpose; Kailash v. Nanhku (2005) addresses when trial commences; and Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh (2006) is cited on that proposition. A general assertion of care is insufficient without particulars establishing due diligence.
members.conclusion: The defendants were not entitled to leave to amend their written statement, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_suit_amendment_request and post_trial_request and proposed_matter_known_earlier and no_particularized_due_diligence_explanation

predicates.civil_suit_amendment_request: A party in a civil suit applied to amend its pleadings.
predicates.post_trial_request: The party applied after the suit had reached the stage of trial.
predicates.proposed_matter_known_earlier: The party knew of the matter it sought to add before trial commenced.
predicates.no_particularized_due_diligence_explanat: The party did not provide particulars showing that, despite due diligence, it could not have raised the matter before trial commenced.

members.legal_issue: A pleading amendment sought after trial has commenced is unavailable when the applicant could have raised the matter earlier through reasonable diligence.
material_facts: A defendant sought to amend her written statement in a suit concerning use of a shared driveway, relying on an agreement that she said had been located among her deceased son's papers.
The suit and the defendant's written statement dated from 1986, but the amendment application was filed in 2004, after the parties had completed their evidence and arguments.
The alleged agreement was not mentioned in the original written statement or in the defendant's testimony, where she described the partition as oral.

The defendant's son, who had handled the litigation, was a chartered accountant, and another son was also available; no steps to raise the agreement were taken before or after the first son's death in 1998.
The plaintiff denied that the agreement was genuine, and the proposed amendment would have departed from the defendant's earlier position.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendments at any stage, but its proviso bars an amendment after trial has commenced unless the court is satisfied that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier. Due diligence requires reasonable diligence, such as a prudent person would exercise in their own affairs; delay and the potential for prejudice are relevant considerations. The court referred to Union of India v. Pramod Gupta (dead) by LRs, (2005) 12 SCC 1, on delay and laches as relevant to deciding an amendment application.
members.conclusion: The defendant did not establish that, despite due diligence, she could not have raised the agreement before trial commenced. The amendment was therefore rightly rejected, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: post_trial_pleading_amendment and material_available_before_trial and omitted_from_original_pleading and not reasonable_explanation_for_delay and amendment_shifts_prior_position

predicates.post_trial_pleading_amendment: A party seeks to amend a pleading after the trial has commenced.
predicates.material_available_before_trial: The material on which the proposed amendment relies was available to the party or its representative before the trial commenced.
predicates.omitted_from_original_pleading: The party did not raise the matter in its original pleading or earlier testimony.
predicates.reasonable_explanation_for_delay: The party provides a reasonable account of why it could not raise the matter earlier despite taking reasonable steps.
predicates.amendment_shifts_prior_position: The proposed amendment departs from a position the party took earlier in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A pleading amendment sought after commencement of trial may be refused when the applicant fails to show due diligence and the amendment is belated, changes the suit’s character, withdraws an admission, and seriously prejudices the opposing party.
material_facts: The suit sought partition and separate possession, and the original pleading proceeded on the basis that the family properties remained joint.
After evidence had been recorded and the suit was listed for final arguments, several plaintiffs sought to amend the plaint to assert that the properties had already been partitioned.
The applicants knew of the asserted earlier partition when a compromise petition referring to it was filed in the suit, but gave no explanation for waiting years to seek amendment.
The opposing plaintiff disputed that any partition had occurred and sought to continue the partition proceedings.
The proposed amendment would replace the original position that partition had not taken place, change the nature of the suit, and seriously prejudice the opposing plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, after trial has commenced an amendment may be allowed only if the applicant satisfies the court that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier. The applicant bears that burden, and amendment is not a matter of right. An amendment may be refused if it introduces a wholly different or inconsistent case, changes the fundamental character of the suit, is not bona fide, or causes prejudice to the other side that cannot be adequately compensated. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The application to amend the plaint was properly rejected; the order setting aside the trial court’s permission to amend was confirmed, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_suit_pleading_amendment and trial_commenced and due_diligence_not_shown and (unexplained_delay or prior_knowledge_not_acted_on) and (changes_suit_character or withdraws_pleading_admission) and causes_serious_prejudice_to_opponent

predicates.civil_suit_pleading_amendment: A party sought to amend a pleading in a civil suit.
predicates.trial_commenced: The application was made after the trial had begun.
predicates.due_diligence_not_shown: The applicant did not establish that, despite acting with due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier.
predicates.unexplained_delay: The applicant waited a substantial time to seek amendment without explaining the delay.
predicates.prior_knowledge_not_acted_on: The applicant knew of the matter later proposed for pleading but did not seek amendment within a reasonable time.
predicates.changes_suit_character: The proposed amendment would fundamentally alter the nature or character of the suit.
predicates.withdraws_pleading_admission: The proposed amendment would retract an admission in the existing pleading.
predicates.causes_serious_prejudice_to_opponent: Allowing the amendment would cause serious prejudice to the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: A proposed plaint amendment may be refused when the applicant knew the relevant facts before filing suit, omitted the relief, and later seeks to add it as a belated afterthought without showing that it could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought to amend their plaint to challenge an old conveyance and add related allegations and relief.
The first plaintiff had been a society office-bearer and was authorized by a society resolution to complete the transaction underlying the conveyance.
The plaintiffs had learned of the conveyance before filing their suit but did not seek relief challenging it in the original plaint.

The amendment was sought after an interim application had been rejected, and the trial court found that the plaintiffs had not shown that they could not raise the proposed matters earlier despite due diligence.
The Supreme Court regarded the proposed amendment as belated and an afterthought intended to avert an adverse consequence.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an amendment application is not allowed merely because a party wishes to make further averments; the court may refuse a belated amendment where the applicant knew the relevant facts, omitted the relief from the original plaint, and fails to show that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order permitting the amendment was set aside, and the trial court’s order refusing the amendment was restored.

rule.if: plaint_amendment_application and prior_knowledge_of_relevant_facts and omitted_relief_from_original_pleading and no_due_diligence_explanation and belated_afterthought

predicates.plaint_amendment_application: A party applied to amend a plaint in a civil suit.
predicates.prior_knowledge_of_relevant_facts: The applicant knew the relevant facts before filing the original plaint.
predicates.omitted_relief_from_original_pleading: The applicant did not seek the proposed relief in the original plaint.
predicates.no_due_diligence_explanation: The applicant did not show that the proposed matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence.
predicates.belated_afterthought: The proposed amendment was sought belatedly as an afterthought to avoid an adverse consequence.

members.legal_issue: An amendment sought after the trial has technically commenced may be allowed when it was sought before evidence was produced and the parties later presented evidence on the proposed amendment without prejudice to the opponent.
material_facts: The amendment application was filed after the case had been fixed for the plaintiff to produce evidence, but before the plaintiff had produced evidence.
The parties subsequently led evidence, and the plaintiff's counsel stated that they had done so in view of the proposed amendment.
The Court found that the opponent was not prejudiced by allowing the amendment.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy, subject to its proviso limiting amendments after trial commences unless the party could not have raised the matter earlier despite due diligence. Salem Advocate Bar Association, T.N. v. Union of India, (2005) 6 SCC 344, explains the proviso's purpose of preventing delay; Rajesh Kumar Aggarwal v. K.K. Modi, (2006) 4 SCC 385, emphasizes amendments necessary to determine the real controversy; Chander Kanta Bansal v. Rajinder Singh Anand, (2008) 5 SCC 117, discusses the purpose and scope of the proviso; and Mahila Ramkali Devi v. Nandram, (2015) 13 SCC 132, reiterates that procedural rules serve justice and amendments should not be rejected on technical grounds absent mala fides or uncompensable injury. In the circumstances here, the Court held that the purpose of the proviso did not bar the amendment because it preceded the evidence and the opponent suffered no prejudice.
members.conclusion: The amendment application was not barred by the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 and was allowed.

rule.if: civil_suit_with_pleadings_amendment and amendment_sought_after_trial_technically_commenced and amendment_sought_before_evidence and parties_later_led_evidence_on_proposed_amendment and opponent_not_prejudiced

predicates.civil_suit_with_pleadings_amendment: A party in a civil suit sought to amend its pleadings.
predicates.amendment_sought_after_trial_technically: The party sought the amendment after the case had reached the stage at which trial had technically commenced.
predicates.amendment_sought_before_evidence: The party sought the amendment before evidence was produced in the suit.
predicates.parties_later_led_evidence_on_proposed_a: After the application, the parties presented evidence addressing the proposed amendment.
predicates.opponent_not_prejudiced: Allowing the amendment did not cause prejudice to the opposing party.

members.legal_issue: A pleading amendment sought after trial has commenced is not permitted when the applicant could have raised the matter earlier despite having relevant knowledge and seeks materially different relief.
material_facts: The plaintiff originally sought a declaration of exclusive rights over the property.
Before filing suit, the plaintiff had been told that another company was occupying the property and conducting mining operations under a lease from the government.
The government’s written statement also described the lease and its transfer to that company.
Despite this information, the plaintiff did not seek possession or damages in the original suit and proceeded through the evidence.
After the evidence had closed and arguments were underway, the plaintiff sought to add claims for possession and damages.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 CPC, as substituted by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2002 with effect from 1 July 2002, permits amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy, but an amendment after trial has commenced may be allowed only if the court is satisfied that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier. Pre-trial amendments are to be considered more liberally. The Court also noted that amendment may be refused where it changes the nature of the claim, introduces a new cause of action intended to prejudice the other party, or defeats limitation. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff did not satisfy the requirement that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence. The amendment was also sought at a late stage and added substantive relief beyond the original claim. The High Court therefore rightly set aside the order allowing the amendment, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_suit_amendment_request and trial_commenced and applicant_lacked_due_diligence and amendment_added_distinct_substantive_relief

predicates.civil_suit_amendment_request: A party in a civil suit sought to amend its pleading.
predicates.trial_commenced: The applicant sought the amendment after the evidence had closed and arguments were underway.
predicates.applicant_lacked_due_diligence: The applicant knew the relevant facts before trial but did not seek the amendment until arguments were underway.
predicates.amendment_added_distinct_substantive_rel: The proposed amendment added claims for possession and damages to a suit that had originally sought declaratory relief.

members.legal_issue: A plaint amendment sought after trial has commenced may be allowed where the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence and the amendment assists determination of the real controversy without changing the suit’s character or prejudicing the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellants brought a civil suit to set aside an earlier ex parte decree, and the record of the suit in which that decree had been made was untraceable.
After issues were framed and two official witnesses had been examined, the appellants sought to amend the plaint to add particulars of the land and related allegations.
The court considered that the missing record could have prevented the appellants from obtaining correct particulars earlier.
The proposed amendment did not change the character or nature of the suit and introduced no fresh ground.
The amendment would not prejudice the defendants, and the trial had progressed only to the examination of two official witnesses.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended, an amendment sought after commencement of trial requires the court to be satisfied that despite due diligence the party could not have raised the matter earlier. Amendments necessary to determine the real question in controversy should generally be allowed where they cause no injustice or prejudice. The Court relied on Abdul Rehman v. Mohd. Ruldu, J. Samuel v. Gattu Mahesh, and Rameshkumar Agarwal v. Rajmala Exports (P) Ltd.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the application to amend the plaint was accepted, and the trial court was directed to proceed on the amended plaint.

rule.if: civil_plaint_amendment and trial_commenced and earlier_details_unavailable_despite_diligence and amendment_preserves_suit_character and amendment_adds_no_fresh_ground and no_opponent_prejudice and trial_at_early_stage

predicates.civil_plaint_amendment: A party in a civil suit sought to amend the plaint.
predicates.trial_commenced: The court had begun the trial before the amendment application was made.
predicates.earlier_details_unavailable_despite_dili: The party could not obtain or raise the relevant matter before trial began despite diligence.
predicates.amendment_preserves_suit_character: The proposed amendment leaves the character and nature of the suit unchanged.
predicates.amendment_adds_no_fresh_ground: The proposed amendment does not introduce a fresh ground of claim.
predicates.no_opponent_prejudice: The proposed amendment would not prejudice the opposing party.
predicates.trial_at_early_stage: Only a limited portion of the trial had taken place when amendment was sought.
