members.legal_issue: A request to amend pleadings after trial has commenced is barred unless the party establishes that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier.
material_facts: The application to amend the written statement was filed after issues had been framed and the parties had submitted affidavits of evidence, with cross-examination dates fixed.
The trial court found that the matters sought to be added were within the applicants’ knowledge, or could have been known to them, before the written statement was filed.
The applicants did not establish that due diligence had prevented them from raising those matters before trial commenced.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended by the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, 2002, bars amendment after commencement of trial unless the court concludes that, despite due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter earlier. The proviso restricts the court’s jurisdiction. The Court relied on Ajendraprasadji N. Pandey v. Swami Keshavprakeshdasji N. and Salem Advocate Bar Assn. v. Union of India, and distinguished Baldev Singh v. Manohar Singh, where the parties had yet to file their documents.
members.conclusion: The mandatory condition in the proviso to Order VI Rule 17 was not satisfied, so the amendment could not be allowed; the High Court’s order allowing it was set aside.

predicates.civil_suit_pleading_amendment: A party in a civil suit applied to amend its pleadings.
predicates.trial_commenced: The suit had reached the stage at which trial had commenced.
predicates.party_failed_to_show_due_diligence_preve: The party did not establish that, despite due diligence, it could not have raised the proposed matter before trial commenced.

members.legal_issue: A pleading amendment sought after trial has concluded may be allowed only when the applicant establishes that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised before trial.
material_facts: The claimants brought a suit for specific performance, but their original plaint omitted an averment that they had performed or had always been ready and willing to perform their essential contractual obligations.
The parties completed their evidence and arguments, and the matter was reserved for judgment before the claimants applied to amend the plaint.
The claimants attributed the omission to a typing mistake, although the omitted averment was substantive and could have been noticed and corrected when the plaint was prepared, signed, and verified.

The claimants relied on references to readiness and willingness in a prior legal notice and in their evidence, but the court held that those matters did not satisfy the requirements for allowing the amendment.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 CPC permits amendment of pleadings, but its proviso bars an amendment after commencement of trial unless the court is satisfied that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised before trial. Due diligence requires reasonable investigation and cannot be dispensed with. A substantive omission that could have been found by reviewing the pleading is not a typographical error. In a specific-performance suit, Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act requires the claimant to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform; Explanation (ii) requires the relevant averment, and Form 47 in Appendix A to the CPC prescribes it. The amendment rule aims to prevent late amendments, surprise, and delay. The Court referred to Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha, Ajendraprasadji N. Pandey v. Swami Keshavprakeshdasji N., Chander Kanta Bansal v. Rajinder Singh Anand, Rajkumar Guraward v. S.K. Sarwagi and Company Private Limited, Vidyabai v. Padmalatha, and Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha.
members.conclusion: The amendment should not have been allowed. The explanation of a typing mistake did not establish due diligence, so the High Court’s order allowing the amendment was set aside.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and amendment_sought_after_trial and essential_readiness_plea_omitted and omission_preventable_by_ordinary_review and typing_mistake_explanation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.amendment_sought_after_trial: The claimant sought to amend the pleading after the trial and arguments had concluded and the matter had been reserved for decision.
predicates.essential_readiness_plea_omitted: The original pleading did not state that the claimant had performed or had always been ready and willing to perform the claimant’s essential contractual obligations.
predicates.omission_preventable_by_ordinary_review: The omitted substantive averment could have been noticed and included by reviewing the pleading before it was filed.
predicates.typing_mistake_explanation: The claimant attributed the omission to a typing mistake.

members.legal_issue: A stranger to a possession decree who claims an independent interest in the property and resists execution before being dispossessed may have that claim adjudicated before delivery of possession.
material_facts: A possession decree had been made against a judgment-debtor, and execution was commenced to deliver the property to the decree-holder.
A person who was not a party to the decree claimed an independent interest in the property and resisted the bailiff’s attempt to execute the warrant.
Before actual delivery of possession, the objector asked the executing court to decide his objections, but the court rejected the request solely because he had not yet been dispossessed.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rules 97, 98, 99 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure establish procedures for adjudicating resistance before dispossession and claims for restoration after dispossession. Rule 97 applies when execution is resisted; Rule 99 applies when a person other than the judgment-debtor has already been dispossessed. The executing court must adjudicate relevant questions of right, title or interest, and refusing to hear a timely objector would also offend natural justice. The Court relied on Bhanwar Lal v. Satyanarain and Another, which recognized that a person resisting execution may raise an independent claim under Rule 97.
members.conclusion: The objector was entitled to have his claim adjudicated before delivery of possession; he was not required to wait until dispossession and then apply for restoration.

rule.if: possession_decree_execution and stranger_claims_independent_interest and stranger_resists_execution and stranger_seeks_adjudication_before_dispossession

predicates.possession_decree_execution: A decree-holder is seeking to obtain possession of immovable property through execution of a possession decree.
predicates.stranger_claims_independent_interest: A person who is not bound by the decree claims an interest in the property independent of the judgment-debtor.
predicates.stranger_resists_execution: That person resists or obstructs the attempt to execute the possession decree.
predicates.stranger_seeks_adjudication_before_dispo: That person asks the executing court to decide the claim before being dispossessed.
predicates.independent_claim_adjudicated_before_del: The executing court decides the stranger’s claim before delivering possession under the decree.

members.legal_issue: A person in possession who claims an independent right in immovable property may resist an attempted dispossession in execution, and the executing court must adjudicate the objection rather than dismiss it as non-maintainable.
material_facts: The objectors claimed that they had acquired the land from pattadars and that their rights arose before the partition suit and its decree.
They claimed to be in possession and to have built houses on the land, and resisted delivery of possession under the decree to its assignees.
The lower courts dismissed their objections as non-maintainable without deciding their claims, reasoning that they claimed through persons who were parties to the suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 21 Rules 97 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the executing court must determine questions relevant to an objection to execution, including questions of right, title or interest, rather than requiring a separate suit. A person claiming an independent right may object before being dispossessed; Rule 99 concerns an application after dispossession. The Court relied on Silverline Forum Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajiv Trust, (1998) 3 SCC 723; Shreenath v. Rajesh, (1998) 4 SCC 543; and Anwarbi v. Pramod D.A. Joshi, (2000) 10 SCC 405. It also referred to Order 21 Rules 35, 36, 99 and 103, and to Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act in discussing transferees pendente lite.
members.conclusion: The dismissal as non-maintainable was unsustainable. The orders were set aside and the objections were remitted for fresh consideration; the Court did not decide the objectors’ title on the merits.

rule.if: execution_for_possession and objector_in_possession and claims_independent_property_right and resists_attempted_dispossession

predicates.execution_for_possession: The proceeding seeks delivery of possession of immovable property under a decree.
predicates.objector_in_possession: A person other than the judgment-debtor claims to be in possession of the property.
predicates.claims_independent_property_right: The objector asserts a right in the property independent of the judgment-debtor’s right under the decree.
predicates.resists_attempted_dispossession: The objector opposes an attempt to dispossess them in execution of the decree.
predicates.executing_court_must_adjudicate_objectio: The executing court determines the objection and relevant questions of right, title or interest instead of dismissing it as non-maintainable.

members.legal_issue: An executing court must adjudicate an independent claim to immovable property raised by a person resisting delivery of possession, and cannot reject that claim solely because related proceedings were previously decided where those proceedings do not bind the claimant.
material_facts: The appellant resisted execution, asserting an independent right and possession in land he claimed was distinct from the properties covered by the possession decree.
The appellant was not a party to the possession suit or appeal, and the earlier writ proceedings recorded no adverse finding or relief against his father.
The executing court rejected the objection as already decided in earlier proceedings without adjudicating the appellant’s independent claim.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rules 97, 98, 100, 101, 103 and 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure require the executing court to determine relevant questions of right, title or interest raised in proceedings resisting or complaining of dispossession. The determination has the force of a decree and is appealable; a separate suit is not the prescribed means of resolving the claim. The 1976 amendment removed the former separate-suit remedy under Order 21 Rule 103 of the 1908 Code. The procedure is intended to provide effective adjudication and shorten execution litigation. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The executing court was required to adjudicate the independent claim under the execution procedure. The earlier proceedings did not justify refusing that adjudication, and the matter was remitted to the executing court.

rule.if: execution_obstruction_proceeding and independent_property_claim and claimant_in_possession and no_binding_adverse_determination

predicates.execution_obstruction_proceeding: A person in possession applies during execution of a possession decree to resist delivery of immovable property.
predicates.independent_property_claim: The person claims a right, title, or interest in the disputed property independently of the judgment-debtor.
predicates.claimant_in_possession: The person asserting the independent claim is in possession of the disputed property.
predicates.no_binding_adverse_determination: Earlier proceedings neither bound the claimant through an adverse determination nor decided the claimant’s asserted right against them.

members.legal_issue: A third party claiming an independent right to possession may be heard before an order is made on a decree-holder’s application concerning obstruction to delivery of possession.
material_facts: A decree-holder sought delivery of property under an execution proceeding and described obstruction by the appellant.
The appellant claimed an independent right to the property and asserted that it was in possession.
The appellant had asked to be heard before an order was passed on the decree-holder’s request.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 97 applies where a decree-holder faces resistance or obstruction by any person in possession, including a person not bound by the decree. Shreemath and Anr. v. Rajesh and Ors., 1998 (4) SCC 543, supports the inclusion of such persons and the resolution of their claims at the execution stage.
members.conclusion: The appellant was entitled to be heard before the executing court passed an order on the decree-holder’s application.

predicates.execution_of_possession_decree: A decree-holder sought to execute a decree requiring delivery of immovable property.
predicates.decree_holder_alleges_obstruction: The decree-holder told the executing court that a person was obstructing delivery of the property.
predicates.third_party_claims_independent_possessio: A person other than the judgment debtor claimed an independent right to the property and asserted possession of it.

members.legal_issue: A third party resisting delivery of possession need not wait to be dispossessed before seeking adjudication of the obstruction in the execution proceeding.
material_facts: The appellant claimed an independent right to the property and asserted that it remained in possession.
The decree-holder sought delivery of possession despite the asserted obstruction.
The executing court treated an application after dispossession as the appellant’s only remedy.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 97 provides for adjudication when a decree-holder faces resistance or obstruction, while Rule 99 provides a remedy to a person other than the judgment debtor who has been dispossessed. Brahmdeo Chaudhary v. Rishikesh Prasad Jaiswal and Anr., 1997 (3) SCC 694, holds that an objector should not be required to surrender possession first and complain of dispossession later under Rule 99.
members.conclusion: The appellant was not required to wait for dispossession and then seek relief; the obstruction could be adjudicated before dispossession.

predicates.execution_of_possession_decree: A decree-holder sought to execute a decree requiring delivery of immovable property.
predicates.third_party_claims_independent_possessio: A person other than the judgment debtor claimed an independent right to the property and asserted possession of it.
predicates.delivery_is_being_resisted: The third party was resisting or obstructing delivery of the property before being dispossessed.

members.legal_issue: Execution courts must comprehensively determine a third party’s objection concerning an independent claim to property rather than reject it without proper consideration.
material_facts: The objector brought an objection under Order XXI Rule 58 CPC, claiming an independent interest in property sought to be attached for a money decree.
The objection raised questions about the objector’s transaction, possession, and the judgment debtor’s lack of title to the property.
The executing court rejected the objection by relying on the proposition that a power of attorney did not confer ownership, without adequately determining the issues raised.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rules 58 and 97 to 104 CPC require questions arising in execution to be determined in the execution proceedings rather than by a separate suit. The Court relied on Brahmdeo Chaudhary v. Rishikesh Prasad Jaiswal, Shreenath v. Rajesh, and Tanzeem-e-sufia v. Bibi Haliman, and noted that Rule 103 gives specified orders the force and appealability of a decree.
members.conclusion: The objection required determination on its merits; the lower courts’ cursory rejection was erroneous, and the objection was allowed without setting aside the underlying decree.

predicates.execution_objection_case: The proceeding concerns an objection raised during execution of a decree.
predicates.objection_raises_independent_property_cl: The objector asserts an interest in the property distinct from the judgment debtor’s interest.
predicates.objection_not_comprehensively_examined: The execution court has not adequately assessed the material facts and evidence bearing on the objection.

members.legal_issue: A stranger to a decree who resists delivery of property may have an independent claim adjudicated in execution proceedings before being dispossessed.
material_facts: The claimants were not parties to the decree for possession.
They obstructed delivery of the property and applied in the execution proceedings before being dispossessed.
They sought to establish an independent right to remain in possession.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rules 97, 101 and 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provide for adjudication of resistance to possession, including an independent claim by a stranger to the decree, and treat the resulting order as a decree. Brahmdeo Chaudhary v Rishikesh Prasad Jaiswal, Shreenath v Rajesh and Har Vilas v Mahendra Nath establish that a stranger may seek adjudication before actual delivery of possession and is not confined to the post-dispossession remedy.
members.conclusion: The claimants could have their independent claim adjudicated in the execution proceedings before dispossession; the remedy was not limited to an application after dispossession.

predicates.execution_obstruction_proceeding: A decree holder seeks delivery of immovable property through execution proceedings.
predicates.claimant_is_stranger_to_decree: The person asserting a right to the property was not a party to the decree.
predicates.claimant_resists_delivery_before_disposs: The person objects to delivery of the property before being dispossessed.

members.legal_issue: A nonparty in possession who claims an independent right in property may seek adjudication of an objection to delivery of possession in the execution proceeding before being dispossessed.
material_facts: A decree directed delivery of vacant possession of mortgaged property, but the objectors were not parties to the suit that produced the decree.
The objectors claimed that they had occupied the shop as tenants since before the mortgage and asserted rights independent of the judgment debtor.
When delivery of vacant possession was sought, the objectors resisted and applied for their objections to be adjudicated under the execution procedure.
The executing court and the High Court rejected the objections without deciding their merits, relying on a Full Bench ruling that a third party could seek adjudication only after dispossession.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 21, Rules 97(1), 97(2) and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the expression “any person” includes a nonparty claiming an independent right, including a tenant, who resists delivery of possession. The executing court must adjudicate the claim in the execution proceeding; the objector need not await dispossession. Rule 35 concerns removal of persons bound by the decree, while Rule 36 provides for symbolic delivery where property is occupied by a person not bound to relinquish occupancy. The corresponding pre-amendment provisions also permitted adjudication of such a claim under Rules 97 and 99. The Court relied on Noorduddin v. Dr. K.L. Anand and Brahmdeo Chaudhary v. Rishikesh Prasad Jaiswal, and held that the contrary interpretation in Smt. Usha Jain v. Manmohan Bajaj was not good law.
members.conclusion: The Court held that a person in possession claiming an independent right may object before dispossession and have the claim adjudicated by the executing court. It quashed the lower-court orders and directed the executing court to consider and decide the objections after hearing the parties.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and nonparty_in_possession and claims_independent_right and resists_delivery and seeks_execution_adjudication

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder is seeking delivery of immovable property through an execution proceeding.
predicates.nonparty_in_possession: A person who was not a party to the decree is in possession of the property.
predicates.claims_independent_right: The person in possession claims a right to the property independent of the judgment debtor.
predicates.resists_delivery: The person in possession resists or obstructs delivery of the property to the decree-holder.
predicates.seeks_execution_adjudication: The person in possession asks the executing court to adjudicate the objection.

members.legal_issue: A person resisting delivery of immovable property in execution may have the resistance adjudicated even if that person is not bound by the decree or asserts an independent right.
material_facts: A final decree for possession was being executed.
A person who was not a judgment-debtor obstructed delivery of possession.
The obstruction was not shown to arise from a right derived from the judgment-debtor.
members.legal_principle: Order 21, Rule 35(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure authorizes steps to deliver possession where the person in possession is bound by the decree. Order 21, Rule 97(1) permits the decree-holder to complain of resistance by any person, and Rule 97(2), read with Rules 98 to 103, provides for adjudication. The court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The summary delivery procedure under Order 21, Rule 35(3) applies only where the person in possession is bound by the decree. Under Order 21, Rule 97, the executing court may enquire into resistance by any person, including one asserting a right independent of the judgment-debtor.

predicates.execution_of_possession_decree: A decree-holder is seeking delivery of immovable property under a possession decree.
predicates.obstruction_by_person: A person resists or obstructs delivery of the property.
predicates.obstructor_not_bound_by_decree: The person resisting delivery is not bound by the possession decree.

members.legal_issue: A mandatory compensation formula for acquired property that caps compensation by reference to a remote requisition-date value, without a rational connection to the property's value when acquired, violates the pre-amendment constitutional guarantee of a just equivalent.
material_facts: The land had been requisitioned years before it was acquired, and its acquisition triggered the right to compensation.
The statute required the arbitrator to award the lesser of the property's open-market price on the acquisition date and twice its open-market price on the requisition date.
The arbitrator had no discretion to use the acquisition-date valuation if the requisition-date formula produced a lower amount.
No circumstances or rational basis were shown for using the requisition date to determine the value payable on acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) before the Fourth Amendment, compensation for compulsory acquisition had to be a just equivalent of the property taken. Legislative principles for determining compensation were reviewable to determine whether they accounted for the property's true value. Fixing value at an anterior date with no relevant connection to acquisition was arbitrary. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, and N. B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector; it distinguished East Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. v. State of Madras because the person to be compensated there could choose among valuation methods. It also held that the phrase “have regard to,” read in context with the mandatory valuation provisions, did not give the arbitrator discretion to disregard the prescribed formula, consistent with Ryots of Garabandho v. Zamindar of Parlakimedi.
members.conclusion: The impugned compensation formula was arbitrary and violated Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it stood before the Fourth Amendment; the challenged provision was void.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: The proceeding challenges the legal basis for determining compensation for property compulsorily acquired.
predicates.mandatory_lower_of_valuation_methods: The decision-maker was required to award the lower amount produced by two prescribed valuation methods and could not select the other method as fairer.
predicates.requisition_date_unrelated_to_acquisitio: The prescribed requisition-date valuation had no demonstrated rational connection to the property's value when it was acquired.

members.legal_issue: A compulsory-acquisition law that fixes compensation by reference to an unrelated earlier valuation date, without relevant circumstances justifying that date, does not provide compensation as required by the applicable legislative limitation.
material_facts: Land was compulsorily acquired for a housing scheme after a notification under the general acquisition law.

The amending law required compensation to be based on the land's value on a fixed date earlier than the acquisition notification, whichever valuation was lower, and removed the additional amount otherwise payable for compulsory acquisition.
The earlier date had no relevant connection to the acquisition or to circumstances requiring the value to be assessed at that time.
members.legal_principle: The court applied section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and held that its compensation requirement was pari materia with Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it stood before amendment. Following State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, compensation must be a just equivalent of the property taken; whether the stated principles account for relevant elements of value is justiciable. A fixed anterior valuation date without relevant justification is arbitrary. The rule does not differ merely because the law is temporary rather than permanent.
members.conclusion: The amending law did not provide compensation that was the just equivalent of what the owner was deprived of and was void for contravening the legislative limitation on compulsory acquisition.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: The case challenges a law governing compensation for compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.compensation_uses_unrelated_earlier_valu: The law bases compensation on a valuation date earlier than the acquisition notification, without tying that date to the acquisition process.
predicates.no_relevant_reason_for_earlier_date: No relevant circumstance requires the property's value to be assessed on the earlier date.

members.legal_issue: A law that fixes compensation for compulsory acquisition by reference to a substantially earlier market value, without establishing that the amount remains a just equivalent at acquisition, violates the applicable property guarantee.
material_facts: The acquisition law fixed compensation by reference to the land’s market value on a date many years before acquisition notifications were issued.
The law denied owners increases in land value between that fixed date and the acquisition notifications.

The State presented no material showing that the earlier value gave owners a just monetary equivalent when their interests were acquired or that later appreciation was attributable to a proposed acquisition scheme.
The law took effect before the later constitutional amendment, which was not retrospective.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, compensation had to be a just equivalent of the property taken. State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee held that an arbitrary ceiling based on an anterior value, without reference to value at acquisition, was not due compensation. Although a rise in value attributable to a known acquisition scheme may be disregarded, a principle denying all increments from a fixed date to the acquisition notification is prima facie insufficient; the State must show that the earlier valuation nevertheless provides a just equivalent. The Court also relied on Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India and State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose concerning the constitutional protection against compulsory deprivation of property.
members.conclusion: The provision fixing compensation by reference to the earlier market value was invalid under the property guarantee applicable when the law took effect.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: An owner challenges the compensation basis in a law authorising compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.earlier_property_guarantee_applies: The acquisition law took effect before a later constitutional change that was not made retrospective.
predicates.compensation_uses_substantially_earlier_: The law fixes compensation by reference to market value on a date substantially before the acquisition notification and denies later increases in value.
predicates.no_evidence_earlier_value_is_just_equiva: The State provides no evidence that the earlier valuation gives the owner a just monetary equivalent at acquisition or that later appreciation resulted from a known acquisition scheme.

members.legal_issue: A law that excludes the value of acquired non-agricultural improvements from compensation denies just compensation under the applicable property guarantee.
material_facts: The acquisition included the owner’s interest in the land and things attached to it, including buildings and other structures.
The compensation law excluded the value of non-agricultural improvements made after its specified benchmark date.
The owner could be deprived of those improvements without receiving their value, whether or not the owner could remove them.
The law took effect before the later constitutional amendment, which was not retrospective.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, required just indemnification for compulsory acquisition. Section 3(a) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, defined land to include benefits arising from land and things attached to the earth; acquisition therefore included the owner’s interest in buildings and other structures. Excluding their value denied compensation for part of the property taken. The Court relied on the just-equivalent principle in State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee and the constitutional property principles discussed in Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India and State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose.
members.conclusion: The provision excluding the value of non-agricultural improvements from compensation was invalid under the property guarantee applicable when the law took effect.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: An owner challenges the compensation basis in a law authorising compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.earlier_property_guarantee_applies: The acquisition law took effect before a later constitutional change that was not made retrospective.
predicates.non_agricultural_improvements_are_acquir: The acquisition takes the owner’s non-agricultural improvements along with the land.
predicates.compensation_excludes_their_value: The compensation calculation omits the value of those improvements, leaving the owner without payment for them.

members.legal_issue: A mandatory ceiling based on the value of property at requisition, rather than its value at acquisition, fails to provide a just equivalent when no relevant circumstance justifies using the earlier value.
material_facts: The land was requisitioned many years before it was acquired.
The compensation formula required comparison of the property's open-market value at acquisition with twice its open-market value at requisition and payment of whichever figure was lower.
No circumstance was shown that connected the requisition date with the property's true value at acquisition.
The Court noted the substantial rise in land values after the war.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, compensation had to be a just equivalent of the property taken, and whether the prescribed principles achieved that result was justiciable. A valuation fixed at an anterior date without a relevant basis could deny the owner later increments in value. The Court relied on The State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, and N. B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector.
members.conclusion: The impugned compensation formula was arbitrary and violated the constitutional requirement that compensation be a just equivalent of the property acquired.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: The proceeding challenges the basis used to determine compensation for acquired property.
predicates.requisition_precedes_acquisition: The property was requisitioned before it was acquired.
predicates.compensation_capped_by_requisition_date_: The compensation calculation limits the acquisition-date value by reference to the property's value when it was requisitioned.
predicates.no_relevant_basis_for_earlier_valuation: No relevant circumstance connects the earlier valuation date to the property's true value when acquired.

members.legal_issue: A compensation ceiling based on a historical market value that may bear no relation to the value when property is acquired is arbitrary and does not satisfy the constitutional compensation requirement.
material_facts: The challenged law was permanent and allowed land to be acquired many years after its enactment.
It capped compensation at the land’s market value on a fixed historical date, regardless of the value when acquisition occurred.
The value of land could increase substantially between the historical date and acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) requires compensation to be a just equivalent of the property taken. Although an earlier valuation date may be permissible in circumstances such as a known acquisition scheme causing a sharp anticipatory rise in prices, fixing a ceiling at a date that may have no relation to value at acquisition is arbitrary and fails to meet that requirement. The principles must account for the property’s true value and are subject to judicial review.
members.conclusion: The provision capping compensation at the historical market value was unconstitutional and void.

predicates.constitutional_property_acquisition_chal: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.permanent_acquisition_law: The law remains in force and permits acquisitions at times substantially later than its enactment.
predicates.compensation_ceiling_uses_historical_val: The law caps compensation by reference to a past valuation that may bear no relation to the property's value when it is acquired.

members.legal_issue: A validating law that preserves acquisitions based on an exhausted notification, without reviving that notification or providing a legislative basis for the later acquisitions, impermissibly fixes compensation by reference to an anterior valuation date.
material_facts: A first declaration had been made for part of the land covered by an earlier notification, after which the notification was exhausted under the prior Supreme Court ruling.

The validating law purported to preserve later acquisitions and declarations based on that notification but did not retrospectively amend the relevant provisions or otherwise revive the exhausted notification.

The later acquisitions could therefore proceed without a fresh notification, and compensation would continue to be based on the value at the date of the exhausted notification despite intervening appreciation in land values.
members.legal_principle: In the dissent's view, the constitutional requirement of compensation continued to require a just equivalent, even though adequacy itself was not reviewable. A law that in substance fixes compensation by reference to a date unconnected to the later acquisition, while omitting a legislative provision to revive the exhausted notification, fails that requirement. The dissent relied on State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector, and Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India.
members.conclusion: The dissenting judges would have held the validating provision invalid because it both failed to revive the exhausted notification and derogated from the constitutional compensation guarantee.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validation_o: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law validating land acquisitions.
predicates.earlier_notification_was_exhausted_after: A prior declaration acquired part of the land and, under the governing interpretation, exhausted the notification for the remaining land.
predicates.validation_does_not_legislatively_revive: The validating law preserves later actions without providing a legislative basis that revives the exhausted notification.
predicates.later_acquisitions_use_the_old_valuation: Later acquisitions rely on the valuation date of the exhausted notification despite appreciation in the property's value before those acquisitions.

members.legal_issue: A pre-amendment acquisition law violates the compensation requirement when its prescribed compensation does not ensure a just equivalent of the property taken.
material_facts: The acquisition law predated the constitutional amendment that changed Article 31(2), so its validity was judged under Article 31(2) as it then stood.
For land, the law capped compensation at a fixed multiple of annual land revenue, although land values had increased substantially since revenue assessments were made.
For buildings or structures, the law based compensation on the sale proceeds of their materials plus an additional percentage, rather than their value as buildings or structures at acquisition.
The State did not show that these measures bore a relation to market value or ensured a just equivalent of the property taken.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) as it stood before the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, the principles for determining compensation had to ensure a just equivalent of the property taken. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, [1954] SCR 558, and State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, [1964] 6 SCR 936.
members.conclusion: The law did not ensure payment of a just equivalent of the property appropriated and violated Article 31(2) as it stood before the Fourth Amendment.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_pre_amendment_acquisition_law and compensation_capped_by_old_revenue_assessment and building_payment_based_on_materials and not state_shows_just_equivalent

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_pre_amendmen: A party challenged an acquisition law enacted before a constitutional change to the applicable compensation requirement.
predicates.compensation_capped_by_old_revenue_asses: The law capped land compensation by reference to revenue assessments that did not reflect the land's value at acquisition.
predicates.building_payment_based_on_materials: The law measured compensation for a building or structure by the value of its materials rather than its value as a building or structure.
predicates.state_shows_just_equivalent: The State demonstrated that the statutory compensation measures ensured a just equivalent of the property taken.

members.legal_issue: A law providing for deprivation of property is invalid when it neither fixes compensation nor specifies principles and a method sufficient to determine or give compensation.
material_facts: The statute allowed the government to transfer other property said to be nearly of the same value, but did not specify when value was to be assessed.
Alternatively, the statute allowed cash to be paid having regard to the property's value, without requiring payment of the full value or specifying how the amount was to be determined.
After substitute property or cash was granted, the rightful owner's title to the original property was extinguished.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) required a law to provide for compensation by fixing its amount or specifying the principles on which, and the manner in which, it was to be determined or given. A reference to value without identifying the relevant time for valuation, or permitting cash merely having regard to value without requiring an equivalent amount, did not satisfy that requirement.
members.conclusion: The statute failed to provide compensation or principles for determining it as required by Article 31(2), and was invalid.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law that permits property to be taken or withheld from its owner.
predicates.law_extinguishes_owner_title: The law provides that the owner's title to the original property is extinguished after the government grants a substitute or payment.
predicates.compensation_amount_or_determination_met: The law does not fix compensation or provide sufficiently definite principles and a method for determining or giving it.

members.legal_issue: An alibi is not established when the accused provides no evidence supporting the claim that they were elsewhere at the time of the offence.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that he was away preparing his thesis and was not present in the village on the night of the offence.
He produced no evidence that he was staying elsewhere, and there was no evidence about the distance between his educational institution and the village.
The Supreme Court held that the alibi plea was not proved.
members.legal_principle: A bare assertion of absence from the scene does not establish an alibi; the court assessed the claim against the absence of supporting evidence and found it unproved.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s alibi plea was rejected as unproved.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the accused’s presence at the relevant place and time is in issue.
predicates.accused_claims_presence_elsewhere: The accused asserts that they were somewhere other than the scene when the offence occurred.
predicates.no_evidence_supports_claimed_absence: The accused provides no evidence supporting the assertion of presence elsewhere.

members.legal_issue: A plea of alibi is not established when its supporting evidence does not reliably place the accused elsewhere at the time of the occurrence and credible eyewitnesses place the accused at the scene.
material_facts: The accused claimed he was training at an athletic venue several kilometres from the scene when the occurrence took place.
His supporting witness admitted that the usual training hours ended well before the occurrence and that he had not earlier reported the accused’s claimed presence there.
The injured eyewitnesses and the informant placed the accused at the scene.
members.legal_principle: The court assesses the evidence offered for an alibi against the timing and circumstances of the occurrence and the prosecution evidence placing the accused at the scene; the Court relied on the trial court’s assessment of the defence evidence and the eyewitness testimony.
members.conclusion: The plea of alibi was rightly rejected.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and alibi_claimed and alibi_evidence_does_not_cover_occurrence_time and credible_witnesses_place_accused_at_scene

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.alibi_claimed: The accused claims to have been elsewhere when the alleged offence occurred.
predicates.alibi_evidence_does_not_cover_occurrence: The evidence supporting the claim does not reliably place the accused elsewhere at the time of the occurrence.
predicates.credible_witnesses_place_accused_at_scen: Credible witnesses place the accused at the scene of the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: Alibi evidence that is vague, unreliable or unsupported by the best-informed witness does not establish that the accused was elsewhere when the offence occurred.
material_facts: One appellant claimed to have been away threshing a relative's crop, supported by two witnesses whose accounts were found inherently flimsy and unreliable.
Those witnesses had difficulty recalling dates, had limited connection with the relevant location and had not reported the claimed presence to the investigating officer.
The appellant did not call his brother, who was said to have informed him of the accusation and was the best-informed witness about his whereabouts.
Another appellant claimed to have been at a market, but his supporting witness could not reliably recall attendance on other dates and had no particular reason to remember the date in question.
The market was close enough to the village that travel from the scene to the market within a short time was possible.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the credibility and reliability of the supporting evidence and whether it established even a reasonable probability that the accused was elsewhere. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for its assessment.
members.conclusion: The Court held that neither appellant had established the claimed alibi, and the alibi evidence did not warrant disturbing the convictions.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.alibi_claim: The accused claims to have been somewhere other than the scene when the offence occurred.
predicates.alibi_support_is_unreliable: The evidence offered to support the claim is vague, contradicted, unsupported by an important available witness, or otherwise not dependable.

members.legal_issue: A rejected alibi is not established merely because other accused persons’ alibis were accepted; the alibi evidence must create reasonable doubt about the prosecution evidence of presence.
material_facts: The appellant’s alibi was based on a certificate stating that he served as a guard during the period that included the date of the offence.

The courts found no material showing that he was at the school throughout the relevant day, no appointment letter was produced, the certificate’s description of a one-week appointment as regular was implausible, and the attendance-register signatures were not accepted.
The trial court and High Court gave cogent reasons for rejecting this appellant’s alibi, although they accepted the pleas of two other accused persons.
members.legal_principle: Where the accused’s presence is satisfactorily established, the court need not accept an alibi unless the supporting evidence is of such quality as to create reasonable doubt about the prosecution case. Acceptance of another accused’s alibi does not itself establish the alibi of a different accused. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld rejection of the appellant’s alibi; the acceptance of other accused persons’ pleas did not require acceptance of his plea.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_establishes_accused: The prosecution evidence satisfactorily places the accused at the scene or otherwise establishes the accused’s presence when the offence occurred.
predicates.alibi_evidence_does_not_create_reasonabl: The evidence offered for the alibi is not sufficient to create reasonable doubt about the prosecution evidence of presence.

members.legal_issue: An alibi is not established by an approximate account of the alleged occurrence when the accused does not prove absence so as to exclude the possibility of presence.
material_facts: The defence relied on the public servant’s alleged election duty on two dates as an alibi for an earlier demand.
The complaint did not specify the exact date of that earlier demand, and the evidence described a further visit and demand later.
The public servant did not claim or prove absence on the later visit and did not establish beyond doubt that he was absent when the demand was made.
members.legal_principle: A plea of alibi must be proved with certainty so as to completely exclude the possibility of the accused’s presence at the place of occurrence. The Court relied on Jitendra Kumar v. State of Haryana.
members.conclusion: The alibi was not established, and the possibility that the public servant was present could not be rejected on that basis.

predicates.criminal_corruption_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution alleging corruption.
predicates.alibi_depends_on_an_approximate_occurren: The accused relies on absence at an approximate date rather than establishing the precise time of the alleged occurrence.
predicates.accused_does_not_exclude_possibility_of_: The accused fails to prove absence so as to exclude the possibility of being present when the alleged conduct occurred.

members.legal_issue: An alibi is not established merely by evidence that an accused’s children studied in another locality when that evidence does not show that the accused was there at the time of the offence.
material_facts: Two accused relied on evidence that their children attended a college in another locality and asserted that they lived there.
The witnesses did not establish that the accused themselves were residing there at the time of the occurrence.
No other evidence was led to establish their absence from the scene.
members.legal_principle: An alibi must be established on the evidence; proof that an accused’s children studied elsewhere does not, without evidence of the accused’s own presence there, establish the accused’s absence from the scene. The Court assessed the evidence on the stated standard of preponderance of probability and cited no earlier case for this application.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish the alibis, and the convictions were not disturbed on that ground.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and alibi_claimed and evidence_shows_children_studied_elsewhere and no_evidence_places_accused_elsewhere_at_offence_time

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction and relied on an alibi.
predicates.alibi_claimed: The accused asserted that they were elsewhere when the offence occurred.
predicates.evidence_shows_children_studied_elsewher: Evidence showed that the accused’s children studied in another locality.
predicates.no_evidence_places_accused_elsewhere_at_: The evidence did not establish that the accused themselves were elsewhere when the offence occurred.

members.legal_issue: An alibi is not established by evidence that is inconsistent, introduced as an apparent afterthought, or otherwise too weak to show that the accused could not have been at the scene.
material_facts: Two accused claimed they were at a hospital at the time of the occurrence.
The witness supporting that account gave shifting versions, had not mentioned the asserted observation in earlier statements or reports, and was found to be supporting the defence.
A defence witness’s account of learning about the occurrence from another person was hearsay, and the account was not reflected in the accused persons’ own statements.
The hospital was close enough to the village that a person could travel between them within the time available.
members.legal_principle: An alibi must be supported by credible evidence showing that the accused was elsewhere at the relevant time; unreliable or belated testimony and evidence of presence at a nearby location do not establish that the accused could not have participated.
members.conclusion: The accused who pleaded alibi failed to substantiate it.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which an accused claims to have been elsewhere during the offence.
predicates.alibi_evidence_inconsistent_or_belated: The evidence offered for the alibi is inconsistent, was not disclosed when it would naturally have been mentioned, or otherwise lacks reliability.
predicates.claimed_location_reachable_in_available_: The distance and available time do not rule out the accused travelling from the claimed location to the scene.

members.legal_issue: An accused’s alibi does not create a basis to disturb a conviction when the accused could have reached the scene and other evidence establishes participation.
material_facts: The accused relied on their employment locations or postings to claim they were elsewhere when the crimes occurred.
The Court found that the accused could have reached the scene in time, including because some workplaces were close to the scene and travel from another location remained possible.
The alibi pleas were not raised before the committing Magistrate.
Other evidence, including eyewitness testimony, a recovered cap, and an accused’s conduct after arrest, supported participation by the accused.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the alibi claims against the evidence about the accused’s locations, their ability to reach the scene, and the evidence of participation. It cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The alibi arguments did not undermine the convictions.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_convictions and accused_raises_alibi and (accused_could_reach_scene or independent_evidence_shows_participation)

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_convictions: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging convictions.
predicates.accused_raises_alibi: An accused claims to have been elsewhere when the crime occurred.
predicates.accused_could_reach_scene: The accused’s location and available travel time permitted the accused to reach the scene in time.
predicates.independent_evidence_shows_participation: Evidence apart from the alibi claim supports the accused’s participation in the crime.

members.legal_issue: An accused who relies on an alibi must establish that the accused could not have been present at the occurrence, and a rejection of the alibi is not disturbed on special-leave appeal absent a cogent ground to re-examine the evidence.
material_facts: The accused relied on evidence of medical examinations and an operation, but the evidence did not specify their timing sufficiently to establish that he could not have been at the scene.
A witness who testified that the accused had rented a room could not say whether he had seen the accused around the time of the occurrence.
The trial court rejected the alibi and the High Court upheld that finding; the Supreme Court found no infirmity warranting re-examination.
members.legal_principle: The burden of establishing an alibi rests on the accused. On a special-leave appeal, the Court will not re-examine the evidence underlying concurrent findings where no cogent ground or infirmity justifies interference. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The accused did not discharge the burden of establishing the alibi, and there was no cogent ground to interfere with the concurrent rejection of it.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_conviction and alibi_claimed and defence_evidence_did_not_exclude_presence and lower_courts_rejected_alibi

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal by special leave from a criminal conviction.
predicates.alibi_claimed: The accused asserted that the accused was elsewhere and could not have been present at the occurrence.
predicates.defence_evidence_did_not_exclude_presenc: The defence evidence did not establish that the accused could not have been present at the occurrence.
predicates.lower_courts_rejected_alibi: The lower courts rejected the accused's alibi.

members.legal_issue: Possession of acquired land may be established through official records and the circumstances of a large public acquisition, resulting in vesting even without proof of the owner’s personal physical dispossession.
material_facts: The land was acquired as part of a large tract for a planned development scheme, and an award was made.
The acquisition officer referred the dispute over compensation and deposited the compensation in court.
The acquisition officer’s record showed delivery of possession of the acquired land to the public housing body.
The scheme was developed on the acquired tract, with many houses constructed and the disputed land set apart for a public park.
The claimant had acknowledged the public body’s title in a letter requesting an alternative site, and there was no evidence that he resisted the taking of possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 11, 16 and 30 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, following an award and the taking of possession, the land vests in the State free from encumbrances; compensation disputed by claimants is deposited and referred as required. Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act permits a presumption that official acts were regularly performed. Taking possession need not invariably involve physical dispossession of every occupant or physical occupation of every part of a large tract; a memorandum or Panchnama made by the acquisition officer in the presence of witnesses is an accepted mode. The approach must be pragmatic and depend on the nature and circumstances of the land. The Court considered Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, (1975) Supp. SCR 250, including its discussion of the modes of taking possession, but did not treat any one method as an absolute rule.
members.conclusion: Possession of the disputed land was taken and delivered to the public body; the land consequently vested free from encumbrances, and the claimant’s contrary claim of continuing title could not succeed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and award_made and compensation_dispute_referred_or_deposited and official_possession_record_and_delivery and (large_tract_public_scheme or claimant_acknowledged_public_title)

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The dispute arises from a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.award_made: The acquisition officer made an award for the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_dispute_referred_or_deposit: The acquisition officer referred a dispute concerning compensation or deposited the compensation in court.
predicates.official_possession_record_and_delivery: The acquisition officer recorded the taking of possession and delivered the land to the public body.
predicates.large_tract_public_scheme: The land formed part of a large tract being developed under a public scheme.
predicates.claimant_acknowledged_public_title: The claimant acknowledged the public body’s title or acted inconsistently with a claim that title remained with him.
predicates.acquired_land_vested_in_public_authority: The acquired land vested in the public authority after possession was taken.

members.legal_issue: Taking possession of acquired land requires actual possession on the spot, with the sufficient act depending on the nature of the land.
material_facts: The land was waste or arable, lay fallow, and had no crop on it at the relevant time.
The acquisition officer directed the local revenue officer to take possession and deliver it to the public institution for which it was acquired.
The revenue officer went onto the land, inspected it to determine the area to be taken, and handed that area over to the institution.
The occupant was not present when possession was taken.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 9(1) and 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, possession for the purpose of vesting must be actual possession on the spot, not possession merely on paper or symbolic possession in the sense used in civil procedure. The act sufficient to take possession depends on the nature of the land; no universal act is prescribed. The owner’s or occupant’s presence and notice of the precise time are not legal requirements, though notice may be desirable to guard against paper possession.
members.conclusion: The inspection and determination of the area on the spot were sufficient, in the circumstances, to constitute actual possession. The occupant’s presence and advance notice of the precise time of taking possession were not legally necessary.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: An authority was taking possession of land in a proceeding to acquire it for a public purpose.
predicates.authority_entered_land: The authority went onto the land as part of taking possession.
predicates.land_inspection_suited_to_its_nature: The land’s condition and use made inspection on the spot to identify the area being taken an act suited to taking possession.

members.legal_issue: A panchnama recording possession is ordinarily sufficient evidence that physical possession was taken where the acquired land is vacant and open.
material_facts: The acquired land was an open piece of land.
A panchnama recorded that possession had been recovered and handed over to government representatives and was signed by the relevant officers.
The landowners disputed that possession had been taken in accordance with law.
members.legal_principle: Raghbir Singh Sehrawat v. State of Haryana, applying the propositions in Banda Development Authority v. Moti Lal Agarwal and the cases reviewed there, holds that for vacant acquired land, the authority’s visit to the site and preparation of a panchnama will ordinarily suffice to establish possession. Different steps may be required where crops or structures are present.
members.conclusion: Physical possession had been taken because the land was open and vacant and the panchnama recorded the taking and handover of possession.

predicates.acquisition_possession_assessment: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether possession of acquired land was taken.
predicates.acquired_land_open_and_vacant: The acquired land was open and vacant, without crops or structures requiring additional possession-taking steps.
predicates.possession_panchnama_records_taking: The authority prepared a panchnama recording that possession was taken.
predicates.physical_possession_treated_as_taken: Physical possession is treated as having been taken.

members.legal_issue: Recorded taking of possession following completion of acquisition proceedings supports the finding that possession and title vested in the acquiring authority.
material_facts: An award covered the disputed land, and the award amount was deposited in court.
A panchanama recorded that possession was taken, and a later statutory notification disclosed the taking of possession.
The acquiring authority subsequently formed a road and developed and allotted sites, while the claimant maintained that possession remained with it.
The single judge found that possession had been taken, and the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with that finding.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the completed acquisition proceedings and the evidence of possession, including the panchanama and the statutory notification recording possession, together with the award and subsequent development and allotment of the land. On those facts, it upheld the finding that possession had been taken and that title and possession had vested in the acquiring authority.
members.conclusion: The finding that possession was taken was upheld, and the Court held that title and possession had vested in the acquiring authority.

predicates.acquisition_appeal_contests_possession_f: An appeal concerning a land acquisition challenges a finding about whether possession was taken.
predicates.award_was_made_and_compensation_deposite: An award was made for the acquired land and the compensation was deposited.
predicates.possession_was_recorded_in_acquisition_d: Acquisition records, including a possession record or notification, documented that possession was taken.
predicates.land_was_subsequently_developed_or_allot: The acquiring authority subsequently developed the land or allotted sites on it.

members.legal_issue: A witnessed possession memorandum, considered with the surrounding official records and circumstances, can establish that possession of acquired open land was taken and delivered.
material_facts: A possession memorandum recorded that an officer took possession of open land in the presence of two witnesses and delivered it to the acquiring company’s representative.
The memorandum was signed by the officers involved, and a possession receipt was also signed.
The revenue records showed the acquiring company as being in possession; the land had no construction or crops when possession was taken.
The challengers later filed witness affidavits contradicting the memorandum, but the Court found them unpersuasive.
members.legal_principle: In Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, the Court explained that taking possession depends on the nature of the land and that the owner’s presence is not essential. Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. Viswam and Balmokand Khatri Educational and Industrial Trust v. State of Punjab recognise a witnessed panchnama or possession memorandum as an accepted mode of taking possession; continued occupation thereafter may be unlawful possession. The Court cautioned that a High Court should not disregard the memorandum and revenue record on the basis of contradictory affidavits.
members.conclusion: Possession had been taken and delivered; the High Court was wrong to find otherwise.

predicates.acquired_land_possession_dispute: The parties dispute whether possession of land acquired by the government was taken.
predicates.witnessed_possession_record_exists: An official memorandum records the taking of possession in the presence of witnesses.
predicates.official_records_support_transfer: Other official records support that possession was transferred to the acquiring body.

members.legal_issue: Possession of a large tract of land may be taken through a properly executed panchnama when the taking is documented and the panchnama is not challenged.
material_facts: The State asserted that it took possession of the surplus land through a panchnama signed by witnesses.
The owners were not in possession when the State asserted that possession was taken.
The appellants did not challenge the panchnama in any proceeding.
The land comprised a large tract.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that possession of a large tract may be taken by a properly executed panchnama, relying on Sita Ram Bhandar Society, New Delhi v. Lieutenant Governor, Government of NCT of Delhi (2009) 10 SCC 501. It upheld the finding that possession had been taken where the panchnama was signed by witnesses and had not been challenged.
members.conclusion: The State had legally and validly taken possession through the panchnama.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and large_tract_of_land and possession_documented_by_panchnama and panchnama_signed_by_witnesses and panchnama_not_challenged

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The matter is an appeal arising from the dismissal of writ proceedings that challenge the State's taking of possession.
predicates.large_tract_of_land: The land from which possession was taken comprises a large tract.
predicates.possession_documented_by_panchnama: The State recorded the taking of possession in a panchnama.
predicates.panchnama_signed_by_witnesses: Witnesses signed the panchnama recording the taking of possession.
predicates.panchnama_not_challenged: The affected parties did not challenge the panchnama in any proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Possession of acquired land may be found to have been taken where the acquiring authorities record its delivery and the subsequent conduct and use of the land support that finding.
material_facts: The authorities recorded that possession of the acquired land had been taken at the site and delivered to the development authority; the record included a field book and a report of a site inspection.
The development authority had deposited 80 percent of the compensation and subsequently constructed roads and utility works, developed the land, and allotted plots and flats.

The landowner disputed that physical possession had been taken, but his earlier pleading referred to the land having been demarcated and to construction being imminent; the Court also considered photographs showing development on the land.
members.legal_principle: There is no hard-and-fast rule for what act constitutes taking possession. For vacant land, going to the site and preparing a panchnama will ordinarily suffice; where crops or structures exist, further steps such as notice and recording possession in the presence of independent witnesses will ordinarily be appropriate. For a large tract, possession may be recorded through an appropriate document rather than by separately taking possession of every parcel. Where a State agency is the beneficiary, 80 percent of the compensation has been deposited and a substantial part of the land has been used for the public purpose, possession may reasonably be presumed. The Court relied on Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, Balmokand Khatri Educational and Industrial Trust v. State of Punjab, P.K. Kalburqi v. State of Karnataka, NTPC v. Mahesh Dutta, Sita Ram Bhandar Society v. Government of NCT, Delhi, Omprakash Verma v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Brij Pal Bhargava v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The site records and use of the land for the residential scheme established that actual possession had been taken and delivered to the development authority.

rule.if: public_purpose_acquisition and site_possession_record and (substantial_public_use or advance_compensation_deposited)

predicates.public_purpose_acquisition: The land is acquired for a public purpose, with a public agency or instrumentality as the beneficiary.
predicates.site_possession_record: The authorities go to the land and prepare a record showing that possession was taken or delivered.
predicates.substantial_public_use: A substantial part of the acquired land is used to carry out the public purpose.
predicates.advance_compensation_deposited: The beneficiary deposits a substantial advance portion of the compensation payable for the land.

members.legal_issue: For compulsory acquisition, symbolic possession is sufficient for vacant and unoccupied land in appropriate circumstances, but actual physical possession is required for cultivated land or land with structures unless the authority already holds it or another recognized circumstance applies.
material_facts: The disputed land was agricultural and contained standing crops and numerous dwelling houses.
The original tenure holders remained in possession, continued cultivation, and had not been offered the promised rehabilitation land.
A court-appointed inspection confirmed that the tenure holders, rather than the acquiring authority, were in actual physical possession.
Revenue-record entries and mutation did not establish that possession had been taken.
members.legal_principle: There is no universal formula for possession under Sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Symbolic possession may suffice for vacant, unoccupied land, while actual physical possession is required where crops or structures remain, unless the acquiring authority already possesses the land or a comparable circumstance applies. Revenue mutation does not create or establish title or possession. The Court relied on Sections 16, 17 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, State of Tamil Nadu v. Mahalakshmi Ammal, Balmokand Khatri Educational and Industrial Trust v. State of Punjab, P.K. Kalburqui v. State of Karnataka, National Thermal Power Corporation v. Mahesh Datta, and Suman Verma v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: Actual physical possession had not been taken, and the land had not vested in the State on that basis; the State could therefore withdraw the acquisition proceedings, subject to the separate ruling concerning submergence and the dwelling units.

predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition: A public authority seeks to acquire land compulsorily.
predicates.cultivated_or_built_land: The land contains crops or structures rather than being vacant and unoccupied.
predicates.landholders_remain_in_actual_possession: The former landholders continue to occupy or use the land and the authority has not taken actual physical possession.

members.legal_issue: A properly recorded possession memorandum is an accepted means of taking possession of acquired land, with the required steps depending on the land’s condition.
material_facts: The Court considered how possession is taken when the State acquires land, including open land, land with crops or structures, and large tracts that cannot practically be occupied parcel by parcel.
It considered possession memoranda prepared by officials and signed by witnesses, and prior decisions accepting that method of taking possession.
It rejected the view that photographs showing later occupation necessarily negate an earlier recorded taking of possession.
members.legal_principle: Sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for vesting upon taking possession. The Court applied the principles in Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. A. Viswam, and Banda Development Authority v. Moti Lal Agarwal. Banda sets out the differing approach for vacant land, occupied land, and large tracts. The Court held that Velaxan Kumar v. Union of India was contrary to the settled approach and overruled it.
members.conclusion: A possession memorandum or panchnama is ordinarily sufficient for vacant land and can establish symbolic possession of a large tract. Where crops or structures are present, the authority ordinarily must give notice and take possession in the presence of independent witnesses; an owner’s refusal to cooperate does not necessarily defeat possession.

rule.if: acquisition_possession_dispute and ((vacant_land and official_possession_memorandum) or (occupied_land_notice_and_witnesses) or large_tract_symbolic_possession_recorded)

predicates.acquisition_possession_dispute: The issue is whether possession was taken in a land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.vacant_land: The acquired land was vacant when the authority went to take possession.
predicates.official_possession_memorandum: The authority recorded a memorandum or panchnama of taking possession.
predicates.occupied_land_notice_and_witnesses: For land with crops or structures, the authority gave notice and recorded possession in the presence of independent witnesses.
predicates.large_tract_symbolic_possession_recorded: The acquisition covered a large tract and the authority recorded symbolic possession in an appropriate document.

members.legal_issue: A tenant may be given time to relocate before an eviction order is executed when the circumstances make immediate relocation difficult.
material_facts: The tenant had operated a thriving cloth business with established goodwill for nearly thirty years.
The Court noted the scarcity of accommodation and the difficulty of finding suitable alternative premises.
The Court dismissed the tenant's appeal but postponed execution of the eviction order to allow time to secure alternative accommodation.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised equitable discretion in light of the tenant's established business and the stated scarcity of accommodation, while leaving the eviction order in force.
members.conclusion: The Court deferred execution of the eviction order to give the tenant time to find suitable alternative accommodation.

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_decree_is_dismis: The tenant's appeal against the eviction decree is dismissed.
predicates.tenant_has_longstanding_thriving_busines: The tenant has operated a thriving business for a substantial period and has goodwill associated with it.
predicates.suitable_alternative_accommodation_is_di: Suitable alternative accommodation is difficult to obtain because accommodation is scarce.

members.legal_issue: A tenant operating a hotel business may be granted time to surrender possession after an eviction order is restored, subject to conditions protecting the premises and the landlord’s interest.
material_facts: The respondent sought time to surrender vacant possession after the Supreme Court restored the eviction order.
The respondent was carrying on a hotel business in the premises.

The Court allowed the respondent to remain temporarily, required surrender of vacant and peaceful possession by the specified deadline, prohibited creation of third-party rights and damage to the property, and required an undertaking.
members.legal_principle: Having regard to the respondent’s hotel business, the Court exercised its discretion to allow temporary continuation in the premises while requiring an undertaking and safeguards against third-party rights and damage; no earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this direction.
members.conclusion: The respondent was permitted to remain in the premises temporarily, subject to surrendering possession by the specified deadline and complying with the stated safeguards.

predicates.eviction_order_restored: The court restored an order requiring the tenant to give up possession of the premises.
predicates.tenant_requested_time: The tenant asked the court for additional time before surrendering possession.
predicates.tenant_operates_hotel_business: The tenant was carrying on a hotel business in the premises.

members.legal_issue: A tenant may be granted additional time to vacate when the tenant has occupied the premises for a long period, subject to compliance with conditions imposed by the court.
material_facts: The tenants had occupied the premises for nearly two decades and remained in possession.

The High Court had previously granted time to vacate, and the Supreme Court extended the time subject to the tenants filing an undertaking and continuing to pay rent, with arrears to be paid within the specified time.
members.legal_principle: In making its final directions, the Court considered the tenants’ nearly two decades of occupation and continued possession, and conditioned the extension on an undertaking and payment of rent and arrears.
members.conclusion: The tenants were granted additional time to vacate, subject to filing the required undertaking and paying rent and arrears as directed.

rule.if: appeal_in_eviction_proceeding and tenant_remains_in_possession and long_period_of_occupation and tenant_complies_with_vacating_conditions

predicates.appeal_in_eviction_proceeding: A tenant brought an appeal in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.tenant_remains_in_possession: The tenant continued to occupy the premises when the court considered the appeal.
predicates.long_period_of_occupation: The tenant had occupied the premises for a substantial period.
predicates.tenant_complies_with_vacating_conditions: The tenant filed the required undertaking and complied with the court’s directions concerning rent and arrears.

members.legal_issue: Recovery of possession may be postponed and conditioned on undertakings when the tenant has been conducting business in the premises.
