material_facts: The tenant had been conducting business for some years in the shop subject to the eviction proceedings.
The Court directed that the landlord not recover possession until the end of 1977, and the tenant undertook to surrender possession by then.
The landlord undertook to give the tenant the first option to rent any part of the building that was let, at fair rent, before letting it to someone else.
The tenant undertook not to obstruct reconstruction so long as possession was not interfered with and the shop’s walls or roof were not damaged.
members.legal_principle: The Court, having regard to the tenant’s ongoing business in the shop, ordered a temporary postponement of recovery of possession and recorded the parties’ undertakings. The judgment identifies no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this direction.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed subject to postponing recovery of possession and recording the parties’ undertakings concerning surrender, a first option to rent, and reconstruction.

rule.if: eviction_appeal and tenant_has_conducted_business_in_premises and tenant_undertakes_to_surrender and landlord_undertakes_first_rental_option and tenant_undertakes_not_to_obstruct_safe_reconstruction

predicates.eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from an eviction case.
predicates.tenant_has_conducted_business_in_premise: The tenant has conducted business for some time in the premises subject to eviction.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s long-standing occupation and the hardship of immediate eviction may justify allowing time to surrender possession when the tenant undertakes to vacate by a later date.
material_facts: The tenant had carried on a hardware trade in the premises for 27 years.
The Court considered that outright eviction would cause hardship.
The tenant, through counsel, undertook to give vacant possession by a specified later date.
members.legal_principle: The Court granted time in light of the hardship of immediate eviction after long occupation and the tenant’s undertaking to surrender possession. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case in making this order.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the tenant time to surrender vacant possession and directed that the landlord take no eviction proceedings until that time, relying on the tenant’s undertaking.

members.legal_issue: A tenant carrying on business in premises subject to an eviction order may be granted a limited opportunity to vacate on conditions imposed by the Court.
material_facts: The tenant had been carrying on business in the shop.
The release application had been pending for many years.
The tenant requested time to vacate after the appeal was dismissed.
The Court conditioned the postponement of eviction on payment of the awarded costs and filing an undertaking.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion to allow time for a business tenant to vacate, subject to compliance with conditions; the judgment states no separate statutory test or earlier case governing this relief.
members.conclusion: The Court postponed enforcement of the eviction order for a limited period, subject to the tenant depositing the costs and filing an undertaking within the specified time.

members.legal_issue: A tenant facing eviction may be allowed time to vacate when the tenant requests that accommodation and undertakes to comply with the condition imposed by the court.
material_facts: The respondents remained in possession of the shop and requested time to vacate, stating that they had carried on business there for a long time.
The Court allowed them to remain in possession for a limited period on condition that they file an undertaking before the trial court.
members.legal_principle: The Court granted the respondents’ request for time to vacate on the condition that they provide an undertaking to the trial court; no separate statutory test or earlier case was stated for this discretionary relief.
members.conclusion: The respondents were allowed to remain in possession for one year from the judgment, conditional on filing the required undertaking within four weeks.

members.legal_issue: An affected tenant operating a longstanding business may be given alternative business premises while the planning scheme is implemented and until the alternative premises are provided.
material_facts: The appellant had occupied the premises as a tenant for many years and operated a continuing business there.
The scheme would terminate the appellant’s possession and adversely affect the business.

The Court declined to interfere with the scheme and directed the respondent to provide a suitable alternative shop, put the appellant in possession, and allow continued occupation of the existing premises until then.
members.legal_principle: In granting relief in this appeal, the Court directed alternative premises for the affected tenant and continued occupation of the existing premises pending provision of those premises; it also stated that summary eviction would be open if the appellant did not vacate or obstruct possession.
members.conclusion: The respondent was directed to provide a suitable alternative shop and place the appellant in possession of it, while permitting occupation of the existing premises until that occurred.

members.legal_issue: A tenant may be given time to leave premises subject to an undertaking to deliver possession and not transfer possession to another person.
material_facts: The tenant and landlord agreed that the tenant could remain in the premises temporarily before handing over possession.
The Supreme Court conditioned that arrangement on the tenant undertaking to hand over vacant and peaceful possession and not to induct another person or otherwise part with possession.
The Court provided that failure to give the undertaking or breach of its conditions would end the protection allowing the tenant to remain.
members.legal_principle: The Court made a conditional order in accordance with the parties’ agreement, requiring an undertaking to hand over possession and not to induct another person or otherwise part with possession. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this arrangement.
members.conclusion: The tenant was allowed to remain temporarily, subject to giving the required undertaking and complying with its conditions; otherwise, the order granting time to vacate would cease to apply.

members.legal_issue: Different compensation rates may be justified for lands in the same village when their locations or qualities differ.
material_facts: The acquired lands were in the same village but were located differently.
The High Court had assigned different compensation rates to the lands, taking their locations into account.
members.legal_principle: Lands within one village need not have the same market value; location and potentiality can affect value. The court relied on Tarlochan Singh v. State of Punjab, (1995) 2 SCC 424, Basant Kumar, and Kanwar Singh v. Union of India, (1998) 8 SCC 136.
members.conclusion: The court held that different compensation rates for lands in the same village were permissible where the lands differed in location or quality.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land may be assessed by belts reflecting differences in land quality rather than at a uniform rate when the record does not support uniform valuation.
material_facts: Approximately 331 acres were acquired for a residential-cum-commercial complex.
The Collector divided the land into three belts, and the courts below maintained or revised the belting while setting different rates for the belts.
The claimants argued that the land’s intended building use and its location alongside a major road warranted uniform compensation.
The Court considered the land’s differing quality and the absence of supporting material for uniform valuation.
members.legal_principle: In determining compensation for acquired land, the land’s quality and productive characteristics may be considered even when it is acquired for building purposes. A claim for uniform valuation must have supporting material in the record. No provision or earlier case was cited for this reasoning.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to discard the belting system or apply a uniform rate, finding no basis in the record to interfere with the High Court’s assessment.

members.legal_issue: Adjacent lands acquired under the same notification need not receive identical compensation when a material legal restriction makes their uses and market values different.
material_facts: The disputed land and adjoining land were acquired under the same notification.
The disputed land was restricted to agricultural use, while the adjoining land was not subject to that restriction and had development potential.
The landowner relied on the principle of uniform compensation for similarly situated lands.
members.legal_principle: Similarly situated lands with the same advantages and potentialities may warrant the same compensation: K. Periasami v. Sub-Tehsildar (Land Acquisition) and Delhi Development Authority v. Bali Ram Sharma. But land subject to a material restriction on use is not comparable in value to unrestricted adjoining land. Subh Ram v. State of Haryana explains that the quality, situation, and access of land are relevant, and that acquisition for the same purpose does not eliminate differences in the lands themselves.
members.conclusion: The lands were not comparable for valuation purposes because the restriction on the disputed land materially affected its use and market value; the same compensation was therefore not required for both.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for a large acquired area containing land with different locations and characteristics must be determined by reasonable classification rather than by applying one uniform rate.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large area containing lands abutting a national highway bypass and lands in the interior.
The land had been classified into different categories, and the court found that location and land category affected market value.
The High Court had applied a uniform rate to all the lands.
The Court considered the sale evidence unreliable in part, including a deed it described as fake.
members.legal_principle: Market value is assessed by considering whether a willing and prudent purchaser would buy the land, with its existing features, at the proposed value. Although valuation involves some guesswork, it must have a reasonable basis and avoid imagination. Where a large acquisition includes land abutting a main road and land in the interior, reasonable demarcation or classification is necessary because the lands do not have uniform market value.
members.conclusion: The uniform rate was based on an incorrect principle. The lands had to be classified by location and category: land within about 500 yards of the main road was to receive the higher rate regardless of soil quality, while other lands were to receive rates according to their category.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional guarantee of equality does not require a uniform compensation rate for acquired lands that differ in characteristics and market value.
material_facts: The claimants argued that different rates for different land classes were arbitrary and violated equality.
The acquired lands differed in location and other characteristics, and the Court found that they would not command the same market value in an open-market sale.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the equality guarantee does not apply to require identical compensation where lands are not equal in all relevant respects and would not command the same market value when sold by a willing vendor to a willing purchaser.
members.conclusion: The equality guarantee did not require the same compensation rate for all the acquired lands, and classification with different rates was not invalid on that ground.

members.legal_issue: Different rates of compensation may be fixed for land included in one acquisition when its characteristics, location, and comparative advantages differ.
material_facts: The lands in the two outer estates were agricultural, lay away from the town centre on its outer periphery, and did not have the same potential as the lands in the Hisar estate.
The valuation decision-makers considered differences in the lands’ nature, present state, location, and comparative advantages and disadvantages.
The claimants argued that the lands formed a block and should receive the same rate, but the courts below maintained different rates.
members.legal_principle: A compact acquisition does not require a single rate where material differences between the lands justify separate valuations. The Court relied on Union of India v. Mangatu Ram, AIR 1997 SC 2704, which concerned nearby acquired lands and supported distinguishing their values.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim for a uniform rate and found no error in principle in the different rates upheld by the High Court.

members.legal_issue: Market value should be assessed by belts rather than at a uniform rate where evidence shows that land abutting a road commands a higher price than interior land.
material_facts: Sale deeds showed higher prices for land abutting roads than for land situated farther inside, including transactions on the same day.
The Single Judge relied on that evidence to distinguish the road-adjoining land from the interior land.
The Division Bench awarded a uniform rate for the entire area based on general propositions, without examining the intrinsic evidence of differing prices.
members.legal_principle: Market value must be determined from the evidence in the particular case. Where intrinsic sale evidence establishes different prices for road-adjoining and interior land, applying a uniform rate or an average without regard to that difference is erroneous; the court may use belting to determine value. The judgment refers generally to earlier decisions but identifies none by name for this holding.
members.conclusion: The uniform rate was erroneous; the land up to 100 yards from the road was valued at Rs. 1,50,000 per acre and the remaining land at Rs. 80,000 per acre.

members.legal_issue: A single block of acquired land may be valued in distinct categories when its parts differ materially in location, accessibility, and potential advantages.
material_facts: The acquired area included land treated as potential building area and land treated as agricultural land.
The parts adjoining roads and nearby habitation had greater building potential and advantages than the land in the rear.
The rear land was away from habitation, inaccessible from the roads, and lacked roads within it.
The lower courts accepted the distinction between the categories.
members.legal_principle: The principle of belting does not apply merely because several plots form one block where the land differs in situation and advantages. Land adjoining an important road may have greater value than land in the rear because of its potential use or commercial exploitation, as applied in Mirza Nausherwan Khan v. The Collector (Land Acquisition), Hyderabad.
members.conclusion: The land’s status as one block did not require uniform compensation; the agricultural land could not be valued at the rate applicable to the better-situated potential building area.

members.legal_issue: Intentionally inflicting fatal injuries while exceeding a right of private defence supports a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Part I.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence came from interested witnesses, and most of the accused had also sustained injuries that the witnesses did not truthfully explain.
The evidence indicated that a melee arose from an altercation and that the respondents probably used force while exercising a right of private defence.
The circumstances did not justify causing death, and the respondents exceeded that right.
The injuries were intentionally inflicted and were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Under section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code, culpable homicide not amounting to murder is punishable where the act is done with the requisite intention. A person who uses force in private defence but exceeds that right may be liable for the resulting culpable homicide. The Court maintained the conviction under section 304 Part I rather than the original conviction under section 302.
members.conclusion: The respondents’ convictions under section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code were maintained.

members.legal_issue: Circumstances showing a right to defend property, despite recklessly excessive force that does not qualify for the applicable exception to murder, may warrant commutation of a death sentence.
material_facts: The appeal was limited to the sentences imposed after the appellants were convicted of four murders and sentenced to death.
The appellants were in effective physical possession of the disputed land and the crop when the opposing group arrived.
The opposing group was armed and intoxicated and had gone to remove the crop by force.
A fight occurred, and both sides sustained injuries; the injuries inflicted by the appellants on the deceased were much greater in number and severity than the injuries the appellants received.
The evidence did not rule out the participation of another person armed with a sharp-edged weapon.
The appellants had a right to defend their possession and property, but used recklessly excessive force.
members.legal_principle: The right of private defence of property and circumstances showing its exercise may be considered in sentencing even when the force used is recklessly excessive and Exception II to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code therefore does not apply. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The convictions were maintained, but each death sentence was commuted to imprisonment for life. The appellants were not entitled to the benefit of Exception II to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code because their force was recklessly excessive; the circumstances showing their right of private defence of property could nevertheless be considered in deciding whether to impose the extreme penalty.

members.legal_issue: A fatal stabbing inflicted after an attack with a stick, in the exercise but excessive use of private defence, is culpable homicide under the first part of Section 304 rather than murder.
material_facts: The accused was struck several times with a stick by the deceased before stabbing him with a knife.
The knife wound pierced the deceased’s heart and was fatal.
The court found that the accused acted in private defence but exceeded that right by stabbing the deceased in the heart.
The accused had been convicted of murder, and the appeal was confined to the nature of the offence and the sentence.
members.legal_principle: Applying Sections 302 and 304, first part, of the Indian Penal Code, the court held that the accused’s act was committed in the exercise of private defence, but that he exceeded that right in responding to the attack with a fatal knife blow. The court therefore treated the offence as falling under the first part of Section 304 rather than Section 302. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction was altered to a conviction under the first part of Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code. The court imposed rigorous imprisonment for five years and a fine of Rs. 2,500, with a further two years’ rigorous imprisonment in default of payment.

members.legal_issue: A person may act in private defence against an immediate threat to another's person, but force exceeding what is justified by the threat may still result in criminal liability for culpable homicide.
material_facts: The accused used a spear against the deceased after the deceased had struck the accused's father and appeared about to deliver a second blow with a stick.
The accused was entitled to defend his father's person against an immediate threat and was not required to weigh his response with precision in the moment.
The father had only one simple injury on the back of his head, and the evidence did not establish a reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt or death warranting the spear blow.
The accused caused the death without premeditation and without intending to cause more harm than was necessary for defence, but the Court found that he exceeded the right of private defence.
members.legal_principle: The right of private defence is available when a threat to the person being defended is real and immediate, and the defender need not weigh the instrument and force used with precision at the spur of the moment. Where the accused exceeds that right and causes death without premeditation or intention to cause more harm than necessary for defence, the conviction under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code may stand. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: The accused had a right of private defence but exceeded it; his conviction under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code was upheld.

members.legal_issue: A person who causes a death while acting in private defence but exceeds that right may be convicted of culpable homicide rather than murder.
material_facts: The evidence accepted by the court indicated that the deceased had first assaulted the accused's brother and that the accused then fatally assaulted the deceased in the family land.
Neither the accused nor his brother received injuries.
The accused relied on private defence, and the court found that he had exceeded that right.
members.legal_principle: Under section 99 of the Indian Penal Code, the right of private defence is subject to limits. Applying that principle, the court held that the fatal assault exceeded the right of private defence and altered the conviction under section 302 to one under section 304 Part II. The judgment cites no earlier case for this issue.
members.conclusion: The accused exceeded the right of private defence, so the murder conviction was altered to a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 304 Part II of the Penal Code.

members.legal_issue: An accused who acts in private defence but exceeds its limits may have a murder conviction reduced where the circumstances support the defence and the force used went beyond what it permitted.
material_facts: The accused and a co-accused were injured during the same occurrence, and the prosecution did not explain their injuries.
The occurrence arose suddenly; even the prosecution case was that the accused arrived unarmed and picked up objects at the scene.
The accused inflicted fatal injuries on two people and injured another person.
members.legal_principle: The accused need not establish private defence beyond reasonable doubt; it is sufficient if the defence is supported on a preponderance of probabilities, and unexplained injuries sustained by the accused in the occurrence are relevant to that assessment. Where private defence is available but exceeded, Exception 2 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code applies, and the offence is punishable under Section 304 Part I. The Court referred generally to earlier decisions on the burden of proving private defence but did not identify any by name.
members.conclusion: The accused had a right of private defence but exceeded it. His conviction for murder was set aside and replaced with a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder; his convictions for attempted murder and house trespass were left undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: Exceeding the limits of an otherwise accrued right of private defence may be taken into account in mitigation of sentence.
material_facts: The accused faced an unlawful group threat that gave rise to a right of private defence of the body.
The accused exceeded that right by firing three shots in quick succession, although the circumstances did not justify causing death.
The High Court had imposed a seven-year term of rigorous imprisonment.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the limits on private defence in Sections 99 and 101 of the Penal Code and treated the accused’s excess of an accrued right, in circumstances where he acted in fear, as a mitigating circumstance. A person in peril is not expected to measure necessary force with exact precision, and the excess could therefore be considered in sentencing.
members.conclusion: The court maintained the conviction but reduced the sentence to six months’ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10,000, with the fine payable as compensation to the deceased’s widow or immediate heirs if she was unavailable.

members.legal_issue: An accused who participates in a fatal attack while acting in defence of another person or property is liable when the force used exceeds the right of private defence.
material_facts: The two accused who remained convicted were found to have participated in the occurrence and attacked the deceased with axes.
The first accused, their father, had a minor injury to his finger, and the court accepted that the deceased had bitten it.
The attack occurred during a dispute over crops and possession of land.
The court agreed that the two accused had exceeded the right of private defence of their father's body and of property.
members.legal_principle: The right of private defence of the body and property does not justify force that exceeds that right. The court applied that principle and retained the convictions under Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The convictions of the two accused under Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code and their five-year prison sentences were retained.

members.legal_issue: A person exercising the right to defend property may not inflict more harm than necessary, and an excessive fatal attack may warrant conviction for culpable homicide rather than murder.
material_facts: The court found that the accused had a right to defend the property but did not accept the accused’s account of the incident in its entirety.
The deceased sustained 15 injuries, including an injury that was individually sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The number and nature of the injuries showed that the accused exceeded the right to defend property; the court considered that the attack continued after the deceased had fallen.
The second accused was present and participated in the attack.
members.legal_principle: Section 99 of the Indian Penal Code limits the right of private defence by providing that it does not extend to inflicting more harm than is necessary for defence. Applying that restriction alongside the right to defend property under Section 97, the court held that the force used exceeded the right and altered the convictions from Section 302 read with Section 34 to Part I of Section 304. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The court set aside the murder convictions and sentences and convicted the accused under Part I of Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code, imposing seven years’ rigorous imprisonment on each.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_had_right_to_defend_property and fatal_attack_was_excessive and multiple_accused_participated

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.accused_had_right_to_defend_property: The accused had a right to defend the property involved in the incident.
predicates.fatal_attack_was_excessive: The accused inflicted fatal harm beyond what was necessary to defend the property.
predicates.multiple_accused_participated: More than one accused participated in the fatal attack.
predicates.conviction_modified_to_culpable_homicide: The court replaces the murder conviction with a conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

members.legal_issue: The availability of a civil remedy does not by itself justify quashing a criminal complaint that prima facie alleges an offence.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that the accused had fraudulently induced the complainant’s father to execute a gift deed.
After a remand, the Magistrate issued process for alleged offences of cheating, forgery and conspiracy.
The High Court quashed the complaint because it considered the allegations to disclose a civil wrong and continuation of the prosecution to be an abuse of process.
The High Court did not find that the complaint’s allegations disclosed no offence.
members.legal_principle: A set of facts may give rise both to a civil claim and to criminal liability; the availability of a civil remedy does not preclude criminal prosecution where the alleged conduct also makes out an offence. The Court relied on Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal, which held that even arbitration is not an effective substitute for criminal prosecution when the conduct also constitutes an offence. The inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure may be used to prevent abuse of process, but the complaint cannot be quashed merely because a civil remedy is available.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the complaint solely because the facts also gave rise to a civil claim. Its order was set aside and the trial court was directed to proceed with the complaint in accordance with law.

rule.if: criminal_complaint_proceeding and civil_claim_available and prima_facie_offence_alleged and not finding_that_allegations_disclose_no_offence

predicates.criminal_complaint_proceeding: A complainant has initiated a criminal proceeding alleging that another person committed an offence.
predicates.civil_claim_available: The alleged facts also provide a basis for pursuing a civil claim.
predicates.prima_facie_offence_alleged: The complaint’s allegations, at the preliminary stage, indicate conduct that may constitute an offence.
predicates.finding_that_allegations_disclose_no_off: The court has found that the complaint’s allegations do not disclose any offence.
predicates.civil_remedy_exists: A civil remedy is available in respect of the alleged conduct.

members.legal_issue: A criminal complaint cannot be quashed solely because the dispute appears civil in nature when its allegations prima facie disclose the ingredients of an offence.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that the accused forged and prepared false documents to bring about a development agreement.
The High Court accepted the accused's contention that the dispute was entirely civil and quashed the criminal process.
The Supreme Court found that the complaint prima facie disclosed the alleged offences and held that their truth had to be decided at trial.
members.legal_principle: Quashing is appropriate where a complaint discloses no offence or is frivolous, vexatious, or oppressive, and the High Court may quash when the alleged facts do not constitute the offence. But a civil character to the dispute alone does not justify quashing if the complaint prima facie discloses the offence's ingredients. The judgment relies on Sonu Gupta v. Deepak Gupta, (2015) 3 SCC 424.
members.conclusion: The criminal proceedings could not be interdicted merely because the allegations appeared civil in nature; the appeal was allowed and the High Court's judgment was set aside.

predicates.quashing_challenge_in_criminal_complaint: A party seeks to quash criminal proceedings initiated by a complaint.
predicates.complaint_discloses_offence_elements: The complainant's allegations, considered with the sworn statement, set out facts that prima facie disclose an offence.
predicates.dispute_appears_civil: The dispute also appears to concern civil rights or obligations.
predicates.criminal_proceeding_is_not_quashed_solel: The criminal proceeding is not quashed solely because the dispute appears civil.

members.legal_issue: A criminal complaint and investigation alleging dishonest inducement to part with money cannot be quashed at the preliminary stage merely because the transaction also involves a civil dispute, where the allegations taken at face value prima facie disclose a cognizable offence.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that two persons represented that a plot of land could be sold to him and thereby induced him to enter into an agreement and pay money.
The complainant alleged that the persons had no valid title to the property and had conspired to induce payment without intending to complete the sale.
The complaint was referred for police investigation, and the High Court quashed the complaint proceedings and the resulting investigation before they could proceed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court ordinarily should not quash a criminal proceeding or FIR if the allegations, taken at face value and as a whole, disclose a cognizable offence. The power must be exercised sparingly; except in very exceptional circumstances, the court should not rely on defence documents or go beyond the allegations to decide the absence of mens rea or actus reus. A civil dispute does not by itself bar criminal proceedings. The Court relied on R. Kalyani v. Janak C. Mehta (2009) 1 SCC 516 and Mahesh Chaudhary v. State of Rajasthan (2009) 4 SCC 443, and distinguished Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168, Murari Lal Gupta v. Gopi Singh (2005) 13 SCC 699, and Ram Biraji Devi v. Umesh Kumar Singh (2006) 6 SCC 669 on their facts.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court's order quashing the proceedings was set aside, and the investigation was permitted to proceed.

rule.if: quashing_challenge_during_investigation and dishonest_inducement_alleged and money_paid_in_reliance and allegations_taken_at_face_value_disclose_cognizable_offence

predicates.quashing_challenge_during_investigation: The matter is a challenge to the quashing of a criminal complaint or investigation before the investigation has run its course.
predicates.dishonest_inducement_alleged: The complainant alleges that a person dishonestly induced the complainant through representations made without an intention to perform the promised transaction.
predicates.money_paid_in_reliance: The complainant alleges that money was paid in reliance on the representations.
predicates.allegations_taken_at_face_value_disclose: Taking the complaint's allegations as true and reading them as a whole, they describe conduct that may amount to a cognizable offence.

members.legal_issue: A complaint cannot be quashed at the prima facie stage merely because a related civil dispute is pending, without examining whether the complaint’s allegations make out the alleged offences.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that the accused committed offences involving voluntarily causing hurt and theft with common intention.
The Magistrate found a prima facie case and took cognizance.
The High Court quashed the complaint after emphasizing the pending landlord-tenant and property disputes, without determining whether the complaint’s allegations made out the alleged offences.
members.legal_principle: At the stage of deciding whether a prima facie case is made out, the court must examine the allegations in the complaint. Mere pendency of a civil suit does not answer whether the alleged criminal offences are made out. The Court referred to State of Haryana v. Ch. Bhajan Lal (AIR 1992 SC 604), which the High Court had cited but failed to apply. The alleged offences were under Sections 323 and 379 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order was legally unsustainable because it did not assess the complaint’s allegations; the Magistrate’s order taking cognizance was restored.

rule.if: complaint_quashing_proceeding and complaint_alleges_criminal_offences and quashing_court_relies_on_civil_dispute and not quashing_court_assesses_complaint_allegations

predicates.complaint_quashing_proceeding: A complaint alleging criminal offences is challenged for quashing before trial.
predicates.complaint_alleges_criminal_offences: The complainant sets out allegations that the accused committed criminal offences.
predicates.quashing_court_relies_on_civil_dispute: The court quashing the complaint relies on a related civil dispute as a basis for its decision.
predicates.quashing_court_assesses_complaint_allega: The court quashing the complaint examines whether the allegations make out a prima facie case for the alleged offences.

members.legal_issue: A criminal prosecution is not barred merely because the same facts also involve a civil dispute, where the allegations disclose criminality and the ingredients of an offence.
material_facts: The allegations concerned property dealings and a dispute over possession of a home, but also included claims of deceptive signatures, withheld money and papers, threats, and conduct said to have contributed to a suicide.
The trial court had framed charges relating to abetment of suicide and criminal trespass.
The High Court treated the matter as substantially civil while acknowledging that some aspects required a full trial.
members.legal_principle: Civil and criminal liability may arise from the same facts. If the record discloses a criminal offence and its ingredients are satisfied, proceedings cannot be quashed merely because a civil claim is also available; courts must not use their powers to stifle a legitimate prosecution. The judgment relies on Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd. and explains the treatment of predominantly civil disputes by reference to Madhavrao Jiwaji Rao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, State of Bihar v. P.P. Sharma, and M.N. Damani v. S.K. Sinha.
members.conclusion: The property-related and civil aspects did not justify quashing the criminal charge because the allegations also raised an element of criminality and could satisfy the charged offence’s ingredients.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding and same_facts_support_civil_claim and allegations_disclose_criminality and offence_ingredients_broadly_satisfied

predicates.criminal_proceeding: A prosecution has been brought alleging a criminal offence.
predicates.same_facts_support_civil_claim: The facts underlying the prosecution also give rise to a civil claim or dispute.
predicates.allegations_disclose_criminality: The prosecution allegations, taken as a whole, describe conduct with a criminal element.
predicates.offence_ingredients_broadly_satisfied: The allegations broadly satisfy the essential ingredients of the charged offence.

members.legal_issue: A criminal prosecution should not be quashed merely because the transaction also gives rise to a civil or commercial dispute when the allegations and material disclose a prima facie criminal offence.
material_facts: The Magistrate considered the final report, the case diary, the protest petition and recorded statements before taking cognizance of alleged cheating and criminal breach of trust.
The investigation included material indicating that the accused had concealed information about the property and that the complainant had paid them money in connection with the proposed sale.

The High Court quashed the cognizance order as against one accused, although the complaint and investigation material were found to allege criminal conduct and the courts below had found a prima facie case.
The Supreme Court found no basis to treat the complaint as mala fide, frivolous or vexatious and held that the High Court had not applied sound principles in quashing the order.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution and Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court must exercise its quashing power cautiously and must not conduct a meticulous assessment of whether conviction is likely. It should not stifle a legitimate prosecution where the allegations, taken as a whole, disclose the ingredients of an offence and the complaint is not shown to be mala fide, frivolous or vexatious. A civil or commercial dispute may also contain criminal ingredients. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, Central Bureau of Investigation v. Ravi Shankar Srivastava, R. Kalyani v. Janak C. Mehta, Gian Singh v. State of Punjab, Mohammed Ibrahim v. State of Bihar, G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P., Indian Oil Corpn. v. NEPC India Ltd., and Rajesh Bajaj v. State NCT of Delhi.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order quashing cognizance was set aside, and the Magistrate was directed to proceed in accordance with law.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_quashing_of_cognizance and prima_facie_offence_disclosed and not complaint_shown_mala_fide

predicates.appeal_challenges_quashing_of_cognizance: An appeal challenges a higher court’s order quashing a lower court’s order taking cognizance of an alleged offence.
predicates.prima_facie_offence_disclosed: The complaint and material considered at the cognizance stage allege facts that, taken as a whole, disclose the ingredients of a criminal offence.
predicates.complaint_shown_mala_fide: The complaint is shown to be mala fide, frivolous or vexatious.

members.legal_issue: Pending civil litigation over the same property does not by itself justify quashing criminal proceedings where the first information report contains specific, serious allegations that prima facie disclose criminal offences and are not frivolous or mala fide.
material_facts: The first information report alleged that the appellant fraudulently procured a power of attorney by forging the signatures of the persons said to have executed it, and then sold the land under that authority.
The report alleged that one purported signatory was a minor when the document was said to have been signed and that another purported signatory was outside India at the time.
A civil suit seeking cancellation of the power of attorney was pending; another suit referred to by the appellant had been dismissed for non-prosecution, with no evidence that it had been restored.
The High Court declined to quash the criminal proceedings, and the Supreme Court considered an appeal from that refusal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, inherent powers to quash proceedings at the initial stage are to be exercised sparingly, including where the allegations, taken at face value and in their entirety, do not prima facie disclose an offence. Disputed or controversial facts cannot form the basis for quashing. A criminal complaint is not to be quashed merely because a civil suit is pending if the allegations are not frivolous, mala fide, or vexatious. The Court relied on Arun Bhandari v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2013) 2 SCC 801, and Kamaladevi Agarwal v. State of W.B., (2002) 1 SCC 555.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the refusal to quash the criminal proceedings and dismissed the appeal, holding that the pending civil suit did not warrant quashing in light of the serious allegations.

rule.if: appeal_from_refusal_to_quash and fir_alleges_forged_authority_document and fir_alleges_signer_was_a_minor and fir_alleges_another_signer_was_abroad and civil_suit_concerns_the_same_dispute

predicates.appeal_from_refusal_to_quash: The accused appealed after a court refused to quash the criminal proceedings.
predicates.fir_alleges_forged_authority_document: The first information report alleged that the accused procured an authority document by forging the signatures of purported signatories.
predicates.fir_alleges_signer_was_a_minor: The first information report alleged that one purported signatory was a minor when the document was said to have been signed.
predicates.fir_alleges_another_signer_was_abroad: The first information report alleged that another purported signatory was outside the country when the document was said to have been signed.
predicates.civil_suit_concerns_the_same_dispute: A civil suit concerning the property or authority document underlying the criminal allegations was pending.

members.legal_issue: A criminal prosecution arising from a commercial contract may not be quashed solely because the dispute also has a civil remedy or is subject to arbitration when the allegations prima facie disclose criminal offences.
material_facts: The complaint, FIR and charge-sheet alleged that the seller obtained substantial payments under an agreement to sell, failed to complete required steps, withheld material information about the property's mortgage and its discharge, and later terminated the agreement.
The charge-sheet also referred to alleged conduct concerning the property's subdivision and an earlier transaction involving the same property.
The High Court quashed the proceedings on the grounds that the dispute arose from a terminated contract and arbitration was pending.
The Supreme Court found that the allegations could disclose the ingredients of cheating and criminal breach of trust, while leaving their truth to be determined at trial.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 CrPC, inherent powers are extraordinary and must be used with care, consistently with the illustrative categories in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal. A commercial transaction may also involve an offence, and arbitration does not substitute for criminal prosecution of an alleged offence: Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal. Whether allegations are true is ordinarily for trial, not a reason to quash where the complaint discloses an offence: Nagpur Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. P. Radhakrishna. The Court also referred to the illustrations of cheating in Sections 415, 418 and 420 IPC and considered the alleged offences under Sections 406, 420 and 34 IPC.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the criminal proceedings merely because the transaction was commercial, the agreement had been terminated, or arbitration was pending; the appeal was allowed and the proceedings restored.

rule.if: criminal_quashing_appeal and allegations_prima_facie_disclose_offence and (commercial_transaction or civil_remedy_available or arbitration_pending)

predicates.criminal_quashing_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order that quashed criminal proceedings.
predicates.allegations_prima_facie_disclose_offence: The complaint, FIR or charge-sheet alleges facts that, taken at face value, may satisfy the elements of a criminal offence.
predicates.commercial_transaction: The alleged conduct arose in the course of a commercial transaction.
predicates.civil_remedy_available: The parties have a civil remedy concerning the same dispute.
predicates.arbitration_pending: Arbitral proceedings concerning the dispute have been initiated or are pending.
predicates.criminal_proceedings_must_not_be_quashed: The criminal proceedings are not to be quashed solely because the dispute is commercial, a civil remedy exists, or arbitration is pending.

members.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus is unavailable unless the applicant establishes a legally protected and judicially enforceable right.
material_facts: The lessee sought a writ compelling the authority and the State Government to withdraw the notification and the refusal to approve the building plan.
The contractual FSI limit had not been authorized by the required governmental sanction, so it did not confer a legally enforceable right.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that a person seeking a writ of mandamus must prove a legally protected and judicially enforceable right. The statutory setting included sections 31(6) and 37(2) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, under which the sanctioned development plan and sanctioned modifications bind the planning authority. No earlier case is cited for the mandamus principle.
members.conclusion: The requested relief was unavailable because the lessee had not established a legally protected and judicially enforceable right.

predicates.writ_mandamus_claim: An applicant asks a court to issue a writ compelling a public authority to act.
predicates.applicant_lacks_legally_protected_enforc: The applicant has no legally protected right that a court can enforce.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising writ jurisdiction cannot direct a statutory licensing authority to grant a licence before that authority has performed its statutory decision-making function.
material_facts: The challenged order remitted the licence application to the licensing authority for reconsideration.
The High Court directed the authority to grant the licence even though the authority had not yet completed its statutory consideration of the application.
members.legal_principle: Where a statute confers a power and requires an authority to perform a function before exercising that power, a court in writ jurisdiction cannot supplant the authority and perform that function itself.
members.conclusion: The High Court could quash the remand order if it was legally erroneous, but it could not take over the licensing authority’s function and direct it to grant the licence; the mandamus was set aside to that extent.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenges_remand: A person brought a writ proceeding challenging an order that sent a licensing matter back for reconsideration.
predicates.statutory_authority_has_not_decided_lice: The statutory licensing authority had not yet completed its consideration of the licence application.

members.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus cannot be used to create a right or to have a court substitute its decision for that of the competent statutory authority.
material_facts: The society did not apply to the authority responsible for the acquisition seeking release of the land.

The society had applied to other authorities for scheme approval and conversion of land use, and later sent a telegram to the Chief Secretary alleging injustice without adequate details of the discrimination claimed.
The High Court ordered the land released rather than leaving any statutory question of release to the competent authority.
members.legal_principle: A writ exists to enforce an established legal right and corresponding duty, not to create a right. A mandamus ordinarily requires a clear demand to an authority with power to act and a refusal of that demand, unless demand is manifestly futile or an empty formality. If a matter has been placed before the appropriate authority and remains undecided, the court may direct that authority to decide it by a reasoned order, but should not decide the matter itself. The Court relied on Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Govardhandas Bhanji, Praga Tools Corporation v. C.V. Imanual, Punjab Financial Corporation v. Garg Steel, Union of India v. Arulmozhi Iniarasu, Khela Banerjee v. City Montessori School, G. Veerappa Pillai v. Raman and Raman, Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Asha Ramchandra Ambedkar, H.P. Public Service Commission v. Mukesh Thakur, and Manohar Lal v. Ugrasen.
members.conclusion: The society had not established a basis for the High Court to order release, and the High Court could not itself take over the task of the statutory authority.

rule.if: writ_seeking_mandamus and (not established_legal_right_or_duty or (not clear_demand_to_competent_authority and demand_not_excused) or not authority_refused_demand)

predicates.writ_seeking_mandamus: A proceeding asks a court to compel a public authority to perform an act.
predicates.established_legal_right_or_duty: The applicant establishes an existing legal right or a corresponding duty of the authority.
predicates.clear_demand_to_competent_authority: The applicant makes a clear demand to an authority empowered to perform the requested act.
predicates.demand_not_excused: The facts do not make a demand unnecessary because it would be futile or an empty formality.
predicates.authority_refused_demand: The competent authority has rejected the demand, by words or conduct.

members.legal_issue: Mandamus is unavailable to compel performance of an obligation unless a law imposes a duty and the claimant has a legal right to enforce that duty.
material_facts: The claimant sought an order compelling the authorities to execute the fishery lease and place it in possession.
No statute or rule having the force of law was shown to impose the asserted duty on the authorities.
The asserted obligation arose from the proposed settlement, which was not binding and enforceable.
members.legal_principle: Mandamus compels performance of public duties prescribed by law. The claimant must show a legal duty imposed by statute and a corresponding legal right to enforce its performance. The court referred to Lekhraj Satramdas Lalvani v. Deputy Custodian-cum-Managing Officer, Dr. Rai Shivendra Bahadur v. Governing Body of Nalanda College, and Dr. Umakant Saran v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to mandamus, and the High Court was not competent to issue it.

predicates.mandamus_proceeding: The claimant seeks an order compelling a public authority to perform an act.
predicates.statutory_duty_not_shown: No law imposing the asserted duty on the authority has been established.
predicates.claimant_legal_right_not_shown: The claimant has not established a legal right under that law to enforce performance of the duty.

members.legal_issue: Mandamus cannot compel delivery of property when the applicant has no present right to possession established by a court.
material_facts: The applicant sought mandamus compelling the government department to hand over management and possession of the property.
The pre-constitutional order required a claimant to establish a right to possession in the civil courts before seeking restoration.
No civil court decision declared the applicant’s right to possession.
members.legal_principle: Mandamus cannot issue where the applicant has no present right to demand the act sought. Under the sovereign order, a claimant’s right to possession remained in abeyance until established in the civil courts; the Court did not decide whether mandamus would be an appropriate remedy if such a right were later established.
members.conclusion: The applicant had no present right to possession, so mandamus could not issue.

predicates.mandamus_application: A person applies for mandamus seeking an order that a public authority deliver property or its management.
predicates.possession_right_conditioned_on_court_es: An order governing the property makes restoration of possession dependent on the claimant establishing a right in court.
predicates.no_court_declaration_of_applicant_right: No court has declared that the applicant is entitled to possession.

members.legal_issue: Mandamus is unavailable unless the applicant establishes non-compliance with a mandatory duty owed by the authority.
material_facts: The applicants sought mandamus against the recovery authority.
They did not establish that the authority had failed to comply with a mandatory provision imposing an obligation toward them.
members.legal_principle: Mandamus requires a showing that a mandatory provision has not been complied with and that an obligation toward the applicant has consequently not been carried out.
members.conclusion: No occasion arose to issue mandamus because the applicants had not shown non-compliance with a mandatory provision or an unperformed obligation owed to them.

predicates.mandamus_sought: The applicant asked a court to compel an authority to act.
predicates.mandatory_duty_breach_shown: The applicant established that the authority failed to comply with a mandatory duty owed to the applicant.

members.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus cannot compel a public authority to transfer property when the authority has no applicable statutory duty to do so and the claimant has no legal right to require the transfer.
material_facts: The claimants sought a writ compelling the authorities to transfer the allotted premises on a hire-purchase basis.
The governing law did not impose a duty on the authorities to transfer the premises to the claimants.
The claimants had no legal right to require such a transfer because the empowered body had not decided to transfer the property.
members.legal_principle: The Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Cooperative Society Ltd. v. Sipahi Singh, AIR 1977 SC 2149, establishes that mandamus requires a statutory duty imposed on the authority and a corresponding legal right in the claimant. The applicable provisions did not impose a duty to make the claimed transfer, and the claimants had no corresponding right.
members.conclusion: The requested writ of mandamus could not be granted.

predicates.mandamus_claim: A claimant asks a court to compel a public authority to transfer property.
predicates.no_statutory_transfer_duty: The applicable law does not require the authority to make the transfer sought.
predicates.no_claimant_right_to_transfer: The claimant has no legal right to require the authority to make the transfer.

members.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus requires a subsisting legally enforceable right and cannot compel performance contrary to binding law.
material_facts: The respondents sought a fresh mandamus requiring the State to make interim payments under the Act.
Their claimed right depended on the amendments being constitutionally invalid and interim payments continuing beyond the Director’s determination.
The Supreme Court had upheld the amendments and declared that interim payments ended upon the Director’s original determination.
The claimed right therefore did not subsist when the later mandamus was sought.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs, including mandamus, for fundamental rights and other legal purposes, subject to recognised limits. Mandamus requires a subsisting legal right in the applicant and a corresponding legal duty in the respondent public authority. The Court relied on Kalyan Singh v. State of U.P. for the requirement that the right subsist on the date of the petition.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not issue mandamus because the respondents had no subsisting legally enforceable right to the payments they claimed.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_mandamus: A party seeks a judicial command requiring a public authority to act.
predicates.claimed_right_no_longer_subsists: The legal right relied on by the applicant had ceased to be enforceable by the time the writ was sought.
predicates.public_authority_is_asked_to_perform_cor: The requested command would require a public authority to perform a duty said to correspond to the claimed right.

members.legal_issue: Readiness and willingness in a specific-performance suit may be shown by the substance of the plaint as a whole and the evidence, without prescribed wording or a specific formula.
material_facts: The claimant paid two-thirds of the consideration when the written agreement was executed, leaving only the balance to be paid.
The plaint, read as a whole, stated that the claimant demanded that the seller accept the balance and execute the sale deed.
The claimant and another witness gave evidence in support of readiness and willingness.
The claimant had deposited the balance pursuant to the trial court's decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the plaintiff to aver and prove that he has performed, or has always been and is willing to perform, the essential terms of the contract. No specific phraseology or form is required if the plaint as a whole conveys that substance, and readiness and willingness are assessed from the relevant facts and conduct. The Court relied on Ramesh Chandra Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal and the three-Judge decision in Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty. It distinguished Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley and Abdul Khader Rowther v. P.K. Sara Bai, which concerned different pleading circumstances.
members.conclusion: The plaint and evidence sufficiently established the claimant's readiness and willingness to perform his obligations.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaint_as_whole_indicates_willingness and claimant_demanded_contractual_performance and evidence_supports_readiness and claimant_paid_substantial_consideration

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for sale.
predicates.plaint_as_whole_indicates_willingness: The claimant's plaint, read as a whole, described willingness to perform the claimant's contractual obligations.
predicates.claimant_demanded_contractual_performanc: The claimant asked the other contracting party to accept the balance consideration and complete the sale.
predicates.evidence_supports_readiness: The claimant presented evidence supporting readiness and willingness to perform.
predicates.claimant_paid_substantial_consideration: The claimant had paid a substantial part of the agreed consideration before seeking completion of the contract.

members.legal_issue: In a suit for specific performance, readiness and willingness may be sufficiently averred and proved through the substance of the pleadings and the buyer’s conduct, without using a prescribed verbal formula.
material_facts: The buyer sued to enforce an agreement to sell property, with six months allowed for completion.

The plaint stated that the buyer was ready to complete the purchase, described repeated requests to the seller to execute the sale deed, and referred to a lawyer’s notice sent immediately after the completion period expired.
The buyer deposited the balance of the purchase price in court when filing the suit.
The trial court denied specific performance for failure to plead and prove continuing readiness and willingness, but the High Court granted the relief.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with Explanation (ii), requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to aver and prove that the plaintiff performed or was always ready and willing to perform the essential contractual obligations. Under Explanation (i), actual tender or deposit of money is not essential unless the court directs it. Readiness and willingness must be assessed from the substance of the pleadings as a whole and the relevant conduct and circumstances; no particular words or formula are required. The plaintiff must establish continuous readiness and willingness from the contract to the hearing. The Court relied on Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon, AIR 1928 PC 208, approved in Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing and Construction (Private) Ltd., AIR 1968 SC 1355; Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, (1970) 3 SCC 140; Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, (1999) 6 SCC 337; Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi, (2000) 6 SCC 420; and Surya Narain Upadhyaya v. Ram Roop Pandey, AIR 1994 SC 105.
members.conclusion: The pleadings and the surrounding conduct sufficiently established readiness and willingness; the High Court’s decree for specific performance was upheld and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and substantive_readiness_pleading and post_deadline_demand and repeated_completion_requests and balance_deposited_with_suit

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A buyer brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.substantive_readiness_pleading: The buyer’s pleading, read as a whole, conveyed readiness and willingness to perform the buyer’s contractual obligations.
predicates.post_deadline_demand: After the contractual completion period ended, the buyer sent a notice requiring the seller to execute the sale deed.
predicates.repeated_completion_requests: The buyer repeatedly met the seller and requested execution of the sale deed.
predicates.balance_deposited_with_suit: The buyer deposited the unpaid purchase price in court when filing the suit.

members.legal_issue: The requirement to plead and prove readiness and willingness is met when the pleadings, read as a whole, convey that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform, even without prescribed words or phraseology.
material_facts: The plaintiff pleaded that he was always ready and willing to perform the agreement and described the steps he took to have the sale deed executed and registered.
The plaintiff had paid most of the agreed consideration, with the balance payable at execution of the sale deed.
The trial court and first appellate court found, on the evidence, that the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires an averment and proof of performance or readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract. Under Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, pleadings must be read as a whole and compliance is assessed by their pith and substance; no particular phraseology is required unless the statute requires a particular form. Under C.S. Venkatesh v. A.S.C. Murthy, readiness and willingness may be inferred from the plaintiff’s conduct before and after suit and the surrounding circumstances; the plaintiff need not produce ready money but must prove means to generate the consideration.
members.conclusion: The pleadings and evidence satisfied the readiness-and-willingness requirement; the High Court erred in finding otherwise based on the absence of specific words in the plaint.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The plaintiff brought a claim seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.pleadings_read_as_whole_convey_readiness: The plaintiff’s pleadings, considered as a whole, conveyed readiness and willingness to perform, even if they did not use prescribed words.
predicates.evidence_supports_ability_and_willingnes: The evidence, including the plaintiff’s conduct and capacity to meet the remaining obligation, supported readiness and willingness to perform.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff’s readiness and willingness to perform an agreement is assessed from the pleadings, evidence, and overall conduct, and does not require incessant demands or acts during every part of the limitation period.
material_facts: The plaintiffs pleaded that they were ready to perform and that they had repeatedly asked the vendors to execute the sale deed; the vendors did not specifically deny that plea.
The plaintiffs paid an initial amount and made a further payment before the date fixed for execution of the sale deed.

After the sale deed was not executed by the stipulated date, the plaintiffs sent a notice seeking execution; the parties then executed a supplementary agreement and the plaintiffs made another payment.
The supplementary agreement recorded an adjustment for encumbrances, leaving approximately half the sale price to be paid.
The suit was filed within the limitation period, and the evidence did not establish that the remaining payment was beyond the plaintiffs’ means or that they were unwilling to perform.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to aver and prove readiness and willingness. This is a question of fact determined from the pleadings, evidence, surrounding circumstances, and conduct; continuous approaches or incessant requests are not required. Where a suit is filed within limitation, delay alone does not defeat the claim. The Court relied on Mademsetty Satyanarayana v. G. Yelloji Rao, AIR 1965 SC 1405, and R. Lakshmikantham v. Devaraji, Civil Appeal No. 2420 of 2018, and considered Azhar Sultana v. B. Rajamani, (2009) 17 SCC 27, Veerayee Ammal v. Seeni Ammal, (2002) 1 SCC 134, and Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James, (2002) 9 SCC 582, as fact-specific decisions.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs proved readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract, and no personal bar prevented their claim for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaintiff_pleaded_readiness and plaintiff_made_part_payments and plaintiff_sought_performance_after_due_date and suit_filed_within_limitation and evidence_does_not_show_inability_or_unwillingness

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_pleaded_readiness: The plaintiff pleaded that they were ready and willing to perform their contractual obligations.
predicates.plaintiff_made_part_payments: The plaintiff made payments toward the agreed consideration before the dispute was resolved.
predicates.plaintiff_sought_performance_after_due_d: After the agreed date for performance passed without completion, the plaintiff called on the other party to perform.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation: The plaintiff filed the suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.evidence_does_not_show_inability_or_unwi: The evidence, considered as a whole, did not establish that the plaintiff lacked the means or willingness to perform.

members.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance cannot be entered on deemed admissions without examining whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform when the pleadings disclose a material factual dispute bearing on that requirement.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement that required the defendants to obtain tax permission and send it to him before he paid a further part of the sale price.
The plaintiff alleged that the permission had not been obtained or sent, while also pleading that the defendants asserted that they had obtained and sent it.
The dispute about obtaining and sending the permission could bear on whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act requires the plaintiff in a specific-performance suit to plead and establish readiness and willingness to perform. Under Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may require proof of facts despite deemed admissions. The court also relied on Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum and Section 58 of the Evidence Act concerning the court’s discretion to require proof of admitted facts.
members.conclusion: The disputed facts bearing on readiness and willingness had to be proved; the court could not decree specific performance merely because the defendants had filed no written statement.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.pleadings_disclose_dispute_material_to_r: The pleadings disclose a material factual dispute that bears on whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff’s readiness and willingness to perform a contract for specific performance must be assessed from the pleadings and evidence of ability and willingness to perform, rather than inferred from a delay in making up a court-fee deficiency.
material_facts: The plaintiff pleaded that he had always been ready and willing to perform the contract and was ready to pay the balance consideration.
The plaintiff deposited the balance consideration within the time allowed by the trial court.
The High Court treated the initial shortfall in court fee and the delay in making it good as evidence that the plaintiff lacked the capacity and willingness to perform.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to plead and establish by evidence that he has always been ready and willing to perform his part of the contract. Failure to meet that requirement is fatal, but the evidence here, including the timely deposit of the balance consideration, established compliance.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff had established that he was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract; the court-fee shortfall and delay did not justify the contrary inference.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaintiff_pleaded_continuing_readiness: The plaintiff stated in the pleadings that they had always been ready and willing to perform their contractual obligations.
predicates.plaintiff_deposited_balance_within_allow: The plaintiff deposited the unpaid contract consideration within the time allowed by the court.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff’s readiness and willingness to perform a contract may be established by pleadings read as a whole and need not be expressed in prescribed words.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement to sell and stated in the plaint that she had throughout been ready and willing to complete the sale.
The plaintiff also led evidence concerning her readiness and willingness to perform her part of the agreement.
The trial court and the first appellate court found in the plaintiff’s favour.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with its explanations, requires the plaintiff to aver and prove that she has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms to be performed by her. The pleading is read as a whole for its substance, not tested by a mechanical requirement for particular words. The Court relied on Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon, Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing and Construction (P) Ltd., Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, Syed Dastagir v. T.R. Gopalakrishna Setty, Motilal Jain v. Ramdasi Devi, Surya Narain Upadhyaya v. Ram Roop Pandey, and Aniglase Yohannan v. Ramlatha.
members.conclusion: The pleadings and evidence sufficiently established readiness and willingness; the High Court erred in finding that the requirement was not met merely because the plaint did not use a particular form of words.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.plaint_read_as_a_whole_shows_readiness: The plaintiff’s pleadings, read as a whole, conveyed readiness and willingness to perform her contractual obligations.
predicates.evidence_supports_readiness: The plaintiff presented evidence supporting her readiness and willingness to perform her contractual obligations.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser’s readiness and willingness to perform must be assessed from the entirety of the relevant facts and conduct, rather than by a fixed formula.
material_facts: The purchasers informed prospective buyers that the plot was subject to their agreement and made inquiries about the required approval.

They wrote that they would pay the balance once the vendors obtained the approval, and they promptly sued for specific performance after learning that approval had been granted without notice to them.
The purchasers had paid the earnest money, had funds available, and were carrying on a business from which they could arrange any remaining balance.
members.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness are not determined by a straight-jacket formula; they must be assessed from the entirety of the facts and circumstances relevant to the party’s intention and conduct. The court treated specific performance as discretionary relief, but discretion must be exercised according to sound and reasonable judicial principles rather than arbitrarily. The Specific Relief Act provisions raised at trial were sections 21 and 22; no earlier case was relied on for this readiness-and-willingness principle.
members.conclusion: The purchasers were ready and willing to perform their part of the contract.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_affirmed_willingness_to_pay and purchaser_protected_contract_interest and purchaser_promptly_sought_enforcement and purchaser_could_arrange_balance

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.purchaser_affirmed_willingness_to_pay: The purchaser communicated willingness to pay the balance when the agreed conditions for completion were met.
predicates.purchaser_protected_contract_interest: The purchaser took steps such as informing prospective buyers of the agreement or inquiring about a required approval.
predicates.purchaser_promptly_sought_enforcement: The purchaser promptly brought proceedings to enforce the agreement after learning that completion could proceed.
predicates.purchaser_could_arrange_balance: The purchaser had funds or a demonstrated ability to arrange the balance of the purchase price.

members.legal_issue: A petitioner seeking discretionary appellate relief must disclose interim court orders that materially bear on the issue raised, and suppression of those orders may warrant dismissal of the petition.
material_facts: The petitioners sought special leave to challenge the dismissal of their challenge to a land acquisition, arguing that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed because the awards were not made within the prescribed time.
Interim orders had stayed or affected proceedings concerning the lands: an earlier order directed status quo as to possession, and later orders stayed further acquisition proceedings.
The special leave petitions did not disclose those interim orders; the respondents brought them to the Court's attention in their counter-affidavit.

The interim orders were material because, under the explanation to Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, time during which action or proceedings pursuant to a declaration were stayed by a court order was excluded.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary, and a petitioner seeking it must make frank and full disclosure of material facts; suppression of facts directly bearing on the question raised may justify dismissal. The explanation to Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, excludes from the relevant period time during which action or proceedings pursuant to a declaration are stayed by a court order. Section 36 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976, applied the Land Acquisition Act provisions, so far as applicable, to acquisitions otherwise than by agreement. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The special leave petitions were dismissed because the petitioners suppressed material facts. Relief under Article 136 is discretionary, and a petitioner seeking it must make frank and full disclosure.

predicates.discretionary_appellate_relief_sought: The applicant seeks discretionary appellate relief from a court.
predicates.material_interim_orders_exist: Interim court orders exist that bear directly on an issue raised in the proceeding.
predicates.material_interim_orders_not_disclosed: The applicant does not disclose those material interim orders in the application.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking extraordinary or equitable relief must candidly disclose material facts, and suppression or distortion of those facts may justify dismissal without adjudicating the merits.
material_facts: The borrower sought writ relief without disclosing that it had created third-party interests in property mortgaged to the bank, despite an undertaking concerning that property.
The borrower had shifted machinery and materials without informing the bank, and third parties claimed tenancy rights in mortgaged property.
The Court found that material facts had been suppressed and that the borrower had not candidly placed its position before the courts.
members.legal_principle: A writ remedy under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and equitable, as is relief under Article 136.
