members.legal_issue: A stipulated period for completing a contract to sell immovable property does not, by itself, make time essential to the contract.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property and required the purchaser to complete registration within a stated period, failing which the earnest money would be forfeited.
The agreement also provided that the purchaser could compel the sellers to execute the sale deed if they evaded doing so.
The agreement did not state unmistakably that time was essential, and the court found no sufficiently strong circumstances displacing the normal presumption.
members.legal_principle: For a contract concerning the sale of immovable property, time is normally presumed not to be of the essence. Fixing a period for performance does not displace that presumption; sufficiently strong circumstances may do so. The Court applied Gomathinarayana Pillai & Ors. v. Palaniswami Nadar, [1967] 1 SCR 227, 233. No statutory provision is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: Time was not of the essence of the contract.

rule.if: sale_of_immovable_property_contract and fixed_performance_period and not unmistakable_time_essential_language and not strong_circumstances_showing_time_essential

predicates.sale_of_immovable_property_contract: The parties made a contract for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.fixed_performance_period: The contract set a period within which performance was to be completed.
predicates.unmistakable_time_essential_language: The contract stated unmistakably that time was essential to performance.
predicates.strong_circumstances_showing_time_essent: The circumstances were sufficiently strong to show that the parties intended time to be essential.

members.legal_issue: In a contract for the sale of immovable property, fixing completion dates and providing for a penalty do not by themselves make time essential.
material_facts: The parties orally agreed to sell a plot of land without fixing a completion date, then made written agreements fixing completion dates and providing for a penalty if either party failed to complete the sale.
The agreements did not state in unmistakable terms that time was essential.
Although the sellers urgently needed money, the circumstances did not show that the parties intended time to be essential.
members.legal_principle: Under section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872, failure to perform by a specified time makes a contract voidable for that reason only if the parties intended time to be essential. In a sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily presumed not to be essential; that presumption may be displaced by unmistakable express language or sufficiently strong circumstances. Fixing a completion date or including a penalty clause is not, by itself, enough. The court relied on Jamshed Khodaram Irani v. Burjorji Dhunjibhai and Stickney v. Keeble.
members.conclusion: Time was not of the essence of the contract.

predicates.contract_for_land_sale: The parties agreed to sell immovable property under a contract.
predicates.no_unmistakable_time_term: The contract did not express in unmistakable terms that the parties intended time to be essential.
predicates.no_strong_circumstances_making_time_esse: The circumstances surrounding the contract were not sufficiently strong to show that the parties intended time to be essential.

members.legal_issue: When time is not essential to a contract for the sale of land, delay alone does not establish default unless the other party gives notice requiring completion within a reasonable time.
material_facts: Time was not of the essence of the agreement.
The sellers did not give notice fixing a reasonable time for the purchaser to complete the sale.
The sellers instead sent a letter treating the agreement as cancelled, and the purchaser had delayed calling for completion.
members.legal_principle: Where time was not originally of the essence, default cannot be inferred merely from delay. A party seeking to bring the contract to an end must give notice requiring completion within a reasonable fixed time and the other party must fail to comply. The court relied on section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872, and Stickney v. Keeble.
members.conclusion: The purchaser's delay in calling for completion did not, by itself, establish default; the sellers' cancellation letter did not determine the purchaser's right to specific performance on that basis.

predicates.contract_did_not_make_time_essential: The parties' contract did not make timely completion essential.
predicates.other_party_gave_no_reasonable_completio: The other contracting party did not give notice requiring completion within a reasonable time.
predicates.delay_occurred: The party required to complete the contract delayed taking steps to do so.

members.legal_issue: Time may be the essence of a contract for the sale of immovable property when the agreement and surrounding circumstances show that the parties intended the specified payment deadline to be fundamental.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property and required a substantial part of the price to be paid within ten days.
The agreement used the word “only” both to qualify the payment amount and to qualify the ten-day period.
The vendor’s obligations to redeem the mortgage and obtain the income-tax clearance arose after payment of that sum.
The buyer did not make the payment by the deadline and sought to make it conditional on delivery of possession and completion of other obligations.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 55 of the Contract Act, a failure to perform by a specified time makes the contract voidable only if the parties intended time to be of the essence. In sales of immovable property, the usual presumption is that time is not essential; that presumption may be displaced by unequivocal language or by the contract’s terms, the nature of the property, and surrounding circumstances. The Court relied on Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Pallaniswami Nadar, Govind Prasad Chaturvedi v. Hari Dutt Shastri, Hind Construction Contractors v. State of Maharashtra, Indira Kaur v. Sheo Lal Kapoor, and Jamshed Khodaram Irani v. Burjorji Dhunjibhai.
members.conclusion: Although time is not ordinarily presumed to be of the essence in a sale of immovable property, the parties intended the payment deadline to be essential under this agreement.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_for_sale_of_immovable_property and substantial_payment_due_within_fixed_period and contract_language_emphasizes_payment_period and vendor_obligations_follow_payment

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.contract_for_sale_of_immovable_property: The agreement was for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.substantial_payment_due_within_fixed_per: The agreement required a substantial part of the price to be paid within a specified period.
predicates.contract_language_emphasizes_payment_per: The agreement’s wording treated the specified payment period as a distinct and emphasized term.
predicates.vendor_obligations_follow_payment: The agreement made the vendor’s relevant clearance or redemption obligations arise after the specified payment.

members.legal_issue: A stipulated deadline does not make time essential to a contract for sale of immovable property when the contract and the parties' case do not establish that intention.
material_facts: The agreement required the property to be conveyed within ten years.
The defendant did not plead or testify that time was essential, and the agreement did not unmistakably express that intention.
The lower courts nevertheless treated time as essential.
members.legal_principle: The normal presumption for an agreement to sell immovable property is that time is not of the essence; the parties' intention must be assessed from the contract and the circumstances. The Court relied on Govind Prasad Chaturvedi v. Hari Dutt Shastri, which also cautions against deciding that time is essential when the issue was not pleaded or tried.
members.conclusion: The lower courts erred in treating time as essential to the contract.

predicates.immovable_property_sale_agreement: The parties made an agreement for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.no_unmistakable_time_essential_term: The agreement does not unmistakably state that timely performance is essential to the bargain.
predicates.no_party_asserted_time_essential: No party pleaded or advanced the case that time was essential to the contract.

members.legal_issue: When time is not of the essence in a contract for the sale of immovable property, a buyer seeking specific performance must act within a reasonable time assessed in light of the circumstances.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of land and specified a date for completion, although the courts found that time was not of the essence.
The seller had undertaken to remove an obstruction from the property; the lower courts found that it was removed before the buyer demanded completion.
The buyer demanded execution of the sale deed after the obstruction was removed, gave public notice of the agreement, and filed suit in the same month after the seller did not complete the sale.
members.legal_principle: Even when time is not of the essence, a party seeking specific performance must perform its part within a reasonable time. Reasonableness is assessed from all the facts and circumstances, including the express terms of the contract, the nature of the property, the object of the agreement, and the surrounding circumstances. The Court relied on Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani and K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan.
members.conclusion: The buyer commenced legal action without delay and within a reasonable time. The second appellate court was not justified in disturbing the lower courts’ finding on that point.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and immovable_property_sale and time_not_essential and seller_completed_preparatory_obligation and buyer_demanded_transfer_promptly and buyer_filed_suit_promptly

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.immovable_property_sale: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property.
predicates.time_not_essential: The circumstances establish that time was not of the essence of the agreement.
predicates.seller_completed_preparatory_obligation: The seller completed an agreed preparatory obligation affecting the property before the buyer demanded completion.
predicates.buyer_demanded_transfer_promptly: The buyer promptly demanded transfer after the relevant preparatory obligation was completed.
predicates.buyer_filed_suit_promptly: The buyer promptly filed suit after the seller failed to complete the sale following the demand.

members.legal_issue: Even when time is not expressly made essential to a contract for the sale of immovable property, the parties must perform within a reasonable time assessed in light of the agreement and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The agreement did not state a fixed deadline for performance, but contemplated that plans and clearances would be obtained and construction completed within a period that indicated an expectation of performance within a few years.
The purchaser was responsible for securing the necessary approvals and clearances.
The transaction remained incomplete for several years before litigation began.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the court's discretion must be exercised with regard to the agreement's time limits and all relevant circumstances. Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani establishes that time is not presumed to be of the essence in sales of immovable property, but reasonable time may be inferred from the agreement, the property, and surrounding circumstances. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan holds that contractual time limits cannot be ignored and that reasonable time must be assessed in context.
members.conclusion: The purchaser's delay in performing its obligations was not reasonable, notwithstanding the absence of an express fixed deadline for completing the agreement.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and immovable_property_sale_contract and contract_does_not_expressly_make_time_essential and agreement_indicates_expected_timing_for_performance and purchaser_delayed_beyond_reasonable_time_in_context

members.legal_issue: A first appellate court deciding whether time was intended to be essential in a contract for the sale of immovable property must apply the presumption against time being essential and assess the parties' intention from the contract and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The dispute arose from a contract for the sale of immovable property that made obtaining the required permission by a specified time a condition, with the possibility of mutual extension and a consequence for failure to obtain permission.
The High Court considered earlier authorities but did not consider the Constitution Bench decision in Chand Rani, which the Supreme Court said governed the applicable legal test.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether time was the essence of this particular contract.
members.legal_principle: Under Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, time is not presumed to be of the essence in a contract for the sale of immovable property. An intention to make time essential must be expressed unequivocally; even where time is not essential, performance within a reasonable time may be inferred from the contract's express terms, the nature of the property, and the surrounding circumstances. K.S. Vidyanandam v. Vairavan followed the Constitution Bench rule.
members.conclusion: The High Court ought to have considered the Constitution Bench rule when assessing the contract; the Supreme Court expressed no view on the merits of whether time was essential in this case.

predicates.first_appeal: The court is hearing the first appeal in the case.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_contract: The dispute concerns a contract for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.time_essence_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether the contract made performance by a particular time essential.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for attempted murder must be reduced where a grievous, life-endangering injury does not establish an intention to cause death, while the evidence supports grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon.
material_facts: The appellant thrust a spear into the victim’s chest, causing a grievous wound that endangered the victim’s life.
The other three recorded injuries were simple, and the court found that the chest injury was not shown to be one that would necessarily have caused death without timely medical aid.
The evidence therefore did not establish the intention to cause death required to sustain the attempted-murder conviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code requires the intent or knowledge specified for an attempt to murder. On these facts, that intent was not established beyond doubt; the grievous injury caused by the spear instead supported conviction under Section 326 IPC.
members.conclusion: The attempted-murder conviction was replaced with a conviction for grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon, and the sentence was reduced from five years to three years of rigorous imprisonment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_attempted_murder_co: The case is a criminal appeal challenging an attempted-murder conviction.
predicates.grievous_injury_caused_by_dangerous_weap: The accused caused grievous hurt using a dangerous weapon.
predicates.death_intent_not_established: The evidence does not establish an intention or knowledge sufficient to support an attempted-murder conviction.

members.legal_issue: An assault causing simple hurt with a weapon likely to cause death when used as a weapon of offence supports conviction for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon rather than attempted murder.
material_facts: The appellant struck the victim on the head with a farasa.
The resulting scalp wound was classified as a simple injury.
The court found that the weapon, used as a weapon of offence, was likely to cause death, but the injury did not support the attempted-murder conviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 324 of the Indian Penal Code applies to voluntarily causing hurt with an instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death. The court applied that provision because the injury was simple but the weapon met that description; it did not cite an earlier case.
members.conclusion: The attempted-murder conviction was replaced with a conviction for voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon, and the sentence was reduced from six years to two years of rigorous imprisonment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_attempted_murder_co: The case is a criminal appeal challenging an attempted-murder conviction.

predicates.weapon_used_as_weapon_likely_to_cause_de: The instrument, used as it was in the assault, was likely to cause death.

members.legal_issue: Instigating an assault with deadly weapons, without sufficient proof that the instigation was to kill, supports conviction for abetting hurt with a dangerous weapon rather than abetting attempted murder.
material_facts: The appellant instigated the others to assault the victim, and the assault was carried out with deadly weapons.
The victim’s testimony described the instigation as an order to kill, but the earlier recorded statement described it as an order to assault.
The court treated the established instigation as one to assault with deadly weapons and did not find the more serious allegation sufficient to sustain abetment of attempted murder.
members.legal_principle: Sections 324 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code apply to abetment of voluntarily causing hurt with an instrument used as a weapon of offence and likely to cause death. The conflicting accounts of the instigation supported the lesser offence rather than abetment of attempted murder. The judgment cites no earlier case.
members.conclusion: The conviction for abetting attempted murder was replaced with a conviction for abetting voluntarily causing hurt by a dangerous weapon; the two-year sentence was unchanged.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_abetment_of_attempt: The case is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for abetting attempted murder.
predicates.accused_instigated_assault_with_dangerou: The accused instigated an assault that was carried out with dangerous weapons.
predicates.instigation_to_kill_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the accused instigated the assailants to kill the victim.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for attempted murder may be sustained where the accused’s intention to kill is established from the circumstances and the accused committed an overt act in execution of that intention, even if the victim’s injuries were not independently proved through every available medical record.
material_facts: The accused struck the victim on the head with a pharsi.
The victim became unconscious and deeply comatose and had a large extradural haematoma that required urgent surgery.
A neurosurgeon testified that without the operation the head injury would have caused the victim’s death.
Two injured eyewitnesses described the assault, and their evidence was corroborated by medical evidence.
The victim did not testify, and the defence relied on the absence of certain scan, X-ray and operation records.
members.legal_principle: Section 307 IPC requires proof of an intention to commit murder and an act done in furtherance of that intention; a fatal or otherwise death-capable injury is not essential. Intention may be inferred from circumstances including the weapon used, the part of the body targeted and the nature and severity of the injuries. The Court relied on State of M.P. v. Kashiram, State of Maharashtra v. Balram Bama Patil, Girija Shanker v. State of U.P., R. Prakash v. State of Karnataka and State of M.P. v. Saleem. It also held that injured eyewitnesses’ evidence is entitled to great weight and requires cogent and convincing grounds to discard when it is credible and medically corroborated.
members.conclusion: The conviction for attempted murder was upheld because the weapon, the head injury, the severity of the blows and the medical evidence supported the finding of an intention to kill and an overt act in execution of that intention.

members.legal_issue: An attempt-to-murder conviction requires proof of the intention or knowledge necessary to constitute murder, assessed from all the circumstances and not merely from the injury caused.
material_facts: The accused took part in a sudden fight in which both sides sustained injuries.
Although the accused had weapons with sharp edges, they used only the blunt sides, including when attacked by the other side.
The court found no motive or intention to kill.
members.legal_principle: Under section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, the act must be done with the intention or knowledge, and in the circumstances, necessary to constitute murder. Intention is gathered from all the circumstances, including the weapon and manner of its use, motive, severity and location of the injury, and not merely from the consequences. No earlier cases are relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The acquittal on the attempt-to-murder charge was not disturbed because the circumstances did not establish the intention or knowledge necessary to constitute murder.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for attempted murder is not sustained where the accused’s responsibility for the grievous injury is not established, although the evidence establishes that the accused caused simple hurt with a sharp weapon.
material_facts: The accused was found to have inflicted one of two spear injuries on the victim.
One injury was grievous and located on the chest, while the other was simple and located on the thigh.
The eyewitness did not identify which injury the accused inflicted.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the offence under Section 307 of the Penal Code from causing hurt with a sharp weapon under Section 324. Because the evidence did not identify the grievous injury as the one inflicted by the accused, the Court, as a matter of caution, convicted him only for causing simple hurt with a sharp weapon. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The attempted-murder conviction was altered to a conviction for causing simple hurt with a sharp weapon, and the sentence was reduced.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for attempted murder is sustainable where the evidence establishes an intentional murderous assault, although the sentence may be reduced in light of the circumstances.
material_facts: The accused attacked his wife with a sharp-edged weapon and caused numerous serious injuries, including deep cuts to her head and injuries to several other parts of her body.
The wife survived and testified about the attack; other witnesses corroborated her account.
The medical evidence documented the injuries, and the Court found no reason to interfere with the attempted-murder conviction.
The Court considered a sentence of seven years' rigorous imprisonment sufficient in place of the ten-year sentence imposed below.
members.legal_principle: Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code governs attempted murder. Intention may be inferred from the circumstances, including the weapon used and the parts of the body struck; the Court found the evidence of the deliberate assault and the serious injuries sufficient to sustain the conviction. It nevertheless reduced the sentence in the circumstances of the case.
members.conclusion: The conviction for attempted murder of the wife was upheld, but the sentence was reduced from ten years to seven years' rigorous imprisonment.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for attempt to murder with common intention may be affirmed while the sentence is reduced.
material_facts: One injured witness sustained several contusions and a lacerated wound, and medical examination disclosed fractures in the arm and hand bones.
The High Court had convicted both accused under Section 307 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for causing injuries to that witness.
The Supreme Court confirmed the conviction but reduced one accused's sentence.
members.legal_principle: The Court confirmed the conviction under Sections 307 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code and reduced the sentence. The judgment gives no separate explanation for the sentence reduction and cites no earlier cases for it.
members.conclusion: The conviction under Section 307 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code was confirmed, while the sentence imposed on the accused whose appeal was allowed in part was reduced.

members.legal_issue: An unexplained and inordinate delay in filing a second appeal is not condonable when the appellant knew of the adverse decision, had the capacity and duty to manage its legal matters diligently, and relies on counsel’s inaction without timely follow-up.
material_facts: The appellant had contested the suit and first appeal and knew of the adverse first-appellate decision.
The appellant was a statutory authority with an established legal department and panel of lawyers.
The second appeal was filed 1,942 days late.
The appellant attributed the delay to its lawyer’s failure to take timely steps, but did not ensure prompt filing or engage another lawyer when necessary.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, delay may be condoned only where sufficient cause is shown. An appellant must act with due diligence to ensure an appeal is filed on time; blaming counsel does not constitute sufficient cause where the appellant knew of the adverse decision and failed to supervise the matter or take timely steps to secure filing.
members.conclusion: The explanation did not establish sufficient cause, so the delay was rightly not condoned and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: second_appeal_delay_petition and inordinate_delay and inadequate_explanation and appellant_knew_adverse_decision and institutional_legal_capacity and counsel_blame_without_diligent_follow_up

predicates.counsel_blame_without_diligent_follow_up: The appellant blamed counsel for the delay but did not promptly ensure filing or take steps to replace or supervise counsel.
predicates.delay_not_condoned: The delay is not excused and the delayed appeal is not entertained.

members.legal_issue: An appeal filed after an inordinate delay should not be admitted where the applicant fails to give a plausible explanation and its account is contradicted by its prior knowledge and conduct.
material_facts: The institutional respondent appealed a trial-court decree more than four years after it was made.

The respondent’s officers had been aware of both the original and subsequent proceedings, had instructed advocates, and had received information about hearing dates, but did not ensure that the case was defended or that an appeal was filed promptly.
The respondent claimed that its legal department learned of the decree only years later, an assertion the Court found false in light of the record.
The opposing party filed a detailed reply to the delay application, but the High Court overlooked it and also proceeded on an incorrect understanding of the length of the delay.
members.legal_principle: Limitation serves public policy by requiring legal remedies to be pursued within a fixed period, while allowing courts to excuse delay for sufficient cause. Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the approach may be liberal for short delays but must be stricter for inordinate delays; no hard-and-fast rule applies. The same standard applies to private litigants and the State, although some latitude may be appropriate for the State’s collective responsibilities and administrative processes. That latitude does not excuse an implausible or false explanation. The Court relied on Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji; N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy; Vedabai v. Shantaram Baburao Patil; G. Ramegowda v. Special Land Acquisition Officer; State of Haryana v. Chandra Mani; State of U.P. v. Harish Chandra; State of Bihar v. Ratan Lal Sahu; State of Nagaland v. Lipok Ao; and State (NCT of Delhi) v. Ahmed Jaan. The application was made under Order 41 Rule 3A of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order condoning the delay was set aside. The application for condonation was dismissed, and the appeal against the trial-court decree stood dismissed as barred by time.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_decree: An institutional litigant filed an appeal against a trial-court decree.

predicates.materially_false_delay_account: The litigant gave an account of when it learned of the decision that was contradicted by the record.
predicates.high_court_overlooked_opposition: The court condoning the delay failed to consider the opposing party’s reply and relevant facts about the delay.

members.legal_issue: A prolonged delay in applying to substitute a deceased respondent in an appeal is not excused when the applicant had reason to know of the death and the circumstances do not adequately explain the delay.
material_facts: A respondent died while the appeal was pending, but the application to bring his legal representatives on record was filed several years later.
Even after excluding the time taken to obtain the High Court certificate, the application was delayed by about three and a half years.
The deceased was a prominent local resident, news of his death appeared in newspapers, and the applicant lived nearby.
The applicant had conducted the litigation for many years, remained in contact with her advocates, and had a son-in-law helping her.
The applicant relied on her poverty, illiteracy, lack of a male family member to manage the litigation, and the fact that the representatives had been added in later final decree proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XVI, rule 14 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, an application to bring a deceased respondent’s legal representatives on record must be made within the prescribed period, excluding time taken to obtain the High Court certificate. On the circumstances presented, the applicant’s asserted hardship did not sufficiently explain the substantial delay.
members.conclusion: There was no sufficient ground to excuse the delay in bringing the deceased respondent’s legal representatives on record in the appeal.

predicates.substitution_delay_application_in_appeal: The applicant sought to add a deceased respondent’s legal representatives to an appeal after the respondent died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.substantial_delay: The application was filed substantially beyond the prescribed time, even after excluding time taken to obtain a required certificate.
predicates.applicant_had_notice_of_death: The circumstances, including the public reporting of the death and the applicant’s proximity to the deceased, indicated that the applicant knew or could have learned of the death.
predicates.applicant_was_actively_conducting_litiga: The applicant had long conducted the litigation, maintained contact with legal representatives, and received assistance from a family member.

members.legal_issue: A public university’s delay in filing an intra-court appeal is not condonable when the extensive delay is supported only by inadequate administrative explanations and the surrounding circumstances show that the delay was not reasonably accounted for.
material_facts: The university filed its intra-court appeal 916 days after dismissal of its writ petition.
The university attributed the delay to deliberations by its authorities, the vacancy in the Vice-Chancellor’s office, committee reports, and the need for Executive Council approval.

The Vice-Chancellor who had overseen the writ proceedings remained in office for about six months after the judgment, and the Executive Council approved filing the appeal more than a year before it was filed.
The record did not adequately explain the delay at each stage, including the substantial period after the Executive Council’s approval.
The public transport body had received substantial funds for the project, which were being used for metro services to the public.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits condonation where sufficient cause is shown. Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Katiji supports a liberal, justice-oriented approach, but does not make condonation automatic; Postmaster General v. Living Media India Ltd. establishes that routine administrative delay is insufficient without a reasonable explanation and bona fide effort. The Court also relied on the principle that accrued consequences and the facts of each case must be weighed carefully.
members.conclusion: The university failed to establish sufficient cause for the 916-day delay, and the High Court was justified in refusing to condone it.

members.legal_issue: A delayed application to bring the legal representatives of a deceased sole appellant on record should be refused where the applicants fail to establish a bona fide and plausible sufficient cause for the delay.
material_facts: The sole appellant died while the appeal was pending, but the legal representatives did not apply to be brought on record for a considerable period.
The legal representatives attributed the delay to not knowing that the appeal was pending, but their accounts about their residences and knowledge were inconsistent.
One legal representative had testified in the trial, undermining the claim that the family was unaware of the proceedings.
The applicants did not explain why they failed to notify counsel of the death or why they did not promptly act after learning the appeal was pending.
The applications lacked supporting material for the alleged communication from counsel and contained averments the Court found untrue.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22 Rules 3 and 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Section 5 of the Limitation Act, an application to set aside abatement and bring legal representatives on record requires sufficient cause. The expression is to be applied reasonably and, where appropriate, liberally to advance substantial justice, but liberal construction does not excuse negligence, inaction, lack of bona fides, or an implausible explanation. The decisive consideration is the sufficiency of the explanation, assessed with the applicant’s conduct and the other party’s accrued rights, rather than the length of delay alone. The Court relied on Union of India v. Ram Charan, Ramlal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd., P.K. Ramachandran v. State of Kerala, Mithailal Dalsangar Singh v. Annabai Devram Kini, Perumon Bhagvathy Devaswom v. Bhargavi Amma, and Katari Suryanarayana v. Koppisetti Subba Rao; it also discussed the distinct facts of other cited decisions.
members.conclusion: The applicants failed to show sufficient cause, so the application to condone the delay was dismissed; the related application to bring the legal representatives on record did not survive.

rule.if: appeal_after_sole_appellant_death and delayed_substitution_request and (inconsistent_heir_accounts or heir_knew_of_proceeding) and unexplained_post_knowledge_inaction

predicates.appeal_after_sole_appellant_death: An appeal was pending when its sole appellant died.

members.legal_issue: A substantial delay in filing an appeal cannot be condoned when a material period remains unexplained and the applicant's conduct shows gross negligence or want of due diligence.
material_facts: The applicants sought to file a second appeal approximately 1011 days after the first appellate court's decision.
Their delay application referred to illness and advised bed rest only until 15 March 2017, but did not explain the period from then until the second appeal was filed in 2021.
The High Court condoned the delay on the grounds that the appeal should be heard on its merits, there was no wilful negligence or want of due diligence, and costs could compensate the opposing party.
The Supreme Court found no sufficient or satisfactory explanation for the unexplained period and found gross negligence or want of due diligence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, condonation depends on sufficient cause and the court must exercise its discretion judicially. Ramlal, Motilal and Chhotelal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd. recognizes both the decree-holder's accrued right after limitation expires and the court's discretion to advance substantial justice where sufficient cause exists and negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides is not imputable. P.K. Ramachandran v. State of Kerala requires a reasonable, satisfactory, or appropriate explanation and rejects condonation on equitable grounds alone. Pundlik Jalam Patil v. Executive Engineer, Jalgaon Medium Project emphasizes limitation's public-policy purpose and that courts do not assist stale claims. Basawaraj v. Special Land Acquisition Officer holds that sufficient cause cannot be liberally interpreted where negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides is present, and that conditions cannot justify condonation where no sufficient cause is shown.
members.conclusion: The High Court had not exercised its discretion judiciously. Its order condoning the delay was set aside, and the second appeal was dismissed as delayed.

rule.if: appellate_review_of_delay_condonation and substantial_appeal_delay and material_period_unexplained and applicant_negligent

predicates.appellate_review_of_delay_condonation: A higher court is reviewing an order that condoned delay in filing an appeal.
predicates.substantial_appeal_delay: The applicant filed the appeal after a substantial delay.
predicates.material_period_unexplained: The applicant did not explain a material period of the delay.
predicates.applicant_negligent: The applicant's conduct showed gross negligence or want of due diligence.
predicates.delay_condonation_order_set_aside_and_ap: The order condoning delay is set aside and the delayed appeal is dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Delay cannot be condoned when the applicant’s prolonged default is attributable to gross negligence and no reasonable explanation establishes sufficient cause.
material_facts: In a civil appeal, the sole respondent died and the appellants were informed of the death but did not take timely steps to bring the legal representatives on record.
The court directed the appellants to take the required steps, but they did not comply, and the appeal stood dismissed after abatement.
The appellants later sought to set aside the dismissal and abatement, with applications involving delays of 883 days and 3703 days.

The explanation attributed the omissions to the inaction and inefficiency of officials and government pleaders; the High Court itself described the delay as unjustifiable but nevertheless condoned it.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act permits condonation only where sufficient cause is shown. A liberal, justice-oriented approach does not dispense with reasonable conduct or justify unexplained delay caused by negligence, default, or inaction, particularly when a valuable right has accrued to the opposing party. Order XXII CPC is intended to facilitate effective adjudication, but its flexibility does not eliminate the requirement to explain delay. The Court relied on Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Katiji, N. Balakrishnan v. M. Krishnamurthy, Mithailal Dalsangar Singh v. Annabai Devram Kini, Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta, and Balwant Singh v. Jagdish Singh.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in condoning the delay; its order allowing the applications was set aside.

rule.if: civil_appeal_after_sole_respondent_died and (prolonged_delay or procedural_default) and not adequate_explanation

predicates.civil_appeal_after_sole_respondent_died: The matter is a civil appeal in which the sole respondent has died.
predicates.prolonged_delay: The applicant waited a substantial time before seeking the procedural relief.
predicates.procedural_default: The applicant failed to take required steps despite being informed of the death or directed by the court to act.

members.legal_issue: A delayed appeal should not receive condonation where the applicants had prior knowledge of the proceedings and judgment, gave an incorrect account of when they learned of the judgment, and were negligent in pursuing the case.
material_facts: The applicants sought condonation of a 349-day delay in appealing an ex-parte decree, claiming they first learned of it from a constable shortly before filing their appeal.
Court records showed the applicants were present during the proceedings before the decree and had opportunities to participate but did not do so.
The applicants had also referred to the decree in another proceeding before the date on which they claimed to have first learned of it.
The underlying suit had previously been remanded at the applicants’ instance, but they did not file a written statement despite opportunities and did not diligently pursue the remanded proceedings.
The lower courts found the applicants’ account incorrect and their conduct negligent.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, delay may be condoned when sufficient cause is shown. The applicants did not show sufficient cause where the record established prior knowledge, their explanation was incorrect, and they were negligent in pursuing the matter. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The refusal to condone the delay was correct, and the appeal challenging that refusal was dismissed.

rule.if: delayed_appeal_condonation_request and applicants_had_prior_knowledge and (applicants_gave_incorrect_account or applicants_neglected_case)

predicates.delayed_appeal_condonation_request: The applicants sought permission to pursue an appeal filed after the applicable time limit.
predicates.applicants_had_prior_knowledge: The applicants knew of the relevant proceedings or judgment before the time they claimed to have first learned of it.
predicates.applicants_gave_incorrect_account: The applicants gave an account of when or how they learned of the judgment that was contradicted by the record.
predicates.applicants_neglected_case: The applicants failed to participate in or diligently pursue the case despite opportunities to do so.
predicates.delay_condonation_refused: The court declines to excuse the delay in filing the appeal.

members.legal_issue: Exempting agricultural property and certain commercial or public-use premises from an urban-property pre-emption law does not make the law discriminatory when those properties form distinct classes from private residential property.
material_facts: The challenged law applied to urban immovable property but excluded agricultural property and premises such as shops, inns, market enclosures, places of worship, and similar buildings.
The Court treated agricultural property as a distinct class and treated the other exempted premises as places to which the public resorted, distinct from private residential property.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and held that the excluded properties could be treated as distinct classes from private residential property. It referred to Karim Ahmad v. Rahmat Elahi in discussing the meaning of a market enclosure.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the challenged provision did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality on account of those exclusions.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge_to_pro: A party alleged that a property pre-emption law discriminated between classes of property owners or properties.
predicates.law_distinguishes_private_residences_fro: The law excludes agricultural property or premises to which the public resorts while applying to private residential property.
predicates.those_property_types_are_distinct_classe: The excluded agricultural or public-use premises differ in relevant character from private residential property.

members.legal_issue: A preventive procedure for restricting premises may create distinct procedural classes without violating the constitutional guarantee of equality when the classification has a reasonable relation to the provision’s purpose.
material_facts: The challenged provision covered both cases in which conduct could also be prosecuted under separate penal provisions and cases involving only the preventive premises measure.
The penal provisions required a regular trial and allowed an appeal, while the premises procedure was preventive, summary, and directed at the use of premises.

The premises measure was intended to reduce the likelihood of brothels or prostitution being conducted near public places, and the elements of the penal offences were not identical to those required for the premises measure.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification based on a real and substantial distinction that bears a reasonable relation to the object of the law. Section 18 of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, addressed premises through a preventive summary procedure, whereas sections 3 and 7 imposed punishment for offences through regular trials with rights of appeal. The classification therefore had a rational connection to the distinct purposes of those provisions and did not offend the principle in State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar.
members.conclusion: The classification under section 18 was reasonable and did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_premises_procedure and (case_involves_premises_measure_with_penal_offence or case_involves_premises_measure_only) and procedure_tracks_distinct_purposes

predicates.equality_challenge_to_premises_procedure: A person challenges an enactment’s premises-related procedure as denying equal protection.
predicates.case_involves_premises_measure_with_pena: The case concerns premises subject to a preventive measure and conduct that may also constitute a separately punishable offence.
predicates.case_involves_premises_measure_only: The case concerns premises subject to a preventive measure without a separately prosecuted offence.
predicates.procedure_tracks_distinct_purposes: The law provides different procedures that correspond to the distinct preventive and punitive purposes of the measures.

members.legal_issue: Exempting public housing property from rent-control protections does not deny equal protection merely because tenants of cooperative housing societies remain protected when the societies and their tenants are not shown to be similarly situated.
material_facts: The challenged amendment excluded land and buildings belonging to or vested in the housing board from rent-control protections.
The board was established to frame housing schemes and address an acute shortage of accommodation, was controlled by the government, and had no shareholders interested in distributing profits.

Cooperative housing societies could earn profits distributable to their members, and no evidence established that they had tenants in a relationship comparable to the occupants of the board's properties.
members.legal_principle: Under article 14 of the Constitution, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia that distinguishes the grouped persons or things from others and must bear a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court relied on article 14 and section 3-A of the Bombay Housing Board Act, inserted by the 1951 amendment; it relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The comparison with cooperative housing societies did not establish discrimination, and the amendment was not unconstitutional on this ground.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption and public_housing_body and board_has_no_profit_motive and cooperative_societies_may_distribute_profits and no_evidence_of_comparable_tenancy

predicates.equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption: A litigant challenged an exemption from rent-control protections as unequal treatment under a constitutional equality guarantee.
predicates.public_housing_body: A public body was created to address housing needs through housing schemes.
predicates.board_has_no_profit_motive: The public housing body was government-controlled and had no shareholders interested in distributing profits.
predicates.cooperative_societies_may_distribute_pro: The compared cooperative societies could earn profits distributable to their members.
predicates.no_evidence_of_comparable_tenancy: The litigant produced no evidence that the compared societies had tenants in a relationship comparable to the occupants of the public body's property.

members.legal_issue: Exempting tenants of government or public-authority housing from rent-control protections while protecting tenants of private landlords does not deny equal protection when the classes are differently situated and the distinction serves the public housing purpose.
material_facts: The rent-control law exempted premises belonging to the government or a local authority, and the amendment expressly extended an exemption to land and buildings belonging to or vested in the housing board.
The board was established to address an acute shortage of accommodation and was controlled by the government.

The Court considered that government and public housing bodies would not be expected to act from a profit-making motive to raise rents unduly or eject tenants, unlike private landlords who might do so.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification based on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court held that tenants of government, local-authority, or housing-board property were not on an equal footing with tenants of private landlords because public bodies served a housing purpose and were not expected to act for profit. The Court relied on article 14, section 4 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and section 3-A of the Bombay Housing Board Act; it relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The difference in treatment rested on an intelligible distinction rationally related to the public purpose of addressing the need for housing; neither section 4 nor section 3-A violated article 14.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption and public_housing_body and public_body_has_housing_mandate and public_body_not_expected_to_seek_profit and private_landlords_may_seek_profit

predicates.equality_challenge_to_rent_exemption: A litigant challenged an exemption from rent-control protections as unequal treatment under a constitutional equality guarantee.
predicates.public_housing_body: A public body owned or managed housing property.
predicates.public_body_has_housing_mandate: The public body was established to address housing needs and accommodation shortages.
predicates.public_body_not_expected_to_seek_profit: The public body was not expected to act from a profit-making motive to raise rents unduly or eject occupants.
predicates.private_landlords_may_seek_profit: Private landlords could act from a profit-making motive in setting rents or seeking to remove tenants.

members.legal_issue: Classifying buildings for a housing-safety levy by residential use, tenancy, age, and construction does not violate equal protection where those distinctions relate to the danger addressed and the measure is directed to a feasible part of that problem.
material_facts: The legislation focused on existing residential buildings occupied by tenants, although dangerous buildings also existed among non-residential properties and buildings constructed later.
Government and municipal studies described recurrent collapses, the age and construction of many residential buildings, and the urgency of addressing the danger to their occupants.
The legislation divided taxable buildings into categories based on when and how they were built, and imposed the levy by reference to each building’s rateable value.

Buildings within the same category could differ in their actual condition, and some buildings did not need repairs; the levy’s primary purpose was to prevent collapses, not to ensure that every taxpayer received an individual repair benefit.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to taxing laws, but the legislature has substantial latitude in fiscal classification. A classification must rest on an intelligible differentia related to the law’s objective; a legislature may tax some objects without taxing all, and differences in burden or benefit within a class do not alone establish discrimination. The Court relied on K. T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, Raja Jagannath v. State of U.P., East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Khandige Sham Bhatt v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Nalla Raja Reddy, Ravi Varma v. Union of India, and Twyford Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Kerala. It held Moopil Nair and New Manek Chowk Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad inapplicable.
members.conclusion: The classifications were based on intelligible differences connected to the legislation’s objectives and feasibility. Differences in actual condition or in the individual benefit received did not make the classifications discriminatory.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_law and existing_tenant_housing_faces_a_housing_safety_hazard and the_legislature_prioritizes_a_feasible_part_of_that_hazard and classification_tracks_building_age_or_construction_or_occupancy and levy_is_assessed_by_property_value

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_law: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law imposing a tax.
predicates.existing_tenant_housing_faces_a_housing_: Existing housing occupied by tenants presents a danger to occupants from unsafe buildings or potential collapse.
predicates.the_legislature_prioritizes_a_feasible_p: The legislature chooses to address a practicable part of a wider safety problem as a priority.
predicates.classification_tracks_building_age_or_co: The tax categories distinguish buildings by characteristics such as their age, construction, or occupancy.
predicates.levy_is_assessed_by_property_value: The levy is calculated by reference to the value assigned to each property.

members.legal_issue: Exempting property groups with materially different uses, occupancy relationships, or regulatory circumstances from a housing-safety levy does not violate equal protection.
material_facts: The legislation exempted, among other groups, owner-occupied buildings, buildings used exclusively for non-residential purposes, buildings occupied on leave and licence, buildings belonging to or leased to cooperative societies, and buildings constructed after the legislation began.

The Court found that these groups differed from residential buildings occupied by tenants in relevant ways, including the application of rent controls, the rights and security of occupants, and the relationship between cooperative societies and their members.
The legislation addressed the particular circumstances associated with residential tenancies and the reluctance or inability of landlords to maintain such buildings.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits different treatment where an exemption distinguishes a class on an intelligible basis connected to the law’s purpose. Buildings outside the targeted residential-tenancy problem, and those with materially different occupancy or regulatory relationships, need not be treated as equivalent to tenanted residential buildings. The Court applied the classification principles stated in Khandige Sham Bhatt v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer and its discussion of Article 14 in relation to taxing laws.
members.conclusion: The exempted groups formed distinct classes relevant to the legislation’s purpose, and the exemptions did not violate equal protection.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_exemptio: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of an exemption from a tax.
predicates.the_levy_targets_a_defined_housing_or_oc: The tax is directed at a defined problem associated with a particular kind of housing or occupancy.
predicates.exempted_properties_have_materially_dist: The exempted properties differ from the taxed properties in their use, occupancy relationships, or applicable regulatory circumstances.

members.legal_issue: Different prices for public housing do not violate equal treatment where pricing distinguishes projects and reflects relevant differences, without unequal treatment among allottees in the comparable project class.
material_facts: The purchasers compared surcharge-bearing flats with flats in other schemes or at other times, including flats in an area where construction costs were higher because of rocky land.
The Authority’s pricing factors included land, materials, labour, transport, land availability, supervision, and management, which varied by time and place.

The surcharge was applied to the relevant schemes to help reduce the cost of housing for lower-income groups, while allottees in the comparable project class were not shown to have received unequal treatment.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unequal treatment within a class unless justified by a valid classification; persons similarly situated must be assessed in relation to the purpose of the classification. Executive price fixation allows wide discretion, and courts do not ordinarily review economic pricing mechanics absent statutory control or patent hostile discrimination. The Court relied on Prag Ice & Oil Mills v. Union of India, Avinder Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills, and East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the comparison across income groups alone was insufficient: a relevant pricing class could be defined by income group, area, time, and scheme, and the challenged pricing did not establish discrimination within that class.

rule.if: public_housing_price_equality_challenge and project_specific_pricing and relevant_costs_vary and not unequal_treatment_within_comparable_project

predicates.public_housing_price_equality_challenge: A purchaser challenged different prices charged for housing provided by a public authority.
predicates.project_specific_pricing: The authority set prices by reference to distinct housing projects or schemes.
predicates.relevant_costs_vary: Relevant land, construction, labour, transport, or management costs differed between projects, locations, or periods.
predicates.unequal_treatment_within_comparable_proj: Allottees in the same comparable project class were treated differently in price without justification.

members.legal_issue: Different rent-fixation procedures for older and newly constructed premises do not violate equal protection when the classification is reasonable and the criteria for fixing rent are substantially similar.
material_facts: The rent-control scheme assigned rent fixation for premises completed before the specified commencement date to courts, and rent fixation for premises completed later to a rent controller.
The criteria for fixing rent for older and newer premises were substantially similar, although the scheme included some differences in timing and returns on improvements.
The court accepted that differences in construction costs, investment returns, housing shortage, and the possibility of excessive rents for newly built premises justified the classification.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification based on intelligible differentia with a rational connection to the law’s objectives. The criteria for older and newer premises were substantially similar, and the differences were justifiable in light of their different circumstances. The court approved G.D. Soni v. S. N. Bhalla, A.I.R. 1959 Punj. 381, and relied on the safeguards requiring reasons, consideration of all circumstances, and an appeal.
members.conclusion: The provisions governing rent fixation for newly constructed premises were not unconstitutional under Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_fixatio: A party challenges the constitutionality of a scheme that fixes standard rent for premises.
predicates.premises_are_classified_by_construction_: The scheme treats premises differently according to whether construction was completed before or after a specified dividing point.
predicates.rent_criteria_are_substantially_similar: The criteria used to fix rent for the two groups of premises are substantially alike.
predicates.classification_has_a_rational_basis: The difference in treatment is connected to relevant differences in the circumstances of the two groups or to the scheme’s objectives.

members.legal_issue: An application filed under an earlier notice cannot be considered when the governing direction requires a fresh notice and applications under that fresh notice.
material_facts: An earlier Supreme Court judgment permitted a fresh notice for grant of the lease in accordance with the applicable procedure.
The pending application had been filed under an earlier notice.
The High Court directed the authority to decide that earlier application, although the fresh-notice process had not been completed.
members.legal_principle: The Court read its earlier judgment, Prem Nath Sharma v. State of U.P., (1997) 4 SCC 552, as requiring a fresh notice in accordance with Rule 72 of the Uttar Pradesh Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963. Accordingly, applications arising from earlier notices could not be substituted for applications invited through the required fresh process.
members.conclusion: The authority must issue a fresh notice and consider applications filed pursuant to it; applications filed under earlier notices or otherwise must not be considered.

predicates.appeal_challenges_direction_to_consider_: An appeal challenges an order directing an authority to decide an existing lease application.
predicates.prior_direction_requires_fresh_notice: An earlier appellate direction requires the authority to invite applications through a fresh notice.
predicates.old_application_filed_under_earlier_noti: The application the authority was directed to consider was filed pursuant to an earlier notice.
predicates.old_application_not_considered_and_fresh: The earlier application is not considered, and the authority considers applications filed in response to the fresh notice.

members.legal_issue: A mining-lease recommendation is invalid when the authority selects applicants using past investments and applicant categories instead of applying the governing statutory criteria.
material_facts: The State considered applications from 111 applicants for mining leases over a notified area.
The Chief Minister’s proceedings divided applicants into groups and ultimately preferred companies with existing steel-plant investments, including the selected applicants.
The proceedings did not adequately assess the statutory factors for comparing applicants, and gave no clear reasons for preferring the selected applicants over others.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2 and 11(3)–(5) of the MMDR Act and the Mineral Concession Rules form the governing scheme; the State acts as a delegate and must exercise its power in the manner prescribed by that scheme. It cannot rely on criteria outside the Act and Rules or frame a policy de hors them. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd., Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. State of Bihar, State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta, Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar, C.I.T. Mumbai v. Anjum M.H. Ghaswala, Captain Sube Singh v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, and State of U.P. v. Singhara Singh.
members.conclusion: The State’s recommendation was contrary to the statutory scheme and could not be sustained.

rule.if: mining_lease_allocation and applications_evaluated_in_stages and selection_based_on_past_plant_investment and statutory_merits_not_assessed

predicates.mining_lease_allocation: The authority considered competing applications for mining leases over an area.
predicates.applications_evaluated_in_stages: The authority divided the applicants into categories and evaluated those categories in successive stages.
predicates.selection_based_on_past_plant_investment: The authority preferred applicants because they had already invested in plants based on the mineral.
predicates.statutory_merits_not_assessed: The authority did not adequately assess the applicants using the governing statutory merits criteria.

members.legal_issue: An application filed before public notification of a previously held area cannot be entertained alongside applications filed in response to that notification.
material_facts: The area sought had previously been held under a mining lease and was later notified as available for regrant.
One applicant had applied for a lease before the notification but did not apply in response to it.
Other applicants applied after the notification.
members.legal_principle: Section 11(4) of the MMDR Act governs applications for notified areas covered by Rule 59(1); only applications made pursuant to the notification are considered together. Rules 59 and 60 require notification before a previously held area becomes available and provide that premature applications shall not be entertained. The first proviso to Section 11(2) concerns virgin areas, not areas governed by Rule 59. The Court relied on Amritlal Nathubhai Shah v. Union Government of India, State of Tamil Nadu v. M.S. Hindstone, State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya, and Gujarat Pradesh Panchayat Parishad v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The pre-notification application was premature and could not be entertained with the applications made in response to the notification.

rule.if: mining_lease_grant_proceeding and previously_held_area and public_notification_required and application_preceded_notification

predicates.mining_lease_grant_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an application for grant of a mining lease.
predicates.previously_held_area: The area had previously been held under a mining lease or otherwise falls within a category requiring public notice before regrant.
predicates.public_notification_required: The area could not be granted until its availability had been publicly notified.
predicates.application_preceded_notification: The applicant filed the grant application before the public notification.

members.legal_issue: A direction to consider applications in accordance with law does not authorize consideration of applications filed before the notification opening a previously held area for grant.
material_facts: An earlier court order directed consideration of applications in accordance with the governing law and referred to applications made pursuant to the notification.
The order did not direct the authority to consider all applications filed before the notification.
The applicant whose application predated the notification relied on that order to support consideration of its application.
members.legal_principle: A court direction to consider applications in accordance with the MMDR Act and the Mineral Concession Rules does not displace the limits imposed by Section 11 and Rules 59 and 60. The order at issue had not decided the interpretation of those provisions and contained no mandamus requiring consideration of prior applications.
members.conclusion: The earlier order did not permit consideration of the pre-notification application.

predicates.mining_lease_allocation: The proceeding concerns competing applications for a mining lease.
predicates.earlier_order_requires_lawful_considerat: An earlier court order directed the authority to consider applications in accordance with law.
predicates.earlier_order_does_not_direct_considerat: The earlier order did not expressly direct consideration of applications filed before the relevant notification.
predicates.application_preceded_notification: The application relied on was filed before the notification opening the area for grant.

members.legal_issue: Past investment and captive consumption in existing plants cannot substitute for proposed investment as a basis for preferring an applicant in an initial grant of a mining lease.
material_facts: The State preferred applicants because they had already established steel plants and sought ore for captive consumption and value addition.
The grant at issue was an initial grant, not a renewal of an existing lease.
The applicants proposed to use the mineral in the steel industry, but the State relied on their past investments rather than assessing proposed investment under the statutory criteria.
members.legal_principle: Section 11(3)(d) refers to investment an applicant proposes to make, not past investment. Rule 35 concerns end use, not the extent of an applicant’s existing investment, and does not expand the proposed-investment factor. TISCO v. Union of India concerned a second renewal under Section 8(3), where the broad criterion of mineral development permitted consideration of captive consumption; it did not govern an initial grant under Section 11. Indian Charge Chrome Ltd. v. Union of India also held that captive mining cannot be the controlling factor for a grant.
members.conclusion: Past investments and captive consumption in existing plants were not valid grounds for the preference given in this initial grant.

predicates.initial_mining_lease_grant: The proceeding concerns an initial grant of a mining lease rather than renewal of an existing lease.
predicates.preference_based_on_existing_plant_or_ca: The authority preferred an applicant because of an existing plant or a need to consume the mineral captively.
predicates.proposed_investment_not_the_basis: The preference was not based on the investment the applicant proposed to make in the mine and related industry.

members.legal_issue: Past commitments by the State to an applicant cannot justify a mining-lease grant contrary to the governing statutory criteria.
material_facts: The selected applicants relied on alleged State commitments connected with their existing steel plants and need for iron ore.
The State had notified the area for grant and considered competing applications.
The statutory scheme supplied the criteria for deciding among those applications.
members.legal_principle: The MMDR Act and Mineral Concession Rules constitute the governing scheme for mining-lease grants, and the State cannot act inconsistently with that scheme or make commitments that displace its criteria. The Court relied on State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta, Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar, M.A. Tulloch, Baijnath Kedia, Kesoram Industries, Bharat Coking Coal, Anjum M.H. Ghaswala, Captain Sube Singh, and Singhara Singh.
members.conclusion: Any past commitments by the State were irrelevant to the grant and could not justify preferring the selected applicants.

predicates.mining_lease_grant_under_statutory_schem: The proceeding concerns a mining-lease grant governed by a statutory allocation scheme.
predicates.authority_relied_on_past_state_commitmen: The authority relied on an earlier State commitment to justify preferring an applicant.

members.legal_issue: Equitable considerations cannot preserve a mining-lease recommendation that violates the governing statute.
material_facts: The recommendation in favour of the selected applicants was made under a statutory scheme governing mining-lease grants.
The recommendation was inconsistent with the scheme’s requirements and criteria.
The selected applicants relied on equitable considerations, including commitments and existing investments.
members.legal_principle: Equity is excluded where a matter is governed by statute and cannot validate action contrary to statutory requirements. The Court relied on Kedar Lal v. Hari Lal Sea and Raja Ram v. Aba Maruti Mali.
members.conclusion: Equity could not save the recommendation because the field was governed by statute and the recommendation violated that statute.

predicates.statutory_scheme_governs_mining_lease_gr: A statutory scheme governs the grant of the mining lease.
predicates.recommendation_conflicts_with_statutory_: The recommendation was made contrary to the requirements of that scheme.
predicates.equitable_relief_invoked: A party relied on equitable considerations to preserve the recommendation.

members.legal_issue: A past governmental commitment cannot displace the governing statutory criteria for deciding mining-lease applications after an area has been notified for re-grant.
material_facts: A State Government had allegedly committed to grant mining leases in the future in connection with a proposed project.
The commitment was invoked years later, after commercial operations at the project had begun.
The area was notified for re-grant and applications were invited from the mining public.
The review petitioner sought to reargue the effect of the commitment, which had already been considered in the earlier judgment.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Sections 2, 11(1), and 11(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. It held that the State Government acts as a statutory delegate, cannot act inconsistently with the Act, and has no authority under that framework to promise a future mining lease in return for investment. Once an area is notified for re-grant, applications must be decided under the Act and rules rather than on the basis of such a commitment.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the applications had to be decided under the governing Act and rules, and that the State Government could not grant a lease on the basis of a past commitment in disregard of the statutory criteria.

rule.if: review_proceeding and area_notified_for_regrant and prior_commitment_invoked and competing_applications_require_decision

predicates.review_proceeding: A party has filed a petition asking the court to review its earlier judgment.
predicates.area_notified_for_regrant: The government has made an area available again for grant and invited applications for it.
predicates.prior_commitment_invoked: An applicant relies on a government promise made earlier to obtain a lease.
predicates.competing_applications_require_decision: Applications from multiple applicants must be considered for the lease.

members.legal_issue: A delay in filing an insolvency application may be condoned for sufficient cause even without a formal written application seeking condonation.
material_facts: The financial creditor filed an application to initiate insolvency proceedings after more than three years had elapsed from the date its borrower’s account was declared non-performing.
The creditor had initiated enforcement proceedings within the limitation period, pursued them, and was later prevented from proceeding by an interim court order.
The creditor had not filed a separate formal application for condonation of delay.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 gives the adjudicating authority discretion to admit an application after limitation where sufficient cause is shown, but does not require a formal written condonation application. The Court relied on B.K. Educational Services Private Limited v. Parag Gupta and Associates, Ramlal Motilal and Chhotelal v. Rewa Coalfields Ltd., Krishna v. Chattappan, Shakuntla Devi Jain v. Kuntal Kumar, and State of West Bengal v. Administrator, Howrah Municipality.
members.conclusion: A formal written application for condonation is not mandatory; the adjudicating authority may condone delay if sufficient cause is shown by the material before it. Condonation is not available as of right, and the authority may require an application or affidavit explaining the delay.

rule.if: insolvency_application_by_financial_creditor and limitation_period_expired and sufficient_cause_material_on_record and not formal_condonation_application_filed

predicates.insolvency_application_by_financial_cred: A financial creditor filed an application seeking commencement of an insolvency resolution process against a corporate debtor.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The application was filed after the prescribed limitation period had elapsed, before accounting for any permissible extension or exclusion.
predicates.sufficient_cause_material_on_record: The applicant placed material before the adjudicating authority showing a sufficient cause for not filing within time.
predicates.formal_condonation_application_filed: The applicant filed a separate formal application asking the adjudicating authority to condone the delay.

members.legal_issue: The time limit for filing a written statement is directory rather than an absolute bar, and a court retains power to receive a late written statement in an exceptional case.
material_facts: The appellants were defendants in a civil suit and sought additional time to file their written statements.
The trial court had fixed a filing date beyond the ordinary 90-day period, and the written statements were filed after that period.
The courts below treated the 90-day limit as leaving no scope to receive a written statement filed later.
members.legal_principle: Order VIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a defendant to file a written statement within 30 days and permits an extension up to 90 days, but it does not expressly remove the court's power to receive a later filing. Its procedural character and purpose of expediting proceedings without sacrificing fairness mean that the limit is directory, not an absolute bar. The court applies the principles in Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur, Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kailash v. Nanhku, Rani Kusum v. Kanchan Devi, Salem Advocate Bar Association, Tamil Nadu v. Union of India, Sushil Kumar Sen v. State of Bihar, and Shreenath v. Rajesh.
members.conclusion: The 90-day limit does not absolutely bar a court from receiving a written statement after that period; the procedural provision is directory, and the court retains discretion to act in exceptional circumstances.

predicates.civil_suit_written_statement: A defendant in a civil suit is required to file a written statement of defence.
predicates.written_statement_filed_after_ordinary_l: The defendant filed the written statement after the ordinary period allowed for filing it had passed.
predicates.exceptional_circumstances: Circumstances of the case make it just to consider receiving the late written statement rather than treating the time limit as an absolute bar.
predicates.late_written_statement_may_be_received: The court may receive the late written statement.

members.legal_issue: Bona fide pursuit of another remedy may constitute sufficient cause to excuse delay in filing a statutory revision.
material_facts: The respondents had bona fide pursued their remedy in the High Court.
The time ordinarily allowed for filing a revision had expired.
The respondents expressed concern that a revision might therefore be rejected as late, and the Court invited them to file it within four weeks.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Rule 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 empowered the revising authority to condone delay where sufficient cause prevented timely filing.
