The Court held that bona fide pursuit of a remedy in the High Court would constitute sufficient cause in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The respondents’ bona fide pursuit of the High Court remedy would be sufficient cause to condone the delay, and the revision should not be dismissed as time-barred if filed within four weeks.

predicates.late_statutory_revision: A party filed, or sought to file, a statutory revision after the ordinary filing period had expired.
predicates.bona_fide_pursuit_of_other_remedy: The party had bona fide pursued another remedy before seeking the statutory revision.

members.legal_issue: Delay in filing special leave petitions may be condoned when the litigants pursued review before the High Court.
material_facts: The special leave petitions were filed late.
Before approaching the Supreme Court, the litigants had sought review before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The court condoned the delay because the litigants had moved the High Court in review; the judgment cites no separate provision or earlier case for this determination.
members.conclusion: The delay in the special leave petitions was condoned.

predicates.delayed_special_leave_petitions: The litigants filed special leave petitions after the applicable filing time had elapsed.
predicates.high_court_review_pursued: The litigants sought review of the challenged orders before the High Court.

members.legal_issue: Sufficient cause for a late application to restore a struck-out defence is established when the applicant bona fide pursues a pending revision that could provide effective relief, is delayed by that proceeding, and promptly applies after it is dismissed.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the order striking out his defence by revision, and further proceedings in the eviction suit were stayed while that revision was pending.
The tenant did not apply under the newly introduced remedial provision while pursuing the revision because he was advised incorrectly about the legal position.
The tenant applied under that provision within 30 days after the revision was dismissed.
The Court found that the tenant had acted bona fide and had sufficient cause for missing the prescribed period.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a court may admit a late application if sufficient cause is shown for not filing it within the prescribed period. The Court held that bona fide pursuit of a revision capable of giving effective relief, together with the stay of further proceedings and a prompt application after the revision was dismissed, constituted sufficient cause in this case.
members.conclusion: The delay was condoned, the application to set aside the order striking out the defence was allowed, and the matter was remitted for the eviction suit to be decided in accordance with law.

rule.if: application_to_restore_struck_defence and revision_pending_with_proceedings_stayed and bona_fide_pursuit_of_effective_remedy and prompt_application_after_revision_dismissal

predicates.application_to_restore_struck_defence: A party makes a late application seeking restoration of a defence that was struck out.
predicates.revision_pending_with_proceedings_stayed: The party has a revision challenging the striking-out order pending, and further proceedings in the underlying suit are stayed.
predicates.bona_fide_pursuit_of_effective_remedy: The party pursues the revision in good faith because success could provide effective relief, and does not make the restorative application while awaiting its outcome.
predicates.prompt_application_after_revision_dismis: The party makes the restorative application promptly after the revision is dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Condoning delay does not enlarge the prescribed limitation period but permits the court to treat the late proceeding as if it had been filed within that period when sufficient cause is shown.
material_facts: The tenant’s application was filed after the prescribed period.
The Court found sufficient cause for the delay because the tenant had bona fide pursued a revision that could provide effective relief and applied promptly after it was dismissed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, condonation does not extend the period of limitation prescribed by law. If sufficient cause is shown, the court may treat the proceeding as if it were filed within time.
members.conclusion: The delay was condoned by treating the application as if it had been filed within the prescribed period, not by extending that period.

predicates.late_proceeding: A party files a proceeding after the applicable deadline.
predicates.sufficient_cause_shown: The party establishes a sufficient reason for not filing within the applicable deadline.

members.legal_issue: The time limit for filing a written statement is directory, and a court may accept a late written statement when exceptional circumstances establish sufficient cause for the delay.
material_facts: The defendant sought permission to file a written statement after the period specified in Order 8 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure had expired.
The defendant said he had followed his trial counsel’s advice to wait for the decision of a pending appeal against an injunction before filing the written statement.
The appeal was being handled by another lawyer, who had the defendant’s case records, leaving the records unavailable to the lawyer conducting the suit at the trial court.
The defendant filed the written statement after obtaining the records and applying for condonation of the delay.
members.legal_principle: Order 8 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including its proviso, is directory rather than mandatory. As held in Salem Advocate Bar Association, Tamil Nadu v. Union of India, AIR 2005 SC 3353, the word “shall” is not conclusive; the provision must be interpreted in light of its purpose and context. A court may accept a written statement after the stated period in exceptionally hard cases where sufficient cause is shown. Procedural rules should advance justice and should not be interpreted to leave a court powerless in extraordinary situations.
members.conclusion: The delay was supported by sufficient cause in an exceptional situation. The application to condone the delay was allowed, the written statement was accepted, and the orders refusing it were set aside.

predicates.civil_suit_defendant_seeks_acceptance_of: A defendant in a civil suit seeks permission to file a written statement after the ordinary filing period has expired.
predicates.exceptional_cause_prevented_timely_filin: An exceptional circumstance, such as case records being held by counsel handling a pending appeal while the defendant followed counsel’s advice to wait, prevented timely filing.
predicates.late_written_statement_may_be_accepted: The court may accept the written statement despite its late filing.

members.legal_issue: A sufficiently explained delay in filing a review petition may be condoned.
material_facts: The review petition was filed 320 days late.
The materials submitted showed that steps had been taken at various levels within the Ministry.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered whether sufficient cause had been shown for the delay and accepted the explanation supported by the application for condonation.
members.conclusion: The Court accepted the explanation and condoned the delay.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party has filed a petition asking the court to review its earlier judgment.
predicates.delay_in_filing: The review petition was filed after the applicable filing period.
predicates.explanation_shows_steps_taken_to_file: The explanation for the delay describes steps taken within the petitioning institution to prepare and file the petition.

members.legal_issue: A person alleging adoption to displace natural succession must prove the adoption with evidence sufficient to meet a grave and serious burden of proof.
material_facts: The alleged adoption had occurred within about a decade before the suit, when witnesses to the giving and taking would normally have been available.
No witness who had seen the adoption ceremony was produced, and no explanation was given for that absence.
The evidence relied on included the alleged adoptive father's statement in his will and testimony from a person who attested the will.
members.legal_principle: Evidence supporting adoption must satisfy the grave and serious burden resting on a person who seeks to displace natural succession by alleging adoption (Mulla's Hindu Law, 14th ed., Article 512). A testator's statement about an adoption is admissible evidence but is not conclusive; there is no rule of law or prudence requiring it to be treated as conclusive (Chandreshwar Prasad Narain Singh v. Bisheshwar Pratap Narain Singh). Greater allowance for missing evidence may be appropriate when a very long time has elapsed since the alleged adoption, but that circumstance was absent here.
members.conclusion: The alleged adoption was not established.

rule.if: adoption_dispute_in_succession_case and adoption_claimed_to_displace_natural_succession and adoption_recent_enough_for_ceremony_witnesses and not ceremony_witnesses_produced and not absence_of_witnesses_explained

predicates.adoption_dispute_in_succession_case: A party in a succession dispute asserted that an adoption determined who inherited the property.
predicates.adoption_claimed_to_displace_natural_suc: The asserted adoption would displace the succession that otherwise followed from natural relationships.
predicates.adoption_recent_enough_for_ceremony_witn: The alleged adoption occurred sufficiently recently that witnesses to its ceremony would normally have been available.
predicates.ceremony_witnesses_produced: A witness who saw the giving and taking at the adoption ceremony was produced.
predicates.absence_of_witnesses_explained: The party relying on the adoption explained why no witness to the ceremony was produced.

members.legal_issue: An alleged adoption that changes the course of succession must be established by evidence sufficiently consistent and probable to leave no reasonable occasion for doubt.
material_facts: The alleged adoption was supported by oral testimony that was insufficient and contradictory about its details and ceremonies.
No contemporary documents or accounts substantiated the alleged adoption, although the relevant family maintained detailed accounts.
The alleged adoptee returned to his birth family after the alleged adoption, and a school record identified him as the son of his birth father.
A later sale deed described an adoption by the widow after her husband's death, rather than the lifetime adoption pleaded in the case.
members.legal_principle: Because adoption changes the course of succession and may deprive others of inheritance rights, proof must be free from suspicion and sufficiently consistent and probable to leave no occasion for doubt. The Court relied on Sootrugun v. Sabitra, Diwakar Rao v. Chandanlal Rao, Kishorilal v. Chunilal, Lal Kunwar v. Charanji Lal, and Padamlal v. Fakira Debya on the significance of accounts and proof; it also applied the principle in Tayammaul v. Sashachalla Naiker that funeral rites do not sustain an adoption unless the adoption itself is proved to have been validly performed.
members.conclusion: The alleged adoption was not established, and the High Court correctly rejected the claim that the appellant had been adopted by the deceased during his lifetime.

predicates.adoption_claim_in_succession_dispute: A person claims an adoption as the basis for a right to property in a succession dispute.
predicates.adoption_evidence_is_inconsistent: Witnesses who support the alleged adoption give inconsistent or insufficient accounts of its circumstances or ceremonies.
predicates.relevant_contemporary_records_are_missin: Relevant records or accounts that could substantiate the alleged adoption are not produced despite being ordinarily maintained or available.
predicates.contemporaneous_record_conflicts_with_cl: A contemporaneous record identifies a different parentage or describes a materially different adoption from the one claimed.

members.legal_issue: An adoption is proved and valid when the required transfer and acceptance of the child are established by reliable evidence and the applicable custom does not require an additional ceremony.
material_facts: The appellant claimed to have been adopted by a childless couple, and the central factual dispute was whether the adoption ceremony had occurred.

The trial court accepted evidence that the natural parent gave the appellant and the adoptive parents received him, and relied on oral and documentary evidence, including a deed signed by both adoptive parents on the day of the alleged adoption and a later letter in which the adoptive father accepted the appellant as his son.

The trial court found that the appellant’s community custom required the ceremony of giving and taking but not the datta homam ceremony; the Supreme Court found nothing showing that an additional ceremony was necessary.
The adoptive mother was seriously ill, and the circumstances did not permit elaborate arrangements, invitations, or ceremonies.
members.legal_principle: A person alleging adoption bears the burden of proving both the factum and validity of the adoption. The evidence must be free from suspicion of fraud and sufficiently consistent and probable, but adoption is proved in the same way as any other fact. Under Hindu law, actual giving and taking is an essential requisite in every adoption; consent or an executed deed alone does not suffice. No particular form is prescribed, and the ceremony may vary with the circumstances. A further datta homam ceremony is required only where applicable law or custom requires it. The Court relied on A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Kishori Lal v. Chaltibai, Shoshinath v. Krishnasunder, Lakshman Singh v. Smt. Rupkanwar, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shriniwas Pandit.
members.conclusion: The adoption was proved in fact and was valid in law; the trial court’s finding was restored.

rule.if: adoption_claim_in_property_dispute and actual_giving_and_taking_proved and adoption_evidence_consistent_and_probable and applicable_custom_requires_no_additional_ceremony

predicates.adoption_claim_in_property_dispute: A party claims adoption as the basis for a right in a property dispute.
predicates.actual_giving_and_taking_proved: Evidence establishes that the natural parent transferred the child and the adoptive parent received the child.
predicates.adoption_evidence_consistent_and_probabl: The evidence of adoption is consistent and probable and does not give reason to suspect fraud.
predicates.applicable_custom_requires_no_additional: The applicable custom does not require a ceremony beyond giving and taking.

members.legal_issue: A claimed adoption that would displace natural succession must be proved as a fact, and a valid adoption requires the actual physical giving and acceptance of the child; an additional ceremony is required only when the applicable law or custom makes it necessary.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that he had been adopted by a childless couple and relied on oral testimony about the adoption and the physical act of giving and taking.
The trial court found the adoption proved after considering the testimony, an adoption deed signed by the couple, other documents, and the circumstances surrounding the adoption.

The appellate court rejected the adoption, but its assessment failed to account for material evidence and applied a standard of proof unsuited to circumstances in which the adoptive mother was seriously ill and elaborate arrangements were not feasible.

The evidence supported the trial court’s finding that the physical act of adoption occurred; the claimant relied on a community custom under which giving and taking sufficed, and no evidence showed that an additional fire ceremony was necessary.
members.legal_principle: A person alleging adoption to displace natural succession bears the burden of proving both the factum and validity of the adoption, and the evidence must be free from suspicion and consistent and probable, but adoption is proved in the same way as any other fact. Actual delivery and acceptance of the child is an essential requisite in every adoption, notwithstanding consent or a deed. No particular form is prescribed for giving and taking. A datta homam is not necessary where the applicable custom suffices or, for the twice-born classes, where the adopted boy belongs to the adoptive father’s gotra. The Court relied on A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Kishori Lal v. Chaltibai, Shoshinath v. Krishnasunder, Lakshman Singh v. Smt. Rupkanwar, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shrinivas Pandit; it also considered Sutroogan v. Sabitra concerning suspicious circumstances and proof.
members.conclusion: The adoption was proved in fact and was valid; the trial court’s finding was restored.

rule.if: adoption_claim_in_succession_dispute and actual_giving_and_acceptance and reliable_contextual_proof and no_evidence_additional_rite_required

predicates.adoption_claim_in_succession_dispute: A person claimed adoption as a basis for displacing the ordinary course of succession to property.
predicates.actual_giving_and_acceptance: The child was physically delivered by the natural parent and accepted by the adoptive parent as part of an adoption ceremony.
predicates.reliable_contextual_proof: The evidence of adoption was consistent and probable when assessed against the surrounding circumstances and the whole record.
predicates.no_evidence_additional_rite_required: The record did not show that an additional religious ceremony was required under the applicable custom or circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking to displace natural succession by alleging an adoption must prove the fact and validity of the adoption.
material_facts: The appellants alleged that a child had been adopted by a family member, thereby affecting the succession to property.
The trial court and the High Court disbelieved the witnesses supporting the alleged adoption and found the documentary record and subsequent conduct inconsistent or inconclusive.
The Supreme Court found no exceptional basis to disturb those concurrent findings.
members.legal_principle: A person seeking to displace natural succession by alleging adoption bears the burden of proving both the factum and validity of the adoption. The Court applied the general distinction between the fixed burden of proof and a shifting evidentiary onus.
members.conclusion: The alleged adoption was not established, and the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proving its fact and validity.

predicates.adoption_claimed_to_displace_natural_suc: A party alleges an adoption as a basis for changing the ordinary course of succession to property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_the_fact_and_va: The party alleging adoption did not establish that the adoption occurred and was valid.

members.legal_issue: Whether an alleged adoption affecting succession was established by the evidence presented.
material_facts: The adoption claim was supported by the claimant's testimony and that of one other witness whose evidence the Court found inherently inconsistent and unreliable.
Three deceased witnesses' testimony from an earlier suit was offered in corroboration, but the controversy over the adoption had already arisen when that testimony was recorded.
A letter describing its sender in a way said to indicate the adoption did not permit a clear or firm conclusion that the adoption had occurred.
The claimant's evidence, once the other material was rejected or found inconclusive, stood isolated.
members.legal_principle: Because adoption changes the course of succession and may divert property, evidence supporting it must be consistent and sufficiently reliable to leave no reasonable doubt. Courts must exercise caution where an adoption is supported only by oral evidence, particularly where suspicious circumstances exist or there is no registered document or other clinching evidence; the person asserting the adoption must dispel such suspicion. The Court relied on Kishori Lal v. Mst. Chaltibai and Rahasa Pandiani v. Gokulananda Panda.
members.conclusion: The alleged adoption was not proved.

predicates.adoption_claim_affecting_succession: A party claims an adoption that would affect the course of succession to property.
predicates.supporting_testimony_unreliable: The testimony offered to establish the adoption is unreliable because of material inconsistencies or other deficiencies.
predicates.no_clinching_admissible_corroboration: No admissible and conclusive corroborating evidence establishes that the adoption occurred.

members.legal_issue: An adoption is established where credible evidence proves the giving and taking of the child, supported by a deed executed at the time of the adoption.
material_facts: The adoptive widow and several witnesses described the adoption ceremony and the giving and taking of the child.
The witnesses’ evidence was accepted as credible, and the scribe explained his presence at the ceremony.
A deed of adoption was executed on the same day as the ceremony and registered later.
The adoptive widow testified to the adoption even though it divested her of her interest in the property.
members.legal_principle: Giving and taking is the essence of adoption. Credible testimony describing that ceremony can establish the adoption, and a deed executed contemporaneously with the adoption provides supporting evidence.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding that the adoption had in fact taken place.

predicates.adoption_status_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether an adoption took place.
predicates.witnesses_described_giving_and_taking: The adoptive parent and other witnesses described the child being given and taken in the adoption ceremony.
predicates.contemporaneous_adoption_deed: A deed recording the adoption was executed at the time of the ceremony.

members.legal_issue: Actual giving and taking in a formal adoption ceremony establishes the intent to transfer a child from the birth family to the adoptive family, and references to customary adoption do not negate that intent when the record shows a formal adoption.
material_facts: The adoptive father took the child into his lap from the child’s parents, who gave the child to him in adoption.
Witnesses described the parents’ participation and statements that they were giving their son to the adoptive father.
The adoption deed described the child as an adopted son, referred to the adoptive father taking him from his parents, and identified itself as an adoption deed.
The deed also referred to custom, and the adoptive father had been governed by customary law.

The finding that giving and taking had occurred was not disputed before the Supreme Court; the appellate court had nevertheless concluded that there was no intent to transfer the child to the adoptive family.
members.legal_principle: Section 11(vi) of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, requires intent to transfer the child from the family of birth to the adoptive family; the Court held that this language indicates the result of actual giving and taking by the parents or guardians. When a formal adoption ceremony is performed and giving and taking occur, the transfer itself establishes the relevant intent. Under section 4, customs or rules of Hindu law cease to apply to matters provided for by the Act. The Court relied on Abdhur Rehmani Khan v. Raghbir Singh (51 PLR 119) for the distinction between customary appointment of an heir and formal adoption, and referred to the adoption principles described in Mayne’s Hindu Law, including the texts of Manu and the Mitakshara.
members.conclusion: The intent to transfer the child to the adoptive family was established. The customary-law background and references to custom did not undermine that conclusion, and the decision restoring the single judge’s judgment was upheld.

predicates.adoption_validity_dispute: A proceeding challenges whether a child was validly adopted.
predicates.formal_adoption_ceremony_performed: The parties performed a ceremony to adopt the child.
predicates.giving_and_taking_occurred: The child’s parent or guardian gave the child to the adopter, and the adopter received the child.

members.legal_issue: A successful claimant in a suit for title and recovery of possession may obtain an inquiry into mesne profits for the period specified by the governing procedural provision.
material_facts: The plaintiff succeeded in establishing title and obtaining a decree for possession of property occupied by the defendant.
The plaintiff sought mesne profits in connection with the recovery-of-possession suit.
members.legal_principle: Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a decree for an inquiry into mesne profits in a suit for recovery of possession. The Court relied on that provision and cited no earlier case on this issue.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to an inquiry into mesne profits under Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, for the period between the suit and delivery of possession pursuant to the decree.

predicates.appeal_in_possession_suit: The matter is an appeal arising from a suit seeking recovery of possession.
predicates.claimant_succeeds_in_title_and_possessio: The claimant establishes title and obtains a decree for possession.
predicates.defendant_occupied_property: The defendant occupied the property for which possession is decreed.

members.legal_issue: A successful claim for possession may include mesne profits for past and continuing occupation, with future profits determined through an inquiry.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of a house and damages for its use and occupation.
The High Court stayed the trial court’s decree while the appeal was pending, and the defendant remained in possession.
By the time the Supreme Court decided the appeals, nearly twenty years had passed from the institution of the suit.
The Supreme Court ordered mesne profits for the period up to its judgment and directed the trial court to inquire into future mesne profits until possession was delivered.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 20, Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may direct an inquiry to determine mesne profits after judgment until delivery of possession. Given the prolonged occupation while the decree was stayed, the Court ordered past mesne profits and directed an inquiry into future profits.
members.conclusion: The defendant was ordered to pay mesne profits for past occupation, and the trial court was directed to determine future mesne profits until delivery of possession.

rule.if: suit_for_possession and claimant_entitled_to_possession and defendant_remained_in_occupation_during_appeal and prolonged_delay_before_final_decision

predicates.suit_for_possession: The proceeding sought recovery of possession of property.
predicates.claimant_entitled_to_possession: The court determined that the claimant was entitled to possession.
predicates.defendant_remained_in_occupation_during_: The defendant continued to occupy the property while an appeal was pending.
predicates.prolonged_delay_before_final_decision: A substantial period of occupation passed before the final decision.

members.legal_issue: A successful claimant to possession is entitled to mesne profits for the period of wrongful occupation, with future mesne profits determined through an inquiry.
material_facts: The second plaintiff was entitled to possession of the house, while the defendant continued to occupy it during the litigation.

The trial court had awarded damages for use and occupation, and the Supreme Court directed payment of mesne profits through the date of its judgment and an inquiry into future mesne profits until possession was delivered.
members.legal_principle: Order 20, Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an inquiry to determine mesne profits continuing after judgment until delivery of possession. A successful claimant to possession may recover mesne profits for the wrongful occupation.
members.conclusion: The defendant was directed to pay mesne profits for the period specified by the Court, with future mesne profits to be determined by the trial court under Order 20, Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.appeal_arises_from_suit_for_possession: The appeal arises from a suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.claimant_is_entitled_to_possession: The court determines that the claimant is entitled to possession of the property.
predicates.opposing_party_continues_in_occupation: The party opposing the claim remains in occupation of the property while possession is withheld.

members.legal_issue: A direction for an inquiry into future mesne profits in a possession suit is governed by the statutory outer limit even if the direction is expressed as continuing until delivery of possession.
material_facts: A preliminary decree in a suit for possession and mesne profits directed an inquiry into future mesne profits from the institution of the suit until delivery of possession.
Possession of some of the properties was delivered more than three years after the preliminary decree.
The final decree included mesne profits for a period extending beyond three years from the preliminary decree.
The majority construed the preliminary direction consistently with the governing rule rather than as authorizing recovery beyond its limit.
members.legal_principle: Order XX, rule 12(1)(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure directs an inquiry into future mesne profits until the first of the specified terminating events, including the expiration of three years from the decree; rule 12(2) provides for a final decree based on the inquiry. A direction that does not set out all the alternatives is construed in conformity with the rule. The Court relied on Girish Chunder Lahiri v. Shoshi Shikhareswar Roy and the line of cases applying that construction, including Venkata Kumara v. Subbayamma, Uttamram v. Kishordas, Trailokya v. Jogendra, Godayarti Raja v. Ramachandraswami, Narayan v. Sono, Kunwar Jagdish Chandra v. Bulaqi Das and Kanai Lal v. Shyam Kishore.
members.conclusion: By majority, the decree-holder could not recover future mesne profits for a period beyond the three-year limit running from the preliminary decree.

predicates.suit_for_possession_and_mesne_profits: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking possession of immovable property and mesne profits.
predicates.future_profit_inquiry_ordered: The court directed an inquiry into mesne profits accruing after the proceeding began.
predicates.possession_not_delivered_within_outer_li: The person entitled to possession did not receive it before the legally prescribed outer limit for the future-profit inquiry.

members.legal_issue: A court may direct an inquiry into future mesne profits without a specific prayer for them when the suit is for possession of immovable property and mesne profits.
material_facts: The suit sought recovery of possession of immovable property and pleaded an entitlement to an account of mesne profits.
The plaintiffs claimed mesne profits for three years before the suit, valued that claim and paid court fees on it.
The plaint did not specifically ask for future mesne profits, but included a request for such other relief as the court considered fit.
The High Court directed an inquiry into future mesne profits, and the appellants did not contend that the High Court had exercised its discretion improperly or erroneously.
members.legal_principle: Order 20, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a decree for past and future mesne profits in a suit for possession of immovable property and rent or mesne profits. Past mesne profits require an existing cause of action to be pleaded, specifically claimed, approximately valued and subjected to court fees under Order 7, rules 1, 2 and 7 of the Code and section 7(1) of the Court Fees Act. Future mesne profits have not accrued when the suit is instituted, so they need not be specifically pleaded, valued or fee-paid; in a qualifying suit the court may grant the general relief of an inquiry into them. The Court relied on Basavayya v. Guruvayya, the observations in Fakharuddin Mahomed Ahsan v. Official Trustee of Bengal, and Atchamma v. Rami Reddy; it distinguished Mohd. Yamin v. Vakil Ahmed because that suit did not claim past or future mesne profits or rent.
members.conclusion: The suit fell within Order 20, rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the court had discretionary power to direct an inquiry into future mesne profits even though the plaint did not specifically seek them. The Court saw no reason to interfere with the decree.

predicates.suit_for_possession_and_mesne_profits: The proceeding is a suit for recovery of possession of immovable property and for rent or mesne profits.
predicates.plaint_claimed_past_mesne_profits: The plaint claimed mesne profits that had accrued before the suit was instituted.
predicates.specific_future_profit_prayer_absent: The plaint did not specifically request mesne profits accruing after the suit was instituted.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff unable to recover possession because land vested in the State may still recover mesne profits for the period of the defendants' wrongful possession before vesting, subject to the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed mesne profits against the defendants, whose possession the plaint alleged had become unlawful.
The land vested in the State on January 26, 1955, preventing the plaintiffs from obtaining possession from the defendants.

The Court held that the plaintiffs could recover mesne profits for the three years before the suit was instituted up to the vesting date, and specified that the recoverable period in this case was May 26, 1950, to January 26, 1955.
The amount of mesne profits was to be determined according to law by the court dealing with the proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The fact that land reform vesting prevents an owner from obtaining possession does not by itself prevent recovery of mesne profits from defendants whose possession became wrongful. Recovery is subject to the applicable limitation period and ends when the land vests in the State.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were entitled to mesne profits from the defendants only for May 26, 1950, through January 26, 1955, with the amount to be determined according to law.

rule.if: mesne_profits_claim and defendants_possession_became_wrongful and land_vested_in_state and claim_within_limitation_period

predicates.mesne_profits_claim: The plaintiff claimed compensation for the defendants' use or occupation of land.
predicates.defendants_possession_became_wrongful: The defendants remained in possession after their possession had become wrongful in relation to the plaintiff.
predicates.land_vested_in_state: The land vested in the State under land reform legislation.
predicates.claim_within_limitation_period: The claimed period of wrongful possession fell within the period recoverable under the applicable limitation law.

members.legal_issue: A claimant is entitled to mesne profits for a period during which the opposing party wrongfully possessed the property before it vested in the state.
material_facts: The opposing parties were wrongfully in possession of the properties during the period for which mesne profits were claimed.
The claimed period ran from the filing of the suit until the properties vested in the state.
The court directed an inquiry into mesne profits limited to that period.
members.legal_principle: A person whose property is wrongfully possessed by another is entitled to mesne profits for the period of that wrongful possession; the court limited the award to the period before vesting in accordance with Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to an inquiry and decree for mesne profits for the period of wrongful possession before vesting, but not beyond that period.

predicates.mesne_profit_claim_in_property_suit: The claimant seeks mesne profits in a proceeding concerning property.
predicates.wrongful_possession_during_claimed_perio: The opposing party wrongfully possessed the property during the period for which mesne profits are sought.
predicates.claimed_period_before_state_vesting: The period for which mesne profits are sought falls before the property vested in the state.
predicates.mesne_profits_awarded_for_prevesting_per: Mesne profits are awarded for the period of wrongful possession before the property vested in the state.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff who succeeds in a suit for possession may receive mesne profits from the filing of the suit when no mesne profits for an earlier period were claimed.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of the properties but did not claim mesne profits for a period before filing suit.
An interim order had directed ascertainment of profits, and the court stated that the plaintiffs could receive a decree for mesne profits upon payment of the appropriate stamp.
members.legal_principle: In a suit seeking possession, the successful plaintiffs were entitled to mesne profits from the filing of the suit where they had not sought mesne profits for an earlier period; the court had directed ascertainment of profits and made the decree subject to payment of the appropriate stamp.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were entitled to mesne profits from the date the suit was filed, subject to payment of the appropriate stamp.

predicates.possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_entitled_to_possession: The court determined that the plaintiff was entitled to possession of the property.
predicates.no_pre_suit_mesne_profits_claimed: The plaintiff did not claim mesne profits for a period before filing the suit.

members.legal_issue: An accused relying on private defence must establish a factual basis for that defence on a preponderance of probabilities, but need not prove it beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the deceased fired at him and that he returned fire in self-defence, and also claimed that the deceased was stealing paddy from a field in which the accused had a property interest.
Medical expert evidence supported the finding that the accused’s injuries were not caused by gunshots in the manner he claimed and had been fabricated to create a defence.

The accused did not produce the alleged nearby witnesses or elicit evidence from prosecution witnesses establishing that the deceased fired at him, stole or attempted to steal paddy, or that the accused was entitled to the paddy.
Prosecution witnesses denied that the deceased fired a weapon or that the deceased and another person stole paddy.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, but the accused’s burden to establish private defence is less onerous and may be discharged by showing a mere preponderance of probabilities, either through cross-examination of prosecution witnesses or by adducing defence evidence. The accused need not establish the plea to the hilt. The Court relied on Partap v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1976 SC 966, and Munshi Ram & Ors. v. Delhi Administration, [1968] 2 SCR 455.
members.conclusion: The accused did not discharge the burden of establishing a factual basis for private defence of either person or property.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the accused’s criminal liability is being determined.
predicates.accused_claimed_private_defence: The accused asserted that the force used was justified to defend a person or property.
predicates.defence_basis_established_on_preponderan: The accused produced or elicited evidence making it more probable than not that circumstances justifying private defence existed.
predicates.private_defence_not_established: The accused’s claim of private defence is not accepted as established.

members.legal_issue: An accused’s failure to explain a circumstance within their special knowledge cannot complete a circumstantial-evidence case when the prosecution has not established the other links in the chain.
material_facts: The prosecution argued that the appellant had a duty to explain how the fire began because she was in the house with the deceased and children.
The appellant gave no explanation for the eruption of the fire.
The other circumstances relied on by the prosecution had not been satisfactorily established or connected to the appellant.
members.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not relieve the prosecution of its burden to prove its case. Under Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, a false or absent explanation may be considered only as an additional link after the prosecution has satisfactorily proved the other links, the circumstances point with reasonable definiteness to guilt, and the circumstance is proximate in time and situation. Shankarlal confirms that a false plea cannot take the place of proof of facts the prosecution must establish.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s failure to explain the cause of the fire could not be used against her as an additional link because the other circumstances in the chain were not established.

rule.if: circumstantial_case and fact_within_accused_special_knowledge and accused_gave_no_explanation and prosecution_links_not_established

predicates.circumstantial_case: The prosecution seeks to establish guilt through circumstances rather than direct evidence of the act.
predicates.fact_within_accused_special_knowledge: The prosecution relies on a circumstance whose explanation is especially within the accused’s knowledge.
predicates.accused_gave_no_explanation: The accused did not explain the circumstance relied on by the prosecution.
predicates.prosecution_links_not_established: The prosecution has not satisfactorily established the other links needed to connect the accused to the crime.

members.legal_issue: An accused who invokes a general exception bears a burden of establishing the supporting circumstances on a balance of probabilities, without displacing the prosecution’s burden to prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused relied on private defence after firing the shot that caused the deceased’s death.
The prosecution’s eyewitnesses established that the accused fired three shots and that one hit and killed the deceased.
The court considered the accused’s account, the prosecution evidence, and other circumstances in assessing the private-defence plea.
members.legal_principle: Section 105 of the Evidence Act places on an accused the burden of establishing circumstances bringing the case within a general exception. Under Sections 3 and 5 of that Act, the relevant standard is that of a prudent person and may be met by a balance of probabilities. This does not shift the prosecution’s burden to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt. The accused may rely on evidence from either side, cross-examination, presumptions, or the accused’s own recorded statement. Even if the exception is not established, the evidence may raise a reasonable doubt about an element of the offence. The court relied on Dahyabhai v. State of Gujarat, State of U.P. v. Ram Swarup, and Pratap v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The accused had to make the circumstances supporting private defence sufficiently probable, while the prosecution retained the burden of proving every element of culpable homicide beyond reasonable doubt. Evidence insufficient to establish an exception could nevertheless raise a reasonable doubt about an element of the offence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the accused faces a charge.
predicates.accused_invokes_general_exception: The accused relies on circumstances said to bring the conduct within a general exception.

members.legal_issue: An accused who bears the burden of establishing a defence or an exception need only establish it on a preponderance of probabilities, while the prosecution retains the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that entrusted public money had been dishonestly retained.
The accused gave an explanation for the money’s custody, supported by prosecution testimony and documents.
The lower courts required the accused to prove his explanation with excessive strictness and treated its alleged falsity as sufficient to establish guilt.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and cannot rely on weakness or falsity in the defence to establish guilt; the accused is presumed innocent and the prosecution’s onus never shifts. Although Evidence Act section 105 places the burden of proving an exception on the accused, it does not prescribe a standard equivalent to the prosecution’s. Preponderance of probabilities is sufficient under Evidence Act section 5. Applied Harbhajan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1965] 3 SCR 235, and State of U.P. v. Ram Swarup, [1975] 1 SCR 409.
members.conclusion: The accused was not required to prove his explanation beyond reasonable doubt; a version that was probable enough to raise doubt in the prosecution case was sufficient, and the prosecution’s burden never shifted.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution alleges guilt.
predicates.accused_relies_on_defence_or_exception: The accused relies on a defence or an exception for which the law places a burden on the accused.
predicates.defence_version_is_probable: The facts supporting the accused’s version make it at least as probable as the competing account.

members.legal_issue: An accused has no obligation to produce defence evidence, and the prosecution cannot establish its case by inviting an adverse inference from the accused’s failure to do so.
material_facts: The courts below drew an adverse inference because the accused did not produce evidence supporting his explanation.
The accused could rely on admissions by prosecution witnesses and documents produced by the prosecution to support that explanation.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must stand on its own legs and prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; an accused may establish a defence by relying on prosecution evidence and is not obliged to call evidence. The prosecution cannot derive support from weakness in the defence. These conclusions follow from the presumption of innocence and the rule that the prosecution’s onus never shifts.
members.conclusion: The courts below were not justified in drawing an adverse inference against the accused for failing to produce defence evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution alleges guilt.
predicates.accused_does_not_call_defence_evidence: The accused does not produce witnesses or other evidence in support of the defence.
predicates.prosecution_case_depends_on_defence_weak: The prosecution seeks to rely on the absence or weakness of defence evidence rather than proving its own case.

members.legal_issue: An accused who raises a plea of private defence bears the burden of making that defence probable, but need not prove it beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused relied on a plea of private defence of person and property at trial.
The Court considered the burden and standard applicable to that plea.
members.legal_principle: The burden to probabilise a plea of private defence lies on the accused. The plea may be assessed from salient facts and circumstances appearing in the prosecution case or from defence evidence. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The accused bears the burden of establishing the plea as probable, but is not required to establish it beyond reasonable doubt.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which an accused's liability is being determined.
predicates.accused_raises_private_defence: The accused relies on private defence as a basis for resisting criminal liability.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s burden to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt is not relieved by the accused’s failure to raise a defence during questioning, and an accused need not prove a plausible defence beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused did not raise their defence under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The evidence established that the accused had made a report about the same occurrence and had received hospital treatment for injuries sustained in it.
The prosecution did not investigate that report or produce the injury report, and could not answer the resulting doubts.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and cannot rely on weaknesses in the defence to make up for a failure to do so. Under Sections 101 and 105 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the prosecution’s burden is more onerous than the accused’s burden to establish a defence, which may be discharged on a preponderance of probabilities. The Court relied on Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand (2013) 4 SCC 422 and Partap v. State of U.P. (1976) 2 SCC 798, and addressed the effect of a defence not being raised under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
members.conclusion: The accused’s failure to raise a defence during questioning did not relieve the prosecution of its burden. Where a defence is not improbable, appears likely, and has supporting material, the accused need not prove anything further; the benefit of doubt follows unless the prosecution proves its case beyond reasonable doubt.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and accused_did_not_raise_defence_during_questioning and defence_is_not_improbable and material_supports_defence and prosecution_cannot_answer_material_evidence

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution in a criminal case.
predicates.accused_did_not_raise_defence_during_que: The accused did not raise the defence when questioned during the criminal proceeding.
predicates.defence_is_not_improbable: The defence is not improbable and appears likely in the circumstances.
predicates.material_supports_defence: There is evidence or other material supporting the defence.
predicates.prosecution_cannot_answer_material_evide: The prosecution cannot explain or answer material evidence that casts doubt on its case.

members.legal_issue: The accused’s failure to explain facts within special knowledge does not relieve the prosecution of its obligation to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The State argued that the accused had not discharged their burden and had not explained matters in their statements under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
The Court found that the prosecution had not first proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt before the burden concerning facts within the accused’s special knowledge under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 can shift. Section 106 does not relieve the prosecution of its burden: Joydeb Patra v. State of West Bengal, relying on Sucha Singh v. State of Punjab and Vikramjit Singh v. State of Punjab. The prosecution must stand on its own evidence, and a weak defence cannot cure a failure of proof: Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, which also refers to Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand.
members.conclusion: The accused’s failure to explain could not make up for the prosecution’s failure to prove its case, and the burden did not shift to the accused.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution bears the burden of proving guilt.
predicates.prosecution_has_not_proved_guilt_beyond_: The prosecution has not established the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.accused_has_not_explained_special_knowle: The accused has not explained facts said to be within their special knowledge.
predicates.burden_does_not_shift_to_accused: The accused’s failure to explain does not shift the burden or cure the prosecution’s failure of proof.

members.legal_issue: Civil recovery proceedings and decrees do not, by themselves, override or preclude a criminal prosecution arising from the same transactions.
material_facts: The bank obtained decrees against borrowers for repayment of the loans, including simple money decrees and mortgage decrees.
The decrees did not result in full repayment; only one borrower had liquidated the loan, and the bank had suffered a loss of interest.
The criminal prosecution concerned the alleged dishonest loan scheme and the conduct of the accused, rather than merely the borrowers’ civil liability for repayment.
members.legal_principle: A civil claim or decree does not override a criminal prosecution. The Court relied on K.G. Premshanker v. Inspector of Police, (2002) 8 SCC 87, and R. Venkatkrishnan v. CBI, (2009) 11 SCC 737.
members.conclusion: The civil decrees did not defeat or override the criminal prosecution.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_arises_from_transac: A criminal prosecution concerns transactions for which a civil recovery claim or proceeding also exists.
predicates.civil_decree_does_not_resolve_criminal_l: The civil decree addresses recovery but does not determine whether the accused committed the alleged criminal acts.

members.legal_issue: Findings of fact in civil proceedings are not binding in criminal proceedings concerning the same subject matter.
material_facts: A civil court had rejected the allegation that the agreement to sell was forged or fabricated, and its decree was under appeal.
The criminal complaint alleged forgery of the same agreement, and the High Court quashed the criminal proceedings by relying on the civil court’s finding.
members.legal_principle: Civil and criminal proceedings may proceed simultaneously, and findings in one are not final or binding in the other because the standards of proof differ: preponderance of probabilities in civil cases and proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases. Sections 41 to 43 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 may make previous judgments relevant in limited circumstances. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras, K.G. Premshankar v. Inspector of Police, Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, Syed Aksari Hadi Ali Augustine Imam v. State (Delhi Administration), Vishnu Dutt Sharma v. Daya Prasad, and P. Swaroopa Rani v. M. Hari Narayana; it held that Karamchand Ganga Pershad v. Union of India was per incuriam and that V.M. Shah v. State of Maharashtra was not approved.
members.conclusion: The civil court’s factual findings did not bind the criminal court; each proceeding had to be decided on the evidence adduced in it. The High Court’s reliance on the civil finding as a basis for quashing was legally unsustainable.

predicates.parallel_civil_criminal_proceedings: A civil proceeding and a criminal proceeding concerning the dispute are pursued in parallel.
predicates.same_subject_matter: The civil and criminal proceedings concern the same subject matter.

members.legal_issue: Findings or evidence in a criminal proceeding cannot, without an independent finding by the civil court, conclusively establish the existence of an agreement for specific performance.
material_facts: The same written agreement was considered in a criminal proceeding and observations about its execution were recorded there.
The High Court treated those observations as supporting proof of execution in the civil suit for specific performance.
The Supreme Court held that the criminal court’s evidence and findings could not conclusively prove the existence of the agreement in the civil suit without an independent civil finding.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act was invoked in the High Court’s treatment of the criminal court’s observations. The Supreme Court held that evidence and findings recorded by criminal courts cannot be conclusive proof of a fact, particularly the existence of an agreement relied on to obtain specific performance, in the absence of an independent finding by the civil court. The criminal proceeding’s findings therefore do not replace the civil court’s own assessment of the evidence.
members.conclusion: The criminal court’s findings could not be treated as conclusive proof of the agreement’s existence for granting specific performance without an independent finding by the civil court.

predicates.civil_specific_performance_proceeding: A civil proceeding seeks specific performance of an alleged agreement.
predicates.criminal_court_findings_about_agreement_: A party or court relies on findings or evidence from a criminal proceeding concerning the alleged agreement.
predicates.independent_civil_finding_on_agreement_a: The civil court has not independently found, on its own assessment of the evidence, that the agreement exists.

members.legal_issue: The civil character of a contractual transaction and the existence of parallel civil or negotiable-instrument proceedings do not by themselves prevent criminal proceedings where fraud or cheating is alleged.
material_facts: The dispute arose from agreements to procure and transfer land in return for a substantial advance.
The complainant also pursued a civil recovery suit and a complaint concerning the security cheques.
The criminal complaints alleged cheating, fraud and conspiracy in connection with the agreements and payment.
members.legal_principle: A contractual breach does not automatically amount to a criminal offence, but a contractual transaction may also involve criminal conduct if the required element of cheating or fraud is alleged. The existence of civil remedies or proceedings, including a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is by itself no ground to quash criminal proceedings. The Court considered S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar (2002) 1 SCC 241 and Anil Mahajan v. Bhor Industries Ltd. (2005) 10 SCC 228.
members.conclusion: The civil suit, the negotiable-instrument complaint, and the civil nature of the contract were not by themselves grounds to quash the criminal complaints.

rule.if: appeal_from_criminal_complaint_quashing and contractual_dispute_exists and complaint_alleges_fraud_or_cheating and parallel_civil_or_cheque_proceedings_exist

predicates.appeal_from_criminal_complaint_quashing: The proceeding is an appeal from an order quashing a criminal complaint.

predicates.complaint_alleges_fraud_or_cheating: The complaint alleges fraud or cheating in connection with the contractual dealings.
predicates.parallel_civil_or_cheque_proceedings_exi: A civil recovery proceeding or a proceeding concerning a cheque also exists.

members.legal_issue: A civil proceeding and an independent criminal investigation concerning related facts may proceed simultaneously, and the civil proceeding alone does not justify staying the investigation.
material_facts: A civil suit for specific performance was dismissed after the trial court found that a receipt relied on to establish an additional payment and delivery of possession was forged or not proved authentic.
The property owner lodged a criminal complaint alleging that the receipt was fabricated, and the police registered a case and began an investigation.
During the appeal from the civil judgment, the High Court stayed the criminal investigation.
members.legal_principle: Whether civil or criminal proceedings should be stayed depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. There is no general bar to simultaneous proceedings, and findings in one proceeding are not final or binding in the other because the standards of proof differ. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras, Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, and Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Assn. of Chartered Certified Accountants. It distinguished Mahar Jahan v. State of Delhi, which concerned a summary possession proceeding under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure while a civil suit concerning possession was pending.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not correct in staying the investigation; the civil appeal and the criminal investigation could proceed simultaneously.

predicates.civil_criminal_parallel_case: A civil proceeding and a criminal proceeding concerning related events are both pending.
predicates.criminal_investigation_independently_all: The criminal investigation concerns an allegation that a document involved in the civil dispute was forged.

members.legal_issue: A pending civil suit concerning the same underlying dispute does not oust the criminal court’s jurisdiction over alleged criminal conduct.
material_facts: A civil suit relating to the dispute was pending while the criminal complaint proceeded.
The complainant’s allegations included cheating and criminal breach of trust.
members.legal_principle: Civil and criminal proceedings are separate and independent, and the pendency of a civil suit does not, by itself, oust the jurisdiction of the criminal court where an offence may have been committed. The judgment cites no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The pending civil suit did not oust the criminal court’s jurisdiction or defeat the criminal proceeding; the civil and criminal proceedings were separate and independent.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_concerns_alleged_cri: A criminal proceeding concerns conduct alleged to constitute an offence.
predicates.civil_suit_concerning_the_dispute_is_pen: A civil suit concerning the same underlying dispute is pending.

members.legal_issue: Findings in civil proceedings do not bind criminal proceedings merely because both concern the same alleged conduct.
material_facts: The alleged forgery was disputed in probate proceedings and was also the subject of a criminal complaint.
The civil and criminal proceedings would apply different standards of proof and decide their cases on the evidence presented in each.
members.legal_principle: Civil cases are decided on the preponderance of evidence, while criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt, with the burden on the prosecution. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras for the principle that the possibility of conflicting decisions is not itself a relevant reason to defer one proceeding, and that the proceedings are decided independently on their evidence.
members.conclusion: There is no statutory provision or legal principle making findings in one proceeding final or binding in the other; the possibility of conflicting findings is not, by itself, a reason to prevent the criminal proceeding.

predicates.civil_and_criminal_proceedings: Civil and criminal proceedings address the same or related alleged conduct.
predicates.each_proceeding_has_its_own_evidence: Each proceeding is decided on the evidence adduced in that proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The exception for culpable homicide committed in a sudden fight does not apply when armed accused prepare for a fight, provoke the confrontation, and take undue advantage of an unarmed victim.
material_facts: The accused went armed to the complainant party’s home, provoked the occupants, and initiated the confrontation.
A mutual fight followed, but the deceased was unarmed and was attacked at the outset with deadly blows.
The deceased was selected as a target despite being unarmed.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies where culpable homicide is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. Its explanation makes it immaterial which party provoked the quarrel or committed the first assault. The Court held that a mutual fight alone is not a sudden fight preceded by a sudden quarrel, and that the accused had taken undue advantage.
members.conclusion: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC did not apply, and the offence could not be reduced to culpable homicide on that basis.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_murder_conviction and accused_prepared_for_fight and accused_provoked_confrontation and unarmed_victim_targeted and accused_took_undue_advantage

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_murder_convictio: The proceeding is an accused’s appeal against a murder conviction.

predicates.accused_provoked_confrontation: The accused provoked the confrontation that led to the fight.
predicates.unarmed_victim_targeted: The accused attacked a victim who was unarmed.
predicates.accused_took_undue_advantage: The accused used the victim’s unarmed condition to attack him in a way that took undue advantage.

members.legal_issue: The sudden-fight exception does not apply when the accused takes undue advantage or acts cruelly or unusually, even if the fatal attack follows a sudden quarrel without premeditation.
material_facts: The accused used a sharp-edged deadly weapon against a victim who was unarmed and had caused no injury to the accused.
The first blow caused the victim to fall, but the accused continued to inflict two more blows while the victim lay on the ground.
The third blow inflicted on the fallen victim was fatal.
The accused relied on the sudden quarrel and heat of passion to claim the benefit of the exception.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC requires that the act be committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. The court relied on Pandurang Narayan Jawalekar v. State of Maharashtra, [1979] 1 SCC 132. Whether the offender took undue advantage depends on the weapons used, the parties’ relative ability to defend themselves, and the manner of the attack; using a deadly weapon against an unarmed person and continuing to attack a fallen victim can establish undue advantage and cruel conduct.
members.conclusion: The accused took undue advantage and acted cruelly; the sudden-fight exception did not apply, and the offence remained murder.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and sudden_fight_exception_claimed and sudden_quarrel and deadly_weapon_used_against_unarmed_victim and further_blows_delivered_to_fallen_victim

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.sudden_fight_exception_claimed: The accused claims that the killing occurred in circumstances of a sudden fight or quarrel.
predicates.sudden_quarrel: The attack followed a sudden quarrel between the accused and the victim.
predicates.deadly_weapon_used_against_unarmed_victi: The accused used a deadly weapon against a victim who was unarmed.
predicates.further_blows_delivered_to_fallen_victim: After the victim fell, the accused inflicted further blows while the victim was on the ground.

members.legal_issue: A sudden quarrel does not bring a killing within the sudden-fight exception when there was no bilateral exchange of blows and the accused inflicted multiple fatal blows with a formidable weapon on an unarmed victim.
material_facts: A quarrel broke out suddenly between the deceased's mother and the accused's companion.
The deceased was unarmed and did not injure the appellant or his companions.
The appellant inflicted three blows to the deceased's head with an axe, including one with its sharp side, and the deceased died at the scene.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Penal Code requires more than a sudden quarrel: there must be a sudden fight, which involves a bilateral transaction in which blows are exchanged. The judgment also considered that the deceased was unarmed and the appellant inflicted three fatal injuries with a formidable weapon. No earlier cases are relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The sudden-fight exception did not apply; the appellant's murder conviction was upheld.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and sudden_quarrel and not blows_exchanged and victim_unarmed and multiple_fatal_weapon_blows

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal against a conviction for murder.

predicates.blows_exchanged: The accused and the victim both exchanged blows during the incident.
predicates.victim_unarmed: The person attacked was not armed.

members.legal_issue: The sudden-fight exception to murder does not apply when the circumstances do not establish its required conditions, including a sudden unpremeditated assault without undue advantage or cruelty.
material_facts: The prosecution party was ploughing its own land when the accused objected.
After the prosecution party did not stop, the accused went to a nearby plot, obtained weapons, and assaulted the prosecution party, who were unarmed.
The assault injured several people and caused one person's death.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code requires a sudden fight, absence of premeditation, and absence of undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct; the occasion must be sudden and not a cloak for pre-existing malice. All the requirements must be present. The court applied that provision to the circumstances of the assault.
members.conclusion: The sudden-fight exception did not apply because the circumstances did not establish the required conditions for it.

rule.if: homicide_prosecution and attackers_obtained_weapons_before_assault and victim_party_unarmed and attack_caused_death

predicates.homicide_prosecution: The proceeding concerns a prosecution for a homicide.
predicates.attackers_obtained_weapons_before_assaul: The attackers went to obtain weapons before carrying out the assault.
predicates.victim_party_unarmed: The party attacked was unarmed when the assault occurred.
predicates.attack_caused_death: The assault caused a person's death.

members.legal_issue: The sudden-fight exception to murder does not apply where the deceased was not a participant in the fight and the accused took undue advantage by stabbing an unarmed person who posed no threat.
material_facts: The accused and another person were involved in a quarrel after the accused had pelted that person with stones and the other person had slapped the accused.
The deceased intervened only to tell the other person to stop fighting and offered to resolve the dispute.
The deceased did not take part in the fight or make threatening gestures.
The accused drew a penknife and stabbed the deceased. The court rejected the accused's account that the deceased had attacked and grappled with him.
members.legal_principle: The fourth exception to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code requires, among other things, that the offender not take undue advantage and that the fight be with the person killed. A fight between the accused and someone else does not satisfy that requirement merely because the accused acted during that quarrel. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The sudden-fight exception did not apply, and the murder conviction was upheld.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_killed_person_outside_fight and victim_made_no_threatening_gesture and accused_used_weapon_against_unarmed_victim

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.accused_killed_person_outside_fight: The accused killed a person who was not a participant in the fight.
predicates.victim_made_no_threatening_gesture: The person killed made no threatening gesture toward the accused.
predicates.accused_used_weapon_against_unarmed_vict: The accused used a weapon against a person who was unarmed.

members.legal_issue: A sudden quarrel does not reduce a killing to culpable homicide when the offender acts in a cruel or unusual manner.
material_facts: After an exchange of abuses during a dispute, the accused struck the deceased on the neck with a pharsa, causing death.
The occurrence was not premeditated and involved a sudden quarrel, and the accused inflicted a single blow.
The trial court found that the accused acted in a cruel and unusual manner and convicted him of murder.
The prosecution eyewitness accounts and medical evidence supported the finding that the accused caused the death.
members.legal_principle: Section 300, Exception 4, requires that the offender not take undue advantage or act in a cruel or unusual manner. The trial court found that condition was not met, so the sudden quarrel did not bring the killing within the exception. The murder conviction was therefore sustained under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code was upheld; the Court found no reason to differ from the lower courts on guilt.

rule.if: murder_trial and sudden_quarrel and cruel_or_unusual_manner and evidence_supports_killing

predicates.murder_trial: The proceeding is a trial or appeal concerning a murder charge.
predicates.sudden_quarrel: The killing followed a sudden quarrel rather than premeditation.
predicates.cruel_or_unusual_manner: The offender acted in a cruel or unusual manner or took undue advantage.
predicates.evidence_supports_killing: The eyewitness and medical evidence support the finding that the accused caused the death.

members.legal_issue: The sudden-fight exception to murder does not apply unless all its requirements are met, including that the offender did not take undue advantage or act cruelly or unusually.
material_facts: A dispute over a field boundary led to an exchange of hot words.
A pistol was handed to the offender, who fired at two people, killing them.
The accused appealed the murder conviction and relied on the sudden quarrel to invoke the exception.
members.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code applies only where death is caused without premeditation in a sudden fight, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel or unusual manner, and the fight is with the person killed. A sudden fight entails mutual provocation and blows on each side; a sudden quarrel and absence of premeditation alone are insufficient. “Undue advantage” means unfair advantage. The Court relied on Dhirajbhai Gorakhbhai Nayak v. State of Gujarat (2003).
members.conclusion: The sudden-fight exception did not apply to the facts, and the appeal against the conviction was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A court must independently determine that the price offered for a company’s property in liquidation is adequate before confirming a sale that is subject to its confirmation.
material_facts: The sale was of a company’s assets in liquidation, and acceptance of an offer by the commissioners was subject to confirmation by the court.
The agreed advertising requirements were not fully followed, the initial process attracted only one offer, and the court received higher offers after the sale process had begun.
The court had information indicating that the property might be worth more than the accepted offer.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, sales may be conducted by public auction, sealed tenders, or another manner directed by the Judge. Confirmation is a safeguard against an inadequate sale price, and the court must exercise its discretion judicially, having regard to the interests of the company and its creditors. The Court relied on Gordhan Das Chuni Lal v. T. Sriman Kanthimathinatha Pillai, AIR 1921 Mad 286; Rathnaswami Pillai v. Sadapathi Pillai, AIR 1925 Mad 318; S. Soundarajan v. M/s. Roshan & Co., AIR 1951 Mad 986; and A. Subbaraya Mudaliar v. K. Sundarajan, cited in the judgment as AIR 1951 Mad 1986.
members.conclusion: The initial offer should not have been confirmed without the court being satisfied that the price was adequate; in the circumstances, the sale required a fresh process.

predicates.company_property_sale_in_liquidation: A company’s property is being sold as part of its liquidation.
predicates.court_confirmation_required: The terms of the sale make the court’s confirmation a condition of the sale.
predicates.offered_price_not_reasonable: The circumstances relied on by the court show that the offered price is not reasonable having regard to the property’s market value.

members.legal_issue: A financial corporation enforcing security over charged assets must conduct a reasonable sale that seeks the best possible price and realizes sale proceeds for distribution among those entitled to them.
material_facts: The corporation held the first charge over the flour mill’s assets, while another creditor held a second charge.

The corporation agreed to transfer the assets without obtaining or producing a valuation, and the proposed consideration was pegged to the corporation’s debt and included a promise to pay the second creditor rather than realized proceeds.
The assets were handed to the proposed buyer before the tender deadline and before the bids were opened.
The corporation did not call for matching offers from the company’s directors, promoters or guarantors.
The corporation did not realize and distribute the full sale consideration.
members.legal_principle: Under section 29(1) and (4) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, a corporation enforcing its security must sell the charged property and apply realized proceeds first to its properly incurred costs and its debt, with the residue paid to those entitled to it. A charge creates a right to payment from the property or its proceeds, not an interest in the property itself (Transfer of Property Act, section 100). The corporation must seek the best possible price, understood as fair market value; adequate publicity and maximum participation in a public sale help achieve it. The Court relied on M/s S.J.S. Business Enterprises (P) Ltd. v. State of Bihar, which affirmed the approach in Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd. and Haryana Financial State Corporation v. Jagdamba Oil Mills; it also relied on Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India on abuse of statutory power, Rajah Kishendatt Ram v. Rajah Mumtaz Ali Khan on the treatment of surplus proceeds, and M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore and Subbu Chetti v. Arunachalam Chettiar on promises to discharge a third party’s debt.
members.conclusion: The agreement and transfer breached the corporation’s statutory duties and were invalid; the corporation had failed to act fairly or reasonably to secure the best possible price and protect the interests of the subsequent charge-holder and the mortgagor.
