members.legal_issue: A court confirming the sale of a company’s assets in liquidation must independently ensure that the sale is for a reasonable price through proper disclosure and judicial scrutiny of a reliable valuation.
material_facts: The court-appointed valuer produced a report that was not disclosed to the secured creditor before the sale was confirmed.
The report relied on unverified local estimates and treated long-term leasehold land as having a value based on rent, without adequately considering the land area or the lease-renewal condition.
The court accepted the report’s final valuation figure without examining its reasoning, and no reserve price was fixed for the sale.
The company’s property was sold as a going concern on the basis of an offer matching the report’s valuation, and the secured creditor challenged the confirmation.
members.legal_principle: In a winding-up sale, the court acts as custodian of the interests of the company and its creditors and must exercise judicial discretion to ensure a reasonable price. It must obtain and examine an expert valuation and disclose it to secured creditors and other interested persons; this duty applies even if objections are not raised. Under M/s Navlakha & Sons v. Sri Ramayana Das & Ors. (1969), confirmation does not give an offeror an automatic right to the property, and the court must satisfy itself that the price is reasonable. This principle was also relied on in Allahabad Bank v. Bengal Paper Mills Co. Ltd. (1999), Gordhan Das Chuni Lal v. T. Sriman Kanthimathinatha Pillai, Rathnaswami Pillai v. Sadapathy Pillai, S. Soundararajan v. Roshan & Co., and A. Subbaraya Mudaliar v. K. Sundararajan. Kayjay Industries (P) Ltd. v. Asnew Drums (P) Ltd. does not remove the duty to assess price; a failure to consider material factors may amount to material irregularity, particularly where the price is substantially inadequate.
members.conclusion: The confirmation of the sale was set aside because the court had not applied its mind to whether the price was reasonable, had not disclosed the valuation report to interested parties, and had proceeded without a reserve price. The property was to be revalued by another reliable expert and resold after disclosure of the valuation and appropriate advertisement.

predicates.valuation_report_materially_unreliable: The valuation report used materially inadequate or unsupported methods or assumptions.

members.legal_issue: A financial corporation’s sale of a defaulting unit or secured property must be conducted fairly and in a manner that gives the debtor a meaningful opportunity to protect the property’s value and offer to pay the debt.
material_facts: The corporation invited tenders and accepted a tender after negotiation, allowing payment over time.
The accepted offer was substantially below the appellant’s earlier proposed payment in settlement, and the appellant was not given notice or an opportunity to respond before acceptance.
The sale was made without a fair opportunity for the appellant to submit an offer or bring forward a higher offer.
members.legal_principle: Section 29 does not exclude natural justice. The corporation must act as a prudent trustee, seek competitive offers and the maximum reasonable price, and give the debtor relevant valuation and tender information and an opportunity to respond. Sale by public auction is the preferred method; a departure must be justified, and private negotiation is confined to exceptional large or specialised concerns with broad advertising. These requirements draw on Fertiliser Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India, Ram & Shyam Co. v. State of Haryana, Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal, Haji T.M. Hassan v. Kerala Financial Corporation, and Lakshmanasami Gounder v. C.I.T.
members.conclusion: The sale was unjust and unreasonable, was vitiated, and was set aside; the corporation was directed to resume possession and, if it later sold the property, to do so by open auction with wide publicity.

predicates.financial_corporation_sale_proceeding: A financial corporation sells a defaulting industrial unit or property securing a loan.
predicates.debtor_was_not_given_notice_or_opportuni: The corporation did not inform the debtor of the proposed acceptance or give the debtor an opportunity to respond or make an offer before the sale.
predicates.sale_process_was_not_fairly_competitive: The sale process did not fairly invite and assess competitive offers or otherwise reasonably seek the best available price.

members.legal_issue: A court confirming a sale of a company’s assets in liquidation must ensure that the sale is conducted so as to realise the best possible price for the creditors.
material_facts: The sale of the company’s assets was advertised only once in three newspapers, at least two of which were local.
A valuation report had been obtained but was not disclosed to the secured creditors, and the valuation did not account for the company’s leasehold land adequately.
No reserve price was fixed, and the sale order did not state that the accepted price was fair or adequate in light of the assets’ valuation.
The successful offer proposed payment terms that differed from the published terms, and another offer was not meaningfully compared with it.

The sale order did not assess the total claims against the company or the interests of unsecured creditors, and possession was ordered to be handed over promptly despite only part of the price having been paid.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, sales by the Official Liquidator are subject to court-approved terms and court confirmation. The confirmation requirement safeguards against an inadequate price, and the court must satisfy itself that the price is reasonable and the best that could be obtained, whether or not fraud or irregularity is alleged. The court acts as custodian of the company and its creditors, including unsecured creditors. These principles are stated in Navalkha & Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das, which relied on Gordhan Das Chuni Lal v. T. Sriman Kanthimathinatha Pillai, Rathnaswami Pillai v. Sadapathi Pillai, S. Soundarajan v. M/s Roshan & Co., and A. Subbaraya Mudaliar v. K. Sundarajan.
members.conclusion: The sale was liable to be set aside because the process did not ensure that the best possible price was obtained for the benefit of the creditors; the assets had to be revalued, a reserve bid fixed, and the sale readvertised.

predicates.liquidation_sale_confirmation_appeal: An appeal concerns a court’s confirmation of a sale of a company’s assets in liquidation.
predicates.sale_publicity_inadequate: The sale was not publicised sufficiently to give potential purchasers a fair opportunity to bid.
predicates.sale_value_not_properly_assessed: The court confirmed the sale without adequately assessing the assets’ value and whether the accepted price was the best reasonably obtainable.

members.legal_issue: When a Company Court considers a private disposition of company assets in winding-up proceedings, it must scrutinize the interests of creditors and the adequacy of the price before approving the transaction.
material_facts: The proposed transaction was a private sale of company land, rather than an auction conducted by an Official Liquidator.
The company opposed the proposed purchaser’s application and was not itself the applicant.
Secured creditors had substantial claims, and the sale proceeds were not shown to be sufficient to meet the company’s liabilities.
The Company Court directed execution of the sale deed without adequately considering creditor interests or the adequacy of the price.
members.legal_principle: A Company Court exercising discretion over a private sale must act with circumspection, consider the company’s and creditors’ interests, and satisfy itself that the price is reasonable in light of market value and applicable creditor priorities, including Section 529-A of the Companies Act, 1956. Section 536(2) is not intended to benefit a purchaser at the expense of creditors. The Court relied on M/s Kayjay Industries (P) Ltd. v. M/s Asnew Drums (P) Ltd., State of Punjab v. Yoginder Sharma Onkar Rai & Co., Allahabad Bank v. Bengal Paper Mills Co. Ltd., Andhra Bank v. Official Liquidator, and the principles discussed in Pankaj Mehra v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the Company Court had jurisdiction, its order could not stand because it had not fairly and carefully considered the creditors’ interests and whether the price was reasonable.

predicates.company_court_considers_private_asset_sa: The Company Court is asked to approve a private disposition of a company’s assets in winding-up proceedings.
predicates.creditor_claims_are_at_stake: Creditors have claims against the company that may be affected by the disposition.
predicates.sale_price_not_scrutinized: The court has not assessed whether the proposed price is reasonable and whether the transaction protects creditor interests.
predicates.sale_approval_is_improper_without_credit: The sale should not be approved without adequate review of creditor interests and price.

members.legal_issue: A financial corporation’s sale of a defaulting borrower’s assets is valid when it follows a fair, transparent process aimed at securing the best price and the borrower fails to use an opportunity to purchase on the accepted terms.
material_facts: The borrower defaulted on its loan, and the corporation took possession of its unit to recover the debt.
The corporation advertised the unit for sale three times over about a year, negotiated with prospective purchasers, and accepted the purchaser’s increased offer.
The borrower challenged the sale but did not produce a concrete better offer.
The Single Judge gave the borrower an opportunity to purchase on the purchaser’s terms, or to bring a better offer, and specified a payment deadline.
The borrower did not make the required payment, seek an extension, or bring a better offer before the corporation sold the unit to the purchaser.
The High Court directed the corporation to repeat the sale process because it considered the procedure inconsistent with guidelines in an earlier decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 authorizes a financial corporation, following default, to take possession of and sell the industrial concern’s assets. Under Article 226, a writ court does not sit as an appellate authority over the corporation’s commercial decisions; intervention is limited to statutory violation or unfair or unreasonable conduct. Sale of public property should aim to secure the best price through transparent procedures and due publicity, with maximum public participation where possible; auction is not the only permissible method, and tenders and negotiations may also be used. Reasonableness is assessed against the objective of securing the best price, and fairness does not prevent recovery of amounts due. Gem Cap (India) supports the limits on writ review; Naini Oxygen & Acetylene Gas cautions courts against substituting their commercial judgment; Contromix recognizes that tenders and negotiations can secure the best price and considers the borrower’s opportunity to produce a higher offer; Micro Cast Rubber reiterates that the corporation’s conduct should be assessed against the applicable guidelines and limits on review; Jagdamba Oil Mills overruled Mahesh Chandra and rejected its overly restrictive approach to the corporation’s sale powers; and S.J.S. Business Enterprises reiterates that reasonableness is tested against the dominant consideration of securing the best price.
members.conclusion: The corporation acted bona fide, and the sale to the purchaser was valid and legal. The High Court’s direction to repeat the sale process was set aside.

members.legal_issue: An autonomous district council cannot make laws granting or regulating mining leases in a field governed by national mining legislation.
material_facts: An autonomous district council claimed authority over land and mining matters in its district.
The national legislation governed regulation and development of minerals, and the constitutional schedule provided that district council laws could not prevail over inconsistent governing law.
The council’s cited rules concerned trade and did not confer authority to grant mining leases.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Entry 54 of List I, Entry 23 of List II, Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, and Paragraphs 3, 9 and 12A of the Sixth Schedule. It held that Union control under the national legislation denuded the corresponding legislative power of the State and district council in that field.
members.conclusion: The autonomous district council has no power to make laws concerning the grant of mining leases in the field governed by the national mining legislation.

predicates.appeal_concerning_district_council_minin: A party appealed a decision concerning a district council’s authority over mining.
predicates.national_mining_law_governs_mineral_regu: National legislation governed regulation and development of the minerals at issue.

members.legal_issue: A state government cannot use executive power to regulate or grant rights over a subject from which the state legislature has been excluded by parliamentary control.
material_facts: The State Government granted settlements or leases authorising collection of slurry discharged from coal washeries.
The slurry was mine waste whose disposal fell within the subject controlled by parliamentary legislation.
The State Legislature lacked power to regulate that disposal under the parliamentary declaration and the governing Act.
members.legal_principle: Article 162 makes state executive power co-extensive with state legislative power and subject to constitutional and parliamentary limits. Executive action cannot infringe rights where it is unsupported by legislative authority, and the State’s executive power cannot extend into a field taken over by parliamentary legislation. The Court relied on Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Thakur Bharat Singh, and applied Articles 162, 245 and 246, Entry 23 of List II, Entry 54 of List I, and Sections 2 and 18 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.
members.conclusion: The State Government had no executive authority to grant leases or settlements for collecting the slurry.

predicates.challenge_concerns_state_executive_grant: A proceeding challenges a state government's executive grant of rights to collect material discharged as mine waste.
predicates.parliamentary_control_covers_the_subject: Parliamentary legislation covers regulation of the relevant mine-waste disposal.
predicates.state_legislature_lacks_power_over_the_s: The state legislature has been excluded from legislating on the subject covered by parliamentary control.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot regulate mining leases for minor minerals in a field that parliamentary legislation has taken under central control.
material_facts: The leases concerned quarrying minor minerals and were granted before the state amendment and rules at issue.

After the central statute declared that the Union would control mine regulation and mineral development to the extent provided in that statute, it provided that state governments could make rules regulating the grant of prospecting licences and mining leases for minor minerals and for connected purposes.
The state amended its land-reform statute to substitute terms of existing minor-mineral leases that conflicted with state rules.
members.legal_principle: Under Constitution, Seventh Schedule, List I Entry 54 and List II Entry 23, a parliamentary declaration under section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 withdraws from the states the legislative field covered by that Act. Sections 14 and 15 address minor minerals and place regulation of the grant of their prospecting licences and mining leases, and connected purposes, within the statutory scheme. The Court applied Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa and State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co. It rejected the argument that the amendment was principally about land and land tenures: once mining leases exist, their regulation falls under the mining entry, even if it incidentally affects land; parliamentary control also counts as control by the Union.
members.conclusion: The state amendment was beyond the state legislature’s competence and invalid because parliamentary legislation had covered the relevant field of minor-mineral regulation.

predicates.minor_mineral_lease_regulation: The challenged law regulates leases for the extraction of minor minerals.

members.legal_issue: A state-made rule cannot alter the terms of existing mining leases without legislative authority from a competent legislature.
material_facts: The leases were granted before the state rules were made and remained in force when the rules were amended.
The amended rule purported to apply rent, royalty, and surface-rent terms to leases that already existed.

The parliamentary statute authorized modification of certain earlier leases but did not provide authority to alter leases of minor minerals granted after the specified cutoff; Parliament had not enacted a provision authorizing alteration of the leases at issue.
The state amendment that purported to authorize substitution of existing lease terms was invalid.
members.legal_principle: Vested interests cannot be taken away except under authority of law; rule-making power alone is insufficient. Sections 15 and 16 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 did not authorize the state rule to alter existing leases of the kind at issue: section 15 concerned rules regulating the grant of leases and connected purposes, while section 16 provided for modification only of leases granted before its specified cutoff. The Court also relied on the principle, applied in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa and State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., that the parliamentary legislation had withdrawn the relevant minor-mineral field from state legislative competence.
members.conclusion: The amended rule was ineffective to alter the terms of the existing leases because it lacked support from a competent legislative enactment.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot regulate the landlord-tenant relationship for house accommodation in cantonment areas where that subject falls within Parliament’s exclusive legislative authority.
material_facts: The premises were situated in a cantonment area and were occupied by a tenant under a private letting.
A state tenancy law had been extended to the cantonment area, and the tenant relied on its protections.
The owner challenged the validity of that extension on the ground that regulation of cantonment housing was within Parliament’s legislative field.
The High Court held the extension notification invalid, and the appeal challenged that decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 246, Parliament’s exclusive authority over matters in List I prevails over state legislative powers, including powers associated with land and landlord-tenant relations under Entry 18 of List II and transfer of property and contracts under Entries 6 and 7 of List III, insofar as they concern cantonment housing. The Court approved Nawal Mal v. Nathu Lal and disapproved A.C. Patel v. Vishwanath Chada, F.E. Darukhanawalla v. Khemchand Lalchand, Kewalchand v. Dashrathlal, and Babu Jagtanand v. Sri Satyanarayanji and Lakshmiji.
members.conclusion: Parliament has exclusive authority to legislate on the landlord-tenant relationship insofar as it concerns house accommodation in cantonment areas; the state law’s extension to the cantonment area was ultra vires and void, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_tenanc: The proceeding challenges the validity of applying a state tenancy law to premises in a cantonment area.
predicates.premises_in_cantonment: The premises governed by the disputed law are situated within a cantonment area.
predicates.state_law_governs_landlord_tenant_relati: The state law regulates the relationship between a landlord and a tenant concerning those premises.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot amend the terms of leases for minor minerals in a field that parliamentary legislation has occupied and withdrawn from state legislative competence.
material_facts: The leases concerned quarrying minor minerals and were granted before the challenged state amendment and rules.
After the estates vested, the state became the lessor under the existing leases.
The state amendment provided that inconsistent lease terms concerning minor minerals would be replaced by terms prescribed under state rules.

The parliamentary statute declared central control over regulation of mines and mineral development and provided that state governments could make rules regulating the grant of minor-mineral leases and related purposes.
members.legal_principle: Under Entries 54 of the Union List and 23 of the State List, a parliamentary declaration and legislation occupy the field to the extent provided by that legislation, leaving no state legislative competence within the occupied field. Sections 2, 14 and 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 covered regulation of minor-mineral leases and empowered state governments to make rules, but did not restore legislative power to state legislatures. The Court applied Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa and State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co. It also held that the amendment's substance concerned regulation of mining leases, not land tenures, notwithstanding its incidental effect on land.
members.conclusion: The state legislature lacked competence to enact the amendment, which was invalid, and the state could not enforce it against the leaseholders.

members.legal_issue: A state rule cannot alter vested terms of an existing mining lease without authority in a law enacted by a competent legislature.
material_facts: The leases were granted before the state rules that prescribed revised dead rent, royalty and surface rent.
The state added a rule applying those prescribed charges to leases already subsisting when the rules commenced.
The leases were outside the class of older leases for which the parliamentary statute expressly provided for modification.
No valid legislative enactment authorized alteration of the terms of these existing leases; the state amendment relied on for that purpose was invalid.
members.legal_principle: Vested rights under existing leases cannot be taken away except under authority of law; rulemaking power alone is insufficient. Section 16 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 provided for modification of leases granted before the specified historical cutoff, but did not authorize modification of the leases at issue. Section 15's rulemaking authority did not itself empower the state to alter those vested lease terms. Because the state amendment was invalid, it could not supply the missing authority for the rule. The Court also relied on the principle that a field occupied by parliamentary legislation cannot be supplemented by state legislation where no room remains for it.
members.conclusion: The rule applying the revised terms to existing leases was ineffective, and the state could not enforce it against the leaseholders.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires property from a party while a suit concerning that property is pending is bound by the resulting decision in the circumstances addressed by the court.
material_facts: A purchaser acquired the property from a person who was a party to an earlier suit while that suit was pending.
The purchaser claimed through that party, and the prior decrees addressed rights in the property; a later injunction suit also included the purchaser.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC binds parties and their privies to final decisions on issues directly and substantially determined in earlier proceedings. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act applies the doctrine of lis pendens to a transfer of property during the pendency of a suit concerning rights in that property.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was bound by the prior decrees as a successor in title and was also affected by the doctrine of lis pendens.

rule.if: property_suit_pending and transfer_from_party_during_suit and transferee_claims_through_party and prior_decision_finally_determines_property_issue

predicates.prior_decision_finally_determines_proper: The resulting final decision determined an issue concerning rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: An interest acquired from a party to litigation in property that remains in dispute during the litigation is subject to the outcome of that litigation.
material_facts: A party to a pending partition proceeding sold the disputed land to the claimant while the appeal in that proceeding was pending.
The claim to the land had not been finally decided when the sale occurred.
The pending proceeding later ended in a compromise decree concerning rights in the property.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that the compromise decree related back to the institution of the suit between the parties and that the purchaser's claim, acquired from a party while the dispute remained pending, was governed by the result of that proceeding. The Court did not identify a particular provision or earlier case as the basis for this application.
members.conclusion: The claimant's alleged interest under the sale had to abide by the outcome of the pending proceeding, which culminated in the compromise decree.

predicates.property_transfer_during_pending_propert: A transfer of property occurs while litigation concerning that property is pending.
predicates.transferor_is_party_to_litigation: The person who transfers the property is a party to the pending litigation.
predicates.transferred_property_is_in_dispute: The transferred property is among the property whose rights are being contested in the pending litigation.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires property during a pending suit concerning it is bound by the result of that litigation.
material_facts: The original purchaser filed a suit asserting title to the property.
The property was transferred to the appellants and their predecessors while that suit was pending.
The evidence and findings showed that the later purchasers had notice of the earlier sale and the pending suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 bars a transfer of immovable property during litigation from affecting the rights of the other parties under the decree. Section 3 addresses notice, including notice arising where a transaction affecting immovable property has been effected by a registered instrument. The Court also relied on Mangru Mahto v. Shri Thakur Taraknathji Tarakeshwar Math concerning the effect of a transfer made during mortgage litigation.
members.conclusion: The appellants and their predecessors were bound by the decree because they purchased pendente lite, with notice of the prior sale.

predicates.suit_concerning_property_is_pending: A suit concerning rights in the property is pending before a court.
predicates.property_transferred_during_suit: The property is transferred while that suit remains pending.
predicates.transferee_claims_under_that_transfer: The transferee bases a claim to the property on the transfer made during the suit.

members.legal_issue: A transferee that acquires disputed property while an appeal concerning it is pending takes subject to the litigation and cannot obtain success in its appeal merely by virtue of the transfer.
material_facts: The State transferred the suit land to a corporation while the appeal concerning the land was pending in the High Court.
The corporation appealed against the judgment in favour of the plaintiffs.
The State’s appeal was dismissed.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of lis pendens applies to a transfer of property made while litigation concerning that property is pending. The Court also relied on the consequence of dismissing the transferor State’s appeal when dismissing the transferee corporation’s appeal.
members.conclusion: The transfer was hit by lis pendens, and the corporation’s appeal was dismissed following dismissal of the State’s appeal.

predicates.property_appeal_pending: An appeal concerning rights to particular property was pending.
predicates.property_transferred_during_appeal: A party to the dispute transferred the property while that appeal was pending.
predicates.transferor_appeal_dismissed: The appeal brought by the party that transferred the property was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires property while litigation concerning it is pending is bound by the final order in that litigation.
material_facts: The acquisition de-notification was challenged by the beneficiary society, and that challenge was pending before the Supreme Court when the petitioners purchased the land.
The Supreme Court later quashed the de-notification, thereby reviving the acquisition proceedings.
The petitioners argued that they were not bound because no interim order had prevented the purchase.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 embodies the doctrine of lis pendens. A transferee pendente lite is bound by the decree as if a party to the litigation; a transfer cannot defeat the other party’s rights under the decree unless made with the court’s permission. The Court relied on K. Adivi Naidu v. E. Duruvasulu Naidu, Venkatrao Anantdeo Joshi v. Malatibai, Raj Kumar v. Sardari Lal, Sanjay Verma v. Manik Roy, Rajender Singh v. Santa Singh, and T.G. Ashok Kumar v. Govindammal.
members.conclusion: The petitioners were bound by the Supreme Court’s final order despite having purchased the land during the pending litigation and despite the absence of an interim order.

rule.if: property_rights_litigation_pending and property_transferred_during_litigation and not transfer_with_court_permission and proceeding_to_apply_final_order

predicates.proceeding_to_apply_final_order: A proceeding seeks to apply the final order made in the property litigation.
predicates.transferee_bound_by_final_order: The transferee is bound by the final order in the property litigation.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made while litigation concerning the property is pending is not void merely because it is pendente lite, but the transferee is bound by the result of that litigation.
material_facts: The owner transferred the land to a purchaser while a suit concerning ownership of the land was pending.
The lower courts treated the transfer as hit by the doctrine of lis pendens.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 prohibits a transfer during pending litigation from defeating the rights determined in that litigation, but does not itself declare the transfer void.
members.conclusion: The transfer was not rendered void or ineffective merely by the pending litigation; the purchaser remained bound by the result of that litigation.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_a_transfer_durin: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning a transfer made while a property dispute was pending.
predicates.transfer_made_during_pending_suit: The property was transferred while a suit concerning it was pending.
predicates.pending_suit_determines_rights_in_proper: The pending suit concerns the rights in the property transferred.

members.legal_issue: Persons who acquire interests in property while litigation concerning that property is pending are bound by the final orders in that litigation.
material_facts: The challenged orders determined claims concerning the acquired land after considering the claims of persons who had objected to the acquisition.
Some applicants had purchased land while proceedings concerning it were pending.
The applicants relied on their purchases and subsequent circumstances to resist implementation of the orders.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the binding effect of final adjudications and held that a purchaser during pending proceedings is bound by the orders concerning the property. It relied on the finality principles stated in T.R. Dhananjaya v. J. Vasudevan and Prithawi Nath Ram v. State of Jharkhand.
members.conclusion: The applicants who purchased land during the pending proceedings were bound by the orders and could not rely on their purchases or changed circumstances to defeat those orders.

predicates.proceeding_enforces_final_order: The proceeding seeks enforcement of a final order concerning property.
predicates.property_litigation_pending_at_purchase: A person acquired an interest in the property while litigation concerning it was pending.

members.legal_issue: Oral evidence may be given to show that a written document was not intended to operate as an agreement but was a sham.
material_facts: The appellant asserted that the written agency-and-licence agreement was a sham and was not intended to be acted upon.
Evidence showed that the appellant submitted accounts and paid commissions in accordance with the agreement.
The appellant’s account of why the agreement was allegedly a sham was rejected on the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, require the writing to prove its terms and generally bar oral evidence that contradicts or varies those terms. They do not bar a party from proving that a document was never intended to operate as an agreement and was merely a sham. The Court relied on Smt. Gangabai v. Smt. Chhabubai and Ishwar Dass Jain v. Sohan Lal.
members.conclusion: The bar on varying written terms did not prevent oral evidence to show that the document was a sham, although the evidence in this case did not establish that claim.

predicates.dispute_over_written_agreement: The proceeding concerns the effect of a written agreement between parties.
predicates.party_claims_document_was_sham: A party asserts that the written document was not intended to operate as an agreement and was only a sham.

members.legal_issue: The bar on oral evidence concerning the terms of a written transaction does not prevent a party from proving that the transaction recorded in the document was never intended to operate and that a different transaction was made.
material_facts: A document purported to record a sale and a rent arrangement.
The party resisting the document’s effect alleged that it was nominal, was never intended to be acted upon, and that the actual arrangement was a loan secured by the property.
The trial court permitted oral evidence supporting that allegation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92(1) of the Indian Evidence Act require the terms and nature of a transaction to be derived from the document when a party relies on it, and generally bar oral evidence between the parties to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from its terms. That bar does not apply when a party asserts that the transaction recorded in the document was never intended to operate and that a different transaction altogether was made. The Court followed Tyagaraja Mudaliyar v. Vedathanni and also noted the first proviso to section 92, which permits proof of facts that invalidate a document or entitle a person to related relief.
members.conclusion: Section 92(1) did not bar the oral evidence; the evidence was admissible to show that the document was a sham and that a different transaction had been made.

predicates.written_transaction_dispute: Parties dispute the effect of a document that purports to record a transaction between them.
predicates.party_alleges_sham_document: A party to the transaction says the document was never intended by the parties to operate.
predicates.party_asserts_different_transaction: That party says the parties made a different transaction from the one recorded in the document.

members.legal_issue: A defendant who is not a party to a transfer may plead and prove that the transfer deed is fictitious, sham, or collusive.
material_facts: The defendant challenging the sale was not a party to the sale between the vendor and the purchaser.
The defendant alleged that the sale deed was fictitious because the full consideration had not been paid.
The Court distinguished a deed intended to effect a genuine transfer from one never intended to operate as a transfer of title.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to apply the broad formulation in Lal Achal Ram v. Raja Kazim Hussain Khan so as to prevent every challenge by a stranger. It approved the approach in Kamini Kumar Deb v. Durga Charan Nag, Saradindu Mukherjee v. S.M. Kunja Katnini Roy, Jugal Kishore Tiwari v. Umesh Chandra Tiwari, and Sanatan Mohapatra v. Hakim Mohammad Kazim Mohammad: a defendant may raise a legitimate plea that a deed was void, fictitious, or collusive, and whether the deed was genuine depends on the pleadings, nature of the suit and deed, evidence, and surrounding circumstances.
members.conclusion: A defendant may raise a legitimate defence that a deed is void, fictitious, or collusive, including when the defendant is a stranger to that deed.

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute was heard as a civil suit.
predicates.challenger_is_not_party_to_deed: The defendant challenging the deed was not a party to the transaction recorded in it.
predicates.deed_is_alleged_to_be_sham_or_collusive: The defendant alleged that the deed was not intended to effect a genuine transfer of title.

members.legal_issue: A person who is not a party to a written transaction may challenge it as sham and adduce evidence that its apparent terms were not intended to be acted upon.
material_facts: The occupants were not parties to the registered lease between the owners and the tenant.
The occupants alleged that the lease was a sham arrangement intended to avoid rent-control protections, rather than seeking to vary or contradict its written terms.
members.legal_principle: Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872 did not apply because the occupants were not parties to the lease and were not seeking to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from its terms. A party may challenge the apparent validity of a document by alleging that the transaction it records was fictitious or not intended to be acted upon, but bears the burden of proving that allegation.
members.conclusion: The occupants were permitted to plead that the lease was sham and to adduce evidence in support; the rules governing proof of the written terms did not bar that challenge.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.challenger_is_not_party_to_document: The person challenging a written transaction was not a party to that document.
predicates.challenge_alleges_transaction_was_sham: The challenger alleges that the transaction recorded in the document was not genuine or was not intended to be acted upon.

members.legal_issue: A defendant resisting a title claim based on a sale deed may contend that the deed is fictitious, collusive, nominal, not acted upon, or not binding on the defendant without first bringing a separate proceeding to set it aside.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership based on registered sale deeds.
The person whose interest was said to be affected by the earlier sale deed had not signed it.
The defendants contended that the earlier deed was nominal and not acted upon, and that it did not bind them.
The defendants had not brought separate proceedings to set aside the deeds.
members.legal_principle: A defendant may raise any legitimate plea available in law to defeat the plaintiff’s claim, including that a deed relied upon to establish title is void, fictitious, collusive, nominal, not intended to be acted upon, or not binding on the defendant. The Court relied on Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao and Another.
members.conclusion: The defendants could raise those defences in the title suit without independently challenging the sale deed by a separate suit or counterclaim.

predicates.declaration_suit_based_on_sale_deed: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership based on a sale deed.
predicates.defendant_not_bound_by_deed: The defendant was not a party to, or otherwise bound by, the deed relied upon by the plaintiff.
predicates.defendant_disputes_deed_as_not_genuine_o: The defendant contended that the deed was not genuine, was not intended to operate, or did not bind the defendant.

members.legal_issue: The rule against using extrinsic evidence to vary written terms does not bar evidence concerning a preliminary recital of past fact or evidence showing that a writing’s apparent character does not reflect the real transaction.
material_facts: The deed contained a preliminary recital describing a prior request to live separately after division, as well as operative provisions allocating land.
The dispute concerned whether the recital and the deed’s maintenance terminology reflected the actual transaction and whether the family’s joint status had already been severed.
The Court used the recital, surrounding circumstances, and subsequent conduct to determine the deed’s true character without varying its operative terms.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Evidence Act bars evidence that varies, contradicts, adds to, or subtracts from the terms of a written disposition, but does not bar evidence concerning a preliminary recital of past fact that is not itself a dispositive term. Evidence de hors the document may also be led where the dispute concerns whether the writing is an illusory or colourable device that cloaks the real transaction. The Court relied on Chandi Prasad Singh v. Piari Bidi and Bhagwan Dayal v. Mst. Reoti Devi.
members.conclusion: The evidentiary bar did not prevent consideration of extrinsic evidence concerning the preliminary recital or the true character of the transaction.

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning competing claims to property.
predicates.disputed_writing_exists: The parties dispute the meaning or character of a written transaction.
predicates.writing_contains_preliminary_past_fact_r: The writing includes a preliminary account of an event or communication that occurred before the writing was made.
predicates.extrinsic_evidence_tests_recital_or_true: A party offers evidence from outside the writing to test the truth of the preliminary recital or the writing’s apparent character.
predicates.extrinsic_evidence_varies_dispositive_te: The offered evidence would contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the writing’s operative disposition of property.

members.legal_issue: Oral evidence is admissible to show that a document, though executed, was never intended to operate and recorded a sham transaction.
material_facts: The defendant admitted execution of the mortgage deed but alleged that it was not intended to operate as a mortgage.
The defendant alleged that the deed was executed only as collateral security and that the transaction was intended to avoid rent-control protections.
members.legal_principle: Section 92(1) of the Evidence Act bars evidence that varies, contradicts, adds to, or subtracts from the terms of a document relied on as recording the transaction. It does not bar oral evidence where a party contends that the recorded transaction was never intended to be acted upon and that the document was sham. The Court relied on Gangabai v. Chhabubai.
members.conclusion: Section 92(1) of the Evidence Act did not bar oral evidence offered to prove that the mortgage deed was a sham document.

predicates.party_to_document: The person offering the evidence was a party to the document.
predicates.alleges_document_never_intended_to_opera: The party alleged that the executed document was never intended to take effect.
predicates.alleges_different_real_transaction: The party alleged that the actual transaction differed from the one recorded in the document.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be granted for the performable part of a contract when the seller cannot perform the whole, the purchaser accepts exclusion of the unperformable part, and the purchaser satisfies the applicable consideration and relinquishment requirements.
material_facts: A minor held a share in the property, and the court refused permission to sell that share during the suit.
The other sellers could convey their own shares.
The purchaser sought a sale of the other sellers’ shares, relinquished any claim to the minor’s share, and sought to pay the consideration reduced by the proportionate value of that share.
The purchaser was found to have been ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance of the part a defaulting party can perform when the other party meets the applicable payment requirement and relinquishes claims to performance and compensation for the unperformed part. The Court relied on Sardar Singh v. Krishna Devi (Smt.) and Another and Rachakonda Narayana v. Ponthala Parvathamma and Another; Rachakonda states that specific performance is ordinarily granted when the statutory requirements are met, unless delay, laches, or another disability exists. The Court also considered Surinder Singh v. Kapoor Singh (Dead) through LRs. and Others.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance of the part of the agreement that the sellers could perform, excluding the minor’s share and adjusting the consideration accordingly.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and seller_cannot_perform_entire_contract and seller_can_transfer_performable_part and buyer_relinquishes_unperformable_part and buyer_pays_adjusted_consideration and buyer_ready_and_willing

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.seller_cannot_perform_entire_contract: A seller was unable to convey the whole property covered by the agreement.
predicates.seller_can_transfer_performable_part: The seller could convey a distinct part of the agreed property.
predicates.buyer_relinquishes_unperformable_part: The purchaser gave up claims to performance and compensation concerning the part that could not be conveyed.
predicates.buyer_pays_adjusted_consideration: The purchaser offered to pay the agreed consideration adjusted as required for the part to be conveyed.
predicates.buyer_ready_and_willing: The purchaser remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations.

members.legal_issue: A contract for the sale of jointly owned property may be specifically enforced against the contracting co-owner’s identifiable share when that co-owner lacked authority to bind the other owner.
material_facts: The agreement covered the whole property, which was owned in equal shares by the contracting seller and his sister.
The seller purported to contract on his sister’s behalf but had no authority to do so.
The seller’s own share was identifiable, and the purchasers sought specific performance limited to that share.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(2) and 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance of the performable part may be granted when the defendant cannot perform the whole contract and the statutory conditions for partial performance are met. Kartar Singh v. Harjinder Singh was confined to its facts: there, the non-signing co-owner had not contracted at all and the contracting party’s agreement to sell his own share was separate and severable. It does not establish that Section 12 is inapplicable whenever a co-owner lacks authority to sell another owner’s share. Rachakonda Narayana v. Ponthala Parvathamma explains the conditions for partial performance.
members.conclusion: Section 12 applied because the agreement covered the whole property but the seller could not perform the part relating to his sister’s share. Specific performance could therefore be granted against the seller’s share, subject to the purchasers satisfying the requirements for partial performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and agreement_covers_multiple_owners_shares and seller_lacks_authority_for_another_share and seller_owns_identifiable_share and purchaser_accepts_performable_share and purchaser_relinquishes_remaining_performance_and_compensation

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: A party seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.agreement_covers_multiple_owners_shares: The agreement purports to cover shares owned by more than one person.
predicates.seller_lacks_authority_for_another_share: The person who made the agreement lacked authority to bind another owner as to that owner’s share.
predicates.seller_owns_identifiable_share: The contracting seller owns a share that can be distinguished from the other owner’s share.
predicates.purchaser_accepts_performable_share: The purchaser seeks performance only of the part the seller can perform.
predicates.purchaser_relinquishes_remaining_perform: The purchaser gives up any claim to performance of the unperformable part and any claim to compensation for its non-performance.

members.legal_issue: A buyer may obtain specific performance of the part of a contract the seller can perform when the seller is unable to perform the whole contract and the buyer satisfies the required consideration and relinquishment conditions.
material_facts: The agreement covered two parcels, but the seller was unable to transfer one of them because he had no title to it.
The buyer agreed to take the parcel the seller could transfer, deposited the full contract price, and relinquished any claim to the other parcel and to compensation.
The first appellate court granted specific performance for the parcel the seller could transfer.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance of the part a defaulting party can perform if the other party satisfies the applicable consideration requirement and relinquishes claims to performance of the remaining part and compensation. For a part that admits of compensation, the consideration is the contract consideration reduced by that attributable to the part left unperformed; for a part that does not admit of compensation, the consideration for the whole contract is required. The relief is discretionary and is ordinarily granted if there is no delay, laches, or other disability affecting the claimant.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court was justified in granting specific performance of the performable part of the contract on these facts.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and seller_unable_to_perform_part and buyer_pays_required_consideration and buyer_relinquishes_remaining_performance_and_compensation and no_delay_laches_or_other_disability

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A buyer brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.seller_unable_to_perform_part: The seller was unable to perform part of the contract.
predicates.buyer_pays_required_consideration: The buyer paid or agreed to pay the consideration required for the part the seller could perform.
predicates.buyer_relinquishes_remaining_performance: The buyer gave up claims to performance of the remaining part and to compensation for its non-performance.
predicates.no_delay_laches_or_other_disability: The buyer was not affected by delay, laches, or another disability that would weigh against the discretionary relief.

members.legal_issue: A contract for the sale of an entire divisible property by a person who owns only part of it and lacks the consent of a co-owner cannot support specific performance against the non-consenting co-owner, but may be specifically enforced as to the seller’s share.
material_facts: The seller contracted to sell the entire house, but the appellant owned half of it and had not consented to the sale.
The house was divisible, and the sale agreement did not bind the appellant as to his half share.
The purchaser and her husband were neighbours, and the property’s joint mutation and joint possession provided indications of joint ownership.
The courts below ordered specific performance of the contract for the entire property.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary; that discretion must be exercised on sound and reasonable judicial principles, considering the circumstances, the parties’ conduct, and their respective interests. Section 12(1) generally bars specific performance of only part of a contract, but Section 12(4) permits it where the part that can and ought to be performed stands on a separate and independent footing from the part that cannot or ought not to be performed. Section 10(b) concerns whether monetary compensation would afford adequate relief. Applying these provisions, the Court held that equity and justice required partial enforcement because the property was divisible and the seller could not contract on behalf of the non-consenting co-owner.
members.conclusion: The decree for specific performance of the entire property was erroneous. The contract could be specifically enforced only in respect of the seller’s half share, and not against the appellant’s share.

members.legal_issue: A court may order specific performance of the part of a contract for sale of land that remains performable when the seller has transferred another part to a third party, with a proportionate reduction in consideration for the part that cannot be conveyed.
material_facts: The seller agreed to sell the entire property for a lump sum and accepted a substantial part of the consideration.
After making that agreement, the seller conveyed one-third of the property to another purchaser by a registered deed.
The original purchaser had tendered the remaining consideration, which the seller did not accept.
The seller retained ownership and control of the balance of the property, and the trial court ordered conveyance of that balance at a proportionately reduced consideration.
members.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, permits specific performance in part in the circumstances it specifies. The Court construed Section 12 purposively to allow performance of the part still capable of performance and to prevent a seller from deliberately frustrating the whole contract by transferring part of the property. The Court also referred to Section 10 as it stood before the 2018 amendment; it cited no earlier case on this issue.
members.conclusion: The decree for specific performance of the remaining property at a reduced consideration was properly upheld.

predicates.remaining_property_still_performable: The seller retained a part of the contracted property that could still be conveyed to the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_paid_or_tendered_consideration: The purchaser paid or offered the consideration required for the contracted sale.

predicates.partial_specific_performance_may_be_orde: The court may order specific performance of the part of the contract that remains performable, with an appropriate reduction in consideration.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be granted for the identifiable share that a contracting seller can convey even though other co-owners did not agree to the sale.
material_facts: The seller agreed to sell land held in the names of himself, his brother, and his minor son.
The brother did not agree to the sale, and no decree was made for his share; the purchaser did not appeal the denial of relief for that share.
The trial court ordered specific performance for the seller’s share, and the High Court also granted relief for the son’s share after finding that the seller owned it beneficially.
The shares were identifiable, and a purchaser of a share could seek partition to have it demarcated.
members.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Jammu and Kashmir Specific Relief Act, 1977 allows a court, in the circumstances it specifies, to direct performance of the part of a contract that a defaulting party can perform. The Court relied on Kartar Singh v. Harjinder Singh, which held that an agreement may be enforced against the co-owner who signed it where that owner’s share is identifiable; such relief is performance of the contract as between the contracting parties, rather than partial performance of the kind addressed by Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. A purchaser of a share may seek partition to have it demarcated.
members.conclusion: There was no bar to specific performance for the share or shares the contracting seller could convey; the absence of the other co-owner’s agreement did not make the contract indivisible for that purpose.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be granted to the extent of the contracting co-owners’ undivided shares even when the other co-owners did not join the agreement.
material_facts: The agreement to sell was executed by some, but not all, of the co-owners.
The property was jointly owned, and the agreement provided for a conveyance of absolute title, including by having other persons join if necessary.
The seller co-owners’ interests were capable of being transferred, although the non-contracting co-owners disputed the transaction.
The purchaser sought specific performance and was willing to accept the contracting co-owners’ shares.
members.legal_principle: Under the equitable principle applied in Kartar Singh v. Harjinder Singh, Sardar Singh v. Krishna Devi, A. Abdul Rashid Khan v. P.A.K.A. Shahul Hamid, Surinder Singh v. Kapoor Singh, and Gajara Vishnu Gosavi v. Prakash Nanasaheb Kamble, an agreement made by a co-owner can be specifically enforced to the extent of that co-owner’s share even if other co-owners did not join. Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, is consistent with transfer of an undivided interest. Article 2177 of the Portuguese Civil Code, 1867, does not prohibit alienation of an undivided interest; a purchaser of such an interest may seek partition, but cannot obtain possession of a specified part before partition.
members.conclusion: The decree for specific performance to the extent of the contracting co-owners’ shares was not disturbed; the purchaser was not entitled to specific performance of the entire property.

members.legal_issue: Prolonged and continuous cohabitation as spouses, in the absence of an insurmountable obstacle to marriage, gives rise to a presumption of lawful marriage and supports the legitimacy of children born of the union.
material_facts: The woman and the deceased lived openly together as husband and wife for 23 to 24 years, and children were born to them.
Their children and the woman lived in the family home, and relatives and friends treated them as a family.
A property sale deed described two of the children as the deceased’s sons, and the settlement deed described the woman as his widow and the children as his children.
The evidence that the woman had been married to another man who was still alive was disbelieved, and no insurmountable obstacle to marriage was established.
members.legal_principle: Under Mahomedan law, prolonged and continuous cohabitation as husband and wife, where there is no insurmountable obstacle to marriage, supports a presumption that a lawful marriage took place. The presumption does not arise from mere casual concubinage or where an insurmountable obstacle exists, and may not apply where the parties’ conduct is incompatible with marriage. The Court relied on Khaja Hidayut Oollah v. Rai Jan Khanam (1844) 3 Moore’s Indian Appeals 295 and referred to the Privy Council decisions reported at 21 Indian Appeals 56 and 37 Indian Appeals 105, as well as Mulla’s Mahomedan Law, section 268.
members.conclusion: The presumption of lawful marriage arose; the woman was the deceased’s lawfully wedded wife and the children born of the union were legitimate.

predicates.marital_status_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over marital status and the legitimacy of children in an inheritance claim.
predicates.prolonged_continuous_cohabitation_as_spo: A man and woman cohabit continuously for a prolonged period and are treated as spouses.
predicates.insurmountable_obstacle_to_marriage: An obstacle exists that makes marriage between the man and woman impossible.

members.legal_issue: Long and continuous cohabitation as spouses, together with recognition of the relationship, gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of a valid marriage.
material_facts: The woman began living with the man as his wife after his first wife died and continued living with him in the family household.
They had a son together, and their relationship as husband and wife was not denied by the persons concerned.
The challenger relied on the absence of direct proof of a valid marriage but produced no unimpeachable evidence rebutting the presumption.
members.legal_principle: The law presumes marriage rather than concubinage where a man and woman have cohabited continuously for a long time; the presumption is rebuttable, but a party seeking to deny the relationship's legal origin bears a heavy burden and must provide clear, unimpeachable evidence. The Court relied on A. Dinohamy v. W.L. Balahamy, AIR 1927 PC 185, and Gokal Chand v. Parvin Kumari, AIR 1952 SC 231.
members.conclusion: The presumption of a valid marriage was not rebutted, and the woman was held to be the man's legally wedded wife.

members.legal_issue: Prolonged cohabitation and social treatment as spouses do not establish a lawful marriage when the surrounding evidence cumulatively rebuts the presumption arising from that cohabitation.
material_facts: The claimant said that he had married the deceased and sought to inherit her property as her husband.
The claimant and the deceased had lived together for several years and were treated by others as husband and wife; they had a daughter.
The court found the testimony of the witnesses who claimed to have attended the wedding unconvincing.
The claimant did not call close relatives, villagers, or the deceased’s relatives to corroborate the alleged marriage.
The deceased’s mother denied that the deceased had married the claimant, and the deceased’s will also stated that she had not married him.
The claimant did not visit or make inquiries about the deceased or their alleged daughter during the years they lived apart.
The court found that the properties had been acquired for the deceased by another person, rather than with the claimant’s money.
members.legal_principle: Long and continuous cohabitation may support a rebuttable presumption of marriage, but the court must consider circumstances that weaken or destroy that presumption. The court considered the Indian Evidence Act, section 50, but held that the question of the relevance of particular witnesses’ relationship opinions was academic; the decision rested on the evidence as a whole. No earlier case was cited for the presumption of marriage applied here.
members.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish that the deceased was his lawfully wedded wife, and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Prolonged living together as husband and wife gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of a valid marriage, and the evidence relied on did not rebut that presumption.
material_facts: The couple had lived together as husband and wife for many years, and it was undisputed that the child was born to them.
The woman and her child were not mentioned in the father’s will or in the family partition compromise.
The witnesses’ depositions did not state that the couple had not lived together.
The first appellate court found a valid marriage by applying the presumption, but the High Court reversed that finding in a second appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Gokal Chand v. Parvin Kumari, prolonged cohabitation as husband and wife raises a rebuttable presumption of a valid marriage. On the facts here, omission from the father’s will and family compromise did not rebut the presumption, and the witness testimony did not contradict the cohabitation. The High Court was therefore not justified in interfering with the first appellate court’s factual finding.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in treating the presumption as rebutted on these circumstances. The Supreme Court restored the first appellate court’s finding.

members.legal_issue: Long-term cohabitation as spouses gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of marriage, and children born of that relationship are not presumed illegitimate.
material_facts: The recorded landholder and the children's mother lived together as husband and wife for a long period after his first wife's death.
Their relationship was accepted as a marital relationship by family members and the community.
The claimants and other children were born from the relationship.
The challengers relied on contradictory age documents, but did not produce unimpeachable evidence rebutting the relationship or the presumption arising from it.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, cohabitation under the same roof for a number of years permits a presumption that the couple lived as husband and wife and that their children are not illegitimate. The law favours marriage over concubinage where a man and woman have cohabited continuously for years, although the presumption may be rebutted by unimpeachable evidence. The court relied on S.P.S. Balasubramanyam v. Suruttayan, AIR 1992 SC 756 and (1994) 1 SCC 460; Mohabbat Ali Khan v. Mohd. Ibrahim Khan, AIR 1929 PC 135; Gokalchand v. Parvin Kumar, AIR 1952 SC 231; Ranganath Parmeshwar Panditrao Mali v. Eknath Gajanan Kulkarni, (1996) 7 SCC 681; and Sobha Hymavathi Devi v. Setti Gangadhara Swamy, (2005) 2 SCC 244. It also referred to S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal, (2010) 5 SCC 600, relying on Lata Singh v. State of U.P., AIR 2006 SC 2522, concerning live-in relationships between unmarried adults of different sexes.
members.conclusion: The long-standing relationship gave rise to a presumption of marriage, and the children could not be treated as illegitimate on the material relied on by the challengers; their claim to be recorded as heirs was not disproved.

members.legal_issue: Continuous cohabitation as spouses supports a presumption of a marital relationship and the legitimacy of their children, and omissions in earlier documents or evidence that does not deny cohabitation do not rebut that presumption.
material_facts: The man and the woman lived together under the same roof and cohabited for many years.
Children, including the person through whom the claimant derived title, were born to them.
A will and a later compromise did not mention the woman or her children.
The witnesses relied on to challenge the relationship did not deny that the man and woman lived together.
The first appellate court accepted the presumption and decreed the title suit, but the High Court reversed that decision; the matter reached the Supreme Court in an appeal concerning the title suit.
members.legal_principle: Continuous cohabitation and living together as husband and wife give rise to a presumption of a marital relationship. The absence of references to the woman or her children in a will or compromise, and testimony that does not deny their cohabitation, do not rebut that presumption or undermine the legitimacy of the children. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The circumstances relied on to rebut the presumption were not relevant or sufficient to destroy it. The appeal was allowed, and the first appellate court’s decree was restored.

predicates.title_suit_appeal: A civil appeal concerns a title suit in which a lower appellate court accepted a marital-relationship presumption and the High Court reversed that decision.

members.legal_issue: Long-term cohabitation as spouses, supported by evidence, raises a rebuttable presumption of a valid marriage and legitimacy that may establish a child’s right to share in family property.
material_facts: The suit concerned family property governed by Mitakshara law, and the plaintiffs claimed a share through the first plaintiff’s asserted parentage.
The High Court accepted that the first plaintiff was the son of the deceased family member but denied partition because it found no proof that his parents had married or cohabited as spouses.
A witness testified that the parents had married and lived together as husband and wife.

Documents created before the dispute, including birth, electoral, service, and death records, identified the parents’ relationship; letters and other evidence also supported the claim that the mother received money from the family.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence established long cohabitation and that the defendants had not rebutted the presumption of marriage.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, long cohabitation as husband and wife gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of marriage. The law presumes marriage rather than concubinage and favours legitimacy; a heavy burden rests on a party seeking to deny the relationship’s legal origin. The Court relied on Andrahennedige Dinohamy v. Wijetunge Liyanapatabendige Balahamy, Mohabbat Ali Khan v. Mohd. Ibrahim Khan, Badri Prasad v. Dy. Director of Consolidation, S.P.S. Balasubramanyam v. Suruttayan, Gokul Chand v. Parvin Kumari, Tulsa v. Durghatiya, Challamma v. Tilaga, Madan Mohan Singh v. Rajni Kant, and Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the partition decree. The appeals were allowed and the Trial Court’s decree granting the plaintiffs a share was restored.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of co-sharers in urban property is a reasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted a pre-emption right to co-sharers in urban property.
The sale of a share to an outsider could introduce a stranger into shared ownership and make common management difficult.
The property at issue was a house, and the provision concerned urban property.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5), holding that the benefit of preserving common ownership and facilitating management could outweigh the restrictions on the vendor and purchaser. It approved the treatment of co-sharer pre-emption in Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh and Sardha Ram v. Haji Abdul Majid Mohd. Amir Khan.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the co-sharer ground was valid and did not violate the constitutional property right.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_favours_existing_coshareholde: The law gives persons who already share ownership priority to acquire the interest being sold.
predicates.sale_would_introduce_an_outsider_into_sh: Without the pre-emption right, a purchaser outside the existing group of co-owners could become a co-owner.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of owners whose properties share a staircase with the property being sold is a reasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted pre-emption to owners of other properties sharing a staircase with the property being sold.
The Court considered that sale to a stranger could give that stranger a right to use the common staircase and cause serious inconvenience to the other owners.
members.legal_principle: Applying Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5), the Court treated the shared-staircase ground as practically analogous to co-sharer pre-emption because it protects the owners' shared use of property and avoids the disadvantages of introducing an outsider. The Court applied its reasoning on co-sharer rights, including that reflected in Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh and Sardha Ram v. Haji Abdul Majid Mohd. Amir Khan.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the common-staircase ground was valid and did not violate the constitutional property right.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_favours_owners_of_properties_: The law gives owners of other properties using the same staircase priority to acquire the property being sold.
predicates.sale_would_give_an_outsider_shared_stair: Without the pre-emption right, the purchaser would acquire a property carrying a right to use a staircase shared with other owners.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of owners of properties sharing a common entrance from the street with the property being sold is a reasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted pre-emption to owners of other properties sharing a common entrance from the street with the property being sold.
The Court considered that the shared entrance placed the owners in a position similar to co-sharers and that sale to a stranger could disrupt their shared arrangement.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5). It held that owners sharing a private entrance from a public street were sufficiently similar to co-sharers for the same public-interest reasoning to apply. The Court applied its reasoning on co-sharer rights, including that reflected in Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh and Sardha Ram v. Haji Abdul Majid Mohd. Amir Khan.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the common-entrance ground was valid and did not violate the constitutional property right.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_favours_owners_of_properties_: The law gives owners of other properties sharing an entrance priority to acquire the property being sold.
predicates.sale_would_introduce_an_outsider_to_the_: Without the pre-emption right, the purchaser would become an owner using an entrance shared with the other properties.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption right among occupants of agricultural land within a survey unit is a reasonable restriction when the occupants are co-sharers or akin to co-sharers and the right promotes consolidation of holdings.
material_facts: The right applied to unalienated land held for agricultural purposes and was limited to occupants holding interests within the same survey number.
The holders of a survey number were jointly responsible for the land revenue, and holders of subdivisions within it were akin to co-sharers.
The right applied to specified transfers to strangers and did not arise for an exchange of land with an occupant of another survey number.
Exercising the right could consolidate agricultural holdings within the survey number.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(f), subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under Article 19(5), the Court held that a right confined to co-sharers or persons akin to co-sharers could protect common ownership and promote consolidation of agricultural holdings. It approved Ramchandra Krishnaji Dhagale v. Janardan Krishnappa Marwar.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the pre-emption provisions as constitutional and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.preemption_is_limited_to_occupants_of_on: The right applies to occupants whose interests lie within the same defined agricultural survey unit.
predicates.occupants_are_coshare_like: The occupants share responsibilities or interests that make them co-sharers or akin to co-sharers.
predicates.preemption_promotes_consolidation_of_hol: Exercising the right can consolidate agricultural holdings within the survey unit.

members.legal_issue: A right of prior purchase for properties sharing a common outer entrance is a reasonable restriction on the purchaser's property right.
material_facts: The sale concerned a house whose owners and the claimant's house owners had access through a common passage and outer entrance.
The passage was private property, and the owners of houses opening onto it had rights of way over it.
The appellant argued that the prior-purchase provision imposed an unreasonable restriction on the right to property.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and followed Bhau Ram v. Baijnath, which upheld analogous grounds of pre-emption for co-sharers, owners of common staircases, and owners of properties with a common entrance. Owners of buildings sharing a common entrance stand more or less in the position of co-sharers, making the restriction sustainable. The court also referred to Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh for the nature of pre-emption as a right of substitution, and to Govind Dayal v. Inayatullah for the description of that right.
members.conclusion: The restriction imposed by the prior-purchase provision for properties sharing a common outer entrance is reasonable and constitutionally valid.

members.legal_issue: A statutory pre-emption right confined to near family members who would inherit the property is a reasonable restriction on free alienation in the interest of the general public.
material_facts: The property was agricultural land sold by its owner.
The claimant asserted a right to pre-empt as the vendor’s son or another close family member entitled to succeed to the property under the applicable order of succession.
The statutory right was confined to members of the vendor’s family who would have been entitled to inherit, and the claim was challenged as an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(5) of the Constitution, the restriction was justified by the purposes of preserving village and community integrity and, independently, allowing the next in succession a chance to retain family property. The Court relied on Bhau Ram v. Baij Nath and Uttam Singh v. Kartar Singh, and distinguished a right granted broadly to relatives from one confined to likely heirs.
members.conclusion: The pre-emption provision, both as originally framed and in its amended form, was a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public and did not violate the constitutional protection of property rights.
