predicates.restriction_serves_village_cohesion_or_f: The restriction is directed at preserving village-community cohesion or giving likely family successors a chance to retain family property.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emption right in favour of an owner within an assessed land unit is a reasonable restriction on the vendor’s right to alienate property when owners in that unit share liability for its land revenue.
material_facts: The claimant owned land within an estate, while the purchaser did not own land there.
The estate was an assessment unit, and its landowners were jointly and severally liable for the land revenue assessed on it.
The purchaser challenged the pre-emption right as an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the shared liability of landowners within an estate as making the claimant’s position akin to that of a co-sharer, and held the resulting restriction reasonable. It relied on Bhau Ram v. Baij Nath.
members.conclusion: The restriction on the vendor’s right was reasonable and was not repugnant to the constitutional protection of property rights.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may obtain an eviction decree by impleading an occupying joint tenant without impleading every heir, and the decree binds the joint tenants.
material_facts: An eviction decree was obtained after one of the tenants was a party to the proceedings; another heir of the deceased tenant was not impleaded.
The omitted heir objected during execution, claiming an interest in and possession of the premises.
The objector produced only two old rent receipts as evidence of possession and acknowledged a dispute with the other tenant and that they had parted ways.
members.legal_principle: Because the tenancy inherited by the heirs is a single joint tenancy, occupation by one joint tenant is occupation on behalf of all, and an eviction petition against one joint tenant is sufficient to bind all. The landlord need not implead every heir, including heirs not occupying the premises. The Court applied H.C. Pandey v. G.C. Paul and its conclusion that the tenancy does not split into separate tenancies among the heirs.
members.conclusion: It was sufficient to implead an occupying joint tenant; the landlord was not required to implead every heir, whether or not they occupied the premises. The eviction decree bound all joint tenants, and the omitted heir’s objection failed.

predicates.at_least_one_occupying_joint_tenant_is_n: The landlord included at least one joint tenant who occupied the premises as a party to the eviction proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A notice seeking a tenant’s eviction is valid when given by co-owner landlords, even if it is not shown to have been given on behalf of every co-owner.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought by co-owner landlords under the tenancy legislation.

The notice named all the co-owner landlords, including the minor co-owners, and was signed by a co-owner acting for himself and as attorney for others, by a guardian for a minor, and by another co-owner.
One co-owner’s signature did not expressly state that it was also made on behalf of his minor son, whose name appeared in the notice.
The lower courts held that the notice was not given on behalf of that minor co-owner.
members.legal_principle: The notice must be assessed in light of its contents and the capacity in which it was signed; express repetition at the foot of the notice that a co-owner signed for a minor is unnecessary when the minor is identified in the notice. Further, relying on Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, the Court held that a notice remains valid even if it is not given on behalf of one co-owner.
members.conclusion: The lower courts were wrong to find the notice invalid: it was given on behalf of all the co-owner landlords, and it would have been valid even if it had not been given on behalf of one co-owner.

predicates.notice_given_by_at_least_one_coowner: At least one co-owner landlord gives the eviction notice.
predicates.notice_valid: The eviction notice is legally valid.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner may maintain an eviction proceeding without joining every other co-owner where the other co-owners do not object, and omission does not defeat the proceeding where the omitted co-owner is later joined.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought by heirs who had become co-owners of the premises.
Another heir was initially not a party, but was later added to the eviction proceedings.
The tenant had not raised the non-joinder objection before the lower courts.
members.legal_principle: Under Dhannalal v. Kalawathibai (2002) 6 SCC 16, applying Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath (1976) 4 SCC 184, Kanta Goel v. B.P. Pathak (1977) 2 SCC 814, and Pal Singh v. Sunder Singh (1989) 1 SCC 444, one co-owner may sue for eviction in their own right without joining the others if they do not object. The later joinder of the omitted co-owner also removed the objection in this case.
members.conclusion: The omission of the other co-owner did not make the eviction petition unmaintainable; the High Court’s contrary ruling was reversed.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and petitioner_is_coowner and (other_coowners_do_not_object or omitted_coowner_later_joined)

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding was brought to evict a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.petitioner_is_coowner: The person bringing the eviction proceeding held a co-ownership interest in the premises.
predicates.other_coowners_do_not_object: The other co-owners did not object to the petitioner bringing the eviction proceeding alone.
predicates.omitted_coowner_later_joined: A co-owner who was initially omitted was later added to the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner who is the acknowledged landlord may seek eviction without joining the other co-owners when they do not oppose the proceeding.
material_facts: The respondent was one of the deceased owner’s heirs and a co-owner of the premises.
The respondent collected rent from the tenant as part of the body of landlords.
The other co-heirs were joined at the High Court stage, and the record did not show that they opposed the respondent’s claim.
members.legal_principle: A co-owner owns every part of the composite property along with the other co-owners and is not merely a fractional owner. Under Sri Ram Pasricha, a co-owner who is also the acknowledged landlord need not establish sole ownership to sue for eviction. The Court left open the situation in which other co-owners oppose the eviction.
members.conclusion: The respondent’s status as a co-owner and the absence of the other co-owners at the initial stage did not disentitle him from suing for eviction.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and claimant_is_co_owner and claimant_is_acknowledged_landlord and other_co_owners_do_not_oppose

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.claimant_is_co_owner: The person bringing the proceeding owns the premises together with other co-owners.
predicates.claimant_is_acknowledged_landlord: The tenant recognizes the person bringing the proceeding as a landlord.
predicates.other_co_owners_do_not_oppose: The other co-owners do not oppose the requested eviction.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner may institute eviction proceedings against a tenant without proving the consent of the other co-owners, unless another co-owner objects.
material_facts: The landlord owned the shop jointly with his four sisters.
He sought eviction of the tenant for his own bona fide business requirement.
There was no evidence that any of his sisters objected to the eviction proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13 of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, an eviction proceeding may be brought by a co-owner. Applying the doctrine of agency, one co-owner acts on his own behalf and as agent for the others; their consent is presumed unless it is shown that they objected. The Court relied on India Umbrella Manufacturing Co. v. Bhagabandei Agarwalla, which in turn referred to Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath and Dhannalal v. Kalawatibai.
members.conclusion: The eviction proceeding was maintainable even though the landlord had not shown that his sisters had consented to it.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and applicant_is_co_owner and not other_co_owner_objected

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is one brought by a landlord to evict a tenant from rented property.
predicates.applicant_is_co_owner: The person bringing the proceeding owns the property jointly with one or more other people.
predicates.other_co_owner_objected: Another co-owner opposed the eviction proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner who jointly sought eviction may continue the claim after another co-owner transfers her interest and the transferee opposes eviction, unless a later event ends the co-owners’ collective entitlement.
material_facts: The two co-owners jointly filed suits to evict their tenants.
After the suits were dismissed, one co-owner transferred her share to persons associated with a tenant.
The transferee opposed eviction, while the other co-owner continued to pursue the appeals.
members.legal_principle: A co-owner may sue to evict a tenant on behalf of the co-owners under the doctrine of agency, and the other co-owners’ consent is presumed unless disagreement is shown. Once a joint suit is filed, the parties’ rights are ordinarily assessed as of its institution; a later event matters only if it ends the co-owners’ entitlement by act of parties or operation of law. The Court relied on Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath and Dhannalal v. Kalawatibai.
members.conclusion: The objection did not make the continuing co-owner’s eviction claim incompetent; consent to the joint claim could not be withdrawn midway to prejudice that co-owner.

rule.if: coowner_eviction_case and coowners_jointly_sought_eviction and continuing_coowner_pursued_claim and another_coowner_or_successor_opposed_eviction and not collective_entitlement_later_ended

predicates.coowner_eviction_case: The proceeding is a claim by co-owners to evict a tenant from jointly owned property.
predicates.coowners_jointly_sought_eviction: The co-owners jointly sought eviction when the claim was filed.
predicates.continuing_coowner_pursued_claim: One co-owner continued to pursue the eviction claim after it was filed.
predicates.another_coowner_or_successor_opposed_evi: Another co-owner or a successor to that co-owner opposed eviction after the joint claim began.
predicates.collective_entitlement_later_ended: A later event ended the co-owners’ collective entitlement to seek eviction.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner who is acknowledged as a landlord may maintain an eviction proceeding without joining the other co-owners when they do not object to the eviction.
material_facts: The claimant and another purchaser jointly acquired the property, and the claimant filed the eviction petition without joining the other co-owner or her heirs.
The tenant had paid rent to the claimant, and there was no evidence that the other co-owner or her heirs wanted the tenant to remain.
The rooms and courtyard in dispute fell to the claimant’s share; the other co-owner’s specific-performance suit concerned a different portion.
members.legal_principle: A co-owner is an owner of the entire property along with the other co-owners, and need not establish sole ownership to seek eviction. A co-owner may maintain the proceeding where the others do not object; Kanta Goel v. B.P. Pathak and Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagan Nath are relied on. The court distinguished the situation in which another co-owner opposes eviction, which Kanta Goel left open.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to maintain the eviction petition alone because the other co-owners did not object to eviction.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and claimant_is_coowner and claimant_is_acknowledged_as_landlord and other_coowners_do_not_object and disputed_premises_fall_to_claimant_share

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.claimant_is_coowner: The person seeking eviction owns the premises jointly with at least one other person.
predicates.claimant_is_acknowledged_as_landlord: The tenant has recognized the claimant as a landlord, including by paying rent to the claimant.
predicates.other_coowners_do_not_object: The other co-owners have not objected to the eviction claim or sought to keep the tenant in the premises.
predicates.disputed_premises_fall_to_claimant_share: The premises sought to be recovered fall within the claimant’s share of the jointly owned property.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered lease document for a one-year term cannot be used to prove a lease from year to year on the basis of its annual-rent terms.
material_facts: The rent document stated a one-year term and annual rent payable in advance, but was not registered.
The tenant relied on the document’s annual-rent terms to argue that the tenancy was from year to year.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 17 of the Registration Act, the document could not establish a lease from year to year without registration. The tenant cited Sajid Mia Majumdar v. Abdul Sattar Gani, Babulal Somalal v. Kantilal Hargovindas, and Chittiapalli Mathai v. Chittilapalli Kochouseph; the Court did not rely on those decisions as the basis for its ruling.
members.conclusion: The document could not be used as evidence of a lease from year to year based on annual rent; it evidenced a lease for one year, which ended on expiry of that term.

predicates.eviction_appeal: A tenant appealed an order granting eviction on the ground of rent arrears.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The parties' lease document was not registered.
predicates.document_claimed_yearly_tenancy: A party relied on the document's annual-rent terms to claim a tenancy from year to year.

members.legal_issue: A lease of immovable property for a term exceeding one year cannot confer enforceable lease rights when it is evidenced by unregistered documents.
material_facts: The firm relied on three written documents as evidence of the lease and its terms.
Under the terms relied on by the firm, the first rent payment covered the period from commencement of the lease through a date fifteen months later.
The documents evidencing the lease were not registered.
members.legal_principle: Sections 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and 2(7) of the Registration Act require registration of an instrument creating a lease for a term exceeding one year. A party relying on written documents as evidence of the lease and its terms cannot avoid that requirement by denying that the documents constitute the completed lease.
members.conclusion: The lease was for at least fifteen months and required a registered instrument; the firm could not enforce rights under the unregistered lease. Because the firm relied on the documents as evidence of the lease and its terms, it could not avoid registration by contending that they did not constitute the completed lease.

rule.if: suit_to_enforce_lease_rights and immovable_property_lease and written_documents_relied_on_as_lease_terms and first_rent_period_exceeds_one_year and lease_documents_unregistered

predicates.suit_to_enforce_lease_rights: A party brought a suit seeking to enforce rights under an asserted lease.
predicates.immovable_property_lease: The asserted lease concerned immovable property.
predicates.written_documents_relied_on_as_lease_ter: The party seeking lease rights relied on written documents as evidence of the lease and its terms.
predicates.first_rent_period_exceeds_one_year: The terms relied on provided for the first rent payment to cover a period exceeding one year from commencement of the lease.
predicates.lease_documents_unregistered: The documents relied on as evidencing the lease were not registered.

members.legal_issue: A lease for a term shorter than one year is not compulsorily registrable on the basis of its term alone.
material_facts: One fishing-right grant was treated as a lease with a term of nine months.
The Court proceeded on the premise that it was a lease because the lease-or-licence issue had not been raised before the Division Bench and the instrument was not produced before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act requires registration of leases of immovable property from year to year, for a term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent. The Court held that the nine-month lease was not compulsorily registrable under that provision. The obligation to pay stamp duty is distinct from compulsory registration.
members.conclusion: The nine-month lease was not compulsorily registrable, although it remained subject to stamp duty.

predicates.appeal_concerning_lease_registration: The matter is an appeal concerning whether a lease instrument must be registered.
predicates.grant_treated_as_lease: The grant is treated as a lease for deciding the dispute.
predicates.lease_term_is_less_than_one_year: The lease term is shorter than one year.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered lease document offered to prove the lease terms and rent that form the basis of a rent-arrears claim cannot be treated as evidence merely for a collateral purpose.
material_facts: The suits sought arrears of rent, and the unregistered document was relied on to establish the lease, its terms, and the rate of rent.
The document was offered to support the principal rent claim, not to prove a separate collateral transaction.
The appellants argued that the document could be relied on for a collateral purpose.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, read with Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, prevent an unregistered instrument from proving the transaction and terms for which registration is required, while the proviso to Section 49 permits specified collateral use. In Kaladevi v. V.R. Somasundaram, an unregistered sale deed could be received in a specific-performance suit as evidence of an oral agreement of sale, a collateral transaction. That case did not apply because the rent document here was offered to prove the main claim and rent terms. The Court also relied on Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons concerning the effect of an unregistered lease document.
members.conclusion: The collateral-purpose argument was rejected. The unregistered document could not be used to prove the lease terms or rent forming the basis of the claim, though the arrears could be established through the tenant’s admissions and other evidence.

predicates.rent_arrears_case: The proceeding seeks recovery of rent said to be unpaid by a tenant.
predicates.unregistered_lease_document_offered_for_: A party offers an unregistered lease document to prove the lease terms or rent that form the basis of the claim.

members.legal_issue: An important tenancy term in an unregistered lease that is required to be registered cannot be admitted as evidence merely by describing it as collateral.
material_facts: The parties’ tenancy memorandum was unregistered.
The memorandum restricted occupation to a particular employee and his family, and required the landlord’s written consent before another employee could occupy the premises.
The landlord relied on that restriction to argue that the tenant could not retain or reallot the premises after the named employee left, and sought eviction on that basis.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, a lease requiring registration cannot be proved through an unregistered instrument; Section 49 of the Registration Act permits such an instrument to be used for a collateral transaction, but that transaction must be independent of or divisible from the transaction requiring registration and must not itself create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish an interest in immovable property. An important lease term is not collateral merely because it is invoked for that purpose. The Court relied on Haran Chandra Chakravarti v. Kaliprasanna Sarkar, Ratan Lal v. Harisankar, Bajaj Auto Ltd. v. Behari Lal Kohli, Rai Chand Jain v. Chandra Kanta Khosla, and Rana Vidya Bhushan Singh v. Ratiram. It distinguished Smt. Juthika Mulick v. Dr. Mahendra Yashwant Bal, which concerned a registered lease.
members.conclusion: The restriction was an important term of the tenancy, not a collateral matter, and could not be relied on to establish a right to evict.

rule.if: landlord_eviction_proceeding and lease_document_unregistered and lease_requires_registration and relied_on_occupancy_restriction and restriction_is_important_tenancy_term

predicates.landlord_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking to evict a tenant.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The document recording the lease was not registered.
predicates.lease_requires_registration: The lease was of a kind for which the law required a registered instrument.
predicates.relied_on_occupancy_restriction: The landlord relied on a restriction in the lease about who could occupy the premises to support eviction.
predicates.restriction_is_important_tenancy_term: The restriction formed an important term of the tenancy rather than a matter independent of the lease transaction.

members.legal_issue: A term permitting subletting that forms part of an unregistered lease cannot be relied on when the lease is inadmissible for non-registration.
material_facts: The lease deed was unregistered.
The tenant relied on a clause in that deed permitting it to part with possession to associate concerns without the landlord’s consent.
The court treated the permission clause as a term of the lease transaction, not as a separate collateral matter.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the rule that where a lease document is inadmissible for want of registration, its terms cannot be admitted separately, including a term concerning the landlord’s permission to sublet. It referred to Sachindra Mohan Ghose v. Ramesh Agarwalla, AIR 1932 Patna 97. Although the tenant invoked Section 49 of the Registration Act, the court rejected the argument that the clause could be used for a collateral purpose because it was a term of the lease transaction.
members.conclusion: The tenant could not rely on the permission clause because all terms of a lease document inadmissible for non-registration are also inadmissible, including a term concerning permission to sublet.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The dispute arose in a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The document recording the lease was not registered.
predicates.permission_clause_is_lease_term: The permission to sublet was expressed as a term of the lease document.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that compulsorily requires registration cannot itself create the lease it purports to record or be used as evidence of that lease.
material_facts: The parties executed an instrument purporting to grant a lease for five years.
The instrument was not registered.
Neither party relied on an exception in the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 107, first paragraph, of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, 1908, require registration of leases from year to year, for a term exceeding one year, or reserving yearly rent. Under Section 49 of the Registration Act, an unregistered document required to be registered cannot affect the property or be received as evidence of the transaction, subject to the stated proviso. The Court relied on Smt. Shantabai v. State of Bombay, Satish Chand Makhan v. Govardhan Das Byas, and Bajaj Auto Limited v. Behari Lal Kohli.
members.conclusion: The instrument could not create the purported five-year lease and could not be used as evidence of a lease created by that instrument.

predicates.compulsory_registration_lease_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an instrument purporting to grant a lease created that lease.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The parties did not register the instrument purporting to grant the lease.
predicates.lease_document_requires_registration: The purported lease is of a kind for which the law requires a registered instrument.

members.legal_issue: Including surplus agricultural land in a ceiling scheme for redistribution does not violate the constitutional right to life merely because the landholder claims that the deprivation impairs livelihood.
material_facts: The landholders argued that losing surplus land deprived them of their livelihood and therefore violated Article 21.
The surplus land was to vest in the State for redistribution to poor and downtrodden agricultural labourers.
The Court relied on earlier decisions rejecting the proposition that livelihood is included in the meaning of life under Article 21.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on In re Sant Ram and A.V. Nachane v. Union of India, which held that livelihood is not included in “life” for the purpose of Article 21, and distinguished Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India because it had not considered Sant Ram. It also referred to Article 39 and the redistribution of surplus land for the benefit of poor agricultural labourers.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the Article 21 challenge and held that Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India did not govern the issue; it also considered the deprivation protected in light of Article 39.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: A person’s landholding was assessed in a proceeding to determine the applicable agricultural land ceiling.
predicates.surplus_land_taken_for_redistribution: Land found to exceed the ceiling was taken for redistribution to disadvantaged agricultural labourers.
predicates.article_21_claim_based_on_livelihood_los: A landholder claimed that losing the land impaired livelihood and thereby violated the right to life.

members.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition for a public purpose, subject to payment of compensation, does not infringe the guaranteed rights to property, and a dispute about compensation must be pursued before the authority or court competent to determine it.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition for road widening, a public purpose.
A declaration was made that the land was needed for that purpose, and compensation was determined.
The appellants were tenants of structures on the land, not its owners.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 19 and 31(2) of the Constitution, compulsory acquisition for a public purpose subject to compensation did not infringe the rights asserted here. Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, the declaration that the land was needed for a public purpose was conclusive evidence of that need. A dispute about compensation belonged before the competent compensation authorities or courts.
members.conclusion: The acquisition did not infringe the appellants’ guaranteed rights to property. Any grievance they were entitled to raise about compensation had to be taken to the authorities or courts competent to determine compensation.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the taking of property through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_for_public_purpose: The land is acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.compensation_determined: Compensation payable for the acquired land has been determined.

members.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition for a public purpose does not violate the owner's right to life merely because it removes land that was the owner's means of livelihood, where acquisition follows lawful procedure and compensation is provided.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that the acquired land was their only source of livelihood.
The land was compulsorily acquired for the public purpose of providing housing.
The acquisition procedure provided for compensation, solatium, and interest.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that, for a public purpose, an individual's ownership right must yield to the public purpose when the State exercises its power of eminent domain according to law. Sections 23, 23(1-A), 28, and 31 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for compensation and related recompense. The Court distinguished lawful acquisition from deprivation of livelihood contrary to Article 21 and considered the principles in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation concerning livelihood as part of the right to life.
members.conclusion: The claim that acquisition deprived the appellants of their right to livelihood under Article 21 was unsustainable.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_appeal and owner_lost_land_used_for_livelihood and acquisition_served_a_public_purpose and lawful_procedure_was_followed and compensation_and_related_recompense_were_provided

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.owner_lost_land_used_for_livelihood: The owner lost land that was used as a means of livelihood.
predicates.acquisition_served_a_public_purpose: The acquisition served a public purpose.
predicates.lawful_procedure_was_followed: The acquisition was carried out according to the applicable legal procedure.
predicates.compensation_and_related_recompense_were: The acquisition law provided compensation and related recompense for the loss.

members.legal_issue: Displacement caused by a development project does not, by itself, violate affected people’s fundamental rights when rehabilitation provides for their resettlement and improvement of their living conditions.
material_facts: The project would displace tribal and other families from homes and agricultural land.
The tribunal’s award provided for resettlement, land and house plots for qualifying families, rehabilitation grants, and civic amenities.

The States had expanded rehabilitation benefits, and the Court found that the resettlement package could provide affected families with better amenities and living conditions than those in their former settlements.
members.legal_principle: Article 21 of the Constitution protects life and human rights, and the Court accepted that international treaties may inform domestic law, referring to Gramophone Co. of India Ltd. v. B.B. Pandey, (1984) 2 SCC 534, PUCL v. Union of India, (1997) 3 SCC 433, and CERC v. Union of India, (1995) 3 SCC 42. Article 12 of ILO Convention No. 107 contemplates removal in exceptional circumstances under national law and provides for land of at least equal quality and compensation for resulting loss or injury. The Court applied these principles to the rehabilitation arrangements and did not treat displacement per se as a rights violation.
members.conclusion: Displacement alone did not establish a violation of fundamental or other rights; the relevant concern was whether affected people were properly rehabilitated and were better off after resettlement.

predicates.development_project_displaces_people: A public development project requires people to leave their homes or land.
predicates.rehabilitation_package_provides_resettle: The project authorities provide affected people with resettlement arrangements and basic amenities.
predicates.rehabilitation_can_improve_living_condit: The resettlement arrangements are capable of improving affected people’s living conditions compared with their former circumstances.

members.legal_issue: Article 21 does not invalidate land-acquisition or housing legislation merely because it deprives an owner of property, where the deprivation does not result in loss of life, liberty, or livelihood and the acquisition is intended to improve living conditions for a larger population.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of land to provide housing accommodation.
The case did not involve deprivation of property that would lead to deprivation of life, liberty, or livelihood.
The acquisition was intended to improve the living conditions of a larger number of people.
members.legal_principle: Article 21 essentially concerns personal liberty and does not, by itself, protect the right to own property in the circumstances presented. The Court distinguished property deprivation that would lead to deprivation of life, liberty, or livelihood from acquisition intended to improve conditions for a larger population.
members.conclusion: Article 21 did not provide a basis for striking down the challenged provisions.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_a_land_acqui: A party invokes the constitutional protection of personal liberty to challenge a land-acquisition or housing law.
predicates.property_deprivation_does_not_deprive_li: The property loss does not also deprive the affected person of life, personal liberty, or livelihood.
predicates.acquisition_improves_living_conditions_f: The property is acquired to improve living conditions for a larger group of people.

members.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition for a public purpose does not violate the right to life merely because it deprives an owner of shelter or livelihood.
material_facts: The owner held a flat in a building notified for acquisition for a public purpose.
The owner argued that acquisition would deprive him of shelter and violate his dignity and rights to life and livelihood.
The Court found that the property was being deprived according to law and that the acquisition was for a public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Article 21 of the Constitution does not circumscribe the State's power of eminent domain when property is acquired according to law for a public purpose. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for determination of compensation under section 23, including solatium for compulsory acquisition under section 23(2); a claimant who disputes the amount may pursue a reference under sections 18 and 23(1). The Court distinguished prior decisions concerning alternative sites, noting that they did not decide the validity of acquisition on Article 21 grounds.
members.conclusion: The acquisition did not violate the constitutional right to life, livelihood, shelter, or personal dignity merely because the owner could be rendered shelterless.

predicates.lawful_public_purpose_acquisition: The State acquires the owner's property according to law for a public purpose.
predicates.owner_deprived_of_shelter: The acquisition deprives the owner of a home or may leave the owner without shelter.

members.legal_issue: Lawful acquisition of property does not, by itself, violate the displaced owner's fundamental right to life, although the owner remains entitled to resettlement and rehabilitation under the applicable policy.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a public project, displacing people whose residence or livelihood was connected to it.
The displaced persons claimed that displacement without proper rehabilitation violated their right to life.
The project had a rehabilitation and resettlement policy applicable to its oustees.
members.legal_principle: The right to property under Article 300-A is a constitutional right, and deprivation of property under lawful acquisition does not, by itself, establish a violation of Article 21. Displaced persons are nevertheless entitled to rehabilitation under the applicable policy. The Court relied on Article 21 and Article 300-A of the Constitution, Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), State of Kerala v. Peoples Union for Civil Liberties, Chameli Singh v. State of U.P., and Samatha v. State of A.P.
members.conclusion: Acquisition does not itself violate a constitutional or fundamental right of displaced persons, but they are entitled to resettlement and rehabilitation under the policy applicable to the project.

predicates.constitutional_claim_based_on_lawful_lan: A displaced person claims a constitutional violation on the basis that property was lawfully acquired for a project.
predicates.applicable_rehabilitation_policy: A rehabilitation policy applies to the people displaced by the project.

members.legal_issue: A substantial interpretive dispute about the computation of vacant land under the ceiling law should be referred for consideration by a larger bench when the relevant earlier decisions conflict and a larger-bench decision bears on the dispute.
material_facts: The appeal concerned whether land occupied by a factory and land appurtenant to it had to be included when calculating the vacant land held by the landholder.
The competent authority had found vacant land in excess of the ceiling, while the appellate court disagreed with its interpretation of the statutory provisions.
The Court considered earlier decisions that addressed the computation question differently and noted that one relevant decision had been given by a three-judge bench.
The Court found force in the contention that an earlier decision had considered the provisions at issue more broadly than a later decision appeared to recognize.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(q)(ii) and 2(q)(iii), read with Section 4(9) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, govern the dispute over whether land occupied by a building and its appurtenant land are included in calculating vacant land. State of U.P. v. L.J. Johnson and Meera Gupta v. State of West Bengal had addressed the issue in ways that raised a conflict; Meera Gupta was decided by a three-judge bench. The Court therefore considered that the interpretive contention should be considered by a larger bench rather than deciding it in this appeal.
members.conclusion: The Court did not resolve the substantive computation question. It directed that the case be placed before the Chief Justice for an appropriate direction because the contention should be considered by a larger bench.

predicates.appeal_involves_statutory_interpretation: The proceeding is an appeal in which the application of statutory provisions to a disputed legal issue must be interpreted.
predicates.earlier_decisions_conflict: Earlier judicial decisions address the relevant interpretive issue in conflicting ways.
predicates.larger_bench_decided_related_issue: A larger bench has decided an earlier case that bears on the interpretive issue.

members.legal_issue: A coordinate bench that cannot distinguish an earlier decision of a coordinate bench and considers it wrong should refer the issue to a larger bench rather than disregard the earlier decision.
material_facts: An earlier decision of a division bench of the same High Court addressed the legal status of an occupant who remained in possession after termination of a tenancy.
A later division bench considered the earlier decision inapplicable because a particular argument had not been addressed in it, and proceeded without referring the issue to a larger bench.
members.legal_principle: Judicial decorum and legal certainty require a coordinate bench that disagrees with an earlier decision of the same court, and cannot distinguish it, to refer the issue to a larger bench. The Court relied on Smt. Sommavanti v. State of Punjab regarding the binding effect of a decision and Mahadeolal Kanodia v. Administrator-General of West Bengal regarding the proper procedure for addressing disagreement with a coordinate-bench decision.
members.conclusion: The later division bench should have referred the matter to a larger bench rather than bypassing the earlier decision.

predicates.coordinate_bench_proceeding: A case is being considered by a bench of the same court with authority coordinate to an earlier bench.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_decision_on_issue: An earlier coordinate bench has decided the legal issue presented in the later case.
predicates.later_bench_cannot_distinguish_and_disag: The later bench considers the earlier decision wrong but cannot distinguish it on the issue before it.

members.legal_issue: A conflict between single-judge decisions on whether an applicant for accommodation is entitled to notice of a hearing in a statutory allotment proceeding should be resolved by a Division Bench.
material_facts: The disputed question arose in an allotment proceeding under Section 16 of the U.P. Act 13 of 1972.
One single judge had held that an applicant for allotment on the ground of deemed vacancy was entitled to be heard before an order was made.
That view appeared to conflict with an earlier decision of another single judge.
members.legal_principle: The judgment identifies the conflicting single-judge decisions, including Munu Lal v. District Judge, and directs that the conflict on the question arising under Section 16 of the U.P. Act 13 of 1972 be resolved by a Division Bench. It does not state the substantive rule on the applicant's entitlement to a hearing.
members.conclusion: The conflict on the right to notice was to be resolved by a Division Bench of the High Court; the Supreme Court did not decide whether the applicant was entitled to notice.

predicates.statutory_accommodation_allotment_procee: The case concerns an application for allotment of accommodation under a statutory scheme.
predicates.conflicting_single_judge_views_on_hearin: Single judges have reached conflicting views on whether an allotment applicant must receive a hearing before the relevant decision.
predicates.hearing_right_conflict_referred_to_divis: The conflict on the hearing right is referred for resolution by a Division Bench.

members.legal_issue: A smaller bench may validly refer a substantial legal issue to a larger bench when it considers conflicting precedent to require reconsideration.
material_facts: A two-judge bench considered conflicting Supreme Court decisions on the application of the amended solatium provisions.
The bench concluded that the legal question required reconsideration by a larger bench and made a reference.
A preliminary objection challenged the validity of that reference.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the established practice of referring questions to a larger bench supports consistency and certainty in the law. Where a smaller bench doubts the correctness of a decision by a larger bench, it cannot overrule that decision and may refer the issue for reconsideration. The Court applied the principles governing the binding effect of Supreme Court precedent and the practice described in Article 141 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The preliminary objection was overruled. The reference to the larger bench was justified by the nature and potential significance of the questions raised.

predicates.supreme_court_reference_proceeding: The matter is before a larger bench following a reference from a smaller Supreme Court bench.
predicates.smaller_bench_faces_conflicting_preceden: The referring bench encountered conflicting earlier decisions on the legal issue.
predicates.issue_requires_reconsideration: The referring bench considered the legal issue to warrant reconsideration by a larger bench.
predicates.reference_to_larger_bench_is_valid: The reference to the larger bench is procedurally valid.

members.legal_issue: Conflicting opinions on the legal effect of non-payment in an emergency acquisition require referral to a larger Bench.
material_facts: The two judges reached conflicting conclusions about whether advance payment was a condition precedent to possession and vesting.
They also disagreed on whether non-payment invalidated the acquisition and on the appropriate relief.
members.legal_principle: The judges expressly directed referral because their separate judgments diverged on the conclusions and legal questions. No statutory provision or earlier case was identified as the basis for this referral.
members.conclusion: The judges referred the matter to the Chief Justice of India for placement before a larger Bench to resolve their divergent views and answer the questions of law; the appeal was not conclusively disposed of by a majority ruling in this judgment.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.separate_judgments_conflict_on_questions: The judges delivered separate judgments that reached conflicting conclusions on legal questions.

members.legal_issue: A matter involving a prima facie conflict between decisions of different-sized benches should be placed before a larger bench for consideration.
material_facts: The Court was considering multiple appeals and petitions involving questions about the nature of mining royalty and the scope of legislative powers over mineral development.
The Court observed a prima facie conflict between a decision of a five-judge bench and a decision of a seven-judge bench.
The Court considered that the questions should be considered by a nine-judge bench and directed that the matter be placed before the Chief Justice for appropriate orders.
members.legal_principle: As stated with reference to Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v. State of Maharashtra, 2005 (2) SCC 673, where a five-judge bench has a doubt concerning a decision under consideration, it should invite the Chief Justice’s attention and request placement before a bench larger than the bench whose decision is in issue. The Court applied that procedure because it saw a prima facie conflict between five-judge and seven-judge decisions.
members.conclusion: The Court requested that the matter be considered by a nine-judge bench and directed that it be placed before the Chief Justice for appropriate orders; it did not decide the substantive questions referred for consideration.

predicates.bench_considering_precedent_conflict: A court bench is considering a matter in which the consistency of judicial decisions is in issue.
predicates.apparent_conflict_between_different_size: The court identifies a prima facie conflict between decisions delivered by benches of different sizes.

members.legal_issue: A High Court bench that is confronted with conflicting decisions of coordinate benches on a question of law should refer the question to a Full Bench rather than choose between the conflicting decisions itself.
material_facts: The High Court bench faced conflicting Division Bench decisions about whether a widow could sell usufructuary-mortgaged property for necessity.
The bench declined to refer the question to a larger bench and instead followed the earlier decision over the later conflicting decision.
The Supreme Court considered the proper practice for a bench facing conflicting decisions of coordinate benches.
members.legal_principle: A decision on a question of law by one High Court bench should generally be followed by another bench; if the later bench has reason to differ, it should refer the question to a Full Bench. Where conflicting decisions are before the later bench, it should refer the matter rather than choose between them. The Court relied on Buddha Singh v. Laltu Singh and Seshamma v. Venkata Narasimharao, and considered Bilimoria v. Central Bank of India and Virayya v. Venkata Subbayya.
members.conclusion: The proper course in the face of conflicting coordinate-bench decisions is to refer the question to a Full Bench without deciding which decision to follow.

predicates.later_high_court_bench_decides_question_: A later bench of a High Court is deciding a question of law.
predicates.conflicting_coordinate_bench_decisions_b: The later bench has before it conflicting decisions on that question from benches of coordinate authority.

members.legal_issue: Information from an accused in police custody may be admitted to the extent that it distinctly relates to a fact discovered in consequence of that information.
material_facts: A co-accused, while in police custody, led the investigating officer and others to a dumping site where concealed pieces of blanket, saree, and rope were found after the ground was unearthed.
Witnesses identified the recovered items as materials used to wrap the deceased's body.
The Supreme Court found the recovery and the evidence about it credible despite the absence of a public witness.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Evidence Act applies when the person giving information is an accused and is in police custody; information is admissible to the extent it relates distinctly to a fact discovered in consequence of it. Discovery provides assurance that the information was true. The Court distinguished Nari Santa v. Emperor and Abdul Sattar v. Union Territory, Chandigarh, where the circumstances of discovery differed.
members.conclusion: The recovery was properly treated as a discovery of incriminating material and the challenge to it was rejected.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution relies on information given by an accused in custody.
predicates.accused_in_police_custody: The person giving the information is an accused and is in police custody when the information is given.
predicates.information_leads_to_concealed_fact_disc: The information leads investigators to discover a previously concealed fact or item connected with the crime.

members.legal_issue: Information given by an accused in police custody is admissible only to the extent that it relates distinctly to a fact discovered because of that information.
material_facts: The accused appeared before the investigating officer and was taken into custody.
Following information given by the accused, the deceased’s gold articles, a weapon, and the accused’s bloodstained clothing were recovered from places associated with the accused.
Witness testimony supported the recoveries, and forensic examination confirmed bloodstains on the seized clothing.
members.legal_principle: Sections 25 and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 generally bar proof of confessions made to police or while in police custody; Section 27 permits proof of only so much information as relates distinctly to a fact discovered in consequence of it. The discovered fact includes the place from which an object is produced and the accused’s knowledge of that place, not merely the object itself. The Court relied on Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Deoman Upadhyaya, Mohmed Inayatullah v. State of Maharashtra, Earabhadrappa alias Krishnappa v. State of Karnataka, and State of Maharashtra v. Damu.
members.conclusion: The discovery-related information and resulting recoveries were admissible to the extent they related distinctly to the facts discovered.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_accused_led_dis: The criminal proceeding relies on a discovery made after information from the accused.
predicates.accused_in_police_custody: The accused gave the information while in police custody.
predicates.information_caused_discovery: The information led investigators to discover a fact or object not previously located by them.
predicates.information_distinctly_related_to_discov: The information directly identified the discovered fact, including the relevant place or the accused’s knowledge of it.

members.legal_issue: Under the rule governing information supplied by an accused in custody, the fact discovered is not equivalent to the object recovered, and only information distinctly related to the discovered fact is admissible.
material_facts: An accused in custody stated that he had concealed a firearm beneath a heap of wood behind an old house.
Police found the firearm at the stated location.
Other evidence established that the firearm had been used in the attack.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Evidence Act operates as a proviso to Sections 25 and 26, permitting the admissibility of the portion of an accused’s statement that distinctly relates to a fact discovered as a result of information supplied in custody. Discovery of a fact cannot be equated with recovery or production of an object, though recovery may help establish the fact discovered. The Court reaffirmed Pulikuri Kottaya v. Emperor, AIR 1947 PC 67, which it said had been repeatedly approved by this Court, including in Jaffar Hussain Dastagir v. State of Maharashtra, State of Rajasthan v. Bhup Singh, Shamshul Kanwar v. State of U.P., and State of Maharashtra v. Damn. It also relied on State of Bombay v. Chhaganlal Gangaram Lavar, AIR 1955 Bombay 1, for the principle that a precedent remains binding unless a superior court takes a different view.
members.conclusion: The discovered fact was that the accused knew the firearm was concealed at that location, not merely the recovery of the firearm; the rule in Pulikuri Kottaya remained binding and the High Court was wrong to depart from it.

predicates.custodial_disclosure_case: The case concerns information supplied by an accused while in custody.
predicates.accused_identified_a_concealed_object_lo: The accused stated that an object was concealed at a particular location.
predicates.police_found_object_at_that_location: The police found an object at the location identified by the accused.

members.legal_issue: Incriminating statements made by an accused to a police officer about an object's past use and the accused's ownership of recovered items are inadmissible when they do not distinctly relate to a fact discovered.
material_facts: The accused was interrogated by a police officer and was said to have stated that the recovered axe was the one used to commit the murder and that the blood-stained clothes belonged to him.
The axe and clothes were subsequently produced from the accused's house.
The statements about the axe's use and the clothes' ownership did not lead to a discovery within the meaning of the applicable discovery rule.
members.legal_principle: Sections 25 and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act exclude incriminating statements made to a police officer, and section 27 permits proof only of the part of information from an accused in police custody that relates distinctly to a fact discovered in consequence of that information. Under Pulukuri Kotayya v. King Emperor, the discovered fact includes the place from which an object is produced and the accused's knowledge of that place; statements about the object's past use do not relate to its discovery. The Court distinguished State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya, where the circumstantial chain did not depend merely on production of a blood-stained weapon.
members.conclusion: The statements were inadmissible under sections 25 and 26 of the Evidence Act and were not made admissible by section 27, because they did not distinctly relate to a fact discovered.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding and accused_in_police_custody and incriminating_statement_to_police and statement_asserts_past_use_or_ownership and statement_does_not_distinctly_relate_to_discovered_fact

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal proceeding.
predicates.accused_in_police_custody: The person who made the statement was an accused in police custody.
predicates.incriminating_statement_to_police: The accused made an incriminating statement to a police officer.
predicates.statement_asserts_past_use_or_ownership: The statement asserts an item's past use in an offence or the accused's ownership of an item.
predicates.statement_does_not_distinctly_relate_to_: The statement does not distinctly relate to a fact discovered as a consequence of the information given.

members.legal_issue: Information given by an accused in police custody is admissible to the extent that it distinctly leads to discovery of a concealed place and the objects or remains found there, even if investigators already suspected that something had been concealed.
material_facts: During police interrogation, the accused described where his wife’s body had been buried and offered to show the place.
The accused pointed out and marked the precise location in the backyard; the buried box and human remains were recovered there.
The exhumation was conducted in the presence of officials and was videographed.
The judgment treated the confession to police as inadmissible, but considered the portion leading to discovery.
members.legal_principle: Sections 25 and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act render police confessions inadmissible, subject to the limited exception in Section 27 for information that distinctly relates to a fact discovered in consequence of it. The discovered fact includes the place from which an object is produced and the accused’s knowledge of that place, not merely the object itself. The Court relied on Pulukuri Kottaya v. King Emperor and its approval in Jaffar Hussain Dastagir v. State of Maharashtra, Shamshuk Kanwar v. State of U.P., and State of Maharashtra v. Damu.
members.conclusion: The accused’s identification of the precise burial site and the recovery of the remains and articles from it were admissible as discovery evidence; the rest of his police confession was not admissible.

rule.if: criminal_trial and custodial_information_led_to_discovery and accused_identified_precise_concealed_location and concealed_evidence_recovered

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which evidence obtained after questioning an accused in police custody is offered.
predicates.custodial_information_led_to_discovery: The accused gave information in police custody that led investigators to a previously concealed fact.
predicates.accused_identified_precise_concealed_loc: The accused identified the particular place where the concealed evidence was located.
predicates.concealed_evidence_recovered: Investigators recovered evidence from the place identified by the accused.

members.legal_issue: Information from an accused in police custody may be admitted to the extent that it distinctly relates to a fact discovered in consequence of that information.
material_facts: The report identified locations where the dead bodies and a concealed weapon could be found.
The police later went with the accused to those locations, and the bodies and weapon were found there.
The Court assumed for purposes of the case that the accused was constructively in police custody when he gave the information.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, partially lifts the exclusion under sections 24, 25 and 26 for so much of information received from an accused in police custody as relates distinctly to a fact discovered in consequence of it. The Court referred to State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya on the custody question and proceeded on an assumption of constructive custody without deciding that question.
members.conclusion: The information in the report that led to the discovery of the bodies and the weapon was admissible to the extent that it related distinctly to those discoveries.

rule.if: criminal_trial and accused_in_police_custody and information_caused_discovery and information_distinctly_related_to_discovered_fact

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which information is offered against an accused.
predicates.accused_in_police_custody: The accused was in police custody when the information was given.
predicates.information_caused_discovery: A fact was discovered in consequence of information given by the accused.
predicates.information_distinctly_related_to_discov: The offered portion of the information related distinctly to the fact that was discovered.

members.legal_issue: Information supplied by an accused in custody is admissible as discovery evidence only to the extent that it distinctly relates to a fact discovered, and recoveries from places accessible to all cannot reliably corroborate guilt in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on an arrest-cum-recovery memo recording statements that the accused had committed the murders and could produce the weapons.
No public witness named in the memo was examined to support the recoveries.
One weapon was recovered from a room and the others from an open field behind the place of the murders, places accessible to others.
The alleged bloodstained clothes were not recovered on a memorandum of the accused, and the forensic reports concerning them were inconclusive.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, only information that distinctly relates to the fact discovered is admissible; a confession or account of past use is not made admissible merely because it accompanies discovery. Pulukuri Kottayya v. King Emperor explains that the discovered fact includes the place of discovery and the accused’s knowledge of it. The Court considered the absence of supporting public witnesses and the accessibility of the recovery locations in assessing whether the recoveries could be relied on.
members.conclusion: The statements about committing the crime were not admissible as discovery information, and the circumstances of the recoveries did not permit reliance on them; the clothes could not be used against the accused as discovery evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial_relies_on_discovery_recov: The prosecution in a criminal trial relies on objects allegedly recovered following information from an accused in custody.
predicates.custodial_statement_includes_confession: The information attributed to the accused includes a confession or an account of committing the offence beyond the fact of discovery.
predicates.recovery_place_accessible_to_others: The object is recovered from a place accessible to people other than the accused.
predicates.confessional_statement_inadmissible_and_: The confession is not admissible as discovery information and the recovery cannot be relied on as reliable corroboration.

members.legal_issue: A court may refuse specific performance and award monetary compensation instead when the parties’ serious misconduct and the circumstances make specific enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: Both sides initiated numerous proceedings, suppressed material facts, and abused the judicial process.
The Court found the purchasers responsible for demolishing the building for purposes of the case.
The purchasers had paid a substantial advance, and the property’s value had risen substantially.
The Court found both sides blameworthy and concluded that monetary relief would better balance the equities than compelling a sale.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary and requires the discretion to be sound and guided by judicial principles; it permits refusal in specified circumstances of unfair advantage, hardship, or inequity. Compensation may be awarded in substitution for specific performance, with the amount and form of relief assessed in light of the circumstances and balance of hardship. The Court relied on Snell’s Equity, Spry’s Equitable Remedies, Gillett v. Holt, Malhotra v. Choudhury, Lalit Kumar Jain v. Jaipur Traders Corporation, P.D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation, and Surinder Singh v. Kapoor Singh.
members.conclusion: The Court refused specific performance and directed repayment of the advance with interest and payment of additional compensation.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and serious_misconduct_by_both_sides and claimant_responsible_for_demolition_for_civil_dispute and monetary_relief_can_balance_the_equities

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The claimant seeks specific performance of a property-sale agreement.
predicates.serious_misconduct_by_both_sides: Both sides engaged in serious misconduct, including abuse of the judicial process or suppression of material facts.
predicates.claimant_responsible_for_demolition_for_: The claimant was found responsible for demolition of the building for purposes of the civil dispute.
predicates.monetary_relief_can_balance_the_equities: The circumstances permit monetary relief to address the parties’ competing interests more fairly than specific enforcement.

members.legal_issue: The Court may grant monetary relief in place of specific performance to do complete justice when the agreement cannot be enforced.
material_facts: The plaintiff had paid the agreed consideration under the unenforceable agreement.
The Trial Court had ordered repayment of the amount paid, while the High Court had ordered conveyance of the property.
The property’s substantial value and the amount paid were before the Court, as were the parties’ conduct and the evidence concerning the transaction.
The Court allowed the appeals, dismissed the specific-performance suit, and ordered a larger monetary payment to the plaintiff’s legal representatives.
members.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution of India empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice between the parties. In exercising that power, the Court considered the evidence, the parties’ conduct, the payment made under the agreement, and the value of the property. The Court also considered the nature of its jurisdiction under Article 136.
members.conclusion: The specific-performance suit was dismissed, but the appellants were ordered to pay the plaintiff’s legal representatives a sum of money to do complete justice between the parties.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and specific_performance_refused and payment_made_under_agreement and circumstances_support_complete_justice_relief

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter came before the Supreme Court in an appeal.
predicates.specific_performance_refused: The Court refused to order specific performance.
predicates.payment_made_under_agreement: The claimant had paid money under the agreement that could not be enforced.
predicates.circumstances_support_complete_justice_r: The evidence and circumstances led the Court to grant monetary relief to achieve complete justice.

members.legal_issue: When acquisition of the subject land makes specific performance impossible without fault on the claimant’s part, the specific-performance decree cannot be maintained and may be replaced with compensation payable from the acquisition proceeds.
material_facts: The sellers agreed to sell their share of the land, received the full purchase price, and delivered possession to the buyer, who built shops on the land.
The sellers later gifted the land to another recipient; the courts below declared the gift void as to the share already agreed to be sold and granted specific performance.
The land and shops were acquired while the second appeal was pending, and compensation was determined in the gift recipient’s favour because its name appeared in the revenue records.
The record did not establish whether the gift recipient had received the compensation.

The claimant had not caused the impossibility of specific performance. The Court considered the acquisition compensation and the parties’ respective rights in directing that compensation be paid to the claimant and the true landowners, rather than the gift recipient.
members.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits compensation in lieu of specific performance where the contract becomes incapable of specific performance without fault of the plaintiff; its Explanation confirms that incapability does not bar the court from exercising that jurisdiction. Under Section 21(4), compensation is assessed by the principles in Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. In Jagdish Singh v. Nathu Singh, 1992 (1) SCC 647, the Court held that acquisition making performance impossible without the plaintiff’s fault may justify compensation in lieu of performance, measured by acquisition compensation subject to appropriate deductions. Kanshi Ram v. Om Prakash Jawal, 1996 (4) SCC 593, states that equitable relief is discretionary and guided by justice, equity, good conscience, and fairness. Applying those principles to the invalid gift and the parties’ respective rights, the Court directed that compensation be shared between the claimant and the true landowners, not the gift recipient.
members.conclusion: The specific-performance decree could not be maintained after acquisition made performance impossible. In its place, the claimant was awarded compensation from the acquisition proceeds, with the remaining compensation payable to the true landowners; the gift recipient, whose gift had been declared void, was not entitled to retain the compensation.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and valid_sale_contract_and_breach and land_acquired_making_performance_impossible and claimant_not_at_fault_for_impossibility and adverse_transfer_declared_void and acquisition_compensation_determined

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.valid_sale_contract_and_breach: The sellers agreed to sell the property, received the agreed consideration, and did not complete the sale.
predicates.land_acquired_making_performance_impossi: The property was acquired, making the agreed transfer through specific performance impossible.
predicates.claimant_not_at_fault_for_impossibility: The claimant did not cause the circumstance that made specific performance impossible.
predicates.adverse_transfer_declared_void: A later transfer of the contracted property to another recipient was declared void as to the property covered by the sale agreement.
predicates.acquisition_compensation_determined: Compensation was determined for the acquired property.

members.legal_issue: Even when specific performance is otherwise established, monetary compensation may be granted in its place when the circumstances make specific performance inappropriate and monetary relief meets the ends of justice.
material_facts: The agreements had been made decades earlier, and the plaintiffs had paid only part of the agreed price.
The vendors and later purchasers remained in effective possession, and the later purchasers had possessed the property for many years.
The property’s value had increased substantially by the time of the High Court’s decision.

The plaintiffs had expressly claimed alternative recovery of the money paid and compensation; a plaintiff also testified that alternative relief and compensation could be granted if specific performance was refused.
The High Court granted specific performance on an enhanced price, but the Supreme Court found that monetary compensation would better meet the ends of justice in light of the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Sections 21 and 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as applicable to the suit, address compensation for breach and alternative relief, including recovery of earnest money or a deposit. The Court considered the pleaded alternative relief and balanced the circumstances of the case, including the long passage of time, possession, increased value, and the parties’ positions, in deciding that compensation rather than specific performance was appropriate.
members.conclusion: The decree for specific performance was set aside and compensation was awarded in lieu of specific performance and any other claim concerning the land.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_unperformed_for_decades and third_party_possession_persisted_for_years and property_value_increased_substantially and plaintiff_claimed_alternative_monetary_relief

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract to transfer property.
predicates.contract_unperformed_for_decades: The contract remained unperformed for several decades before final adjudication.
predicates.third_party_possession_persisted_for_yea: A later purchaser or other third party remained in possession of the property for many years.
predicates.property_value_increased_substantially: The property’s value had increased substantially by the time the court considered the remedy.
predicates.plaintiff_claimed_alternative_monetary_r: The plaintiff claimed monetary relief as an alternative to specific performance.

members.legal_issue: Compensation may be awarded in lieu of specific performance when the contract becomes incapable of performance without fault of the plaintiff.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued for specific performance and was found ready and willing to perform the agreement.
During the second appeal, the State acquired the property for a public purpose, making specific performance impossible.
The plaintiff had not caused the impossibility by choosing to make specific performance unavailable.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(2), (4) and (5) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, including its explanation, permits compensation where specific performance becomes impossible without the plaintiff’s fault. Section 73 of the Contract Act governs assessment. The Court explained Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon, distinguished Piarey Lal v. Hori Lal, and disapproved the contrary reasoning in Mohamad Abdul Jabbar v. Lalmia. It distinguished Indian law from Lord Cairns’ Act, 1858, under which compensation was unavailable when performance became impossible.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff could receive compensation in lieu and substitution of specific performance despite the property’s acquisition.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.performance_became_impossible_without_pl: An event outside the claimant’s fault made performance of the contract impossible.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_choose_impossibility: The claimant did not cause the impossibility by abandoning or otherwise choosing to make specific performance unavailable.

members.legal_issue: A court may award compensation in substitution for specific performance even when the contract has become incapable of specific performance.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed compensation as an alternative or additional remedy in its suit.
The court refused specific performance and found the contract incapable of precise performance in the circumstances.
The court considered compensation appropriate and awarded it in substitution for specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 authorizes compensation in addition to or in substitution for specific performance. Its explanation makes clear that a contract's incapacity for specific performance does not preclude the court from awarding compensation.
members.conclusion: The court awarded compensation in substitution for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and contract_incapable_of_specific_performance and compensation_claimed and court_finds_compensation_appropriate

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A party sought a decree compelling performance of a contract.
predicates.contract_incapable_of_specific_performan: The contract could not be specifically performed in the circumstances.
predicates.compensation_claimed: The claimant sought compensation in the proceedings.
predicates.court_finds_compensation_appropriate: The court determined that compensation should be awarded in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: The equitable discretion to decree specific performance permits substitution of alternative monetary relief when enforcement would be unjust and unfair in the circumstances.
material_facts: An agreement provided for the sale of immovable property, and earnest money was paid.
The purchaser sued for specific performance and, alternatively, damages.
The courts below decreed specific performance.
By the time of the appeal, substantial time had elapsed since the agreement, and the seller offered monetary compensation in place of performance.
The Court considered specific performance inequitable and unjust in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Specific performance is discretionary, not automatic, and must be granted on sound principles with regard to justice, equity, good conscience, and fairness to both parties. A rise in property prices alone is not a sufficient reason to refuse specific performance, but where the circumstances make it unrealistic and unfair, and the claimant has sought damages in the alternative, the court may grant alternative monetary relief. No statutory provision is identified. S. Rangaraju Naidu v. S. Thiruvarakkarasu, AIR 1995 SC 1769, was cited by counsel; the judgment states the governing principle as the settled law on equitable discretion.
members.conclusion: The decree for specific performance was set aside and replaced with a conditional monetary award. The seller was to pay the specified compensation, and could deposit it in court if the purchasers avoided receipt; if the required payment or deposit was not made, the decree for specific performance would stand confirmed. The seller was also restrained from selling the property for the specified period.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and alternative_damages_claimed and prolonged_time_elapsed and seller_offered_monetary_compensation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.alternative_damages_claimed: The claimant also sought monetary damages as an alternative to performance.
predicates.prolonged_time_elapsed: A substantial period passed between the agreement and the court's consideration of the requested remedy.
predicates.seller_offered_monetary_compensation: The party resisting specific performance offered monetary compensation in its place.

members.legal_issue: Non-payment of rent to the landlord is not wilful default when the tenant reasonably refrains from payment under an attachment order or is directed to pay rent to a tax authority by an effective garnishment notice.
material_facts: After receiving an earlier prohibitory order, the tenant believed he could not pay rent to the landlord, kept the rent in bank deposits, and the landlord did not demand it during that period.
A later notice required the tenant to pay amounts then or subsequently due to the landlord to the tax authority, and the tenant paid rent to that authority.
The later notice remained effective, the landlord had not paid the tax arrears specified in it, and there was no evidence that the authority had withdrawn the notice.
The eviction proceeding alleged wilful default in payment of rent.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and its proviso distinguish a simple default from wilful default; wilfulness involves intentional or conscious violation, or conduct showing supine indifference, callousness, or recalcitrance. Default arising from ignorance, accident, compulsion, or circumstances beyond the tenant’s control is not wilful, depending on the facts. The Court relied on Section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, including its provision discharging the payer’s liability to the assessee to the extent paid, and treated that provision as analogous to Order 21 Rule 46 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It also relied on V.N. Vasudeva v. Kiroi Mal Luhariwala, which held that a garnishee notice prevents the person served from paying the landlord while the notice stands.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s non-payment to the landlord during the period covered by the earlier order was not wilful because his belief that payment was prohibited had a reasonable basis. While the later garnishment notice remained effective and the tax arrears remained unpaid, non-payment to the landlord did not establish wilful default or give the landlord a cause of action for eviction on that ground.
