rule.if: rent_control_eviction_for_rent_default and ((ambiguous_attachment_order_served and tenant_reasonably_understood_payment_barred and landlord_made_no_demand) or (garnishment_notice_served and notice_directed_future_payments and notice_remained_effective and tax_arrears_unpaid))

predicates.rent_control_eviction_for_rent_default: A landlord seeks eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the ground that the tenant failed to pay rent.
predicates.ambiguous_attachment_order_served: The tenant received an attachment order whose terms could reasonably be understood to prohibit payment of rent to the landlord.
predicates.tenant_reasonably_understood_payment_bar: The tenant believed that the attachment order prevented payment of rent to the landlord.
predicates.landlord_made_no_demand: The landlord did not demand rent from the tenant during the period in question.
predicates.garnishment_notice_served: The tenant received a notice requiring payment of money owed to the landlord to a tax authority.
predicates.notice_directed_future_payments: The notice expressly required payment of amounts that would subsequently become due to the landlord.
predicates.notice_remained_effective: The tax authority had not withdrawn the notice and the relevant tax arrears had not been cleared.
predicates.tax_arrears_unpaid: The landlord had not paid the tax arrears for which the tenant’s payments were being required.

members.legal_issue: A brief non-payment of rent is not wilful default when the circumstances do not show an intentional and conscious failure to pay without lawful cause.
material_facts: The alleged non-payment concerned one month’s rent for one premises and two months’ rent for the other.
The landlord acknowledged that rent was commonly collected from the tenants once every two months.
There was no established demand notice from the landlords, or service of such a notice was doubtful.
The tenants faced competing pressure about the payment and apportionment of rent, including a demand and threat of eviction from the municipal owner if arrears were not paid directly to it.
The tenants disputed the rate and amount claimed and said they were prepared to pay rent at the rate previously paid.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 requires wilful default for eviction on the ground of non-payment; its proviso permits time to pay when the default is not wilful. In S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman, the Court explained that wilful default is intentional, deliberate, calculated, and conscious, with knowledge of the legal consequences. The parties’ established course of collecting rent and the surrounding circumstances are relevant. The Court relied on Premchand Ranka v. A. Vasanthraj Khatod and D.C. Oswal v. V.K. Subbiah for the relevance of a practice of accepting rent in lumpsums or at intervals.
members.conclusion: The short periods of non-payment did not amount to wilful default, so eviction on that ground was not justified.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and short_rent_nonpayment and (landlord_customarily_collected_rent_at_intervals or rent_demand_or_notice_was_uncertain or tenant_faced_competing_payment_demands)

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The landlord sought eviction of a tenant through a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.short_rent_nonpayment: The tenant failed to pay rent for only a short period.
predicates.landlord_customarily_collected_rent_at_i: The landlord had accepted rent through a regular practice of collecting it at intervals rather than monthly.
predicates.rent_demand_or_notice_was_uncertain: There was no clear proof that the landlord demanded the rent or that a demand notice reached the tenant.
predicates.tenant_faced_competing_payment_demands: The tenant faced competing claims or threats concerning to whom rent should be paid.

members.legal_issue: A rent default becomes wilful only if it continues for two months after the landlord gives notice claiming the rent.
material_facts: The landlord issued a notice claiming arrears of rent.
The landlord filed the eviction proceeding before two months had elapsed after issuing the notice.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 10(2)(i), Explanation I, of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, a default is construed as wilful if it continues after the landlord has given two months’ notice claiming the rent. The tenant must therefore have an opportunity to pay within that period before the default can mature into a wilful default.
members.conclusion: The default could not be treated as wilful when the eviction proceeding was filed before the two-month period expired.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground of unpaid rent under a rent-control regime.
predicates.landlord_gave_notice_claiming_rent: The landlord gave the tenant notice claiming unpaid rent.
predicates.proceeding_filed_before_notice_period_ex: The landlord filed the eviction proceeding before the period allowed after the notice had elapsed.
predicates.default_not_wilful: The rent default is not treated as wilful.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s failure to pay rent is not a wilful default when the circumstances do not show an intentional and conscious decision not to pay.
material_facts: The tenant had regularly paid rent over a long period before the disputed arrears arose.
The landlord’s agent had previously collected rent, but did not come to collect the rent for the earlier part of the disputed period.
The amount claimed for a later part of the period was subject to a genuine dispute about the rent rate.
The tenant deposited the rent fixed during the proceeding as interim rent as soon as it was adjudicated and continued paying rent thereafter.
The eviction proceeding was filed before two months had elapsed after the notice claiming arrears.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, read with Explanation I, governs wilful default. In S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman, (1985) 1 SCC 591, the Court explained that wilful default means an intentional, deliberate, calculated and conscious default, with knowledge of its legal consequences. The tenant’s history of regular payment, the landlord’s agent’s failure to collect rent, the genuine dispute over the rent claimed, payment after interim rent was determined, and the premature filing of the proceeding cumulatively showed no wilful default.
members.conclusion: Considering the circumstances cumulatively, the tenant was not a wilful defaulter, and the orders finding wilful default were set aside.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and prior_regular_rent_payment and landlord_agent_failed_to_collect_rent and genuine_dispute_over_rent_claimed and tenant_paid_after_interim_rent_determination and proceeding_filed_before_notice_period_expired

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground of unpaid rent under a rent-control regime.
predicates.prior_regular_rent_payment: The tenant had regularly paid rent before the period of disputed arrears.
predicates.landlord_agent_failed_to_collect_rent: An agent who had previously collected rent did not come to collect it during part of the period in which arrears accrued.
predicates.genuine_dispute_over_rent_claimed: The tenant and landlord had a genuine dispute about the rent rate used to calculate part of the claimed arrears.
predicates.tenant_paid_after_interim_rent_determina: The tenant paid the rent after it was determined during the proceeding.
predicates.proceeding_filed_before_notice_period_ex: The landlord filed the eviction proceeding before the period allowed after the notice had elapsed.
predicates.default_not_wilful: The rent default is not treated as wilful.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s failure to pay rent is not wilful when the tenant genuinely believed, on the basis of a prior purchase agreement and earnest money paid, that there was no obligation to pay rent.
material_facts: The tenant did not pay rent for the period claimed by the landlords.
The tenant asserted that the former owners had orally agreed to sell the property to him before selling it to the landlords.
The tenant had paid earnest money under the asserted agreement and genuinely believed he was entitled to purchase the property and was not obliged to pay rent.
The tenant’s suit for specific performance had been dismissed, but an appeal was pending.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 10(2)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, read with its proviso, a tenant whose rent default is not wilful may be given a reasonable time to pay or tender the arrears, and the eviction application must be rejected if payment or tender is made within that time. A default is wilful only if it is intentional, deliberate, calculated and conscious, with full knowledge of its legal consequences. The Court relied on S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman, which considered the meaning of “wilful default.”
members.conclusion: The default was not wilful. The tenant was entitled to a reasonable opportunity to pay the arrears, so the eviction decree was set aside and the matter was remitted to the Controller to give him that opportunity.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_for_rent_default and rent_not_paid and bona_fide_belief_of_purchase_right and earnest_money_paid and believed_no_rent_obligation

predicates.tenant_eviction_for_rent_default: A landlord sought to evict a tenant on the ground that rent had not been paid.
predicates.rent_not_paid: The tenant did not pay or tender the rent claimed by the landlord.
predicates.bona_fide_belief_of_purchase_right: The tenant genuinely believed that a prior agreement gave the tenant a right to purchase the property.
predicates.earnest_money_paid: The tenant had paid earnest money under the asserted purchase agreement.
predicates.believed_no_rent_obligation: The tenant genuinely believed that the asserted right to purchase meant the tenant was not obliged to pay rent.

members.legal_issue: A tenant's failure to clear rent arrears after a two-month landlord's notice is wilful unless the tenant proves inability to pay due to unavoidable circumstances.
material_facts: The tenant owed monthly rent and agreed property-tax payments, both of which the Court treated as rent.
The landlord served a notice demanding the arrears and waited the required two-month period before starting eviction proceedings.
The tenant tendered only the monthly rent and did not pay the property-tax arrears, so the full amount demanded remained unpaid.
The tenant did not claim that unavoidable circumstances had made the tenant incapable of paying.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, and its Explanation, default continuing after a landlord's two-month notice to clear arrears is wilful. S. Sundaram v. V.R. Pattabhiraman holds that such continued non-payment is conclusive proof of wilfulness unless the tenant proves inability to pay because of unavoidable circumstances.
members.conclusion: The tenant committed wilful default and was liable to eviction; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and landlord_gave_two_month_arrears_notice and rent_arrears_remained_after_notice and not tenant_proved_unavoidable_inability

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.landlord_gave_two_month_arrears_notice: The landlord gave the tenant two months' notice demanding payment of rent arrears.
predicates.rent_arrears_remained_after_notice: The tenant did not clear all rent arrears after receiving the notice.
predicates.tenant_proved_unavoidable_inability: The tenant proved that unavoidable circumstances made the tenant incapable of paying the rent.

members.legal_issue: Wilful default in a rent-arrears eviction proceeding is assessed differently depending on whether the landlord gave the tenant a two-month notice demanding the arrears.
material_facts: Tenants failed to pay rent by the applicable due dates, and landlords sought eviction on the ground of wilful default.
Some landlords issued a two-month demand notice; some tenants remained in arrears after receiving notice, while others paid or tendered the arrears within the notice period.
In other cases, landlords filed eviction petitions without giving the notice, and the courts had to assess the tenants’ conduct and explanations.
members.legal_principle: Under section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, read with its proviso and Explanation, wilful default means an intentional, deliberate, conscious default made with knowledge of its consequences. The Explanation clarifies the proviso; it does not eliminate the Controller’s duty to determine wilfulness. Where the specified notice has been given and the tenant remains in default after it, the conduct supports a presumption of wilfulness, subject to proof of sufficient cause or circumstances beyond the tenant’s control. Without such notice, wilfulness must be assessed on the facts, including whether the default was deliberate and without lawful or reasonable cause; if it was not wilful, the proviso permits an opportunity to pay within the statutory period. The Court relied on N. Ramaswami Reddiar v. S.N. Periamuthu Nadar, 1980 Law Weekly 577, and Khivraj Chordia v. C. Maniklal Bhattad, AIR 1966 Madras 67, and referred to Rajeswari v. Vasumal Lalchand, AIR 1983 Madras 97. Its construction of provisos drew on Local Government Board v. South Stoneham Union [1909] AC 57; Ishverlal Thakorelal Almala v. Motibhai Nagjibhai [1966] 1 SCR 367; Madras and Southern Maharatta Railway Co. Ltd. v. Bezwada Municipality, AIR 1944 PC 71; West Derby v. Metropolitan Life Assurance Co. [1897] AC 647; Rhodda Urban District Council v. Taff Vale Railway Co. [1909] AC 253; Jennings v. Kelly [1940] AC 206; Commissioner of Income Tax v. Indo Mercantile Bank Ltd. [1959] 2 SCR 256; Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills v. Subhash Chandra Yograj Sinha [1962] 2 SCR 159; State of Rajasthan v. Leela Jain [1965] 1 SCR 276; Sales Tax Officer v. Hanuman Prasad [1967] 1 SCR 831; Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. R.S. Jhaver [1968] 1 SCR 148; Dwarka Prasad v. Dwarka Das Saraf [1976] 1 SCC 128; and Hiralal Rattanlal v. State of U.P. [1973] 1 SCC 216. On the function of an Explanation, it relied on Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distributing Co. v. Commercial Tax Officer [1961] 1 SCR 902; Bihta Cooperative Development Cane Marketing Union Ltd. v. Bank of Bihar [1967] 1 SCR 848; and Dattatraya Govind Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra [1977] 2 SCR 790. The Court also noted the analogous provisions concerning wilful default in the Andhra Pradesh, Orissa and Pondicherry rent-control enactments.
members.conclusion: Without the notice, the Controller must independently decide whether the default was wilful and may allow a tenant whose default was not wilful a reasonable period, not exceeding fifteen days, to pay the rent. If the landlord gives the notice and the tenant remains in default after it, the default is presumed wilful unless the tenant proves sufficient cause or circumstances beyond the tenant’s control prevented payment.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_for_rent_arrears and rent_default_occurred and (no_two_month_demand_notice or (two_month_demand_notice_given and arrears_unpaid_after_notice))

predicates.rent_control_eviction_for_rent_arrears: A landlord brought a rent-control proceeding seeking eviction because the tenant had not paid rent.
predicates.rent_default_occurred: The tenant did not pay or tender rent by the applicable due date.
predicates.no_two_month_demand_notice: The landlord did not give the tenant a two-month notice demanding the arrears.
predicates.two_month_demand_notice_given: The landlord gave the tenant a two-month notice demanding the arrears.
predicates.arrears_unpaid_after_notice: The tenant remained in arrears after the two-month notice period ended.

members.legal_issue: Lands granted as remuneration for a village office belong to the office’s emoluments rather than to the officeholder’s family as divisible family property.
material_facts: Historical records and revenue proceedings described the lands as granted in lieu of remuneration for performing the village office.
The family’s own statements in the revenue proceedings treated the lands as emoluments for that office.
The office was held by family members in rotation, and a former officeholder retained the emoluments when it was another member’s turn to perform the duties.
The claimant was not the person performing the office when the revenue authorities made the impugned order.
members.legal_principle: The 1859 Inam Rules, particularly Rules II, VI(2), VI(8), XIV(2) and XXI(2), do not give a non-serving family member a right to share service emoluments; Rule VI(2) concerns service that has been dispensed with or discontinued. Sections 3 and 9 of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900, provide for rotational office and enjoyment of the office’s emoluments by the person holding office. The distinction between a grant remunerating an office and a grant of land burdened with service is recognized in Lakhamgouda Basavaprabhu Sardesai v. Baswantrao; Venkata Jagannadha v. Veerabhadrayya is also discussed in relation to service lands.
members.conclusion: The lands were service emoluments attached to the office, not family lands burdened with service; a family member who was not the officeholder had no right to a share in them.

predicates.civil_appeal_over_family_share_in_servic: The matter is a civil appeal concerning a family member’s claim to a share in lands associated with a village office.
predicates.historical_records_show_service_remunera: Records and statements by members of the family described the lands as remuneration for performing the village office.
predicates.claimant_is_not_current_officeholder: The family member claiming a share was not the person then holding and performing the village office.

members.legal_issue: Revenue authorities may resume and regrant service lands when the person claiming them is not entitled to hold the service emoluments and the lands are administered as attached to the office.
material_facts: The revenue authorities determined that the person performing the village office was entitled to its emoluments and that the claimant was not entitled to retain the lands.
The claimant possessed the lands after a family partition but did not perform the office when the authorities ordered resumption and regrant.
The authorities ordered the lands resumed and regranted them to the person performing the office.
members.legal_principle: Section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, permits forfeiture of alienated land granted on condition that services be rendered when the holder fails to render them or transfers the land in a way likely to defeat the grant’s purpose; forfeited land is regranted on the original conditions. Sections 9–11 of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900, regulate enjoyment and alienation of office emoluments. The court held that these provisions applied to the service grant at issue.
members.conclusion: The revenue authorities had authority to resume the lands and regrant them to the working officeholder, and the orders were not invalid for want of jurisdiction.

predicates.appeal_challenging_revenue_resumption: The matter is an appeal challenging a revenue authority’s resumption and regrant of lands.
predicates.lands_are_service_emoluments: The lands were granted as emoluments for performing the duties of an office.
predicates.claimant_does_not_perform_required_servi: The person claiming to retain the lands did not perform the service for which they were granted.
predicates.revenue_authority_regrants_to_working_of: The revenue authority regranted the lands to the person performing the office.

members.legal_issue: A personal land grant burdened with religious service is not covered by the statutory power to resume grants made for the performance of religious charity or service.
material_facts: The grant comprised both warams and was found to be personal to the grantees, rather than an emolument for holding a service office.
The grantees were required to perform service for the temples, but the grant also contained a personal element for their benefit.
After the grantees alienated part of the land and stopped performing the service, revenue authorities ordered resumption and regrant of the land to the temples under the Act.
The alienees challenged the revenue authorities’ jurisdiction to resume the grant under that provision.
members.legal_principle: Section 44-B(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, read with sections 44-B(2)(a)(iii), 44-B(2)(f)(i) and (ii), applies to inams granted directly to a temple, service inams, and inams whose whole income is intended for charity, not personal inams merely burdened with service. The structure of the resumption and regrant provisions supports that construction. A personal grant burdened with service is distinct from a service grant; whether the former is resumable for failure to perform service depends on whether the circumstances of the grant made it conditional on performance. The Court referred to Shrimant Lakhamgouda Basavprabhu Sardesai v. Raosaheb Baswantrao and to Board’s Standing Order 54, class (b), as amended.
members.conclusion: The personal inam burdened with service did not fall within section 44-B; the revenue authorities could not resume and regrant it under that section. Such inams remained governed by Board’s Standing Order 54, class (b), and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.challenge_to_public_resumption: A party challenged the authority of public officials to resume and regrant land under a power concerning religious or charitable grants.
predicates.personal_grant_with_service_burden: The land was granted personally to an individual, who was also required to perform service for a religious institution.
predicates.grant_included_personal_benefit: The grant was not wholly intended as income for the religious institution or as emoluments for performing its service.

members.legal_issue: An inam granted to hereditary office-holders as remuneration for services connected with a religious institution falls within the statutory resumption scheme, unlike land granted personally subject only to a service condition.
material_facts: The temple trustees appointed persons to perform services connected with the temple and placed the inams in their possession as remuneration for those services.
The inams were confirmed in the names of hereditary office-holders rendering the services, with holders of an office recorded as enjoying shares.
The claimants contended that the inams were personal grants burdened with conditions of service.
members.legal_principle: There is a distinction between land granted personally subject to a service condition and land granted as remuneration for holding an office. The latter, when the office and services relate to a math or temple, is within section 44-B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. The Court relied on Forbes v. Noor Mahomed Tuquee and P. V. Bheemsena Rao v. Sirigiri Pedda Yella Reddi.
members.conclusion: The inams were granted to office-holders as remuneration for services connected with the temple, rather than as personal inams burdened with a service condition, and were within the scope of the resumption scheme.

rule.if: religious_service_inam_resumption_case and office_holders_received_land_as_service_remuneration and services_connected_to_religious_institution and not personal_grant_merely_burdened_by_service

predicates.religious_service_inam_resumption_case: The proceeding concerns whether an inam connected with services to a religious institution may be resumed.
predicates.office_holders_received_land_as_service_: The holders received the land as remuneration for holding offices and performing associated services.
predicates.services_connected_to_religious_institut: The offices and services were connected with a religious institution.
predicates.personal_grant_merely_burdened_by_servic: The land was granted personally to its holder and was merely subject to a condition to perform services.
predicates.office_holder_inam_falls_within_resumpti: An inam granted to an office-holder as service remuneration falls within the resumption scheme.

members.legal_issue: An inam granted to remunerate service attached to a religious institution is not a personal inam and may be resumed when it is alienated.
material_facts: The official records described the inam as a temple endowment for archaka service and recorded the grantees in their capacity as temple officeholders.
The records and a statement by a person enjoying the inam showed that it was treated as remuneration for performing temple services.
The holders alienated the lands, and the Mission possessed them as an alienee.
The inam was not shown to have been granted personally to an individual independently of the temple office.
members.legal_principle: A grant to an officeholder to remunerate service is a service inam rather than a personal inam, and it is resumable when the service or office conditions are not met. Section 44-B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 authorized resumption on specified grounds, including alienation. P. B. Bheemsena Rao v. Sirigiri Paddayella Reddi distinguishes a proper service inam from a personal grant burdened with service; the Court also relied on the records and the earlier treatment of such grants under the Board of Revenue's Standing Order Rule 54.
members.conclusion: The inam was a service inam, not a personal inam, and its alienation made it liable to resumption.

predicates.service_inam_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an inam granted in connection with institutional service may be resumed.
predicates.grant_attached_to_temple_office: The grant records or other evidence connect the inam to service performed through a temple office rather than to the grantee personally.
predicates.service_grant_alienated: The holder or a successor transferred the inam or the land interest covered by it.

members.legal_issue: A grant made as remuneration for village-office service is a service emolument, not family land merely burdened with service, and may be resumed and regranted when held by a person not entitled to its emoluments.
material_facts: The ancient grant provided land in lieu of wages or emoluments for the patel’s service and was independent of the village jagir.
Historical records and the parties’ statements in revenue proceedings described the land as remuneration for the patel’s work.
The claimant acquired the disputed land through a family partition but had never served as patel; the revenue authorities resumed it and regranted it to the working patel.
members.legal_principle: The distinction is between a grant of an office remunerated by land, which is prima facie resumable, and a grant of land burdened with service, which is not prima facie resumable absent terms or circumstances establishing that result: Lakhamgouda Basavaprabhu Sardesai v. Baswantrao. The historical documents and the parties’ understanding of the grant may establish its character when the original sanads are unavailable. The Inam Rules, 1859, and the Patel and Patwaris Law, 1900, treat service grants as emoluments attached to office and restrict their alienation; section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, authorises forfeiture and regrant in the specified circumstances.
members.conclusion: The lands were a service grant in the nature of emoluments for the office, not family property burdened with service; they could not be freely alienated, and the Government could resume and regrant them to the person entitled to the office’s emoluments.

predicates.civil_challenge_to_revenue_resumption: A person brought a civil challenge to revenue authorities’ resumption of land granted for village-office service.
predicates.service_emolument_grant: The grant gave land in place of wages or emoluments for performing a village office, rather than giving family land subject to a service burden.
predicates.nonofficiating_claimant_holds_land: A person who was not performing the office held land granted as its emoluments.

members.legal_issue: A High Court deciding whether to confirm a death sentence must independently examine the case and carefully consider the relevant evidence, circumstances, and arguments.
material_facts: The trial court imposed death sentences, which were referred to the High Court for confirmation.
The High Court considered the evidence, the arguments for the accused, the evidentiary infirmities, and the enmity between the factions.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had carefully examined the case and had not overlooked the relevant points.
members.legal_principle: Sections 374 and 375 of the Code of Criminal Procedure require the High Court to consider a death-sentence reference for itself, with power to take additional evidence if necessary. Jumman v. State of Punjab, AIR 1957 SC 469, was relied on for the independent and careful scrutiny required in such proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the High Court had discharged its duty in the death-sentence proceedings and rejected the challenge to the adequacy of its review.

predicates.death_sentence_confirmation_proceeding: The proceeding requires a High Court to decide whether a trial court’s death sentence should be confirmed.
predicates.high_court_examined_evidence_and_materia: The High Court independently examined the evidence, relevant circumstances, and material arguments raised for the accused.
predicates.high_court_review_is_adequate: The High Court has fulfilled its duty of review.

members.legal_issue: A High Court dealing with a reference arising from a judge’s disagreement with a jury verdict must consider the entire evidence, give due weight to the opinions of the judge and jury, and reach its own conclusion before deciding whether to uphold the verdict.
material_facts: The accused were tried by a jury, which returned a majority verdict of guilty.
The trial judge disagreed with the jury’s verdict and referred the case to the High Court.
The High Court considered only the objection to the jury charge, accepted the majority verdict, and convicted the accused without considering the entire evidence.
The Supreme Court held that it was not appropriate for it to consider the entire evidence in the first instance and remanded the case to the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 307(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the High Court, when dealing with a reference, to consider the entire evidence, give due weight to the opinions of the Sessions Judge and jury, and decide whether to acquit or convict. As stated in Akyhlakali Hayatalli v. The State of Bombay, applying Ramanugrah Singh v. The Emperor, if the evidence can properly support either view, the jury’s view must prevail; if no reasonable body of men could have reached the jury’s conclusion, the verdict may be disregarded. The High Court must assess the whole case under that standard.
members.conclusion: The High Court violated its statutory duty by accepting the jury verdict without considering the entire evidence; its convictions and sentences were set aside, and the case was remanded for the High Court to reconsider in accordance with law.

predicates.jury_verdict_reference: A trial judge disagreed with a jury verdict and referred the case to a higher court for decision.
predicates.high_court_accepted_jury_verdict: The higher court accepted the jury’s verdict and convicted the accused.
predicates.high_court_did_not_consider_entire_evide: The higher court decided the reference without considering all the evidence in the case.

members.legal_issue: A High Court deciding a reference arising from disagreement between a trial judge and a jury must consider the entire evidence and the charge before reaching its own conclusion.
material_facts: The jury returned a majority verdict finding the accused guilty, but the trial judge disagreed and referred the case to the High Court.
Before the High Court, counsel argued only that the charge to the jury was defective and did not invite consideration of the entire evidence.
The High Court considered the objections to the charge, accepted the jury’s verdict, and convicted the accused without considering the entire evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 307(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure required the High Court to consider the entire evidence and the charge as framed and placed before the jury, give due weight to the opinions of the trial judge and jury, and reach its own conclusion. Applying Akhlakali Hayatalli v. State of Bombay and Ramanugrah Singh v. The Emperor, the Court explained that where the evidence can properly support either view, the jury’s view generally prevails; where no reasonable body could have reached the jury’s conclusion, the verdict may be disregarded in the interests of justice.
members.conclusion: The High Court violated its statutory duty by convicting the accused without considering the entire evidence; its judgment and the convictions and sentences were set aside.

predicates.jury_reference_case: A criminal case was referred to the High Court after the trial judge disagreed with a jury verdict.
predicates.high_court_omitted_full_evidence_review: The High Court decided the reference without considering the entire evidence.

members.legal_issue: A High Court deciding a reference for confirmation of a death sentence must independently consider the entire evidence, including defence evidence.
material_facts: The trial court's death sentences were referred to the High Court for confirmation.
The High Court did not address the defence evidence supporting the alibis.
The case had already been pending for six years, and the Supreme Court considered that remitting it would cause unnecessary hardship.
The Supreme Court examined the defence evidence itself and found that it did not establish the alibis.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a confirmation reference is a continuation of the trial on the same or additional evidence. The High Court must reappraise the entire evidence, consider the case in all its aspects, and reach an independent conclusion. No earlier case was identified by name.
members.conclusion: The High Court's failure to consider the defence evidence was contrary to the settled practice, but the Supreme Court examined the record itself rather than remitting the case because remittal would cause unnecessary hardship.

predicates.death_sentence_confirmation_reference: The proceeding is a reference to a High Court to confirm a death sentence.
predicates.high_court_omits_defence_evidence: The High Court does not consider evidence offered by the defence when independently reviewing the case.
predicates.remittal_would_cause_unnecessary_hardshi: Sending the case back for reconsideration would cause unnecessary hardship in the circumstances.
predicates.reviewing_court_assesses_record_without_: The reviewing court examines the omitted evidence itself instead of remitting the case.

members.legal_issue: When a High Court considers a reference for confirmation of a death sentence alongside an appeal, it must independently assess the proceedings and evidence.
material_facts: The High Court considered the accused's appeal together with a reference for confirmation of their death sentences.
Its judgment gave only a general statement that the eyewitnesses inspired confidence and did not meaningfully discuss their evidence.
The Supreme Court examined the evidence itself rather than remanding the case.
members.legal_principle: Under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court dealing with a death-sentence confirmation reference must independently consider the proceedings and material, while being assisted but not bound by the Sessions Judge's opinion. The Court relied on Jumman & Ors. v. State of Punjab, AIR 1957 SC 469, and Bhupendra Singh v. State of Punjab, [1968] 3 SCR 404. Although an appellate court ordinarily need not examine the entire record when deciding a criminal appeal against conviction, the confirmation reference requires an independent conclusion. In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court does not normally reassess witness credibility, but it did so here because of the High Court's failure to conduct the required assessment.
members.conclusion: The High Court was required to consider the proceedings in all their aspects and reach its own independent conclusion on the material; its failure to do so was an infirmity, so the Supreme Court examined the evidence itself.

predicates.death_sentence_confirmation_reference: The proceeding before the High Court included a reference requiring confirmation of a death sentence.
predicates.high_court_gave_no_substantive_evidence_: The High Court did not meaningfully assess the evidence before reaching its conclusion.

members.legal_issue: A High Court considering an appeal alongside a reference to confirm a death sentence must independently examine the case, and it may dispense with further inquiry or additional evidence when neither is needed to determine guilt or innocence.
material_facts: The High Court considered the appellants’ appeal together with a reference to confirm death sentences imposed on two appellants.
The High Court examined the case for itself and found the prosecution case proved beyond reasonable doubt.
The Supreme Court found that no further inquiry or additional evidence was necessary.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 374, 375 and 376 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court dealing with a death-sentence confirmation reference must examine the case for itself and may direct further inquiry or additional evidence if desirable to determine guilt or innocence. Section 423, as discussed in Bhupendra Singh v. State of Punjab, does not ordinarily require an appellate court to examine the entire record independently in a criminal appeal, but the duty is different when a death-sentence reference is also before the High Court.
members.conclusion: The High Court substantially discharged its duty of independent examination, and no further inquiry or additional evidence was called for.

predicates.death_sentence_confirmation_reference_an: The proceeding included an appeal by a convicted person and a reference for confirmation of a death sentence.
predicates.high_court_independently_examined_case: The High Court examined the case for itself rather than merely reviewing the trial court’s decision.
predicates.no_further_inquiry_or_evidence_needed: The evidence and circumstances did not call for further inquiry or additional evidence to determine guilt or innocence.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming through a party to an appeal may be added to the appeal to protect an interest acquired through that party.
material_facts: A company in possession of the property had granted mortgages over it to a bank.
The bank later obtained a mortgage decree, purchased the property at the mortgage sale, and took possession.
The bank conveyed the property and its interest to the proposed respondents while the appeal was pending.
The proposed respondents were added to the appeal, subject to the decree-holder’s right to object to their standing.
members.legal_principle: Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits proceedings to be taken by or against persons claiming under a party. An appeal is a proceeding for this purpose. Following Saila Bala Dassi v. Nirmala Sundari Dassi, [1958] S.C.R. 1287, the Court applied that principle to allow persons claiming through a party to be brought onto the appeal.
members.conclusion: The proposed respondents were properly added to the appeal because they claimed through a party whose interest in the property was involved in the dispute.

predicates.pending_appeal: An appeal is pending concerning rights or interests involved in the dispute.
predicates.applicant_claims_through_a_party: The applicant acquired or claims an interest through a party to the appeal or that party’s successor in interest.
predicates.applicant_seeks_to_participate_in_appeal: The applicant seeks to be added as a party to the pending appeal.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming through a transferor may continue an appeal filed by the transferor when the transferred interest carries the right to pursue that appeal.
material_facts: The owner transferred the properties to the claimant.
The transferor had filed an appeal concerning execution of a decree affecting those properties.
The claimant sought to be added to the pending appeal, although the claimant had not filed a separate appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure allows a proceeding that may be taken by a person to be taken by a person claiming under that person. An appeal is a proceeding for this purpose, and “claiming under” includes devolution and assignment of an interest. The provision is to be construed liberally to facilitate the exercise of rights acquired by devolution or assignment. The Court relied on Sitharamaswami v. Lakshmi Narasimha, approved in Jugalkishore Saraf v. Raw Cotton Co., Ltd., and on Muthiah Chettiar v. Govinddoss Krishnadoss; it also referred to Moidin Kutty v. Doraiswami.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled under section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be brought on record and to continue the appeal filed by the transferor.

predicates.pending_appeal: An appeal filed by one person remains pending before the court.
predicates.transferor_filed_appeal: The person from whom the claimant derives an interest filed the pending appeal.
predicates.claimant_succeeded_to_transferor_interes: The claimant acquired by transfer or devolution an interest held by the person who filed the appeal.

members.legal_issue: When a party joined as the karta of a continuing Hindu undivided family dies during an appeal, the succeeding karta may be substituted under the procedure for substitution of a deceased party, and the substitution may suffice despite use of an incorrect procedure.
material_facts: A respondent joined in the appeals as the karta of a joint Hindu family business died while the appeals were pending.

The family continued to exist, and its succeeding karta was brought on record through applications made under the procedure for devolution of interest rather than the procedure for substitution of a deceased party.
The applications appeared to have been made after the limitation period, but the succeeding karta was already on record when the objection was considered.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXII Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where a party joined as karta dies and the undivided Hindu family continues, the succeeding karta can be substituted for the deceased karta. An application under Order XXII Rule 10 is not the correct procedure for that substitution, but the court may overrule a technical objection where the succeeding karta has already been brought on record.
members.conclusion: The applications under the procedure for devolution of interest were not the correct procedure; an application for substitution under Order XXII Rule 4 should have been made. However, because the succeeding karta had been brought on record, the court overruled the objection.

predicates.appeal_involving_karta_party: The proceeding is an appeal in which a party was joined in the capacity of karta of an undivided Hindu family.
predicates.family_continued_after_karta_death: The undivided Hindu family continued to exist after the karta died during the appeal.
predicates.successor_karta_brought_on_record: The succeeding karta was brought on record in place of the deceased karta, although the application used was not the correct procedure for substitution.

members.legal_issue: An heir who is allowed to prosecute an appeal on the merits may be treated as substituted despite the absence of a formal substitution order, and the deceased appellant’s widow may also be substituted and heard.
material_facts: The sole appellant died while the appeal was pending.
A son filed an application seeking substitution and claiming the deceased’s estate under an alleged will.
The son was allowed to press the appeal on its merits, although no formal order had been made on the substitution application.
The widow disputed the son’s claim and expressed her desire to challenge the eviction decree.
The Court decided to substitute the widow and permitted her counsel to argue the appeal afresh.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the son as substituted in substance because he had been allowed to prosecute the appeal, notwithstanding the lack of a formal order; it also decided to substitute the widow and permit a fresh argument. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The son was deemed to have been substituted because he was allowed to press the appeal, and the Court also substituted the widow and allowed her to argue the appeal afresh.

rule.if: appeal_pending_at_appellant_death and heir_substitution_application_filed and heir_permitted_to_press_appeal and widow_seeks_substitution

predicates.appeal_pending_at_appellant_death: The appellant died while an appeal was pending.
predicates.heir_substitution_application_filed: An heir filed an application seeking substitution for the deceased appellant.
predicates.heir_permitted_to_press_appeal: The heir was allowed to argue the appeal on its merits.
predicates.widow_seeks_substitution: The deceased appellant’s widow sought substitution and an opportunity to argue the appeal.

members.legal_issue: When a party sued in a representative capacity dies during a pending appeal and the interest in the subject matter passes to a successor, the appeal is governed by the rule for devolution of interest rather than the rules for substitution of legal representatives on death.
material_facts: The suit sought possession and management of a religious institution and its properties, with the plaintiff claiming to be its de jure head and the defendant being sued as its de facto head.
The defendant died while the plaintiff’s appeal was pending, and a successor was elected as the institution’s head.
The application to implead the successor was made after the period prescribed for an application under the rules concerning legal representatives.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where a person is sued in a representative capacity and that person’s interest in the subject matter devolves on another, the proceeding may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the court’s leave. This applies whether the devolution results from death or another event. The Court relied on and approved Rajnam Pillai v. Natraja Desikar, Thirumalai v. Arunachella, and Roshan Lal v. Kapur Chand.
members.conclusion: The interest in the subject matter devolved on the successor, so the appeal could be continued against him under Order 22, rule 10, with the court’s leave; it did not abate merely because the application was late under Order 22, rules 3 or 4.

predicates.civil_appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the disputed subject matter was pending when the relevant party died.
predicates.representative_capacity_case: A party was sued in a representative role concerning the subject matter, rather than in a personal capacity.
predicates.subject_matter_interest_devolved_to_succ: The interest of the deceased party in the disputed subject matter passed to a successor.

members.legal_issue: A transferee of a party’s interest in a suit may be added to the proceedings and maintain an appeal even if not formally substituted before the original party’s death.
material_facts: The original plaintiff transferred his right, title and interest in the suit property to the appellant.
The original plaintiff died, and the appellant had not been formally substituted in his place.
The appellant sought to maintain the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rule 10 permits substitution where an interest in the subject matter is transferred during the proceedings. Order 1 Rule 10 permits an appropriate application to add a person whose interest warrants participation. The Court treated the appellant, who had acquired the original plaintiff’s interest, as entitled to seek participation and maintain the appeal.
members.conclusion: The appellant had standing to maintain the appeal: substitution could have been sought under Order 22 Rule 10, and an application to be added under Order 1 Rule 10 was maintainable even though formal substitution had not occurred.

predicates.transferee_acquired_interest_in_suit: A person acquired a party’s interest in the subject matter while the suit was pending.
predicates.original_party_died: The party whose interest was transferred died before the appeal was pursued.
predicates.transferee_not_formally_substituted: The transferee had not been formally substituted for the original party.

members.legal_issue: A notice correctly addressed and returned unclaimed after an attempted delivery and postal intimation may be presumed served without examining the postman.
material_facts: The purchaser sent a lawyer's notice asking the seller to execute the sale deed.
The notice was correctly addressed, an attempt to deliver it was made, and an intimation was left when the seller was absent.
The notice was returned unclaimed, after which the purchaser sent a telegram and a copy of the notice by certificate of posting.
The High Court considered examination of the postman necessary, but the Supreme Court held that it was not.
members.legal_principle: The presumption under Section 27 of the Post Office Act applies where a notice is correctly addressed and sent through the post; the presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act operates independently. On the facts, the postal endorsement and intimation supported the presumption of service, and the postman did not have to be examined.
members.conclusion: Service could be presumed, and the purchaser was not required to examine the postman to establish service.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and notice_correctly_addressed and delivery_attempted_with_intimation and notice_returned_unclaimed

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought court enforcement of an obligation to execute a document.
predicates.notice_correctly_addressed: The sender addressed the notice correctly to the person required to act.
predicates.delivery_attempted_with_intimation: Postal delivery was attempted and an intimation was left when delivery could not be completed.
predicates.notice_returned_unclaimed: The notice was returned without delivery as unclaimed.

members.legal_issue: Properly addressed, prepaid summons sent by registered post with acknowledgement due may be presumed served when the acknowledgement is not received, unless the recipient rebuts that presumption with convincing evidence.
material_facts: The summonses were sent by registered post with acknowledgement due to the defendants’ correct addresses, and it was not disputed that they were properly addressed, prepaid, and duly sent.
One defendant gave only a bare statement that he had not received the registered letter and did not call the postman, while the other defendant gave no evidence to rebut service.
The defendants occupied the premises jointly, and the circumstances made it inherently improbable that the registered summons would have been served on one but not the other.
members.legal_principle: The second proviso to Order 5 Rule 19A of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provide for a presumption of due service when summons is properly addressed, prepaid, and duly sent by registered post with acknowledgement due, even if the acknowledgement is not received within the specified period. The presumption is rebuttable, and the recipient must produce convincing and cogent evidence to rebut it. Under Order 9 Rule 13, an applicant must establish both that summons was not duly served and that sufficient cause prevented appearance; the latter condition was not at issue here. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The presumption of service was not rebutted; the registered summonses were treated as duly served, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: ex_parte_decree_set_aside_proceeding and registered_summons_correctly_addressed and registered_summons_prepaid_and_duly_sent and acknowledgment_not_received and service_presumption_not_rebutted

predicates.ex_parte_decree_set_aside_proceeding: A party sought to set aside a decree entered when that party did not appear.
predicates.registered_summons_correctly_addressed: The summons sent by registered post was addressed to the recipient’s correct address.
predicates.registered_summons_prepaid_and_duly_sent: The registered summons was prepaid and duly sent with acknowledgement due.
predicates.acknowledgment_not_received: The court did not receive the acknowledgement of delivery within the applicable period.
predicates.service_presumption_not_rebutted: The recipient did not provide convincing and cogent evidence showing that the registered summons was not served.

members.legal_issue: A registered notice returned undelivered is deemed served when it was sent to the recipient's proper address and the recipient does not rebut that basis for service.
material_facts: The buyer sent two registered letters to the seller's address, but they were returned with remarks that the seller had not received them for the preceding week.
The seller later received a legal notice at that same address.
The seller provided no evidence that the address was incorrect.
members.legal_principle: A registered letter sent to the recipient's proper address is deemed served when it is returned with the stated remarks, unless the recipient proves otherwise. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this rule.
members.conclusion: The returned registered letters were deemed served on the seller.

rule.if: registered_notice_case and registered_letter_returned and same_address_later_used_for_received_notice and recipient_did_not_rebut_address

predicates.registered_notice_case: The proceeding concerns whether a registered notice was served on its intended recipient.
predicates.registered_letter_returned: The sender dispatched a registered letter to the recipient, and it was returned without delivery.
predicates.same_address_later_used_for_received_not: The recipient later received another notice at the same address.
predicates.recipient_did_not_rebut_address: The recipient provided no evidence that the address used for the returned letter was not the proper address.

members.legal_issue: A correctly addressed notice sent by registered post and returned because the recipient was unavailable may be treated as properly sent when the recipient does not substantiate a challenge to the return endorsement.
material_facts: The sellers sent registered notices to the purchaser’s correct residential address requiring him to proceed with execution of the sale deed.
The notices were returned with an endorsement that the purchaser was unavailable at home.
The purchaser did not produce evidence that the endorsement was wrong.
members.legal_principle: Where a communication is properly addressed and sent by registered post with acknowledgment due, and is returned because the addressee was unavailable, the sender need do nothing further unless the recipient challenges the endorsement and supports that challenge with evidence. The Court applied this principle in assessing the evidence relevant to readiness and willingness.
members.conclusion: The sellers were not required to take further steps after the notices were returned, and the purchaser’s unsubstantiated account did not establish that the notices were ineffective.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and notice_correctly_addressed and notice_sent_by_registered_post and notice_returned_recipient_unavailable and recipient_did_not_prove_endorsement_wrong

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.notice_correctly_addressed: The sender directed the notice to the recipient’s correct address.
predicates.notice_sent_by_registered_post: The sender dispatched the notice by registered post.
predicates.notice_returned_recipient_unavailable: The postal return stated that the recipient was unavailable at the address.
predicates.recipient_did_not_prove_endorsement_wron: The recipient did not provide evidence that the postal endorsement was incorrect.

members.legal_issue: A notice sent by registered post to the addressee’s correct address gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of service.
material_facts: The authority stated that it sent the allotment letter by registered post to the applicant’s address and produced dispatch records in support.

The applicant did not controvert that account before the lower authorities, and the High Court relied on the dispatch register in finding that the letter had not been sent to the correct person and address.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and Section 114 illustration (f) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, support a presumption of service when a notice is sent by registered post to the correct address. The presumption is rebuttable and is not compulsory: Harihar Banerjee v. Ramshashi Roy; Mst. L.M.S. Ummu Saleema v. B.B. Gujral; C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed; Gujarat Electricity Board v. Atmaram Sungomal Poshani; Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (Admn.), Bangalore v. V.K. Gururaj; Poonam Verma v. Delhi Development Authority; Sarav Investment & Financial Consultancy Private Limited v. Llyods Register of Shipping Indian Office Staff Provident Fund; Union of India v. S.P. Singh; Municipal Corporation, Ludhiana v. Inderjit Singh; and V.N. Bharat v. Delhi Development Authority.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have assessed the evidence in light of the rebuttable presumption arising from registered post; the presumption is permissible, not inevitable, and may be rebutted by evidence.

predicates.administrative_notice_service_dispute: A dispute arose in an administrative proceeding about whether a notice was served on its recipient.
predicates.notice_sent_by_registered_post: The sender dispatched the notice to the recipient by registered post.
predicates.addressee_address_was_correct: The notice was addressed to the recipient at the recipient’s correct address.

members.legal_issue: A notice returned after the addressee refuses to accept it may be presumed served, and its relevant averments may be treated as part of the pleading when relied on in the pleading.
material_facts: Before filing suit, the plaintiff sent two notices stating that he was ready and willing to perform the agreement.
The notices were returned unserved after the defendant refused to accept them.
The plaintiff referred to and relied on the notices in the suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides the basis for presuming service where a notice is refused; averments in notices referred to and relied on in the plaint may be treated as part of it.
members.conclusion: The notices were presumed to have been served, and the High Court could rely on their averments as part of the plaint.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.notice_refused_by_addressee: The addressee refused to accept a notice sent by the claimant.
predicates.notice_relied_on_in_pleading: The claimant referred to and relied on the notice in the pleading.

members.legal_issue: A daughter is entitled to equal rights in coparcenary property under the amended succession law when a partition suit has reached only the preliminary-decree stage and no legally completed partition occurred before the statutory cutoff.
material_facts: The dispute concerned coparcenary property in a partition suit brought by a son against his father, brother, and sisters.
A preliminary decree determining shares was passed and later amended, but no final decree partitioning the property had been passed.
The amendment came into force while the proceedings for the final decree were pending.
The sisters sought equal shares under the amendment, and the property had not been partitioned by a registered instrument or court decree before the statutory cutoff.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, gives a daughter the same coparcenary rights and liabilities as a son. Under Section 6(5) and its Explanation, the exclusion for an earlier partition applies to a partition effected before the cutoff by a duly registered partition deed or a court decree. A preliminary decree declaring shares does not itself complete partition. The Court applied S. Sai Reddy v. S. Narayana Reddy, which held that daughters could claim the benefit of a beneficial amendment before final partition, and relied on the principles concerning preliminary decrees in Phoolchand v. Gopal Lal.
members.conclusion: The sisters were entitled to equal shares in the coparcenary property under the amended law; the preliminary decree could not deprive them of those rights because no partition had been completed before the statutory cutoff.

rule.if: partition_suit and daughter_of_coparcener and coparcenary_property and amendment_applies_before_final_partition and not completed_partition_before_cutoff

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit to partition family property.
predicates.daughter_of_coparcener: A woman claiming a share is the daughter of a member of the coparcenary.
predicates.coparcenary_property: The property in dispute is coparcenary property.
predicates.amendment_applies_before_final_partition: The amended rule took effect while the partition proceeding remained incomplete.
predicates.completed_partition_before_cutoff: The property was partitioned before the relevant cutoff by a legally recognized completed partition.

members.legal_issue: An unmarried daughter may obtain an enhanced share under a statutory change to coparcenary rights in pending final-decree proceedings in a partition suit where the property has not yet been partitioned, notwithstanding that the preliminary decree has become final as to the shares it determined.
material_facts: A partition suit resulted in a preliminary decree determining the parties’ shares, and that decree was affirmed on appeal.
When the statutory amendment granting daughters coparcenary rights came into force, final-decree proceedings were pending and the property had not been divided by metes and bounds.
The daughter was unmarried when the amendment came into force and sought an equal share in the pending final-decree proceedings.
The application was rejected on the grounds that the preliminary decree had become final and the amendment could not be applied in the final-decree proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6A of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, inserted by the Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) Act, 1990, an unmarried daughter acquired coparcenary rights equal to those of a son. Articles 14, 15(1) and 15(3) of the Constitution support giving effect to the amendment’s equality-enhancing purpose. A partition suit proceeds in stages: a preliminary decree is conclusive as to the matters it decides, but the suit is not fully and completely decided until the final decree. Under Phoolchand v. Gopal Lal and S. Sai Reddy v. S. Narayana Reddy, a court may vary shares or pass a further preliminary decree in a partition suit when an intervening event changes the parties’ rights before final partition. Venkata Reddy v. Pethi Reddy and Gyarsi Bai v. Dhansukh Lal concern the finality of matters decided in a preliminary decree and do not prevent giving effect to a later statutory change in a pending partition suit; Mool Chand v. Deputy Director, Consolidation does not establish otherwise. The court also relied on the absence of a bar under the Code of Civil Procedure to varying shares in this situation and allowed relief under Sections 151, 152 and 153 CPC.
members.conclusion: The daughter could claim the enhanced share in the pending final-decree proceedings. The application was allowed, and the final decree was to be made or amended to give effect to her right.

rule.if: partition_suit and preliminary_decree_passed and partition_not_completed and final_decree_proceedings_pending_when_law_changed and law_change_grants_daughters_coparcenary_rights and daughter_unmarried_when_law_changed

predicates.partition_suit: A party brought a suit seeking partition of joint family property.
predicates.preliminary_decree_passed: The court passed a preliminary decree specifying the parties’ shares.
predicates.partition_not_completed: The property had not been divided by metes and bounds among the parties.
predicates.final_decree_proceedings_pending_when_la: Final-decree proceedings were pending when the change in the governing law took effect.
predicates.law_change_grants_daughters_coparcenary_: The legislature changed the governing law to grant daughters coparcenary rights equal to those of sons.
predicates.daughter_unmarried_when_law_changed: The daughter whose share is claimed was unmarried when the change in law took effect.
predicates.daughter_entitled_to_equal_share_in_fina: The daughter is entitled to an equal share to be given effect in the final decree.

members.legal_issue: A daughter in a Mitakshara coparcenary acquires coparcenary status by birth with the same rights and liabilities as a son, whether she was born before or after the amendment and whether her father was alive when it commenced.
material_facts: The connected disputes concerned daughters claiming shares in Mitakshara coparcenary property.
Some daughters were born before the amendment, and in some cases the father or another coparcener had died before it commenced.
The Court found that the daughters claiming rights were alive when the amendment commenced.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1)(a)–(c) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted, confers coparcenary status by birth and equal rights and liabilities. The Court relied on the birthright and nature of Mitakshara coparcenary discussed in Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash and Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy, and agreed with the relevant reasoning in Danamma @ Suman Surpur v. Amar. The contrary living-father requirement in Prakash v. Phulavati and Mangammal v. T.B. Raju was overruled.
members.conclusion: A daughter is a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son, with equal rights and liabilities; her father need not have been alive when the amendment commenced.

predicates.mitakshara_coparcenary_exists: The property was held in a Mitakshara coparcenary.
predicates.daughter_alive_when_amendment_commenced: The daughter claiming the right was alive when the change in law commenced.
predicates.daughter_is_descendant_of_coparcener: The claimant was a daughter of a coparcener in that coparcenary.

members.legal_issue: The daughter’s newly recognized coparcenary rights may be claimed from the commencement of the amendment, while specified earlier dispositions and partitions remain protected.
material_facts: The amendment recognized daughters as coparceners based on birth, including daughters born before it commenced.
The disputes raised whether recognizing those rights would reopen earlier transactions involving coparcenary property.
The amendment expressly preserved specified dispositions, alienations, partitions, and testamentary dispositions made before the stated cutoff.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1), including its proviso, and section 6(5) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as substituted, govern the commencement and savings. The Court characterized the provision as retroactive in operation because the rights claimed from commencement depend on the antecedent fact of birth, not as retrospective reopening of settled transactions. It relied on the distinction between retrospective and retroactive operation discussed in Darshan Singh v. Ram Pal Singh and explained the operation of the amendment in light of G. Sekar v. Geetha.
members.conclusion: A daughter born earlier may claim the rights from the amendment’s commencement, but the specified earlier transactions are not invalidated or reopened.

predicates.coparcenary_property_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to rights in coparcenary property.
predicates.daughter_claims_amended_right: A daughter claims the coparcenary rights recognized by the amended law.
predicates.transaction_completed_before_saving_cuto: A disposition, alienation, partition, or testamentary disposition covered by the statutory saving was completed before the specified cutoff.

members.legal_issue: A notional partition used to ascertain a deceased coparcener’s share does not itself effect an actual partition or end the coparcenary, and a pending partition proceeding must account for the daughter’s amended rights until actual partition is complete.
material_facts: Under the earlier law, a notional partition could be assumed to ascertain the share of a deceased coparcener in specified circumstances.
The connected disputes included partition proceedings in which preliminary decrees had been passed but final decrees or actual divisions by metes and bounds had not been completed.
The Court considered whether the notional partition or preliminary decree prevented daughters from receiving the benefit of the amended law.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the earlier section 6 and its Explanation, and substituted section 6, including sections 6(1), 6(3), and 6(5). It relied on Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum for the limited purpose of the notional-partition fiction; on S. Sai Reddy v. S. Narayana Reddy and Ganduri Koteshwaramma v. Chakiri Yanadi for the incompleteness of partition before a final decree; and on Phoolchand v. Gopal Lal and Prema v. Nanje Gowda concerning adjustment of shares when circumstances or law change before final decree. A preliminary decree declares shares but does not complete partition.
members.conclusion: The statutory fiction of partition only ascertains the deceased coparcener’s share and does not disrupt the coparcenary. A daughter’s equal share must be recognized in pending final-decree proceedings or appeals even if a preliminary decree has already been passed.

rule.if: pending_partition_proceeding and preliminary_decree_passed and actual_partition_incomplete and daughter_entitled_under_amended_law

predicates.pending_partition_proceeding: A suit or appeal concerning partition remained pending.
predicates.preliminary_decree_passed: The court had declared the parties’ shares in a preliminary decree.
predicates.actual_partition_incomplete: The property had not been finally divided and allotted by metes and bounds.
predicates.daughter_entitled_under_amended_law: A daughter was entitled to an equal coparcenary share under the amended law.

members.legal_issue: Daughters born before the 2005 amendment may receive the same coparcenary share as sons when the amendment takes effect while a partition suit remains pending and the partition has not become final.
material_facts: The two daughters were born before the original succession legislation and their father died in 2001.
They claimed shares in properties found to belong to the joint family.
The partition suit was filed in 2002, but the trial court’s decree was passed in 2007, after the 2005 amendment had taken effect.
The Court found that the daughters were entitled to shares and directed that the partition decree be drawn accordingly.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, as amended in 2005, makes a daughter a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son, with the same rights and liabilities; Section 6(3) provides for equal allotment to daughters and sons on a deemed partition. The Court relied on Prakash v. Phulavati for the application of the amendment irrespective of when daughters were born, and on Ganduri Koteshwaramma v. Chakiri Yanadi for the rule that daughters’ amended rights are not lost by a preliminary decree and may require its amendment before final partition. It also referred to State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram on coparcenary incidents, including the right to seek partition. The judgment recited Prakash’s holding concerning living daughters of living coparceners, but in this case treated the daughters’ rights as crystallized during the pending suit.
members.conclusion: The daughters were entitled to equal shares as coparceners, notwithstanding their birth before the original legislation. Because the partition suit remained pending when the amendment took effect and the partition was not final, their rights had to be reflected in the partition decree.

rule.if: partition_suit and coparcenary_property and amendment_took_effect_during_pending_suit and partition_not_final

predicates.partition_suit: A party brought a suit seeking partition of property held by a joint family.
predicates.coparcenary_property: The property in dispute was found to be coparcenary property.
predicates.amendment_took_effect_during_pending_sui: A legal amendment conferring equal coparcenary rights on daughters took effect while the partition suit was still pending.
predicates.partition_not_final: The partition had not become final when the amendment took effect.

members.legal_issue: A gift to a Hindu woman conveyed an absolute, heritable and transferable estate where the instrument described her as owner and neither its language nor its context limited her interest, despite the gift being made for maintenance or residence.
material_facts: A guardian acting for a minor transferred a house and shop to a widowed female relative through a deed described as a Tamliknama.

The deed stated that the donee was made the owner (Malik) of the properties and that they were provided for her residence; a contemporaneous deed recorded her relinquishment of claims to the wider estate.

The documents arose from an effort to resolve disputes over the estate and secure the minor's title. The surrounding circumstances did not indicate that the donee's interest was limited to her lifetime.
The deed contained no express words making the gift heritable or transferable, but it also contained no words limiting the interest to a life estate.
members.legal_principle: A document must be construed by ascertaining intention from the words used, with surrounding circumstances considered to determine their meaning. Under Hindu law, a gift to a female is not presumed to be limited: words conveying full ownership suffice, and no express power of alienation is necessary. The word “Malik” ordinarily indicates full proprietary ownership, including alienability, unless context or surrounding circumstances show otherwise. A maintenance or residence purpose ordinarily explains the motive for the grant and does not itself limit the estate when the dispositive language conveys absolute ownership. The Court relied on Rajendra Prasad v. Gopal Prasad, Kollani Koer v. Luchmee Parsad, Tagore v. Tagore, Sasiman Chowdhurain v. Shib Narayan, and Bishunath Prasad v. Chandrika; it distinguished Raja Ram Buksh v. Arjun and Woodoyaditta Deb v. Mukoond, which concerned maintenance grants in impartible estates and different circumstances. Section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act was cited as embodying the general principle that a transfer carries the full interest in the absence of a contrary intention.
members.conclusion: The donee acquired full heritable and transferable title to the properties. The appeal was allowed and the trial court's decree was restored; the limitation issue did not require determination.

rule.if: gift_interest_construction_case and document_uses_malik and not document_limits_interest_to_life and not context_indicates_limited_interest

predicates.gift_interest_construction_case: The proceeding concerned the extent of the interest conveyed to a donee by a gift of property.
predicates.document_uses_malik: The transfer document described the donee as Malik or owner of the property.
predicates.document_limits_interest_to_life: The transfer document states that the donee may enjoy the property only during her lifetime.
predicates.context_indicates_limited_interest: The document's context or surrounding circumstances indicate that the donor intended to confer only a limited interest.

members.legal_issue: An award granting property to a woman as its permanent owner confers an absolute estate when its operative words are clear and the other passages do not unambiguously qualify them.
material_facts: The award allotted the disputed properties to a daughter and described each recipient as the permanent owner of the allotted share.
Other passages in the award referred to the nature of the properties, the arbitrator’s view of inheritance, and a possible later devolution to the daughter’s son.
Those passages did not unambiguously qualify the operative grant.
members.legal_principle: A document must be construed according to its clear operative language; surrounding passages do not qualify that language unless they do so unambiguously. The Court relied on Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal (1950) S.C.R. 766 at 778 and Bishunath Prasad Singh v. Chandika Prasad Kumari (1933) 60 I.A. 56 at 61–62.
members.conclusion: The award granted the daughter an absolute estate in the disputed properties.

predicates.award_interpretation_case: The court is deciding the meaning of an award or comparable written instrument.
predicates.operative_words_confer_permanent_ownersh: The instrument’s operative words describe the recipient as the permanent owner of the property allotted to that recipient.
predicates.surrounding_passages_do_not_unambiguousl: Other passages in the instrument do not clearly and unambiguously limit the ownership stated in its operative words.

members.legal_issue: A grant of property to a Hindu female gives her an absolute and alienable estate when its words and context convey full ownership, because there is no presumption that a female receives only a limited estate.
material_facts: The deceased owner made an oral will in favour of his daughter, and the women who executed the registered deed did so to carry out that will rather than to convey an estate of their own.
The deed recited that the daughter could deal with the property in any way she liked.
The daughter was the sole object of the owner’s bounty, and the circumstances showed that he intended to give her the same title he held.
The plaintiff claimed the property as an heir on the basis that the daughter had received only a limited estate; after her death, her husband mortgaged and sold the property.
members.legal_principle: There is no presumption that a grant of immovable property to a Hindu female is limited or inalienable, and there is no difference in this respect between a male and a female grantee.
