Words sufficient to convey full ownership to a male also convey full ownership to a female. The Court relied on section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act and Tagore v. Tagore, Mst. Kollani Kuar v. Luchmi Kuar, Mahomed Shumsool v. Shewukram, Nagammal v. Subbalakshmi Ammal, and Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal; it treated the principle drawn from Mahomed Shumsool as clarified by later authority and settled by Ram Gopal.
members.conclusion: The daughter became the absolute owner of the property, and her husband had full right to alienate it; the plaintiff had no title to the property. The appeal was allowed and the trial court’s dismissal of the suit was restored.

rule.if: hindu_property_grant_to_female and grant_interpretation_proceeding and grant_words_convey_full_ownership and context_shows_intention_to_grant_full_title and no_conflicting_context

predicates.hindu_property_grant_to_female: A grant of property is made to a Hindu female.
predicates.grant_interpretation_proceeding: A court is deciding the nature of the estate conveyed by a property grant.
predicates.grant_words_convey_full_ownership: The words used in the grant are sufficient to convey full ownership.
predicates.context_shows_intention_to_grant_full_ti: The surrounding circumstances show that the grantor intended to give the grantee the full title held by the grantor.
predicates.no_conflicting_context: The grant contains no conflicting context that limits the estate conveyed.

members.legal_issue: A compromise deed granting property to a widow in unqualified terms of absolute ownership confers an absolute estate when its language and context do not qualify the grant.
material_facts: The compromise deed stated that the properties allotted to the widow were to be enjoyed by her as “Malik Mustakil.”
The widow gave up claims to a substantial portion of the disputed property in return for an absolute interest in the portion allotted to her.
The deed’s language and the circumstances of the compromise did not qualify the estate granted.
members.legal_principle: A document is ordinarily construed according to the normal and natural meaning of its words. Dhyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore and Bishunath Prasad Singh v. Chandika Prasad Kumar support treating the unqualified expression “Malik Mustakil” as conferring an absolute estate unless other words or circumstances qualify it.
members.conclusion: The widow received an absolute estate in the properties allotted to her under the compromise.

predicates.compromise_deed_uses_unqualified_absolut: The deed describes the recipient’s ownership of the allotted property in unqualified terms of absolute ownership.
predicates.deed_context_does_not_qualify_grant: The circumstances surrounding the deed do not indicate that the recipient’s ownership is limited.

members.legal_issue: A deed granting property to a wife in absolute terms transfers full ownership to her, and a recital explaining the circumstances of the gift does not make the gift a trust or a transfer to the son.
material_facts: The husband’s deed stated that he gifted the scheduled property to his wife and that she could enjoy it with absolute rights.
The deed referred to the wife’s minor son and her wish to be provided for, but the court found that this recital explained the circumstances prompting the gift.
The deed did not express an intention to create a trust for the son or convey the husband’s share to him.
members.legal_principle: The court construed the deed according to its clear and unequivocal terms: an absolute grant to the wife was not converted into a trust or a conveyance to the son merely by mentioning him in the recital. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this construction.
members.conclusion: The deed was a valid absolute gift to the wife, who acquired full title to the properties.

predicates.property_gift_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over title to property transferred by a gift deed.
predicates.deed_grants_absolute_ownership: The gift deed expressly grants the recipient absolute ownership of the property.
predicates.son_is_mentioned_only_as_gift_context: The deed mentions the donor’s son as part of the circumstances explaining the gift, without expressing an intention to benefit him or create a trust for him.

members.legal_issue: An award granting a person a share as its permanent owner conveys an absolute estate when the operative language is clear and the other parts of the award do not unambiguously qualify it.
material_facts: The award stated in its operative part that each recipient had become the permanent owner of the share allotted to them.
The award's other passages included views about the character of the properties and their expected devolution, but the court found those passages did not clearly qualify the operative language.
members.legal_principle: The words used in an instrument are interpreted in their usual sense when they are clear and unambiguous; other words or circumstances in the same instrument may qualify them only if they do so unambiguously. The court relied on Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal and Bishunath Prasad Singh v. Chandika Prasad Kumari in considering the meaning of “malik mustaqil.”
members.conclusion: The award gave the recipient an absolute estate in the allotted property.

rule.if: award_interpretation_case and operative_language_clear and not unambiguous_qualifying_context

predicates.award_interpretation_case: The dispute requires a court to determine the nature of an estate granted by an award.
predicates.operative_language_clear: The award's operative words clearly describe the recipient as the permanent owner of the allotted property.
predicates.unambiguous_qualifying_context: Other language or circumstances in the award clearly limits the estate described in its operative words.

members.legal_issue: A prior Supreme Court decision is binding for the legal principle it actually decided when that principle governs the issue before the Court.
material_facts: A three-judge Supreme Court bench had considered whether owners whose property was acquired under a similar statutory scheme could receive solatium and interest.
That bench considered the relevant statutory provisions and prior authorities and held that solatium and interest were not payable under that scheme.
A later two-judge decision had applied that holding to the statutory scheme at issue in this appeal.
The respondents argued that the earlier decision was not a binding precedent and conflicted with another decision concerning a different statutory scheme.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 141 of the Constitution, the binding force of a decision lies in its ratio decidendi: the principle derived from applying law to the material facts and deciding the issue before the court. A judgment must be read in light of its facts and issue, rather than treating every observation as law. The Court held that Hari Kishan Khosla decided the issue of entitlement under the Central Act and that Satinder Singh concerned a materially different statute that expressly incorporated a compensation provision.
members.conclusion: The earlier three-judge decision was a binding precedent on the issue it had decided; it was neither per incuriam nor in conflict with the decision relied on by the respondents.

rule.if: acquisition_appeal and prior_supreme_court_decision and same_controlling_issue and prior_decision_deliberately_decided_issue

predicates.acquisition_appeal: The proceeding challenges an award of compensation under a statutory acquisition scheme.
predicates.prior_supreme_court_decision: A prior Supreme Court decision addressed the legal issue relevant to the proceeding.
predicates.same_controlling_issue: The issue before the Court is materially the same as the issue decided in the prior decision.
predicates.prior_decision_deliberately_decided_issu: The prior court considered the relevant law and facts and deliberately resolved that issue.

members.legal_issue: A High Court is bound by a Supreme Court Constitution Bench’s declared law and cannot decide inconsistently with it.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a High Court judgment that invalidated provisions establishing a land reforms tribunal and transferring certain pending cases.
The High Court treated the relevant directions in an earlier Constitution Bench judgment as not binding law and reached a view inconsistent with those directions.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 141, law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. The Court held that the reasoning and directions in paragraphs 98 and 99 of L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) 3 SCC 261 constituted such declared law.
members.conclusion: The Constitution Bench’s relevant opinion and directions were law declared under Article 141, binding on the High Court; the inconsistent findings and directions had to be set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_decision: A party appealed a High Court decision to a higher court.
predicates.binding_supreme_court_law_applies: An applicable Supreme Court ruling declared a legal principle binding on courts.
predicates.high_court_departed_from_that_law: The High Court adopted a position inconsistent with the applicable Supreme Court ruling.

members.legal_issue: A High Court must follow a Supreme Court declaration of law that applies to the relevant issue, even where an earlier High Court decision conflicts with that declaration.
material_facts: The Supreme Court had previously applied its interpretation of a rent-law exclusion to the corresponding exclusion in the state rent law.
That application conflicted with an earlier High Court decision concerning the state-law exclusion.
The High Court relied on the earlier High Court decision and directed the parties to pursue eviction remedies before the rent court.
members.legal_principle: Article 141 makes law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India. The Court relied on its prior decision in Shobha Surendar, which applied D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India to Section 31 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act; Padmanabha Rao v. State of Karnataka was impliedly overruled to the extent that it was inconsistent. The Court also referred to Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, but held that the High Court could not use it to depart from the Supreme Court’s declaration.
members.conclusion: The High Court was bound by the Supreme Court’s declaration and could not prefer or distinguish the conflicting High Court decision; the earlier High Court decision stood impliedly overruled to the extent of the conflict.

predicates.high_court_case: The matter is before a High Court.
predicates.supreme_court_declaration_applies: The Supreme Court has declared law that applies to the issue before the High Court.
predicates.high_court_relies_on_conflicting_precede: The High Court relies on a precedent that conflicts with the applicable Supreme Court declaration.
predicates.high_court_must_follow_supreme_court_dec: The High Court is required to follow the applicable Supreme Court declaration.

members.legal_issue: A lower court must follow a binding higher-court decision that directly resolves the legal issue before it when the decisions said to conflict address distinct questions.
material_facts: A Full Bench considered whether a lease made in breach of statutory letting requirements was void and enforceable.
The Supreme Court had already directly addressed those questions in a binding decision.
The Full Bench regarded other Supreme Court decisions as conflicting, but those decisions concerned distinct legal questions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied judicial discipline and the binding force of Supreme Court precedent. It held that Nanakram v. Kundalrai, (1986) 3 SCC 83, directly decided the relevant questions and bound the Full Bench. Waman Shriniwas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co., (1959) Supp. 2 SCR 217, Sri Krishna Khanna v. A.D.M., Kanpur, (1975) 2 SCC 361, and Mannalal Khetan v. Kedar Nath Khetan, (1977) 2 SCC 424, addressed different issues and were not contrary authorities on those questions.
members.conclusion: The Full Bench was bound to follow the directly applicable Supreme Court authority and was not entitled to take a contrary view; the decisions it cited did not create a conflict on the question decided in that authority.

predicates.lower_court_is_resolving_legal_issue: A lower court is deciding a legal issue in a case before it.
predicates.binding_higher_court_authority_directly_: A binding decision of a higher court has directly resolved the same legal issue.
predicates.purportedly_conflicting_decisions_addres: Other decisions said to conflict address legal questions distinct from the issue already resolved.

members.legal_issue: A prior decision of the same court on indistinguishable facts and law binds the court in a later case presenting the same points.
material_facts: The earlier appeal and the remaining appeals arose from the same High Court judgment.
The appellants represented that the points in the appeals were common and that nothing required decision in one appeal that was not common to the others.
The Court found that the earlier decision had been rendered on facts and law indistinguishable from those in the remaining appeals.
members.legal_principle: A decision once rendered ordinarily binds the court in like cases, and a prior decision of the Court on identical facts and law binds it on the same points in a later case. The Court referred to Cassel & Co. Ltd. v. Broome, Young v. Bristol Aeroplane Co. Ltd., Nicholas v. Penny, and The Bengal Immunity Company Ltd. Case in discussing the limits of departing from precedent and the per incuriam doctrine.
members.conclusion: The earlier decision bound the Court in the remaining appeals.

predicates.later_case_before_same_court: A later case or proceeding is before the same court that decided an earlier case.
predicates.prior_decision_on_identical_facts_and_la: The earlier decision was made on facts and law indistinguishable from those in the later case.
predicates.same_points_in_issue: The later case presents the same points that the earlier decision resolved.

members.legal_issue: A High Court must follow a Supreme Court precedent that has considered and distinguished earlier decisions when that precedent governs the same issue.
material_facts: The High Court relied on earlier Supreme Court decisions concerning acquisitions under the Land Acquisition Act to hold that the subsequent allottee could participate in the compensation proceedings.
A later Supreme Court decision had considered and distinguished those earlier decisions and had ruled on the rights of a subsequent allottee in acquisitions under the industrial development statute.
The High Court did not follow that later decision, although it addressed the same statutory setting and issue.
members.legal_principle: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India. Where a later Supreme Court decision considers and distinguishes earlier authorities while deciding the same issue in the relevant statutory setting, the later decision governs. The Court relied on Peerappa Hanmantha Harijan v. State of Karnataka as the controlling decision and referred to Director of Settlements, A.P. v. M.R. Apparao, Rashmi Metaliks Ltd. v. Kolkata Metropolitan Development Authority, and Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar on the binding force of Supreme Court precedent.
members.conclusion: The High Court was bound by the later Supreme Court decision; its failure to follow that precedent was contrary to Article 141 of the Constitution.

predicates.high_court_case: A High Court decides a case involving an issue of law.
predicates.controlling_later_supreme_court_preceden: A later Supreme Court decision governs the same issue in the relevant legal setting.
predicates.later_precedent_distinguished_earlier_ca: The later Supreme Court decision considered and distinguished earlier decisions on which a party or court relies.

members.legal_issue: A decree granting ejectment must provide compensation for the occupant's continued use of the property after the decree until possession is delivered.
material_facts: The plaintiff became entitled to eject the defendant.
The defendant remained in possession after the decree for ejectment.
The trial court had assessed a reasonable monthly amount for use and occupation, and the Supreme Court saw no reason to differ from that assessment.
members.legal_principle: Once ejectment is granted, an occupant who remains in possession despite the decree must pay mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the date of the decree until delivery of possession. A decree for ejectment in such a case must include a direction for that payment.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was awarded future mesne profits at the trial court's assessed rate from the date of its ejectment decree until delivery of possession.

predicates.ejectment_proceeding: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession from an occupant.
predicates.ejectment_decree_granted: The court has granted an order requiring the occupant to give up possession.
predicates.occupant_remains_in_possession_after_dec: The occupant continues to hold the property after the ejectment order.

members.legal_issue: An ejectment decree for an occupant who remains in possession must provide for mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the decree until delivery of possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff became entitled to ejectment of the defendant.
The defendant remained in possession after the ejectment decree.
The High Court had rejected the claim for future mesne profits, but the Supreme Court held that the ejectment decree could not stand without a direction covering post-decree occupation.
members.legal_principle: Once a claimant is entitled to ejectment, an occupant who remains in possession after the decree must pay mesne profits or damages for use and occupation until possession is delivered. An ejectment decree in those circumstances must include a direction for that payment.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was awarded future mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the date of the trial court’s ejectment decree until delivery of possession.

predicates.ejectment_decree_awarded: The court granted a decree requiring the occupant to give up possession of the property.
predicates.occupant_remains_in_possession_after_dec: The occupant continued to hold the property after the ejectment decree.

members.legal_issue: A person remaining in possession during delayed enforcement of an eviction decree may be directed to pay interim compensation to protect the decree-holder from continuing injury.
material_facts: The eviction decree had remained unexecuted for a lengthy period.
The occupant continued to hold the property and claimed to have obtained possession through a party against whom the eviction decree had been made.
The occupant’s declaratory suit remained pending, so the Court did not resolve the merits of the claimed tenancy rights.
The decree-holder sought possession and payment for the period during which the property was held.
members.legal_principle: To protect a judgment creditor from continuing injury when enforcement of a decree for possession is delayed, a court may order reasonable mesne profits or compensation, which may be equivalent to market rent. In an appropriate case, it may appoint a receiver and require the person holding the property to act as the receiver’s agent and deposit a fixed royalty, or make another suitable order. No earlier cases or specific statutory provision are cited as the basis for these principles.
members.conclusion: The Court directed the occupants to pay mesne profits or compensation at the rates it specified, with prior payments adjusted and arrears paid in instalments.

rule.if: decree_execution_proceeding and eviction_decree_unexecuted and person_holds_property and enforcement_delay_continues

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a decree for possession of property.
predicates.eviction_decree_unexecuted: A party obtained an eviction decree, but delivery of possession under it has not occurred.
predicates.person_holds_property: A person other than the decree-holder continues to possess the property.
predicates.enforcement_delay_continues: Enforcement of the decree has been delayed while the person continues to hold the property.

members.legal_issue: A court staying execution of an eviction decree may require the occupant to pay compensation for post-decree use and occupation above the contractual rent.
material_facts: An eviction decree had been passed and its execution was stayed while an appeal was pending.
The occupants continued to possess the premises after the decree and argued that they should pay no more than the standard rent.
The premises had been let at a low contractual rent, and the landlords sought compensation for the delay in recovering possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd., a court staying execution of an eviction decree may impose reasonable terms to compensate the decree-holder for delay if the appeal fails. From the date of the eviction decree, compensation may reflect the rate at which the landlord could have let the premises after they were vacated; the prior contractual rent is not controlling.
members.conclusion: The occupants could be required to pay reasonable compensation for post-decree use and occupation; the contractual rent did not cap that amount.

predicates.eviction_appeal_stay: An appeal against an eviction decree is pending and execution of the decree has been stayed.
predicates.eviction_decree_passed: A court has passed a decree for eviction against the occupant.
predicates.continued_occupation_delays_possession: The occupant continues to use the premises, delaying the decree-holder's recovery of possession.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may condition a stay of an eviction order on payment of reasonable compensation for continued occupation, even when that compensation exceeds the contractual rent.
material_facts: The tenant appealed an eviction order and sought to remain in possession while the appeal was pending.
The tribunal stayed eviction on condition that the tenant make monthly deposits in addition to the contractual rent, with the deposits held until the appeal was decided.
The premises were commercial property, the contractual rent had remained very low for decades, and evidence indicated that comparable nearby premises were let at substantially higher rent.
The tenant did not contend that the amount fixed by the tribunal was unreasonable or grossly excessive.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 38(3) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the tribunal has the powers of a court under the Code of Civil Procedure, including the power under Order 41 Rule 5 to stay execution. A stay is discretionary and equitable, not an automatic right; Order 41 Rule 5(3) requires consideration of substantial loss, delay, and security. The court may impose reasonable terms to compensate the successful decree-holder for loss caused by the stay. South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P. supports restorative compensation for benefits or losses resulting from interim orders; Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd. supports reasonable mesne profits, potentially equivalent to market rent, when execution of a possession decree is delayed. The court may also consider common knowledge and judicially noticeable facts, as recognized in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation.
members.conclusion: The tribunal had power to condition the stay on reasonable compensation for the landlord’s loss from delayed execution, and the High Court erred in setting aside the condition solely because it exceeded the contractual rent. The tribunal’s order was restored.

rule.if: eviction_appeal_stay_application and eviction_order_under_appeal and tenant_seeks_continued_occupation and landlord_succeeded_below

predicates.eviction_appeal_stay_application: A party pursued an appeal from an eviction order and asked the appellate court to stay its execution.
predicates.eviction_order_under_appeal: An eviction order had been made against the party seeking the stay.
predicates.tenant_seeks_continued_occupation: The tenant sought to remain in occupation while the appeal was pending.
predicates.landlord_succeeded_below: The landlord had obtained the eviction order from the lower forum.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may require a tenant to pay reasonable mesne profits or compensation while a stay prevents execution of an eviction decree.
material_facts: The trial court granted an eviction decree, which was confirmed on appeal.
A further appeal was pending and the eviction decree was stayed.
The landlord sought mesne profits during the continuation of the stay.
The High Court directed payment of mesne profits while the stay remained in force.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 5 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appellate court granting a stay may impose reasonable terms to compensate the decree-holder for loss caused by delayed execution. Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd. and Another, (1999) 2 SCC 325, recognizes the need for reasonable mesne profits when execution of a possession decree is delayed. Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd., (2005) 1 SCC 705, holds that compensation may reflect the amount for which the premises could presently be let. State of Maharashtra v. Super Max International Pvt. Ltd. and others, (2009) 9 SCC 772, reaffirmed that view. After an eviction decree, the tenancy terminates and the landlord may receive mesne profits or compensation for loss of use.
members.conclusion: The direction to pay mesne profits or compensation during the stay was consistent with the governing law.

predicates.appeal_seeks_to_continue_stay_of_evictio: An appeal concerns a request to continue a stay against execution of an eviction decree.
predicates.eviction_decree_has_been_passed: A court has granted a decree for eviction.
predicates.stay_delays_possession_and_execution: A stay prevents the decree-holder from obtaining possession and delays execution of the decree.

members.legal_issue: An allegation that execution property sold for a low price does not establish a basis to set aside the sale when the challenge is not brought on the ground of fraud or material irregularity in conducting the sale and substantial injury is not established.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor sought to set aside the execution sale by an application treated by the courts as one under section 47 CPC, not Order XXI Rule 90 CPC.
The judgment-debtors asserted that valuable property had been sold for a low price.
The courts did not determine whether fraud or material irregularity had occurred in publishing or conducting the sale, or whether substantial injury had resulted.
members.legal_principle: Section 47 CPC provides for execution-related objections. Under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC, a sale may be set aside for fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting it only where the applicant also proves substantial injury caused by that fraud or irregularity. The court relied on these provisions and noted that the application and decisions below did not address those matters.
members.conclusion: The low-price contention was not open on the materials before the court because the application was not under Order XXI Rule 90 and there was no evidence or finding of sale irregularity or fraud and resulting substantial injury.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and challenge_brought_as_execution_objection and low_sale_price_alleged and no_evidence_of_sale_fraud_or_irregularity and no_finding_of_substantial_injury

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A judgment-debtor challenges a sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.challenge_brought_as_execution_objection: The challenge is presented as an objection concerning execution rather than as a claim based on fraud or material irregularity in the sale.
predicates.low_sale_price_alleged: The judgment-debtor alleges that the property sold for a low price.
predicates.no_evidence_of_sale_fraud_or_irregularit: No evidence is led to establish fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
predicates.no_finding_of_substantial_injury: There is no finding that substantial injury was caused by fraud or material irregularity in the sale.

members.legal_issue: Mere inadequacy of the price obtained at a court sale does not by itself invalidate the sale.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor alleged that the property was worth substantially more than the price obtained at auction.
The Court identified independent procedural defects and excessive execution as grounds for setting aside the sale.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 21 Rule 90, material irregularity or fraud in publicity or conduct must be proved, and the applicant must show substantial injury. Kayjay Industries (P) Ltd. v. Asnew Drums (P) Ltd. holds that a court sale is a forced sale, that the best market price may not be obtained, and that mere inadequacy of price does not invalidate it. The Court also considered Janak Rai v. Gurdial Singh.
members.conclusion: Inadequacy of price alone is not sufficient to set aside a court sale; the sale in this case was set aside on other grounds.

predicates.court_execution_sale: The proceeding concerns a sale conducted by a court in execution.
predicates.only_ground_is_inadequate_price: The only asserted ground for setting aside the sale is that the price obtained was inadequate.

members.legal_issue: Inadequacy of the price obtained at a court auction does not alone justify setting aside the sale.
material_facts: The respondents sought to set aside a court auction sale and relied on the alleged inadequacy of the sale price.
They did not allege fraud or material irregularity in the conduct of the sale that caused them injustice.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a court auction sale cannot be set aside merely because the price was inadequate when no fraud or material irregularity in the conduct of the sale causing injustice is alleged. No specific statutory provision or earlier decision was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: Mere inadequacy of price was not a sufficient ground to set aside the court sale.

predicates.court_auction_sale_challenged: A party challenged a sale conducted by a court through auction.
predicates.price_inadequacy_is_only_ground: The challenging party relied only on the contention that the auction price was inadequate.
predicates.no_fraud_or_material_irregularity_causin: The challenging party did not allege fraud or a material irregularity in the sale’s conduct that caused injustice.

members.legal_issue: The sale was not liable to be set aside because the objections did not establish a material irregularity or fraud causing substantial injury.
material_facts: The executing court found the debtor's objections to the sale procedure and price unsupported and dismissed the application to set aside the sale.
The sale proclamation was issued sufficiently before the sale, and the Supreme Court treated the period as running from the date the proclamation order was issued.
The record showed publicity by newspaper and beat of drums, and seven bidders participated in the auction.
The sale papers disclosed valuations, and the debtor produced no evidence or bidder offering a higher price than the auction bid.
The debtor did not raise a plea of fraud.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 21 Rules 64 and 66 to 68 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the sale must follow the prescribed procedure. Order 21 Rule 67(1), read with Rule 54(2), provides for publication of the proclamation by a customary mode, including beat of drum, and by affixing copies at specified places; newspaper publication requires a specific court direction. Applying Order 21 Rule 90(2) and Saheb Khan v. Mohd. Yousufuddin, the Court held that the sale could not be set aside without a material irregularity or fraud that caused substantial injury. It found the objections meritless on the evidence and distinguished the other cases cited by the debtor on their facts.
members.conclusion: The debtor had not made out a ground under Order 21 Rule 90(2) to set aside the sale. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and restored the executing court's order dismissing the application.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and sale_procedure_complied and notice_period_sufficient and adequate_sale_publicity and multiple_bidders_participated and sale_valuations_disclosed and no_evidence_of_higher_value and not fraud_pleaded

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A judgment debtor applies to set aside an immovable-property auction sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.sale_procedure_complied: The executing court follows the prescribed procedure for settling and publishing the sale proclamation and conducting the sale.
predicates.notice_period_sufficient: The sale is fixed sufficiently after the order issuing the proclamation, when the notice period is counted from that order.
predicates.adequate_sale_publicity: The sale is publicized by the means used in the locality and in any other manner required by the court's directions.
predicates.multiple_bidders_participated: More than one bidder participates in the auction after the sale is publicized.
predicates.sale_valuations_disclosed: The sale documents disclose valuations of the property to prospective bidders.
predicates.no_evidence_of_higher_value: The debtor produces no evidence supporting the claimed higher market value or showing that a higher price could have been obtained at the sale.
predicates.fraud_pleaded: The debtor does not allege fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.

members.legal_issue: An assertedly inadequate sale price does not invalidate a sale without evidence that the property was worth substantially more or that the sale involved fraud.
material_facts: The appellant asserted that property said to be worth a much higher amount had been sold for a low price.
The evidence did not establish that the property was worth more than the value stated in the appellant’s own earlier account.
The property was subject to mortgages in favour of the government and private parties, and the trial court found no fraud.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the claim of inadequate price against the evidence of the property’s value and its existing mortgage encumbrances. It found no proof of fraud and no adequate evidentiary basis to conclude that the sale price was low.
members.conclusion: The Court was not satisfied that the property had been sold at a low price and rejected this ground for invalidating the sale.

rule.if: revenue_sale_challenged and sale_price_claimed_inadequate and no_reliable_evidence_of_higher_value and property_subject_to_mortgages and fraud_not_proved

predicates.revenue_sale_challenged: A party challenged the validity of a sale conducted to recover a debt through a revenue-sale process.
predicates.sale_price_claimed_inadequate: The challenger asserted that the sale price was too low compared with the property's value.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_higher_value: The evidence did not reliably establish that the property was worth substantially more than the value supported by the record.
predicates.property_subject_to_mortgages: The property was subject to mortgage interests when it was sold.
predicates.fraud_not_proved: The evidence did not establish fraud in connection with the sale.

members.legal_issue: An allegedly inadequate sale price, standing alone, does not invalidate a revenue sale.
material_facts: A house was sold in a revenue sale to a private purchaser for an amount alleged to be less than its estimated value.
No other irregularity that would invalidate the house sale was identified.
members.legal_principle: An allegation that the price obtained at a sale was inadequate does not, standing alone, establish a ground for declaring the sale void.
members.conclusion: The complaint that the house sold for an inadequate amount did not justify holding that sale void, and the claim concerning the house was dismissed.

predicates.revenue_sale_case: A public authority conducts a sale of property to recover a public revenue debt.
predicates.only_challenge_is_inadequate_price: The sole asserted defect is that the sale price was inadequate, with no other invalidating irregularity identified.
predicates.sale_not_void_for_inadequate_price_alone: The sale is not void solely because the price obtained was inadequate.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar on challenging orders made in exercise of statutory powers does not prevent a challenge to an acquisition order made without an essential statutory prerequisite.
material_facts: The acquisition order was made before any effective requisition under the statutory scheme that authorized acquisition only of land so requisitioned.
The governing Act contained a clause barring court challenges to decisions or orders made in exercise of powers conferred by or under that Act.
The affected owners challenged the validity of the acquisition, and the objection was considered in the statutory reference proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, bars challenges only to decisions or orders made in exercise of a power conferred by or under the Act. Because section 4 authorized acquisition only of land requisitioned under section 3, an acquisition order made without an effective section 3 requisition did not fall within that bar. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The statutory bar did not prevent the objection because the acquisition order, made without the required prior requisition, was not made in exercise of a power conferred by or under the Act.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_acquisition_order: A person challenges an order acquiring land under a statutory scheme.
predicates.statutory_bar_limited_to_orders_within_c: The applicable statutory bar covers only decisions or orders made in exercise of powers conferred by or under the scheme.
predicates.required_acquisition_prerequisite_absent: An essential condition for exercising the acquisition power was not satisfied when the acquisition order was made.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar on questioning an administrative order in court does not prevent a civil court from examining whether the authority acted without jurisdiction because the required vacancy did not exist.
material_facts: The officer declared the premises vacant and allotted them to another person.
The tenant brought a civil suit seeking a declaration that he remained the tenant and was entitled to occupy the premises.
The civil court found that the tenant had never vacated the premises and that his tenancy had not been terminated.
The officer’s power to allot the premises depended on a vacancy, and the statutory bar applied to orders made within the officer’s jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 7A of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, authorized action on the existence of a vacancy, while section 16 barred challenge to an order only when it was made with jurisdiction. An authority cannot acquire jurisdiction by wrongly deciding that a jurisdictional fact exists. The Court relied on Reg v. Commissioner of Income-tax (21 Q.B.D. 313), approved in Ebrahim Aboobakar & Anr. v. Custodian-General of Evacuee Property ([1952] S.C.R. 696), and referred to Chaube Jagdish Prasad v. Ganga Prasad Chaturvedi ((1959) Supp. (1) S.C.R. 733).
members.conclusion: The civil suit was maintainable because the officer had no jurisdiction to make the allotment order in the absence of a vacancy; the statutory bar did not prevent the civil court from examining that jurisdictional defect.

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_rent_allotment_or: A person brings a civil suit challenging an official order that allotted premises under a rent-control system.
predicates.official_power_requires_vacancy: The official’s power to allot the premises depends on whether they are vacant.
predicates.vacancy_did_not_occur: The tenant remained in occupation and the tenancy had not ended, so the premises had not become vacant.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar on challenging rent-fixing orders does not exclude civil court jurisdiction over a challenge to an order made without relevant evidence and in violation of fundamental principles of judicial procedure.
material_facts: A civil suit challenged a government notification fixing reduced rents for land in a village.

The notification rested on the Special Officer’s determination, which was based solely on a settlement-register entry for a different village and lacked relevant evidence connecting that entry to the village in question.
The statute barred court challenges to orders made under its rent-fixing provision.
members.legal_principle: Under section 8(1), an order made under section 3(2) was not liable to be questioned in court. But the exclusion of civil court jurisdiction is not readily inferred, and even where jurisdiction is excluded, courts may examine whether statutory provisions were complied with and whether the tribunal acted in conformity with fundamental principles of judicial procedure. The Court applied Secretary of State v. Mask and Company and followed Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh; it also referred to O. K. Muthuswamy Mudaliar v. State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The statutory bar did not apply to the impugned notification, and civil court jurisdiction to entertain the challenge was not excluded.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_rent_fixing_order: A plaintiff brings a civil suit challenging an order fixing reduced rents.
predicates.order_based_on_determination_without_rel: The challenged order rests on an administrative determination that lacks relevant evidentiary support.
predicates.determination_violated_fundamental_proce: The determination was made in a way that violated fundamental principles of judicial procedure.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar on civil suits concerning hereditary-office property does not prevent a civil court from hearing a suit in which the Government is only a formal party and the substantive relief is against private occupants, including where the court must determine whether a limited tribunal exceeded its authority.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession and related relief against the private occupants of the land.
The Government was joined, but it did not possess the land or actively obstruct recovery of possession; the court treated it as a formal party.
The challenged later orders were alleged to be beyond the Government’s jurisdiction and void.
The suit did not require substantive relief against the Government.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(a) of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, bars specified claims against the Government relating to hereditary-office property, but did not apply where the Government was merely a formal party and no substantive relief was sought against it. Civil courts retain jurisdiction to determine whether a tribunal of limited jurisdiction acted within its statutory powers. The Court relied on Ramrao Jankiram Kadam v. State of Bombay, Province of Bombay v. Hormusji Manekji, and The Secretary of State v. Musk & Co.; it distinguished Shrimant Sardan Bhujangarao Daulatrao Ghorpade v. Shrimant Malojirao Daulatrao Ghorpade on the basis that the claim there could not be separated from the relief sought against the Government.
members.conclusion: The statutory exclusion did not bar the suit because no relief was in fact sought against the Government; the civil court could determine whether the authority had exceeded its statutory powers.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_limited_authority: A civil suit asks the court to determine whether a tribunal or authority acted within the powers granted to it.
predicates.government_is_only_formal_party: The Government is joined in the suit but no substantive relief is sought against it.
predicates.substantive_relief_targets_private_occup: The substantive relief sought is directed against private persons possessing or obstructing access to the property.

members.legal_issue: The statutory bar on questioning administrative orders in court does not prevent a court from setting aside an order made in breach of natural justice, but it prevents review of the order’s propriety when the authority properly exercised its jurisdiction.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the provision barring court challenges to orders made under the Act prevented a court from considering the State Government’s order.
The Court considered the effect of that bar and the scope of judicial scrutiny of an order made under the State Government’s revisionary power.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, does not exclude judicial review of an order made in violation of natural justice. However, once the jurisdiction under that section is properly exercised, the court cannot examine the order’s propriety. Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand was considered.
members.conclusion: An order made in breach of natural justice may be quashed; where the State Government has properly exercised its jurisdiction, a court cannot examine the propriety of its order.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_order: A party asked a court to review an order made by an administrative authority under the governing rent-control scheme.
predicates.order_made_without_reasonable_opportunit: The authority made its order without giving both affected parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar does not exclude a civil court from examining whether a demolition action falls outside the statute or is affected by a jurisdictional error.
material_facts: The statute provided an appeal from a demolition order to an appellate tribunal and a further appeal to an administrator, and purported to bar civil suits concerning demolition proceedings.
The statutory scheme regulated the pre-existing common-law right to construct buildings rather than creating the right or liability itself.
The dispute concerned whether civil courts could examine demolition actions despite the statutory bar.
members.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure preserves civil jurisdiction except where it is expressly or impliedly barred. Sections 343(4)–(5) and 347E of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act bar suits concerning specified demolition proceedings, but the bar does not prevent examination of jurisdictional questions where the statute regulates a pre-existing common-law right. The Court relied on the principles in Secretary of State v. Mask & Co., Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Katikara Chintamani Dora v. Guatreddi Annamanaidu, Desika Charyulu v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Pyx Granite Co. Ltd. v. Ministry of Housing and Local Government, and Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission.
members.conclusion: A court should ordinarily direct a person aggrieved by demolition proceedings to the statutory appellate remedies. It may entertain a suit challenging a demolition order only if it is prima facie of the opinion that the order is a nullity because of jurisdictional error or is outside the statute; it may also examine whether vital procedural requirements were not followed.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenging_demolition_action and (action_outside_statutory_scope or jurisdictional_error_established or vital_procedure_not_followed)

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_demolition_action: A person brought a civil suit challenging an action or order concerning demolition of a building.
predicates.action_outside_statutory_scope: The challenged action or order concerned a building or matter to which the statutory scheme did not apply.
predicates.jurisdictional_error_established: The authority's challenged action or order was affected by an error in the exercise of its jurisdiction.
predicates.vital_procedure_not_followed: The authority did not follow a procedural requirement fundamental to the action it took.

members.legal_issue: A decision on the merits in a contested constitutional writ proceeding can bar a later regular suit between the same parties on the same matter under the general principles of res judicata.
material_facts: The claimant sought relief in a writ petition on the ground that the State’s conduct in allowing contractors to dispose of attached goods had discharged his liability as their surety.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the merits after hearing the parties and rejecting the contention that the claimant had been discharged from liability.
The claimant later brought a suit against the State seeking relief on the same ground, and the same question of discharge from liability was directly in issue.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is not exhaustive of the application of res judicata to decisions in earlier proceedings. Under the general principle, grounded in public policy and finality of decisions, a matter decided after full contest or a fair opportunity to prove the parties’ cases by a competent court binds the same parties in a later regular suit concerning the same matter, even if the earlier proceeding was not a suit and the earlier court could not try the later suit. The court relied on Daryao v. State of U.P., Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha, and earlier authorities including Hook v. Administrator-General of Bengal, Ramachandra Rao v. Ramachandra Rao, and Mst. Bhagwati v. Mst. Ram Kali.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s decision on the merits in the writ petition operated as res judicata in the subsequent suit, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: prior_writ_proceeding and later_regular_suit and same_parties and same_matter and prior_decision_on_merits and fair_opportunity_to_contest

predicates.prior_writ_proceeding: The earlier proceeding was a constitutional writ proceeding between the parties.
predicates.later_regular_suit: A party later brought a regular suit concerning a matter addressed in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later suit were the same parties as in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_matter: The same matter was directly in issue in both proceedings.
predicates.prior_decision_on_merits: The earlier court decided the matter on its merits.
predicates.fair_opportunity_to_contest: The parties had a full contest or a fair opportunity to present their cases in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The general doctrine of res judicata applies to petitions seeking constitutional writs and prevents relitigation of the same matter after a contested decision on its merits.
material_facts: A prior constitutional writ petition challenging the tax notices had been contested and decided on its merits.
The earlier decision had not been reversed or modified through an appropriate proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The general principle of res judicata applies to constitutional writ petitions. The Court relied on Pandit M. S. M. Sharma v. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha, which applied the principle to a petition under Article 32, and on Raj Lakshmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen for the principle underlying res judicata. Daryao v. The State of U.P. held that a contested merits dismissal of an Article 226 petition binds the parties unless reversed or modified through an appropriate constitutional remedy.
members.conclusion: Res judicata applies to petitions under Articles 32 and 226; a merits decision in a prior writ proceeding binds the parties on the same matter unless it is reversed or modified.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and prior_contested_merits_decision and same_matter and not prior_decision_reversed

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A party brings a petition seeking a constitutional writ.
predicates.prior_contested_merits_decision: A court previously decided the matter on its merits after the parties contested it.
predicates.same_matter: The later proceeding seeks to relitigate the matter decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_decision_reversed: The earlier decision was reversed or modified through an appropriate proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A final merits dismissal of a contested writ petition bars the same parties from bringing a later original petition to enforce fundamental rights on the same facts for the same or similar relief.
material_facts: The petitioners had previously sought writ relief from a High Court concerning the same underlying decision and on the same grounds as in their later Supreme Court petitions.

In the relevant prior proceedings, the High Court considered the matters on their merits and dismissed the petitions; in one instance, counsel did not press the petition after the High Court’s prior interpretation of the relevant law had defeated the petitioners’ contentions.
The later petitions sought the same or similar relief on the same facts.
members.legal_principle: The general principle of res judicata applies to original petitions under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution. Its foundation is public policy and the rule of law: final decisions of competent courts bind the parties, and a person should not be vexed twice over by the same litigation. The Court relied on the Duchess of Kingston’s case, Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha, and Raj Lakshmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen; it also referred to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure while explaining that the principle is not confined to its technical requirements. A High Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 may decide the same cause and grant relief of the same character as a petition under Article 32, so its merits decision may bind the parties in the later proceeding.
members.conclusion: The merits decisions bound the parties unless modified or reversed through an appropriate procedure, and the later petitions on the same facts and for the same or similar relief were barred by res judicata.

rule.if: later_original_fundamental_rights_petition and prior_high_court_writ_dismissed_on_merits and same_parties and same_facts_and_same_or_similar_relief

predicates.later_original_fundamental_rights_petiti: A party brings an original court proceeding seeking relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.prior_high_court_writ_dismissed_on_merit: The same party previously brought a contested writ proceeding in a High Court, and the court decided the merits before dismissing it.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later proceeding are the same as the parties bound by the earlier decision.
predicates.same_facts_and_same_or_similar_relief: The later proceeding rests on the same facts and seeks the same or similar relief as the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A final decision on an issue directly contested between the same States in an earlier constitutional proceeding operates as res judicata in their later suit.
material_facts: In an earlier proceeding between the same States, the safety of the dam at the proposed higher water level was directly contested.
The Court considered evidence and expert reports and permitted the water level to be raised to the level it found safe.
The earlier judgment became final after a review petition was dismissed.
The later suit raised the same safety issue between the same States.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation VIII, expresses the public-policy rule of res judicata. A decision in a proceeding under Article 32 or Article 226 can bind the parties in a later suit. The Court relied on Duchess of Kingston, Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Prashad Narayan Singh, Daryao v. State of U.P., Gulab Chand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Bombay, Union of India v. Nanak Singh, and State of Punjab v. Bua Das Kaushal. A final safety finding may be reconsidered by the Court in changed circumstances, but not displaced unilaterally by a legislature; N.D. Jayal v. Union of India was read consistently with that principle.
members.conclusion: The earlier judgment operated as res judicata on the safety issue, and the defendant could not re-agitate the issues already decided.

predicates.later_suit_between_same_parties: The parties to a later suit are the same as, or claim under the same titles as, the parties to an earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue_directly_decided_in_prior_pro: The issue in the later suit was directly and substantially contested and decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_decision_final: The earlier decision became final and was not set aside in an available review process.

members.legal_issue: A final decision by a competent court on an issue directly and substantially in dispute between parties or their privies bars that issue from being relitigated in a later suit.
material_facts: In an earlier suit, the first appellant and another plaintiff claimed ownership of educational institutions and asserted that they, rather than the respondent society, were their educational agency.

The earlier proceedings determined that the respondent society was the educational agency and owner of the relevant institutions, that the first appellant acted as its agent, and that the second appellant trust did not exist as a legally constituted trust.
The earlier decision was affirmed through the appellate proceedings and became final.
The later suit concerned the parties’ claims to the same institutions, properties, and educational-agency status.
The civil court had jurisdiction to decide the earlier dispute.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the rule that an issue directly and substantially decided by a competent court between the same parties or their privies cannot be tried again in subsequent litigation. The rule promotes finality and prevents repeated litigation. The Court relied on Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar, and Ishwardas v. State of Madhya Pradesh. A judgment of a court lacking inherent jurisdiction would be a nullity and would not create a res judicata bar, but the earlier court had jurisdiction here.
members.conclusion: The findings in the earlier proceedings were binding in the later suit under the doctrine of res judicata, and the appellants could not reopen the matters already determined.

rule.if: later_civil_suit and prior_final_judgment_by_competent_court and same_parties_or_privies and same_issue_directly_and_substantially_decided

predicates.later_civil_suit: A civil suit is brought after an earlier proceeding between the relevant parties or their privies.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_by_competent_court: A court with jurisdiction has issued a final judgment in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The parties to the later proceeding are the same as, or claim through, parties to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue_directly_and_substantially_de: The issue sought to be raised again was directly and substantially in dispute and was decided in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The principle of res judicata can bar a later suit when a competent quasi-judicial tribunal has finally decided the same issue between the same parties, even if the earlier proceeding was not a suit within the terms of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
material_facts: The landlord applied to the competent authority for permission to execute an eviction decree covering all the premises.
The authority permitted execution for some rooms but expressly refused it for the rooms later claimed in the suit, and the decision was confirmed on appeal.
The later suit involved the same parties and sought possession of the rooms for which permission had been refused.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not exhaustive; its underlying principle may extend beyond proceedings that fall within its precise terms. The principle applies where the issues in the later proceeding are identical to those previously decided, the proceedings are between the same parties, and the earlier decision was final and made by a competent quasi-judicial tribunal. It is founded on public interest, equity, justice, and good conscience, and prevents repeated litigation of a decided issue.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred by a principle analogous to res judicata because the same issue between the same parties had been finally decided by a competent quasi-judicial tribunal.

rule.if: later_civil_suit_after_quasi_judicial_decision and same_parties and same_issue and earlier_decision_final_and_competent

predicates.later_civil_suit_after_quasi_judicial_de: A party brings a civil suit after a quasi-judicial tribunal has decided a related proceeding.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later suit are the same parties as those to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.same_issue: The later suit raises an issue that was also determined in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_decision_final_and_competent: A competent quasi-judicial tribunal finally decided the issue in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action must be decided from the plaint’s averments, without relying on the defendant’s defence.
material_facts: The owner applied under Order VII Rule 11 on the ground that the plaint disclosed no cause of action against it.
The plaintiff relied on material outside the plaint in support of its claim, and the applications concerning rejection, amendment and interim relief were considered together.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court examines the plaint and not the defence when deciding whether it discloses a cause of action or appears barred by law. The power may be exercised at any stage before trial concludes: Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra; Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property; Mayar (H.K.) Ltd. v. Owners & Parties, Vessel M.V. Fortune Express. A meaningful, rather than merely formal, reading is required, and a meritless plaint that creates only an illusion of a cause of action should be rejected: T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal.
members.conclusion: The application had to be decided on the plaint averments alone; the defendant’s written statement and other material outside the plaint were irrelevant to that inquiry. The power may be exercised at any stage before the conclusion of the trial.

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A defendant asks the court to reject a plaint in a civil suit.
predicates.cause_of_action_ground: The application asserts that the plaint does not disclose a cause of action.
predicates.apparent_legal_bar: The application asserts that the plaint itself shows that the suit is barred by law.

members.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint must be decided from the plaint read as a whole together with documents relied on by the plaintiff, without relying on the defendant’s disputed merits, and the plaint must be rejected when those materials show no cause of action or a legal bar.
material_facts: The purchasers sought rejection of the plaint on the grounds that it disclosed no cause of action and was barred by limitation.
The sale deed was filed with and relied on in the plaint, and its recitals acknowledged receipt of the full consideration and transfer of possession.
The courts below relied on the plaint and the sale deed in rejecting the plaint.
members.legal_principle: Order VII Rules 11(a) and 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure require rejection where the plaint discloses no cause of action or appears from its statements to be barred by law. Under Order VII Rule 14(1), documents relied on by the plaintiff and filed with the plaint may be considered, and a document forming the basis of the plaint is treated as part of it. The court assumes the plaint’s factual allegations to be true and reads them as a whole, but may reject a sham or illusory claim. The defendant’s written statement and disputed merits are irrelevant at this stage. The remedy is mandatory when a ground is made out and may be used at any stage. The Court relied on Azhar Hussain v. Rajiv Gandhi, Liverpool & London S.P. & I Assn. Ltd. v. M.V. Sea Success I, Hardesh Ores (P.) Ltd. v. Hede & Co., Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal, and Madanuri Sri Ramachandra Murthy v. Syed Jalal.
members.conclusion: The courts below properly considered the plaint and its supporting documents and rejected it at the threshold; the Supreme Court affirmed that result.

predicates.plaint_shows_legal_bar: The plaint and its supporting documents show that a law bars the suit.

members.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint must be decided by reading the plaint as a whole and assessing its pleaded cause of action, rather than by isolating parts of the pleading or relying on the defendant’s version.
material_facts: The defendants sought rejection of the plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action and because the suit was said to be barred by law.
The plaint alleged a continuing tenancy, forcible eviction, and interference with possession and business.
The lower courts rejected the plaint after considering the reliefs and jurisdictional objections.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court considers the plaint’s averments, not the written statement, and reads the plaint meaningfully and as a whole. A real cause of action must be distinguished from an illusory one created by clever drafting. Order VI Rule 2 requires material facts, not evidence; Order VI Rule 16 provides for striking out improper matter, while Order VII Rule 11 does not permit rejection of only part of a plaint. The Court relied on Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill, Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, and Samant N. Balkrishna v. George Fernandez.
members.conclusion: The lower courts were not justified in rejecting the plaint on the basis of the approach they adopted; the plaint had to be considered as a whole, and the suit could not be rejected merely because some reliefs might not be available in the civil court.

predicates.plaint_rejection_proceeding: A party asks the court to reject a plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action or because the suit appears barred by law.
predicates.plaint_read_as_a_whole: The court considers the entire plaint together rather than isolating a sentence, paragraph, or relief.
predicates.pleaded_facts_are_assessed_without_relyi: The court assesses the plaint’s allegations without using the defendant’s written statement to decide the application.

members.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action or because the suit is barred by law must be decided from the plaint’s allegations, without awaiting the defendant’s written statement.
material_facts: A defendant applied to have the plaint rejected, asserting that it disclosed no cause of action and that the suit was barred by law.
The trial court directed the defendant to file a written statement without first deciding the rejection application.
The High Court upheld that direction and instructed the trial court to frame and decide preliminary issues.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the relevant material for deciding whether a plaint discloses a cause of action or appears barred by law is the plaint’s averments; the defendant’s written statement is wholly irrelevant at that stage. The court may exercise this power at any stage before conclusion of the trial. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The rejection application had to be decided on the plaint’s allegations, and the defendant’s written statement was irrelevant to that decision. Requiring the written statement without deciding the application was a procedural irregularity and a failure to exercise jurisdiction. The challenged order was set aside, and the cases were remitted for the trial court to decide the application after hearing the parties.

predicates.application_alleges_no_cause_or_legal_ba: The application asserts that the plaint discloses no cause of action or that the suit is barred by law.

members.legal_issue: An application seeking rejection of a plaint cannot be decided by relying on evidence recorded outside the plaint.
material_facts: During the plaintiff’s evidence, the defendant applied for rejection of the plaint based on the plaintiff’s cross-examination answer about the property’s market value.
The Trial Court considered the plaint and rejected the application, observing that the evidence led by the parties could not be considered for that application.
The High Court relied on the cross-examination answer and ordered the plaint returned; the Supreme Court set that order aside and restored the Trial Court’s order.
members.legal_principle: For an application under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the plaint is to be considered; the defendant’s pleadings and evidence led by the parties are not to be considered. The Court applied this principle in approving the Trial Court’s rejection of the application based on material elicited in cross-examination.
members.conclusion: The Trial Court rightly rejected the application, and its order was restored.

members.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint must be decided from the plaint’s averments, without relying on pleas or materials supplied by the defendant.
material_facts: The defendant applied to reject the plaint, relying in part on grounds drawn from the defence and materials outside the plaint.
The trial court allowed the application, but the appellate court set that order aside and remitted the case for consideration of all issues.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the court examines the averments in the plaint and does not rely on the defendant’s written statement. The Court relied on C. Natrajan v. Ashim Bai, (2007) 14 SCC 183; Ram Prakash Gupta v. Rajiv Kumar Gupta, (2007) 10 SCC 59; Hardesh Ores (P) Ltd. v. Hede and Company, (2007) 5 SCC 614; Mayar (H.K.) Ltd. v. Owners & Parties, Vessel M.V. Fortune Express, (2006) 3 SCC 100; Sopan Sukhdeo Sable v. Assistant Charity Commissioner, (2004) 3 SCC 137; Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, (2003) 1 SCC 557; and The Church of Christ Charitable Trust & Educational Charitable Society v. M/s Ponniamman Educational Trust, 2012 (6) JT 149.
members.conclusion: The plaint’s averments alone could be examined on the application; the defendant’s written-statement pleas were irrelevant. The High Court was justified in affirming the remittal for consideration of all issues.

members.legal_issue: The statutory power to restrict or control exports includes the power to channel export trade through selected agencies and to limit which persons may participate.
material_facts: The governing statute authorized the government to prohibit, restrict, or otherwise control exports of specified goods.
An order made under that statute required licences for exporting specified goods and allowed licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
The government restricted manganese ore exports through quotas and selected groups of exporters, including a state trading corporation.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, authorizes control of exports that may include restrictions on the persons permitted to export and channeling trade through selected agencies. Clause 6(h) of the Export Control Order, 1958, was within that authority. The Court relied on Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India for the established validity of the canalising power. An agency may be “special” because it is selected to advance the purpose of channeling, and need not necessarily have prior expertise in that trade.
members.conclusion: The statutory power encompassed channeling exports through selected agencies and classifying who could participate, so the relevant provision was within the authority conferred by the statute.

predicates.export_control_case: The case challenges a restriction or control imposed on the export of goods.
predicates.government_has_power_to_control_exports: The governing law authorizes the government to prohibit, restrict, or control exports.
predicates.trade_is_channelled_through_selected_age: The government directs exports of a commodity through agencies it has selected.

members.legal_issue: The exclusion of new entrants from manganese ore exports and the preference given to a state trading corporation did not, in the circumstances, impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on business.
material_facts: The internal market for manganese ore was negligible, and the ore was principally produced for export.
The export policy initially allocated quotas to established exporters and mineowners with export performance in specified years, as well as to the state trading corporation.
The appellant had no export performance in the specified years and was excluded from direct export participation.
The government selected the state trading corporation to help secure regular supplies of uniform quality, maintain continuity in foreign trade, and increase export earnings.
The appellant did not allege that established exporters or mineowners who received quotas had been improperly included in the eligible groups.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) guarantees the right to carry on business, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under the first part of Article 19(6). The state-trade provision in Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself authorize a monopoly by administrative action; however, a restriction may still be valid under the general reasonable-restrictions provision. Where export control may lawfully take the form of channeling, excluding some groups is an inherent consequence. The government may classify participants according to the nature of the commodity and the circumstances of its export trade. The Court considered the need for regular supplies of uniform quality and continuity in trade, and found a rational basis for the selection made.
members.conclusion: The majority held that the exclusion of newcomers and the selection of the state trading corporation were lawful restrictions in the circumstances and did not violate an enforceable right of the appellant.

members.legal_issue: The statutory power to control exports includes the power to regulate who may participate and to channel exports through selected agencies.
material_facts: A mine owner sought a licence to export manganese ore under a system that restricted exports through quotas and selected categories of exporters.
The export-control order allowed the licensing authority to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
The statutory scheme empowered the government to prohibit, restrict or otherwise control exports.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947, control of exports may extend to persons participating in export trade, and canalisation is one permissible form of that control. The Court relied on Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India, which had upheld the validity of the canalisation provision in the Export Control Order.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the statutory power covered canalisation, including restrictions on the persons permitted to export, and that the provision authorising canalisation was within the government’s rule-making power.

predicates.export_control_challenge: A person challenges the legal authority for restrictions imposed on the export of goods.
predicates.exports_are_restricted: The government limits the quantity or circumstances in which goods may be exported.
predicates.exports_are_channelled_through_selected_: The government directs that exports may be conducted through selected agencies or channels.

members.legal_issue: Canalising exports through a state trading agency and excluding new entrants from direct export may be a reasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade when it serves the public interest in reliable, quality-controlled exports and foreign-exchange earnings.
material_facts: There was little domestic demand for the ore, and it was produced mainly for export.

New mine owners without export performance during the selected earlier years were excluded from direct export quotas and could sell their ore only to established exporters or the state trading corporation.
Foreign buyers sought regular supplies of ore of uniform quality, and there had been complaints about supplies not matching samples.
The government sought to maximise foreign-exchange earnings and considered the state trading corporation better placed to advance those objectives.
The appellant did not allege that the established shippers and mine owners included in the export scheme had been improperly selected.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on trade, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under the first part of Article 19(6). Canalisation necessarily entails excluding some groups; the government may select an agency more likely to achieve the purpose of canalisation. The majority concluded that a monopoly or near-monopoly created by these restrictions could be sustained as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6), without relying on Article 19(6)(ii). Subba Rao J. considered that a state monopoly could not be justified by the specific exception in Article 19(6)(ii) without a law, but assessed the restrictions under the general reasonable-restriction test. He referred to Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh in discussing the constitutional amendment and the statutory basis for state monopolies.
members.conclusion: The majority held that the canalisation scheme, including the preference for the state trading corporation and the consequent exclusion of new entrants, was a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public and did not violate the right to carry on trade. Subba Rao J. dissented, concluding that the scheme’s effects on excluded mine owners were unreasonable.
