members.legal_issue: The power to control exports includes the power to channel export trade through selected agencies or channels.
material_facts: The challenge concerned export controls imposed under an order made pursuant to legislation empowering the government to prohibit, restrict, or otherwise control exports.
The order permitted licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947 conferred broad power to prohibit, restrict, or control exports. Control over export quantities may necessarily extend to persons participating in the trade, including their classification and the conditions on which they may export; canalisation is one method of exercising that control. The Court relied on Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India, which had upheld the constitutional validity of the canalisation provision.
members.conclusion: The export-control legislation authorised canalisation, and the relevant provision of the order was within the delegated rule-making power.

predicates.export_control_case: The proceeding challenges a measure governing the export of goods.
predicates.government_controls_export_trade: The government regulates whether, how much, or through whom goods may be exported.
predicates.channeling_selects_export_participants: The measure directs exports through selected participants or channels, thereby excluding other participants.

members.legal_issue: Selecting a public trading agency as the principal export channel and excluding new entrants was not shown to be an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on business in the circumstances of the export trade.
material_facts: The commodity had a very limited domestic market, and most production was intended for export.
The government sought to improve foreign-exchange earnings and maintain regular supplies of consistent quality to foreign buyers.
The government selected a public trading corporation as a principal export agency and granted it export quotas on an ad hoc basis.
Mine-owners without export performance during the specified earlier years were excluded from direct participation and had to sell to authorised exporters or the public corporation.
The appellant did not establish that the established exporters were improperly included or that the selected corporation was an unsuitable channel for the stated export objectives.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) guarantees the right to carry on business, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public under the first part of Article 19(6). Canalisation necessarily excludes some groups, and a person does not establish an unlawful restriction merely by showing that they were excluded. The government may consider the nature of the commodity and trade, foreign-market requirements, continuity and quality of supply, and the suitability of selected agencies. The Court distinguished the State-trade provision in Article 19(6)(ii): the challenged arrangement was sustained as a reasonable restriction under the general part of Article 19(6), rather than as a statutory grant of a State monopoly.
members.conclusion: The selection of the public trading corporation and the resulting exclusion of new entrants were legally permissible in the circumstances; no legally enforceable right of the appellant was violated.

members.legal_issue: A separation from a joint Hindu family by unilateral intention requires a clear and unequivocal communication of that intention to the affected co-sharers.
material_facts: A trust deed contained a declaration of an intention to separate if the alleged adoption were later declared valid.
There was no evidence that the intention to separate was communicated to the appellant when the trust was created.
members.legal_principle: A separation is effected by a clear and unequivocal intimation of the member’s desire to sever to the co-sharers; the intention must be manifested to the knowledge of the persons affected, since an uncommunicated intention has no effect. The Court relied on Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Bal Krishan v. Ram Krishan, A. Raghavamma v. Chenchamma, Puttrangamma v. M.S. Ranganna, and Kalyani v. Narayanan.
members.conclusion: The declaration in the trust deed did not effect a separation because the intention to separate was not communicated to the co-sharer.

predicates.joint_family_separation_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim that a member separated from a joint Hindu family.
predicates.unilateral_intention_to_separate: A member expressed a clear and unequivocal intention to separate from the family.
predicates.intention_communicated_to_affected_co_sh: The member communicated the intention to separate to the co-sharer affected by it.

members.legal_issue: A member of a joint Hindu family effects separation by clearly communicating an unequivocal intention to separate to the co-sharer affected; an uncommunicated declaration does not effect separation.
material_facts: A trust deed contained a declaration of an intention to separate if the adoption were held valid.
The declaration was conditional and was not communicated to the co-sharer whose interest would be affected.
There was no evidence that the co-sharer otherwise learned of the intention to separate.
members.legal_principle: Separation from a joint Hindu family requires a clear and unequivocal intimation of the member’s desire to separate to the co-sharers; a mere uncommunicated declaration is only an unexpressed intention. The Court relied on Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Bal Krishan v. Ram Krishan, A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Puttrangamma v. M.S. Ranganna, and Kalyani v. Narayanan.
members.conclusion: The declaration in the trust deed did not effect a partition or separation.

predicates.joint_family_separation_dispute: The dispute concerned whether a member had separated from a joint Hindu family.
predicates.unequivocal_intention_declared: A member made a clear and unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate.
predicates.intention_communicated_to_affected_co_sh: The member communicated the intention to separate to the co-sharer whose interest was affected.

members.legal_issue: A coparcener’s clear communication of an intention to separate can sever Mitakshara joint-family status even when a subsequent written allotment is described as being for maintenance.
material_facts: The brothers belonged to an undivided Mitakshara joint family, and the family property was not subject to a proved custom of impartibility or primogeniture.

The deed recited that one brother had recently desired to live separately after division and permanently allotted identified lands to him and his male descendants, without reserving a right of reversion.
The brother held and enjoyed the allotted lands exclusively for decades, with revenue records in his name.
After abolition of the watan system, he alone sought regrant of the allotted lands; the other family members knew of this and did not object, while they sought regrant of other lands without him.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, partition includes severance of joint status and does not require an immediate division of property by metes and bounds. A coparcener can cause severance by clearly communicating an intention to separate and enjoy his share separately; the communication and its effect may be inferred from the document, surrounding circumstances, and subsequent conduct. Once severance occurs, it cannot be undone by mere withdrawal of the communication, absent reunion. The Court relied on Appavier v. Rama Subha Aiyan, Giria Bai v. Sadashiv, Bhagwan Dayal v. Mst. Reoti Devi, Puttorangamma v. Ranganna, and the principles stated in Mulla’s and Mayne’s Hindu Law.
members.conclusion: The brothers’ joint-family status had been severed before the deed was executed, and the lands allotted by the deed were the separate property of the brother who received them.

members.legal_issue: An unequivocal unilateral declaration of an intention to separate severs a member’s status in a Mitakshara joint Hindu family when the intention is made known to the other affected members.
material_facts: The family had continued as a joint Hindu family, and the plaintiff was its karta.
The plaintiff issued notices stating unequivocally that he intended to separate from the family.
Although the notices were intercepted before delivery, the evidence established that the other members had knowledge of their contents and of the plaintiff’s intention.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, a coparcener’s unequivocal declaration of an intention to hold his share separately effects severance of status once that intention is made known to the members from whom he seeks to separate. Communication need not take the form of formal dispatch or receipt; it must reach the affected members by a process appropriate to the circumstances. The Court relied on Suraj Narain v. Iqbal Narain, Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Syed Kasam v. Jorawar Singh, and Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff’s status in the joint family was severed because his unequivocal intention to separate had been made known to the other members; formal dispatch to or receipt by them was not essential.

predicates.joint_family_severance_dispute: The case concerns whether a member of a joint Hindu family became separate in status.
predicates.unequivocal_intention_to_separate: A family member clearly and unambiguously declared an intention to separate and hold a share separately.
predicates.intention_made_known_to_affected_members: The declared intention reached the family members affected by it through a process appropriate to the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A member of a joint Hindu family effects severance in status through a definite and unequivocal intention to separate that is brought to the knowledge of the affected family members.
material_facts: A family member executed a will that the appellants relied on as a declaration of an intention to separate.

There were only two relevant members of the joint family for the issue, and the appellants did not establish that the surviving member or his guardian knew the contents of the will before the testator died.
The guardian’s presence inside the house when the will was executed did not establish knowledge of its contents.
members.legal_principle: A member of a joint Hindu family may unilaterally separate by a definite and unequivocal declaration of an intention to hold a share separately, but the declaration must be communicated to the affected members. The Court relied on Hindu law texts, including the Mitakshara, Saraswati Vilasa, Viramitrodaya, and Vyavahara Mayukha, and on Suraj Narain v. Iqbal Narain, Girija Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Kawal Nain v. Budh Singh, Ramalinga Annavi v. Narayana Annavi, Sayed Kasam v. Jorawar Singh, Soundararayan v. Arunachalam Chetty, Bal Krishna v. Ram Krishna, Babu Ramasaray Prasad Choudhary v. Radhika Devi, Kamepalli Avilamma v. Mannem Venkataswamy, and Adujallath Kathusumma v. Adujalath Beechu. The Court rejected the contrary approach in Narayana Rao v. Purushothama Rao and did not accept it insofar as Indira v. Sivaprasada Rao followed that approach.
members.conclusion: An uncommunicated declaration does not effect severance in status; the declaration must reach the person or persons affected by an appropriate process.

predicates.joint_family_member_makes_a_definite_une: A member of a joint family clearly and unequivocally expresses an intention to separate and hold a share separately.
predicates.affected_member_does_not_learn_of_it_bef: The family member affected by the declaration does not learn of it before the person making it dies.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument effects a severance in a joint family only when it clearly and unequivocally expresses an intention to separate.
material_facts: The properties were found to be joint family properties of the deceased and his brother.
The will asserted that there was no ancestral property, referred to property as joint, and directed that the remaining property be kept joint until the deceased’s son attained majority.
The will did not expressly state an intention to end the coparcenary.
members.legal_principle: Under A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, a member of a joint Hindu family may bring about separation in status by a definite and unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate, even in a will; the expression of that intention must be brought home to the persons affected. The terms of this will did not establish such an intention.
members.conclusion: The will did not effect a severance in the status of the joint family.

members.legal_issue: Whether a stipulated completion period is essential to a construction contract when the contract also provides for extensions of time and compensation for delay.
material_facts: The contract required the construction work to be completed within twelve months and expressly described time as essential.
The contract allowed the engineer to extend the completion period on reasonable grounds and provided for compensation for each day the work remained unfinished after the stipulated date.
The parties allowed some work to continue after the stipulated period had expired.
members.legal_principle: Whether time is of the essence depends on the parties’ intention gathered from the contract as a whole. Even an express stipulation that time is essential may be displaced by other provisions, including provisions for extensions or compensation for delay. The Court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 4, para. 1179, and the principles based on Lamprell v. Billericay Union, Webb v. Hughes, and Charles Rickards Ltd. v. Oppenheim; it cited no statutory provision.
members.conclusion: The twelve-month period was not intended to be of the essence of the contract; the extension and delay-compensation provisions, considered with the other terms, displaced that inference.

members.legal_issue: Whether an employer may rescind a construction contract for delay without first fixing a further reasonable completion period as essential.
material_facts: The contract provided for extensions of time and compensation for delay, and the contractor was allowed to continue work after the original completion period expired.
The contractor requested an extension before the original period expired.
The employer rescinded the contract without fixing a further period for completion and making that period essential.
members.legal_principle: Where time was not originally of the essence, or the stipulated time has ceased to apply by waiver, the employer must fix a reasonable time for completion and make time essential before rescinding for failure to complete within that further period. The Court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 4, para. 1179. It held that the question was whether rescission was wrongful and illegal, not whether it was mala fide or merely unreasonable.
members.conclusion: The rescission was wrongful and illegal because the employer did not first set a further reasonable completion period and make time essential for that period.

members.legal_issue: Whether an employer may forfeit a contractor’s security deposit after wrongfully rescinding the construction contract.
material_facts: The employer rescinded the contract without first fixing a further period for completion and making time essential for that period.
The employer forfeited the contractor’s security deposit when it rescinded the contract.
The contractor was entitled to a refund of the security deposit following the wrongful rescission.
members.legal_principle: Because the employer’s rescission was wrongful and constituted a breach of contract, it could not forfeit the security deposit on the basis that the contractor had breached the contract. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this consequence.
members.conclusion: The employer was not entitled to forfeit the security deposit, which had to be refunded to the contractor.

members.legal_issue: A stipulated completion period is not necessarily fundamental where the contract’s other terms provide for extensions or compensation for delay.
material_facts: The construction contract expressly described time as essential and set a completion period.
The contract also allowed the engineer to extend the completion period on reasonable grounds and provided for compensation while work remained unfinished after the stipulated date.
The contractor was permitted to continue working after the stipulated completion period.
members.legal_principle: Whether time is of the essence depends on the parties’ intention ascertained by construing the contract as a whole. An express time-essential term may be displaced by other provisions, including provisions for extensions or delay compensation. The Court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England and the principles reflected in Lamprell v. Billericay Union, Webb v. Hughes, and Charles Rickards Ltd. v. Oppenheim; it applied Clauses 2 and 6 of the contract.
members.conclusion: The completion period was not intended to be of the essence of the contract; alternatively, the stipulated time had been waived.

members.legal_issue: An employer cannot rescind a contract for delay without first fixing a reasonable further period for completion when the original deadline is not fundamental or has ceased to apply.
material_facts: The contractor sought extensions before the stipulated completion period expired, and departmental officers recommended extensions.
The employer allowed some work to continue after the stipulated period.
The employer rescinded the contract without setting a further period for completion and making time essential for that period.
members.legal_principle: Where time has not been made of the essence, or the fixed time has ceased to apply by waiver, the employer must give notice fixing a reasonable time for completion and may rescind for non-completion within that time. The Court relied on the rule stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England and applied the contract’s extension and delay provisions.
members.conclusion: The rescission was wrongful and illegal because the employer did not fix a reasonable further period for completion and make time essential before rescinding.

members.legal_issue: An employer that wrongfully rescinds a construction contract cannot forfeit the contractor’s security, and the contractor may recover the established unpaid amount for completed work and damages.
material_facts: The contractor had provided a security deposit, which the employer forfeited when it rescinded the contract.
The contractor had performed work for which part of the bill remained unpaid.
The trial court found that the contractor was entitled to nominal damages, and the Supreme Court restored that decree after finding the rescission wrongful.
members.legal_principle: Because the employer’s rescission was wrongful, the employer could not forfeit the security deposit on the basis of the contractor’s alleged breach. The Court restored the trial court’s award for return of the deposit, the unpaid balance for work performed, and nominal damages.
members.conclusion: The employer was not entitled to forfeit the security deposit; the contractor was entitled to its return, the established balance due for work performed, and nominal damages.

members.legal_issue: A court ordinarily gives deference to a High Court’s settled interpretation of a local statute, particularly when people have arranged their affairs in reliance on that interpretation.
material_facts: The appeals challenged High Court judgments interpreting a local building-tax statute.
The relevant High Court interpretations had stood for a period of time, and the court noted that people arrange their affairs based on the existing legal position.
members.legal_principle: The court cited State of Gujarat v. Zinabhai Ranchhodji Darji (1972) 1 SCC 233, Bishamber Dass Kohli v. Satya Bhalla (1993) 1 SCC 566, Duroflex Coir Industries Ltd. v. CST, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 568, State of Karnataka v. G. Seenappa, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 648, and Bonam Satyavathi v. Addala Raghavulu, 1994 Supp (2) SCC 556, for the ordinary deference due to a High Court’s interpretation of a local statute, especially where that interpretation has stood the test of time.
members.conclusion: The court considered deference to the High Court’s interpretation an additional reason to sustain the judgments under review.

predicates.appeal_challenges_high_court_interpretat: A party appeals against a High Court’s interpretation of a local statute.
predicates.interpretation_has_stood_over_time: The High Court’s interpretation has remained established over time.

members.legal_issue: A long-standing administrative construction of an unclear statutory provision may support leaving that construction undisturbed.
material_facts: The Court assumed, in the alternative, that the statutory language could be read as placing primary tax liability on the tenant who constructed the building.
The municipal authorities had for a long period treated the land and tenant-built structure as a single unit and charged the tax to the landowner in such cases.
The appeal challenged the construction previously adopted by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Where an enactment is obscure, the Court may consider its contemporary construction as evidenced by long-standing official usage and conduct, expressed by the maxim optima legum interpres est consuetudo. The Court relied on Ohlson’s case, [1891] 1 Q.B. 485, 489, and Clyde Navigation Trustees v. Laird, 8 A.C. 658, 670, while recognizing that practice does not bind a court to perpetuate a mistaken interpretation.
members.conclusion: Even on the assumption that the statutory meaning was obscure, the Court would not interfere with the established construction supported by the authorities’ long-standing practice.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_statutory_interpretation and statutory_meaning_unclear and longstanding_municipal_practice and existing_interpretation_matches_practice

predicates.appeal_challenging_statutory_interpretat: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an interpretation of a statutory provision.
predicates.statutory_meaning_unclear: The statutory language is capable of more than one reasonable interpretation.
predicates.longstanding_municipal_practice: The relevant municipal authorities followed the same construction through their usage and conduct for a long period.
predicates.existing_interpretation_matches_practice: The interpretation under challenge accords with the authorities’ long-standing practice.

members.legal_issue: A long-standing judicial interpretation of an ambiguous statute should not be displaced without exceptional reason when people have relied on it and it is not clearly erroneous.
material_facts: Several courts had adopted the interpretation that the registration requirement regulated the business of money-lending and did not invalidate isolated transactions.
The interpretation had prevailed for a considerable period, during which people had arranged property dealings and contracts in reliance on it.
The challenged interpretation was not patently erroneous, the breach of the registration requirement was a penal offence, and legislative amendments had not changed the relevant requirement.
members.legal_principle: Where statutory language is ambiguous and a higher court’s interpretation has stood for a considerable period, courts ordinarily should not adopt a materially different interpretation that would unsettle transactions made in reliance on the established view, absent exceptional reason. The Court also regarded the penal consequence of contravention and the legislature’s decision not to amend the relevant provision, despite amending other provisions, as reasons for caution. It relied on the established interpretations in Patiram v. Baliram, Janki Bai v. Ratan Melu and Hajarimal v. Hari Narayan.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to overturn the established interpretation and applied it to the dispute.

predicates.appeal_seeks_to_overturn_settled_interpr: A party in an appeal asks the court to replace a judicial interpretation that has been applied over a considerable period.
predicates.statutory_meaning_is_ambiguous: The statutory language is capable of more than one reasonable interpretation.
predicates.settled_interpretation_relied_on_in_tran: People have arranged transactions in reliance on the interpretation adopted by the courts.
predicates.interpretation_not_clearly_erroneous: The established interpretation is not so clearly and patently erroneous that it must be rejected.

members.legal_issue: A court should not reopen a long-settled rule of Hindu law by reconsidering ancient texts where legal transactions and property titles have long relied on that rule.
material_facts: The sons asked the Court to examine ancient Hindu law texts rather than follow the established judicial rule requiring proof of the alienee's knowledge.
The rule in Suraj Bunsi Koer had been followed without doubt or dissent for more than three quarters of a century.
Transactions involving family immovable property and titles in favour of alienees had proceeded on the understanding that the established rule represented the law.
The Court considered it difficult and inappropriate to determine the texts' effect in isolation from the judicially developed principles and customary practices.
members.legal_principle: The principle of stare decisis supports preserving an established legal rule where it has governed transactions and property titles over a long period. The Court relied on the settled principles in Suraj Bunsi Koer v. Sheo Proshad Singh (1879) and Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923), and held that any anomalies in the law were for the legislature to address.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to reconsider the rule solely by reference to ancient texts and applied the settled judicial position, leaving correction of any anomalies to the legislature.

predicates.court_is_asked_to_reconsider_settled_rul: A party asks a court to replace an established legal rule by reconsidering its underlying sources.
predicates.rule_has_been_followed_for_long_period: Courts have followed the rule for a lengthy period without doubt or dissent.
predicates.property_transactions_rely_on_rule: Property transactions and titles have proceeded on the understanding that the rule governs them.

members.legal_issue: A long-standing and uniform interpretation affecting property rights and transactions should not be disturbed without a compelling public-interest reason, even if its reasoning is open to question.
material_facts: The main lease covered agricultural land and a homestead, and the homestead was later separately leased to the appellants.
For about 55 years, courts had consistently treated subleases of portions of an agricultural lease as agricultural leases, even when the subleased portion was only a homestead.
The first appellate court followed that established interpretation, but a Full Bench departed from it and allowed the claim for possession.
The relevant tenancy legislation had been amended several times without the legislature changing the rule reflected in the earlier decisions.
The Court considered the earlier decisions’ reasoning open to question but found no compelling reason to disturb the established interpretation, which affected property rights and transactions.
members.legal_principle: Questions of law settled by a long course of consistent decisions should not ordinarily be disturbed, particularly where the interpretation affects property rights and titles founded on it, unless public interest requires departure. The Court relied on the line of decisions beginning with Babu Ram Roy v. Mahendra Nath Sarnanta and including Abdul Karim Patwari v. Abdul Rahaman, Krishna Kanta Ghosh v. Jadu Kasya, Kadrutulla v. Upendra Kumar Chowdhury, Arun Kumar Sinha v. Durga Charan Basu, Mian Ahir v. Paramhans Pathak, and Shrikishun Lal v. Harihar Sah. It distinguished Lallu Singh v. Gur Narain and Tricomdas Cooverji Bhoja v. Sri Gopinath Jiu Thakur, explaining with reference to Arthur John Pate v. W.C. Pate that the principle permitting correction of a settled interpretation contrary to clear statutory language does not apply where titles and transactions have been founded on that interpretation. The established rule concerned the application of the Bihar Tenancy Act, including its relationship to section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act, to subleases of parts of an agricultural lease.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in departing from the settled interpretation. The appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_departure and property_rights_dispute and long_uniform_interpretation and transactions_founded_on_interpretation and legislature_left_rule_unchanged and not compelling_public_interest_need

predicates.appeal_from_departure: An appellate proceeding challenges a decision that departed from an established interpretation.
predicates.property_rights_dispute: The dispute concerns rights in property.
predicates.long_uniform_interpretation: Courts have consistently applied the same interpretation over a long period.

predicates.legislature_left_rule_unchanged: The legislature amended the relevant law without changing the rule reflected in the established interpretation.

members.legal_issue: A long-standing High Court interpretation of a local statute should normally be followed by a superior court when disturbing it would unsettle settled law and transactions.
material_facts: Two Full Bench decisions of the High Court had interpreted the relevant provisions of the local tenancy statute and had established the principles governing mortgages of occupancy holdings and recovery of possession.
The parties did not challenge the correctness of those established principles, and transactions might have been entered into in reliance on them.
members.legal_principle: In interpreting a local statute, a superior court should normally adhere to a High Court interpretation followed over a number of years where a different view would create uncertainty or unsettle transactions. The Court relied on the Full Bench decisions in Ghassu v. Babu Ram and Mahabal Singh v. Ram Rai, and referred to Brownsea Haven Properties v. Poole Corporation.
members.conclusion: The Court followed the Full Bench decisions, holding that the doctrine of stare decisis should be applied and that the established interpretation should not be disturbed.

members.legal_issue: A covenant recognizing property as a ruler’s private property did not guarantee that the property could never be acquired, and a dispute arising from the covenant was not justiciable.
material_facts: A merger covenant recognized the properties as the ruler’s private property rather than State property.
The acquisition law treated the properties as private property and sought to acquire them on that basis.
The petitioners relied on the constitutional assurance concerning rulers’ personal rights, privileges and dignities.
The dispute concerned the effect of the covenant.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied articles 362 and 363 of the Constitution. Article 362 did not guarantee the perpetual existence of property recognized as private property, and article 363 barred judicial determination of disputes arising from the covenant. Das J. also stated that the assurance related to personal rights, privileges and dignities qua ruler and did not bar acquisition of private property.
members.conclusion: The covenant did not prevent acquisition of the private property, and the covenant-based dispute was not justiciable.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenged a law that acquires property.
predicates.merger_covenant_recognizes_private_owner: A merger covenant recognizes the property as the ruler’s private property rather than State property.
predicates.acquisition_treats_property_as_private: The acquisition proceeds on the basis that the property is privately owned.
predicates.dispute_depends_on_covenant: The asserted bar to acquisition depends on interpreting or enforcing the merger covenant.

members.legal_issue: Acquiring property recognized as a former ruler’s private property under a merger covenant does not, without more, breach the ruler’s constitutional guarantees when the property is acquired in the same capacity as other private property.
material_facts: The properties had been recognized as the former rulers’ private property under merger arrangements.
The acquisition laws acquired those properties as private property and provided for compensation on that basis.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated acquisition of recognized private property in the same manner as other privately owned property as distinct from a breach of a guarantee preserving the ruler’s personal rights. It also noted the limits on judicial intervention in disputes concerning merger covenants and related agreements.
members.conclusion: The acquisition did not contravene the asserted guarantee concerning the rulers’ personal rights or assurances under the merger arrangements.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.property_recognized_as_former_ruler_priv: The property had been recognized as the private property of a former ruler under a merger arrangement.
predicates.acquired_in_same_capacity_as_other_priva: The State acquired the property in its capacity as private property and on the same basis as other privately owned property.

members.legal_issue: A covenant recognizing a ruler’s property as private property does not prevent the State from acquiring that property under a law of general application.
material_facts: The covenant of merger recognized certain properties as the ruler’s private properties rather than State properties.
The challenged law treated the properties as private property and sought to acquire them along with other proprietary interests.
The petitioners relied on the constitutional assurance concerning rulers’ personal rights, privileges and dignities.
members.legal_principle: Article 362 requires due regard to relevant guarantees or assurances concerning a ruler’s personal rights, privileges and dignities; it does not prevent acquisition of property recognized as private or guarantee that property against acquisition. The Court also referred to article 363 as barring judicial determination of disputes arising out of the covenant.
members.conclusion: Article 362 did not prohibit acquisition of the recognized private properties or guarantee their perpetual existence.

predicates.challenge_based_on_merger_covenant: A party challenges acquisition by relying on a covenant made in connection with a merger.
predicates.covenant_recognizes_private_property: The covenant recognizes the property as the ruler’s private property rather than State property.
predicates.state_law_acquires_property_as_private: The State law acquires the property on the basis that it is private property.

members.legal_issue: Acquiring a former ruler’s property as that ruler’s recognized private property, on the same basis as other owners’ property, does not contravene an assurance of private-property recognition in a merger covenant.
material_facts: The merger arrangements recognized the relevant properties as the former rulers’ private property.
The acquisition laws sought to acquire the properties in their capacity as private property and provided compensation on the same basis as for other owners.
The challengers alleged that the acquisition violated guarantees or assurances associated with the merger arrangements.
members.legal_principle: An acquisition of property in the capacity in which it was recognized under the merger arrangement does not breach an assurance merely because the property is later acquired under a general law. The court also noted the asserted factual allegation concerning the relationship between a ruler’s privy purse and property lacked supporting material.
members.conclusion: The acquisition did not contravene the asserted guarantee or assurance.

predicates.owner_receives_same_compensation_basis_a: The owner’s entitlement is treated on the same compensation basis as that of other property owners.

members.legal_issue: A private covenant guaranteeing ownership and enjoyment of property does not prevent a competent legislature from acquiring that property under a later law, and a dispute arising from the covenant may fall outside the Court's jurisdiction.
material_facts: A covenant identified certain property as the ruler's private property and guaranteed its ownership, use, and enjoyment.
The acquisition law treated the property as private property and provided compensation for its acquisition.
The Government denied that the privy purse had been fixed in reliance on income from the property, and no material was produced to displace that denial.
The Government of India signed the covenant as a guarantor and concurring party.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that article 362 did not invalidate the acquisition in these circumstances: the property was treated as private property and acquired on that basis, while article 362 imposed no enforceable legal obligation on the legislature. It further held that article 363 applied to a dispute arising out of the covenant because the Government of India was a party to it. The Court relied on its earlier treatment of a similar issue in the Madhya Pradesh petitions.
members.conclusion: The Act did not breach the guarantee; the claim based on the alleged privy-purse arrangement was unsupported, and article 363 barred the Court from deciding the covenant dispute.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_of_covenant_gua: A party challenges acquisition of property said to be protected by a covenant with a ruler.
predicates.property_treated_as_private_and_compensa: The acquisition law recognizes the property as private property and provides compensation for its acquisition.
predicates.government_was_party_to_covenant: The government was a party to or guarantor of the covenant relied upon.

members.legal_issue: A claim based on guarantees in a merger covenant does not prevent acquisition when the property is treated as private property and the dispute falls within the constitutional bar on judicial jurisdiction over covenant disputes.
material_facts: A ruler’s property had been identified under a merger covenant as private property, and the Act proceeded to acquire it while treating it as private property and providing compensation.
The ruler claimed that the property and its income were protected by the covenant and related constitutional guarantees.
The Government disputed the assertion that the privy purse had been fixed in reliance on the income from the property.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that Article 362 did not impose a legally enforceable obligation on Parliament or a State Legislature and that Article 363 barred jurisdiction over disputes arising out of the covenant. It also reasoned that treating the property as private property and offering compensation recognized the ruler’s ownership.
members.conclusion: The covenant-based challenge failed; the Court held that Article 362 did not impose a legal obligation on the legislature and that Article 363 barred judicial jurisdiction over the dispute arising from the covenant.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_relies_on_merger_c: A person challenges an acquisition by relying on guarantees in a merger covenant.
predicates.property_is_treated_as_private_and_compe: The acquisition treats the property as private property and provides compensation for it.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_covenant: Resolving the claim would require deciding a dispute arising from the covenant.

members.legal_issue: A coparcener’s separate property becomes joint family property only upon a clear intention to relinquish separate rights, not through physical mixing or ambiguous descriptions alone.
material_facts: The business had been started and conducted as the proprietor’s separate business.
Documents and communications continued to describe him as the proprietor, and he conducted himself as the sole proprietor.

Some instruments described the business or property as being for family benefit, but the courts found those recitals could have been made to obtain loans and did not establish an intention to surrender separate rights.
The claimant did not establish that the proprietor intended to place the business in the common stock.
members.legal_principle: Separate property of a Hindu coparcener acquires the character of joint family or ancestral property through the coparcener’s volition and intention to waive or surrender the special right in it, not by mere physical mixing. The intention must be established; mere recitals or dealings describing self-acquired property as joint family property are not by themselves sufficient. The Court relied on Hurpurshad v. Sheo Dyal, 3 I.A. 219; Lal Bahadur v. Kanhaiya Lal, 34 I.A. 65; Lola Muddun Gopal v. Khikhinda Koeri, 18 I.A. 9; and Naina Pilla v. Daiyanai Ammal, AIR 1936 Mad 177.
members.conclusion: The business was not converted into joint family property because there was no clear intention by its proprietor to relinquish his separate rights.

predicates.property_began_as_separate_property: The property was originally acquired or conducted as one coparcener’s separate property.
predicates.clear_intent_to_relinquish_separate_righ: The coparcener clearly intended to waive or surrender his separate rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: A member’s separate or self-acquired property becomes joint family property by blending only when the owner voluntarily places it into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon separate rights in it.
material_facts: The claimants argued that, even if the disputed property had originally been self-acquired, its owner had blended it with joint family property.
The claimants presented no evidence that the owner voluntarily placed the property into the common stock or clearly intended to abandon separate rights in it.
members.legal_principle: A member’s separate or self-acquired property may acquire the character of joint family property if the owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock with the intention of abandoning separate rights. That intention must be clearly established. Joint use by family members, generosity in using income to support them, or failure to keep separate accounts does not by itself establish abandonment. The Court relied on Lakkireddi Chinna Venkata Reddy v. Lakkireddi Lakshamama and K.V. Narayanan v. K.V. Ranganadhan.
members.conclusion: The disputed property could not be held to have been blended with joint family property because the claimants did not establish a clear intention to abandon the owner’s separate rights.

predicates.partition_suit_claiming_blending_of_sepa: A claimant seeks recognition of property as joint family property on the basis that its owner blended it with the family property.
predicates.owner_had_separate_property: The property was separate or self-acquired property of its owner.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_righ: Evidence establishes that the owner voluntarily placed the property into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon separate rights in it.

members.legal_issue: A member’s separate property does not become joint family property by blending unless the member clearly intends to abandon the separate rights in it.
material_facts: The property had been allotted to the member as his separate property.
There was no evidence that he intended to abandon his separate rights in the property.
He had not entered the property separately in account books or maintained separate accounts for its earnings.
members.legal_principle: Separate property may be impressed with the character of joint family property when its owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon separate rights. That intention is a question of fact and cannot be inferred merely from physical mixing, family members’ joint use, generosity in applying income, or failure to maintain separate accounts (Lakkireddi Chinna Venkata Reddi v. Lakkireddi Lakshmama; G. Narayana Ram v. G. Chamaraju).
members.conclusion: The property did not become joint family property; the absence of separate entries or accounts did not alter its separate character.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute arises in a proceeding seeking division of family property.
predicates.separately_owned_property: The property was held by a family member as separate property before the alleged blending.
predicates.no_clear_abandonment_intent: The owner did not clearly intend to give up separate rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: Separate property is not converted into joint family property by blending unless its owner voluntarily puts it into the common stock with a clear intention to abandon the separate claim.
material_facts: A family member had received property under a will as separate property and was a member of a joint family.
There was no evidence that the owner consciously surrendered his separate interest or otherwise acted with the intention of blending the property with the joint family estate.
The evidence did not clearly establish how the property was dealt with or how its income was appropriated.
members.legal_principle: Separate or self-acquired property may become joint family property if its owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock intending to abandon the separate claim. The intention to waive separate rights must be clear; joint use by family members, use of income to support them out of generosity, or failure to keep separate accounts does not by itself establish abandonment.
members.conclusion: The property devised under the will was not shown to have been blended with the joint family estate, and the widow was entitled to a fourth share in that property.

rule.if: partition_suit and property_separately_devised and not clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_claim

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of family property.
predicates.property_separately_devised: The property was received by a family member as separate property under a devise.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_clai: The owner clearly and voluntarily intended to give up the separate claim and put the property into the family’s common stock.
predicates.property_retains_separate_character: The property remains separate property rather than becoming joint family property.

members.legal_issue: A member’s separate or self-acquired property does not become joint family property through family use or support alone; blending requires a clear intention to abandon separate rights and place the property in the common stock.
material_facts: The disputed properties had been received by the father under a settlement from a person who was not his direct male ancestor, and were found to be his self-acquired properties.
The father executed settlement deeds and a will dealing with the properties in favour of one son.
The family members lived together and loans were taken in connection with the properties, but the evidence did not establish a clear intention by the father to abandon his separate rights.
The trial court and the first appellate court found that the properties had not been blended with joint family property.
members.legal_principle: A separate or self-acquired property of a member of a joint Hindu family may acquire the character of joint family property if its owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock with the intention of abandoning separate rights. That intention must be clearly established; it cannot be inferred merely from allowing family members to use the property or from using its income to support them. The Court applied this settled principle without citing a particular earlier case for it.
members.conclusion: The properties were not proved to have been blended with joint family property, and the High Court was not justified in overturning the lower courts’ findings on that issue.

rule.if: partition_property_dispute and property_separately_acquired and not clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_rights and (family_use_or_support or family_related_loans)

predicates.partition_property_dispute: The proceeding concerned a claim to divide property said to belong to a joint family.
predicates.property_separately_acquired: The property was acquired separately by an individual rather than received from direct male ancestors as ancestral property.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_righ: The owner clearly intended to give up separate rights in the property and place it in the family common stock.
predicates.family_use_or_support: Other family members used the property or received support from its income.
predicates.family_related_loans: Family members living together took loans connected with the property or its use.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent transferee may be directed to join in the conveyance required to give effect to a decree for specific performance.
material_facts: The property had been transferred by the vendor to a subsequent purchaser.
The decree required the vendor to perform the sale agreement with the plaintiff.
The subsequent purchaser held title that needed to be passed on to the plaintiff to complete the conveyance.
members.legal_principle: The proper form of a decree for specific performance is to direct performance of the contract between the vendor and the plaintiff and require the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance so as to pass the title held by the transferee, without joining in special covenants between the plaintiff and vendor. The Court relied on Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, AIR 1954 SC 75.
members.conclusion: The direction requiring the vendor and the subsequent purchaser to execute the conveyance was permissible and was upheld.

predicates.specific_performance_decree: The court has decreed specific performance of a contract for the property.
predicates.property_transferred_to_subsequent_trans: The vendor transferred the property to another person after entering the contract with the plaintiff.
predicates.transferee_holds_title_needed_for_convey: The subsequent transferee holds title that must be conveyed to the plaintiff to complete the transfer.

members.legal_issue: When a subsequent purchaser holds title to property that must be retransferred under a decree, the vendor and the subsequent purchaser may be directed to join in the conveyance so that title passes to the person entitled to the property.
material_facts: The decree required the land to be retransferred to the party entitled to redeem it after payment of the mortgage amount.
The mortgagee had transferred the land to a subsequent purchaser, who therefore held the title to be conveyed.
The Court directed the seller and the subsequent purchaser jointly to execute the sale deed and hand over possession after the required deposits, to bring the litigation to an end.
members.legal_principle: Applying the form of decree discussed in Durga Prasad v. Deep Chand, the Court stated that a subsequent transferee should join in the conveyance to pass the title residing in that transferee, without joining in special covenants between the original parties. The Court also relied on Article 142 of the Constitution to frame directions that would do complete justice and end the litigation.
members.conclusion: The seller and the subsequent purchaser were directed jointly to execute the conveyance and deliver possession to the party redeeming the mortgage.

predicates.property_retransfer_required: The decree requires the property to be transferred back to the person entitled to it.
predicates.subsequent_transferee_holds_title: A later purchaser holds title to the property that must be transferred.
predicates.decree_requires_transfer_to_entitled_cla: The court directs transfer of the property to the person entitled to receive it under the decree.

members.legal_issue: A vendor is a necessary party to a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement where the property has subsequently been transferred to another purchaser.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought specific performance of an agreement against the original vendor and subsequent purchasers.
The requested conveyance could require the vendor to give effect to terms of the original agreement, while the subsequent purchasers would join to pass their title.
The plaintiffs also sought, in the alternative, repayment of amounts from the vendor.
members.legal_principle: A decree for specific performance should put the purchaser in the position they would have occupied had the contracting parties completed the sale; the vendor must therefore join in the conveyance, while a subsequent transferee joins to pass the title vested in them. The Court applied Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, [1954] S.C.R. 360, and R. C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, [1971] 2 S.C.R. 573. It also relied on the need for the vendor's presence to grant alternative relief against the vendor.
members.conclusion: The vendor was a necessary party because the conveyance required his participation and the alternative monetary relief could not be granted in his absence.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property that has been transferred to a subsequent purchaser.
predicates.vendor_is_to_execute_conveyance: The original vendor must participate in executing the conveyance, including to give effect to terms of the original sale agreement.
predicates.alternative_repayment_is_sought_from_ven: The claimant seeks repayment of money from the original vendor as alternative relief.

members.legal_issue: When property subject to an agreement of sale has been transferred to a subsequent transferee, the decree for specific performance may direct that transferee to join in the conveyance to pass title to the purchaser.
material_facts: The vendors had transferred the property to a subsequent transferee before the decree for specific performance was made.
members.legal_principle: Under Lal Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, [1954] S.C.R. 360, the decree may direct the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance so as to pass the title residing in that transferee to the purchaser. The transferee does not join in any special covenants between the purchaser and the vendor; the transferee’s role is to pass on the title.
members.conclusion: The decree should direct specific performance between the vendors and the purchasers and require the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance to pass on the title held by that transferee.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.property_transferred_to_subsequent_trans: The vendor transferred the property to another person after entering the agreement with the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: When specific performance is sought against a seller and a subsequent transferee whose title has passed to them, the decree should require the seller to perform the original contract and the transferee to join the conveyance to pass that title to the purchaser.
material_facts: The seller had made an earlier contract to sell the property to the plaintiff and subsequently conveyed the property to the appealing purchasers.
The court concluded that the earlier contract was binding and entitled the plaintiff to specific performance.
The title resided in the subsequent transferees, while the original contract’s terms and covenants were between the seller and the plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: Sections 91 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, 3 illustration (g) and 27 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and 40 of the Transfer of Property Act address the subsequent transferee’s obligation and when it may be enforced, but do not directly prescribe the form of decree. The decree should avoid cancelling the later transfer, which may disturb equities between its parties, and should not force the transferee to assume covenants from a contract to which they were not a party. The court followed Kafiladdin v. Samiraddin, A.I.R. 1931 Cal. 67, and the English practice reflected in Potter v. Sanders, 67 E.R. 1057, and declined the approach in Kali Charan v. Janak Deo, A.I.R. 1932 All. 694, which involved cancellation of the later sale.
members.conclusion: The seller was to execute a sale deed in accordance with the original contract, and the subsequent transferees were to join the conveyance solely to pass their title to the plaintiff.

predicates.purchaser_sued_for_specific_performance: A purchaser sued to compel performance of an earlier contract for sale.
predicates.later_transferee_holds_title_under_subse: A subsequent transferee holds title to the property under a later transfer from the seller.

members.legal_issue: A criminal conspiracy may be proved by circumstantial evidence establishing a meeting of minds to commit an illegal act or to act by illegal means.
material_facts: The manager and beneficiary met on several occasions.
Evidence showed that the beneficiary paid money to the manager on multiple occasions.
The manager sanctioned loans whose proceeds were transferred to the beneficiary’s account.
The circumstances surrounding the loans and the absence of promised plots and security supported an inference that the two acted together.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 120-A of the Indian Penal Code, conspiracy requires a meeting of minds of two or more persons to do, or cause to be done, an illegal act or an act by illegal means. Because conspiracy is generally hatched in secrecy, substantial direct evidence may not be available and the offence may be proved by circumstantial evidence. The Court applied the principles discussed in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Sheetla Sahai, (2009) 8 SCC 617.
members.conclusion: The proved circumstances permitted the Court to infer that the manager and beneficiary had conspired.

predicates.criminal_conspiracy_prosecution: The proceeding alleges that two or more people agreed to pursue an illegal act or an act by illegal means.
predicates.direct_evidence_of_agreement_is_unavaila: The alleged agreement was made secretly and no substantial direct evidence of the agreement is available.
predicates.circumstantial_evidence_shows_joint_acti: Evidence shows coordinated conduct, such as repeated meetings, transfers of proceeds, or payments between the alleged participants.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to commit a serious offence constitutes criminal conspiracy without proof of an overt act, and the agreement may be proved by circumstantial evidence.
material_facts: The evidence showed coordinated conduct by the accused before and after the killings, including preparations for the crimes, assistance with disposing of a body, and conduct connected with the children's deaths.
The courts found that the accused had agreed to eliminate the victims and that their conduct and surrounding circumstances supported that agreement.
The Supreme Court found the evidence sufficient to establish the conspiracy.
members.legal_principle: Sections 120-A and 120-B of the Penal Code define and punish criminal conspiracy. Where the agreement is to commit an offence, proof of an overt act is unnecessary; the agreement itself is the essential ingredient. Conspiracy may be inferred from circumstantial evidence, including surrounding circumstances and antecedent and subsequent conduct, but the inference must rest on solid facts. The Court relied on Noor Mohd. Mohd. Yusuf Momin v. State of Maharashtra and V.C. Shukla v. State (Delhi Administration).
members.conclusion: The convictions for criminal conspiracy were upheld.

predicates.criminal_trial_for_conspiracy: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the accused are charged with agreeing to commit an offence.
predicates.agreement_to_commit_offence_proved: The evidence establishes an agreement between at least two persons to commit an offence.
predicates.agreement_inferred_from_solid_circumstan: The agreement is established by reliable surrounding circumstances or conduct before or after the offence.

members.legal_issue: A criminal conspiracy charge requires evidence capable of establishing an agreement to commit an illegal act or to do a lawful act by illegal means.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the accused official participated in a plan involving a raid and the extraction of illegal gratification through a private intermediary.
The call said to convey the successful completion of the alleged plan was ambiguous and could not reliably be connected to the raid or a bribe agreement.
The other relied-on call indicated that the accused was not involved in the discussion about the raid and alleged settlement.
The Court found no direct or circumstantial evidence establishing the accused’s knowledge of or agreement to the alleged conspiracy.
members.legal_principle: A conspiracy requires an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or to do an act that is not illegal by illegal means. Under Central Bureau of Investigation, Hyderabad v. K. Narayana Rao, (2012) 9 SCC 512, an agreement may be proved by direct or circumstantial evidence, but proved circumstances must support the inference of agreement and be incapable of another reasonable explanation; suspicion and surmise are insufficient.
members.conclusion: There was no material evidence to bring home the conspiracy charge against the accused.

predicates.prosecution_for_conspiracy: The proceeding includes a charge that the accused agreed with another person to commit an illegal act or to use illegal means.
predicates.no_evidence_of_agreement: The prosecution has no direct or circumstantial evidence that the accused agreed to the alleged criminal plan.
predicates.circumstances_allow_other_reasonable_exp: The circumstances relied on by the prosecution are reasonably capable of an explanation other than the accused’s participation in the alleged agreement.

members.legal_issue: A criminal conspiracy to secure an unlawful property benefit may be proved by inferring agreement and prior concert from the participants’ coordinated conduct and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: One public servant sought and received successive conversions and allotments that departed from the applicable rules.
The other public servant, who headed the authority, approved key steps, including conversion of the plot’s use, its allotment, and the grant of additional area.
Records concerning the plot and its layout were altered, and the allotments were processed with unusual haste.
The resulting allotment gave one participant a valuable property and a substantial pecuniary advantage.
The participants’ actions were connected at multiple stages, although direct evidence of an express agreement was not produced.
members.legal_principle: Section 120-B IPC requires an agreement between two or more persons to do, or cause to be done, an illegal act or an act that is not illegal in itself by illegal means. Direct evidence of a conspiracy is often difficult to obtain, so its existence and object may be inferred from surrounding circumstances and the accused persons’ conduct. The Court relied on Yash Pal Mittal v. State of Punjab, (1977) 4 SCC 540; Ajay Aggarwal v. Union of India, (1993) 3 SCC 609; State of Maharashtra v. Som Nath Thapa, (1996) 4 SCC 659; and Ram Narain Popli v. Central Bureau of Investigation, (2003) 3 SCC 641. Knowledge of the unlawful act or unlawful means is necessary, and where the ultimate offence consists of a chain of actions, it is not necessary to prove that each conspirator knew every step the collaborator would take.
members.conclusion: The surrounding circumstances and coordinated acts established the appellants’ prior concert and supported their convictions for criminal conspiracy.

rule.if: public_servant_conspiracy_case and coordinated_official_actions and unlawful_property_benefit and (records_manipulated or undue_haste or repeated_rule_deviations)

predicates.public_servant_conspiracy_case: The proceeding concerns an alleged agreement between public servants to secure a property benefit through unlawful conduct or unlawful means.
predicates.coordinated_official_actions: Two or more participants took connected actions at different stages that facilitated the same benefit.
predicates.unlawful_property_benefit: The coordinated conduct resulted in a valuable property or pecuniary advantage being obtained through unlawful means.
predicates.records_manipulated: Records relating to the property or its allocation were deliberately altered or concealed.
predicates.undue_haste: The relevant authority processed connected requests unusually quickly without an adequate explanation for the urgency.
predicates.repeated_rule_deviations: The participants repeatedly departed from applicable rules in carrying out the connected actions.

members.legal_issue: Criminal conspiracy is a substantive offence established by agreement, and the agreement may be proved by circumstantial evidence, including surrounding circumstances and antecedent and subsequent conduct.
material_facts: The accused had longstanding disputes with the deceased and made statements urging others to kill him.

The accused was seen following the deceased with others shortly before the killing, and the court considered this conduct together with the other circumstances as establishing the accused’s involvement in a plan to kill the deceased.
members.legal_principle: Sections 120-B and 107 of the Indian Penal Code distinguish the substantive offence of criminal conspiracy from abetment by conspiracy: conspiracy requires an agreement to do, or cause to be done, an illegal act or an act not illegal by illegal means, and the agreement itself is an offence even if no step is taken to carry it out. Conspiracy may be proved by circumstantial evidence; surrounding circumstances and antecedent and subsequent conduct are relevant. Once reasonable grounds exist to believe that persons conspired to commit an offence, evidence of acts done by them in reference to their common intention may be relevant to prove the conspiracy and offences committed pursuant to it. The judgment cites no earlier decisions for these principles.
members.conclusion: The conviction for criminal conspiracy was upheld.

rule.if: appeal_against_conspiracy_conviction and accused_urged_others_to_kill and accused_followed_victim_with_others and victim_was_killed_afterward

predicates.appeal_against_conspiracy_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction for agreeing with others to commit an offence.
predicates.accused_urged_others_to_kill: The accused urged other people to kill the intended victim.
predicates.accused_followed_victim_with_others: The accused followed the intended victim together with other people shortly before the victim was killed.
predicates.victim_was_killed_afterward: The intended victim was killed after the accused’s urging and the group’s pursuit.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator exceeds jurisdiction by awarding a claim contrary to the contract or by departing from a contractual formula that governs the claim.
material_facts: The contract set a fixed price for the slabs and did not permit escalation for them; it also excluded price adjustments not provided for in the contract.
The contract required the contractor to arrange its own water supply and contained no provision for payment for additional water lead.
The contract placed responsibility for maintaining haul roads on the contractor and did not provide for the additional payment awarded for canal-slope work.
For labour escalation, the contract prescribed a specific calculation formula, but the arbitrator used a different formula.

The High Court set aside the awards for slab escalation, extra water lead, and canal-slope work, but upheld the labour-escalation award; the Supreme Court upheld the former decisions and set aside the labour-escalation award.
members.legal_principle: An arbitrator derives authority from the parties’ contract and must decide within its bounds. An error in construing the contract is ordinarily within jurisdiction, but deciding a matter not allotted by the contract, or disregarding a contractually prescribed formula, is jurisdictional error. Manifest disregard of the contract vitiates the award. The court relied on Jivarajbhai v. Chintamanrao and discussed the Arbitration Act, 1940, as governing the arbitrator’s authority; it also referred to Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission, Pearlman v. Keepers and Governors of Harrow School, Lee v. Showmen’s Guild of Great Britain, M.L. Sethi v. R.P. Kapur, The Managing Director, J. and K. Handicrafts v. Good Luck Carpets, and State of Andhra Pradesh v. R.V. Rayanim.
members.conclusion: The awards for slab escalation, additional water lead, canal-slope work, and labour escalation calculated by a different formula were beyond the arbitrator’s jurisdiction and could not stand.

predicates.arbitration_award_review: A court is reviewing an award made in an arbitration proceeding.
predicates.contract_excludes_claim_or_prescribes_me: The parties’ contract excludes the claimed payment or specifies the method by which it must be calculated.
predicates.arbitrator_awarded_contrary_to_contract: The arbitrator granted the claim despite the exclusion or used a method different from the one specified by the contract.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator cannot award completion costs under a contractual risk-and-expense clause while disregarding the clause’s requirements and the contractually assigned role of the architect.
material_facts: The contract contained provisions governing termination for failure to proceed with due diligence and completion of the remaining work at the contractor’s risk and expense.
The relevant completion-cost provision contemplated an architect’s certification or an estimate approved under the contract.
The arbitrators treated the architect’s certification requirement as inapplicable because construction had been permitted by an interim arbitral direction that was itself beyond jurisdiction.
The arbitrators did not properly consider the contractual conditions for termination and recovery of completion costs.
members.legal_principle: An arbitrator derives authority from the contract and must decide within its terms. Ignoring a relevant contractual condition or awarding an item contrary to the contract can be a jurisdictional error or legal misconduct. The Court relied on Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. J.C. Budharaja, Government and Mining Contractor; Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. M/s Annapurna Construction; Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v. L.K. Ahuja & Co.; Associated Engineering v. Government of Andhra Pradesh; and the other contract-and-arbitration authorities cited. It also held that the architect’s role under the completion-cost clause could not be bypassed merely because an interim arbitral order had permitted construction to proceed.
members.conclusion: The arbitrators’ failure to consider and apply the relevant contractual provisions amounted to legal misconduct, and the award of completion costs could not stand.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party challenged an arbitral award in a proceeding seeking judicial review of the award.
predicates.risk_cost_claim_awarded: The arbitrator awarded a party the cost of completing unfinished contractual work at the other party’s risk and expense.
predicates.contract_sets_conditions_for_risk_cost_r: The contract specifies conditions or procedures that must be followed before completion costs may be recovered from the contractor.
predicates.arbitrator_disregarded_contractual_condi: The arbitrator did not apply the relevant contractual conditions when deciding the completion-cost claim.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator exceeds jurisdiction by awarding relief beyond the claim presented, including by relying on an unpleaded change to the amount credited as paid or by granting escalation beyond the amount claimed.
material_facts: The arbitration claim statement stated the total amount claimed after crediting the employer with payments of Rs.1,49,88,566.90.
During the arbitration, the claimant asserted that a portion of those payments related to other contracts, but did not amend the claim statement.
The arbitrator used the reduced payment credit and thereby awarded more on the relevant work claims than the claim statement allowed.
The total award exceeded the total claim, and the escalation awarded was calculated at a rate exceeding the rates claimed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an award may be set aside on the specified grounds, including legal misconduct. An arbitrator cannot grant more than the relief claimed or proceed on a material alteration of the claim that was not made by amendment. The award of escalation beyond the amount or rate claimed likewise exceeds jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The portions of the award exceeding the claims were invalid because the arbitrator exceeded jurisdiction and committed legal misconduct.

rule.if: arbitration_award_under_review and (award_exceeds_claimed_relief or award_uses_unpleaded_payment_credit or escalation_exceeds_claimed_relief)

predicates.arbitration_award_under_review: A court is reviewing an award made in an arbitration proceeding.
predicates.award_exceeds_claimed_relief: The arbitrator awarded relief greater than the claimant had sought.
predicates.award_uses_unpleaded_payment_credit: The arbitrator calculated the award using a changed payment credit that the claimant had not incorporated into an amended claim.
predicates.escalation_exceeds_claimed_relief: The arbitrator awarded escalation greater than the escalation sought by the claimant.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal exceeds the scope of its submission when it awards compensation for a loss that was not part of the dispute referred to arbitration.
material_facts: The arbitration agreement referred the parties’ disputes in the pending writ proceeding to arbitration.

The writ proceeding sought damages for damage to houses, crops and an orchard, and reclamation of agricultural land rendered unfit for cultivation; it did not claim compensation for loss of the land’s potential or plead that such compensation as an alternative.
The arbitral tribunal awarded compensation for loss of the land’s potential, together with interest on that amount.
The respondent objected that the compensation for loss of potential was beyond the scope of the reference.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34(2)(iv) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an award may be set aside insofar as it decides a dispute not contemplated by, or beyond the scope of, the submission to arbitration. The proviso permits only the portion dealing with matters beyond the submission to be set aside when that portion can be separated from decisions on matters submitted. The scope of the submission here was determined by the arbitration agreement read with the dispute in the underlying writ proceeding. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The award of compensation for loss of the land’s potential and the interest on that compensation fell outside the scope of the arbitration reference and was set aside.

rule.if: award_challenge_pending and arbitration_reference_limited_to_underlying_claim and land_potential_compensation_not_claimed and award_grants_land_potential_compensation

predicates.award_challenge_pending: A court is considering a challenge to an arbitral award.
predicates.arbitration_reference_limited_to_underly: The parties referred to arbitration the dispute raised in an underlying proceeding.
predicates.land_potential_compensation_not_claimed: The claimant did not seek or plead, in the underlying proceeding, compensation for the land’s lost potential.
predicates.award_grants_land_potential_compensation: The arbitral tribunal awarded compensation for the land’s lost potential.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator exceeds the authority conferred by a reference when the reference requires compliance with specified valuation methods and the arbitrator uses a method outside those limits.
material_facts: The reference required the final accounts to be prepared, as far as possible, according to the partnership agreement, incorporating its valuation terms.

The agreement prescribed the net profits of the preceding five years as the value of goodwill, debts at a specified percentage of book value, stock at book value, and immovable property at book value or purchase price.
The arbitrator stated that the goodwill valuation included depreciation and appreciation of property, dead stock, and recoverable dues.
members.legal_principle: Under section 30 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940, an award may be set aside on the recognized grounds, including where the arbitrator acts beyond the authority conferred by the reference. Where the reference incorporates contractual limits, the court determines those limits and may find excess of jurisdiction when the arbitrator acts outside them. A mere error in reaching a conclusion is not enough: under Champsey Bhara and Company v. Jivraj Balloo Spinning and Weaving Company Ltd. (L.R. 50 I.A. 324), an error apparent on the face of the award must disclose an erroneous legal proposition forming its basis. Cruikshank v. Sutherland ((1923) 92 L.J. Ch. 136) was distinguishable because the agreement there did not prescribe the valuation method.
members.conclusion: The arbitrator exceeded the authority conferred by the reference, making the award invalid to the extent of that excess.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party asks a court to set aside an arbitration award.
predicates.reference_requires_specific_valuation_me: The parties’ reference requires the arbitrator to follow a specified method for valuing assets or accounts.
predicates.arbitrator_uses_unpermitted_asset_adjust: The arbitrator includes asset adjustments that the specified valuation method does not permit.

members.legal_issue: A one-off acquisition and resale of land constitutes an adventure in the nature of trade when the transaction’s purpose and conduct, considered together, show an organised profit-making scheme.
material_facts: The taxpayer agreed to acquire a large estate for a price far beyond his financial resources and paid an advance, with the conveyance permitted to be made to him or his nominees.
The taxpayer divided the estate into 23 plots and arranged purchasers for 22 plots before conveyance; those plots were conveyed to the purchasers and the remaining plot was conveyed to the taxpayer.
The taxpayer lacked the resources to cultivate the estate himself, and the arrangement and subdivision showed planning and organisation directed to resale.
members.legal_principle: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade depends on the total impression and effect of all relevant facts and circumstances; no single abstract test or formula governs.
