Relevant considerations include the transaction’s relation to the taxpayer’s ordinary business, the nature and scale of the acquisition, the taxpayer’s intention, subsequent dealings, organisation, and manner of disposal. The Court applied section 34(1)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, in the assessment context and relied on California Copper Syndicate v. Harris, Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, Leeming v. Jones, Saroj Kumar Mazumdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Raja J. Rameshwar Rao v. Commissioner of Income-tax.
members.conclusion: The transactions were an adventure in the nature of trade, carried out as part of a profit-making scheme, and the resulting profit was taxable.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and land_acquired_for_profit_resale and land_divided_into_plots and purchasers_arranged_for_most_plots and taxpayer_lacked_means_to_cultivate_land

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The taxpayer was involved in an income-tax assessment concerning gains from a transaction.
predicates.land_acquired_for_profit_resale: The taxpayer acquired land under an arrangement indicating an intention to resell it for profit.
predicates.land_divided_into_plots: The taxpayer divided the acquired land into separate plots.
predicates.purchasers_arranged_for_most_plots: The taxpayer arranged purchasers for most of the plots before conveyance.
predicates.taxpayer_lacked_means_to_cultivate_land: The taxpayer lacked the means to cultivate the land personally.

members.legal_issue: Whether a property purchase and resale is an adventure in the nature of trade depends on the total effect of the relevant facts and circumstances, and the transaction here was part of a profit-making scheme.
material_facts: The firm purchased an industrial factory and its associated property using borrowed money and invested little of its own funds.
The income from the property was about one-sixth of the interest payable on the borrowed money.
The firm began selling part of the property within about three months of the purchase.
It used sale proceeds to pay purchase debts and amounts due to the government, and had sold substantial property while still owing money.
The evidence did not establish that the firm bought the factory to establish a cycle factory or another industry.
members.legal_principle: The meaning of “business” in section 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, includes an adventure in the nature of trade; the equivalent provisions of the Hyderabad Income Tax Act also applied to one assessment year. Whether a transaction falls within that expression depends on the total impression and effect of all relevant facts, not an abstract formula. A land transaction is not, without more, presumed to be an adventure in the nature of trade. The Court applied Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and referred to Californian Copper Syndicate v. Harris, Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, Leeming v. Jones, Saroj Kumar Mazumdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold.
members.conclusion: Considering the total effect of the established facts, the purchase and resale of the property was an adventure in the nature of trade and part of a profit-making scheme; the resulting profit was assessable.

rule.if: taxable_profit_classification_case and property_purchased_and_partly_resold and purchase_financed_by_borrowing and own_funds_inadequate_for_permanent_investment and property_yield_far_below_financing_cost and resale_began_soon_after_purchase and sale_proceeds_used_to_repay_debts and no_evidence_established_intended_industrial_use

predicates.taxable_profit_classification_case: A tax proceeding concerns whether profit from purchasing and reselling an asset is taxable as business profit.
predicates.property_purchased_and_partly_resold: The taxpayer bought property and later sold part of it.
predicates.purchase_financed_by_borrowing: The taxpayer used borrowed money to finance the purchase.
predicates.own_funds_inadequate_for_permanent_inves: The taxpayer lacked sufficient own financial resources to make the purchase as a permanent investment.
predicates.property_yield_far_below_financing_cost: The income from the property was substantially lower than the cost of financing its purchase.
predicates.resale_began_soon_after_purchase: The taxpayer began reselling part of the property shortly after acquiring it.
predicates.sale_proceeds_used_to_repay_debts: The taxpayer used proceeds from sales to discharge purchase-related debts or amounts due to the seller.
predicates.no_evidence_established_intended_industr: The evidence did not establish that the taxpayer acquired the property to use it for an intended industrial purpose.

members.legal_issue: A single land-development venture involving subdivision and sale of plots may constitute a business, and evidence of that activity may support treating the resulting proceeds as business income.
material_facts: The taxpayer acquired a village interest and a large area of land, developed part of the land, laid out the remaining land in plots, and sold those plots for a profit.
The tax tribunal found that the proceeds were income from business, and the High Court found evidence supporting that conclusion.
members.legal_principle: Even a single venture may be in the nature of trade or business. Acquiring land to develop and sell, then subdividing and developing it and selling it in parcels rather than as acquired, is dealing with the land as stock-in-trade. On a tax reference asking whether evidence supported the tribunal’s finding, the court examines whether the record supports that finding. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly upheld the finding that the proceeds from the plot sales were business income; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: income_tax_reference_appeal and land_acquired_for_resale and land_subdivided_and_developed and plots_sold_separately

predicates.income_tax_reference_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal concerning a finding made in an income-tax reference.
predicates.land_acquired_for_resale: The taxpayer acquired land with a view to developing and selling it.
predicates.land_subdivided_and_developed: The taxpayer divided the land into plots and developed the area to make it more attractive.
predicates.plots_sold_separately: The taxpayer sold the land in separate plots rather than as a single unit.

members.legal_issue: Whether profits from purchasing land, subdividing it, and selling the resulting plots constitute profits from an adventure in the nature of trade.
material_facts: The purchasers acquired land and, shortly afterward, divided it into four plots.
They sold the plots within a few months of acquiring the land.
The total sale consideration was substantially greater than the purchase price.
The tax tribunal had treated the purchase as an investment, but the High Court concluded that the purchasers intended to resell the land.
members.legal_principle: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade is assessed from its facts and circumstances. The prompt subdivision and resale of the land, considered with the other circumstances, were more consistent with an intention to resell than with an investment. The matter came before the High Court by reference under Section 256(1) of the Income Tax Act; the Supreme Court relied on no earlier cases in deciding this issue.
members.conclusion: The transaction constituted an adventure in the nature of trade, and the Court found no ground to interfere with the High Court’s conclusion.

rule.if: income_tax_reference_appeal and land_subdivided_soon_after_purchase and plots_sold_within_months and resale_gain

predicates.income_tax_reference_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a High Court’s answer to a referred income-tax question.
predicates.land_subdivided_soon_after_purchase: The purchasers divided the land into plots shortly after acquiring it.
predicates.plots_sold_within_months: The purchasers sold the plots within a few months of acquiring the land.
predicates.resale_gain: The purchasers received more for the land on resale than they had paid to acquire it.

members.legal_issue: A profit from an isolated purchase and resale of property is business income when the transaction, considered as a whole, has essential features of trade.
material_facts: A firm whose ordinary business did not include investing in land acquired adjoining plots over a period of time and later sold them to a company it managed for substantially more than their purchase price.
The fact-finder found that the plots were acquired solely to resell them to the company at a profit, and rejected explanations that they were acquired as an investment or to provide housing.

The firm did not cultivate or develop the plots or otherwise use them; the surrounding circumstances supported the finding that the acquisitions formed a profit-making scheme, and no relevant circumstances offset the presumption arising from the sole resale intention.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(4) and 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, an isolated transaction may be an adventure in the nature of trade if it has some essential features of trade or business. The character of a transaction depends on the total effect of all relevant circumstances, not a mechanical count of factors. A sole and exclusive intention to resell at a profit, coupled with no intention to hold, enjoy, or use the property, raises a strong but rebuttable presumption of an adventure in the nature of trade. The Court considered, among other authorities, The Californian Copper Syndicate v. Harris, Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Livingston, Rutledge v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Balgownie Land Trust Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Martin v. Lowry, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, and Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold.
members.conclusion: The transaction was an adventure in the nature of trade, and the resulting profit was properly assessed as business income.

rule.if: income_tax_business_income_classification and isolated_property_purchase_resale and sole_resale_profit_intent and no_intention_to_hold_or_use and profit_making_scheme and no_countervailing_factors_rebut_presumption

predicates.income_tax_business_income_classificatio: The dispute concerns whether profit from a transaction is taxable as income from a business.
predicates.isolated_property_purchase_resale: A person acquired property in an isolated transaction and later resold it.
predicates.sole_resale_profit_intent: The fact-finder found that the person acquired the property solely to resell it at a profit.
predicates.no_intention_to_hold_or_use: The person had no intention of retaining, enjoying, or using the property.
predicates.profit_making_scheme: The circumstances showed that the acquisition and resale formed part of a scheme to make a profit.
predicates.no_countervailing_factors_rebut_presumpt: The other relevant circumstances did not rebut the presumption arising from the sole intention to resell at a profit.

members.legal_issue: A person whose interests may be adversely affected by a decision in an administrative proceeding must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard, even if that person has not acquired a legal right to the property at issue.
material_facts: After the first auction sale was cancelled, other bidders made the highest bid at a later auction, their bid was provisionally accepted, and they made an initial deposit.
The bidders were in possession of the property, and restoring the earlier sale could prevent them from obtaining it and adversely affect them.
The authority decided the earlier purchaser’s petition without notifying the later bidders or giving them an opportunity to be heard.
members.legal_principle: A highest bidder does not acquire a right or interest in property until the sale is approved and confirmed and a sale deed is executed, as explained in Bombay Salt and Chemical v. Johnson. But a person may have sufficient interest to participate where the outcome may prejudice them; natural justice requires that such an affected person receive notice and an opportunity to be heard.
members.conclusion: The later bidders had sufficient interest to be heard, and the authority’s orders were properly quashed for failure to give them that opportunity; the petition must be considered afresh after notice and a hearing.

rule.if: administrative_review_affects_competing_bidders and later_bid_was_provisionally_accepted and bidders_made_initial_deposit and decision_may_prejudice_bidders and bidders_received_no_hearing

predicates.administrative_review_affects_competing_: The proceeding asks an authority to reconsider a decision affecting property that was later offered to competing bidders.
predicates.later_bid_was_provisionally_accepted: The competing bidders’ highest bid at a later sale was provisionally accepted.
predicates.bidders_made_initial_deposit: The competing bidders paid an initial portion of their bid.
predicates.decision_may_prejudice_bidders: The requested decision could adversely affect the competing bidders’ ability to obtain or retain the property.
predicates.bidders_received_no_hearing: The authority decided the matter without giving the competing bidders notice and an opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary whose interests may be substantially affected must be given an opportunity to be heard before the Government withdraws an acquisition in which possession has not been taken.
material_facts: The association was the beneficiary of the acquisition, which was intended to provide housing sites to its members.
The acquisition had progressed through the declaration, award and payment of the acquisition costs by the association.
The Government withdrew the acquisition without giving the association notice or an opportunity to be heard.
The landowners had a statutory route to claim compensation for damage or costs resulting from the acquisition, but no similar remedy was available to the beneficiary.
members.legal_principle: Natural justice is ordinarily read into a statutory power unless excluded expressly or by necessary implication. Under Union of India v. Col. J.N. Sinha, Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation and C.B. Gautam v. Union of India, the ordinary rule is that a person likely to be affected must have an opportunity to be heard, and the party asserting an exception bears the burden of establishing it. Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act did not exclude a beneficiary’s hearing. The distinction between a landowner, whose interests are addressed by Section 48(2), and a beneficiary was recognized in Amar Nath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of U.P., Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Godrej & Boyce and Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The Government could not withdraw the acquisition without first hearing the beneficiary; the withdrawal was vitiated because the association was not heard.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_acquisition_withdrawal and beneficiary_materially_affected and acquisition_steps_substantially_advanced and beneficiary_not_heard

predicates.appeal_challenges_acquisition_withdrawal: The proceeding challenges a government decision to withdraw an acquisition before possession has been taken.
predicates.beneficiary_materially_affected: The proposed withdrawal may cause substantial loss to the person or body for whose benefit the acquisition was undertaken.
predicates.acquisition_steps_substantially_advanced: The acquisition has proceeded through substantial formal steps, and the beneficiary has incurred costs toward it.
predicates.beneficiary_not_heard: The government withdrew the acquisition without giving the beneficiary notice or an opportunity to present its position.

members.legal_issue: A company for whose benefit acquisition proceedings have reached the statutory consent and agreement stages must be given an opportunity to oppose the government’s proposed withdrawal.
material_facts: The land was proposed to be acquired for the company’s housing colony after the required inquiries and company-acquisition procedures had been completed.
The State Government decided to withdraw some of the land without giving the company notice or an opportunity to respond.
The company asserted that the released land was needed for its housing scheme and that its release would prejudice the scheme.
members.legal_principle: Sections 39–42 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require prior government consent, an inquiry, an agreement with the company, and publication of the agreement in the Official Gazette for an acquisition for a company. Rules 3 and 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 provide for a committee and an inquiry into specified matters. Once these requirements have been completed and a Section 6 declaration is made, a valuable right accrues to the company to oppose proposed withdrawal. In Amarnath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of Uttar Pradesh, the Court distinguished the company beneficiary’s position from that of a landowner and recognised the possibility of substantial prejudice to the company.
members.conclusion: The withdrawal decisions were unlawful because the company had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed withdrawal.

rule.if: company_beneficiary_acquisition and company_acquisition_procedures_completed and proposed_withdrawal_may_prejudice_company and company_given_no_opportunity_to_respond

predicates.company_beneficiary_acquisition: The acquisition is being undertaken for the benefit of a company.
predicates.company_acquisition_procedures_completed: The statutory procedures applicable to acquiring land for a company have been completed.
predicates.proposed_withdrawal_may_prejudice_compan: The proposed release of the land may adversely affect the company’s intended use or plans for the acquisition.
predicates.company_given_no_opportunity_to_respond: The government makes its withdrawal decision without giving the company an opportunity to oppose it.

members.legal_issue: A tenant whose possession or tenancy rights may be affected by a decision in a title dispute must be treated as an interested party and given notice and an opportunity to be heard in the statutory revision proceeding.
material_facts: The appellants claimed to occupy disputed land as tenants under leases granted by the Gram Panchayat, including annual leases or pattas.

In proceedings brought by persons claiming ownership, the Director decided a title dispute between those claimants and the Gram Panchayat and ordered distribution of the land without hearing the appellants.
The decision could affect the appellants’ possession or tenancy rights, and they claimed that they remained in possession as tenants.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 makes notice and an opportunity to be heard conditions precedent to varying or reversing an order for parties interested. A person is interested if likely to be affected by the decision. The court relied on Northern India Caterers P. Ltd. v. State of Punjab and Haryana and Mohan Lal v. State of Punjab on lawful process and hearing; Paras Ram v. State of Punjab and Gram Panchayat of Village Serohi Behali v. Har Lal on the broad meaning of interested parties; and Mukhtiar Singh v. State of Punjab and Chet Singh v. State of Punjab on the statutory requirement for a hearing under Section 42.
members.conclusion: The appellants were interested parties entitled to notice and an opportunity to be heard before an order was passed. The orders were set aside and the matters remanded for fresh consideration after hearing the appellants and other necessary parties, including consideration of whether any appellants remained in possession as tenants and how their rights could be protected.

predicates.section_42_revision: The proceeding is a statutory revision concerning an order, scheme, or repartition in a land-consolidation matter.
predicates.tenant_claims_interest_in_land: A person claims to hold a tenancy or leasehold interest in the land under consideration.
predicates.decision_may_affect_tenancy_or_possessio: The decision may adversely affect that person's tenancy rights or possession of the land.

members.legal_issue: A tenant or sub-tenant with a lease-based interest who is in possession when a town-planning scheme is published is a person interested and entitled to notice and an opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The appellant was a tenant in possession of premises affected by the scheme, and the scheme affected the appellant’s possession and business.
The Court treated possession on the date the scheme was notified in the official gazette as the relevant point for entitlement to notice and an opportunity to be heard.
members.legal_principle: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act recognises that a lease creates an interest in enjoyment of the property and entitles a tenant to remain in possession until lawful termination and eviction. Read with Rule 21(3) and (4) of the Bombay Town Planning Rules, 1955, this makes a tenant or sub-tenant in possession a person interested for these purposes; entitlement is limited to those in possession when the scheme is notified in the official gazette.
members.conclusion: A tenant or sub-tenant in possession on the date the scheme is published is a person interested and is entitled to the prescribed notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond.

predicates.town_planning_scheme_proceeding: A planning officer is preparing or finalising a scheme that may alter plots or affect interests in property.
predicates.lease_based_possession_on_publication_da: A tenant or sub-tenant holds possession under a lease when the scheme is published.

members.legal_issue: An invalid portion of an amended statute may be severed when the valid remainder is complete and workable, and the original enactment can remain valid independently of the defective amendment.
material_facts: The original enactment imposed a tax on urban land and was within the State Legislature’s competence.
A later amendment introduced provisions that could operate as a tax on the combined value of a person’s lands and buildings.
A subsequent corrective amendment retrospectively omitted the offending proviso and clarified that properties were taxed separately as units.
The remaining provisions formed a workable scheme without the omitted proviso.
members.legal_principle: Whether valid and invalid parts are severable depends on legislative intention, including whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part without the invalid part. If the valid provisions are distinct and form a complete code after the invalid portion is removed, they may stand; if the provisions are inextricably mixed, the whole enactment fails. The Court relied on M.P.V. Sundara Ramaiar and Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh and R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The offending portion was severable, and the remaining charging and supporting provisions were valid and workable.

rule.if: statute_validity_challenge and defective_part_separable and valid_remainder_complete_and_workable and original_enactment_independently_valid

predicates.statute_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a statute containing both valid and defective parts.
predicates.defective_part_separable: The defective part can be removed without making the remaining provisions dependent on it.
predicates.valid_remainder_complete_and_workable: After the defective part is removed, the remaining provisions form a complete and workable scheme.
predicates.original_enactment_independently_valid: The enactment before the defective amendment was itself within the legislature’s competence.
predicates.valid_remainder_remains_enforceable: The valid remainder continues to have legal effect and may be enforced.

members.legal_issue: A defective amendment does not make an independently valid enactment permanently still-born when a corrective amendment removes the defect retrospectively before a court declares the enactment invalid.
material_facts: The original enactment was independently valid and had not yet been brought into operation when the later amendment introduced the defect.

Before a court had declared the enactment invalid, a corrective ordinance and replacement enactment retrospectively removed the offending provision and clarified the tax’s operation on separate units.
The provisions remaining after correction formed a complete and workable scheme.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may correct an amendment that exceeds its competence where the valid original enactment can stand independently and the defective portion is severable. A valid and complete remainder survives removal of the defect; the Court distinguished M/s. West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras and Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which did not prevent the legislature from correcting its error before a judicial verdict.
members.conclusion: The original enactment was not still-born; the retrospective corrective measure restored the enforceability of the valid scheme, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: challenge_to_amended_enactment and original_enactment_independently_valid and defect_introduced_by_later_amendment and retrospective_correction_before_judicial_invalidation and corrected_remainder_complete_and_workable

predicates.challenge_to_amended_enactment: A party challenges an enactment as amended by a later legislative measure.
predicates.original_enactment_independently_valid: The enactment before the later amendment was itself within the legislature’s competence.
predicates.defect_introduced_by_later_amendment: The defect arose from a subsequent amendment rather than from the original enactment.
predicates.retrospective_correction_before_judicial: The legislature retrospectively corrected the defect before a court declared the enactment invalid.
predicates.corrected_remainder_complete_and_workabl: After correction, the remaining provisions form a complete and workable scheme.
predicates.corrected_enactment_remains_enforceable: The enactment, as corrected, continues to have legal effect and may be enforced.

members.legal_issue: An unauthorized provision in a lease does not invalidate the entire lease if the provision can be severed and the remainder remains workable.
material_facts: A lease contained a clause postponing minimum royalty payments based on an unauthorized modification.
The clause could be removed without disturbing the remaining terms of the lease.
The lease without the clause remained valid and was more advantageous to the ward.
members.legal_principle: An unauthorized clause does not invalidate an entire deed unless it is so integral to the transaction that the valid and invalid parts cannot be separated. The remaining lease terms may stand when they remain effective without the invalid clause.
members.conclusion: The unauthorized clause was inoperative, but it did not invalidate the remainder of the lease.

predicates.lease_contains_unauthorized_clause: A lease includes a provision that was not authorized.
predicates.clause_is_severable: The unauthorized provision can be removed without making the rest of the transaction inseparable or incoherent.
predicates.remainder_is_workable: The remaining lease terms continue to operate effectively without the unauthorized provision.

members.legal_issue: Invalid acquisition provisions may be severed from the remainder of a land-reform law when the remaining provisions can operate independently.
material_facts: The majority held the provisions transferring pre-vesting rent arrears and deducting presumed costs for works benefiting tenants invalid.
The remainder of the land-reform law provided for the transfer of estates and related matters and could continue to operate without those provisions.
members.legal_principle: A statute need not be invalidated in its entirety if the invalid provisions are not so inextricably bound up with the valid provisions that the remainder cannot independently survive. The court applied the severability test based on whether the legislature would have enacted the surviving provisions without the invalid parts.
members.conclusion: The invalid provisions were severable, and the rest of the law remained valid.

predicates.a_challenge_to_partial_invalidity: The proceeding challenges whether invalid provisions require the whole enactment to be struck down.
predicates.invalid_provisions_are_separable: The invalid provisions can be removed without defeating the operation of the rest of the enactment.
predicates.remaining_law_can_operate_independently: The surviving provisions can function as a law without the invalid provisions.

members.legal_issue: An illegal condition attached to an assignment may be severed while the valid assignment remains in force if the condition is separable and its removal leaves the assignment effective.
material_facts: The assignment of land to a person entitled to preferential consideration included an invalid condition restricting the timber entitlement.
The condition was not an integral part of the assignment, and deleting it left the assignment effective and complete.
The challenge in the writ proceeding was directed at the condition.
members.legal_principle: The appropriate relief depends on the circumstances, including whether the valid and invalid parts of an order are severable and whether the remainder remains viable and self-contained. The Court relied on Mahaboob Sheriff v. Mysore State Transport Authority, where the illegal part of an order was severed and quashed while the lawful remainder stood. It held that R. M. D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India was not in point.
members.conclusion: The invalid condition could be quashed without quashing the assignment; the assignment remained valid without that condition.

rule.if: assignment_challenged_in_writ_proceeding and illegal_condition_attached and condition_severable and remaining_assignment_effective

predicates.assignment_challenged_in_writ_proceeding: A person challenged an assignment in a writ proceeding.
predicates.illegal_condition_attached: The assignment included a condition that was unlawful.
predicates.condition_severable: The unlawful condition could be removed without making the rest of the assignment truncated or ineffective.
predicates.remaining_assignment_effective: The assignment remained viable and complete after removal of the unlawful condition.

members.legal_issue: The land was held as a public religious endowment for the temple rather than as the personal property of its manager.
material_facts: The suit sought relief concerning the management of a temple and its endowed property as a public religious trust.

Settlement records stated that the revenue-free status of part of the estate depended on the temple being maintained and described the manager as an ostensible owner, with real ownership vested in the trust.
The deceased manager stated that the property belonged to the deity and that he was only its custodian; the successor affirmed the correctness of that statement in evidence.
The successor also made applications and declarations treating the deity or trust as owner and himself as manager, and representing that the property’s income was used for religious purposes.
members.legal_principle: The settlement records, including a village administration record carrying a presumption of correctness, and the managers’ admissions supported the conclusion that the property vested in the temple or math as a juristic person. An evidentiary admission is not conclusive, but it raises an estoppel and shifts the burden to the person making it or that person’s representative to explain or disprove it; unless explained or shown to be wrong, it is effective proof. The Court distinguished Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop on its different facts. The dispute arose in a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The estate was a public religious trust or endowment dedicated to the deity, not the personal property of the successor manager.

predicates.public_religious_endowment_dispute: A proceeding concerns whether property associated with a religious institution is a public endowment or the personal property of its manager.
predicates.official_records_connect_property_to_tem: Official settlement or administration records connect the property or its continued revenue-free status to the temple and its maintenance.
predicates.predecessor_admitted_deity_ownership: The former manager stated that the property belonged to the deity and that the manager held it only as custodian.
predicates.successor_confirmed_admission: The successor manager confirmed the former manager’s statement or otherwise treated the deity or trust as owner and himself as manager.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired or held in a Mahant’s name may be found to belong to the math where the evidence shows institutional use and the claimant does not establish personal acquisition or ownership.
material_facts: The properties were claimed by the appellant as personal or private properties, but documents concerning acquisitions were generally in the names of the Mahants.
A gift deed referred to the benefit of disciples and their successors in perpetuity and concerned land forming part of the math site.
Other documents connected property with religious services, offerings, food distribution, or assignment to the math.
The Mahants were ascetics and heads of the institution; the evidence did not show that the disputed purchases were made from their personal assets.

The plaintiff did not produce all relevant documents, acquisition-funding accounts, expenditure accounts, or the consolidated budget, and evidence showed that private and math accounts had been mingled.
The record included a grant directing property income toward religious offerings and distribution of food among visiting Vaishnavas.
members.legal_principle: The name in which property is acquired does not by itself establish that it was acquired for the Mahant’s personal use; an acquisition for the math may be equally or more probable where the Mahant acted as its head and representative. The Court relied on Sitaram Days Banasi v. H.R.E. Board Madras and Raghbir Lala v. Mohammad Said for the significance of an acquirer’s status as an ascetic and institutional head. The purpose and use shown by the documents, the absence of evidence tracing acquisitions to personal assets, and the failure to produce relevant accounts and documents supported treating the properties as math properties.
members.conclusion: The disputed properties were properties of the math rather than the personal properties of the Mahant; the evidence did not support the appellant’s claims that the properties were personal or private.

rule.if: property_ownership_dispute and property_acquired_or_held_in_institutional_head_name and evidence_shows_institutional_use and not claimant_shows_personal_funding_or_use

predicates.property_ownership_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property belongs personally to an institutional head or to the institution.
predicates.property_acquired_or_held_in_institution: The property was acquired or held in the name of the person who headed the institution.
predicates.evidence_shows_institutional_use: Documents or other evidence connect the property or its proceeds with the institution’s religious, charitable, or operational purposes.
predicates.claimant_shows_personal_funding_or_use: The claimant establishes that the property was acquired from personal assets or was held for personal use.

members.legal_issue: The temple was a public religious institution, and its property belonged to the shrine rather than to its hereditary manager.
material_facts: Historical grants and records showed that land and other resources were provided for the temple and its religious purposes.
The temple had become a major place of worship visited by many devotees, and offerings were made for the temple.
The governing royal order declared the shrine a religious institution, its dedicated property to be shrine property, and its hereditary head to be its custodian, manager, and trustee.
The evidence did not establish that admission or worship was controlled in a manner showing that the temple was private.
members.legal_principle: Whether a Hindu temple is public or private depends on the facts relating to its foundation, grants, use, access, worship, and public participation; its appearance alone is not decisive. The Court treated the governing royal order as controlling and also relied on the documentary evidence of grants for the shrine.
members.conclusion: The temple was a public temple, and the hereditary head had no ownership of its property merely by holding his office.

rule.if: temple_status_proceeding and (temple_property_was_dedicated_for_public_religious_use or governing_order_declared_shrine_public) and not evidence_established_private_access_control

predicates.temple_status_proceeding: The case concerns whether a temple and its property are public or private.
predicates.temple_property_was_dedicated_for_public: Rulers or donors provided property for the temple or its religious purposes.
predicates.governing_order_declared_shrine_public: A governing order declared the shrine a public religious institution and its dedicated property to be shrine property.
predicates.evidence_established_private_access_cont: Evidence showed that the public's access to worship was restricted in a way establishing that the temple was private.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired by a Mahant from offerings made for a Math belongs to the Math when the evidence shows it was acquired and held for the institution, not for personal benefit.
material_facts: The evidence established that the Math was a monastic religious institution and that the disputed house was acquired by its Mahant using offerings made by disciples.
The offerings were blended with the Math’s funds and used for its purposes; there was no reliable evidence that the property was acquired for the Mahant’s personal benefit.
The claimant’s natural son asserted that the property was the Mahant’s personal property and should pass to him by inheritance.
members.legal_principle: A Math is a religious institution with legal personality, and its property is attached to the office of Mahant. A Mahant has an estate for life in permanent endowments and an absolute property in offerings income, subject to maintaining the institution; property acquired from offerings for the institution is not thereby the Mahant’s personal property. An ascetic’s after-acquired property passes to spiritual, not natural, heirs. The Court relied on Sammantha Pandara v. Sellappa Chetti, Gyanasambhandan Pandara Sannadhi v. Kandaswami Tambiram, Vidya Purna Thirthaswami v. Vidyanidhi Thirtha Swami, Ram Prakash Das v. Anand Das and Vidya Varuthi Thirtha v. Baluswami Iyer.
members.conclusion: The disputed house was Math property and an accretion to the endowment; the Mahant’s natural heir had no claim to it as personal property.

rule.if: math_property_case and math_exists and property_acquired_from_devotee_offerings and offerings_used_for_math_purposes and not evidence_of_personal_acquisition

predicates.math_property_case: The dispute concerns whether property held or acquired by a religious head belongs to a Math or to the head personally or his natural heirs.
predicates.math_exists: A monastic religious institution exists and is presided over by a religious head.
predicates.property_acquired_from_devotee_offerings: The property was acquired using offerings made by the institution’s followers to its religious head.
predicates.offerings_used_for_math_purposes: The offerings were treated as institutional funds or used for the institution’s purposes.
predicates.evidence_of_personal_acquisition: Evidence shows that the property was acquired or held for the religious head’s personal benefit rather than for the institution.

members.legal_issue: Properties shown by the evidence to have been acquired, maintained, or treated for the temple belong to the temple rather than to its religious head personally.
material_facts: Separate accounts were maintained for the temple and the religious head, and the evidence showed that the temple received gifts and contributions and had resources for acquisitions.
The properties were recorded, used, or accounted for as temple property, and some had been expressly gifted or purchased for the temple.
The religious head failed to produce some relevant accounts and documents, and documents produced were found to have been altered or tampered with.
The appellant did not establish that the properties were her personal property.
members.legal_principle: The ownership of religious endowment property is determined from the evidence, including the source of acquisition, gifts, accounts, records, use, and the manner in which the property was dealt with. The Court accepted an adverse inference from the deliberate non-production of relevant accounts and documents and relied on the distinction between temple and personal accounts. The principles concerning public and private endowments in Deoki Nandan v. Murlidar and Mundancheri Koman v. Achutan Nair informed the Court’s assessment.
members.conclusion: All the properties listed in the suit schedules were properties of the temple.

predicates.proceeding_determines_temple_property_ow: The proceeding requires a decision whether disputed properties belong to a temple or its manager personally.
predicates.temple_and_manager_have_separate_account: Separate accounts are maintained for the temple’s affairs and the manager’s personal affairs.
predicates.properties_are_acquired_or_treated_for_t: The properties are acquired with temple resources, dedicated to the temple, used for temple purposes, or consistently recorded and managed as temple property.
predicates.manager_does_not_establish_personal_owne: The manager does not establish that the disputed properties are personal property.

members.legal_issue: Whether special leave should be revoked when the applicant materially misstates a fact and misrepresents a publication as having been made under the court’s authority.
material_facts: The applicant stated that the sale proclamation did not say the property was being sold subject to a mortgage charge, although the proclamation contained such a note.
The applicant published a public notice captioned as a court notice, presenting it as though it had been published under the court’s orders.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the applicant’s material misstatement and its publication of a notice as though it had been issued under the Court’s orders as sufficient reasons to revoke special leave. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The Court revoked the special leave, dismissed the appeal arising from it, and held that the stay already granted stood vacated.

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding in which special leave has been granted for an appeal.
predicates.material_fact_misstated: The applicant stated a material fact that was contradicted by the relevant record.
predicates.false_court_authority_notice_published: The applicant published a notice in a way that represented it as having been issued under the court’s authority.

members.legal_issue: Special leave may be revoked when it was obtained on the basis of a false and materially misleading factual assertion in the petition.
material_facts: The petitioner sought special leave after the High Court dismissed his second appeal in an eviction suit.
The special leave petition asserted that a rent note did not state that the landlord’s predecessor owned the shop.
The rent note expressly identified the predecessor as the owner, and that fact was decisive to the only issue said to arise in the case.
The petitioner offered no sufficient explanation for the false assertion.
members.legal_principle: The Court’s discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 is exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases. A person invoking it must come with clean hands; a material false or misleading statement that bears on the exercise of the Court’s discretion justifies refusing relief or revoking leave already granted. The Court followed and reiterated Hari Narain v. Badri Das, [1964] 2 SCR 203 at 209, and Rajabhai Abdul Rehman Munshi v. Vasudev Dhanjibhai Mody, [1964] 3 SCR 481 at 488 and 493.
members.conclusion: The Court revoked the special leave, rejected the special leave petition, and vacated the stay.

predicates.special_leave_petition: A party asked the Supreme Court for special leave to appeal.
predicates.false_factual_assertion: The petitioner made a factual assertion that was contradicted by the relevant record.
predicates.assertion_material_to_grant: The contradicted assertion concerned a fact bearing decisively on whether leave should be granted.
predicates.special_leave_revoked: The Supreme Court withdrew the special leave it had granted.

members.legal_issue: Materially inaccurate, untrue, or misleading factual statements in an application for special leave justify revoking leave granted on that application.
material_facts: The applicant’s special-leave petition asserted that the landlord had not relied on earlier rent defaults, although the plaint expressly relied on those defaults.
The petition also asserted that the applicant had made no default after a specified date, while omitting that a court deposit had been accepted without prejudice.
The respondent sought revocation of the special leave, and the Court found the statements materially inaccurate and untrue.
The applicant argued that counsel had not relied on the statements when leave was granted and that the statements had been copied from the earlier appeal.
members.legal_principle: When considering an application for special leave, the Court takes the petition’s factual statements and grounds at face value. Applicants must take care not to make material statements that are inaccurate, untrue, or misleading; doing so betrays the Court’s confidence and may justify revoking leave. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle, and did not decide the underlying merits.
members.conclusion: The Court revoked the special leave and dismissed the appeal; it held that the arguments about what counsel urged at admission and where the statements originated did not answer the respondent’s request for revocation.

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: The matter before the Court is an appeal for which special leave was sought and granted.
predicates.petition_contains_material_falsehoods: The applicant made materially inaccurate, untrue, or misleading factual statements in the petition seeking special leave.
predicates.falsehoods_could_support_requested_leave: The false statements, if taken at face value, could assist the applicant in obtaining the requested leave.

members.legal_issue: Special leave obtained through deliberate withholding or misrepresentation of material facts may be revoked.
material_facts: A tenant had deposited money in an earlier proceeding but withdrew it before the trial court decided the later eviction suit.

The tenant knew that the money had been withdrawn, but his special leave petition omitted that fact and presented the deposit as available to the landlord, relying on the High Court’s statement that the record did not prove withdrawal.
The Supreme Court granted special leave on the misleading presentation; disclosure of the withdrawal would have affected whether the Court exercised its discretion to grant leave.
members.legal_principle: The jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary, is exercised sparingly, and is not a general appellate jurisdiction. An applicant invoking that discretion must approach the Court candidly and disclose information that may bear on its decision. If the applicant deliberately misleads the Court or withholds material information to obtain leave, the Court may refuse leave or revoke leave already granted, including at the hearing of the appeal. The Court relied on Har Narain v. Badri Das and approved S. B. Shetty v. Phirozeshah Nursservanji Colabawalla.
members.conclusion: The Court revoked the special leave and ordered the appellant to pay the respondent’s costs.

rule.if: special_leave_proceeding and leave_granted and applicant_knew_material_fact and material_fact_withheld and fact_could_affect_leave_discretion and misleading_presentation

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: The matter is an application or appeal for which the court’s special leave is sought.
predicates.leave_granted: The court granted special leave after considering the applicant’s presentation.
predicates.applicant_knew_material_fact: The applicant knew a fact relevant to the matter when making the presentation to the court.
predicates.material_fact_withheld: The applicant did not disclose that relevant fact to the court.
predicates.fact_could_affect_leave_discretion: The undisclosed fact could have affected the court’s decision whether to grant leave.
predicates.misleading_presentation: The applicant presented the matter in a way that created a materially false impression about the relevant facts.

members.legal_issue: A special-leave order may be revoked when the petition contains material statements that are misleading and bear on the Court’s decision to grant leave.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the refusal to grant a certificate after the High Court had dismissed a writ petition concerning land-acquisition proceedings.
The certificate application to the High Court had been made only under the constitutional ground concerning a question of general importance.
The special-leave petition did not specify that limited ground and stated that the appellant was entitled to a certificate as of right under alternative value-based grounds.
The Court granted special leave without being told that the certificate application had been made only on the limited ground.
The Court had separately refused leave to appeal against the dismissal of the writ petition.
members.legal_principle: An applicant seeking special leave must correctly state all material facts bearing on the Court’s exercise of discretion and on maintainability. A statement calculated or likely to mislead on such a matter may justify revoking leave. The Court relied on Rajabhai Abdul Rehman Munshi v. Vasudev Dhanjibhai Mody and Hari Narain v. Badri Das (1964) 3 SCR 203, and applied this principle to the special-leave jurisdiction under Article 136; the certificate application had been made under Article 133(1)(c), whereas the petition asserted entitlement under Article 133(1)(a) or (b).
members.conclusion: The Court revoked the order granting special leave and dismissed the appeal with costs.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and certificate_application_limited and petition_omits_application_limit and petition_claims_alternative_entitlement and statements_likely_to_mislead

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The applicant seeks appellate review after the Court has granted special leave.
predicates.certificate_application_limited: The applicant's earlier application for a certificate was made only on a limited ground.
predicates.petition_omits_application_limit: The special-leave petition does not disclose the limited ground on which the earlier certificate application was made.
predicates.petition_claims_alternative_entitlement: The special-leave petition asserts entitlement to a certificate on alternative grounds not stated in the earlier application.
predicates.statements_likely_to_mislead: The petition's statements are calculated or likely to mislead the Court on a matter bearing on its decision to grant leave.

members.legal_issue: A former minor’s suit to set aside a guardian’s transfer of immovable property and recover possession is governed by the limitation rule for setting aside a guardian’s transfer.
material_facts: The plaintiffs challenged transfers made by their mother, who was their natural guardian, of property in which they claimed shares.
The suit sought to set aside the transfers and recover possession.
The transfers were alleged to have been made without legal necessity and without the required court permission.
members.legal_principle: Sections 8(1) and 8(2)(a) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, govern the natural guardian’s authority to deal with a minor’s property and the required permission for a sale. A transfer in contravention of those requirements is voidable and must be set aside before possession can be recovered. Article 60 of the Limitation Act applies to a former minor’s suit to set aside a guardian’s transfer, including where possession is sought as consequential relief. Article 109 concerns a father’s alienation of ancestral property; Article 110 concerns enforcing a share after exclusion from joint-family property; Article 113 is residual and does not apply where Article 60 governs. No earlier cases are cited or relied on.
members.conclusion: The suit was governed by Article 60 of the Limitation Act, 1963, rather than Articles 109, 110 or 113. A former minor challenging a transfer made by a guardian in contravention of Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, and seeking possession must sue within the period prescribed by Article 60 after attaining majority.

rule.if: suit_challenges_guardian_transfer and claimant_was_minor_when_transfer and transfer_breached_guardian_authority_requirements and relief_seeks_to_set_aside_transfer

predicates.suit_challenges_guardian_transfer: The proceeding is a suit challenging a transfer of property made by a guardian.
predicates.claimant_was_minor_when_transfer: The claimant whose property interest is challenged was a minor when the transfer occurred.
predicates.transfer_breached_guardian_authority_req: The guardian made the transfer without satisfying the requirements governing dealings with the minor’s property.
predicates.relief_seeks_to_set_aside_transfer: The claimant seeks to set aside the transfer, whether or not possession is also sought.

members.legal_issue: A mother may act as the natural guardian of a minor whose share is relinquished in a family settlement, and the resulting disposition is voidable rather than void when the required court permission was not obtained.
material_facts: A mother executed a registered release on behalf of her minor daughter, relinquishing the daughter’s share in favour of other family members.
The release formed part of an arrangement dissolving or settling the family’s interests in the property.
The Karta was among the persons in whose favour the minor’s share was relinquished, creating a conflict if the Karta were treated as the minor’s guardian.
No court permission was obtained for the disposition.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6 and 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 govern natural guardianship and a natural guardian’s powers. Section 6 excludes a minor’s undivided interest in joint family property from its general rule, but a Karta is the manager of the joint family, not the guardian of its minor members. Where a family settlement relinquishes a minor’s share in favour of the Karta, the conflict prevents the Karta from acting for the minor; the mother is the natural guardian. Under Section 8, a disposition of a minor’s immovable property without the required prior court permission is voidable at the minor’s instance, not void.
members.conclusion: The mother, not the Karta, could act as the minor’s natural guardian in the circumstances; the release was not void ab initio but was at most voidable.

rule.if: minor_property_release_dispute and mother_executed_release_for_minor and minor_share_relinquished_in_family_settlement and no_court_permission_was_obtained

predicates.minor_property_release_dispute: The proceeding concerns a disposition of property belonging to a minor.
predicates.mother_executed_release_for_minor: The minor’s mother executed a release on the minor’s behalf.
predicates.minor_share_relinquished_in_family_settl: The minor’s share was relinquished as part of a family settlement in favour of another family member.
predicates.no_court_permission_was_obtained: The required prior court permission for the disposition was not obtained.

members.legal_issue: A transferee from a person who has attained majority may sue to set aside an unauthorized alienation of that person’s property made by a natural guardian during minority when the transferred right is an interest in property rather than a bare right to sue.
material_facts: A natural guardian sold the minor’s immovable property without obtaining the required court permission and without legal necessity.
After attaining majority, the former minor transferred the property to the plaintiff within the applicable limitation period.
The plaintiff sued to set aside the guardian’s sale and recover possession of the property.
members.legal_principle: Under section 8(3) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a disposal of immovable property by a natural guardian contrary to the statutory requirements is voidable at the instance of the minor or any person claiming under the minor; that expression includes a purchaser from the former minor. Section 6(e) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which bars transfer of a mere right to sue, must be read harmoniously with section 8(3): the right to defeat an adverse claim arising from a voidable guardian’s sale is an assignable interest in property, not a bare right to litigate. Section 5(b) of the Guardianship Act supports avoiding an unduly restrictive construction of the Act’s protections. The Court followed The J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Punjab National Bank, Palaniappa Goundan v. Nallappa Goundan, and P. Kamaraju v. C. Gunnayya, and rejected the contrary approach in Jhaverbhai Hathibhai Patel v. Kabhai Bechar Patel, Mon Mohan Bhattacharjee v. Bidhu Bhusan Dutta, and Palani Goundan v. Vanjiakkal.
members.conclusion: The transferee was competent to bring the suit. The former minor had transferred an assignable interest in the property, not merely a bare right to sue, so the bar on transferring a mere right to sue did not prevent the action.

rule.if: suit_challenges_guardian_alienation and guardian_was_natural_guardian and (guardian_lacked_required_approval or alienation_lacked_minor_benefit) and former_minor_transferred_property_interest and suit_brought_within_limitation

predicates.suit_challenges_guardian_alienation: The claimant brought a suit seeking to undo a transfer of property made during the owner’s minority by a guardian.
predicates.guardian_was_natural_guardian: The person who made the transfer acted as the minor’s natural guardian.
predicates.guardian_lacked_required_approval: The natural guardian made the property transfer without obtaining the required court approval.
predicates.alienation_lacked_minor_benefit: The guardian’s transfer was not made for the minor’s benefit or legal necessity.
predicates.former_minor_transferred_property_intere: After attaining majority, the former minor transferred to the claimant an interest in the property affected by the guardian’s sale.
predicates.suit_brought_within_limitation: The claimant brought the suit within the applicable limitation period.

members.legal_issue: A claim to recover property conveyed by a natural guardian in a voidable transfer is governed by the limitation period for setting aside that transfer, rather than the period for possession based on title.
material_facts: A natural guardian conveyed the minor’s immovable property by sale deeds without obtaining the court’s permission.
The minor died before attaining majority.
The persons claiming through the minor filed suit more than three years after the minor’s death, seeking declaration and possession without setting aside the sale deeds.
members.legal_principle: Article 60(b)(ii) of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a three-year period from the ward’s death for a suit to set aside a transfer made by the guardian when the ward dies before attaining majority. A suit seeking possession by avoiding a guardian’s transfer is, in substance, a suit to set aside that transfer, and Article 65 does not govern it. The Court relied on Madhukar Vishwanath v. Madahav and Narayan v. Babasaheb.
members.conclusion: The claim was governed by Article 60 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and was time-barred; Article 65 did not apply.

rule.if: minor_guardian_transfer_suit and transfer_made_by_natural_guardian and ward_died_before_majority and claim_filed_after_limitation

predicates.minor_guardian_transfer_suit: The proceeding is a claim to recover property transferred by a guardian of a minor.
predicates.transfer_made_by_natural_guardian: A natural guardian transferred the minor’s immovable property.
predicates.ward_died_before_majority: The minor died before reaching majority.
predicates.claim_filed_after_limitation: The persons claiming through the minor brought the claim after the applicable limitation period had elapsed.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of a minor’s immovable property by a natural guardian without the required prior permission is voidable, not void, and must be set aside before the minor can recover the property from the transferee.
material_facts: The minors’ mother, acting as their natural guardian, sold portions of their immovable property without obtaining prior court permission.
The courts found that the sales were not supported by legal necessity.
The plaintiffs sought possession from the purchasers while initially asserting that the transfers were void and could be ignored.
members.legal_principle: Section 8(2) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 prohibits a natural guardian from transferring a minor’s immovable property by sale without previous court permission. Section 8(3) expressly makes a disposal in contravention of that requirement voidable at the instance of the minor or a person claiming under the minor. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The transfers were voidable at the instance of the minors, so the plaintiffs had to obtain an order setting them aside before claiming recovery of the transferred property.

predicates.suit_seeks_recovery_under_guardian_trans: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking to recover property transferred by a guardian of a minor.
predicates.natural_guardian_sold_minor_immovable_pr: A natural guardian sold a minor’s immovable property without obtaining the permission required for that sale.

members.legal_issue: A revenue mutation entry is to be treated as correct unless the contrary is established, and an unchallenged entry cannot simply be disregarded.
material_facts: The trial court accepted one mutation entry as conveying title but doubted a later mutation entry in the widow’s favour.
The later entry had remained unchallenged, and the trial court placed on the appellants the burden of proving the entries correct.
The Supreme Court held that the trial court had not applied a consistent standard to the entries.
members.legal_principle: Gurbaksh Singh v. Nikka Singh holds that mutation entries must be taken as correct unless the contrary is established. An affected person must challenge an entry through the procedure provided by law; an unchallenged entry cannot be brushed aside. This evidentiary effect does not make mutation an instrument that creates or extinguishes title.
members.conclusion: Mutation entries must be taken as correct unless the contrary is established, and the unchallenged later entry could not be ignored, although mutation entries do not themselves convey title.

rule.if: dispute_involves_revenue_entries and revenue_entry_exists and contrary_to_entry_is_not_established and entry_remains_unchallenged

predicates.dispute_involves_revenue_entries: The proceeding involves a dispute about entries in revenue records.
predicates.revenue_entry_exists: A mutation entry concerning the property has been made in the revenue records.
predicates.contrary_to_entry_is_not_established: No evidence establishes that the entry is incorrect.
predicates.entry_remains_unchallenged: A person affected by the entry has not challenged it through the available legal procedure.

members.legal_issue: A registered instrument remains binding unless it is avoided by a proper declaration, and merely pleading that it is void does not establish that it is void.
material_facts: The plaintiff argued that the later sale deed was void because it had been executed to stifle a prosecution and that she could seek only a declaration of ownership while remaining in possession.
The registered deed recited valuable consideration and the discharge of pre-existing debts.
No issue was raised, and no finding was made, that the deed was void under section 23 of the Contract Act; the plaintiff's pleading alone did not establish that claim.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Evidence Act barred oral evidence contradicting the deed's recitals. Section 23 of the Contract Act was not a basis for treating the deed as void because no issue or finding to that effect existed; pleading alone was insufficient. A duly registered instrument remains valid and binding until avoided by proper declaration. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The court rejected the argument that the plaintiff could avoid the deed without seeking its avoidance or cancellation. Until avoided by a proper declaration, the duly registered deed remained valid and binding.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenging_registered_instrument and instrument_is_registered and invalidity_is_only_pleaded and instrument_not_avoided_by_court

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_registered_instru: A party brought a civil suit challenging the effect or validity of an instrument.
predicates.invalidity_is_only_pleaded: The party alleged that the instrument was invalid, but the allegation was not established by an adjudication that it was void.
predicates.instrument_not_avoided_by_court: A court had not avoided or cancelled the instrument by a proper declaration.

members.legal_issue: A registered instrument is presumed to have been validly executed unless the party challenging it rebuts that presumption.
material_facts: The plaintiff challenged the sale deed.
The deed was treated as a registered document, and the plaintiff failed to rebut the presumption of valid execution.
members.legal_principle: A registered document is presumed to have been validly executed and is prima facie valid in law; the party adducing evidence to challenge it bears the burden of rebutting that presumption.
members.conclusion: The presumption that the registered deed was validly executed stood unrebutted, and the burden of rebutting it rested on the plaintiff.

predicates.registered_instrument_challenged: A party brought a claim challenging an instrument that had been registered.
predicates.challenger_fails_to_rebut_valid_executio: The party challenging the instrument did not rebut the presumption that it was validly executed.

members.legal_issue: A substituted revenue entry supported by facts proved before the revenue authorities is presumed correct unless the party challenging it proves otherwise.
material_facts: The original revenue entry incorrectly recorded the whole land in the name of one co-sharer, although the co-sharers' partition allocated shares of one-eighth and seven-eighths.
A corrected entry was made following an inquiry by a subordinate revenue officer whose report and annexures recited the partition and the co-sharers' application for mutation.
The transferor's admission occurred after he had transferred his interest and could not by itself bind the purchaser.
The purchaser adduced no evidence to rebut the presumption arising from the corrected entry.
members.legal_principle: Section 37(a) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 permits entries to be made in accordance with facts proved or admitted to have occurred. Under section 44, an entry made in accordance with the law is presumed true until the contrary is proved or a new entry is lawfully substituted. Although an admission by a person made after parting with an interest cannot itself bind a purchaser, other evidence proving the relevant facts may support the entry and give rise to the presumption.
members.conclusion: The corrected entry was made in accordance with facts proved before the revenue authorities, was presumed correct, and was not rebutted by the purchaser.

predicates.corrected_revenue_entry_disputed: A party disputes the correctness of a substituted entry in a revenue record.
predicates.substituted_entry_supported_by_facts_pro: The substituted entry was made on the basis of facts proved before the authorities responsible for the record.
predicates.challenger_adduced_no_rebuttal_evidence: The party challenging the entry presented no evidence sufficient to disprove it.

members.legal_issue: A registered sale deed is presumed validly executed unless the person challenging it rebuts that presumption with reliable evidence.
material_facts: The disputed property was conveyed by a registered sale deed that recited the consideration and the vendor’s voluntary execution of it.
The person who prepared and witnessed the deed testified that the vendor executed it on his instructions and of his own free will; the trial court found this evidence credible.

The challenger relied on a doctor’s evidence and a medical certificate, but the doctor had prepared the certificate from memory and the trial court did not find the evidence sufficient to show that the vendor could not understand the deed.
The trial court found the deed valid, but the first appellate court and the High Court held it invalid and placed the burden of proving its validity on the purchaser.
members.legal_principle: A registered document carries a presumption of valid execution, and the burden of rebutting it lies on the person challenging the transaction. The Court relied on Prem Singh v. Birbal (2006) 5 SCC 353 and Vishwanath Bapurao Sabale v. Shalinibai Nagappa Sabale (2009) 12 SCC 101.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court and the High Court erred in holding the registered sale deed invalid and in placing the burden of proof on the purchaser; the challenger did not rebut the presumption of valid execution.

rule.if: civil_property_dispute and registered_sale_deed and execution_supported_by_credible_evidence and challenger_lacks_reliable_rebuttal

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The parties litigate rights in property through a civil proceeding.
predicates.registered_sale_deed: The disputed transfer is recorded in a registered sale deed.
predicates.execution_supported_by_credible_evidence: Evidence from a person involved in preparing or witnessing the deed supports that the transferor executed it voluntarily.
predicates.challenger_lacks_reliable_rebuttal: The person challenging the deed does not produce reliable evidence sufficient to rebut valid execution.

members.legal_issue: A revisional order setting aside a decision without deciding the relevant claims on their merits after considering the evidence must be set aside and the matter remanded for a merits determination.
material_facts: The revisional authority did not consider the issues concerning two landholdings on their merits.
It set aside the Assistant Settlement Officer’s order without proper consideration of the matter.
Oral and documentary evidence concerning those landholdings remained to be considered.
members.legal_principle: The revisional authority must consider the relevant issues on their merits and assess the pertinent evidence before setting aside the decision under review. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The orders of the High Court and the revisional authority, insofar as they concerned the two landholdings, were set aside, and the revision was remanded to the revisional authority for a decision on the merits after considering the oral and documentary evidence.

predicates.consolidation_revision: The proceeding is a revision concerning a consolidation matter.
predicates.material_issue_not_decided_on_merits: The revisional authority did not decide a material issue in the revision on its merits.
predicates.relevant_evidence_not_considered: The revisional authority did not consider relevant oral or documentary evidence before making its decision.
predicates.decision_set_aside_and_case_remanded_for: The decision is set aside and the matter is returned to the revisional authority for a merits decision.

members.legal_issue: When a supervisory court's decision is set aside and a disputed issue remains undecided, the proceeding may be remitted for fresh determination of that issue.
material_facts: The High Court had not considered the parties' disputed claims about whether either of them had other premises available.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment after rejecting its reason for overturning the appellate court's finding.
The dispute about other available premises remained for determination.
members.legal_principle: Where an appellate court sets aside a decision but a material disputed point has not yet been considered, it may remit the proceeding for that point to be decided afresh. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this remand direction.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court judgment was set aside, and the writ petition was remitted to the High Court to decide the remaining disputed issue.

predicates.appeal_against_supervisory_decision: An appeal challenges a decision made by a court exercising supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.supervisory_decision_set_aside: The appellate court sets aside the supervisory court's decision.
predicates.material_disputed_issue_remains_undecide: A material disputed issue that requires determination has not been decided.

members.legal_issue: Documents admitted as additional evidence must be proved before they can be considered, and the matter may be remanded to allow that proof and a fresh decision.
material_facts: The Court allowed the claimant to bring the proposed sale deeds and certified copies of awards on record as additional evidence.
The documents had not yet been proved as to their existence, authenticity, genuineness, or contents.
The Reference Court needed to receive and assess the proof before determining compensation afresh.
members.legal_principle: Allowing an application under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC does not itself establish additional documents or permit them to be taken into consideration without proof. The applicant must prove their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents in accordance with law. The Court relied on Uttaradi Mutt v. Raghavendra Swamy Mutt, (2018) 10 SCC 484.
members.conclusion: Admission of the documents did not make them automatically exhibitable or establish their contents. The claimant had to prove them in accordance with law before they could be considered, and the matter was remanded to the Reference Court for that purpose and a fresh decision.

predicates.civil_appeal_with_additional_documents_a: A court in a civil appeal admits documents as additional evidence.
predicates.documents_not_yet_proved: The admitted documents have not yet been proved as to their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents.

members.legal_issue: Where additional evidence is admitted and the circumstances make a fresh determination necessary, the matter may be remanded for a new decision on the merits without relying on the decisions set aside.
material_facts: The trial court had dismissed the suit on limitation and title, and the High Court had dismissed the first appeal.
The Court admitted additional evidence relevant to the ownership dispute and afforded the respondents an opportunity to offer rebuttal evidence.
Having regard to the controversy and the manner in which the suit and appeal had been decided, the Court chose to remand the suit to the trial court for retrial.
The Court made no finding on the merits of the ownership dispute.
members.legal_principle: After allowing additional evidence and providing for rebuttal, the Court must ensure the dispute is determined on the resulting record. In this case, given the nature of the controversy and the manner in which the proceedings had been decided, the appropriate course was to set aside the judgments and remand the suit for a fresh decision on the merits; no view was expressed on those merits.
members.conclusion: The judgments below were set aside, the suit was restored for retrial on the merits, and the trial court was directed to decide it on the pleadings and evidence without being influenced by the findings set aside.

predicates.civil_suit_decided_below: A civil suit has already been decided by a trial court and reviewed on appeal.
predicates.additional_evidence_admitted: Additional evidence is admitted for consideration in resolving the dispute.
predicates.fresh_merits_determination_needed: The dispute requires a fresh decision on the merits in light of the evidence and the manner in which the earlier proceedings were decided.

members.legal_issue: A revisional decision that leaves the scope of remand unclear and may constrain reconsideration should be set aside for fresh consideration.
material_facts: The Supreme Court was hearing an appeal against the Custodian-General’s revisional decision.
The decision set aside a confirmation order and remitted the matter, but it was unclear whether the remand was general or limited.
The Custodian-General had made findings and expressed views that could make it difficult for the authority reconsidering the matter to address the issues afresh.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its appellate jurisdiction, the Court held that the unclear scope and reasoning of the revisional decision made it difficult to maintain. It directed fresh consideration and stated that, if the matter were remanded again, the matters to be considered should be clearly indicated. The Court expressed no opinion on the disputed merits of the confirmation.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the revisional decision and remitted the matter to the Custodian-General for fresh consideration, with an opportunity for both sides to present their views and clarification of any further remand.

predicates.appeal_against_revisional_decision: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an authority’s revisional decision.
predicates.remand_scope_unclear: The revisional decision does not make clear whether its remand is general or limited.
predicates.findings_may_constrain_reconsideration: The decision includes findings or views that may prevent the matter from being reconsidered openly.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking inheritance must prove when the person whose estate is claimed died if that fact is essential to the succession, because the presumption arising from prolonged absence does not establish the exact time of death.
