material_facts: The claimant sought succession to a person's estate as a collateral relative.
The person had not been heard from for more than seven years.
The claimant neither pleaded nor proved the date of that person's death.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 107 and 108 of the Evidence Act, prolonged absence may give rise to a presumption of death, but Section 108 does not presume the exact time of death. The person claiming a right for which the date of death is essential bears the burden of proving that date. The Court relied on Sri Vidya Mandir Education Society (Regd.) v. Malleswaram Sangeetha Sabha and Others, which noticed Lal Chand Marwari v. Mahant Ramrup Gir and Another.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not establish that succession to the estate had opened by the date the suit was filed, and the lower courts erred in treating the suit filing date as the date of death.

predicates.succession_claim: A person sought to inherit an estate through a claimed relationship to the person whose estate was at issue.
predicates.death_date_essential_to_claim: The claimed succession depended on establishing when the person whose estate was claimed died.
predicates.exact_death_date_not_proved: The claimant did not establish the exact date of that person's death.

members.legal_issue: The presumption arising from a person being unheard of for seven years does not establish the date of death, so a claimant whose title depends on death after a legally significant change must prove that timing.
material_facts: Two brothers acquired the disputed property as joint family property, and one brother was a coparcener.
The missing brother was last heard of in 1930, and his wife later sold an interest in the property to the plaintiffs’ predecessor.
The plaintiffs’ claimed interest depended on the missing brother having died after the relevant property law came into force, so that his wife acquired an interest.
The plaintiffs relied on the fact that the missing brother had not been heard of for more than seven years and produced no evidence establishing when he died.
The surviving coparcener later sold the property to the first defendant.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 107 and 108 of the Indian Evidence Act, proof that a person has not been heard of for seven years by those who would naturally have heard from him shifts the burden of proving that he is alive and supports a presumption of death when the question arises. It does not presume the date of death, whether during the seven-year period or at its end; a party whose claim depends on death at a particular time must prove that fact. The Court applied the Privy Council’s decision in Lal Chand Marwari v. Mahant Ramrup Gir, which states that the fact of death may be presumed but its timing is a matter of proof.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs did not prove that the missing brother died after the relevant law came into force. The presumption of death did not establish a particular date of death, so the wife was not shown to have acquired an interest to convey. The surviving coparcener was entitled to convey the property, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: property_title_appeal and person_unheard_seven_years and title_depends_on_death_after_legal_change and no_evidence_of_death_time and claimant_relies_only_on_absence

predicates.property_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning competing claims to title in property.
predicates.person_unheard_seven_years: A person was not heard of for at least seven years by people who would naturally have heard from that person if alive.
predicates.title_depends_on_death_after_legal_chang: A claimant's asserted property interest depends on the person's having died after a legally significant change.
predicates.no_evidence_of_death_time: The claimant offers no evidence establishing when the person died.
predicates.claimant_relies_only_on_absence: The claimant relies only on the person's prolonged absence to establish the timing of death.
predicates.claimant_cannot_establish_title_through_: The claimant cannot establish title through an interest allegedly acquired by the missing person's spouse.

members.legal_issue: A claimant relying on a presumption of death to establish a timely right to possession must prove the time of death when the limitation period depends on when that right accrued.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession of ancestral property after obtaining a declaratory decree concerning an earlier alienation.
The right to seek possession accrued when the last owner died and the line of succession became extinct.
The last owner had not been heard of for more than seven years, but the plaintiffs did not prove when within that period he died.
The applicable limitation period for a possession suit following a declaratory decree was three years from accrual of the right to sue.
members.legal_principle: Article 2(b) of the Schedule to the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 required suit within three years of accrual of the right to sue. Under section 108 of the Evidence Act, 1872, seven years without being heard of permits a presumption of death, but does not presume the precise time of death; a claimant whose right depends on death at a particular time must prove that timing. The Court relied on Nepean v. Doe D. Knight, Jayawant Jivarao Deshpande v. Ramachandra Narayan Joshi, Lalchand Marwari v. Ramrup Gir, Jiwan Singh v. Kuar Reoti Singh, Kottappalli Venkateswarlu v. Kottapalli Bapayya, Punjab v. Natha, and Ram Kali v. Narain Singh.
members.conclusion: The presumption that the missing owner was dead did not establish the time of death. Because the plaintiffs did not prove that he died within three years before filing, they failed to establish that the suits were timely.

rule.if: ancestral_property_possession_suit_after_declaratory_decree and right_to_sue_depends_on_owner_death and owner_unheard_for_seven_years and not evidence_places_death_within_limitation_period

predicates.ancestral_property_possession_suit_after: The plaintiffs brought a possession suit concerning ancestral property after a declaratory decree had been obtained concerning its alienation.
predicates.right_to_sue_depends_on_owner_death: The plaintiffs’ right to seek possession depended on the last owner’s death and the resulting opening of succession.
predicates.owner_unheard_for_seven_years: The plaintiffs established that the owner had not been heard of for at least seven years by those who would naturally have heard of him if he were alive.
predicates.evidence_places_death_within_limitation_: The plaintiffs produced evidence establishing that the owner died within the period that would make the possession suit timely.

members.legal_issue: A presumption of death arising from a person not being heard of for seven years does not establish the date on which that person died.
material_facts: The life-interest holder had not been heard of for more than seven years by people who would naturally have heard from her if she were alive.
Neither side proved her actual date of death.
The dispute involved the date of death, rather than whether she was presumed to be dead.
members.legal_principle: Sections 107 and 108 of the Indian Evidence Act distinguish the presumption that a person is dead from proof of the time of death. The person asserting death at a particular time bears the burden of proving it. The Court relied on Lal Chand Marwari v. Mahant Ramrups Gir and LIC of India v. Anuradha.
members.conclusion: The court could presume that she was dead once the required seven-year absence had elapsed, but could not presume that she died at any particular time during that period or seven years before the suit.

predicates.civil_case_requires_determination_of_dea: A civil dispute requires the court to determine when a person died.
predicates.person_unheard_for_seven_years_by_those_: The person had not been heard of for at least seven years by people who would naturally have heard from the person if alive.
predicates.death_time_not_proved: No party proved the person’s death at a particular time.

members.legal_issue: Death cannot be presumed from a person’s disappearance when the person has been unheard of for less than seven years by those who would naturally have heard from them if alive.
material_facts: The deceased disappeared and could not be traced after a police inquiry.
The question of death arose about two years after the disappearance.
The court considered whether a presumption of death arose from the disappearance.
members.legal_principle: A presumption of death may arise when a person has not been heard of for seven years by those who would naturally have heard from that person if they had been alive. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: No presumption of death arose because the deceased had been unheard of for only about two years.

predicates.death_determination_proceeding: A proceeding requires a decision about whether or when a missing person died.
predicates.missing_person_unheard_of_by_natural_con: People who would naturally have heard from the missing person if that person were alive have heard nothing from them.
predicates.unheard_for_under_seven_years: The period during which the person has been unheard of is less than seven years.

members.legal_issue: At the discharge stage, the court must assess the prosecution material on its face value for grounds to presume that an offence was committed, rather than conduct a mini trial or assess whether conviction is certain.
material_facts: The respondent sought discharge under Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The charge sheet referred to material apart from the spy-camera recording.
The High Court rejected the prosecution's reliance on that other material as unconvincing without assessing it under the discharge-stage standard.
The trial court had dismissed the discharge application.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court considers whether the facts emerging from the prosecution material, taken at face value, disclose the ingredients of the offence and whether there is ground for presuming that the accused committed it. The court may consider the probative value of the material but must not decide whether it warrants conviction or conduct a mini trial. State of Tamil Nadu v N Suresh Rajan states this standard.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in quashing the proceedings. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and maintained the trial court's dismissal of the discharge application.

predicates.discharge_application_proceeding: The court was deciding an application to discharge an accused before trial.
predicates.charge_sheet_contains_prosecution_materi: The prosecution's charge sheet included material on which it relied to support the alleged offence.
predicates.face_value_material_discloses_offence_in: Taken at face value, the prosecution material disclosed the ingredients of the alleged offence.

members.legal_issue: At the charge stage, a court may not discharge accused by deciding the merits without evidence being tried when the prosecution materials disclose a prima facie case.
material_facts: The prosecution records disclosed alleged wrongful demarcations, cutting of government trees, improper compounding of an offence, and a forged agreement and application.
The Special Judge assessed the merits, relied on assumptions and surmises, and discharged the accused without recording evidence.
The court found that the question whether the charges would ultimately be proved could be decided only after evidence was recorded.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, discharge is available when the charge is groundless. At the charge stage, the court asks whether a prima facie case is made out; it must not determine whether the charges will ultimately be proved or decide the case on its merits without evidence. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The discharge order was unsustainable; the case had to be restored for charges to be framed and the trial to proceed.

predicates.case_is_at_charge_stage: The court was deciding whether the accused should be charged and tried.
predicates.prosecution_material_discloses_prima_fac: The prosecution materials, if considered at the threshold, disclosed a prima facie case against the accused.
predicates.judge_decided_merits_without_trial_evide: The judge resolved the merits of the allegations without first recording evidence at trial.

members.legal_issue: A judge considering whether to frame a charge must independently assess whether the record provides sufficient ground to proceed, rather than automatically accepting the prosecution’s case.
material_facts: The prosecution submitted a charge-sheet to a Special Judge alleging offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act and conspiracy.
The Special Judge considered the charge-sheet, witness statements recorded by police, and other documents before discharging the accused.
The proceedings before the Special Judge followed the procedure applicable to sessions trials.
members.legal_principle: Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 applies mutatis mutandis to proceedings before a Special Judge after submission of the charge-sheet. The judge may sift and weigh evidence for the limited purpose of deciding whether a prima facie case exists, and must consider broad probabilities, the total effect of the evidence and documents, and basic infirmities without conducting a trial or a roving inquiry. The Court applied State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh, K. P. Raghavan v. M. H. Abbas, and Almohan Das v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The Special Judge must sift the material for the limited purpose of deciding whether sufficient ground exists to proceed. Grave suspicion that remains unexplained can justify framing a charge, but if the evidence gives rise only to some suspicion, two views are equally possible, and the judge is satisfied there is no sufficient ground to proceed, discharge is justified.

rule.if: pretrial_charge_stage and evidence_only_some_suspicion and two_views_equally_possible and no_sufficient_ground_to_proceed

predicates.pretrial_charge_stage: The court is considering whether to proceed to trial on the material submitted by the prosecution.
predicates.evidence_only_some_suspicion: The prosecution material raises some suspicion against the accused but does not disclose grave suspicion.
predicates.two_views_equally_possible: The material reasonably permits two competing views of the case.
predicates.no_sufficient_ground_to_proceed: The judge concludes, after assessing the material for the limited pretrial purpose, that there is not sufficient ground to proceed against the accused.

members.legal_issue: At the pre-charge stage of a sessions trial, the judge must independently assess whether the prosecution materials provide sufficient ground to proceed, without conducting a full trial of the evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution filed a charge-sheet alleging that the accused had conspired to obtain compensation through the acquisition of land.
The Special Judge considered the charge-sheet, police statements and other documents before discharging the accused.
The proceedings before the Special Judge followed sessions-trial procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 requires the judge to consider the record, accompanying documents and submissions, and to discharge the accused if there is not sufficient ground to proceed. Under State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh, strong suspicion may justify framing a charge but does not replace proof at trial; if the prosecution evidence, even accepted as it stands, cannot show commission of the offence, there is no sufficient ground to proceed. K.P. Raghavan v. M.H. Abbas and Almohan Das v. State of West Bengal support the principle that the judge is not a mere recording machine and may assess whether a prima facie case exists, without deciding whether the evidence is sufficient for conviction.
members.conclusion: The judge is not required to frame a charge at the prosecution’s request. The judge may sift and weigh the materials for the limited purpose of deciding whether a prima facie case exists; the judge must discharge the accused if there is no sufficient ground for proceeding and record reasons.

predicates.sessions_procedure_precharge: The matter is before the judge responsible for a sessions trial, or a proceeding that applies sessions procedure, before charges are framed.
predicates.no_prima_facie_evidence: The materials, even if accepted as presented, do not disclose a prima facie case that the accused committed an offence.
predicates.two_views_equally_possible: The materials permit two views that are equally possible at the pre-charge stage.
predicates.suspicion_not_grave: The materials give rise to suspicion against the accused, but not grave suspicion.

members.legal_issue: An accused should not be discharged at the preliminary stage when the allegations, if true, disclose the charged offences and the preliminary record makes out a prima facie case, merely because the dispute also involves civil title.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that the accused trespassed on an orchard, destroyed it, and removed trees, and charged them with offences including mischief, criminal trespass, and theft committed with common intention.
The complainant gave evidence and produced revenue records and witnesses concerning possession of the land.
The preliminary court found a prima facie case against some accused, and the Magistrate declined to discharge them.
The High Court discharged the accused after relying on the history and outcome of civil litigation concerning the land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 253(2) of the CrPC, where the allegations, if true, disclose the offences charged and the preliminary material makes out a prima facie case, the accused must stand trial. The possibility of a dispute over civil title does not justify discharge on these facts; the Supreme Court did not decide the title question. The alleged offences were under Sections 427, 447, 379 and 34 of the IPC. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in discharging the accused under Section 253(2) of the CrPC. The discharge order was set aside and the trial was directed to proceed.

predicates.criminal_complaint_discharge_proceeding: A criminal complaint is before the court and an application seeks discharge of the accused at the preliminary stage.
predicates.allegations_if_true_disclose_charged_off: The complaint alleges conduct which, if true, constitutes the offences charged.
predicates.preliminary_record_supports_allegations: The preliminary evidence and material support the complaint allegations sufficiently to make out a prima facie case.
predicates.accused_must_stand_trial: The accused are not discharged at the preliminary stage and the prosecution proceeds to trial.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot rely on account books that were not proved at trial when doing so deprives the opposing party of an opportunity to challenge the material.
material_facts: The claimant relied at trial on extracts that he said he had prepared from his account books, but the original books were not produced and the extracts were not shown to have been verified against them.
The extracts were not established as admissible evidence at trial.

On appeal, the High Court inspected the original books and relied on them to find that the claimed earnest money had been paid, without giving the opposing party an opportunity to cross-examine the claimant about the books or their entries.
members.legal_principle: Account books that have not been proved in evidence cannot be used to establish the asserted transactions merely because an appellate court later inspects them. Where material is considered without the opposing party having an opportunity to challenge it through cross-examination, the appellate court cannot rely on it to determine the issue. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in inspecting and relying on the books of account in those circumstances; the books had not been proved at trial and the extracts were inadmissible.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_decision: The matter is an appeal from a decision made after a trial.
predicates.account_books_not_proved_at_trial: A party did not prove the account books at trial, and any extracts were not established as admissible evidence.
predicates.appellate_court_relies_on_books_without_: The appellate court relies on the books without allowing the opposing party an opportunity to challenge them.
predicates.appellate_court_must_not_rely_on_unprove: The appellate court must not rely on the unproved books to decide the issue.

members.legal_issue: A first appellate court cannot rely on additional evidence against a party without giving that party an opportunity to adduce rebuttal evidence.
material_facts: In appeals from the dismissal of four civil suits, the plaintiffs were permitted to introduce additional evidence for the first time at the appellate stage.
The first appellate court relied on that evidence to allow the appeals and decree the suits without giving the defendants an opportunity to present rebuttal evidence.
The defendants were prejudiced by the adverse decision based on evidence they had no opportunity to counter.
members.legal_principle: When additional evidence is admitted in an appeal under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the opposing party must have an opportunity to meet that evidence, including by adducing rebuttal evidence. The Court relied on Land Acquisition Officer, City Improvement Trust Board v. H. Narayanaiah, (1976) 4 SCC 9; Shalimar Chemical Works Ltd. v. Surendra Oil & Dal Mills (Refineries), (2010) 8 SCC 423; and Akhilesh Singh v. Lal Babu Singh, (2018) 4 SCC 759.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court’s decision on the merits could not be sustained because it relied on additional evidence without giving the opposing party an opportunity to rebut it.

rule.if: first_appeal and additional_evidence_admitted and not rebuttal_opportunity

predicates.first_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a trial court’s decision.
predicates.additional_evidence_admitted: The appellate court admits additional evidence and relies on it in deciding the appeal.
predicates.rebuttal_opportunity: The party opposing the additional evidence is given an opportunity to present evidence to counter it.

members.legal_issue: A revisional decision based on new documentary evidence cannot stand when the affected party is denied a fair opportunity to meet that evidence.
material_facts: The State relied on copies of documents to support its claim to the property, and the Custodian-General relied on those documents in reaching the decision.
The documents were introduced in the revision proceeding, and the originals were not produced there.
The affected parties were not told that the copies had been admitted and were not given an opportunity to inspect the documents or present evidence in rejoinder.
The Custodian-General set aside the earlier order on the basis of the State’s case.
members.legal_principle: The rules of natural justice require a fair opportunity to answer evidence relied on against a party. Under rule 31(9) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Central Rules, 1950, the revisional authority may admit additional evidence in an appropriate case, but a party has no right to have additional evidence admitted. The authority must decide whether to admit it in the interests of justice, and an affected party must be allowed to meet evidence that is admitted and relied on.
members.conclusion: The procedure violated natural justice; the Custodian-General’s order was set aside and the matter was remanded for the documents to be formally tendered and both sides to have an opportunity to present evidence and submissions.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A revisional authority is deciding whether to disturb an earlier order.
predicates.new_evidence_relied_on: A party presents evidence not previously on the record, and the revisional authority relies on it in deciding the matter.
predicates.affected_party_denied_opportunity_to_ans: The party affected by the new evidence is not given a fair chance to inspect, rebut, or respond to it.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court may not rely on additional documents that have not been formally admitted and proved in evidence without giving the opposing party an opportunity to respond.
material_facts: The landlord filed a copy of his wife’s will and related documents with an application for additional evidence in the High Court.

The High Court considered the will although the application had not been formally allowed, the documents had not been admitted and proved in evidence, and the tenant had not been afforded an opportunity to adduce evidence in response.

The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in considering the will, but held that excluding the documents did not alter the result because the remaining material supported eviction.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the application under Order 41 Rule 27 read with Section 151 CPC and held that additional documents cannot be treated as evidence without formal admission and proof and an opportunity for the opposing party to respond. The Court did not rely on the will in sustaining the ultimate eviction finding.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in considering the unadmitted will, but the eviction order remained sustainable without those documents.

rule.if: eviction_revision_case and additional_documents_considered and documents_not_admitted_or_proved and opposing_party_denied_response_opportunity

predicates.eviction_revision_case: The proceeding is a revision concerning an eviction order.
predicates.additional_documents_considered: The revisional court takes additional documents into account in deciding the proceeding.
predicates.documents_not_admitted_or_proved: The additional documents have not been formally admitted and proved as evidence.
predicates.opposing_party_denied_response_opportuni: The opposing party has not been given an opportunity to adduce evidence in response to the additional documents.

members.legal_issue: A court may not rely on fresh documents considered outside the record without admitting them as evidence and giving the opposing party an opportunity to rebut them.
material_facts: The High Court considered documents that were not part of the record.
The documents were considered after the arguments had concluded.
The appellants were not given an opportunity to rebut conclusions drawn from those documents.
members.legal_principle: If a court wishes to take fresh evidence into consideration, it must admit that evidence in accordance with law and give the opposing party an opportunity to rebut it. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have relied on the documents; they were excluded from consideration, although their exclusion did not assist the appellants in the result.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and fresh_documents_considered and documents_not_admitted_as_evidence and opposing_party_denied_chance_to_rebut

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is being considered by an appellate court.
predicates.fresh_documents_considered: The court considered documents that had not previously formed part of the record.
predicates.documents_not_admitted_as_evidence: The documents were not admitted as evidence in accordance with law.
predicates.opposing_party_denied_chance_to_rebut: The opposing party was not given an opportunity to answer or rebut the documents.

members.legal_issue: Applying a tenancy reform enactment to one region of a state does not deny equal protection when the relevant tenancies in that region are materially different from those in other regions and the challenger has not established that the groups are similarly situated.
material_facts: The enactment applied to the Cochin region rather than throughout the state.
The Board claimed that this regional application discriminated against landholders compared with landholders in Travancore and Malabar.
The governing legal regimes and incidents of kanam tenure differed among the three regions, including differences concerning renewal fees and security of tenure.
The Board did not plead or establish sufficient facts showing that landholders across the regions were similarly situated.
The High Court’s findings concerning the differences among the regional regimes were not challenged.
members.legal_principle: A claimant alleging a breach of Article 14 must plead and establish with sufficient particulars that persons subjected to different treatment are similarly situated and that the discrimination lacks an intelligible basis. If similarity is established, the State may have to show that the distinction rests on a rational basis related to the legislative object. The Court considered the distinct historical and statutory regimes governing kanam tenancies in Cochin, Travancore, and Malabar. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The enactment does not infringe the guarantee of equal protection under Article 14.

rule.if: regional_legislation_equality_challenge and enactment_limited_to_one_region and regional_tenure_regimes_differ and challenger_fails_to_establish_similarity

predicates.regional_legislation_equality_challenge: The proceeding challenges the equal-protection validity of legislation that applies differently across regions.
predicates.enactment_limited_to_one_region: The challenged enactment applies in one region but not throughout the wider state.
predicates.regional_tenure_regimes_differ: The legal rules or material incidents governing the relevant tenancies differ between the regions compared.
predicates.challenger_fails_to_establish_similarity: The challenger does not plead and establish that the people receiving different treatment are similarly situated.

members.legal_issue: Differences between the rent-regulation laws of different States do not, by themselves, make one State's law invalid under Article 14.
material_facts: The petitioner argued that rent-fixation provisions in other States were fairer, more just, and more reasonable than the challenged provision.
The challenged law and the laws from other States had been enacted by different legislatures, each choosing a method it considered suited to its State.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not authorize invalidating one State's law through a comparative study of laws enacted by different legislatures, and legislative choice among methods suited to different States is not a ground for challenging validity. The Court relied on Prabhakaran Nair v. State of Tamil Nadu and others, [1987] 4 SCC 238.
members.conclusion: Article 14 does not permit a State law to be struck down merely because its provisions differ from those of laws on the same subject in other States.

predicates.state_law_validity_challenge: A person brought a proceeding challenging the validity of a law enacted by a State legislature.
predicates.cross_state_comparison_only: The challenger relied on differences between the challenged law and laws on the same subject enacted by other States.

members.legal_issue: A difference between one state's rent-control law and the laws of other states does not, by itself, establish an equality violation.
material_facts: The challengers relied on the fact that rent-control laws in several other states provided for tenants to return to premises after reconstruction, while the challenged law did not.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not permit a law of one state to be struck down merely because it differs from a law on the same subject enacted by another state; the Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. G.C. Mandawar.
members.conclusion: The difference between the challenged law and rent laws enacted by other states does not by itself make the challenged law unconstitutional under Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law enacted by a state.
predicates.challenged_law_differs_from_other_states: The challenged law differs from laws on the same subject enacted by other states.

members.legal_issue: Territorial application of tenancy legislation does not deny equality solely because it applies to only part of a state.
material_facts: The challenged rent-settlement scheme applied to the former territory of Marwar and not to every area of the larger state.
The respondents stated that rents and cesses in the relevant tenancy area had been higher than those in other areas and that earlier local laws had addressed those differences.
The petitioners neither alleged nor proved that conditions in the other areas were similar to those in the area covered by the scheme; the other areas also had their own rent laws.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits unequal treatment of persons similarly situated. Territorial classification is permissible when germane to the enactment's purpose, and tenancy legislation is not invalid merely because it does not cover an entire state. The Court referred to Bowman v. Lewis, and applied the principles in Biswambhar Singh v. The State of Orissa and Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan.
members.conclusion: The scheme did not violate Article 14 merely because it applied to only part of the state; the petitioners had not established that persons in the differently treated areas were similarly situated.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_regional_ten: A party challenged the constitutionality of a tenancy law that applies to only part of a larger state.
predicates.local_tenancy_conditions_differ: The tenancy conditions in the covered area differed from conditions in areas outside the law's coverage.
predicates.comparable_conditions_not_proved: The challenger did not establish that conditions in the covered and uncovered areas were similar.

members.legal_issue: Historical differences between parallel laws in different regions of a reorganized state do not, by themselves, violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The state was formed from regions that had previously belonged to different states and therefore had different laws governing religious trusts.
The challenged differences between the regional laws arose from that historical background.
The state was considering steps to assimilate the laws.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Article 14 and Bhaiyalal Shukla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 257, which upheld parallel but differing laws in regions of a reorganized state where the distinction arose from historical reasons. State of Rajasthan v. Rao Manohar Singhji, [1954] S.C.R. 996, was distinguished because it concerned a group singled out for unequal treatment without a real and substantial basis.
members.conclusion: The differences between the laws did not violate Article 14.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_parallel_regional_: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of different laws applying in different regions of the same state.
predicates.laws_differ_between_regions: The regions have different laws governing the same general subject.
predicates.difference_arose_from_historical_state_r: The differing laws remained in place because the regions previously belonged to different states.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s rights in premises governed by the Act could not be transferred by will to take effect after the tenant’s death.
material_facts: The deceased tenant carried on business in the shop.
The claimant asserted that a will conveyed the tenancy rights to him.
The Act’s scheme restricted a tenant’s ability to transfer or sublet tenancy rights and regulated occupation by persons outside the tenant’s family.
The Court found that the will, on its plain reading, concerned other property and the business but did not dispose of the tenancy rights.
members.legal_principle: Sections 11, 12, 13 and 15 of the Act, read with Section 3(g), restrict the transfer or subletting of tenancy rights and regulate occupation by persons outside the tenant’s family. From this scheme, the Court concluded that a tenant could not transfer tenancy rights and that the scheme did not permit such a transfer to take effect after the tenant’s lifetime.
members.conclusion: The tenancy rights could not be transferred by will to take effect after the tenant’s death; in any event, the will did not cover the tenancy rights.

predicates.testamentary_tenancy_claim: A claimant relied on a will as the basis for acquiring a tenant’s rights in the premises.
predicates.tenancy_transfer_restricted_by_occupancy: The governing occupancy scheme restricted the tenant’s transfer or subletting of tenancy rights.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s agricultural tenancy interest cannot be transferred through a testamentary bequest as a means of obtaining tenancy rights.
material_facts: A tenant applied for occupancy rights in agricultural land under the governing land-reform scheme.
While the application was pending, the tenant made a will bequeathing his tenancy rights; a later claimant asserted rights through a further will made by the first beneficiary.
The tenant’s wife and children were awarded occupancy rights by the Land Tribunal, and the appellate authority and High Court left that decision undisturbed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 21 and 24 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 must be read together: Section 21 prohibits assignment of an interest in the tenanted land, subject to its specified family and heir exceptions, while Section 24 continues the tenancy after the tenant’s death on the same terms for the heirs. The relevant heirs are determined by personal law but remain subject to Section 21. A devise under a will is an assignment for this purpose because it deals with and disposes of the tenancy interest, and allowing it would permit strangers to enter the land. The Court regarded Timmakka Kom Venkanna Naik v. The Land Tribunal as the better view and declined to follow the broader statements in Shivanna v. Rachiah and Dhareppa v. State of Karnataka. Angurbala Mullick v. Debabrata Mullick did not assist the appellant because the issue was whether the devise was barred, not whether the word “heir” could have a broad meaning.
members.conclusion: The Court held that a testamentary disposition of the tenancy interest amounts to an assignment prohibited by Section 21 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961. On the tenant’s death, the tenancy continues under Section 24 for heirs determined under personal law, subject to Section 21; a will cannot confer the tenancy interest on a legatee as a testamentary transfer. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.occupancy_rights_proceeding: The proceeding sought recognition of occupancy rights arising from an agricultural tenancy.
predicates.will_based_tenancy_claim: A claimant relied on a tenant’s will to claim the tenant’s tenancy interest.
predicates.testamentary_claim_cannot_transfer_tenan: A testamentary claim does not transfer the tenant’s tenancy rights.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary bequest of tenancy rights falls within the statutory restriction on assigning or transferring tenancy rights.
material_facts: The deceased tenants’ wills purported to bequeath their tenancy rights in the premises.
The claimants sought to rely on those bequests to assert rights in the tenancies.
The dispute concerned residential premises governed by rent-control legislation.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 prohibits a tenant from assigning or transferring the premises, subject to a contract to the contrary. The phrase “in any other manner” gives “transfer” a generic meaning broad enough to include a testamentary transfer. The Transfer of Property Act’s treatment of transfers inter vivos does not govern the meaning of “transfer” under this rent-control legislation. The Court followed Bhavarlal L. Shah v. Kanaiyalal N. Intawala and the reasoning approved there from Anant T. Sabnis (Dr) v. Vasant Pratap Pandit.
members.conclusion: The statutory restriction on assignment or transfer includes a transfer by testamentary bequest, so the bequests could not confer the claimed tenancy rights.

predicates.rent_control_tenancy_dispute: The dispute concerns tenancy rights in premises governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.tenant_bequeaths_tenancy_rights: A tenant purports by will to pass tenancy rights in the premises to another person.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on assignment of land acquired through statutory tenant-purchase provisions includes testamentary dispositions.
material_facts: The land had been acquired by a cultivating tenant through the statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
The tenant bequeathed the land by will to a person who was not an agriculturist.
The required prior approval for the disposition had not been obtained.
members.legal_principle: The court construed the restriction on transfer, including assignment, in light of the statutory scheme granting ownership to cultivating tenants and requiring purchasers to comply with obligations such as personal cultivation. It relied on Sangappa Kalyanappa Bangi v. Land Tribunal, Jamkhandi, Jayamma v. Maria Bai, and Bhavarlal Labhchand Shah v. Kanaiyalal Nathalal Intawala, and held Mahadeo v. Shakuntalabai incorrectly decided because it had not considered the earlier decisions and was inconsistent with the applicable principles. The restriction and its invalidity consequence are set out in Sections 43(1) and 43(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 as applicable in Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The restriction on transfer of land acquired through the statutory tenant-purchase scheme applies to a testamentary disposition; without the required prior approval, the disposition is invalid.

rule.if: agricultural_tenancy_appeal and statutory_purchase_land and testamentary_bequest and approval_not_obtained

predicates.agricultural_tenancy_appeal: The dispute reached the reviewing court through an appeal concerning restrictions on dispositions of agricultural land under a tenancy statute.
predicates.statutory_purchase_land: A tenant acquired the land through a statutory scheme that conferred ownership on cultivating tenants.
predicates.testamentary_bequest: The holder of the land made a will bequeathing it to another person.
predicates.approval_not_obtained: The required prior approval for the disposition had not been obtained.

members.legal_issue: The bar on specified transfers of agricultural land in favour of ineligible persons applies to testamentary dispositions.
material_facts: The holder of agricultural land bequeathed it by will to a person who was not an agriculturist.
The required permission for the disposition had not been obtained.
The dispute concerned whether the statutory restrictions on transfers applied to a bequest taking effect after the holder's death.
members.legal_principle: The court adopted a purposive construction of the transfer restrictions, considering the statutory objective of preserving agricultural land for cultivation and preventing the scheme protecting cultivating tenants from being defeated by bequests to ineligible persons. It relied on Sangappa Kalyanappa Bangi v. Land Tribunal, Jamkhandi, Jayamma v. Maria Bai, Amar Singh v. State of Punjab, and Dayandeo Ganpat Jadhav v. Madhav Vithal Bhaskar, and agreed with the High Court's interpretation of Section 63 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 as applicable in Gujarat. It distinguished decisions concerning testamentary devolution where no statutory prohibition on such a disposition was involved, including State of West Bengal v. Kailash Chandra Kapur and S. Rathinam v. L.S. Mariappan.
members.conclusion: The statutory bar on transfers of agricultural land to a non-agriculturist applies to a testamentary disposition, subject to the statutory permission mechanism.

rule.if: agricultural_tenancy_appeal and agricultural_land and testamentary_bequest and beneficiary_not_eligible and permission_not_obtained

predicates.agricultural_tenancy_appeal: The dispute reached the reviewing court through an appeal concerning statutory restrictions on agricultural land dispositions.
predicates.agricultural_land: The property at issue was agricultural land.
predicates.testamentary_bequest: The holder of the land made a will bequeathing it to another person.
predicates.beneficiary_not_eligible: The beneficiary did not meet the statutory eligibility requirements for receiving the land.
predicates.permission_not_obtained: The required permission for the disposition had not been obtained.

members.legal_issue: A court reviewing a challenge to an administrative tribunal decision must give reasons showing application of mind and address a material objection before disposing of the challenge.
material_facts: A tribunal had decided an application concerning registration as occupant of land.
A writ petition challenging the tribunal’s decision was filed about nineteen years later against the original applicant, who had died.
The State and its officials informed the Single Judge of the applicant’s death, but the applicant’s legal representatives were not brought on record or given notice.
The Single Judge remitted the matter to the tribunal without addressing the delay objection, reasoning that the legal representatives would suffer no prejudice.
The legal representatives specifically raised the unexplained delay before the Division Bench, which dismissed their appeal without giving reasons or addressing that objection.
members.legal_principle: Reasons are an indispensable part of sound judicial decision-making: they show application of mind, enable affected parties to understand the decision, and permit effective appellate review or judicial review. Failure to give reasons may amount to a denial of justice. The Court relied on Breen v. Amalgamated Engineering Union and Alexander Machinery (Dudley) Ltd. v. Crabtree; it also stated that the High Court should have addressed the specifically raised objection of unexplained delay.
members.conclusion: The Single Judge’s order and the Division Bench’s judgment were set aside, and the matter was remitted to the Single Judge for a fresh decision after considering the material and evidence placed on record.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_tribunal_decision and material_delay_objection_raised and delay_objection_not_addressed and (affected_legal_representatives_not_given_notice or appellate_order_lacks_reasons)

predicates.writ_challenge_to_tribunal_decision: A party filed a writ petition challenging a decision made by an administrative tribunal.
predicates.material_delay_objection_raised: An affected party argued that the challenge was filed after a long period of unexplained delay.
predicates.delay_objection_not_addressed: The court disposing of the challenge did not consider or decide the objection about delay.
predicates.affected_legal_representatives_not_given: The original party had died, and the court disposed of the proceeding without giving notice to that party’s legal representatives.
predicates.appellate_order_lacks_reasons: The appellate court affirmed the order without explaining why it rejected the challenge or addressing the material objection.
predicates.lower_court_orders_set_aside_and_matter_: The orders under review are set aside and the matter is sent back for a fresh decision.

members.legal_issue: A judicial order rejecting an application must give reasons that disclose proper consideration of the issue.
material_facts: The High Court rejected the request to modify its earlier order but did not give valid, specific reasons for rejecting the expert committee’s recommendation or for refusing the requested modification.
The stated grounds, including preserving greenery and avoiding brisk activities, were unsupported by the facts concerning the proposed replacement of dilapidated structures.
members.legal_principle: Giving reasons is an essential requirement of judicial decision-making and a principle of natural justice; reasons promote transparency and fairness and show that the court applied its mind. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. Dhaniram Luhar, AIR 2004 SC 1794; State of Rajasthan v. Sohan Lal, (2004) 5 SCC 573; Raj Kishore Jha v. State of Bihar, AIR 2003 SC 4664; Vishnu Dev Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2008) 3 SCC 172; Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. Sales Tax Officer, Rourkela I Circle, (2008) 9 SCC 407; State of Uttaranchal v. Sunil Kumar Singh Negi, AIR 2008 SC 2026; U.P.S.R.T.C. v. Jagdish Prasad Gupta, AIR 2009 SC 2328; Ram Phal v. State of Haryana, (2009) 3 SCC 258; Mohammed Yusuf v. Faij Mohammad, (2009) 3 SCC 513; and State of Himachal Pradesh v. Sada Ram, (2009) 4 SCC 422.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s orders on the construction issue were unsustainable because they did not state valid reasons for their conclusions.

predicates.appeal_challenges_judicial_rejection: A party appeals a judicial decision rejecting its application or deciding an issue against it.
predicates.application_or_issue_is_adversely_decide: The court's decision adversely affects a party's application or position.
predicates.court_gives_no_valid_reasons: The court does not state valid reasons that explain its conclusion on the issue.

members.legal_issue: A judicial order deciding an issue must give reasons that disclose the court’s application of mind to the material findings and submissions.
material_facts: The statutory authorities gave reasons for refusing approval, including findings concerning the society’s management, its activities, demands for member payments, and the absence of progress in construction.
The reviewing court set aside those orders without addressing the authorities’ reasons or identifying a reasoned basis for doing so.
members.legal_principle: Judicial as well as administrative orders must be supported by recorded reasons. Reasons demonstrate application of mind, promote transparency and fairness, and allow an affected person to understand the decision. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. Dhaniram Luhar; State of Rajasthan v. Sohan Lal; Vishnu Dev Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh; Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. Sales Tax Officer; State of Uttaranchal v. Sunil Kumar Singh Negi; U.P.S.R.T.C. v. Jagdish Prasad Gupta; Ram Phal v. State of Haryana; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Sada Ram; and Secretary and Curator, Victoria Memorial Hall v. Howrah Ganatantrik Nagrik Samity.
members.conclusion: The reviewing court’s judgment was unsustainable because it did not give reasons addressing the material findings and the issue before it.

predicates.judicial_order_decides_contested_issue: A court makes an order deciding a contested issue.
predicates.material_findings_are_before_court: Material findings or reasons from the decision under review are available for the court’s consideration.
predicates.order_does_not_give_reasons_addressing_t: The court does not explain its decision by addressing those material findings or reasons.

members.legal_issue: A refusal to grant leave to appeal against an acquittal must state reasons sufficient to show that the court applied its mind.
material_facts: The State sought leave to appeal against an acquittal.

The trial court had considered an admission of encroachment, official witness testimony and documentary evidence, but acquitted the accused on grounds concerning proof of notification and compliance with prescribed procedures.
The High Court refused leave in a one-line order without giving reasons.
The Supreme Court considered the evidentiary and legal questions substantial enough to require adjudication in an appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 378(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court considering leave to appeal against an acquittal must give reasons indicating application of mind. Reasons enable the affected party to understand the decision and allow appellate or judicial review; they are an essential feature of judicial decision-making. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Battan, State of Maharashtra v. Vithal Rao Pritirao Chawan, Jawahar Lal Singh v. Naresh Singh, Raj Kishore Jha v. State of Bihar and State of Punjab v. Bhag Singh, and referred to the duty to follow this Court’s declarations under Article 141 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The unreasoned refusal was unsustainable and was set aside.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal against an acquittal.
predicates.leave_sought: The appellant asks the High Court for leave to appeal against the acquittal.
predicates.refusal_without_reasons: The High Court refuses leave without stating reasons that indicate application of its mind.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising supervisory jurisdiction should not dismiss a challenge in limine without reasons when the challenge raises material contentions requiring a decision.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the allotment authority’s eviction order under Article 227 of the Constitution.
The challenge raised material contentions, including the landlord’s assurance and the absence of an established allotment order.
The High Court dismissed the challenge in limine without giving reasons.
members.legal_principle: A court considering a supervisory challenge must give a reasoned decision, or a brief speaking order explaining why the material contentions do not succeed, rather than dismissing such a challenge in limine without reasons.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in dismissing the challenge in limine; the contentions required a reasoned decision or at least a brief speaking order.

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_eviction_order: A person challenged an eviction order in a court exercising supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.material_contentions_require_decision: The challenge raised substantial contentions that required judicial consideration.
predicates.court_dismissed_without_reasons: The court dismissed the challenge without explaining why the contentions did not succeed.

members.legal_issue: Appeals and petitions concerning provisions that have been replaced during their pendency are infructuous when the challenged provisions no longer survive for consideration.
material_facts: The pending appeals and special leave petitions challenged judgments concerning provisions introduced by an earlier amendment.
A later amendment substituted the disputed provisions while those matters were pending.
The Court found that the earlier provisions no longer survived for consideration.
members.legal_principle: Where legislation has been amended so that the provisions challenged in pending proceedings no longer exist in the form under review, the challenge to those provisions does not survive for consideration.
members.conclusion: The appeals and special leave petitions concerning the superseded provisions were dismissed as infructuous.

predicates.pending_appeal_or_petition_challenges_am: A party had an appeal or petition pending that challenged provisions of an earlier amendment.
predicates.later_law_replaces_challenged_provisions: A later enactment replaced the provisions challenged in the pending proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to an ordinance becomes infructuous when the ordinance has been replaced by legislation and no action taken under the ordinance remains for adjudication.
material_facts: A writ petition challenged an ordinance that was later replaced by an Act of Parliament.
The grounds challenging the ordinance were also raised in a separate petition challenging the Act.
No action taken under the ordinance remained whose legality required adjudication after the ordinance ceased to operate.
members.legal_principle: When a challenged ordinance has ceased to operate after replacement by an Act, and no action taken under the ordinance remains to be adjudicated, the challenge to the ordinance is infructuous; the merits can be considered in a challenge to the replacement Act.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the ordinance was disposed of as infructuous without adjudication on its merits.

predicates.ordinance_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of an ordinance.
predicates.ordinance_replaced_by_legislation: The ordinance ceased to operate after being replaced by legislation.
predicates.no_surviving_action_under_ordinance: No action taken under the ordinance remains whose legality requires adjudication.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to a former provision requiring transfer of pending suits need not be decided after that provision has been omitted with retrospective effect.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the provision under which their pending civil suit had been transferred to a revenue authority.
While the appeal was pending, legislation omitted that transfer provision with retrospective effect.
The Court concluded that the constitutional validity of the omitted provision no longer needed consideration and addressed the civil court's jurisdiction under the amended law instead.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the retrospective omission of the former transfer provision as making its constitutional validity unnecessary to decide in the appeal. It then considered jurisdiction under the amended section 13, including clauses (a)(i) and (a)(ii), of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Court did not decide the constitutional validity of the former transfer provision because it had been omitted with retrospective effect.

predicates.appeal_challenges_transfer_order: A party appeals an order transferring a pending civil suit under a statutory transfer provision.
predicates.transfer_provision_omitted_retroactively: The transfer provision is omitted with retrospective effect while the appeal is pending.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional petition is not entertained to challenge the validity of a provision that is no longer in force.
material_facts: The claimants filed a petition under Article 32 challenging the validity of the unamended compensation-limit provision.
That provision had ceased to be in force when the Court considered the petition.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 32 and held that it would not examine the validity of the challenged provision at a time when that provision no longer subsisted.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the Article 32 petition and dismissed it.

predicates.constitutional_original_petition: A petitioner invoked the Supreme Court’s original constitutional jurisdiction to challenge a legal provision.
predicates.challenged_provision_no_longer_in_force: The provision whose validity was challenged had ceased to be in force when the Court considered the petition.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional writ challenging statutory provisions becomes infructuous when the challenged provisions have been repealed.
material_facts: The landlords filed a writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of a rent-control statute and a provision requiring prior permission before eviction.
The statute was repealed while the petition was pending.

The landlords argued that orders made under the repealed statute remained in force and might obstruct relief under the new law; the court noted that they could seek relief under the new law if new circumstances had arisen.
members.legal_principle: The court treated repeal of the challenged statutory provisions as making the constitutional challenge infructuous. It did not decide the constitutional claims. It observed that relief could be sought under the new law if new circumstances had arisen. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was dismissed as infructuous, with the parties bearing their own costs.

predicates.constitutional_validity_writ: A party has brought a writ proceeding to challenge the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.challenged_law_repealed: The law whose validity is challenged has been repealed.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to sell immovable property that provides for possession to be delivered without requiring execution of a conveyance is chargeable to stamp duty as a conveyance when the agreement contemplates delivery of possession within a stipulated time.
material_facts: The purchasers entered into a written agreement to buy a flat for a stated price, which the agreement said had been paid in the specified manner.
The agreement provided for possession to be delivered by a specified date, subject to payment of amounts due and force majeure.
The agreement did not provide for execution of a conveyance, and it stated that it was not itself a grant or transfer of the property.
The agreement was referred for determination of the property's market value and was treated as chargeable to duty as a conveyance.
members.legal_principle: Under Explanation I to Article 25 of Schedule I of the Bombay Stamp Act, 1958, an agreement to sell immovable property is deemed to be a conveyance where possession is transferred before, at, or after execution of the agreement without a conveyance being executed. The Court construed the Explanation to cover an agreement that itself contemplates delivery of possession within a stipulated time without requiring a conveyance. Section 32A applies to such an agreement mutatis mutandis. The Court also considered the provisions of Sections 4 and 11 of the Maharashtra Ownership Flats Act, 1963, but held that the agreement's execution under that Act did not prevent the stamp-duty rule from applying. No earlier cases are relied upon.
members.conclusion: The agreement fell within Explanation I to Article 25 of Schedule I and was chargeable to stamp duty as a conveyance.

rule.if: stamp_duty_review_of_sale_agreement and agreement_for_immovable_sale and possession_delivery_contemplated and possession_not_conditioned_on_conveyance

predicates.stamp_duty_review_of_sale_agreement: The proceeding concerns the stamp-duty treatment of an agreement to sell.
predicates.agreement_for_immovable_sale: The parties made an agreement for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.possession_delivery_contemplated: The agreement provides for possession to be delivered to the purchaser within a specified time or in specified circumstances.
predicates.possession_not_conditioned_on_conveyance: The agreement does not make delivery of possession dependent on execution of a conveyance.

members.legal_issue: Stamp duty imposed on an agreement that is deemed to be a conveyance because it provides for sale and possession is a duty on the instrument, not an unconstitutional duty on the underlying transaction.
material_facts: The purchasers argued that the agreement was only a contract for sale and transferred no right, title, or interest, so duty equivalent to conveyance duty would be imposed on the transaction rather than on an instrument.
The agreement stated the sale price and provided for delivery of possession by a specified date, without providing for a later conveyance.
The stamp-duty provision deemed qualifying agreements to be conveyances and applied conveyance duty to them.
members.legal_principle: Entry 44 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution permits the levy of stamp duties on instruments, subject to the constitutional allocation of matters in Entry 91 of List I. Section 3 of the Bombay Stamp Act, 1958 charges instruments within its scope, and Explanation I to Article 25 of Schedule I deems a qualifying agreement to sell to be a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes. The legislature may select such an instrument for conveyance-equivalent duty where the agreement manifests an intention to sell and contemplates delivery of possession, even though title has not passed. No earlier cases are relied upon.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge, holding that the levy was on the instrument and that the legislature could impose conveyance-equivalent duty on an agreement meeting the statutory conditions even if title had not passed.

rule.if: stamp_duty_challenge_proceeding and written_sale_agreement and sale_intention_expressed and possession_delivery_contemplated and duty_imposed_on_agreement

predicates.stamp_duty_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenges the validity of stamp duty imposed on a written instrument.
predicates.written_sale_agreement: The instrument is a written agreement for the sale of property.
predicates.sale_intention_expressed: The agreement expresses the parties' intention that the property be sold to the purchaser.
predicates.possession_delivery_contemplated: The agreement contemplates delivery of possession to the purchaser.
predicates.duty_imposed_on_agreement: The stamp duty is imposed on the agreement itself by treating it as an instrument in a specified class.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to sell immovable property under which possession is transferred without a conveyance is treated as a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes.
material_facts: The instrument was an agreement to sell immovable property.
The agreement provided for transfer of possession, and possession was delivered to the purchaser.
No conveyance was executed, and the agreement was tendered as evidence in a civil suit.
members.legal_principle: The explanation to Article 23 of Schedule IA of the Stamp Act, as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act No. 19 of 1989, creates a legal fiction under which an agreement to sell immovable property accompanied by transfer of possession without execution of a conveyance is treated as a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes.
members.conclusion: The agreement was deemed to be a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes and was chargeable with the duty applicable to a conveyance.

predicates.agreement_to_sell_immovable_property: The parties made an agreement for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.possession_transferred_under_agreement: The seller transferred possession of the property to the purchaser under the agreement.

members.legal_issue: An agreement for the sale of immovable property that records transfer of possession is treated as a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes and, if insufficiently stamped, is inadmissible until the required duty and penalty are paid.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property and recorded payment of part of the consideration and delivery of physical possession to the purchaser.

The applicable Madhya Pradesh stamp-law amendment treated an agreement to sell immovable property as a conveyance where possession was transferred before or after the agreement without execution of a conveyance.
The agreement bore only a nominal stamp, which was insufficient for the duty chargeable as on a conveyance.
The question arose while the trial court was deciding whether to admit the agreement in evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(10) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 defines conveyance to include an instrument transferring property inter vivos. Section 3 makes chargeable instruments liable to duty, and the Explanation to Article 23 of Schedule 1-A, as substituted by the Madhya Pradesh Indian Stamp (Madhya Pradesh Second Amendment) Act, 1990, deems an agreement to sell immovable property to be a conveyance where possession is transferred without a conveyance being executed. Section 35 bars admission of an instrument that is not duly stamped, while permitting admission on payment of the required duty or deficient portion and penalty. The court relied on Avinash Kumar Chauhan v. Vijay Krishna Mishra, (2009) 2 SCC 532.
members.conclusion: The agreement was a conveyance for stamp-duty purposes and was insufficiently stamped; the trial court rightly refused to admit it, subject to the statutory procedure for admission upon payment of the deficient duty and penalty.

members.legal_issue: A consent decree whose terms themselves transfer title to immovable property between living parties falls within the definitions of conveyance and instrument and is subject to stamp duty.
material_facts: The decrees were made before the 1985 amendment to the statutory definition of conveyance.
The consent terms provided that the defendants granted, sold, conveyed and transferred the immovable property to the plaintiffs, and that the decree itself would operate as the conveyance.
The terms recorded that the full purchase price had been paid and that vacant possession had been delivered.
The dispute concerned whether the decrees were liable to stamp duty.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(g) and 2(1) of the Bombay Stamps Act, 1958, the inclusive definitions of conveyance and instrument are broad enough to cover a consent decree when its terms effect a transfer of property between living parties. The substance and terms of the document, rather than its label or the court stamp, determine its character; a compromise decree does not stand above the agreement on which it is based. The 1985 amendment was made out of abundant caution and did not mean that such a decree was previously excluded. Sharanbasappa Tippanna Indi v. Sanganbasappa Sridramappa Shahapur was distinguished because it concerned a decree creating a charge on property that was not the subject matter of the suit, not a decree operating as a conveyance.
members.conclusion: The consent decrees qualified as both conveyances and instruments under the definitions then in force and were liable to stamp duty under Entry 25 of Schedule I.

members.legal_issue: Parties cannot use an arbitration agreement to remove a possession dispute covered by the rent-control scheme from the exclusive jurisdiction of the statutory rent forum.
material_facts: The agreement contained an arbitration clause covering disputes between the parties.
The licensee claimed deemed-tenant protection, and the dispute concerned possession of the licensed studios and other premises together with machinery and equipment.
The agreement’s composite character did not change the fact that the studios and other premises had been licensed for business.
members.legal_principle: Section 28(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, both confers jurisdiction on the statutory rent forum and excludes other forums for covered disputes. The Act’s tenant-protection purpose and public policy prevent parties from contracting out of that legislative scheme. The Court relied on Deccan Merchants Cooperative Bank Ltd. v. M/s Dalichand Jugraj Jain & Ors. and considered Babulal Bhuramal & Anr. v. Nandram Shivram & Ors., Raizada Topandas & Anr. v. M/s Gorakhram Gokalchand, and Vasudev Gopalkrishna Tamwekar v. The Board of Liquidators, Happy Home Cooperative Housing Society; Sabavva Kom Hanmappa Simpiger v. Basappa Andaneppa Chiniwar was also directly relevant to the exclusion of arbitration for disputes within section 28.
members.conclusion: The Court of Small Causes alone had jurisdiction to decide whether the licensor was entitled to possession; the arbitrator had none, and the arbitration clause was inoperative for the dispute.

predicates.rent_control_possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns possession of premises in a dispute to which rent-control protection may apply.
predicates.protected_tenant_status: A party occupies the premises with a claimed status protected by the rent-control scheme, including status arising by statutory deeming.
predicates.arbitration_clause_covers_dispute: The parties’ agreement contains an arbitration clause purporting to cover the possession dispute.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s suit to recover possession in a tenancy dispute governed by a law reserving that decision to a court cannot be referred to arbitration despite an arbitration agreement.
material_facts: The landlords sued to evict their tenants from a shop premises and sought other reliefs as well.
The tenancy agreement contained an arbitration clause covering disputes arising from the agreement.
The applicable tenancy law provided that, notwithstanding a contract, possession could be recovered only by an order or decree of the Civil Judge in a suit brought by the landlord.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 overrides contrary contractual terms and reserves recovery of possession to the Civil Judge in a landlord’s suit. Section 2(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 preserves laws that make certain disputes non-arbitrable, and Section 8 does not require referral where such a statutory bar applies. Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios supports the principle that statutory tenant protections and the exclusive jurisdiction conferred to enforce them prevail over an arbitration agreement. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Pinkcity Midway Petroleums, Agri Gold Exims Ltd. v. Sri Lakshmi Knits & Wovens, and Branch Manager, Magma Leasing & Finance Ltd. v. Potluri Madhavilata were distinguished because they involved no comparable statutory bar to arbitration.
members.conclusion: The statutory restriction overrode the arbitration clause, so the possession-recovery suit could not be referred to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

members.legal_issue: A contractual arbitration clause does not displace the civil court’s jurisdiction over a landlord-tenant dispute seeking eviction and related reliefs.
material_facts: The landlord filed a civil suit seeking the tenant’s eviction, unpaid rent and a permanent injunction concerning leased commercial premises.
The lease had expired, no renewed lease was executed, and the tenancy continued monthly.
The lease contained an arbitration clause covering disputes arising from it.
The tenant sought referral to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
members.legal_principle: Applying Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios, which held that a landlord-tenant possession dispute was for the designated court and not an arbitrator, and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., which identifies certain eviction and tenancy disputes as non-arbitrable, the Court held that an arbitration clause did not require this eviction dispute to be referred to arbitration. Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 did not require referral in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The civil suit was maintainable, and the tenant’s application for referral to arbitration was correctly dismissed.

rule.if: defendant_sought_arbitration_referral and landlord_tenant_relationship and eviction_or_possession_dispute and lease_contains_arbitration_clause

members.legal_issue: Exclusion of premises from rent-control legislation does not make a landlord-tenant eviction or rent dispute arbitrable merely because the lease contains an arbitration clause.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the Delhi Rent Act did not apply to the premises because they fell within an exclusion in that Act.
The suit sought eviction and ancillary reliefs concerning a tenancy for which no renewed lease had been executed after the original term expired.
The lease contained an arbitration clause.

The Court stated that, where the rent-control statute does not apply to premises, the parties’ rights are governed by the Transfer of Property Act and the civil suit is triable by a civil court, not an arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 3 of the Delhi Rent Act, 1955, and held that its non-application to particular premises does not, by itself, confer jurisdiction on an arbitrator. For premises outside the Act’s application, rights are governed by the Transfer of Property Act and a civil suit is triable by the civil court. The Court relied on Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd. in holding that the dispute was not to be referred to arbitration.
members.conclusion: The rent-control exclusion did not make the arbitration law applicable so as to confer jurisdiction on an arbitrator; the dispute was triable by the civil court.

predicates.rent_control_exclusion: The premises fall outside the coverage of the rent-control regime governing the tenancy.
predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_or_eviction_dispute: The dispute concerns rent, eviction, or possession between a landlord and a tenant.
predicates.civil_suit_filed: A party brought the landlord-tenant dispute in a civil court.

members.legal_issue: A proceeding by a landlord to recover possession from a tenant of premises covered by rent-control legislation falls within the exclusive jurisdiction conferred on the designated rent court, rather than cooperative arbitration.
material_facts: The bank, as the party claiming to be landlord, sought to eject occupants who claimed to be tenants.
The premises were covered by the Bombay Rent Act.
The occupants’ status and possession were disputed, and the bank sought to have the dispute determined through cooperative arbitration.
The rent legislation provided special protections for tenants and assigned landlord-tenant possession proceedings to the Court of Small Causes.
members.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, assigns landlord-tenant proceedings concerning recovery of possession of covered premises to the specified court and excludes other courts. Although Section 91 of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, also contains overriding language, the provisions must be harmonised in light of their respective purposes: rent-control matters are to be dealt with under the Rent Act so that its tenant protections and procedures apply. The Court relied on the principle stated in Shri Ram Narain v. Simla Banking and Industrial Co. Ltd. that competing overriding provisions should be assessed by considering the purpose and policy of the Acts and the language used. It noted Thakur Jugal Kishore Sinha v. Sitamarhi Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. on the status of a Registrar acting under another cooperative statute, but found it unnecessary to decide whether the Registrar was a court for purposes of the Rent Act.
members.conclusion: Section 28 of the Rent Act gave the Court of Small Causes exclusive jurisdiction over the ejectment proceeding, and Section 91 of the cooperative societies legislation did not displace that jurisdiction.

predicates.landlord_tenant_ejectment_proceeding: A landlord seeks to eject a person who claims to be a tenant.
predicates.premises_covered_by_rent_control: The premises involved are covered by rent-control legislation.
