members.legal_issue: Rights arising under the laws of a territory before its conquest are not enforceable against the successor government unless that government recognizes them.
material_facts: A person obtained titles of manifest under the former sovereign’s mining laws and transferred them to the claimant before the territory was conquered.
The claimant applied for mining concessions under those laws before the conquest, but no concessions had been granted.
The successor government did not recognize the claimed entitlement and later stated that applications based on titles of manifest had lapsed.
members.legal_principle: On acquisition of territory by conquest, rights against the former sovereign do not pass to the new sovereign unless recognized. Continuing former laws does not itself recognize rights that arose under them; recognition may instead occur through a regrant, executive action, or a statutory saving provision that covers the rights in question. Section 5(1) of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Act, 1962 and section 4(2) of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Laws) Regulation, 1962 did not recognize rights arising before the conquest. The Court applied Pema Chibar v. Union of India and relied on the principle in Vajesingji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State, followed in State of Gujarat v. Vora Fiddali and other cases.
members.conclusion: The titles and pending applications did not give the claimant a right enforceable against the successor government because the claimed right had not been recognized by that government.

predicates.territory_acquired_by_conquest: The territory in which the claimed right arose was acquired by another government through conquest.

members.legal_issue: An alleged land grant by a former sovereign is unenforceable against a successor government that has not accepted it.
material_facts: The claimants sought a declaration of title based on an alleged grant by a former sovereign.
The successor government did not approve the order that purported to recognize the grant.
The order recognizing the alleged grant was held up for review after the former sovereign directed that post-covenant orders be scrutinized.
The appellate courts rejected the oral evidence offered to prove the grant, and the Supreme Court considered the recognition order of limited significance in light of the subsequent order.
The alleged grantee had not entered possession of the lands pursuant to the alleged grant.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle in State of Gujarat v. Vora Fiddali Badruddin Mithibarwala that a claim based on a grant by a former sovereign is unenforceable when the successor government has not accepted the grant.
members.conclusion: Even assuming that the grant had been made, it was unenforceable because the successor government had not accepted it. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.title_claim_based_on_prior_grant: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking title to land on the basis of an alleged grant by a former sovereign.
predicates.grant_not_accepted_by_successor_governme: The government succeeding the former sovereign did not accept the alleged grant.

members.legal_issue: After territorial cession, an inhabitant cannot enforce proprietary rights in municipal courts merely because a treaty or proclamation generally promises to respect existing rights; the claimant must establish that the new sovereign recognized the rights.
material_facts: A treaty governing the territorial transfer provided for respect of existing leases and for new grants concerning rent-free lands, jagirs, perquisites and hereditary claims.
After the transfer, the British Government investigated the estates and their tenures and decided that the zamindars, apart from a specified chief, were to be treated as ordinary British subjects.
The claimants did not prove that the British Government had acknowledged or recognized sovereign rights held by their ancestors.
members.legal_principle: On acquisition of territory by conquest, cession or otherwise, an inhabitant may enforce in municipal courts only proprietary rights conferred or recognized by the new sovereign. A general treaty or proclamation promising recognition of existing rights means that the government will recognize rights found to exist after investigation; it does not itself confer enforceable rights on inhabitants. The burden of proving recognition rested on the claimants. The Court relied on Vajesingji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India in Council, Bir Bikram Deo v. Secretary of State for India in Council, and Martand Rao v. Malhar Rao.
members.conclusion: The treaty’s general promise to respect existing rights did not establish enforceable sovereign rights for the claimants, and they failed to prove that the new sovereign had recognized such rights.

predicates.territorial_cession_dispute: A person asserted rights over property in territory transferred to a new sovereign.
predicates.treaty_generally_promised_respect_for_ex: The transfer agreement generally promised to respect rights that existed before the transfer.
predicates.new_sovereign_recognized_claimed_rights: The new sovereign recognized the rights asserted by the claimant after investigating the relevant title or tenure.

members.legal_issue: Rights granted by a former sovereign cannot be enforced against a successor sovereign unless the successor sovereign has recognized them.
material_facts: A former ruler granted forest rights to holders of specified tenures, who later contracted with the claimants to cut and remove timber.
Forest officials permitted some cutting only temporarily, subject to undertakings that the claimants would abide by the government’s eventual decision.
The successor government did not recognize the forest rights and ultimately rejected them.
members.legal_principle: Under the rule applied in Secretary of State in Council for India v. Kamachee Boye Sahiba, Secretary of State v. Bai Rajbai, Vajesinghji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India, Secretary of State v. Sardar Rustam Khan, and Asrar Ahmed v. Durgah Committee, rights derived from a former sovereign are enforceable against the successor only if the successor recognizes them expressly or by implication. The Court applied that rule consistently with M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, State of Saurashtra v. Memon Haji Ismail Haji, Jagan Nath Agarwala v. State of Orissa, State of Saurashtra v. Jamadar Mohamed Abdulla, and Promod Chandra Deb v. State of Orissa, and disapproved the contrary approach in Virendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh. Recognition must be attributable to the successor sovereign; conditional action by subordinate officers does not suffice.
members.conclusion: The forest rights could not be enforced against the successor government. The temporary permissions given by subordinate forest officials did not recognize the rights or waive the government’s position.

predicates.civil_claim_to_enforce_former_sovereign_: A claimant brought a civil proceeding seeking to enforce against a successor government a right granted by a former sovereign.
predicates.successor_did_not_recognize_grant: The successor government did not expressly or impliedly recognize the claimed right.
predicates.officials_allowed_work_only_conditionall: Subordinate officials allowed the claimant to work the resource temporarily, subject to the government’s later decision and an undertaking to abide by it.

members.legal_issue: A former state's inhabitants can enforce pre-existing property rights against a new sovereign only if that sovereign recognizes those rights, and the property-rights protection does not itself create rights.
material_facts: The respondents claimed property under grants made by the former ruler.
The administrator's orders repudiated rather than recognized those grants.
The respondents argued that they could rely on the protection against deprivation of property without lawful authority after the new power assumed sovereignty.
members.legal_principle: The separate opinion applied the rule that inhabitants of acquired territory may enforce against the new sovereign only rights that it has recognized, expressly or impliedly, or conferred by legislation. It relied on Cook v. Sprigg, Vajesinghji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India, Secretary of State for India v. Bai Rajbai, M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Jagannath Agarwala v. State of Orissa. Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935 protected existing property rights but did not create or enlarge them.
members.conclusion: In the separate opinion of Justices Sarkar and Mudholkar, the respondents could not enforce the unrecognized grants against the new sovereign, and the property-rights protection did not enlarge their rights; it protected only rights they already possessed against that sovereign.

members.legal_issue: Property inherited from paternal ancestors is ancestral only in relation to the holder’s male issue and is separate property in relation to other heirs when the holder leaves no male issue.
material_facts: The disputed properties had originally belonged to the deceased holder’s paternal ancestors.
The deceased was the last male holder and left no male issue.
No surviving member of a joint family could take the properties by survivorship.
The competing claimants were paternal collaterals and the claimant was the deceased’s sister.

For purposes of deciding the case, the court proceeded on the basis that the applicable custom preferred collaterals to a sister only for ancestral property, and preferred a sister to collaterals for non-ancestral property.
members.legal_principle: Property inherited from paternal ancestors is ancestral as regards the holder’s male issue, but is the holder’s absolute property as regards other relations. If the holder dies without male issue, the property passes by succession as separate property in relation to those other relations. The court relied on Mulla, Principles of Hindu Law, 15th ed., pp. 289 and 291, and applied the assumed custom distinguishing the heirs to ancestral and non-ancestral property.
members.conclusion: As against the paternal collaterals, the properties were not ancestral property; the sister was the preferential heir and was entitled to all the disputed properties.

members.legal_issue: Property inherited by a male descendant under pre-statutory Mitakshara law from a paternal ancestor, and later allotted to his ancestor on partition, remains coparcenary property as to the male descendant.
material_facts: Succession to the property opened under the old Mitakshara law when the original owner died before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The original owner’s son inherited the property, and the property was later partitioned among his sons.
The property allotted to the descendant’s father on partition was claimed by the descendant, who was born before his father’s purported sale of it.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, property inherited by a male Hindu from a paternal ancestor within the relevant degrees is ancestral, and his male descendants acquire an interest in it by birth. Where succession opened before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, that character is not altered by the Act’s later commencement. A share allotted on partition remains coparcenary property as regards the allottee’s male issue. The Court relied on Shyam Narayan Prasad v. Krisha Prasad, Yudhishter v. Ashok Kumar, and Valliammai Achi v. Nagappa Chettiar, as well as Mulla on Hindu Law; it distinguished Uttam v. Saubhag Singh because succession there opened after the Act came into force.
members.conclusion: The property allotted to the father remained coparcenary property as against his son, who acquired an interest in it by birth.

predicates.inherited_from_paternal_ancestor: A male ancestor inherited the property from a paternal ancestor.
predicates.share_received_on_partition: The ancestor later received the property or a share of it on partition.

members.legal_issue: Ancestral property allotted to a sole surviving coparcener in partition is separate property while he remains the sole coparcener, but becomes coparcenary property when a son is subsequently born to him.
material_facts: The father received ancestral property in a partition while he was unmarried and the sole surviving coparcener in respect of that property.
The plaintiff was born to the father after the partition.
members.legal_principle: A sole surviving coparcener may treat property allotted to him in partition as his separate property, but the coparcenary revives when a son is born to him, and the son then acquires an interest in the property. The Court relied on M. Yogendra v. Leelamma, (2009) 15 SCC 184. It distinguished Bhanwar Singh v. Puran, (2008) 3 SCC 87, because that case concerned succession, whereas this case concerned the status of a son in relation to his father and property allotted on partition. The Court also noted the pre-amendment position under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, that male members acquired an interest in coparcenary property by birth.
members.conclusion: The property was the father's separate property until the plaintiff was born; upon the plaintiff's birth, it became coparcenary property in which the plaintiff acquired an interest.

rule.if: civil_appeal_in_property_dispute and ancestral_property_allotted_in_partition and recipient_was_sole_surviving_coparcener and son_born_after_partition

predicates.civil_appeal_in_property_dispute: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal concerning rights in property.

predicates.son_born_after_partition: A son was born to the recipient after the partition.

members.legal_issue: Property inherited by a sole holder that becomes Mitakshara coparcenary property on the birth of a son is governed, on the holder’s later death, by the rules for devolution of coparcenary interest rather than the general rules for separate property.
material_facts: The property had been inherited by a member of a Mitakshara family when he had no son, so it was then his separate property.
A son was born to him before the Hindu Succession Act came into force, and the property thereafter became coparcenary property under Mitakshara law.
The holder died intestate leaving sons and daughters, including female heirs specified in Class I of the Schedule.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, property inherited by a person from a paternal ancestor may remain separate while he has no son, but becomes coparcenary property as against a son when one is born. Krishna Prasad v. C.I.T., Bangalore, and the authorities discussed in Pratap Narain v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, U.P., support the property’s ancestral or coparcenary character. Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act governs a deceased coparcener’s interest, and its proviso requires intestate or testamentary succession rather than survivorship when a Class I female relative survives. Section 8 governs property devolving as separate property; under Chander Sen, property inherited under Section 8 is taken individually, not as karta of the heir’s own family. Eramma v. Veerupana and Daya Singh v. Dhan Kaur establish that the Act is not retrospective and does not apply where succession opened before it came into force. Section 4 gives the Act overriding effect over inconsistent prior Hindu law. The 2005 amendment did not apply because succession had already opened before that amendment.
members.conclusion: The property was coparcenary property when the holder died. His coparcenary interest was governed by Section 6, and because he left female Class I heirs, that interest devolved by intestate succession rather than survivorship. Section 8 did not govern that coparcenary interest; the holder’s half share devolved upon his heirs and legal representatives.

members.legal_issue: A share of ancestral property allotted to a male coparcener on partition remains coparcenary property in relation to his male descendants, giving them an interest in it.
material_facts: An ancestor and his sons partitioned ancestral property, and one son received the property at issue.
That son had sons and a grandson, who brought the suit challenging a later transfer of the property.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, property inherited from a father or other specified paternal ancestor is ancestral, and a coparcener’s share of ancestral property remains ancestral as regards his male issue. The Court relied on C. Krishna Prasad v. C.I.T., Bangalore, M. Yogendra v. Leelamma N., and Rohit Chauhan v. Surinder Singh.
members.conclusion: The property allotted to the son retained its coparcenary character as regards his male descendants, who had an interest in it; the suit was maintainable.

predicates.ancestral_family_partition_dispute: Family members disputed rights in property treated as ancestral and divided by partition.
predicates.share_derived_from_ancestral_property: A male family member received a share of the ancestral property in the partition.
predicates.male_descendants_of_allottee_exist: The allottee had male descendants who claimed an interest in the property.

members.legal_issue: A final land-acquisition compensation award cannot be reopened through redetermination where the applicant had already sought a reference to the civil court.
material_facts: The applicants had sought references under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and received enhanced compensation from the civil court and the High Court.
The High Court’s judgment had become final because the applicants did not seek special leave within the applicable period.
The applicants were not the inarticulate and poor landowners for whose benefit section 28A was intended.

Section 28A provides for redetermination by the Collector, subject to its conditions, for persons who had not applied for a section 18 reference; section 25 would benefit an applicant using that redetermination remedy.
members.legal_principle: Sections 18, 25 and 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 operate together: section 28A provides a limited redetermination remedy for eligible persons who did not seek a section 18 reference and who apply within the prescribed time, while section 25 may benefit a person proceeding through that remedy. The Act provides no other means to reopen an award that has become final and conclusive.
members.conclusion: Section 28A did not apply to the applicants, and there was no other provision for reopening their final award; section 25 did not provide an independent basis to do so.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.final_compensation_award: The compensation award has become final and conclusive.
predicates.applicant_previously_sought_reference: The applicant previously sought a reference to a civil court to determine compensation.

members.legal_issue: Statutory additions to compensation are not an independent entitlement, and a court cannot award them when the underlying redetermination award was made without jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Collector made a redetermination award based on later enhancement decisions even though the earliest qualifying enhancement award predated the redetermination scheme.
The Collector did not include statutory additions to compensation.
The claimants sought those additions in a writ petition, and the High Court directed that they be awarded.
The underlying redetermination award was without jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 28-A(3), 18 to 28, 23(1), 23(1-A), and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act provide for statutory additions in connection with a court’s determination of compensation exceeding the Collector’s section 11 award; they do not create an independent power to award those additions. Because the Collector lacked jurisdiction to make the underlying redetermination, the High Court also erred in granting the additions.
members.conclusion: The Collector’s redetermination award was a nullity, and neither the Collector nor the High Court could award statutory additions independently of a valid enhancement of compensation.

predicates.land_acquisition_redetermination_proceed: The proceeding concerns redetermination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.underlying_redetermination_lacked_jurisd: The Collector based the redetermination on enhancement decisions that did not provide a valid basis for reopening the original compensation award.
predicates.statutory_additions_sought_without_valid: The claimant sought statutory additions without a valid court determination enhancing compensation above the original award.

members.legal_issue: An application for re-determination of compensation filed after the prescribed period is barred.
material_facts: Interested persons applied for re-determination on the basis of reference-court awards.
The applications were filed more than three months after the relevant awards, after accounting for the time excluded under the statutory computation rule.
The Collector nevertheless granted enhanced compensation on some applications.
members.legal_principle: Section 28-A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires a written application within three months of the reference court's award. The proviso excludes the day the award was pronounced and the time required to obtain a copy; an application outside the resulting period is barred.
members.conclusion: The late applications were barred, and compensation granted on their basis was illegal; the challenged orders granting that compensation were set aside.

predicates.compensation_redetermination_proceeding: The proceeding seeks re-determination of compensation by the acquiring authority on the basis of a court award.
predicates.interested_owner_did_not_seek_reference: The interested person did not seek a reference against the original compensation award.
predicates.application_outside_computed_limit: The person filed the written application after the applicable time limit, computed after excluding the specified time for the award and obtaining its copy.

members.legal_issue: A reference court lacks jurisdiction to reopen a completed compensation decree to award additional statutory benefits through a fresh application rather than a permitted correction.
material_facts: A court hearing a land acquisition compensation reference had made an award enhancing compensation, and that award had become final.
After an amendment introduced additional compensation benefits, the claimants applied to the reference court for those benefits.
The application sought substantive additional relief, not correction of a clerical or arithmetic mistake.
The reference court allowed the application, and the High Court summarily dismissed the State’s appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 18 and 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the reference court determines compensation within the powers conferred by the Act. Under section 26(2), its award is deemed a decree. After that decree, correction is confined to the statutory correction power under section 13-A of the Act and section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 151 CPC, which preserves inherent power to prevent abuse of process or meet the ends of justice, does not confer jurisdiction to grant fresh substantive relief where the Act expressly defines the court’s powers. The additional amounts under section 23(1-A) and (2) are additional to, rather than components of, the compensation determined under section 23(1); interest under section 28 is consequential on an enhancement of compensation. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The reference court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the application for additional benefits; its order was void. The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the reference court and the High Court and dismissed the application.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_reference and final_compensation_decree and post_decree_application and seeks_new_substantive_benefits and not limited_to_permitted_correction

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference: The proceeding is a court reference to determine compensation for acquired land.
predicates.final_compensation_decree: The court has made a compensation award that has become a decree.
predicates.post_decree_application: A party applies for relief after the compensation decree has been made.
predicates.seeks_new_substantive_benefits: The application seeks additional compensation benefits rather than enforcement of relief already awarded.
predicates.limited_to_permitted_correction: The application is confined to correcting a clerical or arithmetic error in the decree.
predicates.reference_court_lacks_jurisdiction_to_aw: The reference court has no jurisdiction to award new substantive benefits after the compensation decree.

members.legal_issue: A final land-acquisition compensation decree cannot be reopened through an independent application to obtain statutory benefits introduced by a later amendment.
material_facts: The reference court enhanced compensation and made its award and decree before the statutory amendments took effect; the State's appeal was dismissed and the decree became final.
After the amendments took effect, the claimants applied in the disposed appeal for additional statutory benefits, and the High Court granted them.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 23(1-A), 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended, the court may award the relevant statutory benefits in the compensation proceedings when applicable; it cannot use Sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure to alter a decree that has become final or independently award amended benefits. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Babu Singh, Union of India v. Swaran Singh, and Sarup Singh v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to grant the additional benefits through the later application, and its resulting decree was a nullity.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land compulsorily acquired by the government.
predicates.compensation_decree_final_before_later_a: The compensation award and decree became final before a later application was filed.
predicates.later_application_seeks_benefits_from_am: A party later applied for compensation benefits introduced by a change in the law after the decree became final.
predicates.application_does_not_seek_only_clerical_: The later application seeks a substantive change in the decree rather than correction of a clerical or arithmetic mistake.

members.legal_issue: A stipulated sum payable upon breach of an agreement to transfer immovable property does not, by itself, rebut the presumption that monetary compensation is inadequate when the agreement does not make payment an alternative to performance.
material_facts: The agreement to sell the property required the seller, in the event of breach, to refund the advance and pay an additional stipulated sum as damages.
The agreement did not give the seller an option to pay the stipulated sum instead of completing the sale.
The courts found that the seller had not established fraud, misrepresentation, or an unfair advantage obtained by the buyer.
members.legal_principle: Under section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, the court presumes that breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by monetary compensation unless the contrary is proved. Section 20 permits specific performance despite a sum named for breach, unless the contract makes payment an alternative to performance; section 22 makes specific relief discretionary on sound judicial grounds. The corresponding provisions are sections 10, 23, and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The court also relied on the distinction described in Sir Edward Fry’s treatise between a sum securing performance and payment as an elected alternative to performance.
members.conclusion: The stipulated damages clause was only evidence bearing on whether the presumption was rebutted; it was not conclusive, and the presumption was not rebutted in this case.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_transfer and breach_sum_stipulated and no_payment_option

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to transfer immovable property.
predicates.immovable_property_transfer: The agreement required one party to transfer immovable property to another.
predicates.breach_sum_stipulated: The agreement named a sum payable in the event of breach.
predicates.no_payment_option: The agreement did not allow the party in default to choose payment of the stipulated sum instead of performance.

members.legal_issue: A sum stipulated for breach does not make damages an alternative to specific performance when the stipulation is intended only to secure performance.
material_facts: The sellers relied on a clause in the sale contract providing for payment of damages in case of breach.
The court found from the contract’s terms that the clause was included to secure performance, not to give the sellers an option to pay money instead of performing.
members.legal_principle: A stipulated sum for breach does not bar specific performance when, on the construction of the contract, it serves to secure performance rather than provide the promisor an option to pay damages instead. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The damages clause did not prevent the purchaser from seeking enforcement of the agreement by specific performance.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks enforcement of an agreement by requiring conveyance of property.
predicates.breach_sum_clause: The agreement specifies a sum payable in the event of breach.
predicates.clause_secures_performance_only: The agreement shows that the stipulated sum is intended to secure performance and not to give the promisor an option to pay instead of performing.
predicates.damages_clause_does_not_exclude_specific: The stipulated sum does not prevent the court from ordering specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A contractual provision for damages does not by itself exclude specific performance unless the agreement clearly makes monetary payment an exclusive remedy or gives the party in default an option to pay money instead of performing.
material_facts: The agreement did not expressly provide for specific performance or expressly bar it.
The agreement provided for payment of damages if the vendor defaulted and forfeiture of earnest money if the purchaser defaulted.
The damages provision did not give the vendor an option to pay money in lieu of performing the sale.
members.legal_principle: Sections 10, 21(2), 21(5), and 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permit specific performance where the statutory requirements are met, even if the contract names an amount payable on breach and does not separately provide for specific performance. Under Section 23, a named sum bars specific performance only where the contract shows that the sum gives the defaulting party an option to pay money instead of performing; compensation may otherwise be considered under Section 21 where specific performance is refused and compensation has been claimed.
members.conclusion: The damages provision did not prevent the purchaser from seeking specific performance, subject to proving the vendor’s breach and the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_names_damages_for_breach and not contract_makes_money_an_exclusive_remedy

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.contract_names_damages_for_breach: The contract specifies a monetary consequence for breach.
predicates.contract_makes_money_an_exclusive_remedy: The contract clearly makes payment of money the exclusive remedy or gives the defaulting party an option to pay instead of performing.

members.legal_issue: A contractual sum stipulated for breach does not preclude specific performance when it is a penalty securing performance rather than an alternative to performance.
material_facts: The agreement for sale required a party violating its terms to pay a specified sum as a penalty.
The agreement did not state that the seller could choose to pay that sum instead of conveying the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Jammu and Kashmir Specific Relief Act, 1977 (1920 A.D.) permits specific performance of an otherwise enforceable contract despite a sum being named for breach. The Court applied the distinction between a penalty securing performance, liquidated damages, and a sum payable as an alternative to performance discussed in M.L. Devender Singh v. Syed Khaji, relying on Sir Edward Fry’s treatise; it also relied on Prakash Chand v. Angad Lal. A stipulated sum does not by itself displace the presumption referred to in Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as discussed in M.L. Devender Singh.
members.conclusion: The penalty clause did not prevent a decree for specific performance.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks an order requiring a party to perform a contract for the transfer of property.
predicates.stipulated_sum_secures_performance: The contract stipulates a sum payable for breach as security for performance.
predicates.contract_does_not_offer_payment_as_an_al: The contract does not give the party an option to pay the stipulated sum instead of performing the transfer.

members.legal_issue: A clause providing for a payment on breach does not bar specific performance unless the contract gives the defaulting party an option to pay that amount instead of performing.
material_facts: The agreement required the seller to discharge the mortgage and provided for return of the advance and liquidated damages if the seller breached and failed to sell.
The clause did not state that the seller could elect to pay the specified amount instead of conveying the property.
The buyer sought specific performance despite the clause.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance where a sum is named for breach if the sum secures performance rather than giving the defaulting party an option to pay money in lieu of performance. M.L. Devender Singh v. Syed Khaja distinguishes a security or damages stipulation from a contractual alternative to performance and treats the stated sum as evidence, not a conclusive answer. Manzoor Ahmed Magray v. Gulam Hassan Aram and A. Abdul Rashid Khan v. P.A.K.A. Shahul Hamid reiterate that approach. Dadarao v. Ramrao was distinguished and held per incuriam because it did not consider Section 23 or the earlier binding decision in M.L. Devender Singh.
members.conclusion: The damages clause did not make the specific-performance suit unmaintainable; it secured performance rather than giving the seller an option to substitute payment for the sale.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_contains_breach_payment_clause and clause_secures_performance and not seller_has_payment_instead_option

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a claim by a buyer for specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.contract_contains_breach_payment_clause: The agreement specifies a payment or repayment consequence if a party breaches it.
predicates.clause_secures_performance: The payment consequence is intended to secure performance or compensate for breach rather than define an alternative performance.
predicates.seller_has_payment_instead_option: The agreement expressly allows the seller to choose payment instead of conveying the property.

members.legal_issue: The validity of a will challenged on suspicious circumstances depends on the cumulative assessment of the circumstances surrounding its execution, rather than the effect of any single circumstance.
material_facts: The will excluded the testator’s sons and left property to her daughter and granddaughter, stating reasons for that disposition.
A prior will had substantially identical contents, and the reasons for excluding the sons were apparent from the will.

The daughter participated in arranging the will’s execution and registration, and the testator’s friend attested it; the Court found these circumstances did not warrant an adverse conclusion in the context of the earlier will and the evidence.
The original will was missing from the testator’s custody, and the explanation that it was lost before her death was not disbelieved merely because no police report had been made.

The discrepancy concerning the place of execution was explained by the use of a standard verification form, and evidence described the Sub-Registrar’s usual practice of ascertaining or explaining the will’s contents to the testator.
The other unusual circumstances, including the changed attesting witnesses and the non-examination of one attesting witness, were found capable of explanation.
members.legal_principle: A court must scrutinize unusual features and suspicious circumstances surrounding a will and assess their cumulative effect; no single feature or circumstance is determinative. The Court applied the principles in H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Bharpur Singh v. Shamsher Singh, Rani Purnima Debi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Deb, Apoline D’souza v. John D’souza, Pentakota Satyanarayana v. Pentakota Seetharatnam, Mahesh Kumar v. Vinod Kumar, and Ved Mitra Verma v. Dharam Deo Verma. Sections 281 and 282 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, were referred to in connection with the verification accompanying the probate petition.
members.conclusion: The suspicious circumstances did not justify rejecting the will; the High Court was right to accept it as valid.

rule.if: will_validity_contested and suspicious_circumstances_present and circumstances_reasonably_explained and will_contents_clear_and_reasons_apparent

predicates.will_validity_contested: A party to a proceeding disputing a will challenges whether it was validly executed.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_present: The will’s features or the circumstances surrounding its execution appear unusual or suspicious.
predicates.circumstances_reasonably_explained: The evidence provides reasonable explanations for the unusual features and circumstances when they are assessed together.
predicates.will_contents_clear_and_reasons_apparent: The will clearly expresses the testator’s disposition and makes its reasons apparent.

members.legal_issue: Excluding or reducing the share of a natural heir does not, by itself, make a will suspicious; the circumstances surrounding the disposition must be considered as a whole.
material_facts: The will preferred the testator’s sister’s children and their children, who had cared for and supported him while he was ill and dependent on them.
The testator’s son had not cared for him or met his treatment expenses, and the will provided for a payment to the son.
The testator lived for seven years after making the registered will and did not cancel it.
The challengers also relied on the testator’s illness, the beneficiaries’ relationship to the will, the choice of witnesses, and the circumstances of execution.
members.legal_principle: The propounder must explain suspicious circumstances to the court’s satisfaction, but the exclusion of natural heirs or the grant of a lesser share to them is not, without more, suspicious. The court must assess the relevant background and circumstances rationally. It relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Ramabai Padmakar Patil v. Rukminibai Vishnu Vekhande, S. Sundaresa Pai v. Sumangala T. Pai, and Gurdial Kaur v. Kartar Kaur.
members.conclusion: The court found no suspicious circumstance that prevented acceptance of the will, and held that the exclusion of a natural heir alone was insufficient to invalidate it.

rule.if: will_validity_contested and natural_heir_excluded and beneficiaries_supported_testator and natural_heir_failed_to_care_for_testator

predicates.will_validity_contested: A party challenged whether a will was validly made.
predicates.natural_heir_excluded: The will excluded a natural heir or gave that heir less than the heir might otherwise receive.
predicates.beneficiaries_supported_testator: The beneficiaries had cared for or supported the testator.
predicates.natural_heir_failed_to_care_for_testator: The natural heir had not cared for or supported the testator.

members.legal_issue: Unequal distribution of a testator’s assets among family members does not, by itself, make a will unnatural or create suspicion about its execution.
material_facts: The will distributed immovable property unevenly among the children, gave nothing to the husband and one daughter, and distributed movable property equally among the sons.
The daughter who received nothing supported the will rather than challenging it.
The challenging daughter had received some property by gift during the testator’s lifetime, and the record disclosed acrimony between her and her father.
members.legal_principle: The choice of how to distribute property under a will lies within the testator’s discretion. Unequal distribution among children, by itself, is not a suspicious circumstance surrounding execution. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The uneven distribution, by itself, did not make the will unnatural or create suspicion about its execution; the contrary finding could not be sustained.

predicates.will_challenged_in_civil_suit: A person challenged a will in a civil suit.
predicates.unequal_distribution_among_family_member: The will distributed the testator’s property unevenly among family members.
predicates.unequal_distribution_is_only_basis_for_s: The claim that execution was suspicious rested only on the uneven distribution of property.

members.legal_issue: The failure to register a will does not, by itself, create doubt about its execution merely because another family member’s will was registered.
material_facts: The testator’s will was unregistered, while her husband’s will was registered.
An attesting witness to both wills explained that the husband had insisted on registration of his will because litigation had arisen over his wife’s will.
members.legal_principle: The fact that one will was registered and another was not does not, without more, cast doubt on execution; the judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The difference in registration did not create doubt about the due execution of the testator’s will.

rule.if: will_challenged_in_civil_suit and will_is_unregistered and related_will_is_registered and reason_for_registration_difference_was_explained

predicates.will_challenged_in_civil_suit: A person challenged a will in a civil suit.
predicates.will_is_unregistered: The challenged will was not registered.
predicates.related_will_is_registered: A related family member’s will was registered.
predicates.reason_for_registration_difference_was_e: A witness gave an explanation for why the related will was registered but the challenged will was not.

members.legal_issue: The exclusion or omission of natural heirs from a Will does not, by itself, establish a suspicious circumstance invalidating the Will.
material_facts: The Will did not mention the testator's wife or one of his sons.
The High Court treated that omission as a suspicious circumstance, while the defendants relied on evidence that the testator had separated his sons and settled his daughters during his lifetime.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee, which explains that excluding natural heirs is inherent in the purpose of a Will and is not by itself suspicious, and Ved Mitra Verma v. Dharam Deo Verma, which likewise holds that exclusion of children alone is insufficient. Under Leela Rajagopal v. Kamala Menon Cocharan, the court must assess the cumulative effect of unusual features and surrounding circumstances rather than rely on a single feature.
members.conclusion: The omission of natural heirs was not, by itself, a sufficient reason to treat the Will as suspicious; suspicious circumstances must be assessed cumulatively.

predicates.will_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity or genuineness of a Will.
predicates.will_omits_natural_heirs: The Will excludes or does not mention one or more persons who would otherwise be natural heirs.

members.legal_issue: The statutory ceiling on land held for personal cultivation applies whenever a landowner or tenant holds land above the permissible limit, including when the excess arises after the ceiling provisions take effect.
material_facts: Land that had been mortgaged with possession was excluded from the landowner’s holding for the ceiling calculation while the mortgage subsisted.
After the landowner redeemed the mortgage and regained possession, his total holding exceeded the permissible limit.
The revenue authorities sought surrender of the excess land, although the Act then provided no express machinery for this type of case.
members.legal_principle: Section 32-A imposes a continuing ceiling on land held for personal cultivation, not merely a ceiling measured when the provision came into force. The Court followed Vidya Vati v. The State of Punjab & Ors., which held that the ban applies whenever a person is found to hold land in personal cultivation above the permissible limit. Sections 32-L and 32-M address particular kinds of later acquisitions but do not restrict section 32-A’s general operation. A court must give effect to section 32-A’s plain words even where express enforcement machinery is absent.
members.conclusion: The landowner became liable to surrender the surplus land under the ceiling provision; the absence of an express procedure did not permit the court to disregard the provision’s plain terms.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter concerns whether land held above a permissible ceiling must be surrendered.
predicates.personal_holding_exceeds_permissible_lim: A landowner or tenant holds land for personal cultivation in excess of the applicable permissible limit.

members.legal_issue: The permissible area is subject to both a standard-acre limit and an ordinary-acre ceiling, even when the holding is below the standard-acre limit.
material_facts: Each allottee held about 24 standard acres, but the holdings exceeded 60 ordinary acres when converted.
The allottees relied on their holdings being below 30 standard acres to claim small-landowner status and seek a tenant’s ejectment.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(3) of the Punjab Security of Lands Tenure Act, 1953, sets a limit of 30 standard acres or, where conversion produces a greater area, 60 ordinary acres. A standard acre reflects the qualitative features of the land, while the ordinary-acre maximum reflects the quantitative limit.
members.conclusion: The ordinary-acre ceiling applies even where the holding is below 30 standard acres; the definition does not guarantee an irreducible minimum of 30 standard acres.

predicates.is_land_tenure_permissible_area_determin: The proceeding requires the permissible area of a landowner or tenant to be determined under a land-tenure regime.
predicates.converted_holding_exceeds_ordinary_area_: The holding, when converted from standard acres into ordinary acres, exceeds the applicable ordinary-acre ceiling.
predicates.permissible_area_is_limited_by_ordinary_: The permissible area is limited by the ordinary-acre ceiling despite the holding being below the standard-acre limit.

members.legal_issue: The agricultural-land ceiling scheme permits a holder to acquire land only up to the applicable ceiling and makes any excess holding liable to surrender.
material_facts: The legislation imposed a maximum limit on agricultural-land holdings and provided for acquisition and distribution of land held in excess of that limit.
The court considered the statutory restriction on acquiring land where the holder’s existing land, together with the proposed acquisition, would exceed the ceiling.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 5 establish the prohibition on holdings beyond the ceiling and the ceiling area, while Section 9 bars an acquisition that would cause the holder’s total holding to exceed that area. The Act’s purpose is to acquire and distribute land held in excess of the ceiling. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: A person or family unit may acquire land only up to the ceiling limit; land held in excess of the limit is liable to be surrendered under the Act.

predicates.agricultural_land_ceiling_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the application of a statutory ceiling on agricultural-land holdings.
predicates.existing_holding_at_or_below_ceiling: The person or family unit holds no more land than the applicable ceiling before the proposed acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_would_exceed_ceiling: The proposed acquisition would cause the total holding to exceed the applicable ceiling.

members.legal_issue: The permissible holding under the applicable land-ceiling definition was limited to the ordinary-acre ceiling where the standard-acre conversion exceeded that ceiling.
material_facts: The statutory definition provided for thirty standard acres, but applied a sixty-ordinary-acre limit where conversion of thirty standard acres exceeded sixty ordinary acres.
The landowner held 93.80 ordinary acres, and the Collector’s earlier decision had treated the permissible limit as thirty standard acres.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(2) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act defined permissible area as thirty standard acres, subject to a limit of sixty ordinary acres where conversion of thirty standard acres exceeded sixty ordinary acres.
members.conclusion: The applicable permissible limit was sixty ordinary acres, and the earlier no-surplus decision was based on a mistaken understanding of that limit.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: An authority determined the permissible holding and surplus land of a landowner.
predicates.standard_area_conversion_exceeds_ordinar: Conversion of the stated standard-acre allowance into ordinary acres would exceed the applicable ordinary-acre limit.

members.legal_issue: A ceiling on agricultural land held for personal cultivation applies whenever a person holds land exceeding the permissible limit, not only to holdings exceeding the limit when the ceiling regime commenced.
material_facts: The landowner owned agricultural land exceeding the applicable ceiling but was dispossessed by trespassers when the earlier law required landowners to select land for personal cultivation.
The landowner was restored to possession after the ceiling provisions had taken effect.
The land was declared to exceed the applicable ceiling, and the landowner challenged that determination.
members.legal_principle: Section 32-A(1) imposes a continuing restriction in its plain terms. Sections 32-L and 32-M address particular subsequent acquisitions but do not restrict the general operation of section 32-A(1). The scheme of Chapters II, III and IV, as originally enacted, allowed selection of land for personal cultivation and tenant purchase of unselected land; Chapter IV-A changed that scheme by imposing a ceiling and providing for surplus land to be appropriated to the State. Section 32-B provides machinery for holdings existing at commencement but does not limit section 32-A to that date. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The ceiling applies whenever a person is found to own or hold land under personal cultivation exceeding the permissible limit; its operation is not confined to the commencement date.

predicates.ceiling_landholding_proceeding: The proceeding determines whether a person's agricultural landholding exceeds an applicable ceiling.
predicates.personal_cultivation_exceeds_limit: A person owns or holds agricultural land under personal cultivation in an aggregate area above the applicable permissible limit.

members.legal_issue: The characterization of a transaction as an adventure in the nature of trade is a mixed question of law and fact that may be challenged in a statutory tax reference.
material_facts: The Tribunal classified the purchase of an industrial property and its subsequent partial sale as an adventure in the nature of trade.
The reference asked whether the purchase was part of a profit-making scheme or an adventure in the nature of trade.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the statutory expression “adventure in the nature of trade” requires applying the legal principles associated with trade to primary facts. Section 66(1) permits a challenge in a reference to a decision on this mixed question. The Court relied on Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal must find the primary evidentiary facts and apply the legal meaning of the statutory expression; its decision on that mixed question is open to challenge under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.

predicates.tax_reference_from_tribunal: A party brings a statutory tax reference challenging the Tribunal’s decision.
predicates.transaction_classification_requires_prim: The classification of the transaction depends on primary evidentiary facts and the application of a legal standard.

members.legal_issue: Whether deciding if a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade involves a mixed question of law and fact.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a Tribunal finding that a single land transaction was an adventure in the nature of trade.
The classification required findings about the transaction and the taxpayer’s circumstances, followed by application of the legal meaning of an adventure in the nature of trade.
members.legal_principle: Determining whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade requires the fact-finding body to find primary evidentiary facts and then apply the legal principles conveyed by that expression in section 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax was relied on for this approach.
members.conclusion: The question whether the transaction was an adventure in the nature of trade was a mixed question of law and fact and was open to examination by the Court.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_tax_tribunal: A party seeks review of a tax tribunal’s classification of a transaction as an adventure in the nature of trade.
predicates.classification_requires_primary_facts_an: Deciding the classification requires findings about what happened and application of a legal standard to those findings.

members.legal_issue: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade is a mixed question of law and fact reviewable in a statutory income-tax reference.
material_facts: The fact-finder made findings about the acquisitions, the intended resale, the use of the property, and the circumstances of the sale.
The reference challenged whether those facts justified treating the transaction as an adventure in the nature of trade.
Deciding that characterization required applying the legal meaning of trade to the primary facts.
members.legal_principle: Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, permits consideration of questions of law in a reference. Under Meenakshi Mills, Madurai v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Oriental Investment Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, the legal effect of facts and the correct application of legal principles may raise a question of law even where primary factual findings are accepted. The Court considered Edwards v. Bairstow and held it consistent with treating the characterization of a transaction as a mixed question of law and fact.
members.conclusion: The transaction’s characterization was a mixed question of law and fact and could be examined in the reference; the appropriate inquiry was whether the inference of an adventure in the nature of trade was justified in law on the proved facts.

predicates.income_tax_reference_proceeding: A party sought review of an income-tax determination through a statutory reference procedure.
predicates.transaction_characterization_requires_le: Deciding the transaction’s character required applying legal criteria concerning the nature of trade or business.
predicates.primary_facts_are_found: The fact-finder made findings about the circumstances and conduct underlying the transaction.

members.legal_issue: Whether the classification of transactions as investment or dealing, and the treatment of resulting profits as business profits, is a mixed question of law and fact reviewable by the High Court on a tax reference.
material_facts: The company had held substantial share investments for many years, made relatively few purchases, and disposed of shares in connection with changes in the interests of the group associated with those shares.
The Tribunal classified the company as a dealer, relying in part on its objects and its earlier assertions that it was a dealer.
The dispute concerned the legal effect of the facts found by the Tribunal and whether the profits and losses could be treated as business profits.
members.legal_principle: Under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, a question involving the application of law to facts is reviewable as a question of law. The High Court accepts the Tribunal's primary factual findings but may review its application of the relevant legal principles. The Court relied on G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. C.I.T., 35 I.T.R. 594.
members.conclusion: The classification and tax treatment involve mixed questions of law and fact. The High Court must accept the Tribunal's findings on primary facts but may examine whether the Tribunal applied the relevant legal principles correctly. The Court did not decide the merits of the classification in these appeals.

predicates.tax_reference_proceeding: The matter comes before the High Court as a reference arising from a tax assessment dispute.
predicates.tribunal_found_primary_facts: The tribunal made findings about the primary facts underlying the disputed transactions.
predicates.ultimate_classification_requires_legal_p: The ultimate classification of the transactions depends on applying legal principles to the primary facts.

members.legal_issue: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade is a mixed question of fact and law, so a High Court hearing a tax reference may review the Tribunal's conclusion if it misdirected itself in law.
material_facts: The appeals arose from tax references concerning whether transactions in assets were investment realisations or adventures in the nature of trade.
The Tribunal treated its conclusions about the transactions as factual, and the High Court declined to interfere on the ground that the findings were supported by evidence.
The Supreme Court concluded that the Tribunal had misapplied the law to the facts and that the High Court could have reviewed its findings.
members.legal_principle: The expression “adventure in the nature of trade” entails legal elements that give a transaction the character of trade or business. The ultimate conclusion drawn by applying those legal elements to established facts is a mixed question of fact and law and is reviewable in a tax reference where the Tribunal misdirects itself in law. The court relied on Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. C.I.T., Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. v. C.I.T., and Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. C.I.T.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to treat the Tribunal's conclusions as unreviewable findings of pure fact; it could review the mixed question where the Tribunal misdirected itself in law.

predicates.tax_reference_on_trade_character_of_tran: A High Court is hearing a tax reference about whether transactions were investments or adventures in the nature of trade.
predicates.tribunal_conclusion_applies_legal_test_t: The Tribunal's conclusion applies a legal test to facts it has found.
predicates.tribunal_misdirected_itself_in_law: The Tribunal misapplied or misunderstood the law when reaching its conclusion.

members.legal_issue: A mistaken reference in a tax notification to a statutory clause does not invalidate the tax when the municipality had power to impose the tax on the subject described in the notification.
material_facts: The notification described a tax for removing nightsoil and rubbish from buildings in the selected area but referred to the clause concerning cleaning latrines and privies.
The municipality stated that the clause reference was a mistake and that the broader scavenging-tax clause was intended.
The municipality collected nightsoil and rubbish from each bungalow, a combined service that the court held fell within its power to impose a scavenging tax.
members.legal_principle: The validity of a tax depends on whether the taxing authority has power to tax the subject; a mistaken statutory reference does not defeat an existing power to impose the tax. The court distinguished the scavenging-tax power in section 128(1)(xi) of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act from the power in section 128(1)(xii) to tax the cleaning of latrines and privies, and held the described combined service within the former power.
members.conclusion: The municipality had power to impose the scavenging tax, and the mistaken reference to another clause in the notification did not affect that power or invalidate the tax.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_tax_notification: A taxpayer challenges a municipal tax because the notification imposing it refers to a statutory clause.
predicates.notification_describes_a_taxable_municip: The notification describes a municipal service that is the subject of the tax.
predicates.municipality_has_power_to_tax_that_servi: The municipality has statutory authority to impose a tax on the service described.
predicates.notification_cites_the_wrong_taxing_clau: The notification cites a clause other than the one that supplies the municipality’s authority to impose the tax.

members.legal_issue: Procedural defects in imposing a municipal tax do not invalidate the levy when the defects are not fundamental and cause no substantial prejudice, and an official notification of imposition is conclusive proof that the statutory steps were taken.
material_facts: The Board had authority to impose the water tax and passed the special resolution directing its imposition.
The prescribed authority notified the imposition of the tax in the official gazette.
There were procedural defects in publishing the preliminary proposal, the modified proposal, and the special resolution.
The inhabitants had notice of the proposal and the imposition, and the defects did not cause substantial prejudice.
members.legal_principle: Under section 135(3) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, notification under section 135(2) is conclusive proof that the tax was imposed in accordance with the Act. Procedural defects that are not fundamental and cause no substantial prejudice to inhabitants are cured and do not invalidate the levy. The Court applied Municipal Board v. Raghuvendra, [1966] 1 S.C.R. 950; Buland Sugar v. Municipal Board, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 970; and Berar Swadeshi Vanaspathi v. Municipal Committee, Shegaon, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 596.
members.conclusion: The procedural defects did not invalidate the tax levy; the notification of imposition was conclusive proof that the necessary steps had been taken.

rule.if: municipal_tax_levy_challenge and board_authorized_to_levy_tax and imposition_resolution_passed and official_imposition_notification_issued and not fundamental_procedural_defect and not substantial_prejudice

predicates.municipal_tax_levy_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of a municipal tax levy.
predicates.board_authorized_to_levy_tax: The municipal body had authority to impose the tax.
predicates.imposition_resolution_passed: The municipal body passed a resolution directing imposition of the tax.
predicates.official_imposition_notification_issued: The prescribed authority issued an official notification imposing the tax.
predicates.fundamental_procedural_defect: A defect in the procedure for imposing the tax was fundamental.
predicates.substantial_prejudice: The procedural defect caused substantial prejudice to the municipality’s inhabitants.
predicates.procedural_defects_do_not_invalidate_tax: The procedural defects do not invalidate the tax levy.

members.legal_issue: Failure to publish a modified tax proposal does not invalidate the levy when inhabitants had an opportunity to object to the original rate and exemption limit and the modification caused no prejudice.
material_facts: The original proposal set a higher tax rate and a lower exemption limit than the modified proposal.
The Board considered inhabitants’ objections and reduced the proposed rate and raised the exemption limit.
The modified proposal was not separately published, so inhabitants were not invited to file fresh objections.
Inhabitants had previously been able to object to the proposed rate and exemption limit, and no prejudice resulted from the omission.
members.legal_principle: Section 132(2) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, required publication of a modified proposal. However, where inhabitants had an opportunity to object to the original rate and exemption limit, and the modification reduced the rate or raised the exemption limit without causing prejudice, non-publication is an irregularity cured by section 135(3). The Court also noted that a later amendment to section 132(2) exempted publication where a modification reduced the tax, although that amendment was not in force at the relevant time.
members.conclusion: Non-publication of the modified proposal was a mere irregularity, and the defect was cured.

rule.if: municipal_tax_levy_challenge and original_rate_and_exemption_open_to_objection and modification_reduced_rate_or_raised_exemption and no_fresh_objections_invited and no_prejudice_from_nonpublication

predicates.municipal_tax_levy_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of a municipal tax levy.
predicates.original_rate_and_exemption_open_to_obje: Inhabitants had an opportunity to object to the originally proposed tax rate and exemption limit.
predicates.modification_reduced_rate_or_raised_exem: The modification reduced the proposed tax rate or raised the exemption limit.
predicates.no_fresh_objections_invited: Inhabitants were not invited to submit fresh objections to the modified proposal.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_nonpublication: The failure to publish the modified proposal caused no prejudice to inhabitants.
predicates.modified_proposal_nonpublication_is_irre: Failure to publish the modified proposal is a mere irregularity.

members.legal_issue: Failure to publish the resolution directing imposition of a tax does not invalidate the levy when the governing provision does not require publication and inhabitants receive official notice of the imposition.
material_facts: The provision authorizing the Board to direct imposition of the tax did not require publication of that resolution.
The resolution directing imposition was not published in the manner prescribed by the general publication provision.
The inhabitants had no right to file objections to that resolution.
The prescribed authority published an official notification of the imposition of the tax.
members.legal_principle: Section 134(2) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, does not provide for publication of the resolution directing imposition of the tax. Even assuming section 94 required such publication, its omission is an irregularity cured by section 135(3), where inhabitants had no right to object to the resolution and had notice of the imposition through the official notification.
members.conclusion: Even assuming publication of the resolution was required, its non-publication was a mere irregularity cured by section 135(3).

rule.if: municipal_tax_levy_challenge and imposition_resolution_not_published and inhabitants_had_no_right_to_object_to_resolution and official_imposition_notice_given

predicates.municipal_tax_levy_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of a municipal tax levy.
predicates.imposition_resolution_not_published: The resolution directing imposition of the tax was not published.
predicates.inhabitants_had_no_right_to_object_to_re: Inhabitants had no right to submit objections to the resolution directing imposition.
predicates.official_imposition_notice_given: Inhabitants received notice of the tax imposition through an official notification.
predicates.resolution_nonpublication_does_not_inval: Failure to publish the imposition resolution does not invalidate the tax levy.

members.legal_issue: An omission of territorial boundaries from a tax notification does not invalidate the levy when the intended local area is clear from the notification and existing designation, the proposed levy was published for objections, and the boundaries are later supplied consistently with that designation.
material_facts: A draft of the tax rules was published and invited objections and representations to the proposed levy.
The final notification identified the local area in which the tax was to operate and included a schedule of tax rates, but omitted a second schedule referring to the area's boundaries.
The boundaries had already been set out in a valid area designation, so there was no real doubt about the local area covered by the levy.
A later notification inserted the same boundaries into the tax notification.
The governing enactment made the published final notification conclusive proof that the tax had been imposed in accordance with the Act.
members.legal_principle: Sections 39(2) and 39(3) of the U.P. Town Area Act, 1914 governed the making and prior publication of tax rules; section 15B(4) made the published notification conclusive proof that the tax was imposed in accordance with the Act. The court held that the omission did not defeat the levy because the notification identified the local area, the boundaries were established by the existing area designation, the public had been invited to object to the proposed levy, and the later insertion matched those boundaries.
members.conclusion: The omission of the second schedule was an inconsequential mistake; the tax notification was valid and effective, and the later notification could supply the boundaries.

rule.if: challenge_to_local_tax_levy and draft_levy_published_for_objections and final_levy_notification_published and local_area_unambiguously_identifiable and omitted_boundaries_later_supplied_consistently

predicates.challenge_to_local_tax_levy: A proceeding challenges a local tax imposed by a published notification.
predicates.draft_levy_published_for_objections: A draft setting out the proposed tax rules was published and the public was invited to object or make representations.
predicates.final_levy_notification_published: The final tax notification was officially published.
predicates.local_area_unambiguously_identifiable: The notification and an existing valid area designation leave no real doubt about the local area in which the tax applies.
predicates.omitted_boundaries_later_supplied_consis: A boundary schedule omitted from the final notification was later added with boundaries matching the existing valid area designation.

members.legal_issue: A jagirdar is entitled to compensation for unbuilt village-site land in which the jagirdar had a right or interest extinguished by abolition.
material_facts: The abolition vested unbuilt village-site lands in the State and extinguished rights held by jagirdars in that property.
The jagirdars claimed compensation for unbuilt village-site lands in which they had rights or interests.
members.legal_principle: Section 8 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 vested the specified properties, including unbuilt village-site lands, in the State and extinguished jagirdars’ rights. Section 11(3) is to be construed as entitling a jagirdar to compensation for rights or interests in such property under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, subject to the exceptions in section 11(3)(i) to (iii).
members.conclusion: The jagirdars were entitled to compensation for all unbuilt village-site lands in which they could prove a right or interest.

predicates.jagir_abolition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for rights or interests extinguished when jagir property vested in the State.
predicates.unbuilt_village_site_land_vested_in_stat: The land at issue is unbuilt village-site land that vested in the State on abolition.
predicates.jagirdar_proved_extinguished_interest: The jagirdar proved a right or interest in the land that was extinguished.

members.legal_issue: A claimant’s established right to enjoy land without liability for assessment is an interest in property modified to the claimant’s disadvantage when abolition of a jagir makes the land assessable.
material_facts: The claimant held, under a compromise decree, the right to own and possess certain Gharkhed lands free from assessment.
After the jagir was abolished, the lands became liable to assessment under the Act.
The claimant was not the jagirdar, and compensation for this modification had not been provided under the Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) permits a person other than a jagirdar to apply for compensation when the Act abolishes, extinguishes or modifies that person’s right to or interest in property and the Act provides no compensation for that change. Section 4 made jagir villages liable to land revenue. Enjoying land free from assessment is more valuable than enjoying it subject to assessment, so imposing assessment modifies the holder’s interest to his disadvantage. The Court distinguished State of Gujarat v. Vakhatsinghji Sursinghji Vaghela, where reduced assessment had been a concession rather than an established right, and explained Shapurji Jivanji v. Collector of Bombay as recognizing that the right to collect assessment may be relinquished by contract or legislation.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to claim compensation under section 14(1) for the modification of his interest in the lands.

rule.if: compensation_claim_under_jagir_abolition_law and claimant_is_not_jagirdar and land_was_enjoyed_free_of_assessment_as_an_established_right and abolition_made_the_land_assessable and no_compensation_was_provided_for_the_change

predicates.compensation_claim_under_jagir_abolition: A person sought compensation for a change to a property interest caused by a law abolishing jagirs.
predicates.claimant_is_not_jagirdar: The person seeking compensation was not the jagirdar.
predicates.land_was_enjoyed_free_of_assessment_as_a: The claimant held and exercised an established right to enjoy land without paying assessment.
predicates.abolition_made_the_land_assessable: Following abolition, the land became subject to assessment payable by the claimant.
predicates.no_compensation_was_provided_for_the_cha: The law provided no compensation for the change to the claimant’s property interest.

members.legal_issue: A holder of a grant of land burdened with service is entitled to compensation when abolition extinguishes or modifies rights in the land, where the grant does not authorize resumption in the circumstances of abolition.
material_facts: The grants originated before British rule and were continued to induce the grantees to settle on the land and abandon predatory activities, rather than primarily to remunerate specific services.
The grants were of villages or land itself, not merely the profits or revenue from land, and the grant terms distinguished the land from its income.

The grantees were required to render services, but the grant did not provide for resumption merely because services were not required or were not rendered; it provided for forfeiture or attachment for breach of specified conditions.
The abolition extinguished the service obligation and resumed the land, thereby affecting the grantees’ property rights.
The holders applied for compensation, and the High Court held that they were entitled to compensation and remitted the matters for determination of its amount.
members.legal_principle: Under section 7(1) of the Bombay Bhil Naik Inam Abolition Act, 1955, a person may claim compensation where the Act abolishes, extinguishes or modifies that person’s rights to or interest in property. A grant of land burdened with service cannot be resumed unless the grant specifically provides for resumption; this differs from a grant of land profits as remuneration for an office, which is resumable. The Court applied Lakhamgouda Basayprabhu Sardesai v. Baswantrao and Others, AIR 1931 PC 157, and approved the Bombay High Court’s decision in First Appeal No. 326 of 1953 concerning a grant in the same form.
members.conclusion: The grants were of land burdened with service, not grants of revenue or profits as remuneration for an office. Their abolition affected property rights, so the holders were entitled to compensation; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: compensation_claim_after_abolition and grant_was_of_land_itself and grant_was_burdened_by_service and grant_lacked_resumption_authority_for_the_abolition_circumstance and abolition_affected_property_rights

predicates.compensation_claim_after_abolition: A holder sought compensation after a grant was abolished.
predicates.grant_was_of_land_itself: The grant conveyed the land itself rather than only its profits or revenue.
predicates.grant_was_burdened_by_service: The holder was required to render service in connection with the land grant.
predicates.grant_lacked_resumption_authority_for_th: The grant did not authorize resumption in the circumstance that led to its abolition.
predicates.abolition_affected_property_rights: The abolition extinguished or modified the holder’s rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: A claimant’s right to use land without liability to pay assessment is an interest in property modified when abolition of the estate makes the land assessable, entitling the claimant to compensation if the statutory conditions are met.
material_facts: The claimant was not the holder of the abolished estate and sought compensation for rights affected by its abolition.
A consent decree gave the claimant and his brothers the right to own and possess specified lands without paying assessment.
The claimant enjoyed the lands free of assessment when the abolition law came into force; thereafter assessment became payable on them.
There was no material showing that the estate holder could collect assessment on those lands despite the decree, and the arrangement was not merely a suspension of land revenue.
No compensation for this modification was otherwise provided.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act provides compensation to a person other than a jagirdar who is aggrieved by the Act’s abolition, extinguishment or modification of a right to or interest in property, where compensation is not otherwise provided.
