A right to enjoy land without assessment is more valuable than the right to enjoy it subject to assessment, so the change modifies an interest in property; it was unnecessary to decide whether that interest was itself a right in the property. Section 3’s abolition of jagirs and associated rights supplied the context for the change. State of Gujarat v. Vakhatsinghji Vajesinghji Vaghela was distinguishable because it concerned materially different statutory language and a concession rather than a right. Shapurji Jivanji v. Collector of Bombay did not establish that the right to collect assessment could never be given up; the decision proceeded on the basis that it could be relinquished by contract or legislation.
members.conclusion: The right to enjoy the lands without liability to pay assessment was an interest in property that was modified by the imposition of assessment. The claimant was entitled to compensation under Section 14(1), with the amount to be determined on further inquiry.

rule.if: claim_for_abolition_related_compensation and claimant_is_not_abolished_estate_holder and assessment_free_land_use_before_abolition and assessment_liability_imposed_after_abolition and not mere_temporary_suspension and no_other_compensation_provided

predicates.claim_for_abolition_related_compensation: A person seeks compensation for an effect of abolishing an estate or its associated rights.
predicates.claimant_is_not_abolished_estate_holder: The person seeking compensation is not the holder of the abolished estate.
predicates.assessment_free_land_use_before_abolitio: The claimant was entitled to use the land without paying assessment before the abolition took effect.
predicates.assessment_liability_imposed_after_aboli: After the abolition took effect, assessment became payable on the land used by the claimant.
predicates.mere_temporary_suspension: The absence of assessment before abolition was only a temporary suspension of a liability that remained enforceable.
predicates.no_other_compensation_provided: No other provision provides compensation for the relevant modification.

members.legal_issue: A right to receive payment from an estate is an interest in property when the payment is charged on the estate and is not merely the estate holder’s personal liability, so its abolition may entitle the claimant to compensation.
material_facts: The claimant was not the holder of the abolished estate and sought compensation for rights affected by its abolition.
A consent decree entitled the claimant and his brothers to receive an annual cash allowance from the estate.
The allowance was payable from the estate and was a charge on it, rather than a personal liability of the estate holder.
No compensation for the abolition of this right was otherwise provided.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act provides compensation to a person other than a jagirdar aggrieved by the Act’s abolition, extinguishment or modification of a right to or interest in property, where compensation is not otherwise provided. A payment right charged on the estate, rather than a personal liability of its holder, is an interest in property.
members.conclusion: The right to receive the cash allowance was an interest in property and was compensable under Section 14(1).

rule.if: claim_for_abolition_related_compensation and claimant_is_not_abolished_estate_holder and payment_right_existed_before_abolition and payment_was_charged_on_estate and not payment_was_only_personal_liability and no_other_compensation_provided

predicates.claim_for_abolition_related_compensation: A person seeks compensation for an effect of abolishing an estate or its associated rights.
predicates.claimant_is_not_abolished_estate_holder: The person seeking compensation is not the holder of the abolished estate.
predicates.payment_right_existed_before_abolition: The claimant had a right to receive payment from the estate before its abolition.
predicates.payment_was_charged_on_estate: The payment was secured or imposed as a charge on the estate.
predicates.payment_was_only_personal_liability: The payment obligation was only a personal liability of the estate holder and was not a charge on the estate.
predicates.no_other_compensation_provided: No other provision provides compensation for the abolition or modification of the payment right.

members.legal_issue: A building plan must be considered under the building regulations in force when it is sanctioned, rather than regulations that have ceased to apply.
material_facts: The applicants relied on plans submitted before the first scheme of restrictions was introduced.
The plans had not been finally sanctioned, and the applicants had not submitted fresh plans conforming to the intervening schemes.
The earlier bye-laws were superseded, and the 1988 bye-laws were in force when any fresh plans would be considered.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 181(2) and 181A of the Cantonments Act, 1924, concerning schemes of building restrictions, and Sections 186 and 283 concerning bye-laws. It held that the 1988 bye-laws superseded the earlier bye-laws and that a plan is governed by the regulations prevailing at the time of sanction.
members.conclusion: Any fresh plans submitted by the applicants had to be governed by the building regulations in force when those plans were considered for sanction.

predicates.building_plan_approval_dispute: The proceeding concerns which building regulations govern approval of a building plan.
predicates.plan_not_finally_sanctioned: The plan had not received final sanction.
predicates.building_regulations_changed_before_sanc: The applicable building regulations changed before the plan was sanctioned.

members.legal_issue: A building-plan application must be decided under the law applicable when permission is granted, including any statutory change that has become effective by then.
material_facts: The application for building-plan approval remained pending while a revised development plan was under consideration.
The proposed revision had not been brought into force when the authority rejected the application.
The Court stated that building-plan applications are to be decided according to the law applicable on the day permission is granted.
members.legal_principle: An application does not confer a vested right to obtain approval under the rules in force when it was filed. In Howrah Municipal Corporation v. Ganges Rope Co. Ltd., the Court held that a settled expectation cannot prevail over statutory rules that are amended during the pendency of an application. Director of Public Works v. Ho Po Sang was cited on the distinction between a mere expectation and an acquired right. The Court stated that the law applicable on the date permission is granted governs the application, and relied on Kuldeep Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi concerning the authority’s duty to exercise its jurisdiction within a reasonable time.
members.conclusion: The application had to be considered under the law in force when permission was to be granted, not under a proposed plan that had not become effective.

predicates.building_plan_application_pending: An application for approval of building plans remained undecided.
predicates.planning_law_changes_before_decision: The governing planning law changed after the application was filed but before it was decided.
predicates.new_rule_effective_when_permission_is_co: The new rule had become legally effective by the time permission was considered.

members.legal_issue: A right to have a pending application determined with the benefit of finality does not vest before the determination is made.
material_facts: An application for confirmation was filed under the earlier law and remained pending when later legislation came into force.
No confirmation order had been made before the earlier law was replaced.
The confirmation order was made after the successor legislation had taken effect.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5-B of the East Punjab Evacuees’ (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, finality attached when an order was made. The Court distinguished Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. v. Irving, which concerned a right of appeal in a pending action, and Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. v. Income-Tax Commissioner, where final orders already existed. A right to finality, if it exists, arises only when the determination is actually made.
members.conclusion: The applicant had no vested right, upon filing the application, to a determination carrying the finality provided by the earlier law.

predicates.pending_statutory_application: A person filed an application under a statute that remained undecided.
predicates.no_determination_before_law_change: The statute changed before any decision was made on the application.

members.legal_issue: A pending application for building permission creates no vested right to approval, and it must be decided under the law applicable when the authority considers it.
material_facts: An application for permission to develop land remained undecided after it was submitted.
The applicant sought an order requiring the application to be considered under the law applicable at an earlier point, rather than the law applicable when the authority considered it.
The statutory steps required for permission had not been completed, and no permission had been granted on the pending application.
members.legal_principle: A pending application or settled expectation does not create a vested right to approval before the statutory conditions are satisfied. The application is determined under the law applicable when the authority considers it. The Court relied on Director of Public Works v. Ho Po Sang, Howrah Municipal Corporation v. Ganges Rope Co. Ltd., Union of India v. Indian Charge Chrome, S.B. International Ltd. v. Assistant Director General of Foreign Trade, and Kuldeep Singh v. Government of NCT of Delhi.
members.conclusion: The pending application did not confer a vested right to permission, and it must be considered under the law applicable when the authority is called upon to apply its mind to it.

predicates.appeal_concerning_pending_permission_app: The case is an appeal concerning a pending application for permission.
predicates.permission_application_remained_undecide: The authority had not decided the permission application.
predicates.statutory_conditions_for_permission_were: The statutory steps required to establish an entitlement to permission had not been completed.

members.legal_issue: A pending application and a court-ordered deadline for its consideration do not create a vested right to have it decided under superseded building rules.
material_facts: Permission had been granted for construction up to four floors, while the applicant was left free to apply for permission for further floors.
A later court order expressed an expectation that the further application would be decided within a stated period but did not direct that permission be granted.

Before the further application was decided, the building rules were amended and a municipal resolution, approved by the relevant executive body, restricted building heights in specified areas because of limited civic services.
The proposed additional construction was contrary to the restrictions in force when the authority refused permission.
members.legal_principle: The Act and Building Rules regulate construction in the public interest and do not give an applicant a vested right to approval under the rules in force on the application date. A court order allowing an applicant to apply or requiring timely consideration does not direct approval or freeze the applicable rules. Usman Gani J. Khatri v. Cantonment Board and State of West Bengal v. Terra Firma Investment and Trading Pvt. Ltd. establish that building plans are governed by the regulations in force at the time of sanction and that no legal right to approval arises merely from submitting a plan. The restrictions were imposed under Rule 20(3), with the required approval, in response to civic-service concerns; public interest and convenience prevail over a claimed settled expectation.
members.conclusion: The rules in force when sanction is granted or refused govern the application; the applicant had no vested right to sanction under the earlier rules, and the later restrictions applied to the pending application.

rule.if: building_sanction_proceeding and application_pending_when_rules_changed and court_order_only_allowed_application_or_required_consideration and new_restrictions_in_force_at_decision

predicates.building_sanction_proceeding: A person sought permission from a public authority to construct or alter a building.
predicates.application_pending_when_rules_changed: The building-sanction application remained pending when the governing construction rules changed.
predicates.court_order_only_allowed_application_or_: A court order allowed the applicant to seek further approval or required the authority to consider the application, without directing that approval be granted.
predicates.new_restrictions_in_force_at_decision: When the authority decided the application, changed rules restricted the proposed construction.
predicates.superseded_rules_do_not_create_entitleme: The applicant has no entitlement to approval under rules that were replaced before the application was decided.

members.legal_issue: A government order cannot be given retrospective effect without authority conferred by the legislature.
material_facts: A later government order stated that the building was exempt from specified development-control rules and purported to take effect from an earlier date.
The governing legislation did not confer authority to issue that order with retrospective effect.
members.legal_principle: Retrospective operation must be authorized by the legislature; the Court relied on State of M.P. v. Tikamdas, AIR 1975 SC 1429, and Bakul Cashew Co. v. Sales Tax Officer, Quilon, AIR 1987 SC 2239.
members.conclusion: The later government order was legally unsustainable insofar as it purported to operate retrospectively.

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_government_or: A proceeding challenged a government order that purported to operate from an earlier time.
predicates.order_claimed_earlier_effect: The government order stated that it would take effect before it was issued.
predicates.no_legislative_authority_for_retrospecti: The legislature had not authorized the government to give the order retrospective effect.

members.legal_issue: A delegated executive authority cannot give a later policy decision retrospective effect without statutory authorization.
material_facts: The registrants' defaults occurred before the authority adopted the later policy orders.
The orders applied a new pricing condition to defaults and restoration matters arising before the orders were made.
No provision in the governing Act or regulations authorized the delegatee to alter the contractual terms retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: A delegatee must act within the authority conferred by statute, and in the absence of legislative authorization cannot give delegated legislation or an executive decision retrospective effect. The Court relied on Vice Chancellor, M.D. University, Rohtak v. Jahan Singh, 2007 (4) SCALE 226, and Ashok Lanka v. Rishi Dixit, (2005) 5 SCC 598, and considered Sections 52 and 57 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957.
members.conclusion: The later policy could not validly be applied retrospectively to the registrants' earlier defaults and allocations.

rule.if: delegated_authority_action and policy_created_after_relevant_default and policy_applied_to_preexisting_contractual_rights and no_statutory_authority_for_retroactivity

predicates.delegated_authority_action: An authority acted under powers delegated to it by a statute.
predicates.policy_created_after_relevant_default: The authority adopted the policy after the relevant default or event had occurred.
predicates.policy_applied_to_preexisting_contractua: The authority applied the later policy to rights or obligations already arising under an existing contract.
predicates.no_statutory_authority_for_retroactivity: No governing statute authorized the authority to apply the policy retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: A delegated rule-making authority cannot give a rule retrospective effect unless the enabling law expressly or by necessary implication authorizes retrospective rule-making.
material_facts: The governing rule provided for compensation of a displaced person with a verified agricultural-land claim, as far as possible, by allotment of agricultural land.
An amendment added an explanation limiting agricultural land under the rules to land in a rural area and purported to deem the explanation always to have been inserted.
The government relied on the retrospective explanation to cancel an allotment of land that was in an urban area.
The enabling Act authorized rules to carry out its purposes but contained no express or implied authority to make rules with retrospective effect.
members.legal_principle: The scope of delegated rule-making power is governed by the enabling provision, and subordinate legislation cannot operate retrospectively without express authorization or authorization by necessary implication. The Court relied on section 40 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and referred to Cannapore Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd. v. Collector of Customs and Central Excise, Cochin, The Income Tax Officer, Alleppy v. M. C. Ponnoose, and B. S. Vadera v. Union of India, distinguishing the latter because the language of article 309 supported retrospective rules in that case.
members.conclusion: The retrospective operation of the explanation was beyond the rule-making power; it could operate only prospectively from the date it was added. The cancellation orders based on it were quashed.

rule.if: delegated_rule_challenge and enabling_law_lacks_retroactive_authority and rule_given_retroactive_effect and decision_relies_on_retroactive_rule

predicates.delegated_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a rule made by an authority exercising delegated rule-making power.
predicates.enabling_law_lacks_retroactive_authority: The law granting rule-making power does not authorize retrospective rules expressly or by necessary implication.
predicates.rule_given_retroactive_effect: The rule purports to apply to a period before it was made or amended.
predicates.decision_relies_on_retroactive_rule: The challenged decision relies on the rule's purported retrospective operation.

members.legal_issue: A delegated rule cannot retrospectively impose a contribution liability when the parent statute does not authorize retrospective rulemaking.
material_facts: A 2015 rule for coal, lignite, and sand for stowing made payment commence from the later of the rule’s commencement and the state notification establishing the foundation.
A later notification substituted that commencement rule and required contributions to be paid from an earlier date, 12 January 2015.
The parent legislation did not expressly or by necessary implication authorize the central government to impose the contribution retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: Delegated legislation is ordinarily prospective and cannot operate retrospectively unless the parent statute expressly or by necessary implication authorizes it. The Court applied Hukum Chand v. Union of India, Mahabir Vegetable Oils (P) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, Panchi Devi v. State of Rajasthan, and Vatika Township, alongside the limits on rulemaking under Sections 9B(5) and (6) and 13(2)(qqa) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.
members.conclusion: The notification of 31 August 2016 was beyond the central government’s rulemaking power and was struck down; the earlier commencement rule remained in force.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_contribution_rule: A party in a proceeding challenges a government rule made under delegated legislative authority.
predicates.rule_imposes_contribution_for_an_earlier: The challenged rule requires payment for a period preceding the rule’s otherwise applicable commencement.
predicates.parent_law_does_not_authorize_retroactiv: The legislation authorizing the rule does not expressly or by necessary implication permit retrospective rulemaking.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment to subordinate legislation cannot remove rights conferred under existing rules unless the parent statute authorizes retrospective rule-making at the time of the amendment.
material_facts: A transitional note in the rules recognized sales-tax benefits for qualifying investment made before the relevant industry was added to the excluded list.
The note was later omitted with purported retrospective effect, before the parent statute expressly authorized retrospective rule-making for the relevant rules.
The entrepreneurs relied on the existing rules and the transitional note, and the Court found that rights had been conferred under the note.
members.legal_principle: Subordinate legislation may operate retrospectively only when the parent statute confers that power. A statute is not construed to have retrospective operation unless that construction is clear from its terms or follows by necessary and distinct implication. The Court relied on Section 64(2A) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973, and West v. Gwynne, and held that the relevant retrospective rule-making power became available only after Section 64(2A) came into force. A delegatee may make rules only within the limits of the parent statute.
members.conclusion: The amendments made before the parent statute authorized retrospective rule-making could not retrospectively take away the entrepreneurs’ rights under the transitional note.

predicates.subordinate_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a retrospective change to a rule made under delegated legislative authority.
predicates.accrued_incentive_right_under_existing_r: An existing rule conferred an incentive-related right on the affected person before the change.
predicates.parent_law_lacked_retrospective_rulemaki: The parent law did not authorize retrospective rule-making when the amendment was made.

members.legal_issue: A renewed writ petition cannot be used to obtain review of a decision or direction that has already been considered, including after a full hearing.
material_facts: The petitioners again sought review of an earlier decision after an earlier set of review petitions had been dismissed.
The challenged direction to relocate the graves had been made after a full hearing of the affected group.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the petitions as a second attempt to obtain review of matters already considered and held that a direction made after a full hearing could not be made the subject of review through these petitions. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The renewed challenge to the earlier decision and the grave-relocation direction was rejected.

predicates.renewed_review_proceeding: The petitioners brought a further proceeding seeking review of an earlier decision or direction.
predicates.prior_review_attempt_dismissed: An earlier attempt by the petitioners to obtain review of the challenged matter had been dismissed.
predicates.challenged_direction_fully_heard: The court had considered the challenged direction after hearing the affected persons.

members.legal_issue: A litigant who unsuccessfully challenged an exemption measure cannot later renew the same constitutional challenge on grounds that could have been raised earlier.
material_facts: Some petitioners had previously challenged the validity of the exemption-authorizing provision and the same notification, and the Court had upheld them.
Those petitioners raised additional grounds in later proceedings that were available when they brought their earlier challenge.
members.legal_principle: Finality in litigation and public policy prevent successive challenges to the same measure on grounds that could have been raised earlier. The binding effect of a decision under Article 141 does not depend on whether a particular argument was considered, if the point to which it relates was decided. The Court relied on Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab, T. Govindaraja Mudaliar v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Anil Kumar Neotia v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The renewed challenges by those petitioners were barred by res judicata and the binding effect of the Court's earlier decision.

predicates.repeat_constitutional_challenge: The litigant brings a later constitutional proceeding challenging the same measure that was challenged in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_challenge_decided: The earlier proceeding by that litigant resulted in a decision upholding the challenged measure.
predicates.omitted_ground_available: The ground raised later could have been raised in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A claimant may not raise in a later writ proceeding a ground that was available but omitted from an earlier proceeding based on the same cause of action.
material_facts: The claimants had an earlier writ proceeding challenging the property declaration.
The contention that the required notice procedure had not been followed was available to them in the earlier proceeding but was not raised there.
They later sought to raise that contention in a subsequent writ petition by amendment.
members.legal_principle: Constructive res judicata in writ proceedings prevents a party from taking successive proceedings on the same cause of action and raising grounds that could and should have been raised earlier. The Court relied on Devilal Modi, Proprietor, M/s Daluram Pannalal Modi v. Sales Tax Officer, Ratlam.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in allowing the omitted ground to be raised and decided in the later proceeding because the ground was barred by principles analogous to constructive res judicata.

rule.if: later_writ_proceeding and same_cause_of_action and ground_available_earlier and not ground_raised_earlier

predicates.later_writ_proceeding: A claimant brings a writ proceeding after an earlier writ proceeding involving the challenged action.
predicates.same_cause_of_action: The later proceeding seeks relief based on the same underlying challenged action as the earlier proceeding.
predicates.ground_available_earlier: The factual or legal ground relied on in the later proceeding could have been raised in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.ground_raised_earlier: The claimant actually raised that ground in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A writ petitioner cannot relitigate a matter already decided, or a matter that could and ought to have been raised in the earlier proceeding.
material_facts: The challenged acquisition and the contention that the land fell outside the project agreement had been litigated in earlier proceedings.
The Supreme Court had previously rejected the contention that land beyond the main road alignment was outside the integrated project and had upheld the acquisition.
The appellant knew the contents of the project agreement and could have raised the relevant contention in the earlier proceedings but gave no reasonable explanation for not doing so.
The appellant brought a further writ proceeding raising the same acquisition issues.
members.legal_principle: Constructive res judicata under Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to writ petitions. An adjudication is conclusive not only as to matters actually decided but also as to matters that the parties might and ought to have litigated as part of the same controversy. The Court relied on State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organisation, Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v. State of Maharashtra, State of U.P. v. Nawab Hussain, Devilal Modi v. Sales Tax Officer, Daryao v. State of U.P., Greenhalgh v. Mallard, and Sheoparsan Singh v. Rammanandan Prasad Singh. Relitigation may also be an abuse of process even when it is not technically barred by res judicata, as explained in K.K. Modi v. K.N. Modi.
members.conclusion: The renewed challenge was barred by res judicata and constructive res judicata; those principles apply to writ petitions, and the further proceeding was also an abuse of the process of the court.

rule.if: writ_challenge and prior_final_adjudication and (same_issue_decided or omitted_issue_could_and_ought_to_have_been_raised) and no_reason_for_omission

predicates.writ_challenge: A party brings a writ proceeding to challenge a matter previously litigated.
predicates.prior_final_adjudication: A competent court has finally adjudicated an earlier proceeding concerning the matter.
predicates.same_issue_decided: The issue raised in the later proceeding was decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.omitted_issue_could_and_ought_to_have_be: The later issue was part of the earlier controversy and could and ought to have been raised there.
predicates.no_reason_for_omission: The party offers no reasonable explanation for not raising the issue in the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a government grant cannot be raised in later proceedings on a ground that was available but omitted from an earlier challenge to the same grant.
material_facts: The claimants had earlier challenged the government grant in court.
They did not raise in that challenge the contention that restrictions on acquiring, holding, or transferring agricultural land invalidated the grant for house sites.
They later relied on that contention to challenge the same grant.
members.legal_principle: Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies constructive res judicata and applies to writ proceedings. It bars a matter that might and ought to have been raised in the earlier proceeding. The Court relied on Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v. State of Maharashtra and Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal. A fresh cause of action may support a new proceeding, but it does not permit reopening issues or grounds barred by res judicata or constructive res judicata.
members.conclusion: The omitted ground could not be raised in the later proceeding because of constructive res judicata.

predicates.later_challenge_to_same_grant: A claimant challenged the same government grant in a later proceeding.
predicates.earlier_challenge_to_grant: The claimant had previously brought a proceeding challenging that grant.
predicates.available_ground_omitted: The claimant could have raised a ground in the earlier proceeding but did not do so.

members.legal_issue: Eliminating intermediaries and establishing direct relations between cultivators and the State constitutes a public purpose for land acquisition.
material_facts: The law sought to eliminate intermediary holders between the State and cultivators.
It aimed to establish direct contact between cultivators and the Government, improve tenants’ land status, and place village affairs and common lands under democratic village management.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its reasoning in the Bihar case and held that land-tenure reform establishing direct relations between cultivators and the State was for the general public benefit.
members.conclusion: The law served a public purpose and the objection that it did not was rejected.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of land rights.
predicates.law_aims_to_eliminate_land_intermediarie: The law seeks to remove intermediary holders between the State and cultivators.
predicates.law_directly_benefits_cultivators: The law seeks to improve cultivators’ position or establish direct relations between them and the State.

members.legal_issue: Acquiring estates to eliminate intermediaries, reform land distribution, and bring occupants into direct relations with the State serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The Act sought to abolish zamindari and other proprietary interests, eliminate intermediaries, and bring occupants into direct relations with the Government.
The reform was directed at changing the distribution and control of land and other material resources for the community’s benefit.
members.legal_principle: The requirement of public purpose is assessed in light of the general interest of the community and the social conditions at the time of the legislation. The Court relied on the constitutional objectives in articles 38 and 39, including distributing material resources to serve the common good and preventing concentration of wealth. It referred to Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India for the proposition that public purpose concerns the general interest of the community, while recognizing that the concept changes over time.
members.conclusion: The acquisition of estates under the land-reform scheme was for a public purpose.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_case and (purpose_eliminates_intermediaries or purpose_reforms_land_distribution) and purpose_serves_general_community_interest

predicates.estate_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a law acquiring estates or comparable land interests.
predicates.purpose_eliminates_intermediaries: The law seeks to remove intermediaries between occupants and the State.
predicates.purpose_reforms_land_distribution: The law seeks to alter land distribution or control as part of a land-reform scheme.
predicates.purpose_serves_general_community_interes: The law’s objective is directed to the general benefit of the community rather than a private interest.

members.legal_issue: The acquisition of intermediary estates to reform land distribution and bring cultivators into direct relation with the State serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The laws sought to abolish zamindari and other intermediary interests and transfer those interests to the State.
The stated scheme aimed to alter land distribution and bring cultivators into a direct relationship with the State.
The Constitution’s Directive Principles address distribution of community resources for the common good and preventing concentration of wealth and means of production.
members.legal_principle: Public purpose is assessed in light of the general interest of the community and may evolve with social and economic conditions. The court relied on the constitutional preamble and article 39, and referred to Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India and the reasoning in the High Court decisions concerning the land-reform legislation.
members.conclusion: The acquisition of the estates for the land-reform scheme was for a public purpose.

predicates.a_challenge_to_estate_acquisition: The proceeding challenges the validity of a law acquiring intermediary landholdings.
predicates.acquisition_targets_intermediary_landhol: The law transfers the interests of landlords or other intermediaries in estates to the State.
predicates.scheme_aims_to_reform_land_distribution_: The acquisition scheme seeks to alter land distribution for the general benefit of the community.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of estates to reform land tenure, raise the status of cultivators, and manage land for the community is for a public purpose even when private individuals receive tenure rights after acquisition.
material_facts: The law vested estates in the State and provided for land to vest in village bodies for management under State supervision.
It created or enlarged cultivators' tenure rights and provided for agrarian reforms, including cooperative farming and village self-government.
The acquired property was not taken for the private benefit of a particular individual, and the reform applied to people already in possession of land.
members.legal_principle: The meaning of public purpose is elastic and depends on the statute, the time, and society's needs; the inquiry is whether the acquisition serves the general interest of the community rather than an individual's private interest. The Court considered the constitutional objectives and the Act as a whole, and distinguished redistribution for community-wide agrarian reform from taking one person's property solely for another's private use. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.
members.conclusion: The acquisition had a public purpose and was not invalid for want of one.

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition_for_: A party challenges compulsory acquisition undertaken as part of land-tenure reform.
predicates.acquisition_serves_community_wide_tenure: The acquisition enables reforms intended to change tenure arrangements and benefit the community generally.
predicates.property_not_transferred_for_private_ben: The acquired property is not taken to give it for the private benefit of a particular person.

members.legal_issue: A state acquisition of intermediary estates for agrarian reform serves a public purpose when it advances the interests of the community rather than the private interest of an individual.
material_facts: The legislation acquired intermediaries’ interests in estates and changed the land-tenure system, including by raising the status of cultivators and providing for village bodies and cooperative farming.

The acquired property was to vest in the State or village bodies subject to State supervision, and the scheme did not transfer particular property to an individual for that individual’s private purposes.
members.legal_principle: The meaning of “public purpose” is elastic and depends on the statute, the time, and society’s needs; the test is whether the acquisition serves the general interest of the community rather than an individual’s private interest. The Court applied this principle in interpreting the constitutional requirement in Article 31(2), while holding that the Act was protected from challenge under Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B.
members.conclusion: The acquisition served a public purpose, and the Act was not invalid for want of one.

predicates.state_acquires_intermediary_estates: The government acquires the interests of intermediaries in landed estates.
predicates.agrarian_reform_benefits_the_community: The acquisition forms part of a scheme to reform land tenure or improve the position of cultivators for the community’s benefit.
predicates.property_is_not_transferred_for_an_indiv: The acquired property is not taken to give it to an individual for that individual’s private purposes.

members.legal_issue: A former statement cannot be used to contradict a witness unless it is legally proved and the witness's attention is drawn to the specific parts relied on for contradiction.
material_facts: The defence sought to use a statement allegedly made by an injured prosecution witness to a magistrate on the day of the occurrence.

The magistrate's evidence did not establish the statement's authenticity: it lacked the relevant official signature or seal, and the magistrate did not say who identified the witness before recording it.
At trial, the witness was not confronted with the specific passage said to contradict his testimony; he was only asked generally whether he had made a statement about an accused.
As to the principal accused's alleged assault on the deceased, the former statement and the witness's trial evidence were not inconsistent.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 145 of the Evidence Act, a witness intended to be contradicted by a prior written statement must have attention drawn to the specific parts to be used for contradiction. Tahsildar Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Binay Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar explain this requirement; Bhagwan Singh v. State of Punjab was distinguished on its facts. A statement must also be legally proved before it can be used for that purpose.
members.conclusion: The former statement could not be used to impeach the witness: it was not satisfactorily proved, the witness was not confronted with the relevant passage as required, and there was no material variance concerning the principal accused.

predicates.criminal_trial_and_prior_statement_offer: In a criminal proceeding, a party offers a witness's prior statement to contradict that witness.
predicates.prior_statement_not_reliably_proved: The evidence does not reliably establish that the prior statement was authentic and made by the witness.
predicates.witness_not_confronted_with_specific_pas: The witness was not directed to the specific passage relied on for contradiction.

members.legal_issue: A prior statement may not be used against a witness as an admission when it concerns an unrelated issue, is not a clear admission, or is not put to the witness for an opportunity to explain it before it is proved.
material_facts: The earlier deposition concerned a dispute over different survey numbers from those at issue in the later proceeding.
Read as a whole, the deposition did not clearly admit a landlord-tenant relationship; it stated that no rent was received and that the land was fallow.
The witness was not shown the deposition during cross-examination, and a certified copy was placed on record after his evidence had concluded.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17 of the Indian Evidence Act, an admission must concern a fact in issue or relevant fact. Admissions must be clear to be used against their maker; under section 145, a witness must be given an opportunity to address a writing intended to contradict him. The Court applied Bharat Singh v. Bhagirathi and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shrinivas Pandit, including the principle that a witness should see and be able to answer a statement before it is used against him.
members.conclusion: The earlier deposition was not a usable admission against the witness, and the argument that he was bound by it was rejected.

rule.if: prior_statement_offered_as_admission and (statement_concerned_unrelated_issue or statement_was_ambiguous or witness_not_confronted_before_proof)

predicates.prior_statement_offered_as_admission: A party offered an earlier statement made by a witness as an admission against that witness.
predicates.statement_concerned_unrelated_issue: The earlier statement concerned a matter that was neither in issue nor relevant in the proceeding where it was offered.
predicates.statement_was_ambiguous: The earlier statement, read in context, did not clearly and unequivocally admit the fact for which it was offered.
predicates.witness_not_confronted_before_proof: The witness was not shown the statement and given an opportunity to explain it before it was proved and relied on against the witness.
predicates.prior_statement_not_used_against_witness: The earlier statement is not used against its maker as an admission.

members.legal_issue: A witness's prior statement may be used to contradict the witness only after the witness's attention is drawn to the specific parts relied on, and the prior statement is not substantive evidence.
material_facts: Some witnesses had signed statements recorded by military authorities, but disputed the contents or denied the statements' significance at trial.

The Court explained that a signed statement could establish that a statement was recorded and signed, but that a writing intended for contradiction had to be put to the witness by drawing attention to the relevant parts.
Only the parts properly put to the witness could be considered with the witness's evidence in assessing veracity.
members.legal_principle: Section 145 of the Evidence Act permits contradiction by a prior written statement only when the witness's attention is drawn to the specific parts intended to be used. Proof that a witness signed a statement does not, by itself, make its contents substantive evidence.
members.conclusion: Prior statements could be used only in the prescribed manner to contradict witnesses; the parts put to the witnesses could be considered with their evidence, but the prior statements could not be treated as substantive evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which a witness gives evidence.
predicates.prior_written_statement_used_for_contrad: A party relies on an earlier written statement to challenge the witness's testimony.
predicates.witness_attention_drawn_to_relevant_part: The witness is directed to the specific portions of the earlier statement relied on for contradiction.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s prior written statement may be used to contradict the witness only after the witness’s attention is drawn to the relevant part, and it is not substantive evidence of the facts stated.
material_facts: Some witnesses had signed statements previously recorded by military authorities.
The Court considered whether those statements could be used without confronting the witnesses with the relevant passages during their testimony.
members.legal_principle: Section 145 of the Evidence Act governs contradiction by a prior written statement: the witness’s attention must be drawn to the specific part relied upon. A statement used in that way is considered with the witness’s testimony in assessing credibility, but the whole statement is not substantive evidence.
members.conclusion: A prior statement may be used to contradict a witness only in the manner prescribed by the Evidence Act; the relevant passage must be put to the witness, and the statement is not substantive evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial or an appeal arising from one.
predicates.prior_writing_used_to_contradict_witness: A party relies on a witness’s earlier written statement to challenge the witness’s testimony.
predicates.attention_called_to_relevant_passage: The witness is directed to the specific passage in the earlier writing relied upon for contradiction.

members.legal_issue: A contradiction in a witness's earlier statement cannot be used against the witness when it has not been properly put to the witness or proved through the person who recorded the earlier statement.
material_facts: The surviving witness's testimony referred to three fuel containers, while her earlier recorded declaration referred to one.
The alleged contradiction was not put to the Magistrate who recorded the earlier declaration.
The witness was not specifically given an opportunity to explain the difference.
The court also found that the three containers had been recovered at the scene and that the discrepancy did not undermine the witness's credibility.
members.legal_principle: A prior inconsistent statement must be put to the witness so that the witness has an opportunity to explain it; where the alleged contradiction concerns a recorded statement, it must be proved by putting it to the person who recorded that statement. The Court relied on this procedure in assessing the evidence, without citing a specific provision for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The alleged discrepancy could not be relied on as a contradiction because it had not been properly proved or put to the witness for explanation.

rule.if: criminal_evidence_case and prior_statement_conflicts_with_testimony and contradiction_not_put_to_recorder and witness_not_given_opportunity_to_explain

predicates.criminal_evidence_case: The court is assessing witness evidence in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.prior_statement_conflicts_with_testimony: A witness's earlier recorded statement appears to differ from the witness's testimony at trial.
predicates.contradiction_not_put_to_recorder: The alleged difference was not put to the person who recorded the earlier statement to prove it.
predicates.witness_not_given_opportunity_to_explain: The witness was not specifically asked to explain the alleged difference.

members.legal_issue: A state that owns mineral-bearing land may reserve it for public-sector exploitation without thereby violating the central statutory regime governing mines and mineral development, unless that regime has displaced the state's ownership-based authority.
material_facts: The mineral-bearing land and minerals had vested in the state, and the state owned the area when it issued the reservation notifications.
The notifications reserved iron-ore-bearing areas for exploitation in the public sector before the later statutory scheme expressly regulated state reservations for public-sector mining.
The later state referred to and reaffirmed the continuing reservations, and no competent authority had repealed or altered them.
members.legal_principle: The constitutional allocation of legislative power under Entry 54 of List I and Entry 23 of List II, read with the declaration in Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, removes state legislative power only to the extent that the Union has assumed control under that Act. The Act and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 regulate mining but do not divest the state of ownership or expressly extinguish its authority to reserve its own mineral-bearing land. The Court relied on Amritlal Nathubhai Shah v. Union of India, which recognized the state's ownership-based reservation power and the relevance of Rule 59; it distinguished the occupied-field decisions in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., and Baijnath Kadio v. State of Bihar. It also relied on Indian Metals and Ferro Alloys Ltd. v. Union of India in holding that pre-existing reservations survived the later changes to Rule 58 and the introduction of Section 17A.
members.conclusion: The earlier reservation notifications were valid exercises of the state's authority as owner of the mines and minerals, were not inconsistent with the central statutory regime, and remained operative.

rule.if: mining_lease_appeal and state_owned_mineral_area and reservation_for_public_sector and ownership_authority_not_displaced

predicates.mining_lease_appeal: The proceeding challenges the refusal or withdrawal of proposals for private mining leases.
predicates.state_owned_mineral_area: The mineral-bearing land and minerals were owned by the state.
predicates.reservation_for_public_sector: The state set aside the mineral-bearing area for exploitation in the public sector.
predicates.ownership_authority_not_displaced: No applicable law expressly removed the state's ownership-based authority to reserve its own mineral-bearing land.

members.legal_issue: A State Government may reserve mineral-bearing land owned by the State for exploitation in the public sector and refuse private applications for mineral concessions over that land.
material_facts: The State Government owned the minerals and mines in the areas concerned.
The State Government notified that the areas were reserved for exploitation of bauxite in the public sector.
Private applicants sought mining leases over the reserved areas, and the State Government refused their applications on that ground.
members.legal_principle: The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 declared under section 2 that regulation of mines and mineral development was to be under Union control to the extent provided by the Act, displacing the State Legislature’s power under Entry 23 of List II in that field. That did not divest the State of ownership of minerals within its territory. Sections 4 and 10 and the Rules govern private prospecting and mining concessions; section 10’s power to entertain applications includes power to refuse a concession because the land is unavailable after reservation. Section 17(2) and (4) do not exhaust the State’s authority to reserve land for itself. Rule 59 contemplates State reservation for any purpose. The Court distinguished State of Orissa v. Union of India, AIR 1972 Orissa 68, and found that M/s S. Lal and Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, AIR 1975 Patna 44, did not assist the applicants.
members.conclusion: The State Government had authority to reserve the areas and refuse the applications while the areas remained reserved.

predicates.mineral_concession_refusal_appeal: A party appealed from the refusal of an application for a prospecting licence or mining lease over mineral-bearing land.
predicates.state_owns_minerals: The State Government owned the minerals and mines in the area concerned.
predicates.state_reserved_area_for_public_exploitat: The State Government reserved the area for exploitation in the public sector.

members.legal_issue: A state government’s ownership of land and minerals does not make its proposal to reserve the area for a state-owned undertaking binding on the central government.
material_facts: The state government proposed that land be reserved for exploitation by a state-owned company.
The proposed land was not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease, but the central government did not approve the proposal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 17A(2) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, the state government may propose reservation of land not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease for operations through a state-owned or controlled government company or corporation, but only with central government approval. The Act places regulation of mines and mineral development within the Union’s domain under Section 2. Indian Metals and Ferro Alloys Ltd. v. Union of India, Indian Charge Chrome Ltd. v. Union of India, State of T.N. v. M.P.P. Kavery Chetty, and State of Kerala v. Kerala Rare Earth & Minerals Ltd. support the requirement of central approval.
members.conclusion: The state government may propose reservation of eligible land for a state-owned undertaking, but reservation requires the central government’s approval.

predicates.state_government_seeks_reservation_for_s: A state government asks that an area be reserved for prospecting or mining through a government company or corporation owned or controlled by it.
predicates.proposed_area_not_held_under_prospecting: The proposed area is not held under a prospecting licence or mining lease.

members.legal_issue: The procedure for central-government mining operations does not govern a State government's decision to reserve an area for exploitation in the public sector.
material_facts: The State government reserved the mining area for exploitation in the public sector.
The Central Government had not proposed to undertake prospecting or mining operations in the area.
members.legal_principle: Section 17 applies when the Central Government proposes to undertake prospecting or mining operations in an area not already held under a prospecting licence or mining lease. It does not concern the distinction between public and private sectors.
members.conclusion: Section 17 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 had no bearing on the dispute and did not require compliance in order to reserve the area for public-sector exploitation.

predicates.mineral_concession_dispute: The proceeding concerns a decision about a mineral concession.
predicates.area_reserved_for_public_sector: The government reserves the area for exploitation in the public sector.
predicates.central_government_not_proposing_operati: The Central Government has not proposed to undertake prospecting or mining operations in the area.

members.legal_issue: State ownership of mineral deposits on government land is not displaced by legislation regulating mines and mineral development.
material_facts: The mineral deposits at issue were located on land owned by the State.
The dispute concerned applications for mining leases, and the applicants did not seriously dispute the State’s ownership of the minerals.
members.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, read with Entry 54 of List I and Entry 23 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, places regulation and development of mines and minerals under Union control to the extent provided by the Act; it does not transfer State ownership of minerals. The Court relied on Monnet Ispat and Energy Limited v. Union of India and Amritlal Nathubhai Shah v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The State owns mineral deposits in government-owned land within its territory, while the applicable legislation regulates their development without divesting that ownership.

predicates.mining_lease_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over the grant or refusal of a mining lease.
predicates.mineral_deposits_on_government_owned_lan: The mineral deposits are located on land owned by the State.

members.legal_issue: Identification in court may support a conviction despite the absence of identification at a test identification parade when the identification evidence is otherwise reliable and corroborated.
material_facts: One accused was not identified by a witness at the identification parade.
That witness was not examined at trial, and the court did not rely on his recorded statement.
Several other witnesses identified the accused in court, and the court found their identifications reliable.
members.legal_principle: The Code of Criminal Procedure does not require an identification parade. Such a parade is an investigative tool, and identification at the parade is corroborative of identification in court. Identification in court for the first time is not ordinarily a sufficient basis for conviction without corroboration, but that is a rule of prudence subject to exceptions (Munshi Singh Gautam v. State of M.P.; Sheo Shankar Singh v. State of Jharkhand).
members.conclusion: The failure to identify the accused at the parade was inconsequential and did not undermine the conviction.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and identification_parade_not_supportive and reliable_court_identification and identification_corroborated_by_other_evidence

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.identification_parade_not_supportive: A test identification parade did not identify the accused or otherwise support the prosecution identification evidence.
predicates.reliable_court_identification: Witnesses reliably identified the accused in court.
predicates.identification_corroborated_by_other_evi: Other evidence supports the identification of the accused.

members.legal_issue: Identification evidence from a properly conducted test identification parade, followed by identification in court, is not inherently weak and may be believed unless the witness’s evidence has another infirmity.
material_facts: Witnesses who were not previously acquainted with the accused identified him at test identification parades and later in court.
The relevant witnesses had an opportunity to observe the accused for a substantial time in daylight while he arranged to hire a taxi.
The evidence showed that precautions were taken to keep the accused concealed from the witnesses before the parades.
The High Court rejected the identification evidence by treating it as universally weak and by relying on speculative possibilities that the witnesses had previously seen the accused.
members.legal_principle: Identification at a test parade conducted by a magistrate with essential formalities and precautions, followed by identification in court, can be believed unless there is another infirmity. A witness’s opportunity to observe the accused for some time in daylight strengthens the evidence. Budh Sen v. State of U.P. was explained as concerning first-time identification in court without a prior parade, not as establishing a universal rule. Ramanathan v. State of Tamil Nadu was followed; State of Rajasthan v. Ranjita was approved; Dhokal Singh v. The State was disapproved. The court also accepted that formal entries in police or jail records documenting precautions to keep an accused concealed are not invariably required.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the identification evidence against the principal accused was reliable and rejected the High Court’s universal rule that identification evidence is weak.

rule.if: test_identification_parade_conducted_with_precautions and later_identification_in_court and adequate_opportunity_to_observe and not other_identification_infirmity

predicates.test_identification_parade_conducted_wit: The accused was identified at a test parade conducted with essential formalities and precautions against prior exposure to witnesses.
predicates.later_identification_in_court: The witness also identified the accused in court.
predicates.adequate_opportunity_to_observe: The witness had a meaningful opportunity to observe the accused, such as for some time in daylight.
predicates.other_identification_infirmity: The identification evidence suffers from an additional infirmity apart from the fact that it is identification evidence.

members.legal_issue: Unreliable test identification evidence does not prevent a finding of identity when credible in-court identification is supported by reliable circumstantial evidence.
material_facts: Three witnesses testified that they saw the assault and identified the accused in court; their presence near the scene was natural, and they had no apparent animus against him.

The court considered the identification parades of little value, but the witnesses’ in-court identifications were supported by evidence that the accused had purchased the iron pipe used in the assault, led police to its recovery, and had human blood on his clothes when arrested.
Medical evidence showed that the victim’s injuries could have been caused by the recovered pipe and were sufficient to cause death.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 9 of the Evidence Act, test identification evidence is admissible but is only supporting evidence: it may corroborate a witness’s substantive in-court identification, and has no independent value by itself. Test identification is not the only means of confirmation; circumstantial evidence may also establish identity. The court cited no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The identification parades were of little value, but the credible in-court identifications, corroborating circumstances, and medical evidence reliably established the accused’s identity and guilt.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and credible_in_court_identification and reliable_circumstantial_corroboration and medical_evidence_supports_the_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: A person challenged a criminal conviction in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.credible_in_court_identification: Witnesses who were naturally present at the scene identified the accused in court, and the court found their testimony trustworthy.
predicates.reliable_circumstantial_corroboration: Independent circumstances linked the accused to the weapon or its recovery and to physical evidence connected with the assault.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_the_account: Medical evidence was consistent with the described weapon and injuries and supported the cause of death.
predicates.conviction_supported_by_reliable_evidenc: The conviction rests on reliable evidence establishing the accused’s guilt.

members.legal_issue: A conviction may be affirmed when the accepted identification evidence is reliable despite the identifying witness not seeing the assailant’s face.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a murder conviction based principally on one witness’s testimony.
The witness was closely familiar with the accused and had met him repeatedly shortly before the offence.
Although the witness did not see the assailant’s face, he identified him by voice and gait; he had heard him speak about the dispute immediately before the shooting.
The trial court and the High Court accepted the witness’s testimony, and the Supreme Court found no ground to disturb their assessment.
members.legal_principle: The Supreme Court normally does not review evidence in a criminal appeal unless the trial was vitiated by procedural illegality or irregularity, was unfair, or resulted in a gross miscarriage of justice. Recognition by voice may be risky when the recognizer is unfamiliar with the person, but familiarity and prior opportunities to hear and observe the person may support the identification. No specific provision or earlier case was relied on for this evidentiary ruling.
members.conclusion: The identification evidence did not justify overturning the concurrent findings; the conviction and death sentence were affirmed.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and witness_familiar_with_accused and identification_based_on_voice_or_gait and identification_consistent_with_prior_familiarity and concurrent_fact_findings and not (trial_vitiated_by_procedural_illegality or unfair_trial or gross_miscarriage_of_justice)

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.witness_familiar_with_accused: A witness who identifies the accused was already familiar with that person.
predicates.identification_based_on_voice_or_gait: The witness identifies the accused from the person’s voice, gait, or both, rather than from seeing the person’s face.
predicates.identification_consistent_with_prior_fam: The circumstances of the identification are consistent with the witness’s prior familiarity with the accused.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The trial court and the appellate court below both accept the material identification evidence.
predicates.trial_vitiated_by_procedural_illegality: A procedural illegality or irregularity has vitiated the trial.
predicates.gross_miscarriage_of_justice: The judgment has resulted in a gross miscarriage of justice.
predicates.conviction_and_sentence_affirmed: The conviction and sentence are left undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a test identification parade reduces the evidentiary value of an identification made in court, but does not make that identification insufficient when it is corroborated by other evidence.
material_facts: One eyewitness identified several accused in court about three years after the incident, and no test identification parade had been held.
The court found that this identification was corroborated by another eyewitness and by confessions it held admissible, voluntary and believable.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principle in the identification case cited as Kanan (AIR 1980 SC 1382): absence of a test identification parade diminishes the evidentiary value of in-court identification. It nevertheless held that corroboration by another eyewitness and by admissible, voluntary and believable confessions could make the identification sufficient.
members.conclusion: The in-court identification was not sufficient by itself, but its corroboration made it sufficient to support the relevant findings.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.in_court_identification_without_test_par: A witness identified an accused in court without an earlier test identification parade.
predicates.identification_corroborated_by_independe: Other evidence corroborated the witness’s identification.

members.legal_issue: A court may initiate a complaint procedure for alleged false evidence in a judicial proceeding only when the material supports a prima facie case and the court separately finds an inquiry expedient in the interests of justice.
material_facts: In a civil proceeding, a litigant submitted signed written statements and an affidavit supporting one side, then sought to disown those documents and submitted a contradictory version supporting the other side.

The High Court treated the contradictory documents and declarations as grounds to direct a complaint, but did not adequately follow the required process for forming an opinion on expediency and deciding whether to make a complaint.
The parties later amicably settled some of their disputes.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 340(1) and 195(1)(b)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court must have material making out a prima facie case of an offence within the provision and must form the further opinion that an inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice. A contradictory statement alone is not always enough: intentional falsity or fabricated evidence for use in judicial proceedings must be shown. The court must then decide separately whether to make a complaint. The Court relied on K.T.M.S. Mohd. v. Union of India, Pritish v. State of Maharashtra, and Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah.
members.conclusion: The direction to initiate proceedings was set aside because the required process for forming an opinion on expediency and deciding whether to make a complaint had not been followed; in light of the subject matter and subsequent developments, the matter was laid to rest.

rule.if: section_340_proceeding and (no_prima_facie_basis or no_separate_expediency_assessment) and complaint_directed

predicates.section_340_proceeding: A court is considering a complaint procedure for an offence allegedly committed in or in relation to a judicial proceeding.
predicates.no_prima_facie_basis: The material before the court does not establish a prima facie basis for an inquiry into an offence covered by the complaint procedure.
predicates.no_separate_expediency_assessment: The court has not separately assessed whether an inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice.
predicates.complaint_directed: The court has directed that a complaint be made.

members.legal_issue: A complaint alleging false evidence or a false evidentiary declaration may be directed where the court has found the material allegations in the supporting affidavit untrue and there is a prima facie basis for prosecution.
material_facts: An affidavit verified the allegations in an application for contempt as true to the deponent’s knowledge.
The allegations that the persons accused of contempt had broken a gate, cut down a tree and disturbed possession were found by the High Court not to be true and not reasonably believable.
The High Court considered the inquiry and the evidence, including that the contemporaneous police report did not mention the alleged damage.
members.legal_principle: Sections 193 and 199 of the Indian Penal Code concern, respectively, giving false evidence and making a false statement in a declaration receivable as evidence. Sarkar held that the High Court’s finding that the allegations were not true supplied the necessary finding of falsity. Mudholkar considered the crucial allegations to be those of interference with possession and damage, and concluded that their falsity supported a prima facie case under sections 193 and 199. Hidayatullah stated that review of an order directing prosecution ordinarily asks whether the High Court fairly considered the case, found prima facie good reason and a reasonable prospect of conviction, and considered prosecution expedient in the interests of justice.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s direction to file a complaint for false evidence and a false declaration had a prima facie basis, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_against_order_directing_prosecution and affidavit_used_in_judicial_proceeding and material_allegations_found_untrue and court_fairly_considered_evidence

predicates.appeal_against_order_directing_prosecuti: A person appeals from an order directing that a prosecution be initiated against them.
predicates.affidavit_used_in_judicial_proceeding: A person submits an affidavit for use in a judicial proceeding and verifies its factual statements.
predicates.material_allegations_found_untrue: The court finds that material factual allegations in the affidavit are not true.
predicates.court_fairly_considered_evidence: The court considers the evidence bearing on the alleged falsity before directing a prosecution.

members.legal_issue: Prima facie evidence that a party has tampered with judicial records or filed false affidavits warrants setting the criminal law in motion to protect the administration of justice.
material_facts: The Court found that the tenant had tampered with the Rent Controller's record and that a document had been interpolated into the Rent Tribunal's record.
The Court found that the visa and immigration stamp relied on by the tenant were not genuine and that false affidavits had been filed in support of the appeal.
The Court considered that the conduct was intended to mislead the Court and obstruct the course of justice.
members.legal_principle: Tampering with judicial records and filing false affidavits obstruct the due course of justice and undermine the rule of law. Where the Court is prima facie satisfied that such conduct occurred, it may direct that a complaint be filed to initiate criminal proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Court directed its Registrar to file a complaint before the appropriate court and set the criminal law in motion; it did not determine criminal guilt.

rule.if: court_proceeding and (judicial_record_tampering_found or false_affidavit_filed) and prima_facie_evidence_of_obstruction

predicates.court_proceeding: A matter is before a court exercising judicial authority.
predicates.judicial_record_tampering_found: The court record contains alterations or interpolations attributable to a party or someone acting for that party.
predicates.false_affidavit_filed: A party has filed an affidavit containing statements the court finds false.
predicates.prima_facie_evidence_of_obstruction: The circumstances provide an initial evidentiary basis to find that the conduct was intended to mislead the court or obstruct justice.

members.legal_issue: A prima facie case of fabricating evidence in court proceedings, coupled with the expediency of action in the interests of justice, warrants a complaint for perjury.
material_facts: The application alleged that a balance sheet filed in the higher court proceedings had been altered by hand, changing the description of the share figures in a way that addressed a discrepancy relied on below.
The original balance sheet and other copies exhibited in the trial court record did not contain the handwritten alteration, while the copies filed in the higher court did.
The court found the altered wording materially significant because the original figures and the earnings-per-share calculation were based on the same share count despite an asserted share buy-back.

The company’s director had sworn to the veracity of the facts and documents filed in the higher court proceedings, although he had relied on the unaltered auditor’s report in his trial-court evidence.
The court found a prima facie case that evidence had been fabricated for the higher court proceedings and that action was expedient in the interests of justice.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 340 and 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court considers whether a prima facie case exists that an offence concerning evidence in a judicial proceeding has been committed and whether action is expedient in the interests of justice. The court relied on In Re: Suo Motu Proceedings against R. Karuppan, Advocate, (2001) 5 SCC 289, in directing an officer to file a complaint. It directed complaints under Sections 193 and 199 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The court allowed the application and directed an officer of the court to file complaints against the company and its director for perjury-related offences before a competent Magistrate.

rule.if: perjury_proceeding and (court_record_versions_differ_materially and alteration_first_appeared_in_higher_court_filing) and alteration_could_mislead_court and action_expedient_in_justice

predicates.perjury_proceeding: The matter was an application seeking criminal action for alleged false evidence submitted in court proceedings.
predicates.court_record_versions_differ_materially: The court found that a document in the original lower-court record differed materially from the version filed in the higher court.
predicates.alteration_first_appeared_in_higher_cour: The court found that the alteration was absent from the versions exhibited below and appeared in the version filed in the higher court.
predicates.alteration_could_mislead_court: The alteration changed significant wording in a document in a way that could address an evidentiary discrepancy relevant to the proceedings.
predicates.action_expedient_in_justice: The court found that the circumstances made action appropriate in the interests of justice.

members.legal_issue: The intended industrial or commercial use of acquired agricultural land does not, by itself, justify increasing its market value, though its inherent non-agricultural potential may be relevant.
material_facts: The acquired lands were agricultural when acquired.
The land was acquired for extending an industrial estate and was intended for industrial use.
Development expenditure would be required for industrial use, but development charges had not been deducted in the valuation under review.
The court separately recognized the lands’ non-agricultural potential and location when adjusting compensation.
members.legal_principle: The owner is compensated for what was lost, not by reference to the purpose of acquisition; that purpose cannot itself increase market value. The court relied on Hookiyar Singh v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, (1996) 3 SCC 766, and explained the qualification to the discussion in Subh Ram v. State of Haryana, (2010) 1 SCC 444. Development expenditure is relevant to determining compensation, while inherent potentiality may also be considered.
members.conclusion: The intended use or purpose of acquisition could not itself be used to increase market value; the court nevertheless accounted for the lands’ non-agricultural potential in the valuation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.agricultural_land_at_acquisition: The land was agricultural when it was acquired.
predicates.industrial_or_commercial_future_use: The acquiring body intended to use the land for industrial or commercial purposes.

members.legal_issue: Agricultural land with only a future possibility of building use is not to be valued as already developed land.
material_facts: The acquired lands were agricultural lands on the notification date.
The claimants produced no evidence that their lands were developed or fit for construction of houses.
The land had potential for building use only in the future.
members.legal_principle: Market value under Section 23(1) is assessed with reference to the land's condition and situation on the notification date. For land that is already developed, the nature and cost of development and the land's circumstances must be considered. For land requiring development, the Court stated that at least one-third is to be deducted for amenities and noted that deductions as high as 60% had been upheld. Future potential alone does not make agricultural land developed land.
members.conclusion: The land was correctly valued as agricultural land on a per-bigha basis, and its future potential for building use did not justify valuing it as developed land.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding seeks judicial determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_is_agricultural_on_valuation_date: The acquired land is agricultural when its market value is assessed.
predicates.building_use_is_only_future_potential: The land's building use is prospective rather than an existing developed use.
