members.legal_issue: The acquired land had non-agricultural potential beyond the portion formally converted for non-agricultural use.
material_facts: A portion of the acquired land had been converted for use by a sugar factory, while the owners claimed that the remaining land was also used for non-agricultural purposes.
The factory project report and approved scheme showed that land was required for raw materials, buildings, a workshop, staff quarters, parking, and other factory purposes.
The State produced no evidence that the remaining land was mainly used for agriculture.
Both courts below found that the remaining land had potential for non-agricultural use.
members.legal_principle: The Court saw no reason to disturb concurrent factual findings supported by the factory project materials and not rebutted by evidence from the State.
members.conclusion: The finding that the remaining land had non-agricultural potential was affirmed.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.factory_plans_show_non_agricultural_use: The project materials show that the land was intended for factory-related buildings, storage, access, or other non-agricultural uses.
predicates.state_lacks_evidence_of_agricultural_use: The acquiring authority produces no evidence that the disputed land was mainly used for agriculture.
predicates.concurrent_non_agricultural_potential_fi: The courts below both find that the disputed land has potential for non-agricultural use.

members.legal_issue: Agricultural land may have potential value for non-agricultural uses despite its existing use and the absence of an approved building plan.
material_facts: The acquired land was agricultural on the notification date, and its owners had no sanctioned plan to sell it for building purposes.
The land was within municipal limits and near built-up areas, roads, residential houses, cinema houses, a residential colony, a thermal colony and an aviation centre.
members.legal_principle: In determining market value in a land-acquisition compensation proceeding, the land's potential uses may be considered alongside its existing agricultural use. The judgment refers to the acquisition notification under section 4(1) and the reference under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act; it identifies no earlier case by name for this holding.
members.conclusion: The land possessed potential value for residential or commercial purposes.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.agricultural_land_near_built_up_area: The acquired land was agricultural and situated near built-up areas.
predicates.surrounding_development_indicates_nonagr: Nearby development included features associated with residential or other non-agricultural uses.

members.legal_issue: Multiple principals may jointly appoint one agent through a common power of attorney.
material_facts: The plaintiff, his father, and his stepbrother jointly executed a power of attorney appointing one agent to act for them.
The challenge to the appointment relied on the fact that several principals had jointly granted the authority; no violation of contract law was shown.
members.legal_principle: Agency arises by contract when an agent has authority to act for a principal and consents to do so. Co-principals may jointly appoint an agent and become jointly liable to, and jointly sue, that agent. The Court relied on the general law of contract and Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol. 1, 4th ed., para. 726.
members.conclusion: The joint appointment of one agent by the three principals was legally permissible.

predicates.joint_agent_appointment_disputed: A challenge was made to the validity of appointing one agent for multiple principals.
predicates.multiple_principals_jointly_authorized_a: Multiple principals jointly authorized one agent to act for them.

members.legal_issue: The scope of a jointly granted power of attorney may extend to each principal's separate property where its terms and the circumstances show that intention.
material_facts: The principals each had separate lands and had no identified joint property, business, or venture.
They could not readily reach or manage their own lands and were contemplating migration.
They jointly granted the power of attorney for convenience, and the circumstances indicated that each wanted the agent to deal with his individual property.
The instrument used collective expressions such as acting on the principals' behalf.
members.legal_principle: The authority conferred by a power of attorney depends on its terms and the purpose for which it was executed, and the instrument is ordinarily construed strictly. Surrounding circumstances may nevertheless be considered to ascertain the parties' intention. The Court relied on Bryant, Powis and Bryant Ltd. v. La Banque du Peuple, 1893 A.C. 170 at 177, and Modi & Co. v. Union of India, [1963] 2 S.C.R. 565.
members.conclusion: The power of attorney authorized the agent to act in respect of each principal's individual property, not merely their joint affairs or property.

predicates.scope_of_joint_power_disputed: A dispute arose over whether a jointly granted authority covered only joint affairs or also separate affairs.
predicates.principals_owned_separate_properties: The principals each owned property separately rather than holding only joint property.
predicates.principals_could_not_manage_their_proper: The principals could not readily access or manage their separate properties.
predicates.circumstances_show_individual_dealing_pu: The circumstances surrounding the appointment showed that each principal intended the agent to deal with that principal's own property.

members.legal_issue: Multiple principals may jointly appoint one agent by a power of attorney.
material_facts: Three principals jointly executed a power of attorney appointing one agent.
No provision of contract law or general contract law was shown to make their joint appointment impermissible.
members.legal_principle: An agency arises when an agent has authority to act on behalf of a principal and consents to do so; co-principals may jointly appoint an agent. The Court agreed with the proposition stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England, Fourth Edition, Volume 1, paragraph 726.
members.conclusion: The joint appointment was legally permissible.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.multiple_principals_jointly_appointed_on: Multiple principals jointly appointed one agent to act on their behalf.

members.legal_issue: A power of attorney executed jointly by co-principals may authorize the agent to deal with each principal’s individual property when its terms and the circumstances show that this was the intended scope.
material_facts: The principals had separate lands and no evidence showed that they owned joint property or carried on a joint business or venture.
They faced difficulty accessing or managing their respective lands and executed one power of attorney for convenience.
The instrument authorized the agent to act on their behalf, and the circumstances showed that each principal intended the agent to deal with that principal’s property.
members.legal_principle: A power of attorney is ordinarily construed strictly: Bryant, Powis and Bryant Ltd. v. La Banque du Peuple, [1893] A.C. 170 at 177. Its scope depends on its terms and purpose, and surrounding circumstances may be considered to ascertain the parties’ intention: Modi & Co. v. Union of India. The instrument must be considered as a whole.
members.conclusion: The power of attorney was not confined to joint affairs or jointly owned property; it authorized the agent to act in respect of each principal’s individual property.

rule.if: civil_appeal and jointly_executed_agency_document and principals_owned_separate_property and circumstances_show_individual_property_purpose

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.jointly_executed_agency_document: Multiple principals jointly executed an instrument appointing an agent.
predicates.principals_owned_separate_property: The principals had separate property rather than only property held jointly.
predicates.circumstances_show_individual_property_p: The circumstances showed that the principals appointed the agent so that each could have their individual property managed or dealt with.

members.legal_issue: A pending application for a discretionary mining lease is governed by the rules in force when the application is disposed of, and a prior order directing consideration does not preserve a right to grant under a repealed rule.
material_facts: The applicant sought a quarry lease under a rule that empowered the government to grant or renew leases in special cases.
A court had directed the government to consider and dispose of the application, but had not adjudicated an entitlement to a lease.
The rule was repealed before the government disposed of the application, which it then rejected.
The applicant claimed that the application should be considered under the rule as it stood when the application was made.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 39 of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, the State Government had power to grant or renew a lease or permission in special cases. No one has a vested right to the grant or renewal of a mining lease, or to have an application decided under the rules in force when it was made. A pending application is dealt with under the rules in force on the date of disposal. The Court relied on State of Tamil Nadu v. M/s. Hind Stone, (1981) 2 SCC 205, and P.T.R. Exports (Madras) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 268. It distinguished decisions concerning changes to the basis of rights already decided, because the earlier order here required only consideration of the application and had not established a right to a lease.
members.conclusion: The repeal removed the basis for granting the application under the former rule; the applicant had no vested right to a mining lease, and the authority could not grant the lease under that repealed rule.

predicates.discretionary_mining_lease_application_p: An applicant had a pending request for a mining lease that could be granted in special cases.
predicates.prior_order_only_required_consideration: A court had directed the authority to consider the application but had not decided that the applicant was entitled to a lease.
predicates.governing_rule_repealed_before_disposal: The rule under which the application was made was repealed before the authority disposed of it.
predicates.application_governed_by_rules_at_disposa: The authority must decide the pending application under the rules in force when it disposes of the application.

members.legal_issue: A pending application for a mineral lease or renewal is governed by the rules in force when the application is decided, even if it was filed before a later rule came into force.
material_facts: Some applications for new leases or renewals were filed before the rule barring private black-granite leases came into force.
The applications remained pending and were decided after that rule came into force.
The applicants argued that delay in deciding their applications entitled them to have them considered under the earlier rules.
The applicants had no vested right to obtain a lease or renewal.
members.legal_principle: No applicant has a vested right to the grant or renewal of a lease, or to have an application decided under the rules in force when it was filed. An application must be decided under the rules in force when it is disposed of, although it should be dealt with within a reasonable time.
members.conclusion: The applications had to be decided under the rules in force on the date of disposal; the applicants’ right to a timely decision did not give them a vested right to have the earlier rules applied.

predicates.pending_mineral_lease_application: An application for a new mineral lease or renewal remained undecided.
predicates.later_rule_in_force_before_decision: A new rule relevant to the application came into force before the authority decided it.
predicates.no_vested_right_to_lease: The applicant had no vested right to receive the lease or renewal.

members.legal_issue: Rules governing mining leases apply to a mining sublease made after those rules take effect, even if the lessee’s own lease predates them.
material_facts: The company’s original mining lease was granted before the Act and the Rules came into force in the relevant area.
The company granted the sublease after the Act and the Rules had come into force there.
The sublease was a mining lease within the statutory definition, and the challenged prosecution concerned the later grant rather than a change to the terms of the original lease.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 6 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, authorize rules governing mining leases. Section 7 concerns modifying or altering the terms of mining leases granted before the Act commenced; it does not prevent rules under sections 5 and 6 from applying to a distinct mining sublease made after the Act and Rules have come into force. Because a sublease is itself a mining lease under section 3(d), applying the rules to the later sublease does not modify the earlier lease.
members.conclusion: Rules made under sections 5 and 6 apply to a mining sublease granted after the Act and the Rules come into force, notwithstanding that the underlying lease predates them.

rule.if: mining_sublease_transaction and underlying_lease_preexisting and mining_rules_were_in_force and sublease_made_after_rules_took_effect

predicates.mining_sublease_transaction: A lessee transfers an interest in leased property to another person for mineral-related purposes.
predicates.underlying_lease_preexisting: The transferor’s own lease was granted before the relevant mining rules took effect.
predicates.mining_rules_were_in_force: Rules regulating mining leases had taken effect in the area covered by the transferred interest.
predicates.sublease_made_after_rules_took_effect: The lessee granted the sublease after those rules had taken effect in that area.

members.legal_issue: Amended rules governing the term of a mineral lease apply when they come into force while an appeal against refusal of the lease remains pending.
material_facts: The tender for a sand quarry was rejected before the rules were amended.
The applicant appealed the rejection, and that appeal remained pending when the amendment took effect.
The amendment provided that the lease period would commence on execution of the lease deed.
The appellate authority disposed of the appeal after the amendment took effect, but limited the lease to the period stated in the original advertisement.
The original advertisement was issued to implement the governing rules.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 8(8)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, as amended, the lease period begins on execution of the lease deed. State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone establishes that an application must be decided under the rules in force at the time of disposal, and that an appeal is a continuation of the proceeding begun by the application. Accordingly, an amendment taking effect during a pending appeal applies when that appeal is decided; administrative instructions or inconsistent advertisement terms cannot displace the governing rules.
members.conclusion: The amended rules applied to the pending appeal, and the three-year lease period had to run from execution of the lease deed; the advertisement could not be read in isolation from the rules.

predicates.mineral_lease_appeal: An applicant appealed the refusal of an application for a mineral lease.
predicates.appeal_pending_when_rules_amended: The appeal remained undecided when the rules governing the lease were amended.

members.legal_issue: A pre-constitutional law continued in force after the Constitution cannot, by itself, authorize a local tax on Union property contrary to the constitutional exemption.
material_facts: The municipality sought taxes on railway property owned by the Union.
The asserted liability arose under a pre-constitutional law and a notification issued under that law.
Parliament had not enacted a post-constitutional law authorizing the tax.
members.legal_principle: Article 285(1) exempts Union property from taxes imposed by a State or an authority within a State unless Parliament provides otherwise by law. Under Article 372(1), existing laws continue only subject to the other provisions of the Constitution; the pre-constitutional Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act could not prevail over Article 285(1).
members.conclusion: The pre-constitutional law did not take the Union property outside the exemption from local taxes.

predicates.local_tax_claim_on_union_property: A local authority sought to impose or collect a tax on property owned by the Union.
predicates.preconstitutional_law_is_only_authority: The asserted authority for the tax was a law in force before the Constitution, and Parliament had not afterward enacted a law authorizing the tax.

members.legal_issue: A municipality cannot impose property tax on an occupier of Union-owned property when doing so would defeat the constitutional exemption applicable to the property.
material_facts: The Union owned the land and godowns, while the appellant occupied and used the godowns for storage of food grains.
The appellant occupied the property on behalf of the Union and was not shown to be a lessee paying rent.
The property was exempt from property tax under Article 285(1).
The municipal corporation relied on the statutory rule assigning primary responsibility for property taxes to certain occupiers.
members.legal_principle: Article 285(1) protects Union property from local property tax, and the municipal statute governing primary responsibility for property taxes must be construed consistently with that constitutional protection. The provision assigning responsibility to an occupier cannot be used to make the exemption ineffective. The Court distinguished Food Corporation of India v. Municipal Committee, Jalalabad (1999) 6 SCC 74 and Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. v. Secretary, Revenue Department, Government of Andhra Pradesh (1999) 4 SCC 458, which concerned property belonging to separate legal entities rather than Union-owned property.
members.conclusion: The occupier was not liable for property tax under the municipal statute because applying that provision to charge the occupier would defeat the constitutional exemption for the Union-owned property.

rule.if: municipal_property_tax_appeal and union_owned_property and property_tax_exemption_applies and occupier_holds_directly_from_government and occupier_uses_property_for_government

predicates.municipal_property_tax_appeal: The proceeding challenges a municipal demand for property tax on property.
predicates.union_owned_property: The property on which tax is demanded is owned by the Union.
predicates.property_tax_exemption_applies: The property is constitutionally exempt from the disputed property tax.
predicates.occupier_holds_directly_from_government: The occupier holds the property immediately from the government.
predicates.occupier_uses_property_for_government: The occupier uses the property on behalf of the government.

members.legal_issue: A pre-constitutional central law imposing liability for taxes on Union property does not override the constitutional exemption unless Parliament provides otherwise after the Constitution.
material_facts: The railway property was originally owned by a non-government company and was taxed under a local law and a notification.
After the railway became government-owned, a central law and a later notification provided for payment of local taxes.
The municipality relied on that law to claim taxes on the government-owned railway property.
Parliament had not enacted a post-constitutional law making the Union property liable for the taxes claimed.
members.legal_principle: Article 285(1) exempts Union property from taxes imposed by a State or an authority within a State unless Parliament provides otherwise by law. Under Article 372(1), existing laws continued only subject to the Constitution. The Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act, 1941, was repugnant to Article 285(1) to the extent it imposed taxes on Union property, and was not a post-constitutional law of Parliament providing otherwise.
members.conclusion: The pre-constitutional law could not displace the exemption for Union property under Article 285(1); the property was exempt unless the claim qualified under Article 285(2).

predicates.municipal_tax_claim_against_union_proper: A local authority claims a tax on property owned by the Union.
predicates.liability_based_only_on_preconstitutiona: The claimed tax liability rests only on a central law made before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.postconstitutional_parliamentary_law: Parliament has enacted a law after the Constitution came into force providing for the claimed tax on Union property.

members.legal_issue: Railway property acquired after the applicable constitutional tax-exemption cutoff is not liable to municipal tax under an earlier notification unless a later law or notification makes it liable.
material_facts: The railway administration constructed the assessed buildings after 1 April 1937; some were also constructed after the Constitution commenced.
A 1911 notification under the Indian Railways Act, 1890, had declared the railway administration liable for specified municipal taxes, including taxes in the municipality concerned.
No notification under section 3 of the Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act, 1941, declared the railway property liable for the taxes, and no other applicable law provided for its taxation.
The municipality assessed the buildings and sought to collect municipal tax; the railway administration challenged that liability.
members.legal_principle: Section 154 of the Government of India Act, 1935, exempted Union property from provincial and local taxes, subject to the proviso preserving liability only for property that was already liable immediately before Part III commenced. Article 285 of the Constitution similarly exempts Union property, with clause (2) preserving only pre-existing tax liability. Section 4 of the Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act, 1941, permits revocation or variation of notifications issued under section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890; it does not itself impose tax liability on later-acquired property. Section 3 of the 1941 Act requires a notification declaring railway property liable. The Court applied Corporation of Calcutta v. Governors of St. Thomas’ School, Calcutta, which held that government-built structures not taxable before the 1935 Act commenced were not brought within the grandfathering proviso.
members.conclusion: The buildings were exempt from municipal tax, and the municipality could not levy or collect the tax on them. The earlier notification did not make later-acquired railway property liable.

predicates.railway_municipal_tax_appeal: The proceeding challenges a municipality’s levy or collection of tax on property held for railway administration purposes.
predicates.property_acquired_after_exemption_cutoff: The property was not in existence and was not liable to the relevant local tax when the applicable constitutional exemption took effect.
predicates.no_later_tax_authorization: No later law or notification made the property liable to the local tax.

members.legal_issue: A court must record a compromise in pending litigation when it is satisfied that the compromise is genuine and lawful.
material_facts: The parties signed and accepted a compromise covering the entire subject matter of the litigation.
The compromise stated that each son had received payment in exchange for relinquishing his interest.
One son later disputed receiving the stipulated payment and opposed recording the compromise.
The Court found the compromise genuine and lawful.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution and Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, once the Court is satisfied that a compromise is genuine and lawful, it must record it. The Court approved the principle in Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. v. Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Orissa 108.
members.conclusion: The compromise had to be accepted and recorded, and the suit disposed of in accordance with its terms.

predicates.compromise_recording_proceeding: A party asks a court to record a compromise in pending litigation.
predicates.compromise_signed_and_accepted: The parties signed the compromise and accepted its terms.
predicates.court_satisfied_genuine_and_lawful: The court found that the compromise was genuine and lawful.

members.legal_issue: A writ court may record and give effect to a compromise without requiring strict compliance with the formal requirements for compromises in civil suits.
material_facts: The writ petition was disposed of after counsel for both sides asked the court to record the terms in a government memorandum that had been issued following the Endowments Commissioner’s proposal.
The memorandum set out the proposed terms in writing, and the respondent accepted those terms during the writ proceedings.
The appellants did not contend that their counsel lacked authority to consent; the order recorded that the parties had sought disposal on the compromise terms.
The allegation that the Advocate General had not appeared was raised only later, and the court record stated that the State was represented.
members.legal_principle: Rule 24 of the Andhra Pradesh Writ Proceedings Rules applies the CPC as far as possible, while Section 141 CPC excludes Article 226 proceedings from the expression “proceedings”; Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC therefore does not control the High Court’s power under Article 226 to dispose of a matter by consent. The court relied on Byram Pestonji Gariwala v. Union Bank of India for the authority of counsel to act for a client, and State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak for the principle that a court’s record of what occurred before it is conclusive unless corrected by that court.
members.conclusion: The writ court’s consent order was not invalid merely because the compromise was not separately signed by the parties. The requirements of Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC did not have to be mandatorily followed in the Article 226 proceedings, and the recorded account of what occurred in court could not be contradicted in the appeal.

predicates.article_226_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding before a court exercising constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.consent_terms_recorded_by_court: The court records that the parties, through counsel, agreed to disposal on stated compromise terms.
predicates.counsel_authority_undisputed: The party does not establish that the counsel who consented lacked authority to act for it.

members.legal_issue: A court hearing an appeal must give effect to a proved, lawful compromise that settles the appeal.
material_facts: The parties entered into a written compromise settling their pending disputes, including the dispute in the appeal, and providing that the respondent would withdraw the appeal.
The respondent refused to withdraw the appeal, and the appellant asked the appellate court to dispose of it in accordance with the compromise.
The fact and validity of the compromise were not disputed.
members.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the court, when satisfied that a suit has been settled wholly or in part by a lawful agreement, to record the compromise and pass a decree in accordance with it so far as it relates to the suit. For this purpose, “suit” includes an appeal. The provision is mandatory. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The appellate court was bound to accept the compromise and dismiss the appeal in accordance with its terms; the High Court erred in setting aside that dismissal.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter before the court is an appeal.
predicates.lawful_compromise_covers_appeal: The parties made a lawful compromise that settles the dispute in the appeal.
predicates.compromise_proved: The compromise was proved to the court's satisfaction.

members.legal_issue: A court recording a compromise is not required to state expressly that it is satisfied that the compromise is lawful.
material_facts: The suit was disposed of by a compromise decree, but the order did not expressly record satisfaction that the compromise was lawful.
No contrary showing that the compromise was unlawful was identified.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a compromise must be lawful, but the court need not state expressly that it has satisfied itself of that requirement; such satisfaction is presumed unless the contrary is shown. This approach is consistent with Roshan Lal v. Madan Lal and Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam.
members.conclusion: The court is presumed to have been satisfied that the compromise was lawful unless the contrary is shown.

predicates.compromise_recorded_in_civil_suit: The parties compromised a civil suit and the court recorded the compromise.
predicates.evidence_compromise_unlawful: The material shows that the compromise was unlawful.

members.legal_issue: A case need not be remitted for further examination of an independent property claim when concurrent findings have already rejected that claim and remittal would serve no purpose.
material_facts: The trial court found against the claimant on his right, title, and interest in the property under the sale deed.
The appellate court did not disturb that finding.
The matter had been pending for many years, and the Court concluded that remitting it for further examination would serve no purpose in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the concurrent adverse findings of the courts below and the circumstances of the case, including the lengthy pendency, to conclude that remittal would serve no purpose. No specific provision or earlier case was cited for this determination.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to remit the matter for independent examination of the claimant's property-rights claim and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.appeal_seeks_remand_for_independent_prop: An appeal asks for a matter to be remitted so that an independent claim to property can be examined.
predicates.lower_courts_concurrently_rejected_claim: The trial court rejected the claimant's asserted title and the appellate court left that finding undisturbed.
predicates.remand_would_serve_no_purpose: The circumstances indicate that sending the matter back for further examination would not serve a useful purpose.

members.legal_issue: A case need not be remanded for reconsideration of a factual ground for eviction when concurrent factual findings support that ground and no formulated question of law challenges those findings.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court both found that the claimant bona fide required the building for the claimant’s own business.
The second appeal did not formulate a question of law concerning that finding.
The matter reached the Supreme Court after the High Court reversed the lower courts’ decision on the claimant’s title.
members.legal_principle: Where concurrent factual findings support a ground for eviction and no formulated question of law in the second appeal concerns those findings, there is no purpose in remanding the case to reconsider that ground.
members.conclusion: A remand was unnecessary, and the trial court’s eviction decree as confirmed by the first appellate court was restored.

predicates.second_appeal_in_eviction_case: The matter is a second appeal in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings_support_bona: The trial court and first appellate court both found that the claimant had a bona fide need for the premises.
predicates.no_formulated_law_question_challenges_ne: No question of law formulated in the second appeal challenges the finding on the claimant’s need.

members.legal_issue: A remand is unnecessary when the material findings supporting an eviction decree remain undisturbed and the small causes court need not finally determine title to decide the claim.
material_facts: The trial court found that the claimant owned the premises, had inducted the tenant, and was entitled to eviction.
The revisional court had not disturbed the trial court’s findings on the merits and had ultimately decreed eviction.
The High Court quashed the revisional order and remanded the matter for fresh decision, although final determination of title was not needed for the eviction proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances, the remand was unnecessary because the trial court’s findings on the merits had not been disturbed and title could be considered incidentally. It allowed the appeal and confirmed the revisional court’s eviction decree. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s remand was unnecessary and its order was set aside; the revisional decree of eviction was confirmed.

predicates.challenge_to_eviction_order: A party challenged an order concerning an eviction decree, and the challenged decision had remanded the matter for fresh proceedings.
predicates.material_trial_findings_undisturbed: The findings supporting the eviction decree had not been set aside or disturbed on their merits.
predicates.final_title_determination_not_necessary: The eviction claim could be decided without finally determining title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A grant determination need not be remanded for failure to frame formal issues or take evidence when no disputed question of fact was raised and the challenge presents only a question of law.
material_facts: The State sought a remand, arguing that the grant officer had not treated the application and objection as pleadings, framed issues, or taken evidence as in a civil suit.
The State had not disputed the customary maintenance right in its written objection.
No disputed question of fact was raised before the grant officer, and the challenge concerned a question of law.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the asserted procedural irregularities did not require a remand where the written objection raised no disputed question of fact and the award was challenged only on a question of law. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this procedural conclusion.
members.conclusion: Remand was not warranted because there were no disputed factual questions requiring issues or evidence.

rule.if: grant_determination_appeal and formal_issues_or_evidence_omitted and no_disputed_factual_issue and challenge_only_legal

predicates.grant_determination_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a determination made on a rehabilitation-grant application.
predicates.formal_issues_or_evidence_omitted: The decision-maker did not frame formal issues or take evidence in the manner used in a civil suit.
predicates.no_disputed_factual_issue: The objection raised no disputed question of fact requiring evidence.
predicates.challenge_only_legal: The challenge to the determination presented only a question of law.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may enhance damages for use and occupation when it has authority to determine the matter with the parties’ consent and the record supports the increased amount.
material_facts: The parties consented to the High Court deciding the merits and exercising its appellate powers under Order 41, Rules 30, 32 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
The High Court found that the premises would ordinarily have generated a higher monthly amount than the trial court had awarded.
The evidence and the parties’ position supported the High Court’s assessment of the amount for use and occupation.
The appellant challenged the enhancement, but the Supreme Court found no basis to interfere.
members.legal_principle: Order 41, Rules 30, 32 and 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, empowered the High Court to decide the appeal and make an appropriate decree; in this case the parties consented to its exercise of those powers. The Court upheld the assessment because the record supported the increased damages.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s enhanced award of damages for use and occupation was upheld.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerns_use_and_occupation: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil dispute that includes damages for use and occupation of premises.
predicates.parties_consent_to_appellate_merits_deci: The parties consent to the appellate court deciding the merits and exercising its appellate powers to make a decree.
predicates.record_supports_higher_compensation: The evidence supports a higher amount of compensation for use and occupation than the amount fixed below.

members.legal_issue: A court may require a lawful tenant to pay increased future rent when the existing payment is inadequate in light of the premises and their commercial setting.
material_facts: The Supreme Court concluded that the occupant was a tenant who would remain in lawful possession after the appeal.
The Court considered the existing monthly payment very low in view of the size of the premises and their location in a busy commercial locality.
The Court directed payment of Rs. 2,000 per month from 1 April 2004 for as long as the occupant remained in lawful possession, while preserving liability for any earlier arrears at the agreed rate.
members.legal_principle: Having allowed the appeal and confirmed the occupant’s lawful status as a tenant, the Court considered the existing payment inadequate in view of the premises’ size and busy commercial location, and directed a higher future payment while leaving earlier arrears payable at the agreed rate.
members.conclusion: The occupant was directed to pay Rs. 2,000 per month as rent from 1 April 2004 for as long as he remained in lawful possession, in addition to clearing any earlier arrears at the agreed rate.

predicates.tenant_remains_in_lawful_possession: The occupant is a tenant who will remain in lawful possession of the premises.
predicates.existing_rent_is_inadequate_for_premises: The court finds the existing rent inadequate in light of the premises’ size and commercial setting.
predicates.supreme_court_is_deciding_an_appeal: The Supreme Court is deciding an appeal concerning the occupant’s right to remain in the premises.

members.legal_issue: A court may increase the rent payable for an allotted building when the locality is important and the existing rent is palpably low.
material_facts: The building was in an important locality.
The Court considered the rent then being paid palpably low.
The Court heard counsel for both sides on the rent issue.
members.legal_principle: The Court adjusted the rent in the interests of justice after hearing counsel, taking account of the importance of the locality and the palpably low rent. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this adjustment.
members.conclusion: The Court increased the monthly rent payable for the building, effective from the date it specified in its order.

rule.if: appellate_court_considers_rent and locality_is_important and existing_rent_is_palpably_low and both_sides_heard_on_rent

predicates.appellate_court_considers_rent: An appellate court considers the rent payable for a building in the proceeding before it.
predicates.locality_is_important: The building is situated in a locality the court considers important.
predicates.existing_rent_is_palpably_low: The rent being paid for the building is palpably low.
predicates.both_sides_heard_on_rent: The court hears both sides on whether the rent should be adjusted.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court exercising special-leave jurisdiction may enhance rent when the circumstances show a substantial increase in prevailing rents.
material_facts: While allowing the appeal and setting aside the eviction order, the Court noted that rents in the area had increased enormously.
The Court exercised its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution and directed an increase in the rent or mesne profit payable.
members.legal_principle: In exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court may adjust the rent or mesne profit payable in light of the substantial increase in rents. The judgment cites no earlier case for this direction.
members.conclusion: The Court enhanced the rent or mesne profit payable in the circumstances of the case.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The Court was deciding an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.court_found_prevailing_rents_had_increas: The Court found that prevailing rents had increased substantially.

members.legal_issue: An authority deciding a statutory review that may displace an existing mining lease acts quasi-judicially and must give the affected grantee a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: A state government granted the appellant mining leases for five areas and delivered possession to him.
A competing applicant sought statutory review of the grants, and the reviewing authority cancelled the leases for two areas and directed that leases be granted to the competing applicant.
The reviewing authority made its decision without giving the appellant an opportunity to present his case, despite his request to be heard.
members.legal_principle: Under rules 52–55 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, made under section 6 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1941, a statutory review initiated by an aggrieved party creates a lis between that party and the grantee. The grant is effective unless displaced on review, so the grantee has an interest in the review’s outcome and a right to represent his case. Applying Province of Bombay v. Kushaldas S. Advani, which adopted the test in R. v. Electricity Commissioners, an authority determining contested rights under legal authority must act judicially unless the governing law indicates otherwise. The reviewing rules did not negate that duty; the failure to provide a reasonable opportunity to be heard therefore justified quashing the order.
members.conclusion: The reviewing authority acted quasi-judicially and was required to give the affected grantee a reasonable opportunity to represent his case. Because it did not do so, its order was quashed, with liberty to decide the review afresh after providing that opportunity.

rule.if: statutory_review_of_mining_lease and review_challenges_existing_grant and grantee_has_interest_in_outcome and not grantee_given_opportunity_to_be_heard

predicates.statutory_review_of_mining_lease: A reviewing authority is deciding a statutory review concerning a mining lease.
predicates.review_challenges_existing_grant: The review seeks to displace a lease already granted to another person.
predicates.grantee_has_interest_in_outcome: The existing grantee has an interest in the review because its decision may affect the grant.
predicates.grantee_given_opportunity_to_be_heard: The reviewing authority gave the affected grantee a reasonable opportunity to present their case.

members.legal_issue: A lessee affected by an executive decision to terminate a mining lease prematurely must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the final decision.
material_facts: The leases were terminated prematurely by executive action.
The lessees were affected by the termination.
The lessees received no prior notice and no opportunity to present their cases.
The Court found no indication that the governing provision excluded the affected lessees’ right to be heard.
members.legal_principle: The principles of natural justice apply where the exercise of power has civil consequences unless their application is specifically excluded. The Court relied on Baldev Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh, [1987] 2 SCC 510. It distinguished the legislative activity considered in Union of India v. Cynamide India Ltd., AIR 1987 SC 1802, and discussed D.C. Saxena v. State of Haryana, AIR 1987 SC 1463, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone, [1981] 2 SCR 742.
members.conclusion: A final decision to terminate a lease prematurely can be made only after notice to the lessee and an opportunity for the lessee to present its case.

rule.if: challenge_to_premature_lease_termination and executive_authority_proposes_to_end_lease_early and lessee_will_face_civil_consequences and governing_law_does_not_exclude_a_hearing

predicates.challenge_to_premature_lease_termination: A party challenges a decision to end a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.executive_authority_proposes_to_end_leas: An executive authority proposes to terminate a mining lease before its scheduled expiry.
predicates.lessee_will_face_civil_consequences: The proposed termination will adversely affect the lessee’s rights or interests.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_exclude_a_hearing: The governing law does not expressly exclude the affected lessee’s right to be heard.
predicates.lessee_must_receive_prior_notice_and_opp: The affected lessee must receive notice and an opportunity to present its case before the final termination decision.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing authority exercising quasi-judicial revision over a mining-lease decision must give reasons for its decision, including when it affirms the original decision.
material_facts: The State Government preferred another applicant for the mining lease, giving only brief reasons based on that applicant’s experience, technical knowledge and history as a lessee.
The unsuccessful applicant challenged the decision in revision and submitted comments and rejoinders, including material not before the State Government.
The Central Government rejected the revision by stating that it found no valid ground to interfere, without setting out reasons or expressly adopting the State Government’s reasons.
The revision decision was subject to further challenge before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Under section 30 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, and Rules 54 and 55 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, the Central Government exercises quasi-judicial revisional functions and considers the record, including comments and counter-comments from the parties. Rule 26 requires the State Government to give reasons when refusing a lease, but the absence of an express reasons requirement in Rule 55 does not remove the reviewing authority’s duty to explain its decision. Reasons are needed to disclose the authority’s reasoning, allow parties to understand the decision, and enable effective appellate or supervisory review under Articles 136 and 227. The Court followed Shivji Nathubhai v. Union of India, M.P. Industries v. Union, Harinagar Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Shyam Sundar Jhunjhunwala, and Sardar Govindrao v. State; it distinguished Nandram Hunatram, Calcutta v. Union of India and Commissioner of Income-tax v. K. V. Pilliah.
members.conclusion: The Central Government was required to make a speaking order. Its unexplained rejection was set aside, and the revision applications were remitted for fresh decision.

rule.if: revision_proceeding and quasi_judicial_adjudication and important_rights_determined and further_challenge_available and (fresh_material_submitted or original_reasons_inadequate) and no_reasoned_decision

predicates.revision_proceeding: An unsuccessful applicant sought revision of a decision granting a mining lease to another applicant.
predicates.quasi_judicial_adjudication: The reviewing authority resolved competing claims in a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity.
predicates.important_rights_determined: The decision determined important rights of the competing applicants.
predicates.further_challenge_available: The reviewing authority’s decision could be challenged before a higher court.
predicates.fresh_material_submitted: The parties submitted comments or counter-comments containing material not before the original decision-maker.
predicates.original_reasons_inadequate: The original decision-maker gave brief or unclear reasons for preferring one applicant over another.
predicates.no_reasoned_decision: The reviewing authority neither stated its own reasons nor expressly adopted adequate reasons given by the original decision-maker.

members.legal_issue: A government must give the holder a reasonable opportunity to be heard before prematurely terminating a mining lease under the applicable statutory scheme.
material_facts: The government prematurely terminated the mining leases and granted fresh leases over the same areas to a government company.
The lease holder was not given notice or an opportunity to be heard before termination.
The proceeding challenged the premature termination order.
members.legal_principle: Section 4-A of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, as introduced by the 1972 amendment, did not exclude a hearing; it was interpreted to require one consistently with natural justice. State of Haryana v. Ram Kishan, [1988] 3 SCC 416, held that affected lessees must be heard before a decision to terminate their leases prematurely. The later insertion of section 4-A(3) by the 1986 amendment, expressly requiring a reasonable opportunity of hearing, supported the statutory intention to provide a hearing.
members.conclusion: The termination order was null and void because it was made without giving the lease holder an opportunity to be heard, contrary to the principles of natural justice.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_premature_lease_te: A proceeding challenges a government decision to end a lease before its ordinary expiry.
predicates.government_terminated_lease_early: The government ended the lease before its ordinary expiry.
predicates.lease_holder_not_given_hearing: The government did not give the lease holder an opportunity to be heard before ending the lease.

members.legal_issue: Legal representatives joined to a civil suit may raise an independent title defence in their additional pleading when the court can determine that title and the defence is not inconsistent with the deceased defendant’s position.
material_facts: The deceased defendant had pleaded that the tenant surrendered the premises and that the premises were later occupied with his permission, but had not claimed ownership of the property.
After being joined as legal representatives, the heirs pleaded that the property had been allotted to some of them through inventory proceedings approved by the court.
The plaintiffs did not object when the additional written statement was filed and led evidence with that pleading on record.
The action was before a civil court capable of determining the asserted title.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a person joined as a legal representative to make a defence appropriate to that capacity. J.C. Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan recognizes that legal representatives may also set up an independent title, subject to the court’s ability to determine it. Bal Kishan v. Om Parkash limits that principle where the forum lacks jurisdiction to decide independent title, and Vidyawati v. Man Mohan distinguishes an independent claim that is not consonant with the deceased defendant’s defence.
members.conclusion: The heirs’ title plea was not inconsistent with the deceased defendant’s defence, and the High Court was not justified in striking the additional written statement on that basis.

predicates.legal_representatives_joined_in_civil_su: Persons were joined in a civil suit as the legal representatives of a deceased defendant.
predicates.court_can_determine_independent_title: The court hearing the suit has authority to decide the independent title asserted by the legal representatives.
predicates.independent_title_defence_not_inconsiste: The legal representatives’ asserted title does not contradict the material defence taken by the deceased defendant.

members.legal_issue: Legal representatives substituted in a suit may raise available defences and file an additional written statement when they have a plausible interest in the property in dispute.
material_facts: A suit for specific performance was pending when the defendant died, and his legal representatives were brought on record.
The legal representatives sought permission to file an additional written statement and raise available defences.
A registered sale deed referred to the disputed property as purchased by the deceased and his sons, giving the sons a prima facie basis to claim an interest in it.
The lower courts rejected the application, preventing the legal representatives from presenting the defence and evidence.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rule 4(2) CPC does not confine a legal representative to pleas appropriate only to that representative’s character as such. A party must have an opportunity to present a defence, consistently with natural justice and the CPC. The court relied on the registered sale deed as showing a prima facie interest, without finally deciding ownership.
members.conclusion: The legal representatives were entitled to file an additional written statement and adduce evidence; whether their defence succeeds is for the trial court to decide.

rule.if: suit_for_specific_performance and defendant_died_during_suit and successors_joined_as_parties and successors_have_plausible_property_interest

predicates.suit_for_specific_performance: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.defendant_died_during_suit: The defendant died while the suit was pending.
predicates.successors_joined_as_parties: The deceased defendant’s successors were brought into the suit as parties.
predicates.successors_have_plausible_property_inter: The successors have a factual basis, such as a property document naming them as purchasers, for claiming an interest in the disputed property.
predicates.successors_may_file_additional_defence: The successors may file an additional written statement and present their available defence and evidence.

members.legal_issue: A legal representative substituted for a deceased defendant may raise pleas available to the deceased, except pleas personal to the deceased.
material_facts: The claimant was brought into the suit as the legal representative of a deceased defendant and sought to file an additional written statement based on a will.
The deceased defendant had a life interest under the will, and the claimant's asserted interest was also said to arise under that will.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 4(2) permits a legal representative to raise pleas available to the deceased defendant, except those personal to the deceased. The Court relied on Bal Kishan v. Om Parkash, AIR 1986 SC 1952, and Jagdish Chander Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan, 1973 (1) SCR 850.
members.conclusion: A legal representative may raise all pleas the deceased defendant had or could have raised, except pleas personal to the deceased.

predicates.civil_suit_with_substituted_representati: A defendant in a civil suit dies and another person is substituted to represent that defendant's estate.
predicates.plea_available_to_deceased: The substituted representative seeks to raise a plea that the deceased defendant had or could have raised.
predicates.plea_not_personal_to_deceased: The plea does not depend on a right or defence personal to the deceased defendant.

members.legal_issue: A legal representative cannot assert a title independent of the deceased defendant's title solely in the representative capacity, but may pursue that title after personal joinder or in a separate suit.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a right to the property under the will that was independent of the deceased defendant's life interest.
She sought to assert that right through an additional written statement while acting as the deceased defendant's legal representative.
The Court left the claimant's independent title to be considered in a later proceeding and upheld the refusal to permit her to assert it solely as legal representative.
members.legal_principle: Order I Rule 10 permits a person asserting an independent interest to be joined in that person's own capacity. The Court relied on Jagdish Chander Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan, 1973 (1) SCR 850, which recognizes that legal representatives may also set up their own independent title if impleaded in their personal capacity, avoiding the need for a separate suit.
members.conclusion: The claimant could assert her independent title by being impleaded in her personal capacity or by bringing a separate suit, but could not assert it solely as the deceased defendant's legal representative.

predicates.civil_suit_with_substituted_representati: A defendant in a civil suit dies and another person is substituted to represent that defendant's estate.
predicates.representative_asserts_title_independent: The substituted representative seeks to claim a property interest that does not derive from the deceased defendant's interest.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot extend a deadline fixed by agreement in a compromise decree, and an unchallenged order doing so cannot modify the decree or bar its enforcement.
material_facts: The compromise decree required payment within a period agreed by the parties, rather than a period fixed by the court for performing an act prescribed or allowed by the Code of Civil Procedure.
During execution, the executing court granted the tenant additional time to deposit the balance of the arrears.
The landlord did not challenge that extension order, and the High Court treated this as acquiescence.
members.legal_principle: Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a court to enlarge a period fixed or granted by the court for doing an act prescribed or allowed by that Code; it does not authorize enlargement of a time limit agreed by the parties in a compromise decree. Hukumchand v. Bansilal, AIR 1968 SC 86, supports that limitation. An executing court cannot go behind or modify the decree and must execute it as it stands, as stated in Deepa Bhargava v. Mahesh Bhargava (2009) 2 SCC 294. A void order creates no legal rights or obligations.
members.conclusion: The executing court’s extension of the agreed deadline was beyond its jurisdiction and a nullity. The landlord’s failure to challenge that order did not modify the decree or bar recovery of possession.

rule.if: decree_execution and deadline_set_by_party_agreement and execution_court_extended_agreed_deadline and extension_order_not_challenged

predicates.decree_execution: A court is being asked to enforce a decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.deadline_set_by_party_agreement: The deadline for performance in the decree was fixed by agreement between the parties, not by the court.
predicates.execution_court_extended_agreed_deadline: The court conducting execution gave additional time to perform the agreed obligation.
predicates.extension_order_not_challenged: The party seeking enforcement did not challenge the order granting additional time.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot extend a statutory period for payment or go behind an unchallenged eviction order when enforcing it.
material_facts: The eviction order specified the payment required to avoid eviction and the statutory payment period.
Neither party challenged the eviction order.
In execution, the Controller found that the tenant's deposit was short but gave additional time to make up the deficiency.
The High Court reconsidered the meaning of the amount due while reviewing the execution decision.
members.legal_principle: The third proviso to Section 14(2)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, fixes the payment period by statute, leaving no power to enlarge it. Shri Krishnan Kumar v. Shri Gurbux Singh, 1977 (2) R.C.R. 62, was approved. Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, (1980) 2 SCC 151; Miss Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash, (1980) 3 SCC 610; Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath, (1984) 3 SCC 111; and Ganesh Prasad Sah Kesari v. Lakshmi Narayan Gupta, (1985) 3 SCC 53, were distinguished because the statutes in those cases provided for continuing rent payments and gave courts discretion over the consequences of default.
members.conclusion: The executing court had no jurisdiction to extend the statutory payment period or go behind the unchallenged eviction order, and the High Court could not reconsider the order’s efficacy at that stage.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_execution and unchallenged_eviction_order and statute_fixes_payment_period and tenant_made_short_deposit

predicates.rent_control_eviction_execution: The proceeding is execution of an eviction order made under rent-control legislation.
predicates.unchallenged_eviction_order: The parties did not challenge the eviction order before execution began.
predicates.statute_fixes_payment_period: The governing law itself sets the period for payment after the eviction order.
predicates.tenant_made_short_deposit: The tenant deposited less than the amount required by the eviction order.

members.legal_issue: Tenant-protection purposes do not permit an executing court to refuse enforcement of an eviction order where the statutory ground has been established and the governing law gives no discretion to consider comparative hardship.
material_facts: The Controller had ordered eviction after finding rent default.
The tenant had continued to leave rent unpaid, and the landlords had to pursue further proceedings to recover rent.
The matter was before the courts at the execution stage, and the governing provision did not confer a comparative-hardship discretion.
members.legal_principle: The Court recognized rent-control legislation as social legislation protecting tenants, but held that its protection is bounded by the statutory conditions. Where the applicable law provides no discretion to refuse eviction on comparative-hardship grounds, the executing court must execute the order. The Court agreed with Shri Krishnan Kumar v. Shri Gurbux Singh, 1977 (2) R.C.R. 62.
members.conclusion: Once the eviction ground is established and an eviction order is made under a law without a hardship-based discretion, the executing court must enforce the order; equity or hardship is not a basis to refuse execution.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and eviction_ground_established and execution_stage_reached and no_hardship_discretion

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control legislation.
predicates.eviction_ground_established: The decision-maker finds a statutory ground for eviction established.
predicates.execution_stage_reached: An eviction order has been made and enforcement is being sought.
predicates.no_hardship_discretion: The governing law does not authorize refusal of eviction based on comparative hardship.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot extend a deposit period fixed by consent of the parties when the parties do not consent to a further extension.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors withdrew their challenge to the sale under an agreement by which they were given time to deposit the amount due by a specified date.
They did not deposit the amount by that date, and the decree-holder and auction purchaser opposed their request for more time.
The deposit was not made before the executing court considered confirmation of the sale.
members.legal_principle: Order XXXIV, Rule 5(1) recognizes a judgment-debtor’s right in an execution relating to a mortgage decree for sale to deposit the amount due before confirmation, but it does not empower the court to extend time after the final decree or postpone confirmation to accommodate the judgment-debtor. Section 148 did not apply to extend a period granted by consent when the other parties opposed further extension.
members.conclusion: The executing court was correct to refuse further time; Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not permit extension of the period fixed by the parties’ compromise in these circumstances.

predicates.mortgage_sale_execution: The proceeding is an execution concerning a sale under a mortgage decree.
predicates.deposit_deadline_set_by_party_compromise: The parties agreed to a deadline for the judgment-debtor to deposit the amount due.
predicates.further_extension_opposed: The other parties opposed the judgment-debtor’s request for more time.

members.legal_issue: A valid power to extend existing enactments to a territory may include authority to extend later enactments or amendments to those laws.
material_facts: The executive had authority to extend existing laws to a territory without its own legislature.
Parliament’s limited time to consider the territory’s legislative needs also made it difficult to consider later amendments to laws selected for extension.
The challenged extension concerned an amendment enacted after the original law.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied In re Delhi Laws Act, [1951] SCR 747, and reasoned that if the executive may extend an existing law because Parliament lacks time to consider it, the executive may also extend later amendments to that law for the same reason. The delegated power remains subject to the policy and limits that make the original extension power valid.
members.conclusion: Authority to extend future enactments or amendments is a necessary corollary of a valid power to extend existing laws.

predicates.challenge_to_future_law_extension: A proceeding challenges the executive’s authority to extend a law enacted after the original grant of extension authority.
predicates.valid_power_to_extend_existing_laws: The executive has a valid authority to extend existing laws to the territory.
predicates.later_law_amends_or_supplements_an_exten: The later enactment amends or supplements a law that has been extended to the territory.
predicates.extension_serves_the_same_local_legislat: Extending the later enactment addresses the same need to provide suitable laws for the territory without requiring Parliament to consider every legislative detail.

members.legal_issue: An enactment may be extended to a territory even where related legislation already applies there, provided the new provisions do not repeal, conflict with, or become repugnant to the existing law.
material_facts: An existing parliamentary enactment governed rent matters in the territory.
The later enactment sought to be extended added provisions addressing aspects not covered by the existing enactment.
The added provisions were not inconsistent with the existing enactment and did not displace it.
The challenge argued that extension was impermissible because legislation on the broader subject already applied in the territory.
members.legal_principle: Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 permits extension of an enactment that adds to existing law so long as it does not expressly or impliedly repeal, conflict with, or become repugnant to that law. The Court applied a constructive interpretation of the provision and relied on Hari Shankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1955] 1 SCR 380, and Lachmi Narain v. Union of India, [1976] 2 SCR 795.
members.conclusion: The existence of related legislation did not bar extension of provisions that supplemented it without conflict or repeal.

rule.if: challenge_to_extension_into_territory_with_existing_law and existing_law_applies_to_related_subject and extended_law_adds_uncovered_provisions and no_repeal_conflict_or_repugnance

predicates.challenge_to_extension_into_territory_wi: A proceeding challenges an extension of an enactment to a territory where related legislation already applies.
predicates.existing_law_applies_to_related_subject: A law already applicable in the territory addresses the same broad subject as the enactment proposed for extension.
predicates.extended_law_adds_uncovered_provisions: The enactment proposed for extension adds provisions addressing matters not covered by the existing law.
predicates.no_repeal_conflict_or_repugnance: The added provisions neither expressly or impliedly repeal nor conflict with or become repugnant to the existing law.

members.legal_issue: An executive notification extending rent-law amendments to a territory is valid when the amendments supplement the rent law already applicable there without conflict and the notification makes only minor modifications.
material_facts: A parliamentary enactment had extended the principal rent law to the territory.
The State legislature later amended that rent law, and the executive issued a notification extending those amendments to the territory.
The amendments added provisions concerning aspects not covered by the parliamentary enactment and were not inconsistent with it.
The notification extended the amendments with only very minor modifications.
The appeals and petitions challenged the notification’s validity.
members.legal_principle: Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 permits extension of an enactment in force in a State, including later amendments, where the additions do not repeal or conflict with existing law. Any modifications in the notification must remain incidental and must not substantially deviate from the extended enactment. The Court relied on In re Delhi Laws Act, [1951] SCR 747, Lachmi Narain v. Union of India, [1976] 2 SCR 795, and Hari Shankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1955] 1 SCR 380.
members.conclusion: The notification was valid; the appeals and writ petitions were dismissed.

rule.if: challenge_to_rent_law_extension_notification and existing_rent_law_applies_in_territory and amendments_add_uncovered_matters and no_conflict_with_existing_rent_law and notification_changes_are_minor

predicates.challenge_to_rent_law_extension_notifica: A proceeding challenges an executive notification extending rent-law amendments to a territory.
predicates.existing_rent_law_applies_in_territory: A rent law is already applicable in the territory.
predicates.amendments_add_uncovered_matters: The amendments add provisions concerning matters not addressed by the rent law already applicable in the territory.
predicates.no_conflict_with_existing_rent_law: The amendments do not repeal, conflict with, or become repugnant to the existing rent law.
predicates.notification_changes_are_minor: The notification’s modifications to the enactment being extended are only minor.

members.legal_issue: An executive may extend a later amendment of an existing law to a union territory under a statutory power to extend laws when the extension supplements, rather than conflicts with or repeals, the law already in force there.
material_facts: The legislature had established a policy of applying the relevant rent legislation in the union territory, and Parliament had extended the principal rent law there.
The challenged notification extended a later amendment that added provisions concerning a subject not covered by the law already extended to the territory.
The Court found that the extended provisions did not conflict with, repeal, or displace the existing law.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, the Central Government may extend laws in force in a state to Chandigarh, subject to appropriate restrictions or modifications. The power is a form of conditional legislation when it applies an already enacted law to a territory; it is not an unrestricted power to make substantive law. Re Delhi Laws Act, 1912, Ajmer-Merwara (Extension of Laws) Act, 1947 and Part C States (Laws) Act, 1950; R. v. Burah; Ramesh Birch v. Union of India; Vasu Dev Singh v. Union of India; Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India; and Hari Shankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh support the distinction between permissible extension and impermissible repeal or substantive alteration, and the rule that an extension adding provisions may stand alongside existing law if it does not conflict with it.
members.conclusion: The notification extending the amendment was valid; the challenge based on excessive delegation and related grounds was rejected.

rule.if: extension_challenge and extension_policy_previously_set and later_rules_add_uncovered_subject and not conflict_with_existing_law

predicates.extension_challenge: A party challenges an executive act extending a later amendment of a law to a territory.
predicates.extension_policy_previously_set: The legislature has established a policy of applying laws from another jurisdiction to the territory by extension.
predicates.later_rules_add_uncovered_subject: The later amendment adds rules about a matter not covered by the law already in force in the territory.
predicates.conflict_with_existing_law: The extended rules repeal, displace, or directly conflict with law already in force in the territory.

members.legal_issue: A person who exercised a claimed right on the footing that the land was their own cannot establish that same use as a prescriptive easement over another’s land after failing to establish ownership.
material_facts: The claimant maintained in evidence that the strip was included in the lease and that his rights over it arose under the lease, not later.
He did not claim that he had exercised the disputed rights on the footing that the strip belonged to someone else.
The claimant failed to establish that the strip was included in the lease or acquired as an accession.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 15 of the Easements Act govern who may acquire an easement and the method of acquisition. A prescriptive easement requires a conscious, hostile exercise of the claimed right over another person’s property. A claimant may plead ownership and easement in the alternative, but use exercised on the footing of ownership is not use as an easement. The Court relied on Rayachand v. Maniklal. It noted conflicting High Court views in Abdul Rashid v. Brahman Saron and Ambaram v. Budhalal on a lessee’s ability to acquire certain easements, but found it unnecessary to resolve that conflict.
members.conclusion: The claimant could not rely on the same use to establish prescriptive easements after failing to prove his claim that the strip was part of his leased land.

rule.if: civil_appeal_on_land_and_easement_claims and prescriptive_easement_claim and claimant_asserted_land_was_their_own_or_leased and no_conscious_use_as_another_persons_land and ownership_claim_failed

predicates.civil_appeal_on_land_and_easement_claims: The proceeding is a civil appeal involving a claim to land and an alternative claim to easementary rights over it.
predicates.prescriptive_easement_claim: The claimant sought to establish an easement based on long use.
predicates.claimant_asserted_land_was_their_own_or_: The claimant maintained that the land was owned or leased by them, rather than treating it as another person’s property.
predicates.no_conscious_use_as_another_persons_land: The claimant did not establish a conscious exercise of the claimed right over land understood to belong to someone else.
predicates.ownership_claim_failed: The claimant failed to prove that the land was theirs or included in their lease.

members.legal_issue: Use of another person’s land as a passage does not establish a prescriptive easement when the use was permissive or was not proved to be uninterrupted use as of right for the required period.
material_facts: The claimant used the strip as a passage to reach a well on the other plot and a structure that had stood there under a separate tenancy.
The claimant and his predecessor had permission to draw water from the well, and the passage use was incidental to that permission.
The claimant acknowledged the separate tenancy and rent for the structure on the other plot.
The evidence did not establish continuous, uninterrupted use of the strip as a passage as of right for the statutory period.
members.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Easements Act requires access or use as an easement, without interruption, for the prescribed period. The enjoyment must be as of right and not permissive under a licence or agreement. The Court concluded that the passage use was permissive and therefore could not establish the claimed easement.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not acquire a prescriptive right of passage over the strip.

predicates.civil_appeal_on_easement_claims: The proceeding is a civil appeal involving a claim to acquire an easement by long use.
predicates.passage_easement_claimed_by_prescription: The claimant sought a right of passage based on use over time.
predicates.passage_use_was_permissive_or_not_proved: The passage use was allowed as a matter of permission or was not proved to have been uninterrupted use as of right for the required period.

members.legal_issue: Common use of a passage does not establish a granted easement where no grant was pleaded or supported by evidence.
material_facts: The tenants argued that the passage was used under an easement of right of way granted to them and other tenants.
They had not made that case in the courts below, and the record contained no material from which a grant could be inferred.
The passage had been used in common by the owner and the tenants to access their respective premises.
members.legal_principle: A grant of an easement cannot be inferred without a pleaded case and supporting material; common use by the owner and tenants may instead show a bare licence that creates no interest in the passage. The Court relied on no cited provision or earlier case.
members.conclusion: The claimed granted easement was not established; the common use showed a bare licence to use the passage for access, without an interest in it.

rule.if: granted_easement_claim and claim_not_raised_below and no_evidence_of_grant and passage_used_in_common

predicates.granted_easement_claim: A party claimed that a right to use a passage had been granted as an easement.
predicates.claim_not_raised_below: The party did not advance the granted-easement claim in the lower courts.
predicates.no_evidence_of_grant: The record contained no material showing that an easement had been granted.
predicates.passage_used_in_common: The owner and multiple occupants used the passage to reach their respective premises.

members.legal_issue: A prescriptive easement of access is not established without specific pleadings and evidence that the access was used openly, peaceably, as of right, and without interruption for the required period.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of a motorable right of way through the defendants’ property by prescription.

Although the plaintiff alleged long use of the access, the plaint and witness statements did not specifically state that it had been used as of right for the required period or identify the period of such use.
The evidence indicated that the plaintiff had an opening and access on the southern side of her property and that use of the disputed access through the defendants’ property began only in 1984.
The defendants obstructed the disputed access after discovering its use, and the evidence did not establish the required period of uninterrupted use.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 15 of the Easements Act, 1882, a prescriptive easement requires use openly, peaceably, as of right, and without interruption for 20 years.
