Gordhandas Bhanji, [1952] S.C.R. 135, and State of Punjab v. Hari Kishan Sharma, A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1081.
members.conclusion: The challenged orders were invalid because the Chief Minister, rather than the Cane Commissioner, exercised the statutory power, and the Commissioner did not exercise his own judgment.

rule.if: challenge_to_modified_sugarcane_reservation and superior_directed_the_outcome and delegated_official_opposed_the_change and delegated_official_followed_the_direction and not binding_superior_instruction_authorized

predicates.challenge_to_modified_sugarcane_reservat: A party challenged an order changing an existing sugarcane reservation.
predicates.superior_directed_the_outcome: A superior official directed how the disputed reservation should be changed.
predicates.delegated_official_opposed_the_change: The official entrusted with the decision had expressed the view that the existing reservation should not be changed.
predicates.delegated_official_followed_the_directio: The entrusted official issued an order implementing the superior official’s direction.
predicates.binding_superior_instruction_authorized: A governing legal rule authorized the superior official to give binding instructions on the decision.

members.legal_issue: When one person supplies the purchase money for property transferred in another person’s name, the circumstances and the contributor’s intention determine whether the named person has a beneficial share.
material_facts: The purchaser paid the entire consideration for the property, which was conveyed in the purchaser’s joint name and the claimant’s name.
The claimant did not contribute to the purchase price and relied on an asserted entitlement to a half share.

The claimant’s pleading did not explain adequately the basis for the claimed share, and the lower appellate court found the claimant’s evidence meagre and unsatisfactory to establish that the purchaser intended the claimant to benefit.
The lower appellate court found that the purchaser did not intend to acquire the property for the claimant’s benefit.
members.legal_principle: Under Bhim Singh v. Kan Singh, the person asserting that a transaction is benami bears the burden of showing that it is so; where the purchase money came from someone other than the person in whose favour the property was transferred, the purchase is prima facie presumed to be for the benefit of the person who supplied the money, unless evidence shows otherwise. The contributor’s intention is determined from surrounding circumstances, the parties’ relationship, their motives and subsequent conduct. The Court also relied on The Controller of Estate Duty, Lucknow v. Aloke Mitra and the line of Privy Council authorities including Gopeekrist Gosain v. Gungapersaud Gosain, Sura Lakshmiah Chetty v. Kothandarama Pillai, and Guran Ditta v. Ram Ditta. The doctrine of advancement does not apply in India to presume a gift merely from the relationship between the parties or the transfer into another’s name; the asserted gift must be established.
members.conclusion: The lower appellate court’s finding that the purchase was benami and that the claimant had not established a beneficial share was restored.

predicates.benami_ownership_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property transferred in a person’s name was acquired for that person or for the benefit of someone else.
predicates.purchase_money_supplied_by_someone_other: A person other than the named claimant supplied the purchase money.
predicates.claimant_did_not_contribute_to_purchase: The named claimant supplied none of the money used to acquire the property.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_contributor_: The evidence does not establish that the person who supplied the money intended the named claimant to receive a beneficial share.

members.legal_issue: Whether a property purchased with one person’s money in the names of others was held benami depends on the purchaser’s intention, assessed from the surrounding circumstances and the parties’ conduct.
material_facts: The property was purchased with money provided by the deceased relative, and the title document was issued in the names of the plaintiffs at his request.
The deceased relative was a bachelor, while the second plaintiff was a young child living under his care; the second plaintiff’s father was in indigent circumstances.
The deceased relative gave the original title document to the second plaintiff after he passed an examination.
Witnesses testified that the deceased relative said the house belonged to the second plaintiff and that he intended the second plaintiff to receive his property.
The defendant alleged political circumstances explained why the title document was issued in the plaintiffs’ names but did not substantiate those circumstances.
The deceased relative had no evident reason to conceal his ownership from the government that sold him the property.
members.legal_principle: The person asserting that a transaction is benami bears the burden of proving it. Where the purchase money is provided by someone other than the named transferee, the purchase is prima facie presumed to benefit the person who supplied the money unless evidence shows otherwise; the contributor’s intention is determined from the surrounding circumstances, relationship, motives and subsequent conduct. Section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, recognizes the principle that a transferee must hold property for the benefit of the person providing consideration if that person did not intend the consideration to benefit the transferee. The Court relied on Meenakshi Mills v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Manmohan Dass v. Ramdei, Mohammad Sadiq Ali Khan v. Fakhr Jahan Begum, and Jayadayal Poddar v. Bibi Hazara. It also held that the English doctrine of advancement was not in vogue in India.
members.conclusion: The purchase was not benami; the deceased relative intended the second plaintiff to be the beneficial owner, who was entitled to possession.

predicates.benami_dispute_in_a_property_title_case: The parties to a dispute over property title disputed whether the named transferee held the property benami for another person.
predicates.purchase_money_supplied_by_someone_other: A person other than the named transferee supplied the purchase money.
predicates.named_transferee_received_title_document: The person named in the title document received or retained that document from the person who arranged the purchase.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_show_contribut: The contributor’s statements, conduct, relationship with the named transferee, and other circumstances indicated an intention to benefit the named transferee.

members.legal_issue: A purchase in one person’s name may be found to have been made benami for another person when the evidence shows who supplied the purchase money and who enjoyed the property’s benefits.
material_facts: The property was purchased in the son’s name when he was 18 years old and had no established independent funds.
The son did not reliably establish the source of the purchase money; his accounts of the payment and its sources were inconsistent and unexplained.
The father’s proved statements and account records showed that he paid for the property from his own funds and treated the property’s income as his own.
The son did not prove that he enjoyed the benefits of the property.
members.legal_principle: The source of the consideration and the enjoyment of the benefits are the principal tests for determining whether a transaction is benami (Gangadara Ayyar v. Subramania Sastrigal; Meenakshi Mills v. Commissioner of Income-Tax). The party alleging a benami transaction bears the initial burden, but the burden may shift as evidence is led. Where the evidence does not conclusively establish or rebut the allegation, the court assesses reasonable probabilities and legal inferences from proved or admitted facts; once evidence is before the court, the issue is decided on that evidence rather than abstract considerations of onus (Kalwa Devadattam v. Union of India).
members.conclusion: The father was the real owner and the son was only the ostensible owner or benamidar.

rule.if: civil_property_ownership_dispute and purchase_in_another_persons_name and (alleged_real_owner_funded_purchase or named_purchaser_failed_to_establish_funding) and alleged_real_owner_enjoyed_property_benefits

predicates.civil_property_ownership_dispute: The proceeding concerns who owns property that was purchased in one person’s name.
predicates.purchase_in_another_persons_name: The property was acquired in the name of someone other than the person alleged to be its real owner.
predicates.alleged_real_owner_funded_purchase: The person alleged to be the real owner supplied the purchase consideration.
predicates.named_purchaser_failed_to_establish_fund: The person named as purchaser failed to establish a credible source for the purchase consideration.
predicates.alleged_real_owner_enjoyed_property_bene: The person alleged to be the real owner received or treated the benefits of the property as their own.

members.legal_issue: The real ownership of property acquired in one person's name is determined by the source of the consideration and who enjoyed the benefits of the property, assessed on the whole evidence.
material_facts: The son was about eighteen when the property was purchased and had no established independent means to pay the purchase price.
The son's explanations about receiving the purchase money from relatives were not reliably supported, and he did not prove that he enjoyed the property's benefits.
The father's proved statements and tax records showed that he paid for the property in his son's name and treated its income as his own.
The evidence as a whole supported the finding that the son held the property for the father.
members.legal_principle: Under Gangadara Ayyar v. Subramania Sastrigal and Meenakshi Mills v. Commissioner of Income-tax, the source of the consideration and enjoyment of the benefits are central tests for determining whether a purchase in one person's name was for another's benefit. The burden initially lies on the party alleging benami, but it may shift as evidence is led; where the evidence does not conclusively establish the allegation either way, the court decides on reasonable probabilities and legal inferences from proved or admitted facts. Kalwa Devadattam v. Union of India requires the court to assess the evidence as a whole rather than rely on abstract considerations of onus once the parties have led their evidence.
members.conclusion: The father was the real owner and the son was merely a benamidar.

rule.if: benami_claim_in_civil_suit and ostensible_buyer_lacked_independent_means and ostensible_buyer_failed_to_explain_funding and alleged_owner_paid_purchase_consideration and alleged_owner_received_property_income

predicates.benami_claim_in_civil_suit: A party in a civil suit alleged that property acquired in one person's name was in reality acquired for another person's benefit.
predicates.ostensible_buyer_lacked_independent_mean: The person named as buyer had no established independent means to fund the purchase.
predicates.ostensible_buyer_failed_to_explain_fundi: The person named as buyer failed to give a reliable account of the source of the purchase money.
predicates.alleged_owner_paid_purchase_consideratio: Evidence showed that the person alleged to be the real owner supplied the purchase money.
predicates.alleged_owner_received_property_income: Evidence showed that the person alleged to be the real owner treated income from the property as their own.

members.legal_issue: Omission of a full property description from attachment material is an irregularity rather than a ground to invalidate a sale where the property remains identifiable and bidders are not misled.
material_facts: The execution material identified the property by its plot number and area but did not fully describe it in the attachment order.
A plan with a fuller description was attached to the execution petition.
The property was identifiable and the bidders were not misled.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Form 24 contemplates a full description of property, but an omission is only an irregularity where the property is identifiable and the bidders are not misled.
members.conclusion: The omission of a fuller description was an irregularity and did not invalidate the sale.

rule.if: execution_sale and property_description_incomplete and property_identifiable and bidders_not_misled

predicates.execution_sale: The proceeding involves a sale in execution of a decree.
predicates.property_description_incomplete: The sale or attachment material does not give a full description of the property.
predicates.property_identifiable: The property can nevertheless be identified from the available information.
predicates.bidders_not_misled: The bidders were not misled by the incomplete description.

members.legal_issue: An error in the survey numbers in a sale proclamation does not invalidate a sale when the property’s identity is otherwise clear and the error causes no prejudice.
material_facts: The proclamation misstated the survey numbers of two plots, but otherwise described their area, tenure, and other identifying details.
The owner testified that he knew which plots were being sold, and the evidence showed that no one was misled about their identity.
The court found the proclamation satisfied the applicable requirements for describing the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(2) of the Travancore Revenue Recovery Regulation required a sale notice to specify the defaulter, the position, tenure and extent of the land and buildings, the revenue assessed, and the time, place and conditions of sale. Where the property’s identity is clear and there is only a misdescription, the error is an irregularity rather than a ground to treat the sale as having occurred without a proclamation. The Court applied Sheodhyan Singh v. Muhammat Kuer, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 753, and Thakur Barmha v. Jiban Ram Marwari, (1913) L.R. 41 I.A. 38.
members.conclusion: The sale was not invalidated by the erroneous survey numbers because the errors were misdescriptions, not mistaken identifications.

rule.if: revenue_sale_challenged and survey_numbers_misstated and property_identity_clear and no_material_prejudice

predicates.revenue_sale_challenged: A party challenged the validity of a sale conducted to recover a debt through a revenue-sale process.
predicates.survey_numbers_misstated: The sale notice gave incorrect survey numbers for the land offered for sale.
predicates.property_identity_clear: The land’s area, tenure, or other identifying details made clear which property was being sold.
predicates.no_material_prejudice: The error did not mislead interested persons or cause material prejudice to the person challenging the sale.

members.legal_issue: An inadvertent error in a property identifier does not invalidate a secured-property auction when the property is otherwise unambiguously described and no prejudice is shown.
material_facts: The property identifier in the recovery and auction notices contained an inadvertent typographical error.
The notices also gave the property’s measurements, boundaries, and other identifying details, which were sufficient to identify it.

No other property with the erroneous identifier existed in the locality, and the borrowers did not show that bidders were misled, that the property was ambiguous, or that the error caused a loss in value.
members.legal_principle: A secured creditor is obliged to check the description of the mortgaged property in the initial and subsequent proceedings. However, an inadvertent error that causes no demonstrated prejudice does not, by itself, justify annulling an otherwise compliant process. Where the property’s detailed description is unambiguous, a typographical error in its identifier does not vitiate the auction under the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002.
members.conclusion: The typographical error was inconsequential and did not vitiate the auction proceedings.

rule.if: secured_property_e_auction_challenge and inadvertent_identifier_error and complete_identifying_details and no_competing_property_with_error_identifier and no_prejudice_demonstrated

predicates.secured_property_e_auction_challenge: A challenge was made to an auction of property offered as security for a debt.
predicates.inadvertent_identifier_error: The property identifier contained an inadvertent typographical error.
predicates.complete_identifying_details: The auction materials included other details sufficient to identify the property unambiguously.
predicates.no_competing_property_with_error_identif: No other property in the locality had the erroneous identifier.
predicates.no_prejudice_demonstrated: The borrowers did not establish that the error misled participants, caused ambiguity, or reduced the property’s sale value.

members.legal_issue: An erroneous property number in a sale decree and certificate does not defeat the sale when the property’s identity is otherwise clearly established.
material_facts: The final decree and sale certificate stated plot number 160, while the property intended was plot 1060.
The khata number, area, and boundaries in those documents corresponded to plot 1060, and there was no plot 160 in that khata.
The writ for delivery of possession and the later sale deed correctly identified plot 1060.
members.legal_principle: Under Thakur Barhma v. Jibon Marware and Gossain Das Kundu v. Mrithujoy Agran Sarda, a fully identified property may be treated as sold despite a misdescription that does not create doubt about its identity. Rambhadra Naidu v. Kadiruja Sami Naicker was distinguished because it involved a dispute about the identity of the property, rather than a mere error in its description.
members.conclusion: The number was a mere misdescription, not an uncertainty about the property’s identity, so the appellants’ challenge to the respondents’ claim to the plot failed.

predicates.appeal_against_possession_decree: A party appealed from a decree granting possession of property.
predicates.sale_documents_contain_property_number_e: The decree or sale certificate contained an incorrect property number.
predicates.other_description_details_match_one_prop: The other identifying details in the sale documents corresponded to a particular property.
predicates.no_property_has_the_stated_number_in_the: No property with the number stated in the documents existed in the relevant record.

members.legal_issue: A civil court must refer a contested issue assigned exclusively to a tenancy authority even when that issue arises in a properly constituted suit for specific performance.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of agreements to sell agricultural land governed by the tenancy legislation.
The defendant contested the suit on the ground that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist and was therefore barred from purchasing the land.
The trial court and the High Court decided the plaintiff’s agriculturist status themselves, treating it as an incidental issue in the civil suit.
The legislation assigned the determination of whether a person was an agriculturist to the Mamlatdar and barred civil courts from deciding matters assigned to the statutory authorities.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 70(a), 85 and 85A of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the Mamlatdar has exclusive jurisdiction to decide whether a person is an agriculturist; when that issue arises upon contest in a civil suit, the civil court must stay the suit, refer the issue to the competent authority, and thereafter dispose of the suit consistently with its decision. Although exclusion of civil jurisdiction is not readily inferred (Secretary of State v. Mask), the express statutory bar and referral scheme require it even when the issue is incidental to a suit otherwise cognizable by a civil court. The court approved Dhondi Tukaram Mali v. Dadoo Piraji Adgale and Trimbak Sopana Girme v. Gangaram Mhataraba Yadav, and relied on Bhimaji Shanker Kulkarni v. Dundappa Vithappa Udapudi, Ishverlal Thakorelal Almaula v. Motibhai Nagjibhai, and Noor Mohd. Khan Ghouse Khan Soudagar v. Fakirappa Bharmappa Machenahalli. It explained that Jambu Rao Satappa Kocheri v. Neminath Appayya Hanammannaver concerned a different issue arising after acquisition and did not displace the rule; it also distinguished Mussamiya Imam Haider Bax Razvi v. Rabari Govindbhai Ratnabhai in light of the statutory provisions and issue there considered.
members.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to decide the contested issue of agriculturist status and was required to stay the suit and refer that issue to the competent authority. The appeal was allowed, the decrees dismissing the suit were set aside, and the suit was remanded for further proceedings in accordance with the authority’s decision.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and agricultural_land_sale and contested_agriculturist_status_issue and status_question_assigned_to_exclusive_authority

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a civil suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.agricultural_land_sale: The agreement concerned the transfer of land used for agricultural purposes.
predicates.contested_agriculturist_status_issue: A party disputed whether the person seeking the transfer qualified as an agriculturist, and that status had to be determined to resolve the dispute.
predicates.status_question_assigned_to_exclusive_au: The governing law assigned determination of the disputed status to a designated authority rather than the civil court.

members.legal_issue: A civil court hearing a properly instituted possession suit must refer tenancy issues assigned to a special revenue forum to that forum and then decide the suit in light of its determination, rather than dismissing the suit for want of jurisdiction.
material_facts: The landlord properly instituted a civil suit for possession and mesne profits.
The tenant relied on statutory tenancy protection, raising issues concerning whether the tenancy subsisted and whether it had been validly determined.

The tenancy legislation assigned the determination of whether a person was a tenant or protected tenant to the Mamlatdar and excluded civil-court jurisdiction over questions assigned to the statutory authorities.
A later amendment provided that when an issue assigned to a competent authority arose in a civil suit, the civil court had to stay the suit and refer the issue to that authority.
The District Judge dismissed the suit instead of referring the tenancy issues for determination.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 70 and 85 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, questions assigned to the Mamlatdar, including whether a person is a tenant or protected tenant, are outside the civil court’s authority to decide. Section 85A requires a civil court in a properly instituted suit to stay proceedings and refer such issues to the competent authority, then dispose of the suit in accordance with that authority’s decision. The Court agreed with Pandurang Hari v. Shanker Maruti and Kalicharan Bhajanlal Bhayya v. Bai Mahalaxmi that a properly instituted suit should not be dismissed merely because tenant rights were restored, but rejected their view that the civil court could decide the issues assigned to the revenue court.
members.conclusion: The dismissal could not stand. The civil court had to refer the tenancy issues to the Mamlatdar as a revenue court and thereafter dispose of the suit consistently with that determination.

rule.if: civil_possession_suit and suit_properly_instituted and tenancy_issue_arose and issue_assigned_to_special_forum and referral_procedure_applies

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A landlord brought a civil suit seeking possession of land occupied by a tenant.
predicates.suit_properly_instituted: The civil suit was properly brought in the civil court when it was instituted.
predicates.tenancy_issue_arose: The tenant’s claim raised an issue about tenancy status or the determination of the tenancy.
predicates.issue_assigned_to_special_forum: The governing law assigned that tenancy issue to a designated authority rather than the civil court.
predicates.referral_procedure_applies: A procedure requiring the civil court to refer assigned issues to the designated authority applied to the suit.

members.legal_issue: A civil court must refer a tenancy issue to the competent authority when the issue arises in a civil suit and the law assigns its determination to that authority, even if the issue arises incidentally.
material_facts: The landlords leased the land to the respondents’ predecessor, and later sued for possession after the lease ended.
The respondents disputed the civil court’s jurisdiction and contended that the tenancy legislation applied to the land.
The High Court remanded the suit with directions to refer any issues reserved for the competent authority, including tenancy issues, for determination.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 70(b), 85 and 85A of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, as amended to include whether a person was at any time in the past a tenant, a civil court cannot determine an assigned tenancy issue, even if it arises incidentally, and must refer it to the competent authority. The court relies on G.S. Shinde v. R.B. Joshi and Bhimaji Shanker Kulkarni v. Dundappa Vithappa Udapudi; it explains that Mussamiya Imam Haider Bax Razvi v. Rabari Govindhai Ratnabhai concerned the earlier statutory position.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly directed the trial court to refer any issue required to be determined exclusively by the competent authority and to dispose of the suit in accordance with that authority’s decision.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_tenancy_issue: A party to a civil suit raises a dispute about whether a person is or was a tenant.
predicates.law_assigns_issue_to_special_authority: The law assigns determination of that tenancy issue to a competent specialist authority rather than the civil court.

members.legal_issue: When a pending suit was properly instituted but a later change in law places the entire dispute outside civil-court jurisdiction and provides the claimant a remedy before a special forum, the civil court should not nonsuit the claimant and should follow the procedure for directing the claim to the proper forum.
material_facts: The Court considered the situation in which a suit had been instituted in a competent civil court before a change in law.
It explained that a deemed tenant evicted from land may have a remedy for recovery of possession entirely under the tenancy law, with civil-court jurisdiction barred.
The Court stated that it would be unfair to nonsuit a plaintiff for a loss of jurisdiction caused by a subsequent change in law.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4, 8(2) and 58(2) of the Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act provide an exclusive statutory remedy for recovery of possession by a qualifying deemed tenant and bar civil-court jurisdiction over that remedy. For a pending suit originally filed in a competent court, the Court directed that the procedure in Order 7 Rules 10 and 10A of the Code of Civil Procedure be followed in spirit rather than nonsuiting the plaintiff.
members.conclusion: Where the entire dispute falls outside civil-court jurisdiction because of the change in law, the proper course is to follow in spirit the procedure outlined in Order 7 Rules 10 and 10A of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.pending_suit_originally_within_civil_jur: A suit was pending in a civil court that had jurisdiction when the suit was filed.
predicates.entire_dispute_now_outside_civil_jurisdi: A later change in law places the whole dispute beyond the civil court’s authority.
predicates.claimant_has_remedy_before_special_forum: The governing law provides the claimant a remedy before a special forum.

members.legal_issue: Children born from a void or voidable marriage may claim rights in their parents’ property, including the parents’ interest in ancestral property, but not in the property of other persons.
material_facts: A man’s second marriage occurred while his first marriage was subsisting, and the children of the second marriage were treated as children of a void marriage.
The dispute concerned partition of property found to be ancestral property.
The children sought a share in the property of their father.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(1) and (2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, confer legitimacy on children of void or voidable marriages, and Section 16(3) limits their property rights to the property of their parents without distinguishing between self-acquired and ancestral property. The Court relied on the purposive and beneficial interpretation discussed in Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v. K. Devi, including its recognition that the legal fiction extends to succession to parents’ property. It considered Jinia Keotin v. Kumar Sitaram Manjhi, Neelamma v. Sarojamma, and Bharatha Matha v. R. Vijaya Renganathan to have adopted an unduly narrow interpretation requiring reconsideration. The Court also referred to Articles 37, 39(f), and 300A of the Constitution and the discussion of judicial application of Directive Principles in Kesavananda Bharati.
members.conclusion: The Court expressed the view that the children could claim rights in their parents’ property, whether self-acquired or ancestral, but not in the property of anyone other than their parents. Because this view differed from earlier Supreme Court decisions, the Court referred the matter for reconsideration by a larger Bench rather than finally disposing of the appeal.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: A dispute concerns a child’s claimed rights in property.
predicates.child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage: The child was born from a marriage that is void or voidable.
predicates.parental_property_claim: The child claims property belonging to one or both parents.

members.legal_issue: A child born from a void or voidable marriage cannot claim property belonging to someone other than the child’s parents under the statutory legitimacy rule.
material_facts: The children’s claimed rights arose from their father’s second marriage, which was treated as void.
The property dispute concerned the father’s property; the Court considered whether the statutory rights could extend beyond the parents’ property.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, expressly preserves rights only in the property of the parents and excludes rights in the property of any other person. In Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v. K. Devi, the Court recognized that the legitimacy fiction operates for succession to the parents’ property but not to the property of other relations. The Court considered the contrary or narrower reasoning in Jinia Keotin v. Kumar Sitaram Manjhi, Neelamma v. Sarojamma, and Bharatha Matha v. R. Vijaya Renganathan and referred the matter for larger-Bench reconsideration.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the statutory property rights of such children are confined to the property of their parents and do not extend to the property of another person. The Court referred its differing interpretation of the statutory scheme to a larger Bench for reconsideration.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: A dispute concerns a child’s claimed rights in property.
predicates.child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage: The child was born from a marriage that is void or voidable.
predicates.property_belongs_to_nonparent: The property claimed belongs to someone other than the child’s parent or parents.

members.legal_issue: A child born from a void or voidable marriage may claim only the share of joint family property that becomes the parent’s property and cannot demand partition of that property during the parent’s lifetime.
material_facts: The children sought partition of ancestral joint family property during their father’s lifetime.
The Court considered their entitlement in joint family property to be confined to the property falling to their parent’s share.
The father was alive when the partition claim was made.
members.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, gives children of void or voidable marriages rights in their parents’ property. Applying that provision to joint family property, the Court reasoned that the child’s right is limited to the parent’s share, which becomes the parent’s absolute property upon partition, and that the child cannot demand partition while the parent is alive. The Court’s purposive approach drew on Parayankandiyal Eravath Kanapravan Kalliani Amma v. K. Devi and the constitutional values discussed under Articles 37 and 39(f); it expressed disagreement with the narrower approach in Jinia Keotin, Neelamma, and Bharatha Matha and referred the issue to a larger Bench.
members.conclusion: The Court expressed the view that such children cannot claim partition by their own right during their parent’s lifetime and may exercise their right only after the parent’s death; their entitlement is to the property that becomes the parent’s property. The Court referred the matter to a larger Bench for reconsideration and did not finally dispose of the appeal.

rule.if: partition_dispute and child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage and joint_family_property and parent_alive

predicates.partition_dispute: A proceeding seeks partition of property.
predicates.child_from_void_or_voidable_marriage: The child was born from a marriage that is void or voidable.
predicates.joint_family_property: The property sought to be partitioned is joint family property.
predicates.parent_alive: The parent whose share is claimed is alive when partition is sought.

members.legal_issue: Children deemed legitimate because they were born from a void marriage do not thereby acquire rights in property belonging to persons other than their parents.
material_facts: The children were born from a marriage that was void because an earlier marriage was still subsisting.
They claimed shares in ancestral coparcenary property shared with persons other than their parents.
The courts below denied the children shares in that coparcenary property, and they appealed that decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(1) and (2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, as amended by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976, deem children of a void or annulled marriage legitimate. But Section 16(3), which applies notwithstanding those subsections, expressly prevents that status from conferring rights in the property of anyone other than the parents where the children would otherwise have been incapable of acquiring those rights because they were not legitimate. The protective purpose of Section 16 cannot be used to extend rights beyond the statutory limit. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The children could not claim shares in the coparcenary property under Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act; their statutory rights were confined to the property of their parents. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_against_denial: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision that denied children a claimed share in property.
predicates.children_from_void_marriage: The children were born from a marriage that was void.
predicates.claim_to_property_of_nonparents: The children claimed rights in property belonging, at least in part, to persons other than their parents.

members.legal_issue: A request to add omitted necessary parties at a very late stage may be refused when those parties were omitted from both the original certiorari petition and the subsequent special leave petition.
material_facts: The appellant had omitted the two individuals who succeeded before the revenue authorities from the High Court certiorari petition and had not applied to add them there.
The appellant also did not join those individuals in the special leave petition.
At the hearing of the appeal, the appellant asked the Court to direct that the individuals be added and to remand the matter to the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court may allow proper parties to be added to settle all questions in a proceeding, either on its own initiative or on an application, but it refused the request in these circumstances because it was made at a very late stage. The decision arose in an appeal by special leave from the dismissal of a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court refused the request to add the omitted parties and remand the matter, holding that the request was belated.

predicates.appeal_from_dismissal_of_certiorari_peti: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a petition seeking certiorari.
predicates.omitted_parties_not_joined_in_original_p: Persons whose interests required their presence were not joined in the original certiorari petition.
predicates.omitted_parties_not_joined_in_special_le: Those omitted persons were also not joined in the petition seeking special leave to appeal.
predicates.late_request_to_add_parties: The request to add the omitted persons was first made at a very late stage of the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A plaint amendment may be refused when it is sought very late in the proceedings and is unnecessary to decide the suit.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to amend the plaint in a partition suit when the trial was almost over and the case was fixed for final arguments.
The Supreme Court considered the amendment unnecessary because the suit could be decided without it.
The trial court had rejected the amendment application, but the High Court set aside that order and allowed the amendment.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a plaint amendment may be refused where the application is wholly belated, is made when the trial is almost over, and is not required to determine the issues in the suit. The judgment cites no statutory provisions or earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the trial court’s rejection of the amendment application was restored.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_allowed_plaint_amendment and amendment_application_wholly_belated and trial_almost_over and suit_decidable_without_amendment

predicates.appeal_challenges_allowed_plaint_amendme: The appeal challenges an order allowing a plaintiff’s application to amend a plaint after a trial court rejected it.
predicates.amendment_application_wholly_belated: The plaintiff filed the amendment application very late in the proceedings.
predicates.trial_almost_over: The trial was almost over and the case was fixed for final arguments when the amendment was sought.
predicates.suit_decidable_without_amendment: The suit could be decided without the proposed amendment.

members.legal_issue: A request to remand a case to permit evidence on an asserted deemed resignation may be refused when that ground was not specifically pleaded and the request is made late in the proceedings.
material_facts: The appellants sought a remand to present evidence on whether the settlor had deemedly resigned as trustee.
The appellants had not specifically pleaded deemed resignation in their written statement.
The request was made at a late stage, and the Court considered the passage of time and the absence of a specific plea.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to permit a late evidentiary remand where the proposed ground had not been specifically pleaded, particularly at the distance of time involved. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court refused the request to remand the case for further evidence.

predicates.appeal_in_which_remand_is_sought: The proceeding is an appeal in which a party asks for the case to be remanded so it can present further evidence.
predicates.no_specific_plea_on_proposed_ground: The party did not specifically plead the ground on which it now seeks to introduce evidence.
predicates.late_request_for_additional_evidence: The party makes its request to present additional evidence at a late stage of the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A request to summon evidence may be refused when it is made after the evidence has closed to prove a factual basis that was known but was not pleaded in the suit.
material_facts: The suit challenged a registered adoption deed, which stated when the adoption ceremony occurred.
After the evidence had closed and the suit was listed for final arguments, the plaintiffs sought records concerning whether a defendant was on duty on the date of the ceremony.
The plaintiffs had not pleaded that the defendant's presence or duty status on that date undermined the adoption.
An application to amend the plaint to add the relevant allegation had been dismissed, and that dismissal had become final.
The suit was subject to directions for expeditious disposal.
members.legal_principle: Evidence cannot assist a party in the absence of a pleading to support it. The court also relied on the fact that the relevant event was disclosed in the deed, the request came after evidence had closed, and expeditious disposal had been directed. The judgment identifies no statutory provision or earlier case as authority for this principle.
members.conclusion: The refusal to summon the records was proper, and the appeals challenging that refusal were dismissed.

rule.if: civil_suit_evidence_request and evidence_closed and relevant_fact_known_at_filing and not supporting_pleading and request_is_late

predicates.civil_suit_evidence_request: A party in a civil suit asks the court to summon records as evidence.
predicates.evidence_closed: The evidence in the suit has closed before the party makes the request.
predicates.relevant_fact_known_at_filing: The party knew the factual basis for the proposed evidence when filing the suit.
predicates.supporting_pleading: The party pleaded the factual basis for the proposed evidence in the suit.
predicates.request_is_late: The party makes the request at a late stage of the suit.

members.legal_issue: A summary eviction procedure cannot be used where the person in possession raises a bona fide dispute over ownership that requires adjudication by a civil court.
material_facts: The occupants traced their claim to ownership through a documented chain of conveyances and long-standing possession.
The government asserted ownership and relied on an earlier resumption notice, but that notice had been quashed by the High Court as lacking authority of law.
The history of prior proceedings and the parties’ competing claims established a bona fide, long-standing dispute over ownership.
The government had earlier told the Supreme Court that it would seek dispossession in accordance with law, including, if necessary, by filing a civil suit.
The Estate Officer issued a notice seeking eviction through the summary procedure, and the occupants challenged it by writ petition.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(e) and 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, the summary procedure is not suited to deciding complicated questions of title where an occupant makes a bona fide claim to possession. Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1986) 1 SCC 133, holds that a lessor seeking to enforce a disputed right of re-entry must proceed by suit, while preserving the availability of the Act where unauthorized occupation of public premises is admitted. State of Rajasthan v. Padmavati Devi, 1995 Supp (2) SCC 872, applying Government of A.P. v. Thummala Krishna Rao, (1982) 2 SCC 134, and State of U.P. v. Zia Khan, (1998) 8 SCC 483, holds that summary eviction is unavailable where a bona fide claim requires ordinary adjudication. Kaiser-I-Hind Pvt. Ltd. v. National Textile Corp. (Maharashtra North) Ltd., (2002) 8 SCC 182, and Northern India Caterers (P) Ltd. v. State of Punjab, AIR 1967 SC 1581, explain that the Act supplies a faster remedy for an existing right rather than creating a new right of eviction. The Estate Officer’s authority must be assessed consistently with these principles; Chaube Jagdish Prasad v. Ganga Prasad Chaturvedi, 1959 Supp (1) SCR 733, did not govern this issue.
members.conclusion: The Estate Officer had no jurisdiction to use the summary procedure to evict the occupants in the presence of the bona fide ownership dispute; the notice was quashed, leaving the ownership question for determination by a civil court.

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: A public authority sought to remove an occupant through a summary eviction process.
predicates.bona_fide_title_dispute: The occupant and the public authority each asserted ownership, and the occupant’s claim was supported by circumstances showing a genuine dispute requiring ordinary adjudication.

members.legal_issue: Summary eviction from land cannot be used to resolve a bona fide dispute over whether the land belongs to the government.
material_facts: The government sought to evict occupants summarily from land whose inclusion in an earlier acquisition was disputed.

A prior suit brought by the university for whose benefit acquisition was claimed had been dismissed: one plot was found not to have been acquired, and as to the other plots the university had failed to establish possession within the limitation period.
The government had not been a party to that suit, and the occupants and their predecessors had possessed the land for an appreciable period.

The occupants claimed through the original owner, and deciding the government’s title required resolving whether the land had been acquired and whether title had later been perfected by adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2 and 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, the summary eviction power in section 6 applies to unauthorised occupation of land that is government property and for which assessment is payable; section 7 requires notice before proceedings. Where government title is genuinely disputed and the occupant has a bona fide claim, the government cannot decide title unilaterally and then rely on section 6. Summary proceedings are not suited to adjudicating complicated title questions and are not due process for that purpose. The court cited no earlier case as the basis for this holding.
members.conclusion: The government could not evict the occupants summarily while the genuine dispute over title remained unresolved; the title questions had to be decided through an appropriate ordinary court proceeding.

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The government sought to remove an occupant through a summary statutory eviction process.
predicates.bona_fide_title_dispute: The government and occupant genuinely disputed whether the land belonged to the government, including whether it had been acquired or whether the occupant's predecessor had obtained title through long possession.
predicates.occupant_claims_title: The occupant asserted a claim to the land rather than occupying it without any claim of right.

members.legal_issue: Summary eviction proceedings cannot be used to remove an occupant who raises a bona fide claim to remain in possession that requires adjudication of complex questions of law or fact.
material_facts: The authorities initiated summary proceedings to evict the respondent from land recorded as government land.
The respondent claimed a right to remain in possession based on an earlier government grant, tenancy rules and enactments, revenue records, and other documents.
Determining the respondent’s claim required interpreting laws and documents and investigating disputed facts through evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956 provides a summary procedure for evicting a person in unauthorised occupation of government land, but that procedure is unsuitable for adjudicating a bona fide claim to possession involving complicated questions of title. Relying on the analogous rule under Section 6 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1945, stated in Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Thummala Krishna Rao, 1982 (3) SCR 5000, the Court held that such a claim must be resolved through ordinary proceedings before an appropriate forum.
members.conclusion: The summary proceedings were invalid, and the orders made in those proceedings were set aside. The Court did not determine the parties’ rights to the land, leaving the State free to pursue an appropriate remedy before a competent forum.

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: Authorities initiated a summary proceeding to remove a person alleged to occupy government land without authority.
predicates.occupant_raises_bona_fide_possession_cla: The occupant asserted a bona fide legal basis for remaining in possession of the land.
predicates.claim_requires_complex_adjudication: Resolving the occupant’s claim required adjudicating complex questions of law or fact, including investigation of disputed facts.

members.legal_issue: A summary land-revenue procedure for determining whether land belongs to the government cannot be used to adjudicate a genuine dispute over title to land recorded as privately owned.
material_facts: The government initiated summary proceedings against occupants after a complaint challenged the ownership of an estate conveyed more than a century earlier.
The estate had been divided and transferred through registered transactions, and the government had acquired portions of it while paying compensation to members of the private owner's family.
The proceedings included directions to evict occupants and deliver the land to the government.
members.legal_principle: Section 67(1) and (2) of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 applies to public lands and lands that are not the property of individuals or other legally capable owners; it does not empower the revenue authority to decide a dispute over private title. The Court relied on the text of Section 67 and the established private ownership and transfers in this case.
members.conclusion: The summary proceedings were without jurisdiction because the statutory procedure did not authorize adjudication of a title dispute between the government and private individuals.

predicates.summary_revenue_proceeding: The government used a summary land-revenue procedure to assert a claim to land.
predicates.private_ownership_evidence: Documents or official conduct showed that individuals held the land as private property.
predicates.title_dispute_between_state_and_individu: The government and individuals asserted competing claims of ownership over the land.

members.legal_issue: A public servant is protected from criminal cognizance without prior governmental sanction when the acts alleged have a reasonable connection with the discharge or purported discharge of official duties.
material_facts: The accused was a Sub-Divisional Officer and was present in his official capacity to supervise a drive to remove encroachments from government roadside land.

During the operation, the complainant alleged that the accused and accompanying officials entered the complainant’s clinic, used abusive language, directed that the complainant be removed, and carried out demolitions.
The alleged conduct occurred in the course of the encroachment-removal operation, which the accused was supervising as part of his official duties.
No prior sanction for prosecution had been obtained.
members.legal_principle: Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure bars a court from taking cognizance without prior governmental sanction where the accused is a public servant removable only by or with governmental sanction and the alleged offence was committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. The alleged act must have a reasonable connection with the duty; it need not be strictly necessary to perform that duty, and an act that exceeds what the duty requires may still be protected if it is sufficiently interrelated with the duty. The protection does not place an official above the law for acts unconnected with official duty. Section 197 is an exception to the general cognizance power under Section 190. The court may consider whether sanction is required at any stage, and the question concerns the court’s jurisdiction. The court relied on Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari, Suresh Kumar Bhikamchand Jain v. Pandey Ajay Bhushan, State through the CBI v. B.L. Verma, and N.K. Ogle v. Sanwaldas Alias Sanwalmal Ahuja.
members.conclusion: The allegations had a reasonable nexus with the accused’s official duty, so cognizance could not be taken without prior sanction. The High Court’s order was set aside and the cognizance order was quashed, without preventing the competent authority from obtaining sanction and proceeding in accordance with law.

rule.if: criminal_cognizance_proceeding and protected_public_servant and acts_during_official_task and not prior_sanction

predicates.criminal_cognizance_proceeding: A criminal proceeding seeks a court’s cognizance of alleged offences by a public servant.
predicates.protected_public_servant: The accused is a public servant who can be removed from office only by or with governmental sanction.
predicates.acts_during_official_task: The conduct complained of occurred while the public servant was carrying out or purporting to carry out an assigned official task.
predicates.prior_sanction: The competent government authority granted sanction for prosecution before the court took cognizance.
predicates.cognizance_cannot_be_taken_without_prior: A court cannot take cognizance of the alleged offence unless prior governmental sanction has been obtained.

members.legal_issue: Prior sanction is required when the alleged conduct of a public servant who falls within the protected category was done or purportedly done in the discharge of official duty, even if the conduct is alleged to have involved excesses.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that senior district and police officials intervened to prevent municipal staff from removing an unauthorised structure and that officials assaulted and threatened the complainant and others.
The witnesses’ accounts described the officials taking control of the site amid a gathering crowd and tension over the proposed removal.
The alleged conduct was connected to the officials’ intervention in a developing public-order situation; the Court considered it prima facie to have been done or purportedly done in official duties.
The Court left the justification for the conduct and whether the officials committed excesses to be determined at trial after the required sanction was obtained.
members.legal_principle: Section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to a public servant not removable from office save by or with government sanction when the alleged offence concerns an act done or purportedly done in the discharge of official duty. The act need not itself be an official duty, and an alleged excess may still be protected if sufficiently connected with or purportedly undertaken in official duty; an act wholly in a private capacity is not protected. The Court relied on Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari, including its statement that the connection to duty may become apparent as the case progresses, and Pukhraj v. State of Rajasthan, which distinguishes excess in purported official action from conduct having no semblance of official duty. It also relied on S.B. Saha concerning consideration of materials available when the sanction question arises.
members.conclusion: A case for sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was prima facie made out, so the appeals were dismissed; the Court expressed no opinion on the merits of the allegations.

predicates.criminal_complaint_proceeding: A criminal complaint proceeding is before a court for consideration of cognizance or continuation of the case.
predicates.protected_public_servant: The accused is a public servant who cannot be removed from office except by or with government sanction.
predicates.alleged_conduct_purports_to_be_official_: The alleged conduct is connected with an act the public servant did or purported to do in carrying out official duties, rather than an act wholly in a private capacity.

members.legal_issue: Prior government sanction is required before taking cognizance of alleged offences against public servants when the charged conduct has a reasonable connection with the discharge of their official duties.
material_facts: The accused were public servants whose official roles included processing, approving, or communicating the proposed transfer of the property.
The prosecution alleged that the officials conspired to transfer the property unlawfully and obtain an undue pecuniary benefit.
The charge-sheet alleged that the offences were committed in the discharge of the officials’ duties.
The trial court took cognizance and issued summons without prior sanction from the Central Government.
members.legal_principle: Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure protects qualifying public servants from prosecution for alleged offences committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. The court must examine the nature of the alleged act and its connection to official functions: there must be a reasonable, not fanciful or pretended, connection, and the act must be directly concerned with the official duty such that it could reasonably be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office. The protection is not limited to proper performance; an act alleged to be dishonest may still be an official act for this purpose. Whether sanction is required depends on the facts and the quality of the act, not merely the offence charged. Sanction must precede cognizance, and the issue may be considered at any stage. The court relied on R.R. Chari v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. State of Bombay, Amrik Singh v. State of Pepsu, Hori Ram Singh v. Emperor, H.H.B. Gill v. The King, Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari, Satwant Singh v. State of Punjab, Baijnath Gupta v. State of Madhya Pradesh, B. Saha v. M.S. Kochar, and Prakash Singh Badal v. Union of India. It applied Section 197 CrPC to the allegations of conspiracy under Section 120B IPC and held that sanction from the Central Government was required before cognizance was taken.
members.conclusion: The required prior sanction had not been obtained, so the cognizance order and criminal proceedings against the appellants were quashed; the appeals were allowed.

rule.if: public_servant_prosecution and official_duty_connection and cognizance_challenged and prior_sanction_absent

predicates.public_servant_prosecution: The accused persons were public servants prosecuted for alleged offences.
predicates.official_duty_connection: The prosecution alleged conduct connected to the accused persons’ official functions, and the alleged acts could reasonably be claimed to have been done in the course of those functions.
predicates.cognizance_challenged: A court took cognizance and issued process against the accused, and that step was challenged.
predicates.prior_sanction_absent: The competent government authority had not given prior approval for the prosecution.
predicates.cognizance_and_proceedings_quashed: The cognizance order and the criminal proceedings are set aside.

members.legal_issue: Prior sanction is required before prosecuting a public servant for alleged misconduct in processing an official matter when the charged acts have a reasonable connection with the servant’s assigned duties.
material_facts: The accused public servant was a clerk whose assigned work included land allotment, regularisation, and conversion matters.
The allegations concerned his processing of a land application, including failing to bring irregularities to superiors’ attention and conspiring with them in connection with a disputed lease.
The application passed through the relevant officials, and other officials involved in the same transaction had received protection from prosecution without challenge to those orders.
No prior sanction had been obtained to prosecute the accused.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 197 of the CrPC, prior sanction is required for cognisance of an offence alleged against a public servant when the act or omission has a reasonable connection with, and is directly concerned with, the discharge of official duties. The court applies the prima facie reasonable-connection test stated in State of Maharashtra v. Dr. Budhikota Subbarao and the approach to official-duty connection in B. Saha v. M.S. Kochar. Section 197 protects public servants from malicious or vexatious prosecution, but does not shield corruption, cheating, fabrication, or misappropriation merely because the accused is a public servant; the provision must be construed consistently with honesty, justice, and good governance, as stated in Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh.
members.conclusion: The accused was entitled to the same protection as the other officials involved in the transaction; prior sanction was required before cognisance could be taken, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: public_servant_prosecution and official_work_connection and same_transaction_officials_protected and prior_sanction_absent

predicates.public_servant_prosecution: The proceeding seeks to prosecute a person who held public office for an alleged offence.
predicates.official_work_connection: The alleged acts or omissions occurred in processing a matter within the person’s assigned work and were reasonably connected with that work.
predicates.same_transaction_officials_protected: Other officials who handled the same transaction received protection from prosecution, and that protection was not challenged.
predicates.prior_sanction_absent: The competent authority had not given prior approval for the prosecution.

members.legal_issue: A statutory first charge for tax dues on a dealer’s property extends to the whole property and takes priority over a mortgage created before the charge arose.
material_facts: A bank advanced money under a cash credit facility secured by a mortgage over the debtor’s factory property.
The mortgage was created before a statutory provision made tax dues a first charge on the dealer’s property.
The tax authority claimed unpaid sales tax from the proceeds of a court-ordered sale of the mortgaged property, and the lower courts gave the tax claim priority over the bank’s mortgage claim.
The bank appealed the decision on priority.
members.legal_principle: Section 11-AAAA of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954, creates a first charge on the dealer’s property for tax and other sums due under the Act. Under Sections 58 and 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, a mortgage transfers an interest in property, while a charge secures payment without such a transfer. Dattatreya Shanker Mote v. Anand Chintaman Datar (1974) explains that a charge is wider than a mortgage and includes a mortgage. The Court also relied on Westminster City Council v. Haymarket Publishing Ltd. (1981), which held that a statutory charge on land could take priority over a pre-existing mortgage and extend to all existing estates and interests in the property.
members.conclusion: The statutory first charge applies to the entire property, including the mortgagee’s interest, and has priority over the earlier mortgage; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: tax_debt_on_dealer_property and statute_creates_first_charge and prior_mortgage and appeal_over_sale_proceeds_priority

predicates.tax_debt_on_dealer_property: A dealer incurred tax or other statutory dues payable in respect of the dealer’s property.
predicates.statute_creates_first_charge: A statute made the relevant dues a first charge on the dealer’s property.
predicates.prior_mortgage: The dealer had mortgaged the property before the statutory first charge arose.
predicates.appeal_over_sale_proceeds_priority: A party appealed a decision determining whether the statutory dues or the mortgage claim had priority in sale proceeds.

members.legal_issue: A statutory first charge over a debtor’s property makes the tax authority a secured creditor in insolvency proceedings.
material_facts: The debtor owed statutory sales-tax dues to the state.
A state law made unpaid tax, interest, and penalties a first charge on the dealer’s property.
The tax authority sought recognition of its claim during the debtor’s insolvency resolution process.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(30) and 3(31) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, a security interest may arise by operation of law, and the definition of secured creditor does not exclude a government authority. Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act creates a first charge, bringing the state within those definitions. Section 53(1)(b)(ii) ranks the relevant secured debts equally; its non-obstante clause does not make Section 48 inconsistent with or overridden by Section 53.
members.conclusion: The statutory charge created a security interest, making the state a secured creditor; a creditor’s status as an operational creditor does not negate its status as a secured creditor. The statutory charge was not displaced by the liquidation distribution provisions, and the state’s secured debt ranked with the other debts specified for secured creditors that relinquish security.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_resolution: The proceeding concerns insolvency resolution of a corporate debtor.
predicates.statutory_tax_debt_owed: The debtor owes a public authority taxes or related statutory amounts.
predicates.law_creates_first_charge_on_debtor_prope: A law makes the unpaid statutory amounts a first charge on the debtor’s property.

members.legal_issue: A statutory first charge for tax debts on a debtor’s property takes priority over a mortgage created before the charge, and extends to the property as a whole rather than only the debtor’s equity of redemption.
material_facts: A bank had taken a mortgage over a business’s factory premises as security for advances before the tax authority’s statutory first charge came into force.
The business owed sales tax, and the tax authority claimed priority over the bank in the proceeds from the court-ordered sale of the mortgaged premises.
The governing law made tax and other amounts due under the tax legislation a first charge on the property of the person liable to pay them.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11-AAAA of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954, tax and other sums payable under that Act are a first charge on the liable person’s property. Sections 58 and 100 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguish a mortgage, which transfers an interest in specific immovable property as security, from a charge; a charge is wider and includes a mortgage. Relying on Dattatreya Shanker Mote v. Anand Chintaman Datar, the Court held that a charge on property reaches the property despite a prior mortgage, and that a statutory first charge therefore takes priority over that mortgage. The Court also referred to Fisher and Lightwood’s Law of Mortgage and Westminster City Council v. Haymarket Publishing Ltd. in support of the priority of a statutory charge over an existing mortgage.
members.conclusion: The statutory first charge had priority over the earlier mortgage and operated on the entire property, including the mortgagee’s interest, rather than only on the equity of redemption.

rule.if: sale_proceeds_priority_dispute and competing_claims_on_same_property and law_makes_tax_debt_a_first_charge_on_owner_property and mortgage_predates_tax_charge

predicates.sale_proceeds_priority_dispute: A dispute arises over the priority of claims to proceeds from the sale of property.
predicates.competing_claims_on_same_property: A tax authority and a mortgagee assert claims against the same property.
predicates.law_makes_tax_debt_a_first_charge_on_own: The governing law makes tax debts owed by a property owner a first charge on that owner’s property.
predicates.mortgage_predates_tax_charge: The mortgagee created its mortgage before the statutory charge arose.

members.legal_issue: A statutory claim for tax recoverable as a public demand may take priority over a previously created mortgage when legislation expressly gives that claim precedence over mortgage debts.
material_facts: The bank held a mortgage over property belonging to the firm’s partners, created before the State sought to attach and sell the property for the firm’s sales-tax arrears.

The sales-tax legislation allowed the arrears to be recovered as an arrear of land revenue, and the land-revenue legislation gave claims recoverable under its recovery chapter precedence over other claims, expressly including mortgage claims.
members.legal_principle: The common-law priority of Crown debts does not, by itself, extend over a mortgagee or other secured creditor; it ordinarily applies against unsecured creditors. A statute may expressly extend the State’s priority to secured debts. Under sections 13(3)(a) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, and 190(c) and 158(1) of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964, the tax arrears were recoverable under the land-revenue recovery provisions and had precedence over mortgage claims. The Court relied on M/s Builders Supply Corporation v. Union of India, Collector of Aurangabad v. Central Bank of India, Bank of Bihar v. State of Bihar, and Giles v. Grover.
members.conclusion: The State’s claim for the sales-tax arrears had statutory priority over the bank’s secured mortgage claim.

predicates.tax_priority_dispute_in_secured_creditor: A secured creditor and a public authority asserted competing claims to property in a dispute about priority for a tax debt.
predicates.tax_debt_recoverable_through_public_dema: The governing law allowed the tax debt to be recovered through a procedure for collecting public demands.
predicates.law_expressly_prioritizes_that_demand_ov: The governing law expressly gave demands recoverable through that procedure precedence over mortgage claims.

members.legal_issue: A presumption of a lost grant cannot be made when the evidence does not establish its factual basis or the proposed grant would have been legally impossible.
material_facts: The defendants claimed that they and their predecessors held the lands under a rent-free grant made before the permanent settlement, but the lands had been found to be assessed lands included in the estate at that settlement.

The defendants’ documents asserting a Lakheraj title were not shown to relate to the suit lands, and there was no proof that they asserted a hostile title to the plaintiff’s knowledge before the 1931 record of rights.
The duration of possession was not precisely found; the evidence established only possession for a considerable period without payment of rent.
The defendants denied the title of both the estate owner and the religious institution, then sought to rely on a presumed grant from them after that denial failed.
The proposed Lakheraj grant by the head of the religious institution would have been unsupported by consideration and beyond his powers.
members.legal_principle: A lost grant may be presumed where ancient and continued possession is held under an unchallenged assertion of title derived from the owner and cannot otherwise reasonably be explained, but the presumption is not irrebuttable and need not be made where the evidence contradicts it or a legal impediment makes the grant impossible. An assessed estate could not be treated as containing pre-settlement Lakheraj lands consistently with section 36 of Regulation No. 8 of 1793. A party who denies the title of a person cannot, after failing on that denial, rely on a presumed grant from that person. A manager of a religious institution cannot bind it by a perpetual grant absent compelling necessity or benefit; a gratuitous Lakheraj grant is beyond that power. The Court relied on Attorney-General v. Simpson, Raja Braja Sundar Deb v. Moni Behara, Barker v. Richardson, The Rochdale Canal Company v. Radcliffe, and Palaniappa Chetty v. Sreenath Devasikamony.
members.conclusion: The courts below were not entitled to presume a lost grant in favour of the defendants; the plaintiff was entitled to assessment of fair and equitable rent.

rule.if: lost_grant_dispute and (land_assessed_at_settlement or grantor_title_denied or proposed_grantor_lacked_legal_power or (no_proved_hostile_assertion and possession_duration_unascertained))

predicates.lost_grant_dispute: The proceeding involves a claim that a grant should be presumed from long possession.
predicates.land_assessed_at_settlement: The land was included as revenue-assessed land in a settlement that excluded existing rent-free land from assessment.
predicates.grantor_title_denied: The claimant denied the title of the person from whom the claimant later sought to derive a presumed grant.
predicates.proposed_grantor_lacked_legal_power: The proposed grantor could not legally make the grant pleaded, including because it would bind a religious institution without necessity or benefit.
predicates.no_proved_hostile_assertion: The evidence did not establish an unchallenged assertion of the claimed title known to the owner.
predicates.possession_duration_unascertained: The evidence showed lengthy possession but did not establish its precise duration.

members.legal_issue: The presumption of a lost grant is unavailable when the claimant’s possession is explained by a known lease rather than immemorial, open, exclusive, and uninterrupted use under an unexplained assertion of title.
material_facts: The claimant traced his possession to a lease from an alleged Inamdar beginning in the 1950s.
The claimant relied on that explained source of possession when asserting title.
The record did not establish the kind of immemorial, unexplained possession required for a presumed lost grant.
members.legal_principle: A lost grant may be presumed to account for ancient and continued possession exercised openly and exclusively under an assertion of title, where that possession cannot otherwise reasonably be explained. It is not an irrebuttable presumption and should not be made when the evidence is inconsistent with a grant or the possession has an explained source. The Court applied the principle explained by the Constitution Bench in Monohar Das Mohanta v. Charu Chandra Pal.
members.conclusion: The claimant could not rely on the presumption of a lost grant.

predicates.lost_grant_claim: A party asks the court to presume that a grant existed but was lost.
predicates.possession_has_explained_source: The party’s possession is explained by a known lease or another identified source rather than ancient, unexplained use.

members.legal_issue: Long and quiet possession does not support a presumption of a lost grant in favour of possessors when convincing evidence establishes the nature of the grant and identifies its grantee.
material_facts: The original grant document was unavailable, and the archakas and their predecessors had possessed the properties for a long time.
The Inam Register and the archakas’ predecessors’ statement from the Inam inquiry identified the temple as the grantee and did not identify the archakas as grantees or holders of an interest.
members.legal_principle: A presumption of lawful title based on long and quiet possession may support possessory rights when actual proof of title is absent, but it cannot be made where sufficient and convincing evidence establishes the grant’s nature and grantee. The Court referred generally to judicial decisions supporting the lost-grant presumption but named no such decisions. The Inam inquiry and register were considered in the context of the temple’s notification under Chapter VIA of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927.
members.conclusion: The evidence identifying the temple as grantee precluded a presumption of a lost grant in favour of the archakas; the deity was the grantee.

predicates.temple_property_possession_suit: A suit is brought to recover possession of property claimed for a temple.
predicates.long_quiet_possession: The possessors or their predecessors have held the property for a long time and quietly.
predicates.convincing_grant_evidence_identifies_ano: Reliable evidence establishes the grant’s nature and identifies someone other than the possessors as its grantee.

members.legal_issue: The presumption of a lost grant is unavailable when acceptable evidence establishes the terms of the grant.
material_facts: The trustees produced extracts from the inam register and statements made during the inam inquiry concerning the temple lands.
The Court found that the records clearly established the terms of the grants to the deities.
members.legal_principle: A lost grant may be presumed to support long and quiet possession when actual evidence of title or the grant’s terms is unavailable. It cannot be presumed where sufficient and convincing evidence establishes the grant’s nature and the person to whom it was made. The Court relied on Sankaranarayana Pillayan v. H.R.E. Board, Madras; Buddu Satyanarayana v. Konduru Venkatapayya; Maginiram Sitaram v. Kasturbai Manibhai; and Mohamed Muzafar Ali Musavi v. Jabeda Khatun.
members.conclusion: The doctrine of lost grant could not be invoked because acceptable evidence of the terms of the grants was available.

predicates.temple_endowment_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over title to property granted for a temple endowment.
predicates.reliable_evidence_of_grant_terms: The parties produced acceptable records that establish the terms of the original grant.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on private coal mining operations includes the extraction of coking coal.
material_facts: Private operators claimed that the 1976 amendment prohibited mining ordinary coal but did not apply to coking coal mines.
The material they sought to extract was coking coal, which is a form of coal.
The governing legislation defined a coal mine broadly by the existence of one or more coal seams, and the related legislation defined a coking coal mine as a coal mine containing coking coal seams.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, as amended by the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, uses sweeping language prohibiting coal mining operations by persons outside the specified exceptions. Section 2(b) of the 1973 Act defines a coal mine by the existence of one or more coal seams, and section 3(c) of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, treats a coking coal mine as a coal mine. The Court considered the statutory text, the statutory purpose and the rule in Heydon's case; it held that legislative history could illuminate, but not confine, the interpretation.
members.conclusion: The prohibition on coal mining operations applies to coking coal mining as well as other coal mining.

predicates.challenge_to_coal_mining_restriction: A proceeding challenges a restriction on coal mining operations.
predicates.private_operator_seeks_mining: A private operator seeks to carry on mining operations.
predicates.material_is_coking_coal: The material the operator seeks to mine is coking coal, a form of coal.

members.legal_issue: A court may not appoint a receiver or otherwise authorize coal extraction prohibited by the coal-mining restriction.
material_facts: Receivers appointed by courts had been working mines and extracting coal or coking coal.
