The statutory prohibition was imperative and comprehensive, and contravention was punishable.
The Court stated that the prohibition had been constitutionally upheld.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, as amended by the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, comprehensively prohibits the specified coal-mining operations; section 4 provides punishment for contravention. Because the prohibition had been constitutionally upheld, a court could not authorize conduct that would violate it or sanction the commission of a crime.
members.conclusion: No court may appoint a receiver or otherwise permit the extraction of coal or coking coal contrary to the prohibition.

predicates.request_for_court_authorization: A proceeding asks a court to appoint a receiver or otherwise authorize mining.
predicates.proposed_extraction_is_coal: The proposed mining would extract coal or coking coal.
predicates.extraction_is_barred_and_punishable: The proposed extraction is barred by an enforceable and punishable mining restriction.

members.legal_issue: The statutory prohibition on coal mining by operators outside the permitted classes is mandatory and bars their extraction of coal.
material_facts: The operators associated with the alleged workers were not among the classes permitted to carry on coal mining.
The materials before the Court showed no lawful sanction for the mining operations, and the statutory scheme made contravention punishable.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act, 1976 expressly prohibited coal mining by persons outside the specified classes; Section 4 made contravention punishable with imprisonment. The Court treated the prohibition as part of a public-interest policy for conserving a vital national resource and planning its use.
members.conclusion: The prohibition is peremptory and mandatory, and operators outside the permitted classes cannot extract coal.

predicates.coal_mining_prohibition_case: The proceeding concerns whether coal mining may be carried on despite a statutory prohibition.
predicates.operator_outside_permitted_classes: The operator does not belong to a class legally permitted to carry on the mining activity.
predicates.coal_extraction_is_sought: The operator or another person seeks to extract coal from the mine.
predicates.unauthorized_coal_extraction_is_prohibit: Coal extraction by an operator outside the permitted classes is not allowed.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot appoint a receiver or otherwise authorize coal extraction that a mandatory statutory prohibition forbids.
material_facts: Receivers and other court officers had been appointed in some matters, and coal extraction was reportedly continuing under those arrangements.
The statutory prohibition on mining by unauthorized operators was mandatory and punishable.
The Court had upheld the validity of the prohibition.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act, 1976 imposed a mandatory prohibition, and Section 4 made breach punishable. The Court had upheld the statute's constitutionality and held that judicial orders could not authorize conduct the statute prohibited.
members.conclusion: No court may appoint a receiver or otherwise permit coal extraction contrary to the prohibition, and existing interim orders permitting extraction were vacated.

predicates.court_receiver_or_permission_case: The proceeding concerns a court-appointed receiver or another judicial authorization relating to mining.
predicates.coal_extraction_is_sought: A receiver, officer, or other person seeks to extract coal from a mine.
predicates.statutory_prohibition_is_mandatory_and_c: A mandatory prohibition on the mining activity has been upheld as constitutionally valid.
predicates.courts_may_not_authorize_prohibited_coal: A court cannot authorize coal extraction that the mandatory prohibition forbids.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional writ is not an available substitute for an ordinary civil action to enforce a private right to immovable property against private individuals, absent an alleged breach of statutory duty by a public authority.
material_facts: The dispute concerned possession and access to part of a house property between private individuals.
An eviction suit concerning the property was already pending, and an ordinary civil remedy was available for the disputed property claim.

The property owner sought writ directions against the private individuals, while also alleging that police assistance had been given to them; no breach of a statutory duty by a public authority was alleged as the basis for the property relief.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court's special and extraordinary jurisdiction is not ordinarily available to settle property-right disputes between private persons or to replace remedies available under general law. A writ may be appropriate where a breach of statutory duty by a statutory authority is alleged, in which case directions may be issued to that authority. The Court referred to repeated holdings of the Supreme Court and various High Courts but identified no specific earlier case.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in issuing a writ direction against the private individuals. A regular civil suit, rather than a writ petition, was the appropriate remedy for the property dispute.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_petition and private_immovable_property_dispute and private_parties and ordinary_civil_remedy_available and not statutory_duty_breach_alleged

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: A party sought relief through a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.private_immovable_property_dispute: The relief sought concerned a disputed right to or possession of immovable property.
predicates.private_parties: The property right was claimed by and against private individuals.
predicates.ordinary_civil_remedy_available: A civil remedy under the general law was available to resolve the property dispute.
predicates.statutory_duty_breach_alleged: A breach of statutory duty by a statutory authority was alleged as the basis for the requested relief.
predicates.writ_relief_unavailable: The requested writ relief is unavailable for resolving the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition is not an appropriate remedy for a private property dispute between private parties when no public or statutory duty, statutory infraction, or collusion with the State is involved.
material_facts: The underlying case was a landlord-tenant dispute concerning possession of premises and alleged damage to property.
The dispute was between private parties, and the landlord was the only respondent to the High Court petition.
The respondent was not shown to be performing a public or statutory duty, acting in collusion with the State, or involved in an infraction of statute.
The petition expressly invoked writ jurisdiction and sought to set aside the lower appellate court’s decision.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 provides a public-law remedy, not a forum to decide private property rights. Ordinarily a writ cannot issue against a private person unless that person performs a public or statutory duty; a private person may be amenable where there is collusion with the State. The Court relied on Sohan Lal v. Union of India, AIR 1957 SC 529; Engineering Mazdoor Sabha v. Hind Cycles Ltd., AIR 1963 SC 874; Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. Rohtas Industries Staff Union, (1976) 2 SCC 82; Mohammed Hanif v. State of Assam, (1969) 2 SCC 782; T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa, AIR 1954 SC 440; Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. Kalyani Banerjee, (1973) 1 SCC 273; State of Rajasthan v. Bhawani Singh, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 306; Mohan Pandey v. Usha Rani Rajgaria, (1992) 4 SCC 61; Prasanna Kumar Roy Karmakar v. State of W.B., (1996) 3 SCC 403; and P.R. Murlidharan v. Swami Dharmananda Theertha Padar, (2006) 4 SCC 501.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in entertaining the writ petition in this private landlord-tenant dispute. Its refusal to interfere with the concurrent factual findings was nevertheless unexceptionable, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: article_226_writ_petition and private_property_dispute and private_respondent and not respondent_performs_public_or_statutory_duty and not state_collusion and not statutory_infraction

predicates.article_226_writ_petition: The applicant seeks relief through the High Court’s original writ jurisdiction.
predicates.private_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns property rights disputed between private individuals.
predicates.private_respondent: The person against whom relief is sought is a private individual.
predicates.respondent_performs_public_or_statutory_: The respondent performs a public or statutory duty relevant to the requested relief.
predicates.state_collusion: The private respondent acts in collusion with the State in the conduct challenged.
predicates.statutory_infraction: The challenged conduct involves an infraction of statute.

members.legal_issue: Constitutional writ or supervisory jurisdiction cannot be used to decide a private landlord-tenant dispute or an intensely disputed factual question about alleged harassment when no excess of jurisdiction by the subordinate court is alleged.
material_facts: The dispute involved competing claims concerning occupation and ownership of a shop, including an asserted landlord-tenant relationship.
The respondent alleged that the appellant had obtained court orders against another person deceitfully to harass the respondent and close the respondent’s business.
Whether the orders were obtained with an intent to harass was a factual issue; no issue had been framed and no evidence had been produced to establish that allegation.
The respondent was not a party to the suits in which the challenged orders were made and could have challenged those orders before an appropriate forum.
The respondent did not contend that the subordinate court had acted without jurisdiction or exceeded its jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a petition cannot be used to determine a landlord-tenant dispute or an intense dispute between private individuals. Under Article 227, as explained in Jai Singh v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, (2010) 9 SCC 385, supervisory jurisdiction ensures that subordinate courts act within the bounds of their authority; it is exercised with care and is not a general means of correcting errors by courts acting within their jurisdiction. Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil, (2010) 8 SCC 329, was relied on for the limits on writ intervention in private landlord-tenant disputes.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not entertain the petition to determine the private dispute or the disputed allegation of harassment; its judgment was set aside.

predicates.constitutional_petition_concerns_private: A person brings a constitutional petition seeking relief concerning a dispute between private individuals.
predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: The private dispute concerns the parties’ asserted landlord-tenant relationship or occupation of rented premises.
predicates.intensely_disputed_harassment_facts: A party alleges harassment or improper purpose, and deciding the allegation requires resolving disputed facts.
predicates.subordinate_court_jurisdictional_excess_: The petitioner alleges that the subordinate court acted without jurisdiction or beyond the limits of its jurisdiction.
predicates.constitutional_court_cannot_use_writ_or_: The constitutional court does not use writ or supervisory jurisdiction to decide the private dispute or resolve its disputed factual allegations.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional writ petition is not maintainable to resolve a disputed property-possession claim between private parties when the dispute can be determined through ordinary proceedings and no breach of statutory duty by a public authority is alleged.
material_facts: The claimant sought restoration of possession of a flat through a writ petition against another private individual and public authorities.
The private individuals disputed their rights to ownership and possession of the flat, including whether the claimant had been in possession.
A civil suit concerning the flat was already pending, and a civil suit was available to determine the parties’ claims.
No violation of a statutory duty by a public authority was alleged as the basis for the possession claim.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, extraordinary writ jurisdiction is not a substitute for ordinary civil or criminal remedies for disputes between private persons. Property-rights and possession questions requiring determination of disputed facts and evidence are for the competent ordinary court. Article 226 may support directions to a statutory authority where breach of a statutory duty is alleged. The Court relied on Mohan Pande v. Usha Rani, (1992) 4 SCC 61, and Dwarka Prasad Agrawal v. B.D. Agrawal, (2003) 6 SCC 230; it also noted that a possession dispute may be decided in civil proceedings or proceedings under Section 145 CrPC.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was not maintainable and should have been dismissed; the parties remained free to pursue appropriate civil proceedings.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_for_property_possession and private_parties_dispute_property_rights and possession_or_ownership_facts_are_disputed and ordinary_court_remedy_available and not statutory_duty_breach_alleged

predicates.constitutional_writ_for_property_possess: A claimant brought a constitutional writ petition seeking possession-related relief concerning property.
predicates.private_parties_dispute_property_rights: Private individuals asserted competing rights to ownership or possession of the property.
predicates.possession_or_ownership_facts_are_disput: The parties disputed facts about ownership, possession, or the circumstances of possession.
predicates.ordinary_court_remedy_available: An ordinary civil or criminal proceeding was available to determine the relevant dispute.
predicates.statutory_duty_breach_alleged: The claimant alleged that a public authority breached a statutory duty in a way material to the relief sought.

members.legal_issue: A government disposing of public property to obtain revenue must use a fair, non-arbitrary process that gives the public an opportunity to compete and secures the best available price, rather than accepting a privately offered bid through a secret selection.
material_facts: The State auctioned a mineral quarry, and the appellant made the highest bid at the later auction.

The State declined to confirm that bid, considering it inadequate, and subsequently accepted a higher private offer made directly to the Chief Minister without reopening the process to public competition.
The recipient was not selected to achieve a special public purpose or to benefit a weaker section of society.
In the Supreme Court hearing, open bidding between the appellant and the recipient rose substantially above the privately offered amount.
members.legal_principle: Public property is held and disposed of in the public interest. Where disposal is for revenue, the State must seek the best available market price and act fairly under non-arbitrary standards; a lower price may be justified where a defined public purpose warrants it. Rule 28 of the Punjab Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964 permits disposal by auction or tender, with tender meaning an invitation to intending contractors rather than a secret private deal. The Court relied on K.N. Guruswamy v. The State of Mysore, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. The International Airport Authority of India, Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir, Nand Kishore Saraf v. State of Rajasthan, Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Shiv Charan Sharma. It distinguished decisions recognizing the State’s power to reject the highest bid because the question was not whether the highest bid could be rejected, but whether the State could then make a secret private grant without a fair process.
members.conclusion: The private grant was arbitrary and impermissible; the grant was quashed, and the Court directed the State to grant the quarry right to the appellant on the terms stated in its order.

predicates.government_disposes_public_resource_for_: The government disposes of a public resource for the purpose of obtaining revenue.
predicates.auction_highest_bid_rejected_as_inadequa: The government rejects the highest bid on the ground that it does not provide adequate consideration.
predicates.private_offer_accepted_without_open_comp: The government accepts a private offer without giving interested members of the public an opportunity to compete.
predicates.no_special_public_purpose_justifies_priv: The recipient is not selected to achieve a defined public purpose that could justify a departure from obtaining the best available price.

members.legal_issue: A government need not invariably use public auction or tenders to allocate public property for a socioeconomic purpose, provided the departure from the ordinary method is rational, in the public interest, and not discriminatory or suggestive of bias or favoritism.
material_facts: The government sought to promote tourism by facilitating construction of a five-star hotel and negotiated with established hotel groups that had come forward with proposals.
No other leading hotelier had shown an inclination to make a proposal, and the nature of the project required expertise and financial capacity.
The process was open and extended, and no person claimed that they had been discriminated against or denied a right to carry on business.
The Court found negotiation to be a rational and practical method in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Public property is not at the executive's absolute discretion: public interest is paramount, and public auction or tenders are ordinary methods, but not invariable requirements. A departure requires rational reasons and must not suggest discrimination, bias, jobbery, or nepotism. The Court relied on Rash Bihari Panda v. State of Orissa, R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority, Kasturi Lal Laxmi Reddy v. State of Jammu & Kashmir, State of Haryana v. Jage Ram, Ram & Shyam Co. v. State of Haryana, and Chenchu Rami Reddy v. Government of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The government was justified in negotiating without inviting tenders or holding a public auction; the method adopted was not discriminatory or improper.

rule.if: public_property_allocation_proceeding and specific_socioeconomic_objective and negotiation_rational_in_circumstances and no_comparable_competitors_excluded and no_discriminatory_or_favoritist_process

predicates.public_property_allocation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a government's allocation of public property.
predicates.specific_socioeconomic_objective: The government allocated the property to pursue a specific socioeconomic objective rather than simply to maximize revenue.
predicates.negotiation_rational_in_circumstances: Negotiation with those who came forward was a rational and practical method in the circumstances of the project.
predicates.no_comparable_competitors_excluded: No comparable prospective participant was excluded from an opportunity to propose the project.
predicates.no_discriminatory_or_favoritist_process: The allocation process was not discriminatory and did not suggest bias, jobbery, or nepotism.

members.legal_issue: A sale of seized assets should use a transparent process that encourages competition and seeks the best obtainable price, with appropriate publicity.
material_facts: The corporation had taken possession of an industrial unit securing an unpaid loan and contemplated its disposal.
The Court considered the need to recover public funds while ensuring that disposal of the seized unit obtained the highest price.
members.legal_principle: Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 authorizes realization of secured property. In considering disposal of public property, the Court relied on The Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd., which explains that public auction after adequate publicity generally promotes participation and the best price, while tenders or another suitable method may be appropriate in some circumstances if adequate publicity is given.
members.conclusion: The corporation must use a transparent and acceptable disposal procedure intended to realize the highest price, with due publicity wherever possible; public auction is generally effective, but another suitable method may be used where an auction is unsuitable or unlikely to secure the best price.

predicates.seized_asset_is_to_be_sold: A lender is disposing of an asset it has seized to recover a debt.
predicates.sale_process_can_be_made_competitive: The disposal can be conducted through a process that allows interested purchasers a fair opportunity to participate.
predicates.best_price_is_the_disposal_objective: The seller seeks to obtain the highest price reasonably available for the asset.

members.legal_issue: Public property should ordinarily be disposed of through public auction or tenders, while a departure from that method requires compelling, rational reasons and must remain fair and non-discriminatory.
material_facts: A state financial corporation owned the property after purchasing it in execution of a decree and sought to sell it to recover its money.
The corporation invited tenders for the property and later negotiated with the next-highest tenderer after the highest tenderer failed to pay.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 requires state action, including a public authority’s dealings with property, to be reasonable, rational, non-arbitrary and non-discriminatory, and to serve the public interest. Public auction or tenders are the ordinary means of seeking the best price and ensuring fairness, but are not invariable requirements where compelling, rational reasons justify another method. The Court applied K.N. Guruswamy v. State of Mysore; Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner; R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India; Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir; Fertilizer Corporation Kamagar Union v. Union of India; Ram and Shyam Company v. State of Haryana; and Shri Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: Public property should generally be sold by public auction or by inviting tenders; private negotiation may be used where compelling reasons justify the departure, rather than mere convenience, and the action remains fair and free from apparent discrimination, bias, favouritism or nepotism.

predicates.public_property_disposal: A state body or public authority disposes of property it owns or controls.
predicates.public_authority_action: A public authority takes action in dealing with that property.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit for redemption is not barred by the one-year limitation period for setting aside an official order when the earlier summary application was rejected because the dispute required determination by a civil court, without deciding the right to redeem.
material_facts: The claimants applied to an official for summary redemption of a mortgage, and the application was rejected because the dispute raised complicated questions of fact and law that could not be tried in summary proceedings.
The official directed the claimants to file a civil suit and did not determine their entitlement to redeem the mortgage.
The claimants later brought a civil suit for redemption, and the mortgagees argued that it was barred because it had not been filed within one year of the rejection of the application.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4, 9 and 12 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913, an official may dismiss a summary redemption petition on specified grounds, and a party aggrieved by an order under Sections 6 to 11 may sue to establish rights in respect of the mortgage. Article 14 of Schedule I to the Limitation Act, 1908 applies to a suit seeking to set aside an official order, not to a suit for redemption where the official merely declines summary adjudication and leaves the parties to pursue their rights in civil court. An order must be one the officer had jurisdiction to make and one that bars relief unless set aside to require such a suit. The Court relied on Tulsi Das v. Diala Ram and Dewan Chand v. Raghbir Singh.
members.conclusion: The rejection did not have to be set aside and did not bar the civil suit for redemption; the one-year limitation period for suits to set aside official orders did not apply. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_redemption_suit and prior_summary_redemption_application and official_referred_complex_dispute_to_civil_court and official_did_not_decide_redemption_rights

predicates.civil_redemption_suit: A person claiming a right to redeem brought a civil suit seeking redemption.
predicates.prior_summary_redemption_application: The person had previously applied to an official for summary redemption of the mortgage.
predicates.official_referred_complex_dispute_to_civ: The official rejected the summary application because the dispute was too complex for summary determination and directed the person to pursue a civil suit.
predicates.official_did_not_decide_redemption_right: The official did not determine whether the person was entitled to redeem the mortgage.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit for redemption is not subject to the one-year limitation period for setting aside an officer’s order when the officer merely declines summary jurisdiction and relegates the parties to a civil suit without deciding the redemption claim.
material_facts: The claimants applied for redemption under the statutory summary procedure.
The officer rejected the application because it raised complicated questions of fact and law that could not be tried summarily, and directed the claimants to file a civil suit.
The officer did not decide the merits of the claimants’ right to redeem.
The claimants later filed a civil suit seeking redemption, and the defendants argued that it was barred because it was not brought within one year of the officer’s order.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 9 and 12 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913, an officer’s order dismissing a summary application for a ground within section 9 may be subject to a suit to establish rights under section 12. Article 14 of Schedule I to the Limitation Act, 1908 applies to a suit seeking to set aside an officer’s order, not to a suit for redemption where the officer merely refers the parties to a civil court without deciding against the mortgagor. The substance, not the form, of the order determines whether it must be set aside. The Court followed Tulsi Das v. Diala Ram and Dewan Chand v. Raghbir Singh.
members.conclusion: The civil suit for redemption was not barred by limitation; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: redemption_suit and summary_application_referred_to_civil_court and no_merits_decision_against_mortgagor and suit_seeks_redemption_not_annulment

predicates.redemption_suit: A party brings a civil suit seeking redemption of a mortgage.
predicates.summary_application_referred_to_civil_co: An officer handling a summary redemption application declines to try it summarily and directs the applicant to pursue the matter in a civil court.
predicates.no_merits_decision_against_mortgagor: The officer does not decide the merits of the applicant’s right to redeem.
predicates.suit_seeks_redemption_not_annulment: The civil suit seeks redemption and does not seek to set aside the officer’s order.
predicates.redemption_suit_not_barred_by_order_base: The civil suit for redemption is not barred by the limitation period for setting aside an officer’s order.

members.legal_issue: The period for bringing a mortgage-redemption suit is not enlarged merely because a statutory summary application was dismissed and the suit was brought within the period for challenging that dismissal.
material_facts: The claimants applied under a statutory summary procedure concerning redemption, and their application was dismissed.

The subsequent redemption suit was brought within one year of the dismissal, but the claim was otherwise barred by the limitation period for a redemption suit, even after excluding the time spent pursuing the application.
members.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913 makes an order under sections 6 to 11 conclusive unless a suit to establish rights in respect of the mortgage is brought within the prescribed period. It does not extend the limitation period applicable to a suit for redemption. The court considered prior Lahore High Court decisions on the effect of failing to bring a suit under section 12 but found they did not support an extension of the redemption limitation period.
members.conclusion: The time allowed to sue to establish rights after the summary order did not enlarge the limitation period for a redemption suit, and the suit was dismissed as time-barred.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_suit and summary_redemption_application_dismissed and ordinary_redemption_limitation_expired and suit_within_period_to_challenge_order

predicates.mortgage_redemption_suit: The claimant brought a suit to redeem a mortgage.
predicates.summary_redemption_application_dismissed: The claimant’s application under a summary redemption procedure was dismissed.
predicates.ordinary_redemption_limitation_expired: The limitation period for bringing the redemption suit had expired.
predicates.suit_within_period_to_challenge_order: The claimant brought the suit within the period allowed to challenge the summary order.

members.legal_issue: Dismissal of a summary application for mortgage redemption does not bar a later civil suit for redemption when the suit does not seek to reopen an adjudication of the underlying mortgage right and is filed within the ordinary limitation period.
material_facts: The mortgagor applied for summary redemption, agreed to pay the amount determined in a compromise, and the Collector dismissed the applications after the mortgagor defaulted on payment.
The mortgagor’s successors later filed civil suits seeking redemption and accepted the amount determined in the summary proceedings rather than challenging that determination.
The civil suits were within the limitation period applicable to ordinary mortgage-redemption suits, though they were brought more than one year after the Collector’s orders.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 13 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913 make an order conclusive as to the matters decided and bar a further application under that Act, but do not extinguish the ordinary civil remedy of redemption. Article 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908, equivalent to Article 100 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies to a suit to set aside an official order, not to a suit that does not challenge the order’s adjudication. The ordinary limitation provisions for redemption govern a civil suit seeking redemption and possession. The Court relied on Tulsi Dass @ Nirmal Das v. Diala Ram and Sheo Lal v. Sultan, which distinguish an order’s substance from its form and hold that a dismissal which does not adjudicate the underlying right need not be set aside before a redemption suit is brought.
members.conclusion: The one-year period for challenging an order under the Punjab Act did not bar the civil suits. The Collector’s orders were conclusive as to what they decided, but the suits sought redemption rather than the setting aside of those orders; the suits were within ordinary limitation.

predicates.civil_suit_for_mortgage_redemption: A party brought a civil suit seeking redemption of a mortgage.
predicates.prior_summary_redemption_application_dis: A summary application seeking redemption of the mortgage was dismissed.
predicates.suit_does_not_seek_to_reopen_underlying_: The civil suit seeks redemption without asking the court to set aside or reconsider an adjudication of the underlying mortgage right.
predicates.suit_within_ordinary_limitation: The civil suit was filed within the limitation period applicable to an ordinary claim for mortgage redemption.

members.legal_issue: A contract made in the exercise of government executive power is unenforceable if it does not satisfy the required formalities for making and executing that contract.
material_facts: The government communicated a decision to settle the fishery rights with the claimant.
The settlement was not made and executed in the prescribed constitutional manner.
members.legal_principle: Article 299 of the Constitution requires a government contract to be expressly made by the President or Governor, executed on their behalf, and executed by an authorized person and in an authorized manner. Non-compliance makes the contract void and unenforceable. The court relied on State of Bihar v. Karam Chand Thapar & Brothers Ltd., Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India, State of West Bengal v. B. K. Mondal & Sons, and Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh; it noted that estoppel or ratification cannot cure non-compliance.
members.conclusion: The settlement was not valid or binding on the government, and the claimant could not base an enforceable claim on it.

predicates.government_executive_contract: The agreement was made in the exercise of government executive power.
predicates.required_contract_formalities_not_follow: The agreement was not made and executed in the prescribed manner.

members.legal_issue: A government agreement that does not comply with the constitutionally prescribed form cannot be treated as an implied contract or used as the contractual basis for recovering money from the other party.
material_facts: At a forest-contract auction, the bidder made the highest bids and signed the contract forms, but the contracts required acceptance by a higher government authority.
Before that authority accepted the contracts, a dispute arose over the marking of trees, and the bidder refused to complete the contracts or pay the first instalments.

The contracts were cancelled and re-auctioned, producing a deficiency that the State sought to recover as arrears of land revenue under the auction conditions and the provision concerning money due under a grant, lease, or contract.
No contract satisfying the constitutional requirements had been completed between the bidder and the Government.
members.legal_principle: Article 299(1) of the Constitution requires a government contract to be expressed as made by the President or Governor, executed on their behalf, and executed by an authorized person in the authorized manner. A contract not in full compliance is no contract and cannot be enforced as one; the requirements also preclude inferring an implied government contract. Section 155(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code permits recovery as arrears of land revenue of money due under a grant, lease, or contract, but cannot apply where the asserted basis is an implied contract. The Court applied the principles in State of Bihar v. Karam Chand Thapar, Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India, State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal and Sons, Chaturbhuj Vithaldas Josani v. Moreshwar Prashram, and Union of India v. A.L. Rallia Ram concerning the corresponding requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935.
members.conclusion: The constitutional requirements for a government contract are mandatory; no implied contract could be inferred where those requirements were not met, and the provision for recovering money due under a contract did not permit recovery on the basis of an implied contract.

predicates.government_recovery_appeal: A party appealed a decision concerning the government's demand to recover money from that party.
predicates.required_government_contract_form_not_co: The purported agreement with the Government was not completed in the form and manner required for a binding government contract.
predicates.recovery_claimed_on_implied_contract: The Government relied on an agreement inferred from the parties' conduct rather than a completed contract in the required form as the basis for recovery.

members.legal_issue: A government contract made in the exercise of provincial executive authority is void if it is not expressed to be made by the Governor or is not executed by a person authorized to act on the Governor’s behalf.
material_facts: The water-supply arrangement was made between the government and the applicant outside the irrigation statute and therefore in the exercise of provincial executive authority.
The documents did not express the contract to be made in the Governor’s name.
The record did not establish that the Superintending Engineer was legally authorized to enter into that contract on the government’s behalf.
members.legal_principle: Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, required contracts made in the exercise of a Province’s executive authority to be expressed as made by the Governor and executed on the Governor’s behalf by a person and in a manner authorized by the Governor. The provision is mandatory. Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India and New Marine Coal Co. v. Union of India held that contracts not meeting these requirements are void. Union of India v. Rallia Ram permits the requirements to be assessed by a fair reading of the documents, but does not dispense with them.
members.conclusion: The agreement was void because it neither complied with the required form of expression nor was shown to have been executed by an authorized person.

rule.if: civil_appeal_concerning_state_contract and executive_authority_contract and (not expressed_in_governor_name or not executed_by_authorized_person)

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_state_contract: The matter is a civil appeal concerning a contract made by the government.
predicates.executive_authority_contract: The contract was made in the exercise of the government’s executive authority.
predicates.expressed_in_governor_name: The contract was expressed to be made in the Governor’s name.
predicates.executed_by_authorized_person: The contract was executed on the Governor’s behalf by a person authorized to do so.

members.legal_issue: A contract with the government that does not comply with mandatory constitutional execution formalities is void and cannot be validated by estoppel or ratification.
material_facts: The claimant paid a deposit after an official accepted the bid for rights to collect lac from the forests.
The claimant collected some lac under the arrangement.
The parties did not dispute that the formal requirements for government contracts in Article 299(1) had not been complied with.
members.legal_principle: Article 299(1) of the Constitution, like section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, imposes mandatory formal requirements for government contracts. Those requirements protect the government and the public from unauthorised contracts, so they cannot be waived or dispensed with. The court relied on Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India and State of West Bengal v. B. K. Mondal & Sons.
members.conclusion: The contract was void because it did not comply with Article 299(1), and neither estoppel nor ratification could validate it.

predicates.government_contract_dispute: The case concerns whether an agreement made with the government is legally effective.
predicates.agreement_made_with_government: A person entered an agreement with the government through an official acting for it.
predicates.mandatory_execution_formalities_absent: The agreement did not satisfy the mandatory formal requirements for government contracts.

members.legal_issue: A creditor’s defence that a transfer was fraudulent under the law governing transfers to defeat or delay creditors is sufficiently raised when the pleading alleges that the transfer was sham and, alternatively, that even if genuine it was made to defraud creditors.
material_facts: The creditor’s written statement alleged that the sale was sham and nominal, and also alleged that even if it was genuine it was made to defraud creditors.
The parties presented evidence and contested whether the sale was fraudulent under the provision governing transfers intended to defeat or delay creditors.
members.legal_principle: The court distinguishes a sham transfer, not intended to pass title, from a genuine transfer that is voidable as a fraud on creditors under section 53(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. A pleading that raises both grounds in the alternative permits the court to grant relief if the fraudulent-transfer ground is proved.
members.conclusion: The alternative allegation sufficiently raised the fraudulent-transfer defence, despite the imprecise drafting of the written statement.

predicates.claim_order_challenge_suit: A purchaser brings a suit to challenge an order rejecting a claim to property attached for a debt.
predicates.pleading_alleges_sham_transfer: The creditor alleges that the purported transfer was nominal and was not intended to pass title.
predicates.pleading_alternatively_alleges_creditor_: The creditor alleges that, even if the transfer was genuine, it was made to defraud creditors.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made with intent to defeat or delay creditors is voidable even if it covers less than all of the debtor’s property, unless adequate and readily available property remains to make the transfer immaterial to creditors.
material_facts: The partnership was operating at a loss and had substantial debts when the property was transferred.
Creditors had pursued claims against the partnership, and a creditor had obtained an attachment order concerning the property.
The sale converted immovable property into cash, and no evidence showed that the proceeds were applied to pay particular debts.
There was no definite evidence of other property available to creditors after the sale; the purchaser did not call the vendor as a witness or produce the partnership accounts.
The sale and its registration took place in circumstances from which the court inferred an intention to keep the property beyond creditors’ reach.
members.legal_principle: Section 53(1) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 applies where a transfer is intended to defeat or delay creditors; delay alone is sufficient. The transfer of less than all the debtor’s property does not by itself take the transaction outside the section. The principle in Ramaswami Chettiar v. Mallappa Reddiar, (1920) I.L.R. 43 Mad. 760, was approved: adequate property readily available to creditors must be proved to render the transfer immaterial.
members.conclusion: The sale was made with intent to put the property beyond the reach of creditors and was voidable at the instance of the creditor; the fact that other property might have existed did not defeat that conclusion without proof that it was sufficient in value and readily available.

rule.if: creditor_fraud_transfer_dispute and debtor_financially_distressed and transfer_puts_property_beyond_creditors and not proven_adequate_readily_available_assets

predicates.creditor_fraud_transfer_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a transfer is voidable because it was intended to defeat or delay creditors.
predicates.debtor_financially_distressed: The debtor was losing money or substantially indebted when the transfer was made.
predicates.transfer_puts_property_beyond_creditors: The transfer converted or placed property beyond the practical reach of creditors, without evidence that its proceeds were applied to discharge particular debts.
predicates.proven_adequate_readily_available_assets: Evidence establishes that other property remained which was sufficient in value and readily available to creditors.

members.legal_issue: A conveyance made through a sham transaction to put a debtor’s property beyond creditors’ reach is ineffective against those creditors.
material_facts: The debtor’s property had been attached for unpaid tax liabilities, and an objection seeking its release had been rejected without a successful challenge.
After further tax assessments and a recovery certificate, the property was transferred to a company formed shortly before the transfer.
The company was dominated by the debtor’s close relations, did not pay the stated price in cash, and failed to show that it conducted substantial business.
The timing and circumstances of the transfer showed an effort to prevent the property from being sold to satisfy the debtor’s tax arrears.
members.legal_principle: The court upheld the finding that the transfer was a sham designed to defeat or delay creditors. The circumstances supporting that finding included the debtor’s unpaid liabilities, the attachment and unsuccessful release objection, the timing of the transfer, the transferee company’s control by the debtor’s relatives, the absence of cash payment, and the company’s failure to establish substantial business activity.
members.conclusion: The transfer was sham and ineffective against the debtor’s creditors; the property remained available for attachment and sale to satisfy the arrears.

rule.if: creditor_challenges_property_transfer and property_was_subject_to_debt_recovery and transfer_followed_unsuccessful_effort_to_release_property and transferee_was_family_controlled_entity and (stated_price_not_paid_in_cash or transferee_lacked_substantial_business)

predicates.creditor_challenges_property_transfer: A creditor challenges a transfer of a debtor’s property as an attempt to place it beyond creditors’ reach.
predicates.property_was_subject_to_debt_recovery: The property was subject to steps to recover an unpaid debt from its owner.
predicates.transfer_followed_unsuccessful_effort_to: The transfer took place after an effort to secure the property’s release from recovery measures had failed.
predicates.transferee_was_family_controlled_entity: The transferee was an entity controlled by the debtor’s close relations.
predicates.stated_price_not_paid_in_cash: The stated price for the transfer was not paid in cash.
predicates.transferee_lacked_substantial_business: The transferee failed to show that it conducted substantial business.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made to place a debtor's property beyond creditors' reach may be found sham and ineffective against those creditors when the surrounding circumstances show that the transfer was designed to defeat or delay recovery.
material_facts: The property had been attached for the debtor's unpaid tax liabilities, and an objection seeking its release had failed.
While tax assessment and recovery proceedings were continuing, the nominal owner transferred the property to a company formed shortly beforehand.
The company was dominated by the debtor and close relations, did not pay the price in cash, and failed to show that it conducted substantial business.
The circumstances supported the finding that the company was formed to shield the property from attachment and sale.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the transaction from its timing and surrounding circumstances, including the unsuccessful effort to release the property from attachment, the company's control and activity, and the absence of cash payment. Those facts supported the trial court's finding that the transfer was sham and intended to defeat or delay creditors.
members.conclusion: The transfer to the company was a sham transaction intended to defeat and delay the debtor's creditors, and the decree declaring it ineffective against the creditors was restored.

rule.if: creditor_challenges_debtor_property_transfer and transfer_followed_failed_release_from_attachment and transfer_occurred_during_recovery_proceedings and transferee_controlled_by_debtor_or_relations and consideration_not_paid_in_cash and transferee_lacked_substantial_business_activity

predicates.creditor_challenges_debtor_property_tran: A creditor brought proceedings challenging a transfer of property associated with a debtor.
predicates.transfer_followed_failed_release_from_at: The transfer followed an unsuccessful effort to obtain release of the property from attachment.
predicates.transfer_occurred_during_recovery_procee: The transfer occurred while proceedings to assess or recover the debtor's liability were continuing.
predicates.transferee_controlled_by_debtor_or_relat: The transferee was controlled by the debtor or the debtor's close relations.
predicates.consideration_not_paid_in_cash: The transferee did not pay the stated consideration in cash.
predicates.transferee_lacked_substantial_business_a: The transferee failed to show that it conducted substantial business activity.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s voluntary delivery of possession does not validate a surrender that fails the statutory formalities or permit a landlord to take possession without an order of the competent authority.
material_facts: The tenants held the land as tenants.
They delivered possession to the landlord, who took possession without an order of the Tahsildar.
The surrender was neither in writing nor verified before the Tahsildar in the prescribed manner.
After the landlord later leased the land to another person, the tenants applied for restoration of possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958 requires a surrender to be in writing and verified in the prescribed manner. Section 36(2) prohibits a landlord from obtaining possession of land held by a tenant except under an order of the Tahsildar, and section 36(1) permits a tenant evicted in contravention of that prohibition to apply for possession. Consent or voluntary delivery does not make possession valid without the required formal surrender and order. The Court followed Madho S/o Tatya Sonar v. Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal & Ors. It expressed no opinion on whether verification alone, without an order authorising possession, would prevent a tenant from seeking restoration.
members.conclusion: The surrender was ineffective and the landlord’s possession was unlawful; the tenants could apply for restoration under section 36(1).

rule.if: tenant_held_land and restoration_application_after_eviction and surrender_not_written and surrender_not_verified and landlord_lacked_possession_order

predicates.tenant_held_land: A person held the land as a tenant.
predicates.restoration_application_after_eviction: A tenant applied for restoration after being dispossessed from the land.
predicates.surrender_not_written: The tenant’s surrender of the tenancy was not made in writing.
predicates.surrender_not_verified: The tenant’s surrender was not verified by the competent authority in the prescribed manner.
predicates.landlord_lacked_possession_order: The landlord obtained possession without an order from the competent authority.

members.legal_issue: A protected tenant’s tenancy rights cannot be surrendered orally or transferred without compliance with the statutory surrender procedure, and a later administrative approval does not validate a defective surrender.
material_facts: The purchaser relied on an alleged oral surrender of the protected tenancy in 1954 and a 1957 document purporting to transfer the tenancy rights.
The surrender was not recorded as a bona fide surrender by the competent authority before it was purportedly made.
A later application seeking approval of the surrender was dealt with in 1989, after the alleged surrender and transfer.
members.legal_principle: Section 38-E(5) of the Telangana Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 requires an inquiry into the genuineness of a protected tenant’s surrender, read with Section 19(1)(a), which requires a written surrender admitted by the tenant and found to be in good faith by the competent authority. The inquiry must precede the surrender; later approval cannot cure non-compliance. The former Section 47 also restricted transfers of agricultural land. The Court applied Sada v. Tahsildar, Kotaiah v. Property Association of the Baptist Churches, Edukanti Kistamma v. S. Venkatareddy, and B. Bal Reddy v. Teegala Narayana Reddy on the protection of protected tenants and the need for lawful termination of their rights.
members.conclusion: The alleged surrender and transfer were ineffective, and the protected tenant’s rights were not extinguished by the later administrative proceedings.

predicates.protected_tenancy_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a person holding protected-tenant status retained rights in agricultural land.
predicates.oral_surrender_claimed: A landholder or purchaser relies on an alleged oral surrender of the protected tenant’s rights.
predicates.tenancy_rights_transferred_without_requi: A protected tenant’s rights were purportedly transferred without following the legally required procedure.
predicates.no_prior_good_faith_authority_approval: The competent authority did not, before the purported surrender, determine that it was made in writing and in good faith.

members.legal_issue: A tenant does not terminate a tenancy by unilaterally announcing departure and transferring possession to another person without completing the required termination and surrender to the landlord.
material_facts: A company was the tenant of a shop and informed the landlord that it intended to close its business there and that another person would occupy the shop and pay rent personally.
The landlord objected to the proposed transfer and stated that the company remained responsible unless it delivered vacant possession.
The company delivered possession to the other person, not to the landlord, and did not serve the notice required by law or obtain the landlord’s agreement to terminate the tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Under section 108(q) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a tenant must put the landlord in possession on determination of the tenancy. Unless possession is delivered to the landlord before expiry of the required notice period, the tenant continues to hold the premises as tenant. An assignment differs from a surrender: an assignment does not itself end the tenant’s obligations, whereas surrender or relinquishment must be to the lessor or a person holding the lessor’s interest and requires mutual agreement. The Court relied on W. H. King v. Republic of India, [1952] S.C.R. 419.
members.conclusion: The company did not cease to be the tenant; its transfer of rights did not terminate the tenancy, and the person placed in possession was an assignee rather than a trespasser.

rule.if: tenancy_termination_dispute and tenant_announced_departure and tenant_transferred_possession_to_another and required_notice_was_not_served and not landlord_received_possession and not landlord_accepted_surrender

predicates.tenancy_termination_dispute: The case concerned whether a tenant’s tenancy had ended after the tenant announced its departure and another person took possession.
predicates.tenant_announced_departure: The tenant informed the landlord that it intended to stop occupying the premises.
predicates.tenant_transferred_possession_to_another: The tenant placed another person in possession of the premises as a transferee of its tenancy rights.
predicates.required_notice_was_not_served: The tenant did not serve the notice required to terminate the tenancy.
predicates.landlord_received_possession: The landlord received possession of the premises from the tenant before termination.
predicates.landlord_accepted_surrender: The landlord agreed to accept the tenant’s surrender of the tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s surrender of a tenancy is ineffective when the prescribed verification and recording requirements are not complied with.
material_facts: The landlord submitted a written surrender document bearing the tenant’s thumb-impression and asked the Mamlatdar to verify the surrender.
The Mamlatdar did not verify the surrender or pass a final order on the application.

A Circle Officer recorded statements from the tenant and landlord and ordered that possession be handed over to the landlord, but did not record that he was satisfied that the tenant understood the nature and consequences of surrender and acted voluntarily.
The Circle Officer did not endorse the required findings on the surrender document.
The Deputy Collector and Revenue Tribunal found that the surrender had not been verified as required; the High Court upheld the conclusion that the surrender was invalid.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(3)(b) of the Bombay Tenancy Act and Rule 2-A require a surrender to be in writing, verified by the Mamlatdar after satisfying himself that the tenant understands its nature and consequences and that it is voluntary, and endorsed with those findings on the surrender document. These requirements are mandatory in light of their peremptory language and protective purpose. Where the law prescribes a manner for exercising a power, it must be exercised in that manner or not at all. The Court relied on Liverpool Borough Bank v. Turner and Craies on Statute Law on determining whether a provision is mandatory, and Taylor v. Taylor, Nazir Ahmed v. Emperor, Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of U.P., and Deep Chand v. State of Rajasthan on the prescribed-manner rule.
members.conclusion: The surrender was invalid and ineffective because the mandatory verification and endorsement requirements had not been met; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: tenancy_surrender_proceeding and surrender_attempted and (not required_verification_completed or not required_finding_endorsed)

predicates.tenancy_surrender_proceeding: The matter concerns a tenant’s surrender of a tenancy to a landlord.
predicates.surrender_attempted: The tenant purported to surrender the tenancy.
predicates.required_verification_completed: An authorized officer verified the surrender after determining that the tenant understood its nature and consequences and acted voluntarily.
predicates.required_finding_endorsed: The authorized officer recorded the required findings on the surrender document.

members.legal_issue: A landlord occupying one part of a building is entitled to nominate the tenant for another part being allotted, and the authority must provide an opportunity to exercise that right.
material_facts: The landlord occupied the ground floor of the building while the first floor was considered for allotment.
The authority knew that the landlord occupied part of the building but gave him no opportunity to nominate a tenant before allotting the first floor to the appellant.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires allotment of another part of a building in favour of a person nominated by the landlord when the landlord occupies a part for residential purposes. The authority must afford the landlord the opportunity to nominate, and must allot to the nominee if one is put forward. The Court relied on Babu Singh Chauhan v. Rajkumar Jain & Ors. and also discussed the notice requirement in Yoginder Tiwari v. District Judge, Gorakhpur and Ors.
members.conclusion: The landlord was entitled to nominate a tenant of his choice, and the allotment made without affording that opportunity was without jurisdiction.

predicates.rental_allotment_proceeding: An authority is considering applications to allot a vacant rental building or part of one.
predicates.landlord_occupies_another_part_for_resid: The landlord occupies another part of the same building for residential purposes.
predicates.landlord_denied_opportunity_to_nominate: The landlord was not given an opportunity to nominate a tenant before the authority made the allotment.

members.legal_issue: A transferee landlord who occupies part of a building retains the right to nominate a tenant for another part even if the former landlord's application for release was rejected.
material_facts: The former landlord's application to have the vacant first floor released to him had been rejected before he sold the building.
The transferee acquired the building, occupied the ground floor, and became its landlord before the allotment applications were reconsidered.
The transferee was not given an opportunity to nominate a tenant for the first floor.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, a landlord occupying a part of a building for residential purposes may nominate a tenant for another part being allotted. The Court held that the transferee landlord could exercise that right despite the former landlord's unsuccessful release application; it relied on Babu Singh Chauhan v. Rajkumar Jain & Ors. in explaining the purpose of the nomination right.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the former landlord's release application did not prevent the transferee landlord from exercising the right to nominate a tenant.

predicates.rental_allotment_proceeding: An authority is reconsidering applications to allot a vacant rental building or part of one.
predicates.former_landlord_release_request_was_reje: The former landlord's request to have the vacant premises released to him was rejected.
predicates.transferee_became_landlord_before_recons: A person acquired the building and became its landlord before the allotment applications were reconsidered.
predicates.transferee_occupies_part_for_residence: The transferee landlord occupies another part of the same building for residential purposes.

members.legal_issue: An allotment cannot be made without serving the landlord notice of the date on which allotment will be considered, so that the landlord can seek release of the building.
material_facts: The allotment authority did not serve the landlord with the notice required to inform him of the date on which the question of allotment would be considered.
The landlord was therefore not given the opportunity at that stage to seek release of the building for a qualifying purpose.
members.legal_principle: Rule 9(3) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Rules, 1972 requires notice to the landlord of the date fixed for considering allotment. In response, the landlord may seek release under Section 16(1)(b) for the purposes provided in Section 16(2). The allotment authority performs a quasi-judicial function and must observe natural justice.
members.conclusion: The landlord was entitled to notice of the date fixed for considering allotment, and the allotment order made without that notice and the resulting opportunity was a nullity.

predicates.building_allotment_proceeding: The authority is considering whether to allot a building that is vacant or treated as vacant.
predicates.landlord_not_served_notice_of_allotment_: The landlord was not served notice of the date on which the authority would consider allotment.

members.legal_issue: A rent-control authority cannot allot a newly vacant part of a building to someone other than the landlord’s nominee without giving the landlord an opportunity to nominate a tenant when the statutory conditions for nomination are met.
material_facts: A tenant gave notice that he intended to vacate premises forming part of a building associated with the landlady’s residential occupation.
The authority allotted the premises to the appellant without informing the landlady or asking her to nominate a tenant.
The landlady was not living in the premises, but they were locked and contained her household effects.
The landlady’s request to release the premises was not granted, and the authorities nevertheless re-allotted them to the appellant without giving her an opportunity to nominate a tenant.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires allotment of the remaining part of a building to a person nominated by the landlord where the statutory residential-occupation or release conditions apply. The provision protects the landlord from having an unwanted tenant or neighbour imposed on them. A refusal of release under Section 16(1)(b) does not excuse the authorities from complying with Section 17(2). No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The allotment to the appellant was without jurisdiction because the authorities did not comply with the landlord’s nomination entitlement; the High Court was justified in quashing the orders and remanding the matter for fresh consideration.

predicates.rent_control_vacancy_allotment_proceedin: The matter concerned an authority’s allotment of premises that had become vacant in a building subject to rent control.
predicates.landlord_entitled_to_nominate: The landlord occupied another part of the building for residential purposes, or the relevant part had been released to the landlord for residential purposes, so the landlord was entitled to nominate a tenant for the remaining part.
predicates.authorities_skipped_nomination_opportuni: The authorities allotted the vacant premises without first giving the landlord an opportunity to nominate a tenant.

members.legal_issue: Successive limited-term lettings under statutory permission do not, without more, establish that the owner committed fraud by intending from the outset to let the premises indefinitely.
material_facts: The owner let the premises to the same tenant for successive limited periods after obtaining permission for each letting.
The tenant vacated between some of the periods and later sought to rent the premises again.
The owner stated that she expected to need the premises for family occupation in the future, and the circumstances affecting that expectation changed over time.
The record did not establish that the owner had intended from the outset never to occupy the premises or had concealed material facts when seeking the later permission.
The tenant challenged the permission in an execution proceeding, alleging fraud, and the Supreme Court rejected that objection.
members.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, circumstances must be examined as they stood on each occasion permission was sought. Changing circumstances and uncertainty about future needs may justify successive limited-term lettings; the fact of repeated lettings alone cannot establish an original intention to let indefinitely. The supplied judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish fraud or that the permission was a nullity; repeated limited-term lettings alone did not justify the inference that the premises had been available for indefinite letting from the beginning. The objection was rejected and the possession application was allowed.

rule.if: execution_proceeding_challenges_limited_term_permission and successive_limited_term_lettings_occurred and owner_expected_later_occupation and circumstances_changed_over_time and no_evidence_of_original_intent_never_to_occupy and no_material_facts_concealed

predicates.execution_proceeding_challenges_limited_: A party objects in an execution proceeding that permission for a limited-term letting was obtained by fraud.
predicates.successive_limited_term_lettings_occurre: The owner let the premises for successive limited periods after obtaining permission for each period.
predicates.owner_expected_later_occupation: The owner represented that the premises were expected to be needed for the owner's or family's later occupation.
predicates.circumstances_changed_over_time: The circumstances relevant to the owner's ability or need to occupy the premises changed over time.
predicates.no_evidence_of_original_intent_never_to_: The record contains no evidence that the owner intended from the beginning never to occupy the premises.
predicates.no_material_facts_concealed: The record does not establish that the owner concealed material facts when applying for permission.

members.legal_issue: A limited residential tenancy permission is valid even when the landlord does not state why the premises are not required for the specified period, unless the statutory conditions are absent or the permission is impeached by evidence of fraud, collusion, falsehood, or compulsion.
material_facts: The landlord sought permission to let a newly built premises for the first time for a limited period and stated that it was not required during that period.
The tenant accepted the landlord’s statement, agreed to residential use for the fixed period, and undertook to vacate when it ended.
The Controller recorded that the landlord did not then require the premises and permitted the limited tenancy.

The landlord did not state why the premises were not required for that period, but there was no evidence that the statement was false, that the parties colluded, or that the tenant was compelled or unable to understand the arrangement.
members.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the landlord must not require the premises for a particular period, obtain the Controller’s permission, let the premises for residence, and agree the period in writing. The landlord’s statement must be bona fide, and fraud or collusion cannot validate a permission made without the statutory conditions. Permission is presumed regular, and the party challenging it must establish facts showing invalidity. The Court applied Nagindas Ramdass v. Dalpatram Ichharam on the effect of admissions and statutory grounds; S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna on the Controller’s scrutiny, the presumption of regularity, and fraud or collusion; and distinguished V.S. Rahi v. Smt. Ram Chambeli, J.R. Vohra v. India Export House Pvt. Ltd., and Smt. Dhanwanti v. D.D. Gupta on their facts.
members.conclusion: The permission was valid. The landlord was not required to state reasons for not requiring the premises, and the tenant had not rebutted the presumption that the permission was regular.

rule.if: limited_residential_tenancy_case and landlord_stated_temporary_nonneed and tenant_accepted_statement and residential_use_agreed and fixed_period_agreed_in_writing and controller_granted_permission and (not evidence_of_fraud_or_collusion_or_compulsion)

predicates.limited_residential_tenancy_case: The proceeding concerns permission to create a limited tenancy for residential use.
predicates.landlord_stated_temporary_nonneed: The landlord stated that the premises were not required for a particular period.
predicates.tenant_accepted_statement: The tenant accepted the landlord’s statement about not requiring the premises.
predicates.residential_use_agreed: The landlord and tenant agreed that the premises would be used for residence.
predicates.fixed_period_agreed_in_writing: The landlord and tenant agreed in writing on a fixed period of letting.
predicates.controller_granted_permission: The Controller granted permission after considering the parties’ statements.
predicates.evidence_of_fraud_or_collusion_or_compul: Evidence shows that the landlord’s statement was false or not bona fide, that the parties colluded, or that the tenant was compelled or unable to understand the arrangement.

members.legal_issue: Permission for a limited-period tenancy is presumed valid and remains enforceable unless the tenant obtains a declaration of invalidity in proper proceedings.
material_facts: The landlord sought recovery of possession under the Controller’s earlier permission after the limited tenancy expired.
The tenant objected to recovery but did not prove the absence of a jurisdictional fact that would invalidate the permission.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and the principle, discussed in Wade’s Administrative Law, that an order remains effective for its ostensible purpose unless its invalidity is established in competent proceedings. It relied on S.B. Naronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna, V.S. Rahi v. Smt. Ram Chambeli, Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna, and J.R. Vohra v. India Export House (P) Ltd.
members.conclusion: The permission was presumed valid, and the tenant bore the burden of raising and establishing its invalidity; until declared invalid, it remained enforceable.

predicates.limited_term_possession_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery of premises after a tenancy created for a limited period.
predicates.permission_granted: A competent authority previously permitted the creation of the limited-period tenancy.
predicates.tenant_contests_enforcement: The tenant objects to the landlord’s recovery of possession under the permission.

members.legal_issue: A limited-tenancy permission is not invalidated as fraudulent merely because the landlord has previously obtained permissions for other limited lettings, where the alleged abuse is unsupported by adequate factual evidence.
material_facts: The landlord sought permission to let part of a house for a limited residential period and explained that he was living in government accommodation and needed to allow for the possibility that it might be cancelled.
The tenant accepted the landlord’s statement and undertook to vacate when the agreed period ended.

Although the tenant alleged that the landlord had obtained similar permissions for other lettings, the tenant did not cross-examine the landlord about those lettings or provide independent evidence that they involved abuse of the law.

There was no material before the Rent Controller establishing or arousing suspicion of fraud, and repeated limited lettings did not necessarily show that the premises had been available for indefinite letting.
members.legal_principle: A fraud allegation is a mixed question of fact and law and requires a factual foundation showing wilful contravention or abuse. Under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the limited tenancy must be bona fide, for residential purposes, and supported by the Controller’s permission; the landlord’s statement must be bona fide and there must be no fraud or collusion, though the permission is presumed regular. S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna was applied; V.S. Rahi v. Ram Chambeli was distinguished because it involved false declarations; and Dhanwanti v. D.D. Gupta was relied on for the principle that repeated limited lettings do not by themselves establish that the premises were available indefinitely.
members.conclusion: The allegation of fraud was not established, and the permission was not vitiated on that ground.

rule.if: limited_tenancy_possession_execution and fraud_alleged and (fraud_evidence_absent or repeated_limited_lettings_only)

predicates.limited_tenancy_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession after a tenancy granted for a limited period has ended.
predicates.fraud_alleged: The tenant alleged that the landlord obtained the limited-tenancy permission by abusing the law.
predicates.fraud_evidence_absent: The tenant did not provide adequate evidence establishing that the landlord’s conduct involved fraud or abuse.
predicates.repeated_limited_lettings_only: The allegation of abuse rested on the landlord having made other limited lettings, without proof that those lettings were fraudulent.

members.legal_issue: A common manager holding agricultural land on behalf of co-owners jointly interested in the land or its income is assessable for the aggregate tax payable by the owners on their respective shares.
material_facts: The owners jointly held agricultural land and appointed a common manager to supervise cultivation and manage the agricultural properties.
The common manager managed the agricultural operations, and the resulting profits were distributed to the owners according to their respective shares.
The concern was a co-ownership arrangement rather than a partnership.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act applies where a common manager appointed under law or agreement holds land from which agricultural income is derived on behalf of persons jointly interested in the land or its income. The aggregate of the tax payable by each such person on the income derived from the land and received by that person is assessed on the manager, who is deemed the assessee for that tax and is liable to pay it. The State conceded that section 13 applied if the concern was co-ownership; the assessee conceded that the section did not apply if the concern was a partnership.
members.conclusion: The common manager was assessable under section 13 in respect of the aggregate agricultural income tax payable by the co-owners on their respective shares.

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_assessment: A taxing authority assesses income derived from agricultural land.
predicates.concern_is_co_ownership: The land or the income from it is held jointly by co-owners rather than through a partnership.
predicates.manager_holds_land_for_jointly_intereste: A manager appointed under law or agreement holds or manages the land on behalf of persons jointly interested in it or its agricultural income.
predicates.owners_receive_agricultural_income_from_: The persons jointly interested receive agricultural income derived from the land.

members.legal_issue: Whether jointly owned agricultural operations conducted through a common manager constituted a partnership or a co-ownership concern.
material_facts: Two owners held agricultural land in unequal shares and jointly cultivated it through a common manager appointed for convenience of management.
The record showed no agreement between the owners to form a partnership and no facts establishing that either owner acted as agent for the other.
The owners shared the profits in proportion to their ownership shares; the appointment of the common manager and the sharing of profits were consistent with co-ownership as well as partnership.
The concern was described as a firm in a printed return, but the return provided no separate option for a co-ownership concern.
members.legal_principle: Under section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, partnership is a relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all; the definition of firm in section 2(k) of the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948 takes its meaning from that Act. Partnership requires agreement and agency between partners, whereas co-ownership does not necessarily arise from agreement or involve community of profit or loss, and a co-owner may transfer an interest without the consent of the other co-owner. As discussed in Lindley on Partnership, these are material distinctions. A common manager and profit-sharing in proportion to ownership are not, by themselves, decisive evidence of partnership.
members.conclusion: The concern was a co-ownership concern, not a partnership. The appointment of a common manager, sharing profits or losses in proportion to ownership shares, and describing the concern as a firm did not establish a partnership on these facts.

rule.if: agricultural_tax_classification_case and jointly_owned_agricultural_property and coowners_appointed_common_manager and no_partnership_agreement_evidenced and no_agency_between_owners_evidenced

predicates.agricultural_tax_classification_case: The proceeding concerns whether agricultural operations are taxable as a partnership or as a co-ownership concern.
predicates.jointly_owned_agricultural_property: Two or more persons jointly own agricultural property used to derive agricultural income.
