predicates.coowners_appointed_common_manager: The co-owners appointed a common manager to conduct or manage the agricultural operations.
predicates.no_partnership_agreement_evidenced: The record contains no evidence that the co-owners agreed to form a partnership.
predicates.no_agency_between_owners_evidenced: The record contains no evidence that one co-owner acted as agent for the other.

members.legal_issue: Whether a common manager holding agricultural land for persons jointly interested in it may be assessed for the tax payable by those persons when their concern is one of co-ownership.
material_facts: The owners jointly held interests in agricultural land and derived agricultural income from it.
They appointed a common manager to manage the agricultural operations on their behalf.
The concern was found to be co-ownership rather than partnership; the State conceded that the common-manager assessment provision applied if the concern was co-ownership.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948 provides that where a common manager holds land from which agricultural income is derived on behalf of persons jointly interested in the land or its income, the aggregate of the tax payable by each person on the income derived from the land and received by that person is assessed on the common manager, who is deemed the assessee for and is liable to pay that tax. The Court noted that section 13 did not apply to a partnership firm.
members.conclusion: The common manager was liable to assessment under section 13 in respect of the agricultural income tax payable by each co-owner.

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_case: The proceeding concerns assessment of tax on income derived from agricultural land.
predicates.common_manager_holds_land_for_jointly_in: A common manager holds or manages land on behalf of persons jointly interested in that land or its agricultural income.
predicates.agricultural_income_derived_from_that_la: Agricultural income is derived from the land managed on behalf of the jointly interested persons.
predicates.concern_is_coownership_not_partnership: The arrangement is one of co-ownership rather than partnership.

members.legal_issue: The special method for assessing agricultural income tax on a person holding land for others applies only when that person holds the land on their behalf and those others have joint interests in the land or its agricultural income.
material_facts: The trustees were the legal owners of the trust estate and managed it under a will that gave them powers of absolute owners.
The will directed the trustees to pay specified annuities from the estate’s net rents and profits to individual beneficiaries.
Each annuitant had an individual interest in the agricultural income to the extent of that person’s annuity; the annuitants did not share an undivided interest in the land or income.
The assessing authority assessed the trustees on the total agricultural income received from the estate.
members.legal_principle: Under section 11(1) of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, the special assessment method applies when a person holds land as a common manager, receiver, administrator or the like on behalf of persons jointly interested in the land or its agricultural income. “On behalf of” denotes an agency or representative relationship, not merely holding property for another’s benefit. Under section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, the trustee is the owner of trust property and the beneficiary has a right against the trustee as owner; accordingly, a trustee holds the property in the trustee’s own right, though for the beneficiaries’ benefit. “Jointly interested” denotes an undivided interest, rather than separate individual interests. Sections 2(11) and 3 of the U.P. Act establish the general definition of a person and the charging liability. Lister v. Pickford was considered but distinguished because its observations concerned limitation and adverse possession.
members.conclusion: The trustees did not hold the land on behalf of the annuitants, and the annuitants were not jointly interested in the land or its agricultural income. The special assessment method therefore did not apply, and the trustees were liable to tax on the total agricultural income received by them; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: agricultural_income_tax_assessment and trustee_is_legal_owner and trustee_holds_for_benefit_not_as_agent and beneficiaries_have_separate_interests

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_assessment: An agricultural income tax assessment concerns income derived from land managed or held by a trustee for beneficiaries.
predicates.trustee_is_legal_owner: The trustee holds legal ownership of the trust property.
predicates.trustee_holds_for_benefit_not_as_agent: The trustee holds the property for the beneficiaries’ benefit but does not hold it as their agent or representative.
predicates.beneficiaries_have_separate_interests: Each beneficiary has an individual interest in the property’s income rather than an undivided interest shared with the other beneficiaries.

members.legal_issue: A charge for obtaining illegal gratification under the relevant corruption offences cannot stand without evidence of a demand for the gratification.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that gratification was negotiated and collected through a private intermediary in connection with an official raid.
The evidence did not establish that the accused demanded or agreed to demand illegal gratification, or that the accused accepted or obtained it.
The intercepted calls relied on by the prosecution did not reliably connect the accused to the alleged demand or settlement.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d)(i) and (ii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, proof of demand is indispensable; mere possession, recovery or acceptance of money without proof of demand is insufficient. P. Satyanarayana Murthy v. District Inspector of Police, State of A.P., (2015) 10 SCC 152, applying B. Jayaraj, also holds that the presumption under Section 20 applies only to an offence under Section 7 and depends on proof of acceptance, which in turn requires proof of demand.
members.conclusion: There was no evidence that the accused demanded or accepted illegal gratification, and the prosecution material did not support the charge against the accused.

predicates.prosecution_for_illegal_gratification: The proceeding includes a charge that the accused sought, accepted or obtained illegal gratification.
predicates.no_evidence_of_demand: The prosecution evidence does not establish that the accused demanded illegal gratification.

members.legal_issue: A corruption conviction cannot rest on recovery of money when the evidence does not prove demand and voluntary acceptance of the gratification beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The complainant and the accompanying witness were declared hostile and denied or repudiated essential parts of the prosecution account of demand and acceptance.
The accompanying witness denied being present when the money was demanded or accepted.
The officials who testified about the trap were not present for the alleged demand or acceptance, and their account of those events was based on what others told them.

Although the marked currency was recovered from the accused, the complainant also testified that she had placed the money on the table after an altercation, and the prosecution had no reliable independent evidence establishing demand and voluntary acceptance.
members.legal_principle: For an offence under Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 5(1)(d), read with Section 5(2), of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, proof of demand and voluntary acceptance of illegal gratification is essential. The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt by reliable direct or circumstantial evidence; recovery alone is insufficient. The Court relied on Suraj Mal v. State (Delhi Administration), Sita Ram v. State of Rajasthan, M.K. Harshan v. State of Kerala and C.M. Girish Babu v. CBI. It also referred to M. Narsinga Rao v. State of A.P. and Madhukar Bhaskarrao Joshi v. State of Maharashtra on the presumption that may follow once payment or acceptance of gratification is established, while noting that the presumption in Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 is absent from the 1947 Act.
members.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove demand and voluntary acceptance in accordance with law; the conviction could not stand, and the accused was acquitted of the charges.

rule.if: corruption_conviction_appeal and marked_money_recovered and complainant_denied_or_withdrew_essential_testimony and corroborating_witness_denied_presence_at_demand_or_acceptance and official_witnesses_lacked_firsthand_knowledge

predicates.corruption_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for a corruption offence.
predicates.marked_money_recovered: Investigators recovered marked money from the accused.
predicates.complainant_denied_or_withdrew_essential: The complainant denied or withdrew essential testimony about the accused demanding or accepting the money.
predicates.corroborating_witness_denied_presence_at: A witness relied on to corroborate the allegation denied being present when the money was demanded or accepted.
predicates.official_witnesses_lacked_firsthand_know: The officials who testified about demand or acceptance were not present for those events and relied on what others told them.

members.legal_issue: Demand and acceptance of illegal gratification must be established by evidence and cannot be inferred from recovery alone.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses testified that the public servant demanded and accepted the marked money after receiving the document and registration fee.
The eyewitness accounts were corroborated by other material witnesses and by the evidence of the trap officials.
The chemical test was positive, and the recovery of the marked money from the public servant’s desk drawer was not challenged.
members.legal_principle: For offences under Sections 7, 11 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, demand and acceptance of illegal gratification are essential ingredients, and mere recovery of tainted money is not sufficient. The prosecution must prove the demand and acceptance on facts. The Court relied on Narendra Champaklal Trivedi v. State of Gujarat and State of Punjab v. Madan Mohan Lal Verma.
members.conclusion: The prosecution proved the demand and acceptance of illegal gratification; the recovery and chemical test supported that finding but recovery alone would not have been sufficient.

predicates.corruption_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution alleging corruption by a public servant.
predicates.eyewitnesses_testify_to_demand_and_accep: Witnesses who observed the transaction testify that the public servant demanded and accepted the money.
predicates.material_witnesses_corroborate_the_trans: Other material witnesses corroborate the evidence about the transaction.
predicates.marked_money_recovery_is_unchallenged: The recovery of the marked money from the public servant or a place under the public servant’s control is not challenged.

members.legal_issue: Receipt of money is insufficient to establish a corruption offence when the prosecution does not prove that it was demanded or accepted as illegal gratification and a probable non-bribe explanation exists.
material_facts: The accused received money from the complainant during a trap, and the money was recovered from him after chemically treated notes were used.
The accused immediately explained that the money had been paid through the complainant towards another person’s temple lease arrears.
Evidence showed that the other person owed lease arrears, and a temple clerk testified that the complainant had earlier said he would bring money for those arrears.
The complainant and associated witnesses had prior grievances against the accused.
The trial court found the explanation reasonable and the prosecution had not proved demand and acceptance of illegal gratification beyond reasonable doubt.
members.legal_principle: For an offence under Sections 5(1)(a) or 5(1)(d), read with Section 5(2), of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, mere receipt of money does not establish guilt without proof that it was demanded and accepted as illegal gratification. A probable explanation may be established on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt, and may displace the statutory presumption under Section 4(1). The Court relied on Punjabrao v. State of Maharashtra, which states the accused’s burden is discharged on a preponderance of probabilities, and Chaturdas Bhagwandas Patel v. State of Gujarat, which describes the burden of rebutting the presumption and the need for evidence showing that the money was received other than as a motive or reward under Section 161 IPC.
members.conclusion: The prosecution did not prove that the money was received as illegal gratification, and the accused was entitled to acquittal.

rule.if: corruption_prosecution and money_received and no_proof_of_bribe_demand_or_character and probable_non_bribe_explanation

predicates.corruption_prosecution: The proceeding prosecutes a person for receiving money as illegal gratification connected with an official act.
predicates.money_received: The accused received money from the person who paid it.
predicates.no_proof_of_bribe_demand_or_character: The evidence does not establish that the money was demanded or received as a reward for an official favour.
predicates.probable_non_bribe_explanation: The accused gave an explanation that the money was for a non-bribery purpose, and the circumstances make that explanation reasonably probable.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot grant judgment merely because the defendant did not file a written statement when material facts in the plaintiff’s case require proof.
material_facts: The defendants were served, appeared through counsel, and did not file a written statement despite repeated opportunities.
The plaintiff sought partition on the basis that the property was joint family property and had not previously been partitioned.

The plaintiff relied on an affidavit and documents, but the trial court did not adequately explain how the evidence established that the property remained joint or that no earlier partition had occurred.
The trial court granted a decree without critically assessing the evidence or giving sufficient reasons.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court may proceed when a written statement is not filed, but must not pass judgment mechanically. Under Balraj Taneja v. Sunil Madan, the court must determine whether the plaint’s facts, even if treated as admitted, permit judgment without proof; where material factual issues require proof, the plaintiff must prove them and the court must assess that proof. An uncontested decree may be appropriate where the plaintiff’s case is unimpeachable and the defendant’s conduct is dilatory.
members.conclusion: The trial court’s decree was unsound because the absence of a written statement did not relieve the plaintiff of proving material facts that required proof; the court had to assess the evidence before granting judgment.

predicates.civil_suit_without_written_statement: A civil suit proceeded to judgment without the defendant filing a written statement.
predicates.material_facts_need_proof: The plaintiff’s claim depends on material factual assertions that cannot be resolved solely by treating the absence of a written statement as an admission.

members.legal_issue: A defendant’s nonappearance or failure to file a written statement does not automatically entitle a claimant to a decree.
material_facts: The underlying money suit proceeded ex parte after the defendant stopped appearing.
The trial court accepted the alleged payment without insisting on proof, and the defendant’s wife, who was said to hold title to the property, had not been impleaded.
The decree holder’s claim and supporting evidence had not been scrutinized sufficiently, and no appeal had tested the decree.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VIII Rule 10 and Order IX CPC, the court must diligently ensure that the plaint is proved and that the relief sought is justified, even when the defendant fails to file a written statement or is proceeded against ex parte. The Court relied on Shantilal Gulabchand Mutha v. Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company Limited, (2013) 4 SCC 396.
members.conclusion: The trial court remained obliged to satisfy itself that the claim was proved and legally justified; nonappearance did not warrant an automatic decree.

predicates.civil_claim_proceeding: The proceeding is a civil claim for relief by a plaintiff against a defendant.
predicates.defendant_fails_to_appear_or_file_writte: The defendant does not participate fully, including by failing to appear or file a written statement.
predicates.claim_not_proved_by_sufficient_evidence: The plaintiff has not established the factual and legal basis for the relief with sufficient evidence.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot enter judgment against a defendant solely because no written statement was filed without considering whether the plaint supports judgment or whether facts require proof.
material_facts: The defendants did not file a written statement despite receiving time and a further opportunity to do so.
The suit was decreed under Order 8 Rule 10 because of the defendants’ failure to file a written statement.
The plaint itself disclosed a material factual dispute about whether the defendants had obtained and sent the required tax permission to the plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit judgment on the plaint or another appropriate order when no written statement is filed, but preserve the court’s discretion to require proof. Order 12 Rule 6 and Section 58 of the Evidence Act likewise allow a court to require proof despite admissions. The court relied on Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah, which explains the judicial discretion under Order 8 Rule 10, and Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum, which recognizes that admissions do not invariably dispense with proof.
members.conclusion: The decree could not properly be entered merely because the written statement was not filed; the court had to consider the plaint and determine whether any facts required proof, and could instead make another appropriate order.

predicates.defendant_filed_no_written_statement: The defendant did not file a written statement in the civil suit.
predicates.plaint_discloses_material_factual_disput: The plaintiff’s own pleading discloses a material factual dispute relevant to deciding the claim.

members.legal_issue: A judgment must state the material facts, the controversy resolved, and the reasoning for the decision, including when the case is decided after a defendant fails to file a written statement.
material_facts: The trial court decreed the suit in a brief order that focused on the defendants’ failure to file a written statement and did not set out the facts or reasoning supporting the decree.
The appellate court affirmed the decree without addressing the material factual dispute disclosed by the plaint.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines a judgment as a statement of the grounds for a decree or order; Order 20 Rule 4(2) requires a concise statement of the case, points for determination, decisions, and reasons. These requirements apply to contested cases, ex parte cases, and cases decided under Order 8 Rule 10. The court relied on Nanhe v. Saiyad Tasadduq Husain, Thippaiah v. Kuri Obaiah, and Dineshwar Prasad Bakshi v. Parmeshwar Prasad Sinha.
members.conclusion: The judgments were legally deficient because they did not set out the facts, controversy, and reasoning supporting the decision.

predicates.civil_judgment_is_pronounced: A court pronounces a judgment in a civil proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A party’s admissible prior admission is substantive evidence and need not be put to its maker before the court may rely on it.
material_facts: In a partition suit, the courts relied on earlier statements made by a plaintiff and the plaintiffs’ father in a prior suit, including testimony and a written statement, in finding that disputed properties did not belong to the joint family.
The statements were not put to the plaintiff when he testified in the present suit, and the father was not called to explain them.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 17 and 21 of the Indian Evidence Act, an admission that satisfies the Act’s requirements is substantive evidence, though it is not conclusive proof. Section 145 applies when a prior statement is used to contradict and discredit a witness. The court followed Bharat Singh v. Bhagirathi, which explains this distinction.
members.conclusion: The statements could be used as substantive evidence against their makers without first being put to them; the requirement to put a prior statement to a witness applies when it is used to contradict the witness, not when a party’s admission is relied on as evidence.

rule.if: civil_property_suit and party_authored_admission and admission_is_admissible and maker_not_confronted

predicates.civil_property_suit: The dispute was brought as a civil suit concerning rights in property.
predicates.party_authored_admission: A party made an earlier statement admitting a fact relevant to the dispute.
predicates.admission_is_admissible: The party’s admission satisfied the applicable requirements for admissibility.
predicates.maker_not_confronted: The admission was not put to its maker for explanation or confrontation in the present proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A party’s proved prior statements are admissible against that party as admissions even if the party did not testify, was not confronted with the statements, or the statements were not against that party’s interest when made.
material_facts: The alleged real owner had made statements identifying himself as the person who bought the property using his own funds, and records showed that he had charged the property’s expenditure and income to himself.
The statements and records were proved in evidence.
The maker had been served and had an opportunity to contest the suit but did not appear; efforts to secure his attendance as a witness were unsuccessful.
members.legal_principle: Under the law of admissions in the Evidence Act, a proved admission is substantive evidence against its maker (Bharat Singh v. Bhagirath; Ajodhya Prasad Bhargava v. Bhawani Shanker Bhargava). Its admissibility does not depend on the maker testifying, being confronted with it, or having made a statement adverse to his interest at the time. Section 33 of the Evidence Act concerns statements of persons who cannot be called as witnesses and does not restrict or override the rules governing admissions.
members.conclusion: The statements were admissible against their maker and provided evidence that he owned the property; they were not relied on as evidence against the other defendant.

predicates.civil_case: The proceeding is a civil case.
predicates.prior_statement_proved: A prior statement by a party has been established in evidence.
predicates.statement_made_by_party_against_whom_off: The party against whom the statement is offered made the statement.

members.legal_issue: A party’s duly proved and clear admissions are substantive evidence even if the party is not confronted with them while testifying.
material_facts: The respondent made statements in documents describing the family or firm as joint, including statements in pleadings and an agreement concerning arbitration.
Evidence was given to prove those documents and the respondent’s connection to their contents.
The respondent was not confronted with the admissions when she entered the witness box.
The respondent’s statement that her husband had separated from his brothers before her marriage did not adequately explain or clearly deny the facts admitted.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 17 and 21 of the Indian Evidence Act, admissions are substantive evidence of the facts admitted, although they are not conclusive proof. Section 145 serves the different purpose of contradicting a witness; a prior statement used for contradiction does not thereby become substantive evidence. The Court discussed Firm Malik Des Rai v. Firm Piara Lal, Ayodhya Prasad v. Bhawani Shanker, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shrinivas Pandit, and held that the latter did not directly decide the admissibility of duly proved admissions not put to their maker in testimony. Admissions must be clear to be used against their maker, and their weight is distinct from their admissibility.
members.conclusion: The duly proved admissions could be used as evidence against the respondent despite her not having been confronted with them while testifying.

predicates.party_admission_evidence_dispute: The proceeding involves whether a party’s prior statement may be used as an admission.
predicates.admission_duly_proved: Evidence establishes that the party made the prior statement.
predicates.admission_clear: The statement clearly supports the fact for which it is relied on.

members.legal_issue: A party's duly proved admission may be substantive evidence against its maker even if the maker does not testify, is not confronted with the statement, or the admission was not against the maker's interest when made.
material_facts: The father made proved statements to an income-tax officer that he had purchased the property in his son's name using money from his own bank accounts.
The father did not appear to contest the suit, despite having an opportunity to do so, and could not be secured to testify.
The admissions were considered against the father, not against his son.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 33 of the Evidence Act were considered. Under Bharat Singh v. Bhagirath, a duly proved admission is substantive evidence of the fact admitted and may be used against its maker irrespective of whether the maker testifies or is confronted with it. The Evidence Act does not require that the admission have been against the maker's interest when made. Section 33 concerns statements of persons who cannot be called as witnesses and does not restrict or override the rules governing admissions.
members.conclusion: The father's duly proved admissions were admissible as substantive evidence against him; section 33 of the Evidence Act did not restrict their admissibility.

predicates.party_made_admission_of_material_fact: A party made a statement admitting a fact material to the dispute.
predicates.admission_duly_proved: Evidence established that the party made the admission.
predicates.admission_offered_against_its_maker: A litigant offered the admission as evidence against the party who made it.

members.legal_issue: A decree declaring title to money or property is not a decree for money or other property for the purpose of value-based court fees.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declarations of ownership of property and sought to have an earlier decree declaring another person's ownership adjudged ineffective.
The plaintiff sought no order for recovery of money or property.
The property was valued in the plaint, but the relief claimed was declaratory.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as enacted by the U.P. Legislature, a 'decree for money or other property' means a decree for recovery of money or property, not a decree concerning title to it. The Court read 'for' consistently with its use elsewhere in Section 7, where it denotes obtaining a decree ordering payment or recovery. The declaratory claim was prima facie of the description in Schedule II, clause 17(iii). No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The challenged decree was not a decree for money or other property within the meaning of Section 7(iv-A), so the value-based court fee under that provision did not apply to the declaratory claim.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_prior_decree: A party brought a civil suit seeking to challenge the effect of an earlier decree.
predicates.challenged_decree_declares_title: The earlier decree declared a person's title to money or property.
predicates.relief_seeks_no_recovery: The claimant sought a declaration of title without seeking an order for recovery of money or property.
predicates.declaratory_title_decree_is_not_decree_f: A decree declaring title is not treated as a decree ordering recovery of money or property.

members.legal_issue: A court decree is not an instrument securing money or property merely because it records an adjudication of rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to have an earlier decree adjudged void or ineffective as against his claimed rights in property.
The earlier decree was passed ex parte and was a formal adjudication by the court, not a consent decree recording a contract between the parties.
members.legal_principle: Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as enacted by the U.P. Legislature, applies to an instrument securing money or other property having market value. A decree made after adjudication is a record of the court's formal determination of a claimed right and does not by its own force secure money or property. A consent decree may be regarded as such an instrument where it records a contract that secures money or property, because the court's seal is superadded to the parties' contract. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The earlier decree was not an instrument securing money or other property within the meaning of Section 7(iv-A).

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_prior_decree: A party brought a civil suit seeking to challenge the effect of an earlier decree.
predicates.prior_decree_is_adjudication: The earlier decree records a court's formal adjudication of a claimed right.
predicates.prior_decree_is_not_consent_contract: The earlier decree does not record a contract between the parties that secures money or property.
predicates.prior_decree_is_not_instrument_securing_: The earlier decree is not treated as an instrument securing money or property.

members.legal_issue: A decree declaring title to property is not a decree for property within the provision requiring court fees based on the value of the property.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declarations of ownership over properties and sought to have an earlier decree declaring another person the owner adjudged void.
The earlier decree declared title but did not order the recovery of money or property.
The plaintiff claimed declaratory relief, and the dispute concerned the court fee payable on the plaint.
members.legal_principle: Section 7(iv-A) of the Court-Fees Act, as amended by the U.P. Legislature, applies to a decree for recovery of money or other property, not to a decree merely concerning title to property. The Court read “for” consistently with its use in the other clauses of Section 7, where it denotes obtaining a decree ordering payment or recovery. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The provision concerning cancellation of or adjudging void a decree for money or other property did not apply because the challenged decree declared title rather than ordering recovery of property; the court fee paid was proper.

rule.if: court_fee_classification_dispute and declaratory_title_suit and relief_seeks_voiding_prior_decree and prior_decree_declares_title_only

predicates.court_fee_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns the court fee payable on a plaint.
predicates.declaratory_title_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.relief_seeks_voiding_prior_decree: The plaintiff sought to have an earlier decree adjudged void or voidable.
predicates.prior_decree_declares_title_only: The earlier decree declared a person's title to property without ordering its recovery.

members.legal_issue: A decree made in an opposed proceeding is not an instrument securing money or property merely because it records an adjudication concerning rights to property.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to have an earlier decree adjudged void or voidable.
The earlier decree was an adjudication made by the court in an opposed proceeding, rather than a record of a contract between the parties.
The dispute concerned whether the decree fell within the instrument limb of the court-fee provision.
members.legal_principle: Section 7(iv-A) of the Court-Fees Act, as amended by the U.P. Legislature, addresses an instrument securing money or property. A decree made in an opposed proceeding records the court's formal adjudication and does not by its own force secure money or property. A consent decree may be treated as such an instrument where it records a contract that has that effect. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The earlier decree was not an instrument securing money or property, and the instrument limb of the provision did not apply.

predicates.court_fee_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns the court fee payable on a plaint.
predicates.relief_challenges_property_related_decre: The plaintiff sought to have a decree concerning rights to property adjudged void or voidable.
predicates.prior_decree_is_involuntary: The decree was made by the court in an opposed proceeding rather than by recording a contract between the parties.

members.legal_issue: Applicants do not acquire an enforceable right or legitimate expectation to receive public land merely by applying and succeeding in a provisional allotment draw when the authority has disclaimed any obligation to allot and required land-use approval remains outstanding.
material_facts: The application form stated that accepting an application and earnest money did not oblige the Corporation to allot a plot.
The later notice stated that the draw was provisional, that success in the draw created no right to allotment, and that applicants could seek a refund before allotment letters were issued.
The proposed residential layouts were subject to approval of a change in land use, which had not been granted.
The applicants applied and were named in a provisional list, but no allotment letters were issued for the plots at issue.
members.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel requires a clear and unequivocal promise intended to be acted upon and actual reliance that alters the promisee's position; it cannot compel a public authority to act contrary to law or public interest. Legitimate expectation does not itself create a right and depends on a representation or established practice, reliance, detriment, and consideration of the public interest. The Court relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P. (1979) 2 SCC 409, Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India Ltd. (1985) 4 SCC 369, Hira Tikoo v. Union Territory, Chandigarh (2004) 6 SCC 765, Food Corporation of India v. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993) 1 SCC 71, Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corporation (1993) 1 SCC 499, and Sethi Auto Service Station v. DDA (2009) 1 SCC 180.
members.conclusion: The applicants had no enforceable promise or legitimate expectation entitling them to allotment, and the Corporation could not be compelled to allot the plots.

predicates.proceeding_seeking_compelled_public_land: The proceeding sought to compel a public authority to allot land to applicants.
predicates.application_disclaimed_allotment_obligat: The authority told applicants that accepting their applications and deposits did not oblige it to allot land.
predicates.draw_was_provisional: The authority told applicants that the allotment draw was provisional and did not confer a right to allotment.
predicates.required_land_use_approval_was_pending: Approval required for the proposed use of the land had not been granted.

members.legal_issue: Selection through a draw does not itself create an enforceable right to an allotment, and an allotment requiring acceptance does not become effective as a concluded contract without the required acceptance.
material_facts: The applicant was selected for a flat through a draw and was later sent a formal allotment letter.
The allotment letter required the applicant to communicate acceptance and make a payment within the specified period.
The applicant neither communicated acceptance nor made the required payment or executed the hire-purchase agreement.
members.legal_principle: A draw of lots is a method of selection, not an allotment that by itself creates a legal right: Delhi Development Authority v. Pushpendra Kumar Jain. An order does not become effective, and does not create an enforceable right, until communicated: Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab; State of Punjab v. Amar Singh Harika; Union of India v. Dinanath Shantaram Karekar; State of West Bengal v. M.R. Mondal; and Laxminarayan R. Bhattad v. State of Maharashtra. Here the allotment also expressly required acceptance, which was not sent.
members.conclusion: The draw only identified a prospective allottee; it did not confer a right to the flat. In the absence of the required acceptance, no concluded contract arose.

predicates.public_housing_allotment_proceeding: An authority considered an application for a dwelling under a public housing allotment process.
predicates.selection_was_only_by_draw: The applicant was identified for possible allotment through a draw, without the draw itself completing the allotment.
predicates.required_acceptance_was_not_sent: The selected applicant did not communicate acceptance required by the allotment terms.

members.legal_issue: Selection by lottery does not itself create a right to allotment at the price prevailing on the date of selection.
material_facts: A public authority selected an applicant for a housing flat through a draw of lots.
The authority revised land rates after the draw but before communicating the allotment.
The allocation scheme described estimated prices as subject to revision and did not fix the applicable price by reference to the draw date.
members.legal_principle: A draw of lots is a method of identifying or selecting an allottee, not the allotment itself. The right to the flat arises only when the allotment letter is communicated. Under the scheme, which described prices as illustrative and subject to revision, the price prevailing on communication applied unless the scheme provided otherwise. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The applicant acquired no vested right to allotment at the price prevailing on the draw date; the price prevailing when the allotment was communicated applied, unless the scheme provided otherwise.

rule.if: appeal_against_writ_order and public_authority_uses_lottery_selection and scheme_does_not_fix_price_by_draw and allotment_communicated_after_price_revision

predicates.appeal_against_writ_order: The matter is an appeal from an order allowing a writ petition.
predicates.public_authority_uses_lottery_selection: A public authority uses a lottery to select applicants for a limited number of available flats.
predicates.scheme_does_not_fix_price_by_draw: The governing allocation scheme does not state that the price is fixed by the date of the selection draw.
predicates.allotment_communicated_after_price_revis: The authority communicates the allotment after the applicable price has been revised.

members.legal_issue: Selection in a preliminary draw does not create a right to obtain a site without official communication of the allotment.
material_facts: The applicants were selected in a preliminary draw for larger sites.
The administration did not issue allotment letters or otherwise officially communicate an allotment to them.
The applicants claimed a right to take possession based on the draw.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 8(3) of the Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973, the allotment must be communicated by registered post with particulars of the site and premium. The Court held that such intimation confers the right to obtain possession. No earlier case was cited for this point.
members.conclusion: The applicants had no right to obtain transfer of the sites because no official allotment communication had been issued.

predicates.appeal_claims_site_transfer_from_prelimi: An appeal claims a right to obtain a site based on selection in a preliminary draw.
predicates.no_official_allotment_communication: The administration did not officially communicate the allotment and its particulars to the applicant.

members.legal_issue: A court has discretion to award post-suit interest on a mortgage at a reasonable rate rather than at the contractual rate.
material_facts: The mortgage provided for interest at 12 percent per annum with monthly rests.
The High Court allowed interest at the contractual rate after the suit was filed.
The Supreme Court considered the post-suit interest and found simple interest at 6 percent per annum on the principal sum adjudged appropriate until redemption.
members.legal_principle: Order 34, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, inserted by the 1929 amendment, provides that the court may order interest up to the payment date at the rate payable on the principal and gives the court discretion over pendente lite and subsequent interest. Applying Jaigobind Singh v. Lachmi Narain Ram, the Court held that contractual interest is not invariably obligatory after suit, even if the rate is not penal, excessive, or substantially unfair under the Usurious Loans Act, 1918. The Court distinguished the earlier position under section 34 and the pre-amendment mortgage rules.
members.conclusion: The contractual rate was not required to apply after the suit was filed. In the circumstances, simple interest at 6 percent per annum on the principal sum adjudged was appropriate from the suit date through the date of redemption.

predicates.mortgage_suit: A proceeding was brought to enforce a mortgage.
predicates.post_suit_interest_at_issue: The amount or rate of interest after commencement of the suit was disputed or required determination.
predicates.mortgage_contract_sets_interest_rate: The mortgage agreement specified a rate of interest on the principal.
predicates.court_may_award_post_suit_interest_at_a_: The court may determine post-suit interest at a rate it considers reasonable rather than necessarily applying the contractual rate.

members.legal_issue: A court deciding interest in a mortgage suit may award post-filing interest below the contractual rate when it exercises its discretion under the mortgage-specific rule.
material_facts: The loan was secured by an equitable mortgage.

The trial court considered the interest issue, expressly exercised its discretion, and awarded simple interest at six per cent after the suit was filed rather than the contractual rate of 16.5 per cent.
The High Court replaced that rate with the contractual rate.
members.legal_principle: Order 34 Rule 11 CPC uses the word “may,” which confers discretion over interest for the periods addressed by clauses (a) and (b). After the 1929 amendment, awarding the contractual rate after suit is not obligatory even where the rate is not penal, excessive, or substantially unfair under the Usurious Loans Act, 1918. The Court relied on Jaigobind Singh v. Lachmi Narain Ram, Soli Pestonji Majoo v. Gangadhar Khemka, Srinivasa Vardachariar v. Gopala Menon, and K. Manickchand v. Elias Saleh Mohamed Sait.
members.conclusion: The court had discretion to award post-filing interest below the contractual rate, and it was not bound to award the contractual rate in all circumstances.

predicates.mortgage_recovery_proceeding: A creditor brought a proceeding to recover a debt on the basis of a mortgage.
predicates.court_is_fixing_post_filing_interest: The court is determining the rate of interest for a period after the proceeding was filed.

members.legal_issue: The rate of post-decree interest on a mortgage debt may be fixed at a fair rate under applicable lending protections rather than the contractual rate, with a reasonable rate applying to later interest.
material_facts: The mortgage deeds provided for interest at one per cent per month.
The court determined that the applicable money-lending and usury protections made nine per cent per annum the fair rate for interest on the principal from the decree to the date fixed for payment.
The court directed six per cent per annum on the allowed costs, charges, and expenses and on the relevant sums from the date fixed for payment until realization.
members.legal_principle: Order 34, rule 11(a)(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for interest on the mortgage principal from decree to the date fixed for payment at the rate payable on the principal or, if none is fixed, at a reasonable rate. The Mysore Money Lenders Act, 1939, read with the Mysore Usurious Loans Act, 1923, informed the court’s determination of the fair rate. Order 34, rule 11(a)(ii) provides for interest on costs, charges, and expenses, and rule 11(b) governs interest thereafter. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: Post-decree interest on the mortgage principal was to be calculated at the fair rate of nine per cent per annum, while the court directed six per cent per annum for the specified costs and for the period after the date fixed for payment until realization.

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_suit: A creditor brings a proceeding to enforce a mortgage.
predicates.contractual_interest_rate_is_found_unfai: The court finds that the contractual interest rate is not a fair rate under the applicable protections for borrowers.

members.legal_issue: A court making an equitable adjustment may award simple interest rather than the contractual compound rate applicable to a mortgage.
material_facts: The alienee relied on a mortgage stipulating compound interest.
The decree allowing recovery of the mortgage debt was made in the trust suit to adjust equities after the transfer was set aside, not in an action brought by the alienee as mortgagee.
The High Court substituted simple interest for compound interest.
members.legal_principle: A mortgagee is ordinarily entitled to contractual interest in a mortgage action, as recognized in Jagannath Prasad Singh Chowdhury v. Surajmal Jalal. But when recovery is granted as equitable relief in an action setting aside an alienation, the court may determine the appropriate interest as part of its equitable adjustment rather than apply the contractual compound rate.
members.conclusion: The High Court could award simple interest as part of the equitable adjustment, and its modification was upheld.

predicates.recovery_awarded_as_equitable_relief: The court allowed recovery of a debt as equitable relief in adjusting the parties’ rights.
predicates.claim_not_brought_as_mortgage_action: The proceeding was not an action brought by the claimant to enforce the mortgage as mortgagee.

members.legal_issue: A suit that in substance seeks to avoid an instrument is governed by the limitation period for cancellation when the plaintiff knew of the instrument.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership under an earlier sale deed and sought a declaration that a later registered sale deed did not bind her.
She had knowledge of the later deed when it was executed and registered.
The present suit was filed long after that knowledge; an earlier suit had been withdrawn with liberty to file afresh.
members.legal_principle: Article 59 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to a claim to cancel or set aside an instrument, with time running from when the plaintiff first becomes entitled to seek that relief and knows the relevant facts. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because it was, in substance, a claim to avoid or cancel the later instrument and was not brought within the applicable period after the plaintiff knew of it.

predicates.instrument_avoidance_suit: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking relief that would avoid or cancel an instrument.
predicates.plaintiff_knew_of_instrument: The plaintiff knew of the instrument and the relevant basis for seeking to avoid it.
predicates.suit_filed_after_applicable_limit: The plaintiff filed the suit after the applicable limitation period had run from that knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration that a lease termination was invalid must be brought within the limitation period measured from when the right to sue first accrued.
material_facts: The lease termination took effect in 1978, and the lessee could have challenged it then, whether or not she had also been dispossessed.
The lessee acknowledged that possession had been taken in 1978.
The transferee filed the declaratory suit in 1996, seeking a declaration that the lease continued to subsist and challenging the termination.
members.legal_principle: Article 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires a suit for a declaration not otherwise covered by the Schedule to be filed within three years from when the right to sue first accrues. Under State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, Daya Singh v. Gurdev Singh, Bolo v. Koklan, C. Mohammad Yunus v. Syed Unnissa, and Khatri Hotels v. Union of India, that right accrues when the asserted right is infringed or is met by a clear and unequivocal threat; successive violations do not restart time. The right accrued on termination, and even if accrual were measured from dispossession, the suit was still late.
members.conclusion: The declaratory suit was barred by limitation because it was filed more than three years after the right to sue first accrued.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration about the continued validity of a lease.
predicates.right_to_sue_first_accrued_on_terminatio: The lease termination first infringed the claimant’s asserted right to have the lease treated as subsisting.
predicates.claim_filed_beyond_limitation_period: The claimant filed the declaratory suit after the applicable limitation period had run from the first accrual of the right to sue.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking to avoid a voidable partition deed must be brought within the limitation period running from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to avoid it became known.
material_facts: The suit sought partition despite an earlier partition deed that the Court found was voidable rather than void ab initio.
The challengers had knowledge of the partition deed before bringing suit, as shown by documents and transactions recognizing or acting on it.
The suit was brought after the applicable limitation period had elapsed from that knowledge.
members.legal_principle: Article 59 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act applies to a suit to cancel or set aside an instrument and runs from when the relevant facts first become known to the plaintiff. Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act provides for relief setting aside an instrument. The Court relied on Prem Singh v. Birbal, M/s. Bay Berry Apartments Pvt. Ltd. v. Shobha, and Utha Moidu Haji v. Kuningarath Kunhabdulla.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because the voidable partition deed had not been set aside within the applicable period.

predicates.suit_to_partition_challenging_voidable_d: The proceeding seeks partition while challenging a deed that is voidable rather than void ab initio.
predicates.plaintiff_knew_facts_entitling_avoidance: The plaintiff knew the facts that entitled the plaintiff to seek avoidance of the deed.
predicates.suit_filed_after_limitation_period: The plaintiff filed the suit after the applicable limitation period had elapsed from that knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A suit to obtain a declaration concerning an instrument or to cancel or set it aside must be brought within the applicable three-year limitation period running from accrual of the right to sue or knowledge of the relevant facts.
material_facts: The suit sought declarations that the mortgage and sale documents were void and sought cancellation of the sale deed.
The claimant admitted that he learned of the sale deed shortly after his father’s death.
The suit was filed more than three years after that knowledge and after the dates on which the claimant pleaded that the cause of action arose.
members.legal_principle: Articles 58 and 59 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 prescribe a three-year limitation period for the relevant declaratory and cancellation claims, running respectively from when the right to sue accrues and when the facts entitling the plaintiff to seek cancellation or setting aside first become known.
members.conclusion: The suit challenging the validity of the mortgage and sale documents was barred by limitation.

predicates.suit_seeks_declaration_or_cancellation_o: A civil suit seeks a declaration concerning an instrument or seeks to cancel or set it aside.
predicates.plaintiff_knew_relevant_facts: The plaintiff knew the facts that entitled the plaintiff to bring the relevant claim.
predicates.more_than_three_years_elapsed_before_fil: More than three years passed after the applicable starting point before the suit was filed.

members.legal_issue: The civil court retains jurisdiction over an eviction suit after the statutory authority’s eviction power is removed, and a bar on challenging official orders does not itself bar that suit.
material_facts: The statutory power to decide eviction cases had been vested in a labour authority, but the provision conferring that power was deleted before the eviction suit was filed.
No replacement authority was given power to decide eviction cases after that deletion.
The suit sought eviction from accommodation and damages for its use and occupation; it did not seek to challenge an order made by the State or the labour authority.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil courts may try suits of a civil nature unless their jurisdiction is expressly or impliedly barred. The deletion of Section 21 of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Housing Act removed the labour authority’s eviction jurisdiction without conferring it on another authority, restoring jurisdiction to the civil court. Section 13 of that Act restricts challenges to orders made by the State or labour authority and injunctions concerning actions under the Act; it does not oust jurisdiction over an employer’s eviction suit. Exclusion of civil jurisdiction is not readily inferred, must be explicit or clearly implied, and is construed strictly. No earlier judicial cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The civil suit was within the civil court’s jurisdiction and was not barred by the statutory provision restricting challenges to official orders or actions.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and former_eviction_authority_power_removed and no_successor_eviction_forum_created and statutory_bar_limited_to_official_actions

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A claimant filed a civil suit seeking eviction from accommodation.
predicates.former_eviction_authority_power_removed: The law removed the specialized authority’s power to decide eviction cases.
predicates.no_successor_eviction_forum_created: The law did not give another specialized authority power to decide those eviction cases.
predicates.statutory_bar_limited_to_official_action: The statutory restriction concerned challenges to official orders or actions and did not cover the claimant’s eviction suit.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar on civil suits concerning matters assigned to a special authority does not oust civil court jurisdiction over a disputed claim of title to immovable property when that authority can only order summary eviction and cannot determine title.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that long possession had given rise to title by adverse possession to land owned by the State.
The relevant statutory procedure empowered an authority to order summary eviction of persons occupying land without right or title.
The special procedure did not provide a mechanism for determining competing claims of title to immovable property.
members.legal_principle: A statutory jurisdiction bar does not exclude civil court adjudication of title where the special forum is empowered only to determine matters within its statutory remit and has no machinery to resolve title disputes. The Court relied on Abdul Waheed Khan v. Bhawani, Firm and Illuri Subbayya Chetty & Sons v. State of Andhra Pradesh, State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam, and Dhulabhai.
members.conclusion: The civil court's jurisdiction to determine the disputed title claim was not ousted.

rule.if: civil_suit_seeking_title_determination and title_dispute_concerns_immovable_property and special_proceeding_allows_only_summary_eviction and special_forum_cannot_determine_title

predicates.civil_suit_seeking_title_determination: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking determination of title.
predicates.title_dispute_concerns_immovable_propert: The competing claims concern title to immovable property.
predicates.special_proceeding_allows_only_summary_e: The special statutory proceeding provides only a summary process for eviction.
predicates.special_forum_cannot_determine_title: The special forum has no procedure or authority to decide the competing title claims.

members.legal_issue: A statute providing for summary eviction of unauthorized occupants does not prevent a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
material_facts: A party argued that a statute providing for summary eviction of unauthorized occupants barred the pending suit for eviction.
The suit sought eviction of an occupant whose claim to remain was based on tenancy.
members.legal_principle: The court held that the U.P. Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1972, which provides for summary eviction of unauthorized occupants, did not bar a suit for eviction of a tenant.
members.conclusion: The summary-eviction statute did not obstruct the suit for eviction of a tenant.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: An owner has brought a civil suit seeking eviction from property.
predicates.occupant_claimed_as_tenant: The occupant claims a right to remain in possession as a tenant.
predicates.summary_eviction_law_targets_unauthorize: A separate law provides a summary process for evicting unauthorized occupants.

members.legal_issue: The civil-court bar on suits for eviction of statutory tenants does not bar a suit against a person who no longer falls within the statutory definition of tenant.
material_facts: The owner sought possession in an ordinary civil court on the ground that the occupant was a trespasser following an earlier eviction decree.
The occupant relied on the civil-court bar in the rent law, but the earlier decree meant that he was excluded from the statutory definition of tenant.
members.legal_principle: Section 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 bars a civil suit for eviction of a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1), but does not bar a suit against a person who is not such a tenant. Under ordinary landlord-and-tenant law, a person against whom an eviction decree has been made no longer possesses the rights of a tenant.
members.conclusion: The rent law did not bar the civil suit because the occupant was not a tenant as defined by that law.

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: A claimant brings a civil-court suit seeking possession from an occupant.
predicates.defendant_excluded_from_tenant_definitio: The occupant is excluded from the applicable statutory definition of tenant.

members.legal_issue: An equitable assignee of a decree who cannot proceed under the ordinary decree-transfer procedure may execute the decree under the general provision allowing a person claiming under a decree-holder to apply for execution.
material_facts: The bank had an equitable assignment of the decree proceeds to the extent needed to discharge the debtor’s debt.
The decree had not been legally transferred to the bank, so the bank could not rely on the ordinary procedure for execution by a transferee.
members.legal_principle: Under Jugulkishore Saraf v. Raw Cotton Co. Ltd., [1955] 1 S.C.R. 1369, an equitable assignee of a decree who cannot obtain the benefit of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure may nevertheless execute the decree under section 146 of the Code.
members.conclusion: The bank could execute the decree in its own right under section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: A person sought to have a decree executed.
predicates.equitable_assignee_of_decree: The person seeking execution held an equitable assignment of an interest in the decree.
predicates.ordinary_transferee_procedure_unavailabl: The person could not use the ordinary procedure for execution by a transferee of the decree.

members.legal_issue: An execution application filed in the decree-holder’s name by an agent may continue when the agent is also entitled to execute the decree in its own right as an equitable assignee.
material_facts: The bank initially filed the execution application in the decree-holder’s name, and its manager signed as the decree-holder’s attorney.
The dispute between the decree-holder and the bank arose while execution was pending.
The bank held an equitable assignment of decree proceeds and could execute the decree in its own right.
members.legal_principle: The Court looked to the substance rather than the form of the execution application. Applying the principle in Jugulkishore Saraf v. Raw Cotton Co. Ltd., [1955] 1 S.C.R. 1369, it held that the bank’s entitlement as equitable assignee to execute in its own right made it unnecessary to close an application initially presented in the decree-holder’s name.
members.conclusion: The application did not have to be closed because it was filed in the decree-holder’s name; the bank was entitled to carry it on in its own right.

rule.if: decree_execution_proceeding and application_filed_in_decree_holders_name_by_agent and agent_is_equitable_assignee and dispute_arises_during_pending_execution

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: A person sought to have a decree executed.
predicates.application_filed_in_decree_holders_name: An agent filed an execution application in the decree-holder’s name and acted under the decree-holder’s authority.
predicates.agent_is_equitable_assignee: The agent held an equitable assignment of an interest in the decree.
predicates.dispute_arises_during_pending_execution: A dispute between the decree-holder and the agent arose after the execution application was filed and while it remained pending.

members.legal_issue: An equitable assignee who cannot use the procedure for a formal transfer of a decree may execute it under the procedural provision allowing proceedings by a person claiming under the decree-holder.
material_facts: The bank held an equitable assignment of the decree proceeds to the extent of the debtor’s debt to it.
The bank could not obtain the benefit of the procedure for execution by a transferee of a formally transferred decree.
The decree-holder objected to the bank proceeding with execution.
members.legal_principle: In Jugalkishore Saraf v. Raw Cotton Co. Ltd., this Court held that an equitable assignee of a decree who cannot obtain the benefit of Order XXI, Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure may nevertheless execute the decree under Section 146 of the Code. The Court followed that binding decision and found no compelling reason to reconsider it.
members.conclusion: The bank could execute the decree in its own right under Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure despite being unable to proceed under Order XXI, Rule 16.

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: The proceeding is for execution of a decree.
predicates.equitable_assignee_of_decree: A person has an equitable assignment of the decree or its proceeds.
predicates.formal_transferee_procedure_unavailable: The equitable assignee cannot use the procedure available to a transferee of a formally transferred decree.

members.legal_issue: An execution application filed in the decree-holder’s name may continue for the equitable assignee where its original form followed the parties’ arrangement and the dispute arose only after filing.
material_facts: The bank initially filed the execution application in the decree-holder’s name, with the bank manager signing as attorney under the power of attorney.
There was no dispute between the debtor and the bank when the application was filed, and the form of the application followed the power of attorney.
The dispute arose while execution was pending, after which the bank asserted its own rights as equitable assignee.
members.legal_principle: The Court looked to the substance of the execution rather than its form. Since the application was filed in the decree-holder’s name as required by the power of attorney before any dispute arose, it served no useful purpose to close it; the bank could continue it in its own right as equitable assignee.
members.conclusion: The application could continue, and its form did not prevent the bank from executing the decree in its own right.

rule.if: decree_execution_proceeding and application_filed_in_decree_holder_name_under_authority and no_dispute_when_application_filed and dispute_arose_while_execution_pending and equitable_assignee_may_execute

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: The proceeding is for execution of a decree.
predicates.application_filed_in_decree_holder_name_: The application was filed in the decree-holder’s name in accordance with authority given to the applicant or its agent.
predicates.no_dispute_when_application_filed: The decree-holder and the person acting under the authority were not in dispute when the application was filed.
predicates.dispute_arose_while_execution_pending: The dispute between the decree-holder and the person claiming an interest arose after the execution application was filed and while it remained pending.
predicates.equitable_assignee_may_execute: The person claiming to continue execution has an equitable assignment and may execute the decree in its own right.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who abuses the court process and does not approach the court with clear hands is not entitled to equitable relief under the Specific Relief Act.
material_facts: The claimant pursued different proceedings within a short time and made inconsistent allegations about possession and the timing of dispossession.
The claimant gave no explanation for the discrepancies between the pleadings, including the differing statements about when the cause of action arose.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the principle that a litigant who abuses the process of the court and does not come to court with clear hands is not entitled to equitable relief under the Specific Relief Act.
members.conclusion: The claimant had abused the process of the court and was not entitled to equitable relief under the Specific Relief Act.

predicates.specific_relief_claim: The claimant sought relief under the law governing specific relief.
predicates.claimant_pursued_inconsistent_proceeding: The claimant pursued multiple proceedings containing inconsistent allegations about the claim.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_explain_material_inco: The claimant did not explain material inconsistencies in the allegations or pleadings.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who relies on false factual allegations is not entitled to the equitable relief of specific performance, and the discretion to grant that relief must be exercised on sound legal principles.
material_facts: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.

The claimant alleged that possession of a property portion had been delivered under the agreement, but the evidence showed that the portion was delivered to the sellers after the tenant vacated it and was later handed to the purchaser.
The claimant alleged that he had informed the purchaser of the agreement, but did not testify to having done so, and the purchaser denied receiving that information.
The claimant alleged an additional payment that was not pleaded in the plaint.
The lower courts refused specific performance, finding that the claimant had made false allegations.
members.legal_principle: Specific performance is an equitable relief governed by the court’s discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. That discretion cannot be refused arbitrarily and must be exercised on sound principles of law capable of correction by an appellate court. A party seeking equitable relief must come with clean hands, and a party who makes false allegations is not entitled to specific performance. The Court states that this principle has been repeatedly affirmed, but cites no earlier cases by name.
members.conclusion: The refusal to grant specific performance was justified because the claimant did not come to court with clean hands; the discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, was exercised on sound legal principles and not arbitrarily.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant sought a decree requiring performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.claimant_made_false_factual_allegations: The claimant made factual allegations about the transaction that the court found false.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who participates in a fraudulent, sham transaction and does not approach the court with clean hands cannot obtain the protection of part performance.
material_facts: The claimant sought protection based on an agreement made with the judgment debtor's wife after the land had been attached.
The High Court found that the agreement was sham and fraudulent, that no consideration had been paid, and that it was brought into existence to defeat the creditors' rights.
The High Court found that the claimant was privy to the fraud and that his alleged possession was a device to protect the debtor's property.
The claimant sought a declaration and injunctions rather than relying on part performance only as a defence to retain possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act protects a transferee in possession only when the statutory conditions are met, including performance or continuing willingness to perform the transferee's obligations; the protection is equitable and requires the claimant to come to court with clean hands. The Court explained that the section imposes a bar on the transferor and does not create title, and relied on the principles in Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai and the other authorities addressing the defensive scope of Section 53-A.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to protection under Section 53-A, and the Court dismissed the petition challenging the High Court's decision.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_part_performance_protec: The claimant sought to rely on possession under an agreement to transfer property for protection against enforcement concerning that property.
predicates.claimant_is_party_to_sham_or_fraudulent_: The claimant participated in a sham or fraudulent transaction brought about to defeat another person's lawful claim.
predicates.claimant_lacks_clean_hands: The claimant's conduct in obtaining or relying on the transaction was inequitable.

members.legal_issue: A person whose claim for equitable protection rests on a false account and who does not approach the court with clean hands is not entitled to relief under principles of justice, equity and good conscience.
material_facts: The respondent denied that he was a licensee or had received permission to occupy the land and raise temporary structures.
He claimed instead that he occupied the land as a prospective purchaser under an oral sale agreement.
The courts found the oral sale agreement account false, and the respondent's challenge to the dismissal of his specific-performance suit was unsuccessful.
The respondent sought equitable protection against eviction on the basis of the alleged permanent construction.
members.legal_principle: A court applying equity must promote honesty and good faith and prevent legal fraud; a party seeking equitable relief must come to court with clean hands. The Court considered the equitable principles associated with Section 60(b) of the Easements Act and distinguished Jagat Singh v. District Board, where the licensee had acted on the licence and made permanent works at considerable cost, unlike the respondent's position and conduct.
members.conclusion: Even assuming that analogous equitable principles could apply, the respondent was not entitled to relief because his claim rested on a false account and he did not come to court with clean hands.

predicates.equitable_relief_sought: A party asks a court to grant relief on equitable grounds.
predicates.claimant_denied_permission_and_claimed_p: The party denied receiving permission to occupy the property and claimed instead to occupy it under a purchase agreement.
predicates.purchase_claim_found_false: The courts found the party's claimed purchase agreement account false.

members.legal_issue: The government may withdraw land from acquisition only before possession has been taken.
material_facts: The acquiring company had been put in possession of part of the land under a witnessed possession memorandum.
The State Government later decided to withdraw that land from acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits withdrawal from acquisition where possession of the land has not been taken. The Court relied on U.P. Jal Nigam v. Kalra Properties for the principle that, once possession has been taken and the land has vested in the State, it cannot be divested except through a valid withdrawal under Section 48 before possession is taken.
members.conclusion: Withdrawal from acquisition was impermissible to the extent that possession had already been taken.

predicates.statutory_acquisition_withdrawal: The government decides to withdraw land from an acquisition governed by a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.possession_already_taken: The government or acquiring body has already taken possession of the land.

members.legal_issue: A tentative governmental decision to release acquired land does not constitute a final decision to withdraw from the acquisition.
material_facts: A minister recommended releasing land, and the recommendation received approval from the head of government.
Before the proposed release was implemented, the government sought information about development works, expenditure, and possession so that the authority could be dealt with before land was returned.
The proposed release was not implemented, and the government later reversed course.
members.legal_principle: For a governmental decision to effect withdrawal from an acquisition, the decision must be final rather than provisional or tentative. The court found it unnecessary to decide whether the tentative decision had been communicated.
members.conclusion: There had been no final decision to release the land; a tentative decision was insufficient to establish withdrawal from the acquisition.

predicates.withdrawal_from_acquisition_claimed: A party claimed that the government had withdrawn from an acquisition.
predicates.release_decision_tentative: The government's decision to release the land remained provisional rather than final.
predicates.implementation_steps_remained_pending: Further governmental steps, such as obtaining information needed before returning the land, remained outstanding.

members.legal_issue: The government may withdraw land from acquisition before taking possession without first hearing the landowner.
material_facts: Acquisition notifications and notices had been issued, but the government had not taken possession of the land.
The government withdrew the land from acquisition and did not give the owner an opportunity to be heard beforehand.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 6 and 9 of the Land Acquisition Act, the notifications and notices do not divest the owner of rights in the land; section 16 provides that title vests in the government only when possession is taken. Section 48 permits withdrawal before possession, and the court held that this power may be exercised unilaterally. It relied on Trustees of Bai Smarth Jain Shvetamber Murtipujak Gyanodhyaya Trust v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1981 Gujarat 107.
members.conclusion: The government could withdraw unilaterally before taking possession, and no hearing for the owner had to be implied.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The government had not taken possession of the land when it withdrew from acquisition.

members.legal_issue: The Government may withdraw land from acquisition if possession has not been taken under the applicable vesting provisions.
material_facts: The Government withdrew a substantial portion of the lands that had been notified for acquisition after deciding that acquiring the entire area was not worthwhile.
The appellant sought compensation for the withdrawn lands.
The record did not establish possession taken under section 17(1), and the alleged earlier possession was not satisfactorily proved in the writ proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act permits the Government to withdraw from acquisition any land of which possession has not been taken, subject to the exception in section 36, which was not relevant. For this purpose, possession means possession taken under section 16 or section 17(1); until such possession is taken, the land does not vest absolutely in the Government. Lt. Governor of Himachal Pradesh v. Avinash Sharma was distinguished because the relevant possession and statutory action were present there but not established here.
members.conclusion: The Government was competent to withdraw the lands from acquisition because possession under the applicable vesting provisions had not been established; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and government_withdrew_from_acquisition and not possession_taken_under_vesting_procedure

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns land sought to be acquired by the Government.
predicates.government_withdrew_from_acquisition: The Government withdraws the land from the acquisition.
predicates.possession_taken_under_vesting_procedure: The Collector has taken possession of the land under a procedure that vests it in the Government.

members.legal_issue: A presumptive reversioner’s receipt of a benefit or failure to challenge an alienation does not, without informed assent to the transaction, ratify the alienation and bar a later challenge when the reversion falls open.
material_facts: The reversioner was a minor when the widows made the settlement and was not a party to the settlement or the later transactions implementing it.

He received and enjoyed a house under the arrangement, but the evidence did not establish that he knew of his rights as a possible reversioner or understood that the widows intended to convey absolute titles.
The Collector’s certificate followed registration in the ordinary course, and the reversioner’s other conduct did not establish informed assent to the alienation.
The reversioner sued after the widow’s death to recover property alienated by her.
