members.legal_principle: A widow’s alienation is voidable by reversioners, who may be barred by express ratification or conduct demonstrating informed assent and election to treat the alienation as binding. Mere receipt of a benefit or failure to challenge the transaction is insufficient; whether conduct amounts to ratification is a question of fact. The Court applied Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram, Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal, Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden, and Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb.
members.conclusion: The reversioner had not ratified the alienation and was not precluded from challenging it; the alienation was not binding on him.

predicates.reversioner_suit_to_avoid_widow_alienati: A person claiming as reversioner sued to avoid an alienation made by a widow of the deceased holder’s property.
predicates.reversioner_was_not_a_party: The reversioner did not participate in the transaction or arrangement that effected the alienation.
predicates.reversioner_lacked_knowledge_of_reversio: The reversioner did not know of the rights on which a later challenge as reversioner could be based.
predicates.benefit_was_only_a_gift: The reversioner received a benefit that, without further conduct, indicated assent only to that benefit and not to the wider transaction.

members.legal_issue: A presumptive reversioner who knowingly assents to, adopts, or ratifies a widow’s otherwise voidable alienation cannot later challenge it upon succession opening.
material_facts: The widows held only a widow’s estate, and the challenged alienations were not made for necessity of the estate, so the alienations were prima facie not binding on reversioners.

One presumptive reversioner, with knowledge of the existing alienations, accepted an agreement affirming them and obtained substantial property; he later dealt with property received under that agreement.

Other presumptive reversioners were minors when their guardian entered into an arrangement under which they received property. After attaining majority, they retained and dealt with that property rather than renouncing the arrangement.
The agreements and subsequent dealings showed that the presumptive reversioners accepted the arrangements and the benefits they provided.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, an alienation by a widow in excess of her powers is voidable at the instance of the reversioners, who may be precluded from avoiding it by express assent, conduct treating it as valid, election, or ratification. A presumptive reversioner has no vested right before succession opens but may elect to stand by or ratify a transaction. A minor cannot be compelled to accept a benefit that would deprive the minor of later legal rights; after attaining majority, however, the minor may ratify the guardian’s transaction, and continued enjoyment of a benefit originally conferred on the minor may itself suffice. The Court relied on Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb, T. V. R. Subbu Chetty’s Family Charities v. M. Raghava Mudaliar, Fateh Singh v. Thakur Rukmini Ramanji Maharaj, Jagarlapudi Seetharamayya v. Sarva Chandrayya, Makineni Virayya v. Madamanchi Bapayya, and Krishna Beharilal v. Gulab Chand; it also discussed the categories of estoppel under section 115 of the Evidence Act.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were precluded from challenging the alienations. An alienation by a Hindu widow is voidable, not void, and a reversioner who assents to or ratifies it, or elects to retain benefits under the relevant transaction, cannot later repudiate it.

rule.if: reversioner_challenges_widow_alienation and (knowingly_assented_to_alienation or (minor_when_benefit_received and attained_majority and retained_and_dealt_with_benefit))

predicates.reversioner_challenges_widow_alienation: A person claiming as a reversioner seeks to challenge an alienation made by a widow holding a limited estate.
predicates.knowingly_assented_to_alienation: The presumptive reversioner, knowing of the alienation, accepted or affirmed its validity in a transaction.
predicates.minor_when_benefit_received: The presumptive reversioner was a minor when a guardian entered into a transaction conferring a benefit on that minor.
predicates.attained_majority: The presumptive reversioner later attained legal majority.
predicates.retained_and_dealt_with_benefit: After attaining majority, the presumptive reversioner retained the benefit and dealt with it as the recipient of the transaction.

members.legal_issue: A presumptive reversioner’s consent to a widow’s alienation raises a rebuttable presumption but does not prevent the actual reversioner from proving that the alienation lacked legal necessity and proper inquiry.
material_facts: The person who was the immediate presumptive reversioner joined the widow in executing the security bond.
The evidence established that there was no legal necessity and no proper bona fide inquiry by the mortgagee.
The courts found that the presumption arising from the presumptive reversioner’s consent had been rebutted.
members.legal_principle: Consent by an immediate reversioner may raise a presumption that the alienation was for legal necessity or that the alienee made proper and bona fide inquiry, but that presumption is rebuttable. The actual reversioner may prove the absence of necessity and inquiry. The Court relied on Debi Prasad Chowdhury v. Golap Bhagat and Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden.
members.conclusion: The presumptive reversioner’s consent did not make the security bond binding on the actual reversioners.

predicates.widow_alienation_dispute: A reversioner challenges an alienation made by a widow of inherited property.
predicates.presumptive_reversioner_joined: The person who was then the immediate presumptive reversioner joined in the widow’s alienation.
predicates.presumption_rebutted: Evidence established that the alienation lacked legal necessity and that the alienee had not made proper bona fide inquiry.
predicates.presumptive_reversioner_consent_does_not: The consent does not prevent the actual reversioner from challenging the alienation.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner who knowingly and unequivocally assents to a transaction that is voidable at his instance may be precluded from later avoiding it, even if he assented before becoming entitled to the estate.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s interest as reversioner became operative only after the limited estates ended.
Before then, he expressly assented to the absolute titles of other family members and engaged in a long course of dealings asserting absolute titles himself.
The plaintiff represented the arrangement to a lender, demonstrating knowledge of its nature, and accepted benefits under the arrangement.
The Court found that the plaintiff’s assent was to the family arrangement as a whole, rather than only to an individual gift.
members.legal_principle: An alienation by a widow beyond her powers is voidable by the reversioner, not void; a reversioner may be precluded from avoiding it by ratification or conduct treating it as binding. A person who, with full knowledge of his rights, elects to assent to a voidable transaction cannot later reverse that election. Assent may be given before the reversioner becomes entitled to sue, and may be inferred from conduct amounting to an actual election, but must clearly relate to the transaction in question. The Court relied on Raja Modhu Sudan Singh v. Rooke, [1897] 24 I.A. 164; Bijoy Gopal v. Krishna, [1906] 34 I.A. 87; Ramgouda Annagowda v. Bhausaheb, [1927] 54 I.A. 396; Rangaswami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden, [1918] 46 I.A. 72; and Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, 1952 S.C.R. 478.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff, having knowingly and unequivocally assented to the arrangement and accepted benefits under it, was precluded from avoiding it after the succession opened.

rule.if: reversioner_challenges_voidable_transaction and reversioner_knew_material_facts and reversioner_unequivocally_assented and assent_related_to_whole_transaction and reversioner_accepted_benefit

predicates.reversioner_challenges_voidable_transact: A person who has become entitled as reversioner seeks to avoid a transaction affecting the estate.
predicates.reversioner_knew_material_facts: The reversioner knew the material facts about the transaction and the rights he could assert against it.
predicates.reversioner_unequivocally_assented: The reversioner clearly acted in a way showing assent to the transaction.
predicates.assent_related_to_whole_transaction: The reversioner’s assent concerned the overall transaction rather than only a separate disposition within it.
predicates.reversioner_accepted_benefit: The reversioner received or accepted a benefit under the transaction.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration together with consequential relief is not barred from being heard merely because the plaintiff fails to prove the consequential relief.
material_facts: The suit sought a declaration of ownership and an injunction against interference with the property.
The plaintiff failed to prove possession, so the injunction could not be granted.
The trial court found that the plaintiff had proved ownership.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the proviso bars a declaration where a plaintiff able to seek further relief seeks only a declaration and omits that relief. Whether the proviso applies is assessed from the plaint as framed. Where consequential relief is claimed, failure to prove that relief does not make the suit unmaintainable. The Court relied on M. K. Rappai v. John, Ram Saran v. Smt. Ganga Devi, Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra, and Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy, and rejected the contrary approach in Sri Aralappa v. Sri Jagannath.
members.conclusion: The suit could not be dismissed as not maintainable under the proviso to Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, because the plaint sought consequential relief as well as a declaration; failure on the consequential relief was a matter of merits, not maintainability.

predicates.declaratory_suit_with_consequential_clai: The plaintiff filed a suit seeking a declaration of a right together with relief intended to give effect to that right.
predicates.consequential_relief_unproved: The plaintiff failed to establish the facts necessary to obtain the consequential relief sought.

members.legal_issue: A proven ownership claim may support a declaration of ownership even when the plaintiff has failed to prove possession and cannot obtain consequential relief.
material_facts: The trial court found that the plaintiff had proved ownership of the property, and that finding was not displaced on appeal.
The plaintiff failed to prove possession and therefore could not obtain an injunction against interference.
The request to add a claim for possession at the appellate stage was rejected.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 does not prohibit a standalone declaratory decree where the proviso does not apply. A declaration may be granted on a proven right even if it is non-executable or the plaintiff fails on consequential relief. The Court relied on the principles in M. K. Rappai v. John, Ram Saran v. Smt. Ganga Devi, Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra, and Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy, and held that Sri Aralappa v. Sri Jagannath was not good law insofar as it required dismissal of the declaration claim in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to a declaration of ownership notwithstanding the failure to establish possession or obtain consequential relief.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit seeking a declaration of a right to property.
predicates.ownership_established: The fact-finding court found that the claimant had proved ownership, and that finding was not displaced on appeal.
predicates.consequential_relief_unproved: The claimant failed to establish the facts necessary to obtain the consequential relief sought.

members.legal_issue: Omission of further or consequential relief does not justify rejecting a declaratory plaint at the threshold when entitlement to the declaration has not yet been determined.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declaratory reliefs without also seeking further consequential relief.
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to the declarations had not been decided.
The omission was raised as a ground for rejecting the plaint.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act bars a declaration where a plaintiff able to seek further relief omits it. Whether further relief is required arises for consideration at final adjudication, because the need for such relief depends on whether the declaration is granted.
members.conclusion: Whether further relief was required could be considered at final adjudication, and its omission did not justify rejecting the plaint at that stage.

predicates.declaratory_civil_suit: The plaintiff has filed a civil suit seeking a declaration.
predicates.further_relief_omitted: The plaintiff has not also sought further relief that may accompany the declaration.
predicates.entitlement_to_declaration_not_yet_decid: The court has not yet determined whether the plaintiff is entitled to the declaration.

members.legal_issue: A plaint seeking interconnected reliefs, including an injunction based on alleged possession under an agreement, cannot be rejected at the threshold merely because the requested declaration under part performance may not be maintainable; entitlement to relief is for trial.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration and confirmation of possession based on an agreement, specific performance of that agreement, and a permanent injunction.
They alleged that they were in possession under the agreement, had developed the property, had remained in possession for more than twelve years, and paid municipal taxes.
They alleged that the cause of action for the injunction arose when their possession was sought to be disturbed.
The High Court rejected the plaint on the basis that a declaration under the part-performance provision would not be maintainable against the owner.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. Where the plaint also seeks an injunction and alleges possession under an agreement, with the cause of action for the injunction arising when possession is disturbed, the suit cannot be treated as barred on the stated basis at the rejection stage. A plaint cannot be rejected partially, and whether the plaintiffs ultimately qualify for relief under Section 53A must be decided at trial. The Court distinguished the High Court’s reliance on Delhi Motor Company v. U.A. Basrurkar, AIR 1968 SC 794, because the pleadings included the injunction claim and related allegations of possession.
members.conclusion: The maintainability of the claimed relief under the part-performance provision was to be considered at trial; it did not justify rejecting the plaint at this stage. The interconnected reliefs could not be rejected partially, and the plaint was restored for trial.

rule.if: plaint_rejection_application and claim_includes_declaration_based_on_part_performance and claim_includes_injunction_based_on_possession and plaintiffs_allege_possession_under_agreement and reliefs_are_interconnected

predicates.plaint_rejection_application: A defendant applies to have a plaint rejected before trial.
predicates.claim_includes_declaration_based_on_part: The plaintiffs seek a declaration based on their alleged performance of an agreement.
predicates.claim_includes_injunction_based_on_posse: The plaintiffs also seek an injunction to protect their alleged possession.
predicates.plaintiffs_allege_possession_under_agree: The plaintiffs allege that they possess the property pursuant to an agreement.
predicates.reliefs_are_interconnected: The pleaded declaration and injunction claims are related to the same alleged agreement and possession.

members.legal_issue: A prior judicial decision cannot be relied on without considering whether its factual context fits the case being decided.
material_facts: The High Court granted relief by relying on decisions concerning ownership of reserved trees that had been rendered in writ proceedings.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not examined whether the factual situations in those decisions matched the present case.
members.legal_principle: A decision is binding for its ratio decidendi and what it actually decides, not for every observation or expression in the judgment. Judicial decisions must be read in the context of their facts, and courts must assess whether the factual situation fits before relying on a precedent. The Court relied on State of Orissa v. Sudhansu Sekhar Misra, Union of India v. Dhanwanti Devi, Quinn v. Leathem, London Graving Dock Co. Ltd. v. Horton, Home Office v. Dorset Yacht Co., and Herrington v. British Railways Board.
members.conclusion: Reliance on the earlier decisions without examining their factual context was impermissible.

predicates.court_relies_on_prior_decisions: The court bases its decision in part on one or more earlier judicial decisions.
predicates.precedent_factual_context_not_examined: The court does not examine whether the facts of the earlier decisions fit the facts of the case before it.

members.legal_issue: A court must compare the material facts and legal context before applying an earlier decision as a precedent.
material_facts: The High Court relied on Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Dolly Das to order eviction.
The earlier decision did not consider tenant protections corresponding to Sections 3 and 9 of the applicable tenant-protection law.
The High Court did not consider the effect of those protections before applying the earlier decision.
members.legal_principle: Judgments are not statutes, and judicial observations must be read in their context. A precedent should be applied only after assessing how its facts and legal setting fit the case at hand; even a significant difference may change the result. The Court relied on the contextual cautions expressed in London Graving Dock Co. Ltd. v. Horton, Home Office v. Dorset Yacht Co., Herrington v. British Railways Board, and the cited observations of Lord Denning on distinguishing cases.
members.conclusion: The earlier decision did not justify the eviction order because the legal and factual context differed, and the High Court had not considered that difference.

predicates.precedent_based_adjudication: A court relied on an earlier decision to resolve a later case.
predicates.precedent_material_facts_not_compared: The court did not assess whether the material facts and legal setting of the earlier decision matched the later case.
predicates.current_case_has_materially_different_le: The later case involved legal protections that were not considered in the earlier decision.

members.legal_issue: A court must apply precedent in the context of the facts and issue it decided rather than treating judicial observations as statutory rules.
material_facts: The lower courts relied on an earlier decision to restrain the sale without addressing how its factual setting matched this case.
The earlier decision’s broad guidelines had been expressed without accounting for the statutory purpose and practical circumstances relevant to the present recovery action.
members.legal_principle: Judgments are to be understood in the setting of their facts, and even a significant factual difference may change the result. The Court relied on London Graving Dock Co. Ltd. v. Horton, Home Office v. Dorset Yacht Co., Herrington v. British Railways Board, and the principle stated by Lord Denning that precedent should be followed only so far as it serves the path of justice.
members.conclusion: Courts must examine the factual fit of a precedent and read judicial observations in context; decisions cannot be applied mechanically as though their words were statutory provisions.

predicates.court_relies_on_prior_judgment: A court uses an earlier judgment as a basis for deciding the dispute before it.
predicates.material_factual_fit_is_not_examined: The court does not assess whether the facts and issue of the earlier judgment correspond to the case being decided.

members.legal_issue: A prior case’s factual outcome does not determine the factual result in a later case, which must be assessed on its own circumstances.
material_facts: A prior decision was invoked in argument concerning the relevance of municipal approval to a landlord’s rebuilding claim.
The Supreme Court noted that the facts of that prior decision were not fully stated and that the present case involved its own evidence and circumstances.
members.legal_principle: A case is not authority on a point of fact. A factual question must be decided in light of the circumstances and evidence in the case being considered.
members.conclusion: The prior decision could not serve as authority on the factual question; the circumstances of each case had to be examined individually.

predicates.court_deciding_fact_dependent_reconstruc: The court is deciding a rebuilding claim whose outcome depends on the facts.
predicates.prior_case_invoked_as_proof_of_factual_n: A party relies on the factual outcome of an earlier case to support the claimed need for rebuilding.

members.legal_issue: A statutory process permitting arrest and detention to recover public tax dues is constitutionally valid when it includes safeguards against arbitrary detention.
material_facts: Tax dues were recoverable as public arrears, and the recovery law authorized arrest and detention as one means of collection.
The law limited the duration of detention and exempted specified categories of persons from arrest and detention.

The rules required the arrested defaulter to be brought promptly before the issuing officer and prohibited detention unless the officer had reason to believe it would compel payment of the whole or a substantial part of the arrears.
The court considered arrest and detention a coercive means of recovering public dues, not punishment for mere default.
members.legal_principle: A restriction on freedom of movement must not be arbitrary or excessive; its reasonableness is assessed by balancing individual freedom against the public interest in light of the circumstances. Coercive recovery of public dues may be reasonable when adequate safeguards govern detention. The court applied State of Madras v. V.G. Row, The Collector of Malabar v. Erimal Ebrahim Hajee, and Sangam Lal Gupta v. Sales Tax Officer, and followed Purshottam Govindji Halai on a State's ability to devise machinery for recovering its public demands.
members.conclusion: The statutory recovery process was not violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(d), or 21 of the Constitution.

rule.if: public_dues_recovery_proceeding and arrest_and_detention_are_authorized and detention_is_time_limited and protected_persons_are_exempt and detention_requires_a_productivity_finding

predicates.public_dues_recovery_proceeding: An authority is seeking to recover dues owed to the government as public arrears.
predicates.arrest_and_detention_are_authorized: The recovery process permits arrest and detention as a means of collecting the arrears.
predicates.detention_is_time_limited: The governing process limits how long a defaulter may be detained.
predicates.protected_persons_are_exempt: The governing process exempts specified categories of persons from arrest or detention.
predicates.detention_requires_a_productivity_findin: The officer must determine that detention is likely to compel payment of the whole or a substantial part of the arrears before ordering detention.

members.legal_issue: Statutory authority to recover public dues by arrest and detention of a defaulter is constitutionally valid.
material_facts: The petitioners owed dues to a bank that were recoverable through statutory recovery proceedings.
The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of provisions authorising arrest and detention to recover those dues, fearing they would be arrested and detained.
The Court had upheld the constitutional validity of the challenged provisions in an earlier judgment delivered the same day.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its holding in Ram Narayan Agarwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Writ Petitions Nos. 1110 of 1980 and connected matters, decided the same day, that Section 279(1)(b) and Section 281 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, which authorise recovery of arrears by arrest and detention, are constitutionally valid. The dues were recoverable under the U.P. Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972, read with Section 279 of the 1950 Act.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the constitutional challenge and dismissed the petitions, leaving the revenue authorities free to recover the dues according to law and in light of the earlier judgment.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_arrest_fo: A person brought a constitutional writ challenging statutory authority to arrest and detain a defaulter to recover dues.
predicates.dues_are_recoverable_through_statutory_p: The dues at issue were recoverable through statutory proceedings conducted by revenue authorities.
predicates.precedent_upheld_same_recovery_authority: The Court had already upheld the constitutional validity of the same recovery authority in an earlier decision.

members.legal_issue: Detention to recover unpaid tax does not violate personal liberty when it is carried out under valid laws that establish the procedure for the detention.
material_facts: A collector issued an arrest warrant under a land-revenue law to recover unpaid tax certified for collection under the tax statute.
The petitioner challenged the resulting arrest and detention as inconsistent with the constitutional guarantee of personal liberty.
The court upheld the challenged tax-recovery provision and found that the applicable land-revenue provision supplied the procedure for arrest and detention.
members.legal_principle: Article 21 prohibits deprivation of personal liberty except in accordance with procedure established by law. The court held that where the applicable statutory recovery provisions stand, and provide the procedure under which arrest and detention occur, the resulting detention does not infringe Article 21. The court considered the validity of the provisions under Article 14 before rejecting the Article 21 challenge.
members.conclusion: There was no violation of Article 21 because the arrest and detention were carried out under laws that constituted a procedure established by law.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_recovery: A person challenges detention carried out to recover unpaid tax.
predicates.detention_carried_out_under_valid_recove: The detention is carried out under recovery laws that the court finds valid and that establish a procedure for detention.

members.legal_issue: The statutory process of arrest and detention for recovering public electricity dues is constitutionally valid.
material_facts: The petitioners owed dues to the State Electricity Board.
The petitioners apprehended that revenue authorities would recover the dues by arrest and detention under the challenged recovery process.
The Supreme Court had, in an earlier decision, upheld the constitutional validity of the same process.
The constitutional validity of the process was the only point pressed in these petitions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its earlier decision in Ram Narayan Agarwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which upheld the constitutional validity of the process prescribed by Section 279(1)(b), read with Section 281, of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. Recovery of the electricity dues was pursued under the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958, read with Section 279 of the 1950 Act.
members.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was rejected and the petitions were dismissed. The revenue authorities could proceed to recover the dues by issuing a fresh process in light of the earlier judgment.

predicates.recovery_proceeding_challenges_arrest_pr: The debtors brought a proceeding challenging the constitutionality of arrest and detention as a means of recovering public dues.
predicates.petitioners_owe_recoverable_dues: The persons challenging the recovery process owed dues to a public electricity board.
predicates.same_process_previously_upheld: The Supreme Court had previously considered and upheld the constitutionality of the same arrest-and-detention recovery process.
predicates.challenged_recovery_process_is_constitut: The challenged process of arrest and detention for recovering the dues is constitutionally valid.

members.legal_issue: Market compensation for subsequently acquired land may be increased by applying escalation to an established value for earlier acquired land.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the compensation determined for land acquired for construction of a road.
The Court had, in a separate judgment concerning an earlier acquisition, determined compensation for land at Rs. 5 per square foot.
The acquisition under appeal was made later, and the Court held that the landowners were entitled to the benefit of escalation in land prices.
members.legal_principle: Market-value assessment must account for escalation in land prices. The rate of increase depends on the land’s location, surrounding development, availability of land and demand. ONGC Ltd. v. Rameshbhai Jivanbhai Patel (2008) 14 SCC 745 explains that escalation is generally faster in urban and semi-urban areas than in rural areas, and that a general rural-area estimate may be used absent clear, specific evidence. Specific evidence or special reasons may justify a different rate. Applying escalation from older comparable transactions becomes unsafe as the time gap grows, particularly beyond four to five years. The Court also relied on Ranjit Singh v. UT of Chandigarh (1992) 4 SCC 659, Land Acquisition Officer v. Ramanjulu (2005) 9 SCC 594, Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Bipin Kumar (2004) 2 SCC 283, Sardar Jogendra Singh v. State of U.P. (2008) 17 SCC 133, and Revenue Divisional Officer-cum-LAO v. Sk. Azam Saheb (2009) 4 SCC 395. The judgment ordered interest on solatium without separately explaining the legal basis for that part of the award.
members.conclusion: The landowners were awarded compensation calculated by applying annual escalation to the compensation determined for the earlier acquisition, together with interest on solatium.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and later_acquisition_for_public_infrastructure and earlier_land_value_established and land_price_escalation_applies

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: A landowner appealed the compensation determined for land acquired by the government.
predicates.later_acquisition_for_public_infrastruct: The land in the appeal was acquired later for a public infrastructure project.
predicates.earlier_land_value_established: A value for land acquired earlier was established and available for comparison.
predicates.land_price_escalation_applies: The Court found that escalation in land prices was relevant to determining compensation for the later acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Landowners whose acquired land is comparable to land acquired earlier are entitled to a notional increase in market value for the intervening period.
material_facts: The landowners appealed the compensation fixed for their acquired land.
The acquired land was undisputedly similar to land for which compensation had previously been assessed.
The comparable land had been acquired earlier than the land at issue.
The High Court fixed compensation by reference to the earlier assessment but did not allow an increase for the intervening period.
members.legal_principle: Applying the principle of notional increase in market value where comparable land was acquired earlier, the Court held that an annual increase should be allowed for the period between the comparable acquisition and the acquisition at issue. It relied on Ranjit Singh v. U.T. of Chandigarh (1992) 4 SCC 659, Land Acquisition Officer v. Ramanjulu (2005) 9 SCC 594, Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Bipin Kumar (2004) 2 SCC 283, Sardar Jogendra Singh v. State of U.P. (2008) 17 SCC 133, Revenue Divl. Officer-cum-LAO v. Sk. Azam Saheb (2009) 4 SCC 395, ONGC Ltd. v. Rameshbhai Jivanbhai Patel (2008) 14 SCC 745, and Valliyammal v. Special Tahsildar (Land Acquisition) (2011) 8 SCC 91. The acquisition was referred under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; the judgment does not rely on that provision as the basis for the notional increase.
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed, and the landowners were held entitled to compensation at Rs.49 per square yard, reflecting a 12% per annum increase rounded off. The acquiring authority was directed to pay the enhanced compensation with statutory benefits.

rule.if: land_compensation_appeal and comparable_land_is_similar and comparable_land_acquired_earlier and later_acquisition_at_issue

predicates.land_compensation_appeal: Landowners brought an appeal concerning the compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_land_is_similar: The parties did not dispute that the acquired land was similar to land used as a compensation comparator.
predicates.comparable_land_acquired_earlier: The land used as a comparator had been acquired before the land at issue.
predicates.later_acquisition_at_issue: The landowners' land was acquired after the comparable land.

members.legal_issue: A later acquisition notification for land acquired for the same purpose justifies an increase in market value to account for price escalation.
material_facts: The land in this group of appeals was acquired for the same purpose as land covered by the earlier benchmark determination.
Its acquisition notification was issued after the notification underlying that determination.
The Court considered that prices would have escalated and allowed a 5% increase over the benchmark market value.
members.legal_principle: Where land is acquired for the same purpose under a subsequent notification, the Court may account for the intervening escalation in prices by increasing the benchmark market value. The Court applied the benchmark established for the earlier notification and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its provision for statutory benefits.
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed and compensation was reduced to the benchmark market value with a 5% increase, together with statutory benefits calculated on the modified amount.

predicates.appeal_challenging_enhanced_compensation: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an award that enhanced compensation for acquired land.
predicates.same_acquisition_purpose: The land was acquired for the same purpose as land used for an earlier market-value benchmark.
predicates.later_acquisition_notification: The notification acquiring the land was issued after the notification underlying the benchmark.

members.legal_issue: A later acquisition notification for land acquired for the same purpose justifies an increase in market value to account for price escalation.
material_facts: The land in this appeal was acquired for the same purpose as land covered by the earlier benchmark determination.
Its acquisition notification was issued after the notification underlying that determination and later than the notification applicable to the other subsequent-acquisition group.
The Court considered that prices would have escalated and allowed a 10% increase over the benchmark market value.
members.legal_principle: Where land is acquired for the same purpose under a subsequent notification, the Court may account for the intervening escalation in prices by increasing the benchmark market value. The Court applied the benchmark established for the earlier notification and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its provision for statutory benefits.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and compensation was reduced to the benchmark market value with a 10% increase, together with statutory benefits calculated on the modified amount.

predicates.appeal_challenging_enhanced_compensation: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an award that enhanced compensation for acquired land.
predicates.same_acquisition_purpose: The land was acquired for the same purpose as land used for an earlier market-value benchmark.
predicates.later_acquisition_notification: The notification acquiring the land was issued after the notification underlying the benchmark.

members.legal_issue: A state may impose non-agricultural assessment on government-owned land leased for a business purpose and recover it from an incorporated lessee that is legally distinct from the government.
material_facts: The land was owned by the Union Government and leased to an incorporated company for establishing and operating an industrial plant.
The company’s shares were wholly owned by the Union Government, but the company was a separate legal entity.

The amended assessment scheme included a qualifying government-land lessee within the definition of owner and applied to government land leased for commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural purposes.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(j), 3 and 12 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, as amended, a lessee of government land leased for a commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural purpose could be treated as the owner liable for assessment. Article 285 of the Constitution did not exempt property merely because the shares of the incorporated lessee were wholly held by the Union Government. The Court relied on Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar for the distinct legal personality of an incorporated company and the distinction between company property and shareholder property.
members.conclusion: For the period governed by the amendments, the company was liable as the lessee to pay non-agricultural assessment on qualifying land. Article 285 did not bar the assessment because the land was owned by the Union Government, not by the company, and the company was legally distinct from its shareholder.

rule.if: state_non_agricultural_assessment_proceeding and government_owned_land and land_leased_to_incorporated_company and lease_for_non_agricultural_business and lessee_falls_within_assessment_liability

predicates.state_non_agricultural_assessment_procee: A state authority seeks non-agricultural assessment in a proceeding concerning land.
predicates.government_owned_land: The land is owned by a government.
predicates.land_leased_to_incorporated_company: A government leases the land to a company incorporated as a legal entity distinct from its shareholders.
predicates.lease_for_non_agricultural_business: The land is leased for a commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural purpose.
predicates.lessee_falls_within_assessment_liability: The applicable assessment scheme treats a lessee in these circumstances as liable to pay the assessment.

members.legal_issue: Assessment on leased government land may be imposed only on the portion actually used for a commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural purpose.
material_facts: The leased area included land covered by buildings and roads, land said to be reserved for future expansion, and land said to be used for agriculture.
The extent actually used for qualifying purposes and the applicable rate had not been determined by the assessing authority.
The company was permitted to pursue those matters in an appeal under the assessment scheme.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3 and 12 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, as amended, assessment could be levied only on government land leased for a qualifying purpose and actually used for a commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural purpose. The extent of such land and the appropriate rate were matters for determination in the statutory appeal.
members.conclusion: Only land actually used for a commercial, industrial or other non-agricultural purpose could be assessed. The companies could establish the actual extent of qualifying land and contest the applicable rate in statutory appeals.

members.legal_issue: A lessee of government-owned land leased for a non-agricultural purpose is liable for assessment when the governing law treats that lessee as the owner.
material_facts: The Central Government owned the land and had leased it to the appellant company for industrial and commercial use.
The amended law included a lessee of government land leased for a commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purpose within the definition of owner.
The company challenged demands for non-agricultural assessment on the land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(j) and 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, as amended, treated a lessee of government land leased for a commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purpose as an owner liable to pay assessment. Section 12, as amended, brought such leased government land within the Act. The Court also applied the principle that a company is a separate legal entity from its government shareholder, relying on Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Korba, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: For periods to which the amendment applied, the company was treated as the owner and was liable for assessment on the qualifying leased land.

predicates.law_treats_lessee_as_owner: The applicable law treats a lessee of such government land as an owner liable for assessment.

members.legal_issue: Assessment on leased land covered by the Act is confined to the land actually used for a specified non-agricultural purpose, and the extent and applicable rate may be determined on appeal.
material_facts: The company claimed that only some portions of the land were used for buildings, roads, or other purposes, while some land was reserved for future expansion or used for agriculture.
The High Court left the actual extent of qualifying land and the applicable rate to be determined by the statutory appellate authority.
The Supreme Court allowed the companies to appeal on those matters and stated that assessment could be levied only on qualifying land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(j), 3, and 12 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, as amended, apply to the relevant leased government land and impose assessment liability on the statutory owner. The assessment is limited to land actually used for the specified commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purposes. The actual extent and applicable rate may be canvassed before and decided by the statutory appellate authority.
members.conclusion: Assessment could be levied only on the extent actually used for commercial, industrial, or other non-agricultural purposes; the companies could appeal to establish that extent and contest the applicable rate.

members.legal_issue: A legislative bill was validly passed despite the official record omitting an entry that the final motion was put and carried.
material_facts: The Speaker certified on the printed bill soon after the legislative proceedings that the bill had been passed.
The later printed proceedings omitted any statement that the final motion had been put to a vote or carried.
The recorded speeches at the final stage supported passage, and no member opposed the bill.
The Speaker signed the proceedings months after certifying the bill.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Speaker’s contemporaneous certification and parliamentary practice, as discussed in Craies’ Statute Law and May’s Parliamentary Practice. Das J. additionally held that any omission was an irregularity of procedure cured by article 212 of the Constitution; the later confirmation under the former rule 115 did not displace the earlier certification.
members.conclusion: The omission did not establish that the bill had not been passed; the Speaker’s certification was accepted and the omission was treated as an accidental procedural lapse.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_enacted_law and speaker_certified_passage and later_record_omitted_final_vote and recorded_debate_supported_passage

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enacted_law: A person challenging an enacted law alleged that the legislature had not validly passed it.

predicates.recorded_debate_supported_passage: The recorded debate at the final stage showed support for passage and no opposition.

members.legal_issue: A failure to record the formal putting of a motion does not invalidate legislation when the authenticated bill establishes that it was passed and the omission is only a procedural irregularity.
material_facts: The official report of legislative proceedings did not record that the Speaker formally put the motion to pass the bill.
The authenticated bill bore the Speaker’s endorsement that the Assembly had passed it, and the proceedings showed no dissent to the motion.
members.legal_principle: Article 212(1) bars courts from inquiring into legislative proceedings on the ground of an alleged irregularity of procedure. The authenticated bill and the Speaker’s endorsement supported the conclusion that the bill had been passed.
members.conclusion: The omission did not invalidate the Act; at most, it was an irregularity of legislative procedure.

predicates.legislative_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law based on how the legislature conducted its proceedings.
predicates.authenticated_bill_records_passage: The bill authenticated by the presiding officer records that the legislature passed it.
predicates.only_defect_is_omitted_formal_record_of_: The asserted defect is only that the formal putting or recording of the motion is absent from the official proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A bill is duly passed when the Speaker certifies that it was passed, despite the official proceedings omitting a record that the final motion was put and carried.
material_facts: The Assembly considered the bill through its final reading, and the proceedings recorded the motion that it be passed and speeches supporting it without recording a final vote or declaration that it carried.
The Speaker certified on the printed bill that it had been passed; that certification was made before the Speaker later signed the printed proceedings.
The speeches and the course of the Assembly proceedings disclosed no opposition to passing the bill.
members.legal_principle: The Speaker’s authentication of a bill as passed is conclusive evidence of passage, consistently with the parliamentary practice described in Craies’ Statute Law and May’s Parliamentary Practice. The Court also treated any procedural omission as an irregularity rather than a defect invalidating the enactment, referring to article 212 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Speaker’s certificate was conclusive proof that the bill was passed, and the omission in the proceedings did not invalidate the Act; in any event, any failure formally to put the motion was only a procedural irregularity.

predicates.proceedings_omit_final_vote_record: The official proceedings do not record that the final motion was put to a vote or carried.
predicates.final_vote_not_formally_put: The final motion may not have been formally put to the legislature.

members.legal_issue: The omission to formally put a motion for passage of a bill to the legislative assembly is a procedural irregularity where the bill was authenticated as passed and the assembly’s support was overwhelming.
material_facts: At the bill’s third reading, the Speaker read the motion that the bill be passed, after which members spoke in support amid general acclamation.
The official report did not record that the Speaker formally put the question or that the motion was carried.
The Speaker authenticated the bill with an endorsement that the assembly had passed it, and no dissenting voice was raised.
members.legal_principle: Article 212(1) bars judicial inquiry into mere irregularities of legislative procedure. The court relied on the Speaker’s authenticated endorsement and the circumstances showing the assembly’s support, and held that the omission did not establish that the bill had failed to pass.
members.conclusion: The omission did not invalidate the law; at most, it was an irregularity of procedure.

members.legal_issue: A bill reserved by a Governor for presidential consideration and assented to by the President need not first receive the Governor’s assent or be submitted to the President a second time.
material_facts: The legislative assembly passed the bill and the Governor reserved it for the President’s consideration.
The President assented to the bill.
The bill was not first assented to by the Governor and then reserved again for presidential consideration.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed articles 200, 201, 31(3) and 31(4) of the Constitution together. A bill reserved by the Governor may become law through the President’s assent, and requiring the President to assent twice to the same bill would be a meaningless formality.
members.conclusion: The presidential assent was sufficient; the Constitution did not require a preliminary gubernatorial assent or a second reservation and assent.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the validity of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.governor_reserved_passed_bill: The Governor reserved a bill passed by the legislature for presidential consideration.
predicates.president_assented_to_reserved_bill: The President assented to the bill that had been reserved.

members.legal_issue: A State law reserved for the President’s consideration and assented to by the President need not first receive the Governor’s assent to have effect under the constitutional requirement for acquisition laws.
material_facts: The State acquisition bills were passed by their respective State Legislatures and reserved by the Governors for the President’s consideration.
The challengers argued that the bills also required the Governors’ assent before presidential assent.
members.legal_principle: Articles 31(3) and 200 contemplate reservation of a bill by the Governor for the President’s consideration without the Governor first assenting to it. The Court interpreted the constitutional references to a law and a bill in their procedural context and rejected the proposed requirement of two assents.
members.conclusion: The constitutional requirement was satisfied by reservation of the bill and the President’s assent; an additional prior assent by the Governor was not required.

rule.if: state_acquisition_bill_challenged and bill_reserved_for_president and president_assented and challenge_requires_additional_governor_assent

predicates.state_acquisition_bill_challenged: A party challenged the validity of a State law authorizing compulsory acquisition.

predicates.president_assented: The President assented to the reserved bill.
predicates.challenge_requires_additional_governor_a: The challenger claimed that the Governor must also have assented before the bill was reserved.

members.legal_issue: A state bill reserved for the President’s consideration may become law upon presidential assent without prior gubernatorial assent or a second reservation for presidential consideration.
material_facts: After the Assembly passed the bill, the Governor reserved it for the President’s consideration rather than first assenting to it.
The President assented to the bill, which was then published as an Act.
members.legal_principle: Articles 31(3) and 31(4), read with articles 200 and 201 of the Constitution, allow the Governor to reserve a passed bill for the President and the President to assent to it. The President may perform the relevant functions at the same time, and the term “Legislature” in article 31(4) refers to the legislative House or Houses, not the Governor.
members.conclusion: The President’s assent was sufficient; the Constitution did not require prior assent by the Governor or a second reservation and assent.

predicates.president_assented: The President assented to the bill.

members.legal_issue: A State law requiring presidential assent for effect may be reserved by the Governor as a bill without first receiving the Governor’s assent.
material_facts: The relevant State bills were passed by the legislative houses and reserved by the Governors for the President’s consideration.
The Presidents assented to the bills, and the challengers argued that the Governors’ assent was also required before presidential assent.
members.legal_principle: Under articles 200 and 31(3), a Governor may reserve a bill for presidential consideration; a bill reserved in that way can become law upon presidential assent without a prior gubernatorial assent. The court distinguished a bill reserved for assent from a law already assented to by the Governor.
members.conclusion: The Constitution did not require both the Governor’s assent and the President’s assent in those circumstances.

predicates.president_assents_to_bill: The President gives assent to the reserved bill.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may leave the executive to determine details of compensation payment after the legislature has fixed the governing method and essential terms.
material_facts: The statute authorized compensation to be paid in cash, bonds, or a combination of both, specified the nature of the bonds and the instalment structure, and provided for interest.
The executive was left to determine the proportion payable in cash and bonds and the manner of payment, matters connected with the State’s available funds.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may delegate details after settling the policy and essential principles of the law. The Court relied on The State of Bombay v. Narottamdas Jethabai and Queen v. Burah. It distinguished an impermissible transfer of essential legislative functions from a limited administrative discretion concerning implementation.
members.conclusion: The delegation of those payment details to the State Government was valid and did not amount to an abdication of essential legislative power.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.legislature_fixed_compensation_payment_o: The legislature specified the available forms of payment and the essential terms governing compensation.
predicates.executive_discretion_limited_to_payment_: The executive was left to decide implementation details such as the proportion and manner of payment.

members.legal_issue: Delegating the choice of the proportion of compensation paid in cash or bonds and the detailed timing of bond payments is permissible when the legislature establishes the basic payment framework and policy.
material_facts: The Bihar law specified that compensation could be paid in cash, bonds, or a combination of both.
It prescribed the nature of the bonds, the number of equal instalments, and the interest payable.
It left to the State Government the proportion paid in cash and bonds and details of payment, which depended on the State’s financial resources.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may delegate matters of detail after settling the policy and essential framework of the law. The court relied on The State of Bombay v. Narottamdas Jethabai and Queen v. Burah, and distinguished essential legislative functions from implementation details.
members.conclusion: The delegation of those payment details to the executive was valid.

predicates.a_challenge_to_delegated_rulemaking: The proceeding challenges a law on the ground that the legislature delegated lawmaking authority to the executive.
predicates.legislature_sets_basic_compensation_fram: The legislature specifies the permissible forms of payment and the essential terms of any bonds or instalments.
predicates.executive_receives_only_payment_details_: The executive is left to determine payment proportions or timing that depend on administrative or financial circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may delegate rulemaking about implementation details when the statute itself establishes the main legislative principles.
material_facts: The Act established the main principles governing acquisition and compensation.
It left details such as interest rates and the form, proportion, and timing of compensation payments to executive rules.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may set the main principles and leave matters of detail to rulemaking. The Court considered sections 6(e), 6(g), and 68 of the Act and held that the matters left to the Government were details rather than essential legislative choices. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.
members.conclusion: The delegation was within permissible limits and did not delegate essential legislative power.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_rulemaking: A party challenges authority delegated by a statute to the executive to make rules.
predicates.statute_sets_main_legislative_principles: The statute itself establishes the principal policy and governing standards.
predicates.delegated_matters_are_implementation_det: The delegated matters concern details for implementing the statutory scheme.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may leave administrative details to the executive when the legislature itself has laid down the main principles governing the matter.
material_facts: The Act set out the main principles concerning the acquisition and compensation scheme.
It left details, including matters concerning interest and the form or timing of payment, to be prescribed by the executive.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may prescribe the governing principles and delegate matters of detail to rule-making authorities. The Court considered the Act’s provisions, including sections 6(e), 6(g) and 68, in light of the legislative powers concerning acquisition and compensation under List II, Entry 36 and List III, Entry 42.
members.conclusion: The delegation was within permissible limits and did not delegate essential legislative power.

predicates.legislature_sets_main_principles: The legislature itself establishes the principal rules governing the legislative scheme.
predicates.executive_is_left_only_administrative_de: The executive is authorized to prescribe implementation details rather than decide the scheme’s essential policy.

members.legal_issue: A customary holder of ancestral agricultural land may transfer it for consideration without the consent of descendants or reversionary heirs, unless the transfer is for an immoral purpose.
material_facts: The appellants, who were the holder’s sons, challenged his sale of ancestral agricultural land to the purchasers.
The parties were Jats, and the land was held in the relevant customary-law area.
The appellants alleged that the sale was for immoral purposes, but the courts found that it was not.
Numerous earlier decisions had consistently recognized an unrestricted customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration, and customary-law records supported that understanding.
The trial court and the High Court rejected the challenge to the sale.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the local customary law as shown by the Riwaj-i-am for Rohtak District, Joseph’s Customary Law Manual, and Tupper’s Statements of Customary Law, together with the consistent line of decisions including Telu v. Chuni, Pahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh, Sheoji v. Fajar Ali Khan, and other cited cases. It declined to revive the contrary view in Budal v. Kirpa Ram, which had not been followed and was considered unsatisfactory.
members.conclusion: The customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration was established, and the sale could not be set aside on the grounds advanced because it was not for an immoral purpose.

rule.if: ancestral_transfer_challenge and customary_power_supported_by_settled_authorities and transfer_for_consideration and transfer_not_for_immoral_purpose

predicates.ancestral_transfer_challenge: Descendants or reversionary heirs brought a proceeding challenging a holder’s transfer of ancestral land.
predicates.customary_power_supported_by_settled_aut: The applicable customary records and a consistent body of decisions support the holder’s power to transfer ancestral land for consideration.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The holder transferred the ancestral land in exchange for consideration.
predicates.transfer_not_for_immoral_purpose: The court found that the transfer was not made for an immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: The customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration does not differ according to whether the holder has sons.
material_facts: The holder who sold the ancestral land had sons, who were the appellants challenging the sale.
The customary-law manual described the power of a holder with sons as doubtful, but also contained broader statements supporting the power to alienate land.
Earlier decisions had consistently recognized the power even where the holder had sons, without distinguishing between holders with and without sons.
The court found no adequate customary record supporting a distinction based on the existence of sons.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on the settled line of customary-law decisions recognizing the power of a holder with sons, the absence of a supported distinction in the customary records, Tupper’s general account of sales and mortgages, and the agnatic theory discussed in Gujar v. Sham Das. It held that a doubtful statement in Joseph’s Manual was insufficient to displace the settled law.
members.conclusion: The existence of sons does not restrict the holder’s customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration.

predicates.ancestral_transfer_challenge: Descendants or reversionary heirs brought a proceeding challenging a holder’s transfer of ancestral land.
predicates.holder_has_sons: The holder of the ancestral land had sons when making the transfer.
predicates.customary_authorities_recognize_transfer: The applicable customary records and settled decisions recognize the holder’s transfer power without distinguishing between holders who have sons and those who do not.

members.legal_issue: A customary holder of ancestral agricultural land may transfer it for consideration, and the transfer is not liable to be set aside by an heir unless it was for an immoral purpose.
material_facts: The land was ancestral agricultural land held by Jats of the relevant customary community.
The holder sold the land for consideration.
The holder’s sons and other reversionary heirs sought to have the sale declared void against them.
Although the heirs alleged an immoral purpose, the courts found that the sale was not for such a purpose.
The courts below found that the applicable custom permitted the holder to transfer the land, consistently with numerous earlier decisions.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on the Rohtak customary records, including the Riwaj-i-am recorded in Joseph’s Customary Law Manual and Tupper’s Statements of Customary Law, and on the consistent line of decisions recognizing the holder’s power, including Telu v. Chuni, Giani v. Tek Chand, Behari v. Bhola, Abdul Rafi Khan v. Lakshmi Chand, Ram Datt v. Khushi Ram, Pahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh, Sohan Lal v. Rati Ram, Suraj Mal v. Birju, and Sheoji v. Fajar Ali Khan. It held that Budal v. Kirpa Ram, which had taken a contrary view, had not been followed and was not a satisfactory basis for reviving that view.
members.conclusion: The holder had customary power to transfer the ancestral land for consideration, and the sale was not liable to be set aside at the instance of his sons or other reversionary heirs because it was not for an immoral purpose.

rule.if: heir_challenge_to_transfer and customary_transfer_power and transfer_for_consideration and not immoral_purpose

predicates.heir_challenge_to_transfer: An heir seeks to have a holder’s transfer of ancestral land declared ineffective against the heir.
predicates.customary_transfer_power: The applicable custom permits the holder to transfer the ancestral land for consideration.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The holder transferred the land in exchange for consideration.
predicates.immoral_purpose: The transfer was made for an immoral purpose.
predicates.transfer_not_set_aside_at_heirs_instance: The transfer is not set aside at the instance of an heir.

members.legal_issue: Under the applicable custom, the holder’s power to transfer ancestral land for consideration does not depend on whether the holder has a son.
material_facts: The holder had sons who challenged his sale of ancestral agricultural land.
The applicable customary records did not establish a distinction between a holder with sons and one without sons.
Courts had consistently recognized the power to transfer ancestral property for consideration even when the holder had sons.
The court considered the view that restrictions on alienation, where they exist, rest on an agnatic theory and do not justify distinguishing holders by whether they have sons.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on the customary records and the consistent decisions recognizing the power of holders with sons, and declined to treat the doubt expressed in Joseph’s Customary Law Manual as sufficient to unsettle that settled law. It also referred to the agnatic theory discussed in Gujar v. Sham Das. Budal v. Kirpa Ram was not followed because it had not been followed in later decisions and was an unsatisfactory authority.
members.conclusion: The existence of sons does not restrict the holder’s customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration.

predicates.customary_transfer_power: The applicable custom permits the holder to transfer the ancestral land for consideration.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The holder transferred the land in exchange for consideration.
predicates.sons_do_not_limit_transfer_power: The holder’s sons do not restrict the holder’s power to make the transfer.

members.legal_issue: Self-acquired immovable property can become part of a customary impartible estate when its holder intends to incorporate it.
material_facts: The estate was ancestral, belonged to an undivided Hindu family, and descended by primogeniture.
The dispute concerned whether immovable properties acquired after the original grant had become part of the impartible estate.
The Court found that incorporation depends on the intention of the holder, which may be inferred from conduct and other evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi, a customary impartible ancestral estate remains joint family property insofar as the right of survivorship survives, even though partition and certain other ordinary joint-family rights do not. The power to incorporate self-acquired immovable property depends on the holder’s intention and may be excluded by statute or custom. The Court also referred to Collector of Madura v. Mootoo Ramalinga Sathupathy on the recognition of proven usage.
members.conclusion: A holder of a customary impartible estate may incorporate self-acquired immovable property into it by declaring that intention; the property then acquires the estate’s incidents, including impartibility and descent by primogeniture, unless statute or custom excludes that power.

rule.if: partition_suit and customary_impartible_estate and self_acquired_immovable_property and holder_intended_incorporation and not incorporation_power_excluded

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.customary_impartible_estate: The family holds an estate that custom makes indivisible and that descends to a single heir.
predicates.self_acquired_immovable_property: The holder acquired the immovable property separately rather than receiving it as part of the estate.
predicates.holder_intended_incorporation: The holder’s declaration, conduct, or other evidence shows an intention to make the acquired property part of the impartible estate.
predicates.incorporation_power_excluded: A statute or family custom prevents the holder from incorporating the property.

members.legal_issue: Property is incorporated into an impartible estate only when the evidence shows the holder intended to make it part of the estate.
material_facts: The Prince of Wales Market was built on land belonging to the estate to provide a public amenity in the estate’s principal town, and both lower courts found it had been incorporated.

The leasehold rights in nine villages arose from a settlement involving the estate; the estate holder actively participated, the lessee was treated as a nominee, and the rights were administered and treated as part of the estate.
The Court upheld the findings that the market and village leasehold rights were incorporated.
members.legal_principle: The decisive test for incorporation of immovable property is the holder’s intention, assessed from the evidence as a whole. Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi recognises the power to incorporate self-acquired immovable property into a customary impartible estate. Where both lower courts have found incorporation on the evidence, the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb the concurrent finding concerning the market.
members.conclusion: The Prince of Wales Market and the permanent leasehold rights in the nine villages were incorporated into the impartible estate.

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.customary_impartible_estate: The family holds an estate that custom makes indivisible and that descends to a single heir.
predicates.property_built_on_estate_land_for_public: The holder built the property on estate land to provide a public amenity in the estate’s principal town.
predicates.acquired_rights_administered_and_treated: The holder actively participated in acquiring the rights, and the rights were subsequently administered and treated as part of the estate.

members.legal_issue: Immovable property acquired by the holder may become part of an impartible estate when the holder intended to incorporate it into that estate.
material_facts: Additional lands were acquired from income derived from the impartible estate.
The properties were treated as incorporated into the estate, and the Court found them to be part of it.
The properties were claimed as divisible family property.
members.legal_principle: Incorporation of immovable property into an impartible estate depends on the holder’s intention, which may be express or inferred from conduct and treatment of the property. Income from the estate does not by itself make an acquisition part of the estate. The Court relied on Smt. Rani Prabha Kumari Dibi v. Jagdish Chunder Dhabal, Janki Pershad Singh v. Dwarka Pershad Singh, Murtaza Husain Khan v. Mohd. Yasin Ali Khan, Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, and Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj v. Shri Pushavathi Visweswar Gajapathi Raj.
members.conclusion: The acquired lands found to have been incorporated into the estate were part of the impartible estate and were not partible.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A family member brought a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.immovable_property_acquired_by_estate_ho: The holder of an impartible estate acquired immovable property.
predicates.holder_intended_incorporation: The holder’s intention to incorporate the acquired property into the estate was shown by express evidence or by the holder’s conduct and treatment of it.

members.legal_issue: A holder of a customary impartible estate may incorporate subsequently acquired immovable property into it by demonstrating an intention to do so, and property incorporated before the governing enactment is included in the scheduled estate.
material_facts: The estate was a customary impartible estate included in the schedule to the earlier enactment.
The holder had acquired immovable property after the original grant and before the enactment.
The parties disputed whether scheduled-estate status was confined to the property described in the original grant.
members.legal_principle: Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi establishes that, unless excluded by statute or custom, a holder of a customary impartible estate may incorporate self-acquired immovable property by declaring an intention to do so. Incorporation turns on intention, which may be established by conduct or other evidence. Sections 2(2), 2(3), and 3 of the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904 did not restrict the scheduled estate to the original grant; property incorporated before that Act could form an integral part of the scheduled estate. The principle does not apply to movable property, which may be impartible only if a family custom to that effect is proved.
members.conclusion: The enactment did not confine the estate to the original grant; immovable property incorporated into the estate before the enactment could form part of the scheduled estate, with incorporation determined on the facts of each property.

rule.if: customary_impartible_estate and subsequently_acquired_immovable_property and incorporation_intended and incorporation_before_enactment

predicates.customary_impartible_estate: The estate is treated as indivisible under a family custom.
predicates.subsequently_acquired_immovable_property: The holder acquired immovable property after the original estate had been granted.
predicates.incorporation_intended: The holder's declaration, conduct, or other evidence shows an intention to make the acquisition part of the impartible estate.
predicates.incorporation_before_enactment: The holder's incorporation of the property occurred before the enactment governing the scheduled estate.

members.legal_issue: Differential valuation by belting may be used for an extensive parcel where local circumstances support a higher value for land adjoining an important road, and the value of a tiny plot is not a proper measure for a large acquisition.
material_facts: The acquired property was extensive and included a strip adjoining a road that was valued more highly than the land behind it.
The owner had sought application of the belting method at an earlier stage and later objected to it.
The land was uneven, with differences in level and scattered boulders, and the courts considered the local circumstances and the distinction between a tiny plot and a large acquired area.
members.legal_principle: The appropriate method of valuation depends on local circumstances, and land adjoining an important road may have greater value because of its potential use or commercial exploitation. The Court referred to Mohini Mohan v. Province of Bengal, AIR 1951 Cal. 246, and Kunjukrishna v. State, AIR 1953 T.C. 177, while noting the limitations on the principle; it also recognized that the value of a tiny plot is not a proper measure for an extensive acquisition.
members.conclusion: The belting method was not an error in these circumstances, and the owner’s objection to it was rejected.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and extensive_parcel_acquired and (roadside_strip_has_distinct_value or parcel_has_differing_local_features) and owner_earlier_sought_belting

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the State.
predicates.extensive_parcel_acquired: The acquisition concerns a large parcel rather than a small plot.
predicates.roadside_strip_has_distinct_value: A strip adjoining an important road has a distinct potential-use or commercial value compared with land farther from the road.
predicates.parcel_has_differing_local_features: The parcel’s local physical or situational features bear on the relative value of different parts of it.
predicates.owner_earlier_sought_belting: The owner sought application of differential valuation by belting at an earlier stage of the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: The belting system is an appropriate method for valuing a large acquired tract when its parcels differ in location and roadside frontage.
material_facts: The acquisition comprised a large tract assembled from land belonging to several owners, with parcels at different locations and one side abutting a road.
The land abutting the road had a higher value than land farther inside the tract.
The landowners did not object to the classification before the Collector and did not show why applying the method was improper.
members.legal_principle: The belting system is a judicially accepted method where different parcels with different locations form a large, non-compact acquired tract; roadside land may have greater value than land farther from the road. The Court relied on Union of India v. Mangatu Ram (1997) 6 SCC 59 and Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Ltd. v. G. Mohan Reddy (2010) 15 SCC 412.
members.conclusion: The courts below were justified in applying the belting system to determine the market value of the acquired land.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and large_noncompact_tract and parcels_differ_in_location and (roadside_frontage_creates_value_difference or landowners_fail_to_show_method_improper)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.large_noncompact_tract: The acquired land forms a large tract that is not a single compact block.
predicates.parcels_differ_in_location: The acquired parcels occupy different locations within the tract.
predicates.roadside_frontage_creates_value_differen: Some acquired land abuts a road and is more valuable than land farther from it.
predicates.landowners_fail_to_show_method_improper: The landowners do not establish why applying the belting system is improper.

members.legal_issue: The belting method is appropriate for valuing a large area of urban land where frontage land is more attractive than interior land.
material_facts: The acquired urban tract was large and had frontages on two roads as well as substantial interior land.
The tribunal divided the land into frontage and interior belts and applied lower per-unit values to belts farther from the roads.
The parties did not challenge the use of the belting method or the depth and relative valuation of the belts.
members.legal_principle: Market value for compulsory acquisition is assessed under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as modified by the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911. Where a large area in an urban locality is acquired, the belting method is appropriate because land fronting main roads is ordinarily more attractive than land without such frontage.
members.conclusion: The belting method was appropriate for determining the market value of the large urban tract.

predicates.large_urban_land_acquisition: A large area of land in an urban locality is being valued for acquisition.
