predicates.agent_has_interest_in_agency_subject_mat: The agent has an interest in the property or fund that is the subject matter of the agency.
predicates.authority_given_to_protect_that_interest: The principal gave the agent authority to deal with that property or fund to secure or satisfy the agent’s interest.

members.legal_issue: Different practical effects within a territorially defined taxpayer class do not amount to unjust discrimination when the measure applies uniformly and the differences arise incidentally from variations in crop timing.
material_facts: The measure applied to taxpayers throughout the newly added territory and imposed the same tax treatment on them.

Evidence showed that crop-harvesting seasons varied, but most crops were harvested during similar periods across the territory; the asserted difference principally concerned one crop in part of the territory.
The resulting differences in taxpayers’ income timing were not shown to result from taxpayers being singled out for different treatment.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a law’s real effect is decisive, but equality and uniformity within a class are not defeated by advantages or disadvantages arising incidentally from a peculiar situation, so long as persons are not singled out for special treatment. This principle applies to taxation laws, subject to the requirements of reasonable classification. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, Purshottam Govindji Halai v. Shree B. M. Desai, and Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The differences in crop timing did not establish unjust discrimination between taxpayers within the class covered by the measure.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_challenge and uniform_treatment_within_tax_class and practical_difference_from_crop_timing and no_individuals_singled_out

predicates.constitutional_tax_challenge: A person challenges a tax measure on equality grounds.
predicates.uniform_treatment_within_tax_class: The measure gives taxpayers in the relevant class the same legal treatment.
predicates.practical_difference_from_crop_timing: Taxpayers experience different practical effects because their crops are harvested at different times.
predicates.no_individuals_singled_out: The measure does not select particular taxpayers within the class for special treatment.

members.legal_issue: Applying a uniform levy to a class of landholdings is not discriminatory merely because the quality of their produce differs.
material_facts: The same method of levy applied to the tea estates in the relevant class, although the quality of tea produced by different estates could vary.
The petitioners did not establish hostile or unequal treatment resulting from that difference.
members.legal_principle: The burden rests on the person alleging discrimination to prove hostile unequal treatment, not merely a possible difference in outcomes. The Court applied the principle stated in Twyford Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Kerala and Anr. and recognized that a legislature may use a uniform method inherent in a tax scheme.
members.conclusion: The uniform method of levy was not shown to be discriminatory.

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_tax and same_tax_method_applies_to_class and produce_quality_differs and not hostile_unequal_treatment_proved

predicates.equality_challenge_to_tax: A constitutional challenge alleges that a tax treats members of a class unequally.
predicates.same_tax_method_applies_to_class: The same method of taxation is applied to the relevant class of properties or taxpayers.
predicates.produce_quality_differs: The quality of produce varies among members of the taxed class.
predicates.hostile_unequal_treatment_proved: The challenger establishes hostile or unequal treatment among members of the class.

members.legal_issue: A uniform tax on different crop-yielding plantations does not violate equality merely because the plantations differ in yield or profitability when the tax scheme uses measures intended to equalize the burden and hostile unequal treatment is not established.
material_facts: The tax applied to land used for specified plantations, and only land on which crops had begun to yield was included.

For several plantation types, the taxable extent was calculated by converting the number of yielding plants or trees into an area; for tea and cardamom, the taxable extent was the land on which the plants were grown and had begun to yield crops.
The petitioners relied on differing yields and profits among tea estates and argued that the uniform rate treated unequal plantations alike.
The Court found that the legislature had attempted to equalize the tax burden across plantation types and that the evidence did not establish hostile or unequal treatment among plantations.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to taxation, but legislatures have wide latitude to select taxable subjects, methods, and rates. A person challenging a tax bears a heavy burden to establish hostile unequal treatment, not merely possible inequality. Differences in treatment must be reasonably explained by the legislation’s object, and where different subjects are treated equally there must be a reasonable basis for equalizing their differences. The Court applied Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, East Indian Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income Tax Officer; it distinguished Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Nalla Raja Reddy, New Manek Chowk Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, and State of Kerala v. Haji K. Kutty Naha.
members.conclusion: The majority held that the uniform tax was not shown to be discriminatory and rejected the equality challenge.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax: A person challenges a tax measure on constitutional equality grounds.
predicates.tax_limited_to_yielding_plantations: The taxing authority imposes the tax only on land used for specified crops that have begun to yield.
predicates.plantation_extent_measured_to_equalize_b: The taxing authority uses measures such as yielding-plant counts or crop-yielding land area to compare plantation extents for taxation.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_establish_hostile_une: The person challenging the tax does not conclusively establish that similarly situated taxpayers were treated unequally or that unequal treatment was hostile.

members.legal_issue: A public-interest petitioner has standing to seek review of an exercise of official power that raises a question of public importance.
material_facts: The petitioner was a public-spirited organisation that engaged in public welfare activities.
It challenged the allotment of public land and had also challenged another similar allotment.
The challenge raised issues concerning the exercise of power by State officials.
members.legal_principle: A person may raise a question of public importance involving the exercise of power by public officials even if the person also has a private interest in the matter. The Court relied on Shivajirao Nilangekar Patil v. Mahesh Madhav Gosavi (1987) 1 SCC 227.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the petitioner's standing was rejected.

predicates.public_law_petition_challenging_official: A proceeding asks a court to review the exercise of power by public officials.
predicates.petitioner_is_public_spirited: The petitioner engages in public-interest or public-welfare activity.
predicates.issue_involves_public_importance: The challenge raises a matter of public importance concerning official power.

members.legal_issue: A public-interest organization with a genuine and particular concern in the use of public property may challenge government allotments of that property.
material_facts: The petitioner was a society formed by retired civil servants, journalists and other residents, and challenged government housing arrangements said to affect public property and the State exchequer.
The petition disclosed no personal grievance or oblique motive, and the court considered the concern raised to be just and proper.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 32, a petitioner with a special interest or a concern deeper than that of a busybody may have standing to raise a justiciable public issue. The Court relied on Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union (Regd.) Sindri v. Union of India, (1981) 1 SCC 568, and S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981 Supp SCC 87.
members.conclusion: The petitioner had locus standi and the public-interest petition was maintainable.

predicates.public_interest_petition: An organization brings a public-interest proceeding challenging the use or allocation of public resources.
predicates.organization_special_interest: The organization has a particular concern in the subject matter beyond the general interest shared by the public at large.
predicates.no_oblique_motive: The organization brought the proceeding without an improper personal or collateral motive.

members.legal_issue: A public interest petitioner has standing to challenge an improper disposition of public property.
material_facts: The petition challenged the municipal authority's decision to grant public property to an applicant whose predecessor had not acquired title through the auction.
The petition alleged that the authority's decision was improper and contrary to the Corporation's interests.
The High Court found that the authority had acted against the public interest in disposing of valuable public property.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted public interest standing where petitioners challenged an allegedly improper disposition of public property and the decision implicated the public interest. It relied on Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Muddappa for the principle that public authorities must exercise discretion over public property objectively, rationally, fairly and without arbitrariness.
members.conclusion: The public interest petition was properly entertained, and the petitioners had standing to maintain it.

predicates.public_interest_challenge: The proceeding is a public interest petition challenging a public authority's decision.
predicates.alleged_improper_disposal_of_public_prop: The petition alleges that a public authority improperly disposed of property held for public purposes.

members.legal_issue: Requiring open-auction sales in regulated market yards is within the rule-making power and is not an unreasonable restriction on the right to trade.
material_facts: The rule required consignments of specified agricultural produce brought for sale into principal or sub-market yards to be sold by open auction, except for retail sales specified in the by-laws.
The Act authorized the making of rules to carry out its purposes and contemplated regulation of sale transactions in the market yards.
The Act’s licensing provisions, which restricted trading to licensed persons and made licences subject to rules, were not challenged.
The stated purpose of open auction was to help producers obtain the best price and reduce malpractices associated with private sales by individual negotiation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 9(2), 17 and 40, including section 40(2)(xxvii), supported the rule prescribing the mode of sale. The Court considered open auction a reasonable means of pursuing the Act’s purpose of securing the best price for producers and preventing malpractices; the retail-sale proviso limited the restriction. It distinguished Lala Hari Chand Sarda and Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia, which concerned different licensing defects and did not establish that this sale method was unreasonable.
members.conclusion: The open-auction rule was within the rule-making power and did not violate the traders’ right to carry on business.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and sale_rule_requires_open_auction and sale_method_is_within_rulemaking_authority and auction_advances_producer_protection and retail_sales_are_exempted

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: Traders or other affected persons challenged the constitutionality of a regulated market scheme.
predicates.sale_rule_requires_open_auction: A market rule requires goods brought for sale in regulated yards to be sold through open bidding.
predicates.sale_method_is_within_rulemaking_authori: The governing law authorizes rules to carry out the scheme’s purposes and to prescribe the mode of sale.
predicates.auction_advances_producer_protection: Open bidding is used to help producers obtain better prices and to reduce malpractices associated with private negotiation.
predicates.retail_sales_are_exempted: The rule does not apply its open-bidding requirement to specified retail sales.

members.legal_issue: A rule requiring marketing of declared agricultural produce to take place only in designated markets is within the rule-making authority and is not inconsistent with the licensing provision.
material_facts: Traders were directed to conduct regulated wholesale business only in designated principal or subsidiary markets.
The applicable rule barred marketing declared agricultural produce elsewhere in the market area, while the statute made licensing subject to rules regulating marketing in that area.
members.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1963 authorised rules to carry out the Act's purposes. Section 6 was expressly subject to rules regulating marketing in the market area, so it applied both before and after markets were established and did not conflict with the rule prescribing where marketing must occur. The Court also relied on the Act's scheme of regulated markets and on Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab for the need to confine effective supervision to specified places.
members.conclusion: The rule was within the rule-making authority, consistent with the statute, and reasonable.

predicates.challenge_to_market_only_rule: A proceeding challenges a rule requiring regulated marketing to occur only in designated markets.
predicates.rule_confines_marketing_to_designated_ma: The rule directs persons to conduct regulated marketing in designated markets rather than elsewhere in the market area.
predicates.statute_makes_licensing_subject_to_marke: The governing scheme makes licensing subject to rules that regulate where marketing may occur.

members.legal_issue: Requiring sales and purchases of agricultural produce, including trader-to-trader transactions, to occur in designated markets is not an excessive restriction on the right to carry on trade.
material_facts: The challenged requirement confined marketing transactions to designated markets.

The Court found that dispersing traders across the market area would make supervision difficult, increase the resources required for control, and reduce the availability of market facilities and effective competition for producers.
The market system provided services and facilities that benefited traders as well as producers and consumers.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the constitutional protection of the right to carry on trade and held that localising transactions in markets was helpful and necessary for regulation, control, supervision, and provision of facilities. It reasoned that effective control was less practicable if traders were dispersed throughout a market area and that the market system served traders as well as producers and consumers.
members.conclusion: The requirement that transactions occur in the market was not harsh or an excessive restriction on the right to carry on trade.

predicates.challenge_to_trade_restriction: A proceeding challenges a requirement affecting where a person may conduct trade in regulated produce.
predicates.regulated_transactions_confined_to_marke: The requirement confines regulated transactions to designated markets.
predicates.market_localization_enables_effective_co: Concentrating transactions in designated markets makes supervision, control, or provision of market facilities more effective.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff who is treated as a party to the transaction and seeks to avoid a document must pay court fee for cancellation even when the relief is framed as a declaration that the document is null and void.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declarations that several sale deeds were null and void and also sought a permanent injunction.
The plaintiff alleged that sale documents had been fabricated using signatures obtained on blank papers in connection with a proposed loan and agreement for sale.
The defendants sought rejection of the plaint unless court fee was paid under the provision governing cancellation of documents.
The Court treated the plaintiff as a party to the transaction and held that the substance of the relief sought was cancellation of the sale deeds.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 40 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, a suit for cancellation of a document is valued by reference to the value of the subject matter of the document. A party to a document who seeks to avoid it must seek cancellation; framing the relief as a declaration does not change its substance. A non-executant seeking only a declaration that a document is invalid or not binding is differently situated and may be governed by Section 25(d). The Court relied on Chellakannu v. Kolanji and the distinction stated in Suhrid Singh alias Sardool Singh v. Randhir Singh, and considered Siddha Construction and G. Seethadevi; it also distinguished Shailendra Bhardwaj because that case concerned a state amendment not applicable here.
members.conclusion: The court fee was payable under Section 40 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, notwithstanding that the relief was framed as a declaration that the sale deeds were null and void. The orders refusing the defendants’ application were set aside, and the trial court was directed to allow time to pay the requisite court fee.

predicates.document_invalidation_suit: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking to invalidate a document affecting rights in property.
predicates.plaintiff_party_to_impugned_transaction: The plaintiff is treated as a party to the transaction from which the challenged document arose.
predicates.plaintiff_seeks_to_avoid_document: The plaintiff seeks relief that would set aside or avoid the challenged document, even if the requested relief is described as a declaration.

members.legal_issue: The court fee for a non-executant seeking a declaration that transfer deeds do not bind him or his share, together with consequential possession, is determined under the rules for declaratory suits with consequential relief rather than as a suit to cancel the deeds.
material_facts: The plaintiff had not executed the sale deeds at issue.
The plaint sought a declaration that the deeds did not bind the co-parcenary and sought joint possession; it did not seek cancellation of the deeds.
The lower courts treated the prayers as seeking cancellation and required court fees based on the consideration stated in the deeds.
members.legal_principle: Under the Court-fees Act, 1870 as amended in Punjab, an executant seeking to avoid a deed must seek its cancellation and pay ad valorem court fee on the consideration stated in it. A non-executant seeking a declaration that a deed is invalid or not binding does not seek cancellation. If that non-executant is in possession and seeks only a declaration, the fixed fee under Entry 17(iii) of the Second Schedule applies; if not in possession and seeking consequential possession, section 7(iv)(c) applies, subject to its second proviso requiring valuation not below the value calculated under section 7(v). No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The court fee was to be calculated under section 7(iv)(c) read with section 7(v), with reference to the plaint averments, rather than on the sale consideration stated in the deeds.

rule.if: suit_court_fee_dispute and plaintiff_is_non_executant and seeks_declaration_deed_not_binding and seeks_consequential_possession and not seeks_cancellation

predicates.suit_court_fee_dispute: The proceeding is a suit in which the court fee payable for the reliefs sought is disputed.
predicates.plaintiff_is_non_executant: The plaintiff did not execute the transfer deed whose effect is challenged.
predicates.seeks_declaration_deed_not_binding: The plaintiff seeks a declaration that the deed is invalid or does not bind the plaintiff or the plaintiff’s share.
predicates.seeks_consequential_possession: The plaintiff seeks possession as consequential relief to the declaration.
predicates.seeks_cancellation: The plaintiff asks the court to cancel the deed.
predicates.court_fee_assessed_under_declaratory_con: The court fee is assessed under the method applicable to a declaratory decree with consequential relief, subject to the applicable property-valuation rules.

members.legal_issue: A declaratory suit seeking to invalidate a will and sale deed is subject to the fee provision specifically covering cancellation of valuable instruments, even when no consequential relief is sought.
material_facts: The suit sought declarations that a will and a sale deed were void and their cancellation, but sought no consequential relief.
The suit was brought after the testator’s death and concerned property covered by the will.
The plaintiffs valued the property at Rs. 30,00,000 for jurisdiction but paid a fixed court fee under the declaratory-suit provision.
The applicable state amendment specifically provided for court fees in suits involving cancellation or invalidation of instruments relating to property with monetary value.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as amended in Uttar Pradesh, a suit for or involving cancellation or adjudging void or voidable an instrument securing money or other property having value is subject to court fees computed by reference to the subject matter’s value. Article 17(iii) of Schedule II applies to a declaratory suit without consequential relief only where no other provision of the Act provides for the relief claimed. The Court distinguished Suhrid Singh v. Randhir Singh, (2010) 12 SCC 12, because it considered provisions applicable in Punjab and did not examine the Uttar Pradesh amendment.
members.conclusion: The specific cancellation provision applied, and the court fee had to be computed according to the value of the subject matter; the fixed-fee declaratory provision did not apply.

predicates.declaratory_cancellation_suit: The plaintiff sought a declaration invalidating an instrument and its cancellation.
predicates.instrument_concerns_valuable_property: The instrument at issue secured or related to property having monetary value.
predicates.local_cancellation_fee_rule_applies: The fee rules applicable to the suit specifically provided for cancellation or invalidation suits involving valuable instruments.

members.legal_issue: An auction purchaser who is a distinct third party does not become liable for a former consumer’s electricity arrears merely by purchasing the premises and seeking a new supply or reconnection.
material_facts: The former occupants had received electricity at the premises and left consumption charges unpaid; the Board disconnected the supply for non-payment.
The properties were sold by a financial corporation in statutory recovery proceedings, and the purchasers sought electricity supply for the same premises.
The purchasers were not the former consumers, had no connection with them, and had not assumed their electricity debts under the sale terms or a contract with the Board.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(c) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, a consumer is a person supplied with energy or whose premises are connected to receive it; Rule 2(af) defines an occupier. Sections 22 and 3(2)(f), read with Clause VI of the Schedule, and Section 26 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, concern the obligation to supply subject to applicable requirements. Section 24 permits disconnection for a consumer’s non-payment, but does not make a third-party purchaser liable for that consumer’s contractual debt or create a charge on the premises. The principle is consistent with Souriyar Luka v. Kerala Electricity Board; State of U.P. v. Hindustan Aluminium Corporation explains the interaction of Sections 22 and 26 and Clause VI; Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. v. A.P. State Electricity Board concerns supply on prescribed terms; and Bihar State Electricity Board v. Green Rubber Industries describes the Board-consumer relationship as contractual. A sale under Section 29 of the financial corporation legislation does not, without assumption of the debt, transfer the former consumer’s liability.
members.conclusion: The Board cannot require a distinct auction purchaser to pay the former consumer’s arrears as a condition of supplying electricity to the premises. The former consumer’s contractual liability cannot be enforced against the purchaser, and the purchaser’s bona fides do not alter that rule.

predicates.auction_purchaser_seeks_supply_for_premi: A person who purchased premises at an auction seeks electricity supply or reconnection for those premises.
predicates.prior_consumer_left_unpaid_electricity_c: The former consumer used electricity at the premises and left charges for that use unpaid.
predicates.purchaser_is_distinct_from_prior_consume: The purchaser is a separate person or entity, rather than a continuation of the former consumer.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_assume_old_debt: The purchaser did not agree to take responsibility for the former consumer’s electricity debt.

members.legal_issue: An electricity distributor cannot deny an auction purchaser a fresh connection solely because the former owner left unpaid electricity arrears when the purchaser did not undertake to discharge those arrears.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the property at an auction advertised on an “as is where is” basis.
The purchaser applied for a fresh domestic electricity connection to the acquired property.
The purchaser was unconnected to the former owner and had not undertaken to pay the former owner's electricity arrears.
The distributor refused to release the connection because the former owner’s electricity charges remained unpaid.
The High Court ordered that the connection not be withheld, and the distributor appealed.
members.legal_principle: An auction purchaser who seeks a fresh electricity connection is not liable for the previous owner’s electricity arrears, and the connection cannot be refused solely for non-payment of those arrears where the purchaser did not undertake to pay them. The Court applied Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board, (1995) 2 SCC 648; Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. v. Gujarat Inns (P) Ltd., (2004) 3 SCC 587; and NESCO v. Raghunath Paper Mills (P) Ltd., (2012) 13 SCC 479. Although the auction arose under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, the judgment does not rely on a specific statutory provision as the basis for its ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed, and the distributor could not withhold the purchaser’s fresh electricity connection on account of the former owner’s arrears.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_denial_of_fresh_connection and auction_purchaser_seeks_fresh_connection and sale_notice_says_as_is_where_is and purchaser_unconnected_to_former_owner and purchaser_did_not_assume_former_owner_arrears

predicates.appeal_challenges_denial_of_fresh_connec: A party appeals a ruling that prevented it from denying a fresh electricity connection because of a former consumer’s arrears.
predicates.auction_purchaser_seeks_fresh_connection: A purchaser who acquired property at auction applies for a fresh electricity connection to that property.
predicates.sale_notice_says_as_is_where_is: The auction sale notice states that the property is sold on an “as is where is” basis.
predicates.purchaser_unconnected_to_former_owner: The auction purchaser has no connection to the former owner of the property.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_assume_former_owner_ar: The purchaser did not undertake to discharge the former owner’s electricity arrears.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser cannot be required to pay a previous occupant’s electricity arrears unless an applicable statutory rule or binding term of supply authorizes recovery from the purchaser.
material_facts: A financial corporation auctioned the premises of a borrower to recover its dues, and the purchaser paid the full auction price.
Electricity supply had been disconnected before the auction; the purchaser took possession and obtained a new electricity connection in its own name.
The electricity supplier later demanded arrears incurred by the previous owner and disconnected supply when the purchaser did not pay.
The supplier did not plead or identify any statutory rule or binding term of supply authorizing it to demand the previous owner’s arrears from the purchaser.

The supplier had not demanded those arrears when the purchaser obtained the new connection; the enabling term referred to in the cited later decision had been introduced after the connection was obtained.
members.legal_principle: Electricity arrears do not, as a matter of general law, constitute a charge on the premises, and a purchaser with no contractual relationship to the previous occupant is not ordinarily liable for that occupant’s dues. Under Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board, a fresh connection cannot be made conditional on payment of prior arrears absent a charge or an authorizing statutory rule. Paramount Polymers distinguished Isha Marbles where a binding term of supply expressly authorized recovery from a transferee; Hyderabad Vanaspati Ltd. v. A.P. SEB held that terms notified under Section 49 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 are statutory in character. Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Excel Buildcon Pvt. Ltd. followed Paramount Polymers. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. reiterated that prior dues are not a charge, but may be demanded where applicable rules or binding terms authorize it, provided they are not arbitrary or unreasonable. The court found no such authorization applicable to this case; it did not need to decide whether an authorized term would be invalid on other grounds.
members.conclusion: The previous owner’s electricity arrears could not be enforced against the purchaser on these facts, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: prior_electricity_dues_recovery_claim and subsequent_purchaser_seeks_supply and purchaser_not_previous_consumer and not binding_supply_rule_authorizes_prior_dues

predicates.prior_electricity_dues_recovery_claim: An electricity supplier sought to recover charges incurred by a previous occupant from a later purchaser of the premises.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_seeks_supply: A purchaser of premises sought a new or restored electricity supply for those premises.
predicates.purchaser_not_previous_consumer: The purchaser was not the consumer who incurred the electricity charges and had no contractual relationship with that consumer’s supplier.
predicates.binding_supply_rule_authorizes_prior_due: An applicable binding rule or term of supply authorized the supplier to require payment of the previous occupant’s arrears from the purchaser.
predicates.previous_occupant_dues_not_recoverable_f: The previous occupant’s electricity arrears cannot be recovered from the subsequent purchaser.

members.legal_issue: A cheque-dishonour complaint should not be quashed on disputed factual grounds before the accused has had an opportunity to rebut the presumption arising from admitted cheque issuance.
material_facts: The accused admitted issuing the cheques relied on in the cheque-dishonour complaint.
The accused disputed that the cheques represented an enforceable debt and claimed they had been issued to assist with a land purchase.
That defense required evidence, and the accused had not yet rebutted the statutory presumption in the complaint proceedings.
The High Court quashed the complaint because of the dispute concerning the receipts, but the Supreme Court held that the complaint should proceed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, admission or proof of cheque issuance raises a rebuttable presumption in favour of the holder. The presumption under Section 139 and Section 118(a) of the Indian Evidence Act continues until the accused adduces evidence to rebut it. Disputed factual questions requiring evidence are not a basis to quash a complaint under Section 138 by exercising power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; legal issues such as limitation may be considered separately. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The cheque-dishonour complaint should not have been quashed on the basis of the inter-party dispute and unresolved factual questions. The complaint was restored for adjudication after both sides had an opportunity to present evidence.

rule.if: appeal_from_quashed_cheque_complaint and cheque_issuance_admitted and accused_has_not_rebutted_presumption and disputed_facts_require_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_quashed_cheque_complaint: An appeal challenges an order quashing a cheque-dishonour complaint.
predicates.cheque_issuance_admitted: The accused admits having issued the cheque or cheques relied on in the complaint.
predicates.accused_has_not_rebutted_presumption: The accused has disputed that an enforceable debt existed but has not yet adduced evidence to rebut the presumption arising from cheque issuance.
predicates.disputed_facts_require_evidence: The competing accounts depend on disputed facts that require evidence to resolve.

members.legal_issue: A probable defence supported by the evidence and surrounding circumstances can rebut the presumptions that a cheque was issued for consideration and in discharge of a debt or liability.
material_facts: The cheque was dishonoured for insufficient funds, and the prosecution alleged that it repaid a loan.
The accused’s defence was that the cheque had been provided as security in connection with a property sale, not for repayment of a loan.

Evidence supported the property-sale account, including testimony from the accused and other witnesses, a sale document executed on the cheque date, and evidence that the cheque and document were written with the same pen.
The complainant acknowledged receiving later payments but did not establish the other transaction he claimed those payments concerned.
The trial court found the defence probable and acquitted the accused; the High Court reversed without addressing the trial court’s reasoning.
members.legal_principle: Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 create rebuttable presumptions; Section 138 concerns a cheque issued for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Under M.S. Narayana Menon Alias Mani v. State of Kerala and Another, (2006) 6 SCC 39, the accused rebuts the presumptions on a preponderance of probabilities and may rely on the evidence as a whole, including the complainant’s evidence and surrounding circumstances. The accused need not testify or prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt; once the presumption is rebutted, the complainant must prove the debt without relying on the presumption.
members.conclusion: The defence was sufficiently probable to rebut the statutory presumptions. The burden therefore returned to the complainant to establish the alleged debt, and the High Court was wrong to overturn the acquittal on the reasoning it gave.

predicates.cheque_dishonour_prosecution: The case is a prosecution alleging that a dishonoured cheque was issued to discharge a debt or liability.
predicates.accused_presents_probable_alternative_tr: The accused presents an account of a different transaction explaining why the cheque was given.
predicates.defence_supported_by_evidence_or_circums: Evidence or surrounding circumstances support the accused’s alternative account sufficiently to make it probable.

members.legal_issue: An admitted signature on a dishonoured cheque gives rise to presumptions of consideration and discharge of a debt or liability, which remain unless the accused raises a probable defence sufficient to rebut them.
material_facts: The accused admitted the signature on the dishonoured cheque and the agreement recording the underlying transaction.
The complainant testified that he had advanced money under an agreement for a proposed sale and that the cheque was issued towards repayment of part of the advance when the sale could not proceed.
The accused did not present rebuttal evidence at trial or raise the later account of coercion in the trial or first appeal; he first raised it during arguments in revision.
The notice demanding payment was received but not answered, and the record did not support the claim that the complainant’s relative had used a position of influence to obtain the signatures.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, admission of execution or signature raises rebuttable presumptions that a negotiable instrument was made for consideration and that a cheque was received for discharge of a debt or liability. The accused bears an evidentiary burden to raise a probable defence, assessed on a preponderance of probabilities, and may rely on the complainant’s evidence or other circumstances without testifying. The Court applied K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan, (1999) 7 SCC 510, and the principles summarized in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa, (2019) 5 SCC 418.
members.conclusion: The presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act were not rebutted, so the High Court was wrong to set aside the conviction on that basis.

rule.if: cheque_dishonour_prosecution and accused_admitted_cheque_signature and complainant_evidence_supported_underlying_transaction and no_probable_rebuttal_defence

predicates.cheque_dishonour_prosecution: The proceeding prosecutes an accused for an offence involving a dishonoured cheque.
predicates.accused_admitted_cheque_signature: The accused admitted signing the cheque on which the prosecution is based.
predicates.complainant_evidence_supported_underlyin: The complainant gave evidence and produced material supporting the transaction said to give rise to the cheque liability.
predicates.no_probable_rebuttal_defence: The accused did not present evidence or circumstances sufficient to make a defence probable.

members.legal_issue: An order refusing to recognize a claimed statutory right to review finally determines that right and is a judgment appealable under the applicable Letters Patent and court rules.
material_facts: A party applied to review an earlier order quashing an assessment, asserting that a later enactment conferred a statutory right to review.
The single judge dismissed the application because the enactment did not confer that right in the circumstances.
The appellate bench held that the dismissal was not a judgment and therefore was not appealable.
members.legal_principle: Under clause 10 of the Letters Patent and Chapter VIII, rule 5, an order is a judgment, even on the narrower approach to that term, when it finally determines a substantive right or liability between the parties. The court considered the approaches in The Justices of the Peace for Calcutta v. The Oriental Gas Co., Hadjee Ismael v. Hadjee Mahommed, Tuljaram v. Alagappa, and Manohar v. Baliram, but found it unnecessary to reconcile them or state a general definition.
members.conclusion: The single judge’s order was a judgment under clause 10 of the Letters Patent and Chapter VIII, rule 5 of the court rules; the appellate bench was wrong to hold that no appeal lay.

predicates.special_appeal_from_single_judge_order: A party seeks a special appeal from an order made by a single judge.
predicates.statutory_review_right_claimed: A party claims that a statute gives it a right to have an earlier decision reviewed.
predicates.order_finally_denies_claimed_right: The order finally rejects the claimed statutory right to review.

members.legal_issue: An order deciding an application to set aside an execution auction sale determines substantive rights and is a judgment appealable under the applicable Letters Patent clause.
material_facts: A judgment-debtor applied to set aside an execution auction sale in which the decree-holder had become the purchaser.
A single judge allowed the application, thereby affecting the purchaser’s right to have the sale confirmed and the judgment-debtor’s right to have the sale set aside.
The purchaser challenged the single judge’s order by a Letters Patent appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under clause 10 of the Allahabad High Court Letters Patent, an order is a judgment where it determines a substantive right or liability, even if it does not terminate the underlying suit. An order under Order XXI, rule 90, affects the purchaser’s right to confirmation under rule 92 and the judgment-debtor’s right to seek the sale’s setting aside. The Court relied on the rights-based approach discussed in Justices of the Peace for Calcutta v. Oriental Gas Co. and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Vijay Anand Maharaj, and distinguished the transfer order considered in Asrumati Debi v. Kumar Rupendra Deb Raikot; it also considered Standard Glass Beads Factory v. Shri Dhar.
members.conclusion: The order in the sale-setting-aside proceeding was a judgment, and a Letters Patent appeal against it was maintainable.

predicates.execution_sale_challenge_proceeding: The order arose in a proceeding challenging an auction sale conducted to enforce a judgment or decree.
predicates.order_determines_substantive_sale_rights: The order determined the purchaser’s right to confirmation of the sale or the debtor’s right to have it set aside.

members.legal_issue: An executing court's order setting aside an auction sale as a nullity is appealable when it finally determines the rights of the judgment-debtor and auction purchaser concerning that sale.
material_facts: An auction sale of a judgment-debtor's factory was held in execution of a decree, and a respondent was the highest bidder.
The executing judge set aside the sale as a nullity and ordered a resale; the auction purchaser appealed that order.

The dispute over whether the auction sale was a nullity finally determined the rights of the judgment-debtor and auction purchaser concerning that sale, even though execution proceedings would continue and a resale was ordered.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(2) and 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read together, treat as a decree an execution order that conclusively determines a question relating to execution between the parties, including an auction purchaser. Such a decree is appealable under section 96. The Court applied the finality approach in Jethanand & Sons v. State of Uttar Pradesh and rejected the contrary view in Mrs. Peliti v. Kanshi Gopal; it also relied on the broad construction of section 47 and the inclusion of an execution-sale purchaser as a party. Manilal Mohanlal Shah was followed on the nullity of a sale where mandatory auction requirements are not met.
members.conclusion: The order was a final determination of the parties' rights concerning the sale, fell within the definition of a decree read with the provision governing questions arising in execution, and was appealable.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court is enforcing a decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.order_sets_aside_auction_sale: The executing court makes an order setting aside a property auction sale.
predicates.order_finally_determines_sale_rights_bet: The order conclusively determines the judgment-debtor's and auction purchaser's rights concerning the sale, leaving no further issue between them about that sale.

members.legal_issue: A counterclaim based on a cause of action that accrued before the defendant delivered its defence may be entertained after issues have been framed when the plaintiff’s evidence is still underway and no material prejudice is shown.
material_facts: The defendants filed their counterclaim about two and a half years after issues had been framed.
The cause of action underlying the counterclaim accrued before the defendants filed their written statement.
When the counterclaim was filed, the plaintiff’s evidence had begun but was not complete, and the defendants’ evidence had not begun.
No prejudice to the plaintiff from adjudicating the counterclaim along with the suit was shown.
members.legal_principle: Order VIII Rule 6A(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a defendant to set up a counterclaim for a cause of action accruing before the defendant delivers its defence. Under Rule 6A(2)–(4), the counterclaim has the effect of a cross-suit, and is treated as a plaint. Applying Bollepanda P. Poonacha v. K.M. Madapa, (2008) 13 SCC 179, the Court held that the cause of action must accrue before the defence is delivered. Rohit Singh v. State of Bihar, (2006) 12 SCC 734, did not bar this counterclaim: there, evidence had closed and arguments had been heard, whereas evidence in this suit was ongoing. The Court also found no serious injustice, irreparable loss, or demonstrated prejudice that would justify rejecting the counterclaim.
members.conclusion: The counterclaim was maintainable; the High Court’s order rejecting it was set aside and the trial court’s order accepting it was restored.

rule.if: counterclaim_in_civil_suit and cause_accrued_before_defence and counterclaim_filed_after_issues and plaintiff_evidence_incomplete and defence_evidence_not_started and prejudice_not_shown

predicates.counterclaim_in_civil_suit: A defendant in a civil suit asserts a counterclaim against the plaintiff.
predicates.cause_accrued_before_defence: The cause of action supporting the counterclaim accrued before the defendant delivered its defence.
predicates.counterclaim_filed_after_issues: The defendant filed the counterclaim after the court framed issues in the suit.
predicates.plaintiff_evidence_incomplete: The plaintiff’s evidence had begun but had not been completed when the counterclaim was filed.
predicates.defence_evidence_not_started: The defendant’s evidence had not begun when the counterclaim was filed.
predicates.prejudice_not_shown: The opposing party did not show that adjudicating the counterclaim with the suit would prejudice it.

members.legal_issue: A counterclaim is not barred merely because it is filed after the written defence when its cause of action accrued by the time the defence was delivered or was due, and the counterclaim is within the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The competing claimants filed their written statement denying the plaintiffs’ claim and asserting title to the treasure.
After filing the written statement, the claimants filed a counterclaim seeking title to the treasure.
The cause of action for the counterclaim had arisen before the written statement was filed.
The counterclaim was filed within the applicable limitation period.
members.legal_principle: Order VIII, Rule 6A(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not prohibit filing a counterclaim after delivery of the written statement; it requires that the cause of action have accrued before the defendant delivered the defence or before the time limited for delivering it expired. Under section 3(2)(b) of the Limitation Act, 1963, a counterclaim is treated as a suit for limitation purposes, and Article 113 provides the applicable period where no other period is specified. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The counterclaim was maintainable notwithstanding that it was filed after the written statement.

rule.if: civil_suit_with_counterclaim and counterclaim_filed_after_defence and counterclaim_cause_accrued_by_defence_deadline and counterclaim_within_applicable_limitation

predicates.civil_suit_with_counterclaim: A defendant in a civil suit asserted an independent claim against the plaintiff by counterclaim.
predicates.counterclaim_filed_after_defence: The defendant filed the counterclaim after delivering the written defence.
predicates.counterclaim_cause_accrued_by_defence_de: The cause of action for the counterclaim had accrued before the defence was delivered or before the time allowed for delivering it expired.
predicates.counterclaim_within_applicable_limitatio: The defendant filed the counterclaim within the limitation period applicable to that claim.

members.legal_issue: A counterclaim may be filed after the written statement when its cause of action continued until the time for filing the written statement or its permitted extension.
material_facts: A defendant applied to file a counterclaim after filing a written statement in a pending civil suit.
The application was made on a cause of action alleged to have arisen before or after the suit was instituted and to have continued until the written statement or the extended time for filing it.
The lower court held that the application was not barred merely because it was filed after the written statement.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VIII Rule 6A of the Code of Civil Procedure, the right to file a counterclaim is referable to the accrual of its cause of action. Following Mahendra Kumar v. State of Madhya Pradesh, a counterclaim may be filed after the written statement if its cause of action arose before or after institution of the suit and continued until the written statement or the extended date for filing it.
members.conclusion: The application was not ex facie barred by Order VIII Rule 6A of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the order allowing it to proceed was not interfered with.

predicates.defendant_counterclaim_in_pending_civil_: A defendant in a pending civil suit seeks to bring a counterclaim in that proceeding.
predicates.counterclaim_filed_after_written_stateme: The defendant files the counterclaim after filing the written statement.
predicates.cause_of_action_continued_until_written_: The cause of action for the counterclaim continued until the written statement was filed or the permitted time for filing it expired.

members.legal_issue: Legislation that singles out particular succession claimants, dismisses their claims, and prevents them from establishing their rights in court violates the constitutional guarantee of equal protection when the distinction has no rational basis.
material_facts: A law dismissed the succession claims of two women and their children while leaving other claimants to the estate unaffected.
The excluded claimants asserted that they were entitled to inherit under the personal law governing their community, and no competent court had determined their claims.
The legislation was intended to end a private succession dispute and relied on an adverse report by a non-judicial authority.
The dispute’s lengthy duration did not give it exceptional features warranting different treatment from other succession disputes.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 13(2) and 14 of the Constitution, legislation must not infringe the equal-protection guarantee. A legislature may classify persons to address particular objects, and differentiation alone is not discrimination; the classification must have a rational basis related to the legislative object and must not be arbitrary. In Chiranjit Lal v. Union of India, the Court recognized the presumption of constitutionality and that legislation may concern a single person or entity, but explained that whether those propositions apply depends on the circumstances. They did not justify selecting private succession claimants for exclusion based on a non-judicial report. The State’s legislative power is subject to fundamental rights.
members.conclusion: The legislation was discriminatory and had no rational or reasonable basis, so it violated Article 14 and was void to the extent that it dismissed the claimants’ succession claims.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_law and law_targets_specific_succession_claimants and law_dismisses_their_claims and law_prevents_court_adjudication and law_purpose_is_ending_private_dispute and law_relies_on_nonjudicial_adverse_report and no_exceptional_basis_for_differential_treatment

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law in a court proceeding.
predicates.law_targets_specific_succession_claimant: The law selects particular people asserting rights to inherit an estate for different treatment from other claimants.
predicates.law_dismisses_their_claims: The law itself rejects the selected claimants’ asserted inheritance claims.
predicates.law_prevents_court_adjudication: The law prevents the selected claimants from establishing their asserted rights through ordinary court proceedings.
predicates.law_purpose_is_ending_private_dispute: The law’s purpose is to end a dispute between private claimants rather than to secure a public advantage.
predicates.law_relies_on_nonjudicial_adverse_report: The law’s treatment of the selected claimants rests on an adverse finding by an authority that did not decide the dispute as a court.
predicates.no_exceptional_basis_for_differential_tr: The dispute’s circumstances do not provide a rational and exceptional basis for treating the selected claimants differently from others in the same position.

members.legal_issue: A law that singles out particular persons in a private legal dispute, denies them judicial determination of their rights, and lacks a rational basis for distinguishing them from comparable persons violates the guarantee of equal protection.
material_facts: A public authority had settled land with the affected persons, who took possession and paid rent.
The legislature enacted a law declaring that particular settlement void and directing the affected persons’ eviction, without a judicial determination of the disputed rights.
Other persons held similar settlements, but their settlements were not subjected to the enactment.
The law deprived the affected persons of the ordinary opportunity to have the legality of the settlement and their rights determined by a court.
No rational classification or differentiating attribute was shown to justify singling out the affected persons.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits legislative classification only when it is non-arbitrary and rests on a rational basis related to the legislative object. A law that singles out particular persons, imposes a disability not imposed on comparable persons, and removes their ability to obtain judicial determination of a private dispute is discriminatory. Although legislation is presumed constitutional, that presumption provides little or no assistance where the law contains no classification based on a differentiating attribute. Under Article 13, a law that abridges a fundamental right is void. The Court applied Ameerunnissa Begum v. Mahboob Begum and referred to Gulf of Colorado etc. Co. v. Ellis; it distinguished Chiran v. The Union of India.
members.conclusion: The enactment was discriminatory and void for violating Article 14. The appeal was allowed, and a writ of mandamus was issued restraining action under the enactment and interference with the affected persons’ possession.

rule.if: equal_protection_challenge and private_legal_dispute and law_targets_specific_parties and comparable_parties_not_targeted and judicial_determination_denied and not rational_classification

predicates.equal_protection_challenge: A person challenges a law on the ground that it denies equal protection.
predicates.private_legal_dispute: The law concerns a dispute between private parties over disputed legal rights.
predicates.law_targets_specific_parties: The law singles out particular persons or a particular transaction for a special legal disability.
predicates.comparable_parties_not_targeted: Other persons in materially similar circumstances are not subjected to the same legal disability.
predicates.judicial_determination_denied: The law prevents the affected persons from obtaining ordinary judicial determination of their disputed rights.
predicates.rational_classification: The law distinguishes the affected persons by a rational attribute related to its legislative object.

members.legal_issue: A law that imposes a collection disability on one group but not on comparable groups violates the guarantee of equal protection when no reasonable basis for the distinction is established.
material_facts: A law required the government to collect revenue previously collected by jagirdars and, after deducting expenses, pay it to the jagirdars; an amendment extended the provision to taxes, cesses and forest revenue.
After territorial integration, jagirdars in the area governed by the provision faced this collection disability, while jagirdars in other areas of the same State did not.
The State did not allege or substantiate that the affected jagirdars or their tenures had any substantial distinguishing feature that justified the different treatment.
The challenged provisions remained in force when the Constitution commenced, and the affected holder sought relief against their operation.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 13(1) and 14 of the Constitution, a law in force that is inconsistent with the guarantee of equality is void to the extent of the inconsistency. A classification must bear a reasonable and just relation to the subject of the law, and unequal treatment requires a substantial distinction supporting it. The Court distinguished Frank J. Bowman v. Edward A. Lewis (101 U.S. 22; 25 Law. Ed. 989), where territorial arrangements could be justified by municipal considerations; Ramjilal v. Income Tax Officer, Mohindargarh ([1951] S.C.R. 127), which concerned a reasonable classification for concluding pending proceedings under the law applicable when rights or liabilities accrued; and The State of Punjab v. Ajaib Singh ([1953] S.C.R. 254), where a geographical classification was justified by the similar interests of the class concerned. The Court also noted that Thakur Madan Singh v. Collector of Sikar (Rajasthan Law Weekly, 1954, p. 1) involved a supported basis for classification and distinguished the challenged provision here.
members.conclusion: The provision as amended was void because it contravened the guarantee of equality and equal protection; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_law and unequal_collection_disability_imposed_on_one_group and comparable_groups_left_unburdened and no_substantial_distinction_shown

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A person challenged the validity of a law on the ground that it denied equal protection.
predicates.unequal_collection_disability_imposed_on: The law required one group to surrender or lose control over collection of revenue that it had previously collected.
predicates.comparable_groups_left_unburdened: The law left comparable groups outside the affected group free from the same collection disability.
predicates.no_substantial_distinction_shown: The government did not establish a substantial difference between the affected group and the unburdened groups that justified their different treatment.

members.legal_issue: Publication of a notification covering property for the displaced-persons compensation scheme extinguishes the former owner’s interest and vests the property in the Central Government.
material_facts: A notification covering the properties was published under the displaced-persons compensation and rehabilitation legislation.
The heirs sought possession of the properties after that notification.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, provides for the extinguishment and vesting consequences of a published notification. The Court relied on Basant Ram v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: On publication of the notification, the former owner’s right, title, or interest in the properties was extinguished, and the properties vested absolutely in the Central Government free from encumbrances.

predicates.compensation_scheme_property_case: The proceeding concerns property included in the displaced-persons compensation and rehabilitation scheme.
predicates.notification_covering_property_published: A notification covering the property was published under the applicable compensation and rehabilitation legislation.

members.legal_issue: Publication of a notification vesting property under the displaced-persons compensation scheme extinguished the former owner’s rights in that property.
material_facts: A notification under the displaced-persons compensation legislation was published in respect of the properties.
The former owner’s heirs later sought possession of those properties.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 provided for property covered by a notification under section 12 to vest absolutely in the Central Government, free from encumbrances. The Court relied on Basant Ram v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: On publication of the notification, the former owner’s right, title, or interest in the properties was extinguished, and the properties vested absolutely in the Central Government free from encumbrances.

predicates.civil_claim_for_property: A claimant brings a civil claim seeking property or an interest in it.
predicates.property_included_in_compensation_scheme: A notification under a compensation and rehabilitation scheme covers the property.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of property validly declared evacuee property vests it in the central government and ends its status as evacuee property and the custodian's authority over it.
material_facts: The property had been validly declared evacuee property.
The central government published a notification under the displaced-persons legislation acquiring the property for rehabilitation purposes.
The property was acquired and allotted for the rehabilitation of displaced persons.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(1) and (2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 authorizes acquisition of evacuee property for the specified public purpose and provides that publication extinguishes the evacuee's right, title, and interest and vests the property absolutely in the central government free from encumbrances. Such acquisition requires that the property be evacuee property. The consequence is to divest the custodian of the rights arising from vesting under the evacuee-property legislation. The Court relied on Major Gopal Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property; Basant Ram v. Union of India; Dafedar Niranjan Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property; Haji Siddik Haji Umar v. Union of India; and Dr. Zafar Ali Shah v. Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property.
members.conclusion: Upon publication of the acquisition notification, the property vested absolutely in the central government, ceased to be evacuee property, and was no longer subject to the custodian's powers under the evacuee-property legislation.

predicates.valid_evacuee_property_declaration: The property has been validly declared to have the statutory status that permits its acquisition for displaced-person rehabilitation.
predicates.central_government_acquisition_notificat: The central government publishes a notification acquiring the property for rehabilitation purposes.

members.legal_issue: A written notice given before a change in the governing rent-control framework can satisfy the notice requirement for a later fair-rent proceeding without a fresh notice.
material_facts: The tenant gave the landlord written notice before filing an initial fair-rent suit under the then-existing framework.
After the governing framework changed, the initial plaint was returned for want of jurisdiction and the tenant filed a fresh proceeding before the Rent Controller without giving another notice.
The courts below treated the earlier notice as proper, and the Supreme Court found no basis to hold it insufficient.
members.legal_principle: Section 7(2) of the United State of Gwalior, Indore and Malwa (Madhya Bharat) Accommodation Control Act, Samvat 2006 requires notice in writing but prescribes neither a particular form nor that notice be given after the Act came into force. The Court relied on the provision's text and cited no earlier cases on this point.
members.conclusion: The earlier notice was sufficient; the governing provision did not require that notice be issued in a particular form or after the new framework came into force.

predicates.fair_rent_fixation_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding to have rent fixed for accommodation.
predicates.written_notice_given_before_first_filing: The party seeking rent fixation gave the other party written notice before filing the initial proceeding.
predicates.first_plaint_returned_after_governing_fr: The governing framework changed after the initial proceeding was filed, and the initial plaint was returned before a fresh proceeding was filed.

members.legal_issue: A demand notice served before the amendment remains sufficient for an eviction suit instituted after the amendment when it satisfies the notice requirements that remained unchanged.
material_facts: The landlords served a written demand notice before the amendment took effect.
The notice demanded rent arrears, and the tenant did not pay the demanded arrears within one month after service.
The landlords instituted the eviction suit after the amendment took effect.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(2) was not amended when section 12(3) was amended. Section 12(3)(a) refers to a notice served as required by section 12(2), which did not require the landlord to warn the tenant of the consequences of non-payment. Accordingly, a pre-amendment notice meeting section 12(2) sufficed. The earlier decisions in Dayaram Kashiram Shimpi v. Bansilal Raghunath Marwari and Laxminarayan Nandkishore Shravagi v. Keshardev Baijnath Narsaria concerned the meaning of “at the hearing of the suit” under the earlier law, not a requirement for a new notice after amendment.
members.conclusion: The landlords were not required to serve a fresh notice after the amendment; the earlier notice satisfied the statutory notice requirement.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.demand_notice_before_change: The landlord served a written demand notice before the relevant change in the law took effect.
predicates.notice_met_existing_requirements: The notice made a written demand for rent, and the tenant did not pay the demanded rent within one month after service.

members.legal_issue: A written demand notice served before an amendment remains sufficient for a later eviction suit when the amendment leaves the statutory notice requirement unchanged.
material_facts: The landlord served a written notice demanding rent arrears before the amendment took effect.
The tenant did not pay the demanded arrears within one month after service of the notice.
The amendment changed the provision governing eviction for arrears but did not change the provision requiring the pre-suit notice.
The landlord filed the eviction suit after the amendment took effect.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 12(2) and 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, section 12(3)(a) refers to the notice required by section 12(2). Because the amendment did not alter section 12(2), a notice meeting that section’s requirements remained sufficient. The landlord was not required to tell the tenant what consequences would follow from non-payment.
members.conclusion: The earlier notice satisfied the statutory notice requirement; a fresh notice after the amendment was not required.

rule.if: rent_arrears_eviction_suit and written_demand_before_suit and notice_met_demand_requirements and tenant_unpaid_within_notice_period and amendment_left_notice_requirement_unchanged

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_suit: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding against a tenant on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.written_demand_before_suit: The landlord served the tenant with a written demand for rent before bringing the proceeding.
predicates.notice_met_demand_requirements: The written demand met the requirements that applied to a pre-suit rent notice.
predicates.tenant_unpaid_within_notice_period: The tenant did not pay the demanded rent within the period following service of the notice.
predicates.amendment_left_notice_requirement_unchan: A legislative amendment changed the eviction rule but left the pre-suit notice requirement unchanged.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of a debtor’s property made for adequate consideration to discharge genuine debts is not voidable merely because some creditors are paid while another remains unpaid, where the debtor retains no benefit.
material_facts: The company transferred its assets and used the sale proceeds to pay genuine debts owed to its creditors.
The tax claim remained unpaid after the proceeds were distributed.
The High Court found that the consideration was not inadequate and that the proceeds were used to pay the company’s creditors.
members.legal_principle: Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act makes a transfer intended to defeat or delay creditors voidable, but preferring one creditor over another is not by itself fraudulent if the transfer is for adequate consideration in satisfaction of genuine debts and the debtor retains no benefit. The Court relied on Musahar Sahu v. Hakim Lal, In re Moroney, Middleton v. Pollock, and MA PWA MAY v. S.R.M.M.A. Chettyar Firm.
members.conclusion: The transfer was not voidable under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act merely because the tax creditor remained unpaid after other creditors were paid.

rule.if: creditor_transfer_challenge and genuine_debts_paid and adequate_consideration and debtor_retained_no_benefit

predicates.creditor_transfer_challenge: A creditor challenges a debtor’s transfer of property on the ground that it defeats or delays creditors.
predicates.genuine_debts_paid: The transfer proceeds are applied to discharge genuine debts owed by the debtor.
predicates.adequate_consideration: The debtor receives consideration that is not inadequate for the transferred property.
predicates.debtor_retained_no_benefit: The debtor does not reserve or retain a benefit in the transferred property or its proceeds.
predicates.transfer_not_voidable_merely_for_prefere: The transfer is not voidable merely because some creditors are paid while another creditor remains unpaid.

members.legal_issue: A transfer to a person who is not a creditor is not invalid merely because the transferee is not a creditor when the transfer is for adequate consideration and its proceeds discharge genuine debts without a benefit being retained by the debtor.
material_facts: The company transferred its assets to a firm that was not itself a creditor.
The High Court found that the sale was made to discharge the company’s debts, that the proceeds were used to pay creditors, and that the consideration was not inadequate.
members.legal_principle: Under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, a transfer made for adequate consideration to pay genuine debts, without the debtor retaining a benefit, is not impeachable merely because the transferee is not a creditor. This follows the principle in Musahar Sahu v. Hakim Lal, In re Moroney, Middleton v. Pollock, and MA PWA MAY v. S.R.M.M.A. Chettyar Firm.
members.conclusion: The transferee’s status as a non-creditor did not make the transfer voidable under section 53 on these facts.

rule.if: creditor_transfer_challenge and genuine_debts_paid and adequate_consideration and debtor_retained_no_benefit and transferee_not_creditor

predicates.creditor_transfer_challenge: A creditor challenges a debtor’s transfer of property on the ground that it defeats or delays creditors.
predicates.genuine_debts_paid: The transfer proceeds are applied to discharge genuine debts owed by the debtor.
predicates.adequate_consideration: The debtor receives consideration that is not inadequate for the transferred property.
predicates.debtor_retained_no_benefit: The debtor does not reserve or retain a benefit in the transferred property or its proceeds.
predicates.transferee_not_creditor: The person receiving the transferred property is not one of the debtor’s creditors.
predicates.transfer_not_voidable_solely_because_tra: The transfer is not voidable solely because the recipient is not a creditor.

members.legal_issue: A transfer supported by valuable consideration and made honestly by a transferee who was not shown to share the debtor's intent to defeat or delay creditors cannot be annulled on the evidence in this case.
material_facts: The lender's evidence, receipts, account entries, and evidence from third parties established that the full consideration was paid.
Before lending, the lender's sons made inquiries about the borrowers' standing, business reputation, and property, and reported their findings to the lender.
The lender was a stranger to the borrowers and there was no evidence that he knew their true financial position or shared an intent to screen assets from creditors.
The receiver did not adequately investigate the debtors' accounts or establish that the transaction lacked consideration or that the lender acted dishonestly.
The lower courts assessed good faith using the due-care test and had placed the burden of proof on the transferee.
members.legal_principle: Under s. 35 of the Travancore Insolvency Regulation, the receiver could establish grounds for annulment by proving lack of consideration, consideration so inadequate as to support an inference of bad faith, or that the transferee honestly participated in a transaction intended to shield the debtor's assets from creditors. The burden remained on the receiver. Applying the honesty test of s. 2(22) of the Indian General Clauses Act, 1897, the court found that the evidence established consideration and did not establish dishonesty by the transferee.
members.conclusion: The receiver had not proved that the transfer was unsupported by consideration or made in bad faith. The judgments annulling the mortgage were set aside, and the mortgage and the connected leaseback were held binding on the insolvent estate.

rule.if: insolvency_transfer_annulment and valuable_consideration_paid and transferee_acted_honestly and receiver_did_not_prove_transferee_shared_debtor_intent

predicates.insolvency_transfer_annulment: A receiver seeks to annul a debtor's transfer in an insolvency proceeding.
predicates.valuable_consideration_paid: The transferee paid valuable consideration for the transfer.
predicates.transferee_acted_honestly: The transferee acted honestly in entering into the transaction.
predicates.receiver_did_not_prove_transferee_shared: The receiver did not prove that the transferee shared the debtor's intent to shield assets from creditors.

members.legal_issue: The urban land ceiling law does not displace the agricultural ceiling law as to agricultural land merely because that land lies within an urban agglomeration.
material_facts: The disputed lands lay within an urban agglomeration covered by the urban land ceiling law.
The urban land ceiling law excluded land mainly used for agriculture from its relevant definitions of urban or vacant land.
The lands were bid lands that fell within the agricultural land definitions of the unamended agricultural ceiling law.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(o), 2(q), and 6 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, together with the explanations to Section 2(o), exclude qualifying agricultural land from the urban ceiling regime. Article 252(1) and (2) of the Constitution govern legislation enacted following a State resolution. Thumati Venkaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh explains that an agricultural ceiling law may operate on land before the urban ceiling law applies to land within its field; Union of India v. Valluri Basavaiah Chowdhary addresses the scope of Parliament’s authority under Article 252. The Court held that the unamended agricultural ceiling law continued to operate on agricultural land outside the urban law’s effective reach.
members.conclusion: The urban land ceiling law did not prevent the agricultural ceiling law, in its unamended form, from applying to the agricultural lands.

rule.if: challenge_to_agricultural_ceiling_action and land_is_agricultural and land_within_urban_agglomeration and urban_ceiling_law_excludes_agricultural_land

predicates.challenge_to_agricultural_ceiling_action: A party challenged action taken to determine or acquire land exceeding an agricultural ceiling.
predicates.land_is_agricultural: The land was used or capable of being used for agriculture, including grazing or raising grass.
predicates.land_within_urban_agglomeration: The land lay within an area treated as an urban agglomeration.
predicates.urban_ceiling_law_excludes_agricultural_: The urban land ceiling regime excluded land mainly used for agriculture from its coverage.

members.legal_issue: A state agricultural land ceiling law is not wholly beyond legislative competence merely because it covers land in areas that may later be designated as urban agglomerations, and it cannot govern land already within urban agglomerations covered by the parliamentary ceiling regime.
material_facts: The state enacted a law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings across the state.
State legislative resolutions had transferred to Parliament the subject of ceilings on urban immovable property and related matters.
The parliamentary law covered specified urban agglomerations and allowed other areas to be declared urban agglomerations by notification.
The state law had become operative before any later notification could bring an additional area within the parliamentary law.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 252(1) and (2), resolutions by state legislatures surrender those legislatures’ power over the matter specified, leaving Parliament alone competent to legislate on it; the resolutions here concerned ceilings on urban immovable property and connected matters. The Court relied on Union of India v. V.V. Chaudhary for the effect of such resolutions. A possible future designation of an area as an urban agglomeration does not remove state legislative competence before that designation; the state law cannot operate in areas already covered by the parliamentary regime.
members.conclusion: The state law was not wholly invalid. It did not apply to land in the urban agglomerations already covered by the parliamentary law, but remained within the state legislature’s competence for other areas until they were designated as urban agglomerations; the parliamentary law would then govern land remaining there.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_agricu: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of a state law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings.
predicates.state_law_covers_agricultural_land_acros: The state law applied to agricultural land across the state.
predicates.parliamentary_ceiling_regime_covers_only: The parliamentary ceiling regime applied to specified urban areas and to other areas only after they were designated as urban agglomerations.
