members.legal_issue: The State’s land-ceiling provisions do not govern the imposition of a ceiling on land within an urban agglomeration when that subject has been assigned to Parliament.
material_facts: The relevant State legislative resolution assigned Parliament the regulation of ceilings on urban immovable property and acquisition of property above those ceilings.
The land in question was within an urban agglomeration covered by the parliamentary ceiling law.
The State land-reform law also contained provisions imposing ceilings on landholdings.
members.legal_principle: Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on the distinct subject transferred by State resolutions, and the State legislature is denuded of competence over that transferred subject. The resolution transferred the imposition of ceilings on urban immovable property and related matters, not all subjects concerning land under Entry 18 of List II. The Court relied on Articles 246 and 252, Entry 18 of List II, and Thumati Venkaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Union of India v. Valluri Basavaiah Chowdhary.
members.conclusion: For land within an urban agglomeration, the parliamentary ceiling law governs the imposition of the ceiling; the State law’s ceiling provisions do not apply to that extent.

predicates.ceiling_determination_concerns_land: A proceeding determines whether land is held above a legally imposed ceiling.
predicates.land_is_urban_agglomeration: The land is situated within an area treated as an urban agglomeration.
predicates.urban_ceiling_subject_was_transferred_to: State resolutions assigned the regulation of urban-property ceilings to Parliament.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition should not be used to resolve a contractual dispute or challenge a contractual allotment decision where the allottee has available statutory or contractual remedies.
material_facts: The company challenged the cancellation of its land allotment by writ petition.
The dispute concerned compliance with the lease and the authority's contractual and rule-based power to cancel the allotment.
The rules provided for review and appeal, and the lease contained an arbitration clause.
The company did not use those remedies before filing its writ petition.
members.legal_principle: Contractual disputes and disputes over interpretation or implementation of contract terms ordinarily cannot be resolved through a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. A claimant should resort to available statutory or contractual remedies; the Court relied on Article 226, Rule 24(aa) and Rule 24(bb)(ii) of the Rajasthan State Industrial & Investment Corporation Limited (Disposal of Land) Rules, 1979, the lease's arbitration clause, Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajay Pal Singh, AIR 1989 SC 1076; State of U.P. v. Bridge & Roof Co. (India) Ltd., AIR 1996 SC 3515; and Kerala State Electricity Board v. Kurien E. Kalathil, AIR 2000 SC 2573.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition, and the company should have pursued the available alternative remedies.

predicates.writ_challenges_contractual_allotment_ac: The proceeding is a writ petition challenging an action concerning a contractual land allotment.
predicates.contractual_terms_are_in_dispute: The dispute turns on the interpretation or performance of the allotment's contractual terms.
predicates.effective_alternative_remedies_are_avail: The claimant has available statutory or contractual procedures for review, appeal, or resolution of the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A contractual writ petition should not be rejected solely because a civil remedy is available when recognised grounds for writ intervention are made out.
material_facts: A public development corporation cancelled completed plot-allotment arrangements, relying on the absence of a tender.

The affected parties challenged the cancellation by writ petitions, alleging that the corporation lacked authority to undo the concluded arrangements, denied them a fair hearing, and treated them differently from comparable allotment holders.
The High Court rejected the petitions solely because a civil suit was available.
The Supreme Court held that the circumstances bringing the petitions within the recognised exceptions to the alternative-remedy rule were made out.
members.legal_principle: The availability of an alternative remedy does not bar relief under Article 226 in every case. Under the exceptions identified in Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trademarks, Mumbai, (1998) 8 SCC 1, a writ petition may be entertained in a contractual matter where, among other recognised grounds, the challenged action is without jurisdiction, natural justice has been violated, or fundamental rights have been infringed. The Court held that three such grounds were made out here.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the writ petitions on the ground of an alternative civil remedy. The petitions were maintainable and were restored for the High Court to decide on their merits.

rule.if: contractual_writ_challenge and alternative_civil_remedy_available and (authority_resiled_from_concluded_contract or affected_person_denied_hearing or comparable_parties_treated_differently)

predicates.contractual_writ_challenge: An affected person brought a writ petition challenging action taken in a contractual dispute.
predicates.alternative_civil_remedy_available: A civil suit was available to the affected person as an alternative remedy.
predicates.authority_resiled_from_concluded_contrac: A public authority acted to undo a concluded contractual arrangement.
predicates.affected_person_denied_hearing: The affected person was not given a fair opportunity to be heard before the challenged action was taken.
predicates.comparable_parties_treated_differently: The authority left comparable parties’ arrangements undisturbed while taking adverse action against the affected person.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition is not an appropriate means to challenge an arbitral award when a comprehensive statutory process provides for challenging the award and the dispute arises from contractual obligations.
material_facts: The lessee sought writ relief to quash a demand based on the decision made under the lease’s dispute-resolution term.
The decision-maker’s decision was an arbitral award under the lease term.
The Arbitration Act, 1940, provided procedures for challenging an award, including under Section 33, and Section 32 barred other suits to contest or affect an award.
The royalty obligation and the dispute-resolution mechanism arose from the lease contract.
members.legal_principle: The Arbitration Act, 1940, is a self-contained and exhaustive code governing arbitral awards: Section 33 provides a means to challenge an award, and Section 32 bars contesting or affecting an award otherwise than as provided by that Act. The Court also held that writ jurisdiction under Article 226 is not intended to facilitate avoidance of voluntarily incurred contractual obligations, relying on Har Shankar v. The Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner.
members.conclusion: The High Court rightly declined to entertain the writ petition, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenges_arbitral_awar: A party brought a writ proceeding seeking to challenge an arbitral award.
predicates.arbitration_statute_provides_award_chall: The applicable arbitration law provides a process for challenging or setting aside the award and excludes other means of contesting it.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_voluntary_contract: The disputed right or obligation arises from a contract voluntarily entered into by the parties.

members.legal_issue: A bill passed by a provincial legislative chamber and awaiting assent when the Constitution commenced could be continued by the corresponding State legislature.
material_facts: The provincial assembly passed the acquisition bill and it was reserved for consideration by the Governor-General.
The Governor-General returned the bill to the Governor with a suggestion that it be reserved for the President, and the bill was in transit when the Constitution commenced.
The Governor-General neither assented to the bill nor expressly withheld assent, and his suggestion showed an intention that it remain pending.
After the Constitution commenced, the Governor reserved the bill for the President; the State assembly considered proposed alterations, passed the amended bill, and the President assented to it.
members.legal_principle: Article 389 keeps alive a bill pending in the predecessor legislature and permits its continuation by the corresponding State legislature. Under sections 18, 60, 75 and 76 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Governor or Governor-General represented the sovereign, who formed part of the legislature; a bill presented for assent remained pending until assent was given or withheld. The meaning of “Legislature” depends on context and, in Article 389, includes the machinery involved in the entire legislative process. A suggestion to reserve a bill for further consideration, without a positive declaration withholding assent, does not terminate it. The Court distinguished the broader contextual reading from the passage in Visweshwar Rao v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1952] S.C.R. 1020.
members.conclusion: The bill remained pending before the provincial legislature when the Constitution commenced and was validly continued and enacted by the corresponding State legislature.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and predecessor_chamber_passed_bill and bill_awaited_assent_at_constitutional_transition and assent_not_expressly_withheld

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law on the ground that its enactment process was defective.
predicates.predecessor_chamber_passed_bill: The predecessor legislature's chamber passed the bill before the constitutional transition.
predicates.bill_awaited_assent_at_constitutional_tr: The bill had reached the assent stage and remained unresolved when the constitutional transition occurred.
predicates.assent_not_expressly_withheld: The authority considering the bill did not expressly withhold assent and instead indicated that further consideration was intended.

members.legal_issue: A bill pending before a State Legislature does not lapse merely because the House is prorogued before the Constitution commences.
material_facts: The Bill had been introduced and was pending before the State Legislature when the House was prorogued.
The Bill was later reintroduced and enacted.
members.legal_principle: Section 73 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and article 196 of the Constitution provide that a pending Bill does not lapse by reason of prorogation of the House or Houses. The Court rejected the argument that prorogation caused this Bill to lapse.
members.conclusion: The Bill remained pending despite prorogation and therefore was pending when the Constitution commenced.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_acquis: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law enacted by a State Legislature to acquire property.
predicates.state_legislative_bill_pending: The Bill that became the challenged law was pending before the State Legislature.
predicates.house_prorogued_before_constitution_comm: The House was prorogued before the Constitution commenced.

members.legal_issue: A bill awaiting the President’s assent does not lapse when the State Legislative Assembly is dissolved.
material_facts: The Assembly passed the bill and the Governor reserved it for the President’s assent.
The Assembly was dissolved while the bill was awaiting that assent.
The President later returned the bill with a message, and a newly elected Assembly reconsidered and passed it.
members.legal_principle: Article 196(5) exhaustively identifies the bills that lapse on dissolution and refers to bills pending in the Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council, not bills pending assent. Article 196(3) also departs from the English rule by providing that prorogation does not cause pending bills to lapse. Articles 200 and 201 impose no time limit for the Governor or President to decide on a bill. Article 194(3), concerning legislative powers, privileges and immunities, does not import the English convention on dissolution into legislative procedure.
members.conclusion: The bill did not lapse on dissolution, and the President could validly consider it and give assent after its reconsideration.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_enactment and bill_passed_by_assembly and bill_pending_for_head_of_state_assent and assembly_dissolved

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_enactment: A party in a constitutional challenge to an enactment disputes the validity of the enactment’s passage.
predicates.bill_passed_by_assembly: The legislature passed the bill before it was sent for assent.
predicates.bill_pending_for_head_of_state_assent: The bill was awaiting the head of state’s decision on assent when the legislature was dissolved.
predicates.assembly_dissolved: The legislative assembly was dissolved while the bill was awaiting assent.

members.legal_issue: A court may refuse discretionary writ relief where quashing an unlawful order would restore an earlier unlawful order and defeat a valid decision of the competent body.
material_facts: Both the government’s earlier cancellation order and its later review order were unlawful for different reasons.
The local governing body had validly resolved to locate the health centre at the alternative place.
Quashing the later order would have restored the earlier order and displaced the local governing body’s valid resolution.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 confers extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction. The Court may decline to grant relief where quashing the challenged order would revive an unlawful order and produce a result contrary to a valid resolution of the competent statutory body.
members.conclusion: The High Court properly refused to quash the later order in the exercise of its extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A party seeks discretionary constitutional writ relief against an authority's order.
predicates.challenged_order_unlawful: The order challenged in the writ proceeding is unlawful.
predicates.quashing_would_restore_unlawful_prior_or: Quashing the challenged order would restore an earlier unlawful order.
predicates.valid_competent_body_decision_would_be_d: Restoring the earlier order would defeat a valid decision of the body legally empowered to decide the matter.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court may decline to quash an order made without jurisdiction when doing so would restore an unlawful payment or determination.
material_facts: The Member of the Board of Revenue directed steps to recover compensation paid in excess of the amount legally payable.
The governing Act specified the relevant authorities and their powers but did not confer power on the Board of Revenue to issue that direction.
Quashing the direction would have removed the recovery notice and revived the higher compensation assessment, which the Court considered unlawful.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the discretionary nature of extraordinary judicial review and relied on Gadde Venkateswara Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1966 SC 828, and Mohammad Swalleh v. IIIrd Additional District Judge, Meerut, AIR 1988 SC 94: a court may refuse relief against an order made without jurisdiction when granting relief would revive an invalid or unlawful order.
members.conclusion: The direction was upheld notwithstanding the Board Member’s lack of jurisdiction, because setting it aside would have restored an unlawful order for excess compensation.

predicates.administrative_compensation_recovery_pro: The matter is a proceeding concerning recovery of compensation paid under a statutory compensation assessment.
predicates.challenged_order_made_without_authority: An authority issued the challenged direction without power under the governing law.
predicates.quashing_would_restore_unlawful_compensa: Setting aside the challenged direction would revive a compensation determination or payment that the court considers unlawful.
predicates.court_may_refuse_to_quash_challenged_ord: The court may decline to set aside the challenged order.

members.legal_issue: A court may refuse to set aside an administrative order for a procedural defect when doing so would restore an earlier order that is illegal or otherwise not in accordance with law.
material_facts: The show-cause notice alleged that the Sub-Divisional Officer was not authorized to grant the land, but did not specify the earlier proceedings withdrawing that officer's powers.
The final order referred to those earlier proceedings.
The underlying allotment and transfer orders were invalid and without jurisdiction.
Setting aside the Collector's order would have restored those invalid orders.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a court need not set aside an order merely because of a breach of natural justice where doing so would restore an earlier unlawful order. The Court relied on Venkateswara Rao v. Government of A.P. and M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, which recognize that discretionary writ relief may be refused in those circumstances.
members.conclusion: Even if the omission in the show-cause notice amounted to a technical breach of natural justice, it did not justify interference because that would restore orders that were not in accordance with law.

rule.if: writ_review_of_administrative_order and specific_ground_omitted_from_notice and earlier_order_is_unlawful and quashing_would_restore_earlier_order

predicates.writ_review_of_administrative_order: A party asked a court to review an administrative order through its writ jurisdiction.
predicates.specific_ground_omitted_from_notice: The notice did not identify a specific ground later referred to in the final administrative order.
predicates.earlier_order_is_unlawful: The earlier order in the party's favour was illegal or otherwise not in accordance with law.
predicates.quashing_would_restore_earlier_order: Setting aside the challenged administrative order would restore the earlier order.

members.legal_issue: A compact disc containing a relevant recorded conversation may be received as evidence when the speakers’ voices are identified and the recording’s accuracy is established.
material_facts: The defendant sought to rely on compact discs containing conversations in which the plaintiff and an attesting witness allegedly admitted that the payment was a loan and the sale agreement was security for repayment.
The recordings were made after the witnesses had given evidence, and the plaintiff disputed that the conversations or admissions had occurred.
members.legal_principle: The amended definition of evidence in section 3 of the Evidence Act, 1872, read with the definition of electronic record in section 2(t) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, includes a compact disc containing an electronic conversation. Under section 8 of the Evidence Act, relevant conduct may be considered. R.M. Malkani v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1973 SC 157, holds that a relevant contemporaneous electronic recording is admissible when the voice is identified and the recording’s accuracy is proved, including by eliminating the possibility of erasure, addition, or manipulation.
members.conclusion: An electronically recorded conversation is capable of being received as evidence if it is relevant, the voice is identified, and the accuracy of the recording is proved by eliminating the possibility of erasure, addition, or manipulation.

rule.if: civil_trial and recorded_conversation_relevant and speaker_voice_identified and recording_accuracy_proved

predicates.civil_trial: The proceeding is a civil trial in which evidence is being considered.
predicates.recorded_conversation_relevant: A party offers a recorded conversation that bears on a fact in issue or a relevant fact.
predicates.speaker_voice_identified: The voice in the recording is identified as that of the person whose conversation is relied on.
predicates.recording_accuracy_proved: The party relying on the recording establishes its accuracy and eliminates the possibility of erasure, addition, or manipulation.

members.legal_issue: A contemporaneous tape recording of a relevant conversation is admissible when its recording and integrity are adequately proved.
material_facts: A concealed microphone and tape recorder captured a conversation during which a bribe was offered and handed over.
A competent witness proved how the recording was made, and the speakers’ voices were identified.
Although the tape was not sealed, other evidence supported that it had not been tampered with, and the defence did not suggest that it had been altered.
The dialogue was proved by the recipient of the bribe, and the recording corroborated that witness’s testimony.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 7 and 8 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a contemporaneous record of a relevant event or conversation may itself be a relevant fact, and a contemporaneous dialogue may form part of the res gestae. The court approved Rup Chand v. Mahabir Parshad and Mahindra Nath v. Biswanath Kundu, and followed S. Pratap Singh v. State of Punjab and R. v. Maqsud Ali. Because magnetic recording can be erased and reused, the time, place, accuracy, and identification of voices must be proved, and the court must be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the recording was not tampered with.
members.conclusion: The dialogue was relevant as part of the res gestae, and the tape recording was admissible and could corroborate the witness’s testimony. The court must receive tape evidence cautiously and be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that it has not been tampered with; the recording met that standard here.

rule.if: criminal_evidence_proceeding and conversation_relevant_to_offence and contemporaneous_conversation_recorded and recording_method_proved_by_competent_witness and speakers_identified and recording_integrity_proved_beyond_reasonable_doubt

predicates.criminal_evidence_proceeding: The recording is offered as evidence in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.conversation_relevant_to_offence: The recorded conversation concerns an event relevant to the alleged offence.
predicates.contemporaneous_conversation_recorded: A recording device captured the conversation as it occurred.
predicates.recording_method_proved_by_competent_wit: A competent witness explained when, where, and how the recording was made and reproduced.
predicates.speakers_identified: A witness identified the voices recorded.
predicates.recording_integrity_proved_beyond_reason: The evidence satisfies the court beyond reasonable doubt that the recording was not altered or tampered with.

members.legal_issue: A compact disc containing a recorded conversation is a document for evidentiary purposes.
material_facts: The defence sought to introduce a compact disc containing a recorded conversation.
The compact disc was tendered in an ongoing criminal trial.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 defines a document to include matter expressed or described on a substance for recording purposes. In R.M. Malkani v. State of Maharashtra and Ziyauddin Barhanuddin Bukhari v. Brijmohan Ramdass Mehra, the Court treated tape-recorded conversations as documents and described conditions relevant to their admissibility, including voice identification, accuracy and relevance.
members.conclusion: The compact disc is a document.

predicates.recorded_conversation: A conversation was recorded and stored on a physical medium.
predicates.recording_stored_on_physical_medium: The recorded matter was preserved on a medium capable of being presented as evidence.

members.legal_issue: Entries in an inam register are significant evidence of the nature of an inam grant but are not conclusive when considered in isolation.
material_facts: The inam register described the grant as religious and permanent.
Other records, including historical grant documents, a title deed, administrative documents and earlier court proceedings, bore on who received the original grant.
The original title deed was unavailable, so the register entries had to be assessed alongside the other evidence.
members.legal_principle: The entries in an Inam Fair Register are acts of the State and may have great evidentiary value, particularly when considered with survey and settlement records. They are not conclusive merely because they describe an inam as religious or permanent; the entries must be read with the other evidence and with due regard to the context of the recorded information. Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshitulu and Jammi Raja Rao v. Sri Anjaneyaswami Temple support the importance of inam-register entries. Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal explains the evidentiary significance of the register, while Poohari Fakir Sadavarthy of Bondilipuram v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments establishes that entries in particular columns cannot be accepted at face value without considering other recorded matters.
members.conclusion: The inam-register entries had to be given due weight but could not alone determine the nature of the grant; they had to be read with the other evidence.

predicates.minor_inam_pattta_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning entitlement to a land-settlement patta for a minor inam.
predicates.inam_register_entries_bear_on_grant: The inam register contains entries relevant to the character or recipient of the grant.
predicates.other_relevant_grant_evidence_exists: Evidence other than the inam-register entries bears on the original grant or the nature of the inam.

members.legal_issue: An entry in an alienation register classifying a grant as a personal inam is descriptive and is not conclusive of the grant’s character.
material_facts: The grant was entered in the alienation register as a personal inam.
The governing law contemplated that the register entry would be treated as amended if the government decided the classification question differently.
The register principally served the purpose of realizing land revenue.
members.legal_principle: Explanation I to section 2(1)(e) of the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, provides that an entry in the alienation register is deemed amended if the State Government decides the question differently, showing that the entry is not an unchangeable element of the definition. Section 53 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code concerns the register, whose principal function is connected with land-revenue administration.
members.conclusion: The register entry was not sacrosanct or conclusive; it was descriptive and could be changed consistently with a government decision on the classification.

predicates.inam_classification_is_disputed: A dispute arises over whether a grant is personal or religious in character.
predicates.register_records_the_grant_as_personal: The administrative register classifies the grant as a personal inam.
predicates.register_entry_can_be_amended_after_clas: The governing process treats the register as amended when a classification decision differs from its existing entry.

members.legal_issue: Entries in an Inam Register have substantial evidentiary value but must be assessed in the context of the other information in the register and the evidence about the grant, rather than accepted at face value in isolation.
material_facts: The register entries referred to the shrine and its worship, but also recorded that grants had been made for charitable feeding and support of the institution.
The original grants predated the shrine's construction, and other recorded details indicated that the grants were for the institution or its head rather than for the shrine.
Some descriptions of grants as supporting a temple or being dedicated to God were inconsistent with the chronology and with other details recorded in the entries.
members.legal_principle: Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal recognizes the substantial evidentiary value of an Inam Register prepared after official inquiry, particularly where original grants are unavailable, while also recognizing that such a report does not displace authentic evidence. The Court applied the principle that the register must be read as a whole and in context, not by isolating an entry in a particular column. The relevant inam-settlement rule referred to in the judgment was rule 3(1), concerning continuation of inams granted for religious or charitable objects or services.
members.conclusion: The register entries were of great evidentiary value, but the entries in particular columns could not be accepted at face value without considering the other matters recorded in the entries and the surrounding evidence.

predicates.inam_register_evidence_assessment: The proceeding requires the court to assess entries in a register concerning an inam grant.
predicates.isolated_entry_conflicts_with_other_regi: An entry in one part of the register conflicts with other information recorded in the same register.
predicates.grant_context_undercuts_isolated_entry: The chronology or other evidence about the grant undermines the meaning suggested by an isolated register entry.

members.legal_issue: A widow in possession of inherited property when the Hindu Succession Act came into force became its absolute owner where a mutation entry, without an effective transfer of title, was the basis for the competing claim.
material_facts: A widow inherited land after her husband died without children and was recorded as having transferred it to two minors by mutation, purportedly in accordance with her husband’s wish to adopt them.
The alleged adoption was found not proved in earlier litigation, and the widow continued to live with the minors and manage the property.
The courts below treated the mutation as having divested the widow of title and possession, but the Supreme Court held that the mutation did not convey title or divest her.
The widow was treated as remaining in possession when the Hindu Succession Act came into force and later executed gifts of the land.
Reversioners brought a suit for possession after the widow’s death, challenging the gifts.
members.legal_principle: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 enlarged the widow’s limited interest because she continued to possess the property. As held in Smt. Sawarni v. Smt. Inder Kaur, mutation in revenue records neither creates nor extinguishes title and serves the purpose of land-revenue collection. Because the mutation did not transfer title, the widow was not divested of title or possession by it.
members.conclusion: The widow remained in possession and her limited interest enlarged into absolute ownership when the Hindu Succession Act came into force; she was authorized to deal with the property by gift.

rule.if: reversioner_possession_suit and widow_had_limited_inherited_interest and widow_possessed_property_at_succession_change and competing_title_claim_rested_on_mutation and mutation_did_not_transfer_title

predicates.reversioner_possession_suit: The proceeding is a suit by reversioners seeking possession after a widow’s death and challenging her transfer of inherited property.
predicates.widow_had_limited_inherited_interest: A widow held a limited interest in property inherited from her deceased husband.
predicates.widow_possessed_property_at_succession_c: The widow possessed the property when the succession law came into force.
predicates.competing_title_claim_rested_on_mutation: The competing claim that the widow had lost her title relied on a mutation in revenue records.
predicates.mutation_did_not_transfer_title: The mutation was not an effective transfer of ownership of the property.

members.legal_issue: A widow who has validly transferred property and later occupies it wrongfully does not acquire full ownership under the Hindu Succession Act merely because she remains in possession when the Act comes into force.
material_facts: The widow validly gifted the property to her daughter and the daughter took possession under the gift.
After the daughter’s death, the widow wrongfully retook possession from the daughter’s children and remained in possession when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The widow had no right to possess the property when she retook it.
members.legal_principle: For property to be ‘possessed’ by a Hindu woman within section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, she must both have a right to possess it and be in actual or constructive possession. The Court relied on S. S. Munna Lal v. S. S. Rajkumar and Kuldip Singh v. Surain Singh. Because the widow lacked a right to possession, she acquired no ownership under the Act; the appellants’ reliance on section 14(2) did not alter that result.
members.conclusion: The widow’s later possession was that of a trespasser, not possession that could enlarge her interest under the Hindu Succession Act; she did not become the full owner.

predicates.claim_under_womens_property_succession_l: The dispute concerns whether a woman’s possession gives her an enlarged ownership interest under succession law.
predicates.valid_gift_and_delivery: The woman transferred the property by a valid gift and the donee took possession under it.
predicates.widow_reentered_wrongfully: The woman later retook possession without a right to do so.
predicates.widow_remained_in_possession_at_commence: The woman continued to occupy the property when the relevant succession law came into force.

members.legal_issue: A widow whose pre-Act gift was declared ineffective became absolute owner under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and could dispose of the property by a later will.
material_facts: The widow inherited the property from her husband in 1942 with only a life interest.
Although she had made a gift before the Act, the compromise decree declared the gift ineffective, so she remained the limited owner of the property until the Act came into force.
She made a will after the Act came into force, and the lower courts found the will genuine and properly executed.
The High Court nevertheless awarded the respondents possession of half the land that had been the subject of the earlier gift.
members.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 converts a female Hindu’s limited estate into an absolute estate where she retains the property. Because the gift here had been declared legally ineffective, the widow remained its owner until the Act applied and could later dispose of it by will. The Court distinguished Lachhman v. Thunia, A.I.R. 1972 H.P. 69, where the property was treated as no longer in the widow’s possession at her death; that reasoning did not apply when the widow remained owner after the purported gift was held ineffective.
members.conclusion: Section 14 enlarged the widow’s limited estate into an absolute estate because the ineffective gift had not divested her of the property; she therefore had full capacity to make the later will, and the legatees’ claim under it could not be disputed.

rule.if: property_succession_dispute and widow_inherited_property_with_limited_interest and earlier_gift_was_legally_ineffective and widow_retained_property_at_statutory_change and later_will_was_genuine

predicates.property_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property through succession.
predicates.widow_inherited_property_with_limited_in: A widow inherited property but initially held only a limited interest in it.
predicates.earlier_gift_was_legally_ineffective: A prior gift by the widow was held legally ineffective, leaving her interest in the property intact.
predicates.widow_retained_property_at_statutory_cha: The widow still held the property when the change governing her estate took effect.
predicates.later_will_was_genuine: The widow made a later will that was found genuine and properly executed.

members.legal_issue: On the death of a tenant, the succeeding heirs hold the tenancy as joint tenants in relation to the landlord, rather than as tenants-in-common.
material_facts: The premises were let jointly to the deceased tenant and another tenant.
After the deceased tenant died, one of his heirs succeeded to the tenancy; the other original joint tenant remained a tenant.
The dispute arose in eviction proceedings concerning the premises.
members.legal_principle: Under H.C. Pandey v. G.C. Paul, on the death of the original tenant the tenancy devolves as a single tenancy on the heirs, who succeed as joint tenants as between themselves and the landlord. Section 19 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, which provides for heirs to take as tenants-in-common, concerns the rights of heirs inter se and does not determine their relationship with a landlord, as explained in Mst. Surayya Begum v. Mohd. Usman. The Court also relied on the principles in Boddu Venkatakrishna Rao v. Smt. Boddu Satyavathi, Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, Mohd. Usman v. (Mst.) Surayya Begum, and Harish Tandon v. Addl. District Magistrate.
members.conclusion: The heirs inherited the tenancy as joint tenants. The tenancy remained a single tenancy and was not divided into separate tenancies among the heirs.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The landlord brought proceedings seeking eviction from rented premises.
predicates.premises_jointly_let: The premises were let to the deceased tenant together with another tenant.
predicates.original_tenant_died_leaving_heirs: The original tenant died and left heirs who succeeded to the tenancy.

members.legal_issue: On the death of a tenant, the tenancy devolves on the heirs as a single joint tenancy unless succession is excluded or limited.
material_facts: The original tenant died, leaving heirs who inherited the tenancy.
The tenancy remained a single tenancy, with no division of the premises or of the rent payable.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, absent a provision excluding or limiting succession, the tenancy devolves on the heirs with the same incidence as it had for the original tenant; it remains a single tenancy without division of the premises or rent. The Court affirmed Shrimati Vishnawati v. Bhagwat Vithu Chowdhry, [1969] A.L.J. 1131, and overruled Ramesh Chand Bose v. Gopeshwar Prasad Sharma, AIR 1977 Allahabad 38.
members.conclusion: The heirs succeeded to the tenancy as joint tenants, not as tenants in common.

rule.if: original_tenant_died and heirs_succeeded_to_tenancy and no_succession_exclusion_or_limit and tenancy_remained_undivided

predicates.original_tenant_died: The person who held the tenancy died.
predicates.heirs_succeeded_to_tenancy: The deceased tenant's heirs succeeded to the tenancy.
predicates.no_succession_exclusion_or_limit: No applicable provision excluded or limited the heirs' succession to the tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_remained_undivided: The tenancy remained single, without division of the premises or the rent payable.

members.legal_issue: After an original tenant dies, the tenancy devolves on the heirs as a single joint tenancy rather than as separate tenancies, so a tenancy breach by one heir can affect the tenancy of all heirs.
material_facts: The original tenant died leaving multiple heirs.
The heirs continued to hold and use the same premises under the tenancy, with no division of the premises or the rent payable to the landlord.
One heir admitted a person outside the tenant’s family as a partner in the business conducted in the premises.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 12, 20 and 25 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, and held that the tenancy rights devolve on the heirs jointly, with the same incidents as the original tenancy and no division of premises or rent. It approved H.C. Pandey v. G.C. Paul as laying down the correct law and held that Mohd. Azeem v. District Judge, Aligarh did not. Its reasoning also accords with the general proposition in Smt. Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar that the consequences of a deceased tenant’s succession depend on the governing rent legislation. Treating heirs as separate tenants would create an unprovided-for division of liability and could produce absurd results.
members.conclusion: The heirs succeeded to the tenancy jointly as a single tenancy, and the breach by one heir could result in the consequences prescribed for that tenancy as a whole.

rule.if: rent_control_tenancy_succession_dispute and original_tenant_died and multiple_heirs_succeeded_to_one_undivided_tenancy and one_heir_committed_tenancy_breach

predicates.rent_control_tenancy_succession_dispute: The dispute concerns the succession to a tenancy governed by rent-control law.
predicates.original_tenant_died: The original tenant died while the tenancy existed.
predicates.multiple_heirs_succeeded_to_one_undivide: Multiple heirs succeeded to the same tenancy without a division of the premises or the rent payable to the landlord.
predicates.one_heir_committed_tenancy_breach: One of the heirs committed a breach of a condition governing the tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A court may refuse to enforce a mortgage term that unreasonably restricts redemption even when the governing mortgage statute does not apply, where civil courts apply principles of justice, equity and good conscience and no contrary local rule is established.
material_facts: The suit sought redemption of a transaction treated as a mortgage, and the deed provided that the mortgagee would become the owner if the debt was not repaid within 15 years.
The Court accepted that this term was a clog on the equity of redemption because it extinguished the mortgagor’s right to redeem for failure to repay within the fixed period.
The Transfer of Property Act did not apply in the territory when the mortgage was made or when the stipulated period expired.
The appellant produced no material establishing that local law required enforcement of the term or excluded equitable principles.
The Court noted the consistent application of equitable principles by civil courts in mortgage cases, including in a substantial part of Rajasthan, and relied on Namdeo Lokman Lodhi v. Narmadabai.
members.legal_principle: Civil courts in India apply justice, equity and good conscience to disputes where no applicable statutory rule governs. In Namdeo Lokman Lodhi v. Narmadabai, the Court stated that courts must apply those principles even when the Transfer of Property Act does not apply. The Court relied on the consistent Indian High Court practice of refusing to enforce unreasonable restraints on redemption, including the approach in Venkata Reddy v. Parvati Ammal, Ramji bin Tukaram v. Chinto Sakharam, Bapuji Apaji v. Sonavaraji Marvadi and Ramasami Sastrigal v. Samiyappanayakan. It distinguished the strict approach in Pattabhiramier v. Vencatarow Naicken and Thumbusawmy Moodelly v. Hossain Rowthen in light of that established judicial practice. It also referred to decisions applying the principle underlying section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act where that Act was not in force.
members.conclusion: The equitable principle applied despite the non-application of the Transfer of Property Act; the clog could not bar redemption, subject to the general law of limitation, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_proceeding and term_unreasonably_restricts_redemption and no_applicable_mortgage_statute and civil_courts_apply_equity_in_legal_gaps and no_contrary_local_rule_established

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: A party brings a proceeding to redeem property given as security for a debt.
predicates.term_unreasonably_restricts_redemption: The mortgage term unreasonably restricts the mortgagor’s ability to redeem the property.
predicates.no_applicable_mortgage_statute: No applicable enacted mortgage rule governs the dispute.
predicates.civil_courts_apply_equity_in_legal_gaps: Civil courts apply principles of justice, equity and good conscience when no specific rule governs the dispute.
predicates.no_contrary_local_rule_established: No party establishes a local rule that requires enforcement of the restrictive term or excludes equitable principles.

members.legal_issue: The equitable protection of the right to redeem applies to a mortgage containing a term that restricts redemption even where the applicable property-transfer statute does not govern the transaction.
material_facts: The mortgage deed provided that the mortgagee would become the absolute owner if the debt was not repaid within the specified period, a restriction on the mortgagor’s right to redeem.
The property was in a territory where the Transfer of Property Act did not apply when the mortgage was made or when the repayment period expired.

The Court found that courts in India had consistently applied equitable principles against unreasonable restrictions on redemption, and that no material established that those principles were irrelevant in the territory concerned.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the general equitable principle underlying section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, including the mortgagor’s right to redeem, and on provisions directing courts to decide according to justice, equity and good conscience. It relied on Namdeo Lokman Lodhi v. Narmadabai for the proposition that courts apply those principles even where the Act does not apply; on the established practice of the Madras and Bombay High Courts against enforcing oppressive restrictions on redemption; and on the Rajasthan High Court decisions in Amba Lal v. Amba Lal and Seleh Raj v. Chandan Mal, as well as Nainu v. Kishan Singh. The Court distinguished the Privy Council decisions in Pattabhiramier v. Vencatarow Naicken, Thumbusawmy Moodelly v. Hossain Rowthen, Kader Moideen v. Nepean, and Mehrban Khan v. Makhna, noting the applicable statutory or established-practice context in those decisions.
members.conclusion: The equitable principle applied despite the non-application of the Transfer of Property Act; the restrictive term could not bar the claim for redemption, subject to the general law of limitation.

rule.if: mortgage_redemption_proceeding and clause_restricts_equity_of_redemption and transfer_statute_inapplicable and equitable_practice_supported

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: A claimant seeks to redeem property held under a mortgage.
predicates.clause_restricts_equity_of_redemption: The mortgage instrument contains a term that unreasonably restricts the mortgagor’s ability to redeem the property.
predicates.transfer_statute_inapplicable: The statute governing transfers of property does not govern the mortgage transaction.
predicates.equitable_practice_supported: The record supports that courts apply equitable principles to mortgage disputes and contains no material showing that those principles are unavailable.

members.legal_issue: Equitable principles of mortgage redemption may be applied by a civil court even when the statutory provision governing redemption does not apply in the jurisdiction.
material_facts: The suits sought redemption of mortgages and recovery of the mortgaged property.
The Transfer of Property Act provision on redemption did not apply in the jurisdiction at the relevant time.
The Court found that the principles governing redemption in that provision were consistent with justice, equity and good conscience.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles of justice, equity and good conscience to recognize the right of redemption reflected in Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, notwithstanding that the Act did not apply per se. It relied on Mussammat Bhagwan Devi v. Mussammat Bunyadi Khanum, Safdar Ali v. Ghulam Mohi-ud-din, Mian Nizam & Din Mohammad v. Lala Ram Sukh Das, Milkha Singh v. Mst. Shankari, M/s Ram Gopal Dula Singh v. Sardar Gurbux Singh Jiwan Singh, Atma Singh & Gian Singh v. Mangal Singh, and Ganeshi Lal v. Jyoti Pershad; it also referred to Suryanarayan v. Sriramulu.
members.conclusion: Although the statutory provision did not apply per se, its principles applied as rules of justice, equity and good conscience, and the civil court had jurisdiction to grant decrees of redemption.

predicates.civil_suit_for_mortgage_redemption: A party brought a civil suit seeking redemption of a mortgage.
predicates.statutory_redemption_rule_not_applicable: The statutory rule specifically governing mortgage redemption did not apply in the jurisdiction.
predicates.mortgage_redemption_principle_consistent: The principle recognizing redemption of the mortgage is consistent with justice, equity and good conscience.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on reopening bank transactions because interest is excessive applies to loans made by banking companies to both agriculturists and non-agriculturists.
material_facts: The borrower disputed the interest charged on a bank loan.
The High Court relied on the constitutional allocation of agricultural debt relief to the States when declaring the restriction invalid.
members.legal_principle: Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act provides that a transaction between a banking company and its debtor cannot be reopened by a court on the ground that the charged interest rate is excessive. The provision applies to all such loans; Entry 30 of List II does not change its scope. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The provision applies to all types of loans granted by a banking company, whether the borrower is an agriculturist or a non-agriculturist.

predicates.loan_granted_by_banking_company: A banking company granted the loan to its borrower.
predicates.court_considers_excessive_interest: A court is asked to reopen the transaction on the ground that its interest rate is excessive.

members.legal_issue: Banks are bound by Reserve Bank directions governing the structure of interest on loans, and courts may disallow interest charged in contravention of those directions notwithstanding the restriction on reopening transactions merely because interest is excessive.
material_facts: The Reserve Bank issued directions under statutory powers governing interest on bank loans and advances.
In the agricultural-loan appeal, the bank charged interest with six-monthly rests contrary to the applicable directions.
The borrower sought relief from interest charged in excess of what the directions permitted.
members.legal_principle: Sections 21 and 35-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 empower the Reserve Bank to issue directions regulating interest on loans and advances; those directions have statutory flavour. Section 47-A provides for penalties for non-compliance. The Court agreed with the interpretation in H.P. Krishna Reddy v. Canara Bank and Bank of India v. Kamam Ranga Rao that Section 21-A does not prevent relief where a bank charges interest contrary to a Reserve Bank direction.
members.conclusion: Banks must follow applicable Reserve Bank directions, and a court may disallow interest charged contrary to them despite Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

predicates.bank_loan_recovery_proceeding: A bank brought or defended a proceeding to recover a loan or advance.
predicates.applicable_directive_governs_interest: The central banking regulator issued an applicable direction governing the interest structure for the loan.
predicates.bank_charged_interest_contrary_to_direct: The bank charged interest in a manner that the applicable direction did not permit.

members.legal_issue: A court may not reopen a bank transaction merely because the interest rate is excessive when the Reserve Bank has fixed a maximum rate and the bank has charged no more than that rate.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a bank loan-recovery proceeding and a challenge that the agreed interest rate was excessive.
The Reserve Bank directions fixed a maximum interest rate and permitted the periodic rests at issue.
The bank's claimed rate and rests complied with those directions.
members.legal_principle: Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 prevents courts from reopening transactions between banks and debtors merely on the ground that the interest charged is excessive, notwithstanding the Usurious Loans Act, 1918 or similar State laws. The Court agreed with the interpretation in H.P. Krishna Reddy v. Canara Bank and clarified that this bar applies where the Reserve Bank has fixed a maximum rate; it expressed no opinion on directions that set only a minimum and leave the bank discretion to charge more.
members.conclusion: Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 bars reopening the transaction on the ground that the interest rate is excessive when the Reserve Bank has fixed a maximum rate and the bank has stayed within it.

rule.if: bank_loan_recovery_proceeding and excessive_interest_challenge and regulator_fixed_maximum_rate and bank_charged_no_more_than_maximum

predicates.bank_loan_recovery_proceeding: A bank brought or defended a proceeding to recover a loan or advance.
predicates.excessive_interest_challenge: The debtor asked the court to reopen the transaction on the ground that the interest rate was excessive.
predicates.regulator_fixed_maximum_rate: The central banking regulator fixed a maximum interest rate applicable to the loan.
predicates.bank_charged_no_more_than_maximum: The bank charged interest at or below the applicable maximum rate.

members.legal_issue: A challenge based on alleged noncompliance with the village tribunal’s decision-recording rules fails where the decision and any dissent were recorded as required and no breach is shown.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the village tribunal’s compliance with rules governing its decisions.
The full-bench decision was signed by its members, and the dissenting members’ minute was recorded under their signatures.
No material was presented showing that the relevant rules had been violated.
members.legal_principle: Rule 60(2) of the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules, 1949 required the full-bench decision to be signed by its members and a dissenting minute to be recorded under the dissenting members’ signatures. The Court found those requirements fulfilled and found no material establishing a violation of rules 60 or 61.
members.conclusion: The procedural challenge was rejected because the stated recording requirements were fulfilled and no violation of the rules was shown.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_village_tribunal and decision_signed_by_members and dissent_recorded_under_dissenters_signatures and no_material_shows_rule_breach

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_village_tribunal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning a criminal decision made by a village tribunal.
predicates.decision_signed_by_members: The members who made the full-bench decision signed it.
predicates.dissent_recorded_under_dissenters_signat: The dissenting members’ minute was recorded under their signatures.
predicates.no_material_shows_rule_breach: The challenger presented no material showing that the applicable decision-recording rules had been violated.

members.legal_issue: A challenge alleging that a municipal tax was imposed contrary to statutory procedure fails when the alleged procedural violation is not established by the record.
material_facts: The petitioner alleged that the municipal proposals did not contain all required details, and the municipality denied that allegation.
A municipal resolution referred to draft proposals for revising the tax, but those drafts were not before the court.
The petitioner did not specifically allege that the government had failed to make rules in accordance with the statutory procedure.
The taxes had been imposed long before the challenge, but the court treated the passage of time as insufficient to excuse an established departure from statutory requirements.
members.legal_principle: No tax may be levied or collected except in accordance with law, and an established departure from statutory requirements may infringe Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. A statutory authority’s order is presumed to have followed the prescribed procedure, but long acquiescence cannot cure an established illegality. The court considered sections 131–136 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act and found no established procedural breach.
members.conclusion: It was not established that the taxes had been imposed in violation of the statutory procedure, so the challenge based on infringement of the right under Article 19(1)(f) failed.

predicates.challenge_to_municipal_tax_procedure: A taxpayer challenges a municipal tax on the ground that the statutory procedure for imposing it was not followed.
predicates.municipal_record_refers_to_required_prop: The municipal record contains a resolution referring to draft proposals for the tax.
predicates.no_evidence_establishes_procedural_failu: The record does not establish that the municipality omitted a required procedural step.
predicates.no_specific_allegation_identifies_anothe: The taxpayer does not specifically allege a separate procedural defect for which the record supplies no proof.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the local court’s compliance with procedural requirements fails when the record shows that those requirements were fulfilled and no violation is established.
material_facts: The appellants relied on rules requiring the full-bench decision to be signed by its members and any dissenting minute to be signed by the dissenting members.
The Court found that these requirements had been fulfilled and that no material showed a violation of the relevant rules.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied rules 60 and 61 of the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules, 1949, noting the requirements for signatures on the full-bench decision and on any dissenting minute. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The appellants did not establish that the procedural rules had been violated.

predicates.challenge_to_local_court_procedure: A party challenges the procedural regularity of a local court’s decision.
predicates.required_decision_signatures_are_present: The members who are required to sign the decision have signed it.
predicates.required_dissent_signatures_are_present: The members who are required to sign a dissenting minute have signed it.

members.legal_issue: The validity of a statutory administrative order must be assessed by the reasons recorded when it was made and cannot be rescued by new reasons supplied later in litigation.
material_facts: The contemporaneous government direction described the transaction as a special case and referred to the original purchaser’s financial incapacity.
The order and direction did not state several additional grounds later advanced by the State in affidavits, including policy, delay, and the State’s anticipated commercial interest.
The State relied on those additional grounds to defend the challenged decision in court.
members.legal_principle: A public order made under statutory authority must be construed objectively by reference to its own terms and cannot be supplemented by later explanations. Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Gordhandas Bhanji and Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner establish that an order’s validity is judged by the grounds stated when it was made, not by fresh grounds supplied later.
members.conclusion: The State could not improve the challenged orders by relying on reasons introduced in later affidavits; their validity had to be judged on the reasons recorded at the time.

predicates.statutory_administrative_order_is_challe: A proceeding challenges an order made by a public authority exercising statutory power.
predicates.contemporaneous_order_omits_later_relied: The order, when made, does not record reasons subsequently invoked to defend it.
predicates.authority_relies_on_later_explanations: The public authority relies in litigation on explanations or grounds not stated in the original order.

members.legal_issue: An administrative order must be assessed on the reasons recorded when it was made and cannot be validated by reasons added later.
material_facts: The recorded reason for ordering a re-auction was that the highest bids were only marginally above the reserve prices.
The decision record did not cite cartelization or grouping as a reason for the re-auction, although that justification was advanced later in court.
members.legal_principle: Under Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) 2 SCR 272, applying the principle stated in Gordhandas Bhanji (1952) 1 SCR 135, an order must be judged by the reasons it states and cannot be supplemented later by affidavit or otherwise.
members.conclusion: The re-auction decision could not be supported by the later contention that the bidders had engaged in cartelization or grouping; its validity had to be judged by the reason recorded at the time.

predicates.administrative_order_challenged: A party challenged an administrative order in court.
predicates.contemporaneous_reasons_recorded: The decision-maker recorded reasons for the order when making it.
predicates.later_reason_advanced: A party later relied on a reason that was not recorded when the order was made.

members.legal_issue: The validity of an administrative cancellation order must be assessed on the reasons stated in that order, not on additional reasons later supplied in a court response.
material_facts: The show-cause notice and final cancellation order relied on the absence of a tender as the ground for cancellation.
In its response to the writ petitions, the authority sought to rely on additional grounds to justify the cancellation.
members.legal_principle: An order made on stated grounds must be judged by those grounds and cannot be supplemented later with fresh reasons. The Court applied the principle stated in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner, New Delhi, (1978) 1 SCC 405.
members.conclusion: The authority could not support the cancellation order by adding grounds in its response that were not stated in the notice or final order.

predicates.judicial_review_of_cancellation_order: A person sought judicial review of an authority’s order cancelling an arrangement.
predicates.order_stated_limited_ground: The cancellation notice and order gave a limited set of reasons for the cancellation.
predicates.authority_later_added_grounds: The authority later relied on additional reasons in its response to the judicial challenge.

members.legal_issue: A review petition may be allowed to correct a clear error in an earlier judgment.
material_facts: The earlier judgment inaccurately described the Board as an institution dating from 1949 and as composed of the seniormost members of the family branches.
The Court found that the Board had instead been constituted under an earlier royal proclamation and that seniormost membership was not required.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that when a clear error in its judgment is revealed, it may review and correct the judgment in order to be ultimately right. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The review petition was allowed in substantial part, including to correct the inaccurate description of the Board and clarify the earlier judgment.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party asks the court to review an earlier judgment.
predicates.clear_error_in_earlier_judgment_shown: The reviewing court finds a clear error in the earlier judgment.

members.legal_issue: A review may correct a self-evident error where a later legal change applies to a proceeding that had not reached finality and the change was not available for consideration in the original decision.
material_facts: The tenant’s application to purchase the land remained pending when the statutory amendment took effect.
The amendment and the resulting exemption for qualifying religious institutions had not been available when the earlier decisions were made.
The materials before the reviewing court showed that the landlord institution fell within the amended provision.
members.legal_principle: Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC permits review for newly discovered important matter or evidence despite due diligence, mistake, error apparent on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason. An apparent error must be manifest and not one that must be found through further investigation; review is not a rehearing of the same issue. The Court applied the principles described in Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala concerning review after summary dismissal of a special leave petition.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in allowing review because the intervening amendment made the earlier decision an apparent error in the circumstances, and the issue could be resolved from the record without a rehearing.

rule.if: review_application and later_law_applies_to_pending_proceeding and later_law_was_unavailable_at_original_decision and record_makes_error_self_evident

predicates.review_application: A party sought review of an earlier court decision.
predicates.later_law_applies_to_pending_proceeding: A later legal change governs a proceeding that had not reached finality when the change took effect.
predicates.later_law_was_unavailable_at_original_de: The legal change had not been enacted or was otherwise unavailable for consideration when the original decision was made.
predicates.record_makes_error_self_evident: The materials already on the record make the error apparent without further investigation or a rehearing.

members.legal_issue: A judgment may be reviewed when it overlooks a retrospectively operative amendment that governed the transaction and could change the result.
material_facts: The Court had previously dismissed an appeal on the ground that the sale of standing trees was not a sale of goods chargeable to sales tax.
Before the appeal was decided, a state amendment took retrospective effect to include standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
The amendment was not brought to the Court’s attention when it decided the appeal.
members.legal_principle: A judgment that suffers from an error apparent on the face of the record may be reviewed. The Court applied that principle because the overlooked amendment had retrospective operation and governed the transaction at issue.
members.conclusion: The Court reviewed its judgment because the omission of the applicable retrospective amendment was an error apparent on the face of the record.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party asks the court to review a judgment it previously issued.
predicates.retrospective_amendment_applied: An amendment applied retrospectively to the transaction decided in the prior judgment.
predicates.amendment_overlooked: The prior judgment was issued without the court being informed of the applicable amendment.

members.legal_issue: A requirement that a landholder or a member of the landholder's family reside in the locality for most of the year, where the land is held for personal cultivation and agriculture is the principal source of income, is a reasonable restriction on residence and occupational rights.
material_facts: The challenged condition required the landholder or a family member to reside in the locality where the land was situated for the greater part of the year.
The condition also required the principal source of income to come from the land.
The tenant was not barred from pursuing another occupation, and the tenant could reside elsewhere for part of the year.
The family definition permitted a family member, rather than the tenant personally, to satisfy the residence condition.
The Court found the condition connected to personal cultivation, the prevention of absentee landholding, and the public interest in agrarian reform.
members.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(e) and 19(1)(g) are subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(4) and 19(5). The Court applied the contextual reasonableness approach in State of Madras v. V.G. Row, considering the nature of the rights, the purpose of the restriction, its extent, and the conditions addressed. It held that the restriction was partial, served agrarian reform and public interest, and was not disproportionate.
members.conclusion: The residence and income conditions were reasonable restrictions and did not violate the rights to reside anywhere in India or to carry on an occupation.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_residence_and_occupation_condition and land_is_reserved_for_personal_cultivation and agriculture_is_principal_income_source and tenant_or_family_member_must_reside_locally_most_of_year and condition_allows_other_occupation_and_part_year_absence

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_residence_an: A person brought a constitutional proceeding challenging a condition affecting where a landholder may reside and what occupation the landholder may pursue.
predicates.land_is_reserved_for_personal_cultivatio: The land is made available to a holder on the basis that it will be personally cultivated.
predicates.agriculture_is_principal_income_source: The condition is limited to a holder whose principal source of income comes from the land.
predicates.tenant_or_family_member_must_reside_loca: The condition requires the holder or a member of the holder's family to reside in the locality for most of the year.
predicates.condition_allows_other_occupation_and_pa: The condition does not prohibit other occupations or require residence in the locality throughout the entire year.

members.legal_issue: A requirement that a landholder reside near the land for most of the year and derive the principal source of income from it is valid where it supports personal cultivation and the legislation serves the common-good objective of distributing material resources.
material_facts: The challenged provision required the landholder or a family member to reside for the greater part of the year in the locality where the land was situated and required the principal source of income to come from that land.
The provision was intended to ensure that a landholder cultivating the land gave it attention rather than remaining an absentee landholder pursuing other occupations.
The provision formed part of legislation directed at distributing agricultural resources for the common good.
members.legal_principle: Where legislation has a close nexus to the objectives in Article 39(b), Article 31C protects it from the covered fundamental-rights challenges. A requirement that a cultivator reside near the land for most of the year can further effective cultivation, agricultural production, and equitable distribution. The Court relied on Article 39(b), Article 31C, and its reasoning in Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The residence requirement was not an impermissible ground for invalidating the legislation; Article 31C barred the fundamental-rights challenge, and the requirement was also reasonable and beneficial to cultivation.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_reform and owner_residence_and_income_condition and condition_supports_personal_cultivation and close_nexus_to_common_good

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: Landholders brought a constitutional challenge to legislation reforming agricultural landholding.
predicates.owner_residence_and_income_condition: The legislation required an owner or a family member to live near the land for most of the year and required the land to be the principal source of income.
predicates.condition_supports_personal_cultivation: The residence and income requirements were intended to ensure attention to the land and its cultivation.
predicates.close_nexus_to_common_good: The legislation’s measures were closely connected to distributing material resources for the common good.

members.legal_issue: A requirement that an owner-cultivator reside in the locality of the land for most of the year is not arbitrary or unduly harsh when it advances effective cultivation and the common good.
material_facts: The challenged law required the landowner or a family member to reside in the locality where the land was situated for the greater part of the year.
The law linked that requirement to cultivation of the land and to ensuring that the cultivator gave adequate attention to it.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 39(b) and Article 31C, concluding that a law advancing Article 39(b) could not be challenged under Articles 14, 19 or 31, and that requiring residence near the land supported cultivation and productive use. It applied Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The residence requirement was not harsh or arbitrary. It was a beneficial measure intended to ensure attention to cultivation and to promote effective use of agricultural resources.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law reforming agricultural land ownership or cultivation.
predicates.cultivator_must_reside_near_land_for_mos: The law requires the owner-cultivator or a family member to reside near the land for most of the year.
predicates.residence_requirement_supports_effective: The residence requirement is intended to ensure the cultivator attends to the land and cultivates it effectively.

members.legal_issue: Allegations of fraud do not by themselves justify refusing arbitration when they are not serious and complex enough to require court determination and can be examined by the arbitrator.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged fraud and misrepresentation in connection with the equipment purchase and lease transactions.
The allegations against the appellants included that they induced the plaintiffs to pay a higher price for equipment.
A criminal complaint had resulted in a registered case, and proceedings concerning that case remained pending.
The commercial agreements contained arbitration clauses, and the court found that the allegations were not so serious as to prevent reference and could be examined by the arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, mere allegations of fraud do not nullify an arbitration agreement. Ayyasamy v. A. Paramasivam (2016) 10 SCC 386 holds that reference may be refused only where the allegations are serious and complicated, amount to a virtual case of criminal offence, and are more appropriately determined by a court after appraisal of evidence. The court must also give commercial agreements a sense of business efficacy; an arbitrator may examine allegations that do not meet that serious-and-complicated threshold.
members.conclusion: The fraud allegations did not justify refusing reference to arbitration; the arbitrator could examine them.

rule.if: section_8_reference_application_in_suit and arbitration_agreement_covers_dispute and fraud_is_alleged and not serious_complex_fraud_requires_court_determination

predicates.section_8_reference_application_in_suit: A party to a suit applied for the disputes to be referred to arbitration under an arbitration agreement.
predicates.arbitration_agreement_covers_dispute: The parties made an arbitration agreement covering the dispute being litigated.
predicates.fraud_is_alleged: A party alleged that another party committed fraud in connection with the transaction.
predicates.serious_complex_fraud_requires_court_det: The alleged fraud is so serious and complex that deciding it requires a court to assess evidence rather than an arbitrator.

members.legal_issue: Allegations of fraud in a civil or contractual dispute do not by themselves make the dispute non-arbitrable.
material_facts: The Court considered earlier decisions treating serious fraud allegations as a reason to refuse arbitration.
It distinguished fraud that invalidates the arbitration agreement itself from fraud allegations concerning the parties’ civil or contractual dealings.
It also considered claims involving public-law allegations against the State or its instrumentalities.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 8 and 16 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act and the principles of separability and competence-competence. It relied on A. Ayyasamy v. A. Paramasivam, Avitel Post Studioz Ltd. v. HSBC PI Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd., and Rashid Raza v. Sadaf Akhthar. The relevant considerations are whether the fraud makes the arbitration agreement itself invalid or whether the allegations concern public-law conduct rather than a civil or contractual dispute.
members.conclusion: Civil fraud disputes are arbitrable unless the fraud vitiates the arbitration agreement itself or the allegations raise a public-law controversy requiring adjudication by a public court. Seriousness, complexity, or the mere possibility of criminal proceedings does not alone make a civil dispute non-arbitrable. The Court overruled N. Radhakrishnan v. Maestro Engineers on this point.

rule.if: civil_contract_dispute and fraud_concerns_parties_private_dealings and not (fraud_vitiates_arbitration_agreement or fraud_requires_public_law_adjudication)

predicates.civil_contract_dispute: The dispute arises from a civil or contractual relationship between the parties.
predicates.fraud_concerns_parties_private_dealings: The alleged fraud concerns dealings between the parties rather than conduct requiring adjudication in the public-law domain.
predicates.fraud_vitiates_arbitration_agreement: The alleged fraud makes the arbitration agreement itself invalid or shows that it was never agreed to.
predicates.fraud_requires_public_law_adjudication: The allegations concern public-law conduct requiring determination by a public court.

members.legal_issue: Allegations of fraud do not make a dispute non-arbitrable when the arbitration agreement was executed and the dispute has no public overtones.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that the assignment and confirmation documents were procured by misrepresentation and concealment concerning a partner’s role and authority.
The claimant did not allege that the assignment agreement or confirmation deed had never been entered into.
The dispute was between the parties to the agreements and did not involve public overtones.
members.legal_principle: Following Avitel Post Studioz Limited v. HSBC PI Holding (Mauritius) Ltd., the Court held that fraud within section 17 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and fraud in performance amounting to the civil wrong of deceit, are arbitrable. Criminal overtones alone do not make a dispute non-arbitrable. The fraud exception does not apply on these facts; if the agreement itself had never been executed, the arbitration clause would not exist. The Court held that N. Radhakrishnan v. Maestro Engineers no longer had precedential force, and distinguished State of A.P. v. T. Suryachandra Rao as irrelevant to the issue.
members.conclusion: The fraud allegations did not oust the arbitrator’s jurisdiction, and the dispute was arbitrable.

rule.if: arbitration_referral_proceeding and arbitration_clause_in_executed_agreement and fraud_dispute_is_between_parties and not agreement_execution_denied and not dispute_has_public_overtones

predicates.arbitration_referral_proceeding: A party asked a judicial authority to refer a civil dispute to arbitration.
predicates.arbitration_clause_in_executed_agreement: The parties entered into an agreement containing a clause to arbitrate disputes within its scope.
