predicates.fraud_dispute_is_between_parties: The alleged fraud concerns the rights and conduct of parties to the agreement.
predicates.agreement_execution_denied: A party asserted that the agreement containing the arbitration clause was never entered into.
predicates.dispute_has_public_overtones: The dispute has ramifications beyond the parties, rather than being confined to their private rights.

members.legal_issue: A land-assessment scheme violates equality when it leaves assessment to uncontrolled official discretion without procedures enabling affected landholders to challenge material assessment decisions.
material_facts: The scheme did not prescribe a procedure for making assessments or identify the officer responsible for making them.
It provided no notice or opportunity for a landholder to contest the assessment, classification, or calculation.
The available appeal concerned notifications identifying irrigation sources, not the correctness of individual land assessments.
The State argued that existing administrative standing orders supplied the procedure, but the Court held that the statutory language did not incorporate those orders.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary official action as well as unreasonable statutory discrimination. A fiscal law must provide a fair and workable assessment procedure and cannot leave important assessment decisions uncontrolled. The Court applied the equality principles discussed in Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer.
members.conclusion: The scheme left assessment to arbitrary and uncontrolled discretion without an effective means to challenge its correctness, and therefore violated the constitutional guarantee of equality.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_assessm: A party challenged the constitutionality of a scheme imposing assessments on land.
predicates.assessment_officer_or_process_not_specif: The scheme did not identify the responsible assessment officer or prescribe how individual assessments were to be made.
predicates.no_effective_opportunity_to_contest_asse: Affected landholders had no effective procedure to receive notice and challenge the assessment or its material components.

members.legal_issue: A power to take over land management based on an officer’s subjective assessment, without objective standards or adequate procedures for determining inefficient agricultural use, is arbitrary and invalid.
material_facts: The holders ploughed their land, sowed grass seed, harvested the grass, and used it as fodder for their cattle.
The authority considered the land capable of producing food crops or fruit and concluded that growing grass did not constitute full and efficient agricultural use.
The authority did not identify evidence that the grass was agriculturally unnecessary or inefficiently grown.

The law provided no objective criteria for deciding what counted as efficient cultivation, when a different kind of cultivation could be imposed, or what standards the State’s manager had to meet; it also did not provide the cultivator an opportunity to change the kind of cultivation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(1) and 2(5) of the agricultural tenancy statute include the raising of grass within agriculture and cultivation. The challenged addition to section 65 supplied no objective tests for inefficient cultivation, no clear basis for imposing a different kind of cultivation, and no adequate process for determining those matters. The Court held that a power affecting property cannot rest merely on an officer’s subjective preference among agricultural uses; clear standards and a clear determination are required.
members.conclusion: The amendment conferred arbitrary and unreasonable power and was ultra vires; the orders taking over management of the lands were quashed.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_management_takeover and holder_cultivates_land and authority_relies_on_subjective_view and no_objective_efficiency_standards and inadequate_determination_process

predicates.challenge_to_state_management_takeover: A party challenges a State order taking over management of agricultural land.
predicates.holder_cultivates_land: The holder carries on an agricultural use of the land, including growing and harvesting grass.
predicates.authority_relies_on_subjective_view: The authority bases its decision on its own assessment that another agricultural use would be preferable or more productive.
predicates.no_objective_efficiency_standards: The governing law supplies no objective criteria for deciding whether the existing agricultural use is inefficient or when another use may be required.
predicates.inadequate_determination_process: The governing arrangements lack a sufficient process for determining inefficient use and do not provide an adequate opportunity to address a proposed change in cultivation.
predicates.management_power_invalid_and_takeover_or: The management-taking power is invalid and orders made under it cannot stand.

members.legal_issue: Property valuations based on an unscientific process conducted by untrained personnel under a delegation that leaves the responsible valuation authority without control are arbitrary and violate equality.
material_facts: The Board relied on data gathered through door-to-door surveys by casual municipal employees whose training and qualifications were not established.
The Board had delegated the survey work to the Municipality and had no demonstrated control over the employees or supervision of their work.
The valuations were not shown to rest on an expert or scientific method, and the valuation demands varied extremely across holdings.
The governing municipal legislation identified factors relevant to determining annual valuation.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary state action. Valuation is an expert exercise that must use a rational, non-haphazard method and relevant valuation factors; a statutory authority cannot evade its responsibility through an uncontrolled delegation. The Court relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, AIR 1978 SC 597; Dr. Balbir Singh v. M.C.D. (1985) 1 SCC 167; Krishna Mohan (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi (2003) 7 SCC 151; and Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980) 1 SCC 685, and considered the valuation requirements under section 106 of the West Bengal Municipal Act, 1993 and section 9 of the West Bengal Central Valuation Board Act, 1978.
members.conclusion: The valuation method used was arbitrary and unconstitutional under Article 14.

rule.if: challenge_to_property_valuation_method and valuation_data_was_collected_by_untrained_workers and responsible_authority_lacked_control_over_survey and no_scientific_expert_basis_was_shown and valuation_demands_varied_extremely

predicates.challenge_to_property_valuation_method: The proceeding challenged the method used to determine property valuations for municipal taxation.
predicates.valuation_data_was_collected_by_untraine: The municipal authority used casual workers whose relevant training and qualifications were not established to collect property data.
predicates.responsible_authority_lacked_control_ove: The authority responsible for valuation delegated survey work and did not demonstrate control or supervision over the people carrying it out.
predicates.no_scientific_expert_basis_was_shown: The valuation authority did not establish that its valuations rested on an expert, scientific, or otherwise rational method.
predicates.valuation_demands_varied_extremely: The resulting valuation demands differed extremely across the properties assessed.

members.legal_issue: Landlord-tenant disputes governed by general property law are arbitrable, but disputes assigned exclusively to a rent-control forum are not.
material_facts: The reference challenged the rule in Himangni Enterprises that landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act were non-arbitrable.
The Court distinguished tenancies governed by general property law from tenancies protected by rent-control legislation that gives a specified court or forum exclusive jurisdiction.
The dispute described in Himangni Enterprises concerned eviction, rent arrears, and an injunction in a tenancy not protected by rent-control legislation.
members.legal_principle: Applying the four-fold test and Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc., the Court held that ordinary landlord-tenant claims concern subordinate rights in personam, ordinarily do not affect third parties, and can be enforced like a civil-court decree. The Transfer of Property Act does not expressly or by necessary implication prohibit arbitration, and an arbitrator must apply its tenant-protective provisions. The Court overruled Himangni Enterprises v. Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia. It preserved the exception identified in Booz Allen for special-statute tenancies where tenants enjoy statutory protection and only specified courts have jurisdiction; Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios concerned such a statutory tenancy.
members.conclusion: Landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable. Disputes governed by rent-control legislation are not arbitrable where that legislation gives a specified court or forum exclusive jurisdiction over the special rights and obligations.

predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: The dispute concerns rights or obligations between a landlord and a tenant.
predicates.governed_by_general_property_law: The tenancy is governed by general property law rather than a special rent-control regime assigning exclusive jurisdiction.
predicates.rent_control_forum_has_exclusive_jurisdi: A rent-control law gives a specified court or forum exclusive authority to decide the tenancy dispute.

members.legal_issue: Disputes between a landlord and tenant under the general law governing leases are arbitrable when no special statutory regime reserves them to an exclusive court.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a lease of premises and the tenant’s failure to deliver possession after the lease expired.
The lease contained an arbitration clause covering disputes arising from the agreement or its subject matter.
The dispute was governed by the Transfer of Property Act, and no special rent statute conferred exclusive jurisdiction on a specified court.
The applicable law provided limited relief against forfeiture, but the Court found that this did not exclude arbitration.
members.legal_principle: Under Booz Allen and Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., civil and commercial disputes are in principle arbitrable unless legislation expressly or by necessary implication reserves them to public fora. The non-arbitrability example in Booz Allen concerns tenancy matters governed by special statutes that protect tenants against eviction and confer jurisdiction on specified courts; Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios involved such an exclusive statutory forum. Sections 111, 114 and 114A of the Transfer of Property Act identify grounds for lease determination and limited relief against forfeiture, but do not make those disputes triable only by a civil court. The Act is silent on arbitrability and does not negate it. The Court also relied on Olympus Superstructures Pvt. Ltd. v. Meena Vijay Khetan in rejecting the proposition that statutory discretion alone bars arbitration.
members.conclusion: Disputes about determination of a lease under the Transfer of Property Act, including grounds considered alongside the statutory reliefs against forfeiture, are arbitrable. The Court considered the contrary reasoning in Himangni Enterprises to require reconsideration by a larger Bench.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_dispute and ordinary_property_lease and arbitration_agreement_exists and no_exclusive_tenant_forum

predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: A dispute arose between a landlord and a tenant concerning their lease relationship.
predicates.ordinary_property_lease: The lease and dispute were governed by general property law rather than a special tenancy regime.
predicates.arbitration_agreement_exists: The parties agreed to refer disputes arising from their agreement or its subject matter to arbitration.
predicates.no_exclusive_tenant_forum: No applicable special law both protected the tenant against eviction and reserved the dispute to a specified court.

members.legal_issue: Disputes concerning leases governed by general property law are arbitrable when the tenancy is not governed by a special statute that provides statutory protection against eviction and an exclusive forum.
material_facts: The dispute arose from a sub-lease containing an arbitration clause.
The premises and tenancy were not governed by a special rent statute and were governed by general property law.
The parties had agreed to arbitrate disputes arising out of or in connection with the sub-lease.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle in Booz Allen and Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., disputes are generally arbitrable unless expressly or by necessary implication reserved for public fora. Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios and Booz Allen concern tenancies governed by special statutes, not ordinary leases governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation clarified that such ordinary lease disputes are arbitrable and overruled the contrary observations in Himangni Enterprises v. Kamaljeet Singh Ahluwalia. Where a special rent statute applies, its statutory tenant protections and exclusive forum make the dispute non-arbitrable.
members.conclusion: The dispute was arbitrable, and there was no impediment to invoking the arbitration clause.

rule.if: tenancy_arbitrability_proceeding and lease_governed_by_general_property_law and not special_statutory_tenant_protection_applies and arbitration_agreement_exists

predicates.tenancy_arbitrability_proceeding: A proceeding concerns whether a dispute arising from a landlord-tenant relationship may be resolved by arbitration.
predicates.lease_governed_by_general_property_law: The lease and tenancy are governed by general property law rather than a special rent statute.
predicates.special_statutory_tenant_protection_appl: A special statute provides the tenant statutory protection against eviction and assigns adjudication to a specified court or forum.
predicates.arbitration_agreement_exists: The landlord and tenant agreed to arbitrate disputes arising from their lease.

members.legal_issue: The absence of blood at the alleged place of assault, alongside blood at another location, does not establish that the prosecution misstated the place of occurrence when the circumstances explain the physical evidence.
material_facts: The investigating officer found no blood where the deceased was said to have been assaulted but found blood in the courtyard of the accused's house.
The courts below found that heavy rain had made the assault site muddy and could explain the absence of blood there.
They also found that the injured woman could have returned to the house after being wounded, explaining the blood in the courtyard.
members.legal_principle: Physical evidence concerning the location of blood must be assessed in light of the circumstances that may explain its presence or absence; the court relied on the findings about rain, mud, and the injured woman's movement.
members.conclusion: The blood evidence did not establish that the prosecution had changed the place of occurrence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and blood_absent_at_alleged_scene and blood_found_elsewhere and (rain_or_conditions_could_remove_scene_blood or injured_person_could_have_moved_to_other_location)

predicates.criminal_appeal: The matter is an appeal arising from a criminal prosecution.
predicates.blood_absent_at_alleged_scene: No blood was found at the location where the prosecution said the assault occurred.
predicates.blood_found_elsewhere: Blood was found at a different location connected with the incident.
predicates.rain_or_conditions_could_remove_scene_bl: Rain or other site conditions could explain why blood was not found at the alleged scene.
predicates.injured_person_could_have_moved_to_other: A person injured during the incident could have moved to the location where blood was found.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution may establish the time and place of an occurrence despite the absence of blood or bullets at the scene when the evidence and surrounding circumstances reasonably account for those absences.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses placed the shooting and assault at the alleged location and time.
The deceased was taken for medical treatment after the attack and died later.
The bullets that struck the deceased were recovered from his injuries, while no bullets or substantial quantity of blood were found at the scene.
The road was unpaved and dusty, passers-by had crossed the scene, and the deceased’s injuries caused internal bleeding; the investigating officer was not asked whether he had searched for bullets.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the prosecution evidence as a whole and treated the absence of physical traces at the scene as not decisive where the circumstances and medical evidence reasonably explained it. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The courts below rightly found that the occurrence took place at the time and place alleged by the prosecution.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and eyewitnesses_place_occurrence and medical_evidence_supports_assault and missing_scene_traces_reasonably_explained

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.eyewitnesses_place_occurrence: Witnesses who claimed to see the event placed it at the location and time alleged by the prosecution.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_assault: Medical findings are consistent with the assault described by the witnesses.
predicates.missing_scene_traces_reasonably_explaine: The circumstances provide a reasonable explanation for the absence or loss of physical traces at the scene.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a visible blood trail does not by itself undermine the prosecution account when the body was dragged and blood-stained earth was recovered at the scene or nearby.
material_facts: The informant said the accused dragged the deceased’s body to another house.
The trial court considered that dragging the body could stain the accused persons’ clothes rather than leave a trail of blood.
The investigating officer testified that he collected blood-stained earth from several places.
The High Court did not explain why it disagreed with the trial court’s assessment.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the alleged absence of a blood trail in light of the evidence that the body was dragged and that blood-stained earth was collected at several places; it noted that the case therefore did not involve an absence of blood at the occurrence site or nearby. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s treatment of the absence of a blood trail was unsustainable.

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The prosecution appeals against an acquittal.
predicates.body_dragged_from_occurrence_site: The evidence is that the body was dragged from the place of occurrence.
predicates.blood_stained_earth_recovered_nearby: The investigating officer recovers blood-stained earth at the occurrence site or nearby.

members.legal_issue: An alienation of joint family property is not binding on the sons when it is unsupported by legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or payment of an antecedent debt.
material_facts: The father and his sons sold the remaining agricultural lands to purchasers in separate transactions.
The High Court found that those sales were not for legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or payment of an antecedent debt.
The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and agreed that those sales had no connection to the earlier loan or any other antecedent debt.
members.legal_principle: An alienation of joint family property must be supported by a legally sufficient ground, such as legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or payment of an antecedent debt; the Court found none of those grounds for these sales. Its discussion of antecedent debt relied on Mulla, Principles of Hindu Law, 15th edition, paragraph 295, and Raja Brij Narain v. Mangala Prasad, AIR 1924 PC 50.
members.conclusion: The sales of the remaining agricultural lands were not binding on the sons, and the decree for possession of those lands was maintained.

rule.if: joint_family_property_alienation_challenge and alienation_lacks_legal_necessity and not alienation_benefits_estate and not alienation_discharges_antecedent_debt

predicates.joint_family_property_alienation_challen: Members of a joint family challenged an alienation of joint family property.
predicates.alienation_lacks_legal_necessity: The alienation was not made for legal necessity.
predicates.alienation_benefits_estate: The alienation benefited the joint family estate.
predicates.alienation_discharges_antecedent_debt: The alienation discharged an independent debt that arose before it.

members.legal_issue: An alienation of coparcenary property is invalid when the alienee does not establish legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or adequate bona fide inquiry into either.
material_facts: The father sold property that remained coparcenary property as against his son.
The son had acquired an interest in the property by birth before the purported sale.
The purported buyer admitted that she paid no consideration, and the father also testified that no consideration was paid.
The buyer did not establish legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or bona fide inquiries into either.
members.legal_principle: A manager’s power to alienate coparcenary property is restricted to cases of legal necessity or benefit to the estate. The alienee bears the burden of establishing necessity or benefit, either by proving actual necessity or by showing proper and bona fide inquiries and reasonable steps to satisfy herself that necessity existed. The Court relied on Rani v. Santa Bala Debnath and Vijay A. Mittal v. Kulwant Rai, and on Mulla on Hindu Law.
members.conclusion: The sale deeds were illegal, null and void, and were cancelled.

rule.if: coparcenary_alienation_dispute and manager_alienated_joint_property and alienee_failed_to_prove_necessity_or_estate_benefit_or_bona_fide_inquiry and no_consideration_paid

predicates.coparcenary_alienation_dispute: The case concerns an alleged alienation of coparcenary property.
predicates.manager_alienated_joint_property: A person managing the coparcenary property purported to transfer it.
predicates.alienee_failed_to_prove_necessity_or_est: The transferee did not prove legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or reasonable bona fide inquiry into either.
predicates.no_consideration_paid: The purported transfer was made without payment of consideration.

members.legal_issue: A father's alienation of coparcenary property after a son is born is invalid to the extent of the coparcenary property when it is not made for legal necessity.
material_facts: After the plaintiff's birth, his father executed sale deeds and a release deed affecting the property.
The father had been the sole surviving coparcener until the plaintiff was born, after which the plaintiff acquired an interest in the property.
The parties did not claim that the father executed the deeds as karta for legal necessity.
members.legal_principle: After a son is born and acquires an interest in property that had been held by his father as a sole surviving coparcener, the father may alienate the coparcenary property only as karta for legal necessity. An alienation made before the son's birth cannot be challenged by the son on that basis, but a post-birth alienation without legal necessity is invalid as to the coparcenary property. The Court applied the principle supported by M. Yogendra v. Leelamma, (2009) 15 SCC 184.
members.conclusion: The sale deeds and release deed were illegal, null and void to the extent of the entire coparcenary property; the parties could pursue remedies in an appropriate proceeding regarding the property that would have fallen to the father's share when the deeds were executed.

rule.if: civil_appeal_in_property_dispute and son_acquired_interest_by_birth and father_alienated_property_after_son_birth and not alienation_for_legal_necessity

predicates.civil_appeal_in_property_dispute: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal concerning rights in property.
predicates.son_acquired_interest_by_birth: A son was born while his father held property allotted from ancestral property, and the son thereby acquired an interest in it.
predicates.father_alienated_property_after_son_birt: The father transferred or released property after the son was born.
predicates.alienation_for_legal_necessity: The father made the transfer as manager of the family property for a necessary family purpose.

members.legal_issue: A notification that identifies a company's project and provides for the company to bear the entire compensation is an acquisition for a company, even if it describes the purpose as public.
material_facts: The notification described the acquisition as being for a public purpose but identified staff quarters, hostel buildings and a playground for a society.
The agreement preceding the notification provided that the society would pay all compensation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6(1) and the proviso to it, a public-purpose acquisition requires compensation to be paid wholly or partly from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority, whereas an acquisition for a company may be paid for by the company. As explained in Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab, R.L. Arora v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Smt. Somawanti v. State of Punjab, an acquisition primarily for a company can also be for a public purpose if the statutory public-funding condition is met. The notification must be read fairly to determine which kind of acquisition it declares.
members.conclusion: The notification, read fairly and together with the preceding agreement, was for acquisition for a company at that company's expense, so compliance with the company-acquisition procedure was necessary.

predicates.company_acquisition_proceeding: The government undertook a land acquisition proceeding for a project proposed by a company or comparable entity.
predicates.notification_identifies_company_project: The acquisition notification identifies a project belonging to the company or comparable entity.
predicates.company_pays_all_compensation: The agreement or other acquisition record provides that the company or comparable entity will pay all compensation.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition made specifically for a private company, at its instance and for a site selected by it, is an acquisition for a company rather than a public-purpose acquisition where the asserted public scheme and qualifying public funding are not established.
material_facts: The company proposed a small-car project and identified the project site after discussions with the State.
Cabinet records and acquisition notifications connected the land to the company’s specific project.
The State-owned corporation raised the acquisition cost through loans; the State did not itself contribute the money, and the corporation was not a local authority for this purpose.
The procedures for acquisition for a company were not followed.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(f) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, excludes acquisition for companies from public purpose; Sections 39–41 and Rules 3–5 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 govern acquisition for a company. Justice Gowda relied on Devender Singh v. State of Punjab, Royal Orchid Hotels Ltd. v. G. Jayaram Reddy, and the statutory scheme as explained in R.L. Arora. He distinguished pre-amendment authorities including Pandit Jhandu Lal, Somawanti, and Jage Ram, and considered Pratibha Nema distinguishable. Justice Mishra relied on Section 3(f), Section 6 and its Explanation 2, and the principle in Pratibha Nema that the source of acquisition funds is the principal distinction between the procedures; he also relied on Amarnath Ashram, Sooraram Pratap Reddy, Urmila Roy, and Nand Kishore Gupta.
members.conclusion: Justice V. Gopala Gowda held that the acquisition was for the company, not for a public purpose, and was invalid because the mandatory company-acquisition procedure was not followed. Justice Arun Mishra disagreed and held that it was a public-purpose acquisition; there was no common conclusion between the two opinions on this issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.company_selected_project_site: A private company identified or selected the site used for the project for which the land was acquired.
predicates.acquisition_was_for_specific_company_pro: The acquisition records connected the land to a particular private company’s project.
predicates.acquisition_cost_not_paid_from_qualifyin: The acquisition cost was not paid from funds treated as public funds under the applicable acquisition scheme.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition funded entirely by its beneficiary and conducted under the requirements for acquiring land for a company remains an acquisition for a company despite a preliminary notice describing the purpose as public.
material_facts: A registered society operating a school sought adjacent land for a playground, and the society was to bear the entire acquisition cost.
The acquisition process included an agreement for the society to pay the cost and a declaration referring to the company-acquisition inquiry and agreement.
The preliminary notification described the playground as a public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(e)(ii), 40(1), and Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, an acquisition whose entire cost is borne by the beneficiary is an acquisition for a company; the preliminary notification's description of the purpose does not change that classification. Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab establishes that State contribution can make an acquisition one for a public purpose, but does not require State contribution in every company acquisition. The observation in Srinivasa Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Madam Gurumurthy Sastry concerning public use was made in the context of section 40 and does not make the provisions for company acquisitions redundant.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was for a company under Part VII, not an acquisition for a public purpose requiring the State to contribute to its cost.

rule.if: company_land_acquisition_proceeding and beneficiary_is_statutory_company and beneficiary_funds_entire_cost and preliminary_notice_describes_public_purpose

predicates.company_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition of land for the benefit of an organization.
predicates.beneficiary_is_statutory_company: The organization benefiting from the acquisition falls within the statutory category of a company for land-acquisition purposes.
predicates.beneficiary_funds_entire_cost: The beneficiary organization is to pay the entire cost of the acquisition.
predicates.preliminary_notice_describes_public_purp: The preliminary notice describes the proposed use of the land as a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: Delay and laches do not bar constitutional relief where an unlawful deprivation of property is continuing and the demand for justice is compelling.
material_facts: The owner was an illiterate rural widow who had not sought relief for many years after the State took her land.
The State had admitted that it took the land without acquisition proceedings or another process known to law.
The owner remained uncompensated, and the Court treated the cause of action as continuing.
The High Court had declined to determine the claim in writ proceedings on the basis of disputed questions and delay.
members.legal_principle: Delay and laches do not necessarily bar relief for a continuing cause of action or where the circumstances shock the judicial conscience. Whether delay should be condoned depends on the circumstances, including the breach of fundamental rights, the remedy sought, and the reason for the delay; there is no prescribed limitation period for constitutional courts exercising their jurisdiction to do substantial justice. The Court relied on Tukaram Kana Joshi v. M.I.D.C. and referred to P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of T.N.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the State’s delay-and-laches objection and exercised its extraordinary jurisdiction to grant relief.

predicates.constitutional_relief_proceeding: The claimant seeks relief in a constitutional proceeding concerning deprivation of property.
predicates.continuing_unlawful_property_deprivation: The claimant remains deprived of property taken without legal sanction and has not received compensation.
predicates.compelling_demand_for_justice: The circumstances make the demand for judicial relief compelling.

members.legal_issue: Delay and laches do not bar constitutional relief where the State has taken private property without lawful process or compensation and its own conduct has perpetuated the injustice.
material_facts: The State used the land for a public road without initiating acquisition proceedings or paying compensation, and the owners sought relief decades after the land was taken.
The State initiated acquisition proceedings for some landowners only after they approached courts, while other landowners whose land was used for the same road did not receive that benefit.
The State relied on alleged verbal consent but produced no material to support it.
members.legal_principle: Laches is an equitable, not arbitrary or technical, doctrine; its application depends on the length of delay and the nature of conduct during the interval and must be assessed by balancing justice. Delay does not defeat relief where the circumstances make the demand for justice compelling or the cause is continuing. The State must act lawfully when depriving a person of property under Article 31, as applicable at the time, and Article 300-A. The Court relied on Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation v. Balwant Regular Motor Service, State of U.P. v. Manohar, Tukaram Kana Joshi v. MIDC, and Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh, including its reliance on P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of T.N.; constitutional writ jurisdiction under Article 226 remains available to promote justice.
members.conclusion: The State could not rely on delay and laches to avoid its responsibility, and the circumstances warranted constitutional relief despite the delay.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_disposal and state_took_private_property_without_lawful_process and compensation_was_unpaid and state_failed_to_support_consent_or_acquisition and state_selectively_compensated_similarly_placed_owners and claim_followed_long_delay

predicates.appeal_from_writ_disposal: The claimant appealed after a court disposed of a constitutional writ proceeding without granting the requested relief.
predicates.state_took_private_property_without_lawf: The State took and used a person's private property without following a lawful process for acquiring it.
predicates.compensation_was_unpaid: The State did not pay the owner compensation for the property it took and used.
predicates.state_failed_to_support_consent_or_acqui: The State produced no supporting material showing that the owner consented to give up the property or that it was acquired lawfully.
predicates.state_selectively_compensated_similarly_: The State provided acquisition or compensation benefits to some similarly placed owners after court intervention but did not extend them to other owners.
predicates.claim_followed_long_delay: The owner sought judicial relief a long time after the State took the property.

members.legal_issue: Delay and laches do not bar constitutional relief when the State has continuously deprived a person of property without lawful authority and the circumstances make refusal of relief unjust.
material_facts: The authorities took possession of the land without completing acquisition proceedings and transferred it for public development.
The owners repeatedly sought compensation and pursued the authorities; a later attempt to acquire the land also lapsed.
The owners were illiterate and inarticulate, and the State conceded their ownership.
The High Court rejected their claim on delay and missing-record grounds, although no third-party interest was identified.
members.legal_principle: The discretion to refuse relief under Article 226 for delay must be exercised fairly and on the facts; delay is not an absolute bar where the cause of action continues, the claim is legally sustainable, and substantial justice requires relief. The Court relied on P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of T.N., State of M.P. v. Nandlal Jaiswal, Tridip Kumar Dingal v. State of West Bengal, Durga Prasad v. Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Co. v. District Board, Dayal Singh v. Union of India, Shankara Co-op Housing Society v. M. Prabhakar, and H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in refusing relief on the grounds of delay and missing records; the claim was not barred by delay and laches.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_claim and state_possession_without_law and continuing_claim_efforts and no_third_party_interest

predicates.constitutional_writ_claim: The claimant seeks constitutional-court relief concerning the State's treatment of property.
predicates.state_possession_without_law: State authorities took possession of a person's property without completing a legally authorized process.
predicates.continuing_claim_efforts: The affected person continued to seek relief from the authorities after the property was taken.
predicates.no_third_party_interest: No third party acquired an interest that would be harmed by granting relief.

members.legal_issue: Statutory provisions governing public charitable institutions and endowments do not apply to property found to be an absolute private gift unconnected with a public endowment.
material_facts: The final findings in the earlier litigation established that the land had been gifted absolutely to an individual and that the temple constructed on part of it was private.
The gift deed did not create an endowment, and the Government had no interest in the land.

The appellants relied on the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, including its provisions concerning administration and adjudication of endowment matters.
The fact that the premises had been used as a dharamshala for years was relied on as suggesting a public endowment.
members.legal_principle: Section 1(3) of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987 applies to public charitable institutions and endowments. The court relied on Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar for the distinction between private and public trusts, and Kuldip Chand v. Advocate-General to hold that long use of property as a dharamshala, by itself, does not establish dedication to the public.
members.conclusion: The Act did not apply to the property, so the appellants’ reliance on its provisions did not undermine the consent order or the prior findings.

predicates.property_found_to_be_absolute_private_gi: The evidence and binding findings establish that the property was given absolutely to a private recipient.
predicates.temple_found_to_be_private: The place of worship on the property is found to be private rather than public.
predicates.no_public_endowment_established: The facts do not establish that the property was dedicated for the benefit of the public as a class.

members.legal_issue: The statutory definition of a religious trust does not extend the regulatory scheme to private religious trusts.
material_facts: The statute defined a religious trust in broad terms but excluded a private endowment for worship of a family idol where the public had no interest.

The statute also contained provisions concerning public supervision, applications by persons interested in a trust, and schemes for trust administration, which the court considered inconsistent with applying it to private trusts.
The legislative history and earlier enactments concerning religious and charitable trusts addressed public trusts.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a public trust has beneficial interests vested in an uncertain and fluctuating body of people, such as the public or a substantial section of it; a private trust has definite and ascertainable beneficiaries. A religious group or sect may itself constitute the relevant public. The Court construed the definition in section 2(1) in light of section 4(5), sections 29, 30, 32 and 48, the Act’s purpose, and the legislative history of the Religious Endowments Act, 1863, the Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, and section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, all of which concerned public trusts. It also relied on the distinction described in Nabi Shirazi v. Province of Bengal and the Hindu-law authorities discussed in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The Act applies to public religious trusts and does not apply to private religious trusts.

predicates.religious_trust_regulation_scope_dispute: A court is asked to decide whether a regulatory scheme for religious trusts covers a particular trust.
predicates.statutory_scheme_concerns_public_trusts: The scheme’s legislative context and operative provisions are directed to trusts involving public interests and supervision.
predicates.beneficiaries_are_definite_individuals: The trust’s beneficial interests belong to identified individuals or a class that can be definitely ascertained.

members.legal_issue: The statutory scheme for regulating Hindu religious trusts does not apply to private endowments.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the endowment was private and therefore outside the Act.
The Court determined that the endowment created by the deed was public, so it did not qualify for the exclusion applicable to private endowments.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S. P. Sahi, which held that the Act does not apply to private endowments.
members.conclusion: The Act does not apply to private endowments; because this endowment was public, that exclusion did not prevent the proceedings against it.

predicates.religious_trust_regulation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the application of a regulatory scheme to a religious endowment.
predicates.private_endowment: The endowment confines its purposes and rights of worship to specified individuals or a family rather than the public or a section of the public.

members.legal_issue: The minor censure imposed on an officer did not warrant upward revision because the choice of penalty was not shown to violate Wednesbury principles.
material_facts: The disciplinary authority found misconduct proved but imposed censure, a minor punishment.
The authority took account of the complicated stage at which the officer handled the matter and the absence of malafides as mitigating circumstances.
The authority considered an inquiry report, a commission report, advice from the public service commission, and the views of a committee of secretaries, which were not all against the officer.
The earlier direction in the proceedings was that only a minor punishment could be imposed.
members.legal_principle: A court reviewing disciplinary punishment for arbitrariness applies Wednesbury principles and does not select a different permissible punishment merely because it might have chosen a more severe one. The court relied on Union of India v. Ganayutham, B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India, and Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The court declined to refer the punishment for upward revision because it could not find that selecting censure from the permissible minor punishments violated Wednesbury principles or was shockingly disproportionate.

rule.if: disciplinary_punishment_review and minor_penalty_imposed and mitigating_circumstances_considered and mixed_record_considered

predicates.disciplinary_punishment_review: A court considered whether to increase a punishment imposed in disciplinary proceedings.
predicates.minor_penalty_imposed: The disciplinary authority imposed a minor punishment for proved misconduct.
predicates.mitigating_circumstances_considered: The disciplinary authority considered circumstances mitigating the officer's responsibility.
predicates.mixed_record_considered: The disciplinary authority considered material that included findings or views both adverse and favorable to the officer.

members.legal_issue: A major disciplinary punishment did not warrant further upward revision where the disciplinary authority's decision was not shown to violate Wednesbury principles.
material_facts: The disciplinary authority found misconduct and imposed a major punishment.
The commission and inquiry reports were adverse to the officer, while the public service commission's recommendations were favorable on both occasions.
The court considered the authority's decision in light of that record.
members.legal_principle: A court reviewing the quantum of disciplinary punishment for arbitrariness performs a secondary Wednesbury review and does not substitute its assessment for the disciplinary authority's primary decision absent a reviewable defect. The court relied on Union of India v. Ganayutham and the Wednesbury principles.
members.conclusion: The court declined to refer the punishment for further upward revision because the administrator's decision was not shown to violate Wednesbury principles.

predicates.disciplinary_punishment_review: A court considered whether to increase a punishment imposed in disciplinary proceedings.
predicates.major_penalty_imposed: The disciplinary authority imposed a major punishment for misconduct.
predicates.decisionmaker_considered_mixed_record: The disciplinary authority considered material that included findings or recommendations both adverse and favorable to the officer.

members.legal_issue: Further enhancement of a major disciplinary punishment was not considered where the punishment was already major and a challenge to it was pending before the appropriate tribunal.
material_facts: A major punishment had been imposed on the officer.
The officer's challenge seeking reduction of the punishment was pending before the administrative tribunal.
members.legal_principle: The court did not further enhance a punishment where a major penalty had already been imposed and a challenge to that punishment was pending before the tribunal; the tribunal was to consider the pending matter in accordance with law.
members.conclusion: The court declined to consider further enhancement and left the tribunal to consider the officer's pending challenge in accordance with law.

predicates.disciplinary_punishment_proceeding: An officer's punishment arose from disciplinary proceedings.
predicates.major_penalty_imposed: The disciplinary authority imposed a major punishment for misconduct.
predicates.reduction_challenge_pending_before_tribu: The officer had challenged the punishment before a tribunal, and that challenge remained pending.

members.legal_issue: A State's refusal to be bound by a private contract or licence does not infringe a fundamental right when the State has not acquired or taken possession of that contract or licence.
material_facts: The claimants argued that the State had to honor agreements made by former proprietors.

The Court held that, if the agreements created only contractual rights or licences rather than proprietary rights, the State had not acquired or taken possession of those rights under the abolition legislation.
The petitions sought enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 32.
members.legal_principle: Under Ananda Behera v. State of Orissa and Shrimathi Shantabai v. State of Bombay, a State that does not acquire or take possession of a private contract or licence, but merely declines to be bound by it, has not thereby infringed a fundamental right. A licence also comes to an end with the extinction of the licensor's title.
members.conclusion: If the agreements created only contractual rights or licences, the State's refusal to be bound by them did not infringe a fundamental right supporting relief under Article 32.

predicates.article_32_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.claimant_right_is_only_contractual_or_li: The claimant's entitlement is only a personal contractual right or licence, not a proprietary right in the land or its resources.
predicates.state_did_not_acquire_or_take_possession: The State did not take possession of or acquire the claimant's contract or licence, but declined to be bound by it.

members.legal_issue: The State's mere refusal to recognize a contract does not infringe fundamental rights when it neither takes the contract nor claims its benefits, and an ineffective transfer gives the claimants no enforceable property right.
material_facts: The claim was brought to enforce fundamental rights.
The purported fishery transfers were oral and did not pass title or interest.
The State refused to recognize the contracts and was preparing to auction the fishery rights again.
The State did not take possession of the contracts or claim the payments or other benefits under them.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(1) of the Constitution, a fundamental-rights claim requires a relevant property interest and State action taking or interfering with it in the manner alleged. The court held that the invalid transfers conferred no enforceable interest. It further held that, even assuming a contract could be property, mere refusal to recognize it was not confiscation, acquisition or taking possession of it; a contractual remedy might instead be pursued by suit.
members.conclusion: The State's refusal to recognize the contracts did not violate the asserted fundamental rights, and the petition was dismissed; any remedy for breach of contract lay, if available, in a civil action.

rule.if: constitutional_enforcement_petition and (transfer_formality_unsatisfied or (contract_assumed_property and state_only_declined_recognition and state_neither_took_contract_nor_claimed_benefits))

predicates.constitutional_enforcement_petition: A claimant seeks relief for an alleged infringement of fundamental rights in a constitutional enforcement proceeding.
predicates.transfer_formality_unsatisfied: The purported transfer was oral and lacked the written and registered instrument required for that transfer.
predicates.contract_assumed_property: The claimant's contract is treated, for purposes of the alternative analysis, as property.
predicates.state_only_declined_recognition: The State refused to recognize the contract and did not assume its obligations.
predicates.state_neither_took_contract_nor_claimed_: The State did not take possession of the contract or claim benefits paid or due under it.

members.legal_issue: A claim to cut and appropriate forest produce under an unregistered grant does not establish an infringement of fundamental rights when the grant, under any available construction, gives no enforceable property right against the State.
material_facts: The claimant relied on an unregistered instrument granting rights to take wood and other forest produce from land for a period of years.
Proprietary rights in the land vested in the State under a later enactment.
The claimant alleged that the State forest officer’s order stopping the cutting infringed her rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g).
members.legal_principle: A petition under Article 32 requires an infringement of a fundamental right. Under the Registration Act, an unregistered instrument does not affect immovable property or transfer an interest in it. Section 3 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 vested proprietary rights in the State. A profit à prendre is an interest in immovable property and requires registration. A purely personal contractual right does not become a fundamental right merely because its performance is obstructed; its enforcement or breach is ordinarily pursued by suit. The Court followed Ananda Behera v. State of Orissa and did not follow Chhotabai Jethabai Patel and Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The order did not infringe the claimed fundamental rights, and the Article 32 petition was dismissed. Depending on the instrument’s construction, a proprietary interest was ineffective for want of registration and, in any event, vested in the State; a licence ended when the grantor’s proprietary rights vested; a profit à prendre was an unregistered interest in immovable property; or a purely personal contractual right remained with the claimant and could be pursued through an ordinary suit, not as a fundamental-rights claim against the State.

rule.if: article_32_fundamental_rights_petition and rights_claimed_under_unregistered_forest_grant and ((grant_conveys_proprietary_interest and proprietary_interest_vested_in_state) or (grant_creates_profit_a_prendre and profit_is_immovable_property) or (grant_is_pure_license and grantor_proprietary_rights_vested_in_state) or (grant_is_personal_contract and state_not_party_to_contract and state_did_not_acquire_contract))

predicates.article_32_fundamental_rights_petition: The claimant brought a constitutional petition seeking relief for an alleged infringement of fundamental rights.
predicates.rights_claimed_under_unregistered_forest: The claimant based the asserted rights to enter forest land and take its produce on an instrument that was not registered.
predicates.grant_conveys_proprietary_interest: The instrument, as construed, purports to transfer a proprietary interest in land.
predicates.proprietary_interest_vested_in_state: The proprietary interest in the land vested in the State under a later enactment.
predicates.grant_creates_profit_a_prendre: The instrument, as construed, grants a right to enter land and take produce from it.
predicates.profit_is_immovable_property: The granted right is an interest in land treated as immovable property.
predicates.grant_is_pure_license: The instrument, as construed, grants only permission to enter the land.
predicates.grantor_proprietary_rights_vested_in_sta: The grantor’s proprietary rights in the land vested in the State.
predicates.grant_is_personal_contract: The instrument, as construed, gives the claimant only a personal contractual right.
predicates.state_not_party_to_contract: The State was not a party to the contract.
predicates.state_did_not_acquire_contract: The State did not acquire or take possession of the claimant’s contractual right.

members.legal_issue: A law authorizing premature termination of a lease for extracting minerals is protected from constitutional challenge on specified individual-rights grounds when mineral extraction falls within the constitutional protection for winning minerals.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the 1957 mining statute on the ground that it permitted premature termination of a mineral lease without compensation.
The lease concerned the extraction of minerals from a mine.
members.legal_principle: The dissent applied Article 31A(1)(e) of the Constitution and section 3(d) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, giving “winning” its popular sense of getting or extracting a mineral. It considered Lewis v. Fothergill and Lord Rokeby’s case but declined to adopt a narrower meaning. The majority left the issue undecided.
members.conclusion: The dissent held that extracting a mineral falls within the constitutional expression concerning winning minerals and that a law providing for premature termination of such a lease was protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31. The majority did not decide this contention.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_mineral_leas: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law governing termination of mineral leases.
predicates.law_authorized_premature_termination: The challenged law authorized termination of a mineral lease before its stated expiry.
predicates.lease_concerned_mineral_extraction: The lease concerned obtaining or extracting minerals from a mine.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for laws modifying mineral rights applies to leases for extracting minerals and related purposes, not only to the initial preparation of a mine for working.
material_facts: The lease authorized excavation of white clay and its removal from the leased land.
The challenged rules modified the lease, including its duration and royalty terms.
The appellant argued that the lease covered extraction and removal, not merely the narrow process of making a mine workable.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(e) uses “winning” broadly to mean getting or extracting minerals from mines and purposes incidental to that activity. Definitions of “winning” or “win” in statutes and rules are framed for their own limited purposes and do not control the meaning of the constitutional provision. The court distinguished the narrow, lease-specific usage in Lewis v. Fothergill and Lord Rokeby v. Elliot.
members.conclusion: The lease was for winning minerals within Article 31A(1)(e), so the modification rules were not invalid on the ground that they abridged rights under Articles 14, 19 or 31.

predicates.appeal_challenging_mining_lease_modifica: A party appealed an order modifying the terms of a mining lease.
predicates.lease_authorized_mineral_extraction: The lease authorized the lessee to extract minerals from the leased area.
predicates.modification_related_to_mining_rights: The challenged modification governed rights connected with extracting minerals or related mining activity.

members.legal_issue: A temporary restriction on rights under a mineral lease is a modification of those rights and is protected from the specified constitutional challenge by the constitutional protection for laws modifying mineral-searching or mineral-winning rights.
material_facts: The notice and the statutory prohibition prevented the petitioners from working their mines for a limited period.
The petitioners argued that a temporary suspension of their rights was not a modification of those rights.
The disputed rights arose under mining leases.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(e) protects laws providing for the modification of rights under agreements, leases or licences for searching for or winning minerals from challenges based on the specified constitutional rights. “Modification” includes alteration, limitation or restriction and need not be permanent. The Court distinguished Thakur Raghbir Singh v. Court of Wards, Ajmer, and relied on Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, Atma Ram v. State of Punjab, and In re Delhi Laws Act, 1912, in considering the meaning of modification and the limited scope of the earlier decision.
members.conclusion: The temporary restriction modified the petitioners' lease rights, and Article 31A(1)(e) barred a challenge to sections 4 and 5 on the ground that they infringed Article 31(2).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_temporary_mi: A person challenges a temporary restriction on rights held under an agreement, lease or licence for mineral exploration or extraction.
predicates.restriction_alters_lease_rights: The restriction limits or otherwise alters the holder's rights under the mineral agreement, lease or licence.
predicates.restriction_is_temporary: The restriction applies for a limited period rather than permanently.
predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_restriction_: The specified constitutional challenge to the restriction cannot be maintained.

members.legal_issue: A notation in a government file does not become a binding government order unless it is finalized and communicated to the person affected.
material_facts: The consumer fora relied on a notation by an administrator stating that no decision would be taken until clear directions were received from the central government.
The notation was an internal part of the decision-making process and was not shown to have been communicated as a final order to the affected applicants.
members.legal_principle: In Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab, relying also on State of Punjab v. Sodhi Sukhdev Singh, the Court held that an internal file opinion remains provisional until a final decision is made and communicated to the affected person. The judgment applied that principle to the notation relied on by the consumer fora.
members.conclusion: The internal notation could not, by itself, support a finding of deficiency in service or be treated as a binding government order.

predicates.government_order_status_is_in_issue: A party relies on an internal government notation as though it were a final government decision.
predicates.only_internal_file_notation_exists: The asserted decision appears only as a notation in an administrative file.
predicates.notation_was_not_communicated: The notation was not communicated to the person affected as a final order.

members.legal_issue: An inter-departmental communication or file noting is not a decision of the Government affecting rights unless the decision is formally expressed and authenticated as required for executive action.
material_facts: The District Magistrate sent an inter-departmental communication recommending payment of compensation.
The Government rejected that recommendation as improper.
The High Court treated the recommendation as an order of the Government, although it was not expressed and authenticated as a Government order.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 77(1) and 77(2), and Articles 166(1) and 166(2) of the Constitution, executive action must be expressed in the name of the President or Governor, as applicable, and authenticated in the prescribed manner to be treated as an order of the Government. A file noting is only an expression of an individual’s opinion and does not become a Government decision affecting rights unless acted upon through a properly expressed and authenticated order. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Sodhi Sukhdev Singh, Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Bihar v. Kripalu Shankar, Rajasthan Housing Board v. Shri Kishan, Sethi Auto Service Station v. DDA, and Shanti Sports Club v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The recommendation could not be treated as an order on behalf of the Government or relied on as a Government decision affecting the parties’ rights.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_writ_direction: The proceeding is an appeal from a High Court direction that relies on a communication as a Government decision.
predicates.communication_claimed_as_government_deci: A party or court treats an official communication or file record as a Government decision affecting rights.
predicates.communication_not_formally_expressed_and: The communication was not expressed and authenticated in the prescribed manner as an executive order.

members.legal_issue: A departmental communication that is neither expressed in the Governor’s name nor authenticated as required cannot be treated as a government policy decision.
material_facts: A ministerial committee recommended measures to regularize constructions and occupations involving acquired land.
A departmental official sent a letter describing the committee’s recommendations and decisions.
The letter was not expressed in the Governor’s name and was not authenticated in the prescribed manner.
No material showed that the committee’s recommendations had been approved by the State Government.
members.legal_principle: Articles 166(1) and 166(2) of the Constitution require executive action to be expressed in the Governor’s name and orders and instruments to be authenticated as prescribed; Article 166(3) concerns rules for the transaction of government business. Relying on State of Bihar v. Kripalu Shankar (1987) 3 SCC 34, the Court held that a departmental communication lacking these features is not a government order.
members.conclusion: The letter could not be treated as a policy decision of the State Government.

rule.if: government_policy_review and departmental_communication_only and not expressed_in_governor_name and not authenticated_as_prescribed

predicates.government_policy_review: A court is asked to determine whether a communication represents a government policy decision.
predicates.departmental_communication_only: The asserted decision appears only in a communication from a departmental official describing recommendations or discussions.
predicates.expressed_in_governor_name: The communication expresses the executive action in the Governor’s name.
predicates.authenticated_as_prescribed: The communication is authenticated in the manner prescribed for government orders.

members.legal_issue: A widow holding her husband's property only as a life tenant without power to devise it cannot pass that property by will, and the reversioners succeed to it.
material_facts: The widow had inherited the property from her husband on his death, subject to a life tenure.
She had no right to devise the husband's property, and no necessity supporting an alienation was established.
She attempted to devise the property by will.
The beneficiary's asserted adoption was not proved.
members.legal_principle: Under the applicable Hindu law, a widow who takes her husband's property only for life lacks power to devise it and may not alienate it except for necessity. The court noted that the result would have differed if the adoption had been proved, because the beneficiary would then have succeeded as the sole reversioner.
members.conclusion: The widow's will was inoperative as to the husband's property, and the reversioners, rather than the devisee, succeeded to it.

rule.if: will_dispute and property_inherited_from_husband_as_life_tenant and not power_to_devise_or_proven_necessity and adoption_not_proved

predicates.will_dispute: The dispute concerns a will purporting to dispose of property inherited from a deceased husband.
predicates.property_inherited_from_husband_as_life_: The woman received her husband's property only as a life tenant.
predicates.power_to_devise_or_proven_necessity: The woman had power to devise the property or a necessity justifying its alienation was established.
predicates.adoption_not_proved: The alleged adoption that could make the devisee the reversioner was not established.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner cannot obtain compensation from a widow's separate property for loss to the inherited estate caused by her negligence merely because the reversioner later succeeds to the estate.
material_facts: A widow held and enjoyed her deceased husband's estate, while the reversionary interest remained a possibility during her lifetime.
Some land was lost in a revenue sale after the widow failed to pay the land revenue.
The reversioners sought to debit the lost land against the widow's share in properties, but the case lacked the necessary allegations to establish wilful waste.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a widow is entitled to beneficial enjoyment of the estate and is not a trustee for future reversioners. While she is alive, a reversioner's interest is only a spes successionis; the reversioner is entitled to the property left at her death. A suit to prevent waste during her lifetime is a distinct matter, and the Court observed that a claim based on wilful waste would require the necessary allegations.
members.conclusion: The reversioners were entitled only to the property left when the widow died and could not obtain compensation for the loss from her separate property on the facts pleaded.

predicates.reversionary_claim_after_widow_death: A person claiming as a reversioner seeks relief after the widow's death.
predicates.loss_during_widow_enjoyment: Property in the inherited estate was lost while the widow was enjoying that estate.
predicates.no_wilful_waste_established: The claim does not establish wilful waste by the widow with the necessary allegations.

members.legal_issue: A transferee cannot defeat a reversioner's right to recover property by relying solely on adverse possession attributable to a widow's acts or omissions during her limited estate.
material_facts: The property had been inherited by a widow from her husband as a limited owner.
The respondent claimed that possession following the exchange had continued long enough to establish adverse possession against the reversioners.
The plaintiffs were the next reversioners and brought their claim within twelve years after the widow's death.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and principles of Hindu law: a reversioner's right is in the nature of a spes successionis and is not traced through the widow, so the reversioner does not lose that right through the widow's negligence or sufferance. It relied on Kalipada Chakraborti v. Palani Bala Devi and referred to Mulla's Hindu Law.
members.conclusion: The respondent could not rely on adverse possession during the widow's lifetime to defeat the reversioners' claim, and the claim brought within twelve years of the widow's death was not barred.

predicates.reversioner_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding is brought by a reversioner to recover immovable property after the limited estate holder's death.
predicates.property_inherited_by_limited_estate_hol: The property was inherited by a person holding only a limited estate.
predicates.adverse_possession_depends_on_limited_ho: The opposing claim of adverse possession rests on possession arising from the limited estate holder's acts or omissions.
predicates.claim_brought_within_limitation_after_de: The reversioner's recovery claim is brought within the applicable limitation period measured from the limited estate holder's death.

members.legal_issue: Central control of an industry and a central levy on its product do not displace State competence to tax the land on which the industry operates.
material_facts: The central legislation provided for control of the tea industry, including cultivation, and authorized a central excise cess on tea produced in India.
The State levy was imposed on land comprised in a tea estate and was measured by the estate’s green-leaf yield.
The Court treated the central excise levy and the State land cess as distinct in character and purpose.
members.legal_principle: Legislative competence depends on the true subject of the levy, not merely on the industry that ultimately bears its economic effect. A central levy on tea or tea leaves for the purposes of the central enactment is distinct from a State tax on land. The Court relied on the distinction between taxable subjects and aspects explained in Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Association v. Union of India, and considered the Tea Act, 1953, including Sections 2, 3(n), 10, 12–16, 16B–16D, and 25, alongside Entry 49 of List II and the relevant Union entries.
members.conclusion: The central legislation and central levy did not deprive the State legislature of competence to impose the land cess.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_land_levy and state_levy_is_on_land and central_law_controls_industry_or_product and central_levy_has_distinct_subject

predicates.challenge_to_state_land_levy: A constitutional challenge is made to a State levy imposed in relation to land used by an industry.
predicates.state_levy_is_on_land: The State levy is, in its true character, imposed on land rather than on the industry’s product or activity.
predicates.central_law_controls_industry_or_product: A central law regulates the relevant industry, its cultivation, or its product.
predicates.central_levy_has_distinct_subject: Any central levy concerns a taxable subject distinct from the land taxed by the State.

members.legal_issue: The State’s power to tax land and buildings for municipal administration is not displaced merely because the property is used for mining subject to central regulation and development.
material_facts: The taxed lands and buildings were used for, or covered by, coal mines.
The tax was imposed as a tax on land and buildings by an authority performing municipal functions.
The challenge asserted that the tax conflicted with central powers over coal-mine regulation and development.
No evidence was presented that the tax impeded the achievement of the objectives of the central mining legislation.
members.legal_principle: The State Legislature’s powers over local government under Entry 5 and taxes on lands and buildings under Entry 49 of List II remain distinct from the Union’s powers over mine regulation and development under Entry 54 of List I. The declaration in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 does not occupy the field of municipal administration or invalidate a legitimate tax on land. The Court relied on H.R.S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittoor, State of Haryana v. Chanan Mal, and Ishwari Khetan Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and distinguished Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar. It also considered the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, 1973.
members.conclusion: The State’s power to confer the property-tax power on the authority did not conflict with the Union’s power to regulate and develop coal mines, and the tax did not defeat the purpose of the central legislation.

rule.if: mining_tax_challenge and local_land_building_tax and tax_supports_municipal_functions and no_shown_mining_impediment

predicates.mining_tax_challenge: The proceeding challenges a local tax on the ground that it conflicts with central regulation of mining.
predicates.local_land_building_tax: The challenged levy is a tax on land or buildings.
predicates.tax_supports_municipal_functions: The authority imposing the tax performs municipal functions.
predicates.no_shown_mining_impediment: The record does not show that the tax impedes the objectives of central mining regulation or development.

members.legal_issue: Central control of mining and mineral development does not, without a parliamentary limitation on taxation, automatically extinguish a State's separate power to tax land or mineral rights.
material_facts: The challenges concerned State levies on mineral-bearing land, mineral rights, and material extracted from land.
The central mining legislation declared Union control over mining and mineral development to the extent provided by that legislation.
The Court found no applicable parliamentary limitation that barred the challenged State levies as taxes.
The Court distinguished the power to regulate and control from the power to tax.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 245, 246, and 248, legislative fields and heads of taxation are distinct. Entries 49 and 50 of List II give States taxing powers over land and mineral rights, while Entries 52 and 54 of List I concern Union control and regulation. Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, limits State legislative power only to the extent provided by the Act; Sections 13, 18, and 25 do not create a general central tax on minerals. The Court applied the pith-and-substance approach in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. and M.A. Tulloch and distinguished India Cement and Orissa Cement.
members.conclusion: The central declaration did not by itself invalidate the State levies; State taxation remained available within the fields assigned to the State, subject to any parliamentary limitations and without interference with Union regulation.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_mining_levy and central_mining_control_declared and state_tax_field_independently_available and no_parliamentary_tax_limitation and levy_does_not_interfere_with_union_regulation

predicates.challenge_to_state_mining_levy: The proceeding challenges a State levy connected with land or mineral rights in a mining context.
predicates.central_mining_control_declared: A central law declares Union control over mining or mineral development to the extent specified in that law.
predicates.state_tax_field_independently_available: The levy falls in a field of taxation assigned to the State rather than a general field of regulation.
predicates.no_parliamentary_tax_limitation: No applicable parliamentary law imposes a limitation that bars the State from imposing the particular tax.
predicates.levy_does_not_interfere_with_union_regul: The State levy does not itself disrupt or control the mining regulation exercised by the Union.

members.legal_issue: An unsatisfied decretal debt may be considered for statutory scaling where the operative decree falls within the debt-relief law as extended by the later amendment, subject to the debtor proving eligibility.
material_facts: The operative preliminary decree was made by the appellate court after the principal debt-relief law came into force, and a final decree followed.
The final decree had not been satisfied in full when the amending law came into force.
The applicant sought to scale down the decretal debt, but the court had not yet determined whether the applicant was an eligible agriculturist.
members.legal_principle: Sections 19(2) and 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, as amended by Madras Act 23 of 1948, apply to a decree passed after the principal Act commenced where the decree remained unsatisfied in full when the amendment commenced. The word “debt” includes a decretal debt. The Court followed Narayanan Chettiar v. Annamalai Chettiar on the scope of clause (iii) and the meaning of debt.
members.conclusion: The applicant was entitled to have the scaling application considered under the amended law, provided he established that he was an agriculturist entitled to its benefit.

rule.if: application_to_scale_decretal_debt and operative_decree_passed_after_relief_law_started and decree_not_fully_satisfied_at_amendment and debtor_is_eligible_agriculturist

predicates.application_to_scale_decretal_debt: The debtor applied for statutory scaling of a debt embodied in a decree.
predicates.operative_decree_passed_after_relief_law: The operative decree was passed after the debt-relief law had commenced.
predicates.decree_not_fully_satisfied_at_amendment: The decree had not been satisfied in full when the later amendment commenced.
predicates.debtor_is_eligible_agriculturist: The debtor is an agriculturist eligible for the debt-relief benefit.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree that remained unexecuted or unsatisfied in part when the amending law commenced was subject to debt scaling, just as a decree passed after contest was.
material_facts: The debt decree was made by compromise before the amending law commenced.
Some payments had been made, but the decree had not been executed or satisfied in full when the amending law commenced.
The debtors later applied to have the decree scaled down.
