members.legal_principle: Section 19(2) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, as amended, and section 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948, apply to decrees not executed or satisfied in full before the amending law commenced. The proviso protects creditors from having to refund sums already paid or realized. The court held that compromise decrees are not distinguished from decrees passed after contest for this purpose, and relied on Venkataratnam v. Seshamma, I.L.R. (1952) Mad. 492.
members.conclusion: The application was governed by section 16(iii), read with section 19(2), and the compromise decree was subject to scaling down; amounts already paid or realized did not have to be refunded.

predicates.debt_scaling_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to scale down a debt embodied in a decree.
predicates.money_decree_unexecuted_or_partly_unsati: The money decree had not been executed or satisfied in full when the relevant amending law commenced.

members.legal_issue: Debtors who qualify as agriculturists may obtain scaling down of a decree that remains subject to the amended debt-relief law, unless a legally sufficient bar prevents the claim.
material_facts: The debtors qualified as agriculturists because the assessment attributable to each of their defined shares was below the disqualifying limit.
The compromise decree had not been executed or satisfied in full when the amending law commenced.
The compromise did not amount to a judicial determination of the debtors' entitlement to scaling down, and no conduct-based estoppel had been pleaded and tried.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(ii), 19(2), and 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, as amended by the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948, entitled qualifying agriculturists to seek scaling down of an eligible decree. The court described the relief as protection for petty agriculturists from oppressive loans at usurious rates of interest and applied its rulings on agriculturist status, decrees not fully executed or satisfied, and res judicata.
members.conclusion: The debtors were entitled to have the decree scaled down, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: debt_scaling_proceeding and debtors_are_agriculturists and decree_is_subject_to_scaling_down and no_prior_judicial_bar_to_the_claim

predicates.debt_scaling_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to scale down a debt embodied in a decree.
predicates.debtors_are_agriculturists: The debtors meet the applicable criteria for agriculturist status.
predicates.decree_is_subject_to_scaling_down: The decree remains eligible for scaling down because it was not executed or satisfied in full when the relevant amending law commenced.
predicates.no_prior_judicial_bar_to_the_claim: No prior judicial determination bars the debtors from raising their claim to scaling down.

members.legal_issue: The evidence supported the forgery convictions and the conviction for abetting forgery.
material_facts: The sale deed purported to convey land belonging to a person who had died years earlier, and the second accused impersonated that person to execute it.
The first accused participated in arranging the transaction and assisted the forgery; the second accused executed the forged deed.
The High Court found both accused guilty of forgery-related offences, although it acquitted the first accused on a procedural ground.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 467 and 114 of the Indian Penal Code, forgery of a valuable security and abetment of that forgery are punishable offences. When an appellate court agrees with the trial court’s view of the evidence, it need not repeat the evidence or the reasons already given; Girija Nandini Devi v. Bigendra Nandini Choudry was relied on for that approach.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court sustained the second accused’s conviction for forgery and convicted the first accused of abetting forgery, setting aside his acquittal on that charge.

predicates.criminal_appeal_reviewing_forgery_convic: The proceeding is an appeal asking a court to review convictions for forgery-related conduct.
predicates.evidence_establishes_forgery: The evidence establishes that a document was forged.
predicates.evidence_establishes_each_accused_role: The evidence establishes each accused’s role in committing or abetting the forgery.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for abetting forgery and cheating may stand where an accused identified an impostor as a genuine executant and the claimed honest mistake was unsupported by evidence.
material_facts: The accused, a village Lambardar, identified a woman who was impersonating the actual co-owner as that co-owner during execution and registration of a mortgage deed.
The Sub-Registrar would not have registered the deed but for the accused’s identification.
The accused was expected to know the actual co-owner, and the evidence did not support his claim that he innocently believed the impersonator was her.
The trial court convicted the accused, the High Court affirmed the conviction while reducing the sentence, and the Supreme Court considered his appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 34(3) and 35(1) of the Registration Act, the registering officer must inquire whether a document was executed by the persons said to have executed it and satisfy himself as to the identity of those appearing. The accused’s identification enabled registration; his position and expected knowledge of the true executant, together with the absence of evidence supporting his asserted innocent mistake, supported the conviction under Sections 467 and 417 read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court found no ground to interfere with the concurrent findings, affirmed the conviction, and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and accused_identified_impostor_as_genuine_executant and identification_enabled_registration and accused_expected_to_know_true_executant and no_evidence_supports_innocent_mistake

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed against a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_identified_impostor_as_genuine_e: The accused identified a person impersonating the true executant as that genuine executant.
predicates.identification_enabled_registration: The registering officer would not have registered the document without the accused’s identification.
predicates.accused_expected_to_know_true_executant: The accused’s role or circumstances gave reason to expect that he knew the true executant.
predicates.no_evidence_supports_innocent_mistake: The evidence did not support the accused’s claim that he innocently mistook the impostor for the true executant.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for abetting forgery may be sustained when the evidence establishes the accused’s assistance in procuring the forged document even though the person who physically forged it is not identified.
material_facts: The complainant denied executing the sale deed or appearing for its registration.
A fingerprint expert concluded that the thumb impression on the deed was not the complainant’s.
The accused maintained that the complainant had executed the deed, and two accused had identified the impersonator as the complainant.
One accused had obtained the deed and used it to seek a change to revenue entries.
The evidence did not identify who physically forged the deed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 109 and 465 of the Indian Penal Code apply where evidence establishes assistance or abetment in the commission of forgery. The person who physically made the forged document need not be identified for the accused’s abetment to be established. The court found the evidence, including the complainant’s denial, the fingerprint evidence, the false identification and the accused’s conduct concerning the deed, sufficient to leave no reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: The evidence supported the finding that all three accused abetted forgery, and the convictions under Sections 109 and 465 of the Penal Code were upheld.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction_for_abetting_forgery and forged_document_used_to_claim_property and complainant_denied_executing_document and expert_excluded_complainant_fingerprint and accused_assisted_procurement_or_use

members.legal_issue: A notice terminating a month-to-month tenancy created by holding over must expire at the end of the correctly calculated tenancy month.
material_facts: The lease was for one year and commenced on April 9, 1945; the lease document stated that possession was to be delivered on April 9, 1946.
The lease was not for a manufacturing purpose, and the tenant held over after the one-year term, creating a month-to-month tenancy.
The rent receipts and the fair-rent order supported tenancy months running from the tenth day of one month through the ninth day of the following month.
The landlord’s notice provided the required notice period but purported to terminate the tenancy on the eighth day, rather than at the end of the tenancy month.
members.legal_principle: Under section 110 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the date on which a lease term commences is excluded when computing its duration. The one-year term therefore ended on the corresponding date the following year, and the monthly tenancy created by holding over ran from the following day through the corresponding day of the next month. For a non-manufacturing lease held over under section 116, the resulting month-to-month tenancy is terminable under section 106 by fifteen days’ notice expiring with the tenancy month. Benoy Krishna Das v. Salsiccioni was applied in support of the calculation of the tenancy period.
members.conclusion: The notice did not validly terminate the contractual tenancy because it did not expire at the end of the tenancy month.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and nonmanufacturing_lease and tenant_held_over_after_fixed_term and monthly_tenancy_cycle_followed_term and notice_expired_before_tenancy_month_end

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The dispute concerns a landlord’s attempt to obtain eviction of a tenant.
predicates.nonmanufacturing_lease: The lease was not granted for a manufacturing purpose.
predicates.tenant_held_over_after_fixed_term: The tenant remained in possession after the fixed lease term ended.
predicates.monthly_tenancy_cycle_followed_term: After the fixed term, the tenancy months ran from the day after the term ended through the corresponding day of the following month.
predicates.notice_expired_before_tenancy_month_end: The landlord’s notice purported to end the tenancy before the correctly calculated end of a tenancy month.

members.legal_issue: A notice terminating a month-to-month tenancy is construed as a whole and in the context of the facts and the parties to whom it is addressed.
material_facts: After the fixed lease term expired, the tenancy continued from month to month.
The landlord sent the termination notice to the lessee, not separately to the sublessee.
Different paragraphs of the notice referred to surrender on the expiry of one day and delivery of possession on the following day, while also requiring removal of structures and other property.
Read together, the paragraphs directed the lessee to hand over the property on the stated termination date.
members.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 governs termination of the tenancy by notice. Under Harihar Banerji v. Ramasashi Roy, a notice is construed in light of the facts and circumstances known to the tenant and with a view to making it effective rather than finding defects. Mangilal v. Suganchand Rathi applied the requirement that a section 106 notice comply with the applicable notice period; the Court distinguished that case because the notice there did not provide the required clear notice period. The Court also referred to Subadini v. Durga Charan Law and Gobinda Chandra Saha v. Dwarka Nath Patita on calculating the notice period.
members.conclusion: Read as a whole and in context, the notice validly terminated the tenancy.

rule.if: notice_validity_dispute and month_to_month_tenancy and notice_sent_to_tenant and notice_paragraphs_read_together_identify_surrender_date

predicates.notice_validity_dispute: The case concerns whether a notice terminated a tenancy.
predicates.month_to_month_tenancy: The tenancy continued from month to month after the fixed lease term ended.
predicates.notice_sent_to_tenant: The landlord sent the termination notice to the tenant.
predicates.notice_paragraphs_read_together_identify: The notice contained directions in multiple paragraphs which, read together, identified when the tenant was to surrender the property.

members.legal_issue: A notice to terminate a monthly tenancy is valid when, construed in a common-sense manner, it makes clear that the tenant may remain until the end of the tenancy month and that the tenancy ends only then.
material_facts: The tenancy was a monthly tenancy.
The notice required the tenants to vacate within October and said they would be treated as trespassers from 1 November if they did not do so.
The notice was given on 25 September, and the stated date for treating the tenants as trespassers was after the end of October.
members.legal_principle: Under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, a monthly tenancy must be terminated by notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. A notice to quit is construed ut res magis valeat quam pereat, in a common-sense rather than hyper-critical manner. Applying Sidebotham v. Holland and Harihar Banerji v. Ramsashi Roy, the Court held that requiring vacation within the month, while stating that the tenants would be trespassers from the first day of the next month, showed that the tenancy ended only at the month's end.
members.conclusion: The notice was valid and determined the tenancy with effect from the end of 31 October.

predicates.monthly_tenancy_notice_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a notice validly terminates a monthly tenancy.
predicates.notice_allows_occupancy_through_month_en: The notice permits the tenant to remain in possession through the end of the tenancy month.
predicates.trespasser_status_begins_next_month: The notice states that the tenant will be treated as a trespasser beginning only in the month after the stated tenancy month.

members.legal_issue: The court may disregard a company’s separate personality when its corporate form is used as a cloak for fraud or improper conduct.
material_facts: The contemnor and family members controlled several companies holding or dealing with assets relevant to claims by defrauded purchasers.
A property held in a company’s name had been leased by the contemnor, while the company’s directorship had shifted to family members without a satisfactory explanation of the changes.
The Court found that the company and changes in shareholding or directorship were devices to screen the property and its income from creditors.
members.legal_principle: The ordinary rule of separate corporate personality does not prevent courts from looking behind the corporate veil when incorporation is used to commit illegality, perpetrate fraud, evade obligations, or protect improper conduct. The Court relied on Aron Salomon v. Salomon & Co.; Tata Engineering and Locomotive Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar; and the discussion in Gower and Palmer. It also referred to DHN Food Distributors Ltd. v. London Borough of Tower Hamlets concerning the economic reality of a group of companies.
members.conclusion: The Court disregarded the corporate form in relation to the property and treated it as belonging to the contemnor and family for purposes of securing the purchasers’ claims.

predicates.fraud_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding seeks relief for people who were defrauded and recovery of assets connected with that fraud.
predicates.corporate_entity_used_to_screen_assets: An asset is held through a company in circumstances that obscure who beneficially owns or controls it.
predicates.controlling_persons_used_corporate_form_: The people controlling the company used its separate legal form to facilitate fraud, evade obligations, or shield assets from claimants.

members.legal_issue: A court may lift the corporate veil when those controlling a company use its separate personality to advance their own dishonest or fraudulent purposes.
material_facts: The promoters were the company’s only subscribers and shareholders, and they controlled its board with their son.
The promoters executed the disputed sale agreement as directors after the company had resolved to sell the property.
The Court found that the promoters used the company’s personality to further their personal objectives and fraudulent design.
members.legal_principle: The corporate veil may be pierced where a corporate entity is abused for an unjust or inequitable purpose, so that the court can identify those responsible. The Court relied on Kapila Hingorani v. State of Bihar, State of U.P. v. Renusagar Power Co., Union of India v. Playworld Electronics Pvt. Ltd., and Yukong Line Ltd. v. Rendsburg Investments Corp.
members.conclusion: The corporate veil was applicable to be lifted, and the promoters could not take a position inconsistent with the company’s interests by relying on its separate personality.

predicates.company_control_dispute: The dispute concerns conduct undertaken through a company and the relationship between the company and its controllers.
predicates.company_controlled_by_claiming_parties: The parties whose conduct is challenged controlled the company and its decision-making.
predicates.corporate_personality_used_for_personal_: The controllers used the company’s separate personality to advance their own dishonest or fraudulent purpose.

members.legal_issue: The corporate veil may be lifted where corporate entities and share transactions are used to conceal the effective sale or transfer of assets or to further a dishonest design.
material_facts: The allottee company’s parent transferred subsidiaries, including the Indian subsidiary, to another company, and the evidence described the sale of those subsidiaries and the transfer of their liabilities.
Affidavits also described a transaction involving a further investor and control over the relevant corporate assets.
The allottee withheld details of the transaction despite a direction to disclose them, and its account conflicted with statements in the affidavits placed before the Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Juggilal Kamlapat v. Commissioner of Income-tax, U.P., AIR 1969 SC 932; Jai Narain Parasrampuria (Dead) v. Pushpa Devi Saraf, (2006) 7 SCC 756; State of U.P. v. Renusagar Power Co., AIR 1988 SC 1737; and Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd., AIR 1986 SC 1370, a court may lift the corporate veil when it is used to perpetrate fraud, evade tax, or further a dishonest or fraudulent design.
members.conclusion: The Court lifted the corporate veil and treated the evidence of the transactions as revealing their true character; the respondent had also suppressed material facts and violated the Court’s disclosure direction.

predicates.corporate_relationships_used_to_effect_t: Related corporate entities used their ownership or control relationships to carry out the transaction under examination.
predicates.evidence_showed_asset_or_subsidiary_sale: Evidence before the Court showed that corporate assets or subsidiaries had been sold or transferred.
predicates.material_transaction_details_withheld: A party withheld material details of the transaction despite a direction to disclose them.

members.legal_issue: Compensation is treated as paid for deemed-lapse purposes only when it is delivered to the interested person or, where payment is prevented by a recognized contingency, offered and deposited in the appropriate court.
material_facts: An award had been made, but compensation was neither delivered to the appellants nor deposited in court.
The authority retained the compensation until the appellants applied for it and submitted title documents and a surety bond; the appellants did not complete those steps.
The authority stated that other landowners who completed those steps received their compensation.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 must be read with Section 31(1) and (2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Under Section 31, the Collector must tender compensation and, if prevented from paying by the specified contingencies, deposit it in the court to which a reference may be made. A treasury deposit or mere retention by the authority is insufficient. The Court applied Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki, which binds coordinate and lesser Benches, and relied also on IVO Agnelo Santimano Fernandes v. State of Goa and Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India Ltd.; it reiterated the principle in Nazir Ahmad that a prescribed procedure must be followed in the prescribed manner.
members.conclusion: The authority’s retention of the compensation pending an application did not amount to payment; payment required delivery to the interested person or, where a recognized contingency prevented payment, an offer followed by deposit in the appropriate court.

predicates.compensation_payment_assessment_in_acqui: The court is assessing whether compensation was paid in an acquisition proceeding in which deemed lapse is in issue.
predicates.compensation_delivered: The authority delivered the compensation to the person entitled to it.
predicates.compensation_offered: The authority offered the compensation to the person entitled to it.
predicates.recognized_payment_impediment: A lack of consent to receive payment, absence of a person competent to alienate the land, or a dispute over entitlement or apportionment prevented payment.
predicates.compensation_deposited_in_reference_cour: After payment was prevented, the authority deposited the compensation in the court where a reference concerning the award could be made.

members.legal_issue: Compensation is not treated as paid merely because it was deposited in a treasury; the authority must tender payment and, when a statutory impediment prevents payment, deposit the compensation in the court designated to receive it.
material_facts: The acquiring authority was not ready with the compensation when the award was made and supplied it to the Collector years later.
The Collector did not tender or pay the compensation to the original landowners.

The compensation was deposited in a treasury rather than in the court designated for a reference, and the authorities relied on a local standing order permitting treasury deposits in specified circumstances.

The court found that the standing order treated treasury deposit as a last resort after efforts to secure the payees’ attendance and did not make it a substitute for deposit in the reference court when the statutory contingencies applied.
members.legal_principle: Sections 31(1) and 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require the Collector to tender compensation to persons entitled to it and, when payment is prevented by the specified contingencies, to deposit it in the reference court. Section 34 concerns interest when compensation is not paid or deposited by the time possession is taken. Pune Municipal Corporation v. H.M. Solanki holds that compensation is treated as paid when it is tendered and, where a Section 31(2) contingency prevents payment, deposited in the reference court; a treasury deposit is insufficient. The Court also relied on Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor for the principle that a prescribed statutory procedure must be followed, and on Agnelo Santimano Fernandes and Prem Nath Kapur for the ineffectiveness of a deposit in the State’s revenue account.
members.conclusion: The treasury deposit did not amount to payment of compensation for the purpose of determining lapse; compensation had not been paid as required.

rule.if: legacy_acquisition_case and (compensation_not_tendered_to_entitled_person or (payment_prevented_by_statutory_contingency and not compensation_deposited_in_reference_court) or compensation_deposited_only_in_treasury)

predicates.legacy_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns an acquisition initiated under an earlier land acquisition regime.
predicates.compensation_not_tendered_to_entitled_pe: The acquiring authority did not offer the compensation to the person entitled to receive it.
predicates.payment_prevented_by_statutory_contingen: A legally recognized impediment prevented the acquiring authority from paying the person entitled to compensation.
predicates.compensation_deposited_in_reference_cour: The acquiring authority deposited the compensation in the court designated to receive it for a compensation reference.
predicates.compensation_deposited_only_in_treasury: The acquiring authority placed the compensation in a government treasury without making the required payment or court deposit.
predicates.compensation_not_paid_as_required: Compensation has not been paid in the legally prescribed manner.

members.legal_issue: Compensation is treated as paid for transitional land-acquisition purposes only when it is tendered to the interested person and, if a statutory impediment prevents payment, deposited in court for that person.
material_facts: An award had been made under the former acquisition law, and the acquiring authority notified the landowners to collect compensation.
The landowners did not receive the compensation, and the authority deposited the amount in the government treasury rather than in court.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act must be read with Section 31 of the 1894 Act: Section 31(1) requires tender and payment, while Section 31(2) requires a court deposit when a specified contingency prevents payment. Sections 32 and 33 support the requirement that money deposited be available for the interested persons. The Court relied on Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor for the principle that a prescribed statutory procedure must be followed, and on Ivo Agnelo Santimano Fernandes and Prem Nath Kapur for the rule that a deposit in the State’s revenue account does not satisfy the payment obligation.
members.conclusion: A treasury deposit is not equivalent to payment. Compensation is treated as paid when it has been offered to the interested person and, if a statutory contingency prevents actual payment, deposited in the court where a compensation reference may be made.

rule.if: old_acquisition_proceeding and compensation_tendered and (compensation_received or (payment_prevented_by_statutory_contingency and compensation_deposited_in_reference_court))

predicates.old_acquisition_proceeding: The acquiring authority began the land-acquisition proceeding under the former acquisition law.
predicates.compensation_tendered: The acquiring authority offered the awarded compensation to the interested person.
predicates.compensation_received: The interested person received the offered compensation.
predicates.payment_prevented_by_statutory_contingen: A circumstance specified by the former law prevented the acquiring authority from paying the compensation directly to the interested person.
predicates.compensation_deposited_in_reference_cour: The acquiring authority deposited the compensation with the court where a reference concerning it could be made.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit cannot be used to set aside or modify a tax assessment made under the governing tax legislation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sued to have tax assessments against their family declared unenforceable against property and to restrain the revenue authorities from selling or confirming sales of that property.
The tax assessments had been made under the tax legislation, and the plaintiffs alleged that the tax officer had failed to inquire into a claimed partition.
members.legal_principle: Section 67 of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922 bars a civil suit to set aside or modify an assessment made under that Act. The assessment procedure and remedies are prescribed by the Act, including an appeal under section 30. Relying on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Tribune Trust, Lahore, the Court held that the taxpayer’s remedies must be found within the Act.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred insofar as it sought to set aside or modify the assessments; any error in assessment had to be addressed through the remedies provided by the tax legislation.

predicates.tax_assessment_challenge_suit: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking to invalidate or alter a tax assessment.
predicates.assessment_made_under_tax_law: The challenged assessment was made by a tax authority under the governing tax legislation.
predicates.civil_suit_barred: The civil suit cannot be used to set aside or modify the assessment.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit cannot be used to challenge the correctness of a mine-profit assessment’s computation when a self-contained statutory scheme provides remedies for that challenge and the aggrieved person did not pursue those remedies on that issue.
material_facts: The company challenged the valuation used to compute the colliery’s profits, including the use of the controlled rate for coal supplied to its factories.
The statutory scheme provided a process for objections to a valuation and an appeal, with the appellate decision being final.
The company did not raise its complaint about the mode of computation before the assessing authority and the appellate authority through the prescribed procedure.

The company’s complaint was about the interpretation and application of the computation provisions, rather than a claim that the authority had violated a provision of the Act or fundamental principles of judicial procedure.
members.legal_principle: Sections 75 and 102 of the Bengal Cess Act, 1880 provided for valuation by the Collector, objections, an appeal, and finality of the appellate decision. A special statutory scheme that creates a liability and provides its own remedies for errors in enforcement must be followed rather than bypassed by suit. Under Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1968] 3 S.C.R. 662, civil jurisdiction is excluded where statutory orders are final and an adequate remedy is provided. Collector of South Arcot v. Mask & Co., 67 I.A. 222, recognizes that exclusion is not readily inferred and that civil courts may still examine statutory noncompliance or failure to follow fundamental principles of judicial procedure; that exception did not apply because the complaint concerned computation and interpretation, not such a failure.
members.conclusion: The company could not raise its computation challenge in the civil suit; the civil courts had no jurisdiction to examine the correctness of the authorities’ computation of net profits in these circumstances.

rule.if: mine_cess_assessment_proceeding and statutory_scheme_provides_objection_and_appeal_with_finality and computation_challenge_not_pursued_through_statutory_remedies and challenge_is_to_assessment_correctness and not alleged_statutory_noncompliance_or_fundamental_procedural_failure

predicates.mine_cess_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an assessment of cess by reference to a mine’s profits.
predicates.statutory_scheme_provides_objection_and_: The governing scheme provides a process to object to the assessment and appeal, and makes the resulting decision final.
predicates.computation_challenge_not_pursued_throug: The taxpayer did not use the prescribed objection and appeal process to raise the particular complaint about computation.
predicates.challenge_is_to_assessment_correctness: The complaint concerns the correctness of the assessment’s computation rather than the validity of the governing law.
predicates.not_alleged_statutory_noncompliance_or_f: The taxpayer does not allege that the authority failed to comply with the statute or with fundamental principles of judicial procedure.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit challenging a municipal property-tax revision is barred where the governing statutory scheme makes the assessment final and provides remedies for challenging it, and the pleaded grounds do not bring the case within a recognized exception to the bar.
material_facts: The property tax was revised after the prior revision five years earlier.
The plaintiffs did not use the statutory appeal process and instead filed a representative civil suit.
The plaint alleged that the increase was excessive, arbitrary, and unreasonable, and that assessors inspected properties without prior notice.

The plaint did not allege non-compliance with a fundamental statutory requirement, a breach of fundamental principles of judicial procedure, an invalid law, or another recognized ground for civil-court intervention.
The statutory scheme provided appeals to a taxation appeals committee and then to a district court, and made the assessment or demand final subject to specified decisions and orders.
members.legal_principle: Under Rule 25 of Part I of Schedule III to the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976, assessments are final subject to the specified statutory orders and decisions. Sections 108, 109, 117, 147 and 148 and Rules 1, 2, 5–8, 18–20 and 22 establish the assessment and review scheme. Under Dhulabhai v. State of M.P., civil jurisdiction is excluded where a statute gives finality to a tribunal's decision and provides an adequate remedy, except, among other recognized cases, where fundamental statutory provisions were not complied with or the tribunal did not follow fundamental principles of judicial procedure. Mere disagreement with the correctness or extent of an assessment is for the statutory authorities. These principles were reaffirmed in Shiv Kumar Chadha v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi.
members.conclusion: The suit was not maintainable in the civil court because the allegations of excessive, arbitrary, or unreasonable enhancement did not overcome the statutory bar.

rule.if: municipal_tax_assessment_challenge and statutory_scheme_provides_assessment_appeals_and_finality and pleaded_ground_is_only_excessiveness_or_unreasonableness and not alleged_fundamental_statutory_breach and not alleged_fundamental_procedural_breach

predicates.municipal_tax_assessment_challenge: The proceeding is a civil suit challenging a municipal property-tax assessment or revision.
predicates.statutory_scheme_provides_assessment_app: The governing statutory scheme provides a process for assessing the tax, appeals against the assessment, and finality subject to specified statutory review or appeal decisions.
predicates.pleaded_ground_is_only_excessiveness_or_: The challengers allege that the assessment is excessive, arbitrary, or unreasonable, without pleading another recognized ground for civil-court intervention.
predicates.not_alleged_fundamental_statutory_breach: The challengers do not allege that a fundamental statutory requirement was disregarded so as to make the proceedings illegal and without jurisdiction.
predicates.not_alleged_fundamental_procedural_breac: The challengers do not allege that the statutory decision-maker failed to follow fundamental principles of judicial procedure.

members.legal_issue: Provision for the wakif or the wakif’s family is not a religious purpose merely because it is regarded as a pious act under Muslim law.
material_facts: The deeds provided for the maintenance or benefit of the wakifs’ families while also providing for charitable or religious expenditure.
The family-benefit provisions remained operative, and no religious worship, teaching, service, or performance of religious rites was involved in providing for the families.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(n) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 defines religious purpose by reference to religious worship, teaching, service, or performance of religious rites. Under section 6(1)(i), the relevant holding must be exclusively for a religious or charitable purpose. Family maintenance does not become religious worship or a religious rite merely because it may be regarded as sadaqah or pious under Muslim law; the Court relied on the reasoning in Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Bussomoy Dhur Chowdry and Syed Mohiuddin Ahmed v. Sofia Khatun.
members.conclusion: The family provisions did not constitute religious purposes, and the deeds were not exclusively for religious purposes.

predicates.claim_under_retention_exemption: The proceeding involved a claim to retain property under an exemption from a property-vesting law.
predicates.family_or_self_support_provided: The trust or endowment provided benefits or maintenance for its founder or the founder’s family.
predicates.family_support_unconnected_to_religious_: The provision for the founder or family was not itself connected with religious worship, teaching, service, or performance of religious rites.

members.legal_issue: Private provision for the wakif or the wakif’s family is not a charitable purpose merely because Muslim law permits a family wakf.
material_facts: The deeds provided substantial continuing benefits for the wakifs’ families, including maintenance and other family allowances.
The deeds also directed expenditure toward charitable or religious purposes, but the family benefits were not shown to have ended or become inoperative.
The family provisions were not shown to be directed to poor or needy family members.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(c) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 includes relief of the poor, medical relief, advancement of education, and other objects of general public utility within charitable purpose. Section 6(1)(i) requires an exclusive charitable or religious purpose. The Court relied on Commissioners for Special Purposes of Income Tax v. Pemsel for the recognized heads of charity; Tribune Press Trustees, Lahore v. Income-tax Commissioner for the need to assess public benefit under the statutory test; D.V. Arur v. Commissioner of Income-tax and In re Mercantile Bank of India (Agency) Ltd. for the public-benefit requirement; and Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Bussomoy Dhur Chowdry, Syed Mohiuddin Ahmed v. Sofia Khatun, and Mujibunnissa v. Abdul Rahim for the conclusion that private family gifts are not charitable in the legal sense. The Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913 and the Shariat Act, 1937 did not give private family gifts a new meaning as charitable purposes.
members.conclusion: The family provisions were not charitable purposes because they were not relief of the poor, medical relief, advancement of education, or expenditure on an object of general public utility.

rule.if: claim_under_retention_exemption and private_family_benefits_provided and family_benefits_not_for_poor_or_needy and no_general_public_benefit

predicates.claim_under_retention_exemption: The proceeding involved a claim to retain property under an exemption from a property-vesting law.
predicates.private_family_benefits_provided: The trust or endowment provided benefits for the founder or the founder’s family as private beneficiaries.
predicates.family_benefits_not_for_poor_or_needy: The family benefits were not limited to relieving poverty or meeting the needs of poor or needy beneficiaries.
predicates.no_general_public_benefit: The family provision did not serve an object of general public utility or otherwise confer the relevant public benefit.

members.legal_issue: A wakf chiefly benefiting the settlor’s descendants does not qualify as a gift to religious or charitable uses merely because it provides for limited charity or ultimately directs property to charity.
material_facts: The wakf devoted only an insignificant part of the income to religious or charitable purposes during the family’s existence.
Most of the income was directed to the settlor and his descendants from generation to generation.
The broader charitable or religious application of the income was postponed until the family line became extinct.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed “religious or charitable uses” in section 18 in the context of an Act applying to talukdars of all religions; provision for one’s descendants was not such a use. Section 18 dealt with the procedure for gifts of that kind, while the power to make gifts arose under section 11, and section 12 applied to transfers under the Act. Sections 3 and 4 of the Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, validated wakfs-alal-aulad in specified circumstances but did not make family support itself a religious or charitable purpose under section 18. The Court considered Bikani Mia v. Shuklal Poddar and relied on the Privy Council’s decision in Abul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Russomoy Dhur Chowdry.
members.conclusion: The wakf was not a gift to religious or charitable uses within section 18 of the Oudh Estates Act; section 18 prescribed the procedure for such gifts and did not exempt them from section 12.

predicates.estate_transfer_validity_dispute: The case concerned whether a transfer of regulated estate property was valid.
predicates.family_descendants_are_primary_beneficia: The deed directed the main benefit of the property’s income to the settlor and descendants over generations.
predicates.charitable_use_is_insignificant_or_postp: The deed provided only limited charitable or religious use while the family survived and reserved broader such use until the family line ended.

members.legal_issue: A State law on a concurrent subject ceases to operate when an applicable Central law contains repugnant provisions on that subject.
material_facts: The State law and the Central law both governed land acquisition, a subject in the Concurrent List.
The Central law became applicable in the State and its provisions were substantially different from those of the State law.
The parties accepted that the State law stood repealed when the Central law became applicable.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 254 of the Constitution, repugnancy between an applicable Central law and a State law on a concurrent subject results in the State law being displaced. That consequence operates automatically and may arise by necessary implication; the Court relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 8.
members.conclusion: The State law stood repealed by operation of Article 254 when the repugnant Central law became applicable; no express provision repealing the State law was necessary.

predicates.concurrent_subject_law: The State law and the Central law both regulate a subject on which both legislatures may make laws.
predicates.central_law_applies: The Central law has become applicable to the territory governed by the State law.
predicates.provisions_conflict: The applicable Central law contains provisions repugnant to provisions of the State law on the same subject.

members.legal_issue: A later parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject prevails over inconsistent State laws on that subject.
material_facts: The corporation invoked a parliamentary law providing for eviction from public premises.
State laws also provided procedures for eviction from public premises, and the parties disputed which laws governed the eviction.
The parliamentary law was enacted after the relevant State laws.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 254(1), a parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject prevails over a repugnant State law. Article 254(2) did not apply because the State laws were not repugnant to an earlier parliamentary or existing law; its proviso also permits Parliament to enact a later law on the same matter, which prevails even without express amendment or repeal of the State law. The judgment relies on Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State and Hoechst Pharmaceuticals v. State.
members.conclusion: The parliamentary law prevailed over the State laws and was rightly invoked.

predicates.appeal_disputes_which_eviction_law_appli: A party in an appeal disputes which of competing eviction laws governs the proceeding.
predicates.parliamentary_and_state_laws_cover_the_s: A parliamentary law and State laws address the same subject within the Concurrent List.
predicates.parliamentary_law_was_enacted_after_stat: The parliamentary law was enacted after the relevant State laws.

members.legal_issue: A state enactment may be repugnant to a parliamentary enactment on a concurrent subject because of direct conflict, occupation of the whole field, or regulation of the same subject matter.
material_facts: The state and parliamentary enactments substantially overlapped in regulating the relationship between promoters and purchasers.
The enactments also differed on matters including parking, the scope of force majeure, the regulatory authority’s functions, and compensation adjudication.
The state enactment had not received presidential assent.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Article 254(1) and (2), explaining that repugnancy may arise from irreconcilable conflict, Parliament’s intention to occupy the whole field, or overlapping regulation of the same subject. It emphasized considering both the text and context of the parliamentary enactment and that repugnancy is not the first choice where harmonisation is possible. It relied on Zaverbhai Amaldas v State of Bombay, Tika Ramji v State of Uttar Pradesh, Deep Chand v State of Uttar Pradesh, M Karunanidhi v Union of India, State of Orissa v M.A. Tulloch, Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v State of Bihar, State of Kerala v Mar Appraem Kuri Company Ltd., and Innoventive Industries Ltd. v ICICI Bank.
members.conclusion: The court restated that repugnancy under Article 254 may arise from direct inconsistency, an exhaustive parliamentary code, or state and parliamentary laws regulating an identical subject; a state law is void to the extent of repugnancy, subject to the constitutional rule concerning presidential assent.

rule.if: constitutional_conflict_review and not state_law_received_presidential_assent and (direct_irreconcilable_conflict or parliamentary_law_is_exhaustive_code or both_laws_regulate_identical_subject)

predicates.constitutional_conflict_review: A court is reviewing whether a state enactment conflicts with a parliamentary enactment on a concurrent subject.
predicates.state_law_received_presidential_assent: The state enactment received presidential assent in the circumstances specified by the constitutional rule for state laws on concurrent subjects.
predicates.direct_irreconcilable_conflict: The provisions produce conflicting legal results on the same facts such that compliance with one requires disobedience of the other.
predicates.parliamentary_law_is_exhaustive_code: The parliamentary enactment, considered in its text and context, is intended to provide a complete and exhaustive code on the subject.
predicates.both_laws_regulate_identical_subject: The state and parliamentary enactments regulate the same subject matter rather than distinct, merely allied matters.
predicates.state_law_yields_to_parliamentary_law_to: The state enactment gives way to the parliamentary enactment to the extent the two are repugnant.

members.legal_issue: A finding on an issue that was unnecessary to the decision and was not directly and substantially in issue does not operate as res judicata so as to support an appeal against that finding alone.
material_facts: The trial court’s decree restricted recovery to the father’s interest because the mortgage debt was not binding on the sons’ interests.
Whether the later partition was genuine did not affect that decree; even a genuine partition would not have made the mortgage binding on the sons’ interests.
The finding about the partition was unnecessary to the decision and the partition issue was not directly and substantially in issue in the suit.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the submission relying on Harchandra Das v. Bholanath Day, where the possibility of an appeal against a finding was linked to whether it would operate as res judicata. It did not decide whether that general view was correct; it held that the finding in this case was unnecessary to the decree and that the partition matter was not directly and substantially in issue, so the finding could not operate as res judicata.
members.conclusion: The finding that the partition was a sham could not operate as res judicata, and the appeal against that finding was not maintainable on that basis.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and appeal_targets_only_a_finding and finding_unnecessary_to_decree and issue_not_directly_and_substantially_in_issue

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party brings an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.appeal_targets_only_a_finding: The appeal challenges a finding but does not challenge a decree or an appealable order.
predicates.finding_unnecessary_to_decree: The finding does not affect the decree because the same decree would follow even if the finding were resolved differently.
predicates.issue_not_directly_and_substantially_in_: The issue addressed by the finding was not directly and substantially in issue in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Findings on issues unnecessary to an appeal’s disposition on a threshold ground are not to be considered in pending or future proceedings between the parties.
material_facts: The High Court considered the occupants’ derivative title and other issues in reviewing the eviction direction.
The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal because the official who issued the direction lacked authority.
Some of the other issues were pending in separate proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Where an appeal can be disposed of on a threshold ground, it is unnecessary to decide other issues, particularly issues that are sub judice in separate proceedings. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this direction.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s observations and conclusions on the other issues were not to be taken into consideration in proceedings pending or to be taken in the future.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment deciding a writ petition.
predicates.appeal_resolved_on_threshold_ground: The appeal is disposed of on a ground that makes it unnecessary to resolve other issues.
predicates.lower_court_decided_unnecessary_issues: The lower court made findings on issues that were unnecessary to the appeal’s disposition, including issues pending in separate proceedings.
predicates.lower_court_other_issue_findings_not_con: The lower court’s findings on those other issues are not considered in pending or future related proceedings.

members.legal_issue: An unnecessary observation in an appeal brought by one defendant does not operate as res judicata against other defendants in a later suit when those defendants could not challenge the appellate decree, or when the observation was made without pleadings or evidence raising a dispute between them.
material_facts: In the earlier suit, the trial court held that the two defendants were not sub-tenants and dismissed the ejectment claim against them; the plaintiff did not appeal that finding.

A different defendant appealed the rent decree against him. The appellate court dismissed his appeal, affirming the trial court’s decree, but observed that the other defendants appeared to possess the property on his behalf.
The other defendants were not parties aggrieved by the dismissal of that appeal and could not challenge its decree.

The appealing defendant had filed no written statement raising a dispute between himself and the other defendants, and there was no pleading or evidence requiring the appellate court to decide whether they possessed the property on his behalf.
In a later suit, the plaintiff relied on the appellate observation to seek ejectment of those defendants as licensees.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles of res judicata reflected in Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a finding does not bind a party who had no opportunity to challenge it by appeal; an unnecessary observation made without pleadings or evidence raising the relevant dispute likewise cannot operate as res judicata. Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria, [1953] SCR 154, was distinguished: it states the binding effect of a decision in a subsequent suit but did not assist the appellant on these facts.
members.conclusion: The appellate observation did not operate as res judicata against the defendants in the later suit. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: later_suit_relies_on_prior_appellate_finding and prior_observation_was_unnecessary and (affected_parties_could_not_appeal or (no_interparty_pleading and no_interparty_evidence))

predicates.later_suit_relies_on_prior_appellate_fin: In a later suit, a party relied on an observation made in an earlier appeal as a basis for its claim against other defendants.
predicates.prior_observation_was_unnecessary: The appellate court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the trial decree, while making an observation that was unnecessary to decide that appeal.
predicates.affected_parties_could_not_appeal: The defendants against whom the observation was later used were not aggrieved by the appellate decree and could not challenge it by appeal.
predicates.no_interparty_pleading: The appealing defendant had filed no pleading raising a dispute between himself and the other defendants about whose behalf they possessed the property.
predicates.no_interparty_evidence: No evidence was led on a dispute between the appealing defendant and the other defendants about whose behalf they possessed the property.
predicates.prior_finding_not_binding_as_res_judicat: The earlier appellate observation does not bind the affected defendants as res judicata in the later suit.

members.legal_issue: A judgment of a lower bench that has been overruled by a larger bench no longer remains the law to be followed.
material_facts: A Division Bench decided the interpretation of a territorial-jurisdiction provision.
A Full Bench of the same High Court later held that the Division Bench decision was contrary to the law laid down by the Supreme Court and was not correctly decided.
The High Court Registry was nevertheless being asked to comply with directions in the Division Bench judgment.
members.legal_principle: A judgment is the judgment of the court, not of the individual judge. It remains effective until set aside or its correctness is doubted by a higher court; once overruled by a larger bench, it no longer remains law and is treated as non-est. Judicial propriety requires judges to follow the governing law rather than persist in directions based on an overruled decision.
members.conclusion: The overruled judgment was no longer the law of the land and was to be treated as non-est; judicial propriety required the judges concerned to follow the law laid down by the larger bench.

predicates.intra_court_precedent_conflict: Different benches of the same court have addressed the same legal issue.
predicates.smaller_bench_judgment_overruled_by_larg: A larger bench has held that the smaller bench’s judgment was not correctly decided.

members.legal_issue: A judgment cannot remain in force when it conflicts with a later ruling of a larger bench on the same issue.
material_facts: Different benches of equal strength had reached conflicting conclusions about the pricing of flats under the same scheme.
A Full Bench later upheld the revised pricing and rejected the challenge to it.
The appeals concerned an earlier judgment that had reached the opposite conclusion, and the challenge to the Full Bench ruling had been dismissed.
members.legal_principle: A larger bench resolves a conflict between decisions of benches of equal strength. Contradictory rulings on the same point should not be allowed to operate simultaneously; consistency and certainty require the conflicting judgment to yield to the larger-bench ruling.
members.conclusion: The conflicting judgment was set aside, and the writ petitions were disposed of in accordance with the Full Bench ruling.

predicates.appeal_against_conflicting_judgment: A party appealed from a judgment that decided an issue also addressed by a larger bench.
predicates.later_larger_bench_decided_same_issue: A larger bench later decided the same issue.
predicates.larger_bench_ruling_conflicts: The larger bench reached a conclusion inconsistent with the judgment under appeal.

members.legal_issue: An earlier unappealed judgment does not preserve an enforceable direction when its sole legal basis is later displaced by a binding Supreme Court decision.
material_facts: The respondents obtained mandamus based on a High Court decision that held the amendments invalid.
The State did not appeal the mandamus granted to the respondents, and it became final between them.
The Supreme Court later reversed the High Court decision and held the amendments constitutionally valid.
The respondents sought to enforce their earlier direction after that Supreme Court decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 141, a Supreme Court declaration of law binds everyone, including persons whose similar High Court judgments were not appealed. In M/s Shenoy & Co. v. Commercial Tax Officer, the Court held that a mandamus based on a law declared invalid by a High Court becomes ineffective when the Supreme Court holds that law valid. The Court distinguished the finality and res judicata principles discussed in Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajin Debi, State of West Bengal v. Hemant Kumar Bhattacharjee, and Authorised Officer (Land Reforms) v. M.M. Krishnamurthy Chetty, and applied Shenoy.
members.conclusion: The earlier mandamus did not give the respondents an indefeasible right enforceable after the Supreme Court decision displaced the legal basis for it.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_enforcement_of_unappeal: A party seeks to enforce a judgment that the opposing party did not appeal.
predicates.earlier_direction_depended_solely_on_rev: The earlier direction rested solely on a legal conclusion later displaced by a higher court.
predicates.supreme_court_declared_different_binding: The Supreme Court later declared a legal rule that conflicts with the basis of the earlier direction.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking relief under the procedure for public trusts cannot proceed unless the property is shown to be held in a public trust.
material_facts: The suit sought relief on the allegation that the premises had been dedicated to the public as a trust.
The evidence did not establish complete public dedication; the owners retained control and the premises’ use by the public was limited.
The High Court had treated the premises as a public trust and set aside the trial court’s judgment, but the Supreme Court found that conclusion unsustainable.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to public trusts, not private trusts. The Court relied on Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S.P. Sahi and Bihar State Board Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das, which recognize that Hindu law permits private as well as public trusts and that the statutory provisions in this field apply to public trusts alone.
members.conclusion: Because a public trust was not established, the suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure could not be maintained on the facts of this case, and the High Court’s judgment could not stand.

predicates.public_trust_remedy_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking the special remedy available for administering or protecting a public trust.
predicates.property_shown_to_be_publicly_dedicated: The evidence showed that the property had been completely dedicated to a public trust.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking relief for the administration of a public religious or charitable trust cannot proceed when no breach of trust is proved and no directions for administration are sought.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a trust-management suit alleging misconduct and breach of trust by the person managing the institution and seeking his removal, accounts, and a management scheme.
The courts concurrently found that the alleged misconduct and breach of trust were not proved.
The plaintiffs did not claim that directions were necessary for the proper administration of the trust.
members.legal_principle: Under section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code, a suit of this special character presupposes a public religious or charitable trust and can proceed only where a breach of trust is alleged or directions are necessary for its administration, and the plaintiff seeks one or more of the reliefs specified in that section.
members.conclusion: The foundation for a suit of this kind was absent, and the plaintiffs had no cause of action for the suit.

predicates.special_public_trust_management_suit: The plaintiffs brought a special suit seeking relief concerning the management of an alleged public religious or charitable trust.
predicates.trust_breach_not_proved: The courts found that the alleged breach of trust was not established.
predicates.administration_directions_not_sought: The plaintiffs did not claim that directions were needed for the proper administration of the trust.

members.legal_issue: A suit brought under the special public-trust procedure must fail when the alleged breach is not proved and the request for administrative directions has no factual foundation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that the incumbent had committed breaches of trust, but the trial court and the High Court found no evidence substantiating those allegations.

The plaint asserted that court directions were necessary for trust administration but gave no reasons or factual particulars showing maladministration or a defect in the administrative arrangements requiring correction.
The courts found the request for directions to be unsupported and made only to bring the suit within the special procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a suit to rest on an allegation of breach of a public trust or a demonstrated need for directions for its administration, and to seek one or more of the reliefs specified in that section. The plaint is considered in the first instance to assess whether the suit falls within the section; however, if evidence shows that the alleged breach was not made out and the request for directions is vague and without a factual or reasoned foundation, the suit must be dismissed. The Court referred to Association of B.D.B. Bagga Singh v. Gurnam Singh, AIR 1972 Rajasthan 263, Vahan Singh v. Achhar Singh, AIR 1968 Punjab and Haryana 463, and Radha Krishna v. Lachmi Narain, AIR 1948 Oudh 203. It did not decide the broader meaning of the statutory phrase concerning directions necessary for trust administration.
members.conclusion: The alleged breach was not substantiated and the request for directions lacked a factual basis, so the foundation for a suit under Section 92 failed and the suit was not maintainable under that section.

predicates.public_trust_procedure_suit: The proceeding is brought as a suit concerning the administration of a public trust under a special public-trust procedure.
predicates.alleged_trust_breach_is_not_proved: The evidence does not establish the breach of trust alleged by the plaintiffs.
predicates.administrative_direction_request_lacks_f: The plaintiffs request administrative directions without facts or reasons showing why the directions are needed.

members.legal_issue: Absconding alone and the non-recovery of a vehicle, without evidence that it would contain incriminating traces, do not establish guilt.
material_facts: The accused did not promptly appear before the authorities, but the majority held that absconding by itself was hardly evidence of guilt.
The police could not find the accused’s jeep.
There was no evidence that the jeep, if found, would have contained human blood or shown that it was used to remove bodies.
members.legal_principle: In assessing circumstantial evidence, absconding may lend weight to other evidence but cannot by itself establish guilt. The inability to recover a vehicle does not prove that it would have supplied incriminating evidence. The majority cited no earlier case for these propositions.
members.conclusion: Absconding could add weight to other evidence establishing guilt, but by itself it was hardly evidence of guilt; the jeep’s non-recovery had no evidentiary value on the facts proved.

rule.if: circumstantial_guilt_assessment and accused_absconded and vehicle_not_recovered and no_evidence_vehicle_would_contain_incriminating_traces

predicates.circumstantial_guilt_assessment: The court is assessing guilt from circumstantial evidence.
predicates.accused_absconded: The accused avoided or delayed appearing before the authorities.
predicates.vehicle_not_recovered: A vehicle associated with the accused was not found by investigators.
predicates.no_evidence_vehicle_would_contain_incrim: There is no evidence that the missing vehicle would contain traces connecting it to the alleged offence.

members.legal_issue: An accused's failure to surrender or apparent absconding cannot by itself establish guilt.
material_facts: The accused was not traceable or did not surrender for nearly a year after the murder.
The prosecution also relied on the accused's relatives' lack of apparent efforts to obstruct the prosecution, while the principal prosecution evidence was unreliable.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Prakash Mahadeo Godse v. State of Maharashtra for the principle that an accused's conduct, including hiding after an offence, does not by itself conclude the question of guilt; suspicious conduct cannot replace proof by credible evidence.
members.conclusion: The accused's failure to surrender and the conduct of his relatives could not prove guilt or overcome the failure of the prosecution evidence.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the accused's guilt must be determined.
predicates.accused_did_not_surrender_or_was_abscond: The accused failed to surrender or was not traceable after the alleged offence.

members.legal_issue: A person’s absconding after an offence, by itself, does not establish guilt or complete a circumstantial chain of evidence.
material_facts: The accused was arrested six days after the offence and had remained untraceable during that period.
The lower courts considered his absence, but the Supreme Court held that it could not be used as a circumstance against him by itself.
The circumstance of absence had not been put to the accused, and the Court found that this omission was inconsequential because absence alone could not establish guilt.
members.legal_principle: Absconding is relevant only for consideration with the other evidence and its value depends on the circumstances of the case; it is not, by itself, conclusive proof of guilt or a determining link in a circumstantial chain. The Court relied on Matru v. State of U.P., AIR 1971 SC 1050; Rahman v. State of U.P., AIR 1972 SC 110; State of M.P. v. Paltan Mallah, AIR 2005 SC 733; and Bipin Kumar Mondal v. State of West Bengal, JT 2010 (7) SC 379.
members.conclusion: The Court held that absconding alone was not proof of guilt and could not be a determining link in the circumstantial evidence chain.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns determination of criminal guilt.
predicates.accused_absconds_after_offence: The accused remains away or untraceable after the offence.

members.legal_issue: Removing a landlord’s ability to seek eviction for bona fide personal use from non-residential premises, while retaining that ground for residential premises, violates the constitutional guarantee of equality when the distinction has no rational connection to the rent-control law’s purpose.
material_facts: The rent-control law originally allowed a landlord to seek eviction for bona fide personal use from both residential and non-residential premises.
An amendment removed that ground of eviction for non-residential premises while retaining it for residential premises.
The law’s stated purposes included controlling rents and protecting tenants against mala fide attempts by landlords to obtain eviction.
The amendment’s stated reasons included hardship to tenants of non-residential premises and misuse of the personal-use ground by some landlords.
The landlord asserted that, after retiring from government service, he bona fide required the rented shop for his own use.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those grouped together from those left out, and that differentia must have a rational relation to the statute’s object. The Court relied on Budhan Choudhary v. State of Bihar, Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar, U.P. Electric Power and Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P., and Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar for the classification test. It also relied on Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, which invalidated an unrelated distinction between residential and non-residential tenants, and Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, which observed that a landlord’s bona fide need stands on the same footing for residential and commercial premises.
members.conclusion: The provisions removing the personal-use eviction ground for non-residential premises were declared constitutionally invalid and struck down. The original provisions were restored, so a landlord may seek eviction from non-residential premises on the ground that the landlord requires them for personal use.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_rent_control_rule and commercial_personal_need_eviction_removed and residential_personal_need_eviction_retained and rent_protections_apply_to_both_building_types and law_aims_to_protect_tenants_from_mala_fide_eviction and building_use_type_does_not_distinguish_bona_fide_owner_need

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_control: A party challenges the constitutionality of a rule governing eviction of tenants from rented premises.
predicates.commercial_personal_need_eviction_remove: The legislature removes a landlord’s ability to seek eviction of a tenant from premises used for business on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide personal need.
predicates.residential_personal_need_eviction_retai: The law continues to allow a landlord to seek eviction from residential premises on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide personal need.
predicates.rent_protections_apply_to_both_building_: The law’s other rent and tenancy protections apply to both residential and business premises.
predicates.law_aims_to_protect_tenants_from_mala_fi: The law is intended, among other things, to protect tenants from landlords’ mala fide attempts to obtain eviction.
predicates.building_use_type_does_not_distinguish_b: The use of a building as residential or business premises does not make a landlord’s bona fide need for personal use materially different.

members.legal_issue: Restricting eviction for a landlord’s bona fide personal or family need to residential premises, while excluding non-residential premises, violates the constitutional guarantee of equality when the distinction no longer has a rational basis.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of premises used as a shop and a clinic for her bona fide need and the needs of dependent family members; the need was found to be bona fide, but eviction was refused because the premises were let for non-residential purposes.
The rent-control law’s general scheme treated residential and non-residential premises alike in several respects, while allowing eviction for bona fide need only for residential premises.
The historical concern about resettling refugees and protecting commercial tenants had substantially receded, and the availability of premises suitable for commercial use had increased.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification only where it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational relation to the law’s object. A classification that may have been justified when enacted can become arbitrary when its rationale disappears with changed circumstances. Applying the principles in Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar, Harbilas Rai Bansal v. State of Punjab, Rattan Arya v. State of Tamil Nadu, Rakesh Vij v. Dr. Ravinder Pal Singh Sethi, Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, and Joginder Pal v. Naval Kishore Behal, the Court held that the distinction no longer had a rational basis. The Court also relied on the principle, illustrated by State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhopal Sugar Industries and Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, that a classification may lose its validity as circumstances change.
members.conclusion: The exclusion of non-residential premises from the bona fide-need ground of eviction discriminated irrationally between residential and non-residential premises and violated Article 14. The Court invalidated only the discriminatory limitation, not the whole eviction provision.

rule.if: rental_law_equality_challenge and bona_fide_eviction_ground_confined_by_premises_use and premises_types_otherwise_treated_alike and historical_rationale_no_longer_valid and availability_of_commercial_premises_increased

predicates.rental_law_equality_challenge: A proceeding challenges whether a law governing eviction of tenants complies with the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.bona_fide_eviction_ground_confined_by_pr: The law allows a landlord to recover possession for a genuine personal or family need only when the premises were let for residential use.
predicates.premises_types_otherwise_treated_alike: The law otherwise treats residential and non-residential premises alike in relevant aspects of the landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.historical_rationale_no_longer_valid: The circumstances that originally supported treating the two types of premises differently have materially changed or ceased to exist.
predicates.availability_of_commercial_premises_incr: The availability of premises suitable for commercial or other non-residential use has substantially increased.

members.legal_issue: The exclusion of residential tenants from rent-control protection above a rent threshold, while tenants of non-residential buildings remain protected regardless of rent, lacks a reasonable basis and violates equal protection.
material_facts: The rent-control law generally regulated tenancy, controlled rents, and prevented unreasonable eviction for residential and non-residential buildings.
The challenged provision excluded residential buildings or parts occupied by a tenant paying rent above the prescribed threshold from the law’s protections.
The rent-based exception for non-residential buildings had been removed, so tenants of those buildings remained protected regardless of the rent they paid.

The State did not show that residential tenants were less in need of protection than non-residential tenants, or that excluding higher-rent residential tenants would protect weaker sections of society.
The threshold had been set years earlier, and the Court took judicial notice that rents had increased substantially, making the threshold artificial and irrelevant in practice.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the law’s objective. The Court found no reasonable nexus between the distinction based on building use and rent and the Act’s objectives of regulating tenancies, controlling rents, and preventing unreasonable eviction. A provision that was valid when enacted may become discriminatory and unconstitutional as circumstances change; the Court relied on Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1984] 1 SCC 222, for that principle. It distinguished Raval & Co. v. Ramachandran, [1974] 2 SCR 629, because the observations there were made in a different context and not on a challenge under Article 14.
members.conclusion: The Court struck down the residential rent-based exemption as unconstitutional because it violated Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_based_t: A constitutional challenge is brought against an exemption from tenant-protection rules based on rent.
predicates.residential_tenants_above_rent_threshold: Residential tenants paying rent above a threshold are excluded from the protections available to other tenants.
predicates.nonresidential_tenants_remain_protected_: Tenants of non-residential buildings remain protected regardless of the rent they pay.
predicates.state_did_not_show_residential_tenants_n: The government did not establish that residential tenants need less protection than tenants of non-residential buildings.
predicates.rent_threshold_became_unrealistic: Substantial rent increases made the threshold unrealistic in relation to prevailing rents.

members.legal_issue: A prosecution cannot rely on recovered weapons to establish their connection to an offence when the evidence does not link them to it, and withholding vital forensic evidence warrants an adverse inference.
material_facts: The doctor said the injuries could have been caused by the recovered weapons but found no visible bloodstains or other marks on them.
The purported chemical analyst report was not available in the case record, and the prosecution did not otherwise establish a forensic link between the weapons and the offence.
The prosecution withheld forensic evidence relating to a seized shirt.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish the evidentiary link on which it relies; withholding vital evidence permits an adverse inference against it.
members.conclusion: The recovered weapons were not linked to the offence, and an adverse inference had to be drawn against the prosecution for withholding vital forensic evidence.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution relies on evidence to establish guilt.
predicates.weapon_forensic_link_absent: The prosecution does not establish a forensic or other evidentiary link between recovered weapons and the offence.
predicates.vital_forensic_evidence_withheld: The prosecution withholds forensic evidence material to determining whether an accused or an exhibit was connected to the offence.

members.legal_issue: Possession of weapons and ammunition does not connect an accused to an offence without reliable evidence linking the weapons to the occurrence.
material_facts: Two accused possessed licensed guns and live cartridges, but the prosecution did not provide reliable evidence that the guns had recently been fired.
The Court disbelieved the account that the accused were produced with the weapons before the police, and the alleged production of the weapons was treated as an unreliable embellishment.
members.legal_principle: Possession of a weapon and ammunition, without reliable evidence linking the weapon to the offence, is insufficient by itself to connect an accused to the crime. The Court relied on its assessment of the evidence and cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this point.
members.conclusion: The possession of the guns and live cartridges did not connect the accused with the crime.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.accused_possessed_weapons: One or more accused possessed weapons or ammunition relevant to the alleged offence.
