predicates.no_reliable_link_to_offence: The evidence does not reliably show that the weapons were used in the offence or otherwise link them to it.

members.legal_issue: Production of a weapon is insufficient to establish guilt when no statement connecting the accused to its discovery is shown and the weapon was not proved to have been concealed at a place known only to the accused.
material_facts: The accused took an axe from beneath his cot and produced it to the police.
There was no evidence that the accused had made a statement relating to the recovery, and no evidence that he had concealed the axe at a place known only to him.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Evidence Act requires a statement by the accused relating to a discovery before the discovery fact can be admitted under that provision. The Court also held that mere production of an object is insufficient to convict where it is not shown to have been concealed at a place known only to the accused. Although the High Court had referred to Section 8 of the Evidence Act, the Supreme Court found the recovery insufficient on the facts before it.
members.conclusion: The recovery could not be admitted under Section 27 of the Evidence Act in the absence of a statement relating to it, and mere production of the axe was insufficient to convict the accused in the circumstances.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and no_statement_linking_accused_to_discovery and weapon_taken_from_nonexclusive_location and exclusive_knowledge_not_shown

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.no_statement_linking_accused_to_discover: The accused made no statement connecting the accused to the discovery of the weapon.
predicates.weapon_taken_from_nonexclusive_location: The weapon was produced from a location not shown to be concealed or inaccessible to others.
predicates.exclusive_knowledge_not_shown: There was no evidence that only the accused knew where the weapon was located.

members.legal_issue: A finding that an accused committed rape cannot be sustained when no charge of rape was framed and the evidence does not establish the offence.
material_facts: No charge of rape was framed against the accused.
The medical evidence indicated only that the possibility of rape could not be ruled out.
The child eyewitness did not testify to any rape by the accused or anyone else.
members.legal_principle: A finding of guilt for rape cannot stand in the absence of a charge under Section 376 IPC and evidence supporting the offence. The Court cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The finding that the accused committed rape was unsustainable.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal in a criminal case from a conviction.
predicates.rape_charge_not_framed: The accused was not charged with committing rape.
predicates.evidence_of_rape_absent: The evidence did not establish that the accused or another person committed rape.
predicates.rape_finding_cannot_be_sustained: A finding that the accused committed rape cannot stand.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for rape cannot stand when the evidence establishes, at most, that intercourse occurred but does not establish that it was without consent or against the victim’s will.
material_facts: The deceased’s vaginal swab and underwear contained semen, but the evidence did not establish that intercourse was without her consent or against her will.
The non-firearm injuries found on the deceased did not indicate an attempt to rape or the commission of rape.
The accused was not medically examined after recovering from his serious gunshot injury.
members.legal_principle: The evidence must support the element that intercourse was without the victim’s consent or against her will. Evidence of semen may indicate intercourse, but does not by itself establish that element; the Court found no other evidence sufficient to do so.
members.conclusion: The conviction for rape was set aside and the accused was acquitted of that charge.

predicates.appeal_from_rape_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a rape conviction.
predicates.evidence_of_intercourse: The evidence indicates that intercourse occurred.
predicates.no_evidence_of_lack_of_consent: The evidence does not establish that the intercourse was without the victim’s consent or against the victim’s will.

members.legal_issue: A rape conviction cannot stand where the complainant was above the age at which consent is legally relevant and the evidence leaves a reasonable view that the intercourse was consensual.
material_facts: The trial court found the complainant was about 18 years old at the relevant time and acquitted the accused; the High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted him.
The complainant testified that she had sexual intercourse with the accused on several occasions, and the prosecution alleged that he had promised to marry her.
The complaint was lodged more than eight months after the alleged sexual relationship began and only a few days before the child’s birth.
The Supreme Court considered that a consensual-intercourse view was reasonably possible on the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code, sexual intercourse with a woman above 16 years of age is not rape if she consents. In a criminal case, where two views are reasonably possible on the evidence—one pointing to guilt and the other to innocence—the accused receives the benefit of doubt. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt; the appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment and order were set aside.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_after_acquittal_reversed and complainant_above_consent_relevant_age and complainant_described_repeated_intercourse and complaint_followed_long_delay and consensual_intercourse_view_reasonably_possible

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal_reversed: The case was a criminal appeal in which an appellate court had reversed a trial court acquittal and convicted the accused.
predicates.complainant_above_consent_relevant_age: The complainant was found to be above the age at which consent is legally relevant to whether intercourse constitutes rape.
predicates.complainant_described_repeated_intercour: The complainant testified that she had sexual intercourse with the accused on several occasions.
predicates.complaint_followed_long_delay: The complaint was made more than eight months after the alleged sexual relationship began and shortly before the child’s birth.
predicates.consensual_intercourse_view_reasonably_p: The evidence permitted a reasonable view that the complainant had consented to the intercourse.

members.legal_issue: A conviction resting solely on a child eyewitness's identification is unsafe when the evidence does not establish a prior opportunity to know the accused, the initial identification was prompted, and the delay in recording the investigative statement is unexplained.
material_facts: The prosecution case against the accused depended on the testimony of a child who was the sole eyewitness and was injured during the incident.
The child had arrived at the scene on the evening before the occurrence, and the evidence did not establish that she had previously seen or known the accused.
In the child's first recorded statement, her father suggested the accused's involvement through a leading question, and the child then identified him.
The investigating officer recorded the child's statement three days after the occurrence, without an explanation for the delay, although she was conscious and fit to make a statement.
The later statements and trial testimony contained omissions and differences concerning how the child knew the accused.
There was no evidence connecting the accused to items recovered from the scene, and the other principal witness was discredited.
members.legal_principle: A sole eyewitness's testimony may support a conviction if there is reliable evidence that the witness had an opportunity to see and identify the accused. Where that opportunity is unproved and the circumstances of identification and the unexplained delay in recording the witness's statement raise serious doubts, the conviction is unsafe and the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt. The Court considered the delay in recording the statement under Section 161 CrPC and cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court found it unsafe to sustain the conviction on the child's testimony, gave the accused the benefit of doubt, allowed the appeal, and acquitted him.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and sole_child_witness_evidence and prior_identification_opportunity_unproved and initial_accusation_prompted and investigative_statement_delayed_without_explanation

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a conviction.
predicates.sole_child_witness_evidence: The case against the accused rests on the testimony of a child who is the sole eyewitness.
predicates.prior_identification_opportunity_unprove: The evidence does not establish that the child had an opportunity to see or know the accused before the incident.
predicates.initial_accusation_prompted: Another person suggested the accused's involvement to the child when her first statement was recorded.
predicates.investigative_statement_delayed_without_: The investigating officer recorded the child's statement only after a delay for which no explanation was given.
predicates.conviction_unsafe_and_acquittal_on_benef: The conviction is unsafe and the accused is acquitted because the evidence leaves a reasonable doubt.

members.legal_issue: Dock identification by a young witness is unreliable where no identification parade was held and the witness’s prior familiarity with the accused is not established.
material_facts: The child had named the accused in a statement to the police, but no identification parade was held.
The child identified the accused in court after they appeared in the dock.
The child lived with his parents away from the village where the crime occurred and visited that village only occasionally with his mother.
The evidence did not establish that the child knew all the accused before the incident; residence in the same village did not establish that he was acquainted with them.
members.legal_principle: Where identity is disputed, dock identification may be unreliable when the witness had no established prior familiarity with the accused and no identification parade was held. The Court relied on Japal Singh v. State of Punjab, 1996(4) Crimes 74 (SC), and held that the circumstances did not justify dispensing with an identification parade.
members.conclusion: The court could not safely rely on the child’s dock identification of the accused.

rule.if: criminal_case and identification_is_material and witness_is_a_young_child and no_identification_parade_was_held and not prior_familiarity_with_accused_is_established and identification_occurred_only_in_court

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the identity of the alleged perpetrator is in issue.
predicates.identification_is_material: The prosecution relies on the witness’s identification to connect the accused with the crime.
predicates.witness_is_a_young_child: The identifying witness was a young child whose age and understanding bear on the reliability of identification.
predicates.no_identification_parade_was_held: The authorities did not arrange a procedure for the witness to identify the suspect before trial.
predicates.prior_familiarity_with_accused_is_establ: Evidence establishes that the witness knew the accused before the incident well enough to recognize them reliably.
predicates.identification_occurred_only_in_court: The witness identified the accused for the first time, or only reliably, when the accused appeared in court.

members.legal_issue: Identification evidence may be unsafe where a single eyewitness’s identification is uncertain and an identification procedure requested by the accused did not test that witness.
material_facts: One eyewitness could not identify the accused at the identification parade and said that she had not known him beforehand.
The other eyewitness’s evidence was the only identification evidence against him that the Court considered reliable enough to assess.
That eyewitness had not been asked to identify him at the parade, although he had requested a parade and the prosecution could have produced her.
The Court could not safely exclude an honest mistake because the witness had only limited prior familiarity with him.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove identification and participation beyond reasonable doubt. Where a single witness’s identification may be mistaken and the circumstances do not provide adequate assurance, it is unsafe to convict on that testimony alone.
members.conclusion: The Court gave the accused the benefit of doubt, set aside his conviction and sentence, and acquitted him.

predicates.criminal_conviction_depends_on_identific: The prosecution’s case against the accused depends materially on identifying the accused as a participant.
predicates.single_identification_witness: Only one witness supplies reliable identification evidence against the accused.
predicates.identification_uncertainty: The circumstances leave a reasonable possibility that the witness honestly misidentified the accused.
predicates.requested_test_not_conducted_with_that_w: A requested identification procedure did not ask the witness relied on at trial to identify the accused.

members.legal_issue: A secured-asset sale conducted without the mandatory notice period, and without a waiver of that requirement, is invalid.
material_facts: The secured property was offered for public auction after the bank published notice providing less than 30 days before the sale.
The bank did not obtain a fresh valuation before the sale, and the High Court also identified defects in the vernacular-language publication and missing payment records.
The borrower had not waived the mandatory notice requirement for the sale.
members.legal_principle: Rules 8(5) and 8(6) and 9(1) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 require compliance with the prescribed sale procedure, including the applicable 30-day notice period. The Court applied Mathew Varghese v. M. Amritha Kumar and J. Rajiv Subramaniyan v. M/s Pandiyas, which held that the statutory sale procedure is mandatory and that a sale made without compliance is null and void. Section 13(1) of the SARFAESI Act permits enforcement without court or tribunal intervention only in conformity with the Act; the Court also referred to Section 13(8) and Article 300A in explaining the protection of the borrower’s interest in the secured asset. Ikbal recognizes waiver of protections that benefit the borrower, but no waiver was established here.
members.conclusion: The sale was null and void, and the order setting it aside was upheld.

predicates.secured_asset_public_auction: A creditor put property given as security up for public auction to recover a debt.
predicates.sale_notice_period_was_short: The creditor gave less than the required notice period before the auction.
predicates.borrower_did_not_waive_notice_protection: The borrower did not knowingly and intentionally relinquish the right to the required notice.

members.legal_issue: A statutory financial corporation's sale of secured property is invalid when the sale process is unreasonable and unexplained in circumstances indicating that it did not provide a fair opportunity for effective participation and the best price.
material_facts: A financial corporation exercising statutory recovery powers advertised the property for sale and initially allowed about four weeks for offers.
For a later sale notice, it allowed fewer than three days to submit offers, including two public holidays, and gave no satisfactory reason for the haste.
Valuations obtained over several months differed substantially, including a valuation far higher than the valuation shortly before the sale.

The successful bidder made an offer on the day the later notice was published and paid the entire consideration before the deadline for offers and before the offer could have been accepted; part of that payment had been made before the notice.
The corporation gave no credible explanation for these departures from the ordinary sale process.
members.legal_principle: Statutory powers under section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 must be exercised bona fide and fairly. Under Article 226, unreasonable action may be reviewed. Reasonableness is assessed against the dominant consideration of securing the best price, which requires maximum participation, adequate publicity, and a fair and practical period for prospective purchasers to inspect the property and make considered offers. Although restrictions stated in Mahesh Chandra v. Regional Manager, U.P. Financial Corporation, 1993 (2) SCC 279, were no longer in place after Haryana Financial State Corporation v. Jagdamba Oils Mills, the Court affirmed Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT, Madras v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd., 1995 (4) SCC 595, on fair and reasonable sale conduct. The presumption that public officials act honestly may be rebutted by circumstances reasonably indicating abuse of power; absent a credible explanation, the court may infer impropriety, as stated in M/s. Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India, AIR 1957 SC 397, 409.
members.conclusion: The sale was unfair and invalid, and the sale to the successful bidder could not be sustained.

rule.if: statutory_recovery_sale_challenge and sale_notice_inadequate and sale_irregularities_unexplained and (valuations_varied_substantially or buyer_paid_before_offer_deadline)

predicates.statutory_recovery_sale_challenge: A party challenged in court a sale of secured property conducted by a financial corporation using statutory recovery powers.
predicates.sale_notice_inadequate: The corporation gave prospective purchasers too little practical time to inspect the property, arrange financing, and submit offers.
predicates.sale_irregularities_unexplained: The sale process departed from ordinary practice in ways suggesting unfairness, and the corporation gave no credible explanation for those departures.
predicates.valuations_varied_substantially: The property's valuations obtained for the sale differed substantially over a relatively short period.
predicates.buyer_paid_before_offer_deadline: The successful bidder paid the full offered price before the deadline for offers and before its offer could have been accepted.

members.legal_issue: A secured asset sold by private treaty without written terms settled between the relevant parties is an invalid sale.
material_facts: The borrowers asked the bank for permission to sell the secured assets by private treaty.
The bank and its resolution agent decided to sell the assets to the purchasers without including the borrowers in their meeting.
The parties did not dispute that no written terms for a private-treaty sale had been settled between them.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 13(1) and 13(8) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, a secured creditor may enforce its security without court intervention only in conformity with the Act, and the borrower must be given the prescribed opportunity to redeem the asset. Rules 8 and 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 prescribe mandatory sale procedures; Rule 8(8) requires a sale by a method other than public auction or public tender to be on terms settled between the parties in writing. Non-compliance invalidates the sale and may violate the borrower's protection under Article 300A of the Constitution. The Court relied on Mathew Varghese v. M. Amritha Kumar, which held that the statutory sale requirements are mandatory and that a sale in breach of them is null and void.
members.conclusion: The sale was null and void and was set aside.

predicates.secured_asset_enforcement_proceeding: A secured creditor pursued enforcement against a borrower's secured asset.
predicates.secured_asset_sold_by_private_treaty: The secured asset was sold through a privately arranged sale rather than public auction or public tender.
predicates.no_written_terms_settled_between_parties: The creditor and the borrower did not settle the terms of the private sale in writing.

members.legal_issue: A lower court judgment does not merge into a superior court’s order when the superior court disposes of the appeal without deciding the merits of the issues resolved below.
material_facts: The High Court had quashed the government’s resumption notice.
The Supreme Court later disposed of the government’s appeals after the government stated that it would seek dispossession in accordance with law and, if necessary, by civil suit.
The Supreme Court did not examine the merits of the issues decided by the High Court or record findings on them.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger applies when the superior court considers the merits of the issues decided by the subordinate court and records a finding on them. Where the superior court disposes of the matter without doing so, merger does not occur. The Court relied on Shanmugaval Nadar v. State of Tamil Nadu, (1989) 4 SCC 187.
members.conclusion: The High Court judgment did not merge into the Supreme Court’s later order and continued to hold the field.

predicates.appeal_against_lower_court_order: A party brought an appeal seeking review of an order made by a lower court.
predicates.superior_court_disposed_without_merits_r: The superior court disposed of the appeal without examining the merits of the issues decided below or recording findings on them.

members.legal_issue: A superior court’s limited alteration of an appealed order does not make the lower court’s unadopted reasoning a declaration of law by the superior court.
material_facts: An appeal concerned a High Court judgment about redistribution of unused land.
The Supreme Court removed only the High Court’s direction imposing a time limit for redistribution proceedings.
The Supreme Court did not consider or approve the High Court’s reasoning on whether unused land could be redistributed.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger concerns the operative part of the order, and the reasoning of the lower court does not become the reasoning of the superior court unless the superior court adopts, reiterates, or expressly approves it. A declaration of law under Article 141 requires a decision that expressly or necessarily considers the point. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, S. Shanmugavel Nadar v. State of Tamil Nadu, V.M. Salgaocar & Bros. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Kaikhosrou (Chick) Kavasji Framji v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s reasoning was not affirmed as a Supreme Court precedent; only the operative order resulting from the Supreme Court’s limited alteration governed.

predicates.appeal_against_lower_court_order: A party appeals a lower court’s order to a superior court.
predicates.higher_court_alters_only_a_limited_part: The superior court changes only a limited operative direction in the order.
predicates.higher_court_does_not_consider_or_adopt_: The superior court neither considers the relevant reasoning on its merits nor adopts or expressly approves it.

members.legal_issue: A superior court’s dismissal of an appeal on a procedural ground does not merge or affirm the lower court’s reasoning when the merits were not considered.
material_facts: The High Court had upheld the constitutional validity of a State law.
The Supreme Court dismissed appeals against that decision because the State, a necessary party to the challenge, had not been impleaded.
The Supreme Court did not consider the merits, the High Court’s reasoning, or the validity of the law.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger is not universal: its application depends on the nature and scope of the superior court’s jurisdiction and the subject matter it considered. Ordinarily, the operative part merges, while reasoning merges only if the superior court adopts, reiterates, or expressly approves it. A dismissal that does not consider the merits does not declare law under Article 141. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Mohammad Nooh, State of Madras v. Madurai Mills Co. Ltd., Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, Krishen Kumar v. Union of India, State of U.P. v. Synthetics and Chemicals, M/s. Rup Diamonds v. Union of India, Supreme Court Employees Welfare Association v. Union of India, Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of Bihar, and B. Shama Rao v. Union Territory of Pondicherry.
members.conclusion: Only the operative part of the High Court’s decision merged in the Supreme Court’s order; its reasoning did not, and the order did not declare that reasoning to be law under Article 141.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a State law.
predicates.superior_appeal_dismissed_for_party_defe: A superior court dismisses an appeal because a necessary party was not joined.
predicates.superior_court_did_not_consider_merits: The superior court does not examine the merits or the lower court’s reasons.

members.legal_issue: The export-channeling policy was an unreasonable restriction when it left mineowners without a dependable outlet or safeguards for fair treatment.
material_facts: The domestic market for manganese ore was practically nonexistent.
Mineowners without prior export performance could not export directly and had to depend on established exporters or the state trading corporation to buy their ore.
Those buyers were not required to purchase a mineowner’s ore, and the mineowner could be left with no effective market or compelled to accept terms set by the available buyers.

The policy progressively reduced private quotas and later channelled exports through the state trading corporation without definite rules ensuring quotas, purchases, or fair prices for affected mineowners.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(g), a restriction on business must satisfy the reasonable-restrictions standard in the first part of Article 19(6). Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself confer authority to create a monopoly by administrative action, though an administrative restriction may still be assessed under the general standard in Article 19(6). A scheme channeling exports should provide definite rules that protect affected producers through fair treatment and appropriate safeguards. Subba Rao J. referred to Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P. in discussing the constitutional protection for restrictions on business.
members.conclusion: In his dissent, Subba Rao J. concluded that the policy infringed the appellant’s fundamental right by imposing an unreasonable restriction; he nevertheless considered the application for the expired licensing period infructuous and dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_export_restriction and negligible_domestic_market and producers_cannot_export_directly and no_buyer_must_purchase_producers_goods and no_fair_treatment_safeguards

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_export_restr: A person challenges an export restriction as an infringement of the right to carry on business.
predicates.negligible_domestic_market: There is little or no domestic market for the commodity, making export an important outlet for its producers.
predicates.producers_cannot_export_directly: The policy prevents affected producers from exporting their goods themselves.
predicates.no_buyer_must_purchase_producers_goods: The available authorized buyers are not required to purchase the affected producers’ goods.
predicates.no_fair_treatment_safeguards: The scheme lacks definite safeguards for fair treatment, such as dependable allocation or fair pricing arrangements.

members.legal_issue: Can administrative export controls that exclude mine owners from direct export and leave them without a guaranteed purchaser or fair terms impose an unreasonable restriction on their right to carry on trade.
material_facts: The ore had little domestic market, so excluded mine owners depended on established exporters or the state trading corporation as purchasers.
Neither the established exporters nor the corporation was required to purchase any particular quantity from the excluded mine owners.
The excluded mine owners could be left without a buyer or required to accept prices dictated by the available purchasers.
The restrictions progressively reduced private export participation and eventually left the state trading corporation with a virtual monopoly.
No definite rules guaranteed excluded mine owners quotas, purchases, or fair prices.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the right to carry on trade, and restrictions must satisfy the general reasonable-restriction requirement in Article 19(6). Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself confer power to create a state monopoly by administrative action; it protects a monopoly created by a valid law. Subba Rao J. considered that an export-canalisation scheme should provide definite safeguards, such as fair allocation and treatment, rather than leave producers dependent on purchasers’ discretion. He discussed Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh in relation to the constitutional treatment of state monopolies.
members.conclusion: Subba Rao J. concluded that the restrictions destroyed or crippled the trade of mine owners in the appellant’s position and were unreasonable under Article 19(1)(g), although the majority rejected that conclusion.

rule.if: export_control_challenge and newcomers_excluded and no_guaranteed_purchase and producers_depend_on_purchasers_for_prices and no_definite_fairness_safeguards

predicates.export_control_challenge: A person challenges export restrictions as an interference with the right to carry on trade.
predicates.newcomers_excluded: Producers without prior export performance are excluded from direct participation in export trade.
predicates.no_guaranteed_purchase: The selected exporters or agencies are not required to buy goods from the excluded producers.
predicates.producers_depend_on_purchasers_for_price: The excluded producers have no effective market and must depend on selected purchasers to sell their goods.
predicates.no_definite_fairness_safeguards: The scheme contains no definite safeguards ensuring fair allocation, purchase arrangements, or prices for excluded producers.

members.legal_issue: A canalisation policy that leaves producers with no viable market, no assured purchaser, and no safeguards for fair allocation or prices may impose an unreasonable restriction on their business rights.
material_facts: The dissent considered a commodity for which there was practically no domestic market.
Producers excluded from direct exports depended on authorised exporters, and those exporters were not bound to purchase their output.
The authorised buyers could dictate terms, and the policy ultimately left the public trading corporation as the sole practical purchaser.
The policy did not provide definite rules guaranteeing producers a fair allocation, a reasonable price, or stable treatment.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 19(1)(g), a restriction on business must satisfy the general public-interest and reasonableness standard in Article 19(6). Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself authorise a monopoly by administrative action, although administrative interference may still be assessed under the general reasonableness standard. The dissent relied on Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P., [1955] 1 SCR 707, 727, in discussing the constitutional protection of business rights, and considered that a canalisation scheme should provide definite safeguards for fair allocation and prices.
members.conclusion: In dissent, Justice Subba Rao considered the implementation of the policy an unreasonable restriction on the producers’ right to carry on business, although he agreed that the appeal should be dismissed because the requested licence period had expired.

rule.if: export_control_case and producer_has_no_viable_domestic_market and authorized_buyers_need_not_purchase_output and policy_creates_a_single_practical_buyer and fair_allocation_and_price_safeguards_are_absent

predicates.export_control_case: The proceeding challenges a policy restricting producers’ access to export markets.
predicates.producer_has_no_viable_domestic_market: The producers cannot realistically sell their output in a domestic market.
predicates.authorized_buyers_need_not_purchase_outp: The persons permitted to export are not required to buy the producers’ goods.
predicates.policy_creates_a_single_practical_buyer: The restrictions leave one buyer as the producers’ only practical outlet.
predicates.fair_allocation_and_price_safeguards_are: The policy provides no definite safeguards ensuring fair allocation, prices, or stable treatment for affected producers.

members.legal_issue: An unpaid money judgment, decree, or recovery certificate gives a creditor a fresh cause of action to apply for corporate insolvency resolution.
material_facts: A tribunal entered a final money judgment and issued a recovery certificate in favour of the creditor.
The debtor did not pay the amount due under the judgment or recovery certificate.
The creditor applied to commence insolvency proceedings within three years of the judgment or recovery certificate.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(6), 3(10), 3(11), 3(12), and 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, a claim may be reduced to judgment, a decree-holder is a creditor, and non-payment of a debt due and payable is a default. Section 238A applies the Limitation Act, and Article 137 supplies the three-year limitation period. The Court applied the principle recognized in Ferro Alloys Corporation Ltd. v. Rajhans Steel Ltd., which was relied on in Jignesh Shah v. Union of India, and held that a final adjudication or recovery certificate for unpaid money creates a fresh right to recover that amount through insolvency proceedings.
members.conclusion: An unpaid final money judgment or decree, or an unpaid recovery certificate, gives rise to a fresh cause of action for an insolvency application, which may be filed within three years of the judgment, decree, or certificate.

predicates.financial_creditor_insolvency_applicatio: A financial creditor applied to commence insolvency resolution proceedings against a debtor.
predicates.unpaid_final_money_judgment_or_recovery_: A court or tribunal entered a final money judgment or decree, or issued a recovery certificate, and the debtor left the amount due under it unpaid in whole or in part.
predicates.application_within_three_years_of_judgme: The financial creditor filed the insolvency application within three years after the final judgment, decree, or recovery certificate.

members.legal_issue: Issuance of a recovery certificate for an unpaid debt gives rise to a fresh cause of action for an insolvency application, which is timely when filed within the applicable period measured from the certificate.
material_facts: The recovery certificates were issued in 2017, and the creditor filed its insolvency application in 2018.
The certified dues remained unpaid when the application was filed.
The appellate tribunal treated limitation as running from the earlier default, rather than from issuance of the recovery certificates.
members.legal_principle: Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to applications under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and Section 238A makes the Limitation Act applicable to proceedings under the Code. Ordinarily, limitation runs from default, but a final adjudication and recovery certificate for unpaid dues gives rise to a fresh cause of action; the application may be brought within three years from the judgment, decree, or certificate. The Court affirmed Dena Bank (Now Bank of Baroda) v C. Shivakumar Reddy, and relied on the limitation principles in B.K. Educational Services (P) Ltd. v Parag Gupta & Associates, Jignesh Shah v Union of India, Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd., Vashdeo R. Bhojwani v Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., and Balakrishna Savalram Pujari Waghmare v Shree Dhyaneshwar Maharaj Sansthan.
members.conclusion: The insolvency application was within limitation because it was filed within three years from issuance of the recovery certificates.

rule.if: insolvency_process_application and recovery_certificate_issued and certified_debt_remains_unpaid and application_filed_within_three_years_after_certificate

predicates.insolvency_process_application: A creditor filed an application seeking insolvency resolution against a corporate debtor.
predicates.recovery_certificate_issued: A recovery tribunal issued a certificate specifying the debt owed to the creditor.
predicates.certified_debt_remains_unpaid: Some or all of the debt specified in the certificate remained unpaid.
predicates.application_filed_within_three_years_aft: The creditor filed the insolvency application within three years after the recovery certificate was issued.

members.legal_issue: The rule that an unpaid adjudicated debt or recovery certificate can provide a fresh cause of action for an insolvency application is not per incuriam and is not inconsistent with earlier decisions addressing limitation from the original default.
material_facts: Dena Bank held that a final judgment or recovery certificate for unpaid dues gives the creditor a fresh cause of action to initiate insolvency proceedings within three years of the judgment or certificate.
The respondents argued that this holding conflicted with earlier larger-bench decisions and overlooked relevant statutory provisions.

The Court found that the earlier decisions relied on did not decide whether a judgment or recovery certificate for unpaid dues gives rise to a fresh cause of action, and that Dena Bank had considered the relevant statutory provisions.
members.legal_principle: A decision is per incuriam where it overlooks a relevant statutory provision or cannot be reconciled with an earlier decision of a co-equal or larger bench. A precedent binds for the legal principle actually decided, not for observations on issues that did not arise; the rule must be derived by applying law to the facts. The Court applied these principles from Secretary to Govt. of Kerala, Irrigation Department v James Varghese, Union of India v Dhanwanti Devi, and Regional Manager v Pawan Kumar Dubey, and distinguished Jignesh Shah and Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave because neither addressed the effect of a decree or recovery certificate on limitation.
members.conclusion: Dena Bank correctly stated the law and was not per incuriam; its rule was affirmed.

predicates.challenge_to_insolvency_precedent: A party challenging an insolvency ruling argued that the ruling was legally invalid because of earlier decisions or overlooked law.
predicates.prior_decisions_did_not_decide_certifica: The earlier decisions addressed limitation from default but did not decide whether an adjudication or recovery certificate creates a fresh limitation period.
predicates.precedent_considered_relevant_statutes: The challenged precedent considered the statutory provisions relevant to the effect of an adjudication or recovery certificate.

members.legal_issue: A child born during a valid marriage is presumed legitimate unless it is established that the spouses had no access when the child could have been begotten.
material_facts: The child was born during the subsistence of the marriage.
The spouses had disputes and were said to be living apart, but they lived in the same village.
The courts below found no evidence establishing that the husband had no access to the wife during the period when the child could have been begotten.
members.legal_principle: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 creates a conclusive presumption of legitimacy for a child born during a valid marriage unless it is shown that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. Non-access may be proved by relevant direct or circumstantial evidence, but the proof must be clear and satisfactory. The Court relied on Chilukuri Venkateswarlu v. Chilukuri Venkatanarayana, [1954] S.C.R. 425, Karapaya v. Mayandi, I.L.R. 12 Rang. 243 (P.C.), and Ammathayee v. Kumaresain, [1967] 1 S.C.R. 363.
members.conclusion: The presumption of legitimacy was not displaced, and the child could not be held illegitimate.

rule.if: legitimacy_dispute_in_family_property_claim and valid_marriage and child_born_during_marriage and no_access_not_established

predicates.legitimacy_dispute_in_family_property_cl: A child's legitimacy is disputed in a claim concerning family property or status.
predicates.valid_marriage: The child's parents were in a valid marriage.
predicates.child_born_during_marriage: The child was born while that marriage subsisted.
predicates.no_access_not_established: It was not established that the parents had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.

members.legal_issue: A child born during a valid marriage is presumed to be the husband’s legitimate child unless non-access at any time when the child could have been conceived is proved.
material_facts: The child was born while his mother’s valid marriage to the deceased was continuing.
The deceased denied paternity, but the mother testified that the child was his and that she had not left the marital home.

The mother lived at her father’s house about a furlong from the deceased’s home, and the evidence did not establish that the spouses had no access to each other when the child could have been conceived.
members.legal_principle: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes birth during the continuance of a valid marriage conclusive proof of legitimacy, rebuttable only by proof that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. The court relied on no earlier case on this issue.
members.conclusion: The presumption of legitimacy was not rebutted, and the concurrent finding that the child was the deceased’s legitimate son was left undisturbed.

rule.if: inheritance_claim_by_child and child_born_during_valid_marriage and not nonaccess_proven

predicates.inheritance_claim_by_child: A child claims an inheritance while another party disputes that the deceased was the child’s parent.
predicates.child_born_during_valid_marriage: The child was born while the mother’s valid marriage to the alleged father was continuing.
predicates.nonaccess_proven: Evidence establishes that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been conceived.

members.legal_issue: A child born during the continuance of a lawful marriage is presumed legitimate unless non-access at the possible time of conception is proved.
material_facts: The child was born while the mother and the alleged father were in a lawful marriage.
The alleged father denied paternity, placing legitimacy in dispute.
The alleged father bore the burden of proving non-access at a time when he could have fathered the child.
members.legal_principle: Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act creates a conclusive presumption of legitimacy for a child born during lawful wedlock, displaced only by proof of non-access when the husband could, in the ordinary course of nature, have fathered the child. Access and non-access mean the existence and non-existence of opportunities for marital intercourse, as explained in Karapaya v. Mayandy.
members.conclusion: The presumption of legitimacy under section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act applied and could be displaced only by proof of non-access at the material time.

rule.if: legitimacy_proceeding and child_born_during_lawful_marriage and not clear_nonaccess_proven

predicates.legitimacy_proceeding: A proceeding concerns whether a child is legitimate.
predicates.child_born_during_lawful_marriage: The child was born while the child's mother and alleged father were lawfully married.
predicates.clear_nonaccess_proven: Evidence clearly and satisfactorily establishes that the spouses had no opportunity for marital intercourse at a time when the husband could have fathered the child.

members.legal_issue: Civil courts cannot entertain a suit concerning land rights where the dispute could or ought to have been adjudicated in consolidation proceedings.
material_facts: The land was in an area covered by a consolidation notification.
A claimant asserted an interest in the land based on family relationship and argued that the recorded holder held it in a representative capacity.
The consolidation authorities adjudicated the competing claims to the land.
A civil suit was later brought seeking a declaration that the consolidation order was without jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(2), 5(2), and 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, as amended, assign consolidation authorities the adjudication of rights and interests in land within a notified area, including questions of title that could or ought to be raised in consolidation proceedings, and bar civil or revenue court proceedings on those matters. The Court relied on Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh and Gorakh Nath Dube v. Hari Narain Singh. It distinguished Suba Singh v. Mahendra Singh, which concerned a dispute arising after consolidation operations had been completed under the earlier statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred because the claims concerned rights in land that fell within the adjudicatory functions of the consolidation authorities.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenges_consolidation_order and land_is_in_notified_consolidation_area and dispute_concerns_land_rights and dispute_could_or_ought_to_be_adjudicated_in_consolidation_proceedings

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_consolidation_orde: A person brought a civil suit challenging an order made in consolidation proceedings as beyond the authority of the decision-maker.
predicates.land_is_in_notified_consolidation_area: The land at issue lies in an area covered by a notification initiating consolidation proceedings.
predicates.dispute_concerns_land_rights: The dispute concerns a person's rights or interests in land, including a claim based on title, family relationship, or representative ownership.
predicates.dispute_could_or_ought_to_be_adjudicated: The disputed right is one that could or ought to have been raised and adjudicated by the consolidation authorities.

members.legal_issue: A final allotment made in consolidation proceedings cannot be challenged through a later civil or revenue suit concerning rights in the land or a matter that could or ought to have been addressed in those proceedings.
material_facts: The consolidation authorities allotted the disputed plots to the respondents.
The village was later denotified, and the allotment had become final.
The appellants subsequently filed a suit seeking possession and disputing the respondents’ right to retain the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, bars civil and revenue courts from entertaining suits or proceedings concerning rights in land in a notified consolidation area, or other matters for which a proceeding could or ought to have been taken under that Act. Once the village was denotified and the allotment became final, the allotment could not be challenged by a later suit.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred because the final allotment could not be questioned in a civil or revenue court.

predicates.land_rights_suit: A party brings a civil or revenue suit concerning rights in land or a matter dealt with in consolidation proceedings.
predicates.consolidation_proceedings_completed: The consolidation proceedings for the relevant area have concluded.
predicates.final_land_allotment: The consolidation authorities made an allotment of the land that became final.

members.legal_issue: A party is barred from raising in a later civil suit a matter that could and ought to have been raised in earlier revenue proceedings within the revenue authorities’ jurisdiction, where those proceedings attained finality and their legality was not challenged.
material_facts: The revenue authorities conducted proceedings concerning cancellation of the appellant’s allotment and proceedings concerning mutation of the land.
The appellant could have challenged the respondent’s claimed relationship to the original allottee in those proceedings but did not do so.
The revenue authorities’ decisions were upheld, and the appellant’s review application was dismissed.
The later civil suit did not challenge the legality or validity of the earlier revenue proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The principle of constructive res judicata bars matters that could and ought to have been raised in earlier proceedings before a competent authority. The revenue authorities had jurisdiction over the land-settlement and mutation proceedings and the jurisdictional question whether the land was subject to escheat, subject to review of the legality or validity of those proceedings in an appropriate civil suit. State of U.P. v. Amar Singh and Balwant Singh v. Daulat Singh were cited for the proposition that a mutation entry alone does not confer title; the Court distinguished that proposition from the effect of the final adjudications in this case.
members.conclusion: The later challenge to the respondent’s relationship with the original allottee was barred by constructive res judicata.

rule.if: later_civil_suit_after_revenue_adjudication and revenue_authority_had_jurisdiction and party_could_raise_related_issue_earlier and earlier_decision_became_final and earlier_proceedings_not_challenged_in_later_suit

predicates.later_civil_suit_after_revenue_adjudicat: A party brought a civil suit after revenue authorities had adjudicated proceedings concerning the same land.
predicates.revenue_authority_had_jurisdiction: The revenue authorities had jurisdiction over the earlier land-settlement or mutation proceedings and the relevant jurisdictional question.
predicates.party_could_raise_related_issue_earlier: The party had an opportunity to raise the related issue in the earlier proceedings but did not do so.
predicates.earlier_decision_became_final: The earlier adjudication was not displaced and attained finality.
predicates.earlier_proceedings_not_challenged_in_la: The later civil suit did not challenge the legality or validity of the earlier proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be maintained when the accused deliberately inflicts a brutal, fatal attack on a helpless victim in circumstances showing a pre-existing motive.
material_facts: The accused inflicted a brutal and fatal spear wound on the deceased while he was lying helpless on the ground.
The Court considered that the accused was actuated by pre-existing enmity and intended to finish the deceased.
The High Court had imposed a death sentence, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disagree with it.
members.legal_principle: The Court found no reason to interfere with the sentence in light of the deliberate, brutal and fatal nature of the attack and the circumstances indicating motive. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case in reaching this sentencing conclusion.
members.conclusion: The death sentence imposed on the accused was maintained.

predicates.criminal_sentencing_case: The case involves review of a sentence imposed following a criminal conviction.
predicates.deliberate_brutal_fatal_attack_on_helple: The offender deliberately inflicted a brutal fatal attack while the victim was helpless.
predicates.pre_existing_motive: The circumstances showed that the offender acted from a motive that existed before the attack.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence is justified when the accused are proved to have inflicted the fatal injuries in a brutal and callous murder.
material_facts: Medical evidence established that two injuries were necessarily fatal.
The courts accepted the evidence identifying two accused as the authors of those fatal injuries.
The Court described the murder as brutal and callous and noted that the death sentences were imposed only on the two accused who inflicted the fatal injuries.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and held that the sentences were justified without resort to Section 34. It explained that Section 34 concerns constructive liability for persons acting with a common intention and noted that the other participants had not received the extreme penalty. Although the appellant cited decisions, the supplied judgment does not identify them or rely on a particular earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The death sentences were justified, and the Court rejected the challenge to sentence.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_death_sentence and accused_individually_attributed_fatal_injuries and fatal_nature_of_injuries_established and murder_found_brutal_and_callous

predicates.appeal_challenging_death_sentence: The matter is an appeal challenging a death sentence for murder.
predicates.accused_individually_attributed_fatal_in: The evidence accepted by the court identifies the accused as the persons who inflicted the fatal injuries.
predicates.fatal_nature_of_injuries_established: The medical evidence establishes that the injuries inflicted were fatal.
predicates.murder_found_brutal_and_callous: The court finds the murder brutal and callous.

members.legal_issue: A death sentence may be maintained for an offender whose property-driven attack involved brutal and determined killings.
material_facts: The offender and his father were interested in obtaining property that could be claimed by the deceased family.
The offender killed two members of that family, including a close relative and a young woman.
He chopped the man's neck and inflicted repeated blows on the young woman.
The offender's death sentences had been confirmed on appeal.
members.legal_principle: In considering whether death was justified, the Court referred to Dalbir Singh & Ors. v. State of Punjab, [1979] 3 SCR 1059, concerning reasons that may weigh in favour of a death sentence. It relied on the offender's property-related motive and the brutal, determined manner in which he killed two victims. The convictions arose under Sections 302 and 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The Court saw no reason to alter the death sentence imposed on this offender.

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The case is an appeal challenging a death sentence.
predicates.offender_had_property_based_motive: The offender acted in pursuit of a motive to obtain property or defeat another person's claim to it.
predicates.offender_committed_brutal_determined_kil: The offender personally carried out killings in a brutal and determined manner.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent judicial decision determining rights that affect taxable income can constitute definite information for reopening an assessment.
material_facts: The taxpayer's ownership of the mill and entitlement to its income were subject to litigation when the original returns were filed.
The taxpayer did not disclose the compromise under which he became entitled to the mill's income.
A later Privy Council decision determined that the vendor had been the absolute owner of the mill and that the vendor's sons had no interest in it.
The tax officer relied on that decision to initiate reassessment proceedings for income received from the mill.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34(1)(b) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, information includes information about the true state of the law and relevant judicial decisions. The principle in Maharaj Kumar Kamal Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax also establishes that income may have escaped assessment even where a return was filed, if assessable income was erroneously left untaxed.
members.conclusion: The later judicial decision was definite information, and the reassessment proceedings were validly initiated.

predicates.reassessment_proceeding: A tax authority initiated proceedings to reassess income for a prior assessment period.
predicates.later_judicial_decision_determines_tax_r: A later judicial decision determined rights that bear on who owned an income-producing asset or was entitled to its income.
predicates.decision_reveals_income_liable_to_assess: The judicial decision supplied information showing that income was liable to assessment but had not been assessed.

members.legal_issue: Once reassessment is validly reopened for income that escaped assessment, the reassessment is not limited to the portion that initially justified reopening.
material_facts: The tax authority reopened the assessment after a judicial decision supplied information concerning income from the mill.
The taxpayer argued that any reassessment should be confined to the portion of the income that had escaped assessment under the earlier understanding of the parties' rights.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, once a valid notice reopens an assessment, the previous under-assessment is set aside and the assessment proceedings begin afresh; the tax authority's jurisdiction is not confined to the part of the income that initially supported reopening.
members.conclusion: The tax authority could reassess the whole assessment and had a duty to tax the entire income that had escaped assessment for the year.

predicates.reassessment_proceeding: A tax authority initiated proceedings to reassess income for a prior assessment period.
predicates.valid_reopening: The reassessment was validly reopened on information that justified reassessment.
predicates.income_escaped_assessment: Some income liable to assessment for the year had not been assessed.

members.legal_issue: A later judicial decision finally determining ownership and the correct legal position constitutes definite information for reopening an assessment, and a valid reopening permits reassessment of the entire income that escaped assessment.
material_facts: The taxpayer had not included income from the mill in the original assessment while litigation over ownership was pending.
A later decision of the Privy Council finally determined that the vendor owned the mill and that the taxpayer had acquired it from him.
After that decision, the tax authority issued a reassessment notice for income from the mill.
The taxpayer had not disclosed the compromise under which he obtained release of the vendor’s sons’ claims to the mill and its income.
members.legal_principle: Under section 34(1)(b) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, information includes information about the true state of the law conveyed by a relevant judicial decision. Income may have escaped assessment even if a return was filed, where assessable income was omitted or not taxed. Under section 34 read with section 22(2), valid reopening sets aside the prior underassessment and begins the assessment afresh, allowing the authority to assess the entire escaped income. The Court followed Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax and referred to Kamakhya Narain Singh’s case.
members.conclusion: The later judicial decision constituted definite information and the reassessment proceedings were valid. Once validly reopened, the assessment began afresh and the tax authority had jurisdiction and a duty to assess the entire income that had escaped assessment for the year.

predicates.reassessment_proceeding: The tax authority initiated a proceeding to reassess income for a tax year.
predicates.later_judicial_decision_determines_relev: A later judicial decision finally determined rights or the legal position relevant to the income being assessed.
predicates.income_escaped_assessment: Income that was assessable for the year was omitted from assessment or was underassessed.

members.legal_issue: A landowner need not receive a further hearing after the officer has completed the objections inquiry and submitted the report to the government.
material_facts: The challengers had filed objections and received a full opportunity to present them in the inquiry.
The officer submitted a report to the government, after which the government considered the report and proceeded with the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and held that the government considers the officer's report and decides how to proceed; there is no additional hearing requirement after the report. It relied on State of Gujarat v. Ambalal Haiderbhai for the principle that an inquiry, whether administrative or judicial, must comply with natural justice.
members.conclusion: The law did not require a further opportunity to make submissions after the report was submitted to the government.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and objections_inquired_into and objectors_given_full_opportunity and report_submitted_to_government

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.objections_inquired_into: An officer conducts an inquiry into the objections to the acquisition.
predicates.objectors_given_full_opportunity: The objectors receive a full opportunity to present their objections during the inquiry.
predicates.report_submitted_to_government: The officer submits the inquiry report to the government for consideration.

members.legal_issue: The government is not required to conduct a second hearing after receiving the collector’s report before deciding whether to declare land acquisition.
material_facts: The collector heard the objector and submitted a report to the government.
The government considered the report before issuing the acquisition declaration.
The objector argued that a further hearing by the government was required.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 do not require a second hearing by the government at the stage when it considers the collector’s report and decides whether to issue a declaration. The Court followed Abdul Husein Tayabali & Ors. v. State of Gujarat & Ors., [1968] 1 S.C.R. 597.
members.conclusion: A second hearing by the government after it receives and considers the collector’s report is not necessary.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a proposed acquisition of land.
predicates.collector_heard_objector: The collector heard the objector in the acquisition inquiry.
predicates.government_considered_collector_report: The government considered the collector’s report before deciding whether to proceed with the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Landowners who have been heard in the objection inquiry and whose objections are placed before the government are not entitled to a further hearing before the final acquisition declaration.
material_facts: The landowners appeared in the objection inquiry, were heard, and had their objections recorded.
The inquiry report and the record, including the landowners’ objections, were sent to the government.
The government considered the material and then issued the final declaration that the land was needed.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 5A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the objections and inquiry record accompany the report to enable the government to form its own satisfaction; the report is recommendatory and does not bind the government. Neither section 5A nor another provision requires a second hearing before the section 6 declaration. The court also noted that the landowners had in fact been heard during the objection inquiry.
members.conclusion: The landowners had an opportunity to be heard, and no second opportunity was required before the final declaration.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the proposed compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.landowners_heard_in_objection_inquiry: The affected landowners are given an opportunity to present their objections in the inquiry.
predicates.objections_recorded_and_sent_to_decision: The landowners’ objections are recorded and transmitted with the inquiry material to the government making the acquisition decision.
predicates.decision_maker_considered_objection_reco: The government has the objection record before it when independently deciding whether the land is needed.

members.legal_issue: A sale cannot be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale when the sale and the condition for repurchase are set out in separate documents.
material_facts: The property was conveyed by a sale deed, while the covenant granting the right to reconveyance was contained in a separate document.
The claimant sought to establish that the transaction was in the nature of a mortgage by conditional sale.
members.legal_principle: Under section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as applied by the Court, a sale and the condition for repurchase must be contained in the same document for the transaction to be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale; separate documents do not permit proof of that characterization.
members.conclusion: The claim that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale was inadmissible because the sale deed and the covenant for reconveyance were in separate documents.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding_involves: A proceeding seeking specific performance of reconveyance also involves a claim that the sale was a mortgage by conditional sale.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_characterize_sale_as_c: The claimant seeks to establish that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale.
predicates.sale_and_repurchase_condition_are_in_sep: The sale and the condition for repurchase were recorded in separate documents.

members.legal_issue: A sale accompanied by a separate agreement to reconvey is not a mortgage by conditional sale when the reconveyance condition is not included in the document that effects or purports to effect the sale.
material_facts: The parties executed a deed of sale and a separate agreement to reconvey the property on the same day.
The reconveyance condition was contained in the separate agreement rather than in the deed of sale.
The claimant nevertheless asserted that the transaction was a mortgage securing a loan.
members.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 58(c), provides that a transaction is not a mortgage by conditional sale where the condition for transfer back is not embodied in the document that effects or purports to effect the sale. A mortgage leaves a debt and a right to redeem; a sale with a condition of repurchase does not create a debt and gives only a personal right enforceable according to the agreement. The Court relied on Pandit Chunchun Jha v. Sheikh Ebadat Ali, Shri Bhaskar Waman Joshi v. Shri Narayan Rambilas Agarwal, K. Simrathmull v. Nanjalingiah Gowder, Mushir Mohammed Khan v. Sajeda Bano, and Tamboli Ramanlal Motilal v. Ghanchi Chimanlal Keshavlal.
members.conclusion: The transaction was a sale with a condition of repurchase, not a mortgage by conditional sale.

predicates.sale_with_repurchase_arrangement: The parties completed a transfer of property and agreed that the transferor could later obtain a transfer back.
predicates.reconveyance_condition_in_separate_docum: The condition for transferring the property back appeared in a document separate from the document effecting the sale.

members.legal_issue: A sale accompanied by a separate agreement to reconvey cannot be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale when the condition of reconveyance is absent from the document effecting the sale.
material_facts: The seller executed a registered sale deed transferring the house to the buyer.
Several days later, the buyer executed a separate agreement to reconvey the house if the original price was repaid within the agreed period.
The sale deed and the reconveyance agreement were registered on the same day, but the condition of reconveyance was not included in the sale deed.
The seller sought redemption on the basis that the transaction was a mortgage.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, a transaction cannot be deemed a mortgage by conditional sale unless the condition is embodied in the document effecting or purporting to effect the sale. The parties' intention is assessed from the language of the document in light of surrounding circumstances, but the statutory proviso applies when the condition is in a separate document. The Court relied on Chunchun Jha v. Ebadat Ali, Bhaskar Waman Joshi v. Shrinarayan Rambilas Agarwal, P.L. Bapuswami v. N. Pattay Gounder, and Vidhyadhar v. Mankikrao.
members.conclusion: The documents read together did not create a mortgage by conditional sale because the condition for reconveyance was not embodied in the sale document.

predicates.redemption_suit_appeal: A party appeals in a suit seeking redemption of property on the basis that a transfer was a mortgage.
predicates.sale_document_lacks_repurchase_condition: The document transferring the property does not contain the condition that the property may be repurchased or reconveyed.
predicates.separate_repurchase_agreement: The parties make a separate agreement for reconveyance of the transferred property.

members.legal_issue: A legal representative substituted in a property-based rent eviction proceeding cannot, in that representative capacity, defeat the proceeding by claiming to be a trespasser or asserting an independent title that the rent forum has no jurisdiction to determine.
material_facts: The tenant died while a rent eviction petition concerning leased property was pending, and the right to sue survived.
The successor was added to the proceeding only as the tenant’s legal representative.
The successor claimed that, as the heir of a tenant of commercial premises, he was a trespasser and that the rent authority lacked jurisdiction.
Determining the successor’s asserted independent title would have been outside the rent authority’s jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 4(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires substitution of a deceased defendant’s legal representative where the right to sue survives, and Rule 4(2) permits that representative to raise defenses available to the deceased except those personal to the deceased. Under Jagdish Chander Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan, heirs may also be impleaded in their personal capacity to assert independent title where the court has jurisdiction to determine that title; that principle does not permit such joinder before a rent authority lacking that jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The rent authority properly continued the proceeding against the legal representative, who could not raise the trespasser plea in that capacity or defeat the proceeding on that basis. The successor also could not be joined personally to assert independent title because the rent authority lacked jurisdiction to determine that issue.

rule.if: property_rent_eviction_proceeding_after_defendant_death and right_to_sue_survives and successor_added_only_as_legal_representative and (successor_claims_trespasser_status or successor_asserts_independent_title) and forum_lacks_jurisdiction_over_independent_title

members.legal_issue: Joining a person claiming through a tenant as a proper party to an ejectment suit does not change the suit's character or remove it from the court's statutory jurisdiction.
material_facts: The landlords brought an ejectment suit against the tenant and the subtenant, who claimed through the tenant.
The subtenant was joined so that the dispute about the landlords' right to possession and the subtenant's claimed protection could be determined in that person's presence.
members.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, governs the qualifying landlord-tenant suit. Under the ordinary law, a possession decree against a tenant binds a person claiming under or through that tenant even if that person is not joined; such a person may nevertheless be joined as a proper party to contest the landlord's entitlement to possession and seek any available statutory protection. Joinder of a proper party does not change the suit's character or defeat the court's jurisdiction. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: Although the subtenant was not a necessary party, the subtenant was a proper party, and joining that party did not alter the character of the suit or take it outside section 28.

predicates.landlord_tenant_ejectment_suit: A landlord brought an ejectment suit against a tenant seeking possession of premises covered by the relevant statutory jurisdiction.
predicates.claimant_through_tenant_joined_as_party: A person claiming through the tenant was joined so that the person's position concerning possession or statutory protection could be considered in the suit.

members.legal_issue: Joining an invalid subtenant to a landlord’s eviction suit against the tenant does not convert the suit into a proceeding against a trespasser or remove it from the rent-control court’s jurisdiction.
material_facts: The landlords brought an eviction suit against the appellant and the other occupants, including the original tenant.
The appellant was alleged to occupy the premises under an invalid subtenancy.
The eviction suit was decreed, and the appellant argued that the rent-control court lacked jurisdiction because the suit against him was one against a trespasser.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act, as explained in Importers and Manufacturers Ltd. v. Pheroz Framroze Taraporewala, joining a subtenant whose subtenancy is invalid does not alter the character of a suit between landlord and tenant or take it outside the Rent Act. Hiralal Vallabhram v. Kastorbhai Lalbhai is distinguishable: there the appellate court ordered eviction of the subtenant alone as a trespasser and made no eviction order against the tenants-in-chief, making the proceeding one between an owner and a trespasser.
members.conclusion: The rent-control court had jurisdiction; joining the appellant as an invalid subtenant did not change the character of the suit.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: The landlord brought an eviction proceeding under the rent-control regime.
predicates.landlord_seeks_eviction_of_tenant_and_su: The landlord sought eviction of both the tenant and the subtenant in the same proceeding.
predicates.subtenant_is_joined_as_invalid_occupant: The subtenant was joined as an occupant whose subtenancy was invalid.

members.legal_issue: A will is not presumed to have been duly executed and attested merely because it is more than thirty years old.
material_facts: The disputed will was more than thirty years old when it was relied on in the suit.
The beneficiaries relied on the document’s age to seek a presumption that it had been duly executed and attested.
members.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act does not create a presumption of due execution and attestation for a will. A will must be proved in accordance with Section 63(c) of the Succession Act read with Section 68 of the Evidence Act. The Court relied on Bharpur Singh v. Shamsher Singh.
members.conclusion: The presumption for documents more than thirty years old does not establish due execution or attestation of a will; the will must be proved under the requirements applicable to wills.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party to a proceeding disputes whether a will was duly executed and proved.
predicates.will_is_more_than_thirty_years_old: The will relied on in the proceeding is more than thirty years old.

members.legal_issue: A copy of an old document does not, merely because it is more than thirty years old, attract the presumption of due execution of the original when the copy is not properly admissible as secondary evidence.
material_facts: The defendants relied on a translation of an alleged copy of a will said to have been executed in 1911 to show that the deceased Mahant had taken the defendant as a disciple.
The original will and a certified copy were not produced, the document had not been proved by a witness, and no foundation had been laid for its admission as secondary evidence.
The Court found that the translation of the alleged copy could not be treated as secondary evidence within the Evidence Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Indian Evidence Act requires production of the particular document for which the presumption is sought; production of an admissible copy may at most support a presumption concerning the copy’s authenticating signatures, not due execution of the original. A copy must also qualify as secondary evidence under sections 63 and 65. The Court relied on Basant Singh v. Brij Raj Saran Singh, AIR 1935 PC 132.
members.conclusion: The alleged 1911 will was not proved, and its translation was excluded from consideration.

rule.if: civil_evidentiary_dispute and party_relies_on_old_document and only_unproved_copy_produced and copy_not_admissible_as_secondary_evidence

predicates.civil_evidentiary_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to decide whether a document proves a disputed fact.
predicates.party_relies_on_old_document: A party relies on a document said to be more than thirty years old.
predicates.only_unproved_copy_produced: The party produces only a copy that has not otherwise been proved.
predicates.copy_not_admissible_as_secondary_evidenc: The requirements for admitting the copy as secondary evidence have not been established.

members.legal_issue: The presumption of due execution and attestation for an ancient document does not apply to a copy merely because the copy is admitted as secondary evidence.
material_facts: The original will was not produced, and the courts below found that it had been deliberately withheld by the appellants.
A certified copy obtained from the court record of an earlier suit was admitted as secondary evidence of the will’s contents.
The copy was more than thirty years old and came from proper custody.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 65 and 90 of the Evidence Act, a copy may be admitted as secondary evidence where the requirements for secondary evidence are met. The presumption under section 90 as to execution and attestation applies to an original document, not a copy. For a copy admitted under section 65 and produced from proper custody, only the signatures authenticating the copy may be presumed genuine. The Court followed Harihar Prasad v. Must. of Munshi Nath Prasad and relied on Munnalal v. Krishibai and Basant Singh v. Brij Raj.
members.conclusion: The copy could be admitted as secondary evidence of the will’s contents, but its age and custody did not permit a presumption that the original will had been duly executed and attested.

rule.if: testamentary_validity_dispute and original_will_not_produced and copy_admitted_as_secondary_evidence and copy_more_than_thirty_years_old and copy_from_proper_custody

predicates.testamentary_validity_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a will is valid.
predicates.original_will_not_produced: The original will is not produced in evidence.
predicates.copy_admitted_as_secondary_evidence: A copy of the will is admitted as secondary evidence of its contents.
predicates.copy_more_than_thirty_years_old: The copy is more than thirty years old.
