predicates.copy_from_proper_custody: The copy is produced from proper custody.

members.legal_issue: A purported partition deed made to defeat family members’ rights and not acted upon is a sham transaction.
material_facts: The two brothers divided the lands unequally, while the deed made no provision for division of the family house.
The brothers continued in joint possession of the lands, lived in the same house, and maintained a joint mess after the deed.
The circumstances supported the finding that the deed was intended to limit the widows’ claims to the smaller share and avoid consequences of a possible adoption.
Both lower courts found the deed was not genuine.
members.legal_principle: The Court ordinarily accepts concurrent findings of fact in an appeal by special leave unless they lack evidentiary support. The evidence supported the finding that the deed was a sham, including the unequal division and the family’s continued joint living and possession. The uncertainty before Anant v. Shankar, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 196, concerning the effect of a widow’s adoption on family property also supported the inference that the deed was intended to avoid possible legal consequences.
members.conclusion: The partition deed was sham and was not intended to be effective.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_challenges_concurrent_finding and partition_deed_dispute and unequal_division and continued_joint_living and continued_joint_possession and deed_intended_to_defeat_family_claims

predicates.special_leave_appeal_challenges_concurre: The proceeding is an appeal by special leave challenging a factual finding reached by both lower courts.
predicates.partition_deed_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a document purporting to divide family property was a genuine partition.
predicates.unequal_division: The purported partition allocated substantially unequal shares of the family lands.
predicates.continued_joint_living: The family members continued living together in the same home after the document was made.
predicates.continued_joint_possession: The family members continued possessing the lands jointly after the document was made.
predicates.deed_intended_to_defeat_family_claims: The circumstances showed that the document was intended to defeat or restrict the claims of other family members.

members.legal_issue: A sham expression of an intention to partition does not sever joint family status.
material_facts: The brothers relied on the purported partition deed as an expression of an intention to separate.
The deed was found to be a sham and was not intended to be effective.
The brothers continued in joint possession and continued living together after the deed.
members.legal_principle: A definite and unequivocal indication by one coparcener of an intention to separate can sever joint status without the assent of the others, once clearly communicated. But an expression of intention that is merely a pretence or sham has no such effect. The Court applied Merla Ramanna v. Chelikani Jagannadha Rao, A.I.R. 1941 P.C. 48.
members.conclusion: The sham deed did not sever the joint family status.

predicates.joint_family_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether members of a family remained joint in status.
predicates.purported_separation_expression: A family member relied on an expressed intention or document as showing an intention to separate.
predicates.expression_was_sham: The expression or document was not genuine and was merely a pretence.

members.legal_issue: A purported partition does not sever joint-family status when the expressed intention to separate is merely sham or pretended.
material_facts: The family members relied on the purported partition deed as expressing an intention to separate.
The courts found the deed sham and intended to defeat the widows’ rights, not to effect a genuine separation.
The family members continued in joint possession and continued living and dining together.
members.legal_principle: A definite and unambiguous intention by a member to separate, clearly communicated to the other coparceners, can sever joint status without their assent. But an expression of intention that is merely a pretence or sham does not effect severance. The Court relied on Merla Ranumna v. Chelikani Jagannadha Rao and Others.
members.conclusion: The sham deed did not sever the joint-family status.

predicates.property_partition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a dispute over partition of family property.
predicates.purported_separation: A family member or members expressed an intention to separate from the joint family.
predicates.sham_intention: The expressed intention to separate was a pretence and was not genuinely meant to divide the family or its property.

members.legal_issue: An executive decision cannot authorize a land use that conflicts with the applicable development plan where the governing law provides no authority or procedure for that change.
material_facts: The land was within a development scheme and was reserved for an auditorium and cinema for public and semi-public purposes.
The newspaper allotment was for a printing press, which the judgment treated as an industrial use.
The State directed the allotment, but no statutory power or procedure authorizing the change of use was shown.
members.legal_principle: The Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, establishes the development-plan framework and regulates land use and development. The Court held that, absent a statutory provision and compliance with any applicable requirements for changing use, executive action cannot authorize a use contrary to the plan. It relied on Friends Colony Development Committee v. State of Orissa for the importance of planned development and land-use regulation.
members.conclusion: The State could not, through executive action, authorize use of the land for an industrial purpose contrary to the development plan without following a lawful change-of-use process.

rule.if: public_interest_land_use_challenge and development_plan_specifies_use and proposed_use_conflicts and no_lawful_change_process

predicates.public_interest_land_use_challenge: A public-interest proceeding challenges land use authorized through an allotment.
predicates.development_plan_specifies_use: The applicable development plan specifies the permitted or intended use of the land.
predicates.proposed_use_conflicts: The use authorized by the allotment conflicts with the use specified in the development plan.
predicates.no_lawful_change_process: No applicable statutory authority or procedure for changing the specified use was shown to have been followed.

members.legal_issue: A development authority cannot permit commercial or other non-residential use of land designated for residential use unless the governing plan is lawfully amended through the prescribed process.
material_facts: The operative master plan designated the relevant sector for residential use alone.
Residential plots were used for banks and other commercial businesses without specific permission under a finalized plan or other lawful authorization.
A public notice invited suggestions about possible mixed use, but the proposal was never finalized through the statutory process.
The leases also required the premises to be used for residential purposes.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6(2)(b) and 6(2)(h), 7, 8, 14, 18 and 19 of the U.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, read with Regulations 2, 3–11 of the New Okhla Industrial Development Area (Preparation and Finalization of Plan) Regulations, 1991, and Regulation 3.22 of the 2006 Building Regulations, make the plan and its designated uses binding. An executive or policy decision cannot alter a statutory plan, and the authority must comply with the prescribed amendment process. The Court relied on NOIDA Entrepreneurs Association v. NOIDA, NDMC v. Tanvi Trading, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Mudappa, S.N. Chandrashekar v. State of Karnataka, Shabi Construction Company v. CIDCO, K.K. Bhalla v. State of M.P., Dr. G.N. Khajuria v. DDA and ITC Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: Commercial and other non-residential activity in a sector designated for residential use is impermissible, and the authority has no discretion to authorize it contrary to the operative plan. A change of use requires amendment of the relevant plan and, where necessary, other governing instruments through the prescribed legal process.

rule.if: residential_land_use_case and site_designated_residential and nonresidential_commercial_activity and not plan_lawfully_amended

predicates.residential_land_use_case: The proceeding concerns the regulation of land use by a development authority in an area governed by a development plan.
predicates.site_designated_residential: The operative development plan designates the site or sector for residential use.
predicates.nonresidential_commercial_activity: An occupant or lessee uses the residential site for a commercial or other non-residential activity.
predicates.plan_lawfully_amended: The authority has amended the governing plan through the legally prescribed process to allow the activity.

members.legal_issue: A change from a development plan’s designated land-use category must be authorized under the statutory route governing changes from that plan and cannot be granted through ordinary permission where the proposed use is prohibited by the applicable zoning regulations.
material_facts: The land was designated for residential use, and the proposed restaurant use was not permitted in that zone under either category of use in the zoning regulations.
The planning and government authorities approved a change from residential to commercial use, treating the application as one to change the development plan’s designated use.

The approval did not identify any qualifying circumstance necessitating a change to the plan, and the record did not establish the required public-interest basis or compliance with the other statutory conditions.
The planning authority’s officers had identified the prospect of increased traffic and parking problems, but the approval did not explain how those concerns were addressed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1), 14(2) and 15 of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 govern changes that conform to the development plan and zoning regulations; they do not authorize a use prohibited by those regulations. Section 14-A governs changes from the Outline Development Plan and requires a specified basis for the change, public interest, consistency with other applicable laws, and publication inviting objections. Section 15(2)’s deemed-permission mechanism is subject to conformity with the plan and regulations under Section 13(3). The court relied on Ashok Leyland Ltd. v. State of T.N. on giving effect to the words “subject to,” and considered Special Deputy Commissioner v. Bhargavi Madhavan and Sri Krishnapur Mutt v. N. Vijayendra Shetty in addressing the statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The ordinary permission provisions and the provision for changes from the development plan operate in different fields. Because the proposed use was not permitted by the zoning regulations and the statutory requirements for changing the plan were not met, the conversion approval could not stand.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and land_use_change_from_development_plan and proposed_use_barred_by_zoning and not qualifying_basis_for_plan_change

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: A party appeals after a court has dismissed a challenge to an administrative land-use conversion.
predicates.land_use_change_from_development_plan: The proposed conversion changes the use designated for the land in the applicable development plan.
predicates.proposed_use_barred_by_zoning: The proposed use is not permitted by the applicable zoning regulations.
predicates.qualifying_basis_for_plan_change: The authorities identify and establish a qualifying circumstance that necessitates changing the development plan’s designated use.

members.legal_issue: An eviction proceeding need not be ended outright when a subsequent event defeats the ground originally pleaded but another legally permissible ground may be raised by amendment.
material_facts: The landlord’s acquisition of another non-residential accommodation during the proceeding disabled him from pursuing eviction on the ground originally invoked.
The High Court had made an adverse finding about that disability, and the Supreme Court held that the finding could not be reopened.
The litigation had already been prolonged, and the landlord might have another legally permissible ground for eviction.
The parties could be given an opportunity to file additional pleadings and lead evidence on any permitted amended ground.
members.legal_principle: To avoid driving parties into new litigation of unknown duration, the court may mould relief to promote substantial justice while preserving fairness to both sides. The statutory disability arising under section 10(3)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 had to be taken into account, but other legally permissible grounds could be pursued through amendment with a fair opportunity for further pleadings and evidence.
members.conclusion: The revision was to stand dismissed, but the eviction proceeding was not to be terminated outright: the Rent Controller was to take account of the established disability, the landlord could amend the petition on another legally permissible ground, and both sides were to have a fair opportunity to plead and present evidence. The established finding of disability could not be reopened.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and later_event_defeats_pleaded_ground and another_legal_ground_may_be_available and fair_opportunity_for_amendment_and_evidence

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.later_event_defeats_pleaded_ground: A fact arising during the proceeding makes the ground originally pleaded unavailable.
predicates.another_legal_ground_may_be_available: The party seeking eviction may have another legally permissible ground to pursue.
predicates.fair_opportunity_for_amendment_and_evide: The parties can be given a fair opportunity to amend pleadings and present evidence on the permitted ground.

members.legal_issue: A pending eviction suit originally pleaded on superseded grounds may proceed on fresh pleadings under the amended grounds, with institution for the new grounds treated as occurring when those pleadings are filed.
material_facts: The transferee-landlords had filed eviction suits under the earlier version of the law, before the amended grounds existed.

The amendment applied to pending suits and appeals and restricted suits based on the amended grounds during a post-transfer waiting period, subject to an exception for certain safety-related cases with permission.
The landlords could not have pleaded the amended requirements when they first filed their suits.
By the time fresh pleadings could be filed in the cases before the Court, the waiting period after the transfers had elapsed.
The Court directed that the tenants be allowed to respond and that the parties be allowed to present additional evidence.
members.legal_principle: The majority construed “institute” in its natural and grammatical sense as beginning proceedings on the specified grounds. Because the earlier suits were pleaded on grounds that were not the amended grounds, the new restriction on institution did not attach to them until fresh pleadings were filed. The Court preferred a construction that gives effect to the tenant protections while avoiding needless re-litigation, and allowed further pleadings, responsive pleadings, and additional evidence.
members.conclusion: The landlords may file fresh pleadings setting out the applicable amended grounds in the pending suit or appeal; the suit is treated as instituted on those grounds when the fresh pleading is filed, subject to the waiting-period requirement or the applicable safety-related permission.

rule.if: pending_transferee_landlord_eviction_case and original_pleading_uses_superseded_grounds and landlord_files_fresh_pleading_on_amended_grounds and (post_transfer_wait_elapsed or safety_permission_obtained)

predicates.pending_transferee_landlord_eviction_cas: An eviction suit or appeal by a landlord who acquired the premises by transfer is pending.
predicates.original_pleading_uses_superseded_ground: The landlord’s original pleading relies on grounds that the amendment replaced or altered.
predicates.landlord_files_fresh_pleading_on_amended: The landlord files a new pleading setting out the eviction grounds required by the amended law.
predicates.post_transfer_wait_elapsed: The period that must pass after the landlord acquired the premises has elapsed before the new pleading is filed.
predicates.safety_permission_obtained: The landlord obtained the required permission for an early suit based on a safety-related need for building work.

members.legal_issue: On remand of an eviction proceeding, a landlord may be permitted, on application, to plead an alternative statutory ground for eviction.
material_facts: The case was remitted for fresh disposal of the new-construction exemption claim.
It was submitted that the landlady’s son needed the premises for his personal requirement.
The Court permitted the trial court to allow the landlady, if she applied, to plead an alternative ground for eviction under the Act.
members.legal_principle: The Court noted that, even if the rent-control law applied, eviction could be sought on a ground specified by that law, and permitted alternative pleading on remand to avoid prolixity and delay. No specific provision or earlier case is cited for this permission.
members.conclusion: The trial court could allow the landlady, on application, to plead any specified statutory ground for eviction as an alternative basis.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_remitted: An eviction proceeding has been sent back to the trial court for fresh consideration.
predicates.landlord_applies_to_plead_alternative_st: The landlord asks to plead a statutory ground for eviction as an alternative basis.

members.legal_issue: A custodial sentence should be enhanced when the sentence imposed is grossly inadequate in light of the gravity and circumstances of the offence.
material_facts: The respondents had served less than six months in custody, and the High Court reduced their imprisonment to the period already undergone.
The offence was grave, and the High Court gave no particular reason for imposing such a short custodial sentence.
The Supreme Court concluded that the sentence was grossly and entirely inadequate and enhanced it to five years’ rigorous imprisonment.
members.legal_principle: In fixing punishment, a court should consider the nature of the offence, the circumstances in which it was committed, and the degree of deliberation shown by the offender. The punishment should be proportionate to the gravity of the offence; a sentence that is grossly and entirely inadequate may involve a failure of justice.
members.conclusion: The custodial sentence was enhanced to five years’ rigorous imprisonment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and grave_offence and sentence_limited_to_short_time_served and no_reason_given_for_short_sentence

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case was a criminal appeal concerning the sentence imposed on the accused.
predicates.grave_offence: The offence for which the accused were sentenced was grave.
predicates.sentence_limited_to_short_time_served: The custodial sentence was limited to a short period that the accused had already served.
predicates.no_reason_given_for_short_sentence: The court imposing the short sentence gave no particular reason for doing so.

members.legal_issue: A sentence for a fatal culpable-homicide offence must be increased when the original sentence is grossly inadequate and unreasonable in the circumstances.
material_facts: The trial court imposed two years’ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500 for the culpable-homicide conviction.

The Supreme Court found that sentence grossly inadequate and unreasonable and, considering the circumstances, substituted six years’ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000, with four months’ rigorous imprisonment in default of payment.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the punishment imposed was grossly inadequate and unreasonable in light of the circumstances, and substituted what it considered a proper sentence. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for the sentencing decision.
members.conclusion: The sentence was increased to six years’ rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000, with four months’ rigorous imprisonment in default of payment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and fatal_culpable_homicide and original_sentence_was_brief and circumstances_make_sentence_grossly_inadequate

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The case is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction and its sentence.
predicates.fatal_culpable_homicide: The accused was convicted of a culpable-homicide offence that resulted in the victim’s death.
predicates.original_sentence_was_brief: The trial court imposed a comparatively short custodial sentence and a fine.
predicates.circumstances_make_sentence_grossly_inad: The circumstances of the offence make the punishment originally imposed grossly inadequate and unreasonable.

members.legal_issue: A sentence that is manifestly inadequate in light of the gravity and consequences of a brutal offence must be replaced with a proportionate custodial sentence, and the discretion to impose sentence must be exercised on judicial reasons rather than whim.
material_facts: The offence involved a sword attack that severed the injured person’s hand at the wrist and permanently deprived him of its use.
The High Court reduced the custodial sentence to the period already undergone, which was only a few days, and did not give reasons for that reduction.
The High Court relied on a fine, but the Court found that a fine or compensation alone would not meet the demands of justice.
members.legal_principle: Sentencing must take account of the nature and gravity of the offence, the manner in which it was committed, its impact on the victim and society, and the need for proportionate punishment, protection of society, and deterrence. Judicial discretion must be guided by law and relevant reasons, not whim or caprice; undue sympathy resulting in an inadequate sentence may undermine public confidence and the administration of justice. The Court relied on Sham Sunder v. Puran, Sevaka Perumal v. State of Tamil Nadu, State of M.P. v. Saleem, Ravji v. State of Rajasthan, State of Karnataka v. Krishnappa, Jameel v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Shyam Narain v. State (NCT of Delhi), Guru Basavaraj v. State of Karnataka, Rattiram v. State of M.P., State of Madhya Pradesh v. Najab Khan, Hazara Singh v. Raj Kumar, Ramji Dayawala & Sons v. Invest Import, and M/s. Aero Traders Pvt. Ltd. v. Ravinder Kumar Suri.
members.conclusion: The Court held the sentence manifestly inadequate and modified it to require a proportionate term of rigorous imprisonment in addition to the fine imposed by the trial court.

predicates.appeal_against_inadequate_sentence: An appeal challenges a sentence as inadequate.
predicates.brutal_offence_caused_permanent_grievous: The offence was committed brutally and caused a permanent, grievous injury to the victim.
predicates.lower_court_imposed_minimal_custody_with: The lower court imposed only minimal custodial punishment without giving reasons for its leniency.
predicates.fine_alone_would_not_address_gravity: The gravity and consequences of the offence could not be adequately addressed by a fine alone.

members.legal_issue: The statutory bar on certain proceedings against a sick company does not prevent a landlord from pursuing eviction proceedings against it.
material_facts: The tenant was treated as a sick company under the applicable industrial-company legislation.
The landlord's proceeding sought eviction and possession of the premises.
The trial court made recovery of mesne profits subject to obtaining the competent authority's permission.
members.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Sick Industrial Companies Act, 1985, did not bar the eviction proceeding. The Court relied on Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. v. Church of South India Trust Association, (1992) 3 SCC 1. The trial court separately made recovery of mesne profits conditional on obtaining permission from the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction.
members.conclusion: The sick-company provision did not bar the eviction proceeding, although recovery of mesne profits was subject to the required permission.

predicates.sick_company_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued eviction proceedings against a company treated as sick under the applicable industrial-company law.
predicates.claim_seeks_possession_not_money_recover: The proceeding sought possession of premises rather than recovery of money.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s proceeding to evict a sick industrial company from rented premises is not a proceeding for execution, distress, or a like process against the company’s property.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction of the industrial company for default in payment of rent.
The company was occupying the premises as a statutory tenant under rent-control protection.
At the time the eviction order was made, proceedings concerning the company were pending before the statutory body.
members.legal_principle: Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 suspends specified proceedings, including proceedings for execution, distress, or the like against the company’s property, when a qualifying matter is pending or a sanctioned scheme is being implemented, unless the relevant authority consents. The words “or the like” are read with “execution” and “distress” and concern processes for recovering dues against property. The Act’s purpose is to protect the consideration and implementation of measures for sick companies, not to allow a tenant company to incur further rent liabilities while requiring the landlord to keep providing premises.
members.conclusion: Section 22(1) did not automatically suspend the landlord’s eviction proceeding, and the eviction order was not passed in contravention of that provision.

rule.if: landlord_eviction_proceeding and sick_industrial_company_tenant and eviction_seeks_possession_not_recovery_by_execution and qualifying_statutory_matter_pending

predicates.landlord_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding to obtain possession of premises from a tenant.
predicates.sick_industrial_company_tenant: The tenant in the eviction proceeding is a sick industrial company.
predicates.eviction_seeks_possession_not_recovery_b: The landlord seeks eviction and possession rather than recovery of dues through execution, distress, or a similar process against the company’s property.
predicates.qualifying_statutory_matter_pending: A qualifying inquiry, scheme-related matter, or appeal concerning the company is pending before the relevant statutory body, or a sanctioned scheme is being implemented.

members.legal_issue: The statutory suspension of proceedings concerning a sick industrial company does not bar a landlord’s proceeding to evict the company from leased premises.
material_facts: The tenant was declared a sick industrial company and proceedings concerning its rehabilitation were pending.
The landlords brought rent-control petitions seeking eviction from the leased premises.
members.legal_principle: Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 suspends specified proceedings, including proceedings for execution, distress, or similar recovery against company property, but does not encompass a landlord’s eviction proceeding. The Court relied on Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. v. Church of South India Trust Association, Gujarat Steel Tube Co. Ltd. v. Virchandbhai B. Shah, and Carona Ltd. v. Parvathy Swaminathan and Sons.
members.conclusion: The rehabilitation proceedings did not bar the eviction petitions.

predicates.landlord_eviction_proceeding_against_sic: A landlord brings a proceeding to evict a tenant company that is subject to proceedings concerning its financial rehabilitation.

members.legal_issue: Agreed rent is the fair-rent measure for municipal valuation while the tenancy law’s initial agreed-rent deeming window applies.
material_facts: The building had been constructed and let, but the assessing authority had not determined when it was first let.
The tenancy law’s proviso treated the rent agreed when the premises were first let as fair rent during an initial period.
The Court held that the first letting date had to be determined to establish whether that treatment applied.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 8(1)(d) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, deems the rent agreed when premises are first let to be fair rent during the specified initial period. Because municipal annual value is determined by reference to fair rent under Section 168 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, that deemed fair rent is the relevant measure during that window.
members.conclusion: If the initial agreed-rent deeming window applies, the agreed rent must be used as the fair-rent basis for annual value; the assessing authority must determine when the property was first let before making the fresh assessment.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns assessment of municipal property tax on a building or land.
predicates.initial_agreed_rent_window_applies: The premises were first let and the tenancy law treats the rent agreed at that first letting as fair rent for the period currently being assessed.

members.legal_issue: After the tenancy law’s initial agreed-rent deeming window ends, municipal annual value is based on the fair rent calculated under its cost-based measure.
material_facts: The tenancy law provided a cost-based method for calculating fair rent for premises constructed and let after that law commenced.
The Court held that after the initial agreed-rent treatment ceased to apply, annual value had to be determined under that cost-based method.
The date of first letting was unknown, so the assessing authority had to establish whether the initial window had ended.
members.legal_principle: Section 8(1)(d) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, provides a cost-based formula for fair rent for qualifying premises, including the cost of construction, the land’s market price at commencement of construction, and a share of municipal rates and taxes. Read with Section 168 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, that fair rent is the basis for annual value after the proviso’s agreed-rent treatment ceases to apply.
members.conclusion: Once the initial agreed-rent deeming window has ended, the annual value must be determined using the cost-based fair-rent measure in the tenancy law.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns assessment of municipal property tax on a building or land.
predicates.rent_control_law_applies: The property is subject to a rent-control regime that provides a method for determining fair rent.
predicates.initial_agreed_rent_window_has_ended: The period during which the rent agreed at first letting is treated as fair rent has ended.

members.legal_issue: The rent-control law governing a municipal valuation is the law in force during the period for which the assessment is made.
material_facts: The municipal revision was made in 1960, after a new rent-control Act had come into force.
The lower courts relied on rent-control Acts that had been in force before the new Act.

The Court held that the fair rent for an earlier assessment period must be determined under the rent-control law then in force, and that the law in force during a later assessment period governs that period.
The assessment books were ordinarily revised every five years, but the applicable rules provided a procedure for changing an assessment when a case for change was made out.
members.legal_principle: Section 82(2) of the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, requires valuation by reference to the rent lawfully obtainable, and the applicable fair-rent measure is supplied by the rent-control law in force during the assessment period. Although the Fourth Schedule rules provided for quinquennial revision of assessment books, they also provided a procedure for changing assessments when warranted. The Court relied on the principle in Corporation of Calcutta v. Sm. Padma Debi & Ors. [1962] 3 S.C.R. 49.
members.conclusion: A municipal valuation must be determined in accordance with the rent-control law in force during the period of assessment.

predicates.municipal_tax_assessment: A municipality is determining the taxable annual value of premises.
predicates.assessment_period_has_rent_control_law: A rent-control law governs the period for which the municipal valuation is being assessed.

members.legal_issue: The absence of compensation for some properties within an acquired estate does not establish a violation of the compensation requirement where compensation is provided for the estate as a whole.
material_facts: The appellants contended that some properties included in an inam received no compensation.
The applicable law provided for compensation to be determined for each inam as a whole, and that provision was not challenged.
The Court proceeded on the assumption that some properties received no separate compensation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects qualifying estate acquisitions from a challenge under Article 31(2). The law provided for compensation to be determined for the inam as a whole rather than separately for each interest.
members.conclusion: The contention did not establish a violation of Article 31(2), because compensation was provided for the inam as a whole and Article 31A barred the challenge.

predicates.estate_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a challenge to the acquisition of an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.compensation_provided_for_estate_as_a_wh: The acquisition scheme provides compensation determined for the estate as a whole.
predicates.no_separate_compensation_for_some_proper: Some property or interests within the estate receive no separate compensation.

members.legal_issue: A compensation scheme for acquisition of an entire estate is not illusory merely because it values compensation by reference to net income and provides no separate payment for non-income-producing components.
material_facts: The law acquired estates as a whole, including income-producing and non-income-producing property.
It calculated compensation by reference to the estate's net assets and made compensation payable to each intermediary.
Compensation became due upon vesting, and the amount was determined by an assessment officer subject to appeal.
The law allowed payment in cash, bonds, or a combination, with the method to be prescribed by the Government.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied article 31(2) and the legislative entries concerning acquisition and compensation, while holding that article 31(4) answered challenges to the adequacy of compensation in these appeals. It distinguished acquisition of an entire estate, valued on net income, from acquisition of separate pieces of property. The statutory provisions made payment obligatory, and the compensation amount was determined by an officer with an appeal available.
members.conclusion: The compensation provisions were not illusory or invalid merely because they did not provide an equivalent market value or separately compensate non-income-producing property; compensation was legally due. Rules prescribing an unreasonably remote time for payment could separately be challenged as an abuse of power.

rule.if: challenge_to_compensation_for_estate_acquisition and entire_estate_acquired and compensation_legally_due and compensation_amount_assessed_with_appeal

predicates.challenge_to_compensation_for_estate_acq: A party challenges the compensation provided for acquisition of an estate.
predicates.entire_estate_acquired: The acquisition covers the estate as a whole rather than separate, selected pieces of property.
predicates.compensation_legally_due: The law makes payment of compensation obligatory upon acquisition.
predicates.compensation_amount_assessed_with_appeal: An official determines the compensation amount and the affected person can appeal that determination.

members.legal_issue: When the State acquires an entire estate and compensation is calculated by reference to its net income, the absence of separate compensation for non-income-producing parts does not by itself make the acquisition confiscatory.
material_facts: The Act acquired estates as wholes, including both income-producing and non-income-producing property.
Compensation was calculated by reference to the net income of the estate as a whole.
The appellants argued that particular non-income-producing property, including waste land, received no separate compensation.
members.legal_principle: Where an entire estate is acquired and compensation is based on the net income of that estate, the estate’s non-income-producing components may be considered as part of the whole; the absence of separate compensation for those components does not alone make the legislation confiscatory. The Court contrasted this with a case in which separate pieces of property, rather than the estate as a whole, were acquired.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was not confiscatory merely because non-income-producing properties within the estates received no separate compensation.

predicates.entire_estate_is_acquired: The State acquires the estate as a whole rather than selecting individual pieces of it.
predicates.compensation_is_based_on_estate_wide_net: The compensation calculation uses the net income of the estate as a whole.
predicates.some_estate_property_produces_no_income: Some property within the acquired estate does not itself produce income.

members.legal_issue: A person who receives only part of a deceased person’s estate under a will may be a legal representative of the deceased’s estate.
material_facts: Several persons were joined in the earlier suits as legal representatives because they held different parts of the deceased’s property under a settlement deed and a registered will.
The persons holding property under the will argued that receiving only part of the estate did not make them legal representatives.
The court concluded that the estate need not be represented by a single person holding the whole estate.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(11) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines a legal representative to include a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person and a person who intermeddles with the estate. The definition includes legatees of separate portions of an estate, just as it includes persons who intermeddle with part of the estate. The court relied on the reasoning in Dinamoni Chaudhurani v. Elahandut Khan and disapproved the contrary observation in Natesa Sastrigal v. Alamelu Achi.
members.conclusion: Legatees who receive separate portions of a deceased person’s estate under a will are included among legal representatives; the estate need not mean the whole estate.

predicates.estate_claim_against_successors: A claim concerning a deceased person’s estate is brought against persons said to represent that estate.
predicates.persons_received_separate_estate_portion: Different persons received separate portions of the deceased person’s estate under a will.

members.legal_issue: A person who represents a deceased party’s estate may qualify as a legal representative even if that person is not the head or administrator of the family.
material_facts: The defendant died while a recovery suit was pending.
Under the inheritance law applicable to the estate, the defendant’s widow held a share in it, while the remaining share devolved on the defendant’s children.
The widow was proposed as a substitute for the deceased defendant, although she was not the head of the family or administrator of the other heirs.
members.legal_principle: The Civil Procedure Code’s definition of “legal representative” in Section 2(11) is inclusive and broad: it covers a person who represents the deceased’s estate, whether or not that person is an heir, and may include an heir who represents the estate. The Court relied on Daya Ram v. Shyam Sundari, [1965] 1 SCR 231, and N.K. Mohd. Sulaiman v. N.C. Mohd. Ismail, [1966] 1 SCR 937.
members.conclusion: The widow qualified as a legal representative because her share in the estate meant that she represented the deceased defendant’s estate.

predicates.pending_civil_suit_when_party_died: A party died while a civil suit against that party was pending.
predicates.proposed_representative_had_a_share_in_t: The person proposed to represent the deceased party held a share in the deceased party’s estate.

members.legal_issue: A legatee who intends to represent a deceased person's estate may qualify as that person's legal representative by intermeddling with the estate.
material_facts: The deceased's nieces and nephews claimed that she had bequeathed the suit property to them and sought to come on record to represent her estate.
The competing claimants disputed whether the nieces and nephews or the deceased's husband should represent the estate.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(11) of the Code of Civil Procedure includes within the definition of legal representative a person who intermeddles with the deceased's estate. A legatee intending to represent the testator's estate falls within that definition.
members.conclusion: A legatee who intends to represent the deceased testator's estate is an intermeddler and may be a legal representative, subject to the court determining the representation question.

predicates.deceased_party_in_pending_case: A party to a pending case has died and the estate requires representation.
predicates.legatee_intends_to_represent_estate: A person claiming a legacy intends to represent the deceased person's estate in the pending case.

members.legal_issue: A general delegated legislative measure withdrawing an exemption does not require an individual hearing or reasons unless the governing law requires them.
material_facts: The exemption was withdrawn by a notification made under delegated statutory authority.
The statute contained no requirement to provide an affected person a hearing or to record reasons before withdrawing the exemption.
members.legal_principle: Delegated legislation is legislative in character. In the absence of a statutory requirement, the principles of natural justice do not require a hearing before such legislation is made, and the legislature or its delegate need not give reasons while discharging a legislative function. The court relied on State of Punjab v. Tehal Singh; West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission v. CESC Ltd.; Pune Municipal Corporation v. Promoters and Builders Association; and Bihar State Electricity Board v. Pulak Enterprises.
members.conclusion: A hearing and recorded reasons were not preconditions to withdrawing the exemption by notification.

predicates.challenge_to_general_legislative_measure: An affected person challenges a general measure made through legislative or delegated legislative authority.
predicates.measure_withdraws_exemption: The measure withdraws an exemption previously available under the statutory scheme.
predicates.no_hearing_or_reasons_requirement: The governing law does not require an individual hearing or recorded reasons before the measure is made.

members.legal_issue: A government exercising delegated legislative power is not required to provide an individual hearing unless the governing law expressly requires one.
material_facts: The government published a draft proposal to merge several municipal areas into a corporation and received objections and representations.
The government considered the representations and ultimately excluded one municipal area from the corporation.
One federation received a personal hearing following an assurance given in earlier proceedings, but other objectors did not receive personal hearings.
The High Court directed the government to provide affected parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard before making a further decision.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, the government’s formation of a corporation is legislative or conditional legislative action. Natural justice does not imply a hearing requirement for plenary or subordinate legislative action unless a hearing is expressly prescribed. The Court relied on Tulsipur Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Notified Area Committee, Tulsipur, Baldev Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh, and the legislative-action reasoning in Bates v. Lord Hailsham of St. Marylebone.
members.conclusion: The government’s decision under the municipal corporation legislation was legislative in character, and natural justice did not require it to hear the objectors. The High Court erred in directing that hearings be provided.

predicates.appeal_from_order_directing_hearing: A party appealed an order made in a judicial review proceeding that directed the government to hear affected objectors.
predicates.challenged_action_is_legislative: The government made a general area-formation decision through delegated lawmaking power.
predicates.hearing_not_expressly_required: The governing law provided a process for publishing a proposal and considering objections but did not expressly require an individual hearing.

members.legal_issue: A public hearing is not required before final government sanction of delegated planning legislation when the governing enactment does not provide for one.
material_facts: The planning authority invited objections and suggestions and gave affected persons an opportunity to be heard before submitting the proposed modification.
The enactment provided for government inquiry as the government considered necessary but did not prescribe a hearing before final sanction.
The challenge asserted that affected persons had to be heard again before the government sanctioned the modification.
members.legal_principle: Delegated legislation is not invalid for failure to comply with natural justice in its making unless the statute requires notice or a hearing. An enabling provision allowing the subordinate legislative body to make such inquiry as it considers necessary facilitates obtaining information and does not itself create a hearing right. The Court relied on Union of India v. Cynamide India Ltd., HSSK Niyami v. Union of India, and Canara Bank v. Debasis Das.
members.conclusion: The enactment did not require a hearing before final sanction, and natural justice could not be read into this legislative process to create such a requirement.

predicates.delegated_rulemaking_challenge: A party challenged the making of delegated legislation.
predicates.enactment_silent_on_hearing_at_final_san: The governing enactment did not require notice or a hearing before the final sanction of the delegated legislation.
predicates.hearing_not_required_at_final_sanction: A hearing is not required before final sanction.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who discovers facts suggesting that the original permission for a limited-term tenancy was vitiated should seek adjudication promptly during the tenancy, although a plea raised at the possession stage may be considered.
material_facts: The tenant alleged that the landlord had suppressed an earlier unsuccessful application for permission and that the later permission was therefore procured by fraud.
The tenant did not approach the Rent Controller during the three-year tenancy to have the alleged fraud adjudicated, despite the asserted facts relating to the grant of permission.

The tenant raised the fraud plea after the landlord applied for possession and the warrant had been executed; the High Court remanded the matter for the Rent Controller to consider the tenant’s objections, and the Supreme Court did not disturb that remand.
members.legal_principle: Section 21’s special procedure requires prompt recourse where facts suggest that permission was obtained through fraud or collusion, or granted mechanically. S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna recognizes that such pleas may be considered when raised at the possession stage and that the initial permission is presumed regular; it does not require the Controller to issue notice inviting such pleas in every case. The tenant should seek adjudication when the relevant facts are discovered, rather than wait until the landlord applies for possession after the fixed term.
members.conclusion: A tenant should approach the Rent Controller during the limited tenancy as soon as facts tending to vitiate the original permission are discovered. If the tenant independently raises a plea of fraud or collusion when possession is sought, the Controller may inquire into it, but the tenant risks having a delayed plea rejected as an afterthought.

predicates.limited_term_tenancy_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a tenancy authorized for a limited fixed term.
predicates.tenant_discovers_facts_tending_to_invali: During the tenancy, the tenant learns facts that may show that permission for the tenancy was obtained or granted improperly.

members.legal_issue: A tenant cannot ordinarily challenge the validity of a limited-tenancy permission collaterally after the limited tenancy has expired, but must promptly seek adjudication of the alleged defect during the tenancy.
material_facts: The tenant admitted that the earlier limited tenancy commenced on the date that meant it had expired before the application for the later permission was made.

The tenant challenged the later permission on grounds including that the premises were not vacant and that the landlord had misrepresented the intended use, but did not seek adjudication of those grounds during the later limited tenancy.
The tenant raised the challenge in objections to execution after the limited tenancy had expired, and the Court found no exceptional circumstance justifying that delay.
The Court also found that both landlord and tenant were present before the Rent Controller when the later permission was granted and that there was no factual concealment by the landlord.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a tenant who discovers facts said to vitiate permission must approach the Rent Controller for adjudication during the currency of the limited tenancy, as soon as the facts are discovered or could be discovered with due diligence. The permission is presumed valid until set aside, and a collateral challenge after expiry is ordinarily unavailable. The Court relied on J.R. Vohra v. Indian Export House Pvt. Ltd., Pankaj Bhargava v. Mohinder Nath, and Shrisht Dhawan v. M/s. Shaw Brothers; the latter recognizes that a post-expiry objection may be permitted in exceptional circumstances, which were not shown here.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to challenge the permission on these grounds after expiry of the limited tenancy; the objections were rejected, the appeal was dismissed, and possession was to be delivered to the landlord.

rule.if: limited_tenancy_permission_challenge_case and tenancy_expired and challenge_ground_known_during_tenancy and challenge_not_brought_promptly and not exceptional_circumstances

predicates.limited_tenancy_permission_challenge_cas: The proceeding concerns a tenant's challenge to permission for a tenancy fixed for a limited period.
predicates.tenancy_expired: The fixed period of the tenancy has ended before the tenant seeks adjudication of the challenge.
predicates.challenge_ground_known_during_tenancy: The tenant knew, or could with due diligence have discovered, the facts said to invalidate the permission while the tenancy was still running.
predicates.challenge_not_brought_promptly: The tenant did not promptly ask the Rent Controller to adjudicate the alleged defect during the tenancy.
predicates.exceptional_circumstances: Circumstances exist that exceptionally justify allowing the tenant to challenge the permission after the tenancy has expired.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s challenge to the validity of a limited tenancy must ordinarily be raised before the tenancy expires and cannot be raised as a defence to a later application for possession, except in a narrowly limited case where the tenant establishes that there was no earlier opportunity to learn the relevant facts and learned them only later.
material_facts: The landlord and tenant appeared before the Rent Controller, who approved a residential limited tenancy for a fixed two-year term after recording their statements.
The tenant remained in the premises after the term expired, and the landlord then applied for possession.
The tenant first objected to the validity of the limited tenancy in response to the post-expiry application for possession.
The tenant did not establish that he had no opportunity to learn the relevant facts before the tenancy expired or that he learned them only afterward.
members.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a challenge to the validity of a limited tenancy should be brought during the tenancy, when the tenant becomes aware, or with diligence could become aware, of facts supporting the challenge. The exception is confined to an exceptional case in which the tenant satisfies the Controller that there was no opportunity to know the facts earlier and that awareness arose only later. Section 21 provides a limited-tenancy procedure distinct from the ordinary protection against eviction under section 14. The Court confined S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna, [1980] 1 SCR 281, to its facts and relied on J.R. Vohra v. India Export House Pvt. Ltd., [1985] 2 SCR 899, Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna, [1987] 4 SCC 1, and Shiv Chander Kapoor v. Amar Bose, JT 1989 (4) SC 471; it treated suggestions in Vohra and Shiv Chander Kapoor that a post-expiry objection might be examined as obiter, subject to the narrow exception.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s belated objection should not have been entertained, and the landlord’s application for possession should have been granted.

predicates.limited_tenancy_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a tenancy created for a fixed limited term under a special procedure that provides for possession at the end of the term.
predicates.tenant_challenged_validity_after_expiry: The tenant first challenged the validity of the limited tenancy after its term had expired, in response to an application for possession.
predicates.tenant_had_earlier_opportunity_to_learn_: The tenant had an opportunity to learn the facts supporting the challenge before the term expired, rather than establishing that those facts became knowable only afterward.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for damage caused by overhead electrical lines must be determined on the circumstances of each property rather than by a fixed formula or rate of return.
material_facts: Trees were cut and removed to draw an overhead high-voltage electrical line across private property.
The compensation assessments had used differing approaches, including annuity calculations based on different rates of return and different percentages of diminution in land value.

The relevant circumstances could include the land’s location and value, the line’s distance above and extent across the land, whether it passed over a small strip or through the middle of the property, and any loss of the owner’s ability to use the land for its intended purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(d) and 16(3) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, compensation for damage from exercising the power to place a line is determined by the District Judge if disputed. Section 51 of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 permits the relevant powers of the telegraph authority to be conferred for placing electrical lines. The Court held that the statutory purpose and the circumstances of the individual case guide compensation; the approaches in Kerala Electricity Board v. Thomas, K.S.E. Board v. Marthoma Rubber Co. Ltd., and Kumba Amma v. K.S.E.B. may assist but do not establish a universal formula. The Court also referred to Land Acquisition Officer v. Kamandana Ramakrishna Rao, Kapur Singh Mistry v. Financial Commission, State of Haryana v. Gurcharan Singh, and Airports Authority of India v. Satyagopal Roy in recognizing yield as a relevant compensation method.
members.conclusion: The amount of compensation could not be determined by a fixed formula or rate applicable to every case. The assessments had to be reconsidered on the merits of each case, having regard to its particular facts.

rule.if: compensation_appeal_for_overhead_line and private_property_is_crossed_by_line and (property_value_or_use_is_affected or trees_are_removed)

predicates.compensation_appeal_for_overhead_line: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for an overhead electrical line.
predicates.private_property_is_crossed_by_line: An overhead line is placed across or over property belonging to a private owner.
predicates.property_value_or_use_is_affected: The line’s placement diminishes the property’s value or impairs its intended use.
predicates.trees_are_removed: Trees on the property are cut or removed for the line.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for consumer loss or injury cannot be awarded at a uniform interest rate without assessment of the circumstances of each case.
material_facts: The National Commission had repeatedly awarded or affirmed interest at 18% per annum in varied cases without examining their individual facts.
The cases involved different forms and degrees of delay, cancellation, refusal or delivery of possession, construction defects, additional demands, and refund claims.
Some awards had been increased to 18% even though only the authority had appealed and the lower forum had awarded a lower rate.
members.legal_principle: Under the Consumer Protection Act, compensation is recompense for loss or injury and must correlate with the loss or injury established. The Court relied on Bihar State Housing Board v. Prio Ranjan Roy, which requires an indication of the basis for damages and the relationship between the award and the default, delay, or harassment, and Prashant Kumar Shahi v. Ghaziabad Development Authority, which requires consideration of who was responsible for the alleged delay. The Court also distinguished the fact-specific awards in Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Dhanesh Chand Goel and Haryana Urban Development Authority v. Rajnish Chander Sharde from a general rule requiring 18% interest in every case.
members.conclusion: A uniform award of interest at 18% per annum as compensation is unsustainable; compensation must be assessed according to the loss or injury shown in each case.

predicates.consumer_compensation_proceeding: A consumer proceeding seeks an award for loss or injury caused by a service failure or public-authority conduct.
predicates.compensation_loss_varies_by_case: The nature or extent of the consumer’s loss or injury differs according to the circumstances of the case.
predicates.uniform_interest_rate_used_without_indiv: The forum applies the same interest rate without assessing the particular loss, injury, or responsibility shown in the case.

members.legal_issue: Consumer forums cannot award a fixed rate of interest irrespective of the circumstances and loss or injury in each case.
material_facts: The National Commission increased the interest award to 18% per annum.
The record containing the complaint and supporting evidence was not before the Supreme Court.
The Court found that a fixed 18% rate could not be sustained without regard to the facts of each case.
members.legal_principle: Under Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh, a consumer forum must determine whether there was deficiency in service or misfeasance in public office and whether it caused loss or injury. Compensation for mental agony or harassment is recompense for loss or injury and must be based on, and correlated with, that loss or injury; a uniform interest rate cannot be imposed irrespective of the facts.
members.conclusion: The National Commission's blanket award of 18% interest could not be sustained; compensation must be assessed in light of the circumstances and the loss or injury established.

predicates.consumer_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an award of compensation by a consumer forum or commission.
predicates.fixed_interest_rate_awarded_without_case: A consumer forum or commission awarded a fixed interest rate without assessing the circumstances and loss or injury in the individual case.

members.legal_issue: Failure to lay a published notification before the legislature does not invalidate it when the laying requirement does not make prior legislative approval a condition of its effectiveness.
material_facts: The State Government issued and published a notification withdrawing the exemption.
The notification had not initially been laid before the State Legislature.
The laying provision allowed the Houses to modify or annul a notification after it was laid, and the Court directed that it be placed before both Houses.
members.legal_principle: The effect of a laying clause depends on its wording and the degree of legislative control it establishes. In Jan Mohammad Noor Mohammad Bagban v. State of Gujarat, failure to lay rules did not invalidate them. Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana held that non-compliance with a laying clause did not invalidate an order. Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar held that an omission to lay a notification did not affect its validity and could be addressed by later placement before the legislature.
members.conclusion: The failure to lay the notification did not invalidate it or the action taken under it, and the defect was curable.

predicates.notification_validity_challenge: A person challenges a notification on the ground that it was not placed before the legislature.
predicates.notification_was_published: The executive published the notification in the official gazette.
predicates.laying_clause_allows_later_legislative_m: The laying procedure permits the legislature to modify or annul the notification after it has been placed before it.

members.legal_issue: A requirement that an exemption order be laid before the legislature, where the requirement provides for simple laying, is not mandatory and non-laying alone does not invalidate the order.
material_facts: The statute required exemption orders to be laid before the Legislative Assembly for a specified period.
The legislature could modify or annul an order laid before it.
The challenge included the failure to lay the relevant order before the Assembly.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the requirement as simple laying, without a further procedure making the order dependent on legislative approval. It followed M/s. Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana and noted the consistent approach in D.K. Krishnan v. Secretary, Regional Transport Authority, Chittoor.
members.conclusion: Non-laying did not by itself make an exemption order ineffective or unenforceable.

predicates.statutory_exemption_order_dispute: The proceeding concerns the validity or enforceability of an order made under a statutory exemption power.
predicates.simple_laying_requirement: The law requires the order to be placed before the legislature but does not make its operation dependent on an affirmative approval procedure.
predicates.order_not_laid: The order was not placed before the legislature as required.

members.legal_issue: Failure to place a State notification before the State Legislature as required does not invalidate the notification when the placement requirement is directory.
material_facts: One of the challenged notifications was required to be placed before the State Legislature.
The notification had been referred to in departmental administrative reports, but the Court found that it had not actually been placed before the Legislature as required.
The governing provision required placement but did not make the notification subject to legislative approval or modification.
members.legal_principle: Section 28(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, requires State rules and notifications to be laid before the State Legislature. Unlike Section 28(1), it does not provide for legislative approval or modification. The Court held that placement nevertheless operates as a check on the State and is not futile, but that the requirement is directory, so non-placement does not invalidate the notification. It relied on Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana, which treated a comparable laying requirement as directory.
members.conclusion: The omission to place the notification did not invalidate it; the State was directed to place it before the Legislature at the earliest and to comply with the requirement in future.

predicates.validity_challenge_to_state_delegated_no: The proceeding challenges the validity of a notification made by the State under delegated authority.
predicates.notification_was_not_formally_placed_bef: The State did not formally place the notification before the Legislature as required.
predicates.placement_requirement_is_directory: The requirement to place the notification before the Legislature does not make legislative approval a condition of the notification’s validity.

members.legal_issue: A co-owner may invoke the statutory pre-emption remedy against a stranger transferee of an undivided share in a family dwelling house during execution of a partition decree, until the decree is fully executed and satisfied.
material_facts: The property was found to be a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family.
A co-owner obtained a final partition decree for an undivided share and later gifted that share to a person who was not a member of the family.
The transferee sought execution of the decree, but the property had not yet been divided by metes and bounds or delivered into the respective shareholders’ possession.
A remaining family shareholder applied to buy the transferee’s share before execution was complete.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893, read with Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, protects members of an undivided family from a stranger’s entry into their common dwelling house by permitting a family shareholder to buy the stranger’s share. The words “sues for partition” are not limited to filing an original partition suit and include a transferee’s pursuit of execution of a partition decree. The court relied on CPC Section 38, Explanation VII to Section 11, Order 22 Rules 10 and 12, Order 21 Rule 16, and the explanation to TPA Section 52 in recognizing that litigation may extend through execution until full satisfaction. It approved Harendra Nath Mukharjee v. Shyam Sunder Kuer, Satya Narayan Chakravarty v. Biswanath Paul, and Boto Krishna Ghose v. Akhoy Kumar Ghose, and rejected the contrary view in Abdul Sathar v. Al Nawab. It applied a beneficial construction consistent with the provision’s purpose of preserving the peaceful enjoyment of a family dwelling house.
members.conclusion: The application was maintainable: seeking execution of the partition decree to obtain separation and possession of the transferred share amounted to suing for partition. The right could be invoked while execution remained incomplete, but not after the decree had been fully satisfied by division and delivery of possession.

rule.if: partition_decree_execution and undivided_family_dwelling and share_transferred_to_outsider and outsider_seeks_partition and family_shareholder_undertakes_purchase and not decree_fully_satisfied

predicates.partition_decree_execution: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a decree ordering partition of property.
predicates.undivided_family_dwelling: The property is a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family.
predicates.share_transferred_to_outsider: A shareholder transferred an undivided share in the dwelling house to a person outside the family.
predicates.outsider_seeks_partition: The outsider seeks separation and possession of the transferred share, including by pursuing execution of a partition decree.
predicates.family_shareholder_undertakes_purchase: A shareholder who is a member of the family undertakes to buy the outsider’s share.
predicates.decree_fully_satisfied: The partition decree has been fully carried out by division of the property and delivery of the shareholders’ respective portions.

members.legal_issue: The statutory pre-emption remedy for a stranger’s share in a family dwelling house ends once the partition decree has been fully executed and the respective shareholders have received possession of their separated portions.
material_facts: The court distinguished the pending execution in this case from a situation in which a partition decree has been fully executed.

It explained that after division by metes and bounds and delivery of possession, the common dwelling house ceases to belong to an undivided family for purposes of the stranger transferee’s separated portion.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893, read with Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, applies while the property remains a common dwelling house belonging to an undivided family and the partition litigation remains unfinished. Once execution fully separates the portions and puts the shareholders in possession, the common dwelling-house character relevant to the remedy ends, the litigation reaches its terminus, and there is no remaining subject matter on which the remedy can operate.
members.conclusion: After the partition decree has been fully executed and satisfied by division and delivery of possession, the statutory pre-emption remedy is no longer available against a later transfer of the stranger’s separated portion.

rule.if: partition_decree_execution and undivided_family_dwelling and share_transferred_to_outsider and outsider_seeks_partition and family_shareholder_undertakes_purchase and decree_fully_satisfied

predicates.partition_decree_execution: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a decree ordering partition of property.
predicates.undivided_family_dwelling: The property is a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family.
predicates.share_transferred_to_outsider: A shareholder transferred an undivided share in the dwelling house to a person outside the family.
predicates.outsider_seeks_partition: The outsider seeks separation and possession of the transferred share, including by pursuing execution of a partition decree.
predicates.family_shareholder_undertakes_purchase: A shareholder who is a member of the family undertakes to buy the outsider’s share.
predicates.decree_fully_satisfied: The partition decree has been fully carried out by division of the property and delivery of the shareholders’ respective portions.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer may exercise the statutory right to purchase a stranger’s share in an undivided family dwelling house only when the stranger seeks actual partition and separation and possession of that share.
material_facts: The transferee acquired a share in the dwelling house and was a party to the partition suit.
In the written statements and evidence, the transferee asserted his share but did not ask for partition or demand separation and possession of it.
The other co-sharers sought to purchase the transferee’s share under Section 4 of the Partition Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Partition Act applies where a share in a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family is transferred to a non-member and the transferee sues for partition. Under Ghantesher Ghosh v. Madan Mohan Ghosh, the statutory conditions must be met, and the right may arise at any stage, including execution, if the transferee seeks separation and possession. A mere assertion of a share is not a demand for partition. Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act protects the family from an outsider’s joint possession, while Section 4 provides the purchase right only when its conditions are fulfilled. The Court agreed with Babu Lal v. Hablnoor Khan that a view allowing pre-emption without the stranger seeking partition conflicts with Ghantesher Ghosh.
members.conclusion: Because the transferee had not sought partition or separation and possession of his share, the co-sharers’ application to purchase it was premature and had to be dismissed. The co-sharers could apply under Section 4 if the transferee later sought partition and separation and possession.

rule.if: partition_suit and undivided_family_dwelling_house and outsider_transferee and co_sharer_offers_to_purchase and not transferee_seeks_separation_and_possession

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit for partition of property that includes a dwelling house.
predicates.undivided_family_dwelling_house: The dwelling house belongs to an undivided family.
predicates.outsider_transferee: A person who is not a member of the owning family has acquired a share in the dwelling house.
predicates.co_sharer_offers_to_purchase: A family co-sharer undertakes to purchase the outsider’s share.
predicates.transferee_seeks_separation_and_possessi: The transferee asks, in the suit or in execution proceedings, for actual division and separation and possession of the transferee’s share.

members.legal_issue: A registered sale deed transfers title when its terms show an absolute sale and do not make transfer conditional on payment or performance of a further obligation.
material_facts: The sellers executed and registered a deed stating that they absolutely sold the property for the specified consideration and put the purchasers in possession.
The deed provided for part of the consideration to be applied to the mortgage debt, part to be set off against an amount owed to the purchasers, and the remainder to be paid to the sellers.
The High Court found that the purchasers paid the disputed cash amount, and the purchasers deposited the remaining balance in court.
The deed contained no term making transfer of title conditional on full payment, payment of the mortgage debt, or delivery of the registration receipt.
The sellers retained the registration receipt, but the court treated this as resulting from subsequent events rather than evidence of a condition on transfer.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 8 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, ownership and transferable interests pass on a registered sale unless a different intention is expressed or necessarily implied. The party asserting that title did not pass must establish that intention from the deed or, if it is ambiguous, from attending circumstances, subject to Section 92 of the Evidence Act. Panchoo Sahu v. Janki Mandar illustrates a deed expressly conditioning passage of title on payment; Hara Bewa v. Banchanidhi Barik illustrates resort to surrounding circumstances where the deed is ambiguous. The court also found the other cited decisions consistent with this approach.
members.conclusion: Title passed to the purchasers upon execution and registration of the sale deed.

rule.if: sale_title_dispute and registered_sale_deed and deed_expresses_absolute_sale and possession_delivered and no_title_condition_in_deed

predicates.sale_title_dispute: A proceeding concerns whether a purchaser acquired title to property under a sale.
predicates.registered_sale_deed: The seller executed and registered a deed of sale for the property.
predicates.deed_expresses_absolute_sale: The deed describes the transfer as an absolute sale rather than a conditional transfer.
predicates.possession_delivered: The seller put the purchaser in possession of the property.
predicates.no_title_condition_in_deed: The deed does not state that title will pass only after payment or performance of a further obligation.

members.legal_issue: A sale deed executed alongside an agreement to reconvey constitutes an outright sale rather than a nominal sale securing a loan when the deed and surrounding circumstances show an intention to transfer ownership absolutely.
material_facts: The property owner had borrowed money and had earlier mortgaged the property to the lenders.
On the same day, the owner executed a sale deed and an agreement to reconvey the property.
The sale deed recited an absolute transfer for consideration, stated that the owner and his heirs retained no right or interest, and provided for enjoyment and disposal by the purchasers.
The owner had already delivered possession and handed over property-related certificates, and the evidence did not contradict the sale deed’s terms.
The execution of the agreement to reconvey was established.
members.legal_principle: The true character of a transaction is determined from the document’s terms considered with the surrounding circumstances. Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, where the sale and the agreement concerning reconveyance are embodied in separate documents executed on the same day, the transaction cannot be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this issue.
members.conclusion: The sale deed was an outright sale, not a nominal deed or security for the loan; the established agreement to reconvey did not make the sale deed nominal.

rule.if: specific_performance_dispute and same_day_sale_and_reconveyance_documents and sale_deed_has_absolute_transfer_terms and surrounding_evidence_supports_absolute_transfer

predicates.specific_performance_dispute: The claimant sought enforcement of an agreement concerning reconveyance of property.
predicates.same_day_sale_and_reconveyance_documents: The parties executed a sale deed and a related agreement to reconvey the property on the same day.
predicates.sale_deed_has_absolute_transfer_terms: The sale deed described an absolute transfer of ownership and denied the transferor any continuing right or interest.
predicates.surrounding_evidence_supports_absolute_t: The surrounding circumstances and evidence supported the sale deed’s description of an absolute transfer.

members.legal_issue: A deed transferring specified property in exchange for rights in other property conveyed the specified property outright when its terms did not make the transfer temporary or conditional.
material_facts: A deed allocated specified land to a family branch in exchange for that branch’s share of income and property rights elsewhere.
The deed stated that the transferors had no inheritance claim over the allocated land.
Possession of part of the land was delayed because it was subject to a mortgage, but the deed did not say that the land would be returned when possession of the other property became available.
The defendants’ branch had possessed the disputed land as owners since the deed was made.
The plaintiff sought possession of the land, claiming it had been given only provisionally or for maintenance.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed the deed according to its plain terms.
