members.legal_issue: A belting system and a 50 percent deduction were inappropriate for partially developed land where the smallness of comparable sale plots could be addressed by a one-third deduction.
material_facts: The acquired land was acquired for residential and commercial development and was already developed to some extent.
The High Court used a belting system, awarding different values for land abutting a highway and the remainder.
The High Court imposed a 50 percent deduction, while the comparable sale plots were smaller than the acquired land.
The Court held that belting was improper and that a one-third deduction appropriately accounted for the smallness of the sale exhibits.
The Court used the comparative prices and an annual increase to assess compensation at Rs. 350 per square yard.
members.legal_principle: Market value is determined by considering comparable sales, the acquired land’s development and potential, and appropriate deductions for differences between sale plots and acquired land. The Court applied Sections 23(1-A), 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and relied on General Manager, Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Rameshbhai Jivanbhai Patel and Udho Dass v. State of Haryana on escalation and land-value considerations.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected belting and assessed compensation at Rs. 350 per square yard after applying a one-third deduction.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and acquired_land_is_partially_developed and comparable_plots_are_smaller and belting_does_not_reflect_land_value

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_is_partially_developed: The acquired land has already been developed to some extent.
predicates.comparable_plots_are_smaller: The sale plots used for comparison are smaller than the acquired land.
predicates.belting_does_not_reflect_land_value: Dividing the land into zones would not fairly reflect its value.

members.legal_issue: An estate agent authorised to negotiate a property sale and secure a buyer is not authorised to conclude a binding sale contract unless the principal’s instructions clearly confer that authority.
material_facts: The principal authorised an estate agent in writing to negotiate the sale of property and stated a minimum price, that the property would be free from encumbrances, and that good title would be made out.
The instructions did not specify important terms of the sale, including payment, investigation and approval of title, conveyance, and related costs.
The agent exchanged letters with prospective buyers purporting to conclude a sale contract, but the courts found that the agent lacked authority to bind the principal to that contract.
members.legal_principle: An estate agent’s authority to negotiate a sale or find a purchaser does not, without clear words, include authority to bind the owner to a sale contract. The court relied on Chadburn v. Moore (67 L.T. 257), Rosenbaum v. Belson ([1900] 2 Ch. 267), and Durga Charan Mitra v. Rajendra Narayan Sinha (36 C.L.J. 467), and distinguished authority to negotiate from authority to conclude a sale. The court also noted that the detailed terms ordinarily required for a transfer of real property support this distinction.
members.conclusion: The commission note did not authorise the agent to conclude a binding contract of sale on the principal’s behalf.

predicates.estate_sale_agency_case: The dispute concerns an agent engaged to arrange the sale of real property for a principal.
predicates.instructions_authorise_negotiation_or_bu: The principal instructed the agent to negotiate a sale or find a buyer.
predicates.instructions_clearly_authorise_binding_s: The principal expressly authorised the agent to conclude a binding sale contract on the principal’s behalf.
predicates.material_sale_terms_left_for_later_agree: Important terms of the property sale were not settled in the instructions and remained for later agreement between the principal and buyer.

members.legal_issue: General authority to manage a partnership’s affairs does not, without express authority, empower a partner to transfer immovable property belonging to the firm.
material_facts: The partnership deed stated that a named partner would manage the partnership’s affairs and that what he did would bind the partners.
The deed did not expressly authorise that partner to transfer the firm’s immovable property.
The builder relied on that clause to argue that the partner’s dealings with the property bound the other partners.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 19(1) of the Partnership Act, acts done by a partner in the usual way of the firm’s business bind the firm. Section 19(2)(g) provides that, absent a contrary usage or custom, that authority does not include transferring immovable property belonging to the firm; such authority must be expressly given.
members.conclusion: The management clause did not prima facie authorise the partner to transfer the partnership’s immovable property or bind the other partners to such a transfer.

rule.if: interlocutory_injunction_appeal and partner_received_general_management_authority and firm_property_was_immovable and deed_lacked_express_transfer_authority

predicates.interlocutory_injunction_appeal: The authority question arose in an appeal concerning temporary relief pending a suit.
predicates.partner_received_general_management_auth: The partnership deed gave a partner general authority to manage the firm’s affairs and made his acts binding on the partners.
predicates.firm_property_was_immovable: The property the partner purported to deal with belonged to the firm and was immovable property.
predicates.deed_lacked_express_transfer_authority: The partnership deed contained no express authority for the partner to transfer the firm’s immovable property.

members.legal_issue: An agent’s authority to sell immovable property cannot be inferred from a power of attorney that grants other powers but does not expressly authorize a sale.
material_facts: The property was jointly inherited by two sisters, and one sister gave the other a power of attorney.
The document expressly authorized leasing, borrowing and executing or registering related documents, but did not authorize the agent to sell the property.
The agent nevertheless executed transfers, and the purchasers later transferred the property to another purchaser.
members.legal_principle: A power of attorney is ordinarily construed strictly, and authority to sell must be expressly granted rather than inferred from powers to lease property or execute documents for borrowing or registration. The Court relied on Church of Christ Charitable Trust and Educational Charitable Society v. Ponniamman Educational Trust, which requires express authority to execute a sale deed, present it for registration and admit its execution; it also considered Delhi Development Authority v. Durga Chand Kaushish and Syed Abdul Khader v. Rami Reddy. Under the principle nemo dat quod non habet, a transferor cannot convey a title that the transferor does not possess.
members.conclusion: The agent had no authority to sell the property; the sale conveyed no valid title to the subsequent purchaser.

predicates.agent_executed_property_sale: An agent executed a sale of immovable property on behalf of a principal.
predicates.power_document_omitted_express_sale_auth: The document appointing the agent granted other powers but did not expressly authorize the agent to sell the property.

members.legal_issue: In an inquiry into whether a religious endowment is public, the authority asserting that status bears the burden of establishing it, and may discharge that burden with reliable evidence of dedication for public use or benefit.
material_facts: The charity authority initiated an inquiry into the status of the temples and asserted that they were public religious trusts.

The authority relied on evidence of construction with state funds, long and unobstructed public worship, public contributions and maintenance, and records identifying the deities as owners and the ruler as manager.
The Court found that this evidence was clear, consistent, reliable, and sufficient to establish dedication for public use and benefit.
members.legal_principle: The authority asserting the existence of a public endowment bears the burden of proving it. The burden may be discharged through evidence from which dedication can be inferred, including long and uninterrupted public use and the other circumstances relevant to the temple’s origin, management, funding, and worship. The Court considered whether the burden had been met in determining public-trust status under sections 2(17) and 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, applying the principles discussed in Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchhoddas Kalidas, and the other authorities cited in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The burden rested on the charity authority, and it discharged that burden with the evidence in the record.

predicates.public_endowment_inquiry: The proceeding concerned whether a religious endowment was public or private.
predicates.authority_asserted_public_status: The authority conducting or pursuing the inquiry asserted that the endowment was public.
predicates.reliable_evidence_of_public_dedication: The authority presented reliable evidence, such as public funding, public worship as of right, public contributions, or long unobstructed public use, indicating dedication for public benefit.

members.legal_issue: In an inquiry into whether a religious institution is a public trust, the burden of proving its public character rests on the party asserting that character.
material_facts: The proceeding arose from an application seeking a determination that the institution was private, after which the authorities found it to be a public trust.
No member of the public appeared or gave evidence that the public worshipped there as of right, and the evidence that visitors came with the family’s permission was unchallenged.

Although the Charity Commissioner initially recognized that the burden rested on the party asserting a public trust, the decision ultimately faulted the private claimant for not producing title documents.
members.legal_principle: In the proceeding under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, the Court treated the burden of proving the asserted public-trust character as resting on the party making that assertion. Sections 18 and 72 provide the procedural context for the application and reference in this case; the judgment identifies no separate statutory provision as the source of the burden rule.
members.conclusion: The Charity Commissioner wrongly shifted the burden of proof to the private claimant; the burden of establishing that a public trust existed lay on the party asserting that it did.

predicates.public_trust_status_inquiry: A proceeding requires a determination whether a religious institution is a public trust or private property.
predicates.public_trust_character_asserted: A party in the proceeding asserts that the institution is a public trust.

members.legal_issue: The party alleging that property held by a religious head is subject to a public religious or charitable trust bears the burden of proving that character, and the holder’s failure to produce unavailable founding grants does not by itself justify an adverse inference.
material_facts: The properties had been in the possession and management of successive religious heads since the founding head acquired them.
The founding grants were not produced because they could not be traced.
The party alleging a public trust did not attempt to obtain the relevant estate records, which could have contained copies of the grants.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(1) of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1951, the relevant statutory definition concerns public trusts and does not include private trusts, as held in Mahant Ramsaroop Das Ji v. S. P. Sahi, 1959 Supp. 2 S.C.R. 583. Where properties are in the religious head’s possession, the party asserting that they are held for public purposes must prove that assertion. Parmanand v. Nihal Chand, [1938] I.L.R. 65 I.A. 252, is relied on in addressing the burden and the unavailable grants.
members.conclusion: The burden of proving that the properties were held on trust for public religious or charitable purposes rested on the party alleging the trust. The trial court erred in drawing an adverse inference against the religious head merely because he did not produce the unavailable grants.

rule.if: public_trust_status_dispute and properties_possessed_by_religious_head and claimant_alleges_public_purpose and founding_grants_unavailable and claimant_did_not_seek_available_records

predicates.public_trust_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether property held by a religious institution or its head is subject to a public trust.
predicates.properties_possessed_by_religious_head: A religious head and predecessors in that office have possessed and managed the properties.
predicates.claimant_alleges_public_purpose: A claimant asserts that the properties are held for public religious or charitable purposes.
predicates.founding_grants_unavailable: The original instruments by which the founding religious head acquired the properties cannot be produced because they cannot be traced.
predicates.claimant_did_not_seek_available_records: The claimant did not attempt to obtain other records that might contain evidence of the founding grants.

members.legal_issue: Refusal to permit legal representation in a departmental inquiry does not invalidate the proceedings where the applicable rule makes permission discretionary and the employee has not shown that the refusal caused prejudice.
material_facts: The employee requested permission to engage a lawyer, and the disciplinary authority refused.
The presenting officer was a serving judicial officer, not a practicing lawyer, and the employee was himself a judicial officer with comparable professional qualifications.
The employee could have sought assistance from another government or judicial officer but did not do so.
The charge was not complicated, the employee participated in the inquiry without further protest, and he did not establish that the refusal prejudiced his defence.
members.legal_principle: Rule 14(8) of the Madhya Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1966 permits assistance from another government servant and permits engagement of a legal practitioner when the presenting officer is a legal practitioner or the disciplinary authority allows it in light of the circumstances. The word “may” confers discretion rather than an absolute right. A serving judge is not a “legal practitioner” within the meaning of section 2(i) of the Advocates Act, 1961. The court must consider the circumstances and whether refusal caused prejudice. The court applied Sarla Goel v. Kishan Chand and Malaysian Airlines Systems BHD (II) v. Stic Travels on construing “may”; Muddada Chayanna v. K. Narayana and Bhavnagar University v. Palitana Sugar Mills on contextual interpretation; and distinguished J.K. Aggarwal v. Haryana Seeds Development Corporation and Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay v. Dilipkumar Raghavendranath Nadkarni, where the presenting officers were legally trained or experienced and the circumstances supported a finding of unfairness.
members.conclusion: The refusal was a proper exercise of discretion and did not violate natural justice or invalidate the disciplinary proceedings.

rule.if: departmental_disciplinary_inquiry and legal_representation_requested and presenting_officer_is_serving_judge and employee_is_comparably_qualified and no_prejudice_from_refusal_shown

predicates.departmental_disciplinary_inquiry: An employer conducted a disciplinary inquiry into an employee's alleged misconduct.
predicates.legal_representation_requested: The employee asked to be represented by a lawyer in the inquiry.
predicates.presenting_officer_is_serving_judge: The person presenting the employer's case was a serving judicial officer rather than a practicing lawyer.
predicates.employee_is_comparably_qualified: The employee had professional qualifications and experience comparable to those of the presenting officer.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_refusal_shown: The employee did not establish that being refused a lawyer impaired the ability to defend against the charge.

members.legal_issue: A procedural defect in a disciplinary enquiry does not automatically invalidate the enquiry or punishment when the employee nevertheless receives a fair hearing and the defect causes no demonstrated prejudice.
material_facts: The governing service regulation required copies of earlier witness statements to be supplied at least three days before examination of witnesses; it separately gave the employee a right to inspect and take notes of listed documents.

Copies of the witness statements and other listed materials were not supplied, but the employee was allowed to inspect them and take notes more than three days before the relevant witnesses testified.
The complainant whose statement was not supplied did not testify at the regular enquiry; the Patwari whose statement was not supplied did testify.
The employee did not object during the enquiry that the absence of copies impaired cross-examination or his defence.
The lower appellate court asserted prejudice but did not identify a specific way in which the employee’s defence had been impaired.
members.legal_principle: For a disciplinary enquiry, a breach of a substantive requirement must ordinarily be treated differently from a breach of a procedural requirement. A procedural breach generally calls for examination of whether the employee was prejudiced and, considering the circumstances as a whole, received a fair hearing; substantial compliance may suffice. A breach falling within the categories of no notice, no opportunity, or no hearing, or a breach of a procedural requirement fundamental in nature, may not be assessed in the same way. For a mandatory procedural requirement designed for the employee’s benefit, waiver may also be relevant. The Court relied on Regulation 68(b)(i) and (iii) of the State Bank of Patiala (Officers’) Service Regulations, 1979; sections 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure and 465 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as illustrations of the approach to procedural error; and Ridge v. Baldwin, Vasudevan Pillai v. City Council of Singapore, Calvin v. Carr, Janakinath Sarangi v. State of Orissa, K.L. Tripathi v. State Bank of India, Managing Director, ECIL v. B. Karunakar, Dhirendra Nath Gorai v. Sudhir Chandra Ghosh, and Krishan Lal v. State of Jammu and Kashmir.
members.conclusion: The documents did not have to be supplied as copies under the regulation, and although the witness statements were not supplied as required, the employee had substantial access to them and no prejudice was established. The enquiry was fair, the punishment was not invalidated, and the suit challenging it was dismissed.

rule.if: disciplinary_enquiry and procedural_copy_requirement_applied and required_copies_not_supplied and materials_reviewed_before_relevant_testimony and employee_did_not_claim_defence_impairment_during_enquiry and no_specific_defence_impairment_identified

predicates.disciplinary_enquiry: An employer conducted a disciplinary enquiry into alleged employee misconduct.
predicates.procedural_copy_requirement_applied: The procedure governing the enquiry required copies of earlier witness statements to be provided to the employee before witness examination.
predicates.required_copies_not_supplied: The employer did not provide the required copies of the earlier witness statements to the employee.
predicates.materials_reviewed_before_relevant_testi: The employee was allowed to inspect the relevant materials and take notes before the witnesses testified.
predicates.employee_did_not_claim_defence_impairmen: The employee did not tell the enquiry that the absence of copies impaired the ability to cross-examine witnesses or present a defence.
predicates.no_specific_defence_impairment_identifie: The courts reviewing the enquiry did not identify a specific way in which the employee’s defence was impaired.

members.legal_issue: Refusing an employee legal representation does not deny a reasonable opportunity to defend where the governing rules do not provide for it and the enquiry presents no legal complexity requiring a lawyer.
material_facts: The employee requested the assistance of an advocate and the request was refused.
The enquiry concerned the employee’s own assessment records and explanations of apparent errors in them.
The case did not involve oral evidence requiring cross-examination or legal complexity requiring trained counsel.
The applicable rules did not entitle the employee to an advocate in the enquiry.
members.legal_principle: Natural justice requires a reasonable opportunity to defend, not invariably representation by an advocate. Whether representation is needed depends on the applicable rules and the nature and complexity of the enquiry.
members.conclusion: Refusal of legal representation did not deprive the employee of a reasonable opportunity to defend himself.

rule.if: disciplinary_enquiry_challenge and legal_representation_refused and rules_do_not_provide_advocate and (record_based_explanations_sufficient or no_material_legal_complexity)

predicates.disciplinary_enquiry_challenge: The proceeding challenges the fairness or validity of a disciplinary enquiry.
predicates.legal_representation_refused: The employee asked to be represented by an advocate and the request was refused.
predicates.rules_do_not_provide_advocate: The rules governing the enquiry did not entitle the employee to an advocate.
predicates.record_based_explanations_sufficient: The employee’s defence principally required explaining records and decisions that he had made.
predicates.no_material_legal_complexity: The enquiry involved no legal complexity or witness cross-examination that made trained legal assistance necessary.

members.legal_issue: A reasoned government policy adopted in the public interest to prevent private monopolisation may override a contractual right to participate in future port tenders without a separate legislative measure.
material_facts: The licence agreements granted operators rights to participate in future tenders, while other terms restricted bidding for additional facilities.

The government changed its policy to prevent concentration of control over port facilities and promote competition, including by excluding an existing operator from the immediately following tender while permitting participation in a later tender.
The policy was directed at risks to competition and the shipping industry, including the ability of operators to favour their own ships and affect access to port facilities.
The Court found no arbitrariness in the policy change and considered the larger public interest it served.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, courts ordinarily do not interfere with government policy unless it is arbitrary or constitutionally infirm. The government may change policy with changing circumstances, and a reasoned policy serving the general public interest may override private contractual rights. The change must be free from arbitrariness, irrationality, bias and malice and satisfy Wednesbury reasonableness. The Court relied on Shimnit Utsch India Private Ltd. v. West Bengal Transport Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. and the earlier P&O Ports litigation, in which exclusion of an existing operator to prevent monopolisation had been upheld.
members.conclusion: The policy was a valid exercise of government power and could prevail over contractual bid rights; a policy change for this purpose did not require legislation, provided it was reasoned and non-arbitrary.

rule.if: port_tender_eligibility_challenge and contract_grants_future_bid_right and policy_serves_public_interest and policy_has_reasoned_competition_basis and policy_is_non_arbitrary

predicates.port_tender_eligibility_challenge: An operator challenged its exclusion from a public tender for port facilities.
predicates.contract_grants_future_bid_right: The operator's contract granted it a right to participate in future tenders.
predicates.policy_serves_public_interest: The government adopted the policy to protect the public interest in the use and operation of port facilities.
predicates.policy_has_reasoned_competition_basis: The policy was based on promoting competition and preventing private concentration of control over port facilities.
predicates.policy_is_non_arbitrary: The Court found the policy change to be reasoned and not arbitrary.

members.legal_issue: A legitimate expectation based on a contractual right to bid does not prevent exclusion under a reasoned policy adopted in the public interest unless the government action amounts to an abuse of power.
material_facts: The operator relied on contractual clauses allowing it to participate in future tenders and on its prior participation in the tender process.
The government adopted a policy to prevent port facilities from being concentrated in the hands of a private group or consortium and to promote competition.
The Court found that the policy served the public interest and that the decision to exclude the operator was not arbitrary or unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: As explained in Sethi Auto Service Station v. Delhi Development Authority, legitimate expectation has no role where state action is based on public policy and public interest, unless the action amounts to an abuse of power. A change in policy may defeat a substantive legitimate expectation if the change is justified by Wednesbury reasonableness.
members.conclusion: The asserted legitimate expectation did not warrant interference with the exclusion decision, and the challenge to that decision was dismissed.

rule.if: public_tender_exclusion_challenge and claimant_relies_on_prior_bid_expectation and policy_serves_public_interest and policy_change_is_reasoned and no_abuse_of_power

predicates.public_tender_exclusion_challenge: An operator challenged its exclusion from a public tender.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_prior_bid_expectation: The operator relied on a contractual right or prior treatment as creating an expectation of being permitted to bid.
predicates.policy_serves_public_interest: The government based its tender policy on a public interest in preventing concentration of control and promoting competition.
predicates.policy_change_is_reasoned: The government supported the policy change with reasons that satisfy the applicable standard of reasonableness.
predicates.no_abuse_of_power: The Court found no abuse of power in the government's action.

members.legal_issue: A reasoned change in government policy made in the general public interest may prevail over inconsistent contractual terms between a public authority and private allottees.
material_facts: The allottees had received allotments and entered into long-term leases setting out the amounts payable for the land.

After landowners’ agitation stalled development, the allottees or their representatives approached the government or its authorities seeking a solution, and some expressed willingness to cooperate with a decision on compensation.

Following committee deliberations, the government adopted a policy requiring additional payments from allottees to help fund increased compensation for landowners, and the public authority issued additional demands.
The allottees challenged those demands on the ground that their contracts were concluded and could not be changed unilaterally.
members.legal_principle: A government policy change may override private treaties when it serves the general public interest and is guided by reason: APM Terminals B.V. v. Union of India. Promissory estoppel is equitable and cannot compel the government to maintain a representation where, in the circumstances, equity and the public good require otherwise: Kasinka Trading v. Union of India, following the principles in Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of U.P., Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India, and related decisions. The judgment also notes that, in a conflict between public and personal interests, public interest prevails, referring to ITC Ltd. v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The allottees’ contractual arrangements did not prevent implementation of the policy; the policy could prevail over inconsistent private contractual interests because it was reasoned and adopted in the general public interest.

rule.if: appeal_from_additional_public_demand and government_policy_changed_after_contract and policy_served_general_public_interest and policy_was_guided_by_reason

predicates.appeal_from_additional_public_demand: A party appealed a judgment concerning an additional public-authority demand challenged by private allottees.
predicates.government_policy_changed_after_contract: A government adopted a policy after private parties had entered into contracts with a public authority, and the policy imposed a requirement inconsistent with the parties’ contractual expectations.
predicates.policy_served_general_public_interest: The policy addressed a public problem affecting a broader group of people and supported the continuation of development.
predicates.policy_was_guided_by_reason: The policy followed consideration of relevant circumstances and stakeholder submissions through a deliberative process.

members.legal_issue: A Collector must defer redetermination while an appeal concerning the court award relied on for redetermination remains pending.
material_facts: Applications for redetermination were made while appeals challenging the enhanced original-court awards were pending.
An appellate court could affirm, vary, or set aside the award on which the applications relied.
The Collector made an award in one matter before the pending appeal had been decided.
members.legal_principle: An appeal is a continuation of the original proceeding, and the appellate decree is the executable decree. Deferring redetermination avoids inconsistent outcomes and unnecessary public expenditure. The Collector should obtain information or an affidavit concerning any appeal and proceed on the final appellate determination.
members.conclusion: The Collector must keep timely redetermination applications pending until the appeal is finally decided, and must then determine compensation by reference to the final judgment and decree.

predicates.is_redetermination_application_case: A person applied to have compensation for acquired land reconsidered on the basis of another owner’s court award.
predicates.appeal_pending_against_award_relied_on: An appeal challenging the court award relied on for redetermination remained undecided when the Collector considered the application.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition collector must defer redetermination of compensation when the judicial award relied upon is under appeal.
material_facts: An application for redetermination was filed on the basis of a reference court award.
The reference court award was under appeal when the collector decided the application.
The appellate court later altered the compensation fixed by the reference court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the final determination is that of the appellate forum: the reference court decree merges in the appellate decree, which is the executable decree. In Babua Ram v. State of U.P., the Court held that the collector must keep a timely Section 28A application pending while an appeal is unresolved and redetermine compensation on the final appellate judgment. U.P. State Industrial Development Corporation v. State of U.P. reiterated that course. Union of India v. Munshi Ram held that Section 28A applicants are entitled to the compensation finally payable to reference claimants, including where superior courts reduce compensation. Kendriya Karamchari Sehkari Grah Nirman Samiti Ltd. v. State of U.P. confirmed that withholding a decision pending appeal accords with this principle.
members.conclusion: The collector should have kept the application pending until the appeals were decided and then redetermined compensation on the basis of the final appellate judgment.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_redetermin: A person sought redetermination of land acquisition compensation by relying on a court's award.
predicates.relied_on_award_is_under_appeal: The award relied upon for redetermination was being challenged in an unresolved appeal.

members.legal_issue: When the collector prematurely decides a timely redetermination application while the relied-on award is under appeal, the original application must be reconsidered using the final appellate judgment.
material_facts: A timely initial application sought redetermination based on a reference court award.
The collector decided that application while appeals from the reference court award were pending.
After the appeals were resolved, the applicant filed a further application based on the appellate judgment.
The collector's premature decision meant the applicant's original application had not been determined on the basis of the final appellate outcome.
members.legal_principle: The one-application rule in Section 28A, as stated in Union of India v. Pradeep Kumari, does not make a claimant bear the consequences of the collector's failure to keep the original application pending during an appeal. Under Babua Ram v. State of U.P. and the related authorities, the collector should defer decision until the appeal is resolved. Given the collector's premature decision and the beneficial nature of Section 28A, the Court directed reconsideration of the original application on the final appellate judgment rather than permitting a successive application.
members.conclusion: The further application remained not maintainable, but the original application was to be considered afresh in light of the appellate judgment; the collector's earlier award was set aside, with amounts already paid to be adjusted.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_redetermin: A person sought redetermination of land acquisition compensation by relying on a court's award.
predicates.timely_initial_application: The applicant filed the original redetermination application within the applicable filing period.
predicates.initial_application_decided_while_award_: The collector decided the original application while an appeal from the relied-on award remained unresolved.
predicates.later_application_based_on_appellate_jud: After the appeal concluded, the applicant filed a further application seeking compensation based on the appellate judgment.

members.legal_issue: A partial partition of property that is capable of physical division is not recognized for income-tax purposes unless the property itself is physically divided.
material_facts: In an income-tax assessment, the family claimed an oral partial partition of eighteen immovable properties among its members.
The members received proportionate undivided shares in each property and separately accounted for and divided the income, but the properties were not physically divided.
The evidence supported the finding that the properties could be apportioned into lots on an equitable basis, with cash payments if needed to equalize the shares, without impairing their utility.
The family did not seriously attempt physical division; it relied on arbitration awards and evidence stating that individual properties could not be divided into ten shares.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 171 and Explanation (a)(i) to the Income-tax Act, 1961, where property admits of physical division, the property must be physically divided; dividing only its income is not partition. Where there are multiple properties, equitable apportionment among the members may constitute physical division, including equalization by cash payments. Hindu law may recognize partition without physical division, as described in Appovier v. Rama Subba Aiyan, but the tax statute imposes additional conditions. Charandas Haridas v. Commissioner of Income-tax was distinguishable because physical division of the relevant managing-agency rights would have required dissolution and reconstitution of firms, and the family had taken the fullest measure possible to divide its interest.
members.conclusion: The properties admitted of physical division, and the claimed arrangement did not satisfy the statutory definition of partition. Mere allocation of undivided shares or division of income was insufficient, so the claim of partial partition was correctly rejected.

rule.if: tax_assessment_partition_claim and multiple_assets and physical_apportionment_feasible and only_undivided_shares_allocated and no_serious_physical_division_attempt

predicates.tax_assessment_partition_claim: A family previously assessed as undivided claims a partial partition in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.multiple_assets: The claimed partition concerns multiple income-producing assets.
predicates.physical_apportionment_feasible: The assets can be physically apportioned among the members, including through equitable allocation and any needed equalization payments.
predicates.only_undivided_shares_allocated: The members are allocated undivided shares or income rather than physically apportioned property.
predicates.no_serious_physical_division_attempt: The family does not seriously attempt physical apportionment and relies instead on evidence or arrangements for holding undivided shares.

members.legal_issue: A claimed partition of property belonging to a Hindu undivided family is not recognized for income-tax purposes merely because the family’s status has been severed under Hindu law; the property must be divided in the manner its physical characteristics permit.
material_facts: The family had previously been assessed as an undivided family and claimed a partial partition of eighteen immovable properties among its members.
The family said the properties could not be physically divided and claimed that the members instead held defined shares and separately divided the income.
The Tribunal and the High Court found that the properties could be apportioned among the members, with monetary adjustments to equalize their shares, without impairing their utility.
No actual physical division or apportionment of the properties had been attempted.
members.legal_principle: Section 171(1) and the Explanation, particularly clauses (a)(i), (a)(ii) and (b), require an Income-tax Officer to record a finding of partition before a previously assessed Hindu undivided family is treated as divided for tax purposes. Where property admits of physical division, the property must be physically divided; where it does not, the division it admits of must take place. Division of income alone and mere severance of status under Hindu law are insufficient. Hindu law does not invariably require division by metes and bounds, as explained in Appovier v. Rama Subba Aiyan, but section 171 imposes additional conditions. The Court distinguished Charandas Haridas v. Commissioner of Income-tax, where the family had taken the fullest measure possible to divide an indivisible interest.
members.conclusion: The claimed partial partition did not satisfy the requirements for recognition under section 171, so the properties could not be treated as partitioned for income-tax purposes.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_with_partition_claim and previously_assessed_undivided_family and partial_partition_claimed and ((property_admits_physical_division and not physical_property_division) or (not property_admits_physical_division and not division_as_property_admits))

predicates.income_tax_assessment_with_partition_cla: An income-tax assessment proceeding involved a claim that family property had been partitioned.
predicates.previously_assessed_undivided_family: The family had previously been assessed as an undivided family.
predicates.partial_partition_claimed: A family member claimed that a partition had taken place in respect of some family members or property, or both.
predicates.property_admits_physical_division: The property could be physically divided or apportioned among those entitled to shares.
predicates.physical_property_division: The property was physically divided or apportioned among those entitled to shares.
predicates.division_as_property_admits: Where the property could not be physically divided, the parties carried out the form of division that its nature permitted.

members.legal_issue: For income-tax assessment, a Hindu undivided family is not treated as partitioned merely because of an agreement, a court decree, or a severance of status; the required division of property must be proved.
material_facts: The family had previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
A member relied on a partition agreement and a civil court decree, but the decree was preliminary and no physical division of the properties by metes and bounds had occurred.
The member first raised the partition claim in the assessments at issue.
members.legal_principle: Section 171 and its Explanation give “partition” a special meaning for income-tax purposes, distinct from the general principles of Hindu law: where property admits of physical division, physical division is required; where it does not, the property must be divided to the extent possible. A mere division of income or severance of status is insufficient. The assessee claiming partition bears the burden of proving the required division. The Court followed Kaloomal Tapeshwar Prasad v. C.I.T., Kanpur, 133 I.T.R. 690; it distinguished Parameswaran Nambudiripad v. Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, 72 I.T.R. 644, and Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax and Sales Tax (Special), Kozhikode v. Poomulli Manekkal Parameswaran Namboodiripad, 83 I.T.R. 108, because those cases concerned a different statutory scheme. It also referred to Sunder Singh Majithia v. Commissioner of Income Tax, 10 I.T.R. 457, and Shankar Narayanan v. Income Tax Officer, 153 I.T.R. 562.
members.conclusion: Because no physical division of the properties had taken place, the family’s status was not disrupted for tax assessment purposes, and income from the properties retained its Hindu undivided family character.

rule.if: hindu_family_tax_assessment and partition_claimed and not qualifying_property_division_proved

predicates.hindu_family_tax_assessment: A family previously assessed as a Hindu undivided family is being assessed for tax.
predicates.partition_claimed: A family member claims that the family property has been partitioned.
predicates.qualifying_property_division_proved: The claimant proves physical division of property that can be physically divided, or division to the extent possible of property that cannot be physically divided.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for delayed possession in this project is to be calculated by interest from the end of the developer’s agreed possession period, with a later starting date for a transferee and interest continuing through the specified period after an offer of possession.
material_facts: The appeals concerned complaints seeking possession of units in a housing project where the developer had an available possession period of three years under the agreement.
The developer stated that the flats were complete and occupation certificates had been obtained, and the Court directed that a copy of the certificate accompany the offer of possession.
Earlier appeals concerning the same project had been resolved on terms providing for interest at nine per cent from expiry of the three-year period, or from the date of transfer if later.
The Court directed that interest at that rate continue for two months from the offer of possession in all situations, while necessary maintenance work was to be completed within those two months.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the settlement terms in DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. v. Himanshu Arora and DLF Homes Panchkula (P.) Ltd. v. Sushila Devi, which provided for interest at nine per cent in possession cases after the developer’s three-year period and, for a transferee, from the later of expiry of that period or transfer. The Court also directed that interest continue for two months after the offer of possession, regardless of circumstances.
members.conclusion: The developer was directed to pay interest as compensation for delay from expiry of the three-year period, or from the transferee’s later transfer date, and to continue payment for two months from the offer of possession.

predicates.possession_claim_in_delayed_project: A consumer seeks possession of a unit in a housing project in which delivery was delayed.
predicates.possession_period_exceeded: The developer’s agreed period for delivering possession has expired.
predicates.possession_offered: The developer has made an offer of possession of the unit.
predicates.applicable_start_date: The relevant starting point is expiry of the developer’s agreed possession period, or a later transfer date where the claimant is a transferee.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for delayed possession is reckoned only after the developer’s contractual period for making possession available has expired.
material_facts: Some purchasers sought possession rather than a refund and sought compensation for delayed delivery.
The agreement allowed the developer two years to deliver possession, with an option to extend that period by one year.
The parties agreed that the three-year contractual period would not count when calculating delay compensation and that compensation would run at 9% thereafter.
members.legal_principle: The Court adopted the parties’ agreed calculation framework. Its earlier decision in Himanshu Arora confirmed a 9% interest direction and adjusted the period to conform to the State Commission’s order; no statutory provision was identified as the basis for the agreed contractual-period calculation.
members.conclusion: For possession claims, compensation at 9% is calculated only for the period after expiry of the three-year contractual period.

rule.if: is_consumer_housing_possession_case and purchaser_sought_possession and contractual_possession_period_expired and parties_agreed_to_possession_compensation_framework

predicates.is_consumer_housing_possession_case: A purchaser pursued a consumer proceeding concerning delayed possession of a housing unit.
predicates.purchaser_sought_possession: The purchaser asked to receive the housing unit rather than recover the purchase payments as a refund.
predicates.contractual_possession_period_expired: The period allowed by the agreement for delivering possession had elapsed.
predicates.parties_agreed_to_possession_compensatio: The parties accepted a framework that excludes the agreed possession period from the compensation calculation.

members.legal_issue: For a transferee seeking possession, delayed-possession compensation begins on the later of the transfer date and expiry of the contractual possession period.
material_facts: The agreed framework addressed possession claims in which a transferee had stepped into the original allottee’s position.
The parties agreed that compensation would begin after the contractual possession period expired or on the transfer date, whichever occurred later.
members.legal_principle: The Court adopted the parties’ agreed framework for transferred allotments. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was identified as the basis for this specific rule.
members.conclusion: In a possession case involving a transferee, compensation is reckoned from the later of the transfer date and expiry of the contractual possession period.

rule.if: is_consumer_housing_possession_case and purchaser_sought_possession and transferee_succeeded_to_original_allottee and parties_agreed_to_transfer_possession_framework

predicates.is_consumer_housing_possession_case: A purchaser pursued a consumer proceeding concerning delayed possession of a housing unit.
predicates.purchaser_sought_possession: The purchaser asked to receive the housing unit rather than recover the purchase payments as a refund.
predicates.transferee_succeeded_to_original_allotte: A subsequent purchaser took the original allottee’s position in relation to the housing unit.
predicates.parties_agreed_to_transfer_possession_fr: The parties accepted a framework that sets the starting point for a transferee’s possession compensation by reference to both transfer and contractual expiry.

members.legal_issue: A public servant commits criminal misconduct by abusing official position to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for another person.
material_facts: The public servant applied for a plot under a scheme limited to specified sectors and was allotted a plot in one of those sectors on an as-is-where-is basis.
Despite the scheme and allotment terms not permitting the requested changes, the allotment was converted twice, ultimately securing a plot in a developed sector.
The plot was converted from a guest-house use to residential use and allotted to the public servant at a substantially lower premium than the rate applicable to that sector.
The plot’s area and layout were repeatedly altered without reasonable justification, and additional area was allotted after the lease had been executed.
The public servant’s official position was used to facilitate the allotments and conversions, and the public servant thereby obtained a valuable property and pecuniary advantage.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(d)(i)–(iii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, each of the three alternatives is independent and disjunctive: obtaining a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage by corrupt or illegal means, by abusing public office, or for another person without public interest is sufficient. Section 13(2) provides the punishment. The Court also applied the principle in Noida Entrepreneurs Association v. NOIDA, (2011) 6 SCC 508, that public power is held in trust and must be exercised reasonably, in good faith, and for the purpose for which it was conferred.
members.conclusion: The public servant abused his position to obtain a valuable thing and pecuniary advantage; the conviction for criminal misconduct was properly sustained.

rule.if: public_servant_corruption_case and official_position_abused and valuable_advantage_obtained and (allocation_rules_bypassed or preferential_pricing or unjustified_property_alterations)

predicates.public_servant_corruption_case: The proceeding concerns an allegation that a public servant obtained a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage through the exercise of public office.
predicates.official_position_abused: The public servant used official authority or influence to facilitate a benefit for himself or another person.
predicates.valuable_advantage_obtained: The public servant or another person obtained valuable property or a pecuniary benefit.
predicates.allocation_rules_bypassed: The benefit was provided through allotments or conversions that did not comply with the applicable scheme or rules.
predicates.preferential_pricing: The property was obtained at a price materially below the rate applied to comparable property in its location.
predicates.unjustified_property_alterations: The property’s use, area, or layout was altered without a reasonable justification in a way that benefited the recipient.

members.legal_issue: A public servant commits criminal misconduct by abusing official position to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for themselves or another person, and any one of the independent alternatives in the governing provision is sufficient.
material_facts: The appellant was the public authority’s chairperson-cum-chief executive officer and used her position to have a defective, undated application processed after the scheme’s closing date, despite an improper and late-cleared cheque.

She obtained conversion of her plot to a larger plot in a developed sector and approved a layout change that enlarged it further, made it a corner plot and reduced other land available to the authority.

Her two dependent daughters received shops and residential plots through defective applications and functional certificates; the evidence showed that the appellant and her husband funded the transactions and that the shops were used to obtain eligibility for residential plots.
The allotments and layout changes contravened the authority’s rules, gave valuable advantages to the appellant and her daughters, and caused loss to the authority.
The trial court and High Court convicted the appellant, and the Supreme Court found no error in their concurrent assessment of the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(d)(i), (ii) and (iii) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, the three alternatives are independent and disjunctive: obtaining a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage by corrupt or illegal means, by abusing public position, or for any person without public interest is sufficient to constitute criminal misconduct. Section 13(2) prescribes the punishment. The Court also referred to Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014) 9 SCC 1, Niranjan Hemchandra Sashittal v. State of Maharashtra (2013) 4 SCC 642, Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh (2012) 3 SCC 64 and K.C. Sareen v. C.B.I. (2001) 6 SCC 584 in discussing the serious public harm caused by corruption; the elements applied to the conviction were those in Section 13(1)(d).
members.conclusion: The conviction for criminal misconduct was confirmed because the appellant abused her public position to obtain valuable things or pecuniary advantages for herself and her daughters.

rule.if: appeal_against_corruption_conviction and public_servant and official_position_abused and valuable_advantage_obtained_for_self_or_another

predicates.appeal_against_corruption_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction for corruption-related criminal misconduct.
predicates.public_servant: The accused held public office when the relevant conduct occurred.
predicates.official_position_abused: The public servant used the authority or influence of the office improperly in the relevant dealings.
predicates.valuable_advantage_obtained_for_self_or_: The public servant obtained a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for themselves or another person.

members.legal_issue: Dishonest abuse of public office to obtain an advantage for another, including by causing government property to be parted with, falls within criminal misconduct.
material_facts: The accused was a public servant responsible for land assignments.
He caused government land to be assigned to his brother-in-law without disclosing their relationship and dishonestly understated the trees and their value to meet the rules for assignment.
The courts below found that he understated the extent and value of the trees to help his brother-in-law.
members.legal_principle: A penal statute must be construed strictly: the charged conduct must fall within both the words and the spirit of the enactment, as explained in Dyke v. Elliot, (1872) L.R. 4 P.C. 184. Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, is to be read in light of the Act’s purpose of preventing bribery and corruption. “Otherwise” covers abuses of official position beyond corrupt or illegal means, but its context and the dishonesty implicit in “abuse” require dishonest intent; innocuous acts are not covered. The provision reaches advantages obtained for another through abuse of office, including conduct causing wrongful loss to government. Ram Krishan v. State of Delhi, [1956] S.C.R. 182, and Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena v. Delhi Administration, [1962] 3 S.C.R. 259, support its broad scope.
members.conclusion: Section 5(1)(d) covers a public servant who dishonestly abuses his position to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for another; it is not confined to benefits received from a third party and includes wrongful loss caused to the government. The conduct, if established, constitutes an offence under that provision.

predicates.public_servant_misconduct_case: The proceeding concerns alleged criminal misconduct by a public servant.
predicates.public_servant_abused_position_dishonest: The public servant dishonestly used official position for a purpose for which it was not intended.
predicates.advantage_obtained_for_another: The public servant's conduct secured a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for another person.

members.legal_issue: Judicial officers who decided civil proceedings should not be named as parties merely because their orders are challenged in a writ petition or special leave petition.
material_facts: The judicial officers who had decided matters in the civil proceedings were named as respondents in the writ petition and the special leave petition challenging those proceedings.
The judgment found no necessity or justification for joining those officers as parties.
members.legal_principle: A judicial officer who decides a civil proceeding is not to be treated as a government official for the purpose of naming parties to a challenge to the proceeding. The court referred to writ petitions under Article 226 and special leave petitions under Article 138 of the Constitution of India in condemning the practice.
members.conclusion: The court deprecated the practice and stated that judicial officers who dispose of civil proceedings should not be impleaded as parties in such writ petitions or special leave petitions.

predicates.challenge_to_civil_proceeding_order: A litigant brings a writ petition or special leave petition challenging an order made in a civil proceeding.
predicates.judicial_officers_named_only_because_the: The judicial officers are made parties solely because they decided the civil proceeding being challenged.
predicates.judicial_officers_should_not_be_joined_a: The judicial officers should not be impleaded as parties to the challenge.

members.legal_issue: Judges who decide a contempt matter should not be made parties to a proceeding challenging that decision when no relief is claimed against them.
material_facts: The magistrate appealed his contempt conviction and named the Chief Justice and judges of the court that convicted him as respondents.
No relief was claimed against those judges; they had decided the contempt matter in their judicial capacity.
The court noted the English practice of styling such proceedings as being in re the alleged contemnor and referred to the differing party practice in Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago.
members.legal_principle: Parties to a suit or appeal are those who claim relief, against whom relief is given or sought, or who have a right to be heard because of an interest in the result. Judges who decide a contempt matter have no such litigant's interest merely by virtue of their decision. The court endorsed the English practice of using an in re title and referred to Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago as an example of a different party practice in an appeal.
members.conclusion: The Chief Justice and judges should not be made parties to a contempt proceeding or an appeal from it when no relief is claimed against them; the proceeding should be titled in re the alleged contemnor. The existing practice of joining the judges should be discontinued.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an alleged contempt of court or a challenge to a contempt decision.
predicates.no_relief_claimed_against_judges: No party seeks relief against the judges who decided the contempt matter.
predicates.judges_not_parties_and_title_identifies_: The deciding judges are not joined as parties, and the proceeding is titled to identify the alleged contemnor.

members.legal_issue: Judges who decide a contempt proceeding should not be named as parties to an appeal from that decision when no relief is sought against them.
material_facts: The Chief Justice and Judges who had convicted the appellant of contempt were made respondents to the appeal.
No relief was claimed against those Judges, and their decision did not give them an interest in the appeal in the sense in which a litigant has an interest.
members.legal_principle: Persons who claim relief, against whom relief is sought, or who have or claim a right to be heard because of an interest in the outcome should be parties. Judges deciding a case are not interested in its outcome as litigants, and they should not be parties unless relief is claimed against them. Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago was noted as an example of a different party being named, but the Court did not rely on it as the basis for this rule; no statutory provision was applied to this issue.
members.conclusion: The practice of making the Chief Justice and Judges parties to an appeal from a contempt decision should be discontinued; such proceedings should instead be titled in the name of the alleged contemner.

predicates.contempt_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision in a contempt proceeding.
predicates.judges_named_as_parties: The judges who made the decision being appealed are named as parties to the appeal.
predicates.no_relief_sought_against_judges: The appellant seeks no relief against the judges who made the decision.

members.legal_issue: A governmental exemption from hill-station building controls is invalid when the decision is made without proper consideration of the governing requirements and on irrelevant grounds.
material_facts: The hotel sought approval for a revised building plan, but its application was treated as a request for exemption from building rules.
The expert committee recommended rejection after identifying extensive violations, including excess floor-space index and building height.

The minister relied on considerations including the high cost of the land and its optimum use, while overlooking the expert committee’s recommendation, the applicable master plan, and environmental and ecological requirements.
The statutory validation of the government’s power to grant exemptions did not prevent a challenge to an individual exemption order for irrelevant considerations or non-application of mind.
members.legal_principle: Under Chapter X-A of the Tamil Nadu District Municipalities Act, 1920, including Sections 217-B, 217-C, 217-D, 217-K and 217-Q, and Rules 26 and 27 of the Tamil Nadu District Municipalities (Hill Stations) Building Rules, 1993, building decisions must address the prescribed requirements, including protection of hill-station scenery, environment, and ecosystem. The validation clause in Section 3 of Tamil Nadu Act 52 of 1994 validated the existence of the exemption power but did not immunize an individual order from challenge for irrelevant considerations or non-application of mind.
members.conclusion: The order granting the exemption was illegal, invalid, and arbitrary, and was properly quashed.

rule.if: challenge_to_building_exemption_order and request_was_for_plan_approval_not_exemption and expert_committee_found_major_violations and decision_relied_on_irrelevant_factors and decision_ignored_environmental_requirements

predicates.challenge_to_building_exemption_order: A proceeding challenged a government order exempting a building from applicable building controls.
predicates.request_was_for_plan_approval_not_exempt: The applicant sought approval of a revised building plan rather than an exemption from the rules.
predicates.expert_committee_found_major_violations: An expert committee identified substantial violations when reviewing the building proposal.
predicates.decision_relied_on_irrelevant_factors: The decision-maker relied on considerations unrelated to the governing building-control requirements.
predicates.decision_ignored_environmental_requireme: The decision-maker failed to address environmental, ecological, or applicable planning requirements.

members.legal_issue: An individual exemption from tenant protections is invalid when the reasons supporting it are not relevant to the legislation’s purpose and relevant circumstances have not been considered.
material_facts: A tenant had accepted a fixed-term lease after declining an offered longer lease and remained in possession after the term expired, relying on statutory protection.
The government exempted the building based on the tenant’s choice of a shorter lease, the expiry of the lease, the tenant’s other businesses, and the tenant’s continued possession.
The government did not consider whether the tenant could obtain alternative premises to continue the business conducted in the building.

The majority held that the tenant’s continued possession and exercise of statutory rights did not justify withdrawing protection; two judges dissented and considered the exemption lawful in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: The exemption discretion must be exercised consistently with the policy and purpose of preventing unreasonable eviction and controlling rents. An individual order may be reviewed for discrimination, reliance on irrelevant grounds, or mala fides. The mere expiry of a tenancy, a tenant’s refusal of a longer lease, and the tenant’s exercise of statutory protection do not by themselves justify exemption; the tenant’s ability to obtain alternative accommodation for the relevant business is material. The majority applied Article 14 and the guidance principles in Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar, [1959] SCR 279, and Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1957] SCR 605. The dissent considered all relevant circumstances, including whether eviction would be unreasonable and whether the protection could enable exploitation, and concluded the order was within the statutory purpose.
members.conclusion: By majority, the exemption order was ultra vires and void because the stated reasons were not germane to the legislation’s purpose; the appeal was dismissed. Two judges would have allowed the appeal and upheld the order.

predicates.individual_building_exemption: The government exempted a particular building from protections otherwise available to its tenant.
predicates.tenant_protected_after_lease_expiry: A tenant remained in possession after a fixed-term lease ended under a statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.exemption_reasons_rely_on_expiry_or_exer: The government relied on the lease ending or the tenant's continued possession under statutory protection as grounds for exemption.
predicates.relevant_alternative_accommodation_not_c: The government did not consider whether the tenant could obtain alternative premises for the business conducted in the building.

members.legal_issue: An exemption from rent-control protections is invalid when the government grants it without considering whether the applicant has shown a ground relevant to the purpose of the legislation.
material_facts: A public educational trust owned rental property and used the rental income for the school it maintained.
The trust sought an exemption, asserting that the rental income was devoted to the trust’s expenses.
The trust did not claim that it needed the premises for its own use or that the rent was inadequate to meet the trust’s expenses.
The government granted the exemption, but its returns did not disclose a policy-relevant ground for doing so or establish that it had applied its mind to the relevant considerations.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, the government’s exemption power must be exercised consistently with the policy and purpose of the Act. The fact that an institution falls within a qualifying category and uses the property’s income for its purposes permits it to apply, but does not by itself justify an exemption; the government must consider relevant grounds for granting it. The Court relied on P. J. Irani v. State of Madras, which held that an exemption under the analogous Section 13 of the Madras Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1949, could be ultra vires if its grounds were not germane to the Act’s policy, and on Sadhu Singh v. District Board, Gurdaspur.
members.conclusion: The exemption notification was properly quashed because the government had not applied its mind to whether a ground germane to the Act’s policy justified the exemption; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_against_quashing_of_rent_control_: The proceeding is an appeal against a decision quashing an exemption from rent-control protections.
predicates.applicant_only_showed_qualifying_institu: The applicant relied on its qualifying institutional status and use of property income for its purposes, without showing why an exemption was needed on a ground relevant to the law’s purpose.
predicates.government_record_disclosed_no_relevant_: The government’s record disclosed no relevant ground showing that it had considered why the exemption should be granted.

members.legal_issue: Mere presence at an unlawful assembly does not establish membership when a person may have been only a spectator.
material_facts: The incident occurred in a village where an unusual and serious event could draw curious spectators.
A large crowd gathered, and the evidence did not establish that every person present participated in the occurrence or shared the assembly’s purpose.
The Court found that some accused treated as assembly members were in fact mere spectators.
members.legal_principle: For the purposes of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, mere presence in an assembly is not by itself proof of membership; the court must distinguish members from people who were merely spectators. The Court relied on Masalti v. State of U.P. in addressing proof of individual roles in a large assembly.
members.conclusion: Mere presence at the scene or in a crowd was not enough to establish membership in the unlawful assembly.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The proceeding concerns alleged membership of an unlawful assembly and liability for offences associated with it.
predicates.person_was_only_present_as_spectator: The person was present at the occurrence only as a spectator and was not shown to have joined the assembly.

members.legal_issue: Mere presence in an unlawful assembly does not establish membership unless conduct or a legally recognized circumstance shows that the person joined the assembly.
material_facts: The case involved convictions for offences committed by an unlawful assembly.
The assembly was alleged to have included many residents whose homes surrounded the place of the attack, and the prosecution evidence against some accused was general rather than individualized.

Four appellants had no particular part or overt act attributed to them and might have been spectators; other appellants were linked to specific conduct, including attacking victims, inciting the mob, concealing the crime, or disposing of the bodies.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 149 and 142 of the Indian Penal Code, mere presence in an assembly does not make a person a member of an unlawful assembly unless the person does something or omits to do something that makes them a member, or the case falls within Section 142. Evidence in general terms that people were present and armed must be closely scrutinized, and each accused’s case must be considered individually. Conduct connected with disposing of the victims’ bodies could support membership where that conduct furthered the assembly’s common object.
members.conclusion: Mere presence was insufficient to establish membership in the unlawful assembly. The four appellants against whom no particular part or overt act was attributed were acquitted, while the convictions of the other appellants were maintained where the evidence showed participation or other conduct supporting membership.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_prosecution: The proceeding involves criminal liability for offences alleged to have been committed by an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_presence_is_shown: The evidence places the accused at or among the people assembled at the scene.
predicates.no_individual_conduct_or_other_membershi: The evidence shows no conduct or omission by the accused establishing membership and no legally recognized basis for treating the accused as a member.

members.legal_issue: An accused person's presence at a violent assembly, together with evidence connecting the person to it and the surrounding circumstances, can establish membership and the assembly's common object despite the absence of weapons recovered from that person's possession.
material_facts: The accused were found injured at the scene, away from the inhabited part of the village, after the mob dispersed.
Some accused were tenants facing dispossession, and the others were close relations of those tenants.
The Court accepted oral testimony of their participation and considered their presence and relationships inconsistent with their being mere curious onlookers.
Weapons were found in the field, but the evidence did not establish that they had been recovered from the accused persons' possession.
The mob had attacked the people seeking to take possession, and the Court found that the accused joined the assembly with the common object attributed to it.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated membership and common object as questions of fact, assessed on the accepted oral evidence and all surrounding circumstances. It found that the erroneous view that weapons had been recovered from the accused did not prevent the Court from independently accepting the evidence of participation. Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code were applied to the assembly and offences committed in prosecution of its common object.
members.conclusion: The accused were members of the unlawful assembly with the common object found by the courts below, and their convictions on that basis were upheld.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_unlawful_assembly_c: The proceeding is an appeal from convictions based on membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.credible_evidence_identifies_participati: Accepted oral evidence identifies the accused as participants in the assembly or its actions.
predicates.accused_found_injured_at_remote_scene: The accused were found injured at the scene, away from the inhabited part of the locality, after the assembly dispersed.
predicates.accused_connected_to_people_defending_po: The accused were tenants facing dispossession or close relations of those tenants.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_support_member: The circumstances made innocent presence as mere onlookers unlikely.

members.legal_issue: Industries requiring operating consent must keep primary effluent treatment plants functional, and defaulting industries may be restrained from operating.
material_facts: The petition sought directions requiring industries that need operating consent to have functional effluent treatment plants.

The parties did not dispute that industries requiring operating consent had primary effluent treatment plants when consent was granted, but the continuing functionality of those plants after operations began was in issue.

The Court directed notice to the relevant industries, inspections after the notice period, and restraint of industrial activity where a plant was not made fully operational; electricity could be disconnected on the Pollution Control Board's recommendation.
members.legal_principle: An industry that requires operating consent may operate only while its primary effluent treatment plant is functional. The Court relied on that condition for operation and issued directions to secure compliance; it cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this direction.
members.conclusion: Pollution Control Boards must give the specified notice, inspect the relevant industries, and restrain any industry whose primary effluent treatment plant is not functional; the electricity agency must disconnect supply when the Board recommends disconnection for that reason.

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_writ and industry_requires_operating_consent and primary_treatment_functionality_is_required_for_operation and (plant_not_functional_after_notice or inspection_finds_plant_not_fully_operational)

predicates.environmental_public_interest_writ: A writ proceeding seeks directions to secure environmental compliance across industries or public authorities.
predicates.industry_requires_operating_consent: An industry must obtain operating consent from a pollution-control authority to function.
predicates.primary_treatment_functionality_is_requi: The industry is required to have a functional primary effluent treatment plant to operate.
predicates.plant_not_functional_after_notice: The industry has not made its primary effluent treatment plant fully operational within the period allowed after notice.
predicates.inspection_finds_plant_not_fully_operati: The pollution-control authority inspects the industry and finds that its primary effluent treatment plant is not fully operational.

members.legal_issue: An industry restrained because its primary effluent treatment plant is non-functional may resume industrial activity only after restoring the plant and obtaining fresh operating consent.
material_facts: The Court directed that an industry disabled from carrying on industrial activity could make its primary effluent treatment plant functional to the required capacity and seek fresh operating consent.
The Court specified that industrial activity could resume only after fresh consent was received.
members.legal_principle: Operation requires both a functional primary effluent treatment plant and operating consent from the relevant Pollution Control Board. The Court cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this direction.
members.conclusion: A restrained industry may resume industrial activity only after its primary effluent treatment plant is functional to the required capacity and it receives fresh operating consent.

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_writ and industry_was_restrained_for_nonfunctional_primary_treatment and plant_restored_to_required_capacity and fresh_operating_consent_received

predicates.environmental_public_interest_writ: A writ proceeding seeks directions to secure environmental compliance across industries or public authorities.
