predicates.plant_restored_to_required_capacity: The industry has made its primary effluent treatment plant functional to the required capacity.
predicates.fresh_operating_consent_received: The industry has received fresh operating consent from the relevant pollution-control authority.

members.legal_issue: Industries causing pollution may be required to install effective pollution-control devices and obtain operating consent, and may be closed if they fail to do so.
material_facts: Many tanneries had failed over several years, despite repeated opportunities and notices, to establish satisfactory individual treatment plants or connect to common treatment plants.
Reports showed that treatment plants were not consistently operating satisfactorily and that water near tannery clusters was unfit for drinking.
The Court directed the tanneries to install individual or common pollution-control systems, obtain the Board’s consent to operate, and face closure if they failed to obtain consent.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974, which restricts the use of streams and wells for polluting discharges and requires consent for outlets and effluent discharges, and on sections 5 and 7 of the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, which permit directions including closure and prohibit discharges exceeding prescribed standards. The Court also relied on its prior orders in the proceeding and expert reports documenting inadequate treatment and pollution.
members.conclusion: The tanneries were required to install the necessary pollution-control devices and obtain the Board’s consent to operate; those that failed to obtain consent were to be closed.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.industrial_pollution: An industrial activity is causing or contributing to pollution.
predicates.pollution_controls_inadequate: The industry’s pollution-control equipment or treatment arrangements are absent or do not adequately control its discharges.

members.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not interfere with an appellate court’s discretionary refusal to receive additional evidence when the application is very belated.
material_facts: An application to receive additional evidence was made in the High Court many years after the suit began and years after the appeal was filed.
The principal evidence sought was an alleged letter to a bank nominating a person entitled to the deposited funds.
The letter was not attached to the application; the applicant asked the High Court to summon it from the bank.
The High Court refused the application, and the Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with that discretionary decision.
members.legal_principle: The Supreme Court will not interfere with the High Court’s exercise of discretion to refuse additional evidence where the application is made very late.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not interfere with the High Court’s discretionary refusal to receive the additional evidence.

predicates.appellate_additional_evidence_applicatio: A party seeks to introduce additional evidence in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.application_very_belated: The application to introduce the evidence is made many years after the suit began and after a substantial period has passed since the appeal was filed.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court should not interfere at an interim stage with an appellate court’s order on additional evidence when the appellate court is acting within its jurisdiction and the appeal remains pending.
material_facts: During a first appeal from dismissal of a suit, the appellant asked to have a disputed will’s signature examined by a handwriting expert.
The first appellate court allowed the request for additional evidence.
While the appeal was still pending, the opposing party challenged that order in revision, and the High Court set it aside.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a revisional court should not interfere at an interim stage with an order made within the appellate court’s jurisdiction on an application under Order XLI Rule 27, particularly when the appeal remains pending and the challenged decision can be contested in accordance with law after the appellate decree. The Court relied on Mahavir Singh v. Naresh Chandra (2001) 1 SCC 309 and Gurdev Singh v. Mehnga Ram (1997) 6 SCC 507.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s revisional order was set aside, and the first appellate court was directed to decide the additional-evidence application afresh.

predicates.civil_appeal_pending: A civil appeal was pending before an appellate court.
predicates.appellate_court_ordered_additional_evide: The appellate court made an order on a party’s request to present additional evidence.
predicates.revision_challenged_interim_order: A party challenged that order in revision before the appeal had been finally decided.
predicates.revision_interference_set_aside_and_appl: The revisional interference is set aside and the appellate court is directed to reconsider the additional-evidence application.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court should not interfere with a first appellate court’s discretionary decision to admit additional evidence when that decision rests on the evidence’s materiality and its unavailability despite due diligence or later creation.
material_facts: The first appellate court allowed additional evidence after finding that the documents were material to the landlord’s bona fide need and that the tenant could not have produced them earlier despite due diligence, or that they were created after the trial decree.
The High Court set aside that order in revision.
The Supreme Court found the first appellate court’s exercise of discretion justified and the High Court’s interference unjustified.
members.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs revisional jurisdiction. Where a first appellate court exercises its discretion to permit additional evidence on grounds supported by the record, interference in revision is not justified merely because the revisional court would assess that discretion differently.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the first appellate court’s order, and the order allowing additional evidence was restored.

predicates.revision_from_additional_evidence_order: A party seeks revision of a first appellate court’s order allowing additional evidence.
predicates.appellate_court_exercised_discretion_on_: The first appellate court relied on the evidence’s materiality and its unavailability despite due diligence or its creation after the trial decree when allowing it.

members.legal_issue: A petition under Article 32 is unavailable to challenge government action unless the action violates a fundamental right.
material_facts: The petitioners sought relief under Article 32 concerning the government’s grant of a lease to another operator.
The petitioners did not establish a fundamental right to have the disputed area leased to them or otherwise show that the grant infringed a fundamental right.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 relief requires an infringement of a fundamental right; illegality of government action, without such an infringement, is insufficient to maintain the petition.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the government’s action had been illegal, the petition could not be maintained under Article 32 without a violation of a fundamental right.

predicates.article_32_petition: The claimants sought a constitutional writ through a petition invoking the constitutional remedy for fundamental-rights violations.
predicates.no_fundamental_right_violation_shown: The claimants did not establish that the challenged government action violated a fundamental right.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot establish an infringement of a fundamental right through an Article 32 petition when the claimed right depends on an underlying status or entitlement that a competent authority has finally determined against that person, unless that determination is shown to be void or is otherwise set aside.
material_facts: The petitioner’s husband transferred his interest in land to her.
After notice was issued to the petitioner and her husband, the competent authority declared the husband an evacuee and the land evacuee property.
The petitioner appeared in response to the notice and challenged the determination on its merits before the appellate and revisional authorities, but those challenges failed.
The petitioner’s application for restoration of the property was also rejected.
The petitioner did not obtain a decision setting aside the Custodian-General’s determination through an appropriate challenge, and the determination became final.
The petitioner’s claims under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 depended on establishing that the land was not evacuee property.

The petitioner alleged procedural defects in the notice but did not raise a jurisdictional objection during the proceedings before the authorities; the Court found no jurisdictional defect and no constitutional challenge to the relevant law.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 provides a remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights, but where a competent authority has finally determined an underlying question so that the alleged right does not exist, its infringement cannot be asserted under Article 32 while that determination stands, unless the determination is a nullity or is otherwise got rid of. A challenge to the correctness of the determination on its merits must be brought through an appropriate proceeding. The Court applied Sahibzada Saiyed Muhammed Amirabbas Abbasi v. State of Madhya Bharat, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 138. It considered the claims under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and the determinations under sections 2(d) and 2(f) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950; section 28 did not remove the constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 32, 136, 226 or 227, but the final determination still meant that no infringement was established on these facts.
members.conclusion: The Article 32 petition was incompetent because the final determination by competent authorities negated the right on which the claimed fundamental-right infringement depended, and that determination had not been shown to be void or otherwise set aside.

rule.if: art32_fundamental_right_petition and competent_authority_decided_underlying_entitlement and decision_is_final and claimed_right_depends_on_that_entitlement and jurisdictional_nullity_not_established and decision_not_otherwise_set_aside

predicates.art32_fundamental_right_petition: The proceeding is a petition seeking enforcement of a fundamental right under Article 32.
predicates.competent_authority_decided_underlying_e: An authority competent to decide the matter determined an underlying status or entitlement on which the claimed right depends.
predicates.decision_is_final: The determination has become final in the proceedings available to challenge it.
predicates.claimed_right_depends_on_that_entitlemen: The asserted fundamental right depends on the existence of the status or entitlement decided by the authority.
predicates.jurisdictional_nullity_not_established: The petitioner has not established that the authority’s determination is void for want of jurisdiction.
predicates.decision_not_otherwise_set_aside: The determination has not otherwise been set aside through an appropriate proceeding.
predicates.art32_claim_not_maintainable: The claimed infringement cannot be pursued through the Article 32 petition while the final determination stands.

members.legal_issue: A claim that government action is illegal does not make a petition under Article 32 maintainable unless the action violates a fundamental right.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the government’s grant of a mineral lease as illegal under mining legislation and rules.
The Court found no fundamental right infringed by the grant of the lease.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 relief requires a violation of a fundamental right; alleged illegality by itself is insufficient. The Court relied on Article 32 and cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the grant was illegal, the petitioners could not obtain relief under Article 32 without a violation of a fundamental right.

rule.if: article_32_petition and government_action_alleged_illegal and not fundamental_right_violated

predicates.government_action_alleged_illegal: The petitioner alleges that government action is illegal.
predicates.fundamental_right_violated: The challenged action violates a fundamental right of the petitioner.

members.legal_issue: Expenses incurred to maintain immature, non-bearing plantation trees are deductible when they are non-capital, non-personal expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for the plantation.
material_facts: The estate included rubber plantations, including 235 acres occupied by immature, non-bearing rubber trees.
The assessee claimed deductions for expenses relating to the upkeep and maintenance of the immature trees, including forking and manuring.

The agricultural income-tax tribunal treated expenses on the rubber plantation as deductible and remanded for calculation of expenses relating to the immature areas; the High Court upheld deductibility.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(e) of the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955 permits deduction of expenditure that is not capital expenditure or personal expenses and is laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation. The Court applied its decision on the corresponding issue under section 5(j) of the Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, in Civil Appeals Nos. 290–292 of 1959.
members.conclusion: The expenses for upkeep of the immature rubber trees were deductible, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: plantation_tax_deduction_case and immature_nonbearing_trees and upkeep_expense_incurred and plantation_purpose_expense and noncapital_nonpersonal_expense

predicates.plantation_tax_deduction_case: The proceeding concerns whether expenditure may be deducted in computing agricultural income from a plantation.
predicates.immature_nonbearing_trees: The plantation includes trees that are immature and not yet bearing produce.
predicates.upkeep_expense_incurred: The taxpayer incurred expenditure to maintain or care for the immature, non-bearing trees.
predicates.plantation_purpose_expense: The expenditure was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation.
predicates.noncapital_nonpersonal_expense: The expenditure was neither capital expenditure nor a personal expense of the taxpayer.
predicates.immature_tree_upkeep_expense_deductible: The expenditure for upkeep of the immature, non-bearing trees is deductible.

members.legal_issue: Maintenance expenditure on immature trees in an income-producing plantation is deductible even when those trees yield no income in the accounting year.
material_facts: The taxpayer operated rubber plantations containing both mature, yielding trees and immature trees that had not begun to yield rubber.
The taxpayer incurred expenditure on the upkeep and maintenance of the immature trees.
The expenditure was wholly and exclusively incurred for deriving agricultural income, and was not disputed to be so.
The immature trees produced no return in the accounting years in question.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, expenditure other than capital expenditure or personal expenses, laid out wholly and exclusively for deriving agricultural income, is deductible. The deduction is not limited to expenditure that produces a return in the same accounting year. The Court followed Vallambrosa Rubber Co. Ltd. v. Farmer, (1910) 5 T.C. 529, and held Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, West Bengal, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 972, inapplicable because that case concerned capital expenditure incurred to acquire an income-earning asset.
members.conclusion: The expenditure on maintaining the immature trees was a permissible deduction, notwithstanding that those trees produced no income in the relevant accounting year.

predicates.immature_trees_yield_no_current_income: The immature trees produce no income during the accounting year for which the deduction is claimed.

members.legal_issue: Expenditure on maintaining immature, non-bearing rubber trees is deductible in computing agricultural income when the applicable plantation-expense test is no narrower than the test applied in the controlling precedent.
material_facts: The assessee claimed expenses for the maintenance and upkeep of immature, non-bearing rubber trees on its rubber plantation.
The agricultural income-tax tribunal and the High Court allowed the claimed expenditure, with the tribunal directing that expenses for forking and manuring the immature areas be ascertained.

The applicable deduction provision used wording that was the same as the provision considered in an earlier decision except for its closing phrase, which the Court regarded as more favourable to the assessee.
The earlier decision had decided the deductibility of expenditure for forking, manuring, and similar work on immature rubber trees.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(e) of the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955 permits deduction of expenditure, other than capital expenditure or personal expenses, laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation. Because its test was the same as, and in its closing words more favourable than, the test in section 5(j) of the Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, the Court applied Travancore Rubber & Tea Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax, Kerala, [1961] 3 S.C.R. 279, which decided the deductibility of expenses for work on immature rubber trees.
members.conclusion: The earlier decision governed the case, so the expenditure was deductible and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired from a predecessor's personal assets remains personal property where the evidence, considered as a whole, does not establish that it was acquired from institutional funds.
material_facts: The disputed properties were purchased using a fund left by a predecessor Mahant, which included personal gifts and inherited personal assets.
The successor Mahant inherited that fund and used it to purchase the disputed properties.
The record did not establish that the Math's income left an appreciable surplus after its religious and other obligations were met.
Revenue records named the Mahant, rather than the Math or deity, as owner, and transfers of parts of the properties were not challenged.
The Mahant's will provided for the disputed properties to pass to the respondent.
members.legal_principle: Whether property was acquired by applying an institutional nucleus must be determined by considering all the facts and circumstances and balancing the entire evidence; no presumption applies either way, and the claimant bears the burden of proof. The Court relied on the principles stated in Sushil Chandra Sen v. Gobind Chandra Das and Gurcharan Prasad v. Krishnanand concerning personal property ownership by ascetics, and on Dr. B.K. Mukherjee's Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts concerning the absence of a presumption that a Mahant's property is institutional.
members.conclusion: The disputed properties were the Mahant's personal and separate properties, not properties of the Math or deity, and they devolved on the respondent under the will.

rule.if: civil_property_ownership_claim and purchase_funded_by_predecessor_assets and predecessor_assets_were_personal and not appreciable_institutional_surplus_shown

predicates.civil_property_ownership_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to ownership or possession of property.
predicates.purchase_funded_by_predecessor_assets: The disputed property was purchased using a fund left by a predecessor.
predicates.predecessor_assets_were_personal: The fund left by the predecessor consisted of personal gifts, inherited personal assets, or other personal wealth.
predicates.appreciable_institutional_surplus_shown: The evidence establishes that institutional income left an appreciable surplus available to fund the purchase.

members.legal_issue: A family member's property is not joint family property merely because another family member had substantial earnings, where the purchaser had independent income and the evidence attributes the purchase to personal resources.
material_facts: The appellant sought inclusion in the partition of two properties standing in the second defendant's name.
The second defendant was educated, employed, and testified that he paid for the properties from his own resources, including income earned while working abroad.
The properties were acquired at different times, and the trial court's contrary conclusion relied substantially on the deceased father's success as a lawyer and politician.
The Court found no merit in treating the second defendant's properties as joint family property on that basis.
members.legal_principle: Even where a joint family exists, a co-owner may acquire independent or separate property. The fact that another family member had substantial earnings does not, by itself, establish that a family member's property was acquired with joint family funds. The Court cited no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The second defendant's properties were properly excluded from the partition of the deceased father's properties.

predicates.partition_suit: The plaintiffs brought a suit seeking division of property among persons claiming interests in it.
predicates.purchaser_had_independent_income: The person who acquired the disputed property had employment or another independent source of income.
predicates.purchase_funds_attributed_to_personal_re: The evidence attributed payment for the property to the purchaser's own resources.
predicates.family_earnings_only_basis_for_joint_cha: The claim that the property was jointly owned rested on another family member's earnings rather than evidence tracing joint family funds into the purchase.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired by an individual from personal earnings is self-acquired when there is no evidence that ancestral family assets funded the acquisition.
material_facts: The testator received a salary and remuneration for service to the Maharaja in addition to income from his profession.
The evidence showed that the Maharaja gave land and constructed a building before giving it to the testator.
There was no evidence that family jewels or cash were used to acquire the property, and there was hardly any evidence of an ancestral nucleus.
The lower courts found the property to be the testator’s self-acquisition.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that earnings from practising a hereditary profession were not joint family property and relied on the testator’s means and the absence of evidence that an ancestral nucleus was used to acquire the property.
members.conclusion: The finding that the property in item 1(a) was the testator’s self-acquired property was confirmed.

predicates.appeal_disputes_property_character: An appeal disputes whether property is an individual’s separate property or joint family property.
predicates.individual_had_personal_means: The individual had personal earnings or other means capable of funding the acquisition.
predicates.no_evidence_ancestral_assets_funded_acqu: There is no evidence that ancestral family assets were used to fund the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A contract to cut standing trees does not transfer ownership of the timber as goods before the trees are identified and felled where the contract leaves part of each tree standing.
material_facts: The contract entitled the claimant to cut teak trees meeting a stated girth description, so the qualifying trees had to be identified.
The contract required the stumps to remain above the ground, meaning the whole trees were not to be removed.
The trees had not been felled before the estate vested in the State.
members.legal_principle: Under section 19 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, property in unascertained goods does not pass until the goods are ascertained. Trees agreed to be severed may be goods, but here the trees had not been ascertained and the contract did not provide for sale of the whole trees. Property in the cut timber could pass at the earliest upon felling. Sections 3 and 4 of the Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 governed vesting of the forest and trees in the State; the Court also relied on Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, State of M.P. v. Yakinuddin, and Mulamchand v. State of M.P. on vesting.
members.conclusion: The claimant had not become the owner of the trees as goods; property in the timber could pass only when the trees were felled, and the trees had vested in the State before that occurred.

predicates.claim_to_enforce_tree_cutting_contract_a: A claimant seeks to enforce against the State a contract granting a right to cut trees.
predicates.standing_trees_required_identification_b: The contract describes the trees to be cut by characteristics that must be checked to identify the qualifying trees.
predicates.contract_required_trees_to_be_felled_bef: The contract contemplates that trees are to be felled before the timber is removed.
predicates.estate_vested_before_felling: The estate vested in the State before the contracted trees were felled.

members.legal_issue: A forest contract that leaves title to standing trees with the seller until the trees are felled, checked, and removed does not make the buyer liable to purchase tax on standing trees agreed to be severed.
material_facts: The forest contracts were subject to conditions governing payment, the commencement of work, felling, routes of removal, inspection, and removal from the contract area.
The contractor could lose the right to trees not removed within the contract period, and forest officers controlled and supervised the operations.
The contractor acquired the trees only after felling, compliance with the contract conditions, inspection, and removal from the contract area.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 18–23 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the passing of property depends on whether goods are specific or ascertained, whether the contract is unconditional, whether the goods are in a deliverable state, and the parties’ intention as shown by the contract, conduct, and circumstances. The Court relied on Badri Prasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh in considering when property in standing trees passes.
members.conclusion: The timber contracts were agreements to sell standing trees, not completed purchases of standing trees agreed to be severed; the challenged purchase-tax provisions did not apply to those transactions.

predicates.forest_contract_purchase_tax_dispute: The dispute concerns purchase tax claimed in connection with a contract for acquiring forest trees.
predicates.contract_conditions_prevent_immediate_fe: The buyer must satisfy contractual conditions and follow prescribed controls before felling and removing the trees.
predicates.title_passes_only_after_felling_inspecti: The parties’ arrangements provide that the buyer acquires the trees only after felling, inspection, and removal.

members.legal_issue: A buyer under a contract for future timber does not acquire title to uncut standing trees where the timber remains unascertained and the seller must cut and prepare it for delivery before the estate vests in the State.
material_facts: The contract covered logs meeting a specified girth, to be cut by the seller from trees in the seller’s forests and supplied in stages; the buyer had no right under the deed to cut the trees.
The logs had not been cut and appropriated to the contract before the estate vested in the State.
The agreement did not show an intention that title should pass before the timber was cut, identified, and put into a deliverable state.
The buyer sought compensation from the State for timber that remained standing when the estate vested.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(7), 18, and 21 of the Sale of Goods Act, things attached to land may be goods if agreed to be severed, but title to unascertained goods does not pass until they are ascertained and, where the seller must act to put them into a deliverable state, that act is completed and the buyer is informed. The court also applied sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, under which proprietary rights including rights in trees vested in the State free of encumbrances. It relied on Badische Anilin Fabrik v. Hickson, Kursell v. Timber Operators and Contractors Ltd., Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel & Company v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Shrimati Shantabai v. State of Bombay, Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Yakunuddin.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that title to the logs had not passed to the buyer before vesting and upheld the rejection of the buyer’s claim to cut the standing trees after vesting.

predicates.suit_or_appeal_claims_right_to_cut_stand: The proceeding concerns a buyer’s claim to cut standing timber after the estate containing it has vested in the State.
predicates.contract_covers_unascertained_future_goo: The contract concerns future goods not individually identified when the contract is made.
predicates.seller_must_cut_or_prepare_goods_for_del: The seller is required to cut or otherwise prepare the goods before delivery.
predicates.goods_not_severed_and_appropriated_befor: The goods were neither separated from the land nor appropriated to the contract before the estate vested.

members.legal_issue: A person who receives rent as the tenant’s recognized landlord may qualify as a landlord under rent-control law even when acting for a deceased owner’s estate or other persons.
material_facts: The deceased owner had let the premises to the tenant.
After the owner’s death, the tenant paid rent to the respondent, who initially received it on behalf of the deceased owner’s estate and later issued receipts in his own name.
The respondent functioned as the person receiving rent from the tenant.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(e) and 2(l) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, define landlord and tenant by reference to the receipt or entitlement to receive rent and the person by whom or on whose behalf rent is payable. In rent-control proceedings before a special tribunal, the practical relationship between the rent collector and the tenant governs; concepts of estoppel or the Transfer of Property Act need not be imported inflexibly.
members.conclusion: The respondent qualified as the landlord for purposes of the rent-control proceedings.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_to_claimant: The tenant paid rent to the person claiming the right to bring the eviction proceeding.
predicates.claimant_received_rent_as_recognized_lan: The person claiming eviction received rent in a capacity recognized by the tenant as landlord, including on behalf of an estate or other persons.

members.legal_issue: A usufructuary mortgagee entitled to possess the premises and receive their rent is a landlord within the rent-control statute’s definition.
material_facts: The owner granted the respondents a usufructuary mortgage over the premises occupied by a tenant.
The mortgage entitled the respondents to possession and to receive the property’s rents and profits on their own account.
The respondents sought eviction of the tenant under the rent-control statute.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(h) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 defines landlord inclusively to cover a person receiving or entitled to receive rent. Under Section 58(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a usufructuary mortgagee is entitled to possession or to receive rents and profits and apply them to interest or the mortgage money. The Court’s conclusion accords with V. Baluswamy Servai v. N. Raju Servai, T. Ezhumalai v. Padmavathi Ammal, Aswatharamiah v. Special Deputy Commissioner, and the Full Bench ruling in R. Vijendra v. H.R. & A.C.
members.conclusion: A usufructuary mortgagee with possession is a landlord within the statutory definition because the mortgagee is entitled to receive rent on their own account.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and usufructuary_mortgage and entitled_to_possession and entitled_to_rent_on_own_account

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A person seeks to evict a tenant in a proceeding under rent-control law.
predicates.usufructuary_mortgage: The property owner has granted a mortgage under which the mortgagee receives the property’s usufruct.
predicates.entitled_to_possession: The mortgagee is entitled to possess the mortgaged property.
predicates.entitled_to_rent_on_own_account: The mortgagee is entitled to receive the premises’ rent on the mortgagee’s own account.

members.legal_issue: A trustee who receives rent on behalf of a trust falls within the statutory meaning of landlord.
material_facts: The person charged was a trustee of the trust that owned the premises.
He received rent on account of and on behalf of the trust.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(3) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 defines “landlord” to include a person who receives, or is entitled to receive, rent on account of, on behalf of, or for the benefit of another person, or as trustee for another person.
members.conclusion: The person came within the statutory definition of landlord.

predicates.rental_control_offence_case: The proceeding concerns an alleged rent-control offense based on receipt of an additional payment in connection with a tenancy.
predicates.trustee_received_rent_for_another: A trustee received rent for premises on behalf of, or for the benefit of, another person or trust.

members.legal_issue: An entire law must be struck down when its unconstitutional ceiling and compensation mechanisms are pivotal provisions on which the law's operation depends.
material_facts: The law's operation depended on its provisions fixing the ceiling on land holdings and determining compensation for acquired land.
The Court found both mechanisms discriminatory and unconstitutional.
The ceiling and compensation provisions were pivotal to the law's operation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that when pivotal provisions are unconstitutional and the working of the entire law depends on them, the whole law must fall. It treated the ceiling and compensation provisions as essential to the law's operation after holding them violative of Article 14.
members.conclusion: The entire law had to be struck down as unconstitutional.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_integrated_land_reform_law and ceiling_mechanism_unconstitutional and compensation_mechanism_unconstitutional and entire_law_depends_on_both_mechanisms

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_integrated_l: A constitutional challenge concerned a law whose provisions formed an integrated land-reform scheme.
predicates.ceiling_mechanism_unconstitutional: The court determined that the law's mechanism for limiting land holdings was unconstitutional.
predicates.compensation_mechanism_unconstitutional: The court determined that the law's mechanism for compensating acquired land was unconstitutional.
predicates.entire_law_depends_on_both_mechanisms: The court found that the law's overall operation depended on both mechanisms and that they were pivotal provisions.

members.legal_issue: A property-transfer scheme that cannot be separated into valid and invalid applications is invalid as a whole when its operation includes acquisitions requiring constitutional property-taking safeguards.
material_facts: The law applied where the rightful owner's title could be extinguished after substitute property or cash was provided.
The Court observed that, where the property remained in the compensation pool, extinguishing the owner's title would vest the property in the government.
The Court acknowledged that a case in which title had vested in a displaced person might fall under a different constitutional provision, but held that the law was not severable.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Article 31(2A) of the Constitution, under which some transfers of title to a displaced person might be treated differently, but held that the challenged section was not severable. The Court therefore declared the section void as a whole under Article 31(2).
members.conclusion: The law was not severable and had to be declared invalid as a whole.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_integrated_p: A party in a constitutional challenge disputes a single scheme for transferring property and extinguishing the former owner's title.
predicates.scheme_covers_government_and_private_ves: The scheme operates in circumstances where title may vest in the government and in circumstances where title may vest in a private recipient.
predicates.scheme_is_not_severable: The scheme's valid and invalid applications cannot be separated from one another.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition statute is invalid in its entirety when its central transfer and compensation provisions are invalid and cannot be severed from the rest of the statute.
material_facts: The transfer and vesting provisions and the compensation provisions formed the central mechanism of the statute.
Those provisions impaired the constitutional guarantee of compensation.
The central provisions were not severable from the remaining provisions.
members.legal_principle: Where the provisions that effect the acquisition and prescribe compensation are invalid and are not severable from the remaining statutory scheme, the statute as a whole cannot stand.
members.conclusion: The statute was invalid in its entirety, and action taken under it was unauthorised.

rule.if: statutory_validity_challenge and central_transfer_provisions_invalid and central_compensation_provisions_invalid and provisions_not_severable

predicates.statutory_validity_challenge: A person challenged the validity of a statute that transferred an undertaking and provided for compensation.
predicates.central_transfer_provisions_invalid: The statutory provisions effecting the transfer and vesting were held constitutionally invalid.
predicates.central_compensation_provisions_invalid: The statutory provisions determining compensation were held constitutionally invalid.
predicates.provisions_not_severable: The invalid transfer and compensation provisions could not be separated from the rest of the statutory scheme.

members.legal_issue: A court may treat a counterclaim included in a written statement as a plaint in a cross-suit when the pleading in substance states a claim and contains the necessary particulars for the relief sought.
material_facts: The defendants included a claim for accounts of a dissolved partnership in their written statement and described it as a counterclaim.
They valued the claim and paid the court fee applicable to a plaint seeking that relief.
The counterclaim was held not maintainable as a counterclaim, and the defendants asked that it be treated as a plaint in a cross-suit.
members.legal_principle: A counterclaim is statutory, and the claim here was not within Order VIII, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. But that does not prevent a court from construing pleadings reasonably: where what is in substance a plaint is made part of a written statement, the court may treat it as a plaint and grant relief available on that pleading. Saya Bya v. Maung Kyaw Shun was relied on in support of this approach; Currimbhoy and Co. Ltd. v. Creet and (Mian) Pir Bux v. Mohomed Tahar establish that an unsupported counterclaim is not maintainable, but do not preclude its treatment as a cross-suit. Gour Chandra Goswami v. Chairman of the Nabadwip Municipality was distinguished.
members.conclusion: There was no legal objection to treating the counterclaim as a plaint in a cross-suit, and the High Court's order to do so was upheld.

rule.if: counterclaim_conversion_request and pleading_contains_independent_claim and pleading_supports_claimed_relief and cross_claim_properly_valued_and_fee_paid

predicates.counterclaim_conversion_request: A defendant asked the court to treat a claim included in a written statement as a plaint in a cross-suit.
predicates.pleading_contains_independent_claim: The written statement included a claim for relief independent of the plaintiff's claim.
predicates.pleading_supports_claimed_relief: The allegations in the written statement set out a claim capable of supporting the relief sought.
predicates.cross_claim_properly_valued_and_fee_paid: The defendant valued the cross-claim and paid the court fee applicable to the relief sought.

members.legal_issue: For limitation purposes, a cross-suit formed by treating a counterclaim as a plaint is treated as filed when the written statement containing the counterclaim was filed, if conversion adds no allegations or relief.
material_facts: The defendants' written statement contained the claim for partnership accounts and was filed within the applicable limitation period.
The defendants later requested that the counterclaim be treated as a plaint in a cross-suit.
They sought no new allegations or relief in the conversion, and the claim had already been valued and stamped as a plaint.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, leave to amend will ordinarily be refused where an amendment takes away a legal right accrued by lapse of time, save in exceptional cases. That principle applies to added allegations or fresh relief, not a clarification that does not substantively add to or alter the original pleading. The Court approved the rule in the Bombay High Court decision in Bai Bhuri v. Rai Ambalal Chotalal. It also referred to Article 106 of the Limitation Act when considering the limitation period for the accounting claim.
members.conclusion: The cross-suit was treated as filed on the date the written statement containing the counterclaim was filed, not on the date the court ordered conversion.

predicates.counterclaim_conversion_request: A defendant asked the court to treat a claim included in a written statement as a plaint in a cross-suit.
predicates.original_pleading_contains_claim: The written statement already contained the claim later treated as a cross-suit.
predicates.conversion_adds_no_allegations_or_relief: Treating the claim as a plaint does not add allegations or seek relief not contained in the original pleading.

members.legal_issue: When a counterclaim is treated as a plaint in a cross-suit, both sides may be allowed to file fresh pleadings that conform to their new procedural roles, provided the claim is not substantially changed.
material_facts: The plaintiff's reply had been filed in response to a counterclaim rather than a plaint in a cross-suit.
The defendants sought permission to replace the counterclaim with a pleading in the form of a plaint.
The defendants' replacement pleading was to contain no substantial variation in allegations or relief.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that fairness required the plaintiff to have an opportunity to plead defences to the claim as a cross-suit. It permitted the defendants to recast their pleading in the form of a plaint subject to the stated restriction, without limiting the court's power to permit later amendment under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was allowed to file a fresh written statement, and the defendants were allowed to file a fresh plaint provided there was no substantial variation in their allegations or relief.

predicates.counterclaim_treated_as_cross_suit: The court treated a claim included in a written statement as a plaint in a cross-suit.
predicates.existing_reply_filed_to_counterclaim: The plaintiff's existing response was filed on the footing that the claim was a counterclaim.
predicates.replacement_claim_substantially_unchange: The replacement pleading makes no substantial variation in the allegations or relief sought.

members.legal_issue: An inaccurate statement in a by-law’s preamble about the source of authority does not invalidate the by-law when the authority exists elsewhere.
material_facts: The by-laws’ preamble cited statutory clauses that did not apply.
The municipality nevertheless had power under other provisions to make the challenged by-laws.
members.legal_principle: The validity of a by-law is tested by whether the body had power to make it, not by whether its preamble accurately identifies the source of that power. The Court relied on P. Balakotaiah v. Union of India & Ors., [1958] S.C.R. 1052.
members.conclusion: The incorrect citation of authority in the preamble did not affect the validity of the by-laws.

predicates.bylaw_has_independent_authority: The body that made the by-law possessed authority under a provision other than the one cited in the preamble.
predicates.preamble_cites_inapplicable_power: The by-law’s preamble identifies a source of authority that does not apply.

members.legal_issue: A municipal notice is not invalid merely because it cites a different source of authority when the action is authorized under another applicable power.
material_facts: The municipality issued the challenged notice under a provision concerning unauthorized building work.
The notice was not issued under the separate provision that made the current owner liable for unauthorized work.
The statutory scheme authorized the municipality to require the current owner to address the unauthorized work.
members.legal_principle: A statutory provision may be read with other provisions of the same enactment, and a lawful exercise of power may be supported by the power that authorizes it even if the notice cited a different provision. The Court relied on Pitamber Vajirshet v. Dhondu Navalapa, L. Hazari Mal Kuthiala v. Income-tax Officer, Special Circle, Ambala Cantt., Hukumchand Mills Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Nani Gopal Biswas v. The Municipality of Howrah. It also applied the principle that statutory language may receive an extended meaning when fairly susceptible of it to advance legislative purpose, but may not be strained to include cases plainly omitted from its natural meaning.
members.conclusion: The notice was not unauthorized or illegal merely because it was not issued under the provision relied on to support its validity.

predicates.municipal_notice_validity_challenge: A person challenged the validity of a municipal notice.
predicates.notice_cites_different_power: The notice identified a source of authority different from the one supporting the challenged action.
predicates.alternative_lawful_authority_exists: The applicable legal framework empowered the municipality to take the challenged action under another source of authority.

members.legal_issue: A demolition notice is not invalid merely because it cites an incorrect statutory source if the power to issue it is traceable to a valid source.
material_facts: A demolition notice identified the applicable town-planning scheme and stated that the land and temporary structure were affected by it.

The notice referred to a municipal provision as the source for carrying out demolition, but the notice was in substance issued under a special regulation incorporated into the town-planning legislation.
The special regulation supplied authority to require removal of temporary structures subject to a removal condition.
members.legal_principle: The notice was issued under Special Regulation 36, which became part of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 under section 51(3). Regulations 36 and 38, section 55(1)(a), and Rule 28 made under section 87 supported enforcement. An incorrect citation does not vitiate an exercise of power when the power can be traced to a legitimate source. Afzal Ullah v. State of Uttar Pradesh, J.K. Steel Ltd. v. Union of India, N.B. Sanjana v. Elphinstone Mill, and H.L. Mehra v. Union of India were cited.
members.conclusion: The notice was validly issued under the special regulation, and the mistaken reference to the municipal provision did not invalidate it.

rule.if: demolition_notice_case and notice_identifies_applicable_scheme and valid_law_authorizes_demolition_notice and notice_cites_wrong_power

predicates.demolition_notice_case: The case concerns the validity of a notice directing removal or demolition of a structure.
predicates.notice_identifies_applicable_scheme: The notice identifies the public scheme affecting the land or structure.
predicates.valid_law_authorizes_demolition_notice: A valid legal source authorizes the authority to require removal or demolition in the circumstances.
predicates.notice_cites_wrong_power: The notice refers to an incorrect legal power despite being traceable to a valid source.

members.legal_issue: A transitional provision continuing existing municipal taxes does not authorize a tax in a newly included area where that tax was not being levied there when the successor law took effect.
material_facts: The properties at issue were in villages that were outside the municipality before their inclusion.
The property owners had paid taxes to the village panchayat, but no municipal property tax was being levied on their properties when the successor municipal law took effect in the villages.
The municipality demanded property tax for the period beginning when the villages were included, relying on the transitional provision for continuing existing taxes.
members.legal_principle: Clause 12 of Schedule IX of the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, was a transitional provision authorizing continuation of taxes lawfully being levied at the commencement of the Act, provided they could lawfully be levied under the Act. It did not authorize a tax on property in an area where that tax was not then being levied.
members.conclusion: The transitional provision did not authorize the municipality to levy property tax on the newly included properties for that earlier period.

rule.if: municipal_tax_continuation_case and property_area_newly_added and not tax_being_levied_in_area_at_transition

predicates.municipal_tax_continuation_case: The proceeding concerns whether a municipality may continue a tax under a transitional arrangement.
predicates.property_area_newly_added: The property subject to the proposed tax is in an area newly brought within the municipality.
predicates.tax_being_levied_in_area_at_transition: A municipal council was levying the relevant tax on the property in that area when the successor municipal regime took effect.

members.legal_issue: An opportunity to object to the inclusion of an area within a municipality is not an opportunity to object to a later property tax imposed on that area.
material_facts: The government published a notification stating its intention to include the villages within the municipality.
Residents could object to matters contained in that notification, which concerned the proposed inclusion of the villages.
The municipality later sought to impose property tax on the newly included area without providing the separate tax-objection process for the period in dispute.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(2) and 3(3) of the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, allowed objections to the proposed inclusion of an area. Those objections concerned the contents of the inclusion notification, not a proposed tax. A tax question arose after the final inclusion notification, and a tax resolution then had to comply with section 81, including its first-time tax objection procedure.
members.conclusion: The inclusion notification did not replace the required opportunity to object to the imposition of property tax.

predicates.municipal_tax_objection_case: The proceeding concerns whether residents had a proper opportunity to object to a municipal tax.
predicates.residents_could_object_only_to_area_incl: Residents were invited to object to a proposal to add their area to a municipality, rather than to a proposal to impose a tax there.
predicates.tax_objection_process_not_separately_pro: The municipality did not separately invite and consider objections to the proposed tax.

members.legal_issue: Including an area within a municipality does not automatically extend an existing municipal tax or an earlier tax resolution to that area.
material_facts: The government issued a final notification including the villages within the municipality.
The municipality had previously levied property tax in its existing areas but had not imposed it in the newly included villages.
The council later adopted a resolution to impose property tax in the newly included area after considering objections, but demanded tax for an earlier period.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(4) of the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, brought the Act's provisions into force in an included area, including sections 81 and 83. It did not extend earlier tax resolutions automatically to that area. The tax-imposition procedures in sections 81 and 83 had to be followed. The Court explained Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana, which likewise held that inclusion of an area did not by itself authorize a tax levy without the required tax procedure.
members.conclusion: The inclusion of the villages did not automatically extend the existing tax or prior tax resolutions to them; the municipality had to follow the statutory tax-imposition procedure for the new area.

predicates.municipal_tax_extension_case: The proceeding concerns whether an existing municipal tax or resolution extends to a newly added area.
predicates.area_added_to_municipality: The government included a local area within an existing municipality.
predicates.tax_resolution_predated_area_inclusion: The council adopted the relevant tax resolution before the local area was included in the municipality.

members.legal_issue: Succession to an estate held by a female limited owner opens when she dies, and the law then in force governs who succeeds to the estate, provided it had not already vested in another person.
material_facts: The last male owner died before the Hindu Succession Act commenced, and his widow inherited the estate as a limited owner.
The widow was not in possession of the property when the Act commenced because of the earlier gift and decree.
The widow made a second gift after the Act commenced and died afterward.
The appellants claimed as reversioners under the earlier customary law; the respondent was the daughter of the last male owner.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed Moniram Kolita v. Keri Kolitani and Duni Chand v. Anar Kali: succession to the last male owner's estate opens on the termination of the female limited owner's estate, and the heirs are determined as if the last male owner had died at that time. The words “dying intestate” in section 8 describe intestacy and do not make the section retrospective; section 6, by contrast, expressly refers to a male Hindu dying after commencement. The Court explained and distinguished Eramma v. Verrupanna, approved Banso v. Charan Singh and Kuldip Singh v. Karnail Singh, and overruled Kempiah v. Girigamma. It also relied on Eastend Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and Venkatachalam v. Bombay Dyeing & Manufacturing Co. Ltd. concerning the consequences of a legal fiction. A right that had already vested under the earlier law could not be divested.
members.conclusion: Succession opened when the widow died and was governed by section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, not by the earlier customary law. The appeal was dismissed because the appellants' reversionary interest was only a chance of succession, not a vested right.

rule.if: limited_owner_succession_case and limited_owner_inherited_last_owner_estate and limited_owner_died_after_legal_change and claimants_had_no_vested_right

predicates.limited_owner_succession_case: The proceeding concerns who succeeds to an estate after the death of a female limited owner.
predicates.limited_owner_inherited_last_owner_estat: A female limited owner held the estate by succeeding to its last full owner.
predicates.limited_owner_died_after_legal_change: The female limited owner died after a change in the law governing succession had taken effect.
predicates.claimants_had_no_vested_right: The competing claimants held only a contingent chance of succession before the female limited owner died.

members.legal_issue: The succession rules in force when a female life-estate holder dies govern succession to the estate of a Hindu male who died intestate before those rules came into force.
material_facts: The last male owner held the property absolutely and died intestate before the succession reform came into force.
His mother held the property for life and died after the reform came into force; his sister then held the property for life and died later.
The claimant was the last male owner's sister's son, while the competing claimant was his paternal uncle.
The courts found that the property was not coparcenary property and had not been disposed of by will.
members.legal_principle: Under the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, section 1(2), the Act applies to Mitakshara separate property not held in coparcenary and not disposed of by will; section 3 places the specified relations, including a sister's son, ahead of a paternal uncle. Following Lala Duni Chand v. Musammat Anar Kali, the relevant time is when succession opens on termination of the female life estate, not the earlier death of the male owner. The Court also relied on Annagouda Nathgouda Patil v. Court of Wards for the Act's scope and referred to Shrimati Shakuntala Devi v. Kaushalya Devi, Rajpali Kunwar v. Sarju Rai, Pokhan Dusadh v. Mst. Manoa, Lakshmi v. Anantharama, and Bindeshari Singh v. Baij Nath Singh in support of when succession opens. The earlier contrary views in Krishnan Chettiar v. Manikammal and Kanhaiya Lal v. Mst. Champa Devi had been overruled by later Full Bench decisions.
members.conclusion: The succession opened when the female life estate terminated, so the reform applied notwithstanding that the last male owner had died earlier. The sister's son was preferred to the paternal uncle, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_succession_appeal and male_owner_died_intestate and property_was_separate and property_was_not_willed and succession_reform_was_in_force_when_life_estate_ended and claimant_is_sisters_son and competing_heir_is_paternal_uncle

predicates.civil_succession_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning competing claims to succeed to a deceased person's estate.
predicates.male_owner_died_intestate: The last male owner died without leaving a will.
predicates.property_was_separate: The property belonged separately to the last male owner and was not held in coparcenary.
predicates.property_was_not_willed: The last male owner did not dispose of the property by will.
predicates.succession_reform_was_in_force_when_life: The succession reform was in force when the female holder's life estate ended.
predicates.claimant_is_sisters_son: The claimant is the sister's son of the last male owner.
predicates.competing_heir_is_paternal_uncle: The competing heir is the last male owner's paternal uncle.

members.legal_issue: When a female life estate ends after the succession reform has come into force, the last male owner's sister may succeed in her own right as a preferential heir and take a life estate.
material_facts: The last male owner died intestate, and his mother held the property for life.
The mother's life estate ended after the succession reform had come into force.
The last male owner's sister was the next female holder of the property, and the Court stated that she succeeded as a preferential heir, though her interest was itself a life estate.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that the sister's succession could be regarded as opening on termination of the mother's life estate and that the sister succeeded under section 3(b) of the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, with only a life estate. This statement was made although the point had not been raised by the parties.
members.conclusion: Succession could be treated as having opened when the mother's life estate ended, at which point the sister succeeded in her own right as a preferential heir with a life estate.

predicates.female_life_estate_ended_after_reform: A female holder's life estate ended after the succession reform came into force.
predicates.claimant_is_sister_of_last_male_owner: The person claiming through the ended life estate is the last male owner's sister.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may remain in legal possession of residential premises while living elsewhere if the premises are retained under the landlord’s control.
material_facts: The landlady lived in another town and did not actually reside in the premises at the time.
The premises were locked and contained her household effects.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, occupation for residential purposes is not limited to an owner’s physical presence. A landlord may retain possession while away by keeping household effects in locked premises or leaving the premises in another’s charge. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The landlady’s absence from the premises did not mean that she was not in possession of them; her possession remained sufficient for the landlord-nomination provision to apply.

predicates.rent_control_allotment_proceeding: The matter concerned the allotment of premises that had become vacant under a rent-control regime.
predicates.landlord_resided_elsewhere: The landlord lived elsewhere rather than physically residing in the premises.
predicates.landlord_retained_control_of_premises: The landlord kept the premises under their control, including by leaving household effects there or keeping them locked.

members.legal_issue: A landlord who retains control of part of a residential building may be treated as occupying it even without actually residing there, allowing release of the tenanted part under the statutory rule.
material_facts: The landlord retained part of the house when letting another part to a tenant.
The landlord kept household effects in the retained part and made casual visits, although he generally lived elsewhere with relatives.
The landlord sought release of the tenanted part so he could occupy the whole house.
The tenant argued that the landlord was not in actual physical occupation and that the retained portion was insufficient for the landlord’s needs.
members.legal_principle: Explanation (iv) to section 21(1)(b) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 treats the landlord’s occupation of the remaining residential part as conclusive proof of bona fide requirement of the tenanted part. In Babu Singh Chauhan v. Rajkumari Jain, the Court treated possession as synonymous with occupation and held that keeping household effects in locked premises can amount to occupation. A tenant has no right to interfere with the landlord’s choice of how to use the property.
members.conclusion: Occupation includes constructive occupation through retained control, including keeping household effects in the premises; the landlord’s lack of actual residence did not prevent application of Explanation (iv), and the entire tenanted premises were ordered released. A tenant cannot dictate how the landlord uses or lives in the landlord’s property.

predicates.residential_part_release_proceeding: A landlord sought release of a tenanted part of a building for residential use.

predicates.tenant_occupies_other_part: The tenant occupied another part of the same building.

members.legal_issue: When the whole building is one unit and the landlord occupies part of it, the landlord may obtain release of the other part occupied by the tenant.
material_facts: The trial court, relying on a commissioner’s report, found that the entire building constituted one single unit.
The landlord occupied one part of the building, while the tenant occupied the other part.
The landlord sought release of the tenant’s part.
members.legal_principle: Under Explanation (iv) to section 21(1)(b) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the landlord’s occupation of the remaining residential part conclusively establishes bona fide requirement of the tenanted part. Applying its decision in the companion appeal, the Court held that occupation of part of a single-unit building entitled the landlord to release of the other part.
members.conclusion: Because the building was one unit and the landlord occupied part of it, the landlord was entitled to release of the remaining part occupied by the tenant.
