members.legal_issue: Land capable of cultivation may be treated as arable for an urgent acquisition even when it is situated in an urban area and includes some buildings.
material_facts: The acquired tract included six acres belonging to the respondents and formed part of a larger area.
The respondents' land consisted of open land as well as buildings and servant quarters, but the buildings were not acquired for the public purpose and only the servant quarters were acquired.
The land was capable of raising crops, although it was situated in an urban area.
The High Court held that the land was not arable or waste land and that dispensing with the inquiry was unlawful.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17(4) and 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 govern dispensing with the inquiry. Whether land is arable or waste is a mixed question of fact and law that depends on the circumstances; a pragmatic assessment is required, and land capable of raising crops may be arable even in an urban area. The Court relied on Ishwarlal Girdharilal Joshi v. State of Gujarat, (1968) 2 SCR 267, and Raja Anand Brahma Shah v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1967 SC 1801.
members.conclusion: The land was arable because it was capable of cultivation, and the exercise of the power to dispense with the inquiry was not bad in law; the High Court's contrary view was erroneous.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_case: The government acquired land for a public purpose using an urgent procedure that dispensed with the usual inquiry.
predicates.land_capable_of_cultivation: The acquired land was capable of being cultivated, whether or not it was situated in an urban area.

members.legal_issue: A few structures within a large tract acquired for urgent planned urban development do not require the structured portions to be excluded from the development scheme, and the land's general nature and condition determine whether it is waste or arable.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large tract for planned urban development.
The tract was generally described as arable, although a few structures stood on small portions of it.
Separating the small built-up portions from the rest would impede applying the urgent acquisition process consistently across the scheme.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and held that, for a large urgent planned-development scheme, it would not be proper to leave small portions containing superstructures outside the scheme. Whether land is waste or arable is assessed by its general nature and condition.
members.conclusion: The presence of a few structures did not justify excluding those small portions from the acquisition; the general nature and condition of the land govern its characterization as waste or arable.

predicates.urgent_planned_urban_development: The land is being acquired for an urgent planned urban-development scheme.
predicates.large_tract_acquired: The acquisition covers a large tract of land.
predicates.only_small_portions_have_structures: Structures stand on only small portions of the larger tract.

members.legal_issue: Land actually under cultivation is arable land for the purpose of the urgency possession procedure.
material_facts: The land at issue was under cultivation.
The acquisition proceeded under the statutory urgency procedure, which permitted early possession of waste or arable land.
The Act provided for compensation for standing crops and trees on land taken under the urgency procedure.
members.legal_principle: The Court interpreted section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including section 17(3), which provides for compensation for standing crops and trees. The reference to crops shows that arable land may be cultivated or fallow; land on which crops are grown is not excluded from being arable. The Court approved Baldeo Singh v. State of U.P., A.I.R. 1965 All. 433, Smt. Lakshmi Devi v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1965 Pat. 400, and Guntur Ramalakshmamma v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, A.I.R. 1967 A.P. 280, and overruled Sadruddin Suleman v. J.H. Patwardhan, A.I.R. 1965 Bom. 224.
members.conclusion: Arable land includes land actually under cultivation as well as land capable of cultivation.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned acquisition of land under a procedure allowing early possession of land of a specified kind.
predicates.land_actually_cultivated: The land was actually being cultivated.
predicates.land_fit_for_cultivation: The land was capable of or fit for cultivation.

members.legal_issue: A change in the statutory vesting of village common land does not by itself alter the land’s character or extinguish established community rights.
material_facts: The ponds and canals were recorded as common lands and had long been used by local people.
A respondent argued that repeal of the earlier land law and vesting of the land in the State ended the community’s rights.
The Court found that the change in statutory vesting did not alter the land’s character contrary to the revenue records or defeat long-established rights.
members.legal_principle: Relying on Chigurupati Venkata Subbayya v. Palaguda Anjayya, (1972) 1 SCC 521, the Court held that the transfer of land to the Government, even where a law extinguishes rights created by former landholders, does not necessarily extinguish community rights that originated independently. The repeal of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 and the vesting provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Revenue Code, 2006 did not change the land’s character or defeat established communal rights.
members.conclusion: The repeal and transfer of title to the State did not extinguish the local community’s established rights in the common water bodies.

predicates.appeal_concerning_village_commons: A party brought an appeal concerning land used as a village common.
predicates.land_has_longstanding_community_use: Local people had established community use of the land over a long period.
predicates.statutory_change_transfers_title_to_stat: A statutory change transferred title to the land to the State.

members.legal_issue: A declaration that communal land is no longer needed for its original purpose does not by itself convert the land to another use or extinguish its communal character.
material_facts: The lands had been set apart and used for irrigation and drainage, and their communal character had been accepted in the proceedings.
The Collector declared that some of the lands were no longer needed for their original purpose but made no further written direction concerning their use or conversion.
The remaining lands continued to be treated as communal lands, and no conversion order was made for them.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(16), 20-A(1)(a) and (b), and 20-A(2) of the Madras Estates Land Act, a declaration that communal land is no longer needed for its original purpose must be followed by a written direction specifying another communal purpose or converting it to ryotwari or landholder's ryoti land; absent that direction, the land cannot be assigned or used for another purpose.
members.conclusion: The lands remained communal because the Collector had not made the further written direction required to change their use or convert them.

predicates.communal_land_set_apart_for_common_use: The land had been set apart for and used for a purpose shared by the local community.
predicates.collector_declared_original_purpose_unne: The Collector declared that the land was no longer needed for the purpose for which it had originally been set apart.
predicates.collector_made_no_written_direction: The Collector made no written direction specifying another communal use or converting the land to a private agricultural category.

members.legal_issue: Vesting of an estate in the Government does not by itself extinguish community rights over communal land that were not created by a landholder.
material_facts: The abolition enactment transferred the estate, including communal lands, to the Government.
The community's rights over the disputed lands were not created by the principal landholder or another landholder.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 transferred the estate to the Government and ended rights and interests created by the principal or another landholder; it did not abrogate community rights that were not created by a landholder.
members.conclusion: The vesting of the lands in the Government did not extinguish the community's rights over them.

predicates.estate_vested_in_government: An enactment transferred the estate, including communal land, to the Government.
predicates.community_rights_were_not_created_by_lan: The community's rights over the land did not originate in an act of the principal landholder or another landholder.

members.legal_issue: A tenant of agricultural land governed by the tenancy legislation on the statutory vesting day becomes its deemed purchaser by operation of law, and the purchase-price inquiry proceeds unless the purchase is rendered ineffective under the legislation.
material_facts: The land was agricultural land governed by the tenancy legislation and was not exempt under the existing reservation notification.
The tenant held the land on the statutory vesting day.
An inquiry to determine the purchase price was pending.
members.legal_principle: Section 32 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, as amended, provided for transfer of ownership to the tenant by operation of law on the tillers' day. Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay explained that the purchase is effective unless it is rendered ineffective in the circumstances specified by the legislation. Section 32G provides for determination of the purchase price.
members.conclusion: The tenant became the deemed purchaser and the tribunal must proceed with the inquiry to determine the price.

rule.if: tenancy_purchase_inquiry and agricultural_land_governed_by_tenancy_law and tenant_held_land_on_vesting_day and purchase_not_rendered_ineffective

predicates.tenancy_purchase_inquiry: The proceeding is an inquiry to determine the purchase price of land under a statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
predicates.agricultural_land_governed_by_tenancy_la: The land is agricultural land governed by the tenancy legislation and is not exempt from it.
predicates.tenant_held_land_on_vesting_day: A tenant held the land on the day ownership was statutorily transferred to tenants.
predicates.purchase_not_rendered_ineffective: The tenant did not decline the purchase or commit a default that rendered it ineffective under the legislation.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s ownership acquired under a statutory land-purchase scheme cannot be defeated by the landlord’s death during an appeal when the tenant had qualified to purchase and deposited the first instalment before that death.
material_facts: The landlord was a large landowner when the tenants applied to purchase the land, and the tenants were found eligible.
The purchase price and instalments were fixed, and each tenant deposited the first instalment.
Under the statutory scheme, depositing the first instalment caused ownership to vest in the tenant.
The landlord died while the appeals were pending, and the heirs’ shares made them small landowners.
The heirs argued that the appeal was a continuation of the original proceeding and that their later status as small landowners deprived the tenants of the right to purchase.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 18(1) and 18(4) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a qualifying tenant of a landlord who is not a small landowner is entitled to purchase the land, and deposit of the first instalment makes the tenant its owner. Section 2(2) defines the small-landowner category. Rights are generally determined by the facts existing when the proceeding is instituted; later events may exceptionally affect the form of relief, including where the relief becomes obsolete, is discretionary, or the governing statute makes later facts relevant. But later events cannot divest a statutory right that has already vested, except where a change in law is made applicable at any stage. The Court relied on P. Venkateswarlu v. Motor & General Traders, Bhajan Lal v. State of Punjab, Patterson v. State of Alabama, Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, and Ramji Lal v. State of Punjab, and applied the principle that an act of the court shall prejudice no one.
members.conclusion: The tenants’ ownership had vested upon deposit of the first instalment and was not undone by the landlord’s subsequent death or the heirs’ resulting status as small landowners. The appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: tenant_purchase_proceeding and tenant_eligible_when_applied and landlord_large_at_application and tenant_deposited_first_installment and first_installment_triggers_ownership and landlord_died_during_appeal and heirs_became_small_landowners

predicates.tenant_purchase_proceeding: A tenant sought to purchase land from a landlord under a statutory land-purchase scheme.
predicates.tenant_eligible_when_applied: The tenant met the scheme’s eligibility requirements when applying to purchase the land.
predicates.landlord_large_at_application: The landlord was not within the scheme’s small-landowner category when the tenant applied.
predicates.tenant_deposited_first_installment: The tenant deposited the first instalment of the purchase price.
predicates.first_installment_triggers_ownership: The applicable purchase scheme provided that depositing the first instalment vested ownership in the tenant.
predicates.landlord_died_during_appeal: The landlord died while an appeal concerning the purchase was pending.
predicates.heirs_became_small_landowners: Succession divided the landlord’s holding so that the heirs fell within the small-landowner category.
predicates.vested_tenant_ownership_survives_later_l: The tenant’s ownership, once vested, is not defeated by the landlord’s later death or a resulting change in the heirs’ landowner status.

members.legal_issue: A tenant becomes the deemed owner of tenanted land, extinguishing the former landowner’s interest, upon depositing the purchase price or first instalment fixed by the competent authority, unless the deposit is made while the fixing order is stayed.
material_facts: The tenant had a statutory right to purchase the tenanted land and applied to the competent authority for that purchase.
The authority fixed the purchase price and permitted payment in instalments.
The tenant deposited the first instalment fixed by the authority before the time allowed, and the order fixing the purchase price was not stayed.
The landowner’s challenge to the tenant’s purchase right had been dismissed, and the tenant’s purchase order had become final.
members.legal_principle: Section 18(1)–(4) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, gives an eligible tenant the right to purchase, provides for determination of the land’s value and purchase price, and declares the tenant to be the owner on deposit of the purchase price or first instalment. Section 18(4)(c) permits recovery of unpaid instalments as arrears of land revenue, confirming that non-payment of a later instalment does not postpone ownership. The Court distinguished Deonandan Prashad Singh v. Ramdhari Chowdhri and Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh, which concerned when a pre-emptor becomes owner under a pre-emption decree, not the effect of a deposit under the Tenures Act.
members.conclusion: On deposit of the purchase price or the first instalment fixed by the Assistant Collector, the tenant became the deemed owner and the landowner ceased to have any interest in the land. A deposit made while the fixing order was stayed would not have that effect.

predicates.purchase_price_fixed_by_competent_author: The competent authority determined the purchase price payable for the land.
predicates.required_deposit_made: The tenant deposited the purchase price or the first instalment fixed by the competent authority.
predicates.deposit_not_made_during_stay: The tenant made the deposit while no competent authority or court had stayed the order fixing the purchase price.

members.legal_issue: Vacant land used for quarrying is not a commercial site merely because quarrying is carried on for profit or rock is broken into smaller pieces.
material_facts: The appellant sought to use land, exempt as a plantation, for quarrying operations involving digging and breaking rocks into pieces for sale.
The respondents challenged the environmental-clearance recommendation on the ground that the land could not be used for a purpose other than plantation.
The appellant argued that quarrying was a commercial activity and that breaking rock was manufacture.
The statute’s principal purpose was to limit landholdings and distribute excess land to landless people.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(5) and 81(1)(q) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 must be read in the context of the Act’s purpose. A beneficial or social-welfare statute is construed purposefully to advance its remedial object, while its exemptions are construed strictly. The distinction between ‘lands’ and ‘sites’ in Section 81 indicates that a commercial site is land occupied by a structure used for an industrial or commercial purpose, not vacant land used for quarrying. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K. A. Gangadharan; Regional Executive, Kerala Fishermen’s Welfare Fund Board v. Fancy Food; Bombay Anand Bhavan Restaurant v. ESI Corporation; Union of India v. Prabhakaran Vijay Kumar; Bharat Singh v. Management of New Delhi Tuberculosis Centre; Workmen v. American Express International Banking Corpn.; Indian Performing Rights Society v. Sanjay Dalia; and Shivram A. Shiroor v. Radhabai Shantram Kowshik.
members.conclusion: Quarry land is not a commercial site and is not exempt from the Act on that ground; the High Court majority’s conclusion was upheld.

predicates.land_ceiling_exemption_appeal: A party appeals a ruling on whether land is exempt from a statutory landholding ceiling.
predicates.vacant_land_used_for_quarrying: The land is vacant and is used for extracting and breaking rock in quarrying operations.
predicates.quarry_land_is_not_exempt_as_a_commercia: Vacant land used for quarrying does not qualify as an exempt commercial site.

members.legal_issue: A provision exempting land set apart for an existing commercial or industrial undertaking does not establish that vacant quarry land is a commercial site.
material_facts: The dissenting opinion relied on the exemption for land belonging to an industrial or commercial undertaking and set apart for its use.

The Court explained that this category concerns an undertaking existing when the Act commenced and land set apart for that undertaking, subject to the land being used for its intended purpose within the specified time.
The appellant’s claim that quarry land was a commercial site was not supported by that distinct category.
members.legal_principle: Section 81(1)(k) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 addresses land belonging to an industrial or commercial undertaking at the commencement of the Act and set apart for its use, with the exemption ceasing if the land is not used for that purpose within the specified time. That distinct category does not enlarge the meaning of ‘commercial site’ in Section 81(1)(q).
members.conclusion: The exemption for land set apart for an existing undertaking does not support treating quarry land as a commercial site.

predicates.land_ceiling_exemption_appeal: A party appeals a ruling on whether land is exempt from a statutory landholding ceiling.
predicates.undertaking_land_exemption_used_to_suppo: A party relies on an exemption for land set apart for an undertaking to argue that a separate category of commercial sites has a broader meaning.
predicates.undertaking_land_exemption_does_not_expa: An exemption for land set apart for an undertaking does not broaden the separate category of commercial sites.

members.legal_issue: Breaking rock into smaller pieces in quarrying is not manufacture when the end product remains stone and no distinct commercial product is created.
material_facts: The appellant argued that quarrying involved manufacture because rocks were broken into smaller pieces for sale.
The Court found that the end product remained stone and retained its original identity.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Rajasthan SEB v. Associated Stone Industries, which held that cutting and polishing stones into slabs was not manufacture because no new and distinct commercial product came into existence and the product retained its identity as stone.
members.conclusion: Breaking rock into smaller pieces is not a manufacturing activity in these circumstances.

predicates.land_ceiling_exemption_appeal: A party appeals a ruling on whether land is exempt from a statutory landholding ceiling.
predicates.rocks_broken_into_smaller_pieces: The activity breaks rocks into smaller pieces.
predicates.no_distinct_product_created: The end product remains the same material and no new distinct commercial product is created.
predicates.rock_breaking_is_not_manufacture: Breaking rock into smaller pieces is not manufacture.

members.legal_issue: Granting a long-term lease for a premium can amount to a transfer of a capital asset for capital gains purposes even though the owner retains the underlying property.
material_facts: The assessee developed land into building sites and leased plots to various parties for 99 years.
The leases required payment of a premium and transferred rights to possession and enjoyment of the plots for the lease term, subject to conditions for termination.
The question before the Court was whether granting those leases amounted to a transfer, although the leases conveyed leasehold interests rather than the complete interests of the owner.
members.legal_principle: Section 12-B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, imposed tax on profits or gains arising from the transfer of a capital asset; Section 2(4A) defined a capital asset. Applying the principle in Traders and Miners Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bihar and Orissa, [1955] 27 ITR 341, the Court held that a long lease for a premium, under which rights of possession and enjoyment of an enduring nature were parted with, could constitute a transfer.
members.conclusion: The grant of the leases amounted to a transfer of capital assets for the purposes of capital gains taxation.

rule.if: capital_gains_proceeding and long_term_lease and premium_received and enduring_property_rights_transferred

predicates.capital_gains_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a transaction gives rise to taxable capital gains.
predicates.long_term_lease: The owner granted another person the right to use property for a lengthy fixed term.
predicates.premium_received: The owner received a premium for granting the lease.
predicates.enduring_property_rights_transferred: The lease gave the lessee rights to possess and enjoy the property for the lease term, subject to termination conditions.

members.legal_issue: Granting a mining lease transfers a capital asset and may give rise to taxable capital gains.
material_facts: The assessee purchased land and later granted a mining lease permitting a company to extract clay in return for a premium and royalty.
The lease transferred to the lessee a right to exploit the land, a right flowing from the assessee’s ownership of it.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(14), 2(47) and 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, property of any kind is a capital asset, and transfer includes the grant of a lease that conveys an interest in land. The Court relied on Traders and Mining Ltd. v. C.I.T. and R.K. Palshikar (HUF) v. Commissioner of Income Tax in treating a lease as a transfer of an asset.
members.conclusion: The right to exploit the land was a capital asset, and granting the mining lease transferred that asset for consideration, giving rise to capital gains taxable under section 45.

predicates.capital_gains_tax_case: The proceeding concerns whether consideration from transferring an asset is chargeable as capital gains.
predicates.land_owner_grants_mining_lease: The owner of land grants another person a lease to conduct mining on the land.
predicates.lease_conveys_land_exploitation_right: The lease gives the lessee a right to exploit the land by extracting its resources.

members.legal_issue: The cost of acquiring the right to grant a mining lease can be valued and apportioned, allowing capital gains to be computed.
material_facts: The assessee acquired the land for a stated purchase price that included a bundle of rights, including the right to grant a lease.
The right to excavate clay had a monetary value, although valuing it could be difficult.
The cost attributable to the leasehold right could be apportioned on the evidence, using the best valuation possible.
The right to grant the lease was acquired when the assessee acquired the freehold rights.
members.legal_principle: The cost of an interest transferred by a lease may be apportioned from the acquisition cost of the land because the purchase acquired a bundle of rights that included the right to grant the lease. Apportionment is a question of fact for the tax authority, based on evidence, and the best possible valuation must be made even if it is not mathematically exact; Gold Coast Selection Trust Ltd. v. Inspector of Taxes supports that approach. Because the cost was ascertainable and the right was acquired with the land, the computation provisions and section 45 applied. C.I.T. v. B.C. Srinivas Shetty was distinguished because the asset there had no determinable cost of acquisition.
members.conclusion: The cost attributable to the leasehold right was capable of determination, so the computation provisions applied and section 45 was attracted. The acquisition date for the right to grant the lease was the date the freehold rights were acquired; C.I.T. v. B.C. Srinivas Shetty was distinguishable because the cost of the right here could be determined.

rule.if: capital_gains_computation_case and land_acquired_with_bundle_of_rights and bundle_includes_right_to_grant_lease and evidence_supports_valuation

predicates.capital_gains_computation_case: The proceeding concerns whether a gain from transferring a lease-related right can be computed for capital gains purposes.
predicates.land_acquired_with_bundle_of_rights: A person acquired land together with the rights attached to ownership of that land.
predicates.bundle_includes_right_to_grant_lease: The ownership rights acquired with the land included the right to grant a lease over it.
predicates.evidence_supports_valuation: Evidence permits a best-possible monetary valuation and apportionment of the cost attributable to the transferred right.

members.legal_issue: Failure to determine the origin of blood on a recovered weapon does not eliminate the weapon’s circumstantial evidentiary value when the failure may result from disintegration of the blood.
material_facts: Two axes were recovered after the accused gave information that they had concealed them.
Blood was detected on both axes; the blood on one was found to be human, while the origin of the blood on the other could not be determined because it had disintegrated.
members.legal_principle: A failure to identify the origin of blood because a stain is insufficient or has undergone hematological changes does not establish that it was not human blood and does not invariably deprive recovery evidence of value. Prabhu Babaji v. State of Bombay, AIR 1956 SC 51, and Raghav Prapanna Tripathi v. State of U.P., AIR 1963 SC 74, were decided on materially different facts and do not establish such a categorical rule. A court should assess the circumstance objectively rather than entertain imaginative doubts.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in substantially discounting the recovery evidence because the origin of the blood on one axe could not be determined; the recovery remained a circumstance for consideration.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerned a criminal prosecution based on alleged fatal assaults.
predicates.accused_concealed_weapons_recovered_on_i: Weapons were recovered from places where the accused said they had concealed them.
predicates.blood_found_on_weapons: Blood was detected on the recovered weapons.
predicates.blood_origin_unascertainable_due_to_disi: The origin of blood on a recovered weapon could not be determined because the blood had disintegrated.

members.legal_issue: Failure to determine the origin of blood on a recovered weapon does not automatically deprive the recovery of evidentiary value.
material_facts: Two axes were recovered after the accused gave information about where they had concealed them.
Both axes had bloodstains; the blood on one was identified as human, while the origin of the blood on the other could not be determined because it had disintegrated.
The High Court treated the uncertain origin of one stain and uncertainty about which accused possessed the human-blood-stained axe as reasons to discount the recoveries.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, a fact discovered following information from an accused may be relevant. Failure by a serologist to determine the origin of blood, owing to insufficiency or deterioration, does not establish that the blood was non-human or invariably make the recovery worthless. The Court distinguished Prabhu Babaji v. State of Bombay and Raghav Prapanna Tripathi v. State of U.P. as decisions dependent on their particular facts, not a universal rule that such evidence has no value.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating the inconclusive serological result as making the recovery evidence unusable; the recoveries and the other circumstances had to be assessed together.

predicates.weapon_recovered_after_accused_disclosed: A weapon was recovered from a place of concealment after an accused disclosed information leading to its discovery.
predicates.weapon_bore_bloodstain: The recovered weapon had a bloodstain on it.
predicates.blood_origin_inconclusive: Testing did not establish the origin of the bloodstain.

members.legal_issue: Failure to identify the origin of blood on a recovered item does not by itself deprive the recovery evidence of probative value.
material_facts: The accused made a disclosure that led to recovery of a sheet concealed in his house and of the weapon.
The sheet and other articles were found to bear human blood, but the origin of the blood could not be determined after the passage of time.
The recoveries and the related disclosure evidence were accepted by the courts.
members.legal_principle: Applying State of Rajasthan v. Teja Ram, and distinguishing the fact-specific circumstances in Prabhu Babaji Navle v. State of Bombay, Raghav Prapanna Tripathi v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Kansa Behera v. State of Orissa, the court held that failure to determine the origin of blood due to disintegration does not mean the blood was not human or automatically render a recovery valueless. The evidence must be assessed in the circumstances of the case, rather than discarded on that ground alone.
members.conclusion: The inability to determine the blood’s origin did not entitle the accused to an acquittal or require the recovery evidence to be rejected.

predicates.criminal_case_based_on_circumstantial_ev: The prosecution seeks to prove the offence through circumstantial evidence rather than eyewitness testimony.
predicates.item_recovered_at_accused_disclosure: The accused gave information that led to the discovery and recovery of an item.
predicates.blood_detected_on_item: Testing detected blood on the recovered item.
predicates.blood_origin_unidentified_due_to_degrada: The origin of the blood could not be determined because it had degraded or disintegrated.

members.legal_issue: A family custom, rather than incorporation, may make a category of movable property impartible if the custom is adequately proved.
material_facts: The partition dispute concerned jewels claimed to be ceremonial regalia of the estate.

Evidence included a family member’s will describing state jewels as regalia and impartible, a list of jewels used at an installation ceremony, and family members’ statements and conduct treating ceremonial jewels as belonging to the estate.
The Court found the evidence sufficient to establish a family custom concerning some ceremonial jewels and upheld the finding that 38 jewels were regalia.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that incorporation applies to immovable, not movable, property. A family custom modifying ordinary law must be ancient and invariable and established by clear and unambiguous evidence. In assessing a family custom, the consensus, traditional beliefs, statements, and conduct of family members are relevant; fewer instances may suffice than for a territorial or community custom. The Court relied on Ramalakhmi Ammal v. Sivanantha Perumal Sethurayar and Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona.
members.conclusion: The doctrine of incorporation does not apply to movable property, but a proved family custom may make a category of movables impartible; the finding that 38 jewels were impartible regalia was upheld.

predicates.partition_suit: The dispute arises in a suit seeking partition of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.movable_property_claimed_as_family_regal: A party claims that movable property belongs to a ceremonial or regalia category that is not available for partition.
predicates.family_members_consistently_treated_the_: Family members’ beliefs, statements, or conduct show that they treated the relevant category of movables as belonging to the estate rather than as divisible family property.
predicates.clear_evidence_establishes_an_ancient_in: Clear and unambiguous evidence establishes a family practice as ancient and invariable.

members.legal_issue: Movable property does not become part of an impartible estate merely because it was acquired from estate income, unless a family custom or other sufficient evidence establishes its incorporation.
material_facts: The disputed jewellery and utensils were movable property.
There was no finding of a family custom treating the movables as part of the estate’s regalia.
The junior family member had received jewellery at marriage.
The movables were claimed for partition.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of incorporation ordinarily applies to immovable property, not movables; movables may form part of an impartible estate if a family custom or other sufficient evidence establishes that result. The Court relied on Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi and Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj v. Shri Pushavathi Visweswar Gajapathi Raj.
members.conclusion: The jewellery and utensils were personal property and were not liable to partition.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A family member brought a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.disputed_property_is_movable: The property claimed for partition consists of movable items.
predicates.no_custom_or_evidence_of_incorporation: No family custom or other sufficient evidence shows that the movables were incorporated into the impartible estate.

members.legal_issue: A family custom may make identified ceremonial movable property impartible, and the custom may continue after the circumstances that gave rise to it have changed.
material_facts: The dispute concerned jewels alleged to be regalia and therefore unavailable for partition.
Family documents and conduct before and after an adoption showed that certain ceremonial jewels were treated as state regalia and family heirlooms.
An earlier family member described specified jewels as regalia, and a later list recorded jewels taken out for an installation ceremony.
The family’s treatment of ceremonial jewels continued after the estate was abolished.
The lower appellate court identified 38 jewels as regalia, and the Supreme Court found no sufficient basis to disturb that factual conclusion.
members.legal_principle: Movable property cannot become part of an impartible estate through the doctrine of incorporation; a family custom of impartibility must be proved. Ramalakshmi Ammal v. Sivanantha Perumal Sethurayar requires clear and unambiguous proof that a custom is ancient and invariable. For a family custom, the family’s consensus, traditional belief, statements, and conduct are relevant; Abdul Hussain Khan v. Bibi Sona Daro is cited on proof of family custom. Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi states the broader law of impartible estates. Rai Kishore Singh v. Mst. Gahenabai supports the principle that a custom may outlive the condition that gave rise to it. The evidence supported the continuing family custom and the identification of the ceremonial jewels.
members.conclusion: The 38 identified jewels were properly treated as regalia and excluded from partition as impartible property.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and movable_property_claimed_as_regalia and family_consistently_treated_ceremonial_items_as_regalia and custom_continued_after_change_in_circumstances and evidence_clearly_proves_custom

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute is being determined in a proceeding seeking partition of family property.
predicates.movable_property_claimed_as_regalia: A party claims that movable family property is ceremonial regalia and is not available for partition.

predicates.evidence_clearly_proves_custom: The evidence of family belief, statements, and conduct clearly establishes the claimed custom.

members.legal_issue: A contract styled as a forest lease constitutes a sale of goods for sales-tax purposes when, in substance, it transfers the right to cut and remove specified timber that is to be severed under the contract.
material_facts: The contract allowed the buyer to cut and remove specified species of timber and required payment calculated by the timber extracted and removed.
The buyer received no possession of the forest land as land; its rights extended only to the specified timber, and other contractors could work in the same area.
The timber remained the State's property until severance, when ownership passed to the buyer.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act and section 2(g) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, trees agreed to be severed before or under a contract of sale are goods. Standing timber is movable property for this purpose if it is to be severed while it still belongs to the contracting seller. The sale, sale-price and turnover definitions in sections 2(n), 2(o) and 2(t) of the Madhya Pradesh Act apply where the contract transfers the timber for consideration. The Court distinguished Raja Bahadur Kamakshya Narain Singh, which concerned income tax and a different deed, and treated Badri Prasad as recognizing that trees to be severed are goods, while distinguishing its facts.
members.conclusion: The transaction was a sale of bamboo and salai wood under the contract, notwithstanding its description as a lease, and the Forest Department was liable to sales tax on those sales.

predicates.sales_tax_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning sales tax claimed on timber transferred under an agreement styled as a lease.
predicates.specified_timber_is_to_be_severed_under_: The agreement identifies timber that the buyer is to cut or sever pursuant to the agreement.
predicates.timber_remains_seller_property_until_sev: The seller retains ownership of the timber until the buyer severs it.
predicates.buyer_lacks_possession_of_land_as_land: The buyer is not given possession of the land itself as land.
predicates.buyer_rights_are_limited_to_cutting_and_: The buyer's rights in the area are confined to cutting and removing specified timber.

members.legal_issue: Standing timber attached to land is goods for sales-tax purposes when the sale contract requires it to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
material_facts: The sale concerned timber standing on land.
The contract expressly provided that the timber was to be severed under the contract of sale.
A retrospective state amendment included standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale in the definition of goods.
The dispute arose in an appeal concerning whether the sale was chargeable to sales tax.
members.legal_principle: The expression “sale of goods” in Entry 54 of List II has the same meaning as in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930; a State Legislature cannot extend it to transactions that are not sales of goods within that Act. Under section 2(7) of that Act, however, things attached to land are included as goods when the contract provides for their severance before sale or under the contract of sale. The Court relied on The State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. and Pandit Banarsi Das Bhanot v. The State of Madhya Pradesh for the meaning of “sale of goods,” and on the inclusive definition in section 2(7) to find the timber covered here.
members.conclusion: The timber was goods within the meaning of the Sale of Goods Act, the state amendment was valid as applied to the transaction, and the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: sales_tax_appeal and standing_timber_attached_to_land and contract_requires_severance and state_definition_covers_severable_timber

predicates.sales_tax_appeal: The case is an appeal about whether a transaction is chargeable to sales tax.
predicates.standing_timber_attached_to_land: The subject of the sale is timber that remains standing and attached to land.
predicates.contract_requires_severance: The sale contract provides that the timber is to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
predicates.state_definition_covers_severable_timber: A state enactment includes standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale in its definition of goods.

members.legal_issue: A purchase-tax notification covering standing trees or bamboos agreed to be severed is valid when it taxes a completed purchase of goods rather than an agreement to sever.
material_facts: The challenged notifications declared standing trees and bamboos agreed to be severed liable to purchase tax.
The statutory definitions of goods included things attached to land that were agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
The notifications, read as a whole, taxed the turnover of purchases, and the purchase could be completed before severance.
members.legal_principle: Entry 54 of List II permits taxation of sales or purchases of goods, but not transactions that are not sales or purchases of goods under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Sections 3B and 5(1) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947, operate on the turnover of purchases and the rate of tax. Under sections 4 and 18–23 of the Sale of Goods Act, property may pass before severance when the goods are specific or ascertained, the contract is unconditional, and the goods are in a deliverable state, unless a different intention appears. The Court relied on State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co., The Sales Tax Officer v. Budh Prakash Jai Prakash, Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd. v. D.P. Dube, K.L. Johar & Co. v. Deputy Commercial Tax Officer, Joint Commercial Tax Officer v. Young Men’s Indian Association, and State of Maharashtra v. Champalal Kishanlal Mohta.
members.conclusion: The challenged notifications and entries were constitutional and valid; their subject matter was goods and the taxable event was a completed purchase, not an agreement to sever.

predicates.challenge_to_purchase_tax_notification: A party challenged a government notification imposing purchase tax on a category of goods.
predicates.notification_covers_goods_agreed_to_be_s: The notification covers things attached to land that the parties have agreed will be severed.
predicates.purchase_is_completed_before_severance: The contract and circumstances make the purchase complete before the goods are severed.

members.legal_issue: Depriving a person of property that supports the person's livelihood engages the right to life and requires adequate compensation and rehabilitation.
material_facts: The owners were farmers whose land was taken without compensation or replacement land.
They had no other vocation or business to rely on for their livelihood.
The authorities did not provide compensation or rehabilitation despite the owners' efforts.
members.legal_principle: Article 21 protects the right to life, which the Court applied to the circumstances of persons deprived of property on which their livelihood depended. In a welfare State, statutory authorities must provide adequate compensation and rehabilitate persons uprooted by State action. The Court also relied on K. Krishna Reddy v. Special Deputy Collector, Land Acquisition, which emphasized that compensation should be determined without delay because its value and utility diminish over time.
members.conclusion: The deprivation violated Article 21, and the State had a legal obligation to provide adequate compensation and rehabilitate the persons uprooted by its actions.

predicates.property_deprivation_claim: A person claims that the State deprived that person of property.
predicates.livelihood_depends_on_property: The affected person's livelihood depends on the property taken.
predicates.state_caused_displacement: The State's taking of the property uprooted the affected person without providing a substitute means of support.

members.legal_issue: The right to life includes the right to livelihood where deprivation of livelihood would deprive a person of the means to live.
material_facts: The petitioners lived in pavement or slum dwellings near their work because their modest means made other housing and commuting impracticable.
The evidence and circumstances showed that eviction would cause many people in their position to lose their jobs and means of livelihood.
Their occupations were not alleged to be illegal or immoral.
members.legal_principle: The Court interpreted Article 21 in light of Articles 37, 39(a) and 41. It relied on Munn v. Illinois and Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and distinguished In Re: Sant Ram because the petitioners did not claim livelihood through an illegal or immoral occupation.
members.conclusion: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, and deprivation of livelihood must be according to just, fair and reasonable procedure established by law.

predicates.constitutional_right_to_life_claim: A person claims that public action threatens the constitutional right to life.
predicates.livelihood_is_a_means_of_survival: The person's work or livelihood provides the means necessary to live.
predicates.threatened_deprivation_would_remove_that: The threatened action would deprive the person of that means of livelihood.

members.legal_issue: The right to life includes the right to livelihood, and an eviction that puts that right in jeopardy may violate constitutional protections.
material_facts: The petitions challenged the eviction of slum and pavement dwellers under state laws governing slums, public-land encroachments, municipal streets and town planning.
The petitioners sought protection from eviction without alternative accommodation and sought basic amenities for slum dwellers.
The Court held that the constitutional points decided in the pavement- and slum-dweller cases concerning Bombay governed these petitions.
members.legal_principle: Article 21 protects more than mere physical existence: the right to livelihood is an integral component of the right to life. The Court applied Olga Tellis & Ors. v. Bombay Municipal Corporation & Ors. and applied the constitutional ruling to eviction under the Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, read with the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, the Madras City Municipal Corporation Act, 1919, and the Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning Act, 1971. The judgment also describes Section 11(a) of the 1971 Slum Areas Act as providing for a slum-clearance declaration after the specified opportunity for landowners to show cause.
members.conclusion: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood because a person cannot live without the means of living. An eviction that puts that right in jeopardy is violative of Articles 21 and 19(1)(e) and (g).

predicates.eviction_challenge: A person brings a proceeding challenging eviction from a slum or pavement.
predicates.livelihood_at_stake: The eviction deprives the affected person of the means of livelihood and thereby puts the person's ability to live in jeopardy.

members.legal_issue: Voluntary transfers made after the date on which the land ceiling and surrender obligation are fixed do not reduce the transferor’s liability to surrender the excess, even when the transfers fall within an exception to the restriction on transfers.
material_facts: The landholder owned land exceeding the applicable ceiling on the notified date.
After that date, he executed gifts of land to his children, including children who had been minors on the notified date and attained majority later.
The Land Board required surrender of land associated with the gifts to the children who had been minors on the notified date, while the High Court relieved the landholder of the surrender obligation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 82, 83 and 85 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964 fix the applicable ceiling and surrender obligation by reference to the notified date; section 86 provides for vesting after determination, and section 87 addresses later acquisitions. Section 84 was enacted to prevent circumvention of the ceiling scheme: transfers between publication of the Bill and the notified date are taken into account unless within an enumerated exception, but transfers after the notified date, even of an excepted kind, cannot alter the obligation already fixed. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. Philomina for the principle that the ceiling and surrender obligation are determined as at the notified date.
members.conclusion: The later gifts could not affect the landholder’s obligation to surrender the excess land determined by reference to his holdings on the notified date. The High Court’s judgment was set aside and the appeal was allowed.

predicates.ceiling_surrender_proceeding: A proceeding concerns whether a landholder must surrender land exceeding an applicable land ceiling.
predicates.land_exceeded_ceiling_on_cutoff: The landholder held land exceeding the applicable ceiling on the date used to determine the ceiling and surrender obligation.
predicates.voluntary_transfer_after_cutoff: The landholder voluntarily transferred land after the date used to determine the ceiling and surrender obligation.
predicates.transferor_remains_liable_for_cutoff_exc: The transferor remains liable to surrender the excess measured on the date used to determine the ceiling and surrender obligation.

members.legal_issue: Transfers made after the date on which the ceiling obligation becomes operative must be disregarded when determining the landholder's liability, even if they fall within a category of transfers otherwise excepted from invalidation.
material_facts: Landholders made gift transfers after the date on which the ceiling obligation became operative.
The transfers were claimed to be of a kind excepted under the transfer provision.
The Taluk Land Board and High Court did not exclude the gifted land from the ceiling determination.
members.legal_principle: Sections 83, 84 and 85 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 apply. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K. A. Gangadharan, which held that transfers made after the operative date are to be ignored for the ceiling determination even when they are of an excepted variety mentioned in section 84.
members.conclusion: The transfers were to be ignored in determining liability to surrender excess land, even if they were of an otherwise excepted variety.

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding determines a holder's liability to surrender land exceeding a statutory ceiling.
predicates.transfer_made_after_ceiling_obligation_b: The landholder transferred land after the statutory ceiling obligation became operative.

members.legal_issue: A land transfer made after the statutory cutoff by a predecessor-in-interest must be disregarded when determining a successor’s ceiling area if the successor inherited the land before the assessment date and the transfer is not within an applicable exception.
material_facts: The landowner executed a gift of land after the statutory cutoff, and the land would have been surplus absent the gift.
The donor died before the assessment date, and the successor inherited the land before that date.
The transfer did not fall within either applicable exception.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5(6) of the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, a transfer made after January 24, 1971, of land that would otherwise have been declared surplus is ignored, subject to the proviso’s exceptions. The provision applies to any transfer, not only one made by the tenure-holder whose ceiling area is being determined; it also reaches a transfer by that holder’s predecessor-in-interest where the holder inherited the land before June 8, 1973. This interpretation advances the provision’s purpose of preventing evasion of ceiling limits. Arjan Singh v. State of Punjab was distinguishable because it turned on the construction of a different statutory provision and did not govern this issue.
members.conclusion: The gift had to be ignored in determining the successor’s ceiling area. The gifted land was treated as remaining with the donor until death, then inherited by the successor, and counted in the successor’s holding on the assessment date.

members.legal_issue: A former coparcener in possession of joint family property must account to the other co-owners for income received from that property pending partition.
material_facts: The joint family assets included movable and immovable properties, stocks, shares, and securities in the parties’ possession or control when the joint status was severed.
The parties continued to possess family assets after severance and received rents, income, profits, or dividends from those assets before final partition.
The Court directed that the family assets and liabilities be accounted for and that each party account for income received from joint family property in that party’s possession.
members.legal_principle: Following severance, the family members hold the family property as tenants in common. A member possessing family property must account for its rents and profits received, although the funds in that member’s hands are not thereby impressed with a trust and separate acquisitions are not automatically family property. The Court relied on Gulabrao Fakirrao v. Baburao Fakirrao and John Kennedy v. Mery Annette De Trafford.
members.conclusion: The parties had to account for rents, income, profits, and dividends received from joint family property in their possession after severance and before final partition.

predicates.joint_family_partition_case: The proceeding concerns partition of property formerly held by a joint family.
predicates.joint_status_was_severed: The family members’ joint status ended before final partition.
predicates.co_owner_received_income_from_joint_prop: A co-owner received rents, profits, dividends, or other income from family property in that co-owner’s possession after severance and before partition.

members.legal_issue: A claimant's receipt of income from some family property does not release the family members managing the estate from accounting for their dealings after the claim for partition.
material_facts: The claimant had received income from some of the family property and possessed some portion of it.
Other family members had managed the family estate.

The claimant sought accounts from the time the parties had separated in estate and mess and residence, and the decree required accounts from the relevant demand for partition rather than for earlier dealings.
members.legal_principle: A co-sharer’s possession of some family property or receipt of income from it does not by itself absolve those managing the family estate from accounting for their dealings after the claimant's separation and demand for partition. The value or income received by the claimant is considered in the final adjustment of the account, and past dealings are not included where the claim is limited to the period after separation.
members.conclusion: The claimant's receipt of income from some property did not absolve the managers from rendering accounts for their dealings after the demand for partition; the claimant's possession was to be considered in adjusting the account.

predicates.claimant_received_income_from_some_famil: The claimant possessed some family property or received income from it.
predicates.others_managed_family_estate: Other family members managed the family estate.
predicates.account_claim_is_for_post_demand_dealing: The account sought concerns dealings after the claimant's separation and demand for partition.

members.legal_issue: A co-sharer in possession of joint family property must account to the other co-sharers for income received from that property from severance of joint status until final partition.
material_facts: The prior decree fixed the date from which the family members held the joint family properties as tenants in common.
The decree required accounting for rents, income, profits, and dividends received from joint family properties in each party’s possession until final partition.
The defendants disputed their obligation to account for income from the joint properties after the date of severance.
members.legal_principle: After severance of joint status, the members become tenants in common. A member in possession who receives rents and profits from joint property must account for those receipts to the other co-sharers. The Court applied the binding prior decision in M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty, which relied on John Kennedy v. Mary Annette De Trafford and referred to Gulabrao Fakirrao v. Baburao Fakirrao.
members.conclusion: The parties in possession were liable to account to the others for rents, income, profits, and dividends received from joint family properties from the date of severance until the final decree.

predicates.partition_proceeding_after_severance: The dispute concerns the division of property after the co-owners’ joint status has ended.
predicates.co_sharer_received_income_from_joint_pro: A co-sharer in possession received rent, income, profits, or dividends from property that remained joint property pending partition.

members.legal_issue: A change in the number of judges assigned to hear an appeal does not take away a vested right of appeal or require the appeal to be heard by the panel composition prescribed when the suit or appeal was instituted.
material_facts: When the suit and the appeal were instituted, the governing law required appeals of the relevant value to be heard by a Division Bench.
Before the appeals were heard, a new law expanded the jurisdiction of a single Judge to hear appeals of that value.
The appeal remained available and was heard and decided by a single Judge.
The appellant argued that the earlier panel-composition rule gave him a vested right to a Division Bench.
members.legal_principle: The right of appeal is a substantive right, preserved under the principle stated in Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbaiah Choudhury, but the number of judges who hear an appeal is procedural. The Travancore-Cochin High Court Act regulated High Court procedure and did not confer a right of appeal; the right to appeal from the first-instance judgment arose under s. 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Following Ittavira Mathai v. Varkey Varkey and the procedural approach in Mahendra v. Darsan, the Court rejected Radhakrishan v. Shridhar.
members.conclusion: The appellant had no vested right to have the appeal heard by a specified number of judges, and the appeal was rightly heard by a single Judge under the law in force when it was heard.

rule.if: high_court_appeal and appeal_filed_before_panel_change and panel_change_took_effect_before_hearing and appeal_remained_available

predicates.high_court_appeal: A party pursued an appeal before a High Court.
predicates.appeal_filed_before_panel_change: The appeal was filed before a change in the rules assigning appeals to panels of different sizes.
predicates.panel_change_took_effect_before_hearing: The changed panel-assignment rule was in force when the appeal was heard.
predicates.appeal_remained_available: The change in panel assignment did not remove the party’s appeal.

members.legal_issue: Changing an appeal from a multi-judge hearing to a single-judge hearing does not itself create or impair a vested right to appeal to the Supreme Court under the Constitution.
material_facts: The High Court appeal was heard and decided by a single Judge under the law in force at the time of hearing.
The appellant argued that losing a Division Bench hearing also affected a further appeal to the Supreme Court.
The judgment states that Parliament had not enacted a law permitting an appeal to the Supreme Court from a judgment of one High Court Judge.
members.legal_principle: Article 133(3) provides that an appeal does not lie to the Supreme Court from a judgment, decree, or final order of one High Court Judge unless Parliament provides otherwise. Because a party has no vested right to have a High Court appeal heard by more than one Judge, the appellant could not claim a vested further appeal on that basis.
members.conclusion: No right to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133 vested on the basis of an asserted right to have the High Court appeal heard by a Division Bench.

predicates.constitutional_appeal_sought: A party sought a further appeal to the Supreme Court under the Constitution.
predicates.high_court_single_judge_decision: The High Court decided the case through a single Judge.
predicates.no_law_authorizes_appeal_from_single_jud: No law authorizes a further appeal to the Supreme Court from that single-Judge decision.

members.legal_issue: A party has no vested right to have an appeal heard by a specified number of judges when the governing tribunal or its procedure has changed under competent legislation.
material_facts: The appeal was heard by a two-judge bench of the successor High Court rather than by a three-judge bench under the former High Court's law.
The former High Court had been abolished and a successor High Court established after the merger of the states.

The legislation governing appeals in the successor High Court replaced the earlier provisions, and the provision requiring a full bench for the relevant category had been repealed before the appeal was filed.
The appellant did not contend that the repeal was unconstitutional.
members.legal_principle: A right of appeal may be affected by competent legislation, and a litigant has no right to prevent abolition of the tribunal that existed when the suit was instituted. The right to appeal to a High Court does not confer a vested right to have the appeal heard by a specified number of judges; the composition of the bench is procedural. The Court relied on the legislation governing the successor High Court and noted that the repeal had not been challenged as unconstitutional.
members.conclusion: The appeal was rightly heard and decided by a two-judge bench; the appellant had no vested right to a bench of three judges.

rule.if: appeal_to_successor_high_court and former_tribunal_abolished_by_competent_law and bench_composition_is_procedural and no_vested_right_to_specific_bench

predicates.appeal_to_successor_high_court: The proceeding is an appeal before a High Court established as the successor to an earlier tribunal.
predicates.former_tribunal_abolished_by_competent_l: Competent legislation abolished the tribunal that existed when the original suit was instituted.
predicates.bench_composition_is_procedural: The number of judges assigned to hear the appeal is a matter of procedure.
predicates.no_vested_right_to_specific_bench: The party has no vested right to have the appeal heard by a particular number of judges.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu female’s property may be treated as possessed by her for conversion of a limited interest into full ownership even when she lacks actual or constructive possession, if she retains ownership rights and can enforce a right to recover the property.
material_facts: A widow inherited land from her husband and possessed it until other persons dispossessed her.
She brought a suit to recover the land, which remained pending when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The first appellate court found that she had not remarried and had not lost her rights in the land.
She died while the recovery suit was pending, and the question of her daughter’s succession arose while the land remained recoverable through the widow’s claim.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act uses “possessed by” more broadly than actual or constructive possession and includes possession in law where the female Hindu retains ownership rights, including an enforceable right to recover property from a trespasser. The provision does not apply where she has parted with her rights so completely that she can no longer exercise them, or where she has no title and is merely a trespasser. The Court applied S. S. Munna Lal v. S. S. Rajkumar and Eramma v. Veerupana, and relied on the broad interpretation of “possessed” in Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veerayya; it distinguished Brahmdeo Singh v. Deomani Missir, where the widow had alienated her rights.
members.conclusion: The widow’s retained ownership rights meant that the land was possessed by her for the purposes of section 14(1), so her limited interest became full ownership and the property passed to her daughter.

rule.if: hindu_female_property_conversion_case and ownership_rights_persist_at_relevant_time and (actual_or_constructive_possession or enforceable_right_to_recover_possession) and not rights_completely_parted_with

predicates.hindu_female_property_conversion_case: The proceeding concerns whether a Hindu female’s interest in property is converted from a limited interest into full ownership.
predicates.ownership_rights_persist_at_relevant_tim: The female retained ownership rights in the property when the question of conversion arose.
predicates.actual_or_constructive_possession: The female physically possessed the property or possessed it through another person holding it for her.
predicates.enforceable_right_to_recover_possession: Although out of possession, the female retained an enforceable right to recover the property.
predicates.rights_completely_parted_with: The female had given up her rights so completely that she could no longer exercise ownership rights in the property.

members.legal_issue: A female Hindu need not have physical or constructive possession of property when the relevant legal change takes effect if she has acquired and possesses a legal interest in it when her title is challenged.
material_facts: The widow was not in possession of the property when the Hindu Succession Act came into force because she had previously transferred it.
The transferee later reconveyed the property to her, and she had reacquired and was possessed of it when her title was challenged.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) applies to property possessed by a female Hindu whether acquired before or after the Act commenced. The Court interpreted “possessed of” as referring to a right or interest in the property, rather than requiring physical possession at commencement. Kotturuswamy v. Veeravva was distinguished because possession obtained by trespass without title was not a lawful acquisition.
members.conclusion: Possession, physical or constructive, at the commencement of the Act was not a prerequisite to full ownership; possession in the legal sense when title is called into question is sufficient, provided the property was lawfully acquired.

predicates.property_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a disputed claim to ownership of property.
predicates.female_acquired_property: A female Hindu acquired an interest in the property by a lawful means.
predicates.female_had_legal_possession_when_title_w: The female Hindu had a legal right or interest in the property when her title was challenged, even if she lacked physical or constructive possession when the relevant legal change took effect.

members.legal_issue: Possession for the enlargement of a female Hindu’s estate includes constructive possession and is not confined to actual physical possession.
material_facts: The widow had acquired her deceased husband’s estate before the succession legislation came into force.
The alleged adopted son was said to be in actual possession, but his possession was permissive under an agreement that left the widow in possession and enjoyment of the estate.
The court considered the possession issue on the assumption that the adoption was invalid.
members.legal_principle: Under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property possessed by a female Hindu is held by her as full owner. The court approved the interpretation in Gostha Behari v. Haridas Samanta that possession may be actual or constructive, or in any form recognised by law. It also referred to Gaddam Venkayamma v. Gaddam Veerayya, while stating that it need not adopt the full extent of that decision. An appellate court may take account of a change in law, as held in Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri.
members.conclusion: The statutory term “possessed” has a broad meaning that includes actual, constructive, or other possession recognised by law; the widow was in constructive possession through the permissive holder.

predicates.female_estate_enlargement_claim: A claim concerns whether a female Hindu’s property interest is enlarged under a rule that applies to property she possesses.
predicates.female_hindu_has_property: A female Hindu has a property interest in the property at issue.
predicates.female_hindu_has_actual_possession: The female Hindu physically possesses the property.
predicates.another_person_has_only_permissive_posse: Another person holds the property with the female Hindu’s permission and has not displaced her legally recognised possession.

members.legal_issue: A shared household is not limited to a home owned or rented by the husband or to joint-family property in which he has a share, but must be a dwelling in which the aggrieved person lived in a domestic relationship with some degree of permanence.
material_facts: The daughter-in-law had lived in the father-in-law’s house since her marriage and continued to occupy part of it.
The father-in-law claimed exclusive ownership, and the husband was said to have no share in the property.
The daughter-in-law claimed a right of residence and alleged domestic violence in proceedings under the domestic-violence legislation.
members.legal_principle: The exhaustive definition in Section 2(s), read with Sections 17 and 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, does not require the aggrieved person or her husband to hold an ownership interest. Its requirement is a household where the aggrieved person lives or has lived in a domestic relationship, subject to the nature and permanence of the residence. The Court relied on the interpretive approach to “means” and “includes” in Bharat Coop. Bank (Mumbai) Ltd. v. Coop. Bank Employees Union and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India, and on the purpose of the Act discussed in Kunapareddy Alias Nookala Shanka Balaji v. Kunapareddy Swarna Kumari and Manmohan Attavar v. Neelam Manmohan Attavar. It held that S.R. Batra v. Taruna Batra did not correctly interpret Section 2(s).
members.conclusion: A shared household need not be owned or rented by the husband or belong to a joint family of which he is a member. The contrary interpretation in S.R. Batra v. Taruna Batra was incorrect. The phrase covering a household where the aggrieved person has lived does not make every place of fleeting or casual residence a shared household; the character and permanence of the living arrangement and the parties’ intention must be considered.

predicates.domestic_violence_residence_case: The proceeding concerns a person seeking a right of residence on the basis of domestic violence within a domestic relationship.
predicates.aggrieved_person_lived_in_domestic_relat: The person seeking residence lived in the household in a domestic relationship with the respondent, either alone or with the respondent.
predicates.residence_was_not_merely_casual: The person’s living arrangement had some permanence, assessed in light of the parties’ intention and the nature of the household.

members.legal_issue: An aggrieved woman need not actually reside with the respondent when the alleged domestic violence occurs or when she seeks relief, if she has the relevant domestic relationship and right to reside in a shared household.
material_facts: The aggrieved person was married to the respondent’s son, who died shortly after the marriage.
She alleged that the respondent and other family members harassed and mentally tortured her, causing her to leave the matrimonial home, and that she was living elsewhere when she applied for relief.
The lower courts denied relief in part because they found that she had not shared a household with the respondents.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(a), 2(f), 2(s), 17 and 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, read together, protect a woman in a qualifying domestic relationship and do not make actual co-residence at the time of violence a condition for relief. Section 17(1) gives every woman in a domestic relationship a right to reside in a shared household irrespective of her legal or beneficial interest in it; that right is not confined to actual residence. The Court relied on Juveria Abdul Majid Patni v. Atif Iqbal Mansoori, Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja, Vandhana v. T. Srikanth and Smt. Bharati Naik v. Shri Ravi Ramnath Halarnkar.
members.conclusion: Actual residence with the respondent at the time of the alleged violence is not mandatory; a woman with the right to reside in a shared household may seek relief under the Act even if she is not actually living there.

rule.if: domestic_violence_application and qualifying_domestic_relationship and alleged_domestic_violence and right_to_reside_in_shared_household and not residing_with_respondent_when_violence_occurred

predicates.domestic_violence_application: A woman or someone acting on her behalf sought relief from a Magistrate for alleged domestic violence.
predicates.qualifying_domestic_relationship: The woman is or has been related to the respondent through a legally recognized domestic relationship and has lived in, or has the right to reside in, a shared household.
predicates.alleged_domestic_violence: The woman alleged conduct by the respondent amounting to domestic violence.
predicates.right_to_reside_in_shared_household: The woman had a right to reside in a household shared by virtue of the domestic relationship, regardless of ownership or other legal interest.
predicates.residing_with_respondent_when_violence_o: The woman was actually residing with the respondent when the alleged domestic violence occurred.

members.legal_issue: A domestic relationship need not still exist when an application for relief is filed if the alleged domestic violence relates to the relationship or is later inflicted on account of it.
material_facts: The aggrieved person’s husband died shortly after their marriage, before she filed her application for relief.
She alleged that her in-laws harassed her after his death and that she was forced to leave the matrimonial home.
The lower courts treated the absence of a current domestic relationship and the fact that she was living separately as grounds to deny relief.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(a) and 2(f) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, define an aggrieved person and domestic relationship to include past relationships; the phrase “have at any point of time, lived together” does not require the relationship to subsist when the application is made. Violence must, however, relate to the domestic relationship. The Court relied on Juveria Abdul Majid Patni v. Atif Iqbal Mansoori, which recognized claims based on past domestic relationships and later conduct related to them; Krishna Bhattacharjee v. Sarathi Choudhury, which held that judicial separation does not end the domestic relationship; Saraswathy v. Babu; and V.D. Bhanot v. Savita Bhanot.
members.conclusion: A woman may apply under the Act even if the domestic relationship has ended by the time of filing, provided the alleged domestic violence relates to the period of that relationship or is later inflicted on account of it.

rule.if: domestic_violence_application and past_qualifying_domestic_relationship and not relationship_subsisting_when_filed and alleged_violence_related_to_relationship

predicates.domestic_violence_application: A woman or someone acting on her behalf sought relief from a Magistrate for alleged domestic violence.
predicates.past_qualifying_domestic_relationship: The woman and respondent had previously lived together in a shared household while related through a qualifying domestic relationship.
predicates.relationship_subsisting_when_filed: The qualifying domestic relationship still existed when the woman filed her application.
predicates.alleged_violence_related_to_relationship: The alleged domestic violence occurred during the domestic relationship or was later inflicted on account of that relationship.

members.legal_issue: An aggrieved person may seek residence relief in an existing civil proceeding, and the civil court must consider a pleaded claim that the property is a shared household rather than leave it undecided merely because a separate domestic-violence proceeding is pending.
material_facts: The owner brought a civil suit seeking removal of the daughter-in-law from the house.
In her written statement, she asserted that the house was a shared household and that she had a right to reside there.
A separate application under the domestic-violence legislation was also pending.
members.legal_principle: Section 26 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 permits relief available under Sections 18 to 22, including residence relief under Section 19, to be sought in a legal proceeding before a civil, family, or criminal court, in addition to other relief. In Vaishali Abhimanyu Joshi v. Nanasaheb Gopal Joshi, the Court held that Section 26 must be interpreted to effectuate the Act’s purpose and that considering the claim in the existing proceeding avoids multiplicity of proceedings.
members.conclusion: The residence claim could be considered in the civil suit under Section 26, and the Trial Court’s failure to consider it defeated a right protected by the Act.

predicates.civil_proceeding_affects_aggrieved_perso: A civil court proceeding concerns the aggrieved person’s occupancy or other rights in the property.
