predicates.defendant_pleads_shared_household_reside: The defendant asserts in the civil proceeding that the home is a shared household and that she is entitled to reside there.

members.legal_issue: A property owner may be treated as a respondent for deciding a pleaded residence claim in a civil suit, but residence relief requires the claimant to plead and prove the statutory conditions, including domestic violence by the person against whom relief is sought.
material_facts: The daughter-in-law had lived in the property with her husband and had named the father-in-law as a respondent in her application under Section 12.
In the civil suit, she relied on her asserted right of residence to resist the owner’s claim.
The Magistrate’s order was interim and rested on a prima facie assessment; the civil court had to decide the residence claim on the material before it.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(a) and 2(q) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, read with the striking down of the words “adult male” in Section 2(q) by Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora, allow a respondent to be a person in a domestic relationship against whom relief is sought. Sections 17, 19, and 26 permit residence relief to be considered in a civil proceeding, but relief depends on proof of the statutory requirements, including domestic violence. A prima facie interim order in the separate proceeding does not itself establish those requirements for the civil court’s decision.
members.conclusion: For deciding the daughter-in-law’s claim under Sections 17 and 19 read with Section 26 in the suit, the owner could be treated as a respondent. But the claimant had to plead and prove the necessary conditions for relief, including that the person treated as respondent had committed an act of domestic violence.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_domestic_violence_re: The civil suit requires determination of a claimed right of residence arising under domestic-violence law.
predicates.property_owner_was_in_domestic_relations: The property owner lived with the claimant in a household in a relationship falling within the statutory definition of domestic relationship.
predicates.claimant_seeks_relief_against_owner: The claimant seeks relief against the property owner, either in the domestic-violence proceeding or by relying on the claimed right in the civil suit.
predicates.claimant_proves_domestic_violence_by_own: The claimant establishes in the proceeding that the property owner committed an act of domestic violence against her.

members.legal_issue: Pending domestic-violence proceedings and orders granting interim or final residence relief do not bar related civil proceedings; those orders are relevant evidence, but the civil court must decide the civil issues on the evidence before it and is not bound by the domestic-violence court’s findings.
material_facts: The daughter-in-law’s application under the domestic-violence legislation was pending when the owner filed the civil suit.
The Magistrate had made an interim order against dispossession without an order of a competent court.
The civil suit concerned the same property and the claimed right of residence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17, 19, 25, 26, 28, and 36 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 contemplate independent proceedings and do not bar civil proceedings; Section 43 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes the domestic-violence order relevant in the circumstances described. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras, K.G. Premshankar v. Inspector of Police, Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, Seth Ramdayal Jat v. Laxmi Prasad, and the principles concerning the limited evidentiary effect of criminal-court orders discussed in Shanti Kumar Panda v. Shakuntala Devi. The two proceedings must be decided on the evidence before their respective courts; a domestic-violence order is not conclusive in the civil suit.
members.conclusion: The civil suit could be initiated and continued. Any interim or final order under Section 19 was relevant and had to be given due weight as evidence, but it did not bind the civil court or prevent it from deciding the issues independently on the evidence led there.

predicates.civil_proceeding_and_domestic_violence_p: A civil proceeding and a domestic-violence proceeding concern the same home or claimed right of residence.
predicates.domestic_violence_court_has_made_residen: The court in the domestic-violence proceeding has made an interim or final order concerning residence.

members.legal_issue: A timely, undecided application for the first renewal of a mining lease can result in a deemed extension, but that extension is limited by the governing renewal rules.
material_facts: The applicable version of Rule 24A(6) deemed a lease extended when a timely renewal application had not been decided before the lease expired.
The Court interpreted the earlier and amended versions of the rule together and accepted that the deemed-extension benefit applied to first renewals.
The amended rule provided a limited further extension for qualifying first-renewal applications that remained pending.
members.legal_principle: Rule 24A(1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 required a renewal application to be made at least twelve months before expiry. The former Rule 24A(6) deemed an eligible lease extended until the State Government decided the application; the amended Rule 24A(6) limited the extension and specified treatment for pending first-renewal applications. The Court read the provisions in sequence and applied them to first renewals.
members.conclusion: A leaseholder with a timely, undecided application for a first renewal may rely on the applicable deemed-extension regime; the extension is not unlimited.

predicates.lease_extension_dispute: A court proceeding concerned whether a mining lease continued after its stated expiry.
predicates.timely_first_renewal_application: The leaseholder applied for the first renewal sufficiently before the existing lease was due to expire.
predicates.first_renewal_application_undecided: The first-renewal application had not been rejected or finally decided.

members.legal_issue: The statutory extension regime for pre-amendment mining leases can apply even when the lease or its renewal expired before the amendment, if a valid renewal application remained undecided and the lease conditions were met.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether the amended statutory extension regime covered only leases subsisting when the amendment commenced.
Some leaseholders had made renewal applications at least twelve months before expiry, and those applications remained undecided.
The Court held that expiry of the grant or renewal was not, by itself, rejection, determination or lapse within the statutory exclusion.
The Court made entitlement subject to compliance with all lease terms and conditions, including required clearances and approvals.
members.legal_principle: Sections 8A(5), 8A(6) and 8A(9) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 provide extensions for qualifying pre-amendment leases and exclude leases whose renewal was rejected, which were determined, or which lapsed. The Court treated those terms as distinct from mere expiry. It relied on the statutory text and the amendment's Objects and Reasons, which addressed pending renewal applications and hardship caused by administrative delay. Extension remained subject to compliance with all lease terms and conditions.
members.conclusion: The amended extension regime can benefit a leaseholder whose lease or renewal had expired before the amendment if a valid, timely renewal application remained undecided and the lease conditions were complied with; leases rejected, determined or lapsed are excluded.

rule.if: lease_extension_dispute and pre_amendment_lease_expired and timely_renewal_application_pending and lease_terms_complied and lease_not_rejected_determined_or_lapsed

predicates.lease_extension_dispute: A court proceeding concerned the continued validity or extension of a mining lease.
predicates.pre_amendment_lease_expired: A mining lease granted before a statutory change had expired before that change took effect.
predicates.timely_renewal_application_pending: The leaseholder had applied for renewal sufficiently before expiry and the application remained undecided.
predicates.lease_terms_complied: The leaseholder had complied with the applicable terms and conditions of the lease, including required operational clearances and approvals.
predicates.lease_not_rejected_determined_or_lapsed: The renewal had not been rejected and the lease had not been formally brought to an end or lapsed under the applicable process.

members.legal_issue: A timely application seeking continuation of a lease because mining operations could not be conducted prevents lapse while the application awaits decision, subject to the prescribed limit.
material_facts: Rule 28 allowed a leaseholder to apply for continuation where mining operations could not be commenced or had been discontinued for reasons beyond the leaseholder's control.

Rule 28(4) provided that if the State Government did not decide the application before the lease would otherwise lapse, the lease was deemed extended until the decision or the prescribed outer limit, whichever came first.
The Court relied on that provision in rejecting the claim that lapse was automatic.
members.legal_principle: Rule 28(2) and Rule 28(4) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 permit an application for relief from lapse and deem the lease extended if the State Government has not decided the application by the date it would otherwise lapse. The deemed continuation lasts until the State Government decides the application or the prescribed outer limit is reached, whichever occurs first.
members.conclusion: When such an application is pending, the lease is deemed to continue during the period specified by the rule, unless and until the applicable limit is reached.

predicates.lease_lapse_dispute: A court proceeding concerned whether a mining lease had lapsed because operations had not commenced or had been discontinued.
predicates.timely_lapse_relief_application: The leaseholder applied within the required time for relief from lapse based on reasons beyond the leaseholder's control.
predicates.application_undecided: The State Government had not yet decided the application for relief from lapse.

members.legal_issue: Land may be requisitioned for a public purpose that is permanent in character under a power authorizing requisition for any public purpose.
material_facts: An authority requisitioned privately owned land to establish a new village site and build houses for people whose homes had been destroyed or seriously damaged by floods.
Rehabilitation at a new site was urgently needed before the next monsoon, and the need for the land for that public purpose was undisputed.
The requisitioning law was temporary in duration, and the lower court considered that the new village site was a permanent purpose.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 authorizes requisition where the authority considers it necessary or expedient and the purpose is public; its words “any land for any public purpose” do not limit the purpose to one that is temporary. Section 4(5) defines requisition as taking possession of land or requiring it to be placed at the State Government’s disposal. Section 9 provides for restoration of the land to its owner as far as possible when it is released, but does not restrict the character of the purpose for which it may be requisitioned. The temporary life of the law and the nature of the purpose are distinct. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The power to requisition was not limited to temporary purposes. Requisition for the permanent public purpose of rehabilitating flood victims was not, on that ground, an abuse of or unjustified under the law.

rule.if: requisition_order_appeal and requisition_law_covers_any_public_purpose and authority_considered_requisition_necessary_or_expedient and purpose_is_public and purpose_is_permanent

predicates.requisition_order_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an order requisitioning land.
predicates.requisition_law_covers_any_public_purpos: The law under which the land was requisitioned authorizes requisition for any public purpose.
predicates.authority_considered_requisition_necessa: The authority considered requisitioning the land necessary or expedient.
predicates.purpose_is_public: The land was requisitioned for a public purpose.
predicates.purpose_is_permanent: The public purpose for which the land was requisitioned was permanent in character.

members.legal_issue: Property may be requisitioned for a permanent public purpose, although the requisition remains temporary in duration.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned property requisitioned under the state legislation and allotted for residential accommodation or for fair-price ration shops.
The petitioners argued that requisition could not continue to serve the public purposes for which the premises were being used.
members.legal_principle: The words authorising requisition for a public purpose do not restrict the purpose to one that is temporary. Collector of Akola v. Ramchandra held that the purpose may be permanent, and Jiwani Kumar Paraki v. First Land Acquisition Collector supports distinguishing the purpose of requisition from its duration. Requisition differs from acquisition because title remains with the owner; H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra remains correct as to the temporary character of requisition, but not as to a bar on permanent purposes.
members.conclusion: A permanent public purpose may support an order of requisition; the earlier decision was not to be reconsidered on that basis, and its statement that requisition orders cannot be made for a permanent purpose was not approved.

predicates.requisition_order_case: The matter concerns an order taking possession or control of property for a public purpose without transferring ownership.
predicates.public_purpose_is_permanent: The public purpose for which the property is used is enduring rather than temporary.

members.legal_issue: Requisition is temporary in nature and cannot be used to serve a permanent purpose or continue for an unreasonably long period.
material_facts: The flat was requisitioned and allotted to an occupant who remained in possession under the requisition.
The requisition continued for about thirty years.
Even assuming the original purpose was to house a homeless person, the requisition continued long after that initial purpose could justify it.
members.legal_principle: Acquisition transfers the owner's title and is permanent, whereas requisition takes control without transferring ownership and must be temporary. Requisition may be used only for a transitory public purpose; a permanent purpose from the outset makes requisition an improper use of the power, and a requisition cannot continue indefinitely. The Court relied on Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule and the original Article 31(2) of the Constitution, and referred to Chiranjitlal's case.
members.conclusion: Even if valid when made, the requisition ceased to be valid and effective after a reasonable period; it could not continue for about thirty years, and the State had to revoke it, remove the allottee, and return vacant possession to the owner.

predicates.requisition_order_challenged: A person with an interest in property challenged an order requisitioning that property.
predicates.permanent_purpose_from_inception: The property was required from the outset for a purpose that was permanent or likely to continue indefinitely.
predicates.continued_for_unreasonable_time: The requisition remained in force for a period that was unreasonably long in the circumstances.
predicates.requisition_order_ceases_to_be_effective: The requisition order is no longer valid and effective.

members.legal_issue: Requisition cannot continue indefinitely or for an unreasonable period, even when it serves a permanent public purpose.
material_facts: Some residential and commercial premises had been requisitioned and occupied for decades, including premises requisitioned more than 45 years earlier.
Many residential premises had been requisitioned in or before 1960, and the requisition orders had not been replaced by acquisition.
The State continued to rely on public needs, including accommodation and the operation of fair-price shops.
members.legal_principle: Requisition is temporary in contrast to acquisition, which transfers title. Indefinite or unreasonably prolonged requisition may effectively deprive the owner of the rights of possession and enjoyment without acquisition and due compensation. H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra correctly states that requisition cannot continue indefinitely; Jiwani Kumar Paraki v. First Land Acquisition Collector and Mangilal Karwa v. State of M.P. support the distinction between requisition and acquisition. Collector of Akola v. Ramchandra does not conflict because it concerned the permissible nature of the purpose, not indefinite duration. The reasonable period depends on the circumstances, and is ordinarily for the Government to decide.
members.conclusion: A requisition order may continue only for a reasonable period in the circumstances of the particular case. Continuation for about 30 years was unreasonable, but 30 years is not a fixed outer limit applicable to every case.

predicates.requisition_order_continuation_case: The matter concerns whether an existing requisition order may continue.
predicates.continuation_is_indefinite: The requisition is being continued without a meaningful limit on its duration.
predicates.continuation_is_unreasonable_in_case_cir: The duration of the requisition is unreasonable in light of the circumstances of the particular case.

members.legal_issue: A renewed lease that incorporates the original lease covenants without reservation may preserve an unexhausted option to renew, while the resulting further lease need not itself provide another renewal option.
material_facts: The original lease contained an option to renew for a further term.
The first renewal was executed in a fresh deed that incorporated all covenants and stipulations of the original lease without reservation.
The lessee exercised the option for another renewal, and the State’s officials had recommended or supported renewal before the State disputed the entitlement.
The State had not exercised a right of re-entry before the lessee exercised the renewal option.
members.legal_principle: Whether a renewal covenant carries into a renewed lease depends on the language of the original covenant, the renewed deed, the parties’ intention and the surrounding circumstances, read as a whole. A renewal requires a fresh lease deed. Although the law does not prohibit a perpetual lease, courts lean against perpetual renewal and generally require clear and unambiguous language to establish it. The Court agreed with Syed Jaleel Zane v. P. Venkata Murlidhar & Ors. and Secretary of State for India in Council v. A.H. Forbes; it also relied on Green v. Palmer and referred to Baker v. Merckel and Mulla on the Transfer of Property Act. The principle in Green v. Palmer supports including a renewal covenant in the renewed lease where the original language requires it, without thereby creating an endless succession of renewals.
members.conclusion: The lessee was entitled to a further 50-year renewal commencing May 20, 1987. The lease granted for that term need not include a further renewal covenant, so the ruling does not create a right to successive renewals under that new lease.

rule.if: lease_renewal_appeal and original_lease_allowed_renewal and first_renewal_incorporated_original_covenants_without_reservation and lessee_exercised_further_option

predicates.lease_renewal_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a lessee’s claimed right to renew a lease.
predicates.original_lease_allowed_renewal: The original lease gave the lessee an option to renew.
predicates.first_renewal_incorporated_original_cove: The deed for the first renewal incorporated the original lease’s covenants without reserving an exception for the renewal covenant.
predicates.lessee_exercised_further_option: The lessee exercised the claimed option for a further renewal.

members.legal_issue: Fixing a term in a fresh lease does not, by itself, exclude a renewal option incorporated from the original lease.
material_facts: The compromise fixed the period during which the occupants could remain as lessees.
It incorporated the original lease terms for matters not specifically covered by the compromise.
The original lease contained a renewal option.
members.legal_principle: A renewal option is independent of the duration fixed for the initial lease term. Incorporating the original lease terms for matters not otherwise covered therefore carries the renewal option into the fresh lease, notwithstanding the fixed term. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied upon for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The renewal option remained one of the terms of the fresh lease despite the fixed term stated in the compromise.

rule.if: lease_created_by_compromise and original_lease_terms_incorporated_for_unaddressed_matters and original_lease_contains_renewal_option and initial_lease_term_fixed

predicates.lease_created_by_compromise: The parties’ compromise established a lease.
predicates.original_lease_terms_incorporated_for_un: The compromise adopted the original lease terms for matters it did not otherwise address.
predicates.original_lease_contains_renewal_option: The original lease gives the lessee an option to renew.
predicates.initial_lease_term_fixed: The compromise specifies the duration of the initial lease term.

members.legal_issue: State-owned property situated in a Union Territory is exempt from property taxes imposed under parliamentary authority.
material_facts: The municipal committee assessed property tax on immovable properties owned and occupied by State Governments within a Union Territory.
The States challenged the assessments and demands, claiming the constitutional exemption from Union taxation.
members.legal_principle: Article 289(1) exempts State property from Union taxation, and the term “Union Taxation” includes taxes leviable under parliamentary laws applicable to Union Territories, including laws made under Article 246(4). The Court relied on the ratio of In Re The Bill to amend Section 20 of the Sea Customs Act (the Sea Customs case), reaffirmed in Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation v. Income Tax Officer (the APSRTC case), and on the continuity between Section 155 of the Government of India Act, 1935 and Article 289(1).
members.conclusion: The States are exempt from property taxes imposed on their properties in Union Territories under laws made by Parliament.

predicates.constitutional_tax_immunity_appeal: A proceeding challenges a tax assessment on the ground that constitutional immunity protects the property from that tax.
predicates.state_owned_property_in_union_territory: A State Government owns property situated within a Union Territory.
predicates.property_tax_imposed_under_parliamentary: A property tax is imposed in the territory under authority derived from parliamentary law.

members.legal_issue: Municipal property taxes imposed in a Union Territory fall within the Union-tax exemption for State property.
material_facts: A municipal committee imposed property tax under a municipal enactment on property owned and occupied by State Governments in a Union Territory.
The municipal enactment directed the collected sums to a municipal fund and assigned municipal functions for collecting and applying those sums.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 265, 289(1), 243X and 243ZB, a municipality does not have an independent plenary power to tax; its taxing power is conferred by the relevant legislature. Taxation by authorities within a State is State taxation, while municipal taxes in a Union Territory are within Union taxation. The Court relied on the structure of Articles 285 and 289 and the interpretation of Article 289(1) in the Sea Customs and APSRTC cases.
members.conclusion: Municipal property taxes imposed in Union Territories are within the exemption in Article 289(1), and State property is exempt from them.

predicates.constitutional_tax_immunity_appeal: A proceeding challenges a tax assessment on the ground that constitutional immunity protects the property from that tax.
predicates.state_owned_property_in_union_territory: A State Government owns property situated within a Union Territory.
predicates.municipal_body_imposed_property_tax: A municipality imposed a property tax under authority granted by a legislature.

members.legal_issue: Taxes imposed under laws governing a union territory constitute Union taxation for purposes of the constitutional immunity of state property.
material_facts: Municipal laws in force in the territory imposed property taxes on land and buildings, including property owned by state governments.
The municipal law governing one area had been extended to the territory by parliamentary legislation, and the municipal laws governing the other areas were enacted by Parliament.
The dispute concerned property taxes imposed on state-owned property situated within a union territory.
members.legal_principle: Article 289(1) exempts state property from Union taxation. Under Article 246(4), Parliament has power to legislate for territories outside the States, including on matters in the State List. The Court relied on the majority ruling in In Re the Sea Customs Act that state property in a union territory is exempt from Union taxation on property, reaffirmed in Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation v. Income Tax Officer. It also relied on T.M. Kanniyan v. Income Tax Officer for Parliament’s plenary legislative power over union territories, and Mithan Lal v. State of Delhi for the principle that a law extended to a territory by Parliament derives force there from the parliamentary enactment.
members.conclusion: The property taxes imposed under the municipal laws constitute Union taxation.

predicates.property_tax_dispute_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a tax imposed on property.
predicates.state_owned_property_in_union_territory: A state government owns property situated in a territory that is not part of a State.
predicates.taxing_law_has_parliamentary_force: The law imposing the tax was enacted by Parliament or was extended to the territory by parliamentary legislation.

members.legal_issue: An actor whose unauthorized interference with a natural watercourse causes environmental damage must bear the cost of restoring the damaged environment.
material_facts: The motel constructed embankments and other works along the river and dredged and channelized its flow, including works that blocked the mouth of a natural spill channel.
The motel undertook the works without permission from the relevant department and without expert advice.
The court found that the motel’s constructions and interference with the river’s natural flow degraded the environment and ecology of the area.
The court directed the motel to pay compensation for environmental restitution and directed an expert assessment of the likely restoration cost.
members.legal_principle: The polluter-pays principle means that liability for environmental harm includes both compensation to affected persons and the cost of restoring the damaged environment. A person carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is liable for harm caused by that activity irrespective of whether reasonable care was taken. The Court relied on Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, which recognized the precautionary and polluter-pays principles as essential features of sustainable development and part of Indian law, and Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, which applied the polluter-pays principle and absolute liability.
members.conclusion: The motel was directed to pay the cost of restitution of the environment and ecology damaged by its works, with the amount to be assessed. It was also directed to show cause why an additional pollution fine should not be imposed.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The matter was brought as a public-interest proceeding concerning environmental protection.
predicates.actor_interferes_with_natural_watercours: An actor carried out works that interfered with a natural watercourse without authorization.
predicates.actor_causes_environmental_damage: The actor’s works caused damage to the environment or ecology.

members.legal_issue: The polluter pays principle makes a polluting actor liable both to compensate affected persons and to pay the cost of restoring environmental damage, including damage caused in the past.
material_facts: Tannery effluent had polluted water and soil, impaired agricultural land, and caused hardship and health risks for residents.
The tanneries had operated and polluted the area for years, including some that had by then installed pollution-control equipment.
The Court directed assessment of compensation for affected persons and the cost of reversing environmental damage.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the polluter pays principle as an essential feature of sustainable development and part of domestic environmental law. It relied on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, J.T. 1996 (2) 196, which applied absolute liability to hazardous or inherently dangerous activities regardless of reasonable care. The Court also relied on Article 21 and Articles 47, 48A, and 51A(g) of the Constitution, environmental legislation, and the rule that customary international law forms part of domestic law when not contrary to municipal law.
members.conclusion: Polluting industries are absolutely liable to compensate affected persons and to pay the cost of restoring the damaged environment; liability for past pollution remains even if an industry has since installed pollution-control devices.

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The proceeding concerns public interests affected by environmental conditions.
predicates.polluting_activity: An actor’s activity releases pollutants into the environment.
predicates.environmental_or_personal_harm: The pollution has harmed the environment or people affected by it.

members.legal_issue: An operator responsible for pollution must compensate affected people and pay the cost of restoring the damaged environment.
material_facts: Reports attributed pollution, salinisation, ecological degradation, and loss of livelihood to commercial aquaculture operations.
The court found that commercial aquaculture farms had operated in coastal areas in violation of applicable environmental requirements and that affected people had suffered harm.
The court directed an authority to assess both the loss to ecology and the compensation owed to affected individuals and families, with recovery from polluters.
members.legal_principle: Under the polluter-pays principle, as explained in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India and Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, liability extends beyond compensation to victims to the cost of reversing environmental degradation. The court also applied the principle of absolute liability for harm caused by hazardous or inherently dangerous activity.
members.conclusion: Polluting aquaculture operators are liable to compensate affected people and to pay the cost of restoring the damaged environment.

predicates.public_interest_environment_proceeding: A public-interest proceeding seeks relief for environmental pollution or degradation.
predicates.operator_activity_causes_pollution_harm: An operator's activity causes pollution or environmental harm.
predicates.affected_people_or_ecology_suffer_loss: People or the environment suffer loss as a result of the pollution or harm.

members.legal_issue: A person who causes pollution may be required to pay compensation for restoring the environment and ecology and for losses suffered by victims.
material_facts: The Court had found that the motel interfered with the river’s natural flow and disturbed the environment and ecology of the area.
The earlier judgment directed the motel to pay compensation towards restoring the environment and ecology, with the amount still to be assessed.
members.legal_principle: Under the polluter pays principle, a polluter must make good the environmental damage caused. Pollution is a civil wrong against the community, and the Court may award damages in a public-interest or writ proceeding under Article 32. The Court relied on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, (1996) 3 SCC 212, and Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 647.
members.conclusion: The Court reaffirmed that a person responsible for pollution must pay compensation for environmental restoration and may also be liable for losses suffered by those harmed by the pollution.

predicates.constitutional_public_interest_proceedin: The matter is a public-interest proceeding before a constitutional court.
predicates.environmental_or_personal_loss_resulted: The pollution caused environmental damage or loss to persons.

members.legal_issue: Deliberate conduct that exceeds permission to repair a structure and damages mangroves or obstructs natural water flow constitutes willful disobedience of the applicable orders.
material_facts: The appellants were permitted to repair an existing bund, subject to conditions that they carry out no other construction, not destroy mangroves or vegetation, and not raise the bund’s existing height.

Inspection reports and a court-directed site inspection found that the appellants had widened and raised the bund, built platforms, dumped debris and boulders, closed culverts, obstructed the natural flow of water, and cut or damaged mangroves.
The reports described the work as extensive and the Court found the disobedience deliberate.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated contempt proceedings as quasi-criminal and found that the documented, deliberate departures from the repair-only permission and its conditions established contumacious conduct. It also held that an unlawful action cannot be validated by describing it as repair work.
members.conclusion: The appellants were guilty of willful defiance of the Court’s orders and the District Collector’s order, and the contempt proceedings brought against them were allowed.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding_for_order_disobedience and permission_limited_to_repair_existing_structure and conditions_prohibited_expansion_or_ecological_damage and (party_expanded_structure_or_blocked_water_flow or party_damaged_protected_vegetation) and inspection_evidence_confirmed_violations

predicates.contempt_proceeding_for_order_disobedien: The proceeding alleges disobedience of an order made by a court or public authority.
predicates.permission_limited_to_repair_existing_st: A party was allowed to repair an existing structure, rather than to undertake new or expanded construction.
predicates.conditions_prohibited_expansion_or_ecolo: The permission required the party not to expand the structure or damage protected vegetation or ecological conditions.
predicates.party_expanded_structure_or_blocked_wate: The party expanded the structure or obstructed the natural flow of water while carrying out the work.
predicates.party_damaged_protected_vegetation: The party cut, destroyed, or otherwise damaged protected vegetation while carrying out the work.
predicates.inspection_evidence_confirmed_violations: Inspection evidence confirmed the prohibited work or resulting ecological damage.

members.legal_issue: Substantial construction carried out contrary to a court’s restraint order constitutes disobedience of that order.
material_facts: A court had restrained construction on the land and required prior permission for work there.
Government reports and an expert committee’s inspection described extensive concrete and brick construction, requiring construction machinery and a large workforce.
The government acknowledged that the work had stopped by late July, and the court related the inspected construction to the period in which the restraint was in force.
members.legal_principle: A party must obey the terms of a court order; substantial construction undertaken while an order restrains construction is a violation of that order. The court relied on its own earlier orders and the factual material, including the government’s reports and the expert committee’s report.
members.conclusion: The construction was substantial and was carried out in violation of the court’s orders.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.court_order_restrained_construction: A court had ordered that construction on the land must not proceed without the court’s permission.
predicates.substantial_construction_occurred_while_: Extensive construction was carried out on the land while the restraint order remained in force.

members.legal_issue: A tenancy created by a mortgagee in possession ordinarily ends when the mortgagee’s interest ends, unless the mortgagor or successor adopts or recreates the tenancy, or the lease binds as a prudent act of management.
material_facts: A mortgagee in possession leased an urban cinema property to a head lessee, who sublet it.
The lease imposed a low rent and provided for a lengthy term, including renewals; the property could have obtained a substantially higher rent.
The property was sold to satisfy the mortgage debt, extinguishing the mortgagee’s interest, and the purchaser did not adopt or recreate the tenancies.
The mortgagor had cancelled an earlier rent note and permitted the mortgagees to lease the property, but had not expressly agreed to a tenancy continuing beyond the mortgage.
members.legal_principle: A person cannot confer a better title than that person holds. A mortgagee’s interest as lessor is ordinarily coterminous with the mortgage interest, and under section 111(c) of the Transfer of Property Act a lease determines when the lessor’s interest terminates. Under section 76(a), a mortgagee in possession must manage the property as a person of ordinary prudence would manage it; a bona fide and prudent act in the ordinary course of management may bind successors after the mortgage ends. That exception did not apply to this long, low-rent lease. The Court relied on Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh, [1952] S.C.R. 775, and Asaram v. Mst. Ram Kali, [1958] S.C.R. 986.
members.conclusion: The tenancies did not bind the purchaser after the mortgagee’s interest ended. The purchaser was entitled to possession before the stated lease term and renewals expired.

rule.if: possession_suit_after_mortgage_interest_ended and mortgagee_created_tenancy and successor_did_not_adopt_tenancy and (lease_not_prudent_management or no_express_post_mortgage_consent)

predicates.possession_suit_after_mortgage_interest_: A person claiming through ownership sought possession after the mortgage interest had ended.
predicates.mortgagee_created_tenancy: A mortgagee in possession created a tenancy over the mortgaged property.
predicates.successor_did_not_adopt_tenancy: The person succeeding to the mortgagor’s interest did not adopt or recreate the tenancy.
predicates.lease_not_prudent_management: The mortgagee granted a lease on terms that were not a prudent act of ordinary property management.
predicates.no_express_post_mortgage_consent: The mortgagor did not expressly agree that the tenancy would continue beyond the mortgage.

members.legal_issue: A lease made by a mortgagee in possession binds the mortgagor after redemption only if it was made in the course of prudent management.
material_facts: The mortgagees in possession let the mortgaged shop to a tenant during the mortgage.
The courts below found that the letting was not a prudent act in the ordinary course of management.
That finding was not challenged and became final.
members.legal_principle: Section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, requires a mortgagee in possession to manage the property as a person of ordinary prudence would manage their own property. A lease that meets that standard may bind the mortgagor after redemption, but the person claiming the benefit of this exception must strictly establish it. The Court relied on Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh, Harihar Prasad Singh v. Must. Of Munshi Nath Prasad, and Asa Ram v. Mst. Ram Kali.
members.conclusion: The letting was not an act of prudent management and did not bind the mortgagor after redemption.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: The proceeding sought redemption of a mortgage and recovery of the property for the owner.
predicates.mortgagee_created_lease: The mortgagee in possession let the property to a tenant during the mortgage.
predicates.lease_not_prudent_management: The lease was not made as an act of prudent management in the ordinary course.

members.legal_issue: An agricultural lease created by a mortgagee in possession binds the mortgagor after redemption only when it is a transaction that a prudent owner would make in the usual course of managing the property.
material_facts: The mortgagors had held the agricultural land as home-farm land, and it was entered as the mortgagees’ Khudkasht after the mortgage was made.
The mortgagees accepted the tenants’ written undertaking and received rent under it.
The rent fixed by the arrangement was not shown to be fair in light of the land’s likely net yield; comparison with the circle rate alone did not establish that it was reasonable.

The land was fertile, had canal irrigation, and was not shown to be an economic choice for leasing to tenants; the evidence did not establish exceptional grounds for the mortgagees’ decision to lease it.
After redemption, the mortgagors’ representatives sought possession, and the tenants claimed that the lease bound the owners.
members.legal_principle: Under section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a mortgagee in possession must manage the property as a person of ordinary prudence would manage their own property. Although a mortgagee’s agricultural lease may remain binding on the mortgagor after redemption, the party claiming that benefit must strictly establish that the lease was one a prudent owner would make in the usual course of management. The absence of a prohibition on leasing in the mortgage deed does not establish that the lease is binding. In Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh, the Court held that a lease prohibited by the mortgage deed is not binding; the Court explained that a lease not protected by section 76(a), or not bona fide, likewise does not bind the mortgagor.
members.conclusion: The lease was not a prudent transaction in the usual course of management and did not bind the mortgagors after redemption.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_binding_effect_of_agricultural_lease_after_mortgage_redemption and lease_created_by_mortgagee_in_possession and mortgage_redeemed and (lease_terms_were_not_shown_to_be_fair_against_likely_property_income or lease_put_owner_protected_home_farm_interests_at_risk_without_exceptional_grounds)

predicates.appeal_challenges_binding_effect_of_agri: The proceeding challenges whether an agricultural lease remains binding on the owner after a mortgage is redeemed.
predicates.lease_created_by_mortgagee_in_possession: A mortgagee in possession created an agricultural lease over the mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgage_redeemed: The mortgagor or the mortgagor’s successor redeemed the mortgage.
predicates.lease_terms_were_not_shown_to_be_fair_ag: The party relying on the lease did not establish that its terms were fair in light of the income a prudent owner could obtain from the property.
predicates.lease_put_owner_protected_home_farm_inte: The lease put the owner’s interests in home-farm land at risk, and no exceptional grounds justified that action.

members.legal_issue: A lease granted by a mortgagor in possession after the mortgage binds the mortgagee only when it is made in the ordinary course of management.
material_facts: The mortgage was created before the lease was granted, and the mortgagor remained in possession.
The mortgagor granted a permanent lease of the mortgaged villages.
The lessees did not allege or establish that the lease was granted on usual terms in the ordinary course of management.
The mortgagee’s successor purchased the mortgaged property at an execution sale and sought possession from the lessees.
members.legal_principle: For leases granted before section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the mortgagor in possession could bind the mortgagee by dealing with the property in the usual course of management, as an agent or bailiff might. A lease on unusual terms, or one that changes the character or use of the property, does not bind the mortgagee merely because it does not impair the security; section 66, which concerns waste, does not govern the power to lease. The lessee bears the burden of establishing that the lease was made on usual terms in the ordinary course of management. The Court approved Madan Mohan Singh v. Raj Kishore Kumari (1916) 21 C.W.N. 88, dissented from Balmukund v. Motilal (1915) 20 C.W.N. 350, and explained Banee Pershad v. Beet Bhunjun Singh (1868) 10 W.R. 325. It also referred to Corbett v. Plowden, Pope v. Briggs, and Moreland v. Richardson in describing the mortgagee’s paramount position and the mortgagor’s authority in ordinary management.
members.conclusion: The permanent lease was not binding on the mortgagee’s successor, and the successor was entitled to possession.

rule.if: mortgagee_possession_claim and mortgage_preceded_lease and mortgagor_in_possession and lessee_failed_usual_management_proof

predicates.mortgagee_possession_claim: A mortgagee or a successor to the mortgagee seeks possession against a person claiming under a lease granted by the mortgagor.
predicates.mortgage_preceded_lease: The lease was granted after the mortgage was created.
predicates.mortgagor_in_possession: The mortgagor remained in possession when the lease was granted.
predicates.lessee_failed_usual_management_proof: The lessee did not establish that the lease was on usual terms and made in the ordinary course of management.

members.legal_issue: A lease granted by a mortgagor outside the ordinary course of management does not bind the mortgagee or an auction-purchaser who acquires the mortgagee’s interest.
material_facts: The relevant mortgages predated the statutory provision conferring a power on a mortgagor in possession to lease mortgaged property.
The mortgagor granted leases that purported to be permanent, some for premiums, after the property had been advertised for sale in execution of the mortgage decree.
The leases were found to have been created in bad faith and outside the ordinary course of management.
The property was purchased at an execution sale by the mortgagee.
members.legal_principle: Section 65A of the Transfer of Property Act was inserted by the Transfer of Property (Amendment) Act, 1929, and the saving provision preserved the incidents of mortgages made before that amendment. Under the earlier law, a mortgagor in possession could make leases binding on the mortgagee only in the ordinary course of management, acting as the mortgagee’s agent or bailiff. The Court relied on Madan Mohan Singh v. Raj Kishori Kumari, Raja Kamakshya Narayan Singh Bahadur v. Chohan Ram, and Gobinda Chandra Saha v. Sasadhar Mandal. An auction-purchaser at a mortgage execution sale acquires both the mortgagor’s and the mortgagee’s interests; a lease that does not bind the mortgagee does not bind that purchaser.
members.conclusion: The later-enacted leasing provision did not govern the leases; under the applicable earlier law, the leases were not in the ordinary course of management and were not binding on the mortgagee or the auction-purchaser.

rule.if: mortgage_enforcement_case and lease_under_preexisting_mortgage_regime and lease_outside_ordinary_management and property_acquired_at_mortgage_sale

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_case: The dispute concerns enforcement of a mortgage over property in the mortgagor’s possession.
predicates.lease_under_preexisting_mortgage_regime: The lease was made under a mortgage whose legal incidents were governed by the law before a later statutory leasing power took effect.
predicates.lease_outside_ordinary_management: The mortgagor granted a lease on terms or in circumstances outside the ordinary management of the property as the mortgagee’s agent or bailiff.
predicates.property_acquired_at_mortgage_sale: The property was purchased at a sale held to enforce the mortgage.

members.legal_issue: A request to bring a deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives on record may be treated as a request to set aside abatement of the entire suit, even when it expressly concerns only that plaintiff.
material_facts: Three purchasers jointly sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell.
One plaintiff died while the suit was pending.
The deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives applied to be brought on record and sought condonation of delay and setting aside of abatement only as to the deceased plaintiff.
The trial judge found sufficient cause for the delay, set aside the abatement as to the deceased plaintiff, and allowed the legal representatives to be brought on record.
The Division Bench treated the suit as having abated in its entirety because the surviving plaintiffs had not separately sought to set aside abatement.
members.legal_principle: Abatement provisions must be construed strictly because abatement denies a hearing on the merits, while applications to set aside abatement should be considered liberally. An application to bring legal representatives on record may in substance include a request to set aside abatement, and an application concerning one plaintiff may be construed as seeking relief for the entire suit. The Court applied Order 22 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and rejected an unduly technical approach.
members.conclusion: The application and the order allowing it had the effect of setting aside abatement of the suit in its entirety; the suit was revived with the legal representatives on record.

rule.if: death_in_multi_plaintiff_suit and (representatives_seek_substitution or representatives_brought_on_record) and delay_found_sufficient

predicates.death_in_multi_plaintiff_suit: One plaintiff died while a suit brought by multiple plaintiffs was pending.
predicates.representatives_seek_substitution: The deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives applied to be brought on record in the suit.
predicates.representatives_brought_on_record: The court allowed the deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives to be brought on record.
predicates.delay_found_sufficient: The court found sufficient cause for the delay in applying to bring the legal representatives on record.

members.legal_issue: Bringing a deceased party’s legal representatives on record in an appeal arising from a suit also brings them on record for the suit.
material_facts: An appeal concerning an interim injunction in the suit was pending when one plaintiff died.
The defendants who had filed that appeal applied to bring the deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives on record as respondents in the appeal.
The legal representatives also applied to be brought on record in the suit, and their application was not opposed by the co-plaintiffs.

The Court reasoned that allowing the defendants’ application in the appeal would bring the legal representatives on record for the suit as well, making the later delay in applying in the suit immaterial.
members.legal_principle: Bringing legal representatives on record at any stage of proceedings enures to the benefit of the entire proceedings; an order allowing substitution in an appeal arising from a suit has effect in the suit as well.
members.conclusion: If the application to bring the legal representatives on record in the related appeal is allowed, their addition enures to the benefit of the suit as well, and a later application in the suit is unnecessary for that purpose.

predicates.related_appeal_pending: An appeal arising from the suit was pending when a party died.
predicates.defendants_seek_substitution_in_appeal: The defendants who brought the related appeal applied to bring the deceased party’s legal representatives on record in that appeal.
predicates.substitution_application_allowed: The court allowed the application to bring the legal representatives on record in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: An ancestral estate that is impartible by custom remains joint family property for the purpose of survivorship unless the right to succeed to it has been renounced or surrendered.
material_facts: The court found that the estate was ancestral and impartible by custom.
The family’s joint status continued, and no partition had occurred.
The record did not establish that the junior family members had renounced or surrendered their right to succeed to the estate.
The estate holder died after the Hindu Succession Act came into force, and the court rejected the contention that the estate was exclusively his property for succession purposes.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj Manne Sultan Bahadur v. Shri Pushavathi Visweswar Gajapathi Raj, which relied on Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi: an ancestral estate impartible by custom is not the holder’s separate property, and the right of survivorship remains an incident of joint family ownership. Chinnathayal alias Veeralakshmi v. Kulasekara Pandiya Naicker requires proof of an express or implied intention to renounce or surrender the right to succeed before the estate can be treated as separate for succession. The court also recognized that a holder may alienate an impartible estate by gift or will unless restricted by family custom or tenure. Sections 4 and 6 of the Hindu Succession Act govern the displacement of custom and statutory devolution, respectively.
members.conclusion: The estate remained joint family property for the purpose of survivorship, although it was impartible and the customary rule of primogeniture no longer governed succession under the Hindu Succession Act.

rule.if: succession_in_impartible_estate and ancestral_estate and customary_impartibility and joint_family_status_continued and not succession_right_renounced

predicates.succession_in_impartible_estate: The proceeding concerns succession to an estate that is asserted to be impartible.
predicates.ancestral_estate: The estate came to its holder as ancestral family property.
predicates.customary_impartibility: A custom made the estate impartible.
predicates.joint_family_status_continued: The family remained joint, with no partition ending that status.
predicates.succession_right_renounced: The junior family members expressly or impliedly renounced or surrendered their right to succeed to the estate.

members.legal_issue: A family arrangement that settles immediate possession and allocates other properties does not, without clear evidence of an intention to renounce succession, convert an impartible estate into the separate property of the current holder’s branch.
material_facts: The zamindari was an impartible estate owned by a Hindu joint family, and the junior branches could not demand its partition.

The 1890 arrangements gave the holder possession after the widow’s lifetime and allocated other properties, but did not expressly renounce the junior branches’ contingent right to succeed if the holder’s line became extinct.
Family members described the family as undivided and referred to the person next entitled to succeed; the evidence did not show a clear intention to end the joint family character of the zamindari.
The widow claimed the zamindari as the separate property of her husband, while members of other branches asserted succession through the family.
members.legal_principle: To establish that an impartible estate has ceased to be joint family property for succession, the party asserting separation must prove an express or implied intention to renounce the chance of succession and to impress the estate with the character of separate property. A power to alienate an impartible estate does not imply a power to partition it. The Court relied on Konammal v. Annadana, Collector of Gorakhpur v. Ram Sundar Mal, and Sri Raja Lakshmi Devi Garu v. Sri Raja Surya Narayana, and distinguished Vadrevu Ranganayakamma, Sivagnana Tevar, and Thakurani Tara Kumari.
members.conclusion: The 1890 arrangement did not prove a partition or renunciation of the junior branches’ expectancy of succession. The zamindari remained joint family property for succession purposes, and the widow’s claim to it as her husband’s separate property failed.

rule.if: impartible_estate_succession_dispute and family_members_preserved_contingent_succession and not clear_intention_to_sever_estate and holder_power_to_alienate

predicates.impartible_estate_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns succession to an impartible estate held by a family.
predicates.family_members_preserved_contingent_succ: Family members’ statements or arrangements preserved succession rights if the current holder’s line failed.
predicates.clear_intention_to_sever_estate: The evidence clearly shows an intention to end the estate’s joint family character and make it separate property.
predicates.holder_power_to_alienate: The holder had power to alienate the impartible estate.

members.legal_issue: The impartibility of an ancestral estate and succession by primogeniture do not by themselves end the joint-family character of the estate or the right of survivorship; ending that status requires proof that junior family members intended to renounce succession.
material_facts: The inam estate was ancestral, impartible and devolved under a rule of lineal primogeniture.
The evidence showed that the family treated the estate and property acquired from its income as joint family property.
The trial court found that the alleged partition had not occurred, and that finding was not reversed.
The record did not establish that the junior members had renounced their right of succession.
members.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, an ancestral estate does not become the holder’s separate property merely because it is impartible: custom may displace ordinary incidents of joint property, but survivorship remains unless renounced. Nagesh Bisto Desai v. Khando Tirmal Desai reaffirmed that principle. To establish that a Mitakshara family holding an impartible estate has ceased to be joint, an express or implied intention by junior members to renounce succession must be proved.
members.conclusion: The estate retained its character as joint family property, with survivorship governed by the applicable rule of succession; impartibility alone did not make it the separate property of the holder.

predicates.ancestral_impartible_estate_dispute: The proceeding concerns an ancestral estate that is impartible under its governing custom or grant.
predicates.estate_descended_within_family: The estate passed among members of the family under a succession rule applicable to the family estate.
predicates.junior_members_did_not_renounce_successi: The junior family members did not expressly or impliedly give up their right to succeed to the estate.

members.legal_issue: An ancestral estate that is impartible by custom and devolves by primogeniture remains joint family property for purposes of the junior members’ rights of maintenance and survivorship.
material_facts: The estate was impartible by custom and had passed as an ancestral estate through primogeniture.
The deed described the eldest son as succeeding to the estate and the younger sons as having a right to maintenance and a reasonable share in lieu of that right.
members.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi, an ancestral impartible estate held by succession through primogeniture is part of the undivided Hindu family estate. Rani Sartaj Kuari v. Deoraj Kuari and the First Pittapur case establish that the rights to partition and to restrain alienations do not apply in the ordinary way to an impartible estate. Collector of Gorakhpur v. Ram Sunder Mal and Baijnath Prasad Singh v. Tej Bali Singh affirm that maintenance and survivorship remain and that junior members’ maintenance right rests on joint ownership; survivorship is distinct from a mere spes successionis and can be surrendered. The Court also referred to Raja Yarlagadda Mallikarjuna Prasad Nayadu v. Raja Yarlagadda Durga Prasad Nayadu and Protap Chandra Deo v. Jagadish Chandra Deo.
members.conclusion: The estate was not the holder’s separate or exclusive property: although partition and restraint of alienation were inconsistent with its impartibility, the rights of maintenance and survivorship remained, and the junior members’ maintenance right was based on their joint ownership.

predicates.impartible_estate_dispute: The proceeding concerns an estate that is impartible under custom.
predicates.ancestral_estate: The holder received the estate as ancestral property.
predicates.holder_succeeded_by_primogeniture: The holder succeeded to the ancestral estate by primogeniture.

members.legal_issue: An ancestral estate that is impartible by custom and descends by primogeniture remains joint family property, although most ordinary coparcenary rights do not apply to it.
material_facts: The estate was ancestral and descended by primogeniture under a family custom.
The family remained undivided when the estate was held as impartible.
The dispute arose in a partition suit concerning the family estate.
members.legal_principle: Under Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, an ancestral customary impartible estate descending by primogeniture remains joint family property. The rights of partition, restraint of alienation, and maintenance do not apply in the ordinary way to impartible property, but survivorship remains; that right is distinct from a mere spes successionis and may be renounced or surrendered. Rani Sartaj Kuari v. Deoraj Kuari and the First Pittapur case address the incompatibility of partition and restraint of alienation with impartibility, while the Second Pittapur case addresses maintenance.
members.conclusion: The estate was not the holder’s separate or exclusive property; it remained joint family property, with survivorship as the relevant continuing coparcenary right.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and ancestral_estate and impartibility_by_custom and descent_by_primogeniture

predicates.partition_proceeding: The dispute is being determined in a proceeding seeking partition of family property.
predicates.ancestral_estate: The property came down through the family as ancestral property.
predicates.impartibility_by_custom: The family custom treated the estate as indivisible.
predicates.descent_by_primogeniture: The estate descended to a single heir under a primogeniture rule.

members.legal_issue: An ancestral impartible estate does not become the separate property of its current holder merely because it is impartible, and its joint-family character continues unless junior members renounce their right of succession.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that the family estate was impartible and that succession followed lineal primogeniture, making him entitled to exclusive possession as the current office-holder.

The lower courts found that the alleged custom of impartibility and primogeniture had not been proved; the legal argument before the Supreme Court proceeded on the assumption that the estate was impartible.
The claimant and the other parties descended from a common family ancestor.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, custom may displace some ordinary incidents of joint-family property in an impartible estate, but survivorship remains unless renounced. The Court relied principally on Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, Baijnath Prasad Singh v. Tej Bali Singh, Collector of Gorakhpur v. Ram Sunder Mal, Anant Bhikappa Patil v. Shankar Ramchandra Patil, and Chinnathayi v. Kulasekara Pandiya Naicker; it distinguished Mirza Raja Shri Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Raj Manne Sultan Bahadur and Rajah Velugoti Kumara Krishna Yachendra Varu because those cases concerned different statutory schemes and facts.
members.conclusion: Even if an ancestral estate is impartible, impartibility alone does not make it the separate property of the holder or destroy the right of survivorship. The family ceases to be joint in respect of the estate only if the junior members expressly or impliedly renounce their succession rights.

rule.if: ancestral_family_estate and impartible_estate and not junior_members_renounced_succession

predicates.ancestral_family_estate: The estate descended within a family as ancestral property.
predicates.impartible_estate: The estate could not be divided under a custom or other rule governing its tenure or succession.
predicates.junior_members_renounced_succession: The junior members expressly or impliedly gave up their right to succeed to the estate.

members.legal_issue: A junior family member has no right to partition an ancestral estate made impartible by grant and succession under primogeniture, although a right of succession may continue unless renounced.
material_facts: A permanent grant provided for enjoyment and succession from generation to generation.
The estate passed through successive generations to the eldest male descendant under primogeniture.
The junior family member received maintenance from the estate and sought a partition share.
There was no evidence that the junior family member had expressly or by implication renounced a right of succession.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law as modified by the custom of impartibility, an impartible estate is not subject to partition or ordinary joint enjoyment, while the right of survivorship may remain. Renunciation of that succession right must be proved to establish that the family has ceased to be joint for purposes of succession. The Court relied on Baijnath Prasad Singh v. Tej Bali Singh, Katama Natchiar v. Raja of Shivganga, Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi, Chinnathayi v. Kulasekara Pandiya Naicker, and Anant Bhikkappa Patil v. Shankar Ramchandra Patil.
members.conclusion: The estate was indivisible and impartible, devolving on the eldest lineal descendant under primogeniture; the junior family member was not entitled to a partition share in it.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A family member brought a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.ancestral_impartible_grant: The property was an ancestral estate granted or held as indivisible and impartible.
predicates.primogeniture_succession: The estate passed to the eldest male lineal descendant under a rule of primogeniture.

members.legal_issue: Properties incorporated into an ancient impartible estate retain their impartible character when they do not vest in the government, and junior family members acquire no right by birth to partition them.
material_facts: The properties claimed for partition were outside the territorial limits of the estate and did not vest in the government under the abolition legislation.
The properties had been incorporated into the impartible estate.
The estate was impartible by ancient custom.
The claimants sought partition as junior members of the family.
members.legal_principle: The abolition legislation repealed the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, in its application to the estate transferred to the government, but did not affect properties outside that transferred estate; the 1904 Act continued to apply to those properties. Incorporated property acquired the impartible character of the estate, which could not be lost without statutory intervention. Custom may outlive the conditions that gave rise to it; the maxim cessante ratione legis cessat ipsa lex did not apply. Junior members of an ancient impartible joint-family estate acquire no right in the property by birth and therefore have no right to partition. The court relied on sections 3(b) and 66 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, section 4 of the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, Rai Kishore Singh v. Mst. Gahanabai, C.I.T. Punjab v. Dewan Krishna Kishore, Raja Velugoti v. Raja Rajeshwara Rao, Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Rai Maina v. Pushavathi Visweswar, and Anant Bhikappa v. Shankar Ramchandra.
members.conclusion: The properties retained their impartible character, and the junior members had no right to partition them.

rule.if: partition_claim_over_family_property and property_was_incorporated_into_impartible_estate and property_did_not_vest_in_government and estate_is_impartible_by_custom

predicates.partition_claim_over_family_property: Junior members of a family sought partition of family property.
predicates.property_was_incorporated_into_impartibl: The property had been incorporated into an impartible estate.
predicates.property_did_not_vest_in_government: The property was not transferred to the government under the abolition measure.
predicates.estate_is_impartible_by_custom: The estate had been found to be impartible by custom.

members.legal_issue: Average annual forest income must be determined by considering both historical income and an appraisal of annual yield, but their figures must not be added together.
material_facts: The compensation officer calculated historical income over a period before vesting and separately appraised annual yield at vesting.
The officer added the results of those two calculations to determine average annual forest income.
The High Court assessed evidence about the forests’ recent felling and growth, and the Supreme Court found no error in that assessment.
members.legal_principle: Section 39(1)(e)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, provides for using income over a reasonable period of agricultural years preceding vesting and calculating its average. Section 39(1)(e)(ii) provides for appraising annual yield at vesting, taking account, among other things, of the number and age of trees, cultivated area, and produce. The provisions require recourse to both methods, not arithmetical addition of their results. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The compensation officer must use both the historical-income method and the annual-yield appraisal to compute average annual forest income, but must not add the figures produced by the two methods.

predicates.forest_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation for a forest that vested in the state.
predicates.historical_forest_income_assessed: The decision-maker determines income derived from the forest over a period before vesting and calculates an average.
predicates.current_forest_yield_appraised: The decision-maker appraises the forest’s annual yield as at vesting, including relevant features such as its trees, area, and produce.

members.legal_issue: Average annual income from a forest must be assessed using both its income over the relevant preceding years and the appraised annual yield of the forest on the date of vesting.
material_facts: The Compensation Officer calculated average income from past forest-sale proceeds but did not appraise the forest’s annual yield on the date of vesting.
The High Court appraised the yield at vesting, considered evidence about the forest and a post-vesting sale of a forest coupe, and combined that appraisal with the historical-income calculation.
members.legal_principle: Section 39(1)(e)(i) and (ii) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, provides cumulative rather than alternative methods: the word “and” requires both factors to be considered. Using the at-vesting yield helps keep compensation proportionate to the forest’s actual and potential value and counteracts distortions caused by unusually heavy or light exploitation. The Court relied on Ganga Devi v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which held that both sub-clauses must be referred to and that the at-vesting yield is appraised by considering matters including the number and age of trees, the forest area, and its produce.
members.conclusion: The Compensation Officer was required to consider both historical income and the appraised annual yield at vesting; the High Court’s resulting assessment was not disturbed.

predicates.forest_compensation_assessment: A decision-maker is assessing forest income in a compensation proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Computing average annual income from a forest for compensation requires consideration of both its historical income and its appraised annual yield when it vested, with the average determined from both measures.
material_facts: A forest vested in the State, and compensation was assessed for its former owners.
The compensation officer assessed historical income using the forest’s accounts and separately assessed its annual yield at vesting, then averaged the two figures.
On appeal, the High Court reassessed the annual yield at vesting and calculated average annual income by averaging that figure with the historical-income figure.
The former owners challenged the use of the vesting-date yield, contending that the historical-income measure alone should be used.
members.legal_principle: Section 39(1)(e) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 requires the compensation officer to consider both historical income under clause (i) and the appraised annual yield at vesting under clause (ii); the two are cumulative, not alternative, and “average” means their arithmetic mean. Appraisal of yield at vesting may take account of the number and age of trees, the forest area, and its produce. The Court applied Durgi Devi v. State of U.P. ([1978] 3 SCR 595; [1978] 3 SCC 101) and Ganga Devi v. State of U.P. ([1972] 3 SCC 126).
members.conclusion: The Court held that both measures had to be considered and that the average annual income was properly calculated by taking their arithmetic mean. It dismissed the appeals with costs.

predicates.forest_compensation_appeal: An appeal concerns the calculation of compensation for a forest that vested in the State.
predicates.historical_forest_income_assessed: The compensation authority assessed the forest’s income over a preceding period.
predicates.vesting_date_forest_yield_appraised: The compensation authority appraised the forest’s annual yield as of the time it vested.
predicates.average_forest_income_uses_both_measures: The average annual income for compensation is calculated using both the historical income and the appraised yield at vesting.

members.legal_issue: An unstamped and unregistered sale deed that cannot convey title may be considered to determine the collateral matter of the nature of possession.
material_facts: The parties did not dispute execution of a written sale deed, but it was unstamped and unregistered.
The deed could not convey title, but it recorded the basis on which the purchasers entered possession.
The deed was considered to determine whether the initial possession was illegal or unauthorized.
members.legal_principle: A sale deed must be properly stamped and registered to convey title. Even if such a document is inadmissible in evidence for that purpose, it may be considered for a collateral purpose, including the nature of possession. No earlier cases were relied on for this proposition in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The deed could not convey title, but it could be looked at for the collateral purpose of determining the nature of possession.

predicates.civil_land_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over rights in land.
predicates.instrument_unstamped_or_unregistered: A party relies on a written transfer instrument that is unstamped or unregistered.
predicates.purpose_is_collateral: The instrument is offered to establish a matter collateral to whether it conveyed title, such as the nature of possession.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered document requiring registration may be used to establish a collateral matter, including the nature of a person’s possession, but not as evidence of the transaction affecting the property.
material_facts: The maintenance deed was unstamped and unregistered, although it required registration.
The deed could not be received as evidence of a transaction affecting the land.
The nature of the defendant’s possession was a collateral matter for which the deed was relied on.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 49 of the Indian Registration Act require registration of specified documents and restrict the use of an unregistered document as evidence of a transaction affecting immovable property. The proviso to section 49 permits its use as evidence of a collateral transaction or purpose that does not itself require a registered instrument.
members.conclusion: The maintenance deed could be considered for the collateral purpose of ascertaining the nature of the defendant’s possession.

rule.if: registration_evidence_dispute and document_requires_registration and document_unregistered and collateral_possession_purpose

predicates.registration_evidence_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a document may be used as evidence about possession of property.
predicates.document_requires_registration: The document is of a kind that the law requires to be registered.
predicates.collateral_possession_purpose: The document is offered to establish the nature of possession rather than to prove the transaction affecting the property.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered lease instrument cannot establish its contractual terms, but may be considered to determine the nature and character of possession.
material_facts: The parties executed an indenture for a lease exceeding one year, but the indenture was not registered.
The tenant’s written statement separately admitted that it occupied the property under the lease for a fixed term and that the term had expired.
members.legal_principle: Sections 107 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and 17 and 49 of the Registration Act 1908 require registration of a lease for a term exceeding one year and render an unregistered instrument inadmissible to prove the terms of the transaction, subject to its use for a collateral purpose such as assessing the nature and character of possession. The Court applied Satish Chand Makhan v Govardhan Das Byas, (1984) 1 SCC 369, and distinguished Park Street Properties Private Limited v Dipak Kumar Singh, (2016) 9 SCC 268, which recognizes that tenancy may be determined from other evidence, including the parties’ conduct.
members.conclusion: The contents of the unregistered indenture were inadmissible to determine the lease’s contractual terms; the indenture could be considered only to assess the nature and character of possession.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_possession: A civil suit concerns recovery of possession of property occupied by a person under an alleged lease.
predicates.lease_term_exceeds_one_year: The alleged lease is for a term exceeding one year.
