State of Haryana (2010) 8 SCC 536, Sidhartha Vashisht @ Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2010) 6 SCC 1, and Ramkrushna v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 13 SCC 525.
members.conclusion: The hostile witnesses’ evidence was admissible and could be relied on to the extent that it supported the prosecution and was corroborated by other reliable evidence.

rule.if: criminal_trial and witness_declared_hostile and testimony_supports_prosecution and corroborated_by_reliable_evidence

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: The prosecution asked the court to treat a witness as hostile, and the court did so.
predicates.testimony_supports_prosecution: Part of the witness’s testimony supports the prosecution’s account of the incident.
predicates.corroborated_by_reliable_evidence: Other reliable evidence supports the relevant part of the witness’s testimony.

members.legal_issue: Declaring a witness hostile does not by itself make the witness’s evidence unreliable or exclude it from consideration.
material_facts: Several prosecution witnesses were declared hostile after giving testimony favourable to the defence.
Their testimony included evidence about directions to pursue compensation payments and efforts to persuade affected landowners to accept compensation.
members.legal_principle: A hostile declaration does not efface a witness’s evidence or create a legal bar to relying on it; its weight must be assessed, and it may support a finding if it is corroborated by other reliable evidence. Applied Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, [1976] 1 SCC 389.
members.conclusion: The evidence of a hostile witness remains admissible and may be considered; the witnesses’ evidence in this case should not have been rejected merely because they were declared hostile.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which a witness gives evidence.
predicates.witness_is_declared_hostile: The court permits the party who called a witness to cross-examine that witness.

members.legal_issue: The testimony of a prosecution witness who is declared hostile is not automatically erased and may be relied on in part if that part remains credible.
material_facts: A prosecution witness did not support the prosecution’s account of the actual assault and was cross-examined by the prosecutor with the court’s permission.
The witness nevertheless gave evidence about the presence of another eyewitness, the accused appearing at the scene, and the deceased later being found bleeding.
Those portions were supported by the other eyewitness and by physical evidence recovered from the scene.
members.legal_principle: Under Satpaul v. Delhi Administration, AIR 1976 SC 294, a witness’s evidence is not washed off the record merely because the witness is cross-examined by the party calling them with the court’s permission; the fact-finder may accept a credible part with due care. Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, AIR 1976 SC 202, likewise holds that such evidence remains admissible and may support a conviction if corroborated by other reliable evidence.
members.conclusion: The trial court was wrong to discard the witness’s evidence altogether; the credible portions supporting the prosecution could be considered.

rule.if: criminal_trial_for_offence and prosecution_witness_declared_hostile and part_of_testimony_remains_credible and credible_part_is_corroborated

predicates.criminal_trial_for_offence: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to prove an accused person’s guilt.
predicates.prosecution_witness_declared_hostile: A prosecution witness did not support the prosecution’s account and was permitted to be cross-examined by the prosecutor.
predicates.part_of_testimony_remains_credible: Some of the witness’s testimony remained believable despite the witness not supporting the prosecution on the whole incident.
predicates.credible_part_is_corroborated: Other reliable evidence supported the portion of the witness’s testimony that remained credible.

members.legal_issue: A hostile witness’s testimony may be relied on to the extent that it supports the prosecution case.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses did not fully support the prosecution case at trial.
The court found that other witnesses had independently proved the relevant facts and that portions of the hostile witnesses’ testimony also supported the prosecution case.
members.legal_principle: A court may rely on the part of a hostile witness’s testimony that supports the prosecution case; the court applied Govindaraju @ Govinda v. State by Sriramapuram P.S. & Anr.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ hostile testimony did not undermine the prosecution case, and its supportive portions could be considered.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and witness_declared_hostile and testimony_partly_supports_prosecution and other_evidence_proves_relevant_facts

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: A prosecution witness did not support the prosecution case in full and was treated as hostile.
predicates.testimony_partly_supports_prosecution: Part of the witness’s testimony supports the prosecution account.
predicates.other_evidence_proves_relevant_facts: Other evidence independently establishes the facts the witness was expected to prove.

members.legal_issue: A witness who is hostile at trial need not have all of their testimony discarded if it still establishes relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The person who drove the vehicle did not support the prosecution’s account in full at trial and differed from an earlier account given to police.
At trial, the driver nevertheless testified to circumstances including that the complainant and the official travelled together and that money was handed over and thrown by the official.
The Court considered the trial testimony as evidence of relevant circumstances while noting that the official’s defence was total denial.
members.legal_principle: A witness’s testimony is not rendered wholly unusable merely because the witness turns hostile; the court may consider the parts of the testimony given in court that it finds relevant and reliable. The judgment refers to the witness’s earlier statement under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but does not treat that statement as the basis for the ruling. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The driver’s testimony was not to be discarded altogether and could be considered for the relevant circumstances it established.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.hostile_witness_gave_relevant_trial_test: A witness who did not support the prosecution in full at trial nevertheless gave testimony establishing circumstances relevant to the case.

members.legal_issue: Permission to cross-examine a party’s own witness does not automatically erase that witness’s evidence, and a credible part of the evidence may still be relied on.
material_facts: A prosecution witness supported the allegation that the accused had confessed.
The prosecutor was permitted to cross-examine that witness only concerning a discrepancy about when the first information report was lodged.
The witness’s account of the confession was not the subject of that limited cross-examination and remained credible in the courts’ assessment.
members.legal_principle: Sections 142 and 154 of the Indian Evidence Act govern leading questions and a party’s ability to cross-examine its own witness; Section 155 concerns impeaching a witness’s credit. As explained in Sat Paul v. Delhi Administration, Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, and Rabindra Kumar Dey v. State of Orissa, permission to cross-examine a witness does not wash the evidence off the record. The fact-finder may rely on a creditworthy part after considering the testimony as a whole, with due caution. Permission under Section 154 is discretionary and must be exercised judicially, not granted merely on a party’s request.
members.conclusion: The witness’s evidence about the confession was admissible and could be relied on; the witness’s limited cross-examination did not erase that evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which a witness gives evidence.
predicates.witness_cross_examined_by_calling_party: The court permits the party that called a witness to question that witness in the manner of cross-examination.
predicates.testimony_part_remains_credible: After considering the testimony as a whole and the effect of the questioning, the fact-finder finds a part of the witness’s evidence credible.

members.legal_issue: A witness’s evidence is not erased merely because the witness is declared hostile, and the court may rely on portions found dependable after careful scrutiny.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses did not support the prosecution in court; several denied being present, while the complainant and another injured witness admitted their presence and injuries but denied the accused’s involvement.

The complainant admitted that he had lodged the prompt report naming the accused and explained that he had named him at the urging of people in the crowd, though he said he had not seen the accused fire.
The complainant and another witness acknowledged that a family dispute concerned the division of immovable property, and witnesses testified that a Panchayat had pardoned the accused.
The witnesses’ medical examinations corroborated that the complainant and another witness had suffered injuries in the incident.
members.legal_principle: A hostile witness’s evidence is not effaced or washed off the record. It must be assessed as a whole and with caution, and the court should normally seek corroboration before acting on it. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Anirudhsing, (1997) 6 SCC 514; State of Rajasthan v. Bhawani, (2003) 7 SCC 291; Radha Mohan Singh v. State of U.P., (2006) 2 SCC 450; Mahesh v. State of Maharashtra, (2008) 13 SCC 271; Rajendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2009) 13 SCC 480; and Govindappa v. State of Karnataka, (2010) 6 SCC 533.
members.conclusion: The Court held that hostile testimony was not to be rejected en bloc and could be accepted to the extent it was dependable; it found that the witnesses had concealed material facts to protect the accused.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which witness testimony is being assessed.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: A witness is declared hostile after giving evidence that departs from the prosecution account.
predicates.testimony_contains_dependable_portions: The witness’s testimony contains portions that remain dependable on careful scrutiny.

members.legal_issue: An approver’s evidence may support a conviction when it is reliable and receives sufficient corroboration on material particulars.
material_facts: The conviction rested mainly on the approver’s account of a poisoning plot.

The High Court found the account of the poisoning plot reliable and corroborated on material particulars by credible prosecution evidence, including evidence concerning the purchase of arsenic and the sweets and the approver’s journey.
The Supreme Court found no error in the High Court’s decision to uphold the conviction.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, as explained and applied in Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] SCR 953, the court must first find the approver reliable, meaning the evidence is not inherently improbable and the approver has not been found to have given false evidence. The court must then find sufficient corroboration, a requirement particular to approver evidence and satisfied by corroboration on material particulars.
members.conclusion: The approver’s evidence met both required tests, so the conviction was properly upheld and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_approver_bas: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction based on an approver’s testimony.
predicates.approver_testimony_reliable: The court finds the approver’s testimony not inherently improbable and has not found that the approver gave false evidence.
predicates.material_particulars_corroborated: Credible evidence corroborates the approver’s account on material particulars.

members.legal_issue: A conviction resting on accomplice testimony requires the accomplice to be reliable and the testimony to be corroborated in material particulars that connect the accused with the crime.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended principally on testimony from an accomplice who had participated in the events and later became an approver.
The court found the approver reliable and considered whether other evidence confirmed the part of his account implicating the accused in the crime.
members.legal_principle: Sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act permit accomplice testimony but embody a rule of caution against conviction on that testimony alone. Corroboration may come from another witness or from circumstances, including the accused’s conduct, and must tend to connect the accused with the crime. The court relied on Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] S.C.R. 953, for the requirement to assess the accomplice’s reliability before considering corroboration, and Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab, [1967] 1 S.C.R. 243, for the reliability test and need for material corroboration.
members.conclusion: An accomplice is competent to testify, but a conviction should not rest on accomplice testimony alone; after finding the accomplice reliable, the court must find reliable corroboration in material particulars connecting the accused with the crime. Corroboration must confirm the crime-implicating part of the account, not merely a collateral part.

predicates.proceeding_relies_on_accomplice_testimon: The prosecution in the criminal proceeding relies on testimony from a participant in the crime who has become an approver.
predicates.accomplice_found_reliable: The court finds that the approver is a reliable witness and that the account is not inherently impossible.
predicates.independent_evidence_confirms_crime_impl: Other testimony or circumstances confirm the part of the approver’s account that implicates the accused in committing the crime.

members.legal_issue: An approver's evidence may support a conviction when it is trustworthy, with corroboration in material particulars ordinarily required as a rule of prudence.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on the testimony of an accomplice who had accepted a pardon.
The trial court and High Court found his evidence consistent on material aspects and corroborated by independent witnesses and other evidence connecting the appellants to the crimes.
The Supreme Court found the corroboration sufficient in material particulars.
members.legal_principle: Section 133 of the Evidence Act makes an accomplice a competent witness and provides that a conviction is not illegal merely because it rests on uncorroborated accomplice testimony. Read with Section 114, illustration (b), the ordinary rule of prudence is that an accomplice should be corroborated in material particulars, including as to each accused. In exceptional circumstances, trustworthy approver evidence may be acted on without corroboration. The Court relied on Bhiva Doulu Patil v. State of Maharashtra, Ram Narain v. State of Rajasthan, and Ravinder Singh v. State of Haryana.
members.conclusion: The approver's evidence was properly relied on because it was credible and corroborated on material particulars.

rule.if: criminal_trial and approver_testimony_relied_on and approver_testimony_trustworthy and material_corroboration_present

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution relies on an accomplice who received a pardon.
predicates.approver_testimony_relied_on: The prosecution asks the court to rely on the evidence of a person involved in the crime who has accepted a pardon.
predicates.approver_testimony_trustworthy: The court finds the approver's account credible and intrinsically reliable.
predicates.material_corroboration_present: Independent evidence corroborates material particulars of the approver's account and connects the accused to the crime.

members.legal_issue: A conviction resting substantially on an approver’s testimony requires material corroboration, particularly when the approver has retracted a confession and is otherwise untrustworthy.
material_facts: The prosecution’s substantial evidence against the appellants was the testimony of an approver who had participated in the crime and retracted his confession before the committal court.
The approver was also involved in illicit liquor manufacture and had a bad character.
The other witnesses did not corroborate the approver on material particulars, and one witness contradicted an important part of his account.
The co-accused confessions were not safe corroboration of the approver’s testimony.
members.legal_principle: Section 133 of the Evidence Act does not bar conviction on an accomplice’s evidence alone, but section 114(b) supports the rule of prudence that an accomplice’s evidence should be corroborated in material particulars. The need is greater where the approver has retracted a confession and is not a person of truth. The Court relied on Bhuboni Sahu v. The King and Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The approver’s evidence, without safe corroboration in material particulars, could not sustain the appellants’ convictions; the convictions and sentences were set aside.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and conviction_depended_on_approver and approver_retracted_confession and no_material_independent_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.conviction_depended_on_approver: The prosecution’s case against the accused depended substantially on an accomplice who testified for the prosecution.
predicates.approver_retracted_confession: The testifying accomplice had retracted a confession before the committal court.
predicates.no_material_independent_corroboration: The other evidence did not independently corroborate the accomplice on material particulars.

members.legal_issue: An approver’s testimony may support a conviction when the testimony is reliable and receives sufficient corroboration in material particulars.
material_facts: The approver gave an account of the poisoning plot that the High Court found reliable and convincing.
Other prosecution witnesses corroborated material parts of the account, including the purchase of the sweets and the approver’s journey to deliver them.
The High Court found those corroborating witnesses reliable.
Some details, including the mixing of poison and delivery of the sweets, had no independent corroboration; the court considered those acts naturally unlikely to have been witnessed by others.
members.legal_principle: Under Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] S.C.R. 953, an approver’s evidence must first be reliable, as evidence from any witness, and must also receive sufficient corroboration, a distinct requirement for an approver. Corroboration is required in material particulars, not necessarily for every detail; the absence of witnesses to acts naturally carried out in private does not by itself defeat the evidence.
members.conclusion: The approver’s evidence satisfied the applicable tests, and the conviction based on it was properly upheld.

rule.if: conviction_appeal and approver_testimony_used and approver_account_reliable and material_particulars_corroborated

predicates.conviction_appeal: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.approver_testimony_used: The prosecution relied on testimony from a participant in the offence who gave evidence for the prosecution.
predicates.approver_account_reliable: The court found that the approver’s account was not inherently improbable and was reliable.
predicates.material_particulars_corroborated: Reliable evidence from other sources supported material particulars of the approver’s account.

members.legal_issue: A retracted judicial confession cannot safely support a conviction unless the court carefully establishes its voluntariness and truth and obtains substantial independent corroboration, particularly when objective circumstances surrounding its retraction remain unexamined.
material_facts: The accused made the judicial confession after being produced from police custody and later retracted it, alleging that he had been taken to a police station and tortured before the confession was recorded.
The accused maintained that allegation in his retraction and in his examination at trial; the prosecution did not adequately disprove it.

Records sought from the jail that could have assisted in determining the accused’s movements before the confession were not produced, and the trial court did not take adequate steps to obtain or investigate those records.
The confession was retracted, and the prosecution did not provide substantial independent and cogent evidence corroborating its material account of the murder and the accused’s role.
The courts below treated the confession as a principal source from which to construct the other evidentiary links rather than first testing the other evidence independently.
members.legal_principle: A judicial confession must comply with Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but procedural compliance alone does not establish voluntariness or truth. The court must probe whether it was voluntary and free of inducement, threat, or torture, consistently with Article 20(3) and Article 21 of the Constitution and Sections 24–26 of the Evidence Act. A retracted confession ordinarily requires substantial independent corroboration, and objective material bearing on the circumstances of its making and retraction must be examined; when relevant records are withheld, the court should not resolve the uncertainty against the accused. The Court relied on Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani, State (N.C.T. of Delhi) v. Navjot Sandhu, Shankaria v. State of Rajasthan, Muthuswami v. State of Madras, Paramananda Pegu v. State of Assam, Bharat v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Babubhai Udesinh Parmar v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The retracted judicial confession was not a safe basis for conviction; the unresolved concerns about voluntariness and the absence of adequate independent corroboration required the accused to receive the benefit of doubt.

rule.if: criminal_case_relying_on_retracted_judicial_confession and confession_made_after_police_custody and voluntariness_material_unresolved and independent_corroboration_insufficient

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_retracted_judic: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution relies on a judicial confession that the accused later withdrew.
predicates.confession_made_after_police_custody: The accused was produced from police custody or was otherwise in circumstances requiring careful scrutiny of possible police influence when the confession was recorded.
predicates.voluntariness_material_unresolved: An allegation or objective circumstance casting doubt on voluntariness remains unresolved after adequate inquiry.
predicates.independent_corroboration_insufficient: Independent evidence does not substantially corroborate the material particulars of the confession and the accused’s role.

members.legal_issue: A retracted judicial confession may be acted upon when it was voluntary and true and receives sufficient independent corroboration in material particulars.
material_facts: Two accused made judicial confessions before magistrates and later retracted them.
The magistrates gave evidence about the precautions taken in recording the confessions, and the courts found the confessions voluntary.
The confessions described the accused’s participation in the killings and related events.

Witness testimony, recoveries, forensic and medical evidence, and circumstances concerning the victims’ last appearances and the disposal or discovery of their bodies supported material parts of the confessions.
members.legal_principle: A confession must be a direct acknowledgement of guilt and must be voluntary, meaning it was not caused by inducement, threat or promise. A retracted judicial confession must be true and, as a rule of prudence, receive sufficient corroboration in material particulars from independent evidence. Corroboration of every circumstance is unnecessary; general corroboration of important incidents may suffice. The Court relied on Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Ediga Anamma v. State of A.P. and State of U.P. v. Boota Singh.
members.conclusion: The retracted confessions were true and voluntary and sufficiently corroborated; they could be acted upon and supported the findings of guilt against the confessing accused.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_review and judicial_confession_retracted and confession_voluntary_and_true and independent_material_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing a conviction in a criminal appeal.
predicates.judicial_confession_retracted: An accused made a judicial confession and later withdrew or denied it.
predicates.confession_voluntary_and_true: The court found that the confession was freely made and was true.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration: Independent evidence supported important parts of the confession.

members.legal_issue: A voluntary and legally recorded confession that is generally corroborated may support conviction despite being retracted.
material_facts: The accused later retracted their confessions, which the court found had been made voluntarily and legally recorded.
The confessions described the accused's participation in the attack, their associates, the planning and execution of the crime, and their contacts with criminal leaders.

Other evidence generally corroborated the confessions, including evidence placing the accused near the crime, their association with the other participants, weapon recoveries, identification evidence, and testimony concerning the motive.
members.legal_principle: A retracted confession may be relied on if it was voluntary and lawful. Corroboration is a rule of prudence, not a rule of law, and general corroboration may suffice depending on the circumstances. Under Section 15 of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, a qualifying confession is substantive evidence against its maker and may also be used against a co-accused. The court relied on S.N. Dube v. N.B. Bhoir, State v. Nalini, Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, and the treatment of corroboration in the authorities discussed in those cases.
members.conclusion: The confessions were sufficiently corroborated and could support conviction; the trial court erred in rejecting them, and the accused were convicted of the charged offences.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and confession_voluntary and confession_legally_recorded and confession_retracted and confession_generally_corroborated

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The matter came before the court in an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.confession_voluntary: The accused made the confession of their own free will, without threat, inducement, or pressure.
predicates.confession_legally_recorded: The confession was recorded in accordance with the applicable legal safeguards.
predicates.confession_retracted: The accused later withdrew or denied the confession.
predicates.confession_generally_corroborated: Other evidence supported the confession in material respects.

members.legal_issue: A retracted confession may be acted upon only when it is voluntary and is substantially corroborated by independent circumstances, though corroboration need not extend to every material particular.
material_facts: The principal accused made a confession before a magistrate and later retracted it.
Before recording it, the magistrate warned the accused, questioned him about voluntariness, ensured police were not present, and allowed time for reflection.
The High Court inferred coercion from circumstances without supporting evidence, while the magistrate’s evidence and other circumstances contradicted that inference.
Independent evidence corroborated important incidents in the confession, including the motive, hiring of the taxi, the journey, and the later concealment and attempted sale of the vehicle.
members.legal_principle: A retracted confession requires substantial corroboration by independent circumstances. It is unnecessary to corroborate every material particular if there is general corroboration of the important incidents. The court should assess the confession and then consider how far independent evidence corroborates it.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the confession was voluntary and could be acted upon because independent evidence substantially corroborated its important incidents.

predicates.retracted_confession: The accused later withdraws or disavows a confession made earlier.
predicates.confession_made_voluntarily: The confession was made voluntarily, as assessed from the circumstances in which it was recorded.
predicates.independent_evidence_corroborates_import: Independent evidence generally supports important incidents described in the confession.

members.legal_issue: A retracted judicial confession may support a conviction when it was voluntary and true and receives sufficient independent corroboration in material particulars.
material_facts: Two accused made judicial confessions before magistrates after the required precautions and opportunities for reflection.
The court found the confessions voluntary and true despite their later retraction.
Witness testimony, surrounding circumstances, and recoveries corroborated material aspects of the confessions, including the crimes and the accused persons’ participation.
members.legal_principle: A judicial confession must be voluntary and true. Although it is not illegal to convict on an uncorroborated confession, prudence requires corroboration before acting on a retracted confession; general corroboration of important incidents in material particulars is sufficient and need not independently establish every detail or itself be enough for conviction. The court relied on Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, Swaran Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and State of Uttar Pradesh v. Boota Singh.
members.conclusion: The retracted confessions, which the court found voluntary, true, and materially corroborated, supported the convictions.

rule.if: criminal_appeal and judicial_confession_retracted and confession_voluntary_and_true and independent_material_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal prosecution.
predicates.judicial_confession_retracted: An accused made a judicial confession and later withdrew or disowned it.
predicates.confession_voluntary_and_true: The court found that the confession was voluntary and true.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration: Independent evidence corroborated important parts of the confession in material particulars.

members.legal_issue: An approver's testimony may support a conviction when the approver is credible and the evidence corroborates both the approver's participation and the accused's participation in material particulars.
material_facts: The prosecution case had no eyewitness other than the approver, whose account implicated the appellants in the murders.
The majority considered the approver's account credible despite challenges to his character, a discrepancy about lighting, and his minimisation of his own role.

The approver's account was supported by discoveries and other evidence concerning his participation and the appellants' involvement, including evidence relating to motive, bloodstained clothing, fingerprints, and a weapon.
The lower courts had assessed the approver's credibility, general corroboration, and corroboration connecting each appellant to the crime.
members.legal_principle: Sections 133 and 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, govern accomplice testimony: an accomplice is competent to testify and an uncorroborated accomplice account does not by itself make a conviction illegal, but the Court ordinarily seeks corroboration in material particulars. The majority required the account to be credible and considered the corroborative evidence generally and as it connected each accused with the crime. The majority did not cite an earlier case for this application.
members.conclusion: The majority accepted the approver's testimony and held that its corroboration supported the appellants' convictions.

rule.if: approver_testimony_case and approver_account_credible and approver_participation_corroborated and accused_participation_corroborated

predicates.approver_testimony_case: The prosecution relies materially on testimony from a person who participated in the crime and testified for the prosecution as an approver.
predicates.approver_account_credible: The approver's account is credible when assessed in light of its substance, probabilities, and the evidence as a whole.
predicates.approver_participation_corroborated: Evidence independent of the approver's account supports that the approver took part in the crime.
predicates.accused_participation_corroborated: Evidence independent of the approver's account connects the accused with participation in the crime.

members.legal_issue: An accomplice’s testimony may support a conviction when it is reliable and is corroborated in material particulars connecting each accused with the crime.
material_facts: The approver had participated in the criminal activities and killings described by the prosecution.
The approver gave evidence about the killings of three victims in one incident and three other victims in separate incidents.

Independent witnesses, including eyewitnesses to the attacks, supported material parts of his account; other evidence included recoveries, identification evidence, medical evidence and circumstances surrounding the killings and disposal of the bodies.
The courts below had examined the evidence and found the approver’s account reliable and sufficiently corroborated.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Evidence Act, an accomplice is a competent witness and conviction on uncorroborated accomplice evidence is not illegal, but settled practice requires the evidence to be reliable and sufficiently corroborated. Corroboration must be independent, material and connect or tend to connect each accused with the crime; it need not independently prove the offence or confirm every circumstance. The Court relied on Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Lachhi Ram v. State of Punjab, Mohd. Husain Umar Kochra v. K.S. Dalipsinghji, Ravinder Singh v. State of Haryana, Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, Tribhuvan Nath v. State of Maharashtra and Vemireddy Satyanarayan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad.
members.conclusion: The approver’s testimony, supported by independent evidence in material particulars, was safe to act upon and established the relevant appellants’ guilt in the killings to which his evidence related.

predicates.criminal_appeal_review: The court is reviewing convictions in a criminal appeal.
predicates.accomplice_testimony_reliable: An accomplice gave testimony that the court found reliable.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration_conne: Independent evidence supported material parts of the accomplice’s account and connected the accused with the crime.

members.legal_issue: An accomplice’s testimony can support a conviction when independent evidence corroborates material particulars connecting each accused to the crime.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended in part on an approver who admitted participating in a scheme involving forged cheques and fictitious bank accounts; his participation was independently established by documents and evidence of funds he possessed.

Evidence connected one accused to the opening of a fictitious account through testimony that he filled in the account-opening form and supplied money, corroborated by handwriting evidence and other witnesses.

Evidence connected another accused to the scheme through a fictitious bank introduction and testimony from bank employees that he intervened to identify the fictitious account-holder and assist in cashing cheques.
The Supreme Court found the evidence sufficiently corroborated the approver’s testimony as to each accused and upheld the convictions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirement that an approver’s evidence be corroborated in material particulars connecting each accused with the crime. The judgment cites no provision or earlier case for this requirement.
members.conclusion: The convictions and sentences of the two appellants were confirmed, and their appeals were dismissed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.accomplice_testimony_used: The prosecution relied on testimony from a participant in the crime who testified as an approver.
predicates.approver_participation_independently_est: Evidence apart from the approver’s account established that the approver participated in the criminal scheme.
predicates.each_accused_materially_connected_by_cor: Independent evidence corroborated material particulars of the approver’s account connecting each accused to the crime.

members.legal_issue: An accomplice’s testimony may support a conviction when it is reliable and independently corroborated in material particulars connecting each accused with the crime.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on testimony from a participant in the crimes who testified as an approver.
The approver’s account of the crimes and the accused persons’ involvement was supported by eyewitnesses, witnesses to surrounding circumstances, recoveries, and other evidence.
The court found the approver’s testimony reliable and sufficient corroboration as to the accused persons implicated.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 133 of the Evidence Act, a conviction based on uncorroborated accomplice testimony is not illegal; however, the practice reflected in illustration (b) to Section 114 is to seek corroboration. The testimony must be reliable and corroborated in material particulars so as to connect the accused with the crime, but corroboration need not independently establish every circumstance or be sufficient by itself to convict. The court relied on Swaran Singh Rattan Singh v. State of Punjab, Lachhi Ram v. State of Punjab, Mohd. Hussain v. State, Ravindra Singh v. State of Punjab, Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, Tribhuvan Nath v. State of Maharashtra, and Vemireddy Satyanarayan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad.
members.conclusion: The approver’s testimony, with the corroboration found in this case, supported the convictions.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The case is an appeal in a criminal prosecution.
predicates.accomplice_testimony_reliable: A participant in the crime gave testimony that the court found reliable.
predicates.independent_material_corroboration_conne: Independent evidence corroborated material parts of the testimony and connected the accused with the crime.

members.legal_issue: A bribery conviction may be based on reliable testimony from a bribe-giver without a fixed requirement of corroboration in material particulars, with the need and extent of corroboration assessed in the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The complainant had to obtain a land title and testified that the senior official demanded a bribe and directed him to hand the money to the assistant.

The complainant approached the vigilance authorities before paying and participated in a trap; the marked money was recovered from the assistant, who admitted receiving it on the senior official’s instructions.

The complainant consistently testified to the demand, had no apparent motive against the senior official, and the surrounding evidence, including testimony from other witnesses, supported the prosecution case.
The assistant claimed he believed the money was repayment of a loan, but the supporting witness established only that a provident-fund loan had been sanctioned.
The trial court and the High Court found both officials guilty, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb those findings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 133 and 114, Illustration (b), of the Evidence Act permit conviction on an accomplice’s evidence but counsel caution: corroboration is ordinarily sought as a rule of prudence, and whether it is needed depends on the evidence and circumstances. A bribe-giver who is coerced or unwilling and approaches authorities before paying is not automatically to be treated like a willing participant in the crime; the evidence must be carefully assessed, and any corroboration may be circumstantial. The court relied on Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan and King v. Baskerville on accomplice evidence and corroboration; State of Bihar v. Basawan Singh and later decisions including Bhanuprasad Hanprasad Dave, Dalpat Singh, Maha Singh and Hazari Lal on trap witnesses; and distinguished Panalal Damodar Rathi v. State of Maharashtra on its facts.
members.conclusion: The convictions were upheld. The complainant’s evidence was not subject to an inflexible requirement of corroboration in material particulars, and the recovery and surrounding circumstances supported his account of the demand and payment on the senior official’s instructions.

rule.if: bribery_trap_conviction_appeal and complainant_approached_authorities_before_payment and complainant_testified_to_official_demand and complainant_testimony_was_reliable and money_recovered_from_intermediary and surrounding_evidence_supported_account

predicates.bribery_trap_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction arising from a bribery trap.
predicates.complainant_approached_authorities_befor: The complainant went to the authorities before paying the demanded money.
predicates.complainant_testified_to_official_demand: The complainant testified that an official demanded a bribe.
predicates.complainant_testimony_was_reliable: The court found the complainant’s account sufficiently reliable to act upon.
predicates.money_recovered_from_intermediary: The money paid in the trap was recovered from a person alleged to have received it for an official.
predicates.surrounding_evidence_supported_account: Other evidence or circumstances supported the complainant’s account of the demand or payment.

members.legal_issue: A corruption conviction may be sustained on an interested complainant’s testimony when material evidence corroborates the demand and acceptance of the bribe.
material_facts: The complainant testified that the public official demanded money for assistance and later accepted the money during a police trap.
Police officers testified that the official threw the money when the trap party intervened, and the recovered notes matched the numbers recorded before the trap.
A witness to the ride testified to relevant circumstances, and the Supreme Court accepted the evidence of another witness to the seizure.
The discrepancies in the police witnesses’ accounts concerned minor details and did not affect their evidence about the throwing and recovery of the notes.
members.legal_principle: For the offence under Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act read with Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, an interested complainant’s evidence must be considered with great caution and ordinarily should not be accepted without material corroboration. The Court found corroboration in the other evidence, including the police officers’ account and the matching recovered notes. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The corroborated evidence was sufficient to sustain the conviction and sentence, so the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.interested_complainant_testified_to_brib: A complainant with an interest in the case testified that the accused demanded or accepted a bribe.
predicates.material_corroboration_supports_bribe: Other material evidence supports the complainant’s account of the bribe demand or acceptance.

members.legal_issue: Credible testimony corroborated by recovery evidence is sufficient to sustain convictions for receiving illegal gratification.
material_facts: The complainant testified that the public servant demanded money for supplying a land record copy and accepted the agreed amount.
Marked currency notes were recovered from the public servant's coat pocket after the payment.
The chemical test of the public servant's fingers and the coat pocket turned pink.
The public servant gave no explanation for possessing the money, and no suggestion was made to any witness that he had not received it.
The asserted motive of enmity was not established; the timing of the complainant's land sale was unclear, and the alleged relationship between the supporting witnesses was unsupported.
The trial court and the High Court believed the witnesses, and the Supreme Court found no reason to reject their evidence.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the offences charged under Section 5(1)(d) read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and Section 161 IPC to the accepted evidence of demand, receipt, and recovery of the money. It found the challenges to witness credibility unpersuasive in light of the corroborating chemical test and the absence of an explanation for possession. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The convictions under Section 5(1)(d) read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and Section 161 IPC were affirmed.

rule.if: appeal_from_corruption_conviction and credible_testimony_of_demand_and_acceptance and marked_money_recovered_from_accused and chemical_test_corrobates_contact and no_explanation_for_possession

predicates.appeal_from_corruption_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for receiving illegal gratification.
predicates.credible_testimony_of_demand_and_accepta: The complainant gives testimony accepted by the courts that the accused demanded and accepted money.
predicates.marked_money_recovered_from_accused: Marked money paid in the transaction is recovered from the accused.
predicates.chemical_test_corrobates_contact: A chemical test of the accused or an item holding the money supports contact with the marked money.
predicates.no_explanation_for_possession: The accused provides no explanation for possessing the recovered money.

members.legal_issue: A witness's testimony cannot be rejected solely because the witness was declared hostile.
material_facts: Two prosecution witnesses were declared hostile and permitted to be cross-examined by the prosecution.
The trial court treated their testimony as part of the prosecution's version, while the reviewing court considered the evidence of a hostile witness together with corroborating testimony.
members.legal_principle: A hostile witness's evidence is not to be rejected on that ground alone; the court must assess it on its merits. The judgment relies on no earlier case for this proposition.
members.conclusion: Declaring a witness hostile does not by itself justify rejecting that witness's evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: A witness who testified for the prosecution was declared hostile.

members.legal_issue: A trial court cannot treat the version of a prosecution witness declared hostile as the prosecution's own version.
material_facts: The prosecution declared two of its witnesses hostile, and the court permitted it to cross-examine them.
The trial court relied on those witnesses' accounts as spokesmen for the prosecution case when finding that the prosecution had presented contradictory versions.
members.legal_principle: Declaring a prosecution witness hostile exhibits the prosecution's intention not to rely on that witness's evidence as its case, although the evidence is not thereby automatically rejected.
members.conclusion: The trial court was not justified in treating the hostile witnesses' version as the prosecution's version.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.prosecution_witness_declared_hostile: A witness called by the prosecution was declared hostile.
predicates.prosecution_cross_examined_witness: The prosecution was permitted to cross-examine the witness.

members.legal_issue: Identification of accused persons is established where they were named in the earliest account, were known to the witnesses, and witnesses later identified their presence and participation.
material_facts: The accused were named in the earliest account of the occurrence and were co-villagers known to the witnesses.
The witnesses later named the accused and attributed presence and participation to them.
The accused did not challenge their identification during the investigation or at trial.
members.legal_principle: Identification is assessed in the circumstances of the case. Here, naming the accused in the earliest account, the witnesses’ prior familiarity with them, and later testimony identifying their participation supported the finding of identification.
members.conclusion: The identification challenge was without substance.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and accused_named_in_earliest_account and accused_known_to_witnesses and witnesses_later_identified_participation and identification_not_challenged

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_named_in_earliest_account: The accused were named in the earliest account of the occurrence.
predicates.accused_known_to_witnesses: The accused were already known to the witnesses.
predicates.witnesses_later_identified_participation: Witnesses later named the accused and described their presence and participation.
predicates.identification_not_challenged: The accused did not challenge their identification during the investigation or at trial.

members.legal_issue: A conviction is supported where prosecution witnesses identify the accused as participating in the offence.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses identified one appellant as having forcibly cut and removed the crops.
The Court held that this appellant was rightly convicted.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the prosecution evidence identifying the appellant and concluded that his conviction was justified. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s conviction was upheld.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: An accused appeals a conviction entered by a local adjudicatory body.
predicates.prosecution_witnesses_identify_accused_a: The prosecution witnesses identify the accused as participating in the alleged offence.

members.legal_issue: Evidence from a related witness and from witnesses declared hostile may be relied on to establish an accused’s participation when the dependable parts of their testimony are corroborated by other evidence.
material_facts: A brother of the deceased testified that all three accused were present and attacked the deceased.

Four labourers were declared hostile, but their testimony supported that two accused were present and confronted the deceased; one labourer also testified that he later saw three persons surrounding the deceased.
Weapons were recovered from the accused, including a cutting weapon from the accused whose presence was disputed.
Medical evidence attributed the death to head injuries and haemorrhage and was consistent with the account of an attack.
members.legal_principle: A related witness’s evidence is scrutinized with care as a rule of prudence, not rejected merely because of the relationship; a court may rely on a sole related witness whose testimony is trustworthy and corroborated (Mano Dutt v. State of Uttar Pradesh, relying on Anil Phukan v. State of Assam). A hostile witness’s evidence is not effaced or rejected en bloc; the court may accept the dependable portions after careful scrutiny and ordinarily look for corroboration (Paramjeet Singh alias Pamma v. State of Uttarakhand; State of Rajasthan v. Bhawani; Radha Mohan Singh v. State of U.P.; Mahesh v. State of Maharashtra; Rajendra v. State of U.P.; Govindappa v. State of Karnataka; Mrinal Das v. State of Tripura; Khachar Dipu alias Dilipbhai Nakubhai v. State of Gujarat).
members.conclusion: The relationship of the principal witness to the deceased did not by itself make his evidence unreliable, and the dependable portions of the hostile witnesses’ evidence were not erased from the record. Considered with the recoveries and medical evidence, the evidence established the accused’s participation, including that of the accused whose presence was disputed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.related_witness_gave_testimony_about_the: A witness related to the victim testified about the accused’s presence or conduct during the attack.
predicates.hostile_witnesses_supported_material_par: Witnesses declared hostile testified to material circumstances such as the accused’s presence, confrontation with the victim, or surrounding the victim.
predicates.weapon_recovery_connected_accused_to_the: A weapon connected with the attack was recovered from an accused.
predicates.medical_findings_corresponded_to_the_acc: Medical findings were consistent with the account of the attack and its fatal injuries.

members.legal_issue: The reliable and corroborated portions of testimony from a witness declared hostile may be relied on to support a conviction.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses were declared hostile, but each maintained that the accused assaulted the deceased; parts of their testimony identifying the assault remained unshaken in cross-examination.
Another eyewitness described the assault, and the eyewitness accounts were consistent on the material point that the accused struck the deceased.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 154 of the Evidence Act, declaring a witness hostile does not efface the witness’s testimony. The reliable portions may be accepted on careful scrutiny and may support a conviction when corroborated by other reliable evidence; portions of examination-in-chief left unshaken in cross-examination may be relied on. The Court relied on Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana, (1976) 1 SCC 389; Rabindra Kumar Dey v. State of Orissa, (1976) 4 SCC 233; Syad Akbar v. State of Karnataka, (1980) 1 SCC 30; Khujji v. State of M.P., (1991) 3 SCC 627; and Vinod Kumar v. State of Punjab, (2015) 3 SCC 220.
members.conclusion: The courts below were entitled to rely on the unshaken portions of the hostile witnesses’ evidence, which were corroborated by other reliable evidence.

predicates.criminal_conviction_case: The proceeding concerns whether evidence supports a criminal conviction.
predicates.hostile_testimony_unshaken: A witness declared hostile maintained material testimony identifying the accused’s conduct despite cross-examination.
predicates.hostile_testimony_corroborated: Other reliable evidence supported the material part of the hostile witness’s testimony.

members.legal_issue: Claimants seeking enhanced compensation for acquired land must establish that the acquisition award is inadequate, and a higher court should not disturb a compensation assessment that applies the relevant principles and is supported by the record.
material_facts: The acquired land was agricultural and lacked facilities available to some of the lands in the sale transactions relied on for enhancement.
The land-acquisition officer relied on a recent sale of a small plot but did not adequately explain why numerous sales, including sales of larger extents, were excluded.
The reference court did not properly compare the sale transactions with the acquired land or adequately explain how the claimants had proved their entitlement to enhancement.
Some similarly situated landowners had agreed to compensation at a rate higher than the award, and there was no showing that their agreement was coerced.
The High Court restored the land-acquisition officer’s award, and the Supreme Court found that award to be just on the record as a whole.
members.legal_principle: The burden rests initially on claimants under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act to prove that the award is inadequate and what higher compensation is justified; only after that burden is discharged does the burden shift to the State. Small-plot sales are not categorically inadmissible as a basis for valuing larger acquisitions, but larger-extent sales will normally be more prudent comparators, and relevant differences require appropriate adjustment. Under Section 25, the State cannot seek compensation below the amount awarded by the land-acquisition officer. In considering appellate interference with market-value findings, the Court relied on Thakur Kanta Prasad Singh (dead) by L.Rs. v. State of Bihar, which recognizes the element of estimation in valuation and counsels against disturbing an assessment that considers relevant statutory factors; it also considered Ravinder Narain v. Union of India on the use of small-plot sales.
members.conclusion: The claimants did not establish entitlement to enhanced compensation. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s decision restoring the land-acquisition officer’s award and dismissed the appeals concerning this acquisition.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_acquisition_compe: The case is an appeal from a High Court decision determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimants_bear_initial_burden: The claimants seeking enhanced compensation are required to establish that the acquisition award is inadequate.
predicates.claimants_fail_to_prove_inadequacy: The claimants do not establish with acceptable evidence that the award is inadequate or what higher compensation is justified.
predicates.high_court_assessment_supported_by_relev: The High Court’s compensation decision is consistent with the relevant valuation principles and the evidentiary record.

members.legal_issue: A reference seeking enhanced land-acquisition compensation is an original proceeding in which market value must be determined afresh on evidence produced and proved before the court.
material_facts: The landowner challenged the compensation offered by the acquisition officer and sought a reference for determination of market value.
The trial court had treated the acquisition officer’s award substantially as a judgment under appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, a reference is not an appeal against the acquisition officer’s award. The claimant is in the position of a plaintiff who must show that the offer is inadequate on the material produced in court; material produced and proved by either side may be considered.
members.conclusion: The reference court must determine market value afresh and cannot treat the acquisition officer’s award as an appellate decision or rely on material used for that award unless that material is produced and proved before it.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A landowner brings a reference seeking judicial determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimant_seeks_higher_compensation: The landowner contends that the compensation offered for the land is inadequate.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking enhanced compensation in a reference proceeding must prove that the compensation awarded is inadequate before the court may grant an enhancement.
material_facts: The landowners sought enhanced compensation in references under the land acquisition law.
They adduced no evidence before the Reference Court to show that the acquired land's market value exceeded the amount awarded by the Collector.
The Reference Court enhanced compensation by relying on the Collector's draft award, while the State adduced no evidence before the Reference Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 18, 23 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, a reference on compensation is an original proceeding, not an appeal from the Collector's award. The claimant bears the initial burden, as a plaintiff would, of proving inadequacy and the amount properly payable; the court must determine market value from material produced and proved before it, and cannot rely on the Collector's award materials unless they are produced and proved. The Court relied on Chimanlal Hargovinddas v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Siddappa Omanna Tumari, and Major Pakhar Singh Atwal v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The Reference Court was not justified in enhancing compensation without evidence establishing that the Collector's award was inadequate.

predicates.compensation_reference_proceeding: The proceeding is a reference seeking determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimant_did_not_prove_award_inadequacy: The claimant did not establish through evidence before the reference court that the compensation awarded was inadequate.

members.legal_issue: A court deciding a compensation reference cannot award more than the original award without finding, on relevant material, that the award was inadequate.
material_facts: The claimants sought increased compensation for acquired land through references after rejecting the acquisition officer’s award.
The officer had valued the land by reference to compensation agreed for similar land acquired under the same notification.
The claimants relied on a sale of a small plot and an expert report based on that sale, but the sale’s authenticity and circumstances were not established.
The lower courts increased compensation without adequately considering the material supporting the officer’s award.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 11, 12, 18 and 19 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a claimant seeking a reference bears the initial burden of showing that the award was inadequate, by reference to the award itself or other evidence. The award has final and conclusive evidentiary effect unless that burden is discharged. If inadequacy is established, the burden shifts to the acquiring authority to support the award. Sections 15, 23 and 24 guide valuation. No earlier case is relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: A court cannot determine compensation exceeding the officer’s award unless it finds, on relevant material, that the award was inadequate; the claimants must first prove inadequacy.

predicates.compensation_reference: A claimant seeks a court’s determination of compensation after declining the acquisition officer’s award.
predicates.claimant_proves_award_inadequate: The claimant establishes, using relevant material, that the acquisition officer’s compensation award was inadequate.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking increased compensation in a land acquisition reference must prove that the compensation awarded is inadequate with reliable evidence of comparable land values.
material_facts: The claimants sought further compensation for acquired land.
They did not examine witnesses to prove the prevailing market value of the acquired land or comparable nearby land.
They relied on mutation entries and on sale transactions mentioned in the Land Acquisition Officer’s award, but did not independently place those transactions in evidence.
members.legal_principle: A reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act is an original proceeding, not an appeal. The claimant bears the burden of proving inadequacy by relevant and acceptable evidence, such as comparable sale transactions supported by evidence of the transaction, proximity, and similarity of the lands. Mutation entries are inadmissible for this purpose, and sale transactions mentioned in the Collector’s award cannot be relied on as evidence when they have not been independently proved before the Tribunal.
members.conclusion: The claimants did not establish a basis for increasing the compensation determined by the Tribunal.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference: The matter is a reference proceeding to determine compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimant_seeks_higher_compensation: The claimant asks for compensation above the amount already determined.
predicates.comparable_sales_not_proved: The claimant does not prove reliable comparable land sales through acceptable evidence.

members.legal_issue: Market value for acquired land must be assessed with reference to its value at the time of the acquisition notification, rather than later price increases.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition around 1978 and 1979.
The High Court found that prices in the area began rising and development began after 1980.
The High Court assessed the land by reference to its value at the time of the notifications, and the Supreme Court found no basis to disturb that assessment.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as at the date of the acquisition notification. Later price increases are not the guideline for that assessment. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly did not use post-1980 valuation as a guideline, and its market-value finding was not disturbed.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.prices_increased_after_valuation_time: Prices in the area rose after the time at which the acquired land's value had to be assessed.
predicates.development_began_after_valuation_time: Development in the area began after the time at which the acquired land's value had to be assessed.
predicates.high_court_assessed_value_at_valuation_t: The High Court assessed the land's value by reference to its value at the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must reflect its market value at the time of the acquisition notification and cannot be increased merely because the land was later developed and sold at a higher price.
material_facts: The land was treated as agricultural, and no evidence showed that it had non-agricultural potential or that the owners suffered special damage.
The owners produced no comparable sale near the notification date or other evidence supporting their claimed higher value.
They relied on later sales of developed land at a much higher price and on a High Court determination of value for land in the same village acquired under the same notification.
The Court adopted that High Court determination and enhanced the market value from Rs. 6,500 to Rs. 7,000 per bigha.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as at the date of publication of the Section 4(1) notification, with any proven acquisition-related damage also considered. Valuation may be based on expert opinion, bona fide comparable sales made within a reasonable time, or capitalisation and potential value. A later price for land after development does not establish its value at the acquisition date. In the absence of other evidence, the Court relied on the High Court's determination for land in the same village acquired under the same notification.
members.conclusion: The later sale price of developed land did not justify higher compensation; the market value was fixed at Rs. 7,000 per bigha on the basis of the comparable determination for land acquired under the same notification.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding challenges the compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.no_reliable_contemporaneous_valuation_ev: The claimant has not produced reliable evidence of market value near the acquisition notification date or other evidence supporting a higher value.
predicates.same_notification_comparable_determinati: A determination of market value exists for comparable land in the same locality acquired under the same notification.
predicates.later_high_price_reflects_development: The higher price relied on was obtained later, after the land had been developed.

members.legal_issue: Post-notification land transactions may be used to determine acquired land’s market value only when the required evidence establishes that land prices did not appreciate between the acquisition notification and the transactions.
material_facts: The compensation appeal concerned land acquired by compulsory notification.
The claimants relied on leases executed after the acquisition notification for land said to be near the acquired land.
No sale transaction on or about the notification date was available as a guide to market value.
The claimants did not produce evidence that land prices had not risen between the notification and the dates of the leases.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, market value is assessed as at the date of the Section 4 notification, and bona fide transactions on or near that date are generally the best evidence. When such transactions are unavailable, comparable transactions may be considered; a post-notification transaction may be relied upon in appropriate circumstances if reliable evidence shows that prices did not appreciate between the notification and the transaction. Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, AIR 1988 SC 943, states that subsequent transactions may be used where the market was stable and prices did not fluctuate. State of U.P. v. Major Jitendra Kumar, AIR 1982 SC 876, and Mehta Ravindrarai Ajitrai v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1989 SC 2051, did not resolve the disputed question of who bore the burden of establishing no post-notification price rise and therefore did not assist the claimants.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly rejected the post-notification leases because the claimants had not established that land prices had not appreciated in the intervening period.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.no_comparable_transaction_near_notificat: No comparable sale transaction on or near the acquisition notification date is available as a guide to market value.
predicates.post_notification_comparable_sales_relie: A party relies on comparable land sales made after the acquisition notification.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_price_stability: The party relying on those sales has not produced reliable evidence that prices did not appreciate between the notification and the sales.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land must be assessed by reference to comparable acquisitions from the relevant period, rather than a higher award arising from a materially later acquisition or an unnoticed mistake.
material_facts: The land was acquired in 1976, and the landowners challenged the compensation determined by the Land Acquisition Officer and the Reference Court.

The landowners sought compensation at the rate awarded in Mangu, which principally concerned land acquired in 1991; certain appeals concerning 1977 acquisitions had been disposed of with that case without the acquisition-year difference being noticed.

The High Court’s award in Jagmal of a higher rate for a 1976 acquisition was later reviewed and reduced to the rate consistently awarded for 1976–1977 acquisitions; that reviewed determination was confirmed by the Supreme Court.
Several other decisions concerning acquisitions in 1976–1977, including acquisitions in the same or nearby villages, fixed compensation at the same rate.
The landowners alternatively relied on an award for land acquired in 1983, but development had taken place after 1980 and a development plan was in place by the time of that acquisition.
members.legal_principle: In determining compensation on a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, the relevant basis is comparable land and circumstances at the time of the acquisition; compensation awarded for a materially later acquisition is not comparable merely because a depreciation formula is proposed, particularly where development occurred in the intervening period. A party cannot claim parity from an award that resulted from an inadvertent failure to notice material differences in the acquisitions. The Court relied on the reviewed determination in Jagmal and the consistent determinations for 1976–1977 acquisitions, while distinguishing Mangu and Khazan because of the different acquisition periods and circumstances.
members.conclusion: The appeals were partly allowed, and compensation for the land acquired in 1976 was enhanced to Rs.28.12 per square yard, with applicable statutory benefits on the enhanced compensation. The higher awards relied on by the landowners did not justify compensation at Rs.297 per square yard.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The landowners appealed a determination of compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.claimed_comparator_is_from_materially_la: The landowners relied on an award for land acquired materially later than their land, after intervening development or other relevant changes.
predicates.claimed_comparator_award_reflects_unnoti: The landowners relied on an award that was made without the court noticing a material difference in the acquisition periods or circumstances.
predicates.comparable_same_period_awards_support_an: Other decisions concerning comparable acquisitions from the relevant period consistently supported a different compensation rate.

members.legal_issue: Where the pre-amendment compensation-claim limit applies, compensation awarded by the court cannot exceed the amount claimed in the circumstances specified by that limit.
material_facts: The compensation proceedings arose before the 1984 amendment to the Land Acquisition Act, and the Court held that the earlier version of Section 25 governed.
The claimants had sought specified compensation before the Collector, while the High Court awarded a higher amount.

The High Court found that notice under Sections 9 and 10 had not been served, but the Collector's awards recorded that notice had been issued; the Court held that notice and participation facts required reconsideration.
members.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as it stood before the 1984 amendment, imposed limits on the amount the court could award depending on whether the claimant made a claim pursuant to notice, refused or omitted to make a claim, or had sufficient reason for omission. The Court held that this provision was substantive and that the pre-amendment version applied to the proceedings. It relied on Land Acquisition Officer-cum-DSWO v. B.V. Reddy and Sons and Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Kanhaiya Lal, and discussed the purpose of Section 9 notice, participation with knowledge of the proceedings, and prejudice.
members.conclusion: If the unamended Section 25 applies, the High Court could not award compensation above the amount claimed where the applicable statutory conditions were met. The High Court had to reconsider whether notice had been served and whether the relevant statutory conditions applied.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and pre_amendment_claim_limit_applies and compensation_claim_made and notice_or_participation_condition_met

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.pre_amendment_claim_limit_applies: The proceeding is governed by the earlier compensation-claim limit rather than a later amendment.
predicates.compensation_claim_made: The claimant stated an amount sought as compensation before the acquiring authority.
predicates.notice_or_participation_condition_met: The claimant received the relevant notice or participated in the proceeding with knowledge sufficient to serve the notice's purpose.

members.legal_issue: A court determining compensation on reference cannot award more than the amount claimed in response to the acquisition notice.
material_facts: In response to the acquisition notice, the landowners claimed compensation at a specified per-acre rate.
The District Judge awarded compensation at a per-acre rate substantially above the amount claimed.
The Supreme Court held that the District Judge had acted contrary to the statutory limit, although it separately considered the proper valuation of the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 25(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, provides that the court shall not award an applicant compensation in excess of the amount claimed pursuant to a notice under Section 9.
members.conclusion: The District Judge was not permitted to award compensation exceeding the amount claimed in response to the notice.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference: The proceeding is a reference for determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claim_made_after_notice: The claimant states the compensation sought in response to the acquisition notice.
predicates.reference_court_award_exceeds_claim: The court deciding the reference awards compensation greater than the amount the claimant sought.

members.legal_issue: The pre-amendment compensation limit was substantive and prevented a reference court from awarding more than the compensation claimed after a claim had been made in response to notice.
material_facts: The land was acquired and a compensation claim was made before the statutory amendment took effect.
The owners claimed compensation of Rs. 30,000 per acre in response to notice, and did not challenge the making of that claim in their reference application.
Although the reference court assessed the land at a higher market value, the High Court awarded compensation above the amount claimed.
members.legal_principle: Section 25(1), read with Sections 9, 11 and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, imposed a substantive limit on the reference court’s power where a claimant had made a claim in response to notice. Section 25(5) concerned a claimant who had omitted to claim for a sufficient reason and did not displace the limit in Section 25(1). The Court approved Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Kanhaiya Lal on the substantive nature of Section 25 and relied on Dadoo Yogendrenath Singh v. The Collector concerning the statutory limit.
members.conclusion: The limit was substantive, not procedural. Under the law in force when the claim was made, the court could not award more than the amount claimed; the owners were entitled to compensation only at the claimed rate.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A claimant in a land acquisition matter sought a court determination of compensation after the initial award.
predicates.pre_change_compensation_limit_applies: The compensation limit in force before a statutory change governed the acquisition.
predicates.claimant_made_claim_after_notice: The claimant made a compensation claim in response to notice concerning the acquisition.
