members.legal_issue: Under the applicable earlier version of the compensation-claim limitation, an award cannot exceed the amount claimed where the required notice was served, and an unamended appeal memorandum does not itself amend the original claim pleadings.
material_facts: The compensation proceedings arose before the 1984 amendment to the land-acquisition law, and the earlier version of the claim-limitation provision applied.
The claimants had stated lower amounts in their claims before the Collector than the amounts later awarded by the High Court.
The High Court allowed amendments to the appeal and reference materials and awarded compensation above the amounts claimed.
Whether notice had been served was disputed and had to be determined from the Collector’s records; the Collector’s awards recorded that notices had been issued.
The Court noted that the amendments had not been carried out within the time required after leave to amend.
members.legal_principle: The earlier version of section 25 of the Land Acquisition Act is substantive and applies to proceedings governed by it; where its conditions are met, the claimant is restricted by the amount claimed. Section 53 makes civil procedure applicable, but an appeal amendment does not itself alter the original pleadings. Amendment requires judicial consideration of relevant factors, including admissions and delay, and must be carried out as required by the procedural rules. The Court relied on Land Acquisition Officer v. B.V. Reddy and Sons, Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Kanhaiya Lal, M/s. Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills v. M/s. Ladha Ram, Heeralal v. Kalyan Mal, Sangramsinh P. Gaekwad v. Shantadevi P. Gaekwad, and Order VI Rules 17 and 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The earlier version of the claim-limitation provision governed. If its notice-related conditions were met, the compensation could not exceed the amount claimed. Amending a memorandum of appeal did not, by itself, amend the original claim pleadings, and the High Court had to reconsider the notice and amendment issues.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_reference and earlier_claim_limit_applies and required_notice_served and claimant_claimed_lower_amount

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference: The proceeding is a reference or appeal determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.earlier_claim_limit_applies: The governing law limits an award by reference to the amount claimed by the claimant.
predicates.required_notice_served: The claimant received the notice required for the claim limitation to apply.
predicates.claimant_claimed_lower_amount: The claimant sought a specified amount lower than the amount later awarded.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking enhanced land-acquisition compensation cannot establish a higher market value by relying on other lands without evidence that they are comparable in location, quality, and potential.
material_facts: The claimant appealed seeking compensation above the amount assessed by the High Court, relying on decisions concerning land in the same village and in neighboring villages.

The Reference Court found that the acquired land was agricultural, lacked electrical and municipal water connections, and was about six kilometres from the main road; some lands relied on as comparators were closer to the road and to developed areas.
The claimant produced no site plan or other evidence establishing that the acquired land was similarly situated to land in another village whose award he relied on.
The High Court had assessed compensation at the rate sought by the claimant, relying on an earlier judgment concerning land in the same village.
The Supreme Court found no cogent basis to interfere with the Reference Court’s findings or to award further enhancement.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as at the notification date, from the perspective of the owner who parts with the land, taking account of its existing use, geographical situation, advantages, disadvantages, and potential that is not remote, while excluding advantages arising from the acquisition purpose. A claimant bears the burden of producing relevant evidence, and a court cannot grant compensation merely on the claimant’s request or on conjecture unsupported by the record. Comparator transactions or awards can guide valuation only where the lands are shown to be similar; location, distance, frontage, and other advantages may justify different values, and belting may be appropriate for large or non-contiguous acquisitions. The Court relied on Sections 9 and 23 and on Raja Vyricheria Narayana Gajapatraju Bahadur Garu v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Vizianagaram, AIR 1939 PC 98; Adusumilli Gopalkrishna v. Spl. Deputy Collector (Land Acquisition), AIR 1980 SC 1870; Thakur Kamta Prasad Singh v. State of Bihar, AIR 1976 SC 2219; Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Karigowda, AIR 2010 SC 2322; Charan Das v. H.P. Housing & Urban Development Authority, (2010) 13 SCC 398; Trishala Jain v. State of Uttaranchal, AIR 2011 SC 2458; Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat, AIR 2005 SC 2214; Executive Engineer, Karnataka Housing Board v. Land Acquisition Officer, AIR 2011 SC 781; Bilkis v. State of Maharashtra, (2011) 12 SCC 646; Sabhia Mohammed Yusuf Abdul Hamid Mulla v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, AIR 2012 SC 2709; Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Ltd. v. G. Mohan Reddy, (2010) 15 SCC 412; Ashrafi v. State of Haryana, AIR 2013 SC 3654; Sher Singh v. State of Haryana, AIR 1991 SC 2048; Executive Engineer (Electrical), Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner & Land Acquisition Officer, (2010) 15 SCC 60; Ramanlal Deochand Shah v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2013 SC 3452; Jawajee Nagnatham v. Revenue Divisional Officer, (1994) 4 SCC 595; and Land Acquisition Officer & Sub-Collector, Gadwal v. Sreelatha Bhoopal, (1997) 9 SCC 628.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not establish that the comparator lands were sufficiently similar to justify the higher valuation sought; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: land_compensation_appeal and claimant_seeks_enhancement and claimant_lacks_comparator_similarity_proof and comparator_lands_have_location_advantages

predicates.land_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking review of compensation fixed for compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.claimant_seeks_enhancement: The claimant asked for compensation higher than the amount already assessed.
predicates.claimant_lacks_comparator_similarity_pro: The claimant did not provide evidence establishing that the acquired land was comparable to the lands relied on for a higher valuation.
predicates.comparator_lands_have_location_advantage: The record showed that the comparator lands had location advantages not shared by the acquired land.
predicates.enhancement_denied: The court denies the claimant’s request for a higher valuation.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land cannot be fixed merely by matching awards for land in adjoining villages unless comparable situation and potentiality are established.
material_facts: The acquired land was in one village, while the awards relied on by the claimants concerned land in adjoining villages.
The High Court found that the situation and potentiality of the acquired land differed from those in the adjoining villages, and the Supreme Court found that conclusion supported by the evidence.
The awards for the adjoining villages had not resulted from a substantive examination of the true market value on comparable local sale evidence.
Sale instances relating to the acquired village were available.
members.legal_principle: Market value is assessed as of the date immediately before the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, on evidence of the price a willing buyer and willing seller would agree. Bona fide sales of similar land with similar advantages, at or near the notification, are appropriate evidence. Awards concerning other villages do not establish the acquired land’s market value unless comparable situation and potentiality are shown. The Court relied on no earlier judicial decision as an authority for this principle; it considered the cited High Court judgments as evidence of the outcomes in other acquisition matters and explained why they were not reliable comparators here.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the adjoining villages’ compensation rates merely to achieve uniformity; the High Court correctly declined to rely on those awards.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and neighboring_award_relied_on and (neighboring_land_comparability_unproven or neighboring_award_not_based_on_comparable_market_value) and local_sale_evidence_available

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.neighboring_award_relied_on: A claimant relies on an award for land in an adjoining area to support the claimed compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.neighboring_land_comparability_unproven: The claimant has not established that the acquired land and the adjoining land have comparable situation and potentiality.
predicates.neighboring_award_not_based_on_comparabl: The adjoining-area award was not made after a substantive assessment of market value using comparable evidence for the acquired land.
predicates.local_sale_evidence_available: Evidence of sale transactions relating to the area of the acquired land is available.

members.legal_issue: A compensation award cannot be enhanced on the basis of an award for other land unless the comparator land is shown to be comparable in nature and potentiality.
material_facts: The claimants relied on a certified award relating to land about 150 feet from the acquired land.
The comparator land had been acquired for a road and was three feet higher than the acquired land.
No evidence established that the comparator land and the acquired land were similar in nature and potentiality.
members.legal_principle: Market value is most reliably determined by comparable sales of the same or adjacent land made near the notification date. A comparison is valid only where the lands are comparable in nature and potentiality; an award relating to other land cannot establish that comparability without supporting evidence.
members.conclusion: The other award was properly not relied on, and the reference court's compensation award was upheld without further enhancement.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparator_award_relied_on and (comparable_nature_unproved or comparable_potentiality_unproved)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparator_award_relied_on: A party relies on an award concerning other land to support the claimed market value.
predicates.comparable_nature_unproved: The evidence does not establish that the comparator land is similar in nature to the acquired land.
predicates.comparable_potentiality_unproved: The evidence does not establish that the comparator land has similar potential to the acquired land.
predicates.enhancement_denied: The claim for compensation beyond the amount already awarded is rejected.

members.legal_issue: Enhanced compensation may be upheld when comparable transactions, awards for similar nearby land, and the land's potentiality support the valuation, even if the lower court used an excessive capitalization multiplier or the appellate court gave inadequate reasons.
material_facts: A sale transaction showed a price of Rs. 19,800 per acre for land in a nearby village.

Reference Court awards for land acquired for the same purpose in nearby or the same village set compensation at Rs. 22,000 per acre, and the High Court had dismissed an appeal concerning one such award.
The acquiring authority had itself awarded Rs. 12,000 per acre for other land in the same village.
The land had crop and cashew-nut cultivation, and the Reference Court's finding that there were no cashew trees was factually incorrect.

The High Court awarded Rs. 22,000 per acre, although it did not give adequate reasons; the Supreme Court considered the valuation and the land's potentiality and utility and found the award adequate and reasonable.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as of the notification date. T. Adinarayan Setty identifies expert opinion, bona fide comparable transactions, and capitalization of actual or immediately prospective profits as valuation methods; Tribeni Devi permits consideration of other circumstances to reach the nearest correct market value. The Court may consider land potentiality and utility alongside yield valuation. The principles in P. Veerabhadarappa and the later multiplier cases establish the appropriate multiplier for yield-based valuation, but an excessive multiplier does not require disturbing an award otherwise supported by comparable evidence and the circumstances of the land.
members.conclusion: The enhanced compensation of Rs. 22,000 per acre was upheld and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and comparable_transaction_evidence and comparable_award_evidence and land_potentiality_supported

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: An acquiring authority appeals an enhanced determination of compensation for land taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.comparable_transaction_evidence: Evidence shows bona fide transactions for land with similar advantages in the relevant area.
predicates.comparable_award_evidence: Awards for nearby or otherwise similar land acquired for a comparable purpose support the valuation.
predicates.land_potentiality_supported: Evidence about the land's use, productivity, or utility supports the assessed market value.

members.legal_issue: Where comparable sale evidence and annual appreciation support a higher valuation, compensation may be increased above the amount awarded by the High Court.
material_facts: Land in Ambala was acquired for development of residential areas.
The High Court had awarded Rs. 110 per square yard, while the landowners claimed Rs. 300 per square yard.
A sale conveyance predating acquisition and sale deeds from the acquisition year were relied on as evidence of higher land values.
The Court considered the sale prices and an annual compounded increase, and found Rs. 180 per square yard appropriate on a uniform basis.
members.legal_principle: Market value may be assessed by comparing relevant sales and allowing for changes in value over time. The Court applied the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and its general valuation approach, including annual appreciation where appropriate.
members.conclusion: The Court assessed compensation for the relevant Ambala lands at Rs. 180 per square yard on a uniform basis.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.relevant_sale_evidence_shows_higher_valu: Sale evidence relevant to the acquired land indicates a higher value than the award under appeal.
predicates.annual_appreciation_supports_revision: Allowing for appreciation between the sale evidence and the valuation date supports a revised value.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land not growing the recurring grass crop may be upheld where assessments and comparable transactions support a value above the amount awarded by the Collector.
material_facts: The issue concerned the remaining danga land that was not cultivated with sabai grass.
A revenue official had assessed danga land at Rs. 75 per acre.
Documents showed sales of danga land, or land including danga land, at values supporting a higher valuation.
The High Court awarded Rs. 100 per acre for the remaining danga land.
members.legal_principle: In the compensation references under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, the Court relied on assessments and transaction documents as evidence bearing on the land’s value. It used those materials to support the High Court’s valuation. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this issue.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was justified in awarding Rs. 100 per acre for the remaining danga land and upheld that award.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.local_land_assessment_supports_higher_va: A local assessment places the land’s value above the amount awarded by the Collector.
predicates.comparable_transaction_evidence_supports: Transaction documents for comparable or partly comparable land support a higher value than the Collector’s award.

members.legal_issue: Prior compensation judgments concerning other land acquisitions do not conclusively determine the market value or entitlement to compensation in a separate acquisition proceeding.
material_facts: The lower courts relied on judgments and awards concerning land in nearby villages when determining compensation.
The High Court treated those earlier judgments and awards as creating res judicata and barred the acquiring authority's appeals.
The earlier judgments and awards were evidence about comparable land, not final determinations of the same inter-party dispute in the present proceeding.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata applies when the same lis between the parties has attained finality on the issues in dispute. It does not ordinarily apply to a pure question of law, a judgment of a court lacking jurisdiction, or a non-speaking judgment. Comparable acquisition judgments and awards have evidentiary value, not automatic preclusive effect. The Court relied on Government of West Bengal v. Tarun K. Roy, State of Maharashtra v. Digambar, State of Bihar v. Ramdeo Yadav, Nathi, Shakuntala Devi, and Ramnik Vallabhdas Madhvani.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in applying res judicata. Earlier judgments and awards may be admitted as evidence, but do not by themselves prevent the acquiring authority from disputing the claim or presenting other relevant material; the principle also did not bar the claimants' cross-objections.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.earlier_awards_concern_other_acquisition: The earlier compensation judgments or awards concern separate acquisitions, including acquisitions of allegedly similar land.
predicates.earlier_awards_do_not_finally_determine_: The earlier judgments or awards do not finally determine the same dispute between the parties in the present proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Awards and judgments concerning other land acquisitions are evidentiary material and do not, merely because they were unchallenged or involved similar land, bar reconsideration of compensation or entitlement in a separate acquisition proceeding.
material_facts: The compensation awards relied on by the High Court concerned acquisitions involving other claimants and land in neighbouring villages.
The High Court treated those decisions as creating res judicata and dismissed the acquiring authorities’ appeals as not maintainable.
The parties conceded that res judicata and issue estoppel did not apply to the case.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata applies where the same lis between the same parties has reached finality on the issue; it does not apply where the earlier court lacked jurisdiction, the issue is a pure question of law, or the earlier judgment is non-speaking. Awards from other acquisitions may have evidentiary value but are not, by themselves, conclusive. The Court relied on Government of West Bengal v. Tarun K. Roy, State of Maharashtra v. Digambar, State of Bihar v. Ramdeo Yadav, Nathi, Shakuntala Devi, Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal, and Ramnik Vallabhdas Madhvani.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in applying res judicata. Decisions concerning other acquisitions may be evidence of market value, but they do not prevent the acquiring authorities from disputing entitlement, statutory limits, or the similarity of the lands. The principle also did not bar the claimants’ cross-objections.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.other_acquisition_awards_relied_on: A party relies on judgments or awards concerning compensation for other acquired land.
predicates.prior_decision_not_between_same_parties: The earlier decision did not finally determine the same dispute between the same parties.

members.legal_issue: The enhancement of compensation cannot exceed the rate claimed when the claimant limited the claim to that rate and did not seek a higher award in the appellate proceedings.
material_facts: The Court's valuation analysis supported a rate higher than the rate claimed before the reference court.
The claimants had limited their claim to a lower rate and made no application in the High Court or Supreme Court seeking compensation at a higher rate.
members.legal_principle: Although the evidence and valuation principles may support a higher market value, the Court restricted relief to the claim actually pursued because no higher compensation had been sought in the appellate proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Court restricted the enhanced compensation to the rate the claimants had claimed.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking increased compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimant_limited_the_compensation_claim: The claimant expressly confined the compensation sought to a particular rate before the reference court.
predicates.no_higher_claim_was_pursued_on_appeal: The claimant did not apply in the appellate proceedings for compensation at a rate above the amount originally claimed.

members.legal_issue: Compensation awarded on appeal cannot exceed the amount the claimant sought in that appeal.
material_facts: Some claimants sought compensation at a stated rate in their first appeals to the High Court.
The High Court awarded compensation for their potential building land at a higher rate than they had claimed.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that claimants who limited the compensation sought in their appeals could not be awarded more than they claimed.
members.conclusion: The State’s appeals were allowed to the extent that the compensation exceeded the rate claimed by those claimants.

predicates.compensation_award_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an award of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claimant_limited_compensation_claim: The claimant sought compensation only up to a stated level in the relevant appeal.
predicates.award_exceeded_claim: The award granted compensation beyond the level the claimant sought.

members.legal_issue: A compensation determination that changes land value or diminution without reasons or analysis of the supporting material cannot be sustained.
material_facts: A lower court had fixed a land value and a percentage of diminution in value.
A High Court judgment increased both figures without giving reasons or analyzing the material on record.
The appeals concerned compensation assessments that the Supreme Court directed the High Court to reconsider on the merits of each case.
members.legal_principle: Compensation must be determined with regard to the purpose of the governing law and the facts and material in the particular case. A change to compensation figures requires an assessment grounded in the relevant circumstances and record, rather than an unexplained alteration. The Court applied Sections 10(d) and 16(3) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, and its case-specific approach to compensation.
members.conclusion: The impugned determinations could not be sustained; they were set aside and the matters were remitted for fresh consideration on their individual merits.

predicates.compensation_appeal_involves_changed_ass: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a changed determination of compensation.
predicates.changed_assessment_lacks_reasons_or_mate: The court that changed the assessment gave no reasons or failed to analyze the supporting material.

members.legal_issue: A compensation determination cannot reject supported expert valuation evidence or impose substantial deductions through an unexplained rough method.
material_facts: A government-approved valuer gave evidence and provided a valuation report addressing the land's location, amenities and comparable property values.
The judgment records that cross-examination did not elicit anything undermining the valuer's evidence.
The High Court rejected the valuation evidence and reduced the compensation using cumulative deductions without cogent reasons.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the approved valuer as an expert whose opinion should not be rejected without reason. A compensation determination must have a cogent evidentiary basis; rough and ready deductions are impermissible. The Court applied the valuation framework in Sections 23 and 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
members.conclusion: The High Court's unsupported reduction was set aside. The expert evidence should not have been rejected without adequate reasons, and the Court reassessed compensation on the evidence.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.expert_valuation_evidence_is_supported: A valuation expert has given evidence and supplied a report supported by relevant valuation factors.
predicates.expert_evidence_is_not_materially_underm: The opposing evidence or cross-examination has not materially discredited the expert's valuation evidence.
predicates.compensation_reduction_uses_unexplained_: The compensation was reduced by deductions that lack cogent reasons or a sound evidentiary basis.

members.legal_issue: A later eviction proceeding based on bona fide requirement is not barred by the rule against reopening finally decided issues when the earlier proceeding was disposed of without deciding any issue.
material_facts: The landlord's earlier eviction proceeding was not pressed and was disposed of without a decision on the merits.
The landlord later initiated another eviction proceeding against the occupant of the same premises based on a bona fide requirement.
members.legal_principle: Section 45 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, incorporates principles of res judicata and permits summary rejection only where proceedings involve the same parties or their privies and substantially the same issues have been finally decided in a former proceeding. Because the earlier proceeding was disposed of without deciding any issue, the provision did not apply.
members.conclusion: The finality provision did not bar the later proceeding because no issue had been finally decided in the earlier proceeding.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a rent-control regime.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The successive proceedings involve the same parties or persons claiming under them.
predicates.former_proceeding_disposed_without_decis: The earlier proceeding was disposed of without deciding any issue.

members.legal_issue: A later suit challenging a threat to disconnect and the resulting disconnection is not barred by res judicata when the earlier suit concerned a different matter and sought different relief.
material_facts: An earlier suit sought a permanent injunction against enforcement of a demand for the previous occupant’s electricity arrears and was dismissed, with the dismissal affirmed.
The later suit challenged a threat to disconnect the electricity supply and the resulting disconnection, and sought a declaration and consequential relief.
The matters directly and substantially in issue, and the reliefs sought, differed between the two suits.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata does not bar a subsequent suit when the matter directly and substantially in issue in it is different from the matter in the earlier suit; the court also relied on the difference in relief sought in the two suits.
members.conclusion: The later suit was not barred by res judicata.

rule.if: successive_civil_suits and earlier_suit_final and issues_materially_differ and reliefs_differ

predicates.successive_civil_suits: A party brought a later civil suit after an earlier civil suit concerning the same dispute.
predicates.earlier_suit_final: The earlier suit ended in a final decision.
predicates.issues_materially_differ: The matters directly and substantially in issue in the two suits were different.
predicates.reliefs_differ: The relief sought in the later suit differed from the relief sought in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A prior dismissal of an eviction suit on personal-need grounds does not bar a later eviction suit when the later need is different and is assessed as of the later suit’s filing.
material_facts: An earlier eviction suit based on the landlord’s need was dismissed.
The requirement pleaded in the later eviction suit was different from the requirement pleaded in the earlier suit.
The lower courts considered the landlord’s bona fide need with reference to the time the later suit was filed.
members.legal_principle: A landlord’s bona fide need is considered with reference to the time the eviction suit is filed; an earlier decision against necessity does not establish that the landlord can never have a genuine need in the future. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The earlier dismissal did not bar the later suit, and the courts below were correct to reject the plea of res judicata.

predicates.eviction_appeal: A party appealed in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.earlier_eviction_suit_dismissed: An earlier eviction suit based on the landlord’s need was dismissed.
predicates.later_requirement_different: The requirement pleaded in the later eviction suit differed from the requirement pleaded in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A later rent-control eviction petition based on a distinct period of non-occupation is not barred by res judicata merely because an earlier petition raised the same statutory ground.
material_facts: The earlier petitions alleged cessation of occupation beginning in an earlier period, while the later petitions alleged cessation beginning in September 2001 and continuing until they were filed.

In the earlier proceedings, the premises had been kept open and available for operation for a time; in the later proceedings, the tenant produced no adequate evidence of occupation during the later period.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata did not apply because the later petitions concerned a distinct period of non-occupation and rested on a different cause from the earlier petitions; the evidence relevant to the later period also differed.
members.conclusion: The later petitions were based on different causes and were not barred by res judicata.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_petition: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.earlier_eviction_petition_decided: An earlier eviction petition between the same parties has been decided.
predicates.current_petition_relies_on_later_nonoccu: The current petition relies on non-occupation during a period later than the period alleged in the earlier petition.

members.legal_issue: An earlier representative suit for administration of a trust does not bar a later suit concerning title when the earlier decision did not conclusively determine the title now in issue.
material_facts: The earlier suit was brought representatively by persons interested in a mosque and sought a scheme for its administration and management of its properties.

The property in dispute was considered in the earlier suit, but the court described the predecessor’s right as prima facie and left open steps concerning whether the terms of the grant had been fulfilled.
The earlier suit did not determine whether the predecessor had absolute title or decide the terms or character of the grant.
The later suit sought a declaration concerning the property and possession, and the property had been notified as wakf property after the earlier decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC, including Explanation VI, makes a decree in a bona fide representative suit binding on persons interested in the common right; Explanation VIII addresses issues decided by courts of limited jurisdiction. A court considering a scheme under Section 92 CPC may decide a contested title issue when necessary to determine whether the property belongs to the trust, but a finding that is merely incidental or not necessary and essential to the judgment does not ordinarily operate as res judicata. Mahant Pragdasji Guru Bhagwandasji v. Patel Ishwarlalbhai Narsibhai addresses the scope of Section 92 suits; Raje Anandrao v. Shamrao, Ahmad Adam Sait v. M.E. Makhri, R. Venugopala Naidu v. Venkatarayulu Naidu Charities, and Shiromani Gurdwara Parbhandhak Committee v. Mahant Harnam Singh address the binding effect of representative suits. Sajjadanashin Syed M.D.B.E. Edr. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer states the necessity and essentiality tests; Gram Panchayat of Village Naulakha v. Ujagar Singh and Nand Ram v. Jagdish Prasad address findings that are collateral or not conclusively decided.
members.conclusion: The earlier representative suit did not bar the later suit because it did not conclusively decide the predecessor’s absolute title, and the matters in issue were distinct.

rule.if: civil_suit_following_a_representative_trust_suit and prior_suit_sought_trust_administration and later_suit_seeks_title_or_possession and prior_decision_was_only_prima_facie and prior_decision_did_not_determine_absolute_title and property_status_changed_after_prior_decision

predicates.civil_suit_following_a_representative_tr: A civil suit was brought after an earlier representative proceeding concerning the administration of a trust.
predicates.prior_suit_sought_trust_administration: The earlier proceeding sought a scheme for administering a trust and its property.
predicates.later_suit_seeks_title_or_possession: The later proceeding seeks a determination of title, possession, or both concerning the property.
predicates.prior_decision_was_only_prima_facie: The earlier court described the interested person’s right to the property as prima facie rather than conclusive.
predicates.prior_decision_did_not_determine_absolut: The earlier judgment did not decide that the interested person held absolute title to the property.
predicates.property_status_changed_after_prior_deci: The property was given a changed legal or recorded status after the earlier judgment.

members.legal_issue: A decision in an earlier suit for dissolution and accounts does not bar a later suit concerning entitlement to compensation for an acquired undertaking when the later entitlement was not decided in the earlier suit.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought dissolution of the partnership and an accounting while the licence and undertaking were still in existence.
The later suit sought a declaration that the licensee alone was entitled to compensation after the licence was revoked and the undertaking was taken over by the government.
Although the suits had some issues in common, the earlier suit did not determine whether the other contributors could recover their respective shares from the compensation.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the general doctrine of res judicata prevent re-litigation of a matter finally decided between the parties; the relevant test is whether the issue was in substance tried and decided before. The Court discussed Lakshmi v. Bhuli and Narhari v. Sankar, and distinguished Sheodan Singh v. Mst. Daryao Kaur. It did not decide the broader question whether dismissal of one of multiple appeals from a common judgment necessarily bars another appeal, because the subject matter of the two suits differed.
members.conclusion: The appeals concerning the later compensation suit were not barred by res judicata.

predicates.appeal_from_later_compensation_suit: A party appeals in a suit concerning who is entitled to compensation for an acquired undertaking.
predicates.earlier_suit_sought_dissolution_and_acco: An earlier suit between relevant parties sought dissolution of a business arrangement and an accounting.
predicates.later_suit_sought_exclusive_compensation: The later suit sought a determination that one person alone was entitled to compensation for the undertaking.
predicates.compensation_entitlement_not_decided_ear: The earlier suit did not decide whether other contributors could claim shares of the compensation.

members.legal_issue: A prior suit based on a claim to the entire property under a settlement deed does not bar a later partition suit based on a co-owner’s separate entitlement to a share when the causes of action differ.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought possession of the entire property on the basis of a settlement deed and was dismissed after the court did not accept the deed’s genuineness.
The later suit sought partition of a claimed half share based on the plaintiff’s asserted right as a co-owner.
The court found that the basis and cause of action of the two suits were different.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 bars relitigation of an issue directly and substantially decided between the parties, but the bar requires that the subsequent claim be founded on the same cause of action and that the relief sought was available in the former proceeding. The court relied on Sulochanna Amma v. Narayanan Nair, Jaswant Singh v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, and Kunjan Nair Sivaraman Nair v. Narayanan Nair; cause of action comprises the facts necessary to support the claim to judgment.
members.conclusion: The earlier dismissal did not bar the later partition claim by res judicata.

predicates.partition_suit_after_prior_suit: A party brings a suit for partition after an earlier suit involving the same property and parties.
predicates.different_basis_of_claim: The later partition claim rests on a basis of entitlement distinct from the basis of the earlier claim for possession.

members.legal_issue: A later suit for specific performance is not barred by the rule against splitting claims when it is founded on a cause of action distinct from the earlier suit for an injunction.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought an injunction against interference with possession after alleged threats to dispossess the plaintiff.
The later suit sought specific performance after the vendor allegedly failed to perform the sale agreement despite a demand to execute the sale deed.
The suits involved different causes of action and different requirements for obtaining the reliefs sought.
members.legal_principle: Under Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the defendant must establish, among other things, that the later suit is based on the same cause of action as the earlier suit and that the plaintiff omitted a relief available on that cause of action. The Constitution Bench in Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, AIR 1964 SC 1810, set out these requirements; Virgo Industries (Eng.) P. Ltd. v. Venturetech Solutions P. Ltd., (2013) 1 SCC 625, reaffirmed that identity of causes of action is essential. Similar pleadings do not establish identity of causes of action.
members.conclusion: The later suit for specific performance was not barred by the rule against splitting claims, and no leave to bring that suit was required.

predicates.two_suits_concern_same_transaction: The plaintiff brought one suit for an injunction and another for specific performance concerning the same property and agreement.
predicates.different_claim_triggers: The injunction claim arose from alleged threats to possession, while the specific-performance claim arose from alleged failure to perform the agreement after a demand.
predicates.injunction_suit_precedes_specific_perfor: The plaintiff filed the injunction suit before filing the suit for specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A prior suit does not bar a later suit under the rule against splitting claims when the suits arise from different causes of action.
material_facts: Earlier suits concerning the defendants’ use and occupation of the land ended in compromise decrees.
The defendants did not carry out the terms of those compromise decrees.

The cause of action in the suit for possession was different from the causes of action in the compromised suits, and the failure to comply with the compromise terms formed part of the later suit’s cause of action.
members.legal_principle: Order 2, Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply where the later suit arises from a cause of action different from those in the earlier suits; failure to perform the compromise decrees formed part of the cause of action in the later suit.
members.conclusion: The rule against splitting claims did not bar the suit for possession.

predicates.later_suit_after_prior_compromised_suits: The proceeding is a later suit brought after earlier suits between the parties ended in compromise decrees.
predicates.causes_of_action_are_different: The later suit and the earlier suits arise from different causes of action.
predicates.nonperformance_of_prior_compromise_terms: A party’s failure to perform the earlier compromise terms forms part of the cause of action in the later suit.

members.legal_issue: Omitting or relinquishing one of several distinct causes of action does not bar a later claim based on that distinct cause under the rule against splitting claims.
material_facts: The landlord initially sought eviction on three distinct grounds, then withdrew the personal-need and repair grounds before the tenant had been served or participated.
The landlord later sought to restore the personal-need ground in the same proceedings after withdrawing the ground based on her husband's need to leave government accommodation.
The tenant objected that restoring the personal-need ground was barred by the rule against splitting claims.
members.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies when a plaintiff omits or relinquishes part of a claim arising from the same cause of action; it does not prevent a later suit or claim based on a separate and distinct cause of action. The Court applied the principles in Mohammad Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Khan, including that the causes of action are distinct where the claims rest on different facts or evidence.
members.conclusion: The later amendment was not barred because the personal-need ground was a distinct cause of action from the other grounds.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.distinct_causes_of_action: The landlord's eviction grounds rested on separate and distinct causes of action.
predicates.cause_relinquished_before_opponent_parti: The landlord relinquished the cause later claimed before the tenant had participated in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The bar on bringing a fresh suit after dismissal for the plaintiff's default does not apply when the earlier proceeding was not dismissed in the circumstances specified by the relevant procedural rule.
material_facts: The earlier eviction proceeding was dismissed for default by the prescribed authority.
The proceeding was not dismissed because the plaintiff failed to appear when the defendant appeared, which is the circumstance addressed by Order IX Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The State later initiated a further eviction proceeding.
members.legal_principle: Order IX Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a fresh suit on the same cause of action when the earlier suit was wholly or partly dismissed under Order IX Rule 8, and permits an application to set that dismissal aside for sufficient cause. Because the earlier proceeding was not dismissed under Rule 8, the Court held Rule 9 inapplicable.
members.conclusion: Order IX Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not apply to bar the later proceeding.

predicates.later_statutory_eviction_proceeding: A public authority initiates a statutory proceeding seeking eviction.
predicates.prior_proceeding_dismissed_for_default: An earlier proceeding was dismissed for default.
predicates.prior_dismissal_not_due_to_plaintiff_abs: The earlier proceeding was not dismissed because the plaintiff failed to appear when the defendant appeared.

members.legal_issue: A previous proceeding dismissed for default or withdrawn does not bar a current suit where the earlier proceeding has been restored and the suits concern different properties.
material_facts: A previous suit was dismissed for default and later restored, and it remained pending when the defendant applied to reject the current plaint.
The relief in the previous suit and the relief in the current suit concerned different properties.
The defendant relied on the earlier proceedings to argue that the current plaint was barred.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that Order IX Rules 8 and 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 did not apply because the earlier suit had been restored and was pending; in any event, the earlier and current suits concerned different properties. For the same reasons, Order XXIII Rule 1(3) and Rule 4(b) did not apply.
members.conclusion: The provisions concerning dismissal for default and withdrawal did not bar the current suit on these facts. The case was properly remitted for the trial court to consider all issues.

predicates.plaint_rejection_application: A defendant applied for rejection of a plaint.
predicates.earlier_suit_dismissed_for_default_and_r: An earlier suit was dismissed for default and later restored.
predicates.different_properties: The earlier suit and the current suit concerned different properties.

members.legal_issue: A common judgment disposing of separate suits does not make a final adjudication in one suit a bar to appeals arising from other suits when the adjudications involve different parties or different matters.
material_facts: Twelve suits concerned different sets of plots and were tried together because they raised similar issues.
The suits were disposed of by a common judgment, but separate decrees were prepared for them.
Three appeals involving a defendant who was not a party to the other suits were dismissed for default; the remaining appeals were decided on their merits.
The Board of Revenue dismissed the later appeals as barred by the finality of the three dismissals, although those dismissals concerned different parties and different plots.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata requires that the previous adjudication have been between the same parties and concern the same matter. A common judgment resolving several separate suits ordinarily amounts to as many judgments as there are suits. The Court relied on Badri Narayan Singh v. Kamdeo Prasad Singh, (1962) 3 S.C.R. 759.
members.conclusion: The Board of Revenue was wrong to hold that the appeals were barred by res judicata; the appeals were allowed and remanded for further hearing and decision.

predicates.appeal_challenging_res_judicata_dismissa: A party appealed a decision dismissing its case on the ground that an earlier adjudication barred it.
predicates.prior_adjudication_involved_different_pa: The earlier adjudication was between parties different from those in the proceeding under appeal.
predicates.prior_adjudication_concerned_different_s: The earlier adjudication concerned a different subject matter from the proceeding under appeal.

members.legal_issue: A decision on a request for relief in one jointly tried suit does not, merely because the suits were tried together, bar a separate request for relief in another suit.
material_facts: Several suits were ordered to be tried jointly, with evidence in the main suit treated as evidence in the connected suits.
An application seeking restoration of a dismissed suit was decided separately from the later application to set aside an ex parte decree in another suit.
The applications concerned relief specific to their respective suits, although they relied on similar facts.
members.legal_principle: Section 11's res judicata principle requires identity of the matter decided and does not make a decision on an application in one suit binding in another merely because the suits were consolidated or tried jointly. Each suit's relief and the issue arising under the applicable provision must be considered separately.
members.conclusion: The decision in the restoration application for one suit did not operate as res judicata against the application to set aside the ex parte decree in the other suit.

predicates.separate_civil_suits_jointly_tried: Distinct suits are directed to be tried together or share evidence.
predicates.relief_specific_to_each_suit: The applications seek remedies that arise separately in their respective suits.
predicates.decision_in_one_suit_invoked_against_app: A party relies on a decision in one suit to bar an application in a different suit.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner’s suit for possession is not barred by a predecessor’s failure to sue when the predecessor had no cause of action against persons who were not yet in possession and the reversionary right accrued later.
material_facts: The persons later resisting possession were not in possession during the predecessor’s lifetime.
The predecessor therefore had no cause of action to eject them during that lifetime.
The claimant’s right as the next reversioner arose only upon the death of the intervening holder.
The opposing side had earlier abandoned limitation and adverse-possession pleas, and those pleas had been rejected in the acquisition proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the asserted limitation premise was incorrect because the predecessor had no cause of action while the opposing claimants were not in possession. The reversioner’s title to seek possession arose only when succession opened. The Court also noted that limitation and adverse-possession pleas had been abandoned earlier and rejected in the land acquisition proceedings.
members.conclusion: The predecessor’s failure to sue did not bar the claimant’s later suit, and the possession during the intervening holder’s lifetime did not confer title against the claimant.

predicates.reversioner_possession_suit: A claimant sued for possession in the capacity of a person entitled to succeed after an intervening holder.
predicates.defendants_not_in_possession_during_pred: The persons resisting the later suit were not in possession while the predecessor was alive.
predicates.reversionary_right_accrued_later: The claimant’s right to possession arose only after the intervening holder’s death.

members.legal_issue: When a surrender has not accelerated succession, a claim by a reversioner is not barred by adverse possession that began before the estate vested in the reversioners.
material_facts: Because there was no valid surrender, the estate vested in the nearest reversioners only when the widow died.
The trial court had found that the opposing claimants were in adverse possession from the widow’s death in 1927.
The suit was brought within a few months of the widow’s death.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, absent a valid surrender, succession to the estate vested in the nearest reversioners only on the widow’s death; adverse possession could not bar their claim before that vesting. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited on this point.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because succession had not vested before the widow’s death and the suit was brought within a few months thereafter.

predicates.reversionary_estate_claim: The claimant seeks an estate as a reversioner.
predicates.no_valid_surrender_preceded_vesting: No valid surrender caused the estate to vest in the reversioners before the life holder died.
predicates.suit_filed_within_months_after_vesting: The claimant filed suit within a few months after the estate vested in the reversioners.

members.legal_issue: A later possession suit is not barred by the rule requiring execution of an earlier decree when a compromise made that decree unexecutable and the claimant’s later right gave rise to a fresh cause of action.
material_facts: An earlier decree for possession had been affected by a compromise in appeal and the property was partitioned under the compromise.
The compromise was later declared inoperative against the claimant.
The earlier decree had become unexecutable after the compromise, and the claimant sought possession on a later-accruing right.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that section 47 did not bar a separate suit where the earlier possession decree became unexecutable because of a compromise that was later held not binding on the claimant, and the claimant had a fresh cause of action for possession. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The later suit was not barred by section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the claimant could bring a separate suit for possession.

rule.if: subsequent_possession_suit and earlier_possession_decree and compromise_made_decree_unexecutable and compromise_not_binding_on_claimant and fresh_cause_of_action

predicates.subsequent_possession_suit: A claimant brought a later suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.earlier_possession_decree: A decree for possession had been made in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.compromise_made_decree_unexecutable: A compromise altered the position so that the earlier decree could no longer be executed to obtain the claimed possession.
predicates.compromise_not_binding_on_claimant: The compromise was held not to bind the claimant.
predicates.fresh_cause_of_action: A later-accruing right gave the claimant a new basis to seek possession.

members.legal_issue: A fresh suit for possession of property allotted under a partition compromise is not barred by the execution requirement when the claimant remained in constructive possession and the occupants held permissively.
material_facts: A partition suit was compromised and the plaint property was allotted to the claimant, but no formal decree was drawn because the parties did not provide the required stamp paper.
The occupants remained physically on the property with permission until they removed a structure they had built there.

The occupants claimed only that they held as tenants; their claim that the claimant had put them in possession under a lease was rejected, and they did not assert a right to possess the property as their own.
The claimant was therefore in constructive possession after the compromise.
members.legal_principle: Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not bar a fresh suit for possession in these circumstances where the claimant remained in constructive possession and the opposing parties’ physical occupation was permissive, rather than possession asserted against the claimant’s title. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The claimant’s suit for recovery of khas possession was not barred by section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: partition_compromise_possession_suit and no_formal_decree_drawn and claimant_constructively_possessed and occupants_remained_permissively and occupants_acknowledged_claimant_title

predicates.partition_compromise_possession_suit: A claimant brings a suit for possession of property allotted to the claimant under a partition compromise.
predicates.no_formal_decree_drawn: No formal decree was drawn up after the compromise.
predicates.claimant_constructively_possessed: The claimant retained constructive possession of the property after the compromise.
predicates.occupants_remained_permissively: The opposing occupants remained physically on the property with permission rather than intending to possess it as their own.
predicates.occupants_acknowledged_claimant_title: The opposing occupants claimed no right to remain in possession other than a derivative right, and their asserted basis for that right was not established.

members.legal_issue: A later suit seeking recovery after actual dispossession is not barred for omission of relief where the earlier suit arose from a threat of dispossession and sought protection of possession.
material_facts: The earlier suit was based on an apprehension that the defendants would forcibly dispossess the plaintiff and sought an injunction.
The later suit alleged that the plaintiff had actually been dispossessed and sought restoration of possession.
The later suit therefore relied on an asserted event and sought relief not present in the earlier suit.
members.legal_principle: Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure prevents a plaintiff from splitting reliefs arising from the same cause of action without leave, but does not bar a later suit founded on a distinct cause of action. Unlike res judicata, which concerns grounds supporting a claim, Order 2 Rule 2 concerns reliefs arising from the same cause of action.
members.conclusion: The later suit was based on a distinct cause of action and was not barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.subsequent_suit_after_prior_suit: A party brought a later suit after an earlier suit concerning the same property.
predicates.prior_suit_based_on_threatened_disposses: The earlier suit alleged a threat to possession and sought protection against a future dispossession.
predicates.later_suit_based_on_actual_dispossession: The later suit alleged that dispossession had occurred and sought recovery of possession.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent suit for specific performance is not barred when it is founded on a cause of action distinct from that of an earlier suit for injunction and the plaintiff did not intentionally omit the later relief from the earlier suit.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought an injunction against threatened forcible dispossession and was founded on the defendant’s attempts to take possession of the property.

The later suit sought specific performance after the plaintiff learned that the housing authority had transferred the property to the defendant and the defendant denied, including in response to a legal notice, that he would perform the sale agreement.
The facts and evidence needed to support the injunction claim differed from those needed to support specific performance.
The Supreme Court found nothing in the earlier injunction plaint showing an intentional relinquishment of the specific-performance claim.
members.legal_principle: Order 2 Rule 2 CPC requires a plaintiff to include the whole claim arising from the same cause of action, and bars a later suit for an omitted relief only where the later and earlier suits share the same cause of action and the plaintiff, being entitled to multiple reliefs, omitted the later relief without leave. The defendant must establish the precise cause of action in the earlier suit and its identity with that in the later suit; the bar is technical and cannot be presumed. A cause of action is the bundle of facts necessary to prove the right to judgment, and distinct causes may be shown where the evidence supporting the claims differs. The Court relied on Mohd. Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian, Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti, Deva Ram v. Ishwar Chand, Sidramappa v. Rajashetty, and State of M.P. v. State of Maharashtra. It distinguished Virgo Industries (Eng.) (P) Ltd. v. Venturetech Solutions (P) Ltd. on its facts and noted that precedent must be applied in the context of the facts of the case.
members.conclusion: The subsequent specific-performance suit was not barred by Order 2 Rule 2 CPC. The High Court’s contrary finding was set aside.

rule.if: subsequent_specific_performance_suit and earlier_injunction_suit and distinct_causes_of_action and not intentional_omission_of_later_relief

predicates.subsequent_specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a later proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.earlier_injunction_suit: The plaintiff had earlier brought a proceeding seeking an injunction against interference with possession or threatened dispossession.
predicates.distinct_causes_of_action: The earlier claim rested on facts about threatened dispossession, while the later claim rested on different facts giving rise to the demand for performance, such as disclosure of a transfer and refusal to perform.
predicates.intentional_omission_of_later_relief: The plaintiff intentionally left the later relief out of the earlier proceeding despite being entitled to seek it on the same cause of action.

members.legal_issue: A pending earlier eviction proceeding on a different ground does not bar a later proceeding based on the special recovery right.
material_facts: The landlord had an earlier eviction petition pending against the tenant.
The later petition relied on the special right arising from the landlord's occupation of authority-allotted accommodation and the requirement to vacate it.
The earlier petition relied on different grounds.
members.legal_principle: Section 14A confers a distinct right based on circumstances different from the grounds in the earlier petition; the earlier proceeding therefore did not bar the later petition.
members.conclusion: The pending earlier petition did not prevent the landlord from bringing the special recovery proceeding.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.earlier_eviction_case_pending: A proceeding seeking eviction of the same tenant from the premises was already pending.
predicates.earlier_and_later_cases_have_different_b: The earlier proceeding relied on grounds different from the special right relied on in the later proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Earlier proceedings under general rent-recovery provisions do not by themselves bar a later application under the special recovery procedure.
material_facts: A landlord had previously pursued ejectment proceedings under the general provisions of the rent law.
The landlord later sought recovery under the special procedure for the specially classified landlord category.
The tenant argued that the earlier proceedings barred the later application.
members.legal_principle: The special procedure under Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 is distinct from proceedings under the general provisions, and earlier general proceedings do not by themselves prevent use of the special procedure.
members.conclusion: The earlier proceedings do not bar an application under the special procedure.

predicates.special_nri_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking expedited recovery of rented premises by a landlord in the specially classified returning-resident category.
predicates.earlier_general_eviction_proceeding_exis: The landlord previously pursued recovery of the premises under general rent-recovery grounds.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s construction supports eviction only when it is likely to cause a substantial diminution in the building’s value or utility.
material_facts: The tenant installed a wooden parchhati in the leased shop to store clothes, with wooden beams resting in holes made in the walls.
The tenant’s expert testified that the structure was temporary, removable, and did not affect the shop’s structural soundness or utility; the landlord produced no contrary expert evidence.
The Rent Controller and Appellate Authority found material impairment, and the High Court affirmed those findings.
members.legal_principle: Under section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, it is not enough that a tenant’s construction affects or diminishes value or utility: the impairment must be substantial and significant, assessed from the commercial, monetary, or utilitarian perspective. The Court applied the reasoning on material alteration in Om Prakash v. Amar Singh, [1987] 1 SCC 458, and Brijendra Nath Bhargava v. Harsh Wardhan, [1988] 1 SCC 454, and referred to Govindaswamy Naidu v. Pushpalammal, AIR 1952 Mad 181; Smt. Savitri Devi v. U.S. Bajpai, AIR 1956 Nag 60; Charan Singh v. Shrimati Ananthi, [1966] 6 PLR 780; G. Natarajan v. P. Thandavarayan, [1969] RCJ 733; Shri Anup Chand v. Shri Trilok Singh, [1977] 1 RCJ 752; and Gobind Ram v. Smt. Kaushalya Rani, [1983] 1 RCJ 295.
members.conclusion: The parchhati did not establish a ground for eviction because the evidence did not show substantial impairment of the building’s value or utility; the eviction petition was dismissed.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and tenant_made_construction and temporary_removable_structure and not substantial_impairment_shown

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction on the basis of a tenant’s construction in leased premises.
predicates.tenant_made_construction: The tenant made a construction in the leased premises.
predicates.temporary_removable_structure: The construction was temporary and could be removed without materially affecting the building.
predicates.substantial_impairment_shown: Evidence showed that the construction substantially diminished the building’s value or utility.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s act of waste warrants eviction only when it is reasonably probable to impair the building’s value or utility to a material and substantial degree.
material_facts: An Advocate-Commissioner reported uneven concrete flooring, a hole in the floor for a pipe, nail-holes, no damage to the roof or walls, and only slight vibration at the parapet while the machinery operated.
The rent-control court and appellate authority found the observed defects trivial and concluded that they would not affect the building’s value or utility.
The High Court treated the holes and spaces between the shutter and wall as proof of qualifying damage, displacing the concurrent findings.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 requires acts of waste likely to impair materially the value or utility of the building. The impairment must be reasonably probable and substantial. In Om Pal v. Anand Swarup, the Court held that material impairment must substantially diminish value or utility and that the landlord bears the burden of proving it.
members.conclusion: The observed defects did not establish acts of waste likely to materially impair the building’s value or utility, and the High Court improperly substituted its findings for those of the lower courts.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.alleged_building_damage_is_trivial: The observed defects to the building are minor rather than substantial.
predicates.no_reasonably_probable_material_impairme: The evidence does not show that the defects are reasonably likely to substantially reduce the building’s value or utility.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s permanent structural alterations that substantially diminish a rented building’s value or utility constitute a ground for eviction.
material_facts: The tenants removed the original roofs, partition walls and doors of several shops, replaced the roofs, and merged the shops with the adjoining verandah, changing the premises’ layout and character.
The tenants demolished part of a boundary wall, created access from adjoining property, and constructed a room and staircase.
Inspection reports, witness testimony and municipal notices supported the finding that the alterations had been made by the tenants.
Even assuming the landlord had consented to construction of a shed over part of the open land, the remaining permanent alterations to the shops and verandah were not covered by that consent.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949, a tenant is liable to eviction for acts likely to impair materially the value or utility of the building or rented land. “Impair materially” means a substantial diminution in quality, strength or value, assessed by comparing the premises before and after the alterations. The assessment is from the landlord’s point of view, as stated in Vipin Kumar v. Roshan Lal Anand, (1993) 2 SCC 614. Whether the alterations materially impair value or utility is a mixed question of law and fact; the nature and permanence of the construction are relevant.
members.conclusion: The permanent alterations were acts likely to impair materially the value or utility of the premises, viewed from the landlords’ perspective. The eviction application was allowed; the tenants were directed to vacate, subject to a temporary opportunity to remain upon furnishing an undertaking.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.tenant_made_permanent_structural_changes: The tenant made permanent structural changes to the rented premises, including removing and replacing structural elements and changing the layout.
predicates.alterations_substantially_impair_value_o: The changes substantially diminished the premises’ value or utility when assessed from the landlord’s point of view.

members.legal_issue: Eviction for a tenant’s alterations requires proof that the tenant’s use materially and permanently destroyed or reduced the building’s value or utility.
material_facts: The tenant took an old room for a jewellery business and made changes including bricking up a door and windows, lowering the floor, cutting rafters, erecting pillars and installing a rolling shutter.
The bricked-up openings could be restored, and the floor could be restored without structural impairment; the rolling shutter provided added security for the jewellery business.

The landlord did not plead that the changes materially and permanently destroyed or reduced the building’s value or utility, and the evidence did not establish that effect. The landlord admitted that the room could command higher rent if let again.
members.legal_principle: Section 11(4)(ii) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 requires both material and permanent destruction or reduction of value or utility; the requirements are cumulative. The effect is assessed from the landlord’s standpoint, and the landlord must prove it. The inquiry depends on the facts, including the building’s nature, the purpose of letting, the contract terms and the nature of the interference. The Court relied on the Kerala decisions in Ahammad Kanna v. Muhammed Haneef, Ayissabeevi v. Aboobaker, Shanmugam v. Rao Saheb, Prabodhini v. Rajammal, Thankappan v. Reji Xavier, Mathew v. Gilbert, Aboobacker v. Nanu and Seethalakshmi Ammal v. Nabeesath Beevi. It also considered Manmohan Das v. Bishun Das, Om Prakash v. Amar Singh, Brijendra Nath v. Harsh Wardhan, Arunachalam v. Thondarperienambi, Vipin Kumar v. Roshan Lal Anand and Waryam Singh v. Baldev Singh, noting that provisions in other enactments may differ and that the governing statutory language controls.
members.conclusion: The landlord failed to prove material and permanent destruction or reduction of the building’s value or utility, so eviction on this ground was set aside.

predicates.rent_control_alteration_eviction_case: The proceeding sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the tenant’s use or alteration of rented premises damaged their value or utility.
predicates.tenant_altered_the_building: The tenant made physical changes to the rented building.
predicates.landlord_proved_material_and_permanent_i: The landlord established that the tenant’s use materially and permanently destroyed or reduced the building’s value or utility.

members.legal_issue: A tenant's transfer of possession or subletting without the landlord's written consent establishes a ground for eviction, and oral consent cannot replace the required written consent.
material_facts: The lease prohibited the tenant from subletting any part of the premises.
The tenant placed the occupants in possession of cabins and gave them rights to use those cabins under written occupation agreements.
The landlord's written consent to subletting was not present.
The High Court relied on alleged oral consent when rejecting this ground for eviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 provides a ground for eviction where a tenant transfers rights under the lease or sublets the building or a portion of it without the landlord's written consent. Where the law requires written consent, oral consent does not satisfy that requirement.
members.conclusion: The ground for eviction based on unauthorized subletting was established, and the High Court could not substitute oral consent for written consent.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute is a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_places_others_in_possession_of_pr: The tenant places other persons in possession of the premises or a portion of them.
predicates.landlord_written_consent_absent: The landlord has not given written consent to that placement or subletting.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s subletting without the landlord’s prior written consent, or failure to follow the prescribed procedure for a consented subtenancy, provides a ground for eviction.
material_facts: The tenant created a subtenancy without the previous landlord’s written consent.
The subtenancy was created after the Act came into force, and the required procedure for notifying the landlord was not followed.
The trial court found that the subletting had occurred.
members.legal_principle: Sections 13(1)(a), 16(1) and 16(2) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 require prior written consent for subletting and prescribe notification procedures for subtenancies. The requirement of written consent serves a public purpose, and mere permission or acquiescence is insufficient; the Court relied on M/s Shalimar Tar Products Ltd. v. H.C. Sharma & Ors., [1988] 1 SCC 70.
members.conclusion: The absence of prior written consent was a ground for eviction, and the failure to comply with the prescribed procedure for the subtenancy was an additional reason the tenant could not avoid eviction. Mere knowledge of the subletting or acceptance of rent did not defeat the landlord’s right to eviction.

predicates.subletting_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant created a subtenancy.
predicates.tenant_created_subtenancy: The tenant created a subtenancy of the rented premises.
predicates.prior_written_consent_absent: The landlord had not given written consent before the subtenancy was created.
predicates.consented_subtenancy_notice_procedure_no: Although the landlord had given written consent, the tenant and subtenant did not follow the required procedure for notifying the landlord of the subtenancy.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s subletting is actionable when the landlord has not given written consent specifically covering that subletting.
material_facts: The tenant let an incorporated company occupy part of the premises, and the courts below found that the company had been given exclusive possession.
The lease allowed the tenant’s contractors to share the premises with the landlord’s permission, but that permission did not specifically authorize leasing the premises to the incorporated company.
There was no written consent specifically authorizing that subletting; the landlord objected after learning of it.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1)(b), 16(2) and 16(3) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 require written landlord consent for subletting; consent must relate to the specific subletting, and mere permission or acquiescence is insufficient. Section 16(3) expressly requires previous written consent for sublettings within its scope, while the distinction between subsections 16(2) and 16(3) means that prior consent is not invariably required under subsection 16(2). The Court relied on South Asia Industries Private Ltd. v. S. Sarup Singh and approved Raja Ram Goyal v. Ashok Kumar, Kartar Singh v. Shri Vijay Kumar, and Delhi Vanaspati Syndicate v. Bhagwan Dass Faquir Chand.
members.conclusion: The subletting was without the required written consent and constituted a breach supporting eviction.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_appeal and subletting_found and not written_consent_to_specific_subletting

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a rent-control eviction case.
predicates.subletting_found: The tenant has sublet the premises or a part of them to another occupant.
predicates.written_consent_to_specific_subletting: The landlord gave written consent specifically covering the subletting at issue.
predicates.eviction_ground_established: The subletting establishes a ground for eviction.

members.legal_issue: Material impairment of a rented building’s value or utility is assessed from the landlord’s perspective and may be inferred from proved effects of a tenant’s acts.
material_facts: The tenant constructed a wall in a verandah and installed a door without the landlord’s consent.
The construction stopped the flow of light and air, and the tenant removed fixtures.
The lower courts found that the construction materially affected the value or utility of the building.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, acts likely to materially impair a building’s value or utility can justify eviction. Impairment is assessed from the landlord’s perspective and is an inferential fact that may be deduced from proved facts. Om Parkash v. Amar Singh, concerning material alteration under a different statute, did not assist on these facts.
members.conclusion: The proved effects permitted the courts to infer material impairment from the landlord’s perspective, without requiring separate direct evidence from the landlord of the resulting loss in value or utility.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_made_structural_change and change_obstructed_light_or_air and change_removed_fixtures

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.tenant_made_structural_change: The tenant made a structural change to the rented premises.
predicates.change_obstructed_light_or_air: The structural change obstructed the flow of light or air in the building.
predicates.change_removed_fixtures: The tenant removed fixtures from the premises.
predicates.material_impairment_may_be_inferred: The building’s material loss of value or utility may be inferred from the proved effects of the tenant’s acts, assessed from the landlord’s perspective.

members.legal_issue: Enclosing a verandah warrants eviction for material alteration only when the landlord proves that the tenant made the alteration without consent and that it materially impaired the premises’ value or utility; the impairment cannot be presumed from the alteration alone.
