material_facts: The third party’s visiting cards identified his own jewellery business and gave the premises as its address.
A subscriber list associated the same premises and telephone number with a business previously conducted there by the third party.
The tenant asserted that the third party was an employee paid by commission, but produced no evidence of salary or commission.
The third party was responsible for opening and closing the shop and had admitted conducting business there.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, subletting or otherwise parting with possession without the landlord’s written consent is a ground for eviction. Applying the burden-shifting principles in Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, Kala v. Madho Parshad Vaidya, and Vaishakhi Ram v. Sanjeev Kumar Bhatiani, proof of exclusive possession shifts the onus to the tenant; failure to explain it permits an inference of subletting, even without direct proof of payment.
members.conclusion: The evidence established that the third party was in exclusive possession and conducting an independent business, and the tenant failed to rebut the resulting inference of subletting; the eviction order was therefore upheld.

predicates.subletting_eviction_appeal: The case is an appeal in an eviction proceeding based on alleged subletting or parting with possession.
predicates.third_party_independent_business_evidenc: Evidence shows that a third party used the premises for an independent business and identified the premises as the business address.
predicates.tenant_fails_to_explain_exclusive_posses: After the third party’s exclusive possession is shown, the tenant does not substantiate an explanation for that possession.

members.legal_issue: A landlord proves subletting when the evidence establishes that a third party was given possession of part of the rented premises and supports an inference that the possession was for consideration, and the tenant fails to substantiate the explanation that the third party was an employee.
material_facts: The eviction suit alleged that the tenant had allowed a third party to use part of the shop for watch repairs and was receiving daily payment from him.
The tenant admitted the third party’s presence and said he worked in the shop as an employee, but produced no salary or attendance records or other evidence supporting that claim.

The trial court found that the third party had partial possession, was carrying on repair work in the shop, and was paying consideration to the tenant; the landlord’s witness also supported the allegation of payment.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 20(2)(e) and 25 of the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, subletting requires the tenant to part with possession of the whole or part of the premises in favour of a third party for consideration. The landlord bears the initial burden of proving exclusive possession and consideration; proof of parting with possession may shift the evidential burden to the tenant to explain the third party’s presence. Since such arrangements are often clandestine, consideration may be inferred from the proved facts rather than established by direct evidence. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, Jagdish Prasad v. Smt. Angoori Devi, Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakraborty, Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s S. Chokesiri and Co., Kala v. Madho Parshad Vaidya, Joginder Singh Sodhi v. Amar Kaur, Mahendra Saree Emporium (II) v. G.V. Srinivasa Murthy, Bharat Sales Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, and Krishnawati v. Hans Raj. It also relied on Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in explaining the right to enjoy property that a sublease transfers.
members.conclusion: Subletting was proved. The High Court erred in finding that the landlord had not pleaded or proved parting with possession, and the trial court’s eviction decision on that ground was restored.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_suit_based_on_subletting and landlord_proved_third_party_partial_possession and third_party_used_part_of_premises_for_own_business and evidence_supported_payment_for_possession and tenant_failed_to_substantiate_employment_explanation

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit_based_on_subletting: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet all or part of the rented premises.
predicates.landlord_proved_third_party_partial_poss: The landlord’s evidence establishes that a third party was given possession of part of the rented premises.
predicates.third_party_used_part_of_premises_for_ow: The third party used the premises to carry on a business of his or her own.
predicates.evidence_supported_payment_for_possessio: The evidence supports an inference that the third party’s possession was for payment or other consideration.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_substantiate_employment: The tenant claimed that the third party was an employee but failed to produce evidence that would substantiate that claim.

members.legal_issue: Allowing a substantially identical entity to use rented premises does not amount to subletting, assignment, or parting with possession when the tenant remains in occupation and retains legal possession.
material_facts: The tenant firm continued to occupy the premises after the company began operating there; neither entity ceased its presence.
The company was formed by the tenant firm’s partners, who became its directors, and the two entities operated from the same premises, displayed signboards there, and appointed each other as agents.
The court found substantial identity between the firm and the company, describing the company as the firm’s alter ego and corporate reflection.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, subletting requires the tenant to part with legal possession; permitting another to use the premises while the tenant retains legal possession is insufficient. Mere occupation by a different firm does not itself prove subletting, particularly where the tenant remains in possession. The court relied on Murli Dhar v. Chuni Lal, G. Rangamannar v. Desu Ragiah, Vishwanath v. Chaman Lal, and Reliable Finance Corporation v. Clearing House.
members.conclusion: There was no subletting, assignment, or parting with possession by the tenant, so the eviction ground was not established. The appeal was allowed.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_claim_for_unauthor: A landlord sought eviction on the basis that the tenant had unlawfully sublet, assigned, or parted with possession of rented premises.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_occupation: The tenant continued to occupy the premises after another entity began using them.
predicates.entities_substantially_identical: The tenant and the other entity had substantial practical identity, including through common control or closely connected operations.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s permission for a partnership firm to use leased premises does not amount to subletting if the tenant remains in legal possession.
material_facts: The business operating in the premises was a partnership in which the tenant was a partner.
The tenant contributed the tenancy of the premises for use by the partnership and retained legal possession.
The other partners’ use of the premises was for the partnership business.
members.legal_principle: Under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, subletting requires the tenant to part with legal possession; another person’s use of the premises is insufficient if the tenant retains that possession. The Court relied on Madras Bangalore Transport Co. (West) v. Inder Singh, Mehta Jagjivan Vanechand v. Doshi Vanechand Harakhchand, and Gundalapalli Rangamannar Chetty v. Desu Rangiah.
members.conclusion: There was no subletting merely because the partnership firm used the premises while the tenant retained legal possession.

rule.if: eviction_subletting_proceeding and tenant_is_partner and partnership_uses_premises and tenant_retains_legal_possession

predicates.eviction_subletting_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet the premises.
predicates.tenant_is_partner: The tenant is a partner in the business using the premises.
predicates.partnership_uses_premises: The partnership business uses the leased premises.
predicates.tenant_retains_legal_possession: The tenant has not parted with legal possession of the premises.

members.legal_issue: A tenant does not part with possession merely because another person uses the premises when the tenant retains the legal right to possess them.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had parted with possession to his sons, who ran a partnership business from the premises.
The tenant had earlier run a business there and later sold that business to his sons, who continued the business from the same premises.

Although the tenant had retired from the business, the Court found that he had not been shown to have divested himself of the legal right to possess the premises and could displace his sons from possession.
The premises were used by the father and sons in the context of their joint family business; there was no evidence of subletting or assignment, and the landlord had not given written consent.
members.legal_principle: Parting with possession requires the tenant to vest possession in another person by divesting himself of both physical possession and the right to possession. Another person's use of the premises is insufficient while the tenant retains the legal right to possession. The Court applied section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and relied on Smt. Krishnawati v. Shri Hans Raj, [1974] 1 SCC 289, concerning the need for evidence before inferring that use by another amounts to letting.
members.conclusion: The tenant had not parted with possession within the meaning of the eviction ground, so the eviction order on that ground could not stand.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The dispute was an eviction proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.eviction_sought_for_parting_with_possess: The landlord sought eviction on the basis that the tenant had transferred possession to another person.
predicates.tenant_retained_legal_right_to_possessio: The tenant retained the legal right to possess the premises, including the ability to displace the other occupant.

members.legal_issue: A tenant parts with possession only when the tenant transfers legal possession of the premises or a part of them, excluding the tenant, rather than merely allowing a third party to use a display board while the tenant retains possession and uses the premises for the tenant’s own business.
material_facts: The tenant operated an optical business and also carried on an advertising business, maintaining display boards at various locations.
The tenant installed and maintained a board on the roof area and charged for advertising, including amounts for painting and other expenses.

The tenant testified that the roof had not been given to anyone and that the tenant retained possession; the evidence did not establish that the advertiser had exclusive possession or a right to exclude the tenant.
The landlord’s letter from the advertising company stating that it had the site was written after the eviction suit had been filed, and the landlord did not submit to cross-examination after remand.
The other asserted grounds did not support eviction: no default warranting eviction was found, and the appellate court had rejected material alteration.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 requires an assignment, subletting, or other parting with possession of the whole or part of the premises without the landlord’s permission. Subletting requires transfer of an exclusive right to enjoy the property; parting with possession requires transfer of legal possession to the exclusion of the tenant. Mere occupation or use by another, or the tenant’s receipt of money, is insufficient without the requisite transfer. The Court relied on Shalimar Tar Products v. H.C. Sharma, Gundalpalli Rangamannar Chetty v. Desu Rangiah, Jackson v. Simons, Chaplin v. Smith, Vishwa Nath v. Chaman Lal, Madras Bangalore Transport Co. v. Inder Singh, Dr. Vijay Kumar v. M/s. Raghbir Singh Anokh Singh, B.M. Lal v. Dunlop Rubber & Co., Rajbir Kaur v. M/s. S. Chokosiri and Co., Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakroborty, Associated Hotel of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, and Krishnawati v. Hans Raj. The inquiry depends on the quality of the occupation and whether the tenant retained legal possession and control.
members.conclusion: The display board and receipt of advertising charges did not establish an assignment, subletting, or parting with possession under section 13(1)(e). The eviction order could not stand, and the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_on_transfer_ground and tenant_retained_legal_possession and advertiser_lacked_exclusive_possession and tenant_used_premises_for_own_business

predicates.eviction_proceeding_on_transfer_ground: The proceeding sought eviction on the basis that the tenant had assigned, sublet, or otherwise parted with possession of the premises or part of them.
predicates.tenant_retained_legal_possession: The tenant remained in legal possession and control of the area used for the display board.
predicates.advertiser_lacked_exclusive_possession: The advertiser was not shown to have an exclusive right to possess the area or to exclude the tenant from it.
predicates.tenant_used_premises_for_own_business: The tenant used the premises or the display board in carrying on the tenant’s own business.

members.legal_issue: A tenant parts with possession of leased premises when a third party regularly uses a major portion of them and the tenant does not retain effective exclusive control, even if no rent-paying subletting is proved.
material_facts: The lease prohibited subletting.
A social club regularly used the premises to assemble and play games, and its name board was displayed there.
The club had its registered office at the premises and was subject to statutory requirements relating to records, inspections and service of documents there.
The tenant retained no demonstrated practice of locking the premises and denying the club members entry, though he said he conducted business in a small portion.
The lower courts found no subletting for rent, but the appellate court found that possession had been parted with.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(e) independently covers assigning, subletting, or otherwise parting with possession of all or any part of the premises without the landlord’s permission; consequently, absence of proof of rent or a conventional sublease does not defeat eviction if possession was otherwise parted with. The club’s registered office and the Companies Act, 1956, including Section 146 and the related requirements concerning company records, inspection and service, supported the inference that it had possession. Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s. S. Chokesiri & Co. was distinguished because it concerned occupants shown to be licensees and a different rent statute whose provision did not include the phrase “otherwise parting with the possession.”
members.conclusion: The tenant had parted with possession of a major portion of the premises to the club, making him liable for eviction under Section 13(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950; proof of rent-paying subletting was unnecessary.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_case and third_party_regularly_uses_major_portion and tenant_does_not_exercise_exclusive_control and third_party_has_registered_office_there and landlord_permission_not_shown

predicates.tenant_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.third_party_regularly_uses_major_portion: A third party regularly uses a major portion of the premises.
predicates.tenant_does_not_exercise_exclusive_contr: The tenant does not demonstrate that the tenant keeps the premises under exclusive control by excluding the third party.
predicates.third_party_has_registered_office_there: The third party maintains its registered office at the premises, with the resulting need to use them for its official functions.
predicates.landlord_permission_not_shown: The tenant has not shown that the landlord permitted the transfer of possession.

members.legal_issue: Regular occupation of a distinct part of rented premises by third parties for their independent professional practice, without adequate proof that the tenant retained control or that the arrangement was without consideration, constitutes subletting.
material_facts: The occupation of part of the rented premises by three medical practitioners was admitted.
The practitioners used individual cabins on a mezzanine floor to conduct their practices, and each had a separate telephone connection.
The tenant allowed the practitioners to practise there at regular intervals and permitted them to display their names and practice timings.
The Appellate Tribunal found that the practitioners had exclusive possession while practising and inferred that consideration had passed under the arrangement.
The High Court set aside the Tribunal’s eviction order after reassessing the evidence; the Supreme Court held that the Tribunal’s finding was not perverse.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, subletting involves parting with possession to a third party without the landlord’s consent. Ram Murti Devi v. Pushpa Devi states that the landlord must prove a third party’s exclusive possession of all or part of the premises and monetary consideration; once parting with possession is established, the burden shifts to the tenant to explain. Flora Elias Nahoum v. Idrish Ali Laskar states that where the third party’s presence is admitted, the tenant must establish the nature and capacity of that presence. Bharat Sales Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India explains that direct proof of consideration may be difficult and that a court may infer it from proved facts, including delivery of exclusive possession.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal’s finding of subletting was restored; the eviction ground based on subletting therefore stood established.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_on_subletting_ground: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet all or part of the rented premises.
predicates.third_party_exclusive_possession: A third party occupies a distinct part of the premises to the exclusion of the tenant while using it for the third party’s own purposes.
predicates.monetary_consideration_reasonably_inferr: The proved circumstances support an inference that the tenant received or was promised consideration for allowing the third party to occupy the premises.

members.legal_issue: An arrangement framed as an agency constitutes subletting when its substance and the parties’ conduct show that a third party has the exclusive use of the premises and the tenant does not retain actual control.
material_facts: The agreement stated that the premises were to be used for the third party’s business, whose goods, staff, sales, accounts, and sewing school were under its control.
The third party’s employees held the keys and opened and locked the premises each day.

Although the agreement contained terms describing the tenant as an agent and stating that the tenant retained control, the rent authorities and the High Court found that the third party had the right to exclusive use of the premises for its own business.
The courts assessed the agreement together with oral evidence and the surrounding circumstances and found that the agency arrangement was intended to camouflage a sub-tenancy.
members.legal_principle: The character of an arrangement is determined from its terms, evidence, and circumstances as a whole, rather than from its label. The court treated the third party’s right of exclusive use and its actual control of the premises as showing subletting despite contrary agency clauses. No earlier cases or specific statutory provision governing the substantive test were relied on in deciding this issue.
members.conclusion: The finding that the premises had been sublet was upheld; the agreement’s agency form did not reflect the arrangement’s substance.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_dispute and third_party_exclusive_use and third_party_controlled_premises and tenant_lacked_actual_control and agreement_form_conflicted_with_actual_arrangement

predicates.tenant_eviction_dispute: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.third_party_exclusive_use: A third party was entitled to use the premises exclusively for its own business.
predicates.third_party_controlled_premises: The third party or its employees exercised actual control over access to or use of the premises.
predicates.tenant_lacked_actual_control: The tenant did not in practice retain control over the premises.
predicates.agreement_form_conflicted_with_actual_ar: The agreement’s stated agency terms conflicted with the arrangement shown by its other terms, the evidence, and the parties’ conduct.

members.legal_issue: A property owner is not estopped from denying a claimant’s title merely because rent receipts indicate payment to the owner when the owner’s knowledge and consent are not proved.
material_facts: Rent receipts indicated that the appellant had paid rents to the owner.
There was no evidence that the rents were collected with the owner’s knowledge and consent, and the receipts were not put to the owner or her husband at trial.
The owner’s case was that rent collectors had collected the rents without accounting to her or handing them over.
members.legal_principle: The court rejected estoppel because there was no evidence that rent was collected from the claimant with the owner’s knowledge and consent. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish estoppel against the owner.

predicates.estoppel_defense_in_property_dispute: A claimant in a property dispute argues that the owner is estopped from denying the claimant’s title.
predicates.rent_receipts_indicate_payment_to_owner: Receipts indicate that the claimant paid rent to the owner.
predicates.owner_knowledge_and_consent_not_proved: The evidence does not establish that the owner knew of and consented to the rent collection.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s permission for subletting is not established merely by the landlord’s receipt of rent after the subletting when the landlord’s clear knowledge of the sublease is not proved.
material_facts: The tenant sublet two shops to another person.
The tenant did not plead that the landlord had permitted the subletting, and no issue on permission was framed.
The landlord received rent after the subletting, but there was no proof that the landlord then had clear knowledge of the sublease.
members.legal_principle: Permission cannot be inferred merely from a landlord’s receipt of rent after subletting unless the landlord’s clear knowledge of the sublease is proved. The Court also treated the absence of a pleading and an issue on permission as a reason the lower courts erred in making that finding. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: The lower courts erred in finding that the subletting was permitted; receipt of rent alone did not establish permission without proof of the landlord’s clear knowledge of the sublease.

rule.if: rent_control_ejectment_case and subletting_disputed and consent_not_pleaded and rent_received_without_proven_knowledge

predicates.rent_control_ejectment_case: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.subletting_disputed: The parties dispute whether the tenant sublet the premises or whether the subletting was permitted.
predicates.consent_not_pleaded: The tenant did not plead that the landlord permitted the subletting.
predicates.rent_received_without_proven_knowledge: The landlord received rent after the subletting, but clear knowledge of the sublease was not proved.

members.legal_issue: Knowledge that another person occupies premises does not, without evidence that the person occupies as a subtenant, establish a landlord’s acquiescence in the subletting.
material_facts: The occupant had initially worked in the premises in connection with the tenant’s activities and had an arrangement under which office accommodation was provided by the tenant.
After the tenant moved to other premises, the occupant remained and conducted business there, including work for the tenant, and later used the premises solely for the occupant’s own purposes.
The evidence showed that the landlord knew the occupant was present, but did not establish that the landlord knew the occupant was there as a subtenant.
The landlord did not accept rent after the occupant began using the premises solely for the occupant’s own purposes.
members.legal_principle: Acquiescence is a legal inference from the facts, not an inference that necessarily follows from knowledge that someone is in possession: Lala Beni Ram v. Kundan Lal. Under section 35 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, the High Court may interfere in revision where an acquiescence finding has no evidence to support it; this is consistent with Pooran Chand v. Motilal and the distinction drawn in Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Choudhary.
members.conclusion: The appellate finding of acquiescence was unsupported by evidence, and the occupant had not established the landlord’s acquiescence in the subletting.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and landlord_knew_occupant_was_present and (occupant_used_premises_for_tenant_work or landlord_lacked_evidence_of_knowledge_of_subtenancy) and landlord_received_no_rent_after_occupant_used_premises_independently

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord sought eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the ground of subletting.
predicates.landlord_knew_occupant_was_present: The landlord knew that a person other than the tenant was occupying the premises.
predicates.occupant_used_premises_for_tenant_work: The occupant used the premises for work connected with the tenant’s activities.
predicates.landlord_lacked_evidence_of_knowledge_of: The evidence did not show that the landlord knew the occupant was in possession as a subtenant.
predicates.landlord_received_no_rent_after_occupant: The landlord did not accept rent after the occupant began using the premises solely for the occupant’s own purposes.

members.legal_issue: Subletting may be established by inferring monetary consideration from exclusive possession and the tenant’s failure to provide an acceptable explanation, without direct proof of payment.
material_facts: The lease document stated that the tenant took the premises for his own business and undertook not to part with possession or permit another person to occupy them.
The tenant’s son was found in exclusive possession, conducting an independent business and living separately from the tenant.
The tenant’s explanation that he had taken the premises for his son was rejected.
There was no direct evidence of payment or a promise of payment by the son to the tenant.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Control Act, the landlord bears the burden of proving subletting. Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh and Shama Prashant Raje v. Ganpatrao state that parting with possession and monetary consideration are the two ingredients. Bharat Sales Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India explains that the clandestine nature of subletting can make direct proof of an agreement or payment difficult, and that payment may be inferred from proved facts, including exclusive possession. Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s S. Chokesiri and Co. permits an inference of monetary consideration from exclusive possession and an unacceptable explanation, while Kala v. Madho Parshad Vaidya states that, once parting with possession is established, the evidential onus shifts to the tenant to explain the possession. Direct proof of monetary consideration is not a sine qua non.
members.conclusion: The finding of subletting was lawful because the tenant had parted with possession and the son’s exclusive possession, together with the rejected explanation, permitted an inference of monetary consideration despite the absence of direct proof of payment.

rule.if: eviction_case_based_on_subletting and tenant_parted_possession and occupant_exclusive_possession and tenant_explanation_rejected

predicates.eviction_case_based_on_subletting: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.tenant_parted_possession: The tenant gave up possession of the premises, wholly or in part, to another person.
predicates.occupant_exclusive_possession: Another person was found in exclusive possession of the premises or the relevant part.
predicates.tenant_explanation_rejected: The tenant’s explanation for the other person’s possession was not accepted.

members.legal_issue: Direct proof of monetary consideration is not invariably required to establish subletting when a tenant has given another person exclusive possession of the premises.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of subletting.
The Rent Controller and the Rent Control Appellate Tribunal found that the tenant had sublet the premises, and the High Court did not interfere with that finding.
The tenant challenged the finding on the ground that there was no positive finding or direct proof that the alleged sub-tenants paid consideration.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, subletting involves the tenant giving up possession of the premises, wholly or in part, and putting another person in exclusive possession. Although payment of rent or monetary consideration is an essential element and may be paid, promised, or provided in cash or kind, it need not invariably be proved by affirmative direct evidence because such arrangements may be clandestine. A court may infer consideration from the facts proved, including exclusive possession. The Court relied on Rajbir Kaur v. S. Chokesiri & Co. (1989) 1 SCC 19 and distinguished Delhi Stationers & Printers v. Rajendra Kumar (1990) 2 SCC 331, Jagan Nath v. Chander Bhan (1988) 3 SCC 57, Smt. Krishnavati v. Hans Raj (1974) 1 SCC 289, Gopal Saran v. Satyanarayana (1989) 3 SCC 56, and United Bank of India v. Cooks and Kelvey Properties (P) Ltd. (1994) 5 SCC 9. United Bank did not establish that direct proof of consideration is required in every case; its result rested on facts showing retained control and constructive possession.
members.conclusion: The Court held that consideration may be inferred from proved facts, including delivery of exclusive possession, and dismissed the challenge to the concurrent finding of subletting.

rule.if: challenge_to_eviction_for_subletting and tenant_parted_with_possession and another_person_in_exclusive_possession and direct_consideration_proof_absent and lower_courts_found_subletting

predicates.challenge_to_eviction_for_subletting: The proceeding challenges an eviction decision made on the ground that the tenant sublet the premises.
predicates.tenant_parted_with_possession: The tenant gave up possession of all or part of the premises to another person.
predicates.another_person_in_exclusive_possession: A person other than the tenant was in exclusive possession of the premises or part of them.
predicates.direct_consideration_proof_absent: The landlord did not establish payment of consideration through direct affirmative evidence.
predicates.lower_courts_found_subletting: The lower courts found that the tenant had sublet the premises.

members.legal_issue: Subletting requires a transfer of the right to enjoy the premises for consideration, and exclusive occupation alone does not establish it when the tenant retains legal control and no consideration is paid.
material_facts: The tenant permitted an employees’ trade union to occupy the premises exclusively for union activities.
The tenant received no monetary consideration from the union.
The tenant retained the right to require the union to vacate, maintained the premises at its own expense, and paid the electricity charges for the union’s use.
The union undertook to vacate when required, and its membership was confined to the tenant’s employees.
The landlord relied on the union’s exclusive occupation to establish subletting.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, read with Sections 14 and 13(3), and the definition of a lease in Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, subletting entails a transfer of the right to enjoy the premises for consideration. Rajbir Kaur v. S. Chokesiri and Co. explains that consideration may be inferred from exclusive possession and the circumstances, but that inference may be rebutted. Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakraborty and Jagan Nath v. Chander Bhan recognize exclusive possession and consideration as essential ingredients. Gopal Saran v. Satyanarayana and Delhi Stationers and Printers v. Rajendra Kumar establish that occupation alone is insufficient and that parting with legal possession involves a right to include and exclude others. Bhairab Chandra Nandan v. Ranadhir Chandra Dutta was also considered.
members.conclusion: Subletting was not established because the tenant retained legal control and the union did not receive a transfer of the right to enjoy the premises for consideration. The appeal was allowed and the eviction decree on that ground was set aside.

rule.if: tenancy_eviction_proceeding and third_party_has_exclusive_occupation and tenant_retains_legal_control and no_consideration_for_occupation

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought to recover possession from a tenant on the basis of alleged subletting.
predicates.third_party_has_exclusive_occupation: A person other than the tenant occupies the premises exclusively.
predicates.tenant_retains_legal_control: The tenant retains control over the occupation, including the ability to require the occupant to leave.
predicates.no_consideration_for_occupation: The occupant gives the tenant no money or other consideration for occupying the premises.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s entry into a partnership with another person does not, by itself, establish that the tenant sublet the premises or parted with possession.
material_facts: The deceased tenant and another person had entered into a partnership concerning the business carried on at the premises.
After the tenant died, the tenant’s widow, acting for herself and the minor child, entered into another partnership with the other person.
The landlord alleged subletting, but the courts below had not assessed that allegation on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(2)(ii)(a) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, transferring rights under a lease or subletting without the landlord’s written consent may constitute a ground for eviction. A partnership may be genuine, with the tenant retaining use and control, or may disguise a transfer of possession or control for consideration. The court must examine the actual transaction rather than infer subletting merely from the partnership deed.
members.conclusion: The existence of a partnership does not necessarily establish subletting or parting with possession. If the tenant remains actively associated with the business and retains use and control of the premises, the partnership alone may not amount to parting with possession; the real nature of the arrangement must be assessed where control or use has been transferred under cover of a partnership.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on an allegation of subletting or transfer of tenancy rights.
predicates.tenant_entered_partnership: The tenant entered into a partnership with another person concerning business at the rented premises.
predicates.tenant_retained_use_and_control: The tenant remained actively associated with the business and retained use and control of the rented premises.

members.legal_issue: A tenant's participation with family members in a partnership operating the existing business in the rented premises does not establish unlawful subletting without proof that the tenant parted with legal possession or the right to enjoy the premises.
material_facts: The premises had been rented for a business that continued to operate there after the business was converted from a sole proprietorship to a partnership.
The tenant joined the partnership with family members, including brothers, a brother's wife, and a cousin.
The tenant's family was joint, depended on the business for its livelihood, and included sixteen members.
There was no evidence that the tenant withdrew from the business, that the partners alone carried it on, or that the partners had exclusive possession of the premises.
There was no evidence that the partnership was a device concealing a transfer of possession or the right to use the premises.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(f) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 covers unlawful subletting of all or part of the premises and assignment or transfer of the tenant's interest in another manner. Under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease entails a transfer of the right to enjoy property, and parting with that right is essential to a sub-lease. The landlord bears the burden of proving subletting; prima facie proof that another occupant has exclusive possession for valuable consideration may discharge that burden and call for rebuttal. A change in the constitution of a partnership, or the tenant's entry into partnership to conduct business on the premises, does not alone establish subletting while the tenant retains legal possession. The court may look past a partnership arrangement if it conceals a transfer of possession or the right to use the premises. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, Krishnawati v. Hans Raj, Murlidhar v. Chuni Lal, Helper Girdharbhai v. Saiyed Mohmad Mirasaheb Kadri, and Parvinder Singh v. Renu Gautam.
members.conclusion: The landlord did not establish unlawful subletting under Section 21(1)(f) of the former Act; the eviction ground was not made out, and the eviction proceedings were dismissed.

rule.if: eviction_claim_based_on_unlawful_subletting and partnership_operates_in_tenanted_premises and tenant_actively_participates_in_business and tenant_retains_legal_possession and no_evidence_of_partners_exclusive_possession_or_concealed_transfer

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_unlawful_sublett: The landlord sought eviction on the basis that the tenant had unlawfully sublet or transferred an interest in the premises.
predicates.partnership_operates_in_tenanted_premise: A partnership conducted business in the premises that had been rented to the tenant.
predicates.tenant_actively_participates_in_business: The tenant remained associated with the partnership's business activity in the premises.
predicates.tenant_retains_legal_possession: The tenant retained legal possession or control of the premises rather than parting with the right to enjoy them.
predicates.no_evidence_of_partners_exclusive_posses: There was no evidence that the partners had exclusive possession or that the partnership concealed a transfer of possession or the right to use the premises.

members.legal_issue: A requirement to give notice before an occupant must vacate, or the occupant’s exclusive use of a stall, does not by itself establish a lease.
material_facts: The agreements required notice before a stall-holder could be required to vacate, including 30 days’ notice when the landlord required the stall.
Each stall-holder had exclusive use of the stall during market hours, but could not use it at will, remain there overnight, or enter after the market closed.
The stall-holders’ use was subject to the owners’ continuing responsibilities for the market.
members.legal_principle: The decisive consideration remains the parties’ intention. A contractual licence may require notice before termination or vacation, and section 62(c) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 recognises that a licence may be revoked when a specified condition is fulfilled. Exclusive possession is not conclusive of a tenancy, though it is an important consideration; when coupled with an interest in the property it supports construing the arrangement as a lease. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, Errington v. Errington and Woods, Cobb v. Lane, Close v. Theatrical Properties Ltd. and Westby & Co. Ltd., and Smith & Son v. The Assessment Committee for the Parish of Lambeth.
members.conclusion: Neither the notice requirement nor exclusive use alone established a lease; exclusive possession would point to a lease if coupled with an interest in the property.

predicates.stall_occupation_classification_dispute: The parties dispute whether an arrangement for occupying a stall gives the occupant a lease or only a licence.
predicates.notice_required_before_vacating: The arrangement requires notice before the occupant can be required to vacate.
predicates.exclusive_use_of_stall: The occupant has exclusive use of the stall, whether or not that use is restricted in time or subject to the owners’ control.

members.legal_issue: Exclusive possession alone does not establish that the occupant is a tenant.
material_facts: An interim injunction order in an earlier suit treated exclusive possession as giving rise to a presumption of tenancy.
That order expressed only a prima facie view, and the court in the present proceeding found that the interim order did not decide the tenancy question on evidence.
The rent-control proceeding relied on by the trial court had also not decided whether the claimant was a tenant.
members.legal_principle: The court held that exclusive possession by itself does not give rise to a presumption of tenancy. A prima facie observation in an interim injunction order is not a final determination of tenancy, and an order restoring electricity that does not decide tenancy cannot be treated as such a determination.
members.conclusion: The trial court erred in treating exclusive possession alone, or the earlier interim order, as establishing tenancy.

predicates.tenancy_status_dispute: A court is asked to determine whether an occupant’s possession is based on a tenancy.
predicates.exclusive_possession_is_the_only_basis_f: The asserted tenancy rests only on the occupant’s exclusive possession, without other proof establishing the tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A recital that an occupant is in possession of property does not, without independent evidence, establish that the occupant is a tenant.
material_facts: The sale deed stated that the defendant was in possession of the shop but did not state that he occupied it as a tenant.
The defendant produced no rent receipts or lease deed and did not examine the alleged landlord to prove that a tenancy had been created.
The defendant’s pleaded case was adverse possession, not tenancy, but the High Court inferred tenancy from the sale deed’s recital of possession.
members.legal_principle: A party claiming tenancy must prove the creation of the tenancy with evidence; a document that merely recites possession does not confer tenant status. The judgment cites no particular provision or earlier case for this evidentiary principle.
members.conclusion: The sale deed’s recital of possession did not establish tenancy, and the High Court’s finding that the defendant was a tenant was unsupported by evidence.

predicates.civil_possession_case: The proceeding is a civil dispute seeking possession of property in which the occupant’s status is material.
predicates.conveyance_recites_only_occupant_possess: A conveyance states that the occupant possesses the property but does not state that the occupant is a tenant.
predicates.no_independent_tenancy_evidence: The party asserting tenancy presents no independent evidence of its creation, such as rental documents or testimony from the alleged landlord.

members.legal_issue: A recital that vacant possession was given does not necessarily establish that a property was physically vacant, and evidence may explain what possession the recital conveyed.
material_facts: A registered document relied on by the tenant recited that vacant possession of another house had been given.
The landlord disputed that the house had been physically vacant, and oral evidence indicated otherwise.
The appellate authority accepted evidence that the house was not physically vacant.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that language in a document of this kind could refer to the legal right of possession without establishing actual physical vacant possession. It relied on Lachhman Das v. Rent Control and Eviction Officer for the permissibility of evidence explaining the recital.
members.conclusion: The recital could refer to transfer of the legal right to possession rather than actual physical possession, and oral evidence was admissible to explain it.

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction from residential premises and the landlord’s availability of another house.

members.legal_issue: A registering authority cannot serve as a statutory attesting witness to prove a will when the attesting witnesses do not support its execution.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether a will disposing of property was validly proved.
Neither of the two attesting witnesses supported the will’s execution.
The trial court relied on the registering authority’s statement to find that the will had been proved.
The lower appellate court and the High Court found that the Registrar could not be a statutory attesting witness.
members.legal_principle: A Registrar cannot be treated as a statutory attesting witness to establish due execution of a will. The Court relied on M. L. Abdul Jabhar Sahib v. H. V. Venkata Sastri & Sons and Beni Chand (since dead) now by Lrs. v. Smt. Kamla Kunwar; the judgment does not identify specific statutory provisions.
members.conclusion: The finding that the will had not been duly proved was correct, and the appeal concerning the agricultural property was dismissed.

predicates.will_validity_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether a will was validly proved.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_do_not_support_execu: The witnesses who attested the will do not support its execution.
predicates.proof_depends_on_registering_authority_a: A party relies on the registering authority as an attesting witness to prove the will.

members.legal_issue: A registering officer’s statutory acts do not by themselves make the officer an attesting witness to a will.
material_facts: The registering officer recorded an admission of execution and performed registration duties.
The officer’s signature was made in the course of those duties, and the evidence did not establish that the officer intended to attest the will.
The officer did not personally know the testatrix, and the Court found the officer’s evidence insufficient to prove execution or attestation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 52 and 58 of the Registration Act, 1908 set out duties and endorsements involved in registration. A signature made in performance of a statutory duty does not itself constitute attestation under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925; attestation requires an intention to attest (animus attestandi). The Court relied on Dharam Singh v. Aso and referred to M.L. Abdul Jabhar Sahib v. H.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons and Seth Beni Chand v. Kamla Kunwar.
members.conclusion: The registering officer was not an attesting witness, and the registration evidence did not prove due execution or attestation of the will.

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought recognition of a will in a proceeding concerning the will.
predicates.registering_officer_signed_only_in_offic: The registering officer signed or made an endorsement while carrying out the officer’s statutory registration duties.
predicates.no_intention_to_attest_proved: The evidence did not establish that the registering officer signed with the intention of witnessing and attesting execution.
predicates.registration_does_not_prove_attestation: The registration act or endorsement does not, by itself, establish attestation of the will.

members.legal_issue: A person’s signature on a will does not amount to attestation merely because the person drafted the document or performed a statutory registration function.
material_facts: The will bore the signature of an advocate whom the trial court regarded as having signed as draftsman and counsel, rather than as an attesting witness.
The registration official testified about the will’s registration, but the evidence did not establish that the official signed with the intention of attesting the testator’s signature.
The High Court relied in part on the advocate’s signature and the registration process in treating the will as attested by two witnesses.
members.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act requires attestation by two or more witnesses. Attestation requires animus attestandi: the witness must sign intending to attest that the executant signed or acknowledged the document. A registration officer’s statutory acts under Sections 52 and 58 of the Registration Act, 1908, do not by themselves make the officer an attesting witness; likewise, a draftsman or advocate is not an attesting witness merely by signing the document. The Court relied on Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda, Dharam Singh v. Aso, and Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini.
members.conclusion: Attestation requires the person to sign with the intention of witnessing the testator’s signature or acknowledgment; a signature made only in the course of drafting or performing a registration duty does not by itself satisfy that requirement.

predicates.will_execution_disputed: A party disputes whether a will was executed and attested as required.
predicates.signature_made_only_for_drafting_or_regi: A person signed the document only while drafting it or performing a registration-related duty.
predicates.no_intention_to_attest: The person did not sign intending to witness the testator’s signature or acknowledgment.

members.legal_issue: A registered attested document other than a will need not be proved through an attesting witness when its execution is not specifically denied, and allegations of forgery or fabrication without adequate supporting evidence do not establish such a denial or prove forgery.
material_facts: The gift deed was registered and was required to be attested; the trial court found that the requirements for its execution had been met.

The plaintiffs' pleadings alleged forgery and fabrication and questioned the circumstances of the gift, but the Court found that they had not specifically denied execution in clear and categorical terms.
The plaintiffs did not provide cogent evidence of forgery, such as specimen signatures, a handwriting opinion, or a request for forensic examination.
The trial court did not find that the deed was forged, and the plaintiffs' challenge was based on allegations and surrounding circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act requires an attesting witness for a document required by law to be attested, but its proviso dispenses with that requirement for a registered document other than a will unless execution is specifically denied. A specific denial must be an unambiguous, categorical, and definite statement that the alleged executant did not execute the document. Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act requires a gift of this kind to be attested. The Court applied the principles in Kannan Nambiar v. Narayani Amma and Dashrath Prasad Bajooram v. Lallosingh, and distinguished Rosammal Issetheenammal Fernandez v. Joosa Mariyan Fernandez and K. Laxmanan v. Thekkayil Padmini, where execution had been specifically denied. It also relied on Order VI Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, requiring particulars of allegations such as fraud, and Order VIII Rule 3, requiring specific treatment of factual allegations; it referred to Badat and Co. v. East India Trading Co. The party alleging forgery bears the burden of proving it with cogent evidence.
members.conclusion: Execution was not specifically denied, and forgery was not proved; the donee was therefore not required to call an attesting witness to prove the registered gift deed.

predicates.civil_challenge_to_registered_attested_n: A party challenges a registered document, other than a will, that is required by law to be attested.
predicates.execution_not_categorically_denied: The challenging party does not make a clear and categorical statement that the purported executant did not execute the document.
predicates.forgery_not_proved_by_cogent_evidence: The party alleging forgery does not prove it through cogent supporting evidence.

members.legal_issue: A registered attested document other than a will cannot be admitted without proof by an attesting witness when its execution is specifically denied.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a gift deed treated as a registered document and required by law to be attested.
The pleadings alleged that the deed was brought into existence fraudulently, that the alleged executant was bedridden and unable to execute it, and that his signature had been forged.
The High Court inferred from witness testimony that execution had not been specifically denied, without adequately considering the pleadings.
Neither attesting witness was produced to prove execution of the deed.
The appeal challenged the High Court’s application of the exception to the requirement for attesting-witness proof.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, a document required by law to be attested cannot be used in evidence unless at least one available and capable attesting witness is called to prove execution. The proviso removes that requirement for a registered document other than a will only when execution is not specifically denied. Whether there is a specific denial must be decided clearly and specifically, with consideration of the pleadings; it cannot rest on a vague or negative inference from testimony alone. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The pleadings clearly and specifically denied execution, so the exception did not apply. Because no attesting witness was produced, execution of the deed was not proved; the deed failed and conferred no right over the property it covered.

predicates.appeal_challenges_document_admissibility: A party appealed a decision admitting or relying on a disputed document.
predicates.document_requires_attestation: The disputed document was of a kind that the law required to be attested.
predicates.registered_nonwill_document: The disputed document was registered and was not a will.
predicates.execution_specifically_denied_in_pleadin: A party’s pleadings specifically denied that the person named as executant had executed the document.
predicates.no_attesting_witness_examined: The party relying on the document did not call an attesting witness to prove its execution.

members.legal_issue: A registered, attested mortgage deed may be proved by a certified copy without calling an attesting witness when execution is not specifically denied.
material_facts: The plaintiff produced a certified copy of the registered mortgage deed and called on the defendant to produce the original, which the defendant did not do.
The defendant admitted in the written statement and in evidence that the mortgage deed had been executed, while contending that it was a sham transaction.
The deed was attested by two witnesses, but the plaintiff did not call an attesting witness.
members.legal_principle: Section 65(a) of the Evidence Act permits secondary evidence where the original is in the possession or control of the opposing party and is not produced after notice. Under Section 68 of the Evidence Act, an attesting witness ordinarily must be called to prove an attested document, but its proviso dispenses with that requirement for a registered document other than a will unless execution is specifically denied. Section 59 of the Transfer of Property Act requires a mortgage of this kind to be attested. The Court concluded that the certified copy was admissible and execution was not specifically denied.
members.conclusion: The mortgage was proved by the certified copy, and the plaintiff was not required to call an attesting witness because execution had not been specifically denied.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a will was not proved genuine should not be displaced when the reviewing court fails to give proper weight to the cumulative suspicious circumstances and evidentiary deficiencies identified by the fact-finding court.
material_facts: The testator’s will stated that he had been seriously ill, and he died eight days after the will was made, but satisfactory evidence about the illness and his mental capacity was not produced.
The will incorrectly stated that the testator had no sister and described the sole beneficiary as his real brother, while giving no reason for excluding the natural heir.
A scribe testified that the testator was literate and had written receipts, but the will bore only a thumb impression and no satisfactory explanation was given for not obtaining his signature.
The beneficiary’s son brought the writing book used for the will, the will was made outside the beneficiary’s residence, and the beneficiary gave contradictory accounts of whether he was present.
Only two of the five attesting witnesses were examined; those witnesses sought to deny the testator’s illness and departed from earlier statements made during mutation proceedings.
The first appellate court found the will not proved genuine; the High Court restored the trial court’s finding of due execution without adequately addressing the suspicious circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Applying the principles under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and the burden on a propounder to remove legitimate suspicion, the Court held that the cumulative circumstances required satisfactory evidence about the testator’s illness and capacity, an explanation for the thumb impression, and scrutiny of the beneficiary’s role and the witness evidence. The Court followed H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Rani Purnima Devi v. Kumar Khagendra Narayan Dev, and Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the first appellate court’s finding that the will was not proved to be genuine. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s judgment and restored the dismissal of the suit based on the will.

predicates.second_appeal_review: A High Court reviews a first appellate court’s decision in a second appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_found_will_unproved: The first appellate court finds that the propounder has not proved the will genuine.
predicates.high_court_disregarded_cumulative_suspic: The High Court restores a finding that the will was valid without giving sufficient weight to the combined suspicious circumstances identified by the first appellate court.
predicates.serious_illness_near_execution: The testator was described as seriously ill when making the will and died soon afterward, without satisfactory evidence about the illness or the testator’s mental capacity.
predicates.inaccurate_family_recitals: The will contains material inaccuracies about the testator’s family relationships or the beneficiary’s relationship to the testator.
predicates.literate_testator_used_thumbprint: Evidence indicates that the testator was literate, but the will bears a thumb impression rather than a signature and no satisfactory explanation is given.
predicates.beneficiary_involved_in_preparation: The sole beneficiary, or someone closely connected to the beneficiary, played a role in arranging or preparing the will.
predicates.beneficiary_gave_contradictory_accounts: The beneficiary gave conflicting accounts about being present when the will was executed.
predicates.incomplete_attesting_witness_evidence: The propounder examines only some of the attesting witnesses, despite circumstances making further witness evidence relevant.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_departed_from_prior_: Attesting witnesses give evidence inconsistent with their earlier accounts about circumstances surrounding execution of the will.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a later will was not duly proved is not disturbed in a further appeal when the propounder did not establish due execution and dispel suspicious circumstances and the finding is supported by the record without perversity or manifest error.
material_facts: The appellant relied on a later will to challenge the earlier will that had been upheld in separate proceedings.
The High Court found that the propounder of the later will had not proved due execution or dispelled suspicious circumstances.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court’s factual finding was supported by the record and disclosed no perversity or manifest error.
members.legal_principle: A will’s propounder must prove due execution and dispel suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution. A supported factual finding in a further appeal is not reopened absent perversity or manifest error.
members.conclusion: The later will could not be treated as duly proved, and the finding rejecting it was not disturbed.

predicates.further_appeal_from_will_finding: The proceeding is a further appeal challenging a court’s finding about whether a will was proved.
predicates.propounder_failed_to_prove_execution_or_: The person relying on the will failed to prove due execution or to dispel suspicious circumstances.
predicates.finding_supported_by_record_without_perv: The challenged finding is supported by the record and is not perverse or affected by manifest error.

members.legal_issue: A will’s due execution may be established by credible testimony from an attesting witness, and the witness’s evidence cannot be rejected solely on the circumstances relied on in this case.
material_facts: An attesting witness testified about the will’s due execution and the testator’s testamentary capacity.
The trial judge, who saw the witness testify, believed that evidence and found that the will had been duly executed and that the testator had a sound disposing mind.

The High Court rejected the witness’s evidence based on the will being unregistered, the disposition being considered unnatural, the absence of a temple during the testator’s lifetime, the witness’s professional and personal association with the executor’s family, and alleged family discord.

The Supreme Court found those circumstances insufficient to justify disbelieving the witness; it noted, among other things, that a will need not be registered, that the will provided for the daughter, and that evidence showed the family disputes had been composed.
members.legal_principle: In a probate case, due execution and testamentary capacity must be proved, and the credibility of an attesting witness is assessed on the evidence and surrounding circumstances. Non-registration of a will does not, by itself, support an inference against genuineness because the law does not require registration of a will. The circumstances identified by the High Court did not justify rejecting testimony accepted by the trial judge who had seen the witness. No earlier case was relied on for this evidentiary conclusion.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in rejecting the attesting witness’s evidence on the stated grounds; the appeal was allowed and probate was directed to issue.

rule.if: probate_appeal and attesting_witness_testified_to_execution and trial_judge_credited_attesting_witness and sound_disposing_mind_found and appellate_rejection_based_on_nonregistration_or_disposition_or_delayed_temple_or_association_or_family_discord

predicates.probate_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the grant or refusal of probate.
predicates.attesting_witness_testified_to_execution: A witness who attested the will testified about its execution.
predicates.trial_judge_credited_attesting_witness: The trial judge who observed the witness accepted the witness’s testimony.
predicates.sound_disposing_mind_found: The trial court found that the testator had a sound disposing mind when the will was executed.
predicates.appellate_rejection_based_on_nonregistra: The appellate court rejected the witness’s evidence on grounds such as non-registration, the character or timing of the disposition, the witness’s associations, or family discord.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a will was unproved cannot stand where an attesting witness formally proved execution and the circumstances relied on to discredit the will did not establish suspicion sufficient to overturn the trial court’s finding.
material_facts: The trial court found the will duly proved after relying on an attesting witness’s testimony.
The appellate court accepted that there was formal evidence of execution but reversed the trial court based on the will’s distribution and other asserted circumstances.
The Supreme Court found that the uneven distribution and the other circumstances relied on did not sustain the finding that the will was unnatural or unproved.
members.legal_principle: The judgment relied on the attesting witness’s formal evidence of execution and held that the identified circumstances did not justify rejecting the will. It cites no statutory provision or earlier case in reaching this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The finding that the will had not been proved was set aside, the trial court’s judgment was restored, and the appeal was allowed.

predicates.appeal_against_reversal_of_trial_court_w: An appeal challenges an appellate decision that reversed a trial court’s finding that a will was proved.
predicates.attesting_witness_formally_proved_execut: An attesting witness gave formal evidence that the testator and witnesses signed the will in each other’s presence.
predicates.relied_on_circumstances_do_not_establish: The circumstances relied on to reject the will do not establish suspicion sufficient to discredit its execution.

members.legal_issue: A will requiring attestation is not duly proved by the evidence of its scribe alone when the named attesting witnesses are not examined and the scribe signed only as its writer, without an established intention to attest.
material_facts: The dispute required proof of a will relied on to support a claim to property.
The will named two attesting witnesses, but neither was examined, and no attempt was made to summon either one.
The party did not establish that the attesting witnesses were unavailable after an honest and diligent search.
The scribe testified that he wrote the will and signed it as the writer; the will also described him as its writer.
Although the scribe testified about the execution, the document did not establish that he subscribed his signature with an intention to attest as a witness.
members.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act requires a will to be attested by two or more witnesses in the prescribed manner. Section 68 of the Evidence Act requires at least one available and capable attesting witness to be called to prove execution. Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act defines attestation and requires a witness to sign with animo attestandi, or an intention to attest. A scribe’s signature for the purpose of writing or identifying the document is not, without the required intention, an attesting signature. The Court relied on M.L. Abdul Jabhar Sahib v. H.V. Venkata Sastri & Sons (1969 (3) SCR 513), Girja Datt v. Gangotri Datt (AIR 1955 SC 346), and H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma (1959 Supp. (1) SCR 426).
members.conclusion: The scribe’s signature and evidence did not satisfy the statutory requirement of attestation or proof of the will; the will was not duly proved and could not have the claimed legal effect.

members.legal_issue: Signatures placed on a registration endorsement by persons identifying a testator do not, without evidence that they signed as attesting witnesses, prove due attestation of a will.
material_facts: The testator acknowledged execution of the will before a registrar.
Two persons who identified the testator signed beneath the registrar’s endorsement.
Neither identifier was called to testify about attesting the will, and the record did not establish that either signed in the capacity of an attesting witness.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, attestation requires the prescribed witnessing and signing acts. A signature on a registration endorsement cannot simply be presumed to have been made animo attestandi, or in the capacity of an attesting witness. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act requires an attesting witness to be called to prove due execution and attestation. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The identifiers’ signatures on the registration endorsement did not prove due attestation of the will.

predicates.will_attestation_proof_dispute: A party disputed whether a will had been duly attested.
predicates.identifiers_signed_a_registration_endors: People who identified the testator signed beneath an endorsement made during registration of the will.
predicates.no_evidence_shows_they_signed_as_attesti: The evidence did not establish that those people signed with the intention of attesting the will.
predicates.identifiers_were_not_called_to_testify: Those people were not called as witnesses to prove that they attested the will.

members.legal_issue: A will is not proved when the evidence does not establish its execution and attestation.
material_facts: The appeal challenged the finding that the will had not been proved.
The appellants relied only on one attesting witness to prove execution and attestation.
That witness was not present when the testatrix placed her thumb impression on the will and did not see the other attesting witness sign it.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the evidence established execution and attestation of the will. It relied on the testimony of the sole witness offered for that purpose, which did not establish that the other attesting witness signed the will. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The appellants failed to prove the execution and attestation of the will, so the will was not proved; it was unnecessary to decide separately whether it was genuine.

predicates.civil_appeal_challenges_will_proof: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which a party challenges a finding about proof of a will.
predicates.sole_attesting_witness_lacks_personal_kn: The only attesting witness relied on to prove the will was not present when the testator executed it.
predicates.witness_did_not_observe_other_attestor_s: The witness did not see the other attesting witness sign the will.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary instrument is not legally proved when the attesting witness examined fails to establish that the required witnesses attested it in the legally prescribed manner.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned applications for probate of competing wills, and the disputed will was required to be attested by two witnesses.

Only one of the two named attesting witnesses was examined. He testified that the testator signed in his presence, but did not establish that the other named witness had attested the will in the required manner; his account was inconsistent with the will’s recital that the testator signed before both witnesses and both then signed.
The will named the other attesting witness as executor, but it was produced from the custody of the witness who testified, and that custody was not explained.
The will’s author and typist were unknown. The propounders had previously asserted in other proceedings that the testator had left no will, and did not explain that assertion in the probate evidence.

The will left the entire property to the propounders, who were not Class I heirs, excluding the testator’s sister; the sister had lived near and cared for the testator, while the propounders lived elsewhere.
The Court found numerous suspicious circumstances on the face of the will and in the evidence, in addition to the failure to prove the statutory requirements for execution.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, an unprivileged will must be attested by two or more witnesses, each satisfying the prescribed witnessing and signing requirements. Section 68 of the Evidence Act permits proof by examining at least one attesting witness, but that witness must establish due execution, including the required attestation by both witnesses; if the witness examined does not do so, an available other attesting witness must be called to complete the proof. A testator’s signature alone does not prove due execution. The propounder must also satisfy the court that the will is ordinarily free from genuine suspicious circumstances and remove such circumstances. The Court applied Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda, Ramabai Padmakar Patil v. Rukminibai Vishnu Vekhande, Anil Kak v. Kumari Sharada Raje, and Babu Singh v. Ram Sahai; it also referred to Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act for the meaning of attestation.
members.conclusion: The will dated 18 June 1995 was not legally proved. The judgment granting probate of it could not stand, and the appeal was allowed.

predicates.probate_proceeding: A person sought probate of a testamentary instrument.
predicates.testamentary_instrument_requires_two_att: The testamentary instrument was subject to a requirement that two witnesses attest it in the prescribed manner.
predicates.only_one_attesting_witness_examined: The person seeking probate examined only one of the instrument’s attesting witnesses.
predicates.examined_witness_failed_to_prove_attesta: The attesting witness examined did not establish that both required witnesses attested the instrument in the prescribed manner.
predicates.will_not_legally_proved: The court ruled that the testamentary instrument had not been legally proved.

members.legal_issue: Other evidence cannot be used to prove a will under the fallback evidentiary rule when an available attesting witness has not been called and no attesting witness examined has denied or failed to recollect execution.
material_facts: The propounded will identified the claimant’s brother-in-law as an attesting witness, but he was not summoned or examined.
The claimant relied on the fact that the other alleged attesting witness, an advocate, had not been served and examined.
No attesting witness testified to denying or failing to recollect the will’s execution.
The High Court treated the will as proved through registration and other evidence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act and 68 and 71 of the Evidence Act require proof of a will through at least one attesting witness, if one is available and capable of giving evidence. Section 71 is a limited safeguard that applies when an attesting witness who has been called denies or cannot recollect execution; it does not excuse failure to call another available attesting witness. The Court relied on Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam, Jagdish Chand Sharma v. Narain Singh Saini, and Benga Behera v. Braja Kishore Nanda.
members.conclusion: The fallback rule for proving execution through other evidence was unavailable because the available attesting witness had not been examined and no examined attesting witness had denied or failed to recollect execution.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: A party seeks to establish a will in a dispute about its execution or validity.
predicates.available_attesting_witness_not_examined: The party relying on the will does not call an available attesting witness who can give evidence.
predicates.no_examined_attester_denied_or_forgot_ex: No attesting witness who was examined expressly denied execution or said that they could not recollect it.

members.legal_issue: The alternative proof permitted when an attesting witness denies or cannot recall execution is unavailable when the witness does neither.
material_facts: The scribe-attesting witness testified that the testatrix put her thumb impression only after he had signed the will.
He did not deny execution of the will or say that he could not recall it.
The witness’s account failed to prove the attestation required for execution of the will.
members.legal_principle: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 permits other evidence of execution when an attesting witness denies or does not recollect execution; it is a safeguard to the mandatory proof requirement in Section 68, not a general substitute when a witness fails to prove the required attestation. The Court applied Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam and considered Ittoop Varghese v. Poulose and Others.
members.conclusion: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act did not apply to permit proof of execution by other evidence on these facts.

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought recognition of a will in a proceeding concerning the will.
predicates.attesting_witness_neither_denied_nor_for: The attesting witness neither denied that the document was executed nor said that the witness could not recall its execution.
predicates.witness_failed_to_prove_attestation: The attesting witness’s evidence did not establish the legally required attestation.
predicates.alternative_proof_under_witness_failure_: The failure to prove attestation cannot be cured by relying on the special alternative proof available for denial or lack of recollection.

members.legal_issue: Other evidence may be used to prove a will when an attesting witness denies its execution or genuinely cannot recall it, but not merely when the witness’s evidence fails to prove execution and attestation.
material_facts: The propounder examined both attesting witnesses.
Neither witness denied that the instrument had been executed, nor did either fail to recollect the event of execution; their evidence was instead deficient in establishing execution and attestation.
The propounder sought to rely on the registering officer’s evidence as other evidence to establish the will.
members.legal_principle: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, permits other evidence if an attesting witness denies or does not recollect execution. It is a limited safeguard, not a substitute for Sections 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and 68 of the Evidence Act, and cannot be used merely because the witness’s evidence is inadequate.
