The Court relied on Janki Narayan Bhoir v. Narayan Namdeo Kadam and distinguished M. B. Ramesh v. K. M. Veeraje Urs, where the witness’s evidence indicated a genuine failure to recollect a fact.
members.conclusion: The statutory route for proving execution through other evidence was unavailable, and the registering officer’s evidence could not cure the deficiencies in the attesting evidence.

rule.if: testamentary_proceeding and attesting_witnesses_examined and testimony_fails_to_prove_execution and witnesses_neither_deny_nor_forget_execution

predicates.testamentary_proceeding: A person seeks a grant of administration or other testamentary relief on the basis of an instrument said to be a will.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_examined: One or more available attesting witnesses are called to give evidence about the instrument.
predicates.testimony_fails_to_prove_execution: The testimony of the attesting witnesses does not establish the execution and attestation required for the instrument.
predicates.witnesses_neither_deny_nor_forget_execut: The witnesses neither deny the execution of the instrument nor genuinely fail to remember that event.

members.legal_issue: The fallback of proving execution through other evidence does not excuse failure to examine another available attesting witness when the witness called does not prove due execution.
material_facts: The sole attesting witness examined did not prove that the other attesting witness had attested the will.
The other attesting witness was available but was not called.
The party seeking to prove the will relied on testimony from other witnesses, including the scribe.
members.legal_principle: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, is a safeguard that permits other evidence when an attesting witness who has been called denies or does not recollect execution and the party is otherwise unable to prove it through the attesting witnesses. It does not relieve a party of the requirements of Section 68 when another attesting witness is available but has not been called. The Court approved the approach in Vishnu Ramkrishna v. Nathu Vithal (AIR 1949 Bom. 266) and held the view in Mt. Manki Kaur v. Hansraj Singh (AIR 1938 Pat. 301) on Section 71 to be incorrect.
members.conclusion: Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act did not permit the party to substitute other evidence for the unexamined, available attesting witness in these circumstances.

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and attesting_witness_called and witness_failed_to_prove_due_execution and other_attesting_witness_available and other_attesting_witness_not_examined

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought to establish a will in court.
predicates.attesting_witness_called: The party seeking to prove the will called an attesting witness to testify.
predicates.witness_failed_to_prove_due_execution: The witness called did not establish execution of the will with the required attestations.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_available: Another attesting witness was alive and capable of being called to give evidence.
predicates.other_attesting_witness_not_examined: The party seeking to prove the will did not examine the other available attesting witness.

members.legal_issue: A will requiring attestation is not proved unless the evidence establishes due attestation and execution in accordance with the applicable legal requirements.
material_facts: The defendants relied on a will allegedly executed by the deceased in favour of his grandson.
The witnesses called about the will did not testify that the deceased signed it in their presence or otherwise establish the required attestation.
One witness discussed the will in connection with the adoption, but did not say that the deceased signed the will in his presence.
The High Court inferred due execution from the evidence about the adoption, whereas the trial court and first appellate court found that the will had not been proved.
members.legal_principle: Section 68 of the Evidence Act requires at least one attesting witness to be called to prove a document required by law to be attested, where such a witness is alive, subject to the court’s process, and capable of giving evidence. Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 sets out the requirements for attestation of an unprivileged will, and Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act defines attestation. Attestation and execution are distinct acts; execution is not proved without proof of due attestation, and a court cannot assume a requirement that the evidence does not establish.
members.conclusion: The will was not proved in accordance with law; the High Court could not assume the required execution and attestation from the evidence about the adoption.

predicates.will_claim: A party relies on an alleged will to establish rights in property.
predicates.will_requires_attestation: The alleged will is a document that must be attested by law.
predicates.witnesses_failed_to_prove_attestation: The witnesses’ evidence does not establish that the testator signed or acknowledged the will in the required manner and that the witnesses attested it.

members.legal_issue: A will is not proved unless its execution is established in accordance with the statutory requirements for testamentary documents.
material_facts: The trial court accepted wills propounded in support of the appellant’s claimed shares, but the High Court found their execution unproved.

The evidence concerning the first will included contradictions between the witnesses and scribe; one attesting witness was related to the appellant, and the scribe was connected to the appellant’s family.
The evidence concerning another will led the High Court to find that its execution had been manoeuvred and was not acceptable.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s factual findings on the wills.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, the propounder must call at least one attesting witness to prove execution. The propounder must establish the testator’s signature, testamentary capacity, sound and disposing state of mind, understanding of the disposition, and free will; suspicious circumstances must be explained to the court’s satisfaction. The judgment also refers to the provisions of the Indian Succession Act and applies Savithri v. Karthyayani Amma, (2007) 11 SCC 621, for these requirements.
members.conclusion: The wills were not proved, and the High Court’s findings rejecting them were left undisturbed.

predicates.will_proof_dispute: The proceeding required the court to decide whether a will had been proved.
predicates.will_propounded: A party relied on a will to support a claimed entitlement to property.
predicates.attesting_witness_not_reliably_establish: The evidence of the attesting witness or other execution evidence did not reliably establish that the will was executed as alleged.

members.legal_issue: Registration of a will or codicil does not replace proof of its execution and attestation where the law requires attestation.
material_facts: The will and the disputed codicil were registered.
The will’s execution and attestation were admitted, but the execution and attestation of the codicil were disputed.
No attesting witness to the codicil was examined in court.
members.legal_principle: Section 68 of the Evidence Act, 1872, requires a document that must be attested to be proved through at least one available attesting witness; a will is excluded from the registration-based dispensation described in the proviso to that section. Sections 52, 58, 59 and 60 of the Registration Act, 1908, govern the registrar’s endorsements and certification. Section 114, illustration (e), of the Evidence Act permits a presumption that official acts were regularly performed, but the registration endorsements concern registration and do not establish attestation. Kunwar Surendra Bahadur Singh v. Thakur Behari Singh, AIR 1989 PC 117, is relied on for the limited relevance of those endorsements.
members.conclusion: Registration and the registrar’s endorsements did not dispense with the need to prove the codicil’s execution and attestation in the manner required by law.

predicates.registered_testamentary_instrument_proof: The proceeding concerns proof of a registered will or codicil.
predicates.instrument_requires_attestation: The instrument is one that the law requires to be attested.

members.legal_issue: A contested will is duly proved only when the statutory requirements for its execution and proof are established; registration alone does not establish due execution.
material_facts: The will was contested, and the two attesting witnesses gave contradictory accounts about whether the testator signed the will and whether they signed it in the testator’s presence.
The registrar’s endorsement established that the witnesses signed the endorsement in the testator’s presence, but did not establish the attestation required for due execution of the will.
The will was registered, but the trial court found due execution unproved and the first appellate court affirmed that finding.
members.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires attestation by at least two witnesses in the manner it specifies. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one available and capable attesting witness must be called to prove execution of a document required by law to be attested. The proviso to Section 68 concerning registered documents does not apply to wills. The court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: Due execution of the will was not proved; its registration did not cure the failure of proof.

predicates.contested_will_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a dispute over whether a will was duly executed.
predicates.attesting_witnesses_contradict_each_othe: The attesting witnesses give conflicting accounts about the testator’s signing or the witnesses’ attestation in the testator’s presence.
predicates.required_attestation_unproved: The evidence does not establish that the testator and witnesses completed the required acts of signing or acknowledgment and attestation.
predicates.registrar_endorsement_proves_only_endors: The registration-related endorsement establishes only that witnesses signed the endorsement in the testator’s presence, not that the will was duly attested.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for statutes specifically listed in the constitutional schedule operates independently of the protection for laws concerning acquisition of estates.
material_facts: The State relied on decisions concerning laws included in the constitutional schedule to argue that constitutional protection for scheduled laws supported its interpretation of the separate protection for estate-acquisition laws.

The court held that the provision protecting scheduled laws gives those specified statutes protection from attacks based on Part III even when they do not fall within the separate estate-acquisition protection.
members.legal_principle: The court construed Articles 31-A and 31-B together, relying on Article 31-B's express protection for the statutes specified in the Ninth Schedule, including protection notwithstanding court judgments. The words 'without prejudice to the generality' indicate that the specified statutes may have immunity even if they do not attract Article 31-A. The court distinguished Dhiruba Devisingh Gohil v. State of Bombay and State of U.P. v. H. H. Maharaja Brijendra Singh on this basis.
members.conclusion: Article 31-B is an independent constitutional device that protects the specified statutes from attacks on the ground that they infringe Part III; it is not governed by Article 31-A or merely illustrative of its scope.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The case challenges a statute on the ground that it violates constitutional rights in Part III.
predicates.statute_is_specifically_listed_in_consti: The statute challenged is one specifically listed in the constitutional schedule that provides it protection.

members.legal_issue: Protection of a scheduled statute under article 31-B is independent of article 31-A and can apply to scheduled property even if it is not an estate within article 31-A’s definition.
material_facts: The challenged Act was specified in the Ninth Schedule.
Some acquired villages were conceded not to fall within the relevant land-tenure definition of an estate.
The petitioners argued that article 31-B was merely illustrative of, and limited by, article 31-A.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed articles 31-A and 31-B as independent protections and relied on King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee, holding that the analogy to the phrase “without prejudice to the generality” did not make article 31-B merely illustrative. Article 31-B specifically protected the scheduled Acts.
members.conclusion: Article 31-B operated independently of article 31-A, and the challenged Act could not be questioned under Part III in respect of the villages outside article 31-A’s estate definition.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_scheduled_la: A person challenged a law listed for constitutional protection.
predicates.law_is_listed_for_constitutional_protect: The challenged law is expressly included in the constitutional list of protected laws.
predicates.acquired_property_falls_outside_estate_d: The acquired property does not fall within the applicable definition of an estate.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional provision specifically validating listed laws applies to a listed law even if the property acquired by that law does not fall within the separate constitutional definition of an estate.
material_facts: The Madhya Pradesh acquisition law was specifically listed among the laws protected by the constitutional amendment.
Some acquired malguzari lands were conceded not to be estates under the relevant local land-tenure law.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-B independently validates the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule against challenges based on Part III; its application is not restricted to laws concerning estates under article 31-A. The opening words of article 31-B preserve the generality of article 31-A rather than narrowing the specific validation in article 31-B.
members.conclusion: The specific validation of the listed law applied notwithstanding that the particular lands were not estates.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.law_specifically_listed_for_constitution: The law was specifically named in a constitutional schedule validating specified laws.
predicates.acquired_property_not_an_estate: The particular property acquired does not qualify as an estate under the applicable local land-tenure law.

members.legal_issue: A law specifically protected by the constitutional schedule may remain valid as applied to land that does not fall within the constitutional definition of an estate.
material_facts: The law was specified in the Ninth Schedule.
Some acquired malguzari villages were accepted as falling outside the relevant statutory definition of an estate.
The petitioners argued that the constitutional protection for estates therefore did not protect acquisition of those villages.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-B is an independent provision and is not merely illustrative of or limited by article 31-A, notwithstanding its opening words, “without prejudice to the generality” of article 31-A. The Court relied on King Emperor v. Sibnath Banerjee for the distinction between an independent provision and one that merely illustrates another provision, and held that article 31(4) was not confined to estates.
members.conclusion: Article 31-B independently validated the Act in respect of the malguzari villages, and article 31(4) also saved the law in its entirety.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges the application of a law on constitutional grounds.
predicates.law_listed_for_constitutional_protection: The challenged law is specifically included among laws receiving constitutional protection.
predicates.acquired_land_outside_estate_definition: The acquired land does not fall within the relevant constitutional definition of an estate.

members.legal_issue: The sequence of land-revenue measures and acquisition legislation did not establish that the acquisition law was a fraud on the Constitution.
material_facts: The legislature had enacted earlier measures that increased land revenue or withdrew exemptions before enacting the acquisition law.
The earlier measures were within the Government’s power, and most preceded the Constitution’s commencement.
The Court found no evidence that the measures were enacted with a fraudulent design to defeat constitutional compensation requirements.
The acquisition law itself provided for positive compensation.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on its reasoning in the Bihar case and held that the sequence of legislation could have been undertaken in good faith; the mere existence of revenue changes and acquisition legislation did not prove a fraudulent design.
members.conclusion: The fraud-on-the-Constitution objection was rejected.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A person challenged a law that provides for acquisition of land rights.
predicates.prior_revenue_measures_preceded_acquisit: The government changed land-revenue obligations before enacting the acquisition law.
predicates.no_evidence_of_fraudulent_design: The evidence did not establish that the measures were devised to defeat constitutional guarantees.

members.legal_issue: A law is not a fraud on the Constitution merely because earlier legislation is alleged to have reduced the value or income of property later acquired.
material_facts: The appellants pointed to several earlier enactments and alleged that they formed a scheme to deprive landowners of compensation.
The cited enactments predated the Constitution and were not shown to be connected with acquisition under the challenged Act.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the allegation as founded on a confusion of thought: the earlier enactments were enacted before the Constitution and were not shown to have any connection with acquisition of the properties under the challenged statute. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.
members.conclusion: The fraud-on-the-Constitution contention failed because the earlier enactments had no demonstrated connection with the acquisition law.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_law_as_constitu: A party alleges that an acquisition law is a fraud on the Constitution.
predicates.alleged_prior_measures_predate_constitut: The earlier measures relied on by the party were enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.no_connection_shown_between_prior_measur: The party does not show that the earlier measures were connected with the acquisition under the challenged law.

members.legal_issue: Estate-acquisition legislation is not a fraud on the Constitution merely because earlier laws affecting landowners preceded it.
material_facts: The appellants relied on earlier provincial enactments and alleged that they were part of a plan to reduce landowners’ incomes before acquiring their estates.
The earlier enactments were passed before the Constitution came into force and were not shown to be connected with the acquisition legislation.
members.legal_principle: A fraud-on-the-Constitution allegation must be supported by facts connecting the impugned legislation to the asserted evasion; the earlier enactments identified in this case did not establish such a connection. The Court rejected the allegation and upheld the Act as a whole.
members.conclusion: The Act was not a fraud on the Constitution on the basis of the earlier enactments relied upon.

predicates.constitutional_fraud_claim: A person alleges that legislation was enacted as a device to evade constitutional limits.
predicates.claim_relies_on_prior_laws: The allegation relies on earlier enactments as evidence of the asserted device.
predicates.prior_laws_are_unconnected_to_the_acquis: The earlier enactments are not shown to be connected with the challenged acquisition scheme.

members.legal_issue: The provision permitting inquiry into and annulment of specified transfers does not impose an unconstitutional restriction when it forms part of a valid estate-acquisition law protected by the Constitution.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the Collector's power to investigate and annul the transfer, arguing that the notice threatened their ability to receive rent and that no appeal or review was provided.
The provision required notice to and a hearing for affected parties, prior State Government sanction, and terms considered fair and equitable by the Collector.
The challenged power formed part of the machinery for acquiring estates under the Act.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the safeguards requiring notice, hearing and prior State Government sanction, as well as the provision's role as an integral part of a valid law for acquisition of estates. It held that the Act, including section 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, was protected by Article 31-A of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The challenge failed: the Collector's power was not as absolute or arbitrary as alleged, and the Act, including the challenged provision, was protected by Article 31-A of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_estate_acqui: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law used to acquire estates.
predicates.annulment_power_is_integral_to_acquisiti: The power to review and annul specified transfers forms part of the machinery for acquiring estates.
predicates.affected_parties_receive_notice_and_hear: The decision-maker must give affected parties notice and an opportunity to be heard before annulling a transfer.
predicates.government_approval_is_required: The decision-maker must obtain the government's prior approval before annulling a transfer.
predicates.acquisition_law_is_constitutionally_prot: The governing law for acquiring estates is protected by the Constitution from the asserted fundamental-rights challenge.

members.legal_issue: A power to annul transfers designed to defeat an estate-acquisition law is protected from challenge under fundamental-rights guarantees when it is an integral, ancillary part of that law.
material_facts: The estate in which the disputed plots were situated vested in the State under the land reform law.
The Collector found that the claimed settlement was a paper transaction made to defeat the law and annulled it.
The annulment power was intended to prevent anticipatory transfers and to make the estate-acquisition law effective.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for State acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or extinguishment or modification of those rights, from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. A provision that is ancillary to and integral with such a law is assessed in the setting of the law as a whole, rather than in isolation. The Court applied Thakur Raghubir Singh v. State of Ajmer, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 478.
members.conclusion: The annulment power was protected by Article 31A and could not be invalidated on the grounds that it infringed Articles 14, 19 or 31.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenges the validity of a power forming part of a law directed to land reform.
predicates.measure_acquires_estate_rights: The law provides for the State to acquire an estate or rights in an estate.
predicates.measure_extinguishes_estate_rights: The law provides for rights in an estate to be extinguished or modified.
predicates.annulment_power_is_integral_to_measure: The annulment power is an ancillary part of the law, intended to prevent transfers that would defeat its estate-reform purpose.

members.legal_issue: The remaining provisions of an estate-abolition enactment are constitutionally valid where they fall within the constitutional protection for laws relating to the acquisition of estates.
material_facts: The enactment abolished jagirs and provided for resumption of jagir lands and compensation.
A jagirdar challenged the provisions upheld by the Judicial Commissioner, but did not press his appeal in the Supreme Court.
The Court held that the enactment as a whole fell within the protection of Article 31A and relied on earlier decisions concerning similar legislation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects laws providing for the acquisition of estates and provisions incidental to that acquisition. The Court relied on The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh [1952] SCR 889; Visweshwar Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh [1952] SCR 1020; Raja Suriya Pal Singh v. State of U.P. [1952] SCR 1056; K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa [1954] SCR 1; Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan [1955] 2 SCR 303; Raja Bhairebendra Narayan Bhup v. State of Assam [1956] SCR 303; Sri Ram Ram Narain v. State of Bombay [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 499; Raghubir Singh v. State of Ajmer (now Rajasthan) [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 478; and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 748.
members.conclusion: The jagirdar’s appeal was dismissed, and the Court upheld the constitutional validity of the rest of the enactment.

predicates.individual_appeal_against_upholding_vali: An individual appealed a decision that had upheld the validity of an enactment.
predicates.estate_abolition_enactment: The enactment provided for abolishing an estate and acquiring or resuming the estate’s land.
predicates.enactment_protected_as_estate_acquisitio: The enactment and its relevant provisions concerned the acquisition of estates and were within the constitutional protection for such laws.

members.legal_issue: Forest land forming part of a janmam estate qualifies as an estate under Article 31A(2)(a)(i) without independently satisfying Article 31A(2)(a)(iii).
material_facts: The forest parcels were part of janmam estates.
The relevant janmam rights remained in existence after the resettlement.
The constitutional definition separately included janmam rights in the relevant states and also described certain agricultural and forest lands.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(2)(a)(i) includes janmam rights in the relevant states. Land forming part of such a janmam estate falls within that clause, so it is unnecessary to establish that it is also land held or let for agriculture or an ancillary purpose under Article 31A(2)(a)(iii).
members.conclusion: Forest land forming part of a janmam estate is an estate under Article 31A(2)(a)(i), and need not separately satisfy clause (iii).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law acquiring land.
predicates.forest_land_is_part_of_janmam_estate: The forest land being acquired forms part of a janmam estate.

members.legal_issue: Private forest land held under an included hereditary land tenure may qualify as an estate for acquisition protection without separately meeting the constitutional category for agricultural land.
material_facts: The private forests at issue were held under janmam rights, which the court treated as hereditary proprietorship rights in land.
The statute transferred ownership and possession of the private forests to the State.
The statute also provided for an agrarian reform scheme.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(2)(a) defines an estate inclusively, and Article 31A(2)(a)(i) expressly includes janmam rights in the relevant States. The court relied on Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, State of U.P. v. Raja Anand Brahma Shah, and Balmadies Plantations Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu. Acquisition of an estate still had to be linked to agrarian reform to receive Article 31A(1) protection.
members.conclusion: The janmam rights brought the forests within the constitutional definition of an estate, and it was unnecessary to establish separately that the forests fell within the agricultural-land category.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_challenge and land_held_under_included_hereditary_tenure and law_transfers_land_to_state and law_is_for_agrarian_reform

predicates.estate_acquisition_challenge: A constitutional challenge concerns a law that acquires land held as an estate.
predicates.land_held_under_included_hereditary_tenu: The land is held under a hereditary land tenure that is included in the constitutional definition of an estate.
predicates.law_transfers_land_to_state: The challenged law transfers ownership or possession of the land to the State.
predicates.law_is_for_agrarian_reform: The acquisition law provides for a genuine scheme of agrarian reform.

members.legal_issue: Agricultural land in the villages fell within the constitutional meaning of an estate even though the local landholding system did not establish an equivalent land-tenure estate.
material_facts: The properties were village holdings in a territory where land was dealt with by grants of permanent or period leases or by sale, rather than under a law of land tenures.
Payments to the government were rent or a percentage of presumable income from land, not land revenue under a land-tenure system.
The bulk of the village land was devoted to agriculture or pasture, and some was used for horticulture or purposes ancillary to agriculture.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A(2)(a) defines an estate by reference to local land-tenure law and also includes the specified grants, ryotwari land, and land held or let for agriculture or ancillary purposes. An estate in the ordinary Indian revenue-law sense requires land paying land revenue and held under a law relating to land tenures. The Court considered Sri Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay, Mahadeo Paikaji Kolhe v. State of Bombay, Atma Ram v. State of Punjab, K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, N. B. Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector, and Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The holdings did not qualify as estates by equivalence to the local land-tenure law and were not held under ryotwari settlement. However, land held or let for agriculture or ancillary purposes fell within the constitutional definition of an estate, so its acquisition or extinguishment was protected to that extent.

predicates.agrarian_reform_proceeding: The case concerns a measure abolishing village proprietorship as part of agrarian reform.
predicates.local_land_tenure_system_absent: The land was held through leases or purchase, without a local law of land tenures or a land-revenue tenure system.
predicates.land_held_or_let_for_agriculture_or_anci: The land was held or let for agriculture or a purpose ancillary to agriculture.

members.legal_issue: An executive notification issued under a statute protected against a property-rights challenge cannot be invalidated on that ground merely because it exercises the authority conferred by the statute.
material_facts: The statute was protected by a constitutional provision that placed it in a protected schedule.
The challenged notification was issued under the statute’s delegated power to set a lower maximum rent.
The challengers argued that the notification infringed constitutional property rights.
members.legal_principle: Where the statute is protected by the constitutional schedule, a notification issued through a valid exercise of power conferred by that statute cannot be treated as fresh legislation and challenged on the ground that it infringes the constitutional property-rights provision.
members.conclusion: The notification could not be challenged as infringing constitutional property rights because the statute and the power it conferred were protected.

predicates.property_rights_challenge_to_notificatio: The proceeding challenges an executive notification on the ground that it violates constitutional property rights.
predicates.parent_statute_constitutionally_protecte: The statute authorizing the notification is constitutionally protected against that kind of challenge.
predicates.notification_issued_under_parent_statute: The executive issued the notification under authority conferred by the protected statute.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notification authorized by a valid statute is not invalid merely because the notification itself is not independently protected from a fundamental-rights challenge.
material_facts: The Act authorized the State Government to issue a notification bringing estates within the acquisition scheme.
The challenge to the notification rested on the contention that it was not protected by provisions that sheltered the Act.
members.legal_principle: A notification that is consequential to a valid statute does not become invalid merely because it is an executive act; the Court rejected the challenge as dependent on an erroneous separation of the notification from the statute that authorized it. No earlier case is cited on this issue in the supplied text.
members.conclusion: The notification could not be held invalid on that ground because it was consequential to a valid statute.

predicates.challenge_to_notification_under_acquisit: A party challenges an executive notification issued under an acquisition statute.
predicates.statute_is_valid: The statute authorizing the notification is valid.
predicates.notification_is_consequential_to_statute: The notification implements or follows from the statute's authorization.

members.legal_issue: A law depriving a person of property is not insulated from other fundamental rights guarantees merely because it operates under authority of law.
material_facts: The respondents argued that the property deprivation authorized by the challenged law was governed exclusively by the constitutional provision concerning deprivation of property and therefore did not have to satisfy the guarantee of the right to hold and dispose of property.
The constitutional amendment had separated compulsory acquisition and requisition from other forms of deprivation of property.
The majority found that the challenged law deprived the sthanee of property, and that the estate-related protection did not apply.
members.legal_principle: The majority held that a law must be within the legislature’s competence and must not infringe fundamental rights, subject to applicable constitutional exceptions. It relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income-tax for the limits imposed on legislation by the Constitution and fundamental rights. It distinguished A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras because the relevant personal-liberty provisions formed a different constitutional scheme, and held State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji inapplicable after the constitutional amendment separating acquisition and requisition from other deprivation. It also considered State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose and referred to Narendra Kumar v. Union of India on the possibility that even a prohibition may qualify as a restriction if reasonable.
members.conclusion: The authority-of-law requirement did not exclude review under the property-rights guarantee; a property-deprivation law had to comply with the applicable fundamental rights guarantees unless a specific constitutional exception applied.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A party challenged a law that deprived a person of property on constitutional grounds.
predicates.constitutional_text_separates_acquisitio: The constitutional scheme treats compulsory acquisition or requisition as distinct from other forms of deprivation of property.
predicates.law_deprives_person_of_property: The law takes property from a person or materially removes that person’s property interest.

members.legal_issue: A law providing for compulsory acquisition of property is not insulated from challenge under the fundamental right to property merely because it concerns acquisition.
material_facts: The petitioner challenged legislation that transferred private bank undertakings to state-controlled corporations.
The challenge alleged that the acquisition impaired constitutional protections for property.
members.legal_principle: The effect of state action on an individual's rights, rather than the legislature's object or the form of the action, determines the protection available. The property-right guarantees and the acquisition provisions form parts of a related constitutional scheme. Acquisition for a public purpose may ordinarily be presumed to impose a permissible substantive restriction, but formal compliance with acquisition requirements does not exclude review of other constitutional guarantees or procedural reasonableness. The Court rejected the exclusive-code approach associated with A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras and discussed Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, Swami Motor Transport Co. v. Sri Sankaraswamigal Mutt, and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Ranojirao Shinde.
members.conclusion: The protections in the property-right provisions are not mutually exclusive; acquisition legislation must be assessed by its effect on the individual's rights and may be tested against the relevant fundamental-right guarantees.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_a: A person challenged a law that compulsorily transferred private property to the State or a state-controlled body.
predicates.property_rights_implicated: The challenged transfer affected an individual's constitutionally protected interests in property.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for laws acquiring, extinguishing, or modifying rights in an estate does not extend to a law that transfers a holder’s property to family members without changing the land-tenure relationships associated with the estate.
material_facts: The respondents relied on the constitutional protection for laws affecting estates and the petitioner’s properties were assumed, for deciding that argument, to be held in janmam right.
The challenged law deemed qualifying sthanams to be tarwads and their properties to belong to the tarwads, thereby giving the tarwad members rights in property previously held by the sthanee.
The law did not regulate relations between landlords and tenants, change the incidents of janmam rights, or implement agrarian reform; it transferred property interests between family members.
members.legal_principle: The majority construed the estate-related protection as addressing acquisition of an estate or modification or extinguishment of rights pertaining to land tenure, including relations between landlords and subordinate tenure-holders. It relied on Aswini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose for the limited use of legislative objects and reasons to identify the circumstances and purpose of a constitutional amendment, and distinguished Sri Ram Ram Narain v. State of Bombay and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab as cases involving legislation regulating land-tenure rights and agrarian reform. Justices Imam and Sarkar dissented, reading the protection more broadly to cover modification of a holder’s rights by transferring them to joint holders.
members.conclusion: The challenged law did not fall within the constitutional protection for laws affecting estates and could not, on that ground, avoid review under the fundamental rights guarantees.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_law: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law that affected property rights.
predicates.law_transfers_estate_property_between_fa: The law transferred property held by one family member to other family members or made them joint holders.
predicates.law_changes_land_tenure_relations: The law altered land-tenure rights or relationships, such as the rights between a landholder and subordinate tenure-holders.

members.legal_issue: A law that suspends a proprietor’s management of an estate without acquiring or extinguishing proprietary rights is outside the constitutional saving for laws concerning acquisition, extinguishment or modification of such rights.
material_facts: The challenged measure permitted the Court of Wards to assume superintendence of a proprietor’s property because of habitual infringement of tenants’ rights.
The measure suspended the proprietor’s possession and management but did not acquire the estate for the State or extinguish the proprietor’s ownership.
The suspension of management could continue for a definite or indefinite period.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects qualifying laws providing for State acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or for extinguishment or modification of such rights. The Court interpreted “modification” in that context as a change to the proprietary right, comparable to its extinguishment, and held that a mere suspension of management for a time did not qualify. It considered section 112 of the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The challenged law was not saved by article 31-A because a suspension of management was not an acquisition, extinguishment or modification of proprietary rights within that article.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and law_suspends_management and ownership_remains_with_proprietor and no_state_acquisition_of_estate_or_rights

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a law under constitutional property protections.
predicates.law_suspends_management: The law suspends the proprietor’s management of the property for a period.
predicates.ownership_remains_with_proprietor: The proprietor retains ownership of the property despite the suspension of management.
predicates.no_state_acquisition_of_estate_or_rights: The law does not provide for the State to acquire the estate or rights in it.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a public purpose does not invalidate an acquisition law that is protected as a law acquiring rights in an estate.
material_facts: The amendments transferred to the State the right to hold fairs, a transfer that could augment State revenue.
The Court considered whether the acquisition could be invalid because it was not for a public purpose.
The Court determined that the acquisition fell within the constitutional protection for laws acquiring rights in an estate.
members.legal_principle: After the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, Article 31(2) expressly made public purpose a condition of compulsory acquisition, while Article 31A protected qualifying estate-acquisition laws from invalidation under Article 31. The Court held that Article 31A therefore covered an acquisition even if it was not for a public purpose. It considered The State of Bihar v. Sir Kameshwar Singh, [1952] S.C.R. 880, and held that the later constitutional amendments had removed the basis for the earlier argument that public purpose could be judicially required in this context. The Court also relied on Entry 42 of the Concurrent List as amended by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act.
members.conclusion: The law was not invalid merely because the acquisition was not for a public purpose.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition law.
predicates.acquisition_lacks_public_purpose: The acquisition is not for a public purpose.
predicates.acquisition_is_protected_estate_acquisit: The acquisition is of rights in an estate and falls within the constitutional protection for estate-acquisition laws.

members.legal_issue: Once an estate-acquisition law is protected by Article 31A, the absence of compensation does not invalidate it under the fundamental-rights provisions displaced by that protection.
material_facts: The statute transferred ownership and possession of the forests to the State without providing compensation.
The court found that the acquired land qualified as an estate and that the statute provided for agrarian reform.
The owners challenged the statute under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects qualifying acquisition laws against challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31. The concurring opinion referred to Khajamian Wakf Estates v. State of Madras, which had not decided whether Article 31A protects a law providing no compensation, and stated that a court may not strike down a protected statute for non-payment, while expressing the expectation that just payment ordinarily be provided except in exceptional socio-historical circumstances.
members.conclusion: The absence of compensation did not invalidate the statute once it was protected by Article 31A; the concurring opinion added that legislatures should ordinarily provide just payment except in exceptional circumstances, but that this was not a basis to strike down the statute.

rule.if: no_compensation_challenge and estate_acquisition_law_challenge and land_qualifies_as_estate and law_is_protected_as_agrarian_reform

predicates.no_compensation_challenge: A constitutional challenge alleges that an acquisition law is invalid because it provides no compensation.
predicates.estate_acquisition_law_challenge: The challenged law acquires land that qualifies as an estate.
predicates.land_qualifies_as_estate: The acquired land falls within the constitutional definition of an estate.
predicates.law_is_protected_as_agrarian_reform: The acquisition law is protected because it provides for a genuine scheme of agrarian reform.

members.legal_issue: A respondent who has obtained a favorable judgment may support it on a ground decided against that respondent without filing a separate appeal.
material_facts: The election petition was dismissed, and the returned candidate sought to support that favorable judgment on factual findings the High Court had made against him.
The matter reached the Supreme Court in an appeal under the election law, and the respondent had not filed a separate appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 116C of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 makes the Code of Civil Procedure applicable, as far as possible, to an appeal under section 116A. In the absence of relevant Supreme Court rules, Order 41 Rule 22 CPC allows a respondent to support the judgment on a ground decided against that respondent. The Court relied on Ramanbhai Ashabhai Patel v. Dabhi Ajitkumar Fulsinji and T. N. Angami v. Smt. Ravalu alias Renu M. Shaiza.
members.conclusion: The respondent could support the High Court’s judgment on grounds decided against him without preferring an appeal.

predicates.election_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from an election petition.
predicates.respondent_succeeded_below: The respondent obtained a judgment in that respondent’s favor in the court below.
predicates.adverse_finding_was_made_against_respond: The court below made a finding against the respondent on a ground that could support the favorable judgment.

members.legal_issue: A respondent who has obtained a favorable order may support it on an alternative ground decided against the respondent below without filing a separate appeal or cross-objection.
material_facts: The trust relied on decisions in which respondents had been permitted to challenge adverse findings while supporting favorable final orders.
The court distinguished that situation from the trust’s cross-objections, which sought to challenge the decision itself and restore a less favorable result.
members.legal_principle: A party with an order in its favor may defend that order on an alternative ground decided against it below as a matter of general principles applicable to superior courts, not because Order 41 Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, applies to appeals under Article 136. The court relied on Ramanbhai Ashabhai Patel, Management of Northern Railway Co-operative Society Ltd., Bharat Kala Bhandar Ltd., Nalakath Sainuddin v. Koorikadan Sulaiman, and Banarsi v. Ram Phal.
members.conclusion: A respondent may support a favorable order by seeking reversal of an adverse finding on another ground, but that principle does not make cross-objections maintainable in an appeal by special leave.

predicates.appeal_or_revision_before_superior_court: A superior court is hearing an appeal or revision concerning a lower court’s decision.
predicates.respondent_has_favorable_order: The respondent obtained a final order in its favor below.
predicates.respondent_seeks_only_to_support_that_or: The respondent seeks to preserve the favorable order by relying on a different ground, rather than to obtain a more favorable order.

members.legal_issue: A respondent whose decree is entirely favorable is not required to appeal or file cross-objections solely to contest an adverse finding and may challenge that finding while supporting the decree in the appellant’s appeal.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the first and second suits in their entirety, but made findings adverse to the State on whether the disputed land formed part of government land.
The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal decrees, and the State sought to dispute the adverse findings in those appeals.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(2) and 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal lies against a decree, not a mere finding. Order XLI Rule 22, as amended, permits a respondent to file cross-objections against an adverse finding, but a respondent whose decree is entirely favorable may support it without cross-objections. Order XLI Rule 33 also empowers the appellate court to make an appropriate order. The Court applied Banarsi v. Ram Phal and Hardevinder Singh v. Paramjit Singh, and referred to Sri Nazeer Ahmed v. State Bank of Mysore.
members.conclusion: The State was not obliged to appeal or file cross-objections to challenge the findings while supporting the decrees dismissing the suits.

rule.if: appeal_against_dismissal_decree and decree_entirely_favors_respondent and adverse_finding_against_respondent and respondent_seeks_to_support_decree

predicates.appeal_against_dismissal_decree: A plaintiff appeals a decree dismissing the plaintiff’s suit.
predicates.decree_entirely_favors_respondent: The decree grants the respondent all the relief available under it.
predicates.adverse_finding_against_respondent: The trial court records a finding on an issue against the respondent despite granting a wholly favorable decree.
predicates.respondent_seeks_to_support_decree: The respondent seeks to uphold the decree in the plaintiff’s appeal.
predicates.respondent_may_challenge_adverse_finding: The respondent may contest the adverse finding without filing cross-objections when doing so to support the favorable decree.

members.legal_issue: A respondent may challenge an adverse finding to support a decree in the respondent’s favour without filing cross-objections when seeking no additional relief.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the bank’s suit, leaving the decree in the borrower’s favour, although it rejected the borrower’s plea that the suit was barred by the rule against splitting claims.
The bank appealed, and the borrower relied on the rejected plea to resist the bank’s appeal.
The borrower sought to uphold the decree, not to obtain relief beyond it.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a respondent may support the decree by challenging a finding against them without cross-objections. Cross-objections are needed when the respondent seeks relief beyond what the decree has already granted.
members.conclusion: The borrower was entitled to challenge the trial court’s adverse finding without filing cross-objections.

predicates.appeal_from_favorable_decree: The opposing party appealed from a decree that was ultimately in the respondent’s favour.
predicates.respondent_challenges_adverse_finding: The respondent challenged a finding made against them by the lower court.
predicates.respondent_seeks_only_to_uphold_decree: The respondent sought to preserve the decree and did not seek additional relief.

members.legal_issue: A respondent may support a judgment dismissing a suit on an alternative ground without separately appealing the rejection of an application raising that ground when the respondent obtained the dismissal sought.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the plaintiff’s suit while also rejecting the defendants’ application based on the consolidation provisions.
The defendants had obtained the dismissal of the suit and did not separately appeal the rejection of their application.
In the plaintiff’s appeal, the defendants relied on the consolidation provisions as an alternative basis for maintaining the dismissal.
members.legal_principle: A respondent who obtained the disposition sought may support the judgment on another available ground without separately appealing an order rejecting that ground, where there is no adverse judgment requiring an appeal and no res judicata against the respondent. The objection here arose under Sections 4 and 5 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act.
members.conclusion: The defendants were not precluded from raising the preliminary objection in the appeal.

rule.if: appeal_against_dismissal and respondent_obtained_dismissal_sought and respondent_raises_alternative_ground and no_adverse_judgment_on_alternative_ground

predicates.appeal_against_dismissal: An appeal was brought against a judgment dismissing the claimant’s suit.
predicates.respondent_obtained_dismissal_sought: The respondent had obtained the dismissal of the suit in the judgment under appeal.
predicates.respondent_raises_alternative_ground: The respondent relied on another available ground to support that dismissal.
predicates.no_adverse_judgment_on_alternative_groun: The respondent faced no adverse judgment on the alternative ground that required a separate appeal.

members.legal_issue: A pure question of law may be considered for the first time before the court of last resort when its factual foundation is established and deciding it requires no resolution of disputed factual questions.
material_facts: The argument that subletting one room could justify eviction from all rooms was raised at the final appellate stage, with permission sought and granted to urge additional grounds.
The single tenancy, the different alleged violations in the rooms, and the subletting finding for one room were established or undisputed; deciding the argument required no further factual findings.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law can be examined at any stage if its factual foundation has been laid and its legal consequences have not been considered. The court relied on Yeswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, Connecticut Fire Insurance Co. v. Kavanagh, and Chittoori Subbanna v. Kudappa Subbanna, including the principle that permission to urge additional grounds may be sought by a separate application.
members.conclusion: The court considered the newly raised legal argument because it rested on established facts and raised no factual questions requiring resolution.

rule.if: final_appellate_proceeding and pure_question_of_law and factual_foundation_established and no_disputed_factual_questions

predicates.final_appellate_proceeding: The matter is before a court exercising final appellate review.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The issue concerns the legal consequences of established facts rather than a dispute about what happened.
predicates.factual_foundation_established: The facts necessary to assess the legal issue have been established or are undisputed.
predicates.no_disputed_factual_questions: Deciding the issue does not require resolving disputed factual questions.

members.legal_issue: A pure question of law may be considered for the first time by a court of last resort when it turns on construction or on facts admitted or proved beyond controversy.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the rate of interest in the court of last resort although the rate issue had not been specifically raised in the cross-objections below.
The High Court had in fact considered and decided the rate issue.
The question turned on the construction of the applicable provision, rather than on a disputed factual finding.
members.legal_principle: A question of law first raised in a court of last resort may be entertained when it concerns construction of a document or rests on facts admitted or proved beyond controversy. The Court relied on Connecticut Fire Insurance Co. v. Kavanagh.
members.conclusion: There was no bar to considering the rate-of-interest point, and it was proper to entertain it.

predicates.appeal_before_court_of_last_resort: The proceeding is an appeal before a court of last resort.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The newly raised point concerns a question of law rather than a disputed factual issue.
predicates.question_depends_only_on_construction_or: The point depends only on construing a document or on facts admitted or proved beyond controversy.

members.legal_issue: A pure question of law based on admitted or undisputed facts may be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The challenge based on the constitutional role of district planning bodies was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The issue rested on facts admitted or established by the record and did not require an inquiry into new facts.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law that goes to the root of the matter may be raised at any stage when the facts are admitted or proved beyond controversy. The Court relied on Connecticut Fire Insurance Co. v. Kavanagh, Gurcharan Singh v. Kamla Singh, V.L.S. Finance Ltd. v. Union of India, Greater Mohali Area Development Authority v. Manju Jain, and National Textile Corporation Ltd. v. Naresh Kumar Badrikumar Jagad; it distinguished new factual pleas requiring investigation.
members.conclusion: The Court entertained the new legal ground.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: A party has brought an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The proposed ground raises a legal issue that can be decided without investigating new facts.
predicates.facts_admitted_or_undisputed: The facts necessary to decide the proposed ground are admitted or established beyond controversy.

members.legal_issue: A pure question of law that requires no investigation of facts may be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The respondent raised in the Supreme Court a legal objection that had not been taken in the courts below.
The objection could be decided without investigating facts.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law arising on the facts and circumstances of a case may be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if deciding it does not require investigation of facts. The Court applied Yaswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, Raja Sri Sailendra Narayan Bhanja Deo v. State of Orissa, Seth Badri Prasad v. Seth Nagarmal, State of U.P. v. Anand Swarup, and T. G. Appanda Mudaliar v. State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The Court permitted the objection to be raised.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and pure_question_of_law and not factual_investigation_needed

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The newly raised plea concerns a question of law arising on the case's facts.
predicates.factual_investigation_needed: Deciding the newly raised plea requires further investigation of facts.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may consider a new legal ground that depends only on admitted facts and requires no investigation or proof of additional facts.
material_facts: The landlord raised in the Supreme Court the contention that the rent-control law did not apply to the premises.
The contention depended on the premises’ location and appropriation and on the legal effect of the extension of the rent-control law, matters the Court treated as undisputed or admitted.
The landlord had pleaded that the tenancy was terminated by notice, and the tenant had not put that fact in issue.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law may be raised at the appellate stage when its determination does not require investigation into or proof of new facts. The Court applied this principle to the admitted facts before it and cited no earlier case for this point.
members.conclusion: The Court permitted consideration of the new contention because it was a question of law that required no investigation into or proof of new facts.

rule.if: appellate_challenge_to_eviction and new_ground_is_a_question_of_law and material_facts_are_admitted and deciding_ground_requires_no_new_fact_finding

predicates.appellate_challenge_to_eviction: The proceeding is an appellate challenge to a decision in an eviction dispute.
predicates.new_ground_is_a_question_of_law: A party raises a legal ground that was not relied on in the courts below.
predicates.material_facts_are_admitted: The facts necessary to decide the new ground are admitted or undisputed.
predicates.deciding_ground_requires_no_new_fact_fin: The court can decide the ground without investigating or proving any additional facts.

members.legal_issue: A new contention about the legal effect of a grant may be considered on appeal when it turns solely on construing the document and does not depend on disputed facts.
material_facts: The defendants raised the contention that the grant incorporated the lands into an existing Patni only in appeal, not in the trial court.
The contention depended on construing the grant, and there was no dispute about how its terms related to existing facts.
No objection was made when the contention was raised in the first appeal.
members.legal_principle: The construction of a contract or grant must be based on the document's terms; evidence is inadmissible on that question where there is no dispute about how the document relates to existing facts. The Court relied on Balkishen Das v. Legge (1899) and Maung Kyin v. Ma Shwe La (1917).
members.conclusion: The appellate court was right to allow the contention to be raised.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and new_document_construction_ground and document_terms_undisputed and no_factual_evidence_needed

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is being considered in an appeal.
predicates.new_document_construction_ground: A party raises a contention on appeal about the legal effect of a document that was not raised at trial.
predicates.document_terms_undisputed: The parties do not dispute the document's terms or how those terms relate to existing facts.
predicates.no_factual_evidence_needed: Deciding the contention requires no factual inquiry or evidence beyond construing the document.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may determine the legal character of an offence from proved facts even when the specific legal point was not clearly raised in the courts below.
material_facts: The lower courts’ findings established the circumstances of the fatal injury and the nature of the fight.
The applicability of the sudden-fight exception had not been clearly raised in the High Court.
Determining the offence from the established facts was a question of law.
members.legal_principle: Where the question is the legal nature of an offence deducible from proved facts, it is a question of law, and an appellate court may decide it by examining the findings even if the point was not clearly elucidated in the courts below. The court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The court was not precluded from deciding the exact nature of the offence on the basis of the findings, although the point had not been clearly raised below.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is before an appellate court.
predicates.offense_characterization_depends_on_prov: The legal nature of the offence can be determined from facts already found proved.
predicates.legal_point_not_clearly_raised_below: The specific legal point was not clearly raised or explained in the courts below.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may permit a new pure question of law to be raised for the first time when deciding it requires no investigation of facts.
material_facts: A party raised an objection for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The objection was a pure question of law and did not require investigation of facts.
The court permitted the party to argue the objection.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law that does not require factual investigation may be raised for the first time in an appellate court. The court relied on Yaswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, Raja Sri Sailendra Narayan Bhanja Deo v. State of Orissa, Seth Badri Prasad v. Seth Nagarmal, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Anand Swarup, and T.G. Appanda Mudaliar v. State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The court permitted the new legal objection to be raised because it involved no investigation of facts.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party raised the ground while a court was hearing an appeal.
predicates.new_ground_raises_pure_question_of_law: The ground had not been raised in the courts below and presented a pure question of law.
predicates.deciding_ground_requires_no_factual_inve: The court could decide the ground without investigating facts.

members.legal_issue: A respondent who seeks relief beyond the decree under appeal must challenge the adverse part of the decree by appeal or cross-objection.
material_facts: The trial court awarded the plaintiff monetary relief and made specific performance conditional on the defendants failing to pay or deposit the money in time.
The plaintiff did not appeal or file a cross-objection against the refusal to grant an unconditional decree for specific performance.
The defendants appealed, and the first appellate court dismissed their appeals but replaced the trial court’s decree with an unconditional decree for specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Sections 96 and 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure provide appeals from decrees, and a person may appeal only if aggrieved by the decree. Under Order 41 Rule 22, a respondent may support a decree without cross-objection, including by challenging an adverse finding, but must appeal or cross-object to obtain alteration of a part of the decree adverse to them. A cross-objection is an exercise of the right of appeal. The 1976 amendment to Rule 22 did not change that requirement for challenging an adverse part of a decree. The Court relied on Phoolchand v. Gopal Lal, Smt. Jatan Kanwar Golcha v. M/s Golcha Properties (P) Ltd., Smt. Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, and Sahadu Gangaram Bhagade v. Special Deputy Collector.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court could not grant the plaintiff the greater relief of unconditional specific performance when he had not appealed or filed a cross-objection; the Supreme Court set aside that modification and restored the trial court’s decree.

rule.if: defendant_appeal_against_decree and respondent_denied_greater_relief and respondent_filed_no_appeal_or_cross_objection and greater_relief_is_separable

predicates.defendant_appeal_against_decree: A defendant appealed from a decree that granted the opposing party some relief.
predicates.respondent_denied_greater_relief: The decree denied the respondent a greater form of relief than the relief it granted.
predicates.respondent_filed_no_appeal_or_cross_obje: The respondent did not appeal or file a cross-objection challenging the part of the decree that denied the greater relief.
predicates.greater_relief_is_separable: The greater relief sought by the respondent was independent of the relief granted by the decree.

members.legal_issue: A respondent who seeks relief altering a costs order on appeal must challenge that order by cross-objection.
material_facts: The trial court had awarded two sets of costs, and the High Court modified the order to allow only one set.
Respondents sought further relief concerning the costs order in the Supreme Court but had not filed cross-objections to the High Court's decision.
members.legal_principle: A respondent seeking relief against an order made by the court below must challenge that order by cross-objection; absent such an objection, the appellate court granted no relief on costs.
members.conclusion: No further relief concerning costs could be granted to those respondents because they had not cross-objected to the High Court's order.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.respondent_seeks_change_to_costs_order: A respondent asks the appellate court to alter a costs order made below.
predicates.no_cross_objection: The respondent did not file a cross-objection challenging that order.

members.legal_issue: A respondent cannot obtain a change to a costs order in an appeal without challenging that order by cross-objection.
material_facts: The trial court awarded two sets of costs, and the High Court modified the award to one set.
The respondents who sought further relief on costs did not file a cross-objection to the High Court’s decision.
members.legal_principle: The court declined to vary the High Court’s costs decision in the absence of a cross-objection by the respondents seeking that relief.
members.conclusion: No further relief on costs could be granted to those respondents because they had not filed a cross-objection.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.respondent_seeks_costs_variation: A respondent asked the appellate court to alter the costs order in the respondent’s favour.
predicates.no_cross_objection: The respondent did not file a cross-objection challenging the costs decision.

members.legal_issue: A pure question of law based on undisputed or proven facts may be raised at a late appellate stage when entertaining it causes no unfair prejudice.
material_facts: The land-reform-law argument was raised for the first time in a Letters Patent Appeal.
The argument arose from the parties’ common case and depended on facts that had been found or were undisputed.
No unfair prejudice from considering the argument was established.
members.legal_principle: A pure question of law going to the root of the case may be raised even in a court of last resort if it rests on admitted or proved facts and the opposing party is not taken by surprise or unfairly prejudiced. The Court relied on Connecticut Fire Insurance Company v. Kavanach, [1892] A.C. 473, 480.
members.conclusion: The appellate court was entitled to consider the new legal plea.

rule.if: appeal_at_late_stage and pure_question_of_law and facts_undisputed_or_proven and not unfair_prejudice

predicates.appeal_at_late_stage: The matter is an appeal in which a party raises a legal plea at a late stage.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The new plea raises a question of law rather than a dispute requiring new factual findings.
predicates.facts_undisputed_or_proven: The facts needed to decide the plea are admitted or established by the record.
predicates.unfair_prejudice: Allowing the plea would take the opposing party by surprise or otherwise unfairly prejudice that party.
predicates.late_legal_plea_may_be_considered: The court may consider the late legal plea.

members.legal_issue: A court may permit a pure question of law requiring no further factual investigation to be raised for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The objection that the suit was barred by section 47 had not been raised in the written statement and was advanced at the second-appeal stage.
The issue required no further investigation of facts and had been argued as a question of law.
The allegations in the plaint concerning the issue were obscure enough that the appellant might have missed their import.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion to permit a new legal contention on appeal where it required no further investigation of facts and had been understood and debated as a question of law. The judgment does not cite a specific statutory provision or earlier case for this procedural ruling.
members.conclusion: The appellant was permitted to raise the section 47 objection because it was a pure question of law requiring no further factual investigation.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal in which a party seeks to advance a contention not raised earlier.
predicates.new_contention_is_pure_question_of_law: The new contention can be decided as a question of law on the existing record.
predicates.no_further_fact_investigation_required: Deciding the contention requires no further investigation of facts.

members.legal_issue: A pure question of law based on admitted or undisputed facts may be raised for the first time during an appeal when refusing permission to raise it would not be justified by waiver or prejudice to the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellant did not include the objection concerning the permissible period for mesne profits in the memorandum of appeal and first sought to raise it when the appeal was argued.
The objection presented a question of law that did not depend on resolving disputed facts.
The parties had not previously disputed the permissible period, so the appellant’s silence did not amount to a concession or election on that question.
The respondent could not have been prejudiced by the late objection because a separate claim for the relevant mesne profits was already time-barred.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court has discretion to permit an additional ground, but a pure question of law resting on admitted or proved undisputed facts may be raised at a later stage, including in a final appeal. The refusal of permission may be interfered with when it disregards that principle. The Court relied on Wilson v. United Counties Bank Ltd., Yeswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, M. K. Ranganathan v. Government of Madras, Ittyavira Mathai v. Varkey Varkey and Rehmat-un-Nissa Begam v. Price; it distinguished a mixed question of law and fact.
members.conclusion: By majority, the High Court was wrong to refuse permission to raise the additional ground; the appellant was entitled to urge it in the appeal.

rule.if: appeal_from_final_decree and pure_question_of_law and facts_admitted_or_undisputed and opponent_not_prejudiced

predicates.appeal_from_final_decree: A party appealed from a final decree and sought to raise an additional ground during the appeal.
predicates.pure_question_of_law: The additional ground raised a question of law rather than a question requiring factual determination.
predicates.facts_admitted_or_undisputed: The facts needed to decide the additional ground were admitted or established without controversy.
predicates.opponent_not_prejudiced: Allowing the additional ground would not impair the opposing party’s ability to meet it or deprive that party of an available claim.

members.legal_issue: A respondent may rely on a ground raised below but rejected or left undecided to support a decree, so long as reliance on it does not mutilate or destroy the decree.
material_facts: The respondent relied on the ground that the premises had not been shown to be government premises.
That ground had been raised before the High Court, which did not decide it.
The respondent relied on the ground to support the decree under appeal.
members.legal_principle: On the analogy of Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a party may support a decree on a ground raised and decided against that party below, or not considered below. The limitation is that the ground cannot be used to mutilate or destroy the decree.
members.conclusion: The respondent was entitled to recanvass the ground in the Supreme Court to support the decree.

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.respondent_seeks_to_support_decree_on_gr: The respondent relies on a ground to uphold the decree under appeal.
predicates.ground_raised_below_but_rejected_or_unco: The ground was raised below and either rejected or not decided.
predicates.reliance_does_not_mutilate_or_destroy_de: Relying on the ground would not mutilate or destroy the decree.

members.legal_issue: A party may rely on a ground pleaded in the original petition to support relief on appeal even if the lower court did not consider it, where the opposing party did not answer the pleaded ground.
material_facts: The purchaser’s petition expressly alleged that the cancellation order was made without an opportunity to respond.
The forest authorities did not answer that allegation.
The lower courts did not decide the hearing issue, but it was relied on in support of the order under appeal.
members.legal_principle: The Court permitted reliance on a ground prominently raised in the petition and left unanswered, finding no reason to reject its truth merely because the High Court had not considered it.
members.conclusion: The purchaser could rely on the pleaded hearing ground in support of the order on appeal despite the lower court’s failure to consider it.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and ground_pleaded_in_original_petition and opposing_party_did_not_answer_ground and lower_court_did_not_consider_ground

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: A party appeals from the dismissal of a writ petition.
predicates.ground_pleaded_in_original_petition: The party expressly raised the ground in the original writ petition.
predicates.opposing_party_did_not_answer_ground: The opposing party filed no response to that pleaded ground.
predicates.lower_court_did_not_consider_ground: The lower court did not decide the pleaded ground.

members.legal_issue: A respondent who has not appealed or filed a cross-objection may support the decree on grounds decided against it below but may not use that power to challenge the decree.
material_facts: The landholder appealed the Collector’s order on several grounds but did not challenge the finding that allotted him a specified number of land units.
The State did not appeal or file a cross-objection and submitted to the Collector’s order.
The Commissioner set aside the Collector’s order, including the unchallenged finding about the land units.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XLI, Rule 22(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a respondent may support a decree on grounds decided in its favour or against it, but may challenge the decree only by appeal or cross-objection. Rule 49 of the Bihar Land Reforms Rules, 1963 made Order XLI applicable to appeals under the land-reform scheme.
members.conclusion: The Commissioner could not reverse the finding in the landholder’s favour under Order XLI, Rule 22, because the State had filed neither an appeal nor a cross-objection.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is an appeal in which the applicable procedure permits a respondent to support or challenge the decision under review.
predicates.respondent_filed_no_appeal_or_cross_obje: The respondent filed neither an appeal nor a cross-objection against the decision under review.
predicates.appellate_court_reversed_unappealed_favo: The appellate court reversed a finding favorable to the appealing party that the appellant had not challenged.
predicates.respondent_cannot_challenge_decree_witho: A respondent without an appeal or cross-objection cannot use the power to support a decision to challenge it.

members.legal_issue: A respondent may support a judgment on an available ground but cannot challenge an adverse finding without filing a cross-objection.
