material_facts: The High Court found that the agreement price was 17,000.
The respondent sought to challenge that finding in the appeal but had not filed a cross-objection against it.
members.legal_principle: A respondent may support the judgment under appeal on any ground open under that judgment, but an adverse finding cannot be challenged without a cross-objection.
members.conclusion: The respondent could not challenge the finding about the agreement price, although a respondent may support the judgment on a ground available under it.

predicates.appeal_from_judgment: The proceeding is an appeal from a judgment.
predicates.respondent_challenged_adverse_finding: The respondent sought to contest a finding adverse to the respondent in the judgment under appeal.
predicates.respondent_filed_no_cross_objection: The respondent did not file a cross-objection against that finding.
predicates.challenge_to_adverse_finding_not_permitt: The respondent cannot challenge the adverse finding in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who, after a genuine dispute over who is entitled to receive rent or an unjustified refusal by the landlord to accept it, deposits rent in court may be treated as having paid it and protected from eviction for rent arrears.
material_facts: After the original landlord died, several heirs succeeded to ownership, leaving the tenant uncertain who was entitled to receive rent.
The tenant attempted to tender rent to one heir, who refused it, and the tenant was permitted to deposit rent in court.
After receiving the landlords’ demand notice, the tenant offered in writing to pay the rent if the heir confirmed willingness to accept it, and said otherwise he would deposit it in court.
The landlords did not respond to that offer and instead sued for eviction; the tenant deposited the arrears in court.
The courts below ordered eviction for default, but the Supreme Court found that the tenant had been ready and willing to pay and that his court deposits were justified.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 20(2)(a), 20(4), 30(1) and 30(6), 39 and 40 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, a tenant ordinarily must pay rent to the landlord and may face eviction for qualifying arrears after demand and failure to pay within the prescribed time. But where a bona fide dispute exists about the person entitled to receive rent, or the landlord unjustifiably refuses to accept it, the tenant may use the court-deposit procedure; a deposit within that procedure is deemed payment to the landlord. The Act’s tenant-protective scheme should be interpreted to advance its purpose rather than by a narrow or technical approach. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s deposits were justified and were to be treated as payment to the landlords; he was not in arrears so as to be evicted on that ground. The appeal was allowed, the orders below were set aside, and the eviction suit was dismissed.

rule.if: eviction_claim_based_on_rent_arrears and tenant_ready_to_pay and (bona_fide_dispute_over_rent_recipient or landlord_refused_tender) and tenant_offered_payment_to_landlord and landlord_did_not_respond_to_offer and tenant_deposited_rent_in_court

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_rent_arrears: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of the tenant on the basis of unpaid rent.
predicates.tenant_ready_to_pay: The tenant remained willing to pay rent to the person entitled to receive it.
predicates.bona_fide_dispute_over_rent_recipient: There was a genuine uncertainty or dispute about which claimant was entitled to receive the rent.
predicates.landlord_refused_tender: The landlord or a person claiming entitlement to receive rent refused the tenant’s tender.
predicates.tenant_offered_payment_to_landlord: The tenant told the landlord or claimant that the tenant was willing to pay the rent.
predicates.landlord_did_not_respond_to_offer: The landlord or claimant did not respond to the tenant’s offer to pay.
predicates.tenant_deposited_rent_in_court: The tenant deposited the rent in court after the tender or offer was not accepted.

members.legal_issue: A tenant is in arrears for purposes of eviction for rent default only when rent remains unpaid to the person entitled to receive it, taking account of payments and court-authorised deposits made amid a bona fide dispute over entitlement to rent.
material_facts: The premises were allocated to another partner under a partnership dissolution deed, and the claimant admitted that the premises formed part of that partner’s share.
The tenants had paid rent to the claimant and to the other partner at different times, including a period of double payment.
Because the two claimants made conflicting demands for rent, a court found a bona fide dispute over title and permitted the tenants to deposit rent in court.
The tenants deposited substantial rent in court and produced bank records supporting further payments to the claimant.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972, arrears means rent in arrears to the landlord. The Court considered the court-authorised deposits under Section 30(2) of that Act, made in the context of a bona fide dispute over entitlement to rent, together with the other payments. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The tenants were not in arrears of rent to the claimant, and the claimant had no right to recover rent or obtain eviction on that basis.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and bona_fide_dispute_over_rent_recipient and (rent_paid_to_claimant_or_competing_claimant or rent_deposited_in_court) and claimant_not_entitled_to_rent

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground that rent was not paid.
predicates.bona_fide_dispute_over_rent_recipient: The tenant faces genuine competing claims from different persons to receive rent.
predicates.rent_paid_to_claimant_or_competing_claim: The tenant paid rent to the claimant or to another person asserting entitlement to it.
predicates.rent_deposited_in_court: The tenant deposited rent in court after being permitted to do so in the dispute over who was entitled to receive it.
predicates.claimant_not_entitled_to_rent: The person seeking eviction was not entitled to receive rent for the premises.
predicates.tenant_is_not_in_arrears_to_claimant: The tenant does not owe rent in arrears to the person seeking eviction.

members.legal_issue: A rent deposit made because of a bona fide dispute over who is entitled to receive rent is credited as payment when assessing whether a tenant has paid the arrears required for protection from eviction.
material_facts: The tenant deposited rent in court after the Municipal Board demanded rent following expiry of the landlord’s lease.
The tenant relied on those deposits, along with the amount deposited at the first hearing, to contend that no rent remained due.
The trial court found that the tenant had deposited more than the amount claimed in the suit.
The revisional court excluded the deposits made during the dispute over entitlement to rent, and the High Court upheld that approach.
members.legal_principle: Section 30(6) treats rent deposited under Section 30(2) as paid to the landlord on the date of deposit. Section 20(4), which permits deduction of deposits under Section 30(1), must be read with Section 30(6); the omission of an express reference to Section 30(2) does not negate the statutory effect of those deposits. Related provisions must be read harmoniously and not in isolation. The Court relied on R.S. Raghunath v. State of Karnataka, M. Pentiah v. Muddala Veeramallappa, Canada Sugar Refining Company v. R., Gammon India Ltd. v. Union of India, Mysore State Road Transport Corporation v. Mira Khasivali Ven, Commissioner of Income Tax v. National Taj Traders, Sultana Begum v. Prem Chand Jain, O.P. Singhla v. Union of India, Raj Krushna v. Vinod Kanungo, and Mohd. Sher Khan v. Raja Seth.
members.conclusion: The deposits made during the dispute over entitlement to rent had to be accounted for as payment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and restored the trial court’s order.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction on the ground that the tenant had defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.tenant_deposited_rent_due_to_entitlement: The tenant deposited rent in court because a bona fide doubt or dispute had arisen about who was entitled to receive it.
predicates.deposit_treated_as_payment: The governing rent-deposit scheme treats the tenant as having paid the landlord when the disputed rent is deposited.

members.legal_issue: A deposit of rent with the court handling the landlord's eviction proceeding is a permissible form of payment when the deposit is available to the landlord without hindrance and the landlord knows of it.
material_facts: The tenant deposited the rent arrears with the Rent Controller who was handling the landlord's eviction application.
The deposit remained in the Controller's custody and the landlord could withdraw it.
The Controller informed the landlord's counsel of the deposit on the first hearing date.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, uses the alternatives of paying or tendering and does not prescribe a particular method of deposit. A tenant may tender payment to the landlord or deposit it in the court handling the eviction case, provided the deposit is available to the landlord without hindrance and the landlord knows of it. The Court distinguished Vidya Prachar Trust v. Basant Ram, where the deposit was made in a different court in unrelated proceedings and was not available to the landlord in the same way, and followed Duli Chand v. Maman Chand.
members.conclusion: The deposit with the Rent Controller was a valid mode of payment under the statutory proviso.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.tenant_deposited_rent_with_court_handlin: The tenant placed the rent deposit with the court handling the landlord's eviction proceeding.
predicates.deposit_was_available_to_landlord_withou: The court held the money so that the landlord could obtain it without impediment.
predicates.landlord_knew_of_deposit: The landlord or the landlord's representative knew that the deposit had been made.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s deposit of rent and related amounts with the court hearing an eviction proceeding can substantially satisfy the first-hearing tender requirement when the funds are under that court’s control and available to the landlord.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of unpaid rent.
The tenant deposited the rent and related amounts to the landlord’s credit in the same court that later heard the eviction proceeding.
At the first hearing, the landlord was informed that the deposit could be withdrawn.
The deposited funds were in the court’s custody and could be paid to the landlord at that hearing.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949 gives a defaulting tenant a final opportunity to avoid eviction by paying or tendering the arrears, interest and costs at the first hearing. A deposit in the custody and control of the court hearing the eviction proceeding, available for payment to the landlord at that hearing, may substantially satisfy that requirement. The Court distinguished Shri Vidya Prachar Trust v. Pandit Basant Ram on the facts and found it unnecessary to reconsider that decision; the earlier Punjab High Court decisions discussed there did not govern the outcome.
members.conclusion: The tenant substantially complied with the tender requirement, so the eviction application could not succeed on the asserted failure to tender the arrears. The appeal was dismissed, and a remand to determine whether the landlord had earlier refused monthly tenders was unnecessary.

rule.if: rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding and tenant_deposited_rent_and_related_amounts and deposit_held_by_eviction_court and funds_available_at_first_hearing and landlord_informed_of_withdrawal

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.tenant_deposited_rent_and_related_amount: The tenant deposited the rent due and the related amounts required to address the arrears.
predicates.deposit_held_by_eviction_court: The tenant placed the deposit in the custody of the court hearing the eviction proceeding.
predicates.funds_available_at_first_hearing: The deposited funds could be paid to the landlord at the first hearing.
predicates.landlord_informed_of_withdrawal: The tenant informed the landlord at the first hearing that the deposited funds could be withdrawn.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s deposit of rent arrears through a general court-deposit mechanism is a valid tender when the receiving court is also exercising rent-control jurisdiction.
material_facts: The tenants deposited rent owed to the landlord in court under a provision allowing a person who owes money to deposit it for the creditor.
The court receiving the deposit was presided over by a judge who also functioned as the rent controller for the area.
The landlord was informed of the deposit, which was available for withdrawal.
members.legal_principle: The broad wording of Section 31 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934 covers any person who owes money, including a tenant owing rent. Read with the notification appointing subordinate judges as controllers and the relevant Punjab Courts Act arrangements, Section 31 provides machinery for receiving money for creditors; a qualifying deposit is treated as a deposit to the landlord’s credit. The Court followed Kuldip Singh v. The State of Punjab, Mam Chand v. Chhotu Ram, and Khushi Ram v. Shanti Rani, and overruled Vidya Prachar Trust v. Pandit Basarat Ram.
members.conclusion: The deposit was a valid tender of the rent arrears for the purposes of the rent-control law.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and tenant_owed_rent_arrears and deposited_for_creditor_in_dual_function_court and creditor_notified_of_deposit

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.tenant_owed_rent_arrears: The tenant owed rent arrears to the landlord.
predicates.deposited_for_creditor_in_dual_function_: The tenant deposited the arrears in court for the landlord, and the receiving court was also exercising rent-control jurisdiction.
predicates.creditor_notified_of_deposit: The creditor was informed that the deposited money was available for withdrawal.
predicates.rent_deposit_is_valid_tender: The rent deposit counts as a valid tender of the arrears.

members.legal_issue: A court may extend the time for payment or deposit of monthly rent falling due after an eviction suit is filed.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit that included a claim based on non-payment of rent.
While the suit and the landlord’s appeal were pending, the tenant sometimes deposited monthly rent one to three days after the prescribed date.
The tenant applied for condonation of the delays, and the court received the deposits and the landlord withdrew them without protest.
The High Court held that the court had no power to extend the time and decreed eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 13(1) and 13(6) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, the court’s discretion not to strike out a tenant’s defence for default necessarily implies discretion to condone the default and extend the time to pay or deposit rent. This construction gives effect to the Act’s purpose of protecting tenants. The court disapproved Jagdish Kapoor v. New Education Society and referred to B. C. Kame v. Nem Chand Jain.
members.conclusion: The court has jurisdiction to extend the time for payment or deposit of monthly rent falling due after the suit is filed.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and post_filing_monthly_rent_due and tenant_defaulted_on_monthly_deposit and court_has_discretion_over_striking_defence

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.post_filing_monthly_rent_due: Monthly rent became payable after the eviction proceeding was filed.
predicates.tenant_defaulted_on_monthly_deposit: The tenant failed to deposit or pay a monthly rent instalment by the prescribed time.
predicates.court_has_discretion_over_striking_defen: The governing rule gives the court discretion whether to strike out the tenant’s defence after a rent-payment default.

members.legal_issue: A court may extend the time for a tenant to pay or deposit rent after an eviction suit is instituted, but a late payment does not protect the tenant from eviction unless the court grants an extension.
material_facts: The eviction suits were based on the tenant’s failure to pay rent.
The tenant deposited the arrears after the statutory initial period had expired, without applying for an extension.
The tenant did not thereafter pay rent regularly as it fell due.
The tenant later applied for an extension, and the court rejected the application because the circumstances did not justify extending time.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(1)(a) and 12(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, payment within the prescribed demand-notice period prevents an eviction suit on the rent-default ground. Under Section 13(1), after a suit is instituted the tenant must pay or deposit the arrears within one month of service of summons and continue paying rent as it falls due, unless the court allows further time on application. Sections 13(5) and 13(6) provide that compliance prevents a possession decree on the rent-default ground, while failure to pay as required may result in the defence being struck out. A payment made after the initial period assists the tenant only if the court extends the time; extension is discretionary, not automatic. No earlier cases are relied on in deciding this issue.
members.conclusion: The court had jurisdiction to extend the time on an application, but no basis was shown to exercise that discretion in the tenant’s favour; the decrees for eviction were therefore restored.

rule.if: eviction_for_rent_default and late_initial_payment and not court_extended_deadline

predicates.eviction_for_rent_default: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant failed to pay rent.
predicates.late_initial_payment: The tenant paid or deposited the required arrears after the initial payment period had expired.
predicates.court_extended_deadline: The court granted the tenant additional time to make the required payment or deposit.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s failure to pay rent in time or deposit it as prescribed gives the landlord grounds to seek eviction, but does not require eviction and cannot alone justify refusing to consider discretionary time to pay.
material_facts: The tenant did not pay the rent within the required time or deposit its market value in court, but sent the landlord a money order for the tenant’s calculation of the landlord’s share.
The landlord had refused to cooperate in division of the crop and refused the money order.
The Revenue Divisional Officer refused to consider giving the tenant time to pay because the tenant had not made a court deposit.
The High Court set aside the eviction order after finding that the officer had misunderstood the scope of that discretion.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(2) and 3(3) of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 address rent arrears and deposit of rent payable in kind. Section 3(4)(b) gives the Revenue Divisional Officer discretion to allow time for payment, considering the relative circumstances of landlord and tenant. That discretion operates where the tenant has not made the deposit and must be exercised by considering the circumstances of the case. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The landlord had grounds to apply for eviction, but the Revenue Divisional Officer was required to consider whether to give the tenant time to pay, having regard to the circumstances; failure to make a court deposit could not itself be a reason to refuse to exercise that discretion.

predicates.cultivating_tenant_eviction_case: A landlord seeks the eviction of a cultivating tenant from a holding.
predicates.rent_unpaid_or_undeposited: The tenant fails to pay rent in time or to deposit it, and the landlord seeks eviction on that basis.
predicates.officer_refused_time_to_pay_solely_for_n: The decision-maker refuses to consider allowing time to pay solely because the tenant did not make a deposit.

members.legal_issue: A revenue officer has discretion, rather than an obligation, to give a cultivating tenant time to pay rent arrears during a landlord’s eviction proceeding when the tenant has not used the separate deposit procedure.
material_facts: The landlords sought eviction on the ground of rent arrears.
The tenants had not availed themselves of the statutory procedure for depositing rent before the eviction applications were brought.
The revenue officer did allow the tenants time to pay in these cases.
members.legal_principle: The majority, applying the distinction in the language between section 3(3)(b), which says the court shall allow time when a tenant has used that procedure and further rent is due, and section 3(4)(b), which says the revenue officer may allow time in the eviction proceeding, held that the latter confers discretion. Koshal and Misra JJ. formed the majority on this point; Desai J. dissented.
members.conclusion: The majority held that the revenue officer may grant or refuse time in such circumstances; the tenant is not entitled to time as of right. Desai J. took the contrary view that granting time was obligatory.

predicates.cultivating_tenant_eviction_case: A landlord sought to evict a tenant who cultivates the land.
predicates.rent_default_is_ground: The landlord relied on the tenant’s failure to pay rent as a ground for eviction.
predicates.prior_rent_deposit_procedure_not_used: Before the eviction application, the tenant had not used the separate procedure for depositing rent and seeking a determination of any further sum due.

members.legal_issue: A tenant is habitually in arrears where the tenant repeatedly fails to pay rent by the agreed monthly due date, even if the tenancy terms separately allow notice and a period to settle arrears before termination.
material_facts: The lease required the tenant to pay rent before the tenth day of each calendar month.
The tenant paid the rent for September through November 1984 in December, after a distress warrant had been obtained.
The record also showed further failures to pay rent on the schedule specified in the lease.
The Rent Controller found habitual default, and the Supreme Court upheld that finding under the applicable rent-control ground.
members.legal_principle: Clause 13(3)(ii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, requires the Controller to be satisfied that the tenant is habitually in arrears. “Habitually” connotes continuity. A tenant who repeatedly fails to meet the monthly rent date may be habitually in arrears even if rent is later paid, including after enforcement steps; a separate term allowing notice and time to settle arrears does not change the monthly payment obligation.
members.conclusion: The tenant was habitually in arrears because the repeated failures to pay rent by the agreed due date showed continuity of default; the later notice-and-settlement term did not grant an additional four months for paying rent.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: A rent-control proceeding concerned whether a tenant’s payment conduct amounted to habitual default.
predicates.rent_due_on_fixed_monthly_date: The tenancy required rent to be paid by a specified day in each month.
predicates.tenant_repeatedly_failed_to_pay_by_due_d: The tenant failed on multiple occasions to pay rent by the agreed monthly due date.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s repeated arrears in monthly rent can sustain eviction when the tenant relies on the absence of an agreed payment date or on depositing rent in the Treasury after the landlord refused payment.
material_facts: The tenant was found by the trial court to have been in arrears for more than two months on several occasions.
The courts below found that rent was payable month by month, despite there being no express agreement fixing the time for payment.
The tenant claimed that the landlord had refused rent and that the tenant had deposited rent in the Treasury; the trial court found those deposits ineffective under the amended law.
The tenant appealed the eviction decree, and the appellate courts’ findings were upheld as reasonable on the record.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11(1)(d) of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, as amended, the courts below treated repeated arrears of more than two months as a ground for eviction. The absence of an express agreement fixing the payment date did not excuse the tenant from paying rent regularly each month. Where a landlord refused rent, the trial court held that depositing it in the Treasury was ineffective and that the tenant’s course was to remit it by postal money order. The Supreme Court found the courts below’ findings reasonable; no earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The Court dismissed the appeal and left the eviction decree in force.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_appeal and lower_courts_found_repeated_arrears and rent_was_payable_monthly and treasury_deposit_treated_as_ineffective

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: A tenant appealed a decree ordering eviction for rent default.
predicates.lower_courts_found_repeated_arrears: The courts below found that the tenant had been in arrears for more than two months on repeated occasions.
predicates.rent_was_payable_monthly: The courts below found that rent was payable regularly each month despite no express agreement fixing the payment date.
predicates.treasury_deposit_treated_as_ineffective: The tenant deposited rent in the Treasury after claiming that the landlord refused payment, and the trial court treated that method as ineffective.

members.legal_issue: A timely tender of rent that the landlord refuses can support subsequent deposits with the rent authority, and deposits made within the applicable time do not establish the rent default required for eviction.
material_facts: Rent was payable monthly, and no contract fixed a different payment time.
The tenant sent the rent for one month by money order within the applicable time, but the landlord refused it.
The tenant later deposited that month's rent with the rent authority and deposited the rents for subsequent months; the court found those subsequent deposits were not late.
The High Court treated the deposits as invalid because it considered them unpreceded by a valid tender, despite finding that the initial money-order tender was timely.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4, 13(1)(i), 21 and 22 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, a tenant's eviction for rent default requires the specified pattern of defaults. A timely tender refused by the landlord permits the tenant to deposit rent with the rent authority; after a valid tender is refused, Section 21(4A) allows deposits for subsequent months without further tenders. The court relied on the statutory requirements and did not cite an earlier case.
members.conclusion: The initial tender was valid, the High Court's basis for treating the deposits as invalid was incorrect, and there was no default of the kind required for eviction. The appeal was allowed and the eviction suit dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_eviction_decree and monthly_rent_payable and timely_initial_rent_tender and landlord_refused_initial_tender and rent_deposited_with_authority and subsequent_rent_deposits_timely

predicates.appeal_from_eviction_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree ordering eviction for rent default.
predicates.monthly_rent_payable: The tenancy requires rent to be paid monthly.
predicates.timely_initial_rent_tender: The tenant tendered the rent for a month within the applicable payment time.
predicates.landlord_refused_initial_tender: The landlord refused the timely tender of rent.
predicates.rent_deposited_with_authority: The tenant deposited the refused rent with the rent authority.
predicates.subsequent_rent_deposits_timely: The tenant deposited the rents for subsequent months within the applicable time.

members.legal_issue: After a landlord refuses a valid tender of rent, subsequent monthly rents may be deposited with the rent authority within the applicable deposit period rather than the deadline for tendering rent to the landlord.
material_facts: The landlord refused a timely tender of rent for one month.
The tenant thereafter deposited rent for subsequent months with the rent authority without making further tenders to the landlord.
The landlord argued that the later deposits had to be made by the deadline for payment of rent to the landlord; the court rejected that construction of Sections 21 and 22.
members.legal_principle: Sections 21 and 22 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, read together, permit deposits for subsequent months without further tenders after refusal of a valid tender and apply the statutory time limit for deposits with the rent authority. The court relied on the plain reading of those provisions and cited no earlier case.
members.conclusion: The subsequent deposits were not required to meet the deadline for tendering rent to the landlord; the applicable deposit period governs.

predicates.appeal_from_eviction_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree ordering eviction for rent default.
predicates.landlord_refused_valid_rent_tender: The landlord refused a tender of rent that was made within the applicable time.
predicates.subsequent_rents_deposited_with_authorit: The tenant deposited rents for later months with the rent authority after the refusal.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s deposit of rent in court may be treated as payment to the landlord when physical tender is impracticable and the statutory conditions for deposit are met, but a court deposit is not automatically sufficient.
material_facts: The tenant and landlady had extremely strained relations, including criminal proceedings, and lived in adjacent premises.
The tenant regularly deposited rent in court rather than paying it directly to the landlady.
The lower courts held that the deposits did not amount to payment to the landlady, but did not consider whether other means of direct payment were practicable or had been refused.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(1)(a), 7-C(1) and 7-C(6) of the United Provinces (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, the expression concerning rent paid to the landlord must be construed liberally and in light of the parties’ circumstances. Physical, person-to-person tender is not required where it is impracticable; payment may be attempted by money order, messenger, or by asking the landlord to nominate a bank account. A court deposit is permissible where the landlord refuses rent tendered through such means, and a deposit made in accordance with Section 7-C(1) is deemed duly paid under Section 7-C(6). A tenant may not, however, deposit rent in court without meeting the statutory conditions. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The lower courts construed the deposit provisions too narrowly. Because they had not considered whether the circumstances justified court deposits after accounting for other possible means of payment, the finding was set aside and the case remanded for that determination. If no circumstance justifying court deposit was established, the eviction decree would stand; otherwise, the eviction petition would be dismissed.

predicates.arrears_eviction_proceeding: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that rent was in arrears.
predicates.relationship_makes_physical_tender_impra: The tenant and landlord had relations so strained that physically tendering rent to the landlord was impracticable.
predicates.tenant_regularly_deposited_rent_in_court: The tenant regularly placed the rent in court instead of paying it directly to the landlord.
predicates.lower_courts_did_not_assess_alternative_: The lower courts did not determine whether other ways of paying rent were available or whether the landlord had refused payment through those means.
predicates.case_remanded_for_assessment_of_whether_: The case is sent back for a determination of whether the circumstances justified depositing the rent in court.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s court deposit of rent counts as payment under the statutory protection only when the statutory conditions for depositing rent in court are satisfied.
material_facts: The tenant had previously received protection from eviction after a rent default.
For a later period, the tenant claimed to have paid five months of rent in cash, but the court rejected that claim on the evidence.
The tenant deposited rent for May through October directly in court on October 29, 1982.

The tenant had not remitted the rent by postal money order that was returned with the specified postal endorsement, had not asked the landlords to specify a bank account, and did not claim a bona fide doubt about who was entitled to the rent.
The tenant accepted that the conditions for depositing rent in court under Section 19-A(3)(c) were not satisfied.
The rent for the six-month period remained unpaid by a method recognized under the Act.
members.legal_principle: Sections 19-A(3) and 19-A(4) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950 prescribe the methods by which rent may be paid, remitted, or deposited and deem rent paid only when one of those methods is used. A court deposit under Section 19-A(3)(c) is available only when its stated conditions are met. A legal fiction must be confined to the purpose for which it was created and not extended beyond its legitimate field (The Bengal Immunity Company Limited v. The State of Bihar & Ors., 1955 (2) SCR 603 at 646). Duli Chand v. Maman Chand, 1980 (1) SCC 246, and Sheo Narain v. Sher Singh, 1980 (1) SCR 836, concerned a different statutory scheme and did not justify treating this non-compliant deposit as payment.
members.conclusion: The direct court deposit was not a deposit under Section 19-A(3)(c), so the tenant could not rely on the deemed-payment protection in Section 19-A(4); the tenant had committed a second six-month default and the eviction decree was rightly passed.

rule.if: repeat_default_eviction_proceeding and tenant_previously_received_default_protection and tenant_deposited_rent_directly_in_court and statutory_conditions_for_court_deposit_unsatisfied and rent_unpaid_for_six_months

predicates.repeat_default_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction based on a later alleged rent default after an earlier default proceeding.
predicates.tenant_previously_received_default_prote: The tenant had previously obtained protection from eviction after a rent default.
predicates.tenant_deposited_rent_directly_in_court: The tenant deposited rent directly with a court rather than using another recognized method of payment or remittance.
predicates.statutory_conditions_for_court_deposit_u: The tenant had not fulfilled the prescribed circumstances that permit rent to be deposited in court.
predicates.rent_unpaid_for_six_months: Rent for a continuous period of six months remained unpaid by a recognized method.
predicates.tenant_remains_in_default_despite_court_: The non-compliant court deposit does not prevent the tenant from being treated as in default.

members.legal_issue: A tenant's deposit of the full rent arrears, interest, and assessed costs with the Rent Controller before the first hearing satisfies the statutory payment requirement when the deposit remains available to the landlord and the landlord is informed of it at the first hearing.
material_facts: A landlord filed an application to evict a tenant for non-payment of rent.
Before the first hearing, the tenant deposited the rent arrears, calculated at the fair rent fixed by the Rent Controller, with that Controller.
The deposit included the required interest and costs and remained with the Controller on the first hearing date.
At the first hearing, the Controller informed the landlord's counsel that the amount had been deposited and was available to the landlord.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, payment or tender of the arrears, interest, and costs by the first hearing deems the rent to have been paid within the required time. A deposit made before the hearing counts as a deposit on the hearing date if it remains in court and is available to the landlord, who is informed of it. The Court distinguished Vidya Prachar Trust v. Basant Ram because that case involved a partial tender and a deposit in a different court under unrelated proceedings, and followed Duli Chand v. Maman Chand. It overruled Mehnga Singh v. Dewan Dilbagh Rai.
members.conclusion: The tenant fulfilled the statutory payment requirement and was protected from eviction on the ground of rent default; the landlord's eviction application had to be dismissed.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and tenant_deposited_full_arrears_before_first_hearing and deposit_included_required_interest_and_costs and deposit_remained_available_at_first_hearing and landlord_was_informed_of_deposit

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.tenant_deposited_full_arrears_before_fir: The tenant deposited the full rent arrears with the court handling the eviction proceeding before its first hearing.
predicates.deposit_included_required_interest_and_c: The tenant's deposit included the interest and costs required for the rent-default proceeding.
predicates.deposit_remained_available_at_first_hear: The deposited money remained with the court and could be paid to the landlord at the first hearing.
predicates.landlord_was_informed_of_deposit: The court informed the landlord or the landlord's representative at the first hearing that the deposit had been made.

members.legal_issue: Payment of the rent arrears, interest, and costs on or before the first hearing satisfies the tenant’s payment condition even if the arrears were deposited earlier.
material_facts: The tenants deposited the arrears of rent before the eviction proceeding was filed and deposited future rent as well.
The tenants paid the interest and costs on the first hearing.
The deposited arrears and the payment of interest and costs were available to the landlord by the first hearing.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 13(2) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires the rent arrears, interest, and assessed costs to be paid or tendered on or before the first hearing. Its protective purpose must not be frustrated by a hypertechnical construction; an earlier deposit that remains available to the landlord suffices. The Court applied Sheo Narain v. Sher Singh.
members.conclusion: The tenants complied with the payment condition and were protected from eviction for default; the eviction suit had to be dismissed.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and rent_default_alleged and arrears_interest_and_costs_paid_or_deposited_by_first_hearing and payment_available_to_landlord

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.rent_default_alleged: The landlord alleged that the tenant had defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.arrears_interest_and_costs_paid_or_depos: The tenant paid or deposited all rent arrears, interest, and assessed costs no later than the first hearing.
predicates.payment_available_to_landlord: The money paid or deposited was available to the landlord by the first hearing.
predicates.tenant_satisfies_payment_condition_and_i: The tenant has met the payment condition and is protected from eviction on the ground of rent default.

members.legal_issue: A prior acquisition attempt that was abandoned does not by itself bar a later acquisition of the same land for a public purpose.
material_facts: An earlier attempt to acquire the land had been dropped after a court order restrained construction in the area.
After that order was modified, the State made a fresh decision to acquire the land for development of the tourist complex.
The landowner argued that the earlier abandonment showed that the later acquisition was not bona fide.
members.legal_principle: State of Haryana v. Vinod Oil and General Mills (2014) 15 SCC 410 holds that there is no bar to a subsequent acquisition after land has been released from an earlier acquisition. In this case, the Court also relied on the changed circumstances following modification of the order that had restrained construction.
members.conclusion: The earlier acquisition proceedings having been dropped did not bar the later acquisition, which was made after the relevant court order had been modified and for a public purpose.

predicates.acquisition_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.earlier_acquisition_abandoned: An earlier attempt to acquire the same land was discontinued.
predicates.later_public_purpose_decision_after_chan: The acquiring authority made a later decision to acquire the land for a public purpose after circumstances relevant to the earlier discontinuance had changed.

members.legal_issue: The record did not establish that abandonment of an earlier acquisition proceeding barred a fresh proceeding for the same land.
material_facts: An earlier acquisition proceeding had been abandoned, and a fresh proceeding was later started for some of the same land.
The earlier officer’s report was not before the Court, and the record did not establish that the government had accepted that report as the reason for abandoning the earlier proceeding.
The later proceeding covered a smaller area than the earlier one.
members.legal_principle: The Court did not decide the merits of whether a prior decision on objections could bar fresh acquisition proceedings. It held that such a conclusion could not be reached without evidence showing the contents and acceptance of the earlier report and what had led the government to abandon the earlier proceeding.
members.conclusion: The Court could not hold on the available evidence that the government was prohibited from commencing a fresh acquisition proceeding.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated compulsory acquisition proceedings for land.
predicates.fresh_proceeding_follows_abandoned_proce: The government began a fresh acquisition proceeding after abandoning an earlier proceeding concerning the land.
predicates.record_does_not_show_prior_report_was_ac: The court record does not establish that the government accepted the earlier officer’s report or what prompted abandonment.

members.legal_issue: Requisitioning land does not preclude later compulsory acquisition of the same land under a separate acquisition power.
material_facts: The land was first requisitioned for a public purpose.
The State later initiated compulsory acquisition proceedings in respect of the same land.
The laws providing for requisition and compulsory acquisition contained no provision making the exercise of one power prevent the exercise of the other.
members.legal_principle: The Bombay Land Requisition Act and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 contain no provision that makes action under one preclude action under the other. Part VI of the Land Acquisition Act provides for temporary occupation of certain land for a public purpose or a company, but does not establish an incompatibility between requisition and compulsory acquisition. The court cited no earlier cases on this issue.
members.conclusion: Requisitioning the land did not exhaust or make incompatible the power to initiate compulsory acquisition proceedings later; the later proceedings did not, by themselves, establish an abuse of the requisition power.

predicates.requisition_acquisition_compatibility_ap: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether requisition and later compulsory acquisition are compatible.
predicates.land_was_requisitioned: The land was requisitioned for a public purpose.
predicates.later_acquisition_was_initiated: The government later initiated compulsory acquisition proceedings for the same land.
predicates.laws_do_not_make_powers_mutually_exclusi: The laws governing the two powers do not provide that exercising one prevents exercising the other.

members.legal_issue: The decision not to acquire some land covered by a notification does not by itself invalidate the acquisition of other land covered by the same notification.
material_facts: Some land that had also been proposed for acquisition under the notification was later excluded from acquisition.
The landowner argued that this exclusion undermined the validity of the acquisition of the land at issue.
The statutory objection process allowed interested persons to object, after which the Collector made recommendations and the Government decided whether to proceed.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act provides for objections by interested persons, a hearing and recommendations by the Collector, and a decision by the appropriate Government. The Government may accept some objections and reject others; the differing outcomes alone do not establish an inherent defect in the acquisition of other land.
members.conclusion: The exclusion of other land did not militate against the validity of the acquisition of the land at issue.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition of land.
predicates.other_notified_land_is_excluded: Some other land covered by the same acquisition notification is later not acquired.
predicates.objections_are_decided_for_individual_la: Objections to acquisition are considered and decided in relation to the land concerned.

members.legal_issue: Quashing an acquisition at the instance of some landowners does not, without more, nullify the acquisition of land belonging to owners who did not challenge it.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large area, and only some landowners challenged it.

The relief sought by the owner whose case was later relied on was limited to quashing the declaration as it related to his own land; he did not seek quashing of the preliminary notification or the entire acquisition.
The landowners seeking reconveyance had not challenged the acquisition, and the record did not establish that the earlier court orders had quashed the acquisition in its entirety.
A substantial portion of the acquired land had already been used for housing and other purposes.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Shyamnandan Prasad v. State of Bihar (1999) 4 SCC 255, Abhey Ram v. Union of India (1997) 5 SCC 421, and Delhi Administration v. Gurdip Singh Uban (1999) 7 SCC 44 and (2000) 7 SCC 296 for the principle that quashing acquisition proceedings at the instance of one or a few landowners does not nullify the entire acquisition. The scope of relief is also confined by the challenge and relief actually sought.
members.conclusion: The earlier order quashing the acquisition for a particular landowner did not nullify the acquisition of the land belonging to the other landowners.

predicates.acquisition_challenged_by_some_owners: Some owners challenged the acquisition of land that formed part of a larger acquisition.
predicates.relief_limited_to_challengers_land: The challenger sought relief limited to the land belonging to that challenger.
predicates.other_owners_did_not_challenge: The owners whose land is in dispute did not challenge the acquisition.
predicates.whole_acquisition_quashing_not_establish: The record did not establish that a court had quashed the acquisition as a whole.

members.legal_issue: A later invalid release of part of the land does not invalidate the original acquisition notification when the release was a separate, subsequent act.
material_facts: The original acquisition notification covered the land, including the portion later released.
The release occurred years after the original notification and was a separate subsequent act.
The challenge to the acquisition did not rest on a discriminatory distinction made when the original notification was issued.
members.legal_principle: Under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the invalidity of a separate, subsequent release does not invalidate the original Section 4 notification; the release is treated as non est and the land remains within the acquisition. Lila Ram v. Union of India was distinguished because it concerned the specificity of the public purpose for a large area, not a later release of land.
members.conclusion: The original acquisition notification remained valid, and the released land continued to form part of the acquisition.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a government proceeding to acquire land.
predicates.original_notification_included_released_: The original acquisition notification included the land that was later released.
predicates.release_was_separate_subsequent_act: The government released the land in a distinct act after issuing the original acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: A change in the public use of land during acquisition under the town-planning statute does not invalidate an acquisition completed by the statutory declaration.
material_facts: The landowner served a purchase notice, and acquisition proceedings were commenced for land reserved for a public purpose.
The public use designated for the land changed from a garden to a primary school before the acquisition award.
A declaration under the town-planning statute read with the land-acquisition statute had been issued, but possession had not been taken.
The landowner accepted the compensation, while later joining tenants in challenging the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Sections 126 and 128 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 establish an acquisition scheme distinct from the general Land Acquisition Act scheme; under section 126, vesting may occur at the specified statutory stage and does not depend on the original public purpose continuing until possession. A changed public need does not invalidate an otherwise valid acquisition. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., including its approval of the principle in Ghulam Mustafa v. State of Maharashtra, Mangal Oram v. State of Orissa, Collector of 24 Parganas v. Lalit Mohan Mullick, and State of Maharashtra v. Mahadeo Deoman Rai. It also relied on Girnar Traders (3) v. State of Maharashtra concerning the distinct acquisition scheme under the Act.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was complete upon the statutory declaration and remained valid despite the change in the designated public use.

rule.if: acquisition_validity_challenge and acquisition_under_planning_statute and statutory_acquisition_declaration_issued and public_purpose_changed_during_acquisition

predicates.acquisition_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition undertaken for planned development.
predicates.acquisition_under_planning_statute: The acquisition was undertaken through the special statutory process for land designated in a plan.
predicates.statutory_acquisition_declaration_issued: The required declaration completing the relevant statutory acquisition stage was issued.
predicates.public_purpose_changed_during_acquisitio: The designated public use of the land changed while acquisition proceedings were underway.

members.legal_issue: A later unlawful release of land does not invalidate an acquisition that was initially made for a genuine public purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition had been initiated and completed for a genuine public purpose of developing urban sectors.
The abuse arose from later events, including the release of acquired land to the developer and the associated licences and transfers.
The High Court had quashed the acquisition in its entirety, but the Supreme Court distinguished the valid acquisition from the later unlawful actions.
members.legal_principle: A valid acquisition for a public purpose is distinct from subsequent unlawful action to release the acquired land to a private party. Where the release is mala fide or arbitrary, the acquisition of the released land stands revived. The Court applied the scheme of Sections 4, 6, 16 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and relied on the principle in Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi that an unlawful release does not prevent the acquisition from standing.
members.conclusion: The acquisition notifications and awards were upheld, and the land vested in HUDA. The release orders, licences and transactions in favour of the developer were quashed.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_and_later_relea: A party challenged both a land acquisition and a later release of the acquired land.
predicates.acquisition_had_genuine_public_purpose: The land was initially acquired to fulfil a genuine public purpose.
predicates.later_release_was_abusive: The state later released the acquired land through an arbitrary or mala fide exercise of power.

members.legal_issue: Later diversion of acquired land to another public purpose does not invalidate an acquisition that was valid when made and had vested title in the acquiring authority.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a village market and the Court held it valid.
After the acquisition, title had vested in the municipality, which parcelled out and sold excess land for a housing colony.
The Court regarded a housing colony as a public necessity.
members.legal_principle: Once a valid compulsory acquisition has vested title in the requiring authority, a later diversion of the land to a different public purpose does not void the acquisition; the original owner cannot rely on that later use to invalidate it. The judgment cites no earlier cases on this issue.
members.conclusion: The municipality’s later use of the excess land for a housing colony did not invalidate the original acquisition.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and acquisition_was_valid_when_made and title_vested_in_acquiring_authority and later_use_was_for_another_public_purpose

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_was_valid_when_made: The acquisition was valid for its stated purpose when it was made.
predicates.title_vested_in_acquiring_authority: Title to the acquired land vested in the authority for which it was acquired.
predicates.later_use_was_for_another_public_purpose: The acquiring authority later used the land for a public purpose different from the one originally stated.

members.legal_issue: A valid tender of compensation satisfies the payment condition even when the landholder refuses to accept the amount.
material_facts: The Court considered acquisitions in which compensation was tendered to the persons entitled to receive it but was refused.
The earlier acquisition regime required the acquiring authority to tender payment and to pay the amount unless prevented by specified circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Section 31(1) of the 1894 Act requires tender and payment, while Section 31(2) addresses circumstances preventing payment. The Court construed “paid” in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act in the context of those provisions and relied on Benares State Bank Ltd. v. CIT, Collector of Central Excise v. Elphinstone Spg. & Wvg. Mills Co. Ltd., and J. Dalmia v. Commissioner of Income Tax.
members.conclusion: Compensation is treated as paid when it has been tendered and made available to the person entitled to it; a landholder cannot establish non-payment merely by refusing the tender.

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.compensation_tendered_and_available: The acquiring authority offered the compensation unconditionally and made it available to the person entitled to receive it.
predicates.landholder_refused_tender: The person entitled to compensation declined to accept the amount offered.

members.legal_issue: An unconditional tender of compensation constitutes payment even when the landholder refuses it, and failure to deposit compensation in court does not by itself cause an acquisition to lapse.
material_facts: The Court considered proceedings in which compensation under the earlier acquisition law had been tendered but refused, as well as cases in which compensation had not been deposited in court.
The statutory scheme separately addressed tender or payment, court deposit in specified circumstances, and interest where compensation remained unpaid or undeposited.
Rules and orders governing public funds provided for treasury deposits in circumstances where compensation was not collected and no reference to court was sought.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 31(1), 31(2) and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, tender, court deposit and the interest consequence of non-payment are distinct; section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 uses “paid,” not “deposited.” Section 77 and section 80 of the 2013 Act similarly distinguish tender or payment from deposit and interest. The Court relied on Straw Board Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Gobind, Management of Delhi Transport Undertaking v. Industrial Tribunal, Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. Narayan Bhoumik, and J. Dalmia v. Commissioner of Income Tax for the principle that tender making money unconditionally available can amount to payment. It applied harmonious and ordinary construction, including Raj Krushna v. Binod Kanungo and Sultana Begum v. Premchand Jain, and held the contrary ruling in Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki to be per incuriam by majority; one judge disagreed only with that characterization.
members.conclusion: For the lapse provision, payment means an unconditional tender that makes compensation available to the landholder; court deposit is not included in that meaning. A failure to deposit in court does not itself cause lapse, and a landholder who refuses a proper tender cannot rely on that refusal to obtain lapse.

predicates.legacy_acquisition_lapse_claim: A claimant seeks to have an acquisition under an earlier land-acquisition regime treated as lapsed under a later transition rule.
predicates.compensation_unconditionally_tendered: The acquiring authority offered the compensation unconditionally and made it available to the person entitled to receive it.
predicates.compensation_refused: The person entitled to compensation declined to accept the amount offered.

members.legal_issue: Compensation based on market value on the date of the acquisition notification is not invalid merely because possession and extinguishment of title occur later.
material_facts: The owners argued that a time lag could arise between the acquisition notification and the taking of possession, when title was extinguished.
Compensation was determined by reference to market value on the date of the acquisition notification.
The owners relied on the requirement that compensation be a just equivalent of the land taken.
members.legal_principle: P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector held that determining market value as at the date of the acquisition notification did not offend the constitutional requirement of compensation. The Court therefore rejected the argument that a later taking of possession made that valuation date invalid.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge to using the notification date as the valuation date, relying on its prior decision in Vajravelu.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_case: A proceeding concerns compensation for compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.compensation_based_on_notification_date: Compensation is assessed using market value on the date the acquisition notification is issued.
predicates.later_possession_or_title_extinguishment: Possession is taken or title is extinguished after the notification date.

members.legal_issue: Validating later parcel-by-parcel acquisitions under an earlier notification does not violate the constitutional guarantee concerning compensation when the governing compensation principles remain unchanged and the notification date remains relevant to valuation.
material_facts: The acquisitions were made for the same public purpose stated in the original notification.
The law validated multiple declarations for different parcels under that notification and did not expressly change the compensation provisions or the principles for determining compensation.
The existing acquisition law used the value prevailing at the notification date as the basis for valuation.
The acquisition concerned a large planned development that the State could not necessarily undertake all at once because of planning and resource constraints.
members.legal_principle: After the constitutional amendment of 1955, the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable, but the law must provide compensation or principles for determining it. The Court considered the existing notification-date valuation principle relevant and found that validation of successive declarations did not introduce a different public purpose or alter the compensation principle. Sections 4 and 23 of the Land Acquisition Act were protected by Article 31(5)(a), while the amendments concerned the procedure for reports and declarations. The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, and P.V. Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector.
members.conclusion: The validating law did not violate the constitutional guarantee concerning compensation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: A party challenges the constitutionality of compensation in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.successive_parcels_serve_the_same_public: The parcels acquired through successive steps serve the same public purpose identified for the acquisition.
predicates.existing_compensation_principles_are_unc: The validating law does not alter the existing principles for determining compensation.
predicates.notification_date_is_relevant_to_the_acq: The date used to value the property is connected to the commencement of the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.phased_acquisition_is_consistent_with_pl: The acquisition is carried out in stages for reasons connected with planning or the State's available resources.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition for planned development of a large area is not invalid merely because the particular use of each parcel has not been specified in the development plans when the acquisition is initiated.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large area comprising numerous plots for the stated public purpose of planned development.
The land in question had not been specifically allocated to a particular use in the relevant development plans, and some of it lay within a cantonment area.
The development plans and related planning activities were to be implemented after the land became available through acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(f) and 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, planned development is a public purpose. For an acquisition of a large area comprising plots belonging to different owners, identifying the particular use of every parcel is not a condition precedent to initiating acquisition. The planning details may be worked out after acquisition. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor, Smt. Ratni Devi v. Chief Commissioner, Pt. Lila Ram v. Union of India, Om Prakash v. Union of India, Ram Chand v. Union of India, State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Krishanan, and Jai Narain v. Union of India; it also noted that Section 12(3)(ii) of the Delhi Development Act addresses development in cantonment areas.
members.conclusion: The acquisition notification was not invalid because it did not particularise the intended use of the specific land; the specified purpose of planned development was a public purpose.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_land_acquisition and acquisition_for_planned_development and acquisition_covers_large_area_with_multiple_plots and public_purpose_is_specified and individual_parcel_use_is_not_specified

predicates.appeal_challenges_land_acquisition: An appeal challenges the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_for_planned_development: The acquiring authority seeks land for planned development.
predicates.acquisition_covers_large_area_with_multi: The acquisition covers a large area comprising multiple plots.
predicates.public_purpose_is_specified: The acquisition notice identifies a public purpose for which the land is sought.
predicates.individual_parcel_use_is_not_specified: The intended specific use of each individual parcel has not been identified when acquisition is initiated.

members.legal_issue: A mismatch between the proposed public use of acquired land and the use allowed by the applicable development plan does not by itself invalidate the acquisition.
material_facts: The acquired land was shown in the development plan for light industries and later as a green belt, while the acquisition was for a market yard.
The acquisition was for a public purpose, and the proposed user differed from the user then permitted by the plan.
The beneficiary could seek approval from the competent planning authority to modify the plan for the proposed use.
members.legal_principle: Acquisition for a public purpose and approval to change the use permitted by a development plan are separate matters; acquisition may precede development and is not invalid merely because the plan then permits a different use. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, which discussed Sections 12 and 15 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, and on Patna Improvement Trust v. Smt. Lakshmi Devi and Kendriya Karamchari Evam Mura Sahkari Avas Samithi Ltd. v. State of U.P.; the latter addressed modification under Section 13 of the U.P. Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973.
members.conclusion: The acquisition remained valid despite the plan’s different land-use designation; the beneficiary was required to seek the necessary planning approval for the proposed use.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government pursued an acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_public_purpose: The land was acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.proposed_use_differs_from_plan_use: The use proposed for the acquired land differed from the use permitted by the applicable development plan.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition for a public purpose is not a mala fide or colourable exercise of power merely because a prior attempt to purchase the land by negotiation failed.
material_facts: A public trust sought the land to provide a road connecting two temples.
The trust had earlier attempted to purchase the property by negotiation, but the Charity Commissioner refused permission for the purchase.
After that refusal, the trust asked the government to acquire the land, and the government exercised its acquisition power.
The owners operated a flower-selling business and a small hotel on the property and alleged that the acquisition would deprive them of their livelihood.
members.legal_principle: The exercise of acquisition power is open to judicial review, but a declaration of public purpose is not invalid merely because the land is acquired for a trust rather than directly for the government. It may be challenged if the stated purpose is actually private, is no purpose at all, or the power is exercised mala fide or colourably. A failed effort to purchase land by agreement does not, by itself, establish such misuse. The Court relied on Somavanti v. State of Punjab, Abdul Husein Tayabali v. State of Gujarat, and Tata Cellular v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was neither mala fide nor a colourable exercise of power, and the failed negotiations did not make the acquisition invalid.

rule.if: acquisition_notification_challenge and government_exercised_acquisition_power and purpose_served_general_interest and negotiated_purchase_failed

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges the government's exercise of power to acquire land.
predicates.government_exercised_acquisition_power: The government used its statutory acquisition power after the land was sought for a public project.
predicates.purpose_served_general_interest: The proposed use of the land served the general interest of the community rather than an individual interest.
predicates.negotiated_purchase_failed: An earlier attempt to purchase the land by agreement did not succeed.

members.legal_issue: A title dispute or earlier requisition history does not establish mala fides where the challenged acquisition covers the properties for a public purpose.
material_facts: The owner alleged that the acquisition was mala fide.
There had been earlier requisition of the flats for a public purpose and litigation concerning that history.
There was also a dispute between the owner and his predecessor in title.
The acquisition covered all the flats, including the owner's flat, for a public purpose.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the title dispute was not a ground for finding mala fides and that the acquisition of all the flats for a public purpose left no basis for the allegation in this case.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no substance in the allegation of mala fides.

predicates.mala_fides_challenge: The owner alleges that the acquisition was undertaken in bad faith.
predicates.acquisition_covers_all_affected_units_fo: The acquisition covers the affected units for a stated public purpose.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_title_dispute_or_pri: The owner relies on a title dispute or the history of an earlier requisition to support the allegation.

members.legal_issue: The former owner’s intention to use land for a different public purpose does not invalidate an acquisition that is itself for a public purpose.
material_facts: The former owner intended to use the land to establish a factory but was prevented from doing so by restrictions associated with nearby military installations.
The land was acquired for another factory that the Court found would serve a public purpose.
The former owner’s objection was that land intended for one public purpose should not be acquired for another.
members.legal_principle: The validity of an acquisition depends on whether it is required for a public purpose, not on the former owner’s intended use. An owner may object to the proposed acquisition through the procedure provided for objections, but a competing intended use does not by itself invalidate an acquisition found to be for a public purpose. The Court distinguished Province of Bombay v. Kusaldas S. Advani.
members.conclusion: The former owner’s intended use does not affect the validity of an acquisition that is itself for a public purpose; an objection to whether the land should be acquired may be raised in the statutory objection process.

predicates.challenge_to_public_purpose_acquisition: A party challenges the validity of a compulsory acquisition said to serve a public purpose.
predicates.acquisition_serves_public_purpose: The acquisition is in fact for a public purpose.
predicates.former_owner_intended_a_different_public: The former owner intended to use the land for a different purpose that also served a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition for a public purpose is not invalid merely because the land is already used for a beneficial purpose or that existing use is considered more useful.
material_facts: The land included a polo ground used for sport.
The landowners argued that this existing use served a more useful and important public purpose than the proposed acquisition.
The stated acquisition purposes included development and construction of residential, commercial and administrative buildings.
members.legal_principle: Once an acquisition is found to be for a public purpose, the Court does not assess the comparative utility of competing public purposes, and an existing beneficial use of the land does not by itself invalidate the acquisition.
members.conclusion: The Court would not compare the relative utility of the public purposes; the existing beneficial use did not invalidate an acquisition found to be for a public purpose.

rule.if: challenge_to_public_purpose_acquisition and acquisition_is_for_public_purpose and land_has_existing_beneficial_use and challenge_relies_on_comparative_utility

predicates.challenge_to_public_purpose_acquisition: The proceeding challenges an acquisition said to be for a public purpose.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_public_purpose: The acquisition is for a public purpose.
predicates.land_has_existing_beneficial_use: The land is already being used for a beneficial purpose.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_comparative_utility: The challenge argues that the land’s existing use is more useful or important than the proposed public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A representation by an official that permission to change land use would follow a gift of land does not make a later acquisition by the State illegal.
material_facts: The landowners gave strips of land to a local body for widening a passage after a planning official represented that permission to change the land use would be granted.
The State later included their land in an acquisition for an industrial estate.
The landowners relied on the representation to argue that the State was estopped from acquiring their land.
members.legal_principle: A representation by the Director of Town and Country Planning concerning permission to change land use could not be enforced against the State to prevent acquisition. A possible challenge to the gifts for failure to fulfil the commitment does not invalidate the acquisition.
members.conclusion: The representation was not enforceable against the State so as to invalidate the acquisition; the landowners could seek to challenge the gifts, but that did not make the acquisition proceedings illegal.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the acquisition of their land.
predicates.official_made_conditional_land_use_repre: An official represented that permission to change land use would be granted on a stated condition.
predicates.land_was_gifted_in_reliance: The person gave land to a local body in reliance on that representation.

members.legal_issue: Permission to change the use of land does not, by itself, invalidate a subsequent acquisition of that land.
material_facts: The landowner had received permission to change the use of the land for a proposed hotel project.
The acquisition was made for a public development project.
The Court noted that construction had not commenced in accordance with the conditions attached to the change-of-use permission.
members.legal_principle: State of Haryana v. Vinod Oil and General Mills (2014) 15 SCC 410 holds that permission for change of land use has no relevance to the validity of a land acquisition. Clause (f) of Rule 26-D of the Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction of Unregulated Development Rules, 1965 required construction to start within six months and be completed within two years from the change-of-use order; the Court noted that construction had not been undertaken in accordance with that condition.
members.conclusion: The change-of-use permission did not provide a basis for invalidating the acquisition.

predicates.acquisition_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.land_use_permission: The landowner received official permission to use the land for a proposed development.
predicates.acquisition_for_public_purpose: The land was acquired for a project serving a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A ceiling law can apply to a covered urban agglomeration even if there is no master plan or the plan does not designate land for compulsory acquisition.
material_facts: The relevant urban agglomeration was specified in the Act’s Schedule.
A master plan had been prepared and later revised and sanctioned for the town.
The challenge asserted that the master plan did not satisfy a local-law requirement to designate land for compulsory acquisition.
The plan contained development proposals, and the municipality had power to acquire land needed to implement such proposals.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(h), 2(o), 2(n), 3 and 4 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act define the relevant land, agglomerations and ceiling regime. Section 2(o) provides for urban land both where a master plan identifies it and where there is no plan or the plan does not do so. The word “shall” in Section 244(1)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh (Telengana Area) District Municipalities Act, 1956 is directory in context; a plan is not invalid merely because it omits a proposal designating land for compulsory acquisition. The municipality’s acquisition power under Section 250 supports implementation of a scheme without such designation in the plan. No earlier case is relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The alleged deficiency did not prevent the Act from applying to the urban agglomeration. The Act’s application did not depend on the existence of a master plan; where there is no plan, or it does not refer to land as urban land, the Act applies to qualifying land within the local limits of the relevant municipality or other local authority.

predicates.challenge_to_urban_ceiling_law: A party challenged the application of a ceiling law to an urban agglomeration.
predicates.urban_agglomeration_covered_by_law: The urban agglomeration falls within the areas covered by the law.
predicates.applicability_challenged_for_master_plan: The challenge asserts that the master plan is absent or deficient, including because it omits designation of land for compulsory acquisition.

members.legal_issue: The applicability of the urban land ceiling law to a covered urban agglomeration does not invariably depend on the existence of a master plan.
material_facts: The law identified the urban agglomeration at issue in its schedule.

The law defined urban land by reference to land identified in a master plan where one existed, and provided a local-authority-limits alternative where no master plan existed or it did not identify land as urban.
The High Court held that the law could not apply to the urban agglomeration because of a claimed deficiency concerning its master plan.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(o) and 2(n) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 provide the relevant definitions of urban land and urban agglomeration.
