predicates.original_ejectment_application: The landlord is initiating an original application seeking an order of ejectment rather than enforcing an existing decree.
predicates.transitional_challenge_not_pursued: The judgment-debtor did not use an available transitional procedure to challenge the existing decree.

members.legal_issue: A civil court retains jurisdiction over a claim to recover land or evict a tenant, and a patta does not nullify a civil decree on that claim.
material_facts: A landholder brought a civil suit seeking recovery of land from a tenant on grounds including non-payment of rent, and obtained a decree.
Before the decree, a settlement authority had issued a joint patta identifying the tenant in relation to the building and the landholder in relation to the site.
The execution court treated the patta as changing the tenant's status and preventing execution of the decree.
The civil claim concerned recovery and eviction, matters not determined by the patta grant.
members.legal_principle: Sections 43(1) and 43(2) of the Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 make decisions binding only on matters within the respective statutory and civil-court jurisdictions. Section 46 gives finality to decisions only on matters to be determined for the purposes of the Act. The Court relied on State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam, AIR 1986 SC 794, and distinguished Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu, [1991] 2 SCR 531, because the dispute here concerned a landlord's claim to recover land from a tenant rather than a matter entrusted to the settlement authorities.
members.conclusion: The civil court's jurisdiction was not ousted, and the patta did not make the decree a nullity or prevent its execution; the matter was remitted for fresh disposal.

predicates.civil_recovery_or_eviction_proceeding: A civil proceeding seeks recovery of land or eviction of a tenant.
predicates.civil_decree_on_recovery_or_eviction: A civil court has issued a decree deciding the recovery or eviction claim.
predicates.revenue_patta_does_not_determine_that_cl: A revenue authority has issued a patta, but its decision does not address the civil recovery or eviction claim.

members.legal_issue: A civil court retains jurisdiction over a commercial loan-recovery suit when the claim does not arise under agricultural-tenancy law and the security is merely collateral to the debt.
material_facts: A bank advanced a demand loan to an agriculturist in the ordinary course of its commercial business, and the borrower executed a promissory note.
The borrower hypothecated standing crops and mortgaged agricultural land as security for repayment; two other defendants guaranteed repayment.
After the loan was not repaid, the bank sued to recover the debt on the promissory note and guarantees, with sale of the mortgaged property sought only if the decree was not paid.
The suit was primarily for recovery of the loan and was not a suit to enforce a mortgage created under the agricultural-tenancy legislation.
No applicable listed suit or other remedy under that legislation covered the bank’s commercial debt-recovery claim.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 207 and 256 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, civil-court jurisdiction is barred for suits specified in the Third Schedule, suits based on a cause of action for which relief could be obtained in such a suit, and matters arising under the Act for which it provides a remedy. Entry 35 of the Third Schedule applies only to a matter arising under the Act. Section 43 concerns specified mortgages or hypothecations of tenancy interests for obtaining specified loans; a commercial bank loan does not become a matter arising under the Act merely because agricultural land is offered as collateral. Jurisdiction depends on the substance, not the form, of the suit. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the bank’s suit. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the trial court’s judgment was restored.

rule.if: civil_recovery_suit and commercial_lending_transaction and primary_claim_is_debt_repayment and security_is_collateral and claim_outside_special_tenancy_remedies

predicates.civil_recovery_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking recovery of a debt.
predicates.commercial_lending_transaction: A lender advanced money in the ordinary course of its commercial lending business.
predicates.primary_claim_is_debt_repayment: The claim was primarily based on the borrower’s promise to repay and any guarantees, rather than on enforcement of security.
predicates.security_is_collateral: The borrower provided property or other security only as collateral for repayment of the debt.
predicates.claim_outside_special_tenancy_remedies: The debt-recovery claim did not concern a matter arising under the special agricultural-tenancy regime and was not one for which that regime provided a remedy.

members.legal_issue: A civil court retains jurisdiction over a suit to recover agricultural land from a trespasser when no issue requiring decision by the special tenancy forum arises.
material_facts: The court considered a suit seeking recovery of agricultural land from a person alleged to be a trespasser.
The court distinguished cases in which no dispute arises that must be decided by the special machinery under the tenancy law.
members.legal_principle: The tenancy law excludes civil-court jurisdiction only over questions assigned to the special forum. The Court stated that a suit to recover agricultural land from a trespasser may continue in the civil court if no such question arises.
members.conclusion: If no issue assigned to the special forum arises, the civil court continues to have jurisdiction to decide the possession dispute and grant appropriate relief.

predicates.suit_to_recover_agricultural_land_from_a: A plaintiff brings a civil suit seeking possession of agricultural land from a defendant alleged to be a trespasser.
predicates.no_special_forum_issue_arises: No question arises that the governing tenancy law assigns to a special forum.

members.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate for failure to substitute the legal representatives of a deceased respondent who is unnecessary to the dispute and whose absence cannot produce contradictory decrees.
material_facts: A respondent died while the appeal was pending, and the application to substitute that respondent’s legal representatives was dismissed.
The decree under appeal granted relief against other defendants, not the deceased respondent.
The relief sought in the appeal could be granted between the remaining parties without contradictory decrees.
members.legal_principle: An appeal may proceed without substituting the legal representatives of a deceased party where that party is unnecessary to the dispute and effective relief can be granted among the remaining parties without inconsistent decrees.
members.conclusion: The appeal did not abate because the deceased respondent was unnecessary to its determination.

predicates.appeal_pending_after_party_death: An appeal remains pending when one of its parties dies.
predicates.deceased_party_unnecessary: The deceased party is not necessary to decide the dispute or grant the relief sought.
predicates.relief_severable_without_conflicting_dec: The appeal can be resolved among the remaining parties without producing contradictory decrees.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a deceased defendant’s heirs from an appeal does not defeat the appellants’ claim to dismissal of a suit when the plaintiffs sought no relief against that defendant or those heirs and the relief they sought cannot be granted.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought declaratory relief against the original alienees, asserting that their alienation was not binding, and claimed title to the disputed land.
Although other transferees were joined as parties, the plaintiffs sought no relief against them and pleaded no circumstances explaining their joinder.
The heirs of one such transferee were not brought onto the appellate record; the Court concluded that the plaintiffs’ requested relief against the original alienees could not be granted.
members.legal_principle: Whether the absence of a deceased party’s heirs affects an appeal depends on the relief claimed. Where the plaintiffs claim relief only against the alienees, claim no relief against the deceased party or successors, and cannot obtain the relief sought against the alienees, the omission of those heirs does not prevent the alienees from seeking dismissal. No earlier cases or statutory provisions are cited.
members.conclusion: The absence of the deceased defendant’s heirs did not affect the appellants’ right to seek dismissal of the appeal.

predicates.appeal_involves_nonjoinder_of_deceased_p: The proceeding is an appeal in which the heirs of a deceased party have not been joined.
predicates.plaintiffs_claim_relief_only_against_ali: The plaintiffs seek relief only against the persons who acquired the property through the alienation.
predicates.relief_against_alienees_cannot_be_grante: The relief sought by the plaintiffs against those alienees cannot be granted.

members.legal_issue: An eviction appeal survives the death of a respondent, and the respondent’s legal representatives may raise defenses appropriate to their representative character, but not defenses personal to the deceased.
material_facts: The tenant died while the landlord’s appeal was pending, and the tenant’s heirs were brought on record as legal representatives.
The landlord’s right to pursue the appeal for possession survived the tenant’s death.
The heirs could challenge the termination notice as representatives, but the defense based on the landlord’s personal requirement was personal to the deceased tenant.
members.legal_principle: Order 22 Rules 4 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provide for continuation of a proceeding when the right to sue or appeal survives and permit a legal representative to make a defense appropriate to that character. The Court also recognized that a representative may assert an independent title in a personal capacity, avoiding a separate suit for that determination.
members.conclusion: The appeal could proceed against the legal representatives, who could raise contentions appropriate to their representative character but not contentions personal to the deceased; they could also assert an independent title in their own right.

predicates.eviction_appeal: The matter is an appeal in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.respondent_died_during_appeal: The respondent died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_substituted: The deceased respondent’s legal representatives were brought on record.

members.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate on the death of a respondent when a legal representative is already on record, and remaining representatives may be brought on record after remand.
material_facts: The plaintiff died while the appeals were pending.
His wife was already on record in connected appeals or suits, and the related matters had been clubbed for disposal.
The Supreme Court remanded the pending appeals, allowing consequential steps to bring any remaining legal representatives on record.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances, the presence of one legal representative on record meant the appeal did not abate; the connected proceedings and the opportunity to take consequential steps after remand also supported that conclusion. The judgment cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeals had not abated. The parties could amend the cause title after remand to substitute the surviving wife and any other legal representatives before the second appeals were heard.

rule.if: appeal_pending and respondent_died_during_appeal and legal_representative_already_on_record and (connected_proceedings_grouped or remand_allows_remaining_representatives_to_be_added)

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal is pending when a respondent dies.
predicates.respondent_died_during_appeal: A respondent dies while the appeal is pending.
predicates.legal_representative_already_on_record: At least one legal representative of the deceased respondent is already a party on the record.
predicates.connected_proceedings_grouped: The appeal is being dealt with together with connected proceedings involving the deceased respondent’s legal representative.
predicates.remand_allows_remaining_representatives_: The matter is remanded in circumstances that allow any remaining legal representatives to be added before further hearing.

members.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate in its entirety when a deceased appellant’s interest concerns identifiable property independent of the interests of the other appellants, and the delay in substitution is not excused.
material_facts: A deceased appellant was the donee of specified properties under a separate gift deed, distinct from the properties given to the other donees.
The applications to bring the deceased appellant’s legal representative on record were filed after an unexplained delay of more than twenty-five years.
The decree concerned several reversioners and independent donees with specified interests in identifiable properties.
members.legal_principle: Where a decree is divisible and the deceased party’s interest relates to specific property independent of the other parties’ interests, the abatement is limited to that interest; an unexplained inordinate delay in seeking substitution need not be condoned.
members.conclusion: The delay was not condoned, and the appeal abated only in respect of the properties gifted to the deceased appellant, not as a whole.

rule.if: appeal_from_multi_party_decree and decree_is_divisible and deceased_appellant_had_independent_property_interest and substitution_delay_is_unexplained

predicates.appeal_from_multi_party_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree involving multiple parties.
predicates.decree_is_divisible: The decree separates the parties’ interests into identifiable portions that can be dealt with independently.
predicates.deceased_appellant_had_independent_prope: The deceased appellant held an interest in specified property distinct from the interests of the other appellants.
predicates.substitution_delay_is_unexplained: The party seeking substitution does not provide a satisfactory explanation for the substantial delay.

members.legal_issue: The appeal does not abate as a whole when deceased plaintiffs’ unrepresented interests concern management of property.
material_facts: Some plaintiffs died while the appeal was pending, and their legal representatives were not brought on record.
The plaintiffs had been held to be descendants of the property’s Mutawalis, whose position was managerial.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the Mutawali position as a managerial post and held that the deaths and failure to substitute the deceased plaintiffs’ legal representatives did not cause the appeal as a whole to abate.
members.conclusion: The appeal did not abate as a whole because the interests in question were managerial in nature.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the disputed property is pending.
predicates.deceased_claimants_not_substituted: Some claimants have died during the appeal and their legal representatives have not been brought on record.
predicates.claim_concerns_managerial_position: The claimants’ relevant interest concerns a managerial position relating to the property.

members.legal_issue: An appeal against the remaining defendants may proceed when it has been dismissed as against a respondent who is not a necessary party.
material_facts: The plaintiffs appealed the dismissal of their suit and included the deity as a respondent, although they sought no relief against it.
The appeal was dismissed as against the deity because the plaintiffs did not pay the guardian’s costs.
No party to the appeal had died.
members.legal_principle: A dismissal of an appeal as against a respondent who is not a necessary party does not make the appeal incompetent against the other respondents. Abatement does not arise where no party has died.
members.conclusion: The appeal had not abated, either wholly or in part, and the plaintiffs could prosecute it against the contesting defendants without the deity.

rule.if: civil_appeal and respondent_not_necessary_party and appeal_dismissed_as_to_respondent_for_costs and no_party_died

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a civil suit.
predicates.respondent_not_necessary_party: The respondent against whom the appeal was dismissed was not necessary to determine the relief sought against the other respondents.
predicates.appeal_dismissed_as_to_respondent_for_co: The appeal was dismissed as against that respondent because the appellant did not pay the costs required for the respondent’s representation.
predicates.no_party_died: No party to the appeal died.
predicates.appeal_remains_competent_against_other_p: The appeal may proceed against the other parties.

members.legal_issue: An appeal is not a nullity merely because a person who died before its filing is named as a respondent, if the appeal can proceed against the surviving respondents.
material_facts: The widow died before the petition of appeal was filed in the Supreme Court.
The deceased widow was nevertheless named as a respondent in that petition.
The alienees who were surviving respondents remained parties to the appeal.
members.legal_principle: A person who has died before an appeal is filed cannot be shown as a party respondent. That defect does not prevent the appeal from proceeding against the surviving respondents where it can be adjudicated against them. The Court also noted that the appeal against the deceased respondent had abated after no substitution order was obtained under Order XVI, rule 12(a) of the Supreme Court Rules.
members.conclusion: The deceased person could not be a respondent, but the appeal could proceed against the other respondents on the footing that the deceased person was not a party.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party filed an appeal seeking relief against other parties to the dispute.
predicates.person_died_before_appeal_filing: A person named as a respondent had died before the appeal was filed.
predicates.surviving_respondents_remain: Other respondents against whom the appeal can proceed remained parties.

members.legal_issue: The abatement of an appeal concerning one claimant does not require dismissal of the entire appeal when the claims are distinct and severable and the remaining relief can be granted without producing unenforceable or contradictory decrees.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned the apportionment of compensation among numerous claimants asserting distinct shares in acquired land.
The claimants’ individual claims were combined and decided together because they raised similar issues, but each claimant could have pursued a separate claim and appeal without joining the others.
Five appellants died during the appeals, and their legal representatives were not brought on record within time.
The claims of the remaining appellants were independent, and a decision on those claims could be enforced without negating a decree concerning a deceased appellant.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, abatement as to one party does not automatically abate an appeal as to others. Whether the remaining appeal can proceed depends on the nature of the rights and relief and whether a decree for the remaining parties would be unenforceable or mutually destructive of a decree that has become final. The Court applied the principles in Nathu Ram v. State of Punjab, Ram Sarup v. Munshi, Harihar Prasad Singh v. Balmiki Prasad Singh, and Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. Ram Adhar Singh. It also relied on Sections 11, 18, 30 and 31 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, concerning awards, references and apportionment, and held that consolidated adjudication of distinct compensation claims does not by itself make them a joint and inseverable claim.
members.conclusion: The appeals did not abate in their entirety because of the deaths and non-substitution of the five appellants; they could proceed on the merits for the remaining claimants.

predicates.appeal_from_consolidated_multi_claim_adj: The proceeding is an appeal from a decision that dealt together with claims made by multiple claimants.
predicates.claimants_hold_independent_severable_rig: Each claimant asserts an individual right that can be decided without determining or impairing the rights of the other claimants.
predicates.one_party_dies_without_substitution: A party to the appeal dies and that party’s legal representatives are not brought on record in time.
predicates.remaining_relief_can_be_enforced_without: Relief for the remaining parties can be enforced without negating or making unenforceable a decree concerning the deceased party.

members.legal_issue: The death of a claimant does not require dismissal of an entire appeal when the remaining claimants assert distinct, independent rights and relief for them can be granted without producing an unenforceable or contradictory decree.
material_facts: The compensation apportionment proceedings involved claimants asserting specified, separate shares in the acquired land.
The claimants’ separate claims were heard together and decided in consolidated proceedings.
Five appellants died during the High Court appeals, and their legal representatives were not brought on record within time.
Other appellants had surviving claims based on their own shares, which they could have pursued separately.
The High Court treated the appeals as wholly abated and also dismissed connected appeals raising similar issues.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, abatement against one party does not automatically abate an appeal against others. Whether an appeal can continue depends on the nature of the rights, claims, relief, and decree, including whether granting relief to the surviving parties would make the decree unenforceable or contradictory to a decree that has become final. The Court applied the principles in Nathu Ram v. State of Punjab, Ram Sarup v. Munshi, Harihar Prasad Singh v. Balmiki Prasad Singh, and Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. Ram Adhar Singh, distinguishing cases involving joint and indivisible rights. Sections 11, 18, 30 and 31 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, support treating compensation apportionment as a determination of the respective entitlements of interested persons.
members.conclusion: The appeals did not abate in their entirety merely because the claims of some deceased appellants could not be continued; the surviving appellants’ claims could proceed, and the High Court’s contrary orders were set aside.

rule.if: compensation_apportionment_appeal and claimants_assert_independent_shares and claims_consolidated_for_convenience and some_claimants_unrepresented_after_death and surviving_relief_independently_enforceable

predicates.compensation_apportionment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the allocation of compensation among persons claiming an interest in acquired property.
predicates.claimants_assert_independent_shares: The claimants assert distinct shares or rights that do not depend on one another.
predicates.claims_consolidated_for_convenience: Separate claims are joined or decided together for convenience or because they raise similar issues.
predicates.some_claimants_unrepresented_after_death: One or more claimants die during the proceeding and their legal representatives are not brought on record.
predicates.surviving_relief_independently_enforceab: Relief for the remaining claimants can be enforced without negating or making unenforceable relief that has become final for another claimant.

members.legal_issue: The death of one plaintiff does not cause an appeal to abate when the suit was brought in a representative capacity for the general public.
material_facts: The suit was brought by plaintiffs in a representative capacity on behalf of devotees of the religious institution.
One plaintiff died while the second appeal was pending, and no legal representative was substituted for that plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: A suit prosecuted in a representative capacity for the general public is not a suit prosecuted by individuals for their own interests, and the death of one plaintiff does not make the appeal incompetent. The Court followed Raja Anand Rao v. Ramdas Daduram.
members.conclusion: The death of one plaintiff did not cause the appeal to abate.

predicates.representative_public_proceeding: The proceeding is brought by claimants in a representative capacity for the general public.
predicates.representative_dies_during_appeal: One of the representatives dies while the appeal is pending.

members.legal_issue: The death of one among multiple plaintiffs with separate shares does not abate the entire appeal when the surviving plaintiffs substantially represent the deceased plaintiff’s interest.
material_facts: Several plaintiffs brought the suit as successors claiming shares in the same estate.
One plaintiff died while the appeal was pending in the High Court, and that plaintiff’s legal representatives were not substituted.
The surviving plaintiffs had definite shares in the estate and continued the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXII Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where the right to sue survives to the remaining plaintiffs, the proceedings may continue. Whether an appeal abates in its entirety depends on the circumstances, particularly whether the remaining parties’ decree could be contradictory or inconsistent with a decree concerning the deceased party. The Court applied Budh Ram v. Bansi (2010) 11 SCC 476, Sardar Amarjit Singh Kalra v. Pramod Gupta (2003) 3 SCC 72, Harihar Singh v. Balmiki Prasad Singh (1976) 1 SCC 212, and State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram (1962) 2 SCR 636.
members.conclusion: The appeal did not abate as a whole; the surviving plaintiffs were entitled to proceed.

predicates.multiple_plaintiff_appeal: Multiple plaintiffs brought or continued an appeal arising from the same suit.
predicates.plaintiff_dies_during_appeal: One plaintiff died while the appeal was pending and that plaintiff’s legal representatives were not substituted.
predicates.surviving_sharers_represent_estate: The surviving plaintiffs held distinct shares in the estate and substantially represented the deceased plaintiff’s interest.

members.legal_issue: A person whose lease has expired and who remains in possession without the landlord’s consent cannot rely on statutory protection against termination based merely on expiry when that person has no continuing tenancy.
material_facts: The agricultural lease was for five years and included an option to renew, which the tenant did not exercise; under the earlier statutory deeming provision, the lease term was extended to ten years and expired in 1953.
The tenant had been treated as a protected tenant, but that status ended when the trust-related exemption was introduced in 1956.
The tenant remained in possession after the contractual tenancy had ended, and the landlord had not consented to continued possession.
The landlord had given notices seeking termination and possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 4B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 prevents termination of a tenancy merely because its agreed or customary duration has expired; it does not apply where no tenancy exists. Under the common-law distinction applied by the Court, a person remaining in possession after termination without the landlord’s consent is a tenant by sufferance, whereas consent to continued possession is required for a tenant holding over or a tenant at will. The Court relied on the statutory history under section 23(1)(b) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939, and sections 3A, 4A and 88B of the 1948 Act to determine the duration of the lease and the ending of protected status. It expressed no opinion on the application of section 84 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code or section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, and relied on no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The tenant was in possession as a tenant by sufferance, not as a tenant holding over, and section 4B did not apply because no tenancy remained.

rule.if: tenancy_protection_claim and contractual_lease_expired and protected_status_ended and landlord_did_not_consent_to_continued_possession

predicates.tenancy_protection_claim: A person in possession claims legal protection against termination of a tenancy.
predicates.contractual_lease_expired: The agreed lease term, including any applicable statutory extension of that term, has ended.
predicates.protected_status_ended: A statutory status that had protected the occupant’s tenancy has ceased to apply.
predicates.landlord_did_not_consent_to_continued_po: The landlord did not agree to the occupant remaining in possession after the tenancy ended.
predicates.expiry_based_termination_protection_unav: The occupant cannot rely on protection against termination based merely on expiry because no tenancy remains.

members.legal_issue: A tenant whose oral or unregistered tenancy has expired and who remains in possession only as a tenant in sufferance cannot use rent-control protection to prevent possession under secured-creditor enforcement.
material_facts: The appellant’s alternative account was that the tenancy arose from an oral agreement.
The recovery notice had been issued, and the court found that the alleged oral tenancy carried no implied covenant for renewal.
The appellant had not established a valid continuing lease, and the tenancy relied on had expired by the time of the decision.
members.legal_principle: Sections 13(2) and 13(13) of the SARFAESI Act prevent a borrower from creating further encumbrances after the recovery notice, and Section 35 gives the Act overriding effect over inconsistent laws. Section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act governs the mortgagor’s power to lease; Section 107 addresses the formalities for leases. The court relied on R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P., which describes a tenant in sufferance as one who remains in possession after lawful title expires and notes the little difference between that person and a trespasser. It also referred to Smt. Shanti Devi v. Amal Kumar Banerjee, Murlidhar Jalan v. State of Meghalaya, and D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav. The court applied the overriding effect of the secured-creditor enforcement scheme while recognising that valid tenancy rights under rent legislation must be respected in appropriate cases.
members.conclusion: The appellant, at most, remained as a tenant in sufferance, akin to a trespasser, and could not rely on rent-control protection to prevent delivery of possession to the bank.

predicates.secured_asset_enforcement_proceeding: A secured creditor sought possession of property through proceedings to enforce security over it.
predicates.tenancy_expired: The tenant’s valid term of possession had ended and no valid continuing tenancy was established.
predicates.tenant_remains_only_in_sufferance: The former tenant continued in possession after the lawful tenancy ended without a continuing right to occupy.
predicates.rent_control_protection_does_not_bar_sec: Rent-control protection does not prevent the secured creditor from obtaining possession.

members.legal_issue: A non-statutory tenant whose lease has expired and who remains in possession against the landlord’s wishes is not in lawful possession for the purpose of establishing eligibility for a licence as a non-owner.
material_facts: The applicant was a tenant under a fixed-term lease of the premises and the cinema equipment.
The lease expired, required the tenant to return the property, and the landlord had given notice requiring its return.
The landlord did not assent to the tenant’s continued possession and applied for the licence itself.
The applicant’s only documentary evidence of possession was the expired lease.
The tenancy was not protected by rent-control legislation.
The applicant sought to rely on the protection against forcible dispossession, but the Court found that this protection did not establish lawful possession.
members.legal_principle: Under the second part of Rule 13 of the Madras Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1957, a non-owner must produce documentary evidence, to the licensing authority’s satisfaction, of lawful possession. Lawful possession requires a foundation in a legal right to possess and cannot be equated with juridical possession that merely protects a person against forcible dispossession. Sections 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, prohibit dispossession without due process but do not make continued possession after expiry of a lease lawful. The Court also relied on the lease obligation to return the property and section 108(q) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which requires a lessee, on determination of the lease, to put the lessor in possession. Section 5(1) of the 1955 Act makes the public interest relevant to licensing. The Court distinguished Lalu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, which concerned juridical possession and did not decide whether such possession was lawful for this licensing rule; it also referred to K. K. Verma v. Naraindas Malkani, Yar Mohammad v. Lakshmi Das, Midnapur Zamindary Company Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, and C. Bhavarlal v. Ballay Gounder.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s possession after expiry of the lease was not lawful possession under Rule 13, and the Board of Revenue was right to set aside the renewal.

rule.if: nonowner_cinema_license_application and lease_expired and landlord_withheld_consent and no_statutory_tenancy_protection

predicates.nonowner_cinema_license_application: An applicant who did not own the site, building, or equipment sought a cinema licence and had to establish lawful possession.
predicates.lease_expired: The applicant’s fixed-term lease of the property had ended.
predicates.landlord_withheld_consent: The landlord required return of the property and did not agree to the applicant remaining in possession.
predicates.no_statutory_tenancy_protection: No applicable tenancy law protected the applicant’s continued possession against eviction through lawful process.

members.legal_issue: A statutory tenant whose lease has already determined need not receive a fresh notice to quit before an ejectment action is brought under rent-restriction legislation.
material_facts: The lease expired by efflux of time, and the tenant continued in possession as a statutory tenant.
The landlord commenced an ejectment action under rent-restriction legislation without serving a notice to quit.
The tenant argued that the action was not maintainable without notice.
members.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act concerns termination of a subsisting contractual tenancy by notice; under section 111, a lease may determine by efflux of time or another prescribed mode. Once the lease has determined, the contract has ended, so no further notice is needed to terminate it. The Court followed Kai Khushroo Bezonjee Capadia v. Bai Jerbai Hirjibhoy Warden and affirmed Ganga Dutt Murarka v. Kartik Chandra Das, Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, and Bhaiya Ram v. Mahavir Prasad. It distinguished Mangilal v. Suganchand Rathi, Manujendra Dutt v. Purendu Prosad Roy Chowdhury, and Rawal & Co. v. K. C. Ramachandran, and overruled Lalitha v. Avisumma.
members.conclusion: A fresh notice to quit was not required, and the ejectment action was maintainable without one.

rule.if: rent_act_ejectment_proceeding and lease_already_determined and tenant_remained_as_statutory_tenant and tenant_claimed_notice_was_required

predicates.rent_act_ejectment_proceeding: The landlord brought an ejectment proceeding under legislation protecting tenants from eviction except on specified grounds.
predicates.lease_already_determined: The contractual lease had ended before the ejectment proceeding began.
predicates.tenant_remained_as_statutory_tenant: The tenant remained in possession after the lease ended under statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.tenant_claimed_notice_was_required: The tenant contended that the landlord had to give a notice to quit before bringing the ejectment proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A suit for ejectment following the expiry of a fixed-term lease is maintainable without a notice to quit when the tenancy has not continued by holding over.
material_facts: A registered lease granted possession for a fixed term, with options for two further fixed terms; the lease term commenced when the tenant obtained the required licence.
The lease term expired by efflux of time before the ejectment suit was filed.
The tenant did not claim to be holding over, and there was no allegation that the landlord had assented to continued possession after the lease expired.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 111(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease for a definite term is determined by efflux of time. Section 106 notice is not required when the lease ends in that way. Sections 111(a) and 116 must be read together: continuation by holding over requires possession after determination of the lease and the lessor's express or implied assent. Pleadings cannot alter the intrinsic character of the lease or the rights and obligations arising from it. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The lease expired by efflux of time, so a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 was not necessary and the ejectment suit was maintainable.

rule.if: ejectment_suit_based_on_fixed_term_expiry and fixed_term_lease_expired_by_time and not lessor_assented_to_post_expiry_possession

predicates.ejectment_suit_based_on_fixed_term_expir: The proceeding is an ejectment suit based on the expiry of a fixed-term lease.
predicates.fixed_term_lease_expired_by_time: The lease was for a definite term and that term ended by efflux of time.
predicates.lessor_assented_to_post_expiry_possessio: The lessor expressly or impliedly assented to the tenant's possession after the lease ended.

members.legal_issue: A contractual tenant cannot be treated as a statutory tenant for eviction unless the contractual tenancy has first been terminated by a valid notice or another legally effective mode of termination.
material_facts: The tenant remained in possession under a contractual tenancy after the original fixed term and thereafter held over as a monthly tenant.
The landlord relied on a notice that did not validly terminate the tenancy and argued that the tenant was a statutory tenant for whose eviction no notice was required.
The Supreme Court held that the tenant would become a statutory tenant only if the tenant continued in possession after termination of the contractual tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Under section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a contractual tenancy must be terminated by a valid notice or another mode of termination specified in that section before the tenant can be treated as a statutory tenant on the basis of continued possession after termination. A notice is not required where the lease determines by efflux of the time limited by it. Ganga Dutt Murarka v. Kartik Chandra Das and Pooran Chand v. Motilal were considered but did not support the landlord’s argument; Ganga Dutt Murarka quoted with approval the relevant passage from Kai Khushroo Bezonee Capadia v. Bai Jerbai Hirjibhoy Warden.
members.conclusion: The landlord could not treat the tenant as a statutory tenant or seek eviction on that basis without first terminating the contractual tenancy validly.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and tenant_remains_under_contractual_tenancy and landlord_claims_statutory_tenant_status and contractual_tenancy_not_validly_terminated

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The landlord is seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.tenant_remains_under_contractual_tenancy: The tenant remains in possession under a contractual tenancy that has not yet ended.
predicates.landlord_claims_statutory_tenant_status: The landlord seeks to treat the tenant as a statutory tenant for the purpose of eviction.
predicates.contractual_tenancy_not_validly_terminat: The contractual tenancy has not been terminated by a valid notice or another legally effective mode of termination.

members.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on a landlord’s right to evict a tenant does not displace a contractual requirement to give notice before seeking possession.
material_facts: The proceeding was a landlord’s suit to evict a tenant under a rent-protection law.
The lease required the landlord to give the tenant six months’ notice before requiring the tenant to vacate, including where the lease was not renewed.
The landlord sought eviction on grounds provided by the rent-protection law, but did not give the required notice.
The tenant relied on the lease’s notice requirement.
members.legal_principle: The court construed section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, as imposing additional restrictions on eviction rather than granting landlords new rights or displacing contractual rights. Its non-obstante clause means that a landlord otherwise entitled to possession must still establish a statutory ground for eviction; it does not eliminate a contractual notice requirement. The court relied on Meghji Lakshamshi and Bros. v. Furniture Workshop, Abasbhai v. Gulamnabi, Mangilal v. Sugan Chand, Haji Mohammad v. Rebati Bhushan, and Monmatha Nath v. Banarasi, and considered the contrary view in R. Krishnamurthy v. Parthasarathy incorrect. It also referred to section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in explaining the general requirement to terminate a contractual tenancy before seeking possession.
members.conclusion: The statutory eviction grounds did not excuse compliance with the lease’s notice requirement, and the eviction suit could not succeed because the required notice had not been given.

predicates.eviction_suit_under_rent_protection_law: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant under a rent-protection law.
predicates.lease_requires_notice: The lease required the landlord to give notice before requiring the tenant to vacate.
predicates.required_notice_not_given: The landlord did not give the notice required by the lease before seeking eviction.

members.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction on a ground established under a rent control statute need not first terminate the tenancy by a notice under the general property-transfer law, unless the rent statute itself requires a notice.
material_facts: The landlord applied to evict the tenant under the applicable rent control statute on the ground of personal necessity.

The appellate court found that the premises were bona fide required for personal necessity but dismissed the application because it considered a notice to quit necessary and the notice given defective.
The High Court held that a notice under the general property-transfer law was not required to seek eviction under the rent control statute.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 106 and 111(h) of the Transfer of Property Act, notice may determine a lease where the lease has not otherwise determined. But where a rent control statute permits eviction only on specified grounds, establishing a statutory ground is sufficient; determining the contractual tenancy by a section 106 notice is unnecessary. A notice specifically required by the rent statute must still be given. The Court relied on Rai Brij Raj Krishna v. S. K. Shaw and Brothers, Raval and Co. v. K. G. Ramachandran, Shri Hem Chand v. Shrimati Sham Devi, and Puwada Venkateswara Rao v. Chidamana Venkata Ramana, among other authorities, and rejected earlier decisions on the section 106 notice question, including Bhaiya Punjalal Bhagwanddin, Mangilal, Manujendra Dutt, Isha Valimohamad, P. J. Gupta, Dattopant Gopalyarao Devakate, Ratan Lal, and Sardarilal Vishwanath.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was not necessary to obtain an eviction order under the rent control statute and affirmed the High Court on that point.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and statutory_eviction_ground_established and tenant_continues_under_rent_act and not rent_act_specific_notice_required

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought to evict a tenant under a rent control statute.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_established: The landlord established a ground for eviction specified by the rent control statute.
predicates.tenant_continues_under_rent_act: The rent control statute treats the occupier as a tenant after contractual termination and limits eviction to statutory grounds.
predicates.rent_act_specific_notice_required: The rent control statute expressly requires a particular notice before the landlord may obtain the relief sought.
predicates.section_106_notice_not_required: The landlord may seek eviction without first giving a notice under the general property-transfer law.

members.legal_issue: A special statutory proceeding for eviction that provides a complete procedure does not require a separate notice terminating the tenancy under the general property law.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction through a statutory rent-control proceeding after the tenant defaulted on rent.
The statute provided a special procedure for eviction and contained the requirements for that procedure.

The landlord had sent a notice terminating the tenancy, but the court proceeded on the basis that the statutory eviction process did not require compliance with the general property-law notice provision.
members.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, where the statute provides a complete special procedure for eviction, a separate notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is unnecessary. The Court relied on the principle applied in Ulligamma v. S. Mohan Rao, and on Raval & Co. v. K. C. Ramachandran and Shri Hem Chand v. Shrimati Sham Devi. It distinguished Mangilal v. Sugan Chand Rathi, which concerned an ordinary civil suit and a statutory provision that merely barred such suits subject to exceptions.
members.conclusion: The special statutory eviction proceeding did not require a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act; the High Court correctly applied that principle, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.special_statutory_eviction_proceeding: The party seeking eviction pursued a special statutory proceeding for eviction of a tenant.
predicates.complete_statutory_eviction_process: The statutory process provided the requirements for obtaining eviction through that proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A subletting completed before a law's commencement cannot support eviction merely because the sublease continues afterward, but it can support eviction if a valid retrospective extension makes the law operative before the subletting occurred.
material_facts: The subletting was found to have occurred in 1967.
The rent-control law was first extended to the cantonment prospectively in 1969.
A later notification extended the law retrospectively, with the result that the law was deemed to have commenced there in 1950.
The sublease continued after the law became operative.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 refers to a subletting transaction completed after commencement; subletting is located at the point when the transaction is completed, rather than being a continuing transaction. Although the words “has sub-let” imply that an earlier sublease must subsist when the law commences, the clause's express reference to acts after commencement excludes a transaction completed before commencement. Goppulal v. Thakurji Shriji Shriji Dwarkadheeshji was distinguished because the provision considered there did not contain the same commencement limitation. The amended Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957 authorized retrospective extension, and the later notification made the rent law operative from a date before the subletting.
members.conclusion: Because the valid retrospective extension made the law operative before the 1967 subletting, the landlord could rely on the statutory ground of subletting.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.subletting_is_a_completed_transaction: The tenant completed the act transferring possession by subletting at a definite point in time.
predicates.retrospective_extension_validly_makes_la: A valid retrospective extension made the rent-control law operative before the tenant completed the subletting.

members.legal_issue: The statutory ground of eviction for unauthorized subletting applies to a subletting made before the rent-control statute came into force if the subletting continued into the relevant present period.
material_facts: The tenant had sublet two shops without the landlord’s permission.
The subletting occurred at some point before the rent-control statute came into force, though its precise date was not established.
The landlord sought eviction under the statutory ground for a tenant who has sublet premises without permission.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, uses the words “has sub-let,” which encompass a subletting made in the past and continuing into the present, whether it began before or after the Act came into force. Sections 26 and 27(1) contemplate that grounds of eviction under section 13 may have arisen before the Act commenced. A tenant’s right to sublet under section 108(j) of the Transfer of Property Act does not prevent eviction under section 13(1)(e) when the subletting was without the landlord’s permission.
members.conclusion: The unauthorized subletting could support eviction even if it began before the statute came into force, provided it continued into the present period contemplated by the statutory wording.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_sublet_without_permission: The tenant sublet the premises without the landlord’s permission.
predicates.subletting_continued_into_relevant_prese: The subletting began in the past and continued into the period relevant to the eviction claim.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may pursue eviction under a replacement rent-control enactment for subletting that occurred while the repealed enactment was in force.
material_facts: The tenant’s alleged subletting occurred before the 1959 rent-control enactment was repealed.
The landlord instituted the eviction proceeding after the 1965 enactment came into force.
The former enactment permitted an eviction application on the ground of unauthorized subletting, and the replacement enactment contained an analogous provision.
members.legal_principle: Section 34(1) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, including its proviso, preserved proceedings that could have been brought under the repealed Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1959, for institution under corresponding provisions of the new Act. Section 4 of the Kerala Interpretation and General Clauses Act, 1125, also applied because no contrary intention appeared. The former Act’s section 11(4) was a corresponding provision to the new Act’s section 11(4): corresponding means similar or analogous, not identical. The new Act’s section 11(1) did not displace that saving.
members.conclusion: The saving provision allowed the landlord to pursue eviction under the corresponding provision of the replacement enactment for subletting that occurred under the former enactment.

rule.if: post_repeal_eviction_proceeding and pre_repeal_subletting and old_law_subletting_ground and analogous_new_law_ground

predicates.post_repeal_eviction_proceeding: A landlord instituted an eviction proceeding after a former rent-control enactment had been replaced.
predicates.pre_repeal_subletting: The tenant sublet the premises before the former enactment was replaced.
predicates.old_law_subletting_ground: The former enactment permitted eviction proceedings on the ground of unauthorized subletting.
predicates.analogous_new_law_ground: The replacement enactment contained a provision analogous to the former enactment’s subletting ground.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may enforce a permission to evict that became final under the former rent-control law through an application under the successor law even if a suit based on that permission was filed and dismissed on a technical ground.
material_facts: Permission to seek eviction was granted under the former law and became final after a revision was rejected.
The landlord filed a suit relying on that permission, but the suit was dismissed on a technical ground without a decision on the merits.
The landlord then applied for eviction under the successor law, and the application was rejected on the ground that the permission had been exhausted by filing the suit.
The successor law’s transitional provision was amended to apply whether or not a suit had been instituted, and the amendment was retrospective.
members.legal_principle: Section 43(2)(rr) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 enabled enforcement of a final permission obtained under section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947. The 1976 amendment, which applied whether or not a suit had been instituted, operated retrospectively. A permission granted to achieve eviction is not exhausted when that purpose remains unfulfilled and the suit based on it was dismissed on a technical ground. The Court approved Pahlad Das v. Ganga Saran, AIR 1958 Allahabad 774, and referred to D.K. Soni v. P.K. Mukherjee for the importance of finality in judicial proceedings.
members.conclusion: The application was maintainable. The earlier suit’s technical dismissal did not exhaust the permission or prevent the landlord from seeking eviction under the successor law.

rule.if: transitional_eviction_application and final_former_law_permission and prior_suit_dismissed_on_technical_ground and eviction_not_completed

predicates.transitional_eviction_application: A landlord sought eviction through an application under a successor law that provides for enforcement of a final permission obtained under the former law.
predicates.final_former_law_permission: The permission to seek eviction under the former law had become final.
predicates.prior_suit_dismissed_on_technical_ground: The landlord had filed a suit relying on the permission, and the suit was dismissed on a technical ground without a decision on the merits.
predicates.eviction_not_completed: The tenant had not been evicted, so the purpose for which the permission was granted remained unfulfilled.

members.legal_issue: Written consent to sublet that was given for the contractual tenancy does not authorize a new subletting after that tenancy expires, although the continued possession of a subtenant lawfully inducted during the consent period is not itself a fresh subletting.
material_facts: The tenancy terms gave the tenant an option to sublet during the specified contractual tenancy period.
The contractual tenancy period expired before the tenant inducted a new subtenant into a shop.
The applicable rental law at the time required the landlord’s written consent for subletting.
The earlier subtenancy in that shop had ended before the new subtenancy began, and no written consent for the new subletting was in force.
members.legal_principle: Under clause (iii) of Section 9(2) of the Bangalore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1946, written landlord consent was required for subletting. The landlord’s consent is a voluntary act and, when given for the contractual tenancy, does not ordinarily extend beyond the period for which it was given; statutory tenancy does not continue that permission or confer a right to create a new subtenancy. In Mahabir Prasad Verma v. Dr. Surinder Kaur, a subtenancy created with written consent during the contractual term remained lawful after that term ended, and mere continued possession was not a fresh subletting. The Court distinguished that situation from the new post-expiry subletting here. The Court also explained that Damadilal v. Parashram and the related decisions on the heritable nature of statutory tenancy did not establish a right to create a new subtenancy after contractual tenancy expired.
members.conclusion: The new subletting was unlawful and constituted a ground for eviction.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding under rent-control law.
predicates.subletting_created_after_contractual_ter: The tenant created a new subtenancy after the contractual tenancy had ended.
predicates.prior_written_consent_limited_to_contrac: The landlord’s written permission to sublet was given for the contractual term and did not extend beyond it.
predicates.applicable_rental_law_required_written_c: The rental law governing the creation of the subtenancy required the landlord’s written consent for subletting.

members.legal_issue: A subletting created with the landlord’s written consent while the contractual tenancy subsists does not become unauthorized merely because the contractual tenancy later ends, and continued possession by the lawfully inducted subtenant does not itself establish a new subletting.
material_facts: The written rent agreement authorized the tenant to sublet specified portions of the premises.
The subtenants were inducted in April, while the contractual tenancy was subsisting and the landlord’s written consent was in force.
The finding that further subletting occurred after the contractual tenancy ended was unsupported by proper evidence.
The subtenants continued in possession after the contractual tenancy ended.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 makes unauthorized subletting after commencement of the Act a ground for eviction. Read with the Act’s definitions of landlord and tenant in sections 2(c) and 2(i), a subtenant inducted lawfully with written consent is a tenant under the Act and receives its protection against eviction. Continued possession after the contractual tenancy ends is not a fresh subletting. The judgment discusses V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal and Damadilal v. Parashram in relation to protection after contractual tenancy; it does not decide whether a tenant may create a new subtenancy after that tenancy ends.
members.conclusion: The tenant had not sublet any portion without the landlord’s written consent, so the landlord had no ground to evict the tenant for subletting; the eviction order was set aside.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and written_subletting_consent and subtenant_inducted_during_contractual_tenancy and no_fresh_unauthorized_subletting

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant on a ground relating to subletting.
predicates.written_subletting_consent: The landlord gave written consent for the tenant to sublet the relevant portion.
predicates.subtenant_inducted_during_contractual_te: The tenant inducted the subtenant while the contractual tenancy was still subsisting.
predicates.no_fresh_unauthorized_subletting: After the original lawful subletting, the tenant did not create a new subletting without the landlord’s written consent; the subtenant’s continued possession alone did not involve a new induction.

members.legal_issue: Comparative hardship favors eviction where refusal would leave the landlord without premises for the proposed business while the tenant has other business premises and uses the disputed premises only for storage.
material_facts: The landlord had no other premises for his son's proposed business.
The tenant had purchased adjoining property, had other premises from which he ran his business, and used the disputed premises only to store spare parts.
The tenant was described as a prosperous businessman.
members.legal_principle: In assessing the parties' circumstances on the eviction claim, the Court compared the hardship that refusal or grant of eviction would cause. It found greater hardship to the landlord because he had no alternative premises for the proposed business, whereas the tenant had other premises for his business and used the disputed premises only for storage.
members.conclusion: The landlord would suffer greater hardship if eviction were refused.

rule.if: eviction_application_for_proposed_business and landlord_has_no_alternative_premises and tenant_has_other_business_premises and disputed_premises_used_only_for_storage

predicates.eviction_application_for_proposed_busine: A landlord applied to evict a tenant so the premises could be used for a proposed business.
predicates.landlord_has_no_alternative_premises: The landlord had no other premises available for the proposed business.
predicates.tenant_has_other_business_premises: The tenant had other premises from which the tenant ran the business.
predicates.disputed_premises_used_only_for_storage: The tenant used the premises in dispute only to store goods or parts.

members.legal_issue: A landlord may obtain eviction for personal occupation when the need is reasonable and bona fide and refusing eviction would cause the landlord greater hardship than granting it would cause the tenant.
material_facts: The landlady lived with several family members in a small apartment with one bedroom, while another son lived separately with his own family.
The tenant occupied a flat in the same locality that he admitted had a kitchen and three rooms.
The landlady sought additional accommodation for her family, and the tenant produced no evidence that her demand was made for an oblique motive.
The circumstances showed that refusing eviction would leave the landlady’s family facing greater hardship than the tenant would face upon eviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 requires a reasonable and bona fide need for the landlord’s occupation. Under Section 13(2), eviction is barred if the tenant would suffer greater hardship from eviction than the landlord would suffer from refusal. Reasonableness depends on the circumstances of the case; the Court relied on Krishchand Moorjimal v. Bai Kalavati, Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Jagan Nath Ashok Kumar, and Gujarat Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. Unique Erectors (Gujarat) Pvt. Ltd. The circumstances supported a presumption of bona fides, which remained unrebutted in the absence of evidence of an oblique motive.
members.conclusion: The landlady’s need was reasonable and bona fide, and the comparative hardship did not bar eviction; the eviction decree was restored.

predicates.personal_occupation_eviction_claim: A landlord seeks eviction so that the landlord can occupy the rented premises.
predicates.landlord_has_inadequate_accommodation_fo: The landlord’s existing accommodation is inadequate for the size or needs of the household.
predicates.tenant_has_not_shown_oblique_motive: The tenant has produced no evidence that the landlord’s demand is made for an improper or oblique purpose.
predicates.landlord_would_suffer_greater_hardship_t: Refusing eviction would cause the landlord greater hardship than granting eviction would cause the tenant.
predicates.eviction_for_landlords_occupation_is_jus: The landlord is entitled to eviction for the landlord’s occupation.

members.legal_issue: A decree for eviction on the ground of bona fide personal requirement is not barred by the comparative-hardship requirement when refusing the decree would cause greater hardship to the landlord than granting it would cause to the tenant.
material_facts: The appellate court found that the landlady would suffer greater hardship if the decree were refused than the tenants would suffer if it were granted.
That finding had become final by the time the matter was considered by the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, bars a decree under Section 13(1)(g) when the court is satisfied, considering all the circumstances including the availability of other reasonable accommodation, that greater hardship would result from granting the decree than from refusing it. The final finding that refusal would cause greater hardship to the landlord satisfied this requirement. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The comparative-hardship requirement was satisfied, so it did not prevent a decree for eviction.

predicates.tenant_eviction_case_for_personal_use: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground that the premises were required for personal occupation.
predicates.finding_that_refusal_causes_greater_land: The court found that refusing eviction would cause the landlord greater hardship than granting it would cause the tenant.
predicates.comparative_hardship_does_not_bar_evicti: The comparative-hardship assessment does not prevent the eviction decree.

members.legal_issue: Comparative hardship supports eviction when refusing possession would cause hardship to the landlord and the evidence shows that eviction would not cause hardship to the tenants.
material_facts: The landlord had no other premises of his own and wished to move from a home in an unhygienic location near a drain.
The evidence showed that the tenants would not be put to hardship by eviction from their respective premises.
The High Court considered the circumstances of each tenancy, and the Supreme Court accepted that assessment.
members.legal_principle: In deciding whether eviction is justified, the court must assess the comparative hardship to the landlord and the tenants on the evidence. The Court applied that assessment to the landlord’s lack of other premises and the evidence that the tenants would not be put to hardship. No earlier case was cited for this issue.
members.conclusion: The landlord would suffer hardship if unable to move to the premises, while the tenants would not suffer hardship from eviction; comparative hardship therefore did not prevent eviction.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of tenants through a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.landlord_would_suffer_hardship_without_p: The landlord would face hardship if unable to obtain possession of the premises sought.
predicates.tenants_would_not_suffer_hardship_from_e: The evidence showed that eviction would not cause hardship to the tenants.

members.legal_issue: In an eviction proceeding, partial eviction must be assessed by objectively determining the landlord’s reasonable requirement and whether that requirement would be substantially satisfied by evicting the tenant from only part of the premises.
material_facts: The trial court assessed partial eviction in light of the landlord’s stated requirement, without applying the statutory test of reasonable requirement and substantial satisfaction.
The High Court accepted the trial court’s finding without addressing that test.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 12(1)(c) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1977 requires the court, where the tenant agrees to remain in the rest of the building, to consider whether the landlord’s reasonable requirement would be substantially—not necessarily fully—satisfied by partial eviction. The requirement must be assessed objectively, not by the landlord’s mere desire or assertion.
members.conclusion: The courts must objectively determine the extent of the premises reasonably required and whether partial eviction would substantially satisfy that requirement; the matter was remanded for fresh consideration on the evidence.

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a landlord seeking eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.partial_occupation_would_substantially_s: The court determines that evicting the tenant from only part of the premises would substantially satisfy the landlord’s objectively assessed reasonable requirement.
predicates.tenant_agrees_to_remain_in_rest: The tenant agrees to continue occupying the remaining part of the premises.

members.legal_issue: A court must make a fact-specific inquiry into partial eviction before ordering eviction from the entire premises when the landlord’s need is proved and the tenant agrees to continue in part; it cannot presume that partial eviction is impracticable merely because the premises comprise one room.
material_facts: The premises consisted of a shop measuring 24 by 22 feet with an attached verandah measuring 6 by 22 feet, where the tenant operated a restaurant.
The landlord sought eviction to meet his need for a son to start a television shop, and that need was found proved.
The tenant indicated agreement to continue in occupation of part of the premises, but the landlord did not agree to dividing the premises into two equal halves.

The lower courts ordered eviction from the entire premises without examining whether partial eviction could substantially satisfy the landlord’s need; the High Court relied on a presumption that partial eviction would not suffice where the premises comprised one shop room.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 11(1)(c) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982 requires the court, after finding the landlord’s need proved, to consider whether that need may be substantially satisfied by evicting the tenant from only part of the premises, where the tenant agrees to continue in the remainder. Whether partial eviction is practicable is a question of fact in each case; the fact that premises comprise one room does not create a presumption that partial eviction cannot be ordered. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the orders for eviction from the entire premises were set aside to that extent, and the matter was remitted for an inquiry into whether the premises could be divided so that eviction from only part would substantially satisfy the landlord’s need.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and landlord_need_proved and tenant_agrees_to_partial_occupation and full_eviction_ordered_without_partial_inquiry

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding is a rent-control case seeking eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.landlord_need_proved: The court has found the landlord’s stated need for occupation of the premises proved.
predicates.tenant_agrees_to_partial_occupation: The tenant agrees to continue occupying the remainder if evicted from part of the premises.
predicates.full_eviction_ordered_without_partial_in: The court ordered eviction from the entire premises without examining whether eviction from only part could substantially satisfy the landlord’s need.

members.legal_issue: A court deciding an eviction claim based on the landlord’s reasonable requirement must consider partial eviction even when the tenant has not specifically pleaded for it.
material_facts: The eviction claim was based on the landlord’s reasonable requirement.
Neither the trial court nor the first appellate court considered on the merits whether eviction from only part of the premises could substantially satisfy that requirement.
The lower courts did not take evidence on partial eviction because there had been no specific pleading on the point.
members.legal_principle: The second proviso to the Explanation to section 11(1)(h) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 requires the court to consider whether partial eviction should be ordered or the entire premises vacated. The court must make that determination after hearing evidence from both sides, and the duty applies even without a specific pleading. R. S. Madan v. G. M. Sadiq, 1971 J&K Law Reports 260, was overruled.
members.conclusion: The statutory proviso required the court to determine, after giving both sides an opportunity to lead evidence, whether partial eviction would substantially satisfy the landlord’s reasonable requirement. The absence of a specific pleading did not excuse that inquiry, so the matter was remanded for the first appellate court to decide it.

predicates.landlord_need_eviction_case: The landlord sought eviction on the basis of a reasonable requirement of the premises.
predicates.partial_eviction_feasibility_unexamined: The courts had not assessed, after hearing evidence, whether eviction from part of the premises could substantially satisfy the landlord’s requirement.

members.legal_issue: A commercial tenancy may be released for a landlord’s bona fide business need when the relevant factors, including the tenant’s alternative accommodation and the landlord’s need, support release.
material_facts: The landlady sought release of a shop to establish her unemployed son in a business repairing firearms.
The authorities found the landlady’s need bona fide and genuine; the High Court noted that the son could not obtain the required licence without a vacant shop.
The appellate authority found that the landlady had offered the tenant alternative accommodation and that he refused it.
The tenant challenged the release order, relying on the commercial-premises factors in Rule 16, the length of the tenancy, and the possibility of partial eviction.
members.legal_principle: Rule 16(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 requires consideration of relevant circumstances in a commercial release application; its listed factors are not a sole or mechanical criterion. Under Sushila v. IInd Addl. District Judge, a tenant’s suitable alternative accommodation may reduce the weight of a long tenancy, while a landlord’s substantial existing business may weigh against release. Raghavendra Kumar v. Firm Prem Machinery and Co. recognizes the landlord’s choice of a suitable business location; Gaya Prasad v. Pradeep Shrivastava states that need is assessed as of the application date; and Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan states that bona fide personal need is a factual matter that courts should not ordinarily disturb.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings supporting release disclosed no infirmity warranting interference, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.commercial_release_appeal: The tenant appealed against an order releasing commercial premises to the landlord.
predicates.landlady_sought_business_space_for_unemp: The landlady sought the premises to establish her unemployed son in a business.
predicates.courts_found_bona_fide_need: The deciding authorities found the landlord’s stated need genuine and bona fide.
predicates.tenant_refused_offered_alternative_accom: The tenant declined alternative accommodation offered by the landlord.

members.legal_issue: Comparative hardship must be assessed by weighing the tenant’s length of occupancy against the availability of suitable alternative premises and the landlord’s own need, rather than treating long occupancy as decisive.
material_facts: The tenant’s family had occupied the disputed shop for a long period.
The tenant had another shop available in which he could shift his business; the sale deed established that the property he had purchased included a shop.
The tenant had previously conducted his own business from another shop and had established his son in that shop.
The landlady had no other shop in which to establish her married and unemployed son.
There was no evidence that the landlady’s husband’s existing business was so extensive as to weigh against release under the relevant factor in Rule 16(2).
members.legal_principle: The fourth proviso to Section 21(1) requires consideration of likely hardship to the tenant from granting release as against likely hardship to the landlord from refusing it. Rule 16(2)(a)–(c) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 identifies relevant factors for business premises: longer occupancy weighs against release, suitable alternative accommodation for the tenant weighs in favor of release, and the extent of the landlord’s existing business may also matter. Length of tenancy is one factor, not the sole criterion; availability of suitable alternative accommodation to the tenant can neutralize its weight. No earlier cases were relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: Comparative hardship favored the landlady; the tenant’s long occupancy did not outweigh the availability of another shop to him and the landlady’s lack of another shop for her son.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_release_proceeding and tenant_long_occupancy and tenant_has_suitable_alternative_shop and landlord_lacks_other_suitable_shop and landlord_existing_business_not_extensive

predicates.tenant_eviction_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of business premises occupied by a tenant.
predicates.tenant_long_occupancy: The tenant or the tenant’s predecessor has occupied the premises for a long period.
predicates.tenant_has_suitable_alternative_shop: The tenant has another suitable shop available to which the business can be shifted.
predicates.landlord_lacks_other_suitable_shop: The landlord has no other suitable shop for the proposed use.
predicates.landlord_existing_business_not_extensive: The landlord’s existing business is not shown to be so extensive as to weigh against release.
predicates.comparative_hardship_favors_landlord: The hardship from refusing release to the landlord outweighs the hardship from granting release to the tenant.

members.legal_issue: Comparative hardship in a business-premises release proceeding is assessed by considering the prescribed business-related factors, including tenant occupancy, available alternative accommodation, the landlord’s existing business, and a son’s self-employment need.
material_facts: The tenant had occupied the shop since 1966.
It was undisputed that the tenant had no suitable accommodation to which he could shift.
The District Judge considered the landlord’s existing business.
The landlord’s two adult sons had completed their education, were unemployed, and wanted to carry on business for self-employment.
The District Judge’s order addressed the relevant factors for business premises under Rule 16(2).
members.legal_principle: Rule 16(2) of the Rules under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, identifies factors relevant to comparative hardship for business premises: longer tenant occupation reduces the justification for release; suitable alternative accommodation for the tenant increases it; the landlord’s existing business is relevant; and due consideration is to be given to a son who, after completing technical education, is not in government service and seeks self-employment. Rule 16(1), which concerns residential accommodation, did not apply. The Court distinguished Bishan Chand v. Vth Addl. District Judge because the relevant business-premises factors had not been considered there and an outweighing circumstance was present here.
