members.conclusion: The second accused could not be convicted for murder with the aid of the common-intention provision, and the acquittal was left undisturbed.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_alleging_joint_offen: The proceeding alleges that an accused participated with another person in committing an offence.
predicates.joint_assault_evidence_unreliable: The evidence that the accused joined in the alleged assault is not reliable.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_common_intention: There is no other reliable evidence that the accused shared the intention required for the alleged offence.

members.legal_issue: Joint criminal liability requires participation in the criminal act in furtherance of a common intention, and a conviction cannot stand where such participation is not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused had expressed hostility toward the deceased and was seen following him with others shortly before the killing.
The evidence made it probable that the accused was nearby when the killing occurred, but did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that he was present with the other assailants when it was committed.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code embodies joint liability for a criminal act done in furtherance of a common intention; participation in the commission of the offence is required. The judgment cites no earlier decisions for this principle.
members.conclusion: The conviction for murder on the basis of joint liability was set aside because the accused’s presence and participation at the killing were not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

rule.if: appeal_against_joint_liability_conviction and common_intention_evidence and not participation_at_commission_proved

predicates.appeal_against_joint_liability_convictio: The accused appealed a conviction imposing joint criminal liability for an offence committed by others.
predicates.common_intention_evidence: Evidence showed circumstances suggesting that the accused shared an intention with the persons who committed the offence.
predicates.participation_at_commission_proved: The evidence established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused participated in the criminal act when it was committed.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for murder based on shared intention cannot stand where the evidence does not reliably establish the accused’s participation beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused was alleged to have struck one victim and injured a witness.
The prosecution witnesses did not mention the alleged attack on the victim until their testimony at trial, despite giving detailed accounts of the incident.
The evidence about the alleged injury to the witness was not satisfactory, and that injury was outside the charged common intention and was not the subject of a separate charge.
The court was not satisfied that the evidence safely established that the accused was present and participated in an attack from which a shared intention to murder could be inferred.
members.legal_principle: A conviction under sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of the accused’s participation and the shared intention necessary to impose joint liability. Material omissions in detailed earlier accounts and unsatisfactory evidence of the alleged participation may leave reasonable doubt, entitling the accused to its benefit.
members.conclusion: The case against the accused was not established beyond reasonable doubt; his conviction and sentence were set aside, and he was acquitted and discharged.

predicates.joint_liability_murder_appeal: The case is an appeal from a murder conviction based on alleged shared criminal intention.
predicates.key_alleged_attack_omitted_from_earlier_: Witnesses who gave detailed earlier accounts did not mention a material attack attributed to the accused until trial.
predicates.other_participation_evidence_unsatisfact: Other evidence offered to show the accused’s participation is unreliable or relates to conduct outside the charged shared intention.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_establishes_partici: The remaining evidence does not reliably establish that the accused participated in the attack.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for causing simple injuries in furtherance of a shared intention cannot stand when the evidence supporting the alleged injuries is vague and uncorroborated.
material_facts: A witness alleged that one accused struck him with a stick and that he also received fist blows.
The court found the evidence about the injuries vague and uncorroborated.
The conviction for causing those injuries had been entered against all the accused on a shared-intention basis.
members.legal_principle: The court held the evidence insufficient to sustain the conviction under Sections 323 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code because it was vague and uncorroborated. It cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The court set aside the convictions and sentences of all the accused for causing simple injuries in furtherance of a shared intention.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed from convictions entered by the lower courts.
predicates.injury_evidence_vague: The evidence describing the injuries and how they were caused was vague.
predicates.injury_evidence_uncorroborated: The evidence supporting the alleged injuries was not corroborated.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for a jointly committed assault cannot be maintained where the alleged victim did not testify and the alleged injuries were not proved.
material_facts: The accused were also convicted of assaulting a person who had tried to intervene.
The alleged victim did not testify, and his injuries were not proved.
members.legal_principle: The Court concluded that, in the circumstances, the convictions under Sections 323 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code could and should be set aside because the alleged victim did not testify and his injuries were not proved. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The assault convictions were set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_joint_assault_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction for an assault allegedly committed together.
predicates.alleged_victim_did_not_testify: The person said to have been assaulted did not testify at trial.
predicates.alleged_injuries_not_proved: The injuries said to have resulted from the assault were not proved.

members.legal_issue: A conviction imposing joint criminal responsibility is unsustainable where the case was tried on an individual murder charge and the evidence does not establish a shared intention to cause the death.
material_facts: The accused were tried on a charge of murder, not on a charge alleging joint responsibility.

The evidence attributed different acts to the accused: some allegedly struck the deceased with sticks, while another allegedly arrived later and inflicted the head injuries identified as causing death.

The medical evidence disclosed no leg injuries corresponding to the alleged stick blows, and the record did not establish premeditation, a shared intention to kill, or how the accused who arrived later was connected with the others.
The reviewing court used joint-liability reasoning to convict all the accused.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code was invoked by the reviewing court, but the record contained no evidence of a common intention among the accused to kill, and the alleged acts and arrival of the accused were distinct. In those circumstances, the judgment holds that using Section 34 to convict all the accused was unsustainable. The accused had been tried only on a charge under Section 302 IPC. No earlier case is identified by name in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The joint-liability basis for the conviction was patently unsustainable, and the reviewing court’s judgment was set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to reverse a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.reviewing_court_imposed_joint_responsibi: The reviewing court convicted multiple accused on the basis that they shared responsibility for the offence.
predicates.trial_charge_did_not_allege_joint_respon: The accused were tried on an individual offence charge that did not allege joint responsibility.
predicates.evidence_did_not_establish_shared_intent: The evidence did not establish that the accused shared an intention to cause the victim’s death.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction cannot be sustained on evidence that is rejected as to the alleged fatal assailant when the accused’s own act causing the fatal injuries is not proved and constructive liability is unavailable.
material_facts: The accused was convicted of murder after the High Court acquitted his brother, whom the eyewitnesses identified as inflicting the fatal blows.

The High Court relied on the same eyewitnesses to convict the accused, although their account attributed to him the act of restraining the deceased and did not establish which part of the deceased he struck.
The Supreme Court considered the eyewitness account unreliable against the accused in light of its rejection as to the other accused and found no evidence that the accused caused the fatal injuries.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, substantive murder liability requires evidence that the accused caused the fatal injuries, while constructive liability under Section 34 depends on the basis established for shared participation. On these facts, the acquittal of the alleged fatal assailant left no scope for applying Section 34, and the rejected eyewitness account could not sustain a conviction of the remaining accused. Suspicion cannot take the place of proof. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction could not be sustained: after the alleged fatal assailant was acquitted, constructive liability was unavailable on these facts, and there was no evidence that the accused caused the fatal injuries. The conviction was set aside and the accused was acquitted.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_murder_conviction and alleged_fatal_assailant_acquitted and eyewitness_account_discredited_as_to_assailant and no_evidence_accused_caused_fatal_injuries

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_murder_convictio: The accused brought a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for murder.
predicates.alleged_fatal_assailant_acquitted: The other person identified as inflicting the fatal injuries was acquitted.
predicates.eyewitness_account_discredited_as_to_ass: The court rejected the eyewitness account concerning the alleged fatal assailant.
predicates.no_evidence_accused_caused_fatal_injurie: The evidence did not establish that the accused caused the fatal injuries.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction based on an accused’s attributed individual assault cannot stand when the evidence does not satisfactorily establish that person’s role.
material_facts: The High Court convicted several accused of murder with common-intention liability on the basis that each had actively participated in the assault on the deceased.
The evidence concerning the alleged acts varied by accused and included unsupported testimony, material omissions, or conflicts with medical evidence.
The Supreme Court examined the evidence against each accused separately and found the charge proved against some but not others.
members.legal_principle: Where a conviction under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code rests on an accused’s active participation by an attributed act, the evidence of that person’s role must be assessed individually and must satisfactorily establish the participation. In examining a large group occurrence, the Court also referred to the workable approach in Masalti v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions were sustained only where the evidence satisfactorily established the accused’s participation in the assault; they were set aside where the individual role was not satisfactorily established.

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a murder conviction entered after an acquittal was reversed.
predicates.conviction_based_on_attributed_individua: The conviction rests on a finding that the accused personally participated through an attributed assault.
predicates.individual_role_not_satisfactorily_estab: The evidence, assessed for that accused, does not satisfactorily establish the attributed role.

members.legal_issue: A shared murder conviction cannot stand against an accused where the evidence does not specifically implicate that accused and there is no other evidence against them.
material_facts: The witnesses who spoke of cruel treatment did not specifically state that this accused had treated the deceased cruelly.
The Court found no other evidence against this accused.
The evidence supporting the convictions of the other appellants did not establish this accused’s participation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code but found the evidence insufficient to sustain this accused’s conviction. It cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The accused’s conviction and sentence for murder with common intention were set aside.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The matter is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.no_specific_evidence_of_accuseds_partici: The evidence does not specifically identify the accused as having participated in the relevant conduct.
predicates.no_other_evidence_against_accused: There is no other evidence implicating the accused.

members.legal_issue: A group cannot be convicted on the basis of an unlawful assembly's common object where the assault arose as an exercise of private defence, even though the defence was exceeded.
material_facts: The accused were in possession of the land and the complainant's group entered it to retake possession by force.
The complainant's group was armed, and two members wielded sticks during the mutual fight.
The Court found that the accused acted to defend their person and property, although they exceeded that right.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, on its finding that the accused had exceeded their right of private defence, the common object charged against them failed. It therefore set aside the convictions under Sections 147 and 323/149 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The common object on which the unlawful-assembly charges rested failed, so the convictions under Sections 147 and 323/149 of the Indian Penal Code could not stand and were set aside.

predicates.criminal_group_assault_case: The proceeding concerns an assault by a group charged as an unlawful assembly.
predicates.accused_defended_possession_against_forc: The accused acted to defend their possession after an opposing group entered to take possession by force.
predicates.defence_right_was_exceeded: The accused exceeded the right they had to defend person or property.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on common intention cannot stand when the accused acted in exercise of the right of private defence.
material_facts: The High Court found that the appellants had acted in private defence but convicted them of culpable homicide with the aid of common intention.
The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants were defending their property and persons, rather than acting with a common intention to commit a criminal act.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 96 and 103 of the Indian Penal Code, an act done in exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence, and the right to defend property may extend to causing death subject to Section 99. Common intention under Section 34 cannot be attributed to persons acting in exercise of that right. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Mathu Pandey, which explained that an assertion of a right of private defence within legal limits is not an unlawful common object under Section 141 IPC.
members.conclusion: The conviction for culpable homicide with the aid of common intention was illegal and was set aside.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed against their criminal convictions.
predicates.acts_done_in_private_defence: The accused acted to defend their property or persons from an attack or intrusion.
predicates.conviction_based_on_common_intention: The conviction rested on attributing a common intention to commit the criminal act.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for participation in an unlawful assembly cannot stand where the evidence does not reliably connect the accused to the assembly or the assault.
material_facts: For one appellant, the only name resembling his was an ambiguous name given by a witness, which the prosecution did not clarify; no other eyewitness identified him or other evidence connected him to the assembly.
For the other appellant, one witness named him, but no other eyewitness corroborated that identification or described any act connecting him to the assembly.
The weapons attributed to these appellants were not shown to carry blood stains, and the remaining evidence left reasonable doubt about their presence and participation.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Evidence must be assessed for its quality and the accused’s individual connection to the assembly; an ambiguous or uncorroborated identification, unsupported by other connecting evidence, may leave reasonable doubt. Recovery of a weapon alone does not establish participation where the other evidence does not connect the accused to the crime.
members.conclusion: The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt against these two appellants. Their convictions were set aside and they were acquitted on benefit of doubt.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and (identification_ambiguous or identification_uncorroborated) and no_independent_link_to_assembly

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused challenged a conviction on appeal.
predicates.identification_ambiguous: The evidence identifying the accused was unclear or did not reliably establish that the witness meant that accused.
predicates.identification_uncorroborated: No other witness or material evidence adequately supported the identification of the accused as a participant.
predicates.no_independent_link_to_assembly: No other reliable evidence connected the accused to the assembly or the assault.

members.legal_issue: A conviction based on participation in a group assault cannot stand where the evidence against the accused consists of later, contradictory allegations that are not adequately corroborated and do not reliably establish their participation or shared common object.
material_facts: The victim's initial report assigned specific acts to two male assailants but did not assign any specific role to the three accused women.
At trial, the victim added allegations that one woman struck him with a cutting weapon and that the others kicked and punched him.
The parties had a pre-existing land dispute.

Medical evidence did not convincingly corroborate the later allegations against the women; the injury said to have been caused by the cutting weapon was consistent with a fall, and the other injuries were attributable to the male assailants' alleged acts.
The later allegations came from the victim alone, without support from an independent witness.
The lower courts did not carefully assess the contradictions, medical evidence, and defence that the women were bystanders.
members.legal_principle: An injured witness is generally reliable, but the testimony must still be carefully scrutinized where the circumstances suggest that innocent persons may have been falsely implicated. Material contradictions between an initial account and later testimony, lack of convincing medical corroboration, and the possibility of exaggeration require careful consideration. The court applied this principle to the convictions involving Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not reliably establish the women’s participation in the assault or their sharing a common object with the assailants. Their convictions and sentences were set aside, and they were acquitted of all charges by benefit of doubt.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and initial_account_omitted_specific_roles_for_accused and later_testimony_added_specific_roles_for_accused and medical_evidence_did_not_convincingly_corroborate_later_allegations and later_allegations_lacked_independent_support and evidence_was_not_carefully_scrutinized

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal challenging criminal convictions.
predicates.initial_account_omitted_specific_roles_f: The initial account did not assign specific acts to the accused whose convictions were challenged.
predicates.later_testimony_added_specific_roles_for: The witness later assigned specific acts to those accused in trial testimony.
predicates.medical_evidence_did_not_convincingly_co: The medical evidence did not convincingly support the later allegations about how those accused caused the injuries.
predicates.later_allegations_lacked_independent_sup: The later allegations against those accused came from the witness without support from an independent witness.
predicates.evidence_was_not_carefully_scrutinized: The courts below did not adequately assess the contradictions, medical evidence, and possibility of false implication.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for causing hurt to an alleged victim cannot stand when the prosecution has not established that the victim was present and injured in the occurrence.
material_facts: The first report did not mention that the alleged victim was present or injured.
The alleged victim’s presence and injuries were introduced in a police account that the Court found unreliable.
The Court found that the prosecution had not established the alleged victim’s presence.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish the factual basis for the offence, including the alleged victim’s presence and injury. The Court found that the evidence did not establish those facts and rejected the police-introduced account. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The conviction for causing hurt to the alleged victim and the sentence imposed for that offence were set aside.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_acquittal: The accused challenged a conviction entered after an acquittal in a criminal appeal.
predicates.hurt_conviction_depends_on_victim_presen: The challenged conviction rests on an allegation that a particular victim was present and injured in the occurrence.
predicates.victim_presence_not_established: The prosecution evidence does not establish that the alleged victim was present during the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: A conviction for murder or attempted murder cannot stand when the prosecution evidence does not reliably establish that the accused side initiated the violence and the account of the incident is materially inconsistent with the injury evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on three eyewitnesses, whose account the High Court itself found to contain material improbabilities.
The prosecution side sustained seven injuries, while five members of the accused side sustained 57 injuries; two of those five were severely beaten, and one later died from the injuries.

The prosecution account was that the accused side killed one person and injured another at the outset, after which three people on the prosecution side inflicted the many injuries on five armed members of the accused side without themselves receiving a scratch.

The appellant was convicted of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and attempted murder under Section 307 read with Section 34; the Supreme Court found that the use of guns by the accused side did not, by itself, establish that it was the aggressor or guilty of those offences.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Court assessed the charges under Sections 302 and 307 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code against the reliability of the eyewitness account and the injuries on both sides. Use of a gun alone did not establish that the accused were aggressors or guilty of murder or attempted murder. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; the appeal was allowed and the conviction and sentences were set aside.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.eyewitness_account_materially_improbable: The prosecution’s eyewitness account contains material improbabilities about how the incident occurred.
predicates.injury_pattern_inconsistent_with_prosecu: The number or severity of injuries on the accused side is inconsistent with the prosecution’s account of the incident.

members.legal_issue: A property-right challenge under Article 300A is not fit for determination in a writ proceeding when it is not properly pleaded and depends on disputed title facts that require evidence.
material_facts: The petitioners claimed that property belonging to the society had been taken over.
The Government disputed the petitioners' title to the land, building, and other claimed property.
The petitioners produced no title documents, and the title dispute could not be resolved without evidence.
The Court also noted that the Article 300A claim had not been made out in the writ petition and expressed doubt that the right could be enforced through an Article 32 petition.
members.legal_principle: Article 300A protects persons, including legal persons, from deprivation of property except by authority of law. The Court considered the principles in Board of Trustees, Ayurvedic and Unani Tibia College v. State of Delhi, but held that a claim turning on unpleaded and highly disputed title facts requiring evidence was not suitable for determination in the writ proceeding; it also expressed grave doubt that the property right could be enforced by an Article 32 petition after the Forty-Fourth Amendment.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to adjudicate the Article 300A challenge in the writ proceedings.

rule.if: article_300a_writ_challenge and property_title_disputed and title_requires_evidence and claim_not_properly_pleaded

predicates.article_300a_writ_challenge: The proceeding invokes a constitutional protection against deprivation of property and seeks relief by writ.
predicates.property_title_disputed: The government disputes the claimant's title to the property said to have been taken.
predicates.title_requires_evidence: Resolving the title dispute requires evidence rather than determination on the writ record.
predicates.claim_not_properly_pleaded: The property-right claim was not properly set out in the pleading.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional writ is not an appropriate means to resolve a serious dispute over title and displace a person in possession when the claimant lacks clear and conclusive proof of title.
material_facts: The party opposing the writ was in possession under a mining lease granted by the State and had carried on prospecting operations.
The writ applicants were not in possession and sought orders that would disturb the existing possession.

The opposing party seriously disputed the title on which the writ applicants relied, and the applicants had not produced clear, conclusive and unimpeachable documentary evidence establishing that title.
The writ applicants' earlier possession and their prima facie title were not treated as a final determination of title.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, writ proceedings are not appropriate where serious factual disputes and a contested title would have to be resolved to grant relief that displaces the person in possession. Sohan Lal v. Union of India, [1957] SCR 738, states that a title suit is the proper remedy in such circumstances and that writ relief may be available where the facts are undisputed and title is clear. Mohd. Hanif v. State of Assam, [1969] 2 SCC 782, was distinguished because it concerned executive interference with the petitioner's own possession.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was not competent in these circumstances; the title dispute was left open for determination in a suitably framed civil suit.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenging_property_grant and serious_title_dispute and respondent_in_possession and relief_requires_displacing_possession and not clear_conclusive_title_evidence

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_property: A claimant brings a constitutional writ petition challenging a grant affecting property.
predicates.serious_title_dispute: The parties seriously dispute the claimant's title to the property.
predicates.respondent_in_possession: The person opposing the claim is in possession of the property.
predicates.relief_requires_displacing_possession: The relief sought would require the court to displace the person in possession.
predicates.clear_conclusive_title_evidence: The claimant has produced clear and conclusive evidence establishing title.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional writ protecting possession cannot be issued when the claimant’s asserted right depends on a disputed title that the writ court has declined to determine and no other legal right has been established.
material_facts: The respondents sought writs to prevent the State from dispossessing them after it issued notices resuming the grants under which their predecessors had held the properties.
The respondents claimed the grants gave them proprietary interests, while the State contended that the grants were service tenures resumable at its will.
The High Court declined to decide the disputed nature of the grants and title in writ proceedings, but ordered that the respondents not be dispossessed except in due course of law.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 permits relief beyond enforcement of fundamental rights, but a writ requires an established right that has been illegally invaded or threatened. A writ cannot be issued solely to provide interim relief; under State of Orissa v. Madan Gopal Rungta, interim relief must aid and be auxiliary to relief available after the rights are determined in the substantive proceeding.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in issuing the writs because the respondents had not established a legal right supporting that relief; the orders were set aside.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and title_claim_contested and title_not_determined and no_other_legal_right_established

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: The claimant sought relief through a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.title_claim_contested: The parties disputed whether the claimant held title or another legal interest in the property.
predicates.title_not_determined: The court left the disputed title issue undecided in the proceeding.
predicates.no_other_legal_right_established: No other legal right supporting the requested relief was established in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising constitutional writ jurisdiction may decline to decide a disputed claim of earlier government possession when the evidence does not satisfactorily establish that possession.
material_facts: The appellant alleged that the Forest Department had taken possession of the lands in 1953 or 1954.

The documents relied on included statements by a forest officer that possession had been taken, but the officer explained that he had made them under an erroneous impression about the effect of forest notifications.

The High Court found the evidence insufficient to decide whether possession had been taken, and the Supreme Court agreed that it was justified in declining to decide the factual dispute in the writ proceedings.
members.legal_principle: A disputed factual question that cannot be conclusively decided on the evidence before a court in proceedings under Article 226 need not be determined in those proceedings. The Court left open any other remedy available under law.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in declining to decide whether the Government had taken possession in 1953 or 1954; the appellant remained free to pursue any other remedy available under law.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: The claimant seeks relief in a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.disputed_prior_possession: The claimant alleges that the government took possession before the acquisition proceedings, and that allegation is disputed.
predicates.insufficient_evidence: The evidence before the court does not satisfactorily establish whether the government took that possession.

members.legal_issue: A writ cannot be used to compel a public authority to remedy a breach of a concluded, non-statutory contract where the parties’ rights are governed by the contract and no special statutory obligation applies.
material_facts: The authority’s brochure described the stated housing costs as estimates and reserved the right to change the terms and conditions.
The applicants registered under the brochure terms, which included those reservations, and the authority later notified them of revised costs and instalments.
The authority left applicants free not to proceed on the revised terms; most respondents gave unconditional written acceptance and were allotted houses or flats.
The respondents challenged the revised terms in writ petitions, and the contracts contained no statutory terms or conditions.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a court cannot compel an authority to remedy a breach of a non-statutory, purely contractual obligation where the rights are governed by the contract and no statute imposes a special obligation in that contractual field. The Court relied on Radhakrishna Agarwal v. State of Bihar, Premji Bhai Parmar v. Delhi Development Authority, and D.F.O. v. Biswanath Tea Company Ltd.
members.conclusion: The respondents could claim only the rights conferred by their contracts, and the High Court could not issue a writ directing the authority to remedy a breach of contract pure and simple. The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.

predicates.writ_petition_seeks_contract_remedy: A claimant brought a writ petition seeking a remedy for an alleged breach of an agreement with an authority.
predicates.nonstatutory_concluded_contract: The parties entered a concluded agreement whose terms were not statutory.
predicates.no_special_statutory_obligation: No statute imposed a special obligation on the authority in the contractual relationship.

members.legal_issue: A contractual right ordinarily cannot be enforced through writ jurisdiction when the relief sought depends on the terms of a contract and no independent public-law or statutory ground is established.
material_facts: The company sought repayment of royalty and directions for permits without royalty, relying on a term of its lease.
The applicable regulations prescribed royalty, and their validity was not challenged.
The claim that royalty was not payable depended on the lease term; the asserted statutory basis was only a reproduction of that contractual term.
The company sought relief concerning a contractual dispute that could be pursued through a civil suit.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 permits writs for purposes beyond enforcement of fundamental rights, including where executive action is unsupported by law, equality or equal protection is denied, or a statutory right is enforced. But a contractual claim for specific performance, damages, or refund ordinarily belongs in a civil court. The Court applied Har Shankar v. The Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner and approved Woodcrafts Assam v. Chief Conservator of Forests, Assam.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have dismissed the writ petition at the threshold because the relief sought enforced contractual obligations and was not ordinarily available through writ jurisdiction.

rule.if: writ_proceeding and contractual_relief_sought and right_depends_on_contract and demand_supported_by_law and no_independent_statutory_or_public_law_ground

predicates.writ_proceeding: A claimant sought relief from a High Court through a writ petition.
predicates.contractual_relief_sought: The claimant sought repayment or directions based on an alleged breach of an agreement.
predicates.right_depends_on_contract: The claimed entitlement depended on the terms of a contract between the claimant and the government.
predicates.demand_supported_by_law: The government demand was authorized by applicable law, whose validity was not challenged.
predicates.no_independent_statutory_or_public_law_g: The claimant established no independent statutory right, unlawful executive action, or denial of equality as the basis for relief.

members.legal_issue: A court ordinarily will not use writ jurisdiction to compel amendment of a purely contractual agreement where no public-law element or right to amendment is established.
material_facts: The taxpayer sought writ relief requiring the Government to add a tax-deduction term to executed production-sharing contracts.
The contracts required amendments to be made in writing and signed by all parties, and the Government had not agreed to the requested amendment.
The contracts were formal government contracts, but the dispute concerned contractual rights and did not involve a public-law element warranting writ relief.
The taxpayer had an alternative tax appeal pending.
members.legal_principle: Writ relief is not absolutely barred in contractual disputes involving the State, but it is ordinarily unavailable for a purely contractual claim without a public-law element; the High Court retains discretion and may decline relief where an alternative contractual or statutory remedy exists. A contract requiring a written amendment signed by all parties gives no unilateral right to amendment. Formal government contracts must also satisfy Article 299 of the Constitution, and their novation must meet the applicable procedural requirements. The Court relied on Andi Mukta Sadguru v. R. Rudani (1989) 2 SCC 691; Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajai Pal Singh (1989) 1 SCR 743; Divisional Forest Officer v. Bishwanath Tea Co. Ltd. (1981) 3 SCR 662; Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P. (1991) 1 SCC 212; State of Gujarat v. M.P. Shah Charitable Trust (1994) 3 SCC 552; ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (2004) 3 SCC 553; and LIC of India v. Escorts Ltd. (1986) 1 SCC 264.
members.conclusion: The taxpayer had no right to compel amendment of the contracts, and this was not a fit case for writ relief; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: writ_proceeding_over_state_contract and dispute_is_purely_contractual and no_public_law_element and relief_requires_compelled_amendment and no_mutual_written_amendment_agreement

predicates.writ_proceeding_over_state_contract: A claimant seeks writ relief concerning a contract to which the State or its instrumentality is a party.
predicates.dispute_is_purely_contractual: The claim concerns rights and obligations arising only from the contract.
predicates.no_public_law_element: The challenged conduct does not involve a public-law duty or a demonstrated public-law defect such as arbitrary State action.
predicates.relief_requires_compelled_amendment: The requested relief would require the State to change the terms of an executed contract.
predicates.no_mutual_written_amendment_agreement: The parties have not agreed in a signed writing to the proposed contract amendment.

members.legal_issue: A writ court should not use the right to livelihood to grant relief on a claim founded only on contractual rights when no special circumstance justifies exercising extraordinary jurisdiction.
material_facts: The claim for additional payments arose from the sale of forest produce and the claimant relied on decisions said to govern the payment arrangements.
The High Court treated non-payment of the claimed amounts as a violation of the right to livelihood, but identified no special circumstance warranting writ relief.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court had wrongly assumed jurisdiction, but did not dismiss the claim solely on that ground because the passage of time had made the alternative remedies ineffective; it therefore considered the claim on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Writ jurisdiction is discretionary and may be used to enforce fundamental or legal rights, but ordinarily not mere contractual rights, particularly where an efficacious alternative remedy exists. A court may grant relief despite an alternative remedy in special circumstances, which must be identified. The right to livelihood does not extend to every legal or contractual claim. The judgment refers generally to prior pronouncements on writ jurisdiction but identifies no earlier case as authority for this particular proposition.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in exercising writ jurisdiction to grant relief on the contractual claim by relying on the right to livelihood. The Supreme Court nevertheless declined to dismiss the petition on that procedural ground and decided the merits.

predicates.contractual_writ_claim: A person seeks writ relief on a claim arising from a contractual arrangement.
predicates.no_special_circumstances_found: The writ court identifies no special circumstance justifying relief despite the contractual nature of the claim or the availability of another remedy.
predicates.livelihood_claim_used_as_basis: The writ court relies on an asserted effect on livelihood to justify granting relief on the contractual claim.

members.legal_issue: A writ court ordinarily does not grant specific performance of a contract where the dispute requires adjudication of contractual rights or disputed facts and an appropriate civil remedy is available.
material_facts: The claimant's grievance arose from a development agreement with a state transport corporation.
The claimant sought possession and continuation of a construction project despite the landowner authority's separate lease relationship with the corporation.
The claimant had no contract with the landowner authority.
The dispute involved disputed questions about the agreements, lease rights, breach, and the effect of subsequent events.
The High Court left the claimant free to pursue specific performance or damages in a civil court.
members.legal_principle: Judicial review of contractual action by the State or its instrumentalities is limited to legality, including excess of power, error of law, breach of natural justice, irrationality, or abuse of power; it is not a determination of the merits of contractual performance. A writ court would not normally enforce specific performance where damages or a civil proceeding can provide an appropriate remedy, particularly where disputed facts require trial. The Court relied on Article 226 of the Constitution, Tata Cellular v. Union of India, Ramchandra Murarilal Bhattad v. State of Maharashtra, Noble Resources Ltd. v. State of Orissa, and Rajasthan Housing Board v. G.S. Investments.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to grant specific performance or other writ relief on the contractual claim and left the claimant to pursue an appropriate civil remedy.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_writ_disposition: A party brings a civil appeal challenging a High Court's disposition of a writ proceeding.
predicates.state_contract_dispute: The claim concerns performance of a contract involving the State or one of its instrumentalities.
predicates.specific_performance_or_factfinding_requ: The requested relief requires enforcement of contractual performance or resolution of disputed facts.

members.legal_issue: A writ court should not decide a claimant’s disputed right to resist execution when resolving the dispute requires evidence and an adequate civil remedy is available.
material_facts: An eviction decree had been passed against a tenant, but the claimants were not parties to the eviction suit.
The claimants asserted that they held tenancy rights independently, while the landlords alleged that they had been inducted as sub-tenants.
Determining the claimants’ character of possession required consideration of evidence, and civil procedures were available to resolve the dispute.
The High Court granted relief in a writ petition without deciding the disputed character of possession.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 provides supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction and does not displace civil remedies or legitimate defences in civil proceedings. A writ court should not resolve disputed factual matters requiring evidence when an adequate civil remedy is available. The Court relied on State of Andhra Pradesh v. Chitra Venkata Rao, [1976] 1 SCR 521; Thansingh Nathmal v. A. Mazid, [1964] 6 SCR 654; and M. Naina Mohammed v. K. A. Natarajan, [1976] 1 SCR 102.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have declined to decide the merits in writ jurisdiction and left the claimants to pursue the civil remedy; its judgment was set aside and the writ petition dismissed.

rule.if: writ_proceeding and execution_claimant_dispute and possession_character_requires_evidence and adequate_civil_remedy_available

predicates.writ_proceeding: A party brought a claim for relief before a court exercising supervisory writ jurisdiction.
predicates.execution_claimant_dispute: A person claiming an interest in property disputed whether an existing decree could be executed against them.
predicates.possession_character_requires_evidence: Resolving the dispute about the person’s possession requires the parties to present evidence.
predicates.adequate_civil_remedy_available: A civil procedure provides a remedy capable of addressing the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A writ proceeding ordinarily cannot provide a full adjudication or enforcement of contractual rights where the dispute has no public-law element and the existence of a contract is seriously contested.
material_facts: The bidder pursued a writ proceeding challenging the authority’s cancellation rather than bringing an ordinary civil claim for contractual relief.
The dispute over whether the letter of intent created a concluded contract was seriously contested.
The contractual dispute was not pleaded or argued to have a public-law element.
The authority’s cancellation decision was separately considered under public-law principles and was found not arbitrary or unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 provides public-law review of administrative action, not a full adjudication of contractual rights or ordinary relief for breach of contract. Where a contractual dispute has no public-law element and the existence of a contract is seriously disputed, the court should not assume a valid contract and ordinarily should leave the claimant to pursue the available civil remedy. The Court relied on Kisan Sehkari Chini Mills v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500 and ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd., JT 2013 (10) SC 300.
members.conclusion: The bidder could not obtain full adjudication or enforcement of the disputed contractual claim through the writ proceeding and had chosen the discretionary public-law remedy instead of an ordinary civil remedy.

predicates.contractual_claim_brought_in_writ_procee: A claimant seeks contractual relief through a writ proceeding.
predicates.no_public_law_element_in_contractual_dis: The contractual dispute does not involve a public-law element.
predicates.existence_of_contract_seriously_disputed: The parties seriously dispute whether a contract was formed.

members.legal_issue: The presence of disputed facts does not require a writ court to relegate a claimant to another forum when those facts need not be resolved to grant relief.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether the project was ready for commissioning and whether equipment was missing or had been stolen after inspection.
The record included documentary material concerning inspections, notice and the agreement's default procedure.
The court could decide whether the required default notice had been given and whether the alleged deficiencies could have been remedied without resolving the competing accounts of the equipment.
members.legal_principle: ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. holds that disputed facts are not an automatic bar to writ jurisdiction, particularly where documents permit resolution. Joshi Technologies International Inc. v. Union of India and State of Kerala v. M.K. Jose emphasize that the court may relegate parties where serious, complex factual disputes require evidence. The court applied a case-specific test: whether resolving the disputed facts was necessary to grant the requested relief.
members.conclusion: The disputed factual issues did not require dismissal or relegation to another forum because resolution of those disputes was not indispensable to the relief granted.

predicates.contractual_writ_proceeding: A claimant sought writ relief concerning action taken by the State under a contract.
predicates.disputed_facts_exist: The parties gave conflicting accounts of facts material to the contractual dispute.
predicates.central_relief_can_be_decided_without_re: The court could determine an independent ground for relief from the record without deciding the contested factual issue.

members.legal_issue: Disputed questions of fact or title do not prevent constitutional writ relief when the admitted facts establish bona fide possession and unlawful dispossession, and resolving those disputes is unnecessary to decide the claim.
material_facts: The petitioners sought relief under Article 32 after officials forcibly dispossessed them and transferred possession to the municipality.
The High Court had declined relief because the matter involved disputed questions of fact.
The Supreme Court found it unnecessary to determine the precise rights arising from the original permission or to resolve the disputed questions of fact and title.
The admitted facts established that the petitioners were bona fide in possession and had been removed without authority of law.
members.legal_principle: A writ proceeding need not determine disputed facts or precise title where the admitted facts suffice to establish the infringement of a fundamental right. The Court distinguished the objection based on Sohan Lal v. The Union of India because it was unnecessary to determine title or other disputed questions to grant relief.
members.conclusion: The factual and title disputes did not bar relief; the petitioners could obtain constitutional relief on the admitted facts.

rule.if: article_32_writ_proceeding and bona_fide_possession_established and unlawful_dispossession_established and disputed_title_unnecessary_to_resolve

predicates.article_32_writ_proceeding: The proceeding is a constitutional writ petition seeking enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.bona_fide_possession_established: The admitted facts establish the claimant’s bona fide possession.
predicates.unlawful_dispossession_established: The admitted facts establish that the claimant was dispossessed without lawful authority.
predicates.disputed_title_unnecessary_to_resolve: The court can decide the claim without resolving disputed title or other disputed facts.

members.legal_issue: A writ court is not required to relegate parties to an alternative statutory forum when the dispute can be decided on legal interpretation and documentary material without oral evidence.
material_facts: The challenge concerned the validity of a statutory authority’s notification and involved interpretation of statutes and historical documents.
The High Court examined the parties’ arguments and documents before dismissing the writ petitions.
The Supreme Court found that no oral evidence was necessary to resolve the issues.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 confers broad discretion, and an alternative remedy ordinarily does not bar writ jurisdiction, particularly where an exception to that rule applies. Disputed questions of fact do not by themselves deprive a writ court of jurisdiction, though the court may decline to exercise it where oral evidence is needed. The Court relied on K.K. Kochunni, Committee of Management v. Vice Chancellor, Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, Babubhai Muljibhai Patel v. Nandlal Khodidas Barot, and Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in relegating the parties to the statutory remedy; the dispute was to be examined on its merits.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_public_authority_action and statutory_alternative_remedy_exists and dispute_turns_on_law_and_documents and oral_evidence_is_unnecessary

predicates.writ_challenge_to_public_authority_actio: A party has brought a writ petition challenging an action taken by a public authority.
predicates.statutory_alternative_remedy_exists: A statute provides another forum or remedy for resolving the dispute.
predicates.dispute_turns_on_law_and_documents: The dispute principally requires interpretation of legal rules and documentary material.
predicates.oral_evidence_is_unnecessary: The court can resolve the dispute without receiving oral evidence.

members.legal_issue: Writ jurisdiction is not the appropriate forum for resolving disputed factual allegations of fraud or land undervaluation that require evidence to be assessed.
material_facts: The challenge to the auction relied on allegations of fraud, collusion, and undervaluation that required proof and assessment of evidence.
The challengers sought to establish those allegations through writ proceedings rather than a civil suit in which evidence could be adduced.
Although the High Court considered the factual circumstances, the Supreme Court found no perversity in its conclusions and did not disturb them.
members.legal_principle: Articles 226 and 227 are not the appropriate jurisdiction for trying disputed questions of fact that require evidence, such as allegations of fraud and valuation; such disputes should ordinarily be pursued before a competent civil court. No earlier cases are cited for this issue.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the factual dispute ought not ordinarily to have been entertained under Articles 226 and 227, but declined to interfere with the High Court’s findings after its detailed examination of the matter.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenging_auction: The proceeding invokes writ jurisdiction to challenge a cooperative society land auction.
predicates.disputed_fraud_or_valuation_facts: The challenge depends on contested claims that the auction involved fraud or that the land was undervalued.
predicates.evidence_needed_to_resolve_dispute: Resolving the contested claims requires evidence to be presented and assessed.

members.legal_issue: Extraordinary writ jurisdiction is not an appropriate means to resolve a material dispute about the factual basis for a statutory royalty demand.
material_facts: The claimant sought constitutional writ relief against a demand for royalty on mined gypsum.
The applicable royalty rate depended on whether the gypsum met a specified purity threshold.
The claimant asserted that the gypsum was below the threshold, while the respondents disputed that claim and said adequate laboratory analysis had not been furnished.
A revision challenging the higher royalty rate had been dismissed by the central government.
members.legal_principle: The royalty rate under Section 9(2) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, read with the relevant entry in the Second Schedule, depended on the gypsum’s purity. Determining that purity was a question of fact, and the court upheld the High Court’s refusal to resolve that disputed factual matter in extraordinary jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The court upheld the refusal of writ relief because the gypsum’s purity was a question of fact and found no cogent ground to take a different view from the High Court.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A claimant sought extraordinary constitutional review of an administrative demand.
predicates.disputed_material_fact: The claimant and the government disputed a factual characteristic that determined the amount of the demand.

members.legal_issue: A writ proceeding is not an appropriate means to resolve disputed title where granting possession would require a declaration of title and determination of contested facts.
material_facts: The claimant sought restoration of a house through a constitutional writ petition.
The parties disputed the claimant’s eligibility for allotment, the rights acquired through the allotment process, and the basis on which the claimant had entered possession.
The competing claims required deciding factual and legal questions, and restoration would effectively require a declaration that the claimant had title and a right to possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a writ court should not determine contested questions of fact and law where the requested relief would effectively require a decree declaring title and ordering recovery of property; those questions are appropriately decided by a Civil Court in a properly constituted suit.
members.conclusion: The title and possession disputes should be determined in a properly constituted civil suit, not in the writ proceeding.

predicates.writ_petition: The claimant sought relief through a constitutional writ petition.
predicates.disputed_title_and_material_facts: The parties disputed the claimant’s rights to property and the material facts needed to determine those rights.
predicates.relief_requires_title_declaration: Granting the requested recovery of property would require deciding that the claimant had title or an enforceable right to possession.

members.legal_issue: A writ proceeding is not an appropriate remedy when granting relief requires resolving serious factual disputes or determining disputed title to property.
material_facts: The claimant entered the house after government officials moved his family and belongings there, but no letter of allotment was issued to him.
The government later refused to allot the house, asserting that the claimant was ineligible because he had previously been allotted agricultural land.
The house was subsequently allotted to another applicant, who received possession under an allotment letter.
Determining the parties’ rights required deciding what rights the claimant had acquired and whether the later possessor had a legal right to hold the house against him.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, relief by mandamus or an order in the nature of mandamus is appropriate where the material facts are undisputed and the claimant’s title is clear. Where relief would require resolving disputed facts or declaring title and ordering recovery of possession, the proper remedy is a civil suit.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have used writ proceedings to declare the claimant’s title and order restoration of possession; those matters required determination in a civil suit.

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A claimant sought relief in a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.serious_factual_dispute: The parties disputed facts that had to be determined before their respective rights could be resolved.
predicates.serious_title_dispute: The claimant’s title or right to possess the property was not clear and had to be determined before possession could be restored.

members.legal_issue: A writ court should not adjudicate a private dispute over competing property titles that requires proof of basic facts when no public-law issue or reviewable defect in the authority’s sale process is raised.
material_facts: The property had been mortgaged to secure a loan, and the original owner later transferred it through successive sales while the mortgage remained in place.

After default, the finance corporation took possession and sold the property under its statutory power; the purchaser paid the full offered price, and the corporation confirmed the sale, although no sale deed was executed.

The later purchaser sought cancellation of the corporation’s sale, transfer of the property to him, and restoration of possession, relying on his purchase and claiming lack of knowledge of the mortgage and sale.

Deciding the competing claims required determination of title and proof of basic facts; the writ petition did not challenge the corporation’s authority or the sale process for lack of jurisdiction or abuse of authority.
The High Court cancelled the sale and directed repayment to the corporation’s purchaser, thereby deciding the parties’ competing rights.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a writ proceeding is not an appropriate forum to adjudicate a dispute whose essence is the parties’ competing private-law claims to property and which requires proof of basic facts, absent an issue arising from a public-law function. Even where a statutory authority’s sale is questioned, the writ court’s role is at most judicial review of the administrative action; it does not determine inter se private rights where the authority’s jurisdiction or the sale process is not challenged for lack of jurisdiction or abuse of authority. The Court relied on Godavari Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2011) 2 SCC 439, para 8(vi), and Kisan Sahkari Chini Mills Ltd. v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500, para 23.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have determined the competing title claims in the writ proceeding and should have left the parties to seek remedies before a competent civil forum. The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside.

rule.if: writ_proceeding and competing_private_property_titles and requires_proof_of_basic_facts and not public_law_issue and not authority_or_sale_process_challenged_for_jurisdiction_or_abuse

predicates.writ_proceeding: A party brought the dispute to court by a writ proceeding.
predicates.competing_private_property_titles: The parties asserted competing private claims to ownership or rights in the same property.
predicates.requires_proof_of_basic_facts: Resolving the competing claims required proof of basic facts.
predicates.public_law_issue: The dispute raised an issue arising from a public-law function of the authority.
predicates.authority_or_sale_process_challenged_for: A party challenged the authority’s jurisdiction or the sale process on grounds of lack of jurisdiction or abuse of authority.

members.legal_issue: A writ court may determine disputed questions of fact and should not dismiss a petition in limine solely because factual issues arise.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the petition at the threshold because it considered the demarcation dispute factual and relied on the Collector’s satisfaction about the demarcated area.

The petition raised serious challenges to the acquisition process, many allegations were supported by documentary evidence, and the possible factual conflict concerned publication of the notification.
The High Court dismissed the petition before receiving the respondents’ affidavit in reply.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 gives the High Court jurisdiction to try issues of fact as well as law. That jurisdiction is discretionary and must be exercised on sound judicial principles. A court may decline a writ petition when complex factual disputes require oral evidence or for analogous reasons, but disputed facts alone do not justify summary rejection. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in dismissing the petition in limine on the ground that disputed facts could not be determined; it should have entertained the petition, obtained a reply, and proceeded to decide it.

rule.if: writ_petition_proceeding and serious_reviewable_claim and (documentary_evidence_supports_allegations or factual_dispute_is_limited) and petition_dismissed_only_for_disputed_facts

predicates.writ_petition_proceeding: The proceeding is a petition asking a High Court to exercise its writ jurisdiction.
predicates.serious_reviewable_claim: The petition raises a substantial challenge to the legality of official action.
predicates.documentary_evidence_supports_allegation: Documents are relied on to support a substantial part of the petition’s allegations.
predicates.factual_dispute_is_limited: The factual conflict is confined to an issue that does not make the whole dispute inappropriate for writ adjudication.
predicates.petition_dismissed_only_for_disputed_fac: The court rejects the petition at the outset solely because it considers factual matters disputed.

members.legal_issue: A writ court may not relegate a claimant to a civil suit merely because title or other facts are disputed, without examining whether a genuine dispute requiring that course exists.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a registered deed, earlier proceedings concerning an injunction against construction, and acquisition proceedings in which it had been treated as owner to support its title claim.
The State did not claim title, but argued that the claimant held the land for the benefit of the public and could not use it for construction.
A housing society claimed rights to enjoy the open space, while the municipal corporation asserted that the land had vested in it without explaining how that vesting occurred.
The High Court refused writ relief on the ground that a civil suit was an efficacious alternative remedy, without probing whether there was an actual serious dispute over ownership or title.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a High Court has jurisdiction to determine questions of fact, including disputed questions, although it may decline to do so as a matter of prudence where the dispute is unsuitable for writ adjudication. There is no absolute rule requiring parties to bring a civil suit whenever facts are disputed. The court relied on ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (2004) 3 SCC 553, which discussed Smt. Gunwant Kaur v. Municipal Committee, Bhatinda (1969) 3 SCC 769 and Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. v. Ulhasnagar Municipal Council (1970) 1 SCC 582.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have dismissed the writ petition and relegated the claimant to a civil suit without satisfying itself that a serious dispute over ownership or title existed. The mere raising of disputed facts does not require a writ court to decline jurisdiction.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenges_public_body_a: A claimant brings a writ proceeding challenging action by a public body that allegedly affects the claimant's rights.
predicates.claimant_supports_title_with_documents: The claimant relies on documentary material to support a claim of title to the property.
predicates.public_body_ownership_claim_lacks_explan: A public body asserts that the property has vested in it but does not explain the basis for that assertion.
predicates.high_court_relegates_claimant_without_ex: The High Court directs the claimant to pursue a civil suit without examining whether a serious dispute over title actually exists.

members.legal_issue: A writ proceeding is not the proper forum for relief when the material facts are disputed and deciding the claim requires evidence on complicated questions of fact and law.
material_facts: The proceeding was a writ petition challenging notices requiring transfer of land reserved in colony plans for public purposes.
The parties disputed the nature and extent of their rights in the plots and whether the plots had to be transferred free of cost.
The primary documents concerning the sanctions, their conditions, and the alleged agreements were not in the record before the High Court; documents relied on later were disputed.

The High Court made findings about a trust and the effect of the regulations despite acknowledging that the nature of the trust and its beneficiaries were undetermined and that the relevant agreements were absent.
Determining whether the transfer requirement applied, was incorporated into the sanctions, or had been waived depended on proof of the relevant facts and documents.
members.legal_principle: In a proceeding under Article 226 of the Constitution, when basic facts are disputed and complicated questions of fact and law depend on evidence, the writ court is not the proper forum for relief; it should dismiss the petition without entering into the merits. The Court relied on no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The writ petition should have been dismissed at the threshold without deciding the merits. The Court set aside the High Court’s findings and dismissed both the writ petition and the appeal, leaving the claimant free to seek a remedy by regular suit.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and disputed_foundational_facts and (complicated_questions_require_evidence or primary_evidence_missing)

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A claimant sought relief through a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.disputed_foundational_facts: The parties disputed basic facts material to determining their rights and obligations.
predicates.complicated_questions_require_evidence: Resolving the claim required evidence to decide complicated questions of fact and law.
predicates.primary_evidence_missing: Primary documents material to deciding the claim were absent from the record.

members.legal_issue: A High Court should not determine the contractual merits of a cancellation and guarantee-invocation dispute in writ proceedings when resolving it requires examination of serious, disputed facts.
material_facts: A promoter undertook to submit project materials, obtain clearances and achieve financial closure, and provided a performance guarantee securing those obligations.
The project location changed, and the promoter later stated that it could not proceed at the alternative site because of site conditions.
The public authority cancelled the letter of intent and invoked the guarantee after treating the promoter’s non-performance as a breach.

The promoter challenged the cancellation and invocation in a writ petition, and the High Court addressed whether the cancellation and forfeiture were justified despite disputed questions about the project and performance.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 jurisdiction is discretionary and may be exercised in contractual matters, but, under the principles summarized in Joshi Technologies International Inc. v. Union of India (2015) 7 SCC 728, drawing on ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (2004) 3 SCC 553 and Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks (1998) 8 SCC 1, a court normally will not decide serious and complex factual disputes requiring evidence in writ proceedings. The existence of a contractual dispute does not invariably bar a writ, but writ jurisdiction is not intended to facilitate avoidance of voluntarily incurred contractual obligations.
members.conclusion: The High Court should not have decided in the writ proceeding whether the cancellation was legally justified or whether the underlying circumstances excused the promoter’s non-performance; those matters involved disputed questions of fact and could be pursued in appropriate proceedings.

predicates.contractual_writ_proceeding: A party brought writ proceedings seeking review of a public authority’s action arising from contractual obligations.
predicates.serious_disputed_facts: The dispute over performance or the authority’s action involved serious factual disagreements requiring detailed examination.

members.legal_issue: An injunction cannot protect a claimant with no lawful interest or unlawful possession against the true owner of property.
material_facts: The acquisition and delivery of possession had made the railway authority the lawful owner of the land.
The claimants had no title or other lawful interest because their vendors had none to transfer.

Although a trial court found the claimants in possession, the appellate court found that possession had been delivered to and retained by the railway authority; in any event, the Supreme Court treated any possession by the claimants as unlawful.
The claimants sought an injunction against interference with their possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 41(j) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, an injunction is a discretionary equitable remedy requiring the plaintiff to have a personal interest in the matter. An injunction is not issued against the true owner to protect a claimant who has no lawful interest or is in unlawful possession. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to an injunction against the true owner, even assuming they were in possession, because that possession was unlawful and they had no personal interest in the property.

rule.if: property_injunction_suit and defendant_is_true_owner and (claimant_lacks_lawful_interest or claimant_is_unlawful_trespasser)

predicates.property_injunction_suit: A claimant brings a property suit seeking an injunction to protect possession or prevent interference.
predicates.defendant_is_true_owner: The defendant holds the lawful ownership of the property.
predicates.claimant_lacks_lawful_interest: The claimant has no existing lawful right or personal interest in the property.
predicates.claimant_is_unlawful_trespasser: The claimant possesses the property without a lawful right to do so.

members.legal_issue: A person in unlawful possession cannot obtain an injunction against the true owner merely to protect that possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought an injunction preventing the trust and its representatives from evicting them or interfering with their possession.
The trust disputed the plaintiffs’ right to remain in possession.
The Court stated the rule concerning an unlawful possessor seeking an injunction against the owner but left the disputed facts about possession and eviction to the trial court.
members.legal_principle: Injunction is discretionary and judicial proceedings cannot be used to protect or perpetuate a wrong. The Court relied on Mahadeo Savlaram Sheike v. Pune Municipal Corporation, Shiv Kumar Chadha v. MCD, and Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh.
members.conclusion: An injunction cannot be granted against the true owner at the instance of a person in unlawful possession; the Court left the factual possession dispute for the trial court.

predicates.injunction_claim: A claimant asks a court to restrain another person from acting in relation to property.
predicates.claimant_is_in_unlawful_possession: The claimant’s possession of the property is unlawful.
predicates.injunction_is_sought_against_true_owner: The person whom the claimant seeks to restrain is the true owner of the property.

members.legal_issue: An interim injunction cannot be used to protect a person with no legal right to remain in possession against the rightful owner.
material_facts: The property had been acquired, possession had been taken, and it had been handed to the public authority.
The occupants entered under leave-and-licence arrangements that had expired.
An eviction order against the occupants had become final, leaving them with no legal right to remain in possession.
The occupants relied on municipal resolutions that did not establish a prima facie right to retain the property.
The injunction would restrain the public authority from taking possession for the purpose for which the property had been acquired.
members.legal_principle: Under Shiv Kumar Chadha v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, (1993) 3 SCC 161, and Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh, (1992) 1 SCC 719, interim injunction is discretionary and requires a strong prima facie case, a favourable balance of convenience, and a risk of irreparable injury not adequately remedied by damages. A court must not use its process to protect or perpetuate a wrong, and an injunction cannot be granted against the rightful owner at the instance of persons in unlawful possession.
members.conclusion: The occupants had no basis for an interim injunction against the rightful owner; there was neither a balance of convenience in their favour nor irreparable injury warranting relief. The High Court rightly dissolved the injunction.

predicates.temporary_injunction_sought: A party seeks temporary injunctive relief while a suit is pending.
predicates.applicant_lacks_legal_right_to_possessio: The applicant has no legal entitlement to remain in possession of the property.
predicates.respondent_is_rightful_owner: The respondent is entitled to possession as the rightful owner.

members.legal_issue: A claimant whose title has been decided against them cannot obtain an injunction against the person established to be the true owner merely by asserting possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought cancellation of the registered sale deed and a declaration concerning title, but those claims were rejected and the rejection became final.
The sale deed in favour of the defendant was accepted as valid, including its recording of full consideration, and the defendant was held to be the true and absolute owner.
The lower courts found the plaintiff in possession of part of the land, but the Supreme Court considered the claim even on the assumption that she was in possession.
The plaintiff sought an injunction to prevent the true owner from disturbing that possession.
members.legal_principle: A bare injunction suit may be maintainable in appropriate circumstances, but a claimant cannot maintain one against the true owner after the title dispute has been settled against the claimant. Under Jharkhand State Housing Board v. Didar Singh (2019) 17 SCC 692, a genuine cloud over title may require a declaration; here title was settled against the claimant. A person in possession may have a good title against the world except the rightful owner, as stated in A. Subramanian v. R. Pannerselvam (2021) 3 SCC 675, but cannot use that possession to obtain an injunction against the rightful owner. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594 concerns lawful possession; possession after the claimant has failed to establish title against the true owner is not lawful possession entitling the claimant to an injunction.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to a permanent injunction against the true owner; the injunction decree was unsustainable and was set aside.

predicates.suit_seeks_injunction_against_alleged_tr: The claimant sought an injunction preventing another person alleged to own the property from disturbing the claimant’s possession.
predicates.title_dispute_was_adjudicated_against_cl: A competent court resolved the title dispute against the claimant.
predicates.opposing_owner_was_established_as_true_o: The opposing person was established to hold the rightful title to the property.
predicates.claimant_lacked_independent_legal_entitl: The claimant had no legal entitlement to remain in possession independent of the title claim decided against them.
