members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a permanent injunction to prevent interference with property must prove actual physical possession on the date the suit is filed, and cannot establish that possession merely through inferences from surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The claimant sued for a permanent injunction, asserting that he was a tenant in possession and was carrying on businesses at the premises.

The trial court found that the claimant had not proved actual possession or the businesses he claimed to operate; the premises were found unfit for business, and there was no adequate evidence that he had repaired them.
The claimant had not paid rent for many years and did not rebut the evidence supporting the contention that he had vacated the premises.

The lower appellate court inferred possession from the withdrawal of an earlier suit and the absence of evidence showing that possession had been handed over; the Supreme Court held that this did not establish possession on the date of the later suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, permanent injunction restraining interference with possession may be granted only where the claimant proves actual and physical possession on the date of suit. The burden is on the claimant; possession cannot be established merely by drawing inferences from circumstances. A claimant seeking this equitable relief must also show lawful possession. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The claimant had not proved actual and lawful possession on the date of suit and was not entitled to a permanent injunction. The appeal was allowed, the High Court judgment was set aside, and the suit was dismissed.

predicates.injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a permanent injunction to prevent another person from interfering with claimed possession of property.
predicates.actual_possession_not_proved: The claimant did not establish actual and physical possession of the property on the date the suit was filed.
predicates.lawful_possession_not_established: The claimant did not establish that the claimed possession was lawful.

members.legal_issue: An injunction against interference with property cannot be granted when the claimant has not established possession.
material_facts: The earlier suit for an injunction had been dismissed because the plaintiff failed to establish possession.
In the later suit, the plaintiff did not demonstrate that possession had been recovered after the earlier suit.
The plaintiff had admitted that the opposing party was in possession and cultivating the property.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that injunctive relief against interference with property could not be granted without proof that the plaintiff was in possession. It distinguished Devish v. M. K. Subbiah and Navalram Laxmidas Devmurari v. Vijayaben Jayvantbhai Chavda, where the fact-finding courts had affirmatively found possession, and found that the presumption that possession follows title did not assist the plaintiff in light of the evidence of the opposing party’s possession.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not entitled to the injunction sought because they had not established possession of the property.

predicates.property_injunction_claim: The claimant sought an injunction restraining another person from interfering with the claimant's possession of property.
predicates.claimant_possession_not_established: The claimant did not prove possession of the property, and the evidence showed that another person was in possession.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who is not in possession cannot obtain an injunction against dispossession, and a factual finding of non-possession is not open to interference in constitutional supervisory review.
material_facts: The wife sought an injunction concerning her asserted right to occupy the house.
The Senior Civil Judge found that she was not residing in the house and dismissed her temporary-injunction application.
That finding was challenged in proceedings under Article 227 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the finding that the claimant was not residing in the premises as a finding of fact that could not be interfered with under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution. It further held that a person not in possession cannot claim an injunction restraining dispossession from the property.
members.conclusion: Because the wife was not in possession, she could not obtain an injunction restraining the owners from dispossessing her; the finding of non-possession could not be interfered with in the supervisory proceedings.

rule.if: injunction_claim_depends_on_current_possession and claimant_not_in_possession and non_possession_is_factual_finding and constitutional_supervisory_review

predicates.injunction_claim_depends_on_current_poss: The claimant sought an injunction protecting possession or preventing dispossession from a home.
predicates.claimant_not_in_possession: The claimant was not in possession of the home when the injunction claim was considered.
predicates.non_possession_is_factual_finding: A lower court found as a matter of fact that the claimant was not residing in or possessing the home.
predicates.constitutional_supervisory_review: The challenge to that factual finding was brought in constitutional supervisory proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Possession does not raise a presumption of title in favour of a party when the relevant facts are known and establish that neither party has title.
material_facts: The Society relied on its possession to invoke the presumption described in section 110 of the Evidence Act, 1872.
The facts concerning the parties’ possession and claims were known.
Neither party established title to the land at the relevant time.
members.legal_principle: Section 110 of the Evidence Act, 1872, may support a presumption of ownership from possession, but that presumption does not arise as a substitute for known facts that disclose no title in either party. In that situation, possession decides the contest between them.
members.conclusion: The presumption under section 110 was immaterial; possession alone determined the dispute between the parties.

predicates.possessory_dispute: The parties disputed the right to possess land.
predicates.relevant_facts_known: The material facts about possession and the parties’ claims were known.
predicates.neither_party_has_proven_title: Neither party established title to the disputed land.

members.legal_issue: A defendant who has no better title or authority to possess land cannot defeat a prior possessor’s claim merely by asserting that an unconnected third party owns the land.
material_facts: The plaintiff had possessed the disputed land before the Society took possession.
The Society did not establish title in itself or authority from the State to take the land at the time of the dispossession.
The Society sought to resist the plaintiff’s claim by asserting that the State held title.
Neither party established title to the land at the relevant time.
members.legal_principle: A person in possession has a possessory title good against all persons except the rightful owner, and a defendant without a better title or authority cannot plead the jus tertii against that possession. The Court approved Perry v. Clissold, applied the principle in Asher v. Whitlock, Burling v. Read, and Smith v. Oxenden, and treated the conflicting approach in Doe v. Barnard as displaced. It distinguished Dharani Kanta Lahiri v. Garbar Ali Khan and Mahabir Prasad v. Jamuna Singh. The Court also referred to the declaratory effect of the amended Limitation Act.
members.conclusion: The Society could not rely on the State’s asserted title as a defence to the plaintiff’s claim based on prior possession.

rule.if: possession_recovery_proceeding and claimant_previously_possessed_land and defendant_wrongfully_dispossessed_claimant and defendant_lacks_better_title_or_owner_authority and defendant_relies_only_on_third_party_title

predicates.possession_recovery_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding to recover land from a person in possession.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_land: The claimant possessed the disputed land before the defendant took possession.
predicates.defendant_wrongfully_dispossessed_claima: The defendant took possession in a manner wrongful as against the claimant.
predicates.defendant_lacks_better_title_or_owner_au: The defendant established neither a superior title in itself nor authority from the rightful owner to take possession.
predicates.defendant_relies_only_on_third_party_tit: The defendant relied on an alleged title held by a third party unconnected to the defendant’s own right to possession.

members.legal_issue: A claimant without documentary title can recover immovable property on the basis of prior possession only by proving settled possession, and cannot prevail over a defendant who establishes a better title.
material_facts: The plaintiff had no title document and sought possession based on alleged prior possession and dispossession within twelve years before filing suit.
The evidence relied on by the plaintiff did not establish possession of the disputed plot: the rent note did not identify that plot, and only a small part of a vehicle body lay on its boundary.

The First Appellate Court found that the defendant’s predecessor had possessed the property before selling it to the defendant, and that the defendant had proved title and possession through the sale deeds and other evidence.
The Supreme Court found no material establishing the plaintiff’s settled or established possession and upheld the First Appellate Court’s findings.
members.legal_principle: Section 64 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits a suit for possession based on previous possession, brought within twelve years of dispossession, without initially relying on proprietary title. Under Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, AIR 1968 SC 1165, where a defendant sets up title, the claimant must establish a better title; prior peaceful possession can itself support a claim where no better title is shown. Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu, (2004) 1 SCC 769, explains that settled possession can be protected even against the rightful owner, but it must be effective, undisturbed, and known to the owner or not concealed, and must involve animus possidendi. Stray or casual acts of trespass do not establish settled possession. Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (corresponding to Section 9 of the 1877 Act) concerns the distinct summary remedy for recovery based on possession without adjudicating title. The judgment also refers to Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, AIR 1924 PC 144, for the principle that possession must be obtained through legal process rather than force.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to prove possessory title or a right to recover possession; the suit was dismissed and the First Appellate Court’s judgment was restored.

predicates.possessory_recovery_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking recovery of immovable property on the basis of alleged prior possession.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_settled_possess: The claimant’s evidence did not establish effective, undisturbed possession of the property for a sufficient period with the owner’s knowledge or without concealment.
predicates.defendant_established_better_title: The defendant established a better title to the property through evidence of title and possession, including the possession of a predecessor in title.

members.legal_issue: A declaration of ownership cannot be granted when the claimant has not satisfactorily established title to the property.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration that he was the absolute owner of the site.
The High Court concluded, and the Supreme Court agreed, that the material on record did not satisfactorily establish the plaintiff's title.
members.legal_principle: A claimant seeking a declaration of ownership must satisfy the court that the claimant has good title to the property. No provision or earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to the declaration of ownership, and the suit was dismissed to that extent.

predicates.ownership_declaration_sought: The claimant seeks a declaration that the claimant owns the property.
predicates.title_not_satisfactorily_proved: The evidence does not satisfactorily establish the claimant's title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A title claim cannot be established by an unproved oral arrangement, an unsupported assertion of occupancy, or a mere admission that does not itself transfer title.
material_facts: The claimants alleged occupancy rights over a much larger area than the survey records attributed to their branch; the survey evidence recorded only about nineteen bighas for that branch.
The alleged oral arrangement with the landholder was not established.
The evidence of possession before 1909 was not convincing, and the Court had found that the claimants and their ancestors were not in possession of the disputed land since 1909.
An admission about tenancy rights was made in circumstances the Court regarded as suspicious, was not followed by a formal amendment to the written statement, and had weak evidentiary value.
The claimants did not claim tenancy rights by express grant or adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Title must be established by legally sufficient proof; it does not pass merely by admission. An admission may have weak evidentiary value in the circumstances in which it was made, and mere occupation does not by itself confer tenancy rights.
members.conclusion: The claimants failed to prove title through the alleged occupancy, oral arrangement, or possession. The admission did not establish title, and mere occupation did not confer tenancy rights.

rule.if: civil_property_title_claim and (oral_arrangement_unproved or occupancy_evidence_insufficient or admission_only_supports_title or possession_is_only_basis)

predicates.civil_property_title_claim: A party seeks a declaration or recovery of property on the basis of title.
predicates.oral_arrangement_unproved: The party relies on an alleged oral arrangement that is not proved.
predicates.occupancy_evidence_insufficient: The records and other evidence do not establish the claimed occupancy rights.
predicates.admission_only_supports_title: The party relies on an admission that does not independently establish or transfer title.
predicates.possession_is_only_basis: The party relies on occupation alone without establishing a legal basis for tenancy or ownership.

members.legal_issue: A person who cannot demonstrate any right or connection to property cannot maintain an application seeking a determination of rights over that property.
material_facts: The respondents produced no document showing that the land had been transferred to the society, that the society had allotted the land to them, or that they were society members.
They produced no other document linking them to the land or establishing a claim to it.
The registered sale deed in favour of the appellant’s predecessor had not been challenged before a competent court.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that an applicant must show a basis for an interest in the property to maintain an application concerning it. It also stated that court proceedings should not be used as a means of harassment or persecution, and that courts should not permit litigants to prolong proceedings without a legitimate basis.
members.conclusion: The respondents had no standing to maintain the application, which was not maintainable at their instance.

predicates.property_application_seeking_a_determina: The proceeding is an application asking a court to determine rights concerning property.
predicates.applicant_cannot_show_a_connection_to_th: The applicant produces no evidence linking them to the property or establishing a claimed interest in it.

members.legal_issue: A person who has no established right, title or interest in a housing society’s property cannot claim membership on the basis of that property.
material_facts: The claimant applied to the housing society for membership based on his asserted ownership of the flat.
The asserted ownership rested on an alleged agreement that did not transfer title and was found not to establish a genuine transfer.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the claimed membership as dependent on the claimant’s asserted interest in the property. Once that interest was not established, the claimant could not claim membership on that basis; the judgment cites no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this membership conclusion.
members.conclusion: The claimant had no right, title or interest in the property and therefore could not claim membership of the society.

predicates.housing_society_membership_claim: A person applied to a housing society to be admitted as a member.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_property_ownership: The person based the membership claim on asserted ownership of property associated with the society.
predicates.claimant_produced_no_valid_title_documen: The person produced no valid document establishing title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A claim of adverse possession against a claimant does not arise when that claimant has not established title to the land.
material_facts: The defendants asserted that they or their predecessors had possessed parts of the property for many years and had acquired title by adverse possession.
The Court found that the plaintiffs had not proved that their predecessor acquired title to the disputed land.
The Court therefore held that adverse possession against the plaintiffs did not arise.
members.legal_principle: Adverse possession is a statutory method of acquiring title to land by limitation. It presupposes another person’s ownership and requires possession with an intention to hold the property in opposition to the world, together with the owner’s knowledge of that assertion. The Court also referred to Austin on Jurisprudence.
members.conclusion: Because the plaintiffs had not established title to the disputed land, no question of adverse possession against them arose.

predicates.title_recovery_proceeding: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking title to or possession of land.
predicates.adverse_possession_asserted: An opposing party claimed to have acquired title through long possession adverse to the claimant.
predicates.claimant_lacks_title: The claimant failed to establish ownership of the land against which adverse possession was asserted.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who has not proved title cannot rely on the principle that possession follows title when the defendant is in physical possession, and the defendant need not plead or prove adverse possession.
material_facts: The municipality did not prove title to the disputed land.
Evidence showed that the defendants had physical possession of the land.
The municipality relied on the principle that possession follows title.
members.legal_principle: The principle that possession follows title could not assist a claimant that had not established title where evidence showed physical possession by the defendant. In a suit for possession based on title, failure to prove the claimant's title made it unnecessary for the defendant to plead or prove adverse possession. The Court cited no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The municipality could not rely on possession following title, and because it had not proved title in its possession suit, the defendants did not need to plead or prove adverse possession.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit for possession on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_title: The claimant did not establish title to the disputed property.
predicates.defendant_in_physical_possession: The defendant was in physical possession of the disputed property.

members.legal_issue: A claim of private defence of property fails when the defence does not provide material supporting its claimed possession and the evidence supports the opposing party’s possession and cultivation.
material_facts: The accused claimed that they were in possession of the field and that the deceased came to disturb that possession.
The accused produced neither an order vacating the interim arrangement concerning possession nor records showing that they had raised the crop.
Revenue extracts recorded the deceased as owner, cultivator, and the person who raised the crop.
The injured eyewitness’s evidence that the deceased and she had raised the crop was unrebutted.
Eight accused were harvesting the crop with weapons, while the deceased and his wife were the only opposing persons who came to the field.
members.legal_principle: Under section 97, secondly, read with section 99 of the Indian Penal Code, the asserted right of private defence of property was considered on the material in the record, but the defence had the duty to make the necessary supporting material available. The Court assessed the claim against the possession and cultivation evidence and the surrounding circumstances. No earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The plea of private defence of property was negatived because the accused failed to establish the factual basis for it and the evidence supported the prosecution’s account of possession.

rule.if: criminal_assault_case and private_defence_of_property_claimed and defence_lacks_possession_support and evidence_supports_other_party_possession

predicates.criminal_assault_case: The case concerns an assault arising from a dispute over possession of property.
predicates.private_defence_of_property_claimed: The accused asserted that they used force to protect their possession of property.
predicates.defence_lacks_possession_support: The accused did not produce material supporting their claimed possession or showing that the other party’s asserted entitlement to possession had ended.
predicates.evidence_supports_other_party_possession: Documents, testimony, or surrounding circumstances supported the other party’s possession and cultivation of the property.

members.legal_issue: A claim of title does not establish a right to defend property when the opposing party's possession is proved and the claimant's possession is not.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence, accepted by both lower courts, showed that the deceased owner had possessed and used the disputed grove.
The accused relied on documents relevant to title, but those documents did not establish their possession.
The Supreme Court was prepared to assume, for purposes of argument, that the land belonged to the accused, but the concurrent finding about possession remained unrebutted.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished title from possession in assessing a claim of defence of property. It relied on the concurrent factual finding of possession; it cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The accused had no established right of defence of the property, and their claim of title did not displace the finding that the deceased owner was in possession.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and opposing_party_possession_proved and accused_possession_not_proved and title_evidence_does_not_establish_possession

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction in which a right to defend property is claimed.
predicates.opposing_party_possession_proved: Evidence accepted by the courts shows that the opposing party possessed and used the disputed property.
predicates.accused_possession_not_proved: The accused do not establish that they possessed the disputed property.
predicates.title_evidence_does_not_establish_posses: The evidence relied on to show title does not establish possession of the disputed property.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming as executor or legatee under a will cannot establish that right in court without probate or letters of administration when the will falls within a category subject to the requirement.
material_facts: One petitioner claimed to be the sole beneficiary under a will and sought to establish a right to property under it.
The petitioners argued that the probate requirement prevented a Christian legatee from establishing a right in court without first obtaining probate or letters of administration.
The statutory scheme applied the requirement to Christians and to specified wills of other communities, while exempting other categories of wills.
members.legal_principle: Section 213(1) bars establishment in a court of a right as executor or legatee under a will without probate or letters of administration. Section 213(2), read with Section 57(a), (b) and (c), limits the categories to which that requirement applies. The bar concerns the asserted capacity of executor or legatee, whether the claimant appears as plaintiff or defendant, and does not prohibit consideration of the will for other purposes. The Court also referred to the application of the requirement to specified Parsi wills following the Indian Succession (Amendment) Act, 1962.
members.conclusion: The bar concerns establishing a right as executor or legatee in a court of justice without the required grant. It does not prevent a will from being considered for other purposes, or prevent its reference in administrative or other tribunal proceedings.

predicates.court_proceeding_to_establish_executor_o: A claimant seeks in court to establish a right under a will in the capacity of executor or legatee.
predicates.will_within_compulsory_probate_category: The will falls within a category for which a probate or equivalent grant is required before the testamentary right may be established in court.
predicates.probate_or_letters_not_granted: No probate or letters of administration for the will has been granted by a competent court.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming property through a legatee cannot establish the legatee’s right under an unprobated will when that right is necessary to prove the property title.
material_facts: In a property-title suit, the defendant relied on a will in which the original owner allegedly bequeathed the disputed house to her mother.

The defendant had obtained letters of administration for her mother’s later will, but no probate or letters of administration had been obtained for the earlier will on which the mother’s ownership of the whole house depended.
The defendant could claim the mother’s share as an heir, but establishing the mother’s ownership of the entire house as a legatee depended on the earlier will.
members.legal_principle: Section 213(1) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 bars the establishment in court of a right as executor or legatee under a will unless probate or letters of administration have been obtained. The bar applies whether the claimant is plaintiff or defendant, and also applies when a person must establish another person’s right as legatee to prove a derivative title. Ghanshamdoss v. Gulab Bi Bai, (1927) I.L.R. 50 Mad. 927, was approved. Probate and administration proceedings address due execution of a will, not title to the property included in it.
members.conclusion: The defendant could not establish her mother’s right as a legatee under the unprobated will, and the later letters of administration did not give the defendant title to property that had not belonged to her mother. The bar applied even though the defendant was claiming through the legatee rather than directly as a legatee.

predicates.property_title_suit: A party brought a civil suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.derivative_title_depends_on_unprobated_w: A party’s claimed title depends on establishing that another person acquired the property as a legatee under a will for which no probate or letters of administration were obtained.
predicates.legatee_right_cannot_be_established: The claimed right as legatee cannot be established in court.

members.legal_issue: The benefit of a final order quashing an acquisition declaration does not extend to landowners who were not parties to the successful proceedings when the order was confined to the petitioners and the declaration was not quashed in its entirety.
material_facts: The appellants had not obtained the orders that quashed declarations in proceedings brought by other landowners.
The earlier court orders granted relief to the petitioners before those courts rather than quashing the declarations in their entirety.
The appellants’ lands remained covered by declarations that had not been quashed in their cases.
The Supreme Court had previously held that the benefit of the earlier limited quashing did not enure to landowners who were not parties to those proceedings.
members.legal_principle: In Abhey Ram (Dead by LRs) v. Union of India, a three-judge Bench held that where the operative order quashes a declaration only with respect to the writ petitioners, its benefit does not extend to other landowners; unless the composite declaration is quashed in toto, it remains effective for lands not covered by the quashing order. The Court distinguished the interim effect of a stay, which may inhibit action under a composite notification, from the final relief granted in a particular case. This conclusion also accords with the principle applied in Delhi Administration v. Gurdip Singh Uban that the final benefit is confined to those in whose favour the order was made.
members.conclusion: The appellants could not obtain the benefit of the final quashing orders made in other landowners’ cases.

rule.if: is_land_acquisition_challenge and applicant_not_party_to_successful_case and final_quashing_limited_to_petitioners and declaration_not_quashed_in_entirety

predicates.is_land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges an acquisition of land under a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.applicant_not_party_to_successful_case: The landowner seeking relief was not a petitioner in the proceeding that resulted in the successful final order.
predicates.final_quashing_limited_to_petitioners: The final order granting relief confined its effect to the petitioners before the court.
predicates.declaration_not_quashed_in_entirety: The declaration covering the acquisition was not set aside in its entirety.

members.legal_issue: Quashing acquisition proceedings for landowners whose objections were not properly considered does not extend to nonparties who filed no objections, and a later purchaser cannot rely on that quashing to revive a lost challenge.
material_facts: The original landowners filed no objections under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; their writ petition was dismissed, and their special leave petition was later withdrawn.
The earlier High Court decision quashed proceedings because objections filed by the landowners who brought those petitions had not been properly heard.
The purchaser acquired the land with knowledge of the acquisition dispute and relied on a later High Court order that treated the acquisition as quashed and required repayment of compensation.
The purchaser’s later deposit under that order was the basis on which the High Court declared the acquisition lapsed.
members.legal_principle: A judgment granting relief for an individualized failure to hear objections is in personam unless the acquisition is explicitly quashed in its entirety. Under Abhey Ram v. Union of India and Delhi Administration v. Gurdip Singh Uban (both decisions), landowners who filed no Section 5A objections cannot rely on another landowner’s successful challenge to invalidate the acquisition. Gurdip Singh Uban further confined the effect of the earlier High Court orders to the petitioners and land covered by those petitions. Shyam Nandan Prasad v. State of Bihar, Chairman and Managing Director, Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. S. Saraswathy, and State of Haryana v. Devander Sagar likewise support individualized relief and require an explicit order to quash acquisition proceedings in their entirety. The later decisions in Abhey Ram and Gurdip Singh Uban did not approve the reasoning underlying the order in Balbir Singh; a deposit made under that order cannot revive a challenge already lost.
members.conclusion: The earlier quashing and the order requiring repayment of compensation gave the purchaser no right to claim lapse; the later deposit was inconsequential.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_proceeding: A claimant seeks to invalidate acquisition proceedings by relying on a court order in another landowner’s challenge.
predicates.prior_quashing_for_other_landowners: A court quashed acquisition steps because the objections of landowners who brought that case were not properly heard.
predicates.no_objections_filed_by_predecessor: The claimant’s predecessor in interest filed no objections to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.prior_quashing_does_not_invalidate_acqui: The earlier quashing does not invalidate the acquisition for the claimant.

members.legal_issue: Owners who did not object to an acquisition notification cannot rely on its quashing in other owners’ cases to invalidate the acquisition as against their own land.
material_facts: The landowners did not file objections to the acquisition notification.
A prior judgment had allowed other landowners’ petitions on grounds relating to the inquiry into objections and quashed the later acquisition declaration in those cases.
The landowners relied on that prior judgment, and the High Court treated it as invalidating the declaration for all affected owners.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1), 5A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, persons who filed no objections to the Section 4(1) notification could not challenge the Section 5A inquiry or obtain the benefit of its alleged defects. The Court applied the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram v. Union of India, which held that such owners could not rely on the quashing of the Section 6 declaration in other owners’ cases; it preferred that decision to the two-Judge decision in Delhi Development Authority v. Sudan Singh.
members.conclusion: The landowners could not claim the benefit of the quashing in other owners’ cases. Because they had filed no objections, the declaration remained in force as against them, and the earlier quashing did not cause the initial notification to lapse for their land.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_judgment: The matter is an appeal from a judgment allowing a writ petition concerning an acquisition.
predicates.owners_filed_no_objections: The owners did not submit objections to the notification concerning their land.
predicates.prior_quashing_arose_from_other_owners_c: The earlier quashing followed challenges brought by other owners, rather than by the owners seeking to rely on it.

members.legal_issue: Quashing an acquisition declaration in individual owners’ cases does not, without more, quash the declaration for all owners covered by it.
material_facts: A prior Division Bench had allowed petitions brought by some owners and quashed the acquisition declaration in those cases.
The present landowners had not filed objections and were not among the petitioners in those earlier cases.
The High Court treated the earlier judgment as a judgment applying to all owners, while the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram had interpreted its effect as limited to the cases before that court.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram v. Union of India, which considered the effect of the earlier Division Bench judgment and held that quashing in individual writ petitions did not quash the whole declaration. That larger-Bench decision governed over the two-Judge decision in Delhi Development Authority v. Sudan Singh; dismissal of a special leave petition and non-binding departmental legal opinions could not override it.
members.conclusion: The earlier Division Bench judgment did not quash the entire declaration for all owners. The Court was bound by the three-Judge decision in Abhey Ram, which had interpreted the earlier judgment as case-specific.

predicates.appeal_concerns_same_acquisition: The appeal concerns the same acquisition as the one involved in the earlier judgment.
predicates.earlier_quashing_followed_individual_pet: The earlier declaration was quashed in proceedings brought by individual owners.
predicates.larger_bench_interpreted_earlier_judgmen: A larger judicial bench interpreted the earlier judgment as applying to the individual cases before it rather than to all affected owners.

members.legal_issue: The reasoning that individual stay orders suspended further steps for an integrated acquisition does not make a later quashing in individual cases apply to the entire acquisition declaration.
material_facts: The acquisition was part of an integrated scheme.
The earlier Full Bench considered whether the declaration had been issued outside the applicable time limit and held that individual stay orders prevented further steps on the integrated declaration.
The landowners argued that the same reasoning meant the later quashing in individual petitions must apply to the entire declaration.
members.legal_principle: The Full Bench’s reasoning in Balak Ram Gupta v. Union of India concerned the effect of stay orders on the timing of a declaration for an integrated scheme. It did not determine the effect of later quashing in individual petitions. The Court applied Abhey Ram v. Union of India in holding that case-specific quashing was not quashing of the whole declaration.
members.conclusion: The stay-order reasoning was confined to the time-limit issue and did not establish that quashing in individual cases invalidated the declaration for everyone.

predicates.challenge_concerns_time_limit_for_acquis: The issue under consideration is whether an acquisition declaration was made outside the applicable time limit.
predicates.acquisition_was_an_integrated_scheme: The acquisition formed part of a scheme treated as an integrated whole.
predicates.individual_stays_prevented_further_steps: Stay orders in individual proceedings prevented the authorities from taking further steps on the declaration.

members.legal_issue: A person whose property interest is not affected by an evacuee-property declaration cannot challenge that declaration.
material_facts: The petitioners were not evacuees and held shares in the properties.
The declaration identified only the shares of family members who had migrated as evacuee property.
The declaration did not purport to affect the petitioners’ shares.
members.legal_principle: A person cannot challenge an order in proceedings that did not purport to affect that person’s interest. Because the declaration affected only the evacuees’ shares, the petitioners were not concerned with its validity.
members.conclusion: The petitioners could not challenge the declaration, and the Court did not decide whether the notice underlying it was valid.

predicates.constitutional_property_challenge: A claimant brings a constitutional proceeding to challenge an order concerning property.
predicates.declaration_limited_to_others_interests: The order declares only the interests of other persons to be evacuee property.
predicates.claimant_interest_unaffected: The order does not purport to affect the claimant’s property interest.

members.legal_issue: A party with no interest in the property is not entitled to a declaration that alienations of it are invalid or limited.
material_facts: The appellants sought declarations against alienations made by the widow and the adopted son.
The adopted son was validly adopted and entitled to take the property under the will, leaving the appellants without an interest in the properties.
members.legal_principle: Because the appellants had no interest in the properties, they could not obtain declarations against alienations made by those entitled to the property. The Court accordingly rejected their claim for declarations concerning the alienations.
members.conclusion: The appellants were not entitled to declarations concerning the alienations.

predicates.appeal_seeking_declaration_against_prope: A party appeals seeking a declaration that alienations of property are invalid or do not bind the party's claimed interest.
predicates.challenger_has_no_interest_in_property: The party seeking the declaration has no interest in the property.

members.legal_issue: A person interested in one specifically identified parcel cannot challenge an acquisition notification on the ground that another parcel included in it was ineligible for dispensing with the objection inquiry when the owner of that other parcel has not challenged the acquisition.
material_facts: The challenger was a tenant of a plot that was admittedly arable or waste land and therefore fell within the urgency provision.
The same notification included another plot on which a permanent construction stood, and the challenger argued that the acquisition procedure could not be used for that plot.
The owner of the other plot did not challenge the acquisition and accepted compensation.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, the objection inquiry under section 5A could be dispensed with for the challenger's arable or waste land. The owner of the other plot was the person entitled to object to dispensing with the inquiry for that plot; because that owner did not challenge the acquisition, the challenger could not do so on the owner's behalf. Sarju Prasad v. State of U.P. (AIR 1965 SC 1763) was distinguished: there, the challenger was entitled to object, whereas here the alleged defect concerned land in which the challenger had no relevant interest.
members.conclusion: The challenger could not question the validity of the notification on the basis of the alleged ineligibility of the other plot, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges a notification acquiring land for a public purpose.
predicates.challenger_interested_in_arable_or_waste: The challenger has an interest in a plot that is arable or waste land.
predicates.notice_also_includes_ineligible_other_pl: The challenged notification also includes another plot that is ineligible for the procedure used to dispense with an objection inquiry.
predicates.other_plot_owner_did_not_challenge: The owner of the other plot did not challenge its acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A transferee cannot acquire title through a transfer made after the property has vested in the acquiring authority following acquisition and delivery of possession.
material_facts: The land was acquired, possession was delivered to the railway authority, and the acquisition awards had become final.
The claimants’ vendors purported to purchase the land after the original owner had been divested of title.
The claimants later relied on an agreement with those vendors and sought a declaration of title, having given up their challenge to the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12 and 30 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the awards became binding and final as to the relevant matters; after acquisition and delivery of possession, the land vested in the acquiring authority free of encumbrances. A later transferee from a person who no longer has title obtains no interest in the land. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The vendors had no title or interest to transfer, so the claimants acquired no interest through them and could not obtain the requested declaration.

predicates.suit_claiming_title_through_later_transf: A claimant brings a suit seeking title to property through a transfer from another person.
predicates.property_acquired_and_possession_taken: The property was acquired for a public purpose and possession was delivered to the acquiring authority.
predicates.transfer_occurred_after_acquisition: The purported transferor transferred the property after the acquisition had divested the transferor of title.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser who acquired land after it had vested in the State cannot claim that the acquisition has lapsed.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the land after the acquisition proceedings and the taking of possession.
The purchaser sought a declaration of lapse under the 2013 Act and relied on Government (NCT of Delhi) v. Manav Dharam Trust.
The Court found that the purchaser’s claim was barred by the principles stated in the larger-bench decision in Shiv Kumar v. Union of India.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the 2013 Act, including Section 11(4), restricts transfers of acquired land in the circumstances addressed by the Court. Section 24(2) does not confer on a later purchaser a new right to challenge completed acquisition proceedings or to recover land that has vested in the State. Shiv Kumar v. Union of India held that Manav Dharam Trust was not good law because it failed to follow binding larger- and coordinate-bench decisions, including M. Venkatesh v. Bangalore Development Authority; a later purchaser cannot use Section 24(2) to challenge possession-taking or obtain the land through a void or prohibited transaction.
members.conclusion: The purchaser had no right to claim lapse of the acquisition proceedings.

predicates.lapse_claim_proceeding: A claimant seeks a declaration that a land acquisition has lapsed under a statutory lapse provision.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser: The claimant acquired the land from a person whose interest derived from the original landowner.
predicates.purchase_after_vesting: The claimant acquired the land after possession had been taken and the land had vested in the State.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_cannot_claim_lapse: A later purchaser cannot obtain a declaration that the acquisition has lapsed.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who acquires an interest in land after its acquisition notification and vesting obtains no title enforceable against the acquiring authority.
material_facts: The land had been notified for acquisition before the former owner sold interests in it to the respondents.
Possession had been taken and the land had vested in the acquiring authority before the respondents claimed through those sales.
The respondents relied on sale deeds or agreements with the former owner, who no longer had an interest in the acquired land.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 6 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, publication of the acquisition notification prevents the owner from creating an interest binding on the acquiring authority; under Section 16, vesting following possession is free from encumbrances. A subsequent purchaser acquires no title against the State. The Court relied on Gain Chand v. Gopala, Yadu Nandan Garg v. State of Rajasthan and related decisions, and held that a sale opposed to public policy is void under Section 23 of the Contract Act.
members.conclusion: The respondents acquired no title or right to possession under the sales or agreements; at most, a person entitled under the acquisition law could claim compensation.

predicates.acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a claim to land that was acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.purchase_after_acquisition_notification: The claimant acquired an interest from the former owner after the acquisition notification was published.
predicates.purchase_after_vesting: The claimant acquired an interest from the former owner after the land had vested in the acquiring authority.

members.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires an interest in land after an acquisition notification cannot challenge the acquisition and may only claim compensation.
material_facts: The land was notified for acquisition before the society entered into an agreement to sell with the original landholders.
The agreement to sell did not transfer title to the society, and the original landholders did not join the society's later petition.
members.legal_principle: A transfer made after an acquisition notification is void as against the Government and does not bind it; a subsequent purchaser cannot challenge the acquisition and may claim compensation. The Court relied on Gian Chand v. Gopala, Yadu Nandan Garg v. State of Rajasthan, Jaipur Development Authority v. Mahavir Housing Cooperative Society, Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain, Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, Har Narain v. Mam Chand, and V. Chandrasekaran v. The Administrative Officer. It also relied on Smt. Kalawati v. Bisheshwar and State of Kerala v. M.K. Kunhikannan Nambiar for the meaning of “void.”
members.conclusion: The society could not challenge the acquisition as a subsequent transferee; a transferee in that position may only claim compensation.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_by_transferee: A transferee brings a proceeding challenging the acquisition of the land in which the transferee claims an interest.
predicates.transfer_after_acquisition_notice: The landowner transfers or agrees to transfer an interest in the land after the acquisition notice has been issued.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who acquires land after publication of an acquisition notification has no right to challenge the acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The petitioner purchased the property after publication of the acquisition notification.
The petitioner challenged the notification, declaration, and award.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1), 6, and 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, an alienation after publication of the acquisition notification does not bind the State or the beneficiary, and the purchaser acquires no valid title; once possession is taken after the award, the land vests in the State free of encumbrances. The Court relied on Gurmukh Singh v. State of Haryana, Y.N. Garg v. State of Rajasthan, Sneh Prabha v. State of U.P., and U.P. Jal Nigam v. Kalra Properties (P) Ltd.
members.conclusion: The petitioner had no right to challenge the acquisition proceedings or the award because its purchase after publication of the notification gave it no valid title.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_proceeding: A person seeks to challenge the legality of land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.purchase_after_acquisition_notification: The person acquired the land after the acquisition notification had been published.
predicates.post_notification_purchaser_lacks_right_: A person who acquired the land after publication of the acquisition notification has no right to challenge the acquisition proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A person who purchases land after public notice of its acquisition cannot challenge the acquisition proceedings on the basis of that purchase.
material_facts: The petitioners purchased the land after the preliminary acquisition notification had been issued.
The petitioners sought de-notification and challenged the refusal to give effect to the later de-notification order.
The Court held that the acquisition proceedings had revived after the earlier de-notification was quashed.
members.legal_principle: A purchaser who acquires land after a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does so at their own peril. The purchase does not bind the State or the acquisition beneficiary and confers no title against them, although the purchaser may claim compensation by stepping into the vendor’s shoes. The Court relied on V. Chandrasekaran v. The Administrative Officer and the authorities cited there, including Leela Ram v. Union of India, Smt. Sneh Prabha v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi, and Tika Ram v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The petitioners could not challenge the acquisition proceedings; at most, they could claim compensation on the basis of their vendors’ title.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity or continuation of a land acquisition.
predicates.purchase_after_public_acquisition_notice: The purchaser acquired the land after public notice that it was needed for acquisition.
predicates.purchaser_cannot_challenge_acquisition: The purchaser cannot challenge the acquisition on the basis of the purchase.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser does not acquire cultivatory rights in occupancy land through decree enforcement or insolvency proceedings when the transfer is barred or lacks required revenue-authority permission.
material_facts: The mortgagees purchased one share of the land rights in execution of a civil decree based on an arbitration award and another share in insolvency proceedings.
The rights were cultivatory rights held by occupancy tenants or, alternatively, by ex-proprietary occupancy tenants.
There was no suggestion that the transfers of ex-proprietary occupancy rights had the permission of the appropriate revenue authority.
members.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Central Provinces Tenancy Act barred transfer of an occupancy tenant’s cultivatory rights in execution of a civil-court decree or in insolvency proceedings. Under section 49, an ex-proprietary occupancy tenant’s rights could not be transferred to the mortgagees in these circumstances; section 50 permitted certain transfers only with the appropriate revenue authority’s permission. The court also held that the cultivatory rights did not vest in the Insolvency Court under the Provincial Insolvency Act. It relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The transfers did not vest the cultivatory rights in the mortgagees, and the respondent, as the surviving holder of those rights, was entitled to restoration of possession; the appellants could not claim possession on the basis of the transfers.

rule.if: possession_claim_based_on_purchased_tenancy_rights and transfer_through_decree_or_insolvency and (ordinary_occupancy_tenancy or (ex_proprietary_occupancy_tenancy and not revenue_authority_permission))

predicates.possession_claim_based_on_purchased_tena: A party seeks possession in a suit based on rights it says it purchased from a tenant.
predicates.transfer_through_decree_or_insolvency: The claimed purchase occurred through enforcement of a civil decree or through insolvency proceedings.
predicates.ordinary_occupancy_tenancy: The rights transferred were cultivatory rights held by an occupancy tenant who was not an ex-proprietary occupancy tenant.
predicates.ex_proprietary_occupancy_tenancy: The rights transferred were cultivatory rights held by an ex-proprietary occupancy tenant.
predicates.revenue_authority_permission: The transfer of the ex-proprietary occupancy rights had the permission of the appropriate revenue authority.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot obtain enforceable title through a transferor whose claimed interest derives from a post-notification purchase and an unauthorized allotment of acquired land.
material_facts: The transferor purchased land after publication of the acquisition notification.
The transferor’s claimed interest in the plots depended on an acquisition award and a later allotment of acquired land to him.
The applicants purchased the plots from that transferor.
The Tribunal and trial court found that the transferor had no valid title, and those findings were not successfully challenged.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 and Section 31 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, the acquisition officer had no authority to allot acquired land in the circumstances described. Such an allotment was a nullity, and a post-notification purchase did not create title. The Court relied on Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam (1994) 4 SCC 370 and Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain (1997) 1 SCC 35, as well as Narpat Singh v. Jaipur Development Authority (2002) 4 SCC 666 on the invalidity of such directions and their enforcement.
members.conclusion: The transferor could not convey valid title to the applicants, who therefore had no right to prevent the development authority from auctioning the plots; the High Court erred in granting them relief.

rule.if: auction_challenge_proceeding and acquisition_notice_preceded_transfer and transferor_claim_depended_on_unauthorized_acquired_land_allotment and purchaser_claims_through_transferor

predicates.auction_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges an authority’s proposed auction of land.
predicates.acquisition_notice_preceded_transfer: The transferor’s purchase occurred after public notice that the land was to be acquired.
predicates.transferor_claim_depended_on_unauthorize: The transferor’s claimed interest depended on an award or allotment of acquired land made without authority.
predicates.purchaser_claims_through_transferor: The party challenging the auction claims its interest through a transfer from that transferor.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition declaration is not invalid for failure to consider objections that the affected landowners did not file.
material_facts: The appellants had filed no objections to the proposed acquisition for consideration in an inquiry.
They challenged the declaration in part on the basis that objections had not been properly considered.
members.legal_principle: Section 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 concerns the consideration of objections filed for inquiry. The Court stated that absent objections from the appellants, there was no need to consider their objections. It referred to Delhi Development Authority v. Sudan Singh in discussing this point but held that the case did not apply to the appellants’ circumstances.
members.conclusion: There was no need to consider objections that the appellants had not filed, and the declaration was not vitiated on that ground.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a declaration made in a land-acquisition process.
predicates.affected_claimants_filed_no_objections: The claimants whose land is affected did not submit objections for consideration.
predicates.declaration_challenged_for_nonconsiderat: The claimants allege that the declaration is invalid because their objections were not considered.

members.legal_issue: A failure to provide a hearing under the acquisition objection procedure is not established where the affected owners made no objections and did not seek a hearing.
material_facts: In one petition, the owners raised no objections to the acquisition.
The owners did not request a hearing on the acquisition objections.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the hearing and inquiry procedure under section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and concluded on the record that there were no objections requiring inquiry and no request for a hearing.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that no hearing had been given, noting that the owners had made no objections and had never wanted a hearing.

predicates.land_acquisition_objection_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether an affected owner received a hearing on objections to a proposed land acquisition.
predicates.no_objections_made: The affected owner made no objection to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.no_hearing_requested: The affected owner did not request a hearing on objections.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of land made after publication of an acquisition notification does not bind the acquiring State.
material_facts: An acquisition notification was published before the original owner transferred the properties to the claimants.
A declaration under the acquisition law was published after the transfers.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, a transfer made after publication of the acquisition notification is void as against the State. The Court also noted the subsequent declaration under Section 6. No earlier cases were relied upon.
members.conclusion: The post-notification transfers were void as against the State and did not bind it.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The dispute concerns land acquired through a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.notification_preceded_transfer: An acquisition notification was published before the owner transferred the land.

members.legal_issue: A person who purchases land after publication of a preliminary acquisition notification cannot use that purchase to claim valid title against the acquiring State.
material_facts: A preliminary notification had been published before the appellant purchased the land under a registered sale deed.
The appellant later constructed a house on the land.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, after possession is taken the land vests in the State absolutely, free from encumbrances. A purchase made after the Section 4(1) notification cannot be asserted against the State to obtain title. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s post-notification purchase could not give him valid title against the State; upon acquisition and possession, the land would vest in the State free from encumbrances.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity or effect of a land acquisition.
predicates.purchase_after_initial_notification: The claimant acquired the land after the preliminary acquisition notification had been published.
predicates.post_notification_purchaser_cannot_asser: A purchaser who acquired the land after the preliminary notification cannot assert valid title to it against the acquiring State.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who acquires land after public acquisition notice is ordinarily not entitled to benefits under a policy that reserves alternative developed land for the owner whose land was acquired.
material_facts: The acquisition notice was published before the appellant purchased the land.

The policy provided alternative developed land to qualifying owners whose land was acquired, and the relevant category allowed an owner holding more than two but less than twenty acres to seek a portion of the developed land.

The appellant applied for a policy benefit and deposited compensation she had received, but the Trust learned that she had purchased the land after the acquisition notice only when she later produced her title deed.
No order granting the appellant the policy benefit had been passed and no agreement to lease land to her had been entered into.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, publication of the acquisition notice informs the public that the land is needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose and makes subsequent alienations ineffective against the Government or the acquisition beneficiary; on possession, the land vests in the State free of encumbrances. A subsequent purchaser's rights are subject to the Act and may include a right to compensation, but not an alternative site under a policy conferring that benefit on the owner whose land was acquired. The Court relied on Union of India v. Shri Shivkumar Bhargava and distinguished the limited clarification in the Government Order of June 2, 1972.
members.conclusion: The appellant, as a purchaser after the acquisition notice, was not entitled to the land-policy benefit.

rule.if: policy_claim_by_transferee and purchase_after_public_acquisition_notice and not (timely_policy_application and benefit_order_passed and lease_agreement_entered)

predicates.policy_claim_by_transferee: The proceeding concerns a transferee's claim for an alternative developed site under a policy associated with compulsory acquisition.
predicates.purchase_after_public_acquisition_notice: The claimant acquired the land after public notice of the proposed acquisition had been published.
predicates.timely_policy_application: The claimant applied within the prescribed time to obtain the policy benefit.
predicates.benefit_order_passed: An order granting the claimant the policy benefit had been passed.
predicates.lease_agreement_entered: An agreement to lease the alternative land to the claimant had been entered into.

members.legal_issue: A person who purchases land after publication of an acquisition notification is not entitled under the government policy to an alternative site as the owner whose land was acquired.
material_facts: The claim was made in a writ petition for an alternative site under government policy on the basis that land had been acquired for a public purpose.
The claimant was not the owner when the acquisition notification was published, but became the owner before the acquisition was finalized.
The government policy treated the owner on the date of notification as the person entitled to an alternative site.
members.legal_principle: Under the government policy, the person whose land was acquired means the owner on the date the notification under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act was published. A subsequent purchaser may claim compensation through the rights acquired from the predecessor, but does not qualify as the owner for allotment of an alternative site. The Court also referred to its prior view while considering a Full Bench judgment of the Delhi High Court, without identifying that case in this judgment.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to an alternative site; the direction granting one was quashed and the writ petition was dismissed.

predicates.alternative_site_writ_claim: A claimant sought an alternative site by filing a writ petition under a government policy for acquired land.
predicates.land_acquired_for_public_purpose: The land in question was acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.claimant_bought_after_acquisition_notice: The claimant purchased the land after the acquisition notification was published.
predicates.later_purchaser_not_eligible_for_alterna: A person who purchased the land after the acquisition notification is not eligible for an alternative site under the policy.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution is not subject to an absolute rule requiring it to examine every witness it has cited.
material_facts: The prosecution did not examine three listed witnesses.
The prosecutor represented that two witnesses had been won over and that the third was unable to give a coherent account after suffering severe mental shock.
The trial court found that the witnesses’ evidence was not essential to a just decision, rejected the defence request to call them, and the defence did not call them itself.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must place before the court the material evidence necessary to unfold its case, but there is no general rule that every cited witness must be examined, including a witness whose evidence is not material or who is believed to have been won over or terrorised. Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits the court to call a witness when necessary in the interests of justice.
members.conclusion: The Court held that it would be unsound to require the prosecution in every case to examine every cited witness, particularly where a witness is not material or is believed to have been won over or terrorised; the omission was not a ground for relief in this case.

rule.if: criminal_trial and prosecution_omits_cited_witness and (witness_not_material or prosecutor_bona_fide_believes_witness_won_over_or_terrorised) and defence_can_seek_witness_examination

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.prosecution_omits_cited_witness: The prosecution does not examine a witness it had cited.
predicates.witness_not_material: The omitted witness’s evidence is not material to the just decision of the case.
predicates.prosecutor_bona_fide_believes_witness_wo: The prosecutor honestly and in good faith believes that the witness has been won over or terrorised.
predicates.defence_can_seek_witness_examination: The defence may seek to call the witness, and the court may consider doing so in the interests of justice.
predicates.failure_to_examine_witness_is_not_automa: The prosecution’s failure to examine the witness is not automatically improper.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to examine every witness named in an initial report does not, by itself, require rejection of the evidence of the witnesses who testified.
material_facts: The initial report named three eyewitnesses, but the prosecution did not examine one of them.
The Supreme Court held that the other evidence did not have to be rejected merely because that witness was not examined.
members.legal_principle: The Court relies on Masalti v. State of U.P. for the principle that it is unsound to require examination of every witness mentioned in an initial report in all circumstances.
members.conclusion: There is no general rule requiring examination of every witness named in an initial report, and failure to examine one such witness does not require rejection of all other evidence.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a prosecution for a criminal offence.
predicates.witness_named_in_initial_report: A witness was identified in the initial report of the incident.
predicates.witness_not_examined: The prosecution did not call that witness to testify.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to examine every available or independent witness does not by itself undermine a case supported by truthful, reliable evidence.
material_facts: The prosecution did not examine some witnesses named in the charge sheet.
The prosecutor stated that some witnesses were inimically disposed towards the informant, and the defence produced no material to disprove that explanation.
Several eyewitnesses testified, their accounts were more or less consistent, and the defence did not point to anything discrediting their testimony.
The Court considered that independent witnesses may be reluctant to testify in village disputes involving land.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution is not invariably required to examine every available witness; the quality and intrinsic worth of the evidence matter more than its quantity. Witnesses essential to unfolding the prosecution narrative should be called, and omission may matter where it causes prejudice or leaves an essential account unexplained. The Court relied on Sheelam Ramesh v. State of A.P., Pohlu v. State of Haryana, Balram Singh v. State of Punjab, State of U.P. v. Anil Singh, Habeeb Mohammad v. State of Hyderabad, and Sahaj Ram v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The non-examination of the other witnesses did not warrant an adverse inference or undermine the prosecution case on these facts.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.examined_witnesses_are_truthful_and_reli: The witnesses who testified gave evidence the court found truthful and reliable.
predicates.omitted_witnesses_not_shown_to_be_essent: The omitted witnesses were not shown to be essential to the prosecution narrative or their omission to have prejudiced the accused.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution is not required to call a witness who is not essential to unfolding its case, and failure to call such a witness does not by itself vitiate the trial.
material_facts: The charged offences concerned the assault on a person and his abduction.
The witness arrived only after the assault and abduction had occurred and could not give evidence about those charged events.
The witness’s later involvement in a separate incident was not necessary to prove the charged offences.
The prosecution did not call him, and the accused did not seek to produce him as a defence witness.
members.legal_principle: Under the test stated in Stephen Seneviratne v. The King, A.I.R. 1936 P.C. 289, a material witness for this purpose is one essential to unfolding the narrative on which the prosecution is based, not merely one who might support the defence. As recognized in Habeeb Mohammad v. The State of Hyderabad, [1954] S.C.R. 475, deliberately or unfairly withholding a material witness may cast serious doubt on the propriety of the trial and expose the resulting conviction to challenge. The prosecution must call material witnesses to prove its own case, but need not call witnesses merely to establish the defence or duplicate evidence.
members.conclusion: The witness was not material to the prosecution’s case, the prosecution was not bound to call him, and the trial was not vitiated by his absence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction_f: The accused brought a criminal appeal arguing that the conviction was affected by the prosecution’s failure to call a witness.
predicates.witness_arrived_after_charged_events: The witness came onto the scene only after the events underlying the charged offences had occurred.
predicates.witness_could_not_testify_to_charged_eve: The witness was not in a position to give evidence about the facts on which the prosecution relied to prove the charged offences.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution need not call every person said to have witnessed an offence if it produces the material witnesses and has not deliberately withheld a material witness.
material_facts: The appellant argued that some people named as witnesses in the first information report had not been examined.
The Court found that the appellant had not shown how their absence made the prosecution case less trustworthy or that any material and important witness had been deliberately withheld.
The prosecution had produced witnesses considered necessary to unfold its case.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution is not bound to produce every person said to have witnessed the occurrence. It need produce the material witnesses necessary to unfold its case, without unnecessary or redundant multiplication of witnesses. No earlier case or statutory provision is cited for this proposition.
members.conclusion: The non-examination of the additional persons did not undermine the prosecution case.

rule.if: criminal_trial and some_alleged_witnesses_not_called and material_witnesses_produced and no_material_witness_deliberately_withheld and no_demonstrated_prejudice

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution must prove its case.
predicates.some_alleged_witnesses_not_called: Some people said to have witnessed the occurrence are not called by the prosecution.
predicates.material_witnesses_produced: The prosecution calls the witnesses it considers necessary to present the material account of the offence.
predicates.no_material_witness_deliberately_withhel: The evidence does not show that the prosecution deliberately kept back an important witness.
predicates.no_demonstrated_prejudice: The absence of the uncalled witnesses is not shown to make the prosecution case less trustworthy.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution need not examine every person who witnessed an offence, and the non-examination of additional witnesses does not by itself warrant an adverse inference when the evidence of those examined is sufficient.
material_facts: The prosecution examined three injured eyewitnesses whose accounts corroborated one another.
Two other injured eyewitnesses were not examined after the prosecution stated they had been won over; another person named in the first report was also not examined.
The accused did not call the unexamined eyewitnesses as defence witnesses.
members.legal_principle: Section 134 of the Indian Evidence Act provides that no particular number of witnesses is required to prove a fact. The prosecution must call witnesses essential to unfolding its case, but it need not call every person who witnessed the occurrence. State of U.P. v. Jaggo, AIR 1971 SC 1586, was cited for the duty to call essential witnesses; Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras, AIR 1957 SC 614, and Ramratan v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1962 SC 424, support the rule that evidence is weighed, not counted.
members.conclusion: No adverse inference against the prosecution was justified merely because the additional witnesses were not examined.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the number of witnesses examined is challenged.
predicates.multiple_credible_eyewitnesses_examined: The prosecution has presented more than one credible eyewitness whose account supports its case.
predicates.additional_witnesses_not_examined: Other people who witnessed the occurrence were not called as prosecution witnesses.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution is not invariably required to examine every person who witnessed an occurrence, and omission of a witness is not necessarily fatal to the case.
material_facts: Four eyewitnesses testified about the assault, and the trial court and High Court found their evidence reliable and sufficient to support the convictions.
Other people said to have witnessed or arrived at the occurrence were not examined.
It was not shown that the unexamined witnesses were essential to complete the prosecution narrative or could speak to a matter on which the examined witnesses could not testify.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution and the court share a duty to ensure that full and material facts are placed on the record to avoid miscarriage of justice. There is no absolute rule requiring every person present at an occurrence to testify: the effect of non-examination depends on the circumstances, including whether the witnesses examined provide reliable and sufficient evidence and whether an omitted witness is essential. A witness cannot properly be withheld merely because truthful evidence may favour the accused; where the reason for non-examination is untenable or improper, an adverse inference may be drawn. No earlier case or specific Evidence Act provision is cited in the judgment for this principle.
members.conclusion: The failure to examine the other witnesses did not justify interfering with the convictions. The prosecution must examine witnesses essential to unfolding its case, and the court may draw an adverse inference if witnesses are withheld for improper reasons, including because their evidence would favour the accused.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.examined_eyewitnesses_reliable_and_suffi: The witnesses who testified about the occurrence gave evidence found reliable and sufficient to support the conviction.
predicates.omitted_witnesses_not_shown_essential: The evidence does not show that the unexamined witnesses were essential to complete the case or to address a matter the testifying witnesses could not cover.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution’s failure to examine every material witness does not require rejection of its case when the omission is reasonably explained and credible eyewitness evidence is corroborated.
material_facts: Several witnesses who allegedly saw the occurrence or arrived afterward were not examined.
The prosecutor explained that some were relatives of an accused and others had been won over and were unlikely to speak truthfully.
The two eyewitnesses testified to the occurrence, and their evidence was supported by medical evidence and evidence of weapon recoveries.
The accused did not seek to have the omitted witnesses called before the trial court or the High Court.
members.legal_principle: The prosecution must present material evidence necessary to unfold its case, but it is not a general rule that every witness must be examined, particularly where a witness has been won over or is unlikely to speak truthfully.
