The buyer took no steps to complete the transaction for more than two and a half years and produced no contemporaneous communication supporting his claim that he had repeatedly sought completion.
The buyer had paid only a small part of the agreed consideration and did not tender the balance or arrange the sale documents within the stated period.
The buyer purchased other properties during the period of inactivity.
The value of the urban property rose substantially between the agreement and the buyer’s demand for completion.
The Supreme Court rejected the buyer’s explanation for his inaction and concluded that the delay, together with the rise in value, made specific performance inequitable.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 10 and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is discretionary and must be exercised on sound judicial principles; Sections 21 and 23 address compensation and the effect of a stipulated sum. Section 55 of the Contract Act distinguishes the consequences of failure to perform when time is or is not essential, and Article 54 of the Limitation Act prescribes the period for filing a specific-performance suit. The absence of an essential-time term and filing within limitation do not make the contractual time limits irrelevant or compel a decree. Under Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, even where time is not essential, performance must occur within a reasonable time assessed in light of the contract, the property, and surrounding circumstances. Satyanarayana v. Yellogi Rao explains that delay alone is insufficient without conduct or neglect that prejudices the defendant or makes relief inequitable; here, prolonged inaction coupled with a substantial rise in property values created that inequity. Jiwan Lal was distinguished because the delay there had a reason, while the contrary approach attributed to S. V. Sankaraninga Nadar was not accepted insofar as it excluded rising prices from the discretionary assessment.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the decree granting specific performance was set aside, and the trial court’s decree was restored. The buyer’s prolonged inaction, considered with the contractual timeline and the substantial rise in property values, made specific performance inequitable.

rule.if: appeal_from_specific_performance_decree and immovable_property_sale_agreement and agreement_set_completion_period and buyer_inactive_beyond_completion_period and buyer_did_not_tender_balance_or_prepare_sale_documents and no_credible_reason_for_inactivity and property_value_rose_substantially

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: A party appealed a decree granting specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_agreement: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property.
predicates.agreement_set_completion_period: The parties specified a period for completing the transaction and taking steps toward completion.
predicates.buyer_inactive_beyond_completion_period: The buyer took no meaningful steps to complete the transaction after the agreed completion period expired.
predicates.buyer_did_not_tender_balance_or_prepare_: The buyer neither tendered the remaining consideration nor arranged the documents needed to complete the sale during the relevant period.
predicates.no_credible_reason_for_inactivity: The court rejected the buyer’s explanation for failing to act during the period of inaction.
predicates.property_value_rose_substantially: The property’s value increased substantially while the buyer remained inactive.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused where the circumstances, including prolonged extensions, sharp property-value escalation, and hardship to the seller, make enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The buyers paid most of the recorded sale consideration, but the agreements extended the time for performance repeatedly over a total period of eight years.
The second agreement recorded that the buyers had been unable to pay the balance and complete the sale within the earlier period.
The seller built a house on the property and lived there with his family; the property was his only property and shelter.
The property was in an urban area, and the Court considered the substantial increase in its value over the long passage of time.
The Court considered that enforcement would cause the seller and his family greater hardship than refusal would cause the buyers.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff's part of the contract at all material times. Under Section 20, specific performance is discretionary and is not granted merely because it is lawful to do so; the discretion must be exercised judicially in light of the circumstances, conduct of the parties, agreement recitals, and circumstances outside the contract. Relying on Sardar Singh v. Smt. Krishna Devi and Saradamani Kandaplan v. Rajalakshmi, the Court considered the totality of circumstances, including rapidly escalating urban property values and the hardship of enforcement after a long delay.
members.conclusion: The decree for specific performance was set aside because granting that discretionary relief would be inequitable in the circumstances.

rule.if: suit_for_specific_performance and prolonged_extensions_of_performance and buyer_acknowledged_inability_to_complete and substantial_property_value_escalation and seller_occupies_only_home and enforcement_causes_greater_hardship_to_seller

predicates.suit_for_specific_performance: A buyer brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.prolonged_extensions_of_performance: The parties repeatedly extended the time for completing the sale over a prolonged period.
predicates.buyer_acknowledged_inability_to_complete: The buyer's own conduct or recorded statement showed an inability to pay the balance or complete the sale within the agreed period.
predicates.substantial_property_value_escalation: The property substantially increased in value during the prolonged period before the dispute was decided.
predicates.seller_occupies_only_home: The seller and the seller's family live in a house on the property, which is their only home or property.
predicates.enforcement_causes_greater_hardship_to_s: Enforcing the sale would cause the seller greater hardship than refusing enforcement would cause the buyer.

members.legal_issue: The discretionary remedy of specific performance may be refused where the claimant’s conduct and the circumstances of the transaction make enforcement inequitable, even when time and increased property value are considered.
material_facts: The buyer’s conduct showed prolonged inaction and a lack of demonstrated willingness to complete the transaction.
Several decades had passed since the agreement, during which the property’s value had undoubtedly increased.
The buyer had withdrawn the balance consideration deposited in court.
The court considered the buyer’s conduct in deciding whether to grant specific performance and ordered return of the advance with interest instead.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 confers discretion to grant specific performance, which must be exercised on sound, reasonable, and equitable principles. Delay and price escalation alone do not justify refusal; the court considers the totality of circumstances, including the parties’ conduct, responsibility for delay, unfair advantage, and hardship. The court relied on Zarina Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam, Satya Jain v. Anis Ahmed Rushdie, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P.) Ltd., and K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan.
members.conclusion: The court declined to grant specific performance and directed that the advance be refunded with interest.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and buyer_conduct_inconsistent_with_completion and long_lapse_since_agreement and property_value_rose_substantially

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.buyer_conduct_inconsistent_with_completi: The buyer did not timely pursue completion, delayed bringing the specific-performance claim, and later withdrew the balance deposited in court.
predicates.long_lapse_since_agreement: A substantial period passed between the agreement and the court’s decision on specific performance.
predicates.property_value_rose_substantially: The value of the property increased substantially during the period of delay and litigation.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused when the circumstances make enforcement inequitable and performance would cause greater unforeseen hardship to the defendant than non-performance would cause to the plaintiff.
material_facts: The agreement depended on obtaining several governmental permissions and sanctions, which the purchaser was expected to secure but did not secure within a reasonable time.
Part of the property was subject to legal restrictions on transfer, part was acquired, and the proposed multi-storeyed development appeared impracticable.
The seller remained in possession of most of the property, while the purchaser had possession of only a small part.
The property's value had risen substantially after the agreement, and the purchaser did not show that its conduct made refusal of specific performance inequitable.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary; the discretion must be exercised judicially on sound principles and is subject to appellate correction. Comparative hardship may justify refusal, although mere inadequacy of consideration or an onerous bargain does not by itself establish unfair advantage or unforeseen hardship. The court relied on Lourdu Mari David v. Louis Chinnaya Arogiaswamy, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, and K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, including the principle that the court must consider surrounding circumstances and specified time limits, particularly for urban immovable property.
members.conclusion: The court refused to decree specific performance because, considering the circumstances as a whole, enforcement would cause the seller unforeseen hardship without comparable hardship to the purchaser.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and purchaser_failed_to_perform_within_reasonable_time and (required_approvals_unavailable or subject_property_partly_untransferable or planned_development_impracticable) and unforeseen_hardship_to_seller_exceeds_hardship_to_purchaser and purchaser_did_not_show_inequity_in_refusal

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A party sought a decree compelling performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.purchaser_failed_to_perform_within_reaso: The purchaser did not carry out the obligations needed to complete the transaction within a reasonable time.
predicates.required_approvals_unavailable: Permissions or sanctions needed to carry out the transaction were not obtained.
predicates.subject_property_partly_untransferable: Some of the property covered by the agreement could not be transferred.
predicates.planned_development_impracticable: The proposed development of the property appeared impracticable.
predicates.unforeseen_hardship_to_seller_exceeds_ha: Enforcing the agreement would cause the seller unforeseen hardship greater than the hardship non-enforcement would cause the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_show_inequity_in_refus: The purchaser did not establish that its conduct or reliance made it inequitable to refuse specific performance.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused where the agreement’s terms, the parties’ conduct, and the circumstances in which it was made give the purchaser an unfair advantage or make enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a decree ordering specific performance of an agreement to sell property for a total consideration of ₹1.6 lakh, of which ₹60,000 had been paid in advance and ₹1 lakh remained payable.
The purchaser’s father, who entered into the agreement and testified in support of the claim, carried on a moneylending business.
The sellers consistently maintained that the agreement had been executed as security for a loan; a defence witness testified that the agreement was signed in connection with repayment of a loan.
The sellers produced evidence of the property’s value, including evidence that it was valued at ₹6.3 lakh in 2006 and a document concerning its value in 1999.
Although the trial and appellate courts referred to this evidence, they did not take the relevant circumstances into account when deciding whether to grant specific performance.

The sellers offered ₹10 lakh in lieu of specific performance. The Court substituted compensation of ₹15 lakh, payable within two months, with interest at 9 per cent per annum thereafter until payment or realization.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is discretionary, and that discretion must be sound, reasonable, and guided by judicial principles. Section 20(2)(a) and (c) permit the court to refuse specific performance where the agreement’s terms, the parties’ conduct, or the circumstances give the plaintiff an unfair advantage or make enforcement inequitable. The explanations to Section 20 clarify that mere inadequacy of consideration, an onerous contract, or an increase in property value is not by itself sufficient; the circumstances must be considered as a whole. The Court relied on Parakunnan Veetill Joseph’s Son Mathew v. Nedumbara Kuruvila’s Son, Sardar Singh v. Smt. Krishna Devi, K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd., Lourdu Mari David v. Louis Chinnaya Arogiaswamy, A.C. Arulappan v. Smt. Ahalya Naik, and Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd.
members.conclusion: The terms of the agreement, the parties’ conduct, and the circumstances in which it was made gave the purchaser an unfair advantage and made enforcement inequitable. The decree for specific performance was set aside and replaced with a direction to pay ₹15 lakh in compensation in lieu of specific performance, with interest at 9 per cent per annum after two months until payment or realization.

rule.if: specific_performance_decree_appeal and moneylending_relationship and loan_transaction_defense_supported and price_below_documented_value and lower_courts_omitted_equitable_assessment

predicates.specific_performance_decree_appeal: The matter was an appeal from a decree ordering specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.moneylending_relationship: The purchaser’s father, who entered into the agreement, carried on a moneylending business.
predicates.loan_transaction_defense_supported: The sellers consistently asserted that the agreement was connected to a loan, and a witness testified that it was signed in connection with repayment of a loan.
predicates.price_below_documented_value: The agreed sale price was substantially below the property value indicated by evidence produced by the sellers.
predicates.lower_courts_omitted_equitable_assessmen: The lower courts referred to evidence about the transaction and property value but did not take those circumstances into account in deciding whether to grant specific performance.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance is not automatic merely because it is lawful, and the court may refuse it where the suit’s motive and circumstances show that the remedy would be used oppressively to obtain an unfair advantage.
material_facts: The suit for specific performance was brought after the intended purchaser under the later transaction failed to obtain the estate and the purchaser who obtained the conveyance was unwilling to give it up.
The original contractual right relied on in the suit had been waived, and the claimant relied on an assignment of that right.
The purchaser in possession had obtained the conveyance and made substantial improvements to the estate.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 preserves judicial discretion over specific performance. A court must consider all facts and circumstances, including the motive behind the litigation, and must guard against using the remedy as an instrument of oppression or to secure an unfair advantage. Specific performance is not required merely because it is lawful to grant it.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to specific performance; the decree granting it was reversed and the trial court’s judgment was restored.

predicates.appeal_from_specific_performance_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree granting specific performance.
predicates.claim_based_on_waived_right: The claimant seeks to enforce a contractual right that the original holder waived.
predicates.suit_motive_is_to_gain_unfair_advantage: The suit was brought to obtain an advantage over a person who acquired and retained the property after another intended purchaser failed to obtain it.
predicates.specific_performance_must_be_refused: The court refuses to grant specific performance.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused where enforcing the contract would be inequitable because its public purpose cannot be achieved, implementation is impracticable, or enforcement would confer an unjustified benefit.
material_facts: The development plan in force reserved the land for uses inconsistent with the proposed residential housing.
The scheme therefore could not provide the intended housing benefit to weaker sections under the applicable planning regime.
Construction and later allotment would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to supervise.
The proposed use of a large area of land for a much smaller housing project risked an uncalled-for benefit to the scheme proponent.
The approval relied on to support enforcement was legally erroneous, and the governing legislation had been repealed.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary and requires the discretion to be exercised on sound judicial principles. The Court relied on K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd. in assessing the impracticability of performance and the effect of failed development plans, and held that the failed public purpose, practical obstacles, possible bonanza, and erroneous approval made enforcement inequitable.
members.conclusion: It would be inequitable to maintain the decree for specific performance, and the Court refused that relief.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.public_purpose_cannot_be_achieved: The land-use restrictions prevent the contract from delivering its intended public benefit.
predicates.performance_is_impracticable: The proposed construction and subsequent allocation cannot feasibly be carried out or supervised.
predicates.enforcement_would_create_unjustified_ben: Enforcement would confer a substantial benefit on the claimant out of proportion to the project that can lawfully be carried out.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused when the circumstances and subsequent events make its exercise inequitable.
material_facts: The purchaser was both a tenant of part of the property and a practicing advocate who had advised the executor about the property and a possible sale.

The purchaser's correspondence raised the prospect that the Rent Controller could allot vacant premises to another person, and the court found that he created a scare about that possibility while negotiating to buy the property.
The purchaser drafted the agreement and had an upper hand in the negotiations.
The beneficiaries later obtained a partition decree under which the house was allotted to them according to their shares.
The purchasers had paid nothing to the beneficiaries, and the purchaser did not challenge the partition decree in later proceedings concerning his tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 confers discretionary jurisdiction over specific performance. The court relied on V. Muthusami (Dead) by Lrs. v. Angammal and Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd. in declining to exercise that discretion in light of the purchaser’s conduct and subsequent events.
members.conclusion: In any event, the circumstances and subsequent events made this an unfit case for exercising the discretionary jurisdiction to grant specific performance.

predicates.specific_performance_appeal: An appeal concerns a claim for specific performance of an agreement to convey property.
predicates.purchaser_used_advisory_or_tenant_positi: The purchaser used a position as a tenant, adviser, or both to gain an advantage in negotiations for the property.
predicates.subsequent_partition_decree_allotted_pro: A later partition decree allotted the property to other beneficiaries according to their shares.
predicates.purchaser_paid_no_consideration: The purchaser paid no consideration to the persons to whom the property was later allotted.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who substantially performs and timely tenders the balance of the price is ready and willing to perform a contract for the sale of immovable property where the seller refuses payment and the contract does not expressly provide for cancellation upon delay.
material_facts: The purchaser paid a substantial part of the agreed price when the sale agreement was made and later made a further acknowledged payment.
The purchaser offered the balance within the period for payment asserted by the seller, but the seller refused it; the purchaser also obtained a demand draft for the balance shortly thereafter.
The agreement did not contain the alleged condition that the purchaser first obtain cancellation of an earlier agreement with another buyer.
The trial court and High Court found, on the evidence, that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform.
members.legal_principle: The party making an allegation bears the burden of proving it. Time is not ordinarily of the essence in an agreement to sell immovable property unless the agreement specifically and expressly provides for cancellation as a consequence of failure to meet a stipulated date. The court upheld the finding under the Specific Relief Act as it stood before the 2018 amendment; no earlier case was cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform was supported by the evidence and did not warrant interference.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and substantial_advance_paid and balance_tendered_promptly and seller_refused_payment and not express_cancellation_for_delay

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser brought a claim seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.substantial_advance_paid: The purchaser paid a substantial part of the agreed consideration before the dispute over completion arose.
predicates.balance_tendered_promptly: The purchaser offered the unpaid balance within, or shortly after, the period contemplated for payment.
predicates.seller_refused_payment: The seller refused to accept the purchaser's offered balance.
predicates.express_cancellation_for_delay: The agreement expressly provided that failure to pay by the stipulated date would cancel the agreement.
predicates.buyer_ready_and_willing: The purchaser was ready and willing to perform the purchaser's obligations under the agreement.

members.legal_issue: A buyer remains ready and willing to perform an agreement to sell when the seller has not fulfilled agreed prerequisites to payment and the buyer deposits the balance when directed by the court.
material_facts: The seller admitted that the land was to be measured, the consideration determined, and the original sale deed delivered before completion.
The land was not measured, and the seller did not provide the buyer with the original title deed or final land-ceiling documents.
The buyer repeatedly sought those documents and completion of the agreed steps.
The buyer deposited the balance consideration within the extended time allowed by the trial court.
The trial court and the High Court found that the seller had failed to perform her part of the agreement and that the buyer was ready and willing to perform.
members.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness must be assessed in light of the parties' agreed obligations and their conduct. Where the seller has not fulfilled agreed prerequisites to completion, the buyer is not required to pay the balance before those prerequisites are met. A deposit made when the court directs it supports the buyer's bona fides; the later source of the deposited funds does not, by itself, establish that the buyer was previously unable to pay. The judgment does not apply a statutory provision or earlier case as controlling on this issue; it distinguishes the authorities cited by the seller in light of the concurrent factual findings.
members.conclusion: The buyer's readiness and willingness were established, and the decree for specific performance was upheld. The buyer's failure to demonstrate that he held the balance consideration at an earlier point, including the fact that he later deposited money received from a property sale, did not alter that result.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and seller_admitted_completion_prerequisites and seller_failed_completion_prerequisites and buyer_deposited_balance_when_directed

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.seller_admitted_completion_prerequisites: The seller admitted that specified steps, including measuring the land and delivering title documents, were to be completed before the sale was finalized.
predicates.seller_failed_completion_prerequisites: The seller did not complete the agreed steps before the buyer was required to pay the balance and complete the purchase.
predicates.buyer_deposited_balance_when_directed: The buyer deposited the balance consideration when the court directed the deposit and within the time allowed.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who proves readiness and willingness to perform is not disentitled to specific performance merely because completion was delayed by other co-owners’ refusal to join in the sale.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform and testified that he could pay the consideration.
The purchaser’s testimony about his ability to pay was not challenged in cross-examination, and he had served a notice seeking execution of the sale deed.
The seller stated in his written defence that the deed could not be executed because other co-owners were not prepared to sell, but did not testify.
The purchaser’s suit was within the limitation period, and there was no evidence that the sellers called upon him to complete the transaction.
members.legal_principle: Whether a purchaser was ready and willing, and whether delay disentitles the purchaser to relief, depends on the evidence. The Court found the purchaser’s pleading and testimony supported readiness and willingness, while the seller’s own written statement attributed non-completion to the other co-owners and was not supported by testimony. The suit was within limitation, and no evidence showed that the sellers had called upon the purchaser to complete the sale.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was found ready and willing to perform, and the asserted delay did not disentitle him to equitable relief.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and purchaser_proved_readiness_and_ability_to_perform and noncompletion_was_attributed_to_other_owners and suit_was_within_limitation and seller_did_not_prove_purchaser_caused_delay

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract for the transfer of property.
predicates.purchaser_proved_readiness_and_ability_t: The purchaser pleaded and gave evidence that the purchaser was ready and able to perform, and that evidence was not undermined.
predicates.noncompletion_was_attributed_to_other_ow: The seller attributed non-completion to other owners’ unwillingness to join in the transfer.
predicates.suit_was_within_limitation: The purchaser brought the suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.seller_did_not_prove_purchaser_caused_de: The seller did not provide evidence that the purchaser caused the delay or was called upon to complete but failed to do so.

members.legal_issue: Delay caused by the court process, without more, does not justify denying specific performance to a purchaser who was ready and willing to perform and whose suit was filed within limitation.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded readiness and willingness and deposited the balance consideration in court.
The purchaser filed suit after the vendors failed to complete their contractual obligations.
The findings that the vendors were in breach and the purchaser remained ready and willing were not displaced.
The lengthy passage of time before the appellate decision resulted from the court process, not from default by the purchaser.
members.legal_principle: Under section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as it stood before amendment, discretion to grant specific performance had to be exercised on sound judicial principles; delay caused by the court process was not by itself a ground to refuse relief. Mere delay or escalation in property prices is not alone sufficient. The Court relied on Mademsetty Satyanarayana v. G. Yelloji Rao, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., P. D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, P.S. Ramaswamy Reddy v. M.K. Bhagyalakshmi, Narinderjit Singh v. North Star Estate Promoters Ltd., Satya Jain v. Anis Ahmed Rushdie, and other cases addressing delay, price escalation, and equitable conditions. It distinguished cases involving purchaser default, including K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan and Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi.
members.conclusion: The delay in the court process could not be held against the purchaser to deny specific performance. The Court restored the decree for specific performance and required the purchaser to pay an additional amount offered during the appeal.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit_on_appeal and suit_within_limitation and purchaser_ready_and_willing and vendor_breach and delay_caused_by_court_process

predicates.specific_performance_suit_on_appeal: A suit for specific performance is before an appellate court.
predicates.suit_within_limitation: The purchaser brought the suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.purchaser_ready_and_willing: The purchaser remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s contractual obligations.
predicates.vendor_breach: The vendor failed to perform an obligation required by the sale agreement.
predicates.delay_caused_by_court_process: The time taken to resolve the case resulted from the court process rather than the purchaser’s default.

members.legal_issue: A claimant entitled to relief should not be denied effective relief solely because proceedings consumed time when the delay was not the claimant's fault and no intervening circumstance made relief inequitable or impossible.
material_facts: The appellant pursued legal proceedings, and the delay in their final resolution was not attributable to him.
No auction had taken place and no third-party interest had been created in the mining rights.
The mine remained unoperated during the time the appellant's operation fell short of the three-year term.
The State's intervening order stopping the operation was found unsustainable.
The appellant sought to operate the mine for the balance needed to receive the benefit of the full term, with credit for time already operated.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, relief is assessed by reference to the claimant's position when litigation began, and a successful claimant should, as far as possible, be put in the position they would have occupied absent the wrong. Later events may justify withholding relief if they make it redundant, impossible, or inequitable, including through third-party interests or a changed balance of equities; relief should not be denied solely for time lost in proceedings when the claimant was not at fault. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The appellant was entitled to effective relief and was to be allowed to operate the mine for the balance of the three-year term, subject to adjustment for the time already operated and payment under the lease.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance should not be refused where the claimant acted fairly and the circumstances do not establish equitable grounds for withholding that relief.
material_facts: The purchaser acted fairly and there was no evidence that he encouraged the sellers to convey the property to the subsequent purchasers.
There was no evidence that the purchaser obtained an unfair advantage or that performance would cause the respondents unforeseen hardship.

The subsequent purchasers alleged that they had built on the property, but the court was unable to find that permanent construction had been established; any building material could be removed when possession was delivered.
members.legal_principle: The ordinary rule is that specific performance should be granted and should be denied only when equitable considerations point to refusal and damages would constitute adequate relief. The court applied that principle to the claimant’s conduct and the evidence of hardship and construction. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and claimant_acted_fairly and no_unfair_advantage and no_unforeseen_hardship and permanent_construction_not_proven

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks enforcement of an agreement by requiring conveyance of property.
predicates.claimant_acted_fairly: The claimant acted fairly in relation to the agreement and its performance.
predicates.no_unfair_advantage: There is no evidence that the claimant secured an unfair advantage when entering the agreement.
predicates.no_unforeseen_hardship: There is no evidence that performance would impose unforeseen hardship on the opposing parties.
predicates.permanent_construction_not_proven: The evidence does not establish that permanent construction was made on the property.
predicates.specific_performance_granted: The agreement is enforced by an order requiring its performance.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance should not be refused through an unguided exercise of discretion where the agreement is proved, the plaintiff has performed substantially and is ready and willing to complete performance, and the circumstances favor the plaintiff.
material_facts: The courts below found that the agreement to sell was executed and proved, that a substantial part of the consideration had been paid, and that the plaintiff was ready and willing to pay the balance at execution.
The subsequent purchasers were found to have known of the agreement when they purchased the property, and the consideration stated in their sale deed was doubted.
The subsequent purchasers remained in possession and enjoyed the property during the prolonged litigation, while the plaintiff was kept out of possession.

The High Court relied on the discretionary character of specific performance to refuse relief, although no issue on that ground had been framed and no cogent reasons were given for refusing the decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as applicable to the case, made specific performance discretionary, but that discretion had to be exercised judiciously, soundly and reasonably. Where execution is proved, part consideration is paid, and the plaintiff is ready and willing to perform, the balance should tilt toward the plaintiff rather than reward dishonest conduct by the defendant. The Court noted that the later amendment inserting Section 10(a), though not applied retrospectively, could guide the exercise of discretion; whether it applied retrospectively or to pending proceedings was left open. The Court also held that delay caused by prolonged litigation could not operate to the plaintiff’s disadvantage in the circumstances, particularly where the purchasers had notice of the agreement.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s discretionary refusal of specific performance was unsustainable; the decree for specific performance was restored, and the subsequent purchasers’ possession and the passage of time caused by the litigation did not justify denying relief.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and agreement_execution_proved and substantial_part_of_consideration_paid and plaintiff_ready_and_willing and transferees_purchased_with_notice and equitable_circumstances_favor_plaintiff

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The plaintiff brought a claim seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.agreement_execution_proved: The evidence established that the agreement to sell was executed.
predicates.substantial_part_of_consideration_paid: The plaintiff paid a substantial portion of the agreed consideration before completion.
predicates.plaintiff_ready_and_willing: The plaintiff was ready and willing to perform the remaining obligations under the agreement.
predicates.transferees_purchased_with_notice: The later purchasers knew of the earlier agreement when they acquired the property.
predicates.equitable_circumstances_favor_plaintiff: The surrounding conduct and circumstances favored the plaintiff, including doubtful consideration for the later transfer or delay and deprivation caused by prolonged litigation.

members.legal_issue: A civil eviction suit is barred when the premises are governed by rent-protection legislation and the suit is not founded on a statutory ground permitting eviction.
material_facts: The trial court found that the premises were governed by the Act.
The suit sought possession on the basis that the tenancy had ended by efflux of time and alleged rent arrears.

The plaint did not allege arrears for the statutory minimum period followed by failure to pay within the prescribed time after a demand notice, and the suit was not based on another ground specified in Section 20(2).
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 20(1) and 20(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, an eviction suit concerning a covered building cannot be instituted except on the statutory grounds specified in Section 20(2). The arrears ground in Section 20(2)(a) requires the prescribed period of arrears and failure to pay within the prescribed time after service of a demand notice.
members.conclusion: The trial court should ordinarily have dismissed the suit for want of jurisdiction under Section 20(1), because the suit was not based on a ground specified in Section 20(2).

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and premises_covered_by_rent_law and not permitted_eviction_ground_pleaded

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a civil suit seeking to evict a tenant.
predicates.premises_covered_by_rent_law: The premises were found to be governed by rent-protection legislation.
predicates.permitted_eviction_ground_pleaded: The landlord based the eviction suit on a ground that the rent-protection law permits as a basis for eviction.

members.legal_issue: An ordinary civil court lacks jurisdiction to hear an eviction suit when the governing rent-control scheme assigns that matter exclusively to the rent-control forum.
material_facts: The suit sought recovery of possession of premises occupied by the respondent as a tenant, together with mesne profits.
The Andhra Pradesh Rent Control Act governed the eviction dispute, and the High Court concluded that jurisdiction lay exclusively with the Rent Controller.
The suit had been brought in the City Civil Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Rent Control Act, 1960, formed part of the statutory setting for the dispute. The Court upheld the conclusion that the suit lay exclusively within the Rent Controller’s jurisdiction; a court lacking jurisdiction in law cannot acquire it through res judicata or estoppel.
members.conclusion: The City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit because jurisdiction lay exclusively with the Rent Controller.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: The proceeding seeks eviction in a dispute governed by a rent-control scheme.
predicates.rent_law_assigns_exclusive_forum: The governing rent-control scheme assigns jurisdiction over the eviction dispute exclusively to a designated rent-control forum.
predicates.suit_filed_in_ordinary_civil_court: The eviction suit was filed in an ordinary civil court rather than the designated rent-control forum.

members.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction to grant eviction on a rent-control ground unless the statutory condition permitting recourse to that court has been satisfied.
material_facts: The occupants had entered possession as tenants, and the landlords’ own pleading stated that their possession continued to be that of tenants.
The landlords sought possession by counterclaim, relying on the occupants’ denial of the landlords’ title and claim under an alleged agreement of sale.
No Rent Controller finding had been made that the denial of title was bona fide, and the landlords had not otherwise satisfied the statutory condition for bringing an eviction claim in a civil court.
The trial court granted possession without considering evidence on the counterclaim, and the High Court upheld that grant.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(1) and 10(2)(vi) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, eviction on denial of the landlord’s title is ordinarily for the Rent Controller to determine. The proviso to Section 10(1) permits a civil-court eviction suit only after the Controller finds the denial or claim bona fide. A civil court cannot bypass that condition, and its jurisdiction is barred for an eviction ground governed by the Act. A decree made without jurisdiction is a nullity: Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan; Bihar State Mineral Development Corporation v. Encon Builders; Dwarka Prasad Agarwal v. B.D. Agarwal; Ashok Leyland Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu; and M.D., Army Welfare Housing Organisation v. Sumangal Services.
members.conclusion: The civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the eviction counterclaim on these facts. The decree on the counterclaim was set aside; a decree passed without jurisdiction is a nullity.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_counterclaim and eviction_based_on_title_denial and not required_controller_finding

predicates.rent_control_eviction_counterclaim: The proceeding is a counterclaim seeking eviction from premises governed by rent-control protections.
predicates.eviction_based_on_title_denial: The claimant seeks eviction on the ground that the occupant denied the landlord’s title or claimed a right inconsistent with the tenancy.
predicates.required_controller_finding: The Rent Controller made the statutory finding that permits the landlord to pursue eviction in a civil court.

members.legal_issue: A civil court may order eviction under a rent-control scheme only when the statutory condition for civil-court jurisdiction has been satisfied.
material_facts: The landlord sued in a civil court to recover possession, alleging rent default; the occupant denied being a tenant and claimed an interest as a co-owner or associate.
The rent-control scheme applied to the building after the provision excluding higher-rent premises was declared invalid.
The Controller had not decided that the occupant’s denial or claim was bona fide and recorded a finding to that effect.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(1), including its second proviso, read with sections 14 to 16 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, creates a self-contained scheme that impliedly excludes civil-court jurisdiction over eviction except to the specified extent. The Controller determines only the bona fides of the tenant’s denial or claim, not its correctness or validity; the civil court decides the title issue if the statutory condition is met. The Court applied the jurisdiction-exclusion principles in Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Secretary of State v. Mask & Co., Raleigh Investment Co. v. Governor General in Council and Barraclough v. Brown; it relied on Magiti Sasamal v. Pandab Bissoi concerning the Controller’s limited inquiry and Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan concerning the nullity of a decree made without jurisdiction. It distinguished B.V. Patankar v. C.G. Sastry because the enactment there expressly preserved civil suits for eviction.
members.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction over tenant eviction was barred except where the statutory procedure was followed: the tenant denied the landlord’s title or claimed permanent tenancy, and the Controller decided that the denial or claim was bona fide and recorded that finding. Without that procedure, the civil suit was incompetent and its eviction decree was null and void.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and building_covered_by_rent_control_scheme and not (tenant_denied_landlord_title_or_claimed_permanent_tenancy and controller_recorded_bona_fide_finding)

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding in civil court seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.building_covered_by_rent_control_scheme: The building was within the scope of the special rent-control scheme when the court dealt with the eviction proceeding.
predicates.tenant_denied_landlord_title_or_claimed_: The tenant denied the landlord’s title or claimed a right of permanent tenancy.
predicates.controller_recorded_bona_fide_finding: The Controller decided that the tenant’s denial or claim was bona fide and recorded that finding.

members.legal_issue: A tenant protected by rent-control legislation cannot be evicted through an ordinary civil suit where the legislation requires eviction to be pursued before the rent-control forum.
material_facts: The occupant held the building under a tenancy arising from the owner’s transfer of possession and the payment or agreement to pay rent.
The Rent Act defined a tenant by reference to rent payable for a building and applied to buildings let or to be let.
The landlord brought an ordinary civil suit to recover possession rather than seeking eviction before the Rent Control Court.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(6) and 2(i) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, define tenant and building in terms that require a lease and rent payable for the building. Once a tenancy is established, the Act governs eviction and the landlord must seek eviction before the Rent Control Court on a ground recognised by the Act. The Court relied on Biswabani Pvt. Ltd. v. Santosh Kumar Dutta in recognising continued statutory protection under rent-control legislation.
members.conclusion: The occupant was a tenant protected by the Rent Act, the civil court could not grant the requested eviction, and the suit was dismissed without prejudice to the landlord’s right to seek relief under the Rent Act.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brings an ordinary civil suit seeking to recover possession from an occupant.
predicates.tenancy_established: The occupant holds the property under a landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.rent_control_law_covers_the_tenancy: The applicable rent-control law covers the building and the established tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot entertain a landlord's possession suit against a tenant entitled to protection under the tenancy law.
material_facts: The landlords brought possession suits in the civil court against tenants who remained in possession of the land.
When the appellate court decided the cases, no exclusion notification was in force to remove the land from the tenancy law.
The court held that the tenants could claim the law's protection against eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under the scheme of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, where the Act applies to the tenancy, a possession suit against a protected tenant lies in the revenue court rather than the civil court; the civil court has jurisdiction only where the occupant is a trespasser. The Court treated the failure of these civil suits upon the Act's application as undisputed.
members.conclusion: The tenants could not be ejected through the civil suits, which therefore failed.

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A landlord brings a suit seeking possession in a civil court.
predicates.occupant_is_protected_tenant: The occupant is a tenant entitled to protection under the applicable tenancy law.

members.legal_issue: A decree for recovery of a tenant’s premises is unenforceable when it is made outside the required landlord-initiated proceeding and without a finding of a permitted ground for eviction.
material_facts: The decree directed the tenants to deliver possession of the premises to the landlord.
The decree was passed according to an arbitration award in a proceeding to which the landlord was not a party.
The court had not determined that a permitted ground for eviction existed.
The landlord and the landlord’s son sought to execute the possession direction.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 prohibited a court from decreeing recovery of premises in favour of a landlord against a tenant except in a proceeding instituted by the landlord against the tenant and where the court was satisfied that a prescribed ground for eviction existed. The court relied on Peachey Property Corpn. v. Robinson in treating a judgment made contrary to such a restriction as a nullity. The award-based decree had been made under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, but the landlord was not a party to that proceeding and the required finding had not been made.
members.conclusion: The possession direction was a nullity and could not be executed by either the landlord or the landlord’s son.

rule.if: possession_decree_execution and protected_tenancy and recovery_decree_for_landlord and not landlord_initiated_proceeding and not qualifying_eviction_ground_found

predicates.possession_decree_execution: The proceeding is execution of a decree directing recovery of premises.
predicates.protected_tenancy: The premises and tenancy are subject to a legal restriction on recovery of possession.
predicates.recovery_decree_for_landlord: The decree directs a tenant to deliver possession of premises to a landlord.
predicates.landlord_initiated_proceeding: The proceeding in which the possession decree was made was instituted by the landlord against the tenant.
predicates.qualifying_eviction_ground_found: The court found that a legally permitted ground for eviction existed.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree for recovery of possession against a protected tenant is void and unexecutable when the court has not judicially satisfied itself that a statutory ground for eviction is established.
material_facts: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the allegation that the tenant had sublet the premises, which the tenant denied.
During the suit, the landlord and tenant entered into a compromise, and the court passed a decree for ejectment based on that compromise.

The compromise and the court’s order did not address the alleged subletting, and the court did not determine whether it had occurred or otherwise find that a statutory ground for eviction was established.
In execution, the decree was challenged as a nullity because it had been passed without the satisfaction required for eviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 bars a decree for recovery of possession against a tenant unless the court is satisfied that one or more grounds in the statutory proviso are established; subletting without the landlord’s written consent is one such ground. The court’s jurisdiction to make a possession decree depends on that satisfaction, which cannot be replaced by a compromise alone. The Court relied on Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass and Smt. Kaushalya Devi v. K. L. Bansal, in which decrees made contrary to Section 13(1) were held void and incapable of execution.
members.conclusion: The decree was a nullity and could not be executed; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: possession_decree_execution and rent_control_eviction_case and decree_based_only_on_compromise and not court_found_eviction_ground

predicates.possession_decree_execution: The proceeding concerns execution of a decree for recovery of possession.
predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The possession decree concerns eviction of a tenant protected by rent-control requirements.
predicates.decree_based_only_on_compromise: The court passed the possession decree solely on the parties’ compromise, without determining an asserted ground for eviction.
predicates.court_found_eviction_ground: The court judicially found that a statutory ground for eviction was established.
predicates.decree_is_nullity_and_unexecutable: The possession decree is void and cannot be executed.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree for eviction is invalid when the court passes it without finding that a statutory ground for eviction exists.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit alleging residential need, the tenant’s ownership of suitable alternative accommodation, and rent default.
After issues were framed, the parties filed a compromise providing for eviction after a specified date and fixing the rent.
The court passed a decree in accordance with the compromise without recording that any statutory ground for eviction existed.
The tenant later challenged the decree’s validity in execution proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 forbids a court from passing an eviction decree unless it is satisfied that a statutory ground for eviction exists. A decree passed without that satisfaction is a nullity and cannot be enforced in execution. The Court followed Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass, which applied this principle to a decree passed in terms of an award.
members.conclusion: The decree was a nullity insofar as it directed delivery of possession and could not be executed; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant from rented premises subject to statutory rent-control restrictions.
predicates.compromise_based_eviction_decree: The court passed an eviction decree in accordance with an agreement between the landlord and tenant.
predicates.no_judicial_finding_of_permitted_evictio: The court did not find that a statutory ground permitting eviction existed.

members.legal_issue: A compromise cannot support eviction of a tenant protected by rent-control law unless a statutory ground for eviction is made out.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction under statutory grounds concerning alleged unauthorised transfer or subletting and a need for additional accommodation.
The parties filed a compromise, and the rent controller ordered the tenants to vacate and continue paying rent until they did so.
The compromise order did not identify any particular statutory ground for eviction or indicate that the court was satisfied such a ground existed.
The compromise terms recited in the order did not themselves establish a statutory ground for eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(2)(ii)(a) and 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, eviction may be ordered only when the prescribed ground is made out. A rent court cannot acquire authority to order eviction on a ground outside the statute merely because the parties consent. Under Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must satisfy itself that the compromise is lawful. K.K. Chari v. R.M. Seshadri considered Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass, Kaushalya Devi v. Shri K.L. Bansal and Ferozi Lal Jain v. Man Mal. Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam held that if material before the court supports prima facie satisfaction of a statutory ground, that satisfaction may be presumed; such material may include clear admissions in the compromise, with judicial admissions under Section 58 of the Evidence Act standing as proof. The absence of a statutory ground also permits the decree’s invalidity to be raised in execution.
members.conclusion: A tenant cannot be evicted under the compromise order unless a statutory ground for eviction is made out; the order in this case did not record that any particular ground had been established.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction of a tenant under a rent-control regime.
predicates.compromise_eviction_decree: The court ordered eviction on the basis of an agreement or compromise between the landlord and tenant.
predicates.no_material_supporting_statutory_ground: No evidence, admission, or other material before the court supported a statutory ground for eviction.

members.legal_issue: A rent court cannot make an eviction decree by consent unless there is a material foundation for a statutory ground of eviction.
material_facts: The landlord brought a possession suit alleging rent arrears and a need for personal use.
The parties compromised, and the court entered a decree for possession on the agreed terms.
members.legal_principle: The public policy protecting tenants under sections 12, 13 and 28 of the Bombay Rent Act limits the rent court’s jurisdiction to the statutory grounds for eviction; those grounds are a necessary condition of its authority, and consent cannot enlarge that authority. Under Order 23 Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must satisfy itself that a compromise is lawful, including that its terms are consistent with the Rent Act. The court approved Shah Rasiklal Chunilal v. Sindhi Shyamlal Mulchand and applied Barton v. Fincham.
members.conclusion: The parties’ consent could not itself confer jurisdiction to order eviction, but the decree was valid because material in the record, including admissions in the compromise, could support a statutory ground for eviction.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession of rented premises.
predicates.consent_possession_decree: The court entered a possession decree on terms agreed to by the landlord and tenant.
predicates.material_supports_statutory_ground: Evidence or admissions before the court could provide a prima facie basis for a statutory ground of eviction.

members.legal_issue: In statutory rent-control eviction proceedings, failure to establish a landlord-tenant relationship bars an eviction decree based solely on the claimant’s general title.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought an eviction suit under the state accommodation-control law and sought delivery of possession.
The courts found that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties.

The lower appellate court nevertheless awarded possession on the basis of the plaintiff’s title, while the High Court held that eviction could not be ordered under the rent-control law without the required relationship.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(1)(a) and 12(1)(e) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, read with the Act’s definitions of landlord and tenant, the existence of that relationship is essential to relief under the Act. The court’s inquiry in such a proceeding is limited to the statutory grounds for eviction. Rajendra Tiwary v. Basudeo Prasad distinguishes ordinary civil actions under the Transfer of Property Act, in which an alternative relief may be available under Order VII Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure; Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul and Biswanath Agarwalla v. Sabitri Bera concerned such ordinary civil actions. Dr. Ranbir Singh v. Asharfi Lal and LIC v. India Automobiles & Co. support the limited scope of an eviction action based on a landlord-tenant relationship.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to eviction under the rent-control law because the landlord-tenant relationship was not established; possession could not be awarded in that proceeding merely on the basis of general title.

predicates.statutory_rent_eviction_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking eviction under a statutory rent-control regime.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_established: The evidence established that the claimant and occupant stood in a landlord-tenant relationship.

members.legal_issue: A limited statutory eviction forum cannot determine ownership or adverse possession when the landlord-tenant relationship required for its jurisdiction is not established.
material_facts: The defendant disputed the plaintiff’s title and claimed to have acquired title by adverse possession.
The trial court found for the defendant on adverse possession, and the lower appellate court later rejected that finding and awarded possession based on the plaintiff’s title.
The absence of a landlord-tenant relationship was established, so the statutory eviction proceeding did not require a decision on either party’s title.
The High Court restored the trial court’s decree, including its adverse-possession determination.
members.legal_principle: Under the scheme of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, the statutory court’s inquiry concerns the parties’ status and the grounds for eviction, not final determination of title. Rajendra Tiwary v. Basudeo Prasad explains that a court exercising limited jurisdiction under a special rent law cannot grant an alternative decree on general title under Order VII Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure where that relief is outside the Act. Dr. Ranbir Singh v. Asharfi Lal and LIC v. India Automobiles & Co. explain that title may be considered incidentally in an eviction action only as needed to assess the landlord-tenant relationship, not to determine title finally. Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul and Biswanath Agarwalla v. Sabitri Bera were distinguished because they involved ordinary civil suits.
members.conclusion: The title and adverse-possession questions were outside the limited inquiry in the statutory eviction proceeding and remained open for determination in an ordinary civil suit; the High Court’s affirmation of the trial court’s adverse-possession finding was set aside.

predicates.limited_statutory_eviction_proceeding: The claimant brought an eviction proceeding in a forum whose authority is limited by a special rent-control scheme.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_established: The evidence established that the claimant and occupant stood in a landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.title_or_adverse_possession_claim_disput: A party disputed ownership or asserted that possession had matured into title by adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: A court exercising limited jurisdiction under a rent-control statute cannot grant eviction based on title under the general-relief rule when the landlord-tenant relationship required for statutory eviction has not been established.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a statutory eviction suit alleging rent default, personal requirement, and damage to the premises.
The trial court and first appellate court found that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the plaintiffs and the defendant.
The High Court remanded the case for a finding on title and contemplated eviction based on the plaintiffs’ title.
The Supreme Court held that title was outside the scope of the statutory eviction proceeding and that the plaintiffs could pursue a separate suit for title and possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11(1) of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1982, eviction in a proceeding under that Act depends on establishing a statutory ground and the landlord-tenant relationship; the definitions in Section 2(f) and (h) inform that relationship. A court exercising the Act’s limited jurisdiction cannot grant eviction on a ground outside the Act or decide title when title is not relevant to the statutory inquiry. Order VII Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an appropriate general or smaller relief supported by the case and facts, but does not enlarge a limited statutory court’s jurisdiction. Firm Sriniwas Bam Kumar v. Mahabir Prasad & Ors. recognizes that relief may be granted on an alternative case expressly admitted or advanced by the defendant; Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul explains that relief may be granted where the parties knew the matter was in issue and had an opportunity to lead evidence, subject to avoiding prejudice. Those principles do not authorize title-based eviction in a limited-jurisdiction rent proceeding.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not remand the statutory eviction suit for determination of title or direct an eviction decree based on title under Order VII Rule 7. Its judgment was set aside and the eviction suit was dismissed.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_tenant_relationship_not_established and title_based_eviction_proposed and jurisdiction_limited_to_statutory_grounds

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is a statutory rent-control suit seeking eviction on specified statutory grounds.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_not_establi: The courts found that the alleged landlord-tenant relationship between the claimant and the occupant was not established.
predicates.title_based_eviction_proposed: The proposed eviction relief rests on the claimant’s title rather than an established statutory eviction ground.
predicates.jurisdiction_limited_to_statutory_ground: The court hearing the proceeding has authority confined to the eviction grounds specified by the governing special law.

members.legal_issue: A special rent court hearing a statutory eviction suit lacks jurisdiction to evict an occupant it finds to be a trespasser.
material_facts: The landlords brought an eviction suit in the special rent court under the rent-control statute.
The appellate court treated the occupant as a trespasser because he had not proved an assignment and ordered his eviction.
members.legal_principle: The statutory jurisdiction conferred by section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, permits eviction of a tenant when the requirements of section 12 or section 13 are satisfied; it does not extend to eviction of a trespasser. A special rent court’s appellate jurisdiction is no wider than the trial court’s jurisdiction, and eviction of a trespasser must be pursued in an ordinary civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The appellate court had no jurisdiction in the statutory eviction suit to order the eviction of a person it had found to be a trespasser; such relief could be sought in an ordinary civil suit.

predicates.statutory_rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding in a court exercising special jurisdiction under rent-control law.
predicates.occupant_found_to_be_trespasser: The court found that the occupant possessed the premises without being a tenant or having established a right derived from a tenant.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may not go behind an eviction decree once the decree or the original trial record discloses material that could support a statutory ground for eviction.
material_facts: The decree incorporated the tenant’s admissions about arrears and payment at the contractual rent rate.
The tenant objected in execution that the decree was a nullity because the rent court had not been satisfied that a statutory ground existed.
The decree itself disclosed material supporting a statutory ground for eviction.
members.legal_principle: An executing court must accept and execute a decree that on its face discloses material on which the rent court could have been satisfied of a statutory ground for eviction. If the decree does not disclose such material, the executing court may inspect the original trial record; once it finds prima facie supporting material, it may not go further and reassess the rent court’s satisfaction. The court applied the principle in K. K. Chari v. B. M. Seshadri.
members.conclusion: The executing court was not entitled to question the decree’s validity and had to execute it.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce a possession decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_shows_supporting_material: The decree itself disclosed material capable of supporting a statutory ground for eviction.
predicates.original_record_inspected: The executing court inspected the original trial record because the decree did not disclose supporting material on its face.
predicates.original_record_shows_supporting_materia: The original trial record disclosed material capable of supporting a statutory ground for eviction.

members.legal_issue: A determination in an earlier execution proceeding that a compromise-based eviction decree was valid, reached by considering facts bearing on the court's satisfaction of statutory grounds for eviction, bars a renewed challenge to the decree in a later execution proceeding between the same parties or their privies.
material_facts: A landlord obtained an eviction decree by compromise, and the tenant objected to its execution on the ground that the decree was a nullity because it was not based on findings by the court.

In the first execution proceedings, the executing court and the appellate court considered the circumstances and concluded that the court passing the eviction decree had been satisfied that statutory grounds for eviction existed; that determination was upheld in revision.
In later execution proceedings involving the same judgment-debtors and the decree-holders or their successors, the judgment-debtors renewed the challenge to the decree's validity.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 prohibited an eviction order unless the court was satisfied that one or more statutory grounds existed (Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass). Although Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply in terms to execution proceedings, constructive res judicata applies to them. A mixed question of law and fact determined in earlier proceedings between the same parties cannot be questioned in a later proceeding, as recognized in Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N. B. Jeejeebhoy.
members.conclusion: The earlier determination involved a mixed question of law and fact and operated as constructive res judicata, barring the renewed objection. The appeal was allowed, the High Court's order was set aside, and the orders allowing execution were restored.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and issue_previously_decided and prior_decision_mixed_fact_law and same_parties_or_privies

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is an execution proceeding concerning enforcement of a judgment or decree.
predicates.issue_previously_decided: A party previously raised the same issue in an earlier proceeding, and the court decided it.
predicates.prior_decision_mixed_fact_law: The earlier decision rested on both legal requirements and an assessment of the facts.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The later proceeding involves the same parties as the earlier proceeding or persons claiming through them.

members.legal_issue: The ordinary requirements of planned industrial development do not, without a genuine time-critical exigency, justify invoking urgency powers to dispense with landowners’ objections.
material_facts: The land was acquired for planned industrial development, including infrastructure and the anticipated establishment of private industrial units.
The State relied on anticipated investment and employment, possible encroachment, the size of the affected group, and the time needed to hear objections.
The acquisition proposal had been under consideration for an extended period, and more than a year passed between the completion of preliminary work and publication of the acquisition notification.
The State did not establish that a delay of several weeks to hear objections would frustrate the acquisition’s purpose.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5-A and 17(1), (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 make the opportunity to object the normal procedure and dispensing with it an exceptional power. Urgency to acquire land and the separate need to dispense with objections must both be considered; the latter does not follow automatically from the former. The authority must be satisfied that the time needed for the objection procedure would probably frustrate the public purpose. Planned industrial, residential, commercial, or similar development ordinarily takes time, and generalized claims about investment, employment, encroachment, or the number of objectors do not by themselves establish the required urgency. The Court relied on Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra; Om Prakash v. State of U.P.; Union of India v. Mukesh Hans; Union of India v. Krishan Lal Arneja; Esso Fabs Private Limited v. State of Haryana; Anand Singh v. State of U.P.; and distinguished authorities upholding urgency on materially different circumstances, including State of U.P. v. Pista Devi, Rajasthan Housing Board v. Shri Kishan, and Chameli Singh v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: There was no real and substantive urgency to justify the use of urgency powers, and there was no justification for excluding the landowners’ opportunity to object. The acquisition could not proceed on that basis, although the State remained free to proceed from the preliminary notification stage after complying with the objection procedure.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and urgency_powers_invoked and acquisition_for_planned_industrial_development and (ordinary_long_term_project or generalized_investment_or_employment_claims or generalized_encroachment_or_objections_claims) and no_time_critical_exigency_shown

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.urgency_powers_invoked: The acquiring authority used an urgency procedure that limits the landowner’s opportunity to object.
predicates.acquisition_for_planned_industrial_devel: The land was acquired as part of a planned industrial development project.
predicates.ordinary_long_term_project: The project involves planning and implementation that ordinarily take substantial time.
predicates.generalized_investment_or_employment_cla: The State relied on broad claims about attracting investment or creating employment rather than a specific time-critical need.
predicates.generalized_encroachment_or_objections_c: The State relied on a general risk of encroachment or on the number or volume of objections.
predicates.no_time_critical_exigency_shown: The State did not show that allowing time for objections would probably frustrate the project’s purpose.

members.legal_issue: The government cannot dispense with the ordinary opportunity to object to a land acquisition merely because it invokes urgency when its own prolonged inaction undermines the claim that the hearing must be omitted.
material_facts: Earlier acquisition proceedings concerning the land had lapsed.

A later application to change the land’s use was rejected on the ground that the land was likely to be needed for a public purpose, but the government took no further acquisition steps for about a decade.
The government later sought the land for a public road, invoked urgency, dispensed with the hearing of objections, and issued a final acquisition notification.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4, 5A, 6 and 17(1), (2) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the ordinary process includes an opportunity for interested persons to object and be heard. The existence of urgency or unforeseen emergency does not, by itself, dispense with that opportunity; Section 17(4) gives the government a discretionary power that requires it to consider whether the urgency also makes the hearing unnecessary. Applying Nandeshwar Prasad v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Union of India v. Mukesh Hans, the Court held that the extended inaction in this case did not justify dispensing with the hearing. The Court did not accept that urgency alone made the waiver automatic, and it did not decide the separate question about the timing of publication of the final notification.
members.conclusion: The government was not justified in invoking the urgency provision to dispense with the hearing of objections. The waiver of the hearing and the final acquisition notification were quashed, without preventing the authorities from proceeding under the ordinary statutory procedure.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government commenced a statutory proceeding to acquire privately owned land for a public purpose.
predicates.objection_hearing_dispensed: The government invoked an accelerated acquisition mechanism and omitted the ordinary opportunity for interested persons to object and be heard.
predicates.prolonged_government_inaction: After earlier acquisition action or a stated public need, the government allowed a lengthy period to pass without advancing the acquisition before later invoking urgency.

members.legal_issue: Dispensing with the landowners’ opportunity to object is unjustified when land is acquired for planned residential development and the government does not establish a real urgency requiring the inquiry to be eliminated.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a planned residential colony.
The land-selection process began years before the acquisition notifications, and there was a further delay of more than a year between the notifications and the declaration of acquisition.
The government produced no material showing that it had applied its mind to whether the urgency required eliminating the landowners’ opportunity to object.
The development authority sought the land in part because it lacked a land bank and wished to keep the authority running.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1), 5A, 17(1), 17(1A) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read together, require the government to consider not only whether urgency exists but also whether it is so pressing that the summary inquiry must be dispensed with. The right to object under Section 5A is valuable and may be removed only for good reason supported by material and after application of mind. Planned residential or urban development ordinarily allows time for an expedited inquiry; dispensing with it for such development is exceptional, not routine. The Court followed Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra and Union of India v. Mukesh Hans, and agreed with Om Prakash v. State of U.P. that State of U.P. v. Pista Devi could not establish a contrary general rule. It also considered the principles in Gurdial Singh, Rajasthan Housing Board, and other cited decisions concerning urgency and judicial review.
members.conclusion: The use of urgency powers to dispense with the inquiry was unjustified, and the notifications were legally infirm to the extent that they excluded the inquiry.
