rule.if: challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition and residential_planned_development and (extended_pre_or_post_notification_delay or no_evidence_of_mind_applied_to_waiver)

predicates.challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition: A landowner challenged compulsory acquisition proceedings and the removal of the opportunity to object.
predicates.residential_planned_development: The land was acquired for planned residential or urban development.
predicates.extended_pre_or_post_notification_delay: The acquisition process included a substantial delay before the notification, after it, or both.
predicates.no_evidence_of_mind_applied_to_waiver: The government did not place material before the court showing that it considered whether urgency required eliminating the owners’ opportunity to object.
predicates.dispensing_with_owner_objections_unjusti: The government’s decision to remove the owners’ opportunity to object was unjustified.

members.legal_issue: Emergency powers cannot be used to dispense with the landowner hearing where the record does not establish a real and immediate urgency that would be frustrated by the time needed for an inquiry.
material_facts: The proposal to establish the sub-station had been under consideration for more than five years before the acquisition notification was issued.
More than a year passed after an official request cited the approaching power plant and major event as reasons for urgency before the preliminary notification was issued.
The Government produced no tangible evidence that the project had to be completed on a fixed schedule or that the time needed for objections and an inquiry would frustrate its purpose.
The approval dispensing with the hearing did not show a conscious assessment of why the hearing could not be held.

The project served a public purpose, but the asserted need to supply power and the project’s broad public benefit did not, without evidence of real urgency, establish that the hearing could be omitted.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5A(1) and 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 protect the right to object and be heard. Sections 17(1) and 17(4) confer extraordinary powers that may be used to dispense with that inquiry only in a case of real urgency, where even the time required for the inquiry would probably frustrate the public purpose. The authority must apply its mind to relevant material, and its satisfaction is judicially reviewable. Pre-notification delay has material bearing on urgency, particularly where the Government produces no material justifying the elimination of the inquiry. A laudable public purpose or general public benefit alone does not justify denying a hearing. These principles are drawn from Anand Singh v. State of U.P. (2010) 11 SCC 242, Radhy Shyam v. State of U.P. (2011) 5 SCC 553, Munshi Singh v. Union of India (1973) 2 SCC 337 and State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh (1980) 2 SCC 471; Deepak Pahwa v. Lt. Governor of Delhi (1984) 4 SCC 308 does not make pre-notification delay irrelevant in these circumstances. The Court also noted the protection against deprivation of property without authority of law under Article 300A of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The invocation of the emergency provisions and the resulting dispensation of the landowners’ hearing were unjustified; the acquisition was quashed, without preventing fresh acquisition proceedings in which the landowners could object and be heard.

predicates.emergency_land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked emergency powers and omitted the ordinary hearing of interested landowners.
predicates.extended_pre_notification_delay: The proposal for the acquisition remained under consideration for a substantial period before the preliminary acquisition notification was issued.
predicates.no_evidence_short_hearing_delay_would_fr: The acquiring authority produced no tangible evidence that the time needed for landowners to object and be heard would probably frustrate the public purpose.
predicates.no_conscious_assessment_of_need_to_omit_: The record did not show that the decision-maker consciously assessed why the landowners’ hearing had to be dispensed with.

members.legal_issue: The government cannot dispense with the landowner's objection inquiry on urgency grounds without genuine immediate urgency, particularly after prolonged inaction and without supporting material.
material_facts: The preliminary notification stated that the land was needed for construction of a bus stand, but the government invoked urgency and dispensed with the inquiry only when it made the declaration nearly seven years later.

During that interval, the government took no steps to commence the objection inquiry, although the inquiry could have been completed in a few months and few owners or interested persons were involved.
The government's explanation asserted that urgency was apparent from the public purpose but supplied no material showing that delay for the inquiry would defeat that purpose.
Construction of the proposed bus stand would itself take time.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5-A and 17(1) and (4) of the 1953 Act, read consistently with Article 300-A, require the lawful procedure for compulsory acquisition to be followed. The right to object under Section 5-A is substantial and valuable; dispensing with it is an exceptional power justified only where genuine urgency cannot brook the delay of even a few weeks or months. The government must apply its mind and, when challenged, provide material supporting the urgency; pre- and post-notification delay is relevant, particularly where no such material is produced. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Govt., Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Anand Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Radhy Shyam v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The exercise of urgency powers and dispensation of the objection inquiry were legally unsustainable because real urgency was not established and the landowners' valuable right to object was taken away without justification.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and urgency_power_invoked and objection_inquiry_dispensed and prolonged_inaction and no_inquiry_steps and no_urgency_material and purpose_allows_inquiry_delay

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land compulsorily.
predicates.urgency_power_invoked: The government invoked its special power on the ground that the acquisition was urgent.
predicates.objection_inquiry_dispensed: The government dispensed with the inquiry that would allow interested persons to object to the acquisition.
predicates.prolonged_inaction: A substantial interval passed after the preliminary notice before the government invoked urgency.
predicates.no_inquiry_steps: The government took no steps during that interval to commence the objection inquiry.
predicates.no_urgency_material: The government produced no material showing that conducting the inquiry would defeat the public purpose.
predicates.purpose_allows_inquiry_delay: The nature of the proposed public project allowed time for the objection inquiry to be conducted.

members.legal_issue: Urgency powers cannot routinely be used for a residential development scheme to dispense with the landowner’s opportunity to object unless the government establishes both an immediate need for possession and a need to eliminate the objection process.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a residential scheme and the government invoked urgency powers while dispensing with the opportunity to object to the acquisition.

The notification contained a statement of satisfaction, but there was no other material showing that immediate possession was needed or that completing the objection process would frustrate the scheme.
The government did not show that the scheme could not tolerate the delay of a few months needed to complete the objection process.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5A and 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, dispensing with the objection process is an exceptional power. The government must apply its mind to, and establish, both the need for immediate possession and the need to dispense with the objection process. For a residential scheme or planned development, urgency cannot be invoked routinely; the government bears the burden of justifying it, and a general assertion of urgency is insufficient. The Court applied Anand Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2010) 11 SCC 242, which considered, among other authorities, Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra (1977) 1 SCC 133, State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh (1980) 2 SCC 471, State of U.P. v. Pista Devi (1986) 4 SCC 251, and Om Prakash v. State of U.P. (1998) 6 SCC 1.
members.conclusion: The invocation of urgency powers and the direction dispensing with the objection process were invalid. The relevant direction and the declaration of acquisition concerning the subject land were quashed, and the competent authority could invite objections and proceed according to law.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_challenge and residential_scheme_purpose and urgent_possession_power_invoked and objection_opportunity_dispensed_with and (government_did_not_establish_immediate_possession_need or government_did_not_establish_need_to_dispense_with_objections)

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges a compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.residential_scheme_purpose: The government seeks the land for a residential scheme or planned residential development.
predicates.urgent_possession_power_invoked: The government invokes a power to take possession urgently.
predicates.objection_opportunity_dispensed_with: The government removes the landowner’s opportunity to object to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.government_did_not_establish_immediate_p: The government does not establish, with material, that carrying out the stated purpose requires immediate possession of the land.
predicates.government_did_not_establish_need_to_dis: The government does not establish, with material, that allowing objections to be heard would frustrate the stated purpose.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition authority may not dispense with the landholder’s hearing merely by invoking urgency when the acquisition process has proceeded slowly and no real urgency is demonstrated.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a new jail, a project considered by the government over several years through committees and administrative steps.
The government took nearly a year between publication of the initial acquisition notification and publication of the declaration that the land was needed.
The State did not dispute that interval, and the record showed a slow pace in processing the acquisition.
The hearing on objections was dispensed with, but there was no categorical finding that holding the hearing would harm the public interest.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A confers a substantial right to object and be heard, which must be strictly respected when property is taken; it is akin to a fundamental right when read with Article 300-A. Sections 17(1) and 17(2) do not automatically authorize dispensing with the inquiry under Section 5A: Section 17(4) must be separately justified by real urgency. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Government, Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chennai, Essco Fabs Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana, and Union of India v. Mukesh Hans.
members.conclusion: The State was not justified in dispensing with the hearing on objections under the urgency provision. The acquisition notifications were quashed insofar as they concerned the affected land, without preventing a fresh acquisition proceeding conducted in accordance with law.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land for a public project.
predicates.hearing_dispensed_with: The government omitted the landholders’ opportunity to object and be heard before declaring the land needed.
predicates.prolonged_administrative_delay: The government’s processing of the acquisition proceeded slowly over an extended interval, inconsistent with a need for immediate action.

members.legal_issue: A prolonged and lethargic acquisition process did not justify invoking urgency powers to exclude landowners’ opportunity to object to acquisition for construction of a jail.
material_facts: The acquisition was for construction of a district jail, a public purpose.
The State had proposed acquiring land for the jail several years before issuing the acquisition notifications.
After a further interval, the State began identifying suitable land, and it took about two years after the selection committee recommended land before the notifications were issued.
The State invoked the urgency provisions and excluded the statutory inquiry and hearing on landowners’ objections.
The landowners challenged the acquisition, and the High Court dismissed their challenge.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, urgency powers are exceptional, and exclusion of the inquiry under Section 5-A is not an automatic consequence of invoking Section 17(1). The Government must be satisfied that the time required for the inquiry would in all probability frustrate the public purpose; the public purpose alone does not establish urgency. The statutory power and its exercise are assessed in light of the circumstances and the Government’s application of mind. A prolonged, slow acquisition process can demonstrate that there was no urgency warranting denial of the hearing. The Court applied Radhy Shyam v. State of U.P. (2011) 5 SCC 553 and Dev Sharan v. State of U.P. (2011) 4 SCC 769; it distinguished Deepak Pahwa v. Lt. Governor of Delhi (1984) 4 SCC 308, where delay could increase an urgency that already existed, and noted that Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. (1996) 2 SCC 549 had been distinguished in Radhy Shyam.
members.conclusion: The State was not justified in invoking the urgency provision to dispense with the inquiry and hearing. The landowners could not be denied their right to object, and the appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment set aside.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_appeal and jail_construction_project and urgency_authority_invoked and landowner_hearing_excluded and prolonged_state_inactivity

predicates.acquisition_challenge_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the dismissal of a challenge to a land acquisition.
predicates.jail_construction_project: The land is proposed to be acquired for construction of a jail.
predicates.urgency_authority_invoked: The acquiring authority invokes an urgency procedure to proceed without the ordinary acquisition process.
predicates.landowner_hearing_excluded: The acquiring authority removes the landowners’ opportunity to object and be heard.
predicates.prolonged_state_inactivity: The government’s acquisition process includes substantial periods of delay or slow progress before the acquisition notifications are issued.

members.legal_issue: Dispensing with the statutory objection inquiry in a land acquisition requires a genuine urgency supported by relevant material, and planned development alone does not establish that urgency.
material_facts: The acquisition was for planned industrial development over a large area, but the authorities did not identify a specific urgency that required omitting the opportunity to object.
A prior acquisition from the same village for the same purpose had proceeded with an objection inquiry.
More than a year passed between the development authority’s request for urgent acquisition and the acquisition notification, without an explanation for the delay.
The stated risk of encroachment was the only identified ground for urgency and did not explain why an objection inquiry had to be dispensed with.
There was also an unexplained delay of about a year between the acquisition notification and the declaration notification.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4, 5-A, 6 and 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, read with the Uttar Pradesh amendments, make the objection inquiry the normal procedure and permit its omission only when a genuine urgency, supported by relevant material, warrants it. A court may examine whether relevant material existed, though it does not reappraise a properly supported subjective satisfaction as an appellate authority. Planned development does not automatically justify dispensing with the inquiry. The Court applied Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra, which requires attention to whether urgency warrants eliminating the inquiry; State of U.P. v. Pista Devi and A.P. Sareen v. State of U.P., which recognize that urgency may arise in appropriate development cases but do not establish an automatic rule; Rajasthan Housing Board v. Shri Kisan, where concrete time-bound circumstances supported urgency; and Gurdial Singh v. State of Punjab, concerning the importance of the inquiry and the need for real urgency.
members.conclusion: The State had no relevant material supporting genuine subjective satisfaction that the objection inquiry had to be dispensed with; invoking the urgency power for that purpose was unjustified.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and specific_urgency_material_absent and (encroachment_only_basis or unexplained_acquisition_delay)

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges an acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.specific_urgency_material_absent: The acquiring authority did not have material showing why the circumstances required the ordinary objection process to be omitted.
predicates.encroachment_only_basis: The authority relied on the possibility of encroachment as its stated reason for omitting the objection process.
predicates.unexplained_acquisition_delay: A substantial delay in acting on the acquisition request or completing the acquisition steps was left unexplained.

members.legal_issue: Dispensing with the landowner’s objection inquiry in a supplemental acquisition for a development scheme is unjustified when the record does not establish genuine urgency or show that the authority applied its mind to the need to exclude the inquiry.
material_facts: The acquisition concerned a small additional area for a residential and commercial development scheme, after a larger area had already been acquired for the scheme.

The additional land had initially been left out of the acquisition, and the authorities later gave differing reasons for seeking it, including alleged construction, contiguity with the scheme, and the incompatibility of a cattle market with residential development.
The landowners disputed the authorities’ claim that their land was in the middle of the scheme; the claim that it was at the scheme’s edge was not specifically denied.
The proposal to acquire the additional land had been under consideration for more than two years before the urgency notification was issued.

The declaration following the urgency notification was issued just before the one-year deadline, and the file indicated that it was issued to avoid lapse of the acquisition rather than because immediate possession was required.
The record did not establish exceptional circumstances requiring immediate possession or demonstrate that the authority considered whether even a summary objection inquiry could be held.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5A and 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the right to object and be heard is a valuable safeguard, and dispensing with it is an exceptional, discretionary power that requires genuine urgency, relevant material, and application of mind to whether the inquiry itself must be excluded. A public purpose alone does not establish that urgency. In reviewing the decision, the court considers the total evidence: the challenger cannot succeed on bare assertions, but the State must place before the court facts especially within its knowledge, including material establishing exceptional circumstances. The court applies the approach in Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra, while considering the differing emphases in State of U.P. v. Pista Devi, Rajasthan Housing Board v. Shri Kishan, Chameli Singh v. State of U.P., Om Prakash v. State of U.P., Anand Singh v. State of U.P., and Radhey Shyam v. State of U.P. Sections 101, 102 and 106 of the Evidence Act inform the burden of proof. The existence of a relevant basis and application of mind are required even though the urgency assessment is subjective and courts do not act as appellate authorities over it.
members.conclusion: The decision to dispense with the inquiry was unjustified. The acquisition notifications and proceedings based on them were quashed, and the property was to be returned to the landowners, without prejudice to the authorities’ powers under law.

rule.if: challenge_to_urgent_acquisition and supplemental_land_for_development and (no_material_showing_immediate_need or no_application_of_mind_to_waiving_hearing) and (delay_in_processing or declaration_issued_to_avoid_lapse)

predicates.challenge_to_urgent_acquisition: A person whose land is compulsorily acquired challenges the decision to dispense with the opportunity to object and be heard.
predicates.supplemental_land_for_development: The acquisition concerns additional land sought for a development scheme after land for the scheme has already been acquired.
predicates.no_material_showing_immediate_need: The government record does not establish circumstances showing that immediate possession is necessary to carry out the public purpose.
predicates.no_application_of_mind_to_waiving_hearin: The record does not show that the authority considered whether the objection inquiry itself needed to be excluded.
predicates.delay_in_processing: The authorities allowed substantial time to pass while processing the additional acquisition before invoking urgency.
predicates.declaration_issued_to_avoid_lapse: The record indicates that the declaration was issued to prevent the acquisition from lapsing rather than because immediate possession was needed.

members.legal_issue: Urgency provisions allowing earlier possession of non-waste or non-arable land do not permit the government to dispense with the landowner's objection procedure unless the statutory condition for dispensing with that procedure applies.
material_facts: The land was occupied largely by a mill and godowns, with the remainder open and paved; no part was waste or arable.
The government invoked urgency provisions, including the provision permitting earlier possession of other-than-waste-or-arable land for planned development.
The government directed that objections not be heard and issued a declaration without taking action under the objection procedure.
The landowners had filed objections after receiving possession notices, but no procedure under section 5-A had been followed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5-A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act require the objection procedure before a declaration, unless section 17(4) validly disapplies it. Sections 17(1) and 17(4) are independent: an order permitting earlier possession under section 17(1) does not itself dispense with section 5-A. Section 17(4), as then framed, applied to land covered by section 17(1), namely waste or arable land. The U.P. amendment adding section 17(1-A) permitted earlier possession of other-than-waste-or-arable land in specified circumstances but did not extend section 17(4) to that land. The right to object under section 5-A is substantial and cannot be removed by implication. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The direction dispensing with objections was beyond the government's powers, and the declaration issued without following section 5-A was invalid.

rule.if: land_acquisition_case and land_not_waste_or_arable and urgency_possession_authorized and declaration_issued_without_objection_procedure

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a government acquisition of land under the general land-acquisition law.
predicates.land_not_waste_or_arable: The land is neither waste nor arable, and buildings stand on at least part of it.
predicates.urgency_possession_authorized: The government invoked a provision permitting possession before an award because of urgency or planned development.
predicates.declaration_issued_without_objection_pro: The government issued an acquisition declaration without giving the landowner the statutory opportunity to object.

members.legal_issue: The urgency power to dispense with the objection inquiry does not extend to land outside the categories covered by the original possession provision merely because the acquisition falls within a locally expanded urgency category.
material_facts: The land was not waste or arable, and that fact was not disputed.
The government used the urgency provision to dispense with the statutory objection inquiry for an acquisition treated as falling within the locally expanded category for taking possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5-A and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, the inquiry may be dispensed with only for land to which Section 17(1) or Section 17(2) applies. The Uttar Pradesh amendment adding Section 17(1-A) extended the power to take possession before an award in specified circumstances, but did not extend the separate power under Section 17(4) to dispense with the inquiry. The Court applied Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Government. A declaration under Section 6 made without the obligatory Section 5-A procedure is invalid.
members.conclusion: The direction dispensing with the objection inquiry was invalid. Because the required inquiry had not been held, the subsequent acquisition declaration was also invalid.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and land_is_not_waste_or_arable and acquisition_falls_within_locally_expanded_urgency_category and objection_inquiry_is_dispensed_with

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated compulsory acquisition proceedings for land.
predicates.land_is_not_waste_or_arable: The land being acquired was not waste or arable land.
predicates.acquisition_falls_within_locally_expande: The acquisition fell within a locally expanded category that permitted possession before an award.
predicates.objection_inquiry_is_dispensed_with: The government directed that interested persons would not receive the statutory inquiry into objections.

members.legal_issue: An emergency acquisition notification cannot dispense with the landowner’s right to object when it fails to state the required land qualification and the government’s opinion that immediate possession is urgent.
material_facts: A land-acquisition notification directed that emergency powers be used and that the objection procedure be dispensed with.
The notification did not state that the land was waste or arable, or that the government was of the opinion that there was urgency to take immediate possession.
The notification merely directed the Collector to act under the emergency power on grounds of urgency.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government may dispense with the objection procedure only where the land is waste or arable and urgency requires immediate possession. The landowner’s right to object under Section 5A must not be interfered with casually or cavalierly. A direction to the Collector to take action on grounds of urgency does not by itself fulfill the legal requirements. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The direction dispensing with the objection procedure was invalid; the Court struck down that portion of the notification and allowed the appeal and writ petition.

rule.if: emergency_acquisition_case and objection_opportunity_dispensed and notification_omits_land_qualification and notification_omits_government_urgency_opinion and collector_only_directed_on_urgency

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land using an emergency power to obtain possession.
predicates.objection_opportunity_dispensed: The government’s notification removes the landowner’s opportunity to file an objection.
predicates.notification_omits_land_qualification: The notification does not state that the land is waste or arable.
predicates.notification_omits_government_urgency_op: The notification does not state that the government is of the opinion that urgency requires immediate possession.
predicates.collector_only_directed_on_urgency: The notification merely directs the Collector to act on grounds of urgency.

members.legal_issue: Urgent possession under the special power for arable or waste land is unauthorized when the acquired land is neither arable nor waste.
material_facts: The acquired land was forest land covered with a large number of trees, including about one lakh trees.
The government directed the Collector to take possession before an award, and the Collector did so.
The court found that the land was not mainly used for ploughing and raising crops and was not desolate, barren land with little or no vegetation.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permits urgent possession before an award only of waste or arable land. In that context, arable land means land mainly used for ploughing and raising crops, while waste land means land unfit for cultivation or habitation, desolate and barren, with little or no vegetation. The land’s character is a jurisdictional fact that a court may determine independently on certiorari. The court relied on R. v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White and Collins v. Minister of Health.
members.conclusion: The government’s direction under section 17(1) and the Collector’s taking of possession under that subsection were ultra vires.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The government invokes an urgent land-acquisition procedure permitting possession before an award.
predicates.land_neither_arable_nor_waste: The land is neither mainly used for ploughing and raising crops nor barren, desolate land with little or no vegetation.

members.legal_issue: The power to dispense with objections in an urgent acquisition cannot validly be exercised where the land does not meet the condition for urgent possession and the government has not properly applied its mind to that condition.
material_facts: The land was forest land with a large number of trees, rather than waste or arable land.
The government formed the opinion that the urgent-possession provision applied and directed that the objection procedure be dispensed with.
Because the land did not meet the statutory condition, the court concluded that the government had not honestly formed the relevant opinion or had failed to apply its mind to the relevant facts.
A subsequent declaration and further acquisition proceedings followed the decision to dispense with objections.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, connect the power to dispense with objections under section 5A to the applicability of the urgent-possession provisions. Although the government’s opinion is subjective, it may be challenged if the government did not apply its mind or acted mala fide; the court may infer failure to apply the mind where the land does not satisfy the statutory condition. The court relied on King Emperor v. Shibnath Banerjee, Jaichand Lal Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Estate and Trust Agencies Ltd. v. Singapore Improvement Trust, Ross Clunis v. Papadopoullos, and R. v. Australian Stevedoring Industry Board.
members.conclusion: The direction dispensing with objections was ultra vires; the subsequent declaration and proceedings were invalid and without jurisdiction.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The government invokes an urgent land-acquisition procedure that can dispense with the ordinary objection process.
predicates.land_neither_arable_nor_waste: The land is neither mainly used for ploughing and raising crops nor barren, desolate land with little or no vegetation.
predicates.government_opined_urgent_power_applied: The government states that the urgent-possession procedure applies and dispenses with the ordinary objection process.

members.legal_issue: A government cannot dispense with a landholder’s right to object by relying on an emergency opinion that the land qualifies for emergency powers when the land does not meet the required description.
material_facts: The government formed an opinion that the emergency provision applied and directed that objections need not be heard.
The land was forest land and was neither waste nor arable land.
Dispensing with the objection procedure deprived the appellant of the opportunity to object to the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act permits the government to direct that the section 5A objection procedure does not apply where it considers the emergency provisions applicable. Although that opinion is ordinarily subjective, it may be challenged where the authority did not apply its mind or acted mala fide; the absence of grounds supporting the opinion may permit an inference that it was not honestly formed or that relevant facts were not considered. The Court relied on King Emperor v. Shibnath Banerjee, Jaichand Lal Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Estate and Trust Agencies Ltd. v. Singapore Improvement Trust, Ross Clunis v. Papadopovllos, and R. v. Australian Stevedoring Industry Board.
members.conclusion: The government’s direction dispensing with objections was ultra vires; the related acquisition declaration and subsequent proceedings were also invalid.

predicates.land_acquisition_emergency_exemption_pro: The government used an emergency procedure in an acquisition proceeding to dispense with the ordinary objection process.
predicates.land_not_waste_or_arable: The land did not qualify as either waste land or arable land for the emergency procedure.
predicates.objection_hearing_excluded: The government directed that affected persons would not receive the ordinary opportunity to object to the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: An urgency direction dispensing with the objection inquiry cannot be upheld for only the qualifying portion when the acquisition also covers land outside the qualifying categories.
material_facts: The acquisition notification covered land of which, at most, only part was said to be waste or arable.
The direction dispensing with the inquiry applied to the notified land, and interested persons could not be restricted to objecting only about the non-waste-or-arable portion.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5-A and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, where the government lacks power to dispense with the inquiry for any part of the notified land, the notification cannot be severed so as to dispense with the inquiry for another part. Interested persons must be able to raise objections concerning the notified land as a whole.
members.conclusion: The direction dispensing with the inquiry was invalid for the notified land as a whole and could not be treated as partly valid.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated compulsory acquisition proceedings for land.
predicates.acquisition_notification_covers_mixed_la: The notified land included both land within and land outside the categories for which the inquiry could be dispensed with.
predicates.inquiry_exemption_covers_the_entire_noti: The government purported to dispense with the objection inquiry for all land covered by the notification.

members.legal_issue: A composite acquisition notification cannot be preserved for its preliminary acquisition purpose while being invalidated only insofar as it invokes the urgency power, where the common urgency foundation is invalid and that result would treat similarly situated owners differently.
material_facts: The notification covered multiple properties and relied on one common urgency basis.
The urgency basis was invalid, and the same notification had already been quashed for other owners covered by it.

Preserving the notification for the preliminary acquisition purpose while setting aside only the urgency provisions would leave the affected owners without the consequences of quashing the notification in full.
members.legal_principle: The common notification could not be divided so that its urgency basis was invalid for some properties but valid for others where the basis was the same. Partial invalidation would create an anomalous and unjust result, including leaving owners subject to the acquisition while removing the protections associated with the urgency process. The Court relied on the reasoning in Union of India v. Shakuntala Gupta and the earlier treatment of the same notification in Banwari Lal & Sons v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The notification could not be sustained in part by severing the urgency provisions; it was invalid as a whole.

rule.if: acquisition_case and composite_notification and common_urgency_basis_invalid and notification_already_quashed_for_other_covered_owners

predicates.acquisition_case: The government sought to acquire land under a notification.
predicates.common_urgency_basis_invalid: The common basis relied on to invoke urgency was invalid.
predicates.notification_already_quashed_for_other_c: The same notification had already been quashed for other owners whose properties it covered.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition of one property under a composite notice cannot stand when the common expression of urgency relied on to dispense with objections has already been held insufficient.
material_facts: The property was one of fourteen properties covered by a single acquisition notice, which expressed a common opinion that urgency justified taking possession and dispensing with objections.

The same notice was set aside in a challenge concerning another listed property, in part because its expression of urgency was insufficient; the Supreme Court dismissed the challenge to that decision.
The acquisition of the property at issue was set aside by following the decision concerning the other property, and the order dismissing the appeal was challenged by review.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4, 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the notice relied on a common expression of urgency to invoke the urgency procedure and dispense with objections. Applying the decision in Banwari Lal & Sons v. Union of India, the Court held that the insufficiency of that common expression was not peculiar to one property: it could not be partly valid and partly invalid across properties covered by the composite notice. The Court did not decide whether the broader principles concerning urgency under Section 17 were correctly stated in Banwari Lal.
members.conclusion: The common expression of urgency could not be treated as sufficient for this property after it had been held insufficient for another property covered by the same notice. The order dismissing the appeal was not legally erroneous, and the review application was dismissed without costs.

predicates.review_of_appeal_dismissal: The applicant sought review of an order dismissing an appeal concerning an acquisition.
predicates.composite_notice_covers_multiple_propert: The acquisition notice covered multiple properties in one notice.
predicates.common_urgency_basis: The notice relied on the same expression of urgency for the properties it covered.
predicates.same_urgency_basis_previously_held_insuf: A court had previously set aside action concerning another property under the same notice because the common expression of urgency was insufficient.

members.legal_issue: Dispensing with the statutory hearing in an urgent land acquisition requires the appropriate government to apply its mind separately to whether that hearing must be excluded, and cannot follow automatically from a finding of urgency.
material_facts: The acquisition authorities invoked urgency and the published notification stated that the landowners’ hearing had been dispensed with.
The records before the Lieutenant Governor did not show consideration of the need to dispense with the hearing.
The land had continued to be used for the festival’s concluding ceremony, and there was no material showing that the owners were preventing its use.
An earlier attempt to acquire part of the land for the same purpose had lapsed, but that fact was not placed before the Lieutenant Governor.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5A and 17(1), (2) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the existence of urgency or unforeseen emergency is a condition precedent to dispensing with the hearing but does not, by itself, make dispensation automatic. The appropriate government must also apply its mind to whether the circumstances require the hearing to be excluded; the urgency may itself be sufficiently serious to support that conclusion, but the government must consider that need. The hearing is a valuable substantive right that may be taken away only for good and valid reasons supported by the material before the government. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. State of U.P. for the distinction between urgency powers and dispensing with the hearing, and Munshi Singh v. Union of India for the importance of the hearing right.
members.conclusion: The decision to dispense with the hearing was vitiated by non-application of mind. The appeals were dismissed, leaving in place the High Court’s decision to set aside that decision and permit acquisition proceedings to continue from the preliminary-notification stage.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and urgent_possession_basis_invoked and hearing_dispensed_with and not government_considered_need_to_dispense

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a land acquisition in which the government dispensed with an opportunity for interested persons to object.
predicates.urgent_possession_basis_invoked: The acquiring authority relied on an asserted need for urgent possession or an unforeseen emergency.
predicates.hearing_dispensed_with: The government directed that interested persons would not receive the ordinary opportunity to object and be heard before acquisition proceeded.
predicates.government_considered_need_to_dispense: The government considered, on the relevant material, whether the circumstances required removing the opportunity to object and be heard.

members.legal_issue: Urgency permitting accelerated possession does not by itself justify dispensing with the interested persons’ hearing in a land acquisition; the appropriate government must separately consider and form an opinion that the hearing should be dispensed with.
material_facts: The acquisition authority invoked the urgent-acquisition power and the notification stated that the statutory hearing would not apply.
The record did not show that the decision-maker had considered the distinct need to dispense with the hearing.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1), 17(2) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the power to take possession urgently and the power to dispense with the inquiry under Section 5A are distinct. Section 17(4) makes dispensing with the inquiry discretionary, not automatic upon a finding of urgency. Nandeshwar Prasad v. State of U.P. supports the distinction between invoking the urgent-possession power and separately directing that the Section 5A inquiry not apply. Section 5A provides a valuable substantive opportunity to object, as recognised in Munshi Singh v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The existence of urgency or unforeseen emergency is a condition precedent to dispensing with the hearing, but is not by itself sufficient. The appropriate government must apply its mind to whether the circumstances also warrant dispensing with it; the urgency itself may support that decision if the government makes that assessment.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land by a public authority.
predicates.urgent_possession_need: The appropriate government considers immediate or accelerated possession necessary.
predicates.unforeseen_emergency: The appropriate government considers an unforeseen emergency to require immediate possession.
predicates.government_must_separately_assess_need_t: The appropriate government separately considers whether the circumstances warrant removing the interested persons’ opportunity to object and be heard.

members.legal_issue: Regulation of the duties and functions of religious attendants and a spiritual officeholder does not infringe freedom of religion when the regulating body must observe the applicable religious law and tenets.
material_facts: The challenged provisions authorised the committee to determine the Khadims’ privileges and regulate their presence, and to determine any functions and powers of the Sajjadanashin in relation to the shrine.
The Khadims performed duties by rotation, making regulation of their discharge necessary.
The Act required the committee to observe Muslim law and the tenets of the Chishti saint when conducting and regulating established rites and ceremonies.
members.legal_principle: Article 25(1) protects freedom of conscience and the freedom to profess, practise, and propagate religion, but the powers at issue regulated the discharge of duties and functions rather than prohibiting religious practice. The provisions had to be read together with the Act’s mandatory requirement to observe Muslim law and the saint’s tenets. The Court’s discussion of essential and integral religious practices was consistent with Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, and Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. The State of Mysore, [1958] S.C.R. 895.
members.conclusion: The challenged provisions did not violate Article 25(1).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_regulation_o: A party challenged a law regulating the duties of attendants and the functions of a religious officeholder.
predicates.attendants_performed_duties_by_rotation: The attendants carried out their duties by rotation.
predicates.regulating_body_was_required_to_observe_: The law required the regulating body to observe the applicable religious law and the institution’s religious tenets.

members.legal_issue: General regulatory requirements governing the registration, accounting, audit, investment, inspection, and administration of public religious trusts do not infringe the constitutional freedom of religion or the right to manage religious affairs.
material_facts: The challenged law required trustees of public trusts to register the trusts, keep accounts, have them audited, and comply with rules governing investment and alienation of trust property.
Officials could inspect trust property after reasonable notice and were required to respect the trust’s religious practices and usages.
The law provided for procedural remedies and penalties connected with its administration.
members.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26(b) protect religious belief and acts performed in pursuance of religious belief, while Article 26(d) permits a religious denomination to administer its property in accordance with valid law. Article 25(2)(a) permits regulation of associated secular activities. Applying the principles stated in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, and the discussion of religious practice in Adelaide Company v. The Commonwealth, the Court distinguished protected religious affairs from secular property administration; reasonable controls over trust property and incidental procedural provisions do not, without more, infringe religious freedom.
members.conclusion: The challenged administrative requirements were valid because they regulated the administration of trust property and did not interfere with religious affairs.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_public_trust: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of regulation governing a public trust.
predicates.public_religious_trust: The trust is a public trust established for religious purposes.
predicates.challenged_measures_regulate_property_ad: The challenged measures govern matters such as registration, accounts, audits, investment, inspection, or other administration of trust property.
predicates.not challenged_measures_control_religiou: The challenged measures do not dictate or prohibit religious beliefs, rites, or practices.

members.legal_issue: A statutory scheme may vest temple property in the deity and entrust its administration to a board while preserving religious observances according to established custom.
material_facts: The legislation vested ownership of the temple and its endowments in the deity and gave the board the right to possess and administer the property.
The board was assigned management of the temple's property and secular affairs and responsibility for arranging worship, ceremonies, and festivals according to the denomination's customs and usages.
The legislation preserved established temple usages and customary rights unless expressly displaced.
The board's authority over temple affairs was construed as extending to secular affairs, not as displacing religious observances.
members.legal_principle: The Court read the provisions together and applied the rule that, where two reasonable constructions are available, the construction that preserves constitutionality is preferred. It treated administration of property as secular and protected religious worship and customary rights through the provisions preserving customs and usage.
members.conclusion: The statutory scheme was valid insofar as it provided for board administration of temple property and secular affairs while preserving religious observances and customary rights.

predicates.temple_administration_law_challenge: The case challenges a law providing for administration of a public temple.
predicates.law_vests_property_in_deity: The law recognizes the deity as the owner of the temple's property and endowments.
predicates.board_administers_secular_property_matte: The law assigns a board responsibility for property management and secular administration.
predicates.religious_customs_and_rights_are_preserv: The law protects established religious observances and customary rights except where it expressly provides otherwise.

members.legal_issue: Statutory regulation of the administration of religious trust property does not, by itself, interfere with a denomination’s right to manage its religious affairs.
material_facts: The Jain trust challenged statutory provisions concerning investment and transfer of trust property, accounts, auditing, budgets, court directions, and the appointment of trustees.
The Court found that the challenged provisions regulated trust administration and protection of property rather than religious rites or practices.
The religious materials relied on did not establish a general prohibition on increasing trust property or depositing funds in banks or other specified institutions.
The provisions concerning court directions and trustee appointments required judicial consideration and did not give the administrative officers power to determine those matters themselves.
members.legal_principle: Article 26(b) concerns affairs in matters of religion, such as rites, ceremonies, and festivals; administration of property is dealt with by Article 26(d) and may be regulated by law. Regulation is permissible, but the State cannot altogether take away a denomination’s right to administer its property and vest it in an authority that does not comprise that denomination. The Court relied on Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay, Tilakayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, and Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. State of Mysore.
members.conclusion: The challenged administrative provisions were valid and did not infringe the denomination’s religious freedom.

predicates.religious_trust_property_regulation_chal: A religious denomination challenges legal controls over the administration of its trust property.
predicates.challenged_controls_are_administrative: The challenged controls concern property administration rather than religious rites or practices.
predicates.controls_do_not_displace_denominational_: The controls do not transfer the denomination’s management of religious affairs to an authority outside the denomination.

members.legal_issue: A law may transfer a public temple's secular management to a statutory board without violating religious freedom when it preserves religious worship and ritual practices.
material_facts: The legislation transferred temple administration and management from the existing managers to a board.
The deity retained ownership of the temple and its endowments.
The legislation required worship and rituals to be conducted according to Hindu scriptures, customs, and usage.
Priests remained responsible for performing religious services, and the board and its officers were prohibited from interfering with those duties.
The legislation provided for improved management, safekeeping of property, and facilities for pilgrims.
members.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect religious belief and practices that are integral to religion, but administration and management of a religious institution and its property are secular activities subject to legislation. The Court relied on A.S. Narayana Deekshitulu v. State of A.P., Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of A.P., Sri Sri Sri Lakshmana Yatendrulu v. State of A.P., Bira Kishore Deb v. State of Orissa, and Bhuri Nath v. State of Jammu & Kashmir.
members.conclusion: The legislation did not violate Articles 25 or 26 because it regulated secular administration while preserving religious practices and the performance of worship.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_temple_manag: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law governing the management of a temple.
predicates.law_transfers_only_secular_management: The law transfers administrative and property-management functions without transferring ownership of the temple from the deity.
predicates.religious_worship_is_preserved: The law protects religious worship and ritual performance according to the temple's religious practice.

members.legal_issue: Regulatory supervision of a religious trust does not violate religious freedom or a denomination’s right to manage religious affairs when it preserves religious practices and directs trust property to the purposes established by the founder or usage.
material_facts: The Board could alter or modify a trust budget and give directions to a trustee.

Budget changes could not be inconsistent with the founder’s ascertainable wishes or the governing law, and directions had to be for proper administration in accordance with the governing law and those wishes.
The legislation was directed to administration of the trusts and protection of trust property, not to changing religious practices or diverting trust funds to different purposes.
The appellants identified no provision that interfered with religious practices or with the right to establish and maintain religious institutions.
members.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect religious belief and practice and a denomination’s management of its affairs in matters of religion. The Court relied on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, including its recognition that religious freedom extends to religious practices; Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. The State of Mysore, [1958] S.C.R. 895; and Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. The State of Bombay, [1954] S.C.R. 1055, concerning the use of religious trust property for the founder’s purposes or established usage. A mere apprehension that regulatory powers may be abused does not invalidate the provision.
members.conclusion: The legislation did not contravene the constitutional protections for religious freedom and the management of religious affairs.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_regulation: The litigants challenged a law providing oversight of religious trusts.
predicates.oversight_is_limited_to_proper_trust_adm: The regulator’s powers are confined to proper administration of the trust under its governing law and purposes.
predicates.religious_practices_are_not_interfered_w: The oversight does not interfere with practices regarded by the religious community as part of its religion.
predicates.trust_funds_remain_directed_to_authorize: The oversight does not divert trust property or income from purposes established by the founder or by established usage.

members.legal_issue: A provision for interim arrangements when a religious office becomes vacant does not infringe freedom of religion when it forms part of a procedure for determining succession to that office.
material_facts: The challenged provision authorised the committee to make provisional arrangements for performing the functions of the Sajjadanashin when that office fell vacant.
The same statutory section prescribed the procedure for inviting applications and determining succession to the office.
members.legal_principle: The interim-arrangement provision must be read with the rest of the section, whose principal purpose was to prescribe a procedure for determining succession. A temporary arrangement pending selection of a successor does not, on that reading, interfere with freedom of religion.
members.conclusion: The interim-arrangement provision did not violate Article 25(1).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_interim_arra: A party challenged a law authorising temporary arrangements for the functions of a religious office.
predicates.interim_arrangements_were_part_of_a_succ: The temporary arrangements were provided within a procedure for determining a permanent successor.

members.legal_issue: Temporarily preventing a religious officeholder from performing the office does not violate the freedom to practise and propagate religion when the person remains able to enter the religious institution and is not barred from religious practice.
material_facts: The officeholder was suspended pending an inquiry and another official was placed in charge of day-to-day administration.
Although police guarded the institution, the officeholder was not prohibited from entering it.
The record did not establish that he was barred from professing, practising, or propagating his religion.
members.legal_principle: Article 25(1) protects the freedom to profess, practise, and propagate religion. The Court held that the right was not infringed because the officeholder had not been prohibited from entering the institution or exercising that freedom there.
members.conclusion: The arrangement did not violate the officeholder’s right under Article 25(1) to profess, practise, and propagate religion.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenged an arrangement affecting the exercise of religious freedom.
predicates.religious_officeholder_temporarily_sidel: An authority temporarily prevented the religious officeholder from managing or administering the institution.
predicates.entry_to_religious_site_remained_permitt: The officeholder remained permitted to enter the religious institution.
predicates.religious_practice_not_barred: The authority did not prohibit the officeholder from professing, practising, or propagating the religion.

members.legal_issue: A temporary administrative arrangement does not violate a religious denomination’s autonomy over rites and ceremonies when neither the governing law nor the appointed administrator interferes with deciding or performing those rites and ceremonies.
material_facts: An official was appointed temporarily to attend to the day-to-day administration of the institution and its endowments while the officeholder was suspended.
The officeholder alleged interference with the denomination’s religious autonomy.
Nothing in the challenged provisions empowered the authority to decide which rites and ceremonies were essential to the religion.
No interference with such matters by the authority or the temporary administrator was established.
members.legal_principle: Article 26(b) protects a religious denomination’s autonomy in deciding what rites and ceremonies are essential according to its tenets. Relying on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, the Court held that neither the statutory powers nor their exercise in this case interfered with that autonomy.
members.conclusion: There was no contravention of Article 26(b), because the denomination’s autonomy concerning rites and ceremonies had not been interfered with.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A religious denomination challenged a state arrangement as interfering with its religious autonomy.
predicates.temporary_administrator_appointed: An authority appointed an administrator temporarily to manage the institution’s day-to-day affairs.
predicates.no_interference_with_rites_or_ceremonies: Neither the governing arrangement nor the administrator interfered with the denomination’s decisions about or performance of religious rites and ceremonies.

members.legal_issue: A temporary arrangement for administering religious institutional property does not violate a denomination’s right to administer that property when the arrangement responds to a specified temporary need and does not permanently transfer the right of administration.
material_facts: The officeholder was suspended pending an inquiry into serious charges of misappropriation and defalcation of trust funds and leading an immoral life.
An official was appointed temporarily to manage the institution and its endowments during the inquiry.
The statutory arrangement applied to specified temporary circumstances and lasted only until the relevant disability ceased or another officeholder succeeded.
The arrangement did not permanently vest administration in an authority lacking entitlement under the institution’s customary rules.
members.legal_principle: Article 26(d) protects a religious denomination’s right to administer property according to law, subject to lawful regulation. The Court relied on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, which distinguished a drastic power exercisable without justifying necessity from a limited arrangement for specified circumstances. It also referred to H. H. Sudhundra Thirtha Swamiar v. Commissioner for Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Mysore, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 302, in discussing the officeholder’s duties as trustee. The temporary arrangement did not take administration away altogether or vest it permanently in another authority.
members.conclusion: The temporary administrative arrangement did not contravene Article 26(d).

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and temporary_administrative_need_exists and administration_is_only_temporary and administration_is_not_permanently_transferred

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A religious denomination challenged a state arrangement affecting administration of its property.
predicates.temporary_administrative_need_exists: A temporary vacancy, suspension, succession dispute, or comparable circumstance created a need for an interim administrative arrangement.
predicates.administration_is_only_temporary: The interim administrator’s authority lasts only until the temporary circumstance ends or a successor takes office.
predicates.administration_is_not_permanently_transf: The arrangement does not permanently vest the denomination’s right of administration in an authority not entitled to exercise it under the institution’s customary rules.

members.legal_issue: A law may include a public official on a temple-management board and authorize interim administrative arrangements without infringing religious freedom when those powers concern secular administration.
material_facts: The law made the district collector a statutory board member even if the collector did not follow the denomination.
It required the other board members to belong to the denomination and profess the Hindu religion.
The law authorized interim administration after a board's dissolution and transitional administration before the first board was formed.
The board could appoint and discipline temple staff, including staff who handled valuable property as well as assisted with worship.
The law authorized inspection of temple property and records as an incident of property administration.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Articles 25(1) and 26(b) and held that participation in secular administration, including supervision, inspection, and control of property-related staff, does not itself interfere with religious freedom. It relied on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt in upholding the inspection power and construed the powers consistently with the protection of religious customs and authority.
members.conclusion: The challenged provisions concerning the collector's membership, interim administration, staff, and inspection were valid; the board's authority had to be exercised consistently with the preservation of religious worship and the hereditary head's religious role.

predicates.temple_board_powers_challenge: The case challenges statutory powers or membership arrangements for a public-temple management board.
predicates.challenged_powers_concern_secular_admini: The challenged powers concern property administration, supervision, staff, inspection, or temporary management rather than the conduct of religious rites.
predicates.religious_worship_remains_protected: The legal scheme preserves worship and religious ceremonies according to established custom and usage.

members.legal_issue: A contribution imposed on public trusts to fund the administration and regulation of those trusts is a fee, rather than a tax, when the proceeds are earmarked for that work and correspond to the services provided.
material_facts: The law required public trusts to contribute according to their gross annual income to a special Public Trusts Administration Fund.
The fund was earmarked for expenses incidental to regulating public trusts and carrying out the law, rather than being merged into general public revenue.
The State met certain personnel costs initially, but the special fund was required to meet the administration’s expenses.
members.legal_principle: A tax raises revenue for general public purposes without reference to a special service or benefit to the payer. A fee is connected with a service or work for those from whom it is collected, and the collections must be earmarked for the expenses of providing that service; the levy and expenses must have a correlation, though exact equivalence is not required and payment need not be voluntary. The Court relied on Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar and held that the contribution fell within entry 47 of List III, with the Act also relating to entries 10 and 28 of that List; if it had been a tax outside the specified State fields, legislative competence would instead have depended on Parliament under entry 97 of List I or Article 248(1).
members.conclusion: The contribution was a fee and not a tax, so the provision imposing it was within the State Legislature’s competence and was not ultra vires on that ground.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge_to_trus: The proceeding challenges the legislature’s competence to impose a contribution on public trusts.
predicates.contribution_funds_trust_regulation_serv: The contribution is collected to fund services or work for regulating and administering public trusts.
predicates.proceeds_are_earmarked: The collected money is set apart for those services rather than merged into general public revenue.
predicates.levy_correlates_with_service_expenses: The amount collected has a relationship to the expenses of providing the services, even if the two amounts are not exactly equal.

members.legal_issue: An annual contribution earmarked for the administration of religious institutions is a fee rather than a tax and may be imposed by the legislature with authority over that subject.
material_facts: Institutions above the stated income threshold had to make an annual contribution toward the Commissioner’s office and staff.
The contributions formed part of a special fund used to administer the endowment law and were not merged into general public revenue.
The fund was specifically set apart for the services involved in administering the institutions.
members.legal_principle: A fee is imposed in consideration of services or work for the benefit of those from whom it is demanded, and its proceeds must be specifically appropriated for that purpose rather than merged into general revenue. The distinction between fees and taxes and the application of those principles followed The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, Civil Appeal No. 38 of 1953.
members.conclusion: The contribution was a fee, not a tax, and the legislature was competent to enact it.

predicates.challenge_to_legislative_competence_over: A party challenges the legislature’s competence to impose an annual levy on institutions.
predicates.levy_funds_administration_services_for_c: The levy is collected to fund administration services connected with the contributing institutions.
predicates.proceeds_are_set_apart_for_those_service: The proceeds are specifically appropriated to those services rather than merged into general public revenue.

members.legal_issue: A contribution imposed on religious trusts to meet the expenses of administering a regulatory scheme is a fee rather than a tax when it funds that administration rather than general public revenue or the promotion of a religion.
material_facts: The legislation required trustees to pay a contribution, subject to a limit, for expenses incurred or to be incurred in administering the regulatory scheme.
The contribution was imposed to support the administration of religious trusts and was not for promoting or maintaining a particular religion or denomination.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the distinction between a tax and a fee and relied on Mahant Shri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1046, which upheld an analogous contribution for the administration of religious endowments. Article 27 prohibits specific appropriation of tax proceeds to promote or maintain a particular religion or religious denomination; it did not apply to a fee for secular administration of religious institutions.
members.conclusion: The contribution was a valid fee, not an unauthorized tax, and did not violate the constitutional prohibition on appropriating tax proceeds for the promotion or maintenance of a religion.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_administrat: The litigants challenged a charge imposed on religious trusts in connection with administration of a regulatory scheme.
predicates.charge_funds_administration_of_trust_reg: The charge was collected to meet the expenses of administering the trust-regulation scheme.
predicates.charge_is_not_appropriated_to_promote_a_: The charge was not specifically appropriated to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination.

members.legal_issue: A court charge is a fee rather than a tax when its primary purpose is to provide a special service to a defined class and its total collections broadly correspond to the total cost of that service.
material_facts: The challenged charge was imposed on litigants in connection with the administration of civil justice.
The State presented evidence of receipts from court fees and expenses associated with administering justice.
The Court found that the relevant relationship was between aggregate receipts and aggregate expenses, not the charge paid by an individual litigant and the service received by that litigant.
members.legal_principle: Under Entry 3 of List II of the Seventh Schedule, a legislature may charge fees for the administration of civil justice but may not use such a charge to raise general public revenue. The primary purpose must be a special service for a defined class, with broad aggregate correlation between collections and service costs. Exact arithmetic equivalence is unnecessary: I.M. & M. Industries v. State of Bihar; Government of Madras v. Zenith Lamps; Om Prakash v. Giri Raj Kishori; and P.M. Ashwanatha Narayana Setty v. State of Karnataka.
members.conclusion: A broad and general correlation between total collections and total service costs is sufficient for the charge to retain the character of a fee; exact or individual-level equivalence is unnecessary.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_court_charge: A litigant challenges the legal character or validity of a charge imposed in connection with court proceedings.
predicates.special_service_for_defined_class: The charge is primarily intended to fund a specific service provided to a defined class of persons.
predicates.broad_aggregate_correlation: The total amount collected bears a broad and general relationship to the total cost of providing the service.

members.legal_issue: Abolishing succession to hereditary trusteeship does not violate religious freedom when trusteeship remains open to qualified persons and religious practice remains protected.
material_facts: The law abolished hereditary rights to the office of trustee, including rights arising under earlier arrangements or documents.
A member of the founder's family could still be appointed as a trustee if qualified.
The legislative record included findings that hereditary management could be associated with mismanagement or misappropriation.
The law regulated institutional administration rather than religious beliefs, tenets, usages or practices.
members.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect religious belief and practice, but administration of institutional property is a secular activity that may be regulated by law under Article 25(2) and Article 26(d). The Court relied on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt and Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. The State of Bombay, which distinguish religious affairs from administration of property and reject a law that wholly transfers administration away from the religious body. The Court also considered Article 15(1) and the legislature's authority to end hereditary preference.
members.conclusion: Abolition of hereditary trusteeship was constitutional because it changed the mode of secular administration without abolishing trusteeship or interfering with religious practices.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_hereditary_t: A party challenged a law that ended succession to trusteeship by hereditary right.
predicates.secular_administration_is_regulated: The law regulates the management or administration of institutional property rather than religious belief or practice.
predicates.trusteeship_remains_open_to_qualified_pe: Persons remain eligible to serve as trustees under the law, including qualified members of the founder's family.
predicates.religious_practice_remains_protected: The law leaves the institution's religious beliefs, practices, customs and modes of worship undisturbed.

members.legal_issue: A law may abolish hereditary succession to religious-office appointments without violating religious freedom when it regulates selection of the office-holder while preserving the religious rites and practices themselves.
material_facts: The petitioners claimed hereditary rights to appointments as priests and other temple office-holders, and the associated rights and emoluments.

The law ended hereditary succession and provided for appointments under statutory procedures, while safeguarding the performance of worship and ceremonies according to the practices of each institution.
The priest’s appointment was made by the temple’s secular manager or authority, and the priest remained subject to discipline as an office-holder or servant.
The court accepted that a priest must be proficient in the rituals and practices applicable to the particular temple, but held that hereditary succession was not necessary to secure that competence.
members.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect essential religious beliefs and practices, but do not protect every custom associated with religion; the essential character of a practice must be assessed in context. Shirur Math recognized protection for integral religious practices; Venkataramana Devaru addressed matters of religion; Durgah Committee cautioned that non-essential or secular practices do not obtain religious protection. Seshammal held that appointing a priest is a secular act and that hereditary succession does not make the appointment a religious practice. Gazula Dasaratha Rama Rao held that appointment by descent to a public office is incompatible with constitutional equality. Sections 13 and 142 preserve the institution’s religious practices, while Sections 34 and 35 abolish hereditary rights and regulate appointments.
members.conclusion: Abolition of hereditary rights to appointment as a priest or other temple office-holder is valid and does not violate the constitutional protections for religious freedom or equality.

rule.if: religious_endowment_writ_challenge and hereditary_appointment_challenged and temple_authority_selects_office_holders and religious_rituals_remain_protected

predicates.religious_endowment_writ_challenge: A person challenges a law governing appointments in a religious institution through a writ proceeding.
predicates.hereditary_appointment_challenged: The challenged law ends succession to religious-institution offices by family inheritance or custom.
predicates.temple_authority_selects_office_holders: A temple manager or other secular authority selects the person who holds the office.
predicates.religious_rituals_remain_protected: The law preserves the institution’s established religious worship, ceremonies, and ritual practices.

members.legal_issue: Customary shares in offerings and other emoluments attached to a hereditary temple office may be abolished when the hereditary entitlement is ended and remuneration is provided through service conditions.
material_facts: Priests and other office-holders received shares in offerings, prasadam, lands, or other perquisites because of customary practices, agreements, or their hereditary offices.
The law abolished hereditary rights and separately abolished shares in offerings and other customary emoluments.
The statutory scheme provided for payment of salary to office-holders for their services.
The petitioners identified no independent entitlement to those shares apart from the office and the customary or contractual arrangements associated with it.
members.legal_principle: Section 144 abolishes shares in offerings, prasadam, lands, and other customary emoluments, and operates consequentially to the abolition of hereditary office under Section 34.
