In Gazula Dasaratha Rama Rao, the Court held that emoluments attached to an office are not an independent right apart from the office. Seshammal supports the distinction between the religious service performed and the secular incidents of holding the office.
members.conclusion: The customary rights to shares in offerings and other emoluments attached to the offices were validly abolished; the office-holders’ remuneration is governed by the statutory salary arrangements.

rule.if: religious_endowment_writ_challenge and customary_shares_attached_to_office and hereditary_office_right_abolished and salary_provided_for_service

predicates.religious_endowment_writ_challenge: An office-holder challenges changes to rights connected with service in a religious institution.
predicates.customary_shares_attached_to_office: The office-holder received shares in offerings or other perquisites by virtue of custom, agreement, or the office.
predicates.hereditary_office_right_abolished: The law ends hereditary entitlement to hold the office.
predicates.salary_provided_for_service: The governing scheme provides salary for the service performed in the office.

members.legal_issue: Hereditary control of temple management and hereditary entitlement to perform priestly duties or receive offerings may be regulated or abolished without creating a right to compensation where the legislation preserves worship and permits qualified appointments.
material_facts: The legislation extinguished the appellants' claimed hereditary management rights and placed management with a board.
The appellants claimed customary or hereditary rights as mahants, pandas, or archakas and claimed a right to receive pilgrims' offerings.
The legislation left priests responsible for religious services and permitted eligible persons to be appointed as archakas.
The appellants had not established that they were prevented from worshipping as devotees.
members.legal_principle: The right to manage temple property is secular, and an office or right to offerings dependent on performing temple service is not an independent vested right that prevents statutory regulation or abolition. Articles 25 and 26 protect religious practices, not every secular activity associated with religion. The Court relied on A.S. Narayana Deekshitulu v. State of A.P., Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of A.P., Sri Sri Sri Lakshmana Yatendrulu v. State of A.P., and Bira Kishore Deb v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The hereditary management claims and associated entitlement to offerings were not protected by Articles 25 and 26; the legislation could regulate or abolish those rights without compensation, while the appellants remained free to worship as devotees and could be considered for appointment as archakas if eligible.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_change_in_temple_: A proceeding challenges legislation that changes who manages a temple or performs its priestly services.
predicates.claimed_right_depends_on_hereditary_offi: The claimed management, priestly office, or entitlement to offerings depends on hereditary status or service to the temple.
predicates.religious_worship_remains_available: The legislation does not prevent the claimant from worshipping as a devotee and preserves the performance of religious services.

members.legal_issue: A tax supporting secular administration of religious trusts and institutions does not violate the constitutional prohibition on appropriating tax proceeds for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion.
material_facts: The contribution was imposed to support the proper administration of religious trusts and institutions wherever they existed.
Its purpose was not to foster or preserve Hinduism or any particular religious denomination.
members.legal_principle: Article 27 forbids the specific appropriation of tax proceeds to pay expenses for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion or religious denomination. The Court reasoned that secular administration of religious trusts and institutions, without favouring a religion or denomination, does not attract that prohibition.
members.conclusion: The levy did not fall within the prohibition in Article 27, although it was invalid on the separate ground that the state legislature lacked competence to impose it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_ad: A party challenges a tax imposed to support the administration of religious trusts or institutions.
predicates.tax_proceeds_support_neutral_administrat: The tax proceeds support administration carried out without favouring a religious group.
predicates.proceeds_do_not_promote_or_maintain_a_pa: The tax proceeds are not specifically used to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination.

members.legal_issue: A contribution used for the secular administration of religious institutions does not constitute an appropriation for promoting or maintaining a religion.
material_facts: The contribution funded the Commissioner and the administrative machinery for religious trusts and institutions.
The proceeds were applied to the proper administration of those institutions, not to foster or preserve a religion or denomination.
members.legal_principle: Article 27 prohibits the specific appropriation of tax proceeds to pay expenses for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion or religious denomination. A contribution directed to the secular administration of religious institutions, without favoring a religion or denomination, does not fall within that prohibition.
members.conclusion: The contribution did not violate Article 27.

predicates.challenge_to_a_religious_institution_con: A party challenges a contribution imposed on religious institutions.
predicates.proceeds_fund_secular_administration: The proceeds fund the secular administration of religious trusts and institutions.
predicates.proceeds_do_not_promote_or_maintain_a_re: The proceeds are not used to foster or preserve a religion or religious denomination.

members.legal_issue: Restrictions on a religious-trust manager’s control of trust property are permissible when they reasonably serve proper administration and protection of the trust and include safeguards against misuse of the regulatory powers.
material_facts: The legislation gave the Board supervisory and administrative powers, including powers relating to budgets, inspection, directions to trustees, schemes, and removal of trustees in specified circumstances.
The legislation directed that trusts be properly supervised and that their income be applied to their objects and purposes.

The Board’s powers were subject to safeguards, including consistency with the founder’s ascertainable wishes and the trust’s governing law, and opportunities to seek judicial review of certain decisions.
Before the legislation, section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure provided a court-based procedure to enforce duties relating to public charitable or religious trusts.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f), subject to Article 19(5), allowed reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The Court considered the purpose of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, and its safeguards, and relied on Angurbala Mullick v. Debabrata Mullick, [1951] S.C.R. 1125, concerning a shebait’s mixed duties and beneficial interest. It distinguished The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, and Mahant Shri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1046, where different statutory provisions were held unreasonable.
members.conclusion: The restrictions were reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public and did not violate the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_regulation: The litigants challenged a law regulating the management of religious trusts.
predicates.regulation_limits_trustee_control: The law gave a public regulatory body powers that restricted a trustee’s control over trust affairs or property.
predicates.limits_serve_trust_administration_and_pr: The restrictions were directed to proper administration of the trust and protection or preservation of its property.
predicates.regulatory_powers_have_effective_safegua: The law limited the regulator’s powers and provided safeguards or review against improper exercise.

members.legal_issue: Statutory controls requiring hereditary trustees to share secular administration with other trustees and executive officers are reasonable and in the public interest when they preserve the hereditary trustee’s office and do not interfere with religious functions.
material_facts: The challenged provisions permitted the appointment of non-hereditary trustees and executive officers even where hereditary trustees were in office and no mismanagement had been found.
A hereditary trustee was not removed from office and was to chair the board, alone or by rotation where there was more than one hereditary trustee.
The controls required administration in collaboration with other trustees and placed aspects of management with an executive officer.
The challenged controls concerned secular administration; religious practices and functions were to continue according to the applicable religious rules, usage or custom.
A commission had reported widespread mismanagement of endowment property and misuse of endowment funds.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The Court held that associating non-hereditary trustees and executive officers with management served the purpose of better and more efficient administration; hereditary trustees retained their office and a chairmanship role, and religious matters were not interfered with. Sections 15, 17, 27, 36 and 97 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, were among the challenged provisions. The Court relied on the reported need to address mismanagement and misuse of endowment property.
members.conclusion: Even if the hereditary trustees’ rights constituted property, the restrictions imposed by the Act were reasonable and in the interest of the general public.

predicates.constitutional_appeal_challenging_truste: An appeal challenging statutory controls over the management of an institution or endowment as unconstitutional is before the court.
predicates.statutory_controls_improve_public_admini: The controls associate other administrators with the institution to promote better and more efficient administration.
predicates.hereditary_trustee_retains_office_and_ch: The hereditary trustee keeps the office and has a chairmanship role in the governing board.
predicates.religious_functions_are_untouched: The controls concern secular administration and leave the institution’s religious functions undisturbed.
predicates.management_restrictions_are_reasonable_a: The controls on management are reasonable and serve the interests of the general public.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings under the earlier land acquisition regime lapse when an award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime commenced and either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid.
material_facts: An award had been made in 1987–1988, more than five years before the replacement land acquisition legislation commenced.
Physical possession of the land had not been taken.
Compensation had been deposited with the Revenue Department, but not paid to the landholders; such a deposit was not treated as payment.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 provides for deemed lapse where an award was made five years or more before that Act commenced and either possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid. Under Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki, a deposit in the government treasury is not payment to the landholders. The Court also relied on Bharat Kumar v. State of Haryana and Bimla Devi v. State of Haryana.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were deemed to have lapsed, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: earlier_land_acquisition_case and award_old_enough and (physical_possession_not_taken or compensation_unpaid)

predicates.earlier_land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns an acquisition initiated under an earlier land acquisition regime.
predicates.award_old_enough: The award was made at least five years before the replacement regime commenced.
predicates.physical_possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken physical possession of the land.
predicates.compensation_unpaid: Compensation had not been paid to the landholders; depositing it with a government department did not count as payment.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings covered by an earlier award lapse when the required compensation has not been paid or deposited under the applicable statutory conditions.
material_facts: An award for the acquired land had been made in 2005, more than five years before the 2013 Act came into force.
The acquiring authority admitted that the owners had not been paid compensation and stated that funds remained available with it for owners who came forward to collect them.
The owners sought relief on the basis that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, acquisition proceedings covered by an award made under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 lapse when the statutory conditions are met and compensation has not been paid or deposited as required. The Court relied on Sections 24(2) of the 2013 Act and 11 and 31 of the 1894 Act; it cited no earlier cases. The Court left open whether the manner in which possession was taken satisfied the statutory requirement.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings concerning the owners’ land had lapsed because compensation had not been paid to them; the proceedings were set aside as having lapsed.

predicates.acquisition_lapse_claim: The landowners sought a ruling that compulsory acquisition proceedings concerning their land had lapsed.
predicates.qualifying_prior_award: An award covering the land was made sufficiently before the new acquisition regime took effect to bring the proceedings within its lapse provision.
predicates.compensation_unpaid: The acquiring authority had not paid the required compensation to the landowners.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition under the earlier land-acquisition regime is deemed to have lapsed when the award was made at least five years before commencement of the new regime and either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid.
material_facts: The award was made in 1968, well over five years before the new regime commenced on 1 January 2014.
The compensation was not delivered to the appellants and was not deposited in court; it remained with the authority pending an application by the appellants.
Whether possession had been taken was disputed, and the Court did not decide that question because the compensation had not been paid.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 applies where an award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 predates commencement of the 2013 Act by at least five years and either possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid. The Court applied the meaning of payment set out in Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki and the other decisions it cited, including Union of India v. Shiv Raj, Bimla Devi v. State of Haryana, Competent Automobiles Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, Radiance Fincap (P) Ltd. v. Union of India and Rajiv Chaudhari HUF v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was deemed to have lapsed because the award was sufficiently old and compensation had not been paid. The Government could initiate fresh acquisition proceedings under the new regime if it chose to do so.

rule.if: deemed_lapse_acquisition_proceeding and award_at_least_five_years_old and (possession_not_taken or compensation_not_paid)

predicates.deemed_lapse_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether an acquisition under an earlier land-acquisition regime has lapsed under a later regime.
predicates.award_at_least_five_years_old: The award was made at least five years before the later regime commenced.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: The authority had neither delivered the compensation nor, when payment was prevented by a recognized contingency, offered it and deposited it in the appropriate court.

members.legal_issue: Land-acquisition proceedings under the former regime lapse when an award was made at least five years before the new regime commenced and either physical possession was not taken or compensation was not paid.
material_facts: An award had been made more than five years before the new regime commenced.
The acquiring authorities had not taken physical possession of the land.
Compensation had not been paid to the landowner.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 applies where an award under the former Land Acquisition Act was made five years or more before commencement of the 2013 Act and either possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid. The word “or” makes either failure sufficient. Under Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki, the legal fiction of lapse operates when those conditions are met; Section 114(2) and Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 do not preserve proceedings that have lapsed under Section 24(2). The Court also relied on Bharat Kumar v. State of Haryana, Bimla Devi v. State of Haryana, and Union of India v. Shiv Raj.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were deemed to have lapsed, and the acquisition notification was quashed insofar as it covered the land.

rule.if: legacy_land_acquisition and award_at_least_five_years_old and (physical_possession_not_taken or compensation_not_paid)

predicates.legacy_land_acquisition: The government initiated land-acquisition proceedings under the former land-acquisition regime.
predicates.award_at_least_five_years_old: The acquiring authority made an award at least five years before the new regime commenced.
predicates.physical_possession_not_taken: The acquiring authorities had not taken physical possession of the land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: The acquiring authorities had not paid compensation to the landowner.

members.legal_issue: The lapse condition for an acquisition under the former land acquisition regime is satisfied if either physical possession was not taken or compensation was not paid, provided the award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime commenced.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings were initiated under the former land acquisition law and the award was made more than five years before the replacement legislation commenced.
Physical possession was taken, but compensation had not been tendered or paid to the landowners and had not been deposited in the reference court.
The authorities deposited the compensation in court only immediately before the replacement legislation commenced.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act uses “or” in setting out the two alternative conditions—possession not taken or compensation not paid. Its plain meaning does not permit “or” to be read as “and.” Pune Municipal Corporation v. H.M. Solanki, followed in subsequent cases, establishes that either condition is sufficient where the award was made five years or more before the 2013 Act commenced.
members.conclusion: The conditions for lapse were satisfied because compensation had not been paid as required, even though physical possession had been taken; the acquisition proceedings were deemed to have lapsed.

rule.if: legacy_acquisition_case and award_made_well_before_replacement_regime and (physical_possession_not_taken or compensation_not_paid_as_required)

predicates.legacy_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns an acquisition initiated under an earlier land acquisition regime.
predicates.award_made_well_before_replacement_regim: The acquisition award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime commenced to meet its applicable time threshold.
predicates.physical_possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken physical possession of the land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid_as_required: The acquiring authority had not paid compensation in the legally prescribed manner.
predicates.acquisition_deemed_lapsed: The acquisition proceeding is treated as having lapsed.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition may be deemed to have lapsed for non-payment of compensation even after possession has been taken and the land has vested in the State.
material_facts: A possession record showed that possession of the open land had been taken and handed to government representatives.
Compensation had not been tendered or paid to the landowners in the prescribed manner.
The acquiring authorities argued that vesting made lapse impossible, relying on the rule concerning lapse under the earlier statute.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act expressly deems qualifying proceedings to have lapsed. Its wording differs from Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which uses “lapse.” The Court applied the effect of a statutory deeming fiction and distinguished Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., whose limited ratio was explained in Laxmi Devi v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The deeming provision applies despite prior possession and vesting when compensation has not been paid; the earlier rule concerning lapse under the former statute does not prevent that result.

rule.if: legacy_acquisition_case and award_made_well_before_replacement_regime and possession_taken_and_land_vested and compensation_not_paid_as_required

predicates.legacy_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns an acquisition initiated under an earlier land acquisition regime.
predicates.award_made_well_before_replacement_regim: The acquisition award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime commenced to meet its applicable time threshold.
predicates.possession_taken_and_land_vested: The acquiring authority took possession and the land consequently vested in the State.
predicates.compensation_not_paid_as_required: The acquiring authority had not paid compensation in the legally prescribed manner.
predicates.acquisition_deemed_lapsed_despite_vestin: The acquisition is treated as lapsed even though possession was taken and the land vested in the State.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition under the former land acquisition law lapses when the award was made at least five years before the new law commenced and either physical possession was not taken or compensation was not paid.
material_facts: The acquisition award had been made more than five years before the new law commenced.
The owner had not been paid compensation.
The owner remained in possession, and the Court found that possession had not been taken by the acquiring authority.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 creates a legal fiction of lapse where an award was made five years or more before commencement and either possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid. The Court applied Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki, which held that the conditions are alternatives and that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 is subject to Section 24(2); it also relied on Sree Balaji Nagar Residential Association v. State of Tamil Nadu. The contrary argument based on Satendra Prasad Jain and Sanjeevanagar Medical and Health Employees' Co-operative Housing Society was rejected.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings in respect of the owner's land were deemed to have lapsed, and the acquisition notifications were quashed.

rule.if: former_law_acquisition_proceeding and award_old_enough and (physical_possession_not_taken or compensation_not_paid)

predicates.former_law_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding was for acquisition under the former land acquisition law.
predicates.award_old_enough: The acquisition award was made at least five years before the new land acquisition law commenced.
predicates.physical_possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not actually taken possession of the land from the owner or interested person.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: The compensation awarded for the land had not been paid to the owner or interested person.

members.legal_issue: An old-law land-acquisition proceeding lapses when an award was made at least five years before the new acquisition law commenced and either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid in the legally required manner.
material_facts: The award was made more than five years before the 2013 Act commenced.
The landowners did not receive the compensation, and the unpaid amount was deposited in the government treasury rather than in court.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act provides for deemed lapse where an award under the 1894 Act was made five years or more before commencement of the 2013 Act and either physical possession was not taken or compensation was not paid. The meaning of payment is determined by Section 31 of the 1894 Act, including its requirement of court deposit when a specified contingency prevents payment. Sections 32 and 33 address money deposited in court. The Court relied on Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor, Ivo Agnelo Santimano Fernandes, and Prem Nath Kapur.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were deemed to have lapsed because compensation had neither been paid to the interested persons nor deposited in court; the treasury deposit did not satisfy the payment requirement.

predicates.old_acquisition_proceeding: The acquiring authority began the land-acquisition proceeding under the former acquisition law.
predicates.award_at_least_five_years_old: The authority made the award at least five years before the new acquisition law commenced.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken physical possession of the land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid_or_deposited_in_co: The acquiring authority had neither paid the compensation to the interested persons nor deposited unpaid compensation with the court for their benefit.

members.legal_issue: Land acquisition proceedings under the former acquisition law lapse when an award was made at least five years before the new land acquisition law commenced and either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid.
material_facts: The award for the land was made more than five years before the new land acquisition law commenced.
Compensation for the land had not been paid to the landowner.
The landowner remained in physical possession of the land.

The acquiring authority asserted that possession had been taken, but actual possession had not been taken; the authority had not followed the required procedure for taking possession of a large tract, including a properly executed panchnama attested by independent witnesses.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 deems proceedings under the repealed Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to have lapsed if an award was made five years or more before commencement of the 2013 Act and possession was not taken or compensation was not paid. Under Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misrimal Solanki, the legal fiction operates once those conditions are met, notwithstanding Section 114(2) of the 2013 Act read with Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897. For taking possession of a large tract, a properly executed panchnama attested by independent witnesses is permissible; the Court relied on Sita Ram Bhandar Society v. Lt. Governor, Bhanda Development Authority v. Moti Lal Agarwal, Raghubir Singh Sehrawat v. State of Haryana, and Patasi Devi v. State of Haryana. The Court also followed Bharat Kumar v. State of Haryana, Bimla Devi v. State of Haryana, and Union of India v. Shiv Raj.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings concerning the land had lapsed, and the acquisition notification was quashed insofar as it related to that land.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns acquisition proceedings initiated under an earlier land acquisition regime.
predicates.award_made_at_least_five_years_before_ne: The acquisition award was made at least five years before the replacement land acquisition law commenced.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken actual possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: Compensation for the acquired land had not been paid to the landowner.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings lapse when an award was made at least five years before the new acquisition law commenced and either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid.
material_facts: The acquisition awards were made more than five years before the new law commenced.
The High Court found that possession had not been taken and compensation had not been paid.
The High Court declared the acquisitions lapsed, and the acquiring authorities appealed.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, applies sequentially: the existence of an award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, made at least five years before commencement of the 2013 Act must first be established; then, proof that either possession was not taken or compensation was not paid attracts lapse. The Court relied on Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki, Union of India v. Shiv Raj, Bimla Devi v. State of Haryana, and Rajiv Chowdhrie HUF v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The acquisitions had lapsed, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: section_24_lapse_proceeding and award_at_least_five_years_old and (possession_not_taken or compensation_not_paid)

predicates.section_24_lapse_proceeding: A party sought a determination that existing land acquisition proceedings had lapsed under the new acquisition-law transition provision.
predicates.award_at_least_five_years_old: The acquiring authority made an award at least five years before the new acquisition law commenced.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: The acquiring authority had not paid compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_deemed_lapsed: The acquisition proceedings are treated as having lapsed.

members.legal_issue: Land acquisition proceedings are deemed to have lapsed when the award was made well before the 2013 Act and possession of the affected land was not taken.
material_facts: An award concerning the respondent's land had been passed in 1986.
The acquiring authority conceded that it had not taken possession of 1,100 square yards of the respondent's land.
The High Court declared the acquisition proceedings lapsed, and the acquiring authority appealed.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 applies to the acquisition of land for which an award had been made well before that Act and possession had not been taken. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings in respect of the 1,100 square yards were deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_lapse_declaration and land_acquisition_proceeding and award_preceded_new_act_by_five_years and possession_not_taken

predicates.appeal_challenges_lapse_declaration: The acquiring authority appealed against a declaration that the acquisition proceedings had lapsed.
predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.award_preceded_new_act_by_five_years: An award for the land was made at least five years before the new land-acquisition law took effect.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken possession of the affected land.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings covered by an old award lapse when physical possession has not been taken by the required time.
material_facts: The proceedings to acquire the lands were initiated under the earlier land acquisition law and resulted in awards.
Physical possession of the lands had not been taken within the five years or more before the later acquisition law commenced.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 provides that proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 lapse where an award was made five years or more before commencement of the 2013 Act and possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid. The appropriate Government may initiate fresh acquisition proceedings. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings had lapsed, and the appeals challenging that conclusion were dismissed.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: Proceedings to acquire land were initiated under an earlier land acquisition regime.
predicates.award_made_five_years_before_new_regime: An award in the land acquisition proceeding was made at least five years before the new acquisition regime commenced.
predicates.physical_possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken physical possession of the land by the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition under the earlier land-acquisition regime lapses under the transitional provision only when, in a qualifying pending proceeding, neither possession has been taken nor compensation has been paid.
material_facts: The cases concerned acquisition proceedings initiated under the earlier land-acquisition regime in which an award had been made at least five years before the replacement regime commenced.
The statutory wording joined two negative conditions: possession had not been taken and compensation had not been paid.
Taking possession under the earlier regime could vest the land in the acquiring authority even if compensation remained unpaid.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act is an exception to Section 24(1)(b), and applies to qualifying pending proceedings. Where two negative conditions are joined by “or,” the word may be read conjunctively in context; the Court relied on Patel Chunibhai Dajibha v. Narayanrao Khanderao Jambekar, Punjab Produce & Trading Co. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Brown & Co. v. Harrison, and M/s. Ranchhoddas Atmaram v. Union of India. Sections 16, 31 and 34 of the 1894 Act support the distinction between vesting, payment, and the interest consequence of non-payment.
members.conclusion: The two conditions are cumulative: lapse occurs only if possession has not been taken and compensation has not been paid. If either possession has been taken or compensation has been paid, the acquisition does not lapse under this provision.

rule.if: transitional_acquisition_proceeding and qualifying_old_award and possession_not_taken and compensation_not_paid

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.qualifying_old_award: An award was made sufficiently long before the replacement regime took effect to meet the statutory threshold for possible lapse.
predicates.possession_not_taken: The acquiring authority had not taken possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_not_paid: Compensation had not been paid, including by a legally sufficient tender.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings do not lapse when possession has been taken, even if compensation has not been paid or was only deposited.
material_facts: The acquisition authority’s records and the purchaser’s own submissions showed that possession had been taken of the acquired land; the purchaser also sought a mandamus requiring delivery of possession.
Compensation had been paid for part of the land and deposited with the Land Acquisition Collector for the remainder.
The purchaser relied on a later deposit of money made under the High Court’s order, which was based on an earlier order requiring landowners to return compensation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, as interpreted in Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal, lapse requires both that possession has not been taken and that compensation has not been paid. The word “or” is read as “nor” or “and”; once possession is taken, non-payment or non-deposit does not cause lapse. Possession under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is taken by drawing an inquest report or memorandum, and subsequent re-entry or continued occupation by the former owner does not undo vesting. Indore Development Authority also holds that Section 24(2) does not revive stale or concluded claims, and that a deposit made under an invalid order cannot reopen the acquisition.
members.conclusion: The acquisition did not lapse because possession had been taken. The later deposit did not alter that result.

predicates.lapse_claim_proceeding: A claimant seeks a declaration that a land acquisition has lapsed under a statutory lapse provision.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the acquired land, including by preparing a possession memorandum or inquest record.
predicates.compensation_paid: The acquiring authority paid or tendered the compensation determined for the acquired land.
predicates.acquisition_does_not_lapse: The acquisition proceedings remain in force and do not lapse.

members.legal_issue: Failure to deposit compensation in court does not by itself cause an acquisition to lapse where possession has been taken, although statutory interest may be payable.
material_facts: The earlier regime required a court deposit in specified circumstances, including refusal to accept compensation or a dispute about entitlement or apportionment.
The acquiring authority could take possession and the land could vest in the State despite compensation remaining unpaid or undeposited.
The earlier and replacement regimes provided for interest when compensation was not paid or deposited by the relevant time.
members.legal_principle: Sections 31(2) and 34 of the 1894 Act provide for court deposit in specified circumstances and interest for failure to pay or deposit; Sections 77 and 80 of the 2013 Act carry forward corresponding provisions. The Court relied on Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., Tika Ram v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Pratap v. State of Rajasthan in explaining that non-payment does not undo vesting after possession has been taken.
members.conclusion: Non-deposit in court does not itself lapse the acquisition. Where possession has been taken and compensation remains unpaid or undeposited, the compensation obligation is addressed through interest rather than lapse.

rule.if: transitional_acquisition_proceeding and award_made and possession_taken and compensation_unpaid_and_undeposited

predicates.transitional_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an acquisition begun under an earlier land-acquisition regime and is still pending when a replacement regime takes effect.
predicates.award_made: The acquiring authority made an award determining compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_unpaid_and_undeposited: Compensation remained unpaid and was not deposited with the court in circumstances requiring such a deposit.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition proceeding initiated under the earlier acquisition regime does not lapse merely because no award has been made by the commencement of the later regime, and compensation must be determined under the later regime.
material_facts: The acquisition was initiated under the earlier land acquisition law.
No award had been made under either the earlier or the later law.
The owner disputed whether possession had been taken and compensation had been paid, but the absence of an award was admitted.
members.legal_principle: Section 24(1)(a) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 provides that when proceedings were initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 but no award under Section 11 had been made, the proceedings may continue and compensation is determined under the 2013 Act. Section 24(2) addresses proceedings in which an award had been made at least five years before the 2013 Act commenced and possession had not been taken or compensation had not been paid; its lapse conditions did not apply where no award had been made. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings had not lapsed and could continue, but the award had to be made and compensation determined under the 2013 Act. The authorities were directed to make the award within six months and deposit or disburse the compensation within one month thereafter.

predicates.legacy_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a land acquisition initiated under an earlier acquisition regime.
predicates.no_award_at_transition: No award had been made when the later acquisition regime commenced.
predicates.proceedings_continue_with_compensation_u: The acquisition proceeds without lapsing, and compensation is determined under the later regime.

members.legal_issue: The deadline for making an award in a saved acquisition proceeding in which no award had been made under the repealed law is governed by the compensation provisions of the new law, provided the earlier deadline had not already expired when the new law commenced.
material_facts: Acquisition proceedings had been initiated under the earlier land acquisition law, but no award had been made before that law was repealed.
The earlier statutory period for making an award had not expired by the time the new law commenced.
members.legal_principle: Sections 24(1)(a), 25 and 114 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, read with Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, preserve earlier acquisition proceedings while applying the new law’s provisions relating to compensation. The words “all the provisions” and “relating to” include the award deadline in Section 25. The court followed Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal, (2020) 8 SCC 129, on the operation of Section 24 and the need to give effect to its provisions, and applied principles of limitation and statutory construction, including that a new limitation provision does not revive an already-barred right absent the required legislative intention.
members.conclusion: The new law’s award deadline applies to awards under Section 24(1)(a), and that period runs from the commencement of the new law. Proceedings that had already lapsed under the earlier law before or on the transition date are not revived.

predicates.saved_acquisition_without_prior_award: The acquisition was initiated under an earlier law and remained pending without an award when that law was repealed.
predicates.prior_award_deadline_unexpired_at_transi: The deadline for making an award under the earlier law had not expired when the new law commenced.
predicates.new_compensation_law_deadline_governs_aw: The deadline prescribed by the new law for making an award governs the saved acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for an acquisition that remains valid and for which no award has been made is to be determined under the later fair-compensation and resettlement legislation.
material_facts: The acquisition was upheld, but no award had been made while the litigation was pending.
The Court directed that compensation for the acquisition be determined under the later legislation governing fair compensation, rehabilitation, and resettlement.
The Court expressed no opinion on the parties’ entitlement to apportionment of compensation.
members.legal_principle: The Court expressly directed that compensation for the acquisition be determined in accordance with the 2013 Act; it did not decide how compensation should be apportioned among the parties.
members.conclusion: Compensation for the acquisition is to be determined under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, without deciding apportionment.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation arising from a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_upheld: The acquisition remains valid after judicial review.
predicates.award_not_made: No compensation award had been made before the court resolved the challenge.

members.legal_issue: A reservation of private land in a planning scheme lapses when the land remains unacquired and the authority does not commence acquisition within the period following a valid owner’s notice.
material_facts: Private land was reserved for public purposes in sanctioned development plans and remained unacquired for the initial statutory period.
The owners or persons interested served valid purchase notices on the relevant planning authorities.
Within the period following the notices, the land was not acquired and acquisition proceedings were not commenced by the legally required step.
members.legal_principle: Section 127 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 provides for lapse where land is not acquired within the initial period and, after a valid notice, is not acquired or made subject to commenced acquisition proceedings within the further notice period. Sections 126 and 127 must be read together. The Court applied Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Dr. Hakimwadi Tenants’ Association and the majority judgment in Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra (Girnar Traders II), which it held stated the correct law. The safeguard against indefinite reservation also accords with Article 300A of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The reservations were deemed to have lapsed, and the land was released from reservation and became available for development as otherwise permissible under the relevant plan.

predicates.planning_reservation_lapse_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a reservation of land in a planning scheme has lapsed.
predicates.land_reserved_for_public_purpose_in_sanc: A planning authority designated privately owned land for a public purpose in a sanctioned plan.
predicates.owner_served_valid_notice_after_initial_: An owner or person interested in the land served a valid notice after the initial period for acquiring the reserved land had elapsed.
predicates.no_acquisition_or_commencement_within_no: The authority neither acquired the land nor commenced acquisition proceedings during the period following the notice.

members.legal_issue: A reservation of land lapses when, after the prescribed long period of reservation and service of a valid release notice, the land is neither acquired nor the formal acquisition declaration is published within the notice period.
material_facts: The land remained reserved for a public purpose under the revised development plan for more than ten years without acquisition proceedings being completed.
The owners served a notice seeking release of the land from reservation, and the authority received it on 19 March 2002.

Within six months of the notice, an improvement committee recommended acquisition and the Chief Engineer sent communications concerning acquisition. The Municipal Corporation later authorized its Commissioner to apply for acquisition, but no application by the authorized Commissioner was produced.
No acquisition declaration was published within the six-month period, which expired on 18 September 2002. The State Government published its declaration on 20 November 2002.
members.legal_principle: Sections 126 and 127 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 must be read together. Under Section 127, after the specified period has elapsed and a valid notice is served, acquisition or commencement of the steps for acquisition must occur within the ensuing six months. The steps must be steps towards acquisition that can result in acquisition, not merely preliminary recommendations or requests for time. For acquisition through the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, publication of the declaration under Section 6 is the necessary commencement of acquisition proceedings; a request to the State Government to acquire the land is not enough. The provision safeguards owners against indefinite reservation and must be construed to give effect to that purpose. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Dr. Hakimwadi Tenants’ Association, 1988 (Supp.) SCC 55, and statutory-interpretation principles in Collector of Customs v. Digvijaysinhji Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd., AIR 1961 SC 1549; His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, AIR 1973 SC 1461; Narashimaha Murthy v. Susheelabai, (1996) 3 SCC 644; American Home Products Corporation v. Mac Laboratories Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1986 SC 137; Tirath Singh v. Bachittar Singh, AIR 1955 SC 830; Commissioner of Income Tax v. J.H. Gotla, AIR 1985 SC 1698; and State of Rajasthan v. Leela Jain, AIR 1965 SC 1296.
members.conclusion: The reservation was deemed to have lapsed, the land was released from reservation, and the owners could use it for development as otherwise permissible for adjacent land under the relevant plan.

rule.if: reserved_land_acquisition_case and prescribed_reservation_period_elapsed and owner_served_valid_release_notice and not land_acquired_within_notice_period and not formal_acquisition_declaration_published_within_notice_period

predicates.reserved_land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns land reserved for a public purpose in a planning scheme and the acquisition of that land.
predicates.prescribed_reservation_period_elapsed: The applicable period for acquiring the reserved land or commencing acquisition proceedings had elapsed.
predicates.owner_served_valid_release_notice: The landowner or another interested person served a valid notice seeking release of the land from reservation.
predicates.land_acquired_within_notice_period: The reserved land was acquired within the period following service of the release notice.
predicates.formal_acquisition_declaration_published: The government published the formal declaration commencing acquisition within the period following service of the release notice.

members.legal_issue: After a planning reservation has remained in force for the prescribed long period, a landowner must serve a further purchase notice before relying on the statutory process for lapse of the reservation.
material_facts: The development plan had been in force for more than ten years.
The landowner had served a purchase notice under the process applicable to a confirmed purchase notice, but had not served a further purchase notice after the plan had been in force for ten years.
The acquisition proposal was not followed by effective further steps to acquire the land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 126 and 127 require acquisition steps to be steps that can lead to acquisition; the mere making of an application or sending of a letter is insufficient. Under Section 127, after the prescribed period has elapsed, the owner must give notice and the authority must acquire the land or commence effective acquisition steps within the applicable period. The Court relied on the majority in Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra, (2007) 7 SCC 555, and Shrirampur Municipal Council v. Satyabhamabai Bhimaji Dawkher, (2013) 5 SCC 627. It read Hasmukhrai V. Mehta v. State of Maharashtra, (2015) 3 SCC 154, as having granted relief on its exceptional facts under Article 142, where no further notice had been served.
members.conclusion: In future cases, after ten years have elapsed from publication of the relevant plan, a second purchase notice must be served under Section 127. If the land is not acquired and effective acquisition steps are not commenced within one year after that notice, the reservation lapses. An application or other preliminary step that may not lead to acquisition is not, by itself, an effective step towards acquisition.

rule.if: planning_reservation_lapse_dispute and plan_in_force_for_prescribed_long_period and second_purchase_notice_served and (land_not_acquired or no_effective_acquisition_steps)

predicates.planning_reservation_lapse_dispute: The case concerns whether a planning reservation over land has lapsed.
predicates.plan_in_force_for_prescribed_long_period: The plan containing the reservation has remained in force for the period after which the owner may invoke the statutory lapse process.
predicates.second_purchase_notice_served: The owner served a further notice seeking acquisition or release of the land after that period elapsed.
predicates.land_not_acquired: The authority did not acquire the land within the period following the further notice.
predicates.no_effective_acquisition_steps: The authority did not commence steps that could lead to acquisition within the period following the further notice.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings lapse when the applicable statutory period for making an award expires without an award, after excluding time during which a court stayed the proceedings.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeded under a special law for granting house sites, to which the award-time-limit amendment applied.
Court orders stayed dispossession during parts of the proceedings.
Even after excluding the periods covered by stay orders, the prescribed time for making an award had expired, and no award had been made.
members.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires an award to be made within the prescribed period, with periods during which court proceedings are stayed excluded from the calculation; failure to make an award within the applicable period causes the acquisition proceedings to lapse. The Court held that Section 11-A applied to the special-law acquisition because the special law lacked its own machinery and depended on the general law for acquisition procedure.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings, including the notifications initiating and declaring the acquisition, lapsed.

predicates.special_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land under a special law.
predicates.award_time_limit_applies: The award-making time limit governs the proceeding.
predicates.award_not_made_within_applicable_period_: No award was made before the applicable time limit expired after periods covered by court stays were excluded.

members.legal_issue: Land acquisition proceedings lapse when no award is made within the prescribed period after publication of the acquisition declaration.
material_facts: A declaration in the land acquisition proceeding was published, starting the period for making an award.
The applicable two-year period expired without a final award; the officer had only submitted a proposed award, and prior approval had not been granted.
The court below had directed the authorities to proceed on the basis that an award had been made.
members.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires the Collector to make an award within two years from publication of the declaration. The requirement is mandatory, and if no award is made within that period the acquisition proceedings lapse, subject to the statutory proviso, which was not at issue.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings lapsed when the period expired without an award, and the direction to take further steps on the basis of the proposed award was set aside.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and declaration_published and award_period_expired and no_final_award_made

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.declaration_published: The acquisition declaration was published, starting the period for making an award.
predicates.award_period_expired: The prescribed period for making the award ended.
predicates.no_final_award_made: The land acquisition officer had not completed and issued a final award before the period ended.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may examine whether a decree is void for lack of inherent jurisdiction and refuse to execute it if it is a nullity.
material_facts: A party sought execution of a final eviction decree.
The opposing party objected that the decree was void because the court that passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction.
The objection arose after a retrospective amendment made the rent-control law applicable to the tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Although an executing court generally cannot go behind a decree or question its legality or correctness, it may consider an objection that the decree is a nullity for lack of inherent jurisdiction. The Court followed Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, [1955] 1 SCR 117, and Seth Hiralal Patni v. Sri Kali Nath, [1962] 2 SCR 747.
members.conclusion: The executing court was competent to examine whether the decree was a nullity and, if so, to refuse execution.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce a court decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_lacks_inherent_jurisdiction: The court that passed the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction over the case.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may examine a decree’s validity only when the objection is that the court which passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction, and may decline to enforce the decree if that defect renders it a nullity.
material_facts: The decree-holder sought to execute an ex-parte decree for possession.
The judgment-debtor objected to execution, arguing that the civil court lacked jurisdiction because the land was governed by the land reforms law.
The executing court found that the land had ceased to be agricultural land, and the Supreme Court held that the decree was not a nullity.
members.legal_principle: An executing court generally cannot go behind a decree or question its legality or correctness, but it may refuse execution if the decree is a nullity for want of the passing court’s inherent jurisdiction. The Court relied on Hira Lal Patni v Sri Kali Nath, Sunder Dass v Ram Prakash, Kiran Singh v Chaman Paswan, and Gaon Sabha v Nathi.
members.conclusion: An executing court may consider an objection based on inherent lack of jurisdiction, but the objection in this case failed because no such lack of jurisdiction was established.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is seeking to enforce a court decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_challenged_for_inherent_jurisdict: The objector argues that the court that passed the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction over the subject matter or parties.
predicates.inherent_jurisdiction_absent: The court that passed the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction, making the decree a nullity.

members.legal_issue: An objection that a court inherently lacked jurisdiction may be raised at any stage, including in proceedings to execute its decree.
material_facts: The defendant did not challenge the civil court's jurisdiction in the courts below.
The jurisdictional objection was considered in the Supreme Court appeal.
Counsel for the plaintiffs conceded that an inherent jurisdictional defect could be raised even in execution proceedings on the ground that the decree was a nullity.
members.legal_principle: A court's inherent lack of jurisdiction may be raised at any stage because a decree made without jurisdiction is a nullity; the Court cited no earlier cases for this proposition.
members.conclusion: An objection based on an inherent lack of jurisdiction may be raised at any stage, including in execution proceedings.

predicates.appeal_challenges_decree_of_civil_court: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decree made by a civil court.
predicates.court_inherently_lacked_jurisdiction: The civil court lacked jurisdiction over the kind of suit it entertained.
predicates.jurisdiction_objection_was_not_raised_ea: The jurisdictional objection was not raised in the lower courts.

members.legal_issue: A decree that is a nullity because it was made without jurisdiction may be challenged in execution proceedings.
material_facts: The claimants sought to execute the High Court's later decree granting amended statutory benefits.
The State objected in the execution proceedings that the later decree had been made without jurisdiction and was not enforceable.
The executing court rejected the objection, and the High Court dismissed the State's challenge to that decision.
members.legal_principle: A decree made without jurisdiction is a nullity, does not acquire finality, and may be challenged at any stage, including before the executing court. The Court relied on Union of India v. Swaran Singh and Sarup Singh v. Union of India, and applied the rule that the executing court may consider a plea that the decree it is asked to enforce is a nullity.
members.conclusion: The State could raise the decree's nullity in the execution proceedings; the later decree was not enforceable, and the execution petition seeking its enforcement had to be dismissed.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party asks a court to enforce a decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_sought_to_be_executed_was_made_wi: The decree sought to be enforced was made by a court that lacked jurisdiction to grant the relief.

members.legal_issue: A decree awarding benefits beyond the court’s jurisdiction may be challenged as a nullity in execution even after the decree has become final.
material_facts: The governing acquisition statute did not authorize the additional benefits awarded under the amended central law in this case.
The court nevertheless included those benefits in its order.
The appellant objected to their enforcement in execution under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The lower courts rejected the objection on the ground that the decree had become final.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court may consider whether a decree is a nullity. Sushil Kumar Mehta v. Gobind Ram Bohra and Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam establish that a decree made without inherent jurisdiction may be challenged at execution; Hiralal Moolchand Doshi v. Barotraman Lal Ranchhoddas distinguishes an erroneous decree from one that is ultra vires the court’s authority. Section 144 permits restitution where appropriate.
members.conclusion: The additional-benefit award was without jurisdiction and could be challenged in execution; the objection was to be determined under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, with restitution considered under Section 144 if warranted.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is seeking to enforce or resist enforcement of a decree in execution.
predicates.decree_awards_relief_beyond_court_jurisd: The decree grants relief the court lacked jurisdiction or authority to grant.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may treat a compensation order as a nullity if the court that made it lacked inherent jurisdiction, but it may not otherwise go behind a valid decree.
material_facts: The original compensation judgments had become final, and no appeal was brought against them in the Supreme Court.
After the amendments, claimants sought enhanced solatium and interest through later proceedings, including applications invoking powers to correct or supplement judgments.

The later orders granting the enhanced benefits were made when the underlying awards did not qualify under the transitional provisions, or purported to make substantive changes to final judgments through correction powers.
The executing court refused to enforce the enhanced-benefit orders as nullities, and the High Court upheld that refusal.
members.legal_principle: An executing court ordinarily cannot go behind a decree or grant relief not contained in it, as stated in State of Punjab v. Krishan Dayal Sharma, AIR 1990 SC 2177. However, a decree made without inherent jurisdiction is non est and may be challenged even in execution or collateral proceedings; the defect cannot be cured by consent or waiver. The Court relied on Union of India v. Sube Ram (1997) 9 SCC 69, Amrit Bhikaji Kale v. Kashinath Janardhan Trade (1983) 3 SCC 437, Balvant N. Viswamitra v. Yadav Sadashiv Mule (2004) 8 SCC 706, and Chiranjilal Shrilal Goenka v. Jasjit Singh (1993) 2 SCC 507. It also applied sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and Union of India v. Swaran Singh (1996) 5 SCC 501 and Dwaraka Das v. State of M.P. (1999) 3 SCC 500, holding that those provisions do not permit substantive alteration of a final judgment or decree.
members.conclusion: The executing court and the High Court were justified in treating the orders granting enhanced benefits as without jurisdiction and nullities. Although an executing court ordinarily cannot go behind a decree, a decree or order made without inherent jurisdiction may be challenged at the execution stage.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court is being asked to enforce a judgment or decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.final_compensation_decree: The compensation judgment or decree had become final before the later order was made.
predicates.later_enhancement_order_lacked_inherent_: A later court order granted substantive enhanced compensation benefits even though the underlying case did not qualify for them, or the court used correction powers to alter a final judgment on its merits.

members.legal_issue: An order made without jurisdiction is a nullity that may be challenged when it is sought to be enforced, including during execution or in collateral proceedings, and consent or waiver does not cure the jurisdictional defect.
material_facts: The High Court directed its Court Receiver to sell the property after the recovery proceeding had transferred to the specialist tribunal.
The receiver conducted the sale and a sale certificate was issued to the bank.
The respondent challenged the sale before the tribunal, contending that the former court lacked authority to direct it.
members.legal_principle: Sushil Kumar Mehta v. Gobind Ram Bohra, relying on Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, states that a decree made without jurisdiction is a nullity and may be challenged whenever and wherever it is enforced or relied upon, even at execution or in collateral proceedings; consent cannot cure the defect. The Court also relied on Ledgard v. Bull and Barton v. Fincham for the principle that consent or agreement cannot validate action inconsistent with law.
members.conclusion: The direction to sell and the subsequent sale proceedings were void ab initio, and the challenge was not defeated by the passage of time or by the respondent's earlier conduct.

predicates.execution_or_collateral_challenge: A party challenges a decision when it is being enforced or relied upon in execution or in a collateral proceeding.
predicates.decision_made_without_jurisdiction: The decision was made by a court that lacked authority over the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: An eviction decree passed by a court inherently lacking subject-matter jurisdiction is void and may be challenged when execution is sought.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an ex parte eviction decree from a civil court.
The tenant objected to execution on the ground that the rent-control regime gave the Controller exclusive jurisdiction over eviction.
The civil court had no inherent jurisdiction to entertain the eviction suit.
members.legal_principle: A decree passed without inherent jurisdiction over the subject matter is coram non judice and non est; its invalidity may be raised whenever it is enforced or relied upon, including in execution or collateral proceedings. The Court relied on Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, Ferozi Lal Jain v. Man Mal, Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass, Smt. Kaushalya Devi v. K.L. Bansal, Chandrika Misir v. Bhaiya Lal, and Choudari Rama v. Qureshi Bee. It distinguished defects in the exercise of jurisdiction, such as certain territorial or pecuniary defects, from a defect going to the court’s inherent authority.
members.conclusion: The decree was a nullity and the tenant could challenge it at the execution stage.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The proceeding is one in which enforcement of a decree is sought.
predicates.eviction_decree_passed_by_civil_court: A civil court passed a decree ordering eviction.
predicates.civil_court_lacked_inherent_subject_matt: The civil court lacked authority over the subject matter of the eviction suit, rather than merely making an error while exercising jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: An ejectment decree passed by a civil court lacking jurisdiction over a tenancy protected by rent-control law is a nullity that may be challenged in execution.
material_facts: The premises were let for commercial use and were covered by rent-control law.
The relevant rent-control scheme reserved eviction proceedings to the rent authority and barred civil-court jurisdiction over eviction of protected tenants.
The civil court passed an ejectment decree on the understanding that the commercial tenancy was not heritable.
The judgment-debtors challenged the decree’s executability in execution proceedings, relying on the rule that the commercial tenancy was heritable.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 14 and 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, eviction of a tenant from covered premises could be ordered only by the rent authority, and the civil court’s jurisdiction was barred. Under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court may entertain an objection that a decree is a nullity for want of inherent jurisdiction. Sushil Kumar Mehta v. Govind Ram Bohra holds that such a defect goes to the court’s authority, is not cured by a prior determination of jurisdiction, and may be raised when enforcement is sought, including in execution. Urban Improvement Trust v. Gokul Narain followed that principle. Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar established that the commercial tenancy was heritable; that interpretation applied to the earlier decree as well.
members.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to pass the ejectment decree, so the decree was a nullity and could not be executed; the judgment-debtors could raise that objection in execution.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and rent_law_covers_tenancy and rent_regime_reserves_eviction_to_special_authority and civil_court_issued_ejectment_decree and judgment_debtor_challenged_decree_in_execution

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is an execution proceeding seeking enforcement of an ejectment decree.
predicates.rent_law_covers_tenancy: The premises and tenancy are covered by a rent-control legal regime.
predicates.rent_regime_reserves_eviction_to_special: The governing rent-control regime assigns eviction decisions to a special authority and excludes civil-court jurisdiction over those matters.
predicates.civil_court_issued_ejectment_decree: A civil court issued a decree ordering the tenant’s eviction.
predicates.judgment_debtor_challenged_decree_in_exe: The judgment-debtor objected during execution that the ejectment decree could not be enforced.

members.legal_issue: A decree or award directing delivery of acquired land outside the matters authorized for determination in acquisition proceedings may be challenged as a nullity during execution.
material_facts: The civil court on reference confirmed the acquisition officer’s award, subject to correcting certain deductions.
The award included a direction for allotment of land in lieu of compensation, and the landowners sought delivery of that land in execution.
The acquiring authority objected in execution that the allotment was beyond the officer’s jurisdiction; the High Court held that the objection could not be raised at that stage.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 18 and 26(2), the reference court determines the referred statutory questions, and its award is a decree only to the extent of matters properly determined under the acquisition law. A decree cannot make executable a direction that the acquisition officer lacked jurisdiction to give. The invalidity or nullity of such a decree may be raised during execution. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The allotment direction was a nullity and could be challenged in execution. The execution proceedings seeking delivery of land under that direction were invalid, void and inexecutable.

predicates.land_acquisition_execution_proceeding: A party is seeking execution of a decree or award arising from land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.decree_directs_delivery_of_acquired_land: The decree or award directs delivery of acquired land as an allotment in lieu of compensation.

members.legal_issue: A decree is a nullity for execution purposes only when it was passed by a court lacking inherent jurisdiction, not merely because the court made an error.
material_facts: An eviction decree was passed by a court in a suit brought under rent-control legislation.
The tenant challenged the decree’s executability in execution, alleging that the court had not established the statutory grounds for eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court generally must execute the decree and cannot go behind it unless it is a nullity. A decree is a nullity when the court lacked inherent jurisdiction, rather than when the decree is merely erroneous or voidable.
members.conclusion: The decree was not a nullity merely because of an alleged error in passing it; a decree is a nullity only if it is beyond the powers of the court that passed it.

predicates.execution_challenge: A judgment-debtor challenged the decree’s validity or executability in execution proceedings.
predicates.court_had_inherent_jurisdiction: The court that passed the decree had inherent authority to decide the kind of dispute before it.
predicates.decree_alleged_erroneous: The judgment-debtor alleged that the court made an error in passing the decree.

members.legal_issue: A decree passed by a court with jurisdiction is not a nullity merely because of an alleged defect in notice or procedure, and its validity cannot be challenged collaterally in execution unless the court lacked inherent jurisdiction.
material_facts: A landlord brought a possession suit against the deceased tenant’s heirs for arrears of rent.
The landlord tried to identify and notify the heirs, sent notices by post, and affixed a notice at the premises after other service attempts did not provide the heirs’ details.
An advocate appeared for the defendants, partly cross-examined the landlord’s witness, and later withdrew after stating that he had no instructions.
The trial court had jurisdiction over the subject matter and entered a possession decree; the decree was challenged in execution as void because of alleged defects in notice and the parties named.
members.legal_principle: A decree is a nullity when the court that passed it lacked inherent jurisdiction; a mere error, wrong exercise of jurisdiction, or procedural irregularity does not make it void. An executing court ordinarily cannot go behind the decree, and a jurisdictional defect must be patent for the executing court to treat the decree as a nullity. The Court relied on Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, Seth Hiralal Patni v. Sri Kali Nath, Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v. Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, Rafique Bibi v. Sayed Waliuddin, Malkarjun Bin Shidramappa Pasare v. Narhari Bin Shivappa, Ittavira Mathai v. Varkey Varkey, and Bhawarlal v. Universal Heavy Mechanical Lifting Enterprises.
members.conclusion: The decree was not void or inexecutable. Any challenge to alleged errors or procedural irregularities had to be pursued in appropriate proceedings to set it aside, rather than by a collateral challenge in execution.

predicates.execution_or_collateral_challenge: A person challenges the decree in execution or in another proceeding collateral to the proceeding in which it was entered.
predicates.decree_passed_by_competent_court: The court that entered the decree had jurisdiction over the subject matter of the case.
predicates.alleged_defect_is_nonjurisdictional: The challenge concerns an error or procedural defect rather than a patent lack of the court’s inherent jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A decree entered in a suit barred by limitation is not a nullity when the court had jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties.
material_facts: The appellant argued that an earlier decree on a hypothecation bond was a nullity because the suit had been brought out of time.
The court that entered the earlier decree had jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties.
The limitation objection was not established as a basis for treating that decree as void.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a court must take notice of limitation even if it is not pleaded. As explained in Maqbul Ahmad v. Onkar Pratap Narain Singh, that duty does not mean that failure to enforce limitation deprives the court of jurisdiction. A court with jurisdiction may decide an issue wrongly, and the resulting error of law must be corrected through the procedures provided by the Civil Procedure Code; an unchallenged erroneous decree remains effective.
members.conclusion: Even if the earlier suit was barred by limitation, the decree was not a nullity and could not be ignored in later litigation; the error had to be corrected through an appeal against that decree.

rule.if: later_proceeding_challenges_prior_decree and court_had_subject_matter_jurisdiction and court_had_jurisdiction_over_parties and prior_decree_entered_despite_limitation_bar

predicates.later_proceeding_challenges_prior_decree: The proceeding seeks to avoid or disregard a decree entered in an earlier case.
predicates.court_had_subject_matter_jurisdiction: The court that entered the earlier decree had authority over the kind of dispute before it.
predicates.court_had_jurisdiction_over_parties: The court that entered the earlier decree had authority over the parties to that case.
predicates.prior_decree_entered_despite_limitation_: The court entered the earlier decree even though the suit was barred by limitation.
