members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot entertain an objection that a decree was passed without territorial jurisdiction.
material_facts: A partition decree was passed by a trial court and was later brought before that court for execution.
The judgment-debtor objected under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure that the decree was invalid because the trial court lacked territorial jurisdiction.
The executing court declined to consider the objection, but the High Court directed it to do so.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires an objection to the place of suing to be raised at the earliest opportunity in the court of first instance and permits it to be entertained by an appellate or revisional court only if there has been a consequent failure of justice. Territorial jurisdiction is distinct from inherent jurisdiction over the subject matter. Under Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, an executing court cannot go behind a decree; an objection that requires investigation of facts cannot be raised in execution, and territorial-jurisdiction objections are not an exception to that rule. Kiran Singh v Chaman Paswan, Hiralal v Kalinath, Harshad Chiman Lal Modi v DLF Universal Ltd., Hasham Abbas Sayyad v Usman Abbas Sayyad, and Mantoo Sarkar v Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. support the distinction between territorial jurisdiction and jurisdiction over the subject matter.
members.conclusion: The objection to territorial jurisdiction could not be decided in execution, and the executing court was required to execute the decree as it stood.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The court is dealing with proceedings to execute an existing decree.
predicates.objection_based_on_territorial_jurisdict: A party objects that the court which passed the decree lacked territorial authority to hear the suit.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot entertain a challenge to a decree’s jurisdiction when deciding the challenge requires inquiry into facts not apparent on the face of the record.
material_facts: The decree for ejectment had been affirmed on appeal and in further proceedings, and the jurisdictional objection was first raised when execution was sought.
The alleged lack of jurisdiction depended on interpreting the lease and determining the use of the land, matters requiring examination beyond the face of the record.
members.legal_principle: An executing court must take a decree according to its tenor and cannot go behind it; an erroneous decree remains binding until set aside in an appropriate proceeding. A decree that is a nullity, or that was made by a court lacking inherent jurisdiction, may be challenged in execution when the defect appears on the face of the record. If deciding the objection requires examining matters raised or capable of being raised at trial, the executing court cannot entertain it. The Court referred to Jnanendra Mohan Bhaduri v. Rabindra Nath Chakravarti for a jurisdictional defect apparent on the record. It also explained that sections 5(8) and 6 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, made the court’s jurisdiction depend on the premises and their use; Mst. Subhadra v. Narasaji Chenaji Marwadi was cited concerning the date for determining agricultural use. The Court noted the distinction for objections apparent on the record, subject to the stated exceptions concerning territorial jurisdiction and section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act.
members.conclusion: The executing court could not investigate those facts to decide whether the decree was without jurisdiction, and the jurisdictional objection had to be rejected in execution.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and jurisdiction_objection_requires_fact_inquiry and not jurisdictional_defect_apparent_on_record and decree_not_set_aside

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is asking a court to enforce an existing decree.
predicates.jurisdiction_objection_requires_fact_inq: The party's claim that the decree was made without jurisdiction can be resolved only by examining facts or matters beyond the face of the record.
predicates.jurisdictional_defect_apparent_on_record: The alleged jurisdictional defect is evident from the face of the record.
predicates.decree_not_set_aside: The decree has not been set aside in an appropriate proceeding.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may not treat a decree as a nullity for want of jurisdiction unless the court’s lack of inherent jurisdiction is apparent from the record.
material_facts: The decree was made by a court whose jurisdiction to decide the eviction suit was not disputed.
The judgment debtors did not claim that the eviction ground was unavailable under either the earlier or successor rent-control law.
The asserted jurisdictional defect depended on the court’s failure to provide an opportunity to deposit rent, rather than an absence of jurisdiction apparent from the decree or record.
members.legal_principle: Under the rule in Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v. Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, an objection to a decree for inherent lack of jurisdiction may be raised in execution when the defect appears on the face of the record; if deciding the objection requires examining matters raised or that could have been raised at trial, the executing court cannot entertain it. A decree involving illegality or procedural irregularity is distinct from a decree passed without jurisdiction and must be challenged in appropriate proceedings. The terms “void” and “nullity” are relative to the remedy and proceedings in which relief is sought; a decree of a competent court cannot be defeated by collateral attack.
members.conclusion: The asserted defect did not establish that the decree was without jurisdiction or a nullity. The executing court could not go behind the decree on that basis, and the decree remained enforceable.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and decree_exists and not patent_inherent_jurisdictional_defect

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is asking a court to enforce an existing decree.
predicates.decree_exists: A court has issued a decree in the case.
predicates.patent_inherent_jurisdictional_defect: The record itself shows that the court which issued the decree lacked inherent jurisdiction to do so.
predicates.executing_court_must_enforce_decree: The executing court must enforce the decree rather than invalidate it on a collateral challenge.

members.legal_issue: An executing court cannot decide an objection to a decree that requires determination of the merits of the underlying dispute.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor argued that property relied on to establish the trial court's territorial jurisdiction did not belong to the common ancestor.
Deciding that contention would require consideration of the merits of the property dispute.
A first appeal challenging the decree, in which jurisdiction had also been raised, was pending.
members.legal_principle: Under Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, an executing court must take the decree according to its tenor and cannot go behind it; an objection requiring investigation of facts cannot be decided in execution. The Court stated that the property contention was a matter of merits for the appropriate court in the first appeal.
members.conclusion: The property-related contention was a matter of merits and, if pursued, had to be raised in the first appeal rather than decided by the executing court.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The court is dealing with proceedings to execute an existing decree.
predicates.objection_requires_determination_of_unde: Resolving the objection requires deciding a disputed matter that formed part of the merits of the underlying case.

members.legal_issue: A sale made wholly without jurisdiction is a nullity that may be challenged collaterally and is not barred by the rule requiring execution disputes to be resolved in execution proceedings.
material_facts: A court ordered an execution sale of immovable property despite lacking jurisdiction to do so.
The judgment-debtor's successor later brought a suit seeking a declaration concerning the property and alleging that the sale was void.
The challenge concerned a sale alleged to be wholly without jurisdiction, rather than an irregular or voidable sale.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle stated in Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan, a decree or order made without jurisdiction is a nullity whose invalidity may be raised whenever it is relied upon, including in execution or collateral proceedings. A wholly jurisdictionless sale is distinct from an irregular or voidable sale, which subsists unless set aside. The Court held that the alternative objection under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not survive once the sale was found to be a nullity.
members.conclusion: The sale was non-existent in law and did not need to be set aside; its invalidity could be raised in collateral proceedings, and the suit was not barred by Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.collateral_challenge_to_execution_sale: A person challenged an execution sale in proceedings other than an application to set aside an irregular or voidable sale within the execution process.
predicates.sale_wholly_without_jurisdiction: The court ordering the sale had no jurisdiction to order it.
predicates.sale_is_nullity_open_to_collateral_chall: The sale is a nullity that need not first be set aside and may be challenged collaterally.

members.legal_issue: Occupants affected by a decree made in a suit that the civil court lacked jurisdiction to entertain may challenge the decree’s nullity to defend their possession.
material_facts: The later possession suit was incompetent because the required permission to bring it had not been obtained, and the civil court lacked jurisdiction over the matter assigned to the competent authority.
The decree was made against occupants who were entitled to rely on the statutory protection governing eviction from slum areas.
members.legal_principle: A decree made by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity. The Court held that the affected co-defendants could set up that nullity in order to defend their possession by invoking the protections of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act.
members.conclusion: The decree was non-est, and the surviving occupants could challenge its nullity to defend and protect their possession.

predicates.possession_defense_against_civil_court_d: An occupant relies on a defense in a possession dispute against a civil-court decree.
predicates.decree_made_without_jurisdiction: The civil court made the decree in a matter over which it lacked jurisdiction.
predicates.occupant_affected_by_decree: The decree affects the occupant’s possession or claimed right to remain in possession.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may consider relevant material to decide whether a rent-control eviction decree is a nullity for want of the required statutory basis.
material_facts: The tenant objected to execution on the ground that the eviction decree was a nullity because the tribunal had not independently satisfied itself about the landlord’s bona fide requirement.
The landlord relied on the evidence and documents that had been before the tribunal before the compromise.
The Court rejected the contention that consideration of the nullity objection would require an impermissibly elaborate enquiry.
members.legal_principle: A party may raise before the executing court the objection that a decree is void and therefore inexecutable. In deciding that objection, the executing court may consider relevant material bearing on whether the tribunal had the satisfaction required for an eviction order; the possibility that this requires examining the record does not prevent it from doing so.
members.conclusion: The executing court may adjudicate a plea that an eviction decree is void and consider relevant material to determine whether the tribunal’s required satisfaction existed.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce an eviction decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_challenged_as_statutory_nullity: The opposing party claimed that the eviction decree was void because a required statutory basis for eviction was absent.
predicates.relevant_record_material_exists: Material in the record bears on whether the tribunal considered or was satisfied about the asserted ground for eviction.

members.legal_issue: An executing court deciding whether a decree is a nullity must examine the record on which the decree was based and may not permit the parties to introduce fresh evidence on that objection.
material_facts: The tenant objected in execution that the compromise eviction decree was a nullity.
The executing court allowed the tenant to produce documentary evidence to support the objection.
members.legal_principle: An executing court may examine the decree and the original record to determine whether material supported the court’s authority to pass it, but it cannot sit as an appellate court or permit fresh evidence to relitigate the issue. This principle was applied consistently with the Court’s discussion of Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and its reliance on Nagindass v. Dalpatram.
members.conclusion: Allowing the tenant to lead fresh evidence in execution was unwarranted; the executing court had to assess nullity from the record on which the decree was based.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A court was asked to enforce a decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.decree_challenged_as_nullity: The judgment-debtor contended in execution that the decree was a nullity.
predicates.party_seeks_fresh_evidence: A party sought permission to introduce evidence that was not part of the record on which the decree was based.

members.legal_issue: An invalid declaration of acquisition may be treated as ineffective and replaced by a fresh declaration without withdrawing from the acquisition.
material_facts: The earlier declaration stated that the land was required for a public purpose at the expense of a housing society.
The compensation was not to be paid wholly or partly from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority, so the earlier declaration was invalid.
The Government cancelled the earlier declaration because it was invalid, did not intend to withdraw from the acquisition, and issued a fresh declaration for the same public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a declaration for a public purpose could be made only if compensation was to be paid wholly or partly out of public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority. A declaration made without that authority was invalid and of no effect: Shyam Behari v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Section 48 did not prevent the Government from treating such an invalid declaration as ineffective and issuing an effective replacement; the Court distinguished the unaddressed question of cancelling a lawful and valid declaration without withdrawing from the acquisition.
members.conclusion: The Government could treat the invalid declaration as ineffective and issue a fresh declaration; section 48 did not preclude this, and the cancellation recognized the earlier declaration’s invalidity rather than withdrawing from the acquisition.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_appeal and earlier_declaration_invalid and government_cancels_as_invalid and government_continues_acquisition

predicates.acquisition_challenge_appeal: An appeal challenges steps taken to acquire land.
predicates.earlier_declaration_invalid: The earlier declaration was made without the required basis for payment of compensation from public revenues or a qualifying public fund.
predicates.government_cancels_as_invalid: The government cancels the earlier declaration in recognition that it was invalid.
predicates.government_continues_acquisition: The government does not intend to withdraw from the acquisition and proceeds with the same acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Issuing an invalid declaration does not exhaust the Government’s power to issue a valid declaration for the acquisition.
material_facts: The Government’s first declaration was invalid because the compensation was to be paid at the expense of a housing society rather than from a qualifying public source.
The Government later issued a fresh declaration for the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: A declaration made without the authority required by the proviso to section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is invalid and does not effectively exercise the Government’s power under that section. The Court relied on Shyam Behari v. State of Madhya Pradesh in holding the earlier declaration invalid.
members.conclusion: The first declaration did not effectively exercise the Government’s power, so the Government could issue a fresh declaration.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_appeal: An appeal challenges steps taken to acquire land.
predicates.earlier_declaration_invalid: The earlier declaration was made without the required basis for payment of compensation from public revenues or a qualifying public fund.
predicates.government_issues_replacement_declaratio: The government issues a later declaration for the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Cancelling an invalid acquisition declaration recognizes its invalidity rather than withdrawing from the acquisition, and permits a replacement declaration for the same land under the existing preliminary notification.
material_facts: A preliminary notification covered the land proposed for acquisition.
The Government considered its first declaration of the need to acquire the land invalid, cancelled it, and issued a replacement declaration covering the same land.
The cancellation and replacement occurred while the acquisition process concerning that land remained under consideration.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 6, and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, an invalid declaration under section 6 may be treated as ineffective and replaced by a fresh declaration. Cancelling the invalid declaration merely recognizes its invalidity, and section 48 does not preclude that course. The Court applied Girdharilal Amratlal Shodan v. State of Gujarat and distinguished State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, which concerned successive declarations for different portions of land.
members.conclusion: Cancellation of the first declaration did not amount to withdrawal from acquisition or exhaust the preliminary notification; the Government could issue a fresh declaration for the same land without issuing a fresh preliminary notification.

rule.if: land_acquisition_case and preliminary_notification_covers_land and first_declaration_is_invalid and replacement_declaration_covers_same_land

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.preliminary_notification_covers_land: An earlier preliminary notification identifies the locality containing the land proposed for acquisition.
predicates.first_declaration_is_invalid: The Government treats the first declaration identifying the land needed for acquisition as invalid.
predicates.replacement_declaration_covers_same_land: The Government issues a replacement declaration identifying the same land.

members.legal_issue: A withdrawal of an invalid or ineffective acquisition declaration does not exhaust the notification that preceded it.
material_facts: The lands were covered by an acquisition notification followed by a declaration.
The declaration was challenged because the affected landowners had not been heard on their objections.
The government withdrew the declaration after the procedural illegality was raised, and the landowners were then heard before a fresh declaration was issued.
members.legal_principle: A valid declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 exhausts the scope of the Section 4 notification. That rule does not apply where the declaration is invalid, ineffective or infructuous. There is no distinction between a declaration held invalid by a court and one withdrawn by the government after an obvious illegality is pointed out. The Court followed Girdhari Lal Amrit Lal v. State, State v. Haider Bux and State v. Bhogilal Keshavlal; distinguished State v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma; and disapproved Ajit Singh v. State.
members.conclusion: The withdrawal did not make the original acquisition notification ineffective or infructuous; the notification could support a fresh declaration.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land under a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.court_found_declaration_invalid: A court determined that the acquisition declaration was invalid or ineffective.
predicates.government_withdrew_declaration_after_ob: The government withdrew the acquisition declaration after an obvious illegality in it was pointed out.

members.legal_issue: A fresh declaration may be issued after an earlier invalid declaration, and the preliminary acquisition notice remains available when the earlier declaration did not effectively exercise the acquisition power.
material_facts: The first declaration provided that the entire acquisition expense would be borne by a cooperative housing society, although the governing law did not permit acquisition for a public purpose on that basis.
The government cancelled that declaration and later issued a fresh declaration providing for acquisition at public expense for the housing scheme.
The preliminary notice had not fulfilled its purpose because the first declaration was invalid.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read with the proviso to Section 6, compensation for acquisition for a public purpose must be payable wholly or partly from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority; the government cannot acquire land for a public purpose where compensation is to be paid entirely by a company. Valjibhai Muljibhai Soneji v. State of Bombay and Girdharilal Amratlal Shodan v. State of Gujarat establish that an invalid declaration may be treated as ineffective and followed by a fresh declaration, and that cancellation recognizing its invalidity does not itself amount to withdrawal from the acquisition. Section 48 does not preclude a fresh declaration in those circumstances. State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, which addresses successive declarations following an effective declaration, does not bar a fresh declaration following an invalid one.
members.conclusion: The earlier declaration was invalid and had no effect; the preliminary notice remained in force, and the government could issue a fresh declaration correcting the funding defect. The successive-declaration rule in State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma did not prevent this because the first declaration was invalid.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and first_declaration_invalid_for_private_funding and preliminary_notice_purpose_unfulfilled and fresh_declaration_provides_public_funding

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns the acquisition of land by the government.
predicates.first_declaration_invalid_for_private_fu: The government first declared an acquisition for a public purpose with the entire compensation payable by a private body.
predicates.preliminary_notice_purpose_unfulfilled: The preliminary notice had not fulfilled its purpose because the first declaration was invalid.
predicates.fresh_declaration_provides_public_fundin: The government later issued a fresh declaration providing for acquisition at public expense.

members.legal_issue: A fresh acquisition declaration may be issued after an invalid same-day declaration if the statutory period for making the declaration remains open.
material_facts: The declaration published on the same day as the preliminary notification was invalid.
The Court stated that a fresh declaration could be issued if the statutory period remained available.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that a fresh declaration under Section 6 could be issued within the period contemplated by the proviso to Section 6(1), read with its first Explanation, if the acquiring authority chose to do so.
members.conclusion: The acquiring authority remained free to issue a fresh declaration within the period allowed by the applicable statutory time limit.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a proposed acquisition of land requiring an acquisition declaration.
predicates.prior_declaration_invalid: An earlier acquisition declaration in the proceeding was held invalid.
predicates.statutory_declaration_period_open: The statutory period for making a valid acquisition declaration has not expired.

members.legal_issue: A fresh declaration cannot be made after the statutory time limit has expired, even when an earlier timely declaration has been quashed and a court has directed renewed acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The land was covered by a notification published under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, on 8 September 1982.
A declaration under Section 6 was made within three years, but it was later quashed because of non-compliance with the applicable mandatory procedure.
The three-year period had expired before the High Court directed a fresh enquiry and allowed a further declaration to be issued.
The High Court also directed that an award be passed after any fresh declaration.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, barred a declaration concerning land covered by the relevant Section 4(1) notification after three years from publication. Explanation 1 excluded from the computation only a period during which action or proceedings pursuant to that notification were stayed by a court. The judgment cites no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not authorize a fresh declaration after the three-year period had expired. Its directions for a fresh Section 5A enquiry, a further declaration, and a subsequent award were set aside.

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning proceedings to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.earlier_declaration_quashed: A declaration concerning the land was made but was later set aside.
predicates.declaration_window_expired_before_fresh_: The applicable time window for making a declaration had expired before a fresh declaration could be made.

members.legal_issue: Quashing an acquisition declaration does not restart or extend the statutory period for issuing a fresh declaration.
material_facts: A notification identifying land for acquisition was published, and an initial declaration was issued within the applicable statutory period.
The initial declaration was quashed by a court.
A subsequent declaration was issued after the applicable period measured from publication of the original notification, and the State contended that time should run afresh from the court's order.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its first proviso, imposes a peremptory time limit measured from publication of the notification under Section 4(1); Explanation 1 excludes only a period during which relevant action or proceedings are stayed by a court. The provision is plain and unambiguous, and a court cannot supply a casus omissus or read in a new period after a declaration is quashed. Sections 11 and 23 reinforce the importance of the original notification date because valuation and compensation are tied to that date. A.S. Naidu and Oxford English School were affirmed; N. Narasimhaiah and D.C. Nanjudaiah were overruled. Pooranmal was distinguishable because it concerned a different statutory scheme and waiver. The Court also relied on the principles of statutory construction discussed in Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama, Dr. R. Venkatchalam, and Rishabh Agro Industries.
members.conclusion: A fresh declaration must be made within the period applicable to the original notification, allowing only the exclusion expressly provided for periods when relevant action or proceedings are stayed by a court. A declaration issued after that period is invalid; the subsequent declarations in the appeals were quashed.

predicates.land_acquisition_declaration_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a declaration that land is required for acquisition for a public purpose or a company.
predicates.earlier_declaration_quashed: A court quashed an earlier declaration concerning land covered by the same acquisition notification.
predicates.fresh_declaration_after_original_limit: A later declaration was made after the applicable period measured from publication of the original acquisition notification, accounting for any period that must be excluded because relevant action or proceedings were stayed by a court.
predicates.fresh_declaration_is_invalid: The later declaration is invalid because it was made after the applicable period for the original acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: Quashing an acquisition declaration does not restart the statutory period for issuing a replacement declaration.
material_facts: A land-acquisition notification was published before the 1984 amendment, so the applicable statutory period was three years from publication of that notification.
An initial declaration was made within that period but was later quashed.
A replacement declaration was issued after the applicable period had expired, and the High Court upheld it by applying the view that the period ran from receipt of the court’s order.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its first proviso and Explanation 1, a declaration must be made within the prescribed period calculated from publication of the Section 4(1) notification, excluding only a period during which the relevant action or proceeding was stayed by a court. The time limit is peremptory; a court cannot add a new period triggered by quashing a declaration or supply a casus omissus where the statutory language is plain. Sections 11 and 23 link valuation and compensation to the date of the Section 4(1) notification, supporting the purpose of the time limit. A.S. Naidu and Oxford English School were affirmed; N. Narasimhaiah and D.C. Nanjudaiah were overruled. The Court distinguished Pooran Mal and relied on principles of statutory construction reflected in R. Venkatchalam, Rishabh Agro Industries, Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama, Luke v. I.R.C., and Artemiou v. Procopiou.
members.conclusion: The replacement declaration was invalid because quashing the initial declaration did not provide a fresh period or otherwise extend the deadline running from the original notification.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose or a company.
predicates.prior_declaration_quashed: A court quashed an earlier declaration concerning the land.
predicates.replacement_declaration_outside_original: The replacement declaration was made after the applicable deadline calculated from the original acquisition notification, with any legally excluded stay period left out.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition declaration set aside after the time for making a declaration on the original acquisition notification has passed cannot be replaced by a fresh declaration relying on that notification.
material_facts: The Government issued an initial acquisition notification and later made a declaration under it.
The Court set aside the declaration for failure to comply with the hearing requirement.
By the time the Court considered the matter, the State could not rely on the original notification to make a fresh declaration.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the Constitution Bench ruling in Padma Sundara Rao (Dead) v. State of Tamil Nadu concerning the time limit for making a declaration following an acquisition notification under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
members.conclusion: The State could not rely on the original notification to issue a fresh acquisition declaration, although it remained free to initiate fresh acquisition proceedings in accordance with law.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The State undertook proceedings to acquire privately held property compulsorily.
predicates.acquisition_declaration_set_aside: A court set aside the declaration made in the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.declaration_period_for_original_notice_e: The time allowed for making a declaration based on the original acquisition notice had passed.

members.legal_issue: A substantial delay in completing a land acquisition does not invalidate the acquisition when the awards are made within the statutory time limit and the delay is not shown to result from deliberate bad faith or a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The acquisition covered land in 86 villages for a large planned township, and the project followed consideration of reports by expert committees.
The authorities received and considered more than 25,000 objections and had to plan and acquire a very large area.

Although the proceedings took a long time and the Court considered that they could have been completed earlier, it found no firm basis to conclude that the delay was deliberate or that the acquisition was initiated solely to suppress land prices.
The awards were made within the time allowed by the applicable statutory framework.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, including its proviso, and relied on Kaliyappan v. State of Kerala and Gujarat State Corporation v. Valji Mulji Soneji for the principle that, where the statute prescribes the time within which an award may be made, acquisition completed within that time is not to be set aside merely for delay. Public authorities must act reasonably and fairly, and a colourable or mala fide exercise of power may invalidate an acquisition; Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi was also considered in assessing delay and planning context.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were not invalidated by the delay because they were completed within the statutory time frame and were not shown to have been initiated or prolonged through deliberate bad faith or a colourable exercise of power.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and substantial_delay and award_within_statutory_period and large_scale_planned_project and not deliberate_bad_faith

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.substantial_delay: The acquiring authority took a substantial time to complete the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.award_within_statutory_period: The acquiring authority made the award within the applicable statutory time limit.
predicates.large_scale_planned_project: The acquisition formed part of a large project that had been planned for a public purpose.
predicates.deliberate_bad_faith: The acquiring authority deliberately delayed or used the acquisition power in bad faith or for a colourable purpose.

members.legal_issue: Delay in making an award after the declaration does not invalidate the acquisition on the facts where statutory compensation addresses the delay and the claimants themselves delayed seeking relief.
material_facts: Awards were made in 1983 after declarations made in 1978, and the Court accepted that there had been delay.
The State provision allowed compensation for damage caused when an award was not made within two years, unless the owner materially caused the delay.
The proceedings were pending on the date that made the additional amount under the central statute available, and the claimants had delayed bringing their petitions.
members.legal_principle: Section 48-A of the Land Acquisition Act, as added by the State legislature, provides compensation for damage caused by delay in making an award beyond two years, subject to the owner's responsibility for the delay. Section 23(1-A) provides an additional amount during the specified period of acquisition proceedings. These provisions informed the result in the circumstances, but do not permit indefinite delay. The Court relied on Ram Chand v. Union of India for the obligation to exercise acquisition powers reasonably and fairly.
members.conclusion: The delay in making the awards was not fatal to the acquisition proceedings in these cases, although acquisition proceedings must be concluded without avoidable delay and cannot be delayed indefinitely.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and award_delayed_after_declaration and statutory_delay_compensation_available and claimant_delayed_seeking_relief

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.award_delayed_after_declaration: The award was made after a substantial interval following the formal declaration.
predicates.statutory_delay_compensation_available: The governing law provided compensation or an additional amount addressing loss associated with the acquisition delay.
predicates.claimant_delayed_seeking_relief: The claimant waited an unreasonable period before seeking judicial relief.
predicates.award_delay_not_fatal: The delay in making the award does not invalidate the acquisition in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: Delay in making an award does not justify setting aside the acquisition where the statutory additional amount and interest adequately compensate for the resulting loss.
material_facts: The respondents had been denied enjoyment of the land between the taking of possession and the deposit of compensation.
The award was delayed.
The Court held that the additional amount and interest provided under the amended compensation provisions adequately compensated the respondents for any loss.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(1A) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Act 68 of 1984, provide an additional amount and interest to compensate for delay in making an award and for loss of enjoyment between taking possession and deposit. The Court considered that compensation adequate in this case.
members.conclusion: The respondents were adequately compensated for the delay and were not entitled to have the award set aside or to further compensation on that basis.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: An owner challenges an award made in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.award_delayed: The authority delayed making the award.
predicates.statutory_additional_compensation_and_in: The additional compensation and interest available in the proceeding adequately compensate for the loss caused by the delay.
predicates.delay_does_not_justify_setting_aside_awa: The delay does not justify setting aside the award or granting further compensation on that basis.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition award made within the applicable statutory maximum period is not invalidated solely because it was made after an alleged inordinate delay.
material_facts: The award was made near the end of the two-year period applicable to the acquisition.
The landowners alleged that the time taken to make the award was inordinate and sought to have the acquisition set aside.
The award was nevertheless made within the maximum period prescribed for making it.
members.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 establishes the maximum time for making an award. Where that period has not been exceeded, a court should not invalidate acquisition proceedings merely by applying its own varying standards of speed. The Court noted that requiring an award earlier could deprive claimants of adequate time to present valuation evidence and could prevent due consideration of that evidence.
members.conclusion: The time taken to make the award was not fatal to the acquisition proceedings because the prescribed maximum period had not been exceeded.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the validity of proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.award_within_statutory_outer_limit: The award was made within the maximum period prescribed for making it.
predicates.delay_alleged_without_exceeding_limit: The challenger alleges delay even though the prescribed maximum period was not exceeded.

members.legal_issue: A fresh land-acquisition declaration made within the applicable statutory period is not invalid solely because it followed the initial notice after a long delay.
material_facts: An initial notice proposing acquisition was issued before the 1967 amendment took effect.

The first declaration was invalidated because the acquisition benefited a corporation, no part of the compensation was to come from public revenue, and the requirements for acquisition for a company had not been followed.

After the invalidation, the government gave the affected landholders an opportunity to make further objections and a personal hearing, then issued a fresh declaration within two years of the amendment’s commencement.
The fresh declaration was challenged only on the ground that it came more than fifteen years after the initial notice.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(2) and 6(1), including the proviso added by the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, establish time limits for making a declaration: for an initial notice issued before the Ordinance commenced, the declaration must be made within two years of commencement; for a notice issued after commencement, it must be made within three years of publication. Where the legislature prescribes a period for exercising a power, exercise within that period cannot be invalidated solely as unreasonably delayed. The earlier inter partes decision in Valjibhai Muljibhai Soneji v. State of Bombay invalidated the original declaration because the acquisition benefited a corporation without public revenue contributing to compensation and the requirements of Part VII had not been complied with.
members.conclusion: The fresh declaration was valid and could not be struck down solely for unreasonable or unexplained delay because it was made within the statutory period applicable to notices issued before the amendment.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a challenge to a government declaration made in a land-acquisition process.
predicates.initial_notice_pre_amendment: The initial notice proposing the acquisition was issued before the relevant statutory amendment took effect.
predicates.fresh_declaration_within_transition_peri: The government made the fresh declaration within the transitional period applicable to an initial notice issued before the amendment.

members.legal_issue: Delay in issuing a fresh declaration after cancellation of an invalid declaration does not invalidate the fresh declaration in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The landowner challenged the first declaration, which was invalid because the acquisition was to be funded entirely by the cooperative housing society.
The government cancelled the invalid declaration and later issued a fresh declaration providing for acquisition at public expense.
The landowner had not pleaded unreasonable delay in the writ petition, and the interval between cancellation and the fresh declaration was one year and four months.
members.legal_principle: The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not preclude a fresh declaration when an earlier declaration is ineffective. Whether delay makes a fresh declaration unreasonable depends on the circumstances, including whether delay was pleaded and whether it was attributable to the challenger. Gujarat State Transport Corporation v. Valji Mulji Soneji was cited in support of the conclusion that a substantial interval may not be unreasonable in the circumstances.
members.conclusion: The fresh declaration was not invalid for delay. The landowner had not raised delay as a ground, and the interval between cancellation of the invalid declaration and issuance of the fresh declaration was not unreasonable in the circumstances.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and earlier_declaration_invalid and government_cancelled_earlier_declaration and fresh_declaration_issued_after_cancellation and delay_not_pleaded

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns the acquisition of land by the government.
predicates.earlier_declaration_invalid: The first declaration for the acquisition was legally ineffective.
predicates.government_cancelled_earlier_declaration: The government cancelled the first declaration in recognition of its ineffectiveness.
predicates.fresh_declaration_issued_after_cancellat: The government issued a fresh declaration after cancelling the first declaration.
predicates.delay_not_pleaded: The person challenging the fresh declaration did not plead unreasonable delay as a ground of challenge.

members.legal_issue: A proceeding pending under a repealed rent law ordinarily continues under that law, subject to modifications or clarifications made by the replacement law.
material_facts: The eviction suit was filed under the earlier rent control law and remained pending when the replacement rent control law came into force.
The replacement law’s corresponding eviction provision omitted the word “suitable” from the description of residential accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, read with its first proviso, pending proceedings ordinarily continue under the repealed Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, while slight modifications or clarifications in the replacement Act apply. The Court relied on Karam Singh Sobhi v. Pratap Chand and Brij Kishore v. Vishwa Mitter Kapur.
members.conclusion: The pending suit was to be continued and decided under the earlier law, with any slight modifications or clarifications in the replacement law taken into account; the change at issue did not alter the result in this case.

predicates.pending_eviction_proceeding_under_repeal: An eviction proceeding under an earlier rent law remained pending when that law was repealed.
predicates.replacement_law_slightly_modifies_or_cla: The replacement rent law made only a slight modification or clarification to the relevant prior rule.

members.legal_issue: A later rent-control provision giving a tenant relief for curing a lease-condition breach applies to pending eviction proceedings under the repealed rent-control law when it clarifies or slightly modifies a remedy already available under that law.
material_facts: The eviction proceedings were pending under the earlier rent-control law when the later law came into force.
The later law expressly permitted relief where a tenant complied with the relevant condition or paid compensation directed by the Controller.
The earlier law required prior notice for eviction based on the relevant lease-condition breach, and the court held that relief for curing the breach could already be available under that law.
members.legal_principle: Under section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, pending proceedings ordinarily continue under the repealed Act, but the first proviso requires regard to the new Act's provisions where they slightly modify or clarify the earlier law. In Karam Singh v. Sri Pratap Chand, the Court held that this proviso does not displace the general rule that the old Act governs pending proceedings when the new law makes a radical departure; clarifications and slight modifications are to be applied. The Court found that section 14(11) clarified and slightly modified relief already available under section 13(1)(k) of the 1952 Act.
members.conclusion: The later provision was clarificatory and slightly modificatory, rather than a radical departure, and therefore applied to the pending proceedings under the first proviso to section 57(2).

predicates.pending_case_under_repealed_rent_law: An eviction proceeding under an earlier rent-control law remained pending when a later rent-control law came into force.
predicates.later_law_adds_relief_for_same_kind_of_b: The later rent-control law provides relief to a tenant who cures the kind of breach underlying the eviction claim.
predicates.earlier_law_already_allowed_comparable_r: The earlier rent-control law allowed a court to grant comparable relief against eviction for that kind of breach.

members.legal_issue: A pending eviction proceeding under a repealed rent-control law continues under that law, subject to modifications or clarifications in the replacement law, but not to its creation of entirely new rights or liabilities.
material_facts: An eviction suit was brought under the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and remained pending in revision when the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 came into force.
The alleged subletting had begun before the 1952 Act came into force.
The replacement Act changed the treatment of subletting, including by creating different rights and liabilities for sublettings occurring at different times.
members.legal_principle: Section 57(1) and (2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 repealed the earlier Act but saved pending suits and proceedings for disposal under its provisions. The first proviso to section 57(2), requiring the court to have regard to the replacement Act, must be read harmoniously with that saving: it permits application of slight modifications or clarifications, not provisions creating entirely new rights or liabilities. The Court relied on the ordinary meaning of “have regard to” discussed in Mysore State Electricity Board v. The Bangalore Woollen, Cotton and Silk Mills Ltd. and Ryots of Garbandho v. Zamindar of Parlakimedi, and agreed with the approach in Jhabar Mal Chokhani v. Jinendra Parshad and related Punjab decisions.
members.conclusion: The pending revision was governed by the 1952 Act, with any slight modifications or clarifications in the 1958 Act applied, but the replacement Act’s creation of new rights or liabilities did not override the earlier Act. The landlord could rely on the earlier Act’s eviction exception, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_repealed_rent_: An eviction proceeding under an earlier rent-control law was pending when a replacement rent-control law began.
predicates.replacement_law_modified_or_clarified_pr: The replacement law modified or clarified rules contained in the earlier law.
predicates.replacement_law_created_new_rights_or_li: The replacement law created rights or liabilities that did not exist under the earlier law.
predicates.prior_law_provided_the_applicable_evicti: The earlier law provided the eviction ground relied on in the pending proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A remedial provision in a new rent-control law that clarifies or slightly modifies relief already available under the repealed law may govern pending eviction proceedings under the repealed law.
material_facts: The landlords brought eviction suits under the repealed rent-control law after tenants made structures contrary to conditions imposed on the landlords by the relevant authorities.
The tenants removed the offending structures while the suits were pending, leaving no further danger to the landlords’ leases.
The new rent-control law provided that eviction could be avoided if the tenant complied with the relevant condition or paid compensation as directed by the Controller.
The new provision was held to clarify and slightly modify relief that a court could already grant under the repealed law, by analogy with relief against forfeiture.
members.legal_principle: Under the first proviso to section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, read harmoniously with section 57(2), the repealed law ordinarily governs pending proceedings, but clarifications or slight modifications in the new law may be applied; a radical departure may not. Karam Singh v. Sri Pratap Chand applied this approach. Section 14(11) of the 1958 Act was a clarification and slight modification of the relief that could have been granted under section 13(1)(k) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, by analogy with section 114-A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The court also relied on Uma Kumari v. Jaswant Rai Chopra in treating the eviction ground as analogous to forfeiture for breach of a lease condition.
members.conclusion: The new law’s provision for relief against eviction could be considered in the pending proceedings, and relief could be granted to tenants who remedied the breach.

rule.if: pending_ejectment_proceeding_under_prior_law and remedial_change_is_clarificatory and tenant_removed_offending_structure and breach_no_longer_endangers_lease

predicates.pending_ejectment_proceeding_under_prior: An eviction proceeding under an earlier rent-control law remained pending when a later rent-control law took effect.
predicates.remedial_change_is_clarificatory: The later law's provision for relief clarified or slightly modified relief that could already have been granted under the earlier law.
predicates.tenant_removed_offending_structure: The tenant removed the structure that had breached a condition imposed on the landlord.
predicates.breach_no_longer_endangers_lease: After the tenant remedied the breach, it no longer threatened the landlord's lease.
predicates.tenant_is_not_evicted: The tenant receives relief from eviction.

members.legal_issue: Pending proceedings under a repealed rent-control law continue under that law, subject to applicable slight modifications or clarifications in the replacement law.
material_facts: The eviction suit began under the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952.
The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 came into force while the suit was pending.
The replacement Act omitted the word “suitable” from the corresponding ground for eviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 57(2) and its first proviso of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, preserve pending proceedings under the repealed Act while requiring regard to the replacement Act. Karam Singh Sobhi v. Shri Pratap Chand, [1964] 4 S.C.R. 647, and Brij Kishore v. Vishww Mitter Kapur, as cited in the judgment, establish that the old Act ordinarily governs pending proceedings, with slight modifications or clarifications in the new Act applying harmoniously with that rule.
members.conclusion: The pending proceeding ordinarily continued under the 1952 Act, while slight modifications or clarifications in the 1958 Act were to be applied; whether either Act governed, the result in this case was the same.

predicates.pending_rent_control_proceeding_under_re: A rent-control proceeding was pending under a law when that law was repealed and replaced.
predicates.replacement_law_makes_slight_modificatio: The replacement law makes a slight modification or clarification to the relevant prior provision.

members.legal_issue: The statutory consequences of repeal continue to apply when a repealed enactment is replaced by fresh legislation on the same subject unless the new legislation shows a contrary intention.
material_facts: A temporary ordinance made filing false information about a refugee land claim an offence.
The respondent filed a claim under the ordinance, and the claim was found to be false.
The ordinance was repealed and its provisions were re-enacted in a new Act.
The new Act treated earlier claims as claims under the Act and retained provisions for investigating claims, punishing false information, and cancelling allotments obtained on false claims.
The prosecution was begun after the repeal for the false claim filed while the ordinance was in force.
members.legal_principle: General Clauses Act, 1897, section 6(c), (d) and (e), preserves accrued liabilities, penalties and proceedings on repeal unless a contrary intention appears; section 30 extends the Act to ordinances. The corresponding provision is section 4 of the Punjab General Clauses Act. When repeal is followed by fresh legislation on the same subject, the new legislation must be examined to determine whether it manifests an intention incompatible with the statutory savings; the question is not whether it expressly preserves old liabilities, and the absence of an express saving clause is not decisive. The Court rejected the broad dictum in Danmal Parshotamdas v. Baburam (1935) I.L.R. 58 All. 495 that section 6 does not apply to repeal followed by substitution.
members.conclusion: The repeal did not extinguish the liability incurred under the ordinance. The General Clauses Act applied despite the simultaneous re-enactment, because the new legislation did not manifest an intention to end that liability.

rule.if: prosecution_for_pre_repeal_offense and enactment_repealed_and_replaced and successor_continues_claim_framework and successor_shows_no_incompatible_intention

predicates.prosecution_for_pre_repeal_offense: A prosecution was brought for conduct that occurred before the enactment under which the conduct was criminal was repealed.
predicates.enactment_repealed_and_replaced: The enactment was repealed and fresh legislation on the same subject took its place.
predicates.successor_continues_claim_framework: The replacement legislation continued to recognize claims made under the former enactment and retained mechanisms to investigate and address false claims.
predicates.successor_shows_no_incompatible_intentio: The replacement legislation did not show an intention to extinguish liabilities incurred under the former enactment.

members.legal_issue: The repeal and re-enactment of ceiling legislation did not prevent pending ceiling proceedings from being decided under the repealed law where the new legislation did not manifest a contrary intention.
material_facts: The earlier tenancy legislation imposed a ceiling on agricultural holdings and provided for determination with reference to a notified date.

The later ceiling legislation repealed the earlier ceiling provisions but included provisions preserving certain applications of the old law, including reopening specified decided matters and retaining the old ceiling standard in certain circumstances.
After the later legislation came into force, ceiling proceedings under the earlier law were initiated or continued against landholders.
The landholders argued that the differences between the two statutory schemes and the later law’s overriding clause prevented use of the repealed law in pending cases.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6 of the Rajasthan General Clauses Act, 1955, repeal does not affect accrued rights, incurred liabilities, or proceedings concerning them unless a different intention appears. When repeal is accompanied by re-enactment on the same subject, the new enactment must be examined to determine whether it manifests that different intention; mere omission of an express reference to section 6 is not conclusive. A saving clause is not exhaustive of rights and obligations that survive repeal. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh, B. Bansgopal v. Emperor, Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh, Chief Inspector of Mines v. K.C. Thapar, and I.T. Commissioner, U.P. v. Shah Sadiq and Sons. It found that sections 15(2) and 40(1), read with the second proviso to section 4(1) of the 1973 Act, showed no contrary intention; section 3’s reference to law for the time being in force did not exclude a law deemed to remain in force.
members.conclusion: Pending ceiling proceedings could be initiated or continued under the repealed provisions because the later legislation did not manifest an intention inconsistent with saving the old law for those proceedings.

rule.if: ceiling_proceeding_under_repealed_law and pending_when_repealed and repeal_followed_by_reenactment and new_law_preserved_some_application_of_old_law and not contrary_intention_in_new_law

predicates.ceiling_proceeding_under_repealed_law: A proceeding to determine a ceiling on agricultural holdings was brought under an earlier law.
predicates.pending_when_repealed: The proceeding had not been concluded when the earlier law was repealed.
predicates.repeal_followed_by_reenactment: The legislature repealed the earlier law and enacted a replacement law on the same subject.
predicates.new_law_preserved_some_application_of_ol: The replacement law retained specified applications or remedies under the earlier law.
predicates.contrary_intention_in_new_law: The replacement law’s provisions manifest an intention inconsistent with applying the earlier law to pending proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A restoration application and deposit made under an earlier temporary enactment and still pending when that enactment is repealed may continue under the later enactment.
material_facts: The tenants filed a restoration application under an earlier temporary enactment and deposited the purchase money and interest required for that proceeding.
That application was pending when the earlier enactment was repealed and the later enactment came into force.
The tenants sought to have the earlier application and deposit treated as continuing in the later proceeding, and undertook to pay any deficiency found by the court.
The lower appellate court found the deposit sufficient, subject to deposit of any further interest if restoration was allowed; the High Court did not dislodge that finding.
members.legal_principle: Whether repeal destroys rights or liabilities accrued under an earlier enactment depends on whether the later enactment manifests an intention to destroy them, not merely on whether it expressly preserves them. The Court approved the approach in Parameswaran Nambudiri’s case and relied on State of Punjab v. Mohar Singh. It also applied the requirements of Section 13(B) in the later enactment.
members.conclusion: The earlier pending application and deposit continued unaffected by the later enactment and could support the tenants’ claim for restoration.

rule.if: restoration_proceeding_case and earlier_application_pending_at_repeal and required_deposit_already_made and no_intention_to_destroy_accrued_rights

predicates.restoration_proceeding_case: The proceeding concerns an application to restore a holding after a sale in execution for rent arrears.
predicates.earlier_application_pending_at_repeal: The tenant’s restoration application under the earlier enactment was still pending when that enactment was repealed.
predicates.required_deposit_already_made: The tenant had made the deposit required for the earlier restoration proceeding.
predicates.no_intention_to_destroy_accrued_rights: The later enactment did not manifest an intention to destroy rights and liabilities accrued under the earlier enactment.

members.legal_issue: A proceeding commenced under a law before its repeal may continue in the original court when the repeal does not clearly displace pending proceedings and a later saving provision preserves them.
material_facts: The mortgagor’s successor filed an application to redeem a usufructuary mortgage under the then-applicable law before the repeal was given effect.
The repeal operated retrospectively only from a date after the application was filed.
The new law did not provide for pending proceedings to be transferred to the newly empowered court.
When a later amendment expressly preserved pending proceedings and appeals, the matter was still pending on appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(c) and (e) of the U.P. General Clauses Act, unless a different intention appears, repeal does not affect accrued rights or remedies and does not prevent the continuation and conclusion of proceedings commenced before repeal. The court found no contrary intention in the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act or its 1953 amendment: the repeal was not retrospective to a time before the proceeding began, and there was no provision transferring pending cases. Section 23 of the 1956 amending Act expressly preserved proceedings and appeals already pending, confirming that they continued under the old law. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The original court had jurisdiction to continue and decide the proceeding under the old law; the repeal and the new court’s jurisdiction did not render it incompetent.

rule.if: redemption_proceeding and commenced_before_repeal_took_effect and repeal_did_not_reach_before_commencement and no_transfer_of_pending_proceedings and pending_when_later_saving_applied

predicates.redemption_proceeding: A party commenced a proceeding to redeem a mortgage under the law then in force.
predicates.commenced_before_repeal_took_effect: The party commenced the proceeding before the repeal took effect.
predicates.repeal_did_not_reach_before_commencement: The repeal did not operate from a time earlier than the commencement of the proceeding.
predicates.no_transfer_of_pending_proceedings: The new law did not direct that pending proceedings be transferred to another court or authority.
predicates.pending_when_later_saving_applied: The proceeding or its appeal remained pending when a later enactment expressly preserved pending proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Consumer proceedings and compatible actions taken under the repealed consumer law remain effective under the successor consumer law.
material_facts: The purchasers initiated consumer proceedings under the 1986 consumer law.
The consumer commission issued orders in those proceedings.
The successor consumer law had come into force, and the developer challenged whether the earlier proceedings and orders remained effective.
members.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 107 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 preserve the additional character of consumer remedies and save actions taken under the repealed Consumer Protection Act, 1986 to the extent they are not inconsistent with the successor law. The Court also referred to Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
members.conclusion: The proceedings and resulting actions, including the consumer commission’s orders, were saved.

predicates.consumer_proceeding_under_repealed_law: A consumer complaint was initiated under a consumer law that was later repealed.
predicates.action_taken_in_that_proceeding: A consumer forum took an action or issued an order in the proceeding before or in connection with the repeal.
predicates.action_not_inconsistent_with_successor_l: The earlier action or order is not inconsistent with the successor consumer law.
predicates.proceeding_and_action_remain_saved: The proceeding and compatible actions taken in it remain effective under the successor law.

members.legal_issue: The absence of preliminary procedures under a former forest law does not by itself prevent a notification under that law from being treated as a notification under a corresponding provision of an extended law.
material_facts: Notifications defining forest boundaries were issued under the former state's forest law and were continued under legislation extending a new forest law to the state.
The former law did not prescribe the preliminary procedures required by the extended law before a forest area could be notified.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 4, including the proviso to section 4, of the Part C States (Laws) Act, 1950, an action under a repealed corresponding law may be deemed to have been taken under the extended law. Whether a notification is under a corresponding provision turns on the provision to which it corresponds, not on whether the former law required the same preliminary procedures. The Court relied on the Indian Forest Act, 1927, and the statutory scheme for extending laws to the state.
members.conclusion: The difference in preliminary procedures did not prevent the continued notifications from being treated as notifications under a corresponding provision of the extended law.

predicates.legacy_law_transition_case: The case concerns the transition from a former local law to an extended law that replaces it.
predicates.former_law_notification_continued: A notification made under the former law remained in force after the new law was extended.
predicates.former_law_lacked_preliminary_procedures: The former law did not require preliminary procedures that the extended law prescribed for the comparable notification.

members.legal_issue: A notification preserved by a transition law may be treated as made under a corresponding provision of the replacement law despite differences in the procedures prescribed by the two laws.
material_facts: The former state law authorized the forest-area notifications without the elaborate preliminary procedure prescribed by the replacement law.

The replacement law was extended to the territory, the former law was repealed, and a saving proviso deemed actions taken under the former law to have been taken under corresponding provisions of the replacement law.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 4 of the Part C States (Laws) Act, 1950, including the proviso to section 4, actions under a repealed corresponding law could be deemed to have been taken under the corresponding provision of the extended law. Whether a notification was under a corresponding provision depended on the provision to which it corresponded, not on whether the old law prescribed the same preliminary procedure. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The absence of identical procedural requirements did not prevent the preserved notifications from being treated as notifications under a corresponding provision of the replacement law.

rule.if: replacement_law_extended and former_law_repealed and saving_clause_preserves_actions and notification_validly_made_under_former_law

predicates.replacement_law_extended: A replacement law was extended to the territory governed by the former law.
predicates.former_law_repealed: The former law was repealed because it corresponded to the extended replacement law.
predicates.saving_clause_preserves_actions: The transition law preserved actions taken under the former law by deeming them taken under corresponding provisions of the replacement law.
predicates.notification_validly_made_under_former_l: A notification was validly issued under the former law.

members.legal_issue: A preliminary notification issued under a repealed municipal law may support a valid inclusion under the successor law when the successor law preserves prior administrative actions.
material_facts: The government declared its intention to include two villages within the municipality under the former municipal law.
After the successor municipal law came into force, the government issued a final notification including the villages under that law.
The successor law provided that qualifying actions taken under the former law were to be treated as actions taken under the successor law.
members.legal_principle: Clause 13 of Schedule IX, read with clause 1 of the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, deemed prior actions under the repealed District Municipalities Act, 1920 to have been taken under the successor Act unless inconsistent with it. The preliminary notification was therefore treated as having been issued under section 3(1)(b) of the successor Act.
members.conclusion: The inclusion of the villages within the municipality was valid.

predicates.municipal_boundary_inclusion_case: The proceeding concerns whether a local area was validly included within a municipality.
predicates.government_started_inclusion_under_prior: The government began the process of including a local area under an earlier municipal regime before a successor regime took effect.
predicates.successor_framework_preserved_prior_admi: The successor framework treated qualifying administrative steps taken under the earlier regime as steps taken under the successor regime.

members.legal_issue: Proceedings commenced under a repealed acquisition regime are treated as proceedings under the replacement regime when the replacement law continues prior actions under its provisions.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications and proceedings began under the earlier improvement-trust law.
A replacement law provided that actions and proceedings taken under the earlier law were deemed to have been taken under the replacement law.
The compensation proceedings were pending when the replacement law came into force.
members.legal_principle: Under section 173(2) of the replacement law, actions and proceedings taken under the repealed law were deemed to have been taken under the replacement law. Under clause 6 of the replacement law’s Schedule, section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act was omitted and replaced. This statutory construction did not determine the separate question whether that replacement provision was constitutionally valid.
members.conclusion: The prior proceedings were deemed to have been taken under the replacement law, so the earlier regime did not independently preserve an entitlement to solatium.

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: A proceeding was conducted to determine compensation for compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.proceeding_started_under_earlier_regime: The acquisition proceeding began under an earlier legal regime that was later replaced.
predicates.later_law_continued_prior_proceedings: A later law treated actions and proceedings taken under the earlier regime as taken under the later regime.

members.legal_issue: A scheme saved by a successor statute continues to operate without being reassessed for consistency with that statute unless it is modified through the prescribed procedure.
material_facts: A scheme for the administration of a religious institution was framed under an earlier statute and was confirmed, subject to minor modifications, after a challenge in court.
A later statute repealed and replaced the earlier statute and provided that schemes of this kind would be deemed to have been settled or modified under the later statute.
The later statute separately provided a procedure by which such a scheme could be modified or cancelled.
The challenge sought to test the scheme's consistency with the later statute in writ proceedings, rather than through the procedure for modifying or cancelling the scheme.
members.legal_principle: The court construed section 103(d) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, together with section 62(3)(a). Unlike other clauses of section 103 that expressly addressed consistency with the later Act, section 103(d) contained no such condition. The court considered East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council but held that the deeming provision did not require schemes to be reassessed. A saved scheme continued to operate unless modified or cancelled under the statutory procedure.
members.conclusion: The saving provision continued the scheme as though it had been made under the later statute; it did not require the scheme to be reassessed or reframed for consistency with that statute. The scheme could be modified or cancelled through the procedure specifically provided for that purpose.

predicates.scheme_made_under_repealed_law: A scheme was made under an earlier law before that law was repealed.
predicates.successor_law_saves_schemes: A later law provides that schemes of this kind are to be treated as made under that later law.
predicates.scheme_challenged_outside_modification_p: A party challenges the scheme's continued operation without using the process provided for modifying or cancelling it.

members.legal_issue: A proceeding concerning a right preserved on repeal must be resolved under the repealed law when the saving provision so directs.
material_facts: The tenants claimed a protected right acquired under the earlier tenancy law.
The landlord brought a possession suit concerning that right after the later tenancy law had replaced the earlier law.
members.legal_principle: Section 89(2)(b)(ii) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, required proceedings in respect of a preserved right to be continued and disposed of as if the later Act had not been passed. The Court held that this provision did not limit the independent preservation of accrued rights under section 89(2)(b)(i), and that the present controversy was to be resolved under the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939. It considered the difference from section 7 of the Bombay General Clauses Act but found that it did not change this result.
members.conclusion: The dispute had to be resolved under the earlier law, and the suit for possession was dismissed.

predicates.proceeding_over_repeal_saved_right: The case is a legal proceeding concerning a right claimed to have been preserved when the law creating it was repealed.
predicates.proceeding_concerns_preexisting_tenancy_: The proceeding concerns a tenancy right acquired before the later law came into force.

members.legal_issue: A rent-control law’s new mesne-profit limit does not govern an eviction suit that was pending when the new law commenced and that must continue under the repealed law.
material_facts: The eviction suit was filed under the earlier rent-control law before the new law commenced and was still pending when the new law took effect.
The tenant argued that the new law limited mesne profits for commercial premises to three times the standard rent.
The new law preserved pending suits and proceedings for continuation and disposal under the repealed law.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(3)(a) of the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2001 gives overriding effect to the savings for applications, suits, and proceedings pending when that Act commenced, requiring them to be continued and disposed of under the repealed Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 as if it remained in force. Consequently, Section 20 of the 2001 Act does not govern such a pending suit.
members.conclusion: The new law’s mesne-profit limit did not apply to the pending suit; the suit continued under the earlier law.

predicates.eviction_suit_pending_at_new_law_commenc: An eviction suit was filed under the earlier rent-control regime and remained pending when a replacement rent-control law commenced.
predicates.new_law_preserves_pending_proceedings: The replacement law directs that pending suits continue and be decided under the earlier law.

members.legal_issue: Execution proceedings commenced under a repealed statutory regime and pending before an authority at repeal continue under that regime.
material_facts: Recovery and execution proceedings were initiated under the earlier cooperative-society law, and execution proceedings were pending before the relevant authority when the replacement law came into force.
The execution included proceedings to attach and sell property to satisfy the recovery award.
members.legal_principle: Section 126(6) of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 preserves legal proceedings pending before a court, the Central Registrar, or another authority at commencement, as if the new Act had not been passed. The expression “legal proceeding” is not limited to proceedings in courts: Governor-General in Council v. Shiromani Sugar Mills Ltd., AIR 1946 FC 16, held that it includes proceedings to recover tax dues through administrative authorities, and Binod Mills Co. Ltd. Ujjain v. Suresh Chandra Mahaveer Prasad Mantri, (1987) 3 SCC 99, applied that understanding to execution petitions. Under Section 85(c) of the 1984 Act, an order could be executed by attachment and sale; the later Act’s arbitration scheme and its Section 94 execution provision did not displace proceedings saved by Section 126(6).
