members.conclusion: The pending execution proceedings continued under the earlier law despite its repeal, and the High Court was wrong to set aside the sale on the ground that execution had to proceed under the later arbitration law.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is an execution proceeding to enforce a recovery decision or order.
predicates.initiated_under_prior_recovery_regime: The execution proceeding was initiated under the legal regime that was later repealed.
predicates.pending_before_authority_at_repeal: The execution proceeding remained pending before an authority when the replacement regime came into force.

members.legal_issue: A pending special-leave proceeding under the Constitution survives the repeal of the governing rent-control law when the replacement law does not clearly terminate that constitutional review.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding had been initiated under the former rent-control law, and a High Court revision had resulted in an eviction order before the tenant sought special leave to appeal.
While the special-leave proceeding was pending, the former rent-control law was repealed and a replacement rent-control law came into force.
The premises were outside the replacement law's coverage because their non-residential area exceeded the statutory threshold.

The replacement law provided for abatement of certain pending proceedings concerning premises outside its coverage, but did not clearly direct that a pending proceeding under the Supreme Court's constitutional jurisdiction should abate.
members.legal_principle: Sections 69 and 70 of the Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 govern the transfer, continuation, and abatement of proceedings following repeal of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961. Section 70(2)(c) applies to specified proceedings concerning premises outside the new Act's coverage, while Section 70(3) preserves the residual operation of Sections 6, 8, and 24 of the Karnataka General Clauses Act, 1899. Abatement must be strictly construed and applies only where its reach is clear; absent a contrary legislative intention, it terminates proceedings pending at the relevant stage, not an original case already adjudicated below and reopened for review by a superior forum. Article 136 confers plenary constitutional jurisdiction that subordinate legislation cannot curtail. The Court relied on Durga Shankar Mehta v. Thakur Raghuraj Singh, Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India, S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India, Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai, and Gyan Chand v. Kunjbeharilal; it distinguished Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh, Chattar Singh v. Thakur Prasad Singh, Satyanarayan Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar, and Mst. Bibi Rahmani Khatoon v. Harkoo Gope, which concerned legislation that abated the original case itself.
members.conclusion: The proceeding under Article 136 survived and could be decided on its merits; it did not abate under the replacement law.

rule.if: local_rent_law_repealed_during_review and premises_outside_replacement_rent_regime and article_136_special_leave_review and lower_court_eviction_case_already_adjudicated and no_clear_direction_to_abate_constitutional_review

predicates.local_rent_law_repealed_during_review: A local rent-control law was repealed while a challenge to a decision under that law remained pending.
predicates.premises_outside_replacement_rent_regime: The premises fell outside the coverage of the replacement rent-control regime.
predicates.article_136_special_leave_review: The pending matter was a discretionary special-leave review under the Supreme Court's constitutional jurisdiction, rather than an ordinary appeal as of right.
predicates.lower_court_eviction_case_already_adjudi: The eviction claim had already been adjudicated below, and the pending matter concerned review of that adjudication.
predicates.no_clear_direction_to_abate_constitution: The replacement law did not clearly direct, expressly or by necessary implication, that the pending constitutional review be terminated.
predicates.constitutional_review_survives: The pending constitutional review continues and may be decided on its merits.

members.legal_issue: A scheme commenced under a repealed statute may continue under successor legislation when the scheme’s substantive features have not been shown to have changed.
material_facts: The scheme was first notified under the 1919 Act and was later sanctioned under the 1966 Adhiniyam.

The initial notification was not placed before the Court, and the alleged difference between the scheme descriptions rested on the types of schemes identified in the former Act and a change in the scheme’s Hindi name.
The locality and plots involved were the same in the initial and final notifications.
No substantive alteration to the original scheme was shown.
members.legal_principle: Section 97(3) of the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1966, transferred pending schemes and related proceedings under the U.P. Town Improvement Act, 1919, to the successor Board, which could proceed from the stage reached. The party challenging continuation had to show a substantive change that prevented the scheme from continuing; a different name alone did not establish one.
members.conclusion: The scheme could continue under the successor legislation because no change beyond its name was shown to prevent its continuation.

rule.if: successor_law_continuity_challenge and scheme_started_under_repealed_law and same_area_and_plots and no_substantive_change_shown

predicates.successor_law_continuity_challenge: The case challenges whether a scheme begun under a repealed law may continue under successor legislation.
predicates.scheme_started_under_repealed_law: The scheme was initiated under the former law before that law was repealed.
predicates.same_area_and_plots: The initial and later versions of the scheme concern the same locality and plots.
predicates.no_substantive_change_shown: The challenger has not shown a substantive alteration to the scheme beyond a change in its name or description.

members.legal_issue: Valid steps already taken in a pending acquisition proceeding under a repealed State law remain effective, and the proceeding may continue from the stage it had reached under the applicable Central law.
material_facts: Acquisition proceedings began under the State law, and a preliminary notification and declaration were issued under it.
A challenge to the declaration was dismissed, and the declaration had been upheld by the High Court.
When the Central law became applicable and the State law was repealed, further acquisition proceedings remained pending.
The acquisition officer later issued notice to make an award without issuing a fresh preliminary notification under the Central law.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(b) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides that repeal does not affect the previous operation of the repealed enactment or anything duly done under it, unless a different intention appears. The Court relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 8, which recognized that duly completed steps under a repealed enactment are preserved.
members.conclusion: The valid steps taken under the State law up to the declaration were not effaced by repeal, and the acquisition officer could continue the pending proceeding from the stage it had reached without beginning the procedure afresh.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and proceeding_pending and central_law_applies and state_law_steps_valid

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding is for the acquisition of land.
predicates.proceeding_pending: The proceeding had not reached completion when the replacement law became applicable.
predicates.central_law_applies: A Central law governing the acquisition became applicable while the proceeding was pending.
predicates.state_law_steps_valid: Steps already taken under the State law were legally valid and had not been set aside.

members.legal_issue: A possession application enforcing a tenancy right acquired under a repealed law is treated as a continuation of the earlier proceeding and is decided by the successor authority using the replacement law’s procedure.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an order determining the tenancy under the earlier law before it was repealed.
After the replacement law took effect, the landlord applied for possession under its procedure.
The earlier law provided for a further possession order after the tenancy had been determined.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 132(2) and 132(3) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, acquired rights remain enforceable, while proceedings pending at commencement are transferred to the corresponding authority and disposed of under the replacement Act. The court treated the possession application as a continuation of the proceeding under section 19 of the Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, following Jayantraj Kanakmal Zambad v. Hari Dagdu. The phrase requiring disposal in accordance with the replacement Act attracts its procedural provisions, not new substantive conditions for instituting proceedings.
members.conclusion: The application was to be treated as one under the earlier law and as a continuation of the proceeding concerning the acquired right. The successor authority was competent to hear it and had to follow the replacement law’s procedure while giving effect to the right already acquired.

rule.if: tenancy_possession_enforcement_proceeding and prior_termination_order and possession_application_after_repeal and right_acquired_before_repeal

predicates.tenancy_possession_enforcement_proceedin: The proceeding concerns a landlord’s application to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.prior_termination_order: A landlord obtained an order determining the tenancy under the law then in force before that law was repealed.
predicates.possession_application_after_repeal: A landlord applied for possession after the earlier law had been repealed.
predicates.right_acquired_before_repeal: The landlord’s right to seek possession arose before the earlier law was repealed.

members.legal_issue: A former licensee whose licence has expired may recover possession from the owner through a summary possessory remedy after being dispossessed without consent and otherwise than through lawful process.
material_facts: The bank occupied the premises under an admitted leave-and-licence agreement that expired, and the owner had refused renewal.
The bank stopped conducting business in the premises after a fire and began operating elsewhere; the owner had not used force to remove it.
The bank’s letter described the premises as vacated after the fire, and the owner later restricted access to the premises.
The bank sought recovery of possession through a summary possessory suit.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, a person dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law may seek summary recovery of possession without the court determining title. Justice Kasliwal distinguished a tenant holding over, whose possession may receive statutory protection, from a licensee whose licence has expired: relying on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and the quoted passage from K.K. Verma v. Naraindas C. Malkani, and on D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav, he treated the former licensee’s possession as that of a trespasser and denied recovery against the owner on these facts. Justice Ramaswamy disagreed, relying on the purpose of Section 6 to prevent self-help and on authorities including Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, Rudrappa v. Narsingrao, Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, Ram Ratan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. Rev. Father K.C. Alexander, and Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao; he considered settled possession protected even against the owner until lawful eviction.
members.conclusion: Justice Kasliwal concluded that the bank could not recover possession: in his view, it had vacated because of the fire and had not been dispossessed by force or unlawful means; after the licence expired, it was a trespasser with no right to recover possession from the admitted owner. Justice Ramaswamy reached the opposite conclusion, treating the bank as dispossessed without consent and entitled to recover possession. The judges divided, and the matter was referred to a larger bench; neither view was a majority resolution in this judgment.

rule.if: summary_possession_proceeding and former_licensee and licence_expired and owner_title_admitted and occupant_left_after_unavoidable_event and not owner_used_force_to_remove_occupant

predicates.summary_possession_proceeding: The claimant brought a summary suit seeking recovery of possession of immovable property.
predicates.former_licensee: The claimant had entered and occupied the property under a licence granted by the owner.
predicates.licence_expired: The agreed period of the claimant’s licence ended without an agreed renewal.
predicates.owner_title_admitted: The parties admitted that the defendant owned the property.
predicates.occupant_left_after_unavoidable_event: The claimant stopped using the premises and left them after an event made continued business use impracticable.
predicates.owner_used_force_to_remove_occupant: The owner used force to remove the claimant from the property.

members.legal_issue: A person in settled possession who entered lawfully may recover possession through a summary possessory remedy if the owner retakes possession without consent and otherwise than through lawful process, even after the person’s licence has expired.
material_facts: The bank had entered the premises lawfully under a licence and had occupied them for many years.

After the fire, the bank said it surrendered the premises to allow repairs and renovation and that the owner had undertaken to return possession; the bank’s furniture and other items remained in part of the premises.
The bank claimed a continuing intention to possess and sought recovery after the owner refused to restore access.
In the High Court, the owner’s counsel agreed, for purposes of the suit and without prejudice, to proceed on the footing that the bank had been dispossessed as alleged.
The bank brought its summary possessory suit within six months of the alleged dispossession.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act provides a summary remedy for a person dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law, without regard to either party’s title, if the suit is brought within six months. Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act defines a licence as permission to do something on another’s immovable property without creating an interest in it. Justice Ramaswamy reasoned that, despite the ordinary consequences of an expired licence, settled possession cannot be terminated by self-help and must be ended through lawful process. He relied on Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, Rudrappa v. Narsingrao, Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, Ram Ratan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. Rev. Father K.C. Alexander, Yar Muhammad v. Lakshmi Das, and Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao. He distinguished D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav and rejected the contrary approach attributed to Chandu Lal v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi. Justice Kasliwal took the opposing view, relying on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and D.H. Maniar.
members.conclusion: Justice Ramaswamy concluded that the bank had been dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law, and was entitled to recover possession. Justice Kasliwal disagreed and would have denied relief. Because the judges divided, the matter was referred to a larger bench; Justice Ramaswamy’s conclusion was not a majority resolution in this judgment.

rule.if: summary_possession_proceeding and lawful_initial_entry and long_peaceful_occupation and claimant_retained_intention_to_possess and owner_repossessed_without_judicial_process and suit_brought_within_six_months

predicates.summary_possession_proceeding: The claimant brought a summary suit seeking recovery of possession of immovable property.
predicates.lawful_initial_entry: The claimant first entered the property with the owner’s permission or under an agreement with the owner.
predicates.long_peaceful_occupation: The claimant occupied the property for an extended period without interruption.
predicates.claimant_retained_intention_to_possess: The claimant continued to assert an intention to possess the property, including by retaining belongings or requesting its return.
predicates.owner_repossessed_without_judicial_proce: The owner took or retained possession without obtaining it through a court or other lawful process.
predicates.suit_brought_within_six_months: The claimant filed the suit within six months after the alleged dispossession.

members.legal_issue: A person in settled possession who is dispossessed otherwise than in due course of law may sue to recover possession notwithstanding the title asserted against that person.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that they had been forcibly dispossessed despite their continuing tenancy.
The trust disputed the allegation and maintained that possession had been taken lawfully, including by voluntary surrender in some instances.
The Court left the factual dispute about forcible dispossession for consideration by the trial court.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits a person dispossessed from immovable property without consent and otherwise than in due course of law to sue for possession notwithstanding another title. The Court relied on Yashwant Singh v. Jagdish Singh, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Mrs. Shobha Venkata Rao, Ram Rattan v. State of U.P., State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmender Prasad Singh, and K.K. Verma v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: A claimant who proves settled possession and dispossession otherwise than in due course of law may seek recovery of possession; whether the plaintiffs were forcibly dispossessed was left for the trial court to decide.

predicates.summary_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit seeking recovery of immovable property after being dispossessed.
predicates.claimant_was_in_settled_possession: The claimant had settled possession of the property rather than merely fugitive possession.
predicates.claimant_was_dispossessed_without_consen: The claimant was removed from the property without consent and without use of due legal process.

members.legal_issue: A person in possession may seek restoration against a person who dispossesses them otherwise than through due process of law, even before title by adverse possession is perfected.
material_facts: The Court considered the distinction between a possessory claim based on prior possession and a claim based on title perfected by adverse possession.
It stated that a person in possession cannot be ousted by force and that possession may be protected against an unlawful dispossessor before the possessor's title has ripened.
The Court referred to the statutory possessory remedy and the rule that a wrongdoer cannot justify forcible dispossession merely by asserting that title belongs to someone else.
members.legal_principle: Article 64 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides for a suit based on previous possession, and Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a summary remedy for unlawful dispossession. The Court relied on Lallu Yashwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, Somnath Berman v. Dr. S.P. Raju, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao, and State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh. These authorities establish that possession is protected against forcible dispossession and that a person must obtain possession through lawful process.
members.conclusion: A person dispossessed otherwise than through due process may maintain a possessory suit for restoration, including before title by adverse possession is perfected.

predicates.kind_possessory_claim: The proceeding seeks restoration of possession based on the claimant's prior possession.
predicates.claimant_was_in_possession: The claimant actually possessed the property before the dispossession.
predicates.claimant_was_dispossessed_without_due_pr: Another person removed the claimant from possession without obtaining possession through lawful process.

members.legal_issue: A claimant seeking summary restoration of possession must establish possession in their own right and dispossession within the statutory period.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that he occupied a tuck shop as a tenant, but the trial court found that the pleaded tenancy had not been proved.
The claimant offered no alternative pleaded basis for becoming a tenant of the property owner.
The evidence and records did not establish that the claimant had exclusive possession in his own right.
The court found that the claimant was not in exclusive possession as a tenant and was therefore not entitled to relief in the summary possession suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a summary remedy based on possession and dispossession, rather than on an unproved claim to tenancy. Possession of a servant or agent is, for these purposes, the possession of the master or principal, and the servant or agent cannot sue the master or principal on the basis of that possession: Southern Roadways Ltd., Madurai v. S.M. Krishnan, [1989] 4 SCC 603.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to relief under Section 6 because he failed to establish the necessary possession in his own right.

predicates.section_six_possession_proceeding: The claimant brought a summary proceeding seeking restoration of possession after alleged dispossession.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_independent_exc: The claimant did not establish that the claimed possession was exclusive possession in the claimant’s own right.

members.legal_issue: A limitation defense may be considered even when it was not pleaded in the written statement if the governing law requires dismissal of a suit filed after limitation expires.
material_facts: The defendants did not plead limitation in their written statement.
The suit included claims for rent that the court found were filed after the applicable limitation period had expired.
The court found that the appellants could identify no further evidence they could have adduced on limitation and that the absence of the plea caused no prejudice.
members.legal_principle: Section 184 of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885 requires dismissal of a suit instituted after limitation has expired even if limitation has not been pleaded. The court also relied on the absence of prejudice from allowing the point to be raised.
members.conclusion: The defendants were properly allowed to raise the limitation point despite not pleading it in the written statement.

rule.if: tenancy_suit and limitation_not_pleaded and limitation_period_expired and law_requires_dismissal_after_expiry and no_prejudice_from_late_plea

predicates.tenancy_suit: A claimant brought a suit governed by the tenancy-law limitation regime.
predicates.limitation_not_pleaded: The defendant did not raise limitation in the written statement.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The suit was instituted after the applicable limitation period had expired.
predicates.law_requires_dismissal_after_expiry: The governing law requires dismissal of a suit filed after limitation expires even if limitation was not pleaded.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_late_plea: The party opposing consideration of limitation could identify no further evidence it would have adduced and suffered no prejudice from the point being raised.

members.legal_issue: A court may dismiss a suit as time-barred rather than continue a consent remand for trial when the limitation bar is established by the record, even if limitation was not initially pleaded.
material_facts: The appeal court had remanded the suit for a fresh trial by consent of the parties.
The original plaint, without the amendment, sought only enforcement of the pre-emption right.
The record established that possession had been delivered to the purchaser at the time of the sale and that the suit was filed more than one year later.
The limitation plea had not initially been raised in the written statement.
members.legal_principle: A court must ensure that a suit barred by limitation is dismissed whether or not a party has raised limitation as a plea. Where the record sufficiently establishes the bar, the court need not prolong proceedings under a consent remand. The limitation rule applied was Article 10 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to dismiss the suit as time-barred instead of requiring further proceedings under the consent remand.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.consent_remand_for_trial: The parties consented to an order sending the suit for further trial.
predicates.limitation_bar_established_on_record: The record establishes the facts showing that the suit was filed outside the applicable limitation period.

members.legal_issue: A court must apply an apparent statutory limitation bar even if the applicable limitation provision is not specifically pleaded or named in an issue.
material_facts: The pleadings and issues raised facts relevant to limitation, including the plaintiffs' allegations of possession and dispossession and the defendants' claim of adverse possession.
The defendants had pleaded limitation, and the issues framed addressed the facts relevant to the applicable limitation rule.
The Court held that an issue need not name the legal provision applicable to those facts.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908 requires a court to dismiss a suit instituted after the prescribed limitation period, subject to the Act. The court must apply the bar where it is apparent from the facts; an issue need not cite the relevant legal provision.
members.conclusion: Under section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the court must apply a limitation bar apparent from the facts even if the provision is not specifically pleaded or named in an issue.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.limitation_bar_apparent_from_facts: The facts established or raised in the suit show that the claim is out of time under an applicable limitation rule.

members.legal_issue: A court must determine whether a suit is barred by limitation even when no party has pleaded limitation.
material_facts: The suit sought accounts and other relief relating to a business, and limitation was disputed in the proceedings.
The Court considered whether the suit was time-barred and held that the issue required fresh consideration, including consideration of the relevant limitation articles and the admitted document.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Limitation Act requires the court to determine whether a suit is barred by limitation irrespective of whether the parties have raised the plea. The relevant limitation articles and admissible evidence bearing on limitation must be considered.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the court must determine whether a suit is barred by limitation regardless of whether a party has raised that plea; it did not decide whether this suit was time-barred and remitted the question for fresh consideration.

predicates.civil_suit_before_court: A court is deciding a civil suit or an appeal in which the timeliness of the suit is relevant.

members.legal_issue: In a suit to recover possession based on established title, the defendant bears the burden of proving that adverse possession has displaced that title.
material_facts: The owners’ title had been finally adjudicated in earlier proceedings.
The owners brought a suit to recover possession on the basis of that title.
The claimant argued that the suit was governed by the limitation rule for possession based on prior possession and asserted adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, limitation begins when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse. Once the plaintiff proves title, the burden shifts to the defendant to establish title by adverse possession; the Court relied on M. Durai v. Muthu & Ors. and Saroop Singh v. Banto & Ors.
members.conclusion: The suit attracted Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, and the claimant had to prove possession under a hostile title sufficient to extinguish the owners’ title.

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: The plaintiff brings a proceeding seeking recovery of possession of property.
predicates.plaintiff_title_proved: The plaintiff establishes title to the property.
predicates.defendant_relies_on_adverse_possession: The defendant asserts that possession has extinguished the plaintiff’s title by adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: In a title suit governed by the 1963 limitation law, a plaintiff who proves title need not also prove possession within the twelve years preceding suit; the defendant relying on adverse possession must establish it.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title to the property and relief against a person occupying it.
The first appellate court required the plaintiff to prove title and possession within twelve years before filing suit and treated the claim as time-barred.
The High Court upheld that approach, while the Supreme Court identified it as an error in applying the limitation law.
The Supreme Court did not itself finally determine whether the plaintiff had proved title and remitted the matter for reconsideration.
members.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 changed the position under Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908: in a suit governed by Article 65, the plaintiff succeeds upon proving title, and the defendant bears the burden of proving adverse possession. The defendant must also prove animus possidendi.
members.conclusion: The lower courts applied the wrong principle under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963. If the plaintiff proves title, the defendant must establish adverse possession to defeat that title; the plaintiff need not prove possession within the period preceding suit.

predicates.title_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking relief on the basis of title to property.
predicates.plaintiff_proves_title: The plaintiff establishes title to the property.

members.legal_issue: In a title-based possession suit under the later limitation framework, the defendant bears the burden of proving that title was acquired by adverse possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession based on asserted title to the property.
The Court explained that the applicable limitation framework had changed from the earlier framework, under which a plaintiff had to plead and prove possession within the relevant period.
The Court stated that under the later framework the plaintiff succeeds by proving title, while the defendant must prove adverse possession to defeat that claim.
members.legal_principle: Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 place the burden on the defendant to prove adverse possession when seeking to defeat a plaintiff’s title-based possession claim; this differs from Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908. The Court relied on Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagdish Kalita and also referred to P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, Binapani Paul v. Pratima Ghosh, Kamakshi Builders v. Ambedkar Educational Society, and Bakhtiyar Hussai v. Hafiz Khan.
members.conclusion: For a title-based possession claim under the later framework, the defendant bears the burden of proving acquisition of title by adverse possession.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit_under_later_: The plaintiff brought a suit for possession of property based on title under the later limitation framework.
predicates.defendant_seeks_to_defeat_claim_by_adver: The defendant relied on alleged adverse possession to defeat the plaintiff’s title-based claim.

members.legal_issue: In a suit for possession based on title, the defendant’s possession bars the claim through limitation only if the defendant establishes adverse possession, including the required intention to possess as owner.
material_facts: The plaintiffs established title to the property by inheritance.
The defendant did not plead that he had perfected title by adverse possession and stated that his possession was not adverse to the true owner.
The defendant did not intend to raise an adverse-possession plea before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, limitation for possession based on title begins when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse, and the plaintiff need not prove possession within the preceding twelve years. A defendant relying on adverse possession must plead and prove the facts establishing it, including exclusive possession and animus possidendi. The Court relied on Vasantiben Prahladji Nayak v. Somnath Muljibhai Nayak, Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagdish Kalita, and Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because the plaintiffs had proved title and the defendant had not pleaded adverse possession; the burden to establish adverse possession rested on the defendant.

rule.if: appeal_in_title_based_possession_suit and plaintiffs_proved_title and not defendant_pleaded_adverse_possession

predicates.appeal_in_title_based_possession_suit: The matter is an appeal in a suit seeking possession on the basis of title.
predicates.plaintiffs_proved_title: The claimants established their title to the property.
predicates.defendant_pleaded_adverse_possession: The defendant pleaded that possession had become adverse to the true owner and had perfected title by adverse possession.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking possession based on title is governed by the limitation applicable to title-based possession even when it also seeks a declaration.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought both a declaration concerning their rights and possession of the land based on title.
Possession was handed over to the opposing side in 1978, and the suit was filed in 1987.
The appellants argued that the three-year limitation for a declaratory suit applied.
members.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a twelve-year limitation period for a suit for possession of immovable property based on title, running from when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse. A declaration sought as part of such a possession suit does not make the suit one governed by the shorter period for a declaration alone. The Court distinguished L.C. Hanumanthappa v. H.B. Shivakumar, (2016) 1 SCC 332, because that was a suit for declaration alone, not for both declaration and possession.
members.conclusion: The suit was governed by Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and was within limitation because it was filed within twelve years of the possession becoming adverse.

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_title: The claimant seeks possession of immovable property on the basis of title.
predicates.declaration_also_claimed: The claimant also seeks a declaration concerning title or rights in the property.
predicates.filed_within_adverse_possession_period: The suit is filed within the applicable period measured from when the opposing possession became adverse.

members.legal_issue: A title-based suit seeking possession as a consequence of a declaration of title is governed by the limitation rule for possession claims, not the rule for declaratory relief alone.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title and an injunction, and alternatively sought vacant possession if found to be out of possession.
The claim for possession was framed as consequential to the plaintiff’s asserted title to the property.
The High Court treated the suit principally as one for declaration and applied the limitation rule for declaratory relief.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Article 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which concerns declaratory suits, from Article 65, which concerns possession of immovable property based on title. Where possession is sought as a consequence of declaration of title, Article 58 does not apply to that possession claim.
members.conclusion: The limitation rule for declaratory relief alone did not govern the suit where possession was sought as a consequence of the declaration of title.

predicates.title_based_property_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit asserting title to immovable property.
predicates.possession_sought_as_consequence_of_titl: The plaintiff sought possession of the property as relief consequent on the asserted title.

members.legal_issue: A representative suit seeking recovery of trust property is governed by the limitation rule for possession rather than the rule for a mere declaration.
material_facts: Creditors brought a representative suit seeking a declaration that transferred properties remained subject to a trust, appointment of an administrator, and recovery of the properties into the administrator’s possession.
The suit was valued as a claim for possession, and defendants in possession were joined on that basis.
members.legal_principle: The applicable limitation article depends on the plaint read as a whole and properly construed, including the substance of the relief sought rather than its form. A suit seeking possession of property for delivery to a newly appointed administrator is not a mere declaratory suit. The Court distinguished the rule in Rani Chhatra Kumari Devi v. Prince Mohan Bikram Shah, which concerned a beneficiary’s claim to possession as owner.
members.conclusion: Read as a whole, the suit sought possession as well as a declaration and was governed by Article 134, not Article 120, of the Limitation Act; it was therefore within time.

predicates.representative_trust_suit: Creditors brought the suit on behalf of a general body of creditors under a representative procedure.
predicates.seeks_recovery_of_trust_property: The plaintiffs sought recovery of trust property into the possession of an administrator.
predicates.suit_valued_as_possession_claim: The plaintiffs valued the suit on the basis that possession of the properties was sought.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff in a title-based suit governed by the former limitation regime who admits dispossession or ouster bears the burden of proving possession within the limitation period.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership through a court auction purchaser and sought partition and possession of a share of the house.
The plaint alleged that the defendants asserted ownership, prevented tenants from paying rent to the plaintiff, and obstructed the plaintiff from managing the house and collecting rent.
The defendants pleaded that they had been in adverse possession for more than twelve years.
The plaintiff's own allegations therefore amounted to an admission of dispossession or ouster.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908, as applicable to the case, a title-based plaintiff who admits dispossession must establish possession within twelve years. Section 3 required the court to determine whether the suit was within time. The Court relied on Bindhyachal Chand v. Ram Gharib Chand for the distinction between the burdens under Articles 142 and 144, and distinguished Manikyala Rao v. Narasimhaswami because the pleadings there did not admit dispossession and symbolic possession there interrupted adverse possession within the relevant period. The Court noted that the 1963 Act clarified the position but did not decide the law under that Act.
members.conclusion: The plaint disclosed an admitted dispossession or ouster, so the plaintiff had to prove actual or constructive possession within twelve years; the burden did not shift to the defendants merely because they were co-sharers.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking possession or partition on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.former_limitation_framework: The suit was governed by the former limitation regime applicable to title-based possession claims.
predicates.plaintiff_admitted_dispossession_or_oust: The plaintiff's pleadings acknowledged that another person had excluded the plaintiff from possession or denied the plaintiff's rights in a way amounting to ouster.

members.legal_issue: In an ejectment suit where the defendant admits the plaintiff’s title and claims to have received possession from the plaintiff as a tenant, the limitation rule based on dispossession or discontinuance applies only if such dispossession or discontinuance is alleged.
material_facts: The plaintiff asserted title and continued possession, and sought possession only in the alternative if he were deemed dispossessed because of criminal proceedings.
The defendants admitted the plaintiff’s title and claimed that the plaintiff had given them the land to cultivate as tenants, while also asserting occupancy rights.
Neither side alleged that the plaintiff had been dispossessed or had discontinued possession.
The defendants’ asserted settlement and possession were rejected by the appellate court.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 142 and 144 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, where a defendant admits the plaintiff’s title and admits deriving possession from the plaintiff as a tenant, the case proceeds on the defendant’s plea; for deciding which article applies, dispossession or discontinuance within Article 142 is not assumed when neither party alleges it. The Court approved Jaldhari v. Rajendra Singh, A.I.R. 1958 Pat. 386. It distinguished The Official Receiver of East Godavari v. Chava Govinda Raju, I.L.R. [1940] Mad. 953, and Behari Lal v. Sundar Das, I.L.R. (1935) 16 Lah. 442, where the defendant asserted an independent title. It also referred to Kumbham Lakshmanna v. Tangirala Venkateswarlu, (1948-49) L.R. 76 I.A. 202, Seturatnam Aiyar v. Venkatachala Gounden, (1919) L.R. 47 I.A. 76, and Nainapillai Marakayar v. Romanathan Chettiar, L.R. 51 I.A. 83, concerning the burden where tenants claim occupancy rights.
members.conclusion: Article 144, rather than Article 142 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, applied, and the suit was not barred by limitation.

predicates.ejectment_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking recovery of land from persons in possession.
predicates.defendant_admits_plaintiff_title: The defendant admitted that the plaintiff held title to the land.
predicates.defendant_claims_possession_derived_as_t: The defendant claimed that the plaintiff had given the land to the defendant to cultivate as a tenant.
predicates.neither_side_alleges_dispossession_or_di: Neither party alleged that the plaintiff had been dispossessed or had discontinued possession.

members.legal_issue: A person who has perfected title to immovable property by adverse possession may sue to protect that title or recover possession after it is infringed.
material_facts: The Court considered a common legal question in connected matters about whether a person claiming title through adverse possession could sue for declaration, protection of possession, or restoration of possession.
The question included interference or dispossession by a former owner whose title had been extinguished, or by another person.

Earlier decisions had treated adverse possession as available to a plaintiff as well as a defendant; a contrary observation in a later decision had not been contested or supported by consideration of the earlier authorities.
members.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits a suit for possession based on title, and title includes title perfected by adverse possession. Under Section 27, expiry of the limitation period extinguishes the owner's right; the possessor's perfected right may then be asserted as a plaintiff, not merely raised as a defendant. The Court relied on Sarangadeva Periya Matam v. Ramaswami Goundar, Balkrishan v. Satyaprakash, Des Raj v. Bhagat Ram, Kshitish Chandra Bose v. Commissioner of Ranchi, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, Padminibai v. Tangavva, Mohammed Fateh Nasib v. Swarup Chand Hukum Chand, S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, and Mandal Revenue Officer v. Goundla Venkaiah. It overruled the contrary rule in Gurudwara Sahib v. Gram Panchayat Village Sirthala and decisions relying on it, including State of Uttarakhand v. Mandir Shri Lakshmi Siddh Maharaj and Dharampal v. Punjab Wakf Board.
members.conclusion: A person who has perfected title by adverse possession may use that title as a basis for a suit to protect possession or recover possession, and may sue when any of that person's rights are infringed.

predicates.kind_civil_property_suit: The proceeding is a civil claim concerning possession or other rights in immovable property.
predicates.claimant_perfected_adverse_title: The claimant acquired title through possession that met the requirements for adverse possession for the legally required period.
predicates.claimant_rights_infringed: Another person interfered with the claimant's rights or dispossessed the claimant.

members.legal_issue: A person whose possession has matured into title by adverse possession may sue for possession after dispossession, but must clearly plead and prove adverse possession, including when the possession became adverse.
material_facts: The plaintiff alternatively relied on the alleged real purchaser’s and then the plaintiff’s long possession as having extinguished the certified purchaser’s title.
The plaint stated that the alleged real purchaser continued in possession but did not allege that the possession became hostile to the certified purchaser or state when it became adverse.
The record contained no evidence of when possession became adverse; references to uninterrupted possession for several years and to acquired title appeared only in the relief clause.
members.legal_principle: Under the Limitation Act, possession that ripens into title may support a suit for possession after dispossession, independently of the benami transaction. Adverse possession must be adequate in continuity, publicity, and extent, and the pleading must at least identify when possession became adverse so that the start of limitation can be determined. Long possession alone, or a statement in the prayer for relief, is not enough. The Court referred to Sukan v. Krishanand, Sri Bhagwan Singh v. Ram Basi Kuer, and Bishun Dayal v. Kesho Prasad; it noted that Bishun Dayal did not accept an alternative possession-based claim without a proper plea.
members.conclusion: Although a person whose possession has matured into title may sue for possession after being dispossessed, the alternative claim failed because adverse possession was not adequately pleaded or proved.

rule.if: title_or_possession_suit and adverse_possession_relied_on and hostility_start_not_pleaded and adverse_possession_timing_unproved

predicates.title_or_possession_suit: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking title to property or possession of it.
predicates.adverse_possession_relied_on: The plaintiff relies on possession said to have become adverse to another person’s title.
predicates.hostility_start_not_pleaded: The plaintiff does not clearly plead when possession became hostile to the person whose title is affected.
predicates.adverse_possession_timing_unproved: The evidence does not establish when the possession became adverse.

members.legal_issue: In a suit for possession based on title governed by the applicable title-based limitation rule, the court must determine the claimant's title even if the defendant has not pleaded adverse possession.
material_facts: The municipality filed its possession suit after the Limitation Act, 1963 had come into force.
The suit sought possession on the basis of the municipality's asserted title, which the defendants denied.
The defendants had not pleaded adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applied to the suit for possession based on title. Because the defendants denied the claimant's title, the court had to determine title notwithstanding the absence of a plea of adverse possession. The Court cited no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applied, and the court had to decide whether the municipality had title even though the defendants had not pleaded adverse possession.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit for possession on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.suit_filed_after_limitation_law_commence: The suit was filed after the applicable limitation law came into force.
predicates.defendant_denied_claimant_title: The defendant denied that the claimant held title to the disputed property.

members.legal_issue: In a civil suit for possession based on title, a plaintiff who creates a high degree of probability in favour of title shifts the onus to the defendant, and the plaintiff's burden is discharged if the defendant does not shift the onus back.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession on the basis of ownership and relied on rent records, account books, a rent agreement, tax records, and other evidence of possession through a tenant.
The temple produced no evidence establishing its title to the property.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the plaintiff's evidence created a high degree of probability of title and that the temple had not discharged the onus shifted to it.
The second appellate court reassessed the evidence despite those findings.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 defines when a fact is proved; in civil proceedings, proof is assessed on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. As explained in A. Raghavamma v. Chenchamma, the burden of proof remains on the party asserting a fact, while the onus of proof may shift during the evaluation of evidence. In a title-based possession suit, a high degree of probability supporting the plaintiff's title can shift the onus to the defendant; if the defendant does not shift it back, the plaintiff's burden is treated as discharged. Brahma Nand Puri v. Neki Puri states that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of the title established, not merely on the weakness of the defendant's title.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff's evidence was sufficient to shift the onus to the temple, and the temple's failure to discharge that onus meant the plaintiff's burden of proving title was met.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiff seeks possession of property on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.plaintiff_evidence_creates_high_probabil: The plaintiff's evidence makes it highly probable that the plaintiff holds title to the property.
predicates.defendant_fails_to_discharge_shifted_onu: After the evidence shifts the onus to the defendant, the defendant does not produce evidence sufficient to shift it back.

members.legal_issue: The annual value of a building governed by rent-control legislation cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that legislation, even when standard rent has not been fixed and the landlord may lawfully receive a higher contractual rent.
material_facts: The buildings were subject to rent-control legislation, but no standard rent had been fixed by the Controller.
Some buildings were let at contractual rents that could exceed the standard rent determinable under the rent-control legislation.
The municipal assessments used annual values exceeding the standard rent determinable under that legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3(1)(b) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 and section 116 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, annual value is the rent at which a building may reasonably be expected to let. Rent-control legislation supplies an upper limit on that reasonable expectation, even where standard rent has not yet been fixed. The assessing authority may estimate the determinable standard rent for valuation purposes. The Court applied Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation, [1970] 2 SCC 44, and Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers' Association, [1971] 2 SCR 423; it relied on Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Devi, [1962] 3 SCR 49, and distinguished Municipal Corporation, Indore v. Ratnaprabha, [1977] 1 SCR 1017, because the relevant municipal valuation provisions here had no non-obstante clause.
members.conclusion: The annual value was limited to the standard rent determinable under the rent-control legislation and could not be based on a higher contractual rent.

rule.if: municipal_house_tax_valuation_proceeding and rent_control_law_governs_building and standard_rent_not_fixed and assessed_annual_value_exceeds_determinable_standard_rent

predicates.municipal_house_tax_valuation_proceeding: A municipal authority assesses a building for house tax by determining its annual value.
predicates.rent_control_law_governs_building: Rent-control legislation applies to the building and provides for determination of a standard rent.
predicates.standard_rent_not_fixed: The authority empowered to fix the building's standard rent has not yet done so.
predicates.assessed_annual_value_exceeds_determinab: The assessed annual value is greater than the rent that can be determined by applying the rent-control legislation's standard-rent principles.

members.legal_issue: The reasonable annual rental value of a building for municipal rating cannot be based on rent actually received above the rent lawfully chargeable under rent-control law when a standard rent has been fixed.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the municipal assessment of a house for house-tax purposes under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911.
A fair rent for the house had been fixed under the New Delhi House Rent Control Order, 1939, and that fixation remained valid; no later fair-rent or standard-rent fixation had occurred.
The landlord actually received rent substantially higher than the previously fixed fair rent.
The municipal assessment was enhanced on the basis of the rent actually received.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1)(b) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 bases a building’s annual value on the gross annual rent at which it may reasonably be expected to let. Applying Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, the Court held that reasonable expectation must account for rent-control restrictions and their penal consequences: a landlord is presumed to act prudently and abide by the law, so unlawful excess rent cannot define the rental value for rating. The Court also referred to the rating principles in Patel Gordhandas Hargovindas v. Municipal Commissioner, Ahmedabad, and Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. M/s. Polychem Ltd. Sections 5(1) and 48(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, prohibited claiming or receiving rent above standard rent and provided a penalty; the Court also considered the standard-rent framework in section 6 and explained that the proviso to section 116 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, supported this understanding of reasonable rental value.
members.conclusion: The actual rent received above the standard rent could not determine the rateable value. The assessment had to be based on the standard rent, subject to the applicable statutory deduction, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: municipal_house_tax_valuation_case and rent_control_limits_chargeable_rent and standard_rent_previously_fixed and no_later_rent_fixation and actual_rent_exceeded_standard

predicates.municipal_house_tax_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns the valuation of a building for municipal house-tax rating.
predicates.rent_control_limits_chargeable_rent: The applicable rent-control law limits the rent a landlord may lawfully claim or receive and attaches consequences to exceeding that limit.
predicates.standard_rent_previously_fixed: A fair or standard rent for the building was fixed under the applicable rent-control regime.
predicates.no_later_rent_fixation: No later fixation of fair or standard rent replaced the earlier fixation.
predicates.actual_rent_exceeded_standard: The landlord actually received rent above the fixed fair or standard rent.
predicates.rateable_value_based_on_standard_rent: The building’s rateable value is based on its fixed standard rent rather than unlawful excess rent actually received.

members.legal_issue: Rateable value calculated by reference to reasonable annual rent is limited by the standard rent under applicable rent-control legislation when the municipal law does not provide an independent valuation method or override that limit.
material_facts: The property was assessed for municipal property taxes under a municipal law that calculated rateable value by reference to the annual rent for which the land or building might reasonably be expected to let.

The municipal law did not define rateable value in specific terms or provide a detailed independent method for determining it, and it contained no overriding clause displacing the rent-control legislation.
The Corporation proposed to value land made available for construction by reference to its market value.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, the reasonable annual letting value must be read with the Bombay Rent Act, including Sections 5(10)(b) and 7. A rent-control limit constrains reasonable letting value unless the municipal law supplies a specific independent valuation method or an overriding provision. The Court relied on East India Commercial Co. (P) Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, India Automobiles (1960) Ltd. v. Calcutta Municipal Corporation, Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, and Srikant Kashinath Jituri v. Corporation of the City of Belgaum; it distinguished legislation of the kind considered in Griha Yajamanule Samkhya.
members.conclusion: The rateable value was limited by the standard rent determined or determinable under the applicable rent-control legislation; market value alone could not displace that limit.

rule.if: municipal_property_tax_assessment and valuation_uses_reasonable_annual_rent and rent_control_limits_chargeable_rent and not municipal_law_has_independent_valuation_method and not municipal_law_overrides_rent_control

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: A municipal authority assesses land or a building for property tax.
predicates.valuation_uses_reasonable_annual_rent: The applicable valuation system measures the property by the rent for which it might reasonably be expected to let.
predicates.rent_control_limits_chargeable_rent: A rent-control system limits the rent that may lawfully be charged for the property.
predicates.municipal_law_has_independent_valuation_: The municipal law provides a specific, independent method for determining the property's rateable value.
predicates.municipal_law_overrides_rent_control: The municipal law expressly displaces the applicable rent-control limit.

members.legal_issue: The annual value of rent-controlled premises for municipal property-tax assessment is limited by the fair rent determinable under the applicable rent-control law when the municipal law neither overrides that law nor independently prescribes the valuation method.
material_facts: The property was a building let to tenants on agreed rent, but no fair rent had been fixed under the applicable tenancy law.

The municipal law valued property by the rent it could reasonably be expected to command and contained neither an overriding clause nor an independent method displacing the tenancy law’s fair-rent measure.
The High Court had treated the actual contractual rent as the basis for valuation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 168 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, read with Sections 4 and 8 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, annual value cannot exceed the fair rent determinable under the tenancy law. The Court applied Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation, Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, Dr. Balbir Singh v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, Morvi Municipality v. State of Gujarat, Bhagwant Rai v. State of Punjab, and New Delhi Municipal Committee v. M.N. Soi. It distinguished Municipal Corporation, Indore v. Ratna Prabha and Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation because the municipal law there contained an overriding clause, and Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation for the City of Ahmedabad because that municipal law independently defined annual letting value.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to make actual contractual rent the general basis of annual valuation; the municipal law must be read with the tenancy law, and the annual value is limited to the fair rent determinable under that law.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns assessment of municipal property tax on a building or land.
predicates.rent_control_law_applies: The property is subject to a rent-control regime that governs the rent recoverable from a tenant.
predicates.municipal_law_has_no_override: The applicable municipal law contains neither an overriding rule displacing the rent-control measure nor an independent method for determining annual value.

members.legal_issue: Municipal annual-value assessments of premises governed by rent control cannot exceed the fair rent determinable under the applicable rent-control law, even when a rent controller has not formally fixed the rent.
material_facts: The municipality revised rental values for tax assessment and increased some values beyond the fair rent determinable under the rent-control legislation.
The municipality argued that the rent-control limit applied only after a controller had formally fixed the fair rent.

The Court held that the same fair-rent measure applied whether or not the controller had fixed a rent; where no rent had been fixed, the municipality had to determine it using the statutory fair-rent principles.
members.legal_principle: Section 82(2) of the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, measures annual value by the rent the premises may reasonably be expected to fetch, meaning rent lawfully obtainable from a hypothetical tenant. The municipality cannot use an arbitrary value and is bound by the fair or standard rent under the rent-control law. If no rent has been fixed by the controller, the municipality must determine fair rent by applying the principles in section 4 of the applicable Act. The Court followed Corporation of Calcutta v. Sm. Padma Debi & Ors. [1962] 3 S.C.R. 49.
members.conclusion: A municipality may not assess premises above the fair rent determinable under the rent-control law, regardless of whether a rent controller has formally fixed that rent.

rule.if: municipal_tax_assessment and premises_subject_to_rent_control and (fair_rent_formally_fixed or fair_rent_not_formally_fixed)

predicates.municipal_tax_assessment: A municipality is determining the taxable annual value of premises.
predicates.premises_subject_to_rent_control: The premises are governed by a rent-control regime that limits the rent lawfully obtainable for them.
predicates.fair_rent_formally_fixed: A rent controller has formally fixed the fair rent for the premises.
predicates.fair_rent_not_formally_fixed: A rent controller has not formally fixed the fair rent for the premises.

members.legal_issue: The annual letting value of property governed by rent-control legislation cannot exceed the standard or fair rent permitted under that legislation.
material_facts: The municipalities imposed property tax on the basis of annual letting value under rules that treated actual rent as the basis for valuation in some circumstances, including where actual rent exceeded standard rent.
The challenged rules applied to properties that could be governed by rent-control legislation.
The applicable rent-control legislation limited the rent recoverable for properties within its scope.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(1) and 99(1)(i) of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963, annual letting value means the rent reasonably expected from the property, and property tax may be based on that value. The second proviso to Section 99(1), clause (e), permits a consolidated tax. The Court applied The Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, [1962] 3 SCR 49; Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, [1971] 1 SCR 248; Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers Association, [1971] 2 SCR 423; and Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, [1980] 1 SCC 685, which establish that rent-control limits define the outer limit of reasonable rent for valuation. Municipal Corporation Indore v. Smt. Ratnaprabha, [1976] 4 SCC 622, was distinguished because the statute there contained a non-obstante clause; the Court left open whether such a clause would affect the result.
members.conclusion: For property governed by rent-control legislation, annual letting value must be determined on the basis of the standard or fair rent determined or determinable under that legislation, and cannot be based on actual rent above that limit.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: A local authority assesses property tax by determining the annual letting value of land or buildings.
predicates.rent_control_applies: The property is governed by legislation that restricts the rent recoverable for it.
predicates.actual_rent_exceeds_controlled_rent_limi: The rent actually charged or received for the property exceeds the standard or fair rent permitted under the applicable rent restriction.

members.legal_issue: A municipal rule permitting actual rent to be used to determine annual letting value is applicable to properties outside rent-control legislation, but not to properties governed by it.
material_facts: The municipalities’ rules allowed actual rent to be used to calculate annual letting value, including in circumstances where standard rent had not been determined or actual rent exceeded standard rent.
The High Court had struck down Rule 5, while the municipalities argued that it could operate for properties not governed by rent-control legislation.
Rule 4 prescribed property-tax rates by reference to annual letting value.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(1) and 99(1)(i) of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963, require annual letting value to be determined consistently with the reasonable rent legally available from the property. Rules 4 and 5 must be construed accordingly: Rule 5 may operate for properties outside rent-control legislation, while rent-controlled property is valued by standard or fair rent. The Court relied on The Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, [1962] 3 SCR 49; Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, [1971] 1 SCR 248; Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers Association, [1971] 2 SCR 423; and Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, [1980] 1 SCC 685.
members.conclusion: Rule 5 is not invalid in its entirety: it is to be read as permitting actual rent as the basis for annual letting value only for properties not governed by rent-control legislation. For properties governed by that legislation, valuation must use standard or fair rent. Rule 4 is valid when annual letting value is understood consistently with that limit.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_valuation: A local authority determines annual letting value for a property-tax assessment.
predicates.rent_control_does_not_apply: The property is not governed by legislation restricting the rent recoverable for it.
predicates.actual_rent_used_as_valuation_basis: The local authority uses the rent actually received or charged to determine the property's annual letting value.

members.legal_issue: The annual ratable value of a property subject to rent control is measured by the reasonable standard rent, not by the actual rent received.
material_facts: The owners’ house was assessed for municipal tax using the rent they actually received from a bank tenant.
The applicable valuation definition measured a building by the rent it could reasonably be expected to fetch from year to year, subject to deductions.
The Court found that the valuation authorities had used actual rent rather than the reasonable standard rent determinable under the relevant rent-control law.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3(1)(b) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, annual value is based on the rent at which a building may reasonably be expected to let. Diwan Daulat Rai Kapur v. New Delhi Municipal Committee and Mrs. Shiela Kaushish v. C.I.T. establish that this expectation cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under the relevant Rent Act, even if the actual contractual rent is higher. New Delhi Municipal Committee v. M.N. Soi rejects actual rent as the measure where it reflects rent received in defiance of rent-control law. Balbir Singh v. M/s M.C.D. holds that standard rent is an upper limit and that the reasonable rent may be lower in light of the circumstances.
members.conclusion: The actual rent received was not the proper measure of annual ratable value; the value must be determined by reference to the reasonable standard rent under the relevant Rent Act, and the authorities’ assessment was illegal.

predicates.municipal_property_valuation: The proceeding concerns assessment of a property's annual value for municipal rating.
predicates.property_is_tenanted: The property is let to a tenant.
predicates.property_is_self_occupied: The property is occupied by its owner.
predicates.actual_rent_exceeds_reasonable_standard_: The rent actually received or contracted for exceeds the rent reasonably expected under the applicable rent-control principles.

members.legal_issue: Rateable value under rent-control legislation is based on the rent reasonably expected from a hypothetical tenant, subject to standard rent as an upper limit, and may be lower than that limit.
material_facts: The properties were assessed to property tax under municipal legislation defining rateable value by reference to the annual rent at which the property might reasonably be expected to be let.
The properties were subject to rent-control legislation, and the assessments raised the question whether rateable value must equal standard rent or could be lower.
Some actual or contractual rents, or the standard rent calculated under the rent-control legislation, could exceed the rent reasonably obtainable in light of the property’s circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under section 116(1) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, and the materially similar provisions of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, rateable value is measured by the annual rent reasonably expected from year to year. Where rent control applies, the standard rent is the ceiling on that expectation, not an automatic rateable value. The Court explained Dewan Daulat Ram v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, which held that rateable value cannot exceed standard rent but did not require it to equal standard rent.
members.conclusion: The assessing authority must determine the rent the owner could reasonably expect from a hypothetical tenant; that figure cannot exceed the standard rent determined under the rent-control legislation, but it may be lower.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: A municipal authority assesses land or a building to property tax by reference to its rental value.
predicates.rent_control_applies: Rent-control law limits the rent that may lawfully be recovered for the property.

members.legal_issue: For income from property governed by rent-control legislation, the annual value is measured by the standard rent determinable under that legislation rather than by the higher actual rent received, even when no standard rent has been formally fixed.
material_facts: The assessee owned a warehouse subject to rent-control legislation and had let its portions to a tenant under different tenancies before entering into a lease for the entire warehouse.
For the relevant income-tax assessments, the assessee received actual rent under the lease, but no standard rent had been formally fixed for the warehouse during the periods at issue.
The tax authorities and Tribunal used the actual rent to determine annual value; a later rent-control proceeding fixed a standard rent.
members.legal_principle: Sections 22 and 23(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 make the annual value the amount for which property might reasonably be expected to let from year to year. Applying Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1980), the Court held that where rent-control legislation applies, that amount cannot exceed the standard rent determinable under that legislation, even if standard rent has not been formally fixed or the time to seek its fixation has expired. The annual-value definitions in the municipal legislation considered in Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor were materially identical to section 23(1). The standard rent was to be worked out under section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958; the Court also noted that the later amendment to section 23(1) supported this interpretation.
members.conclusion: The annual value had to be determined using the standard rent of the warehouse portions as determinable under the rent-control legislation, not the actual rent received. The appeals were allowed to that extent.

predicates.income_tax_house_property_assessment: The owner’s income from a building was being assessed under the income-tax rules for house property.
predicates.property_subject_to_rent_control: The building was governed by rent-control legislation that limited the rent reasonably recoverable for it.
predicates.standard_rent_not_formally_fixed: No authority had formally fixed the standard rent for the building during the relevant assessment period.
predicates.annual_value_is_determinable_standard_re: The building’s annual value is measured by the standard rent determinable under the rent-control rules, not by a higher actual rent received.

members.legal_issue: The annual rental value used for municipal property assessment cannot exceed the applicable standard rent when rent above that amount is unlawful.
material_facts: The local authority assessed the premises using a monthly rental value higher than the standard rent subsequently fixed by the rent controller.
The standard rent was fixed before the assessment objections were finally determined.
The rent-control law made rent above the standard rent irrecoverable and penalised a landlord for knowingly receiving it.
members.legal_principle: Under section 127(a) of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923, annual value is based on the gross rent at which property could reasonably be expected to be let, reflecting its value to the owner and the rent realisable by the landlord. Reasonableness is assessed in the circumstances, and the law—including statutory limits and penalties—constrains what rent can reasonably be expected in the open market; hypothetical rent cannot include rent available only through unlawful transactions. The Court approved Corporation of Calcutta v. Ashutosh Deo, Bengal Nagpur Railway Company Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, and Municipal Corporation of the City of Rangoon v. Surati Bara Bazzar Company Ltd.; it distinguished Poplar Assessment Committee v. Roberts on the differences between English rating law and the Indian statutory scheme. It also referred to sections 2(10)(b), 3 and 33(a) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, which defined standard rent, rendered excess rent irrecoverable, and penalised its knowing receipt.
members.conclusion: The annual rental value could not be fixed higher than the standard rent applicable to the premises.

rule.if: municipal_property_assessment and rent_control_applies and standard_rent_fixed and excess_rent_unlawful

predicates.municipal_property_assessment: A local authority is determining a property's annual value for municipal assessment.
predicates.rent_control_applies: A rent-control regime applies to the assessed property.
predicates.standard_rent_fixed: The legally applicable standard rent for the property has been fixed.
predicates.excess_rent_unlawful: The landlord cannot lawfully recover rent above the applicable standard rent.

members.legal_issue: The annual value of rent-controlled premises for municipal assessment is limited by the standard rent even when no order fixing standard rent has been made.
material_facts: The premises were subject to rent control, but no order fixing standard rent had been made.
Under the rent-control statute’s definition, standard rent was the amount that would have been fixed had an application been made.
The tenant paid rent that was treated as the statutorily determined standard rent, while the municipal authority assessed the premises using the higher rent received by the tenant from sub-tenants.
members.legal_principle: Under section 168(1) of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1951, annual value is the gross annual rent at which premises might reasonably be expected to let. The proviso does not alter the meaning of that standard. Applying Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, which interpreted section 127(a) of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923, statutory rent limits the hypothetical rent. Section 2(10)(b) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950 defines standard rent, where no rent has been fixed under section 9, as the rent that would have been fixed if an application had been made under that section.
members.conclusion: The annual value had to be assessed on the basis of the standard rent payable by the tenant to the owner, not the higher subletting receipts.

predicates.municipal_annual_value_assessment: An authority is determining the annual value of premises for municipal assessment.
predicates.rent_control_limits_rent: The premises are subject to a rent-control regime that limits the rent at which they may reasonably be expected to let.
predicates.standard_rent_is_determinable_without_or: The applicable rent-control regime makes it possible to determine standard rent even though no authority has issued an order fixing it.

members.legal_issue: A municipal annual-value provision containing an overriding clause permits reasonable letting value to be determined without applying a statutory standard-rent limit when no standard rent has been fixed and standard-rent fixation does not apply to the building.
material_facts: The provision under consideration deemed annual value to be the reasonable gross annual rent and expressly applied notwithstanding other laws.

The earlier direct decision construed the provision to allow a reasonable-rent criterion without regard to accommodation-control law where no standard rent had been fixed and the building had never been let and was used in circumstances in which standard-rent fixation did not arise.
