The Court held that this construction was a reasonably permissible interpretation of the provision.
members.legal_principle: Municipal Corporation, Indore v. Ratna Prabha held that a fixed standard rent, absent fraud or collusion, represents reasonable letting value; where no standard rent is fixed and standard-rent fixation does not arise, reasonable rent may be assessed without applying the accommodation-control law. The Court distinguished The Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi because the provision there lacked an overriding clause, and noted that Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor, Dr. Balbir Singh, and Morvi Municipality distinguished Ratna Prabha on that basis.
members.conclusion: The interpretation that the overriding clause permits reasonable annual value to be determined without a standard-rent limit in those circumstances was a reasonably permissible construction and was not displaced.

rule.if: municipal_annual_value_uses_reasonable_rent and overriding_clause_applies_despite_other_laws and no_standard_rent_fixed and building_never_let and standard_rent_fixation_does_not_apply

predicates.municipal_annual_value_uses_reasonable_r: The applicable municipal rule measures annual value by the reasonable rent the building could be expected to command.
predicates.overriding_clause_applies_despite_other_: The applicable rule states that its annual-value measure applies notwithstanding other laws.
predicates.no_standard_rent_fixed: No standard rent has been fixed for the building.
predicates.building_never_let: The building has never been let.
predicates.standard_rent_fixation_does_not_apply: The building is used in circumstances in which fixing a standard rent does not arise.

members.legal_issue: The reasonable letting value of a building that has never been let and has no applicable fixed standard rent may be assessed without applying rent-control limits.
material_facts: The building had never been let on rent and was being used by its owners as a hotel.
No standard rent had been fixed for the building, and the question of fixing one did not arise.

The municipal authority assessed the building’s annual value using a reasonable letting value, and the owners challenged that assessment as exceeding the standard rent that could be fixed under rent-control law.
members.legal_principle: Under section 138(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, annual value is based on the gross annual rent at which a building might reasonably be expected to be let, notwithstanding anything in another law. If standard rent has been fixed under section 7 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, and there is no fraud or collusion, that rent represents the reasonable letting value. But where the building has never been let and standard rent does not arise, the non-obstante clause permits assessment without applying that Act. The Court distinguished The Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, and New Delhi Municipal Committee v. M.N. Soi because those cases concerned let premises or statutes without the same non-obstante clause.
members.conclusion: The municipal authority was permitted to determine the building’s reasonable letting value without regard to the rent-control provisions because the building had never been let and no standard rent had been fixed or was required to be fixed.

predicates.municipal_building_value_assessment: A municipal authority is assessing a building’s annual value for property taxation.
predicates.building_never_let: The building has never been let to a tenant.
predicates.standard_rent_not_fixed_or_applicable: No standard rent has been fixed for the building, and fixing one does not arise in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: The annual value of a building that has never been let and for which standard rent has not been fixed may be assessed by a reasonable criterion that does not follow the rent-control standard-rent provisions.
material_facts: The building had never been let and was operated as a hotel by its owners.
No standard rent had been fixed, and the question of fixing standard rent did not arise.
The municipal authority determined annual value using a criterion other than the standard-rent provisions.
members.legal_principle: Section 138(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 requires annual value to be based on the gross annual rent reasonably expected at the time of assessment, while its non-obstante clause permits departure from other laws. Where standard rent has been fixed and there is no fraud or collusion, it represents the reasonable letting value; where it has not been fixed and the question of fixing it does not arise, another suitable criterion may be used without regard to section 7 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, and New Delhi Municipal Committee v. M.N. Soi were distinguished because they concerned rented premises or statutes without the same non-obstante clause.
members.conclusion: The municipal authority was entitled to determine the building’s reasonable letting value without being bound by the standard-rent provisions.

rule.if: property_tax_assessment_dispute and building_never_let and standard_rent_not_fixed and standard_rent_question_does_not_arise

predicates.property_tax_assessment_dispute: A municipal authority is determining a building’s value for property-tax assessment.
predicates.building_never_let: The building has never been let to a tenant.
predicates.standard_rent_not_fixed: No standard rent has been fixed for the building.
predicates.standard_rent_question_does_not_arise: The circumstances are such that fixing standard rent for the building does not arise.
predicates.assessment_may_use_another_reasonable_cr: The assessing authority may determine annual value using another suitable reasonable criterion.

members.legal_issue: A municipal valuation law that displaces rent-control restrictions permits annual rental value to be determined by a reasonable assessment of relevant circumstances rather than by an automatic cap at the standard rent or the rent received by the owner.
material_facts: The owner leased a nine-storeyed commercial building to a tenant at a monthly rent of Rs. 75,000, and the tenant sublet premises to sub-tenants.
The municipal authority assessed annual value by taking account of rent paid by the sub-tenants to the tenant.
The Municipal Assessment Tribunal instead fixed annual value on the basis of rent received by the owner.
The governing municipal valuation provision contained a non-obstante clause displacing the operation of rent-control legislation.
members.legal_principle: Section 174 of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, read with Sections 193 and 194, governs valuation where the municipal law displaces rent-control restrictions. The Court distinguished the first group of cases, including Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers' Association, and Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, where rent-control limits applied, from cases involving municipal provisions that displaced those limits, including Municipal Corporation, Indore v. Ratnaprabha, Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation for the City of Ahmedabad, East India Commercial Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, Balbir Singh v. MCD, Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation, Srikant Kashinath Jituri v. Corporation of the City of Belgaum, and Government Servant Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Union of India. Even where rent-control limits are displaced, a determined fair rent may generally provide a reasonable guide, but it is not an inflexible ceiling; the valuation must reflect the circumstances of the case.
members.conclusion: The municipal authority was not invariably limited by the standard rent or the rent actually received by the owner. It had to determine the reasonable annual rental value by considering all relevant circumstances, including the actual rent received by the owner, any standard rent, rent received by the tenant from sub-tenants, prevailing rents nearby, and the peculiar circumstances of the property.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_valuation: A municipal authority is determining the rental value of land or a building for property taxation.
predicates.rent_restrictions_displaced: The applicable municipal valuation regime displaces rent-control restrictions when determining taxable rental value.
predicates.premises_sublet: A tenant has sublet all or part of premises leased from the owner.

members.legal_issue: A municipal property assessment cannot determine annual rental value by applying a flat rate per unit of floor area without a basis for treating the properties as comparable and deriving a reasonable annual rent.
material_facts: The municipality assessed textile mills and other special properties using fixed rental rates per 100 square feet of floor area.

The properties differed in location, age, construction and other characteristics, and the municipality did not establish that the factories were sufficiently similar for a floor-area method to provide a sound rental valuation.
The municipality did not show that it had derived the rate from the contractor's method or another recognised valuation method.
The governing scheme required the rateable value of each property to be based on the annual rent for which it might reasonably be expected to let from year to year.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(53), 2(54) and 127(3) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, read with rule 7(1) and rule 9(b), required rateable value to be determined by reference to reasonable annual rent. In Lokmanya Mills v. Barsi Borough Municipality, [1962] 1 S.C.R. 306, the Court held that a municipality could not substitute an arbitrary floor-area valuation for a valuation based on a recognised method tied to annual rental value. The floor-area method may be appropriate where properties are sufficiently alike, but it cannot be applied indiscriminately.
members.conclusion: The flat floor-area method was contrary to the Act and the taxation rules; the relevant assessments were invalid and fresh assessment lists had to be prepared.

rule.if: property_tax_assessment_proceeding and rental_value_required and flat_floor_area_rate_used and properties_not_shown_to_be_comparable

predicates.property_tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a municipal assessment of property tax.
predicates.rental_value_required: The applicable assessment scheme requires rateable value to be based on the reasonable annual rent of the property.
predicates.flat_floor_area_rate_used: The assessing authority determined rental value by applying a fixed rate to each unit of floor area.
predicates.properties_not_shown_to_be_comparable: The assessing authority did not establish that the properties were sufficiently alike for the same floor-area rate to provide a reliable rental valuation.

members.legal_issue: A municipality cannot assess a rate on the stated annual letting value of buildings by fixing that value solely by reference to floor area, without a basis connecting the calculation to the rent reasonably expected from letting the buildings.
material_facts: The municipality assessed rates on mills, factories, and related buildings by assigning an annual letting value according to floor area alone.
The affected property included structures of different kinds, including factory buildings, warehouses, godowns, and shops.
There was no evidence that the different structures could reasonably be let at the uniform rate used in the calculation.
Because the assessment turned on floor area rather than rental value, a taxpayer’s objection was effectively confined to the area and not the valuation.
The affected taxpayer paid the demanded taxes under protest and sued to recover the amounts claimed to exceed the taxes lawfully due.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 73, 75, and 78 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, a rate on lands or buildings could be assessed on capital value or annual letting value. Section 3(1) defined annual letting value by reference to the rent for which the property might reasonably be expected to let from year to year. A municipality could not substitute an unsanctioned method that ignored both bases, bore no demonstrated relationship to expected rent, and made the statutory opportunity to object to valuation ineffective. The Privy Council decision in The Madras and Southern Mahratta Railway Co. Ltd. v. The Bezwada Municipality was distinguished because it concerned a different statutory scheme and a recognised method of estimating rent. The approach in The Borough Municipality of Amalner v. The Pratap Spinning, Weaving and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. was not approved. Motiram Keshavdas v. Ahmedabad Municipal Borough was referred to regarding a levy not dependent on property value.
members.conclusion: The floor-area rule was illegal and ultra vires, and the appeals were allowed, restoring the decrees that had restrained demands based on that rule.

rule.if: municipal_rate_assessment_case and annual_rental_value_is_assessment_basis and floor_area_alone_sets_value and (no_evidence_area_method_reflects_expected_rent or materially_dissimilar_buildings_are_assessed_uniformly or taxpayer_objection_is_limited_to_area)

predicates.municipal_rate_assessment_case: A proceeding concerns a municipality’s assessment or demand of a rate on land or buildings.
predicates.annual_rental_value_is_assessment_basis: The municipality assesses the rate on a value stated to represent the rent reasonably expected from letting the property.
predicates.floor_area_alone_sets_value: The municipality fixes the stated value solely by reference to the floor area of the property.
predicates.no_evidence_area_method_reflects_expecte: The municipality offers no evidence that its floor-area calculation reflects the rent reasonably expected from letting the property.
predicates.materially_dissimilar_buildings_are_asse: The municipality applies a uniform calculation to buildings that differ in kind or rental character.
predicates.taxpayer_objection_is_limited_to_area: The assessment process effectively confines the taxpayer’s objection to the property’s area rather than its rental valuation.

members.legal_issue: A municipal authority cannot use subordinate bye-laws to determine property-tax rateable value by a unit-area formula based on property characteristics and value when the governing statute defines rateable value by the rent the property might reasonably be expected to fetch.
material_facts: The governing statute defined rateable value for assessable land and buildings by reference to annual rent reasonably expected from letting the property, subject to a specified deduction.
The impugned bye-laws used a unit-area method that applied assigned values and factors, including area, use, occupancy and age, rather than determining the rent the property could reasonably fetch.

The statute authorized bye-laws on matters relating to taxation under the Act, but the unit-area method was introduced without amending the statutory definition and method of determining rateable value.
members.legal_principle: Rateable value under a statutory formula based on the rent at which property might reasonably be expected to let must reflect the rent realizable by the landlord, not the value of the property. The test is the rent the property could lawfully fetch from a hypothetical tenant. Where property is let, actual rent may guide the assessment unless material shows that a different reasonable rent applies; for self-occupied or vacant property, comparable rents may be relevant. Subordinate bye-laws must remain consistent with the parent statute and cannot replace its prescribed basis of assessment. The Court relied on The Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, The Guntur Municipal Council v. The Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Council, Indian Automobiles Ltd. v. Calcutta Municipal Corporation, State Trading Corporation v. New Delhi Municipal Council, Government Servant Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Union of India, and Mehrasons Jewellers Private Limited; it applied Sections 2(42), 63(1) and 388(1)(A)(9) of the New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994.
members.conclusion: The unit-area bye-laws were ultra vires the governing statute because they substituted a property-value method for the statutory annual-rent method.

predicates.municipal_tax_bye_law_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a subordinate rule used to assess municipal property tax.
predicates.statute_requires_expected_rent: The governing statute requires rateable value to be based on the rent the property might reasonably be expected to fetch from year to year.
predicates.bye_law_uses_property_value_instead_of_e: The subordinate rule assesses value using property characteristics or assigned area values instead of determining the rent the property might reasonably fetch.

members.legal_issue: A tenant's time bar from applying to fix standard rent does not raise the annual value above the determinable standard rent, and the same valuation limit applies to a self-occupied building.
material_facts: For tenanted buildings, the existing tenants were barred by limitation from applying to the Controller to fix standard rent, leaving them liable to pay the contractual rent.
The Court considered that a hypothetical tenant would not share the existing tenant's limitation bar and could seek fixation of standard rent after a hypothetical letting.
One appeal concerned a self-occupied building.
The applicable rent-control legislation provided principles for determining standard rent, although no standard rent had been fixed.
members.legal_principle: The statutory yardstick is the rent reasonably obtainable from a hypothetical tenant, not merely the amount the current tenant is legally obliged to pay. A hypothetical tenant is not subject to the current tenant's expired limitation period, and valuation should not vary according to whether the building is let or owner-occupied. The Court applied Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers' Association, [1971] 2 SCR 423, and Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation, [1970] 2 SCC 44; it considered M. M. Chawla v. J. S. Sethi, [1970] 2 SCR 390, concerning the operation of the rent-control prohibitions and limitation, but held that it did not determine the hypothetical letting value for municipal assessment.
members.conclusion: The limitation bar affecting an existing tenant did not justify valuing a building at the higher contractual rent, and annual value remained limited by determinable standard rent whether the building was tenanted or self-occupied.

rule.if: municipal_house_tax_valuation_proceeding and rent_control_law_governs_building and standard_rent_not_fixed and (existing_tenant_barred_from_fixation_application or building_is_self_occupied)

predicates.municipal_house_tax_valuation_proceeding: A municipal authority assesses a building for house tax by determining its annual value.
predicates.rent_control_law_governs_building: Rent-control legislation applies to the building and provides for determination of a standard rent.
predicates.standard_rent_not_fixed: The authority empowered to fix the building's standard rent has not yet done so.
predicates.existing_tenant_barred_from_fixation_app: The current tenant is prevented by a limitation rule from applying to have the standard rent fixed.
predicates.building_is_self_occupied: The owner occupies the building rather than letting it to a tenant.

members.legal_issue: Rent-control restrictions inform the reasonable letting value even when the assessed premises have never previously been let or are occupied by their owner.
material_facts: The Corporation argued that the rent-control restrictions did not apply because the premises had never been let.
The Court considered the hypothetical rent a tenant would offer and held that the tenant would take applicable rent-control restrictions into account.
The Court also noted that the same valuation approach must apply to premises occupied by their owner.
members.legal_principle: Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act asks what rent the property might reasonably be expected to command. The Court held that the hypothetical tenant would consider the restrictions imposed by the Bombay Rent Act, including Section 7, even if the premises had not previously been let; otherwise owner-occupied premises could escape property taxation. The Court rejected the argument based on Section 6 of the Bombay Rent Act.
members.conclusion: The absence of a prior letting did not make the rent-control restrictions irrelevant to determining rateable value.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: A municipal authority assesses premises for property tax.
predicates.premises_never_previously_let: The premises have not previously been let to a tenant.
predicates.valuation_uses_hypothetical_tenant: The assessment determines reasonable letting value by considering what a hypothetical tenant would offer.

members.legal_issue: The statutory exclusion of appeals and reviews from summary possessory proceedings does not prevent the Supreme Court from exercising its special-leave jurisdiction to examine the resulting decision.
material_facts: The case reached the Supreme Court by special leave from a decree in a summary possessory suit.
The respondent argued that the statutory bar on appeal or review meant that the Supreme Court should not review the High Court’s decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(3) of the Specific Relief Act bars an appeal or review from an order or decree in a suit under that section. Justice Ramaswamy held that this does not restrict the Supreme Court’s plenary judicial-review jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: Justice Ramaswamy rejected the argument, holding that the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction under Article 136 is plenary and is not barred by the statutory prohibition on appeal or review. The judges divided on the principal possession issue and referred the matter to a larger bench.

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: A party sought the Supreme Court’s special-leave jurisdiction to challenge a lower court decision.
predicates.underlying_summary_possession_case: The challenged decision arose from a summary suit for recovery of possession.
predicates.statute_bars_ordinary_appeal_or_review: The governing law prohibits an ordinary appeal or review of the order or decree.

members.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on further appeals does not displace the constitutional jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear an appeal when the constitutional requirements for that appeal are met.
material_facts: The legislation provided for an appeal to the High Court from an order of a District Judge and stated that no appeal would lie from an order made in appeal under that provision.
The appellants argued that the restriction contravened the constitutional provision governing appeals to the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court interpreted the statutory appeal restriction as not overriding Article 133 or any other constitutional provision governing appeals to the Supreme Court. A statute cannot affect the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction where the constitutional requirements for an appeal are fulfilled.
members.conclusion: The restriction did not override the constitutional provisions governing appeals to the Supreme Court and did not affect the Court’s jurisdiction.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_appeal_restrictio: A litigant challenged a statutory provision limiting further appeals from an appellate order.
predicates.statute_limits_further_ordinary_appeals: The statute restricted further appeals within the ordinary statutory appeal process.
predicates.constitutional_appeal_requirements_are_s: The requirements imposed by the Constitution for an appeal to the Supreme Court are fulfilled.

members.legal_issue: The bar on disputing an unappealed remand order does not prevent the Supreme Court, exercising special-leave jurisdiction, from examining that order in an appeal from the decision made after remand.
material_facts: A High Court made an order remanding the case, and that order was not separately appealed.
After proceedings on remand, a later decision was appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave.
The correctness of the earlier remand order was challenged in that appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not bar the Supreme Court from examining an earlier remand order when hearing an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi and discussed Kshitish Chandra Bose v. Commissioner of Ranchi in relation to challenges to illegal or jurisdictionally invalid remand orders.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court could examine the correctness of the earlier remand order; Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, did not bar that examination.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_post_remand_de: A party seeks special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court from a decision made after a case was remanded.
predicates.prior_remand_order_was_not_appealed: The party did not separately appeal the earlier order that remanded the case.
predicates.prior_remand_order_is_challenged: The party asks the Supreme Court to examine the correctness of the earlier remand order in the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A judgment of a single judge in a statutory appeal to a High Court is subject to an intra-court appeal under the court’s charter unless the legislature has removed that right expressly or by necessary implication.
material_facts: The statute provided an appeal from the Tribunal to the High Court, and the High Court’s rules assigned that appeal to a single judge.
The single judge dismissed the statutory appeal, and a further appeal was brought under the High Court’s charter.
members.legal_principle: Under clause 10 of the Letters Patent and section 108 of the Government of India Act, 1915, an appeal to an established High Court is regulated by that court’s practice and procedure. A single judge’s judgment in such an appeal is appealable under the Letters Patent unless the legislature expressly or by necessary implication removes that right. The court relied on National Sewing Thread Co. Ltd. v. James Chadwick & Bros. Ltd., National Telephone Co. Ltd. v. Postmaster-General, R.M.A.R.A. Adaikappa Chettiar v. Ra. Chandrasekhara Thevar, Secretary of State for India v. Chellikani Rama Rao, Maung Ba Thaw v. Ma Pin, and Hem Singh v. Basant Das.
members.conclusion: A statutory appeal heard by a single judge is governed by the High Court’s practice and procedure; if the single judge’s order is a judgment and the legislature has not taken away the further-appeal right, an intra-court appeal lies. The statute at issue did take away that right, as addressed separately.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_to_high_court and heard_by_single_judge and single_judge_order_is_judgment and not legislature_removed_further_appeal

predicates.statutory_appeal_to_high_court: A statute provides an appeal to a High Court from an order of a tribunal or court.
predicates.heard_by_single_judge: The High Court assigns and hears the statutory appeal before a single judge.
predicates.single_judge_order_is_judgment: The single judge makes an order that qualifies as a judgment.
predicates.legislature_removed_further_appeal: The legislature expressly or by necessary implication takes away the right to appeal from the single judge’s judgment.

members.legal_issue: A statutory bar on appeals from orders in summary possession proceedings does not exclude an appeal under a High Court charter from an order made by a single judge exercising original jurisdiction unless the statute expressly excludes charter appeals.
material_facts: The suit was brought under a statutory procedure for recovery of possession, and a single judge of the High Court exercising original jurisdiction decreed it.
An appeal was filed before a division bench under the High Court’s charter.
The respondents argued that the statutory provision barring appeals and revisions made the appeal unmaintainable.
The statutory bar did not expressly exclude appeals under the High Court’s charter.
members.legal_principle: The statutory provision barring an appeal or revision from an order under the summary possession procedure bars an appeal under that provision, but does not cut across the High Court’s constitutional power or exclude an appeal available under its charter unless the statute expressly does so. Under clause 15 of the Letters Patent, an appeal lay from a judgment of a single judge exercising original jurisdiction. The Court relied on section 6(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 and clause 15 of the Letters Patent; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The charter appeal was maintainable, and the matter was restored to the High Court for the appeal to proceed.

rule.if: summary_possession_case and single_judge_original_order and charter_provides_appeal and statutory_bar_not_expressly_covering_charter_appeal

predicates.summary_possession_case: The proceeding was brought under a summary procedure for recovery of possession.
predicates.single_judge_original_order: A single judge made the challenged order while exercising the court’s original jurisdiction.
predicates.charter_provides_appeal: The court’s charter provides an appeal from a judgment of a single judge.
predicates.statutory_bar_not_expressly_covering_cha: The statutory restriction on appeals does not expressly exclude appeals available under the court’s charter.

members.legal_issue: An intra-court appeal from a single judge’s judgment of a High Court is maintainable under the applicable Letters Patent appeal jurisdiction.
material_facts: The respondent challenged the single judge’s decision before a Division Bench by a Letters Patent appeal.
The single judge’s decision was a judgment of the High Court, rather than a decree passed in appeal by a court subordinate to the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Clause 15 of the Letters Patent covers the appeal in question. Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to decrees passed in appeal by a court subordinate to the High Court, so it did not displace the Letters Patent appeal.
members.conclusion: The Letters Patent appeal was maintainable; a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not the required remedy.

predicates.intra_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal within the same High Court from a decision of one of its judges.
predicates.decision_by_single_high_court_judge: A single judge of the High Court issued the decision being appealed.
predicates.intra_court_appeal_maintainable: The appeal within the High Court is maintainable.

members.legal_issue: A further intra-court appeal is unavailable when a single judge decides an appeal brought under the procedural code against an order made appealable by that code.
material_facts: A court auction sale was challenged in an execution proceeding, and the application to set it aside was dismissed.
An appeal from that dismissal was dismissed by a single judge of the High Court.
A further appeal to a division bench was brought under the High Court’s Letters Patent.
members.legal_principle: Sections 104(1) and 104(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order XLIII Rule 1, form an integrated scheme: an appeal from an order listed as appealable is available under the Code, but no further appeal lies from the order made in that appeal. Section 4 does not preserve a further appeal contrary to this specific bar, and Clause 15 of the Letters Patent cannot avoid it. The Court approved Resham Singh Pyara Singh v Abdul Sattar and New Kenilworth Hotel (P) Ltd. v Orissa State Finance Corporation; it also relied on Shah Babulal Khimji v Jayaben D. Kania and the principles in Union of India v Mohindra Supply Company and South Asia Industries Private Ltd. v S.B. Sarup Singh. Gulab Bai v Puniya concerned a different statutory appeal and did not decide this issue.
members.conclusion: The further appeal was barred because the single judge had decided an appeal under the procedural code, and the bar on a further appeal applied.

rule.if: intra_court_appeal_proceeding and single_judge_decided_initial_appeal and initial_appeal_was_under_procedural_code and initial_order_was_made_appealable_by_procedural_code

predicates.intra_court_appeal_proceeding: A party pursued an appeal within the same high court from a single judge to a larger bench.
predicates.single_judge_decided_initial_appeal: A single judge decided an appeal from a lower court’s order.
predicates.initial_appeal_was_under_procedural_code: The appeal decided by the single judge was brought under the general procedural code.
predicates.initial_order_was_made_appealable_by_pro: The lower court’s order was among the orders the procedural code makes appealable.

members.legal_issue: A further intra-court appeal is unavailable from a single judge’s appellate order on an appealable interlocutory injunction order when the governing procedural law bars a further appeal.
material_facts: A company sued to challenge steps taken against it and sought an injunction preserving its possession of a hotel.
The trial court ordered the parties to maintain the existing position, leaving the company in possession.
On the other side’s appeal, a single judge vacated that order while exercising appellate jurisdiction.
The company then filed a Letters Patent Appeal, which the Division Bench held was not maintainable.
members.legal_principle: A right of appeal is statutory. Under Section 104(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, read with Order XLIII Rule 1(r), an appeal lies from an order concerning an injunction under Order XXXIX Rule 1; Section 104(2) bars an appeal from an order passed in an appeal under Section 104. Section 4(1) does not displace that express bar. Clause 10 of the Letters Patent does not provide a further appeal in this circumstance. Resham Singh Pyara Singh v. Abdul Sattar supports the bar on a Letters Patent Appeal from such an appellate order. Shah Babulal Khimji v. Jayaben D.C. Kania concerned a single judge exercising original jurisdiction and does not establish a right of further appeal here merely because the order may be a judgment within Section 2(9) of the Code. The contrary views in Sukuri Dibya and Birendra Kumar Majhi were held not to be good law.
members.conclusion: The Letters Patent Appeal did not lie because the single judge’s order was made in appellate jurisdiction and the statutory bar on a further appeal applied. The appeals were dismissed.

predicates.intra_court_appeal_from_single_judge: A party filed an intra-court appeal from an order made by a single judge.
predicates.single_judge_exercised_appellate_jurisdi: The single judge made the challenged order while deciding an appeal from a lower court’s order.
predicates.underlying_order_concerned_interlocutory: The order challenged before the single judge concerned interim injunctive relief.
predicates.governing_procedure_bars_further_appeal: The procedural law governing the appeal expressly prohibits a further appeal from an order made in that appeal.

members.legal_issue: A further intra-court appeal is not maintainable when a single judge has decided an appeal and the prohibition on a further appeal applies.
material_facts: A single judge of the High Court dismissed an appeal from the trial court’s decision.
The plaintiff then filed an intra-court appeal after the amended no-further-appeal provision had come into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 100-A of the Code of Civil Procedure, as amended by the 2002 amendment and effective from 1 July 2002, bars a further appeal where a single judge decides an appeal from an original or appellate decree or order. Kamla Devi v. Kushal Kanwar and Mohd. Saud v. Dr. (Maj.) Shaikh Mahfooz establish that an intra-court appeal filed after that amendment is not maintainable.
members.conclusion: The intra-court appeal was not maintainable, and its dismissal on that ground was correct.

predicates.intra_court_appeal: A party filed an appeal within the same High Court against a single judge’s decision.
predicates.single_judge_decided_appeal: A single judge decided an appeal from an original or appellate decision.
predicates.further_appeal_bar_applied: The rule barring a further appeal applied when the intra-court appeal was filed.

members.legal_issue: An intra-court appeal is not maintainable when it challenges a single judge’s decision exercising supervisory jurisdiction over an order of a civil court.
material_facts: The respondents challenged an appellate officer’s decision in a writ petition invoking Articles 226 and 227.
The appellate officer was a civil court, and the Single Judge dismissed the challenge to that court’s order.
The nature and substance of the Single Judge’s decision showed that the jurisdiction exercised was supervisory jurisdiction, not jurisdiction to issue a writ under Article 226.
The respondents then brought a Letters Patent Appeal against the Single Judge’s decision.
members.legal_principle: Articles 226 and 227 confer distinct jurisdictions. A judicial order of a civil court is not amenable to a writ under Article 226; a challenge lies, where appropriate, under Article 227, and no intra-court appeal lies from a Single Judge’s decision exercising that supervisory jurisdiction. Whether the Single Judge acted under Article 226, Article 227, or both depends on the pleadings, the jurisdiction invoked, and the true nature and character of the decision and directions. The Court relied on Radhey Shyam v. Chhabi Nath, Ram Kishan Fauji v. State of Haryana, and Jogendrasinghji Vijaysinghji v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The Letters Patent Appeal was not maintainable and should have been dismissed.

rule.if: intra_court_appeal_proceeding and appeal_challenges_single_judge_decision and underlying_order_is_from_civil_court and single_judge_exercised_supervisory_jurisdiction

predicates.intra_court_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an intra-court appeal against a decision of a High Court Single Judge.
predicates.appeal_challenges_single_judge_decision: The appellant seeks review of the Single Judge’s decision by a High Court Division Bench.
predicates.underlying_order_is_from_civil_court: The order challenged before the Single Judge was made by a civil court.
predicates.single_judge_exercised_supervisory_juris: The substance of the Single Judge’s decision shows that the judge exercised supervisory jurisdiction over the civil court.

members.legal_issue: A division-bench appeal does not lie from a single judge’s judgment exercising supervisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts or tribunals when the High Court’s charter excludes such judgments from appeal.
material_facts: The widow’s petition before the single judge was under Article 227 and challenged the Revenue Tribunal’s order.
The single judge set aside the Tribunal’s order and restored the Sub-Divisional Officer’s order.
The appellants’ intra-court appeal was dismissed as not maintainable, and they challenged that dismissal.
members.legal_principle: Article 227 confers supervisory jurisdiction, distinct from the power to issue writs under Article 226, and a proceeding under Article 227 is not an original proceeding. The charter’s exclusion of orders made in the exercise of the power of superintendence is read to cover orders made under Article 227. The court relied on Section 8 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, Section 38 of the Interpretation Act, 1889, National Sewing Thread Co. Ltd. v. James Chadwick & Bros. Ltd., Ahmedabad Mfg. & Calico Ptg. Co. Ltd. v. Ram Tahel Ramnand, Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, and State of Gujarat v. Vakhatsinghji Vajesinghji Veghela.
members.conclusion: No intra-court appeal lies from a single judge’s judgment given in a proceeding under Article 227; the appeal in this case was rightly dismissed as not maintainable.

rule.if: supervisory_review_proceeding and single_judge_disposition and order_exercises_supervisory_power and charter_excludes_supervisory_orders

predicates.supervisory_review_proceeding: The proceeding asks the High Court to supervise whether a subordinate court or tribunal acted within its authority and according to law.
predicates.single_judge_disposition: A single judge of the High Court disposes of the proceeding.
predicates.order_exercises_supervisory_power: The single judge’s order is made in the exercise of supervisory power over a subordinate court or tribunal.
predicates.charter_excludes_supervisory_orders: The High Court’s charter excludes orders made in the exercise of supervisory power from its intra-court appeal provision.

members.legal_issue: A Division Bench lacks jurisdiction to decide the merits of an intra-court appeal that is not maintainable.
material_facts: The Division Bench rejected the objection to maintainability and proceeded to decide the merits of the Letters Patent Appeal.
The appeal challenged a Single Judge’s decision whose substance was an exercise of supervisory jurisdiction over a civil court’s order.
The Supreme Court held that the Letters Patent Appeal was not maintainable.
members.legal_principle: A Division Bench must determine whether an intra-court appeal is maintainable by examining the nature of the jurisdiction exercised by the Single Judge. If the challenged decision is an exercise of supervisory jurisdiction over a civil court’s order, no intra-court appeal lies; the Division Bench cannot then reach the merits. The Court applied Radhey Shyam v. Chhabi Nath, Ram Kishan Fauji v. State of Haryana, and Jogendrasinghji Vijaysinghji v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The Division Bench’s decision on the merits was without jurisdiction and could not stand.

predicates.intra_court_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is an intra-court appeal against a decision of a High Court Single Judge.
predicates.division_bench_decides_merits: The Division Bench considers and rules on the substantive merits of the appeal.
predicates.single_judge_exercised_supervisory_juris: The Single Judge’s decision reviewed an order of a civil court in the exercise of supervisory jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A court that determines it lacks jurisdiction over the subject matter cannot decide a cross-objection on the merits.
material_facts: The High Court concluded that the civil court lacked jurisdiction over the suit.
Despite that conclusion, the High Court dismissed a cross-objection concerning the crediting of a payment against rent or damages.
The cross-objection raised a question on the merits.
members.legal_principle: A court lacking jurisdiction over the subject matter may decide the jurisdictional question but cannot decide a question on the merits. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not decide the cross-objection on the merits, and the order dismissing it was set aside.

predicates.appeal_with_merits_cross_objection: The appeal includes a cross-objection raising a question on the merits.
predicates.court_lacks_subject_matter_jurisdiction: The court determines that it lacks jurisdiction over the subject matter of the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A judgment of a single judge in a petition invoking writ jurisdiction is appealable to a division bench when the High Court’s charter provides an intra-court appeal and no applicable exclusion bars it.
material_facts: The court considered whether a single judge’s judgment in a petition invoking writ jurisdiction could be appealed to a division bench under the High Court’s charter.

The charter provided for an appeal from a single judge’s judgment, subject to specified exclusions, and the court found that a proceeding under Article 226 was not excluded merely because of the jurisdiction exercised.
members.legal_principle: The charter’s appeal provision covers judgments given in any jurisdiction unless that jurisdiction or judgment is expressly excluded. Article 225 preserves the existing High Courts’ powers and the continued operation of their charters and rules; the references in the charter to Section 108 of the Government of India Act, 1915, are read as references to the corresponding provision in Article 225. A proceeding under Article 226 is an original proceeding and, when it concerns civil rights, an original civil proceeding. The court relied on National Sewing Thread Co. Ltd. v. James Chadwick & Bros. Ltd., South Asia Industries Private Ltd. v. S.B. Sarup Singh, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Dr. Vijay Anand Maharaj, Commissioner of Income-tax v. Ishwarlal Bhagwandas, Ramesh v. Seth Gendalal Motilal Patni, Arbind Kumar Singh v. Nand Kishore Prasad, and Ahmedabad Mfg. & Calico Ptg. Co. Ltd. v. Ram Tahel Ramnand.
members.conclusion: An intra-court appeal lies from a single judge’s judgment in a proceeding under Article 226, provided the charter’s conditions are met and the appeal is not otherwise barred.

rule.if: writ_jurisdiction_proceeding and single_judge_judgment and charter_allows_intra_court_appeal and appeal_not_otherwise_barred

predicates.writ_jurisdiction_proceeding: The proceeding asks the High Court to issue a direction, order, or writ to a person, authority, or government.
predicates.single_judge_judgment: A single judge of the High Court decides the proceeding.
predicates.charter_allows_intra_court_appeal: The High Court’s charter provides an appeal from a single judge’s judgment in the relevant category of proceeding.
predicates.appeal_not_otherwise_barred: No applicable exclusion or other enactment bars an appeal from the judgment.

members.legal_issue: A procedural rule assigning certain writ proceedings to a single judge and providing for their final disposal does not, by itself, remove an appeal right granted by the High Court’s charter.
material_facts: The High Court’s rules ordinarily assigned certain applications under Articles 226 and 227 to a division bench.
A rule allowed specified applications to be heard and finally disposed of by a single judge notwithstanding those ordinary assignments.
The appellants relied on the rule’s words concerning final disposal to argue that no further appeal was available.
members.legal_principle: The rule’s non obstante clause permits a single judge to hear and dispose of specified applications, rather than merely issue an initial rule, despite the ordinary assignment of those applications to a division bench. It does not override the charter-based right of appeal. The court relied on Article 225 and the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, particularly Rule 18 of Chapter XVII.
members.conclusion: The words providing for final disposal by a single judge do not themselves bar an intra-court appeal granted by the charter; any applicable bar must arise from the charter or another enactment.

rule.if: specified_constitutional_proceeding and single_judge_final_disposal and procedural_rule_assigns_single_judge and charter_allows_intra_court_appeal and appeal_not_otherwise_barred

predicates.specified_constitutional_proceeding: The proceeding is one of the constitutional applications that the High Court’s procedural rules permit a single judge to decide.
predicates.single_judge_final_disposal: A single judge hears and finally disposes of the proceeding.
predicates.procedural_rule_assigns_single_judge: A High Court procedural rule assigns the proceeding to a single judge despite the ordinary assignment to a division bench.

members.legal_issue: A criminal complaint may be quashed where its allegations do not disclose an offence, but the inherent power to quash cannot be used on that basis unless the complaint’s allegations support that conclusion.
material_facts: The accused sought quashing under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The High Court quashed the complaint on the ground that it disclosed a civil wrong, rather than finding that the allegations made out no offence.
The Supreme Court held that the complaint could not be treated as frivolous at the prima facie stage on the facts presented.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, inherent powers may be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of law and secure the ends of justice. Proceedings may be quashed where the allegations in a complaint or FIR do not constitute the alleged offence or disclose any offence. The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal and K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar for these principles.
members.conclusion: A complaint that does not disclose an offence may be quashed to prevent abuse of process, but that ground did not justify quashing this complaint because the High Court had not found that the allegations disclosed no offence.

predicates.criminal_complaint_proceeding: A complainant has initiated a criminal proceeding alleging that another person committed an offence.
predicates.complaint_allegations_do_not_disclose_of: The facts alleged in the complaint do not constitute or disclose an offence.

members.legal_issue: The inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings may be exercised to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice only in recognized categories of cases.
material_facts: The challenged proceeding arose from a first information report alleging that the accused had made fraudulent representations that induced another person to pay money.
The accused sought quashing before the magistrate had considered the police report on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 preserves the High Court’s inherent power to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, but it cannot be used where the matter is specifically covered by another provision of the Code. The Court relied on In re Shripad G. Chandavarkar, Jagat Chandra Mozumdar v. Queen Empress, Dr. Shankar Singh v. The State of Punjab, Nripendra Bhusan Ray v. Govind Bhandhu Majumdar, and Ramanathan Chettiar v. K. Sivarama Subrahmanya Ayyar.
members.conclusion: Proceedings may be quashed where a legal bar prevents their institution or continuation, where the allegations taken at face value do not disclose the alleged offence, or where there is no legal evidence or the evidence manifestly fails to prove the charge.

members.legal_issue: A criminal prosecution challenged at its initial stage may be quashed when the uncontroverted allegations do not prima facie establish an offence or special features make continuation unjust and unlikely to serve a useful purpose.
material_facts: A private complaint alleged that trust officers and a trustee had acted together to create tenancy documents for a flat forming part of trust property.
The accused challenged the criminal proceedings before the trial was completed, and the matter came before the court under its inherent jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: The court applied section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. It stated the prima facie-allegations test and the additional consideration of special features, oblique purpose, and the likelihood that continuation would serve a useful purpose. Although several decisions were cited by counsel, the court found it unnecessary to refer to them and relied on no earlier case by name.
members.conclusion: At the initial stage, the court must assess whether the uncontroverted allegations prima facie establish an offence and may also consider special features bearing on the expediency and interests of justice in allowing prosecution to continue. It may quash the proceeding if the prospects of conviction are bleak and continuation would serve no useful purpose.

predicates.initial_stage_criminal_quashing: A person facing a criminal prosecution asks the court to quash it before the case has proceeded to completion.
predicates.uncontroverted_allegations_disclose_offe: The allegations, taken as uncontroverted, set out facts that prima facie establish a criminal offence.
predicates.special_features_make_conviction_bleak: Features of the particular case indicate that the prospect of conviction is bleak and that continuing the prosecution would serve no useful purpose or would use the court for an oblique purpose.
predicates.criminal_prosecution_quashed: The criminal prosecution is brought to an end by quashing it.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings may be quashed when the complaint does not prima facie disclose the charged offences and continuation would be an abuse of the court's process.
material_facts: The accused sought quashing of the criminal complaint and the summons issued on it.
The complainant was not a member of the society or a party to the registered sale deeds.
The registered sale deeds had been executed more than twelve years before the complaint, and no court had declared them void.
An earlier complaint to the district authority had been investigated, and the police concluded that no offence was disclosed because the dispute was civil in nature.
The complaint did not allege the ingredients of entrustment, action in a specified capacity, or deception and inducement.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court considering quashing at the initial stage asks whether the uncontroverted allegations prima facie establish an offence and may also consider special features, including whether continuing the prosecution would serve a useful purpose or abuse the process. Mathavrao Jiwajirao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, (1988) 1 SCC 692, states that proceedings may be quashed where the prospect of conviction is bleak and continuation serves no useful purpose. Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal, (2007) 12 SCC 1, holds that the power is to be exercised sparingly and carefully to prevent harassment, private vendetta, or ulterior pressure. Suresh v. Mahadevappa Shivappa Danannava, (2005) 3 SCC 670, quashed a cheating prosecution in light of a ten-year delay.
members.conclusion: The prosecution was an abuse of process; the appeal was allowed and the complaint and orders summoning the accused were quashed.

members.legal_issue: A criminal complaint must be quashed when, even accepting its allegations as true, it does not make out the charged offences.
material_facts: The buyer filed a criminal complaint alleging cheating-related offences, dishonest execution of a transfer deed, forgery, intentional insult, and criminal conspiracy in connection with the land sale.
The complaint did not allege that the sellers intentionally concealed the pending suit to induce the buyer to part with property.
The complaint contained no basic allegations making out the alleged forgery, intentional insult, or conspiracy offences.
The High Court declined to quash the complaint, and the sellers appealed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a criminal proceeding may be quashed where the allegations, taken at face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute an offence. This is the first illustrative category in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal; the power must be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. The Court noted that the principles in Bhajan Lal had been followed in Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill, Rajesh Bajaj v. State (NCT of Delhi), State of Kerala v. O.C. Kuttan, P.S. Rajya v. State of Bihar, and State of Orissa v. Bansidhar Singh.
members.conclusion: The complaint and the proceeding based on it were quashed, and the appeals were allowed.

members.legal_issue: The inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings should be exercised where the complaint discloses no offence and continuing the prosecution would be an abuse of process.
material_facts: The complainant challenged the refusal to quash a complaint and the cognizance taken on it.
The complaint and the statements recorded before cognizance disclosed no criminal offence, and the allegations amounted to civil liability between the parties.
The account of the agreement and payments was self-contradictory.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, quashing is confined to extreme exceptions. As stated in Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal, the civil character of an act alone does not justify quashing if the act is an offence; however, the Court found that no offence was disclosed here and that the cognizance was an abuse of process. The Court also relied on Sections 406, 419, 420 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code as the offences for which cognizance had been taken.
members.conclusion: The proceedings presented an extreme exception warranting intervention; the refusal to quash was set aside, and the complaint, cognizance order and process were quashed.

predicates.appeal_challenges_refusal_to_quash: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision that refused to quash a criminal complaint or the process issued on it.
predicates.complaint_discloses_no_criminal_offence: The complaint, taken at face value, does not allege facts constituting a criminal offence.
predicates.continuation_would_abuse_process: The criminal proceeding rests on material that discloses only civil liability and does not support the offences charged.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings should be quashed where the record, viewed as a whole, shows no criminal intent or act and continuation of the prosecution would amount to an abuse of process.
material_facts: The association obtained leased land to build a cricket stadium, with nominal rent for the stadium land approved under the applicable lease rules for a public purpose.
Additional land for a club house and hotel was leased for commercial use at commercial rates in accordance with the applicable rules.

Senior government officials examined and approved the land arrangements, but the officials who played significant roles in the decisions were not prosecuted or did not receive prosecution sanction; some more junior officials remained accused.
The association’s conversion to a not-for-profit company followed the cricket board’s mandate, and the State retained ownership of the leased land while the facilities were used by the public.
The proceedings alleged criminal conduct in the land arrangements and related acts, but the Court found that the record did not disclose criminal intent or acts constituting an offence.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, inherent power is exercised sparingly and cautiously to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, including where accepted allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence or the proceeding is clearly abusive. The Court applied State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd., Vineet Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and State of Karnataka v. M. Devendrappa. It also considered that the nominal rent for the stadium was authorized under the proviso to Rule 8(1) of the Himachal Pradesh Lease Rules, 1993, and that the association’s conversion was under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court’s refusal to quash the proceedings and quashed both FIRs, holding that no criminal case was made out and that continuation of the proceedings would serve no purpose.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings may be quashed where an unexplained, substantially delayed complaint following defeat in civil litigation is brought to harass the opposing party and abuse the process of law.
material_facts: The complainant’s agreement provided for completion of the sale by 1989, but the complainant did not sue for specific performance until 1996.

The opposing party had filed a civil suit in 1989, which resulted in a decree in its favour in 1996; the complainant later brought a separate suit to set aside that decree, which was dismissed in 2002.
The complainant lodged the criminal complaint in July 2002, shortly after the civil suit was dismissed and an appeal was filed, and gave no plausible explanation for the delay.

The criminal allegations substantially repeated allegations made in the unsuccessful civil suit, and the Court found that the complaint was lodged to harass the opposing party and involve it in prolonged criminal proceedings.
members.legal_principle: A delay in lodging an FIR does not by itself make a complaint improbable when properly explained, but unexplained or deliberate delay may be fatal. Courts should examine whether a frustrated litigant is using criminal proceedings with mala fide intent to harass or exact vengeance; proceedings used in that way may amount to abuse of process. The Court relied on Sahib Singh v. State of Haryana, Chandrapal Singh v. Maharaj Singh, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P., and Gorige Pentaiah v. State of A.P.
members.conclusion: Although the High Court’s reliance on the civil court’s findings was legally unsustainable, the Court declined to interfere with the quashing of the criminal proceedings because the unexplained delay and circumstances showed that the complaint was not bona fide and amounted to an abuse of process.

rule.if: criminal_complaint_quashing_proceeding and substantially_delayed_complaint and no_plausible_delay_explanation and complaint_follows_civil_defeat and harassment_motive

predicates.complaint_follows_civil_defeat: The complaint was made after the complainant had lost relevant civil litigation.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings may be quashed when a complaint concerning transactions already in civil litigation is initiated after a substantial delay with an ulterior motive to harass the accused.
material_facts: Civil suits seeking specific performance of agreements concerning the same transactions had been filed and were being contested.
The complainant had filed written statements in the civil suits denying execution of the agreements before making the criminal complaint.
The criminal complaint was filed substantially later than the institution of the civil suits and the filing of the written statements.
The Court found that the complaint had been filed with an ulterior motive to harass the accused.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, proceedings may be quashed where they are manifestly attended with mala fides or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive to wreak vengeance or pursue a private grudge. State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal identifies this as a category warranting quashing, while cautioning that the power should be exercised sparingly and with circumspection.
members.conclusion: The criminal proceedings were manifestly attended with mala fides and fell within the category of cases in which proceedings may be quashed to prevent abuse of process; the FIRs were quashed.

members.legal_issue: The High Court may use its inherent criminal jurisdiction to quash a prosecution that is an abuse of process, including a prosecution brought by a frustrated litigant after adverse proceedings when the allegations do not substantiate the charged offences.
material_facts: The complainant had unsuccessfully challenged the allotment in the rent-control proceedings before filing the criminal complaint.
A separate civil dispute between the parties was pending.
The complaint followed the adverse allotment proceedings and alleged offences based on affidavits filed in those proceedings.
The allegations did not identify evidence destroyed for the alleged screening offence, and the rejection of a disputed statement did not establish that it was knowingly false.
members.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, permits the High Court to exercise its inherent jurisdiction to prevent abuse of the process of a criminal court. A litigant’s frustration at losing related proceedings does not justify invoking criminal jurisdiction where the complaint’s allegations do not support the charged offences. No earlier case was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The criminal complaint was an abuse of the process of law; the appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the criminal proceedings were quashed.

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal proceeding initiated by a complaint.
predicates.complaint_follows_adverse_related_procee: The complainant brought the criminal complaint after an adverse result in related proceedings.
predicates.complainant_has_pending_related_dispute: A related civil or other dispute between the parties remains pending.
predicates.complainant_is_frustrated_by_adverse_res: The complaint was brought as an expression of frustration at the complainant’s adverse result in related proceedings.
predicates.charged_offences_lack_supporting_allegat: The complaint does not allege facts sufficient to support the offences charged.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings may be quashed against accused persons when the complaint and investigation materials disclose no prima facie offence or participation by them, and their implication is intended to exert pressure in a civil dispute.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that, after buying disputed property, he was dispossessed and threatened. The complaint also alleged that a family member had forged property documents and rented the property to another accused.

The appellants were not parties to, witnesses to, or facilitators of the disputed sale transactions; the materials did not connect them with preparing the allegedly forged documents or delivering possession of the property.

The appellants were not parties to the civil proceedings concerning the property. The Court found that they had been implicated as family members to exert pressure to obtain possession and settle the pending civil dispute.
The appellants challenged the High Court’s refusal to quash the criminal proceedings against them.
members.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure preserves the High Court’s inherent power to prevent abuse of the court’s process and secure the ends of justice. Under State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, illustrative grounds for quashing include allegations that do not prima facie constitute an offence or make out a case against an accused (categories 1 and 3), and proceedings manifestly attended by mala fides or instituted for an ulterior purpose (category 7). Vineet Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2017) 13 SCC 369, relying on State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, (1977) 2 SCC 699, explains that proceedings may be quashed where allowing them to continue would abuse the process of the court or undermine the ends of justice. The Court noted that these principles were followed in Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra, 2021 SCC OnLine SC 315.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have quashed the criminal complaint and all consequential proceedings against the appellants. The appeals were allowed, and the proceedings were quashed as to them; the case against the other accused was left to proceed independently.

predicates.challenge_to_refusal_to_quash_criminal_p: The accused sought review of a decision refusing to terminate criminal proceedings against them.
predicates.complaint_does_not_connect_accused_to_of: The complaint and investigation materials did not connect the accused to the alleged criminal conduct underlying the disputed transaction or documents.
predicates.accused_had_no_role_in_property_transact: The accused were not parties to, witnesses to, or facilitators of the property transfer and were not shown to have prepared the disputed documents or delivered possession.
predicates.accused_implicated_to_pressure_resolutio: The accused were implicated as family members in order to exert pressure over possession of property and settlement of a pending civil dispute.

members.legal_issue: The court may quash a criminal complaint that renews an unsupported allegation already considered in contempt proceedings that were closed at the complainant’s request, where the complaint is an abuse of process in a genuine property dispute.
material_facts: The contempt proceedings concerned the same alleged nondisclosure in the second writ petition and were closed after the complainant said he did not wish to pursue the remedy further.
The complaint under the Act was later based on that same alleged nondisclosure.
The parties had a continuing dispute over rights and possession of land, and the complainant had pursued criminal and revenue proceedings concerning it.

The record did not establish the intentional falsehood, malice, or vexatiousness required for the charged offence; the Court characterized the resort to proceedings as intimidatory and found no justification for launching the criminal prosecution afresh.
members.legal_principle: The inherent power to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice permits quashing a wholly untenable criminal complaint and prevents needless harassment through criminal prosecution. Issue estoppel prevents relitigation of an identical issue of fact determined between the same parties, but the Court noted that the contempt order did not record a finding on the alleged false affidavit; it relied instead on the circumstances of the closure, the absence of the offence’s essential basis, and the abuse of process. A second complaint is not invariably barred, but is not maintainable where the earlier matter was disposed of after full consideration on the merits. The Court relied on Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; Manipur Administration v. Thokchom Bira Singh and other issue-estoppel authorities cited in the judgment; Shiv Shankar Singh v. State of Bihar; Chandrapal Singh v. Maharaj Singh; and the authorities on binding judgments cited in its judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the lower courts’ orders, restored the Magistrate’s order, and quashed the complaint under the Act as an unjustified continuation of criminal process.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings may be quashed where a contractual dispute has been given a criminal character but the allegations and supporting material do not disclose the essential ingredients of an offence.
material_facts: The parties’ dispute arose from development agreements, a power of attorney, and a later memorandum concerning sale of property and payment of a loan.
The landowner alleged unauthorized sales of four flats, while the developer company asserted that additional sales were agreed as an adjustment for payments made toward the loan.

The developer company sought arbitration after the power of attorney was revoked; the landowner filed a criminal complaint during the dispute and withdrew the excess-flat claim from arbitration to pursue it in civil proceedings.
The Court found no dishonest or fraudulent intention and concluded that the dispute was essentially contractual and civil in nature.
members.legal_principle: Section 482 CrPC permits the High Court to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice. Under State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, quashing may be warranted where allegations, taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute an offence, uncontroverted allegations and supporting material disclose no offence, or the allegations are inherently improbable. G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P. and Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd. caution against giving a civil dispute a criminal cloak. The existence of a civil remedy or arbitration does not alone bar a criminal case; Priti Saraf v. State of NCT of Delhi and Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal recognize that civil and criminal proceedings may coexist where an offence is disclosed. Here, the lack of essential criminal ingredients justified quashing.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court’s order and quashed the FIR and the criminal proceedings arising from the charge sheet.

rule.if: criminal_quashing_proceeding and contractual_civil_dispute and no_dishonest_intent_at_inception and allegations_do_not_disclose_offence

predicates.allegations_do_not_disclose_offence: Even accepting the allegations and supporting material as presented, they do not disclose the essential ingredients of a criminal offence.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings for breach of trust should be quashed when the alleged retention of a contractual deposit does not disclose dishonest use or misappropriation and the dispute is civil in nature.
material_facts: A developer paid an interest-free deposit under a development agreement.

The agreement provided for return of the deposit when the developer handed over the constructed area allocated to the owner, but that event had not occurred because the contemplated development had not taken place.
The accused said the deposit was retained as security, including because the complainant remained in part possession of the property and had not fulfilled related obligations.
The complainant maintained that the agreement remained in force and had not demanded return of the deposit; it made no attempt to recover the money through a civil action.

The FIR and charge sheet alleged breach of trust based on retention of the deposit, but the material did not show that the accused had dishonestly used or misappropriated it contrary to law or contract.
members.legal_principle: Sections 405 and 406 of the Indian Penal Code require entrustment and dishonest misappropriation, conversion, use, or disposal of property contrary to a legal direction or contract. Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, proceedings may be quashed where the allegations, even taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute an offence, where uncontroverted allegations and collected evidence disclose no offence, or where the allegations are inherently improbable. State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal identifies these categories for exercise of inherent power; State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy recognizes that proceedings may be quashed to prevent abuse or harassment. Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd. cautions against using criminal prosecution to pressure a party in a civil dispute. The Court also treated the absence of any attempt to recover the deposit through civil action as supporting its conclusion that the prosecution was mala fide.
members.conclusion: The dispute was civil in nature and did not disclose criminal breach of trust; the FIR and charge sheet were quashed as an abuse of process.

members.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings arising from a civil land and contract dispute should be quashed when the allegations, even taken at face value, do not disclose the alleged offences and continuing the prosecution would abuse the court’s process.
material_facts: The dispute concerned land that had been dealt with through a power of attorney and an agreement to sell, and the parties disputed payment, land demarcation, title, and the validity of later sales.
The power of attorney was cancelled after notice, and the agreement to sell the disputed land had been treated by the complainants as terminated after they did not pay the claimed balance.
A civil suit concerning the disputed land and the relevant sale deed was pending.
The FIR alleged cheating, forgery, and conspiracy, but the appellants’ alleged acts of cancelling the power of attorney and selling land did not establish the ingredients of cheating or forgery.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a High Court may quash proceedings to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, but must exercise that inherent power sparingly and cautiously. Under Sections 415 and 420 IPC, cheating requires deception and the relevant inducement; for a promise, fraudulent or dishonest intention must exist when the promise is made, and later failure to perform alone does not establish that intention. Under Section 467 IPC, the prosecution must allege that a document was forged by the accused and that it is a document of a kind specified in that section. The Court applied R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab, State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, Madhavrao Jiwajirao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P., Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd., and Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Mohd. Sharaful Haque.
members.conclusion: The criminal proceedings emanating from the FIR were quashed to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice.

rule.if: section_482_quashing_proceeding and dispute_is_civil_in_substance and (civil_suit_pending or civil_rights_are_contested) and allegations_lack_offence_ingredients

predicates.section_482_quashing_proceeding: A party seeks to quash criminal proceedings by invoking the court’s inherent jurisdiction.
predicates.dispute_is_civil_in_substance: The underlying controversy concerns civil rights or obligations, such as contractual performance, property, or title.
predicates.civil_suit_pending: A civil proceeding concerning the underlying dispute is pending.
predicates.civil_rights_are_contested: The parties dispute civil rights or obligations that require determination on evidence.
predicates.allegations_lack_offence_ingredients: Even if accepted at face value, the allegations do not establish the essential elements of the offences charged.

members.legal_issue: A forgery-related FIR should be quashed where the authenticity of the documents is pending determination in a civil suit and the FIR rests on a handwriting expert’s opinion.
material_facts: A civil recovery suit was pending in which the authenticity of four receipts was directly in issue.

A handwriting expert opined that the signatures on the receipts did not match the purported signer’s signatures, but the opinion was not conclusive and could be challenged by evidence or assessed by the court comparing writings.
The FIR alleging forgery and related offences was registered after the expert’s opinion, while the civil court had not yet determined whether the receipts were genuine.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act, a handwriting expert’s opinion is relevant but not conclusive evidence. Section 73 empowers the court to compare admitted and disputed writings. Where the genuineness of documents is pending in a civil suit, an FIR based on the expert opinion alone should not continue; the Court exercised its power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash it. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The FIR should not continue while the authenticity of the receipts is pending in the civil suit; its continuation would prejudice the parties and amount to an abuse of process. The FIR was quashed.

predicates.petition_to_quash_forgery_fir: A person accused in a forgery-related FIR seeks to have that FIR quashed.
