predicates.sham_arbitration_used: The parties used an ostensible arbitration process to achieve an outcome without genuine adjudication of a dispute.
predicates.material_facts_withheld_from_court: A party suppressed or misrepresented material facts about the dispute or arbitration proceedings when seeking the decree.
predicates.decree_made_on_sham_award_is_invalid: A decree made on the sham award is invalid.

members.legal_issue: An administrative order alleged to be invalid cannot simply be disregarded as void before it is set aside through appropriate proceedings.
material_facts: The original order determining excess land had not been challenged by the landowners in the earlier appeal.
The order stated that notice had been properly sent to the address supplied and treated the owners as served.

The landowners did not raise non-service or lack of hearing in their earlier appeal or revision, and the later revisional authority set the order aside without considering the earlier proceedings and subsequent events.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the principle discussed in Smith v. East Elloe Rural District Council, 1956 AC 736, and State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, (1991) 4 SCC 1: an allegedly invalid order remains effective for its ostensible purpose unless appropriate legal proceedings establish its invalidity and set it aside. A party seeking a declaration of invalidity must use the proper remedy and comply with applicable procedural requirements.
members.conclusion: The original order could not be treated as void or illegal merely on the basis of an allegation of defective notice while it remained unchallenged; it remained effective unless set aside through appropriate proceedings.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_order: A proceeding seeks to challenge an order made by an administrative authority.
predicates.invalidity_is_alleged: A party claims that the order is invalid or unlawful.
predicates.order_has_not_been_set_aside: No competent authority or court has set the challenged order aside through appropriate proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A party affected by an order cannot treat it as non-binding merely because the party considers it void or invalid.
material_facts: The appellants challenged the validity of a notification affecting their land, arguing that it did not state the source of authority and that the required legal procedure had not been followed.
The validity of the notification was pending consideration in a civil suit, and the Court declined to decide that challenge in these proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Kerala v. M.K. Kunhikannan Nambiar, AIR 1996 SC 906; Tayabbhai M. Bagasarwalla v. Hind Rubber Industries Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1997 SC 1240; M. Meenakshi v. Metadin Agarwal, (2006) 7 SCC 470; Sneh Gupta v. Devi Sarup, (2009) 6 SCC 194; State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, AIR 1991 SC 2219; and Sultan Sadik v. Sanjay Raj Subba, AIR 2004 SC 1377. It also referred to Lord Radcliffe’s observation in Smith v. East Elloe Rural District Council, [1956] 1 All ER 855, that an order remains effective for its ostensible purpose unless proceedings establish its invalidity and obtain its setting aside or other relief.
members.conclusion: Even an order or notification alleged to be void or voidable remains binding unless and until a competent court sets it aside or declares it invalid; a party cannot decide for itself to disregard it.

predicates.party_affected_by_order: A person or entity is affected by an order made by an authority or court.
predicates.order_validity_disputed: The affected person or entity disputes the order’s validity or binding effect.

members.legal_issue: An interim order remains operative and must be obeyed while an objection to the issuing forum’s jurisdiction is undecided, unless the order is set aside or modified.
material_facts: The petitioner objected to the company-law forum’s jurisdiction and maintainability but did not obtain an order setting aside its interim directions.
The forum had made interim directions regulating company affairs while the proceedings remained pending.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether the company-law proceedings were ultimately maintainable and left the parties free to raise jurisdictional objections in those proceedings.
members.legal_principle: In Tayabbhai M. Bagasarwalla v. Hind Rubber Industries (P) Ltd., the Court held that an objection to jurisdiction does not immediately disable a forum from making interim orders. Such orders operate until the forum decides that it lacks jurisdiction, though they may then be modified or brought to an end. While in force, they must be obeyed, and a breach committed before the jurisdictional decision may be punished. The Court also noted that the relevant interim powers arose under Sections 397, 398, and 403 of the Companies Act, 1956, but expressly left the ultimate maintainability of the pending proceedings open.
members.conclusion: The jurisdictional objection did not itself invalidate the interim directions; they remained binding while in force, without the Court deciding the ultimate maintainability of the proceedings.

rule.if: pending_interim_order_proceeding and interim_order_made and jurisdiction_objection_undecided and order_not_set_aside_or_modified

predicates.pending_interim_order_proceeding: A proceeding is pending in which a forum has made an interim order while its authority to hear the matter is disputed.
predicates.interim_order_made: The forum has issued an interim order regulating the parties’ conduct or the affairs in dispute.
predicates.jurisdiction_objection_undecided: The objection to the forum’s jurisdiction has not yet been determined.
predicates.order_not_set_aside_or_modified: No competent order has set aside or modified the interim order.

members.legal_issue: An affected party cannot treat an operative order as invalid and disregard it without obtaining a court’s determination setting it aside or declaring it invalid.
material_facts: The lessor issued an order terminating the lease and acted on it by taking possession of the land.
The claimants argued that the termination was illegal and could be ignored while they sought protection of possession.
No court had set aside or declared invalid the termination order before the claimants sought relief against it.
members.legal_principle: An order does not bear a visible label of invalidity and remains effective for its ostensible purpose unless the necessary proceedings establish its invalidity. An aggrieved party must seek relief from a competent court within the prescribed limitation period. The Court relied on Smith v. East Elloe Rural District Council, Krishnadevi Malchand Kamathia v. Bombay Environmental Action Group, Pune Municipal Corporation v. State of Maharashtra, R. Thiruvirkolam v. Presiding Officer, State of Kerala v. M.K. Kunhikannan Nambiar, Tayabbhai M. Bagasarwalla v. Hind Rubber Industries, and State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh. It also held that declaratory relief under the Specific Relief Act is discretionary and that claimed possession could not cure the limitation defect, particularly because possession had been taken over.
members.conclusion: The claimants could not ignore the termination order as non est; they had to seek judicial relief against it, and their asserted possessory rights did not make the late declaratory suit timely.

rule.if: challenge_to_operative_order and claimant_affected_by_order and order_not_set_aside and claimant_seeks_to_disregard_order_as_invalid

predicates.challenge_to_operative_order: The proceeding concerned a claim against an order that had been issued and acted upon.
predicates.claimant_affected_by_order: The claimant’s asserted rights were affected by the order.
predicates.order_not_set_aside: No competent court had set aside the order or declared it invalid.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_disregard_order_as_inv: The claimant sought relief on the basis that the order could be treated as invalid without first obtaining a judicial determination against it.

members.legal_issue: An administrative order described as void does not automatically cease to have effect between parties when its invalidity has not been successfully established in proceedings between them.
material_facts: A land board rejected an application by two persons to participate in ceiling proceedings and found their claimed tenancy unproved and collusive.
Those persons challenged the rejection, and the High Court affirmed it in a revision between them and the State.
In a separate revision brought by the head of the family, the High Court held that the underlying ceiling proceedings were void because they had not been initiated following the required intimation.
The decision affirming rejection of the application to participate was not set aside in proceedings between the State and the two applicants.
members.legal_principle: An invalid administrative order ordinarily remains effective until it is set aside or otherwise held invalid by a competent court; “void” is relative rather than invariably absolute, and the legal effect depends on the nature and gravity of the defect. The Court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England, De Smith, Woolf and Jowell’s Judicial Review of Administrative Action, Wade and Forsyth’s Administrative Law, and Janardhan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad, which held that an appellate court with jurisdiction over an appeal may decide correctly or incorrectly whether the lower tribunal had jurisdiction, and its decision is not thereby a nullity.
members.conclusion: The use of the word “void” did not make the earlier order nonexistent for all purposes. It remained effective between the State and the applicants because it had not been successfully avoided in proceedings between them.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_decision: A party brought a challenge concerning an administrative decision.
predicates.decision_alleged_invalid: A party asserted that the administrative decision was invalid because of a defect in the proceedings.
predicates.decision_set_aside_between_affected_part: A competent court set aside or otherwise held the decision invalid in proceedings between the parties affected by it.

members.legal_issue: An order alleged to be a nullity must still be challenged before it can be treated as having no legal effect.
material_facts: The parties disputed the legal effect and challengeability of earlier orders concerning the property.
The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that an order could simply be disregarded as a nullity, stating that even a null order must be challenged.
The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh.
members.legal_principle: Even an order alleged to be void or a nullity must be challenged; the Court relied on State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh.
members.conclusion: An order cannot be treated as ineffective merely by asserting that it is a nullity; it must be challenged.

predicates.proceeding_concerning_effect_of_order: The proceeding concerns whether an existing order has legal effect.
predicates.operative_order_alleged_to_be_nullity: A party asserts that an existing order is a nullity.
predicates.alleged_nullity_order_must_be_challenged: The order must be challenged rather than simply disregarded as void.

members.legal_issue: A subsisting judicial order must be obeyed unless and until it is set aside, even when a party considers it void or without jurisdiction.
material_facts: A company court granted a creditor permission to pursue debt-recovery proceedings subject to conditions, including that no coercive steps be taken against the company’s assets during or after those proceedings.
The order remained in force and had not been varied or set aside when the recovery officer proceeded with the sale and confirmed it.
The sale and confirmation were treated as contrary to the court’s order.
members.legal_principle: A party or third party cannot decide for itself that a court order is void and disregard it; the party must obtain a declaration or an order setting it aside from a competent court. Until then, the order must be obeyed. The Court relied on Krishnadevi Malchand Kamathia v. Bombay Environmental Action Group, Jehal Tanti v. Nageshwar Singh, and Official Liquidator, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand v. Allahabad Bank.
members.conclusion: The order remained binding while it subsisted, and actions taken in violation of it were liable to be set aside.

predicates.court_order_is_in_force: A court has made an order that remains in force.
predicates.party_or_third_party_considers_order_inv: A party or a third party considers the court’s order invalid or without jurisdiction.
predicates.order_has_not_been_set_aside: No competent court has set aside the order.

members.legal_issue: A court may recall an earlier order obtained by fraud even after a special leave petition challenging that order has been dismissed.
material_facts: The State sought recall of an earlier High Court order after special leave petitions challenging that order had been dismissed.
The High Court considered a CBI report and other material indicating that the landowners and officials had misled the authorities about possession of the land.
The Supreme Court accepted that the earlier order was liable to be recalled because of the fraud found by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136, dismissal of a petition for special leave does not ordinarily attract the doctrine of merger; the order below is not replaced by the Supreme Court's refusal of leave. Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala explains this distinction and considers Abbai Maligai Partnership Firm v. K. Santhakumaran. In any event, fraud is an exception: an order procured by fraud is a nullity and cannot be allowed to stand. The Court also relied on the fraud principles in Lazarus Estates Ltd. v. Beasley, S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) Pvt. Ltd. and United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajendra Singh.
members.conclusion: The dismissal of the special leave petitions did not prevent the High Court from recalling its earlier order in the circumstances, because the order was alleged and found to have been procured by fraud.

predicates.recall_application: A party applied to the court that made an earlier order to have that order recalled.
predicates.special_leave_petition_refused: A petition seeking permission to appeal against the earlier order was refused without the matter proceeding as an appeal.
predicates.fraud_materially_misled_the_court: A party's deliberate deception materially misled the court when it made the earlier order.

members.legal_issue: A court of record may set aside a decision procured by fraud despite the decision's prior finality and earlier unsuccessful proceedings concerning it.
material_facts: The Tribunal's order in the claimant's favour was followed by dismissal of the State's appeal at the admission stage.
The Tribunal later dismissed a review application, and the High Court subsequently refused to condone delay in a further review proceeding.
The High Court issued a mandamus for restoration of the land, and the land was purportedly handed over to the claimant during contempt proceedings.

After finding that the original Tribunal order had been procured by fraud, the High Court exercised its authority as a court of record to set that order aside and directed that the land be taken back.
The earlier refusals to interfere, including the refusal to condone delay, did not prevent the High Court from addressing the fraud.
members.legal_principle: Article 215 of the Constitution gives a High Court, as a court of record, power to undo a decision obtained by fraud on the court. Section 44 of the Evidence Act recognizes that a prior adjudication may be shown to be vitiated by fraud. The proper course is to approach the court that pronounced the decision, or to appeal where an appeal is available: Kinch v. Walcott. The principle that no court will permit itself to be used as an instrument of fraud is also reflected in Guddappa Chikkappa Kurbar v. Balaji Ramji Dange, Hip Foong Hong v. H. Neotia and Company, and Rex v. Recorder of Leicester.
members.conclusion: The High Court had power as a court of record to undo the decision procured by fraud, and the earlier proceedings and orders did not bar that relief.

rule.if: application_to_set_aside_prior_decision_for_fraud and fraud_in_procurement_established and deciding_court_is_court_of_record and prior_proceedings_left_decision_in_place

predicates.application_to_set_aside_prior_decision_: A party asks the court that pronounced a decision, or a court with authority over it, to set that decision aside for fraud.
predicates.fraud_in_procurement_established: The court finds that a party deliberately misled the court to obtain the decision.
predicates.deciding_court_is_court_of_record: The court deciding the challenge is a court of record with authority to undo a decision procured by fraud.
predicates.prior_proceedings_left_decision_in_place: Earlier proceedings, including dismissals or refusals to grant relief, left the challenged decision in place.

members.legal_issue: A court has inherent jurisdiction to address a decree obtained by fraud, and res judicata does not protect a judgment so obtained.
material_facts: In a partition proceeding, a preliminary decree recognized the mortgagor’s sisters as having shares in the property.

The appellant challenged the decree, relying on documents indicating that the sisters had no interest and alleging that material facts, including their father’s death before the applicable succession law came into force, had been suppressed.

The High Court set aside an order allowing the challenge on the ground that the procedural provisions invoked did not empower the court to set aside the preliminary decree for fraud, and relied on earlier orders to bar the challenge.
members.legal_principle: Fraud vitiates judicial acts and cannot be protected by finality or res judicata. Under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, courts have inherent power to recall or set aside an order obtained by fraud on the court; the absence of an express procedural provision does not eliminate that jurisdiction. The court relied on S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) Pvt. Ltd., Smt. Shrisht Dhawan v. M/s. Shaw Brothers, Lazarus Estates Ltd. v. Beasley, Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal, and Sharda v. Dharmpal.
members.conclusion: The court has inherent jurisdiction to address a decree obtained by fraud, including under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If fraud on the court is established, res judicata does not apply; the High Court erred in shutting out the challenge on that basis, and its judgment was set aside for reconsideration.

predicates.challenge_to_judicial_decree: A person brought a court proceeding challenging a judicial decree.
predicates.material_facts_concealed_from_court: A party to the proceeding withheld material facts from the court when seeking the decree.
predicates.false_representation_induced_decree: A party made a false representation that induced the court to grant the decree.

members.legal_issue: A judgment obtained by fraud or collusion may be challenged and cannot be used to prevent a court from examining the matter as res judicata.
material_facts: The appellate court found that the father had used false gift claims or spurious mortgage claims to defraud creditors.
In the former suit, the defendants jointly admitted the plaintiff's claim, and the judgment relied on the alleged gift in that setting.
The evidence in the record supported treating the former suit as collusive or fraudulent.
members.legal_principle: Section 44 of the Evidence Act permits a party to show that a judgment, order, or decree relevant under sections 40, 41, or 42 was obtained by fraud or collusion. Fraud is an extrinsic collateral act that can vitiate judicial proceedings; the court must apply res judicata between co-defendants with care and caution.
members.conclusion: The alleged collusion or fraud was a relevant matter for the court to consider, and the former judgment could not be mechanically applied as res judicata.

predicates.judgment_invoked_as_bar_in_later_proceed: A party relies on an earlier judgment to prevent a court from examining a matter in a later proceeding.
predicates.judgment_obtained_by_fraud_or_collusion: The evidence shows that the earlier judgment was obtained through fraud or collusion.

members.legal_issue: A party may challenge an earlier judgment as fraudulent or collusive in a later proceeding without first bringing an independent suit to set it aside.
material_facts: A party relied on an earlier injunction decree in later statutory proceedings concerning common land.
The Panchayat alleged that the earlier decree had been obtained through collusion with its then representative.
The statutory authorities found collusion, but the High Court allowed a writ petition on the ground that an independent suit was required first.
The High Court did not examine the merits of the statutory authorities’ decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 44 of the Indian Evidence Act permits a party to show in a later proceeding that a relevant judgment was obtained by fraud or collusion; it does not make a prior independent suit to set the judgment aside a condition precedent. This accords with the authorities collected in Sarkar’s Evidence Act, including Bansi v. Dhapo, Rajib v. Lakhan, Parbati v. Gajraj, Prayag v. Siva, Hare Krishna v. Umesh, Aswini v. Banamali, Manchharam v. Kalidas, Ranganath v. Govind, Kamiruddin v. Jhadejanessa, Bhagwandas v. Patel & Co., Bishunath v. Mirchi, and Vijaya v. Padmanabham. The Court also relied on Spencer-Bower and Turner on Res Judicata and the principle that fraud or collusion may defeat an estoppel without active proceedings to rescind the earlier judgment. Section 11 CPC is relevant to the asserted res judicata bar.
members.conclusion: The statutory authorities could consider whether the earlier decree was collusive without requiring the Panchayat first to bring an independent suit. The contrary Full Bench rule was incorrect; the High Court’s judgment was set aside and the writ petition remitted for disposal in accordance with law.

predicates.collateral_proceeding: A party raises an objection to an earlier judgment in a later proceeding rather than in a separate action to set that judgment aside.
predicates.earlier_judgment_invoked_as_bar: A party relies on the earlier judgment as a bar or as the basis of an estoppel in the later proceeding.
predicates.collusion_or_fraud_alleged: A party alleges that the earlier judgment was obtained through fraud or collusion.

members.legal_issue: A party may challenge a decree as fraudulent in a collateral proceeding despite withdrawing an earlier suit that sought to set the decree aside.
material_facts: The purchasers had filed a suit challenging an arbitral award and a decree as fraudulent, then withdrew that suit.
They had already obtained a decree for specific performance in the suit in which they raised the fraud challenge.
The trial court found that material facts had been concealed and that the decree resulted from a collusive and fraudulent proceeding.
members.legal_principle: Section 44 of the Evidence Act permits a party to show that a judgment or decree was obtained by fraud or collusion in a proceeding in which it is relied upon. Fraud vitiates solemn acts, and a plea of fraud may be raised collaterally. The Court rejected the contention that Order 23, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure barred the challenge after withdrawal, and relied on Ram Chandra Singh v. Savitri Devi, Vice Chairman, Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan v. Girdhari Lal Yadav, State of A.P. v. T. Suryachandra Rao, Ishwar Dutt v. Land Acquisition Collector, and the other fraud authorities cited in the judgment.
members.conclusion: Withdrawal of the earlier suit did not prevent the purchasers from raising the fraud challenge in the specific-performance proceeding; a decree obtained by fraud could be treated as a nullity there.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding in which the challenge is raised seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.prior_suit_to_set_aside_decree_withdrawn: The party previously filed, and later withdrew, a suit seeking to set aside the decree.
predicates.decree_relied_on_alleged_to_be_fraudulen: The party alleges that the decree relied on in the current proceeding was obtained by fraud or collusion.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking to prevent the consequences of an operative decision by a competent authority cannot proceed on a suit for permanent injunction alone without seeking a declaration setting that decision aside or establishing its invalidity.
material_facts: The defendants stated that the land had been allotted and selected for the project after deliberation and consultation with an expert committee and by the competent authorities exercising their powers.
The plaintiffs did not challenge those decisions or seek declaratory relief concerning them; they sought only a permanent injunction against starting the project.
members.legal_principle: An operative order or decision remains capable of producing legal consequences unless it is set aside or declared invalid in appropriate proceedings; a party affected by it cannot simply treat it as non-binding. Board of Trustees of Port of Kandla v. Hargovind Jasraj applied that principle, relying on Smith v. East Elloe Rural District Council, Krishnadevi Malchand Kamathia v. Bombay Environmental Action Group, Pune Municipal Corporation v. State of Maharashtra, and other authorities. The Court also referred to Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy on the need for comprehensive declaratory relief where the dispute cannot appropriately be resolved in a bare injunction suit.
members.conclusion: The suit for a permanent injunction simpliciter could not be proceeded with because the plaintiffs had not sought a declaration concerning the competent authorities’ decisions.

predicates.suit_for_injunction_only: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking only an injunction against the consequences of an authority’s decision.
predicates.operative_authority_decision_not_challen: The plaintiff did not seek to have the competent authority’s operative decision set aside or declared invalid.

members.legal_issue: An administrative order cannot be invalidated in a collateral civil proceeding when its validity is not directly in issue and the authority that made it is not a party.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of a sale agreement and did not place the competent authority’s orders for review.
The competent authority was not joined as a party, and the orders were not challenged in an appropriate proceeding.
The orders were not found to be wholly without jurisdiction, and their validity was raised before the appellate bench without having been made an issue in the suit.
members.legal_principle: An order that may be void in relation to one person may be valid in relation to another, and even a void order is not necessarily non est. Its validity cannot be determined collaterally in the absence of the authority that made it. The judgment treats this as a settled principle and cites no earlier case for it.
members.conclusion: The appellate bench could not examine or effectively invalidate the competent authority’s orders in the suit or make strictures against the authority; those orders had to be set aside in an appropriate proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A contract for sale of immovable property does not create a property interest in the proposed purchaser under Indian law.
material_facts: The mortgagee sold the property at auction under a power contained in the mortgage deed.
The appellant was declared the highest bidder and paid the purchase price, but the conveyance had not been completed by a registered instrument.
The appellant argued that the auction contract transferred an interest in the property, relying in part on English decisions.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, expressly provides that a contract for sale does not of itself create any interest in or charge on the property. Indian law does not recognise the English distinction between legal and equitable estates in land; there can be only one owner, the legal owner. The Court followed Rani Chhatra Kumari v. Mohan Bikram and Rambaran Prasad v. Ram Mohit Hazra, and distinguished the English decisions because they applied a different statutory framework.
members.conclusion: The auction contract did not give the appellant an interest or right in the property that extinguished the society’s equity of redemption.

predicates.immovable_property_sale_dispute: The proceeding concerns the sale of immovable property and the rights asserted by a proposed purchaser.
predicates.sale_contract_only: The proposed purchaser’s claim to the property rests on a contract of sale.
predicates.no_completed_transfer: The transfer of ownership has not been completed by the legally required instrument.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to sell, without a completed transfer, does not confer title on the intended purchaser.
material_facts: The vendors had entered into an agreement to sell the land to a cooperative society before executing a registered sale deed in favour of the appellant’s predecessor.
The society had not obtained a decree for specific performance before the registered sale deed was executed.
The respondents produced no evidence that they were members of the society or that the society had allotted the land to them.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled principle that an agreement to sell does not itself create a right or title in favour of the intended buyer. No earlier case or statutory provision is identified in the judgment as the source of this proposition.
members.conclusion: The agreement to sell did not confer title on the society, while title passed under the registered sale deed in favour of the appellant’s predecessor.

predicates.no_completed_transfer_to_the_claimant: The claimant did not obtain a completed transfer of the property.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to sell immovable property does not itself transfer title or create an interest in the property, even if possession is delivered.
material_facts: The transaction form considered by the Court included an agreement confirming the sale terms, payment of the full price, and delivery of possession, with an undertaking to execute a sale deed later.
The purchaser might rely on the agreement as evidence of a completed transfer despite the absence of a registered conveyance.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 states that a contract for sale does not, of itself, create an interest in or charge on immovable property. Section 53A provides a limited protection concerning possession in part performance. The Court relied on Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam and Rambaran Prosad v. Ram Mohit Hazra.
members.conclusion: An agreement to sell does not itself transfer title or create an interest or charge in the property, whether or not it is accompanied by possession, subject to the limited protection available under the law of part performance.

members.legal_issue: A contract for sale of immovable property does not transfer title where the law requires a registered sale deed and no such deed is executed.
material_facts: The disputed land was immovable property valued at more than one hundred rupees.
The owner agreed to sell the land to the intermediate purchaser, but no registered sale deed was executed in that purchaser’s favour.
The intermediate purchaser later agreed to sell the land to the appellant and put him in possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that a contract for sale does not, of itself, create an interest in or charge on immovable property, and that a sale of property valued above one hundred rupees can convey title only by registered instrument. Section 53-A protects possession in the circumstances it covers but does not confer ownership. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. District Judge (1997) 1 SCC 496 for the rule that title remains with the vendor until conveyance by registered sale deed.
members.conclusion: The sale agreements did not transfer title to the intermediate purchaser or the appellant, and ownership remained with the original owner in the absence of a registered sale deed.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered agreement to sell does not transfer ownership or another interest in immovable property so as to defeat recovery proceedings against the property.
material_facts: A bank initiated recovery proceedings against a company and its guarantors, and the property was attached in those proceedings.
The claimant relied on an alleged agreement to sell made before the attachment, but there was no registered deed of conveyance.
The claimant asserted that he had taken possession under the agreement.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 54 and 55 of the Transfer of Property Act, an agreement to sell is not a conveyance and does not transfer title or create an interest in immovable property; a sale requires a registered instrument. Section 53A provides only a limited defence in proceedings brought by the transferor or a person claiming under the transferor. The Court relied on Suraj Lamp & Industries (P) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, (2012) 1 SCC 656.
members.conclusion: The alleged agreement did not transfer any right, title or interest in the property and could not defeat the recovery proceedings. The limited protection under the doctrine of part performance was unavailable in this proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A contract for sale of immovable property does not itself transfer ownership or create an interest or charge in the property.
material_facts: The parties had made a memorandum of understanding and agreements for the sale of the company’s land.
The purchaser relied on those agreements to claim an interest in the land, although the court was not deciding the merits or enforceability of the parties’ contractual rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 distinguishes a sale from a contract for sale and states that a contract for sale does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on the property. The court relied on Rambaran Prosad v. Ram Mohit Hazra and reiterated the position stated in State of U.P. v. District Judge, Dharma Naika v. Rama Naika, and Mrs. Saradamani Kandappan v. Rajalakshmi.
members.conclusion: An agreement to sell does not itself create title, an interest or a charge in the immovable property.

members.legal_issue: The English doctrine of conversion does not give a purchaser equitable ownership of immovable property under Indian law, although a contract may create an enforceable obligation annexed to ownership.
material_facts: The dispute arose from an agreement concerning immovable property.
The agreement provided for the property to be sold to the purchaser or, in an alternative circumstance, sold at auction with the surplus paid to the purchaser.
members.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, sections 40 and 54, distinguish an enforceable obligation annexed to ownership from an interest in the property. The Court relied on Rambaran Prasad v. Ram Mohit Hazra and Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam in rejecting dual legal and equitable ownership under Indian law. Equity may assist in interpreting Indian statutes that incorporate equitable principles, but the English doctrine of conversion cannot be transplanted wholesale.
members.conclusion: The English doctrine of conversion cannot be bodily applied in India, where an agreement to sell immovable property does not itself create an interest in the property. It creates an obligation annexed to ownership that may be enforced against a transferee with notice or a gratuitous transferee.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to sell does not itself constitute a transfer of land or create an interest in land for the purpose of the statutory restriction on transfers.
material_facts: The parties executed agreements to sell a share in land, and the purchaser sought specific performance.
The court found that the agreements did not themselves create an interest in the land and that the secured dues to the Land Development Bank had been repaid.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an agreement to sell does not itself create an interest in immovable property or amount to a sale; it enables the intending purchaser to claim specific performance on proving the agreement. The court relied on this distinction and also noted that the secured dues had been repaid. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The agreements were not barred as transfers under Section 48(d) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, and the purchaser could seek specific performance by proving the agreements’ terms.

members.legal_issue: An alleged contract and equitable part performance do not transfer title to property where the required registered instrument is absent and the statutory conditions for part-performance protection are not satisfied.
material_facts: The claimant’s father allegedly agreed to inherit the property in return for marrying a relative of the property owner and managing the owner’s property.
The claimant relied on the alleged agreement to claim title after the owner’s death, but no registered instrument transferring the property was executed.
Specific performance of the alleged agreement was not sought in the proceeding.
The statutory requirements for protection based on part performance were not satisfied.
members.legal_principle: Under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the English doctrine of equity of part performance could be applied in India only where that section’s requirements were satisfied. Equity could not override a statutory requirement that title be conferred only by a registered instrument. The Court relied on Ariff v. Jadunath Majumdar (1931) and treated Challa Papi Reddi v. Challa Koti Reddi, Bhalla Nahana v. Prabhu Hari, Asita Mohan Ghosh Moulik v. Mohan Ghosh Moulik, and Venkatayyamma Rao v. Appa Rao as inapplicable to the issue before it.
members.conclusion: The alleged contract and equitable considerations did not confer title on the claimant or his heirs. The appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: Delivery of possession of immovable property without an effective conveyance does not constitute a transfer for capital-gains purposes.
material_facts: The seller agreed to sell the factory and its assets, and possession of the land, buildings, and machinery was given to the company during the relevant accounting year.
The company adopted the agreement only after that year, and the registered sale deed for the land was executed later.
No conveyance of the immovable assets was executed and registered during the relevant accounting year.
members.legal_principle: Under section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, capital gains arise in the previous year in which a sale, exchange, or transfer of a capital asset takes place. For immovable property, title must pass by an effective conveyance; delivery of possession alone is not equivalent to conveyance. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax v. Bhurangya Coal Co., 34 I.T.R. 802, and rejected the contention based on section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act that possession alone effected the transfer.
members.conclusion: The land, buildings, machinery, and electrical fittings were not sold or transferred during the relevant accounting year, so no capital gains on those assets arose in that year.

members.legal_issue: An oral sale of land does not transfer title when the applicable law requires a registered instrument for the sale.
material_facts: The landholder purported to sell the land orally to two transferees.
The statutory requirement for a registered instrument had been extended to the relevant territory before the purported sales.
The transferees’ names were later entered in mutation records, but the courts found that the purported sales conveyed no title.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as extended to the relevant territory with effect from April 1, 1955, required a registered instrument for the sales at issue; oral sales could not transfer title.
members.conclusion: The alleged oral sales did not pass title to the transferees.

members.legal_issue: An oral sale of an immovable fishery right for a price, without the required written and registered instrument, transfers no title or interest.
material_facts: The fishery rights were granted orally in exchange for payment.
The value of the transactions exceeded the applicable registration threshold.
No written or registered instrument was executed.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act requires a sale of immovable property for a price to be made by a written and registered instrument when the property is tangible and exceeds the prescribed value; a registered instrument is required for intangible immovable property regardless of value. Because a profit a prendre is immovable property and the transactions were oral, no title or interest passed.
members.conclusion: The transactions did not pass any title or interest to the purchasers.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered transfer does not pass title to immovable property when the applicable law requires a registered sale deed for a transfer of that kind.
material_facts: The claimant said he had purchased land and paid the agreed price, and he took possession.
The land was worth more than the applicable statutory threshold for requiring a registered sale deed.
No registered sale deed was executed in the claimant’s favour before the owner became an evacuee.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirement that a registered sale deed is necessary to pass title to immovable property of the value established in this case. The judgment did not identify a specific statutory section for that requirement or rely on an earlier case for it.
members.conclusion: The claimant had not become the owner because no registered sale deed had been executed.

members.legal_issue: A letter of intent that leaves formal allotment dependent on clearances and subsequent formal steps does not, on those terms, create a concluded contract.
material_facts: The letters of intent stated that formal allotment would follow receipt of general regulatory clearance and that further individual clearances could also be required.
The applicable allotment rules reserved the authority’s power to accept or reject a bid and stated that payment of earnest money and an offered premium created no right or interest in the land.
The rules required approvals from statutory authorities and made allotment subject to approval by the authority’s board or competent authority.
No formal allotment letter or lease was issued, possession was not given, and the remaining premium was not paid before cancellation.
members.legal_principle: Whether a letter of intent is a final acceptance creating a contract or merely expresses an intention to contract later depends on its terms. A letter that makes final allotment conditional on clearances and subsequent formalities ordinarily indicates that the contract is to be made later. The Court relied on Dresser Rand S.A. v. Bindal Agro Chem Ltd. (2006) 1 SCC 751 and Speech & Software Technologies (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Neos Interactive Ltd., and considered the allotment rules’ provisions reserving the right to reject bids and requiring statutory and board approvals.
members.conclusion: The letters of intent expressed an intention to enter into a contract after further formalities and did not create a concluded contract on these facts.

predicates.letter_makes_final_allotment_conditional: The letter states that final allotment depends on receipt of required clearances.
predicates.letter_requires_later_formal_steps: The letter contemplates further formal steps before the parties’ arrangement becomes final.
predicates.formal_allotment_and_lease_were_not_comp: The authority did not issue a formal allotment or complete the contemplated lease before the dispute arose.

members.legal_issue: A preliminary decision to allot property does not create a final allotment or a concluded contract when the terms remain unsettled.
material_facts: The appellant’s appointment as manager was expressly temporary, pending any outright allotment.
Government communications stated that allotment had been decided in principle, that the terms would be communicated later, and that the appellant would meanwhile continue as manager.
The terms and conditions were never finally settled, and the appellant sought possession of the businesses through writ proceedings.
members.legal_principle: A decision in principle, with terms and conditions left for later determination, does not establish a concluded contract of sale or a final allotment. Article 226 does not provide mandamus to enforce a right that has not been established. No earlier case was relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: The communications did not make a final allotment or establish a concluded contract of sale, so the appellant had no legal right to the businesses on that basis and was not entitled to mandamus for possession.

predicates.communications_are_preliminary: The communications described the proposed allotment as a decision in principle and deferred its terms to a later determination.

members.legal_issue: A conditional letter of intent that contemplates a later sale agreement does not create an enforceable right to specific performance when the purchaser has not fulfilled its conditions and no formal sale agreement has been executed.
material_facts: The developer issued letters of intent reserving flats subject to stated conditions, including payment of installments, and contemplated executing sale agreements after payment of the purchase price.
The purchasers stopped paying installments, including amounts due under the original terms, and did not fulfill the conditions in the letters of intent.
No formal sale agreements were executed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4(1) of the Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963, an agreement between a flat purchaser and a developer is to be registered. The conditional letters of intent were not sale agreements: they contemplated a later agreement after payment and fulfillment of conditions. The court held that, absent a registered agreement and fulfillment of the conditions, no enforceable right to specific performance arose.
members.conclusion: The letters of intent did not create a binding contract for sale, and the purchasers were not entitled to specific performance.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that transfers immovable property through an exchange cannot be admitted to prove that transfer.
material_facts: Two parties executed an exchange instrument concerning their respective properties.
The instrument’s terms included a building, and the building’s value exceeded the registration threshold described by the Court.
The instrument was not registered, and one party argued that the exchange concerned only businesses.
members.legal_principle: Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines exchange and requires a transfer completing an exchange to follow the mode applicable to a sale; Sections 54 of that Act and 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 require registration for the transfer at issue. Section 49 of the Registration Act bars an unregistered document required to be registered from affecting the immovable property or being received as evidence of the transaction. The Court relied on Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh and Section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872 concerning proof of the contents of a document.
members.conclusion: The instrument was inadmissible to the extent it purported to transfer the immovable property; it could not be proved by the document or by oral evidence as proof of its contents.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that is required to be registered under the property-transfer law cannot be used as evidence of a transaction affecting the immovable property it concerns.
material_facts: The later document was relied on to establish that the transaction involving the house was an outright sale and to read it together with the registered mortgage deed.
The later document was unregistered, although the sale it purported to record required registration.
The document was offered as evidence of a transaction affecting immovable property.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, read with section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, as amended by section 10 of the Transfer of Property (Amendment) Supplementary Act, 1929, required registration and barred an unregistered document from being received as evidence of a transaction affecting the property. The amendment made clear that section 49 covered documents requiring registration under the Transfer of Property Act even when not independently covered by section 17 of the Registration Act. The Court referred to Sohan Lal v. Mohan Lal and Rama Sahu v. Gowro Ratho as earlier decisions reflecting a contrary view, which the subsequent legislation had superseded.
members.conclusion: The unregistered document was inadmissible as evidence of the transaction affecting the property and could not be read with the registered deed to establish an outright sale.

members.legal_issue: A transfer requiring registration is not complete for the purpose of a statutory right of reconveyance until registration is completed, even if the transferee’s title may relate back to the date of execution.
material_facts: A sale deed was executed and presented for registration, but registration was completed only after the applicant lodged the reconveyance application.
The applicant relied on the rule that, once registration occurred, the transferee’s title related back to the date of execution.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 16(2)(iii) and 16(3) of the Bihar Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling Area and Acquisition of Surplus Land) Act, a transfer requiring registration is not complete before registration. Section 47 of the Registration Act does not alter that result. The Court followed Ram Saran Lal v. Mst. Domini Kuer, Radhakishan L. Toshniwal v. Shridhar, and Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh.
members.conclusion: The transfer was completed only when registration was completed; the relation-back effect did not make the transfer complete on the date the deed was executed.

members.legal_issue: A sale of immovable property that must be made by registered instrument is not complete for purposes of a pre-emption demand until registration of the instrument is complete, even if the instrument, once registered, operates from an earlier date.
material_facts: The parties accepted that the pre-emption right arose only from a valid, complete and bona fide sale, and that the first demand had to be made after completion of the sale.
The sale concerned a house and was made by an instrument that was required to be registered.
The pre-emptor made the first demand after the instrument was executed and presented for registration, but before it was copied into the registration records, when registration became complete.
The instrument stated that it would operate from the date of execution; the court held that this did not make the sale complete before registration was complete.
members.legal_principle: Under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, a sale of tangible immovable property of the relevant value can be made only by a registered instrument. Sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act govern completion of registration, and section 61 provides that registration is complete when the prescribed endorsements and certificate are copied into the register. Section 47 permits a registered document to operate from the time it would have operated had registration not been required, but does not determine when the sale is completed; retrospective operation does not make the sale complete before registration is complete. The first demand under the applicable law of pre-emption must follow completion of the sale. The court approved Tilakdhari Singh v. Gour Narain, Nareshchandra Datta v. Gireeshchandra Das, and Gobardhan Bar v. Guna Dhar Bar, and distinguished Bindeshri v. Somnath Bhadry and Gopal Ram v. Lachmi Misir.
members.conclusion: The sale was complete only when registration was complete. Because the first pre-emption demand was made earlier, it was premature and the pre-emption suit failed.

predicates.sale_requires_registered_instrument: The sale concerned immovable property for which the applicable law required a registered instrument.
predicates.first_demand_preceded_registration_compl: The pre-emptor made the first demand before the instrument was copied into the registration records and registration was complete.

members.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption over immovable property does not accrue from a contract for sale when the governing transfer law requires a registered instrument to transfer ownership.
material_facts: The pre-emption suit was filed on the basis of agreements for sale before a sale deed had been executed.
The agreements for sale did not themselves create an interest in the property or transfer proprietary title.
The sale deed was executed after the suit was filed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, a contract for sale does not of itself create an interest in or charge on immovable property, and a transfer of ownership of the relevant kind must be made by a registered instrument. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act support the requirement that a document requiring registration cannot affect the property unless registered. The statutory pre-emption rights under sections 176 to 178 and 183 of the Berar Land Revenue Code do not broaden the meaning of sale beyond the applicable transfer law, and Mohammedan or other personal law cannot override that law. The Court relied on Immudipattam Thirugnana S. O. Kondema Naik v. Peria Dorasami, Sitaram Bhaurao Deshmukh v. Jiaul Hasan Sirajul Khan, Begum v. Mohammad Yakub, and the reasoning of Mahmood, J., in Janki v. Girjadat.
members.conclusion: No enforceable right of pre-emption had accrued when the suit was filed on the basis of the agreements for sale; the later sale deed could not validate that claim as pleaded.

rule.if: preemption_enforcement_suit and transfer_requires_registered_instrument and suit_filed_before_registered_transfer and claim_based_on_contract_for_sale

predicates.preemption_enforcement_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding to enforce a claimed right to take the place of a property purchaser.
predicates.transfer_requires_registered_instrument: The applicable transfer law requires ownership of property of this kind to be transferred by a registered instrument.
predicates.suit_filed_before_registered_transfer: The claimant filed the proceeding before the ownership transfer was completed by the required instrument.
predicates.claim_based_on_contract_for_sale: The claimant relied on an agreement for sale that had not itself transferred ownership.

members.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption over immovable property does not accrue from an agreement to sell before a valid sale is completed by the required registered conveyance.
material_facts: The pre-emption suit was filed on the basis of agreements to sell agricultural land.
The sale deed for the disputed land was executed only after the suit was filed.
The court treated the agreements as creating no interest in the land and found that no sale had been completed when the suit was brought.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 176 and 183 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, a right of pre-emption could arise on a qualifying transfer. But where the Transfer of Property Act applied, section 54 required a registered instrument to transfer ownership of immovable property of the relevant value, and a contract for sale did not itself create an interest in the property. Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act reinforced the need for registration. The court distinguished the broader approach to identifying a sale under Mohammedan law in Begum v. Mohammad Yakub and considered Sitaram Bhaurao Deshmukh v. Jiaul Hasan Sirajul Khan, Immudipattam Thirugnana S. O. Kondema Naik v. Peria Dorasami, and the reasoning in Janki v. Girjadat concerning the need for a valid and perfected sale before pre-emption could be exercised.
members.conclusion: No enforceable right of pre-emption had accrued when the suit was filed.

predicates.preemption_suit: A claimant brings a proceeding seeking to exercise a right of pre-emption over a property transfer.
predicates.registered_conveyance_required: The relevant transfer of immovable property requires a registered conveyance to pass ownership.
predicates.no_registered_sale_at_filing: No registered instrument completing the sale existed when the pre-emption proceeding was brought.
predicates.preemption_right_not_accrued: The claimant's right to enforce pre-emption had not yet arisen.

members.legal_issue: The existence of a Hindu joint family does not by itself establish that property held by a family member is joint, and the burden of proving that an acquisition was made with joint family funds shifts only when an adequate income-producing nucleus is shown.
material_facts: The family possessed ancestral lands of about 56 acres, but their income was found insufficient even for the members’ maintenance.

The acquisitions and substantial house construction greatly exceeded the value of the ancestral lands’ contribution; the family’s ancestral lands remained intact and their income was used for maintenance.
The acquiring family member had long-term employment income and other resources.
members.legal_principle: Proof of a Hindu joint family does not raise a presumption that every member’s property is joint. The person asserting joint ownership must prove it. If the family has joint property which, by its nature and relative value, could have formed an adequate nucleus for the acquisition, the burden shifts to the person asserting self-acquisition to prove that the acquisition was made without its aid. The Court applied Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti, which states this rule, and referred to Babubhai Girdharlal v. Ujamlal Hargovandas, Venkataramayya v. Seshamma and Vythianatha v. Varadaraja. The adequacy of the nucleus depends on the evidence, particularly its income and the scale and timing of the acquisitions.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not establish a sufficient nucleus to shift the initial burden; even assuming the burden shifted, the evidence established that the disputed purchases and buildings were self-acquisitions, not joint family property.

rule.if: partition_claim and joint_family_exists and (nucleus_insufficient or (nucleus_adequate and self_acquisition_independently_proved))

predicates.partition_claim: A claimant seeks, in a partition proceeding, to treat property acquired or held by a family member as joint family property.
predicates.joint_family_exists: The parties belong to a Hindu joint family.
predicates.nucleus_insufficient: The family’s joint property could not, in light of its nature, income and relative value, reasonably have funded the acquisitions in dispute.
predicates.nucleus_adequate: The family’s joint property could, in light of its nature, income and relative value, reasonably have provided a foundation for the acquisitions in dispute.
predicates.self_acquisition_independently_proved: Evidence shows that the acquisitions were made without aid from joint family property, including that the joint property remained intact and its income was used for family maintenance.

members.legal_issue: A property is not presumed to be joint family property merely because a joint Hindu family exists; the claimant must prove an adequate joint-family nucleus capable of supporting its acquisition before the burden shifts to the person asserting self-acquisition.
material_facts: The property in dispute had been purchased by a family member and was claimed by other family members as joint family property.

The family owned another property that was joint family property, but the claimants presented no evidence that it generated income or had a value sufficient to provide a nucleus for the purchase in dispute.
The claimants presented no other evidence establishing that the disputed property was joint family property.
The person who purchased the disputed property also presented no evidence of separate income.
members.legal_principle: Under Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti, Srinivas Krishnarao Kango v. Narayan Devji Kango, Mudi Gowda Gowdappa Sankh v. Ram Chandra Ravagowda Sankh, Baikuntha Nath Paramanik v. Sashi Bhusan Pramanik, and Surendra Kumar v. Phoolchand, the existence of a joint family alone does not raise a presumption that a member’s property is joint. The person asserting joint-family character initially bears the burden. If that person proves an adequate joint-family nucleus from which the property could have been acquired, a presumption arises and the burden shifts to the person claiming self-acquisition. The adequacy of the nucleus depends on its nature, extent, and income. Mallesappa Bandeppa Desai v. Desai Mallappa, Achuthan Nair v. Chinnammu Amma, and Malappa Girimallappa Betgeri v. R. Yellappagouda Patil do not displace that rule where an adequate nucleus has not been established.
members.conclusion: The claimants did not establish a sufficient nucleus or otherwise prove that the disputed property was joint family property, so their claim to it failed; the purchaser’s failure to prove separate income did not shift the burden.

rule.if: partition_suit_claiming_joint_family_character and claimant_asserts_property_is_joint_family and not adequate_acquisition_nucleus_proved and not other_evidence_of_joint_family_character

predicates.partition_suit_claiming_joint_family_cha: A claimant seeks recognition of property as joint family property in a suit involving partition.
predicates.claimant_asserts_property_is_joint_famil: A claimant alleges that the disputed property belongs to the joint family.
predicates.adequate_acquisition_nucleus_proved: The claimant proves that joint-family property had sufficient value or income to provide a nucleus from which the disputed property could have been acquired.
predicates.other_evidence_of_joint_family_character: The claimant presents evidence, apart from an acquisition nucleus, that the disputed property is joint family property.

members.legal_issue: Later acquisitions are presumed to be joint family property when an adequate family-property nucleus could have funded them and no separate source of funds is established.
material_facts: The family possessed ancestral lands that the lower courts found constituted an adequate nucleus for the later purchases.
The income from the nucleus was more than sufficient to acquire the later lands.
The later acquisitions were made over a period of years, and the claimed separate business income of the acquiring family member was not proved.
members.legal_principle: Joint family status alone creates no presumption that a family possesses joint property or that a member’s acquisition is joint. The person claiming an item as joint family property initially bears the burden of proof. Once an adequate nucleus capable of funding the acquisition is established, the burden shifts to the person claiming self-acquisition to prove that the property was acquired without aid from the family estate. The Court applied Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti, I.L.R. [1948] Mad. 440 (P.C.), and referred to Babubhai Girdharlal v. Ujamlal Hargovandas, Venkataramayya v. Seshamma, and Vythianatha v. Varadaraja.
members.conclusion: The later-acquired lands were joint family properties.

rule.if: partition_property_dispute and adequate_family_nucleus and nucleus_could_fund_acquisition and separate_source_not_proved

predicates.partition_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns the division of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.adequate_family_nucleus: The family possessed joint property that formed an adequate nucleus.
predicates.nucleus_could_fund_acquisition: The income or value of the nucleus was sufficient to fund the disputed acquisition.
predicates.separate_source_not_proved: The person claiming the acquisition as separate property did not prove an independent source of funds.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired in the name of a family member is joint family property when the family had a sufficient nucleus and the purchase was made from joint family funds, unless the party asserting separate ownership establishes otherwise.
material_facts: The family manager purchased the property in the name of a minor family member, and the courts found that the consideration was paid from joint family funds.
The family had sufficient joint property that could have provided a nucleus for the purchase.
The appellant asserted that his maternal grandfather paid the consideration but failed to establish that assertion or that the property was purchased from the appellant’s separate funds.
The trial court and High Court both found the property to be joint family property after considering the evidence.
members.legal_principle: There is no presumption that a joint family possesses joint property merely because the family is joint; the party alleging joint ownership must establish that the family had property whose income could have acquired the disputed property. If the family had joint property that could have formed a sufficient nucleus, the presumption arises that the disputed property was acquired with its aid, and the burden shifts to the party alleging self-acquisition to prove otherwise. The Court applied this principle in declining to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts.
members.conclusion: The property was joint family property, the respondents were each entitled to a share of the compensation, and there was no justification for disturbing the concurrent findings.

rule.if: compensation_apportionment_appeal and joint_family_had_sufficient_nucleus and purchase_made_from_joint_funds and claimant_failed_to_prove_separate_acquisition and concurrent_findings_supported_by_evidence

predicates.compensation_apportionment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning ownership and apportionment of compensation awarded for acquired property.
predicates.joint_family_had_sufficient_nucleus: The family possessed joint property capable, in its nature and relative value, of providing a sufficient nucleus for the disputed purchase.
predicates.purchase_made_from_joint_funds: The family manager paid for the disputed property from joint family funds.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_separate_acquis: The person asserting separate ownership did not establish that the purchase was made from separate funds.
predicates.concurrent_findings_supported_by_evidenc: The lower courts reached the same finding after considering evidence that supported their conclusion.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired in the name of a joint-family member is presumed to be joint-family property only when the family had a sufficient nucleus at the time of acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisitions in dispute were made in the names of a family member’s wife, son, and grandson; the court found that the funds for several of them had been advanced by the family manager.

The evidence showed that family income had been substantially spent on family needs, cultivation, and other land purchases, and that the manager could have accumulated substantial savings from his separate earnings.
For acquisitions made when the son had long been earning independently, it was possible that he had used his own savings.
The court found no sufficient family nucleus available for the disputed acquisitions at the relevant times.
members.legal_principle: Under the rule stated in Amritlal Sen & Ors. v. Surath Lal Sen, A.I.R. 1942 Cal. 553, and Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurthy & Ors., I.L.R. [1948] Mad. (P.C.) 440, property acquired in a joint-family member’s name is presumed to have been acquired from family funds, and to be joint-family property, if the family had a sufficient nucleus at the date of acquisition, unless the contrary is shown. The presumption therefore does not arise without a sufficient nucleus.
members.conclusion: The disputed acquisitions were not shown to have been made from joint-family funds and were not liable to partition as joint-family property.

predicates.partition_suit: A family member brought a suit seeking division of alleged joint-family property.
predicates.property_acquired_in_member_name: The disputed property was acquired in the name of a member of the joint family or a member of that person’s branch.
predicates.family_nucleus_insufficient: The family’s available funds and income at the relevant acquisition time were not sufficient to provide a nucleus for the acquisition.
predicates.disputed_acquisitions_not_established_as: The disputed acquisitions are not treated as joint-family property liable to partition.

members.legal_issue: A member claiming that acquired property is separate must displace the inference of joint-family ownership that arises when the family had an adequate nucleus capable of funding the acquisition.
material_facts: The family possessed ancestral land measuring 151 acres and 27 gunthas, including irrigated land, and the evidence showed substantial income and resources for cultivation.
Twelve additional parcels were acquired over about thirty years for a total price of Rs. 4,800, which the courts found could have been funded from the family property.
The appellants asserted that the acquisitions were made from separate business income but did not establish the nature or source of that income with reliable evidence.
members.legal_principle: Joint-family status alone does not create a presumption that property held by a member is joint property; the person asserting joint ownership initially bears the burden of proof. If an adequate joint-family nucleus is established from which the acquisition could have been made, the burden shifts to the person asserting self-acquisition to prove that the property was acquired without aid from the family estate. The Court relied on Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti and referred to Babubhai Girdharlal v. Ujamlal Hargovandas, Venkataramayya v. Seshamma, and Vythianatha v. Varadaraja.
members.conclusion: The twelve parcels were joint-family property, and the plaintiff was entitled to a share in them on partition.

rule.if: property_partition_appeal and acquired_property_claimed_as_joint and adequate_family_nucleus and nucleus_could_fund_acquisition and no_proof_of_independent_source

predicates.property_partition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a dispute over partition of family property.
predicates.acquired_property_claimed_as_joint: A party to the partition dispute claims that property acquired by a family member belongs to the joint family.
predicates.adequate_family_nucleus: The family possessed joint property of sufficient value or productive capacity to provide a financial nucleus.
predicates.nucleus_could_fund_acquisition: The established family nucleus could have provided the means for the acquisition in dispute.
predicates.no_proof_of_independent_source: The party asserting separate ownership did not prove that the acquisition was made from an independent source without aid from the family estate.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired in the names of family members managing a joint family may be treated as joint family property when the family had a sufficient nucleus to fund the acquisitions.
material_facts: The joint family owned extensive property, and its income was admitted to have supported acquisitions.
The family nucleus was sufficient to fund the acquisitions standing in the names of the family members.
The family members in whose names the acquisitions stood participated in managing family property.
Family account books were not produced, and the member asserting separate income did not produce his own account books.
members.legal_principle: Where a joint family possesses a nucleus sufficient to make an acquisition, a presumption arises that an acquisition standing in the name of a person managing the family property is a family acquisition. The Court relied on this principle; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for it.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding that acquisitions in the names of the family members who managed the family property, made before the division in status, were family acquisitions and liable to partition.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding sought partition of family property.
predicates.joint_family_had_sufficient_nucleus: The joint family possessed property or income sufficient to fund the disputed acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_stood_in_name_of_family_prop: The acquisition stood in the name of a person who managed family property and was made while the family remained joint in status.
predicates.acquisition_is_presumed_joint_family_pro: The acquisition is treated as joint family property unless the presumption is displaced.

members.legal_issue: Property acquired with the aid of a sufficient joint-family nucleus is joint-family property unless the person asserting separate ownership proves that it was acquired without that aid.
material_facts: The family continued to be joint and carried on business together despite documents purporting to record separation.
The court found that the relinquishment documents and trust deed were colourable parts of a scheme to protect family assets from creditors.
The family had extensive property and business income sufficient to provide the funds used for the trust and construction of the house.
No reliable evidence established that the person who executed the trust had separate income sufficient to fund the trust and the house.
Other family members supervised construction, paid contractors, and obtained receipts; the trustees were connected with the family, and the trust was brought to an end.
members.legal_principle: Hindu law presumes a family to be joint, but does not presume that property held by a family member is joint-family property. The person asserting that property is joint-family property bears the initial burden; proof of a sufficient family nucleus from which the property could have been acquired shifts the burden to the person asserting separate ownership to show acquisition without the family’s assistance. A document purporting to effect separation may be shown to be sham and not intended to be acted upon. The court also relied on Alluri Venkatapathi Raju v. Dantuluri Venkatanarasimha Raju when assessing admissions of separation.
members.conclusion: The trust deed was colourable and fictitious, the property was joint-family property, and the respondent was entitled to the declaration sought.

rule.if: suit_to_declare_trust_document_sham and family_remained_joint and sufficient_joint_family_nucleus_existed and claimant_failed_to_prove_acquisition_from_separate_funds and transaction_fitted_family_asset_protection_scheme

predicates.suit_to_declare_trust_document_sham: The proceeding seeks a declaration that a trust document is sham and does not affect the claimant’s rights in the property.
predicates.family_remained_joint: The family members continued to conduct joint affairs and remained connected with the family estate despite documents asserting separation.
predicates.sufficient_joint_family_nucleus_existed: The family had property or income sufficient to provide the funds from which the disputed property could have been acquired.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_prove_acquisition_fro: The person asserting separate ownership did not reliably establish that the property was acquired without assistance from family property or funds.
predicates.transaction_fitted_family_asset_protecti: The trust and related documents formed part of arrangements used to protect family assets from creditors.

members.legal_issue: Properties acquired in the names of individual family members were joint-family acquisitions where the claimant established a sufficient joint-family nucleus and the holders did not prove acquisition from independent funds.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought partition of properties alleged to belong to the joint Hindu family.
The family possessed agricultural properties and had used family resources to establish businesses.
The trial court found that the family had a nucleus capable of funding the disputed acquisitions, which stood in the names of family members and their close relatives.
The defendants produced no evidence that the named holders had independent income or sufficient personal funds to acquire the properties.
The High Court reversed the trial court’s finding and dismissed the suit against the defendants concerned.
members.legal_principle: There is no presumption that property held by a member of a joint Hindu family is joint-family property merely because the family is joint; the person asserting that status bears the initial burden. Once that person establishes that the family possessed a sufficient nucleus from which the property could have been acquired, the burden shifts to the person claiming self-acquisition to prove affirmatively, by cogent evidence, that the property was acquired without assistance from the joint-family property. The Court relied on Srinivas Krishnarao Kango v. Narayan Devli Kango, Mst. Rukhmabai v. Lala Laxminarayan, Achuthan Nair v. Chinnammu Amma, Bhagwant P. Sulakhe v. Digambar Gopal Sulakhe, and Surendra Kumar v. Phoolchand. No statutory provision is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and restored the trial court’s finding that the disputed properties were joint-family acquisitions available for partition.

rule.if: partition_suit and claimant_asserted_joint_family_ownership and property_acquired_in_family_member_name and family_had_sufficient_nucleus and nucleus_could_fund_acquisition and no_cogent_proof_of_independent_acquisition

predicates.partition_suit: A person brought a suit seeking partition of property alleged to belong to a joint Hindu family.
predicates.claimant_asserted_joint_family_ownership: The person seeking partition asserted that the disputed property belonged to the joint Hindu family.
predicates.property_acquired_in_family_member_name: The disputed property was acquired in the name of a member of the family or a person closely connected to a member.
predicates.family_had_sufficient_nucleus: The family possessed joint property or resources that could provide a sufficient financial nucleus.
predicates.nucleus_could_fund_acquisition: The nature and value of the family’s joint property or resources were such that they could have funded the disputed acquisition.
