predicates.underlying_suit_not_decided_on_prelimina: The trial court had dismissed the suit after addressing the issues rather than disposing of it on a preliminary point.
predicates.appellate_court_did_not_reverse_trial_de: The appellate court did not find that the trial court's decree was liable to be reversed.
predicates.appellate_court_did_not_find_retrial_nec: The appellate court did not find that a retrial was necessary.
predicates.remand_was_for_secondary_evidence: The appellate court remanded the suit to permit the parties to adduce secondary evidence.
predicates.evidence_refusal_was_not_set_aside: The appellate court did not set aside the trial court's order refusing the application to adduce secondary evidence.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot remand a case for a new trial without a properly raised and supported basis for remand and a reasoned decision under the applicable remand provisions.
material_facts: No party sought remand before the first appellate court or the High Court, and no complaint was made that the trial had been unsatisfactory or had caused prejudice.
The High Court framed no substantial question of law concerning remand, identified no applicable remand ground, and ordered a de novo trial in all the suits.
The High Court set aside the lower courts’ decisions and remanded the cases of its own initiative.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI Rules 23, 23-A and 25 CPC govern remand by an appellate court. A party seeking remand must raise the plea and establish a factual basis bringing the case within an applicable rule; the appellate court must record reasons for the remand. Section 100 CPC confines a second appeal to formulated questions, so the High Court could not decide an unframed remand issue.
members.conclusion: The remand order was unjustified and beyond the High Court’s jurisdiction in the circumstances; the High Court should have decided the appeals on their merits.

rule.if: appellate_case and remand_not_sought_by_a_party and no_supported_remand_ground and no_remand_question_framed

predicates.appellate_case: The proceeding is an appeal in which a court is considering whether to send the case back for further proceedings.
predicates.remand_not_sought_by_a_party: No party raised a request for remand before the appellate court.
predicates.no_supported_remand_ground: No facts were established showing an applicable basis for remand or prejudice requiring further trial proceedings.
predicates.no_remand_question_framed: The appellate court did not frame a question authorizing it to decide whether remand was warranted.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court that remands a case for a fresh decision should explain why remand is necessary and should not record findings on the merits of the issues left for retrial.
material_facts: The first appellate court remanded the suit so the trial court could decide it afresh on the full evidence.
In its remand judgment, the first appellate court also recorded findings on several merits issues.
members.legal_principle: When an appellate court forms the view that a remand is required, it should give reasons supporting the remand. If the case is being remanded for the trial court to decide the merits afresh, the appellate court need not discuss or record findings on those merits issues.
members.conclusion: The merits findings were unnecessary and uncalled for; the remand was restored with a modification requiring the trial court to decide the suit without being influenced by those findings.

predicates.appellate_court_orders_fresh_trial: An appellate court sends a case back for a fresh trial.
predicates.trial_court_must_decide_merits_afresh: The trial court is to decide the underlying merits after remand.
predicates.appellate_court_records_merits_findings: The appellate court records findings on merits issues that the trial court must decide afresh.

members.legal_issue: A court remanding a case for a procedural hearing should leave the merits open rather than express findings likely to influence the trial court.
material_facts: The High Court set aside the charge order in part on the ground that the accused had been denied an opportunity to be heard and remanded the matter.
While doing so, the High Court expressed the view that there was no prima facie case against the accused.
The Supreme Court concluded that the merits-based observations frustrated the remand and were likely to influence the trial court.
members.legal_principle: A court ordering a procedural remand should not express a strong opinion on the merits that may influence the court conducting the further proceedings or frustrate the purpose of the remand.
members.conclusion: If the High Court remanded the matter because the accused lacked an opportunity to be heard, it should have stopped there and left the merits for the trial court.

predicates.criminal_case_remanded_for_procedural_he: A criminal case is remanded so that a party may receive a procedural hearing.
predicates.remanding_court_expresses_merits_view: The court ordering the remand expresses a view on the merits of the criminal case.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should not conclusively decide a material issue on the merits while remanding a suit when factual issues on the merits remain unresolved.
material_facts: The High Court returned the suit to the trial court, where material issues on the merits remained to be determined.
The High Court nevertheless found that the disputed property was private property and neither a Gurdwara nor a Sikh Gurdwara.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court should not have effectively concluded the suit through that finding.
members.legal_principle: Where a case is remanded and issues of fact on the merits remain for determination, the appellate court should not make a finding that virtually concludes the suit; the unresolved issue must remain open for further consideration.
members.conclusion: The High Court's finding on the property's status was vacated and left open for further consideration.

predicates.appeal_from_remand_order: A party appealed an order returning the case to a lower court for further proceedings.
predicates.merits_factual_issues_unresolved: Material factual issues on the merits remained to be determined after the remand.
predicates.appellate_court_makes_conclusive_merits_: The appellate court made a finding that effectively concluded the unresolved merits issue.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should determine compensation on remand when the reviewing court lacks material and submissions needed to fix the proper amount itself.
material_facts: The claimants’ appeals concerned the amount of compensation for acquired land.
The claimants provided no material on the reviewing court’s record on which it could fix proper compensation and advanced no arguments on that amount.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that it would have determined compensation itself but, because the record contained no material on which to do so and no arguments had been advanced on the amount, it remanded the appeals for determination by the High Court. No provision or earlier case is cited for this procedural ruling.
members.conclusion: The judgments and orders were set aside, and the appeals were remanded for the High Court to determine proper compensation in accordance with law.

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.reviewing_record_lacks_material_to_fix_a: The record before the reviewing court contains no material on which it can determine the proper compensation amount.
predicates.no_arguments_on_amount: The parties advance no arguments before the reviewing court on the proper compensation amount.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should remand a land-acquisition compensation matter when the record and submissions do not enable it to determine the proper compensation.
material_facts: The claimants appealed against the High Court’s compensation determination.
They provided no material on the Supreme Court record on which it could fix proper compensation and advanced no arguments on that determination.
The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgments and orders and remanded the appeals for the High Court to determine proper compensation in accordance with law.
members.legal_principle: Where the appellate record contains no material on which the court can fix proper compensation and no arguments have been advanced on that question, the court may set aside the impugned determination and remand the matter for determination in accordance with law. The judgment cites no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this remedial ruling.
members.conclusion: The impugned judgments and orders were set aside, and the appeals were remanded to the High Court to determine proper compensation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.record_lacks_material_to_fix_compensatio: The record before the appellate court contains no material enabling it to fix proper compensation.
predicates.no_arguments_address_proper_compensation: The appellant advances no arguments on how proper compensation should be determined.
predicates.appeal_is_remanded_for_compensation_dete: The appeal is remanded for determination of proper compensation.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary that was not heard and is adversely affected by a compensation award may challenge it through an appropriate appeal or writ proceeding.
material_facts: The beneficiary had not been joined in the proceedings in which compensation was determined or enhanced.
The beneficiary sought to challenge the resulting awards, including by writ petitions and by seeking to participate in appeals.
The beneficiary would bear the financial burden of the enhanced compensation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(b), 18, 26, 50(2), and 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read with Article 226 of the Constitution and Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, permit a beneficiary that is a person interested to challenge an adverse award when it was not heard. It may seek leave to appeal against an enhanced award, defend the Collector’s award, or invoke writ jurisdiction to challenge an award made without notice; an award of the Collector may also be challenged where vitiated by fraud, collusion, or corruption. The Court relied on Neelagangabai, N. Krishnamachari, and the other beneficiary authorities, and explained that Santosh Kumar concerned a different issue about seeking a reference from the Collector’s award.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary was entitled to challenge an adverse compensation determination, including by seeking leave to appeal or by a writ petition where appropriate. The dismissed writ petitions were directed to be treated as appeals under section 54 and disposed of with the State’s pending appeals.

rule.if: challenge_to_compensation_award and land_acquired_for_beneficiary and beneficiary_bears_compensation and beneficiary_not_heard

predicates.challenge_to_compensation_award: The proceeding seeks review of an award determining compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_acquired_for_beneficiary: The land was acquired for the benefit of a person or entity other than the acquiring authority.
predicates.beneficiary_bears_compensation: The beneficiary is responsible for bearing the compensation payable for the acquired land.
predicates.beneficiary_not_heard: The beneficiary was not given an opportunity to participate and be heard before the compensation award was made.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary excluded from a compensation-reference proceeding after its request to be joined was rejected may be joined and allowed to appeal the resulting compensation judgment.
material_facts: The Union sought impleadment while the landowners’ compensation references were pending because the acquisition was for the benefit of a security force controlled by the Union.
The application for impleadment was rejected, and the compensation was later enhanced without the Union’s participation.
The rejection of impleadment deprived the Union of an opportunity to appeal the enhancement judgment.
members.legal_principle: A person interested in the compensation determination may be impleaded under Order I Rule 10 CPC, read harmoniously with Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Applying Himalayan Tiles and Marbles (P) Ltd. v. Francis Victor Countinho and the later decisions in Neelgangabai v. State of Karnataka and Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti v. Ashok Singhal, the Court rejected the contrary approach in the majority view in M/s Indo Swiss Time Ltd. v. Umrao and in Kulbhushan Kumar and Company v. State of Punjab. Where rejection of impleadment has deprived an interested beneficiary of an opportunity to appeal the compensation judgment, impleadment and the opportunity to appeal should be allowed.
members.conclusion: The impleadment application was allowed, and the Union was entitled to appeal the judgment enhancing compensation.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and beneficiary_is_person_interested and impleadment_denied and compensation_enhanced_without_beneficiary and appeal_opportunity_lost_due_to_exclusion

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: Landowners sought judicial determination of compensation following a state land acquisition.
predicates.beneficiary_is_person_interested: The beneficiary had a direct or indirect interest in the land or the amount of compensation.
predicates.impleadment_denied: The court rejected the beneficiary’s request to be joined in the reference proceeding.
predicates.compensation_enhanced_without_beneficiar: The court enhanced compensation without the beneficiary participating as a party.
predicates.appeal_opportunity_lost_due_to_exclusion: The beneficiary could not appeal the enhanced compensation judgment because its request to be joined had been rejected.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary local authority may appeal an enhanced compensation award when the government does not appeal, but it must obtain leave.
material_facts: The reference tribunal had determined compensation for land acquired for the board.
The board could be prejudicially affected if the reference court enhanced the compensation.
The Court considered the case in which the government does not appeal an enhancement made by the reference court.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the proviso to Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 bars a beneficiary local authority from demanding a reference under Section 18 but does not eliminate the appeal remedy against an enhanced award of the reference court, subject to leave. Union of India v. Sher Singh and Union of India v. Kolluni Ramaiah were considered in addressing the beneficiary body’s ability to challenge an adverse determination. The Court treated the right of appeal as a legal remedy distinct from the prohibited demand for a reference.
members.conclusion: If the reference court enhances compensation and the government does not appeal, a local authority adversely affected by the enhancement may appeal to the High Court after obtaining leave of the court.

rule.if: reference_court_enhanced_compensation and local_authority_adversely_affected and government_did_not_appeal and local_authority_obtains_leave

predicates.reference_court_enhanced_compensation: The reference court increased the compensation awarded for acquired land.
predicates.local_authority_adversely_affected: The increased compensation adversely affects the local authority for whose benefit the land was acquired.
predicates.government_did_not_appeal: The government did not appeal the reference court’s enhancement.
predicates.local_authority_obtains_leave: The local authority obtained the appellate court’s permission to appeal.

members.legal_issue: An acquiring authority that is aggrieved by a compensation award may appeal even if it was not impleaded in the compensation reference.
material_facts: The acquiring authority was not impleaded before the Reference Court and had no opportunity to adduce evidence there.
The acquiring authority challenged the compensation award before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act permits an appeal by a person aggrieved by the award; the acquiring authority's status as an aggrieved person is not defeated merely because it was not impleaded in the reference proceedings.
members.conclusion: The acquiring authority was a person aggrieved and its appeal under Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act was maintainable.

predicates.acquiring_authority_aggrieved_by_award: The authority responsible for the acquisition was adversely affected by the compensation award.
predicates.award_made_without_authority_as_party: The compensation award was made in proceedings in which the acquiring authority was not a party.
predicates.acquiring_authority_appeals: The acquiring authority appealed against the compensation award.

members.legal_issue: A company for whose benefit land is acquired may appeal from a compensation award after contesting the landowners’ reference, despite being barred from seeking its own reference.
material_facts: The company sought references to reduce the Collector’s compensation, but the reference court held those references barred.
The landowners had joined the company as a contesting party in their references, and the company actively contested them before the reference court.
The reference court awarded compensation above the Collector’s award, and the company appealed.
The landowners did not challenge the maintainability of the company’s appeals before the High Court and raised the objection for the first time in the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 bars a company from demanding a reference under Section 18, which prevents it from seeking a reduction below the Collector’s offer. It does not bar an appeal under Section 54 against the court’s award, including an award exceeding the Collector’s amount; Section 25 supports the rule that compensation cannot be reduced below the Collector’s award. The Supreme Court may also, in its discretion under Article 136 of the Constitution, permit a person to appeal. An objection to maintainability not raised in the courts below cannot be raised for the first time at that late stage.
members.conclusion: The company’s appeals were maintainable. The bar on a company seeking a reference did not prevent it from appealing against the court’s award after contesting the landowners’ references; the late objection also could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and company_for_whose_benefit_land_was_acquired and company_contested_landowners_reference and court_award_exceeded_collectors_award and objection_first_raised_in_final_appeal

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.company_for_whose_benefit_land_was_acqui: A company was the beneficiary of the land acquisition.
predicates.company_contested_landowners_reference: The company was joined as a party and actively contested the landowners’ reference before the reference court.
predicates.court_award_exceeded_collectors_award: The reference court awarded more compensation than the Collector had offered.
predicates.objection_first_raised_in_final_appeal: The opposing party did not object to the company’s appeal in the courts below and first raised the objection in the final appeal.

members.legal_issue: A company for whose benefit land is acquired and which has an interest in the land or must pay the compensation is a person interested entitled to challenge a ruling in the acquisition proceeding.
material_facts: The land was acquired for the company's benefit under an agreement providing that it would be transferred to the company after vesting in the government.
Under the agreement, the company was responsible for paying the compensation.
The company appealed a ruling that it lacked standing because it was not a person interested.
members.legal_principle: Section 18(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 uses an inclusive definition of person interested, which must be construed liberally to include persons directly or indirectly interested in title to the land or the amount of compensation. The Court relied on Sunder Lal v. Paramsukhdas, The Hindustan Sanitaryware and Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana, Comilla Electric Supply Ltd. v. East Bengal Bank Ltd., and M. Kuppuswami v. The Special Tahsildar, and rejected the contrary view in State of Orissa v. Amarendra Pratap Singh and the contrary view attributed to the Calcutta High Court.
members.conclusion: The company was a person interested and could maintain its appeal; the High Court erred in dismissing the appeal for lack of locus standi.

rule.if: land_acquired_for_company_benefit and (company_had_contractual_land_interest or company_bound_to_pay_compensation) and company_appealed_acquisition_ruling

predicates.land_acquired_for_company_benefit: The government acquired the land for the benefit of a company.
predicates.company_had_contractual_land_interest: An agreement provided that the land would be transferred to the company after it vested in the government.
predicates.company_bound_to_pay_compensation: An agreement made the company responsible for paying the compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.company_appealed_acquisition_ruling: The company appealed a ruling in the land acquisition proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A person for whose benefit land is acquired and who bears the compensation is a person interested in the acquisition proceedings and may be joined as a proper party.
material_facts: Land was acquired for the appellant company’s benefit, and the company would bear the compensation payable for it.
The lower courts refused to treat the beneficiary as a person interested or to implead it in the compensation proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, contains an inclusive definition that is to be construed liberally. A beneficiary that bears the compensation has a direct interest in both the compensation and the land acquired for its benefit. The Court followed Himalayan Tiles & Marbles (P) Ltd. v. Francis Victor Coutinho, Neelagangabai v. State of Karnataka, Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti v. Ashok Singhal, Union of India v. District Judge, Udhampur, Union of India v. Sher Singh, Bihar State Electricity Board v. State of Bihar, Union of India v. Kolluni Ramaiah, and N. Krishnamachari v. Managing Director, APSRTC. It held Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad v. Chandulal Shamaldas Patel to be no longer good law and distinguished Santosh Kumar v. Central Warehousing Corporation.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary was a person interested under section 3(b) and a proper party under Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure; the contrary orders were set aside.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land and determination of compensation for it.
predicates.land_acquired_for_beneficiary: The land was acquired for the benefit of a person or entity other than the acquiring authority.
predicates.beneficiary_bears_compensation: The beneficiary is responsible for bearing the compensation payable for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary that bears the compensation may participate in compensation proceedings, present and test evidence, and be heard; the statutory right to adduce evidence does not exhaust its procedural rights.
material_facts: The beneficiary sought to participate in pending references to determine compensation, including by adducing evidence.
The lower courts rejected its applications on the ground that it was not a person interested.
The beneficiary would bear any increased compensation, and the government’s participation might not adequately contest claims for an increase.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(b) and 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, must be read together. Section 50(2), which permits a company or local authority to adduce evidence before the Collector or the court, is additional to—not a substitute for—the procedural rights that follow from being a person interested. Those rights include a fair opportunity to be heard, consistent with Article 14 of the Constitution. Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure supports joining the beneficiary as a proper, if not necessary, party. The Court relied on the line of authority beginning with Himalayan Tiles and including Neelagangabai, Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, Union of India v. Sher Singh, and the other beneficiary cases it reviewed.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary was entitled to be impleaded in the pending references, to cross-examine the claimants’ witnesses, to adduce rebuttal evidence, and to be heard on just and proper compensation.

predicates.compensation_determination_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation for acquired land, including a proceeding before the Collector or a court reference.
predicates.land_acquired_for_beneficiary: The land was acquired for the benefit of a person or entity other than the acquiring authority.
predicates.beneficiary_bears_compensation: The beneficiary is responsible for bearing the compensation payable for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary of a land acquisition with a direct or indirect interest in the land or compensation may qualify as a person interested in a compensation reference.
material_facts: The state acquired land for the benefit of a security force controlled by the Union of India, at the Union’s request.
Landowners sought enhancement of compensation through references, and the Union sought to participate because the compensation amount would adversely affect its interests.
members.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 uses an inclusive definition of a person interested, which must be liberally construed to include persons directly or indirectly interested in title to the land or the quantum of compensation. The Court relied on Himalayan Tiles and Marbles (P) Ltd. v. Francis Victor Countinho, Neelgangabai v. State of Karnataka, and Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti v. Ashok Singhal. It distinguished Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad v. Chandulal Shamaldas Patel and overruled the contrary majority views in M/s Indo Swiss Time Ltd. v. Umrao and Kulbhushan Kumar and Company v. State of Punjab; it approved the minority view in Indo Swiss. The provisions of Order I Rule 10 CPC and Section 50(2) of the Act may be read harmoniously.
members.conclusion: The Union of India was a person interested and was entitled to be impleaded in the compensation-reference proceedings.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: Landowners sought judicial determination of compensation following a state land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_for_entity_benefit: The state acquired the land for the benefit of an entity that would use or control it.
predicates.compensation_amount_affects_entity_inter: The amount of compensation would adversely affect the entity’s interests.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary local authority is a proper party in proceedings on a reference concerning compensation.
material_facts: The landowners sought references against the acquisition officer’s compensation award.
The board was not joined in the proceedings before the reference tribunal.
The board was the body responsible for paying compensation and was entitled to present evidence on its determination.
members.legal_principle: Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 gives the beneficiary body the right to appear and adduce evidence before the reference court. Applying the necessary-party and proper-party distinction in Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member, Board of Revenue, the Court held the local authority to be a proper party. The proviso to Section 50(2) prevents it from demanding a reference under Section 18, but does not prevent it from participating in a reference sought by a person interested in the land.
members.conclusion: A local authority for whose benefit land is acquired is a proper party and is entitled to be impleaded in proceedings before the reference court, where it may defend the acquisition officer’s award, oppose an increase in compensation, and adduce evidence.

predicates.compensation_reference_proceeding: A court is hearing a reference concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_acquired_for_local_authority: The land was acquired for the benefit of a local authority.
predicates.local_authority_pays_compensation: The local authority is responsible for paying the compensation.

members.legal_issue: A company for whose benefit land is acquired has the same participation and related procedural rights as a local authority.
material_facts: The judgment considered acquisitions made for a company as well as acquisitions made for a local authority.
The acquiring body is responsible for the compensation and may present evidence concerning its amount.
members.legal_principle: Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 expressly applies to a local authority or company. The Court relied on Himalayan Tiles & Marbles (P) Ltd. v. Francis Victor Countinho for the company’s ability to participate in determining compensation, while explaining that the relevant basis is Section 50(2), rather than treating the company as a person entitled to demand a reference under Section 18.
members.conclusion: The rights and procedural rules stated for a local authority under Section 50(2) apply equally to a company for whose benefit land is acquired.

predicates.land_acquired_for_company: The land was acquired for the benefit of a company.
predicates.company_pays_compensation: The company for whose benefit the land was acquired is responsible for paying the compensation.

members.legal_issue: A body for whose benefit land is acquired may participate in compensation proceedings and must receive notice of the proceedings.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a statutory housing board, which was responsible for paying the compensation.
The board was not given notice of the compensation proceedings before either the acquisition officer or the reference tribunal.
The board had not appeared in those proceedings to present evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 grants the right to appear and adduce evidence, subject to its proviso barring a demand for a reference under Section 18. The notice requirement is implicit in that right. Neelgangabai v. State of Karnataka and Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti v. Ashok Singhal support the consequence of denying the beneficiary body an opportunity to participate; the Court also considered Union of India v. Sher Singh and Union of India v. Kolluni Ramaiah.
members.conclusion: A local authority or company for whose benefit land is acquired may appear and adduce evidence on compensation before the Collector and the reference court. That right includes adequate notice of when compensation will be determined.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: An authority is determining compensation for land acquired for another body’s benefit.
predicates.beneficiary_body_pays_compensation: The body for whose benefit the land is acquired is responsible for paying the compensation.
predicates.beneficiary_body_can_present_evidence: The body for whose benefit the land is acquired seeks to present evidence relevant to compensation.

members.legal_issue: A local authority benefiting from an acquisition and bearing its compensation cost is entitled to notice and an opportunity to adduce evidence in compensation proceedings, and a compensation determination made without that opportunity cannot stand.
material_facts: The agency was a statutory authority responsible for development and had initiated the acquisition for the planned development of the area.
The agency was asked to provide the funds for payment of compensation.
The Collector and the Reference Court did not give the agency notice or an opportunity to adduce evidence.
The agency was not made a party or given notice before the High Court further enhanced the compensation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(aa) and 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 define local authority and person interested inclusively. Section 50(2) gives the local authority or company for whose account land is acquired the right to appear and adduce evidence, and the notice necessary to make that right effective is implicit in the provision and reflects natural justice. The proviso to Section 50(2) bars the local authority from demanding a reference under Section 18, but does not remove its right to participate or its other available remedies. The Court relied on Himalayan Tiles and Marble (P) Ltd. v. Francuis Victor Coutinho, (1980) 3 SCC 223; Union of India v. District Judge, (1994) 4 SCC 737; Neyvely Lignite Corporation Ltd. v. Special Tahsildar (L.A.), (1995) 1 SCC 221; U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Gyan Devi, (1995) 2 SCC 326; Agra Development Authority v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, (2001) 2 SCC 646; Abdul Rasak v. Kerala Water Authority, (2002) 3 SCC 228; Kanak v. U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad, (2003) 7 SCC 693; and Regional Medical Research Centre, Tribals v. Gokaran, (2004) 13 SCC 125. It also relied on P. Kasilingam v. P.S.G. College of Technology, 1995 Supp (2) SCC 348, Bharat Cooperative Bank (Mumbai) Ltd. v. Employees Union, (2007) 4 SCC 685, N.D.P. Namboodripad v. Union of India, (2007) 4 SCC 502, and Hamdard (Wakf) Laboratories v. Dy. Labour Commissioner, (2007) 5 SCC 281, concerning the breadth of inclusive definitions.
members.conclusion: The agency was a local authority and a person interested entitled to participate in the proceedings. The Collector’s failure to give it notice and an opportunity to adduce evidence was fatal to the award; the Reference Court’s decisions without notice were nullities; and the High Court erred in further enhancing compensation without the agency being joined. The decisions were set aside and the references remitted for fresh determination with an opportunity for the parties, including the agency, to adduce evidence.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and beneficiary_is_local_authority and beneficiary_bears_acquisition_cost and (no_notice_before_collector or no_notice_before_reference_court or enhancement_appeal_without_beneficiary_joined)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation for land acquired for a beneficiary.
predicates.beneficiary_is_local_authority: The beneficiary is a public authority with local development functions.
predicates.beneficiary_bears_acquisition_cost: The beneficiary is required to bear the cost of compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.no_notice_before_collector: The beneficiary was not notified of the compensation determination before the acquiring officer.
predicates.no_notice_before_reference_court: The beneficiary was not notified of the compensation determination before the court hearing the reference.
predicates.enhancement_appeal_without_beneficiary_j: A claimant sought enhanced compensation in an appeal without joining the beneficiary or giving it an opportunity to oppose the enhancement.

members.legal_issue: An authority for whose benefit land is acquired and which bears the compensation must be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before a compensation reference is determined, and an award made without that opportunity is not binding on the authority and must be reconsidered.
material_facts: The land was acquired for the requirements of a municipal corporation, which bore the burden of paying compensation.
A court received a reference concerning compensation but issued no notice to the corporation.
The court determined the compensation on the basis of an agreement between the landowners and the State, without taking evidence on valuation.
The corporation was thereby deprived of the opportunity to present its case and evidence on valuation.
The High Court set aside the award and directed that the reference proceedings be reopened to allow the corporation to present evidence.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(c) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as applicable in the State, requires notice to the person or authority for whom an acquisition is made when the acquisition is not for Government. The provision entitled the beneficiary corporation to be heard before determination of the compensation reference. The Court referred to Himalayan Tiles and Marbles (P) Ltd. v. Francis Victor Coutinho, [1980] 3 SCR 235, which interpreted “person interested” broadly, but held that it was unnecessary to interpret section 20(b) because section 20(c) specifically addressed the beneficiary authority.
members.conclusion: The corporation was entitled to notice and a hearing before determination of the reference. The award made without notice was illegal and not binding on the corporation, and the proceedings were properly ordered reopened for fresh determination after the corporation had an opportunity to lead evidence.

rule.if: compensation_reference_case and acquisition_for_non_government_beneficiary and beneficiary_bears_compensation and beneficiary_received_no_notice and beneficiary_denied_opportunity

predicates.compensation_reference_case: A court is determining a reference concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.acquisition_for_non_government_beneficia: The land was acquired for the benefit of a person or authority other than Government.
predicates.beneficiary_bears_compensation: The beneficiary bears the burden of paying the compensation.
predicates.beneficiary_received_no_notice: The court did not notify the beneficiary before determining the reference.
predicates.beneficiary_denied_opportunity: The beneficiary was deprived of an opportunity to present its case before the reference was determined.
predicates.reference_award_is_not_binding_on_benefi: The award is not binding on the beneficiary, and the proceedings must be reopened for a determination that gives the beneficiary an opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: A statutory beneficiary authority that bears liability for enhanced compensation is entitled to notice and participation in the compensation reference proceedings.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a government department before the statutory authority was constituted.
The authority came into existence before the civil court determined the compensation references.
The authority would bear liability for any enhancement beyond the amount awarded by the Collector.
The authority was not given notice or made a party to the reference proceedings in which compensation was enhanced.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read with the scheme of the Act, a local authority liable to pay compensation is a proper party entitled to adequate notice and an opportunity to contest enhancement and adduce evidence. U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Gyan Devi (Dead) by L.Rs. and Ors. recognizes these rights. The authority succeeded to the State's liability for the Collector's award, but liability for subsequent enhancement fell on the authority after its constitution.
members.conclusion: The authority was entitled to notice and to participate as a party in the reference proceedings concerning enhancement, and its absence justified remitting those proceedings for a fresh trial with the authority joined.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference: The proceeding concerns a reference to determine compensation for acquired land.
predicates.authority_bears_enhancement_liability: The statutory beneficiary authority bears liability for compensation beyond the amount initially awarded by the Collector.
predicates.authority_not_given_notice: The beneficiary authority was not given notice of the reference proceedings in which compensation was determined.

members.legal_issue: A tenant with a sufficient subsisting interest in land may challenge acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: One of the challengers was a tenant of land covered by the acquisition notification.
The lower courts did not reject the tenant’s challenge as unmaintainable.
The notification was common to the properties challenged by other owners, and it was quashed in those proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 treats as interested in land a person who would be entitled to claim an interest in compensation if the land were acquired. A tenant with a sufficient subsisting interest may therefore challenge acquisition proceedings in an appropriate case. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s challenge could not be rejected on the categorical ground that a tenant can never challenge acquisition proceedings.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A person challenges compulsory acquisition proceedings affecting land.
predicates.challenger_is_tenant: The person challenging the acquisition occupies the land as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_has_sufficient_subsisting_interes: The tenant has a continuing interest in the land sufficient to support a claim to an interest in compensation if the land is acquired.

members.legal_issue: A person with a subsisting leasehold interest in requisitioned property has standing to challenge the requisition.
material_facts: The claimants had acquired the original lessee's interest in the land, and the leases allowed renewal at the lessee's option up to a maximum term.
The leases were current when the requisition order was made, and there was no evidence that renewal had been refused or that the leases had been terminated or the land resumed.
The authorities had demanded and received rent for the land from the claimants.
members.legal_principle: A person whose subsisting proprietary or leasehold interest is affected by a requisition has standing to challenge it. The Court assessed the claimants' interest as it existed when the order was made, noting the transferable leasehold interest, the renewal options, the absence of evidence of termination or refusal of renewal, and the collection of rent.
members.conclusion: The claimants had sufficient locus standi to challenge the requisition order and seek restoration of their leasehold rights and possession.

predicates.challenge_to_property_requisition: A person challenges an authority's requisition of property in which that person claims an interest.
predicates.claimant_succeeded_to_leasehold_interest: The claimant acquired the leasehold interest from the original lessee.
predicates.leasehold_interest_was_subsisting_when_r: The leasehold interest remained in force when the authority made the requisition, with no established termination or refusal of renewal.

members.legal_issue: A statutory allottee in possession of evacuee property has standing to challenge an order that threatens the allottee’s possessory rights.
material_facts: The occupants held the property under allotments made by the Custodian and were in possession when a claim seeking restoration of the property was allowed.
The order challenged by the occupants would have affected their continued possession, which could be ended only on grounds and by procedures specified in the governing law.
members.legal_principle: Article 226 ordinarily requires an applicant to show an affected legal right. Statutory allottees have enforceable possessory interests even though those interests are not constitutional property rights; those interests are protected under the applicable statutory scheme. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Suraj Prakash Kapur, which drew on Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab, and on Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v. Additional Member Board of Revenue, Bihar & Anr., concerning parties affected by orders challenged through certiorari.
members.conclusion: The allottees had a legal interest sufficient to challenge the adverse order in writ proceedings.

predicates.statutory_allottee_in_possession: The person challenging the order occupies the property under an allotment made by the statutory property administrator.
predicates.challenged_order_threatens_possession: The challenged order could displace the occupant or otherwise impair the occupant’s legally protected possession.

members.legal_issue: An allottee of acquired evacuee property retains sufficient interest to seek judicial review of action affecting the allotted land.
material_facts: The respondents had received an allotment of land and remained in possession under a quasi-permanent tenure.
The Central Government acquired the evacuee property before the respondents filed their writ petition, but the respondents continued in possession on the conditions governing their allotment.
The respondents filed their petition before receiving a sanad, which conferred proprietary rights before the High Court finally disposed of the petition.
members.legal_principle: Sections 10 and 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, read with rule 14(6) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Rules, 1950, preserved an allottee’s valuable quasi-permanent interest while the property remained vested in the Central Government. The Court relied on Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab, which recognized that such rights were entitled to protection by the courts; the subsequent sanad conferred full proprietary rights.
members.conclusion: The respondents had sufficient interest to maintain their petition under Article 226, notwithstanding the acquisition notification issued before they filed it.

rule.if: displaced_person_allotment and acquired_allotted_property and continued_possession and writ_petition

predicates.displaced_person_allotment: A displaced person received an allotment of property under an evacuee-property arrangement.
predicates.acquired_allotted_property: The government acquired the property that had been allotted to the displaced person.
predicates.continued_possession: The allottee remained in possession under the conditions of the allotment after the acquisition.
predicates.writ_petition: The allottee brought a petition seeking judicial review of action affecting the allotted property.
predicates.writ_petition_maintainable: The allottee may maintain the petition seeking judicial review.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser with a documented interest in land being acquired is a person interested for purposes of the acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The claimant purchased the land at an auction and received a sale certificate.
The Collector had sued the claimant for possession of the land, and that suit and the appeal were dismissed.
The Collector later served the claimant with a notice calling for a claim to compensation.
The Collector did not deny the claimant’s entitlement to compensation in the proceedings before the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act includes persons claiming an interest in compensation payable on account of an acquisition. The circumstances, including the sale certificate and the Collector’s conduct acknowledging the claimant’s interest, established that status. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The claimant was a person interested within the meaning of section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government undertook proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.sale_certificate_issued: A purchaser received a sale certificate after buying the land at auction.
predicates.acquisition_authority_acknowledged_inter: The acquisition authority acted in ways acknowledging the claimant’s interest, including suing for possession, seeking a compensation claim, or not denying entitlement to compensation.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming an interest in compensation may be joined in a land acquisition reference when the objection before the court is likely to affect that interest.
material_facts: The acquired land was leased, and the compensation was apportioned between the landowner and the lessee.
The landowner and lessee each sought a reference challenging compensation and its apportionment.
A decree-holder had attached the lessee’s share of the compensation and claimed an interest in it.
The decree-holder’s claim could be affected by the resolution of the objections in the references.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(b), 20 and 21 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the inclusive definition of “person interested” covers a person claiming an interest in compensation, even without an interest in the acquired land. Such a person is interested in an objection concerning the amount or apportionment of compensation if the decision is likely to affect the person’s claim. Section 21 excludes consideration of interests not affected by the objection, but does not restrict the grounds an affected person may raise to protect those interests. The Court followed Grant v. State of Bihar and relied on Golap Khan v. Bholanath Marick and Siva Pratapa Bhattadu v. A.E.L. Mission; it distinguished Manjoor Ahmed v. Rajlaxmi Dasi, Abu Bakar v. Peary Mohan Mukherjee, Gobinda Kumar Roy v. Debendra Kumar Roy Chowdhury, Mahammad Safi v. Haran Chandra and Karuna Sindhu Dhar v. Panna Lal Paramanik.
members.conclusion: The decree-holder was a person interested in the compensation and in the objections, and was entitled to be made a party to the references.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference and claims_interest_in_compensation and (objection_concerns_amount_or_apportionment) and claim_likely_affected

predicates.land_acquisition_reference: A court is determining objections in a reference concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.claims_interest_in_compensation: A person claims an interest in the compensation to be awarded or apportioned.
predicates.objection_concerns_amount_or_apportionme: An objection before the court concerns the amount or apportionment of compensation.
predicates.claim_likely_affected: The decision on the objection is likely to affect the person’s claimed interest in compensation.
predicates.may_be_joined_as_party: The person may be joined as a party to the reference.

members.legal_issue: Joint family property is liable for a debt incurred by the family manager for the legal necessity or benefit of the joint family estate.
material_facts: The land sought to be sold was joint family property, as the plaintiffs had themselves described it as such in an earlier pleading.
The father obtained the loan to improve joint family agricultural land and offered other joint family land as security.
Agriculture was one of the family’s occupations, and the loan was intended to increase the productive potential of family land.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a joint family manager has implied authority to borrow for family purposes, and debts incurred for family legal necessity or the benefit of the estate bind the joint family property. The Court relied on Mulla’s Hindu Law, including paragraphs 240 and 251, and treated a loan to improve family agricultural land as being for legal necessity where agriculture was a family occupation.
members.conclusion: The loan was a joint family debt incurred for the benefit of the joint family estate, and the joint family property was liable for its repayment.

rule.if: joint_family_property and family_manager_borrowed and loan_improves_family_land and agriculture_is_family_occupation

predicates.joint_family_property: The property to be reached for repayment belonged to the joint family.
predicates.family_manager_borrowed: The family manager obtained the loan in circumstances showing that he acted for the family rather than solely for himself.
predicates.loan_improves_family_land: The loan was used or intended to improve land belonging to the joint family.
predicates.agriculture_is_family_occupation: Agriculture was one of the occupations carried on by the family.

members.legal_issue: An alienation of joint Hindu family property for debts must be a prudent transaction supported by adequate consideration, even when the alienation is said to meet a family necessity or discharge debts.
material_facts: The family’s manager and his brother sold nearly all of the family’s land and a house for a price the Court found grossly inadequate compared with the property’s value.
The sale deed omitted several debts, included fictitious debts, and permitted ordinary debts to be paid later, although almost all of the family property was being transferred.
The evidence supported the finding that the sale was nominal and intended to stave off creditors, with an understanding that the property would be reconveyed.
The vendees did not establish that the sale was a prudent disposition for adequate consideration.
members.legal_principle: To uphold an alienation of joint Hindu family property by a father or manager, it is necessary to establish legal necessity and that the father or manager acted prudently rather than sacrificing the property for inadequate consideration. The Court relied on Dudh Nath v. Sat Narain Ram for the prudence and adequate-consideration requirement. It also placed the burden of proving that the sale was valid and binding on the vendees.
members.conclusion: The sale could not be upheld and was set aside.

predicates.challenge_to_joint_family_property_alien: A party challenged a transfer of joint Hindu family property made by a family member managing or representing the family.
predicates.inadequate_consideration: The family property was transferred for consideration substantially below its value.
predicates.nominal_creditor_evasion: The transfer was arranged nominally to stave off creditors rather than as a genuine disposition of the property.

members.legal_issue: A karta’s sale of joint family property is justified by legal necessity when, viewed in the circumstances, it is a prudent act of management that benefits the family, including by disposing of a dilapidated and unproductive property to fund a more advantageous family asset.
material_facts: The property sold was part of joint family property and was in a dilapidated, dangerous condition with no present utility.
The sale proceeds were intended to fund an additional storey on the family’s house in the city where the karta worked and the family lived.
The courts below found that improving the city house was more advantageous to the family than rebuilding the old property.
The karta was the family’s sole adult male member and there was no allegation that he was a profligate or had reason to act to the family’s detriment.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that legal necessity is not to be construed narrowly and that a prudent act of management undertaken to benefit the family may justify an alienation. It approved and applied Nagindas Maneklal v. Mahomed Yusuf Mitchella, which treated disposal of a dilapidated property as potentially justified, and referred to Hunoomanpersaud Pandey v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree for the principle that the actual pressure, danger to be averted, or benefit to be conferred is what matters. The Court stated that the principles governing a karta’s alienation of joint family property are identical to those governing a manager’s alienation for an infant heir.
members.conclusion: The sale was an act of good management for the family’s benefit and was justified by legal necessity.

rule.if: joint_family_property and seller_was_family_manager and sold_property_was_dilapidated_or_unproductive and sale_funded_more_advantageous_family_property and sale_was_prudent_for_family_benefit

predicates.joint_family_property: The property sold belonged to a joint family or coparcenary.
predicates.seller_was_family_manager: The person who made the sale managed the family property and acted for the family.
predicates.sold_property_was_dilapidated_or_unprodu: The property sold was in poor condition or had little or no present utility or income value.
predicates.sale_funded_more_advantageous_family_pro: The sale proceeds were used or intended to be used to create or improve property more advantageous to the family.
predicates.sale_was_prudent_for_family_benefit: In the circumstances, the sale was a sensible management decision that protected or advanced the family’s interests.

members.legal_issue: A family manager may agree to alienate joint family property without legal necessity only where the transaction is shown to confer, or be reasonably expected to confer, a benefit on the family when made.
material_facts: The manager agreed to sell the family’s fractional share of land to a person who already owned most of the land.
There was no legal necessity for the sale.
The claim that the sale benefited the family rested on the small size of its fractional share and the higher price offered than the land’s earlier value.
The pleadings and evidence did not show that the manager considered the property difficult to manage, that retaining it caused loss, or that the proceeds would be invested profitably.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a family manager may alienate joint family property for the family’s benefit even if the transaction is not defensive and there is no compelling necessity. Whether a transaction benefits the family depends on the facts and circumstances, and the court must be satisfied from the material that it conferred or was reasonably expected to confer a benefit when entered into. The Court considered Jagatnarain v. Mathura Das, Hanooman Persaud Pandey v. Babooee Munraj Koonwaree, Sahu Ram Chandra v. Bhup Singh, Palaniappa Chetty v. Sreemath Daiyasikamony Pandara Sannadhi, Sital Prasad Singh v. Ajablal Mander, In the matter of A. V. Vasudevan & Ors. Minors, and Sellappa v. Suppan.
members.conclusion: The transaction was not established to be for the benefit of the family and was not binding on the family.

rule.if: manager_contract_to_sell_joint_family_property and no_legal_necessity and family_benefit_claimed and benefit_not_established_at_transaction

predicates.manager_contract_to_sell_joint_family_pr: A family manager agreed to sell property belonging to the joint family.
predicates.no_legal_necessity: The family had no legal necessity requiring the property to be sold.
predicates.family_benefit_claimed: A party claimed that the proposed sale would benefit the family.
predicates.benefit_not_established_at_transaction: The material did not establish that the sale conferred or was reasonably expected to confer a family benefit when it was made.

members.legal_issue: A manager of a joint Hindu family may surrender a tenancy without the other members’ express consent when the surrender benefits the family estate.
material_facts: The hotel had been closed for several years, while rent liability continued to accrue.
The family member acting as Karta surrendered the tenancy to the landlord.
The person who executed the surrender and the landlord’s representative admitted the surrender document and the transaction.
The Court held that surrendering the unused tenancy benefited the family by ending the continuing rent burden.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the Hindu law principle that a manager may bind the family by a transaction for legal necessity or the benefit of the estate, without obtaining express consent from adult coparceners. It relied on the principles described in Mulla’s Hindu Law and the authorities Suraj Bunsi Koer v. Sheo Proshad, Sahu Ram v. Bhup Singh and Radha Krishnadas v. Kaluram.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the tenancy was connected with a joint family business, the surrender was for the family’s benefit and did not require the express consent of the other coparceners.

rule.if: appeal_from_high_court_order and joint_family_tenancy_assumed and family_business_inactive_for_years and rent_obligation_continued and family_manager_surrendered_tenancy and surrender_document_admitted_by_executor_and_landlord

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_order: A party appealed from a High Court order concerning a tribunal’s decision.
predicates.joint_family_tenancy_assumed: The tenancy is treated, for purposes of the issue, as connected with a joint family.
predicates.family_business_inactive_for_years: The family business conducted from the premises had ceased operating for an extended period.
predicates.rent_obligation_continued: Rent continued to be payable while the premises were unused.
predicates.family_manager_surrendered_tenancy: The person managing the family surrendered the tenancy to the landlord.
predicates.surrender_document_admitted_by_executor_: The person who executed the surrender and the landlord’s representative acknowledged the surrender document.

members.legal_issue: A father's alienation of ancestral property binds his sons when it is made for family necessity or the benefit of the family and is not shown to be for an illegal or immoral purpose.
material_facts: The house was ancestral property, and the father was the manager of the joint Hindu family.
The father sold the house, which was in a dilapidated and ruinous condition, while living with his family elsewhere and earning a modest salary; the sale was recited to be for family necessity.
The purchasers made inquiries about the father's need for money before the sale.
The plaintiffs did not produce cogent evidence rebutting the recital of family necessity or show that the transaction was for an illegal or immoral purpose.
The purchasers substantially reconstructed the house after buying it, and the father stood by the sale for many years before supporting the challenge brought by his sons.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a father who is the manager of a joint family may alienate coparcenary property, including his sons' interests, for legal necessity or the benefit of the family. A father may also alienate it to discharge an antecedent debt, provided that the debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose. The Court referred to Mulla's Hindu Law, 16th edition, paragraphs 242 and 256. It assessed the asserted necessity in light of the sale deed's recital, the surrounding circumstances, the purchasers' inquiries, and the evidence; no earlier case was cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: The alienation was for the benefit of the family and was binding on the plaintiffs; they were not entitled to relief, and their suit was dismissed.

rule.if: ancestral_property_alienation_case and father_was_family_manager and family_necessity_or_benefit and no_illegal_or_immoral_purpose_shown

predicates.ancestral_property_alienation_case: Sons challenged their father's transfer of property in which they claimed interests by birth.
predicates.father_was_family_manager: The father managed the joint family when he made the transfer.
predicates.family_necessity_or_benefit: The transfer met a family need or benefited the family, as supported by the property's condition and the circumstances of the transaction.
predicates.no_illegal_or_immoral_purpose_shown: The challengers did not establish that the transfer was made for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A later alienation of joint family property to discharge a father's independent antecedent personal debt may bind his sons when the debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
material_facts: The father borrowed money for his personal benefit under a conditional sale deed several years before the challenged sale.
The sale proceeds were used to repay the loan and obtain reconveyance of the property for the benefit of the father and the family.
The sons did not establish that the loan was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
members.legal_principle: A father may alienate joint family property to discharge his personal debt if that debt was antecedent to the alienation and was not incurred for an immoral purpose; the sons' pious obligation supports the alienation. The Court relied on Mulla, Principles of Hindu Law, 15th edition, paragraph 295; Raja Brij Narain v. Mangala Prasad, AIR 1924 PC 50; Luhar Amrit Lal Nagji v. Doshi Jayantilal Jethalal, AIR 1960 SC 964; and Vyankates Dhonddeo Deshpande v. Sou. Kusum Dattatraya Kulkarni, [1979] 1 SCR 955. It distinguished Benares Bank Ltd. v. Hari Narain, LIX IA 300.
members.conclusion: The sale of the house and specified agricultural lands to discharge the antecedent debt was valid and binding on the sons.

rule.if: joint_family_property_alienation_challenge and sons_challenge_fathers_alienation and father_contracted_personal_debt and debt_is_antecedent_in_fact_and_time and sale_proceeds_discharge_debt and not debt_for_illegal_or_immoral_purpose

predicates.joint_family_property_alienation_challen: Members of a joint family challenged an alienation of joint family property.
predicates.sons_challenge_fathers_alienation: The sons challenged an alienation made by their father.
predicates.father_contracted_personal_debt: The father contracted the debt for his own personal benefit.
predicates.debt_is_antecedent_in_fact_and_time: The debt was independent of the challenged alienation and arose before it in fact and time.
predicates.sale_proceeds_discharge_debt: The proceeds of the alienation were used to discharge the earlier debt.
predicates.debt_for_illegal_or_immoral_purpose: The debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A father may alienate his sons’ interests in joint Hindu family property to discharge his own antecedent debt if the debt was not incurred for an immoral purpose and the alienation is prudent and supported by adequate consideration.
material_facts: The father incurred debts in connection with a new business conducted for his own benefit, and the debts preceded the challenged sale.
The sons did not allege that their father’s debts had been incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
The sale was intended to discharge debts, but the Court found that its consideration was grossly inadequate and that the transaction was nominal.
members.legal_principle: A father in a joint Hindu family may alienate joint family property, including his sons’ interests, to discharge his own debt if the debt is antecedent in fact and time, independent of the transaction impeached, and not incurred for an immoral purpose. The alienation must also satisfy the requirement of prudent conduct and adequate consideration. The Court relied on Sidheshwar Mukherjee v. Bhubneshwar Prasad Narain Singh, Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, Shanmukam v. Nachu Ammal, and Dudh Nath v. Sat Narain Ram.
members.conclusion: The father’s personal business debts were antecedent debts as against his sons, and the sons were under a pious obligation to discharge non-immoral debts; however, the challenged sale was not upheld because its consideration was inadequate and the transaction was imprudent.

rule.if: father_alienates_sons_interest and personal_debt_precedes_alienation and debt_independent_of_alienation and not immoral_purpose and prudent_adequate_alienation

predicates.father_alienates_sons_interest: A father transferred joint family property that included his sons’ interests.
predicates.personal_debt_precedes_alienation: The father incurred the debt for his own benefit before making the transfer.
predicates.debt_independent_of_alienation: The debt existed independently of, and was not part of, the transaction challenged by the sons.
predicates.immoral_purpose: The father incurred the debt for an immoral purpose.
predicates.prudent_adequate_alienation: The father made the transfer prudently and for adequate consideration.

members.legal_issue: A father’s mortgage of joint family property for a personal debt binds his son’s interest to the extent the mortgage secures a debt that was antecedent in fact and time and independent of the mortgage transaction.
material_facts: The father borrowed money for a new personal business that was not a family necessity or benefit, and the borrowing was not illegal or immoral.
Before the mortgage was created, the father owed the same bank substantial amounts on two overdraft accounts.
The bank handed the father a new loan by a separate draft while the earlier overdraft debts remained outstanding and unsecured.
The father deposited the draft into an overdraft account, and the earlier debts were thereby discharged.
The family was undivided when the mortgage was created; the later partition did not establish a defence to the creditor’s security.
The Court found that the entire new loan was used to discharge the pre-existing debts and that the transactions were factually dissociated.
members.legal_principle: Under Brij Narain v. Mangal Prasad, approved and adopted in Panna Lal v. Mst. Naraini, a father may, while the family remains undivided, alienate joint family property to discharge antecedent personal debts that are not illegal or immoral. A mortgage for a debt incurred at the same time is not binding on the son merely as a mortgage unless it discharges an antecedent debt. Antecedence requires both time and fact: the prior debt must be truly independent of the mortgage debt, and the transactions must be dissociated in fact. Whether that separation exists depends on the nature of the transactions, the parties’ intention, and the form in which they carried out the transaction. The Court also referred to Chidambara Mudaliar v. Kootha Perumal and Venkataramayya v. Venkataramana in discussing the differing historical views on the rule.
members.conclusion: The prior overdraft indebtedness was antecedent in fact and time, notwithstanding that the same bank was the creditor and the new loan was used to pay the earlier debts. The mortgage therefore bound the son’s share to the extent of the loan secured by it, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: mortgage_enforcement_claim_against_sons_share and father_mortgaged_joint_family_property_while_family_was_undivided and debt_was_personal_and_not_illegal_or_immoral and prior_debt_existed_before_mortgage and prior_debt_was_independent_of_mortgage_debt and new_loan_was_used_to_discharge_prior_debt

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_claim_against_sons_: A creditor sought to enforce a mortgage against a son’s interest in joint family property.
predicates.father_mortgaged_joint_family_property_w: A father mortgaged joint family property while the family remained undivided.
predicates.debt_was_personal_and_not_illegal_or_imm: The father incurred the debt for a personal purpose that was neither illegal nor immoral.
predicates.prior_debt_existed_before_mortgage: The father already owed the debt before creating the mortgage.
predicates.prior_debt_was_independent_of_mortgage_d: The earlier debt was a genuinely independent transaction, rather than part of the transaction creating the mortgage debt.
predicates.new_loan_was_used_to_discharge_prior_deb: The father used the new loan to pay off the earlier debt.

members.legal_issue: A son may impeach a mortgage of joint-family property that the father-manager made without legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt, even after a decree on the mortgage has been passed against the father.
material_facts: A father acting as manager mortgaged joint-family property, and a son claimed that the mortgage was neither for legal necessity nor for payment of an antecedent debt.
The mortgagee obtained a decree against the father on the mortgage before the son’s challenge was finally decided.
The son sought a declaration that the mortgage and decree did not bind his interest in the property.
members.legal_principle: The first and third propositions in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, read together, establish that a manager generally cannot burden joint-family property except for legal necessity and that a father-manager’s mortgage must be for legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt to bind the estate. A decree against the father does not itself create or enlarge a mortgage over the son’s interest.
members.conclusion: The decree against the father did not enlarge the mortgagee’s security or make the mortgage binding on the son’s interest; the son remained entitled to challenge the mortgage on the ground that it lacked legal necessity and was not for payment of an antecedent debt.

predicates.son_challenges_family_mortgage_after_dec: A son challenges the effect on his interest of a mortgage of joint-family property after a decree on the mortgage has been passed against his father.
predicates.father_managed_joint_family: The father acted as manager of the joint family when he mortgaged its property.
predicates.mortgage_lacked_legal_necessity_and_ante: The mortgage was neither for legal necessity nor for payment of an antecedent debt.

members.legal_issue: A mortgage securing a father-manager’s loan binds the joint-family property, including the son’s interest, when the loan is used partly to pay antecedent debts and partly for the joint-family business and other legal necessities.
material_facts: The father-manager borrowed money and mortgaged joint-family property to secure repayment.
Part of the loan was used to discharge antecedent debts.
The remaining loan proceeds were used for the joint-family business and other legal necessities, including family maintenance and the son’s education.
The Court found that the father was carrying on the family business and rejected evidence that he had not done so.
members.legal_principle: Under Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, a father-manager may mortgage the joint-family estate for legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt. The Court found the loan was used for antecedent debts and for the family business and other legal necessities, and held that the mortgage therefore bound the property in its entirety.
members.conclusion: The mortgage in its entirety bound the joint-family property, including the son’s interest.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_mortgage_binding and father_mortgaged_joint_family_property and loan_partly_paid_antecedent_debts and remaining_loan_served_family_business_or_legal_necessities

predicates.appeal_challenges_mortgage_binding: A son appeals a ruling about whether a mortgage made by his father binds his interest in joint-family property.
predicates.father_mortgaged_joint_family_property: A father acting as manager mortgaged property belonging to the joint family.
