members.legal_issue: A son's pious obligation to discharge his father's personal debt depends on the debt being vyavaharik and not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
material_facts: The father borrowed money for his personal use in starting a grain business.
The courts found that the father was not indulging in the alleged vices, and the sons' challenge did not establish that the debt was incurred for an immoral or illegal purpose.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine rests on religious considerations and presupposes a vyavaharik debt. The Court relied on Luhar Amrit Lal Nagji v. Doshi Jayantilal Jethalal, AIR 1960 SC 964, and Vyankates Dhonddeo Deshpande v. Sou. Kusum Dattatraya Kulkarni, [1979] 1 SCR 955; it also referred to Mulla, Principles of Hindu Law, 15th edition, paragraph 295.
members.conclusion: The doctrine of pious obligation applies only to a father's debt that is vyavaharik; sons may be liable for their father's personal debt if it is not tainted by illegality or immorality.

rule.if: joint_family_debt_challenge and father_contracted_personal_debt and debt_is_vyavaharik and not debt_for_illegal_or_immoral_purpose

predicates.joint_family_debt_challenge: Sons challenged their liability for a debt contracted by their father while they were members of a joint family.
predicates.father_contracted_personal_debt: The father contracted the debt for his own personal benefit.
predicates.debt_is_vyavaharik: The debt was of a kind to which the doctrine of pious obligation applies.
predicates.debt_for_illegal_or_immoral_purpose: The debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A son's liability for his father's debt under the doctrine of pious obligation is not excluded unless the debt is shown to be tainted by illegality or immorality.
material_facts: The son argued that the debt underlying the execution proceedings was incurred for immoral purposes and therefore could not bind his interest in the family property.
The evidence offered to establish that the father used part of the loan for an immoral purpose came from two witnesses whose testimony the High Court disbelieved.
The Supreme Court found no reason to differ from the High Court's assessment of that evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under the doctrine of pious obligation, a son is liable for his father's debt unless the debt is tainted by illegality or immorality. The Court applied the doctrine as discussed in Girdharee Lall v. Kantoo Lall (1874) 1 I.A. 321, Suraj Bansi Koer v. Sheo Prasad (1880) 6 I.A. 88, Muttayan v. Zamindari of Sivagiri (1883) 9 I.A. 128, and Brij Narain v. Mangal Prasad, 51 I.A. 129, and accepted the High Court's factual finding that the alleged immoral purpose had not been proved.
members.conclusion: The allegation that the debt was tainted by immorality was not established, so immorality did not exclude the son's liability under the doctrine of pious obligation.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_son_liability_fo: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning a son's liability for his father's debt.
predicates.debt_taint_alleged: A party alleges that the father's debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_illegal_or_i: The evidence does not establish that the debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A son cannot restrain execution of a mortgage decree against joint-family property for a debt personally owed by his father if the debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
material_facts: A father who managed a joint family mortgaged its property and personally covenanted to repay the loan.
The mortgagee obtained a decree for sale of the property against the father, and a son sought to stop the sale before it took place.
The debt was admitted to be owing by the father and was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under the second proposition in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad, a father may, by incurring a debt not tainted by an immoral purpose, expose joint-family property to execution for payment of that debt. The principle applies to secured as well as unsecured debts and to execution of a mortgage decree before sale. The Court relied on Luhar Amritlal Nagji v. Doshi Jayantilal Jethalal and the pious-obligation doctrine, and rejected contrary observations in Jagdish Prasad v. Hoshyar Singh, Bharamappa Murdeppa v. Hanmantappa Tippanna, Ganpati v. Rameshwar, and Abdul Hameed Sait v. Provident Investment Co. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The son had no right to obtain an interim or final stay of the sale, even though the sale had not yet occurred and his suit had been filed before the decree for sale.

predicates.son_challenges_mortgage_decree_execution: A son seeks to stop execution of a mortgage decree against joint-family property mortgaged by his father as manager.
predicates.father_personally_owes_debt: The father is personally liable to repay the debt secured by the mortgage.
predicates.debt_not_illegal_or_immoral: The debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A father managing a joint Hindu family may expose the joint family estate to execution for a debt he incurs, including a mortgage debt, if the debt is not for an immoral purpose, even when it was not incurred for legal necessity.
material_facts: The father, who was the manager of the family, mortgaged property that the sons claimed was joint Hindu family property.
The sons alleged that the mortgage was made without consideration and family necessity.
The Court addressed whether a mortgage debt incurred by a father-manager could expose the joint family estate to execution despite the absence of legal necessity.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a father who manages a joint family may incur a debt that exposes the joint family estate to execution, provided the debt is not for an immoral purpose. This applies to a mortgage debt for which the father is personally liable, even if the mortgage was not for legal necessity or payment of an antecedent debt. The Court relied on Faqir Chand v. Harnam Kaur.
members.conclusion: A father-manager’s debt may expose the joint family estate to execution if it was not incurred for an immoral purpose; the absence of legal necessity does not by itself prevent that result, including for a mortgage debt.

members.legal_issue: A genuine partition does not discharge liability for an unpaid pre-partition family debt when no provision for that debt was made at partition, and sons remain liable for an untainted debt of their father to the extent of family property received.
material_facts: A registered partition between the father and his sons took place while the loan remained unpaid.
The partition made no provision for the outstanding family debts.
The debt was incurred before partition and was not shown to have been incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.
members.legal_principle: Hindu law requires provision to be made for joint family debts when the family estate is partitioned; absent such provision, the sons remain liable for pre-partition debts. The pious obligation extends to a father’s debts not tainted with illegality or immorality. The Court relied on Sat Narain v. Das, Pannalal v. Mst. Naraini, Vriddhachalam Pillai v. Shaldean Syrian Bank Ltd., Muttayan v. Zamindar of Sivagiri, and Anthonyswamy v. M. R. Chinnaswamy Koundan.
members.conclusion: The property allotted to the sons remained liable for the pre-partition debt; the sons’ pious obligation to pay their father’s untainted debt continued after partition.

rule.if: pre_partition_debt and partition_made and no_debt_provision_at_partition and not debt_tainted

predicates.pre_partition_debt: The debt was incurred before the family partition.
predicates.partition_made: The family estate was partitioned and property was allotted to the sons.
predicates.no_debt_provision_at_partition: The partition arrangement made no provision for payment of the outstanding debt.
predicates.debt_tainted: The debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A son’s share received on partition remains liable for the father’s pre-partition debt if the debt is neither illegal nor immoral and no proper arrangement for its payment was made at partition.
material_facts: The father incurred the debt before the partition.
The sons received separate shares of family property on partition.
The debt’s legality or morality and whether provision for its payment was made at partition had not been determined.
members.legal_principle: Under the Hindu-law pious obligation, a son’s liability for a father’s debt is limited to liable ancestral property and does not attach to the son’s self-acquisitions or create personal liability. The obligation continues after partition for pre-partition debts that are not illegal or immoral unless a proper arrangement for payment was made at partition. The Court relied on Hindu-law texts, Sat Narain v. Das, and Bankey Lal v. Durga Prasad, and approved the latter decision’s approach.
members.conclusion: A son remains liable after partition for the father’s pre-partition debt if it is not illegal or immoral and no arrangement for its payment was made when the partition took place.

rule.if: claim_for_father_debt_against_separated_son and debt_incurred_before_partition and not debt_illegal_or_immoral and no_payment_arrangement_at_partition

predicates.claim_for_father_debt_against_separated_: A creditor sought payment of a father’s debt from a son who had separated from the father by partition.

predicates.no_payment_arrangement_at_partition: No proper arrangement for payment of the debt was made when the partition took place.

members.legal_issue: A partition does not defeat a creditor’s claim against a son’s share when the son fails to establish that the partition made adequate provision for the father’s debts.
material_facts: A father and his minor son were members of an undivided Hindu family that owned property in more than one state.
After the father incurred debts, a partition deed divided only the family’s property in one state into equal shares and assigned the father responsibility for certain debts.
The father had numerous other debts, and the partition did not provide for all of them.
The son did not establish the value of the property available to the father or that his allotted share was adequate to discharge the debts.
The creditor sought to enforce its security against the son’s share.
members.legal_principle: Under Panna Lal v. Mst. Naraini, a son may remain liable after partition for the father’s pre-partition debts that are not illegal or immoral if no proper arrangement for their payment was made at partition. Whether an arrangement is adequate depends on the circumstances. The son who relies on the partition to discharge his liability must establish that the arrangement made proper and adequate provision. A partition need not be fraudulent to fail to bind a creditor if it makes no adequate provision for the debts.
members.conclusion: The partition was not binding on the creditor. The son bore the burden of establishing that the arrangement made proper and adequate provision for the debts; that burden was not met.

predicates.creditor_claims_against_sons_share_after: A creditor sought to reach property allotted to a son after partition.
predicates.father_had_prepartition_debts: A father owed debts incurred before the partition.
predicates.partition_did_not_make_adequate_provisio: The partition arrangement did not provide adequate property or other provision for payment of all the father’s debts.
predicates.son_failed_to_establish_adequate_provisi: The son relying on the partition did not prove that the arrangement adequately provided for payment of the debts.

members.legal_issue: Partition does not end a son’s liability for a father’s pre-partition debt that is not tainted with immorality or illegality.
material_facts: A payment order was made against the father before the partition suit was filed.
The family property was attached and sale proceedings had begun before the partition suit.
The debt was not shown to have been incurred for an immoral or illegal purpose.
No arrangement for payment of the father’s debt at partition was established.
members.legal_principle: The sons’ liability rests on their pious obligation, not solely on the father’s power to alienate their shares. Partition ends that power of alienation but does not discharge the sons’ liability for a father’s pre-partition debt that is not immoral or illegal, unless payment of the debt was provided for at partition. The Court relied on Panna Lal v. Mst. Naraini and Sudheshwar Mukherji v. Bhubneshwar Prasad Narain Singh, and applied the principles in Nanomi Babuasin v. Modun Mohan and related authorities on a creditor’s ability to proceed against the sons’ interests.
members.conclusion: The sons’ pious obligation continued after partition, and their shares remained liable to satisfy the father’s debt.

rule.if: execution_of_pre_partition_father_debt and debt_not_tainted_with_immorality_or_illegality and partition_after_decree and no_payment_arrangement_at_partition

predicates.debt_not_tainted_with_immorality_or_ille: The father’s debt was not tainted with immorality or illegality.
predicates.partition_after_decree: The family partition occurred after the decree against the father.
predicates.no_payment_arrangement_at_partition: No arrangement for paying the father’s debt was made when the family partitioned.

members.legal_issue: A sale in execution for an untainted pre-partition debt is not invalid merely because it occurs after partition or the sons were not parties to the recovery proceeding.
material_facts: Recovery proceedings for the loan began before the partition, although the sale proclamation for the disputed land was issued later.
The sons knew of the intended sale, and the purchaser was put in possession after the sale was confirmed.
The sons did not establish that the debt was tainted with illegality or immorality.
The sale covered the whole property, which the purchaser intended to buy and did buy.
members.legal_principle: A revenue recovery order for a loan recoverable as arrears of land revenue is equivalent to a decree, and a sale proclamation is execution of that decree. The pious obligation continues after partition, and the whole estate may be sold for an untainted pre-partition debt. The sons’ remedy is to challenge the character of the debt in an appropriate proceeding. The Court relied particularly on S. M. Jakati & Sons v. S. M. Borkar, read with Pannalal v. Mst. Naraini, and applied sections 150 and 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code to the recovery process.
members.conclusion: The sale could not be set aside solely because it occurred after partition or because the sons were not parties to the recovery proceeding; the sons could challenge it by establishing that the debt was tainted.

predicates.sale_challenged_in_suit: The sons brought a proceeding seeking to set aside a sale of family property for their father’s debt.
predicates.revenue_recovery_for_pre_partition_debt: The recovery process concerned a debt incurred before partition and recoverable through revenue procedures.
predicates.property_sold_in_execution: The property was sold through an execution or revenue-sale process and the purchaser acquired possession.
predicates.debt_tainted: The debt was incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser at an execution sale under a decree against a father may acquire his sons’ interests in joint family property for a non-immoral debt even when the father was not the family manager and the sons were not parties to the suit or execution proceedings.
material_facts: The debtor was a father in an undivided Hindu family that included his sons and other coparceners; he was not the family manager.
The father had borrowed money, and the debt was not shown to be immoral or irreligious.
A decree was obtained against the father alone, and the execution sale was found to include the interests of the father’s sons.
The sons had an opportunity in the partition suit to assert that the debt was not binding on them, but did not establish that claim.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara Hindu law, sons’ interests in coparcenary property are liable for their father’s debts that are not tainted with immorality or irreligion. That liability is not limited by the father’s power of voluntary disposition, nor does it depend on his being the karta or on the family consisting only of the father and sons. Under the rule in Nanomi Babuasin v. Modun Mohun, a creditor may have the sons’ interests sold without joining them, subject to their right to establish that the debt is not binding on them. The Court relied also on Pannalal v. Mst. Naraini and approved Lalta Prashad v. Gazadhar, Chhotey Lal v. Ganpat, and Virayya v. Parthasarathi.
members.conclusion: The purchaser acquired the sons’ interests included in the execution sale, and the purchaser was entitled to the claimed one-fourth share.

members.legal_issue: An unsuccessful bidder whose auction sale was not confirmed is entitled to repayment of the earnest money deposited, with interest.
material_facts: The bidder deposited earnest money after the provisional acceptance of the highest bid.
The competent authority did not confirm the sale, and the auction bid was cancelled.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed repayment with interest as relief after finding that the provisional auction sale had not been confirmed; it stated no separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this direction.
members.conclusion: The earnest money was ordered to be refunded with interest from the date of deposit until payment.

predicates.earnest_money_deposited: The bidder paid earnest money in connection with the provisional bid.
predicates.sale_not_confirmed: The competent authority did not confirm the auction sale.

members.legal_issue: An auction purchaser is entitled to repayment with interest when an auction is annulled through no fault of the purchaser.
material_facts: The auction purchaser deposited the purchase price with the authorities.
The auction was annulled because the amendment could not retrospectively govern the property proceedings, and the annulment was through no fault of the purchaser.
members.legal_principle: In the peculiar circumstances, because the auction had to be annulled through no fault of the purchaser, the Court directed repayment of the deposited purchase price with interest. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this direction.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to a refund of the entire amount deposited with interest at six per cent per annum from the auction date until payment, and the Department was directed to pay it within three months.

predicates.auction_annulment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether an annulled auction requires repayment to its purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_deposited_purchase_price: The auction purchaser paid the purchase price to the relevant authorities.
predicates.auction_annulled_without_purchaser_fault: The auction was annulled for reasons not attributable to the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_is_entitled_to_refund_with_int: The purchaser is entitled to repayment of the deposited purchase price together with interest.

members.legal_issue: A deposit retained by a public authority after the auction claim fails must be returned with interest.
material_facts: The bidders had paid 25 per cent of the bid amount.
The authority said it had sent the deposit back by cheque, but the bidders did not accept it.
The deposit remained with the authority for about fourteen years, and the Court dismissed the bidders’ writ petition.
members.legal_principle: Having rejected the claim to the property and found that the deposit remained with the authority, the Court ordered its return with interest. The judgment cites no earlier case or specific provision for that order.
members.conclusion: The authority was directed to return the retained deposit with interest at 9 per cent per annum from the date of the auction until its return.

predicates.auction_claim_failed: The claimant’s demand for the auctioned property or a substitute property was rejected.
predicates.deposit_remained_unreturned: The deposit paid by the claimant remained with the public authority and had not been returned.

members.legal_issue: When an execution sale is set aside, the court may direct repayment of the auction purchaser’s purchase money and account for interest earned or not earned while the money was held.
material_facts: The auction purchaser’s money had remained in court after the sale.
The money was later invested in a fixed deposit and earned interest.
The court directed repayment of the purchase money and the interest earned, and required the judgment debtors to pay interest for the period when the money earned none.
members.legal_principle: Order 21, Rule 93 of the Code of Civil Procedure entitles the court to direct repayment of purchase money when a sale is set aside. The court also addressed the interest consequences according to whether the money held in court was earning interest.
members.conclusion: The auction purchaser could withdraw the purchase money together with the interest earned, while the judgment debtors were directed to pay interest for the period when the money was not earning interest.

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside: The court set aside an execution sale.
predicates.purchaser_money_held_by_court: The auction purchaser’s money remained with the court after the sale.
predicates.interest_accrued_or_was_not_accruing: The money held by the court earned interest during some period or did not earn interest during some period.

members.legal_issue: When an invalidated recovery sale requires the auction purchaser's money to be refunded, equitable interest may be allocated between the taxpayer and the recovery authority according to when the authority was informed that the demand no longer existed.
material_facts: The auction purchaser paid the purchase money, which remained with the tax authorities after the sale was set aside.
The demand had ceased to exist, and the taxpayer had informed the recovery authority of that fact.
The Court directed that the taxpayer bear interest for the period before that notification and that the tax department bear interest thereafter, as equitable relief on the facts of the case.
The Court expressly stated that this interest award did not lay down a principle to be followed as precedent.
members.legal_principle: The Court awarded interest on equitable considerations because the purchaser had been deprived of the use of the deposited money. It allocated responsibility to the taxpayer before the recovery authority was informed that the demand had ceased to exist, and to the tax department after that point, when the authority should have cancelled the recovery certificate. The Court expressly disclaimed laying down a precedent or general principle of law.
members.conclusion: The auction purchaser was entitled to a refund with interest; the taxpayer was responsible for interest before the recovery authority was informed that the demand no longer existed, and the tax department was responsible thereafter. The allocation was made on equitable considerations specific to the case and was not declared a precedent.

members.legal_issue: An auction purchaser whose sale is set aside is not automatically entitled to interest on the refunded purchase price where the purchaser had received possession and the sale terms reserved the court’s power to set the sale aside after payment.
material_facts: The auction sale was set aside on appeal.
The purchaser had paid the purchase price and received possession of the property.
The sale terms expressly allowed the court to set aside the sale even after confirmation or payment.
The purchaser sought interest and recovery of expenditure incurred after the purchase.
members.legal_principle: Motors and Invests Ltd. v. Union Bank of India was distinguishable because possession had been handed over after payment in the present case. Relying on Allahabad Bank v. Bengal Paper Mills Co. Ltd., the Court held that a purchaser who knew or was bound by the possibility of the sale being set aside could not claim interest merely because the sale was later invalidated; the purchaser could separately apply for recovery of expenditure if entitled to it in law. The express sale condition also reserved the court’s power to set aside the sale after confirmation or payment.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to a refund of the amount deposited without interest, but could apply to recover other expenditure if legally entitled to it.

members.legal_issue: Setting aside an execution sale may be conditioned on equitable compensation to the auction-purchaser when the purchaser’s money has remained blocked for a substantial period.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors sought to set aside the execution sale, and the Court concluded that the pending objections did not bar their separate application.
The auction-purchaser’s money had remained blocked for a substantial number of years and was probably more than the amount required by the decree.

The Court directed that the sale be set aside upon payment to the auction-purchaser of the deposited amount with interest, while crediting the judgment-debtors for the amount deposited in court and any interest earned on it.
The Court provided that the appeal would be dismissed if the required payment was not made within the specified time.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied equitable fairness in fashioning relief: setting aside the sale without relief for an auction-purchaser whose money had remained blocked for a substantial period would be unfair. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this equitable condition.
members.conclusion: The sale was to be set aside only if the judgment-debtors paid the auction-purchaser equitable compensation, including interest on the blocked money, with credit for the court deposit and any interest earned on it; otherwise, the appeal would stand dismissed.

predicates.execution_sale_appeal: The case is an appeal concerning a sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.sale_setting_aside_sought: The judgment-debtor seeks to have the execution sale set aside.
predicates.auction_purchaser_funds_blocked_for_subs: The auction-purchaser’s money has remained unavailable to the purchaser for a substantial period.

members.legal_issue: A court may direct compensation for auction purchasers whose purchase money remains blocked when a sale is set aside because a substituted preliminary decree removes the basis for the sale.
material_facts: The auction purchasers’ purchase money had remained deposited in court since the sale proceedings began.
The substituted preliminary decree was satisfied, removing the basis for the final decree sale and its confirmation.
The Court held that the strict compensation provision in Order 34, Rule 5(2) did not apply because that stage had not arrived in law.
The judgment debtor’s appeal was allowed subject to a direction to pay the auction purchasers interest on their blocked purchase money.
members.legal_principle: Order 34, Rule 5(2) provides for a compensatory deposit in the circumstances specified by that rule, but those circumstances had not arisen here because the relevant stage had been rendered non-est. The Court nevertheless exercised its inherent powers under the Code of Civil Procedure and its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to further the cause of complete justice and to be fair to the auction purchasers.
members.conclusion: Although compensation was not due under the strict terms of Order 34, Rule 5(2), the Court directed payment to the auction purchasers of a sum equivalent to the blocked purchase money, exercising its inherent powers under the Code and its powers under Article 142 to do complete justice.

members.legal_issue: Restitution following the setting aside of an execution sale must account for the purchaser’s possession of the property and any improvements made.
material_facts: The sale of the further properties was set aside.
The purchaser asserted that he had possessed the properties and made improvements.
The court directed the executing court to determine possession and the value of any improvements.
members.legal_principle: When an execution sale is set aside, the court should adjust restitution according to possession and improvements: a purchaser who possessed the property may recover the purchase price and the value of improvements upon returning it, without interest on the improvement value; if the purchaser was not in possession, the debtor must refund the purchase price with interest.
members.conclusion: The executing court must inquire into possession and improvements. If the purchaser was in possession, he must return the property and receive the purchase price and the value of improvements, without interest on the improvement value. If he was not in possession, the debtor must repay the purchase price with interest, and no improvement payment arises.

predicates.purchaser_did_not_possess_property: The purchaser did not possess the property after the sale.

members.legal_issue: When specific performance is refused after the plaintiff has paid earnest money and deposited the balance consideration, those sums are to be returned with applicable interest.
material_facts: The plaintiff had paid earnest money under the agreement for sale.
After the first appellate court granted specific performance, the plaintiff deposited the balance consideration with that court.
The Supreme Court set aside the decree for specific performance.
The Court directed the sellers to repay the earnest money with interest and permitted the plaintiff to withdraw the deposited balance with any interest accrued on it.
members.legal_principle: After setting aside the decree for specific performance, the Court directed repayment of the earnest money with interest and allowed withdrawal of the balance consideration deposited in the appellate court. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this direction.
members.conclusion: The sellers were ordered to repay the earnest money with interest at 12% per annum from the agreement date to the judgment date and thereafter at 10% per annum until payment. The plaintiff was permitted to withdraw the deposited balance consideration with any interest accrued on it.

predicates.specific_performance_claim_rejected: The court refused the plaintiff’s claim for specific performance.
predicates.plaintiff_paid_earnest_money: The plaintiff paid earnest money to the other party under the agreement.
predicates.plaintiff_deposited_balance_consideratio: The plaintiff deposited the balance consideration with a court during the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Earnest money may be ordered returned when specific performance is refused and, in the circumstances, the recipient is not entitled to retain it.
material_facts: The purchaser had paid earnest money under the agreement.
The purchaser was denied specific performance because he failed to prove readiness and willingness.
The Court held that, in the circumstances of the case, the sellers were not entitled to keep the earnest money.
members.legal_principle: The Court made an equitable order in the particular circumstances, holding that refusal of specific performance did not entitle the sellers to retain the earnest money. It did not cite a separate statutory provision or earlier case for this refund order.
members.conclusion: The earnest money had to be returned without interest within the time directed by the Court, with interest accruing if repayment was delayed.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and earnest_money_paid and specific_performance_refused and recipient_not_entitled_to_retain_earnest

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.earnest_money_paid: The purchaser paid earnest money under the contract.
predicates.specific_performance_refused: The court refused the requested specific performance.
predicates.recipient_not_entitled_to_retain_earnest: The court found in the circumstances that the recipient was not entitled to keep the earnest money.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser at a judicial sale in execution of a decree later reversed is not protected from restitution if the purchaser was the decree-holder, knew of the pending appeal, or colluded with or acted as a name-lender for the decree-holder.
material_facts: A money decree was executed while the judgment debtor’s appeal against it was pending, and the judgment debtor’s properties were sold at a court auction to a person who was not formally a party to the decree.
The decree was later reversed on appeal, and the judgment debtor sought restitution of the properties.

Evidence showed that the auction purchaser was related by marriage to the decree-holder, lacked money of his own to buy the properties, and joined the decree-holder in an agreement to sell one of the properties.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, courts must remedy injury caused by their proceedings and restore parties, so far as possible, to the position they would have occupied absent the decree. A bona fide stranger purchaser without knowledge of the pending litigation is generally protected when the decree is later reversed or modified, as stated in Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh and Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai. That protection does not extend to a decree-holder purchaser, a purchaser who knew of the pending appeal, or a collusive or nominal purchaser. The Court rejected the contrary approach in R. Raghavachari v. M.A. Pakkiri Mahomed Rowther and relied also on Chhota Nagpur Banking Association v. C.T.M. Smith, Jamnomal Gurdinomal v. Gopaldas, Rodger v. The Comptoir D’Escompte De Paris, and A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak. The procedural provisions in Order 21, rules 89–91 do not require courts to protect a purchaser who is not bona fide when restitution is otherwise warranted.
members.conclusion: The auction purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser, so the sale in his favour had to fall for restitution.

rule.if: execution_sale and decree_later_reversed and (purchaser_is_decree_holder or purchaser_knew_of_pending_appeal or purchaser_colluded_with_decree_holder_or_acted_as_name_lender)

predicates.execution_sale: The property was sold at a judicial sale held to execute a decree.
predicates.decree_later_reversed: The decree under which the sale was held was later reversed or modified.
predicates.purchaser_is_decree_holder: The person who bought the property at the sale was the decree-holder.
predicates.purchaser_knew_of_pending_appeal: The purchaser knew of the pending appeal against the decree when buying the property.
predicates.purchaser_colluded_with_decree_holder_or: The purchaser colluded with the decree-holder or bought the property as the decree-holder’s nominal purchaser.

members.legal_issue: A decree-holder who purchases attached property at a court auction is not protected as a stranger auction purchaser when the underlying decree is set aside on appeal, and cannot acquire an interest the judgment debtor had already transferred before the auction.
material_facts: The mortgagor transferred the equity of redemption to a subsequent purchaser before the creditor’s court auction.
The creditor had obtained an attachment before judgment and later purchased the property himself at auction while his decree was subject to appeal.
The trial decree was set aside on appeal before a later appellate court restored only a reduced money decree.
The property was sold subject to the subsisting mortgage, and the creditor, rather than an independent stranger, was the auction purchaser.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a private transfer of attached property is void against claims enforceable under the attachment, which are the claims for which the decree is made. An attachment before judgment serves as security for satisfaction of that claim and falls when the decree supporting it is set aside on appeal. Although a stranger auction purchaser may be protected where execution proceeds without a stay, a decree-holder who purchases with knowledge that the decree is under appeal is not entitled to that protection. The Court followed Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh and applied Order XXXVIII Rule 5 and Section 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The creditor did not acquire the equity of redemption at the auction and was not entitled to protection as a stranger auction purchaser; his rights did not include ownership of the property.

rule.if: appeal_concerning_court_auction_sale and decree_holder_purchased_attached_property and underlying_decree_set_aside_on_appeal and prior_transfer_of_judgment_debtor_interest and property_sold_subject_to_existing_mortgage

predicates.appeal_concerning_court_auction_sale: The proceeding concerns the effect of a court auction conducted to execute a decree that is challenged in appeal.
predicates.decree_holder_purchased_attached_propert: The person who obtained the decree, rather than an independent stranger, purchased the attached property at the court auction.
predicates.underlying_decree_set_aside_on_appeal: The decree being executed was set aside by an appellate court.
predicates.prior_transfer_of_judgment_debtor_intere: The judgment debtor transferred the relevant property interest before the court auction.
predicates.property_sold_subject_to_existing_mortga: The court auction sale was expressly subject to a mortgage that remained in force.

members.legal_issue: A court auction cannot displace a purchaser’s title acquired under an authorized private sale completed before the auction when the judgment-debtor has no saleable interest at the time of auction, and an auction that breaches a condition imposed on the authorized sale cannot confer valid title.
material_facts: The competent authority permitted the tribal owner to sell the property privately for a specified price.
The owner sold the property to the private purchaser after obtaining permission and before the court auction.
The attachment preceding the private sale was void, and the owner had no saleable interest left when the auction occurred.
The auction was conducted for less than the price required by the permission.
members.legal_principle: A court sale transfers only the judgment-debtor’s right, title, and interest, so an auction purchaser acquires no interest the debtor no longer has. Further, where permission for a private sale is subject to a price condition, an auction sale that violates that condition cannot confer valid title. The Court applied clause 6 of the Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property by Scheduled Tribes Regulation No. 2 of 1956 and Rule 4 made under it.
members.conclusion: The auction sale was invalid and could not displace the private purchaser’s title.

predicates.execution_auction_sale: A court auction transferred property in execution of a money decree.
predicates.prior_authorized_private_transfer: The owner transferred the property privately to a purchaser, after obtaining the competent authority’s permission and before the auction, leaving the judgment-debtor with no interest to sell.
predicates.auction_breached_sale_condition: The auction sale failed to satisfy a condition imposed by the competent authority on the permitted sale.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser at an auction sale generally takes the property subject to defects of title, but that rule does not cover a case in which the judgment debtor had no saleable interest in the property.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the property at a court auction to enforce a mortgage decree.
The dispute concerned whether the property remained subject to a charge for unpaid municipal taxes, not whether the judgment debtor had any saleable interest in it.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the caveat emptor principle to auction purchasers and distinguished the case contemplated by Order 21, Rule 91 of the Code of Civil Procedure, where the judgment debtor had no saleable interest in the property.
members.conclusion: There is no warranty of title in an auction sale, and the purchaser takes the property subject to defects of title; the separate case in which the judgment debtor had no saleable interest is not covered by that rule.

predicates.court_auction_purchase: The purchaser acquired the property at a court-conducted auction.
predicates.judgment_debtor_lacked_saleable_interest: The judgment debtor had no saleable interest in the property sold.

members.legal_issue: Interest may be awarded as restitution on money withdrawn under a decree that is later reversed or varied, when the interest is consequential on that reversal or variation.
material_facts: The receiver collected rent from the defendant and deposited it in court.
After the plaintiff’s suit was dismissed on appeal, the defendant withdrew the deposited rent.
The plaintiff later succeeded in the Supreme Court, and the defendant redeposited the money only after that decree.
The trial court allowed interest for the period between withdrawal and redeposit, but the High Court disallowed it on the stated ground that the Supreme Court did not award it.
members.legal_principle: Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure authorizes orders for restitution consequential on variation or reversal of a decree, including orders for interest, damages, compensation, and mesne profits. In the absence of an express or implied prohibition in the Supreme Court decree, interest could be allowed on the withdrawn deposit as restitution.
members.conclusion: The defendant was liable for interest on the withdrawn sum for the period between withdrawal and redeposit by way of restitution.

predicates.restitution_claim_after_decree_reversal_: A party seeks restitution after a decree has been reversed or varied.
predicates.money_withdrawn_under_earlier_decree: A party withdrew money deposited in court following the earlier decree and later redeposited it after reversal or variation.
predicates.interest_is_consequential: Interest is sought for the period during which the withdrawn money was withheld and is consequential on the reversal or variation.

members.legal_issue: A defendant liable for mesne profits may receive a deduction reflecting interest on purchase-price money that the decree-holder withdrew and later redeposited.
material_facts: The plaintiff withdrew part of the purchase-price deposit after his suit was dismissed on appeal.
He redeposited that sum after succeeding in the Supreme Court.
The defendant was liable for mesne profits during a period that overlapped the withdrawal.
The Court considered it fair to deduct interest on the withdrawn sum for the relevant period, excluding the period during which the property was managed by the receiver.
members.legal_principle: In assessing the parties’ monetary obligations, the Court allowed a fair deduction for the period during which the decree-holder had withdrawn and retained the purchase-price money, subject to excluding the receiver-management period.
members.conclusion: The defendant was allowed a deduction from mesne profits for interest on the purchase-price sum withdrawn and later redeposited.

rule.if: mesne_profits_execution_inquiry and decree_holder_withdrew_purchase_deposit and deposit_later_redeposited and defendant_liable_for_mesne_profits

predicates.mesne_profits_execution_inquiry: A court is determining monetary obligations in an execution or related inquiry under a decree.
predicates.decree_holder_withdrew_purchase_deposit: The decree-holder withdrew money deposited toward the purchase price after an adverse judgment.
predicates.deposit_later_redeposited: The decree-holder later redeposited that money after succeeding on appeal.
predicates.defendant_liable_for_mesne_profits: The defendant is liable for mesne profits during a period that includes the time the deposit was withdrawn.

members.legal_issue: Restoring property sold in execution to an agriculturist debtor, subject to repayment and compensation for improvements, is a reasonable restriction on the purchaser's right to hold property.
material_facts: The law allowed an agriculturist debtor to seek restoration of qualifying property sold in execution of a debt decree.
A decree-holder purchaser could receive the purchase money in instalments, while a stranger purchaser was entitled to the purchase money in a lump sum.
The debtor had to repay the purchase money, and the value of improvements made by the purchaser had to be deposited for payment to the purchaser.
The law was directed at agricultural indebtedness and the severe poverty of indebted agriculturists.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f), read with Article 19(5), permits reasonable restrictions on the right to hold property in the interests of the general public. Reasonableness requires balancing the nature of the right and the harm to its holder against the social purpose, urgency of the problem, and connection between the restriction and that purpose; Articles 38 and 39(b) also inform that assessment. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas, Fatehchand Himmatlal v. State of Maharashtra, Jyoti Prashad v. Administrator for the Union Territory of Delhi, Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar, Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of Madras v. V. G. Row, Narendra Kumar v. Union of India, Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, and O. K. Ghosh v. E. X. Joseph.
members.conclusion: The restriction on the purchasers' property rights was reasonable and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of the right to hold property.

rule.if: challenge_to_property_right_restriction and relief_targets_poor_indebted_agriculturists and purchaser_receives_repayment and (improvements_are_compensated or purchaser_is_paid_before_restoration)

predicates.challenge_to_property_right_restriction: The proceeding challenges a law that restricts a purchaser's ability to retain property acquired at a sale.
predicates.relief_targets_poor_indebted_agriculturi: The law is directed at relieving poor agriculturists burdened by debt and distress sales.
predicates.purchaser_receives_repayment: The law requires the debtor to repay the purchase money to the purchaser.
predicates.improvements_are_compensated: The law requires the debtor to deposit the value of qualifying improvements for payment to the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_is_paid_before_restoration: The law makes restoration conditional on payment of the amount due to the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: Limiting recovery of a reduced secured debt to compensation for resumed property is a reasonable restriction in the general public interest when it supports the rehabilitation of the affected debtor.
material_facts: The law reduced debts secured on resumed property and limited recovery of the reduced amount to compensation and a rehabilitation grant payable for that property.
The property had been taken over for a public purpose at a low valuation.
The secured creditor had primarily looked to the secured property for repayment.
Without the recovery limit, the debtor’s other property, future income, and later-acquired property could be reached, making it difficult to start life afresh.
members.legal_principle: Section 7(2) of the Rajasthan Jagirdars’ Debt Reduction Act was valid as a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public on secured-creditor rights. The Court relied on the provision’s rehabilitative purpose, the public-purpose resumption of the secured property at a low valuation, and the fact that the creditor had primarily relied on that property for repayment. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The recovery limit was valid because it imposed a reasonable restriction in the general public interest on the rights of a secured creditor.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and reduced_secured_debt_concerns_resumed_property and recovery_is_limited_to_property_compensation and resumption_served_public_purpose and broader_recovery_would_reach_other_assets

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law in a proceeding concerning debt relief.
predicates.reduced_secured_debt_concerns_resumed_pr: The debt was secured on property taken over by the state and was reduced under a debt-relief scheme.
predicates.recovery_is_limited_to_property_compensa: The law confined recovery of the reduced debt to compensation or a rehabilitation payment for the resumed property.
predicates.resumption_served_public_purpose: The state took over the secured property for a public purpose and valued it low enough to make rehabilitation relevant.
predicates.broader_recovery_would_reach_other_asset: Without the recovery limit, enforcement could reach the debtor’s other property, future income, or later-acquired property and hinder a fresh start.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired property satisfies the constitutional requirement when it is determined by relevant principles and is not shown to be illusory, even if its adequacy is challenged.
material_facts: The acquisition law set compensation for the scheduled undertakings in specified amounts.
The compensation calculation applied a principle accepted by the Court as relevant to valuing used machinery.
The undertakings had substantial carried-forward losses, had failed to pay cane growers and labour, and remained in serious difficulty despite earlier management intervention.
The appellants challenged the compensation as inadequate and illusory.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as it stood at the relevant time, required compensation for compulsory acquisition. A specified principle is open to challenge if it is irrelevant to determining value or produces illusory compensation, but the Court will not review adequacy where a relevant, recognized principle is applied. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition, Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India, State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas, and His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the compensation under Article 31(2), as it then stood, failed; the adequacy of compensation calculated using the relevant principle was not open to judicial review.

predicates.challenge_to_compensation_in_acquisition: A party challenges the compensation provided in a compulsory-acquisition case.
predicates.compensation_principle_is_relevant: The compensation is determined using a principle relevant to valuing the property acquired.
predicates.compensation_is_not_shown_illusory: The challenger does not establish that applying the principle makes the compensation illusory.

members.legal_issue: A law governing compulsory acquisition must provide for compensation representing a just equivalent, but courts cannot review the adequacy of the compensation or the principles used merely because another method would yield more; they may review illusory compensation or principles unrelated to the property or its value near the time of acquisition.
material_facts: The challenged law set compensation by the lower of the market value at notification or the average market value during the preceding five years.
It reduced the solatium compared with the principal acquisition law and excluded additional value attributable to the land's suitability for a different use.

The Court considered the valuation method sufficiently related to the land and its value at or about the time of acquisition, and treated the disputed exclusions and reduced solatium as matters of adequacy rather than fraud on power.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, requires a law authorizing acquisition to provide compensation or specify principles for determining it. Compensation means a just equivalent, but the adequacy of the compensation and the choice between relevant valuation methods are not justiciable. A court may review whether compensation is illusory or whether the stated principles are irrelevant to the property or its value at or about the time of acquisition; such defects may amount to a fraud on legislative power. The Court followed State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, [1954] S.C.R. 558, and State of Madras v. Namasivaya Mudaliar, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 936, and referred to Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1, and Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. A.P. State Road Transport Corporation, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 319, on colourable legislation and fraud on power.
members.conclusion: The challenged compensation provisions did not violate Article 31(2), because they prescribed valuation principles and did not provide illusory compensation or principles unrelated to the property or its value near the time of acquisition.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.compensation_principles_related_to_prope: The law's compensation principles take account of the kind of property acquired.
predicates.compensation_principles_related_to_value: The law's compensation principles relate to the property's value at or about the time it is acquired.
predicates.compensation_illusory: The law provides compensation that is merely nominal or illusory.

members.legal_issue: A compulsory-acquisition law satisfies the compensation guarantee when it specifies relevant, non-illusory valuation principles, and the resulting amount cannot be challenged merely as inadequate.
material_facts: The legislation adjusted compensation and contributions by comparing the market value of original and reconstituted plots at the date of the declaration of intention to make the scheme.
If an owner received no reconstituted plot, the legislation provided for payment of the value of the original plot using that same valuation date.
The owner challenged the valuation method because it did not provide a just equivalent at the time the owner's interest was extinguished, which occurred many years after the declaration of intention.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, bars judicial review of compensation for inadequacy when the law fixes compensation or specifies principles for determining it. A court may still examine whether the stated principles are irrelevant or whether the supposed compensation is illusory. The Court treated observations in P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector as obiter and overruled Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India Ltd.; it also explained the earlier approach in State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee and State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose in light of the amendment.
members.conclusion: The legislation specified relevant principles for determining compensation, and the compensation was not illusory. The challenge that the resulting compensation was not a just or adequate equivalent could not invalidate the law.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_compensation_case and legislature_set_uniform_valuation_rule and valuation_rule_relevant and compensation_not_illusory and challenge_claims_inadequacy

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding challenges compensation provided for a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.legislature_set_uniform_valuation_rule: The legislature prescribed a general valuation rule for determining what an affected owner is to receive.
predicates.valuation_rule_relevant: The prescribed valuation rule bears a rational relation to determining compensation.
predicates.compensation_not_illusory: The compensation produced by the prescribed rule is not merely nominal or fictitious.
predicates.challenge_claims_inadequacy: The challenger argues that the compensation is inadequate or not a just equivalent.

members.legal_issue: A statutory compensation scheme for compulsory acquisition must use principles relevant to the value of the property at or about the time of acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition law required compensation for the undertaking as a whole, calculated by valuing its assets under separate rules and deducting its liabilities.
Unused machinery in good condition was valued at its original purchase cost, even where that cost could be substantially below its value at acquisition.
Other machinery was valued at its written-down value under income-tax rules, which reflected notional depreciation allowances rather than the machinery's actual value.
Machinery was the most valuable part of the undertaking.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) of the Constitution, a law authorising compulsory acquisition had to provide a just equivalent or specify principles that would lead to that result. The principles themselves were subject to judicial scrutiny for relevance and arbitrariness, although the adequacy of compensation produced by relevant, non-arbitrary principles was not reviewable. A scheme was invalid if its compensation was illusory or its principles were unrelated to the property's value at or about acquisition. The Court relied on The State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, Vajravelu v. Special Deputy Collector, and Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector.
members.conclusion: The machinery valuation rules were irrelevant to determining its value at acquisition and therefore did not provide compensation within the constitutional requirement; the acquisition law was unconstitutional.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorising compulsory acquisition.
predicates.unused_machinery_valued_at_historical_co: The law valued unused machinery in good condition by its original purchase cost rather than its value at acquisition.
predicates.used_machinery_valued_by_tax_written_dow: The law valued used machinery by a written-down amount calculated for taxation purposes.
predicates.valuation_rules_unrelated_to_value_at_ac: The valuation methods did not reflect the property's value at or about the time it was acquired.

members.legal_issue: A compulsory acquisition law must provide compensation through an amount or valuation principles that are relevant and non-arbitrary in relation to the property’s value at or about the time of acquisition.
material_facts: The law acquired an undertaking and calculated compensation by valuing its assets and subtracting its liabilities.
Unused machinery in good condition was valued at its historical purchase cost, while other machinery was valued at its tax written-down value.
The historical-cost method did not account for later increases in machinery prices, and tax depreciation did not necessarily reflect machinery’s actual value.
Machinery was a major part of the undertaking.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) of the Constitution, a law compulsorily acquiring property must provide compensation and either fix its amount or specify principles and a manner for determining it. The principles must be relevant and non-arbitrary and must provide a just equivalent by reference to value at or about acquisition; once they meet that test, the adequacy of the resulting compensation is beyond judicial scrutiny. The Court applied State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, State of Madras v. D. Namasivaya Mudaliar, Vajravelu v. Special Deputy Collector, and Jeejeebhoy v. Assistant Collector.
members.conclusion: The valuation principles for machinery were irrelevant to its value at acquisition and did not provide compensation within the constitutional meaning; the acquisition law was unconstitutional.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_law: A law provides for the compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.unused_equipment_valued_at_historical_co: The law values unused equipment in good condition by the cost incurred to acquire it, without regard to its value at acquisition.
predicates.used_equipment_valued_by_tax_write_down: The law values used equipment by a tax write-down measure rather than its actual value at acquisition.
predicates.valuation_basis_unrelated_to_value_at_ac: The valuation methods do not provide a relevant measure of the property’s value at or about the time it is acquired.
predicates.acquisition_law_unconstitutional: The acquisition law is unconstitutional for failing to provide constitutionally valid compensation.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsory acquisition of an undertaking must be determined by relevant and appropriate principles that value the undertaking as a unit.
material_facts: The legislation acquired each bank's undertaking as a going concern but calculated compensation by valuing specified components separately and subtracting liabilities.
The valuation scheme omitted goodwill and the value of unexpired lease interests.
The prescribed method for valuing land and buildings could produce an illusory result and did not appropriately account for the premises taken as vacant premises.
The method for calculating liabilities included defects in the treatment of contingent liabilities and encumbrances.
members.legal_principle: The constitutional guarantee requires compensation and relevant principles for determining it; inadequacy alone is not justiciable, but principles that are irrelevant to the property or class of property acquired do not satisfy the guarantee. An undertaking acquired as a unit must be valued as a unit, and the aggregate of selected component values need not represent the value of an organised going concern. The Court applied P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Madras and State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas, and discussed State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India, and Trego v. Hunt.
members.conclusion: The compensation scheme violated the constitutional guarantee because the prescribed principles were not relevant and appropriate to valuing the acquired undertakings and did not provide compensation for the undertakings as a whole.

rule.if: constitutional_compensation_challenge and going_concern_acquired_as_unit and compensation_based_on_components and important_value_elements_omitted or constitutional_compensation_challenge and going_concern_acquired_as_unit and prescribed_valuation_principles_irrelevant

predicates.constitutional_compensation_challenge: A person challenged the compensation provided for compulsory acquisition.
predicates.going_concern_acquired_as_unit: The law transferred an organised operating undertaking as a single going concern.
predicates.compensation_based_on_components: The law calculated compensation by valuing selected components separately rather than valuing the undertaking as a whole.
predicates.important_value_elements_omitted: The valuation scheme omitted important elements of the undertaking's value, such as goodwill or unexpired lease interests.
predicates.prescribed_valuation_principles_irreleva: The prescribed methods were not relevant and appropriate to valuing the property or class of property acquired.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for property acquired under a redevelopment scheme is not constitutionally inadequate or illusory when it includes a market-value floor and may share the scheme’s proceeds.
material_facts: Compensation was calculated by reference to the scheme’s income and costs, with the total distributed among persons according to their interests.

The legislation required that an interested person receive no less than the market value of that person’s interest, subject to demolition and removal costs, and separately provided compensation for structures.
The statutory definition of land was broad enough to include buildings.
The Trust had to submit the scheme statement within the prescribed statutory limit, and the scheme could produce compensation exceeding the market-value floor.
The petitioners objected that final compensation could be delayed and that interest was not payable during the delay.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as considered by the Court, was not violated where the statutory method provided at least the market value of the claimant’s interest, subject to specified deductions, and could yield more through sharing scheme proceeds. The Court relied on sections 11–13 and 16 of the Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, and the broad definition of land comparable to section 3(a) of the Land Acquisition Act. It also noted the statutory timetable for submitting the scheme statement. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The compensation was neither inadequate nor illusory and did not violate Article 31(2).

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_compensation and compensation_includes_a_market_value_floor and compensation_can_share_scheme_proceeds and buildings_are_within_compensable_property and scheme_statement_has_a_statutory_submission_limit

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenges the adequacy of compensation for property acquired under a statutory scheme.
predicates.compensation_includes_a_market_value_flo: The compensation method guarantees at least the market value of the claimant’s interest, subject to specified deductions.
predicates.compensation_can_share_scheme_proceeds: The compensation method may distribute surplus scheme income to persons with interests in the acquired property.
predicates.buildings_are_within_compensable_propert: The statutory description of compensable property includes buildings.
predicates.scheme_statement_has_a_statutory_submiss: The scheme authority is subject to a statutory limit for submitting the statement used to determine final compensation.

members.legal_issue: The statutory principles for compensating acquisition of a pipeline right of user and resulting damage, loss, or injury are not invalid or illusory, and the compensation in this case was not inadequate.
material_facts: The compensation scheme provided compensation for actual damage, loss, or injury caused by entry, pipeline-laying, or later pipeline work, separately from compensation for acquisition of the right of user calculated by reference to the land’s market value.
The owners and occupiers retained title and possession, although their use of the land was restricted in order to protect the pipeline.
The parcels were agricultural land when the initial notification was issued; permissions to convert some parcels to non-agricultural use were granted afterward.
Compensation was agreed at rates above the average recorded sale rate, and provisional compensation at a higher rate was deposited while the proceedings were pending.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 10 of the Petroleum and Minerals Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 1962, compensation for actual damage, loss, or injury is distinct from additional compensation for the acquired right of user, calculated by reference to market value. Section 10(3) requires regard to specified forms of loss, including injury to property or earnings. The Court held that permanent impairment may support compensation and distinguished H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra, finding its principle inapplicable. It also relied on the Statement of Objects and Reasons and the separate compensation elements in Section 10.
members.conclusion: The compensation provisions were not invalid or illusory, and the compensation on the record could not be called inadequate.

predicates.pipeline_right_of_user_acquisition: The proceeding concerns acquisition of a limited right to use land for a pipeline.
predicates.actual_loss_is_separately_compensable: The scheme provides compensation for damage, loss, or injury caused by pipeline-related activities apart from compensation for the acquired user right.
predicates.additional_compensation_reflects_land_va: The scheme provides additional compensation for the user right by reference to the land’s market value.
predicates.ownership_and_possession_remain: The landowner or occupier retains title and possession despite the pipeline right being acquired.

members.legal_issue: A complaint that the compensation fixed by an estate-acquisition law is illusory cannot be recast as a colourable exercise of legislative power when legislative competence is not in issue and the law is protected by Article 31-A.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the compensation provisions produced illusory or no compensation and therefore constituted a colourable exercise of legislative power.
The Court found no question of legislative incompetence and treated the complaint as one about the quantum of compensation.
The Court had concluded that the law was protected by Article 31-A.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of colourable legislation concerns legislative competence; it does not provide a basis to challenge the amount of compensation where competence is not in issue. Under Article 31-A, a complaint relating to the quantum of compensation for an acquisition protected by that article is barred. The Court relied on K. C. Gajapati Narain Deb v. State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1.
members.conclusion: The compensation complaint could not invalidate the law as a colourable exercise of legislative power, and the quantum of compensation could not be challenged in view of Article 31-A.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and estate_acquisition_law_protected_from_rights_challenge and compensation_amount_is_complaint and legislative_competence_not_in_issue

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of an enacted law.
predicates.estate_acquisition_law_protected_from_ri: The challenged law provides for acquisition of estates and is protected from a Part III rights challenge.
predicates.compensation_amount_is_complaint: The party's complaint concerns the amount or adequacy of compensation provided for the acquisition.
predicates.legislative_competence_not_in_issue: The challenge does not allege that the legislature lacked authority to enact the law.

members.legal_issue: A court may not examine whether compensation principles are relevant or whether the resulting compensation is illusory when the challenged provisions are protected from the property-rights challenge.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the compensation formula produced illusory compensation by limiting the relevant market value to an earlier valuation benchmark with an addition.
The challenged provisions were part of a law placed in the protected constitutional schedule.
The appeals sought to invalidate those provisions on the basis of the property guarantee in the former constitutional order.
members.legal_principle: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule foreclosed examination of a challenge based on the property guarantee in repealed Article 31 where the challenged provisions enjoyed that protection. The Court treated Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India and State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas as irrelevant to that threshold bar, and agreed with the High Court’s conclusion upholding the provisions.
members.conclusion: The Court could not examine whether the prescribed valuation principles were relevant or whether the compensation was illusory, because the provisions were protected from the asserted property-rights challenge.

predicates.compensation_validity_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the validity of provisions that determine compensation for acquired property.
predicates.protected_compensation_provisions: The challenged compensation provisions are part of a law protected from the asserted rights-based challenge.
predicates.challenge_claims_illusory_compensation: The challenger alleges that the compensation formula produces illusory compensation or uses irrelevant valuation principles.

members.legal_issue: A challenge that statutory compensation is inadequate is barred where the acquisition law is protected from Part III challenges, and a positive compensation entitlement is not illusory merely because it is substantially below the property’s asserted value.
material_facts: The law prescribed compensation calculated by reference to net income and provided that net income could not be reduced below five per cent of gross income.
The petitioner asserted that the compensation for property worth substantially more would be much smaller and payable in instalments.
The law had received presidential assent and was included in the Ninth Schedule.
The compensation formula produced a positive amount rather than zero or a negative amount.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on article 31(4), articles 31-A and 31-B, and its reasoning in the Bihar case. Article 31(4) barred an objection based on article 31(2) where its conditions were met, while articles 31-A and 31-B supplied further protection from Part III challenges. The Court distinguished inadequate compensation from no compensation or illusory compensation.
members.conclusion: The compensation could be described as grossly inadequate, but its adequacy was not justiciable; the compensation was not illusory because the law provided for a positive payment.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenged a law that acquires private property.
predicates.acquisition_law_is_constitutionally_prot: The acquisition law has received the constitutional protection that bars relevant Part III objections.
predicates.law_provides_positive_compensation: The law provides for a compensation payment greater than zero.

members.legal_issue: The adequacy of compensation under a qualifying acquisition law cannot be judicially examined when the constitutional protections governing such laws apply.
material_facts: The challenged law provided compensation calculated under statutory schedules and payable in cash or bonds, potentially in instalments.
The petitioners alleged that the compensation was substantially below the value and income of their property and was therefore inadequate or illusory.
The bill was pending at the commencement of the Constitution, was reserved for the President’s consideration, and received his assent; the Act was also included in the Ninth Schedule.
members.legal_principle: Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B barred an inquiry into the challenge to compensation based on inconsistency with fundamental rights. Article 31(4) applied because the bill was pending at the commencement of the Constitution, was reserved, and received presidential assent; the First Amendment protections also applied to the Act. The Court distinguished inadequate compensation from compensation that was merely illusory, noting that the statute provided for a positive amount.
members.conclusion: The Court had no jurisdiction to inquire into the adequacy of compensation, and the compensation provisions were not illusory on the facts described.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_proceeding and compulsory_property_acquisition and qualifying_constitutional_protection_applies and compensation_is_provided

predicates.constitutional_challenge_proceeding: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law authorizing acquisition of property.
predicates.compulsory_property_acquisition: The challenged law transfers private property to the State by compulsory acquisition.
predicates.qualifying_constitutional_protection_app: The law satisfies the constitutional conditions that protect it from challenge based on fundamental rights.
predicates.compensation_is_provided: The law provides a positive amount of compensation rather than no compensation at all.

members.legal_issue: The adequacy of compensation cannot be challenged against legislation relating to agrarian reform that is protected by the constitutional saving provision.
material_facts: The legislation provided compensation for abolished inams and related rights.
Other provisions removed exemptions for certain religious trust lands under agricultural tenancy and land-ceiling laws.
The appellants alleged that the compensation available for lands covered by those agricultural laws was grossly inadequate.
The legislation was found to relate to agrarian reform and to be protected by the constitutional saving provision.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects legislation relating to agrarian reform from specified constitutional challenges, and the Court held that an objection to the adequacy of compensation could not be agitated against legislation within that protection. The Court also stated that objections based on Articles 14, 19, and 31 were not entertainable in this context.
members.conclusion: The objection based on inadequacy of compensation was not entertainable; objections based on Articles 14, 19, and 31 were also not entertainable against the protected agrarian-reform legislation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law enacted to reform agrarian arrangements.
predicates.law_is_protected_as_agrarian_reform: The law relates to agrarian reform and falls within the constitutional protection for such legislation.
predicates.compensation_is_challenged_as_inadequate: A party claims that the compensation provided for the effects of the law is insufficient.

members.legal_issue: A challenge that estate-acquisition legislation provides inadequate or illusory compensation is barred when the legislation satisfies the constitutional conditions that protect it from such a challenge.
material_facts: The Act provided compensation calculated by reference to the net assets of the acquired estate and made compensation due from the date of vesting, with interest.
The Act provided for payment in cash, bonds, or a combination, and for determination of compensation by an officer with a right of appeal.
The Bill was pending when the Constitution came into force and received the President’s assent.
The appellants argued that compensation was inadequate, that non-income-producing property received no separate compensation, and that payment was left to the Government’s discretion.
members.legal_principle: Articles 31(4), 31-A and 31-B barred the relevant challenge. Article 31-A did not repeal Part III; its proviso preserved the alternative application of Article 31(2), with the President as the decision-maker on compliance for a qualifying State law. The Court also relied on sections 27, 28, 65 and 68 of the Act, which made compensation obligatory and provided for its payment. It rejected the argument that the provisions left payment entirely to the Government’s discretion.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the Act’s validity could not be challenged on the ground that it failed to provide compensation or provided inadequate compensation; it also rejected the contention that the compensation provisions made payment illusory.

predicates.state_estate_acquisition_law: The challenged law provides for the State to acquire estates.
predicates.compensation_challenge_made: A person challenges the law on the ground that compensation is absent, inadequate, or illusory.
