predicates.law_meets_constitutional_protection_cond: The law satisfies the constitutional conditions that protect it from a challenge based on fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: A law certified under the constitutional transitional safeguard cannot be challenged on the ground that it contravened the earlier guarantee concerning compensation for compulsory acquisition.
material_facts: The legislation was enacted before the Constitution came into force and received the Governor-General’s assent under the earlier constitutional framework.
After the Constitution came into force, the legislation was submitted for and received presidential certification within the prescribed period.
The landholders challenged provisions governing compensation as colourable and as contravening the earlier guarantee concerning compensation for compulsory acquisition.
The parties did not dispute that the legislation satisfied the requirements for certification.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(6) of the Constitution bars a court challenge to a qualifying, certified law on the ground that it contravened Article 31(2) or section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The Court distinguished The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh, which concerned legislation enacted under the Constitution and legislative competence under Entry 42 of List III, and referred to Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The challenge based on contravention of the earlier compensation guarantee could not be raised in court, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge and law_enacted_before_new_constitution and law_certified_within_allowed_window and challenge_based_on_earlier_compensation_guarantee

predicates.constitutional_challenge: A person challenges the validity of a state law in constitutional proceedings.
predicates.law_enacted_before_new_constitution: The legislature enacted the law before the new constitutional framework came into force.
predicates.law_certified_within_allowed_window: The law was submitted to and certified by the designated constitutional authority within the permitted period after the new framework came into force.
predicates.challenge_based_on_earlier_compensation_: The challenger alleges that the law contravened the earlier guarantee concerning compensation for compulsory acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A law authorizing the taking of property must fix compensation or prescribe adequate principles for determining it.
material_facts: The law permitted substitute property to be provided, but did not specify when the property's value was to be assessed.
The law also permitted cash to be paid without requiring that it equal the value of the property withheld or prescribing a standard for the amount.
The owner's title to the original property was extinguished after substitute property or cash was provided.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) of the Constitution required a law authorizing acquisition or requisition to fix compensation or specify the principles on which, and the manner in which, compensation was to be determined or given. A direction to provide property of nearly the same value was inadequate without specifying when value was to be assessed; the cash alternative supplied no adequate standard. The Court referred to Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab, [1957] SCR 801, for statutory background, not as the basis for this holding.
members.conclusion: The law violated the compensation requirement because it neither fixed compensation nor prescribed adequate principles for determining it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tak: A party in a constitutional challenge disputes a law that permits property to be taken or withheld from its rightful owner.
predicates.law_lacks_adequate_compensation_standard: The law provides neither a fixed compensation amount nor adequate principles for determining compensation, including a standard for assessing value or the cash amount.

members.legal_issue: A law specifies the principles and manner for determining compulsory-acquisition compensation when it requires full indemnification, provides for an appropriate inquiry, and permits civil-court review of the determination.
material_facts: Street widening could require acquisition of very small, irregular, or otherwise unusual pieces of land for which a single standard valuation method might not be appropriate.
The law set full indemnification for the owner's loss or deprivation as the goal of compensation.
An authorized official was required to hold an inquiry and determine compensation, with appeals to a civil-court judge and a further appeal to the District Court.
The appellate courts were not subject to limits on determining compensation justly and appropriately.
members.legal_principle: Section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and Article 31 of the Constitution required the law to specify the principles and manner of determining compensation. Sections 216 and 389 established full indemnification as the governing goal; sections 390, 391, 411, and 434 provided for an inquiry and civil-court appeals, importing judicial norms into the determination. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Shri Shantilal Mangaldas & Ors. for the meaning of specified principles as general guiding rules and for the use of differing valuation methods according to the property acquired.
members.conclusion: The law specified both the principles and the manner for determining compensation because it required full indemnification using valuation methods appropriate to the property and provided for an inquiry and judicial appeals.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_chal: A proceeding challenges whether a law authorizing compulsory acquisition meets constitutional compensation requirements.
predicates.law_sets_full_indemnity_as_goal: The law makes full indemnification for the owner's loss or deprivation the goal of compensation.
predicates.compensation_is_reviewable_by_civil_cour: The law permits civil courts to review and determine the appropriate compensation on appeal.
predicates.initial_compensation_inquiry_is_required: The law requires an authorized official to hold an inquiry before determining compensation.

members.legal_issue: A land-requisition law satisfies the constitutional compensation requirement when it provides for agreed compensation and court determination in case of disagreement using acquisition-compensation principles with suitable adaptations.
material_facts: The challenged law provided for compensation agreed in writing between the collector and the interested person.
If they disagreed about compensation, the law required the matter to be referred to a court.
The law applied the compensation provisions of the general acquisition law, including its principles for determining compensation, with due alterations for requisition.
For requisition, the relevant compensation could reflect the owner’s temporary loss of possession rather than the permanent loss of the land itself.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) required a law authorizing compulsory acquisition or requisition to provide compensation and either fix its amount or specify the principles and manner for determining and giving it; the adequacy of compensation was not justiciable once those requirements were met. Under sections 7(3), 8(1)(b), and 8(2) of the land-requisition law, compensation could be agreed and disagreements referred to a court, to which the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, applied mutatis mutandis. Sections 23, 24, and 25 of that Act supplied principles that could be adapted to compensate for the temporary loss of possession. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The law did not offend the constitutional compensation requirement because it provided for compensation and a process and principles for determining it when the parties disagreed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_requisition_: A party challenges the validity of a law authorizing compulsory requisition of property.
predicates.law_authorizes_requisition_for_public_pu: The law permits requisition for purposes serving the public interest.
predicates.law_provides_for_agreed_compensation: The law provides for the interested person and the acquiring authority to agree on compensation.
predicates.compensation_disagreement_is_referred_to: The law provides for a court to determine compensation if the parties disagree.
predicates.acquisition_compensation_principles_appl: The law applies principles used to determine compensation for acquisition, with changes suited to the temporary loss caused by requisition.

members.legal_issue: A public-purpose description is not invalid for vagueness when it is understandable in context and the landholders understood the proposed acquisition well enough to make detailed objections without showing substantial prejudice.
material_facts: The notifications described the purpose as establishing a diamond park, and the responsible industrial-development officer was identified in the notification.
The industrial-policy context and the notices issued during the objection process made clear that the project concerned industrial development and diamond-processing units.
The landholders filed detailed objections addressing the acquisition’s purposes and circumstances.
The landholders did not demonstrate that the wording prevented them from effectively objecting or otherwise caused substantial prejudice.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 5A require sufficient specification of the public purpose to enable meaningful objections, assessed in light of the facts and circumstances of the case. A court should not invalidate acquisition proceedings for a theoretical ambiguity without a real and substantial grievance or prejudice. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, Madhya Pradesh Housing Board v. Md. Shafi, and Munshi Singh v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The stated public purpose was not so vague as to invalidate the notification or the subsequent proceedings.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landholders challenged a government acquisition on the ground that its stated purpose was vague.
predicates.purpose_description_understandable_in_co: The stated purpose conveyed its nature when read in the context of the project and the information accompanying the acquisition process.
predicates.objectors_understood_purpose_and_made_de: The landholders understood the proposed use of the land and submitted detailed objections about it.
predicates.no_substantial_prejudice_shown: The landholders did not show that the wording prevented meaningful objections or caused substantial prejudice.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition notifications are not vague when they identify the public purpose and the particular scheme for which the land is proposed to be acquired.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications stated that the acquisition was for a public purpose.
The notifications identified the housing scheme for which the acquisition was proposed.
members.legal_principle: Notifications identifying the public purpose and stating the particular purpose of the proposed acquisition are sufficiently clear; the Court found these notifications similar to those ordinarily issued under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
members.conclusion: The notifications were not vague.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a land acquisition undertaken for a proposed purpose.
predicates.notifications_identify_public_purpose: The acquisition notifications state that the proposed acquisition is for a public purpose.
predicates.notifications_identify_specific_scheme: The acquisition notifications identify the particular scheme for which the land is proposed to be acquired.

members.legal_issue: The preliminary acquisition notice was not shown to be vague where the objector’s own case identified the public purpose and challenged the suitability of the land rather than the clarity of that purpose.
material_facts: The notice referred to the intended uses, including a fire station, workshop, and parking purpose.
In the statement of case, the objector himself described the proposed uses as a fire station, workshop, and parking purpose.
His stated objection was that the land was unsuitable for the fire station, and he had not raised vagueness in his statement of case.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires the preliminary notification to state the public purpose. The Court assessed the claimed vagueness against the objector’s own description of the purpose and the objection he had actually made; it cited no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The challenge that the notice failed to state the public purpose was rejected as having no substance.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and preliminary_notice_identifies_purpose and objector_acknowledges_purpose and objection_concerns_land_suitability

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a land acquisition.
predicates.preliminary_notice_identifies_purpose: The preliminary notice states the intended public use of the land.
predicates.objector_acknowledges_purpose: The objector’s own account identifies the intended public use.
predicates.objection_concerns_land_suitability: The objector’s stated objection concerns whether the land is suitable for the intended use rather than whether the notice identifies that use.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notification is not invalid for vagueness where it identifies a sufficiently precise public purpose and the landowners can make and have their objections considered.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications stated that the land was being acquired for industrial development, including the establishment and development of industrial areas.
The acquisition covered a large area for a project with multiple connected components.
The landowners filed objections and the competent authority considered them after giving an opportunity to object.
The Court found no prejudice from the wording of the notifications.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 28(1) and 28(2) of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, and the principles of natural justice. It relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, which explains that the precision required of a stated purpose depends on the circumstances and that a large acquisition may properly state the purpose by reference to the acquisition as a whole.
members.conclusion: The stated purpose was sufficiently precise, and the notifications were not invalid for vagueness or breach of natural justice.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and large_area_acquisition and notification_states_sufficiently_precise_public_purpose and landowners_can_object and objections_considered and no_material_prejudice_from_wording

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: An appeal challenges the validity of a land acquisition notification.
predicates.large_area_acquisition: The acquisition covers a large area, potentially comprising land belonging to different owners.
predicates.notification_states_sufficiently_precise: The notification identifies a public purpose with sufficient precision in the circumstances of the acquisition.
predicates.landowners_can_object: The landowners have a meaningful opportunity to object to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.objections_considered: The competent authority considers the landowners' objections after giving them an opportunity to present them.
predicates.no_material_prejudice_from_wording: The wording of the notification does not materially prejudice the landowners' ability to object.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition notification is not vague merely because it states the public purpose generally when the notification identifies a public purpose and the record explains the specific public use.
material_facts: The notification stated that the land was likely to be needed for a public purpose for a public trust.
The respondents explained in their counter-affidavit that the land was needed to provide access between two temples.
The land was sought for access to temples visited by large numbers of pilgrims.
members.legal_principle: Under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, public purpose need not be exhaustively defined in the notification. Whether a purpose is public is primarily for the government to determine, and the court does not substitute its assessment unless the acquisition serves a private purpose, no purpose, or involves a colourable exercise of power. A stated public purpose may be explained by the record or a counter-affidavit. The Court relied on Somavanti v. State of Punjab, V.M. Soneji v. State of Bombay, Ratilal Shakarabhai v. State of Gujarat, Jage Ram v. State of Haryana, Gopal Krishan Das v. Sailendra Nath Biswas, Babu Singh v. Union of India, and Srinivasa Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Madam Gurumurthy Sastry. It distinguished M.P. Housing Board v. Mohd. Shafi, where the notification did not identify any public purpose.
members.conclusion: The stated purpose was sufficiently clear and served a public purpose; the notification was not invalid for vagueness.

rule.if: acquisition_notification_challenge and notice_identified_public_purpose and record_explained_specific_use and purpose_served_general_interest

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges a notification authorising the acquisition of land.
predicates.notice_identified_public_purpose: The notification stated that the land was needed for a public purpose.
predicates.record_explained_specific_use: The government or the record explained the particular use for which the land was sought.
predicates.purpose_served_general_interest: The proposed use of the land served the general interest of the community, including by providing public access to places visited by the public.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notice must describe the public purpose with enough specificity to show what the land is proposed to be used for.
material_facts: The initial notice stated the purpose only as “residential,” without identifying the type of accommodation, its intended beneficiaries, or further details.
The declaration described the purpose as a housing scheme, but the notice did not explain the proposed use in a way that enabled affected people to understand or assess it.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 4(2) require the public purpose to be sufficiently particularised, including so that affected people can understand the proposal and consider objections to the land’s suitability. The State cannot acquire land to provide a residence for another unless the acquisition serves the public or an identifiable section of the public. The Court relied on Munshi Singh and Others v. Union of India and Others.
members.conclusion: The stated public purpose was too vague to convey the purpose of the acquisition, rendering the notice and acquisition proceedings invalid.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition of land.
predicates.public_purpose_description_is_vague: The acquisition notice describes the intended public use so generally that affected people cannot understand what use is proposed or for whose benefit.

members.legal_issue: A declaration of acquisition is not invalid merely because it describes the public purpose more narrowly or precisely than the preliminary notification, where both describe substantially the same purpose.
material_facts: The preliminary notification described soil conservation and other improvement works in a catchment area, including raising a green belt.
The declaration described soil conservation measures in that catchment area.
The Court found the purposes consistent and identified no real contradiction between the descriptions.
members.legal_principle: The public purpose stated in the preliminary notification and the declaration must be broad and understandable. The requirement serves to give affected persons an opportunity to object to the proposed acquisition; differing levels of detail do not invalidate the declaration where the stated purposes are substantially the same.
members.conclusion: The descriptions of public purpose did not materially differ, so the declaration was not invalid on that ground.

rule.if: acquisition_notification_challenge and preliminary_purpose_understandable and declared_purpose_substantially_same and no_real_purpose_contradiction

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: An affected person challenged a declaration made in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.preliminary_purpose_understandable: The preliminary notification described the proposed public purpose in terms that could be understood by affected persons.
predicates.declared_purpose_substantially_same: The declaration described a purpose substantially the same as the purpose in the preliminary notification.
predicates.no_real_purpose_contradiction: The two descriptions did not contain a real contradiction about the purpose for which the land was acquired.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition notification must give owners sufficient information to identify whether their land is proposed for acquisition and to exercise their right to object.
material_facts: The notification identified a large survey field and stated areas to be acquired from it, but did not precisely locate the portions proposed for acquisition.
No plans showing the land to be acquired were published or made available to the owners.
The appellants’ plots were within the larger field, and the record did not show that the entire field was to be acquired.
No order dispensing with the objection inquiry was issued.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 4(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, the acquiring authority must publish sufficient information to give owners due notice that their properties are intended to be acquired. Section 5-A gives interested persons an opportunity to object, and the inquiry and report under that section may be dispensed with only through an order under Section 17(4). A declaration under Section 6 follows consideration of the report under Section 5-A unless that inquiry has been dispensed with. No earlier case was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The notification did not give the owners due notice that their lands were intended for acquisition, and the resulting denial of a meaningful opportunity to object raised a serious challenge to the acquisition proceedings; the ultimate validity of those proceedings was left for determination on remand.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and (land_not_precisely_identifiable_from_notice or acquisition_plans_unavailable) and objection_inquiry_not_dispensed_with

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated proceedings to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.land_not_precisely_identifiable_from_not: The notice described the land in a way that did not enable affected owners to identify whether their particular land was included.
predicates.acquisition_plans_unavailable: Plans identifying the land proposed for acquisition were neither published nor made available to affected owners.
predicates.objection_inquiry_not_dispensed_with: The government did not dispense with the statutory objection inquiry.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notification is not vague when it refers to a site plan that identifies the land being acquired.
material_facts: The notification identified the relevant land by field numbers and area and expressly referred to a site plan available for inspection.
The fields' combined area exceeded the area being acquired, but evidence filed for the society stated that the acquired area was exactly one acre.
An official who later attempted to deliver possession had difficulty identifying the acquired portion, but he had not brought the correct plan.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the notification's identification of the land under section 7(1) of the U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, including its express reference to the site plan and the evidence identifying the acquired area. No earlier case is relied on for this conclusion in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The notification had not been shown to be vague, and the court found no sufficient ground to interfere with the finding that it properly identified the land.

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a notification acquiring land.
predicates.notification_references_site_plan: The notification expressly refers to a site plan concerning the land to be acquired.
predicates.evidence_identifies_acquired_land: The available plan or other evidence identifies the land or area being acquired.
predicates.notification_not_shown_vague: The court does not find the notification vague on the basis of the challenge presented.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition notification is sufficiently descriptive when it identifies the land and makes further land plans and details available, and a later objection to its description may be rejected when no such deficiency was raised within the objection period.
material_facts: The notification identified the villages, survey and sub-survey numbers, nature, type, and area of the land proposed for acquisition.
The notification stated that land plans and other details were available for inspection at the competent authority's office.

The initial objectors did not claim that the description prevented them from effectively objecting; some landowners raised that claim only in later representations, outside the statutory objection period.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3A(2) and 3A(3) of the National Highways Act, 1956 require a brief description of the land and publication of the substance of the notification in two local newspapers. Section 3C(1) provides a 21-day period for objections. The notification supplied adequate particulars, and the later complaint was not made within that period.
members.conclusion: The notification was not vague, and the later complaint about its description did not require consideration because it was raised outside the prescribed period.

rule.if: land_acquisition_notification_challenge and notification_identifies_land_particulars and further_land_details_available and no_timely_description_objection and later_description_objection_out_of_time

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: A person challenged a notification proposing the acquisition of land.
predicates.notification_identifies_land_particulars: The notification identifies the affected land by relevant location and parcel details and states its nature and area.
predicates.further_land_details_available: The notification states that plans or additional details of the affected land are available for inspection.
predicates.no_timely_description_objection: The objectors did not claim within the objection period that the description prevented them from effectively objecting.
predicates.later_description_objection_out_of_time: An objector first complained about inadequate description after the period for making objections had expired.

members.legal_issue: The effective land acquisition notice for determining market value is the notice that identifies the land with sufficient precision to inform affected owners and occupiers of the proposed acquisition.
material_facts: The first notice misidentified the owner and extent of the land in the relevant survey number and did not make clear which part of that survey number was to be acquired.
A later notice identified the separate owners and specified the land proposed to be acquired with sufficient precision.
The notice issued to the company under the objection procedure referred to the later notice.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act requires publication in the Gazette and at convenient places in the locality, and the notice must clearly indicate the land proposed for acquisition sufficiently to give owners or occupiers a fair idea of the acquisition and its impact. A material failure to identify the land or its ownership can make a notice defective. Section 21 of the General Clauses Act does not establish that every amending notice automatically replaces the original as the effective notice; the notices must be construed on their terms. Raghunath v. State of Maharashtra was distinguished as a decision resting on its own facts, not a general rule for amendments.
members.conclusion: The notice issued on 28 February 1963 was the effective notice, and market value had to be determined as of that date.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land acquired by the government.
predicates.initial_notice_materially_ambiguous: The initial notice materially fails to identify the land proposed for acquisition or gives inaccurate information about its extent or ownership.
predicates.later_notice_precisely_identifies_land: A later notice identifies the land proposed for acquisition with sufficient precision for affected owners or occupiers to understand the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: An initial acquisition notice stating the public purpose need not also specify whether the purpose will be achieved by government activity or by transferring land to a company.
material_facts: The initial notification stated that the land was required for a public purpose to be achieved for the housing society at the society's cost.
Interested persons were made aware through the notices and objection process of the nature of the proposed acquisition.
The later declaration identified the same public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 requires notification of the Government's intention to acquire land needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose; it does not require the notice at that stage to specify whether the purpose will be achieved through government activity or through a company. The Court referred to Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay in discussing acquisition for a company and the required conditions for proceeding beyond the objection stage.
members.conclusion: The initial notification was not required to specify whether the public purpose would be achieved by government activity or by passing the land to a company, provided the public purpose was stated.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns State acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_intended_for_company: The proposed public purpose is to be achieved through land acquired for a company or an entity treated as a company.
predicates.public_purpose_stated_in_initial_notice: The initial notice identifies the public purpose for which the land is proposed to be acquired.

members.legal_issue: A notification declaring a public purpose is not invalid merely because it does not identify the instrumentality that will carry out that purpose.
material_facts: The challenge to the acquisition notifications asserted that the declaration of public purpose was invalid because it did not identify the instrumentality through which the purpose would be carried out.
The Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court had held that omission of the instrumentality did not invalidate a notification, and the Supreme Court had confirmed that view.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, failure to specify the instrumentality that will execute the public purpose does not affect the validity of the notification. The Court relied on Ramji Popatbhai Patel v. Jamnadas Shah, Kanaiyalal Maneklal Chinai v. State of Gujarat, and Vishnu Prasad Ramdas Gohil v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The omission of the instrumentality from the notification did not invalidate it, and the contention was rejected.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a notification for acquiring land.
predicates.notification_states_public_purpose: The notification identifies the public purpose for which the land is acquired.
predicates.notification_omits_executing_instrumenta: The notification does not identify the body or agency that will carry out the public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition notification is not invalid merely because it does not identify the instrumentality that will carry out the public purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications identified the public purpose but did not specify the instrumentality that would execute it.
The appellants argued that the omission made the notifications unenforceable.
members.legal_principle: The Land Acquisition Act does not require the instrumentality carrying out the public purpose to be specified in notifications under sections 4 and 6. The Court approved Ramji Popatbhai v. Jamnadas Shah, (1969) Guj. L.R. 164, and followed Vishnu Prasad Ramdas Gohil & Others v. The State of Gujarat, C.A. No. 1983 of 1966, decided October 9, 1969.
members.conclusion: The omission of the executing instrumentality did not affect the validity of either notification.

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a land-acquisition notification.
predicates.public_purpose_identified: The notification identifies the public purpose for which the land is sought.
predicates.implementing_instrumentality_omitted: The notification does not identify the instrumentality that will carry out the purpose.

members.legal_issue: General statutory notice of a proposed acquisition is sufficient where the rules do not require special individual notice.
material_facts: The challengers did not dispute compliance with the requirements to publish the notice in the Official Gazette and give public notice of its substance at convenient places in the locality.
The rule relied on by the challengers did not impose a further special-notice requirement.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires publication in the Official Gazette and public notice of the substance of the notification at convenient places in the locality. Rule 30B of the Gujarat Land Acquisition Rules did not add a requirement for special individual notice.
members.conclusion: No special notice to the challengers was required.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.general_notice_given: The substance of the proposed acquisition is publicly notified through the required general methods.
predicates.no_rule_requires_special_notice: The applicable rule does not require a separate special notice to the challenger.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition proceeding is not invalid merely because an interested person did not receive an individual notice of the preliminary intention to acquire when the required public notice was given.
material_facts: The respondents were tenants of acquired land and had erected structures on it at their own expense.
They said they received no individual notice and learned of the acquisition only when their landlord told them that possession was to be handed over.
The acquisition notification was published in the Official Gazette, and the substance of the notification was publicly posted at a convenient place in the locality.
The acquisition authorities also served notices on persons known or believed to be interested, and compliance with the public-notice procedure was not disputed.
The respondents challenged the acquisition proceedings and award, and the High Court set them aside because the respondents had not been individually notified.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires publication in the Official Gazette and public notice of the substance of the notification at convenient places in the locality; Rule 1 of the rules made under section 55 does not add a requirement of personal notice to every interested person. The Court approved Bai Malimabu v. State of Gujarat, which interpreted the similar Rule 30-B consistently with that principle, and overruled Ashokkumar Gordhanbhai v. State of Gujarat; it also noted the consistent view in Vasudev Chunilal Pancholi v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The absence of individual notice to each interested person did not invalidate the acquisition proceedings; the appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment and decree were set aside.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and official_publication_given and locality_public_notice_given and individual_notice_absent

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The challenged proceeding sought to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.official_publication_given: The acquisition notification was published through the prescribed official publication method.
predicates.locality_public_notice_given: The substance of the acquisition notification was publicly communicated at a convenient place in the affected locality.
predicates.individual_notice_absent: An interested person did not receive a separate personal notice of the acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: Failure to serve notice on an interested person during land acquisition does not invalidate the award or subsequent acquisition proceedings when the statutory scheme preserves the person’s ability to claim compensation or seek a reference.
material_facts: The acquisition award covered land belonging to numerous owners and was made for planned industrial development.
The appellant alleged that she had not been served with notice inviting claims to compensation.
The High Court found that notice had been affixed on the land when the appellant was unavailable.
The Court held that even non-service would not invalidate the award or subsequent proceedings, and that an interested person could still pursue compensation-related remedies.
members.legal_principle: Whether a statutory provision is mandatory depends on legislative intent assessed from its language, context, purpose, and the consequences of non-compliance, rather than from the use of “shall” alone. A provision concerning a public duty is generally directory where invalidating proceedings for its breach would cause general inconvenience without furthering the statute’s object. The Court relied on Dattatraya Moreshwar v. State of Bombay, State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya, Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Rampur, State of Mysore v. V.K. Kangan, Sharif-Ud-Din v. Abdul Gani Lone, Balwant Singh v. Anand Kumar Sharma, Bhavnagar University v. Palitana Sugar Mill Pvt. Ltd., Chandrika Prasad Yadav v. State of Bihar, M/s. Rubber House v. M/s. Excellsior Needle Industries Pvt. Ltd., B.S. Khurana v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, State of Haryana v. Raghubir Dayal, and Gullipilli Sowria Raj v. Bandaru Pavani. Under sections 9, 18, 30 and 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, a person interested may pursue compensation or apportionment remedies, and land vests in the State free from encumbrances upon possession being taken. State of Tamil Nadu v. Mahalakshmi Ammal and Nasik Municipal Corporation v. Harbanslal Laikwant Rajpal support treating irregularities in service of notices under sections 9 and 10 as curable and not invalidating the award.
members.conclusion: The notice requirement was directory, and its non-compliance would not invalidate the award or subsequent acquisition proceedings.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land by the State.
predicates.notice_not_served: The acquiring authority did not serve the required claim notice on an interested person.

members.legal_issue: An irregularity in serving notices concerning compensation and persons interested in acquired land is curable and does not by itself invalidate the award.
material_facts: The respondents alleged that notices had been served on many persons on a single day, including a deceased person.
The Court held that even an irregularity in service of the notices would be curable and would not invalidate the award.
members.legal_principle: An irregularity in service of notices under Sections 9 and 10 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is curable and does not invalidate an award made under Section 11.
members.conclusion: Any irregularity in service of the notices did not make the award invalid.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: An authority is making an award in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.compensation_notices_served_irregularly: The authority served notices concerning compensation or interested persons in an irregular manner.
predicates.service_irregularity_is_curable: The defect in service is an irregularity that can be cured.
predicates.award_not_invalidated_by_service_irregul: The award remains valid despite the curable service irregularity.

members.legal_issue: A statutory ground that permits eviction does not itself terminate a periodic tenancy or convert non-payment into a forfeiture of the lease.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the premises under a month-to-month tenancy.
The landlord relied on the tenant’s failure to pay arrears within the period allowed by a demand notice.
The parties’ landlord-tenant relationship continued until a valid termination notice was given.
members.legal_principle: The Court read section 4(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955 together with section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. The statutory ground conditions the landlord’s ordinary right to terminate; it does not turn a periodic tenancy into a fixed or indefinite tenancy or add a re-entry condition. The Court considered forfeiture under section 111(g) and relief under section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and held that the statutory arrears ground did not constitute such a forfeiture.
members.conclusion: The statutory arrears ground only removed the statutory bar to exercising the landlord’s ordinary right to terminate the tenancy; it did not change the periodic character of the tenancy or create a right of re-entry for forfeiture. Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 therefore did not apply as a relief against forfeiture.

predicates.landlord_brought_tenant_eviction_proceed: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_was_periodic: The tenant held the premises under a tenancy that renewed periodically.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_was_establishe: The landlord established a statutory ground that permits seeking the tenant’s eviction.

members.legal_issue: Relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent is unavailable when an eviction suit enforces a statutory rent-default right rather than a forfeiture of the lease.
material_facts: The landlord's suit relied on statutory rent-default provisions and did not claim that the lease had been forfeited under the law governing transfers of property.
The tenants sought relief against forfeiture based on their payment of rent after the suit began.
members.legal_principle: Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, provides relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent where a lease has been determined by forfeiture. Sections 111(g) and 114 concern forfeiture based on breach of an express condition permitting re-entry and the required notice. They do not apply where the landlord sues to enforce a statutory right arising from rent default. The Court considered Praduman Kumar v. Virendra Goyal.
members.conclusion: The tenants could not obtain relief under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act because the suit was not based on forfeiture of the lease.

predicates.rent_eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant for rent default.
predicates.claim_based_on_statutory_default_not_lea: The landlord relied on a statutory rent-default right rather than termination of the lease by forfeiture.
predicates.forfeiture_relief_unavailable: Relief against lease forfeiture cannot be granted in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Relief under the law governing forfeiture of leases does not apply when a tenant's statutory rent default removes the bar to an eviction suit without forfeiting the lease.
material_facts: The landlord sued under statutory provisions governing rent default.
The statutory default removed the bar to the landlord's eviction suit and gave the landlord a right to seek an eviction decree.
The suit did not rely on an express lease condition allowing re-entry for non-payment of rent.
members.legal_principle: Sections 111(g) and 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, apply to forfeiture of a lease, including forfeiture for breach of an express condition permitting re-entry after the required notice. A statutory rent-default regime may remove a bar to an eviction action and confer a right to seek eviction without determining the lease by forfeiture.
members.conclusion: The tenants were not entitled to relief against forfeiture because no forfeiture of the lease was the basis of the suit.

predicates.eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.statutory_default_removes_bar_to_suit: The tenant's statutory default removed a legal bar to the landlord bringing the eviction proceeding.
predicates.lease_not_determined_by_forfeiture: The landlord did not establish that the lease had been determined by forfeiture.
predicates.transfer_of_property_forfeiture_relief_i: The tenant cannot obtain relief against forfeiture under the law governing leases.

members.legal_issue: A tenant in an eviction case governed by rent-control legislation cannot obtain relief against forfeiture under the general forfeiture provision when the governing rent-control legislation supplies the applicable conditions for protection from eviction.
material_facts: The eviction suit was brought under the rent-control legislation for arrears of rent.
The tenant had failed to pay or tender the rent and permitted increases required for protection from eviction.
The tenant sought to resist execution by relying on the general forfeiture-relief provision of the Transfer of Property Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, is a special provision that incorporates the equity of section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in modified form. A tenant governed by the rent-control legislation must meet its requirements and cannot claim double protection under section 114. The Court relied on Pradesh Kumar Bajpai v. Binod Behari Sharkar and distinguished the reliance placed on Krishnabai v. Hari and Gajanand Govind v. Pandurang Keshav.
members.conclusion: The case had to be resolved under section 12(3) of the rent-control legislation, not section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act; the tenant could not obtain the additional protection of section 114.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.tenant_fails_to_meet_statutory_rent_cond: The tenant does not satisfy the rent-payment or tender requirements for protection from eviction under the governing legislation.

members.legal_issue: A tenant cannot obtain additional relief against forfeiture under general property law after the statutory conditions for eviction under rent-control law have been met.
material_facts: The tenant was found to be in arrears of rent for more than three months and did not pay within one month after receiving a demand notice.
The landlord obtained the required permission and brought an eviction suit under the rent-control law.
The tenant sought relief under section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act and tendered the arrears, interest, and costs during the proceedings.
The notice relied on statutory rent default, not forfeiture under the lease; the lease’s forfeiture clause could not authorize immediate possession outside the rent-control procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act restricts eviction to its statutory grounds and procedure, so section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act cannot be read into it to provide additional relief against forfeiture. V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yasodai Ammal rejected the theory of double protection under rent-control law and the Transfer of Property Act.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to relief under section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act; the rent-control law provided the applicable eviction regime, and the tenant could not claim double protection under general property law.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and statutory_eviction_requirements_met and tenant_claims_general_forfeiture_relief and eviction_sought_on_statutory_default

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant under a statutory rent-control regime.
predicates.statutory_eviction_requirements_met: The tenant satisfied the statutory conditions that permit the landlord to bring an eviction suit.
predicates.tenant_claims_general_forfeiture_relief: The tenant sought relief against forfeiture under general property law.
predicates.eviction_sought_on_statutory_default: The landlord based the eviction proceeding on a rent default covered by the rent-control regime rather than on contractual forfeiture.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who satisfies the statutory conditions for eviction for rent default is subject to a mandatory eviction decree, and the alternative protection for other cases does not apply.
material_facts: The eviction suit alleged rent payable monthly, arrears exceeding six months, service of a demand notice, and non-payment within the notice period.
The tenants did not dispute the standard rent or permitted increases within the relevant period.
The tenants paid neither the arrears within the notice period nor the amount required to avoid the statutory consequence under the applicable clause.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(2) and 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the court must decree eviction when rent is payable monthly, there is no dispute about standard rent or permitted increases, arrears have continued for at least six months, and the tenant fails to pay within one month after notice. Section 12(3)(b), beginning with “In any other case,” applies only when clause (a) does not. The Court relied on Harbanslal Jagmohandas v. Prabhudas Shivlal, Jaywant S. Kulkarni v. Minochar Dosabhai Shroff, Ganpat Ladha v. Sashikant Vishnu Shinde, and Ganpat Ram Sharma v. Gayatri Devi.
members.conclusion: The statutory conditions for eviction were met, so the court was required to decree eviction; the alternative clause did not apply because it covered only cases outside the mandatory clause.

rule.if: statutory_rent_eviction_suit and monthly_rent and arrears_for_at_least_six_months and no_rent_amount_dispute and notice_period_expired_without_payment

predicates.statutory_rent_eviction_suit: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on a statutory ground of rent default.
predicates.monthly_rent: The tenant's rent was payable monthly.
predicates.arrears_for_at_least_six_months: The tenant had rent arrears lasting at least six months.
predicates.no_rent_amount_dispute: The tenant did not dispute the amount of standard rent or permitted increases during the relevant period.
predicates.notice_period_expired_without_payment: The tenant did not pay the demanded arrears before the notice period expired.
predicates.mandatory_eviction_decree_required: The court must decree eviction when the stated statutory rent-default conditions are met.

members.legal_issue: When the statutory ground for eviction is established, eviction is required unless another provision provides relief.
material_facts: The eviction suits relied on tenants having used or dealt with the premises contrary to conditions imposed on the landlords by the relevant authorities.
The relevant lease conditions prohibited unauthorised structures, and the landlords relied on the tenants’ breaches as grounds for eviction.
The applicable rent-control provisions allowed relief against eviction where the tenant remedied the breach, and the tenants had removed the offending structures.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, was framed imperatively. Although the proviso to section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, used different language, there was no substantive difference: where its requirements were satisfied, eviction had to follow unless another provision of section 14, including sections 14(2), 14(10), or 14(11), provided otherwise.
members.conclusion: The eviction provisions were mandatory in substance when their requirements were met, but eviction was not required where a provision otherwise allowed relief.

predicates.statutory_ejectment_proceeding: A proceeding seeks eviction on a ground specified by the applicable rent-control law.
predicates.statutory_ejectment_ground_is_establishe: The facts satisfy the statutory requirements for the asserted ground of eviction.
predicates.no_applicable_relief_is_available: No applicable provision permits the tenant to avoid eviction despite the established ground.
predicates.eviction_is_required: The court or authority must order eviction.

members.legal_issue: A subtenant may acquire direct tenancy under a later tenancy law even when an ejectment suit against the subtenant was pending under the repealed law.
material_facts: An ejectment suit against a subtenant was pending when a new tenancy law repealed the law governing the suit, and no eviction decree or order had been made.
While the suit remained pending, the subtenant gave the required notice and applied to the rent authority for recognition as a direct tenant under the superior landlord.
The rent authority declared the subtenant a direct tenant, and the trial court found that the landlord-and-tenant relationship between the parties to the ejectment suit had ceased.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 16(2) and 16(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, a subtenant could, after the prescribed notice and application, be declared a tenant directly under the superior landlord. Section 2(h) included a person continuing in possession until an eviction decree or order was made. Section 40 saved pending proceedings as if the repealed Act remained in force, but did not deny a subtenant the distinct new right conferred by the 1956 Act.
members.conclusion: The pending ejectment suit remained governed by the repealed law, but the savings provision did not prevent the subtenant from acquiring the new law’s right to direct tenancy. The relationship between the parties ceased when the rent authority made its declaration.

rule.if: pending_ejectment_proceeding and subtenant_in_possession and no_eviction_order and new_law_allows_direct_tenancy and rent_authority_declared_direct_tenancy

predicates.pending_ejectment_proceeding: An ejectment proceeding against a subtenant was pending when the governing law changed.
predicates.subtenant_in_possession: The subtenant continued in possession of the premises.
predicates.no_eviction_order: No eviction decree or order had been made against the subtenant when the direct-tenancy declaration was made.
predicates.new_law_allows_direct_tenancy: A law in force gave a subtenant a procedure to become a tenant directly under the superior landlord.
predicates.rent_authority_declared_direct_tenancy: The rent authority declared the subtenant to be a direct tenant under the superior landlord.
predicates.subtenant_becomes_direct_tenant: The subtenant becomes a tenant directly under the superior landlord.

members.legal_issue: A subtenant's statutory entitlement to direct tenancy is not defeated merely because the subletting violated the lease or the landlord sought eviction on account of subletting.
material_facts: The lease prohibited the tenant from subletting the premises or any part of them.
The subtenant claimed direct tenancy after the tenant's tenancy ended.
The landlord argued that the breach of the lease and the eviction provisions prevented the subtenant from acquiring statutory rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950 does not limit protection to subleases lawful under the lease. Section 12(1)(c) preserves the rights and obligations of subtenants under section 13 in the stated eviction context. The Court contrasted this language with section 11(3) of the 1948 Act, which referred to premises lawfully sublet, and held that the 1950 Act deliberately enlarged the protected class. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: A breach of the lease's prohibition on subletting does not by itself prevent the subtenant from acquiring the rights provided by section 13(2); the rights of subtenants remain governed by section 13 even where the landlord brings an eviction suit based on subletting.

predicates.first_degree_sublease: A tenant holding directly from the landlord sublet the premises or part of them.
predicates.lease_prohibited_subletting: The lease barred the tenant from subletting the premises or part of them.
predicates.qualifying_tenancy_termination: The tenant's tenancy ended lawfully, other than through a decree based on the excluded ground described by the law.

members.legal_issue: A subtenant obtains statutory tenant protection only if the premises were lawfully sublet before the applicable statutory cutoff.
material_facts: The petitioner claimed that he had occupied the entire flat as a subtenant from an earlier time and had merely confined his occupation to the portion in question later.
The courts below found that his occupation of the portion then in his possession began in 1962, not earlier.
The subtenancy of that portion therefore began after the applicable cutoff.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, protects a subtenant to whom the premises were lawfully sublet before commencement of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control (Amendment) Ordinance, 1959. Because the courts found that the subtenancy of the premises in question began after that cutoff, the petitioner could not claim the benefit of section 14(1).
members.conclusion: The petitioner was not entitled to statutory protection as a subtenant and had no right to continue in possession on that basis.

predicates.subtenant_protection_claim: The occupant claimed statutory protection on the basis of being a subtenant.
predicates.subtenancy_began_after_statutory_cutoff: The subtenancy of the premises in the occupant’s possession began after the applicable statutory cutoff.

members.legal_issue: A subtenant whose subletting began after the applicable statutory cutoff is not protected from eviction on the basis of that protection.
material_facts: The two lower courts found that the second defendant was sublet the premises after the date relevant to protection under the applicable ordinance.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court could not disturb that factual finding in supervisory review and restored the eviction decree on the ground of unlawful subletting.
members.legal_principle: Under Ordinance No. III of 1959, read with the Bombay Rent Act, the relevant date determined whether the subtenant received the claimed protection. The lower courts found the subletting occurred after that date. The Supreme Court left that factual finding undisturbed because it could not be reappreciated in Article 227 proceedings.
members.conclusion: The second defendant was not entitled to protection under the Ordinance, and the eviction decree was restored on the ground of unlawful subletting.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_based_on_unlawful_su: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant unlawfully sublet the premises.
predicates.subletting_occurred_after_protective_cut: The subletting began after the statutory cutoff for the claimed protection.

members.legal_issue: Permission to receive additional documentary evidence does not itself establish the documents or make them admissible as exhibits without proof.
material_facts: The High Court allowed the applications to produce additional documents but stated that the documents would be subject to proof.
The respondent intended to rely on the documents, and their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents had not been established merely by allowing the applications.
members.legal_principle: An order allowing additional evidence under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the evidence to be tendered; it does not dispense with the ordinary requirements of proof. The party relying on documents must establish their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents as required by law.
members.conclusion: The documents could not be exhibited automatically; the party relying on them had to prove their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents as required by law.

predicates.additional_documents_received_for_consid: An appellate court has permitted documents not previously produced to be brought into the appeal for consideration.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_those_documents: A party asks the court to rely on the documents in deciding the dispute.

members.legal_issue: Admission of secondary evidence does not by itself establish the authenticity, truthfulness, or genuineness of the document.
material_facts: The appellants were permitted to lead secondary evidence of a copy of the will.
The Court clarified that the document’s authenticity, truthfulness, and genuineness would still have to be established at trial.
members.legal_principle: The admission of a document into evidence, including its marking as an exhibit, does not by itself prove it. The document must be proved in accordance with law; permission to use secondary evidence only allows that evidence to be led.
members.conclusion: Permission to lead secondary evidence does not automatically prove the document; its authenticity, truthfulness, and genuineness must be established during trial in accordance with law.

predicates.secondary_evidence_offered: A party offers secondary evidence of a document in a court proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Admission of secondary evidence does not by itself prove the document or establish its genuineness, correctness, or existence.
material_facts: The trial court permitted the defendant to lead secondary evidence of the letter of disclaimer.

The Supreme Court clarified that the document’s genuineness, correctness, and existence still had to be established during the trial and that reasons must be recorded before relying on the secondary evidence.
members.legal_principle: The admission or marking of a document as an exhibit does not dispense with the proof otherwise required by law. The court must assess the document and its contents, and its genuineness, correctness, and existence must be established before reliance. This principle was stated in M. Chandra v. M. Thangamuthu and applied alongside the requirements of Sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act.
members.conclusion: The admission of secondary evidence did not prove the document; its genuineness, correctness, and existence had to be established at trial before the court relied on it.

predicates.secondary_evidence_proceeding: A court proceeding concerns the proposed use of secondary evidence to prove a document.
predicates.secondary_evidence_admitted: The court has allowed secondary evidence of the document to be received.
predicates.document_proof_not_yet_established: The document’s genuineness, correctness, and existence have not yet been established.

members.legal_issue: A document’s admissibility does not establish the truth of its contents, which must still be proved.
material_facts: The High Court held that the disputed agreement could not be relied on because it was unregistered.
The Supreme Court considered that view potentially incorrect, but the party relying on the agreement did not examine its attesting witnesses or prove its contents.
members.legal_principle: Admissibility and probative value are distinct: an admissible document may have little or no probative value, and its contents must be proved. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Radha Krishna Singh, Madan Mohan Singh v. Rajni Kant, H. Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam, and Laxmibai v. Bhagwantbuva.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s view that the document could not be relied on merely because it was unregistered might not be legally correct, but the document’s admissibility did not establish its contents, which remained unproved.

rule.if: civil_case_relying_on_document and document_admissible and not document_contents_proved

predicates.civil_case_relying_on_document: A party in a civil case relies on a document to establish a claim or defence.
predicates.document_admissible: The court permits the document to be received in evidence.
predicates.document_contents_proved: The party relying on the document establishes the truth of its contents.

members.legal_issue: Admission of a document, or of a signature appearing on it, does not by itself prove the document’s contents or establish the probative value of those contents.
material_facts: The property owner acknowledged his signature on the photocopy of the power of attorney but denied admitting its contents or genuineness.
The trial court inferred from the signature admission that the document authorised the representative to sell the property.
The Supreme Court held that the court had to assess the document’s probative value and could not draw that inference from the signature admission alone.
members.legal_principle: Admissibility and probative value are distinct, and a document that is admitted in evidence does not thereby become proof of its contents. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Sri Radha Krishna Singh, AIR 1983 SC 684, and Madan Mohan Singh v. Rajni Kant, AIR 2010 SC 2933.
members.conclusion: The signature admission did not establish the contents of the power of attorney or prove that it authorised a sale; the trial court’s contrary inference was unwarranted.

predicates.civil_evidence_case: A court is deciding a civil dispute using documentary evidence.
predicates.document_admitted: A document or a copy of it has been admitted or received in evidence.
predicates.contents_not_admitted_or_proven: The relevant contents of the document have not themselves been admitted or established by evidence.

members.legal_issue: A party may be permitted to lead secondary evidence when foundational facts account for the original document’s non-production and evidence supports its existence, even if its existence has not been conclusively established before that evidence is received.
material_facts: The appellants sought to prove a copy of a will after the original, which they said had been given to revenue officials, could not be produced.
The officials failed to produce the original after receiving court-issued notices to do so, but neither unequivocally denied that it existed.

One official testified that he could not trace it, in part because the matter was old and he was no longer posted in that area; another acknowledged that a will had been handed to an official for mutation purposes.
The will’s scribe identified it and testified that it bore his signature as scribe and witness.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 65(a) and 66 of the Evidence Act, secondary evidence may be given when the original appears to be held by a person legally bound to produce it and is not produced after notice. A party must establish foundational facts explaining why the original is unavailable. Ashok Dulichand v. Madahavlal Dube and Rakesh Mohindra v. Anita Beri address the conditions for secondary evidence; H. Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam confirms that a plausible reason for non-production and a factual foundation are required. The court must assess the evidence bearing on the original’s existence and non-production; conclusive proof of the document is not a precondition to allowing the secondary evidence to be led.
members.conclusion: The foundational factual basis for secondary evidence had been established, and the appellants had to be given an opportunity to lead it. The refusal to permit secondary evidence was set aside.

rule.if: civil_evidence_appeal and original_not_produced_after_notice and evidence_supports_original_existence and nonproduction_reason_explained

predicates.civil_evidence_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a refusal to permit a party to lead secondary evidence in a civil case.
predicates.original_not_produced_after_notice: A person appearing to hold the original document did not produce it after receiving notice to do so.
predicates.evidence_supports_original_existence: Testimony or other evidence supports that the original document existed.
predicates.nonproduction_reason_explained: Evidence gives a reason why the original document was not produced.

members.legal_issue: Secondary evidence may be admitted when the party establishes a factual basis for the original document’s unavailability despite efforts to produce it.
material_facts: The defendant sought to prove a letter of disclaimer through a photocopy after the original could not be found in the office of the official custodian where the defendant said it had been lodged.
The official custodian produced the office records, including the photocopy, and testified that the original was not in the office.
The trial court considered the evidence about the search for the original and allowed the defendant to lead secondary evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the defendant had made the necessary efforts and that the photocopy came from the official custodian’s records.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 63, 64 and 65(c) of the Evidence Act, documents are ordinarily proved by primary evidence, but secondary evidence may be given when the original is lost or cannot be produced for a reason not arising from the offering party’s default or neglect. The party must lay a factual foundation showing why primary evidence is unavailable, and the court must assess the evidence and the probative value of the document. The principle that exceptions to primary evidence provide relief where a party is genuinely unable to produce the original through no fault of that party was applied in M. Chandra v. M. Thangamuthu. J. Yashoda v. K. Shobha Rani and H. Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam were considered in addressing the requirements for secondary evidence; Rai Baijnath v. Maharaja Sir Pavaneshwar Prasad Singh was cited concerning proof of loss. Illegible signatures on some documents were not, by themselves, a reason to reject the secondary evidence.
members.conclusion: The trial court correctly permitted the defendant to lead secondary evidence, and the High Court’s order setting that permission aside was reversed.

rule.if: secondary_evidence_request_in_civil_proceeding and original_unavailable_despite_efforts and original_unavailability_not_caused_by_offering_party and copy_found_in_custodian_records and custodian_confirmed_original_missing

predicates.secondary_evidence_request_in_civil_proc: A party in a civil proceeding asked the court to permit proof of a document through secondary evidence.
predicates.original_unavailable_despite_efforts: The party made efforts to produce the original but could not do so.
predicates.original_unavailability_not_caused_by_of: The original could not be produced for a reason not caused by the offering party’s default or neglect.
predicates.copy_found_in_custodian_records: A copy of the document was found among records held by the office said to have custody of the original.
predicates.custodian_confirmed_original_missing: The official custodian produced the records and confirmed that the original was not among them.

members.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a lost document may be considered when a party lays a sufficient foundation for its loss, even without filing a separate application for permission to adduce it.
material_facts: The defendants stated that the original Will, which had been in a beneficiary's possession, was lost.
They produced a certified copy from the Sub-Registrar and a photocopy of the Will; the plaintiff had admitted execution but alleged fraud and misrepresentation.
The defendants' witnesses were not cross-examined about the loss of the original, and no application to lead secondary evidence had been filed.
members.legal_principle: Section 65(c) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 permits secondary evidence when an original has been lost. The Court relied on M. Ehtisham Ali v. Jamna Prasad and Aher Rama Gova v. State of Gujarat on proof of loss and admission of secondary evidence, and held that a separate application is not required if the foundation is laid in the pleadings or evidence. Bipin Shantilal Panchal v. State of Gujarat was also relied on regarding the handling of evidentiary objections.
members.conclusion: The evidence laid a sufficient foundation for secondary evidence, and it could not be excluded merely because the defendants had not filed a separate application.

predicates.documentary_proof_proceeding: A party seeks to prove a document in a civil or other evidentiary proceeding.
predicates.original_document_lost: The party offering the document states that the original has been lost.
predicates.secondary_evidence_foundation_laid: The party presents evidence supporting the loss and produces secondary material relating to the document.

members.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a registered will may be admitted when the original was produced in earlier proceedings and is no longer available from the person who had it.
material_facts: The trial court found that the original will had been produced in earlier proceedings.
The executor, who had retained the original, had died.
The executor’s son was asked to produce the original and stated that he did not possess it.
A certified copy of the registered will was tendered as secondary evidence.
members.legal_principle: The Court upheld the concurrent factual finding that the circumstances warranted admitting secondary evidence of the will. It distinguished the question of whether the will was proved from objections to the use of a certified copy, and relied on the evidence concerning the original’s earlier production and subsequent unavailability.
members.conclusion: The admission of the certified copy as secondary evidence was justified, and the contrary view of the High Court could not stand.

rule.if: will_proof_proceeding and original_previously_produced and custodian_unavailable and current_holder_lacks_original and certified_copy_available

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A court is deciding whether a will has been proved.
predicates.original_previously_produced: The original document was produced in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.custodian_unavailable: The person who had custody of the original is no longer available to produce it.
predicates.current_holder_lacks_original: A person asked to produce the original states that they do not possess it.
predicates.certified_copy_available: A certified copy of the document is available for use as secondary evidence.
predicates.secondary_evidence_admissible: The certified copy may be admitted as secondary evidence in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A party relying on an ancient document should have an opportunity to establish the basis for admitting a certified copy as secondary evidence when the original’s availability has not been investigated.
material_facts: The claimant relied on an old lease as the source of the claimed title but did not produce the original.
The claimant belatedly sought to rely on a certified copy, which the trial court excluded for lack of a foundation for secondary evidence.
The courts had not established whether the original document was available or given the claimant an opportunity to lay the necessary foundation.
members.legal_principle: Where an ancient document is relied on to establish title, the court should investigate the availability of the original and give the party an opportunity to lay the foundation for secondary evidence before refusing to consider a certified copy on that ground. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The claimant had to be given an opportunity to produce the original lease or to adduce evidence supporting admission of the certified copy as secondary evidence; admission of the copy was not ordered automatically.

rule.if: title_suit_relies_on_old_document and original_not_produced and original_availability_unexamined and certified_copy_offered

predicates.title_suit_relies_on_old_document: A party in a title suit relies on an old document as evidence of title.
predicates.original_not_produced: The party has not produced the original document.
predicates.original_availability_unexamined: The court has not investigated whether the original document is available.
predicates.certified_copy_offered: The party offers a certified copy of the document.

members.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a document is inadmissible unless the failure to produce the original is accounted for and the copy is supported by foundational evidence establishing its authenticity.
material_facts: The party seeking specific performance relied on a photocopy of a power of attorney to establish that the property owner had authorised a representative to sell the property.
The original power of attorney was not produced, and no factual foundation was laid to justify reliance on secondary evidence.
The property owner admitted his signature on the photocopy but did not admit its contents or genuineness.
members.legal_principle: Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 permits secondary evidence only subject to its statutory conditions. When the original is not produced, its absence must be accounted for, and foundational evidence must establish that the copy is a true copy. The Court relied on The Roman Catholic Mission v. State of Madras, AIR 1966 SC 1457; State of Rajasthan v. Khemraj, AIR 2000 SC 1759; Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Ram Pal Singh Bisen, (2010) 4 SCC 491; and M. Chandra v. M. Thangamuthu, (2010) 9 SCC 712.
members.conclusion: The trial court could not treat the photocopy as proof that the power of attorney authorised the representative to sell the property; secondary evidence could not be relied upon without the required foundation and proof.

rule.if: civil_document_proof_case and secondary_evidence_tendered and original_not_produced and not nonproduction_accounted_for and not copy_authenticated

predicates.civil_document_proof_case: A party in a civil case relies on a document to establish a material fact.
predicates.secondary_evidence_tendered: A party offers a copy or other secondary evidence of the document instead of its original.
predicates.original_not_produced: The original document is not produced in court.
predicates.nonproduction_accounted_for: The party relying on secondary evidence establishes a legally recognised reason why the original is not produced.
predicates.copy_authenticated: Foundational evidence establishes that the offered copy is a true copy of the original.
