members.legal_issue: A copy of a document is inadmissible where the original is not produced and its loss is not properly accounted for.
material_facts: A party relied on a photographic copy of a document said to contain a deceased family member’s later ratification of an arrangement.
The original, which would ordinarily have been in the possession of the party relying on the document, was not produced.
The loss of the original was not properly accounted for.
Both lower courts rejected the copy as inadmissible, and the Supreme Court agreed.
members.legal_principle: The Court upheld the exclusion of the copy because the original was not produced and its loss was not properly accounted for; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this evidentiary ruling.
members.conclusion: The photographic copy was rightly refused admission in evidence.

rule.if: civil_partition_case and party_offered_document_copy and original_not_produced and loss_of_original_not_properly_accounted_for

predicates.civil_partition_case: The proceeding is a civil dispute concerning division of family property.
predicates.party_offered_document_copy: A party offered a copy of a document as evidence.
predicates.original_not_produced: The original document was not produced in evidence.
predicates.loss_of_original_not_properly_accounted_: The party relying on the copy did not properly account for the loss of the original.

members.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a will cannot establish its contents unless the loss of the original is satisfactorily proved.
material_facts: The beneficiary had obtained the original registered will and testified that he showed it to the testatrix.
He could not say where or how the original was lost, and no report of its loss or corroborating evidence was produced.
The beneficiary relied on a certified copy and a purported photocopy in place of the original.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 65(c) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, secondary evidence may be given when the original has been destroyed or lost, or cannot be produced for a reason not arising from the offering party’s default or neglect. The party relying on secondary evidence must first prove the loss of the original.
members.conclusion: The loss of the original was not satisfactorily proved, so the secondary evidence could not establish the will.

predicates.will_proof_proceeding: A party sought recognition of a will in a proceeding concerning the will.
predicates.original_not_produced: The party relying on the will did not produce its original document.
predicates.loss_of_original_not_satisfactorily_prov: The party relying on secondary evidence could not give a satisfactory account or supporting proof of the original’s loss.
predicates.secondary_evidence_cannot_establish_will: The substitute evidence cannot establish the will’s contents or execution.

members.legal_issue: An ordinary copy of a document whose original is unavailable is not admissible as secondary evidence unless its correctness is proved by proper evidence.
material_facts: The claimant relied on an old sale deed as the foundation of title but did not produce the original or a certified copy.
The copy produced was an ordinary copy, without an endorsement establishing it as a true copy or evidence showing that it had been compared with the original.
The witness who produced it had no personal knowledge of its registration and did not produce the register; no evidence established the contents of the original.
members.legal_principle: Sections 63 and 79 of the Indian Evidence Act govern the kinds of secondary evidence and the presumption as to the correctness of certified copies. Correctness is presumed for certified copies within Section 63(1), but other copies must be proved by proper evidence. A certified copy of a registered sale deed may be produced as secondary evidence when the original is unavailable; an unverified ordinary copy is not thereby admissible.
members.conclusion: The ordinary copy was not secondary evidence and could not support the claimant’s title.

rule.if: title_suit_based_on_document and original_unavailable and copy_not_certified and copy_correctness_unproved

predicates.title_suit_based_on_document: A claimant brings a title suit relying on a document as the foundation of title.
predicates.original_unavailable: The original document is not produced.
predicates.copy_not_certified: The copy produced is not certified as a true copy.
predicates.copy_correctness_unproved: No proper evidence establishes that the copy is correct or establishes the contents of the original.

members.legal_issue: When the original document is in the possession or power of the opposing party and is not produced after notice, any secondary evidence of its contents is admissible even if the document is one for which a certified copy may be given in evidence.
material_facts: The opposing party had produced the original deed to a public body, along with a plain copy and an English translation, and endorsed that the copy corresponded to the original.
The original was returned to that party, while the copy and translation were retained by the public body.
At trial, the opposing party did not produce the original despite receiving notice to do so.
No copy of the deed could be traced in the registration office, and the party relying on the deed tendered the retained copy and translation.
Admissions by the opposing party and earlier officeholders, together with other evidence, supported the existence of the deed and the dedication of the properties.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 65(a) and 66 of the Evidence Act, when the original is shown or appears to be in the possession or power of the opposing party and that party does not produce it after the required notice, any secondary evidence of its contents is admissible. Section 65(f) does not control or restrict section 65(a) when both apply. The Court approved In the Matter of a Collision between the Ava and the Brenhilda (1879) I.L.R. 5 Cal. 568, which held that any secondary evidence may be received where the case falls within clauses (a) or (c), even if clause (f) also applies.
members.conclusion: The plain copy was admissible as secondary evidence because the conditions for admission based on the opposing party’s failure to produce the original after notice were satisfied. That rule was not displaced by the possibility that the document also fell within the category for which a certified copy could be given in evidence.

rule.if: secondary_evidence_admissibility_dispute and original_in_opponent_possession_or_power and notice_given and original_not_produced_after_notice and offered_evidence_is_secondary and document_in_certified_copy_category

predicates.secondary_evidence_admissibility_dispute: The proceeding presents a dispute about whether evidence other than an original document may be admitted to prove its contents.
predicates.original_in_opponent_possession_or_power: The original document was shown or appeared to be in the possession or power of the opposing party.
predicates.notice_given: The party seeking to prove the document gave the opposing party notice to produce the original.
predicates.original_not_produced_after_notice: The opposing party did not produce the original after receiving notice.
predicates.offered_evidence_is_secondary: The party seeking to prove the document offered evidence other than the original to establish its contents.
predicates.document_in_certified_copy_category: The document is of a kind for which a certified copy may be given in evidence.

members.legal_issue: Secondary evidence of a public judgment is admissible when the original has been lost and the statutory conditions for secondary evidence are met.
material_facts: The community offered an ordinary copy of the judgment in an earlier suit to establish its contents.
The original judgment was no longer available in the court records, and the certified copy obtained by the community had been lost.
The opposing parties did not deny that the earlier judgment existed or claim that the copy offered was inaccurate.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 65(c) of the Evidence Act, secondary evidence may be given when the original has been lost. That provision operates independently of Section 65(f), so secondary evidence may be admitted even for a public document when the conditions of clause (c) are fulfilled. The Court relied on Mst. Bibi Aisha v. The Bihar Sunni Majlis Avaqaf, AIR 1969 SC 253.
members.conclusion: The ordinary copy of the earlier judgment was admissible as secondary evidence.

predicates.civil_proceeding: A party is offering documentary evidence in a civil proceeding.
predicates.public_judgment_copy_offered: A party offers a copy of a judgment that is a public document to prove its contents.
predicates.original_lost: The original document has been lost or destroyed.

members.legal_issue: A certified copy of a private instrument cannot be admitted as secondary evidence merely because it is a certified copy when the absence of the original has not been adequately explained.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a certified copy of a registered instrument said to transfer a share in the property.
The opposing party denied executing the instrument.

The claimant said the original had been taken from the registrar’s office by the opposing party, but the record did not substantiate that account; the claimant did not seek confirmation from the registrar’s office, and the reported communication came from a petition writer who was not an employee of that office.
The instrument was not a public document, and the courts found that the original’s unavailability had not been properly explained.
members.legal_principle: Section 65(f) of the Evidence Act permits secondary evidence notwithstanding the existence of an original where the document is one for which the Act or another law permits a certified copy to be given in evidence. It does not dispense with an appropriate explanation for the original’s unavailability when the document is a private document. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly held that Section 65(f) of the Evidence Act did not make the certified copy admissible in these circumstances.

rule.if: civil_property_claim and private_instrument_offered_as_secondary_evidence and certified_copy_produced and original_unavailable and not adequate_explanation_for_original_unavailability

predicates.civil_property_claim: A party brought a civil claim asserting an interest in property.
predicates.private_instrument_offered_as_secondary_: A party offered a private instrument as secondary evidence in support of the property claim.
predicates.certified_copy_produced: The party produced a certified copy of the instrument.
predicates.original_unavailable: The original instrument was not produced in court.
predicates.adequate_explanation_for_original_unavai: The party gave an adequately supported explanation for why the original instrument could not be produced.

members.legal_issue: A party's identification of a signature as their own does not, by itself, amount to an admission that they executed the document or accepted its contents.
material_facts: The defendants denied executing the agreement and receipt and claimed that the signature was a clever forgery.
The party identified a signature shown without the rest of the document as their own.
The court treated that identification as an admission of execution.
members.legal_principle: An admission must be a conscious and deliberate act, and an admission that a signature is one's own is distinct from an admission that the document was executed or that its contents are true. The genuineness of an allegedly forged signature must be determined on the evidence, including expert evidence and testimony tested by cross-examination.
members.conclusion: Identification of the signature was not an admission of execution of the agreement or of its contents.

predicates.civil_suit_party_examination: A court examines a party during a civil suit.
predicates.party_identifies_signature_on_disputed_d: A party identifies a signature appearing on a document whose authenticity or execution is disputed.
predicates.execution_is_denied: The party has denied executing the document.

members.legal_issue: Admitting a signature on a document does not, by itself, amount to admitting its execution; execution requires signing with assent to terms understood by the signer.
material_facts: The purported executant admitted that her signatures and fingerprints were on the sale deed but disputed having executed it.

She alleged that the deed had been obtained through fraud and undue influence, that its area and boundaries differed from what had been agreed, that it included her residence, and that the full consideration had not been received.
The Registrar relied on evidence that she had signed the deed and affixed her fingerprints, without finding that she understood and assented to its terms.
members.legal_principle: Sections 35(1)(a) and 35(3)(a) of the Registration Act distinguish admitting a signature from admitting execution. Execution means signing as assent to the terms of a document understood by the signer, not merely affixing a signature. The Court relied on Rajendra Pratap Singh v. Rameshwar Prasad, which treated signature as giving rise to a rebuttable presumption of execution; Puran Chand Nahatta v. Monmotho Nath Mukherji, which explains that execution is more than signing; and the reasoning in Suraj Lamps and Industries Private Limited v. State of Haryana and Bharat Indu v. Hakim Mohammad Hamid Ali Khan concerning the purposes of registration. It also considered Section 68 of the Evidence Act and distinguished the definition of execution in Section 2(12) of the Stamp Act because that Act serves a different purpose.
members.conclusion: The admission of the signatures and fingerprints did not establish execution of the sale deed; execution required assent to the document's terms after understanding them.

rule.if: document_registration_proceeding and signer_admitted_signature and execution_disputed and (understanding_of_terms_denied or assent_to_terms_denied)

predicates.document_registration_proceeding: A registration authority is deciding whether a document presented for registration was executed.
predicates.signer_admitted_signature: The purported executant acknowledged that the signature on the document was theirs.
predicates.execution_disputed: The purported executant maintained that the document had not been executed by them.
predicates.understanding_of_terms_denied: The purported executant maintained that they did not understand the document's terms when signing it.
predicates.assent_to_terms_denied: The purported executant maintained that they did not agree to be bound by the document's terms.

members.legal_issue: A party’s failure to file a replication does not by itself admit facts pleaded in a written statement when the opposing party has otherwise specifically challenged those facts.
material_facts: In a property division suit, a defendant pleaded in the written statement that the deceased had gifted certain properties to him.
The plaintiff did not file a replication but specifically denied the gift’s execution in affidavits concerning injunction applications.
Those affidavits were accepted on the record, and the parties proceeded to trial knowing that execution of the gift deed was disputed and led evidence on that issue.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, pleadings consist of the plaint and written statement; a replication, if permitted, may become part of the pleadings, but its absence does not itself admit facts pleaded in the written statement. Whether execution is specifically denied must be assessed in light of the record and the parties’ conduct. Rosammal Issetheenammal Fernandez v. Joosa Mariyan Fernandez holds that the existence of a specific denial determines whether the proviso to Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, applies.
members.conclusion: The absence of a replication did not amount to an admission of the pleaded gift; the gift’s execution remained contested.

predicates.civil_property_division_proceeding: The parties are litigating a claim to divide property and one party relies on a document pleaded in a written statement.
predicates.no_replication_filed: The opposing party did not file a replication responding to the written statement.
predicates.execution_specifically_denied_elsewhere_: The opposing party specifically challenged execution in another filing accepted by the court or otherwise made clear the challenge at trial.

members.legal_issue: A party’s failure to produce a document in rebuttal does not, by itself, amount to an admission of that document or its contents.
material_facts: The plaintiff produced a Will during the first appeal as additional evidence.
The defendant did not produce a document in rebuttal after the Will was taken on record.
The first appellate court treated the absence of rebuttal evidence as an admission of the Will and its contents, although no admission had been made through the applicable procedure.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17–31 and 58 of the Evidence Act govern admissions; Section 58 dispenses with proof only where a fact is admitted at or before the hearing in the manner contemplated by that provision. Order XII CPC provides procedures for admissions of cases and documents. A failure to prove a defence does not amount to an admission or shift the plaintiff’s burden. The Court relied on Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, L.I.C. of India v. Ram Pal Singh Bisen, and other authorities on admissions.
members.conclusion: The first appellate court erred in treating the defendant’s failure to produce rebuttal evidence as an admission of the Will or its contents.

predicates.civil_proceeding: The dispute is being decided in a civil proceeding.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_a_document: One party relies on a document to establish a fact in dispute.
predicates.the_opposing_party_does_not_produce_rebu: The opposing party does not produce evidence to rebut the document.
predicates.no_admission_was_made_through_the_applic: The opposing party has not admitted the document or its contents through a recognized written, pleading, or hearing procedure.

members.legal_issue: Acquittal of some participants does not automatically entitle the remaining accused to acquittal where the evidence supports their participation in the offence.
material_facts: The injured witness attributed an assault on himself to a group of accused, some of whom were acquitted by the appellate court.
The evidence also implicated the appellants in the fatal attack, and the Court considered the number and extent of the injuries and the circumstances of the assault.
The Court stated that the accused could have formed a common intention or common object at the scene and that the maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus does not apply in India.
members.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not applicable in India; a court may distinguish the evidence against different accused. The acquittal of some accused therefore does not automatically require acquittal of others whose participation is supported by the evidence.
members.conclusion: The acquittal of the other accused did not, by itself, require extending the same benefit to the appellants.

predicates.multi_accused_criminal_case: The criminal case alleges that several persons participated in the offence.
predicates.some_accused_acquitted: The court acquits some of the persons accused of participating in the offence.
predicates.evidence_independently_supports_remainin: Evidence supports the participation of the remaining accused apart from the evidence that led to the acquittals.

members.legal_issue: A court may accept witnesses’ evidence against an accused while rejecting their evidence against another accused when the reasons for rejecting it concern the other accused and do not undermine the evidence against the first accused.
material_facts: The same witnesses gave evidence that the accused ordered the fire to be set and that another person set it.
Some witnesses had omitted or failed to mention that the other person set the fire, but the identified evidentiary infirmities did not apply to their account of the accused’s order.
The appellate court found the witnesses’ evidence consistent against the accused and rejected the allegation against the other person.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that there is no rule of law or prudence requiring a court to accept or reject a witness’s testimony as a whole against all accused persons. Testimony may be accepted against one accused and rejected against another where the court gives reasons and the infirmities relate to the latter allegation.
members.conclusion: There was no violation of law or prudence in accepting the witnesses’ evidence against the accused while rejecting it against the alleged principal offender.

predicates.evidence_consistent_against_accused: The court found the witnesses’ evidence consistent against the accused whose conviction is challenged.

members.legal_issue: The acquittal of one accused does not, by itself, prevent the conviction of another accused in the same criminal occurrence.
material_facts: The appellant and other accused were tried for the same killing, and the appellant was convicted while one alleged participant was tried separately and acquitted.
The acquittal of the separately tried accused became final because the State did not appeal.
members.legal_principle: Criminal liability is generally individual: a person is liable for that person’s own acts, except where vicarious liability is recognized by law and its conditions are proved. Under Sections 34 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code, liability may extend to other participants when the requirements of common intention or unlawful assembly are established. The Court cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: An acquittal of a co-accused does not automatically bar the conviction of another accused; each accused’s liability must be assessed on the evidence and applicable rules of liability.

predicates.multi_accused_criminal_case: Several people were accused of involvement in the same criminal occurrence.
predicates.co_accused_acquitted: A person accused of involvement in the occurrence was acquitted.
predicates.remaining_accused_individually_tried: The liability of another accused was considered separately on the evidence against that accused.

members.legal_issue: The acquittal of some alleged participants does not, by itself, discredit the prosecution evidence against the remaining accused or require their acquittal.
material_facts: The appellants were convicted after a trial in which four co-accused were acquitted, and the convictions were challenged on the ground that witnesses had attributed participation to both the convicted and acquitted accused.
The acquittals rested on differing doubts, including inconsistencies with medical evidence, omissions about how weapons were used, and suspicious or delayed recoveries.
Two neighbours independently witnessed the occurrence, and the prosecution case against the convicted accused was otherwise supported by evidence concerning the occurrence and its scene.
members.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno falsus in omnibus is not applied mechanically. Doubt about particular participants does not necessarily discredit evidence against others; the court must assess the evidence and circumstances as a whole. The Court relied on the independent eyewitness evidence and the particular reasons for the co-accused’s acquittals.
members.conclusion: The acquittals of the four co-accused did not undermine the prosecution case as a whole; the maxim falsus in uno falsus in omnibus did not apply, and the convictions could stand.

predicates.appeal_from_convictions_after_some_acqui: The proceeding is an appeal against convictions entered after some accused in the same case were acquitted.
predicates.independent_witnesses_support_the_occurr: Witnesses independent of the complainant group gave evidence supporting the account of the occurrence.
predicates.other_corroborating_circumstances_suppor: Circumstances concerning the occurrence or its scene supported the prosecution account.
predicates.doubts_are_specific_to_some_participants: The reasons for doubt about acquitted accused concern their individual roles or evidence particular to them.

members.legal_issue: A possible acquittal of an alleged exhorter does not necessarily make witnesses who described that person’s participation unreliable as to the other accused.
material_facts: One acquitted accused was said to have exhorted the deceased, caught his hair, and taken away a rifle after the occurrence.
The trial court regarded these allegations as possible overstatement and was not satisfied of that accused’s criminality, while other evidence supported the account against the appellants.
The Supreme Court considered exhortation in the context of the facts and circumstances rather than treating it as inherently fabricated.
members.legal_principle: Exhortation is not necessarily padding or overstatement and must be evaluated in the facts and circumstances of each case. A possible, cautious view that an alleged exhorter’s participation is not proved does not, by itself, discredit witness testimony about other participants. The Court referred to Jainul Haque v. State of Bihar, AIR 1974 SC 45.
members.conclusion: The trial court could reasonably acquit the alleged exhorter on a cautious assessment without thereby requiring the witnesses to be treated as liars about the other accused.

predicates.appeal_from_convictions_after_some_acqui: The proceeding is an appeal against convictions entered after some accused in the same case were acquitted.
predicates.testimony_attributes_exhortation_to_an_a: Witnesses say that a person who was acquitted exhorted or encouraged an attack.
predicates.evidence_supports_the_other_participants: Evidence apart from the disputed allegation supports the account of the other participants’ involvement.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal of some accused persons does not automatically entitle other accused persons to acquittal when direct evidence establishes their presence and participation.
material_facts: Two accused persons were acquitted, while the courts below found direct evidence establishing the presence and participation of the appellants whose convictions were challenged.
The Supreme Court accepted that evidence.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that the effect of an acquittal depends on the evidence concerning each accused; acquittal of some accused does not displace direct evidence establishing another accused’s presence and participation. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The acquittal of two accused persons did not provide a ground to extend the benefit of acquittal to the appellants.

predicates.some_coaccused_acquitted: One or more people tried with the appellant were acquitted.
predicates.direct_evidence_establishes_appellant_pa: Direct evidence establishes the appellant’s presence and participation in the offence.

members.legal_issue: A court may accept evidence against some accused while acquitting others, because the maxim that false evidence in one respect must be rejected entirely does not apply in criminal trials.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted ten accused but convicted the appellants after considering the case of each accused separately.
The Supreme Court found the eyewitness evidence cogent, consistent, and corroborated by medical and other evidence.
The reasons supporting the acquittals were not applicable to the appellants whose participation the evidence established.
members.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus does not apply in criminal trials. The court must separate truth from falsehood and assess the evidence against each accused. The judgment cites no earlier cases or statutory provisions for this principle.
members.conclusion: The acquittals of other accused did not require the appellants’ acquittal; the convictions of the appellants were upheld on the evidence assessed against them individually.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.some_coaccused_were_acquitted: The trial court acquitted some persons accused in the same case.
predicates.accused_participation_individually_estab: The evidence, assessed against the particular accused, established that person’s participation.

members.legal_issue: The acquittal of one accused does not require acquittal of other accused whose participation is established by a credible part of the evidence.
material_facts: The Court found a reasonable doubt about one accused’s identification but accepted the evidence against the remaining accused.
The remaining convictions rested on evidence the Court considered credible and sufficient.
members.legal_principle: There is no rule that acquitting one accused on evidence open to doubt requires acquitting every accused. The remaining evidence must be scrutinized more closely, and conviction may stand if the court is assured that it is safe to rely on the credible evidence. The Court relied on Sat Kumar v. State of Haryana and Mohammed Moinuddin v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The doubt warranting one accused’s acquittal did not extend to the remaining accused, whose convictions were upheld.

predicates.one_accused_given_benefit_of_doubt: The court acquits or gives the benefit of doubt to one accused because of a defect specific to that accused.
predicates.credible_evidence_separately_proves_othe: The remaining credible evidence independently provides assurance of the other accused’s participation.

members.legal_issue: The acquittal of some accused does not by itself invalidate testimony against other accused when the witness’s account of the latter’s acts is independently supported.
material_facts: The eyewitness said that some of the other accused instigated the attackers.
The High Court acquitted those accused as a matter of abundant caution.
Medical evidence corroborated the account of the appellants’ acts but did not provide the same corroboration against the acquitted accused.
members.legal_principle: An acquittal of some persons implicated by a witness does not necessarily establish that the witness falsely implicated the remaining accused. The evidentiary basis may differ between accused, including where medical evidence corroborates the account against some but not others. The Court relied on no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The acquittal of the other accused did not require rejection of the eyewitness’s testimony against the appellants.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.witness_implicated_multiple_accused: A witness attributes acts or participation to more than one accused.
predicates.corroboration_differs_between_accused: Evidence corroborates the witness’s account against some accused more strongly than against others.

members.legal_issue: Credible and separable evidence against some accused may sustain their convictions even when other accused are acquitted on the same prosecution case.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted several accused but convicted the appellants.
The courts below identified distinguishing features in the evidence concerning the acquitted and convicted accused.
The appellants argued that the acquittals required their convictions to be set aside.
members.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a rule of law in India but a rule of caution; the court must assess the evidence and separate truth from falsehood where possible. A conviction can stand on the credible residue even if evidence against other accused is insufficient, provided the evidence can be separated without reconstructing an entirely new case. The Court relied on Nisar Alli v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1957 SC 366; Gurcharan Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1956 SC 460; Sohrab v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1972) 3 SCC 751; Ugar Ahir v. State of Bihar, AIR 1965 SC 277; Zwingle Ariel v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1954 SC 15; Balaka Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1962 SC; State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki, AIR 1981 SC 1390; Krishna Mochi v. State of Bihar, JT 2002 (4) SC 186; and Gangadhar Behera v. State of Orissa, (2002) 7 Supreme 276.
members.conclusion: The acquittals of other accused did not require the appellants’ convictions to be set aside because the evidence against the appellants was separately found sufficient and credible.

members.legal_issue: Credible eyewitness evidence against an accused need not be rejected merely because the same witnesses' evidence concerning other alleged participants is insufficient.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses consistently identified the accused as having fired the shot that caused the victim's death.
Other alleged participants were acquitted because the witnesses' accounts of their respective roles contained material contradictions, and those persons had no motive against the victim.
members.legal_principle: The reliability of evidence concerning each accused must be assessed in light of the part attributed to that person; discrepancies concerning other alleged participants do not automatically discredit evidence against the accused. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: The contradictions that justified acquitting the other alleged participants did not require rejection of the eyewitness evidence against the accused.

members.legal_issue: The acquittal of some accused does not require acquittal of another where the evidence against that person can be separated and assessed independently.
material_facts: The eyewitness identified one assailant but did not identify the other assailants.
The other accused were acquitted, while the evidence identifying the appellant as an assailant was accepted.
The Court considered whether the accepted portion of the eyewitness’s testimony could be separated from the portion insufficient to establish the guilt of the other accused.
members.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a rule of law in India but a rule of caution concerning the weight of evidence. A court must carefully screen the evidence and may separate reliable evidence from unreliable evidence; if truth and falsehood cannot be separated without reconstructing an entirely new case, the evidence must be discarded in toto. The Court relied on Nisar Alli v. State of Uttar Pradesh (AIR 1957 SC 366), Gurucharan Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1956 SC 460), Sahrab s/s Belli Nayata v. State of Madhya Pradesh ((1972) 3 SCC 751), Umar Ahir v. State of Bihar (AIR 1965 SC 277), Zwieolae Ariel v. State of Madhya Pradesh (AIR 1954 SC 15), Balaka Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1975 SC 1962), and State of Rajasthan v. Smt. Kalki (AIR 1981 SC 1390).
members.conclusion: The acquittal of the other accused did not require the appellant’s acquittal; the conviction could stand on the evidence accepted against him.

members.legal_issue: An acquittal in a group-violence murder case may be set aside for accused whose participation and shared unlawful object are established by reliable evidence, while retained for those not sufficiently linked to the crimes.
material_facts: Three people were killed during a group assault involving multiple assailants and different weapons.
Three eyewitnesses described the assault; two were searching for a missing animal, and the third was a young relative of the victims who had brought them food.
The High Court rejected the eyewitness accounts based on the witnesses’ presence, relationship to the victims, an alleged medical discrepancy, delay in reporting, and lack of proven motive.

The Supreme Court found those criticisms insufficient to discredit the witnesses’ accounts, but found reasonable doubt as to some accused because two were not named in the initial report and the evidence did not establish that two others shared the object of committing murder.
members.legal_principle: An appellate court ordinarily does not interfere with an acquittal, but may do so when the court below overlooked important facts and relied on circumstances that did not impair the probative value of the evidence. A chance witness is not necessarily incredible, though the evidence requires cautious and close scrutiny; relationship alone does not make a witness suspect; discrepancies about which assailant used which weapon are not necessarily fatal in a group assault; and where reliable eyewitness, medical, and prompt-report evidence proves the crimes, motive need not be established. The Court applied Sections 148 and 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. It referred generally to this Court’s repeated statements about related witnesses but named no earlier case.
members.conclusion: The acquittals were set aside and convictions for rioting and murder with a shared unlawful object were entered for the five accused whose participation was established. The acquittals of four others on those charges were upheld.

predicates.individual_participation_proved: The evidence sufficiently identified an accused as participating in the assault.
predicates.shared_unlawful_object_proved: The evidence established that an accused shared the group’s unlawful object to commit the crimes.

members.legal_issue: The acquittal of accused whose participation was consistently described and medically supported could be reversed, while an acquittal had to stand for accused whose individual participation remained in reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted all accused after accepting alibis and private defence, disbelieving the informant’s presence, and rejecting the eyewitnesses as partisan.
The appellate court found those findings unsustainable.
The informant’s presence was probable, the alibi evidence was unreliable, and the private-defence account was improbable.
The accounts assigning acts to three accused remained consistent, and medical evidence supported the weapons and injuries attributed to them.
The accounts concerning three other accused materially changed at trial, and the medical evidence did not resolve their individual participation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied sections 302, 326 and 324 read with section 34 of the Penal Code in place of section 149 for the three accused whose common intention and participation were proved. It found the evidence insufficient to sustain the charges against the other three. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The acquittals of three accused were unsustainable and their convictions were maintained, with their convictions altered to liability for acting in furtherance of common intention; the other three accused were acquitted because their guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

members.legal_issue: A court’s refusal to rely on an uncorroborated part of an approver’s account does not by itself make the approver unreliable or untruthful.
material_facts: The High Court declined to rely on the approver’s account of an earlier attempted shooting because it was not sufficiently corroborated and was not convincing.
The High Court did not find that the earlier-incident account was false.
The High Court accepted the approver’s account of the poisoning plot as reliable and corroborated.
members.legal_principle: The test of reliability concerns whether the approver’s evidence is inherently improbable or has been found false. Applying the caution required when assessing approver evidence under section 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and the approach in Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] SCR 953, a court may decline to act on a particular uncorroborated part without treating the witness as generally unreliable.
members.conclusion: Rejecting the earlier-incident account did not establish that the approver was unreliable or untruthful.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_approver: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution relies on an approver’s testimony.
predicates.approver_segment_excluded_for_lack_of_co: The court declines to rely on a part of the approver’s account because it lacks corroboration or is unconvincing.
predicates.no_finding_segment_false: The court does not find that the excluded part of the approver’s account is false.

members.legal_issue: Rejecting an uncorroborated and unconvincing part of an approver’s account does not, without more, make the approver unreliable as a witness overall.
material_facts: The High Court declined to rely on the approver’s account of an earlier attempted shooting because it lacked corroboration and was not convincing.
The High Court did not find that this account was false.
It found the approver’s account of the later poisoning plot reliable and corroborated in material particulars.
members.legal_principle: Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] S.C.R. 953, requires the court to assess whether an approver is a reliable witness and, separately, whether the approver’s evidence is sufficiently corroborated. Declining to act on one portion for want of corroboration or because it is unconvincing is not equivalent to finding the witness false or unreliable overall.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s rejection of the earlier episode did not make it wrong to rely on the approver’s evidence about the poisoning plot.

members.legal_issue: A prior identification parade is not indispensable when witnesses had repeated opportunities to see and recognize the accused before identifying him in court.
material_facts: Several witnesses had seen the accused on multiple occasions over a number of days before the crime and later identified him in court.
The accused argued that the court identifications were unreliable because no prior identification parade had been held.
The Court found that the witnesses' prior repeated exposure distinguished the case from cases involving a stranger seen only briefly.
members.legal_principle: Identification in court is substantive evidence, while a prompt identification parade ordinarily provides assurance and corroboration when the accused was previously unknown to the witness. The need for a parade may be dispensed with where the witness had repeated opportunities to see and recognize the accused. The Court considered Kanan v. State of Kerala and Mohanlal Gangaram Gehani v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The absence of an identification parade did not make the witnesses' identifications unreliable in these circumstances.

members.legal_issue: Defects in an identification parade do not require rejection of identification evidence independently supported by witnesses' direct observation of the accused during the incident.
material_facts: The prosecution did not establish adequate precautions to prevent witnesses from seeing the accused before the identification parade.
The evidence showed that the appellants were apprehended at the scene and that the witnesses had an opportunity to observe their features.
The second appellant was identified by most eyewitnesses at the parade; the court considered the parade evidence concerning the third accused unreliable.
members.legal_principle: A flawed identification parade may warrant reduced reliance on parade identification, but it does not necessarily defeat identification supported by direct observation at the incident. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The identification parade could not be given much weight in establishing the third accused's identity, but its defects did not justify rejecting the evidence concerning the appellants' participation, which was supported by the witnesses' opportunity to observe them at the scene.

members.legal_issue: A challenged declaration about an injured witness’s own assailant does not displace accepted eyewitness evidence of another assault when the declaration is unreliable and the remaining evidence independently supports the finding.
material_facts: A declaration by an injured witness attributed that witness’s injuries to one accused but did not provide a reliable basis to displace the evidence about the fatal assault.
The trial court did not rely on the declaration, and its recorder was not examined; the declaration indicated that the witness was not fully conscious.
The High Court found sufficient evidence from other eyewitnesses even excluding the challenged witness’s testimony, and the Supreme Court agreed.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the declaration’s reliability in light of the circumstances in which it was recorded and the independent eyewitness evidence. It cited no earlier case or separate statutory provision for this evidentiary assessment.
members.conclusion: The declaration did not justify discarding the accepted eyewitness evidence or overturning the murder convictions.

members.legal_issue: An independent witness’s evidence is not discredited merely because the witness’s presence is challenged as improbable or the witness implicated more accused persons than the appellate court ultimately found proved.
material_facts: A witness testified that he saw the attack on one deceased person while cutting grass near a river.
He explained that he went there because good grass was available at that location.
The witness identified all the accused as participants in the attack, but the High Court acquitted some of them because their names were absent from another injured person’s dying declaration.
That injured person was hovering between life and death when he made the declaration.
The witness was not shown to be friendly with the victims’ group or hostile to the accused.
members.legal_principle: A witness’s presence and credibility must be assessed in light of the explanation given and the circumstances of the evidence. The Court held that the availability of good grass answered the challenge to the witness’s presence, and that the omission of names from a declaration made by a person hovering between life and death did not invalidate the witness’s testimony.
members.conclusion: The criticisms did not provide a valid reason to reject the independent witness’s evidence about the attack.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance cannot be granted when the claimant's conduct shows that the claimant was not continuously ready and willing to perform the contract.
material_facts: The claimant issued a notice rescinding the contract and sought repayment of the advance rather than performance of the sale agreement.
The claimant pursued a suit for repayment of the advance and later sought specific performance.
The claimant's conduct did not show continuing readiness and willingness to perform the claimant's obligations under the agreement.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, including Explanation II, requires a claimant seeking specific performance to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, according to its true construction. The surrounding circumstances must show that readiness and willingness continued from the contract through the hearing. The Court also referred to Forms 47 and 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure as reflecting the required pleadings.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not ready and willing to perform the contract, so specific performance could not be granted and the suit was not maintainable.

members.legal_issue: A specific-performance claim lacks a cause of action when the plaintiff does not allege readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s part of the contract.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of the agreement but did not allege in the plaint that he was ready and willing to perform his part.
The plaintiff alleged instead that the agreement was the product of fraud and undue influence and was not binding on him.
members.legal_principle: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must allege readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s obligations under the contract. The Court relied on Ardeshir Mama v. Flora Sassoon, 55 I.A. 360, which recognized that requirement under Indian law as well as English law, and referred to Karsandas v. Chhotalal, 25 Bom. L.R. 1037. The Court also applied the principle that a party seeking enforcement treats the contract as subsisting and must establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff had no cause of action for specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A buyer who fails to perform within the agreed period and does not establish continuing readiness and willingness to perform is not entitled to specific performance of an immovable-property sale agreement.
material_facts: The agreement fixed a period for completing the sale and provided for a limited extension if required permissions were delayed.
The buyer did not pay the balance consideration or complete the sale within the stipulated and extended period.
The buyer's correspondence showed that he sought further time, and the evidence did not establish that he had the funds or arrangements to pay the balance consideration.
The trial court found that the buyer was not ready and willing to perform, but the first appellate court reversed that finding and granted specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, a plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove readiness and willingness to perform throughout the relevant period, assessed in light of the plaintiff's conduct and the surrounding circumstances. Under Section 55 of the Contract Act, time is not ordinarily of the essence in a sale of immovable property, but the parties' language, the agreement as a whole, and the circumstances may show an intention to require performance within a specified period. The Court applied Smt. Chand Rani v. Smt. Kamal Rani on time stipulations and N.P. Thirugnnam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao and P.R. Deb & Associates v. Sunanda Roy on readiness and willingness.
members.conclusion: The buyer failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform, and the first appellate court erred in granting specific performance; the denial of that relief was restored.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_sale_agreement and agreed_completion_period and buyer_failed_to_complete_within_applicable_period and buyer_did_not_prove_continuing_readiness

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_agreement: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property.
predicates.agreed_completion_period: The parties specified a period for completing the sale, including any agreed extension mechanism.
predicates.buyer_failed_to_complete_within_applicab: The buyer did not complete the required performance within the period fixed by the agreement, including any applicable extension.
predicates.buyer_did_not_prove_continuing_readiness: The buyer's conduct and evidence did not establish readiness and willingness to perform throughout the relevant period.

members.legal_issue: A buyer is not ready and willing to perform an agreement for specific performance when the buyer fails to make the required payment and makes payment conditional on performance of terms not required by the agreement.
material_facts: The buyer did not pay the required sum within the contractual period.
After the seller notified the buyer that payment was due, the buyer did not pay the sum.
The buyer’s notices and evidence showed that payment was being withheld until possession and other requirements were provided or completed.
The agreement did not make those requirements conditions precedent to that payment.
members.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness are assessed from the party’s conduct and the notices exchanged, not merely from an assertion that funds are available. A buyer who withholds a payment due under the agreement while insisting on an unsupported countercondition is not ready and willing to perform. The Court considered Nathulal v. Phoolchand but held that it did not apply to these facts.
members.conclusion: The buyer was not ready and willing to perform the contract and was not entitled to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and buyer_failed_to_make_required_payment and seller_notified_buyer_payment_was_due and buyer_conditioned_payment_on_uncontracted_requirements

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.buyer_failed_to_make_required_payment: The buyer did not make a payment required by the agreement.
predicates.seller_notified_buyer_payment_was_due: The seller informed the buyer that the required payment had not been made and was due.
predicates.buyer_conditioned_payment_on_uncontracte: The buyer made payment dependent on the seller first satisfying requirements that the agreement did not make conditions to payment.

members.legal_issue: A buyer is ready and willing to perform, and the seller is in breach, when the buyer offers payment in the manner required by the agreement but the seller insists on a different manner of payment.
material_facts: The buyer stated in correspondence that he remained ready to pay any requested amount, within the agreed limit, to the tax authorities as the agreement required.
The seller’s demand for a further amount was made directly to the buyer, and the seller did not establish that he had requested payment to the tax authorities under the agreement.
The seller did not proceed with the sale, while the buyer continued to seek completion of the transaction.
members.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness are assessed from the claimant’s overall conduct before and after suit, considered in light of the other party’s conduct; no fixed formula applies. The Court relied on J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao and the earlier decisions R.C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, and P. D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu.
members.conclusion: The buyer was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, and the seller defaulted by insisting on payment in a manner not required by the agreement.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.buyer_offered_contractual_payment: The buyer offered to make payment in the manner and to the recipient specified in the agreement.
predicates.seller_demanded_different_payment_recipi: The seller insisted that the buyer make payment to a recipient different from the one specified in the agreement.
predicates.seller_made_no_contractual_request_to_au: The seller did not request that the buyer make the payment to the authority identified in the agreement.

members.legal_issue: A vendee who fails to perform an essential contractual term and is not ready and willing to perform it may be denied specific performance, particularly where the vendee’s conduct makes enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The vendee took possession of the agricultural land under an obligation to pay customary rent after the delay exceeded one year.
The vendee paid no rent for approximately thirteen years before filing suit and denied liability to pay rent in his replication.
The vendee cultivated and benefited from the land, while the vendor received less than eighteen percent of its market value.
The vendee sought specific performance of the sale agreement.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, including Explanation (ii), requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the essential terms according to the contract’s true construction. Section 20, as applicable to the suit, makes specific performance discretionary and permits refusal where enforcement would be inequitable; Explanation (2) addresses when hardship is assessed. Section 51 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 was also considered in relation to reciprocal promises. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The vendee was not entitled to specific performance because he failed to perform an essential term, failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform it, and his conduct made the discretionary relief inequitable.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and rent_term_unperformed and no_readiness_or_willingness and prolonged_unpaid_occupation and inequitable_hardship

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.rent_term_unperformed: The plaintiff did not pay rent required by an essential term of the contract.
predicates.no_readiness_or_willingness: The plaintiff failed to prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the essential term.
predicates.prolonged_unpaid_occupation: The plaintiff retained and used the property for a prolonged period without paying the agreed rent.
predicates.inequitable_hardship: The plaintiff’s nonperformance and use of the property caused hardship to the other party and made enforcement inequitable.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who does not establish continuing readiness and willingness to perform the agreement is not entitled to discretionary specific performance, particularly where the claimant gives no explanation for a long delay in filing suit.
material_facts: The claimant issued a notice asserting readiness and willingness and relied on an affidavit said to show presence before the registering authority on the contractual performance date.
The claimant filed suit about three years after issuing the notice and gave no explanation for that delay.
The suit was initially framed as one for mandatory injunction and the trial court did not frame an issue on readiness and willingness.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the claimant to aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual obligations. Readiness and willingness must be assessed from the claimant’s conduct, including whether it continued through the institution of the suit. Section 20 makes specific performance discretionary, and the court treated the unexplained delay and the limited evidence of readiness as material to that discretion.
members.conclusion: The notice and affidavit did not establish that the claimant continued to be ready and willing when suit was filed; given the unexplained delay and the claimant’s conduct, the discretionary relief of specific performance was unavailable.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks, in substance, to compel performance of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.readiness_evidence_confined_to_contract_: The claimant’s evidence of readiness and willingness relates only to the contractual performance date and does not establish continuation of that readiness when suit is filed.
predicates.unexplained_delay_after_notice: The claimant waits a substantial period after asserting readiness in a notice before filing suit and gives no explanation for the delay.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who fails to complete a commercial sale of immovable property by an expressly essential deadline may be denied specific performance when the contract permits termination for that failure.
material_facts: The purchaser, which was engaged in building construction, agreed to buy land for a commercial transaction.

The agreement expressly made time essential, set a one-year period for completion, and provided for cancellation and return of the earnest money if the purchaser failed to complete within that period.
The purchaser was responsible for obtaining clearance for part of the land but failed to obtain it within the agreed period.
There was no evidence that the vendor delayed signing necessary applications or petitions.
After the deadline, the vendor cancelled the agreement and sent the earnest money back by cheque, which the purchaser refused to accept.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a defendant may raise a defence available under contract law; Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 makes a contract voidable at the promisee's option when a party fails to perform by the specified time and the parties intended time to be essential. Although time is not normally of the essence in contracts for the sale of immovable property, it may be essential where the agreement clearly says so, the transaction is commercial, and the other terms do not displace that intention. The Court relied on Jamshed Khodaram Irani v. Burjorji Dhunjibhai, Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Palaniswami Nadar, K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, and M/s. Hind Construction Contractors v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The vendor was entitled to terminate the contract, and the purchaser was not entitled to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_sale and commercial_transaction and express_essential_deadline and purchaser_failed_deadline and contract_provided_cancellation and not vendor_caused_delay and not terms_negated_deadline

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.immovable_property_sale: The contract concerns the sale of immovable property.
predicates.commercial_transaction: The purchaser entered into the transaction for a commercial purpose.
predicates.express_essential_deadline: The parties expressly agreed that completion by a specified deadline was essential.
predicates.purchaser_failed_deadline: The purchaser failed to complete its required performance by the agreed deadline.
predicates.contract_provided_cancellation: The contract provided for cancellation if the purchaser failed to complete on time.
predicates.vendor_caused_delay: The vendor delayed the purchaser's performance or the steps needed to complete it.
predicates.terms_negated_deadline: Other contract terms displaced the stated intention that the deadline was essential.

members.legal_issue: A court may refuse specific performance when the contract makes timely completion essential and the purchaser fails to perform within the stipulated time, particularly where the seller urgently needs payment.
material_facts: The agreement required the draft sale deed to be finalized within seven days and the sale deed to be registered within the stipulated period.
The seller urgently needed cash for his daughter’s marriage and insisted on cash payment.
The purchaser did not complete the sale within the stipulated time.
The High Court refused specific performance, and the Supreme Court found that it had exercised its discretion soundly.
members.legal_principle: The court treated execution of the sale deed within the stipulated period as an essential contractual term in light of the seller’s urgent need for cash. Specific performance is discretionary, and the High Court’s sound exercise of judicial discretion in refusing relief was upheld. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The stipulated time was essential in the circumstances, and the High Court was right to refuse specific performance; the challenge to that refusal was dismissed.

rule.if: challenge_to_refusal_of_specific_performance and contract_made_timely_completion_essential and purchaser_missed_stipulated_deadline and seller_needed_prompt_payment

predicates.challenge_to_refusal_of_specific_perform: A party challenged a court’s refusal to order specific performance.
predicates.contract_made_timely_completion_essentia: The contract and surrounding circumstances made completion within the stipulated time essential.
predicates.purchaser_missed_stipulated_deadline: The purchaser failed to complete the required performance within the stipulated time.
predicates.seller_needed_prompt_payment: The seller had an urgent need for prompt payment.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who fails to pay the balance of the sale price within the period expressly agreed in a sale contract has not performed the contract as agreed, making a decree of specific performance on that basis erroneous.
material_facts: The sale agreement required the purchaser to pay the balance consideration within nine months.
The purchaser did not pay the balance within that period and issued a demand for a sale deed only after the period had expired.
The purchaser argued that payment depended on the sellers first measuring the property, but the Court rejected that argument.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the agreed payment period was relevant to the purchaser’s performance and that the clause fell within the first part of Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963. It considered Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, but applied the principle that whether time is of the essence depends on construction of the contract as a whole. It relied on Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Palaniswami Nadar, Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, and Hind Construction Contractors v. State of Maharashtra; the latter authorities explain that contractual provisions may affect whether a time stipulation is fundamental.
members.conclusion: The purchaser had not adhered to the agreed payment period, and the lower courts’ decision granting specific performance was contrary to the agreement and the evidence.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract for the sale of property.
predicates.fixed_payment_deadline: The sale contract set a time by which the buyer had to pay the balance of the sale price.
predicates.buyer_missed_deadline: The buyer did not pay the balance of the sale price within the time set by the contract.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser’s failure to meet expressly fixed payment dates may justify cancellation and defeat specific performance when the agreement makes payment time essential and the payment schedule was not varied.
material_facts: The agreement required payment of the balance price in specified instalments and expressly made payment on the due dates essential, with cancellation available for default.
The purchaser missed part of the second instalment and the entire final instalment.
The courts found that the parties had not agreed to postpone the instalments until the sellers produced original title documents.
The agreement made the timing of the sale deed depend on the purchaser’s convenience but did not make the payment schedule depend on further title review.
members.legal_principle: Section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872 governs failure to perform at a fixed time when time is essential. For sales of immovable property, time is generally presumed not to be essential, but that presumption may be displaced by the contract’s express terms and circumstances. Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, relying on Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Pallaniswami Nadar and Govind Prasad Chaturvedi v. Hari Dutt Shastri, states that fixing a performance period alone is insufficient, but unequivocal terms may make time essential. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan supports giving significance to stipulated periods, applying greater scrutiny to readiness and willingness, and not treating the limitation period as permission to delay. The Court noted that rising property values and prolonged litigation make mechanical reliance on the general presumption inappropriate, while leaving a general reconsideration of the rule for another case. N. Srinivasa v. Kuttukaran Machine Tools Ltd. was distinguished as a conclusion based on that contract’s terms, not a categorical rule that time can never be essential.
members.conclusion: The sellers were justified in cancelling the agreement, and the purchaser was not entitled to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and payment_dates_fixed and payment_time_made_essential and purchaser_missed_due_payments and no_agreed_payment_variation

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.payment_dates_fixed: The agreement set dates for payment of the balance price.
predicates.payment_time_made_essential: The agreement stated that payment on the specified dates was essential and provided for cancellation on default.
predicates.purchaser_missed_due_payments: The purchaser failed to pay some or all instalments when due.
predicates.no_agreed_payment_variation: The parties did not agree to change the payment schedule.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who is unable or unwilling to make an essential part payment within the agreed or reasonable time is not entitled to specific performance of an immovable-property sale contract.
material_facts: The sale agreement required the purchaser to pay a substantial part of the price within five months, stated that time was of the essence, and provided that this payment was not earnest money.

The seller explained that she needed the payment to obtain alternative accommodation before delivering vacant possession and, after the payment deadline passed, gave the purchaser a further short period to pay.

The purchaser did not pay and stated that he could not raise the money unless the seller first made a separate agreement with a proposed cooperative housing society. The agreement did not make that separate agreement a condition precedent to payment.
The proposed society was never registered, and there was no evidence that the purchaser had the money or could pay within a reasonable time.

The trial court found that the purchaser was not ready and willing to perform the agreement, but the High Court granted specific performance. The purchaser also failed to make the payments required by the High Court's decree within its specified period.
members.legal_principle: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must be ready and willing to perform the plaintiff's part of the contract at all material times. Although time is not ordinarily of the essence in a contract for sale of immovable property, the parties' intention that performance occur within a reasonable time may be inferred from the express terms, the nature of the property, and the surrounding circumstances. The Court applied Chand Rani (Smt.) (Dead) by Lrs. v. Kamal Rani (Smt.) (Dead) by Lrs. (1993) 1 SCC 519, which considered those principles and readiness and willingness, and Parakunnan Veetill Joseph's Son Mathew v. Nedumbara Kuruvila's Son, (1987) Supp SCC 340, which requires careful consideration of the facts and circumstances so that specific performance is not used oppressively to secure an unfair advantage.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was not ready and willing to perform the agreement, and specific performance would be unfair and unreasonable. The High Court's decree was set aside and the trial court's dismissal of the suit was restored.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and immovable_property_sale_contract and substantial_part_payment_due_by_fixed_time and contract_or_circumstances_made_payment_time_critical and purchaser_unable_to_pay_within_reasonable_time and purchaser_conditioned_payment_on_unformed_society_agreement and seller_needed_payment_for_alternative_housing

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking an order requiring the seller to complete a property sale.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_contract: The parties made a contract for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.substantial_part_payment_due_by_fixed_ti: The contract required the purchaser to make a substantial part payment by a specified time.
predicates.contract_or_circumstances_made_payment_t: The contract's terms and the circumstances surrounding performance made timely payment important to completion.
predicates.purchaser_unable_to_pay_within_reasonabl: The purchaser did not have, and was not shown to be able to obtain, the required payment within a reasonable time.
predicates.purchaser_conditioned_payment_on_unforme: The purchaser made payment dependent on a separate agreement with a proposed society that was never formed.
predicates.seller_needed_payment_for_alternative_ho: The seller needed the payment to obtain alternative accommodation in order to perform the obligation to deliver vacant possession.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser’s failure to pay the balance of the auction price within the required period, absent a court or tribunal order preventing payment, makes confirmation of the sale illegal.
material_facts: The purchaser deposited 15 percent of the sale price at the auction.
The balance was not deposited within 30 days after the auction; it was deposited after the sale had been confirmed and more than a year after the auction.
No court or tribunal order preventing payment within the period was identified.
The purchaser argued that the delay followed protracted correspondence and that the authority’s acceptance of the late payment made confirmation lawful.
members.legal_principle: Section 36 of the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894 requires the balance of the sale consideration to be remitted within 30 days of the auction. The purchaser is obliged to pay within that period unless prevented by an order of a court or tribunal; non-compliance makes the earnest deposit liable to forfeiture, and confirmation without compliance is illegal. No earlier cases are cited for this holding.
members.conclusion: The balance had to be paid within 30 days unless a court or tribunal order prevented payment. The failure to do so made the deposit liable to forfeiture and confirmation of the sale illegal; the sale was vitiated and was rightly set aside.

predicates.revenue_recovery_auction: The proceeding involved a public auction of a debtor’s property to recover a debt through a revenue recovery process.
predicates.purchaser_missed_balance_deadline: The auction purchaser did not pay the balance of the sale price within the period required by the governing procedure.
predicates.no_judicial_bar_to_payment: No court or tribunal order prevented the purchaser from paying the balance within the required period.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who fails to pay the balance of an auction price within a mandatory deadline does not acquire an interest in the decree-holder’s property through that auction.
material_facts: The first respondent was the highest bidder at an auction of immovable property and paid the required initial portion of the bid.
The applicable auction rules required the balance to be paid within a fixed period and provided for forfeiture and resale upon default.
The first respondent paid the balance years after the deadline.
The municipal officer later accepted the delayed payment and issued a sale certificate, which the first respondent relied on to seek substitution in execution.
members.legal_principle: Rules 8(2) and 8(3) and Rule 13 of the Maharashtra Municipalities (Sale of Distrained or Attached Movable and Immovable Property) Rules, 1967, require timely payment and do not authorize acceptance of a late payment. The Court applied the analogous requirements in Order 21 Rules 84 and 85 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rule in Manilal Mohanlal Shah v. Sardar Syed Ahmed Sayed Mohammed that non-compliance with those requirements renders a sale void. Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh and Sardar Govindrao Mahadid v. Devi Sahai did not assist the purchaser because they concerned a sale validly held.
members.conclusion: The payment deadline was mandatory, the sale became void when the balance was not paid in time, and the first respondent did not acquire the decree-holder’s interest by operation of law.

rule.if: execution_substitution_claim and immovable_property_auction and sale_rules_fixed_payment_deadline and purchaser_paid_balance_late

predicates.execution_substitution_claim: A person sought substitution as the successor to a decree-holder’s interest in execution proceedings.
predicates.immovable_property_auction: The claimed interest arose from an auction of immovable property.
predicates.sale_rules_fixed_payment_deadline: The rules governing the auction required the balance price to be paid within a fixed period and prescribed consequences for failure to pay in time.
predicates.purchaser_paid_balance_late: The purchaser paid the balance price only after the required payment period had expired.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser’s failure to pay the balance of the purchase price within the prescribed time renders a revenue auction sale void.
material_facts: Land was sold at a revenue auction to recover an amount treated as arrears of land revenue.
The auction purchasers paid the required initial deposit on the day of the auction.
They paid the balance after the prescribed payment period had expired.
The authorities accepted the late payment, confirmed the sale, and issued a sale certificate.
members.legal_principle: Sections 85, 86 and 88 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 impose mandatory requirements for the initial deposit and payment of the balance within the prescribed period. Applying Manilal Mohanlal Shah v. Sardar Sayed Ahmed Sayed Mahamad, which construed the analogous requirements in Order XXI Rules 84, 85 and 86 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court held that non-compliance leaves no sale in law, forfeits the purchaser’s claim to the property, and requires resale. The authorities have no discretion to extend the payment time or validate the sale by accepting late payment or confirming it.
members.conclusion: The balance-payment requirement was mandatory, and the late payment rendered the sale void; the subsequent confirmation and sale certificate conferred no title on the purchasers.

predicates.revenue_recovery_auction: The property was sold at an auction conducted to recover an amount treated as public revenue arrears.
predicates.initial_deposit_paid: The purchaser paid the required initial deposit after being declared the successful bidder.
predicates.balance_paid_after_deadline: The purchaser paid the remaining purchase price after the required payment period had expired.

members.legal_issue: Failure to pay the balance of an auction premium by the extended deadline cancels the conditional allotment, and an unregistered long-term lease does not confer title.
material_facts: The auction purchaser paid only part of the premium and did not pay the balance within the additional three months allowed.
The extension expressly provided that the allotment would be cancelled if the balance was not paid within that period.
No registered lease deed was executed, and the purchaser did not pay rent or obtain possession.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 79 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, the statutory requirements for disposal of municipal property had to be fulfilled; under Section 17 of the Registration Act, a lease for a term exceeding one year required a registered instrument. The Court relied on The Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Co-operative Society Ltd. v.
