predicates.plaintiff_made_substantial_payments: The plaintiff paid a substantial part of the agreed consideration before completion of the sale.
predicates.plaintiff_pursued_completion_promptly: The plaintiff took steps to complete the transaction and brought suit promptly after the seller refused or the agreed performance date passed.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser’s financial readiness to perform may be shown by the ability to raise the required funds and does not necessarily require possession of the money or a completed financing arrangement, but the purchaser must prove that ability.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed that she would obtain the balance of the consideration by selling ornaments but did not testify to establish that claim.
The purchaser did not make the required payment when first directed and sought extensions and further orders before eventually depositing the balance.
The record did not establish that the purchaser had sufficient assets or another demonstrated means to obtain the funds when performance was required.
members.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness in a specific-performance claim include the ability to meet the financial obligation, but the plaintiff need not already possess the money or prove a concluded financing scheme if able to raise it when performance is due. Jitendra Nath Roy v. Smt. Maheshwari Bose and Bank of India Ltd. v. Jamsetji A. H. Chinoy were considered.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to establish that she could meet the financial obligation, supporting the finding that she was not ready and willing to perform.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and financial_performance_required and ability_to_raise_funds_not_proved and repeated_failure_to_pay_when_required

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff asked a court to compel performance of a contract.
predicates.financial_performance_required: Performance required the plaintiff to pay money.
predicates.ability_to_raise_funds_not_proved: The plaintiff did not establish that the required money could be obtained when performance was due.
predicates.repeated_failure_to_pay_when_required: The plaintiff failed to pay when directed and sought further time or orders before paying.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance of a contract requiring payment must prove continuous readiness and willingness, including the ability to pay or timely arrange the balance consideration.
material_facts: The purchaser alleged an agreement to buy immovable property and pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform.
The agreement required payment of the balance consideration by a specified date, but the purchaser gave no cogent evidence that he had funds or timely arrangements to obtain them.
The purchaser’s financial records showed that he lacked sufficient funds when performance was due.
The purchaser deposited the balance consideration in court only years after the contractual performance date.
The lower courts relied on a general observation about the purchaser’s business and presumed sources of funds without adequately examining the evidence of his financial capacity.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as it stood before the 2018 amendment, a plaintiff must plead and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, except terms prevented or waived by the defendant. Under the explanations to Section 16(c), actual tender or court deposit is generally unnecessary, but the plaintiff must show that funds were available or could be arranged in time. Readiness concerns capacity, including financial capacity; willingness concerns conduct. The assessment considers the plaintiff’s conduct and the evidence throughout the proceedings, and a later court deposit alone does not prove readiness at the time performance was due. The Court relied on Man Kaur v. Hartar Singh Sangha, Pt. Prem Raj v. D.L.F. Housing and Construction (Private) Ltd., N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan, His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, and Kalawati v. Rakesh Kumar.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness, particularly his readiness to pay the balance consideration, and was not entitled to specific performance. The lower courts’ decrees granting that relief were set aside.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and monetary_obligation_due and (insufficient_funds_at_performance_time or no_proof_of_funds_or_timely_arrangements) and not continuous_readiness_proven

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser seeks an order requiring completion of an agreement to sell.
predicates.monetary_obligation_due: The purchaser's contractual performance requires payment of the remaining purchase money by the time fixed for performance.
predicates.insufficient_funds_at_performance_time: The evidence shows that the purchaser lacked sufficient funds when payment was due.
predicates.no_proof_of_funds_or_timely_arrangements: The purchaser provides no cogent evidence that funds were available or could be arranged in time to make the required payment.
predicates.continuous_readiness_proven: The purchaser establishes by evidence continuous readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser's essential contractual obligations.

members.legal_issue: A buyer seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential contractual obligations, assessed from financial capacity and conduct.
material_facts: The agreement required the buyer to pay the balance consideration within six months and required the sellers, upon receiving it, to execute a sale deed free from encumbrances.
The buyer did not pay or indicate willingness to pay the balance by the contractual deadline and produced no timely communication asking the sellers to clear the mortgage or complete the sale.

The buyer’s first demand for performance came in response to the sellers’ notice rescinding the contract; the buyer first sought an injunction against alienation and filed the specific-performance suit about three years after the contractual deadline.
The buyer relied on bank passbooks for accounts opened after the contractual period and did not produce evidence that he had funds to pay the balance during that period.
The trial court did not frame an issue on readiness and willingness and relied on the buyer’s asserted means without adequately examining his conduct or the contract terms.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the plaintiff to plead and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform essential contractual terms; the plaintiff bears the burden, and actual tender or deposit is generally unnecessary unless directed by the court. Readiness concerns financial capacity, while willingness is assessed from conduct and surrounding circumstances. The court relied on JP Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao, His Holiness Acharya Swami Ganesh Dassji v. Sita Ram Thapar, Atma Ram v. Charanjit Singh, and P. Meenakshisundaram v. P. Vijayakumar.
members.conclusion: The buyer failed to prove that he had continuously been ready and willing to perform the contract, so he was not entitled to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and contract_made_balance_payment_precede_sale_deed and buyer_did_not_offer_balance_by_deadline and buyer_did_not_urge_seller_to_complete_in_time and buyer_lacked_contemporaneous_proof_of_funds and buyer_delayed_specific_performance_action

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.contract_made_balance_payment_precede_sa: The agreement required the buyer to pay the balance before the seller had to execute the sale deed free of encumbrances.
predicates.buyer_did_not_offer_balance_by_deadline: The buyer neither paid nor indicated willingness to pay the balance by the time fixed for performance.
predicates.buyer_did_not_urge_seller_to_complete_in: The buyer did not timely communicate with the seller to request completion of the sale or clearance of the encumbrance.
predicates.buyer_lacked_contemporaneous_proof_of_fu: The buyer produced no evidence showing financial capacity to pay the balance during the contractual period.
predicates.buyer_delayed_specific_performance_actio: The buyer sought an injunction against alienation before later bringing a specific-performance claim, and did not bring that claim until well after the contractual deadline.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s essential contractual obligations, and the court may refuse the discretionary remedy when the purchaser’s capacity and conduct do not establish that readiness and willingness.
material_facts: The plaintiff agreed to purchase a house, paid an advance, and took possession as a tenant pending execution of the sale deed.
The plaintiff did not pay a further contracted advance intended to discharge a mortgage debt; that amount was adjusted toward rent with consent.
The plaintiff failed to pay rent as agreed and had substantial rent arrears.
The plaintiff had limited funds and other financial obligations, and the courts found that he lacked the means to complete the purchase.
Although a witness offered to lend the plaintiff money, the witness did not have the money available and would have had to raise it by mortgaging property.
After being directed to deposit the required amount or furnish a bank guarantee, the plaintiff did neither.
The trial court found that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform, and the appellate court affirmed that finding.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a plaintiff seeking specific performance must plead and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract that the plaintiff must perform, except terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the defendant. Readiness and willingness are assessed from the plaintiff’s conduct before and after filing suit and the attending circumstances; the consideration must be shown to have been available, although the plaintiff need not keep the money physically on hand if the plaintiff has the capacity to raise it. Under Section 20, specific performance is an equitable discretionary remedy and is not automatic merely because a valid agreement exists. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff failed to establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract, so the refusal of specific performance was upheld and the special leave petition was dismissed.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and (funding_capacity_unproved or failed_funding_direction) and contractual_obligations_unperformed

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.funding_capacity_unproved: The purchaser’s evidence and financial circumstances did not establish the capacity to raise the funds required to complete the purchase.
predicates.failed_funding_direction: The purchaser did not deposit the required funds or provide the requested security after the court directed the purchaser to do so.
predicates.contractual_obligations_unperformed: The purchaser failed to perform material contractual obligations, including payment obligations, and the purchaser’s conduct did not show continuing readiness to perform.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, including the capacity to pay the balance consideration.
material_facts: The purchaser relied on a certificate showing his presence before the Sub-Registrar on the contractual execution date, but produced no further evidence of his continuing ability to pay the balance consideration.
The sellers sent registered notices requiring execution of the sale deed, and the purchaser did not establish that he had received or responded to them.
The purchaser did not deposit the balance consideration within the time allowed by the trial court and offered no explanation for that failure.

He sought an extension only after the deadline, saying that the money would otherwise lie in a bank without earning interest; he did not plead special circumstances preventing payment or state that he remained ready and willing.
There was no stay of the decree during the appeal, and the purchaser waited for the appeal’s outcome rather than depositing the balance consideration.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(1)(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 bars specific performance unless the plaintiff avers and proves performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms. Readiness includes capacity to pay, and conduct must be assessed in light of all the pleadings, evidence, and surrounding circumstances. An extension under Section 28 does not by itself establish readiness and willingness; the plaintiff must show sufficient grounds and, where relevant, special circumstances beyond his control. The Court relied on V.S. Palanichamy Chettiar Firm v. C. Alagappan, (1999) 4 SCC 702, Umabai v. Nilkanth Dhondiba Chavan, (2005) 6 SCC 243, and Ramankutty Guptan v. Avara, (1994) 2 SCC 642.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform his obligations, so he was not entitled to specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and no_balance_deposit_without_explanation and extension_sought_after_deadline and weak_extension_reason and no_special_circumstances and no_stay_pending_appeal

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.no_balance_deposit_without_explanation: The purchaser did not pay the balance consideration within the time allowed and gave no explanation for that failure.
predicates.extension_sought_after_deadline: The purchaser sought more time to pay only after the payment deadline had passed.
predicates.weak_extension_reason: The purchaser relied on a reason that did not explain an inability to pay, such as preferring not to have the money remain in a bank without interest.
predicates.no_special_circumstances: The purchaser did not identify circumstances beyond his control that prevented timely payment.
predicates.no_stay_pending_appeal: No appellate order stayed the decree or prevented the purchaser from paying while the appeal was pending.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must establish both the capacity and the willingness to perform the purchaser’s obligations.
material_facts: The agreement required payment of the consideration in cash and contemplated execution of the sale deed within a short stipulated period.
The seller was in urgent need of cash, but the purchaser did not offer the cash payment.
The purchaser did not timely return the approved draft sale deed or complete the steps needed to finalize the sale deed.
The purchaser produced no documentary proof that sufficient funds were available; the account evidence later produced showed funds below the required amount.
The High Court found that the purchaser was not ready and willing to perform, and the Supreme Court agreed.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to prove readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract. Readiness concerns capacity to perform, including financial capacity; willingness is assessed from the plaintiff’s conduct and the surrounding circumstances. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The purchaser did not prove readiness and willingness to perform the contract and was therefore not entitled to specific performance.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser sought a court order compelling performance of a contract.
predicates.purchaser_lacked_financial_capacity: The purchaser lacked, or failed to establish, the financial capacity to meet the payment obligation.
predicates.purchaser_failed_willing_conduct: The purchaser’s conduct, including failure to make the required payment or timely complete required steps, did not show willingness to perform.
predicates.purchaser_failed_readiness_and_willingne: The purchaser did not establish the required readiness and willingness to perform.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who has performed the purchaser’s obligations and established readiness and willingness to pay the balance is entitled to specific performance under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
material_facts: The purchaser paid the earnest money and part of the purchase price.
The purchaser sent a notice expressing readiness and willingness to pay the balance of the consideration, and the vendor acknowledged the notice.
The trial court and the appellate court found that the purchaser had performed her part and fulfilled the requirements of Section 16(c).
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the claimant to establish performance, or continuous readiness and willingness to perform, the essential contractual obligations required of that claimant. The court upheld the findings that the purchaser had performed her part and had conveyed readiness and willingness to pay the balance.
members.conclusion: The purchaser satisfied Section 16(c) and was entitled to the decree for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_paid_earnest_money and purchaser_notified_readiness_to_pay_balance and seller_acknowledged_readiness_notice

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_paid_earnest_money: The purchaser paid the earnest money and part of the purchase price.
predicates.purchaser_notified_readiness_to_pay_bala: The purchaser sent a notice conveying readiness and willingness to pay the remaining consideration.
predicates.seller_acknowledged_readiness_notice: The vendor acknowledged the purchaser’s notice of readiness and willingness.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who remains ready and willing to perform, takes steps to complete a sale, and is prevented from completing it by the sellers’ evasion is entitled to specific performance.
material_facts: The purchaser was a long-standing tenant of the property and paid earnest money under the agreement to buy it.
Before the completion period expired, the purchaser sent letters and notices seeking execution of the sale deed, offered to pay the balance and outstanding rent, and attended the registrar’s office.
The evidence accepted by the Court showed that the purchaser had sufficient funds to complete the transaction.
The Court found that the sellers evaded their responsibility to execute the sale deed.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the correspondence, the purchaser’s efforts to complete the transaction, and the evidence of available funds, and concluded that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform while the sellers evaded performance. It restored the trial court’s decree for specific performance. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this determination.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was always ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, the sellers evaded their responsibility, and the decree for specific performance was restored.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_remained_ready_and_willing and purchaser_took_steps_to_complete and purchaser_had_sufficient_funds and sellers_evaded_execution

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.purchaser_remained_ready_and_willing: The purchaser remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations under the contract.
predicates.purchaser_took_steps_to_complete: The purchaser took steps to complete the transaction, such as requesting execution or attending to registration.
predicates.purchaser_had_sufficient_funds: The purchaser had sufficient funds to perform the purchaser’s payment obligations.
predicates.sellers_evaded_execution: The sellers evaded their responsibility to execute the sale documents.

members.legal_issue: The purchaser established continuous readiness and willingness to perform the sale agreement for purposes of obtaining specific performance.
material_facts: The courts found that the purchaser was in a position to raise the funds needed to perform the agreement.
The time to complete the sale had been extended beyond the date on which the sellers purported to terminate the agreement.
The purchaser brought the specific-performance suit soon after the purported termination and continued to assert the agreement rather than abandon it.
There was no evidence that the post-dated cheque had been dishonoured, and the courts found no unreasonable delay in payment.
members.legal_principle: Under section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, a purchaser seeking specific performance must establish readiness and willingness to fulfil the agreement. It is sufficient to show that the purchaser remained ready and willing to fulfil its terms, did not abandon the contract, and kept it subsisting. The Court relied on Nannapaneni Subayya Chowdary v. Garikapati Veeraya.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was ready and willing to perform the agreement, and the courts below were right to decree specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_could_raise_required_funds and purchaser_did_not_abandon_contract and purchaser_sued_promptly_after_termination and no_unreasonable_payment_delay

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.purchaser_could_raise_required_funds: The purchaser was in a position to obtain the funds needed to perform the agreement.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_abandon_contract: The purchaser continued to assert the agreement and did not abandon it.
predicates.purchaser_sued_promptly_after_terminatio: The purchaser brought suit soon after the seller purported to terminate the agreement.
predicates.no_unreasonable_payment_delay: The evidence did not establish unreasonable delay in payment or dishonour of the tendered post-dated cheque.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser’s continuous readiness and willingness to perform a sale agreement is assessed from the pleadings, evidence, conduct, and surrounding circumstances, including whether the purchaser had the capacity to pay and whether the seller prevented performance.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded that it had always been and remained ready and willing to perform the agreement.
The purchaser produced evidence that it prepared a demand draft for a payment due under the agreement and offered that payment to the seller, who refused it.
The seller denied the agreement and did not permit the purchaser to take possession or proceed with the contemplated development, and the courts found that this prevented further performance.
The trial court found that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform, and the seller did not appeal or cross-object against that finding.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform essential contractual terms, except terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the defendant. Readiness and willingness are not assessed by a straitjacket formula but by considering the party’s conduct and the surrounding circumstances; the purchaser’s capacity, including financial capacity to pay, is relevant. The Court relied on R.C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, (1970) 3 SCC 140; D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, (2004) 6 SCC 649; N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, (1995) 5 SCC 115; and J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao, (2011) 1 SCC 429.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform was supported by the evidence and was properly upheld.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and purchaser_pleaded_continuous_readiness and purchaser_proved_tender_of_due_payment and seller_refused_tender and seller_prevented_subsequent_performance

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The proceeding sought enforcement of an agreement to sell by specific performance.
predicates.purchaser_pleaded_continuous_readiness: The purchaser pleaded that it had always been and remained ready and willing to perform its contractual obligations.
predicates.purchaser_proved_tender_of_due_payment: The purchaser produced evidence that it prepared and offered a payment due under the agreement.
predicates.seller_refused_tender: The seller refused to accept the offered payment.
predicates.seller_prevented_subsequent_performance: The seller’s conduct prevented the purchaser from proceeding with later contractual performance.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance may be found ready and willing where the evidence supports the purchaser’s financial capacity and the alleged abandonment of the contract is not proved.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded that he had always been ready and willing to perform the agreement.
Two witnesses supported his evidence that he had sufficient means to purchase the property.
The seller’s allegation that the purchaser had said she could sell the property to someone else was not established by evidence.
The trial court found the purchaser ready and willing, while the High Court relied on delay and lack of steps to perform to reach the opposite conclusion.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed readiness and willingness from the pleadings and evidence, including evidence of financial capacity and whether the alleged abandonment of the contract was proved. It cited no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this issue.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s finding that the purchaser was not ready and willing was perverse and contrary to the evidence; the trial court’s finding was restored.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and purchaser_claimed_readiness_and_willingness and evidence_supported_financial_capacity and alleged_abandonment_was_not_proved

predicates.specific_performance_claim: A purchaser sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.purchaser_claimed_readiness_and_willingn: The purchaser pleaded that he was ready and willing to perform his contractual obligations.
predicates.evidence_supported_financial_capacity: Witness evidence supported that the purchaser had the means to complete the purchase.
predicates.alleged_abandonment_was_not_proved: The seller’s allegation that the purchaser had given up the contract or permitted a sale to another person was not established by evidence.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must prove personal readiness and willingness through competent evidence, and an agent without personal knowledge cannot ordinarily prove the purchaser’s state of mind or conduct.
material_facts: The purchaser did not testify about his readiness and willingness to complete the sale.

The agent who testified for the purchaser was appointed after the relevant events and acknowledged that he had no personal knowledge of the transaction or of the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.
A different agent had negotiated and executed the agreement, and that agent was not examined.

The property dealer’s evidence could not establish the purchaser’s personal finances or intentions, and the facts did not establish that the purchaser’s affairs were entirely managed by an agent in a way that justified the recognized exception.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires both pleading and proof that the plaintiff performed or was always ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract. Readiness and willingness concern the purchaser’s state of mind, conduct, capacity, and preparedness. Under Order III, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an agent may testify about acts or transactions within the agent’s personal knowledge, but ordinarily cannot testify in place of the principal about matters known personally only to the principal. The Court relied on N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, Pushparani S. Sundaram v. Pauline Manomani James, Manjunath Anandappa v. Tammanasa, Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v. Indusind Bank Ltd., and Shankar Finance & Investments v. State of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to prove readiness and willingness as required for specific performance, and the suit for that relief had to fail.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and principal_did_not_testify_on_readiness and testifying_agent_lacked_personal_knowledge and transaction_agent_was_not_examined and not exclusive_agent_management_exception

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.principal_did_not_testify_on_readiness: The purchaser did not give evidence about the purchaser’s own readiness and willingness to perform.
predicates.testifying_agent_lacked_personal_knowled: The agent who testified lacked personal knowledge of the relevant transaction or the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.
predicates.transaction_agent_was_not_examined: The agent who handled the relevant transaction was not examined as a witness.
predicates.exclusive_agent_management_exception: The purchaser’s affairs were entirely managed by an agent in circumstances that could justify accepting the agent’s evidence about the purchaser’s readiness and willingness.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance must establish readiness and willingness through evidence competent to prove the purchaser’s own knowledge and capacity to perform.
material_facts: The purchaser did not enter the witness box to testify about readiness and willingness or the ability to pay the balance of the price.
The purchaser’s power-of-attorney holder was appointed after the relevant events and lacked personal knowledge of them.
Apart from an assertion in the plaint, no evidence was led to establish readiness and willingness or capacity to perform.
members.legal_principle: Under Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v. Indusind Bank Ltd., a power-of-attorney holder may testify about acts performed by that holder but cannot testify for the principal about the principal’s acts or matters within the principal’s personal knowledge. Under Vidhyadhar v. Manikrao, a party’s failure to testify and submit to cross-examination may support an adverse presumption that the party’s case is incorrect. Applying those principles, the absence of competent evidence of readiness and willingness meant the purchaser had not established entitlement to discretionary specific performance.
members.conclusion: The purchaser failed to establish readiness and willingness, and was not entitled to discretionary specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and purchaser_did_not_testify_personally and agent_lacked_personal_knowledge and no_independent_readiness_evidence

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_testify_personally: The purchaser did not testify about the purchaser’s own readiness, willingness, or ability to perform.
predicates.agent_lacked_personal_knowledge: The purchaser’s agent lacked personal knowledge of the relevant events or matters personal to the purchaser.
predicates.no_independent_readiness_evidence: No other evidence was presented to support the purchaser’s readiness and willingness to perform.

members.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance of a sale agreement requires proof of a concluded, valid and enforceable contract, and the discretionary remedy must be granted according to judicial principles after considering the evidence and circumstances.
material_facts: The claim for specific performance rested on a written sale agreement that referred to an earlier agreement, but the earlier agreement was neither produced nor exhibited.
The trial court found that the later agreement and payment of consideration had not been proved; the High Court reversed that finding and granted specific performance.
The High Court relied in part on a criminal court’s observations about the agreement, while not considering documents from earlier proceedings that bore on the claim concerning possession.

The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not properly considered the evidence and circumstances relevant to whether the alleged agreement was proved and whether specific performance was appropriate.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, specific performance is discretionary and the discretion must be exercised on sound and reasonable judicial principles, not arbitrarily. A plaintiff must establish a valid and enforceable contract, including consensus ad idem on the vital and fundamental terms of sale; a court will not make a contract for the parties. The plaintiff must also establish continued readiness and willingness to perform the plaintiff’s part. An oral agreement may be enforceable, but the party seeking specific performance bears a heavy burden to prove a concluded agreement. The Court applied Koillipara Sriramulu v. T. Aswatha Narayana on oral agreements; Surya Narain Upadhyaya v. Ram Roop Pandey on the statutory discretion; Mayawanti v. Kaushalya Devi on the need for a valid and enforceable contract; and K. Prakash v. B.R. Sampath Kumar and Zarina Siddiqui v. A. Ramalingam on the exercise of discretion and the requirements for specific performance.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s decree for specific performance was set aside, the trial court’s judgment was restored, and the suit was liable to be dismissed.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and alleged_sale_agreement_referred_to_an_earlier_agreement and earlier_agreement_not_produced and criminal_findings_relied_on_for_execution and independent_civil_assessment_of_evidence_inadequate

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property.
predicates.alleged_sale_agreement_referred_to_an_ea: The written agreement relied on by the plaintiff referred to an earlier agreement as part of the claimed transaction.
predicates.earlier_agreement_not_produced: The plaintiff did not produce or exhibit the earlier agreement referred to in the written agreement.
predicates.criminal_findings_relied_on_for_executio: The court granting specific performance relied on observations or findings from a criminal proceeding concerning execution of the agreement.
predicates.independent_civil_assessment_of_evidence: The civil court granting specific performance did not adequately assess the evidence and circumstances independently, including material records bearing on the claim.

members.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance requires a valid and enforceable contract whose material terms are certain and on which the parties reached agreement.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance of a written entry said to record an agreement to sell property and machinery, while the defendant disputed that the agreement covered the building and other parts of the property.
The parties’ correspondence reflected differing understandings of what was to be sold, including whether the building was included.
The entry did not clearly identify the land, define the vendor’s share if the co-owner did not join in the sale, or specify the price for that share.
The terms of an alleged preceding oral agreement were not proved.
members.legal_principle: Specific performance enforces the obligation actually undertaken, so the contract’s terms must be certain and the parties must have reached consensus ad idem; the plaintiff bears the burden of proving those terms and that agreement. A court cannot make a contract for the parties. Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits a defendant to raise any defence available under contract law. The court also described specific-performance jurisdiction as discretionary, drawing on Fry’s Specific Performance, 6th ed., and Halsbury’s Laws of England; no earlier judicial decision was relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff did not establish a valid and enforceable contract on agreed and sufficiently certain terms, so specific performance was unavailable; the appeal was dismissed and the refund decree was upheld.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a proceeding seeking an order requiring another party to perform an alleged contract.
predicates.material_terms_uncertain: The alleged agreement left material matters, such as the property to be transferred, the share to be transferred, or the consideration, unresolved.
predicates.parties_lacked_matching_understanding: The parties’ accounts or communications showed that they understood the subject or terms of the alleged transaction differently.
predicates.specific_performance_unavailable_for_no_: The court does not order specific performance because no valid and enforceable contract on sufficiently certain, mutually agreed terms was established.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance may be granted under the pre-amendment law when the purchaser establishes readiness and willingness and the circumstances do not warrant refusing the discretionary relief.
material_facts: The seller admitted executing the agreement to sell the immovable property.
The purchaser pleaded and proved readiness and willingness, including by making demands for performance during the contractual period.
The seller failed to perform despite those demands.
The trial court had refused specific performance, but the High Court granted it, and the Supreme Court found no illegality or infirmity in that decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 10, 16(c), and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as they stood before the 2018 amendment, specific performance could be granted for transfer of immovable property where money compensation was inadequate, provided the plaintiff satisfied Section 16(c); the court’s discretion under Section 20 had to be sound, reasonable, and guided by judicial principles. The Court relied on Kamal Kumar v. Premlata Joshi, (2019) 3 SCC 704, for the relevant considerations, including the existence of a concluded contract, performance and readiness, hardship, and the parties’ conduct; and referred to K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan, (1997) 3 SCC 1, and Saeadamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi, (2011) 12 SCC 18, on relevant considerations in exercising discretion. The Court also applied the readiness-and-willingness principles in Syed Dastagir and the related cases cited above.
members.conclusion: The decree granting specific performance was upheld.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and valid_contract_for_immovable_property and buyer_satisfies_readiness_requirement and seller_failed_to_perform

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.valid_contract_for_immovable_property: The parties made a valid agreement for the transfer of immovable property.
predicates.buyer_satisfies_readiness_requirement: The purchaser has pleaded and proved readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s essential contractual obligations.
predicates.seller_failed_to_perform: The seller did not perform the seller’s obligations under the agreement.

members.legal_issue: Specific performance is warranted when a valid sale agreement is proved and the purchaser establishes continued readiness and willingness to perform, unless a proper equitable ground justifies refusing relief.
material_facts: The trial court found that the seller had signed the sale agreement and admitted in cross-examination that he had read and signed the papers.
A subsequent letter signed by the seller acknowledged the agreement and receipt of the advance consideration.
The purchaser had paid or arranged substantial amounts toward the transaction and arranged funds for the balance consideration and registration charges.
The purchaser asserted that he remained ready and willing to perform, and the trial court granted specific performance after considering the evidence.

The seller alleged that the agreement was signed under pressure and was intended only to secure a loan; the Supreme Court rejected the High Court’s conclusion that the agreement was executed without free mind and volition.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to prove continued readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract from the contract date through the hearing. Under Section 20, once a valid agreement and the requirements for relief are established, the court should exercise its discretion in favour of specific performance unless a proper equitable consideration justifies otherwise.
members.conclusion: The agreement was validly proved, and the purchaser’s claim for specific performance was allowed, subject to the condition that he pay an increased total consideration.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.sale_agreement_validly_proved: The purchaser proves that the parties entered into a valid sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_continuously_ready_and_willing: The purchaser demonstrates continued readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s contractual obligations.

members.legal_issue: The power to strike a tenant’s defence for non-payment or non-deposit of rent is discretionary and must not be exercised punitively where the tenant acted in good faith and the failure resulted from the advocate’s conduct.
material_facts: The tenant regularly paid the rent arrears by cash or cheque to her advocate, whom she had engaged because she could not attend every hearing.
The advocate did not deposit the money in court or pay it to the landlord.
The tenant complained to the Bar Council after discovering that the money had not been remitted.
The Rent Controller struck out the tenant’s defence, and the tenant ultimately deposited the arrears as directed by the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 uses the word “may” and is directory, not mandatory; it gives the Controller a liberal judicial discretion. Because striking out a defence is a penal and extreme measure that deprives a tenant of the protection of section 14, it must be used with due circumspection and in light of the circumstances. The power is not triggered mechanically by non-payment or non-deposit: the failure must indicate wilfulness, deliberate default, or volitional non-performance, such as defiance or gross neglect. The court relied on V. K. Varma v. Radhey Shyam, AIR 1964 SC 1370, which explained the deliberate change from the mandatory wording of section 13(5) of the 1952 Act to the discretionary wording of section 15(7) of the 1958 Act.
members.conclusion: The tenant had not failed to pay or deposit rent in the relevant sense, and no case for the punitive exercise of discretion was made out. The order striking out her defence was illegal, and she should have an opportunity to contest the eviction claim.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_paid_rent_to_advocate and advocate_failed_to_remit_rent and tenant_acted_in_good_faith and not tenant_wilfully_defaulted

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant in a proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_to_advocate: The tenant paid rent to an advocate engaged to represent and protect the tenant’s interests.
predicates.advocate_failed_to_remit_rent: The advocate did not pay or deposit the rent received from the tenant.
predicates.tenant_acted_in_good_faith: The tenant entrusted the rent to the advocate in good faith and took steps after discovering it had not been remitted.
predicates.tenant_wilfully_defaulted: The tenant deliberately or wilfully failed to pay or deposit rent.

members.legal_issue: The tenant’s payments and the acknowledged excess amount did not establish a deliberate or contumacious default warranting the striking out of the defence.
material_facts: The tenant paid the arrears specified in the Rent Controller’s order on the date the order was made and paid an additional amount covering ten months of rent.
The landlord acknowledged receiving the excess amount, did not refund it, and did not adjust it against future rent.

The tenant made further rent payments, and Justice Thakur considered the total payments sufficient to cover rent due at the time the defence was struck out and for a substantial period beyond that date.
Justice Thakur considered the tenant’s conduct inconsistent with a deliberate or contumacious refusal to pay rent.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, striking out a defence is an exceptional discretionary step justified only where the tenant’s failure is deliberate, contumacious, or negligent. Applying Miss Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash (1980) 3 SCC 610 and Kamla Devi v. Vasdev (1995) 1 SCC 356, Justice Thakur held that the payments and circumstances did not show such conduct. He treated the acknowledged excess payment, in the absence of refund or another direction, as held for the tenant and applicable to future rent.
members.conclusion: Justice Thakur would allow the appeal, set aside the orders striking out the defence, and permit the tenant to contest the eviction proceeding on its merits. He considered the excess amount received and retained by the landlord applicable to future rent.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and ordered_arrears_paid and landlord_retained_acknowledged_excess and total_payments_exceeded_rent_due and not deliberate_or_contumacious_nonpayment

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.ordered_arrears_paid: The tenant paid the arrears required by the rent authority’s order.
predicates.landlord_retained_acknowledged_excess: The landlord acknowledged receiving more than the ordered arrears and neither refunded nor adjusted the excess.
predicates.total_payments_exceeded_rent_due: The tenant’s payments covered rent due at the relevant time and exceeded that amount.
predicates.deliberate_or_contumacious_nonpayment: The tenant deliberately or contumaciously withheld rent that was due.

members.legal_issue: Repeated late payment of future rent without an acceptable explanation justified striking out the tenant’s defence, notwithstanding later payments or excess payments made toward arrears.
material_facts: The Rent Controller ordered future rent to be paid month by month by a specified date.

Justice Khehar found that the tenant paid none of the future rent by the stipulated dates during the twelve-month period considered; payments were made late, including after the landlords applied to strike out the defence.
The tenant did not deposit rent with the Rent Controller or tender it unilaterally on time, and the payments were made when the landlord sought or collected them.
Justice Khehar found no acceptable explanation for the repeated delays.
The tenant had paid extra toward arrears, later paid rent, and offered to increase the rent and pay it in advance; Justice Khehar considered those matters insufficient to cure the prior defaults.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15(1) and 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 make the payment schedule in the Rent Controller’s order the basis for assessing compliance. Payments made toward arrears cannot be credited to future rent, and later payments do not cure earlier violations unless there is an adequate and acceptable explanation for the delay. The discretion under Section 15(7) may be exercised where non-compliance is repeated, shows disregard of the order, or lacks justification; even a single willful, contumacious, negligent, or careless default may suffice. Justice Khehar relied on Miss Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash (1980) 3 SCC 610, Kamla Devi v. Vasdev (1995) 1 SCC 356, Jain Motor Car Co. v. Swayam Prabha Jain (1996) 3 SCC 55, Aero Traders (P) Ltd. v. Ravinder Kumar Suri (2004) 8 SCC 307, and Amrit Lal v. Shiv Narain Gupta (2010) 15 SCC 510.
members.conclusion: Justice Khehar would dismiss the appeal and uphold the orders striking out the tenant’s defence. He held that the repeated, unexplained failures to meet the payment schedule showed contumacious disregard of the Rent Controller’s directions.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and rent_payment_schedule_set and repeated_late_future_rent_payments and no_acceptable_delay_explanation and not tenant_made_timely_unilateral_payments

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.rent_payment_schedule_set: A rent authority directed the tenant to pay future rent according to a specified schedule.
predicates.repeated_late_future_rent_payments: The tenant repeatedly paid future rent after the dates specified in the payment schedule.
predicates.no_acceptable_delay_explanation: The tenant provided no acceptable explanation for the late payments.
predicates.tenant_made_timely_unilateral_payments: The tenant independently paid or deposited future rent by the dates specified in the payment schedule.

members.legal_issue: The power to strike off a tenant’s defence for failure to deposit rent is discretionary, but deliberate default without a good and adequate reason warrants striking off the defence.
material_facts: The defendant made no deposit on the first hearing and did not regularly deposit rent during the suit.
The trial and revisional courts found no evidence of payment to the plaintiff; the Supreme Court found the defendant’s conduct showed volitional non-performance and no good reason for relaxation.
The High Court set aside the strike-off order while finding no bona fide character in the defendant’s pleas, and the Supreme Court held that its grant of indulgence was unsupported by reasons.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XV Rule 5(1) and (2) CPC, the word “may” gives the court discretion; striking off a defence is not mandatory on every default. Under Bimal Chand Jain v. Sri Gopal Agarwal, the court must consider a timely representation and may also rely on good reason apparent from the record. The discretion must be exercised with circumspection, not mechanically, but a deliberate or wilful default, defiance, or gross neglect without a good and adequate reason may warrant the penalty. The Court also referred to Miss Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash and Smt. Kamla Devi v. Vasdev on the discretionary character of such a penalty.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order was set aside and the trial court’s order striking off the defence was restored.

rule.if: eviction_and_rent_recovery_suit and tenant_is_tenant and (first_hearing_deposit_missed or regular_rent_deposits_missed) and deliberate_rent_default and no_good_reason_for_default and appeal_challenges_reversal_of_strikeoff

predicates.eviction_and_rent_recovery_suit: The lessor sought eviction and recovery of rent or compensation for use and occupation from the defendant.
predicates.tenant_is_tenant: The defendant did not deny being a tenant of the premises.
predicates.first_hearing_deposit_missed: The defendant did not deposit the amount due by the first hearing.
predicates.regular_rent_deposits_missed: The defendant did not regularly deposit amounts accruing during the suit.
predicates.deliberate_rent_default: The defendant’s conduct showed deliberate or volitional failure to pay or deposit rent.
predicates.no_good_reason_for_default: The record disclosed no good and adequate reason for excusing the defendant’s default.
predicates.appeal_challenges_reversal_of_strikeoff: An appeal challenged a court order that had reversed an order striking off the defendant’s defence.

members.legal_issue: An irregularity in rent deposits does not require the tenant’s defence to be struck off when the tenant has deposited all arrears and the irregularity does not warrant that consequence.
material_facts: The tenant’s defence in the eviction suit was at risk of being struck off for irregularities in rent deposits.
The tenant had deposited all rent arrears.
The Supreme Court found that the irregularity was not of a nature warranting the striking off of the defence.
members.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, does not require the defence to be struck off for every deposit default. The court retains discretion to relieve against that consequence, including where all arrears have been paid and the irregularity is not sufficiently serious. The Court applied its interpretation of ‘shall’ as directory and relied on the principles in Govindlal Chagganlal Patel v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee and Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, as well as the discretion recognized by Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s defence should not be struck off; the High Court’s direction to treat it as struck off was set aside, and the trial court’s order refusing to strike it off was restored.

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.tenant_deposited_all_arrears: The tenant deposited all rent arrears relevant to the dispute.
predicates.deposit_irregularity_not_serious: The court found that the irregularity in depositing rent was not serious enough to warrant striking off the defence.

members.legal_issue: A court may excuse a tenant’s late or missed rent deposit in an eviction suit when the delay is properly explained, and must not strike out the tenant’s defence in that circumstance.
material_facts: During an eviction suit, the court ordered the tenant to deposit rent monthly.
The tenant missed deposits for two months, believing that the tenant’s son had made them, and later discovered that they had not been made.
The tenant subsequently deposited the missed rent and continued depositing rent for later periods.
The Supreme Court found the delay properly explained, although the trial court had rejected the explanation and struck out the defence.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982 must be read harmoniously with the Act’s purpose of preventing unreasonable eviction. Although it provides for striking out a defence upon non-deposit, the court must assess whether the delay has been reasonably and properly explained. If it has, the court may excuse the delay; if it has not, the court must strike out the defence. The court applied Ganesh Prasad Sah Kesari v. Lakshmi Narayan Gupta, which cautioned against treating non-compliance as invariably requiring striking out; Mrs. Manju Choudhary v. Dulal Kumar Chandra, concerning the consequence of unexplained delay; and M/s B.P. Khemka Pvt. Ltd. v. Birendra Kumar Bhowmick, on construing a rent-deposit default provision in light of justice and the legislation’s purpose.
members.conclusion: The court has discretion to excuse a delay that is properly explained; where the explanation is accepted, the defence must not be struck out. The trial court erred in striking out the defence, and the High Court erred in failing to correct that miscarriage of justice. The orders were set aside and the defence restored.

predicates.eviction_suit_with_rent_deposit_order: A tenant contests an eviction suit in which a court has ordered periodic rent deposits.
predicates.rent_deposit_missed_or_late: The tenant failed to deposit rent by the ordered time or deposited it late.
predicates.delay_properly_explained: The court finds that the tenant has reasonably and acceptably explained the delay or failure to deposit rent.

members.legal_issue: A court may condone delay in depositing rent only when the defaulting tenant pleads justifiable reasons showing that circumstances beyond the tenant’s control prevented timely compliance; unexplained willful default does not warrant condonation.
material_facts: The tenant was directed to pay or deposit monthly rent during the proceeding but failed to do so regularly, and the Nazir’s report showed substantial delays.
The tenant had maintained that he had paid the arrears, but the Rent Controller found that he had not proved payment or tender of rent after the demand notice.
The tenant gave no explanation for the delays in depositing rent, and the Rent Controller denied him the benefit of protection from eviction.
members.legal_principle: In Hem Chand etc. etc. v. The Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. and Anr. etc. etc., the Court had held that there was no discretion to extend time for payment under Section 15(1). Relying on Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas and Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath and Anr., the Court recognized that the Rent Controller may condone default in payment or deposit of future rent. That discretion applies where the tenant seeks condonation and pleads justifiable reasons showing that circumstances beyond the tenant’s control prevented compliance. Under Sections 14(2) and 15(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, compliance with the rent-payment order is required for protection from eviction on the ground of non-payment.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to condonation of the delays or to the benefit of Section 14(2), and the eviction order was not disturbed.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and tenant_delayed_required_rent_deposits and tenant_willfully_defaulted and tenant_offered_no_justifiable_explanation

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding on the ground that a tenant had failed to pay rent.
predicates.tenant_delayed_required_rent_deposits: The tenant deposited rent later than the times required by the court’s rent-payment order.
predicates.tenant_willfully_defaulted: The tenant failed to make the required rent payments despite being ordered to do so.
predicates.tenant_offered_no_justifiable_explanatio: The tenant did not provide a justifiable reason showing that circumstances beyond the tenant’s control prevented timely payment.

members.legal_issue: A rent controller has discretion to strike out a tenant’s defence when the tenant fails to make payments or deposits required by the controller’s order.
material_facts: In an eviction proceeding, the tenant failed to make rent deposits as directed.
The landlord applied to have the tenant’s defence struck out, and the controller did so.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, provides that the controller may strike out the defence and proceed with the hearing if the tenant fails to make a payment or deposit required by an order under section 15(1). The Court relied on the legislative choice of “may,” including its substitution for “shall” in the corresponding provision of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and found no need to construe “may” as “shall.”
members.conclusion: The word “may” gives the controller discretion to strike out the defence or not; striking it out is not mandatory whenever the tenant fails to comply.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_failed_ordered_rent_deposit: The tenant failed to make a rent payment or deposit required by the controller’s order.
predicates.controller_may_strike_tenant_defence: The controller has discretion to strike out the tenant’s defence.

members.legal_issue: Failure to comply with a rent-payment direction does not automatically require a tenant’s defence to be struck out.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding included a claim based on non-payment of rent, and the Rent Controller directed the tenant to pay arrears and future rent.
The tenant did not make every future payment by the date directed, and the landlords sought to have the tenant’s defence struck out.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 uses discretionary language and is directory rather than mandatory; striking out a defence is penal because it deprives the tenant of protection under Section 14. The Court relied on Miss Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash (1980) 3 SCC 610, Kamla Devi v. Vasdev (1995) 1 SCC 356, Jain Motor Car Co. v. Swayam Prabha Jain (1996) 3 SCC 55, Aero Traders (P) Ltd. v. Ravinder Kumar Suri (2004) 8 SCC 307, and Amrit Lal v. Shiv Narain Gupta (2010) 15 SCC 510. It also noted the tenant-protective purpose of rent control legislation, including the principles discussed in Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam (1974) 1 SCC 242 and M/s Rahabhar Productions Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajendra K. Tandon (1998) 4 SCC 49.
members.conclusion: The power to strike out a tenant’s defence is discretionary, not automatic, and is an exceptional measure that must be exercised with care. The default must warrant that measure, such as by showing deliberate, contumacious, negligent, or otherwise seriously unjustified non-compliance.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought recovery of premises from a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_follow_rent_direction: The tenant failed to make a payment or deposit required by a rent authority’s direction.

members.legal_issue: A court retains discretion to relieve a tenant from striking off the defence for failure to comply with a rent-deposit direction in an eviction suit.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit on the ground of non-payment of rent, and the tenant contested the claim.
The court directed the tenant to deposit arrears and continue depositing rent during the suit.
The tenant did not comply with the deposit direction without irregularity, and the landlord sought to have the defence struck off.
The governing rent-control law was enacted to protect tenants from unreasonable eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, the power to direct deposits is accompanied by a sanction for non-compliance, but the direction to strike off the defence is directory, not mandatory. Whether ‘shall’ is mandatory depends on legislative intent, the nature and purpose of the law, and the consequences of the competing constructions. The Court relied on Govindlal Chagganlal Patel v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee, which approved the approach in Crawford on Statutory Construction, and on Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, which recognized a court’s jurisdiction to extend time for rent deposits under a similar provision. Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure also supports the principle that a court may enlarge a period it has fixed.
members.conclusion: The word ‘shall’ does not make striking off the defence an inevitable consequence of every failure to comply. The court retains discretion to grant relief where the circumstances and the ends of justice warrant it.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_suit and rent_deposit_direction and tenant_failed_to_comply and rent_law_aims_to_prevent_unreasonable_eviction

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.rent_deposit_direction: The court directed the tenant to deposit rent during the eviction suit.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_comply: The tenant failed to comply with the court’s rent-deposit direction.
predicates.rent_law_aims_to_prevent_unreasonable_ev: The governing rent law is intended to protect tenants from unreasonable eviction.

members.legal_issue: A court retains discretion not to strike a defendant’s defence for default in depositing rent even when the defendant made no timely representation.
material_facts: A lessor sued to evict a lessee and recover rent arrears.
During the suit, the lessee failed to make regular deposits of monthly rent.
The lessee made no representation within the prescribed time opposing the striking of the defence.
The trial court struck the defence, and the High Court affirmed on the basis that the court had no discretion to do otherwise.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and remanded the case for fresh consideration.
members.legal_principle: Order XV Rule 5(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, as re-enacted by the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act 1976, uses the word “may” and gives the court power, not an obligation, to strike off the defence for deposit default. Under Rule 5(2), the court must consider a timely representation, but the absence of one does not eliminate the court’s discretion to consider material already on the record. Because striking off the defence is penal, the power must not be exercised mechanically. The Court disagreed with and overruled the contrary view in Puran Chand v. Pravin Gupta.
members.conclusion: A court is not obliged to strike off the defence in every case of default, even if the defendant made no timely representation; it retains discretion to decline to do so when the material on the record provides good reason. The appeal was allowed and the case remanded for fresh consideration.

predicates.eviction_rent_suit: A lessor brought a suit seeking eviction of a lessee and recovery of rent or compensation.
predicates.rent_deposit_default: The defendant failed to make a required deposit of rent during the suit.
predicates.no_timely_representation: The defendant did not make a representation opposing the striking of the defence within the prescribed time.
predicates.court_retains_discretion_not_to_strike_d: The court has discretion to decline to strike the defence when the material before it provides good reason.

members.legal_issue: A tenant whose defence against eviction is not struck out retains the opportunity to claim statutory protection, and failure to comply with a rent-deposit order does not by itself require eviction.
material_facts: The tenant had deposited most rent on time but had deposited rent for four consecutive months late.
The Rent Controller refused the landlord’s application to strike out the tenant’s defence, while also ordering eviction for non-compliance with the deposit order.
The Supreme Court held that the tenant’s defence remaining available meant the tenant could still claim protection against eviction, and remitted the matter for reconsideration.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(2), 15(6) and 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act must be construed together. Section 15(7) makes striking out the defence discretionary, while Sections 14(2) and 15(6) make the protection against eviction turn on compliance with the deposit requirements. The phrase “as required” must be construed reasonably, with substantial compliance assessed in light of the Controller’s discretion. Hem Chand v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. also rejected the proposition that failure to comply automatically gives the landlord an indefeasible right to eviction.
members.conclusion: If the tenant’s defence is not struck out, the tenant retains the defences available under the Act, including the right to claim protection against eviction; non-compliance with the deposit order does not automatically entitle the landlord to eviction.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that rent was not paid or tendered.
predicates.tenant_failed_deposit: The tenant failed to pay or deposit rent as required during the eviction proceeding.
predicates.defence_not_struck_out: The Rent Controller did not strike out the tenant’s defence against eviction.
predicates.tenant_retains_right_to_claim_eviction_p: The tenant may still rely on the statutory protection against eviction and the defences available in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A rent controller has discretion, rather than a duty, to strike out a tenant’s defence after the tenant fails to comply with an order to pay or deposit rent, and may allow delayed payment.
material_facts: The tenant had not paid rent and did not pay the arrears within the time directed by the Rent Controller.

The tenant later paid part of the arrears, but a balance remained outstanding; the Rent Controller found that the delay in depositing that balance was not wilful, deliberate, or contumacious and noted that there had been some compromise between the parties.
The matter was treated as a first default, and the Rent Controller condoned the delay and allowed the tenant the statutory protection against eviction.
The Tribunal and the High Court upheld that decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 14(1)(a), 14(2), 15(1), and 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, failure to comply with a rent-payment order does not itself require the defence to be struck out or eviction to follow. Section 15(7) says the Controller “may” strike out the defence, conferring discretion that must be exercised on the circumstances of the case and not mechanically. The Court applied Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, which held under materially similar provisions that discretion not to strike out a defence implies discretion to condone default or extend time; Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath, which applied that principle to the Delhi Act; and Santosh Mehta v. Om Praksh, which treated the power as discretionary and the provision as directory and penal. Hem Chand v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. did not establish that non-compliance requires automatic eviction or mandatory striking out of the defence.
members.conclusion: The Rent Controller was not required automatically to strike out the tenant’s defence for non-compliance with the payment order. The power to strike out the defence is discretionary, and the Controller may, after considering the circumstances, extend time or condone delay. The appeal was dismissed, leaving the tenant’s protection against eviction intact.

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground that the tenant had not paid rent.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_follow_rent_payment_ord: The tenant did not pay or deposit rent as directed by the adjudicator.

members.legal_issue: A rent controller has discretion to retain a tenant’s defence and to extend the time for rent payment or deposit after a default, rather than automatically striking the defence or ordering eviction.
material_facts: The proceeding sought eviction for non-payment of rent, and the controller had directed the tenant to deposit rent monthly by a specified day.
The tenant deposited one month’s rent late.
The lower rent authorities declined to strike out the tenant’s defence, while the High Court treated the default as requiring that result.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(2), 15(1) and 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 provide the tenant a route to protection through payment or deposit, while making striking out the defence discretionary. The Court relied on Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, Ram Murty v. Bhola Nath and Kamla Devi v. Vasdev. It held that the contrary strict approach in Hem Chand v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. could not stand with the later larger-bench decisions. The discretion must be exercised on the facts and not mechanically.
members.conclusion: The controller’s power under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 is discretionary and includes, by necessary implication, power to extend the time for payment or deposit of future rent. A default does not automatically require the defence to be struck out or eviction to follow.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought recovery of premises from a tenant through a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_monthly_rent_by_dea: The tenant did not pay or deposit a required monthly rent amount by the required deadline.

members.legal_issue: A rent controller may condone a tenant’s late deposit of future rent and extend the deadline when the delay resulted from circumstances beyond the tenant’s control.
material_facts: In an eviction proceeding based on rent default, the tenant was ordered to deposit rent monthly by a specified day.
The tenant deposited the rent for four consecutive months late.
The Rent Controller had declined to strike out the tenant’s defence but had treated the late deposits as a basis for eviction.
The Supreme Court remitted the matter for the Rent Controller to consider whether to condone the delay.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(2) and 15(1), (6) and (7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act must be read together to give effect to the protection against eviction and the Controller’s discretion over striking out a defence. The discretionary, penal character of Section 15(7) recognized in Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash supports an implied power to condone a default in appropriate circumstances. The Court applied the reasoning in Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas concerning analogous provisions, and held that Hem Chand v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd., which denied a power to extend time, could not stand with that larger-bench decision on this point.
members.conclusion: The Rent Controller has an implied discretion to condone a delay in depositing future rent and extend the time for deposit where the failure resulted from circumstances beyond the tenant’s control; the matter was remitted for that discretion to be considered.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that rent was not paid or tendered.
predicates.future_rent_deposit_missed: The tenant fails to deposit rent that falls due during the eviction proceeding by the required deadline.
predicates.delay_beyond_tenant_control: The tenant’s failure to meet the deposit deadline resulted from circumstances beyond the tenant’s control.
predicates.controller_may_extend_future_rent_deadli: The Rent Controller may condone the late deposit and extend the deadline for payment or deposit.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s failure to comply with a rent-payment order does not require the Controller to strike out the tenant’s defence, and the Controller may extend the payment time or condone the default after considering the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction for rent default, and the tenant admitted that rent was due.
The Controller ordered the tenant to pay or deposit the arrears within one month and to make subsequent monthly payments.
The tenant paid part of the amount but did not deposit the remaining arrears within the time ordered.

On remand, the Controller found that there had been a compromise between the parties and that the delay in depositing the remaining arrears was not wilful, deliberate, or contumacious; the Controller condoned the delay and allowed the tenant the benefit of the statutory protection against eviction.
The Tribunal and High Court upheld that decision, and the Supreme Court dismissed the landlord’s appeal.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1)(a), 14(2), 15(1), and 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 provide the relevant framework. The word “may” in Section 15(7) makes striking out the defence discretionary. The discretion not to strike out the defence carries, by necessary implication, discretion to condone default or extend time. The Court applied Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, which construed materially similar provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act; followed Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath on the operation of Section 15(7); and relied on Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash for the discretionary, non-mandatory character of striking out the defence. Hem Chand v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd. does not make eviction automatic upon non-compliance: although the Controller cannot treat the payment deadline as automatically extended, the question remains whether to strike out the defence under Section 15(7).
members.conclusion: The Controller’s power to strike out a tenant’s defence is discretionary, not mandatory. The Controller may extend the time for payment or deposit or condone default, but must decide whether to strike out the defence by applying its mind to the circumstances of the case rather than acting mechanically.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought recovery of possession on the ground that the tenant had not paid rent.

members.legal_issue: The direction to strike out a tenant's defence for rent-payment default is discretionary, and the court may condone delay and extend the time for payment when justice and the circumstances of the case warrant it.
material_facts: The tenant paid rent late for two months, with delays of forty-four days and six days.
The defaults concerned belated payments rather than non-payment of the later rent arrears and were considered technical and inconsequential.
The lower courts treated striking out the defence as mandatory.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, is directory: its use of “shall” is read as “may,” leaving the court discretion to strike out or retain the defence in light of the circumstances and the interests of justice. That discretion also permits the court to condone default and extend the time for payment or deposit. The Court relied on Govindlal Chhagganlal Patel v. Agricultural Produce Market Committee, Godhra, [1976] 1 SCR 451; Ganesh Prasad Sah Kesari v. Lakshmi Narain Gupta, [1985] 3 SCC 53; Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdas, [1980] 2 SCR 334; Santosh Mehta v. Om Prakash, [1980] 3 SCR 325; and Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath, [1984] 3 SCR 111.
members.conclusion: Striking out the defence was not warranted in the circumstances; the court had discretion not to strike it out and could condone the delay or extend the time for payment.
