members.legal_issue: A life estate created for a widow by a settlement instrument that expressly limits her interest does not become full ownership under the general enlargement rule when the instrument falls within the statutory exception for restricted estates.
material_facts: A settlement deed granted a widow a life interest in certain properties and provided that they would revert to the settlor or his heirs upon her death.
After the widow died, the settlor’s son claimed the properties under the deed, while the widow’s brother claimed under her will.

The appellant argued that the settlement was in exchange for properties allegedly alienated without authority, and that the widow’s interest in those properties should mean she obtained full title to the settlement properties.
members.legal_principle: Under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a woman’s limited interest may be enlarged into full ownership, but section 14(2) is an exception: where an instrument creates a restricted estate, the enlargement under subsection (1) does not apply. The Court relied on these provisions and cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The settlement deed created a restricted estate within the statutory exception, so the widow did not acquire full or alienable ownership of the properties. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_over_widow_estate: A party appealed a decision resolving competing claims to property after a widow’s death, including a claim based on her will.
predicates.settlement_instrument_created_restricted: A settlor used a settlement instrument to grant a widow a limited interest in property, with the property to revert to the settlor or the settlor’s heirs after her death.
predicates.widow_did_not_acquire_alienable_title: The widow did not acquire full ownership that she could transfer by will.

members.legal_issue: A restriction imposed by a testamentary disposition made after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act remains effective when the female beneficiary acquires no pre-existing right in the property.
material_facts: The property was the testator’s self-acquired property.

The testator’s will gave his widow an interest in the property subject to restrictions, including that the property would pass to other beneficiaries on her death and that she could not sell or mortgage it during her lifetime.
The widow acquired the property under the will after the Hindu Succession Act had commenced; she was not in possession of it when the Act commenced.
Apart from the will, the widow had a right to maintenance, but no charge over the testator’s separate property had been created.
The lower appellate court found the will genuine and duly executed, and the High Court proceeded on the basis that the property came to the widow under that will.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, Section 14(1) applies where a female Hindu possessed property at the commencement of the Act under a semblance of a right, including a pre-existing right; Section 14(2) applies to a later instrument that creates a new restricted interest. A right to maintenance, without a charge or other right in the property, does not itself give a widow a pre-existing right in her husband’s separate property. Section 30 permits a Hindu to dispose of property by will, and a beneficiary takes subject to valid terms of that will. The Court distinguished V. Tulasamma v. V. Shesha Reddi and Raghubar Singh v. Gulab Singh, and relied on Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veeravva, Eramma v. Verrupanna, Dindyal v. Rajaram, Mst. Karmi v. Amru, Bhura v. Kashi Ram and Sharad Subramanyan v. Soumi Mazumdar.
members.conclusion: The widow’s interest was governed by the restrictions in the will. Section 14(1) did not enlarge it into an absolute estate; Section 14(2) applied.

members.legal_issue: A restricted interest granted to a female Hindu under a will that takes effect after the succession-law reform does not enlarge into absolute ownership merely because she possesses the property.
material_facts: A Hindu male executed a will granting each of his two wives a life interest in one half of his property and making his daughter the ultimate beneficiary.
The testator died after the succession-law reform had taken effect, and the will then operated in favour of the wives.
One wife later made a will purporting to bequeath her interest to a person outside the family.
The courts below treated the wife’s life interest as enlarged into absolute ownership, while the High Court held that she received only the interest specified in the testator’s will.
members.legal_principle: Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 recognises a Hindu’s power to dispose of property by will. Section 14(1), including its explanation, broadly enlarges qualifying property held by a female Hindu into full ownership, but Section 14(2) excludes property acquired under a will that prescribes a restricted estate. The exception must be read so it does not defeat Section 14(1), but a restricted estate created by a will that operates after the Act is within Section 14(2); the pre-existing-right reasoning in V. Tulasamma v. Shesha Reddy does not convert such a testamentary grant into an absolute estate. The Court also relied on G. Appaswami Chettiar v. R. Sarangapani Chettiar and Kothi Satyanarayana v. Galla Sithayya concerning restricted interests created by testamentary or other instruments.
members.conclusion: The wife acquired only the life interest granted by the will; it did not enlarge into an absolute estate, and she could not transfer an absolute interest by her own will. The appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A restricted lifetime interest in property created for a Hindu woman by a will or other instrument does not become absolute ownership under the general rule for female Hindu property.
material_facts: The property owner’s 1944 will gave his daughter the right to reside in a house and receive its rental income during her lifetime.
The will prohibited her from alienating, mortgaging, gifting, selling, or transferring the house, and provided that her brother would be its owner subject to her rights.
The daughter claimed that the interest became absolute ownership under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, generally makes property possessed by a female Hindu her full property, but Section 14(2) excepts property acquired under a will, gift, or other instrument that prescribes a restricted estate. Reading Section 14(1) to enlarge an expressly restricted testamentary interest would make Section 14(2) and Section 30 otiose. The Court relied on Mst. Karmi v. Amru, AIR 1971 SC 745; Navneet Lal @ Rangi v. Gokul, AIR 1976 SC 794; Jagan Singh (Dead) Through LRs. v. Dhanwanti, (2012) 2 SCC 628; and Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike, AIR 2006 SC 3282. It distinguished Balwant Kaur v. Chanan Singh, AIR 2000 SC 1908, where the will, read as a whole, gave only a limited estate.
members.conclusion: The interest remained limited to the daughter’s lifetime and did not become absolute ownership.

members.legal_issue: A restricted life interest granted by will to a female Hindu in the testator’s self-acquired property, independently of any pre-existing right, is not enlarged into absolute ownership when the will creates that interest for the first time.
material_facts: The house was the testator’s self-acquired property, which he owned exclusively.

By will, the testator gave the house’s ground and first floors to his son and daughter, respectively, as their absolute property, while giving his wife only a right to reside in the house during her lifetime and use its rental income for her maintenance and the house’s upkeep.
The wife’s interest was granted for the first time by the will and was not given in recognition or satisfaction of a pre-existing right.
The testator gave other property to his wife absolutely, and she did not seek maintenance from him.
The lower courts held that the wife’s interest remained a life interest under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; the appeal challenged that conclusion.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a female Hindu’s limited interest in property held in recognition of a pre-existing right may enlarge into absolute ownership. Section 14(2) applies where a will or other instrument creates a new interest for the first time and expressly restricts it. Section 30 permits a Hindu to dispose of property by will, including by granting only a life interest. V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy explains the distinction between a grant recognizing a pre-existing right and one creating a new restricted interest; Sadhu Singh v. Gurudwara Sahib Narike applies that distinction to a testamentary grant of a restricted interest. The Court also relied on the principles in Gullapalli Krishna Das v. Vishnumolakayya Venkayya, Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, and Thota Sesharathamma v. Thota Manikyamma in noting that the interpretation in V. Tulasamma had been consistently upheld.
members.conclusion: The wife’s life interest fell under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and remained a restricted estate until her death; it was not enlarged into absolute ownership under Section 14(1). The appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A limited interest created for the first time by a will in the owner’s self-acquired property does not become absolute merely because it is granted to a Hindu woman, when the property itself is not given in lieu of maintenance.
material_facts: The testator made a will dividing his self-acquired property between his son and his second wife.
The wife received a restricted life interest, with the property to pass absolutely to the son after her death.
The wife was to receive income from the property for her livelihood; the property itself was not allotted in lieu of maintenance or to satisfy a pre-existing right.
The testator had also provided for the wife’s maintenance needs through the income and allowed her to mortgage property for a daughter’s marriage if necessary.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 must be read so that Section 14(1) enlarges a limited interest where an instrument recognises or confirms a pre-existing right, including a right to maintenance, while Section 14(2) applies when an instrument creates a new and independent title subject to restrictions. Under V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, a maintenance right is pre-existing, and a transfer that merely recognises it does not create a new title. But a property owner may devise self-acquired property by will subject to a limited estate if the property itself is not given in lieu of maintenance. The court distinguished Shakuntla Devi v. Kamla and Jupudy Pardha Sarathy v. Pentapati Rama Krishna, which concerned pre-1956 wills. The word “possessed” in Section 14(1) is wide and does not require physical possession, but the woman must have a vestige of a claim, right, or title.
members.conclusion: The wife’s interest remained a restricted life estate and did not enlarge into absolute ownership; the purchasers from her could not acquire a better title than she held.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary life estate is not enlarged into an absolute estate where the limited interest falls within the statutory exception for interests created by an instrument.
material_facts: The widow's life estate in the property was created under her father's will.
The respondents argued that the life estate became absolute after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to a limited estate created by an instrument and prevents its enlargement under section 14(1). The Court agreed with the High Court that the testamentary life estate fell within section 14(2).
members.conclusion: The life estate was not enlarged into an absolute estate because the interest was created by a will and the statutory exception applied.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu woman given only a life interest under an instrument does not acquire absolute ownership merely by operation of the rule enlarging a Hindu woman’s existing property rights.
material_facts: The earlier judgment concerning the property held that the woman had only a life interest.
The life interest arose under an oral testamentary disposition, and the woman later transferred the property by sale deed.
The courts below relied on the earlier determination that she had no authority to transfer the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is an exception to Section 14(1): where an instrument gives a Hindu woman only a life interest, that interest does not become absolute ownership under Section 14(1). The Court relied on Shivdev Kaur v. R.S. Grewal and the authorities discussed there, including Mst. Karmi v. Amru, Navneet Lal v. Gokul, Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike, and Jagan Singh v. Dhanwanti.
members.conclusion: The life interest did not become absolute ownership, and the transfer made by the life-interest holder could not confer rights beyond those she possessed.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s limited interest in property created by an instrument is not enlarged into full ownership where she had no pre-existing right in the property and the instrument prescribes a restricted estate.
material_facts: The widow’s husband died in 1925, and under the Hindu law then applicable she acquired no share or interest in the house left by him.
A registered award later entitled her to receive the house’s rent in lieu of maintenance for her lifetime and provided that her sons would own the house after her death.
The widow claimed the house in proceedings concerning its attachment and argued that her limited interest had become full ownership.
Her interest ended during the proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) enlarges a woman’s interest where she possesses property in recognition of a pre-existing right, but Section 14(2) applies where a gift, will, instrument, decree, order, or award itself prescribes a restricted estate. Badri Prasad v. Smt. Kanan Devi was distinguished because the widow there acquired a share under the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937, and therefore had a pre-existing right; the widow here had none, and the award created her restricted estate.
members.conclusion: The award created a restricted estate within the scope of Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; Section 14(1) did not enlarge the widow’s interest, which ended on her death. The appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A widow who receives property under a will granting only a life interest does not acquire an absolute estate in that property under the Hindu Succession Act.
material_facts: The property owner’s genuine last will gave his widow a life interest in his estate and directed that it pass to collateral relatives after her death.
The widow later made a will purporting to leave the property to her daughter.
The daughter claimed title under the widow’s later will.
members.legal_principle: The Hindu Succession Act does not enlarge a limited life interest expressly given to a widow under a will into an absolute estate. The Court relied on the Act’s provisions concerning a Hindu woman’s property; it cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The widow’s interest remained a life estate and did not become absolute under the Hindu Succession Act; she therefore could not pass title to the daughter under her will, and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: The exception for property acquired under an instrument prescribing a restricted estate does not displace full ownership where the acquisition recognizes a pre-existing right to maintenance.
material_facts: The husband’s letter entrusted the land to his wife and identified its produce as a source of her maintenance.
The wife had a pre-existing right to maintenance, and the Court found that the land had been given in recognition of that right.
The purchaser argued that the wife had to establish a limited estate without a right of alienation for the statutory enlargement to apply.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property acquired in recognition of a pre-existing right to maintenance is enlarged into full ownership. Section 14(2), which concerns property acquired under a written instrument, decree, order, or award prescribing a restricted estate, is in the nature of an exception and applies where the acquisition is for the first time without a pre-existing right. The Court relied on Badri Pershad v. Kanso Devi, distinguished Naraini Devi v. Rano Devi, and applied the principles in V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi and Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai.
members.conclusion: A separate showing that the wife received a restricted estate was unnecessary. The acquisition was traceable to her pre-existing maintenance right, so the restriction exception did not prevent her interest from becoming full ownership.

members.legal_issue: The restriction on enlargement of a female Hindu's property interest does not apply when an instrument recognizes her pre-existing maintenance right rather than creating a new, restricted title.
material_facts: The partition arrangement allowed the widow to reside in the disputed property and take its income after her husband's death, while limiting the successors' ability to interfere with her enjoyment.
The property had been allotted to her husband at partition, and the widow possessed it with a right to income for her maintenance after his death.
The widow's maintenance right pre-existed the arrangement because her husband had a personal obligation to maintain her.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(2) is an exception to Section 14(1) and applies where an instrument or other specified source creates a restricted interest in property. It does not displace Section 14(1) when property is acquired in recognition of an antecedent right, such as a right to maintenance. The Court relied on V. Tulsamma v. Sesha Reddi and Gulwant Kaur v. Mohinder Singh, and held that Bai Vajia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai did not establish a different rule.
members.conclusion: Section 14(2) did not prevent the widow's interest from becoming full ownership under Section 14(1), because her possession was traceable to her pre-existing maintenance right.

members.legal_issue: Possession alone does not make a female Hindu a full owner under section 14(1) when she had no title to the property.
material_facts: The appellant was in possession of part of the properties after her husband died, but the Hindu Women’s Right to Property Act, 1937 had not then come into force in the relevant territory.
When the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, the appellant had no title to the properties and was in possession without a right to them.
After the respondents sought to execute their decree for possession, the appellant objected, claiming full ownership under section 14(1).
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with its Explanation and subsection (2), enlarges a female Hindu’s existing restricted interest into full ownership; it applies to property in which she has acquired some kind of title, however limited, and does not validate illegal possession or confer title on a trespasser. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s possession alone did not attract section 14(1); the provision did not confer title on her because she had no vestige of title and was a trespasser.

predicates.objection_to_execution_of_property_decre: A person objects to execution of a decree requiring delivery of property.

predicates.no_title_to_property_at_law_commencement: The female Hindu has no legal title or existing interest in the property when that law comes into force.

members.legal_issue: Possession by a female claimant at the commencement of succession legislation does not by itself convert her interest into absolute ownership unless her possession rests on a vestige of claim, right, or title.
material_facts: The appellant claimed absolute ownership based on possession of the disputed property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The alleged oral gift to the appellant’s mother was not proved, and an earlier declaratory decree had limited the mother’s interest to the lifetime of the property owner.
The Court found that the appellant’s possession did not rest on a valid right or title, or on a recognized basis for acquiring property.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) and its Explanation enlarge a female Hindu’s existing limited interest into full ownership when she possesses property under some vestige of claim, right, or title or another recognized mode of acquisition. Mere possession without such an interest does not create title. Section 14(2) concerns instruments or orders creating an independent new title with restrictions; it does not displace Section 14(1) where a document recognizes a pre-existing right. The Court applied Eramma v. Veerupana, AIR 1966 SC 1879, and V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, (1977) 3 SCC 99.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s possession did not give her absolute ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.

members.legal_issue: A minor son remains a member of a family unit for agricultural land-ceiling calculations despite having been separated from the family by partition.
material_facts: A father and his sons had divided property by partition deeds before the land-ceiling law came into force, and the separated minor sons held land separately.
The land-reform authorities aggregated the land held by the family members when determining whether the family unit held land beyond the ceiling.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(f), 3(o), 4, 5(3), 5(4), 8 and 10 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 treat a family unit as distinct from a joint family and require the aggregate land held by its members to be considered. The Court relied on Tumati Venkaish v. State of Andhra Pradesh, approved Kanuru Venkatakrishna Rao v. The Authorised Officer, Land Reforms, Bandar, and followed State of Maharashtra v. Vyasendra.
members.conclusion: A separated minor son is as much a member of the family unit as an undivided minor son, and the land held by the family-unit members must be aggregated for applying the ceiling.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: A person’s landholding was assessed in a proceeding to determine the applicable agricultural land ceiling.
predicates.minor_son_separated_by_partition: A minor son had been separated from the family by a partition before the ceiling assessment.

members.legal_issue: For land-ceiling purposes, a family is a statutory unit based on the specified relationships, and a prior partition does not prevent minor sons’ separately held land from being counted in the family holding.
material_facts: A parent had partitioned property with his two minor sons before the appointed day, and each son held land separately under that partition.
The sons were minor members of the parent’s family on the appointed day.
The land-ceiling authority included the sons’ separately held land when determining the family’s holding.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(10) defines a family by relationships, not by joint title or joint holding. Sections 4(1) and 4(2) make the family the unit for determining the ceiling and deem land held individually or jointly by family members to be held by the family. Section 4(3)(a), which separately addresses an individual’s share in an undivided Hindu family, confirms that the statutory family is distinct from a Hindu joint family. Section 4(4) addresses transfers and partitions made after the appointed day and before the Act commenced; it does not make the existence of a prior partition relevant to whether minor sons fall within the statutory family. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The minor sons’ separate land had to be included in the family holding despite the prior partition.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: An authority or court is determining the land holding of a family for a ceiling limit.

members.legal_issue: Land held by a minor son who has separated from the family through partition is included in the family unit’s holdings for determining the applicable land ceiling.
material_facts: The state law defined a family unit to include minor sons without distinguishing between sons who remained undivided and sons who had separated through partition.
The law applied the ceiling to the aggregate land held by members of the family unit.
A partition before the statutory cutoff was not invalidated, but land obtained by a divided minor son remained held by him.
members.legal_principle: The definition of family unit included minor sons, whether divided or undivided, and the provision applying the ceiling to the aggregate holdings of family-unit members required their lands to be clubbed. This aggregation did not invalidate a partition: the divided minor son could own the land separately while the land was nevertheless counted for the family unit’s ceiling.
members.conclusion: A divided minor son remained a member of the family unit, and land held by him, including land obtained on partition, had to be aggregated with the land of the other members for applying the ceiling.

predicates.minor_son_holds_land_separately_after_pa: The minor son holds land separately after a partition.

members.legal_issue: Land separately owned by a spouse is included when calculating the holding of the statutory family for land-ceiling purposes, even if the spouse acquired it with separate personal funds.
material_facts: The parent’s wife separately owned land that she had purchased using her Sridhanam money.
The parent and his wife were members of the same family for the ceiling determination.
The land-ceiling authority included the wife’s land in calculating the family holding.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(10) and 4(2) define the family by relationship and deem land held individually by family members to be held by the family for ceiling purposes. Explanation IV to section 7(1) proceeds on the basis that separately held land of both spouses is pooled for the ceiling calculation; it allocates any land to be surrendered between them in proportion to their separate holdings. The source of the wife’s funds does not remove her land from the family calculation. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The wife’s separately owned land had to be included in the family holding.

predicates.spouses_hold_land_separately: The spouses each hold land in their own separate ownership.

members.legal_issue: Land held by a member of a family unit must be included in the unit’s holding for ceiling purposes regardless of whether it is that member’s separate or stridhan property.
material_facts: The respondent’s wife held land in her own name, which the respondent claimed was her separate property.
The Tribunal included the wife’s land in the family unit’s total holding when determining whether it exceeded the ceiling.
The respondent, his wife, and their minor children fell within the statutory definition of a family unit.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, deems all land held by each member of a family unit to be held by the unit for determining its ceiling area. The Explanation defines a family unit to include a person, the person’s spouse, and their minor sons and minor unmarried daughters. Read with sections 3(1) and 3(2), which prohibit holdings above the ceiling and treat excess land as surplus, the provision requires aggregation whether land is held jointly or separately. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: All land held by each member of the family unit, jointly or separately, must be pooled when determining the unit’s ceiling holding; the character of a member’s interest in the land is irrelevant.

members.legal_issue: Land held by members of a landowning family must be included in calculating permissible area, subject to the separate-unit treatment for adult sons and the aggregate limit on the family and those units.
material_facts: The landowner’s wife and sons held land in their own names, and the dispute concerned whether their holdings could be excluded when determining the family’s permissible area.
On the appointed day, the family included one adult son and three minor sons.
The revenue authorities treated the family and the adult son as entitled to two units, while the High Court directed that the permissible area be determined separately for the individual petitioners.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(e) and 3(n) define family and person; Section 4(1) sets the permissible area for a family, Section 4(4) treats every adult son as a separate unit subject to an aggregate limit, and Section 4(6) requires the land held by a person who is a family member to be considered together with the land held by the family members. Section 6 imposes the ceiling on land held by a person. The Court held that the plain language of Section 4 did not support treating a wife’s separately held land as outside the family calculation.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating the wife’s separately held land as giving her an independent permissible area and in excluding family members’ holdings from the calculation. A member’s land must be taken into account with the family’s land; an adult son is treated as a separate unit, but the family’s land and the separate units’ land together cannot exceed the aggregate limit.

predicates.adult_son_holds_land: An adult son of a landowner holds land.

members.legal_issue: Defining a family unit to include minor children for agricultural land-ceiling purposes does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The landholders challenged the statutory definition of family unit as discriminatory.
The definition aggregated land held by family members for ceiling purposes as part of an agrarian-reform measure.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and the protections in Articles 31A and 31B of the Constitution. It followed Seth Nand Lal v. State of Haryana, which upheld an agrarian-reform classification based on a family unit, noting the operational role of families in agriculture and the aim of preventing evasion and reducing inequality.
members.conclusion: The definition of family unit, as interpreted by the High Court, does not violate Article 14 and is also protected by Articles 31A and 31B.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: A person’s landholding was assessed in a proceeding to determine the applicable agricultural land ceiling.

predicates.agrarian_reform_measure: The ceiling measure was adopted as part of an agrarian-reform scheme.

members.legal_issue: The distinction between minor sons included in a family unit and major sons excluded from it does not invalidate a protected agrarian reform law on the ground of unequal treatment.
material_facts: Landholders challenged the definition of family unit because it included minor sons but excluded major sons.
The challenged law was an agrarian reform measure.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects qualifying agrarian reform legislation from challenge on the ground that it violates Article 14, among other specified constitutional rights. The Court relied on the discussion of the corresponding contention in the companion Haryana land ceiling judgment delivered by Tulzapurkar J.
members.conclusion: The equality challenge could not succeed because the agrarian reform law was protected against challenge for infraction of Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a law concerning agrarian reform.
predicates.law_is_protected_agrarian_reform_legisla: The challenged law qualifies as protected agrarian reform legislation.
predicates.challenge_alleges_unequal_treatment: The party alleges that the law treats comparable persons unequally.

members.legal_issue: Agricultural ceiling legislation that modifies rights in agricultural land may receive constitutional protection from challenges based on equality, freedom, and property rights, and using a family unit to apply the ceiling does not by itself invalidate the legislation.
material_facts: The legislation imposed ceilings on agricultural holdings and treated a family unit, including a husband, wife, and minor children, as the unit for applying revised ceilings.
The legislation modified rights in agricultural land and was part of an agrarian-reform scheme.
The petitioners challenged the family-unit approach and argued that it violated fundamental rights, including equality.
The Acts were included in the constitutional schedule, and the Court found that the legislation fell within the category of agrarian laws protected by Article 31A.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a) protects laws providing for acquisition of an estate or extinguishment or modification of rights in an estate from being declared void for inconsistency with, or abridgment of, Articles 14, 19, or 31. Article 31A(2)(a)(iii) includes agricultural land within the meaning of an estate. The Court also relied on Dattatraya Govind Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra, which rejected the challenge based on the family-unit ceiling and the second proviso to Article 31A(1), and on the principle that incidental hardship in pursuing agrarian reform does not establish destruction of the equality guarantee.
members.conclusion: The agricultural ceiling Acts were protected by Article 31A from the asserted fundamental-rights challenges, and the family-unit approach did not establish a violation of the relevant constitutional protection.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agricultural: A litigant brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings.
predicates.law_modifies_rights_in_agricultural_land: The law modifies rights in land held or used for agriculture as part of an agrarian-reform scheme.
predicates.law_uses_family_unit_ceiling: The law applies the ceiling by treating a family unit as the operative unit.
predicates.law_not_invalidated_by_asserted_fundamen: The law is not invalidated by the asserted fundamental-rights challenge because it falls within the applicable constitutional protection.

members.legal_issue: Grouping the separate holdings of family members to determine an agricultural land ceiling does not violate the second proviso to Article 31A(1), and the law need not use one uniform ceiling for every individual.
material_facts: The land-ceiling law grouped an individual’s land with separately held land of the individual’s spouse and minor children to determine the family’s ceiling.
The law did not merge or extinguish the family members’ separate ownership or legal personalities, and it allowed holders to select land to retain in proportion to their separate holdings.
The law provided for compensation for land acquired in excess of the ceiling.
The law defined a person to include a joint family, while the General Clauses Act definition included bodies of individuals.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1), including its second proviso, does not prohibit different ceiling limits for individuals or classes of individuals differently situated, and does not require those limits to be prescribed directly in a single provision. The term person has no fixed concept that prevents a law from grouping family members’ separate holdings for ceiling computation. Article 367 applies definitions in the General Clauses Act, 1897, including section 3(42), for interpreting the Constitution, but that definition does not bar such grouping. Section 6(2) of the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act grouped holdings for determining the ceiling without merging separate legal personalities or ownership. Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab was distinguished; Kunjukutty Sahib v. State of Kerala was relied on regarding the effect of a changed ceiling limit.
members.conclusion: The grouping provision was valid. The second proviso to Article 31A(1) neither requires a single uniform ceiling nor prescribes a particular method for imposing different ceilings on differently situated individuals; the statutory grouping did not alter the family members’ separate legal status or ownership.

predicates.land_ceiling_law_challenge: A person challenges a law that limits how much agricultural land may be held.
predicates.separate_family_holdings_grouped_for_cei: The law counts separately held land of family members together when determining the applicable ceiling.
predicates.separate_ownership_preserved: The law leaves the family members’ separate ownership and legal identities intact.
predicates.holders_can_select_land_to_retain: The law allows the holders to select which land to retain, with the retained land reflecting their separate holdings.

members.legal_issue: Treating a defined family as the ceiling unit and aggregating its members' lands does not conflict with the constitutional protection for land within the ceiling applicable to a person.
material_facts: The legislation defined a family unit consisting of a person, spouse, and specified minor children.
It aggregated land held by each family-unit member, jointly or separately, and deemed the aggregate to be held by the family unit.
The ceiling was applied to the family unit, rather than separately to each individual member of that unit.
The legislation aimed, among other things, to prevent avoidance of ceiling limits through transfers to close relatives.
members.legal_principle: The constitutional restriction applies where the land is personally cultivated and is within the ceiling applicable to the person whose land is acquired. When the statute makes the family unit the ceiling unit, an individual member is not separately treated as the unit for applying that ceiling. The Court also relied on the legislative purpose of preventing evasion of ceiling laws through transfers to close relatives and on Hasmukhlal Dayabhai v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The family-unit provisions did not violate the constitutional restriction because the applicable ceiling in such a case was that of the family unit, not that of an individual member.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may define a family for agricultural-ceiling purposes and club family members’ holdings without violating the constitutional protection for land within a ceiling limit.
material_facts: The legislation defined a raiyat’s family to include specified spouses, children and other relatives, and provided for holdings of family members to be clubbed.
The definition included provision for divorced and widowed daughters in specified circumstances and allowed the ceiling area to increase with family size, subject to a maximum.
The ceiling scheme treated the individual raiyat as the unit while accounting for family members.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14K(c) and 14M(2) were components of a law imposing a ceiling, not enlarging the maximum holding. The Court held that defining family and clubbing holdings were necessary to prevent evasion and to implement that ceiling, and that the second proviso to Article 31A(1) did not invalidate those provisions. It also relied on Article 31B as an independent protection.
members.conclusion: The family definition and clubbing provisions did not violate the second proviso to Article 31A(1); in any event, the provisions were protected by Article 31B.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.family_members_hold_land: Two or more people treated as members of a raiyat’s family hold agricultural land.
predicates.family_holdings_are_clubbed_for_a_ceilin: The legislature aggregates family members’ holdings to calculate a maximum holding and allows a limited increase based on family size.

members.legal_issue: Defining a ceiling unit as an individual, that person’s spouse, and their unmarried minor children does not violate equality merely because it excludes major children or joint-family arrangements.
material_facts: The law defined a family by reference to an individual, that individual’s spouse, and their unmarried minor children.
The petitioners argued that the definition treated families with minor children differently from households with adult children or joint-family arrangements when applying the land ceiling.
The Court concluded that the definition did not inevitably cause concentration of wealth and accorded with contemporary urban living conditions.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a legislative classification merely because it draws distinctions among family arrangements; the Court considered whether the definition was arbitrary and whether it necessarily produced the alleged concentration of wealth. Krishna Iyer, J. considered the definition consistent with current urban family conditions.
members.conclusion: The statutory definition of family is not arbitrary or violative of Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_urban_land_c: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of legislation imposing ceilings on urban vacant land.
predicates.ceiling_unit_includes_individual_spouse_: The law calculates the relevant household unit by including an individual, the spouse, and their unmarried minor children.
predicates.definition_does_not_inevitably_concentra: The definition does not necessarily or inevitably permit concentration of land in a few hands.

members.legal_issue: Defining a family for an urban land ceiling as an individual, that individual's spouse, and their unmarried minor children is not, by itself, an unconstitutional or arbitrary classification.
material_facts: The law defined a family as an individual, the individual's spouse, and their unmarried minor children.
The challenge asserted that this definition excluded adult children and joint families and could produce different permitted holdings.
The Court considered that the definition reflected the nuclear family increasingly prevalent in urban life and did not inevitably cause concentration of wealth.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a family definition merely because it excludes adult children or joint-family arrangements. The majority considered the definition in the context of contemporary urban family patterns and the law's distributive purpose under Article 39(b) and (c). Justice Sen also relied on the Court's prior approval of substantially similar family definitions in agrarian ceiling laws and referred to Union of India v. Valluri Basavaiah Chowdhary concerning legislative difficulties in imposing an urban ceiling.
members.conclusion: The family definition was valid and did not violate Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_family_unit_: A litigant challenges the constitutional validity of the family unit used to calculate a land ceiling.
predicates.law_counts_individual_spouse_and_unmarri: The law treats an individual, their spouse, and their unmarried minor children as a single family unit.
predicates.definition_does_not_inevitably_concentra: The definition does not by itself or inevitably produce concentration of wealth contrary to the law's distributive purpose.

members.legal_issue: A land transfer made after the statutory cutoff is included in calculating a holder’s landholding unless it satisfies an applicable exception, even when it is said to implement an earlier family arrangement.
material_facts: The holder executed a registered gift of land to his adult unmarried daughter after the statutory cutoff.
He asserted that the gift implemented an earlier family arrangement intended to provide for his daughter, but did not prove that arrangement or explain the delay in executing the gift.

The authorities found that the transfer was not proved to be in good faith and appeared designed to defeat the ceiling law; the holder and his sons remained in possession and enjoyed the land’s income.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(6) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960 requires a post-cutoff transfer to be ignored in determining the ceiling area unless it falls within an exception in the proviso. The relevant exception requires proof of good faith, adequate consideration and an irrevocable instrument, and excludes benami transfers and transfers for the immediate or deferred benefit of the holder or the holder’s family.
members.conclusion: The gifted land had to be included in calculating the holder’s total landholding because the transfer was not shown to fall within an exception.

predicates.qualifying_protected_transfer: The transfer was proved to be in good faith, for adequate consideration, under an irrevocable instrument, not benami, and not for the immediate or deferred benefit of the landholder or the landholder’s family.

members.legal_issue: An involuntary transfer made after the relevant cutoff is subject to the same conditions as a voluntary transfer before it may be excluded from a tenure-holder’s surplus land calculation.
material_facts: A creditor obtained a court-ordered auction sale of a large area of the tenure-holder’s land after the ceiling proceedings had begun.
The sale was made to the decree-holders for a small sum in relation to the area sold.
The purchasers did not establish that the sale was bona fide and for adequate consideration.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(6) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960 requires post-cutoff transfers to be ignored unless the transfer satisfies the proviso, including good faith, adequate consideration and an irrevocable instrument, and is not benami or for the immediate or deferred benefit of the tenure-holder or family. Explanation II places the burden of proving the exception on the party claiming it. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The auction sale was not exempt from the rules governing transfers merely because it was involuntary; it could be excluded from the surplus calculation only if the required conditions were proved.

members.legal_issue: An affected person must receive a meaningful opportunity to object and be heard when the statutory objection procedure applies to a land acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition was challenged by interested persons who alleged that personal notices were not served, objections were not properly heard, and objectors were not given a proper opportunity to present material.
The acquisition was not described as proceeding under an urgency dispensation from the objection procedure.
members.legal_principle: The applicable version of Section 5A requires personal service on persons known or believed to be interested, permits written objections, and requires an opportunity to be heard in person or through a pleader, further inquiry where necessary, and a decision. The Collector acts in a quasi-judicial capacity. The opportunity is a just and wholesome safeguard for a person whose property is intended to be acquired, unless the Government validly dispenses with it under the urgency provisions of Section 17. The Court relied on Shri Mandir Sita Ramji v. Lt. Governor of Delhi and Farid Ahmed Abdul Samad v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad.
members.conclusion: Compliance with the objection procedure is mandatory, and an objector must be afforded an opportunity to be heard; the procedure cannot be treated lightly or casually.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land by the State.
predicates.affected_person_objects: A person interested in the land submits an objection to the proposed acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A person whose property is proposed to be compulsorily acquired must receive an effective opportunity to be heard on objections before the acquisition declaration is made.
material_facts: The owners submitted written objections to the proposed acquisition.
The acquisition officer adjourned the hearing once but refused a further adjournment requested because the owners’ representative and advocate could not attend.
The officer proceeded without hearing the objectors, and the Government made an acquisition declaration.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5A(1) and 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 give an interested person a substantive right to object and to be heard; the hearing is not an empty formality. Section 6 requires the Government to consider the Collector’s report before making a declaration. Because compulsory-acquisition legislation is ex-proprietary, its requirements are strictly construed. The Court relied on Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Om Prakash v. State of Uttar Pradesh, State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh, Union of India v. Mukesh Hans, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Dev Saran v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Radhy Shyam v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The failure to provide the hearing required by Section 5A(2) invalidated the acquisition declaration.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The State undertook proceedings to acquire privately held property compulsorily.
predicates.affected_person_submitted_objections: A person affected by the proposed acquisition submitted objections to it.
predicates.effective_hearing_denied: The acquisition authority proceeded without giving the objector an effective opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: The statutory opportunity to be heard on an objection to a proposed land acquisition must be provided by the designated inquiry officer, and a hearing by the government does not substitute for it.
material_facts: An objection was filed asserting that the land was attached to a religious institution and fell within an excluded category.
The Collector did not hear the objector before submitting his report.
The government later heard the objection and rejected it before the declaration was upheld by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 places the duty to hear an objector on the Collector, and that duty is mandatory. A government decision on the objection cannot replace the hearing the Collector must provide. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Collector was required to hear the objector, and the government’s later hearing did not cure the failure. The declaration was quashed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_objection_case and objector_filed_objection and not collector_provided_hearing

predicates.land_acquisition_objection_case: The proceeding concerns a proposed acquisition of land and an objection to that proposed acquisition.
predicates.objector_filed_objection: A person whose land was proposed for acquisition submitted an objection to the proposal.
predicates.collector_provided_hearing: The official responsible for hearing and reporting on the objection gave the objector an opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: The acquisition process satisfied the statutory requirements concerning consideration of landowners’ objections where the objections were heard, reports were forwarded, and the appropriate government considered them before approving acquisition.
material_facts: The Land Acquisition Collector heard objections submitted by landowners.
The Collector forwarded the objections and reports to the appropriate government.
The appropriate government examined the objections and accompanying reports before approving the acquisition.
The Supreme Court reviewed the record and found no infirmity in the procedure followed.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires consideration of landowners’ objections through the prescribed process. On the record before it, the Court found that the objections had been heard and placed before the appropriate government with the Collector’s reports, and that the government had applied its mind. The Court expressly left the broader question of the scope and interpretation of Section 5A for other appeals.
members.conclusion: The procedure followed in considering the objections complied fully with the statutory requirements, and the asserted procedural infirmity was not established.

rule.if: is_land_acquisition_challenge and objections_heard_by_collector and reports_forwarded_to_government and government_considered_objections_and_reports

predicates.is_land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges an acquisition of land under a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.objections_heard_by_collector: The official responsible for considering landowners’ objections heard those objections.
predicates.reports_forwarded_to_government: The official forwarded the objections and the related report to the government responsible for deciding whether to proceed.
predicates.government_considered_objections_and_rep: The responsible government examined the objections and reports before approving the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition is not procedurally invalid where objectors receive an opportunity to be heard and their objections are considered.
material_facts: The landowners filed objections to the proposed acquisition.
The appointed officer heard the objectors and submitted a report to the State Government.
The High Court found that the objectors were given an adequate hearing and that their objections were considered.
members.legal_principle: Section 52(3) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 requires the appointed officer to give objectors an opportunity to be heard, consider objections and make any necessary inquiry before submitting the matter and a report to the State Government. The Court upheld the factual findings that these requirements had been met.
members.conclusion: The Court found no infirmity in the findings that the objectors had received an adequate opportunity to be heard and that their objections had been considered.

predicates.acquisition_objection_proceeding: The proceeding concerns objections made to a proposed land acquisition.
predicates.objectors_received_opportunity_to_be_hea: The objectors were given an opportunity to present their objections to the authorized officer.
predicates.objections_considered_by_authorized_offi: The authorized officer considered the objections before reporting to the government.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition is not procedurally vitiated when affected persons receive an opportunity to object and their objections are considered before the declaration.
material_facts: Notices inviting objections were issued to the affected farmers.
The respondent filed an objection, which was taken on record and considered before the declaration was published.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5-A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, the objection process must precede the declaration; the record showed that an objection was filed and considered before the declaration. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The claimed denial of an opportunity to object was not established, and the acquisition procedure was not vitiated on that basis.

rule.if: acquisition_writ_appeal and objection_notice_given and affected_person_objected and objection_considered_before_declaration

predicates.acquisition_writ_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a judgment reviewing land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.objection_notice_given: The acquiring authority gave affected persons notice and an opportunity to raise objections.
predicates.affected_person_objected: An affected person filed an objection to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.objection_considered_before_declaration: The acquiring authority considered the objection before issuing the acquisition declaration.

members.legal_issue: The statutory opportunity to object to a land acquisition requires effective consideration of the objections and the decision-making record when that consideration is challenged.
material_facts: The landowner filed objections disputing the public purpose and the suitability of the land for acquisition.
The Collector conducted an inquiry, made a report and recommendations, and a declaration was subsequently issued.
The landowner later challenged whether the State Government had applied its mind to the objections and the Collector's report.
The court directed production of the State's records, but they were not produced; the State said they were not readily traceable.
The affidavit filed for the State was affirmed by a Deputy Collector and did not establish that he was authorized to speak for the State or knew the relevant decision-making process.
members.legal_principle: Section 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, gives an affected owner a valuable, substantive right to an effective hearing on public purpose and suitability. The Collector must inquire into objections and report to the Government; the Government must independently apply its mind to the objections, report, recommendations and relevant record. When that decision is challenged, the State must justify it, and the court may call for the record. The Act is expropriatory and is strictly construed. The court relied on Article 300A; Munshi Singh v. Union of India; Madhya Pradesh Housing Board v. Mohd. Shafi; State of Tamil Nadu v. A. Mohammed Yousef; Bharat Singh v. State of Haryana; Shri Farid Ahmed Abdul Samad v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad; and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma.
members.conclusion: The State had to demonstrate the validity of its decision, including proper consideration of the objections and the Collector's report. The Collector's affidavit did not satisfy that burden, and the absence of the State's records left the challenged decision unsupported.

rule.if: land_acquisition_review and landowner_raised_objections and government_decision_challenged and government_records_not_produced

predicates.land_acquisition_review: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition seeks judicial review of the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.landowner_raised_objections: The affected landowner submitted objections to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.government_decision_challenged: The landowner challenged whether the government properly considered the objections and the inquiry report before deciding to proceed.
predicates.government_records_not_produced: The government did not produce the records needed to show how it reached the challenged decision.

members.legal_issue: The statutory opportunity to object to a proposed acquisition is a substantive safeguard requiring a genuine hearing, objective consideration of objections, and an independent governmental decision before a final declaration.
material_facts: The Cabinet had already decided to acquire the particular land before the preliminary notification and inquiry.
Landowners and cultivators filed objections, including objections concerning existing uses and livelihoods.
Some objectors were not afforded an effective opportunity to be heard, and the Collector rejected objections without adequately addressing them.
The State mechanically accepted the Collector’s report without independently considering the objections.
The proposed project was later abandoned.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5-A(2) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require the Collector to hear objectors and objectively report on their objections, and require the Government to consider that report and make its own decision before declaring the land needed. The Court relied on Raghubir Singh Sherawat v. State of Haryana, Surinder Singh Brar v. Union of India, Kamal Trading (P) Ltd. v. State of West Bengal, Usha Stud & Agricultural Farms (P) Ltd. v. State of Haryana, Gojer Brothers Private Ltd. v. State of West Bengal, and related decisions. Justice Arun Mishra explained that individual notices are not required for the Section 5-A inquiry if the prescribed public notifications are made, but that the hearing and consideration must be genuine and objective.
members.conclusion: Both opinions found the inquiry and consideration of objections defective and agreed that the acquisition proceedings were vitiated; the Supreme Court quashed the acquisition.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and objections_were_filed and acquisition_decision_preceded_effective_objection_review and objections_not_objectively_considered

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.objections_were_filed: People with interests in the land submitted objections to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_decision_preceded_effective_: The decision to acquire the particular land was made before the statutory objection process could operate meaningfully.
predicates.objections_not_objectively_considered: The Collector or Government failed to give the objections genuine consideration or the Government merely endorsed the Collector’s report.

members.legal_issue: A competent authority must decide objections to a proposed land acquisition after hearing the objectors by making a reasoned order and communicating it to them.
material_facts: The landowners filed written objections and later received a personal hearing, after which they submitted further written objections.
No decision allowing or disallowing the objections was passed after the hearing or communicated to the landowners.
The authority relied on an earlier letter issued before the hearing and on internal file notings recording rejection of the objections; it also stated that no order had been passed after the hearing.
members.legal_principle: Section 20D(2) of the Railways Act, 1989 requires the competent authority, after hearing the objections and making any necessary further inquiry, to allow or disallow them by order. The objection right is a substantive and valuable safeguard, analogous to the right under Section 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and must not be reduced to a formality. A quasi-judicial authority must apply its mind and give a reasoned decision; internal file notings are not an effective order unless finalized and communicated. The Court relied on Union of India v. Shivraj; Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai; Laxmi Devi v. State of Bihar; Raghbir Singh Sehrawat v. State of Haryana; Kranti Associates (P) Ltd. v. Masood Ahmed Khan; Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab; Shanti Sports Club v. Union of India; and Sethi Auto Service Station v. DDA. It also applied the principle that when a statute prescribes how an act must be done, it must be done in that manner, and strictly construed the expropriatory procedure.
members.conclusion: The mandatory objection procedure was not complied with. The pre-hearing letter was not a valid decision, and the internal file notings did not constitute an order deciding the objections.

rule.if: acquisition_objection_appeal and written_objections_submitted and hearing_granted and not post_hearing_reasoned_order and not decision_communicated

predicates.acquisition_objection_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a land acquisition on the basis of how objections to the proposed acquisition were handled.
predicates.written_objections_submitted: Interested landowners submitted written objections to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.hearing_granted: The competent authority gave the objectors an opportunity to be heard.
predicates.post_hearing_reasoned_order: After the hearing, the competent authority made a reasoned decision allowing or disallowing the objections.
predicates.decision_communicated: The competent authority communicated its decision to the objectors.

members.legal_issue: An objector who is clearly notified that a hearing will be available when objections are submitted, but elects to submit written objections by post without appearing, has been given the required opportunity of hearing when those objections are considered.
material_facts: The notice invited the objector to submit objections within the stated period and said that the objector or a representative or advocate would be heard when the objections were produced.
The objector sent written objections by post and did not appear personally or through a representative or advocate to produce them or request a hearing.
The objections were considered and a report was submitted to the government before the acquisition declaration was published.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act requires the Collector to provide an objector an opportunity to be heard in person or through an authorised person or pleader. The right to a hearing is mandatory, but an objector may choose not to avail himself of it. The Court accepted the principle in Shyam Nandan Prasad v. State of Bihar, (1993) 4 SCC 255. The reliance on Sir Farid Ahmed Abdul Samad v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmedabad, (1976) 3 SCC 719, did not require a further hearing date on these facts. Had the objector appeared and requested a hearing but not been heard, the question would have been different.
members.conclusion: The mandatory hearing requirement was complied with; in these circumstances, the authority was not required to fix a further hearing date, and the acquisition declaration was not invalid for want of a hearing.

rule.if: land_acquisition_objection_challenge and notice_offered_hearing_when_objections_were_produced and objector_sent_objections_by_post and objector_did_not_appear and objections_were_considered

predicates.land_acquisition_objection_challenge: A person challenged an acquisition on the ground that the required opportunity to be heard on objections was not provided.
predicates.notice_offered_hearing_when_objections_w: The authority notified the objector that the objector or a representative or advocate could be heard when the objections were produced.
predicates.objector_sent_objections_by_post: The objector submitted the objections by post rather than producing them in person or through a representative or advocate.
predicates.objector_did_not_appear: The objector did not appear, personally or through a representative or advocate, to produce the objections or seek a hearing.
predicates.objections_were_considered: The authority considered the written objections before proceeding with the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: An opportunity to be heard on acquisition objections is afforded when the objector is notified of a hearing, even if the objector does not establish that a representative attended.
material_facts: The company filed written objections to the proposed acquisition.
It was informed that the objections would be heard on a specified date at the Collector’s office.
The company did not establish through an affidavit or the relevant record that a representative attended the hearing.
The Collector’s report showed that objections were considered and recommendations were made, and the company’s written representation was in the file.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act requires the Collector to give an objector an opportunity of being heard, to consider objections, and to report recommendations to the appropriate Government. The Court assessed whether that opportunity was afforded on the evidence in the case and did not treat an unproved claim of attendance as establishing that it was denied.
members.conclusion: There was no force in the contention that the company had not been afforded an opportunity to be heard before the Collector made the report.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and written_objections_filed and hearing_opportunity_notified and no_reliable_proof_of_attendance

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition of land.
predicates.written_objections_filed: The landowner submits written objections to the proposed acquisition.
predicates.hearing_opportunity_notified: The objector is informed of a hearing at which the objections may be presented.
predicates.no_reliable_proof_of_attendance: The objector does not provide reliable evidence that a representative attended the hearing.

members.legal_issue: An erratum correcting the omission of land from an acquisition notification does not invalidate the declaration where the affected owners had the opportunity to participate in, and did participate in, the objection inquiry.
material_facts: An erratum added lands in survey numbers that had been omitted because they lay in adjacent villages.
The respondents had the opportunity to object and in fact participated in the inquiry into objections.
The respondents argued that no separate inquiry was held after publication of the erratum.
members.legal_principle: An erratum correcting an omission in the original notification dates back to that notification and is not a fresh notification. Where affected owners had the opportunity to participate and did participate in the inquiry under Section 5A and Rule 3, the declaration under Section 6 is not vitiated merely because there was no separate inquiry after the erratum.
members.conclusion: The erratum related back to the original notification and was not a fresh notification; the declaration was not invalidated by the absence of a separate inquiry after the erratum.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and erratum_corrected_omitted_land and owners_participated_in_objection_inquiry and no_separate_post_erratum_inquiry

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: An owner challenges a declaration made in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.erratum_corrected_omitted_land: An erratum corrected an omission of the owner’s land from the original notification.
predicates.owners_participated_in_objection_inquiry: The affected owners had the opportunity to object and participated in the inquiry into their objections.
predicates.no_separate_post_erratum_inquiry: No separate objection inquiry was conducted after publication of the erratum.
predicates.declaration_not_invalidated_by_lack_of_n: The declaration remains valid despite the absence of a separate inquiry after the erratum.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notification’s omission of a particular scheme purpose does not invalidate the acquisition where affected owners knew of that purpose and had an effective opportunity to object to it.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications and notice did not disclose that land was also being acquired for shopping sites.
The scheme included shopping sites, and the owners knew this when they filed objections.
The owners objected to the shopping-site component, including by challenging the shops and seeking the relevant land or a shop site.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 16 and 17 of the City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, the scheme is notified and affected persons may object before it is submitted for government approval. An omission in the notification is not a basis to invalidate the acquisition where it caused no prejudice to the affected owners’ opportunity to make representations.
members.conclusion: The omission caused no prejudice because the owners knew of and objected to the shopping-site purpose; the challenge to the notifications on that ground failed.

rule.if: acquisition_scheme_challenge and notification_omitted_scheme_purpose and affected_owners_knew_purpose and affected_owners_objected_to_purpose

predicates.acquisition_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenged an acquisition made under an improvement scheme.
predicates.notification_omitted_scheme_purpose: The notification did not disclose one of the purposes included in the scheme.
predicates.affected_owners_knew_purpose: The affected owners knew of the omitted purpose when they made their representations.
predicates.affected_owners_objected_to_purpose: The affected owners made representations opposing the omitted purpose.

members.legal_issue: A declaration that is conclusive as to the acquisition need and public purpose does not exclude judicial review of the decision-making process, including compliance with the opportunity to object.
material_facts: The landowner objected to the proposed acquisition, disputing the public purpose and the suitability of acquiring that land rather than other available land.
The land was proposed to be acquired for a corporation controlled by the State.
The landowner challenged the acquisition proceedings, including the consideration of the objections.
members.legal_principle: Article 300A permits compulsory acquisition only for a public purpose and with reasonable compensation. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 3(f)(iv), 4, 5-A and 6(3), must be read together: although Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive as to need and purpose, it does not immunize the decision-making process from review for illegality, irrationality or procedural impropriety, including total or substantial non-compliance with Section 5-A. The court relied on Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat; State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh; Om Prakash v. State of U.P.; Union of India v. Krishan Lal Arneja; and Union of India v. Mukesh Hans.
members.conclusion: The statutory conclusiveness of the declaration and the broad definition of public purpose did not bar judicial review. The court could examine whether the decision-making process complied with the law, including whether the objections were properly considered.

predicates.land_acquisition_review: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition seeks judicial review of the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.conclusive_acquisition_declaration: The acquiring authority has issued a declaration treated by statute as conclusive on the acquisition's need and purpose.

members.legal_issue: The conclusive effect of an acquisition declaration does not prevent judicial review where the acquisition involves a jurisdictional defect or a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The acquisition declaration stated that the land was needed for a public purpose.
The agreement placed the acquisition cost on the company, and the State’s nominal contribution was made only after the acquisition had been challenged.
The mandatory company-acquisition procedure had not been followed.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, makes a declaration conclusive evidence of the stated need, but does not insulate an action taken without jurisdiction or through a colourable exercise of power. Authorities must form their opinion on relevant materials and act within the statutory procedure; expropriatory legislation is strictly construed. The Court relied on R.L. Arora v. State of U.P., Somawanti v. State of Punjab, and John v. Rees.
members.conclusion: The declaration’s claimed conclusiveness did not shield the acquisition from review for jurisdictional error or colourable exercise of power.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landowners challenged a compulsory land acquisition in court.
predicates.declaration_claimed_conclusive: The State relied on the formal declaration as conclusive evidence of the stated acquisition purpose.
predicates.jurisdictional_or_colourable_defect_show: The acquisition record showed that authorities acted outside the governing procedure or used their power for a purpose not authorized by that procedure.

members.legal_issue: A person directly affected by a prejudicial building-control order must be given an opportunity to be heard before the order is made final.
material_facts: Permission had been granted for additions to buildings, and the building-control authority’s resolution granting permission could be suspended by a senior authority.

Following suspension, the statutory process provided for directions stopping construction and for the board to be given an opportunity to show cause why an interim direction should not be made absolute.
The affected owners, lessees or occupiers were not given a hearing before the final directions, although the board was given an opportunity to be heard.
The final directions could prevent construction or require alteration or demolition, with statutory compensation contemplated for certain losses.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution incorporates the audi alteram partem rule: an order prejudicial to a person and entailing civil consequences must not be made without an opportunity to be heard. Sections 52(1)(b) and 185(2) of the Cantonments Act, 1924 provide for suspension of the board’s resolution, an opportunity for the board to show cause, communication of the resulting direction to the owner, lessee or occupier, and compensation for specified losses. The compensation provision indicates that the affected person’s rights are at stake; hearing the board alone is inadequate because it may choose not to defend its resolution. The judgment notes that the High Court relied on State of Orissa v. Dr. Ms. Beenapani and refers to the subsequent expansion of Article 14 principles.
members.conclusion: The affected owners, lessees or occupiers were entitled to a hearing before the senior authority made the directions final; the appeals challenging that requirement were dismissed.

rule.if: building_sanction_review_proceeding and affected_non_board_person and adverse_civil_consequences and person_not_heard and board_only_heard

predicates.building_sanction_review_proceeding: The proceeding concerns review of permission for building work and a proposed direction to stop, prohibit, alter or demolish that work.
predicates.affected_non_board_person: A person other than the board owns, leases or occupies the affected land and is directly affected by the proposed direction.
predicates.adverse_civil_consequences: The proposed direction may prejudice that person’s interests or cause civil consequences.
predicates.person_not_heard: The directly affected person was not given an opportunity to be heard before the final direction was made.
predicates.board_only_heard: The board was given an opportunity to show cause, but the directly affected person was not.

members.legal_issue: A person whose assigned interest in land may be affected by a revisional decision must receive a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
material_facts: The State had assigned land to the Corporation after the land vested in the State.
The Corporation paid the occupancy price, received possession, and was undertaking construction activity.
The revisional authority set aside the order concerning the land without making the Corporation a party or giving it notice and an opportunity to be heard.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 34 of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976 requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard for a person affected by a revisional order. The Court applied the principles of natural justice and held that a party with an assigned interest and possession could not be treated as a mere beneficiary without an affected interest.
members.conclusion: The Corporation was an affected party and was entitled to notice and a hearing before the revisional authority decided the matter.

rule.if: administrative_revision_proceeding and third_party_has_assigned_interest and revision_decision_affects_interest and third_party_not_heard
