predicates.administrative_revision_proceeding: A public authority is considering whether to revise an administrative order or proceeding.
predicates.third_party_has_assigned_interest: A person other than the original disputants has received an interest in the subject matter from a public authority.
predicates.revision_decision_affects_interest: The proposed revisional decision may impair or undo that person's interest in the subject matter.
predicates.third_party_not_heard: The person whose interest may be affected was not given notice and a reasonable opportunity to present a case before the decision.

members.legal_issue: A law abolishing personal inams and extinguishing rights in them is constitutionally valid despite the absence of compensation in the law and does not impermissibly vary the terms of a grant recognizing the inam.
material_facts: The holder had acquired a personal inam from the original inamdar, who had received a grant recognizing it.
The challenged law abolished personal inams and extinguished rights in them.

The holder argued that the law was not protected by the constitutional provision concerning estates because the property was not an estate and no compensation was provided, and that the grant could not be varied by legislation.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed Gangadharrao Narayanrao Majumdar v. State of Bombay in upholding the law under Article 31-A. It rejected the argument that a grant recognizing an inam was immutable, following Thakur Jagannath Baksh Singh v. United Provinces and Maharaj Umeg Singh v. State of Bombay; Article 294(b) did not prevent the legislation.
members.conclusion: The constitutional challenge failed; the law was valid and protected by Article 31-A, and the grant did not prevent the State from legislating to alter the rights it recognized.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_inam_aboliti: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law that abolishes personal inams.
predicates.personal_inam_rights_extinguished_by_law: The challenged law extinguishes rights held under a personal inam.
predicates.recognized_grant_challenged_as_immutable: The holder relies on a grant recognizing the inam to argue that legislation cannot alter its terms.
predicates.compensation_or_estate_objection_raised: The holder argues that the law lacks constitutional protection because the property is not an estate or the law provides no compensation.

members.legal_issue: The right of an inam holder to retain the difference between the full land assessment and the reduced payment is a right in an estate protected from constitutional challenge under the estate-law protection.
material_facts: The holders possessed personal inams under which they paid less than the full land assessment and retained the difference.
The challenged enactment extinguished the personal inams, made the lands liable for full land revenue, and ended the holders’ right to retain that difference.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A(1)(a) protects laws providing for the acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or the extinguishment or modification of such rights, from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. Under Article 31-A(2)(a), an estate includes an inam; under Article 31-A(2)(b), rights in an estate include rights or privileges in respect of land revenue. The right also fell within section 3(5) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The inams were estates, and the holders’ right to retain the difference was a right in an estate and a right or privilege in respect of land revenue. The enactment’s extinguishment or modification of that right was protected by Article 31-A.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_law and inam_tenure and holder_retained_revenue_difference and law_extinguished_or_modified_that_right

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A person challenged the constitutionality of a law affecting rights held under a land tenure.
predicates.inam_tenure: The affected land tenure was an inam.
predicates.holder_retained_revenue_difference: The tenure holder paid less than the full land assessment and retained the difference.
predicates.law_extinguished_or_modified_that_right: The challenged law extinguished or modified the holder’s right to retain that difference.

members.legal_issue: The absence of compensation for ending the inam holder’s right to retain the difference between the full assessment and the reduced payment does not invalidate the enactment when the enactment is protected by the estate-law protection.
material_facts: The enactment made the inam lands liable for full assessment, ending the holders’ benefit from paying a reduced amount.

The enactment provided compensation for certain lands vested in the State but expressly denied compensation for the loss of the benefit arising from the difference between the reduced payment and the full assessment.
The enactment extinguished or modified rights in inams, which the Court held were estates and rights in estates protected by Article 31-A.
members.legal_principle: Article 31 provided for compensation, but Article 31-A protected laws concerning the acquisition of estates or rights in them, and the extinguishment or modification of those rights, from challenges under Article 31. Section 17(5) of the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, denied compensation for the loss caused by making previously exempt or partly exempt land subject to full assessment. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The absence of compensation for the loss of the revenue difference did not make the enactment unconstitutional, because Article 31-A protected it from an attack under Article 31.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_law and inam_tenure and law_ended_reduced_revenue_payment and law_extinguished_or_modified_rights_in_the_tenure

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: A person challenged the constitutionality of a law affecting rights held under a land tenure.
predicates.inam_tenure: The affected land tenure was an inam.
predicates.law_ended_reduced_revenue_payment: The law made the land liable for full assessment and ended the holder’s reduced payment.
predicates.law_extinguished_or_modified_rights_in_t: The law extinguished or modified rights held under the inam tenure.

members.legal_issue: The absence of compensation does not by itself invalidate an acquisition under an enactment protected by its inclusion in the constitutional schedule.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the acquisition on the ground that no compensation had been provided for his tree-cutting rights.
The enactment had been included in the Ninth Schedule following the Seventeenth Amendment to the Constitution.
The appellant did not dispute that the absence of compensation would not render the enactment or acquisition unconstitutional after that inclusion.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Seventeenth Amendment and the inclusion of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, in the Ninth Schedule. It recorded that, after that inclusion, the absence of compensation would not render the enactment or acquisition unconstitutional; the appellant did not contest that position.
members.conclusion: The Court treated the constitutional challenge based on the absence of compensation as not requiring determination, given the appellant’s acceptance that the enactment’s inclusion in the Ninth Schedule prevented that ground from invalidating the acquisition.

predicates.constitutional_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the constitutionality of an acquisition.
predicates.enactment_in_constitutional_schedule: The law authorizing the acquisition is included in a constitutional schedule that protects it from the asserted challenge.
predicates.compensation_not_provided: The governing law provides no compensation for the acquired interest.

members.legal_issue: The absence of compensation for unexploited mineral reserves does not make the acquisition law unconstitutional.
material_facts: The minerals for which compensation was claimed had not been exploited or leased when the estate vested, so the former owner had no existing right to income from them at that time.
The statutory scheme provided compensation for existing rights and income, and the Act had been included in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: The Act must be read fairly and as a whole; the court cannot supply compensation that the legislature did not provide. Since the claimed right was not existing at vesting, the absence of compensation for it did not deprive the former owner of an existing right without compensation or expose the Act to constitutional invalidity. The Court also noted that the Act had been incorporated in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Act was not unconstitutional merely because it provided no compensation for minerals that had not been exploited.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law acquiring an estate.
predicates.mineral_right_not_existing_at_vesting: The claimed right to income from the minerals did not exist when the estate vested.
predicates.compensation_provided_for_existing_right: The law provides compensation for existing rights and sources of income.
predicates.law_included_in_constitutional_protectiv: The law was included in a constitutional schedule that the Court treated as relevant to its validity.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of property declared to be evacuee property under a law protected by the constitutional exception is not invalidated by the absence of an agreement providing for compensation.
material_facts: The property had been declared evacuee property and was acquired by a published government notification for the rehabilitation of displaced persons.
The applicable law provided for compensation according to principles and in a manner agreed between the governments of the two countries, but no such agreement had been reached.
The constitutional exception covered laws concerning evacuee property made in pursuance of an agreement or otherwise.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(5)(b)(iii) excluded from the operation of Article 31(2) laws concerning property declared by law to be evacuee property, whether made pursuant to an agreement with another country or otherwise. Sections 12 and 13 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1951 provided for acquisition and for compensation in accordance with principles and a manner agreed between the governments; without that agreement, compensation was not payable under Section 13. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was not open to challenge under Article 31(2), and compensation could not be claimed under the applicable law in the absence of the contemplated agreement.

rule.if: challenge_to_acquisition_of_evacuee_property and acquisition_law_covers_evacuee_property and constitutional_exception_covers_such_laws and not compensation_agreement_exists

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_of_evacuee_prop: A person challenges the acquisition of property that had been declared evacuee property.
predicates.acquisition_law_covers_evacuee_property: The law under which the property was acquired applies to property declared evacuee property.
predicates.constitutional_exception_covers_such_law: The constitutional exception protects laws concerning evacuee property whether made pursuant to an agreement with another country or otherwise.
predicates.compensation_agreement_exists: The governments whose agreement is required have agreed on the principles and manner for paying compensation.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition scheme for slum clearance is not invalid merely because it does not provide solatium for compulsory acquisition.
material_facts: The slum-clearance acquisition provisions were substantially similar to the other special-purpose acquisition scheme, except that they provided no solatium.
The slum-clearance provisions did not require compensation to be paid in instalments.
The Court considered that the acquired land was slum land and that the public interest in maintaining public services also mattered.
members.legal_principle: In Prakash Amichand Shah v. State of Gujarat, a Constitution Bench held that there is no general rule requiring the State always to pay solatium in addition to reasonable compensation, because the public interest is also important. The Court applied that principle to acquisition of slum land and found the absence of solatium not unreasonable.
members.conclusion: The slum-clearance acquisition provisions were intra vires the Constitution notwithstanding the absence of solatium.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_slum_clearan: A person challenges the constitutionality of a statutory scheme for acquiring land for slum clearance.
predicates.scheme_provides_reasonable_compensation: The scheme provides compensation for the acquired land that is otherwise reasonable.
predicates.scheme_does_not_require_installment_paym: The scheme does not require compensation to be paid in instalments.
predicates.scheme_provides_no_solatium: The scheme does not provide an additional payment because the acquisition is compulsory.

members.legal_issue: A statutory omission of solatium and interest from an acquisition compensation scheme does not, on that basis, violate constitutional protections of property or equality.
material_facts: The owners argued that the denial of solatium and interest was discriminatory because owners whose property was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 could receive those payments.
They also argued that the omission was unconstitutional because property rights remained fundamental rights in the relevant constitutional setting.
The governing acquisition statute contained its own compensation scheme and omitted solatium and interest.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed the constitutional ruling in Union of India v. Hari Kishan Khosla and held that the statutory omission did not violate Article 14 or Article 31. Different statutory acquisition schemes may prescribe different principles of compensation; the omission of additions provided by another statute does not itself establish unconstitutional discrimination.
members.conclusion: The omission did not violate Article 14 or Article 31 as applicable to the relevant constitutional setting.

predicates.acquisition_appeal: The proceeding challenges compensation awarded for property acquired under a statutory scheme.
predicates.different_compensation_schemes: The acquisition scheme at issue prescribes compensation differently from another statutory scheme that provides additional payments.
predicates.statutory_omission: The governing scheme omits additional payments that are available under the other scheme.

members.legal_issue: The absence of solatium does not by itself make an otherwise comparable land-acquisition regime unreasonable under the equality guarantee.
material_facts: The challenged slum-clearance provisions were substantially similar to the welfare acquisition provisions considered by the Court.
The slum-clearance provisions did not provide for payment of compensation in instalments.
They also did not provide for solatium in addition to compensation.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require the State invariably to pay solatium in addition to reasonable compensation. The public interest in providing and maintaining public services is also relevant; Prakash Amichand Shah v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The slum-clearance acquisition provisions were constitutional; the absence of solatium did not make them unreasonable.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_a_special_sl: A party challenges the constitutionality of a special regime for acquiring land for slum-related purposes.
predicates.compensation_is_not_deferred_in_instalme: The regime does not require compensation to be deferred through installment payments.
predicates.the_only_relevant_difference_is_no_solat: The regime is otherwise comparable to an acquisition regime upheld by the Court, and the relevant difference is that it provides no solatium.

members.legal_issue: The absence of a solatium under a town-planning scheme does not, by itself, make its compensation mechanism discriminatory.
material_facts: The challenged scheme provided compensation and financial adjustments under its own integrated planning mechanism but did not provide the solatium available under the Land Acquisition Act.
The scheme involved automatic vesting upon the final scheme taking effect, possible allotment of reconstituted plots, and financial adjustments between landowners and the local authority.
It was not shown that the compensation payable was illusory or unreal.
members.legal_principle: A town-planning scheme that operates through automatic vesting, reconstituted plots and financial adjustments is not equivalent to a conventional acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act. The absence of solatium does not alone establish discrimination, and the public interest in providing and maintaining public services is also relevant. The Court distinguished Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, State of Kerala v. T.N. Peter and P.C. Goswami v. Collector of Darrang.
members.conclusion: The absence of solatium did not make the town-planning scheme discriminatory, and the compensation mechanism was not shown to be illusory or unreal.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_challenge and automatic_vesting_with_reconstitution and no_solarium_provided and compensation_not_shown_illusory

predicates.town_planning_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a statutory town-planning scheme.
predicates.automatic_vesting_with_reconstitution: The scheme provides for land to vest by operation of law and allows for reconstituted plots or related financial adjustments.
predicates.no_solarium_provided: The scheme does not provide an additional payment of the kind sometimes awarded alongside compensation.
predicates.compensation_not_shown_illusory: The challenger has not shown that the compensation payable is unreal or illusory.

members.legal_issue: The absence of provisions for solatium and interest in the compensation scheme for acquisition of previously requisitioned property does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The land was requisitioned for a military purpose, and the owners were out of possession while the government possessed and used it.
The land was later acquired under a special statutory scheme that prescribed compensation by reference to the property's condition when it was requisitioned.
The owners had received compensation for the period during which the land was requisitioned.
The owners challenged the absence of solatium and interest by comparing the scheme with the general land-acquisition scheme.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification founded on intelligible differentia that bears a rational relation to the legislation's lawful object. The Court applied Sections 30 and 31 of the Defence of India Act, 1971, and contrasted them with Sections 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It relied on Union of India v. Hari Krishan Khosla and Union of India v. Dhanwanti Devi, which held that solatium and interest under the Land Acquisition Act are not read into a distinct acquisition statute. It distinguished the Nagpur Improvement Trust decisions because those statutes incorporated the Land Acquisition Act's compensation scheme, unlike this self-contained scheme.
members.conclusion: The different compensation schemes were based on a reasonable classification, so the special scheme was not invalid under Article 14 and did not entitle the owners to solatium or interest under the general land-acquisition law.

rule.if: special_requisition_acquisition_case and land_was_requisitioned_before_acquisition and government_possessed_land_during_requisition and owners_were_compensated_for_requisition and acquisition_purpose_was_limited

predicates.special_requisition_acquisition_case: The proceeding challenged the compensation scheme for property acquired after it had been requisitioned under a special statutory scheme.
predicates.land_was_requisitioned_before_acquisitio: The government requisitioned the land before later acquiring it.
predicates.government_possessed_land_during_requisi: The government possessed and used the land while it was requisitioned, leaving the owners out of possession.
predicates.owners_were_compensated_for_requisition: The owners received compensation for the period in which the land was requisitioned.
predicates.acquisition_purpose_was_limited: The statutory scheme permitted acquisition in limited circumstances connected with works constructed during requisition or excessive restoration costs.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional power to acquire property does not itself carry an implied obligation to provide compensation, and a protected acquisition law cannot be challenged for failing to provide or adequately provide compensation.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of estates and specified a compensation scheme that the proprietors argued was illusory or inadequate.
The legislation was pending in the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced, received the President’s assent, and was included in the constitutional schedule protecting specified laws.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) expressly imposes the compensation requirement, while entries 36 of List II and 42 of List III are legislative heads and do not independently impose that duty. Article 31(4) bars challenges to a qualifying law on the ground that it contravenes article 31(2); articles 31-A and 31-B protect the specified acquisition laws from challenges based on Part III. In Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India, the Court upheld the First Amendment that inserted articles 31-A and 31-B. The Court held that Julius v. Bishop of Oxford does not make a legislative entry a power coupled with a duty to legislate.
members.conclusion: The compensation obligation does not arise by implication from the legislative entries on acquisition or compensation; the challenge to the adequacy or absence of compensation was barred by the constitutional protections applicable to the Act.

rule.if: acquisition_law_challenge and (challenge_based_on_missing_or_inadequate_compensation) and (pending_at_constitution_start and presidential_assent and constitutionally_protected_law)

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: A party challenged a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.challenge_based_on_missing_or_inadequate: The challenger claimed that the law failed to provide compensation or provided inadequate compensation.
predicates.pending_at_constitution_start: The acquisition bill was pending in the State Legislature when the Constitution commenced.
predicates.presidential_assent: The bill was reserved for and received the President’s assent.
predicates.constitutionally_protected_law: The law was among the laws protected by the constitutional provisions applicable to specified acquisition laws.

members.legal_issue: The legislative entries authorizing acquisition do not themselves imply requirements of public purpose or compensation, and a state acquisition law within the legislature’s assigned subject is not outside its competence on that basis.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the state legislature’s competence to enact the acquisition law under the relevant legislative entries as they stood when the law was enacted.

They argued that the word “acquisition” necessarily carried requirements of public purpose and compensation, and that the reference to another legislative entry imposed those requirements on state legislation.
The law acquired the inamdars’ rights in estates as part of agrarian reform and had received the President’s assent.

The Constitution separately stated safeguards concerning public purpose and compensation for acquisition, while the legislative entries allocated lawmaking subjects and provided for possible displacement of state legislation by Union legislation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) expressly addressed the safeguards for acquisition, leaving no basis to imply those safeguards into the legislative entries; the maxim expressum facit cessare tacitum supports that reading. The entries define and delimit legislative fields. The words making state acquisition legislation subject to another entry mean that Union legislation may displace or override it, not that the entry itself imposes public-purpose and compensation restrictions. The Court also held that legislation protected by Article 31A cannot be struck down for noncompliance with Article 31(2).
members.conclusion: The word “acquisition” in the legislative entry bears its natural meaning and does not import requirements of public purpose or compensation; the reference to the other entry concerns the possibility that Union legislation may displace state legislation. The law was not beyond the state legislature’s competence.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_state_acquisition_law and law_acquires_estate_rights and law_is_part_of_agrarian_reform and state_law_received_presidential_assent and constitution_separately_states_acquisition_safeguards

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_acquis: A challenger asks a court to invalidate a state law authorizing acquisition on the ground that the state legislature lacked competence.
predicates.law_acquires_estate_rights: The law transfers estate interests or rights in estates to the State, or extinguishes or modifies those rights.
predicates.law_is_part_of_agrarian_reform: The law forms part of a legislative program to reform agrarian relationships, including by abolishing intermediaries.
predicates.state_law_received_presidential_assent: The state law received the President’s assent.
predicates.constitution_separately_states_acquisiti: The constitutional text states safeguards for property acquisition separately from the legislative entries that allocate lawmaking subjects.
predicates.state_law_within_legislative_competence: The state law is not beyond the state legislature’s competence on the ground that the acquisition entry itself implies public-purpose or compensation requirements.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional heads authorizing compulsory acquisition do not themselves imply an obligation to provide compensation, and a legislature’s power to make a law under a legislative head is not a duty to legislate.
material_facts: The acquisition laws were challenged on the ground that the legislative entries concerning acquisition and compensation inherently required just compensation.
The relevant constitutional provisions separately addressed legislative power, compensation requirements, and protection for specified acquisition laws.
members.legal_principle: The legislative entries are heads defining legislative competence, not implied substantive restrictions or duties. Article 31(2) expressly states the compensation requirement, while entries 36 of List II and 42 of List III identify legislative subjects. The court relied on the structure of articles 31(2), 31(4), 31-A and 31-B, and rejected the analogy to a power coupled with a duty in Julius v. Bishop of Oxford and Chief Controlling Revenue Authority v. Maharashtra Sugar Mills Ltd.
members.conclusion: The acquisition entries do not themselves impose an obligation to provide compensation, and the power to legislate on compensation is not a duty to enact a compensation law; the challenge on that basis failed.

predicates.a_legislative_competence_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a legislature had authority to enact a law concerning compulsory acquisition.
predicates.compulsory_acquisition_law: The challenged law authorizes the State to take property without the owner's consent.
predicates.challenge_claims_acquisition_entry_impli: The challenger argues that the legislative subject of acquisition itself requires the law to provide compensation.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of land through compulsory acquisition is not excluded from legislative competence merely because the measure is described as nationalization.
material_facts: The law transferred proprietary land rights to the State.
The petitioners argued that nationalization was a separate legislative subject and that general acquisition did not cover it.
The challenged measure operated through compulsory acquisition.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the cited passage from Stephen’s Commentaries, read in full, did not support excluding nationalization from acquisition, and noted that properties had been nationalized in various countries through powers of compulsory acquisition. It applied entry 36 of List II of the Seventh Schedule.
members.conclusion: The nationalization argument was rejected; the acquisition was within the relevant legislative subject.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: A person challenged a law that compulsorily acquires property.
predicates.law_transfers_property_to_state_by_compu: The law transfers property to the State through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.challenge_labels_measure_nationalization: The challenger argues that the transfer is nationalization rather than acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A landlord proceeding under the special rent-control procedure for a qualifying eviction need not first obtain permission under the slum-area legislation, even when the premises are in a slum area.
material_facts: The premises were within a designated slum area.
The landlord had previously sought permission to institute eviction proceedings under the slum-area legislation, but permission was refused and the refusal was upheld on appeal.
The landlord later brought an eviction proceeding under the special rent-control procedure for a qualifying personal need.
The special rent-control provisions contained a non-obstante clause and were enacted after the relevant slum-area provisions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the non-obstante provisions in sections 14A and 25A–25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and held that the later special procedure prevails over inconsistent provisions, including section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956. It relied on Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal, Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti, and Vinod Kumar Chowdhry v. Narain Devi Taneja, and approved Smt. Krishna Devi Nigam v. Shyam Babu Gupta.
members.conclusion: The special rent-control procedure overrides inconsistent requirements of the slum-area legislation, so prior permission from the competent authority was not required for the eviction proceeding.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_special_rent_p: The landlord brings an eviction proceeding under a special procedure for a qualifying ground of eviction.
predicates.premises_are_in_a_slum_area: The premises are located in an area subject to a statutory slum-area regime.
predicates.special_procedure_conflicts_with_prior_p: The special eviction procedure conflicts with a requirement to obtain prior permission under another law.

members.legal_issue: A special expedited eviction procedure for landlords required to leave allotted government accommodation takes precedence over an earlier law requiring permission before eviction proceedings concerning premises in a protected area.
material_facts: The landlord occupied residential accommodation allotted by the government and was required to vacate it because he owned a residential house.
Tenants occupied part of the landlord’s house, which was situated in a slum area.
The landlord sought eviction through the special procedure available to a landlord required to vacate allotted accommodation.
The tenants argued that the proceeding could not be maintained without prior written permission from the competent authority.
The later special procedure included provisions giving it overriding effect over inconsistent provisions in the rent-control law and other laws.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 14A and 25A–25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, a qualifying landlord’s right to immediate possession is enforced by the special procedure in Chapter IIIA, whose overriding clauses prevail over inconsistent provisions in that Act or another law. Sections 19 and 39 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act were inconsistent to the extent that they required prior permission for these proceedings. Where laws in the same field contain non obstante clauses, their conflict is resolved by considering their language, purpose and policy; the specific purpose of the later special procedure would be frustrated by the prior-permission requirement, and the later enactment therefore prevails. The Court followed Sri Ram Narain v. The Simla Banking & Industrial Co. Ltd. on resolving such conflicts by reference to purpose and policy, and distinguished Jyoti Pershad v. The Administrator for the Union territory of Delhi because it did not consider the later amendments. The Court did not rest its decision on implied repeal.
members.conclusion: The provisions conferring the special right and prescribing its procedure prevailed over the permission requirement in the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act; prior permission was not required, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: special_summary_eviction_proceeding and landlord_required_to_leave_allotted_home and landlord_owns_rented_home and rented_home_in_protected_area and competing_law_requires_permission and later_law_has_override_clause

predicates.special_summary_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding under a special expedited procedure.
predicates.landlord_required_to_leave_allotted_home: A landlord occupying accommodation allotted by a public authority was required to leave it because the landlord owned residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_owns_rented_home: The landlord owned the residential premises occupied by the tenant.
predicates.rented_home_in_protected_area: The rented premises were situated in an area subject to special legal protection.
predicates.competing_law_requires_permission: Another applicable law required written permission before an eviction proceeding concerning premises in the protected area could be instituted.
predicates.later_law_has_override_clause: A later enactment establishing the special procedure stated that it would prevail over inconsistent rules in other laws.

members.legal_issue: Prior permission under slum-protection legislation was not required to execute a rent-control eviction decree based on bona fide requirement.
material_facts: The eviction decree was based on the landlord’s bona fide requirement.
The decree-holder sought permission under slum-protection legislation before seeking execution.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on Ravi Dutt v. Rattan Lal, which held that the Delhi Rent Control Act provisions in Chapter III-A concerning eviction for bona fide requirement had overriding effect and rendered the Slum Act inapplicable. Accordingly, section 19 of the Slum Act did not require permission to execute this decree.
members.conclusion: The court held that permission under the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act was not required to execute this decree.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_execution: The proceeding seeks execution of an eviction decree made under rent-control legislation.
predicates.decree_based_on_bona_fide_requirement: The eviction decree was made on the ground that the landlord required the premises bona fide.

members.legal_issue: The special procedure for specified landlord-need eviction proceedings displaces an inconsistent requirement to obtain prior permission from a slum-area authority.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an eviction order on the ground of bona fide requirement under the special rent-control procedure.
The appeal raised whether the landlord had to obtain prior permission from the competent authority under the slum-area law before instituting eviction proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1)(e), 14A, 25A, 25B and 25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, are special provisions; their non-obstante clause gives priority to the special procedure over inconsistent existing law. Chapter III-A therefore renders the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, inapplicable to the extent of inconsistency, and section 19(1)(a) permission is not a prerequisite to proceedings under sections 14(1)(e) or 14A. The Court relied on Ravi Dutt Sharma v. Ratan Lal Bhargava, [1984] 2 SCR 614.
members.conclusion: For proceedings covered by the special rent-control provisions, the slum-area law does not apply to the extent of inconsistency, and prior permission from the competent authority is not required.

predicates.landlord_seeks_eviction_under_special_pr: The landlord seeks eviction through the special procedure for specified landlord-need grounds.
predicates.special_procedure_has_priority_over_othe: The procedure governing the eviction claim expressly gives its procedure priority over other laws.
predicates.other_law_requires_prior_slum_authority_: Another applicable law requires the landlord to obtain permission from a slum-area authority before bringing the eviction proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The public-premises eviction regime prevails over rent-control protections where both regimes would otherwise apply to premises and an occupant whose authority has ended.
material_facts: The disputed premises fell within the geographic and substantive reach of both enactments.
The occupants had entered as tenants but remained after their tenancies expired or were terminated.

The rent-control enactment regulated landlord-tenant relations, while the public-premises enactment provided a procedure for recovering public premises and barred court proceedings concerning eviction of unauthorised occupants.
Both enactments were enacted by Parliament, and the public-premises enactment was later.
members.legal_principle: Rent control legislation falls within entries 6, 7, and 13 of List III; the public-premises enactment, insofar as it concerns lessees or licensees of premises belonging to entities other than the central government, also rests on concurrent-list powers. Thus, the conflict is not resolved merely by reference to different legislative lists. Both enactments are special in relation to their respective subjects, so the generalia specialibus non derogant exception does not resolve the conflict. Applying the later-law principle, and considering the enactments’ purposes and language, the Court held that the public-premises enactment prevails. Section 15 bars jurisdiction over eviction of unauthorised occupants; the Court considered that provision alongside Sections 14, 22, 50, and 54 of the Delhi Rent Control Act. It relied on J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, U.P. State Electricity Board v. Hari Shankar Jain, Life Insurance Corporation v. D.J. Bahadur, Shri Ram Narain v. Simla Banking and Industrial Co., Kumaon Motor Owners’ Union v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal, Jain Ink Manufacturing Company v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, and the stated objects of both enactments. It rejected the suggestion that the rent-control procedure must first be completed under V. Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, because that would confer duplicative protection inconsistent with the later enactment’s purpose.
members.conclusion: To the extent the enactments cover the same premises, the public-premises eviction regime overrides the rent-control enactment, and an unauthorised occupant cannot invoke rent-control protection.

predicates.overlapping_rent_control_and_public_prem: The proceeding concerns a claim that rent-control protection prevents eviction under a public-premises recovery regime.
predicates.premises_within_both_regimes: The premises and occupation would otherwise fall within the reach of both regimes.
predicates.occupant_authority_ended: The occupant’s authority to remain in the premises has expired or been terminated.

members.legal_issue: The special eviction regime for public premises prevails over the general tenant-protection regime where their application overlaps.
material_facts: The premises were owned by a public corporation and fell within the public-premises eviction regime.
The occupant argued that the tenant-protection law barred recovery of possession except through its own procedure.
The public-premises law was enacted after the tenant-protection law, although it was given retrospective effect from an earlier date.
The public-premises law applied to a limited class of publicly owned premises and provided a summary eviction procedure; the tenant-protection law had broader application.
members.legal_principle: The court considered sections 14, 3(a), and 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. It held that retrospective operation does not change the actual date of enactment; the later, limited and special public-premises regime prevails over the broader tenant-protection regime. Conflicts between laws containing overriding clauses are resolved by their objects, purposes, and policies. The court relied on Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal and Shri Ram Narain v. The Simla Banking & Industrial Co. Ltd.; it also referred to Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab and Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay regarding the distinct class covered and the summary procedure.
members.conclusion: The public-premises eviction law overrides the tenant-protection law, and the latter does not bar proceedings under the former for premises within its scope.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a special regime for publicly owned premises.
predicates.premises_belong_to_covered_public_body: The premises belong to a public body covered by the special eviction regime.
predicates.limited_public_property_eviction_regime_: A later-enacted regime provides a distinct eviction process for a limited class of publicly owned premises.
predicates.overlapping_tenant_protection_regime_is_: A separate tenant-protection regime covers a wider range of premises and its procedure overlaps with the public-premises process.

members.legal_issue: The special eviction regime for public premises prevails over a conflicting statutory restriction on eviction proceedings in slum areas.
material_facts: The premises were within the scope of the public-premises eviction regime.
The occupant argued that the slum-area law required prior written permission before instituting eviction proceedings.
The public-premises eviction law was enacted after the slum-area law as amended and prescribed a forum for eviction of unauthorised occupants of covered premises.
The court found the two regimes directly in conflict and treated the public-premises law as a later law with a limited, special scope.
members.legal_principle: Section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, as amended, required prior written permission to institute certain eviction proceedings concerning buildings or land in slum areas. The court held that this requirement directly conflicted with the forum and eviction process provided for covered premises by the later Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. Applying the same reasoning used to resolve the conflict with the tenant-protection law, the later and specially limited public-premises regime prevailed.
members.conclusion: The public-premises eviction law overrides the conflicting slum-area restriction for premises within its scope.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_proceeding and premises_within_special_public_eviction_regime and slum_area_eviction_restriction_applies and eviction_regimes_directly_conflict and public_eviction_regime_is_later_and_limited

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a special regime for publicly owned premises.
predicates.premises_within_special_public_eviction_: The premises are covered by the special public-premises eviction regime.
predicates.slum_area_eviction_restriction_applies: A separate rule requires prior permission before instituting eviction proceedings concerning the premises.
predicates.eviction_regimes_directly_conflict: The permission requirement conflicts with the forum or process prescribed by the public-premises regime.
predicates.public_eviction_regime_is_later_and_limi: The public-premises regime was enacted later and governs a limited class of premises.

members.legal_issue: A landlord need not obtain the District Magistrate’s permission to sue for eviction on a ground expressly listed among the statutory exceptions to that permission requirement.
material_facts: The landlords sued for eviction on the ground that the tenant had willfully failed to pay rent within the required period after service of a demand notice.
The eviction ground was one of the grounds listed as an exception to the permission requirement.
The landlords had not obtained the District Magistrate’s permission before filing the suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the U.P. Cantonment (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1952 requires permission for an eviction suit based on a ground other than those specified in clauses (a) to (f), but not for a suit based on one of those specified grounds. The Court followed Bhagwan Dass v. Paras Nath, which interpreted the materially similar provision in section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947.
members.conclusion: The suit was maintainable without the District Magistrate’s permission because it was brought on a specified statutory ground.

predicates.eviction_suit_under_cantonment_rent_cont: A landlord brought an eviction suit governed by a rent-control law applicable to cantonment premises.
predicates.eviction_ground_in_listed_exceptions: The landlord relied on a ground that the law expressly lists as an exception to the requirement for prior permission.

members.legal_issue: A landlord does not need prior permission from the District Magistrate to bring an eviction suit on a ground expressly listed in the rent-control statute.
material_facts: The landlords brought an eviction suit on the ground of the tenant’s wilful failure to pay rent after a demand notice.
The landlords had not obtained the District Magistrate’s permission before filing the suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the U.P. Cantonments (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1952 requires the District Magistrate’s permission for an eviction suit only when the landlord relies on a ground other than those specified in clauses (a) to (f). Applying the interpretation of the materially identical provision in Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, the Court relied on Bhagwan Dass v. Paras Nath.
members.conclusion: Permission was not required because the suit was brought on a ground specified in Section 14(1)(a); the Civil Court could entertain it.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: A landlord filed a suit seeking eviction of a tenant under a rent-control law.
predicates.eviction_ground_is_statutorily_listed: The landlord relied on a ground that the rent-control law expressly lists as a basis for eviction.
predicates.prior_district_magistrate_permission_not: The landlord may bring the eviction suit without first obtaining permission from the District Magistrate.

members.legal_issue: A landlord seeking eviction under the special remedy for a returning non-resident owner satisfies the required ownership period, as against a tenant who admits having been inducted by that landlord and remains in possession, without separately proving title against that tenant through documents linking the property to the leased premises.
material_facts: The landlord was a returning non-resident who sought the shop for his own use, and the court accepted his non-resident status and need for it.

The tenant admitted that he occupied the shop as a tenant under the landlord, though he disputed the year in which the tenancy began; even on the tenant’s account, the tenancy began more than five years before the eviction petition.
The tenant continued to occupy the shop and did not claim that a paramount title holder had become entitled to it or that the landlord’s title had ended after the tenancy began.
The landlord’s sale deeds had been proved, but the lower courts considered him not to have sufficiently linked them to the land beneath the shop.
members.legal_principle: Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Land Restriction Act, 1949 permits a returning non-resident Indian owner to seek possession of a let residential or non-residential building required for the owner’s or a dependent’s use, subject to the five-year ownership threshold and the statutory limits on exercising the right. Under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, a tenant cannot, during the tenancy, deny that the landlord had title when the tenancy began. Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath, (1976) 4 SCC 184, reiterates this rule and explains that the landlord’s title is ordinarily irrelevant in an eviction suit. The stated exceptions include valid attornment to a paramount title holder and the landlord’s subsequent loss of title. These general rules of evidence and estoppel apply to tenants of non-resident Indian owners as well.
members.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from denying the landlord’s title while the tenancy continued and possession had not been surrendered. The landlord’s ownership period was therefore established as against the tenant, the lower courts’ decisions were set aside, and eviction was ordered.

rule.if: returned_nonresident_owner_seeks_personal_use_eviction and tenant_admitted_induction_by_landlord and tenancy_continues and tenant_has_not_surrendered_possession and not tenant_shows_paramount_title_attornment and not tenant_shows_subsequent_loss_of_landlord_title

predicates.returned_nonresident_owner_seeks_persona: A returning non-resident owner seeks eviction of a tenant because the owner requires the let premises for personal use or for the use of a dependent.
predicates.tenant_admitted_induction_by_landlord: The tenant admitted that the landlord inducted the tenant into possession as a tenant, even if the tenant disputed when the tenancy began.
predicates.tenancy_continues: The landlord-tenant relationship remained in force when the title dispute was raised.
predicates.tenant_has_not_surrendered_possession: The tenant had not returned possession of the premises to the landlord.
predicates.tenant_shows_paramount_title_attornment: The tenant showed that the tenancy had been validly attorned to a person holding paramount title.
predicates.tenant_shows_subsequent_loss_of_landlord: The tenant showed that the landlord lost title after the tenant was inducted.

members.legal_issue: A landlord-owner seeking possession of non-residential accommodation under the special bona fide-requirement procedure need not plead ownership or independently prove it to succeed.
material_facts: The landlord applied for possession of a shop, saying it was needed to start a business for her sons.
The tenant disputed the landlord’s ownership and bona fide requirement.
The Rent Controller found for the landlord on ownership and bona fide requirement, but the High Court set aside the eviction order because it considered independent proof of ownership necessary.

The special procedure provided for a tenant to obtain leave to contest and treated the landlord’s statements as admitted if leave was not obtained; it also presumed bona fide requirement unless the contrary was proved.
members.legal_principle: Reading Section 23A(b) in the context of the expedited procedure in Sections 23B, 23C and 23D, the court held that requiring a separate pleading and proof of ownership would frustrate the legislative scheme. Section 116 of the Evidence Act may prevent a tenant from denying the landlord’s title. The court referred to Stringer’s Estate, Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath and Krishna v. Barabani Coal Concern Ltd. It also observed that a landlord seeking possession on the same ground under Section 12(1)(f) was not required to plead and prove ownership in that manner.
members.conclusion: The ownership language in Section 23A(b) enables an owner-landlord to apply for possession; it does not require the landlord to plead ownership or adduce independent evidence proving it. A tenant may contest ownership only if not barred from doing so by tenant’s estoppel.

predicates.special_nonresidential_eviction_proceedi: A landlord seeks possession of non-residential accommodation through a special procedure based on bona fide need for a business.
predicates.landlord_is_owner: The applicant landlord owns the accommodation for which possession is sought.

members.legal_issue: An eviction order founded principally on the landlord’s bona fide personal requirement remains an order on that ground when demolition and reconstruction are also mentioned, so the statutory duty to provide the tenants with accommodation in the new building does not apply.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession to locate a gold and silver ornaments factory on the premises after demolishing and reconstructing the building.
The lower courts found the landlord’s personal requirement bona fide and ordered eviction under both the personal-requirement ground and the reconstruction-related ground.
The tenants argued that the reconstruction-related ground made the statutory obligation to provide accommodation in the new building applicable.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 12(1)(f) and 12(1)(h) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, the substance and principal basis of the eviction order determine which ground it rests on. Section 18 was not attracted because the order was substantially based on section 12(1)(f). Applying Ramnilal P. Mehta v. Indradaman Amritlal Sheth, AIR 1964 SC 1676, the Court held that a bona fide requirement for the landlord’s occupation remains such a ground whether occupation is to be without alterations or after necessary alterations; the corresponding Bombay provision was section 13(1)(g).
members.conclusion: The eviction order was in substance based on the landlord’s bona fide personal requirement; the additional reference to the reconstruction-related ground did not make it an order solely on that ground, and the statutory duty to provide accommodation in the new building did not apply.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The tenants challenged an order evicting them from the premises.
predicates.bona_fide_personal_need_primary_ground: The courts found that the landlord principally required the premises bona fide for the landlord’s own proposed use.
predicates.reconstruction_ground_also_cited: The eviction order also referred to a ground involving demolition, reconstruction, or other building work.
predicates.statutory_rehousing_duty_not_triggered: The landlord is not required by the statutory rehousing duty to provide the evicted tenants with accommodation in the replacement building.

members.legal_issue: Requirements governing eviction for reconstruction do not invalidate an eviction decree founded on bona fide personal need when reconstruction was not the basis of the suit and the tenant’s asserted reconstruction requirements were found satisfied in any event.
material_facts: The eviction suit was brought on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide personal requirement, not on a reconstruction ground.
The tenant did not raise the reconstruction-ground plea in the trial court and acknowledged before the appellate court that the suit was not based on that ground.
The appellate court found that the relevant plans and estimates had been prepared and that the landlord had the necessary resources for the proposed changes.
The tenant nevertheless argued on appeal that the decree should fail for non-compliance with the requirements governing reconstruction.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(h) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, concerns eviction for building, rebuilding, or substantial alterations, and subsection (7) prescribes conditions for an eviction order on that ground. Those conditions did not defeat this suit, which was based on bona fide personal need under Section 12(1)(f); additionally, the appellate court found the relevant requirements satisfied. The Supreme Court did not rely on an earlier case for this holding.
members.conclusion: The tenant could not succeed on the reconstruction argument because the suit was not based on reconstruction; in any event, the appellate court had found the relevant requirements satisfied.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: A tenant appealed an eviction decree.
predicates.suit_based_on_personal_need: The landlord brought the suit on the ground of bona fide personal need rather than to carry out reconstruction.
predicates.tenant_disclaimed_reconstruction_ground_: The tenant accepted in the lower appellate court that the suit was not based on a reconstruction ground.
predicates.reconstruction_requirements_found_satisf: The lower appellate court found that the relevant plans, estimates, and resources for the proposed work were in place.

members.legal_issue: A land-ceiling rule that treats a Hindu undivided family as one landholding unit for ceiling purposes is protected from constitutional challenges to property and equality rights when it forms part of agrarian reform.
material_facts: The land was held by a Hindu undivided family, with the land recorded in the name of its head.
The family members argued that each was entitled to retain a separate ceiling area from the family holding.
The challenged rule treated the family holding as the land of the family head for the purposes of the land-reform scheme and prevented descendants from claiming separate ceiling areas.
The scheme limited holdings, acquired surplus land for distribution, and preserved family members’ rights in the retained area and their entitlement to compensation for surplus land.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects laws providing for the acquisition of an estate or rights in it, or the extinguishment or modification of such rights, from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31 when the law concerns agrarian reform. Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab held that land ceilings and related measures can constitute agrarian reform. K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras confined Article 31-A’s protection to measures directed to agrarian reform. Pritam Singh v. State of Punjab upheld the protection of a rule disregarding certain land transfers for surplus-land purposes. The challenged rule prevented a family from multiplying its ceiling area through separate claims by descendants, while leaving their other family-property rights and compensation rights unaffected. The Court also noted that a challenge to Article 31-A itself was unavailable in light of I. C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The rule formed part of agrarian reform and was protected by Article 31-A from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The challenge failed and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: A person challenges a rule governing the maximum landholding and acquisition of surplus land on constitutional-rights grounds.
predicates.joint_family_treated_as_one_unit_for_cei: The rule treats land held by a joint family as one holding for calculating the family’s permissible area.
predicates.rule_aimed_at_surplus_land_distribution: The rule is part of a scheme intended to acquire surplus land and make it available for distribution.
predicates.other_family_property_rights_preserved: The rule leaves family members’ other rights in family property and their entitlement to compensation for acquired surplus land unaffected.

members.legal_issue: Land-rights modifications made through consolidation and village-planning measures that form part of an agrarian-reform scheme are protected against constitutional property-rights challenges when they serve the planned use and welfare of the rural community.
material_facts: During consolidation proceedings, land held by proprietors was reserved for village panchayats and community purposes, including schools, roads, health facilities, manure pits, and other village needs.
Some land was reserved for non-proprietors, including for housing and village services; the affected proprietors received no compensation.

The challenged measures operated together with legislation on consolidation, village panchayats, common lands, and security of land tenure, as part of a wider programme of land redistribution and rural planning.
The proprietors challenged the measures and legislation as unconstitutional for modifying or taking their property without compensation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A, including its provisions concerning acquisition or modification of rights in an estate, is construed broadly to protect legislation forming part of agrarian reform. Such reform can include measures ancillary to land redistribution that plan rural areas and promote the productive use of land and community welfare. The court relied on Atma Ram v. State of Punjab; Gangadhar Narayanrao Majumdar v. State of Bombay; Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay; Sonapur Tea Co. Ltd. v. Must. Mazirunnessa; Burrakur Coal Co. Ltd. v. Union of India; State of Bihar v. Rameshwar Pratap Narain Singh; State of Bihar v. Umesh Jha; and the distinction from K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras. It upheld the High Court’s approach in Jagat Singh v. Punjab State. Relevant provisions included Article 31-A, Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, sections 18, 2(bb) and 23-A of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, section 19 of the Punjab Gram Panchayat Act, and sections 3, 4, 6 and 7 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act.
members.conclusion: The challenged modifications formed part of a general scheme of agrarian reform and were protected by Article 31-A; the challenge based on Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 therefore failed, and the appeals were dismissed. The court distinguished Kochuni because it concerned a bare transfer of rights without a change in tenure or an agrarian-reform purpose.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_realloc: People challenge the constitutionality of measures that reallocate or modify rights in land.
predicates.land_taken_from_proprietors_without_comp: A public authority takes, reserves, or reallocates land held by proprietors without paying them compensation.
predicates.land_reserved_for_village_community_uses: Land is reserved for management by a village body or for facilities and uses that benefit the village community.
predicates.land_allotted_to_nonproprietors: Land is allotted to people who did not previously hold proprietary rights in it.
predicates.measures_form_part_of_integrated_rural_r: The land measures form part of a broader programme of land reform and rural planning, rather than a bare transfer of property rights.

members.legal_issue: A state acquisition law whose dominant purpose is agrarian reform and protection of an estate is protected by the constitutional provision governing acquisition of estates, even if it includes ancillary measures concerning associated valuables.
material_facts: The acquisition law provided for acquisition and management of an estate containing land used for linaloe cultivation and its tree growth.
The stated purposes included preserving the estate and its valuable objects and establishing an art gallery and museum.
The State Legislature passed the law, and the President assented to it.
The court found that preserving and protecting the estate was the law’s dominant purpose and that measures concerning paintings and other valuables were ancillary.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a), read with Article 31A(2)(a)(iii), protects laws directed to acquisition of estates and agrarian reform. Whether a law concerns agrarian reform is determined by its substance and dominant purpose, not merely its outward form; ancillary provisions do not remove the protection. The court relied on State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing (Wvg.) Co.; Kunjukutty Sahib v. State of Kerala; and Mahant Sankarshan Ramanuja Das Goswami v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The acquisition law was protected by Article 31A(1)(a) and was immune from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and dominant_purpose_is_agrarian_reform and ancillary_measures_support_that_purpose and required_presidential_assent_was_obtained

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law providing for acquisition of an estate.
predicates.dominant_purpose_is_agrarian_reform: The law’s primary purpose is to preserve, protect, or reorganize land as part of agrarian reform.
predicates.ancillary_measures_support_that_purpose: The law includes additional measures that support, rather than displace, its primary land-related purpose.
predicates.required_presidential_assent_was_obtaine: The law received presidential assent where the constitutional protection required it.

members.legal_issue: A law providing for land to be reserved for agriculture and the welfare of agricultural populations, and for remaining land to be assigned to agriculturists and agricultural labourers, effects agrarian reform and receives constitutional protection.
material_facts: The law provided for land to be reserved for promoting agriculture and the welfare of the agricultural population to be settled on it.
It provided for remaining lands to be assigned to agriculturists and agricultural labourers.

The Court construed the reservation purposes as limited to purposes directly connected with agricultural promotion or the welfare of agricultural populations, including purposes similar to the common purposes approved in Ranjit Singh.
The Court found that the lands fell within the constitutional category of Janmam rights.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that agrarian reform extends beyond redistribution of land to include certain common purposes promoting agriculture and rural welfare, but a fanciful connection to those purposes is insufficient and land used for unrelated purposes may be restrained. It relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raja Anand, Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma, and P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Madras.
members.conclusion: The three purposes in the law, understood within the limits stated by the Court, were covered by agrarian reform, and the law was protected from constitutional challenge under Article 31A.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_resumpt: A party challenged a law that resumes land to the State.
predicates.land_is_within_janmam_rights: The land falls within the proprietary landholding category considered by the Court to be Janmam rights.
predicates.land_is_reserved_for_direct_agricultural: The law reserves land only for purposes directly connected with promoting agriculture or the welfare of the agricultural population.
predicates.remaining_land_is_assigned_to_agricultur: The law assigns the land remaining after reservation to agriculturists or agricultural labourers.

members.legal_issue: The amendment defining village common land encompasses land reserved for common purposes during consolidation from proprietors’ holdings outside their permissible ceiling limits, and is constitutionally valid as a declaratory measure of agrarian reform.
material_facts: During consolidation, land was reserved for common purposes by applying a pro-rata cut to proprietors’ holdings; the land at issue was outside the proprietors’ permissible ceiling limits.
The Supreme Court had previously held that land reserved in this manner vested in the Panchayat as part of agrarian reform and that compensation was not payable.
The challenged amendment was enacted after receiving the President’s assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects laws forming part of agrarian reform, including an amendment that extends or clarifies the operation of an existing agrarian-reform law when it receives presidential assent. Article 300A does not require compensation where the land had already vested in the Panchayat. The Court relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, which treated land reserved by pro-rata cut outside the applicable ceiling limits as acquired for agrarian reform without compensation, and Mahant Sankarshan Ramanuja Das Goswami v. State of Orissa, on Article 31A’s protection for an assented amending Act.
members.conclusion: The amendment is valid and clarifies the existing legal position: land reserved for common purposes from holdings outside the permissible ceiling limits had already vested in the Panchayat and was not newly acquired by the amendment.

rule.if: challenge_to_common_land_amendment and land_reserved_by_pro_rata_cut and land_outside_permissible_ceiling and amendment_received_presidential_assent

predicates.challenge_to_common_land_amendment: A proceeding challenges a law that defines or regulates village common land.
predicates.land_reserved_by_pro_rata_cut: During consolidation, land was set aside for village common purposes by taking a proportionate share from proprietors’ holdings.
predicates.land_outside_permissible_ceiling: The land taken for common purposes was outside the permissible ceiling limits applicable to the proprietors.
predicates.amendment_received_presidential_assent: The amending law received the required assent before it took effect.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of an estate held under a jagir, inam, or similar grant as a necessary step in agrarian reform is constitutionally protected, and the resulting vesting notifications are valid.
material_facts: The challenged amendment deemed the area to be an estate with retrospective effect and applied to the existing vesting notifications.
The area was held under grants in the nature of a jagir or inam.
The Court regarded acquisition of such grants as a necessary step in implementing agrarian reforms.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A protects laws concerning estates when their acquisition is a necessary step in implementing agrarian reforms. The Court held that acquisition of jagirs, inams, and similar grants met that description.
members.conclusion: The amendment was protected by Article 31A, the vesting notifications were upheld, and the petition challenging them was dismissed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_vesting: A party challenged the validity of a law or notification providing for land to vest in the state.
predicates.grant_estate: The land at issue was held under a grant in the nature of a jagir, inam, or similar grant.
predicates.acquisition_is_a_necessary_step_in_agrar: Acquiring the grant was a necessary step in implementing agrarian reform.
predicates.acquisition_is_constitutionally_protecte: The acquisition is constitutionally protected and the vesting is valid.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for acquisition or modification of estate rights applies only when the measure is connected with agrarian reform.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of land for housing schemes, including schemes that could extend beyond slum clearance to other housing objectives.
The acquisitions were not connected with agrarian reform.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A applies to a law acquiring an estate or rights in an estate, or extinguishing or modifying such rights, only when the measure is connected with agrarian reform. That restriction remains applicable after the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964. Article 31-A is a limited exception to the protections applicable to acquisition under Article 31(2) and (2A), not a general protection for State acquisitions. The Court followed K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 887, and Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 82.
members.conclusion: The law was not protected by the constitutional provision concerning estates because its acquisitions were not connected with agrarian reform.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorizing the State to acquire property.
predicates.acquisition_for_housing: The State sought to acquire property for a housing scheme.
predicates.acquisition_not_connected_to_agrarian_re: The acquisition was not connected with agrarian reform.

members.legal_issue: Legislation that gives effect to the policy of distributing community resources for the common good cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates equality or freedom of trade where the applicable constitutional protection covers it.
material_facts: The Nationalisation Act was enacted to reorganise and rehabilitate sick textile undertakings and to promote production and distribution for the public good.
The Act declared that it gave effect to the policy of the State towards the principles concerning community resources and the common good.
The petitioners did not contend that the Act failed to give effect to that policy.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the Act gave effect to the policy reflected in Article 39(b), concerning ownership and control of material resources and their distribution to best serve the common good. Because the Act was protected by Article 31C, the petitioners could not challenge it for violating Articles 14 and 19. The Court relied on the protection of Article 31C as upheld in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala and discussed in Waman Rao v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The petitioners could not challenge the Act on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_validity_of_public_resour: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law reorganising or nationalising an undertaking.
predicates.law_advances_common_good_distribution_of: The law gives effect to a policy of organising ownership or control of community resources so their distribution serves the common good.
predicates.policy_basis_is_not_disputed: The challenger did not establish that the law failed to give effect to the policy it declared.
predicates.constitutional_protection_for_that_polic: The constitutional protection for laws implementing that policy applies to the law.

members.legal_issue: Agrarian reform provisions that reduce landholders’ retained agricultural land, protect cultivators’ interests, and redistribute surplus agricultural land to landless tillers are protected from constitutional challenge when they have a close nexus to the common-good objective of distributing material resources.
material_facts: The challenged amendments reduced the agricultural land that landholders could retain and regulated the rights of cultivators working the land.

The legislation took surplus agricultural land from landholders and made it available to landless tillers, while leaving landholders land within the prescribed ceiling and not taking their homestead lands or buildings.
The amendments were directed at distributing agricultural land, a material resource, for the common good.
members.legal_principle: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of the community’s material resources to serve the common good. Distribution is not confined to a literal division; it includes allocation, allotment, classification, and apportionment. A broad approach applies when assessing the required nexus between legislation and Article 39(b). Where that nexus exists, Article 31C protects the legislation from challenges based on the fundamental rights it covers. The Court relied on Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Waman Rao v. Union of India, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai, State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India, and Sasanka Sekhar Maity v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The challenged provisions were protected by Article 31C because they gave effect to Article 39(b), and the constitutional challenges to them failed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: Landholders brought a constitutional challenge to legislation reforming agricultural landholding.
predicates.surplus_agricultural_land_taken_from_lan: The legislation took agricultural land above the amount landholders could retain.
predicates.agricultural_land_allocated_to_landless_: The legislation allocated agricultural land to landless people who cultivated it.
predicates.close_nexus_to_common_good: The legislation’s land-distribution measures were closely connected to serving the common good.

members.legal_issue: Agrarian reform measures that reduce land ceilings and confer protected cultivation rights on tillers are constitutionally valid when they distribute agricultural resources for the common good.
material_facts: The challenged amendments reduced the agricultural land that former landlords could retain and provided for cultivation by bargadars, including protection of bargadars’ rights.
The amendments provided for surplus agricultural land to be distributed among landless tillers, while leaving owners homestead land, buildings and land within the applicable ceiling.
The petitioners argued that the amendments caused confiscatory deprivation, lacked a sufficient connection to distributive objectives, and involved no genuine distribution.
members.legal_principle: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of the material resources of the community to serve the common good; distribution is not confined to literal division and includes allocation and apportionment. Article 31C protects laws that give effect to Article 39(b) from challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31. The Court applied Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India, Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Waman Rao v. Union of India, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd., State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavur Bai, and Sasanka Sekhar Maity v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The amendments were valid. They were directed to distributing agricultural resources among tillers for the common good, and the broad conception of distribution includes the allocation of resources in this manner. The challenge based on confiscation, lack of nexus, or absence of a distribution process therefore failed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party brings a constitutional challenge to a law reforming agricultural land ownership or cultivation.
predicates.surplus_agricultural_land_is_allocated_t: The law reallocates surplus agricultural land to people who till the land.
predicates.reform_is_directed_to_serving_the_common: The reform is directed to distributing community resources for the benefit of the community.
