members.legal_issue: A law whose contents provide for acquisition and distribution of land and related amenities for community housing can be protected as implementing the constitutional policy of distributing material resources for the common good, without an express legislative declaration of that purpose.
material_facts: The legislation provided for acquiring private land, developing it, and making housing sites or accommodation available to the community.
It also provided for land and facilities such as community centres, shopping complexes, parks, roads, drains, and playgrounds that serve residents collectively.
The legislation's contents, rather than an express declaration of its purpose, showed its relationship to distribution of material resources.
members.legal_principle: Article 31C applies according to the character and contents of legislation; it does not require an express legislative declaration. Article 39(b)'s reference to distribution of material resources is construed broadly enough to include the acquisition, development, and distribution of land and community amenities. The Court relied on His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalavaru v. State of Kerala, Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, State of Karnataka v. Shri Ranganatha Reddy, and Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Company v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd.
members.conclusion: The legislation implemented the policy in Article 39(b) and was protected by Article 31C against a challenge based on Articles 14 and 19, even assuming an infringement of Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_a_housing_an: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law providing for land acquisition and housing or related development.
predicates.law_provides_for_acquiring_and_developin: The law provides for private land to be acquired and developed for public use.
predicates.developed_land_and_shared_amenities_are_: The law provides for housing sites or accommodation and shared civic facilities to serve the community.

members.legal_issue: The family definition used in an agrarian land-ceiling regime has a sufficient connection to the State’s policy of distributing surplus land for the common good to withstand the constitutional challenge raised against it.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned declaration and distribution of surplus land under a law aimed at agrarian reform.
The challenged family definition determined which landholdings were grouped when calculating a ceiling unit.
The surplus-land provisions were intended to distribute land held by large tenure holders among landless people.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 14, 31B, 31C and 39(b) of the Constitution. It held that the family definition had a clear nexus with the policy of distributing surplus land for the common good. It referred to Tumati Venkaish v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Seth Nand Lal v. State of Haryana, and Waman Rao v. Union of India, which upheld analogous land-ceiling provisions against constitutional challenges.
members.conclusion: The family definition had a clear nexus with the State’s policy of securing the principle in Article 39(b), so the constitutional challenge had no merit.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The proceeding concerns determining surplus land under a land-ceiling regime.
predicates.agrarian_reform_law: The law is directed at agrarian reform.
predicates.surplus_land_distribution_for_common_goo: The law provides for distributing surplus land for the benefit of people without land.

members.legal_issue: A law extinguishing landholder rights in the course of agrarian reform and distributing material resources does not violate the Constitution’s basic structure or fundamental-rights guarantees when protected by the applicable constitutional provisions.
material_facts: The law extinguished former landholders’ interests in land and mineral resources as part of a broader scheme of land-tenure abolition and agrarian reform.
The law was included in the Ninth Schedule and was directed to vesting resources in the State for public use.
The claimants argued that the law violated constitutional protections, including equality and the right to property, and damaged the Constitution’s basic structure.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C, and Articles 39(b) and 39(c), together with the Ninth Schedule. It held that land and embedded mines, minerals, and quarries are material resources of the community, and that their acquisition can be a means of distributing those resources for the common good. It also held that the right to property under Article 300A is not a basic feature or structure of the Constitution. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Waman Rao v. Union of India, State of Tamil Nadu v. L. Abu Kavibai, Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Cooking Coal Ltd., and other decisions concerning agrarian reform, material resources, and constitutional structure.
members.conclusion: The law was protected as part of agrarian reform and did not damage the Constitution’s basic structure; it was also saved by the constitutional protection for laws giving effect to the distribution of material resources for the common good.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_law and law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform and law_distributes_community_resources and law_has_constitutional_protection

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A litigant challenged the constitutional validity of a law affecting land rights.
predicates.law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform: The law forms part of a scheme that abolishes intermediary land tenures or reorganizes land rights.
predicates.law_distributes_community_resources: The law vests or distributes land or embedded natural resources for public use or the common good.
predicates.law_has_constitutional_protection: The law falls within a constitutional protection for agrarian reform or laws directed to distributing material resources for the common good.

members.legal_issue: The amendment abolishing a landlord’s right to resume tenanted land and vesting tenancy land for transfer to cultivating tenants does not violate the Constitution’s basic structure.
material_facts: The amendment ended the landlord’s right to resume tenanted land, including where the landlord bona fide required it for personal cultivation and relied on its income for maintenance.
The amendment provided for tenancy land to vest in the State and for cultivating tenants to obtain occupancy rights.
The law was challenged as not being agrarian reform and as violating the Constitution’s basic structure.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 31-A, 31-B and 31-C, Article 39(b) and (c), and the principles stated in Waman Rao v. Union of India and Kesavananda Bharati. It held that transferring land ownership to the tiller is a means of using a community resource for the common good and that preferring a cultivating tenant over a landlord who did not personally cultivate the land is part of agrarian reform.
members.conclusion: The amendment was a law aimed at agrarian reform and securing the Directive Principles in Articles 39(b) and (c); it did not offend the basic structure of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law that reforms agricultural landholding or tenancy.
predicates.tenant_personally_cultivates_land: A tenant personally cultivates the land at issue.
predicates.landlord_did_not_personally_cultivate_la: The landlord did not personally cultivate the land at issue.
predicates.law_transfers_tenancy_land_for_cultivato: The law provides for tenancy land to be transferred for ownership by the person cultivating it.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional amendments establishing protection for laws concerning acquisition, extinguishment, or modification of rights in agricultural estates do not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure.
material_facts: The challenged constitutional amendments introduced and expanded protection for laws concerning agrarian reform, including the extinguishment or modification of rights in agricultural land.
The amendments were directed at reducing social and economic disparities in agriculture and advancing the distribution of material resources and prevention of wealth concentration.
The petitioners argued that withdrawing fundamental-rights protections for this category of laws damaged the Constitution’s basic structure.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 368, Parliament may amend every constitutional provision, including fundamental-rights provisions, but may not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure. Article 13(2) makes a law void to the extent it abridges or takes away Part III rights, but the withdrawal of a fundamental-rights protection does not invariably damage the basic structure; the inquiry depends on the right affected and whether its withdrawal is essential to that structure. The Court applied Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Smt. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, and Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, and considered the objectives reflected in Article 39(b) and (c).
members.conclusion: The amendments introducing Article 31A and expanding its categories are valid because they do not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: A litigant challenges a constitutional amendment on the ground that it damages or destroys the Constitution’s basic structure.
predicates.amendment_protects_defined_agrarian_refo: The amendment protects a defined category of laws that alter rights in agricultural land as part of agrarian reform.
predicates.amendment_advances_equitable_distributio: The amendment is directed at reducing disparities and promoting a more equitable distribution of resources.
predicates.amendment_valid_under_basic_structure_li: The amendment is valid because it does not damage or destroy the Constitution’s basic structure.

members.legal_issue: A tenant must be granted leave to contest an expedited eviction application when the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that would defeat the landlord’s claim to possession.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest the landlord’s expedited eviction application.
The tenant argued that the building’s mixed commercial and residential use meant the landlord could not rely on the special recovery ground.
The Court held that the building’s character did not defeat the landlord’s claim and that the affidavit disclosed no facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovering possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 25B(5) requires leave where the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession. Disclosure of such facts is a sine qua non for leave. The provision is not to be equated with Order 37, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure: its social setting, subject matter and deliberately narrower language limit the scope for permitting a defence.
members.conclusion: The Controller was justified in refusing leave to contest because the tenant’s affidavit did not disclose facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession.

predicates.special_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks expedited eviction under a special procedure that requires the tenant to obtain leave to contest.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_defeati: The tenant’s affidavit states facts which, if established, would prevent the landlord from obtaining possession on the asserted ground.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who raises a genuine factual dispute about the landlord-tenant relationship and the basis on which possession was obtained must not be denied leave to contest a summary eviction application on the mistaken premise that the relationship was admitted.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest an eviction application and stated that possession had been obtained under an agreement to sell, not as a tenant.
The tenant disputed that a landlord-tenant relationship existed and denied that the alleged tenancy was genuine.
The Rent Controller treated the tenant’s pleadings as admitting the landlord-tenant relationship and refused leave to contest.
The High Court dismissed the revision without addressing that alleged error.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(1), (4), (6), (8) and (10) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a tenant served in a qualifying bona fide-requirement eviction proceeding must seek leave to contest by affidavit. Because refusal results in the landlord’s allegations being deemed admitted, the special procedure requires strict interpretation. On a reasonable and purposeful interpretation, leave must not be refused where the tenant’s application and affidavit disclose a triable case. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The tenant had raised a triable dispute, so refusing leave to contest was unsustainable. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the orders refusing leave and granting eviction.

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_request: A tenant sought permission to contest an eviction application handled through a summary procedure.
predicates.tenant_denied_landlord_tenant_relationsh: The tenant stated that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties.
predicates.tenant_claimed_possession_under_sale_agr: The tenant stated that possession had been obtained under an agreement to sell rather than as a tenant.

members.legal_issue: Leave to contest a special recovery application may be granted only when the tenant's affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession on the special ground.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest the landlord's special recovery application.
The tenant raised objections concerning the landlord's status after retirement, the pending earlier petition, and the premises' mixed residential and professional use.
The Court held that the statutory grounds for leave were confined to facts capable of defeating the landlord's entitlement under the special recovery provision.
members.legal_principle: Section 25B(5) requires leave where the tenant's affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovery on the applicable statutory ground. For a section 14A application, the relevant facts are those negating the landlord's entitlement under that section, such as the required occupation or the qualifying order to vacate. This restricted test is not analogous to leave to defend under Order XXXVII, Rule 2(3), and Rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The scope of leave under section 25B(5) is restricted to cases where the tenant's affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession under section 14A.

predicates.special_eviction_case: The landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of let premises under the special procedure for persons required to leave authority-allotted residential accommodation.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_negatin: The tenant's affidavit stated facts which, if established, would defeat the landlord's entitlement to recover possession under the special ground.

members.legal_issue: A tenant should be granted leave to defend an eviction suit when the landlord relies on bona fide personal requirement and the tenant disputes that ground.
material_facts: The landlords sought eviction on the ground of bona fide personal requirement.
The tenant disputed that ground but was refused leave to defend the eviction suit.
members.legal_principle: The court held that leave to defend should be granted in these circumstances. The judgment cites no statutory provisions or earlier cases in support of this ruling.
members.conclusion: The tenant should have been granted leave to defend and an opportunity to contest the suit; the refusal was set aside.

predicates.eviction_suit_leave_to_defend: A tenant is seeking leave to defend a suit brought by a landlord for eviction.
predicates.landlord_claims_personal_requirement: The landlord seeks eviction on the ground of a bona fide personal requirement.
predicates.tenant_disputes_requirement: The tenant disputes the landlord's claim of bona fide personal requirement.

members.legal_issue: A tenant must receive leave to contest a summary eviction application when the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that, if established at trial, would defeat the landlord’s claim.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession on the ground of bona fide residential need and asserted that no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation was available.
The tenant’s affidavit disputed the purpose for which the premises had been let and alleged that the landlord had other suitable accommodation and had repeatedly let out comparable vacant premises.
The Controller refused leave after deciding disputed factual matters on the affidavits as though they were evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(4)–(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the landlord bears the burden of establishing the statutory grounds for eviction, and the Controller must grant leave if the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that could defeat the claim. The statutory wording requires disclosure, not proof, and differs from the substantial-defence language of Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court relied on Santosh Kumar v. Bhai Mool Singh and approved S. Kanjibhai v. Mohanraj Rajendra Kumar and Kishan Singh v. Mohd. Shafi. It also stressed that rent restriction legislation must not be interpreted so as to make tenant protections illusory, referring to Bahadur Singh v. Muni Sabrat Das, Kaushalya Devi v. R.L. Bansal and Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Rehman.
members.conclusion: The Controller had to grant leave because the tenant disclosed facts which, if believed at trial, could disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession.

predicates.summary_residential_need_eviction_procee: A landlord has brought a summary eviction proceeding based on a claimed bona fide need for residential occupation.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_that_if: The tenant has stated in an affidavit facts which, if established at trial, could defeat the landlord’s claim to possession.
predicates.leave_to_contest_must_be_granted: The tenant is allowed to contest the eviction application.

members.legal_issue: A tenant must receive leave to contest when the affidavit raises substantial disputes about the landlord’s bona fide need and alternative accommodation that require a trial.
material_facts: The landlord had returned and settled in the city but had renewed the tenant’s leave-and-licence arrangement after returning.

The tenant alleged that an identical unit behind the premises had become vacant and had been let to successive tenants, and the landlord acknowledged that the unit was occupied by another tenant until a later period.
The tenant alleged that the landlord had other suitable accommodation and had repeatedly let vacant premises at higher rents.
Although an eviction notice had been served, the landlord did not pursue the claim for several years before serving a further notice.
The landlord did not provide sworn details of his residential requirements or the basis on which he occupied the accommodation where he was then living.
The Controller resolved the disputed allegations on the affidavits and refused leave; the High Court dismissed the revision.
members.legal_principle: Under section 25B(5), allegations concerning alternative accommodation, repeated reletting of comparable premises, conduct bearing on bona fide need, and the landlord’s failure to explain his existing accommodation may disclose facts which, if proved, would defeat a residential-need eviction claim. The Controller must not decide those disputed matters at the leave stage. The Court applied its construction of sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(4)–(5), and the principles in Santosh Kumar v. Bhai Mool Singh and Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah.
members.conclusion: The disclosed facts put the landlord’s bona fides and the availability of suitable alternative accommodation in issue. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the orders refusing leave and granted the tenant leave to contest, remitting the case for proceedings according to law.

predicates.summary_residential_need_eviction_procee: A landlord has brought a summary eviction proceeding based on a claimed bona fide need for residential occupation.
predicates.tenant_discloses_material_doubts_about_b: The tenant’s affidavit raises facts about the landlord’s conduct, existing accommodation or alternative premises that could materially undermine the claimed need if established.
predicates.tenant_must_receive_leave_to_contest: The tenant is allowed to contest the eviction application.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking leave to defend a summary eviction claim based on bona fide requirement must disclose material facts that prima facie raise a triable issue; vague, unsupported assertions about alternative accommodation do not suffice.
material_facts: The landlord placed material before the Rent Controller supporting the claimed bona fide need and the absence of reasonably suitable alternative accommodation.
The tenant alleged that other properties were available but provided no adequate pleadings or supporting material showing that those properties were reasonably suitable.
The landlord denied ownership of the alleged alternative properties, and the Rent Controller found the tenant’s defence to be a moonshine.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the landlord must make out a prima facie case of bona fide need and lack of reasonably suitable accommodation; the tenant must then disclose material of substance that prima facie could disentitle the landlord from eviction. Leave is not granted on mere assertion, but a genuine triable issue warrants leave. Section 19 provides a post-eviction remedy if the premises are not used for the intended purpose and reflects the legislative objective of enabling speedy possession. The Court relied on Inderjeet Kaur v. Nirpal Singh (2001) 1 SCC 706; Anil Bajaj v. Vinod Ahuja (2014) 15 SCC 610; Baldev Singh Bajwa v. Monish Saini (2005) 12 SCC 778; and Ram Krishan Grover v. Union of India (2020) 12 SCC 506. It also held that a tenant cannot dictate how a landlord should use the landlord’s property.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s unsupported allegations did not raise a triable issue requiring leave to defend, and the Rent Controller’s refusal of leave was restored.

predicates.summary_eviction_claim_based_on_bona_fid: The proceeding sought summary eviction on the ground that the landlord had a bona fide requirement for the premises.
predicates.landlord_made_prima_facie_showing_of_nee: The landlord placed material supporting the need for the premises and the lack of reasonably suitable alternative accommodation.
predicates.tenant_relied_on_vague_unsupported_alter: The tenant alleged that other accommodation was available without adequate particulars or supporting material showing its reasonable suitability.

members.legal_issue: A tenant is entitled to leave to contest a summary eviction proceeding when the tenant raises prima facie grounds which, if accepted, could defeat the landlord’s claim to eviction.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the basis of a claimed inheritance through adoption and produced an adoption deed said to have been executed many years earlier.
The tenant disputed the claimant’s ownership and landlord status, had not attorned to the claimant, and challenged whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed between them.
The tenant specifically alleged that alternative accommodation in the building was available to meet the claimed need for the premises.
The lower authorities refused leave without allowing the tenant to contest the eviction claim on its merits.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 25B(4) and 25B(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the authority considering leave to contest should not determine the merits and demerits of the proposed defences. Leave is warranted where the grounds prima facie disclose a defence which, if accepted, may disentitle the landlord to eviction. The eviction claim in this case was brought under Section 14(1)(e). The Court cited no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The tenant had raised prima facie grounds sufficient to obtain leave to contest. The refusal of leave was set aside and the eviction proceeding was restored for decision on its merits. Leave was subject to depositing the rent arrears and continuing to deposit rent; failure to comply would result in refusal to contest.

rule.if: summary_rent_eviction_leave_application and ownership_or_landlord_status_disputed and tenancy_relationship_unproven and alternative_accommodation_specifically_pleaded

predicates.summary_rent_eviction_leave_application: A tenant applied for leave to contest a proceeding in which a landlord sought eviction under a summary rent-control procedure.
predicates.ownership_or_landlord_status_disputed: The tenant disputed the claimant’s ownership of the premises or status as landlord, including by challenging the basis on which that status was claimed.
predicates.tenancy_relationship_unproven: The tenant disputed the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship, and the record did not establish that relationship between the tenant and the claimant.
predicates.alternative_accommodation_specifically_p: The tenant specifically alleged that other suitable accommodation was available to meet the claimant’s stated need.

members.legal_issue: A tenant should be granted leave to defend an eviction action when the tenant raises a material, evidence-dependent dispute about the purpose of letting that could affect the landlord’s entitlement to possession.
material_facts: The landlords sought eviction on the ground of bona fide personal requirement.
The tenants contended that the premises had been let for both residential and commercial purposes, which they said would prevent recovery on the personal-requirement ground.
The Rent Controller refused leave to defend on a prima facie assessment from affidavits that the dominant purpose of letting was residential.
The Supreme Court considered that the competing contentions warranted a full determination, including whether the landlord’s requirement was bona fide and whether the letting was for both purposes.
members.legal_principle: Where a tenant’s defence raises a material dispute that could affect the landlord’s entitlement to eviction and requires determination on evidence, leave to defend is appropriate rather than resolving the dispute on a prima facie assessment of affidavits. The judgment refers generally to the Delhi Rent Control Act but identifies no specific provision or earlier case as the basis for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the orders refusing leave were set aside, and the tenants were granted leave to defend. The Rent Controller was directed to decide the disputed issues after allowing the tenants to file a written statement.

rule.if: appeal_from_refusal_of_leave and eviction_for_personal_requirement and tenant_pleads_mixed_purpose and mixed_purpose_could_bar_eviction and material_dispute_requires_evidence

predicates.appeal_from_refusal_of_leave: The tenant appealed an order refusing permission to defend the eviction action.
predicates.eviction_for_personal_requirement: The landlord sought possession on the ground of personal requirement.
predicates.tenant_pleads_mixed_purpose: The tenant asserted that the premises had been let for both residential and commercial purposes.
predicates.mixed_purpose_could_bar_eviction: The tenant’s asserted purpose of letting, if established, could prevent eviction on the ground relied on by the landlord.
predicates.material_dispute_requires_evidence: The competing claims raised a material issue that required determination beyond a prima facie assessment of affidavits.

members.legal_issue: Leave to defend in a summary eviction proceeding is warranted only when the tenant discloses facts that could disentitle the landlord from eviction and present a genuine issue for trial.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on grounds including personal requirement and rent default.
The tenant sought leave to defend, denying the landlord-tenant relationship and claiming that the property had been purchased from another person.

The tenant’s denial was inconsistent with the tenant’s sworn acknowledgment of the landlord’s title and was unsupported by a credible explanation; the trial court found the defence false, frivolous, and unsustainable.
members.legal_principle: Sub-sections (4) and (5) of Section 14 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982 require the tenant seeking leave to disclose facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining eviction. A court may assess whether an issue raised in the pleadings is genuinely triable; a defence that is sham, illusory, or practically moonshine does not suffice. The Court applied Charan Daas Duggal v. Brahma Nand, [1983] 1 SCC 30, and the Patna High Court decisions in Md. Fahimuddin v. Godhan Pd. Singh, (1992) 2 PLJR 352, and Bijoy Kumar Singh v. The State of Bihar & Ors., (1992) 1 PLJR 123, while holding that those authorities did not prevent the court from assessing whether a real triable issue arose.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s defence did not disclose a triable issue, so the trial court was justified in refusing leave to defend.

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_application: The matter is an application for leave to defend in a summary eviction proceeding.
predicates.tenant_seeks_leave_to_defend: The tenant asks for permission to contest the eviction claim.
predicates.tenant_relies_on_defence_barred_by_tenan: The tenant relies on a denial of the landlord’s title despite facts that estop the tenant from making that denial.
predicates.tenant_discloses_no_other_genuine_fact_t: The tenant discloses no other genuine fact which, if established, could disentitle the landlord from eviction.

members.legal_issue: A tenant is entitled to leave to contest an expedited recovery application when the tenant’s affidavit discloses material facts that, if established, could defeat one of the landlord’s required grounds for recovery.
material_facts: The tenants were required to seek leave to contest by affidavit.
Some tenants challenged the landlord’s status, ownership, return to the country, duration of ownership, or genuineness of need.

The court held that bare assertions, unsupported allegations about other properties, or grounds outside the statutory requirements did not suffice; material, particularized evidence could warrant leave.
members.legal_principle: Sections 18-A(4) and 18-A(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 require the tenant to disclose in an affidavit facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovery under Section 13-B. The inquiry is confined to the matters the landlord must establish under Section 13-B, including qualifying status, return, ownership for the required duration, and genuine need. A bare assertion does not rebut the presumption of genuine need; the tenant must provide necessary facts and particulars, supported by documentary evidence where available.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s defence is confined to the statutory grounds for recovery, and leave is warranted only where the affidavit presents a strong, material challenge to a ground the landlord must establish.

predicates.special_nri_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking expedited recovery of rented premises by a landlord in the specially classified returning-resident category.
predicates.tenant_files_contesting_affidavit: The tenant submits an affidavit seeking permission to contest the recovery application.
predicates.affidavit_discloses_material_facts_chall: The affidavit gives specific, material facts that could defeat a ground the landlord must establish to recover possession.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking leave to contest a summary eviction petition based on the landlord’s bona fide requirement must receive leave when the tenant’s affidavit raises non-frivolous facts that could defeat the landlord’s entitlement and require adjudication at trial.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement and relied on a registered sale deed to establish ownership.

The tenants disputed the landlord’s title, alleging that the property had vested in a public custodian and could not validly have been sold to the landlord; they also challenged the genuineness of the sale deed and the sellers’ title.
The tenants produced a communication from the custodian stating that the property vested in it and that rent was to be collected on its behalf.
The Rent Controller relied on an earlier order under a different property statute declaring the property not to be evacuee property and denied leave to defend; the High Court affirmed.

The Supreme Court held that the questions of vesting, the consequences of vesting, and the sale deed’s authenticity required determination at trial, and that the tenants’ pleas were not frivolous or baseless.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 25B(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, a tenant must be given leave to contest an eviction application under Section 14(1)(e) if the affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession. The leave-stage inquiry is summary and asks whether the tenant has disclosed reasonable grounds; it concerns disclosure of facts, not proof of them. Rent-control legislation should not be construed hyper-technically in a way that frustrates its protective purpose. The Court relied on Mangat Ram v. Kedar Nath, 1980 (4) SCC 276.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the orders denying leave were set aside, and the tenants were granted leave to defend the eviction petition so the rival claims could be decided after the parties had an opportunity to prove their cases.

rule.if: summary_eviction_leave_request and tenant_discloses_material_defense and defense_not_frivolous and defense_requires_trial

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_request: A tenant asks for leave to contest a landlord’s summary eviction petition based on a claimed need for the premises.
predicates.tenant_discloses_material_defense: The tenant’s affidavit sets out facts which, if established, could defeat the landlord’s entitlement to possession.
predicates.defense_not_frivolous: The tenant’s stated grounds have a prima facie basis and are not baseless or unreal.
predicates.defense_requires_trial: The disputed matters require evidence and adjudication rather than resolution in the summary leave inquiry.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking leave to contest a summary residential-eviction application need only disclose facts that prima facie raise a triable issue capable of disentitling the landlord from possession; the tenant need not establish a defence that would ultimately defeat the claim.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction for bona fide residential occupation by himself and dependent family members.
The tenant’s affidavit disputed the landlord’s bona fide need and asserted that the landlord and family were settled abroad, and that the premises had been let for residential-cum-commercial use.
The tenant also raised disputes about the extent of the tenancy and other proceedings between the parties.
members.legal_principle: Sections 25B(4) and 25B(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 require leave where the tenant’s affidavit discloses facts that would disentitle the landlord from possession under Section 14(1)(e). The landlord bears the burden of affirmatively establishing bona fide need. The applicable test is whether a triable issue arises, not whether the tenant is likely to succeed. The Court relied on Charan Dass Duggal v. Brahma Nand, including its reference to Santosh Kumar v. Bhai Mool Singh, and Precision Steel & Engineering Works v. Prem Deva Niranjan Deva Tayal; it also applied the principle of natural justice that a person should have an adequate opportunity to meet a claim carrying serious civil consequences.
members.conclusion: Leave to defend must be granted when the tenant’s affidavit prima facie discloses facts that could disentitle the landlord from obtaining possession; a mere desire for leave is insufficient, but the tenant need not prove the defence at that stage.

predicates.summary_residential_eviction_proceeding: A landlord has brought a summary proceeding seeking possession of residential premises for the landlord’s bona fide occupation or that of a dependent family member.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_prima_facie_t: The tenant’s affidavit states facts which, if established, could defeat the landlord’s entitlement to possession and are not plainly frivolous or untenable.

members.legal_issue: A decree for eviction cannot be entered on admission of the landlord-tenant relationship alone when the tenant raises a disputed defence that goes to the root of the claim.
material_facts: In the eviction suit, the tenant admitted the landlord-tenant relationship and the lease period.
The tenant claimed that the parties had entered into an agreement for sale of the premises and that he had paid a substantial advance under it; the landlord denied that claim.
The tenant had also brought a contested suit for specific performance based on the alleged agreement.
The trial court granted eviction under Order XII Rule 6 CPC, and the Supreme Court found that the disputed issues required the tenant to have an opportunity to contest the suit.
members.legal_principle: Order XII Rule 6 CPC is an enabling and discretionary provision: judgment on admission is not a matter of right, and where a defendant raises objections going to the root of the case, the court should not exercise that discretion merely on the basis of an admission that does not unequivocally establish entitlement to the decree. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The admission of the tenancy relationship was not an unequivocal admission entitling the landlord to an eviction decree under Order XII Rule 6 CPC. The matter was remitted for fresh consideration, subject to the tenant paying the arrears and ongoing compensation specified by the Court; the Court expressed no opinion on the merits.

rule.if: eviction_suit_with_judgment_on_admissions_application and tenancy_relationship_admitted and material_defence_raised and landlord_disputes_material_defence

predicates.eviction_suit_with_judgment_on_admission: A plaintiff seeks eviction and asks the court to decide the claim on admissions.
predicates.tenancy_relationship_admitted: The tenant admits that the landlord-tenant relationship exists.
predicates.material_defence_raised: The tenant raises a defence that, if established, could affect the right to eviction.
predicates.landlord_disputes_material_defence: The landlord contests the tenant’s material defence.

members.legal_issue: A court should not enter judgment on admission in a property suit when the defendant raises a substantial, unresolved defence to dispossession and the asserted admission is not clear, unambiguous, and unconditional.
material_facts: The owner sought mandatory and permanent injunctions to remove his daughter-in-law from part of the house.

The daughter-in-law admitted in separate domestic-violence pleadings that the property stood in the father-in-law’s name, but in her written statement disputed that it was his self-acquired property and asserted that it had been acquired with joint-family funds.
She also asserted a right to reside in the property as a shared household.
The Trial Court decreed the suit under Order XII Rule 6 based on the ownership admission without deciding those defences.
members.legal_principle: Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is discretionary, not a matter of right. Under Himani Alloys Ltd. v. Tata Steel Ltd., an admission relied on for judgment without trial must be clear, unambiguous, unconditional, categorical, and deliberate. S.M. Asif v. Virender Kumar Bajaj holds that judgment on admission is inappropriate where the defence raises objections going to the root of the case. Section 26 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 also permits relevant residence relief to be sought in other legal proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Trial Court’s decree under Order XII Rule 6 was unsustainable; the substantial defences and the claim of residence had to be considered rather than disposed of summarily on the alleged admission.

predicates.civil_property_injunction_case: An owner has brought a civil suit seeking an injunction or possession affecting the defendant’s occupancy of property.
predicates.defendant_disputes_material_property_or_: The defendant contests a material issue about the property or asserts a legal right to remain in the home.
predicates.alleged_admission_does_not_resolve_defen: The statement relied on as an admission does not clearly, unambiguously, and unconditionally dispose of the defendant’s material defence.

members.legal_issue: A possession decree in a landlord-tenant suit cannot be entered on admissions alone when the tenant raises a material and plausible defense based on agreements to sell that requires evidentiary determination.
material_facts: The suit sought possession on the basis of a landlord-tenant relationship. The parties did not dispute the lease agreements, the rent terms, or that rent had not been paid after the extended lease expired.
The tenant relied on several agreements to sell and contended that the sale arrangements and related adjustments changed the parties’ relationship and addressed the accrued rent.
The dispute over the agreements and the tenant’s defense had not been tested by evidence; a suit for specific performance was also pending.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court has discretionary power to enter judgment on admissions, but should exercise it only where the admissions are specific, clear and categorical. Admissions of a landlord-tenant relationship do not by themselves warrant a decree where a material defense requires appreciation of evidence. The Court applied S.M. Asif v. Virendar Kumar Bajaj (2015) 9 SCC 287, and considered the principles in Himani Alloys Ltd. v. Tata Steel Ltd. (2011) 15 SCC 273 and Hari Steel and General Industries Ltd. v. Daljit Singh (2019) 20 SCC 425 concerning the discretionary nature of the power and the need for clear admissions.
members.conclusion: The admissions were not clear and categorical enough to justify a possession decree without considering the defense. The decree was set aside and the suit remitted for trial, with an opportunity for the parties to lead evidence.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s statutory interest in commercial premises remains heritable after termination of the contractual tenancy when the rent-control law does not restrict its inheritance, and the heirs may continue to receive the law’s protection against eviction.
material_facts: The tenant leased a shop for commercial use, and the landlord terminated the lease by notice.
The tenant remained in possession after termination, and the landlord accepted rent from her until her death, leaving her a statutory tenant under the rent-control law.
The heirs succeeded to her interest by intestate succession and remained in possession of the shop.
The heirs had not carried on the business with the tenant during her lifetime.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3(vii)(a) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, a person continuing in possession after termination of tenancy remains a tenant unless a decree for eviction has been passed. Section 13(1) protects a tenant from eviction except on grounds specified by the Act. Applying the ordinary law of succession, including the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Court held that the statutory tenant’s interest in commercial premises is heritable where the Act contains no contrary restriction. The Court relied on Damadilal v. Parashram, which treated a statutory tenant as retaining an interest in the premises; Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, which held that termination does not itself extinguish the tenant’s estate or make commercial tenancy non-heritable; V. Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal; and the earlier cases J.C. Chaterjee v. Sri Kishan and Anand Niwas (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi. It distinguished Bhavarlal Labhchand v. Kanaiyalal Nathalal Intawala, which concerned a testamentary transfer to a stranger.
members.conclusion: The tenancy interest was heritable despite termination of the contractual tenancy, and the heirs succeeded to it and were entitled to the rent-control law’s protection against eviction except in accordance with that law.

members.legal_issue: A protected tenant’s interest in premises may be inherited when the governing rental law treats a person continuing in possession after termination as a tenant and does not limit that interest to a personal right of occupation.
material_facts: The tenants died while their appeal against an eviction decree was pending, and their heirs sought to continue the appeal.

The governing law defined a tenant to include a person continuing in possession after termination of the tenancy, subject to its stated exclusion for a person against whom an eviction order or decree had been made.
The law’s restrictions on subletting applied to tenants as defined, supporting the conclusion that a protected tenant retained an interest in the premises.
members.legal_principle: The incidents of a protected tenancy must be determined from the governing statute, rather than imported from the English concept of statutory tenancy. Under sections 2(i) and 14 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, continued possession after termination was included in the definition of tenant, and the restriction on subletting applied to that defined class. The Court distinguished Anand Nivas (Private) Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi and Jagdish Chander Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan, which proceeded on a different statutory basis and treated the protected tenant’s right as personal; it also referred to the English cases Roe v. Russell, Haskins v. Lewis, Keeves v. Dean and Boyer v. Warbey.
members.conclusion: The tenants’ interest in the premises was heritable, and their heirs were entitled to prosecute the pending appeal.

predicates.tenancy_appeal_after_tenant_death: A tenant died while an appeal concerning the tenancy or the right to remain in the premises was pending.
predicates.governing_law_includes_continuing_posses: The governing rental law treats a person continuing in possession after termination of the tenancy as a tenant, subject to the law’s stated limits.
predicates.subletting_restrictions_apply_to_that_te: The governing rental law applies its restrictions on subletting to the class of tenants that includes persons continuing in possession after termination.

members.legal_issue: A deceased tenant’s commercial tenancy remains heritable after termination of the contractual tenancy, and the heirs inherit the protection against eviction where the governing rent law imposes no restriction on succession to commercial tenancies.
material_facts: The deceased tenant occupied commercial premises and his contractual tenancy had been terminated.
He continued in possession under the protection of the rent-control law when he died during the eviction proceedings.

The governing law treated a person continuing in possession after termination as a tenant and provided no restriction on inheritance of commercial tenancy rights, although it restricted succession to residential tenancies.
The High Court ordered eviction on the ground that the heirs of a tenant whose contractual tenancy had ended did not inherit the tenancy or its statutory protection.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(1)(ii) and 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a person continuing in possession after termination of the contractual tenancy remains a tenant protected against eviction except on grounds specified by the Act. The Act does not, merely by terminating the contractual tenancy, extinguish the tenant’s estate or interest; that interest is heritable unless the Act provides otherwise. Section 2(1)(iii), introduced by the Delhi Rent Control (Amendment) Act, 1976, restricts succession in respect of residential premises but does not restrict inheritance of commercial tenancy rights. In the absence of such a restriction, those rights pass under the ordinary law of succession. The Court followed Damadilal v. Parashram and relied on V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal; it held that contrary observations in Ganpat Ladha v. Sashikant Vishnu Shinde did not state the correct law.
members.conclusion: The tenancy rights in the commercial premises devolved on the deceased tenant’s heirs under the ordinary law of succession, and the heirs inherited the Act’s protection against eviction. The High Court’s order was set aside and the case remanded for the appeal and cross-objection to be decided on their merits.

members.legal_issue: On the death of a tenant of a non-residential building, the heirs who succeed intestate acquire tenancy rights, including the right to continue the business in the premises.
material_facts: The original tenant died intestate while occupying a non-residential building.
The deceased tenant's married daughters were among the heirs who succeeded under the law of succession.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(a)(2) of the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 defines a tenant of a non-residential building to include the deceased tenant's heirs. Read with the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, this gives the heirs who succeed intestate the tenancy rights, not merely the liability to pay rent, but also the right to continue the business until eviction in accordance with the Act. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The heirs who succeeded intestate were tenants under the Act and acquired the deceased tenant's leasehold rights, including the right to continue the business until duly evicted.

predicates.heirs_acquire_tenancy_rights: The heirs who succeeded acquire the tenancy rights, including the right to continue the business until duly evicted.

members.legal_issue: The rights of an ordinary tenant in agricultural land are heritable under the tenant’s personal law unless a special statutory provision provides otherwise.
material_facts: The deceased held rights as an ordinary tenant in agricultural land.
The claimant, as the deceased’s adopted son and successor under personal law, claimed those tenancy rights.
The relevant statute contained provisions on mutation applicable to all classes of tenants but no special rule excluding inheritance of ordinary tenancy rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 86 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 applies to all classes of tenants and contemplates succession or transfer of tenancy rights. Sections 87 and 89 address ordinary tenants and sub-tenants but do not make ordinary tenancy rights non-heritable. In the absence of a special statutory provision, heritability is governed by the tenant’s personal law.
members.conclusion: The ordinary tenancy rights were heritable under personal law, and the adopted son was entitled to succeed to them.

members.legal_issue: The rights of an ordinary tenant are heritable when the governing tenancy law makes no special provision against heritability.
material_facts: The disputed agricultural land was held under ordinary tenancy rights.

The respondent argued that those rights were not heritable because the tenancy law had special provisions concerning the heritability of pakka tenants but no corresponding provision for ordinary tenants.
The Court considered the provisions governing ordinary tenants and mutation of names.
members.legal_principle: Sections 86, 87 and 89 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 support the conclusion that ordinary tenancy rights are not excluded from heritability: section 87 concerns the terms on which an ordinary tenant holds land, while section 86 applies to holders of land generally and contemplates a new holder succeeding to a former holder’s title. In the absence of a special statutory rule, the personal law of the tenants governs heritability.
members.conclusion: The ordinary tenancy rights were heritable, with heritability governed by the tenants’ personal law in the absence of a special statutory provision.

predicates.ordinary_tenancy: The land was held under ordinary tenancy rights rather than a distinct tenancy category with its own special rules.

members.legal_issue: A tenant company’s continued possession of agricultural land after expiry of its lease remains juridical possession where the governing land-reform law provides that expiry alone does not terminate the tenancy, making the company subject to the prohibition on holding land.
material_facts: A registered company leased agricultural land for a fixed term, and the term expired.
The company remained in possession after the lease expired; the landowners were not in possession of the land at the relevant time.
The land-reform law provided that a tenancy could not be terminated merely because its fixed duration had expired.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 5 and 6 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, a tenancy cannot be terminated merely by expiry of its fixed term. Read with Sections 19, 20, 44, 58, 60, 62 and 79-B, the Act allows only a person in possession and personally cultivating land to hold it, while prohibiting a company from holding agricultural land and requiring a company holding land to declare it. The Court distinguished Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, which concerned whether landlord consent created a tenancy after expiry, and M.C. Chockalingam v. V. Manickavasagam, which concerned lawful possession under cinema licensing rules; neither displaced the effect of the statutory continuation of tenancy here.
members.conclusion: The company’s possession remained juridical despite expiry of the lease. It was required to declare the land it held, and the land covered by the declaration vested in the State free from encumbrances.

members.legal_issue: A tenant of agricultural land who remains in possession after a fixed-term lease expires does not thereby become a trespasser and may be evicted only through the applicable agricultural-tenancy process.
material_facts: The landlord’s case was that the agricultural land had been leased to the tenant for fixed terms and that the last lease expired in 2005.
The landlord acknowledged that the tenant had been in possession from 1986 through 2005, and revenue records recorded the tenant’s possession.
The tenant remained in possession after the lease expired and claimed protection under the agricultural-tenancy laws.
The landlord sought possession through a civil-court counterclaim; no eviction through the designated revenue process was shown.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the definition of tenant in section 2(6) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, read with section 4(5) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, and considered sections 8, 9, 14-A and 18 of the 1953 Act and sections 40 and 42 of the 1887 Act. It relied on Bhajan Lal v. State of Punjab, Sanwat Singh v. Zail Singh, Tulsi v. Paro and Ram Lal v. Darshan Lal, and distinguished V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal and R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P. as cases concerning rent-control laws. It expressly disagreed with Sukhdev Singh v. Puran, which had treated a fixed-term agricultural tenancy as ending on expiry of the term, and referred the matter to a larger Bench to resolve the conflict.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the lower courts erred in treating the agricultural tenant as a trespasser merely because the fixed-term lease had expired. In the Court’s view, eviction had to proceed under the applicable tenancy law before the empowered Revenue Court. Because this view conflicted with an earlier Supreme Court decision, the Court referred the matter to a larger Bench.

members.legal_issue: A tenant whose fixed-term lease has expired remains entitled to apply to acquire the landowner’s proprietary rights if the tenancy has not been ended by eviction or relinquishment.
material_facts: The respondent had been inducted as a tenant under a five-year lease, which expired before he applied to acquire the landowner’s proprietary rights.
The finding that the respondent had not relinquished possession and remained a tenant was not contested in the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11(1) of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, a tenant may apply to acquire the landowner’s rights in the tenancy land. Read with Sections 48 to 55 and 62 of that Act, expiry of the lease term alone did not end the tenancy; it continued until eviction by court decree or abandonment or other relinquishment. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The respondent remained a tenant after the lease expired and was entitled to maintain his application for acquisition of the proprietary rights.

members.legal_issue: A person who continues in possession of agricultural land after the deemed lease term with the landlord’s consent retains tenant status and statutory protection against eviction based solely on expiry of the lease.
material_facts: The agricultural lease document was unregistered, so its stated fixed term could not be relied on to establish the lease’s duration.
The tenant remained in possession beyond the deemed lease period with the landlord’s consent; that consent ceased only when the landlord sought possession in the tenant’s injunction suit.
The landlord sought a mandatory injunction based on expiry of the lease, rather than eviction on a statutory ground and through the prescribed procedure.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(6) and 9 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenure Act, 1953, read with Section 4(5) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, a tenant holding over with the landlord’s consent remains within the statutory protection against eviction except on the grounds specified in Section 9. Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 gives legitimacy to possession continued with the landlord’s consent after expiry of the deemed lease term. Section 40 of the 1887 Act, which permits ejectment on expiry of a fixed term, does not override the protection provided by Section 9 of the 1953 Act; eviction must follow the procedure in Section 14-A. The court distinguished the position discussed in Sukhdev Singh (Dead) through Legal Representatives v. Puran, and relied on the holding-over principle in Section 116.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s continued possession with the landlord’s consent made him a tenant holding over and entitled to protection under the 1953 Act. Expiry of the lease alone did not entitle the landlord to evict him; the order against the tenant was set aside.

members.legal_issue: A person who remains in possession after termination of a tenancy remains protected as a tenant against execution of an eviction decree, including a decree entered by compromise, where the rent-control law covers continuing possession and restricts eviction under decrees.
material_facts: An advocate rented a building and agreed in a compromise to vacate it by a specified date; an eviction decree was entered on the compromise before the rent-control law was extended to the area.
The tenant remained continuously in possession after the decree and after the law’s extension.
The landlord did not establish a ground for eviction under the rent-control law.
The parties later agreed to a sale of the property, and the court recorded their agreement as an undertaking; it formally dismissed the appeal because no further relief was needed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(i) and 13(1) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, read together, include a former tenant who continues in possession and prohibit eviction in execution of a decree, whether passed before or after the Act’s commencement, except as the Act permits. The inclusive definition preserves statutory tenant status even if a decree or other process has ended the tenancy under general property law. The Act is beneficial legislation and should be construed liberally to fulfil its protective purpose; interpretative doubt favours the potential evictee unless the language plainly provides for eviction. Subudhi’s case, decided under the Orissa House-Rent Control Act, 1958, was distinguishable because that Act’s definition expressly excluded a person against whom an eviction decree had been made.
members.conclusion: The tenant remained a tenant under the Act despite the compromise decree and continued to enjoy the protection of Section 13(1), so execution of the eviction decree could not proceed. The appeal was formally dismissed following the parties’ settlement.

members.legal_issue: A tenant-protective rent restriction that becomes applicable after a possession decree but before its execution can prevent execution of that decree against a tenant who remains in possession.
material_facts: A possession decree was passed while the premises were outside the area covered by the rent-control regime.
Before execution was completed, the premises came within the regime’s coverage and the tenant remained in possession.
The tenant challenged an order directing delivery of possession under the earlier decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(1) prohibits an order or decree for recovery of possession against a tenant except on the grounds permitted by that provision, and Section 3(r) defines tenant to include a person continuing in possession after termination of the tenancy. Following Mani Subrat Jain v. Raja Ram Vohra, the Court treated a person remaining in possession as protected despite a decree or process that had otherwise ended the tenancy under general property law. Because rent-control legislation is beneficial to tenants, its protection is construed liberally; absent express provision or clear implication to the contrary, a restriction that is prospective in form may displace a landlord’s vested right under a final decree. The Court distinguished Konchada Ramamurty Subudhi v. Gopinath Naik, which concerned the parties’ intention under a compromise decree rather than the legislative purpose of a rent-control provision.
members.conclusion: The later-applicable rent restriction prevented execution of the earlier possession decree against the tenant, so the appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.

predicates.premises_entered_rent_protection_before_: The premises came within a tenant-protective rent regime after the possession decree but before its execution was completed.
predicates.occupant_remained_in_possession_after_te: The occupant continued in possession after the tenancy had otherwise been terminated.

members.legal_issue: A person who becomes a tenant under a lease between the parties remains a tenant protected against an eviction suit requiring prior administrative permission, even if the lease was made without an allotment order.
material_facts: The landlord leased the premises to the occupant, who paid rent under the lease.
No allotment order had been made for the occupant.
The owners brought a civil suit to recover possession without first obtaining the District Magistrate’s permission.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(g) and 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 define a tenant by reference to rent payable and restrict eviction suits without prior permission. Under Udho Dass v. Prem Prakash (1963 A.L.J. 406), a lease made without an allotment order may create a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties even though it does not bind the authorities. Reading the definition and scheme of the Act, a tenant without an allotment order is still protected by Section 3; the landlord is estopped from denying that status.
members.conclusion: The occupant was a tenant for purposes of the statutory protection, and the suit was not maintainable because it had been brought without the required permission.

members.legal_issue: A person who occupies accommodation as a tenant remains within the protection against eviction suits even without an allotment order.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the premises under a lease made without an allotment order.
The tenant paid rent to the original owner and later to the purchasers of the premises.
The purchasers brought a civil suit to recover possession without first obtaining the District Magistrate’s permission.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(g) and 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, together with the scheme of the Act, include a person from whom rent is payable even if the person occupies without an allotment order. The Court approved Udho Dass v. Prem Prakash, (1963) A.L.J. 406, on the validity between the parties of a lease made without the required allotment. Section 3(1) prohibits an eviction suit against a tenant without the District Magistrate’s permission.
members.conclusion: The occupant was a tenant protected by the restriction on eviction suits, and the suit brought without the required permission was not maintainable.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and rent_payable_by_occupant and no_allotment_order and required_permission_not_obtained

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brings a civil proceeding to evict an occupant from accommodation.
predicates.rent_payable_by_occupant: The occupant pays rent, or would owe rent under an express or implied agreement, for the accommodation.
predicates.no_allotment_order: The occupant’s possession was not based on an allotment order from the responsible authority.
predicates.required_permission_not_obtained: The landlord brings the eviction suit without first obtaining the permission required from the responsible authority.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s rights do not merge into ownership when the tenant acquires only a partial ownership interest and the landlord’s interest in the whole property does not vest in the same person.
material_facts: The occupants acquired the tenancy rights and ownership interests transferred by only some co-owners; the landlord’s ownership interest was not transferred to them.
The eviction proceeding proceeded on the basis that the landlord was a co-owner and the occupants had acquired only partial ownership.
members.legal_principle: Section 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires the lessee’s and lessor’s interests in the whole property to vest at the same time in one person in the same right for merger to determine a lease. The Court relied on Badri Narain Jha v. Rameshwar Dayal Singh, Shaikh Faqir Bakhsh v. Murli Dhar, and Nalakath Sainuddin v. Koorikadan Sulaiman; merger is not established when only partial ownership interests are acquired, and it is presumed against where it would operate to a party’s disadvantage.
members.conclusion: The tenancy was not determined by merger, so the occupants remained obliged to deliver possession when the tenancy ended.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and tenancy_rights_acquired and partial_ownership_acquired and landlord_interest_not_acquired

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking eviction from premises held under a tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_rights_acquired: The occupants acquired the tenant’s rights in the premises.
predicates.partial_ownership_acquired: The occupants acquired ownership interests from only some of the co-owners.
predicates.landlord_interest_not_acquired: The landlord’s ownership interest in the property did not vest in the occupants.

members.legal_issue: A joint lessee’s acquisition of only part of the lessor’s interest does not merge or extinguish the lease when the interests in the tenancy and reversion do not fully coincide.
material_facts: The village had originally been granted under one lease, whose interest later devolved among several branches of lessees.
One branch held an eight-anna share of the leasehold and acquired an eight-anna share of the proprietary interest, while other persons continued to hold the remaining interests.
The entire proprietary interest was later sold for unpaid government cess, and the purchasers claimed that the leasehold share had merged into the proprietary interest and passed with it.
The claimants did not allege a fresh contract that extinguished or replaced the existing tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Merger requires the lessee’s and lessor’s interests to coincide; acquiring only part of the reversion does not extinguish a lease held jointly with others. The Court applied the doctrine of merger and relied on the principle concerning joint tenants’ common obligations discussed in White v. Tyndall (13 App. Cas. 263). No statutory provision was relied on.
members.conclusion: The leasehold interest did not merge into the acquired proprietary share, and the later sale of the proprietary interest did not transfer that leasehold interest to the purchasers.

rule.if: merger_based_rent_suit_challenge and lease_created_as_single_contract and joint_leasehold_remained_with_others and acquiring_lessee_did_not_own_entire_reversion and no_fresh_contract_severed_interests

predicates.merger_based_rent_suit_challenge: In a dispute over a rent claim, a party challenges the claim on the ground that acquiring a lessor’s interest extinguished the lease.
predicates.lease_created_as_single_contract: The lessor originally granted the property under one lease, and the leasehold later devolved among multiple holders.
predicates.joint_leasehold_remained_with_others: The lessee who acquired a proprietary interest continued to hold the leasehold jointly with other lessees.
predicates.acquiring_lessee_did_not_own_entire_reve: The lessee acquired only part of the lessor’s interest, while other holders retained the rest.
predicates.no_fresh_contract_severed_interests: No fresh agreement between the relevant holders and the lessor replaced or severed the existing tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s acquisition of only some co-owner landlords’ interests does not determine the tenancy by merger, and the tenant remains subject to rent-control obligations.
material_facts: The occupants held the building under a continuing lease.
They acquired the rights of some, but not all, of the co-owner landlords.
The rights of the remaining co-owner landlords did not vest in the occupants.
The landlords obtained a rent-control order directing the occupants to deposit rent, and the occupants challenged that order on the ground that the tenancy had ended by merger.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 105 and 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, a lease is determined by merger only when the lessee’s and lessor’s interests in the whole property vest simultaneously in one person in the same right, with no intervening estate. Acquisition of only part of the reversion, including the rights of a co-owner, is insufficient. Section 44 does not vest the entire property interest in the acquiring tenant, and Section 109 permits an assignee of the reversion to exercise the lessor’s rights but does not itself extinguish the tenancy. The Court approved T. Lakshmipathi v. P. Nithyananda Reddy and the approach in India Umbrella Manufacturing Co. v. Shagabandei Agarwalla; it held Abul Alim v. Sheikh Jamal Uddin Ansari incorrectly decided on this point, and distinguished Jagdish Dutt v. Dharam Pal because Section 111(d) was not applied there. The principle is also supported by Faquir Baksh v. Murli Dhar, Badri Narain Jha v. Rameshwar Dayal Singh, and Puran Chand v. Kirpal Singh.
members.conclusion: The tenancy was not determined by merger because the occupants acquired only some co-owner landlords’ rights. They remained tenants and were bound to comply with the rent-control requirements, including the rent-deposit order; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.rent_deposit_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a direction to deposit rent in a rent-control matter.
predicates.tenant_acquired_partial_reversion: The tenant acquired the rights of only some of the landlords in the property.
predicates.co_owner_interests_remained_outstanding: The interests of other co-owner landlords remained outstanding and did not vest in the tenant.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s acquisition of only part of a landlord’s interest does not extinguish the tenancy by merger.
material_facts: The property was jointly owned by two co-owners and let to tenants.
Some partners of one tenant firm acquired the share of one co-owner during the litigation.
The tenant-associated purchasers acquired only a share of the property, not the entire landlord interest.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, merger requires the landlord’s interest in its entirety to vest in the tenant’s interest in its entirety. Acquisition of only part of the landlord’s interest, or of one co-landlord’s interest, does not cause merger or extinguish the tenancy.
members.conclusion: The tenancy was not extinguished by merger because the landlord’s interest did not vest entirely in the tenant’s interest.

predicates.landlord_tenant_case: The proceeding concerns a tenancy between a landlord and a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_relationship_exists: A tenancy existed between the parties before the tenant’s acquisition.
predicates.tenant_acquired_only_part_of_landlord_in: The tenant or persons associated with the tenant acquired only part of the landlord’s interest.

members.legal_issue: Abolition of an intermediary land grant does not by itself end an existing landlord–tenant relationship or defeat a tenant’s statutory right to purchase the land.
material_facts: The land was held by its owner as an inam for the performance of services, and the tenants possessed part of it under leases created before the abolition and regrant.
The tenants were declared purchasers under the tenancy legislation, and the tribunal fixed the purchase price.
The owner argued that abolition of the inam ended the tenancies and therefore removed the tenants’ purchase rights.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4–9 of the Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955 abolished alienations and provided for occupancy rights but did not extinguish the relationship between an ex-inamdar and existing tenants. Section 28 preserved the application of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 and the mutual rights and obligations of landlords and tenants except where inconsistent with an express provision of the abolition legislation. Section 32 of the Tenancy Act was not inconsistent with that legislation. The abolition legislation aimed to eliminate intermediaries, not evict tenants. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The tenancies continued after abolition, and the tenants remained entitled to purchase under the tenancy legislation; the tribunal could proceed to fix the purchase price.

rule.if: statutory_tenant_purchase_proceeding and land_was_held_under_an_abolished_intermediary_grant and tenant_held_under_a_preexisting_lease and abolition_law_preserves_tenancy_rights

predicates.statutory_tenant_purchase_proceeding: A tribunal is considering a tenant’s claim to purchase land under a statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
predicates.land_was_held_under_an_abolished_interme: The landowner held the land under an intermediary grant that was later abolished.
predicates.tenant_held_under_a_preexisting_lease: The tenant held the land under a lease that existed before the grant was abolished.
predicates.abolition_law_preserves_tenancy_rights: The law abolishing the intermediary grant preserves tenancy rights except where they conflict with its express provisions.

members.legal_issue: Abolition and vesting do not end the landlord–tenant relationship before the provisions extinguishing that relationship take effect when the governing law preserves mutual rights and those provisions commence later.
material_facts: The law abolished the inams and vested the land in the State when it first came into force, but only some of its provisions commenced at that time.
The provisions preserving the application of tenancy law and the mutual rights and obligations of inamdars and tenants were in force from the initial commencement.
The provisions directing that rents be paid to the State and extinguishing the landlord–tenant relationship did not take effect until the rest of the law commenced.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(1) and 3(2)(b) and section 33 of the Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954, the interests expressly saved from vesting and the mutual rights and obligations under the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 were preserved. Since sections 3(2)(d), (g), (h) and (i), including the provision extinguishing the relationship, commenced later, the relationship continued until then. Section 4 of the 1956 Amendment Act, which treated the inamdar as an occupant for land-revenue purposes during the interval, supported that reading.
members.conclusion: The landlord–tenant relationship continued after abolition and vesting until the delayed provisions took effect.

predicates.statutory_inam_abolition_case: The proceeding concerns a law abolishing inam interests and vesting the land in the State.
predicates.mutual_tenancy_rights_preserved: The law preserves the application of tenancy rules and the mutual rights and obligations between the landholder and tenant.
predicates.relationship_extinction_provision_not_ye: The provision ending the landholder–tenant relationship has not yet taken effect.
predicates.landlord_tenant_relationship_continues_u: The landholder–tenant relationship continues until the provision ending it takes effect.

members.legal_issue: The statutory vesting of an acquired undertaking does not, by itself, terminate an existing tenancy of premises within the undertaking.
material_facts: The occupants were tenants of shops, offices, or storage premises under the former hotel company.
After the undertaking was acquired, the Hotel Authority accepted rent from the occupants and dealt with them as tenants.
The State argued that statutory vesting and the termination of contracts ended the tenancies.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 4(2) of the Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1980, vesting free of encumbrances and deemed termination of contracts did not end the landlord-tenant relationship. A tenancy is not an encumbrance of the kind listed in Section 4(1), and the deemed termination in Section 4(2) did not terminate that relationship. The State stepped into the former company's shoes as landlord.
members.conclusion: The tenancies continued after acquisition, and the State Government took the former company's place as landlord.

predicates.acquisition_tenancy_case: The case concerns whether a tenancy survived the statutory acquisition of an undertaking containing the rented premises.
