predicates.existing_tenant_relationship: The occupant held the premises as a tenant under the former owner before the acquisition.
predicates.rent_accepted_after_acquisition: The new public owner or its representative accepted rent from the occupant after the acquisition.
predicates.landlord_relationship_continued_in_pract: After acquisition, the new public owner or its representative dealt with the occupant in a manner consistent with a continuing landlord-tenant relationship.

members.legal_issue: Service of a notice terminating a tenancy and filing an application for possession do not end the tenancy before possession is ordered, so a tenant who remains in possession at vesting can acquire occupant rights under the abolition law.
material_facts: The appellant served a notice purporting to terminate the tenancy and applied for possession under the tenancy law.
The application for possession was not granted before the land vested in the State.
The other party remained in possession as a tenant when the land vested.
The abolition law granted occupant rights to a qualifying person in possession at vesting.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 44(1) and 32(2) of the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Land Act, 1950, notice and an application for possession do not by themselves terminate the tenancy; the process is not complete until possession is ordered by the competent authority. Rule 28(5) provides that, upon the application for possession being granted, termination takes effect from the commencement of the following year. Accordingly, a tenant still in possession at vesting may acquire occupant rights under section 6(1) of the Hyderabad Abolition of Inams and Cash Grants Act, 1954. The Court doubted the contrary view of the Bombay High Court Full Bench in Dattatraya Sadashiv Dhond v. Ganpati Raghu Gaoli, 67 Bombay Law Reporter 521.
members.conclusion: The tenancy had not ended merely through service of notice and filing the possession application; because the tenant remained in possession at vesting, the tenant acquired the rights of an occupant.

rule.if: proceeding_concerning_occupant_rights_on_vesting and termination_notice_served and possession_application_filed and no_possession_order_before_vesting and tenant_in_possession_at_vesting

predicates.proceeding_concerning_occupant_rights_on: The proceeding determines whether a person acquired occupant rights when land vested under an abolition law.
predicates.termination_notice_served: The landholder served a notice purporting to terminate the tenancy.
predicates.possession_application_filed: The landholder applied to the competent authority for possession of the land.
predicates.no_possession_order_before_vesting: The competent authority had not ordered possession in favour of the landholder before the land vested.
predicates.tenant_in_possession_at_vesting: The tenant remained in possession of the land when vesting occurred.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s right to purchase land is not extinguished by a pending ejectment proceeding or defeated by a later ejectment order if the tenant was still a tenant when the purchase right was exercised.
material_facts: The tenant had continuously occupied the land for the minimum period required to claim the statutory purchase right.
The landowner had begun an ejectment proceeding alleging non-payment of rent, but no ejectment order had been passed when the tenant applied to purchase the land.
The tenant’s purchase application was made before the ejectment order was passed.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 9, 14-A and 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a tenancy is determined only in the prescribed conditions and manner; instituting an ejectment proceeding does not itself terminate the tenancy. A tenant who has completed the continuous occupation period required by section 18 remains entitled to purchase while still a tenant, and a later ejectment order does not retrospectively defeat a purchase right already exercised. Har Sarup v. Financial Commissioner, Revenue, Punjab, (1965) 44 Lah. L.T. 157, was approved.
members.conclusion: The tenant was entitled to exercise the purchase right while the ejectment proceeding was pending, and the later ejectment order did not defeat that right.

rule.if: purchase_claim_in_ejectment_case and six_year_continuous_occupation and tenant_status_at_purchase_claim and no_ejectment_order_at_purchase_claim

predicates.purchase_claim_in_ejectment_case: A tenant’s claim to purchase land is made while an ejectment proceeding concerning that tenancy is pending.
predicates.six_year_continuous_occupation: The tenant has continuously occupied the land for the minimum period required to claim the purchase right.
predicates.tenant_status_at_purchase_claim: The tenant remains a tenant when the purchase claim is made.
predicates.no_ejectment_order_at_purchase_claim: No order ejecting the tenant has been passed when the purchase claim is made.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who is wrongfully dispossessed remains a tenant, and may retain a preferential right to pre-empt a sale, unless the tenancy is lawfully terminated.
material_facts: The lower courts found that the plaintiff was a tenant of the land on the date it was sold.
The vendees forcibly dispossessed the tenant after the sale.
The tenant’s tenancy was not shown to have been terminated on a ground authorized by the applicable tenancy law.
The tenant applied to the revenue authority for restoration of possession.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4, 7 and 7A of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, override inconsistent laws and require a lawful ground and an order or decree for eviction to determine a tenancy. Applying Rikki Ram v. Ram Kumar, the Court held that a person with a right to possess land remains its tenant despite wrongful dispossession, particularly where proceedings to recover possession have been initiated. The tenant must have a subsisting pre-emption right on the material dates, as referred to in Bhagwan Das v. Chet Ram; Dindyal v. Rajaram was also cited. The Court confined its conclusion to the provisions before it.
members.conclusion: The tenant was deemed to remain a tenant on the sale date and the other material dates, and was entitled to pre-empt the land.

rule.if: preemption_suit and tenant_on_sale_date and wrongfully_dispossessed and not tenancy_lawfully_terminated and restoration_proceedings_started

predicates.preemption_suit: The proceeding is a claim to pre-empt a sale of land.
predicates.tenant_on_sale_date: The claimant was a tenant of the land when it was sold.
predicates.wrongfully_dispossessed: The claimant was put out of possession without lawful authority.
predicates.tenancy_lawfully_terminated: The tenancy was terminated on a lawful ground through the required process.
predicates.restoration_proceedings_started: The claimant initiated proceedings to recover possession of the land.
predicates.tenant_remains_eligible_to_preempt: The claimant remains a tenant entitled to exercise the preferential right to pre-empt the sale.

members.legal_issue: A lease and a mortgage of the same property do not merge merely because the rights of the lessee and mortgagee are united in one person.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a lease and usufructuary mortgages relating to the same property.
members.legal_principle: Merger requires a lesser estate and a higher estate to vest in one person at the same time and in the same right, with no interest remaining outstanding. A lease and a mortgage are not higher and lower estates relative to one another: the lessor’s reversion and the mortgagor’s equity of redemption remain outstanding. The Court relied on Narayana Dogra Shetty v. Ramchandra Shivram Hingne, approved in Shah Mathuradas Maganlal & Co. v. Nagappa Shankarappa & Ors. The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Sections 58, 101 and 105, are identified in the judgment’s headnote in connection with the dispute.
members.conclusion: There could be no merger of the lease and the mortgage because neither estate was higher or lower than the other, and the lessor’s reversion and the mortgagor’s equity of redemption remained outstanding.

predicates.lease_and_mortgage_same_property: A lease and a mortgage relate to the same property.
predicates.lease_and_mortgage_estates_are_not_highe: The lease estate and the mortgage estate are not higher and lower estates relative to one another.

members.legal_issue: A leasehold interest and a mortgage interest in the same property do not merge merely because one person holds both interests.
material_facts: The mortgagee relied on the fact that the mortgagee had also been the tenant before the mortgage.
The lease and mortgage arose in different capacities, and neither interest was a higher or lower estate than the other.
members.legal_principle: Under section 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, merger requires the relevant lesser and greater interests in the whole property to vest at the same time in one person in the same right, with no interest remaining outside. A lease and a mortgage do not merge merely by being held by one person because neither is, as against the other, a higher or lower estate. The Court approved Narayan v. Ramchandra, 65 Bom. L.R. 449.
members.conclusion: The lease and mortgage did not merge merely because their interests were held by the same person.

rule.if: lease_and_mortgage_interests_in_same_property and same_person_holds_both_interests and interests_held_in_distinct_capacities and neither_interest_is_higher_or_lesser

predicates.lease_and_mortgage_interests_in_same_pro: The same property is subject both to a leasehold interest and to a mortgage interest.
predicates.same_person_holds_both_interests: One person holds both the leasehold interest and the mortgage interest.
predicates.interests_held_in_distinct_capacities: The person holds the two interests in different legal capacities.
predicates.neither_interest_is_higher_or_lesser: Neither the leasehold interest nor the mortgage interest is a higher or lower estate than the other.

members.legal_issue: A notice requirement that applies only to tenancies created after the statutory purchase day does not apply to a tenancy that existed before that day merely because the land was later regranted to the owner.
material_facts: The tenants’ leases existed before the statutory purchase day and before occupancy rights were regranted to the owner after abolition of the inam.

The owner argued that abolition and regrant created a new landlord–tenant relationship and that the tenants had lost their purchase right by failing to give the notice required for later-created tenancies.
members.legal_principle: Section 32-O of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 applies only to tenancies created after the tillers’ day. Because the existing landlord–tenant relationship did not end upon abolition and regrant, no new tenancy arose that would attract that section. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The tenants’ relationship with the owner did not end and restart upon abolition and regrant; the notice requirement for tenancies created after the statutory purchase day did not apply.

predicates.statutory_tenant_purchase_proceeding: A tribunal is considering a tenant’s claim to purchase land under a statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
predicates.tenancy_existed_before_statutory_purchas: The tenant’s tenancy began before the day on which the statutory purchase scheme took effect.
predicates.abolition_and_regrant_did_not_create_a_n: The intermediary grant was abolished and occupancy rights were regranted, but the tenant’s existing tenancy continued rather than being replaced by a new tenancy.

members.legal_issue: The special recovery remedy for a tenancy created on or after the statutory cutoff does not apply when a valid tenancy was created before that cutoff.
material_facts: The tenant had occupied the land under leases granted by the mother from 1951 onwards.
A written lease for the 1956–57 year was executed in favour of the minor represented by her mother.
The mother was competent to act as the minor’s natural guardian in the circumstances, and the lease was valid and binding.
The landlord sought termination of the tenancy and recovery of possession under the special statutory remedy.
members.legal_principle: Section 39 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958 concerns tenancies created not earlier than April 1, 1957. A valid lease created before that date does not meet that requirement. The Court noted that the question of limitation under section 39 did not arise once the provision was found inapplicable; the possible deemed-tenancy issue under section 6 would matter only if the earlier lease were invalid.
members.conclusion: Because the valid tenancy had been created before the statutory cutoff, the special remedy under section 39 did not apply. The Court did not decide whether the application would have been time-barred if that section applied.

predicates.landlord_tenancy_recovery_proceeding: A landlord seeks termination of a tenancy and recovery of possession through a special tenancy-law remedy.
predicates.valid_tenancy_created_before_cutoff: A valid tenancy was created before the legally relevant cutoff for that special remedy.

members.legal_issue: The transitional provisions governing the additional amount apply to an acquisition proceeding pending when the amendment bill was introduced if the Collector had not yet made an award, even when possession was taken earlier.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeding was pending when the amendment bill was introduced, and the Collector had not made an award by then.
Possession had been taken before the bill was introduced.
The Collector made the award after the bill was introduced but before the amendment came into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) provides a substantive right to an additional amount. Under the transitional provision in Section 30(1)(a) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, Section 23(1-A) applies to a proceeding pending on the date the bill was introduced if the Collector had made no award before that date. Where possession had already been taken, the additional amount runs from the Section 4(1) notification until possession. The Court relied on K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, Special Tahsildar (LA), P.W.D. Schemes, Vijayawada v. M.A. Jabbar, and Khanna Improvement Trust v. Land Acquisition Tribunal.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to the additional amount under Section 23(1-A), calculated from the notification until possession had been taken.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding_pending_at_a: The acquisition proceeding remained pending when the relevant amendment bill was introduced.
predicates.collector_award_not_made_by_cutoff: The Collector had not made an award by the time the bill was introduced.
predicates.possession_taken_before_award: Possession of the acquired land was taken before the Collector made the award.
predicates.claimants_entitled_to_transitional_addit: The claimants receive the additional amount available under the transitional rule.

members.legal_issue: The transitional provisions make the additional acquisition benefit available for land-acquisition proceedings commenced after the applicable transition boundary, whether or not the Collector had already made an award before the amending law commenced.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeding began after the transition boundary identified in the transitional provision.
The Collector made the award before the amending law commenced.
The landowners sought enhanced compensation in a reference proceeding.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1A), read together with Section 30(1)(b) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, applies to acquisition proceedings commenced after 30 April 1982, whether or not the Collector made an award before the amending Act commenced. The Constitution Bench majority in K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala construed these provisions together; Prem Chand v. Union of India applied that interpretation.
members.conclusion: The landowners were entitled to the additional benefit provided by Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding was for the acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_started_after_transition_bou: The acquisition proceeding began after the applicable transitional boundary.

members.legal_issue: A claimant may receive the additional compensation benefit when the Reference Court makes its award after the benefit takes effect, even if the Collector made an earlier award.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the Collector made the compensation award before the 1984 amendments took effect.
The landowners sought a reference under Section 18, and the Reference Court made its award after the amendments took effect.
The Reference Court granted the additional benefit, and the High Court upheld that grant.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) confers a substantive right and places a duty on the Court deciding the reference to award the additional amount. Substantive provisions ordinarily operate prospectively unless the statutory language and context show retrospective intent. The term “Court” refers to the court defined by Section 3(d), which decides a reference under Section 18; it cannot be read as “Collector.” The Court rejected the narrower interpretation in Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama and distinguished the issues addressed in Union of India v. Raghuvir Singh; it referred to K. Kamala Jammannia-varu and Bhag Singh in discussing the statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to the additional amount under Section 23(1-A), and the appeals challenging that entitlement were dismissed.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference: A landowner whose land was acquired sought a court determination of compensation through a reference proceeding.
predicates.reference_court_award_after_benefit_take: The court deciding the compensation reference made its award after the additional-benefit provision took effect.
predicates.collector_award_before_transitional_cuto: The Collector had made the initial compensation award before the statutory transitional cutoff.

members.legal_issue: The transitional provision extends the additional compensation benefit to covered acquisition proceedings even where the reference court had already made its award before the benefit took effect.
material_facts: The Court construed Section 30(1)(a) together with Section 23(1-A).

It considered acquisition proceedings that were pending on the transitional cutoff date and in which the Collector had not yet made an award, including proceedings in which the court had already made an award before the new provision took effect.
members.legal_principle: Section 30(1)(a) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 makes Section 23(1-A) applicable to acquisition proceedings pending on the specified transitional date where the Collector had not made an award by then. Read with the word “also” in Section 30(1) and the plain language of Section 23(1-A), the transitional provision does not exclude a proceeding merely because the court had already made its award. The Court disapproved the contrary narrow approaches in Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama and Jaiwant Laxman P. Sardesai, and noted approval of State of Punjab v. Krishan Lal and Maya Devi v. Union Territory of Chandigarh.
members.conclusion: In those covered proceedings, the additional amount is payable even if the court made its award before the new provision took effect.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns acquisition of land and determination of compensation under the acquisition law.
predicates.proceeding_pending_at_transitional_cutof: The acquisition proceeding remained pending on the statutory transitional cutoff date.
predicates.collector_had_not_awarded_by_cutoff: The Collector had not made an award by that cutoff date.

members.legal_issue: A distance safeguard for new sugar mills applies retrospectively to pending disputes when the governing amendment is clarificatory and retrospective.
material_facts: The challenge to de-licensing rested on the establishment of a sugar mill in the vicinity of an existing mill, though more than the prescribed minimum distance away.
A later amendment specified effective steps for establishing a mill.
A prior Supreme Court decision held that the amendment was clarificatory and retrospective and upheld the minimum-distance requirement.
members.legal_principle: In Ojas Industries P. Ltd. v. Oudh Sugar Mills Ltd., the Court held that the amendments to the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, specifying effective steps, were clarificatory and retrospective and applied to cases pending before courts; it also upheld the minimum-distance requirement between mills.
members.conclusion: The distance safeguard applied retrospectively to pending disputes, substantially removing the basis of the challenge to de-licensing.

predicates.pending_mill_spacing_dispute: A dispute concerning the spacing of a newly established mill was pending before a court.
predicates.clarificatory_amendment_specifies_effect: A later amendment clarified the steps required to establish a mill.
predicates.amendment_applies_retroactively: The amendment was held to apply retrospectively to pending disputes.

members.legal_issue: A clarifying amendment to the law of pre-emption applies retrospectively to pending proceedings even without express language giving it retrospective effect.
material_facts: The claimant's pre-emption suit and subsequent appeals were pending when the 1964 amendment was enacted.
The amendment inserted words clarifying that the relevant children were those of the husband through whom the female seller had inherited the property.
The Court concluded that the claimant was entitled to pre-emption under the law even before the amendment.
members.legal_principle: A curative or declaratory amendment that clarifies the previous law is more readily given retrospective effect than legislation that prejudicially affects past rights and transactions. Section 31, inserted by the 1960 amendment, applied to that amendment and did not itself extend to later amendments. The Court relied on Ram Sarup v. Munshi for the scope of section 31 and on Moti Ram v. Bakhwant Singh for retrospective treatment of a clarifying amendment.
members.conclusion: The 1964 amendment was clarificatory or declaratory and had retrospective effect, so it applied to the pending proceedings.

predicates.preemption_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim to obtain property by exercising a right of pre-emption.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_clarifying_amend: The dispute was still pending when the amendment was enacted.
predicates.amendment_clarifies_existing_law: The amendment clarifies the meaning of the law as it stood before the amendment.
predicates.amendment_applies_retroactively: The amendment governs the pending dispute as well as disputes arising after its enactment.

members.legal_issue: An amendment that clarifies the pre-existing meaning of the law governing pre-emption applies retrospectively.
material_facts: The claimant’s pre-emption suit was pending through appeals when the 1964 amendment was enacted.
The amendment inserted words identifying the relevant husband in the provision governing who could pre-empt a sale by a female vendor.
The Court concluded that the provision already referred to the children of the husband through whom the vendor inherited the property.
members.legal_principle: A curative or declaratory statute is more readily construed as having retrospective operation than legislation that prejudicially affects past rights and transactions. The Court relied on the interpretation of Section 15(2)(b) and the reasoning in Moti Ram v. Bakhwant Singh.
members.conclusion: The 1964 amendment was clarificatory and had retrospective operation; in any event, the claimant was entitled under the provision even before the amendment.

predicates.is_preemption_proceeding: A court is deciding a claim or appeal in a proceeding for pre-emption.
predicates.amendment_clarifies_preexisting_law: A later amendment clarifies the meaning the relevant law already had, rather than changing that meaning.

members.legal_issue: The amendment defining persons treated as owners for house-property taxation was clarificatory and applied retrospectively.
material_facts: At the time the relevant income was assessed, the High Courts had taken conflicting views on whether a person in possession under a sale arrangement, but without a registered conveyance, could be treated as an owner.

The amendment expanded the categories of persons treated as owners, and its explanatory materials described the change as addressing uncertainty and practical problems concerning ownership and taxation of property income.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing declaratory and clarificatory legislation, including those discussed in Crawford's Statutory Construction, Francis Bennion's Statutory Interpretation and G.P. Singh's Principles of Statutory Interpretation. It relied on Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas for the principle that an explanatory enactment may supply an omission or clear up doubt about the meaning of existing law. It concluded that the amendment to Section 27(iii), (iiia) and (iiib) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, clarified the meaning of ownership for Section 22 and therefore operated retrospectively.
members.conclusion: The amendment was declaratory and clarificatory in nature and applied retrospectively insofar as it concerned the specified deemed-owner categories.

predicates.tax_amendment_interpretation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a tax-law amendment applies to periods before its enactment.
predicates.amendment_addresses_uncertainty_in_exist: The amendment was introduced against conflicting interpretations or uncertainty about an existing legal definition.
predicates.amendment_clarifies_existing_rule: The amendment's purpose and effect are to explain or clarify the existing rule rather than to introduce a new rule.

members.legal_issue: Procedural amendments governing recovery of sums payable to a custodian apply to recovery proceedings initiated after the amendments take effect, even when the underlying claim arose earlier.
material_facts: A fresh recovery notice was issued after the amended recovery procedure had come into force.
The claim related to money deposited before the amendment.
members.legal_principle: Procedural amendments apply, absent anything to the contrary, to actions taken after they come into force even if the action began earlier or the claim is anterior. The Court treated sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 48 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, as amended, as procedural.
members.conclusion: The recovery initiated by the later notice could be dealt with under the amended procedural provisions, notwithstanding that the claim arose earlier.

predicates.evacuee_property_recovery_case: A custodian seeks recovery of a sum connected with property of a person treated as an evacuee.
predicates.procedural_change_applies_to_recovery: The change alters the procedure for investigating or recovering the sum rather than the underlying substantive right.
predicates.recovery_initiated_after_change: The recovery proceeding at issue was initiated after the procedural change took effect.

members.legal_issue: A procedural rule governing the valuation of property applies to proceedings that are pending when the rule comes into force.
material_facts: The assessments concerned earlier valuation years, but the assessments in the representative cases were made after the valuation rule had been introduced.
The assessees sought use of the rule’s valuation method, and the dispute over its application proceeded through appeals and references.
The rule governed the method of valuation rather than creating or altering the underlying tax liability.
members.legal_principle: Procedural provisions generally apply to pending proceedings because a litigant has no vested right in procedure; provisions affecting existing substantive rights are not applied retrospectively without express enactment or necessary intendment. The Court relied on Jose Da Costa v. Bascora Sadasiva Sinai Narpomim, Associated Cement Company Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer, Kota, and the principles stated in Halsbury’s Laws of England and Bennion’s Statutory Interpretation. It also applied its conclusion that the valuation rule was procedural and evidentiary.
members.conclusion: The valuation rule applies to pending proceedings, including proceedings concerning earlier valuation years.

predicates.pending_wealth_tax_valuation_proceeding: A proceeding to assess wealth tax or determine an asset’s value was pending when the valuation rule came into force.
predicates.rule_governs_valuation_method: The rule prescribes how an asset’s value is to be determined in the proceeding.
predicates.rule_does_not_alter_substantive_rights: The rule changes the procedure for determining value without changing an existing substantive right or liability.

members.legal_issue: A procedural amendment governing the effect of earlier issue determinations applies to a civil suit that was pending when the amendment took effect, absent an applicable exclusion.
material_facts: The suit in which the earlier determinations were invoked remained pending when the relevant amendment came into force.
The amendment concerned the procedural operation of prior decisions as res judicata.
The amending provisions did not exclude the amendment to the res judicata provision from the general rule governing pending proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 97(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure Amendment Act, 1976 applies the amended Code to pending suits except where otherwise provided. Procedural provisions are generally presumed to apply to pending proceedings unless the text or necessary intendment indicates otherwise. The Court relied on Jose Da Costa v. Bascora Sadasiva Sinai Narcornim, as well as the principles in Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. Ltd. v. Income Tax Commissioner, Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhary, Gurbachan Singh v. Satpal Singh, and the cited English authorities.
members.conclusion: The amended procedural provision applied to the pending suit.

predicates.civil_suit_pending_when_procedural_chang: A civil suit remained pending when a legal change took effect.
predicates.change_concerns_procedure: The legal change concerns the procedure by which a court determines or gives effect to a matter.
predicates.no_exclusion_applies: No applicable provision or necessary implication excludes pending suits from the change.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective legislative amendment to a statutory definition governs pending litigation and may remove an objection that an earlier notification changed the definition.
material_facts: A notification applying the land-reform law to the territory had altered the statutory definition of an estate.
A later amendment substituted a definition that applied retrospectively from before the notification and covered the relevant land interests.
The amendment contained no express saving for pending litigation.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the retrospective terms of the 1958 amending Act and held that a saving for pending litigation could not be implied. It cited K. C. Mukherjee v. Mt. Ramratan Kuer, 63 Ind App 47: (AIR 1936 PC 49).
members.conclusion: The retrospective amendment removed the basis of the definition-related challenge, and no exception for pending litigation could be implied.

predicates.pending_challenge_to_application_of_land: A challenge to the application of a land-reform law remains pending when a later enactment takes effect.
predicates.retrospective_amendment_covers_disputed_: A later enactment retrospectively changes the relevant definition so that it covers the land interests in dispute.
predicates.no_pending_case_saving_expressed: The later enactment does not expressly preserve pending cases from the effect of its retrospective change.

members.legal_issue: Amendments expressly given retroactive effect must be applied from the date from which they are deemed to operate.
material_facts: The 1965 amending legislation stated that the changes to the tenancy provisions were deemed effective from the commencement of the 1956 amending legislation.
The dispute concerned whether land was exempt from the tenancy legislation.
members.legal_principle: The language of sections 7 and 18 of the Gujarat Amendment Act, 1965, gave the amendments to sections 43C and 88(1)(b), including its proviso, retroactive effect from the date the 1956 Amendment Act came into force.
members.conclusion: The amended provisions must be read as having been in force from the commencement of the 1956 amending legislation.

predicates.tenancy_exemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land is exempt from tenancy legislation.
predicates.amendment_declares_earlier_effective_sta: The amending legislation states that its changes are deemed effective from an earlier commencement date.

members.legal_issue: An amendment expressly given retrospective effect must be applied according to its plain terms even when it was enacted on an erroneous view of the law.
material_facts: The legislature enacted an amendment expressly deemed effective from an earlier date.
The amendment changed the requirements governing publication of land acquisition notifications.
The acquiring authority argued that the amendment should not apply retrospectively because the legislature had enacted it on an assumption about the law that was later rejected.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 1(3) and 2 of the Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, the amendment was expressly deemed to have come into force from 12 September 1975, and its plain terms had to be applied. The court rejected the proposed limitation of its retrospective operation because the amendment did not exclude the provision it changed.
members.conclusion: The amendment must be given retrospective effect according to its plain terms; the asserted legislative assumption does not make it prospective or superfluous.

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the validity of notifications issued as part of a land acquisition.
predicates.amendment_enacted: The legislature enacted an amendment changing requirements applicable to the acquisition notifications.
predicates.amendment_expressly_retroactive: The amendment expressly states that it takes effect from an earlier date.

members.legal_issue: A statutory amendment that expressly applies to pending proceedings applies to those proceedings even when the relevant right or cause of action arose before the amendment.
material_facts: The rent suits were pending when the central amending Act took effect.
Section 97(3) stated that the amended principal Act applied to pending suits and proceedings notwithstanding that the relevant right or cause of action had accrued earlier.
members.legal_principle: Section 97(3) expressly applies the principal Act as amended to pending suits, proceedings, appeals, and applications notwithstanding the earlier accrual of the right or cause of action. The Court held that this language gives the amendment retrospective operation and affects vested rights to that extent.
members.conclusion: The amended provisions applied retrospectively to pending proceedings, including proceedings instituted before the relevant state and central amendments took effect.

predicates.civil_proceeding_pending_when_amendment_: A civil suit or other civil proceeding remained pending when the amendment took effect.
predicates.amendment_expressly_covers_pending_proce: The amendment states that it applies to pending proceedings even if the underlying right or cause of action arose earlier.

members.legal_issue: The amendment restricting a purchaser’s right to annul tenures applied retrospectively to ejectment litigation that was pending when the amendment commenced.
material_facts: The purchaser brought an ejectment suit after acquiring an estate at a revenue sale and annulling interests under the law then in force.
When the amendment commenced, the suit was pending in an appeal from the decree for possession.
The disputed property was a tenure that existed when the sale notification was issued, bringing it within an exception to the purchaser’s annulment rights under the amended law.
members.legal_principle: The substituted provision governing annulment rights was prima facie prospective, but section 7 made the amended law applicable to specified pending suits, proceedings, appeals, reviews, and revisions. Read together, sections 4 and 7 applied the amended protection to tenures within the new exceptions even where the revenue sale predated the amendment. The Court cited no earlier case by name on this point.
members.conclusion: Although the provision substituting the amended rule was prima facie prospective, it applied to pending litigation because the amendment’s transitional provision gave it retrospective effect to that extent.

predicates.pending_ejectment_case: An ejectment suit or a proceeding continuing from that suit was pending when the new law took effect.
predicates.protected_tenure: The disputed property was a tenure within an exception to the purchaser’s annulment rights under the amended rule.
predicates.suit_barred_under_amended_rule: Under the amended rule, the purchaser could not validly have brought the ejectment suit.

members.legal_issue: Dismissal of a special leave petition without grant of appellate leave does not prevent a party from seeking review in the court whose decision was challenged.
material_facts: The parties sought special leave to appeal against the High Court’s decision in a second appeal.
The Supreme Court dismissed the special leave petition as withdrawn, without granting leave or giving permission to pursue a further challenge.
The parties then filed a review petition in the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC permits review where no appeal has been preferred; dismissal of a special leave petition without grant of leave does not convert it into an appeal or attract the doctrine of merger. Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala holds that the court whose decision was challenged retains review jurisdiction when special leave is refused. Sarguja Transport Service v. State Transport Appellate Tribunal concerns withdrawal of a writ petition without permission to bring a fresh one and does not bar review of the original decision.
members.conclusion: The review petition was maintainable despite the dismissal of the special leave petition as withdrawn without leave to challenge the High Court’s decision.

predicates.review_filed_in_deciding_court: The party filed a review application in the court that issued the decision being challenged.
predicates.special_leave_petition_dismissed_without: The special leave petition against that decision was dismissed without the Supreme Court granting leave to appeal.
predicates.review_remains_maintainable: The review application is not barred merely because the special leave petition was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A non-speaking dismissal of a special leave petition in another matter does not bar the Supreme Court from examining the merits of a later appeal.
material_facts: The respondents relied on summary dismissals of special leave petitions in similar matters.
The Court considered the issue on its merits in the appeals before it.
members.legal_principle: A dismissal of a special leave petition without a speaking order does not constitute res judicata; the Court may examine the merits in a later matter. The judgment also rejected the contention that the involvement of a local Act made the High Court’s view immune from review under Article 136 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The earlier summary dismissals did not constitute res judicata and did not prevent examination of the appeals on their merits.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_on_merits: A matter is before the Supreme Court for consideration on its merits.
predicates.similar_special_leave_petition_dismissed: A special leave petition in a similar matter was dismissed summarily without a reasoned order.
predicates.prior_dismissal_does_not_bar_merits_revi: The earlier summary dismissal does not prevent the Supreme Court from examining the merits.

members.legal_issue: A summary dismissal of an earlier special leave petition does not bar a later challenge to an issue that was neither raised nor decided in that petition.
material_facts: The Union of India and the Land Acquisition Collector had earlier filed a special leave petition challenging the High Court’s judgment, and it was summarily dismissed.
The earlier petition did not raise whether the beneficiary agency was entitled to notice and an opportunity to adduce evidence in the compensation proceedings.
The Court did not decide that issue in the earlier petition.
members.legal_principle: Under Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, (2000) 6 SCC 359, refusal of special leave does not attract merger; a summary refusal without deciding a question does not make that undecided question res judicata in a later proceeding.
members.conclusion: The earlier summary dismissal did not operate as res judicata against the agency’s challenge, and it did not prevent consideration of the agency’s distinct claim.

predicates.later_challenge_by_an_interested_benefic: A beneficiary with an interest in the compensation determination brings a later challenge.
predicates.earlier_special_leave_petition_summarily: An earlier special leave petition concerning the same underlying judgment was dismissed summarily.
predicates.issue_not_raised_or_decided_earlier: The issue advanced in the later challenge was neither raised nor decided in the earlier petition.

members.legal_issue: A non-speaking dismissal of a petition for special leave does not merge the challenged judgment into the dismissal order.
material_facts: A party challenged an earlier High Court order by filing a petition for special leave.
The Supreme Court dismissed that petition without giving reasons.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, dismissal of a petition for special leave without reasons does not attract the doctrine of merger or declare law under Article 141. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala, Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of Bihar, and Gangadhara Palo v. Revenue Divisional Officer.
members.conclusion: The High Court judgment did not merge into the Supreme Court's non-speaking dismissal order.

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: A party seeks permission to appeal from a judgment by filing a petition for special leave.
predicates.special_leave_dismissed_without_reasons: The court dismisses the petition for special leave without stating reasons.

members.legal_issue: Dismissal of a petition for special leave to appeal without granting leave does not merge the challenged order into the Supreme Court’s order or, by itself, extinguish an otherwise available right to seek review.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the State’s appeal from the Forest Tribunal’s decision.
The State sought special leave to appeal, and the Supreme Court dismissed the petition in a non-speaking order without granting leave.
The State later sought review of the High Court’s decision, relying on a statutory review provision.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 involves two distinct stages: discretionary consideration of whether to grant special leave, followed, if leave is granted, by appellate jurisdiction. Dismissal at the first stage is not dismissal of an appeal and does not attract merger or, without more, res judicata. An available review remedy is not lost merely because special leave was refused. The Court relied on Workmen of Cochin Port Trust, Indian Oil Corporation, Rup Diamonds, V.M. Salgaocar, and the review principles in Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s order did not merge into the Supreme Court’s order dismissing the special leave petition and remained open to review if grounds for review were otherwise made out.

rule.if: special_leave_petition_proceeding and leave_not_granted and dismissal_without_reasons and review_basis_available

predicates.special_leave_petition_proceeding: A party asked the Supreme Court for permission to appeal against an order of a lower court or tribunal.
predicates.leave_not_granted: The Supreme Court refused permission to appeal and did not take up the matter as an appeal.
predicates.dismissal_without_reasons: The Supreme Court dismissed the permission-to-appeal petition without stating reasons.
predicates.review_basis_available: The party seeking review had a ground for review available under the applicable review law.

members.legal_issue: Dismissal of a petition for special leave to appeal does not affirm the challenged judgment or prevent review after leave to appeal has been granted.
material_facts: A petition for special leave challenging the earlier decree had previously been dismissed.
The present proceedings were full appeals after leave to appeal had been granted.
The respondent argued that the dismissal of the earlier petition prevented reconsideration of the interest ruling.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, dismissal of a special-leave petition does not reverse, modify, or affirm the challenged judgment and does not make that judgment res judicata. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court could examine the legality and correctness of the challenged judgment in the full appeals notwithstanding the earlier dismissal of the special-leave petition.

predicates.full_appeal_after_leave_granted: The proceeding was a full appeal heard after leave to appeal had been granted.
predicates.earlier_special_leave_petition_dismissed: A petition for special leave challenging the judgment had previously been dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A non-speaking dismissal of an earlier special leave petition does not establish the correctness of the challenged decision as precedent and need not be treated as a ruling on the legal issue.
material_facts: The bank relied on an earlier special leave petition concerning a similar dispute that had been dismissed without reasons.
The respondents argued that the earlier dismissal and the bank's failure to disclose it barred the later appeals.
The earlier dismissal order contained no reasons.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 141, a non-speaking dismissal of a special leave petition does not lay down law or signify acceptance of the correctness of the decision sought to be appealed. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The non-speaking dismissal did not amount to acceptance of the correctness of the decision challenged in that petition and did not constitute law declared by the Supreme Court. The Court held that the earlier dismissal need not have been disclosed in the later petitions.

predicates.later_appeal_case: The court is deciding a later appeal concerning a legal dispute.
predicates.earlier_special_leave_petition_dismissed: An earlier special leave petition concerning the dispute was dismissed without reasons.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent writ petition is not barred by principles analogous to res judicata when the earlier writ was dismissed without a speaking order, the petitioner then pursued a statutory revision, and the later petition seeks relief not claimed in the earlier proceeding.
material_facts: The first writ petition challenged the cancellation of permanent settlement rights and was dismissed in limine by a non-speaking order.
The petitioner then pursued a statutory revision, which was rejected by the revisional authority.
The later writ petition challenged the revisional order and specifically sought cash compensation, a relief not claimed in the first writ petition.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles in Daryao v. State of U.P., Virudhunagar Steel Rolling Mills Ltd. v. Government of Madras, Tilokchand Motichand v. H.B. Munshi, and P.D. Sharma v. State Bank of India, a writ petition dismissed in limine without a speaking order does not create a res judicata bar. A dismissal on the ground of an available alternative remedy likewise does not bar a later petition after that remedy is pursued. Merger of the original order into a revisional order does not by itself bar the later petition, and a distinct relief not claimed earlier is not barred on that basis.
members.conclusion: The later writ petition was not barred by principles analogous to res judicata, either because the earlier petition was dismissed without a speaking order or because the compensation claim was a separate relief not raised earlier.

predicates.subsequent_writ_after_statutory_revision: A petitioner files a later writ petition after a statutory revisional authority has decided the petitioner's revision.
predicates.earlier_writ_dismissed_without_speaking_: A court dismisses the petitioner's earlier writ petition without giving reasons in a speaking order.
predicates.statutory_remedy_pursued: After the earlier writ is dismissed, the petitioner pursues an available statutory appeal or revision before filing the later writ petition.
predicates.compensation_relief_not_claimed_earlier: The petitioner seeks compensation in the later writ petition but did not seek that relief in the earlier writ petition.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition dismissed in limine without a decision on the merits does not bar a later suit by res judicata.
material_facts: The appellant challenged a consolidation order in a writ petition.
The High Court dismissed that petition in limine by a one-word order, without deciding the merits of the issues.
The appellant later brought a suit challenging the consolidation authority’s power, and the lower courts treated the earlier dismissal as barring the suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the rule of res judicata. As explained in Workmen of Cochin Port Trust v. Board of Trustees of the Cochin Port Trust, a matter decided on the merits by a speaking order in a writ petition may operate as res judicata, but a dismissal in limine or a dismissal on grounds such as laches or an available alternative remedy does not bar another remedy on that basis.
members.conclusion: The summary dismissal of the earlier writ petition did not operate as res judicata, so the suit was not barred on that ground.

rule.if: civil_suit_after_writ and (writ_dismissed_in_limine or writ_dismissed_for_laches or writ_dismissed_for_alternative_remedy) and not writ_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking_order

predicates.civil_suit_after_writ: A person brings a civil suit after previously seeking relief in a writ petition concerning the dispute.
predicates.writ_dismissed_in_limine: The court dismissed the writ petition at the threshold without deciding the issues on their merits.
predicates.writ_dismissed_for_laches: The court dismissed the writ petition because of delay.
predicates.writ_dismissed_for_alternative_remedy: The court dismissed the writ petition because another remedy was available.
predicates.writ_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking: The court gave a reasoned order deciding the issue on its merits in the writ petition.
predicates.earlier_writ_dismissal_does_not_bar_suit: The earlier writ dismissal does not prevent the later suit from proceeding on the ground of res judicata.

members.legal_issue: A prior dismissal of a constitutional petition because the requested relief was considered suitable for a civil suit does not bar a later petition on the same claim where the earlier court did not decide the merits.
material_facts: An earlier petition seeking similar relief was dismissed because title and possession claims were considered more appropriately investigated in a civil suit.
The earlier court did not decide the merits of the petitioner’s claims.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata may apply where a competent court has finally decided against a person’s title to property, but a dismissal that does not decide the merits leaves no basis to invoke the doctrine. The Court cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provisions for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The earlier dismissal did not operate as res judicata, so the present petition was not barred on that ground.

predicates.constitutional_writ_seeking_fundamental_: The proceeding seeks constitutional relief to enforce an asserted fundamental right.
predicates.similar_prior_proceeding: A prior proceeding sought substantially similar relief.
predicates.prior_dismissal_without_merits: The prior proceeding was dismissed as unsuitable for that forum or because another remedy was available, without deciding the merits.

members.legal_issue: A High Court’s dismissal of a writ petition for laches or because an alternative remedy is available does not ordinarily bar a later original fundamental-rights petition.
material_facts: The Court considered the effect of High Court dismissals that rested on delay or the availability of an alternative remedy rather than a decision on the merits.
It recognized that facts found in the earlier proceeding may nevertheless be relevant to the later fundamental-rights proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a merits judgment, which may create res judicata, from a refusal to issue relief because of laches or an alternative remedy. It applied the general res judicata principle to Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, while recognizing the different grounds on which a High Court may decline relief under Article 226.
members.conclusion: A dismissal for laches or an available alternative remedy is not ordinarily a bar to a later petition, except where facts found by the High Court are themselves relevant to the later proceeding.

predicates.later_original_fundamental_rights_petiti: A party brings an original court proceeding seeking relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.prior_writ_dismissed_for_laches_or_alter: The party’s earlier writ proceeding was dismissed because of delay or because another effective remedy was available, rather than after a decision on the merits.
predicates.prior_findings_relevant_to_later_claim: Facts found in the earlier proceeding bear on the later fundamental-rights claim.

members.legal_issue: A non-speaking dismissal in limine or a dismissal after withdrawal does not bar a later original fundamental-rights petition by res judicata.
material_facts: One earlier High Court writ petition was dismissed in limine by an order that stated no reasons.
Another earlier writ petition was withdrawn, and the High Court expressly had not considered its merits.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata requires a judicial determination of the rights in controversy and a final decision on them. Without reasons, the basis of an in-limine dismissal cannot safely be identified as a merits determination; withdrawal likewise leaves no decision on the merits. The Court applied the general principle of res judicata to petitions under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: Neither an unexplained dismissal in limine nor a dismissal after withdrawal creates a bar of res judicata to a later petition.

predicates.later_original_fundamental_rights_petiti: A party brings an original court proceeding seeking relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.prior_writ_dismissed_in_limine_without_r: The earlier writ proceeding was dismissed at the outset without a reasoned order stating the basis for dismissal.
predicates.prior_writ_withdrawn_without_merits_deci: The earlier writ proceeding was withdrawn and the court did not decide the merits.

members.legal_issue: Failure to pursue an available intra-court appeal does not impose an inflexible bar on the Supreme Court’s discretionary consideration of a special-leave appeal.
material_facts: The appellant did not request certification for a further High Court appeal immediately after judgment and gave no explanation for that failure.
The Supreme Court granted special leave, and the case proceeded beyond interim orders and preparation of the record before the preliminary objection was considered.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 confers a wide discretionary jurisdiction, and there is no inflexible rule that special leave must be refused whenever an available Letters Patent appeal was not pursued. The court relied on Penu Balakrishna Iyer v. Sri Ariva M. Ramaswami Iyer and treated the decision whether to exercise jurisdiction as case-specific.
members.conclusion: The failure to pursue the further High Court appeal did not automatically bar the Supreme Court from hearing the special-leave appeal; whether to exercise its jurisdiction depended on the circumstances of the case.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_from_second_appellate_decision and further_high_court_appeal_not_pursued and special_leave_granted and case_progressed_beyond_interim_stage

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_second_appella: A party seeks special leave to challenge a High Court decision in a second appeal.
predicates.further_high_court_appeal_not_pursued: The party did not pursue an available further appeal within the prescribed procedure.
predicates.special_leave_granted: The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal.
predicates.case_progressed_beyond_interim_stage: The case proceeded beyond interim orders and preparation of the record before the objection to its competence was considered.

members.legal_issue: Failure to pursue an available intermediate appeal does not create an absolute bar to special leave or require its automatic revocation.
material_facts: The challenged decision was made by a single judge in a second appeal.
The appellants did not seek leave to pursue an appeal to a division bench under the available Letters Patent procedure before seeking special leave.
The court found the second-appellate judgment’s defect sufficiently serious to warrant setting aside the decree and remitting the matter.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court has wide discretion over whether to exercise its jurisdiction and on what terms. A party would normally be expected to pursue an available Letters Patent appeal before seeking special leave from a second-appellate decision, but there is no inflexible rule barring special leave or requiring its revocation for failure to do so. Article 133(3) reflects the general position against appeals to the Supreme Court from a judgment of one High Court judge. Raruha Singh v. Achal Singh was considered, but its statement about already-granted leave was not treated as laying down an absolute rule.
members.conclusion: The failure to pursue the Letters Patent remedy did not, by itself, require dismissal of the appeal or revocation of special leave; whether to exercise jurisdiction under Article 136 depended on the facts of the case.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_second_appella: A party seeks special leave to appeal from a decision made in a second appeal.
predicates.intermediate_appellate_remedy_not_pursue: The party did not pursue an available appeal to an intermediate appellate bench before seeking special leave.

members.legal_issue: A delay in reporting does not undermine the prosecution case when it is not inordinate and is consistent with efforts to obtain prompt assistance for an injured person.
material_facts: The deceased was alive after the attack, and those present first arranged to take him to the police station or hospital.
The deceased died on the way, and the report was made later that same night, about five hours after the incident.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the delay in light of the circumstances, including the effort to take the injured person for assistance and the fact that the report was made that same night. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The reporting delay was not inordinate and did not require the prosecution case to be viewed with suspicion.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and report_made_same_night and delay_not_inordinate and efforts_made_to_get_assistance

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.report_made_same_night: The report was made on the night of the incident.
predicates.delay_not_inordinate: The time taken before the report was made was not inordinate in the circumstances.
predicates.efforts_made_to_get_assistance: Those present were occupied with efforts to obtain assistance for the injured person.

members.legal_issue: A delay in reporting an incident is sufficiently explained when the circumstances provide cogent reasons for the delay.
material_facts: The first information report was given about twelve hours after the incident.
The deceased and several injured family members required medical attention until the deceased died.
Heavy rain affected travel, and the police station was some distance from the place of occurrence.
The High Court accepted these circumstances as cogent reasons for the delay, and the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere.
members.legal_principle: Whether delay in giving a first information report is sufficiently explained depends on the circumstances. Here, the injuries and need for medical attention, heavy rain affecting travel, and distance to the police station were accepted as cogent reasons. No provision or earlier case was cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The delay in giving the first information report was sufficiently explained and did not warrant interference with the High Court’s conclusion.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_delayed_first_information_report and injured_people_needed_medical_attention and severe_rain_affected_travel and reporting_station_was_distant

predicates.criminal_case_with_delayed_first_informa: The criminal case relies on a first information report made after a delay from the incident.
predicates.injured_people_needed_medical_attention: People injured in the incident required medical attention during the period before the report was made.
predicates.severe_rain_affected_travel: Heavy rain affected the ability to travel and report the incident.
predicates.reporting_station_was_distant: The police station was a considerable distance from the place of occurrence.

members.legal_issue: A delay in lodging a first information report does not make it unreliable when the circumstances reasonably explain why the complainant could not report sooner.
material_facts: The occurrence took place at night in winter, outside the village, and the police station was about 18 kilometres away.
The complainant was injured, one of her minor children was also injured, and she took shelter overnight after two people had been killed.
She travelled to hospital the next morning and made her statement there; the police recorded the report on its basis.
The Supreme Court accepted these circumstances as explaining the delay and rejected the claim that the report was ante-timed.
members.legal_principle: The effect of delay in lodging a first information report depends on the circumstances explaining it. The court must assess those circumstances realistically rather than apply a hyper-technical approach. No earlier case is cited.
members.conclusion: The delay in lodging the report was adequately explained and did not justify treating it as ante-timed or unreliable.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the prosecution of an alleged criminal offence.
predicates.complainant_was_injured_and_sheltered_ov: The complainant was injured and spent the night sheltering after the occurrence.
predicates.prompt_reporting_was_impracticable: Distance, danger, lack of assistance, or similar circumstances made it impracticable for the complainant to report sooner.
predicates.report_was_made_when_reporting_became_pr: The complainant reported the occurrence when circumstances allowed her to reach assistance.

members.legal_issue: Delay in reporting an offence does not by itself make the prosecution case doubtful when the circumstances explain the delay and do not indicate fabrication.
material_facts: Several people, including the first informant and his sons, were injured in the shooting; one later died and another had injuries that were dangerous to life.
The injured were taken first to a hospital for treatment, and the first informant's statement was recorded at the hospital after a doctor confirmed he was fit to give it.
The statement was then carried to the police station, where the formal report was recorded; the special report was sent to the magistrate promptly after that.
The High Court treated the time taken to record the report as a reason to doubt the prosecution, without accounting for the medical emergency and the sequence of events.
members.legal_principle: Delay in lodging a first information report is not automatically fatal; whether it casts doubt on the prosecution depends on the circumstances, including the informant's condition, the injuries, efforts to obtain treatment, and the distances involved. The court must look for indications of fabrication rather than apply a mathematical rule. Tara Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1991 SC 63; Zahoor v. State of U.P., AIR 1991 SC 40; and Jamna v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1994 SC 79, support this principle.
members.conclusion: In the circumstances, there was no basis to draw an adverse inference from the time taken to lodge the report or send the special report.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and delayed_first_report and urgent_medical_care_preceded_reporting and reporting_sequence_explained and not fabrication_indications

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the timing of the first report is relied on to challenge the case.
predicates.delayed_first_report: The first report was made some time after the alleged offence.
predicates.urgent_medical_care_preceded_reporting: The injured people were taken for urgent medical treatment before the report was made.
predicates.reporting_sequence_explained: The circumstances account for the steps and time involved in recording and transmitting the report.
predicates.fabrication_indications: The circumstances indicate that the delay was used to fabricate or alter the prosecution account.

members.legal_issue: A delay in reporting an offence or forwarding the first information report does not discredit the prosecution when the delay is adequately explained by the circumstances and supporting evidence.
material_facts: The witnesses were threatened after the nighttime killings and shut themselves in a room.
The accused remained in their part of the house until morning, and the informant left for a police station about six miles away after they had departed.
The report was lodged at 9 a.m. after the informant set out at about 6 a.m.

The officer explained that the report reached the magistrate later because the magistrate was not in his seat when the officer attended court; the officer then went to another town before delivering it.
The lower courts accepted the officer’s evidence, which was supported by documents.
members.legal_principle: Whether delay in reporting or forwarding a first information report undermines a prosecution depends on the explanation and evidence in the particular case; a sufficiently explained delay does not require rejection of the case.
members.conclusion: The delay in lodging the report and its later delivery to the magistrate were satisfactorily explained and did not undermine the prosecution case.

predicates.criminal_case_with_delayed_report: A criminal case involves a delay in lodging or forwarding the initial report.
predicates.delay_explained_by_safety_or_practical_c: The delay is explained by threats, safety concerns, distance, unavailability of the recipient, or comparable practical circumstances.
predicates.supporting_evidence_accepted: The explanation is supported by evidence or documents accepted by the court.

members.legal_issue: A delay in reporting an occurrence does not undermine the prosecution when the delay is satisfactorily explained and the informant’s presence at the scene is supported by the evidence.
material_facts: The occurrence took place in the morning, and the informant reported it to a village officer several hours later.
The informant said he first arranged for the injured people to be moved and then waited for the officer, who was away in the fields.
The officer confirmed that the informant was waiting when he returned, and police records and testimony supported that the informant had been released from police custody the previous evening.
The informant lived a short distance from the place where he had been questioned and could have returned there before the occurrence.
members.legal_principle: The timing of a report must be assessed in light of the circumstances explaining the delay and the evidence bearing on the informant’s presence; an explained delay is not, by itself, a reason to reject the prosecution case.
members.conclusion: The delay was sufficiently explained and did not make the informant’s presence at the occurrence improbable or undermine the prosecution case.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.report_delay_explained: The informant delayed reporting while attending to the injured, travelling to the reporting officer, or waiting for that officer, and the circumstances support that account.
predicates.informant_presence_supported: Independent or otherwise reliable evidence supports the informant’s presence at the scene at the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: Delay in delivery of a special report to a magistrate does not, by itself, establish that the first information report was recorded later than claimed.
material_facts: The first information report was recorded in the evening, and the special report was entrusted to a constable shortly afterward for delivery to the magistrate.

The constable delivered the report the following morning and gave explanations for the delay, including a punctured bicycle tyre and stomach pain; the court did not need to accept those explanations to assess when the report was entrusted to him.
The informant was not shown to be a false witness, and the challenge to his knowledge of the injured persons’ whereabouts at the hospital had not been put to him.
members.legal_principle: A delayed special report may raise a question about when the first information report was recorded, but the delay does not itself establish later recording. The inference depends on whether the informant’s account is discredited. No particular statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The delay in delivery did not justify inferring that the first information report had not been recorded at the stated time; the challenge based on that delay was rejected.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging criminal convictions.
predicates.special_report_delivery_delayed: A special report was delivered to the magistrate later than the time it was entrusted for delivery.
predicates.informant_not_discredited: The informant’s account of when the first information report was recorded was not shown to be false or discredited.

members.legal_issue: A delay of a few hours in the report reaching the local Magistrate does not, by itself, establish that the report was ante-timed or that the prosecution account was false.
material_facts: A report was made to the police post shortly after the occurrence and registered at the police station later that evening.
The local Magistrate received the report a few hours later.
The court rejected the claim that this delay showed the report had been ante-timed and found the eyewitness evidence truthful.
members.legal_principle: The court assessed the timing objection in light of the evidence and circumstances as a whole and found the delay in receipt by the Magistrate insufficient to support the allegation.
members.conclusion: The timing objection did not justify rejecting the prosecution case or finding that the report was ante-timed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.report_made_and_registered_soon_after_oc: The report was made and registered soon after the occurrence.
predicates.magistrate_received_report_after_a_short: The Magistrate received the report a few hours after it was made or registered.
predicates.credible_evidence_does_not_support_ante_: The credible evidence does not support the allegation that the report was created or dated earlier than it was in fact made.

members.legal_issue: Delay in sending an occurrence report to a magistrate does not by itself taint an investigation or make a prosecution unsupported when the first information report was recorded promptly, the investigation began on its basis, no other infirmity is shown, and no prejudice from the delay is claimed.
material_facts: The occurrence report reached the magistrate at about 6 p.m., several hours after the occurrence.
The first information report had been recorded without undue delay, and the investigation began on its basis.
No other infirmity in the investigation was brought to the Court's notice, and the accused did not claim prejudice from the delayed receipt.
members.legal_principle: Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the police officer to send the occurrence report forthwith to a magistrate empowered to take cognizance. Its purpose is to keep the magistrate informed of the investigation and enable appropriate control or directions under section 159. Delay alone does not establish a tainted investigation or unsupported prosecution where the first information report was recorded promptly, the investigation proceeded on its basis, no other infirmity is shown, and no prejudice is claimed.
members.conclusion: The delayed receipt of the occurrence report, though improper or objectionable, did not by itself justify treating the investigation as tainted or the prosecution as unsupported.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_delayed_occurrence_report and first_information_report_recorded_promptly and investigation_started_on_first_information_report and no_other_investigative_infirmity_shown and no_prejudice_from_delay_claimed

predicates.criminal_case_with_delayed_occurrence_re: The case involved a criminal investigation in which the occurrence report was sent to the magistrate late.
predicates.first_information_report_recorded_prompt: The police recorded the first information report without undue delay after the occurrence.
predicates.investigation_started_on_first_informati: The police began the investigation on the basis of the first information report.
predicates.no_other_investigative_infirmity_shown: No other infirmity in the investigation was brought to the court's notice.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_delay_claimed: The accused did not claim that the late report prejudiced them.
predicates.delay_alone_does_not_make_investigation_: The delay by itself does not make the investigation tainted or the prosecution unsupported.

members.legal_issue: A delay in delivering a special report to a magistrate does not undermine the prosecution when the delay is explained and causes no demonstrated prejudice.
material_facts: The special report reached the magistrate during the night after the constable first delivered it to the Superintendent of Police and then travelled to the magistrate’s residence because the courthouse was locked.
The constable explained that he had waited for the Superintendent of Police to become available and had to locate the duty magistrate.
The statement underlying the report had already been recorded, police had visited the scene, and the inquest reports and seizures had been made.
The appellant identified no prejudice caused by the timing of delivery.
members.legal_principle: Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the prescribed report to be sent to the magistrate. Whether delay in doing so undermines the prosecution must be assessed in context, including the explanation for delay and whether it caused prejudice. No earlier case is cited.
members.conclusion: The delivery of the special report was not unduly delayed; in any event, the explained delay caused no demonstrated prejudice and did not cast doubt on the report.

rule.if: criminal_case and special_report_delivery_was_delayed and delivery_delay_was_explained and no_prejudice_was_shown

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the prosecution of an alleged criminal offence.
predicates.special_report_delivery_was_delayed: The report of the occurrence was delivered to the magistrate later than the time at which it could have been sent.
predicates.delivery_delay_was_explained: The person responsible for delivery gave a circumstantial explanation for the time taken to deliver the report.
predicates.no_prejudice_was_shown: The accused did not demonstrate that the timing of delivery caused prejudice.

members.legal_issue: Delay in forwarding a promptly lodged report and minor investigative omissions do not, without more, make the report or prosecution case unreliable.
material_facts: The report was lodged within hours of the occurrence and the police reached the scene that night and began investigating.
The copy of the report was delayed in reaching the local magistrate, and the crime title was omitted from the inquest reports.
The record did not show that the investigating officer antedated the documents or fabricated the investigation.
members.legal_principle: A delay in forwarding a report or a minor omission in investigative documents must be assessed in the context of the whole record; it does not displace positive, credible evidence merely by its existence. The judgment cites no earlier case for this principle.
members.conclusion: The procedural irregularities did not undermine the report or the otherwise credible prosecution evidence.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and prompt_report_lodged and investigation_began_promptly and forwarding_delay_or_minor_omission and no_evidence_of_fabrication

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed criminal convictions that the prosecution supported with a report and investigation records.
predicates.prompt_report_lodged: A report describing the occurrence was lodged soon after it happened.
predicates.investigation_began_promptly: Investigators reached the scene and began investigative steps soon after the report was made.
predicates.forwarding_delay_or_minor_omission: The report was forwarded late or an investigative document contained a minor omission.
predicates.no_evidence_of_fabrication: The evidence did not show that investigators fabricated or antedated the report or related records.
