rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction_for_murder and rapid_escalation_from_trivial_dispute and uncontrollable_anger_deprives_self_control and no_intention_to_eliminate_victim and knowledge_of_likely_fatal_consequences

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction_for_murd: The case is an appeal by a person convicted of murder.
predicates.rapid_escalation_from_trivial_dispute: A minor dispute quickly escalates into the violent incident.
predicates.uncontrollable_anger_deprives_self_contr: The accused acts in an uncontrollable fit of anger that deprives the accused of self-control.
predicates.no_intention_to_eliminate_victim: The accused does not intend to kill or eliminate the person attacked.
predicates.knowledge_of_likely_fatal_consequences: The accused knows that the conduct is likely to cause fatal consequences.

members.legal_issue: An assault with a common stick causing fatal head injuries, committed without premeditation in a heat of passion, may amount to culpable homicide based on knowledge rather than murder based on intention.
material_facts: A land dispute existed between the parties, and the assault occurred while the deceased was harvesting crops.
The appellant struck the deceased on the head with a lathi during the occurrence.
The deceased suffered head contusions and a fractured parietal bone, and died in hospital the following day.
The appellant also suffered injuries in the occurrence.
The High Court found that the assault was not premeditated and occurred in a heat of passion; the appellant did not continue the assault.
members.legal_principle: Whether an assault with a lathi on the head shows an intention to cause death or only knowledge that death is likely depends on the circumstances, manner of assault, and nature and number of injuries considered cumulatively; a lathi is not, merely because it can be used to assault, a deadly weapon. The Court applied the distinction between intention and knowledge under Sections 302 and 304 Part II of the IPC, relying on Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab, Joseph v. State of Kerala, Chamru Budhwa v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Gurmukh Singh v. State of Haryana, and Mohd. Shakeel v. State of A.P.
members.conclusion: The Court altered the conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II of the IPC. Because the appellant had already undergone the maximum sentence prescribed for that offence, it directed his release unless he was wanted in another case.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and common_stick_used_in_head_assault and fatal_head_injuries_followed and assault_without_premeditation_in_heat_of_passion and accused_also_injured and assault_not_continued

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction for murder.
predicates.common_stick_used_in_head_assault: The accused used a common stick to strike the victim on the head.
predicates.fatal_head_injuries_followed: The victim suffered head injuries in the assault and later died from the consequences.
predicates.assault_without_premeditation_in_heat_of: The assault arose spontaneously in a heat of passion rather than being planned beforehand.
predicates.accused_also_injured: The accused also sustained injuries during the occurrence.
predicates.assault_not_continued: The accused did not continue the assault after the head injury was inflicted.

members.legal_issue: An intentional infliction of injuries likely to cause death, without proof that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death or that the accused intended to kill, warrants conviction for culpable homicide rather than murder.
material_facts: The attack followed a petty quarrel, and the accused fetched a weapon and inflicted several injuries on the deceased.
The accused stopped the attack after his wife intervened and allowed her to take the weapon.
The deceased died about a week later from septicemia arising from infection of the wounds.

The medical evidence did not establish with certainty that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; the evidence also left open that the gall bladder injuries could have occurred from a fall or forceful impact.
The nature of the injuries and the medical evidence showed that the injuries were likely to cause death, and the Court found that the accused intended to inflict them.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 300, clause thirdly, IPC, including its objective test of whether the bodily injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and Section 304 Part I IPC. It distinguished an intention to cause death or an injury meeting that objective test from an intention to cause injuries that were likely to cause death. No earlier case was cited for this classification.
members.conclusion: The conviction for murder was modified to conviction under Section 304 Part I IPC because the accused intended to cause the injuries but the evidence did not establish the required ordinary-course sufficiency for murder.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and attack_followed_sudden_petty_quarrel and accused_intended_to_inflict_injuries and injuries_likely_to_cause_death and ordinary_course_fatality_not_established and evidence_did_not_establish_intent_to_kill and attack_stopped_when_interrupted

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.attack_followed_sudden_petty_quarrel: The attack followed a sudden quarrel over a petty matter.
predicates.accused_intended_to_inflict_injuries: The evidence shows that the accused intended to cause the bodily injuries inflicted.
predicates.injuries_likely_to_cause_death: The nature of the injuries and medical evidence indicate that they were likely to cause death.
predicates.ordinary_course_fatality_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
predicates.evidence_did_not_establish_intent_to_kil: The evidence does not establish an intention to put an end to the victim’s life.
predicates.attack_stopped_when_interrupted: The accused stopped the attack when another person intervened.

members.legal_issue: A death caused with knowledge that the injury may cause death, but without an intention to cause death or an injury likely to cause death, is culpable homicide not amounting to murder under the knowledge-based form of liability.
material_facts: The fatal head injury was a scalp injury, with no skull fracture, and the doctor had not measured its depth.
The deceased sustained only two injuries, and the head injury caused internal bleeding that resulted in death after some time.

The Court considered the force and gravity of the assault insufficient to show an intention to kill or to inflict an injury likely to cause death, while finding that the assailant had knowledge that the weapon used on the head could cause death.
members.legal_principle: Section 304 IPC distinguishes an act done with the intention of causing death or an injury likely to cause death from an act done with knowledge that death is likely but without that intention; the latter falls under Part II. The Court relied on Camilo Vaz v. State of Goa, (2000) 9 SCC 1, on that distinction, and on Deo Nath Rai v. State of Bihar, AIR 2017 SC 5428, in considering a spontaneous, unpremeditated incident. It also assessed the evidence about the injury and its severity when determining whether the required intention was proved.
members.conclusion: The murder convictions were set aside and replaced with convictions under Section 304 Part II IPC.

rule.if: appeal_against_murder_conviction and accused_caused_fatal_injury and injury_created_knowledge_of_likely_death and not intention_to_cause_death and not intention_to_cause_likely_fatal_injury

predicates.appeal_against_murder_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction for murder arising from the death.
predicates.accused_caused_fatal_injury: The accused inflicted an injury that caused the victim's death.
predicates.injury_created_knowledge_of_likely_death: The circumstances of the assault and the injury showed that the accused knew the act could likely cause death.
predicates.intention_to_cause_death: The accused intended to cause the victim's death.
predicates.intention_to_cause_likely_fatal_injury: The accused intended to inflict an injury likely to cause death.
predicates.conviction_is_for_culpable_homicide_not_: The conviction is for culpable homicide not amounting to murder on the basis of knowledge without the required intention.

members.legal_issue: Causing death by firing without an established intention to kill, but with knowledge that the act is likely to cause death, amounts to culpable homicide not amounting to murder in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The accused fired three rounds in quick succession, and one struck and killed the deceased.
The evidence did not establish that the accused deliberately aimed at the deceased or intended to kill a particular person.
The court accepted that the accused fired out of fear, but found that he had exceeded the available right of private defence.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Sections 299 and 300 of the Penal Code to distinguish culpable homicide from murder, and Section 304, Part II, to the case in which the accused had knowledge that the act was likely to cause death but the circumstances did not establish the requisite intention for murder. It agreed with the High Court’s assessment that the accused had fired out of fear and had not deliberately aimed at a particular person.
members.conclusion: The offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and the conviction under Part II of Section 304 of the Penal Code was upheld.

predicates.criminal_appeal_after_homicide_convictio: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for causing a death.
predicates.accused_causes_death_by_firing: The accused fires a weapon and the firing causes a person's death.
predicates.no_intention_to_kill_particular_person_i: The evidence does not establish that the accused intended to kill a particular person.
predicates.accused_knows_act_is_likely_to_cause_dea: The accused acts with knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

members.legal_issue: A murder conviction may be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder where the circumstances leave open the possibility that the accused acted without an intention to cause death.
material_facts: The accused participated in an armed group attack that caused a death, and the court rejected their claim of private defence.
The High Court had convicted two appellants of murder-related offences on the basis of their roles in the incident.

Despite finding the prosecution case established, the Supreme Court considered that, in the particular circumstances, the possibility that those appellants committed the crime without an intention to cause death could not be ruled out.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Sections 302, 304 Part I, 34, and 109 of the Indian Penal Code. It concluded, on the particular facts, that the possibility of an absence of intention to cause death could not be excluded and therefore substituted culpable homicide not amounting to murder for the murder-related convictions of the two appellants. No earlier case was cited as the basis for this specific alteration.
members.conclusion: The convictions of the two appellants were altered from murder-related convictions to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, with liability based on their common intention; the other appellants’ convictions were not disturbed.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction for murder.
predicates.participation_in_attack_proved: The evidence established the accused’s participation in the attack that caused the death.
predicates.lesser_intent_remains_possible_on_the_ci: The circumstances leave open the possibility that the accused acted without an intention to cause death.

members.legal_issue: Where the accused caused injuries resulting in death but the evidence and circumstances did not establish murder, the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
material_facts: The accused were close family members, and the incident arose from a dispute over cultivation and family property.
The Court accepted that two accused caused injuries to one victim and that one accused alone caused injuries to the other victim.

The injuries attributed to the appellants were on the thigh and back; the medical evidence disclosed no firearm wound, and no evidence or finding identified who caused the fatal injuries to the first victim.
The Court considered the weapons and circumstances insufficient to establish an intention to cause death or knowledge that death was likely from the injuries inflicted.
The second victim died about eight days after the incident, and the injuries inflicted on him were not proved to be serious or fatal.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 299, 300, 302 and 304 of the Indian Penal Code and the three-stage analysis in State of Andhra Pradesh v. Rayavarapu Punnayya (1977 (1) SCR 601): determine whether the accused caused the death, whether the act amounts to culpable homicide under Section 299, and whether the case falls within Section 300. The Court concluded on these facts that the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under Section 304, Part I.
members.conclusion: The Court altered the murder convictions to convictions for culpable homicide under Section 299 read with Section 304, Part I, of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: murder_conviction_appeal and accused_caused_death_resulting_injuries and fatal_injury_attribution_unproved and injuries_confined_to_nonvital_parts and circumstances_do_not_establish_murder_intent_or_knowledge

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The accused appealed convictions for murder arising from a criminal proceeding.
predicates.accused_caused_death_resulting_injuries: The accused caused injuries that resulted in a victim's death.
predicates.fatal_injury_attribution_unproved: The evidence did not establish which accused caused the fatal injury or injuries.
predicates.injuries_confined_to_nonvital_parts: The injuries attributed to the accused were confined to parts of the body not shown to be vital.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_establish_murder_in: The weapons, injuries, and surrounding circumstances did not establish an intention to cause death or knowledge that death was likely.

members.legal_issue: A single fatal blow delivered during a sudden altercation, without prior animosity toward the victim, does not establish murder where the circumstances do not establish an intention to kill or the requisite knowledge that death would result.
material_facts: During an altercation involving the victim’s son, the victim came out and questioned why his son was being beaten.
The accused inflicted one severe knife blow to the victim’s abdomen, causing a penetrating injury from which the victim later died.

The court found no animosity between the accused and the victim and concluded that the circumstances did not establish an intention to cause murder or the requisite knowledge that death would be the inevitable result.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Sections 302 and 304 Part II IPC. Considering the single blow, the circumstances in which it was inflicted, and the absence of animosity toward the victim, the court held that the required intention or knowledge for murder was not established. No earlier case is cited for this conclusion in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The murder conviction was set aside and the accused was convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_reviewing_murder_conviction and one_severe_blow and sudden_altercation_context and no_prior_animosity_toward_victim

predicates.criminal_appeal_reviewing_murder_convict: The proceeding is a criminal appeal reviewing a murder conviction.
predicates.one_severe_blow: The accused inflicted one severe blow that caused the victim’s fatal injury.
predicates.sudden_altercation_context: The fatal blow was delivered during a sudden encounter arising from an altercation involving another person.
predicates.no_prior_animosity_toward_victim: The accused had no prior animosity toward the victim.

members.legal_issue: A single fatal blow does not by itself reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder; intention must be inferred from the whole circumstances, including the weapon, force, target, and presence or absence of a sudden fight or provocation.
material_facts: The appellant carried a large dagger and had been involved in an earlier altercation with the deceased’s family shortly before the fatal incident.
The deceased and the two relatives accompanying him were unarmed, and there was no indication that they intended physical harm or retaliation.
The appellant stabbed the deceased with great force just below the neck, causing a deep wound to a vital part of the body that was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The circumstances did not show provocation, a sudden quarrel or fight, or a basis for applying the sudden-fight exception.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 299 and 300 of the Indian Penal Code, the distinction between murder and culpable homicide not amounting to murder turns on the required intention or knowledge and whether a statutory exception applies. Section 300 Exception 4 requires a sudden fight in the heat of passion, without premeditation, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. Section 302 prescribes punishment for murder, while Section 304 Parts I and II address culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Under Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab (AIR 1958 SC 465), the prosecution must establish the injury, its nature, the accused’s intention to inflict that injury, and that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Jagrup Singh v. State of Haryana (AIR 1981 SC 1552) explains that intention is inferred from circumstances including the weapon, the body part struck, force, and surrounding events; a single blow alone does not determine the offence. The Court distinguished Laxman Kalu Nikalje, Randhir Singh, Tholan, and Bagdiram, and referred also to Virsa Singh, Gudar Dusadh, Vasanta, Jai Prakash, and State of Karnataka v. Vedanayagam as examples where a single blow did not preclude a murder conviction.
members.conclusion: The evidence established an intention to cause death or, at least, to cause bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death; the offence remained murder, and the sudden-fight exception did not apply.

rule.if: homicide_conviction_appeal and accused_carried_dangerous_weapon and blow_struck_vital_part_with_great_force and injury_sufficient_to_cause_death and victim_unarmed and sudden_fight_or_grave_provocation_absent

predicates.homicide_conviction_appeal: The case is an appeal challenging a conviction for a homicide offence.
predicates.accused_carried_dangerous_weapon: The accused brought or carried a dangerous weapon to the incident.
predicates.blow_struck_vital_part_with_great_force: The accused struck a vital part of the victim’s body with great force.
predicates.injury_sufficient_to_cause_death: The injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
predicates.victim_unarmed: The victim was not carrying a weapon.
predicates.sudden_fight_or_grave_provocation_absent: The circumstances did not establish a sudden fight or grave and sudden provocation.

members.legal_issue: Whether a conviction for murder should be altered where the fatal injury resulted from a single blow in the circumstances of the incident.
material_facts: The accused struck the deceased on the head with a wooden yoke, and the record described the fatal injury as resulting from a single blow.
The Court considered that the blow was delivered with a small, light wooden yoke and assessed it in the context of the incident as a whole.
The accused had been convicted of murder, and the Court had rejected their claim of private defence.
members.legal_principle: A single blow resulting in death does not invariably exclude murder; the circumstances of each case must be assessed. On the facts here, the Court altered the conviction under Section 302 to Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The conviction was altered from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Part I, and a custodial sentence of ten years was imposed.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and single_fatal_head_blow and blow_delivered_with_small_light_weapon and circumstances_considered_as_a_whole_support_reduced_offence

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.single_fatal_head_blow: The death resulted from a single blow to the head.
predicates.blow_delivered_with_small_light_weapon: The blow was delivered with a small, light weapon.
predicates.circumstances_considered_as_a_whole_supp: The circumstances of the incident, considered as a whole, support treating the offence as culpable homicide rather than murder.

members.legal_issue: A fatal single blow delivered during a sudden, unpremeditated quarrel, considered with the nature of the injury and all surrounding circumstances, may constitute culpable homicide not amounting to murder rather than murder.
material_facts: The accused was convicted of murder for causing the deceased’s fatal head injury during a dispute over construction of a wall.
The quarrel arose suddenly after construction had begun, following an ongoing dispute and an exchange of abuses; the evidence did not indicate premeditation.

Only one blow was inflicted. The witnesses differed about the weapon and the assailants’ roles, and the medical evidence was inconsistent about whether the head wound was incised or caused by a hard, blunt object.

A doctor testified that the injury could not have been caused by a sharp cutting weapon and could have resulted from a fall; another doctor described an incised wound. The possibility that the blow came from the blunt side of an axe could not be ruled out.
A co-accused had an unexplained injury, other accused were acquitted, and much of the prosecution account of their involvement was rejected.
members.legal_principle: Section 300, Exception 4, applies where the act occurs without premeditation, in a sudden fight, without undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct. The court must assess intention and the nature of the offence holistically, considering the weapon, force, injury, suddenness of the quarrel, premeditation, and conduct. A blunt-force wound may resemble an incised wound, as explained in Shankaria v. State of Rajasthan. Under Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab, the elements of the relevant murder clause include intention to inflict the particular injury and that injury’s sufficiency to cause death in the ordinary course. The court also relied on Pappu v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Pulicherla Nagaraju @ Nagaraja Reddy v. State of A.P., and Rajinder v. State of Haryana in assessing the distinction between murder and culpable homicide; Section 304, Part II applies where the circumstances establish the lesser offence without the requisite basis for murder.
members.conclusion: The accused was not guilty of murder but was guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304, Part II of the Indian Penal Code; the appeal was allowed to that extent.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and single_fatal_blow and sudden_quarrel_without_premeditation and not undue_advantage_or_cruel_conduct and surrounding_circumstances_do_not_establish_murder

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.single_fatal_blow: The accused inflicted one blow that caused the victim’s fatal injury.
predicates.sudden_quarrel_without_premeditation: The fatal act occurred in a sudden quarrel and was not premeditated.
predicates.undue_advantage_or_cruel_conduct: The accused took undue advantage or acted cruelly or unusually during the incident.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_do_not_establi: The evidence about the injury, weapon, intention, and incident as a whole does not establish murder.

members.legal_issue: An accused who participated in an assault may be convicted of grievous hurt rather than culpable homicide when the evidence does not reliably connect that accused’s blow to the fatal injury.
material_facts: The courts below found that the appellant assaulted the deceased and that injuries from the assault caused the deceased’s death.
The evidence was general and did not reliably connect the appellant’s blow to the internal injury that caused death.

The High Court had convicted the appellant under Section 304, Part II, IPC. The prosecution accepted that Section 325, read with Section 34, IPC, was the appropriate provision if the fatal injury could not be attributed to the appellant.
The other accused had not been convicted under Section 325, and the prosecution had not appealed against their convictions.
members.legal_principle: Applying Sections 304, Part II, and 325, IPC, the Court held on these facts that the appellant’s participation in the assault supported a conviction for grievous hurt, but the evidence did not support attributing the fatal injury to him so as to sustain the culpable-homicide conviction. Section 34, IPC, was raised in relation to the proposed conviction, but the Court convicted this appellant under Section 325 alone because the other accused had not been convicted under that provision and no prosecution appeal was before it. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Court set aside the conviction under Section 304, Part II, IPC, and convicted the appellant under Section 325, IPC; it did not alter the convictions of the other accused.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed against a conviction arising from an assault.
predicates.appellant_assaulted_deceased: The evidence accepted by the court established that the accused assaulted the deceased.
predicates.evidence_does_not_attribute_fatal_injury: The evidence did not reliably connect the accused’s blow to the injury that caused the deceased’s death.

members.legal_issue: The injuries and the knowledge accompanying their infliction supported conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder rather than grievous hurt.
material_facts: Medical evidence established an incised wound on a deceased person’s scalp that fractured the skull and extended across the skull bones; the trial court found the injury severe enough to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
The injury was attributed to the appellants, and the trial court found they must have had knowledge that it would cause death.

The trial court and the High Court both assessed the evidence and concluded that the offence fell under Section 304, Part II, IPC, rather than Section 302 read with Section 149, IPC or Section 325, IPC.
members.legal_principle: Section 304, Part II, IPC applies where the accused has the knowledge relevant to culpable homicide but the offence does not amount to murder; Section 325, IPC concerns grievous hurt. The Court relied on the medical evidence about the severity of the injury and the concurrent factual findings. It cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the concurrent findings that the appellants were guilty under Section 304, Part II, IPC, and declined to substitute a conviction under Section 325, IPC.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and injury_attributed_to_accused and injury_severe_enough_to_cause_death and accused_knew_injury_would_cause_death and concurrent_findings_support_culpable_homicide

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed against a criminal conviction.
predicates.injury_attributed_to_accused: The courts found that an injury to a deceased person was caused by the accused.
predicates.injury_severe_enough_to_cause_death: Medical evidence showed that the injury was severe enough to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
predicates.accused_knew_injury_would_cause_death: The courts found that the accused had knowledge that the injury would cause death.
predicates.concurrent_findings_support_culpable_hom: The trial and appellate courts both found that the evidence supported culpable homicide rather than murder or grievous hurt.

members.legal_issue: An accused who participates with another in causing a knife injury may be convicted for the assault where the evidence establishes their joint participation but not liability for murder.
material_facts: Two accused were found to have caused an injury to the informant with a knife.
The court treated their conduct as causing an injury rather than as participation in either victim's murder.
They had already spent more than seven years in custody.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Sections 324 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code to the joint infliction of a knife injury. It substituted that conviction for the murder-related conviction and ordered release in light of the custody already served. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The two accused were convicted of the lesser assault offence with joint liability, sentenced to two years' imprisonment, and directed to be released because they had already served more than that period.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed from convictions entered in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.accused_jointly_caused_knife_injury: The accused acted together in causing an injury to a person with a knife.
predicates.injury_did_not_establish_murder_liabilit: The evidence established the knife injury but did not establish that the accused were liable for a victim's murder.

members.legal_issue: An interlocutory order may be challenged in an appeal from the decree in the suit.
material_facts: The lower appellate court rejected a request to revisit the order limiting certain defendants to watching and participating in the proceedings without filing a written statement.
Those defendants challenged the resulting decree in appeals from the decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 105(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an interlocutory order to be challenged in an appeal from the decree, subject to the provision’s requirements.
members.conclusion: The lower appellate court was wrong to treat the interlocutory order as unchallengeable in the appeals from the decree.

predicates.appeal_from_decree: A party appealed from the decree entered in a civil suit.
predicates.interlocutory_order_challenged: The party challenged an interlocutory order in that appeal.

members.legal_issue: A determination firmly made by an appellate court before remand binds the trial court and a later bench hearing the appeal, but it may be challenged in an appeal to the Supreme Court from the final judgment.
material_facts: An earlier appellate judgment expressly considered and finally rejected the tenant’s claim to an occupancy right.
The case was remanded for trial of other issues.
After remand, the trial court and the later appellate bench treated the earlier determination as binding.
The tenant challenged that determination in an appeal to the Supreme Court against the final judgment.
members.legal_principle: A determination finally made on an issue in an earlier stage binds the court conducting proceedings after remand and a later bench hearing the appeal. However, the correctness of that determination may be challenged in an appeal to the Supreme Court against the final judgment. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Sm. Deorajin Debi, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 590.
members.conclusion: The trial court and the later appellate bench were bound by the earlier determination, but the tenant could challenge it in the Supreme Court appeal from the final judgment.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_from_final_judgm: The matter is an appeal to the Supreme Court from a final judgment entered after an earlier appellate decision remanded the case.
predicates.earlier_appellate_decision_firmly_resolv: An earlier appellate decision expressly and finally resolved the issue before the case was remanded for other proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A party may challenge in an appeal the correctness of an earlier order remitting an award when no appeal lay from that remittal order.
material_facts: An earlier order set aside an award and remitted the matter to the arbitrator for a fresh decision.
No appeal lay from that remittal order under section 39 of the Arbitration Act.
The correctness of that order was challenged in an appeal arising from the later decision in the arbitration proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 39 of the Arbitration Act provides that no appeal lies from an order remitting an award under section 16. The Court held that, because the party could not appeal the remittal order when it was made, there was no reason to preclude a challenge to its correctness in the later appeal.
members.conclusion: The appellants were not precluded from challenging the correctness of the earlier remittal order in the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_later_arbitration_decision: A party brings an appeal arising from a later decision in arbitration proceedings.
predicates.earlier_order_remitted_award: An earlier order set aside an award and sent the matter back to the arbitrator for a fresh decision.
predicates.no_appeal_lay_from_remittal_order: The governing appeal rules did not permit an appeal from the earlier remittal order.

members.legal_issue: An interlocutory remand order may be challenged in an appeal from the final judgment in the proceedings.
material_facts: The High Court made a remand order that did not terminate the proceedings.
Further proceedings took place following the remand, and a final decision was later appealed.
The appellants challenged the earlier remand order in their appeal from the later decision.
members.legal_principle: An order of remand that does not terminate the proceedings is an interlocutory judgment and may be challenged in an appeal from the final order. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajin Debi and Kshitish Chandra Bose v. Commissioner of Ranchi, and also referred to Gangadhar v. Shankar Lal in support of allowing the challenge at that stage.
members.conclusion: The appellants were entitled to challenge the interlocutory remand order in the appeal from the final decision; because the remand order was erroneous, the proceedings and orders consequent to it were set aside.

predicates.appeal_from_final_order: A party appealed from a final order in proceedings that had followed a remand.
predicates.earlier_interlocutory_remand: A court had earlier made a remand order that did not terminate the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A party may challenge an interlocutory determination in an appeal from the final judgment in the same litigation even if the earlier determination was not appealed when made.
material_facts: During the suit, the High Court affirmed an order setting aside an arbitrators' award and made a finding about whether the partition could be reopened.
The plaintiff did not appeal that decision at the time, but the parties later challenged the earlier finding in the Supreme Court appeal from the final judgment.
members.legal_principle: An interlocutory decision does not invariably prevent a higher court from considering the matter at a later stage of the same litigation. The Court relied on Satyadhan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajan Devi, Jasraj Indu Singh v. Hem Raj Multan Chand, Margaret Lalita v. Indo Commercial Bank Ltd., and Arjun Singh v. Mohindra Kumar.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the earlier finding could be challenged in the appeal from the final judgment.

predicates.appeal_from_final_judgment_in_same_litig: A party appealed from the final judgment in the same litigation in which the earlier determination was made.
predicates.earlier_interlocutory_determination: A court made an interlocutory determination during the litigation.
predicates.earlier_determination_appealed: A party appealed the earlier determination when it was made.

members.legal_issue: A party may challenge an adverse ruling on an issue when that ruling and the favorable judgment are parts of the same proceeding and the issue was not finally disposed of separately.
material_facts: The court had first addressed the constitutional challenge while leaving the pending appeal for further consideration on its merits.
The later decision in that same appeal granted relief on the merits, and the party seeking to preserve that relief challenged the earlier adverse conclusion without having separately appealed it.
members.legal_principle: Where successive rulings are parts of one continuing proceeding and the relevant matter was not finally disposed of separately, the party may challenge the adverse ruling when defending the favorable judgment; the Court also considered that it was doubtful a separate appeal would have lain from the earlier ruling.
members.conclusion: The party was not precluded from challenging the constitutional ruling and could support the favorable judgment by contesting the adverse conclusion.

predicates.same_proceeding: The earlier ruling and the later favorable judgment were made in the same continuing proceeding.
predicates.earlier_issue_not_finally_disposed: The court left the proceeding pending after its earlier ruling and later considered the matter further.
predicates.party_defends_favorable_judgment: A party seeks to preserve a favorable judgment by contesting an adverse ruling made during that proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A tenant may challenge the dismissal of an interlocutory application for statutory protection in an appeal from the decree in the eviction suit without filing a separate appeal against the dismissal order.
material_facts: The landlords brought an eviction suit, and the tenants filed an application under the tenant-protection legislation in that suit.
The trial court dismissed the application and decreed eviction.
The tenants appealed the decree and challenged the dismissal of their application in the appellate proceedings.
The High Court treated the application as no longer pending because the tenants had not filed a separate appeal against its dismissal.
members.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants’ Protection Act permits a tenant facing an eviction suit to apply to the court for relief. Under Section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a party appealing a decree may challenge the correctness of an interlocutory order made in the suit. That principle applies to an order on a Section 9 application even though Section 9A provides for appeals from specified orders. No earlier case is relied upon for this holding.
members.conclusion: The tenants could challenge the interlocutory order in their appeal against the decree without bringing a separate appeal, and their application was to be treated as pending during the appeal and second appeal. The legal effect of the application remained for the High Court to consider.

rule.if: eviction_suit and tenant_filed_protection_application and application_order_was_interlocutory and tenant_appealed_decree

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.tenant_filed_protection_application: The tenant applied for statutory protection in the eviction suit.
predicates.application_order_was_interlocutory: The court disposed of the tenant’s application as an interlocutory matter in the suit.
predicates.tenant_appealed_decree: The tenant appealed the decree made in the eviction suit.
predicates.interlocutory_order_challengeable_in_dec: The tenant may challenge the interlocutory order in the appeal against the decree without filing a separate appeal against that order.

members.legal_issue: A party may challenge an interlocutory ruling in an appeal from the final decision even though the party did not appeal the interlocutory ruling when it was made.
material_facts: In a remand judgment, the High Court rejected the appellant’s contention that the issue was barred by res judicata.
The appellant did not appeal the remand judgment.
After the proceedings on remand, the High Court issued a final judgment, which the appellant appealed and in which the appellant again challenged the earlier ruling.
members.legal_principle: Under Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajin Debi, an interlocutory order may be challenged in an appeal from the final decree or order, whether no appeal lay from the interlocutory order or an available appeal was not taken.
members.conclusion: The failure to appeal the remand judgment did not prevent the appellant from challenging its ruling in the appeal from the final judgment.

predicates.appeal_from_final_decision: The proceeding is an appeal from a final judgment, decree, or order.
predicates.earlier_interlocutory_ruling_not_appeale: A party did not appeal an earlier interlocutory ruling, whether because no appeal lay or because no appeal was taken.
predicates.party_challenges_earlier_ruling_in_final: In the appeal from the final decision, a party challenges the correctness of the earlier interlocutory ruling.

members.legal_issue: An unappealed interlocutory remand order that does not terminate the proceedings may be challenged in an appeal from the final order.
material_facts: The High Court remanded the tenants’ application after deciding that the statutory remedy remained available.
The landlords did not appeal the remand order.
After remand, the trial court rescinded the ejectment decree, and the landlords challenged that final order.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata promotes finality, and under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure its principle may also apply between stages of the same proceeding. But a non-terminating interlocutory order can be challenged in an appeal from the final order; section 105 of the Code permits objections to interlocutory orders affecting the decision, subject to the special restriction in section 105(2) for an appealable remand order. The Court held that section 105(2) did not bar this challenge before it. It relied on Maharaja Mohesur Singh v. The Bengal Government, Forbes v. Amecroonissa Begum and Sheonath v. Ramnath, and distinguished Ramkripal Shukul v. Mst. Rup Kuari, Bani Ram v. Nanhu Mal and Hook v. Administrator General of Bengal, which concerned decisions that had effectively terminated earlier proceedings.
members.conclusion: The landlords were not precluded from challenging the remand order’s ruling on the statutory remedy in their appeal from the final order.

predicates.appeal_from_final_order: A party brought an appeal against the order that concluded the proceeding or its relevant stage.
predicates.challenged_order_did_not_terminate_proce: The earlier order was interlocutory and left the proceeding to continue toward a final decision.
predicates.no_appeal_lay_from_interlocutory_order: The earlier interlocutory order was not appealable.
predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_order_was_not_: Although an appeal from the earlier interlocutory order was available, the party did not take it.

members.legal_issue: Failure to appeal immediately from an interlocutory provisional-rent order does not bar a tenant from challenging that order in an appeal against the resulting eviction order.
material_facts: The Rent Controller fixed provisional arrears without considering the tenant’s affidavit setting out rent payments and directing the tenant to pay the assessed amount.
The tenant did not immediately appeal the provisional-rent order and did not comply with it, so the Rent Controller ordered eviction.
The tenant appealed the eviction order and also challenged the provisional-rent order in that appeal.
The appellate authority set aside both orders and remanded the matter, but the High Court held that the provisional-rent order could not be reviewed because no immediate appeal had been filed.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(1)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 permits an appeal from an order of the Rent Controller but does not provide that failure to appeal an interlocutory order forfeits the right to challenge it in an appeal from the final order. Unlike Sections 97 and 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, it contains no such bar. An order fixing provisional rent is interlocutory because it does not finally determine the principal matter, even though non-compliance may lead to eviction. The principle against requiring appeals from every interlocutory order is supported by Maharajah Moheshur Sing v. The Bengal Government and the discussion of the competing approaches in Nanibala Dasi v. Ichhamoyee Dasi and Syed Ishak Syed Farid v. Kunjbihari Singh. Rakesh Wadhawan v. Jagdamba Industrial Corporation, affirmed in Vinod Kumar v. Prem Lata, explains the provisional assessment and the consequence of non-compliance; it does not bar review of that assessment in an appeal from eviction.
members.conclusion: The appellate authority may examine the legality and validity of the provisional-rent order when the tenant appeals the eviction order and challenges the provisional-rent order in that appeal, notwithstanding the absence of an immediate appeal.

predicates.eviction_order_appealed: The tenant appealed the resulting eviction order.
predicates.provisional_order_challenged_in_eviction: In the appeal against eviction, the tenant also challenged the correctness of the provisional assessment.

members.legal_issue: An interlocutory remand order that does not terminate the proceedings may be challenged in an appeal from the final order.
material_facts: The High Court's first judgment remanded the case for further consideration and did not finally terminate the proceedings.
The affected party did not appeal the remand order at that stage, but challenged it in an appeal after the proceedings on remand and a subsequent High Court judgment.
members.legal_principle: An interlocutory remand judgment that does not terminate proceedings may be challenged in an appeal from the final order. The Court relied on Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria and Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi.
members.conclusion: The first judgment could be challenged in the appeal from the final judgment; because it was legally erroneous, the subsequent proceedings founded on it were non est.

predicates.appeal_from_final_order_after_remand: The appeal is from a final order made after proceedings following an earlier remand.
predicates.earlier_order_did_not_terminate_proceedi: The earlier order remanded the matter and did not terminate the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to limitation cannot be raised in an appeal confined to an interlocutory order before the final decree, when the remand order holding the final-decree application timely was not challenged at that stage.
material_facts: The trial court had initially dismissed the final-decree application as time-barred, but the appellate court reversed that ruling and remanded the matter for further proceedings.
The High Court upheld the ruling that the final-decree application was not time-barred, and the defendant did not then bring the matter before the Supreme Court.
The present appeal arose from the dismissal of a later interlocutory application, and no final decree had yet been passed.
The appellants also relied on non-payment of redemption money as an additional limitation ground.
members.legal_principle: Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and Satyadhyan Ghosal permit an interlocutory order to be challenged in an appeal from the final decision in the circumstances described by the Court. The limitation issue would arise for consideration only if a final decree were eventually passed against the appellants; the Court expressed no opinion on the merits of either limitation ground.
members.conclusion: The limitation arguments were premature in this appeal and could not be raised in the remanded proceedings; the Court left them open for appropriate future proceedings if a final decree were ultimately passed against the appellants.

rule.if: appeal_from_interlocutory_order and earlier_remand_order_upheld_limitation_finding and no_challenge_to_remand_order_then and no_final_decree_against_appellant

predicates.earlier_remand_order_upheld_limitation_f: An earlier remand order, later upheld on review, held that the final-decree application was not time-barred.
predicates.no_challenge_to_remand_order_then: The affected party did not challenge the remand order when it was made and upheld.
predicates.no_final_decree_against_appellant: No final decree had yet been passed against the affected party.

members.legal_issue: A decision on the merits of an appeal while a challenge to the order condoning delay is pending does not prevent review of the condonation order.
material_facts: The claimants appealed against the order condoning delay in the State’s land acquisition appeals.
While those challenges were pending, the High Court decided the State’s appeals on the merits.
members.legal_principle: An order deciding an appeal on the merits may depend on the order excusing delay; setting aside the latter can undermine the former. Accordingly, deciding the merits appeal in the meantime does not by itself make a challenge to the delay-condonation order infructuous.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s decision on the merits did not bar the Court from considering whether the delay-condonation order was correct; if that order were set aside, the subsequent merits decision could be rendered nugatory.

predicates.appeal_challenges_delay_condonation: A party has appealed against an order excusing delay in filing another appeal.
predicates.main_appeal_decided_on_merits: The court has decided the underlying appeal on its merits while the challenge to the delay order is pending.

members.legal_issue: The question whether to condone delay in an appeal is for the appellate authority to decide, and a challenge to that question is academic when the authority also decides the appeal on its merits.
material_facts: The occupant’s appeal against the order striking out the defence was one day late.
The Rent Control Tribunal dismissed that appeal both as time-barred and on its merits.
The occupant challenged the refusal to condone delay, but the Supreme Court noted that the merits had also been decided.
members.legal_principle: The appellate authority determines whether the explanation establishes sufficient ground to condone delay. The Supreme Court stated that the matter was academic where the appeal had also been considered and dismissed on its merits. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: Whether the delay should have been condoned was within the appellate authority’s discretion, and the issue was of no importance because the Tribunal had also rejected the appeal on its merits.

predicates.rent_control_appeal_against_defence_orde: The occupant appealed an order striking out a defence in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.appeal_filed_late: The occupant filed that appeal after the applicable filing period.
predicates.appellate_authority_decided_merits: The appellate authority considered and decided the appeal on its merits as well as addressing delay.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a remittal in rent-control proceedings does not warrant a direct eviction order when proceedings after remittal have taken place and the related appeal remains available to determine the parties’ remedies.
material_facts: A tenant challenged an eviction order, and the High Court remitted the rent-control matter for a decision after allowing the tenant to file a written statement.
After remittal, the Rent Controller dismissed the eviction application, and an appeal from that dismissal was pending before the District Judge.
The petitioners asked the Supreme Court to direct eviction in light of its decision in the rent-arrears appeals.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to bypass the pending rent-control appeal by ordering eviction through a shortcut based on the decision in the rent-arrears appeals. In light of the subsequent proceedings before the Rent Controller, the challenge to the remittal had become infructuous; the parties were left to pursue their remedies in the pending appeal.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to order eviction directly and left the petitioners to pursue their remedies in the pending rent appeal. The special leave petition challenging the remittal was dismissed as infructuous following the post-remittal rent-control proceedings.

predicates.rent_control_remittal_challenge: The proceeding challenges a decision remitting a rent-control matter for further proceedings.
predicates.post_remittal_controller_proceedings_com: The rent-control authority has acted on the remittal and issued a decision.
predicates.related_rent_appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the post-remittal rent-control decision remains pending.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s share in a deceased coparcener’s property includes both the share she would receive in a partition immediately before his death and her share by succession in his interest in the coparcenary property.
material_facts: The properties were found to belong to a joint family, and no prior partition had taken place.
The deceased had an interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property and died leaving a widow, sons, and daughters, including female heirs in Class I.
The deceased had made no testamentary disposition.
At the notional partition immediately before his death, the widow would have received a share equal to that of a son.
The Court calculated the widow’s share as the share received at the notional partition together with her equal share in the deceased’s interest by intestate succession.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the proviso makes the deceased coparcener’s interest devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, rather than survivorship, when the specified female relative or qualifying male relative survives him. Explanation 1 requires the deceased’s interest to be calculated as the share he would have received in a partition immediately before death. The partition fiction must be given full effect throughout the calculation of the heirs’ shares: its consequences cannot be used to determine the deceased’s share and then disregarded when determining the heirs’ shares. The heir therefore receives the share obtained, or deemed to have been obtained, in the notional partition as well as the heir’s share in the deceased’s interest. Sections 8, 9, and 10 govern the relevant intestate succession calculation. The Court applied Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi v. S. Teja Singh and approved the reasoning in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council on giving full effect to a statutory fiction. It also approved Rangubai Lalji v. Laxman Lalji, Sushilabai Ramachandra Kulkarni v. Narayanrao Gopalrao Deshpande, Vidyaben v. Jagadishchandra N. Bhatt, and Ananda v. Haribandhu.
members.conclusion: The widow was entitled to both her share at the notional partition and her share by succession in the deceased’s coparcenary interest; her total share was 7/24.

predicates.widow_entitled_to_share_at_partition: The widow would have received a share if a partition had taken place immediately before the deceased’s death.

members.legal_issue: When a coparcener dies leaving female Class I heirs, the deceased’s interest devolves by succession rather than survivorship, and the applicable shares are determined by a notional partition followed by succession to that interest.
material_facts: The deceased coparcener died leaving a widow, daughters, and other Class I heirs, including an unmarried daughter and a surviving son who was the other coparcener.
The deceased’s mother and any predeceased son or brother were not surviving.
The High Court calculated the unmarried daughter’s share at the notional partition and each heir’s share in the deceased’s interest as an intestate heir.
The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court’s calculation of the parties’ shares.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gives that Act overriding effect over inconsistent Hindu law. The proviso to Section 6 provides for succession rather than survivorship when a coparcener leaves a female Class I heir, while Explanation 1 to Section 6 requires a notional partition immediately before death. Section 8 of the Mysore Hindu Law Women’s Rights Act, 1933 provides the relevant female shares at partition; Section 8(1)(d) is superseded to the extent that the deceased’s interest does not pass by survivorship. Under Sections 8(1)(a) and 8(2)(c) of the Mysore Act, the unmarried daughter’s partition share is calculated by reference to her brother’s share. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum establishes that a female’s share at the notional partition is additional to her share as an heir; State of Maharashtra v. Narayan Rao is also cited on the effect of the notional partition.
members.conclusion: The female-share provision applicable when joint family property passes to a single coparcener by survivorship did not apply to the deceased’s interest because that interest devolved by succession. The unmarried daughter received a share at the notional partition as well as a share as an heir, and the parties’ calculated shares were affirmed.

predicates.coparcener_dies_with_class_i_female_heir: A coparcener dies leaving female heirs entitled to succeed to his interest.
predicates.deceased_interest_would_otherwise_pass_b: Absent the surviving female heirs, the deceased’s interest would pass to surviving coparceners by survivorship.
predicates.unmarried_daughter_qualifies_for_partiti: The deceased leaves an unmarried daughter who qualifies for a share when the family property is notionally partitioned.
predicates.heirs_succeed_to_deceased_interest: The deceased’s interest passes to his heirs by intestate succession.

members.legal_issue: When a Mitakshara coparcener dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and leaves a qualifying female relative, his interest is determined by a notional partition immediately before his death.
material_facts: The coparcener died after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 had commenced.
His wife and other qualifying female relatives survived him.
The courts had to determine the shares in the joint family property.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, including Explanation 1 and its proviso, requires the deceased coparcener's interest to be calculated as the share he would have received on a partition immediately before his death and, where the proviso applies, to devolve by succession rather than survivorship. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum explains that the hypothetical partition must give the wife a share equal to a son.
members.conclusion: A notional partition immediately before the coparcener's death had to be presumed to determine his interest; the wife was entitled to a share equal to that of a son in the hypothetical partition.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A proceeding seeks partition of property held by a joint family.
predicates.coparcener_died_after_succession_law_com: A coparcener died after the applicable succession law had commenced.
predicates.qualifying_female_relative_survived: A qualifying female relative survived the coparcener.

members.legal_issue: When a Hindu coparcener dies after the Hindu Succession Act applies and leaves a qualifying female relative, the deceased’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property devolves by succession after determining that interest through a notional partition.
material_facts: The property was Mitakshara coparcenary property.
The deceased’s death was determined to have occurred after the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
He left a widow, three sons, and three daughters.
The court determined his interest by considering the share he would have received on a partition immediately before his death, and then determined succession to that interest among his heirs.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, including its proviso and Explanation I, provides that where a male Hindu dies with an interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property and leaves a female relative specified in Class I of the Schedule, his interest devolves by testamentary or intestate succession rather than survivorship. Explanation I determines that interest as the share that would have been allotted to him on a partition immediately before death. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The deceased’s interest devolved by succession rather than survivorship. His widow, sons, and daughters shared that interest equally; the widow also received the share attributed to her on the notional partition.

predicates.inheritance_dispute: A proceeding requires determination of the devolution of a deceased person’s property interest.
predicates.male_hindu_dies_after_succession_law_app: A male Hindu dies after the succession law applies to the succession in question.

predicates.deceased_interest_determined_by_notional: The deceased’s interest is determined by identifying the share that would have been allotted to him on a partition immediately before death.

members.legal_issue: The shares in joint family property must reflect successive intestate devolution of the interests of a deceased coparcener and of a widow who later dies intestate.
material_facts: The deceased coparcener's interest devolved by intestate succession on his surviving heirs, including his widow, mother, children, and descendants of a predeceased child.
The mother had an interest in the property and later died, leaving a daughter and the children of her predeceased son.
The lower courts had awarded the appellants a 37.5% share, but the Supreme Court's calculation of the successive devolution resulted in a 38.1% share for the appellants.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the deceased coparcener's interest devolved by intestate succession because qualifying female relatives survived him. The Court then applied intestate succession to the mother's interest on her death, allocating one-half to her daughter and the other half to the branch of her predeceased son. The calculation also applied the principles in Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum concerning the notional partition.
members.conclusion: The appellants' share in the joint family property was 38.1%, rather than 37.5%, and the decree was modified accordingly.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A proceeding seeks partition of property held by a joint family.
predicates.coparcener_interest_devolved_by_intestat: A deceased coparcener's interest passed by intestate succession to surviving heirs.
predicates.widow_later_died_leaving_daughter_and_pr: A widow who held an interest later died, leaving a daughter and descendants of her predeceased son.

members.legal_issue: A deceased coparcener’s interest that devolves by intestate succession to Class I heirs is inherited individually by those heirs rather than as joint family property.
material_facts: A coparcener died intestate, leaving a wife and daughters who were Class I heirs.
A notional partition immediately before his death would have determined his share in the coparcenary property.
The deceased’s share was claimed by his heirs in a suit for partition.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, including its proviso and Explanation 1, where a male Hindu leaves a Class I female heir, his coparcenary interest devolves by succession, with that interest determined by a notional partition immediately before death. Sections 8 and 19 provide for succession to heirs per capita as tenants in common, and Section 30 treats a coparcener’s interest as disposable property. Section 4(b) displaces inconsistent prior Hindu law. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum explains that the consequences of the deemed partition must be worked out; Commissioner of Wealth Tax v. Chander Sen and Appropriate Authority (IT Deptt) v. M. Arifulla establish that property devolving under Section 8 is individual property held by heirs as tenants in common, not HUF property.
members.conclusion: The deceased’s share devolved under the Hindu Succession Act to his heirs individually, who held it as tenants in common; it did not remain joint family property.

predicates.partition_claim_over_intestate_coparcena: The proceeding seeks partition of an interest in coparcenary property after its holder died intestate.
predicates.deceased_left_class_one_female_heirs: The deceased left one or more female heirs who qualify as Class I heirs.

members.legal_issue: A share that became separate property upon partition devolves by succession under the Hindu Succession Act, including to qualifying female heirs, rather than by survivorship.
material_facts: After the death of the family ancestor, a notional partition under Section 82 of the Madhya Bharat Land Code gave his son, grandson, and widow separate shares.
The son’s share thereby became his separate property and he died after the Hindu Succession Act came into force, leaving a wife and daughter.
The High Court increased the daughter’s share in the family property, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act addresses a Mitakshara coparcener who dies after the Act comes into operation without testamentary disposition of his undivided share. Its proviso provides for the devolution of that interest where the deceased leaves a daughter or another female Class I heir. Here, the earlier partition had made the son’s share separate property, and its devolution was by succession. The court also relied on Section 82 of the Madhya Bharat Land Code in finding that the earlier partition had occurred. No earlier case was cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: The son’s property devolved by succession, not survivorship, and the surviving female heirs were entitled to the shares provided by the Hindu Succession Act.

members.legal_issue: A deceased coparcener's share, after division from the coparcenary, devolves as separate property under intestate succession, and a widow's inherited share devolves to her heirs when she later dies.
material_facts: The ancestral coparcenary property had been divided between the father and his son, with each receiving one half.
The father's half became his separate property and, on his death, passed to his widow, two daughters and son under the rules of intestate succession.
On the widow's later death, her inherited share passed to her three children under the rules governing succession to a female Hindu's property.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the father's separate property devolved among his widow and children. Under Sections 15 and 16, the widow's share devolved among her children when she died. The Court treated the father's share obtained on division as separate property, not as continuing coparcenary property.
members.conclusion: Each daughter received one eighth of the father's half share and one twenty-fourth from the mother's share, for a total of one sixth each. The son received his original one-half share, one eighth from the father's estate and one twenty-fourth from the mother's estate, for a total of two thirds.

rule.if: partition_claim_appeal and coparcenary_share_separated_before_death and deceased_left_widow_and_children and widow_later_died

predicates.partition_claim_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal arising from a suit concerning partition and separate possession.
predicates.coparcenary_share_separated_before_death: The coparcenary property had been divided so that the deceased coparcener held a separate share.
predicates.deceased_left_widow_and_children: The deceased left a widow and children entitled to inherit.
predicates.widow_later_died: The widow who inherited a share later died, leaving children who could inherit from her.

members.legal_issue: When a female Hindu dies intestate and without descendants, property inherited from her husband devolves on his heirs, determined as though he died immediately after her.
material_facts: The widow inherited the land from her husband.
She died intestate and without children or descendants.
The dispute concerned who inherited the land after her death.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(2)(b) of the Hindu Succession Act provides that property inherited by a female Hindu from her husband devolves, in the absence of a son or daughter or their descendants, on the husband’s heirs. Section 16, Rule 3 requires the order of devolution to be determined as if the husband had died intestate immediately after the female intestate.
members.conclusion: The property devolved on the husband’s heirs, with those heirs determined as if the husband had died intestate immediately after the widow’s death.

predicates.female_intestate_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns inheritance to a female Hindu’s estate after she died intestate.
predicates.property_inherited_from_husband: The property at issue was inherited by the female intestate from her husband.
predicates.no_descendants: The female intestate left no son or daughter and no descendants of any predeceased son or daughter.

members.legal_issue: When a female intestate inherited property from her husband and died without descendants, the husband’s heirs are identified by treating him as having died immediately after her, so a relative in the applicable statutory class may succeed ahead of more remote agnates.
material_facts: The deceased female died intestate and without a son or daughter, and the disputed land had been inherited from her husband.
The claimant was the daughter of the husband’s sister; the competing claimants were the husband’s remote agnates.
Neither side fell within Class I of the applicable schedule, while a sister’s daughter was listed in Class II.
The dispute arose in an inheritance suit, and the Supreme Court affirmed the decree granting the claimant the land rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 15(2)(b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, applied because the female intestate had inherited the property from her husband and left no son or daughter. Rule 3 of Section 16 required the husband’s heirs to be determined as if he had died intestate immediately after the female intestate. Under Section 8 and the Schedule, a sister’s daughter is a Class II heir, whereas agnates are reached only after Class I and Class II heirs are absent.
members.conclusion: The husband’s heirs were to be ascertained as if he had died intestate immediately after the female intestate. The claimant, as a Class II heir of the husband, therefore succeeded in preference to the competing agnates.

predicates.competing_claimants_are_husbands_agnates: The competing claimants were agnates of the husband.
predicates.claimant_precedes_competing_agnates: The claimant who is the husband’s Class II relative succeeds ahead of the competing agnates.

members.legal_issue: A widow who acquires an interest in joint family property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 has an unquantified share until partition, at which time she is entitled to the share her husband would have received.
material_facts: The common ancestor died while the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 was in force, leaving a widow and joint family property.
The widow's share had not been determined by a partition.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 gave the widow the same interest in the joint family property as her husband had. In Potti Lakshmi Perumallu v. Potti Krishna Venamma, this Court held that the share is to be determined by reference to the share the husband would have received had he lived until the date partition was claimed.
members.conclusion: The widow acquired an interest in the joint family property on her husband's death, but her share remained undetermined until partition; she was entitled to the share her husband would have received had he lived until the date partition was claimed.

predicates.partition_proceeding: A proceeding seeks partition of property held by a joint family.
predicates.ancestor_died_with_joint_property: An ancestor died while the family held joint family property.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s share in joint family property under the statutory right to claim partition is determined when she claims partition, not when her husband dies.
material_facts: The widow’s husband died while the properties were found to be joint family property held with his brother.
The widow had no issue with her husband; his son from an earlier marriage died after him and before the partition suit.
The widow later sought partition and claimed the share her husband would have had in the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Hindu Women’s Rights to Property Act, 1937, gives the widow the same interest as her husband had, and section 3(3) gives her the right to claim partition. The court treated this as a statutory interest under which the widow, as her husband’s surviving half, is entitled to the share he would have received if alive when she claimed partition. The interest may fluctuate with changes in family membership and property before partition. The court followed the approach reflected in Chinniah Chettiar v. Sivagami Achi and the decisions cited in support of a fluctuating interest, and disapproved the contrary approach in Jadaobai v. Puranmal and Natarajan Chettiar v. Perumal Ammal. It also noted that the widow’s interest had later been enlarged by section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
members.conclusion: The widow was entitled to the share her husband would have been entitled to had he lived on the date she claimed partition; her interest was not fixed by the family’s composition at the date of his death.

predicates.widow_claims_partition_of_joint_family_p: A widow seeks partition of property held by the joint family to which her deceased husband belonged.
predicates.deceased_coparcener_left_widow: A member of the joint family died leaving a widow.
predicates.widow_entitlement_arises_under_statutory: The widow’s asserted entitlement to the property arises from a statutory right associated with her deceased husband’s interest.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s claim for partition defines her statutory interest in coparcenary property, extinguishes the other coparceners’ right to take that interest by survivorship, and permits the interest to devolve to her husband’s heirs on her death even without division by metes and bounds or exclusive possession.
material_facts: The widow’s husband died while holding an interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property; the finding that he had separated from the coparcenary before his death was not established.
By statute, the widow received the same interest in the coparcenary property that her husband had held.
The widow brought a suit seeking partition and separate possession of that interest.
She died while the suit was pending, before the property had been divided by metes and bounds or placed in her exclusive possession.
Her daughters, as heirs of their father, continued the suit.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(2) and 3(3) of the Hindu Women’s Rights to Property Act, 1937, as extended to agricultural lands in Bihar by Bihar Act 6 of 1942, a widow acquired her deceased coparcener husband’s interest and the same right to claim partition as a male owner. A partition claim defines that interest through adjustment of rights; it does not require physical division or exclusive possession. Once defined by the claim, the interest is no longer subject to survivorship and, when the widow’s estate ends, devolves on her husband’s heirs. The Court relied on Lakshmi Perumallu v. Krishnavenamma and Giria Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, approved Parappagari Parappa v. Parappagari Nagamma, distinguished Pratapmull Agarwalla v. Dhanabati Bibi, and disapproved the contrary views in Movva Subba Rao v. Movva Krishna Prasadam, Shamrao Bhagwantrao v. Kashibai, and Bhagabai v. Bhaiyalal.
members.conclusion: The partition claim defined the widow’s interest and extinguished the other coparceners’ right to take it by survivorship. On the widow’s death, that interest devolved upon her husband’s heirs, and the decree granting them the share was upheld.

rule.if: widow_partition_proceeding and deceased_coparcener_left_joint_interest and widow_received_substituted_interest and widow_made_partition_demand

predicates.widow_partition_proceeding: The proceeding is a widow’s claim to partition property held by a coparcenary.
predicates.deceased_coparcener_left_joint_interest: The widow’s husband died while holding an interest in the coparcenary property.
predicates.widow_received_substituted_interest: The widow received the same interest in the coparcenary property that her husband held.
predicates.widow_made_partition_demand: The widow demanded partition of her interest, including by bringing a suit for partition.
predicates.defined_widow_interest_devolves_to_husba: The widow’s defined interest passes to her husband’s heirs when her estate ends, rather than passing to the coparceners by survivorship.

members.legal_issue: A widow is entitled to the applicable share in joint-family property and may maintain a partition suit when the law granting that right applies to her husband’s death.
material_facts: The widow sought partition of joint-family property on the basis that her husband, a member of the joint family, died after the relevant property-right legislation took effect.

The Supreme Court found that the husband died in 1939, relying on the admission in the earlier plaint together with the widow’s and her witnesses’ evidence, and rejecting the defendants’ contrary evidence.
The husband held an eight-annas interest in the joint-family properties, and the property-right legislation applied to the agricultural land at issue.
It was conceded that, after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 took effect, the widow held her share as full owner.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the Hindu Women’s Rights to Property Act, 1937, read with the Bihar Hindu Women’s Rights to Property (Extension to Agricultural Land) Act, 1942, to the widow’s right to a share and to maintain partition. It also noted the concession that section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 made her share her full property.
members.conclusion: The widow was entitled to an eight-annas share in the joint-family estate and could maintain the partition suit. Following her death during the appeal, the purchaser could claim through her sale of the specified property.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and widow_of_joint_family_member and husband_held_joint_family_property_interest and applicable_property_right_law_applied_to_property and husband_died_after_that_law_took_effect
