predicates.partition_proceeding: The proceeding seeks partition of joint-family property.
predicates.widow_of_joint_family_member: The claimant is the widow of a member of the joint family whose property is to be partitioned.
predicates.husband_held_joint_family_property_inter: The husband held an interest in the joint-family property.
predicates.applicable_property_right_law_applied_to: A property-right law granting a widow an interest applies to the property in the proceeding.
predicates.husband_died_after_that_law_took_effect: The husband died after the applicable property-right law took effect.

members.legal_issue: A trial decree merges into the appellate decree when the entire decree is appealed and the appellate court decides the appeal on its merits, even if it affirms the lower court’s decision.
material_facts: A decree for possession was passed in a suit based solely on rent default.
The entire decree was appealed through the lower appellate court to the High Court.
The High Court heard the appeal on its merits and affirmed the decree, while allowing additional time to vacate.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger rests on the principle that there cannot be more than one operative order governing the same subject matter. When an appeal is decided on its merits, the appellate decree is operative even if it merely affirms the trial decree. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. Amritlal Bhogilal & Co., Collector of Customs v. East India Commercial Co. Ltd., Jowad Hussain v. Gendan Singh, Bhup Inder v. Bijai, and Brij Narain v. Tejpal. It distinguished State of U.P. v. Mohammad Nooh and State of Madras v. Madurai Mills Co. Ltd. on their facts and the scope of the proceedings involved.
members.conclusion: The trial court’s decree merged into the High Court’s decree, which became the operative decree capable of execution.

rule.if: civil_decree_appeal and entire_decree_appealed and same_subject_matter and appellate_court_heard_appeal_on_merits

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil case involving a decree.
predicates.entire_decree_appealed: The appellant challenged the entire decree rather than only a distinct part of it.
predicates.same_subject_matter: The appeal and the original case concern the same subject matter.
predicates.appellate_court_heard_appeal_on_merits: The appellate court considered and decided the appeal on its merits.

members.legal_issue: An appellate decree that supersedes a trial court decree is the operative decree for determining when the decree was passed.
material_facts: A preliminary decree was passed by the trial court before the debt-relief law came into force.
Appeals from that decree were pending when the debt-relief law came into force.

The appellate court later issued a preliminary decree that modified the relief granted to some defendants and affirmed the decree against the applicant, and a final decree was subsequently passed on that basis.
members.legal_principle: On appeal, the appellate decree becomes the operative decree and the decree below merges in it. The Court relied on Jowad Hussain v. Gendan Singh, which approved Gajadhar Singh v. Kishan Jiwan Lal on the effect of an appellate decree in mortgage proceedings, and on The Collector of Customs, Calcutta v. The East India Commercial Co. Ltd. for the principle that the appellate order is operative after the appeal is disposed of.
members.conclusion: The trial court decrees were superseded, and the appellate preliminary decree, made final by the later final decree, was the operative decree.

predicates.appeal_from_preliminary_mortgage_decree: The proceeding was an appeal from a preliminary decree in a mortgage suit.
predicates.appellate_court_issued_decree_supersedin: The appellate court issued a decree that replaced or modified the trial court decree.

members.legal_issue: A decree for specific performance that is affirmed on appeal merges into the appellate decree, which is the operative decree for execution.
material_facts: Both sides appealed the trial court’s decree for specific performance, and the appellate court dismissed both appeals while affirming the decree.
The decree-holder sought execution, and the judgment debtor objected that the balance had not been paid within the period stated in the trial court’s decree.
The appellate court decided the appeals before the decree-holder deposited the balance of the sale consideration.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger means that, after an appellate court decides a matter on the merits, its decree is the single operative decree, whether it affirms, modifies or reverses the decree below. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v State of Kerala, Chandi Prasad v Jagdish Prasad, Khoday Distilleries Ltd v Sri Mahadeshwara Sahakara Sakkare Karkhane Ltd, and Shanthi v T D Vishwanathan. Order 41 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that an appeal does not by itself stay execution, but that does not prevent merger when the appeal is decided.
members.conclusion: The trial court’s decree merged into the appellate decree, and the decree-holder’s right to execute the appellate decree could not be defeated on the ground that the trial court’s payment period had elapsed.

predicates.specific_performance_execution: A party is seeking execution of a decree for specific performance.
predicates.appeal_decided_on_merits: An appellate court has decided an appeal concerning the decree on its merits.

members.legal_issue: A trial judgment appealed to and decided by a higher court merges into the appellate judgment, whose determination defines the scope of the earlier suit.
material_facts: A trial court decided an earlier suit concerning the mill as movable property.
An appeal was taken, and the appellate court held that the earlier suit concerned the mill, not the land and building in which it stood.
members.legal_principle: Under the doctrine of merger, once a trial judgment is appealed and the appellate court gives judgment, the appellate judgment is operative. The scope of the earlier litigation is determined from that appellate judgment.
members.conclusion: The trial court's judgment merged into the appellate judgment, and the earlier suit was confined to the mill as movable property.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_judgment: A party appealed a trial court's judgment.
predicates.appellate_judgment_given: The appellate court gave judgment on the appeal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate decree that varies the trial court’s decision on the merits is not a decree of affirmance, even when the variation favors the party seeking further appeal.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the suit after holding that the challenged alienations bound the claimant’s share.
The appellate court held that some alienations did not bind the claimant’s share and granted partition relief for the affected property, while confirming the rest of the trial court’s decree.
The claimant sought a certificate to appeal further, and the appellate court refused it on the ground that its decree was one of affirmance.
The required valuation criterion was satisfied.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 133(1) of the Constitution, the appellate decree must be compared as a whole with the trial court’s decision as a whole. A merits variation means the decree is not one of affirmance, regardless of the variation’s extent or whether it favors the proposed appellant. The Court relied on the plain reading of the provision and the Privy Council decisions in Rajah Tasadduq Rasul Khan v. Manik Chand and Annapurnabai v. Ruprao; it rejected a part-by-part approach and held that the valuation and substantial-question-of-law requirements do not alter this construction.
members.conclusion: The appellate decree was not a decree of affirmance because it varied the trial court’s decision on the merits in the claimant’s favor. The refusal of the certificate was set aside and the matter was remitted for disposal according to law.

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: A party seeks further appellate review of a decree made in a civil proceeding.
predicates.merits_variation_by_adjudication: The appellate court changes the trial court’s decision on the merits through its adjudication, whether the change is small or large and whether it favors or disadvantages the party seeking further appeal.
predicates.appellate_decree_not_one_of_affirmance: The appellate decree is not characterized as affirming the trial court’s decision.

members.legal_issue: Whether an appellate decree is one of affirmance when it changes the trial court’s decision on the merits, including by a change in favour of the party seeking a further appeal.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed a suit for a share of family properties after upholding the challenged alienations.
The appellate court held some alienations not binding on the plaintiff’s share and granted partition relief for the affected properties, while confirming the trial court’s decree as to the rest.
The plaintiff sought a certificate to appeal further, and the High Court refused it on the ground that its decree was one of affirmance.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 133(1) of the Constitution, the words concerning a decree that affirms the decision below refer to the appellate decree and trial court decision taken as wholes; “appealed from” is descriptive, not a limitation to the portion challenged in a further appeal. The natural meaning of “decision” is the decision of the suit as a whole, consistent with Rajah Tasadduq Rasul Khan v. Manik Chand. The Court disapproved the approach in Chittam Subba Rao v. Vela Mankanni Chellamayya and discussed Annapurnabai v. Ruprao as supporting the conclusion that a variation in favour of the intending appellant prevents the decree from being one of affirmance.
members.conclusion: An appellate decree must be compared as a whole with the trial court’s decision as a whole. A merits variation makes it a decree of variation, whether the variation is minor or major and whether it favours or disfavors the party seeking the further appeal. The refusal of the certificate was set aside and the matter remitted to the High Court for disposal according to law.

rule.if: constitutional_civil_appeal and appellate_court_adjudicated_a_merits_variation and not variation_is_only_costs and not variation_is_by_concession_consent_or_withdrawal

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_adjudicated_a_merits_var: The appellate court changed the trial court’s decision through its adjudication of the merits.
predicates.variation_is_only_costs: The only change made by the appellate court concerns costs.
predicates.variation_is_by_concession_consent_or_wi: The change resulted from a concession, the parties’ consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter rather than the appellate court’s decision on the merits.

members.legal_issue: An appellate decree is not one of affirmance when, considered as a whole against the trial court’s decision as a whole, it varies that decision, even if the variation benefits the prospective appellant.
material_facts: The trial court decreed ejectment and awarded a sum for recovery.
The High Court set aside the ejectment decree and reduced the amount awarded.
Those changes benefited the appellants who sought to appeal to the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The character of an appellate decree is determined by comparing the appellate decree in its entirety with the decision below as a whole. Whether a variation favours or disadvantages the intending appellant is irrelevant. The Court followed Tirumalachetti Rajaram v. Tirumalachetti Radhakrishnayya Chetty.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment did not affirm the trial court’s decision, despite the changes being in the appellants’ favour.

predicates.appeal_compares_appellate_and_trial_decr: The appeal requires the appellate decree to be characterized by comparison with the decision below.
predicates.appellate_decree_varies_from_trial_decis: The appellate decree, considered as a whole, changes the decision below in at least one respect.

members.legal_issue: When a statutory appeal is entertained and decided on its merits, the limitation period for executing the decree runs from the appellate decree that supersedes the lower-court decree.
material_facts: A final decree was made in a partition suit, and an appeal against it was entertained and ultimately dismissed on its merits.
A formal decree following the appellate decision was drawn, and an execution application was filed within twelve years of that decree.
The judgment debtors challenged execution as time-barred, and the lower courts rejected that challenge.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period for execution begins when the decree becomes enforceable. A decree under Section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure may be passed by a trial or appellate court. When a statutory appeal is entertained and decided on its merits, the appellate decree merges with and supersedes the lower-court decree whether it affirms, modifies or reverses it; this applies even where the appeal is a second appeal. The court relied on U.J.S. Chopra v. State of Bombay, V.M. Salgaocar and Bros. Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala. It distinguished Ratansingh v. Vijay Singh, where an appeal dismissed as time-barred produced no decree and the doctrine of merger did not apply. Article 182 of the former Limitation Act and Section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure were discussed in explaining the change to the present limitation scheme.
members.conclusion: The appellate decree superseded the lower-court decree, and the execution application was not barred by limitation; the appeal challenging that result was dismissed.

predicates.execution_limitation_dispute: A party disputes whether an application to enforce a decree was filed within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.statutory_appeal_decided_on_merits: A statutory appeal concerning the decree was entertained and decided on its merits, rather than rejected solely as late.
predicates.formal_appellate_decree_drawn: A formal decree was drawn following the appellate court's decision.

members.legal_issue: For execution limitation, an appellate decree that supersedes the lower-court decree is enforceable from its own date, and a later appeal dismissed as time-barred without a decree on the merits does not restart or alter that period.
material_facts: A trial court granted a decree for possession, and the first appellate court dismissed the appeal against it, thereby passing the appellate decree.
A second appeal was dismissed as time-barred after the request to condone delay was refused; no decree was passed in that appeal.
The decree-holder filed the execution application more than twelve years after the first appellate decree became enforceable.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a twelve-year period running from when a decree becomes enforceable. Unlike former Article 182 of the Limitation Act, 1908, Article 136 does not make the filing or dismissal of an appeal a separate starting point. An appeal does not affect enforceability unless its operation is stayed; when an appeal results in a decree, that decree supersedes the lower-court decree and becomes the enforceable decree. When an appeal is dismissed as time-barred without a decree, the lower-court decree remains unaffected. The Court considered the change from former Article 182, the former Section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the explanatory objects and reasons for Article 136. It noted Anandilal v. Ram Narain on broad construction of limitation provisions, while emphasizing that hardship is not a basis to disregard limitation, and found Nagendra Nath Dey inapplicable because it concerned former Article 182.
members.conclusion: The first appellate decree remained enforceable, and the execution application filed more than twelve years after it became enforceable was barred by limitation.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and appellate_decree_superseded_lower_decree and later_appeal_rejected_without_merits and execution_started_after_limitation_period

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder sought to enforce a civil court decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.appellate_decree_superseded_lower_decree: An appellate court decided an appeal by a decree that replaced the lower-court decree as the enforceable decree.
predicates.later_appeal_rejected_without_merits: A later appeal was rejected as late without a decree being made on its merits.
predicates.execution_started_after_limitation_perio: The decree-holder filed for execution after the applicable limitation period had run from when the enforceable decree became enforceable.

members.legal_issue: An appeal concerning a collateral proceeding does not start a fresh limitation period for execution of a decree when the appeal is not from the decree or order sought to be executed.
material_facts: A final mortgage decree was passed, and no appeal was taken from that decree.
The judgment-debtor appealed the dismissal of an application to restore the proceeding seeking to reopen the preliminary decree.
That appeal was dismissed for non-prosecution.
The decree-holder applied to execute the final decree more than three years after it was passed.
members.legal_principle: Article 182, clause 2, of the Limitation Act, 1908, must be read with the article's description of applications for execution of a decree or order. An appeal starts a fresh limitation period only when it is connected directly or immediately with the decree or order sought to be executed; an appeal from an order in a collateral proceeding does not suffice. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The appeal from the order in the collateral proceeding did not provide a fresh starting point for limitation under Article 182, clause 2, of the Limitation Act, 1908; the execution application was time-barred.

predicates.execution_application: A decree-holder applied to execute a decree.
predicates.appeal_from_collateral_proceeding: A party appealed an order made in a proceeding related to, but collateral to, the decree sought to be executed.
predicates.appeal_not_from_decree_sought_to_be_exec: The appeal was not from the decree or order for which execution was sought.

members.legal_issue: A decree in a separate proceeding concerning a third party’s title does not provide a fresh starting point for limitation when it leaves the decree sought to be executed unchanged.
material_facts: The decree-holder sought to execute a foreclosure decree against the judgment debtor.
In a separate suit, the judgment debtor’s son obtained a declaration that the foreclosure decree did not bind him as to his half share and an injunction preventing execution against that share.
The separate proceeding did not reverse, vary, or amend the foreclosure decree as it applied to the judgment debtor.
members.legal_principle: Under clauses 1, 2, and 4 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act 1908, a fresh starting point arises from the decree being executed, an appeal concerning that decree, or an amendment of that decree. A decision in a collateral proceeding that leaves the decree unchanged does not qualify. The Court relied on Bhawanipore Banking Corporation Ltd. v. Gori Shanker Sharma.
members.conclusion: The separate suit’s appellate decree did not provide a fresh starting point for limitation under clauses 1, 2, or 4 of Article 182.

predicates.execution_limitation_case: A decree-holder applies to execute a decree and limitation is disputed.
predicates.separate_proceeding_concerns_third_party: A separate proceeding determines a third party’s rights in property covered by the decree.
predicates.original_execution_decree_unchanged: The separate proceeding does not reverse, vary, or amend the decree as it applies to the judgment debtor.

members.legal_issue: A change confined to costs does not prevent an appellate decree from being treated as a decree of affirmance.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished costs, which are within the court’s discretion under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure, from matters forming part of the dispute between the parties. A costs-only variation does not make the appellate decree one other than affirmance.
members.conclusion: A variation in the costs order alone does not alter the character of an appellate decree that otherwise affirms the trial court’s decision.

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: A party seeks further appellate review of a decree made in a civil proceeding.
predicates.underlying_decision_confirmed: The appellate court confirms the trial court’s decision on the matters in dispute.
predicates.only_costs_order_varied: The appellate court changes only the order as to costs.
predicates.appellate_decree_is_one_of_affirmance: The appellate decree is characterized as affirming the trial court’s decision.

members.legal_issue: Whether a change confined to costs changes an appellate decree that otherwise affirms the trial court’s decision.
material_facts: The Court considered how a change to the costs order affects the character of an appellate decree that otherwise confirms the trial court’s decision.
Costs are within the court’s discretion under the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court discretion over costs; a costs-only variation is not a variation of the decision on the merits for purposes of the affirmance test under Article 133(1) of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: A change confined to costs does not change the character of an appellate decree that is otherwise one of affirmance.

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.appellate_decree_otherwise_affirms_trial: Apart from the costs order, the appellate decree confirms the trial court’s decision.
predicates.variation_is_only_costs: The only change made by the appellate court concerns costs.

members.legal_issue: A merits-related variation in an award of interest prevents an appellate decree from being treated as a decree of affirmance.
members.legal_principle: Unlike costs, interest awarded under section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure can form part of the dispute between the parties. A variation in that part of the decision is therefore a relevant variation for determining whether the appellate decree affirms the trial court’s decision.
members.conclusion: A variation concerning interest that forms part of the dispute between the parties affects the character of the appellate decree and means it is not one of affirmance.

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: A party seeks further appellate review of a decree made in a civil proceeding.
predicates.adjudicated_interest_variation: The appellate court adjudicates a change to an award of interest that forms part of the dispute between the parties.
predicates.appellate_decree_not_one_of_affirmance: The appellate decree is not characterized as affirming the trial court’s decision.

members.legal_issue: Whether a change to an award of interest affects the character of an appellate decree as one of affirmance.
material_facts: The Court distinguished interest from costs, explaining that interest forms part of the dispute between the parties.
The appellate court can award interest under the Code of Civil Procedure, and a change to that award can vary the decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, interest forms part of the dispute between the parties; a change to the interest award is therefore an integral variation of the decision for purposes of Article 133(1) of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: A change to the award of interest affects the character of the appellate decree and makes it a decree of variation rather than affirmance.

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_changed_interest_awarded: The appellate court changed the interest award that formed part of the dispute between the parties.

members.legal_issue: A variation resulting from concession, consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter does not affect whether an appellate decree is one of affirmance.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of affirmance concerns the appellate court’s decision on the merits. A change that does not result from appellate adjudication on the merits is not a merits variation for this purpose.
members.conclusion: A variation made because of a concession, the parties’ consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter does not affect the character of the appellate decree.

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: A party seeks further appellate review of a decree made in a civil proceeding.
predicates.underlying_decision_confirmed: The appellate court confirms the trial court’s decision on the matters in dispute.
predicates.variation_due_to_concession_consent_or_w: Any change in the appellate decree results from a party’s concession, the parties’ consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter, rather than adjudication on the merits.
predicates.appellate_decree_is_one_of_affirmance: The appellate decree is characterized as affirming the trial court’s decision.

members.legal_issue: Whether a change resulting from concession, consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter changes the character of an appellate decree.
material_facts: The Court considered changes made because a party conceded a point, the parties consented to a change, or part of the subject matter covered by the decree was withdrawn.
Such a change does not result from the appellate court’s adjudication of the appeal on the merits.
members.legal_principle: The affirmance test under Article 133(1) of the Constitution concerns the appellate court’s decision on the merits; a change made by concession or consent, or following withdrawal of part of the subject matter, is not a merits variation by the appellate court.
members.conclusion: A change resulting from concession, consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter does not affect the character of the appellate decree.

predicates.constitutional_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the character of an appellate decree matters to a further appeal.
predicates.change_results_from_concession_consent_o: The change resulted from a concession, the parties’ consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter.

members.legal_issue: The statutory time limits and consequences of default in the general land-acquisition law do not apply to an acquisition carried out under a self-contained planned-development statute when importing them would undermine that statute’s scheme.
material_facts: The appeal concerned land included in an acquisition initiated for a development scheme under a state development statute.
The appellant argued that the acquisition had lapsed because the award was made beyond the period prescribed by the general land-acquisition law.
The state statute provided its own scheme for planned development, specified when a scheme would lapse, and applied the general land-acquisition law only so far as its provisions were applicable.
The Court found that importing the general law’s acquisition deadlines and consequences of default could frustrate the planned-development scheme.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 27 and 36 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, the state statute provides a self-contained scheme and applies the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 only so far as its provisions are applicable. Provisions concerning acquisition, compensation and legal remedies may apply where the state statute has no corresponding provisions, but its own scheme and consequences of default exclude incompatible deadlines and lapse provisions such as Section 11A. This approach follows Land Acquisition Officer, City Improvement Trust Board v. H. Narayanaiah, Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka and Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, and is consistent with Girnar Traders III.
members.conclusion: The general law’s time limits and consequences of default, including the provision for lapse of acquisition, cannot be read into acquisitions under the state development statute; the general law’s provision requiring an award within a specified period therefore does not apply.

predicates.acquisition_for_planned_development: The public authority undertook the acquisition as part of a statutory planned-development scheme.
predicates.state_statute_has_its_own_scheme_and_def: The state development statute sets out its own scheme and specifies consequences for failure to carry it out.
predicates.imported_deadline_would_frustrate_the_sc: Applying a deadline from the general acquisition law would undermine or frustrate the state development scheme.

members.legal_issue: The general acquisition statute’s award deadline does not apply to acquisitions conducted under a self-contained development scheme with its own provisions governing lapse.
material_facts: The land was acquired as part of a sanctioned scheme to develop a planned layout under a development-authority enactment.
That enactment provided its own acquisition procedure and stated when failure to execute a scheme would cause the scheme to lapse and acquisition powers to become inoperative.
The award was made after the deadline in Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984.
The development-authority enactment did not expressly adopt that later award deadline, and the scheme could operate without importing it.
members.legal_principle: The Court affirmed Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, which construed Sections 17, 18, 27 and 36 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act alongside the Land Acquisition Act. The development-authority enactment is a special, self-contained law primarily concerned with planned development, with land acquisition incidental to that purpose; its own lapse provision governs. The later amendments to the Land Acquisition Act are not imported absent express language or necessary implication. The Court applied the principles on referential legislation and incorporation in State of M.P. v. M.V. Narasimhan and U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Jainul Islam, and distinguished Mariyappa v. State of Karnataka, which concerned a different enactment that depended on the Land Acquisition Act. It also found no basis in Special Land Acquisition Officer v. P. Govindan or Land Acquisition Officer v. H. Narayanaiah to apply the later award deadline to this distinct statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: Sections 6 and 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, do not apply to acquisitions under the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976; the acquisition therefore did not lapse because the award was made after the Section 11-A deadline.

rule.if: development_scheme_acquisition_proceeding and acquisition_is_incidental_to_planned_development and framework_is_self_contained and framework_has_its_own_lapse_conditions and not framework_adopts_general_award_deadline

predicates.development_scheme_acquisition_proceedin: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land under a development scheme administered by a development authority.
predicates.acquisition_is_incidental_to_planned_dev: The enactment principally provides for planned development, and acquiring land is incidental to that purpose.
predicates.framework_is_self_contained: The enactment provides a distinct and substantially complete procedure for the acquisition involved.
predicates.framework_has_its_own_lapse_conditions: The enactment specifies the circumstances in which failure to carry out the scheme causes it or the related acquisition powers to lapse.
predicates.framework_adopts_general_award_deadline: The enactment expressly or by necessary implication adopts the general acquisition law’s deadline for making an award.

members.legal_issue: The time limit for making an award and the resulting lapse of acquisition proceedings under the central acquisition enactment do not apply to acquisitions governed by the state planning enactment.
material_facts: The reference arose from acquisition of land reserved under a development plan, following a declaration made under the state planning enactment in the manner specified by the central acquisition enactment.
The landowner contended that the central enactment's award deadline applied and that the acquisition had lapsed because the award was made after that deadline.
The planning enactment contained its own timeframes and consequences for specified defaults, including provisions addressing lapse of reservations.
The planning enactment made specific references to parts of the central enactment rather than a general adoption of all its provisions.
The Court concluded that importing the central enactment's award deadline would disrupt the planning enactment's scheme and could frustrate planned development.
members.legal_principle: The planning enactment is a self-contained code with specific timeframes and consequences of default; the central enactment is referred to for limited purposes, not generally adopted. Referential legislation must be interpreted in light of the later law's object, legislative intent, and workability. The Court relied on the distinction between legislation by incorporation and legislation by reference discussed in Secretary of State for India in Council v. Hindusthan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd., Ujagar Prints v. Union of India, and M.V. Narasimhan, as well as on Sant Joginder Singh Kishan Singh v. State of Maharashtra, which it affirmed as correct in result for reasons other than its procedural-substantive distinction.
members.conclusion: The central enactment's award deadline and its consequence of lapse cannot be read into acquisitions under the planning enactment.

predicates.planning_development_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns acquisition undertaken to carry out a plan under a planning law.
predicates.planning_law_sets_its_own_default_conseq: The planning law specifies its own timeframes and consequences for defaults in the planning and acquisition process.
predicates.central_law_is_referred_to_for_specific_: The planning law refers to particular parts or purposes of another enactment rather than adopting that enactment generally.
predicates.importing_external_award_deadline_would_: Applying the other enactment's award deadline and lapse consequence would frustrate or materially impair the planning law's scheme.

members.legal_issue: Time limits and lapse consequences in the general land acquisition law do not govern the preliminary and final stages of acquisition under a self-contained planned-development law when that law provides its own scheme.
material_facts: A development authority issued a preliminary notification to acquire land for a planned urban layout.
The final declaration had not been issued for several years, and landowners argued that the acquisition should lapse by applying time limits from the general land acquisition law.
The planned-development statute contained its own acquisition procedure and consequences for failure to implement a scheme.
members.legal_principle: The planned-development statute is a self-contained code. Under sections 15–19 and 27 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976, read with section 36, provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 apply only insofar as applicable; its distinct time limits and default consequences, including sections 6 and 11A, do not become part of the planned-development statute. The Court relied on Offshore Holdings Private Limited v. Bangalore Development Authority (2011) 3 SCC 139, which approved the self-contained-code principle in Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka (2002) 4 SCC 326 and considered Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority (2010) 7 SCC 129.
members.conclusion: The general land acquisition law’s time limits, including the provisions governing the time for a declaration and lapse of acquisition, could not be imported into the planned-development statute. The authority’s acquisition was governed by that statute’s own scheme, including its provisions concerning implementation and default.

predicates.planned_development_acquisition: A public authority undertook land acquisition as an incident of carrying out planned development.
predicates.special_law_has_its_own_acquisition_sche: The law governing the development project provided its own acquisition procedure and consequences for default.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_general_acquisition_: A party sought to invalidate or lapse the acquisition by relying on time limits in the general land acquisition law.

members.legal_issue: A time limit imposed by the Land Acquisition Act for its own final declaration did not invalidate a final declaration made under a separate acquisition procedure in a development-authority law.
material_facts: The development-authority law contained its own procedure for a preliminary notification and a final declaration.
The final declaration was published a few days more than one year after publication of the preliminary notification.
The development-authority law applied the Land Acquisition Act only so far as its provisions were applicable and used that Act for stages not covered by its own procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 36 of the development-authority law applies the Land Acquisition Act only so far as applicable. Where the development-authority law itself provides for the relevant acquisition stages, the corresponding provisions of the Land Acquisition Act do not apply. Accordingly, the time limit in section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act did not govern a final declaration made under the development-authority law. The court relied on Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, which treated the development-authority law as a special and self-contained code.
members.conclusion: The final declaration was not invalid merely because it was published more than one year after the preliminary notification.

predicates.development_authority_acquisition: The acquisition was undertaken as part of a development scheme under a law governing a development authority.
predicates.governing_law_has_its_own_preliminary_an: The law governing the development authority prescribed its own procedure for preliminary notification and final declaration.
predicates.land_acquisition_act_applies_only_to_unp: The governing law adopted the general acquisition law only for acquisition stages that its own provisions did not address.

members.legal_issue: A statutory deadline for making an acquisition award does not apply merely because substantive compensation principles from the general acquisition law apply to an acquisition under a separate enactment.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeded under a state enactment that expressly incorporated certain provisions of the general acquisition law.
The state enactment did not expressly incorporate the general law's award-making deadline, which was introduced by a later amendment.
In one appeal, the award had not been made within the period specified by that general-law deadline.
The Court accepted that compensation could be determined using the substantive principles governing compensation in the general acquisition law.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished substantive compensation rules from procedural rules governing the time for making an award. It applied the compensation principles in section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, by necessary implication, but held that section 11A was not incorporated into the state enactment. Where provisions of an earlier enactment are incorporated, later amendments to that enactment do not become part of the incorporating enactment unless made applicable; incorporation differs from adoption by reference. The Court relied on Gauri Shankar Gaur v. State of U.P., 1994 (1) SCC 92.
members.conclusion: The award-making deadline in the general acquisition law did not apply to these acquisitions, and the failure to make an award within that period did not cause the acquisition notice to lapse. Applying substantive compensation principles did not import the separate procedural deadline.

rule.if: special_enactment_acquisition_proceeding and award_period_elapsed and selected_general_acquisition_provisions_incorporated and award_deadline_not_incorporated

predicates.special_enactment_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding seeks acquisition under a separate enactment rather than directly under the general acquisition law.
predicates.award_period_elapsed: The period allowed for making an award under the general acquisition law passed before an award was made.
predicates.selected_general_acquisition_provisions_: The separate enactment expressly made some provisions of the general acquisition law part of its own scheme.
predicates.award_deadline_not_incorporated: The separate enactment did not expressly make the general law's award-making deadline applicable to its acquisitions.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment imposing a time limit for making the declaration step in the general acquisition process does not apply to acquisitions under the town-improvement statutes after the acquisition law has been incorporated into those statutes.
material_facts: The relevant notices initiating the acquisitions were followed by declaration-equivalent notices more than three years later.
The challenged acquisitions proceeded under the Nagpur and Uttar Pradesh town-improvement enactments.
The time limit relied on had been added to the general acquisition law after the local enactments were made.
members.legal_principle: As the acquisition law had been incorporated into the local enactments, later amendments to it did not ordinarily affect acquisitions under those enactments. The Court applied the incorporation principles in U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Jainul Islam and State of Madhya Pradesh v. M.V. Narasimhan.
members.conclusion: The later time-limit amendment did not govern the acquisitions, and the declaration-equivalent notices were not invalid merely because they were issued more than three years after the initiating notices.

predicates.town_improvement_acquisition: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition under a town-improvement enactment that adopts the general acquisition law.
predicates.declaration_step_follows_initiating_noti: The local acquisition process uses a later declaration-equivalent step after an initiating notice.
predicates.relied_on_time_limit_was_added_after_loc: The asserted deadline was introduced into the general acquisition law after the local enactment was made.

members.legal_issue: The time-based lapse provisions of the general land acquisition laws do not cause an acquisition under a special industrial development law to lapse where the land vests by final declaration independently of an award.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeded under a special industrial development law, under which land vested in the State upon publication of the final declaration.
No compensation award was made for the owners’ land, and the owners did not receive the compensation.
The authorities deposited compensation in court in light of a dispute about who was entitled to receive it.
The High Court applied the later general land acquisition law’s lapse provision to quash the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: Sections 28(4) and 28(5) of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act provide for vesting upon publication of the final declaration, independently of an award. Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not apply to acquisitions under that special law, as held in M. Nagabhushana v. State of Karnataka, (2011) 3 SCC 408. The Court relied on the related reasoning in Pratap v. State of Rajasthan, (1996) 3 SCC 1; Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, (2002) 4 SCC 326; Offshore Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Bangalore Development Authority, (2011) 3 SCC 139; and Girnar Traders (3) v. State of Maharashtra, (2011) 3 SCC 1. Because the special law is a self-contained code and the general law’s award-time provision does not apply, Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 does not make such an acquisition lapse. The Court also applied the incorporation principle in State of M.P. v. M.V. Narasimhan, (1975) 2 SCC 377; it distinguished Mariyappa v. State of Karnataka, (1998) 3 SCC 276, because the legislation there was not a self-contained code.
members.conclusion: The acquisition had not lapsed under the general land acquisition laws; the High Court’s decision quashing it was set aside.

predicates.acquisition_under_special_industrial_law: The proceeding is an acquisition of land under a special law governing development of industrial areas.
predicates.land_vested_on_final_declaration: The governing law made the land vest in the State upon publication of the final declaration, independently of an award.
predicates.award_not_made: The authority had not made an award determining compensation for the land.

members.legal_issue: The absence of an award within the period prescribed for awards under the general land acquisition law does not lapse an acquisition under a separate enactment when that enactment provides for vesting on publication of the acquisition declaration.
material_facts: The appellant contended that the acquisition had lapsed because no award was made within two years of the acquisition notification.
Under the applicable enactment, publication of the acquisition declaration vested the land in the State free from encumbrances.
The applicable enactment did not make vesting dependent on an award, and the Court treated it as a self-contained code with purposes distinct from the general land acquisition law.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the vesting mechanism under Sections 28(4) and 28(5) of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act from vesting under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Where the special enactment provides that land vests on publication of the declaration, vesting does not depend on an award and the award-period provision in Section 11A of the 1894 Act does not cause the acquisition to lapse. The Court relied on Pratap v. State of Rajasthan, Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, Offshore Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Bangalore Development Authority, and Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra. It distinguished Mariyappa v. State of Karnataka because the enactment considered there was not a self-contained code and was supplemental to the general acquisition law.
members.conclusion: The award-period provision in the general land acquisition law did not apply to the acquisition, which had vested on publication of the declaration, and the acquisition had not lapsed for want of an award within that period.

predicates.special_statutory_acquisition: The proceeding concerns acquisition under a special statutory enactment rather than acquisition solely under the general land acquisition law.
predicates.declaration_publication_vests_land_indep: The special enactment provides that publication of the acquisition declaration vests the land without requiring an award.

members.legal_issue: Once a special acquisition scheme governs land required for its specified purpose, the State cannot acquire that land for the same purpose under the general acquisition law.
material_facts: Land was sought to be acquired under the general acquisition law for a purpose covered by the special acquisition scheme after that scheme had come into force.
The special scheme provided that land required for its specified purpose could be acquired only under its own provisions.
The special scheme was held valid apart from its requirement for payment of compensation in instalments.
members.legal_principle: The exclusivity provision of the special acquisition scheme displaced the general acquisition law for land required for the specified purpose. Because the special scheme remained valid apart from its severed instalment-payment requirement, acquisition for that purpose had to proceed under the special scheme.
members.conclusion: The proceedings under the general acquisition law were quashed because the valid special scheme precluded acquisition for the covered purpose under that law.

predicates.special_acquisition_scheme_is_in_force: A valid special statutory acquisition scheme governs the relevant kind of land acquisition.
predicates.land_is_required_for_purpose_covered_by_: The land is required for a purpose specified in the special scheme.
predicates.general_law_acquisition_is_started_for_t: The State starts or continues acquisition under the general process for that specified purpose.

members.legal_issue: Once a special acquisition law governs land required for its specified welfare purpose, the land cannot instead be acquired for that purpose under the general acquisition law.
material_facts: After the special acquisition law had commenced, the State sought to acquire land under the general acquisition law for the welfare scheme.
The special law provided that land required for that purpose could be acquired only in accordance with its provisions.
The landowner sought to stop the proceedings under the general acquisition law.
members.legal_principle: The special law made its acquisition process exclusive for land required for the specified welfare purpose, displacing the general acquisition law for that purpose.
members.conclusion: The proceedings under the general acquisition law were quashed because the special law governed acquisition for that purpose.

predicates.challenge_to_an_acquisition_proceeding_u: A landowner challenges an acquisition proceeding brought under a general acquisition regime.
predicates.land_is_sought_for_a_purpose_governed_by: The land is being acquired for a purpose covered by a special acquisition regime that is in force.
predicates.special_regime_requires_exclusive_use_of: The special regime requires land acquired for that purpose to be acquired only through its own procedure.

members.legal_issue: The State’s general power to acquire land does not permit it to bypass mandatory procedures governing a scheme implemented under a special planning statute.
material_facts: The State sought to acquire land to implement a new-town scheme governed by the planning statute.
The State relied on its general acquisition power despite the absence of the planning statute’s required declaration of a planning area.
The State had not called on the planning board to select a site, and another authority undertook that task instead.
members.legal_principle: The State’s power of eminent domain does not displace the procedure prescribed by the Punjab Regional and Town Planning and Development Act, 1995 when acquisition is sought to implement a scheme under that Act. Section 42 permits acquisition on the authority’s request for the authority’s purposes, while Sections 14 and 56 provide for the Board’s role in selecting and declaring a planning area. Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 2 SCC 662, and the cases following it, were distinguishable because the Rajasthan statute allowed acquisition on broader terms, including otherwise than on an authority’s request.
members.conclusion: For this acquisition under the new-town scheme, the State had to follow the planning statute’s mandatory procedure and could not rely on its general acquisition power to avoid it.

predicates.acquisition_challenge: A party challenges an acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_under_special_planning_schem: The acquisition is sought to implement a development scheme governed by a special planning framework.
predicates.mandatory_planning_procedure_bypassed: The State proceeds with acquisition without following a procedure required for the scheme under that framework.

members.legal_issue: A transferee cannot rely on the protection for transfers by an ostensible owner without proof that the true owners consented to that person appearing to be the owner and that the transferee took reasonable care to ascertain the authority to transfer.
material_facts: The eldest son mortgaged the entire property as though he were its full owner, although other heirs held beneficial shares.
The other co-sharers permitted him to manage the common property, and the property was recorded in his name.
There was no evidence that the co-sharers had put him forward as the ostensible owner of the entire property.
An enquiry by the mortgagee would have disclosed that he was not the full owner.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act requires proof that the transferor was the ostensible owner with the consent, express or implied, of the persons interested in the property, and that the transferee took reasonable care to ascertain the transferor’s power to transfer and acted in good faith. Permitting a co-sharer to manage common property does not, by itself, create an estoppel or establish that consent.
members.conclusion: The protection under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act did not assist the transferee; management by one co-sharer and an entry in his name did not establish that the others consented to his being held out as full owner, and the required reasonable enquiry was not made.

rule.if: transfer_by_apparent_full_owner and co_owners_have_interests and not co_owners_held_transferor_out_as_full_owner and reasonable_inquiry_would_reveal_limited_title

predicates.transfer_by_apparent_full_owner: A person transfers or mortgages property while appearing to claim full ownership.
predicates.co_owners_have_interests: Other persons hold interests in the property.
predicates.co_owners_held_transferor_out_as_full_ow: The other interest-holders put forward or consented to the transferor appearing to be the full owner.
predicates.reasonable_inquiry_would_reveal_limited_: A reasonable enquiry by the transferee would disclose that the transferor does not own the entire interest.

members.legal_issue: A transferee invoking the protection for a transfer by an ostensible owner must prove the conditions for that protection, and a transferee who knows that the transferor's title is defective cannot establish good faith.
material_facts: The purchaser and transferor belonged to the same village.
The transferor sold the land on the day he was required to appear before revenue authorities considering a challenge to the recorded ownership.
Although the sale deed was executed earlier, the purchaser paid most of the consideration three years later.
The purchaser obtained an indemnity bond from the transferor against loss concerning the land.
These circumstances showed that the purchaser knew the transferor's title was disputed and took a risk in purchasing the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act is an exception to the general rule that a person cannot transfer a better title than that person possesses. The transferee bears the burden of proving that the transferor was the ostensible owner with the consent of the persons interested in the property, and that the transferee took reasonable care to ascertain the transferor's power to transfer and acted in good faith. Knowledge that the transferor's title is disputed is inconsistent with good faith.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser in good faith and could not rely on the ostensible-owner exception to establish title to the whole property.

predicates.ostensible_owner_protection_claimed: A transferee seeks protection for a transfer made by someone who appeared to be the owner.
predicates.transferee_knew_transferor_title_was_def: The transferee knew that the transferor's title was disputed or defective when acquiring the property.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot rely on the protection for a transfer by an ostensible owner when reasonable care would have disclosed that the transferor lacked authority to sell.
material_facts: The purchaser relied on transfers made through an agent whose power of attorney contained no express power of sale.
The document expressly authorized other property-related acts, making the absence of sale authority apparent on examination.
The Court agreed that reasonable care would have disclosed the lack of authority.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 protects a transfer by an ostensible owner only where the statutory requirements are met, including that the transferee takes reasonable care to ascertain the transferor’s power and acts in good faith. A purchaser who could readily discover from the authority document that the agent had no power of sale has not satisfied the reasonable-care requirement.
members.conclusion: The purchaser could not claim protection under the rule for transfers by ostensible owners.

predicates.ostensible_owner_transfer: A person appearing to own immovable property transferred it for consideration.
predicates.authority_document_lacked_sale_power: The document relied on as authority for the transfer did not authorize a sale.
predicates.purchaser_failed_reasonable_inquiry: The purchaser did not take reasonable care to check the transferor’s authority, although the lack of authority could readily have been discovered.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot rely on the rule protecting a transferee from an ostensible owner when the purchaser relied on the transferor’s title rather than a representation by the true owner.
material_facts: The purchasers bought the lands from the government after the government had acquired them through the nominal-bid transactions.
The purchasers relied on their belief that the government had acquired title through those transactions.
The purchasers did not rely on any representation, act, or conduct by the original owner that the government was the owner.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act has no application where the transferee did not rely on a representation, act, or conduct of the person whose title is challenged. If the transferor had no title to convey, the transferee could not acquire title on the basis of a belief that the transferor owned the property.
members.conclusion: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act did not protect the purchasers or prevent the original owner from challenging their title.

rule.if: transfer_from_ostensible_owner and purchaser_reliance_on_transferor_title and not true_owner_representation

predicates.transfer_from_ostensible_owner: A person transfers property while appearing to hold ownership without having acquired valid title.
predicates.purchaser_reliance_on_transferor_title: The purchaser relies on the transferor’s apparent title rather than on conduct by the true owner.
predicates.true_owner_representation: The true owner made a representation, or engaged in conduct, that the transferor owned the property.
predicates.ostensible_owner_protection_does_not_app: The protection for a transferee from an ostensible owner does not apply.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who represents that another person exclusively owns property and may deal with it, thereby inducing a purchaser to proceed with a sale, may be estopped from later asserting an interest in that property.
material_facts: After her husband’s death, the claimant’s name was excluded from the property records, and her son managed and dealt with the property as its owner without objection from her.
During negotiations, the purchaser was still investigating the son’s title and requested records relating to the property.
In the purchaser’s presence, the claimant said that the property belonged to her son and that he could deal with it as he wished.
The claimant did not testify to establish the facts necessary to show that she had inherited a share or had retained that share until the sale.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied estoppel by representation and conduct to the claimant’s clear declaration, acquiescence in the son’s exclusive management, and the purchaser’s reliance while investigating title. It also held that the claimant bore the burden of proving the facts necessary to establish her asserted share under section 3 of the Hindu Women’s Rights to Property Act, 1937; the possibility of her having relinquished that share before the sale was relevant. The Court noted that her asserted interest could have become absolute under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, but did not treat that possibility as relieving her of the burden of proof.
members.conclusion: The claimant was estopped from challenging the sale insofar as her asserted share was concerned; the estoppel did not apply to the minor claimants.

rule.if: third_party_sale_challenged and claimant_declared_seller_exclusive_owner and claimant_authorized_seller_to_deal_with_property and purchaser_was_still_investigating_title and claimant_acquiesced_in_sellers_exclusive_management

predicates.third_party_sale_challenged: A claimant challenges a sale of property made to a third-party purchaser.
predicates.claimant_declared_seller_exclusive_owner: The claimant told the purchaser, or did so in the purchaser’s presence, that the seller exclusively owned the property.
predicates.claimant_authorized_seller_to_deal_with_: The claimant said the seller could deal with the property as the seller wished.
predicates.purchaser_was_still_investigating_title: The purchaser was still making inquiries about the seller’s title when the claimant made the representation.
predicates.claimant_acquiesced_in_sellers_exclusive: The claimant allowed the seller to manage and deal with the property as its exclusive owner without objection.

members.legal_issue: A person who represents that a company owns property and induces another to act on that representation may be estopped from later denying the company’s ownership.
material_facts: The promoters represented in court proceedings, corporate records, and dealings concerning a bank mortgage that the company owned the property.
The promoters signed the company’s pleadings and documents making or repeating those representations.
The purchasers relied on the representations when entering the sale transaction and paying an advance.
The Court found no statutory bar to vesting title in the company.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles of estoppel, acquiescence, and approbation and reprobation, including the rule reflected in Section 116 of the Evidence Act in appropriate circumstances. A mere admission does not create title, but conduct and representations are relevant to determining intention and may prevent a party from taking an inconsistent position where another has acted to their detriment. The Court relied on Bank of India v. O.P. Swarnakar, Gillett v. Holt, Indu Shekhar Singh v. State of U.P., Pawan Alloys v. U.P. State Electricity Board, Taylor Fashions Ltd. v. Liverpool Victoria Trustees Co. Ltd., Amalgamated Investment & Property Co. Ltd. v. Texas Commerce International Bank Ltd., and Sarat Chunder Dey v. Gopal Chunder Laha.
members.conclusion: The promoters were estopped from denying or disputing the company’s title to the property.

rule.if: property_ownership_dispute and party_represented_company_ownership and other_party_relied_on_representation_to_its_detriment and no_statutory_bar

predicates.property_ownership_dispute: The parties disputed who owned the property.
predicates.party_represented_company_ownership: A party represented that the company, rather than that party personally, owned the property.
predicates.other_party_relied_on_representation_to_: Another party relied on the representation and changed its position to its detriment.
predicates.no_statutory_bar: No statutory restriction prevented the company from holding title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A person may be personally estopped from challenging a transfer when he represented the asserted title to a purchaser before the purchaser acquired the property.
material_facts: Before the first defendant acquired the disputed properties, the plaintiff and his brother represented to him that family members held absolute titles under the family arrangement.
The first defendant later acquired the properties through a subsequent sale and, as to another property, through pre-emption.
members.legal_principle: A party’s representation concerning title may prevent that party from denying the represented position against a person who acquired property after the representation. The Court stated that the additional estoppel in this appeal was governed by Dhiyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore, 1952 S.C.R. 478, but did not elaborate because the separate principle of election was sufficient to decide the appeals.
members.conclusion: In the appeal involving those later acquisitions, the Court held that the plaintiff was also personally estopped from challenging the transfers, although it relied on the reversioner’s election as sufficient to dispose of both appeals.

predicates.property_transfer_challenge: A claimant seeks to challenge a transfer of property.
predicates.claimant_represented_absolute_title_to_p: Before the acquisition, the claimant represented to the eventual purchaser that the relevant family members held absolute title.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_property_after_repres: The purchaser acquired the property after the claimant made the representation.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who, by conduct or silence, leads another to rely to that person's detriment on an apparent acceptance of a property transaction may be estopped from later challenging it.
material_facts: The claimant had consented to the regrant of the land to a family member who later transferred it to purchasers.
The claimant lived jointly with the transferring family member and was found to have known of related proceedings concerning the land.
The claimant did not challenge the transfer for about ten years, while the purchasers asserted their rights and participated in successive proceedings concerning the property.
The claimant sought a declaration of absolute ownership, although the property had been described as family property.
members.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 bars a person from denying a fact where that person's declaration, act, or omission caused or permitted another to believe it to be true and act on that belief. Estoppel requires conduct amounting to a representation, action on its faith, and resulting detriment; acquiescence may be inferred from conduct, and silence is relevant where there is a duty to speak. The Court relied on Sunderabai v. Devaji Shankara Deshpande, S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai, Provash Chandra Dalui v. Biswanath Banerjee, and Indira Bai v. Nand Kishore, among other authorities.
members.conclusion: The claimant was estopped from challenging the alienation, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: property_claim_challenging_alienation and claimant_conduct_indicated_assent and claimant_knew_of_transaction_or_proceedings and claimant_failed_to_object and purchaser_relied_to_detriment

predicates.property_claim_challenging_alienation: The proceeding is a property claim in which a claimant seeks to challenge an alienation.
predicates.claimant_conduct_indicated_assent: The claimant's words, acts, or silence reasonably conveyed acceptance of the transaction to the person who later acquired an interest.
predicates.claimant_knew_of_transaction_or_proceedi: The claimant knew of the transaction or of proceedings concerning the property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_object: The claimant did not object to the transaction despite having an opportunity to do so.
predicates.purchaser_relied_to_detriment: The purchaser acted on the apparent acceptance and would suffer detriment if the claimant were permitted to challenge the transaction.

members.legal_issue: A person who accepts a division of disputed property, induces the other claimant to rely on that acceptance to their detriment, and obtains a benefit from it is estopped from later denying the represented facts underlying the other claimant’s title.
material_facts: A claimant seriously asserted a right to the whole estate, while the daughter asserted a right to separate and exclusive possession and to an absolute share.
After the dispute was referred to arbitration and an award divided the estate, the parties accepted the division and acted on it rather than continuing their dispute.
The claimant retained property allotted to him, while the daughter gave up an appreciable portion of the estate and relied on the claimant’s acceptance of her absolute title to her allotment.
The claimant retained the benefit of the division and did not attempt to undo it during his lifetime.
members.legal_principle: Estoppel requires a representation of existing fact, reliance on that representation that induces action, and resulting detriment. Although estoppel does not arise merely on a question of law, conduct may represent an admission of the facts that produce a legal consequence. A party may accept and act on a division even if the underlying award could be challenged. The Court relied on Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal (1919) 45 I.A. 118 and distinguished the question of estoppel from the validity or binding force of the award itself.
members.conclusion: The claimant was estopped from denying the facts that, as recognized through his acceptance of the division, gave the daughter an absolute interest in her allotted properties; the award’s validity or binding effect was not necessary to that conclusion.

rule.if: property_dispute_case and claimant_accepted_property_division and acceptance_represented_existing_facts and other_claimant_relied_and_suffered_detriment and accepting_claimant_received_benefit

predicates.property_dispute_case: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property divided between claimants.
predicates.claimant_accepted_property_division: A claimant accepted and acted on a division of the disputed property instead of pursuing the dispute further.
predicates.acceptance_represented_existing_facts: The claimant’s acceptance represented recognition of existing facts underlying the other claimant’s asserted title.
predicates.other_claimant_relied_and_suffered_detri: The other claimant relied on that acceptance and gave up property or otherwise changed position to their detriment.
predicates.accepting_claimant_received_benefit: The claimant who accepted the division retained or obtained a benefit from it.

members.legal_issue: A party to a property settlement is estopped from denying the settlement's effect after inducing the other party to accept it and change position to their detriment.
material_facts: One party asserted a serious claim to the estate, and the dispute was referred to arbitration.
After the award divided the property, both sides accepted and acted on it rather than continuing to contest the dispute.
The party who received property under the division retained its benefit, while the other party accepted a reduced share and changed position in reliance on the settlement.
members.legal_principle: Estoppel requires a representation of existing fact, belief in that representation leading the other party to act on it, and action to that party's detriment. The court explained that acceptance of the award represented recognition of facts supporting the other party's absolute interest, rather than creating an estoppel on a question of law. It relied on Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal and distinguished the award's imposed form from a voluntary compromise because the parties chose to accept and act on the award.
members.conclusion: The party who induced acceptance of the award was estopped from denying the other party's absolute interest in the property, even if the award was invalid.

rule.if: property_settlement_dispute and party_accepts_award and acceptance_induces_reliance and other_party_changes_position_to_detriment

predicates.property_settlement_dispute: The parties dispute entitlement to property and use an award or settlement to divide it.
predicates.party_accepts_award: A party accepts the award or settlement and acts in accordance with it.
predicates.acceptance_induces_reliance: That party's conduct leads the other party to believe that the division will be accepted as resolving the dispute.
predicates.other_party_changes_position_to_detrimen: The other party relies on that belief, gives up property or another substantial position, and suffers detriment as a result.

members.legal_issue: A party who takes a benefit under a family settlement cannot challenge it after another party has acted on it to that party's detriment.
material_facts: The appellant was a party to the family arrangement and took a benefit under it.
In reliance on the arrangement, another party paid liabilities to obtain the release of property from management by the Court of Wards.
The appellant later challenged the validity of the arrangement.
members.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, prevents a party from denying a representation on which another has acted. The Court also relied on Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb and the principle that the consideration for a family settlement is the expectation of amity and goodwill, so a settlement cannot be impeached after its benefits have been taken and the other disputant has acted on it.
members.conclusion: The appellant was not entitled to challenge the arrangement and was estopped from doing so.

predicates.challenge_to_family_settlement: A party brought a proceeding challenging a family settlement.
predicates.claimant_received_settlement_benefit: The challenging party received a benefit under the settlement.
predicates.another_party_acted_in_reliance: Another party acted on the settlement, including by paying liabilities or taking steps to obtain property released.

members.legal_issue: A property owner who acquiesces in a sale by an ostensible owner and accepts the consideration may not later challenge the transferee's title on the ground that the ostensible owner lacked authority.
material_facts: The plaintiff's father acted as though he owned the land and entered into an agreement to sell it.
The sale was completed for consideration, which the evidence showed was paid to and accepted by the plaintiff in his presence.
The plaintiff knew of and acquiesced in the transaction.
The plaintiff later challenged the sale on the basis that his father lacked authority and the agent had merely completed a sale negotiated by another person.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, protects a transfer for consideration by an ostensible owner where the person interested in the property consented expressly or impliedly to that appearance of ownership. The Court also applied the equitable principle recognized in Ramcoomar v. Macqueen, (1872) I.A. 11, Bengal L.R. 46, and held that acquiescence and acceptance of consideration estopped the plaintiff from contesting the sale.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was estopped from challenging the title transferred through the sale, and the challenge to the transferee's title failed.

rule.if: transferee_title_challenged and another_person_acted_as_ostensible_owner and interested_owner_acquiesced_in_sale and interested_owner_accepted_sale_consideration

predicates.transferee_title_challenged: A person challenged the title acquired by a transferee through a property sale.
predicates.another_person_acted_as_ostensible_owner: Another person acted toward others as though that person owned the property.
predicates.interested_owner_acquiesced_in_sale: The person with an interest in the property knew of and acquiesced in the sale.
predicates.interested_owner_accepted_sale_considera: The person with an interest in the property accepted the consideration paid for the sale.

members.legal_issue: An owner who consents to another person holding themselves out as owner and acquiesces in a transfer for consideration cannot later challenge the transfer on the ground that the apparent owner lacked authority.
material_facts: The owner’s father acted as though he owned the land and entered into an agreement to sell it before the power of attorney was executed.
The sale was completed by the agent under the power of attorney.
The owner was present when consideration was paid and accepted it.
The owner later challenged the sale, including on the ground that the agent merely completed a transaction negotiated by another person.
members.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that a transfer for consideration by an ostensible owner is not voidable for lack of authority where the person interested in the property expressly or impliedly consented to that person’s being ostensible owner. The Court relied on the equitable principle stated in Ramcoomar v. Macqueen (1872) I.A. 11 Bengal L.R. 46.
members.conclusion: The owner was estopped from challenging the sale on the ground that the apparent owner lacked authority or that the agent merely executed the prior agreement; the transfer was protected under the principle codified in Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act.

rule.if: civil_appeal and apparent_owner_held_out_with_owner_consent and transfer_for_consideration and owner_acquiesced_in_transfer

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter was a civil appeal.
predicates.apparent_owner_held_out_with_owner_conse: A person acted as the owner of property with the express or implied consent of the person interested in it.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The apparent owner’s transfer of the property was made for consideration.
predicates.owner_acquiesced_in_transfer: The person interested in the property knew of and acquiesced in the transaction, including by accepting its consideration.

members.legal_issue: A presumptive reversioner who knowingly takes and retains property solely under a division accepted by an earlier holder is estopped from later challenging that division when the reversion opens, including when claiming in the new capacity of reversioner.
material_facts: The son had no independent title to the property allotted to his father when he took possession after his father’s death; he claimed through his father.
He knew of the award and the division made under it, took possession with his brother, and dealt with the property as their own for many years.
He benefited from the property and did not object while the daughter treated her own allotment as absolute property, including when she gifted it to her grandsons.
After the daughter’s son died, the son became the presumptive reversioner, and the reversion opened while the son was alive.
members.legal_principle: An estoppel may bind a successor who takes through the person estopped, and a person who knowingly accepts and benefits from a transaction may be precluded from challenging it even when later claiming in a different capacity. A reversioner who personally consented to and benefited from a transaction may remain estopped when the reversion opens. The Court relied on Kanhai Lal v.
