Brij Lal (1919) 45 I.A. 118 and Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb (1927) 54 I.A. 396 at 403; it distinguished Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden (1919) 46 I.A. 72 and Mt. Binda Kuer v. Lalitha Prasad on the facts concerning independent title and benefit.
members.conclusion: The son was estopped both through his father and by his own conduct, and the estoppel continued after the reversion opened despite his claim in the character of reversioner.

rule.if: reversionary_succession_case and claimant_took_only_through_estopped_predecessor and claimant_knew_of_division and claimant_retained_and_benefited_from_property_under_division and claimant_later_claimed_as_reversioner

predicates.reversionary_succession_case: The proceeding concerns a claim to property after a limited holder’s estate ends and the reversion opens.
predicates.claimant_took_only_through_estopped_pred: The claimant acquired possession or asserted title through a predecessor who was estopped from challenging the division.
predicates.claimant_knew_of_division: The claimant knew of the division under which the property was held.
predicates.claimant_retained_and_benefited_from_pro: The claimant retained and derived benefit from the property on the basis of the division.
predicates.claimant_later_claimed_as_reversioner: The claimant later asserted a right to the property in the capacity of reversioner.

members.legal_issue: A reversioner who claims through a predecessor who accepted and benefited from a property division, or who personally accepted and benefited from it, may be estopped from reopening the division even when claiming in a later capacity.
material_facts: The predecessor accepted the award, obtained and retained property under it, and induced the other party to accept the division.

The successor took possession of property under the award, knew of the division and the other party's reliance on it, retained benefits, and allowed the other party to deal with the allotted property as their own.
The successor later claimed the disputed property as a reversioner, and the plaintiffs claimed through that successor.
The court distinguished cases in which a claimant had an independent title or it could not be established that the claimant had benefited from the compromise.
members.legal_principle: Under Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal, a person who was a party to and acted on a property arrangement may be estopped despite later claiming in the different capacity of reversioner. The court also relied on Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb and distinguished Rangasami Gounden v. Nachiappa Gounden and Mr. Binda Kuer v. Lalitha Prasad, where independent rights or the attribution of the benefit to the compromise were material.
members.conclusion: The successor remained estopped when the reversion opened, and the plaintiffs claiming through that successor were also estopped.

rule.if: reversionary_property_claim and ((claimant_claims_through_predecessor and predecessor_accepted_and_benefited_from_division) or (claimant_accepted_and_benefited_from_division and claimant_knew_of_other_party_reliance))

predicates.reversionary_property_claim: A person claims property as a reversioner after an earlier property division involving a limited estate.
predicates.claimant_claims_through_predecessor: The claimant derives the asserted right through a predecessor who held property under the division.
predicates.predecessor_accepted_and_benefited_from_: The predecessor accepted the division and obtained and retained property under it, inducing the other side to act on the division.
predicates.claimant_accepted_and_benefited_from_div: The claimant personally took or retained property and benefits on the basis of the division.
predicates.claimant_knew_of_other_party_reliance: The claimant knew that the other party had accepted and dealt with the property on the basis of the division.

members.legal_issue: A consent decree recognizing a family-settlement claim to property that was the subject matter of the suit does not require registration where it acknowledges a pre-existing right.
material_facts: The suit concerned the disputed land, and the decree followed the landowner’s admission of the claimant’s claim.
The landowner testified that part of the land was ancestral, and the Court found that this portion came to the claimant under a family settlement.
The Court treated the decree as acknowledging the claimant’s entitlement to that portion under the family settlement, rather than as creating a new right by gift.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, 1908 exempts a court decree concerning property that is the subject matter of the suit from the relevant registration requirement. The Court applied the distinction discussed in Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major, (1995) 5 SCC 709, and K. Raghunandan v. Ali Hussain Sabir, (2008) 13 SCC 102; a three-judge Bench had found no inconsistency between those decisions. A decree acknowledging a pre-existing right under a family settlement is distinct from one creating a new right in the property for the first time.
members.conclusion: The decree concerning the portion transferred under the family settlement did not require compulsory registration.

predicates.consent_decree_dispute: The dispute concerns a consent decree that determines rights in property.
predicates.property_was_suit_subject_matter: The property addressed by the decree was included in the suit.
predicates.decree_acknowledges_preexisting_settleme: The decree recognizes a claim to the property under a family settlement rather than creating a new right by transfer.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree concerning immovable property that was the subject matter of the suit is exempt from compulsory registration when no collusion is alleged.
material_facts: A court had issued a compromise decree declaring rights in land that was the subject matter of the original suit.
The decree was later objected to when it was tendered in evidence, on the ground that it had not been registered.
No allegation was made that the decree was collusive.
The lower courts held registration necessary, relying in part on the view that a title claimed through adverse possession could not have existed before the decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 generally requires registration of instruments affecting rights in immovable property, but Section 17(2)(vi) exempts court decrees except compromise decrees comprising immovable property outside the subject matter of the suit or proceeding. Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major explains that a collusive compromise or one creating rights for the first time may require registration; Som Dev v. Rati Ram confirms that a compromise decree concerning property within the suit does not require registration. The reasoning based on Gurdwara Sahib v. Gram Panchayat Village Sirthala was no longer valid because Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur overruled it and held that perfected adverse possession can support a claim as well as a defence.
members.conclusion: The compromise decree did not require registration and was admissible in evidence; the orders holding otherwise were set aside.

rule.if: civil_appeal_challenges_registration_ruling and decree_is_court_compromise and decree_property_within_original_suit and no_collusion_alleged

predicates.civil_appeal_challenges_registration_rul: A party appeals a ruling that a decree cannot be admitted because it was not registered.
predicates.decree_is_court_compromise: A court issued the decree on the basis of a compromise.
predicates.decree_property_within_original_suit: The immovable property covered by the decree was the subject matter of the original suit or proceeding.
predicates.no_collusion_alleged: No party alleges that the decree was collusive.

members.legal_issue: A court decree that recognizes a pre-existing property right arising from a family arrangement and does not itself create that right is admissible without registration when relied on to establish title in a later pre-emption suit.
material_facts: In an earlier property suit, the claimant and a relative asserted that a family arrangement had already transferred a co-owner’s share to them.
The defendant in that suit admitted the arrangement in a written pleading and in evidence, and the court decreed the claim on that admission.
The decree recognized the asserted pre-existing right in property that was the subject matter of the earlier suit; it did not itself create a new right.
The claimant later relied on the decree to establish co-ownership and seek pre-emption against an assignee of another co-owner’s share.
The decree was not challenged as fraudulent, collusive, or made by a court lacking jurisdiction, and no gift was alleged.
members.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, Section 17(2)(vi), excludes court decrees and orders from compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) and (c), including a compromise decree confined to the suit property. A decree that merely recognizes a pre-existing right does not create a right for the first time. Bhoop Singh v. Ram Singh Major was distinguishable because the decree there created a right for the first time; S. Noordeen v. V.S. Thiru Venkita Reddiar was consistent with distinguishing cases involving a pre-existing right. The Court also relied on the principle that a bona fide family arrangement does not require registration.
members.conclusion: The decree was admissible without registration to establish the claimant’s recognized co-ownership, and the challenge to the claimant’s right of pre-emption failed.

rule.if: later_preemption_suit and earlier_property_suit_decree_relied_on and claim_based_on_preexisting_family_arrangement and opposing_party_admitted_arrangement and decree_only_recognized_existing_claim and property_within_earlier_suit and not gift_alleged

predicates.later_preemption_suit: A claimant brings a suit to enforce pre-emption against an assignee of a co-owner’s share.
predicates.earlier_property_suit_decree_relied_on: A party relies on a decree from an earlier suit concerning the property to establish title in the later suit.
predicates.claim_based_on_preexisting_family_arrang: The claimant in the earlier suit asserted that a family arrangement had already given them an interest in the property before the decree.
predicates.opposing_party_admitted_arrangement: The opposing party in the earlier suit admitted the asserted arrangement in a pleading and in evidence.
predicates.decree_only_recognized_existing_claim: The earlier court granted the claim on the admission and recognized the asserted right rather than creating a new right by the decree.
predicates.property_within_earlier_suit: The property in which the right was recognized was the subject matter of the earlier suit.
predicates.gift_alleged: A party alleged that the transfer of the property was a gift.

members.legal_issue: A court decree or order is exempt from registration under the provisions governing instruments that create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish property rights, subject to the exception for a compromise decree that includes property outside the suit.
material_facts: The earlier decree was based on an admission, not a compromise decree.
The decree concerned property that was the subject matter of the earlier suit.
The asserted right arose from an earlier family arrangement, and no gift, lease, or transfer of a court decree or order was alleged.
members.legal_principle: Registration Act, 1908, Section 17(1)(b) and (c), read with Section 17(2)(vi), exempts court decrees and orders from registration on the basis that they create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish property rights. The exception applies where a compromise decree includes immovable property outside the subject matter of the suit. The exemption does not extend to the separate categories in Section 17(1)(a), (d), and (e), including instruments effecting a gift or qualifying lease, or a transfer of a court decree or order. The Court discussed the legislative history and relied on Rani Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Midnapur Zamindari Company Limited and Mangan Lal Deoshi v. Mohammad Moinul Haque.
members.conclusion: A decree or order, including a compromise decree confined to the property that is the subject matter of the suit, does not require registration under the provisions addressing instruments that create or declare property rights; a compromise decree including property outside the suit falls within the exception.

rule.if: court_decree_or_order and not qualifying_gift_lease_or_decree_transfer and (not compromise_decree or not compromise_includes_outside_suit_property)

predicates.court_decree_or_order: The instrument relied on is a decree or order made by a court.
predicates.qualifying_gift_lease_or_decree_transfer: The decree or order effects a gift, a qualifying lease, or a transfer of a decree or order that creates or alters rights in immovable property.
predicates.compromise_decree: The court decree records a compromise between the parties.
predicates.compromise_includes_outside_suit_propert: The compromise decree includes immovable property that was not the subject matter of the suit or proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide and voluntary family arrangement that fairly resolves family disputes may bind its parties even when a recipient lacks a legal title, if the arrangement recognizes a possible claim or the other parties relinquish their claims in that recipient’s favour.
material_facts: The settlement divided the properties among close members of the deceased owner’s family and gave the recipient a share despite his not then having a certain legal right to inherit while one of the daughters was alive.
The recipient was a grandson and prospective heir, and the daughters relinquished their claims to the properties allotted to him.
The arrangement gave the daughters permanent rights in their allotted properties and was considered fair and equitable in the circumstances.
The parties acted upon the settlement, and the respondents neither pleaded nor proved fraud, coercion, or undue influence.
members.legal_principle: Family arrangements are governed by a special equitable approach and are favoured when honestly made to settle present or possible family disputes. The parties need not all hold an established legal title: a possible claim may suffice, and a title may be assumed where another party relinquishes claims and acknowledges the recipient’s entitlement. The settlement must be bona fide and voluntary, and allegations of fraud or undue influence must be clearly pleaded and proved. Lala Khunni Lal v. Kunwar Gobind Krishna Narain; Mt. Hiran Bibi v. Mt. Sohan Bibi; Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram; Ram Charan Das v. Girjanandini Devi; Tek Bahadur Bhujil v. Devi Singh; Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimham; Krishna Biharilal v. Gulabchand; S. Shanmugam Pillai v. K. Shanmugam Pillai; and Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb.
members.conclusion: The arrangement was bona fide, fair, and binding; the recipient’s possible claim and the relinquishment in his favour were sufficient to support it, and the challenge to its validity failed.

rule.if: family_arrangement_dispute and bona_fide_equitable_settlement and voluntary_agreement and possible_family_claim_acknowledged and no_fraud_or_undue_influence_proved

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns an agreement among family members intended to settle disputes about family property.
predicates.bona_fide_equitable_settlement: The parties made a genuine settlement that fairly allotted property and resolved their competing claims.
predicates.voluntary_agreement: The parties agreed to the settlement voluntarily rather than under coercion or undue influence.
predicates.possible_family_claim_acknowledged: A recipient had a possible family claim, or the other parties relinquished their claims and acknowledged the recipient’s entitlement.
predicates.no_fraud_or_undue_influence_proved: The party challenging the agreement did not establish fraud or undue influence through properly pleaded and proved allegations.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide family arrangement may be valid and binding even when the parties do not have conflicting legal claims to the property.
material_facts: The property had been acquired by the father, who directed that the younger, more capable son should receive a larger share in recognition of his contribution to the family.
After the father’s death, the younger son managed the family properties and businesses on the elder son’s promise that the father’s direction would be respected.
The younger son sought partition, and a substantial amount of property stood in his name, creating a possibility that he would claim it as his own.
To preserve family harmony and secure the younger son’s continued management, the brothers agreed that the elder’s branch would receive two shares and the younger’s branch three shares.
The courts below found that the agreement was genuine and bona fide, and the Supreme Court upheld those findings.
members.legal_principle: Although conflicting legal claims, actual or anticipated, are generally relevant to a family arrangement, they are not essential. Bona fide disputes or apprehensions, including ones that do not involve legal claims, can suffice when family members arrange matters to preserve peace or harmony. Courts favour arrangements that are bona fide and fair in the circumstances. The Court relied on Halsbury’s Laws of England, Ram Nirunjun Singh v. Prayag Singh, Basantakumar Basu v. Ramshankar Ray, Thakur Umrao Singh v. Thakur Lachman Singh, M. Ramayya v. U. Lakshmayya, and Sahu Madho Das v. Mukand Ram.
members.conclusion: The arrangement was a valid family arrangement and was binding on the family members.

rule.if: family_arrangement_challenge and family_members_arranged_property and bona_fide_arrangement and (existing_or_possible_dispute or family_peace_or_harmony_purpose)

predicates.family_arrangement_challenge: A party in a dispute over a family arrangement challenges whether that arrangement is valid or binding.
predicates.family_members_arranged_property: Members of the same family agreed on how family property or interests in it would be allocated.
predicates.bona_fide_arrangement: The family members made the arrangement honestly and its terms were fair in the circumstances.
predicates.existing_or_possible_dispute: The parties faced an actual dispute or a genuine possibility of disagreement over property or its management.
predicates.family_peace_or_harmony_purpose: The arrangement was made to preserve family peace or harmony or to avoid future disputes.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide arrangement among family members to settle existing or apprehended disputes may operate as a family arrangement and recognize an interest in property even where the recipient had no enforceable antecedent title to that property.
material_facts: A family document settled competing claims among members of different branches concerning their status and rights in family properties, including properties held in individual names.

The document recognized that one family member was entitled to a half share in a house, although he had been adopted into another branch and lacked an enforceable legal claim to property acquired by his birth father.
Read as a whole, the document’s recitals and operative terms showed conflicts of interest and a bona fide settlement of existing or apprehended disputes among family members.
members.legal_principle: Under Pullaiah v. Narasimham, A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1837, bona fide present or possible disputes, even if they do not involve enforceable legal claims, can support a family arrangement; such an arrangement may also be made to maintain peace or harmony, if its terms are fair in the circumstances. Sahu Madho Das v. Mukund Ram, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 22, and Rani Mewa Kuwar v. Rani Hulas Kuwar, (1873–74) L.R. 1 I.A. 157 at 166, explain that an arrangement proceeds on an assumption of antecedent title, which need not actually exist in law. The arrangement must be assessed as a whole; disputes need not concern every item or pit every participant against every other participant. Williams v. Williams, (1867) 2 Ch. A. 294, was referred to on family arrangements and the relevance of motive and consideration.
members.conclusion: The document was a valid family arrangement, and the family member acquired the recognized half share in the house under it.

predicates.family_members_settling_property_claims: Members of a family made an arrangement addressing competing claims to family property.
predicates.bona_fide_family_claims_or_counterclaims: Family members made bona fide claims or counterclaims that threatened or could threaten family harmony or property interests.
predicates.whole_arrangement_settles_existing_or_ap: Considered as a whole, the arrangement resolved disputes that existed or were apprehended among family members.
predicates.arrangement_valid_as_family_settlement_a: The arrangement is valid as a family settlement and gives its recipient the interest allocated to that recipient.

members.legal_issue: Agreements between near relations that settle actual or possible disputes in good faith to secure family peace may constitute binding family arrangements even without conflicting vested legal claims.
material_facts: The parties were near relations and had disputes concerning property and claims that would arise when succession opened.
An agreement gave one branch of the family immediate possession of property, while recognizing the widows’ rights to other property and to manage charitable properties.
A later agreement, made after litigation over a purported will, provided property to a presumptive reversioner and recognized the rights of the widows and other recipients of earlier alienations.
The beneficiaries of the agreements subsequently retained and dealt with property received under them.
members.legal_principle: Courts favor bona fide family arrangements that bring about harmony, settle actual or possible disputes, and avoid future litigation. A conflict of present or future legal claims is generally relevant but is not indispensable; bona fide disputes between near relations, even disputes not involving legal claims, may suffice. A family arrangement may be inferred from a long course of dealings, and courts are more ready to uphold an agreement made bona fide on fair terms than to avoid it. The Court relied on Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram, Maturi Pullaiah v. Maturi Narasimhan, Krishna Beharilal v. Gulab Chand, and Ram Charan Das v. Girjanandini Devi.
members.conclusion: The agreements, read together, constituted a family arrangement, and the plaintiffs could not repudiate the arrangements after accepting their benefits.

rule.if: family_arrangement_dispute and near_relations_disputed_property_claims and bona_fide_settlement_to_preserve_harmony and parties_accepted_transactional_benefits

predicates.family_arrangement_dispute: A proceeding disputes whether agreements settling family property claims are effective as a family arrangement.
predicates.near_relations_disputed_property_claims: Near relations had actual or possible disputes over property or claims arising in the future.
predicates.bona_fide_settlement_to_preserve_harmony: The parties entered into the arrangement in good faith to settle disputes, avoid litigation, or preserve family peace.
predicates.parties_accepted_transactional_benefits: The parties accepted benefits under the arrangement and acted on the transactions it established.

members.legal_issue: A prior judgment may be received as evidence of a transaction in which a person asserted a relevant right, even though the judgment is not an admission by that person under the Evidence Act.
material_facts: A prior judgment recorded a spiritual pedigree connecting the deceased Mahant and the claimant through a common spiritual ancestor.
The deceased Mahant had been a plaintiff in that earlier proceeding and had asserted a right as a spiritual collateral of the person whose property alienation was challenged.
The evidence did not establish who had propounded the pedigree recorded in the earlier judgment, so it could not be treated as an admission by the deceased Mahant.
The Court considered the judgment together with the oral evidence supporting the claimant’s spiritual relationship.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act permits evidence of a transaction in which a right was asserted or recognized; the earlier judgment could be used on that basis. The pedigree was not an admission under section 21 because it was not shown to have been propounded by the person against whom it was relied upon.
members.conclusion: The prior judgment was admissible under section 13 as evidence of a transaction asserting the relevant right, though it was not conclusive and had to be weighed with the other evidence.

predicates.civil_proceeding_involves_disputed_right: The proceeding concerns whether a person holds a disputed right.
predicates.prior_judgment_records_transaction_asser: An earlier judgment records a transaction in which a person asserted or obtained recognition of a right relevant to the present dispute.
predicates.judgment_is_not_shown_to_be_party_admiss: The evidence does not show that the relevant statement in the earlier judgment was an admission made or adopted by the party against whom it is now used.

members.legal_issue: A judgment concerning a property right in an earlier proceeding is admissible as evidence of the assertion and recognition of that right even when the current litigant was not a party to the earlier proceeding.
material_facts: An earlier suit had resulted in a judgment declaring the institution’s title to the disputed land.
The plaintiff in the present suit was not a party to the earlier suit.
The institution relied on the earlier judgment as evidence of its title in the present property dispute.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13 of the Evidence Act, a judgment not inter partes may be admitted as evidence of an assertion or recognition of a right to property. The Court relied on Srinivas Krishna Rao Kango v. Narayan Devji Kango, Sital Das v. Sant Ram, Dinamoni v. Brajmohini, and Collector of Gorakhpur v. Ram Sunder.
members.conclusion: The earlier judgment was admissible under Section 13 of the Evidence Act and could be relied on as evidence of the institution’s title, notwithstanding that the present plaintiff was not a party to it.

predicates.property_rights_dispute: The parties are litigating a right to property.
predicates.earlier_judgment_concerns_property_right: A judgment in an earlier proceeding addressed an asserted or recognized right to the property in dispute.
predicates.current_litigant_was_not_party_to_earlie: A litigant in the current dispute was not a party to the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A prior judgment concerning the same will may be relevant evidence in a later dispute between the same parties even when the earlier proceeding concerned different property and does not determine the later dispute by res judicata.
material_facts: The same parties had previously litigated a different property, relying on and disputing the same will.
The earlier court found that the will was duly executed, and that finding was upheld in a later proceeding between the parties.
The earlier judgment was before the courts in the present title suit, but its relevance was overlooked.
The pleadings and issues from the earlier suit were not tendered or shown to have been tried on res judicata in the present suit.
members.legal_principle: Sections 11, 13 and 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 make the earlier judgment relevant evidence in the circumstances described. The Court also referred to Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams v. K.M. Krishnaiah, (1998) 3 SCC 331. Res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law; the Court declined to determine it because it had not been pleaded or tried below and could not be raised for the first time at the hearing before the Court.
members.conclusion: The earlier judgment was relevant evidence with a material bearing on the will’s execution, although the Court did not hold that it was conclusive by res judicata.

predicates.later_civil_dispute_concerns_same_will: The later civil proceeding requires determination of a dispute concerning a will that was also in issue in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_judgment_records_adjudication_of: A judgment from the earlier proceeding records an adjudication concerning that will between the same parties.
predicates.earlier_judgment_is_before_court: The earlier judgment is placed before the court deciding the later proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree made before the narrowing amendment to the decree-registration exception remains within that exception even when it deals with immovable property beyond the subject matter of the suit.
material_facts: The decree was based on a compromise in a suit concerning a disputed portion of a larger area of coal-bearing land.
The compromise decree also dealt with the parties’ rights and obligations concerning the larger area beyond the disputed portion.
The decree was made before the statutory amendment that narrowed the exception for compromise decrees.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17(2)(vi) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, as it stood before the amendment effective on 1 April 1930, a decree or order of court was excepted from the registration requirements in clauses (b) and (c) of section 17(1), including a compromise decree dealing with immovable property beyond the subject matter of the suit. The Court relied on Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Midnapur Zamindari Co.
members.conclusion: The decree-registration exception applicable before the amendment covered the compromise decree even to the extent that it dealt with property outside the subject matter of the suit.

predicates.appeal_contests_registration_of_compromi: A party in an appeal challenged the use of a compromise decree on the ground that it was unregistered.
predicates.decree_predates_narrowing_amendment: The court made the compromise decree before a later amendment narrowed the registration exception for compromise decrees.
predicates.decree_covers_property_outside_suit: The compromise decree dealt with immovable property beyond the property that was the subject of the suit.
predicates.decree_would_otherwise_require_registrat: The decree concerns rights in immovable property of a kind that would otherwise require registration.

members.legal_issue: A family composition deed incorporated into a court decree does not require registration where it rearranges family interests and a provision concerning property outside the suits merely clarifies an earlier transaction.
material_facts: The agreements settled property disputes among members of the same family for their mutual benefit.
The agreements were incorporated into the final court decree.
The only property mentioned in the agreements that was outside the pending suits was covered by a clause that clarified an earlier deal and did not change legal rights in that property.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 generally requires registration of instruments that create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in immovable property. Section 17(2)(i) excepts composition deeds, and Section 17(2)(vi) excepts decrees or orders of a court. The court also applied the principle that family arrangements should be upheld rather than disturbed on technical or trivial grounds, particularly where the parties have received benefits under them. The clause concerning the property outside the suits merely recited existing rights and did not create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in that property.
members.conclusion: The agreements and decree were not invalid for want of registration.

rule.if: family_composition_deed and settlement_for_mutual_family_benefit and decree_incorporates_settlement and outside_property_clause_only_recites_existing_rights

predicates.family_composition_deed: Family members enter into a written composition deed to settle their property disputes.
predicates.settlement_for_mutual_family_benefit: The arrangement is made for the mutual benefit of the participating family members.
predicates.decree_incorporates_settlement: The court incorporates the settlement into its decree.
predicates.outside_property_clause_only_recites_exi: A clause concerning property outside the pending suits merely clarifies an earlier transaction without changing rights in that property.

members.legal_issue: A settlement of a property dispute between near relations may be a family arrangement even if all participants do not belong to one family in the narrow legal sense.
material_facts: The principal parties to the compromise were near relations.
The dispute concerned property originally owned by their common ancestor.
The compromise settled the parties’ competing claims to that property.
members.legal_principle: The word “family” in the context of a family arrangement is not confined to persons with a legal right of succession or a claim to a share in the disputed property. A settlement of a dispute between near relations may qualify. Courts favour family arrangements to preserve harmony and prevent future disputes. The Court relied on Ram Charan Das v. Girjanandini Devi and Sahu Madho Das v. Pandit Mukand Ram.
members.conclusion: The compromise could be treated as a family arrangement, and the suits challenging the resulting alienations were not maintainable.

predicates.civil_property_dispute_between_near_rela: The proceeding concerns a property dispute between people who are near relations.
predicates.dispute_concerns_property_of_common_ance: The disputed property originally belonged to an ancestor common to the parties.
predicates.settlement_resolves_competing_claims: The parties settled their competing claims to the disputed property.

members.legal_issue: A compromise resolving competing property claims among related persons can constitute a final and binding family arrangement.
material_facts: Several related persons asserted competing claims to property, and litigation was pending over those claims.
The compromise document allocated property among the disputants, recorded recognition of their respective claims, and provided for the resolution of the pending suits.
The disputants and the persons interested in the property were parties to the arrangement, and the related withdrawal and compromise of suits formed part of the same transaction.
The appellant was a party to the arrangement and obtained a benefit under it.
members.legal_principle: Courts give effect to family settlements because they resolve existing or future property disputes and promote amity among related persons. “Family” is not limited to persons with a legally established right of succession or a share; a relationship and a possible or even apparent claim may suffice. The Court relied on Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb, which treated connected dispositions as one transaction settling a family dispute.
members.conclusion: The document was in substance a family arrangement intended to settle the disputes finally and was binding on the parties.

predicates.family_property_dispute_settled: Related persons had disputed property claims, and the arrangement was made to resolve those disputes.
predicates.all_interested_parties_joined: The persons interested in the disputed property participated in the arrangement.
predicates.competing_claims_recognized: The arrangement recognized or accommodated the competing claims of the disputants.

members.legal_issue: A substantially delayed challenge to land-acquisition proceedings may be rejected for laches when the delay is not adequately explained.
material_facts: Some appellants filed their writ petitions many years after the acquisition declarations had been issued.
The acquisition proceedings had begun long before those petitions were filed.
The appellants relied on confusion and an asserted period of inactivity to explain their delay, but the High Court found the explanation insufficient.
The Supreme Court found the High Court justified in declining to entertain the delayed petitions.
members.legal_principle: A person challenging administrative action under Articles 226 and 227 must approach the court within a reasonable time and satisfactorily explain the delay. The Court held that the asserted period of uncertainty did not justify the substantial delay in these cases, particularly given the long passage of time since the acquisition proceedings began.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in dismissing the affected petitions on the ground of delay and laches, and the delay was not condoned.

predicates.is_writ_challenge_to_land_acquisition: The proceeding is a writ challenge to land-acquisition action.
predicates.substantial_delay_in_filing: The landowner filed the challenge substantially after the relevant acquisition action gave rise to the claim.
predicates.delay_not_satisfactorily_explained: The landowner’s account of the delay did not adequately justify waiting to bring the challenge.

members.legal_issue: A claimant cannot belatedly challenge an acquisition on the ground that a different procedure applied to acquisition for a private company when that ground was not raised within a reasonable time.
material_facts: The acquisition was undertaken for the benefit of a private company.
The former owners filed their challenge about 17 years after the award and taking of possession.
They had accepted compensation and pursued enhancement without timely challenging the acquisition on the ground that a different procedure applied.
members.legal_principle: A challenge to acquisition proceedings, including one based on the procedure applicable to acquisition for a private company, must be brought within a reasonable time; Article 226 relief may be refused for delay and laches. The Court relied on Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, [1998] 4 SCC 387, and Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co. Pvt. Ltd., [1996] 2 SCC 501.
members.conclusion: The contention about the procedure applicable to acquisition for a private company did not assist the former owners because it was raised too late.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_writ: A claimant filed a writ petition challenging land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.private_company_acquisition: The acquisition was undertaken for the benefit of a private company.
predicates.ground_not_raised_timely: The claimant did not raise the procedural challenge within a reasonable time after the acquisition proceedings began.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to land-acquisition notifications may be dismissed when it is brought after an unreasonable delay, particularly after the acquisition has substantially progressed on the basis of those notifications.
material_facts: The government initiated acquisition proceedings for planned urban development, issued and published an initial acquisition notification, later issued a declaration and notices to claimants, and made an award.
No objection was made during the statutory objection stage.
The challengers filed writ petitions about nine years after the declaration, challenging the acquisition notifications and later notices on grounds available when the notifications were published.
members.legal_principle: A challenge to an acquisition notification and declaration must be brought within a reasonable time. The length of delay matters in light of the acts done in the interval on the basis of the notification and declaration. Allowing the government to complete acquisition proceedings and then challenging instruments on grounds available when they were published would reward dilatory tactics. The Court followed Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, [1975] 1 SCR 802, and referred to the acquisition sequence under sections 4, 5A, 6 and 9 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953.
members.conclusion: The High Court rightly dismissed the petitions for inordinate delay, and the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: acquisition_notification_challenge and unreasonable_delay_after_declaration and (acquisition_process_substantially_completed_before_challenge or government_acted_on_notifications_as_valid) and grounds_available_at_publication

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: The proceeding seeks to invalidate notifications or declarations issued in a land-acquisition process.
predicates.unreasonable_delay_after_declaration: The challengers waited an unreasonable time after the acquisition declaration before bringing their challenge.
predicates.acquisition_process_substantially_comple: The government had substantially advanced the acquisition process before the challengers brought their case.
predicates.government_acted_on_notifications_as_val: The government proceeded with acquisition steps on the basis that the notifications and declaration were valid.
predicates.grounds_available_at_publication: The challengers relied on grounds that were available when the relevant notifications were published.

members.legal_issue: A delayed challenge to an acquisition notification for insufficiently particularized public purpose is barred when the challenger did not raise the alleged prejudice at the appropriate stage.
material_facts: The notification covered a large area comprising plots belonging to different persons and specified the purpose as the planned development of the city.
A declaration covering part of the area was published in 1966, but the challengers waited until 1970 or later to contest the notification.
The challengers did not argue before the High Court that insufficient particulars had prevented them from effectively objecting to the acquisition.
members.legal_principle: A valid notification under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act is a sine qua non for acquisition proceedings, and the particular public purpose must be specified sufficiently to allow meaningful objections under sections 4(2) and 5A. For a large acquisition involving many plots, the purpose may be specified with reference to the area as a whole; whether the specification is sufficient depends on the circumstances. A challenge brought after delay, particularly after the challenger has allowed proceedings to advance and did not raise the asserted prejudice below, may be rejected for laches and acquiescence. The Court relied on Munshi Singh v. Union of India, Arnold Rodricks v. State of Maharashtra, Tilokchand Motichand v. H. B. Munshi, and Rabindranath Bose v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the challenge, holding that the challengers’ delay and failure to raise the alleged prejudice earlier barred it.

rule.if: acquisition_notification_challenge and large_area_multiple_owners and challenge_delayed_after_declaration and alleged_objection_prejudice_not_raised_below

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: A person challenges the validity of a notification initiating compulsory acquisition proceedings.
predicates.large_area_multiple_owners: The acquisition covers a large area made up of plots belonging to multiple owners.
predicates.challenge_delayed_after_declaration: The challenger waits until after a formal declaration advancing the acquisition before challenging the notification.
predicates.alleged_objection_prejudice_not_raised_b: The challenger does not raise before the lower court the claim that the notification prevented an effective objection.

members.legal_issue: A delayed challenge to the authority that issued an acquisition notification may be rejected for laches and acquiescence without deciding whether that authority was authorized to issue it.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was issued by a local administrative officer, while the challengers contended that the development statute assigned the acquisition power to the Central Government.
The challengers did not timely challenge the notification and allowed the acquisition proceedings to advance.
The Court assumed, without deciding, that the officer might not have been authorized and rejected the challenge because of laches and acquiescence.
members.legal_principle: A challenge to the authority responsible for issuing an acquisition notification relates primarily to the validity of that notification. Where the challenger is precluded by laches and acquiescence from questioning the notification, the challenge may be rejected without resolving whether the authority was in fact authorized. Section 15 of the Delhi Development Act was the asserted source of the claimed allocation of power.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge to the issuing officer’s authority because the challengers were precluded by laches and acquiescence from questioning the notification.

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: A person challenges the validity of a notification initiating compulsory acquisition proceedings.
predicates.authority_to_issue_disputed: The challenger claims that the official who issued the notification lacked authority to do so.
predicates.challenge_delayed_after_proceedings_adva: The challenger waits until acquisition proceedings have advanced before contesting the issuing official’s authority.

members.legal_issue: A writ challenge to acquisition notifications may be barred by laches when the challenger waits until the acquisition has proceeded to completion despite grounds for challenge being available earlier.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications and declaration were issued before the challengers filed their writ petition.
The challengers filed the petition only after notices had issued and possession had been taken, although the grounds they raised were available earlier.
members.legal_principle: The Court reiterated that a challenge to acquisition notifications must be brought within a reasonable time. A person cannot wait while the government completes acquisition proceedings on the basis that the notifications are valid and then raise grounds that were already available, since that would reward delay.
members.conclusion: The challenge was barred by laches as well as failing on its other grounds.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: A party brings a writ challenge to notifications or a declaration initiating or advancing a land acquisition.
predicates.challenge_brought_after_proceedings_adva: The challenger waits until the acquisition has substantially proceeded before filing the challenge.
predicates.grounds_available_earlier: The grounds relied on were available to the challenger before the acquisition substantially proceeded.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to public action is barred by laches when the action was publicly knowable well before the petition and the petitioner did not act despite events that should have prompted a challenge.
material_facts: The land was converted to residential use years before the university filed its writ petition.
The public transport body invited bids and conducted a public auction for the land before the petition was filed.
Related litigation concerning the residential development had already occurred, and the development was in the public domain.
The university filed its writ petition years after the conversion and auction, and the writ court found that it suffered from delay and laches.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the equitable principles governing delay and laches and cited M/s Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Company Ltd. v. District Board, Bhojpur for the test that a petitioner should approach the court before a parallel right is created and that the lapse of time should not be attributable to laches or negligence. The Court considered the public availability of the development and the petitioner’s failure to act when events should have prompted it to do so.
members.conclusion: The writ court was justified in finding that the university’s writ petition was hit by delay and laches.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_public_action and public_action_preceded_petition_substantially and public_events_signalled_the_challenge and petitioner_failed_to_act_promptly

predicates.writ_challenge_to_public_action: A petitioner brought a writ proceeding challenging action taken by a public authority.
predicates.public_action_preceded_petition_substant: The challenged action occurred a substantial time before the petitioner filed the writ proceeding.
predicates.public_events_signalled_the_challenge: Publicly visible steps or related proceedings indicated the development or action that the petitioner later challenged.
predicates.petitioner_failed_to_act_promptly: The petitioner did not bring the challenge promptly after those events occurred.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to acquisition proceedings brought after substantial unexplained delay may be rejected for laches when the grounds were available earlier.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was issued in 1959, and the declarations covering the land were issued in 1968 and 1969, but the foundation did not challenge them until 1973.
The grounds later advanced against the earlier notifications were available when those notifications were issued.
The foundation withdrew its first writ petition and later filed another on substantially the same grounds, without identifying a fresh circumstance that justified the later filing.
The later notices concerned only a small portion of the land, while the challenge concerned notifications covering the whole area.
The absence of an award and the fact that the foundation remained in possession did not explain the delay; the foundation had itself sought a stay against making the award and dispossessing it.
The Court relied on Aflatoon & Ors. v. Lt. Governor Delhi & Ors., [1975] 1 SCR 802, which applied laches to a delayed challenge to land-acquisition proceedings.
members.legal_principle: A writ challenge under Article 226 may be rejected for laches where the grounds for challenging acquisition notifications were available when they were issued but the challenger waited without adequate explanation. Later notices relating to only part of the land, continued possession, and the absence of an award do not by themselves justify delay in challenging earlier notifications. The Court applied Aflatoon & Ors. v. Lt. Governor Delhi & Ors., [1975] 1 SCR 802, concerning notifications and declarations under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the acquisition notifications was liable to be dismissed for laches and delay. The appeal was dismissed with costs, and the Court found it unnecessary to decide the other questions of law raised.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_acquisition_proceedings and challenge_grounds_available_earlier and substantial_delay and no_adequate_explanation_for_delay

predicates.writ_challenge_to_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding is a writ challenge to land-acquisition proceedings.
predicates.challenge_grounds_available_earlier: The grounds relied on to challenge the acquisition were available when the challenged notifications were issued.
predicates.substantial_delay: The challenger waited a substantial period before raising those grounds in court.
predicates.no_adequate_explanation_for_delay: The challenger offered no adequate explanation for waiting, and the circumstances relied on did not justify the delay.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition challenge raised only years after the declaration, when the award is imminent or made, may be rejected for laches if the claimant did not object or act at the appropriate time.
material_facts: The landowners did not file objections in the statutory inquiry or raise the challenged grounds before the declarations were made.
The declarations were made in 1978, but the writ petitions were filed in 1982 or 1983, when awards were about to be made or had already been made.
The challenge included grounds that could have been raised earlier, including the alleged vagueness of the public purpose and procedural defects.
members.legal_principle: A claimant who remains inactive after a declaration and challenges the acquisition only near completion of the proceedings may be barred by laches, particularly where the ground was available earlier. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi and its discussion of Tilokchand Motichand v. H.B. Munshi and Rabindranath Bose v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The delayed challenges could not be entertained on the grounds available earlier; the delay and laches were fatal to those claims.

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A claimant sought judicial review of a land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.challenge_filed_years_after_declaration: The claimant brought the challenge years after the formal declaration and near the award stage.
predicates.no_timely_objection_or_challenge: The claimant did not raise the relevant objection or challenge at an earlier appropriate stage.
predicates.late_acquisition_challenge_barred_by_lac: The court will not entertain the delayed challenge on grounds that were available earlier.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who waits years after the acquisition declaration cannot raise a procedural objection to the statutory inquiry for the first time when the award is imminent or has been made.
material_facts: The High Court had found non-compliance with rules requiring notice of the objection hearing to the department and an opportunity for the department to answer objections.
The claimants raised that procedural ground only in writ petitions filed years after the declarations, when awards were imminent or had been made.
The claimants had not raised the ground at the appropriate time.
members.legal_principle: A procedural objection to an acquisition inquiry may be rejected where the claimant remains silent for years and raises it only when the proceedings are nearing completion. The Court relied on the principles of laches applied in Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to decide the merits of the alleged non-compliance because of the claimants' delay and held that they could not raise the contention at that late stage.

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A claimant sought judicial review of a land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.alleged_inquiry_hearing_noncompliance: The claimant alleged that a required participant was not notified of the objection hearing or given an opportunity to respond.
predicates.challenge_filed_years_after_declaration: The claimant brought the challenge years after the formal declaration and near the award stage.
predicates.late_procedural_objection_not_entertaine: The court declines to consider the procedural objection because it was raised too late.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to acquisition notifications may be dismissed when it is brought after an unreasonable, unexplained delay and the acquisition process has been completed in reliance on them.
material_facts: The petition challenging the notifications was filed about six years after their publication and about five years after the award.
No explanation was offered for the delay.
The acquisition process had been completed, and the State had spent a considerable amount carrying out the public purpose.
members.legal_principle: A challenge to an acquisition notification and declaration must be brought within a reasonable time. The length of delay is assessed in light of the acts done in the interval in reliance on the notifications. A person who allows acquisition proceedings to be completed before raising grounds available earlier may not obtain relief through a belated challenge. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi and Indrapuri Griha Nirman Sahakari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan.
members.conclusion: The challenge was liable to be dismissed for delay, providing an additional reason for dismissing the appeal.

rule.if: acquisition_notification_challenge and unreasonable_unexplained_delay and acquisition_process_completed and substantial_public_purpose_expenditure_incurred

predicates.acquisition_notification_challenge: A person challenged notifications issued in a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.unreasonable_unexplained_delay: The person waited an unreasonable time to bring the challenge and offered no explanation for the delay.
predicates.acquisition_process_completed: The acquisition process was completed before the challenge was brought.
predicates.substantial_public_purpose_expenditure_i: The government had spent a substantial amount carrying out the public purpose in reliance on the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A delayed challenge to land acquisition proceedings remains barred by laches even when a fresh challenge has been permitted, unless the challengers overcome the delay-based bar.
material_facts: Possession of the acquired land was taken and compensation was paid.
The claimants pursued compensation references and appeals, and the compensation proceedings attained finality.
Years later, the claimants challenged the acquisition proceedings on the ground that the award was invalid.
The challenge was dismissed as barred by laches, and the dismissal was upheld on appeal.
The claimants had been permitted to pursue appropriate proceedings based on their grievance under the later land acquisition law.
members.legal_principle: A challenge to acquisition proceedings may be rejected for laches when brought after substantial delay, including where possession has been taken and compensation proceedings have been pursued. Permission to bring a fresh proceeding does not itself overcome laches. In affirming the High Court’s delay finding, the Court found no infirmity in its application of the principles reflected in Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, Swaika Properties Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, Sawaran Lata v. State of Haryana, and Banda Development Authority, Banda v. Moti Lal Agarwal.
members.conclusion: The Court upheld the dismissal of the acquisition challenge as barred by laches. Permission to bring a fresh challenge did not remove the need to overcome that bar, and the claimants had not done so.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_proceeding and substantial_delay_in_challenging_acquisition and possession_taken and compensation_paid and compensation_claim_pursued_to_finality and fresh_challenge_permitted

predicates.acquisition_challenge_proceeding: The claimant brings a proceeding challenging the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.substantial_delay_in_challenging_acquisi: The claimant waits a substantial period after the acquisition before challenging it.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority takes possession of the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_paid: The claimant receives compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.compensation_claim_pursued_to_finality: The claimant pursues proceedings seeking compensation, and those proceedings reach finality.
predicates.fresh_challenge_permitted: A court permits the claimant to bring a fresh proceeding concerning the acquisition or a related grievance.
predicates.acquisition_challenge_barred_by_laches: The acquisition challenge is rejected as barred by laches.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to a preliminary acquisition notification based on an alleged public-notice defect cannot be brought after an unreasonable lapse of time when the challenger knew of the notification and acted on it.
material_facts: The challenger knew of the preliminary acquisition notification and filed objections to the proposed acquisition.
The challenger later filed a writ petition challenging the notification, after the subsequent acquisition notification had been published and after an unreasonable lapse of time.
The challenger contended that the required public notice had not been given.
members.legal_principle: A person who knows of a preliminary acquisition notification and files objections must challenge its validity within a reasonable time. The Court found no basis to disturb the notification on the asserted public-notice ground because the challenge was unreasonably delayed.
members.conclusion: The challenger was not entitled to challenge the preliminary notification after an unreasonable lapse of time; a defect in the required public notice should have been challenged within a reasonable time of publication.

rule.if: land_acquisition_notification_challenge and challenger_knew_of_notification and challenger_filed_objections and challenge_unreasonably_delayed

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: A person brings a legal challenge to a preliminary notification for a proposed land acquisition.
predicates.challenger_knew_of_notification: The challenger knew that the preliminary acquisition notification had been issued.
predicates.challenger_filed_objections: The challenger filed objections to the proposed acquisition after learning of the notification.
predicates.challenge_unreasonably_delayed: The challenger waited an unreasonable time after publication before challenging the notification.

members.legal_issue: An amendment that substantively narrows the grounds for eviction does not govern proceedings already pending unless retrospective operation is expressly provided or necessarily implied.
material_facts: The landlord applied for eviction on the ground that the shop was required for reconstruction before the amendment took effect.
The amendment substantially narrowed the circumstances in which a landlord could recover possession for building work.
The proceeding was pending when the amendment took effect, and the amendment contained no express direction that the changed eviction ground applied retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: An amendment affecting substantive rights operates prospectively unless retrospective operation is expressly stated or follows by necessary implication. The Court held that the amendment to s. 13(3)(a)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, was substantive, found no express or necessarily implied retrospective operation, and approved Ram Parshad Halwai, Ludhiana v. Mukhtiar Chand. The Act’s beneficial purpose for tenants did not determine the question of retrospectivity.
members.conclusion: The amended eviction ground did not apply to the pending proceeding, which remained governed by the earlier provision.

rule.if: rent_control_ejectment_case and eviction_application_preceded_substantive_change and proceeding_pending_when_change_took_effect and not express_retroactivity and not necessary_retroactivity

predicates.rent_control_ejectment_case: A landlord sought to evict a tenant in a proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.eviction_application_preceded_substantiv: The landlord applied for eviction before a legislative change altered the substantive grounds for recovering possession.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_change_took_effe: The eviction proceeding remained pending when the substantive change took effect.
predicates.express_retroactivity: The legislative change expressly made the altered eviction ground applicable to earlier proceedings.
predicates.necessary_retroactivity: Applying the altered eviction ground to earlier proceedings was necessary for the change to operate.

members.legal_issue: An amendment that affects substantive compensation rights and contains no express or necessarily implied retrospective operation applies prospectively.
material_facts: The amendment changed the method for determining compensation for mines and minerals and affected the proprietor’s substantive compensation rights.
The amendment stated that it would come into force at once but did not state that it would operate retrospectively.
The compensation entitlement was to be determined under the law applicable when compensation was payable.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the presumption against retrospectivity for legislation affecting substantive rights, relying on Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhury, [1957] SCR 488, and the principles in Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra, [1994] 4 SCC 602. It also relied on Union of India v. C. Rama Swamy, [1997] 4 SCC 647, in rejecting the argument that substitution alone made the amendment retrospective. The relevant provisions were Section 1(2) and Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms (Validation and Amendment) Act, 1974, and Sections 24 and 25 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
members.conclusion: The amendment applied prospectively, so the unamended compensation provision governed the compensation in this case.

predicates.statutory_compensation_proceeding: The matter concerns compensation determined under a statute.
predicates.amendment_affects_substantive_rights: A statutory amendment changes a party’s substantive entitlement to compensation.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent_shown: The amendment contains no express or necessarily implied indication that it applies to past or pending entitlements.
predicates.amendment_applies_prospectively: The amendment governs only prospectively and does not displace the law applicable to the earlier entitlement.

members.legal_issue: Amendments that alter substantive rights do not change the rights governing pending actions unless the legislation clearly makes that change retrospective.
material_facts: The civil suits were instituted before the 1957 amendments came into force and were still pending when those amendments commenced.
The amendments enlarged the definition relevant to the statutory scheme and changed the government’s right to appeal against a Settlement Officer’s decision.
The amendments contained no clear language making them apply to pending or concluded civil actions.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, substantive rights in a pending action are determined under the law in force when the action began unless the later legislation clearly expresses an intention to vary those rights. The Court applied that rule of statutory construction, noting that the 1957 amendments contained no express or necessarily implied retrospective operation and affected substantive rights and obligations.
members.conclusion: The 1957 amendments operated prospectively and did not alter the parties’ rights in the pending suits, which had to be decided under the law applicable when those actions were instituted.

rule.if: civil_action_pending_when_law_changed and (new_law_changes_substantive_rights or new_law_imposes_new_obligations) and not law_clearly_makes_change_retroactive

predicates.civil_action_pending_when_law_changed: A civil action was pending when a later law came into force.
predicates.new_law_changes_substantive_rights: The later law changes substantive rights relevant to the pending action.
predicates.new_law_imposes_new_obligations: The later law imposes obligations or disabilities relevant to the pending action.
predicates.law_clearly_makes_change_retroactive: The later law clearly states, expressly or by necessary implication, that the change applies retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: Amendments that alter substantive rights do not apply retrospectively to determine an earlier decree unless the legislation expressly makes them applicable to pending matters.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court decrees were made after the 1964 Act came into force but before the 1969 amendment took effect.
The leaseholder relied on rights and remedies introduced by the 1969 amendment, including provisions concerning use of the holding, tree cutting and recoverable rent.
The Court found that the relevant amendments operated prospectively and that the leaseholder was not otherwise entitled to the claimed statutory benefits.
members.legal_principle: A statute must be considered in light of its scope, the former law and the legislative changes it makes. Legislation altering substantive rights ordinarily does not affect pending actions or earlier transactions unless it expressly so provides; procedural changes that do not affect rights generally apply to pending and future proceedings. The Court relied on Gardner v. Lucas, Moon v. Durden, Smithies v. National Union of Operative Plasterers, and Re Joseph Sucha & Co. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The earlier decree was correctly made under the law then in force and was not altered by the later substantive amendments.

rule.if: decree_precedes_substantive_amendment and amendment_alters_rights and not express_retrospective_application

predicates.decree_precedes_substantive_amendment: The decree was made before the relevant statutory amendment took effect.
predicates.amendment_alters_rights: The later amendment changes the substantive rights or remedies available to a party.
predicates.express_retrospective_application: The amendment expressly applies its changed rights or remedies to earlier matters or pending proceedings.

members.legal_issue: An amendment affecting a substantive pre-emption right does not apply retrospectively to a pending appeal unless retrospective operation is expressed or necessarily intended.
material_facts: The statutory amendment substituted a provision limiting the right of pre-emption to tenants and thereby removed a co-sharer’s basis for claiming pre-emption.
The amendment took effect after the trial court had decreed the plaintiffs’ suit and while an appeal was pending.
The substituted provision contained no express language or necessary implication making it retrospective.
members.legal_principle: Substantive legislation is presumed prospective unless retrospective operation is expressly stated or follows by necessary intendment. Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry, Dayawati v. Inderjit, Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra, K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, and Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan support that rule. Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri concerns legislation made retrospective and does not require an appellate court to apply a prospective amendment. Shantidevi v. Hukum Chand had already treated the substituted provision as prospective.
members.conclusion: The substituted provision operated prospectively and did not affect the substantive rights fixed when the trial court passed its decree; the appellate court was not required to apply it to the pending appeal.

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: An appeal in a pre-emption proceeding remained undecided when a new law came into force.
predicates.amendment_changes_substantive_right: The new law altered who could claim the substantive right to pre-emption.
predicates.no_express_or_necessary_retroactive_inte: The new law did not expressly or by necessary implication apply to rights already fixed in pending litigation.

members.legal_issue: An amendment requiring permission for executing eviction decrees does not impose a fresh-permission requirement on an execution proceeding already commenced with the required permission, unless the amendment expressly or by necessary implication applies to that pending proceeding.
material_facts: A decree-holder obtained an eviction decree concerning a tenant in a slum area and obtained permission to execute it under the law then in force.
The decree-holder filed an execution application with that permission before the amendment came into force.

While an appeal concerning the execution application was pending, the application was consigned to the record room; a later application was filed to revive it, and the court treated it as a continuation of the original pending proceeding.
The amendment came into force while the original execution proceeding was pending and changed the permission requirements for executing eviction decrees.
The tenant objected that fresh permission under the amended law was required.
members.legal_principle: Under section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, as it stood before its substitution by the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Amendment Act, 1964, a decree-holder required prior written permission to execute an eviction decree. The substituted section 19 also required permission for executing decrees obtained in proceedings instituted before the amendment. However, absent express words or necessary implication that an amendment applies to pending proceedings, the parties’ rights in a proceeding are determined under the law in force when it commenced. The court found no such intention in the substituted section: it neither provided for a stay nor otherwise clearly varied rights in pending proceedings. Applying the amended requirement could also leave a decree-holder without a remedy if a fresh execution application were time-barred. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The amended provision did not affect the pending execution proceeding expressly or by necessary implication. The proceeding remained governed by the law in force when it commenced, so fresh permission was not required and the tenant’s objections were rightly dismissed.

predicates.eviction_decree_execution: The proceeding seeks to execute a decree for eviction of a tenant from premises in a protected area.
predicates.execution_application_started_before_ame: The decree-holder commenced the execution proceeding before a change in the governing law took effect.
predicates.required_permission_obtained_before_appl: The decree-holder obtained the permission required by the law in force before filing the execution application.
predicates.later_application_continues_original_pro: A later filing seeks to revive or continue the original execution proceeding rather than commence a new proceeding.
predicates.amendment_lacks_clear_application_to_pen: The amendment does not expressly or by necessary implication apply its new requirements to proceedings already pending.

members.legal_issue: An amendment cannot be applied retrospectively to impair vested substantive rights unless that intention is expressed in plain and unmistakable language.
material_facts: The property had been allotted and was subject to proceedings for its division under the applicable rules.
After the relevant rule was deleted by amendment, the property was auctioned and purchased by a third party who deposited the purchase price.
A prior decision held that the amendment could not operate retrospectively in these proceedings, restoring the rule to its original position.
members.legal_principle: A statute is not construed retrospectively to take away or impair a vested or substantive right unless that intention is made manifest by plain and unmistakable language. Even where a procedural statute operates retrospectively, it does not affect substantive rights already vested. The Court approved the view in Pt. Dey Ral v. Union of India that the amendment could not retrospectively apply to these proceedings, with the result that Rule 30 was restored for them.
members.conclusion: The amendment did not apply retrospectively to these proceedings; the auction was quashed and the matter was remitted for partition under the applicable rules.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_judgment: The matter is an appeal from a High Court judgment concerning proceedings to allot or divide property under applicable rules.
predicates.amendment_would_impair_vested_substantiv: Applying an amendment to the proceedings would impair substantive rights that had already vested.
predicates.plain_unmistakable_retroactive_intent: The amendment expresses in plain and unmistakable language an intention to impair those vested substantive rights retrospectively.
predicates.auction_proceedings_are_quashed_and_prop: The auction proceedings are set aside and the property is remitted for partition under the rules applicable to the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Jurisdictional amendments assigning tenancy questions to revenue officers do not govern civil appeals already pending when the amendments take effect unless the legislation expressly or by necessary implication makes them applicable.
material_facts: An eviction suit was filed before the 1951 agricultural leases legislation came into force, and the trial court decreed the suit before the 1953 amendments took effect.
When the 1953 amendments came into force, an appeal from the decree was pending in the first appellate court.
The amendments assigned certain tenancy questions to revenue officers and required civil courts to accept their decisions.
members.legal_principle: The legislature must expressly or by necessary implication oust civil-court jurisdiction. Sections 16, 16A and 16B of the amended Act did not indicate that they applied to pending appeals: “suit or proceeding” did not ordinarily indicate appellate proceedings, and section 16B used “entertain” rather than “entertain or try,” as section 15(2) of the 1951 Act had done. The Court inferred that the amendments were not intended to affect pending appeals. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The 1953 amendments did not apply to the appeal already pending when they came into force, so they did not oust the civil court’s jurisdiction in this case.

rule.if: civil_eviction_proceeding and appeal_pending_when_jurisdictional_change_took_effect and change_assigns_issue_to_special_officer and no_clear_retroactive_application

predicates.civil_eviction_proceeding: A civil court was asked to decide an eviction dispute.
predicates.appeal_pending_when_jurisdictional_chang: An appeal from the civil court’s decree was pending when a jurisdictional change took effect.
predicates.change_assigns_issue_to_special_officer: The change assigned determination of an issue in the dispute to a special officer.
predicates.no_clear_retroactive_application: The change contained no express or necessarily implied indication that it applied to appeals already pending.

members.legal_issue: The characterization of an amendment as beneficial does not, by itself, justify construing a clear and unambiguous substantive provision as retrospective.
material_facts: The appellants argued that removing the co-sharer’s pre-emption right benefited the public generally and therefore the amendment should operate retrospectively.
The substituted provision used plain and unambiguous language and did not state that it applied retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: Benevolent construction may assist where statutory language is ambiguous, but it cannot be used to rewrite a plain provision or create an unstated retrospective effect. Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan establishes that a measure’s beneficial character does not determine retrospectivity. Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Chetri was distinguishable because the statutory provisions there indicated an intention to protect earlier transactions; H. Shiva Rao v. Celelia Pereira concerned ambiguous expressions.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument that benevolent construction made the amendment retrospective; doing so would require adding words to the enactment and altering its meaning.

rule.if: pending_preemption_appeal and amendment_is_claimed_to_be_beneficial and provision_is_plain_and_unambiguous and no_retroactive_intent

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: An appeal in a pre-emption proceeding remained undecided when a new law came into force.
predicates.amendment_is_claimed_to_be_beneficial: A party argued that the amendment was enacted for the general benefit of the public.
