predicates.provision_is_plain_and_unambiguous: The new provision’s words have a clear meaning and do not give rise to competing interpretations.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The new provision does not express or necessarily imply that it applies to earlier rights or proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A substituted provision is not declaratory or retrospective merely because it replaces an earlier provision.
material_facts: The amendment replaced the earlier provision governing pre-emption with a provision limiting the right to tenants.
The earlier provision was plain and its meaning was not in doubt; the amendment did not purport to explain an omission or clarify the meaning of the earlier provision.
The amendment contained no express or implied indication that it was intended to operate retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: A declaratory or explanatory enactment generally operates retrospectively when it removes an existing doubt or supplies an obvious omission in earlier law; its substance, not its label, determines its character. Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas and R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan state this principle. Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare was overruled on the relevant point by R. Rajagopal Reddy. A substituted provision is subject to the ordinary rules governing amending enactments.
members.conclusion: The amendment was not declaratory and had no retrospective operation.

rule.if: preemption_law_amended_during_appeal and earlier_provision_was_clear and amendment_does_not_clarify_doubt_or_supply_omission and no_retroactive_intent

predicates.preemption_law_amended_during_appeal: A new provision governing pre-emption came into force while an appeal in a pre-emption proceeding was pending.
predicates.earlier_provision_was_clear: The prior provision had a plain meaning that was not in doubt.
predicates.amendment_does_not_clarify_doubt_or_supp: The amendment does not explain an uncertain earlier provision or fill an obvious gap in it.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The amendment does not expressly or by necessary implication apply to earlier rights or proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A clear amendment affecting substantive rights is not retrospective merely because it substitutes a provision or is beneficial, and it is not declaratory without an intention to clarify or explain the prior law.
material_facts: The amendment substituted a plain and unambiguous provision limiting the right of pre-emption to tenants.
The prior provision was also clear, and the amendment did not expressly or by necessary implication address pending claims or declare what the prior law meant.
The amendment affected the substantive pre-emption rights at issue.
members.legal_principle: A statute affecting substantive rights is presumed prospective unless retrospective operation is expressed or necessarily implied; procedural changes are generally presumed retrospective, subject to limits. A declaratory or explanatory enactment clarifies the prior law or supplies an obvious omission, and its substance—not merely its label—determines its character. Benevolent construction cannot add words to a clear provision or re-legislate it. The Court relied on Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry, Dayawati v. Inderjit, Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra, K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan, Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas and R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan; it distinguished Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Chetri and H. Shiva Rao v. Celelia Pereira, whose statutory contexts or ambiguity differed.
members.conclusion: The amendment was prospective, was not declaratory, and could not be made retrospective through benevolent construction.

rule.if: substantive_right_affected and amendment_text_clear and no_retroactive_intent and no_prior_law_clarification and preemption_case_pending_on_appeal

predicates.substantive_right_affected: The amendment changes a substantive right rather than merely regulating procedure.
predicates.amendment_text_clear: The amendment’s language is plain and unambiguous.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The amendment contains no express or necessarily implied intention to operate retrospectively.
predicates.no_prior_law_clarification: The amendment does not clarify an ambiguity or supply an omission in the prior law.
predicates.preemption_case_pending_on_appeal: A pre-emption claim is pending in an appeal when the amendment takes effect.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment expressly adding a power to condone delay does not govern an appeal arising under the prior law when the amendment is prospective and the prior text was unambiguous.
material_facts: The appeal arose under section 93 as it stood before its amendment.
A later amendment expressly made section 5 of the Limitation Act applicable to appeals and revisions under the special enactment.
The amendment was prospective, and the Court found that the earlier text was unambiguous and that the amendment was not clarificatory.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the amendment to section 93 by the Andhra Pradesh Tenancy Laws (Amendment) Act, 1979 as a prospective change rather than a clarification of the prior law. Because the earlier text was unambiguous and the amendment was prospective, the amended provision did not govern this appeal.
members.conclusion: The later amendment did not assist the appellant; the appeal was governed by section 93 as originally enacted.

rule.if: appeal_under_special_enactment and proceeding_arose_under_prior_law and later_amendment_expressly_added_extension_power and later_amendment_was_prospective and prior_text_was_unambiguous

predicates.appeal_under_special_enactment: The proceeding is an appeal under a special enactment.
predicates.proceeding_arose_under_prior_law: The appeal arose under the law as it stood before a later amendment.
predicates.later_amendment_expressly_added_extensio: A later amendment expressly added power to extend the filing period.
predicates.later_amendment_was_prospective: The later amendment was made to operate prospectively.
predicates.prior_text_was_unambiguous: The text governing the proceeding before the amendment was unambiguous.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment expanding revisional jurisdiction does not apply to a revision concerning an appellate decree that became final under the earlier law before the amendment.
material_facts: The eviction suits were filed before the amendment to the rent statute’s revisional provision.
The appellate court’s decrees became final under the provision as it stood before the amendment.
The revisions were heard after the amendment, and the High Court relied on the amended provision to review the appellate decisions.
members.legal_principle: As held in Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas, an amendment made after an appellate decree has become final under the former Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rent Act cannot be used to set that decree aside. The amendment made by Gujarat Act 18 of 1965 did not govern these proceedings insofar as it purported to enlarge the High Court’s power over the already-final appellate decrees.
members.conclusion: The amended revisional provision could not be used to review the decrees; the High Court could consider the revisions only under its ordinary civil revisional jurisdiction.

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision arising from an appellate decision in a rent-control case.
predicates.appellate_decision_final_before_procedur: The appellate decision became final under the earlier procedural law before a later amendment was enacted.
predicates.revision_considered_after_procedural_ame: The revision was considered after the later procedural amendment was enacted.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment expanding revisional jurisdiction does not apply to a decision that had become final before the amendment, absent a clear indication of retrospective operation.
material_facts: The appellate court had confirmed the trial court’s decision, and that appellate decision had become final subject only to the High Court’s limited revisional jurisdiction under the Code of Civil Procedure.
While the revision petition was pending, an amendment gave the High Court wider power to examine whether the appellate decision was according to law.
The amendment contained no indication that it was to operate retrospectively, but the High Court applied its expanded power and reversed the appellate decision.
members.legal_principle: Under section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, as amended, the High Court received revisional power wider than that available under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the absence of express words or necessary intendment, an enactment that takes away the finality of an existing decision or enlarges jurisdiction over it is not retrospective; such a change is substantive, not merely procedural or explanatory. This applies the principle in Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. v. Irving and Dafedar Niranjan Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, and distinguishes Indira Sohan Lal v. Custodian of Evacuee Property and Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan because in those cases the relevant decision had not become final before the change. Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Safibhai describes the limits of the High Court’s jurisdiction under section 115 in this context.
members.conclusion: The expanded revisional jurisdiction could not be applied to the already-final appellate decision. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the revision petition was remanded for decision under the limited jurisdiction on which it had been filed.

rule.if: rent_appeal_revision and appellate_decision_final_before_later_law and later_law_expands_review_power and no_retroactive_intent

predicates.rent_appeal_revision: The proceeding is a revision arising from an appeal in a rent-control dispute.
predicates.appellate_decision_final_before_later_la: The appellate decision had become final, subject only to the previously available limited review, before the later law took effect.
predicates.later_law_expands_review_power: A later law gives the reviewing court broader power to examine the appellate decision than it previously had.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The later law contains no express or necessarily implied indication that the expanded power applies retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: A later amendment that applies retrospectively to certain statutory-officer decisions does not revive a decision already vacated by a final civil court decree unless the amendment clearly provides for that result.
material_facts: Before the 1960 amendment commenced, final civil court decrees had determined that the village was not an estate and had thereby vacated the Settlement Officer’s earlier decision on that issue.
The amendment addressed certain earlier decisions of Settlement Officers or tribunals, but did not expressly state that it revived decisions already vacated by civil court decrees.
The amendment did not specify a commencement date earlier than its publication.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may alter the basis of a court’s decision, but merely declaring a decision non-binding is not enough to reverse it; the conditions on which the decision rests must be fundamentally altered. Even where legislation has some retrospective operation, it should not be read to interfere with vested rights more than its plain words require. Section 9-A of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, as inserted by the 1960 amendment, covered decisions still subsisting at commencement and did not clearly revive decisions already vacated by competent court decrees. Section 64-A(2) remained relevant to the binding effect of civil court decisions. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, [1970] 1 SCR 388, and Reid v. Reid, (1886) 31 Ch. D. 403 at 408.
members.conclusion: The 1960 amendment applied only to decisions that were still subsisting at its commencement; it did not revive the Settlement Officer’s decision already vacated by the final civil court decrees or affect those decrees’ finality and binding effect.

predicates.civil_decree_preceded_later_amendment: A civil court decree was made before a later amendment came into force.
predicates.decree_vacated_officer_decision: The decree vacated the statutory officer’s decision on the matter.
predicates.amendment_clearly_revives_vacated_decisi: The amendment clearly provides that decisions already vacated by court decrees are revived.

members.legal_issue: Statutory interest on acquisition compensation does not run for a period before the preliminary acquisition notification, although a landowner dispossessed earlier may seek rent or damages for that earlier period.
material_facts: The land was submerged and possession was taken before the preliminary acquisition notification was issued.
The Reference Court and High Court awarded interest on enhanced compensation from the earlier submergence date.

The claimants had not acquired a statutory entitlement to acquisition compensation for the period before the acquisition notification, but the Court directed that they could apply for rent or damages for that period.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(1A), 23(2), 28 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 do not authorize statutory acquisition interest for a period before the preliminary notification. When possession is taken before that notification, title remains with the owner and the owner may seek rent or damages for use and occupation. The Court followed R.L. Jain v. Delhi Development Authority and Lila Ghosh v. State of West Bengal, which treated the earlier view in Special Tahsildar (LA), PWD Schemes v. M.A. Jabbar as correct and rejected the contrary view in Assistant Commissioner, Gadag Sub-Division v. Mathapathi Basavannewwa; it also distinguished Satinder Singh v. Umrao Singh.
members.conclusion: The awards of statutory interest for the period before the notification were set aside. The claimants were permitted to seek rent or damages from the competent authority for the period of earlier dispossession until the notification, with any amounts already paid for that period to be adjusted.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: A court is determining statutory compensation in a compulsory land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.possession_taken_before_preliminary_noti: The acquiring authority took or retained possession of the land before publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: Statutory acquisition interest is unavailable for a period before the preliminary acquisition notice when possession was taken before that notice.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that the land had been submerged before the acquisition process began and sought interest for that earlier period.
The land’s alleged submergence and the date possession was lost were disputed, and evidence indicated that the land may have remained in cultivation.
The High Court had awarded statutory interest from the date of the award.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 28 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, statutory interest runs from when compensation becomes payable, ordinarily from the award; it is not available for a period before acquisition proceedings begin. Lila Ghosh v. State of West Bengal and Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Karigowda support this rule. R.L. Jain v. DDA distinguishes pre-notification possession, for which rent or damages may be claimed, from statutory interest. The urgency procedure in section 17 is an exception under which compensation and interest may be payable from earlier possession; this case was not treated as falling within that exception.
members.conclusion: Interest under the statutory interest provisions cannot be awarded for a period before the preliminary acquisition notice merely because possession was taken earlier.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: A claimant pursued an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.possession_preceded_notice: The claimant alleged that possession of the land was taken before the preliminary acquisition notice.
predicates.interest_claimed_for_pre_notice_period: The claimant sought statutory interest for a period before the preliminary acquisition notice.

members.legal_issue: Statutory interest is unavailable for a period of possession that preceded publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.
material_facts: The claimant was dispossessed before the later acquisition proceedings began.
The earlier acquisition proceedings were declared invalid by a decree that became final.
The Collector’s later award included statutory interest running from the earlier dispossession, and the High Court set that interest aside.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 must be read in the context of the Act’s acquisition and possession provisions: the possession that triggers statutory interest is possession taken lawfully under Sections 16 or 17, after the required acquisition steps. Possession before publication of a Section 4(1) notification is de hors the Act and cannot trigger interest under Section 34; the same understanding of lawful possession informs Section 28. Union of India v. Budh Singh and Smt. Lila Ghosh v. State of West Bengal support this conclusion. Shri Vijay Cotton & Oil Mills v. State of Gujarat did not decide whether statutory interest is payable for pre-notification possession and is not authority for that proposition; the Court also relies on the principle that a decision is authority for what it actually decides, as stated in Krishena Kumar v. Union of India, Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Gurnam Kaur, and M/s. Orient Paper and Industries Ltd. v. State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to interest under the acquisition statute for the period before publication of the preliminary notification; the High Court was correct to set aside that part of the award.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.possession_preceded_acquisition_notice: The state took possession before publication of the preliminary notice that began the acquisition proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Interest under the land acquisition statute is unavailable for a period of possession that precedes publication of the acquisition notification, and a court cannot award interest beyond the statute’s prescribed rate and period.
material_facts: Possession of the land was taken for a public purpose before acquisition proceedings were initiated under the land acquisition statute.
The owners later received compensation following acquisition proceedings initiated by publication of a notification under the statute.
In execution of the decree, the court directed payment of interest at 18% per annum from the date possession was first taken, and the High Court upheld that direction.
members.legal_principle: The Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is a self-contained code governing the State’s liability to pay interest and the owner’s entitlement to it. Sections 4(1), 17, 28 and 34 govern the statutory acquisition process and interest; section 48(2) provides a remedy for damages when acquisition proceedings are withdrawn. Publication of the section 4(1) notification is a condition precedent to possession being treated as possession taken under the Act. Courts cannot use common-law principles of justice, equity and good conscience to award interest contrary to the statute. Vallabhdas Naranji v. Development Officer, Bandra did not decide entitlement to interest for possession predating the notification. Revenue Divisional Officer, Trichinopoly v. Venkatarama Ayyar involved possession connected to the exercise of statutory urgency powers, and State of Punjab v. Raminder Kaur concerned possession taken pursuant to an earlier section 4(1) notification; those decisions were consistent with, rather than contrary to, the statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The owners could not receive statutory interest for the period before publication of the acquisition notification, and the court could not award interest at a rate or for a period beyond that authorized by the statute. The owners were entitled to interest on enhanced compensation at 9% from 16 October 1984; the direction for 18% interest from the date of initial possession was set aside.

rule.if: appeal_from_execution_order and possession_taken_before_acquisition_notification and later_acquisition_proceedings_under_statute and statute_prescribes_interest_entitlement and lower_court_awarded_interest_for_pre_notification_period_or_beyond_statutory_rate

predicates.appeal_from_execution_order: The matter is an appeal concerning an order made in execution of a decree.
predicates.possession_taken_before_acquisition_noti: The acquiring authority took possession before publication of the notification that initiated acquisition under the statute.
predicates.later_acquisition_proceedings_under_stat: Acquisition proceedings under the statute were initiated after possession had been taken.
predicates.statute_prescribes_interest_entitlement: The applicable statute specifies when interest is payable and the rate or manner of its payment.
predicates.lower_court_awarded_interest_for_pre_not: The lower court directed interest for a period before the acquisition notification or at a rate exceeding the statutory entitlement.

members.legal_issue: A person whose immovable property is compulsorily acquired and possessed is entitled to interest on compensation for the period before the compensation is paid or deposited, unless the governing law clearly excludes that entitlement.
material_facts: The State took possession of the claimants' immovable property before paying or depositing the compensation.
The acquisition statute expressly applied section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, but the Court found that this did not exclude the principles underlying sections 28 and 34 of that Act.
The claimants sought interest from the taking of possession until payment or deposit of compensation.

The Court directed interest at four per cent per annum and allocated it according to the parties' respective compensation interests, including the maintenance beneficiary's entitlement to interest on compensation for the village charged for her maintenance.
members.legal_principle: The taking of possession of immovable property generally implies an obligation to pay interest on its value, because interest takes the place of the owner's right to retain possession. The Court applied Swift & Co. v. Board of Trade, Birch v. Joy, and Inglewood Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd. v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, and approved Surjan Singh v. The East Punjab Government. It held that section 5(e) of the 1948 Act, by applying section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, did not exclude the general rule or the principles underlying sections 28 and 34 of that Act. The proviso to section 1 of the Interest Act, 1839, saved interest otherwise payable by law; the Court referred to Bengal Nagpur Railway Co. Ltd. v. Buttanji Ramji on that proviso. It distinguished the relevant observations in Seth Thawardas Pherumal v. The Union of India in light of Nachiappa Chettiar v. Subramaniam Chettiar.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest from the date the State took possession until the compensation was paid or deposited; interest on the compensation for the village charged for maintenance was payable to the maintenance beneficiary, and interest on the other compensation was payable equally to the holder and the reversioner.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_of_immovable_prop: The proceeding concerns immovable property taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.state_took_possession_before_compensatio: The acquiring authority took possession before paying or depositing compensation.
predicates.governing_law_did_not_clearly_exclude_in: The governing law did not clearly show an intention to deny interest for the period between possession and payment.

members.legal_issue: An owner deprived of possession of property through compulsory requisition is entitled to interest on unpaid compensation for the period of deprivation, absent a clear statutory intention to exclude that entitlement.
material_facts: The appeal was confined to whether interest was payable on compensation awarded by an arbitrator for requisition of premises.
The owner had been deprived of possession of the premises, and part of the compensation remained unpaid during the period of deprivation.
The premises were later de-requisitioned and returned to the owner, and the principal compensation was paid by 31 July 1987.
members.legal_principle: Upon a statutory compulsory taking of property, interest on the compensation is ordinarily payable from the date possession is taken because it substitutes for the owner's lost right to retain possession; the taking of possession gives rise to an implied obligation to pay interest. The entitlement is not excluded merely because a statute makes compensation provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 applicable, unless the statute clearly indicates a contrary intention. The Court relied on Satinder Singh v. Amrao Singh, [1961] 3 SCR 676 at 694; National Insurance Co. Ltd., Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, [1963] Supp. 2 SCR 971 at 992; Hirachand Kothari v. State of Rajasthan, [1985] Supp. 1 SCR 644 at 655; and Inglewood Pulp and Paper Co. Ltd. v. New Brunswick Electric Power Commission, AIR 1928 PC 287.
members.conclusion: The appellants were entitled to interest on the unpaid balance of the compensation for the relevant period of deprivation. Interest was payable at 6% per annum from 7 March 1975 to 28 February 1985, and at 12% per annum from 8 August 1985 to 31 July 1987; the latter rate applied only for that period. Interest was calculated on the balance remaining unpaid from the respective dates, and the appeal was disposed of with costs.

rule.if: requisition_compensation_appeal and owner_deprived_of_possession and compensation_unpaid_during_deprivation and no_clear_statutory_exclusion

predicates.requisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding concerns an appeal about interest on compensation awarded for compulsory requisition of property.
predicates.owner_deprived_of_possession: The owner lost possession of the property through the compulsory taking.
predicates.compensation_unpaid_during_deprivation: Some of the compensation remained unpaid while the owner was deprived of possession.
predicates.no_clear_statutory_exclusion: The applicable law did not clearly express an intention to exclude interest for the period of deprivation.

members.legal_issue: A person deprived of immovable property is entitled to reasonable interest on the compensation due, which may be awarded on equitable grounds.
material_facts: The claimant was deprived of possession of property under the failed exchange arrangement.
The State did not deliver the exchange property or pay compensation when the claimant was deprived of the property.
The Court considered interest necessary to compensate for the deprivation and the rise in the property's value.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 1 of the Interest Act, 1839, a court may award interest on equitable grounds. Relying on Satinder Singh v. Amrao Singh, which referred to Swift & Co. v. Board of Trade and Birch v. Joy, the Court applied the principle that taking possession of immovable property generally implies an agreement to pay interest on its value.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to reasonable interest on the compensation, with interest awarded on equitable grounds.

predicates.civil_compensation_claim: A claimant brings a civil claim seeking compensation for property or its value.
predicates.claimant_deprived_of_immovable_property: A claimant is deprived of possession of immovable property by another party.
predicates.compensation_remains_unpaid: The party responsible has not paid compensation for the property taken.

members.legal_issue: The additional statutory amount on market value is unavailable for a period before publication of the preliminary acquisition notification.
material_facts: The claimant was dispossessed before the later acquisition proceedings began.
The Collector’s later award included an additional amount calculated from the earlier dispossession.
The Court considered conflicting decisions on whether that additional amount could cover a pre-notification period.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1-A) ties the additional amount to a period beginning on publication of the notification under Section 4(1). The Court followed Special Tehsildar (LA) PWD Schemes Vijaywada v. M.A. Jabbar and held that the additional amount does not extend to a period before that publication; it rejected the contrary holding in Assistant Commissioner, Gadag, Sub-Division, Gadag v. Mathapathi Basavanewwa.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to the additional statutory amount for the period before publication of the preliminary notification; the contrary view in Assistant Commissioner, Gadag, Sub-Division, Gadag v. Mathapathi Basavanewwa was overruled.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.possession_preceded_acquisition_notice: The state took possession before publication of the preliminary notice that began the acquisition proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Additional compensation for acquired land does not accrue for a period before publication of the acquisition notification, even when possession was taken earlier.
material_facts: Possession of the owners’ land was taken for an irrigation project before publication of the acquisition notification.
The acquisition notification was published later, followed by an award of compensation.
In execution proceedings, the owners claimed additional compensation beginning on the earlier date when possession was taken.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 fixes the beginning of the additional-compensation period at publication of the notification under Section 4(1), and its endpoint at the award or taking of possession, whichever is earlier. Where possession precedes publication, that possession date cannot serve as the endpoint for a period beginning at publication; the award is the available endpoint. The provision’s clear language permits no alternative construction to avoid an allegedly unjust result. The Court approved Special Tahsildar (LA), P.W.D. Schemes v. M.A. Jabbar, [1995] 2 SCC 142, and disapproved Asstt. Commr., Gadag Sub-Division v. Mathapathi Basavannewwa, [1995] 6 SCC 355, and State of H.P. v. Dharam Das, [1995] 5 SCC 683.
members.conclusion: The owners were entitled to additional compensation only for the period beginning on publication of the acquisition notification and ending on the date of the award, because possession had been taken before the notification.

predicates.additional_compensation_claim_in_land_ac: The proceeding concerns a claim for additional compensation in a land acquisition.
predicates.possession_precedes_notice_publication: The acquiring authority took possession of the land before the acquisition notice was published.
predicates.award_follows_notice_publication: The compensation award was made after publication of the acquisition notice.

members.legal_issue: A landowner is entitled to interest when awarded compensation is not paid or deposited before possession is taken.
material_facts: The Trust said it had paid the compensation to the Collector before possession was taken.
The landowner claimed interest, and the High Court upheld that claim and directed the necessary parties to appear before the Executing Court to determine the amount.
The Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s conclusion that interest was due and payable.
members.legal_principle: Sections 31 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require the Collector to tender the compensation or, in the circumstances specified by Section 31, deposit it in court. If compensation is not paid or deposited before possession is taken, Section 34 requires interest. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: Interest is payable to the landowner if the compensation is not paid or deposited before possession is taken; the amount was left for determination by the Executing Court.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by a public authority.
predicates.compensation_not_paid_or_deposited_befor: The awarded compensation was not paid to the interested person or deposited in court before possession of the land was taken.

members.legal_issue: A landowner deprived of advance compensation in an emergency acquisition is entitled to additional interest for the delay in payment.
material_facts: Possession was taken under the emergency procedure before the prescribed advance compensation was received by the landowners.
Funds had been deposited by the beneficiary with State authorities, but the record did not establish that the landowners had received the money before possession or promptly thereafter.
The State paid the award only after a substantial delay.
members.legal_principle: Justice Kumar read Sections 17(1), 17(3A), and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 harmoniously, treating the advance-payment obligation as requiring payment before possession and applying the interest protection in Section 34 to non-compliance. He also applied the principle that, where the law specifies no time for performance, payment must be made within a reasonable time.
members.conclusion: Justice Swatanter Kumar held that, where the prescribed advance compensation was not paid on time, the claimants were entitled to additional interest, applying the enhanced interest rate in the proviso to Section 34 from the relevant emergency-acquisition period until payment. He also held that interest was payable on the balance compensation from possession. The judges' broader disagreement was referred to a larger Bench.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land.
predicates.advance_compensation_received_before_pos: The landowners received the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.

members.legal_issue: The validating effect of the retrospective provision for property that purported to vest as evacuee property under a repealed law does not depend on a defect in that law or its procedure.
material_facts: The properties had been taken over as evacuee properties under an earlier regional law and remained with the Custodian through the subsequent legal transitions.
The heirs challenged the properties’ treatment as evacuee property, including the procedure by which they had been taken over.
members.legal_principle: Section 8(2A) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, read with section 8(2), validates property that purported to vest under a repealed law and actions relating to it, whether or not the earlier law or procedure was defective. The non-obstante clause does not limit that effect. The Court relied on The Dominion of India v. Shrinbai A. Irani, Azeemunnisa v. The Deputy Custodian Evacuee Properties, M/s. Haji Ismail Noor Mohammad & Co. v. The Competent Officer, and approved Ahmedbhai Abdulkadar v. The Custodian of Evacuee Property.
members.conclusion: The validating provision applied even if the earlier law and the taking over were free of defects; it also cured any defects in the vesting or procedure.

predicates.legacy_evacuee_property_case: The proceeding concerns property dealt with as evacuee property under an earlier law that was later repealed.
predicates.property_purported_to_vest_under_repeale: The property purported to vest as evacuee property in a person exercising custodian powers under the earlier law.

members.legal_issue: A validating law that expressly operates notwithstanding court judgments can validate an earlier acquisition previously set aside if the acquisition is complete and satisfies the law’s substantive conditions.
material_facts: A court had previously set aside the acquisition notification.
The validating law expressly applied notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of a court.
The land had vested in the Government, and the acquisition was for a factory serving the public purpose of the company’s industry.
members.legal_principle: A validating enactment that expressly operates notwithstanding judgments is intended to validate actions otherwise held invalid, to the extent of the enactment’s validation. It can reach an acquisition already set aside by a court where the land has vested in the Government and the acquisition satisfies the substantive conditions for validation.
members.conclusion: The previous judgment setting aside the acquisition does not prevent validation because the law expressly operates notwithstanding court judgments, and the completed acquisition satisfied the applicable conditions.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_previously_set_: A party challenges an acquisition that a court previously set aside.
predicates.validating_law_expressly_overrides_court: The validating law expressly states that it operates notwithstanding court judgments or orders.
predicates.land_has_vested_in_government: The acquired land has vested in the Government.
predicates.acquisition_satisfies_public_purpose_con: The acquisition satisfies the substantive conditions requiring the acquired building or work to serve a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A law may validate acquisitions made under an earlier notification despite not giving retrospective effect to amendments that authorize multiple reports and declarations.
material_facts: The earlier acquisition notification had been followed by a first declaration and then by further declarations for other parcels of land.
Under the earlier Supreme Court ruling, those later declarations could not be supported by the original notification.
The validating law provided that acquisitions and related actions would not be invalid merely because multiple declarations had been made under one notification, notwithstanding contrary judgments.
The amendments authorizing multiple reports and declarations were not expressly made retrospective.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may validate past actions either by expressly making an amendment retrospective or by separately providing that past actions are not to be treated as invalid on specified grounds. The power to enact the latter form of validation is ancillary to legislative power over the subject, subject to constitutional limitations. The Court relied on United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum, Piare Dusadh v. The King Emperor, and West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The absence of express retrospective operation for the amendments did not invalidate the separate provision validating past acquisitions and actions.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validation_o: A party challenges a law that validates past land acquisitions.
predicates.one_notification_was_followed_by_multipl: The acquiring authority made more than one declaration concerning parcels covered by the same earlier notification.
predicates.validation_law_expressly_preserves_past_: The legislature expressly provided that past acquisitions and related actions would not be invalid on the specified ground.
predicates.underlying_amendment_is_not_expressly_re: The amendment authorizing the relevant procedure was not expressly given retrospective effect.

members.legal_issue: A validating statute that applies to previously acquired undertakings can retrospectively validate earlier acquisition actions that complied with the earlier enactment and are not inconsistent with the validating statute.
material_facts: The undertaking was taken over under an earlier enactment that was later held invalid.
The later enactment incorporated the acquisition scheme, applied expressly to undertakings already taken over, and included a clause validating prior orders, notifications, proceedings, and acts.
The challenged acquisition notification was issued in the manner contemplated by the earlier enactment and was not shown to conflict with the later enactment.
members.legal_principle: The enactment's definitions and provisions applying to undertakings already taken over showed that its material and operative provisions were retrospective. The validation clause covered prior actions that would have been properly taken under the earlier enactment if it had been valid, subject to consistency with the later enactment. The absence of the usual words deeming prior notifications to have been issued under the new enactment did not alter that effect.
members.conclusion: The later enactment operated retrospectively, and its validation clause deemed the earlier acquisition notification valid under the later enactment.

predicates.acquisition_validation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition action taken before a later enactment that addresses prior acquisitions.
predicates.later_law_covers_prior_acquisitions: The legislature enacted a law whose operative scheme applies to undertakings already taken over.
predicates.prior_action_would_have_been_proper_unde: The acquiring authority took the earlier action in the manner the earlier enactment required, assuming that enactment had been valid.
predicates.prior_action_does_not_conflict_with_late: The earlier acquisition action is not inconsistent with the provisions of the later enactment.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective law validating a property acquisition can satisfy the requirement that a person be deprived of property only by authority of law.
material_facts: The property was taken under an earlier enactment that was void.
A later enactment applied retrospectively and purported to validate the acquisition action.

The constitutional property guarantee required deprivation to be by authority of law, while the separate protection against retrospective criminal punishment expressly referred to a law in force at the time.
members.legal_principle: The property guarantee required deprivation by authority of law but did not use the phrase “law in force at the time.” By contrast, the protection against retrospective criminal punishment used that phrase, indicating that retrospective operation was excluded there. Accordingly, a subsequent law operating retrospectively could validate the acquisition for purposes of the property guarantee.
members.conclusion: The retrospective operation of the later enactment supplied authority of law for the acquisition and satisfied the property guarantee.

predicates.property_deprivation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a deprivation of property on the ground that it lacked legal authority.
predicates.later_law_operates_retrospectively: The legislature enacted a law that applies to events occurring before its enactment.
predicates.later_law_validates_the_acquisition: The later law purports to validate the earlier acquisition action.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective enactment may deem a required acquisition notice to have been issued and validate an acquisition, preventing the acquisition from being challenged solely because the notice was not actually issued.
material_facts: A notice was issued under the general land acquisition law for land needed for coal prospecting, and no objection was filed within the specified period.
The central government later acquired land within the area covered by the original notice without actually issuing the intermediate notice required by the coal-bearing-areas acquisition law.
The acquisition was challenged, and the High Court restrained the acquiring corporation because the intermediate notice had not been issued.

While the appeal was pending, Parliament enacted retrospective provisions deeming the intermediate notice and the absence of an objection, and validating acquisitions within the specified category despite court decisions.
The respondent did not identify a ground on which the amending law could be held invalid, and its legislative competence was conceded.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on section 28(3) and the added section 28(3A) of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, as amended, and section 3 of the 1969 Amendment Act, which retrospectively deemed the relevant notices and objections and validated specified acquisitions notwithstanding court decisions. It also relied on Parliament’s competence to create legal fictions and enact retrospective validation. No earlier cases were cited. The Court did not decide whether the High Court’s original interpretation of the unamended law was correct.
members.conclusion: The retrospective amendments applied to the acquisition and prevented it from being challenged solely on the ground that the intermediate notice had not been issued. The appeal was allowed.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and land_notice_issued and no_objection_filed_within_period and intermediate_notice_not_actually_issued and legislature_retroactively_validated_covered_acquisitions and acquisition_within_validated_category

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: An appeal is brought against an order restraining action under an acquisition.
predicates.land_notice_issued: The government issued an initial notice identifying land for a stated public purpose.
predicates.no_objection_filed_within_period: No affected person filed an objection within the applicable period after the initial notice.
predicates.intermediate_notice_not_actually_issued: The government proceeded with the acquisition without actually issuing a notice required between the initial notice and acquisition.
predicates.legislature_retroactively_validated_cove: The legislature enacted a retrospective law deeming the required procedural steps completed and validating acquisitions in a specified category.
predicates.acquisition_within_validated_category: The challenged acquisition falls within the category of acquisitions covered by the retrospective validation.

members.legal_issue: A validating enactment that retrospectively makes one acquisition procedure govern earlier acquisitions prevents objections based on failure to follow the displaced improvement scheme, while preserving constitutional objections and challenges allowed under the governing acquisition law.
material_facts: The land acquisitions had been undertaken under the general land-acquisition law for purposes connected with the improvement, expansion, or development of a city.
A later validating enactment deemed the earlier acquisitions and related proceedings valid notwithstanding the improvement law and other laws or court orders.
The enactment also preserved challenges under the applicable land-acquisition laws and their rules.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(1)(a) of the Bangalore Acquisition of Lands (Validation) Act, 1962, validated covered acquisitions notwithstanding the City of Bangalore Improvement Act and other laws, judgments, decrees, or orders. Section 2(2) preserved challenges under the Mysore Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and their rules. The words barring challenges on any other ground were read down so that constitutional and fundamental-rights objections remained available.
members.conclusion: Objections based on non-observance of the improvement law had to fail. The broad words barring challenges did not exclude objections based on the Constitution or fundamental rights, or challenges permitted under the land-acquisition laws and rules.

predicates.covered_acquisition_validation_case: The proceeding challenges an earlier land acquisition of the kind addressed by a later enactment that validates acquisitions and related steps.
predicates.validation_law_displaces_improvement_pro: The legislature made the earlier acquisitions valid notwithstanding a separate improvement scheme and provided for them to be governed by the acquisition procedure that had been used.

members.legal_issue: Cancellation of a quasi-permanent evacuee-property allotment under lawful authority does not, in these circumstances, establish a breach of the allottee’s constitutional property right.
material_facts: The allottees held land under a quasi-permanent settlement that did not confer proprietary rights or permanent rights of occupation.
The allotments were subject to the evacuee-property legislation and were cancelled by an authority with jurisdiction after the allottees had an opportunity to present their case.
The allottees challenged the cancellation as a deprivation of their constitutional property right.
members.legal_principle: The quasi-permanent character of the settlement did not make an allotment irrevocable: the land remained subject to the governing evacuee-property legislation and the custodian’s cancellation powers. Because the cancellation was within jurisdiction and the allottees had been heard, the Court found no breach of the property right asserted under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The allottees did not establish a breach of a fundamental right, and the challenged orders were valid and within jurisdiction.

predicates.constitutional_property_right_challenge: The proceeding claims that cancellation of an allotment breached a constitutional property right.
predicates.quasi_permanent_allotment_subject_to_can: The allotment was quasi-permanent and remained subject to the governing authority’s power to cancel it.
predicates.lawful_cancellation_after_opportunity_to: An empowered authority lawfully cancelled the allotment after the allottee had an opportunity to present their case.

members.legal_issue: Cancellation of the allotment did not deprive the applicants of property without authority of law.
material_facts: The allotments were subject to powers of cancellation under the governing law and rules.
The cancellation was made by the responsible authorities as part of a readjustment of land allotments following a higher authority’s direction.
The applicants sought revision, and the reviewing authority heard them before dismissing their challenge.
The cancellation was an exercise of the statutory power governing the allotments, not an usurpation of jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(1) requires both deprivation of property and deprivation without authority of law. The Court applied section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and the rules governing cancellation, including the 1949 allotment conditions and the applicable rules made under the Act. Sections 28 and 46 of the Act made the relevant orders final and barred civil or revenue court challenges to matters entrusted to the authorities. The Court noted the broader view expressed in State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose about deprivation of an individual right within a bundle of property rights, but observed that the other members of the Court had not shared that view; it held that, in any event, the cancellation here was authorized by law. The principle in Julius v. Lord Bishop of Oxford did not establish an indefeasible entitlement to transfer of the allotted land because the allotment remained subject to cancellation under the applicable statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: Even assuming that the allotment interest was property, its cancellation was not a deprivation without authority of law and did not infringe a fundamental right.

predicates.constitutional_petition_challenging_allo: A person sought constitutional relief against cancellation of an allotment of land.
predicates.allotment_rights_are_subject_to_statutor: The allottee's rights were expressly subject to cancellation under the governing scheme.
predicates.cancellation_is_made_by_authorized_offic: An official responsible for administering the allotment scheme cancelled the allotment.
predicates.under_statutory_power: The official relied on a legal power governing cancellation of the allotment.
predicates.order_is_within_authority_jurisdiction: The cancellation was an exercise of the authority's assigned function rather than an usurpation of jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: Cancellation of a quasi-permanent allotment under the law that created it does not deprive the allottee of property without authority of law.
material_facts: The allotments were made under a statutory scheme that made them subject to cancellation or resumption.
The Custodian cancelled the allotments while readjusting land allotments, and the cancellation was affirmed on revision after the parties were heard.
The cancellation was made by the authorities exercising statutory powers, rather than by an usurpation of jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(1) of the Constitution required deprivation to be without authority of law before it could be infringed; deprivation alone was insufficient. The Court treated cancellation as the exercise of a power inherent in the statutory allotment, under section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950. It also noted that sections 28 and 46 of that Act barred the challenged orders from being called into question in the manner attempted, absent an illegal usurpation of jurisdiction. The Court referred to State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose for a broader view of property under Article 31(1), but that view was not shared by the other members of the Court and did not alter the result.
members.conclusion: The cancellation did not violate Article 31(1), because it enforced a power of resumption or cancellation that was an incident of the allotment and was exercised under the law governing it.

rule.if: constitutional_property_petition and statutory_land_allotment and allotment_subject_to_resumption and custodian_cancelled_under_statutory_authority and no_jurisdictional_usurpation

predicates.constitutional_property_petition: A person brought a constitutional proceeding alleging deprivation of a property interest.
predicates.statutory_land_allotment: The person held land under an allotment created by statute.
predicates.allotment_subject_to_resumption: The terms governing the allotment made the interest subject to cancellation or resumption.
predicates.custodian_cancelled_under_statutory_auth: The official responsible for administering the allotted property cancelled the allotment by exercising statutory cancellation authority.
predicates.no_jurisdictional_usurpation: The cancellation was not an illegal assumption of power by an authority lacking jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A deprivation resulting from a property declaration made under a valid law is not a deprivation without authority of law.
material_facts: The petitioner argued that declaring his purchased land to be evacuee property deprived him of property without authority of law.
The declaration was made under a law enacted by Parliament, and the Court rejected the constitutional challenge to the relevant provisions.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(1) prohibits deprivation of property save by authority of law. A deprivation resulting from a declaration made pursuant to a valid law enacted by Parliament is made under authority of law; the result would differ if the law were unconstitutional. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The declaration did not violate the prohibition on deprivation of property without authority of law because it was made pursuant to a law enacted by Parliament.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A person raises a constitutional challenge to being deprived of property.
predicates.deprivation_follows_official_property_de: An official declaration results in the person losing the property or its recognized status.
predicates.declaration_is_pursuant_to_valid_law: The official makes the declaration under a law that is valid.

members.legal_issue: A quasi-permanent allotment of evacuee agricultural land did not constitute property attracting the constitutional protections claimed.
material_facts: The applicants held agricultural land under quasi-permanent allotments made to displaced landholders.
The allotments conferred use and occupation, including rights that could benefit heirs, but the original owners retained ultimate ownership while the land remained evacuee property.
The allotments were subject to statutory cancellation or resumption powers, and the applicants could not ordinarily transfer them by sale, mortgage, gift, or will.
The applicants had not received instruments transferring permanent ownership of the allotted land.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1), 31(2), and 31(2A), and the statutory scheme under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, including sections 8–10, 12, and 16; the 1949 allotment conditions; the relevant rules governing cancellation; and sections 10, 12, and 19 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, together with rules 72(2) and 102. The statutory grant remained provisional and subject to cancellation; it was not transferable or disposable in the ordinary ways required for protection under Article 19(1)(f), and it did not amount to ownership or a right of possession of the kind addressed by Article 31(2). The Court distinguished the stage at which permanent ownership was granted by a sanad. It noted Dunichand Hakim v. Deputy Commissioner as background to the rehabilitation scheme, and disagreed with the view in Suraj Parkash Kapur v. State of Punjab insofar as it treated the allottee’s interest as constitutionally protected property.
members.conclusion: The interest created by a quasi-permanent allotment was not property attracting protection under Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1), or 31(2) of the Constitution.

rule.if: constitutional_petition_challenging_allotment_cancellation and statutory_use_and_occupation_grant and (grantor_retains_cancellation_power and interest_is_not_ordinarily_transferable) and (ultimate_title_remains_with_original_owner or permanent_title_instrument_not_issued)

predicates.constitutional_petition_challenging_allo: A person sought constitutional relief against cancellation of an allotment of land.
predicates.statutory_use_and_occupation_grant: An authority granted a person use and occupation of land under a statutory allotment scheme.
predicates.grantor_retains_cancellation_power: The authority granting the allotment retained power to cancel or resume it.
predicates.interest_is_not_ordinarily_transferable: The allottee could not ordinarily transfer or dispose of the interest in the land.
predicates.ultimate_title_remains_with_original_own: The original owner retained ultimate title to the land while it remained within the scheme.
predicates.permanent_title_instrument_not_issued: The allottee had not received an instrument granting permanent ownership.

members.legal_issue: A quasi-permanent allotment of evacuee agricultural land does not create property protected by the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property.
material_facts: The land was allotted to displaced landholders under a statutory scheme, while ultimate ownership remained with the evacuees.
The allotment was subject to resumption or cancellation for administrative purposes.
The allottees could not ordinarily sell, mortgage, gift or bequeath their allotment rights, and they had not obtained permanent title documents for the land.
members.legal_principle: For Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, property must be capable of acquisition and disposal. An interest granted by statute to a specified class, which an ordinary citizen cannot acquire in normal ways and which the allottee cannot dispose of in normal ways, does not meet that test. The Court relied on the statutory nature and provisional, resumable character of the allotment; it did not rely on an earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The interest created by a quasi-permanent allotment was not property protected by Article 19(1)(f).

rule.if: constitutional_property_petition and quasi_permanent_land_allotment and allotment_subject_to_resumption and allottee_cannot_normally_transfer_interest

predicates.constitutional_property_petition: A person brought a constitutional proceeding seeking protection of an interest in property.
predicates.quasi_permanent_land_allotment: A statutory scheme granted a person provisional use and occupation of land on a quasi-permanent basis.
predicates.allotment_subject_to_resumption: The grant made the person's continued interest in the land subject to resumption or cancellation.
predicates.allottee_cannot_normally_transfer_intere: The person holding the allotment could not ordinarily transfer it by sale, mortgage, gift or will.

members.legal_issue: Cancellation of a quasi-permanent allotment is not an acquisition or requisitioning of property within the protection of Article 31(2).
material_facts: The allottees held a statutory right of use and occupation, while ultimate ownership remained with the evacuees.
The allotment was provisional and subject to cancellation or resumption under the governing scheme.
The challenged cancellation enforced that existing limitation on the allotment rather than transferring ownership of the land to the allottees or acquiring their tenure as ownership.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as it stood before amendment, used concepts of taking possession and acquisition that were inapt for the limited rights comprising a quasi-permanent allotment. The amended Article 31(2), read with Article 31(2A), contemplated acquisition or requisitioning and taking possession as a result of transfer of ownership or of the right to possession; the allotment interest did not fit that description. The Court considered the possible retrospective effect of the amendment but held that the amended provision was inapplicable as well.
members.conclusion: Article 31(2), both before and after its amendment, did not apply to the rights comprising a quasi-permanent allotment.

rule.if: constitutional_property_petition and quasi_permanent_land_allotment and allotment_is_limited_tenure and allotment_subject_to_resumption

predicates.constitutional_property_petition: A person brought a constitutional proceeding alleging that an action concerning property triggered a constitutional acquisition protection.
predicates.quasi_permanent_land_allotment: A statutory scheme granted a person provisional use and occupation of land on a quasi-permanent basis.
predicates.allotment_is_limited_tenure: The person's interest was a limited right of use and occupation rather than ownership of the land.
predicates.allotment_subject_to_resumption: The grant made the person's continued interest in the land subject to resumption or cancellation.

members.legal_issue: Retrospective legislation may constitutionally validate eviction actions taken under an earlier public-premises law by making those actions subject to a replacement law that removes the discriminatory choice between eviction procedures.
material_facts: Eviction orders were made against the occupants under the earlier public-premises law, and appeals from those orders were pending when the replacement law was enacted.

The replacement law applied retrospectively, deemed actions taken under the earlier law to have been taken under its corresponding provisions, and barred courts from entertaining eviction proceedings concerning unauthorised occupation of public premises.
The replacement law provided a single eviction procedure; the procedure, including the right of appeal, was materially the same as the procedure used in the cases.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, the vice identified in Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab, [1967] 3 SCR 399, arose from the availability of both a special eviction procedure and an ordinary-court procedure without guidance for choosing between them. A legislature competent to regulate eviction from public premises may legislate retrospectively and remove that vice by leaving only one procedure. A validating law is sustained where the legislature has competence over the subject and removes the defect identified in the earlier law. The Court relied on M/s West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras, [1963] 2 SCR 747, distinguishing Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma, [1968] 1 SCR 561; it also relied on State of Mysore v. D. Achiah Chetty, [1963] 3 SCR 55, and referred to Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, [1970] 1 SCR 388. The relevant provisions were sections 15 and 20 of the 1971 Act and section 5 of the 1958 Act. Beg J. additionally observed that the 1958 Act had not itself been declared unconstitutional and that the earlier procedure had to satisfy the replacement law's requirements.
members.conclusion: The retrospective replacement law was constitutionally valid, and the earlier eviction actions were to be tested under its provisions; the appeals were dismissed.

predicates.appeal_challenges_eviction_under_earlier: An appeal challenges an eviction action taken under an earlier law governing public premises.
predicates.replacement_law_applies_retroactively: A later law governing eviction from public premises is made applicable to a period that includes the earlier action.
predicates.past_actions_are_deemed_taken_under_repl: The later law treats actions taken under the earlier law as actions taken under its corresponding provisions.
predicates.replacement_law_leaves_one_eviction_proc: The later law leaves a single procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants of public premises rather than a choice between that procedure and an ordinary-court procedure.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_public_pr: The legislature has authority to regulate eviction of unauthorised occupants from public premises.

members.legal_issue: A legislature with authority over acquisition may retrospectively remove discrimination caused by the availability of competing procedures by making the procedure previously followed the only applicable procedure.
material_facts: Two laws provided different procedures for acquiring land for public purposes, and the procedure used for the acquisitions was shorter and more prejudicial to owners.
The legislature later enacted a law that retrospectively made the acquisitions subject to the procedure that had been followed, excluding the competing procedure.
The legislature had authority over the subject of acquisition, and the validating enactment received the required presidential assent.
members.legal_principle: Within its constitutional jurisdiction, the legislature may retrospectively make one of two competing procedures the only applicable procedure, thereby removing discrimination arising from the earlier selection between them. The Court applied Piara Dusadh v. King Emperor, [1944] F.C.R. 61. The Court noted that the required presidential assent had been obtained.
members.conclusion: The legislature could retrospectively remove the procedural discrimination by putting the competing procedure out of action and leaving only the procedure that had been followed; the validating enactment was not invalid on that ground.

rule.if: retrospective_validation_case and legislature_has_acquisition_authority and competing_procedure_removed_retroactively and required_assent_obtained

predicates.retrospective_validation_case: The proceeding challenges a law that retrospectively validates earlier land-acquisition actions.
predicates.legislature_has_acquisition_authority: The legislature enacting the validation law has authority over the subject of land acquisition.
predicates.competing_procedure_removed_retroactivel: The legislature retrospectively removes one of two competing procedures and leaves the procedure previously used as the applicable one.
predicates.required_assent_obtained: The validation law received the assent required for its enactment.

members.legal_issue: Land may be acquired for improvement or another purpose under the governing urban-improvement framework without a scheme having first been framed by the improvement trust.
material_facts: The landowners challenged acquisition under the urban-improvement law on the ground that no scheme had been framed by the improvement trust.
The State Government decided to acquire the land for development and construction of residential, commercial and administrative buildings.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(1)(vi), 29, 52 and 72 of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, improvement may be undertaken by the trust or by a government department; the trust’s scheme-making requirement applies when the trust undertakes the work. Section 52 permits acquisition on a representation from the trust or otherwise, where the land is required for improvement or another purpose under the Act. The word “appears” does not require the Government to frame a detailed scheme before deciding to acquire land.
members.conclusion: The acquisition did not require a prior scheme framed by the trust. The State Government could acquire land for a government improvement or another purpose under the Act, and a detailed scheme or development plan did not have to be prepared before the acquisition decision.

predicates.acquisition_under_urban_improvement_fram: The proceeding challenges a land acquisition carried out under an urban-improvement framework.
predicates.government_or_trust_seeks_land_for_impro: The government or improvement trust seeks land for improvement or another purpose authorized by the framework.
predicates.trust_scheme_not_prepared: The improvement trust has not prepared a scheme before the acquisition decision.

members.legal_issue: Land may be acquired for planned development before development plans are ready or the land has been declared a development area.
material_facts: The Government had decided on planned development before the relevant development statute came into force.
The acquisition notification was issued before a master plan was ready and before the area had been declared a development area.
The challenge concerned acquisition for planned development, rather than the lawfulness of carrying out development without the required approval or sanction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12 and 15 of the Delhi Development Act address different matters: section 12 regulates development, while section 15 provides for acquisition of land required for development or another purpose under that Act. Acquisition may precede development. Land may be acquired for planned development before a master plan is ready, although subsequent development must comply with the applicable requirements, including obtaining the relevant approval or sanction. The Court relied on Patna Improvement Trust v. Smt. Lakshmi Devi.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the absence of a master plan or development-area declaration did not prevent acquisition of land for planned development.

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.purpose_is_planned_development: The land is acquired for a program of planned development.
predicates.development_plan_not_ready: The relevant development plan has not yet been prepared when the land is acquired.

members.legal_issue: Land may be acquired for a public purpose under the urban-improvement law without a formulated improvement scheme.
material_facts: The land was acquired for multipurpose development, including residential, commercial, and industrial construction.
The owners challenged the acquisition on the grounds that no scheme had been framed and that the acquisition was inconsistent with the planned use of the land.
The acquisition notification identified development purposes under the urban-improvement law.
members.legal_principle: Section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act authorizes acquisition when the State Government considers land necessary for improvement or another purpose under the Act. Relying on Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 2 SCC 662, the Court held that framing a scheme is mandatory when the Trust undertakes the work, but the State Government may undertake development without a scheme under Chapter V. The Court considered State of Tamil Nadu v. A. Mohammed Yousef (1991) 4 SCC 224 distinguishable in light of the decision concerning the Rajasthan Act.
members.conclusion: The absence of a formulated or finalized scheme did not invalidate the acquisition for a public purpose under the Act.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a government proceeding to acquire land.
predicates.government_acquired_for_public_purpose: The government acquired land for a development purpose it identified as public.
predicates.no_scheme_was_formulated: No improvement scheme had been prepared or finalized for the proposed work.

members.legal_issue: A scheme for the eventual use or disposal of acquired land is not a legal prerequisite to notifications initiating or declaring a land acquisition.
material_facts: The government had not prepared a scheme for using the developed sites before issuing the acquisition notifications.
The notifications stated that the land was to be developed and used as industrial and residential areas.
members.legal_principle: The Court found no requirement in the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for a scheme to precede notifications under sections 4 and 6. It suggested that a scheme should be prepared before disposal of the developed sites.
members.conclusion: No law required a scheme to be prepared before notifications under sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act were issued, although the Court expected a scheme to exist before the sites were disposed of.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_proceeding: The proceeding concerns notifications initiating or declaring a land acquisition.
predicates.no_prior_use_scheme: No scheme for the eventual use or disposal of the acquired land had been prepared before the notifications.

members.legal_issue: A final and effective scheme under the housing statute is not a prerequisite to acquisition unless the notification identifies the acquisition as being for execution of a formal scheme prepared under that statute.
material_facts: The land was being acquired for the Housing Board, but the notifications did not state that it was for execution of a scheme prepared by the Board under the housing statute.
No final and effective scheme had been completed when the notifications were issued; the schemes were initiated earlier and finalized later.
The housing statute empowered the Board to execute schemes transferred by the Government or a local authority, as well as schemes prepared under its own scheme-making provisions.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act does not expressly or by necessary implication require a final scheme before acquisition. Sections 35(2), 35(3), 36 and 70 of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board Act provide for Board functions and acquisitions beyond schemes prepared under sections 37 to 56. The Court distinguished State of Tamil Nadu v. A. Mohammed Yousef, limiting its scheme requirement to acquisition expressly for execution of a scheme prepared under Chapter VII. Arnold Rodricks v. State of Maharashtra and Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi support the principle that acquisition may precede development or preparation of a development plan; Patna Improvement Trust v. Smt. Lakshmi Devi was also relied on.
members.conclusion: The absence of a final and effective scheme did not invalidate these notifications. The scheme requirement identified in the earlier decision applies when a notification expressly states that the land is being acquired to execute a formal scheme prepared by the Housing Board under the housing statute.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The government initiated a proceeding to acquire land for a public purpose.
predicates.acquisition_for_housing_authority: The land was intended for a housing authority's use.
predicates.notification_identifies_formal_authority: The acquisition notice expressly stated that the land was needed to execute a formal scheme prepared by the housing authority under its governing statute.
predicates.prior_final_scheme_not_required: A completed formal scheme need not exist before the acquisition notice is issued.

members.legal_issue: Land may be acquired for improvement or another purpose under the applicable urban-improvement law without a scheme having been framed or finalized.
material_facts: The land was acquired for improvement of an urban area, including construction of residential, commercial, and industrial buildings.
The appellants relied on a High Court decision to argue that acquisition could not proceed without a sanctioned scheme and that the proposed use had to conform to the Master Plan.

The Supreme Court relied on its earlier decision concerning the same urban-improvement law, which held that a scheme is mandatory when the Trust undertakes the work, but not when the State Government or one of its departments undertakes development.
members.legal_principle: Section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act authorizes acquisition when the State Government considers land necessary for improvement or another purpose under the Act. Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan holds that a scheme is mandatory when the Trust undertakes the work, but the State Government may undertake development without a scheme under Chapter V. The Court also held that the Division Bench decision in Narain v. State of Rajasthan did not state the correct law and had been disapproved by the High Court Full Bench.
members.conclusion: A scheme need not be framed or finalized for the State Government to acquire land under the Act for improvement or another purpose under the Act; the acquisition was not invalid for want of a scheme.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the validity of a land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_for_urban_improvement_or_oth: The government acquired the land for urban improvement or another purpose authorized by the applicable law.
predicates.no_scheme_framed: No scheme for the proposed work had been framed or finalized.

members.legal_issue: Prior permission for regulated-area development is not required merely to initiate land acquisition for a statutory scheme intended to secure regulated development.
material_facts: The land proposed for acquisition was in a regulated area.
The acquisition was initiated for a statutory land-development scheme framed by a public board for regulated development.
The physical development activities governed by the general building-control law had not begun.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the U.P. (Regulation of Building Operations) Act, 1958 governs development activities, not proceedings to acquire land for a scheme that may later lead to those activities. The U.P.
