Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965 is a self-contained special Act; in the absence of a provision making its schemes subject to the general Act, its provisions prevail. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The absence of prior permission under the general building-control law did not make the acquisition proceedings ultra vires.

rule.if: scheme_acquisition_challenge and regulated_area and prior_permission_objection and scheme_for_regulated_development and physical_development_not_started

predicates.scheme_acquisition_challenge: The case challenges land-acquisition proceedings initiated to carry out a statutory housing or improvement scheme.
predicates.regulated_area: The land proposed for acquisition lies in an area subject to regulation of building operations.
predicates.prior_permission_objection: The challenger argues that prior permission for development was not obtained.
predicates.scheme_for_regulated_development: A public body framed the scheme for the purpose of regulated development.
predicates.physical_development_not_started: The physical site or building activities governed by the general development rules had not begun.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition declaration need not expressly recite the government’s satisfaction or use a prescribed formula to be valid.
material_facts: The government issued the declaration after an inquiry and consideration of the report concerning objections to the acquisition.
The declaration stated that the land appeared to be required for a public purpose, rather than expressly stating that the government was satisfied that it was needed for that purpose.
No statutory form for the declaration was prescribed.
The challenge was that the declaration did not itself express the government’s satisfaction; the government’s actual satisfaction was not challenged.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government’s satisfaction after considering any report under section 5A is a condition precedent to a valid declaration, but section 6(1) does not require that satisfaction to be stated in the declaration. Section 6(2) specifies what the declaration must state, and no particular form is required. The Court approved the observations in Ezra v. Secretary of State, I.L.R. 30 Cal. 36, at p. 81, that a section 6 notification need not be in any particular form. The Court did not decide whether “it appears” and “is satisfied” are synonymous.
members.conclusion: The declaration was not invalid merely because it did not expressly state the government’s satisfaction or used different wording. The High Court was wrong to hold that the declaration was invalid on that basis.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and government_actually_satisfied and declaration_states_public_need and no_statutory_form_prescribed

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a government acquisition of land for a public purpose or for a company.
predicates.government_actually_satisfied: The government was in fact satisfied that the land was needed for the stated purpose.
predicates.declaration_states_public_need: The declaration states that the land is needed or required for a public purpose or for a company.
predicates.no_statutory_form_prescribed: No legally prescribed form requires the declaration to recite the government’s satisfaction or use particular words.

members.legal_issue: A notification invoking urgency is not invalid merely because it does not expressly state the nature or existence of the urgency.
material_facts: The notification referred to the urgency provision but did not state the specific urgency said to justify its use.

The Court found the notification invalid because the circumstances and available material did not establish genuine urgency, not merely because the notification omitted an express statement of urgency.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1), 17(1), and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 do not require the notification itself to recite the nature of the urgency. The existence of a proper basis for invoking the urgency power may be assessed from the surrounding circumstances and the records available when the authority formed its satisfaction. The Court relied on Union of India v. Ghanshyam Das Kedia, and distinguished the question of what the notification must recite from whether the urgency power was substantively justified.
members.conclusion: The absence of an express statement of urgency in the notification does not, by itself, invalidate it; the relevant circumstances and available records may establish whether urgency existed.

predicates.acquisition_case: The government issued a notification as part of compulsory acquisition proceedings.
predicates.notification_omits_specific_urgency_stat: The notification does not expressly describe the urgency said to justify dispensing with the ordinary objection process.

members.legal_issue: A land acquisition notification need not state whether the land is arable or waste land.
material_facts: The acquisition notification stated that the land was needed for a public purpose but did not specify whether it was arable or waste land.
The High Court quashed the notification in part because it did not declare the nature of the land.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires publication to notify interested persons that land is needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose, authorise entry for measurement and related work, and notify owners that later encumbrances will not bind the State. It does not require a statement whether the land is arable or waste land.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to require the notification to specify the nature of the land.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification: The government published a notification announcing that land was needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition notification invoking the urgency power need not expressly state that the land is waste or arable.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications did not recite that the land was waste or arable.
The challenge asserted that the absence of that recital invalidated the notifications.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(4) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 does not require the notification itself to recite that the land is waste or arable. Dora Phalauli v. State of Punjab was distinguished because its reasoning also concerned the absence of a statement that the government considered the urgency power applicable.
members.conclusion: The omission of a recital that the land was waste or arable did not invalidate the notification.

predicates.urgency_acquisition_proceeding: The government issued an acquisition notification invoking an urgency procedure that dispenses with an inquiry into objections.
predicates.notification_omits_land_condition_recita: The notification did not state that the land was waste or arable.

members.legal_issue: The urgency power may be exercised for land that is neither waste nor arable when the governing law extends that power to land acquired for qualifying development purposes.
material_facts: The acquired land included houses that were found not to form part of agricultural land.
The land was acquired for planned housing for members of a disadvantaged community.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 17(1-A), as amended by the State Legislature, which extended the power to take possession of land other than waste or arable land when acquired for sanitary improvements or planned development. Since the acquisition was for housing as part of planned development, the land's non-agricultural character did not prevent use of the urgency power.
members.conclusion: The State was statutorily empowered to exercise the urgency power in relation to this land.

predicates.acquisition_validity_appeal: The proceeding challenges the validity of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.land_was_not_waste_or_arable: The acquired land was neither waste nor arable land.
predicates.acquisition_was_for_planned_development_: The land was acquired for planned development or sanitary improvement.

members.legal_issue: When land is acquired for planned development and the urgency power is invoked, possession may be taken of land that is neither waste nor arable, and failure to expressly cite the applicable possession power in the notification is not fatal.
material_facts: The acquisition was for planned development.
The notification invoked the urgency power but did not expressly refer to the provision authorizing possession of land other than waste or arable land.
The land included some portions with structures.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1-A), as inserted by the Land Acquisition (U.P. Amendment) Act, 1954, permits possession of land other than waste or arable land when it is acquired for sanitary improvements or planned development. The Court held that invoking section 17(1) in a planned-development acquisition attracts that power without a further declaration, and that omission to cite section 17(1-A) expressly in the notification is not fatal.
members.conclusion: The omission to refer expressly to the additional possession power did not invalidate the acquisition; the Government could take possession of non-waste and non-arable land for planned development when the urgency power was invoked.

predicates.planned_development_acquisition: The land is acquired for planned development.
predicates.urgency_power_invoked: The Government invokes the urgency power in the acquisition.
predicates.notification_omits_express_reference_to_: The notification does not expressly refer to the power permitting possession of land that is neither waste nor arable.

members.legal_issue: A land-acquisition proceeding that substantially contains the elements of an award may be treated as an award even if it is not in the prescribed form.
material_facts: A prior court order directed the Collector to prepare an award in the acquisition proceedings.

The Collector issued a proceeding dated 31 July 1984 containing the requisites of an award and bearing the Collector's signature, although the signature was illegible and the proceeding was not in Form 15.
The challengers disputed that the proceeding was an award, while the society sought implementation of the earlier court order.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 requires the Collector to make an award under the Collector's hand and sets out the award's substantive contents. The Court treated compliance with the prescribed form as procedural where the proceeding contained the requisites of an award. It also upheld the High Court's authority under Article 215 to issue directions in the circumstances, including where conduct potentially called for contempt proceedings.
members.conclusion: The proceeding was in substance an award, although it was not in Form 15, and the authority could be directed to sign and complete it in accordance with the earlier order.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and prior_court_order_requires_award and proceeding_contains_award_requisites and proceeding_not_in_prescribed_form

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to acquire land.
predicates.prior_court_order_requires_award: A court had previously directed the responsible authority to prepare an award in the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.proceeding_contains_award_requisites: The authority issued a proceeding containing the substantive elements of an award.
predicates.proceeding_not_in_prescribed_form: The issued proceeding did not use the prescribed form.

members.legal_issue: A consent award in a land acquisition proceeding does not require the parties’ agreement to comply with the formal requirements for government contracts or to follow a prescribed form.
material_facts: The compensation awards were made by consent following agreements between the acquiring authority and the landholders.
The landholders contended that the agreements did not meet the formal requirements for government contracts and were not in the prescribed form.
The High Court rejected those contentions.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that Article 299 of the Constitution does not have to be complied with for the purpose of passing a consent award, and that an agreement between the parties need not strictly conform to a prescribed format.
members.conclusion: The agreements did not need to comply with the formal requirements for government contracts or strictly follow a prescribed form for consent awards to be made.

predicates.consent_award_in_land_acquisition_case: The acquiring authority made an award based on an agreement with the landholder.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff who is out of possession cannot maintain a suit seeking only a declaration of title without seeking recovery of possession.
material_facts: The trial court found that the Temple had continuously possessed the disputed property and that the plaintiff was not in possession.
The plaintiff sought a declaration and a mandatory injunction concerning revenue records, but did not seek recovery of possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 bars a declaration when the plaintiff is able to seek further relief but omits it. The Court relied on Ram Saran and Anr. v. Smt. Ganga Devi, AIR 1972 SC 2685, which held that a suit for declaration alone is not maintainable where the plaintiff is out of possession and has not sought possession.
members.conclusion: The suit was not maintainable because the plaintiff, being out of possession, omitted the further relief of recovery of possession.

predicates.civil_property_suit: The plaintiff brought a civil suit asserting a right in property.
predicates.plaintiff_out_of_possession: The plaintiff was not in possession of the property, and another person was found to possess it.
predicates.only_declaration_and_incidental_relief_s: The plaintiff sought a declaration and an incidental form of relief but did not seek recovery of possession.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration of ownership is not maintainable when the defendant possesses part of the disputed property and the plaintiff omits to seek possession of it.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration of ownership but did not seek possession of any part of the property.
The defendant was found to possess property that had been in the possession of the deceased co-owner.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, a declaratory suit is not maintainable when the plaintiff is able to seek further relief but omits to do so. The Court relied on no earlier cases in deciding this issue.
members.conclusion: The suit was not maintainable because the plaintiffs sought only a declaration and omitted the consequential relief of possession.

predicates.declaratory_ownership_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking a declaration of ownership of disputed property.
predicates.defendant_possesses_disputed_property: The defendant possesses at least part of the disputed property.
predicates.plaintiff_omitted_possession_relief: The plaintiff did not seek possession of the part of the disputed property possessed by the defendant.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking only a declaration of title is not maintainable when the plaintiff is out of possession and omits to seek available consequential relief.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership of the land but did not seek possession or another consequential relief.
The plaintiff was admittedly not in possession of the land.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 prevents a court from granting a declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief, omits to do so. The Court relied on Ram Saran v. Smt. Ganga Devi, Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra, and Gian Kaur v. Raghubir Singh.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred because the plaintiff sought a declaration without seeking consequential relief despite not being in possession.

rule.if: declaratory_suit and plaintiff_is_out_of_possession and plaintiff_can_seek_consequential_relief and plaintiff_does_not_seek_consequential_relief

predicates.declaratory_suit: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking a declaration of a right or status.
predicates.plaintiff_is_out_of_possession: The plaintiff is not in possession of the property in dispute.
predicates.plaintiff_can_seek_consequential_relief: The plaintiff is able to seek relief in addition to a declaration, such as recovery of possession.
predicates.plaintiff_does_not_seek_consequential_re: The plaintiff asks only for a declaration and omits available additional relief.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking a declaration cannot obtain it under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act while omitting further relief that the plaintiff is entitled to seek.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration that the transferees were not owners and had no right to redeem the mortgage under the Collector’s order.
They did not seek cancellation or setting aside of the Collector’s order, or an injunction, although the Court considered such relief available to them.
members.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act prevents a court from granting a declaration where the plaintiff is able to seek further relief but omits it. The Court stated that the plaintiffs could have sought the setting aside of the Collector’s order.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not entitled to the declaration because they had omitted further relief; the suit was barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

predicates.declaration_suit_challenging_an_order: The plaintiff brings a suit for a declaration challenging the effect of an order.
predicates.further_relief_is_available: The plaintiff is entitled to seek additional relief addressing the order or its effects.
predicates.further_relief_is_omitted: The plaintiff does not claim that additional relief.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking only a permanent injunction is not maintainable where the plaintiff’s title is genuinely disputed and resolving the title dispute requires a full adjudication.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a permanent injunction without seeking a declaration of title.
The plaintiff and a defendant claimed ownership under competing sale deeds and disputed each other’s title, possession, and account of how the property was acquired.
The defendant alleged that the plaintiff’s vendor lacked title and that documents concerning the plaintiff’s claim were fabricated.
The court found that the plaintiff’s title was not clear and that the dispute required evidence and adjudication of questions of fact and law.
members.legal_principle: Under Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594, a suit for injunction simpliciter may be decided on possession where title is not disputed or under a cloud. Where a genuine cloud over title exists and the dispute involves complicated questions of fact and law, the parties should be relegated to a comprehensive suit for declaration of title. Although a court may decide a simple and straightforward title issue in an injunction suit when there are necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue, that is an exception. Jharkhand State Housing Board v. Didar Singh (2019) 17 SCC 692 confirms that a declaration is necessary when the defendant raises a genuine title dispute and a cloud over the plaintiff’s title.
members.conclusion: The suit for a permanent injunction without a declaration of title was not maintainable on these facts, and the appeal challenging the setting aside of the injunction decree was dismissed.

predicates.bare_injunction_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking an injunction without also seeking a declaration of title.
predicates.genuine_title_dispute: A defendant asserted a competing claim of ownership that the court could not treat as merely vexatious or unfounded.
predicates.title_requires_full_trial: Resolving the competing claims of title required evidence and adjudication of substantial questions of fact or law.
predicates.bare_injunction_suit_not_maintainable: The plaintiff cannot maintain the injunction-only suit without seeking a determination of title.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking only an injunction is not an adequate remedy where possession of a vacant site depends on resolving a serious and complex dispute over title and identification of the property.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed the disputed property under a registered assignment deed and sought an injunction based on his alleged possession.
The defendant disputed the plaintiff’s title and possession, asserting that the property belonged to his family and was not included in the plaintiff’s deed or purchase certificate.

The parties’ descriptions and survey numbers did not clearly identify the disputed property, and the lower courts’ findings relied on a disputed boundary and an inference of possession from an adjoining plot.
The property was a vacant site, so determining de jure possession depended on resolving title; the Court considered that the documentary and oral evidence would require a full trial.
After the High Court remanded the suit, the plaintiff amended the pleadings to seek a declaration of title, and the defendant amended the written statement in response.
members.legal_principle: Under Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594, a suit for injunction simpliciter ordinarily turns on possession, but where a vacant site makes de jure possession dependent on title, title may directly and substantially arise. A court should not decide title in an injunction suit where title is seriously disputed and the matter involves complicated questions of fact and law; the remedy is a comprehensive suit for declaration of title. Although a court may decide a simple and straightforward title issue in an injunction suit where there are necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue, that is an exception. Jharkhand State Housing Board v. Didar Singh, (2019) 17 SCC 692, likewise recognizes that a bare injunction is inadequate when a genuine dispute creates a cloud over title. Here the title and identification disputes were complex, and the plaintiff had amended the suit to seek declaratory relief.
members.conclusion: The bare-injunction suit was not an appropriate vehicle for deciding possession without resolving the serious and complex title dispute. The parties should have their title rights adjudicated in the comprehensive declaratory proceedings, and the High Court’s remand was not disturbed because the pleadings had been amended to seek a declaration of title.

rule.if: bare_injunction_suit and vacant_site and (serious_title_dispute and property_identification_disputed) and possession_depends_on_title and title_issue_requires_full_trial

predicates.bare_injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction without initially seeking a declaration of title.
predicates.vacant_site: The disputed property was a vacant site.
predicates.serious_title_dispute: The opposing party asserted a competing claim of ownership that seriously placed the claimant’s title in dispute.
predicates.property_identification_disputed: The parties disputed whether the property claimed by the claimant was the same property described or identified in the evidence.
predicates.possession_depends_on_title: Determining possession of the property required establishing which party had title to it.
predicates.title_issue_requires_full_trial: Resolving title required consideration of complicated factual or legal matters and a full assessment of documentary and oral evidence.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking only a permanent injunction is not maintainable without a declaration of title when the defendant raises a genuine dispute that creates a cloud over the plaintiff’s title.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed to have purchased the property by registered sale deed and to have possessed it, including by constructing a residence.
The Board asserted that the property had been acquired and possession handed over to it, and relied on acquisition proceedings and a possession certificate.

The lower courts found that the plaintiff’s possession was proved and that the acquisition proceedings had not been shown to have attained finality, but granted an injunction without requiring a declaration of title.
The Supreme Court held that the Board’s reliance on the acquisition proceedings and possession certificate was sufficient to raise a cloud over the plaintiff’s title.
members.legal_principle: Under the settled principles stated in earlier judgments of the Court, a dispute about title does not in every case require the plaintiff to seek a declaration. A bare injunction suit is insufficient where the defendant raises a genuine title dispute that creates a cloud over the plaintiff’s title; in that circumstance, the plaintiff must seek a declaration. No particular provision or earlier case is identified by name in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff should have sought a declaration of title, so the suit for a bare injunction could not be maintained; the decrees below were set aside. The parties were also directed to maintain the status quo as to possession temporarily.

predicates.bare_injunction_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking an injunction to protect possession without seeking a declaration of title.
predicates.defendant_raised_genuine_title_cloud: The defendant relied on evidence or proceedings that genuinely put the plaintiff’s title in doubt.
predicates.declaration_not_sought: The plaintiff did not ask the court to declare the plaintiff’s title.
predicates.bare_injunction_suit_not_maintainable: The suit seeking only an injunction cannot be maintained without a declaration of title.

members.legal_issue: In a bare-injunction suit concerning a vacant site, title may be examined to determine possession only when the title issue is properly raised and is simple; a complex or unpleaded title dispute belongs in a comprehensive title suit.
material_facts: The property was a vacant site, so physical use or occupation did not resolve who possessed it.
The plaintiffs’ claimed possession depended on their title through an alleged oral gift and the claimed protection of an ostensible owner transfer.
The defendant claimed through the person both sides accepted as the original owner, and the evidence and title theories were disputed.
The plaint did not plead the alleged oral gift or the facts needed for protection as a transfer from an ostensible owner, and no title issue was framed.
members.legal_principle: For a vacant site, possession follows title, so title may need to be determined as a prelude to deciding de jure possession. A court may decide title in an injunction suit when the issue is straightforward and the necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue exist. It should relegate the parties to a comprehensive declaratory suit where title involves complicated questions of fact or law, or where the parties did not proceed on the basis that title was at issue. A title finding requires necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue, whether express or implied. The judgment discusses Vanagiri Sri Selliamman Ayyanar Uthirasomasundareswarar Temple v. Rajanga Asari, Sulochana Amma v. Narayanan Nair, Annaimuthu Thevar v. Alagammal, and Sajjadanashin Sayed Md. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer in explaining the treatment of title in injunction suits.
members.conclusion: The court should not decide the disputed title in this injunction suit; the plaintiffs’ remedy was a comprehensive suit for declaration and consequential relief.

rule.if: injunction_suit and vacant_site and title_needed_to_determine_possession and (title_issue_complicated or not title_properly_pleaded_and_raised)

predicates.injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction concerning immovable property.
predicates.vacant_site: The property was vacant and its possession was not established through physical occupation or use.
predicates.title_needed_to_determine_possession: Determining who had possession required determining who had title.
predicates.title_issue_complicated: The title dispute involved complicated questions of fact or law.
predicates.title_properly_pleaded_and_raised: The pleadings and an express or implied issue placed title before the court for determination.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking a declaration of title need not also claim possession when the property is in judicial custody and the defendant is neither in possession nor able to deliver possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs brought a suit seeking a declaration concerning their title to property and the validity of deeds affecting it.
At the time of suit, the property was attached in a criminal proceeding and was in the magistrate’s custody; no party was in possession.
The defendants were not in possession and could not deliver possession, and the magistrate was not a party to the suit.
The High Court set aside the trial court’s decree because the plaintiffs had not sought recovery of possession, without considering the merits.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1887, the further relief contemplated is relief against the defendant. A plaintiff need not claim possession where the defendant is not in possession and cannot deliver possession, including where the property is in custodia legis. The Court relied on Sunder Singh Mallah Singh Sanatan Dharm High School Trust v. Managing Committee, Sunder Singh-Mallah Singh Rajput High School, Nawab Humayun Begam v. Nawab Shah Mohammad Khan, and K. Sundaresa Iyer v. Sarvajana Sowkiabil Virdhi Nidhi Ltd.; it disapproved Dukkan Ram v. Ram Nanda Singh.
members.conclusion: The suit was competent without a claim for delivery of possession; the appeal was allowed and the case remanded for decision on the merits.

rule.if: declaratory_title_suit and property_in_judicial_custody and defendant_not_in_possession and defendant_unable_to_deliver_possession and custodian_not_a_party

predicates.declaratory_title_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.property_in_judicial_custody: The property was held in the custody of a judicial or other legal authority during the suit.
predicates.defendant_not_in_possession: The defendant was not in possession of the property.
predicates.defendant_unable_to_deliver_possession: The defendant was unable to deliver possession of the property to the plaintiff.
predicates.custodian_not_a_party: The authority holding the property in custody was not a party to the suit.

members.legal_issue: A party seeking adjudication of rights to property attached by an Executive Magistrate need not also seek recovery of possession where the property is held in custody of the law.
material_facts: The Magistrate ordered the disputed shop attached as a case of emergency.
The attachment placed the property in the Magistrate’s custody pending determination of the parties’ rights by a competent court.
members.legal_principle: Section 146(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for attachment pending determination of the parties’ rights by a competent court. Because attached property is held in custody of the law for the party who ultimately establishes entitlement to possession, a proceeding seeking determination of that entitlement need not include a separate claim for recovery of possession.
members.conclusion: Where the property is attached and held in custody of the law, it is sufficient for the party seeking relief to ask the competent court to determine the rights concerning entitlement to possession; a separate prayer for recovery of possession is not necessary.

predicates.proceeding_after_property_attachment: A proceeding is brought before a competent court after the disputed property has been attached by an Executive Magistrate.
predicates.property_held_in_legal_custody: The attached property remains in the custody of the law pending determination of the parties’ rights.
predicates.party_seeks_determination_of_possession_: A party asks the competent court to determine who is entitled to possession of the attached property.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking rescission of a contract cannot claim specific performance of that same contract in the alternative.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that the agreement was void and inoperative because it resulted from undue influence and coercion.
In the same suit, the plaintiff alternatively sought specific performance of the agreement to sell plots.
members.legal_principle: Although Order 7, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits inconsistent reliefs, each pleaded relief must independently be maintainable. Section 37 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 expressly permits a plaintiff suing for specific performance to seek rescission in the alternative, but neither that provision nor section 35 permits the converse. The omission is deliberate. Cawley v. Poole, 71 E.R. 23, supports the principle that a claim to set aside a transaction for fraud cannot be combined in the alternative with a claim to enforce it.
members.conclusion: The alternative prayer for specific performance was not maintainable.

predicates.suit_seeks_rescission: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking to undo a contract.
predicates.specific_performance_is_alternative: The plaintiff asks for enforcement of the contract only as an alternative to the requested rescission.
predicates.same_contract_at_issue: The rescission claim and the alternative enforcement claim concern the same contract.
predicates.alternative_specific_performance_unavail: The plaintiff cannot maintain the alternative claim for specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff who has no cause of action for specific performance is not entitled to insist on an election between that relief and rescission.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought rescission of the agreement and alternatively sought specific performance.
The plaintiff did not allege readiness and willingness to perform his part of the agreement, and therefore had no cause of action for specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Election between alternative reliefs arises only if the plaintiff has established a cause of action for each relief at issue. A specific-performance claim requires an allegation of readiness and willingness to perform; without that allegation, the plaintiff has no cause of action for specific performance and cannot demand an election between it and rescission. The Court relied on the specific-performance requirement discussed in Ardeshir Mama v. Flora Sassoon, 55 I.A. 360.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not entitled to be put to an election between the two reliefs.

predicates.suit_claims_alternative_reliefs: The plaintiff seeks alternative remedies in the same suit.
predicates.specific_performance_cause_of_action_abs: The plaintiff has no cause of action for specific performance.
predicates.plaintiff_not_entitled_to_election: The plaintiff cannot insist on being allowed to choose between the claimed remedies.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking to avoid a possession decree for rent default must meet the applicable rent-payment requirements through the suit and appeal.
material_facts: The landlords sought possession in a rent-control proceeding on the ground of rent default.
The tenant had not deposited the full arrears by the first date of hearing.
The tenant did not pay rent month by month during the appeal.
The findings about those defaults were not successfully challenged.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act imposes mandatory requirements that a tenant must strictly comply with during the suit and any appeal when possession is sought on that ground. The Court relied on no earlier case for this issue.
members.conclusion: The courts below were right to decree possession for rent default, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.rent_control_possession_proceeding: The proceeding seeks possession of rented premises under a rent-control regime on the ground of rent default.
predicates.full_arrears_not_deposited_by_first_hear: The tenant did not pay or deposit all rent arrears by the first date of hearing.
predicates.rent_not_paid_during_appeal: The tenant did not continue paying rent during the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking the protection available under the statutory payment procedure must make the required payments or tenders on time and continue making them regularly; failure to do so removes the case from that protection.
material_facts: The court fixed interim rent at ₹25 per month and directed the tenant to deposit both arrears and future rent at that rate.
The tenant did not comply with the deposit directions, and the application in which interim rent had been fixed was later dismissed for non-prosecution.
The tenant admitted that rent had not been paid regularly as contemplated by the court's order.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, bars eviction only where the tenant pays or tenders the rent and permitted increases due by the first hearing or another date fixed by the court, continues to pay or tender them regularly until final decision, and pays costs as directed. Shah Dhansukhlal Chaganlal v. Dalichand Virchand Shroff, [1968] 3 S.C.R. 346, holds that failure to deposit rent regularly as required takes the case outside that protection. The explanation to section 12 provides a rule of evidence concerning readiness and willingness; it does not excuse non-compliance with the payment requirements.
members.conclusion: The tenant did not satisfy the payment requirements for protection under section 12(3)(b), and the defaults deprived him of the Act's protection against eviction.

rule.if: nonpayment_eviction_proceeding and tenant_seeks_payment_based_protection and court_fixed_payment_requirements and tenant_failed_to_pay_or_tender_as_required

predicates.nonpayment_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession because the tenant had not paid rent.
predicates.tenant_seeks_payment_based_protection: The tenant relied on statutory protection that depends on paying or tendering rent during the proceeding.
predicates.court_fixed_payment_requirements: The court specified amounts or timing for payment or deposit of rent during the proceeding.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_or_tender_as_requir: The tenant failed to make the payments or tenders required by the court or to continue them regularly.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking protection from eviction for rent default must pay or tender rent regularly during the suit or appeal, and a court cannot treat persistent payment at irregular intervals as substantial compliance merely because arrears are cleared before judgment.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession on the ground of rent default. The matter proceeded to an appeal that remained pending for about 40 months.
Rent was payable monthly, but the tenant deposited it only 16 times during the appeal, at intervals ranging from two to four months, rather than paying it monthly as it fell due or in advance.
The tenant’s final rent payment was made after final arguments, and the arrears had been cleared by the time judgment was pronounced.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 requires strict compliance with its conditions and creates no discretionary jurisdiction to excuse non-compliance. “Regularly” requires payment or tender with reasonable punctuality and substantial proximity to the intervals at which rent falls due. For monthly rent, the tenant must pay or tender it every month as it falls due or in advance; persistent payments at intervals of two, three, or four months are not substantial compliance, even if arrears are cleared before judgment. The Court relied on Ganpat Ladha v. Sashikant Vishnu Shinde, which followed Shah Dhansukhlal Chagganlal and Harbanslal Jagmohandas v. Prabhudas Shivlal.
members.conclusion: The requirement to pay or tender rent regularly during the suit or appeal is mandatory. Because the tenant paid at persistently irregular intervals, the tenant was not entitled to protection from eviction; the appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and a decree for possession was passed.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought possession because the tenant had defaulted in paying rent, and the matter was before a court in the suit or an appeal.
predicates.tenant_paid_at_persistently_irregular_in: The tenant paid or tendered rent repeatedly at intervals that did not substantially conform to the monthly due sequence, rather than paying monthly as rent fell due or in advance.

members.legal_issue: A tenant obtains the conditional protection against eviction only by paying all rent and permitted increases due by the first hearing and continuing to pay or tender them regularly until the suit is decided.
material_facts: The tenant deposited Rs. 1,000 on the first hearing date, but the total payments and credit fell short of the amounts due by that date.
After the first hearing, several monthly rent payments fell due and remained unpaid when the suit was decided.
The tenant did not regularly pay or tender the amounts that fell due during the suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 requires payment or tender in court of the standard rent and permitted increases then due by the first hearing or another date fixed by the court, followed by regular payment or tender until final decision, as well as payment of costs as directed.
members.conclusion: The tenant did not qualify for protection under section 12(3)(b) because he had not paid all amounts due by the first hearing and did not thereafter pay or tender the amounts falling due regularly.

rule.if: rent_arrears_eviction_suit and (not all_arrears_paid_by_first_hearing or not regular_payments_after_first_hearing)

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking possession on the ground that the tenant had not paid rent or permitted increases.
predicates.all_arrears_paid_by_first_hearing: The tenant paid or tendered in court all rent and permitted increases due by the first hearing or another date fixed by the court.
predicates.regular_payments_after_first_hearing: The tenant continued to pay or tender in court regularly the rent and permitted increases falling due until the suit was finally decided.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who disputes the amount of rent or permitted increases must take the prescribed steps within the notice period to establish readiness and willingness to pay and cannot obtain general rent protection merely by offering arrears later in the suit.
material_facts: The tenant disputed the standard rent and the claimed arrears in his written statement.
He made no application to the court to determine the disputed rent within one month after receiving the demand notice.
He made no payment within that month and deposited only part of the arrears after the suit began.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(1) must be read with its Explanation: where the amount of standard rent or permitted increases is disputed, readiness and willingness to pay requires an application under section 11(3) before the month after notice expires, followed by payment or tender of the amount specified by the court. The Court distinguished Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subbash Chandra Yograj Sinha, and applied Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Safibhai and Mrs. Manorama Masurekar v. Mrs. Dhanlaxmi G. Shah.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to protection under section 12(1) because, despite disputing the rent, he did not apply to the court as required and could not cure that failure by offering payment when the court was about to decree the suit.

rule.if: rent_arrears_eviction_suit and tenant_disputes_rent_amount and not timely_court_application

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking possession on the ground that the tenant had not paid rent or permitted increases.
predicates.tenant_disputes_rent_amount: The tenant disputed the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable.
predicates.timely_court_application: The tenant applied to the court within the notice period to determine the disputed amount.

members.legal_issue: A tenant must initiate a dispute over standard rent within the prescribed notice period to prevent the strict arrears-based eviction provision from applying; raising the dispute for the first time later in the suit is insufficient.
material_facts: In one appeal, the tenants’ alleged letters disputing rent within the notice period were found to be manufactured, and a later letter was sent after that period.
In the other appeal, the tenants did not dispute standard rent within the notice period and first raised the dispute in their written statement.
The landlords’ claims concerned rent arrears, including arrears of at least six months, and the tenants had not made a timely application for fixation of standard rent.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 12(1), 12(2), and 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the strict eviction provision applies where monthly rent is at least six months in arrears, the tenant neglects to pay within the notice period, and there is no dispute about standard rent or permitted increases. Section 12(3)(b) governs other cases and provides protection subject to payment and continued tender of rent and costs. Explanation I to section 12 deems a tenant ready and willing to pay where, before expiry of one month after notice, the tenant applies under section 11(3) for fixation of standard rent and thereafter pays or tenders the amount specified by the court. Sections 11(3) and 11(4) govern interim orders in connection with a rent dispute, but are attracted only where the application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation I. The Court applied Shah Dhansukhlal Chhanganlal v. Dalichand Virchand Shroff, and held that Vora Abbasbhai v. Haji Gulamnabi had not overruled the Gujarat High Court’s conclusion in Ambalal v. Badaldas that the dispute must exist no later than expiry of the one-month period.
members.conclusion: The Court held that a tenant must raise the standard-rent dispute within one month after receiving the notice and apply to the court for fixation of standard rent within that period. A dispute first raised later in a written statement does not prevent application of the strict arrears-based eviction provision. The Court dismissed the Gujarat appeal and allowed the Bombay appeal, restoring the eviction decree in the latter.

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction on the ground that the tenant had failed to pay rent.
predicates.dispute_first_raised_after_notice_deadli: The tenant first disputed the standard rent after the period for making the rent-fixation application had expired.

members.legal_issue: The amount a tenant must pay to obtain protection from eviction for rent default includes rent whose recovery is barred by limitation.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had failed to pay rent arrears after receiving a demand notice.
The landlord relinquished the claim for rent from an earlier period because its recovery was time-barred.
The tenant deposited the rent and damages claimed for the later period, together with interest and costs, but did not include the earlier unpaid rent.
The tenant relied on the deposit to seek relief from eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 20(2)(a) and 20(4) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, a tenant sued for eviction for rent default may obtain relief by unconditionally paying or depositing the entire amount due at the first hearing. A limitation period bars the remedy but does not extinguish the debt, except in circumstances such as those covered by section 28 of the Limitation Act, which do not apply to a debt. The Court relied on Curwen v. Milburn, Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. The State of Bombay, and Ram Nandan Sharma v. Mt. Maya Devi; it also referred to sections 25(3) and 60 of the Contract Act. Accordingly, the entire amount due includes time-barred rent.
members.conclusion: Time-barred rent forms part of the entire amount of rent due for purposes of the statutory relief. Because the tenant omitted that rent from the deposit, the tenant was not entitled to protection from eviction.

rule.if: eviction_suit_for_rent_default and tenant_sought_first_hearing_protection and tenant_had_unpaid_time_barred_rent and tenant_omitted_old_rent_from_deposit

predicates.eviction_suit_for_rent_default: The landlord brought a suit seeking eviction because the tenant had rent arrears and had not paid them after demand.
predicates.tenant_sought_first_hearing_protection: The tenant made a deposit at the first hearing to seek protection from eviction.
predicates.tenant_had_unpaid_time_barred_rent: The tenant had unpaid rent from a period for which recovery by action was barred by limitation.
predicates.tenant_omitted_old_rent_from_deposit: The tenant's deposit did not include the unpaid rent from the time-barred period.
predicates.tenant_not_entitled_to_eviction_protecti: The tenant does not obtain protection from eviction through the statutory deposit procedure.

members.legal_issue: A tenant seeking protection from eviction for rent default must pay all rent due, including rent that has become barred by limitation.
material_facts: The landlords claimed arrears only for a later period, stating that earlier rent had become barred by time.
The High Court held that the tenant had to clear all dues, including rent barred by time.
The Supreme Court stated that the High Court’s view on that point could not be faulted.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(4) requires payment of the entire amount of rent and damages due for the tenant to receive protection from eviction on the ground of rent default. The Court expressly accepted the proposition that this includes arrears barred by limitation.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the view that the tenant had to clear all rent due, including rent barred by time, to obtain the statutory protection from eviction.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction on the ground that the tenant had defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.arrears_include_time_barred_rent: The rent due from the tenant includes arrears that have become barred by limitation.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot require a public authority to perform a promise that is contrary to law or beyond its lawful authority.
material_facts: The authority’s lease agreement stated that the lessee could develop at an FSI of 2.
The State Government had sanctioned a lower FSI for the relevant use, and the authority refused to approve a plan relying on the higher contractual figure.
The lessee invoked estoppel to require the authority to honor the contractual representation.
members.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 concerns estoppel. The Court applied the settled principle that promissory estoppel cannot compel a public body or the Government to carry out a representation or promise that is contrary to law or outside its authority or power. Sections 31(6) and 37(2) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 make the sanctioned development plan and sanctioned modifications binding; section 159 concerns the authority to make regulations. No earlier case is cited in the judgment for this principle.
members.conclusion: The lessee could not invoke promissory estoppel to compel the authority to honor a contractual term that conflicted with the sanctioned development controls.

predicates.writ_mandamus_claim: A person sought a writ requiring a public authority to perform a promise.
predicates.public_authority_made_a_promise: A public authority represented that a person could proceed on a stated basis.
predicates.promise_conflicts_with_binding_law_or_ex: The promised action conflicted with binding legal controls or was beyond the authority’s lawful power.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot compel the State to honour an unauthorized benefit where no specific representation of that benefit was made.
material_facts: The board directed that the recently announced cement package and the scheme would apply, but did not direct that the company receive a 75% subsidy.
The later memorandum of understanding promised incentives permissible under the scheme and the prevalent policy, not a fixed higher subsidy.
The company invested in the project, but no application seeking an increase under the general enhancement mechanism was placed before the competent board while it existed.
The higher subsidy was granted later through screening committee decisions that were unauthorized and inconsistent with the applicable scheme.
members.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel requires a representation that induced a change of position and cannot enforce a promise contrary to law or beyond the authority of the person making it. The Court relied on Dr. Ashok Kumar Maheshwari v. State of U.P., which referred to Kasinka Trading v. Union of India and Shabi Construction Co. v. City & Industrial Development Corporation. A promise limited to benefits permissible under the scheme does not represent that an unauthorized higher benefit will be given; nor does estoppel defeat a revisional power reserved under the scheme.
members.conclusion: Promissory estoppel did not prevent the State from withdrawing the excess subsidy or exercising its revisional power.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim: A beneficiary claims that the State is prevented from withdrawing a benefit because the beneficiary relied on a governmental promise.
predicates.no_specific_representation_of_higher_ben: The State made no specific representation that the beneficiary would receive the higher benefit claimed.
predicates.higher_benefit_granted_without_authority: The higher benefit was granted by an authority acting beyond the benefit permitted by the applicable scheme.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot require a public authority to carry out a promise that it lacks legal power to perform.
material_facts: The predecessor authority adopted a resolution promising to reconvey part of the acquired land subject to conditions.
In reliance on the proposed arrangement, the landowner withdrew compensation-reference proceedings and did not pursue compensation in the ordinary course.
The governing legislation did not authorize the authority to reconvey the acquired land.
The landowner relied on the promise to argue that the authority was barred from resiling from it.
members.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel may bind a public authority where a clear promise is intended to be acted on and the promisee changes position, but it cannot compel an act prohibited by law or beyond the authority's power. The Court relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, A.P. Pollution Control Board II v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu, Sharma Transport v. Government of A.P., and Pune Municipal Corporation v. Promoters and Builders Association. It distinguished State of Punjab v. Nestle India Ltd., where the authority had statutory power to grant the promised exemption.
members.conclusion: Promissory estoppel could not be used to compel the authority to reconvey land contrary to the governing law.

rule.if: public_authority_promise_dispute and clear_promise_made and promisee_changed_position and promised_act_not_authorized_by_law

predicates.public_authority_promise_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a public authority must honor a promise it made.
predicates.clear_promise_made: The authority made a clear promise intended to be acted on by the recipient.
predicates.promisee_changed_position: The recipient acted on the promise and changed position to their detriment.
predicates.promised_act_not_authorized_by_law: The authority lacked legal power to perform the promised act.

members.legal_issue: Promissory or equitable estoppel cannot make an executive representation enforceable when it was made in violation of a mandatory statutory requirement.
material_facts: The government issued an exemption-related order without complying with the statutory requirement for publication in the official gazette.
The industrial undertaking claimed that it had relied on the order and that the government should be prevented from denying the exemption.
The statutory scheme governed the exemption and prescribed how an exemption order had to be made.
members.legal_principle: Where a statute governs the matter and mandates the manner in which an act must be done, estoppel cannot be used to validate an act that violates that requirement or defeat the statute. The Court discussed and distinguished the observations in Collector of Bombay v. Municipal Corporation of the City of Bombay, and rejected reliance on those observations as authority for estoppel in these circumstances. It also referred to Article 162 of the Constitution in explaining the limits of executive action where legislation occupies the field.
members.conclusion: The earlier order could not support promissory or equitable estoppel against the statutory requirements.

predicates.tax_exemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim that a statutory tax or assessment is avoided by an asserted exemption.
predicates.executive_representation_conflicts_with_: The executive made a representation that did not comply with a mandatory legal requirement governing the exemption.
predicates.party_relied_on_representation: The party claiming the exemption says it acted in reliance on the executive representation.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel may bind the government to an authorized representation on which a person has relied, but cannot validate an act beyond the government’s legal power.
material_facts: The ministry responsible for the property granted permission for the additional construction, and the lessee built in reliance on that permission at substantial expense.
The permission was given within the Minister’s authority under the rules governing government business, as found by Justice Sen.
The government later challenged the permission.
members.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel can apply against public authorities, but cannot confer a power that the authority does not possess or legitimate an ultra vires act, and it does not operate to override government policy. The Court relied on Robertson v. Minister of Pensions, Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd., Century Spinning & Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Ulhasnagar Municipal Council, and Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. v. State of Uttar Pradesh. This conclusion was stated by Justice Sen; the other opinions left the contractual questions open.
members.conclusion: Justice Sen held that the Union was precluded by promissory estoppel from denying the authority of the Minister to grant the permission after the lessee had acted on it; the doctrine could not validate an ultra vires act.

predicates.authorized_government_representation: A government authority makes a representation within the scope of its legal power.
predicates.reasonable_reliance_and_change_of_positi: A person reasonably relies on the representation and changes position as a result.
predicates.representation_beyond_legal_power: The representation exceeds the legal power of the authority that made it.

members.legal_issue: A public authority is not estopped from acting according to law when its earlier representation exceeded its authority.
material_facts: The municipal committee advertised plots in the market on the representation that octroi would not be imposed there, and purchasers relied on that representation.
The committee’s original promise of continuing immunity from octroi exceeded its authority to exempt property from the tax.
The committee later recommended that the exemption be cancelled and octroi imposed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 70(2)(c) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, an exemption required a resolution at a special meeting confirmed by the State Government; the municipality could not independently promise permanent immunity from the tax. Estoppel cannot require a public authority to act contrary to law or validate an ultra vires act. The Court relied on Excise Commissioner, U.P. v. Ram Kumar, M. Ramanatha Pillai v. State of Kerala and State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The municipal committee was not estopped from recommending or imposing octroi because its original promise was beyond its authority.

predicates.claim_to_estop_public_authority: A party sought to prevent a public authority from acting by relying on an earlier representation made by that authority.
predicates.public_authority_made_tax_exemption_prom: A public authority represented that a tax would not be imposed on specified persons or property.
predicates.promise_exceeded_authority: The authority lacked legal power to make the tax-exemption promise it gave.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel may constrain an authorized public officer who arbitrarily repudiates a representation relied on to the promisee’s disadvantage, but it cannot bar legislative or statutory functions or validate unauthorized acts.
material_facts: The purchasers relied on the municipal committee’s representation that octroi would not be imposed in the market and claimed to have purchased plots and built establishments on that basis.
The representation at issue was not an authorized undertaking binding the State Government, and the municipality lacked authority to grant the asserted permanent exemption.
The State Government acted in exercising statutory powers when it approved cancellation of the exemption and permitted the tax levy.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that promissory estoppel is unavailable against legislative functions, the discharge of statutory duties, or acts of government officers beyond their authority. Where an authorized officer makes a representation under a scheme and a person relies on it to their disadvantage, a court may require the officer to honour it if the officer repudiates it arbitrarily; the officer may nevertheless change course for special considerations bearing on the State’s general interest. The Court applied Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd. on authorized representations and arbitrary repudiation, while distinguishing its scope; it relied on Howell v. Falmouth Boat Construction Co. Ltd., Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property v. Brij Kishore Agarwala, Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Cooperative Society v. Sipahi Singh, Excise Commissioner, U.P. v. Ram Kumar, M. Ramanatha Pillai v. State of Kerala and State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd. It also considered Article 299(1) of the Constitution, sections 10, 25, 63, 65 and 70 of the Contract Act, and explained and disagreed in part with the approach in Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: Promissory estoppel did not bar the municipal committee or the State Government from acting according to law in this case.

rule.if: public_authority_promise_claim and officer_acted_within_authority and promise_made_under_scheme and promisee_relied_to_disadvantage and officer_repudiated_arbitrarily and not_special_public_interest_justification

predicates.public_authority_promise_claim: A party sought to enforce a representation made by a public authority.
predicates.officer_acted_within_authority: The public officer who made the representation acted within the authority given to that officer.
predicates.promise_made_under_scheme: The officer made the representation as part of an applicable public scheme.
predicates.promisee_relied_to_disadvantage: The person to whom the representation was made relied on it and put themselves in a worse position.
predicates.officer_repudiated_arbitrarily: The officer later refused to honour the representation arbitrarily, without a disclosed justification.
predicates.special_public_interest_justification: The authority had a special consideration affecting the general interest of the State that justified changing course.

members.legal_issue: A public body is not estopped from changing its position when its earlier position supported an action that was contrary to law.
material_facts: The municipal authority initially supported the project and appealed against the High Court judgment, but later withdrew its appeals and supported that judgment.
The builder relied on the authority’s earlier position to argue that it could not change its stance.
The Court found that the project and agreement contravened statutory requirements and were against public interest.
members.legal_principle: A public body cannot be held to an earlier position when doing so would perpetuate conduct contrary to statute. The Court distinguished Union of India v. Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd. (1968) 2 SCR 366 and The Ganges Manufacturing Co. v. Sourujmull (1880) ILR Cal 669, and relied on the principle in Dr. H.S. Rikhy v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, AIR 1962 SC 554, that there is no estoppel against a statute.
members.conclusion: The municipal authority was not estopped from changing its position because estoppel cannot require a public body to maintain an unlawful action.

predicates.public_body_position_challenged: A party argues that a public body must adhere to a position it took earlier in the dispute.
predicates.public_body_previously_supported_action: The public body previously supported or pursued the action that is now challenged.
predicates.earlier_action_contrary_to_law: The action previously supported by the public body is found to contravene governing law.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not bind a public authority to a conditional representation made by an officer who lacks authority to make a binding promise on its behalf.
material_facts: A tenant relied on a letter from an estate manager stating that, after specified conditions were met, the manager would recommend granting a lease in reconstructed premises to the authority’s board.
The tenant paid the requested deposit.
The manager acted as an intermediary who collected information and presented it to the board, rather than as an officer authorized to promise a lease.
The board considered the request and rejected it, deciding that the reconstructed premises would be needed for its staff.
members.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine that can apply against public bodies, but it cannot compel a public authority to perform a promise prohibited by law or made without the officer’s authority. A subordinate officer’s representation does not bind the authority merely because the recipient relied on it; the officer must be competent to make a binding promise. The doctrine must also yield where equity or the public interest requires, although the authority must place relevant grounds and material before the court. The court relied on Union of India v. Indo Afghan Agencies, Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Ulhasnagar Municipal Council, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Jeet Ram v. State of Haryana, Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India Ltd., State of Bihar v. Usha Martin Industries Ltd., Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Dharwar v. Dharmendra Trading Co., Howell v. Falmouth Boat Construction Co. Ltd., and Attorney General for Ceylon v. A.D. Silva.
members.conclusion: The public authority was not bound by the estate manager’s representation, so promissory estoppel could not prevent the authority from seeking the tenant’s ejectment.

rule.if: promissory_estoppel_claim_against_public_body and representation_made_by_officer and representation_only_promised_recommendation and officer_lacked_authority_to_bind_body and public_body_did_not_approve_promise

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_against_public: A party invokes promissory estoppel to prevent a public body from acting inconsistently with a representation.
predicates.representation_made_by_officer: An officer of the public body made a representation to the party.
predicates.representation_only_promised_recommendat: The representation promised only that the officer would recommend the requested benefit for decision by another authority.
predicates.officer_lacked_authority_to_bind_body: The officer was not authorized, actually or ostensibly, to make a binding promise for the public body.
predicates.public_body_did_not_approve_promise: The public body considered the requested benefit but did not approve the representation as a binding commitment.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot be used to prevent the application of a statutory rule.
material_facts: The respondents relied on promissory estoppel to argue that the corporation should not insist on applying the additional floor-space-index requirement to the same plot.
The development control rules were made under statutory authority and had statutory force.
members.legal_principle: Rules made under statutory authority form part of the statute, and promissory estoppel cannot operate against a statute. The Court relied on General Officer Commanding-in-Chief v. Subhash Chandra Yadav, A.P. Pollution Control Board II v. M.V. Nayudu, Sales Tax Officer v. Shree Durga Oil Mills, and Sharma Transport v. Government of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in applying promissory estoppel to prevent the corporation from relying on the statutory rule.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_against_statut: A party invoked promissory estoppel to resist the application of a rule having statutory force.
predicates.rule_made_under_statutory_authority: The rule was made under authority conferred by statute.
predicates.promissory_estoppel_cannot_override_stat: Promissory estoppel cannot prevent the application of the statutory rule.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel cannot compel a public authority to carry out an assurance that conflicts with binding legal procedure or exceeds the authority's power.
material_facts: The applicants relied on the administration's demand for an additional payment and the preliminary draw as assurances that they would receive the larger sites.
No specific assurance promising those particular sites was established.
The claimed assurance would have required the administration to allot particular sites without following the governing allotment procedure.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the rule that promissory estoppel is reliance-based and does not require proof of separate detriment, while holding that it cannot be used to compel a public body to perform a promise contrary to law or beyond its authority. It relied on Delhi Cloth & General Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, Civil Appeal No. 223 of 1974, disposed of on October 8, 1987.
members.conclusion: Promissory estoppel could not require the administration to allot the sites; the applicants had established no specific assurance, and even an assurance contrary to the governing rules could not be enforced.

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_in_public_allo: An applicant invokes promissory estoppel to require a public authority to allot a particular site.
predicates.no_specific_assurance_of_particular_site: The public authority did not specifically assure the applicant that a particular site would be allotted.
predicates.requested_promise_conflicts_with_binding: The requested performance would require the public authority to act contrary to the governing procedure or beyond its authority.

members.legal_issue: A public authority that makes a clear promise, which is acted upon to the promisee's disadvantage, may be prevented by promissory estoppel from withdrawing that promise absent a legal basis to do so.
material_facts: A statutory financial corporation, accepted as an instrumentality of the State, made a loan offer and entered into an agreement to advance the loan in the performance of its statutory role.
The borrower relied on the promise and incurred substantial expenditure and liabilities in undertaking and carrying out the project.
The corporation later decided not to disburse the loan, and the borrower would be placed at a disadvantage if the corporation were permitted to withdraw its promise.
The appeal challenged an order enforcing the corporation's promise.
members.legal_principle: Under the principle stated in Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. v. State of U.P., a clear and unequivocal promise intended to affect legal relations, which is acted upon by the promisee, binds the promisor where it would be inequitable to permit withdrawal. Jeet Ram Shiv Kumar v. State of Haryana does not assist a public authority that withdraws a representation arbitrarily: although estoppel cannot prevent the discharge of functions required by law, an authority cannot ignore an acted-upon promise on whim or undefined grounds to the promisee's prejudice.
members.conclusion: The corporation was estopped from backing out of its obligation arising from its solemn promise.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_enforcement_of_public_promise and public_authority_made_clear_promise and promisee_relied_and_incurred_disadvantage and not withdrawal_required_by_law

predicates.appeal_challenges_enforcement_of_public_: The proceeding is an appeal challenging enforcement of a promise made by a public authority.
predicates.public_authority_made_clear_promise: A public authority made a clear promise intended to affect a legal relationship.
predicates.promisee_relied_and_incurred_disadvantag: The promisee acted on the promise and incurred expenditure, liabilities, or another disadvantage.
predicates.withdrawal_required_by_law: The public authority's withdrawal of the promise was required by law.

members.legal_issue: A public authority cannot displace promissory estoppel by asserting public interest or possible loss to the public treasury without material evidence showing that enforcing the promise would prejudice the public interest.
material_facts: The lessees acted on the allotment and subsequent permissions, paid the required sums, obtained financing, and created third-party interests.
The authority did not produce evidence that the allotment caused a financial loss or that allowing the project to proceed would prejudice a specific public interest.
The authority relied on the possibility that a different land use or tender might have generated greater revenue.
members.legal_principle: Promissory estoppel applies against the government in its public or executive functions when a promise is made and relied upon, subject to the exception that equity or public interest may require otherwise. The government bears the burden of proving with material evidence that public interest would be prejudiced by enforcing the promise, and the Court applies a rigorous standard of proof. The Court relied on Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Union of India v. Godfrey Philips India Ltd., and Vasantkumar Radhakisan Vora v. Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay.
members.conclusion: The unsupported claim of public interest did not displace promissory estoppel, and the authority was required to honour its promises in these circumstances.

rule.if: public_contract_promise_review and promisee materially relied on promise and promisee altered position and authority produced no material proof of public harm

predicates.public_contract_promise_review: The proceeding concerns whether a public authority must honour a promise made in connection with a public contract.
predicates.promisee_materially_relied_on_promise: The promisee acted in reliance on the authority's promise.
predicates.promisee_altered_position: The promisee materially changed its position, such as by making payments, investments, or commitments, in reliance on the promise.
predicates.authority_produced_no_material_proof_of_: The authority did not produce material evidence that honouring the promise would prejudice the public interest.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent the government from claiming damages for unauthorised occupation where it made no inducing representation and the occupant did not change position in reliance on one.
material_facts: The officer had declared that his allotment was subject to the applicable rules and did not notify the authorities of his transfer.
The officer continued occupying the flat and paid normal rent, but the government did not represent that he could remain there on that basis.
There was no evidence that the officer changed his position to his detriment in reliance on any government representation.
members.legal_principle: Estoppel requires a representation of existing fact, belief and action by the other party on the faith of that representation, and resulting detriment. The Court found no representation or conduct intended to induce the officer to believe he could remain in the accommodation on payment of normal rent, and no detrimental change of position in reliance on the government.
members.conclusion: Promissory estoppel did not prevent the government from claiming market-rate damages for the period of unauthorised occupation.

predicates.government_accommodation_retention_case: The case concerns a person retaining government accommodation allotted to that person.
predicates.government_made_no_inducing_representati: The government made no representation intended to lead the occupant to believe that continued occupation was permitted on the terms claimed.
predicates.occupant_did_not_change_position_in_reli: The occupant did not change position to the occupant’s detriment in reliance on a government representation.

members.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent a public authority from withdrawing a representation when the claimant has not materially changed its position to its detriment and the withdrawal is supported by public interest.
material_facts: The bidder relied on a letter of intent that made formal allotment dependent on clearances and further formal steps.
The bidder paid earnest money but did not pay the substantial remaining premium, incur other expenses, assume liabilities, or take steps to implement the project before cancellation.
The value of the public plots had risen substantially during the prolonged delay, and the authority sought to obtain a price reflecting that value.
members.legal_principle: A representation does not attract promissory estoppel where the claimant has not altered its position to its prejudice to an extent that makes enforcement necessary to do justice. A supervening public interest may outweigh individual equity and permit the Government to withdraw a representation. The Court relied on M.P. Mathur v.
