Union of India (2006) 13 SCC 706 and the distinction between administrative-law doctrines and contractual rights explained in Kisan Sehkari Chini Mills v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500.
members.conclusion: The bidder could not invoke promissory estoppel to prevent cancellation; it had not changed its position to its prejudice, and the public interest could justify the authority changing its position.

predicates.public_body_promise_claimed_as_estoppel: A claimant relies on a representation by a public body and seeks to prevent its withdrawal through promissory estoppel.
predicates.claimant_made_no_material_detrimental_ch: The claimant did not materially alter its position to its detriment in reliance on the representation.
predicates.public_interest_favours_withdrawal: The public interest favours the public body withdrawing the representation.

members.legal_issue: The statutory restriction limiting a protected tenant’s ejectment to specified grounds applies to a pre-enactment ejectment suit that is pending when the tenant-protection amendments take effect.
material_facts: The ejectment suit was filed before the original tenant-protection Act came into force and remained pending through appeals when the amendments took effect.
The amendments brought the defendant within the statutory definition of a protected tenant.
The landlord did not establish any of the specified grounds for ejectment.
members.legal_principle: Although statutes are generally not construed retrospectively to defeat vested rights, retrospective operation may follow from express language or necessary implication. The overriding language of section 3—making a protected tenant liable to ejectment only on specified grounds and not otherwise—showed that the restriction applied to pending pre-enactment suits. The Court referred to the general principles in Craies on Statute Law and Halsbury’s Laws of England, and to Knight v. Lee and Beadling v. Goll on retrospective operation and pending claims.
members.conclusion: The tenant could rely on the statutory restriction in the pre-enactment suit, and ejectment was unavailable because the landlord proved none of the permitted grounds.

rule.if: pre_act_ejectment_suit and case_pending_when_tenant_protection_amendment_took_effect and tenant_covered_by_amended_definition and not permitted_eviction_ground_proved

predicates.pre_act_ejectment_suit: A landlord began an ejectment suit before the tenant-protection law came into force.
predicates.case_pending_when_tenant_protection_amen: The suit or an appeal in it was still pending when the relevant tenant-protection amendment took effect.
predicates.tenant_covered_by_amended_definition: The defendant fell within the protected-tenant definition as amended.
predicates.permitted_eviction_ground_proved: The landlord proved at trial at least one ground on which the law permitted the protected tenant to be ejected.

members.legal_issue: A tenant-protection rule barring recovery of possession applies to a pending possession suit when the rule becomes applicable to the area before the decree is passed.
material_facts: The tenant’s fixed-term lease expired, and the landlord then filed a suit to recover possession.
While the suit was pending, a notification made the relevant part of the rent-control law applicable to the area where the premises were situated.
The tenant remained in possession after the lease ended and expressed readiness and willingness to pay rent; the Court found that the tenant fulfilled the conditions for protection.
members.legal_principle: Under section 12(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a landlord is not entitled to recover possession while the tenant pays, or is ready and willing to pay, standard rent and permitted increases and observes the tenancy conditions consistent with the Act. The Act’s definition of tenant includes a person who remains in possession after the lease ends. The point at which section 12(1) operates is when a decree for possession would be passed, so it applies to suits pending when the relevant part of the Act becomes applicable as well as to later suits. Nilkanth Ramachandra v. Rasiklal and Chandrasingh Manibhai v. Surjit Lal Sadhamal Chhabda concerned subsections (2) and (3), not subsection (1), and therefore did not determine this issue.
members.conclusion: The possession restriction applied to the pending suit. Because the tenant fulfilled its conditions, the landlord was not entitled to a decree for possession; the appeal was allowed and the lower courts’ decisions were set aside.

rule.if: pending_possession_suit and rent_protection_became_applicable and tenant_remained_after_lease and tenant_ready_and_willing_to_pay and tenant_observed_tenancy_conditions

predicates.pending_possession_suit: A landlord had brought a suit to recover premises, and the suit remained pending when the court had to decide whether to decree possession.
predicates.rent_protection_became_applicable: A rent-protection rule became applicable to the area where the premises were situated while the possession suit was pending.
predicates.tenant_remained_after_lease: The tenant continued in possession after the lease had ended.
predicates.tenant_ready_and_willing_to_pay: The tenant showed readiness and willingness to pay the rent and permitted increases due.
predicates.tenant_observed_tenancy_conditions: The tenant observed and performed the tenancy conditions consistent with the applicable rent-protection rule.

members.legal_issue: Occupancy-tenant protections apply to a pending civil ejectment case, and the transitional and repeal provisions do not preserve an ejectment claim so as to defeat occupancy rights conferred by the code.
material_facts: An ejectment suit based on the landholder’s claim to recover the land for personal cultivation was pending when the code came into force.
The tenant acquired occupancy-tenant status under the code while the suit was pending.
The claimed right to evict arose under the general law governing landlord and tenant, rather than under a law repealed by the code.
members.legal_principle: Sections 261 and 262(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code do not prevent the application of section 185 to pending ejectment proceedings. Section 261 preserves rights acquired under repealed laws, but the asserted right to evict arose under the general law, not a repealed enactment. Section 262(2) preserves the civil court’s jurisdiction and the applicable procedure for a pending suit; it does not nullify occupancy rights conferred by the code. Under section 193, eviction of an occupancy tenant must be on the grounds specified there, and personal cultivation is not such a ground. The Court also considered the provisions for resuming proceedings after a stay in sections 6 of the 1954 and 1955 protection Acts.
members.conclusion: The pending suit remained with the civil court for disposal under the applicable prior procedure, but the code’s substantive occupancy protections applied; the tenant could not be evicted for the stated personal-cultivation ground.

predicates.pending_civil_ejectment_case: A civil ejectment suit was pending when the new land-revenue regime commenced.
predicates.occupancy_status_conferred: The tenant acquired statutory occupancy rights while the suit was pending.
predicates.personal_cultivation_ejectment_claim: The landholder sought ejectment on the ground of needing the land for personal cultivation.

members.legal_issue: A statutory proviso restoring tenancy rights protects a tenant in a pending possession suit even when an intervening amendment had removed those rights before the restoring proviso was enacted.
material_facts: The land was held for agricultural purposes by the tenant and his predecessor from 1939, and the tenancy continued from year to year.
The tenant acquired rights under the 1948 tenancy legislation, including protection against termination and recovery of possession except in the prescribed manner.
A 1952 amendment excluded the municipal area containing the land from the operation of the 1948 legislation, after which the landlord gave notice terminating the tenancy and filed a possession suit.
A 1956 amendment introduced a proviso preserving rights acquired under the 1948 legislation despite the 1952 amendment; the possession suit was still pending when the 1956 amendment took effect.
The land did not fall within the categories excluded by the 1956 amendments.
members.legal_principle: A proviso ordinarily excepts or qualifies the substantive clause, but its meaning depends on interpretation and it may operate as an independent substantive provision when it addresses a matter unrelated to the main clause. The proviso here expressly preserved rights acquired under the principal tenancy legislation from the effect of the 1952 amendment, retrospectively; those rights could be asserted in a suit not finally disposed of. Section 89(2) of the tenancy legislation did not apply because it concerned rights and proceedings predating commencement of that principal legislation. Section 7 of the Bombay General Clauses Act did not defeat the express contrary intention in the proviso. The Court approved Patel Maganbhai Jethabhai v. Somabhai Sursang.
members.conclusion: The proviso preserved the tenant’s rights despite the 1952 exclusion, and the tenant could rely on those rights in the possession suit because it was still pending when the proviso took effect.

rule.if: pending_civil_possession_suit and tenant_rights_previously_acquired and intervening_law_removed_tenant_protection and restoring_law_took_effect_before_final_disposition

predicates.pending_civil_possession_suit: A landlord brought a civil suit seeking possession of land held by a tenant, and the suit remained pending when the later restoring law took effect.
predicates.tenant_rights_previously_acquired: A tenant had acquired rights under tenancy legislation before those rights were removed by a later change in the law.
predicates.intervening_law_removed_tenant_protectio: A later change in the law removed the statutory protection that had applied to the tenant or the land.
predicates.restoring_law_took_effect_before_final_d: A subsequent law restored the previously acquired rights before the possession suit was finally disposed of.

members.legal_issue: Amended tenant-protection provisions govern the disposal of an ejectment suit that remains pending when the amendments take effect, and an incomplete proceeding under the former scheme must yield to the amended scheme.
material_facts: An ejectment suit was pending when the tenant-protection law was extended to the area, and the tenant applied for an order requiring the landlord to sell the site.
Before the later amendments took effect, a court declared the tenant entitled to purchase the site and directed that its value be determined, but no final order directing conveyance was made.
The amendments changed the purchase scheme and expressly made the amended provisions applicable to pending suits and proceedings.
The proceeding remained incomplete when the amendments took effect.
members.legal_principle: Sections 9 and 10 of the Madras City Tenants’ Protection Act, 1921, as amended by Madras Act XIII of 1960, made the amended scheme applicable to pending ejectment suits and proceedings. The amended section 9 altered the extent of land that could be purchased and the method of determining its price. Under the original section 9(3), the proceeding was not concluded until the court, after payment of the price, directed conveyance. The Court also relied on Gnanaprakasam and Another v. Mahboob Bi and others for the proposition that an application was not at an end before final orders directing conveyance and delivery of possession.
members.conclusion: The amended provisions governed disposal of the pending suit. The earlier order did not conclude the proceeding; it stood superseded, and the court had to proceed under the amended scheme.

predicates.ejectment_case_pending_when_amendment_to: A landlord’s ejectment suit or related proceeding remained pending when the amending law took effect.
predicates.amendment_applied_new_procedure_to_pendi: The amending law provided that its new procedure applied to pending suits or proceedings.
predicates.tenant_purchase_proceeding_not_finalized: The court had not yet made the final order directing conveyance after the tenant paid the price.

members.legal_issue: More protective eviction requirements enacted for tenants apply to eviction proceedings that were pending when the amendment commenced.
material_facts: The amendment replaced an earlier eviction ground with more restrictive requirements for rebuilding and for the landlord’s own occupation.
The amendment expressly provided that its changes applied to pending suits and appeals.
The eviction proceedings had originally been brought under the earlier ground, before the landlords could have anticipated the new requirements.
members.legal_principle: The majority read the express provision covering pending suits and appeals as applying the amended eviction grounds to those proceedings. It treated the more protective requirements as a permissible retrospective change and preferred an interpretation that gives effect to the statute while avoiding unnecessary litigation.
members.conclusion: The new requirements for eviction apply to pending proceedings, and landlords may be given an opportunity to establish the requirements applicable to their cases, with tenants able to rebut that evidence.

predicates.pending_rent_eviction_case: A suit or appeal seeking eviction under a rent-control law remained pending when the amendment commenced.
predicates.amendment_expressly_covers_pending_cases: The amendment states that its changes apply to suits and appeals already pending.
predicates.amended_eviction_criteria_give_tenants_a: The amendment adds stricter requirements that a landlord must satisfy to recover possession.

members.legal_issue: A later rent-control law’s modification of the rules for striking out a tenant’s defence applies to a pending eviction proceeding under the repealed law when the later law requires the court to have regard to its provisions.
material_facts: The eviction suit was pending under the 1952 Act when the 1958 Act came into force.
The former law required the court to strike out the defence upon the tenant’s failure to make a required rent payment or deposit.
The later law made striking out the defence discretionary rather than mandatory.
The tenant paid the overdue rent after the payment deadlines but before the application to strike out the defence was decided.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 57(2) of the 1958 Act, the direction that a court have regard to that Act means that modifications or clarifications of the former law are to be applied in pending proceedings. Karam Singh Sobti v. Pratap Chand governs that interpretation. Comparing Section 13(5) of the 1952 Act with Sections 15(1)–(7) of the 1958 Act, the Court held that Section 15(7)’s change from mandatory to discretionary striking out was a modification to be applied to the pending suit.
members.conclusion: The court was required to apply the later law’s discretionary approach and consider the circumstances, including the tenant’s subsequent payment; it was not bound to strike out the defence merely because payment was late.

predicates.pending_eviction_proceeding_under_repeal: An eviction proceeding remained pending under an earlier rent-control law when a later rent-control law came into force.
predicates.later_law_requires_regard_to_its_provisi: The later law directs the court to have regard to its provisions when deciding the pending proceeding.
predicates.later_law_makes_striking_out_discretiona: The later law allows, but does not require, the court to strike out a tenant’s defence for failure to make a required rent payment or deposit.
predicates.tenant_later_paid_overdue_rent: The tenant paid rent after the required payment deadlines but before the application to strike out the defence was decided.

members.legal_issue: A change in tenancy law that takes effect while an appeal in a possession suit is pending governs the parties’ rights in that appeal, even if the suit was filed before the change took effect.
material_facts: The landlord filed a suit for possession before the statutory protection applied to the premises.
The protection became applicable during the tenant’s pending first appeal and restricted possession decrees to specified grounds.
The eviction ground relied on was not among the statutory exceptions, and the landlord’s notice did not meet the statutory notice requirement.
members.legal_principle: The statutory restriction on making a possession order protects a tenant by limiting the court’s power to make an effective order or decree, and applies to pending matters where its language and purpose so require. A change in law during an appeal governs the parties’ rights because an appeal is a continuation or rehearing of the suit. The Court applied sections 13(1) and 13(6) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, and relied on Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subhash Chandra Yograj Sinha, Mst. Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Cheetri, Ram Sarup v. Munshi, Mula v. Godhu, Amarjit Kaur v. Pritam Singh, and the principles discussed in Dayawati v. Inderjit, Kristnama Chariar v. Mangammal, and Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri.
members.conclusion: The changed law governed the pending appeal. Because no applicable exception displaced the protection and the required notice had not been given, the suit was incompetent and was dismissed.

rule.if: tenant_possession_appeal and suit_preceded_protection and protection_became_applicable_during_appeal and asserted_ground_outside_exceptions and required_notice_not_given

predicates.tenant_possession_appeal: A landlord’s suit seeking possession from a tenant was under appeal.
predicates.suit_preceded_protection: The landlord filed the possession suit before the protective tenancy law became applicable to the premises.
predicates.protection_became_applicable_during_appe: A law restricting possession orders became applicable to the premises while the appeal was pending.
predicates.asserted_ground_outside_exceptions: The landlord relied on a ground that was not within an exception to the law’s restriction on possession orders.
predicates.required_notice_not_given: The landlord did not give the tenant the notice required before filing the possession suit.

members.legal_issue: A statutory protection governing eviction in a suit applies to an appeal that is a continuation and rehearing of that suit when the protection takes effect while the appeal is pending.
material_facts: A landlord obtained an eviction decree, and the tenant appealed against it.

While the appeal arising from the eviction suit was pending, a new provision came into force barring an eviction decree in a pending suit or proceeding unless the landlord had the specified written permission.
The High Court treated the appeal as not being a proceeding pending against the tenant because the tenant had filed it.
members.legal_principle: An appeal is a rehearing and a continuation of the suit, and the appellate court has seisin of the case; accordingly, the word “suit” in clause 13-A of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 includes an appeal. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, Kristnama Chariar v. Mangammal, Garikapati v. Subbiah Chowdhry, Amarjit Kaur v. Pritam Singh, Lakshmi Narayan Guin v. Niranjan Modak, and H. Shiva Rao v. Cecilia Pereira. It distinguished Motiram Ghelabhai v. Jagan Nagar because the particular repeal-and-saving language there displaced the general continuation-of-suit principle.
members.conclusion: The appeal was a continuation and rehearing of the suit, so the new protection applied to it; the High Court was wrong to conclude that no proceeding was pending against the tenant.

predicates.eviction_case_on_appeal: A party is pursuing an appeal arising from a suit seeking the party’s eviction.
predicates.appeal_pending_when_protection_takes_eff: The appeal remains pending when a new eviction protection takes effect.
predicates.protection_requires_permission_before_ev: The new protection bars eviction in the relevant pending proceeding unless the landlord obtains written permission.

members.legal_issue: Tenant-protection provisions covering earlier tenancies apply to an appeal in an ejectment suit that remains pending when the provisions take effect.
material_facts: The landlords sued to evict their tenants after the leases expired, and trial courts decreed eviction before the tenant-protection law took effect.
The tenants appealed, and those appeals were pending when the law took effect.
The leases permitted the tenants to build residential houses, and the appellate courts found that permanent houses had been built within five years of the leases.
The law extended its protection to tenancies created before it took effect and protected qualifying tenants from eviction except for non-payment of rent.
members.legal_principle: A statutory provision operates retrospectively when express terms provide for it or when that intention clearly follows from its words and context. Although legislation affecting vested rights is ordinarily construed prospectively absent such an indication, the Act’s provision applying to tenancies created before its commencement and section 5(1)(a)’s protection of tenants who had already built qualifying structures showed an intention to apply retrospectively. Because an appeal is a continuation of the suit, section 5(1)(a) applied to an appeal pending when the Act took effect. The Court referred to Re Athlumney, Ex parte Wilson, (1898) 2 Q.B.D. 547.
members.conclusion: The tenant-protection provisions applied to the pending appeals, which were continuations of the suits; the appeals were dismissed.

predicates.tenant_protective_law_covers_prior_tenan: The law extends its tenant protections to tenancies created before the law took effect.
predicates.qualifying_structure_built: The tenant built a permanent residential or business structure within the required period under a contractual right or with the landlord’s knowledge and acquiescence.
predicates.ejectment_appeal_pending_at_commencement: An appeal from an ejectment decision remained pending when the tenant-protection law took effect.

members.legal_issue: Amendments governing eviction of tenants apply to pending eviction applications and appeals, requiring a pending appeal to be decided afresh under the amended law.
material_facts: The landlords’ appeal concerned an eviction application and remained pending when the amending legislation took effect.
The amending legislation provided that its amendments applied to pending eviction applications and appeals from orders on those applications.
The amended law changed the governing eviction provisions, and the Court sent the case back to the appellate authority for a fresh decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the amending Act made the amendments applicable to all eviction applications and appeals from orders on such applications that were pending when the Act commenced. The Court therefore required a fresh decision under the amended Section 3; it also noted that Section 7A conferred a related power on the controller.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the lower courts’ decisions were set aside, and the matter was remanded for a fresh decision under the amended law.

predicates.thika_tenancy_ejectment_proceeding: The matter is an application for eviction of a tenant or an appeal from an order on such an application.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_amendment_took_e: The eviction application or appeal remained pending when the amending law took effect.
predicates.proceeding_decided_afresh_under_amended_: The pending matter is decided afresh under the amended law.

members.legal_issue: A newly conferred power of revision applies to a pending eviction proceeding when the appellate order is made after the amendment creating that power has taken effect.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction proceeding before the amendment, and the proceeding remained pending when the amendment took effect.
The amendment created a power for the High Court to examine orders made under the rent law.
The appellate authority made its decision after the amendment took effect.
members.legal_principle: Under Indira Sohanlal v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, Delhi, finality prescribed for a decision arises when the decision is actually made, not earlier. The Court followed that principle and referred to Delhi Cloth and General Mills Co. Ltd. v. Income-tax Commissioner, Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. v. Irving, and Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhury.
members.conclusion: The revision application was competent, and the High Court had jurisdiction to hear it; finality attached to the appellate decision only when that decision was made, by which time the amendment was in force.

predicates.rent_control_ejectment_case: A landlord sought to evict a tenant in a proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_review_power_cre: The eviction proceeding was still pending when a legislative change created a new power to review orders.
predicates.appellate_order_after_review_power_creat: The appellate authority made its order after the new review power took effect.

members.legal_issue: The extended rent-control provisions applied to a pending eviction proceeding when the reviewing authority decided the revision after the provisions had been extended to the area.
material_facts: The landlord filed the eviction application before the relevant provisions had been extended to the cantonment area.
The reviewing authority decided the revision after a later notification extended the Act to cantonments in the state.
members.legal_principle: Under the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, section 3, the Government could extend the rent-control law to cantonments. Applying Jai Singh Jairam Tyagi v. Mamanchand Ratilal Agarwal, the Court held that the provisions of Chapter IV-A applied when the revisional order was made. It declined to interfere on this ground because dismissing the application would have been futile in light of the subsequent extension.
members.conclusion: The provisions applied when the revision was decided, and the objection that the proceeding could not continue because the application predated the extension was rejected.

predicates.rent_control_revision_proceeding: The matter is a revision in a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.initial_application_preceded_extension: The eviction application was filed before the relevant rent-control rules were extended to the area.
predicates.revision_decided_after_extension: The reviewing authority decided the revision after those rules had been extended to the area.
predicates.extended_rent_rules_apply_to_revision: The extended rent-control rules govern the revision.

members.legal_issue: A pending appeal from a possession decree passed before rent-control protection became applicable to the area is governed by the law applicable when the decree was passed, including when the original possession suit was brought under general property law.
material_facts: The landlord brought an ejectment suit under the general law governing property after the tenant’s lease had expired and the tenant did not comply with a notice to vacate.
The trial court entered a possession decree before rent-control protection applied to the area.
The tenant appealed, and rent-control protection was extended to the area while the appeal was pending.
members.legal_principle: Section 50 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, read as a whole with its proviso and the separate paragraph added by Bombay Act 3 of 1949, is an independent substantive saving provision. It extends the Act’s protection to specified pending suits and original proceedings, but excludes appeals arising from decrees or orders passed before the Act applied; those appeals are disposed of under the law previously applicable. This provision applies even when the original suit was brought under the Transfer of Property Act. Although section 12(1) is retrospective in operation under Shah Bhojraj Kuverji Oil Mills and Ginning Factory v. Subhash Chandra Yograj Sinha, and Chandrasingh Manibhai v. Surjit Lal Ladhamal Chhaabda considered the exclusion of appeals under the proviso, the special saving provision in section 50 prevails over the general protection in section 12(1). The Court approved Shankarlal Ramrotan v. Pandharinath Vishnu on the nature of the proviso.
members.conclusion: The appeal had to be decided under the law applicable before rent-control protection was extended to the area. The tenant could not rely on the new protection to defeat the possession decree.

predicates.pending_appeal_from_possession_decree: A tenant appealed from a decree ordering possession, and the appeal remained pending.
predicates.decree_predated_rent_protection: The possession decree was passed before rent-control protection applied to the area.
predicates.protection_extended_during_appeal: Rent-control protection was extended to the area while the appeal was pending.

members.legal_issue: The right of appeal in a suit pending when a replacement rent-control regime came into force remains governed by the appeal provisions preserved for pending proceedings.
material_facts: An ejectment suit was instituted under the earlier rent-control regime and remained pending when a replacement regime came into force.
The tenant applied under the replacement regime for a finding that the suit had abated, and the trial court rejected the application while continuing the suit.

The statutory transition provision required pending suits to be continued and disposed of under the earlier regime, while directing the court to have regard to specified provisions of the replacement regime and preserving the earlier regime’s appeal provisions.
members.legal_principle: Under section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, pending proceedings under the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, were to continue and be disposed of under the 1952 Act, subject to the stated proviso; the second proviso preserved the 1952 Act’s appeal provisions for proceedings disposed of under it. Thus, applying section 50(2) of the 1958 Act in a pending suit did not change the source of the court’s jurisdiction or the governing appeal provisions.
members.conclusion: The right of appeal concerning the pending suit continued to be governed by the earlier regime’s appeal provisions, even though the court considered the replacement regime’s abatement provision.

predicates.pending_rent_proceeding_under_prior_regi: A rent-control proceeding was instituted under an earlier regime and remained pending.
predicates.replacement_regime_takes_effect_during_p: A replacement rent-control regime became applicable while the proceeding was pending.
predicates.transition_preserves_prior_appeal_proces: The transition arrangement continued pending proceedings under the earlier regime and preserved its appeal process for those proceedings.

members.legal_issue: Delay in completing acquisition proceedings does not invalidate the acquisition when the delay is explained by the processing of numerous objections and pending challenges to the proceedings.
material_facts: Approximately 6,000 objections were filed by interested persons.
Several petitions challenging the acquisition proceedings were filed in 1966 and 1967.
The Government waited for the objections and petitions to be dealt with before proceeding further.
members.legal_principle: Whether delay in completing acquisition proceedings is inordinate depends on the circumstances. The Court accepted that the Government necessarily had to wait for numerous objections and pending petitions to be disposed of, and saw no basis to depart from the High Court’s assessment.
members.conclusion: The Court agreed that the Government had not caused inordinate delay in completing the acquisition proceedings.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and numerous_objections_pending and acquisition_challenges_pending and government_waited_for_disposal

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.numerous_objections_pending: A large number of interested persons have filed objections that remain to be dealt with.
predicates.acquisition_challenges_pending: Court challenges to the acquisition proceedings remain pending.
predicates.government_waited_for_disposal: The Government delayed further steps while the objections and court challenges were being dealt with.

members.legal_issue: A delay between the preliminary acquisition notification and the acquisition declaration is not inordinate where the acquisition involves many parcels and objectors, objections require individual hearings, and responsibility for government-caused delay is not established.
material_facts: The acquisition covered land belonging to numerous persons, and individual objections had to be heard.
About two and a half years passed between the preliminary notification and the declaration.
The objector did not produce his written objection, and there was no clear statement showing what delay was attributable to the government or whether the objector contributed to it.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the interval between the notifications was inordinate in light of the scale of the acquisition, the need to hear individual objections, and the evidence about responsibility for delay. It cited no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The delay was not shown to be inordinate in the circumstances.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and many_landowners_affected and individual_objections_required and government_delay_not_clearly_attributed

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a land acquisition.
predicates.many_landowners_affected: The proposed acquisition concerns land belonging to numerous persons.
predicates.individual_objections_required: The objections required hearings on an individual basis.
predicates.government_delay_not_clearly_attributed: The evidence does not clearly establish how much delay was attributable to the government.

members.legal_issue: An interval between a preliminary acquisition notification and a later declaration does not invalidate the acquisition where the interval is explained by preparation and approval of the acquisition scheme, and a later purchaser cannot rely on that interval to challenge the acquisition.
material_facts: The preliminary notification preceded the declaration by a substantial period.
After the preliminary notification, an improvement scheme was prepared and sent to the government for finalisation and approval.
The appellant purchased the land after the preliminary notification.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Sections 4(1) and 6 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953. It held that time taken to prepare and obtain approval for the improvement scheme did not make the valid preliminary notification invalid, and that a purchaser who acquired land after that notification could not rely on the interval between notification and declaration. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The delay did not invalidate the acquisition: the time taken for the scheme’s preparation and approval did not amount to inordinate delay, and the appellant, having purchased after the preliminary notification, could not rely on the interval to challenge it.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity or effect of a land acquisition.
predicates.purchase_after_initial_notification: The claimant acquired the land after the preliminary acquisition notification had been published.
predicates.scheme_preparation_and_approval_accounte: The period before the later declaration was used to prepare and obtain approval for the acquisition scheme.
predicates.interval_does_not_invalidate_acquisition: The interval between the preliminary notification and the later declaration does not invalidate the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A delay in publishing the acquisition declaration does not invalidate the acquisition when the delay is explained by consideration of representations and objections.
material_facts: There was a delay between publication of the acquisition notification and the declaration.
The government’s records showed that representations had been made and that objections to the notification were considered after an inquiry was directed.
The declaration was published after that process.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted the explanation that the declaration followed consideration of the objections and representations. No specific statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The delay did not invalidate the acquisition.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.delay_in_declaration_publication: There was a delay between the initial acquisition notification and publication of the declaration.
predicates.delay_used_to_consider_representations_o: The intervening time was used to consider representations or objections concerning the acquisition.
predicates.declaration_delay_does_not_invalidate_ac: The delay in publishing the declaration does not invalidate the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: Delay, construction of the public-purpose project elsewhere, failure to construct during pending litigation, and increased land prices do not by themselves invalidate an acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings had reached the award and possession stage before the challenge was filed.
The challengers relied on the passage of time and argued that the acquisition's purpose no longer survived.
They also relied on the fact that quarters had been constructed elsewhere and that construction on the acquired land had not occurred while litigation was pending.
The challengers additionally relied on an increase in land prices.
members.legal_principle: A later lapse of time, the fact that the public purpose was served elsewhere, construction not proceeding because of pending litigation, or an increase in land prices does not by itself vitiate a notification under Section 4(1) or a declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act. No earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: Those circumstances did not establish an error of law in the acquisition notifications and did not warrant interference; the acquisition notifications were restored.

rule.if: acquisition_writ_appeal and (prolonged_delay or purpose_served_elsewhere or construction_delayed_by_litigation or land_prices_increased)

predicates.acquisition_writ_appeal: The matter is an appeal from a judgment reviewing land acquisition proceedings.
predicates.prolonged_delay: A challenger relies on the passage of time after the acquisition proceedings began.
predicates.purpose_served_elsewhere: The public purpose was served by carrying out the project at another location.
predicates.construction_delayed_by_litigation: Construction on the acquired land did not proceed while litigation was pending.
predicates.land_prices_increased: The value of the acquired land increased after the acquisition proceedings began.

members.legal_issue: Publication of an acquisition declaration after the statutory deadline does not alone invalidate the acquisition when the declaration itself is distinct from its publication and its untimeliness has not been proved.
material_facts: The scheme’s preliminary notice was treated as equivalent to a preliminary notice under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The final notification under the successor enactment was published after the two-year period prescribed by section 4(2) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967.
The record did not establish when the declaration under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was made.
The challenger neither asserted nor proved that the declaration itself was made after the deadline, and did not challenge its existence or bona fides.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires the declaration that land is needed for a public purpose; sections 6(2) and 6(3) provide for its publication and its effect as conclusive evidence. Section 4(2) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, imposed the deadline on making the declaration, not on publishing it. The Court relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Vishnu Prasad Sharma, [1966] 3 SCR 557, concerning delay in acquisition notifications, while distinguishing a late publication from proof that no timely declaration existed. The challenger bore the burden of proving that the declaration was made late.
members.conclusion: The late publication of the notification did not invalidate the acquisition because the statutory deadline applied to making the declaration, and no proof showed that the declaration was late.

rule.if: acquisition_validity_appeal and preliminary_notice_preceded_deadline_period and final_publication_after_deadline and declaration_distinct_from_publication and no_proof_declaration_late

predicates.acquisition_validity_appeal: The case is an appeal challenging the validity of an acquisition for a public scheme.
predicates.preliminary_notice_preceded_deadline_per: The preliminary notice was issued before the period that triggered the statutory deadline for making the declaration.
predicates.final_publication_after_deadline: The notification publishing the declaration appeared after that deadline.
predicates.declaration_distinct_from_publication: The governing procedure treats making the declaration as a separate act from publishing it.
predicates.no_proof_declaration_late: The challenger neither established nor showed that the declaration itself was made after the deadline.

members.legal_issue: The one-year limit for making a declaration of public purpose runs to the making of the declaration, not its later publication in the official gazette.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette on 4 June 1992, and the substance of the notification was subsequently published locally, including in newspapers on 17 and 19 May 1993.
The declaration was made on 17 May 1994 and published in the official gazette on 24 May 1994.
The High Court treated the gazette publication of the declaration, rather than the date it was made, as decisive and quashed the acquisition proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the one-year limit applies to making the declaration that the land is needed for a public purpose. Section 6(2) requires publication of the declaration but prescribes no time limit for that publication. The Court relied on S.H. Rangappa v. State of Karnataka, Khadim Hussain v. State of U.P., and Sriniwas Ramnath Khatod v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The declaration was made within the prescribed one-year period; its publication in the official gazette after that period did not make the acquisition proceedings invalid.

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and official_notification_published and declaration_made_within_one_year and declaration_published_after_one_year

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.official_notification_published: The government published the acquisition notification in the official gazette.
predicates.declaration_made_within_one_year: The government made the declaration that the land was needed within one year of the legally relevant publication of the acquisition notification.
predicates.declaration_published_after_one_year: The declaration was published after one year had passed, although it had been made within that period.

members.legal_issue: The statutory time limit for making an acquisition declaration does not also limit the time for publishing it.
material_facts: An initial acquisition notification was published, and the declaration was formally made within the applicable one-year period following that publication.
The declaration was published in the Official Gazette after that one-year period.
The landowner challenged the declaration as time-barred because its publication occurred after the period expired.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 6(1), including its first proviso, the prescribed period governs when the declaration must be made. Section 6(2) requires publication of the declaration but sets no time limit for that publication; publication is evidence of the declaration, whose legal effect as conclusive evidence is addressed by Section 6(3). The Court followed the binding four-judge decision in Khadim Hussain v. State of U.P. and held that the contrary observations in other cited cases did not displace it.
members.conclusion: The declaration was valid because it was made within the prescribed period; its later publication did not make it time-barred.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a government's acquisition of land for a public purpose or another permitted acquisition purpose.
predicates.declaration_made_within_applicable_time_: The competent authority formally made the acquisition declaration within the time allowed after publication of the initial acquisition notification.
predicates.declaration_published_after_that_limit: The declaration was published after the time allowed for formally making it had expired.

members.legal_issue: The required publication and local notice for a proposed land acquisition must be contemporaneous, but need not be simultaneous, and a time gap does not by itself invalidate the acquisition.
material_facts: A notification and declaration for a public-purpose land acquisition were published in the official gazette.
Public notice of the substance of the notification was given in the locality 29 days after gazette publication.
The challenge asserted that the interval made the notification invalid.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires both gazette publication and public notice in the locality; section 4(2) action cannot precede their completion. Khub Chand v. State of Rajasthan and Narinderjit Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh establish that both steps are mandatory. State of Mysore v. Abdul Rajak does not establish that every interval is fatal. The Court approved Sanjivaiah Nagar Depressed and Backward Classes Sangh v. District Collector, Hyderabad and the Full Bench decision in Shahnaz Salima v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, and disapproved Satish Kapur v. State of Haryana, Rattan Singh v. State, C. Suryanarayana v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, and Mohammad Khawaza v. Government of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: Both steps are required before further action, but they need not occur at the same time or immediately one after the other. They must be contemporaneous; a gap that breaks continuity and raises a prima facie concern about bona fides may require further inquiry into its cause and any resulting prejudice. The interval alleged here did not make the notification invalid merely by itself.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.gazette_publication_and_local_notice_bot: The government published the acquisition notification in the official gazette and gave notice of its substance in the locality.
predicates.notice_gap_did_not_break_continuity: The interval between publication and local notice was not shown to be so large that it broke the continuity of the acquisition process.

members.legal_issue: A delay between publication of an acquisition notification in the Gazette or newspapers and publication of its substance in the locality does not, by itself, invalidate the notification.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the Gazette and newspapers before its substance was published in the locality.
The interval between those publications was more than six months.
The respondent argued that the interval invalidated the notification.
members.legal_principle: The requirement of local publication under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is mandatory, but the statute does not require simultaneous publication through the different modes. The court applied the contextual approach to mandatory and directory provisions discussed in Raza Buland Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board.
members.conclusion: Local publication need not occur simultaneously with publication in the Gazette or newspapers, and the delay alone did not invalidate the notification.

predicates.land_acquisition_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.section4_locality_notice_published_after: The authority published the substance of the acquisition notification in the locality after publishing the notification in the Gazette or newspapers.

members.legal_issue: Some delay in publishing the substance of an acquisition notification after its official-gazette publication does not by itself invalidate the acquisition proceedings.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was published in the official gazette in June 1992, its substance was posted at conspicuous places in November 1992, and it was later published in local newspapers in May 1993.
The landowners argued that the interval between these publications required the acquisition proceedings to be quashed.
The Court held that, even if there was some delay, the sequence did not require the proceedings to be set aside.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Haryana v. Raghubir Dayal, which supports the conclusion that some delay in the sequence of publication does not, by itself, require the acquisition proceedings to be quashed.
members.conclusion: The acquisition proceedings were not invalid merely because there was some delay in the subsequent publication of the notification’s substance.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.required_publications_occurred: The acquisition notification and its substance were published or notified in the required ways.
predicates.publication_sequence_involved_delay: There was some delay between the required steps for publishing or notifying the substance of the acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: A delay in completing acquisition proceedings does not invalidate an acquisition for an alleged collateral purpose when the evidence does not establish bad faith and the delay is explained by efforts to purchase the land.
material_facts: The land lay within a prescribed street line and could not be put to profitable use without municipal sanction.
After the acquisition notices, the municipality continued trying to purchase the land by private treaty; some land was purchased, and the remaining owners could not be persuaded to sell.
The acquisition authorities proceeded to determine compensation after the private-purchase efforts did not succeed.
The appellants alleged that the notices were issued to hold down the land price, but the Court found no evidence that the acquisition was not pursued bona fide for the stated purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, the declaration that land was needed for a public purpose was conclusive evidence of that need, and no further inquiry into whether the land was needed for that purpose was permissible. The Act contemplated that a declaration would be followed without unreasonable delay by proceedings to determine compensation; a person aggrieved by delay could seek an order compelling completion. The Court found no evidence that these notices were issued in bad faith to peg down prices rather than to acquire the land.
members.conclusion: The notifications were not invalidated on the ground that they were issued to peg down prices or for another collateral purpose. Although acquisition proceedings should proceed to compensation determination without unreasonable delay, the facts did not establish the alleged bad faith; an aggrieved person could seek an order requiring the authorities to complete the proceedings.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_challenge and public_purpose_declared and delay_explained_by_purchase_efforts and no_evidence_of_collateral_purpose

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_challenge: A person challenges the validity of a compulsory-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.public_purpose_declared: The government has declared that the land is needed for a public purpose.
predicates.delay_explained_by_purchase_efforts: The delay in proceeding to compensation determination occurred while the acquiring authority continued efforts to purchase the land privately.
predicates.no_evidence_of_collateral_purpose: The evidence does not show that the acquisition was initiated for a purpose other than the stated public purpose.

members.legal_issue: Delay in deciding representations, without supporting evidence of bad faith, does not establish that acquisition notifications were issued mala fide.
material_facts: The purchaser alleged that the authorities had conspired to deprive him of the colliery, but the allegations were vague.
There was delay in disposing of his representations.
The Coal Board had previously declined to revise its refusal to permit reopening, and the record did not support a conspiracy between the Board and the Government.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that delay by itself is hardly evidence of mala fides, particularly where the relevant authority had already declined to revise its decision. Vague allegations and unrelated personal hostility did not establish bad faith by the Government.
members.conclusion: The acquisition notifications were not vitiated by mala fides.

predicates.acquisition_notifications_challenged_as_: A person challenges acquisition notifications on the ground that they were issued in bad faith.
predicates.representations_delayed: The authorities took time to dispose of the person's representations.
predicates.no_supporting_evidence_of_collusion: The record contains no specific evidence that the relevant authorities colluded to bring about the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: The applicability of rent-control legislation to an eviction suit is determined when the suit is instituted, and expiry of the construction-based exemption while the suit or a related proceeding is pending does not make the legislation applicable to that proceeding.
material_facts: The eviction suit was instituted before ten years had elapsed from completion of the building’s construction.
The ten-year period expired while the suit or subsequent proceedings were pending.
The tenant argued that the Act consequently governed the pending proceedings and restricted eviction to the statutory grounds.
members.legal_principle: The law applicable on the date of institution of the suit governs it. In Nand Kishore Marwah v. Samundri Devi, the Court held that expiry of the ten-year period during a suit, appeal, or revision does not make the Act applicable to the proceeding. The Court agreed with that decision and distinguished the contrary reliance placed on Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera.
members.conclusion: Expiry of the ten-year period during the pendency of the suit, appeal, or revision did not make the Act applicable; the suit had to be decided without reference to it.

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord instituted a suit seeking eviction of a tenant from a building.
predicates.suit_filed_during_construction_exemption: The suit was instituted before ten years had elapsed from completion of the building’s construction.
predicates.exemption_expired_while_proceeding_pendi: Ten years from completion of the building’s construction elapsed while the suit or a related proceeding remained pending.

members.legal_issue: A statutory exemption from rent-control restrictions that applies when an eviction suit is instituted within the exemption period continues to govern that suit until adjudication, even if the period expires while the suit is pending.
material_facts: The landlord filed a civil suit for possession of a rented shop while the building remained within the statutory exemption period for newly constructed buildings.
The exemption period expired while the suit was pending.
The tenant sought dismissal on the ground that the rent-control statute had become applicable after the exemption expired, and the High Court dismissed the suit for want of civil-court jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 1(3) and 13(1) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, read purposively, mean that a suit instituted within the ten-year exemption period is not defeated merely because the period expires during its pendency; the parties' rights crystallise when the suit is instituted, and adjudication must proceed on that basis. The Court relied on Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera, Nand Kishore Marwah v. Samundri Devi, Om Prakash Gupta v. Dig. Vijendrapal Gupta, and Ram Saroop Rai v. Lilavati. It also applied the principle actus curiae neminem gravabit and the purposive approach to interpretation discussed in Poppatlal Shah v. State of Madras and Black-Clawson International Ltd. v. Papierwerke Waldhof-Aschaffenburg A.G.
members.conclusion: The exemption continued to apply to the suit because it had been instituted within the exemption period. The High Court's order was set aside, the Sub-Judge's order was restored, and the suit was to proceed in accordance with law.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord filed a civil-court suit to recover possession of a rented building from a tenant.
predicates.exemption_unexpired_at_filing: The suit was instituted while the building remained within the period during which the rent-control restrictions did not apply to it.
predicates.exemption_expired_while_pending: The period during which the rent-control restrictions did not apply expired while the suit remained pending.

members.legal_issue: An eviction decree remains exempt from rent-control execution restrictions when the eviction suit was filed during the building’s exemption period, even if the decree was passed after that period ended.
material_facts: The building was completed in March 1960 and fell within the class of buildings covered by a government exemption from the rent-control restrictions for five years from completion.
The landlord filed an eviction suit in January 1963, within that five-year period, and obtained an eviction decree in August 1969, after the period had ended.
The executing court refused execution on the ground that the decree did not meet the exemption conditions; the High Court held the decree executable.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 restricts eviction in execution of a decree except as permitted by that section; section 3 empowers the Government to exempt buildings or classes of buildings from provisions of the Act. Under the notification dated July 30, 1965, the relevant timing condition was that the eviction suit be instituted during the exemption period; no deadline was prescribed for passing the decree. The Court read the notification in light of its language and purpose: requiring the decree to be passed within the period would make the separate suit-filing condition redundant and could defeat the exemption where a suit was filed near the period’s end. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The suit had to be filed during the exemption period, but the decree did not have to be passed during that period. The decree was exempt from the restrictions on execution, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_decree_execution and building_within_exempted_construction_class and suit_filed_during_exemption_period and decree_passed_after_exemption_period

predicates.rent_control_eviction_decree_execution: The proceeding concerns execution of a decree ordering a tenant’s eviction where rent-control restrictions would otherwise govern execution.
predicates.building_within_exempted_construction_cl: The building belongs to a class of newly constructed buildings granted a time-limited exemption from rent-control restrictions.
predicates.suit_filed_during_exemption_period: The landlord instituted the eviction suit while the building’s exemption period was still running.
predicates.decree_passed_after_exemption_period: The eviction decree was passed after the building’s exemption period had ended.

members.legal_issue: A landlord who files an eviction suit while a building is exempt from rent-control restrictions may obtain and execute an eviction decree after the exemption period ends.
material_facts: Newly constructed buildings were exempt from eviction restrictions for a fixed period.
Landlords filed eviction suits while the buildings were within the exemption period.
The exemption period expired while the suits were pending.
The notification expressly covered decrees in suits filed during the exemption period, whether passed during that period or afterward.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, and the notification must be read harmoniously and in light of the exemption's purpose of encouraging new construction. A construction that advances the legislation's purpose should be preferred to one that makes the exemption ineffective. The Court relied on Amarnath Basheshar Dass v. Tek Chand and Punjab Tin Supply Company v. Central Government; it distinguished the different statutory schemes considered in Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera and Shiv Kumar v. Jawahar Lal Verma, and also referred to Om Prakash Gupta v. Dig Vijendrapal Gupta, Nand Kishore Marwah v. Samundri Devi, and Atma Ram Mittal v. Ishwar Singh Punja.
members.conclusion: The civil court retained jurisdiction to pass and execute eviction decrees after the exemption expired in suits instituted during the exemption period; the notification did not extend the exemption period indefinitely but preserved the parties' positions as they stood when the suits were filed.

rule.if: eviction_suit and suit_filed_during_exemption and exemption_ends_while_suit_pending and notification_covers_later_decrees

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord brings a civil-court proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant from a building.
predicates.suit_filed_during_exemption: The landlord files the eviction suit while the building is exempt from the relevant eviction restrictions.
predicates.exemption_ends_while_suit_pending: The exemption period ends before the eviction suit is finally decided.
predicates.notification_covers_later_decrees: The exemption measure expressly covers decrees in suits filed during the exemption period even when those decrees are passed afterward.

members.legal_issue: A civil court may continue a validly instituted possession suit and its decree may be executed when a temporary exemption from rent-control protection expires while the suit is pending.
material_facts: The premises were newly constructed buildings that were exempt from the rent-control legislation for a fixed period after construction.
The landlords terminated the tenancies and filed possession suits while the buildings remained exempt.
The exemption period expired before the trial courts passed decrees for possession.
The decrees were upheld on appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 1(3) and 13(1) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, a suit validly instituted while a newly constructed building is exempt may proceed after the exemption expires. Section 13(1) does not expressly bar the civil court from deciding such a suit or prevent execution of its decree. The parties’ rights are determined by the law applicable when the suit is instituted; reading the Act otherwise would defeat the purpose of encouraging new construction and allow a tenant to frustrate that purpose by delaying litigation. The Court applied the reasoning in Firms Amar Nath Basheshar Dass v. Tek Chand, Shri Ram Saroop Rai v. Smt. Lilavati, Mohinder Kumar v. State of Haryana, Nand Kishore Marwah v. Samundri Devi, Atma Ram Mittal v. Ishwar Singh Punia, Kesho Ram & Co. v. Union of India, Suresh Chand v. Gulam Chisti, Ramesh Chandra v. III Additional District Judge, Bhola Nath Varshney v. Mulk Raj Madan, and Parripati Chandrasekharrao & Sons v. Alapati Jalaiah. It rejected the contrary approach in Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera as no longer good law.
members.conclusion: Expiry of the exemption during the pendency of the suits did not deprive the civil courts of jurisdiction to decide them, and the decrees for possession remained executable.

rule.if: civil_possession_suit and tenancy_terminated_before_filing and suit_filed_during_temporary_exemption and exemption_expired_before_decree

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A landlord brought a civil court proceeding seeking possession of rented premises.
predicates.tenancy_terminated_before_filing: The landlord terminated the tenancy before filing the possession suit.
predicates.suit_filed_during_temporary_exemption: The landlord filed the suit while the premises were within a temporary period of exemption from rent-control protection.
predicates.exemption_expired_before_decree: The temporary exemption expired before the court passed its decree.

members.legal_issue: A civil court retains jurisdiction over a validly instituted eviction suit when rent-control protection is extended to the premises during the suit, unless the legislation specifically protects terminated tenancies or pending proceedings.
material_facts: The premises were outside the rent legislation when the landlord instituted the eviction suit after terminating the tenancy.
During the suit, a notification brought the area containing the premises within the rent legislation.
The trial court decreed eviction, and the tenant challenged the decree on the ground that the civil court lost jurisdiction when the notification took effect.
The applicable legislation contained no provision protecting ex-tenants in these circumstances or excluding civil-court jurisdiction over pending suits.
members.legal_principle: The parties’ rights ordinarily crystallise when a valid suit is instituted, and later application of rent-control legislation does not oust the civil court’s jurisdiction over that suit absent a specific statutory provision extending protection to terminated tenancies or pending proceedings. This follows the reasoning in Atma Ram Mittal v. Ishwar Singh Punia, Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera, Ram Saroop Rai v. Lilawati, Shri Kishan alias Krishna Kumar v. Manoj Kumar, and Mansoor Khan v. Moti Ram. The Court distinguished Mani Subrat Jain v. Raja Ram Vohra and Lakshmi Narayan Guin v. Niranjan Modak because the relevant legislation there defined tenants to include ex-tenants and expressly protected against eviction under earlier decrees. The Court considered Sections 1(3) and 13(1) of the Haryana Rent Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, and the absence of a provision ousting civil-court jurisdiction over validly instituted suits.
members.conclusion: The civil court retained jurisdiction to decide the suit. The appeal was allowed, the judgments of the appellate court and High Court were set aside, and the trial court’s decree was restored.

rule.if: eviction_suit_in_civil_court and suit_filed_before_rent_protection and premises_later_brought_under_rent_protection and not statute_protects_terminated_tenancies_in_pending_suits

predicates.eviction_suit_in_civil_court: A landlord instituted a suit in a civil court seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.suit_filed_before_rent_protection: The premises were not covered by rent-control protection when the eviction suit was instituted.
predicates.premises_later_brought_under_rent_protec: During the pending suit, a legal change brought the premises within rent-control protection.
predicates.statute_protects_terminated_tenancies_in: The applicable legislation specifically protects terminated tenancies or pending proceedings from civil-court eviction jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A civil eviction suit validly instituted before rent-control protections are extended to the area may be decided by the civil court after the extension, and a resulting decree remains executable unless the legislation provides otherwise for pending suits or decrees.
material_facts: The landlord filed a civil suit for possession while the premises were outside the area covered by the rent-control legislation, after terminating the tenancy.
While the suit was pending, a notification extended the rent-control legislation to the area.
The civil court passed a possession decree after that extension.

The legislation gave the Rent Tribunal jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes in covered areas but contained no provision barring decision of pending civil suits or execution of decrees in those suits.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 1(2) and 18 of the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2001, the Act applies to areas from the effective date of the relevant notification, and the Rent Tribunal has jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes in areas to which the Act extends. Section 18 does not invalidate or transfer suits already validly instituted in civil court. In the absence of an express or implied provision applying the new regime to pending suits or barring execution of decrees in them, the law applicable when the suit was instituted governs it, and the parties’ rights crystallise on that date. This approach is supported by Nand Kishore Marwah v. Samundri Devi, Ramesh Chandra v. III Additional District Judge, Atma Ram Mittal v. Ishwar Singh Punia, Shri Kishan v. Manoj Kumar, Mansoor Khan v. Motiram Harebhan Kharat, and Rajender Bansal v. Bhuru; Vineet Kumar v. Mangal Sain Wadhera was specifically held not to be good law in Shri Kishan. The Court distinguished statutory schemes that expressly restrict execution of earlier decrees, including Section 13 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
members.conclusion: The civil court could validly pass the decree after the legislation became applicable to the area, and the decree remains executable. The appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and suit_valid_when_filed and rent_protection_extended_during_suit and later_decree_passed and not pending_case_or_decree_bar

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a civil-court suit seeking eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.suit_valid_when_filed: The civil court had jurisdiction when the landlord instituted the suit under the law then applicable to the premises.
predicates.rent_protection_extended_during_suit: Rent-control protections were extended to the area while the civil suit was pending.
predicates.later_decree_passed: The civil court passed an eviction decree after those protections were extended to the area.
predicates.pending_case_or_decree_bar: The legislation expressly or impliedly bars the civil court from deciding the pending suit or bars execution of a decree in such a suit.
predicates.decree_remains_valid_and_executable: The civil-court eviction decree remains legally valid and may be executed.

members.legal_issue: A civil eviction suit may proceed for premises excluded from rent-control protection by the applicable rent-law exclusion.
material_facts: The landlord brought a civil suit seeking possession of commercial premises and relied on an exclusion from rent-control protection for premises above a specified monthly rent.
The Supreme Court’s applicable declaration treated the state-law exclusion as operative, contrary to the High Court’s direction that the parties pursue eviction before the rent court.
The trial court had decreed eviction, and the Supreme Court restored that decree after setting aside the High Court’s order.
members.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act excluded premises above the specified rent from the Act. The Court applied D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India, concerning a similar exclusion under the Delhi Rent Control Act, as applied to the Karnataka provision in Shobha Surendar. It therefore rejected the High Court’s reliance on Padmanabha Rao and restored the civil court’s decree. Section 21 was relevant to eviction under the Rent Control Act, but did not govern premises excluded from that Act.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to direct the parties to seek their remedies under the Rent Control Act, and the trial court’s eviction decree was restored.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord has brought a civil suit seeking eviction or possession of premises.
predicates.premises_excluded_from_rent_control: The premises fall outside rent-control protection under an applicable exclusion.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession: The landlord seeks possession of the premises from the occupant.
predicates.civil_court_may_adjudicate_eviction: The civil court may hear and decide the eviction claim.

members.legal_issue: A building excluded from rent control falls within the jurisdiction of the civil court rather than the rent control authority.
material_facts: The building was constructed in 1958, after the statutory cutoff for the rent control legislation.
The landlord brought a civil suit seeking possession after the rent authority proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction Control) Act, 1960 did not apply to buildings constructed after August 1957. The building’s status under the rent control legislation determined which forum had jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The building was outside the protection of the rent control legislation, so the civil court, not the rent authority, had jurisdiction over it.

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a civil-court suit seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.building_constructed_after_statutory_cut: The building was constructed after the cutoff beyond which the rent control regime did not apply.

members.legal_issue: The rent-control law does not govern a local authority’s suit to recover its land, and the suit need not be brought in the court designated for rent-control matters.
material_facts: A local authority sought ejectment and vacant possession of land belonging to it.
The suit’s claim was for possession of the land.
The tenant relied on the rent-control law and argued that the suit belonged in the court designated for rent-control matters.
The relevant statutory amendment addressed specified buildings, while the suit concerned the land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1), 4(4)(a), and 5(8) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates (Control) Act, 1947, read together, exclude a local authority’s action concerning its land from the Act; section 4(4)(a) addresses specified buildings and does not extend that exclusion to land. The Court relied on Bhatia Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. D. C. Patel, which explained the effect of section 4(1), and Ram Bhagwandas v. Bombay Corporation, which discussed the amendment’s scope. Accordingly, the rent-control court’s jurisdictional requirement did not apply.
members.conclusion: The rent-control law did not prevent the local authority from recovering the land, and the suit was properly brought in the City Civil Court rather than the Small Causes Court.

predicates.local_authority_ejectment_suit: A local authority brought a suit to eject a person and recover possession.
predicates.land_owned_by_local_authority: The land sought to be recovered belonged to the local authority.
predicates.claim_concerns_land: The claim for possession concerned the land rather than a claim to evict occupants from a building.

members.legal_issue: A special rent-control regime excludes the ordinary civil court from ordering eviction where a leased building is covered by the regime, even though a minor part of it lies on municipal land.
material_facts: The landlord leased the shop as a building to the tenant, and the building stood mainly on the landlord’s land, with a small part on municipal land leased to the landlord.
The landlord sought eviction for non-payment of rent.
The applicable rent-control regime provided for eviction through its designated Controller, and the municipal-land exemption did not exempt the building.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(a), 3 and 13 of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, the relevant question was whether the leased building was covered by the Act; an exemption relating to municipal land did not exempt the building on these facts. Where a special statute creates a right and provides the forum and remedy for its enforcement, the ordinary civil court has no jurisdiction to grant that remedy. The Court relied on Hari Parshad Gupta v. Jitender Kumar Kaushik, Barrachlough v. Brown, Doe v. Bridges, and the third proposition in Premier Automobiles v. K.S. Wadke.
members.conclusion: The building was governed by the rent-control regime, whose Controller had exclusive jurisdiction to order eviction; the civil court inherently lacked jurisdiction to entertain the eviction suit.

rule.if: urban_tenancy_eviction_case and building_leased_as_a_building and building_mainly_on_land_owned_by_landlord and small_part_on_municipal_land

predicates.urban_tenancy_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns eviction of a tenant from a building in an urban area.
predicates.building_leased_as_a_building: The landlord leased the premises to the tenant as a building.
predicates.building_mainly_on_land_owned_by_landlor: The building stood mainly on land belonging to the landlord.
predicates.small_part_on_municipal_land: A small part of the building stood on municipal land leased to the landlord.

members.legal_issue: Statutory interest is payable on solatium as part of compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
material_facts: The court awarded solatium on the full market value of the compulsorily acquired land.
Possession had been taken from the landowner before the solatium was paid.
The lower court had awarded interest on compensation, and the Supreme Court directed interest on the solatium from the date possession was taken until payment.
members.legal_principle: Solatium under section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is part of compensation, and sections 28 and 34 provide for interest on compensation. Periyar and Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala, AIR 1990 SC 2192, recognized entitlement to interest on solatium. Although Dr. Shamlal Narula v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Punjab, [1964] 7 SCR 668, characterized statutory interest as interest for delayed payment rather than compensation for loss of possession, the Court held that solatium, being part of compensation, must bear statutory interest from dispossession until payment.
members.conclusion: The landowner was entitled to statutory interest on the solatium from dispossession until payment.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_appe: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land taken compulsorily.
