predicates.solatium_is_awarded: The decision-maker awards an additional sum for the compulsory nature of the acquisition.
predicates.possession_was_taken_before_payment: The acquiring authority took possession of the land before paying the solatium.

members.legal_issue: Interest is payable on statutory solatium that forms part of compensation for acquired land.
material_facts: The claimants had been awarded solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
The High Court refused interest on solatium, relying on Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India.
The claimants challenged that refusal, and the Court considered the Constitution Bench decision in Sunder v. Union of India, which had overruled Prem Nath Kapur.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(2) provides for solatium as part of the compensation, and the Court applied Sunder v. Union of India, which held that the aggregate compensation under Section 23 attracts interest when payment is delayed and overruled Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India. The Court thereby rejected splitting compensation into components to exclude solatium from interest under the applicable interest provision, including Section 28; the reasoning quoted from Sunder also addresses Section 34.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest on solatium.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding was an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.solatium_was_awarded: The claimants had been awarded statutory solatium as part of the compensation.
predicates.interest_on_solatium_was_denied_below: The lower court refused to award interest on the solatium component.

members.legal_issue: Interest on statutory solatium is payable as part of interest on compensation.
material_facts: The claimants sought solatium, interest, and other statutory benefits in connection with compensation for acquired land.
The High Court had held the award of interest on solatium contrary to governing principles.
The Supreme Court directed that the claim for statutory benefits be governed by the principle in Sunder v. Union of India.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(2) provides statutory solatium as part of compensation, and Section 28 authorises interest on compensation, including solatium. The Court applied Sunder v. Union of India, which held that solatium forms an integral statutory part of compensation and that interest on compensation therefore includes interest on solatium.
members.conclusion: Interest is payable on solatium, and the claim for statutory benefits is to be determined in accordance with Sunder v. Union of India.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The case concerns compensation for land taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.statutory_solatium_is_awarded: The compensation includes statutory solatium for the compulsory nature of the acquisition.
predicates.interest_is_claimed_on_compensation: The claimant seeks interest on the compensation awarded.
predicates.interest_payable_on_solatium: Interest on compensation includes interest on statutory solatium.

members.legal_issue: Interest payable on compensation for compulsorily acquired land includes interest on the statutory solatium component.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned compensation for land acquired compulsorily under the land acquisition law.
The compensation included solatium awarded because the acquisition was compulsory.
The dispute was whether interest payable on compensation also accrued on the solatium component.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 23(1), 23(1-A) and 23(2), the amounts awarded under each subsection together constitute the compensation awarded; Sections 28 and 34 provide for interest on that compensation, and do not permit it to be split into components to exclude solatium. Sections 26 and 31 support treating the additional amounts under Section 23 as part of the award and compensation payable. Solatium for compulsory acquisition is distinct from damages for a landowner’s disinclination to part with land, which Section 24 excludes from consideration. Union of India v. Shri Ram Mehar concerned interest on market value under a different amending provision and does not govern interest on compensation under Sections 28 and 34. Periyar & Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. supports interest on solatium; the contrary views in Mir Fazeelath Hussain and Yadavrao P. Pathade are not followed, and the observation in Prem Nath Kapur was made where the question was not directly considered. The Court also noted consistent High Court decisions, including State of Haryana v. Smt. Kailashwati.
members.conclusion: A person entitled to compensation for acquired land is entitled to interest on the aggregate compensation, including solatium, when interest is payable under the applicable statutory provision.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired compulsorily.
predicates.solatium_awarded: The compensation awarded includes an additional amount because the acquisition was compulsory.
predicates.statutory_interest_payable: Interest is payable on the compensation because payment was delayed or an excess compensation amount was awarded.

members.legal_issue: Interest is payable on the solatium component of compensation for acquired land.
material_facts: The claimants were entitled to solatium as part of the compensation for their acquired land.
They sought interest on the solatium component.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sunder v. Union of India, Chimanlal Kuberdas Modi v. Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, Nadirsha Shapurji Patel v. Collector and Land Acquisition Officer, R. Saragapani v. Special Tahsildar, and Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited v. R.S. Avtar Singh and Company, holding that interest is payable on solatium.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest on solatium.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.solatium_is_awarded: The owner is awarded solatium as part of the compensation for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Interest on compensation for compulsory acquisition includes interest on solatium where the governing provision awards interest on excess compensation.
material_facts: The claimant received solatium as part of the additional compensation for the acquired land.
The claimant sought interest on the excess compensation, including solatium, from the date possession was taken until payment.
The governing provision directed interest on excess compensation, and the Court distinguished a precedent concerning interest on market value under a different statutory provision.
members.legal_principle: Section 25(3) of the Kerala Land Acquisition Regulation, 1089 provides interest on excess compensation. The Court held that “compensation” in that provision includes solatium, which forms part of compensation under sections 23(1) and 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It distinguished Union of India v. Shri Ram Mehar, which concerned statutory wording referring to interest on market value rather than compensation.
members.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to interest on the excess compensation including solatium from the taking of possession until payment.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_proc: The proceeding concerns compensation for compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.excess_compensation_includes_solatium: The court determines that excess compensation payable to the claimant includes solatium.
predicates.possession_precedes_payment: The acquiring authority took possession before paying the excess compensation.

members.legal_issue: Interest is payable on the compensation amounts awarded under each of the three compensation sub-sections, including the additional amount and solatium.
material_facts: The claimants sought interest on the additional amount payable under the compensation provision.
The controlling larger-bench decision had held that the total compensation includes the amounts payable under all three compensation sub-sections.
members.legal_principle: The Court followed Sunder v. Union of India, which held that the compensation amount on which interest is payable includes the amounts determined under all three sub-sections of the compensation provision. It also referred to Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India Ltd., whose contrary treatment of interest on the additional amount was superseded by the larger-bench ruling in Sunder.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest on the amount payable under the additional-compensation sub-section, as well as on the other compensation components.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_claim: The proceeding concerns compensation awarded for an acquisition under the general acquisition law.
predicates.compensation_includes_statutory_addition: The awarded compensation includes statutory additions to the basic market-value amount, such as an additional amount or solatium.

members.legal_issue: An increase in compensation for compulsorily acquired land carries the applicable statutory solatium, interest, and additional amount.
material_facts: The court increased the compensation payable for the compulsorily acquired land.

The court stated that the claimants were entitled to solatium under Section 23(2), interest under Section 28 until deposit, and the additional amount under Section 23(1-A) on the enhanced compensation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(2), 28, and 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide the applicable solatium, interest, and additional amount, respectively. The court applied those provisions to the enhanced compensation.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to the statutory solatium, interest, and additional amount on the enhanced compensation.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_awar: The proceeding concerns an award of compensation for land taken by compulsory acquisition.
predicates.compensation_enhanced: The court increases the compensation awarded for the acquired land.
predicates.claimant_entitled_to_statutory_additions: The claimant is entitled to the statutory additions applicable to the enhanced compensation.

members.legal_issue: An amount by which a court enhances land compensation carries solatium and interest.
material_facts: The court enhanced the compensation for the acquired land on appeal.
The court clarified that the enhanced compensation carried solatium and interest.
members.legal_principle: The court directed that the enhanced compensation carry the usual solatium and interest. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this clarification in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The enhanced compensation was to carry solatium at 10 per cent and interest at 4 per cent per annum from the land acquisition officer's award until realization.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.court_enhances_compensation: The court increases the compensation awarded for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Enhanced compensation carries the solatium and interest awarded by the Court.
material_facts: The Court enhanced the compensation payable for the acquired land.
The claimants sought the statutory benefits associated with the enhanced compensation.
members.legal_principle: The Court awarded solatium on the enhanced compensation and interest on the compensation, specifying the applicable rates and periods. The judgment does not identify the statutory provisions supporting this part of the order.
members.conclusion: The claimants were awarded 30% solatium on the enhanced compensation and interest at 9% for one year from possession and 15% thereafter until deposit.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: A claimant appeals a court's determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.enhanced_compensation_awarded: The court increases the compensation payable for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Enhanced compensation for acquired land carries solatium and interest as directed by the court.
material_facts: The court enhanced the compensation payable for the acquired land.
The court directed solatium on the enhanced compensation and interest running from the taking of possession until payment.
members.legal_principle: The court directed solatium on the enhanced compensation and interest from the date of taking possession until payment. The judgment does not identify a statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this direction.
members.conclusion: The appellants were entitled to solatium on the enhanced compensation and interest from the date possession was taken until payment.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_enhanced: The court increases the compensation payable for the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: A claimant awarded compensation for acquired land is entitled to the applicable additional amount, solatium, and interest.
material_facts: The High Court had fixed market value for the acquired land and ordered additional compensation, solatium, and interest.
The Supreme Court affirmed the land valuation and ratified the related orders for those compensation components.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 23(1A) and 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act and affirmed the interest ordered by the High Court.
members.conclusion: The claimant remained entitled to the additional amount under Section 23(1A), solatium under Section 23(2), and the interest ordered by the High Court.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.market_value_awarded: A court has awarded market value for the acquired land.
predicates.statutory_compensation_additions_apply: The claimant qualifies for the additional amount, solatium, and interest associated with the compensation award.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired land is to carry solatium and interest running from the taking of possession.
material_facts: The court fixed compensation for the acquired land.
Possession of the acquired land had been taken.
The trial court had awarded solatium and interest, and the Supreme Court directed that the usual additions be made to the compensation it fixed.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the usual additions of solatium and interest to the compensation award. It cited no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this direction.
members.conclusion: The compensation is to include solatium at 15% and interest at 6% from the date possession was taken.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.compensation_awarded: The court has determined compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.possession_taken: Possession of the acquired land has been taken.

members.legal_issue: A later suit seeking relief concerning a transaction already available to challenge when an earlier suit was filed is barred when both claims arise from the same cause of action and the relief was omitted from the earlier suit.
material_facts: The plaintiffs’ first suit challenged one part of a transfer of ancestral family property, alleging that the transferor had disposed of the property without legal necessity and to the family’s detriment.
Before the first suit was filed, the transferor had also transferred the remaining part of the property to the same defendants.
The pleadings in the two suits relied on virtually identical factual and legal allegations, and the plaintiffs did not seek relief concerning the second transfer in the first suit.

The plaintiffs later brought a separate suit seeking to set aside the second transfer. They argued, among other things, that its different limitation period meant that the later suit had a different cause of action.
members.legal_principle: Under Order II Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaintiff must include the whole claim arising from a cause of action, and omission or intentional relinquishment of part of that claim precludes a later suit for it. Whether causes of action are the same depends on the substance of the factual and legal basis on which the plaintiff seeks relief, not on the relief sought or the defence raised. A different limitation period does not itself make the cause of action different. The Court applied the tests in Mohammad Khalil Khan v. Mehbub Ali Mian and Coffee Board v. Ramesh Exports Private Limited, and relied on Virgo Industries (Eng.) (P) Ltd. v. Venturetech Solutions (P) Ltd. for the distinction between omitted claims and omitted reliefs; it also considered Alka Gupta v. Narender Gupta and the principles discussed in Union of India v. H.K. Dhruv and S. Nazeer Ahmed v. State Bank of Mysore.
members.conclusion: The later suit was barred because the omitted relief arose from the same cause of action and could have been sought in the earlier suit. The appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment was set aside. The Court did not decide the constructive-res-judicata issue.

predicates.subsequent_suit_for_omitted_relief: A plaintiff brings a later suit seeking relief that was not sought in an earlier suit.
predicates.same_cause_of_action: The earlier and later claims rest in substance on the same factual and legal basis for seeking the court’s intervention.
predicates.relief_available_in_earlier_suit: The transaction giving rise to the later claim had occurred, and the plaintiff could have sought the relief, when the earlier suit was filed.

members.legal_issue: A later suit for relief arising from the same cause of action is barred when that relief could and should have been claimed in an earlier suit.
material_facts: An earlier suit seeking an injunction concerning the same land was pending when the present suit was filed.
The present suit sought declaration and injunction relief based on the same alleged transaction underlying the earlier suit.
The Court found that the relief now claimed could and ought to have been claimed in the earlier suit.
members.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a subsequent suit for a portion of a claim or relief arising from the same cause of action where that claim or relief could and should have been included in the earlier suit.
members.conclusion: The later suit was apparently barred by Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.later_civil_suit: A civil suit is brought after an earlier suit concerning the underlying claim.
predicates.earlier_suit_on_same_cause_pending_when_: An earlier suit based on the same cause of action remains pending when the later suit is filed.
predicates.omitted_relief_could_and_should_have_bee: The relief sought later was available and ought to have been included in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A bar for omitting relief in an earlier suit applies only when the later suit concerns the same cause of action, the plaintiff was entitled to multiple reliefs on that cause of action, and the plaintiff omitted the later relief without obtaining leave.
material_facts: The defendant argued that the plaintiff had omitted to claim possession in the earlier suit and was therefore barred from seeking possession in the later suit.

The Court stated the elements required for a bar under Order 2 Rule 2(3), but did not determine whether the two suits were based on the same cause of action because the earlier plaint had not been produced.
members.legal_principle: Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 permits a person entitled to multiple reliefs in respect of the same cause of action to sue for all or any of them, but bars a later suit for an omitted relief if it was omitted without the court’s leave. The defendant bears the burden of establishing the elements. The Court did not resolve the competing views on whether claims for possession and mesne profits arise from the same cause of action, and cited no earlier case as authority for the test.
members.conclusion: To succeed, the defendant must establish all three elements: identity of cause of action, entitlement to more than one relief on that cause of action, and omission of the later relief without leave.

rule.if: defendant_asserts_omission_bar and later_suit_same_cause_of_action and plaintiff_entitled_to_multiple_reliefs and later_relief_omitted_without_leave

predicates.defendant_asserts_omission_bar: In a later civil suit, the defendant claims that the plaintiff omitted the relief now sought from an earlier suit.
predicates.later_suit_same_cause_of_action: The earlier and later suits are based on the same cause of action.
predicates.plaintiff_entitled_to_multiple_reliefs: The plaintiff was entitled to more than one relief in respect of that cause of action.
predicates.later_relief_omitted_without_leave: The plaintiff omitted the relief sought in the later suit from the earlier suit without obtaining leave.

members.legal_issue: A later suit for an omitted relief is barred when it arises from the same cause of action as an earlier suit, the plaintiff was entitled to claim multiple reliefs on that cause, and leave to omit the relief was not obtained.
material_facts: The plaintiff first sued for an injunction based on agreements to sell the properties and omitted to seek specific performance, although the first-suit pleadings alleged conduct showing that the defendant intended to frustrate the agreements.
The plaintiff asked for leave to reserve the specific-performance claim, but the court did not grant leave.
The plaintiff later brought suits for specific performance based on the same agreements and the same events pleaded in the earlier suits.
members.legal_principle: Order II Rules 2(2) and 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure address, respectively, omission of part of a claim and omission of one of several reliefs. Under Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, the party invoking the bar must establish that the suits rest on the same cause of action, that more than one relief was available on that cause, and that the later relief was omitted without leave. The Court also relied on Deva Ram v. Ishwar Chand and M/s Bengal Waterproof Ltd. v. M/s Bombay Waterproof Manufacturing Co. The identity of a cause of action turns on the material facts entitling a plaintiff to relief, as discussed in Church of Christ Charitable Trust v. Ponniamman Educational Trust.
members.conclusion: The later specific-performance suits were barred, and the plaints were struck off.

rule.if: later_specific_performance_suit and same_cause_of_action and multiple_reliefs_available and relief_omitted_without_leave

predicates.later_specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brings a later suit seeking specific performance after an earlier suit concerning the same agreement or transaction.
predicates.same_cause_of_action: The material facts supporting the later claim were also the basis of the earlier suit.
predicates.multiple_reliefs_available: The plaintiff could claim more than one form of relief on the facts supporting the earlier suit.
predicates.relief_omitted_without_leave: The plaintiff omitted the relief later sought and did not obtain the court’s permission to reserve it.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who omits relief available on the same cause of action in an earlier suit, without leave to omit it, cannot seek that relief in a later suit.
material_facts: The earlier partition suit sought division of all family property and determination of the family business accounts.
The claimant limited the accounting relief in the earlier suit to a specified cutoff and did not seek accounts for the later period.
The claimant later sued for accounts for the motor business for that later period.
The later claim arose from the same desire to separate and divide the family property that formed the basis of the earlier suit.
The claimant had no leave of the court to omit the later-period accounting relief.
members.legal_principle: Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that a person who omits, without the court’s leave, relief to which that person is entitled cannot later sue for the omitted relief. The Court held that the cause of action in the later suit was the same as in the earlier partition suit.
members.conclusion: The later suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure because the omitted relief arose from the same cause of action.

rule.if: later_suit_after_prior_partition_suit and same_separation_cause and relief_omitted_from_prior_suit and no_leave_to_omit_relief

predicates.later_suit_after_prior_partition_suit: The claimant brought a later suit after an earlier suit seeking partition of shared family property.
predicates.same_separation_cause: The earlier and later suits arose from the claimant’s wish to separate and divide the shared family property.
predicates.relief_omitted_from_prior_suit: The claimant did not seek in the earlier suit relief that was later sought in the subsequent suit.
predicates.no_leave_to_omit_relief: The claimant had not obtained the court’s permission to omit that relief from the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A borrower who deliberately omits relief available in an earlier suit to reopen loan decrees cannot seek that relief in a successive suit.
material_facts: The borrower first sued for relief concerning a personal decree arising from a mortgage loan and sought reopening of that decree only.
The borrower could have sought reopening of the preliminary and final mortgage decrees in the first suit but deliberately abandoned that relief.
The borrower later brought another suit concerning the same loan transaction to obtain reopening of the preliminary and final mortgage decrees.
members.legal_principle: Section 36 of the Bengal Money-lenders Act, 1940, contemplated one suit, not successive suits, for reopening transactions and decrees. The principles underlying section 11 and Order 2, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, applied: relief available but not claimed or deliberately abandoned in the earlier suit could not be sought in a later suit.
members.conclusion: The later suit was barred; the appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: successive_borrower_relief_suit and prior_borrower_relief_suit and same_loan_transaction and omitted_relief_available_earlier and omitted_relief_deliberately_abandoned

predicates.successive_borrower_relief_suit: The current proceeding is a borrower's suit seeking relief to reopen a loan transaction or decree.
predicates.prior_borrower_relief_suit: The borrower previously brought a suit seeking relief concerning the same loan transaction or its decrees.
predicates.same_loan_transaction: The earlier and later suits concern the same loan transaction.
predicates.omitted_relief_available_earlier: The borrower could have sought the relief claimed in the later suit in the earlier suit.
predicates.omitted_relief_deliberately_abandoned: The borrower deliberately chose not to seek that relief in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who omits a specific-performance claim from a suit after the other party has clearly refused performance cannot later pursue that omitted claim on the same cause of action.
material_facts: The agreement fixed no date for performance.
The seller published a notice asserting ownership and possession and stating that the agreement and related authority had been cancelled.
After that notice, the purchaser filed a suit for declaration of ownership and an injunction but did not seek specific performance.
The purchaser later sought to add specific performance to the suit, rather than having included it when the refusal gave rise to a cause of action.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, when no date is fixed for performance, limitation for a suit for specific performance begins when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. Order 2 Rule 2 CPC embodies the principle that a claimant must include the whole claim arising from a cause of action; its broad, public-policy principles applied even though no later second suit had been filed.
members.conclusion: The purchaser had a cause of action for specific performance when the refusal was made clear, but its omission of that relief from the original suit amounted to relinquishment of that part of its claim and attracted the broad principles of Order 2 Rule 2 CPC.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and refusal_known and no_performance_date_fixed and original_suit_omitted_performance

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant seeks enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.refusal_known: The claimant has notice that the other party refuses to perform the agreement.
predicates.no_performance_date_fixed: The agreement does not specify a date for performance.
predicates.original_suit_omitted_performance: After the cause of action arose, the claimant filed a suit concerning the same transaction but did not include a claim for specific performance.

members.legal_issue: A later claim for compensation that could and ought to have been raised in an earlier execution proceeding is barred by constructive res judicata when it is closely connected to the earlier claim to resist possession.
material_facts: In the earlier execution application, the claimants sought a declaration that they were entitled to remain in possession as lessees and that the decree holders could not dispossess them.
The earlier application did not assert a claim for compensation for improvements under the applicable improvements legislation.
The claimants later sought to remain in possession until compensation for improvements was determined and paid.
The compensation claim was connected to the earlier attempt to resist delivery of possession, and the execution proceedings provided a means to have the claim adjudicated.
members.legal_principle: Section 11, Explanation IV of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 deems a matter directly and substantially in issue if it might and ought to have been raised in the earlier proceeding; the requirements are conjunctive. Whether a matter ought to have been raised depends on the scope of the earlier proceeding and the matter's connection to the controversy. The principle serves finality and prevents multiplicity of proceedings, as explained in Kameswar Pershad v Rajkumari Ruttun Koer, Henderson v Henderson, Greenhalgh v Mallard, Johnson v Gore Wood & Co, State of U.P. v Nawab Hussain, Direct Recruit Class II Engineering Officers' Association v State of Maharashtra and Forward Construction Co. v Prabhat Mandal. Order XXI Rules 97 to 103 provide a complete execution remedy for claims relating to possession. Sections 4 and 5 of the Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958 provide for compensation and continued possession pending eviction, and support raising such a claim in the proceeding determining the right to possession.
members.conclusion: The later compensation claim was barred by constructive res judicata because it could and ought to have been raised in the earlier execution proceedings.

rule.if: execution_obstruction_proceeding and earlier_possession_claim_adjudicated and later_claim_seeks_possession_pending_compensation and compensation_claim_could_have_been_raised_earlier and compensation_claim_ought_to_have_been_raised_earlier

predicates.execution_obstruction_proceeding: A claimant resists delivery of property in a proceeding to execute a decree for possession.
predicates.earlier_possession_claim_adjudicated: The claimant's earlier request to remain in possession was adjudicated in the execution proceeding.
predicates.later_claim_seeks_possession_pending_com: The claimant later seeks to retain possession until compensation for improvements is determined or paid.
predicates.compensation_claim_could_have_been_raise: The claimant had an opportunity to assert the compensation ground in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.compensation_claim_ought_to_have_been_ra: The compensation ground was sufficiently connected to the earlier dispute about possession that it should have been raised there.

members.legal_issue: A later title suit by a successor is barred when the predecessor could and ought to have raised in the earlier suit the ownership-based ground or alternative relief on which the later claim depends.
material_facts: In the earlier suit, the wife claimed that the husband had relinquished his rights in the house and that she and the children occupied it under the settlement.
The husband claimed through an inherited interest in a house allotted to his mother, although the formal conveyance in his favour was obtained later.
The husband and the co-plaintiff sought an injunction based on the mortgage but did not alternatively seek possession on the basis of the husband's claimed rights.
The earlier suit was dismissed and was not appealed.
The later claimant purchased the house from the husband and sought title and possession.
members.legal_principle: Explanation IV to section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure deems a matter that might and ought to have been made a ground of attack or defence in the former suit to have been directly and substantially in issue there. The court applied this principle to the successor claiming through the earlier plaintiff; it also relied on the rule in Sulochana Amma v. Narayan Nair, (1994) 2 SCC 14, concerning the effect of an earlier injunction decision where title was in issue.
members.conclusion: The later purchaser's claim was also barred by constructive res judicata because the ownership-based claim and alternative claim for possession could and ought to have been raised in the earlier suit.

rule.if: earlier_suit_between_predecessors and later_title_suit_by_successor and predecessor_had_ownership_based_claim and opposing_party_asserted_competing_right and alternative_possession_claim_was_available and omitted_claim_could_and_ought_to_have_been_raised

predicates.earlier_suit_between_predecessors: The parties through whom the later claimant and opposing party claim litigated an earlier suit concerning the same property.
predicates.later_title_suit_by_successor: A person claiming through a party to the earlier suit later brought a suit asserting title to the property.
predicates.predecessor_had_ownership_based_claim: The predecessor relied on an existing or claimed right to the property as a basis for relief in the earlier suit.
predicates.opposing_party_asserted_competing_right: The opposing party in the earlier suit asserted a competing right to the property.
predicates.alternative_possession_claim_was_availab: The predecessor could have sought possession as an alternative form of relief based on the claimed right to the property.
predicates.omitted_claim_could_and_ought_to_have_be: The ownership-based ground or alternative relief was available and should have been advanced in the earlier suit but was not.
predicates.later_claim_precluded_as_omitted_ground: The later claim cannot be pursued because it depends on a ground that should have been raised in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot rely in a later suit on a lawful basis of possession that could and ought to have been raised as a defence in an earlier suit between the parties.
material_facts: In the earlier suit, the defendant was found not to be the owner and was found to be occupying the property as a tenant.
The defendant did not put forward a claim that he occupied the property lawfully in some capacity other than as a tenant, although he could have raised that defence in the earlier proceedings.
The defendant later denied the landlord-tenant relationship and disputed the purchaser’s right to possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, particularly Explanation IV, treats as directly and substantially in issue a matter that might and ought to have been made a ground of defence or attack in the former suit. The Court explained that this rule requires parties to raise available grounds of attack or defence in the same suit. It relied on Horo v. Jahan Ara, Jaswant Singh v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, Forward Construction Co. v. Prabhat Mandal, Direct Recruits Class II Engineering Officers’ Association v. State of Maharashtra, and Vijayan v. Kamalakshi.
members.conclusion: The defendant was barred from raising in the later suit a claim to lawful possession in a capacity other than that of a tenant.

rule.if: later_landlord_eviction_suit and same_parties_in_both_suits and prior_suit_decided_defendants_possession_status and alternative_lawful_possession_defence_available and alternative_lawful_possession_defence_omitted

predicates.later_landlord_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a later suit seeking eviction of a person occupying the property.
predicates.same_parties_in_both_suits: The parties to the later suit were parties to the earlier suit.
predicates.prior_suit_decided_defendants_possession: The earlier court decided the basis on which the defendant occupied the property.
predicates.alternative_lawful_possession_defence_av: The defendant could have raised a claim to lawful possession in a capacity other than the one determined in the earlier suit.
predicates.alternative_lawful_possession_defence_om: The defendant did not raise that alternative claim as a defence in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot grant specific performance on the basis of a different agreement pleaded by the defendant when the claimant has not accepted and sought performance of that agreement or pleaded readiness and willingness to perform it.
material_facts: The defendant’s written statement described an agreement to sell part of the property for a specified price, which differed from the oral reconveyance agreement pleaded by the plaintiff.
The plaintiff did not amend the pleadings or otherwise seek relief on the basis of the defendant’s agreement.
The plaintiff did not accept that agreement as true or plead that he was ready and willing to perform it.
The High Court nevertheless ordered a sale on the terms stated in the defendant’s written statement.
members.legal_principle: A specific-performance claim must set out the agreement sued upon and plead that the claimant applied for its performance, that the other party failed to perform, and that the claimant has been and remains ready and willing to perform. The judgment relies on Forms 47 and 48 in the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure and applies Pt. Prem Raj v. The D.L.F. Housing and Construction (Private) Ltd. and distinguishes Srinivas Ram Kumar v. Mahabir Prasad.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to decree specific performance on the basis of the defendant’s different agreement.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.defendant_pleaded_a_different_contract: The defendant described a contract materially different from the contract on which the claimant based the suit.
predicates.claimant_did_not_accept_or_seek_relief_o: The claimant neither accepted the defendant’s version of the contract nor amended the claim to seek relief on its basis.
predicates.claimant_did_not_plead_readiness_and_wil: The claimant did not plead readiness and willingness to perform the contract described by the defendant.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff who declined an opportunity to amend the pleading could not obtain specific performance of a different agreement asserted later.
material_facts: The plaint sought specific performance of an agreement allegedly concluded at the initial meeting.
The High Court gave the plaintiff an opportunity to amend the plaint to claim specific performance of an agreement allegedly concluded at a later meeting.
The plaintiff declined that opportunity and argued in the Supreme Court for relief on the later alleged agreement.
members.legal_principle: Specific performance must be sought on the agreement put in issue by the pleadings; a plaintiff cannot abandon the pleaded agreement and obtain a decree on a different agreement. The Court relied on the strict approach to variance in specific-performance suits described in Gonesh Ram v. Ganpat Rai, Md. Ziaul Haque v. Calcutta Vyapar Pratisthan, and Hawkins v. Maltby.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff could not obtain relief for specific performance of the later alleged agreement after declining to amend the plaint to seek that relief.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an alleged agreement.
predicates.pleaded_agreement_differs_from_later_cla: The agreement identified in the pleading differed from the agreement later relied on for relief.
predicates.plaintiff_refused_amendment: The plaintiff declined an opportunity to amend the pleading to claim relief on the later alleged agreement.

members.legal_issue: In a specific-performance suit, general relief cannot support a decree based on a materially different agreement from the one pleaded and claimed.
material_facts: The plaint specifically alleged that the parties concluded an agreement at the initial meeting and sought specific performance of that agreement.
The plaint did not allege a separate concluded agreement at the later meeting; it described that meeting as involving arrangements for payment and execution.
The plaintiff relied on a general prayer for other relief to seek specific performance of the alleged later agreement.
There was no part performance by delivery of possession, and the difference between the pleaded and asserted agreements was not immaterial.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 7 Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure, general relief must be consistent with the pleaded and proved case and with the specific relief claimed. In specific-performance suits, the agreement to be enforced must conform to the pleadings and proof; a material variance is not cured by a general prayer. The Court relied on Gonesh Ram v. Ganpat Rai, Md. Ziaul Haque v. Calcutta Vyapar Pratisthan, Hawkins v. Maltby, Cargil v. Bower, and Kidar Lall Seal v. Hari Lall Seal.
members.conclusion: The general prayer could not support specific performance of the different agreement, even if evidence had established it.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and pleaded_agreement_differs_from_proved_agreement and no_part_performance and no_immaterial_variation and no_amendment

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an alleged agreement.
predicates.pleaded_agreement_differs_from_proved_ag: The agreement described in the pleading differed materially from the agreement on which the evidence or later argument sought relief.
predicates.no_part_performance: The plaintiff had not partly performed the asserted agreement by taking possession of the property.
predicates.no_immaterial_variation: The difference between the pleaded agreement and the asserted agreement was material rather than insignificant.
predicates.no_amendment: The pleading was not amended to put the different agreement in issue.

members.legal_issue: The rule barring a later claim for a portion omitted from an earlier claim in a suit does not apply to the contents of a constitutional writ petition or to a later suit because of an omission from that petition.
material_facts: The claimant argued that treating the decision in his writ petition as res judicata could also bar a later suit concerning a portion of a claim omitted from the writ petition.
The earlier proceeding was a writ petition, followed by a regular suit.
members.legal_principle: Order 2, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies by its terms to suits: it requires a suit to include the whole claim arising from its cause of action and bars a later suit for a portion omitted or relinquished. Those provisions do not govern the contents of a writ petition. The court referred to Devendra Pratap Narain Rai Sharma v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The provisions governing omission or relinquishment of part of a claim in a suit do not apply to the contents of a writ petition and therefore do not bar a subsequent suit on that basis.

predicates.prior_writ_proceeding: A party first pursued relief in a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.later_regular_suit: A party later brought a regular suit concerning a claim related to the writ proceeding.
predicates.claim_portion_omitted_from_writ: A portion of the claim later raised in the suit was omitted from the earlier writ petition.

members.legal_issue: The bar against omitting a claim or relief in an earlier suit does not apply to an application to amend the pleading in the same pending suit.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought to amend the plaint in the existing suit, which had not yet been adjudicated.
The defendant argued that the claim for increased damages was barred because of the omission or relinquishment contemplated by Order II Rule 2 CPC.
members.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 CPC bars a subsequent suit in specified circumstances, including where a plaintiff omits a relief arising from the same cause of action without leave. A plea under the rule requires proof of the identity of the cause of action and the other statutory conditions; it does not govern amendment of pleadings in the one pending suit. The Court relied on Mohd. Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian, Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal, Upendra Narain Roy v. Rai Janoki Nath Roy, and Vaish Cooperative Adarsh Bank Ltd. v. Geetanjali Despande.
members.conclusion: Order II Rule 2 CPC did not bar the amendment application because the plaintiffs sought amendment in the existing suit rather than bringing a subsequent suit.

predicates.claim_amendment_in_pending_suit: A party seeks to add or alter a claim by amending the pleading in a suit that is still pending.
predicates.subsequent_suit: The party brings a new suit after the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: Proprietary rights in forests and trees conveyed through a proprietor vest in the State when the statutory abolition of those proprietary rights takes effect.
material_facts: The statutory scheme treated forests and trees within an estate as items of proprietary rights belonging to the proprietors.
The agreements conveyed rights to forest produce and associated rights over the land and trees to the claimants.
The claimants challenged the State's action after the statutory vesting of proprietary rights.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 provide for proprietary rights, including the rights and interests of persons claiming through the proprietor, to vest in the State. The Court read these provisions with sections 2(13) and 47(3) and section 202 of the Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1917, which supported the conclusion that forests and trees belonged to proprietors as items of proprietary rights. The Court did not follow Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel and Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, treating its characterization of the grants as bare licences as per incuriam.
members.conclusion: The rights conveyed under the agreements were proprietary rights and vested in the State under sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950.

predicates.statutory_vesting_challenge: The claimant challenges the consequences of a statutory process that transfers proprietary rights in an estate to the State.
predicates.forest_or_tree_rights_belong_to_propriet: The forest or tree rights at issue form part of proprietary rights held by the proprietor of the estate.
predicates.agreement_transfers_proprietary_forest_r: The agreement conveys those proprietary forest or tree rights, or an interest in them, from the proprietor to another person.

members.legal_issue: A right acquired from a proprietor to collect forest produce after proprietary interests in the land pass to the state is a proprietary right that passes to the state.
material_facts: The claimant acquired rights from land proprietors to collect forest produce for years after the proprietary interests in the forests were to vest in the state.
The state took charge of the forests and prevented the claimant from exercising the acquired rights.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1)(a) provides for proprietary rights, including rights in forests, to vest in the state free of encumbrances. State of Madhya Pradesh v. Yakinuddin held that rights to propagate lac and collect forest produce acquired from proprietors were proprietary rights within that provision; it expressly overruled the contrary view in Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh. The court held that the present case was governed by Yakinuddin.
members.conclusion: The right to collect forest produce was a proprietary right and vested in the state under section 4(1)(a) of the Abolition Act; the acquired rights did not fall within the exceptions in section 5.

predicates.forest_produce_rights_case: The dispute concerns rights to collect forest produce from land whose proprietary interests pass to the state.
predicates.rights_acquired_from_proprietor: A person acquired the forest produce rights from the land proprietor.
predicates.exercise_due_after_state_vesting: The acquired rights were to be exercised after the proprietary interests in the land passed to the state.

members.legal_issue: Forests and trees forming part of an estate vested in the State upon the statutory vesting notification despite a prior contract granting a right to cut trees.
material_facts: A contract with the former proprietor granted a right to cut specified teak trees in a forest forming part of a jagir estate.
A notification under the abolition statute vested the estate in the State after the contract was made.
The claimant sought to enforce the forest rights granted by the former proprietor against the State.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4 of the Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 provide for proprietary rights, including rights in forests and trees, to vest in the State upon notification, subject to the Act’s exceptions. The claimed interest was not shown to fall within the saving provisions of section 5. Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, State of M.P. v. Yakinuddin, and Mulamchand v. State of M.P. were followed.
members.conclusion: The forest and trees vested in the State under the Act.

predicates.claim_to_enforce_prevesting_forest_contr: A claimant seeks to enforce against the State forest rights granted by a former proprietor before vesting.
predicates.forest_and_trees_were_part_of_vested_est: The forest and trees were part of an estate in which the former proprietor held proprietary rights.
predicates.vesting_notification_applied_to_estate: A notification took effect that vested the estate in the State.

members.legal_issue: Rights granted by a proprietor in estate land or forest produce cease on statutory vesting and cannot be enforced against the State unless they fall within an interest saved by the governing Act.
material_facts: Proprietors granted rights to propagate lac, collect tendu leaves, and gather fruits and flowers from trees in their estates.
After statutory notifications, the State took possession of the estates and refused to recognise the grantees’ rights.
The claimed rights were derived from the proprietors and were not shown to fall within any of the interests saved by the Act.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 4(1)(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, proprietary rights and interests derived through a proprietor vest in the State free of encumbrances and cease, notwithstanding a contract, grant, or document. The interests saved are those specified in section 5(a)–(h); a claimant must bring the claimed interest within those provisions. The Court applied Shrimati Shantabai v. State of Bombay and Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and overruled Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel and Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The rights ceased upon vesting and could not be enforced against the State; the appeals were allowed and the earlier decision in Chhotabhai Jethabhai Patel and Co. was overruled.

rule.if: abolition_vesting_dispute and proprietor_derived_estate_right and state_took_possession_after_vesting and not interest_within_statutory_savings

predicates.abolition_vesting_dispute: The case concerns whether rights in an estate remain enforceable against the State after statutory abolition and vesting.
predicates.proprietor_derived_estate_right: A person acquired a right in estate land or its produce from a proprietor or through a proprietor.
predicates.state_took_possession_after_vesting: The State took possession of the estate after the statutory vesting event.
predicates.interest_within_statutory_savings: The claimed interest falls within an interest expressly preserved by the governing enactment.

members.legal_issue: A forest contract transferring proprietary rights that were to vest in the State became void on vesting when the contracted trees had not been felled and ascertained by that time.
material_facts: The proprietor contracted to sell standing forest trees, with the contract to continue for a period extending beyond the scheduled vesting of the estate in the State.
The contract required the forest staff to check and pass the logs before their removal; the trees had not been felled and ascertained in accordance with that requirement by the date of vesting.
The contract was made after the statutory cutoff for transfers of rights liable to vest in the State.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, proprietary rights in the estate and its forest vested in the State on the notified date. Section 6(1) made transfers after the statutory cutoff of rights liable to vest void from that date. For property in forest goods to pass under the Sale of Goods Act, the trees had to be felled and ascertained; the contract's requirement that logs be checked and passed meant that they were not ascertained before that occurred. The Court followed Badri Prasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh, which applied the same principles to a forest contract.
members.conclusion: The title to the trees had not passed before vesting, and the contract was void from the date the estate vested in the State.

rule.if: forest_estate_transfer_dispute and transfer_after_statutory_cutoff and forest_rights_scheduled_to_vest and not trees_felled_and_ascertained_by_vesting

predicates.forest_estate_transfer_dispute: The dispute concerns a contract transferring rights in forest property within an estate whose proprietary rights are subject to vesting in the State.
predicates.transfer_after_statutory_cutoff: The proprietor made the transfer after the applicable cutoff for transfers of rights liable to vest in the State.
predicates.forest_rights_scheduled_to_vest: The transferred forest rights were among the proprietary rights scheduled to vest in the State.
predicates.trees_felled_and_ascertained_by_vesting: The contracted trees had been felled and identified as the goods covered by the contract before the rights vested.

members.legal_issue: Agreements granting rights to gather and remove forest produce confer licenses rather than interests in land, trees, or proprietary rights.
material_facts: The agreements gave the holders rights to pluck, collect, cut, gather, and carry away forest produce.
The agreements did not grant an interest in the land or in the trees or plants themselves; any cultivation rights were ancillary to gathering the produce.
The agreements were genuine and were not alleged to be collusive or fraudulent.
members.legal_principle: The nature of an agreement is determined by the rights it creates. The Court applied the reasoning in Mohanlal Hargovind v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Central Provinces and Berar, where agreements for picking and carrying away leaves were treated as granting no interest in land or in the plants themselves. The Court also referred to Baden Powell's account of proprietary rights as one or more interests within a bundle of rights in land.
members.conclusion: The agreements were in substance licenses to cut, gather, and carry away produce, and their holders were not proprietors or persons holding an interest in proprietary rights through the proprietors.

predicates.constitutional_property_writ_petition: The holder seeks constitutional relief to protect contractual rights to forest produce from state interference.
predicates.agreement_grants_only_produce_removal: The agreement gives the holder the right to gather or cut produce and carry it away.
predicates.agreement_grants_no_land_or_tree_interes: The agreement does not give the holder an interest in the land or the trees or plants themselves.

members.legal_issue: A grant to harvest forest produce is a licence rather than a lease when it confers no interest in or exclusive possession of the land and entry onto the land is merely ancillary to harvesting.
material_facts: The agreements ran for nine to ten months and created no estate or interest in the land.
The grantees received no exclusive possession or control of the land, but only the right to pluck, cut, carry away and appropriate forest produce existing or arising during the agreement period.
The right to enter the land was ancillary to harvesting the forest produce.
members.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy immovable property; under section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882, a licence permits an act on another’s property without creating an interest in it. The definitions of immovable property in section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 2(6) of the Registration Act support the distinction. The substance and essence of the agreement, rather than its form, and the parties’ intention determine its character; an interest in the property indicates a lease, whereas permission to use the property while possession remains with the owner indicates a licence. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, Kauri Timber Company Limited v. Commissioner of Taxes, Marshall v. Green and Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and distinguished Mahadeo v. State of Bombay. Article 31(c) of the Stamp Act was therefore inapplicable.
members.conclusion: The agreements were licences, not leases, and did not attract stamp duty applicable to leases under Article 31(c).

rule.if: forest_produce_harvesting_grant and short_term_grant and no_land_interest_created and no_exclusive_land_possession and land_entry_is_ancillary and stamp_duty_classification_dispute

predicates.forest_produce_harvesting_grant: A grant gives the recipient rights to harvest and take away forest produce.
predicates.short_term_grant: The grant is for a short period.
predicates.no_land_interest_created: The agreement creates no estate or other interest in the land.
predicates.no_exclusive_land_possession: The recipient is not given exclusive possession or control of the land.
predicates.land_entry_is_ancillary: Entry onto the land is only incidental to the purpose of harvesting the produce.
predicates.stamp_duty_classification_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an agreement is a lease or licence for stamp-duty purposes.

members.legal_issue: A contractual right to collect natural produce does not constitute a property right in produce that remains attached to the land.
material_facts: The firm held an agreement granting it a right to pluck and carry tendu leaves from specified villages for a fixed term.
The agreement gave the firm no interest in the land or the trees themselves.
When the later law interfered with the firm's asserted right, the relevant leaves had not yet been plucked.
The firm sought to enforce the asserted right through a constitutional petition alleging an invasion of property.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 provides a remedy for enforcement of fundamental rights, but a right to contract is not itself a right to property. A claimant who has only a contractual collection right has no property in natural produce before it is severed. The Court relied on Shantabai v. State of Bombay and Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and explained why Chhotabhai Jethabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh could not establish the contrary proposition; it also referred to Article 19(1)(f) in describing the earlier claims.
members.conclusion: The firm had only a contractual right, not a property right in leaves before they were plucked, and therefore could not invoke constitutional protection of property on that basis.

predicates.constitutional_property_claim: The claimant seeks constitutional relief on the basis that an asserted right to collect natural produce is a property right.
predicates.claimant_has_only_contractual_collection: The claimant's asserted entitlement to collect the produce arises only from a contract and gives no interest in the land or the holding.
predicates.leaves_remain_attached_when_right_is_inv: The produce that the claimant seeks to collect remains attached to the land when the asserted right is interfered with.
predicates.claimant_has_no_interest_in_holding: The claimant has no independent interest in the holding on which the produce grows.

members.legal_issue: A bare licence to work in a forest, or permission that merely avoids penalties under forest legislation, does not transfer ownership of trees or forest produce.
material_facts: The forest officials permitted the petitioners to enter and work in the forest, but lacked authority to grant the trees to them.

The petitioners relied on statutory provisions concerning permitted acts in reserved and protected forests, but the Court found no basis for concluding that the relevant forests had been declared under those provisions and held that the provisions did not deal with the sale of forest produce.
The permissions did not include a grant of the trees or other movable forest produce.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Easements Act defines a licence as a right to do something on another’s immovable property without creating an interest in that property. A licence can transfer movable property only if it is coupled with a grant of that property; Ramakrishna v. Unni Check, I.L.R. 16 Mad. 280, involved such a grant in the terms of the licence. Sections 26(2)(a) and 34 of the Madhya Bharat Forest Act concern permission to do otherwise prohibited acts or relief from penalties; they do not transfer title to forest produce.
members.conclusion: The licence and forest-law permissions did not pass ownership of the trees or products made from them to the petitioners.

predicates.forest_work_licence_only: The claimant was given permission to enter or work in forest land without a grant of the produce.
predicates.no_grant_of_forest_produce: The permission did not include a grant transferring ownership of the trees or other forest produce.
predicates.no_authority_to_grant_forest_produce: The person granting permission lacked authority to transfer ownership of the forest produce.

members.legal_issue: A provision vesting specified tree rights in the government does not impliedly preserve all other tree rights for former tenure holders when the abolition law extinguishes their rights unless expressly saved.
material_facts: The abolition law extinguished the former holders’ rights arising from their jagirs unless a right was expressly preserved.
The law vested specified rights to trees in the government.
The law expressly preserved certain rights concerning mines and mineral products but contained no corresponding express preservation of the former holders’ rights to trees.
The former holders argued that the government’s specified tree rights impliedly left all other tree rights with them.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 extinguished jagirdar rights except where the Act expressly provided otherwise. Section 9 vested specified tree rights in the State Government but did not expressly preserve other tree rights for jagirdars. Section 10’s express preservation of rights to mines and mineral products supported the conclusion that the absence of a comparable provision for trees was significant. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The specified vesting of tree rights in the government did not imply that the former holders retained all other tree rights. Their rights were extinguished because no express provision saved them.

predicates.appeal_concerns_former_holder_tree_right: The proceeding is an appeal concerning tree rights claimed by a person whose former tenure was abolished.
predicates.abolition_extinguished_former_tenure_rig: The legal change abolished the former tenure and extinguished its incidents unless expressly preserved.
predicates.government_was_given_specified_tree_righ: The governing law vested specified rights to trees in the government.
predicates.no_express_saving_of_former_holder_tree_: The governing law did not expressly preserve the former holder’s claimed tree rights, although it expressly preserved other specified rights.

members.legal_issue: A right to remission of land revenue in an estate ends when the recipient's proprietary right in that estate vests in the State and cannot be converted into a right to receive the remitted amount.
material_facts: The recipient was a proprietor of twelve mahals that constituted an estate.
The arrangement granted a remission of part of the land revenue assessed on those mahals, rather than a separate pension payable from the revenue collected on other villages.
The recipient's proprietary right in the twelve mahals vested in the State under the statutory notification.
The recipient sought to claim the amount of the remission as a positive payment after the proprietary right in the mahals had ceased.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(8) and 4 of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, provide for an estate and the vesting of rights in it in the State. Under section 6(b), grants or confirmations of rights or privileges in respect of land in an acquired estate or its land revenue determine. A remission of land revenue is a right directly in respect of revenue from the estate; once the recipient's interest in that estate ceases, the remission cannot be transformed into a positive payment. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The right to remission in respect of the twelve mahals ended upon vesting, and the recipient was not entitled to receive the remitted amount as a payment.

predicates.statutory_estate_vesting_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a statutory vesting of land estates extinguished a pre-existing right.
predicates.recipient_owned_proprietary_interest_in_: The recipient held a proprietary interest in the land treated as an estate.
predicates.claimed_benefit_was_remission_of_revenue: The claimed benefit was a reduction in land revenue payable for the estate, rather than a separate allowance for relinquishing rights in other land.
predicates.proprietary_interest_vested_in_state: The recipient's proprietary interest in the estate vested in the State.

members.legal_issue: A long-term grant of the right to take growing forest produce, together with related land-use rights, is a profit a prendre and not a sale of goods, lease, or easement.
material_facts: The bamboo contract granted an exclusive right and licence to fell, cut, obtain, and remove bamboos over a lengthy period, including bamboos that would grow in the future.
The grantee received ancillary rights to use land, roads, and streams and to construct works for its operations.
The grantee had to pay a minimum royalty that did not correspond to the quantity of bamboos actually cut and removed.
The grantee had no right to exclusive possession of the contract area, and the grant was not for the beneficial enjoyment of other land belonging to it.
members.legal_principle: A profit a prendre is a right to take produce from another’s land and is a benefit arising out of land; under section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, it is immovable property. A profit a prendre is not an easement unless granted for the beneficial enjoyment of the grantee’s land. The Court relied on Ananda Behra v. State of Orissa, Shantabai v. State of Bombay, and Mahadeo v. State of Bombay, and held Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Orient Paper Mills Ltd. not to be good law.
members.conclusion: The bamboo contract was a grant of a profit a prendre, a benefit arising out of land and an interest in immovable property; amounts payable under it could not be taxed as a sale or purchase of goods under the Act or under the State’s power to tax goods.

predicates.bamboo_contract_tax_dispute: The dispute concerns tax imposed on payments under a grant relating to the taking of forest produce.
predicates.long_term_right_to_take_growing_forest_p: The grantee receives a right over an extended period to take produce that exists or will grow on the land.
predicates.ancillary_rights_to_use_land: The grant gives the grantee related rights to use land or access routes for its operations.
predicates.minimum_payment_not_tied_to_actual_quant: The grantee must pay a minimum amount that is not determined by the quantity of produce actually taken.

members.legal_issue: Agreements granting long-term rights to forest produce together with ancillary rights to use land are not contracts for the sale of goods simpliciter.
material_facts: The agreements granted rights over periods extending beyond the immediate collection of leaves.
They covered forest produce beyond tendu leaves, including timber and bamboos, and included rights to prune, coppice and burn trees.
They also permitted the use and occupation of land, construction of storage buildings, and manufacture of bricks for the business.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the definitions of goods and immovable property in the General Clauses Act, the Sale of Goods Act, the Transfer of Property Act and the Registration Act. Because the agreements conveyed rights beyond the collection of leaves, including rights relating to trees, other forest produce and land, they were not merely sales of goods. The Court distinguished the reasoning in Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel and Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and considered the principle in Mohanlal Hargovind of Jubbalpore v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Central Provinces and Berar.
members.conclusion: The agreements could not be characterized as contracts for the sale of goods simpliciter.

predicates.agreement_grants_long_term_forest_produc: The grant gives the recipient rights over forest produce for an extended period, rather than only an immediate purchase of existing produce.
predicates.agreement_includes_ancillary_land_or_tre: The grant also permits use of land or activities involving trees, buildings, or other forest resources.

members.legal_issue: A person acting in private defence does not exceed that right when, in the circumstances, a real and imminent threat reasonably creates apprehension of death or grievous hurt and the force used is no more than necessary to meet it.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, finding that the prosecution had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that he was the aggressor; the High Court accepted that the other person was the aggressor but convicted the accused on the ground that he had exceeded his right of private defence.
The brothers had a history of bitter disputes and quarrels, and the evidence supported the finding that the deceased was the aggressor.

The deceased stooped to pick up a stone of a dangerous size. The eyewitness had not seen the accused draw his knife, and the evidence did not establish that the deceased stooped only after seeing the accused advance with the knife.
The Court found that the accused reasonably apprehended death or grievous hurt from a real and immediate danger and acted to ward it off without inflicting more harm than was necessary.
members.legal_principle: Under the fourth clause of Section 99 of the Indian Penal Code, no more harm may be inflicted than is necessary for the purpose of defence. The right requires a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body from an attempt or threat to commit an offence, and does not arise until that apprehension exists. Whether the force used exceeded the right is a question of fact assessed objectively from the events and surrounding circumstances at the crucial time; no fixed pattern of conduct can be required. Once circumstances show an apprehension of death or grievous hurt, the defender may meet the threat, subject to the limit on necessary harm. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The accused acted within his right of private defence and did not exceed it. The High Court erred in convicting him; the appeal was allowed and the acquittal restored.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction_after_acquittal and attacker_was_aggressor and attacker_reached_for_dangerous_object and defender_reasonably_apprehended_death_or_grievous_hurt and danger_was_real_and_imminent and defensive_force_not_more_than_necessary

predicates.appeal_from_conviction_after_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction entered after a trial court acquitted the accused.
predicates.attacker_was_aggressor: The person posing the threat initiated or was the aggressor in the confrontation.
predicates.attacker_reached_for_dangerous_object: The aggressor reached for or picked up an object capable of causing serious harm.
predicates.defender_reasonably_apprehended_death_or: In the surrounding circumstances, the defender reasonably apprehended death or grievous hurt.
predicates.danger_was_real_and_imminent: The threat to the defender was real and immediate when the defensive act occurred.
predicates.defensive_force_not_more_than_necessary: The defender used no more force than was necessary to ward off the threat.

members.legal_issue: A person may use force in private defence of another when the circumstances create a reasonable apprehension of danger to that person's life.
material_facts: The appellant’s father was being struck with lathis by members of the complainant party when the appellant fired.
A lathi is capable of causing a fatal injury, regardless of whether the injuries actually inflicted were simple or grievous.
The appellant fired to protect his father from further blows.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 96 and 100 of the Indian Penal Code, force used in private defence is justified in the circumstances found here. The relevant consideration is the situation faced when the force was used, including the reasonable apprehension of danger; the fact that the blows actually caused only simple injuries does not determine whether that apprehension was reasonable. No earlier case is cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appellant could reasonably apprehend danger to his father’s life, and firing to defend him was justified; the conviction for murder was set aside.

members.legal_issue: A person may use force, including force causing death, in defence of self or another when a sudden unlawful assault creates a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, provided the force is used to avert the danger and is not wholly disproportionate.
material_facts: The trial court found that the deceased inflicted a serious, bone-deep sharp-weapon injury on the accused's father.
The deceased then advanced toward the accused holding a sharp weapon, and the accused fired at him, causing his death.

The occurrence took place in a field in the accused's father's possession; the Supreme Court accepted the trial court's assessment that the defence version was more probable than the prosecution version.
members.legal_principle: Sections 96 and 97 of the Indian Penal Code recognize the right of private defence of the body, subject to the restrictions in section 99; section 100 permits causing death in specified circumstances, including an assault that reasonably causes apprehension of death or grievous hurt. The right begins with reasonable apprehension, lasts while that apprehension continues, is defensive rather than retaliatory, and does not require a person under attack to measure force with exactness, though the force must not be wholly disproportionate. The accused need not prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt; it may be established on a preponderance of probabilities. The Court relied, among others, on Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, Jagtar Singh v. State of Punjab, Bhagwan Swaroop v. State of Madhya Pradesh, James Martin v. State of Kerala, Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Ramesh, Vidhya Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Jai Dev v. State of Punjab, and Buta Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The accused's act was covered by the right of private defence, and his appeal was allowed on that basis.

members.legal_issue: Deadly force is justified in private defence of the body when an assault creates a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt and the force used does not exceed what is necessary for defence.
material_facts: A large group went to remove a bund by force despite knowing that those guarding it would resist and that one of them had a gun.
The group attacked the defenders, severely beating older members and causing numerous injuries, including injuries to vital parts of the body.
The gun was used against the attacking group when the person using it apprehended grave danger to the lives of the defenders and to himself.
The occupiers had time to seek relief from public authorities or the pending civil court, but instead went to remove the bund by force.
The court found that the person who used the gun did not exceed the right of private defence.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 96 and 97 of the Indian Penal Code, acts done in private defence are not offences and a person may defend their own body or another person's body against offences affecting the human body. Subject to the restrictions in section 99, section 100 permits causing death where an assault reasonably creates an apprehension that death or grievous hurt will otherwise result; section 99 limits the right where there is time to seek public protection and prohibits inflicting more harm than necessary. The right is preventive, not punitive, and must be applied practically; the judgment refers to Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration and Kishna v. State of Rajasthan in describing its social purpose.
members.conclusion: The use of the gun was justified in the exercise of the right of private defence, and the accused were entitled to acquittal.
