members.legal_issue: A person who uses force to repel an imminent attack is entitled to complete acquittal when the circumstances establish the right of private defence.
material_facts: The prosecution party attacked the accused and his brothers with cutting weapons and sticks, causing the accused head injuries and causing one brother severe injuries, including fractures.
The accused was not armed when the occurrence began and did not use his gun while the initial attack was taking place.

After the severely injured brother was left outside the house, the accused and another brother entered the house, while the prosecution party continued pelting bricks and stones and tried to enter by scaling the wall.
The prosecution party threatened to kill the accused and his brother and claimed that they had already killed the brother who was lying outside.
The accused first fired shots in the air to frighten the crowd and fired at it only when it continued toward the house; the resulting injuries to the witnesses were simple.
The accused appealed his convictions, and the Court considered the appeal on the plea of private defence.
members.legal_principle: The right of private defence of the person permits a complete acquittal where the circumstances give rise to a reasonable apprehension of imminent danger and the force used is in response to that danger. The Court relied on the circumstances of the attack, the threats, the attempted entry into the house and the accused's resort to firing only after warning shots proved ineffective. No particular statutory provision or earlier case is cited in the judgment for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The accused was entitled to complete acquittal on the plea of private defence; the convictions and sentences were set aside.

members.legal_issue: A defender does not exceed the right of private defence by using force to repel an imminent threat after lesser measures fail to stop the attack.
material_facts: The prosecution party attacked the accused and his brothers with cutting weapons and sticks, causing the accused head injuries and causing one brother severe injuries, including fractures.
The accused did not use his gun during the initial attack and entered the house with another brother after the severely injured brother was left outside.
The prosecution party continued pelting bricks and stones, tried to enter the house by scaling the wall, and threatened to kill the accused and his brother.
The accused fired shots in the air first and fired at the crowd only when it continued toward the house; the witnesses' resulting injuries were simple.
The accused appealed his convictions, and the State argued that he had exceeded the right of private defence.
members.legal_principle: Whether the right of private defence has been exceeded depends on the circumstances creating the apprehension of imminent danger and the defender's response to it. Here, the Court treated the initial attack, the severe injuries, the pursuit and threats, and the warning shots followed by firing only when the threat persisted as supporting the exercise of the right rather than its excess. No particular statutory provision or earlier case is cited in the judgment for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The accused did not exceed his right of private defence and was entitled to complete acquittal.

members.legal_issue: A person who reasonably apprehends physical harm from an unlawful attempt to restrain or overpower them may defend their body, but may not use lethal force unless the circumstances reasonably create an imminent apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
material_facts: After a heated dispute about payment, five men waited by the road for about 45 to 60 minutes and attempted to stop the accused’s vehicle as it travelled toward the town.
The court found that the group’s purpose was not peaceful persuasion but to restrain or overpower the accused and obtain money by putting him in fear of injury.

The deceased and his companions were not shown to be armed; stone-throwing was possible but did not establish a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, and the accused could have driven through the group.
The accused fired three shots in quick succession, one of which killed the deceased.
members.legal_principle: Sections 99 and 102 of the Penal Code limit private defence to necessary defensive force and provide that the right begins and lasts with a reasonable apprehension of danger. Sections 100 and 101 govern when the right extends to causing death and when it permits lesser harm. The right is defensive, not punitive; it permits no more harm than necessary, though a person acting in good faith need not calculate force with precision. Lethal force requires a reasonable and imminent apprehension of death or grievous hurt, subject to the limits on necessity and proportionality.
members.conclusion: A right of private defence of the body had accrued, but the circumstances did not justify causing death. The accused exceeded the right, and the plea did not displace the homicide conviction.

members.legal_issue: A person defending possession of property may use force causing death when a forcible attempt to take the property is accompanied by an assault creating a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, and the defender does not exceed the right of private defence.
material_facts: The accused were in possession of the land and had grown the ripe paddy crop on it.
The deceased and their group trespassed onto the land and attempted to harvest the crop.
The deceased and their group were the aggressors and used sharp cutting weapons against the accused.
Two accused were first attacked and sustained grievous injuries from sharp weapons, including injuries to vital parts of the body.
The attack occurred before the attackers had retreated.
The trial court acquitted the accused, but the High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted three of them of culpable homicide.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 97 and 99 of the Indian Penal Code, the right of private defence extends to the body and property, subject to the restrictions in Section 99. Under Section 100, the right of defence of the body may extend to voluntarily causing death where an assault may reasonably cause apprehension of death or grievous hurt. Under Section 103, the right of defence of property may extend to causing death in specified circumstances, including theft or mischief where a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt would otherwise arise. A person in possession may use reasonable force to keep away a trespasser; where the facts establish a qualifying threat and the attackers have not retreated, the defender does not exceed the right by causing death. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The accused were entitled to exercise private defence of both person and property, and that right extended to causing death in the circumstances. They had not exceeded that right. The High Court's reversal was set aside and the trial court's acquittal was upheld.

members.legal_issue: A person defending settled possession may use force, including force causing death, where an immediate invasion and a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt justify it, and the response is assessed in the circumstances rather than by exact measurement of each blow.
material_facts: The appellants were in possession of the land and had grown wheat there.
The complainant party went to the land armed with weapons and attempted to destroy the crop and retake possession by force.
Two appellants' associates suffered gunshot injuries, which the prosecution did not explain.
The prosecution's account did not disclose the material origin of the occurrence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 99 to 102 of the Indian Penal Code govern the limitations and operation of private defence. A person facing an immediate attack need not flee to the authorities; where there is an invasion or aggression by a person without a right to possession, there may be no opportunity to seek their aid. Under Jai Dev v. State of Punjab and Amjad Khan v. State, reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt is enough to activate the right, and the response is not judged by weighing blows in golden scales. The right may extend to causing death where that apprehension exists. The Court also followed State of Gujarat v. Sai Fatima on the assessment of injuries to accused persons and the circumstances of an occurrence.
members.conclusion: The appellants were entitled to defend their property and persons, and the Court could not find that they had exceeded that right, including in causing the deaths.

members.legal_issue: Accused in settled possession may use necessary force to defend possession and persons against an intrusion where the circumstances create a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm, and the force used in the heat of the moment is not assessed with exacting precision.
material_facts: The appellants had been in continuous possession of the land as cultivating tenants for many years, and the prosecution party had not established settled possession of it.
The prosecution party had attempted to take possession on the previous day, retreated after protest, and returned the next morning to plough the land.
In the ensuing incident, members of both groups were injured; some appellants had injuries to the head, and the prosecution did not explain those injuries.
The High Court found that the appellants were defending their possession, but held that they had exceeded their right of private defence.
The Supreme Court found that the appellants were the persons defending possession and that the circumstances justified a reasonable apprehension of grievous harm or death.
members.legal_principle: Sections 96 to 106 IPC govern private defence; Section 103 permits the defence of property to extend to causing death in the specified circumstances, subject to Section 99. A person in settled possession may defend that possession even against the rightful owner, while stray or intermittent acts of trespass do not create settled possession. The right is liberally construed, and a person facing imminent peril is not expected to calculate the precise force required. The accused’s burden under Section 105 of the Evidence Act is not as onerous as the prosecution’s burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; unexplained injuries to the accused may support an inference that the prosecution has suppressed the occurrence’s origin or that the defence account is probably true. The Court relied on Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, and Mohd. Ramzani v. State of Delhi.
members.conclusion: The appellants had not exceeded their right of private defence and were entitled to defend their possession and persons; the convictions could not be sustained.

members.legal_issue: The right of private defence of the body begins when a person reasonably apprehends present and imminent danger from an unlawful attempt or threat, and continues while that apprehension lasts.
material_facts: The accused side was in possession of the disputed land.
The opposing side deliberately came to forcibly prevent or obstruct that possession and cultivation, and the obstruction was unlawful.
The courts found that the accused could reasonably apprehend imminent danger to themselves and their companions from the opposing side’s threatened assault.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 102 of the Indian Penal Code, the right of private defence of the body commences when a reasonable apprehension of danger arises from an attempt or threat to commit an offence, even before the offence is committed, and continues while the apprehension lasts. The danger must be present and imminent, not remote or distant. The right protects against apprehended unlawful aggression and is preventive, not punitive. The Court also relied on G. V. Subranmanyam v. State of Andhra Pradesh for the scheme of the right of private defence.
members.conclusion: The right of private defence arose upon the reasonable apprehension of imminent danger; it did not depend on the accused first sustaining a serious injury.

members.legal_issue: The circumstances in which an accused may rely on the right of private defence to justify causing fatal harm.
material_facts: The accused claimed they used force to protect themselves and others after members of the other group had been injured, and some members of the accused group had also suffered injuries.
During the incident, the deceased came to support his injured family members and was struck on the head by the accused with wooden yokes.
The courts found that the accused had not established that the fatal force was necessary to ward off an attack or a continuing reasonable apprehension of danger.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 96–106 of the Indian Penal Code, the right of private defence is defensive, arises when a reasonable apprehension of danger begins, and continues only while that apprehension lasts; it does not justify retaliation after the danger has passed. Under Section 105 of the Evidence Act, the accused bears the burden of establishing the plea, but need only show that it is more probable than not, and may do so through prosecution evidence. Injuries on the accused are relevant but do not automatically establish the defence; the circumstances must make the defensive response reasonable and necessary. The Court relied on Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, State of Gujarat v. Bai Fatima, State of U.P. v. Mohd. Musheer Khan, Mohinder Pal Jolly v. State of Punjab, Salim Zia v. State of U.P., Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar, Jai Dev v. State of Punjab, Biran Singh v. State of Bihar, Wassan Singh v. State of Punjab, Sekar alias Raja Sekharan v. State, Butta Singh v. State of Punjab, and Vidhya Singh v. State of M.P.
members.conclusion: The accused had not established that they were exercising the right of private defence.

members.legal_issue: A temple’s public or private character depends on the intended beneficiaries and the evidence of dedication and public worship, and the evidence did not establish a hereditary trusteeship in the claimant’s family.
material_facts: The official inam-register entries identified the deity as the owner or pattadar of the temple lands and described the endowment as being for the religious institution and the temple’s maintenance.
The entries recorded persons outside the claimant’s family as managers of the temple or its lands.
Witnesses described members of the public, including people from neighbouring villages, as having access to the temple to worship, sometimes using a key left available when the claimant was absent.

The family partition deed, will and register prepared by the claimant’s father did not establish that the family’s claimed hereditary management had been acted upon; the claimed fact that the temple was in the claimant’s residence was not supported by the evidence.
The claimant’s father had earlier sought a determination that the temple was private, but that claim was rejected, and he was later appointed as a trustee for a limited term.
members.legal_principle: Under section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, a public temple is distinguished from a private one by the nature of the beneficiaries and the founder’s intention: an endowment for specified individuals is private, while one for the general body of worshippers is public. Public access alone does not necessarily make a temple public, but public use without interference is cogent evidence of public dedication when the endowment is in favour of the idol (Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar; Babu Bhagwan Gir v. Gir Har Saroon). In the relevant former Madras Presidency region, the court applied the presumption that temples and their endowments are public religious trusts, rebuttable by affirmative and compelling evidence (Mundancheri Koman v. Achutan Nair; T.V. Mahalinga Iyer v. State of Madras). Inam-register entries are important evidence of the history and tenure of property (Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal; Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayah Gosavi), though they must be read with the other recorded circumstances (The Poohari Fakir Sadavarthy of Bondilipuram v. Commissioner, Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments).
members.conclusion: The temple was public, not private, and the claimant failed to establish that he was its hereditary trustee.

members.legal_issue: A temple endowment is public when the dedication and surrounding circumstances show that its beneficiaries are the public or a section of the public, rather than specified individuals or a family.
material_facts: The temples were built with funds from the state treasury, and public funds and subscriptions contributed to their upkeep.
The public, particularly members of a religious community, worshipped at the temples as of right over a long period and participated in festivals and ceremonies without obstruction.
Devotees made offerings that were kept in separate temple accounts and used for the temples’ upkeep and related properties.
Public records listed the deities as owners and the ruler as manager; the temples were situated outside the palace precincts and faced a public road.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(17) and 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, a temple meeting the statutory definition of a temple may fall within the definition of a public trust. The essence of a public endowment is dedication for the public’s use or benefit: its beneficiaries are the public or a section of it, rather than specified individuals. Where there is no written instrument, dedication may be inferred from the historical circumstances, including the temple’s origin, its management, the source and use of funds, devotees’ rights of worship, and long public use. Management by a ruler or family member does not by itself establish private ownership. The Court applied the principles in Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchhoddas Kalidas, and Pujari Lakshmana Goundan v. Subramania Ayyar, among other cited authorities.
members.conclusion: The temples were public temples and the properties attached to them were public religious trusts, not private properties of the ruler or his family.

members.legal_issue: A place used for public religious worship is a public temple and public trust when the evidence shows that the public or a section of it worships there as of right and the surrounding circumstances support dedication for the public’s benefit.
material_facts: The temple was ancient, and its origin was lost in antiquity; no reliable documentary evidence of dedication was available.
Large numbers of people from the Hindu community visited the temple for worship and to fulfil vows, without being prevented from visiting.
A restriction on entry and inside worship was treated as an arrangement for orderly darshan, rather than proof that public access was by permission only.
Rulers provided regular cash grants for the temple, and devotees made offerings and donated land and other property to the deity.
Government and revenue records showed temple property in the deity’s name, and historical records described the temple and public worship there.

The appellants’ family managed the temple and its properties, but that circumstance was not conclusive of private character; prior civil proceedings had not determined the temple’s public or private status.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(17) and 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, a temple is a place used for public religious worship and dedicated to, for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it; a public trust includes such a temple. The distinction is between specific, ascertainable beneficiaries of a private endowment and the general public or an indeterminate class benefiting from a public endowment. Dedication need not be documented and may be inferred from conduct and circumstances. Long use by the public as of right, public or royal grants and gifts, property held in the deity’s name, and the understanding of managers and worshippers are relevant; family management and internal arrangements for orderly worship are not conclusive. The Court applied Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwala v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi, Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S.P. Sahi, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Ranchhoddas Kalidas, State of Bihar v. Charusila Dasi, Bihar State Board of Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das, T.D. Gopalan v. Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Dhaneshwarbuwa Guru Purshottambuwa v. Charity Commissioner, T.V. Mahalinga Iyer v. State of Madras, Sri Radhakanta Deb v. Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments, Hari Bhanu Maharaj of Baroda v. Charity Commissioner, Jammi Raja Rao v. Sri Anjaneyaswami Temple Vahi, and Kapoor Chand v. Ganesh Dutt. The Court also held that the Bombay Presidency Gazette was admissible under sections 35 and 81 of the Evidence Act, 1872, and that its historical statements could be considered with other evidence, though they were not conclusive.
members.conclusion: The temple was a public temple and a public trust, and the High Court correctly upheld its registration as such.

rule.if: public_trust_status_appeal and public_worship_as_right and (long_public_use or large_public_attendance) and (public_or_ruler_support or property_in_deity_name)

predicates.public_trust_status_appeal: A party appealed a determination about whether a religious site was a public trust.
predicates.public_worship_as_right: Members of the public or a section of the religious community used the site for worship as of right, rather than solely by individual permission.
predicates.long_public_use: The public or a section of it had used the site for worship over a long period.
predicates.large_public_attendance: Large numbers of members of the public or a religious community attended the site for worship.
predicates.public_or_ruler_support: Members of the public or rulers provided grants, offerings, donations, or other support for the site.
predicates.property_in_deity_name: Records showed that property associated with the site was held in the name of its deity.

members.legal_issue: A religious endowment is public when the founder intends worship or other benefits to be available to the public or a section of the public, rather than confining them to specified individuals or a family.
material_facts: The deed established separate temples outside the settlor’s residence for a deity and the settlor’s religious preceptor.
The deed provided for worshippers to make offerings, which would become part of the trust estate.
It provided for public festivals and ceremonies, including free distribution of food and water, on a scale intended to allow many people to participate.
The temple committee was to include people outside the settlor’s family.
The deed created an independent trust to establish a hospital for Hindu females and a charitable dispensary for outpatients of any religion or creed.
members.legal_principle: Under Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, the central question is whether worship is intended for specified individuals or for the general public or a section of it. The terms of the deed must be considered as a whole; the location of a temple outside a residence is relevant but not decisive. The Court explained In re Charusila Dasi and distinguished Prasaddas Pal v. Jagannath Pal, where feeding the poor was incidental to family worship rather than an independent public charity.
members.conclusion: The deed created a religious and charitable trust of a public nature, not a private endowment for family worship.

rule.if: trust_deed_case and worship_open_to_public and independent_public_charity and public_participation_or_management

predicates.trust_deed_case: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether an endowment created by a deed is public or private.
predicates.worship_open_to_public: The deed gives the public or a section of the public a right to worship or make offerings at the religious institution.
predicates.independent_public_charity: The deed establishes a distinct charitable purpose for the benefit of members of the public beyond the founder’s family.
predicates.public_participation_or_management: The deed provides for public participation in religious events or gives people outside the founder’s family a role in managing the institution.

members.legal_issue: Whether a religious endowment is public or private depends on whether its intended beneficiaries are the public or a specified individual or family.
material_facts: The founder dedicated property to an idol and provided for the temple's management and continued upkeep beyond the lifetimes of his wives.
The founder had no male issue, and the management arrangements included people unrelated to him.
Witnesses described villagers worshipping at the temple without interference, and evidence indicated that the temple had been built at the villagers' request because the village had no temple.
The idol was ceremoniously installed in a separate building, and the temple's worship was conducted by an appointed priest.
members.legal_principle: The distinction is that beneficiaries of a private endowment are specified individuals, while beneficiaries of a public endowment are the general public or a class of it. Although an idol can hold endowed property as a juristic person, it has no beneficial interest; worshippers are the true beneficiaries, and the purpose is to provide opportunities and facilities for worship. The founder's intention is central. Public use without interference is cogent evidence where the endowment was made to the idol, though later public use alone does not necessarily change an endowment first shown to be private. The court relied on Prosunno Kumari Debya v. Golab Chand Baboo, Maharaja Jagadindra Nath Roy Bahadur v. Bani Hemanta Kumari Debi, Pramatha Nath Mullik v. Pradhyumna Kumar Mullik, Bhupati Nath Smrititirtha v. Ram Lal Maitra, Hindu Religious Endowments Board v. Veeraraghavachariar, Nabi Shirazi v. Province of Bengal, Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroon, Mundancheri Koman v. Achuthan, and Delroos Banoo Begum v. Nawab Syud Ashgur Ally Khan. No particular ceremony is necessary if the intention to dedicate is clear. Uthsarga is distinct from Prasadothsarga; for a temple, Prathista takes the place of Uthsarga, and the performance of Prathista was evidence of dedication to the public.
members.conclusion: The endowment was public, intended for worship by the general public rather than only the founder's family.

rule.if: appeal_on_public_private_endowment and property_dedicated_to_idol and founder_had_no_male_issue and management_included_unrelated_people and endowment_continued_beyond_founders_widows and (public_worship_without_interference or temple_built_for_community_worship or public_dedication_ritual_performed)

predicates.appeal_on_public_private_endowment: An appeal concerns whether a religious endowment is public or private.
predicates.property_dedicated_to_idol: The founder dedicated property to an idol for the purposes of its temple.
predicates.founder_had_no_male_issue: The founder had no male child.
predicates.management_included_unrelated_people: The founder's management arrangements included people who were not related to the founder.
predicates.endowment_continued_beyond_founders_wido: The founder provided for the endowment's management and use to continue after the founder's widows had died.
predicates.public_worship_without_interference: Members of the public worshipped at the temple without interference.
predicates.temple_built_for_community_worship: Evidence showed that the temple was built to provide a place of worship for the community.
predicates.public_dedication_ritual_performed: A temple installation ceremony that the court treated as evidence of dedication to the public was performed.

members.legal_issue: The character of a religious endowment as public or private is determined by the founder’s intended beneficiaries and the surrounding evidence of the endowment’s use, management, and support.
material_facts: The founder intended the deity to be worshipped continually by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public and arranged for regular worship, devotional singing, ceremonies, and processions.
The public worshipped at the temple over a long period without evidence of hindrance or restriction.
The temple received a government land grant in its own name and was managed by successive spiritual successors as managers rather than as personal owners.
Members of the public donated land and contributed subscriptions for worship and ceremonies.
The institution was held out and treated by its managers as a place for public use, and its history contained no evidence that it had been treated as private property.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, a public trust includes an express or constructive trust for a public religious purpose; section 2(17) defines a temple by its use as a place of public religious worship and dedication to, benefit of, or use as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it. The distinction between public and private trusts turns principally on whether the beneficiaries are the general public or an unascertained class, rather than specified or ascertainable individuals, and whether the founder intended the public or a specified portion of it to have the right of worship. Public use without interference is cogent evidence of dedication. The court may also consider the temple’s origin, management, grants and gifts, devotees’ worship rights, and the awareness of managers and devotees of its public character; not every factor must be present. The court relied on Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, State of Bihar v. Charusila Dasi, Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi, Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchhodas Kalidas, and Bihar State Board Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das.
members.conclusion: The endowment was a public trust, not a private religious endowment.

predicates.religious_endowment_classification_proce: The dispute concerns whether a religious endowment is public or private.
predicates.founder_intended_worship_for_indetermina: The founder intended the place or deity to be worshipped by an indeterminate body of public worshippers.
predicates.public_worship_without_interference: Members of the public worshipped at the place over time without interference or restriction.
predicates.public_contributions_supported_worship: Members of the public gave gifts or contributions to support worship or related ceremonies.
predicates.government_grant_recognized_temple_endow: A government grant identified the temple or religious institution as the holder or beneficiary of endowed property.
predicates.succession_managers_treated_property_as_: Successive managers administered the property for the religious institution rather than as their personal property.

members.legal_issue: A mutt may be either private or public, and its character depends on whether the endowment benefits the public or an unascertained class, rather than only the grantee or an ascertained group, assessed from the grant and the institution’s established circumstances.
material_facts: The institution was a religious asthal with a temple and properties managed by its head.
The evidence included the manner in which properties were acquired, managed, and dealt with, and the institution’s practices and use.
The evidence did not establish that the institution’s endowment was intended to benefit the public or an unascertained class.
members.legal_principle: A mutt dedicated for ascetics generally or for the ascetics of a particular sect may be public, while an endowment intended to maintain a particular spiritual family or benefit the grantee or an ascertained group may be private. The court must determine the endowment’s beneficiaries from the grant and the established circumstances, including usage, custom, and dealings with the properties. The Court referred to Matam Nadipudi v. Board of Commissioners for Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras, A.I.R. 1938 Mad. 810, and Missir v. Das, [1949] I.L.R. 28 Pat. 890.
members.conclusion: The Court recognized that a mutt can be private or public and that its character must be determined from the grant or the circumstances, including usage, custom, and the manner in which its properties have been dealt with.

predicates.mutt_public_or_private_status_dispute: A dispute concerns whether a religious mutt or asthal is a public or private institution.
predicates.evidence_about_grant_or_institutional_ci: Evidence is available about the grant, the institution’s usage or custom, or the way its properties have been managed and dealt with.

members.legal_issue: A temple’s public or private character depends on the entire evidence concerning its origin, management, endowments, worshippers’ rights, and the understanding of its managers and devotees.
material_facts: The shrine was constructed on property acquired by the family and was found to have a private origin.
Management and control remained with members of the family throughout.
There was no endowed property, and certain features commonly associated with public temples were absent.
People outside the family worshipped at the shrine and made offerings, and the shrine had some features commonly found in public temples.
The trial court found the evidence of public donations, worship as of right, and other acts said to show dedication to the public insufficiently reliable.
members.legal_principle: Under section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, a public temple is a place used for public religious worship and dedicated or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it for that purpose. The origin of the temple, its management, the nature and extent of gifts, the rights exercised by devotees, and the consciousness of managers and devotees are relevant; no single fact or set of facts is conclusive, and the evidence must be considered as a whole. Where private origin is established, stronger proof is required to establish subsequent dedication to the public: Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop. Public use is significant according to the circumstances showing whether it was as of right, and public worship, participation in festivals as of right, votive offerings, and public contributions may support public character: Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchoddas Kalidas. The Court also referred to Mundancheri Koman v. Achuthan Nair and Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Board v. V. N. D. Ammal.
members.conclusion: The shrine was private in character and was not a public temple within the statutory definition.

rule.if: temple_character_dispute and private_origin_established and family_control_continued and no_endowed_property and public_dedication_evidence_insufficient

predicates.temple_character_dispute: The parties disputed whether a shrine was private or a place of public religious worship.
predicates.private_origin_established: The evidence established that the shrine originated on privately owned property and was established by a family for its own worship.
predicates.family_control_continued: Members of the founding family retained management and control of the shrine.
predicates.no_endowed_property: No property had been endowed for the shrine’s maintenance.
predicates.public_dedication_evidence_insufficient: The evidence did not sufficiently establish public dedication or that outsiders worshipped as of right, notwithstanding evidence of outsider worship or other public-temple features.

members.legal_issue: A temple of unknown or ancient origin is public when the evidence of its use, support, and treatment establishes public worship as of right.
material_facts: The temple’s origin could not be established with certainty and was treated as lost in antiquity.
Followers regularly worshipped there as of right and participated in its ceremonies and festivals.
Devotees made gifts and contributions, and the temple was substantially maintained from those contributions.
Separate accounts and documents treated the deity and temple as distinct from the religious head and his personal affairs.
The temple’s management and devotees treated it as public; the building’s residential appearance did not alter that conclusion.
members.legal_principle: The issue is a mixed question of law and fact. If a temple is shown to have originated as public, nothing further is needed to establish its public character; if its origin is private, unknown, or lost in antiquity, public use and other circumstances must be considered. Relevant factors include origin, management, gifts and contributions, rights exercised by worshippers, and the understanding of the manager and devotees. Public worship as of right is strong evidence, and public offerings and contributions may support a presumption of public character. The Court relied on Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan; Lakshmana v. Subramania; Mundancheri Koman v. Achutan Nair; Deoki Nandan v. Murlidar; and Narayan Bhagwant Rao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi.
members.conclusion: The temple was a public temple.

rule.if: proceeding_determines_whether_a_temple_is_public and temple_origin_is_unknown_or_ancient and worshippers_use_temple_as_of_right and public_contributions_support_temple

predicates.proceeding_determines_whether_a_temple_i: The proceeding requires a decision on whether a temple is public or private.
predicates.temple_origin_is_unknown_or_ancient: The temple’s origin is unknown, lost in antiquity, or not established as private.
predicates.worshippers_use_temple_as_of_right: Members of the public or a section of it regularly worship at the temple as of right.
predicates.public_contributions_support_temple: Devotees make offerings or contributions that support the temple and its activities.

members.legal_issue: A shrine is a public temple under the governing definition only if it is a place of public religious worship and is dedicated to, intended for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it.
material_facts: The shrine was built by the head of an institution whose grants were made for his maintenance and for feeding and aiding religious mendicants and travellers.
The shrine was treated as an adjunct to that institution, and the evidence supported that access depended on the head's permission rather than a public right of entry.
Some income from the grants was spent on worship at the shrine, but the grant records did not establish that the grants were made for the shrine or for public worship there.
The evidence did not establish that members of the public worshipped at the shrine as of right; evidence of visitors or public attendance at festivals did not establish such a right.
members.legal_principle: Section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 requires both a place of public religious worship and its dedication to, benefit of, or use as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it. Evidence that people visit or worship at a shrine is not by itself proof of public use as of right, since visitors may be permitted to enter a private temple. The presumption discussed in Mundancheri Koman v. Achuthan Nair—that temples and their endowments are public charitable trusts in parts of the Madras Presidency where private temples were practically unknown—is rebuttable; the evidence here rebutted it.
members.conclusion: The shrine was not a public temple within the statutory definition, and the order classifying it as a temple was set aside.

rule.if: temple_status_appeal and grants_for_maintenance_and_charity and shrine_as_private_adjunct and access_depended_on_permission and public_dedication_or_benefit_not_established and public_use_as_of_right_not_established

predicates.temple_status_appeal: The proceeding concerns whether a shrine qualifies as a public temple under a statutory definition.
predicates.grants_for_maintenance_and_charity: The grants supporting the institution were made for the head's maintenance and for charitable aid to religious mendicants or travellers.
predicates.shrine_as_private_adjunct: The shrine was established as an adjunct to an institution rather than as a separately endowed public place of worship.
predicates.access_depended_on_permission: People seeking to enter the shrine for worship obtained permission from its head or manager.
predicates.public_dedication_or_benefit_not_establi: The evidence did not establish that the shrine was dedicated to or intended for the benefit of the Hindu community or a section of it.
predicates.public_use_as_of_right_not_established: The evidence did not establish that the Hindu community or a section of it used the shrine for worship as of right.

members.legal_issue: Long-standing public worship and a separate endowment support an inference that a religious institution is public unless contrary circumstances are established.
material_facts: The public had access to the temple throughout the day, and there was no evidence that worshippers had been excluded from worship as a matter of right.
The public had worshipped there continuously for a long period.
The temple was extensive, had facilities for large gatherings, and hosted public festivals, processions, worship and feeding of visitors.
The deity received grants and endowments for worship and festivals, and the institution's administration and history were consistent with public use.
members.legal_principle: Under the definition of a temple in section 9 of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, as discussed in Narayanan v. Hindu Religious Endowments Board, public character may be inferred from the institution's nature, public use and administration. Once long public worship and a separate endowment for the deity are established, dedication for public use may fairly be inferred unless the contrary is shown. Public offerings alone are not necessarily sufficient, as noted in Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop; the extent of the temple, endowments and public use are relevant circumstances.
members.conclusion: The deity and temple were public, and the evidence established a public right of worship.

rule.if: proceeding_to_determine_public_or_private_religious_status and long_public_worship and separate_endowment_for_deity and (public_access_without_exclusion or public_scale_and_rituals)

predicates.proceeding_to_determine_public_or_privat: The proceeding asks whether a religious institution is public or private.
predicates.long_public_worship: Members of the public have worshipped at the institution over a long period.
predicates.separate_endowment_for_deity: Property or income has been set apart for the deity or its worship.
predicates.public_access_without_exclusion: The public has been admitted for worship without evidence of exclusion as a matter of right.
predicates.public_scale_and_rituals: The institution's scale, ceremonies or activities indicate use by a worshipping public beyond a private household.

members.legal_issue: Longstanding public worship as of right, considered with the character and use of a temple, supports the inference that the temple is public.
material_facts: The public had worshipped at the temple for more than 200 years, and there was no evidence that the public had been excluded.
The temple was extensive, included a large assembly hall, and admitted worshippers throughout the day.
Public festivals, processions, ceremonies, offerings, and feeding were conducted at the temple.
Rulers had granted land and money for worship and festivals.
The idol was sometimes moved temporarily for processions or visits, and a substitute was left for worship at the temple.
members.legal_principle: In Narayanan v. Hindu Religious Endowments Board, A.I.R. 1938 Mad. 209, the court treated long public user, a separate endowment, the institution’s character and administration, and the absence of arbitrary exclusion as grounds for inferring public dedication and public use as of right. The court also considered Ram Soondur Thakoor v. Taruk Chunder Turkoruttum (1873), Hari Raghunath v. Anantji Bhikaji (1920), Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925), and Venkatachala v. Sambasiva, A.I.R. 1927 Mad. 465. It held that temporary movement of an idol, the absence of a dome or kalas, and the lack of consecration for a swayambhu deity were not by themselves decisive against public character.
members.conclusion: The temple and deity were public, and the public had a right of worship; temporary movement of the idol did not make the temple private.

rule.if: public_worship_longstanding and no_evidence_of_public_exclusion and temple_has_public_character and public_endowment_or_grants

predicates.public_worship_longstanding: Members of the public worshipped at the institution over a long period.
predicates.no_evidence_of_public_exclusion: The evidence did not show that the institution’s managers excluded members of the public from worship.
predicates.temple_has_public_character: The institution’s scale, layout, ceremonies, or administration were characteristic of a place used for public worship.
predicates.public_endowment_or_grants: The institution received grants or endowments for worship, festivals, or related religious purposes.

members.legal_issue: A court may order eviction from a specified part of a building under a single tenancy, even if the order leaves another part with the tenant.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the first and second floors as a residence and used the ground floor for a drug store belonging to his wife.
The landlord sought possession of the entire building or, alternatively, part of it.
The appellate authority allowed release of the ground floor alone.
members.legal_principle: Section 21(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 authorizes an eviction order from the building under tenancy or any specified part of it. The Court therefore rejected the contention that a single tenancy could not be divided into separate occupied portions for this purpose.
members.conclusion: The partial-release order was permissible; the Act allows eviction from a specified part of a building under tenancy.

predicates.landlord_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery of possession from a tenant in a release proceeding.
predicates.tenancy_covers_building: The tenant's tenancy covers the building from which possession is sought.
predicates.release_sought_for_specified_part: The landlord seeks release of a specified part rather than only the entire building.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot divide a single tenancy let for both residential and non-residential purposes and order eviction under the residential-requirement ground only from the part used as a residence.
material_facts: The premises were let under a single tenancy for both running a school and residence.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the premises were bona fide required for his own residence.
The lower appellate court found that the letting was for both residential and non-residential purposes.
The High Court directed that the residential portion be demarcated and that eviction be ordered in respect of that portion.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(e) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 permits eviction for a landlord’s bona fide residential requirement only where the premises were let for residential purposes; it does not apply to premises let for composite residential and non-residential purposes. In the absence of statutory authority, a court cannot divide a single, indivisible contract of tenancy and grant relief for only a part of the premises. The court followed Dr. Gopal Das Verma v. S. K. Bhardwaj, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 678, approved Kunwar Behari v. Smt. Vindhya Devi, A.I.R. 1966 Punjab 481, and overruled Motilal v. Nanak Chand, (1964) Punj. L.R. 179.
members.conclusion: The court lacked jurisdiction to divide the single tenancy and order eviction of the residential portion under the residential-requirement ground. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the decree dismissing the eviction suit was restored.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_seeks_residential_requirement_eviction and premises_let_for_composite_purposes and tenancy_is_single_and_indivisible and court_proposes_to_separate_residential_portion

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction proceeding concerning premises occupied by a tenant under rent-control protection.
predicates.landlord_seeks_residential_requirement_e: The landlord seeks eviction on the ground that the premises are required for the landlord’s own residence or that of the landlord’s family.
predicates.premises_let_for_composite_purposes: The premises were let for both residential and non-residential purposes.
predicates.tenancy_is_single_and_indivisible: The parties entered into one tenancy contract covering the premises as a whole.
predicates.court_proposes_to_separate_residential_p: The court proposes to divide the premises and order eviction only from the portion used for residence.

members.legal_issue: Where a statute does not permit partial eviction, a landlord whose bona fide and reasonable need is established for most of the leased premises may obtain possession of the whole premises if the part for which need is not established is insubstantial.
material_facts: The eviction petition concerned the entire leased ground floor, and the landlord had not expressly removed the front portion from it.
The Supreme Court directed the High Court to proceed on the basis that bona fide and reasonable need was established for the ground floor except the front portion.
The statute did not provide for partial eviction, and the comparative-hardship issue had been concluded in the landlord's favour.
The record did not establish whether the front portion was a minor or a substantial part of the ground floor.
members.legal_principle: Where a tenancy cannot be split under the applicable statute, a landlord may have to seek possession of the whole premises even if the bona fide need extends only to part of it. Whether the whole premises may be recovered depends on whether the portion for which need is not established is insubstantial or substantial. The Court relied on Mattulal v. Radhe Lal and referred to Sanyal v. Gian Chand in addressing the bar on splitting the tenancy.
members.conclusion: The High Court had to determine the relative size of the front portion on remand: if it was minor, it was to confirm eviction of the entire ground floor; if it was substantial or major, it was to allow the revision and dismiss the eviction petition.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and no_partial_eviction_authority and bona_fide_need_for_substantial_part and need_not_established_for_remaining_part

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant from leased premises.
predicates.no_partial_eviction_authority: The governing law does not authorize an order evicting the tenant from only part of the leased premises.
predicates.bona_fide_need_for_substantial_part: The landlord's bona fide and reasonable need is established for a substantial part of the premises.
predicates.need_not_established_for_remaining_part: The landlord's bona fide and reasonable need is not established for the remaining part of the premises.

members.legal_issue: A single lease of accommodation for both residential and non-residential purposes does not prevent eviction when the landlord establishes the applicable bona fide need for each part.
material_facts: The tenant occupied a building under an integral lease for both residential use and operation of a cloth business.
The landlord sought the ground floor to operate a chemist shop and the first floor for residence.
The final court of fact found both requirements bona fide, and that finding was not challenged in the High Court or in the appeal to the Supreme Court.
The tenant appealed against the eviction decree.
members.legal_principle: Under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, accommodation includes a building or part of a building, whether residential or non-residential. Sections 12(1)(e) and 12(1)(f) permit eviction respectively for a bona fide residential requirement and a bona fide requirement to continue or start a business, subject to the statutory conditions concerning other reasonably suitable accommodation. An integral lease may have dual purposes without being impermissibly split: eviction may be ordered for the relevant residential and non-residential parts when the respective grounds are established. S. Sanyal v. Gian Chand, [1968] 1 S.C.R. 536, was distinguished because the case involved no splitting of the contract.
members.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed and the eviction order was upheld because the residential and non-residential parts each constituted accommodation and the landlord had established the corresponding bona fide requirements.

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_decree: The tenant brought an appeal challenging an eviction decree.
predicates.integral_lease_has_residential_and_busin: The tenant occupied the accommodation under one integral lease for both residential use and a business purpose.
predicates.landlord_bona_fide_needs_both_parts: The landlord established a bona fide need to use the residential part as a residence and the non-residential part for a business.
predicates.factual_finding_of_bona_fide_need_is_unc: The finding that the landlord had the asserted bona fide needs was not challenged in the subsequent appeals.

members.legal_issue: A tenant cannot be evicted solely for acquiring residential accommodation when the tenancy was for both residence and professional use.
material_facts: The rent deed described the premises as being for residence, and a letter from the landlord permitted the tenant to have a professional office there along with his residence.

The tenant used rooms in the premises as his legal practice office while living there with his family; the courts below found that the premises had been let for combined residential and professional purposes.
After the tenant died, his family continued to occupy the premises, and the respondent sons also used them for legal offices.
The respondents had built a residential house, and the landlord sought eviction on the ground that they had acquired residential accommodation.
The courts below made a concurrent finding that the tenancy was for combined residential and professional purposes.
members.legal_principle: Sections 13(1)(h) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, do not permit eviction on the ground of acquiring residential accommodation where the tenancy is for both residence and professional use: residential accommodation alone does not satisfy the professional purpose of that tenancy. The definition of “premises” in Section 2(g) of the earlier Act, unchanged in the replacement Act, accommodates combined uses. The Court applied Dr. Gopal Das Verma v. Dr. S. K. Bhardwaj, rejected a dominant-intention test, and held that the concurrent finding of combined use foreclosed the argument that professional use was merely a personal licence ending on the original tenant’s death.
members.conclusion: Eviction could not be ordered merely because the tenant or his successors had acquired residential accommodation, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding governed by rent control law.
predicates.eviction_sought_for_acquisition_of_resid: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant or the tenant’s successors had acquired residential accommodation.
predicates.tenancy_authorized_for_residence_and_pro: The premises were let or authorized for both living there and carrying on professional work there.

members.legal_issue: A tenancy used for both residence and professional purposes cannot be terminated merely because the tenant has acquired a suitable residence elsewhere.
material_facts: The tenant used the premises both for residence and for his medical profession.
The landlord sought ejectment on the ground that the tenant had acquired another suitable residence.
The tenant’s other residence would not meet the professional purpose for which the tenancy was also used.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(h) permits ejectment where the tenant has acquired a suitable residence. Where the tenancy is created or used for both residence and professional purposes, acquisition of premises suitable for residence alone does not satisfy the purposes of the tenancy and cannot alone justify its termination. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The tenant could not be ejected under Section 13(1)(h) merely because he had acquired a suitable residence.

predicates.acquisition_based_ejectment_claim: The landlord seeks possession on the ground that the tenant has acquired another suitable residence.
predicates.mixed_residential_professional_tenancy: The tenant’s premises are used for both residence and professional purposes.
predicates.tenant_acquired_suitable_residence: The tenant acquired premises suitable for residential use.

members.legal_issue: A tenant or the tenant’s successors cannot be evicted solely for acquiring residential accommodation when the rented premises were let for both residence and professional or business use.
material_facts: The premises were let to a practising lawyer for residence, and the landlord gave written consent for a professional office to be maintained there along with the residence.
The courts below found that the premises had been let for, and used for, both residence and professional purposes; that concurrent finding was accepted as final.
After the original tenant died, his successors continued to live in the premises, and two of them later used it for professional offices.
The successors had built a residential house, and eviction was sought on the ground that they had acquired residential accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Under section 13(1)(h) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and section 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, acquisition of residential accommodation does not justify eviction where the rented premises were let for both residence and professional or business use. The definition of premises in section 2(g) of the 1952 Act and section 2(1) of the 1958 Act accommodates combined uses. The Court applied Dr. Gopal Das Verma v. Dr. S. K. Bhardwaj, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 678, and held that a dominant-intention test did not govern the question. The same position applied to the tenant’s heirs and legal representatives.
members.conclusion: The successors could not be evicted solely because they had acquired residential accommodation, since the tenancy was for the composite purpose of residence and professional use.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.composite_residential_and_professional_l: The premises were let for both residence and professional or business use.
predicates.tenant_or_successors_acquired_residentia: The tenant or the tenant’s successors acquired residential accommodation.

members.legal_issue: Regular and open use of premises let for residence as a boarding house, with the landlord's knowledge and consent, takes the premises outside the residential-premises ground for eviction based on the landlord's residential requirement.
material_facts: The premises were let for residential purposes.
The tenant regularly accommodated foreign students as paying guests and used the premises as a boarding house, rather than merely as a private residence.
The landlord knew or was presumed to know of that use and did not object to it.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground of bona fide residential requirement.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the landlord must establish that the premises were let for residential purposes. Its Explanation preserves that character where premises let for residence are used incidentally for another purpose without the landlord's consent. But regular and open non-residential use ordinarily supports a presumption of the landlord's knowledge and consent; where, as here, the tenant regularly ran a boarding house with the landlord's knowledge and without objection, the Explanation does not preserve the residential eviction ground. The Court relied on Dr. Gopal Dass Verma v. Dr. S.K. Bhardwaj and Kartar Singh v. Chaman Lal; it also referred to Hobson v. Tulloch, Thorn v. Madden and Tendler v. Sproule in describing the boarding-house activity as a species of business.
members.conclusion: The residential personal-requirement ground was unavailable because the landlord's knowledge and implied consent to the regular boarding-house use took the premises outside the relevant category of premises let for residential purposes.

rule.if: residential_personal_need_eviction_case and premises_initially_let_for_residence and regular_open_paid_lodging_use and landlord_awareness_and_nonobjection

predicates.residential_personal_need_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction on a landlord's asserted need to occupy the premises as a residence.
predicates.premises_initially_let_for_residence: The premises were originally let for use as a residence.
predicates.regular_open_paid_lodging_use: The tenant regularly and openly accommodated paying lodgers in the premises as a boarding-house operation.
predicates.landlord_awareness_and_nonobjection: The landlord knew, or was presumed to know, of the lodging use and did not object to it.

members.legal_issue: Premises let for residence but used by the tenant for professional purposes with the landlord’s consent are not recoverable on the ground that the landlord bona fide requires them for residence.
material_facts: A substantial part of the premises had been used by the tenant for his medical profession from the beginning of the tenancy.
The tenant’s professional use was with the landlord’s consent.
The landlord sought possession for his own residential use, but the courts below found that the premises were not let for residence alone.
members.legal_principle: Under the explanation to Section 13(1)(e) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, premises let for residence but used incidentally for professional or other purposes with the landlord’s consent fall outside the category of premises let for residential purposes alone. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The landlord was not entitled to eject the tenant under Section 13(1)(e), even if the landlord established a bona fide residential need.

predicates.residential_need_ejectment_claim: The landlord seeks possession of the premises on the ground of a need to occupy them as a residence.
predicates.residential_let: The premises were let for use as a residence.
predicates.professional_use_with_landlord_consent: The tenant used the premises for professional purposes with the landlord’s consent.

members.legal_issue: A landlord seeking additional accommodation under Section 10(3)(c) may seek possession even when the tenant's use of the remaining part differs from the landlord's intended use.
material_facts: The landlords occupied part of the building for residence and sought the ground floor for additional residential accommodation.
The tenant used the ground floor as a godown for business goods.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(c) applies to a landlord occupying part of a residential or non-residential building and permits an application against any tenant occupying the remaining part for additional residential or business accommodation, as the case may be. Its non-obstante clause overrides the restrictions in Section 10(3)(a)(i) and (iii), including the requirement that the tenant's use correspond to the landlord's need. The words “any tenant” and “as the case may be” do not impose a matching-use restriction. The court approved K. Parasuramaiah v. Lakshmamma and overruled Thirupathi v. Kanta Rao.
members.conclusion: The landlords could invoke Section 10(3)(c) for residential needs even though the tenant used the remaining part for a non-residential purpose.

predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_procee: A landlord seeks eviction to obtain additional accommodation in a building the landlord partly occupies.
predicates.landlord_occupies_part_of_building: The landlord occupies one part of the building from which additional accommodation is sought.
predicates.landlord_has_bona_fide_additional_accomm: The landlord genuinely needs additional accommodation for residential or business purposes.
predicates.tenant_uses_remaining_part_for_different: The tenant uses the remaining part for a purpose different from the landlord's intended use.

members.legal_issue: A landlord occupying part of a building for residential purposes may seek possession for additional residential accommodation of a tenant-occupied part used for non-residential purposes.
material_facts: The landlord and his family occupied the first floor of the building as their residence, while the tenant used the ground floor for banking business.
The landlord sought the ground floor as additional accommodation for residential use, relying on his and his wife's difficulty climbing stairs and the family's increased accommodation needs.
The lower courts had found the landlord's requirement bona fide and reasonable and had found comparative hardship in his favour.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 permits a landlord occupying part of a building to seek additional accommodation for residential purposes from a tenant occupying the whole or part of the remainder, even where that tenant uses it for non-residential purposes. The claim requires bona fide need and that the advantage to the landlord outweigh the hardship to the tenant. The Court relied on Sri Balaganesan Metals v. M.N. Shanmugham Chetty and Ors.
members.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to hold that the landlord could not seek residential accommodation under Section 10(3)(c) from a tenant occupying the remaining part for non-residential use.

rule.if: additional_accommodation_eviction_proceeding and landlord_occupies_part_residentially and tenant_occupies_remaining_part_non_residentially and bona_fide_residential_need and landlord_advantage_outweighs_tenant_hardship

predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_procee: A landlord seeks eviction to obtain additional accommodation in a building of which the landlord already occupies part.
predicates.landlord_occupies_part_residentially: The landlord occupies part of the building for residential purposes.
predicates.tenant_occupies_remaining_part_non_resid: The tenant occupies another part of the building and uses it for non-residential purposes.
predicates.bona_fide_residential_need: The landlord has a bona fide need for additional accommodation for residential purposes.
predicates.landlord_advantage_outweighs_tenant_hard: The advantage to the landlord from eviction outweighs the hardship to the tenant.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that itself allocates specific immovable properties among co-parceners cannot prove title to those properties or that they ceased to be joint property, but may prove an intention to separate in status.
material_facts: In a partition proceeding, the parties relied on a written instrument that allocated specific parcels of land and portions of a house among the co-parceners.
The instrument was not registered.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act requires registration of an instrument that creates or declares rights in immovable property by allocating specific properties. Under Nanni Bai v. Gita Bai, an unregistered instrument of this kind may nevertheless be used to show severance of joint status, but not to establish rights in specific properties or their partition.
members.conclusion: The instrument required registration and was inadmissible to prove title to any particular property or that any property had ceased to be joint property. It was admissible to prove the parties’ intention to become divided in status.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The parties were litigating a division of jointly held family property.
predicates.unregistered_partition_instrument: A party relied on a written instrument that had not been registered.
predicates.instrument_allocates_specific_immovable_: The instrument assigned identified immovable properties to particular co-parceners.
predicates.instrument_admissible_only_to_prove_seve: The instrument may be used to show that the co-parceners intended to separate in status, but not to prove rights in particular properties or that those properties ceased to be joint.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered record of a partition may be used for a limited collateral purpose to show severance in status and the character of possession.
material_facts: The writing recorded the parties’ arrangement concerning the division of the remaining family properties after agricultural lands had been partitioned and the family’s joint status disrupted.
The parties subsequently divided and possessed properties in accordance with the intention to divide recorded in the writing.
The writing was relied on to show the nature and character of possession of the properties allotted to the family members.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 permits an otherwise inadmissible unregistered document to be used as evidence of a collateral transaction not required to be effected by a registered instrument. Such a document may be used for the limited purpose of showing severance in status and the resulting nature of possession, but not to prove a transfer of legal title. The Court relied on Varada Pillai v. Jeevarathnammal and referred to the principles in Rajangam Ayyar v. Rajangam Ayyar and Nani Bai v. Gita Bai.
members.conclusion: Even if unregistered, the writing could be considered for the limited collateral purpose of establishing severance in status and showing that the subsequent division of the properties followed the original intention to divide.

rule.if: civil_appeal and unregistered_partition_record and prior_severance_of_joint_status and later_division_follows_original_intention

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter came before the court as a civil appeal.
predicates.unregistered_partition_record: The parties made a writing about the division of their property that had not been registered.
predicates.prior_severance_of_joint_status: The family members had already separated their joint status.
predicates.later_division_follows_original_intentio: The parties later divided or possessed the properties in accordance with an earlier intention to divide.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered writing may be relied on to establish severance of joint status, but not to prove a formal partition by metes and bounds where it requires registration.
material_facts: A suit sought partition of properties claimed to belong to a joint family.
The defendants relied on an unregistered writing relating to an earlier partition.

The lower courts found a prior partition and separate enjoyment of the properties, supported by evidence of separate possession, cultivation, tax payments, division of a house, separate dealings in properties, separate accounts of acquisition compensation, and separate property records.
The first appellate court relied on the writing to establish severance of joint status, rather than treating it as an admissible deed proving allotments by metes and bounds.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, a writing intended to record a formal partition by allotting specific property and declaring exclusive title requires registration. A partition may be oral, and an unregistered writing that does not itself evidence partition by metes and bounds may be used to establish severance of joint status. The Court relied on Nani Bai v. Gita Bai Kom Rama Gunge, Shiromani v. Hem Kumar, Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh, and Sk. Sattar Sk. Mohd. Choudhari v. Gundappa Amabadas Bukate.
members.conclusion: The unregistered writing could be relied on to establish severance of joint status, although it could not serve as a registered deed proving a formal partition by metes and bounds. The other evidence supported the finding of a prior partition.

predicates.partition_dispute: The parties disputed whether property claimed as joint family property had already been partitioned.
predicates.unregistered_partition_writing: A party relied on a writing about a partition that had not been registered.
predicates.relied_on_to_show_severance: The writing was relied on to show that the family had separated in status, rather than as proof of formal allotments by metes and bounds.

members.legal_issue: A document recording severance of joint status without allotting specific property by metes and bounds is not compulsorily registrable and may be admitted to prove that severance.
material_facts: Documents recorded a separation among members of a Mitakshara coparcenary and were used to show that they became separate in estate.
The documents were not relied on to prove a partition by allotment of specific properties by metes and bounds.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, a written partition by specific allotment of properties is compulsorily registrable. A partition consisting only of severance of joint status and definition of shares, without specific allotments, does not affect rights in immovable property in the manner contemplated by that provision and is not barred from evidence by section 49. The Court applied the distinction between the two forms of partition under Mitakshara law.
members.conclusion: The documents were admissible for the limited purpose of proving severance of joint status, despite being unregistered.

rule.if: document_offered_as_partition_evidence and mitakshara_coparcenary and document_records_status_severance and not document_allots_specific_property

predicates.document_offered_as_partition_evidence: A document is offered as evidence of a partition among family members.
predicates.mitakshara_coparcenary: The family members are governed by the Mitakshara law of coparcenary.
predicates.document_records_status_severance: The document records that a member's joint status has been severed and shares defined.
predicates.document_allots_specific_property: The document allots specific properties to individual members by metes and bounds.

members.legal_issue: An unstamped and unregistered instrument may be received in a partition suit for a collateral purpose, but not to prove division of joint property by metes and bounds, and only subject to impounding, payment of stamp duty and penalty, proof, and relevance.
material_facts: The defendants alternatively sought to use the unregistered and unstamped documents for a collateral purpose.
The documents concerned an alleged earlier partition and the resulting shares and possession.
The court held that the documents could be marked for a collateral purpose after payment of stamp duty and penalty and impounding, subject to proof and relevance.
members.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 permits an unregistered document to be received as evidence of a collateral transaction that does not itself require a registered instrument. In a partition suit, collateral use may concern severance of title or the nature of possession, but not division of joint property by metes and bounds. Under Chinnappa Reddy Gari Muthyala Reddy v. Chinnappa Reddy Gari Vankat Reddy, AIR 1969 A.P. 242, an unstamped instrument cannot be admitted even for a collateral purpose until it is impounded; the required stamp duty and penalty must be paid, and proof and relevance remain necessary.
members.conclusion: The documents were admissible for a collateral purpose subject to payment of stamp duty and penalty, impounding, proof, and relevance.

rule.if: partition_suit_evidence_issue and instrument_is_unregistered and instrument_is_unstamped and collateral_use_is_distinct_from_division_by_metes_and_bounds and stamp_duty_and_penalty_paid and instrument_is_impounded

predicates.partition_suit_evidence_issue: The instrument is tendered as evidence in a proceeding seeking partition of property.
predicates.instrument_is_unregistered: The instrument has not been registered.
predicates.instrument_is_unstamped: The instrument has not been duly stamped.
predicates.collateral_use_is_distinct_from_division: The proposed use concerns a matter such as severance of title or the nature of possession, rather than proving division of joint property by metes and bounds.
predicates.stamp_duty_and_penalty_paid: The party tendering the instrument has paid the required stamp duty and penalty.

members.legal_issue: An unregistered family-settlement instrument may be used for a collateral purpose in a partition-related proceeding only after it is impounded and the required stamp duty and penalty are paid.
material_facts: The document was unregistered and unstamped.
The document was offered in a property dispute, and the Court considered whether it could be used for a purpose collateral to proving the division of property by metes and bounds.
members.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act prevents an unregistered instrument from proving the primary transaction requiring registration, but it may be considered for a collateral purpose, such as severance of title or the nature of possession, rather than division by metes and bounds. Under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, an unstamped instrument cannot be admitted even for a collateral purpose until it is impounded and the required duty and penalty are paid. Yellapu Uma Maheswari v. Buddha Jagadheeswararao (2015) 16 SCC 787, applying Chinnappareddigari Peda Mutyala Reddy v. Chinnappareddigari Venkata Reddy, AIR 1969 AP 242, states these limits.
members.conclusion: The document could be admitted for a collateral purpose, subject to being impounded and payment of stamp duty and penalty, and subject to proof and relevance.

rule.if: partition_related_property_proceeding and unregistered_instrument and unstamped_instrument and collateral_use_sought

predicates.partition_related_property_proceeding: The proceeding concerns rights or possession arising from a claimed partition of property.
predicates.unregistered_instrument: The instrument has not been registered despite being one that requires registration.
predicates.unstamped_instrument: The instrument has not been duly stamped.
predicates.collateral_use_sought: The party seeks to use the instrument for a purpose other than proving the primary division of property by metes and bounds.
