members.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC, read with Explanation VIII, makes a final decision on an issue by a competent court of limited jurisdiction conclusive in a later suit between the same parties or their privies. The Court relied on P.M. Kavade v. A.B. Bokil, Rai Bahadur Singh v. Rai Beni Madho Rakesh Singh, Daryao v. State of U.P., and Gulam Abbas v. State of U.P. in explaining the scope and public-policy basis of res judicata.
members.conclusion: Explanation VIII to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure includes courts of limited pecuniary jurisdiction, so their final decisions can operate as res judicata in later suits even when those courts could not have tried the later suits.

rule.if: limited_jurisdiction_prior_decision and issue_finally_decided and later_suit_between_parties_or_privies and same_issue_raised

predicates.limited_jurisdiction_prior_decision: A court whose jurisdiction was limited, including by pecuniary limits, decided the issue in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.issue_finally_decided: The issue was directly and substantially raised and was finally decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.later_suit_between_parties_or_privies: A later suit was brought between the same parties or persons claiming through them.
predicates.same_issue_raised: The same issue was directly and substantially raised in the later suit.

members.legal_issue: A final determination of an issue by a court competent to decide that issue can bar its relitigation in a subsequent civil suit even when the earlier court could not have tried the subsequent suit, including where the claimant litigates under the title of a party to the earlier proceeding.
material_facts: Earlier civil suits, decided after the parties had an opportunity to contest the issues, determined that one alleged son had not been adopted by the property owner and that another person had been adopted by him.
The earlier determinations concerned issues raised again in the subsequent suit for possession.
The claimant was not personally a party to all the earlier proceedings, but claimed through a person who had been a party to them.
The court deciding the earlier proceedings was competent to decide the issues, although it could not have tried the subsequent suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation VIII, gives effect to final determinations by a court competent to decide the issue, notwithstanding that the court could not try the later suit. Res judicata promotes finality and prevents repeated litigation of the same issue. The Court relied on the general principles discussed in Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Gujarat and on Explanation VIII to Section 11.
members.conclusion: The earlier determinations operated as res judicata against the claimant, who was litigating under the same title as the earlier party, and the issues could not be reopened in the subsequent suit.

rule.if: subsequent_civil_suit_reopens_same_issue and prior_issue_finally_decided_after_fair_hearing and prior_court_competent_to_decide_issue and (claimant_was_prior_party or claimant_claims_under_prior_party)

predicates.subsequent_civil_suit_reopens_same_issue: A party to a later civil suit raises an issue that was determined in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.prior_issue_finally_decided_after_fair_h: The earlier proceeding finally determined the issue after the affected parties had an opportunity to contest it.
predicates.prior_court_competent_to_decide_issue: The court in the earlier proceeding had authority to decide the issue, even if it could not have tried the later suit.
predicates.claimant_was_prior_party: The claimant in the later suit was a party to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.claimant_claims_under_prior_party: The claimant in the later suit claims through a person who was a party to the earlier proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A decision by a court with jurisdiction to decide the issue in a special proceeding can operate as res judicata even if that court could not try the later ordinary suit.
material_facts: A special judge appointed under land acquisition legislation decided the competing title claims in the compensation proceeding.
The special judge had jurisdiction to determine the title issue necessary to resolve the compensation dispute.
The special judge would not have had jurisdiction to try the later ordinary possession suit.
members.legal_principle: For res judicata founded on general principles, the former court must have been competent to decide the matter before it; it need not have jurisdiction to try the later suit. The limitation in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure concerning the former court’s competence to try the later suit applies to suits under that section, not to the general principle. The Court relied on Ramachandra Rao v. Ramachandra Rao and Bhagwati v. Ram Kali.
members.conclusion: The special judge’s decision could operate as res judicata despite the judge’s lack of jurisdiction to try the later suit.

rule.if: special_proceeding and former_court_competent_on_issue and issue_decided_finally and later_suit_raises_same_issue

predicates.special_proceeding: The earlier decision was made in a proceeding exercising a court’s special or exclusive jurisdiction.
predicates.former_court_competent_on_issue: The court had authority to decide the issue that arose in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.issue_decided_finally: The court finally decided that issue.
predicates.later_suit_raises_same_issue: A later ordinary suit raises the issue already decided.

members.legal_issue: For res judicata jurisdiction purposes, the competence of the court that decided the former suit is considered, even when the suit was initially filed in a different court and later transferred.
material_facts: The respondent’s suits were initially filed in a Munsif’s court, transferred to the Additional Civil Judge, and decided by that judge.
The court that decided the respondent’s suits had jurisdiction to try the appellant’s later title suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the court that decided the former suit to have been competent to try the subsequent suit or the issue later raised. The relevant court is the court that decided the former suit, not the court in which it was first filed.
members.conclusion: The initial filing of the respondent’s suits in the Munsif’s court did not prevent the decisions from operating as res judicata, because the court that actually decided them was competent to try the later title suit.

predicates.res_judicata_claim_in_later_proceeding: A party invokes the decision in an earlier proceeding to bar a later proceeding or issue.
predicates.former_suit_decided_by_competent_court: The court that actually decided the earlier suit had jurisdiction to try the later suit or issue.

members.legal_issue: A difference between the courts where related suits were initially filed does not prevent a res judicata bar when both suits are tried by a court competent to decide them.
material_facts: The partition suit and the money suit were initially filed in different courts.
The money suit was transferred to the court hearing the partition suit, and that court tried and decided both suits.
The same issue concerning whether the brothers’ businesses were joint or separate was decided in both suits.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Explanation II, determines a court’s competence irrespective of provisions governing a right of appeal. The relevant competence is that of the court which actually tried the suits. The Court followed Lortankutty v. Thomman and distinguished Narhari v. Shankar; it also noted that decisions made beyond a court’s jurisdiction cannot operate as res judicata.
members.conclusion: The initial difference in the courts’ jurisdiction did not prevent the decisions from supporting a res judicata bar because the court that actually tried both suits was competent to do so.

predicates.appeal_challenges_one_of_related_suits: A party appeals from a decision in one of two related suits.
predicates.both_suits_were_decided_by_a_court_compe: The court that actually heard and decided both suits had authority to decide each of them.
predicates.same_issue_was_decided: The same issue was heard and decided in both suits.

members.legal_issue: A determination of a vital issue in an earlier suit between the same parties may bar its relitigation when the suit was dismissed because the claim was satisfied during its pendency rather than for a defect affecting maintainability.
material_facts: In an earlier suit between the same parties, the tenant disputed the claimant’s ownership on the ground that the property had been bought benami for another person.
The court decided that the claimant owned the property and was entitled to rent, and allowed the claimant to withdraw rent deposited by the tenant during the suit.
The earlier suit was formally dismissed because the tenant had deposited the arrears claimed during the proceedings.
The tenant did not appeal the ownership determination and later challenged the claimant’s title again in a subsequent eviction suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars retrial of an issue directly and substantially in issue between the same parties that was heard and finally decided. A finding on a vital issue can operate as res judicata where the earlier claim ended because its cause of action was extinguished or otherwise satisfied, rather than because the suit was not maintainable. The principle in Midnapur Zamindari Company v. Naresh Narayan Roy (AIR 1922 PC 241) concerns an adverse finding that was unnecessary to a party’s success on an alternative ground; it does not prevent preclusion where the earlier decision on the vital issue formed part of a judgment effectively in that party’s favour.
members.conclusion: The earlier determination of ownership was final and barred the tenant from relitigating the claimant’s title.

predicates.later_suit_between_same_parties: A later proceeding is brought between the same parties as an earlier proceeding.
predicates.vital_issue_directly_and_substantially_i: The issue in the later proceeding was directly and substantially contested in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.vital_issue_decided_finally: The earlier court finally decided the vital issue after hearing the parties.
predicates.prior_suit_ended_because_claim_was_satis: The earlier suit ended because the claim was satisfied or its cause of action otherwise ceased during the proceedings, rather than because the suit was not maintainable.

members.legal_issue: A substantive determination made in an earlier suit can operate as res judicata in a later suit even when the earlier court also found that the plaintiff was not entitled to sue, if the substantive issue was directly tried and no preliminary issue made its determination unnecessary.
material_facts: In the earlier suit, the plaintiff claimed that an estate-holder had only a life interest under a will and a related letter, and sought relief concerning the estate.

The earlier court considered the nature of the estate in detail, held that the estate-holder had obtained absolute ownership, and found that the plaintiff had no present interest entitling him to sue.
The earlier court did not dispose of the case on a preliminary issue that made examination of the estate-holder’s rights unnecessary.
In the later suit, the plaintiff again based his claim on the will and letter, and the court held that the earlier determination barred the claim.
members.legal_principle: Where a court’s final decision rests on determinations of more than one point, each independently sufficient to support that decision, each determination operates as res judicata between the parties. The Court applied Vithal Yeshwant Jathar v. Shikandarkhan Mukhtum-khan, [1963] 2 S.C.R. 285 at 290, and explained and distinguished Shankarlal v. Hiralal, A.I.R. 1950 P.C. 80. It also explained that if a plaint on its face discloses a bar such as failure to comply with section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court should reject it without trying the merits; where the plaint does not facially disclose that bar, the court may decide the issues raised, and its substantive determinations may bind the parties in later litigation.
members.conclusion: The earlier decision operated as res judicata on the nature of the estate, and the later suit was barred.

rule.if: subsequent_suit and same_parties_or_privies and same_substantive_issue_relitigated and prior_court_decided_substantive_issue and not preliminary_issue_made_substantive_decision_unnecessary

predicates.subsequent_suit: The proceeding is a later suit in which a claim is again advanced.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The parties to the later suit are the same as, or legally represented by, parties to the earlier suit.
predicates.same_substantive_issue_relitigated: The later suit raises for determination the same substantive issue that was raised in the earlier suit.
predicates.prior_court_decided_substantive_issue: The earlier court tried and determined the substantive issue between the parties.
predicates.preliminary_issue_made_substantive_decis: A preliminary issue disposed of the earlier suit in a way that made deciding the substantive issue unnecessary.
predicates.subsequent_claim_is_barred: The later claim cannot be tried because the earlier determination binds the parties.

members.legal_issue: A later suit is barred by res judicata when the same issue between the same parties has already been finally decided, even if the suits have different subject matters, additional parties, or different material is placed before the later court.
material_facts: A prior damages suit and the later suit for a declaration involved the same plaintiff and the State as the contesting defendant on the issue of whether the agreement and surety bond were unenforceable for non-compliance with Article 299 of the Constitution.
The prior court rejected that challenge, finding that the agreement had been ratified and acted upon, and its decision was affirmed on appeal.
The later suit included additional parties and did not expressly plead ratification, and the subject matter of the suits differed.
The prior decision was final, and the additional parties and differences between the suits did not alter the identity of the issue between the plaintiff and the State.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, res judicata may apply where the issue in the later suit is the same as an issue previously decided between the same parties, or parties under whom they claim, by a competent court and the other statutory conditions are met. It is not necessary for every party or the overall subject matter of the suits to be identical. Once the issue and parties are the same, the fact that material supporting the earlier decision is not placed before the later court does not prevent the bar from applying.
members.conclusion: The plea of res judicata was properly upheld because the issue in the later suit had already been decided between the same parties in the prior suit.

rule.if: successive_suits and same_parties_on_issue and issue_identical and prior_decision_final and prior_court_competent

predicates.successive_suits: A party raises an issue in a later suit after that issue arose in an earlier suit.
predicates.same_parties_on_issue: The parties contesting the issue in the later suit are the same as those who contested it in the earlier suit, or claim under them.
predicates.issue_identical: The issue in the later suit is the same issue that was determined in the earlier suit.
predicates.prior_decision_final: The earlier court's determination of the issue became final.
predicates.prior_court_competent: The earlier issue was decided by a court competent to determine it.

members.legal_issue: A final determination of entitlement in an earlier suit between the same parties bars relitigation of that issue in a later suit, notwithstanding an observation that the earlier judgment would not prevent a suit for possession.
material_facts: An earlier suit sought permanent injunction concerning management and possession of the Gaddi.
The earlier courts determined that the claimant was not entitled to hold or manage the Gaddi, and the Supreme Court restored the appellate decree containing those findings.
A later suit between the parties sought possession of the properties on the basis of entitlement to the Gaddi.
The earlier Supreme Court judgment stated that it would not come in the way of filing a suit for possession, if the claimant was so advised.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a matter directly and substantially in issue that was heard and finally decided in a former suit between the same parties litigating under the same title before a competent court; Explanation IV extends the bar to matters that might and ought to have been raised. Section 12 addresses suits barred by res judicata. Order II Rule 2 bars a second suit for relief that could but was not claimed in the first suit. A judgment is read in the context of its facts, and an observation does not override the applicable law or the binding ratio. The court relied on Sheodan Singh v. Daryao Kunwar, State of U.P. v. Nawab Hussain, Home Plantations Ltd. v. Talaku Land Board, Fateh Singh v. Jagannath Baksh Singh, and Shiv Kumar Sharma v. Santosh Kumari.
members.conclusion: The earlier determination of entitlement was final and binding, and the later suit was barred by res judicata; the observation about filing a suit for possession did not remove that bar.

rule.if: later_possession_suit and same_parties and prior_entitlement_issue_decided_finally and prior_court_competent and (prior_observation_allows_fresh_suit or not prior_observation_allows_fresh_suit)

predicates.later_possession_suit: A party brought a later suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later suit were the same as, or claimed under, the parties to the earlier suit and litigated under the same title.
predicates.prior_entitlement_issue_decided_finally: The earlier suit directly and substantially raised the parties’ competing entitlement, and that issue was heard and finally decided.
predicates.prior_court_competent: The court deciding the earlier suit was competent to decide the issue and the later suit.
predicates.prior_observation_allows_fresh_suit: The earlier judgment included an observation that a party could bring a fresh suit for possession.
predicates.not_prior_observation_allows_fresh_suit: The earlier judgment did not include an observation that a party could bring a fresh suit for possession.

members.legal_issue: A state law whose predominant purpose is planned development may incidentally provide for land acquisition without being invalid merely because acquisition is also addressed by central legislation, if the laws can operate without irreconcilable conflict.
material_facts: The state statute established a development authority and provided for the formulation and implementation of planned-development schemes.
Land acquisition under that statute was incidental to the schemes’ development purpose.

The appellant contended that acquisition was governed by the concurrent legislative field and that the state statute conflicted with the central land-acquisition law; the state statute had not received presidential assent.
The Court concluded that the state statute was principally concerned with planned development, fell within the state legislative field, and could coexist with the central law.
members.legal_principle: Articles 246 and 254 of the Constitution, read with Entries 5 and 18 of List II and Entry 42 of List III, permit the State Legislature to enact a law principally concerned with local authorities, land and planned development, even if acquisition is an incident of that law. Applying the doctrines of pith and substance, incidental encroachment and harmonious construction, repugnancy requires an actual, irreconcilable conflict; incidental overlap does not suffice. The Court relied on Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, A.S. Krishna v. Madras State, State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd. and Girnar Traders III.
members.conclusion: The state development statute is within the State Legislature’s competence and is not invalid on grounds of repugnancy with the central land-acquisition law.

predicates.state_law_for_planned_development: The challenged state law principally establishes a public authority or scheme for planned development.
predicates.acquisition_is_incidental: The law provides for acquisition as an incident of achieving its planned-development purpose rather than making acquisition its primary object.
predicates.laws_can_operate_without_irreconcilable_: The state law and the central law can operate in their respective fields without an actual, irreconcilable conflict.

members.legal_issue: A state planning law and a central land acquisition law operating in distinct fields can be applied harmoniously without the planning law being invalidated for repugnancy.
material_facts: The state enactment's principal purpose was planned development, while the central enactment's principal purpose was acquisition of land and payment of compensation.
The planning law had a comprehensive scheme and used selected acquisition-law provisions for limited purposes.

The Court found that the enactments could operate in their respective fields, with compatible acquisition and compensation provisions applied without importing provisions that would frustrate the planning scheme.
The Court treated land acquisition as incidental to the planning law's principal purpose and rejected the contention that the central law displaced the relevant planning-law provisions.
members.legal_principle: Legislative entries define fields of legislation and are construed broadly. The Court applied the doctrines of pith and substance and incidental encroachment, seeking to preserve and harmonize legislation where possible. It relied on Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar, Union of India v. Shah Gobardhan L. Kabra Teachers' College, and State of Bombay v. Narottamdas Jethabhai, among other cases.
members.conclusion: The repugnancy challenge fails; the enactments can operate harmoniously, and the planning law remains effective within its legislative field.

predicates.planning_law_and_central_acquisition_law: The dispute involves a state planning law and a central law concerning land acquisition.
predicates.planning_law_is_substantially_about_plan: The planning law, viewed as a whole, principally regulates planned development rather than land acquisition alone.
predicates.acquisition_is_incidental_to_planning: Acquisition under the planning law is a means of implementing its planning purpose rather than its principal object.
predicates.the_laws_can_operate_harmoniously: The two laws can operate in their respective fields by applying compatible provisions without defeating either law's purpose.

members.legal_issue: A state acquisition law is not repugnant to central acquisition legislation merely because both concern acquisition when their dominant purposes differ and they do not occupy the same field incompatibly.
material_facts: The challenged state law primarily sought to preserve and protect an estate governed by land-reform legislation.
The central land-acquisition law concerned acquiring land for public purposes and determining compensation.
The state law also dealt incidentally with acquisition of paintings, artefacts, and other valuables.
The court found the dominant purposes and fields of the two laws materially different.
members.legal_principle: Article 254 applies when state and central laws concern substantially the same subject matter and are fully inconsistent or irreconcilable so that they cannot operate together. The court examined the dominant intention and field of each law. It relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh; Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar; M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India; and Vijay Kumar Sharma v. State of Karnataka.
members.conclusion: There was no repugnancy between the state law and the central land-acquisition law, and assent under Article 254(2) was not required on that ground.

predicates.repugnancy_challenge_to_state_law: A person challenges a state law as repugnant to a central law.
predicates.state_and_central_laws_have_different_do: The state and central laws principally pursue different legislative purposes.
predicates.laws_are_not_irreconcilably_inconsistent: The laws do not create an unavoidable conflict when applied to the same facts.

members.legal_issue: A state amendment is not repugnant to central legislation when the two can operate together and the central legislation does not prohibit the change made by the amendment.
material_facts: The central legislation and the agreement made under it did not provide for modification, variation, or deletion of the agreement’s terms.
The state amendment provided for retrospective modification of such agreements and removed the prohibition on construction in the agreement.
The amendment did not create a direct, irreconcilable conflict with the central legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 254, repugnancy requires clear and direct inconsistency that is irreconcilable and makes it impossible to obey both laws. The Court relied on M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India and Kanaka Gruha Nirmana Sahakara Sangha v. Narayanamma. It considered Sections 41 and 42 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and held that the central legislation was silent on modification of the agreement, so the state amendment did not place the laws in direct conflict.
members.conclusion: The state amendment was not repugnant to the central legislation, so the challenge based on Article 254 failed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_amendm: A party challenges a state legislative measure on the ground that it conflicts with central legislation.
predicates.central_law_is_silent_on_agreement_modif: The central legislation does not address whether the relevant agreement may be changed or its terms deleted.
predicates.state_amendment_adds_modification_mechan: The state legislature enacts a measure providing for changes to agreements made under the central law.
predicates.both_laws_can_operate_together: The central law and the state measure do not impose commands that cannot both be followed.

members.legal_issue: A State law directed principally to agrarian reform is not repugnant to a central law directed principally to forest management where the laws concern different subjects and can operate together.
material_facts: The State legislation principally addressed land tenure and agrarian reform, including the vesting of private forest land as land.
The central legislation principally addressed forests, including their management, preservation, transit, and forest produce.
The central legislation permitted acquisition for its purposes but did not require that all forest acquisitions occur under that process.
The two statutory schemes did not impose irreconcilable obligations or occupy the same field in their dominant purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 254, repugnancy requires laws on a concurrent subject to occupy the same field and to conflict directly and irreconcilably, such that both cannot operate together; a central law intended as an exhaustive code may also exclude a State law. The Court applies the pith-and-substance doctrine and the triple test in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India. It also relies on Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar, Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, Govt. of A.P. v. J.B. Educational Society, and State of Maharashtra v. Bharat Shanti Lal Shah. Incidental overlap between laws with different dominant purposes does not establish repugnancy.
members.conclusion: There is no repugnancy between the two laws, and no presidential assent was required to sustain the State law on that ground.

rule.if: repugnancy_challenge_to_state_law and state_law_targets_land_reform and central_law_targets_forest_management and laws_can_operate_together

predicates.repugnancy_challenge_to_state_law: A party challenges a State law on the ground that it conflicts with a central law.
predicates.state_law_targets_land_reform: The State law principally concerns land tenure and agrarian reform.
predicates.central_law_targets_forest_management: The central law principally concerns forest management, preservation, or forest produce.
predicates.laws_can_operate_together: The two laws can operate without a direct, irreconcilable conflict or one law requiring disobedience of the other.

members.legal_issue: A state law acquiring land for public purposes is not repugnant to a central law controlling an industry when the laws address different matters and the central law does not prohibit acquisition.
material_facts: The central tea-industry law provided for regulation of tea production and cultivation and contemplated that land planted with tea could be compulsorily acquired under another law.
The challenged state law acquired lands and provided for their restoration in specified circumstances and their assignment for agricultural purposes.
The company argued that the Tea Board, rather than the Land Board, should decide what land was necessary for the efficient operation of a plantation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that laws addressing different matters do not conflict merely because one affects the subject regulated by the other. It relied on Paresh Chandra Chatterjee v. The State of Assam and Another, which held that the Tea Act did not prohibit acquisition of land used for tea or for purposes incidental to the tea industry, and noted that the Tea Act contemplated compulsory acquisition and replacement planting.
members.conclusion: There was no repugnance between the state law and the Tea Act because they dealt with different matters, and Parliament had not required the Tea Board to determine what land must remain with a plantation.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisition_law and central_industry_law_regulates_industry and state_law_acquires_land and central_law_does_not_prohibit_acquisition and no_conflict_between_the_laws

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A party brought a constitutional challenge to a law that acquires land.
predicates.central_industry_law_regulates_industry: A central law regulates the relevant industry.
predicates.state_law_acquires_land: The state law acquires land, including land used in the regulated industry.
predicates.central_law_does_not_prohibit_acquisitio: The central law does not prohibit the acquisition of land under another law.
predicates.no_conflict_between_the_laws: The two laws address different matters and can operate without conflicting requirements.

members.legal_issue: A state law acquiring an electricity undertaking is not repugnant to central electricity legislation when the central provisions for purchasing undertakings do not apply to the acquired company and the laws operate in different fields.
material_facts: The state enacted a law to acquire an undertaking involved in completing a hydroelectric project, citing delay, public interest, and an acute power shortage.
The company was not a licensee under the electricity legislation governing supply and use of electrical energy.
The central law’s provisions for purchasing undertakings applied to licensees, and the provisions made applicable to generating companies did not include those purchase provisions.
The state law provided for acquisition of the undertaking and compensation; the central laws made general provision for the supply and use of electrical energy.
members.legal_principle: Articles 245, 246 and 254 of the Constitution allocate legislative powers and govern repugnancy between state and central laws. Repugnancy requires actual inconsistency, occupation of the same field, or an intention by Parliament to enact an exhaustive code; a mere possibility of conflict is insufficient, and courts should, where possible, reconcile the laws. The Court relied on Shyamakant Lal v. Rambhajan Singh, Deepchand v. State of U.P., Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay, and M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India. It considered the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, including sections 6 and 7A, and the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, including sections 2(4A), 2(6), 26A and 37. The purchase provisions in the 1910 Act applied to licensees, while the provisions made applicable to generating companies did not include those provisions. As the company was not a licensee and the state law and central laws operated in different fields, there was no repugnancy. The Court left unresolved whether the state law was referable to the State List entry on water and water power or the Concurrent List entry on electricity.
members.conclusion: The state law did not conflict or create repugnancy with the central electricity laws, and presidential assent was therefore unnecessary. The constitutional challenge failed and the appeals were dismissed. The Court did not decide whether the state law fell under the State List entry on water and water power or the Concurrent List entry on electricity.

predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.state_law_acquires_electricity_undertaki: The challenged state law acquires an electricity undertaking.
predicates.company_not_covered_by_central_purchase_: The company whose undertaking is acquired does not fall within the class of persons to whom the central law’s provisions for purchasing undertakings apply.
predicates.state_and_central_laws_operate_in_differ: The state law addresses acquisition and compensation, while the central laws address the supply and use of electrical energy.

members.legal_issue: A state law may vest ownership of mineral rights in the state without being repugnant to central legislation regulating mines and mineral development when the central law contemplates state vesting and does not itself acquire ownership of the land.
material_facts: The state enacted a law authorizing it to acquire rights to minerals in land, including saltpetre deposits, and issued notifications under that law.
The central legislation regulated mining and mineral development and the grant of mining rights, but did not acquire ownership of mineral-bearing land.

The central legislation required certain mining leases in land vested in a state to be brought into conformity with its provisions, and separately contemplated central mining operations on land in which minerals vested in a state or another person.
The state law made its operation subject to the central legislation.
members.legal_principle: The character of legislation is determined by the substance and effect of its operative provisions, not merely by its stated objects and reasons. The central law's declaration under section 2 must be read with its provisions, including sections 16(1)(b) and 17: those provisions contemplate state vesting of mineral-bearing land while requiring mining rights to be governed by the central law. The central law did not occupy the separate field of acquiring ownership of the land. The Court distinguished the circumstances addressed in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, State of West Bengal v. Union of India, State of Orissa v. M. A. Tulloch & Co., and Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, particularly because the central law had been amended after the earlier decisions.
members.conclusion: The state law was valid and not repugnant to the central legislation; the state could validly acquire ownership rights in the mineral deposits.

rule.if: state_legislation_validity_challenge and state_law_vests_mineral_ownership and central_law_regulates_mining_rights and (central_law_contemplates_state_vesting or central_law_leaves_land_acquisition_unaddressed)

predicates.state_legislation_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of state legislation that concerns mineral-bearing land.
predicates.state_law_vests_mineral_ownership: The state law authorizes the state to acquire ownership of mineral rights in land.
predicates.central_law_regulates_mining_rights: The central law regulates mining operations or the grant of mining rights.
predicates.central_law_contemplates_state_vesting: The central law provides for mining rights in land that has vested in a state to be governed by the central regulatory scheme.
predicates.central_law_leaves_land_acquisition_unad: The central law regulates mining but does not itself acquire ownership of the mineral-bearing land.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature may acquire property belonging to an undertaking in an industry declared for central control when the acquisition is within its independent acquisition power and does not intrude on the field occupied by central regulation.
material_facts: The challenged state law transferred and vested scheduled sugar undertakings in a state corporation.
The central legislation governed the development and regulation of declared industries, including sugar, but did not generally govern ownership of their undertakings.
After the transfer, the undertakings remained subject to central control under the central legislation.
The state law’s provisions, viewed as a whole, dealt with acquisition of the undertakings.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 246 and Entries 24 of List II, 52 of List I, and 42 of List III, acquisition of property is an independent legislative power under Entry 42, exercisable by both Parliament and the States. A declaration under Entry 52 removes state legislative power under Entry 24 only to the extent of the control occupied by the legislation enacted pursuant to the declaration. The law’s pith and substance determines its character, and incidental effects on another field do not invalidate it. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Rajamundry Electric Supply Corporation Ltd. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh, State of West Bengal v. Union of India, Kannan Devan Hills Produce Company Ltd. v. State of Kerala, Baijnath Kedia v. State of Bihar, and State of Haryana v. Chanan Mal.
members.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the acquisition law, and it did not conflict with or intrude upon the field occupied by the central legislation.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_acquisition_law and law_acquires_industrial_property and acquisition_power_is_separate and central_law_regulates_industry_without_acquiring_property

predicates.challenge_to_state_acquisition_law: A party challenges the legislative competence of a state law that acquires an industrial undertaking.
predicates.law_acquires_industrial_property: The law’s provisions, in substance, transfer ownership of property belonging to an industrial undertaking.
predicates.acquisition_power_is_separate: The acquisition is an exercise of legislative power specifically concerning acquisition of property, rather than merely an incident of power over another subject.
predicates.central_law_regulates_industry_without_a: The central law regulates the industry but does not itself acquire the undertaking’s property.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature may acquire land and determine what land is required for a plantation even when the acquisition affects an industry under central control, provided the law is in substance about land and acquisition.
material_facts: The challenged law transferred possession of lands in a defined area to the State, subject to exceptions, and provided for restoration of lands found necessary for specified plantation purposes.
The law provided for the State to determine which lands should be acquired and for remaining lands to be assigned for agricultural purposes.
The company argued that the provisions concerning restoration and hardship regulated the tea industry because plantations operated as integrated units.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the pith-and-substance approach to the legislative entries on land and acquisition. An effect on a matter within central legislative competence does not change the subject matter of an otherwise valid state law. The Court relied on Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Canadian Pacific Railway Company v. Attorney General, and distinguished Baijnath Kedai v. State of Bihar, Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia v. Union of India, and State of Maharashtra v. Madhavrao Damodar Patilchand.
members.conclusion: The State Legislature was competent to enact the law; its provisions concerning land determination were incidental to acquisition and did not become legislation about the controlled industry merely because they affected it.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisition_law and law_concerns_land_rights and state_acquires_land and (land_determination_is_incidental_to_acquisition or effect_on_controlled_industry_is_not_its_subject_matter)

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_acquisi: A party brought a constitutional challenge to a law that acquires land.
predicates.law_concerns_land_rights: The challenged law principally regulates rights in or over land.
predicates.state_acquires_land: The law transfers land or rights in land to the State for acquisition.
predicates.land_determination_is_incidental_to_acqu: The law determines what land is to be acquired as an incident of the acquisition power.
predicates.effect_on_controlled_industry_is_not_its: The law affects a centrally controlled industry, but its subject matter is not the regulation of that industry.

members.legal_issue: A pre-existing state law authorizing land requisition remains within legislative competence after central control is assumed over an industry using the land when the two laws regulate distinct subjects.
material_facts: The land-requisition law was enacted when the relevant state legislature was competent to legislate on compulsory acquisition of land, and no federal law had then declared the industry to be under federal control.
The law dealt with requisition and acquisition of land for public purposes, rather than regulation or development of an industry.
The later central law controlled the industry but did not regulate land requisition or acquisition; it contemplated compulsory acquisition of land and provided for replacement planting elsewhere.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 372, a law valid when enacted continues after the Constitution comes into force until altered, repealed, or amended by a competent legislature or authority. The court considered the legislative fields in Entry 9 of List II and Entry 34 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of India Act, 1935, and Entry 52 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The central industry-control law did not displace the state law because the former regulated the industry while the latter concerned land requisition and acquisition. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The land-requisition law was not beyond the state legislature’s power, and the later central law did not alter, repeal, or amend it; the earlier law continued in force.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preexisting_: A party challenges the continued validity of a pre-existing state law authorizing land requisition.
predicates.original_law_was_within_state_legislativ: The state legislature had authority to enact the land-requisition law when it was made.
predicates.later_central_law_targets_industry_contr: A later central law regulates control of an industry but does not regulate or prohibit land requisition or acquisition.

members.legal_issue: When the Controller is satisfied that a statutory ground for eviction exists, the word “may” does not give the Controller discretion to refuse eviction.
material_facts: The eviction application was allowed on the ground of non-payment of rent.
The tenant argued that the Controller could choose not to order eviction even after finding a ground under the Act.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed Section 14(2) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, in context: the provision directs rejection when the Controller is not satisfied of a ground, so “may” means “shall” when a ground is established. The Court also applied the principle that, where possible, legislation should be interpreted to avoid a construction that would make it unconstitutional under Article 14 of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: Once the Controller is satisfied that a specified ground for eviction exists, the Controller must order eviction; the Controller has no discretion to reject the application on that basis.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction under rent-control legislation.
predicates.controller_satisfied_eviction_ground: The Controller finds that a statutory ground for eviction has been established.

members.legal_issue: When the statutory conditions for eviction for monthly rent arrears without a dispute about the rent are satisfied, the court must order eviction despite the statute’s use of the word “may.”
material_facts: The landlord sued for possession on the ground of unpaid rent.
The tenant disputed the amount of rent and sought to have standard rent fixed, so the case did not fall within the category of undisputed rent arrears addressed by this rule.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, applies where rent is payable monthly, there is no dispute about standard rent or permitted increases, arrears have continued for at least six months, and the tenant neglects to pay within the period after the statutory demand notice. In that context, “may” requires a decree for eviction. The Court relied on Bhaiya Punyalal Bhagwandin v. Bhagwatprasad, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 312.
members.conclusion: The word “may” in section 12(3)(a) is mandatory: when that clause’s conditions are fulfilled, the court must decree eviction.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_suit and rent_payable_monthly and no_rent_amount_dispute and arrears_persist_for_required_period and tenant_neglects_payment_after_demand_notice

predicates.rent_default_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.rent_payable_monthly: The rent was payable by the month.
predicates.no_rent_amount_dispute: The tenant and landlord did not dispute the amount of standard rent or permitted increases.
predicates.arrears_persist_for_required_period: The rent or permitted increases remained unpaid for the statutory duration.
predicates.tenant_neglects_payment_after_demand_not: The tenant failed to pay the arrears before the period following the landlord’s demand notice expired.

members.legal_issue: Where rent is payable monthly, the amount payable is not genuinely disputed, and the tenant neglects to pay arrears of at least six months after the required demand notice, the court must grant eviction under the statutory arrears provision.
material_facts: The rent was payable monthly, and the agreed monthly rent was ₹30.
The tenant's application to fix standard rent was dismissed for non-prosecution, and the court found no real dispute about standard rent or permitted increases.
Rent had remained unpaid for more than six months, and the landlord served a notice demanding payment before bringing the eviction suit.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, applies where rent is payable monthly, there is no dispute about standard rent or permitted increases, arrears have continued for six months or more, and the tenant neglects to pay within one month after the demand notice under section 12(2). Under Vora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Safibhai, [1964] 5 S.C.R. 157, the court is bound to decree eviction when the statutory requirements apply and are not complied with.
members.conclusion: The case fell within section 12(3)(a); because its requirements were not met by the tenant, the court was bound to pass an eviction decree.

rule.if: nonpayment_eviction_proceeding and monthly_rent and no_genuine_rent_dispute and arrears_for_at_least_six_months and demand_notice_served and tenant_neglected_payment_after_notice

predicates.nonpayment_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession because the tenant had not paid rent.
predicates.no_genuine_rent_dispute: The tenant did not establish a genuine dispute about the rent or permitted increases payable.
predicates.arrears_for_at_least_six_months: The rent or permitted increases remained unpaid for six months or longer.
predicates.demand_notice_served: The landlord served the tenant with a written demand for the rent or permitted increases due.
predicates.tenant_neglected_payment_after_notice: The tenant did not pay the amount due within the required period after receiving the demand notice.

members.legal_issue: An eviction decree is mandatory when monthly rent is undisputed as to its standard amount, remains in substantial arrears, and the tenant fails to pay within the period following a written demand notice.
material_facts: The landlord sued to recover possession on, among other grounds, the tenants’ failure to pay rent.
Rent was payable monthly, and the claimed arrears covered more than six months.
The landlord served a written notice demanding the arrears, but the tenants did not pay within the period following the notice.
The tenants did not raise a dispute about the amount of standard rent or permitted increases.

The tenants asserted that the landlord had not provided receipts and had demanded compensation for use and occupation; the courts below nevertheless found neglect to pay, and the Supreme Court upheld their decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 12(2) and 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, where rent is payable monthly, there is no dispute about standard rent or permitted increases, the rent is in arrears for six months or more, and the tenant neglects to pay within one month after the written demand notice, the court shall pass a decree for eviction. The 1963 amendment replaced “may pass” with “shall pass,” making the decree mandatory when those conditions are satisfied. Harbanslal Jagmohandas & Anr. v. Prabhudas Shivlal, [1976] 3 SCR 628, was relied on in applying Section 12(3)(a). Mohan Laxman Hede v. Noormohamed Adam Shaikh, AIR 1988 SC 1111, was distinguished because it concerned regular deposits under Section 12(3)(b), not total failure or neglect to pay under clause (a).
members.conclusion: The statutory conditions for eviction were met, so the courts were bound to pass and uphold the eviction decree; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: possession_suit_for_unpaid_rent and rent_payable_monthly and no_standard_rent_dispute and arrears_for_six_months_or_more and tenant_did_not_pay_after_notice

predicates.possession_suit_for_unpaid_rent: A landlord brought a suit seeking possession on the ground that rent was unpaid.
predicates.rent_payable_monthly: The rent was payable from month to month.
predicates.no_standard_rent_dispute: The tenant did not dispute the amount of standard rent or permitted increases.
predicates.arrears_for_six_months_or_more: The rent or permitted increases remained unpaid for at least six months.
predicates.tenant_did_not_pay_after_notice: The tenant failed to pay the demanded rent within the period following the landlord’s written notice.

members.legal_issue: Payment of rent arrears only after an ejectment suit is filed does not prevent or make discretionary an eviction decree when the statutory conditions for eviction for substantial arrears are satisfied.
material_facts: The landlords brought an ejectment suit after the tenant had failed to pay rent despite a demand notice.
The arrears had remained unpaid for the qualifying period, and the standard rent was not disputed.
The tenant deposited arrears in court after the suit had been instituted.
The courts below decreed ejectment, and the Supreme Court upheld the decree.
members.legal_principle: Under section 12(2) and section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a landlord may sue after the tenant fails to pay within the prescribed time after a demand, and a decree must follow where rent is payable by the month, the qualifying arrears exist, and the tenant has not paid within the time allowed after the demand. Payment after institution of the suit does not undo the basis for eviction. Although section 12(3)(a) uses the word “may,” it does not confer discretion to refuse a decree when its conditions are met; the contrast with section 12(3)(b), which expressly provides a means for a tenant to avoid eviction by paying and continuing to pay, confirms that result. The court also held that section 12 provides no relief against forfeiture in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The post-filing payment did not affect the tenant's liability to eviction or the court's power to decree eviction. Once the statutory conditions were satisfied, the court was bound to pass the decree and had no discretion to refuse it.

rule.if: rent_ejectment_proceeding and monthly_rent and qualifying_rent_arrears and standard_rent_undisputed and demand_deadline_passed_without_payment and arrears_paid_only_after_suit_filed

predicates.rent_ejectment_proceeding: A landlord has brought an ejectment proceeding based on non-payment of rent.
predicates.monthly_rent: The rent is payable by the month.
predicates.qualifying_rent_arrears: The tenant has arrears that meet the applicable statutory threshold for eviction.
predicates.standard_rent_undisputed: The tenant has not disputed the amount of standard rent.
predicates.demand_deadline_passed_without_payment: The tenant failed to pay within the time allowed after receiving a demand for the arrears.
predicates.arrears_paid_only_after_suit_filed: The tenant paid or deposited the arrears only after the landlord had instituted the ejectment suit.

members.legal_issue: The amended rule governs an eviction suit instituted after the amendment and requires eviction when the tenant has substantial undisputed rent arrears and fails to pay them within the notice period, even if the tenant pays before the decree.
material_facts: The eviction suit was instituted after the amendment took effect.
The tenant was in arrears for more than six months, and there was no dispute about the amount of standard rent or permitted increases.
The tenant did not pay the arrears within one month after receiving the written demand notice.
The tenant paid the arrears by instalments before the decree, so no arrears remained due when the decree was passed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12(1), 12(2), and amended 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, governed the dispute. Under section 12(3)(a), where rent arrears of six months or more are undisputed and remain unpaid for one month after the required notice, the court must pass a decree for possession. The suit was instituted after the amendment, so the amended provision governed it; the earlier ability to pay at the hearing under the former section 12(3) did not confer a vested right that altered the amended provision’s effect. The court approved the mandatory reading of “may” in Kurban Hussen Sajuddin v. Ratikant Nilkant and distinguished the earlier decisions in Dayaram Kashiram Shimpi v. Bansilal Raghunath Marwari and Laxminarayan Nandkishore Shravagi v. Keshardev Baijnath Narsaria, which addressed the former law.
members.conclusion: The amended section applied to the suit, and the court was bound to decree eviction because the tenant had not paid within the prescribed time after notice; later payment before the decree did not prevent eviction. The tenant had no vested right to avoid that result by paying at the hearing.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_suit and suit_filed_after_change and arrears_at_least_six_months and rent_amount_undisputed and demand_notice_served and unpaid_through_notice_period

predicates.rent_control_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a suit seeking eviction of a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.suit_filed_after_change: The landlord instituted the suit after the relevant change in the law took effect.
predicates.arrears_at_least_six_months: The tenant owed rent arrears covering six months or more.
predicates.rent_amount_undisputed: The landlord and tenant did not dispute the amount of standard rent or permitted increases due.
predicates.demand_notice_served: The landlord served the tenant with a written demand for the rent arrears before bringing the suit.
predicates.unpaid_through_notice_period: The tenant did not pay the demanded arrears within one month after receiving the notice.

members.legal_issue: Under the amended arrears rule, a court must order eviction when the tenant has the requisite arrears and fails to pay within the notice period, even if the tenant pays before the decree and previously had an opportunity to pay later in the proceedings.
material_facts: The landlord’s written demand claimed rent arrears covering more than six months.
The tenant did not pay the demanded arrears within one month after receiving the notice.
The landlord filed the eviction suit after the amended provision took effect.
The tenant paid all the rent due before the trial court passed its decree.
The courts found that the case met the conditions for eviction under the amended arrears provision, and the Supreme Court dismissed the tenant’s appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(a), read with sections 12(1) and 12(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, required eviction where there was no dispute about the standard rent or permitted increases, the tenant was in arrears for six months or more, and the tenant failed to pay within one month after the required notice. The amended provision applied because the suit was brought after the amendment took effect. The Court followed Kurban Hussen Sajuddin v. Ratikant Nilkant in treating “may” as “must” when the provision’s conditions were met. It distinguished the earlier rule discussed in Dayaram Kashiram Shimpi v. Bansilal Raghunath Marwari and Laxminarayan Nandkishore Shravagi v. Keshardev Baijnath Narsaria concerning payment during the suit or appeal. The provision did not confer a vested right to cure the default by paying later; even if such a right existed, it could not change the provision’s plain effect.
members.conclusion: The amended provision governed the suit and required a decree for eviction; payment of the arrears before the decree did not prevent that result.

rule.if: rent_arrears_eviction_suit and no_dispute_about_rent_amount and arrears_at_least_six_months and compliant_notice_served and tenant_unpaid_within_notice_period and suit_after_amendment and tenant_paid_before_decree

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_suit: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding against a tenant on the ground of unpaid rent.
predicates.no_dispute_about_rent_amount: The landlord and tenant did not dispute the amount of standard rent or permitted increases due.
predicates.arrears_at_least_six_months: The tenant owed rent arrears for six months or more.
predicates.compliant_notice_served: The landlord served the tenant with a written demand that met the applicable notice requirements.
predicates.tenant_unpaid_within_notice_period: The tenant did not pay the demanded rent within the period following service of the notice.
predicates.suit_after_amendment: The landlord brought the eviction proceeding after an amendment to the governing arrears rule took effect.
predicates.tenant_paid_before_decree: The tenant paid the rent due before the court entered its decree.

members.legal_issue: The amended requirement to notify a tenant of each rent default applies to an ejectment proceeding where the tenancy was terminated and the proceeding was brought after the amendment took effect.
material_facts: The tenant had defaulted in rent for three years before the amendment took effect.
The landlord issued the notice terminating the tenancy after the amendment took effect.
The landlord applied for possession after the amendment took effect.
The landlord had not notified the tenant of each default within six months, as the amended proviso required.
members.legal_principle: Section 28(1) of the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, as amended by Section 7 of the 1960 Amendment Act, excluded the statutory relief where the tenant had failed to pay rent for three years and the landlord had not intimated each default within six months. A mere right to take advantage of a statutory provision is not an accrued right. The Court relied on Abbot v. Minister of Land (1895) AC 425, followed in Sakharam v. Manikchand Mothichand Shah, Hungerford Investment Trust Limited v. Haridas Mundhra, and Lalji Raja & Sons v. Hansraj Nathuram. Because both the termination notice and the possession application followed the amendment, the asserted right to institute the proceeding had not accrued before the change.
members.conclusion: The amended proviso applied. The landlord had no accrued right to proceed without complying with its notice requirement, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.ejectment_for_rent_default: The proceeding sought to eject a tenant for nonpayment of rent.
predicates.termination_after_notice_requirement: The landlord terminated the tenancy after a legal change began requiring timely notice of each rent default.
predicates.possession_application_after_notice_requ: The landlord applied for possession after that legal change began requiring timely notice of each rent default.

members.legal_issue: A notice demanding payment for use and occupation at the agreed rent rate can satisfy the requirement for a demand notice for rent arrears when read in its context.
material_facts: The landlord had previously terminated the contractual tenancy, after which the tenant remained as a statutory tenant.
The landlord's notice described the unpaid amount as damages for use and occupation, at a rate equivalent to the agreed rent, and demanded that the arrears be cleared within two months.
The tenant did not pay within that period; a later remittance was refused by the landlord.
The eviction proceeding concerned a further default after the tenant had previously obtained the statutory benefit for an earlier default.
members.legal_principle: Under section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, a landlord may seek recovery of possession where the tenant fails to pay or tender legally recoverable rent arrears within two months after service of a demand notice in the manner provided by section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Section 14(2), including its proviso, governs the tenant's benefit after payment or deposit and excludes that benefit after a further default of three consecutive months. Whether a notice is a demand for rent depends on its substance and context: describing the amount as damages for use and occupation does not prevent it from being a rent demand where the tenant is a statutory tenant and the amount is claimed at the agreed rent rate. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The notice satisfied the requirement for a demand notice for rent arrears. The appeal was allowed, the High Court judgment was set aside, and the matter was remitted to the Controller for further proceedings.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and tenant_is_statutory_tenant and tenancy_was_terminated and notice_describes_arrears_as_use_and_occupation_charges and charges_equal_agreed_rent and notice_demands_arrears_within_two_months

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession based on a tenant's alleged failure to pay rent arrears.
predicates.tenant_is_statutory_tenant: The tenant remained in the premises as a statutory tenant.
predicates.tenancy_was_terminated: The landlord had previously terminated the contractual tenancy.
predicates.notice_describes_arrears_as_use_and_occu: The landlord's notice described the unpaid amount as charges for use and occupation.
predicates.charges_equal_agreed_rent: The amount demanded for use and occupation was at a rate equivalent to the agreed rent.
predicates.notice_demands_arrears_within_two_months: The landlord's notice required the tenant to clear the arrears within two months.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s notices constitute a sufficient demand for rent arrears when, read together and in context, they communicate the arrears and a request for payment in a way an ordinary person would understand as a demand.
material_facts: The lease required rent to be paid in advance by the fifth day of each month.
An earlier notice stated that rent for February and March was unpaid and requested immediate payment of the arrears.
A later notice identified unpaid rent for February, March and April, terminated the tenancy, and requested possession of the premises.
The tenant’s reply acknowledged specified rent arrears as of that date.
The Rent Controller ordered eviction and the Rent Control Tribunal affirmed it, but the High Court set the eviction order aside for want of a proper demand notice.
members.legal_principle: Under section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, recovery of possession for non-payment requires a landlord-tenant relationship, legally recoverable arrears on the date of demand, service of a demand notice in the manner provided by section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and failure to pay or tender the rent within two months of service. A notice must be read from a common-sense point of view, bearing in mind how ordinary people would understand it; a demand may be apparent from notices read together and their context. The Court approved the approach in Shri Ram Sarup v. Shri Sultan Singh and distinguished Mangoo Singh v. The Election Tribunal, Bareilly, Chimanlal v. Mishrilal, and Mangat Ram v. Sardar Meharban Singh.
members.conclusion: The notices, read together and in the context of the tenant’s reply, clearly demanded payment of rent; the relevant notice requirement was fulfilled, and the High Court erred in setting aside the eviction order.

rule.if: rent_eviction_appeal and related_notices_read_together and arrears_identified and payment_requested and nonpayment_consequence_indicated

predicates.rent_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an eviction claim based on a tenant’s failure to pay rent.
predicates.related_notices_read_together: The landlord’s related communications are considered together and in their surrounding context.
predicates.arrears_identified: The communications tell the tenant that rent is in arrears.
predicates.payment_requested: The communications request that the tenant pay the arrears.
predicates.nonpayment_consequence_indicated: The communications indicate that a consequence, such as eviction proceedings, may follow if the arrears are not paid.

members.legal_issue: Eviction for rent default requires both qualifying arrears and failure to pay them to the landlord within the prescribed period after a compliant demand notice.
material_facts: The eviction claimant alleged rent default and served a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
That notice asserted that rent was due but did not satisfy the demand-notice requirements of Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972.
The tenants had made payments and court deposits, and the Court found that they were not in arrears to the claimant.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972 requires proof that the tenant is in arrears for at least four months and has failed to pay the arrears to the landlord within one month after service of a notice of demand. A notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 that merely asserts rent is due does not meet that requirement. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The eviction suit could not succeed because the tenants were not in qualifying arrears and, independently, the notice served was not a demand notice satisfying Section 20(2)(a).

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and (not qualifying_rent_arrears or not compliant_demand_notice)

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking eviction on the ground that rent was not paid.
predicates.qualifying_rent_arrears: The tenant owes the landlord at least the required period of unpaid rent.
predicates.compliant_demand_notice: The landlord served a notice demanding the rent and giving the tenant the required opportunity to pay it.
predicates.eviction_for_rent_default_fails: The landlord cannot obtain eviction on the ground of rent default.

members.legal_issue: A rent controller must order eviction when the tenant has defaulted in paying rent and has not made the full statutory cure at the first hearing.
material_facts: The rent was determined to be Rs. 12 per month, and the purchaser was entitled to rent from the date the sale was confirmed.

The tenant's second court deposit was made after the eviction application had been filed, and the Controller found the total amount deposited was short by Rs. 4-12-0 of the amount required, including rent, interest and application costs.
There was no proof of money-order tenders covering the relevant period.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, provides for eviction for non-payment of rent, subject to the proviso deeming the tenant to have paid in time if, at the first hearing, the tenant pays or tenders the arrears, interest and application costs. In Waryam Singh v. Amarnath, this Court held that a rent controller must order eviction when the statutory default is established and the tenant has not made the required cure; the decision was binding. The Court treated that rule as precluding relief from forfeiture in this case.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to relief from forfeiture, and the eviction order was required to stand.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and rent_default and not full_cure_at_first_hearing

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking to evict a tenant for non-payment of rent.
predicates.rent_default: The tenant failed to pay or tender rent within the time allowed for payment.
predicates.full_cure_at_first_hearing: At the first hearing, the tenant paid or tendered all arrears, interest and application costs.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who remains after a one-year lease expires must pay rent month to month, and eviction for arrears is sustainable when the tenant does not tender the full arrears at the first hearing.
material_facts: The one-year lease expired while the tenant remained in the premises.
The tenant tendered only part of the rent claimed and did not pay the rent due for at least two months after the lease expired.
The lower courts found that the tenant had not tendered the whole amount of arrears on the first day of hearing.
members.legal_principle: After the one-year lease expired, the tenant, even if holding over, was liable to pay rent month to month as contemplated by the Rent Act, with rent payable in the succeeding month before its end. Under Section 13 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, failure to tender the whole arrears on the first day of hearing supported eviction. The Court relied on its application of these statutory provisions and did not cite an earlier case as the basis for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The tenant was in arrears and had not tendered the whole amount due on the first day of hearing, so the eviction order was properly granted under Section 13 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act.

rule.if: eviction_appeal and fixed_term_lease_expired and tenant_remained_in_premises and rent_due_monthly and full_arrears_not_tendered_at_first_hearing

predicates.eviction_appeal: A tenant appealed an order granting eviction on the ground of rent arrears.
predicates.fixed_term_lease_expired: The lease for a fixed term ended.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_premises: The tenant continued occupying the premises after the lease ended.
predicates.rent_due_monthly: The rent payable after the lease ended fell due from month to month.
predicates.full_arrears_not_tendered_at_first_heari: The tenant did not tender the whole amount of rent arrears at the first hearing.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal has full power to review the evidence but must give proper weight to the trial court’s assessment and the safeguards that favour the accused.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused, and the High Court reversed that acquittal after reviewing the evidence.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not paid sufficient attention to important evidentiary problems or observed the caution required when disturbing an acquittal.
members.legal_principle: Sections 417, 418 and 423 of the Code of Criminal Procedure confer full power to review evidence in an appeal against acquittal. Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor establishes that the appellate court must give due weight to the trial judge’s credibility assessments, the presumption of innocence, the benefit of doubt and the trial judge’s opportunity to see the witnesses. Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan confirms that phrases such as “strong reasons” do not limit the power to review the evidence, but the appellate court must consider the record and the trial court’s reasons and explain why the acquittal was unjustified. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Samman Dass reiterates the presumption of innocence, preference for a reasonably possible view favourable to the accused, regard for the trial judge’s opportunity to observe witnesses, and the entitlement to reasonable doubt.
members.conclusion: An appellate court may review the evidence fully, but in deciding an appeal against acquittal it must consider the trial judge’s views on witness credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to observe witnesses; it must explain why the acquittal is unjustified.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to reverse an acquittal.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court reviewing an acquittal may reassess the evidence, but must give due consideration to the trial court’s view, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of doubt, and the advantage the trial court had in seeing the witnesses.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding the prosecution evidence unreliable.
The High Court reassessed the evidence and reversed the acquittal.
The Supreme Court examined the High Court’s judgment and found that it did not depart from the governing principles for appeals against acquittal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court has full power to review the evidence in an appeal against acquittal. In exercising that power, it must give proper weight to the trial judge’s assessment of witness credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s right to the benefit of doubt, and the trial judge’s advantage in seeing the witnesses. The Court relied on Sheo Swarup v. The King Emperor, 61 I.A. 398; Satwant Singh v. State of Rajasthan; and Sohrab v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1972 (3) SCR 751.
members.conclusion: The High Court had full power to review the evidence, and its reversal of the acquittal called for no interference because it gave proper consideration to the relevant matters.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to overturn an acquittal.
predicates.appellate_court_reassesses_evidence: The appellate court reviews the evidence on which the acquittal was based.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse a trial court’s acquittal only after giving due weight to the acquittal and finding substantial and compelling reasons to displace it.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding serious inconsistencies in the prosecution evidence, including medical and ballistic evidence indicating that the fatal bullet injury and the other person’s pellet injuries resulted from different shots fired from different firearms.

The trial court considered the possibility that the complainant’s side had been the aggressor and that the accused had acted in self-defence, and found the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the accused, but did not adequately address or displace the trial court’s reasons.
The Supreme Court considered the trial court’s assessment of the evidence to be a reasonable and plausible view and held that the High Court had no substantial and compelling basis for reversing it.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 378 and 386 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, an appellate court has broad power to review and reappreciate the evidence in an appeal against acquittal. That power must be exercised with due regard to the presumption of innocence, which is strengthened by acquittal, the trial court’s assessment of witness credibility, and the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of reasonable doubt. If two reasonable views are possible, the view supporting acquittal must be preferred; a different view on the evidence alone is insufficient for reversal. Interference requires substantial and compelling reasons, such as a palpably wrong or perverse conclusion, an erroneous view of law, a manifestly illegal approach, or ignored or misread material evidence. The Court relied on Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor, Surajpal Singh v. State, Khedu Mohton v. State of Bihar, Tota Singh v. State of Punjab, Sambasivan v. State of Kerala, State of Goa v. Sanjay Thakran, and Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, among other authorities.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the acquittal. Its judgment was set aside and the trial court’s acquittal was restored.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and two_reasonable_views_possible and not substantial_compelling_reasons_to_reverse

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed a trial court’s acquittal, and the appellate court reversed it.
predicates.two_reasonable_views_possible: The trial court considered the evidence and reached a view supporting acquittal that remained a reasonable interpretation of the record.
predicates.substantial_compelling_reasons_to_revers: The appellate court identified compelling defects in the acquittal, such as a perverse or palpably wrong conclusion, a manifestly illegal approach, or disregard or misreading of material evidence.
