material_facts: The agreement fixed a period for exercising the repurchase option but did not specify a period for executing the reconveyance deed after the option was exercised.
The purchaser refused to execute the deed, and the suit was filed within three years of that refusal.
members.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a three-year limitation period for a suit for specific performance, running from the date fixed for performance or, if no such date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. Because no date was fixed for execution of the reconveyance deed after exercise of the option, the refusal-based part of Article 54 applied.
members.conclusion: The suit was within limitation because time began to run from the refusal to perform.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.no_execution_date_fixed: The agreement does not fix a date or period for completing performance after the relevant option is exercised.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_after_refus: The suit is filed within the applicable limitation period after the other party refuses to perform.

members.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance is timely when no date for performance was fixed and it was brought within three years after the plaintiff had notice that performance was refused.
material_facts: No date for performance was fixed in the agreement relied on by the plaintiff.
The plaintiff received notice in July 1978 that the property had been sold to others.
The plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance on 3 January 1979.
members.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides a three-year limitation period for a suit for specific performance, running from the date fixed for performance or, if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
members.conclusion: The suit was within time because it was filed within three years after the plaintiff had notice of the refusal of performance.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.no_performance_date_fixed: The parties did not fix a date for performance of the contract.
predicates.suit_filed_within_three_years_of_notice_: The plaintiff filed the suit within three years after learning that the other party had refused performance.

members.legal_issue: A specific-performance consumer complaint is timely under the applicable limitation period where no time for performance was agreed, the promisor continued to acknowledge liability until a later notice, and the complaint was filed within three years of that notice.
material_facts: The complaint sought enforcement of an agreement to sell a flat, and the parties had specified no period for specific performance.
The appellants had not denied their liability to execute the sale deed and had acknowledged liability to deliver legal possession up to 30 August 1991.

In a notice dated 30 August 1991, the appellants demanded a disputed balance and required the respondent to take legal possession, after which the respondent could at the latest assume that they were not interested in performing the agreement.
The complaint was filed on 19 June 1992, within three years of that notice.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, under which the limitation period for specific performance runs from the date fixed for performance or, where no date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused. Because no performance date had been agreed and liability continued to be acknowledged, the Court treated the notice of 30 August 1991 as the latest date from which the period could run. The Court made this alternative finding without holding that the Limitation Act applied to consumer complaints.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the Limitation Act applied, the complaint was within time when measured from the date on which the respondent could at the latest treat the appellants as unwilling to perform the agreement.

rule.if: consumer_complaint and specific_performance_claim and no_agreed_performance_deadline and liability_acknowledged_until_later_notice and complaint_within_three_years_of_notice

predicates.consumer_complaint: A consumer brings a complaint before a consumer dispute-resolution body.
predicates.specific_performance_claim: The consumer seeks enforcement of an agreement to transfer property.
predicates.no_agreed_performance_deadline: The parties did not fix a date or period for performance of the agreement.
predicates.liability_acknowledged_until_later_notic: The party required to perform continued to acknowledge its liability until a later communication that could alert the claimant to its unwillingness to perform.
predicates.complaint_within_three_years_of_notice: The claimant filed the complaint within three years after the communication that could alert the claimant to the refusal to perform.

members.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance is timely when the parties have extended the performance period and the suit is filed within three years after the plaintiff receives notice that performance has been refused.
material_facts: The sale agreement stated that the balance payment was due within fourteen months, but the company’s title to the property was not clear and proceedings to resolve title continued.
The purchaser sent repeated requests for a sale deed, and the company gave assurances, including a letter shortly before the refusal that it would honour the agreement.
The courts below found that the parties had extended the time for performance and that the company refused performance on 21 August 1985.
The purchaser filed the specific-performance suit soon after the refusal.
members.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requires a suit to be filed within three years from the date fixed for performance; if no date is fixed, the period runs from when the plaintiff has notice of refusal. Where a date was originally fixed but the parties extend the time, including by conduct or forbearance, limitation runs from notice of refusal. Section 63 of the Contract Act, 1872, permits a promisee to extend the time for performance, and the extension need not be written. The Court applied S. Brahmanand v. K.R. Muthugopal, R.K. Parvatharaj Gupta v. K.C. Jayadeva Reddy and Gunwantbhai Mulchand Shah v. Anton Elis Farel; it distinguished Ramzan v. Hussaini, Tarlok Singh v. Vijay Kumar Sabharwal, T.L. Muddukrishana v. Lalitha Ramchandra Rao and Venkappa Gurappa Hosur v. Kasawwa C/o Rangappa Kulgod on their facts.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because the performance period had been extended and the suit was filed soon after the company refused performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and performance_time_extended and refusal_notified and suit_filed_within_three_years_of_refusal

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.performance_time_extended: The parties extended the time for performance, as shown by their agreement or conduct.
predicates.refusal_notified: The plaintiff received notice that the defendant refused to perform the agreement.
predicates.suit_filed_within_three_years_of_refusal: The plaintiff filed the suit within three years after receiving notice of refusal.

members.legal_issue: The partition suit was not barred by limitation.
material_facts: The trial court held that the suit was not barred by limitation.
The High Court agreed with that conclusion, and no serious argument on limitation was raised in the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court agreed with the lower courts’ limitation determination but stated no further limitation analysis, statutory provision, or earlier case on that issue.
members.conclusion: The Court affirmed the conclusion that the suit was not barred by limitation.

predicates.partition_suit_on_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a suit seeking partition and separate possession.
predicates.trial_court_found_suit_not_time_barred: The trial court found that the suit was not barred by limitation.
predicates.appellate_court_agreed: The appellate court agreed with the trial court’s conclusion on limitation.

members.legal_issue: A partition claim is not barred by limitation merely because a party alleges earlier possession or partition where the right to partition arose only after the estate became partible and the alleged earlier partition was not proved.
material_facts: The suit sought partition after the character of the land changed from impartible to partible following abolition and regrant.
The defendants alleged an earlier partition and continued possession as owners.
The appellate court disbelieved the alleged earlier partition, and the High Court held that the suit was brought after the change that gave rise to the right to partition.
members.legal_principle: The right to seek partition arose when abolition and regrant changed the land’s character from impartible to partible. The Court upheld the finding that the alleged prior partition had not been proved and that the suit was not time-barred; it cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this limitation ruling.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation, and the High Court’s conclusion was upheld.

predicates.partition_claim_after_estate_became_part: A claimant brought a proceeding for partition after the estate had become partible.
predicates.right_to_partition_arose_on_change_to_pa: The claimant’s right to seek partition arose when the estate’s character changed from impartible to partible.
predicates.alleged_earlier_partition_not_proven: The party relying on an earlier partition did not establish that it had occurred.

members.legal_issue: A special-purpose land acquisition scheme is not invalid under equality review merely because it differs from the general acquisition law, where its procedures and compensation provisions are not arbitrary or unreasonable.
material_facts: The scheme authorised acquisition for defined welfare purposes after the landowner and other interested persons were invited to show cause.
The acquiring authority was required to consider the objections before deciding whether acquisition was necessary.
Compensation was based on market value as of the acquisition notice, determined after an inquiry in which interested persons could present their claims and evidence.
A person dissatisfied with the compensation determination could appeal to a court, and a further appeal was available in qualifying cases.
The scheme provided for interest if compensation was not paid or deposited by the time possession was taken.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a statute is invalid if it is so arbitrary or unreasonable that it must be struck down. A law of one State cannot be invalidated merely by comparing it with a law on the same subject derived from another source: State of M.P. v. G.C. Mandawar and Sant Lal Bharti v. State of Punjab. A comparable statute may be considered only as an indication of what may be reasonable. The Court found the acquisition procedure substantially encapsulated the safeguards in Sections 4 to 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; the market-value standard was an adequate compensation principle under State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas. The Court also relied on Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer and Periyar and Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala in considering the compensation inquiry and appeal arrangements.
members.conclusion: The scheme's provisions were not violative of Article 14, except for the provision requiring compensation to be paid in instalments.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_purp: A person challenges the constitutionality of a statutory scheme for acquiring land for a defined public welfare purpose.
predicates.owners_receive_opportunity_to_object: The acquiring authority calls on landowners and other interested persons to explain why their land should not be acquired.
predicates.objections_are_considered_before_acquisi: The acquiring authority considers the objections before deciding whether to acquire the land.
predicates.compensation_is_based_on_market_value_af: The authority determines compensation by reference to market value after an inquiry that allows interested persons to present their claims and evidence.
predicates.dissatisfied_owners_can_seek_judicial_re: A person dissatisfied with the compensation determination can ask a court to review it.

members.legal_issue: A special state law providing for land acquisition to develop planned industrial areas and estates is not procedurally discriminatory merely because it uses a different procedure from the general acquisition law, which provides for acquisition for companies.
material_facts: The challenged law provided its own procedure for acquiring land for industrial areas, industrial estates and other purposes furthering its objectives.
Acquisition under the challenged law was by the State for public purposes, while acquisition under the general law for companies was at a company’s instance and for its benefit.
The challenged law aimed to create planned industrial areas and estates and to promote the orderly development and dispersal of industries.
members.legal_principle: A special law directed to the growth, development and organisation of industries may have its own acquisition procedure. The Court distinguished it from the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which provided for acquisition for companies: under the challenged law the State acquired land for public purposes, whereas under the general law acquisition was at a company’s instance and for its benefit. No earlier cases are relied on in the supplied judgment.
members.conclusion: The two acquisition procedures applied in dissimilar situations and circumstances, so the difference between them did not amount to procedural discrimination.

predicates.procedural_discrimination_challenge_to_l: The proceeding alleges that different procedures for acquiring land under two legal schemes are procedurally discriminatory.
predicates.special_law_targets_planned_industrial_d: One scheme is specially directed to planned industrial development and has its own acquisition procedure.
predicates.state_acquires_for_public_purpose: Under the special scheme, the State acquires land for a public purpose rather than to fulfil a company’s acquisition request.
predicates.general_procedure_serves_company_at_its_: The other scheme permits acquisition initiated by and for the benefit of a company.

members.legal_issue: A special land-acquisition scheme for a welfare purpose is not rendered unreasonable under the equality guarantee merely because its procedures differ from those of the general acquisition law, where affected owners can object and compensation is determined by reference to market value after an inquiry with an appeal available.
material_facts: The scheme required the acquiring authority to notify owners and other interested persons and consider their objections before deciding to acquire land.
Compensation was based on the land’s market value on the date of the acquisition notice, determined after an inquiry in which interested persons could present their claims and evidence.
A court appeal was available against the compensation determination, and a further appeal was available in specified cases.
The scheme differed from the general acquisition law in its procedure and review mechanisms, but its market-value date was more favorable to owners.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not permit one State’s law to be struck down merely by comparing it with another law on a similar subject; The State of Madhya Pradesh v. G.C. Mandawar and Sant Lal Bharti v. State of Punjab. A statute must be so arbitrary or unreasonable that it must be struck down. The specification of market value as the compensation basis is a sufficient guiding principle; State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas. A landowner’s opportunity to establish market value before the prescribed authority, with an appeal from the resulting award, can provide an adequate means of challenging compensation; Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer and Periyar and Pareekanni Rubbers Ltd. v. State of Kerala.
members.conclusion: The scheme’s acquisition and compensation provisions were not unreasonable or arbitrary under Article 14 on these grounds; differences from another acquisition law did not by themselves make it unconstitutional.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_a_special_we: A party challenges the constitutionality of a special land-acquisition scheme enacted for a welfare purpose.
predicates.owners_can_object_before_the_acquisition: The acquiring authority gives owners or interested persons an opportunity to object before deciding to acquire the land.
predicates.compensation_is_market_value_determined_: The authority determines compensation by assessing market value after an inquiry in which interested persons can present their claims and evidence.
predicates.compensation_determination_can_be_appeal: An affected person can appeal the compensation determination to a court.

members.legal_issue: A statutory town-planning scheme does not violate equality or property guarantees merely because land vests through the scheme and compensation is determined under a distinct procedure rather than the general land-acquisition procedure.
material_facts: The challenged scheme formed part of an urban development plan involving allocation and reconstitution of land, rather than an isolated acquisition of land for a single public purpose.
When the final scheme took effect, land required by the local authority vested in it by operation of law.
The scheme provided for reconstituted plots and financial adjustments, including compensation based on the market value of the original and reconstituted plots at the prescribed point.
The land-acquisition procedure and its appeal mechanisms were not applied to vesting under the town-planning scheme.
members.legal_principle: The Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 must be considered as an integrated urban-planning scheme, not as a series of isolated acquisitions. Sections 53, 66, 67, 71 and 73 provide for vesting, contributions, compensation and financial adjustments; the market value of land remains relevant. The distinct procedure is not discriminatory merely because the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its procedures under sections 18 and 54, does not apply. The Court applied State of Gujarat v. Shri Shantilal Mangaldas, Maneklal Chhotalal v. M.G. Makwana and The Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. G.J. Desai.
members.conclusion: The distinct town-planning procedure and compensation mechanism did not make the scheme unconstitutional or discriminatory under Articles 14 or 31 of the Constitution.

rule.if: town_planning_scheme_challenge and integrated_urban_plan and statutory_reconstitution_and_adjustment and market_value_remains_relevant

predicates.town_planning_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a statutory town-planning scheme.
predicates.integrated_urban_plan: The local authority uses the scheme as part of an integrated plan for orderly urban development.
predicates.statutory_reconstitution_and_adjustment: The scheme provides for reconstituted plots or financial adjustments when land is taken or rights are altered.
predicates.market_value_remains_relevant: The compensation or adjustment mechanism takes the market value of the affected land into account.

members.legal_issue: A statutory town-improvement acquisition scheme may use a distinct compensation and review process, including making the tribunal’s award final, without violating the guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The land was acquired under a statutory scheme for town improvement, which required the trust to frame a scheme before proceeding with acquisition.
The statute adopted the general compensation principles of the land-acquisition framework with modifications and supplemental principles suited to town-improvement acquisitions.

A tribunal with a president qualified for appointment as a High Court judge and two assessors heard compensation references, and its award was made final without the statutory appeal available in ordinary land-acquisition proceedings.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14’s rule that a reasonable classification is permissible when it has a rational relation to the object of the law. It relied on the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, particularly sections 59(a) and 59(d), and the Act’s adoption, with modifications, of compensation principles under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including the supplemental principles in paragraph 10 of the Schedule. The Court reasoned that the scheme-based process and its different character justified the classification, and that a right of appeal is statutory rather than a fundamental right. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The distinct statutory process had a rational basis connected to the object of town improvement, and the absence of a further appeal did not violate the guarantee of equality or a fundamental right. The challenged provision was valid.

rule.if: town_improvement_acquisition_case and scheme_precedes_acquisition_notice and compensation_framework_adopts_general_acquisition_principles and specialized_tribunal_hears_compensation_reference and tribunal_award_is_final

predicates.town_improvement_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns land acquired through a statutory process directed to improving towns.
predicates.scheme_precedes_acquisition_notice: The acquiring body must frame a development scheme before publishing the acquisition notice.
predicates.compensation_framework_adopts_general_ac: The statutory process uses general land-compensation principles, with modifications or additions suited to its purpose.
predicates.specialized_tribunal_hears_compensation_: A specialized tribunal hears the landowner’s reference concerning compensation.
predicates.tribunal_award_is_final: The tribunal’s award is final and no further statutory appeal is available.
predicates.distinct_compensation_and_review_process: The distinct compensation and review process does not violate the guarantee of equality.

members.legal_issue: A uniform income-capitalization method for valuing acquired land in municipal areas, distinct from the valuation method for rural land, does not deny equal protection merely because owners of municipal land cannot use every valuation method available under the general land-acquisition regime.
material_facts: The challenged provisions applied one valuation method to land in municipal areas, while a different method applied to rural land.

The municipal-area method calculated the acquisition amount by reference to income derived from the land, including a prescribed deduction for expenses and a method for valuing land that had been vacant or unrented.
The distinction applied uniformly to all land in each category, and municipal land had greater potentialities than rural land.
Capitalization was a recognized method of valuation, and the Court found no adequate material establishing hostile discrimination or that the resulting amount was illusory.
members.legal_principle: Legislation is presumed constitutional, and a challenger must provide adequate material to displace that presumption. Article 14 does not require that every recognized method of determining market value be available in every land category. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Shri Shantilal Mangaldas, Prakash Amichand Shah v. State of Gujarat, Raja Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Union of India v. Shanti Devi, Special Land Acquisition Officer, Davangere v. P. Veerabhadrappa, and Oriental Gas Co. Ltd. v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The challenged valuation provisions did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A party challenges the constitutionality of provisions governing valuation of land acquired by the state.
predicates.municipal_land_is_valued_by_a_uniform_in: The same income-based valuation method is applied to all acquired land in municipal areas.
predicates.municipal_and_rural_land_have_different_: The land in municipal areas has potentialities different from those of land in rural areas.
predicates.capitalization_is_a_recognized_valuation: The method used to value the acquired land is a recognized method of property valuation.
predicates.challenger_lacks_adequate_evidence_of_ho: The challenger does not provide adequate material showing that the valuation scheme discriminates hostilely against the affected landowners.

members.legal_issue: The compensation framework for acquiring property that was previously requisitioned does not violate equality merely because it omits separate awards of solatium and interest available under the general land acquisition law.
material_facts: The property had first been requisitioned, and compensation was payable for the owner’s loss of possession and enjoyment during requisition.

The later acquisition concerned the remaining ownership rights, and the governing framework valued the property by the price it would have fetched in the open market on the acquisition date, assuming it remained in its condition at requisition.
The acquiring authority was required to determine just compensation with regard to the circumstances of the case and the statutory compensation principles.
The owners argued that the absence of separate solatium and interest, unlike under the Land Acquisition Act, amounted to discrimination.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require identical compensation regimes where the acquisitions differ materially. Under Sections 7(3) and 8(1), 8(2) and 8(3)(a) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, an arbitrator determines just compensation in light of the case’s circumstances and the prescribed open-market valuation. Requisition compensation accounts for the earlier loss of possession and enjoyment, so a subsequent acquisition is not equivalent to acquisition of the entire ownership interest under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court distinguished Vajravelu Mudaliar, Balammal, Nagpur Improvement Trust and State of Kerala v. T.M. Peter, and relied on the reasoning in Union of India v. Kamlabhai Harjiwandas Parekh and Prakash Amichand Shah; it also distinguished P.C. Goswami because the Assam statute there permitted application of the Land Acquisition Act. Sections 23 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act do not apply simply by comparison, and solatium is not mandatory in every acquisition.
members.conclusion: The omission of separate solatium and interest under the compensation framework does not make it discriminatory or violative of Article 14. The compensation must be determined under the governing Act; the general land acquisition provisions cannot be imported merely because they provide those additional amounts.

rule.if: acquisition_after_prior_requisition and requisition_compensation_paid_for_possession_and_enjoyment and acquisition_covers_remaining_ownership_rights and compensation_uses_open_market_value and proceeding_challenges_compensation_equality

predicates.acquisition_after_prior_requisition: The property was requisitioned before it was acquired.
predicates.requisition_compensation_paid_for_posses: Compensation was payable for the owner’s loss of possession and enjoyment during requisition.
predicates.acquisition_covers_remaining_ownership_r: The later acquisition concerned ownership rights remaining after the earlier requisition.
predicates.compensation_uses_open_market_value: The compensation framework values the property by its open-market price at acquisition, assessed on the prescribed basis.
predicates.proceeding_challenges_compensation_equal: The proceeding challenges the compensation framework as unequal because it differs from another acquisition regime.

members.legal_issue: A town-planning acquisition does not deny equal protection merely because its compensation method differs from the method used for a separate government acquisition, where the local authority has no choice between methods for the town-planning acquisition.
material_facts: The town-planning legislation prescribed the method for determining compensation for land subject to a town-planning scheme.

A separate acquisition procedure was available for land acquired by the State Government, but the local authority had no option to use that procedure instead of the town-planning legislation for scheme land.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 is not infringed by different compensation procedures where the local authority is required to use the procedure prescribed for town-planning acquisitions and has no arbitrary choice between alternative methods for the same acquisition. The Court distinguished P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, where the State could choose between acquisition procedures without legislative guidance, and applied Taylor v. Taylor.
members.conclusion: The compensation provisions did not violate the guarantee of equality before the law or equal protection of the laws.

predicates.town_planning_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns an acquisition carried out through a town-planning scheme.
predicates.local_authority_has_mandatory_procedure: The local authority is required to use the procedure prescribed for acquisitions under the scheme.
predicates.no_arbitrary_choice_between_methods: The local authority cannot choose among alternative methods for carrying out the same scheme acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A statutory scheme does not create an arbitrary choice between acquisition regimes merely because it incorporates provisions of another redevelopment law.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that the Improvement Trust could choose between the challenged Act and the Punjab Town Improvement Act, with different compensation consequences.

The challenged Act allowed a scheme to provide for matters listed in section 28 of the Punjab Town Improvement Act and treated schemes already framed under that Act as schemes under the challenged Act.
The Court found that these provisions did not give the Trust a choice to acquire property under either law.
members.legal_principle: The Court read section 3 of the Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, as incorporating specified matters from section 28 of the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, and deeming existing schemes under the latter to have been framed under the former. That arrangement did not establish an option to select either law. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The Act gave no arbitrary discretion to choose between the two acquisition regimes; the Article 14 challenge on this ground failed.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenges the validity of a statutory property-acquisition scheme.
predicates.other_law_provisions_are_incorporated_fo: The governing framework uses provisions of another law to identify matters that a scheme may address.
predicates.existing_schemes_under_other_law_are_tre: Schemes already made under another framework are treated as schemes under the governing framework.
predicates.no_choice_between_acquisition_regimes: The acquiring authority is not given an option to acquire the same property under either of two regimes.

members.legal_issue: Providing a special acquisition procedure for town-planning schemes does not create unconstitutional arbitrary choice merely because another acquisition law could theoretically be used.
material_facts: The Town Planning Act provided a specific acquisition mechanism for land required to implement its schemes.
The legislation expressly modified the application of the ordinary acquisition law for those acquisitions.
In one appeal, the authorities used the ordinary acquisition law only after the special mechanism had been invalidated and was unavailable.
The argument that authorities could choose between the two procedures rested on that example and on the theoretical possibility of using either law.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a fanciful possibility of discriminatory choice is insufficient; the real risk of discrimination must be considered in light of normal administrative conduct. Maganlal v. Municipal Corporation was relied on for that approach. Sections 32 and 34 of the Town Planning Act establish a special acquisition and compensation mechanism, with specified modifications to the ordinary acquisition law.
members.conclusion: The court rejected the claim of arbitrary choice: acquisition for a town-planning scheme was to proceed through the special statutory mechanism, and the isolated use of the ordinary law after the special mechanism had been invalidated did not establish a real choice between procedures.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law: An affected person challenges the constitutionality of a law governing town-planning schemes.
predicates.land_is_required_for_a_town_planning_sch: The land is needed to implement a scheme governed by the special planning law.
predicates.the_special_law_provides_an_acquisition_: The planning law provides a specific procedure for acquiring land needed for its schemes.
predicates.ordinary_law_was_used_only_after_the_spe: The authorities used the ordinary acquisition procedure only after the special procedure had been invalidated or otherwise could not be used.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking eviction of a tenant from property related to a waqf is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the civil court when the Act does not require the Waqf Tribunal to determine the eviction dispute.
material_facts: The committee brought an eviction suit against a tenant concerning property described as waqf property.
The tenant denied that the property was waqf property and challenged the Waqf Tribunal’s jurisdiction.
The Tribunal initially directed that the plaint be returned to the civil court, then recalled that order because an issue had been framed about whether the property was waqf property.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6 and 7 of the Waqf Act, 1995 confer Tribunal jurisdiction over specified disputes, including whether property specified in a list of auqaf is waqf property and whether a listed waqf is Shia or Sunni. Sections 83 and 85 do not exclude civil-court jurisdiction for every dispute related to waqf property: under Section 85, jurisdiction is excluded only for matters that the Act requires the Tribunal to determine, and Section 83 does not extend that exclusion. An eviction suit concerning a tenant’s occupation of waqf property is not among the matters assigned to the Tribunal by Sections 6 and 7. The Court followed Ramesh Gobindram (Dead) through LRs v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf, (2010) 8 SCC 726, and held that Bhanwar Lal v. Rajasthan Board of Muslim Wakf, 2013 (11) SCALE 210, was consistent with it; it also noted Board of Wakf, West Bengal v. Anis Fatma Begum, (2010) 14 SCC 588, and Sardar Khan v. Syed Nazmul Hasan, (2007) 10 SCC 727.
members.conclusion: The eviction suit is exclusively triable by the civil court; the Tribunal’s recalled order and the High Court’s decision were set aside, and the order returning the plaint to the civil court was restored.

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A claimant seeks to evict a person alleged to be a tenant from property.
predicates.waqf_related_property: The property in the eviction dispute is described or treated as waqf property.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking possession from a lessee of waqf property is not within the Tribunal’s jurisdiction under the pre-amendment statutory scheme where that scheme did not assign eviction disputes to it.
material_facts: The Board sought possession and an injunction against a person who had occupied the property as its lessee.
The Board claimed that the lease had ended and that the occupant had not returned possession.
The suit was filed before the statutory amendment expressly adding eviction and lessor-lessee disputes to the Tribunal’s jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 83 and 85 of the Wakf Act, 1995, as they stood before the 2013 amendment, civil-court jurisdiction was excluded only for matters required by the Act to be determined by the Tribunal. The Act then provided no Tribunal proceeding for eviction of a tenant or determination of the lessor’s and lessee’s rights and obligations. The Court applied Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf and Faseela M. v. Munnerul Islam Madrasa Committee; it also noted that the 2013 amendment expressly added eviction and lessor-lessee disputes, but did not govern these suits.
members.conclusion: The possession suit was triable by the civil court, and the High Court correctly directed that the plaint be returned for presentation there.

predicates.waqf_suit_seeking_possession_from_lessee: A suit concerning waqf property seeks possession from a person who occupied it as a lessee.
predicates.claim_is_eviction_or_lessor_lessee_dispu: The claim depends on ending the lease or resolving rights and obligations between lessor and lessee.
predicates.tribunal_law_at_filing_did_not_assign_ev: When the suit was filed, the applicable Tribunal jurisdiction did not include eviction or lessor-lessee disputes.

members.legal_issue: The Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes about whether listed property is wakf property and whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni, but that exclusion does not extend to other disputes merely because they concern wakf property.
material_facts: The properties in the eviction suits were admitted to be wakf properties.
The disputes concerned eviction of tenants, not whether the properties were wakf property or whether the wakf was Shia or Sunni.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6(1), 6(5) and 7 of the Wakf Act, 1995 assign the Tribunal disputes about whether listed property is wakf property and whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni, and bar civil proceedings concerning those questions. The exclusion is limited to those specified questions. The Court relied on Board of Muslim Wakfs Rajasthan v. Radha Kishan and Punjab Wakf Board v. Gram Panchayat Alias Gram Sabha in discussing the scope of Section 6.
members.conclusion: The statutory exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction under Sections 6 and 7 is confined to the questions those provisions specify and does not cover tenant-eviction disputes.

predicates.proceeding_is_wakf_status_or_sect_disput: The proceeding concerns whether property listed as wakf property is wakf property or whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni.

members.legal_issue: Civil-court jurisdiction is excluded for a dispute relating to a wakf only when the governing statutory scheme requires the Tribunal to determine that dispute.
material_facts: The eviction suits concerned property admitted to be wakf property.
The Act did not provide for Tribunal proceedings to determine the eviction dispute or the lessor-lessee rights and obligations at issue.
members.legal_principle: Section 85 of the Wakf Act, 1995 bars civil proceedings in respect of matters relating to a wakf or wakf property that are required by or under the Act to be determined by a Tribunal. The general presumption is that civil courts have jurisdiction over civil disputes and that its exclusion is not readily inferred; the party asserting exclusion bears the onus. The Court relied on Rajasthan SRTC v. Bal Mukund Bairwa, Pabbojan Tea Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner, Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya v. Anil Panjwani, Dhulabhai v. State of M.P., Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, State of A.P. v. Manjeti Laxmi Kantha Rao, Dhruv Green Field Ltd. v. Hukam Singh, Dwarka Prasad Agarwal v. Ramesh Chandra Agarwala, and State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam.
members.conclusion: Section 85 excludes civil-court jurisdiction only for matters the Act requires the Tribunal to determine; it does not exclude jurisdiction over the eviction suits.

predicates.proceeding_is_civil_suit_about_wakf_matt: A party has brought a civil suit concerning a wakf, wakf property, or another related matter.
predicates.matter_assigned_to_tribunal: The governing statutory scheme requires the Tribunal to determine the matter in dispute.

members.legal_issue: The provision establishing the Tribunal does not itself exclude civil-court jurisdiction over a tenant-eviction dispute concerning wakf property.
material_facts: The Wakf Board brought suits before the Tribunal seeking eviction of tenants from properties admitted to be wakf properties.
The Act contained no Tribunal procedure for determining eviction of tenants from wakf property or the rights and obligations of its lessor and lessees.
The Tribunal decreed the eviction suits, and the High Court upheld those orders.
members.legal_principle: Section 83 of the Wakf Act, 1995 concerns the constitution, procedure, and powers of Tribunals and does not independently oust civil-court jurisdiction. Read with Sections 6, 7, and 85, the Tribunal may decide only matters assigned to it by the Act or rules. Since no such assignment covered tenant eviction or lessor-lessee rights, the civil court retained jurisdiction. The Court affirmed the approach of the Allahabad, Karnataka, Madras, and Bombay High Courts and rejected the contrary approach of the Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, and Punjab and Haryana High Courts.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to decide the eviction suits; the suits could be brought only in a competent civil court, and the Tribunal and High Court orders were set aside.

predicates.proceeding_is_tenant_eviction_suit: A wakf landlord brings a suit seeking to evict a tenant occupying wakf property.
predicates.property_is_admitted_wakf_property: The parties do not dispute that the property from which eviction is sought is wakf property.
predicates.act_provides_no_tribunal_eviction_procee: The governing statutory scheme provides no Tribunal proceeding to determine the eviction dispute or the lessor-lessee rights and obligations at issue.

members.legal_issue: A Waqf Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide whether disputed property is Waqf property, while the civil court's jurisdiction over that question is barred.
material_facts: The plaintiff, who was the mosque's Mutawali, alleged that the disputed land formed part of the mosque's Waqf property.
The defendants denied that the land was Waqf property and claimed it was privately owned.

The plaintiff brought the suit before the Waqf Tribunal, which decided that the land was Waqf property; the High Court set aside the Tribunal's order on the ground that the dispute belonged before a civil court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 83 of the Waqf Act, 1995, the Tribunal may determine disputes, questions, or other matters relating to a Waqf or Waqf property. Section 85 bars civil-court proceedings concerning matters required by or under the Act to be determined by the Tribunal. Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Hamayun Mirza Waqf, (2010) 8 SCC 726, and Bhanwar Lal v. Rajasthan Board of Muslim Wakf, (2014) 16 SCC 51, support the rule that whether property is Waqf property is for the Tribunal to decide.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide whether the disputed land was Waqf property, and the High Court erred in holding otherwise. The Supreme Court did not decide the merits of the Tribunal's finding on the land's status; it remanded the revision for decision on the merits.

predicates.wakf_property_status_suit: The proceeding is a suit before the specialized tribunal concerning property claimed to be associated with a religious endowment.
predicates.status_of_property_is_disputed: One side claims that the property is part of the endowment, while the opposing side denies that claim.
predicates.tribunal_has_jurisdiction_to_decide_wakf: The specialized tribunal has jurisdiction to decide whether the disputed property is part of the endowment.

members.legal_issue: A dispute over whether property claimed as waqf property is waqf property must be determined by the Waqf Tribunal when that question falls within the Tribunal’s statutory jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Board sued for an injunction concerning land it claimed was waqf property.
The respondent denied that the land was waqf property and challenged the Board’s title.
The suit was transferred to the Tribunal, which rejected the respondent’s challenge to its jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 6(1), 7(1), 83 and 85 of the Wakf Act, 1995, a question whether listed property is waqf property is for the Tribunal, and the civil-court bar applies to matters the Act requires the Tribunal to decide. The explanation to Section 6(1) includes a person interested in the property even if not interested in the waqf, subject to the notice requirement. The Court applied Haryana Wakf Board v. Mahesh Kumar and distinguished the earlier interpretation in Board of Muslim Wakfs, Rajasthan v. Radha Kishan in light of the later statutory explanation.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide whether the land was waqf property, and the civil court’s jurisdiction was barred for that issue; the High Court erred in holding otherwise.

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_claimed_waqf_prope: A civil suit concerns property that one side claims is waqf property.
predicates.defendant_denies_waqf_status: The opposing party asserts that the property is not waqf property.
predicates.status_question_within_tribunal_authorit: The governing waqf framework assigns the disputed question of the property’s waqf status to the Tribunal.

members.legal_issue: A Wakf Tribunal may determine whether disputed premises are Wakf property when that status dispute turns on whether the premises fall within the extent of property identified in the notified Wakf record.
material_facts: The claim sought eviction from premises said to be Wakf property and recovery of an additional portion alleged to have been encroached upon.
The respondent denied that either portion was Wakf property and disputed the notification identifying the extent of the Wakf property.
The Tribunal framed and decided whether the premises formed part of the notified Wakf property, relying on the evidence presented.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6 and 7 of the Wakf Act, 1995 assign to the Tribunal disputes about whether property specified as Wakf property is Wakf property; Section 85 bars civil-court jurisdiction over matters required to be determined under the Act. Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf (2010) 8 SCC 726 concerned eviction from property admitted to be Wakf property and did not govern this dispute about the notified property’s extent. Board of Wakf, West Bengal v. Anis Fatma Begum (2010) 14 SCC 588, Haryana Wakf Board v. Mahesh Kumar (2014) 16 SCC 45, and Punjab Wakf Board v. Sham Singh Harike (2019) 4 SCC 698 support determining whether the Act requires the dispute to be decided by the Tribunal. Faseela M. v. Munnerul Islam Madrasa Committee (2014) 16 SCC 38 was distinguished, and Kiran Devi v. Bihar State Sunni Wakf Board (2021) SCC Online SC 280 confirms that jurisdiction depends on the facts and the statutory framework.
members.conclusion: The suit was maintainable before the Wakf Tribunal, which had jurisdiction to determine whether the disputed premises formed part of the Wakf property.

predicates.waqf_tribunal_possession_suit: A party brought a suit before a Wakf Tribunal seeking possession of premises claimed to belong to a Wakf institution.
predicates.defendant_disputes_waqf_status: The opposing party denied that the premises were Wakf property.
predicates.dispute_concerns_notified_property_exten: The dispute concerned whether the premises fell within the extent of property identified in the notified Wakf record.

members.legal_issue: The Wakf Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes about whether property specified in a published wakf list is wakf property and whether a listed wakf is Shia or Sunni, subject to the saving for earlier pending civil proceedings.
material_facts: The suit raised questions about whether the disputed property was wakf property, although the respondents asserted that its wakf status was not disputed.
The Court considered the statutory scheme governing published lists of wakfs and the Tribunal’s authority to determine disputes about entries in those lists.
The suit had been instituted before the relevant Act commenced, so the statutory saving applied to this case.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6(1), 6(5), 7(1), 7(5), and 85 of the Rajasthan Wakf Act, 1995 assign the specified questions about listed property and the sect of a listed wakf to the Tribunal and bar civil-court proceedings on those questions, while preserving certain proceedings already pending in civil court. Sardar Khan v. Syed Nazmul Hasan (Seth) and Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf support this limited, question-specific allocation of jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: For a proceeding not saved as an earlier pending civil suit, the Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to decide the specified list-related questions; the civil court cannot decide them.

rule.if: wakf_related_proceeding and listed_property_status_question and not preexisting_civil_suit

predicates.wakf_related_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a wakf or property claimed to be wakf property.
predicates.listed_property_status_question: The dispute asks whether property specified in a published wakf list is wakf property or whether a listed wakf belongs to one of the two specified sects.
predicates.preexisting_civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil-court suit instituted before the relevant enactment commenced and saved as an earlier pending suit.

members.legal_issue: A Waqf Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide a dispute about the validity of a sale alleged to involve Waqf property, including whether the sale is void for lack of the required prior sanction.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that the disputed land was part of the mosque's Waqf property and that an individual unconnected with the Waqf had sold it to the defendants.
The plaintiff alleged that the sale was void and sought relief concerning the defendants' possession and the sale.
The defendants denied that the land was Waqf property and disputed the Tribunal's jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Section 51 of the Waqf Act, 1995, provides that a gift, sale, exchange, or mortgage of immovable Waqf property is void unless effected with the Board's prior sanction. Section 52 concerns recovery of Waqf property alienated contrary to Section 51 or Section 56, and Section 83 empowers the Tribunal to determine disputes relating to Waqf property. Section 85 bars civil-court proceedings concerning matters required by or under the Act to be determined by the Tribunal. The Tribunal therefore has jurisdiction over disputes concerning such alienations.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the dispute concerning the alleged sale. The Supreme Court did not decide whether the land was Waqf property or whether the sale was in fact void; it remanded the matter for the High Court to decide the revision on the merits.

predicates.wakf_property_sale_dispute: The proceeding is a dispute before the specialized tribunal about a sale alleged to concern property of a religious endowment.
predicates.sale_validity_turns_on_wakf_status_or_re: Whether the sale is valid depends on whether the property belongs to the endowment or whether the required prior sanction was obtained.
predicates.tribunal_has_jurisdiction_to_decide_wakf: The specialized tribunal has jurisdiction to decide the dispute about the sale's validity.

members.legal_issue: A civil court cannot hear an injunction suit concerning a waqf or waqf property when the dispute falls within the jurisdiction of the Waqf Tribunal.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued for mandatory and permanent injunctions concerning land admitted by the defendant to be waqf property.
The defendant sought rejection of the plaint on the ground that the dispute belonged before the Waqf Tribunal.
The defendant admitted the waqf and its mutawalli but denied that the plaintiff was a beneficiary, raising a dispute about the plaintiff’s relationship to the waqf.
members.legal_principle: Sections 83(1) and 85 of the Waqf Act, 1995 give the Tribunal jurisdiction over any dispute, question or other matter relating to a waqf or waqf property and bar civil-court proceedings within that field; the jurisdiction does not depend on whether the property’s status as waqf property is disputed or admitted. Section 83(5) gives the Tribunal the powers of a civil court under the CPC. The court relied on W.B. Waqf Board v. Anis Fatma Begum and Akkode Jumayath Palli Paripalana Committee, which support Tribunal jurisdiction over injunction disputes, and on Syed Mohideen for the Tribunal’s power to issue temporary injunctions. It explained that the basis of Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Waqf was removed by the 2013 amendment and that its narrower approach could not control; it also considered the treatment of the issue in Punjab Waqf Board v. Sham Singh Harike and Kiran Devi v. Bihar State Sunni Waqf Board. The statutory scheme recognizes limited civil-court proceedings in provisions including Sections 68(6), 86 and 90, but none applied to this injunction suit.
members.conclusion: The Waqf Tribunal had jurisdiction over the dispute, and the civil court could not entertain the injunction suit. The appeal was allowed, and the plaint was to be returned for presentation to the Tribunal.

predicates.civil_court_injunction_suit: A claimant brought an injunction suit in a civil court.
predicates.dispute_concerns_waqf_or_waqf_property: The parties’ dispute concerns a waqf or property associated with a waqf.

members.legal_issue: Disputes seeking removal of wakf trustees or rendition of accounts fall within the Wakf Tribunal’s jurisdiction, subject to the saving for earlier pending civil suits.
material_facts: The suit included claims for removal of trustees and rendition of accounts.
The Court stated that those claims would fall within the Tribunal’s domain, while separately holding that this suit remained in civil court because it had been instituted before the Act commenced.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 85 of the Rajasthan Wakf Act, 1995 govern the Tribunal’s jurisdiction over matters assigned to it by the Act and the corresponding exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction. Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf explains that the Tribunal’s jurisdiction is confined to matters provided for under the Act; the saving for earlier pending suits under Section 7(5) preserves civil-court jurisdiction over such proceedings.
members.conclusion: Claims for removal of trustees and rendition of accounts are for the Tribunal when they arise in a proceeding not saved as an earlier pending civil suit.

rule.if: wakf_related_proceeding and trustee_removal_or_accounts_claim and not preexisting_civil_suit

predicates.wakf_related_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a wakf or property claimed to be wakf property.
predicates.trustee_removal_or_accounts_claim: The claim seeks removal of a wakf trustee or rendition of accounts relating to the wakf.
predicates.preexisting_civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil-court suit instituted before the relevant enactment commenced and saved as an earlier pending suit.

members.legal_issue: Disputes relating to wakf property within the special statutory regime must be brought before the Wakf Tribunal in the first instance rather than directly before a civil court or the High Court.
material_facts: The dispute concerned property constituted as a wakf estate and questions about its division under the wakf deed and the application of the statutory regime to a portion of that property.
The proceeding was commenced after the statutory regime came into force.
The dispute was not an eviction dispute.
members.legal_principle: Section 83(1) of the Wakf Act, 1995 gives the Tribunal jurisdiction to determine any dispute, question or other matter relating to a wakf or wakf property, and section 84 supports that broad jurisdiction. Section 83(9) provides for recourse to the High Court after the Tribunal's decision. Section 83(5) gives the Tribunal civil-court powers, including powers to grant and enforce temporary injunctions. The Court applied the principle that a special statutory forum displaces recourse to the general forum, relying on Justice G.P. Singh's Principles of Statutory Interpretation and Chief Engineer, Hydel Project v. Ravinder Nath. It distinguished Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakf because that case concerned eviction proceedings.
members.conclusion: The Wakf Tribunal had jurisdiction in the first instance, and the parties could not bring this dispute directly before the civil court or the High Court; the High Court judgment was set aside.

rule.if: wakf_related_proceeding and property_is_wakf_property and special_forum_regime_applies and not eviction_dispute

predicates.wakf_related_proceeding: A party brings a proceeding to resolve a dispute, question or other matter relating to a wakf or wakf property.
predicates.property_is_wakf_property: The property involved in the dispute is treated as wakf property.
predicates.special_forum_regime_applies: The proceeding falls within the operation of the special statutory regime that assigns such matters to a Tribunal.
predicates.eviction_dispute: The proceeding concerns eviction from property.
predicates.wakf_tribunal_is_first_instance_forum: The Wakf Tribunal is the forum that must be approached first to determine the dispute.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on enforcing rights in benami property does not bar a recovery suit filed before the prohibition took effect, even if the suit remained pending when it took effect.
material_facts: The claimant filed her suit for a declaration of ownership and related relief on 30 September 1987, before the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 came into force on 5 September 1988.
The suit was pending when the Act came into force.
The trial court dismissed the suit on the basis of Mithilesh Kumari, but the first appellate court later applied R. Rajagopal Reddy, which had overruled that decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) bars the filing or entertaining of a suit, claim, or action to enforce a real owner's right in benami property after the provision takes effect; it does not make a pending suit abate. The Act creates substantive rights and liabilities and is prospective, not retrospective. The Court applied R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, which overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by Section 4 of the Act because it had been filed before the Act came into force; the High Court erred in disregarding the binding decision in R. Rajagopal Reddy.

predicates.real_owner_benami_recovery_suit: A person claiming to be the real owner brings a suit to enforce rights in property held in another person's name.
predicates.suit_filed_before_prohibition_took_effec: The claimant filed the suit before the prohibition on enforcing rights in benami property took effect.
predicates.suit_pending_when_prohibition_took_effec: The suit remained unresolved when the prohibition took effect.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on benami recovery claims does not extinguish a suit instituted before the prohibition took effect, even if that suit remains pending when the prohibition takes effect.
material_facts: The proceedings included suits brought before the relevant prohibition took effect by persons claiming to be the real owners of property held in another person's name.
Some of those suits remained pending at different stages of appeal or revision when the prohibition took effect.
Before the statutory changes, the law recognized a real owner's right to seek recovery of property held benami, including under Section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 7 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 do not expressly terminate pending suits, and the words “no suit ... shall lie” bar suits filed after the provision takes effect rather than suits already instituted. Section 7 repealed Section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, but Section 6(b), (c) and (e) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 preserves accrued rights and permits pending proceedings and remedies to continue unless a different intention appears. A provision affecting substantive rights is not retrospective absent clear language or necessary implication. The Court relied on Garikapati v. N. Sibbiah Choudhary and the interpretive rule stated in Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, and rejected the contrary view in Mithilesh Kumari.
members.conclusion: The prohibition does not apply to suits instituted before it took effect; those pending proceedings may continue, and the earlier contrary ruling in Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare was incorrect on this point.

predicates.benami_recovery_suit: A person claiming to be the real owner brought a suit to enforce a right in property held in another person's name.
predicates.filed_before_recovery_bar: The claimant instituted the suit before the statutory bar on bringing such recovery claims took effect.
predicates.pending_when_bar_began: The suit had not been finally disposed of when the statutory bar took effect.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on enforcing rights in property held benami does not bar a suit instituted before that prohibition applies.
material_facts: The suit sought a declaration of ownership based on the claim that the conveyance in another person's name was security for a loan rather than a transfer of beneficial ownership.
The suit was instituted before the relevant prohibition came into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 is not retrospective and does not bar suits instituted before it came into force. The Court applied R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, (1995) 2 SCC 630, which overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare, (1989) 2 SCC 95, on retrospectivity.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, although that conclusion did not determine whether the claimant had proved the merits of the suit.

predicates.benami_ownership_suit: The claimant brought a suit asserting beneficial ownership of property conveyed in another person's name.
predicates.suit_filed_before_claim_prohibition_appl: The claimant instituted the suit before the restriction on enforcing such claims applied.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on benami recovery claims applies to a suit brought after the prohibition takes effect even when the asserted benami transaction occurred earlier.
material_facts: The Act addressed property held benami without limiting its reach to transactions made after the Act took effect.
The Court considered the example of a real owner bringing a suit after the prohibition took effect to recover property bought benami before that time.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 prohibits a real owner from bringing a suit, claim or action to enforce a right in property held benami. Although the Act is not retrospective as to suits already instituted, Section 4(1) reaches past benami transactions when a suit to enforce the asserted right is brought after the provision takes effect. The words “no suit ... shall lie” prevent such a later suit from being filed or entertained.
members.conclusion: A suit brought after the prohibition takes effect to enforce a right arising from a past benami transaction is barred.

predicates.benami_recovery_suit: A person claiming to be the real owner brought a suit to enforce a right in property held in another person's name.
predicates.transaction_predates_recovery_bar: The alleged benami transaction occurred before the statutory bar on bringing recovery claims took effect.
predicates.filed_after_recovery_bar: The claimant instituted the suit after the statutory bar took effect.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on benami pleas does not prevent adjudication of a plea raised before the relevant commencement date in a proceeding that was already pending on that date.
material_facts: The possession suit was filed before the relevant provisions of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act came into force.
The defendants raised their benami defence before those provisions came into force.
The suit remained pending on the relevant commencement date.
members.legal_principle: Under R. Rajagopala Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, Sections 4(1) and 4(2) do not shut out a benami plea already raised before 19 May 1988 in a proceeding pending on that date. Those provisions bar later pleas to the extent explained in that decision, but do not retrospectively extinguish a plea already raised in a pending proceeding. The Court also relied on Heirs of Vrajlal Ganatra v. Heirs of Parshottam S. Shah and Sankana Hali & Sankana Institute v. Kishori Lal Goenka, and noted that R. Rajagopala Reddy overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare.
members.conclusion: The Act did not preclude the court from deciding the benami defence because it had been raised before the relevant commencement date in a proceeding then pending.

predicates.is_benami_proceeding: The proceeding involves a claim or defence that property held in one person’s name is beneficially owned by another.
predicates.proceeding_pending_at_relevant_commencem: The proceeding was still pending when the relevant prohibition on benami pleas came into force.
predicates.benami_plea_raised_before_relevant_comme: A party raised the benami claim or defence before that prohibition came into force.

members.legal_issue: A defence asserting that property was held benami is not barred in a suit when both the suit and the defence were filed before the statutory prohibition came into force.
material_facts: The property transaction predated the statutory prohibition.
The suit was filed before the prohibition came into force.
The defendant raised the benami defence in a written statement filed before the prohibition came into force, although the trial judgment was delivered afterward.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(2) of the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not operate retrospectively to bar a benami defence already raised before the Act came into force. R. Rajagopal Reddy (Dead) by LRs. v. Padmini Chandrasekharan (Dead) by LRs. held that the Act is prospective, with limited operation in pending suits where the defence had not already been raised; it overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare and was approved in Prabodh Chandra Ghosh v. Urmila Dassi and C. Gangacharan v. C. Narayanan.
members.conclusion: The defendant was entitled to raise and prove the benami defence; the later delivery of the trial judgment did not make the statutory bar applicable to that defence.

predicates.benami_property_dispute: The proceeding is a property dispute in which a party claims that the person named on the title held the property benami.
predicates.suit_filed_before_prohibition: The suit was filed before the statutory prohibition on benami claims came into force.
predicates.benami_defence_raised_before_prohibition: The defendant raised the benami defence before the statutory prohibition came into force.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on benami defences does not undo a defence already allowed in a pending suit before the prohibition took effect.
material_facts: The Court considered pending suits in which a real owner's benami defence had already been allowed before the prohibition took effect, so that an issue had arisen from that defence.
The statutory text barred a defence from being allowed but did not state that an already allowed defence could no longer be continued.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(2) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 bars the allowance of a benami defence after it takes effect; it does not direct that a defence already allowed be withdrawn or that an issue already arising from it be extinguished. The Court also relied on the principle that, absent a contrary legislative intention, repeal does not affect accrued rights or pending proceedings, as reflected in Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
members.conclusion: A benami defence already allowed before the prohibition took effect remains for the court to decide under the law applicable when the defence was allowed.

rule.if: pending_title_suit and real_owner_benami_defence and defence_previously_allowed and prohibition_began_later

predicates.pending_title_suit: A suit concerning title to property was pending when the statutory prohibition on benami defences took effect.
predicates.real_owner_benami_defence: A person claiming to be the real owner relied on a benami transaction as a defence in the suit.
predicates.defence_previously_allowed: The court had permitted the person to raise that defence before the statutory prohibition took effect.
predicates.prohibition_began_later: The statutory prohibition took effect after the defence had been allowed.

members.legal_issue: A benami defence not yet permitted in a pending suit cannot be raised after the prohibition on such defences takes effect.
material_facts: Section 4(2) addresses a defence based on a right in property held benami in a suit, claim or action by or on behalf of a person claiming to be the real owner.
The Court considered pending proceedings in which the stage for raising or permitting the real owner's defence had not been reached when the prohibition took effect.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(2) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 provides that no such defence shall be allowed. The provision applies when the defence is sought to be allowed after it takes effect; it does not state that a defence already allowed in a pending proceeding is to be withdrawn. The Court rejected the view in Mithilesh Kumari that the provision nullifies every benami defence at any later stage of a pending suit.
members.conclusion: In a pending suit, a benami defence that had not already been allowed cannot be allowed after the prohibition takes effect.

rule.if: pending_title_suit and real_owner_seeks_benami_defence and defence_not_previously_allowed and prohibition_in_effect

predicates.pending_title_suit: A suit concerning title to property was pending when the statutory prohibition on benami defences took effect.
predicates.real_owner_seeks_benami_defence: A person claiming to be the real owner sought to defend the suit on the basis that the property was held benami.
predicates.defence_not_previously_allowed: The court had not permitted the person to raise that benami defence before the prohibition took effect.
predicates.prohibition_in_effect: The statutory prohibition on allowing a benami defence had taken effect when permission to raise it was sought.

members.legal_issue: A person who accepts compensation without protest is not entitled to seek a reference for determination of higher compensation.
material_facts: The claimants accepted the compensation awarded for their land without protest.
They later sought a reference to obtain increased compensation.
members.legal_principle: The second proviso to Section 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, precludes a person who receives compensation without protest from seeking a reference under Section 18. The Court relied on no earlier case in stating this principle.
members.conclusion: Claimants who received compensation without protest were not entitled to seek a reference under Section 18.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a reference to determine compensation for acquired land.
predicates.compensation_accepted_without_protest: The claimant accepted the compensation offered without expressing protest.

members.legal_issue: Where compensation is fixed by agreement, a party who accepts the assessment without objection cannot later demand that the compensation dispute be referred to a tribunal.
material_facts: The proprietor accepted the final compensation assessment roll without protest and notified the compensation authority that he would not object to it.
The governing provision allowed compensation for mines and minerals to be fixed by agreement, with a tribunal reference available if no agreement was reached.
The proprietor later sought a higher rate and claimed that the compensation should be referred to a tribunal.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 25(4)(a) of the unamended Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, compensation could be fixed by agreement; under Section 25(4)(b), reference to a tribunal arose only if no agreement was reached. The Court held that acceptance of the final assessment roll without protest established agreement and foreclosed the tribunal route.
members.conclusion: The acceptance of the compensation assessment without objection constituted an agreement, and the proprietor could not require a tribunal reference for determination of the compensation.

predicates.statutory_mines_compensation_proceeding: The matter concerns statutory compensation for mines or minerals.
predicates.final_assessment_accepted_without_object: The recipient accepted the final compensation assessment without objecting to it.
predicates.tribunal_reference_requires_absence_of_a: The governing process provides for tribunal determination only when the parties have not agreed on compensation.
predicates.party_cannot_demand_tribunal_reference: The party cannot later require the compensation dispute to be determined by a tribunal.

members.legal_issue: A landholder who has accepted a consent award cannot obtain a reference to a civil court to determine compensation.
material_facts: The landholders negotiated the compensation with the acquiring authority and consent awards were made on that basis.
They received the awarded compensation in full satisfaction of their claims and agreed not to seek enhancement.
They later applied for references to a civil court, although they had not first challenged the validity of the agreements or awards.
members.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits a reference only where the interested person has not accepted the award. Under Section 11(2), an award made according to a written agreement is a consent award. State of Gujarat v. Daya Shamji Bhai and Ishwarlal Premchand Shah v. State of Gujarat hold that an agreed consent award removes the need for a Section 18 reference. An accepted agreement remains binding unless its validity is challenged and set aside in an appropriate proceeding. Assam Railways & Trading Co. Ltd. v. Collector of Lakhimpur was distinguishable because the negotiations there had not resulted in a binding agreement.
members.conclusion: The applications for reference were not maintainable because the landholders had accepted the awards; the appeals were allowed and the High Court’s orders were set aside.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_application: An interested person in a land acquisition proceeding applied for a reference to a court to determine compensation.
predicates.award_accepted_without_protest: The interested person accepted the award without protest.

members.legal_issue: A landowner who enters a binding written agreement for a consent compensation award and accepts payment under it is not entitled to seek a reference for enhanced compensation.
material_facts: The landowners agreed in writing to accept the compensation determined by the Land Acquisition Officer together with an additional amount and expressly agreed not to seek a reference.
The Land Acquisition Officer made the award in accordance with the agreement, and the landowners received the agreed payment without protest.
The landowners later sought a reference and the reference court enhanced the compensation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Collector may make an award in accordance with the written agreement of the interested persons. Section 18 permits a reference at the request of an interested person who has not accepted the award; Sections 31(2) and 18 make acceptance without protest inconsistent with that entitlement. A consent award under Section 11(2) obviates a reference under Section 18. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The landowners were not entitled to seek a reference for enhanced compensation because the consent award under the agreement foreclosed that right.

rule.if: land_acquisition_case and written_consent_terms and express_reference_waiver and payment_accepted_without_protest

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by the State.
predicates.written_consent_terms: The landowner and the acquiring authority agreed in writing on the compensation terms to be included in the award.
predicates.express_reference_waiver: The landowner expressly agreed not to seek a court reference for increased compensation.
predicates.payment_accepted_without_protest: The landowner accepted payment under the agreed award without protesting its amount.

members.legal_issue: Receipt of compensation without protest bars an application for a reference challenging the compensation award.
material_facts: The claimants received the compensation awarded for their land after signing an agreement accepting the amount, and they did not protest when they received it.

They later objected to the amount and sought a reference for enhanced compensation, claiming that they had protested orally; the High Court found that claim contradicted by the written agreement and evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 31(2) and 18(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, a person who receives compensation otherwise than under protest is not entitled to apply for a reference challenging the award. Receipt under protest is a condition precedent to an application under Section 18; the application must also meet the applicable limitation requirements and state the grounds of objection under Section 18(2). The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The reference application was not maintainable because the claimants had received compensation without protest. The Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with the High Court’s decision.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_reference_: The proceeding concerns a request to refer a dispute about compensation for acquired land for judicial determination.
predicates.compensation_received_without_protest: The claimant received the awarded compensation without protesting at the time of receipt.
predicates.later_application_to_challenge_award: After receiving the compensation, the claimant applied to challenge the award.

members.legal_issue: A landholder who has agreed to compensation under a consent award may not claim statutory compensation benefits beyond the terms of that agreement.
