material_facts: The agreements specified compensation that included solatium and additional market value.
The landholders accepted the consent awards and undertook not to seek enhancement.
The landholders later claimed further statutory benefits, including solatium and interest.
members.legal_principle: Sections 23(2), 23(1-A) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for solatium, additional amounts and interest in the circumstances specified in those provisions. Those benefits may be waived by agreement. State of Gujarat v. Daya Shamji Bhai and Ishwarlal Premchand Shah v. State of Gujarat establish that agreed compensation need not include statutory additions unless they form part of the agreement.
members.conclusion: The landholders could waive statutory benefits by agreement and could not claim benefits beyond the agreed terms of the consent awards.

predicates.consent_award_in_land_acquisition_case: The acquiring authority made an award based on an agreement with the landholder.
predicates.agreed_compensation_terms: The agreement stated the compensation payable and the benefits included in it.
predicates.claimant_accepted_award: The landholder accepted the award based on the agreement.

members.legal_issue: A landowner who accepts agreed acquisition compensation without protest under a written agreement excluding further claims cannot subsequently recover interest for the period before the agreement.
material_facts: The land was taken before compensation was determined and paid.
The landowner entered into a written agreement for compensation under the applicable agreement rules.
The agreement stated that the landowner would not claim any amount beyond the agreed compensation and would accept it without protest.
The landowner accepted the agreed compensation without protest, and it was paid on the date the agreement was signed.
The agreed compensation was a package accepted voluntarily and was higher than the compensation fixed for claimants who did not enter into such agreements.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, interested persons may agree in writing on matters to be included in the award, and the Collector may make an award on those terms. Read with Sections 23 and 34, such an agreement and an award accepted without protest are binding: the agreed compensation is treated as just compensation, including interest due up to the agreement, and a clear undertaking not to claim further amounts bars a later claim for that interest. State of Gujarat v. Daya Shamji Bhai and State of Karnataka v. Sangappa Dyavappa Biradar establish that agreed compensation accepted without protest forecloses further statutory benefits or enhancement; Shree Vijay Cotton & Oil Mills Ltd. v. State of Gujarat was distinguishable because it concerned an ordinary acquisition without an agreement. Equitable considerations did not alter the result given the voluntarily accepted package and payment when the agreement was made.
members.conclusion: The landowner could not claim additional interest for the period between the taking of possession and the agreement and payment; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_case and written_compensation_agreement and agreement_excludes_additional_claims and accepted_without_protest

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired by a public authority.
predicates.written_compensation_agreement: The landowner and the acquiring authority agreed in writing on the compensation to be included in the award.
predicates.agreement_excludes_additional_claims: The agreement states that the landowner will not claim compensation beyond the agreed amount.
predicates.accepted_without_protest: The landowner accepted the agreed compensation without protest.

members.legal_issue: A landowner who agreed to compensation cannot compel the acquiring authority to reopen the agreement solely because a later award grants higher compensation for similar land.
material_facts: The landowners entered into agreements fixing compensation for their acquired land.
They relied on a later arbitral award granting higher compensation for other land and sought a fresh agreement or reopening of the compensation settlement.
There was no finding that the agreements were vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, or a similar defect, and no express statutory right to reopen them.
members.legal_principle: An agreement fixing compensation is ordinarily binding unless vitiated, and changing it requires the parties' agreement. A substantive right to reopen a final compensation determination must be expressly provided by statute and cannot be implied; an unavailable statutory remedy cannot be achieved indirectly. The Court relied on Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama of Vedem Vasco De Gama, Bhavnagar University v. Palitana Sugar Mill, and Unique Butyle Tube Industries v. U.P. Financial Corporation for the principle that clear statutory language cannot be enlarged by implication.
members.conclusion: The landowners had no enforceable right to compel the acquiring authority to reopen their agreements on the basis of the later award.

rule.if: proceeding_to_compel_reopening_of_compensation_agreement and compensation_was_agreed and later_comparable_award_exists and no_agreement_vitiation_is_established and no_express_reopening_right_exists

predicates.proceeding_to_compel_reopening_of_compen: The claimant asked a court to require the acquiring authority to reopen an agreed compensation settlement.
predicates.compensation_was_agreed: The claimant and acquiring authority had agreed on the compensation for the property.
predicates.later_comparable_award_exists: A later award fixed higher compensation for other land said to be comparable.
predicates.no_agreement_vitiation_is_established: No fraud, misrepresentation, or other defect vitiating the agreement was established.
predicates.no_express_reopening_right_exists: The governing law did not expressly give the claimant a right to reopen the agreed determination.

members.legal_issue: A party who accepts a final compensation assessment cannot later challenge it on the ground that a required preliminary procedural step was omitted.
material_facts: The proprietor accepted the final compensation assessment roll.
He later argued that the prescribed preliminary procedure involving a draft in the required form had not been followed.
The Court held that, having accepted the final assessment, he could not raise that procedural objection.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered Rule 18(2) and the prescribed preliminary form, but held that acceptance of the final assessment prevented the proprietor from later relying on the alleged procedural omission.
members.conclusion: The challenge based on noncompliance with the preliminary procedure was rejected.

predicates.statutory_compensation_assessment_procee: The matter concerns an assessment of compensation under a statutory procedure.
predicates.final_assessment_accepted: The party accepted the final compensation assessment.
predicates.later_challenge_based_on_omitted_prelimi: The party later challenged the assessment because an earlier procedural step was allegedly omitted.
predicates.party_cannot_raise_procedural_objection: The party cannot rely on that alleged procedural omission to challenge the accepted assessment.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration recorded by a police officer may be admitted and relied on as the sole basis for conviction when it is reliable, voluntary, and made by a person fit to give a statement.
material_facts: The injured declarant gave a statement in hospital identifying the assailants and describing their actions.
A doctor certified that she was mentally fit to make a statement, and she signed it after it was recorded.
The statement was clear and consistent, and medical evidence showed that she could speak despite her injuries.
The declaration was recorded by an investigating officer rather than a Magistrate; the officer’s account was not materially shaken in cross-examination.
The trial and appellate courts found the declaration credible, and the Supreme Court found no reason to reject it.
members.legal_principle: A dying declaration can alone sustain conviction if, after careful scrutiny, the court is satisfied that it is true, voluntary, coherent, and made by a person in a fit state of mind; corroboration is a rule of prudence, not an absolute requirement. A declaration recorded by a police officer is not automatically inadmissible merely because a Magistrate did not record it. The Court relied on Munnu Raja v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Paras Yadav v. State of Bihar, Balbir Singh v. State of Punjab, State of Karnataka v. Shariff, Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar, Laxman v. State of Maharashtra, State of Rajasthan v. Wakteng, Bijoy Das v. State of West Bengal, Muthu Kutty v. State, Panneerselvam v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Paniben v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The police-recorded dying declaration was admissible and sufficiently reliable to sustain conviction without corroboration; the absence of a Magistrate’s recording did not by itself invalidate it.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and conviction_relies_on_dying_declaration and declaration_recorded_by_police and declarant_medically_fit and declaration_clear_and_consistent and declaration_voluntary and not material_infirmity

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.conviction_relies_on_dying_declaration: The conviction rests on a statement made by a person who later died.
predicates.declaration_recorded_by_police: A police officer recorded the declarant’s statement.
predicates.declarant_medically_fit: Medical evidence or certification indicated that the declarant was fit to make a statement.
predicates.declaration_clear_and_consistent: The declarant gave a coherent account that was not materially contradictory.
predicates.declaration_voluntary: The evidence supported that the declarant spoke freely and was not tutored or prompted.
predicates.material_infirmity: The declaration had a material defect, such as evidence that the declarant was unconscious or unable to make a statement.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration may sustain a conviction without corroboration if it is trustworthy, and multiple dying declarations must each be trustworthy and materially consistent.
material_facts: The deceased made one oral statement to a neighbour and another to her brother shortly before her death, identifying her mother-in-law as the person who poured kerosene on her and her husband as the person who set her on fire.
Witnesses to the statements were found credible after scrutiny, and cross-examination did not discredit their accounts.
The deceased was in a proper mental condition to make the statements, and their voluntariness was not challenged.
The statements related to the circumstances leading to the deceased’s death and were consistent in material particulars.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act makes a deceased person’s oral or written statement about the cause of death or circumstances resulting in death relevant and admissible when the cause of death is in issue, provided the declarant was mentally fit. A true and trustworthy dying declaration, free from embellishment, can by itself support a conviction without corroboration. Where there is more than one declaration, the court must assess the trustworthiness of each and whether they are consistent in material particulars. No earlier case was cited for these principles.
members.conclusion: The oral dying declarations were admissible, voluntary, trustworthy, and consistent, and the Court accepted them as reliable evidence implicating the accused persons.

rule.if: death_cause_in_issue and dying_declaration_about_death_made and declarant_mentally_fit and declaration_voluntary and declaration_witnesses_credible and (single_trustworthy_declaration or multiple_declarations_trustworthy_and_consistent)

predicates.death_cause_in_issue: The proceeding concerned the cause of the declarant’s death.
predicates.dying_declaration_about_death_made: The deceased made a statement about the cause of death or the circumstances leading to it.
predicates.declarant_mentally_fit: The deceased was in a proper mental condition when making the statement.
predicates.declaration_voluntary: The deceased made the statement voluntarily.
predicates.declaration_witnesses_credible: The witnesses who testified to the statement were found credible after careful scrutiny.
predicates.single_trustworthy_declaration: The deceased made one declaration that the court found trustworthy and free from embellishment.
predicates.multiple_declarations_trustworthy_and_co: The deceased made multiple declarations that the court found trustworthy and consistent in material particulars.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration recorded by a magistrate may be relied on despite the non-examination of the doctor who was present, and may alone support a conviction when the magistrate verified the declarant’s ability to make the statement and the declaration is reliable.
material_facts: The magistrate recorded the injured person’s statement within hours of his hospital admission and testified that he had checked the person’s consciousness and ability to make the statement by asking preliminary questions.
A doctor was present and endorsed that the injured person was conscious, but the doctor was not examined at trial.
The declaration implicated the accused and contained relevant details of the incident; the Court found no suspicious feature affecting its credibility.
The declaration did not mention the accused’s lip injury, which the injured person may not have had an opportunity to observe.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled principle that a reliable dying declaration can by itself support a conviction. Under Laxman v. State of Maharashtra, the absence of a doctor’s certification that the declarant was in a fit state of mind is not fatal where the magistrate is satisfied of that fitness; the contrary proposition in P. Rosamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh was no longer good law. Relying on State of Maharashtra v. Krishnamurti, the Court also held that omission to mention injuries to the accused does not require rejection where the declarant may not have been able to observe them.
members.conclusion: The magistrate-recorded dying declaration was reliable despite the doctor’s non-examination and could form the sole basis for a conviction.

rule.if: dying_declaration_conviction_appeal and declaration_recorded_by_magistrate and magistrate_checked_ability_to_make_statement and doctor_not_examined and declaration_has_no_suspicious_features and declaration_omits_accused_injury and declarant_could_not_observe_accused_injury

predicates.dying_declaration_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction that rests on a dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_recorded_by_magistrate: A magistrate recorded the injured person’s statement as a dying declaration.
predicates.magistrate_checked_ability_to_make_state: The magistrate asked questions or otherwise checked that the injured person could make the statement.
predicates.doctor_not_examined: The doctor who was present when the statement was recorded was not examined at trial.
predicates.declaration_has_no_suspicious_features: The declaration contained relevant details and the court found no feature that cast suspicion on its credibility.
predicates.declaration_omits_accused_injury: The dying declaration did not refer to an injury sustained by the accused.
predicates.declarant_could_not_observe_accused_inju: The circumstances did not give the injured person an opportunity to observe the accused’s injury.

members.legal_issue: A reliable dying declaration may support a conviction without corroboration, and corroboration by reliable evidence further supports reliance on it.
material_facts: The victim gave a statement to the doctor who first treated him, and the doctor testified that the victim was in a fit state of mind when making it.
The doctor supported the recording of the statement, and the court found no material showing that the victim was tutored or prompted or that the statement was fabricated.
The reliable eyewitness testimony corroborated the declaration in all material particulars.
members.legal_principle: There is no absolute rule that a dying declaration cannot be the sole basis of conviction unless corroborated. A declaration may be relied on if it is reliable and is not an attempt to conceal the truth or falsely implicate the accused; corroboration by other prosecution evidence provides further support.
members.conclusion: The dying declaration was reliable and could be relied on as evidence supporting the conviction.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the determination of criminal liability.
predicates.dying_declaration_is_reliable: The declaration was made by a person in a fit state of mind and is otherwise found reliable.
predicates.declaration_is_attempt_to_conceal_truth_: The declaration is an attempt to conceal the truth or falsely implicate the accused.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration may be accepted as evidence of guilt when the declarant was conscious and capable of making the statement, and it does not require corroboration as a matter of law.
material_facts: The injured person gave a detailed statement identifying the attackers and describing the assault before dying.
The officers who recorded or witnessed the statement said that the declarant was conscious.
Medical witnesses testified that the injuries did not prevent the declarant from remaining conscious and speaking, and the medical evidence was consistent with the described weapons and injuries.
A witness's statement that the declarant appeared unconscious at an earlier point did not establish that she could not later regain consciousness and speak.
members.legal_principle: A dying declaration that is shown to have been made while the declarant was conscious and capable of speaking may be acted upon without corroboration. The Court relied on Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay and distinguished Padman Meher v. State of Orissa and Darshan Singh v. Punjab, where the medical circumstances differed.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the statement as a dying declaration and held that it was entitled to great weight without requiring corroboration.

predicates.criminal_case_relies_on_dying_declaratio: The prosecution relied on a statement made by an injured person who later died.
predicates.declarant_conscious_when_statement_made: The person making the statement was conscious when it was made.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_capacity_to_sp: Medical evidence supports that the person's injuries did not prevent them from speaking coherently at the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: A true, carefully scrutinized, coherent, consistent, and unprompted dying declaration may by itself support a criminal conviction without corroboration.
material_facts: The High Court relied on the declaration after rejecting the eyewitness testimony.
The Supreme Court found the declaration straightforward, rational, coherent, consistent, and free from any indication of prompting or tutoring.
The declaration described the motive and participants, and the Court found it true and reliable.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act makes a qualifying dying declaration a relevant fact and gives it special evidentiary status. Under Khushal Rao v. State of Bombay, Tarachand Damu Sutar v. State of Maharashtra, and Mannu Raja v. State of Madhya Pradesh, a true dying declaration may support a conviction without corroboration after careful scrutiny. Ram Nath Madhoprasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh was overruled to the extent it required corroboration.
members.conclusion: The declaration was sufficient to sustain the conviction even without corroboration, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: criminal_case_based_on_dying_declaration and declaration_carefully_scrutinized and declaration_true and declaration_coherent_and_consistent and no_prompting_or_tutoring

predicates.criminal_case_based_on_dying_declaration: The proceeding is a criminal case in which a dying declaration is relied on to establish guilt.
predicates.declaration_carefully_scrutinized: The court carefully scrutinizes the dying declaration.
predicates.declaration_true: The court is satisfied that the declaration is true.
predicates.declaration_coherent_and_consistent: The declaration is coherent and consistent.
predicates.no_prompting_or_tutoring: The evidence does not show that the declarant was prompted or tutored to make the statement.

members.legal_issue: A voluntary, truthful, reliable dying declaration may by itself support a conviction when its maker was conscious and fit to make it and the statement was recorded reliably without external influence.
material_facts: The deceased made a statement to a police officer soon after suffering the burns and later made a dying declaration before a judicial officer.
The judicial officer found the deceased conscious and fit to make a statement and recorded it scrupulously.
The dying declaration was consistent with the earlier complaint, and the Court found no doubt about its truthfulness.
members.legal_principle: A dying declaration must be scrutinised carefully because its maker cannot be cross-examined. Under Puran Chand v. State of Haryana, a voluntary and truthful dying declaration, made in a conscious state of mind and free from doubt or influence, may be the sole basis for conviction.
members.conclusion: The conviction could lawfully rest solely on the dying declaration because it was trustworthy, reliable, and free from doubt.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and dying_declaration_voluntary_and_truthful and maker_conscious_and_fit and declaration_recorded_reliably and no_external_influence

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.dying_declaration_voluntary_and_truthful: The deceased made a statement that the court found voluntary and truthful.
predicates.maker_conscious_and_fit: The deceased was conscious and fit to make the statement when it was given.
predicates.declaration_recorded_reliably: The statement was recorded carefully and reliably.
predicates.no_external_influence: The statement was not influenced by relatives, investigators, or another outside source.

members.legal_issue: A conviction may rest on reliable oral and recorded dying-declaration evidence despite defects in the formal recording of the declaration.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness to the attack, but the injured person was conscious and able to speak after being stabbed.
Several witnesses testified that the injured person identified the principal attacker as the person who stabbed him.
A police officer recorded the injured person’s statement at the scene shortly after the attack, and the statement was later treated as a dying declaration.
The injury described in the statements was corroborated by medical evidence.

The investigating officer did not separately record a dying declaration or have a doctor establish the injured person’s fitness to make a statement; the injured person died more than 24 hours after the attack.
members.legal_principle: A statement made by an injured person may be relied on as a dying declaration even if it was recorded as an ordinary police statement rather than expressly as a dying declaration, where the evidence establishes that the person was conscious and fit to speak and the statement is reliable. Investigative omissions should not automatically benefit the accused; the prosecution evidence must be assessed apart from those omissions. The Court relied on Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar and others, J.T. (1998) 3 SC 290, and upheld the conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The conviction of the principal attacker was upheld because the dying-declaration evidence was reliable and corroborated, notwithstanding the investigating officer’s omissions.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and injured_person_was_conscious_and_able_to_speak and multiple_witnesses_recounted_identification_of_fatal_attacker and police_recorded_statement_at_scene and medical_evidence_corrobated_the_injury and investigator_omitted_formal_recording_of_dying_declaration

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.injured_person_was_conscious_and_able_to: The injured person remained conscious and able to speak after being injured.
predicates.multiple_witnesses_recounted_identificat: Several witnesses testified that the injured person identified the person who inflicted the fatal injury.
predicates.police_recorded_statement_at_scene: A police officer recorded a statement from the injured person at the scene of the incident.
predicates.medical_evidence_corrobated_the_injury: Medical evidence supported the account of the injury given in the statements.
predicates.investigator_omitted_formal_recording_of: The investigator did not separately record the statement as a dying declaration or obtain medical confirmation of the speaker’s fitness to make it.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration may be accepted without a doctor's written fitness endorsement when the evidence otherwise establishes the declarant's fitness and the declaration's reliability.
material_facts: A Magistrate recorded declarations from the surviving injured witness and from a victim who later died.
The declarations did not bear a doctor's written endorsement of the declarants' fitness.
The Magistrate testified that he had sought and obtained the doctor's opinion that the declarants were fit to make statements, and that he had taken precautions before recording them.
The Magistrate's evidence on obtaining the doctor's opinion was not challenged in cross-examination.
The court found the declarations voluntary, truthful, and reliable; the declaration of the surviving witness was used as corroboration, while the other declaration was substantive evidence.
members.legal_principle: A doctor's certification is ordinarily relevant to whether a declarant was fit, but it is not indispensable where other evidence establishes fitness and the declaration is reliable. Under Section 157 of the Evidence Act, a Magistrate-recorded declaration by a witness who survives may corroborate that witness's testimony; a declaration by a person who dies may be substantive evidence. The Court relied on the Constitution Bench ruling in Laxman v. State of Maharashtra and also referred to Shanmugham @ Kulandaivelu v. State of Tamil Nadu and P.V. Radhakrishnan v. State of Karnataka.
members.conclusion: The absence of a written medical endorsement did not require rejection of either declaration; the declaration of the victim who died was substantive evidence, and the surviving witness's declaration corroborated her testimony.

rule.if: dying_declaration_case and magistrate_recorded_declaration and doctor_endorsement_absent and declarant_fit_to_speak and declaration_voluntary_and_reliable

predicates.dying_declaration_case: The case involves a statement made by a person who believed death was impending or who later died, or by an injured witness who survived.
predicates.magistrate_recorded_declaration: A Magistrate recorded the declarant's statement.
predicates.doctor_endorsement_absent: The recorded statement did not contain a doctor's written certification of the declarant's fitness.
predicates.declarant_fit_to_speak: Evidence established that the declarant was conscious and mentally fit to make the statement.
predicates.declaration_voluntary_and_reliable: The court found that the statement was voluntary, truthful, and not influenced by another person or circumstance.

members.legal_issue: A dying declaration that the court accepts as truthful can independently support a conviction.
material_facts: The deceased made a declaration to a doctor, who testified that the deceased was conscious when it was made.
The deceased also made a declaration to a magistrate; the Supreme Court found it coherent overall and considered the magistrate an independent and respectable witness.

The declarations identified the accused, and the Supreme Court found the declarations reliable; it excluded a separate declaration because of the doctor’s endorsement that the deceased was not answering questions.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Lallubhai Devchand Shah v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1972 SC 1976, for the principle that a dying declaration accepted as truthful can form the basis of a conviction. The judgment states no statutory provision as the basis for this principle.
members.conclusion: The reliable dying declarations supported the conviction, and a truthful dying declaration may itself form the basis for conviction.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The proceeding is a criminal prosecution in which the court is deciding whether the accused committed an offence.
predicates.truthful_dying_declaration_accepted: The court accepts as truthful a statement made by a person about the cause or circumstances of that person’s impending death.

members.legal_issue: A voluntary and credible extra-judicial confession, assessed with the surrounding evidence, may support a conviction when the evidence as a whole establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused made an oral confession before his brothers, nephew, an intending purchaser, and tenants after giving a false account of the deceased’s whereabouts and being confronted about it.
The witnesses to the confession were found credible, consistent, and not shown to be hostile or motivated to falsely implicate him.
The accused had arranged the sale of the family property, delivered rooms occupied by the deceased, and built and reinforced a platform beneath which the deceased’s body was recovered.
The accused’s statements led to recovery of the body and the deceased’s belongings, and evidence also showed that he disposed of some of those belongings.
The body was identified as the deceased’s, and medical evidence established a homicidal death by throttling.
members.legal_principle: An extra-judicial confession is not to be rejected merely as a weak category of evidence. If voluntary, true, and proved through credible witnesses, it can form the basis of conviction; corroboration is ordinarily a matter of prudence, assessed in the circumstances. Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, only information distinctly related to a fact discovered is admissible, not a narrative of the past crime. The Court relied on State of Rajasthan v. Raja Ram, Gagan Kanojia v. State of Punjab, Heramba Brahma v. State of Assam, State of Maharashtra v. Damu, Anter Singh v. State of Rajasthan, and Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor.
members.conclusion: The conviction of the accused who made the extra-judicial confession was upheld because the confession was voluntary and credible and the surrounding evidence supported his guilt. Only the part of a custodial statement that distinctly related to a discovery could be relied on as discovery evidence; the inadmissible narrative of the crime could not be admitted as part of that statement.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and voluntary_extra_judicial_confession and credible_confession_witnesses and corroborating_circumstances_establish_guilt

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.voluntary_extra_judicial_confession: The accused made an extra-judicial confession voluntarily and in circumstances supporting its reliability.
predicates.credible_confession_witnesses: Witnesses who testified to the confession were credible and were not shown to have a motive to falsely attribute it to the accused.
predicates.corroborating_circumstances_establish_gu: Other circumstances, including discoveries or conduct connected with the crime, supported the confession and established the accused’s guilt.

members.legal_issue: A voluntary and reliable extra-judicial confession may provide the basis for a conviction even without independent corroboration.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness to the killing, and the prosecution relied principally on the accused’s extra-judicial confession and circumstantial evidence.

Two witnesses testified that the accused confessed immediately after the occurrence; the courts found their evidence reliable and the confession voluntary, with no inducement, threat, promise, coercion, or pressure shown.
The confession was supported by evidence of disclosures and recoveries, including the weapon and a bloodstained sheet.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh, Maghar Singh v. State of Punjab, Narayan Singh v. State of M.P., Kishore Chand v. State of H.P., Baldev Raj v. State of Haryana, Piara Singh v. State of Punjab, and Madan Gopal Kakkad v. Naval Dubey, an extra-judicial confession is not inherently weak and may alone sustain conviction if the court finds it true, voluntary, and reliable. The court must examine its circumstances and ensure it was not induced by a threat, promise, or inducement within Section 24 of the Evidence Act or procured in suspicious circumvention of Sections 25 and 26.
members.conclusion: The confession to the reliable witnesses was voluntary and could be relied on; considered with the other proved circumstances, it supported the conviction.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and confession_extra_judicial and confession_voluntary and confession_reliable

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.confession_extra_judicial: The accused made a confession outside a formal judicial proceeding to another person.
predicates.confession_voluntary: The accused made the confession without inducement, threat, promise, coercion, or pressure.
predicates.confession_reliable: The court found the confession and the witness who recounted it credible after considering the circumstances in which it was made.

members.legal_issue: In an eviction proceeding based on personal requirement, the landlord’s requirement must continue until the proceeding is finally decided, and a court must consider subsequent events that may defeat that requirement.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of personal business need.
The landlord obtained vacant possession of a substantial adjoining portion of the building after the trial court’s eviction decree but while the tenant’s appeal remained pending.
The tenant sought to rely on that subsequent event, and the event was admitted and undisputed.
members.legal_principle: The court held that an appeal is a continuation of the suit and that an eviction decree does not become final while an appeal is pending. A requirement based on personal need must exist when the proceeding is finally disposed of; courts must examine subsequent events and mould the decree accordingly. The court followed Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor and General Traders and held that Taramal v. Laxman Sewak was overruled on this point. It also interpreted the statutory definition of tenant to exclude a person only after the eviction decree or order has become final.
members.conclusion: The subsequent acquisition of suitable accommodation had to be considered when deciding the appeal, and the landlord’s business-need claim could not succeed once the need was satisfied.

predicates.personal_requirement_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a tenant-protection law on the ground of the landlord’s personal requirement.
predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal against the eviction decision remains pending, so the eviction decision is not final.
predicates.subsequent_event_satisfies_landlord_need: An event occurring during the proceeding gives the landlord accommodation that satisfies the asserted requirement.

members.legal_issue: A landlord's personal requirement for possession must continue until the proceeding is finally disposed of, unless the governing statute provides otherwise.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought on the ground of the landlord's personal requirement.
The landlord's claim that no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation was available was affected by later events during the proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, which states that, unless the statute provides to the contrary, personal requirement must exist on the date the proceeding is finally disposed of in appeal or revision. Relevant and material subsequent events may therefore be considered; Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders and Variety Emporium v. V.R.M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina were also relied upon.
members.conclusion: In a proceeding for eviction on personal-requirement grounds, the requirement must continue to exist when the proceeding is finally disposed of in appeal or revision, unless the statute provides otherwise.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding_based_on_pers: A landlord seeks to evict a tenant on the ground that the landlord personally requires the premises for residence.

members.legal_issue: A court reviewing an eviction proceeding must consider a material subsequent event that may affect the claimed personal requirement, even when the event occurs during writ review.
material_facts: The eviction application was based on the landlords’ need to conduct a business in the shop.
Both landlords died while the writ petition was pending, and that event was brought to the High Court’s attention.
The landlords’ three daughters were substituted, and the tenants relied on the fact that they were married and living at their marital homes.
The High Court refused to consider the deaths, reasoning that it could not take account of subsequent events in writ proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, parties’ rights are determined as at the institution of the proceeding. However, a court may, and where appropriate must, take cautious account of subsequent events if the original relief has become inappropriate, consideration can shorten litigation, or it is needed to do complete justice, subject to procedural fairness and prompt notice. A personal requirement must continue until final determination. The Court relied on Shikharchand Jain v. Digamber Jain Praband Karini Sabha, Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. Motor & General Traders, Om Prakash Gupta v. Ranbir B. Goyal, and Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad. It distinguished Rameshwar v. Jot Ram, which concerned agrarian reforms, and Gaya Prasad v. Pradeep Srivastava, where the relevant need was not extinguished in the same way.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in law and jurisdiction by refusing to consider the landlords’ deaths. The Supreme Court set aside its order and remitted the matter for consideration of the subsequent event and the applicable law.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and personal_requirement_basis and landlord_died_during_review and material_subsequent_event_brought_to_court and (relief_may_become_inappropriate or consideration_may_shorten_litigation or consideration_needed_for_complete_justice)

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a claim to evict a tenant from premises.
predicates.personal_requirement_basis: The landlord seeks eviction on the basis of a personal requirement for the premises.
predicates.landlord_died_during_review: The landlord whose personal requirement supports the eviction claim died while judicial review of the claim was pending.
predicates.material_subsequent_event_brought_to_cou: A subsequent event capable of affecting the claimed need was brought to the reviewing court’s attention.
predicates.relief_may_become_inappropriate: The subsequent event may make the relief originally sought inappropriate.
predicates.consideration_may_shorten_litigation: Considering the subsequent event may shorten the litigation.
predicates.consideration_needed_for_complete_justic: Considering the subsequent event may be necessary to do complete justice between the parties.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s personal requirement for eviction must continue to exist when the proceeding is finally decided, and relevant subsequent events must be considered in determining whether relief remains justified.
material_facts: During the proceedings, eviction orders against other tenants became final.
Those orders gave the landlord possession of several other premises in the same building.
The Supreme Court found that possession of those premises more than adequately met the landlord’s asserted requirement, while the appellant’s premises remained occupied.
members.legal_principle: In a tenant-eviction proceeding based on personal requirement, the requirement must continue to exist when the proceeding is finally disposed of, unless the governing statute provides otherwise. A court must evaluate subsequent events that may defeat the claimed need and mould relief accordingly. The Court relied on Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, [1981] 3 SCR 605.
members.conclusion: The Court considered the subsequent events and held that there was no justification for evicting the appellant; the eviction petition against the appellant was dismissed.

predicates.personal_requirement_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that the landlord personally requires the premises.
predicates.subsequent_events_provide_other_premises: Events during the proceeding give the landlord possession of other premises.
predicates.other_premises_adequately_meet_claimed_n: The other premises are sufficient to meet the landlord’s asserted personal requirement.

members.legal_issue: Relevant events occurring after the filing of a tenant-eviction suit may be considered when deciding whether the landlord's asserted personal requirement continues to justify eviction.
material_facts: During the appeal, the landlord's husband acquired a plot, built a spacious bungalow, and the landlord's family resided there.
The additional-evidence application placed these developments before the courts, and the landlord did not controvert them.
The High Court considered the later developments while exercising supervisory jurisdiction and found them relevant to the asserted need for an office.
members.legal_principle: In an appropriate case, a court deciding a tenant-eviction proceeding may take cautious account of relevant developments after the suit was filed, with fairness to both sides, because the claimed personal requirement must continue until final disposal. The Court relied on Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 227 of the Constitution, and on M/s Variety Emporium v. V.R.M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina, Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders, Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad, Amarjit Singh v. Smt. Khatoon Quamarain, and Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram.
members.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to consider the relevant subsequent facts placed before it through an application for additional evidence when deciding whether the claimed requirement remained bona fide.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground of personal requirement.
predicates.relevant_subsequent_events: Developments after the suit was filed had a bearing on whether the landlord's asserted requirement continued.
predicates.evidence_properly_brought_on_record: The later developments were placed before the court through an application for additional evidence.

members.legal_issue: In an eviction suit founded on a landlord–tenant relationship, the court determines whether that relationship exists and may consider title only incidentally rather than finally.
material_facts: The claimant brought an eviction suit after purchasing the premises from a person said to have inherited them from the former owner.
The tenant had attorned to the claimant, agreed to pay rent, and paid rent for two months.
An adoption deed and the tenant’s failure to dispute the adoption supported a prima facie basis for the transferor’s succession to the private property.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3(III) and (VII) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, a landlord includes a person entitled to receive rent and a tenant includes a person liable to pay it. In an eviction suit based on the relationship of landlord and tenant, title is not the primary issue; the court makes only a prima facie decision on the collateral question of landlord status. The court relied on L.I.C. v. India Automobiles & Co. and distinguished Rajendra Singh v. Union of India, which held that recognition as ruler did not itself recognize private-property rights. The adoption deed and the surrounding facts supported prima facie succession to the private property.
members.conclusion: The claimant was established as the landlord and the respondent as the tenant; the title inquiry was only prima facie and collateral, not a final adjudication of title.

predicates.eviction_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a person occupying premises as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_attorned_to_claimant: The occupant accepted the claimant as landlord and agreed to pay rent to the claimant.
predicates.claimant_has_prima_facie_basis_for_rent_: The claimant presented evidence supporting an entitlement to receive rent from the occupant.

members.legal_issue: A title question considered in an ordinary eviction proceeding is generally considered only incidentally and is not finally determined there.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the landlord’s ownership could be examined in the eviction proceeding.
The eviction proceeding did not frame an issue of title.
The Court distinguished an exceptional earlier case in which title had been directly and substantially in issue and the finding was held to operate as res judicata.
members.legal_principle: Bhagadi Kannababu v. Vuggina Pydamma, relying on Tej Bhan Madan v. II Additional District Judge, states that an eviction court determines whether the landlord-tenant relationship exists; title may be considered incidentally but is not finally decided. Mohd. Nooman v. Mohd. Jabed Alam was expressly confined to exceptional facts where title was directly and substantially in issue, so its res judicata result does not ordinarily apply. Section 116 of the Evidence Act supports the estoppel principle between landlord and tenant.
members.conclusion: The eviction proceeding could consider title incidentally, but it could not finally determine title in the ordinary circumstances of this case; the exceptional res judicata case did not apply.

predicates.ordinary_eviction_proceeding: A court is deciding a proceeding for eviction rather than a suit principally seeking a final determination of title.
predicates.title_considered_incidentally: The court examines title only as part of deciding the issues necessary to the eviction proceeding.
predicates.title_not_directly_and_substantially_in_: The parties have not made title a directly and substantially framed issue for decision.

members.legal_issue: An eviction proceeding based on the landlord-tenant relationship does not finally determine title to the property, which may be considered incidentally but must be left for comprehensive adjudication.
material_facts: The proceeding sought eviction of tenants on grounds including default and subletting.
The parties disputed whether the claimant and her daughters had inherited the property.
The court considered that the tenancy relationship and the grounds for eviction could be decided without finally determining the daughters’ title or inheritance rights.
members.legal_principle: In an eviction proceeding, the court decides whether the landlord-tenant relationship exists; title may be considered incidentally but cannot be finally decided. A comprehensive suit for title is the appropriate proceeding for final determination of competing title and inheritance claims.
members.conclusion: The eviction proceeding could determine whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether eviction was warranted, but it did not finally determine title or inheritance rights.

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A proceeding was brought to evict a tenant from property under tenancy law.
predicates.competing_title_or_inheritance_claims: The parties disputed who held title to the property or inherited it.
predicates.eviction_decision_turns_on_tenancy_relat: The eviction question could be decided by determining whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether eviction grounds were established.

members.legal_issue: For a rent-control eviction suit based on bona fide need, the relevant date for determining whether the need existed is the date the suit was instituted, and the landlord’s later death does not by itself invalidate a suit validly filed.
material_facts: The landlord instituted an eviction suit alleging a bona fide need to use non-residential premises for business.
The trial court passed an eviction decree before the landlord died during the tenant’s appeal.
The High Court treated the landlord’s death as ending the need and dismissed the suit.
The applicable statute barred filing an eviction suit except on specified grounds, including the bona fide business need described in the case.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 bars the filing of an eviction suit except on specified grounds, and Section 12(1)(f) includes a landlord’s bona fide need for non-residential premises for business. The Court read the statutory bar as governing whether the suit was validly filed, not as requiring the need to persist until the decree becomes final. Kamleshwar Prasad v. Pradumanju Agarwal, Gaya Prasad v. Pradeep Srivastava and G.C. Kapoor v. Nand Kumar Bhasin support assessing bona fide need on the date of the eviction application. The broad observations in P.V. Papanna v. K. Padmanabhaiah that subsequent events may be considered until a final decree were not the correct legal position on this point and were unnecessary to that decision. The Act’s preamble also emphasizes expeditious trial of bona fide-need eviction cases.
members.conclusion: The bona fide need is examined as of the institution of the eviction proceedings; the landlord’s death after an eviction decree has been passed does not make the validly instituted suit unmaintainable.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and bona_fide_need_at_filing and eviction_decree_before_landlord_death and landlord_died_during_appeal

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord has brought an eviction suit governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.bona_fide_need_at_filing: The landlord alleged a bona fide need that existed when the eviction suit was instituted.
predicates.eviction_decree_before_landlord_death: A court passed an eviction decree in the landlord’s favour before the landlord died.
predicates.landlord_died_during_appeal: The landlord died while the tenant’s appeal was pending.

members.legal_issue: A landlord's bona fide need is ordinarily assessed as of the eviction petition, and events during prolonged litigation displace that assessment only when they completely eclipse the need.
material_facts: The landlords sought the premises to start or expand business, and the courts below found the need genuine when the eviction claim was brought.
The litigation continued for a prolonged period, during which the landlords and their sons could not be expected to remain idle.
One son had settled in the United States, but other sons still wanted to expand business at Calicut; the Court found that circumstance did not eclipse the need.
members.legal_principle: The normal rule is that parties' rights and obligations are determined as of the date of the eviction petition. Under the principles in Pratap Rai Tanwani v. Uttam Chand, (2004) 8 SCC 490, and Gaya Prasad v. Pradeep Srivastava, (2001) 2 SCC 604, later events may be considered when moulding relief, but only where their nature and dimension completely eclipse the landlord's need. A landlord should not be penalized for delays in the legal process.
members.conclusion: The need was properly assessed by reference to the date of the eviction petition; the later circumstances shown did not extinguish it.

rule.if: need_based_eviction_proceeding and need_existed_when_petition_filed and not later_event_completely_eclipsed_need

predicates.need_based_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction sought on the landlord's asserted bona fide need.
predicates.need_existed_when_petition_filed: The landlord's asserted need existed when the eviction petition was filed.
predicates.later_event_completely_eclipsed_need: An event occurring during the litigation completely extinguished the landlord's asserted need.

members.legal_issue: The landlord’s bona fide personal need in an eviction proceeding is ordinarily assessed as of the date the eviction petition is filed.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction to use the building for his son’s medical practice and for his own proposed work.
The fact-finding authorities found the need bona fide when the eviction petition was filed.
The tenant relied on the son’s later entry into medical service to challenge the eviction order.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the landlord’s bona fide requirement is ordinarily assessed as of the date of the eviction application. The normal rule is that parties’ rights and obligations are determined as they stood when the litigation began, subject to cautious consideration of subsequent events that materially affect entitlement or the relief; the Court relied on Ramesh Kumar v. Kesho Ram and Kamleshwar Prasad v. Pradumanju Agarwal.
members.conclusion: The date of filing the eviction petition was the crucial date for deciding whether the landlord’s need was bona fide; later developments did not, by themselves, change that assessment.

predicates.personal_need_eviction_case: A landlord brings an eviction proceeding on the ground that the premises are needed for the landlord or a family member.
predicates.need_existed_when_petition_filed: The landlord’s asserted need existed when the eviction petition was filed.

members.legal_issue: An amendment adding a claim that is already time-barred does not relate back to the filing of the original pleading when the court preserves the limitation defence and no special circumstances justify relation back.
material_facts: The original suit sought an injunction, and the later amendment added a declaration of title, introducing a claim for distinct relief.
The amendment was sought after the limitation period for the declaration claim had elapsed from the defendant’s original denial of title.
When allowing the amendment, the High Court expressly permitted the defendant to raise limitation.
The amendment did not involve the exceptional circumstances found in cases where no new material facts were needed and the amendment merely added an alternative legal claim.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendment of pleadings, but relation back is not universal and the court may direct that an amendment take effect from the date it was sought. Sampath Kumar v. Ayyakannu and Siddalingamma v. Mamtha Shenoy recognize that the doctrine may be displaced in an appropriate case. The general approach to amendments that would deprive a defendant of an accrued limitation defence is reflected in Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, L.J. Leach & Co. Ltd. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., Vishwambhar v. Laxminarayan and Van Vibhag Karamchari Griha Nirman Sahkari Sanstha Maryadit v. Ramesh Chander. Exceptional circumstances may justify allowing an amendment despite limitation, but none were present here.
members.conclusion: The amendment did not relate back to the date the original suit was filed. The limitation defence remained available, and the declaration claim was time-barred.

rule.if: civil_pleading_amendment and amendment_adds_time_barred_claim and court_preserves_limitation_defence and not exceptional_amendment_circumstances

predicates.civil_pleading_amendment: A party seeks to amend pleadings in a civil proceeding.
predicates.amendment_adds_time_barred_claim: The amendment adds a claim for which the limitation period has already elapsed.
predicates.court_preserves_limitation_defence: The court allows the amendment while expressly leaving the opposing party free to raise limitation.
predicates.exceptional_amendment_circumstances: Special circumstances exist that justify allowing the amendment despite the accrued limitation defence, such as the amendment adding no new material facts and merely supplying an alternative legal claim.
predicates.amendment_does_not_relate_back: The added claim is treated as brought when the amendment was sought, rather than when the original pleading was filed.

members.legal_issue: An amendment adding a claim for possession may be refused when it is sought after the applicable limitation period has expired.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought, at the appellate stage, to amend the plaint to add an alternative claim for possession.
The plaintiffs had been aware from the earlier proceedings that they were not found to be in possession.
The High Court found the explanation for the delay unsatisfactory, and the amendment was found to be outside the prescribed limitation period.
members.legal_principle: A plaintiff may seek to amend a plaint to add an omitted relief, but the amendment must be saved by limitation. The Court relied on Vinay Krishna v. Keshav Chandra and Venkataraja v. Vidyane Doureradjaperumal; it also referred to Parkash Chand Khurana v. Harnam Singh and State of M.P. v. Mangilal Sharma for the requirement that defendants raise the issue at the earliest.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the amendment seeking possession was upheld because the amendment was not sought within the applicable limitation period.

predicates.appellate_amendment_request: A party asked an appellate court to amend the pleadings in an existing suit.
predicates.added_possession_claim: The requested amendment would add a claim to recover possession of property.
predicates.limitation_period_expired: The time allowed for bringing the added claim had expired before the amendment was sought.

members.legal_issue: An amendment adding a specific-performance claim cannot be allowed when it is sought after the limitation period has expired, even if the original suit sought a different form of relief.
material_facts: The purchasers initially sued for a mandatory injunction directing the seller to comply with requirements in the agreement.
They later applied to amend the plaint to seek specific performance.
The agreement fixed May 28, 1989, as the performance date, and the amendment application was filed on November 5, 1992.
The trial court rejected the amendment, and the High Court affirmed that decision.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a specific-performance claim based on a fixed performance date must be brought within three years from that date. A suit for mandatory injunction is different from a suit for specific performance, and adding the latter by amendment after its limitation period has expired cannot cure the bar. Order VI, Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs amendment of pleadings. K. Raheja Construction Ltd. v. Alliances Ministries and Tarlok Singh v. Vijay Kumar Sabharwal support refusing an amendment that introduces a time-barred specific-performance claim.
members.conclusion: The amendment was sought after the specific-performance claim had become barred by limitation and was properly refused. The appeal was dismissed, subject to the seller’s undertaking to refund the amount paid with interest as stipulated in the contract.

predicates.specific_performance_claim_added_by_amen: A party seeks to add a claim for specific performance by amending a pleading.
predicates.performance_date_fixed: The parties fixed a date for performance, either directly or by reference to an event that makes the date ascertainable.
predicates.amendment_after_limitation_period: The amendment is sought after the limitation period for the specific-performance claim has expired.

members.legal_issue: A plaint amendment adding a new declaration may be refused when it would defeat a limitation right that accrued to the opposing party before the amendment was sought.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a pending partition suit and later sought to add a declaration challenging a registered deed affecting the property.
The opposing parties had pleaded the deed in their written statement, and the amendment application was made about three years after that pleading.
Allowing the amendment would have permitted a claim for declaratory relief after the time for bringing that claim had expired.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendments are ordinarily allowed, but an amendment is refused in exceptional cases where it takes away a legal right accrued through lapse of time. The Court relied on Laxmidas Dahyabhai Kabarwala v. Nunabhai Chunilal Kabarwala, distinguishing a merely clarificatory amendment from one that adds a new claim or relief. Registration of the deed gave notice to persons claiming an interest in the property, and the written statement in any event disclosed the deed to the plaintiff.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly refused because it would defeat the opposing parties’ accrued right to rely on limitation; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: amendment_in_pending_civil_suit and amendment_adds_new_claim_or_relief and limitation_right_accrued and amendment_would_defeat_accrued_right

predicates.amendment_in_pending_civil_suit: A party sought to amend pleadings in a pending civil suit.
predicates.amendment_adds_new_claim_or_relief: The proposed amendment added a claim or relief rather than merely clarifying an existing pleading.
predicates.limitation_right_accrued: The opposing party had acquired a limitation-based right because the time to bring the added claim had expired.
predicates.amendment_would_defeat_accrued_right: Allowing the amendment would take away the opposing party’s accrued limitation-based right.

members.legal_issue: An amendment adding a claim for specific performance is barred when the claim was apparent from the original pleadings but the amendment is sought after the limitation period has expired.
material_facts: The original suit sought a permanent injunction and alleged that a concluded contract for sale existed, that the other side had refused to perform it, and that the claimants were ready and willing to perform their part.
The original plaint did not seek specific performance, although the pleaded refusal was identified as a cause of action.
The claimants sought to amend the plaint to add specific performance about seven years after filing the suit.
The applicable limitation period for the specific-performance claim was three years.
The claimants relied on a later discovery that the competent authority had granted permission for the sale.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an amendment cannot be used on these facts to defeat the valuable limitation right accrued to the opposing party. Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963, provided a three-year limitation period. A.K. Gupta v. D.V.C. (1966 (1) SCR 796) did not apply because the claimant there had expressly reserved the right to claim the amount in the original plaint, whereas no comparable reservation was made here.
members.conclusion: The amendment application was barred by limitation, and the petition was dismissed.

predicates.pending_suit_amendment_request: A party seeks to amend the pleadings in a pending suit.
predicates.original_pleadings_show_concluded_contra: The original pleadings state that a concluded contract existed and that the opposing party refused to perform it.
predicates.specific_performance_omitted_from_origin: The original claim does not seek specific performance despite pleading facts supporting that relief.
predicates.amendment_sought_after_limitation_expire: The party seeks the amendment after the limitation period for the omitted claim has expired.
predicates.specific_performance_amendment_barred_by: The amendment adding specific performance is barred by limitation.

members.legal_issue: An amendment adding a specific-performance claim after the limitation period cannot relate back when it changes the basis or character of the original suit.
material_facts: The purchaser's original suit sought declaration of ownership and an injunction, not specific performance.
The purchaser sought to add specific performance to the suit about eleven years after filing it.
The added relief substantially altered the character of the suit and increased its pecuniary jurisdiction, requiring transfer to another court.
members.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963 bars a specific-performance claim brought after the applicable period. In Vishwambhar v. Laxminarayan, (2001) 6 SCC 163, the Court held that an amendment changing the basis of a suit cannot relate back to cure a limitation defect. In K. Raheja Constructions Ltd. v. Alliance Ministries, 1995 Supp. (3) SCC 17, the Court held that a delayed amendment adding specific performance cannot defeat the other party's accrued limitation rights.
members.conclusion: The amendment could not relate back to the date of the original plaint to cure the limitation defect, and the specific-performance relief could not be granted.

rule.if: pending_suit_amendment and amendment_adds_specific_performance and claim_out_of_time and amendment_changes_suit_character

predicates.pending_suit_amendment: A claimant seeks to amend a suit that is already pending.
predicates.amendment_adds_specific_performance: The amendment adds a claim to enforce an agreement to sell.
predicates.claim_out_of_time: The added claim is brought after the applicable limitation period has expired.
predicates.amendment_changes_suit_character: The added claim changes the basis or character of the original suit.

members.legal_issue: An amendment introducing a specific-performance claim is not allowable when it substitutes a new and inconsistent case based solely on a decree that conferred only a pre-emption right and is sought to avoid limitation.
material_facts: The original suit sought to enforce a pre-emption right created by a compromise decree.
During the appeal, the plaintiff sought to amend the plaint to allege an agreement of sale and claim specific performance.
The amendment relied on the same compromise decree; no separate agreement of sale was pleaded.
The original pre-emption claim faced a limitation bar.
members.legal_principle: An amendment that substitutes a new and inconsistent case and is sought to get around a limitation bar should not be allowed on these facts. A compromise decree providing that parties must sell allotted property among themselves confers a right of pre-emption but does not itself constitute an agreement for sale. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly set aside because it introduced a new and inconsistent claim intended to overcome the limitation bar, and the compromise decree did not constitute an agreement for sale.

rule.if: amendment_application_in_preemption_suit and decree_created_only_preemption_right and no_separate_sale_agreement_pleaded and amendment_sought_to_avoid_limitation

predicates.amendment_application_in_preemption_suit: A party to a suit seeking to enforce a pre-emption right applies to amend the pleading to claim specific performance.
predicates.decree_created_only_preemption_right: The decree relied on provided a right to buy property before it was sold to someone outside the specified group, without creating a sale agreement.
predicates.no_separate_sale_agreement_pleaded: The party seeking amendment does not plead a separate agreement of sale apart from the decree.
predicates.amendment_sought_to_avoid_limitation: The amendment is sought to avoid a limitation bar affecting the original claim.

members.legal_issue: A suit to set aside a decree is barred when it is brought after the applicable limitation period has elapsed from the time the facts entitling the claimant to seek that relief first became known or chargeable to the claimant as knowledge.
material_facts: The claimant was found to have knowledge of the earlier partition proceedings and decrees from the beginning through the benamidar from whom he claimed title.
The claimant filed his suit in 1981, more than three years after the knowledge attributed to him.
The claimant sought to have the preliminary and final decrees set aside.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period for a suit to set aside or cancel a decree begins when the facts entitling the plaintiff to that relief first become known. The court held Article 113 inapplicable and treated the claimant's knowledge through his benamidar as knowledge for this purpose.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because it was filed more than three years after the claimant had knowledge of the facts entitling him to seek the decrees' cancellation.

predicates.suit_seeks_to_set_aside_decree: The claimant brought a suit seeking to set aside an earlier decree.
predicates.claimant_knew_or_was_chargeable_with_kno: The claimant knew, or was treated as knowing, the facts entitling the claimant to seek the decree's cancellation.
predicates.suit_filed_after_applicable_limitation_p: The claimant filed the suit after the applicable limitation period had elapsed from the date of that knowledge.

members.legal_issue: A suit to cancel a conveyance is time-barred when the facts supporting cancellation were known when the conveyance was executed and the suit is brought after the applicable limitation period; later discovery of a document index does not create a new accrual date.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that the bulk of the consideration had not been paid when the last cheques were delivered and the registered sale deed was executed.
The deed identified the cheques and expressly acknowledged receipt of the full consideration.

The plaintiffs alleged that they discovered the fraud only when they obtained an index and a copy of the deed years later, but they did not complain or seek recovery of the alleged unpaid amount during the intervening period.
The suit seeking cancellation was filed beyond three years from the alleged non-payment and execution of the deed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(j) and 3 of the Limitation Act, 1963 define the prescribed period and require dismissal of a suit instituted after it. Articles 58 and 59 prescribe three years for the relevant declaration or cancellation claim, running from when the right to sue first accrues or the facts entitling cancellation first become known. A later or successive event does not restart limitation where the right to sue first accrued earlier. The court examines the plaint to identify when the right to seek relief arose. The Court relied on Khatri Hotels Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, and Raghwendra Sharan Singh v. Ram Prasanna Singh.
members.conclusion: The right to sue arose when the alleged non-payment occurred, not when the plaintiffs later obtained the index; the cancellation claim was barred by limitation under Article 59.

predicates.suit_seeks_cancellation_of_instrument: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking cancellation of an instrument.
predicates.cancellation_facts_known_when_claim_firs: The plaintiff knew the facts alleged to justify cancellation when the asserted injury or non-performance first occurred.
predicates.suit_filed_beyond_applicable_limitation_: The plaintiff filed the suit after the limitation period applicable to the claim had expired.
predicates.later_discovery_is_only_of_document_inde: The plaintiff relies on later receipt of an index or copy of a document, although the underlying facts supporting the claim had already occurred and were known.
predicates.cancellation_claim_is_time_barred: The court holds that the cancellation claim was brought too late.

members.legal_issue: A belated amendment that seeks to withdraw an admission and introduce an entirely new case may be refused.
material_facts: During the appeal, the tenant sought to amend the written statement to assert that the business entity, rather than the tenant, had taken the premises on rent.
The tenant had previously admitted in the written statement that he was the tenant.
The Tribunal considered the proposed amendment belated and found that it would replace the admission with an entirely new case and prejudice the landlord's position.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an amendment seeking to displace an admission and introduce an entirely new case may be refused. The Court relied on Subashini Majumdar v. Krishna Prasad Mahatoo, AIR 1956 Assam 79, and M/s Modi Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. M/s Ladha Ram and Co., [1977] 1 SCR 728.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal was right to refuse the amendment.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: The matter was an appeal in a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.amendment_sought_after_admission: The tenant sought an amendment after having admitted a material fact in the existing pleading.
predicates.amendment_would_introduce_entirely_new_c: The proposed amendment would replace the admission with a substantially different case.

members.legal_issue: A belated proposed amendment may be refused when it seeks to add grounds already concluded by a final prior adjudication and is aimed at avoiding rejection of the plaint.
material_facts: During the appeal, the plaintiff sought to amend the plaint to add grounds that had been raised and rejected in earlier proceedings concerning the decree.
The application was highly belated and was made after the absence of a cause of action had been identified as requiring rejection of the plaint.
members.legal_principle: The Court refused the amendment in light of its lateness, its apparent purpose of avoiding rejection of the plaint, and the fact that the proposed grounds had been concluded by the earlier adjudication. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case as authority for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court refused the application to amend the plaint because it was a belated afterthought and the proposed grounds had already been concluded by the earlier final adjudication.

rule.if: appeal_from_suit_maintainability_order and amendment_sought_during_appeal and amendment_is_highly_belated and proposed_grounds_were_concluded_by_final_prior_adjudication and amendment_aims_to_avoid_plaint_rejection

predicates.appeal_from_suit_maintainability_order: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a lower court’s ruling that a suit is maintainable.
predicates.amendment_sought_during_appeal: The plaintiff applied to amend the plaint while the appeal was being heard.
predicates.amendment_is_highly_belated: The plaintiff sought the amendment only after the case had advanced to the appeal stage.
predicates.proposed_grounds_were_concluded_by_final: The grounds proposed for addition had already been rejected in an earlier adjudication that had become final.
predicates.amendment_aims_to_avoid_plaint_rejection: The proposed amendment was an afterthought intended to avert rejection of the plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s death does not extinguish an eviction claim based on occupation for the landlord and members of the landlord’s family when those family members’ occupation is also a basis of the claim.
material_facts: The court considered a rule applied in an eviction proceeding where the landlord sought residential occupation for himself and members of his family and died while an appeal was pending.

The court held that the statutory wording made the need for occupation the need of both the landlord and the family members, and that family members could continue the proceeding through the senior member of the family.
members.legal_principle: The court interpreted section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which permitted eviction for occupation as a residence for the landlord and members of the landlord’s family. Because the provision included the family members’ occupation, their need did not cease on the landlord’s death. The court overruled Phul Rani & Ors. v. Naubat Rai Ahluwalia.
members.conclusion: The right to sue survives to the landlord’s family members where the claim is for occupation by the landlord and members of the family; the contrary holding in Phul Rani was overruled.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.landlord_dies_while_claim_pending: The landlord dies while the eviction claim is still pending.
predicates.claimed_occupation_includes_family_membe: The claimed occupation is for the landlord and members of the landlord’s family.

members.legal_issue: The landlord’s death during a challenge to an eviction order does not extinguish an established bona fide need to start a business when the business can be carried on by family members.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction to start a business in the premises, and the statutory appellate authority found the requirement bona fide.
The landlord died while the tenant’s writ petition was pending.
The court found that the business could be carried on by the landlord’s widow or an elder son.
members.legal_principle: For an eviction application based on bona fide requirement, the application date is the crucial date for determining whether the tenant incurred liability to be evicted. The subsequent death of the landlord does not extinguish the need where the business can be carried on by the landlord’s widow or an elder son. The judgment relies on Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Act XIII of 1972 and cites no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The landlord’s death did not cause the established bona fide need to lapse, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_for_landlord_business_need and bona_fide_need_found_at_application and landlord_dies_during_challenge and family_can_carry_on_business

predicates.eviction_proceeding_for_landlord_busines: A landlord sought eviction so that the premises could be used to start the landlord’s own business.
predicates.bona_fide_need_found_at_application: The statutory appellate authority found that the landlord genuinely required the premises for the business when the eviction application was made.
predicates.landlord_dies_during_challenge: The landlord died while a challenge to the eviction order was pending.
