predicates.family_can_carry_on_business: The business could be carried on by the landlord’s widow or an elder son.
predicates.landlord_death_does_not_extinguish_bona_: The landlord’s death does not extinguish the established bona fide need to use the premises for the business.

members.legal_issue: The death of a landlord during eviction proceedings does not necessarily substantially diminish the family's need for the premises when the family need continues.
material_facts: The landlord died after the High Court's order, while the matter was proceeding on appeal.
The eviction claim also rested on the increasing accommodation needs of the landlord's family.
The landlord's married sons and their families, as well as his wife, remained beneficiaries of the proceedings, and the family had grown during the litigation.
members.legal_principle: Courts should take subsequent events into account cautiously. The effect of a landlord's death depends on whether the underlying need survives; a death does not substantially alter the need where the claim also rests on continuing family requirements and the family beneficiaries remain.
members.conclusion: The landlord's death did not substantially diminish the accommodation need in this case because the enlarged family and surviving beneficiaries continued to need the premises.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and landlord_dies_during_proceedings and family_need_supports_claim and family_beneficiaries_remain

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant and the proceeding remains unresolved.
predicates.landlord_dies_during_proceedings: The landlord dies while the eviction proceeding is pending.
predicates.family_need_supports_claim: The claimed need for the premises includes the accommodation needs of the landlord's family.
predicates.family_beneficiaries_remain: Family members who benefit from the claimed accommodation need remain after the landlord's death.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s death after an eviction decree has been passed does not prevent the landlord’s heirs from continuing to defend that decree against the tenant’s appeal.
material_facts: A landlord obtained an eviction decree based on a bona fide need to use non-residential premises for business.
The landlord died while the tenant’s appeal against the decree was pending, and the landlord’s heirs were substituted and continued the proceedings.
The High Court dismissed the eviction suit on the ground that the landlord’s personal need had ended on his death.
members.legal_principle: In Smt. Phool Rani v. Naubat Rai Ahluwalia, the Court held that where a possession decree has been passed before the landlord’s death, the landlord’s estate is entitled to the benefit of the decree and the heirs may defend it against an appeal. Shantilal Thakordas v. Chimanlal Maganlal Telwala overruled Phool Rani to the extent that it treated the family’s need as ending with the landlord’s death, and supports the heirs’ ability to continue eviction proceedings. Section 12(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 restricts the grounds on which an eviction suit may be filed; it does not extinguish a decree already obtained when the landlord dies during the tenant’s appeal. The principle actus curiae neminem gravabit also supports preventing the court’s stay of the decree from prejudicing the landlord’s estate.
members.conclusion: The heirs were entitled to defend the eviction decree, and the landlord’s death during the tenant’s appeal did not require dismissal of the suit.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_appeal and eviction_decree_before_landlord_death and landlord_died_during_appeal and heirs_substituted

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: A tenant has appealed against a decree ordering eviction.
predicates.eviction_decree_before_landlord_death: A court passed an eviction decree in the landlord’s favour before the landlord died.
predicates.landlord_died_during_appeal: The landlord died while the tenant’s appeal was pending.
predicates.heirs_substituted: The landlord’s heirs were substituted in the proceedings after the landlord’s death.

members.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption survives the pre-emptor’s death and may be pursued by legal representatives who succeed to the relevant rights by inheritance.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought statutory pre-emption suits based on his relationship to the vendor, and decrees were granted and affirmed on first appeal.
The plaintiff died while second appeals were pending, and his legal representatives were brought on record.
The claim concerned agricultural land and depended on the statutory qualifications governing the pre-emptor and the vendor.
members.legal_principle: The statutory right of pre-emption is not an interest in land, but it attaches to the land and is enforceable against a purchaser. Although the right is personal in the sense that it depends on the pre-emptor’s relationship with the vendor, a successor who takes the relevant land by inheritance takes the rights that go with it. The Court relied on section 306 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and Order XXII, rules 1 and 11, read with rule 10, of the Code of Civil Procedure. It approved Faqir Ali Shah v. Rani Kishan, 133 P.R. 1907, and Wajid Ali v. Shaban, I.L.R. 31 All. 623; it distinguished the rule concerning pre-emption under Mohammedan law discussed in Muhammad Husain v. Niamat-un-nissa, I.L.R. 20 All. 88.
members.conclusion: The right to sue did not abate on the plaintiff’s death, and his legal representatives were properly brought on record in the pending appeals.

rule.if: statutory_preemption_proceeding and qualifying_preemption_relationship and preemptor_dies_while_appeal_pending and legal_representatives_succeed_by_inheritance

predicates.statutory_preemption_proceeding: A claimant brings a proceeding to enforce a statutory right of pre-emption.
predicates.qualifying_preemption_relationship: The claimant and vendor have the relationship and other statutory qualifications on which the asserted pre-emption right depends.
predicates.preemptor_dies_while_appeal_pending: The claimant dies while an appeal in the pre-emption proceeding remains pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_succeed_by_inherit: The claimant’s legal representatives succeed by inheritance to the relevant estate or land rights.

members.legal_issue: The legal representatives of a tenant who dies during a suit to enforce a customary pre-emption right may be substituted and continue the suit when the right to sue survives.
material_facts: The tenant filed a suit to enforce a customary right of pre-emption arising from his tenancy.
The tenant died while the suit was pending, before a decree had been granted.
His legal representatives applied to be substituted so they could prosecute the suit, and the trial court allowed the application.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, legal representatives may be substituted when the right to sue survives. Because the pre-emption right was incidental to a heritable tenancy, the tenant’s death during trial did not extinguish the right to sue. The Court followed Hazari v. Neki, held Chandrup Singh v. Data Ram inconsistent with that decision and overruled it, and distinguished Muhammad Husain v. Niamet-un-nissa as involving a different basis for the claimed right.
members.conclusion: The right to sue survived to the tenant’s legal representatives, who were entitled to be substituted under Order 22, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and continue the suit.

rule.if: preemption_suit and plaintiff_died_while_suit_pending and right_to_sue_is_heritable and applicants_are_legal_representatives

predicates.preemption_suit: The proceeding is a suit to enforce a right of pre-emption.
predicates.plaintiff_died_while_suit_pending: The plaintiff died before the suit was finally decided.
predicates.right_to_sue_is_heritable: The right underlying the suit survives the plaintiff’s death and passes to the plaintiff’s heirs.
predicates.applicants_are_legal_representatives: The persons seeking substitution are the deceased plaintiff’s legal representatives.
predicates.legal_representatives_may_be_substituted: The legal representatives are entitled to replace the deceased plaintiff and prosecute the suit.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s pending rent-control eviction claim founded on the landlord’s own personal residential requirement does not survive to legal representatives when the landlord dies before an eviction decree and their distinct requirements would have to replace the original claim.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the premises were bona fide required for the landlord’s residence with dependent family members and that no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation was available.

The initial eviction application was dismissed on a preliminary issue concerning the notices to quit, and the landlord died while an appeal was pending, before a decision on the merits or an eviction decree.
The landlord’s legal representatives sought to continue the proceeding; determining their requirements and accommodation would involve issues distinct from those pleaded by the landlord.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 22 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, abatement depends on whether the right to sue survives. The right to sue means the right to seek the same relief that the deceased plaintiff asserted at death, as stated in Saraj Chandra v. Nani Mihan. The nature of the pleaded claim determines survival. Here, the landlord’s claim under section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act rested on the landlord’s own bona fide requirement, and replacing it with the legal representatives’ distinct requirements would fundamentally alter the pleadings beyond the permissible scope of Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code. The Court treated section 306 of the Indian Succession Act only as an indirect analogy. It distinguished Motilal Pannalal v. Kailash Narain, Amar Nath Bihari v. Jai Dayal Puri, Smt. Dhan Devi v. Bakshi Ram, Vas Dev v. Sohan Singh, Dr. Muhammad Ibrahim v. Rahiman Khan, and Rameshwar Dayal v. Smt. Mohania because those decisions involved different procedural circumstances or principles.
members.conclusion: The landlord’s right to sue did not survive to the legal representatives, and they could not continue the pending eviction proceeding on the basis of their own distinct requirements.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_died_before_eviction_decree and claim_based_on_landlords_personal_requirement and heirs_require_distinct_factual_inquiry

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding was brought by a landlord to obtain eviction under rent-control law.
predicates.landlord_died_before_eviction_decree: The landlord died while the eviction proceeding was pending and before an eviction decree had been obtained.
predicates.claim_based_on_landlords_personal_requir: The landlord pleaded that the premises were bona fide required for the landlord’s own residence with dependent family members.
predicates.heirs_require_distinct_factual_inquiry: Continuing the proceeding for the legal representatives would require deciding their distinct requirements and accommodation rather than the landlord’s pleaded requirement.

members.legal_issue: After a landlord dies while a personal-requirement release application is pending, the landlord’s legal representatives may continue the proceeding on the basis of their own need in substitution for the deceased landlord’s need.
material_facts: The release application sought possession on the ground of the landlords’ bona fide requirement.
Both landlords died while the litigation was pending, and their three daughters were brought on record as legal representatives.
The tenants argued that the deceased landlords’ requirement no longer survived.
members.legal_principle: The Court read Section 21(1)(a) together with Section 21(7) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. Where possession is sought on the ground of bona fide requirement and the landlord dies during the pendency of the application, the legal representatives may prosecute it on the basis of their own need in substitution for the deceased landlord’s need. The Court also referred to Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad.
members.conclusion: The legal representatives could prosecute the application on the basis of their own need in substitution for the deceased landlords’ need; the High Court had to consider that provision and make a finding on remand.

rule.if: eviction_release_proceeding and personal_requirement_basis and landlord_died_while_claim_pending and legal_representatives_brought_on_record

predicates.eviction_release_proceeding: The proceeding is an application seeking release of rented premises from a tenant.
predicates.personal_requirement_basis: The application seeks possession on the basis of the landlord’s personal bona fide requirement.
predicates.landlord_died_while_claim_pending: The landlord died while the claim for release was pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_brought_on_record: The landlord’s legal representatives were brought into the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s death before the end of an approved fixed-term tenancy does not prevent the landlord’s legal representatives from seeking possession after the tenant fails to vacate.
material_facts: The landlord let residential premises under a written agreement for a fixed period after obtaining the Controller’s permission.
The landlord died before that period expired.
After the period expired, the tenant did not vacate, and the landlord’s legal representatives applied for possession.
The permission was not shown to be vitiated by fraud, misuse, or the creation of a non-genuine tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 is a self-contained exception to Section 14 and is to be construed strictly against attempts to frustrate its purpose. Under Section 2(e), a landlord is the person for the time being receiving, or entitled to receive, rent. Section 21 concerns both the creation of a permitted fixed-term tenancy and the recovery of possession after its expiry; the landlord’s non-requirement of the premises supports the grant of permission, but does not determine who may seek possession later. The right to possession arises from the tenant’s failure to vacate when the term ends. The Court relied on S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna, V.S. Rahe v. Smt. Rem Chambeh, and Shiv Chand Kapoor v. Amar Bose concerning grounds on which permission may be challenged.
members.conclusion: The landlord’s legal representatives could apply for and obtain possession after the tenancy period expired.

rule.if: limited_term_rent_control_possession_case and controller_approved_written_fixed_term_lease and original_landlord_died_before_term_expired and tenant_failed_to_vacate_after_term and successors_entitled_to_receive_rent and permission_not_invalidated

predicates.limited_term_rent_control_possession_cas: The proceeding seeks possession after a fixed-term tenancy created under a rent-control procedure.
predicates.controller_approved_written_fixed_term_l: The landlord and tenant made a written fixed-term lease after the relevant authority approved it.
predicates.original_landlord_died_before_term_expir: The landlord who obtained approval died before the agreed tenancy period ended.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_vacate_after_term: The tenant remained in the premises after the agreed tenancy period ended.
predicates.successors_entitled_to_receive_rent: After the landlord’s death, the landlord’s successors were entitled to receive rent for the premises.
predicates.permission_not_invalidated: The approval was not set aside or shown to be tainted by fraud, misuse, or a non-genuine tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A possession proceeding based on a tenant’s failure to vacate after a fixed-term tenancy does not abate merely because the landlord who obtained permission died.
material_facts: The landlord obtained permission to create a tenancy for a limited period and died before that period expired.
The tenant failed to vacate when the agreed period ended.
The possession claim was based on the tenant’s failure to vacate after expiry, rather than on the deceased landlord’s personal need for the premises.
members.legal_principle: The maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona generally concerns specified personal actions, such as certain claims for damages, and does not apply to proceedings under rent-control legislation of this kind. An eviction action abates only when its cause of action does not survive. The cause for permission arose from the landlord’s non-requirement of the premises during the agreed period, while the cause for possession arose from the tenant’s failure to vacate after that period. The Court relied on Supreme Bank v. P.A. Tendulkar, Phool Rani v. Naubat Rai, and Shanti Lal Thakur Das v. Chaman Lal Magan Lal Telwala.
members.conclusion: The proceeding did not abate on the landlord’s death because the cause of action survived; the doctrine that a personal action dies with the person did not apply.

predicates.rent_control_fixed_term_possession_case: The proceeding seeks possession under rent-control rules after a tenancy for a fixed period.
predicates.original_landlord_died_before_term_expir: The landlord who obtained permission died before the agreed tenancy period ended.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_vacate_after_term: The tenant remained in the premises after the agreed tenancy period ended.
predicates.possession_claim_based_on_post_expiry_no: The claim for possession arose from the tenant’s failure to leave after the agreed period, not from the landlord’s personal need.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition-amount framework is not invalid merely because its payment may be inadequate if, properly construed, it provides a non-arbitrary and non-illusory amount determined through a just-and-reasonable assessment.
material_facts: The legislation provided for an arbitrator to determine the amount payable where agreement was not reached.
The arbitrator was required to determine an amount appearing just and reasonable, considering the circumstances and the scheduled guidance so far as applicable.
The legislation provided for an appeal from the arbitrator’s award to the High Court.
The Court construed the schedule as guidance for the arbitrator rather than an inflexible limit on the amount.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as considered in Kesavananda Bharati, does not permit an amount to be wholly arbitrary or illusory, but does not allow a challenge merely because the amount is inadequate. The Court considered State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India, State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas, and Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India in explaining the constitutional history and effect of the Twenty-fifth Amendment. Reading the amount provisions together, the arbitrator must decide what is just and reasonable on the circumstances, keeping the schedule in mind without being bound to apply it as a fixed measure; “having regard to” makes the schedule a guide, not a fetter. Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. Union of India, Illingworth v. Walmsley, and Perry v. Wright were relied on in construing that expression.
members.conclusion: On the Court’s construction, the amount provisions were not wholly arbitrary or illusory and did not invalidate the law under Article 31(2); inadequacy alone was not a ground for invalidation.

predicates.acquisition_amount_challenge: A party challenged the amount payable for property compulsorily taken.
predicates.amount_framework_provides_independent_as: The payment framework authorizes an independent decision-maker to assess the amount payable.
predicates.arbitrator_must_determine_a_just_and_rea: The decision-maker must determine an amount considered just and reasonable in the circumstances.
predicates.amount_is_not_wholly_arbitrary_or_illuso: The amount framework does not produce a wholly arbitrary or illusory return for the property taken.
predicates.amount_framework_is_not_invalid_merely_f: The amount framework is not invalid merely because the amount may be inadequate.

members.legal_issue: A statutory principle for determining an acquisition amount is valid if it is relevant to the acquisition and is not illusory, even though the resulting amount need not be adequate.
material_facts: The law provided for an amount based on the average net annual income received from the relevant mineral products before vesting.
The claimants argued that the amount was not equivalent to the value of the rights taken and was illusory.
The Court found the income-based principle relevant to determining the amount and the resulting amount not illusory.
members.legal_principle: After the constitutional changes that removed the former compensation guarantee, courts may review whether the principles used to determine an acquisition amount are relevant and whether the amount is illusory, but they may not review adequacy. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, Achutananda Purohit v. State of Orissa, State of Maharashtra v. Basantibai Mohanlal Khetan, and Tinsukhia Electric Supply Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam.
members.conclusion: The statutory principle for determining the amount was valid; its adequacy could not be challenged in court.

rule.if: challenge_to_acquisition_amount and amount_uses_property_related_income_principle and principle_is_relevant and amount_is_not_illusory

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_amount: A litigant challenged the principle used to determine the amount payable for acquired property.
predicates.amount_uses_property_related_income_prin: The amount is determined by reference to income derived from the property or resource before it was taken.
predicates.principle_is_relevant: The chosen principle has a rational connection to determining the amount payable for the property or resource.
predicates.amount_is_not_illusory: The amount produced by the principle is not merely nominal or illusory.

members.legal_issue: A statutory maximum on the amount payable for acquired excess vacant land is not unconstitutional when the amount is not illusory or confiscatory.
material_facts: The law prescribed principles for calculating the amount payable when excess vacant land was acquired and imposed a maximum amount payable in any case.
The petitioners argued that the maximum was arbitrary and illusory because it did not vary with the full extent or market value of the land acquired.
The Court held that the maximum amount was not merely nominal or confiscatory.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as amended by the Twenty-fifth Amendment, made the adequacy of the amount payable non-justiciable; the Court nevertheless considered whether the amount was illusory. The Court relied on the approach to Article 31(2) in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd., and State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy.
members.conclusion: The maximum amount payable is valid and does not violate Articles 14 or 31(2).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_a: A proceeding challenges the constitutionality of the amount payable for compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.law_sets_payment_principles_and_a_maximu: The law specifies a method or principles for calculating payment and also sets a maximum payable amount.
predicates.maximum_amount_is_not_merely_nominal: The amount payable under the maximum is not merely nominal or illusory.

members.legal_issue: A statutory maximum amount payable for acquired excess vacant land is valid when the amount is not illusory or confiscatory.
material_facts: The law set principles for calculating the amount payable for acquired excess vacant land and imposed a maximum payable in any case.
The maximum could be lower than the market value of a large holding, but the Court considered the prescribed amount substantial rather than fictitious or nominal.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as altered by the Twenty-fifth Amendment, permits an amount to be fixed by law and bars a challenge merely that the amount is inadequate; the amount must not be illusory. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd., and State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, and considered the maximum amount substantial in light of the social context. Justice Iyer also reasoned that a ceiling on the maximum is not discriminatory unless the maximum itself is a hoax or trivial.
members.conclusion: The maximum amount provision was valid and was neither illusory nor confiscatory.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A litigant challenges a legal maximum on payment for property acquired by the State.
predicates.law_sets_a_maximum_payment_for_acquired_: The law fixes a maximum amount payable for property acquired under it, even where the property's value may exceed that maximum.
predicates.maximum_payment_is_substantial_rather_th: The maximum amount is more than a fictitious or merely nominal payment.

members.legal_issue: Lowering a ceiling under a later law does not require market-value compensation for the difference from the ceiling under an earlier law.
material_facts: The earlier Act fixed a ceiling that was higher than the ceiling fixed by the amending Act.
The petitioners argued that the reduction required compensation at market value for the difference between the two ceilings.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed the phrase “ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force” in the second proviso to Article 31A(1) as referring to the ceiling imposed by the law fixing the applicable limit, not an earlier law that had been amended or repealed.
members.conclusion: The reduction of the ceiling did not attract the second proviso to Article 31A(1), and compensation for the difference between the earlier and later ceilings was not required.

predicates.challenge_to_reduced_land_ceiling: A landholder challenged a lower ceiling imposed by a later land-reform law.
predicates.later_law_replaced_earlier_ceiling: A later law replaced the ceiling imposed by an earlier law.
predicates.compensation_claim_rests_on_difference_b: The landholder sought compensation on the ground that the later ceiling was lower than the earlier ceiling.

members.legal_issue: Reducing the ceiling limit and acquiring land above the newly applicable limit does not violate the constitutional compensation protection for land within the ceiling.
material_facts: The amended law reduced the ceiling limit and required surrender of land exceeding the new limit.
The land in question exceeded the new limit, although it had been within the limit under the earlier law.
The amended ceiling was not challenged as beyond legislative competence, and it was not contended that the legislature was barred from reducing the earlier ceiling.
members.legal_principle: Under the second proviso to Article 31-A(1), the relevant ceiling is the ceiling under the law for the time being in force. Once a valid amendment replaces the former ceiling, the former ceiling ceases to govern for the future; the compensation protection applies to land within the new applicable ceiling. The Court was not asked to decide whether a law fixing a new ceiling and acquiring the land above it violated another constitutional provision.
members.conclusion: The acquisition of land exceeding the new ceiling did not violate the second proviso to Article 31-A(1) on the ground that it lacked market-value compensation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_reduced_land: A party challenges the constitutionality of reducing a landholding ceiling and requiring surrender of land above it.
predicates.ceiling_reduction_is_not_challenged_as_u: The challenge does not establish that the legislature lacked authority to reduce the former ceiling.
predicates.land_exceeds_new_applicable_ceiling: The land required to be surrendered is above the ceiling limit applicable under the amended law.

members.legal_issue: A revised agricultural ceiling is measured by the ceiling in the law currently in force, and acquisition of surplus land under that ceiling does not require market-value compensation for land within an earlier ceiling.
material_facts: The challenged legislation introduced a new ceiling on agricultural holdings and replaced the earlier ceiling.
Land was to vest in the State only to the extent it exceeded the new ceiling prescribed by the legislation.
members.legal_principle: Article 31A(1), including its second proviso, refers to the ceiling under the law currently in force, not a ceiling under an amended or repealed earlier law. Kunjukutty v. State of Kerala and Malankara Rubber and Produce Co. v. State of Kerala applied that principle. The Court also treated the legislation as agrarian reform protected by Article 31A and, independently, by Article 31B because it was included in the Ninth Schedule; Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala was referred to in connection with the validity of a Ninth Schedule amendment.
members.conclusion: The new ceiling was the ceiling applicable under the law for the time being in force. The second proviso to Article 31A(1) did not require market-value compensation by reference to the earlier ceiling, and the legislation was protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.new_ceiling_is_current_law: The legislature replaces an earlier agricultural ceiling with a new ceiling that is in force when the acquisition occurs.
predicates.acquisition_is_confined_to_land_exceedin: The State acquires only land exceeding the ceiling prescribed by the new law.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional protection concerning land under personal cultivation within the applicable ceiling does not require compensation to be valued on the date of award or possession for land acquired for planned urban development.
material_facts: The land was acquired for planned development rather than agrarian reform.
Some landowners asserted that their land was personally cultivated and within the applicable ceiling limit.
They argued that compensation should reflect the market value when the award was made or possession was taken rather than when the acquisition notification was published.
members.legal_principle: Sections 11(1) and 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for market value by reference to the date of publication of the acquisition notification. The Court held that Article 31-A concerns agrarian reform and does not govern acquisition for planned urban development. It relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, P.V. Mudaliar v. Deputy Collector, Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, Vajravelu v. Special Deputy Collector, and Ram Chand v. Union of India. The second proviso to Article 31-A requires market-value compensation where it applies, but does not shift the valuation date prescribed by the Act in this acquisition.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was not invalid on this ground, and the applicable market value was the value on the date of publication of the acquisition notification.

rule.if: compensation_challenge and acquisition_for_planned_urban_development and acquisition_not_for_agrarian_reform and compensation_value_claimed_at_award_or_possession

predicates.compensation_challenge: The proceeding challenges the basis or amount of compensation for a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_for_planned_urban_developmen: The land was acquired for planned urban development.
predicates.acquisition_not_for_agrarian_reform: The acquisition was not for agrarian reform.
predicates.compensation_value_claimed_at_award_or_p: The landowner seeks valuation by reference to the award or taking of possession rather than the acquisition notification.

members.legal_issue: Limiting additional compensation to the legislatively specified transitional categories does not violate the constitutional guarantee concerning acquisition of certain agricultural land.
material_facts: It was argued that excluding acquisitions with Collector’s awards made before the transitional cutoff would leave compensation below the market value at the time possession was taken.
The challenge relied on the constitutional proviso concerning acquisition of land held under personal cultivation.
The legislation under which the land was acquired was pre-constitutional general land-acquisition legislation, not legislation relating to agrarian reform.
members.legal_principle: The second proviso to Article 31-A(1) concerns laws providing for agrarian reform. The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is not such a law; it is pre-constitutional legislation saved by Article 31(5)(a). Accordingly, Article 31-A does not govern the interpretation of Section 23(1-A) or Section 30(1) of the amending legislation. The Court relied on Atma Ram v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The constitutional guarantee concerning acquisition of agricultural land did not affect the interpretation of the additional-compensation provisions, and the transitional limitation did not violate that guarantee.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The matter concerns compensation for land acquired through a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.acquisition_under_general_preconstitutio: The land was acquired under a general acquisition law enacted before the Constitution and not as part of agrarian reform.
predicates.claimant_invokes_agricultural_land_guara: The claimant argues that limiting compensation violates the constitutional protection concerning certain agricultural land.

members.legal_issue: The statutory scheme for regulating excess vacant land does not violate the constitutional protection against acquisition of agricultural land without compensation at market value.
material_facts: The appellants challenged provisions of the land-ceiling statute under the constitutional protection concerning acquisition of agricultural land.
The land declared excess was treated as excess vacant land, rather than agricultural land acquired by the State.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the second proviso to Article 31-A(1) of the Constitution and on Maharao Saheb Shri Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, which had upheld the statute's validity. The second-proviso argument did not apply because the State took excess vacant land, not agricultural land.
members.conclusion: The constitutional challenge was rejected because the statute's validity had already been upheld and the compensation argument was misconceived in relation to excess vacant land.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_ceiling: The party challenged the constitutionality of a statutory scheme regulating excess land.
predicates.excess_land_is_vacant_land: The land taken by the State was treated as excess vacant land rather than agricultural land.
predicates.prior_binding_upholding_of_scheme: A prior binding decision had upheld the validity of the challenged statutory scheme.

members.legal_issue: An apology does not warrant discharge from criminal contempt when it is not genuine, while the court may impose a fine instead of further substantive imprisonment in light of custody already served and subsequent delivery of possession.
material_facts: The tenant offered an unconditional apology but had earlier made a similar apology while continuing to falsely claim that possession had been delivered.
The tenant had been in custody for some days following his arrest and was later released on bail.
Vacant possession was ultimately delivered to the landlord’s representative.
members.legal_principle: The court may reject an apology that is not genuine and bona fide. In deciding the punishment, the court considered the tenant’s custody already served and the fact that possession had since been delivered, while imposing a fine also to deter others from filing false affidavits.
members.conclusion: The court found the apology not genuine and imposed a fine, with simple imprisonment in default of payment, rather than sending the tenant back to prison; the fine, if realised, was payable to the petitioner as compensation.

rule.if: criminal_contempt_found and apology_not_genuine and contemnor_already_spent_time_in_custody and possession_later_delivered

predicates.criminal_contempt_found: The court has found the litigant guilty of criminal contempt.
predicates.apology_not_genuine: The litigant’s apology is contradicted by continued false statements or other conduct showing it is not bona fide.
predicates.contemnor_already_spent_time_in_custody: The contemnor has already spent some time in custody in connection with the proceedings.
predicates.possession_later_delivered: Vacant possession is eventually delivered after the contemptuous conduct.

members.legal_issue: A tactical or insincere apology does not excuse serious deliberate contempt, and imprisonment may be imposed when a fine would not meet the ends of justice.
material_facts: The respondents tendered an unconditional apology but did so after defending their transactions and when contempt proceedings were under way.
The court found that the apology was a tactical move rather than an expression of genuine contrition.
The court considered the respondents’ deliberate violation of clear orders serious and concluded that a fine would not meet the ends of justice.
members.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 provides for punishment for contempt and permits discharge or remission on an apology satisfactory to the court; its explanation does not require rejection of an apology merely because it is qualified or conditional if it is bona fide. Section 12(3) permits detention in civil prison when a fine will not meet the ends of justice and imprisonment is necessary. Hiren Bose, Re; M.Y. Shareaf v. Hon’ble Judges of the High Court of Nagpur; M.B. Sanghi v. High Court of Punjab & Haryana; T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Ashok Khot; and L.D. Jaikwal v. State of U.P. establish that an apology is not a defence to be used to purge guilt and must reflect genuine contrition. Article 129 of the Constitution recognizes the Supreme Court’s power to punish contempt of itself; Section 94(c) and Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure address disobedience of interim orders and its consequences.
members.conclusion: The court rejected the apology, found the respondents guilty under the applicable contempt provisions, and imposed simple imprisonment.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and serious_deliberate_breach and apology_not_genuine and fine_insufficient

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A proceeding asks the court to punish a person for civil contempt.
predicates.serious_deliberate_breach: The person knowingly and deliberately commits a serious breach of a court order.
predicates.apology_not_genuine: The apology is not a genuine expression of contrition and is instead offered as a tactic to avoid consequences.
predicates.fine_insufficient: The court determines that a fine would not adequately serve the ends of justice.

members.legal_issue: A court may reject an apology for contempt when it is qualified by a defence of the conduct or when the contemnor’s conduct shows persistent disregard for the court’s orders.
material_facts: The respondent tendered an apology while asserting that any breach resulted from mistake, inadvertence, or misunderstanding.
In the same affidavit, the respondent repeated the arguments defending the conduct that the Court had rejected.
The Court found that the respondent had persistently flouted its orders and treated the Court’s authority with disregard.
members.legal_principle: The Court may decline to accept an apology in contempt proceedings where it is not genuine and unconditional or where the contemnor’s conduct makes acceptance inappropriate. No statutory provision or earlier case was identified as the basis for this part of the ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the apology, finding it was not truly unconditional and that the respondent’s conduct would warrant rejection even if it were treated as unconditional.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The proceeding asked the court to determine and address alleged disobedience of a court order.
predicates.apology_qualified_by_defence: The contemnor tendered an apology while continuing to defend the conduct said to breach the order.
predicates.conduct_showed_persistent_disregard: The contemnor’s conduct showed repeated disregard for the court’s orders.

members.legal_issue: A person charged with contempt cannot maintain both that the conduct was justified and that an apology should excuse it.
material_facts: The officials argued that they were justified in acting without official communication of the extended order.
They also offered an apology if their conduct was found improper.
members.legal_principle: In contempt proceedings, justification and apology cannot both be maintained. The Court relied on M. Y. Shareef v. The Hon'ble Judges of the High Court of Nagpur.
members.conclusion: The officials could not rely on both justification and apology.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The case is a proceeding alleging contempt through disobedience of a court order.
predicates.justification_asserted: The person charged contends that the conduct alleged to be contemptuous was justified.
predicates.apology_offered: The person charged offers an apology for the conduct alleged to be contemptuous.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide conditional apology may be accepted after a finding of contempt, resulting in discharge of the rule against the contemnor.
material_facts: The operator tendered a conditional apology, asking to be pardoned if the court found that he had committed contempt.
The court accepted that the apology was bona fide.
members.legal_principle: The Explanation to Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, states that an apology must not be rejected merely because it is qualified or conditional if it is made bona fide.
members.conclusion: The court accepted the apology and discharged the rule against the operator.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter is an application alleging that persons disobeyed a court judgment.
predicates.apology_was_conditional: The person tendered an apology that was expressly conditional on the court finding contempt.
predicates.apology_was_bona_fide: The court found that the apology was made in good faith.
predicates.conditional_apology_accepted_and_rule_di: The court accepts the conditional apology and discharges the rule against the person.

members.legal_issue: A contempt notice alleging delayed implementation of court directions may be discharged after the directions have been complied with and unqualified apologies have been tendered.
material_facts: The Court directed that an employee not be evicted from his government accommodation, be restored to it if already evicted, and be reinstated in service.
The employee was evicted and the directions were not implemented promptly; the responsible officer attributed the delay to communication delays, administrative bottlenecks, and security reasons.
The employee was later reinstated, given similar accommodation, and provided for the rent he had paid for private accommodation.
The respondents tendered unqualified apologies.

There was some material that might have shown the responsible officer knew of the order before the eviction, and an allegation that local officers resented the filing of the writ petition, but the Court declined to investigate these matters further in view of subsequent compliance and the apologies.
members.legal_principle: Court directions must be obeyed by everyone within the framework of the Rule of Law, including public officers, and failure to comply may warrant punishment. In this case, the Court did not pursue the alleged contempt further because there had been compliance and the respondents had tendered unqualified apologies. The judgment’s headnote identifies sections 2 and 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; it relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Court accepted the respondents’ unqualified apologies and discharged the contempt notice. It also directed the responsible officer to pay the petitioners the costs of the proceedings.

predicates.contempt_proceeding_alleges_disobedience: A party initiates a contempt proceeding alleging that a court direction was disobeyed.
predicates.court_direction_was_not_timely_implement: The persons responsible did not implement a court direction when required.
predicates.subsequent_compliance: The persons responsible later implemented the court direction.
predicates.respondents_tendered_unqualified_apologi: The respondents tendered apologies without qualification.
predicates.contempt_notice_discharged: The court discharges the contempt notice.

members.legal_issue: A court may accept an unconditional apology and discharge notices concerning breach of an undertaking when the undertaking is later fulfilled before the relevant event.
material_facts: The respondents undertook through counsel to furnish security within a specified time but did not do so within that time.

After notices issued asking why they should not be punished for breaching the undertaking, the respondents appeared personally, tendered an unconditional apology, and filed an affidavit explaining the delay.
The respondents ultimately furnished security before the announced date of the reauction.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted the apology in light of the circumstances explained in the affidavit and the respondents’ eventual compliance before the reauction. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this disposition.
members.conclusion: The Court accepted the unconditional apology and discharged the notices.

rule.if: contempt_notice_for_breach_of_court_undertaking and undertaking_deadline_missed and later_compliance_before_relevant_event and unconditional_apology

predicates.contempt_notice_for_breach_of_court_unde: A court issued a notice asking a person to show why they should not be punished for breaching an undertaking given to that court.
predicates.undertaking_deadline_missed: The person did not perform the undertaking within the time specified.
predicates.later_compliance_before_relevant_event: The person performed the undertaking before the event for which performance was required.
predicates.unconditional_apology: The person appeared before the court and offered an apology without conditions.

members.legal_issue: Scandalizing a judicial officer in connection with the performance of judicial functions can substantially interfere with or tend substantially to interfere with the due course of justice and therefore be punishable.
material_facts: The appellant recklessly imputed malice and lack of good faith to the judicial officer who had decided cases against him.
The imputations were unsupported and scandalous, and the appellant did not retract them or show remorse.
The notice attacked the officer in relation to the discharge of judicial functions.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 prohibits imposing a sentence unless the contempt is of such a nature that it substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice. The Court held that scandalizing a judicial officer in relation to judicial functions satisfies that threshold because the due course of justice is a facet of the broader administration of justice.
members.conclusion: The contempt substantially interfered or tended substantially to interfere with the due course of justice and was punishable under section 13.

predicates.contempt_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for contempt arising from a communication about a judicial officer.
predicates.scandalizing_conduct_targets_judicial_fu: The contemptuous conduct scandalizes a judicial officer in relation to the performance of judicial functions.
predicates.conduct_substantially_impairs_or_tends_t: The conduct substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice.
predicates.contempt_is_punishable: The contempt may be punished by a court.

members.legal_issue: A contempt finding may be punished only where the contempt substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice, and that threshold is met by publication likely to undermine confidence in the fairness of the courts.
material_facts: The pamphlet accused a judge of having prejudged the case and deliberately reaching a conviction despite there being no evidence.

The criticism was published by a practising lawyer in a small rural community where litigants were largely illiterate or poorly educated and were especially susceptible to doubts about a judge's impartiality.
The Court agreed that the publication was likely to cause litigants to lose confidence in the administration of justice.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 bars punishment unless the contempt substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice. The Court treated likely damage to public confidence in the fairness and impartiality of courts, in the circumstances of the audience and setting, as satisfying that threshold. It applied the principles in Perspective Publications Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra and referred to Baradakanta v. Registrar, Orissa High Court.
members.conclusion: The contempt was of a nature that substantially interfered, or tended substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice, so the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 13.

predicates.criminal_contempt_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a finding of criminal contempt.
predicates.contemptuous_publication: The contemnor published material that scandalised or tended to scandalise a court or judge.
predicates.likely_substantial_interference_with_due: The publication was likely substantially to impair the fair administration of justice, including by undermining litigants' confidence in the courts.

members.legal_issue: A court may impose punishment for contempt only when the conduct substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice, and an unconditional apology does not necessarily excuse such conduct.
material_facts: The Court found that the affidavit contained a deliberate falsehood, but the statement was made in an application for clarification after the transfer order had already been made.
The Court found no definite advantage had been gained through the statement and treated that circumstance as relevant to punishment, not to whether contempt had been committed.
The respondents tendered an unconditional apology.
The Court considered the false sworn statement sufficiently serious to warrant punishment and imposed a fine on each respondent.
members.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 bars punishment unless the contempt substantially interferes, or tends substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice. Rachapudi Subba Rao v. Advocate General, Andhra Pradesh was cited on the scope of that requirement; Legal Remembrancer v. Martial Ghose and Attorney-General v. Times Newspapers Ltd. were cited for the distinction between technical contempt and conduct warranting punishment. Whether a contemnor gained an advantage is immaterial to commission of the offence but relevant to punishment. The Court held that an unconditional apology did not, in the circumstances, exonerate the respondents.
members.conclusion: The apology did not exonerate the respondents; the Court imposed a fine on each of them, with imprisonment in default of payment.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and contemnor_found_guilty and conduct_substantially_interfered_with_justice and unconditional_apology_tendered

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A proceeding was brought before a court alleging contempt.
predicates.contemnor_found_guilty: The court found the person guilty of contempt.
predicates.conduct_substantially_interfered_with_ju: The court found that the contempt substantially interfered, or tended substantially to interfere, with the due course of justice.
predicates.unconditional_apology_tendered: The person tendered an unconditional apology to the court.

members.legal_issue: An unsupported, malicious attack on a judge’s integrity and impartiality in performing judicial functions can scandalize the court and constitute criminal contempt.
material_facts: After losing suits, the appellant sent the deciding judicial officer a notice accusing the officer of inventing facts and intentionally manipulating evidence to help the opposing party.
The notice alleged bad faith, malice, partiality, and dishonesty without providing supporting particulars, and threatened a damages claim.
The notice was sent while execution proceedings and an application to stay execution were pending.
The appellant continued to defend the allegations and did not express contrition.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(c)(i) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 covers conduct that scandalizes or tends to scandalize, or lowers or tends to lower, a court’s authority. Section 2(c)(ii) covers conduct that prejudices or interferes or tends to interfere with the due course of a judicial proceeding. The Court held that unfounded imputations of mala fides, bias, or dishonesty against a judge, including in relation to decided matters, can undermine public confidence and amount to criminal contempt under section 2(c)(i); interference with a pending judicial proceeding can also bring conduct within section 2(c)(ii).
members.conclusion: The notice was a deliberate attempt to scandalize and embarrass the judicial officer and lower the authority of the court, and its issuance constituted criminal contempt.

rule.if: contempt_appeal and communication_attacks_judicial_integrity and accusations_are_unsupported and communication_is_calculated_to_discredit_the_court

predicates.contempt_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for contempt arising from a communication about a judicial officer.
predicates.communication_attacks_judicial_integrity: A person communicated allegations that a judicial officer acted dishonestly, maliciously, or partially in performing judicial functions.
predicates.accusations_are_unsupported: The person provided no adequate factual basis for the allegations.
predicates.communication_is_calculated_to_discredit: The communication is intended or likely to bring the judicial officer and the court into disrespect or disrepute.

members.legal_issue: Publication imputing deliberate bias and prejudgment to a judicial officer, in a setting where it is likely to undermine public confidence in the administration of justice, constitutes criminal contempt rather than fair criticism.
material_facts: A practising advocate published a pamphlet criticizing a judicial decision after the decision had been reversed on appeal.

The pamphlet described the judge as having a wayward mind and suggested that he had deliberately changed the course of his reasoning because he had already resolved to convict despite there being no evidence.

The criticism was directed at the only or one of very few courts serving a rural area where many litigants were illiterate or poorly educated, and the author was a lawyer whose views would attract particular attention.
members.legal_principle: Fair and reasonable criticism of a judicial act is protected by the freedom of speech in Article 19(1)(a) and reflected in section 5 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Criticism may identify errors of fact or law, but attributing improper motives, bias, or prejudgment to a judge is not fair criticism when it is likely to impair public confidence or interfere with the administration of justice. Contempt jurisdiction must be exercised sparingly and with restraint. The Court applied Perspective Publications Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra and referred to Baradakanta v. Registrar, Orissa High Court; Queen v. Gray; Regina v. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis, ex parte Blackburn; and Andre Paul v. Attorney-General.
members.conclusion: The publication scandalised or tended to scandalise the court and substantially interfered with the due course of justice; the contempt conviction was upheld.

rule.if: criminal_contempt_appeal and criticism_of_judicial_act and imputation_of_judicial_motive_or_prejudgment and likely_damage_to_public_confidence

predicates.criminal_contempt_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a finding of criminal contempt.
predicates.criticism_of_judicial_act: The publisher publicly criticized a judicial decision or the conduct of a judge in deciding a case.
predicates.imputation_of_judicial_motive_or_prejudg: The criticism attributed a deliberate improper motive, bias, or prejudgment to the judge.
predicates.likely_damage_to_public_confidence: The publication was likely, in its audience and setting, to weaken confidence in the fairness or integrity of the administration of justice.

members.legal_issue: A possession-recovery suit filed within twelve years after redemption of the mortgage is not barred by limitation on the ground that the claimant was not in possession during that period.
material_facts: The mortgage was redeemed in 1943.
The suit was instituted within twelve years of redemption.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the twelve-year limitation period to the claim and held that the period was satisfied because the suit was brought within twelve years of redemption; no earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation.

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: A claimant brought a suit to recover possession of land.
predicates.claim_follows_mortgage_redemption: The claim to recover possession followed redemption of a mortgage under which the occupants had possessed the land.
predicates.suit_filed_within_applicable_limitation_: The claimant filed the suit within the applicable limitation period measured from the relevant event.

members.legal_issue: Possession is presumed to continue until dispossession, so a possession suit is within limitation when the claimant’s possession continued until the defendant dispossessed the claimant within the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The courts below found that the plaintiff had been in possession during the lifetime of the female donee and continued in possession afterward.
Even if the tenant left the house and the plaintiff did not lock it, there was no established earlier dispossession; the defendant later entered into possession.
The suit was filed within twelve years of the defendant’s entry into possession.
members.legal_principle: The law presumes continuity of possession. If a person’s possession is established, it is presumed to continue until that person is dispossessed.
members.conclusion: The suit was within limitation, and there was no valid ground to disturb the concurrent finding on possession.

rule.if: civil_possession_suit and claimant_possession_established and no_earlier_dispossession_proved and suit_filed_within_limitation_period_after_dispossession

predicates.civil_possession_suit: A claimant brings a civil suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.claimant_possession_established: The claimant’s possession of the property is established.
predicates.no_earlier_dispossession_proved: No dispossession of the claimant before the defendant’s entry is proved.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_period_afte: The claimant files suit within the applicable limitation period after the defendant dispossesses the claimant.

members.legal_issue: A possession suit is not barred by limitation when the affirmed finding is that the defendants began possession only recently enough for the suit to be timely.
material_facts: The Additional Commissioner found that the appellants took possession of the properties only in 1950.
The Board of Revenue treated that finding as a finding of fact binding on it and agreed with the Additional Commissioner’s conclusions.
The appellants’ contention that inadmissible evidence supported the possession finding had not been raised before the Board of Revenue.
The Supreme Court found ample evidence supporting the possession finding and held that, on that finding, the suit was within time.
members.legal_principle: The court accepted the affirmed factual finding about when possession began and concluded that the suit was timely on that basis. It also held that the High Court should not entertain an evidentiary objection that had not been raised before the Board of Revenue. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The suit was within time and was not barred by limitation.

rule.if: tenancy_possession_suit and possession_began_recently_enough_for_suit and possession_finding_supported_by_evidence and evidence_objection_not_raised_before_tribunal

predicates.tenancy_possession_suit: A claimant brought a tenancy proceeding seeking possession of property held by another person.
predicates.possession_began_recently_enough_for_sui: The defendants’ possession began only recently enough that the possession finding made the claimant’s suit timely.
predicates.possession_finding_supported_by_evidence: The finding about when possession began was supported by evidence.
predicates.evidence_objection_not_raised_before_tri: The party challenging the evidence did not raise that objection before the tribunal whose decision was challenged.

members.legal_issue: A suit for recovery is not barred by limitation where the trial court found possession within the applicable limitation period and that finding is not shown to lack evidentiary support.
material_facts: The trial judge expressly found that the plaintiff had been in possession of the disputed land, including the land containing the mines, within the applicable limitation period.
The finding was not shown to have been challenged before the High Court.
The appellant did not contend that there was no evidence supporting possession within the applicable period.
members.legal_principle: For the limitation contention raised under Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, the Court relied on the trial court’s finding of possession and the absence of a showing that the finding lacked evidentiary support. The judgment did not disturb that finding where it had not been challenged before the High Court and the appellant did not establish that there was no evidence for it.
members.conclusion: The limitation plea was rejected because the finding of possession within the applicable period stood and was not shown to be unsupported by evidence.

rule.if: civil_appeal and recovery_suit and trial_court_found_possession_within_applicable_period and finding_not_shown_to_lack_evidence

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal challenging a limitation ruling in a suit for recovery.
predicates.recovery_suit: The underlying suit sought recovery of possession of disputed land.
predicates.trial_court_found_possession_within_appl: The trial court found that the claimant had possessed the disputed land within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.finding_not_shown_to_lack_evidence: The finding was not shown to have been challenged below or to lack evidentiary support.

members.legal_issue: A person suing for possession on the basis of prior possession after the summary remedy period has expired cannot recover possession from a defendant who proves a subsisting title to the property.
material_facts: The plaintiff was dispossessed while a temporary injunction was in force and later sought to amend the suit to claim possession after the summary remedy period had expired.
The suit was therefore considered as a regular suit based on possessory title.
The institution proved that it had title to the land and that its title had not been extinguished.
members.legal_principle: Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander holds that, after the time for a summary possession suit has expired, a dispossessed plaintiff may still sue on prior possession, but the defendant may establish title and remain in possession if that title is proved. The Court also relied on Sections 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, Asher v. Whitlock, and Perry v. Clissold.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff could not recover possession on the basis of prior possession because the institution proved its subsisting title and was entitled to retain possession.

predicates.regular_possession_suit_based_on_prior_p: The proceeding is a regular suit seeking possession on the basis of the plaintiff’s prior possession.
predicates.plaintiff_was_dispossessed: The plaintiff had possession and was later put out of possession by another person.
predicates.summary_possession_remedy_period_expired: The plaintiff sought possession after the period for the summary remedy had expired.
predicates.defendant_proves_subsisting_property_tit: The defendant establishes a valid title to the property that remains in force.

members.legal_issue: A suit for possession based on prior possession is maintainable after the summary possessory remedy’s short filing period has expired, unless the defendant establishes a better title or right to possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued for possession after being dispossessed from land he had previously possessed.
The suit was not brought under the summary remedy corresponding to section 9 of the Specific Relief Act; it was a regular suit for possession.
The Society argued that, after the summary remedy’s six-month period, a suit based on possession alone was incompetent.
Neither party established title to the disputed land, and the Society did not establish a right to possession derived from the State for the period before its later lease.
members.legal_principle: Sections 8 and 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and the corresponding Travancore provisions, provide distinct remedies; section 8 prescribes use of the Code of Civil Procedure and does not bar a regular suit based on prior possession. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars only suits whose cognizance is expressly or impliedly excluded. Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, distinguish a possession-based suit from a title-based suit and were described as declaratory of the law. The Court relied on Mustapha Sahib v. Santha Pillai and Kuttan Narayaman v. Thomman Mathai, and considered Ram Harakh Rai v. Scheodihal Joti and the Allahabad Full Bench decision in Lachman v. Shambu Narain.
members.conclusion: The suit was competent on the basis of prior possession, subject to the defendant’s ability to establish a better title or right to possession.

rule.if: regular_possession_suit and claimant_previously_possessed_land and claimant_dispossessed_by_defendant and suit_within_applicable_limitation and not defendant_establishes_better_right_to_possession

predicates.regular_possession_suit: The claimant brought a regular civil suit seeking possession rather than relying solely on a summary possessory remedy.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_land: The claimant possessed the disputed land before being dispossessed.
predicates.claimant_dispossessed_by_defendant: The defendant dispossessed the claimant from the disputed land.
predicates.suit_within_applicable_limitation: The claimant brought the suit within the limitation period applicable to the possession claim.
predicates.defendant_establishes_better_right_to_po: The defendant proved a title or other right to possession superior to the claimant’s prior possession.

members.legal_issue: A prior possessor who has not proved ownership may recover possession from a wrongdoer on the strength of possessory title, even when the action is brought more than six months after dispossession.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s ownership of the land was not proved.
The evidence established that the plaintiff possessed the land from about 1930 until about 1945, when the second defendant trespassed and took possession.
The suit for possession was instituted in 1949, more than six months after the dispossession.
The defendants’ claim of title by adverse possession was not established.
members.legal_principle: Under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, the summary remedy is distinct from an ordinary action of ejectment: prior possession is sufficient title against a wrongdoer even when the ejectment action is brought more than six months after dispossession. A trespasser cannot defeat the prior possessor by asserting that title and the right to possession belong to a third person. The Court applied Ismail Ariff v. Mohamed Ghouse and approved Narayana Row v. Dharmachar, Krishnarav Yashvant v. Vasudev Apaji Ghotikar, Singh v. Ramji Das, Wali Ahmad Khan v. Ajudhia Khandu, and Subodh Gopal Bose v. Province of Bihar; it held that the contrary Calcutta decisions in Debi Churn Boldo v. Issur Chunder Manjee, Ertaza Hossein v. Bany Mistry, Purmeshur Chowdhry v. Brijo Lal Chowdhry, and Nisa Chand Gaita v. Kanchiram Bagani did not state the law correctly.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff’s prior possession gave him a sufficient title against the defendants, who had not established that they were lawful owners. The decree for possession was upheld and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: ejectment_action and plaintiff_prior_possession and defendant_wrongdoer and not defendant_lawful_title_established

predicates.ejectment_action: The claimant brought an ordinary action seeking recovery of possession from the person in possession.
predicates.plaintiff_prior_possession: The claimant had possession of the property before being dispossessed.
predicates.defendant_wrongdoer: The person in possession took or retained the property by wrongful dispossession rather than under an established lawful right.
predicates.defendant_lawful_title_established: The person in possession established a lawful title or right to possess the property.
predicates.plaintiff_entitled_to_possession: The claimant is entitled to recover possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: A suit for possession brought within the applicable limitation period after dispossession is not time-barred merely because it began as a suit for declaration of title and was later amended to seek possession.
material_facts: The respondents initially sued for a declaration of title and were dispossessed after filing the suit.
They later amended the plaint to seek possession, and the suit was brought within twelve years of their dispossession.
members.legal_principle: Because the suit was outside the scope of the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, limitation was governed by the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. Article 142 applied to the suit for possession, and the suit was within time because it was filed within twelve years of dispossession.
members.conclusion: The suit for possession was not barred by limitation.

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession_after_disposse: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking possession after being dispossessed of land.
predicates.suit_within_applicable_limitation_period: The claimant brought the suit within the limitation period applicable to the possession claim.

members.legal_issue: A later formal amendment adding a possession prayer is not time-barred where the original suit was timely and already pleaded the termination and failure to surrender possession.
material_facts: The suit was filed in 2001, before the landlord added a formal prayer for possession by amendment.
The original pleading alleged that the tenancy had been terminated and that the tenant had not vacated or handed over possession.
The amendment adding the possession prayer was allowed.
members.legal_principle: The court held that the formal addition of the possession prayer was not time-barred because the suit had already been filed and the original pleading had asserted termination of the tenancy and the failure to deliver possession.
members.conclusion: The amended prayer for possession was not barred by limitation.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding and original_suit_timely and possession_cause_pleaded_in_original_suit and possession_prayer_added_by_amendment

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued an eviction claim against a tenant.
predicates.original_suit_timely: The original suit was filed before the applicable limitation period expired.
predicates.possession_cause_pleaded_in_original_sui: The original pleading alleged facts asserting a right to possession, including termination and non-surrender.
predicates.possession_prayer_added_by_amendment: A formal prayer for possession was added to the suit by amendment.

members.legal_issue: A family member who holds land separately is excluded when calculating the family's additional ceiling allowance, but land acquired in that member's name is treated as family land, and the member is counted, when there is no evidence it was held separately.
material_facts: A family member had acquired land in his own name before the appointed day.
The Tribunal found no evidence that the land had been purchased from his separate funds or treated by him or the family as his separate property.
The Tribunal included the land in the family's holding and counted the member in calculating the family's additional ceiling allowance.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 6 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, a member who holds land separately is not regarded as a family member for the purpose of increasing the family's holding beyond the basic ceiling. If the land is treated as family property, it is included in the family's holding and the member is counted for the additional allowance. The Court relied on section 6 and its proviso.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal correctly treated the land as family property, counted the member, and allowed the corresponding additional ceiling area.

predicates.family_ceiling_determination: The proceeding determines a family's ceiling holding and any additional allowance based on its membership.
predicates.land_acquired_in_member_name: Land was acquired in the name of a member of the family.
predicates.no_evidence_land_held_separately: There is no evidence that the member or family treated the land as the member's separate property.
predicates.land_counted_as_family_property_and_memb: The land is counted as family property and the member is counted in calculating the family's additional allowance.

members.legal_issue: A family member’s separate holding of land does not by itself end that person’s membership of the family or entitle that person to a separate ceiling unit.
material_facts: The heirs’ interests in the family property had become fixed after the male member’s death.
The respondents relied on the separate interests to claim individual ceiling units, but the alleged family settlement was not pressed.
The Court considered the proviso to Section 6 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, concerning a member who separately held land.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(11) and 2(22) of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961 define family and person for the Act’s purposes. The proviso to Section 6 is limited to determining the additional ceiling area available to a family with more than five members and does not generally remove a separate landholder from family membership. The Court’s discussion of joint-family membership also relied on Gowli Buddanna, Sitabai, and N. V. Narendranath.
members.conclusion: The proviso to Section 6 of the Ceiling Act applied only when determining an increase in the family’s ceiling area; it did not establish that a member holding separate land ceased to be a family member for all purposes or gained a separate ceiling unit.

predicates.agricultural_ceiling_proceeding: The dispute concerns the application of an agricultural land ceiling to a family’s landholding.
predicates.family_member_holds_land_separately: A person who is a member of a family holds some land separately.

members.legal_issue: Commutation of hereditary service does not by itself change the tenure of land granted as watan property.
material_facts: The land had been granted as remuneration for hereditary village service, and the parties accepted that the grant was of the soil rather than merely a share of revenue.
Under a commutation settlement, the holder was relieved of the service obligation in return for paying a fixed sum.
No express agreement altering the tenure of the land was established.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 15(1)–(3) of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, the watan comprises the watan property, hereditary office, and attached rights and privileges; an hereditary office retains its character even when its service is no longer demanded. Commutation relieves the service obligation but does not alter the tenure absent an express agreement. Section 22 permits the watan rights to be determined by resumption. The Court relied on Appaji Bapuji v. Keshav Shamrav, (1890) I.L.R. 15 Bom. 13, and Bachharam Datta Patil v. Viswanath Pundalik Patil, [1956] S.C.R. 675.
members.conclusion: The commutation relieved the holder and successors of the service obligation but did not, without an express agreement to that effect, change the land’s watan tenure; the watan and its restrictions continued subject to the settlement.

rule.if: watan_tenure_dispute and land_granted_for_hereditary_service and service_obligation_commuted and not express_tenure_change

predicates.watan_tenure_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land granted for hereditary service retained its special tenure after the service obligation ended.
predicates.land_granted_for_hereditary_service: The land was granted as remuneration for duties attached to a hereditary office.
predicates.service_obligation_commuted: The holder agreed to a settlement under which the holder and successors were relieved of the service obligation.
predicates.express_tenure_change: The settlement expressly changed the tenure of the land.

members.legal_issue: Commutation of the services attached to a watan does not, by itself, convert watan land into the watandar’s private property.
material_facts: Service attached to the hereditary office had been commuted in return for a quit-rent on the land.
The office had not thereby been abolished, and the land remained associated with the hereditary office before the later statutory abolition.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles concerning service commutation under the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, and relied on Collector of South Satara v. Laxman Mahadev Deshpande, which approved the relevant reasoning in Appaji Bapuji v. Keshav Shamrav. It also referred to Bachharam Datta Patil v. Vishwanath Pundalik Patil concerning the State’s power to abolish or resume a watan.
