members.conclusion: Commutation relieved the watandars from performing services but did not convert the land into their private property or make it freely alienable; while the office survived, the land retained its character as watan property.

predicates.watan_services_were_commuted: The holder was relieved from performing the services attached to the watan in return for a payment or quit-rent.
predicates.hereditary_office_survived: The hereditary office was not abolished when the services were commuted.

members.legal_issue: Abolition of an impartible hereditary watan does not extinguish the joint family's right to partition the land when it is converted into ordinary cultivable land.
material_facts: The land had been held hereditarily as watan property, with the watan customarily held in the senior family member's name and succession governed by primogeniture.
The land was abolished as watan and converted into rayatwari land.
The High Court had dismissed the partition suit on the ground that abolition extinguished all rights, including the right to partition.
The Supreme Court relied on a Full Bench ruling and its own earlier decision disapproving that view.
members.legal_principle: The Bombay Inferior Village Watans Abolition Act, 1958 (Bom. Act 1 of 1959), read in light of its scheme, did not extinguish the joint family's rights in the former watan land. The Court followed the Full Bench view in Laxmibai v. Ganesh and relied on Nagesh Bisto Desai and Ors. v. Khando Tirmal Desai and Ors., which disapproved the contrary view in this case and approved the Full Bench approach. The Court also rejected the contention that the distinction between the legislation considered in Nagesh Bisto Desai and the legislation concerning these watans changed the result.
members.conclusion: Abolition did not extinguish the family's right to partition the land; the land enured for the benefit of the joint family and was partible.

predicates.partition_suit_appeal: A party appealed in a partition suit after a higher court reversed a decree granting partition.
predicates.hereditary_watan_land: The land had been held hereditarily as watan property for the benefit of the family.
predicates.abolition_converted_land_to_ordinary_cul: Abolition ended the watan tenure and converted the land into ordinary cultivable land.
predicates.former_watan_land_remains_partible_joint: The former watan land remains joint family property capable of partition.

members.legal_issue: Abolition of a watan and regrant of its land to the holder for the time being extinguish watan-specific incidents but do not extinguish the family’s other rights under personal law.
material_facts: The family estate included lands held as watan property.
The claimant was recognized as the watandar after his father’s death and the lands were regranted to him as occupant after the statutory abolition and resumption.
The other family members claimed interests in the properties as members of the joint family.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4(1) of the Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans Abolition Act, 1950, and sections 4 and 7 of the Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, abolish the watan, resume the land, and provide for regrant. They alter the tenure but do not abrogate personal-law rights unrelated to the watan tenure. The Court relied on Collector of South Satara v. Laxman Mahadev Deshpande and approved the reasoning in Laxmibai Sadashiv Date v. Ganesh Shankar Date and Dhondi Vithoba Koli v. Mahadeo Dagdu Koli.
members.conclusion: The abolition and regrant changed the tenure and character of the land as watan property and extinguished incidents attached to the watan, including impartibility and primogeniture insofar as they were such incidents. They did not extinguish other rights under personal law. If the watan land was joint-family property, its regrant to the holder for the time being enured to the benefit of the entire joint family.

predicates.watan_land_was_joint_family_property: Members of a family held the land as joint-family property before its watan tenure ended.
predicates.watan_land_was_resumed: The land was taken back under a measure abolishing the watan tenure.
predicates.watan_land_was_regranted_to_current_hold: The land was granted again as occupancy land to the person who held the watan at the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: A consolidation notification covering land in dispute abates the entire pending civil proceeding, including an appeal challenging a preliminary decree.
material_facts: A civil suit sought determination of rights and shares in land that fell within the consolidation scheme.
A preliminary decree dismissing the suit was challenged in a pending title appeal when a consolidation notification covering the area had been issued.

An application seeking abatement under the consolidation law was filed, but the appellate court treated the matter as abated for non-substitution of a deceased respondent rather than deciding the statutory abatement issue.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 4(c) of the Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956 provide for abatement of pending proceedings concerning rights or interests in land brought within consolidation, so that consolidation authorities can adjudicate those claims without impediment. Statutory abatement under this scheme differs from abatement under the Code of Civil Procedure: it nullifies the civil proceeding as a whole, not merely the pending appeal. The Court applied Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh, Chattar Singh v. Thakur Prasad Singh, Satyanarayan Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar, and Mst. Bibi Rahmani Khatoon v. Harkoo Gope. It rejected the contrary readings in Raja Mahto v. Mangal Mahto and Dr. Jagdish Prasad v. Sardar Satya Narain Singh. The case differed from the final-decree situation discussed in Srinibas Jena, where the preliminary decree had already become final and was not under challenge.
members.conclusion: The suit and the appeal abated in their entirety, and the civil proceeding from its commencement came to a naught.

predicates.consolidation_notification_covers_disput: A notification bringing the disputed land within a consolidation scheme has been issued.
predicates.land_rights_claim_is_within_consolidatio: The pending claim concerns rights or interests in land that consolidation authorities can adjudicate.
predicates.civil_proceeding_is_pending: A civil proceeding concerning that claim remains pending before a court.
predicates.appeal_from_preliminary_decree_is_pendin: An appeal challenging a preliminary decree that determines rights or shares in the disputed land remains pending.
predicates.entire_civil_proceeding_abates: The civil proceeding, including its earlier stages and decisions, comes to an end from its commencement.

members.legal_issue: A consolidation notification abates the entire pending civil proceeding concerning land brought under consolidation, including the decisions at earlier stages, rather than only the pending appeal.
material_facts: The plaintiffs’ civil suit sought a declaration of title and possession to agricultural land, and the defendants disputed rights in that land.
While the defendants’ second appeal concerning one parcel remained pending, a government notification brought the land into consolidation.
The consolidation authorities were empowered to adjudicate the competing rights, and the governing provision allowed the parties to pursue those rights before those authorities.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 4(1)(c) of the Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, read with its proviso and Section 3, a qualifying notification causes pending civil proceedings concerning rights or interests in land to abate so that consolidation authorities can adjudicate those rights without interference from civil-court proceedings. This statutory abatement differs from ordinary civil-law abatement, under which abatement of an appeal leaves the decision appealed from final. The Court relied on Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh, Chattar Singh v. Thakur Prasad Singh, and Satyanarayan Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The second appeal concerning the parcel abated, and the civil proceeding as a whole—including the trial court and first appellate court decisions concerning that parcel—also abated, leaving the parties to pursue their rights before the consolidation authorities.

rule.if: land_rights_civil_proceeding and land_included_in_consolidation and consolidation_notification_issued and proceeding_pending_when_notification_issued

predicates.land_rights_civil_proceeding: The parties were litigating in a civil proceeding over rights or interests in land.
predicates.land_included_in_consolidation: The land involved in the dispute was included in a consolidation process.
predicates.consolidation_notification_issued: The government issued a notification bringing the land into that consolidation process.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_notification_iss: A proceeding concerning the land remained pending before a civil court when the notification was issued.

members.legal_issue: A consolidation notification abates the entire partition suit, including its preliminary decree, when an appeal against that preliminary decree is pending.
material_facts: A preliminary decree had been passed in a partition suit.
An appeal challenging the preliminary decree was pending when the consolidation notification was issued.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(2)(a) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act provides for abatement of covered suits and proceedings pending before a court or authority, and Section 5(2)(b) preserves the right to agitate the disputed rights before consolidation authorities. The court relied on Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh, Chattar Singh v. Thakur Prasad Singh, Munshi Muqbool Raza v. Hasan Raza, Satyanarayan Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar, and Mst. Bibi Rahmani Khatoon v. Harkoo Gope for the principle that pending proceedings abate; it distinguished cases where no appeal against the preliminary decree was pending.
members.conclusion: The notification has the effect of abating the entire suit and proceedings, including the preliminary decree.

rule.if: consolidation_proceeding and consolidation_notification_published and partition_suit and preliminary_decree_already_passed and appeal_from_preliminary_decree_pending

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings affected by the commencement of consolidation operations over land.
predicates.consolidation_notification_published: A notification commencing consolidation operations was published for the area containing the land.
predicates.partition_suit: The underlying suit seeks division of jointly held land and determination of the parties’ shares.
predicates.preliminary_decree_already_passed: The court had passed a preliminary decree declaring the parties’ rights or shares before the notification was published.
predicates.appeal_from_preliminary_decree_pending: An appeal challenging the preliminary decree was pending when the notification was published.

members.legal_issue: A preliminary decree in a partition suit survives a consolidation notification when no appeal against that decree is pending, even though proceedings to prepare or appeal the final decree abate.
material_facts: A preliminary decree in a partition suit had determined the parties’ rights and shares in the land.
No appeal against the preliminary decree was pending when the consolidation notification was issued; proceedings concerning the final decree were pending.
Consolidation authorities relied on the preliminary decree in resolving the parties’ claims.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5(2) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, proceedings concerning declaration or determination of rights in land abate upon the prescribed order, and the affected rights may be pursued before consolidation authorities under Section 5(2)(b). Read with Section 2(2) and Order 20 Rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a preliminary partition decree determines and declares the parties’ rights, while the final decree works out those rights. Sections 97 CPC, Order 26 Rules 13 and 14 CPC, and the principles in Ahmed Musaji Saleji v. Hashim Ebrahim Saleji, Venkata Reddy v. Pothi Reddy, Gyarsi Bai v. Dhansukh Lal, and Shankar Balwant Lokhande v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande support treating an unappealed preliminary decree as final on the matters it decides. The court approved Ruderpal Singh, Satish Kumar and Mohan Lal and disapproved Ram Garib on this point.
members.conclusion: The preliminary decree remains unaffected, while proceedings relating to preparation of the final decree abate; consolidation authorities may give effect to the surviving decree under Sections 9 and 9A of the Act.

rule.if: consolidation_proceeding and consolidation_notification_published and partition_suit and preliminary_decree_already_passed and preliminary_decree_not_under_appeal and final_decree_proceedings_pending

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings affected by the commencement of consolidation operations over land.
predicates.consolidation_notification_published: A notification commencing consolidation operations was published for the area containing the land.
predicates.partition_suit: The underlying suit seeks division of jointly held land and determination of the parties’ shares.
predicates.preliminary_decree_already_passed: The court had passed a preliminary decree declaring the parties’ rights or shares before the notification was published.
predicates.preliminary_decree_not_under_appeal: No appeal challenging the preliminary decree was pending when the notification was published.
predicates.final_decree_proceedings_pending: Proceedings to implement the declared shares or challenge the final decree were pending when the notification was published.

members.legal_issue: A final mortgage decree passed while an appeal from the preliminary decree is pending does not require formal amendment or replacement when the appellate court affirms or varies the preliminary decree without directing a fresh decree.
material_facts: A preliminary decree for sale of mortgaged property was made final while the decree-holder’s appeal was pending.
The appellate court later varied the preliminary decree by allowing interest and appeal costs.
The appellate court gave no direction to prepare a fresh preliminary decree or final decree.
The judgment-debtors objected that the existing final decree could not be executed without a fresh final decree, and the objection was rejected.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXXIV rules 4 and 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the form of final decree in Form No. 6, the final decree depends on and carries out the preliminary decree. Where an appeal confirms or varies the preliminary decree, the existing final decree operates according to the preliminary decree as confirmed or varied, unless the appellate court specifically directs a fresh preliminary decree or otherwise gives directions requiring a new decree. The Court followed Periakaruppan Chettiar v. Venugopal Pillai, Rukhmabai v. Krishnarao, and Gandavarapu Venkata Subba Rao v. Vavilal Kesavayya, and disapproved Ram Nath v. Deoki Nand Krishna, Abdul Jalil v. Amar Chand Paul, and Mewa Singh v. Tara Singh to the extent inconsistent with this approach.
members.conclusion: The existing final decree remained executable without formal amendment or a fresh final decree, but the executing court had to give effect to the appellate variation when carrying out execution.

rule.if: mortgage_sale_proceeding and appeal_from_preliminary_decree and final_decree_passed_before_appeal_decided and appellate_court_confirmed_or_varied_preliminary_decree and not appellate_court_directed_fresh_decree

predicates.mortgage_sale_proceeding: The proceeding seeks sale of property mortgaged as security for a debt.
predicates.appeal_from_preliminary_decree: A party appealed from the preliminary decree in the mortgage proceeding.
predicates.final_decree_passed_before_appeal_decide: The court passed a final decree while the appeal from the preliminary decree was still pending.
predicates.appellate_court_confirmed_or_varied_prel: The appellate court left the preliminary decree in force, either unchanged or with modifications.
predicates.appellate_court_directed_fresh_decree: The appellate court directed that a fresh preliminary decree or other replacement decree be prepared.

members.legal_issue: An appeal that has abated does not merge the decree under appeal into a later judgment in that appeal, and the decree under appeal remains executable.
material_facts: The first appellate court had decreed the suit for specific performance.
The defendant’s second appeal abated after the defendant died and the legal representatives were not brought on record.
The second appellate court nevertheless dismissed the appeal after the defendant’s death.
The decree-holder’s legal representatives sought execution, which the judgment under appeal had treated as unavailable because of merger.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of merger is not rigid or universal; under State of Madras v. Madurai Mills Co. Ltd., its application depends on the nature of the superior court’s order and the scope of its jurisdiction. Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala is also cited on the limits of merger. Rahmani Khatoon v. Harkoo Gope establishes that an appeal’s abatement leaves the judgment or decree challenged in it final. Because the second appeal had abated, there was no effective appellate determination capable of superseding the first appellate decree; Order 22 Rule 9 also prevents the legal representatives’ failure to continue the appeal from adversely affecting the decree-holder in the manner asserted.
members.conclusion: The doctrine of merger did not apply; the first appellate decree remained operative and executable, and the executing court could proceed with execution.

rule.if: second_appeal and underlying_decree and appellant_died_during_appeal and legal_representatives_not_brought_on_record

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding was a second appeal against a lower court’s decree.
predicates.underlying_decree: A lower court had entered a decree that remained the subject of the appeal.
predicates.appellant_died_during_appeal: The appellant died while the second appeal was pending.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_brought_on_rec: The deceased appellant’s legal representatives were not brought on record to continue the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A pending execution application may continue after an appellate court dismisses an appeal and affirms the decree without altering it.
material_facts: The decree-holders had filed an execution application before the judgment-debtors appealed.
The appellate court stayed the pending execution while the appeal was being considered.
The appeal was dismissed, and the decree was affirmed without alteration or modification.
The High Court held that the earlier execution application could not continue because the decree had merged in the appellate decree and a fresh application was required.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine that a decree merges into an appellate decree does not, by itself, make an execution application already pending in respect of that decree unmaintainable. Where the appellate court affirms the decree without alteration, an execution application stayed during the appeal may continue after the stay ends; any necessary information about the appeal may be supplied or the application amended. The Court relied on Order XXI Rule 11(2)(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, which requires information about an appeal from the decree to be stated in an execution application. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The existing execution application remained maintainable and could continue after the appeal was dismissed; a fresh application was not required.

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: A decree-holder seeks enforcement of a decree through an execution proceeding.
predicates.execution_application_was_pending_before: The decree-holder filed an execution application before the judgment-debtor appealed.
predicates.appellate_court_stayed_execution: The appellate court stayed the execution proceeding while the appeal was pending.
predicates.appeal_was_dismissed_affirming_unaltered: The appellate court dismissed the appeal and left the decree unchanged.

members.legal_issue: A pending suit for possession of land abates when it concerns land rights that must be adjudicated in ongoing consolidation operations.
material_facts: The suit sought possession on the basis that the plaintiff held the relevant land right and that the defendant was a trespasser; the defendant disputed the plaintiff’s claim and asserted tenancy rights.
The land was brought under consolidation operations while the appeal from the possession decree was pending.

The consolidation authorities were empowered to determine land rights and related disputes, and the abatement provision preserved the affected parties’ ability to pursue those rights before those authorities.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5(2)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, as amended, pending suits and proceedings concerning rights or interests in land, and other rights that can or ought to be determined under the Act, abate upon the required order. Although possession suits are not expressly named in the amended provision, a possession claim falls within it when deciding possession necessarily requires adjudication of rights or interests in the land. Sections 3, 9, 11, 11A, 24, 28, 40, 48 and 49 support the conclusion that the consolidation authorities can determine disputes of this kind; section 5(2)(b) preserves the parties’ ability to raise the disputed rights before those authorities. The underlying possession claim was brought under section 209 of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The amended abatement provision covered the possession suit because deciding the possession claim required adjudication of rights or interests in the land; the suit and the appeal arising from it therefore abated.

rule.if: appeal_in_possession_suit and consolidation_operations_notified and possession_claim_requires_land_rights_adjudication and dispute_is_within_consolidation_authority

predicates.appeal_in_possession_suit: An appeal was pending from a judgment in a suit seeking possession of land.
predicates.consolidation_operations_notified: The area containing the disputed land was brought under consolidation operations.
predicates.possession_claim_requires_land_rights_ad: Determining the possession claim required the court to decide the parties’ rights or interests in the land.
predicates.dispute_is_within_consolidation_authorit: The dispute concerned rights that the consolidation authorities were empowered to determine.

members.legal_issue: A pending ceiling proceeding that involves a dispute over rights or interests in land within an area undergoing consolidation abates while consolidation operations are in progress.
material_facts: The tenure-holder had not filed its own statement of holdings, and the Prescribed Authority served it with a statement prepared by the authority.
The tenure-holder objected to that statement and disputed whether it held all the listed plots, as well as identifying plots it wished to retain.
Other persons had made claims to the tenure-holder’s plots in consolidation proceedings, and those claims were pending in revisions.
The land was within villages brought under consolidation operations.
The Prescribed Authority’s decision on whether the tenure-holder had an interest in the disputed plots would affect which plots were included in determining its ceiling area and surplus land.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(2) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 provides for abatement of pending proceedings concerning declaration of rights or interests in land within the notified area. A voluntarily filed statement, or acceptance of a statement prepared by the authority, ordinarily presents no dispute about rights or interests; but a contested statement that raises a dispute over whether the tenure-holder has an interest in listed plots does. Sections 10 and 12 of the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960 require the Prescribed Authority to determine that dispute, and section 32 makes the State a party. Section 49 of the Consolidation Act gives the consolidation process priority over overlapping proceedings; section 48A expressly preserves a different authority’s jurisdiction, but contains no similar exception for the Prescribed Authority. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The ceiling proceedings were proceedings in respect of declaration of rights or interests in land and therefore abated under section 5(2) of the Consolidation Act. They could be resumed after consolidation operations ended in the circumstances specified by the Court.

rule.if: ceiling_determination_proceeding and consolidation_notification_covers_land and consolidation_operations_are_pending and ceiling_objection_contests_interest_in_listed_land and competing_claims_to_that_land_are_pending

predicates.ceiling_determination_proceeding: The proceeding determines a tenure-holder’s holdings, ceiling area, or surplus land.
predicates.consolidation_notification_covers_land: A notification has brought the land covered by the ceiling proceeding within a consolidation area.
predicates.consolidation_operations_are_pending: Consolidation operations concerning that land are still in progress.
predicates.ceiling_objection_contests_interest_in_l: The tenure-holder objects to the listed holdings by disputing whether it has an interest in some or all of the land.
predicates.competing_claims_to_that_land_are_pendin: Other persons’ claims to the same land remain pending in the consolidation process.

members.legal_issue: A civil suit to cancel a void transaction concerning land is barred when consolidation proceedings concerning that land are pending, because the transaction's validity can be determined in those proceedings.
material_facts: A suit was brought to cancel a sale deed concerning land.
The plaintiff's claim was that the sale transaction was void because she had been deceived about the character of the document and had not intended to enter into the sale.
Consolidation proceedings concerning the property were pending when the suit was brought.
members.legal_principle: Section 49 bars civil and revenue courts from deciding disputes that could or ought to be taken up under the consolidation legislation. Under Gorakh Nath Dube v. Hari Narain Singh, consolidation authorities can determine whether a transaction is void, while a civil suit may be needed to set aside a voidable document that remains effective until cancelled. Because the transaction here was void, its validity could be adjudicated by the consolidation authorities. Applying Ningawwa v. Byrappa, the misrepresentation about the document's character made the transaction void.
members.conclusion: The civil suit was not maintainable under Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953; the parties could seek appropriate relief from the consolidation authorities, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: civil_suit_to_cancel_document and consolidation_proceedings_pending and land_rights_dispute and transaction_void

predicates.civil_suit_to_cancel_document: A party brings a civil suit seeking cancellation of a document.
predicates.consolidation_proceedings_pending: Proceedings to consolidate landholdings are pending concerning the land at issue.
predicates.land_rights_dispute: The dispute concerns rights or interests in land that are at issue in the consolidation proceedings.
predicates.transaction_void: The transaction embodied in the document is wholly void.
predicates.civil_suit_not_maintainable: The civil suit cannot be maintained to determine the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A pending proceeding concerning rights in land abates during consolidation when the dispute over a transfer’s validity can be adjudicated by the consolidation authorities as part of determining those rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed that the disputed plots had been acquired with joint family funds and that the vendor’s sale of the plaintiff’s claimed share was invalid, inoperative, and void.
The suit sought cancellation of the sale deed to the extent of the claimed share and possession of that share.
The defendants’ second appeal was pending when the area containing the plots was brought under consolidation operations.
The dispute over the claimed share and the alleged invalidity of the sale could be adjudicated by the consolidation authorities.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5(2)(a) and (b) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, proceedings concerning declarations of rights or interests in land that can be decided in consolidation proceedings abate upon the required order, without prejudice to pursuing the dispute before the consolidation authorities. The substance of the claim, not its form, is decisive. A distinction applies between a document that is invalid and may be disregarded, whose effect the consolidation authorities can determine when deciding land rights, and one whose legal effect can be removed only by cancellation. Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh & Ors. held that proceedings involving declaration of land rights may abate; Jagarnath Shukla v. Sita Ram Pande & Ors. supports adjudicating the validity of transfers in consolidation proceedings where that issue arises in determining rights or interests in land.
members.conclusion: The suit abated, and the claims were left for decision by the consolidation authorities; the Court set aside the judgments below so that they would not impede that decision.

predicates.pending_land_rights_proceeding: A proceeding concerning rights or interests in land was pending when the relevant area came under consolidation operations.
predicates.consolidation_operations_cover_land: The land in dispute was within an area undergoing consolidation operations.
predicates.transfer_validity_is_part_of_land_rights: A party’s claimed rights in the land depended on whether a transfer was valid.
predicates.transfer_effect_can_be_adjudicated_witho: The effect of the disputed transfer could be determined as part of deciding the land rights, without first cancelling the document to remove its legal effect.

members.legal_issue: A writ compelling the grant or renewal of a mining lease is unavailable when the purported lease term has expired and no formal lease was executed.
material_facts: The tender for mining rights was accepted and possession of the area was given, but no formal lease was executed.
The purported twenty-year lease term had expired by the time the court considered the appeal.
The appellant sought, among other relief, an order directing the State to grant a lease or recognize an option to renew.
members.legal_principle: Because the purported lease term had expired and no proper lease had been executed, there was no subsisting lease or renewal option on which to base a writ for grant or renewal.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not obtain a writ for grant of the lease or exercise of an option to renew it.

predicates.lease_or_renewal_writ_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a writ compelling the grant or renewal of a mining lease.
predicates.purported_lease_term_expired: The stated term of the purported lease had ended.
predicates.formal_lease_not_executed: The parties had not executed a formal lease.
predicates.lease_or_renewal_writ_unavailable: A writ compelling the grant or renewal of the lease is unavailable.

members.legal_issue: The expiry of a mining lease does not itself entitle the holder to renewal.
material_facts: Some leases for quarries that were otherwise permitted to operate had expired.
Proceedings seeking renewal of those leases were pending before courts.
The court left the renewal question to the appropriate courts for decision according to the law and facts of each case.
members.legal_principle: Whether an expired lease should be renewed depends on the law and facts of the individual case and is for the appropriate court to determine. No earlier cases are cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: An expired lease was not automatically renewed; the appropriate court had to decide any renewal request on its merits.

predicates.environmental_mining_writ: The proceeding concerns the environmental or legal status of mining operations.
predicates.mining_lease_expired: The lease authorizing mining has expired.
predicates.renewal_request_pending: A request for renewal of the expired lease is pending before a court.

members.legal_issue: A lessee cannot obtain renewal of a quarry lease when the lease contains no option of renewal.
material_facts: The lessee applied to renew a quarry lease that did not contain an option of renewal.
The lease form’s renewal-option clause had been deleted.
members.legal_principle: A lessee may seek renewal on the basis of an option only where the lease grants such an option. In the absence of an option, the applicant may seek a fresh lease but cannot claim renewal. The Court applied the terms of the lease in the context of the prescribed lease form under the Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The renewal application was misconceived and could be rejected, notwithstanding that its description of the mineral was adequate.

predicates.quarry_lease_renewal_application: A lessee applies to renew an existing quarry lease.
predicates.lease_contains_renewal_option: The lease gives the lessee an option to obtain a renewal.

members.legal_issue: A mining-concession renewal rule for government grants does not entitle a holder of a statutory mining lease to renewal.
material_facts: Following vesting, the lessee held a statutory lease for the remainder of the original lease term.
The lessee relied on a mining-concession rule providing for renewal of mining leases at the lessee’s option.

The court found that the rule applied to grants made by government, not leases arising by statute; it also observed that, even if the rule applied, the relevant statutory lease period had expired long before the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Rule 40 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 applies to mining leases granted by government and not to statutory leases arising under section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The court further stated that, even assuming the rule applied, the duration of the original lease for this purpose could be no longer than the period from vesting until expiry of the original lease, and the period for which renewal could have been claimed had elapsed.
members.conclusion: The mining-concession rule did not give the lessee a right to renewal of the statutory lease; in any event, the relevant period for a claimed renewal had already expired.

predicates.claim_to_renew_mining_lease: A leaseholder seeks renewal of a mining lease.
predicates.lease_created_by_statutory_operation: The lease arose by operation of legislation rather than by a government grant.
predicates.renewal_claim_relies_on_general_mining_c: The leaseholder relies on a general rule governing renewal of mining leases.

members.legal_issue: A lessee has no right to compel renewal of an expired municipal lease beyond the period authorized by the State when the required approval for a further lease has not been granted.
material_facts: The lease was for a fixed term and had expired.
The lease deed stated that it would be renewed, with rent subject to adjustment, but the municipality could grant a lease exceeding ten years only with prior State permission.
The State had authorized a further lease only through a specified endpoint, and no approval for a lease beyond that endpoint was granted.
The land had been leased for operating an oil mill, but no oil mill remained on the property; the lessee had instead developed a commercial complex and earned rental income.
The property was public land leased at a very low rent, and the municipality required it for educational purposes.
members.legal_principle: Section 65(2) of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963 requires prior State permission for a municipal lease exceeding ten years. A municipality cannot grant such a lease without that permission, and a lease clause referring to renewal does not give the lessee an inherent right to renewal beyond the term authorized by the State. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The lessee was not entitled to renewal as a matter of right, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: renewal_appeal and fixed_term_lease_expired and further_lease_requires_state_approval and not state_approval_covers_further_term

predicates.renewal_appeal: The proceeding challenges the rejection of a claim to renew an expired lease.
predicates.fixed_term_lease_expired: The lessee held a lease for a fixed term, and that term ended.
predicates.further_lease_requires_state_approval: The municipality could grant a lease for a further term only after obtaining State approval.
predicates.state_approval_covers_further_term: The State granted approval covering the proposed further lease term.
predicates.lessee_cannot_compel_renewal: The lessee cannot require the municipality to renew the lease.

members.legal_issue: A mining lease cannot be extended for a period during which operations were obstructed when no statute or lease term grants that extension and the prevailing mining policy requires new leases to be granted through a competitive process.
material_facts: Mining operations under the leases were stopped following an order made in proceedings in which the leaseholders had not been joined.
The interruption was not attributable to the leaseholders, and the lands covered by their leases were ultimately excluded from the relevant forest area.
The lease terms and the applicable statutory rules did not provide a right to extend the leases for the obstructed period.
The mining policy in force when an extension would have to be granted required leases to be granted through e-tendering or e-auction.
The State had agreed to refund relevant security deposits and advance royalties.
members.legal_principle: Under the Uttar Pradesh Mining Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 68 is a restricted relaxation power to be read with the rules governing grants and auctions; it does not create a right to extend an expired lease to compensate for an interruption. A right to extension must arise from statute or the lease terms. Rule 40(h) provides for adjustment of the installment equivalent to the disrupted period. The Court relied on Sukhan Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Mohammad Yunus Hasan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Vijay Kumar Dwivedi v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and applied the principle that clear statutory language is given its literal meaning. The prevailing mining policy requiring competitive allocation also weighed against extension.
members.conclusion: The leases should not be extended for the obstructed period. The applicable rules provide for monetary adjustment of amounts paid for a period when mining could not take place, rather than an extension of the lease.

rule.if: mining_lease_appeal and mining_operations_obstructed and no_lessee_fault and (not statutory_extension_right and not contractual_extension_right) and prevailing_policy_requires_competitive_grant

predicates.mining_lease_appeal: A leaseholder appeals in a proceeding concerning the consequences of an interruption to mining under a mining lease.
predicates.mining_operations_obstructed: Mining operations under the lease were prevented for a period by an order or other restriction.
predicates.no_lessee_fault: The interruption was not caused by wrongdoing or fault of the leaseholder.
predicates.statutory_extension_right: A statute gives the leaseholder a right to extend the lease for the obstructed period.
predicates.contractual_extension_right: The lease terms give the leaseholder a right to extend the lease for the obstructed period.
predicates.prevailing_policy_requires_competitive_g: The policy in force when a new grant or extension would be made requires mining rights to be allocated through a competitive process.
predicates.obstructed_lease_extension_denied: The lease is not extended for the obstructed period.

members.legal_issue: A second renewal is invalid when the State grants it hastily without considering relevant material and without establishing that it serves mineral development.
material_facts: The State granted numerous second renewals in a short period, including after the proposed change to the mining-allocation framework became public.

The State did not await or consider the results of investigations it had initiated into lease-holder violations, despite its policy stating that such violations could exclude lease holders from renewal.
Reports documented widespread mining and environmental violations, and the State did not adequately consider those reports or the environmental degradation they described.
Goan iron ore was principally exported, with little domestic value addition, while the mining lease holders stood to gain commercially.
The State’s decision appeared directed at restoring revenue rather than being based on a holistic assessment of mineral development.
members.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the MMDR Act requires the State to form an opinion that renewal is necessary in the interests of mineral development and to record reasons. Under Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, (1996) 9 SCC 709, mineral development must be considered holistically, including captive mining, industry requirements, and equitable distribution under Article 39(b). Article 14 permits limited review of executive decisions allocating natural resources. Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, (2012) 10 SCC 1, explains that allocation for private commercial profit without a social or welfare purpose may attract Article 14 scrutiny. The State’s own mining policy also made renewal contingent on considering investigations and violations.
members.conclusion: The second renewals were unduly hasty, failed to take relevant material into account, and were not in the interests of mineral development; they were quashed.

rule.if: challenge_to_second_renewal and state_granted_renewals and relevant_investigations_unconsidered and material_violations_unconsidered and mineral_development_not_demonstrated

predicates.challenge_to_second_renewal: A proceeding challenges the State’s decision to grant second renewals of mining leases.
predicates.state_granted_renewals: The State granted second renewals of mining leases.
predicates.relevant_investigations_unconsidered: The State made renewal decisions without awaiting or considering investigations it had initiated into relevant conduct.
predicates.material_violations_unconsidered: The State did not adequately consider documented violations or other relevant environmental and mining evidence.
predicates.mineral_development_not_demonstrated: The State’s decision was not shown to rest on a reasoned assessment that renewal served mineral development.

members.legal_issue: A further renewal of a mining lease is invalid when the required reasons are not recorded or relevant considerations bearing on mineral development are not addressed.
material_facts: The leaseholder sought a second renewal of its lease.
The first government authorization granting the renewal did not state reasons for finding renewal to be in the interest of mineral development.
The later authorization gave reasons for reducing the area but did not consider the earlier committee report, the Supreme Court’s decision relying on that report, or the National Mineral Policy.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 8(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, as applicable to the application, a further renewal may be authorized only if the Central Government considers it necessary in the interests of mineral development and records reasons for doing so. The requirement is a safeguard against arbitrariness and must be followed strictly; the reasons must reflect proper consideration of relevant factors.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside both renewal authorizations because they did not satisfy the requirements of Section 8(3).

predicates.further_lease_renewal_proceeding: A government body considered whether to authorize a further renewal of an existing mining lease.
predicates.reasons_not_recorded: The government body authorized renewal without recording why it considered renewal necessary for mineral development.
predicates.relevant_mineral_development_factors_ign: The government body did not consider relevant policy or prior findings bearing on mineral development.

members.legal_issue: A lease granted by an agent without the authority required by the principal is invalid.
material_facts: The disputed properties were leased by the principal’s agent to the original lessee, rather than by the principal himself.
The agent’s written authority prohibited leasing the properties without the principal’s or his manager’s written consent.
No written consent was produced, and the appellate revenue authority found that the principal had not consented.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the terms of the agent’s written authority: because the authority required written consent before the properties could be leased, a lease granted without that consent was invalid. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The lease in favour of the appellants was invalid because the agent lacked authority to grant it.

predicates.tenancy_possession_suit: A claimant brought a tenancy proceeding seeking possession of property held by another person.
predicates.agent_lease_requires_consent: The principal’s agent was permitted to lease the property only if the principal or an authorised manager consented.
predicates.consent_not_given: The required consent was not given before the agent granted the lease.

members.legal_issue: A lease of minerals granted by holders who lack mineral rights does not entitle the lessee to compel the government to grant mining permission.
material_facts: The holders of the inam granted the respondents mica-mining leases with a term permitting renewal.
The grant did not establish that the inam holders had subsoil mineral rights.
After the estate was taken over, the respondents sought a writ compelling permission to mine on the basis of their leases.
The respondents relied on the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, in seeking permission.
members.legal_principle: A lessor cannot convey mineral rights that the lessor does not possess. Because the inam holders had no established subsoil rights, their leases conveyed no rights in the minerals and could not support a claim to mining permission as of right under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949. The practical difficulty of working mines where surface and subsoil rights are held separately does not make the surface holders co-sharers in the mineral rights. The Court applied Secretary of State for India in Council v. Srinivasa Chariar (1920) L.R. 48 I.A. 56; it did not treat Secretary of State v. Krishna Rao (1945) L.R. 72 I.A. 211 as establishing a different rule about subsoil rights.
members.conclusion: The leases had no legal effect as conveyances of mineral rights and gave the respondents no right to require the government to grant them a mining lease or permission. The State's appeal was allowed and the respondents' appeal was dismissed.

predicates.mining_permission_writ: The proceeding seeks to compel the government by writ to permit mining under a claimed lease.
predicates.lessor_lacked_mineral_rights: The person who granted the mining lease did not possess the mineral rights.
predicates.claim_based_on_lease: The claimant relies on the lease as the basis for seeking mining permission.

members.legal_issue: A statutory power to exempt buildings from rent-control protections is not an excessive delegation when the legislation provides sufficient guidance for its exercise.
material_facts: The tenants challenged the statutory provision authorising the government to exempt a building or class of buildings from all or any of the rent-control law.
The statutory preamble and operative provisions identified the law’s purposes and provided guidance for deciding when exemptions could be granted.
The challenge to the provision was not pressed in light of an earlier decision concerning an identical provision in an earlier enactment.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a statutory delegation is sufficiently guided where the legislation’s preamble and operative provisions indicate the policy and purposes governing the discretion. The power to grant exceptions may address undue hardship or abuse arising from uniform application, but must not subvert the enactment’s general purpose. P.J. Irani v. State of Madras upheld an identical exemption power on this basis; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal likewise upheld a guided exemption power.
members.conclusion: The statutory exemption power does not suffer from excessive delegation and is not invalid under the constitutional guarantee of equality.

predicates.rent_control_delegation_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law that authorises the government to exempt buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.statutory_scheme_supplies_guidance: The legislation’s stated purposes and operative scheme guide the government in deciding when exemptions may be granted.

members.legal_issue: Discretion to exempt land or transfers from a restriction does not deny equal protection when the discretion is guided by the law’s purpose and is subject to safeguards and review.
material_facts: The government could exempt an area or transfer by written order stating reasons, with the law’s objective guiding that power.
The government could also grant exemptions to avoid hardship.
The Collector’s exemption power was limited to specified purposes or purposes prescribed by rules.
A person could appeal the Collector’s exemption decision to the government, and exemption orders were to be placed before the legislature.
The petitioner argued that the exemption power lacked a rational guideline.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not prohibit administrative discretion where the law supplies adequate guidance and safeguards against arbitrary exercise. The court relied on the law’s stated object, the requirement to record reasons, the hardship criterion, the limits on the Collector’s authority, the availability of appeal, legislative oversight, and the rule-making framework. It referred to Article 14 and did not need to decide whether Article 31C protected the law. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The exemption powers were sufficiently guided and controlled and did not violate equal protection.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and exemption_power_exists and exemption_power_has_purpose_or_hardship_guidance and exemption_decisions_are_subject_to_review

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenges the constitutional validity of a restriction on land transfers.
predicates.exemption_power_exists: The law authorizes officials to exempt areas or transfers from the restriction.
predicates.exemption_power_has_purpose_or_hardship_: The law directs exemptions toward its purpose or hardship relief and limits the grounds on which officials may act.
predicates.exemption_decisions_are_subject_to_revie: The law provides review or oversight of exemption decisions, such as an appeal or legislative supervision.

members.legal_issue: The statutory power to exempt buildings from rent-control protections is not an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power or a violation of equality guarantees.
material_facts: The legislation authorized the government to exempt a particular building or class of buildings from rent-control provisions.
Earlier decisions had upheld comparable exemption powers, and an earlier decision had upheld the same statutory power against delegation and equality challenges.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on P. J. Irani v. The State of Madras, which upheld a comparable exemption power, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal, which likewise upheld an exemption power, and Sadhu Singh v. The District Board, Gurdaspur, which held that this statutory power did not involve excessive delegation or violate Article 14. The relevant provision was section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, as modified for the territory.
members.conclusion: The statutory exemption power is valid and does not suffer from excessive delegation or violate the equality guarantee.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_control: A constitutional challenge is brought against the power to exempt buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.legislation_authorizes_executive_exempti: The legislature authorizes the executive to exempt buildings or classes of buildings from rent-control protections.
predicates.comparable_exemption_powers_have_been_up: Earlier court decisions have upheld comparable executive exemption powers.

members.legal_issue: A delegation allowing the executive to lower a statutory maximum rent is valid when the legislation states its policy and provides guidance for exercising the delegated power.
material_facts: The legislation sought to improve peasants’ economic and social conditions and to protect tenants from excessive rent.
It set a maximum rent linked to the crop and the type of land.
It provided a process for fixing reasonable rent and specified factors for that determination, including local rental values, agricultural profits, crop prices, improvements, and land assessment.
It authorized the government to lower the maximum rent for particular areas or on another suitable basis, without prescribing a minimum rent.
The majority treated the policy expressed in the legislation and the factors governing reasonable rent as guidance for the government’s area-specific exercise of the power.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may delegate subsidiary or ancillary powers but may not delegate its essential legislative function. It must state the legislative policy and principle and provide guidance for the delegate. Whether it has done so is assessed from the preamble and relevant provisions read together. The majority relied on Harishankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh and The Edward Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Ajmer, and found that the tenant-protection policy and the factors specified for fixing reasonable rent adequately guided the delegated power.
members.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive; the provision conferring the power was valid, and the absence of a prescribed minimum rent did not alter that conclusion.

rule.if: excessive_delegation_challenge and tenant_protection_policy_declared and crop_linked_rent_ceiling_set and reasonable_rent_factors_provided and area_specific_adjustment_power_conferred

predicates.excessive_delegation_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law on the ground that it delegates legislative power excessively.
predicates.tenant_protection_policy_declared: The legislature stated a policy of protecting tenants and improving their economic or social conditions.
predicates.crop_linked_rent_ceiling_set: The legislature itself set a maximum rent linked to the crop or other characteristics of the land.
predicates.reasonable_rent_factors_provided: The legislation specified factors for authorities to consider when determining reasonable rent.
predicates.area_specific_adjustment_power_conferred: The legislation authorized the government to adjust the maximum rent for particular areas.

members.legal_issue: An exemption power is not unguided for equality purposes when the enactment’s preamble states a policy that governs the exercise of that power.
material_facts: The enactment authorized the government to exempt any person or class of persons from its operation without stating exemption criteria in that provision.
The preamble stated that the enactment was intended to protect tenants from ejectment or dispossession and to grant them relief.
members.legal_principle: A preamble may supply the policy guiding an exemption power and prevent the exercise of that power from being unguided. The Court relied on Harishankar Bagla v. The State of Madhya Pradesh. It also observed that even if the exemption provision were invalid, it was severable from the rest of the enactment.
members.conclusion: The exemption power was not unguided because the preamble sufficiently stated the legislative policy governing it, so the enactment was not invalid under Article 14 on this ground.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge: A party contends that an exemption power violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.exemption_power_has_no_express_criteria: The provision granting exemption power does not itself state the criteria for exercising that power.
predicates.enactment_preamble_states_governing_poli: The enactment’s preamble states a policy that governs the purpose and exercise of the exemption power.

members.legal_issue: A law authorizing the executive to exempt buildings or classes of buildings from rent-control protections is not invalid merely because it does not specify detailed guidelines for exercising that power.
material_facts: The legislature authorized the executive to direct that all or some provisions of the rent-control scheme would not apply to a particular building or class of buildings.
The executive used that authority to exempt newly constructed buildings from eviction restrictions for a limited period, as an incentive for construction.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, Sadhu Singh v. District Board, Gurdaspur, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kanhaiyalal, and Punjab Tin Supply Company v. Central Government, which supported the validity of comparable exemption powers. The Court held that the provision was valid in light of the purpose of encouraging new construction and the resulting increase in accommodation.
members.conclusion: The exemption-authorizing provision was constitutionally valid and did not suffer from excessive delegation of legislative power.

predicates.challenge_to_exemption_authority: A litigant challenges the constitutionality of a law that authorizes executive exemptions from a regulatory scheme.
predicates.executive_exemption_power: The law gives the executive power to exclude particular buildings or classes of buildings from some or all of the scheme's requirements.
predicates.exemption_encourages_new_construction: The executive uses the exemption power to provide an incentive for construction intended to increase available accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A statutory power to exempt individual buildings from rent-control protections is constitutional when the legislation supplies sufficient guidance for exercising that power.
material_facts: The legislation regulated letting, controlled rents, and sought to prevent unreasonable eviction of tenants.
Its tenant protections could cause hardship to landlords or be abused by tenants, and the legislation provided a discretionary exemption power to address such circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, legislation may leave selection or classification to the government if the statute supplies a policy or principle guiding that discretion; executive action that fails to follow the guidance may be invalid even though the statute is valid. The preamble and operative provisions supplied adequate guidance here. The Court relied on Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar, [1959] SCR 279, and Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1957] SCR 605, which also referred to Harishanker Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The exemption power was not arbitrary or unguided and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equal protection.

predicates.rent_control_case: The proceeding concerns legislation regulating rents and protecting tenants from unreasonable eviction.
predicates.statute_policy_is_stated: The legislation states its purposes and contains operative provisions that guide the exercise of the exemption discretion.
predicates.exemption_power_addresses_unforeseen_har: The legislation permits exemptions to address hardship or abuse that its general protections may produce.

members.legal_issue: A statutory discretion to restrict execution of eviction decrees does not violate equal protection when the enactment supplies sufficient guidance through its policy and purpose.
material_facts: The challenged enactment required prior permission before an eviction decree concerning a building in a slum area could be executed.
The enactment’s stated purposes and operative provisions addressed both improvement and clearance of slum areas and protection of tenants from eviction.
The challenge argued that the authority had no statutory criteria governing whether permission should be granted.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a law that gives an authority discretion without any declared policy, intelligible purpose, or guiding standard may permit arbitrary discrimination. Guidance need not be set out expressly in the particular provision conferring discretion; it may be derived from the preamble, surrounding circumstances, other operative provisions, and the enactment’s object. The Court applied the principles discussed in Ramakrishna Dalmia v. Justice Tendolkar, Harishankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, M/s. Dwarka Prasad Laxmi Narain v. State of Uttar Pradesh, State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra, Kedar Nath Bajoria v. State of West Bengal, and Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The discretion was sufficiently guided by the enactment’s policy and purpose, so the provision did not violate Article 14.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_eviction_con: A proceeding challenges a legal regime that conditions execution of eviction decrees on administrative permission.
predicates.law_targets_slum_clearance_and_tenant_pr: The law seeks both to improve or clear slum areas and to protect their residents from eviction.
predicates.administrative_discretion_is_guided_by_l: The authority’s discretion can be guided by the law’s stated policy, purpose, and related operative provisions.

members.legal_issue: A broadly worded statutory power to exempt land or buildings from planning controls is constitutionally valid when the statute’s policy and other provisions provide guidance for its exercise.
material_facts: The challenged provision allowed the government to exempt land or buildings from provisions of the planning legislation and its subordinate rules, subject to conditions.

The legislation’s stated purpose and its provisions established a policy of planned development and regulated land use and construction through planning authorities, development plans, and detailed development rules.
The challengers argued that the exemption power lacked limits and allowed arbitrary departures from the planning regime.
members.legal_principle: A legislature may delegate implementation of its policy but may not abdicate its essential legislative function. Guidance for delegated power may be found in the statute’s express provisions, preamble, scheme, objects, or subject matter. A wide exemption power is valid if it must be exercised consistently with the statute’s policy. The Court relied on State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, In re The Delhi Laws Act, Harishankar Bagla v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, P.J. Irani v. State of Madras, Registrar of Co-operative Societies v. K. Kunhambu, Premium Granites v. State of Tamil Nadu, and distinguished A.N. Parasuraman v. State of Tamil Nadu and Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, where the statutes lacked adequate policy or guidance.
members.conclusion: The exemption provision is valid because the statute’s preamble, objects, and other provisions provide clear policy and guidance, so the power is not unbridled or an excessive delegation of essential legislative function.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_delegated_ex: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law because it delegates power to grant exemptions from statutory requirements.
predicates.statute_states_planning_policy: The statute states a policy of planned development and regulated land use.
predicates.other_statutory_provisions_guide_exercis: The statute’s other provisions and subordinate rules provide standards that guide how the exemption power is to be exercised.

members.legal_issue: Differentiating vacant land by urban location, permissible transfer size, and whether it forms part of a compact block does not deny equal protection when the distinctions are reasonably related to preventing concentration and manipulation of land.
material_facts: The law applied to vacant land in cities and municipal boroughs and to surrounding areas designated by the State with regard to urbanisation and other relevant considerations.
The designated surrounding area could vary by locality, and the State had prescribed greater distances for larger cities and lesser distances for smaller municipal boroughs.

A person could alienate one plot up to a specified area if it did not form part of a compact block; the compact-block definition included contiguous land owned jointly or separately by members of a family unit.
The petitioner argued that the restriction used the same permissible area irrespective of location and land value, and treated land differently depending on whether it formed part of a compact block.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification with a clear nexus to the law’s object. The court found that varying urban boundaries by local conditions was permissible and that excluding compact blocks from the small-plot exception prevented manipulation and concentration. The court relied on Article 14 and the stated objectives associated with Article 39(b) and (c), but did not need to decide whether Article 31C protected the law. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The distinctions were reasonable, had a clear nexus with the law’s objectives, and did not violate equal protection.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and restriction_targets_vacant_urban_land and urban_boundaries_reflect_local_conditions and small_plot_exception_excludes_compact_blocks

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenges the constitutional validity of a restriction on land transfers.
predicates.restriction_targets_vacant_urban_land: The restriction applies to vacant land in urban areas rather than to all land generally.
predicates.urban_boundaries_reflect_local_condition: The areas subject to the restriction are defined with regard to urbanisation or other relevant local considerations.
predicates.small_plot_exception_excludes_compact_bl: A limited plot-transfer exception is unavailable where the land forms part of a larger compact block, including contiguous land held by related owners.

members.legal_issue: Excluding building land and allowing specified public and cooperative transfers from a vacant-land restriction does not deny equal protection when those distinctions advance the restriction’s purpose.
material_facts: The law defined vacant land to exclude land with a building constructed or being constructed in accordance with applicable law, together with the minimum appurtenant land required for it.
The law did not apply to transfers to government bodies, local authorities, government companies, specified public corporations, or approved cooperative housing societies serving weaker sections.
The petitioner argued that excluding building land and allowing those transfers was discriminatory.
The law’s stated objective was to facilitate distribution of material resources for the common good and prevent concentration of wealth.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classifications that are reasonable and have a clear nexus with the legislative object. The court held that excluding building land was consistent with a restriction directed at vacant land, that transfers to public bodies could advance rather than defeat the law’s object, and that cooperative housing societies could help fulfil that object. It referred to Article 14 and the objectives stated in connection with Article 39(b) and (c); it did not need to decide whether Article 31C applied. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The exclusions and permitted transfers were reasonable classifications with a clear nexus to the law’s objectives and did not violate equal protection.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and restriction_targets_vacant_urban_land and building_land_is_excluded and permitted_transfers_advance_common_good

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A person challenges the constitutional validity of a restriction on land transfers.
predicates.restriction_targets_vacant_urban_land: The restriction is directed at vacant land in urban areas.
predicates.building_land_is_excluded: Land with a lawfully constructed or lawfully developing building, and the necessary appurtenant land, is outside the restriction.
predicates.permitted_transfers_advance_common_good: Transfers to designated public bodies or qualifying cooperative housing bodies are permitted because they can advance the restriction’s public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee’s acquisition of occupancy rights through possession under the mortgage does not extinguish the mortgagor’s right to redeem when no legally recognized mode of extinguishment has occurred.
material_facts: The mortgagors were permanent tenants with rights in the land and mortgaged their share in it with possession.
The mortgagees were in possession of the mortgaged share because of the mortgage.
After the land was resumed, the mortgagees obtained a grant of occupancy rights based on their possession, although the mortgagors were entitled to the grant as permanent tenants.
The mortgagors had deposited the occupancy price and sought redemption.
members.legal_principle: A right of redemption ends only by a legally recognized means, such as agreement, merger, or a statutory provision barring redemption; otherwise, the principle is “once a mortgage, always a mortgage.” Under section 8 of the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, tenants’ rights in the watan lands subsisted after abolition. The judgment cites no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The grant did not extinguish the mortgagors’ right to redeem the mortgage.

rule.if: redemption_proceeding and mortgagee_in_possession and grant_derived_from_mortgage_possession and not lawful_extinguishment

predicates.redemption_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding seeking redemption of a mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_in_possession: The mortgagee held possession of the property under the mortgage.
predicates.grant_derived_from_mortgage_possession: The mortgagee obtained a property right because possession under the mortgage enabled the grant.
predicates.lawful_extinguishment: The right to redeem was ended by agreement, merger, or a legal provision barring redemption.
predicates.redemption_right_survives: The mortgagor retains the right to redeem the mortgage.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee’s possession under a tenancy statute and subsequent purchase of the tenant’s estate do not extinguish the mortgagor’s right to redeem where the mortgage rights are preserved and there is no contract or merger ending the mortgage.
material_facts: The tenant mortgaged the land and later fell into rent arrears.
The mortgagee paid arrears and obtained possession under the tenancy statute, which preserved the mortgagee’s existing rights.
After further arrears, the mortgagee purchased the tenant’s estate at a court sale while already in possession as mortgagee.
The purchase was of the tenant’s estate, not the landlord’s estate, and no contract ending the right to redeem was pleaded.
The High Court granted a preliminary decree for redemption, and the mortgagee appealed.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 90 of the Trusts Act, the mortgagee in possession held the property subject to the mortgagor’s right to redeem. Section 225 of the Orissa Tenancy Act made the person obtaining possession under it a statutory mortgagee and, under subsection (2), preserved existing mortgage rights. The principle that a mortgage remains a mortgage applies: absent a contract, merger, court order, or special statutory provision ending redemption, the mortgagee’s purchase of the tenant’s estate did not extinguish the right to redeem. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed and the decree for redemption was upheld.

rule.if: appeal_from_redemption_decree and mortgagee_in_possession and possession_under_tenancy_law and statute_preserves_mortgage_rights and mortgagee_purchased_tenant_estate and not contract_ended_redemption and not mortgage_merged_into_higher_estate

predicates.appeal_from_redemption_decree: A party appeals from a decree granting redemption of mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_in_possession: The mortgagee holds possession of the mortgaged property in the capacity of mortgagee.
predicates.possession_under_tenancy_law: The mortgagee obtained possession under a tenancy-law mechanism.
predicates.statute_preserves_mortgage_rights: The governing law preserves the mortgagee’s existing mortgage rights after possession is obtained.
predicates.mortgagee_purchased_tenant_estate: The mortgagee later purchased the tenant’s estate at a court sale while holding possession as mortgagee.
predicates.contract_ended_redemption: The parties made an agreement ending the mortgagor’s right to redeem.
predicates.mortgage_merged_into_higher_estate: The mortgagee acquired a higher estate into which the mortgage merged.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee's prolonged possession under a void usufructuary mortgage of an occupancy holding does not extinguish the right to recover the holding by paying the mortgage consideration.
material_facts: An occupancy tenant executed a usufructuary mortgage over the holding and put the mortgagee in possession.
The mortgagee and the mortgagee's successors remained in possession for more than twelve years.
The later holders of the occupancy rights sought possession and deposited the mortgage money in court.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles established in the Full Bench decisions in Ghassu v. Babu Ram and Mahabal Singh v. Ram Rai, a usufructuary mortgage of an occupancy holding is void, but the person in possession is analogous to a mortgagee. Possession for more than twelve years does not extinguish the mortgagor's right to recover the holding on payment of the consideration; it only amounts to prescribing for mortgagee rights. The Court considered sections 33, 44, 45, 82 and 180 of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939, and followed the established local interpretation under the doctrine of stare decisis.
members.conclusion: The mortgagee's status was analogous to that of a mortgagee, and prolonged possession did not extinguish the right to recover possession on payment of the mortgage money; the suit was not barred by time.

rule.if: occupancy_holding_redemption_suit and usufructuary_mortgage_created and mortgagee_possession_over_twelve_years and redemption_money_tendered

predicates.occupancy_holding_redemption_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of an occupancy holding by redeeming an earlier mortgage.
predicates.usufructuary_mortgage_created: An occupancy tenant gave possession of the holding under a usufructuary mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_possession_over_twelve_years: The mortgagee or the mortgagee's successors remained in possession for more than twelve years.
predicates.redemption_money_tendered: The person seeking recovery tendered or deposited the money received under the mortgage.

members.legal_issue: Long possession by occupants whose possession began only as mortgagees does not estop the owner from seeking recovery of possession.
material_facts: The defendants’ possession began under the mortgage deeds.
The defendants had no prior connection with the land, and their claimed independent raiyati interest was rejected.
The plaintiffs sought possession after redeeming the mortgages.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that long possession did not estop the claimants in the circumstances because the defendants possessed the land only as mortgagees; no statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The defendants’ long possession did not estop the plaintiffs from recovering possession.

rule.if: possession_recovery_suit and possession_began_under_mortgage and no_independent_land_right and long_possession

predicates.possession_recovery_suit: A claimant brought a suit to recover possession of land.
predicates.possession_began_under_mortgage: The occupants entered possession of the land only by virtue of a mortgage.
predicates.no_independent_land_right: The occupants did not establish an independent right to the land.
predicates.long_possession: The occupants remained in possession for a lengthy period.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagor’s right of redemption is not extinguished merely because a mortgagee exercises a power of sale and sells the mortgaged property at auction; it continues until the sale is completed by a registered conveyance.
material_facts: The society mortgaged its land and incomplete building under a mortgage deed conferring a power of sale without court intervention.
After the society failed to pay the mortgage debt, the mortgagee advertised and held a public auction, and the appellant was declared the highest bidder.
The appellant paid the purchase price and took possession, but no registered conveyance completing the sale had been executed.
The society paid the mortgage debt to the mortgagee before completion of the sale and sought to redeem the property.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 54 and 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a contract for sale does not itself transfer an interest in the property, and the right of redemption continues unless extinguished by an act of the parties or a court decree. Read with section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, transfer of the mortgagor’s interest in immovable property requires a registered instrument; the right is therefore not extinguished by the mortgagee’s auction or by a mere contract for sale. Section 69(3) protects a purchaser’s title from challenge on the ground that no case authorising the sale had arisen, but does not make an auction contract a completed transfer. The Court approved Abraham Ezra Issac Mansoor v. Abdul Latif Usman and Ellappa Naiker v. Sivasubramania Maniagaran, and rejected the contrary view in Meenakshi Velu v. Kasturi Sakunthala. The English decisions in Waring v. London and Manchester Assurance Co. and Property & Bloodstock Ltd. v.
