Emerton were distinguished because they rested on section 100(1)(i) of the English Law of Property Act, 1925.
members.conclusion: The auction and the contract of sale did not extinguish the society’s right of redemption; because the sale had not been completed by a registered conveyance, the society could redeem on payment of the amount due.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a mortgagor may redeem mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_public_auction: The mortgagee exercised a power of sale by putting the mortgaged property up for public auction.
predicates.no_registered_conveyance: No registered conveyance completing the transfer of the mortgagor’s interest had been executed.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagor’s right to redeem is not extinguished merely because property is put up for auction or an agreement for sale is made; absent a completed conveyance, payment of the secured debt preserves the right to redeem.
material_facts: The company’s assets were subject to a mortgage and the company retained an equity of redemption.
The corporation had put the assets up for tender and entered into an agreement for sale, but no conveyance had been executed.
The appellant, acting as a director of the company, paid the corporation’s full dues before the tenders were opened and sought the return of the company’s title documents and assets.
The corporation did not return the assets and instead adjusted the payment to the account of another company.
members.legal_principle: Under the principles governing a mortgagor’s equity of redemption, an agreement for sale does not by itself extinguish that equity; extinguishment requires a completed conveyance. Putting property up for auction likewise does not extinguish the right of redemption. The Court relied on section 69 of the Transfer of Property Act, Mulla on Transfer of Property, and Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam.
members.conclusion: The company retained its right to redeem because no conveyance had extinguished that right; payment of the corporation’s dues required the loan to be treated as repaid, and the assets were to be restored to the company.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_enforcement_sale and mortgaged_assets_have_not_been_conveyed and secured_debt_is_paid and mortgagor_seeks_redemption

predicates.appeal_challenges_enforcement_sale: An appeal challenges a financial corporation’s sale of assets while enforcing security for a debt.
predicates.mortgaged_assets_have_not_been_conveyed: The mortgaged assets have not been transferred by a completed conveyance.
predicates.secured_debt_is_paid: The secured debt is paid on behalf of the mortgagor.
predicates.mortgagor_seeks_redemption: The mortgagor seeks return of the mortgaged assets after paying the secured debt.

members.legal_issue: Confirmation of an execution sale does not prevent a mortgagor from seeking redemption while an appeal challenging the sale remains pending and the right of redemption has not been extinguished.
material_facts: The mortgagor challenged the first auction sale, and the challenge was initially allowed before being reversed on appeal.
The High Court confirmed the first sale while an appeal against its order was pending before the Supreme Court.
A subsequent sale had been held subject to a direction that it not be confirmed.
The mortgagor sought redemption while the appeals remained pending, and the right of redemption had not been extinguished.
members.legal_principle: Order 34 Rule 5 permits payment before confirmation of sale. An order confirming a sale after dismissal of a challenge to the sale does not attain finality for this purpose while an appeal against that dismissal is pending. The Court relied on Chandra Mani v. Anarjan Bibi, Sri Ranga Nilayam Ramkrishan Rao v. Kandokari Chellayamma, S.V. Ramalingam v. K.E. Rajagopalan, and M. Sevugan Chettiar v. V.A. Narayana Raja. Under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, redemption is extinguished only in the circumstances specified there; Raghunath Singh v. Pt. Hansraj Kunwar and Mhadagonda Ramgonda Patil v. Shripal Balwant Rainade were also relied on concerning the survival and extinguishment of that right.
members.conclusion: The confirmation of the first sale had not become absolute while the appeal remained pending, and the mortgagor could still invoke the redemption procedure. The later sale, which had not been confirmed, could not stand once the redemption relief was granted.

predicates.mortgage_execution_sale_proceeding: A sale of mortgaged property was being conducted in execution proceedings.
predicates.sale_challenge_appeal_pending: An appeal challenging the decision on an application to set aside the sale remained pending.
predicates.redemption_right_unextinguished: The mortgagor’s right to redeem had not been extinguished by an act of the parties or a court decree.

members.legal_issue: An execution sale and the recording of satisfaction of the decree cannot be treated as final while an appeal challenging the sale remains undecided.
material_facts: The execution sale was confirmed and satisfaction of the decree was recorded after the application to set aside the sale was dismissed.
An appeal against that dismissal remained pending when the High Court considered the related debt-relief application and sale appeal.
The High Court treated the judgment-debtors as having ceased to own the estate from the sale date while also permitting debt relief on the basis that the decree remained relevant.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI, rule 92, and section 65 of the Code of Civil Procedure govern confirmation and vesting following an execution sale. Where an appeal challenges refusal to set aside the sale, finality awaits the appellate decision; Chandramani Shaha v. Anarjan Bibi supports this approach. The sale and satisfaction of the decree must be treated consistently, and Bhawani Kunwar v. Mathura Prasad Singh concerns the effect of a sale once it has become effective.
members.conclusion: The High Court's treatment was inconsistent: while the challenge to the sale remained pending, neither the sale nor the recorded satisfaction could be treated as final for deciding the related appeals.

predicates.execution_sale_challenge_appeal_pending: A judgment-debtor has appealed the refusal to set aside an execution sale, and that appeal has not been decided.
predicates.sale_confirmation_recorded: The court has recorded an order confirming the execution sale.
predicates.decree_satisfaction_recorded: The court has recorded satisfaction of the decree based on the execution sale.
predicates.sale_and_decree_satisfaction_remain_nonf: The sale and the recorded satisfaction are not final while the challenge to the sale remains pending.

members.legal_issue: A court considering a challenge to an arbitral award cannot set it aside by re-examining and reappraising evidence that the arbitrator considered and believed.
material_facts: The parties referred their disputes to arbitration, and the arbitrator heard and considered substantial oral and documentary evidence.
The arbitrator accepted the Chief Engineer’s evidence and found that the contractor was not entitled to additional payment.
In proceedings to set aside the award, a High Court judge re-examined and reappraised that evidence and set aside part of the award.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, a court hearing a challenge to an award does not exercise appellate jurisdiction over the arbitrator’s assessment of evidence. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not sit in appeal over the arbitrator’s award by reappraising the evidence; the award could not be set aside on that basis.

rule.if: award_challenge_proceeding and arbitrator_considered_evidence and arbitrator_believed_evidence and reviewing_court_reappraised_evidence

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party brought a proceeding to have an arbitral award set aside.
predicates.arbitrator_considered_evidence: The arbitrator considered evidence bearing on the dispute.
predicates.arbitrator_believed_evidence: The arbitrator accepted evidence in reaching the award.
predicates.reviewing_court_reappraised_evidence: The reviewing court reassessed evidence to reach a different view from the arbitrator.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral award cannot be set aside merely because the arbitrator allegedly reached a wrong conclusion, failed to appreciate facts, or acted contrary to a statutory obligation where those objections fall outside the limited grounds for challenge.
material_facts: The parties appeared before an umpire appointed by the Court, who made a reasoned award after lengthy proceedings.

An application was made to set aside the award in whole or in part, including on the grounds that the arbitrator had reached a wrong conclusion, failed to appreciate facts, and acted contrary to Section 70 of the Contract Act.
The Court found that the objections fell outside the limited grounds of challenge available under the Arbitration Act.
members.legal_principle: Under the scheme of the Arbitration Act, the arbitrator is the final arbiter of the dispute, and an award is not open to challenge merely because the arbitrator reached a wrong conclusion or failed to appreciate facts. An objection that the arbitrator acted contrary to Section 70 of the Contract Act is not a permissible ground for challenge on the facts of this case. The Court considered the appellant's reliance on Yogambai Boyee Ammani Animal v. Naina Pillai Markayar, ILR 33 Madras 15, but did not accept that reliance as permitting the challenge.
members.conclusion: The objections were rejected and the award was directed to be made a rule of the Court.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_to_set_aside_arbitral_a: A party applied to have an arbitral award set aside in whole or in part.
predicates.award_is_reasoned: The arbitrator issued an award that gave reasons.
predicates.objections_attack_merits_conclusions: The challenging party objected that the arbitrator reached a wrong conclusion or failed to appreciate the facts.
predicates.objection_alleges_conflict_with_restitut: The challenging party alleged that the arbitrator acted contrary to an obligation to make restitution for a benefit received.

members.legal_issue: A court considering an application to set aside an arbitral award cannot re-examine factual merits that do not fall within a statutory ground for setting aside.
material_facts: The challenge to the awards relied on factual disputes concerning default, whether time was essential, readiness and willingness, termination, and the merits of specific performance.
The Court found no issue showing that the subject matter was incapable of arbitration and no basis for treating the awards as conflicting with public policy.
The challenge did not establish another applicable statutory ground for setting aside the awards.
members.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, provides limited grounds for setting aside an award. Under section 34(2)(b), the relevant grounds are that the subject matter is not capable of arbitration or that the award conflicts with the public policy of India; the statutory explanation identifies fraud, corruption, and specified procedural violations as examples relevant to public policy. Disagreement with factual findings about contractual performance does not, by itself, establish one of those grounds.
members.conclusion: The factual merits raised did not provide a basis to set aside the awards under section 34(2)(b), and the Court rejected the challenge on those grounds.

rule.if: award_set_aside_challenge and challenge_targets_factual_merits and no_non_arbitrability_ground and no_public_policy_ground

predicates.award_set_aside_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award in court seeking to have it set aside.
predicates.challenge_targets_factual_merits: The challenge disputes factual findings about the parties’ performance, default, readiness, or contractual rights.
predicates.no_non_arbitrability_ground: The challenger has not established that the subject matter cannot lawfully be resolved by arbitration.
predicates.no_public_policy_ground: The challenger has not established that the award conflicts with public policy or otherwise identified a public-policy basis for setting it aside.

members.legal_issue: Judicial review of a domestic arbitral award is confined to the statutory grounds for setting it aside and does not permit an appeal on the merits.
material_facts: The dispute arose from a domestic arbitration under a concession agreement.
The award was challenged under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the challenge was considered on appeal under Section 37.
The High Court reassessed factual matters and contractual interpretation when setting aside parts of the award.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5, 34(2), 34(2-A), and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 limit judicial intervention. Patent illegality must go to the root of the matter and does not include mere legal error or reappreciation of evidence; a view that is not even possible, a contract interpretation no fair-minded or reasonable person would adopt, jurisdictional error, absence of reasons, or a finding based on no evidence or ignoring vital evidence may justify intervention. The Court relied on Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Company Limited v. National Highways Authority of India, Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, Uttarakhand Purv Sainik Kalyan Nigam Limited v. Northern Coal Field Limited, Bhaven Construction v. Executive Engineer Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Ltd., Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran, and Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co.
members.conclusion: Courts reviewing an arbitral award must remain within the limited grounds for intervention and must not reappreciate evidence or substitute their view for a reasonable possible view taken by the tribunal.

rule.if: domestic_arbitral_award_challenge and court_reviewing_award and (award_has_statutory_ground_for_interference or not award_has_statutory_ground_for_interference)

predicates.domestic_arbitral_award_challenge: A party challenges a domestic arbitral award in court.
predicates.court_reviewing_award: A court examines the challenged award rather than deciding the underlying dispute anew.
predicates.award_has_statutory_ground_for_interfere: The award has a defect of the kind that permits a court to set it aside.
predicates.not_award_has_statutory_ground_for_inter: The award does not have a defect of the kind that permits a court to set it aside.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot find an error apparent in an arbitral award by inferring the arbitrator’s reasoning or by relying on valuation evidence that was not presented to the arbitrator.
material_facts: The award stated the market values of the properties but did not disclose the arbitrator’s reasoning for arriving at those values.

A valuation statement covering the immovable properties bore the signatures of all parties, and no party produced other valuation evidence before the arbitrator or objected to the stated valuations during the arbitration.
Additional municipal assessment documents were produced in court but had not been produced before the arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 30(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an error on the face of an award may justify setting it aside where the award or an incorporated document states reasons based on an erroneous legal proposition. A court may not infer reasons from a non-speaking award, probe the arbitrator’s mental process, reassess the evidence, or use evidence not presented to the arbitrator to attack the award. The Court relied on Champsey Bhara and Co. v. Jivraj Balloo Spg. and Wvg. Co. Ltd., Jivarajbhai Ujamshi Sheth v. Chintamanrao Balaji, Sudarsan Trading Co. v. Government of Kerala, Raipur Development Authority v. Chokhamal Contractors, and Santa Sila Devi v. Dhirendra Nath Sen.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in examining the valuation as though the award disclosed a reasoned method and in relying on additional valuation evidence; the valuation objection did not establish an error on the face of the award.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party challenged an arbitral award in court.
predicates.award_is_non_speaking: The award states the result but does not set out the arbitrator’s reasoning for it.
predicates.valuation_error_requires_inferred_reason: The alleged valuation error can be found only by inferring the arbitrator’s reasoning from the award or the record.
predicates.valuation_challenge_uses_evidence_not_be: The valuation challenge relies on evidence that was not presented to the arbitrator.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral award is not open to correction for factual mistakes or an alleged error in applying the law unless an erroneous legal proposition appears in the award or an incorporated document and forms the basis of the award.
material_facts: The award stated the requirement under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act that a transferee must have performed or be willing to perform his part of the contract.
The award found that the party in possession had stopped paying the monthly instalments and was not willing to perform that obligation.
The challenge alleged that the arbitrator had erred by treating the monthly payments as still due after the other contracting party repudiated the agreement.
The award contained no erroneous statement of the legal requirement; the alleged error concerned its application to the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an error of law is reviewable when an erroneous legal proposition appears in the award or a document incorporated into it and forms the basis of the award; a mistake of fact is not reviewable merely because a court might assess the facts differently. The court relied on Coimbatore District Podu Thozillar Sangam v. Balasubramania Foundary, Champsey Bhara and Co. v. Jivraj Balloo Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., Kanpur Nagar Mahapalika v. M/s Narain Das Haribansh, State of Orissa v. M/s Lall Brothers, and Union of India v. A. L. Rallia Ram. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act requires a transferee invoking its protection to have performed or be willing to perform his part of the contract.
members.conclusion: The objection did not establish an error of law on the face of the award, so the award was not set aside on that ground.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and award_states_correct_legal_requirement and challenged_error_concerns_application_or_facts and no_erroneous_legal_proposition_in_award

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party seeks to set aside or correct an arbitrator’s award.
predicates.award_states_correct_legal_requirement: The award sets out the legal requirement relevant to the dispute without stating it incorrectly.
predicates.challenged_error_concerns_application_or: The alleged error concerns how the arbitrator applied the legal requirement to the facts or assessed the facts.
predicates.no_erroneous_legal_proposition_in_award: The award and any document incorporated into it contain no erroneous legal proposition that forms the basis of the decision.

members.legal_issue: A court should not disturb the rejection of claims in a non-speaking arbitral award when the arbitrator considered the material and the award discloses no error on its face.
material_facts: The contractor challenged the rejection of three claims concerning alleged loss from delay in receiving the work site, retention of security, and expenses for a truck.
The arbitrator had considered the material placed before him and rejected the claims.
The award gave no reasons, and its face disclosed no error.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that it could not reassess the evidence considered by the arbitrator where the award was non-speaking and disclosed no error on its face. Although the case arose under the Arbitration Act, 1940, the Court cited no particular statutory section or earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the three claims was upheld, and the High Court was justified in affirming the award on those claims.

rule.if: arbitral_award_review and challenged_claims_rejected_by_arbitrator and award_is_non_speaking and arbitrator_considered_material and award_face_discloses_no_error

predicates.arbitral_award_review: A court reviews an arbitral award in a proceeding challenging the award.
predicates.challenged_claims_rejected_by_arbitrator: The arbitrator rejected claims that a party later challenged in court.
predicates.award_is_non_speaking: The award gives no reasons for its decision.
predicates.arbitrator_considered_material: The arbitrator considered the material placed before him or her.
predicates.award_face_discloses_no_error: The face of the award reveals no error.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal must remain within its reference, and a court reviewing an award cannot set it aside on an objection that was not raised before the tribunal.
material_facts: The arbitration concerned the delay in issuing a traffic-restriction notification and the resulting effect on toll collection.
The State did not argue before the tribunal that it had no contractual obligation to issue the notification.
The courts below relied on the absence of such an obligation when setting aside part of the award.
members.legal_principle: An arbitral tribunal derives its authority from the reference and cannot materially enlarge its scope. A court may intervene under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 for an award that exceeds the reference or is patently illegal, including for jurisdictional error. In exceptional circumstances, a tribunal may examine the contract and statutory provisions where a party properly pleads that a demand exceeds them. The Court relied on Grid Corporation of Orissa Ltd. v. Balasore Technical School; Delhi Development Authority v. R.S. Sharma and Company; Associated Engineering Co. v. Government of Andhra Pradesh; and Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. SAW Pipes Ltd.
members.conclusion: The courts below erred in deciding an objection that the State had not raised before the tribunal. An arbitrator cannot decide matters beyond the reference, though a court may intervene where an award exceeds the reference or contains a jurisdictional error.

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: The proceeding challenges an arbitral award before a court.
predicates.objection_not_raised_before_tribunal: A party relies on an objection in court that it did not raise before the arbitral tribunal.

members.legal_issue: An arbitral tribunal cannot replace clear, agreed contractual terms with different terms, and an award doing so may be set aside on the limited grounds for judicial review of arbitral awards.
material_facts: The registered lease fixed the monthly rent and provided for a specified lease period.
The respondent sought an increase in rent and a change to the lease period in arbitration invoked under the separate dealership agreement.
The arbitrator increased the rent and reduced the lease period, although the lease terms had not been altered by agreement of the parties.
The respondent had entered into the lease voluntarily, and the tribunal had not found any term of the dealership agreement unconscionable.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 restrict judicial intervention to the grounds specified in Section 34, including conflict with public policy under Section 34(2)(b)(ii) and, for applicable domestic awards, patent illegality under Section 34(2A). A court does not review the merits or reappraise evidence and ordinarily does not interfere with a reasonable contractual interpretation; however, an award that disregards the contract or rewrites it can be set aside. The Court relied on Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, Ssangyong Engineering and Construction Co. Ltd. v. National Highways Authority of India, PSA SICAL Terminals Pvt. Ltd. v. Board of Trustees of V.O. Chidambranar Port Trust, M.D., Army Welfare Housing Organisation v. Sumangal Service (P) Ltd., and Satyanarayana Construction Co. v. Union of India. It distinguished Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly because the case concerned a voluntary lease, not an employment contract, and there was no finding of an unconscionable term.
members.conclusion: The award’s changes to the lease rent and lease period were in patent disregard of the lease terms and were set aside. The parties remained bound by their agreed lease terms.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party seeks judicial review of an arbitral award.
predicates.contract_terms_are_express: The parties’ contract states the terms governing the matter in dispute.
predicates.tribunal_changes_terms_without_party_agr: The tribunal awards terms different from those in the contract without the parties agreeing to the change.

members.legal_issue: A court may set aside an execution sale for irregularity or fraud only when the applicant proves both the irregularity or fraud and substantial injury caused by it.
material_facts: The judgment debtor applied to set aside a sale of immovable property conducted in execution of a money decree.
The application alleged defects in the sale process and that the property would have fetched a higher price.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 90(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires substantial injury caused by a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting an execution sale. The Court relied on Saheb Khan v. Mohd. Yousufuddin, which applied this requirement, and referred to Dhirendra Nath Gorai v. Sudhir Chandra Ghosh, Jaswantlal Natvarlal Thakkar v. Sushilaben Manilal Dangarwala, and Kadiyala Rama Rao v. Gutala Kahna Rao.
members.conclusion: Proof of a material irregularity or fraud alone is insufficient; the applicant must also establish substantial injury caused by that irregularity or fraud.

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A person affected by an immovable-property sale conducted in execution of a decree applies to have that sale set aside.
predicates.material_sale_irregularity: The applicant proves a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the execution sale.
predicates.sale_fraud: The applicant proves fraud in publishing or conducting the execution sale.
predicates.substantial_injury_caused_by_irregularit: The applicant proves substantial injury caused by the material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.

members.legal_issue: A court sale of immovable property may be set aside for irregularity or fraud in its publication or conduct only when the applicant proves that the defect caused substantial injury.
material_facts: The sale was conducted by an Advocate Commissioner after notice was sent to the parties through their advocates, notices were affixed to the property, and pamphlets were distributed locally.
The applicant alleged collusion but gave no sufficient particulars to support that allegation.
The successful bid exceeded the assessed market value, and the applicant did not establish substantial injury caused by any irregularity or fraud.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 90(1) and (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an affected person to challenge a sale for material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting it, but requires proof that the defect caused substantial injury. A charge of fraud or material irregularity must be supported by sufficient particulars and established facts; bald allegations are insufficient. The Court relied on Dhirendra Nath Gorai and Suibal Chandra Shaw v. Sudhir Chandra Ghosh, (1964) 6 SCC 101; Jaswantlal Natvarlal Thakkar v. Sushilaben Manilal Dangarwala, (1991) Supp. 2 SCC 691; and Kadiyala Rama Rao v. Gutala Kahna Rao, (2000) 3 SCC 87.
members.conclusion: The sale could not be set aside because no material irregularity or fraud causing substantial injury was established; the High Court erred in setting it aside.

predicates.court_sale_challenge: The proceeding challenges a court-conducted sale of immovable property in execution of a decree.
predicates.no_material_defect_proved: The applicant has not proved a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.
predicates.no_substantial_injury_caused_by_defect_p: The applicant has not proved substantial injury caused by an irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.

members.legal_issue: An irregularity in the conduct of an execution sale does not justify setting it aside unless the applicant proves that the irregularity caused substantial injury.
material_facts: The decree holders purchased the property at the court auction after receiving permission to bid at a reduced price without notice to the judgment debtor.
The judgment debtor challenged the sale under Order 21, Rule 90, relying on the absence of notice.
The Court found no sufficient facts showing that the absence of notice caused substantial injury to the judgment debtor.
members.legal_principle: Order 21, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires an applicant challenging an execution sale to prove not only an illegality or material irregularity in the conduct of the sale but also substantial injury caused by it. The Court found no material irregularity or illegality vitiating the sale under the applicable provisions and upheld the rejection of the application.
members.conclusion: The application to set aside the sale was properly rejected because substantial injury resulting from the irregularity was not proved.

rule.if: execution_sale_set_aside_application and sale_conduct_irregularity and not substantial_injury_caused_by_irregularity

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside_application: A person applies to have a sale conducted to enforce a decree set aside.
predicates.sale_conduct_irregularity: An irregularity occurred in the conduct of the execution sale.
predicates.substantial_injury_caused_by_irregularit: The irregularity caused substantial injury to the person challenging the sale.

members.legal_issue: An execution sale cannot be set aside for an irregularity in its proclamation when the applicant did not preserve the objection after notice or has not sustained substantial injury because of the irregularity.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors applied under the civil procedure rule governing applications to set aside execution sales, relying in part on defects in the sale proclamations.
The judgment-debtors had received notice; one did not object to the valuation, and the other, despite filing valuation objections, did not attend when the proclamation was settled.
The lower courts concurrently found that the non-compliance caused no substantial injury to the judgment-debtor.
The subordinate judge found no fraud and found the prices obtained for the properties to be fair.
members.legal_principle: Non-compliance with the sale-proclamation requirements is an irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale and is addressed through Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Under that rule, an applicant must show substantial injury caused by the irregularity; a person who received notice but did not attend the drawing up of the proclamation, or who was present but did not object to the defect then, cannot seek to set the sale aside on that defect. The court approved Manindra Chandra v. Jagdish Chandra and Maniruddin Ahmed v. Umaprasanna, and distinguished Ashram Thikadar v. Vijay Singh Chopra.
members.conclusion: The sales could not be set aside under Order XXI, rule 90, because the applicants did not meet its requirements, including the requirement of substantial injury.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and sale_proclamation_irregularity and ((notice_received and did_not_attend_proclamation) or (present_at_proclamation and no_objection_when_proclamation_set) or not substantial_injury_caused)

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A person affected by an execution sale applied to have the sale set aside.
predicates.sale_proclamation_irregularity: The challenged sale involved an irregularity in the publication or conduct of the sale relating to its proclamation.
predicates.notice_received: The applicant received notice of the drawing up of the sale proclamation.
predicates.did_not_attend_proclamation: The applicant did not attend when the sale proclamation was drawn up.
predicates.present_at_proclamation: The applicant was present when the sale proclamation was drawn up.
predicates.no_objection_when_proclamation_set: The applicant did not object to the relied-on defect when the proclamation was drawn up.
predicates.substantial_injury_caused: The applicant sustained substantial injury because of the sale irregularity.

members.legal_issue: A court sale should not be set aside for an allegedly inadequate price unless a material irregularity in the conduct of the sale caused substantial injury to the judgment-debtor.
material_facts: A finance corporation sought recovery of its loan by attachment and sale of the debtor company's mortgaged industrial property.

The executing court repeatedly postponed earlier auctions in an effort to obtain a better price; the bids eventually levelled off, and the final auction drew numerous bidders, including interested industrial concerns.

The debtor's director attended the final auctions but did not object to the conduct of the sale or seek postponement, and the debtor produced neither a valuation report nor a buyer through private negotiation.

The corporation obtained a valuation substantially above the accepted bid, but the executing court considered the valuation, the actual bids, the difficulties of selling a specialised industrial plant, the prolonged proceedings, and the prospect that further postponements would deter bidders.
The debtor had contributed to delay through litigation, and the court found that the executing judge had consciously sought to maximise the sale price rather than mechanically accepting the bid.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(8) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 applies the Code of Civil Procedure, including Order XXI rule 90, so a sale may be set aside only where material irregularity in the conduct of the sale causes substantial injury. The court's acceptance of a bid is part of the conduct of the sale, and mechanical acceptance of a substantially inadequate bid without considering whether a better price could be obtained may establish both elements. But price inadequacy alone is insufficient: the executing court must make a realistic appraisal of relevant circumstances, including value, actual bids, economic conditions, the burden of raising funds, the likely futility of postponements, and litigation risk. A court need not adjourn sales indefinitely, assess fairness with hindsight, or give a speaking order where it has fairly applied its mind. The court relied on Nayalkha and Sons v. Ramanya Das for the court's duty to ensure an adequate price before confirming a sale.
members.conclusion: The executing court committed no material irregularity in accepting the final bid, and the sale was not liable to be set aside merely because the price was below the estimated market value. The appeal was allowed; the purchaser was directed to deposit the additional amount it had offered, after which it could take possession.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and court_realistically_assessed_bid and repeated_prior_adjournments and bidders_participated and debtor_no_valuation and debtor_no_sale_objection and debtor_litigation_delayed and bid_below_valuation

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A judgment-debtor sought to set aside a sale conducted in execution proceedings.
predicates.court_realistically_assessed_bid: The executing court considered the relevant circumstances before accepting the bid rather than accepting it mechanically.
predicates.repeated_prior_adjournments: The executing court had already postponed earlier sale attempts in an effort to obtain a better price.
predicates.bidders_participated: Interested bidders attended and participated in the sale.
predicates.debtor_no_valuation: The judgment-debtor did not provide a valuation report for the property.
predicates.debtor_no_sale_objection: The judgment-debtor did not object to the conduct of the sale or seek its postponement when present at the auction.
predicates.debtor_litigation_delayed: The judgment-debtor's litigation contributed to delay and to concern that further obstacles might follow the sale.
predicates.bid_below_valuation: The accepted bid was below an estimate of the property's value.

members.legal_issue: An execution auction sale cannot be set aside for irregularity or fraud unless the applicant establishes injury caused by that irregularity or fraud.
material_facts: The notice for the adjourned auction sale did not specify the hour of sale, although the original proclamation had specified the date and hour.
The judgment-debtor sought to set aside the sale, alleging material irregularity and inadequacy of the price paid by the purchaser.
The judgment-debtor relied on a valuation report prepared without notice to the purchaser or an opportunity for the purchaser to object.

No other evidence was led to establish the value of the property share or that the price was inadequate, and the judgment-debtor did not establish that any inadequacy resulted from the omission in the notice.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI, rule 90, as amended by the Allahabad High Court, requires the applicant to satisfy the court that injury was sustained by reason of the irregularity or fraud. Proof of irregularity and injury, including an allegedly inadequate sale price, is not sufficient without a causal connection between them. The Court considered the alleged omission under Order XXI, rule 69, but held that the valuation report, prepared without notice or an opportunity for the purchaser to object, could not establish inadequacy, and there was no other supporting evidence.
members.conclusion: The sale was not liable to be set aside because the judgment-debtor failed to establish inadequacy of price caused by the alleged material irregularity.

rule.if: execution_sale_set_aside_proceeding and material_sale_irregularity and not injury_caused_by_irregularity_proven

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside_proceeding: An applicant sought to set aside an auction sale conducted in execution of a judgment or decree.
predicates.material_sale_irregularity: A material procedural irregularity occurred in the conduct or notice of the auction sale.
predicates.injury_caused_by_irregularity_proven: The applicant established that the irregularity caused injury, such as a reduced sale price.

members.legal_issue: A material irregularity in an execution sale warrants setting it aside when the judgment-debtor proves substantial injury resulting from the sale.
material_facts: The three houses in another sale item were put up separately and realised a total price considerably greater than the value attributed to them when grouped together in the proclamation.
The High Court found that the two bungalows would probably also have fetched a higher price if sold separately.
The judgment-debtors’ assertions about the value and sale of comparable property were not controverted by material from the decree-holders.
The Court found enough evidence of substantial injury from the sale of the two bungalows.
members.legal_principle: In an application under Order 21, Rule 90, Civil Procedure Code, the Court considered whether material irregularity in conducting the execution sale had caused substantial injury. Evidence that separate sales of comparable properties produced substantially more than their grouped valuation, together with a finding that separate sales of the properties in question would probably similarly yield a higher price, was sufficient evidence of substantial injury in this case.
members.conclusion: Substantial injury was shown as to the sale of the two bungalows; the Court set that sale aside and ordered a fresh sale after judicial consideration of whether the bungalows could be sold separately and what particulars should be included in the proclamation.

predicates.execution_auction_sale_challenge: A party applied to set aside an auction sale held to execute a decree.
predicates.sale_irregularity_found: The court found a material irregularity in the conduct of the sale.
predicates.separate_sale_evidence_supports_higher_p: Evidence from separate sales and the court’s assessment supported that separate lots would probably fetch a higher price than a grouped sale.

members.legal_issue: A court conducting an execution sale must sell only the portion of attached property necessary to satisfy the decree when that portion can be separately sold, and a sale of the entire property without considering this requirement is invalid.
material_facts: The execution claim was about Rs. 2,400, while the attached land measured 10 acres and was sold for Rs. 17,000.
The land was not indivisible, and a portion could conveniently have been demarcated and sold.
The executing court did not consider whether selling only a portion would satisfy the execution claim.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the executing court to determine whether the whole attached property or only a portion is necessary to satisfy the decree. This is an obligation, not merely a discretion; even a single property must be sold only in part where a separate portion can be sold lawfully and will suffice. A sale made without examining this requirement is illegal and without jurisdiction. The Court relied on Takkaseela Pedda Subba Reddy v. Pujari Padmavathamma & Ors., [1977] 3 SCC 337, which held that execution sales must stop once the decree is satisfied.
members.conclusion: The sale of the entire property was illegal and without jurisdiction and was set aside.

rule.if: execution_sale and claim_small_relative_to_property and property_portion_separately_saleable and court_failed_to_consider_sufficient_portion

predicates.execution_sale: A court conducted a sale of attached property to execute a decree.
predicates.claim_small_relative_to_property: The execution claim was small in relation to the value or extent of the property sold.
predicates.property_portion_separately_saleable: A portion of the property could be separately sold without violating the law, and division was not impracticable or undesirable.
predicates.court_failed_to_consider_sufficient_port: The court did not consider whether selling only a sufficient portion of the property would satisfy the execution claim.
predicates.execution_sale_is_invalid: The execution sale is illegal and must be set aside.

members.legal_issue: An executing court must sell only the property, or portion of it, necessary to satisfy the decree, and failure to consider a sufficient part may constitute a material irregularity causing substantial injury.
material_facts: The entire commercial plot, measuring 550 square yards, was sold to recover a debt of about Rs 7,780.
The plot was worth substantially more than the debt.
The executing court did not consider whether a smaller portion could satisfy the decree.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 17(4), Rule 64 and Rule 66(2)(a), together with Form 27 of Appendix E, require the executing court to sell only so much property as is necessary to satisfy the decree. The Court relied on Ambati Narasayya v. M. Subba Rao, Mangal Prasad v. Krishna Kumar Maheshwari and Takaseela Pedda Subba Reddy v. Pujari Padmavathamma. Under Order 21 Rule 90, a material irregularity must cause substantial injury to the judgment-debtor.
members.conclusion: Selling the whole plot without considering whether a portion would suffice was a material irregularity causing substantial injury, and the sale was liable to be set aside.

rule.if: immovable_property_execution_sale and whole_property_sold and property_value_greatly_exceeded_debt and court_did_not_consider_partial_sale

predicates.immovable_property_execution_sale: The proceeding is a sale of immovable property in execution of a decree.
predicates.whole_property_sold: The whole property was sold to recover the decree debt.
predicates.property_value_greatly_exceeded_debt: The value of the property greatly exceeded the debt being recovered.
predicates.court_did_not_consider_partial_sale: The executing court did not consider whether selling only part of the property would satisfy the decree.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for seeking enhanced compensation does not begin to run against a claimant who lacked notice or knowledge of the award and whose entitlement to compensation became fixed only after a later determination of competing claims.
material_facts: The claimants did not participate in the inquiry leading to the compensation award and had no knowledge of it until a later proceeding resolved competing claims to the land.
The Collector had made no apportionment because ownership shares were disputed, and the claimants became entitled to compensation only when the later proceeding determined their share.
The claimants sought a reference for enhanced compensation within six weeks after learning of their entitlement.
The High Court held the reference time-barred, and the appeal challenged that ruling.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the expression “date of the award” is not construed mechanically; under Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, it means the date the award is communicated to or becomes actually or constructively known by the claimant. Where entitlement to compensation is unresolved until apportionment, the claimant's right to seek enhanced compensation crystallizes when that entitlement is determined. Sections 18 and 30, read with Dr. G.H. Grant v. State of Bihar, support that conclusion.
members.conclusion: The reference for enhanced compensation was not barred by limitation, and the High Court erred in holding otherwise.

rule.if: appeal_from_reference_limitation_ruling and award_not_communicated_or_known and compensation_entitlement_fixed_only_later and reference_filed_within_six_weeks_after_knowledge

predicates.appeal_from_reference_limitation_ruling: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a ruling that a compensation-enhancement reference was time-barred.
predicates.award_not_communicated_or_known: The claimant was not given notice of the award and did not actually or constructively know of it before a later event.
predicates.compensation_entitlement_fixed_only_late: The claimant's entitlement to receive compensation was determined only after a later resolution of competing claims.
predicates.reference_filed_within_six_weeks_after_k: The claimant sought a reference for enhanced compensation within six weeks after learning of the award and becoming entitled to compensation.

members.legal_issue: A person who had actual or constructive knowledge of an acquisition award cannot obtain a reference by relying on a later notice when the reference application was already outside the applicable limitation period.
material_facts: The society objected to the acquisition before the award was made, and its objections were rejected on the ground that it had no right, title, or interest in the land.
The award was made in favour of the recorded landholders, and the society had constructive knowledge of it when it was made.
The society sought a reference years later, relying on a notice subsequently issued to it.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 12(2) and 18(2) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, limitation runs from actual or constructive knowledge of the award, not necessarily from later formal notice. Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer and Madan v. State of Maharashtra establish that knowledge of the award is essential to commencement of limitation. A party that participated in the acquisition process and knew, or reasonably ought to have known, of the award cannot rely on a later notice to restart limitation.
members.conclusion: The reference application was time-barred, and the Land Acquisition Officer could not validly refer it to the civil court.

predicates.acquisition_reference_proceeding: A person sought a judicial reference to challenge or seek reconsideration of compensation awarded in a land acquisition.
predicates.applicant_participated_before_award: The applicant took part in the acquisition process before the award was made.
predicates.applicant_had_constructive_knowledge_of_: The applicant's participation or circumstances meant that a reasonable person in the applicant's position ought to have known of the award when it was made.
predicates.reference_application_was_outside_time_f: The applicant sought a reference after the applicable period had elapsed from the applicant's actual or constructive knowledge of the award.

members.legal_issue: For an absent claimant who received no award notice, the limitation period for seeking a reference runs from actual or constructive knowledge of the essential contents of the award, not mechanically from the date the award was made.
material_facts: The landowners were not present, personally or through representatives, when the award was made.
They did not receive the notice of the award that would have informed them of its contents.
The Court accepted that they learned of the award’s contents only shortly before applying for a reference.
members.legal_principle: Section 18(2), proviso (b), provides different time limits depending on the claimant’s presence and receipt of notice. Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer held that the date of the award means the date it is communicated or actually or constructively known. State of Punjab v. Mst. Qaisar Jehan Begum clarified that knowledge must concern the essential contents of the award. Those principles were followed in Parsottambhai Maganbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat and Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. S.U.T.N.I. Sangam. Reading the date-of-award language literally where the claimant had no knowledge could produce arbitrary results and risk violating Articles 14 and 300A of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: For an absent claimant who received no notice, the applicable period runs from the date the claimant actually or constructively knew the essential contents of the award.

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_proceeding: A person applied to the Collector to refer a land-acquisition compensation claim to a court.
predicates.claimant_absent_when_award_made: Neither the claimant nor the claimant’s representative was present when the award was made.
predicates.no_award_notice_received: The claimant did not receive notice communicating the award.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for seeking a reference concerning an acquisition award begins when the affected applicant has actual or constructive knowledge of the award if the applicant was not present or represented when it was made and was not served notice of it.
material_facts: The applicants were not present when the award was made and had not been served notice of it.
There was no evidence that notice of the award had been served on the applicants.
The applicants’ assertion that they learned of the award when compensation was paid in July 1988 was not challenged.
They applied for a reference on September 22, 1988, within six months of learning of the award.
The High Court held that the application was time-barred by counting from the date the award was declared.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 18(2)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, where an applicant was not present or represented when the award was made and was not served notice under Section 12(2), the limitation period runs from the date the applicant had actual or constructive knowledge of the award, rather than mechanically from the date it was declared. The Court applied Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. The Deputy Land Acquisition Officer and another, AIR 1961 SC 1500, which held that knowledge or communication of the award is essential and that the date of the award, for this purpose, is when it is communicated or becomes known actually or constructively.
members.conclusion: The application was within time because it was made within six months of the applicants’ knowledge of the award. The finding that it was time-barred was set aside, and the appeals were remitted to the High Court for decision on the merits.

predicates.reference_request_concerning_acquisition: The applicant sought a reference concerning an award made in an acquisition proceeding.
predicates.applicant_absent_or_unrepresented_when_a: The applicant was neither present nor represented when the award was made.
predicates.applicant_not_served_award_notice: The applicant was not served notice of the award.
predicates.application_filed_within_six_months_of_k: The applicant filed the reference request within six months after gaining actual or constructive knowledge of the award.

members.legal_issue: For an interested person who was absent when a land acquisition award was made and received no notice of it, the limitation period for seeking a reference begins when the person learns the essential contents of the award.
material_facts: The interested persons were not notified of the acquisition and were neither present nor represented when the award was made.
They first sought interim payment without knowing the amount of compensation fixed by the award; that request did not establish knowledge of the award’s essential contents.
They learned the essential contents when they received the compensation payment and applied for a reference within six months of that date.
Their evidence about when they learned the award’s contents was not seriously contradicted.
members.legal_principle: Under section 18, proviso clause (b), of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, where the applicant was not present or represented when the award was made and did not receive notice under section 12(2), the period in the second part of clause (b) runs from when the award is communicated to the applicant or becomes actually or constructively known. Following Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. The Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, knowledge must concern the essential contents of the award, not merely the fact that an award was made. The Court did not decide whether a court hearing a reference may itself examine whether the reference was timely.
members.conclusion: The application for a reference was within time. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_request and applicant_absent_from_award and award_notice_not_received and essential_contents_learned_within_limitation_window

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_request: An interested person sought a court reference to challenge compensation fixed in a compulsory land acquisition award.
predicates.applicant_absent_from_award: The interested person was neither personally present nor represented when the award was made.
predicates.award_notice_not_received: The acquiring authority did not give the interested person notice of the award.
predicates.essential_contents_learned_within_limita: The interested person learned the essential contents of the award sufficiently before applying for a reference to meet the applicable time limit.

members.legal_issue: For an application seeking a court reference in a land acquisition matter, the period running from the Collector’s award does not begin before the award is communicated to, or actually or constructively known by, the affected person.
material_facts: The Collector made, signed, and filed an award determining compensation, but the affected owner was not present or represented when it was made.
The Collector did not give the owner notice of the award.
The owner learned of the award later and applied for a reference within six months of learning of it.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 12(1), 12(2), and 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Collector’s award is an offer of compensation on behalf of the Government, and section 12(2) requires immediate notice to interested persons who were not present or represented when it was made. Accordingly, the expression “date of the Collector’s award” in the proviso to section 18 means the date the award is communicated to, or actually or constructively known by, the affected person. The Court applied Ezra v. The Secretary of State and Ezra v. Secretary of State for India, and approved Magdonald v. The Secretary of State for India in Council and Hari Das Pal v. The Municipal Board, Lucknow; it disapproved the contrary approach in Jehangir Bomanji v. G. D. Gaikwad and State of Travancore-Cochin v. Narayani Amma Ponnamma.
members.conclusion: The application was not time-barred because the relevant date of the award was the date when the owner knew of it, not the earlier date when the Collector signed or filed it.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_application and applicant_absent_from_award and award_notice_not_given and application_within_six_months_of_award_knowledge

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_application: A person applied in a land acquisition proceeding for the compensation matter to be referred to a court.
predicates.applicant_absent_from_award: The applicant was neither present nor represented when the award was made.
predicates.award_notice_not_given: The authority did not give the applicant notice of the award after making it.
predicates.application_within_six_months_of_award_k: The applicant filed the reference application within six months after actually or constructively learning of the award.
predicates.application_not_time_barred: The reference application is not barred by the limitation period calculated from the award.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for seeking re-determination of compensation on the basis of an award in another landowner’s reference begins on the date the court pronounced that award, not on the date the applicant learned of it.
material_facts: Land was acquired under a common notification, and a court enhanced compensation in a reference brought by other landowners.
The applicants, who had not sought a reference, applied for re-determination about five years after the court’s award.
The High Court held that the limitation period began when the applicants learned of the award and directed that their applications be entertained.
members.legal_principle: Section 28-A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and its proviso expressly measure the three-month period from the court’s award and exclude the day of pronouncement and the time requisite to obtain a copy. Tola Ram v. State of U.P., Union of India v. Mangatu Ram, and Jose Antonio Cruz Dos R. Rodriguese v. Land Acquisition Collector hold that knowledge does not alter that starting point. Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer, approved in State of Punjab v. Mst. Qaisar Jehan Begum, concerned Section 18 and was distinguished: that provision’s notice-related scheme does not govern an application by a person who was not party to the reference. The beneficial nature of the provision does not excuse failure to act within its prescribed period.
members.conclusion: The period begins on the date the court pronounced the award. In computing it, the day of pronouncement and the time required to obtain a copy of the award are excluded; lack of knowledge does not extend the period. The appeals were allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside.

predicates.redetermination_application_based_on_ano: An applicant sought re-determination of compensation by relying on an award obtained in another landowner’s court reference.
predicates.acquisition_under_same_notification: The applicant’s land and the land in the reference were acquired under the same notification.
predicates.court_award_increased_compensation: A court awarded greater compensation than the original acquisition award.

members.legal_issue: The filing period for a compensation-redetermination application based on another interested person’s court award runs from the date of that award, not from the applicant’s knowledge of it.
material_facts: Other interested persons whose land was covered by the same notification obtained an enhanced-compensation award on 3 April 2006.
The applicants had not sought a reference themselves. Their counsel applied for a certified copy on 17 May 2006; it was ready on 29 May and collected on 3 June.
The applicants filed their redetermination application on 18 July 2006. The Collector rejected it as four days late, and the applicants’ claimed date of acquiring knowledge was not substantiated.
members.legal_principle: Section 28A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires an application within three months from the date of the court’s award, excluding the day of the award and the time requisite for obtaining a copy. Under State of A.P. v. Marri Venkaiah, Union of India v. Mangatu Ram, Tota Ram v. State of U.P., Des Raj v. Union of India, and State of Orissa v. Chitrasen Bhoi, knowledge of the award is irrelevant to that period. Raja Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Deputy Land Acquisition Officer concerned Section 18 and does not govern Section 28A applications.
members.conclusion: The application period began from the date of the court’s award, with the day of the award and the time requisite for obtaining a copy excluded; the applicant’s date of knowledge did not affect the period. The dismissal of the application as late was upheld.

predicates.reassessment_request_based_on_another_in: A person who did not seek a reference requests reassessment based on a court award obtained by another interested person whose land was covered by the same acquisition notification.
predicates.statutory_period_measured_from_court_awa: The governing rule fixes the filing period by reference to the date of the court’s award and excludes the award day and the time requisite to obtain a copy.

members.legal_issue: An interested person who did not seek a reference may obtain re-determination of compensation on the basis of a court award if the land was covered by the same acquisition notification and the application is filed within the prescribed period.
material_facts: Some interested persons had not sought a reference under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Their land was covered by the same notification as land for which a reference court enhanced compensation.
An application for re-determination was filed within three months of the reference court's award, applying the statutory computation rules.
members.legal_principle: Section 28-A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permits interested persons who did not seek a section 18 reference, but whose land was covered by the same section 4(1) notification, to apply to the Collector for re-determination on the basis of the court award. Under the proviso, the day the award was pronounced and the time required to obtain a copy are excluded when computing the three-month period.
members.conclusion: The timely applicant was entitled to re-determination of compensation on the basis of the compensation awarded by the reference court.

rule.if: compensation_redetermination_proceeding and interested_owner_did_not_seek_reference and land_shared_acquisition_notification and application_within_computed_limit

predicates.compensation_redetermination_proceeding: The proceeding seeks re-determination of compensation by the acquiring authority on the basis of a court award.
predicates.interested_owner_did_not_seek_reference: The interested person did not seek a reference against the original compensation award.
predicates.land_shared_acquisition_notification: The person's land was covered by the same acquisition notification as land considered in the court award.
predicates.application_within_computed_limit: The person filed the written application within the applicable time limit, computed after excluding the specified time for the award and obtaining its copy.

members.legal_issue: A person who did not seek a reference may apply for redetermination of compensation on the basis of any qualifying court award made after the redetermination procedure became available, rather than only the first such award.
material_facts: Land was acquired under common notifications, and some landowners obtained enhanced compensation through court references.
The applicants had not sought references against the Collector’s awards and applied for redetermination based on court awards concerning land covered by the same notifications.
The applications were made within three months of the particular awards on which the applicants relied.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 28-A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read in light of its stated purpose of reducing inequality in compensation for similarly situated landowners, the relevant award is any award under Part III allowing compensation above the Collector’s award, not necessarily the first such award after Section 28-A came into force. The application must be made within three months of the relied-on award, concern other land covered by the same notification, be made by a person who did not apply for a reference, and be the applicant’s only application. A beneficial provision should be construed to advance its purpose; the Court relied on Jnan Ranjan Sen Gupta v. Arun Kumar Bose and rejected the contrary approach in Babua Ram v. State of U.P. and Union of India v. Karnail Singh.
members.conclusion: The limitation period runs from the award on which redetermination is sought. An applicant may rely on any qualifying award made after the procedure became available, provided the statutory conditions are met and the applicant makes only one application.

rule.if: land_acquisition_redetermination_application and court_award_after_procedure_available and award_grants_more_than_collector_awarded and applicant_land_covered_by_same_notification and applicant_did_not_seek_reference and application_within_three_months_of_relied_on_award and applicant_has_made_only_one_application

predicates.land_acquisition_redetermination_applica: A person seeks redetermination of compensation for acquired land through the procedure available to a person who did not seek a reference.
predicates.court_award_after_procedure_available: A court made the relied-on award after the redetermination procedure became available.
predicates.award_grants_more_than_collector_awarded: The court award allows the claimant in the reference more compensation than the Collector awarded.

predicates.applicant_did_not_seek_reference: The applicant did not apply for a reference against the Collector’s award.

predicates.applicant_has_made_only_one_application: The applicant has made no more than one application for redetermination under this procedure.

members.legal_issue: The true nature of an occupancy arrangement depends on its substance and the parties’ actual intention, rather than the label given to the document.
material_facts: The occupant had been in possession of the shop for about twenty years before signing a document styled as a licence.
The occupant had exclusive possession and conducted an independent stationery business and related activities in the premises.
The owner did not interfere with or control the occupant’s business or use of the premises.
The occupant remained in possession and continued the same use after the stated licence period expired, and the owner allowed this to continue for about seven years before filing suit.
The occupant paid a monthly amount for use of the premises, and the owner presented no relevant evidence about the nature of the occupation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, the distinction between a lease and a licence is determined by the real intention of the parties, assessed from the whole document and surrounding circumstances. The use of labels such as “lease”, “licence”, “rent” or “licence fee” is not decisive. Exclusive possession is an important consideration: a lease ordinarily gives a right to possess and enjoy the property, whereas a licence gives permission to use it while the owner retains possession and control. The parties’ conduct before and after the arrangement is relevant. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, AIR 1959 SC 1262, and Corporation of Calicut v. K. Sreenivasan, (2002) 5 SCC 361.
members.conclusion: The relationship was that of landlord and tenant, and the occupant possessed the premises as a tenant, not as a licensee.

rule.if: occupancy_classification_is_contested and (occupant_has_exclusive_possession and owner_does_not_retain_control) and occupant_uses_premises_for_independent_business and occupation_predates_document and occupation_continues_after_stated_expiry

predicates.occupancy_classification_is_contested: A court proceeding contests whether an occupant holds premises as a tenant or as a licensee.
predicates.occupant_has_exclusive_possession: The occupant has possession of the premises to the exclusion of the owner and others.
predicates.owner_does_not_retain_control: The owner does not retain control over the occupant’s possession or use of the premises.
predicates.occupant_uses_premises_for_independent_b: The occupant uses the premises for a business independent of the owner’s business.
predicates.occupation_predates_document: The occupant was already in possession before signing the document that describes the arrangement.
predicates.occupation_continues_after_stated_expiry: The occupant remains in possession and continues the same use after the document’s stated period ends.

members.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting occupancy of immovable property creates a lease or a licence depends on the parties' intention, assessed from the agreement and surrounding circumstances; exclusive possession is significant but not conclusive.
material_facts: The written agreement described the arrangement as a leave and licence and stated that the occupant would have no tenancy rights, but those descriptions were not decisive of the parties' intention.
The occupant was given exclusive possession of a loft, and the grantor reserved neither possession of any part of it nor a right of entry.
The loft had a separate entrance used by the occupant's customers, and the occupant's stock remained there after business hours.
The parties were both cloth merchants, the occupant was permitted to use the loft for that business, and the only consideration was a monthly payment.
There was no evidence that the arrangement arose from sympathy, friendship, relationship, or a similar personal motive.
The written terms specified a one-year period, restricted use to cloth trading, prohibited transfer or subletting, and required a month's notice for termination.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Easements Act defines a licence as a right to do something on another's immovable property that does not amount to an easement or an interest in that property. Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act defines a lease as a transfer of a right to enjoy immovable property. The controlling test is whether the agreement, read in light of surrounding circumstances, was intended to create an interest in the property; the parties' labels are evidence but are not decisive. Exclusive possession is significant but not conclusive. The Court relied on Mrs. M. N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 642.
members.conclusion: The agreement created an interest in the loft and operated as a lease, not a licence.

rule.if: occupancy_classification_case and exclusive_possession_granted and grantor_reserved_no_possession_or_entry and occupant_has_independent_access_and_use and payment_is_the_only_consideration and circumstances_indicate_property_interest

predicates.occupancy_classification_case: The dispute requires a court to determine whether an agreement for occupancy of immovable property creates a lease or a licence.
predicates.exclusive_possession_granted: The grantor placed the occupant in exclusive possession of the premises.
predicates.grantor_reserved_no_possession_or_entry: The grantor reserved neither possession of part of the premises nor a right of entry into them.
predicates.occupant_has_independent_access_and_use: The premises had separate access used by the occupant's customers, and the occupant kept business stock there after business hours.
predicates.payment_is_the_only_consideration: The occupant's payment was the only consideration for the arrangement, without evidence of a personal or relational motive for granting occupancy.
predicates.circumstances_indicate_property_interest: The agreement's terms and surrounding circumstances, considered together, indicated that the parties intended to create an interest in the premises despite describing the arrangement as a licence and disclaiming tenancy rights.

members.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting use of premises creates a lease or only a licence depends on the substance of the arrangement and the parties’ intention, rather than the document’s label or exclusive possession alone.
material_facts: The occupant was admitted temporarily to a member’s flat with the housing society’s permission and became a nominal member of the society.

The written agreement described the arrangement as a licence, granted use of the flat together with its furniture and fittings for a limited period, and stated that the occupant would not claim tenancy or sub-tenancy.
The occupant had exclusive possession, but the terms of the agreement and the surrounding circumstances showed an intention to permit temporary use without transferring an interest in the flat.
members.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy immovable property; section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 describes a licence as a permission that does not create an interest in the property. The substance of the agreement and the parties’ intention, gathered from its terms and surrounding, antecedent and subsequent circumstances, control; exclusive possession is significant but not conclusive. The Court relied on Board of Revenue v. A.M. Ansari, Tarkeshwar Sio Thakur Jiu v. Dar Dass Dey & Co., and Sohan Lal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, and considered N.E. Railway v. Hastings, Isaac v. Hotel De Paris Ltd. and Booker v. Palmer. It distinguished Antoniades v. Villiers, where the apparent licence terms were a pretence and the arrangement was intended to create a joint tenancy.
members.conclusion: The agreement created a licence, not a lease.

predicates.temporary_use_was_granted: The grantor permitted the occupant to use the premises temporarily, including with the associated furniture or fittings.
predicates.agreement_disclaimed_tenancy: The parties’ agreement stated that the occupant would not claim tenancy or sub-tenancy.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_showed_no_tran: The surrounding circumstances, including the occupant’s temporary admission and nominal membership, showed that the parties did not intend to transfer an interest in the premises.

members.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting occupation and business use of premises creates a lease or a licence is determined by the parties’ operative intention, gathered from the agreement as a whole and the relevant circumstances.
material_facts: A written agreement granted use of premises and associated equipment for operating a petrol service station, and the occupier was given exclusive possession.
The agreement expressly stated that it was not intended to create a lease or a landlord-tenant relationship and described the payment as a licence fee.
The agreement contemplated a sublease only if the tenant obtained the superior landlord’s consent; that consent was not obtained and no sublease was executed.
The licensor retained responsibility for the premises’ outgoings and could revoke the licence for breach, while the occupier was responsible for maintaining equipment and insuring the business.
The parties were companies, and there was no allegation that the agreement was a sham or camouflage to evade rent-control law.
The trial court treated the agreement as a licence, but the appellate court classified it as a lease, relying principally on exclusive possession.
members.legal_principle: The distinction between a lease and a licence turns on the operative intention of the parties, assessed from the substance and terms of the agreement as a whole; labels alone are not decisive. Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy immovable property, while section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, defines a licence as permission to use property without transferring an interest in it. Exclusive possession is significant but is not conclusive: it may be consistent with a licence where the agreement and circumstances negate an intention to create a tenancy. Where the written terms are clear and no camouflage is alleged, the parties’ stated terms carry weight; where terms are unclear, surrounding circumstances and conduct may assist. Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act addresses the mode of creating leases, and section 14(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, restricts subletting without prior written consent. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, Rajbir Kaur v. S. Chokesiri & Co., Sohan Lal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, and M.N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb for the governing tests and the significance, but not conclusiveness, of exclusive possession.
members.conclusion: The agreement created a licence, not a lease. The appeals were allowed, the appellate judgment was set aside, and the trial court’s order was restored.

rule.if: lease_or_license_appeal and written_agreement_governs_the_relationship and agreement_expressly_disclaims_tenancy and future_sublease_depends_on_consent and no_camouflage_is_alleged and occupier_has_exclusive_possession

predicates.lease_or_license_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which a court must classify an arrangement as a lease or a licence.
predicates.written_agreement_governs_the_relationsh: The parties reduced the terms governing occupation and use of the premises to a written agreement.
predicates.agreement_expressly_disclaims_tenancy: The agreement expressly states that the arrangement does not create a tenancy or landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.future_sublease_depends_on_consent: The agreement provides that a sublease may be created only after the tenant obtains the superior landlord’s consent.
predicates.no_camouflage_is_alleged: No party alleges that the written agreement is a sham intended to conceal a different arrangement or evade legal restrictions.
predicates.occupier_has_exclusive_possession: The person permitted to use the premises has exclusive possession of them.

members.legal_issue: Whether the stall-holders’ arrangement created a lease or only a licence depended on the parties’ intention, assessed from the agreement and, where needed, the surrounding circumstances and conduct.
