material_facts: The written agreements were signed only by the stall-holders, and fresh agreements were executed when the market’s collection contractor changed.

The agreements called the daily payments “rent,” required only 24 hours’ notice for eviction after three days of non-payment, and allowed the landlord to require the stall-holder to vacate on 30 days’ notice.
The stalls were open and separated by low walls. Stall-holders could use them only during market hours, had to leave when the market closed, and could not enter them at night.
The owners were responsible for market cleaning, disinfection, closure, and compliance with municipal requirements, and needed access to the stalls to perform those duties.
The stall-holders had no right to use the stalls whenever they chose or to remain there overnight.
members.legal_principle: The decisive consideration in distinguishing a lease from a licence is the parties’ intention, determined from all relevant terms and, where there is no clear formal agreement, the circumstances and conduct. Exclusive possession is important but is not conclusive; exclusive possession coupled with an interest in the property points to a lease. A requirement to give notice before a licensee must vacate is not inconsistent with a licence, including under section 62(c) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, Errington v. Errington and Woods, Cobb v. Lane, Close v. Theatrical Properties Ltd. and Westby & Co. Ltd., Smith & Son v. The Assessment Committee for the Parish of Lambeth, and Vurum Subba Rao v. The Eluru Municipal Council.
members.conclusion: The parties intended to create licences, not leases; the word “rent” was used loosely to mean a fee.

rule.if: stall_occupation_classification_dispute and (use_limited_to_stated_hours and owners_retain_operational_control) and not stall_holder_has_property_interest

predicates.stall_occupation_classification_dispute: The parties dispute whether an arrangement for occupying a stall gives the occupant a lease or only a licence.
predicates.use_limited_to_stated_hours: The occupant may use the stall only during stated hours and must leave when the premises close.
predicates.owners_retain_operational_control: The owners retain responsibility for operating, maintaining, cleaning, or securing the premises and need access to the stall to perform those responsibilities.
predicates.stall_holder_has_property_interest: The occupant has an interest in the property in addition to the right to use the stall.

members.legal_issue: Whether the arrangement with an occupier amounted to a subletting rather than a licence, and whether consideration could be inferred from the circumstances.
material_facts: A tenant permitted an ice-cream business to operate from a separate portion of the leased commercial premises.
The lower courts found that the ice-cream business had exclusive possession of that portion and rejected the tenant’s explanation for the arrangement as unsatisfactory.
The written agreement described the arrangement as a licence and denied that possession had been transferred, but the landlord was not a party to that agreement.
The evidence included that the ice-cream premises could be locked independently and that the ice-cream business operated separately from the tenant’s business.
members.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy property for consideration; section 52 of the Easements Act distinguishes a licence that creates no interest in the property. Exclusive possession is an important indicator but is not conclusive; the operative intention and substance of the transaction govern, not the label in the agreement. Where a tenant’s explanation is unacceptable after exclusive possession is established, consideration may be inferred from the circumstances and ordinary human conduct. The Court relied on Wood v. Leadbitter, Glenwood Lumber Co. v. Phillips, Associated Hotels of India v. R.N. Kapoor, B.M. Lall v. Dunlop Rubber Co., Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, Board of Revenue v. A.N. Ansari, M.N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, and Dipak Banerjee v. Smt. Lilabati Chakraborty.
members.conclusion: The transaction was subletting: the evidence supported exclusive possession, and the courts could infer that the arrangement was prompted by monetary consideration despite the absence of direct evidence of rent.

predicates.rent_eviction_for_unauthorized_sublettin: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground that a tenant has transferred occupation of part of the premises to another person without authority.
predicates.third_party_exclusive_possession: A third party occupies and controls a distinct part of the premises separately from the tenant.
predicates.tenant_explanation_unacceptable: The tenant’s account of why the third party occupies the premises is rejected as unsatisfactory in light of the evidence.

members.legal_issue: Whether a grant creates a lease or a licence depends on its substance and the parties’ intention, not merely on the form of the document or the fact of occupation.
material_facts: The grant permitted the grantee to open a store room but did not precisely identify the plot or create an interest in it.
The temple retained control of the premises, including a right of entry; the premises were inaccessible to the occupant during part of each night, and temple employees cleaned the area.
The grant did not give the grantee exclusive possession of the premises.
members.legal_principle: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, defines a lease, and section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882, defines a licence. The controlling test is whether the grant creates an interest in immovable property, assessed from its substance and the parties’ intention. Exclusive possession is prima facie evidence of a tenancy but is not conclusive if the circumstances negate an intention to create one. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, Quadrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, Board of Revenue v. A.M. Ansari, Errington v. Errington, Cobb v. Lane, and M.N. Chubwala v. Eide Hussain Sahib.
members.conclusion: The grant created a licence, not a lease.

rule.if: lease_or_licence_characterization_dispute and grant_only_permitted_limited_use and owner_retained_control and occupant_lacked_exclusive_possession

predicates.lease_or_licence_characterization_disput: A dispute arose over whether an instrument granting use of premises created a lease or a licence.
predicates.grant_only_permitted_limited_use: The instrument permitted a specified use of the premises without granting an interest in them.
predicates.owner_retained_control: The owner or its representatives retained control over the premises.
predicates.occupant_lacked_exclusive_possession: The occupant did not have exclusive possession of the premises.

members.legal_issue: Whether an agreement creates a lease or a licence depends on the parties’ operative intent and the rights actually granted, rather than the agreement’s label or stated purpose.
material_facts: The agreement was made in connection with collecting market dues, but it gave the contractor possession and use of shops and sheds as enjoyed by the owner.
The agreement authorized the contractor to let the shops to subtenants for rent and stated that the contractor would remain in possession of the identified areas.
The agreement and its map also included designated open strips and market areas, without distinguishing them from the shops and sheds as to possession.
members.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882, the distinction turns on the operative intent of the parties: a transfer of an interest in immovable property is a lease, while permission to use land without an interest or right to exclusive possession is a licence. The court followed Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, [1959] SCR 265, and treated the agreement’s substance and the rights it granted as controlling.
members.conclusion: The agreement created leases, not merely a licence, over the shops and sheds and the designated open areas.

predicates.contract_characterization_case: The dispute concerns whether an agreement concerning the use of property created a lease or a licence.
predicates.interest_in_property_transferred: The agreement gave the recipient a property interest that entitled the recipient to enjoy the property.
predicates.possession_rights_granted_by_contract: The agreement granted possession or comparable rights over the property beyond permission merely to use it.

members.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting use and occupation of premises creates a lease or only a licence depends on the parties’ intention as shown by the agreement and circumstances.
material_facts: The premises were held by the grantor as a monthly tenant, and the parties made a written agreement allowing the occupant to use the premises for a fixed period to conduct a workshop business.
The agreement described the arrangement as leave and licence, called the parties licensor and licensee, and required monthly compensation rather than rent from the occupant.

The agreement restricted use to the workshop business, limited working hours, allowed the licensor to enter and inspect the premises at any time, and provided that the licensor would pay the rent for the premises.

The occupant was permitted to keep the keys, but the agreement also restricted the occupant’s use and provided for the licensor to revoke the permission and retake possession in specified circumstances.
The grantor brought an ejectment proceeding after the agreed period had ended, and the trial court found that the occupant was a licensee rather than a subtenant.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 105 and 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers an interest in immovable property and entitles the lessee to possession. Section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882 describes a licence as permission to do something on another’s property without creating an interest in it. The decisive consideration is the parties’ intention, assessed from the substance of the agreement and the circumstances, rather than its label alone; exclusive possession is relevant but not conclusive if the circumstances negate an intention to create a tenancy. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, Mrs. M.N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, Sohan Lal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, and Booker v. Palmer, among other cited authorities. Section 41 of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 provides the relevant ejectment procedure for an occupant whose tenancy or permission has ended or been withdrawn.
members.conclusion: The agreement created a licence, not a lease; the occupant was a licensee, and the Court of Small Causes’ ejectment order was upheld.

rule.if: ejectment_proceeding_after_permission_ended and (agreement_shows_permission_without_property_interest or (restricted_business_use and limited_working_hours and licensor_inspection_right))

predicates.ejectment_proceeding_after_permission_en: A grantor brought an ejectment proceeding against an occupant after the occupant’s permission to use the premises had ended or been withdrawn.
predicates.agreement_shows_permission_without_prope: The agreement and surrounding circumstances show that the parties intended permission to use the premises without transferring an interest in the property.
predicates.restricted_business_use: The agreement restricted the occupant’s use of the premises to a specified business purpose.
predicates.limited_working_hours: The agreement limited the hours during which the occupant could work in the premises.
predicates.licensor_inspection_right: The agreement allowed the grantor to enter and inspect the premises at any time.
predicates.occupant_is_a_licensee_not_a_tenant: The occupant’s arrangement is classified as a licence rather than a tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A court may not reexamine the genuineness of the stated need for land after a public-purpose declaration unless the government's action is fraudulent.
material_facts: The government made a declaration that the land was needed for a public purpose.
The appellants disputed whether the need for the scheme was genuine.
The Court found no material indicating that the government had acted fraudulently.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a public purpose; that conclusiveness extends to both need and whether the purpose is public. The Court relied on Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab and recognized an exception where the government's action is fraudulent.
members.conclusion: The Court could not examine whether the need was genuine because no fraud was shown.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a land acquisition undertaken for a proposed purpose.
predicates.official_public_need_declaration: The government formally declares that the land is needed for a public purpose.
predicates.no_evidence_of_fraud: The record contains no evidence that the government acted fraudulently in making the declaration.

members.legal_issue: A statutory declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive as to both the need and the public character of the purpose, except where the declaration is a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The government declared that the land was needed for a public purpose, namely to establish a factory manufacturing refrigeration equipment.
The landowners challenged whether the acquisition was genuinely for a public purpose and argued that the declaration could not prevent judicial examination of that question.
The court found no basis on the record to treat the declaration as a colourable exercise of power.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a declaration is conclusive evidence that land is needed for a public purpose or for a company. The court held that “conclusive evidence” has the same effect as “conclusive proof” under section 4 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872: once the prescribed evidence is produced, contrary evidence is excluded. Sections 4, 5A, 6(1) and 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act show that the declaration covers the need and the character of the purpose together. The exception is a declaration made through fraud or colourable use of the acquisition power. The court distinguished Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India because it did not concern a declaration protected by section 6(3), and distinguished R. L. Arora v. State of Uttar Pradesh because that case concerned the court’s interpretation of the limits on acquisition for a company under Part VII.
members.conclusion: The declaration was conclusive as to both the need for the land and whether the purpose was public, and the court could not examine those questions on their merits; a colourable exercise of power remained open to challenge.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and government_declared_public_need and not colourable_exercise

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A person whose land is subject to compulsory acquisition challenges the acquisition in court.
predicates.government_declared_public_need: The government formally declared that the land was needed for a stated public purpose.
predicates.colourable_exercise: The government used the acquisition power as a sham for a private purpose or for no purpose authorized by the acquisition power.

members.legal_issue: A conclusive declaration that land is needed for a public purpose may be challenged only where the acquisition is a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The government declared the land necessary for limestone quarrying, and the statutory declaration stated that it was needed for a public purpose.
The limestone was used to produce cement, which was sold for profit, but the appellant did not establish that the government’s action was a colourable exercise of power.
The court left open whether producing cement as a commercial enterprise is itself a public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 6(1) and 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government’s declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive, subject to challenge where the power was colourably exercised for a private purpose or no purpose. The court followed Smt. Somavanti v. The State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the public-purpose declaration failed because the appellant did not show a colourable exercise of power; the court did not decide whether commercial cement production is a public purpose.

rule.if: public_purpose_acquisition and conclusive_public_purpose_declaration and not colorable_exercise_shown

predicates.public_purpose_acquisition: The government acquires land on the stated basis that it is needed for a public purpose.
predicates.conclusive_public_purpose_declaration: The government makes a statutory declaration that the land is needed for a public purpose.
predicates.colorable_exercise_shown: The challenger establishes that the government used its acquisition power for a private purpose or no purpose.

members.legal_issue: A government declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive unless the acquisition is shown to be a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications stated that the land was required for a public purpose connected with state transport and for the transport corporation.
The challengers alleged collusion and mala fides, but the lower courts found that they had not substantiated those allegations.
The lower courts made concurrent findings on collusion, and the Supreme Court found no exceptional reason to review the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a government declaration of public purpose is conclusive unless the power was exercised colourably. The Court relied on Smt. Somawanti v. State of Punjab, 1963 (2) SCR 774, and applied the rule that concurrent findings of fact are not ordinarily reviewed absent exceptional reasons.
members.conclusion: The notifications were conclusive that the land was required for a public purpose because collusion or other colourable exercise of power had not been established.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and government_declares_public_purpose and colourable_exercise_not_proved and concurrent_findings_against_collusion and no_exceptional_review_basis

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenged a government proceeding to acquire land.
predicates.government_declares_public_purpose: The government declared that the land was required for a public purpose.
predicates.colourable_exercise_not_proved: The challengers did not establish that the government used its acquisition power as a colourable exercise of power.
predicates.concurrent_findings_against_collusion: The lower courts made concurrent factual findings that collusion had not been proved.
predicates.no_exceptional_review_basis: No exceptional reason was shown for the Supreme Court to review the concurrent findings of fact.

members.legal_issue: A government declaration that a land acquisition serves a public purpose is not open to challenge absent a collateral purpose or a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The land was acquired at public expense to enable the establishment of a manufacturing industry.
The government declared that the acquisition served a public purpose.
The challengers did not establish that the acquisition was for a collateral purpose or involved a colourable exercise of power.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government’s declaration that an acquisition is for a public purpose is conclusive evidence that the land is needed for that purpose, subject to challenge where there is a colourable exercise of power. Whether starting an industry is in the public interest is essentially for the government to decide. The Court relied on Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab and Raja Anand Brahma Shah v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was for a public purpose, and the government’s declaration was not open to challenge on the facts.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_land_acquisition and government_declared_public_purpose and not proven_collateral_or_colorable_purpose

predicates.appeal_challenging_land_acquisition: A party appealed a decision in a proceeding challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.government_declared_public_purpose: The government declared that the acquisition was for a public purpose.
predicates.proven_collateral_or_colorable_purpose: The challenger established that the acquisition was for a collateral purpose or was a colourable exercise of power.

members.legal_issue: A public-purpose acquisition is not a colourable exercise of power absent material showing that the acquisition serves a collateral or private objective.
material_facts: The notifications specified development and use of the land as industrial and residential areas.
The evidence supported a public need for additional residential and industrial development.
No material was placed before the Court showing that the government was pursuing a collateral object.
members.legal_principle: Under Smt. Somawanti v. State of Punjab, a public-purpose declaration is open to challenge for colourable exercise where the asserted purpose is private or nonexistent; otherwise, the declaration is final on that point. The Court found no material of such an improper purpose and had already found a public purpose.
members.conclusion: The notifications were not shown to be a colourable exercise of power and could not be invalidated on that ground.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding challenges the exercise of power to acquire land.
predicates.public_purpose_supported: The stated acquisition purpose is supported as a purpose serving the public interest.
predicates.no_material_of_collateral_object: No material shows that the acquisition was undertaken to serve a collateral or private objective.

members.legal_issue: A statutory declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive against a challenge to the purpose unless the declaration resulted from a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The government declared that the land was needed for a public purpose for a limestone quarry.
The appellant alleged that limestone was used to manufacture cement sold for profit, but did not establish that the government’s action was a colourable exercise of power.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, a declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive evidence of that purpose. It may nevertheless be challenged for colourable exercise of power. The Court relied on Smt. Somavanti v. The State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The challenge to the public-purpose declaration failed because the declaration was conclusive and no colourable exercise of power was shown; the Court expressed no concluded opinion on whether commercial cement production itself was a public purpose.

rule.if: land_acquisition_writ_challenge and public_purpose_declaration_made and not colorable_exercise_shown

predicates.land_acquisition_writ_challenge: A person brought a writ challenge to an acquisition of land.
predicates.public_purpose_declaration_made: The government formally declared that the land was needed for a public purpose.
predicates.colorable_exercise_shown: The challenger established that the government invoked its acquisition power for a private purpose or no genuine purpose.

members.legal_issue: A declaration of public purpose in a land acquisition is conclusive unless the challenger establishes mala fides or a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The Government issued a declaration stating that the land was needed for industrial development at public expense.
The landowners alleged that the stated public purpose was a pretext for benefiting a company.
The High Court found that mala fides or colourable exercise of power had not been established.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act makes a declaration conclusive evidence that land is needed for a public purpose, subject to the exception that the declaration may be challenged for mala fides or colourable exercise of power. The Court relied on Somawanti v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The declaration had to be accepted at face value as to the public purpose because the landowners did not establish the exception for mala fides or colourable exercise of power.

rule.if: land_acquisition_case and public_purpose_declaration and not challenger_proved_bad_faith

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land.
predicates.public_purpose_declaration: The acquiring authority made a formal declaration that the land was needed for a public purpose.
predicates.challenger_proved_bad_faith: The person challenging the acquisition established that the declaration was made in bad faith or through a colourable exercise of power.

members.legal_issue: The Government’s satisfaction that a proposed work is useful to the public does not conclusively determine the meaning of the statutory requirements, and the declaration of acquisition is conclusive only as to the stated need for the land for a company.
material_facts: The Government treated the usefulness of the factory’s products and business-related access to the factory as sufficient to satisfy the requirements for acquisition for a company.
The declaration stated that the land was needed for a company; it was not disputed that the land was needed for that company.
members.legal_principle: Sections 40(1)(b) and 41(5) require the Court to determine the meaning of the statutory terms; the Government’s role is to decide whether the facts and agreement satisfy those terms as correctly interpreted. Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a company, but does not establish that the statutory prerequisites for such an acquisition have been fulfilled. The Court considered Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay and explained that Ezra v. Secretary of State did not establish that the Government’s interpretation of those terms was beyond judicial review.
members.conclusion: The Court, not the Government, determines the meaning of the requirements governing acquisition for a company. The conclusiveness of the declaration did not prevent review of whether those requirements were met, and the Government’s satisfaction based on an incorrect interpretation did not validate the acquisition.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_for_company: A person challenges, in an appeal or other proceeding, a compulsory land acquisition made for a company.
predicates.government_satisfaction_is_based_on_inco: The Government considers the acquisition requirements satisfied by applying a meaning of those requirements that is incorrect.
predicates.declaration_only_establishes_need_for_co: The declaration establishes that the land is needed for a company, while whether the statutory prerequisites were met remains disputed.

members.legal_issue: The government’s satisfaction and a conclusive acquisition declaration do not prevent a court from deciding whether the proposed work and agreement meet the legal requirements for acquisition for a company.
material_facts: The government treated the factory’s products being useful to the public and business-related public access to the factory as sufficient to approve the acquisition.
The land was declared needed for the company, and the challenge concerned whether the proposed acquisition and agreement fell within the governing statutory requirements.
members.legal_principle: Sections 40(1)(b) and 41 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, require the court to determine the meaning of the statutory terms, while the government decides whether the facts satisfy those terms. Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for the stated purpose or company, but does not foreclose review of whether the acquisition satisfies the statutory conditions. The Court rejected the contrary implication of Ezra v. Secretary of State on the question before it.
members.conclusion: The court had jurisdiction to interpret the statutory requirements and determine whether they were met; the government’s satisfaction based on an incorrect interpretation did not validate the acquisition, and the declaration’s conclusiveness did not resolve that question.

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government undertook a compulsory acquisition of land for a company.
predicates.government_satisfaction_based_on_broad_l: The government approved the acquisition on an interpretation that treated indirect public benefit or business-related access as sufficient.
predicates.statutory_conditions_challenged: A person affected by the acquisition challenged whether the proposed work or agreement met the legal conditions for that kind of acquisition.

members.legal_issue: The consent of a majority of the equally near male sapindas is sufficient to satisfy the requirement that a widow consult the nearest sapindas before adopting.
material_facts: Three male sapindas were equally near to the deceased husband.
The consent of two of them was established, while the third sapinda’s consent was not established.
The widow had adopted without authority from her deceased husband.
members.legal_principle: In applying the Hindu-law requirement that a widow without her deceased husband’s authority consult the nearest sapindas, the Court held that the consent of the majority of equally near sapindas is sufficient; the consent of every such sapinda is not essential.
members.conclusion: The consent of two out of the three equally near sapindas was sufficient to satisfy the consultation requirement and support the adoption.

predicates.widow_adoption_without_husbands_authorit: A widow adopted a child without authority from her deceased husband.
predicates.majority_of_equally_near_sapindas_consen: More than half of the equally near sapindas whose consultation was required consented to the adoption.

members.legal_issue: A female sapinda is not required to consent to a widow’s adoption, even if she is nearer in degree than the male sapindas consulted.
material_facts: The widow adopted without authority from her deceased husband.
The deceased husband’s grandmother, a female sapinda nearer in degree than the consenting male sapindas, was alive when the adoption occurred.
The grandmother’s consent was not obtained.
The adoption had the consent of male sapindas.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the Hindu-law rationale that a widow’s need for sapinda consent arises from the law’s view that women cannot exercise independent judgment in this matter; a woman regarded as needing such consent herself is not a competent adviser whose consent must be obtained by another widow. The Court relied on V.T.S. Chandrasekhara Mudaliar v. Kulandai Velu Mudaliar and the Privy Council decisions in The Collector of Madura v. Mootoo Ramalinga Sethupatty, Veera Basavaraju v. Balasurya Prasada Rao, and Ghanta China Ramasubbayya v. Maparthi Chenchuramayya, which interpreted the relevant references to kindred as referring to male agnates. It disapproved contrary observations in Rajah Damara Kumara Venkatappa Nayanim Bahadur Varu v. Damara Renga Rao and Maharajah Kolhapur v. S. Sundaram Ayyar.
members.conclusion: The grandmother’s consent was not required to validate the adoption; the relevant consent was that of male sapindas.

predicates.widow_adoption_without_husbands_authorit: A widow adopted a child without authority from her deceased husband.
predicates.female_sapinda_is_nearer: A female sapinda was nearer in degree to the deceased husband than the male sapindas consulted.
predicates.male_sapindas_consented: Male sapindas whose consent was sought consented to the adoption.

members.legal_issue: A widow's adoption to her deceased husband is valid where the required sapindas were consulted and their refusal of consent was improper.
material_facts: The widow adopted a son before the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 came into force, and no express authority from her husband was established.

The widow consulted the nearer agnates, who refused consent because they feared losing a reversionary interest in the property; evidence also showed they negotiated for payment in exchange for consent.
The courts found that the refusal was improper and that the widow consulted the necessary sapindas; consent of other relevant agnates was obtained or could be inferred from their conduct.
members.legal_principle: Under the pre-codification Hindu law applicable to the adoption, where the husband had not authorized it, a widow was required to obtain the assent of her husband's sapindas. Their role was advisory: the assent assured that the adoption was a bona fide religious act, rather than protecting reversionary property interests. In a divided family the widow should first consult the nearer agnates, but if they withhold consent for improper reasons she may seek the assent of remoter agnates. The Court relied on the Ramnad case, (1868) 12 MIA 397, 442, and approved Balusu Gurulingaswami v. Balusu Ramalakshmamma, I.L.R. 22 Mad. 398; it also referred to Kanakaratnam v. Narasimha Rao, I.L.R. (1942) Mad. 173.
members.conclusion: The refusal of consent for personal property reasons did not invalidate the adoption, and the adoption was valid.

rule.if: pre_codification_widow_adoption and no_husband_authorization and nearer_agnates_consulted and nearer_agnates_refused_for_property_reasons and (relevant_agnates_consented or remoter_agnates_consulted)

predicates.pre_codification_widow_adoption: A widow adopted a child to her deceased husband before the governing personal law was codified for such adoptions.
predicates.no_husband_authorization: The husband had not expressly authorized the adoption.
predicates.nearer_agnates_consulted: The widow consulted the nearer agnates of her husband's family before proceeding with the adoption.
predicates.nearer_agnates_refused_for_property_reas: The nearer agnates withheld consent because they feared losing a property interest or sought payment for their consent.
predicates.relevant_agnates_consented: One or more relevant agnates other than the refusing nearer agnates consented to the adoption.
predicates.remoter_agnates_consulted: After the nearer agnates refused consent, the widow consulted remoter agnates of her husband's family.

members.legal_issue: A widow's adoption of a child to her deceased husband is not valid without the husband's authority under the applicable pre-statutory adoption law.
material_facts: A widow adopted a child decades after her husband had died, purporting to adopt the child to him.
The evidence established the fact of the adoption and the adoption ceremony, but did not establish express authority from the husband to adopt a son to him.
The claimant relied on the adoption to assert rights in the husband's family property.
members.legal_principle: Section 8 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 addresses a widow's right to adopt a child for herself but is silent on adoption to her deceased husband. For the latter, the Court applied the Shastric law requiring the husband's express authority to the widow to adopt a child to him.
members.conclusion: The adoption to the deceased husband was not legally valid because no authority from him to make that adoption was proved.

predicates.adoption_claim_is_to_deceased_husband: The adoption is asserted to have made the child a son of the widow's deceased husband.
predicates.widow_adopted_child_after_husband_died: A widow adopted a child after her husband had died.
predicates.no_authority_from_husband_was_proved: The evidence did not establish that the husband had authorized the widow to adopt a child to him.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s adoption under a legal system requiring her deceased husband’s authority is invalid when that authority has not been proved.
material_facts: The parties were governed by a school of Hindu law under which a widow could not adopt without authority from her deceased husband.
The widow performed the adoption ceremonies, but the evidence of witnesses did not establish that her husband had authorized her to adopt.

The widow later executed a deed of adoption reciting her husband’s desire and applied to be appointed guardian of the child, but there was no evidence that she knew her husband’s authority was legally required.
members.legal_principle: Under the applicable Banaras School of Hindu Law, a widow could not adopt a son without her deceased husband’s authority. The party relying on the adoption had to establish that authority. The widow’s performance of the adoption ceremonies, the deed’s recital, and her guardianship application did not establish authority where she may have acted believing the adoption was valid and there was no evidence she knew authority was required. The judgment relies on no earlier cases or statutory provisions.
members.conclusion: The husband’s authority was not proved, so the adoption was invalid; the widow was entitled to her deceased husband’s full one-third share in the joint family properties.

rule.if: partition_appeal and widow_adoption_disputed and governing_law_requires_husbands_authority and not husbands_authority_proven

predicates.partition_appeal: The dispute arose in an appeal from a partition proceeding.
predicates.widow_adoption_disputed: A party disputed the validity of an adoption made by a widow.
predicates.governing_law_requires_husbands_authorit: The legal system governing the parties required a widow to have her deceased husband’s authority to adopt.
predicates.husbands_authority_proven: Evidence established that the deceased husband authorized the widow to adopt.

members.legal_issue: A widow’s power to adopt to her deceased husband is her own power, subject to the limits imposed by her husband’s authority and the required assent of sapindas.
material_facts: The adoption was made by a widow to her deceased husband, who had died many years earlier.
The case concerned an adoption in a divided family, and no specific authorization by the husband limiting the widow’s choice was identified.
members.legal_principle: Applying Balusu Gurulingaswami v. Balusu Ramalakshmamma (1899) I.L.R. 22 Mad. 398, the Court treated the widow as exercising a power of her own as her husband’s representative. Specific authority from the husband limits her discretion according to its terms; absent such authority, her power is coextensive with his, subject to the required sapinda assent.
members.conclusion: When the husband has not limited the widow’s discretion by specific authorization, her power to adopt is coextensive with his, subject to the assent of sapindas; her discretion whether to adopt is otherwise absolute and she cannot be compelled to adopt.

predicates.widow_adoption_case: A widow seeks to adopt a child to her deceased husband.
predicates.no_restrictive_husband_authority: The husband did not give an authorization that specifically limits the widow’s choice or power to adopt.

members.legal_issue: A widow does not need the consent of her husband's sapindas for an adoption where her husband authorized her to adopt.
material_facts: The widow's husband had authorized her during his lifetime to make an adoption after his death.
The letter and the challenger's witnesses supported the finding of authorization, although the husband had also expressed a preference for a particular boy.
The challenger argued that consent of the husband's sapindas was required if the parties were governed by the Madras School of Mitakshara.
members.legal_principle: Under the Madras School of Mitakshara rule invoked by the challenger, consent of the husband's sapindas is necessary only where the husband has not authorized the widow to adopt. The court therefore found it unnecessary to decide whether that rule otherwise applied or whether the amendment application had been properly rejected; it cited no earlier case for this issue.
members.conclusion: The absence of sapinda consent did not invalidate the adoption because the husband had authorized it.

predicates.widow_adoption_case: The proceeding concerns the validity of an adoption made by a widow after her husband's death.
predicates.husband_authorized_adoption: Before his death, the husband authorized his widow to make an adoption after his death.
predicates.sapinda_consent_not_required: The adoption does not require the consent of the husband's sapindas.

members.legal_issue: A law that separately transfers pre-existing rent arrears to the State without a public purpose is unconstitutional.
material_facts: The Act transferred rent arrears due to proprietors for periods before the estates vested in the State.
The arrears were distinct from the land interests being acquired, and the State was to retain part of their value.
The majority found that taking the arrears did not further the land-reform purpose and instead served to augment State funds or finance compensation.
members.legal_principle: Compulsory acquisition must serve a public purpose. The majority held that arrears of rent were a separate chose in action and that their transfer was not a necessary incident of the estate acquisition or the land-reform scheme. Article 31(4) did not bar review of the absence of a public purpose. Mukherjea J. additionally regarded the provision as a colourable device to deprive the owners of money without genuine compensation. The reasoning referred to the principles of eminent domain discussed in Cooley’s Constitutional Limitations and to the distinction between acquisition for public use and a forced loan.
members.conclusion: The provision acquiring the rent arrears was unconstitutional and void.

rule.if: estate_acquisition_case and pre_existing_rent_debts_transferred_to_state and debts_separate_from_land_interests and no_public_purpose_for_debt_transfer

predicates.estate_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a law acquiring estates or comparable land interests.
predicates.pre_existing_rent_debts_transferred_to_s: The law transfers rent debts owed to former landholders to the State.
predicates.debts_separate_from_land_interests: The transferred debts arose independently of the land interests acquired by the State.
predicates.no_public_purpose_for_debt_transfer: The transfer of the debts does not serve a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: The transfer to the State of landlords’ pre-vesting rent arrears, with only half of those arrears credited to them, is an unconstitutional acquisition when it is independent of the estate transfer and lacks a public purpose.
material_facts: The Bihar law transferred to the State recoverable rent arrears, including debts and certain decrees, that had accrued before the estates vested.
The rent arrears were the landlords’ property independently of their interests in the estates and were not a normal consequence of transferring the estates.
Only half of the arrears was credited to the former landlords; the State retained the remainder.
The majority considered the taking unrelated to land reform and unsupported by a public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Compulsory acquisition must serve a public purpose, and a legislative head concerning acquisition does not authorize taking property merely to augment State revenue or meet the State’s compensation obligations. The majority treated the provision as an independent acquisition and a colourable use of the acquisition power; it relied on the principles concerning eminent domain discussed in Cooley on Constitutional Limitations and on the distinction between acquisition and a forced loan.
members.conclusion: The provision transferring the pre-vesting rent arrears was unconstitutional and inoperative.

predicates.a_challenge_to_compulsory_acquisition_la: The proceeding challenges a provision in a law authorizing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.law_transfers_prevesting_rent_debts_to_s: The law transfers to the State debts for rent that accrued before the relevant estates vested.
predicates.rent_debts_are_independent_of_estate_tra: The transferred debts belong to the former owners independently of their interests in the acquired estates.
predicates.state_retains_part_without_public_purpos: The State retains part of the transferred debts without a purpose benefiting the public.

members.legal_issue: A law that permits deprivation of property for reasons unrelated to a public purpose is invalid under the constitutional requirement of acquisition or requisition for a public purpose.
material_facts: The statute allowed the government to withhold restoration of property whenever it considered restoration not expedient or practicable, including for reasons other than the stated circumstance that a displaced person occupied the property.
The statute permitted substitution of other property or cash when restoration was withheld, thereby allowing the rightful owner to be deprived of the original property.

Rehabilitation of displaced persons was a public purpose, but the statute also allowed withholding restoration for the government's convenience or the convenience of an occupant who was not a displaced person.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) required acquisition or requisition to be for a public purpose. Although rehabilitation of displaced persons served a public purpose, a power to deny restoration for governmental or private convenience could also serve a purpose other than a public purpose. The court referred to Amar Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property, Punjab for the legislative background; its public-purpose holding rested on Article 31(2).
members.conclusion: The statute violated the public-purpose requirement in Article 31(2) and was invalid.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law that permits property to be taken or withheld from its owner.
predicates.law_allows_deprivation_for_nonpublic_con: The law permits property to be withheld from its owner for governmental convenience or the convenience of a private occupant, rather than for a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A law depriving a person of property solely to increase State resources is not a reasonable restriction in the interest of the general public.
material_facts: The enactment extinguished the grantees’ rights to receive money from the State.
The enactment enabled the State to retain resources by ending its liability to pay the grants.
The State relied on the law as authority for depriving the grantees of their property.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(1), a law authorizing deprivation of property must be valid and satisfy Article 19(1)(f), including the requirement in Article 19(5) that a restriction be reasonable and in the interest of the general public. A law permitting the State to appropriate property solely to augment its resources does not meet that requirement. The Court relied on Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh, and Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. State of Bombay.
members.conclusion: The enactment was also invalid under Article 19(1)(f), because the restriction was not saved by Article 19(5).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_dep: A person challenged a law authorizing the State to deprive that person of property.
predicates.state_appropriates_property: The law allows the State to take or retain property belonging to another person.
predicates.state_revenue_is_the_purpose: The State uses the deprivation solely to increase its resources or revenue.

members.legal_issue: A statutory right of pre-emption based solely on ownership of adjoining property is an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property when the law applies broadly to different kinds of property.
material_facts: The challenged law granted pre-emption to owners of adjoining property, including where the purchaser and pre-emptor both owned adjoining property.
The law applied to urban and rural property, including agricultural land and houses.
Even after notice of the proposed sale, a pre-emptor could bring a later suit by alleging that the stated price was not fixed in good faith, exposing the vendor and purchaser to litigation.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) guaranteed the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property, subject under Article 19(5) to reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The majority held that a customary right's earlier acceptance did not determine its reasonableness under the Constitution, and that a broad vicinage rule offered no sufficient general-public advantage to justify its burdens. The majority considered the reasoning in Shri Audh Behari Singh v. Gajadhar Jaipuria, Ibrahim Saib v. Muni Mir Udin Saib, and Mohomed Beg Amin v. Narayan Meghaji Patil; it held that even a right attaching to property could restrict the constitutional right. It also reasoned that excluding strangers from localities could not be justified by the former aim of preserving groups divided by religion, race, or caste, in light of Article 15.
members.conclusion: By a majority, the Court held the vicinage-based pre-emption provision invalid as an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property; the appeal concerning that provision succeeded. The dissenting judges would have upheld it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_based_only_on_adjoining_owner: The law granted the pre-emption right because a claimant owned property adjoining the property being sold.
predicates.law_covers_urban_and_rural_property: The law applied across both urban and rural property, including property beyond agricultural holdings.

members.legal_issue: A statutory pre-emption right based on ownership of property contiguous to the property being sold is an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The challenged provision granted pre-emption to persons owning property contiguous to the property being sold.
The law applied to urban immovable property, and the claimed right was based on vicinage rather than co-ownership or a shared facility.
members.legal_principle: The majority applied Article 19(1)(f) and Article 19(5), holding that pre-emption based on vicinage was not a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public. Its reasoning in the related vicinage challenge included that a prior custom did not conclusively establish constitutional reasonableness and that excluding strangers from an area could not be justified by divisions based on religion, race, or caste, given Article 15. The majority also considered Shri Audh Behari Singh v. Gajadhar Jaipuria, Ibrahim Saib v. Muni Mir Udin Saib, and Mohomed Beg Amin v. Narayan Meghaji Patil.
members.conclusion: By a majority, the Court held the contiguous-property ground invalid for the same reasons that made the other vicinage-based pre-emption provision invalid. The dissenting judges would have upheld it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a right of pre-emption over property.
predicates.preemption_based_only_on_contiguous_owne: The law grants the pre-emption right because the claimant owns property contiguous to the property being sold, without requiring co-ownership or a shared facility.

members.legal_issue: A customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage is invalid when it imposes unreasonable restrictions on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a general local custom of pre-emption based on vicinage and had made the required demands.
The claimant owned a house adjacent to the property sold, and the trial court found him entitled to pre-empt under the custom.
The challenged custom restricted both the seller's ability to transfer the property and the purchaser's ability to acquire it, without an advantage to the general public.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f), 19(5), and 13 of the Constitution, the reasoning in Bhau Ram v. B. Baijnath Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 724, that statutory pre-emption based on vicinage imposes unreasonable restrictions on property rights applies equally to a customary right. Such a restriction is not justified by an asserted aim of preventing people of different religions, races, or castes from acquiring property in an area, in light of Article 15. Digambar Singh v. Ahmad Said Khan, L.R. 42 I.A. 10, was referred to concerning the history of pre-emption.
members.conclusion: The customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage was void, and the decree could not be sustained on that basis.

predicates.customary_preemption_claim_based_on_vici: A claimant in a dispute over a property transfer sought pre-emption under a custom based on being a neighbour.
predicates.restricts_seller_and_buyer_property_righ: The custom limited the seller's ability to transfer the property and the buyer's ability to acquire it.
predicates.lacks_general_public_advantage: The restriction did not provide an advantage to the general public.
predicates.customary_vicinage_preemption_is_void: A customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage is invalid.

members.legal_issue: The constitutional exception for promoting public health or preventing danger to life or property does not protect a law authorising permanent acquisition of property.
material_facts: The law permanently vested acquired land in the State for flood-control and erosion-prevention works.
The State relied on the purpose of preventing danger to life or property to claim protection from the compensation requirement.
The Court distinguished permanent acquisition from destruction, impairment, requisition, or temporary occupation strictly necessary to abate a public menace.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(5)(b)(ii), read in the context of Article 31 before and after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, does not exempt permanent acquisition from Article 31(2). It may protect laws providing for destruction or temporary occupation strictly necessary to abate a public menace. The Court considered State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose, [1954] SCR 587, and Dwarkadas Shrinivas of Bombay v. Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., [1954] SCR 674.
members.conclusion: The law was a law for acquisition of property, not a law for preventing danger to life or property, and was not protected by Article 31(5)(b)(ii).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_law: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorising the State to take private property.
predicates.permanent_state_acquisition: The law permanently transferred the property or its ownership to the State rather than authorising only temporary occupation or a temporary taking.
predicates.public_safety_purpose: The acquisition was intended to promote public health or prevent danger to life or property.

members.legal_issue: A law providing for permanent acquisition of land for town planning is not exempt from the constitutional requirements governing compulsory acquisition merely because it promotes public health.
material_facts: The scheme provided for land needed by the local authority to vest in it when the final scheme came into force.
The town-planning legislation was intended to promote planned urban development, sanitation, and healthier living conditions.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2), compulsory acquisition must be for a public purpose and under a law providing compensation and either fixing its amount or specifying the principles and manner for determining and giving it. The public-health exception in Article 31(5)(b)(ii) does not cover permanent acquisition of property merely because its object is to promote public health. Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma was followed.
members.conclusion: The vesting of land needed by the local authority constituted compulsory acquisition, and the law was not exempt from the requirements governing compulsory acquisition on the ground that it promoted public health.

predicates.town_planning_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a law providing for acquisition of land as part of a town-planning scheme.
predicates.property_vests_in_public_body: The law provides that land needed for a public body vests in that body.

members.legal_issue: A housing scheme of a cooperative society may be treated as a public purpose for land acquisition only after prior approval of the appropriate government, and the public-purpose route cannot be combined with the acquisition procedure for a company.
material_facts: The society was a cooperative society whose paid-up share capital did not meet the threshold for treatment as a state-controlled corporation.
The society sought acquisition of land for a housing scheme for its members.

The society relied on a government order and an agreement made under the company-acquisition procedure, but no separate prior approval of the housing scheme under the public-purpose provision was produced.
The acquisition was ultimately pursued by the government as an acquisition for public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(e)(iii) and 3(f)(vi) of the Land Acquisition Act, a cooperative society not covered by Section 3(cc) is a company for the purposes of Part VII, while land for its housing scheme may separately be acquired as a public purpose only with the appropriate government’s prior approval. That approval is substantive, not a formality. If acquisition proceeds under Part VII, Sections 39 and 40 require previous government consent after the prescribed satisfaction or inquiry, and Section 44-A restricts transfer of the acquired land. The routes are distinct; no earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: Prior approval of the scheme was a condition precedent to acquisition for a cooperative society’s housing scheme as a public purpose; the earlier consent under the company-acquisition procedure did not satisfy that requirement, and the two routes could not be mixed.

rule.if: housing_cooperative_acquisition and acquisition_challenged and public_purpose_treatment and (no_prior_scheme_approval or hybrid_acquisition_route)

predicates.housing_cooperative_acquisition: A cooperative society sought acquisition of land for a housing scheme.
predicates.acquisition_challenged: The acquisition notifications or proceedings were challenged in court.
predicates.public_purpose_treatment: The government treated the acquisition as one for a public purpose.
predicates.no_prior_scheme_approval: The appropriate government had not given prior approval to the housing scheme before acquisition steps began.
predicates.hybrid_acquisition_route: The acquisition combined the public-purpose route with the procedure for acquiring land for a company.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition for a registered society’s housing scheme may qualify as a public purpose where the required prior government approval is given and the society has a housing scheme for which land is sought.
material_facts: The association was registered under the applicable state societies registration law, and its registration had not been cancelled.
Some of the association’s stated objects fell within the objects permitted by that law.
The association submitted a housing scheme, including a layout plan, proposed sites, membership and allotment details, and information about financing and administration.
The Town Planning Authority’s clearance was obtained, and the relevant authorities examined the proposal and found its particulars satisfactory.
The Government’s letter of 15 March 1991 conveyed approval to initiate acquisition for the association’s housing scheme.
The final declaration stated that the acquisition was for the public purpose of providing housing sites to the association’s members.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(f)(vi) of the Land Acquisition Act requires prior approval of the appropriate Government, land for a housing scheme, and sponsorship by a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 or corresponding state law. Sections 4(1) and 6 govern the public-purpose acquisition process, and Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a public purpose. The Court held that Article 166’s requirements are directory and that government action may be established as a matter of fact: Chitralekha v. State of Mysore, Dattatreya v. State of Bombay and Major E.G. Barsay v. State of Bombay. Gulabra v. State of Gujarat was distinguishable on its facts. The Court found the approval and scheme established on the record and did not decide the Article 254 issue.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was properly initiated as a public-purpose acquisition for the association’s housing scheme. The Court did not need to decide whether there was a conflict between the central and state registration provisions or which would prevail under Article 254 of the Constitution.

rule.if: acquisition_for_society_housing_scheme and society_registered_and_registration_uncancelled and housing_scheme_submitted and government_prior_approval_given

predicates.acquisition_for_society_housing_scheme: The acquisition is sought to provide land for a housing scheme sponsored by a society.
predicates.society_registered_and_registration_unca: The society is registered under an applicable registration law, and its registration has not been cancelled.
predicates.housing_scheme_submitted: The society has submitted details of a housing scheme, including its proposed layout and arrangements for allotment and administration.
predicates.government_prior_approval_given: The Government approved the acquisition for the housing scheme before the relevant acquisition notification was issued.

members.legal_issue: A government-sanctioned housing scheme undertaken by a cooperative society qualifies as a public purpose, so acquisition for it does not require the agreements applicable to acquisition for a company.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a housing scheme undertaken by a cooperative society with the State Government's sanction.
The State contributed a substantial sum toward compensation.
The agreements contemplated for acquisition for a company had not been entered into.
members.legal_principle: The Gujarat amendment to Section 3(f) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 included housing schemes undertaken by the State or, with its previous sanction, by a local authority or company within public purpose. The Act's definition of company included a cooperative society. Because the acquisition was for a public purpose rather than for a company, Sections 40 to 42 did not apply. The Court relied on Pt. Jhandulal v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was for a public purpose, and the absence of the company-related agreements did not invalidate it.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and housing_scheme and scheme_undertaken_by_cooperative_entity and scheme_has_prior_government_sanction

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a land acquisition undertaken for a proposed purpose.
predicates.housing_scheme: The proposed use of the acquired land is a scheme to provide housing.
predicates.scheme_undertaken_by_cooperative_entity: A cooperative entity undertakes the housing scheme.
predicates.scheme_has_prior_government_sanction: The government has sanctioned the cooperative entity's housing scheme before it is undertaken.

members.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition for a private cooperative housing society to allot plots to its members is not transformed into a public-purpose acquisition merely because the society is cooperative; the acquisition must fall within the statutory route and purposes applicable to it.
material_facts: The society was registered under cooperative-society legislation and sought land to develop and allot plots to its members for building houses.
There was no group housing scheme approved by the State, and the acquisition was for the society’s members rather than an identified public housing programme.
The agreement made under the company-acquisition provisions was given up, and the acquisition did not satisfy the mandatory requirements applicable to acquisition for a company.
members.legal_principle: The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 distinguishes public-purpose acquisition from acquisition for a company under Part VII. Sections 39–41 impose mandatory requirements for company acquisitions, including prior consent and an agreement, while sections 44-A and 44-B protect the purposes and public interest underlying such acquisitions. The court applied the statutory scheme, including sections 3(e) and 3(f), and relied on Jhandulal v. State of Punjab for the distinction between public-purpose and company acquisitions.
members.conclusion: The acquisition for allotment of plots to the society’s members was a private purpose, not a public purpose. It could not be sustained through the public-purpose route, and the acquisition provisions applicable to companies could not be used to authorize a private purpose outside their permitted categories.

rule.if: compulsory_land_acquisition and private_cooperative_housing_purpose and land_intended_for_member_plots and no_genuine_public_benefit

predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition: The government sought to acquire privately owned land compulsorily.
predicates.private_cooperative_housing_purpose: A private cooperative housing organization sought the land for its housing activities.
predicates.land_intended_for_member_plots: The land was intended to be divided or allotted as plots to the organization’s members.
predicates.no_genuine_public_benefit: The acquisition was not shown to serve a public housing programme or another benefit to the community generally.

members.legal_issue: A housing scheme does not cease to serve a public purpose merely because it benefits a limited group of people.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a housing scheme undertaken by a cooperative society.
The society had about 20 members, and the scheme was intended to benefit them.
members.legal_principle: A need of a section of the public may constitute a public purpose; a purpose need not benefit the public at large. The Court rejected the argument that a housing scheme for a limited number of people could not qualify as a public purpose.
members.conclusion: The limited number of intended beneficiaries did not prevent the housing scheme from being a public purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a land acquisition undertaken for a proposed purpose.
predicates.housing_scheme: The proposed use of the acquired land is a scheme to provide housing.
predicates.scheme_benefits_a_limited_group: The housing scheme is intended to benefit a limited group rather than the public at large.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of land for a cooperative housing scheme serving a section of the public is for a public purpose.
material_facts: The land was proposed to be acquired for a cooperative housing society’s scheme to construct houses for its members.
The scheme served a limited section of the public.
members.legal_principle: The Government is ordinarily the best authority to determine whether a purpose is public; a housing scheme for a limited number of persons is not thereby excluded from being a public purpose, and the needs of a section of the public may constitute a public purpose. The Court relied on Ratilal Shankerbhai v. State of Gujarat, Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab, and Ram Swarup v. District Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: Acquisition for the cooperative housing scheme was for a public purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the proposed compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.cooperative_housing_scheme: The land is proposed to be acquired for a cooperative housing scheme.
predicates.scheme_serves_section_of_public: The housing scheme addresses the needs of a section of the public.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of land for a cooperative housing scheme can serve a public purpose even when the scheme benefits a limited group of people.
material_facts: The cooperative housing society was formed to enable its members to construct houses.
The government declared that the land was needed for the society's housing scheme.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government is the best judge of whether the proposed purpose is public, and the needs of a section of the public may constitute a public purpose. Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab, Ratilal Shankarbhai v. State of Gujarat, Ram Swarup v. District Land Acquisition Officer, and State of Gujarat v. Musamiyan Imam Haider Bux Razvi support the conclusion that acquisition for a cooperative housing society may be for a public purpose.
members.conclusion: Acquisition of land for the cooperative housing society's housing scheme was for a public purpose; a housing scheme does not cease to be a public purpose merely because it serves a limited number of people.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns the acquisition of land by the government.
predicates.acquisition_for_cooperative_housing: The government sought to acquire land for a cooperative housing scheme.
predicates.scheme_meets_housing_needs_of_a_section_: The scheme was intended to meet housing needs of a section of the public, even if its beneficiaries were limited in number.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of land for a state-controlled housing project that substantially provides affordable homes to the community serves a public purpose even when a joint venture participates and may earn profit.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a housing complex intended to address the shortage of housing.
The project was undertaken through a joint sector company formed with a private company, while the State and Housing Board retained control and guidance over the company and project.
The project planned a substantial proportion of homes for lower- and middle-income groups at controlled prices, with revenue from higher-income homes helping subsidise those homes.
The State and Housing Board set conditions for the use of the land and the housing scheme, including eligibility and allotment arrangements.
No ulterior purpose was alleged.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1) and Section 4(1a) of the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 permit requisition and acquisition for specified public purposes, including creating better living conditions through housing. Sections 17, 18 and 27A of the West Bengal Housing Board Act support housing schemes and entrusting their execution to a joint sector company. The Court relied on S.M. Nandy v. State of West Bengal in discussing the Act's validity, and on L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India and Reg. v. Hillingdon L.B.C., Ex p. Puhlhofer for the scope and restraint of judicial review. It also discussed H.D. Vora v. State of Maharashtra on the need for the State to establish a public purpose. The Court held that a profit element does not by itself defeat public purpose where the project is controlled by public authorities and serves community housing needs; courts should not minutely review a policy serving those needs absent grounds such as mala fides, statutory or constitutional conflict, or abuse of power.
members.conclusion: The housing project served a public purpose, and the acquisition and use of the joint sector company did not amount to a colourable exercise, arbitrariness, irrationality, or abuse of power.

rule.if: housing_acquisition_challenge and housing_shortage_addressed and affordable_housing_substantially_provided and public_authority_controls_joint_project

predicates.housing_acquisition_challenge: A proceeding challenges an acquisition made for a housing project.
predicates.housing_shortage_addressed: The project is intended to address a housing need in the community.
predicates.affordable_housing_substantially_provide: The project provides a substantial share of homes on affordable terms for people who otherwise face difficulty obtaining housing.
predicates.public_authority_controls_joint_project: Public authorities retain meaningful control over the joint project and its housing scheme.
predicates.acquisition_serves_public_purpose_and_is: The acquisition serves a public purpose and is not a colourable exercise of power.

members.legal_issue: Acquiring land to provide residential housing for industrial workers serves a public purpose.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a labour colony consisting of residential quarters for industrial workers.
The housing was part of a government-sponsored scheme, and the workers had organized themselves into a cooperative housing society.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Babu Barkaya Thakur v. State of Bombay for the principle that building residential quarters for industrial labour is a public purpose. It also noted that the relevant Punjab amendment expressly included construction of labour colonies under a government-sponsored housing scheme.
members.conclusion: The acquisition served a public purpose, even apart from the provision that expressly included government-sponsored labour colonies among specified purposes.

predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition: A public authority compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.housing_for_industrial_workers: The land was acquired to provide residential housing for industrial workers.

members.legal_issue: Land acquired for staff quarters serving a public scheme may be acquired for a public purpose.
material_facts: The proposed staff quarters were for employees working under the Employees' State Insurance Scheme.
The Court found the quarters closely connected with the scheme's operation and implementation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, under which the declaration is conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a public purpose, and relied on Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab. It also held that staff quarters serving the scheme were themselves a public purpose.
members.conclusion: Acquisition for the staff quarters was for a public purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.staff_housing_serves_public_scheme: The proposed staff housing is for employees whose work serves the public scheme for which the land is acquired.

members.legal_issue: A single judge who considers earlier decisions of the same High Court in need of reconsideration should refer the matter to a larger bench rather than reconsider them alone.
material_facts: A single judge considered earlier High Court decisions holding that the relevant statutory proceedings were administrative rather than quasi-judicial.
The single judge reconsidered those decisions while sitting alone, although they had not been overruled, directly or by necessary implication, by the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that judicial propriety, decorum, and the traditional practice of the courts require a single judge not to undertake alone the reconsideration of earlier High Court decisions, but to refer the issue to a Division Bench or seek the constitution of a larger bench.
members.conclusion: Judicial propriety and decorum require a single judge who considers earlier High Court decisions in need of reconsideration to refer the matter to a Division Bench or, where appropriate, place it before the Chief Justice for constitution of a larger bench.

predicates.single_judge_precedent_reconsideration: A single judge hearing a matter considered whether earlier decisions should be reconsidered.
predicates.earlier_high_court_decisions: Earlier decisions of the same High Court addressed the issue before the single judge.
predicates.no_higher_court_overruling: No higher-court decision had overruled the earlier decisions directly or by necessary implication.
predicates.refer_reconsideration_to_larger_bench: The issue should be referred to a larger bench instead of being reconsidered by the single judge alone.

members.legal_issue: A High Court bench that disagrees with a decision of a co-ordinate bench must refer the question to a larger bench rather than decline to follow that decision.
material_facts: A High Court Division Bench declined to follow an earlier decision of another Division Bench of co-ordinate jurisdiction.
The disagreement concerned the meaning of a statutory term, and the later bench did not refer the issue to a larger bench.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that judicial propriety requires referral to a larger bench when a High Court bench cannot agree with a decision of a co-ordinate bench; otherwise, conflicting decisions undermine public respect for the High Court and make the work of subordinate courts difficult.
members.conclusion: Judicial propriety requires a bench unable to agree with a decision of a co-ordinate bench to refer the question to a larger bench.

predicates.high_court_bench_conflict_case: The case concerns disagreement between benches of the same High Court.
predicates.later_bench_disagrees_with_coordinate_be: A later bench cannot agree with a decision made by a bench of co-ordinate jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A judge should not decide contrary to an applicable decision of the same High Court without referring the matter to a larger bench.
material_facts: A party cited an earlier decision of the same High Court concerning a similar use of a common channel.
The High Court judge decided contrary to that decision without referring the matter to a larger bench.
members.legal_principle: Judicial propriety and decorum require a judge of a High Court not to hold contrary to a decision of that same court; a judge who disagrees should refer the issue to a larger bench. The Court approved Subbiah Goundan v. Ramaswamy Goundan, AIR 1973 Mad. 42.
members.conclusion: The judge should have followed the earlier decision or referred the matter to a larger bench; judicial propriety did not warrant deciding contrary to it.

predicates.intra_court_precedent_issue: The proceeding raises whether a judge was bound by an earlier decision of the same court.
predicates.lower_court_judge_disagrees_with_same_co: A judge decides contrary to an applicable decision of the same court.
predicates.no_larger_bench_reference: The judge does not refer the disagreement to a larger bench.

members.legal_issue: A High Court bench that cannot distinguish an earlier decision of a bench of coordinate jurisdiction and considers it wrong must refer the issue to a larger bench rather than overrule the earlier decision.
material_facts: An earlier decision of a coordinate bench of the High Court addressed the same legal issue.
