The Court identified an apparent error in the wording of a paragraph in India Cement that described royalty itself as a tax.
members.legal_principle: Royalty under a mining lease is a return to the lessor, ordinarily varying with the quantity of minerals extracted or removed, and is not a compulsory tax. The Court relied on D.K. Trivedi & Sons and H.R.S. Murthy, among other authorities, and explained that the relevant passage in India Cement contained an apparent typographical or inadvertent error: it was the cess on royalty, not royalty itself, that was described as a tax.
members.conclusion: Royalty is a payment to the owner for the privilege or use associated with extracting minerals, not a tax; the Court clarified that India Cement did not hold otherwise.

predicates.interpretation_of_mining_lease_royalty: The proceeding requires the court to characterize a payment made under a mining lease.
predicates.payment_proportional_to_mineral_extracte: The lessee pays the owner an amount that varies with the quantity of minerals extracted or removed.

members.legal_issue: A levy earmarked for development of mineral-bearing areas may be a fee, but it is outside State legislative competence when it concerns mineral development in a field occupied by parliamentary legislation.
material_facts: The statute imposed a cess on land held under a mining lease and set its measure by reference to royalty or dead rent.
The proceeds were expressly directed toward development of mineral-bearing areas, supporting treatment of the levy as a fee.
The parliamentary mining legislation declared Union control over mineral development and covered the relevant field.
members.legal_principle: Under Entries 23 and 66 of List II, a fee must concern a matter within the State List. Entry 23 is subject to Union legislation under Entry 54 of List I. A declaration under Entry 54 erodes State competence to the extent of the field assumed by Parliament, assessed by considering the central enactment and matters legitimately within its scope. The Court relied on the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, including sections 2, 9, 9A, 13, 18 and 25, and followed Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., and India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu. It also considered Srinivasa Traders v. State.
members.conclusion: The mineral-areas development cess was invalid because, although it could be treated as a fee, its subject matter fell within the field occupied by parliamentary legislation.

predicates.state_cess_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state levy connected with mining.
predicates.levy_is_earmarked_for_mineral_area_devel: The state directs the proceeds of the levy toward development of mineral-bearing areas.
predicates.central_mining_control_covers_the_field: A central legal regime controls mineral development and covers the subject matter of the state levy.

members.legal_issue: Central legislation regulating mine and mineral development does not impliedly repeal a land-cess levy that serves a separate purpose and does not regulate or develop mines and minerals.
material_facts: The cess was imposed on occupied land and its proceeds were credited to a district fund for local administration and public amenities.
The central enactments concerned regulation and development of mines and minerals.
The land-cess provisions did not concern the development or regulation of mines and minerals.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Hingir Rampur Coal Co. v. State of Orissa, [1961] 2 S.C.R. 537, and State of Orissa v. M. A. Tullock & Co., A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1284. Those cases concerned a state enactment for development of mining areas that overlapped with central mine-and-mineral legislation. The land-cess provisions instead served local administration and were unrelated to mine development or regulation; therefore, there was no overlapping field requiring implied repeal.
members.conclusion: The central enactments did not repeal or displace the land-cess provisions because the levy and the central regulation of mines and minerals did not overlap in purpose or field.

rule.if: challenge_to_land_cess_demand and cess_funds_local_administration and central_law_regulates_mines_or_minerals and cess_provision_does_not_regulate_mines_or_minerals

predicates.challenge_to_land_cess_demand: A person challenges a demand for a cess imposed on occupied land.
predicates.cess_funds_local_administration: The proceeds of the cess are used for local administration or public amenities.
predicates.central_law_regulates_mines_or_minerals: A central enactment regulates or develops mines or minerals.
predicates.cess_provision_does_not_regulate_mines_o: The provision imposing the cess does not regulate mines or minerals.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot use its inherent jurisdiction to review an appealable remand order after an aggrieved party failed to appeal it.
material_facts: The first appellate court made a remand order under Order 41, rule 23, of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The order was appealable, but no appeal was filed against it.
The High Court later reconsidered the correctness of the remand order by invoking its inherent power.
members.legal_principle: Under section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a party who does not appeal an appealable remand order is thereafter precluded from disputing its correctness. Sections 151 and 105(2), read with Order 41, rule 23, and Order 43, do not permit inherent jurisdiction to override a specific procedure in the Code or to function as appellate jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not review the remand order: section 105(2) precluded disputing its correctness, and section 151 could not be used to exercise appellate power or bypass a remedy provided by the Code.

rule.if: civil_proceeding_with_remand_order and remand_order_appealable and aggrieved_party_did_not_appeal and later_court_reexamined_order_under_inherent_power

predicates.civil_proceeding_with_remand_order: A civil court proceeding included an order remanding the case for further decision.
predicates.remand_order_appealable: The remand order could be challenged by an appeal under the applicable procedure.
predicates.aggrieved_party_did_not_appeal: A party aggrieved by the remand order did not appeal it.
predicates.later_court_reexamined_order_under_inher: A later court reconsidered the correctness of the remand order by invoking its inherent power.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot use its inherent powers to reconsider the correctness of an appealable remand order that an aggrieved party did not appeal.
material_facts: The first appellate court made an appealable remand order deciding issues concerning the court’s jurisdiction and the effect of property vesting in the State.
The defendants did not appeal the remand order.
After the case proceeded on remand, the High Court used its inherent powers to reconsider the effect of the property vesting and held that the claimant had lost title.
members.legal_principle: Section 105(2) precludes a party that does not appeal an appealable remand order from later disputing its correctness. Section 151 cannot be used to do what the Code prohibits, where the Code provides a specific remedy that the party neglected to use, or to exercise appellate power. The order was appealable under Order 43, having been made under Order 41, Rule 23. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not reconsider the correctness of the unappealed remand order; the bar in Section 105(2) applied, and Section 151 did not permit the High Court to exercise appellate power.

rule.if: appeal_from_post_remand_decree and prior_remand_order_appealable and prior_remand_not_appealed and reviewing_court_reconsidered_remand_merits

predicates.appeal_from_post_remand_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree made after a case was remanded.
predicates.prior_remand_order_appealable: A court made an earlier remand order that could be appealed.
predicates.prior_remand_not_appealed: The party seeking to challenge the remand order did not appeal it.
predicates.reviewing_court_reconsidered_remand_meri: A reviewing court reconsidered the correctness of the earlier remand order.

members.legal_issue: A party on remand cannot use the proceedings to return to an earlier stage or reopen matters foreclosed by an unappealed appealable remand order.
material_facts: The defendant was placed ex parte, and the plaintiff’s witnesses were examined in the defendant’s absence.
The remand order was appealable and neither party appealed it.
On remand, the defendant sought fresh evidence and to have the plaintiff’s witnesses recalled for cross-examination.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an unappealed appealable remand order becomes final and its correctness cannot later be disputed; the court on remand is bound by its terms. Nainsingh v. Koonwarjee was relied on for that rule. Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah and Arjun Singh v. Mohindra Kumar explain that a party may join proceedings at a later stage but must accept what has already occurred and cannot turn back the clock.
members.conclusion: The remand order had become final and circumscribed the trial court’s jurisdiction; the defendant could not use the remand proceedings to recall the witnesses and set the proceedings back.

rule.if: proceeding_on_remand and remand_order_appealable and remand_order_not_appealed and party_seeks_to_rewind_proceedings

predicates.proceeding_on_remand: The court is conducting proceedings after a case has been remanded to it.
predicates.remand_order_appealable: The order remanding the case could be appealed.
predicates.remand_order_not_appealed: Neither party appealed the remand order.
predicates.party_seeks_to_rewind_proceedings: A party seeks to return to an earlier stage by reopening prior evidence or having witnesses recalled.

members.legal_issue: An unappealed appellate remand in an execution-and-satisfaction proceeding binds the parties on the limitation determination and precludes later challenges to matters covered by the remand.
material_facts: A judgment debtor sought to have a decree recorded as adjusted and satisfied, alleging a compromise and payments, including a final payment that would make the application timely.
The trial court dismissed the application solely on limitation without investigating the alleged compromise or payments.
On appeal, the appellate court held that the application would be timely if the alleged final payment were established and remanded for findings on the compromise and payments.
The decree holder did not appeal the remand order and did not object before the remand that the alleged payments failed to comply with the prescribed mode of payment.
After remand, the trial court found the compromise and payments established, and the appellate court affirmed those findings.
In a second appeal, the High Court accepted the concurrent factual findings but reversed on the ground that the payments did not comply with the prescribed mode.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 47(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an execution, discharge, or satisfaction dispute may be treated as a suit. Order 41 Rule 23 permits an appellate court to remand a matter disposed of on a preliminary point, and Order 43 Rule 1(u) provides for an appeal from an appealable remand order. Under Section 105(2), a party who does not appeal an appealable remand order is thereafter precluded from disputing its correctness. The remand determination therefore bound the parties, including on matters covered by its directions. The Court did not decide the general effect of Order 21 Rule 1 on payments made under a compromise.
members.conclusion: The unappealed remand decision bound the parties on the limitation determination and precluded the decree holder from renewing the limitation objection or raising the payment-mode objection. The High Court erred in disregarding the remand decision and reversing the subordinate courts; its judgment was set aside and the appeal was allowed. The Court expressed no opinion on whether payments made directly under a compromise must, as a matter of general law, comply with the prescribed mode of payment.

rule.if: execution_satisfaction_proceeding and trial_dismissed_on_preliminary_limitation and appellate_remand_fixed_conditional_limitation_basis and remand_order_was_appealable and opposing_party_did_not_appeal_remand and post_remand_courts_confirmed_conditioning_facts and payment_mode_objection_omitted_before_remand and second_appeal_followed

predicates.execution_satisfaction_proceeding: The dispute arose in a proceeding to determine the execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree.
predicates.trial_dismissed_on_preliminary_limitatio: The trial court dismissed the application solely on limitation without deciding the disputed underlying facts.
predicates.appellate_remand_fixed_conditional_limit: The appellate court determined the limitation basis conditionally on proof of a specified payment and remanded for findings on that payment and related facts.
predicates.remand_order_was_appealable: An appeal was available from the appellate court's remand order.
predicates.opposing_party_did_not_appeal_remand: The party opposing the application did not appeal the remand order.
predicates.post_remand_courts_confirmed_conditionin: After remand, the trial court found the facts on which the appellate court had conditioned its limitation determination, and the appellate court affirmed those findings.
predicates.payment_mode_objection_omitted_before_re: The party opposing the application did not raise before the remand that the payments failed to follow the required mode.
predicates.second_appeal_followed: A second appeal was later brought against the decision made after remand.
predicates.remand_determination_binds_parties: The determination made in the unappealed remand order binds the parties in the later proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A later review proceeding cannot be used to indirectly reopen an earlier dismissal of review when the renewed challenge does not establish a valid basis to reconsider that dismissal.
material_facts: Earlier review petitions challenging the compensation judgment had been dismissed because no material was produced to substantiate the claim that the relied-on sale transaction was manipulated.

In the later review petitions, the applicant repeated the challenge and produced additional company records, but those records did not substantiate common control of the companies when the sale price was agreed or an oblique motive for the transaction.
members.legal_principle: Review is a limited statutory power, not an appeal in disguise, and finality of a dismissed review must be respected. The Court relied on Article 137 of the Constitution, Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and Lily Thomas v. Union of India, which states that once a review petition is dismissed, a further review petition cannot be entertained.
members.conclusion: The Court found no valid ground to indirectly review its earlier dismissal and rejected the renewed challenge.

rule.if: later_review_proceeding and prior_review_dismissed and (same_ground_reasserted or new_material_does_not_support_reopening)

predicates.later_review_proceeding: A party brings a later review proceeding seeking to reopen an earlier judgment or review decision.
predicates.prior_review_dismissed: The party's earlier review proceeding challenging the same decision was dismissed.
predicates.same_ground_reasserted: The party renews a ground that was raised in the earlier review proceeding.
predicates.new_material_does_not_support_reopening: Any additional material produced does not substantiate a basis to reopen the earlier dismissal.

members.legal_issue: A second review of the same judgment is not maintainable when the first review has been dismissed and the later application presents no qualifying new evidence or apparent error.
material_facts: The respondents had already sought review of the judgment and their first review applications were dismissed after the grounds raised had been considered.

In the second review applications, the respondents filed certified copies of revenue records, although they had previously filed photocopies of the same records and had several earlier opportunities to produce certified copies.

The respondents did not explain that the documents were unknown to them or could not have been obtained despite due diligence before the judgment, and they identified no error apparent on the face of the record.

The earlier order of the Supreme Court left open the possibility of approaching the High Court with documents said to show surrender, but the documents later produced were not new and had been available earlier.
members.legal_principle: Section 114 and Order XLVII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure permit review only on discovery of new and important matter or evidence that, despite due diligence, was not previously known or could not be produced, an error apparent on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason analogous to those grounds. Review is not an appeal in disguise, does not permit reappreciation of evidence or repetition of rejected arguments, and a dismissed review cannot be followed by another review of the same judgment. The Court relied on Lily Thomas v. Union of India, which states that no further review lies after dismissal of a review; Kamlesh Verma v. Mayawati, which summarizes grounds on which review is and is not maintainable; Parsion Devi v. Sumitri Devi and Thungabhadra Industries Ltd. v. Government of A.P., on the distinction between an apparent error and an erroneous decision; State of West Bengal v. Kamal Sengupta, on the need to show that new evidence was previously unavailable despite due diligence and could have affected the judgment; and Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aribam Pishak Sharma, on the limits of review jurisdiction. The Court also relied on the principles in Col. Avatar Singh Sekhon, Kerala State Electricity Board v. Hitech Electrothermics, Jain Studios, and Chajju Ram v. Neki Ram, among other cited cases.
members.conclusion: The second review applications were not maintainable and amounted to an abuse of the process of the court. The appeals were allowed, the order allowing the second reviews was set aside, and the earlier judgment was restored.

rule.if: second_review_proceeding and first_review_dismissed and documents_previously_available and no_due_diligence_explanation and no_apparent_error_identified

predicates.second_review_proceeding: A party filed a further application seeking review of the same judgment after an earlier review application concerning that judgment.
predicates.first_review_dismissed: The court had dismissed the party's earlier application to review that judgment.
predicates.documents_previously_available: The party relied on documents that it had already possessed, submitted in earlier proceedings, or had earlier opportunities to obtain.
predicates.no_due_diligence_explanation: The party did not explain that the documents were unknown or could not have been obtained earlier despite reasonable diligence.
predicates.no_apparent_error_identified: The party did not identify a patent error evident from the record that required correction.
predicates.second_review_not_maintainable: The further application to review the judgment cannot be entertained.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot indirectly review an earlier decision by revisiting matters determined in that proceeding through a later challenge to post-remand orders.
material_facts: A court had earlier remanded the approval matter for reconsideration by the statutory authority.
After the authority made fresh orders on remand, a later challenge concerned those fresh orders.
The reviewing court relied on delay relating to the earlier proceedings and revisited matters that had been addressed in the earlier proceeding, rather than limiting its review to the fresh orders.
members.legal_principle: What cannot be done directly cannot be done obliquely, and an authority or court cannot evade a legal limit through a shift or contrivance. The Court relied on Jagir Singh v. Ranbir Singh and M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath.
members.conclusion: The reviewing court impermissibly reviewed its earlier decision indirectly; a matter that cannot be reviewed directly cannot be revisited through an indirect or circuitous course.

predicates.later_challenge_to_post_remand_orders: A proceeding challenges orders made after an authority reconsidered a matter on remand.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_resolved_the_revisite: An earlier proceeding addressed the issue later revisited by the reviewing court.
predicates.reviewing_court_reconsiders_that_issue_i: The reviewing court uses the later proceeding to revisit the earlier issue rather than confining itself to the orders under challenge.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot use liberty to mention after final judgment to reopen a matter already decided or review its decision.
material_facts: The High Court’s first judgment directed restoration of the property and granted liberty to mention if clarification was needed.
After the owners disputed who was entitled to receive possession, the High Court issued a second judgment directing restoration to the owners.
The Supreme Court considered the second judgment unwarranted insofar as it reopened an issue already decided, but examined the merits itself under Article 136.
members.legal_principle: A judgment is final once pronounced and signed, and liberty to mention does not confer a right to re-agitate the matter or confer review jurisdiction. Review is not an inherent power and must be conferred by law, including under Order 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court relied on Patel Narshi Thakershi v. Pradyumansinghji Arjunsinghji, AIR 1970 SC 1273, and State of U.P. v. Brahm Datt Sharma, (1987) 2 SCC 179, on the finality of concluded proceedings and the limits on reopening them through a later application.
members.conclusion: Liberty to mention permits clarification of a judgment where needed, but does not authorize reopening a finally decided issue or reviewing the judgment; the Supreme Court nevertheless considered the merits in the appeal.

rule.if: post_judgment_motion_in_concluded_case and final_judgment_pronounced and (matter_already_decided or fresh_issue_requires_separate_proceeding)

predicates.post_judgment_motion_in_concluded_case: A party sought further action in a proceeding after the court had disposed of it.
predicates.final_judgment_pronounced: The court had pronounced and signed its judgment before the later request was made.
predicates.matter_already_decided: The later request sought further adjudication of an issue the court had already decided.
predicates.fresh_issue_requires_separate_proceeding: The later request concerned a new matter or cause of action arising after the proceeding had ended.

members.legal_issue: A deliberate breach of an express undertaking given to a court and incorporated into a consent decree constitutes civil contempt.
material_facts: The respondents expressly undertook not to alienate or encumber specified properties until the decree was satisfied, and the undertaking formed part of the decree.
Before satisfying that decree, the respondents entered into consent terms in another suit that placed the same properties under attachment and allowed them to be sold to satisfy the other decree.
The respondents made no payments under the first decree, and the court found that their conduct was deliberately intended to create obstacles to its execution.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court is civil contempt. Babu Ram Gupta v. Sudhir Bhasin distinguishes breach of an express undertaking from mere non-compliance with a consent order; an undertaking must be clearly given and is not to be implied. Bajranglal Khemka v. Kapurchand Ltd. supports enforcing an undertaking given as part of consent terms. When a court adopts such terms in its decree, breach of the undertaking is contempt of court.
members.conclusion: The respondents wilfully breached their undertaking and committed civil contempt of court.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and express_court_undertaking and undertaking_incorporated_into_decree and deliberate_inconsistent_dealing_with_protected_property

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A party asked a court to address another person's conduct as contempt.
predicates.express_court_undertaking: A person expressly promised the court to refrain from specified conduct until an obligation was satisfied.
predicates.undertaking_incorporated_into_decree: The court adopted the express promise as part of its decree.
predicates.deliberate_inconsistent_dealing_with_pro: Before the obligation was satisfied, the person deliberately dealt with protected property in a way inconsistent with the promise.

members.legal_issue: An express undertaking incorporated into a court order is not reduced to a mere consent order because it induced the parties to agree to the order, and its deliberate breach may constitute contempt of court.
material_facts: The order recorded an express undertaking to vacate the premises after notice, along with undertakings concerning payment and possession.
The court dismissed the pending proceeding in view of the undertakings, which were recorded as undertakings to the court.
After receiving the required notice, the litigant did not comply with the undertaking and argued that the order was merely an agreement between the parties.
The High Court convicted the litigant of contempt, and the matter came before the Supreme Court as an appeal from that conviction.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 19(1)(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, the conviction was appealable. Halsbury’s Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 9, paras. 71 and 75, and Dashwood v. Dashwood (1927) distinguish breach of a mere consent order from breach of an express undertaking in an order. A breach of a mere consent order ordinarily calls for specific performance or an injunction before contempt proceedings; an express undertaking in the order may support an immediate contempt application. An undertaking given to the court on the faith of which the court sanctions a course of action has the same force as an injunction, and its breach may amount to contempt.
members.conclusion: The order contained express undertakings to the court, not merely an agreement with an order appended to it. Their deliberate breach amounted to contempt, and the conviction was affirmed.

rule.if: appeal_from_contempt_conviction and express_undertaking_in_order and court_acted_in_reliance and undertaking_breached and deliberate_breach

predicates.appeal_from_contempt_conviction: The matter is an appeal from a conviction for contempt of court.
predicates.express_undertaking_in_order: A litigant gave an express undertaking to the court that was incorporated into its order.
predicates.court_acted_in_reliance: The court sanctioned a course of action in reliance on the undertaking.
predicates.undertaking_breached: The litigant failed to do what the undertaking required.
predicates.deliberate_breach: The litigant deliberately failed to comply with the undertaking.

members.legal_issue: A wilful breach of a clear undertaking given to the court may amount to contempt.
material_facts: The contempt allegation was based on an asserted undertaking to hand over possession to a receiver.
The record contained no application or affidavit giving that undertaking and the court’s order did not expressly incorporate an oral undertaking to that effect.
The court distinguished a breach of an undertaking to the court from a breach of a consent order between parties.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 applies to wilful breach of a clear undertaking given to the court. The undertaking must be carefully construed to determine its nature and extent; it cannot be assumed from the terms of an order. Bhatnagar & Co. Ltd. v. Union of India supports careful construction of the undertaking, and Aligarh Municipal Board v. Ekka Tanga Mazdoor Union explains the purposes of contempt proceedings and the need for care in exercising the power.
members.conclusion: A wilful breach of an undertaking amounts to contempt when the undertaking was clearly and expressly given to the court, either in a filed application or affidavit or orally and incorporated into the court’s order.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A court is considering whether a person’s conduct amounts to contempt.
predicates.clear_undertaking_given: A person clearly and expressly undertook to the court, in a filed application or affidavit or in an oral statement incorporated into the court’s order, to do or refrain from doing something.
predicates.undertaking_wilfully_breached: The person deliberately failed to honour the undertaking given to the court.

members.legal_issue: Wilful failure to comply with an undertaking accepted by a court in a civil proceeding constitutes contempt and may require an order to purge the contempt as well as a sanction.
material_facts: After dismissing an eviction appeal, the Court allowed the tenant to remain in the premises temporarily on the condition that he and the people staying there undertake to deliver vacant possession when that permission expired.
The tenant gave the undertaking but did not deliver vacant possession as required.
The tenant later asserted that he was not in possession when he gave the undertaking, but the Court rejected that assertion in light of his earlier statements and the record of the proceedings.

The Court found the tenant had wilfully disobeyed the undertaking and ordered him to deliver vacant possession, imposed a fine, and directed the local authorities to evict those in possession if necessary.
members.legal_principle: When a court accepts a party’s undertaking and acts on it, the undertaking is treated, for enforcement, as an order in substance equivalent to an injunction. Its breach in a civil proceeding is misconduct amounting to contempt. The court may direct the contemnor to purge the contempt, impose imprisonment or a fine, or do both; the remedy depends on the circumstances. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this principle.
members.conclusion: The tenant was guilty of contempt for wilful disobedience of the undertaking. A sanction alone would not suffice: he was also required to purge the contempt by delivering vacant possession, with further directions to enforce delivery.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding_for_civil_court_undertaking and court_accepted_undertaking and undertaking_not_performed and wilful_nonperformance

predicates.contempt_proceeding_for_civil_court_unde: A contempt proceeding concerns a person's alleged failure to comply with an undertaking given to a court in a civil proceeding.
predicates.court_accepted_undertaking: The court accepted a party's undertaking and acted on it in permitting or directing a course of action.
predicates.undertaking_not_performed: The party who gave the undertaking did not do what the undertaking required.
predicates.wilful_nonperformance: The party who gave the undertaking deliberately failed to perform it.

members.legal_issue: A minister who gives a personal undertaking to a court and willfully disobeys it may be convicted of contempt.
material_facts: The Chief Minister’s undertaking was both personal and on behalf of the government.
Extensive construction took place in breach of the court’s orders and undertaking.
The Chief Minister did not establish that reasonable steps had been taken to prevent the construction.
The court found a flagrant breach and willful disobedience of the undertaking.
members.legal_principle: A minister is not immune from contempt for a personal element in disobedience of a court order. The court relied on In re M. v. Home Office, (1994) 1 AC 377, and State of Bihar v. Rani Sonabati Kumari, AIR 1961 SC 221, and applied the principle that personal responsibility attaches where the minister personally undertakes compliance and willfully disobeys.
members.conclusion: The Chief Minister was convicted of contempt and sentenced to a token term of imprisonment and a fine.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.minister_personally_undertook_compliance: A minister personally undertook to the court that a court order would be obeyed.
predicates.undertaking_was_wilfully_breached: The undertaking was flagrantly disobeyed, and the minister did not establish that reasonable steps had been taken to prevent the breach.

members.legal_issue: Disobedience of a clear court order known to the person bound by it is civil contempt when the person deliberately acts contrary to the order.
material_facts: The court’s orders clearly prohibited the transactions during the period of absolute restraint and required advance notice before later creation of third-party rights.
The respondents knew of the orders and entered into transactions contrary to them.
The respondents defended the transactions on the ground that the later order did not require prior notice, but the court rejected that interpretation.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil contempt as wilful disobedience of a court judgment, decree, direction, order, writ, or other process, or wilful breach of an undertaking to a court. Wilfulness requires voluntary conduct with the specific intent to disobey or disregard the law. Ashok Paper Kamgar Union v. Dharam Godha explains wilful disobedience; Kapildeo Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar and Anil Ratan Sarkar v. Hirak Ghosh require a clear case of deliberate disobedience and caution that mere disobedience is insufficient. All Bengal Excise Licensees Association v. Raghabendra Singh recognizes that wilful and deliberate violation of an interim order is contempt. Tayabbhai M. Bagasarawala v. Hind Rubber Industries confirms that a party cannot escape consequences for breaching an operative interim order. Commissioner, Karnataka Housing Board v. C. Muddaiah emphasizes that a court order must be obeyed unless challenged through lawful proceedings.
members.conclusion: The respondents’ disobedience was wilful, intentional, and deliberate, and they were guilty of civil contempt.

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A proceeding asks the court to determine whether a person has committed civil contempt.
predicates.clear_order_known_to_bound_person: The person bound by the order knew of a direction whose meaning was clear and unambiguous.
predicates.deliberate_contrary_conduct: The person voluntarily acted in a way that the known direction prohibited or failed to do what it required.

members.legal_issue: Civil contempt requires wilful disobedience of a court order that the person charged could comply with in normal circumstances.
material_facts: The approved revival scheme was not implemented fully, and the unit’s operation was affected by its old machinery, inadequate power supply, restrictions on removing machinery for repairs, and other difficulties.
The record indicated that the respondents were not directly responsible for all factors that prevented full implementation.
The Court found the material insufficient to establish that any respondent deliberately disobeyed the orders.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, civil contempt requires wilful disobedience of a court order or wilful breach of an undertaking. Wilfulness means voluntary and intentional conduct with a specific bad purpose to disobey or disregard the law. The order must be capable of execution by the person charged in normal circumstances, without extraordinary effort or dependence, wholly or partly, on an act or omission of a third party. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The charge of contempt was not established against any respondent, and the petition was dismissed.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and (implementation_depended_on_external_factors or compliance_required_extraordinary_effort) and (respondents_not_directly_responsible or evidence_does_not_establish_deliberate_disobedience)

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A party seeks a finding that a person wilfully disobeyed a court order.
predicates.implementation_depended_on_external_fact: Implementation was affected by events or circumstances beyond the charged persons’ direct control.
predicates.compliance_required_extraordinary_effort: Compliance could not be achieved in ordinary circumstances without extraordinary effort.
predicates.respondents_not_directly_responsible: The charged persons were not directly responsible for the circumstances preventing compliance.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_deliberate_d: The evidence did not establish that the charged persons intentionally disobeyed the order.

members.legal_issue: The availability of execution of a decree does not preclude contempt proceedings for wilful breach of an undertaking given to the court.
material_facts: The respondents had given an undertaking in consent terms that became part of a decree.
The decree holder could pursue execution, but the respondents' conduct breached the undertaking.
The decree holder's ability to execute the decree did not alter the court's concern with the breach of its undertaking.
members.legal_principle: Wilful breach of a court undertaking falls within civil contempt under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Contempt is a matter between the court and the alleged contemnor and is not displaced by the decree holder's separate execution remedy.
members.conclusion: The possibility of executing the decree does not affect liability for contempt arising from a wilful breach of the undertaking.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A party asked a court to address another person's conduct as contempt.
predicates.wilful_breach_of_court_undertaking: A person deliberately failed to comply with an express undertaking given to the court.
predicates.decree_execution_remedy_available: The decree holder could seek enforcement of the decree through execution proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A breach of an undertaking incorporated into a final injunction decree must be pursued through execution rather than through proceedings for breach of an interim injunction or as a means of enforcing the decree through contempt.
material_facts: The civil court disposed of the suit by a final decree based on the defendant’s undertaking not to dispossess the plaintiff.
No interim injunction had been granted during the suit.
After the decree, the plaintiff sought action for breach of the undertaking under a procedure for breach of an interim injunction and through contempt proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Order XXXIX Rule 2A CPC applies to disobedience of an injunction or order made under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 during the pendency of a suit; once the suit is decreed, the interim order merges into the final order. Breach of an injunction decree, including an undertaking that has become part of the decree, is to be addressed through execution under Order XXI Rule 32 CPC. The Court relied on Food Corporation of India v. Sukha Deo Prasad, AIR 2009 SC 2330, and Hungerford Investment Trust Ltd. v. Haridas Mundhra, AIR 1972 SC 1826, among other authorities.
members.conclusion: The post-decree application under Order XXXIX Rule 2A CPC was not maintainable; the remedy for breach of the decree was execution under Order XXI Rule 32 CPC, and contempt jurisdiction could not be used as a mode of executing the decree.

predicates.post_decree_breach_proceeding: A party seeks sanctions for breach after the suit has ended in a final decree.
predicates.final_injunction_decree: The final decree directs a party to refrain from an act or to perform an act.
predicates.undertaking_incorporated_into_decree: A party’s undertaking to the court forms part of the final decree.

members.legal_issue: The general residual limitation article does not govern an application to file an arbitration agreement when the application is made under arbitration legislation rather than the Code of Civil Procedure.
material_facts: The applicants sought a court order to file a written arbitration agreement and refer their dispute to the named arbitrator.
The appellate court held the application time-barred under the general residual limitation article, calculating time from when the dispute arose.

The Supreme Court held that the article had been interpreted as applying only to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure and that no contrary intention making it applicable to this arbitration application appeared in the arbitration legislation.
members.legal_principle: The general residual limitation article applies to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure for which the schedule provides no limitation period, not to applications under other legislation unless that legislation expressly or by clear intendment provides otherwise. The Court relied on Hansraj Gupta v. Official Liquidators of the Dehradun-Mussoorie Electric Tramway Company Ltd., Sha Mulchand & Company Ltd. (in liquidation) v. Jawahar Mills Ltd., and Bombay Gas Company Ltd. v. Gopal Bhiva.
members.conclusion: The application to file the arbitration agreement was not barred by the general residual limitation article.

rule.if: application_to_file_arbitration_agreement and application_made_under_arbitration_law and not application_made_under_civil_procedure_code and not contrary_limitation_intention

predicates.application_to_file_arbitration_agreemen: A party applied to a court to file a written arbitration agreement and refer a dispute to arbitration.
predicates.application_made_under_arbitration_law: The application was made under legislation governing arbitration.
predicates.application_made_under_civil_procedure_c: The application was made under the Code of Civil Procedure.
predicates.contrary_limitation_intention: The governing arbitration law expressly or clearly indicates that the general residual limitation article applies to the application.
predicates.application_not_barred_by_general_residu: The application is not barred by the general residual limitation article.

members.legal_issue: The residual limitation period for applications does not govern an application to file an arbitration agreement when the application is made under a separate arbitration law and no law extends that residual period to it.
material_facts: The parties had a written agreement containing an arbitration clause, and an assignee of the original contractor sought to have the agreement filed and the disputes referred to arbitration.
The disputes arose in 1950, while the application to file the agreement was made in 1955; the opposing party argued that the application was out of time.
The lower appellate court applied the residual limitation period for applications and treated the period as running from when the differences arose.
members.legal_principle: Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908, was construed as applying to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure for which no period was otherwise prescribed, consistent with the line of authority including Bai Manekbai v. Manekji Kayasji, Hansraj Gupta v. Official Liquidators of the Dehradun-Mussoorie Electric Tramway Company Ltd., Sha Mulchand & Company Ltd. v. Jawahar Mills Ltd., and Bombay Gas Company Ltd. v. Gopal Bhiva. The amendments to Articles 158 and 178 made by the Arbitration Act, 1940, did not alter the established meaning of Article 181. Section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, did not extend Article 181 to an application to file an arbitration agreement.
members.conclusion: The residual limitation article did not govern the application to file the arbitration agreement, and the application was not barred under that article.

predicates.is_application_to_file_arbitration_agree: A party applied to a court to file a written arbitration agreement and obtain a reference of the dispute to arbitration.
predicates.is_made_under_separate_arbitration_law: The application was made under a law governing arbitration rather than under the general civil procedure code.
predicates.no_rule_extends_residual_application_lim: No applicable rule expressly or by clear implication extended the residual limitation period for applications to this kind of application.

members.legal_issue: A limitation provision governing arbitration does not authorize a court to reject an application to file an arbitration agreement because the underlying claim may be time-barred.
material_facts: The applicants applied to the court to file an arbitration agreement and refer their dispute to arbitration.
The opposing party argued that the application was barred by limitation because the right to apply had arisen earlier.
The Court held that the limitation provision concerning arbitration governs the arbitrator's decision on the dispute, not the court's decision on the application to file the agreement.

The Court stated that, when considering such an application, the court must satisfy itself that a valid and subsisting written agreement exists, that it was executed before any suit was instituted, and that a dispute within the agreement's subject matter and the court's jurisdiction has arisen.
members.legal_principle: The provision applying limitation law to arbitrations concerns the arbitrator's authority to decide the dispute and does not govern an application to a court to file an arbitration agreement and effect a reference. The Court relied on section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, and explained its background by reference to Ramdutt Ramkissentdass v. F. D. Sasson and Company.
members.conclusion: The court cannot reject an application to file an arbitration agreement on the ground that the underlying claim is time-barred; that limitation question is for the arbitrator.

predicates.application_to_file_arbitration_agreemen: A party applied to a court to file a written arbitration agreement and refer a dispute to arbitration.
predicates.court_objection_based_on_underlying_clai: The court was asked to reject the application because the underlying claim was said to be time-barred.
predicates.limitation_rule_governs_arbitrator_decis: The limitation rule applies to the arbitrator's decision on the dispute referred to arbitration.
predicates.court_must_leave_claim_limitation_questi: The court must leave the question whether the underlying claim is time-barred to the arbitrator.

members.legal_issue: In an application to file an arbitration agreement and refer a dispute, the court must leave the limitation of the underlying claim to the arbitrator rather than reject the application on that ground.
material_facts: The applicants sought to file a written arbitration agreement and refer disputes concerning rights under that agreement to its named arbitrator.
The opposing party argued that the underlying disputes had arisen years before the application and were therefore time-barred.
The agreement was treated as a valid, subsisting written agreement made before the institution of any suit, and the disputes concerned its subject matter.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 20 and 37(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, Section 37(1) requires limitation law to be applied in the arbitration to the dispute referred, but does not authorize the court to refuse an application to file an arbitration agreement because the underlying claim may be time-barred. Section 37(1) reflects the principle discussed in Ramdutt Ramkissendass v. F.D. Sasson and Company that an arbitrator decides according to the law applicable to the dispute. At the filing-and-reference stage, the court must examine the existence of a valid and subsisting written agreement executed before any suit, a dispute within the agreement's subject matter, and the court's jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The court was not to decide whether the underlying claims were time-barred when considering the application; that question was for the arbitrator after the reference. The court had to determine whether a valid, subsisting written agreement existed, whether a dispute within its subject matter had arisen, and whether the dispute was within the court's jurisdiction.

rule.if: is_application_to_file_and_refer_arbitration_agreement and written_agreement_is_valid_and_subsisting and agreement_predates_any_suit and dispute_is_within_agreement_subject_matter and court_has_jurisdiction

predicates.is_application_to_file_and_refer_arbitra: A party applied to a court to file an arbitration agreement and refer a dispute to arbitration.
predicates.written_agreement_is_valid_and_subsistin: The parties had a written arbitration agreement that remained valid and in force.
predicates.agreement_predates_any_suit: The written arbitration agreement was made before any suit was instituted.
predicates.dispute_is_within_agreement_subject_matt: A dispute had arisen concerning a matter covered by the arbitration agreement.
predicates.court_has_jurisdiction: The court considering the application had jurisdiction over the dispute and the application.

members.legal_issue: When the existence or genuineness of an arbitration agreement is denied in an application seeking appointment of an arbitrator, the appointing court must decide that issue and cannot leave it to the arbitrator.
material_facts: The respondents sought appointment of an arbitrator based on a memorandum containing an arbitration clause.
The appellant denied signing or executing the memorandum, and alleged in response to the proceedings that it was forged and fabricated.
The High Court appointed an arbitrator and left the legality, validity, and genuineness of the memorandum and arbitration agreement for the arbitrator to decide.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the Chief Justice or designate must decide whether an arbitration agreement exists and whether the applicant is a party to it; this jurisdictional issue cannot be left to the arbitral tribunal. Where forgery or fabrication is alleged, it is appropriate for the appointing court to decide the issue. The Court applied SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd. (2005) 8 SCC 618, National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Boghara Polyfab (P) Ltd. (2009) 1 SCC 267, and Bharat Rasiklal Ashra v. Gautam Rasiklal Ashra (2012) 2 SCC 144.
members.conclusion: The High Court was required to decide whether the memorandum was a valid and genuine agreement before deciding whether to appoint an arbitrator. Its direction leaving that question to the arbitrator was set aside, and the matter was remanded for the court to decide the question on its merits.

rule.if: arbitrator_appointment_proceeding and agreement_existence_denied and document_forgery_alleged and court_left_threshold_issue_to_arbitrator

predicates.arbitrator_appointment_proceeding: A party applied to a court to appoint an arbitrator.
predicates.agreement_existence_denied: The opposing party denied that it had entered into the alleged arbitration agreement.
predicates.document_forgery_alleged: The opposing party alleged that the document said to contain the agreement was forged or fabricated.
predicates.court_left_threshold_issue_to_arbitrator: The court directed the arbitrator, rather than deciding the issue itself, to determine whether the agreement existed or was genuine.

members.legal_issue: In an application to appoint an arbitrator, the court must finally determine whether an arbitration agreement exists between the relevant parties and cannot leave that question to a provisional determination.
material_facts: The application sought appointment of an arbitrator against a company whose status as a party to the arbitration agreement was disputed.
The appointing court held only that the company was prima facie a party to the agreement and bound by its arbitration clause.
members.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the court considers whether it is the appropriate court and whether an arbitration agreement exists between the relevant parties, including whether the party against whom the application is made is a party to it. The determination of that issue is final and cannot be left for the arbitrator to decide inconsistently. This follows from SBP & Co. v. Patel Engineering Ltd. and National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Boghara Polyfab Pvt. Ltd.
members.conclusion: The appointing court had to decide finally whether the company was a party to the arbitration agreement; a prima facie finding was insufficient.

predicates.arbitrator_appointment_application: A party applied to a court for appointment of an arbitrator.
predicates.respondent_party_status_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether the respondent is a party to the arbitration agreement.

members.legal_issue: A tenant sublets premises when the premises were let to the tenant individually and another business takes exclusive possession, leaving the tenant without a right to possess them.
material_facts: The shop was let to the tenant individually, not to the joint family.
The tenant's business was later taken over by a partnership formed by his father and brothers.
The partnership exclusively occupied the shop, and the tenant was no longer its proprietor or entitled to possession there.
The rent authorities and the High Court found that the tenant had sublet the shop.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 provides for eviction where a tenant sublets the premises without the landlord's written consent. The Court distinguished Hira Singh v. Banarsi Dass, which concerned joint tenants and held that one co-tenant's absence did not, by itself, establish subletting to the others.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the tenant had sublet the shop was supported by the evidence and was unassailable.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and premises_let_to_individual_tenant and business_taken_over_by_another_business and other_business_has_exclusive_occupation and tenant_lacks_right_to_possession

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.premises_let_to_individual_tenant: The premises were let to one tenant individually rather than to the family or business later occupying them.
predicates.business_taken_over_by_another_business: A different business took over the business previously carried on by the tenant in the premises.
predicates.other_business_has_exclusive_occupation: The business that took over occupied the premises exclusively.
predicates.tenant_lacks_right_to_possession: The original tenant no longer had a right to possess the premises.

members.legal_issue: Subletting is established when a tenant parts with possession of the premises to another in return for consideration.
material_facts: The tenant entered into an agreement with a sewing-machine company described as a consignment dealership.
Under the agreement, the company had exclusive possession of the premises and conducted business there.
The tenant received Rs. 1,500 per month, described as commission, for allowing the company to use the premises.
The Supreme Court held that the agreement’s terms showed that the payment was consideration for parting with possession.
members.legal_principle: To establish subletting under Clause 13(3)(iii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, both parting with possession and consideration for that parting must be established. The Court corrected the appellate authority’s conclusion because it was based on a misconstruction of the agreement; it did not rely on the earlier cases cited by counsel.
members.conclusion: The tenant had sublet the premises because the tenant had parted with possession and received consideration for doing so.

predicates.rent_control_subletting_proceeding: A rent-control proceeding concerned whether a tenant had sublet premises.
predicates.tenant_parted_with_possession: The tenant gave another person possession of the premises.
predicates.tenant_received_consideration_for_posses: The tenant received money or other consideration in return for giving the other person possession.

members.legal_issue: A tenant parts with legal possession when another person has exclusive possession and the tenant retains neither control of the premises nor the right to possess them.
material_facts: The tenant's son carried on a sole-proprietary business in the rented shop and had exclusive possession of it.
The tenant had no interest in that business, worked at another shop, and had not retained control of the rented shop.
The tenant was occasionally seen sitting in the shop, but there was no plea of concurrent use or of the son occupying as a licensee while the tenant retained possession.
The tenant did not plead that he had obtained the landlord's written consent.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b), as explained in Jagan Nath (deceased) through L.Rs. v. Chander Bhan & Ors., parting with possession requires the tenant to vest possession in another and divest himself of both physical possession and the right to possession. Another person's use of the premises alone is insufficient if the tenant retains legal possession.
members.conclusion: The tenant had parted with legal possession of the shop, bringing the case within the ground for eviction under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks recovery of rented premises on the ground that the tenant transferred possession to another person.
predicates.another_person_has_exclusive_possession: A person other than the tenant has exclusive possession of the premises.
predicates.tenant_retains_no_right_or_control: The tenant has retained neither the right to possess the premises nor control over them.

members.legal_issue: A tenant parts with possession of a portion of rented premises when that portion is divided off and is exclusively occupied by other persons carrying on a separate business, rather than by the tenant as part of a joint business.
material_facts: The shop was divided by a wooden partition into two portions with separate doors and no direct passage between them.
The tenant occupied one portion as a clinic, while his sons occupied the other portion and conducted a motor-car business there.
Each portion was locked separately, and the sons were found to have exclusive possession of their portion.
The claim that the motor-car business was a joint business was rejected; the tenant had not reported income from it and the business account books were not produced.
The lower authorities' findings were confirmed, and the Supreme Court accepted that the tenant had parted with possession of the sons' portion.
members.legal_principle: Under proviso (b) to Section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the relevant ground is that the tenant has sublet, assigned, or otherwise parted with possession of the premises or a part of them. The court accepted the concurrent factual finding of exclusive possession and rejected the claim of joint business. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The tenant had parted with possession of the portion exclusively occupied by the other occupants, and the ejectment ground under proviso (b) to Section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, was established.

rule.if: rent_control_ejectment_for_parting_with_possession and premises_physically_divided and other_occupants_have_exclusive_possession_of_a_portion and tenant_uses_a_separate_portion and joint_business_claim_not_established

predicates.rent_control_ejectment_for_parting_with_: The proceeding seeks ejectment on the basis that the tenant has transferred or parted with possession of rented premises or part of them.
predicates.premises_physically_divided: The premises are divided into separate portions that do not allow direct passage between them.
predicates.other_occupants_have_exclusive_possessio: Persons other than the tenant exclusively occupy and separately secure one portion of the premises.
predicates.tenant_uses_a_separate_portion: The tenant continues to use a different portion of the premises for the tenant's own activity.
predicates.joint_business_claim_not_established: The claim that the tenant and the other occupants conduct a joint business from the premises is not proved.

members.legal_issue: A tenant creates a sublease by putting an independent dealer in possession of the premises for its own enjoyment in return for fixed rent.
material_facts: The tenant put its dealer in possession of the premises.
The dealer was a separate legal entity and was not a licensee or in possession on the tenant’s behalf.
The dealer paid the tenant a fixed sum as rent, unrelated to vehicle sales; the dealer’s commission did not include a right of enjoyment of the premises.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1), proviso (b), the relevant question is whether the tenant parted with possession by subletting. The court found a sublease where a separate entity occupied the premises in its own right, rather than as a licensee or on the tenant’s behalf; the fact that the occupant was the tenant’s dealer did not change that result.
members.conclusion: The tenant created a sublease and parted with possession within the meaning of Section 14(1), proviso (b), of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

rule.if: eviction_for_subletting and tenant_put_occupant_in_possession and occupant_is_independent_entity and occupant_paid_fixed_rent

predicates.eviction_for_subletting: The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises without consent.
predicates.tenant_put_occupant_in_possession: The tenant placed another entity in possession of the premises.
predicates.occupant_is_independent_entity: The occupant was a separate entity and did not occupy the premises as the tenant’s licensee or on the tenant’s behalf.
predicates.occupant_paid_fixed_rent: The occupant paid the tenant fixed rent that was not dependent on its sales or other business activity.

members.legal_issue: A tenant sublets premises by transferring legal possession, including the right to possess and exclude others, rather than merely allowing another person to use the premises.
material_facts: The company occupied the portion of the premises exclusively, and the tenant had transferred to it the right to possess that portion.
The company’s liquidator took possession on the company’s behalf, supporting the finding that the company held the right to possession.
The tenant argued that retaining the key showed that there had been only permitted use, but the courts below had found subletting.
members.legal_principle: Subletting requires parting with legal possession, meaning possession accompanied by the right to include and exclude others; physical possession or use alone is not enough. Whether legal possession has been transferred is a question of fact. The Court relied on Mehta Jagjivan Vanechand v. Doshi Vanechand and referred to Chaplin v. Smith; it also discussed authorities distinguishing a transfer of possession from permission to use premises. The cited discussion of section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act describes a lease as a transfer of the right to enjoy property.
members.conclusion: The tenant had transferred legal possession to the company, so the arrangement was a subletting.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a rent-control eviction case.
predicates.exclusive_possession_transferred: The tenant gave another occupant exclusive possession of the premises or a part of them.
predicates.tenant_transferred_right_to_exclude: The tenant transferred to the other occupant the right to exclude others from the premises or the relevant part.

members.legal_issue: A tenant unlawfully transfers an interest in rented premises when the tenant withdraws from the business and the premises, leaving others in exclusive independent possession without retaining a right or control to possess them.
material_facts: The premises were let to a tenant under rent notes that prohibited subletting.

The tenant initially carried on business in the premises in partnership with his sons, but later retired from the partnership and handed the shop to two sons who conducted a new partnership business there.
The later partnership deeds gave the tenant no interest in the business or premises.
The sons exercised exclusive control of the premises and paid rent from the new partnership's business; rent receipts continued to be issued in the tenant's name.
The tenant did not pay rent or exercise physical control over the premises, and his occasional visits did not establish that he retained a right to possess them.
The trial court and appellate court ordered eviction, but the High Court reversed those orders in revision.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 13(1)(e) and 15 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a tenant may not sublet, assign, or otherwise transfer an interest in the premises, absent a contract to the contrary. Parting with possession requires divestment of both physical possession and the legal right to possession; another person's use alone is insufficient if the tenant retains that right. A tenant who remains a partner retains legal possession, but a tenant who withdraws and leaves others in independent exclusive possession without control or a right to reclaim possession has transferred the interest. The transfer limb is wider than subletting and is not limited to a transfer for consideration, as explained in Harshachandra Narsibhai Patel and Dudabhai Karsandas Patel. The Court distinguished Jagan Nath v. Chander Bhan, where the tenant had not divested himself of legal possession, and applied the possession principles discussed in Smt. Krishnawati v. Hans Raj and Dipak Banerjee v. Lilaboti Chakraborty; P.A. Thomas v. M. Mohammed Tajuddin was considered irrelevant.
members.conclusion: The tenant had divested himself of possession and transferred his interest in the premises to his sons, entitling the landlord to recover possession. The High Court's judgment was set aside and the eviction orders were restored.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of rented premises on the ground that the tenant had transferred an interest in them.
predicates.tenant_handed_premises_to_others: The tenant withdrew from the business and handed the premises over to other occupants.
predicates.others_exercised_exclusive_independent_p: The other occupants conducted their own business and exercised possession independently of the tenant.
predicates.tenant_lacked_control_or_right_to_retake: The tenant neither controlled the premises nor retained a right to displace the occupants and resume possession.

members.legal_issue: A tenant that has let or licensed the premises to a third party who is in actual physical possession is not entitled to statutory protection that depends on the tenant being in actual physical possession.
material_facts: The leased land had a petrol station operated by a dealer under an arrangement with the tenant company.

The Supreme Court found the dealer agreements identical to agreements considered in an earlier three-judge decision, which held that a tenant not in actual physical possession could not claim the relevant protection.
The tenant company was not in actual physical possession of the premises.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(4)(ii)(b) of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, 1972, the requirement of actual physical possession concerns factual, not merely legal or deemed, possession; a tenant that has let or licensed the premises to a third party in possession does not satisfy it. The related protection under Section 9(1)(a)(ii) likewise requires the lessee to be in actual physical possession. The Court applied Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Nirmala and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. R. Chandramouleeswaran, whose interpretation binds under Article 141 of the Constitution; it also noted the distinction between that protection and possible benefits under Section 2(4)(i) or Section 2(4)(ii)(a).
members.conclusion: The tenant company could not rely on the actual-physical-possession-based protection under the Tenants Act to resist the owner's claim for possession.

predicates.tenancy_protection_dispute: The proceeding concerns a tenant's claim to statutory protection against recovery of leased premises.
predicates.tenant_transferred_use_or_possession: The tenant let or licensed the premises, or otherwise placed them in the use or possession of another.
predicates.third_party_in_actual_physical_possessio: The third party, rather than the tenant, was physically occupying the premises.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who has constructed a building on leased land but is not in actual physical possession of it is not entitled to the statutory protection claimed in an ejectment proceeding.
material_facts: The oil companies had taken land on long-term leases, constructed petrol pumps, and allowed appointed dealers to operate them under dealership agreements.
The leases had expired, the landlords sought possession, and the companies applied for statutory protection and an order for sale of the land.
The companies were not in actual physical possession of the premises occupied by the dealers or other third parties.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(4) and 9, read with the Act's purpose of protecting tenants who occupy and use their buildings, require actual physical possession for the relevant protection in these circumstances. The court applied its earlier ruling in Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Nirmala that the phrase “actual physical possession” requires factual, not merely legal or deemed, possession; that ruling operated as res judicata for parties to that case and as binding precedent under Article 141 for other cases. It also relied on P. Ananthakrishnan Nair v. Dr. G. Ramakrishnan and S.R. Radhakrishnan v. Neelamegam on the protective purpose of Section 9 and the tenant's need to occupy the premises.
members.conclusion: The companies were not entitled to the Act's protection and benefits because they were not in actual physical possession of the buildings; the appeals were dismissed and the High Court orders were upheld.

predicates.tenant_seeks_protection_in_ejectment_pro: A tenant seeks statutory protection while the landlord is pursuing an ejectment or possession proceeding.
predicates.tenant_constructed_building: The tenant constructed a building on the leased land.
predicates.tenant_in_actual_physical_possession: The tenant physically occupies the building rather than having possession held by a third party.

members.legal_issue: A will cannot change joint family property into the absolute property of the son when the testator lacked the right to dispose of the whole property.
material_facts: The properties were found to be joint family properties of the testator and his son.
The testator’s will gave the residue to his son, but the testator was not entitled to dispose of the entire joint family property.
The son obtained probate and carried out the will’s provisions.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, a father’s share in ancestral property remains ancestral property as regards his male issue, who take an interest by birth. The Court relied on Mulla’s Hindu Law, Thirteenth Edition, paragraphs 223(2), 223(4), and 224, and held that a father’s will could not change the character of joint family property which he lacked the right to dispose of as a whole.
members.conclusion: The property retained its character as joint family property in the son’s hands insofar as his male issue was concerned.

predicates.property_was_joint_family_property: The property belonged to a joint family of the testator and his son.
predicates.testator_lacked_right_to_dispose_of_enti: The testator did not have the right to dispose of the entire property by will.
predicates.will_purported_to_give_property_to_son: The testator’s will purported to give the property or its residue to his son.

members.legal_issue: A will by an undivided member does not itself effect severance and cannot dispose of that member’s undivided interest in joint family property.
material_facts: A family member executed a will disposing of property that the appellants claimed belonged to him as a separate share.
The alleged earlier partition had not been proved.
The will’s contents were not shown to have been known to the affected family member or his guardian before the testator died.
members.legal_principle: A will speaks from the testator’s death. An undivided coparcener may execute a will, but cannot validly bequeath an undivided interest in joint family property; the bequest can operate only if the testator was separated before death. A will may be relied on to ascertain an intention to separate, but the declaration must be communicated to the affected member before the testator dies for severance to occur in time to prevent devolution by survivorship.
members.conclusion: The will did not convey the testator’s interest in the joint family property because it was not established that he had become separated before his death.

predicates.a_will_disposes_of_an_undivided_joint_fa: A will purports to dispose of a family member’s interest in property held jointly by an undivided family.
predicates.testator_was_not_proved_separate_before_: The evidence does not establish that the testator became separate from the family before dying.

members.legal_issue: A coparcener cannot make an effective testamentary disposition of ancestral joint family property.
material_facts: The properties were ancestral joint family properties, and the family had expanded its business and acquired further property using the ancestral nucleus.
The father’s document described itself as a will, made bequests to take effect after his death, appointed executors, and asserted that the family properties were his self-acquisitions.
The father had no power under Hindu law to dispose of the joint family property by will.
members.legal_principle: A coparcener cannot devise joint family property by will because, when the will takes effect on the testator’s death, his interest passes by survivorship to the other coparceners. The Court relied on Vittla Bulten v. Yamenamma, Lakshman Dada Naik v. Ramachandra Dada Naik, Paryatibai v. Bhagwant, and Subbarami Reddi v. Ramamma. It distinguished Brijraj Singh v. Sheodan Singh and Lakshmi Chand v. Anandi, in which documents described as wills were given effect as family arrangements that had been acted upon.
members.conclusion: The document was inoperative as a will insofar as it disposed of the joint family properties.

predicates.joint_family_partition_case: The proceeding concerns claims to divide property of a joint family.
predicates.property_is_ancestral_joint_family_prope: The property was ancestral property held as joint family property rather than the individual property of the person making the disposition.
predicates.coparcener_attempted_testamentary_dispos: A coparcener attempted to dispose of the property by a testamentary document intended to take effect after death.

members.legal_issue: A coparcener’s declaration to separate does not effect severance unless it is communicated to the other affected coparcener before the declarant’s death, and a will cannot dispose of an undivided coparcenary interest under the pre-existing law.
material_facts: The parties’ claimed oral partition was not proved.
A newspaper notice purporting to declare separation was dated after the date on which the alleged response from the other coparcener was said to have been sent.
The alleged correspondence showing communication was not produced in the civil proceedings, and the evidence about its dates and contents was inconsistent.
There was no other evidence that the other coparcener knew of the declaration before the declarant died.
The declarant died before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
members.legal_principle: A severance of joint-family status requires an unequivocal intention to separate communicated to the affected coparcener; knowledge must be established, and a later communication cannot defeat rights that vested on the death. A will speaks from the testator’s death, and under the law applicable before Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, a coparcener could not bequeath an undivided interest in joint-family property. The Court relied on Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma, Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, and the principles concerning the effect of severance and joint-family property in Bhagwant P. Sulakhe v. Digambar Gopal Sulakhe.
members.conclusion: The court could not find that severance had been effected before the declarant’s death; consequently, the will could not dispose of the disputed properties as the declarant’s separate property.

rule.if: coparcenary_title_proceeding and no_proved_prior_partition and separation_declaration_not_proved_communicated_before_death and death_before_testamentary_change

predicates.coparcenary_title_proceeding: The proceeding concerns title to property claimed to belong to a Hindu coparcenary.
predicates.no_proved_prior_partition: The asserted earlier partition among the coparceners is not proved.
predicates.separation_declaration_not_proved_commun: The evidence does not establish that the other affected coparcener knew of an unequivocal declaration to separate before the declarant died.
predicates.death_before_testamentary_change: The coparcener died before a change in law permitted testamentary disposition of an undivided coparcenary interest.
predicates.severance_not_established_and_will_canno: The declaration does not establish severance before death, and the will cannot dispose of the undivided interest as separate property.

members.legal_issue: A father governed by Mitakshara law cannot make a testamentary disposition of ancestral property in which his sons have acquired an interest by birth.
material_facts: The father described the properties in the relevant schedules as family or tarvad properties.
The instrument purported to deal with the whole of those properties, including the sons’ interests, rather than only the father’s own undivided share.
The father retained powers of disposition during his lifetime and intended the directions concerning the properties to take effect after his death.
members.legal_principle: A Mitakshara father has no authority to make a will disposing of ancestral property in which his sons have acquired an interest by birth. The Court relied on the characterization of the property as joint family property and distinguished a testamentary disposition of the father’s own undivided share, which was not attempted here.
members.conclusion: The instrument was ineffective as a will insofar as it purported to dispose of ancestral property.
