predicates.validity_of_will_in_joint_family_propert: The proceeding concerns whether an instrument is effective as a will in a dispute over joint family property.
predicates.ancestral_joint_property: The property was ancestral joint family property in which the sons had acquired interests by birth.
predicates.father_attempted_to_dispose_of_sons_inte: The father purported by will to dispose of the sons’ interests in the ancestral property, rather than only his own undivided share.

members.legal_issue: Property received by a son from his father by gift or bequest does not become ancestral property merely because it came from his father.
material_facts: The father held the relevant properties as his self-acquired property.
The son received the properties under his father's will, rather than by inheritance or partition.
The claim for partition depended on treating the properties as ancestral in the son's hands.
members.legal_principle: Under the Mitakshara, including Chapter 1, section 4, placita 1 and 28, a father's gift is a distinct category of property exempt from partition, and the son's interest in property received by gift or bequest depends on the grantor's intention. The mode of transmission matters: property ordinarily becomes ancestral when received by descent as a son or descendant, not simply because it is granted by an ancestor. The Court relied on Rao Balwant v. Rani Kishori for the father's power over his self-acquired property and considered Muddun v. Ram and the conflicting High Court authorities; Lal Ram Singh v. Deputy Commissioner, Partabgarh had left the question open.
members.conclusion: A property gifted or bequeathed by a father to his son does not become ancestral in the son's hands merely because the son received it from his father; the interest taken depends on the grant's terms and the donor's intention.

predicates.property_character_dispute: A party to a dispute over property character claims rights on the basis that the property is ancestral.
predicates.father_transferred_property_by_gift_or_b: A father transferred property to a son by gift or testamentary bequest.
predicates.recipient_received_property_by_grant_not: The son received the property by the father's grant rather than through inheritance by descent.

members.legal_issue: Property purchased by a grandfather and bequeathed to his son does not become ancestral property in the son's hands merely because the son received it from his father.
material_facts: The grandfather had purchased the property himself and later bequeathed it to his son.
The plaintiffs claimed that the property was ancestral, relying in part on a statement that a partition had occurred among the son and his brothers.
The plaintiffs did not produce the grandfather's will or prove that it intended the property to benefit the family as ancestral property.
members.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, a father has full power to dispose of his self-acquired property. Property he bequeaths to a son does not necessarily become ancestral in the son's hands merely because it came from the father; the mode of transmission and the donor's intention matter. The party asserting ancestral character bears the burden of proving it, including any intention that a bequest benefit the family. The Court relied on C.N. Arunachala Mudaliar v. C.A. Muruganatha Mudaliar and Pulavarthi Venkata Subba Rao v. Valluri Jagannadha Rao, and distinguished Shyam Narayan Prasad v. Krishna Prasad because that case concerned property retaining its ancestral character after partition. The judgment also referred to succession under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act.
members.conclusion: The property was the son's separate, self-acquired property; he could dispose of it by gift, and the plaintiffs had not proved that it was ancestral property.

predicates.claim_of_ancestral_property_against_a_la: A party claims that property is ancestral in order to challenge a later transfer by the person who received it.
predicates.grandfather_acquired_property_independen: The prior holder acquired the property independently rather than as ancestral property.
predicates.property_passed_to_son_by_testamentary_b: The prior holder transferred the property to his son through a will.
predicates.proof_of_intention_to_benefit_family_as_: Evidence establishes that the prior holder intended the bequest to benefit the family as ancestral property.

members.legal_issue: Property devolving on a father under statutory succession does not become Hindu joint-family property in his hands as against his own sons merely because it came from his father.
material_facts: The family was governed by the Mitakshara school of Hindu law.
The property in the ancestral house devolved on the landlord’s father on the death of the landlord’s grandfather.
The tenant argued that the landlord had a coparcenary interest in that house and therefore occupied another residential house.
members.legal_principle: Under section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property inherited in the circumstances addressed in Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen is taken by the heir in his individual capacity, not as property of a Hindu undivided family vis-à-vis his own sons. The Court also considered State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram and Sundarsanam Maistri v. Narasimhulu Maistri, and held Rani Sartaj Kuari v. Rani Deoraj Kuari inapplicable.
members.conclusion: The property that devolved on the landlord’s father was not Hindu joint-family property in his hands vis-à-vis his sons, and the appellate authority was right to treat the landlord as occupying the house with his father’s permission.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a landlord may recover residential premises from a tenant.
predicates.property_devolved_on_parent_by_statutory: The property devolved on a parent by statutory succession from an earlier generation.
predicates.claimant_is_parent_descendant: The person claiming a family-property interest is a descendant of the parent who inherited the property.

members.legal_issue: Property inherited by a son from his intestate father under the statutory succession scheme is the son’s individual property and is not property of the son’s Hindu undivided family.
material_facts: A father and son had constituted a Hindu undivided family, but partitioned the family business and thereafter carried it on as a partnership; the family house property remained joint.
The father’s credit balance in the partnership represented capital allotted to him on partition and profits accumulated by him, and was his separate property during his lifetime.
The father died intestate, leaving his son and grandsons. The son inherited the credit balance, while the son’s own Hindu undivided family excluded it from its wealth-tax returns.
The Revenue included the balance in the son’s family’s net wealth; the dispute concerned whether the balance belonged to the son individually or to that family.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, read with the Class I Schedule, govern intestate succession and override inconsistent pre-existing Hindu law. A living son’s son is not a Class I heir to his grandfather’s property, and the son takes property devolving under section 8 individually, not as karta of his own family. Section 19, which provides that heirs succeeding together take as tenants-in-common rather than joint tenants, supports the statutory departure from the former law. The Court approved Commissioner of Income-tax, U.P. v. Ram Rakshpal, Ashok Kumar; Additional Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras v. P.L. Karuppan Chettiar; Shrivallabhdas Modani v. Commissioner of Income-Tax; and Commissioner of Wealth-Tax, A.P.-II v. Mukundgirji, and rejected the contrary view in Commissioner of Income-tax, Gujarat-I v. Dr. Babubhai Mansukhbhai.
members.conclusion: The credit balance devolved on the son in his individual capacity and was not an asset of his Hindu undivided family; it was therefore not includible in that family’s net wealth.

rule.if: wealth_tax_assessment_of_hindu_undivided_family and father_died_intestate and father_owned_property_separately and son_inherited_property and son_was_separated_from_father_by_partition

predicates.wealth_tax_assessment_of_hindu_undivided: A tax assessment determines the net wealth of a Hindu undivided family that includes the inheriting son.
predicates.father_died_intestate: The father died without leaving a will.
predicates.father_owned_property_separately: The property belonged to the father separately during his lifetime.
predicates.son_inherited_property: The son received the property from his father by inheritance.
predicates.son_was_separated_from_father_by_partiti: The son and father had separated their family interests by partition before the father died.

members.legal_issue: The increased statutory solatium and interest apply to compensation proceedings pending at the relevant retroactivity threshold or instituted after it, even when the proceedings ended before the amending legislation commenced.
material_facts: The original compensation awards and an earlier appellate order preceded the relevant retroactivity threshold.
A further appeal was pending at that threshold, and the appellate order in that proceeding was made afterward but before the amending legislation commenced.
A further appeal was pending when the amending legislation commenced.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15(b) and 18(a) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 amended sections 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; section 30(2) made those amended provisions applicable to qualifying awards and appellate orders. The time phrase in section 30(2) governs both awards and appellate orders. Thus, the amendments apply to compensation proceedings pending at the threshold or instituted afterward, even if they terminated before the amending Act commenced. The Court approved State of Punjab v. Mohinder Singh and disagreed with Kamalajammannivaru v. Special Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to solatium and interest under the amended provisions. The Court applied the increased solatium and the amended interest rates, including the applicable higher rate after the first year.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerned the determination of compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.pending_at_retroactivity_threshold: A compensation proceeding was pending when the legislature’s selected threshold for retrospective application was reached.
predicates.instituted_after_retroactivity_threshold: A compensation proceeding was instituted after the legislature’s selected threshold for retrospective application.

members.legal_issue: The increased statutory solatium applies where a land acquisition reference was pending during the period to which the amendment gave limited retrospective effect.
material_facts: The Collector made the award before the amendment's specified period.
The reference court made its award after that period.
The reference remained pending during the period between the amendment's commencement and the end of its specified retrospective period.
members.legal_principle: Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for solatium. Section 30(2) of the 1984 Amendment Act gave the increased rate limited retrospective effect. In Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, the Court confined the benefit to specified awards and appeals; Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama applied the amendment to avoid an anomalous result; and K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala extended the benefit to proceedings pending when the amendment came into force. Applying that interpretation, the increased solatium was available where the reference was pending during the relevant period.
members.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to the increased solatium, and the award was modified accordingly.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.reference_pending_during_amendment_trans: The reference seeking determination of compensation remained pending during the period to which the amendment gave limited retrospective effect.
predicates.increased_solatium_allowed: The owner is entitled to the increased statutory solatium.

members.legal_issue: The availability of amended statutory solatium when the land acquisition award and the decision on the compensation reference preceded the amendment.
material_facts: The acquisition notification was issued in 1971, and the Collector awarded compensation for the land.
The District Judge decided the compensation reference in 1978.
The High Court later increased the compensation and granted solatium on the increase.
The Supreme Court considered the solatium issue in an appeal in which notice was limited to solatium and interest.
members.legal_principle: Applying K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala & Ors. (1994) 5 SCC 593, the Court held that the amended provision for solatium in Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act did not entitle the respondents to solatium in these circumstances. The judgment does not state the broader transitional test from that precedent.
members.conclusion: The respondents were not entitled to solatium, and the High Court’s grant of it was set aside.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and award_pre_amendment and reference_decided_pre_amendment and amended_solatium_granted

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.award_pre_amendment: The initial compensation award was made before the relevant change in the law.
predicates.reference_decided_pre_amendment: The decision on the claimant’s compensation reference was made before the relevant change in the law.
predicates.amended_solatium_granted: A court granted solatium under the changed law.

members.legal_issue: The applicable interest rate when both the initial land acquisition award and the decision on the compensation reference preceded the relevant change in the law.
material_facts: The Collector made the compensation award before 1982, and the District Judge decided the reference before 1982.
The High Court awarded interest at 9% for one year from possession and 5% thereafter until payment.
The Supreme Court considered the interest issue in an appeal in which notice was limited to solatium and interest.
members.legal_principle: Applying K.S. Paripoornan (II) v. State of Kerala & Ors. (1995) 1 SCC 367, the Court held that the higher interest rates were not admissible where the Collector’s award and the decision on the Section 18 reference preceded 1982. The Court confined interest to 6% per annum. The judgment does not identify the statutory provision governing those interest rates.
members.conclusion: The interest rate was confined to 6% per annum, and the High Court’s higher interest award was modified.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal and award_pre_interest_change and reference_decided_pre_interest_change and interest_above_earlier_rate_awarded

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.award_pre_interest_change: The initial compensation award was made before the relevant change in the law governing interest.
predicates.reference_decided_pre_interest_change: The decision on the claimant’s compensation reference was made before the relevant change in the law governing interest.
predicates.interest_above_earlier_rate_awarded: A court awarded interest at a rate higher than the rate applicable before the relevant change.

members.legal_issue: Enhanced statutory solatium and interest are available only when the relevant compensation award falls within the transitional period specified for the amendments.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the 1894 acquisition law, and the Collector’s awards and the reference court’s awards in the relevant cases were made before 30 April 1982.
The claimants later sought enhanced solatium and interest under amendments that came into force on 24 September 1984.
In some cases, a later court order granted the enhanced benefits despite the dates of the underlying awards.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 30(2), 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Act 68 of 1984, the enhanced solatium applies to a Collector’s or court’s award made between 30 April 1982 and 24 September 1984, and to appeals against such awards. The date of the underlying award is decisive; an appellate order made during that period does not qualify an award made before it. The Court applied the five-judge decision in Union of India v. Raghubir Singh (1989) 2 SCC 754. The judgment also considered the amended interest provisions, including section 34.
members.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to the enhanced statutory solatium and interest because none of the relevant Collector’s or reference court’s awards was made within the transitional period.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired under a statutory land acquisition process.
predicates.no_qualifying_award_within_transition_wi: Neither the relevant award made by the acquiring authority nor the relevant award made by the reference court fell within the transitional period.

members.legal_issue: The increased statutory solatium applies only to an award made during the specified transitional period, including an appellate decision arising from such an award.
material_facts: The land was compulsorily acquired, and the Collector made the compensation award before the transitional period.
The reference court enhanced compensation before the transitional period.
An appeal from that award remained pending when the amendment was introduced, and the High Court later applied the increased solatium.
The Court considered conflicting earlier decisions on the meaning of the transitional provision.
members.legal_principle: Sections 30(2) and 15 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, read with sections 23(2) and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, make the increased solatium available only where the Collector’s or Court’s award was made between 30 April 1982 and 24 September 1984. The words “any such award” limit the relevant appellate orders to appeals arising from awards made in that period; the general principle that an appeal is a continuation of the original proceeding cannot displace that statutory limit. The Court followed K. Kamalajammanniavaru and rejected the interpretations in Bhag Singh and State of Punjab v. Mohinder Singh.
members.conclusion: The increased solatium applies to an award made by the Collector or the Court during the period from 30 April 1982 to 24 September 1984, or to an appellate order arising from such an award. It does not apply merely because an appeal from an earlier award was pending or decided during that period. The Court adopted the interpretation in K. Kamalajammanniavaru and overruled the contrary statements in Bhag Singh and Mohinder Singh.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired compulsorily.

members.legal_issue: The applicable amendment entitles claimants to the enhanced statutory solatium and interest when the reference court’s award was made before the amendment.
material_facts: The reference court made its award on November 2, 1973.
The High Court applied Amendment Act 68 of 1984 and awarded enhanced solatium, interest, and an additional amount.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Amendment Act 68 of 1984, holding that it applied in view of the date of the reference court’s award. It relied on no earlier case in deciding this issue.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the amendment applied and that the claimants were entitled to solatium at 15% and interest at 6% on the enhanced compensation from the date possession was taken until the amount was deposited in court.

members.legal_issue: Enhanced statutory solatium and interest apply to a pending land-acquisition appeal only if the governing interpretation gives the amendments retrospective effect for the relevant class of awards.
material_facts: The appeals were pending before the Supreme Court on the specified cutoff date.
The underlying award fell within the period whose treatment under the amendments was in dispute.
A Constitution Bench was expected to decide whether the amendments applied retrospectively to that class of appeal.
members.legal_principle: Section 30(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, read with amended sections 23(2) and 28, governs the transitional entitlement. The court made its conclusion depend on the pending Constitution Bench decision, describing the competing interpretations in Bhag Singh, (1985) 3 SCC 737, and Kamalajammanniavaru, (1985) 1 SCC 582.
members.conclusion: The landowner’s entitlement was left conditional: the enhanced benefits would apply if the Constitution Bench adopted the view in Bhag Singh and overruled Kamalajammanniavaru, and would not apply if it affirmed Kamalajammanniavaru.

members.legal_issue: The entitlement of pending land-compensation appeals to enhanced solatium and interest depends on the Constitution Bench’s determination of the retrospective operation of the amending legislation.
material_facts: The appeals were pending before the Supreme Court on the date relevant to the statutory amendment.

The amendment provided for enhanced solatium and interest, and the Court treated entitlement under its transitional provision as dependent on whether the amendment applied to orders under appeal concerning earlier awards.
A Constitution Bench was expected to decide between the view in Bhag Singh and the view in Kamalajammanniavaru.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 30(2) of the Central Amending Act, 1984, entitlement to the enhanced benefits under amended Sections 23(2) and 28 depended on the amendment’s retrospective operation. The Court left that question to the expected Constitution Bench decision on the differing views in Bhag Singh and Kamalajammanniavaru.
members.conclusion: The appellants would receive the enhanced benefits if the Constitution Bench upheld the view in Bhag Singh and overruled the view in Kamalajammanniavaru; they would not receive those benefits if it affirmed the latter view.

members.legal_issue: Giving non-resident owners a special summary eviction remedy does not violate equal protection when the class is based on an intelligible distinction connected to a legitimate housing need and the remedy is limited by safeguards.
material_facts: The legislature created a special category of non-resident owners who return to India and require their property for their own use or for the use of a dependent ordinarily living with them.
The stated legislative purpose was to address returning owners’ difficulty in recovering their property under ordinary rent procedures.
The special remedy was limited by requirements concerning ownership, genuine need, the number of times and properties for which it could be used, and restrictions after recovery of possession.
Tenants retained the opportunity to challenge the owner’s eligibility and the genuineness of the claimed need.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification founded on intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the object of the law. The assessment is practical and considers the purpose of the law and the circumstances that prompted it; a classification need not be perfect, and legislative choices receive a presumption of constitutionality unless palpably arbitrary. The Court relied on Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar; State of A.P. v. Nallamilli Rami Reddi; Kewal Singh v. Smt. Lajwanti; and Ravi Dutt Sharma v. Ratan Lal Bhargava, and considered the need to balance landlord and tenant interests discussed in Malpe Vishwanath Acharya v. State of Maharashtra, Joginder Pal v. Naval Kishore Behal, Satyawati Sharma v. Union of India, and Vinod Kumar v. Ashok Kumar Gandhi.
members.conclusion: The classification of non-resident owners was not arbitrary and did not violate Article 14; the challenge was rejected.

rule.if: equal_protection_challenge and distinct_returning_owner_class and special_remedy_has_rational_connection_to_rehousing_need and genuine_need_is_required and tenant_can_challenge_claim and misuse_safeguards_exist

predicates.equal_protection_challenge: A party argues that a law’s differential treatment of a defined group violates equal protection.
predicates.distinct_returning_owner_class: The law groups owners who live abroad and return to require their property for themselves or a dependent.
predicates.special_remedy_has_rational_connection_t: The special procedure addresses the group’s identified difficulty in recovering property needed for personal use after return.

predicates.misuse_safeguards_exist: The law restricts repeated use of the remedy or imposes controls on the owner after possession is recovered.

members.legal_issue: A special expedited eviction procedure for landlords seeking possession for specified personal housing needs does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The eviction proceedings concerned a landlord seeking possession for personal bona fide need under a category covered by the special procedure.
The ordinary eviction process could take years, during which the landlord might die or the need for possession might disappear.
The special procedure provided for a tenant to obtain leave to defend before contesting the eviction claim.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits the legislature to create a class of landlords for a special procedure where the classification has a reasonable nexus with the law’s object. The Court relied on Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti, Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal, and Vinod Kumar Chowdhry v. Narain Devi Taneja in upholding the special procedure and its classification.
members.conclusion: The special procedure was enacted in the public interest and did not violate Article 14 because the class of landlords receiving its benefit had a reasonable connection to the legislation’s purpose.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_evic: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a special procedure for eviction proceedings.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession_for_personal_h: The landlord seeks possession of the premises for a qualifying personal housing need.
predicates.ordinary_process_causes_prolonged_delay: The ordinary process for resolving the eviction claim may take so long that the landlord’s need may disappear or the landlord may die before obtaining relief.
predicates.special_procedure_has_a_reasonable_conne: The special procedure is designed to provide landlords with qualifying needs more timely relief.

members.legal_issue: A special summary procedure for eviction on a landlord's bona fide personal-need grounds is not unconstitutional discrimination or an excessive delegation of power when the classification is reasonably connected to its purpose and safeguards remain available to the tenant.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the special eviction procedure as discriminatory because it differed from the procedure available for other eviction grounds.
The special procedure applied to eviction claims based on a landlord's bona fide personal need and was intended to provide quicker relief in such cases.
A tenant could obtain leave to defend by disclosing facts that would defeat the landlord's claim.
The procedure allowed revision by the High Court and review by the Controller in the circumstances specified by the statute.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits hostile discrimination, not reasonable classification; a classification is permissible when it rests on an intelligible distinction with a rational connection to the legislative objective. The Court applied the presumption of constitutionality and the requirement that a challenger plead and prove the necessary facts. It relied on Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India, State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, Mahant Moti Das v. S.P. Sahi, and A.C. Aggarwal v. Mst. Ram Kali. It considered the procedure under Section 25B for claims under Section 14A and clause (e) of the proviso to Section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, and referred to Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahmed Khan concerning the meaningful application of bona fide personal-need grounds.
members.conclusion: The special procedure was constitutionally valid: it did not violate Article 14 or involve excessive delegation of power.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_special_eviction_procedure and procedure_limited_to_personal_need_cases and classification_connected_to_quick_relief and tenant_can_defend_on_disclosing_supporting_facts and review_safeguards_available

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_special_evic: A tenant challenged the constitutionality of a special procedure used in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.procedure_limited_to_personal_need_cases: The special procedure applied to eviction cases based on the landlord's bona fide personal need rather than all eviction grounds.
predicates.classification_connected_to_quick_relief: The special category reflected landlords' particular need for prompt relief.
predicates.tenant_can_defend_on_disclosing_supporti: A tenant could obtain permission to defend by presenting facts that, if established, would defeat the landlord's claim.
predicates.review_safeguards_available: The procedure provided for review by a higher court or the decision-maker in the circumstances available under the law.

members.legal_issue: A special provision governing owners of basti properties does not violate equality when those properties form a distinct class and the owners' position is protected by the provision.
material_facts: The landowner challenged the special treatment of owners of basti properties as discriminatory under Article 14 of the Constitution.
The Court treated bastis and their dwellers as a distinct class and noted that the municipal provision protected the owners' position.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not bar special treatment of a distinct class. The Court held that bastis and their dwellers stood in a separate class and that Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951 protected the owners' position. The Court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Article 14 challenge failed because bastis and their dwellers formed a distinct class and the owners' position was protected by Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951.

predicates.proceeding_is_special_leave_petition: The matter is brought before the court as a petition seeking special leave to appeal.
predicates.equality_challenge_targets_special_treat: The challenger claims that special treatment of owners of basti properties is discriminatory.
predicates.basti_properties_form_a_distinct_class: The properties and their occupants are treated as a distinct social and factual class.
predicates.owners_have_a_protective_recovery_mechan: A legal mechanism protects the owners' position by permitting recovery of attributable municipal rates.

members.legal_issue: A summary eviction procedure for non-resident owners is not arbitrary or unreasonable where tenants can seek leave to defend on relevant grounds and the procedure preserves review and safeguards against misuse.
material_facts: The tenant may apply for leave to contest by affidavit and must disclose facts that could disentitle the owner from obtaining possession.

The grounds available to the tenant include whether the applicant qualifies as a non-resident owner, owns the building for the required period, and genuinely requires it for personal or dependent use.
The Court held that a tenant need show a strong, well-grounded defence raising triable issues, not establish the defence beyond doubt at the leave stage.

The procedure provides for a High Court review, restricts the owner’s use of the remedy, limits dealings with the recovered property, and provides for restoration or punishment in specified cases of misuse.
members.legal_principle: Sections 13-B, 18-A and 19(2-B) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act provide the special remedy, leave-to-defend procedure, review, and safeguards. The claimed need must be genuine and bona fide; a tenant may obtain leave by raising a strong, well-grounded defence on the grounds relevant to eligibility and need, including triable factual disputes. The Court relied on Baldev Singh Bajwa v. Monish Saini; Ravi Dutt Sharma v. Ratan Lal Bhargava; Kewal Singh v. Smt. Lajwanti; Inderjeet Kaur v. Nirpal Singh; Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander; Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan; Surjit Singh Kalra v. Union of India; Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta; and Swami Nath v. Nirmal Singh.
members.conclusion: The summary procedure did not deprive tenants of a legal remedy and was not arbitrary or unreasonable; the constitutional challenge was rejected.

rule.if: tenant_remedy_challenge and summary_eviction_proceeding and tenant_can_seek_leave_to_defend and tenant_can_raise_relevant_triable_defence and review_or_abuse_safeguards_exist

predicates.tenant_remedy_challenge: A party challenges the fairness of a special procedure for eviction by a defined class of landlords.
predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The challenged proceeding is a summary eviction process for a defined class of landlords.
predicates.tenant_can_seek_leave_to_defend: The tenant may ask to contest the eviction claim by presenting grounds in an affidavit.
predicates.tenant_can_raise_relevant_triable_defenc: The tenant may obtain a hearing by raising a well-grounded factual defence relevant to the landlord’s eligibility or genuine need.
predicates.review_or_abuse_safeguards_exist: The process allows judicial review or provides safeguards against an owner’s misuse of the eviction remedy.

members.legal_issue: A statutory summary-eviction procedure that provides notice and an opportunity to respond does not impose an unreasonable restriction on the then-recognised right to hold property.
material_facts: The statute authorised summary eviction of occupants of municipal premises for specified breaches or unauthorised occupation.

Before making an eviction order, the authority had to give written notice of the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to provide an explanation and evidence; the occupant could also be represented in the proceeding.
The occupant received a notice, responded by denying unauthorised occupation, and was later ordered to vacate.
The High Court had invalidated the provision under Article 19(1)(f), while the Supreme Court had upheld materially identical provisions in earlier decisions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Maganlal Chhaganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, which overruled Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab, together with Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation v. Ramanlal Govindram and State of Gujarat v. Patel Beva Karsan. It relied on those decisions’ treatment of materially identical eviction procedures as intra vires, notwithstanding the challenge to the procedure as an unreasonable restriction.
members.conclusion: The provision was not invalid under Article 19(1)(f), and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_appeal and summary_eviction_authority and notice_and_opportunity_provided and comparable_supreme_court_decisions_considered

predicates.constitutional_validity_appeal: A party appealed from a judgment invalidating a statutory summary-eviction procedure.
predicates.summary_eviction_authority: The law authorised a public authority to order eviction of occupants from public premises in specified circumstances.
predicates.notice_and_opportunity_provided: The authority had to give the occupant notice of the grounds and a reasonable opportunity to respond and produce evidence before ordering eviction.
predicates.comparable_supreme_court_decisions_consi: The Supreme Court considered its earlier decisions addressing materially identical statutory eviction procedures.

members.legal_issue: A legislature may provide a reasonable summary procedure for evicting occupants without thereby abridging the constitutional right to property.
material_facts: The challenged law provided a speedier procedure for evicting tenants, sub-tenants, and unauthorised occupants from public premises.
The occupants argued that the summary procedure abridged their property rights.
The Court held that the procedure must be reasonable and conform to the principles of natural justice.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f), as it stood before its deletion, did not prevent the legislature from prescribing an eviction procedure or withdrawing statutory rent protection. A tenant's interest in premises is property, as recognised in Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Lala Pancham, but that does not require the legislature to retain a particular eviction procedure or statutory protection. The Public Premises Act creates a speedier remedy for an existing right of eviction rather than a new right of eviction, as explained in Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: Providing a reasonable summary eviction procedure that conforms to natural justice does not, by itself, abridge the constitutional right to property.

rule.if: eviction_law_challenge and summary_eviction_procedure and procedure_is_reasonable and procedure_observes_natural_justice

predicates.eviction_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges a law that provides for eviction of occupants.
predicates.summary_eviction_procedure: The law provides a summary procedure for evicting occupants.
predicates.procedure_is_reasonable: The procedure prescribed by the law is reasonable.
predicates.procedure_observes_natural_justice: The procedure prescribed by the law conforms to the principles of natural justice.

members.legal_issue: A statutory clearance procedure that gives affected tenants opportunities to object and appeal imposes reasonable restrictions on their property interests.
material_facts: The tenants had interests in the premises that were affected by the clearance order.
The statutory scheme provided for public notice and an opportunity for affected persons to object to the proposed order.
The scheme also provided affected persons a right of appeal against the confirmed order.
members.legal_principle: A tenant’s interest in demised premises is property protected by Article 19(1)(f), but Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The provisions must be read together: public notice permits affected tenants to object, the authority has duties concerning persons likely to be displaced, and an affected person may appeal. Those safeguards make the restrictions reasonable.
members.conclusion: The restrictions on the tenants’ property interests were reasonable, so the statutory provisions were valid.

rule.if: clearance_order_proceeding and tenant_property_interest_affected and tenants_have_objection_opportunity and tenants_have_appeal_opportunity

predicates.clearance_order_proceeding: A public authority undertook a proceeding to clear an area and remove buildings in it.
predicates.tenant_property_interest_affected: Tenants held interests in premises that would be affected by the clearance order.
predicates.tenants_have_objection_opportunity: The procedure gave affected tenants an opportunity to object to the proposed clearance order.
predicates.tenants_have_appeal_opportunity: The procedure gave affected persons an opportunity to appeal the confirmed clearance order.

members.legal_issue: Restrictions on property rights and the right to carry on business are reasonable when they serve planned improvement for the public and affected persons have meaningful opportunities to object and pursue review.
material_facts: The Act enabled planned improvement schemes for damaged areas of the city.
Affected persons could object to schemes before the Trust and the government considered them, participate in compensation inquiries, challenge specified matters before a Tribunal, and pursue appeals.
The Court noted that some buildings might be newly built or undamaged but found that this did not justify blocking a scheme serving a social purpose.
The Trust had assured displaced shop occupants that alternative accommodation or shops would be available, subject to the stated arrangements.
members.legal_principle: The reasonableness of restrictions under Article 19 is assessed by balancing the nature of the right, the purpose of the restrictions, the urgency of the evil, and the necessity of remedying it against the social welfare purpose. Articles 19(5) and 19(6) permit reasonable restrictions in the interests identified there. The Court applied this test without citing an earlier case.
members.conclusion: The restrictions were reasonable and served the general public; they were protected by Articles 19(5) and 19(6) and did not violate Article 19(1)(f) or Article 19(1)(g).

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_redevelopmen: A person challenges restrictions imposed through a statutory redevelopment scheme.
predicates.planned_improvement_serves_public_welfar: The scheme provides for planned improvement directed to a public or social purpose.
predicates.affected_persons_can_object_before_appro: People affected by a scheme can submit objections for consideration before it is approved.
predicates.affected_persons_can_seek_compensation_r: People affected by acquisition can participate in compensation proceedings and seek review of specified compensation matters.
predicates.some_affected_occupants_receive_alternat: The scheme authority assures affected occupants that alternative accommodation will be made available under stated arrangements.

members.legal_issue: A debtor who fails to pursue the prescribed sale-setting-aside remedy and satisfy its payment conditions cannot rely on partial or late payments to reopen a confirmed execution sale.
material_facts: The debtor did not make the deposit required to apply under the prescribed procedure for setting aside the sale.
The debtor’s application to set aside the sale was rejected, and the sale was subsequently confirmed.
The debtor later obtained a conditional order setting aside the sale if he paid the required sum with interest, but did not pay the full amount within the specified time.
The debtor made only partial payments and also relied on an undervaluation claim, although he had not pursued the prescribed remedy in time.
members.legal_principle: Rule 38(4)(a) requires the prescribed deposit, including the amount due to the decree-holder, for an application to set aside a sale; the application and deposit must comply with Rule 38(4)(b). A challenge based on irregularity or fraud is addressed by Rule 38(5), including its requirement of substantial injury. The debtor did not pursue the prescribed remedy and did not comply with the later conditional payment direction. Annapurna v. Mallikarjun concerned Order 21 Rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and did not govern this case.
members.conclusion: The debtor’s partial and late payments did not satisfy the conditions for setting aside the sale, and he could not obtain relief against the confirmed sale on that basis.

rule.if: execution_auction_proceeding and sale_confirmed and debtor_failed_to_make_required_full_deposit and debtor_made_only_partial_or_late_payments

predicates.execution_auction_proceeding: A creditor pursued recovery by auctioning immovable property through an execution process.
predicates.sale_confirmed: The competent recovery authority confirmed the sale in favour of the purchaser.
predicates.debtor_failed_to_make_required_full_depo: The debtor did not deposit the full amount required by the applicable sale-setting-aside procedure or a conditional order.
predicates.debtor_made_only_partial_or_late_payment: The debtor made payments that were incomplete or outside the required time.

members.legal_issue: A judgment debtor seeking to set aside an execution sale must make the required deposits within the applicable period, and an application without those deposits cannot prevent confirmation of the sale.
material_facts: A judgment debtor applied to set aside the execution sale before the sale was confirmed.
The application did not include the deposits required to set aside the sale, and the judgment debtor did not make those deposits within the applicable period.
The judgment debtor later offered to pay the auction purchaser’s amount, with interest and an additional sum, after the applicable period had passed.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 89 CPC requires the judgment debtor to deposit the amount payable to the decree-holder and five per cent of the purchase money for the auction purchaser. The deposit is a condition precedent and must be unconditional and made within the applicable period. Order 21 Rule 92(2), read with Article 127 of the Limitation Act, provides for the relevant period; Jammulu Ramulu, (2001) 7 SCC 71, held that Rule 92(2) does not itself prescribe a separate limitation period for the deposit and that a deposit made within the application period may be considered, subject to the court’s discretion where applicable. The Court also relied on Tribhovandas Purshottamdas Thakkar, AIR 1968 SC 372, and Challamane Huchha Gowda v. M. R. Tirumala, (2004) 1 SCC 453, on the purpose of Rule 89 as a final opportunity to save the property by satisfying the decree-holder and compensating the purchaser. The required deposits were not made within the applicable period, so the application could not be allowed.
members.conclusion: The application could not be entertained without the required timely deposits; the sale could not be set aside on the basis of the application, the later offer was rejected, and the confirmed sale was upheld.

predicates.execution_sale: The property was sold through a court process to enforce a decree.
predicates.judgment_debtor_sought_to_set_aside_sale: The judgment debtor asked the court to set aside the execution sale.
predicates.required_deposits_not_made_within_applic: The judgment debtor did not make the required payments within the period applicable to the request to set aside the sale.

members.legal_issue: A court has discretion over the amount and requirement of a deposit or security for an application to set aside an execution sale and should ordinarily give the applicant an opportunity to comply, particularly when the application predates the condition and the parties proceeded as though it did not apply.
material_facts: The application to set aside the sale was filed several months before the deposit-or-security condition was added.
The parties proceeded before the executing court on the basis that the new condition did not apply, and the court did not call on the applicant to provide security.
The compliance objection was raised for the first time in the High Court.

The High Court refused the applicant’s request for an opportunity to comply, treating compliance as mandatory and beyond the court’s power to permit after the application had been considered on the merits.
members.legal_principle: Order 21, Rule 90’s amended proviso gives the court discretion to determine the amount of the deposit or security, subject to the prescribed maximum, and to dispense with the requirement for recorded reasons. The court ordinarily should give the applicant an opportunity to comply and may reject the application if the applicant still does not comply. The Court relied on the interpretation in Kundan Lal v. Jagan Nath Sharma and held that this approach was particularly appropriate where the application predated the added condition and the parties had proceeded on the assumption that it did not apply.
members.conclusion: The High Court should have remitted the matter to the executing court to exercise its discretion concerning compliance; the appeal was allowed and the case remitted.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and application_predates_compliance_condition and parties_proceeded_without_compliance and court_did_not_seek_compliance

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A party challenges a sale conducted to enforce a judgment.
predicates.application_predates_compliance_conditio: The application was filed before a compliance condition was added to the governing procedure.
predicates.parties_proceeded_without_compliance: The parties conducted the proceedings on the understanding that the added condition did not apply.
predicates.court_did_not_seek_compliance: The court did not call on the applicant to comply before the compliance objection was raised.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to an execution sale cannot succeed on grounds outside the sale-related case advanced in the application, and the application was rightly dismissed where the judgment debtors did not make the deposit required by the court or allege fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
material_facts: The judgment debtors applied to set aside the execution sale, alleging inadequate publication to obtain an adequate market value and alleging fraud in obtaining the decree.
They did not allege fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale, and their principal fraud allegation concerned the decree itself.
They did not deposit the sale consideration with interest as required by the executing court.
The appellate court set aside the dismissal by relying on the purchaser’s relationship to the judgment creditor, a ground not advanced in the sale application.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an application to set aside an execution sale on the ground of material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale. The Court also upheld the executing court’s application of the deposit requirement it attributed to that rule and held that the appellate court had gone beyond the case advanced in the application.
members.conclusion: The executing court rightly dismissed the application to set aside the sale, and the appellate court erred in reversing that dismissal on a ground not raised in the application.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_execution_sale: A party applies to set aside a sale conducted to enforce a court decree.
predicates.no_required_deposit_made: The applicant fails to make the deposit that the court requires for the sale challenge.
predicates.alleged_fraud_concerns_decree_not_sale: The applicant alleges fraud in obtaining the decree rather than fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
predicates.appellate_court_relied_on_ground_not_rai: The appellate court reverses the dismissal by relying on a ground that the applicant did not advance in the application.

members.legal_issue: A later application to set aside an execution sale under the deposit procedure may be made and prosecuted after an earlier application to set aside the sale on other grounds is withdrawn, and is treated as made upon that withdrawal.
material_facts: In execution of a decree, the applicant first sought to set aside the sale under the procedure for challenging a sale on other grounds.
The applicant later filed an application under the deposit procedure, deposited the required amount, and stated in that application that the earlier application was withdrawn.
The court formally dismissed the earlier application only after the later application had been filed.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 89(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, gives effect to both the words “make” and “prosecute”: a person who first applies under Rule 90 cannot make or prosecute an application under Rule 89 unless the earlier application is withdrawn, and an application under Rule 89 made before that withdrawal is treated as made upon withdrawal. The interpretation is supported by the corresponding proviso to section 310A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1882, and Rajendra Nath Haldar v. Nilratan Mitter, ILR 23 Calcutta 958, which construed “make” in that proviso to include carrying on or prosecuting an application.
members.conclusion: The later application was maintainable and was treated as made when the earlier application was withdrawn; the absence of a formal dismissal order at that point did not invalidate it.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and earlier_sale_challenge_filed and later_deposit_application_filed and earlier_application_withdrawn

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: The proceeding concerns an application to set aside a sale made in execution of a decree.
predicates.earlier_sale_challenge_filed: The applicant first filed an application to set aside the execution sale on grounds other than compliance with the deposit procedure.
predicates.later_deposit_application_filed: The applicant later filed an application relying on the deposit procedure to set aside the execution sale.
predicates.earlier_application_withdrawn: The applicant communicated withdrawal of the earlier sale-challenge application.

members.legal_issue: A pending application by one judgment debtor to set aside an execution sale does not bar other judgment debtors from seeking to set aside the sale by making the required deposit.
material_facts: A house was sold in execution of a money decree against several judgment debtors.
One judgment debtor applied to set aside the sale on grounds relating to the sale procedure.
Other judgment debtors later applied to set aside the sale by depositing the decretal amount and the purchaser’s compensation.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 21, Rules 89 and 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an application by one judgment debtor under Rule 90 does not prevent other judgment debtors from applying under Rule 89 when they make the deposit required by that rule. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The application by one judgment debtor did not bar the other judgment debtors’ application, and the sale was set aside.

rule.if: execution_sale_proceeding and one_judgment_debtor_challenges_sale and different_judgment_debtors_seek_sale_relief and required_amount_deposited

predicates.execution_sale_proceeding: Immovable property was sold in execution of a decree.
predicates.one_judgment_debtor_challenges_sale: One judgment debtor applied to have the execution sale set aside.
predicates.different_judgment_debtors_seek_sale_rel: Judgment debtors other than the applicant in the challenge applied for relief from the sale.
predicates.required_amount_deposited: The judgment debtors seeking relief deposited the amounts required for that relief.

members.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor who had an opportunity to challenge a decree but did not do so may be barred from raising that objection later in execution proceedings.
material_facts: The tenant received notice when the arbitration award was placed before the court and did not object that the decree could not be passed without rent-controller permission.
The tenant also did not raise that objection during an earlier execution proceeding, despite opportunities to do so.
The tenant first raised the objection in a later execution proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The principles of constructive res judicata apply in execution proceedings. Mohanlal Goenka v. Benoy Kishna Mukherjee, AIR 1953 SC 65, applied those principles to execution proceedings. An objection available when a decree is made, but not raised despite an opportunity to do so, may not be raised later in execution.
members.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from raising the objection belatedly, and constructive res judicata applies in execution proceedings; the Court considered this an additional ground, though its decision on surrender made it unnecessary to rely on it.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to execute a court decree.
predicates.objection_available_before_decree_was_pa: The judgment-debtor could have raised the objection when the award or proposed decree was before the court.
predicates.judgment_debtor_did_not_raise_objection_: The judgment-debtor received an opportunity to raise the objection but did not do so.
predicates.objection_first_raised_in_later_executio: The judgment-debtor first raised the objection in a later execution proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor who did not raise limitation when challenging steps taken after revival of execution cannot later challenge the revival order on limitation grounds.
material_facts: Execution was revived, property was attached and sold, and the judgment-debtors sought to set aside the sale on the ground that a statutory protection barred the sale.
The judgment-debtors did not argue before the executing court that revival, attachment, or sale was barred by limitation.
members.legal_principle: The principle of res judicata applies to execution proceedings. A party that does not raise a limitation objection in proceedings concerning the revival and subsequent steps in execution cannot later use a separate execution application to contest the unchallenged revival order on that ground.
members.conclusion: The judgment-debtors were barred by res judicata from challenging directly or indirectly the earlier order reviving execution on limitation grounds.

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to execute a decree.
predicates.prior_execution_order_accepted_or_left_u: An earlier order allowing execution to proceed was not challenged by the affected party.
predicates.party_omitted_limitation_objection_when_: The party contested later execution steps without raising a limitation objection.

members.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor may be barred by constructive res judicata from later challenging an executing court’s jurisdiction when the objection could and should have been raised in earlier execution proceedings but was omitted or abandoned.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor received notice of a second execution application but did not then object that the executing court lacked jurisdiction.

The judgment-debtor also received notice of the decree-holder’s application to the court that passed the decree for authority to sell the property, but did not object to the executing court proceeding.
The judgment-debtor challenged sales in several later applications and proceedings, but either omitted the jurisdiction objection or raised it without pressing it; the resulting orders became final.
The judgment-debtor raised the objection in a later application after the property had been sold and the execution proceedings had advanced.
members.legal_principle: The principle of constructive res judicata applies to execution proceedings even though section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not apply to them in terms. Under section 11, Explanation IV, and general principles of res judicata, a party is barred from raising later a matter that could and should have been raised earlier; an objection raised but not pursued may be treated as having been decided against that party. The jurisdictional character of the objection does not by itself prevent the rule from operating in these circumstances. The court relied on Annada Kumar Roy v. Sheik Madan, Mahadeo Prasad Bhagat v. Bhagwat Narain Singh, Ram Kirpal Shukul v. Mussamat Rup Kuari, Raja of Ramnad v. Velusami Tevar, and Sha Shivraj Gopalji v. Edappakath Ayissa Bi; it distinguished Ledgard v. Bull and other authorities, and overruled Raghubir Saran v. Hori Lal.
members.conclusion: The judgment-debtor was precluded from raising the jurisdiction objection at the later stage by constructive res judicata, notwithstanding that the objection concerned the executing court’s jurisdiction.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and party_had_opportunity_to_raise_objection and objection_could_have_been_raised_earlier and (objection_omitted or objection_abandoned) and earlier_proceedings_became_final

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter concerns a court proceeding to enforce a decree.
predicates.party_had_opportunity_to_raise_objection: The party received notice or otherwise had an opportunity to raise the objection in the earlier proceedings.
predicates.objection_could_have_been_raised_earlier: The objection was available to the party at an earlier stage of the proceedings.
predicates.objection_omitted: The party did not raise the objection at an earlier stage when it could have done so.
predicates.objection_abandoned: The party raised the objection earlier but did not pursue it for decision.
predicates.earlier_proceedings_became_final: The earlier proceedings or orders concluded without the objection being determined in the party’s favour.

members.legal_issue: An objection to execution that was previously dismissed for default is not barred by res judicata when the objection was not heard and finally decided.
material_facts: In the course of execution of a mortgage decree, judgment debtors raised an objection that the decree could not be executed under the applicable land-reform law.
Two earlier applications raising the same objection were dismissed for the judgment debtors’ default, without a decision on the objection’s merits.
A later application raised the same objection, which the execution court considered and decided.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata, whether under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure or as a matter of public policy, requires that the issue or plea have been heard and finally decided. The Court relied on Maharaja Radha Parshad Singh v. Lal Sahab Rai, Pulvarthi Venkata Subba Rao v. Velluri Jagannadha Rao, Lakshmibai Anant Kondkar v. Ravji Bhikaji Kondkar, Bahir Das Pal v. Girish Chandra Pal, Bhagwati Prasad Sah v. Radha Kishun Sah, Jethmal v. Mst. Sakina, and Bishwanath Kundu v. Subala Dassi; it disapproved Ramnarain v. Basudeo.
members.conclusion: The objection was not barred by res judicata because the earlier applications had been dismissed for default and the objection had not been heard and finally decided.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The dispute arose in proceedings to execute a decree.
predicates.earlier_objections_dismissed_for_default: The objecting judgment debtor’s earlier applications raising the objection were dismissed for default.
predicates.objection_not_decided_on_merits: The earlier dismissals did not follow a hearing and final decision on the objection’s merits.
predicates.repeated_objection_not_barred_by_res_jud: The same objection may be raised again without being barred by res judicata.

members.legal_issue: A suit challenging an execution sale is not barred by res judicata when the claimants were neither parties to nor represented in the earlier suits, or when those suits were not decided by a court of competent jurisdiction.
material_facts: The claimants were not parties to the earlier suits, and they were not representatives of their father for the purposes of Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The earlier suits were decided by a court that was not competent in relation to the court in which the present suit was filed.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires, among other things, that the matter have been heard and finally decided by a competent court and that the relevant parties or their representatives be bound by that decision. The claimants were not parties or representatives in the earlier suits, and those suits were not decided by a court of competent jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by res judicata.

rule.if: suit_to_challenge_prior_execution_sale and ((not claimant_was_party_to_prior_suits and not claimant_was_represented_in_prior_suits) or prior_court_lacked_competent_jurisdiction)

predicates.suit_to_challenge_prior_execution_sale: A claimant brought a suit challenging an execution sale after earlier suits concerning the property had been decided.
predicates.claimant_was_party_to_prior_suits: The claimant was a party to the earlier suits concerning the property.
predicates.claimant_was_represented_in_prior_suits: The claimant was represented in the earlier suits by a person whose representation bound the claimant.
predicates.prior_court_lacked_competent_jurisdictio: The court that decided the earlier suits lacked competent jurisdiction for the matter at issue.

members.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor’s failure to raise an objection in execution does not operate as actual or constructive res judicata against a person claiming through the judgment-debtor when the validity of the auction sale is the issue and the relevant status and need for sanction were not disputed.
material_facts: The private purchaser claimed through the judgment-debtor.
The judgment-debtor had not raised the particular objections to the auction in the execution proceedings.
Neither the judgment-debtor nor the decree-holder disputed that the judgment-debtor was a member of a Scheduled Tribe, and both were aware that sanction was needed for a sale of the property.
The decree-holder had informed the executing court that permission was needed, and the basic issue later was the validity of the auction sale.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that no question of actual or constructive res judicata arose on these facts: the basic issue was the validity of the auction sale, the purchaser claimed through the judgment-debtor, and the judgment-debtor’s tribal status and the need for sanction had not been disputed.
members.conclusion: The judgment-debtor’s failure to raise the particular objections did not operate as actual or constructive res judicata against the judgment-debtor or the purchaser claiming through him.

rule.if: execution_sale_dispute and claimant_derives_title_from_judgment_debtor and debtor_omitted_objection and tribal_status_was_not_disputed and parties_knew_sanction_was_needed

predicates.execution_sale_dispute: The dispute concerned the validity of a court auction conducted in execution proceedings.
predicates.claimant_derives_title_from_judgment_deb: The person challenging the auction claimed title through the judgment-debtor.
predicates.debtor_omitted_objection: The judgment-debtor did not raise the particular objection to the auction in the execution proceedings.
predicates.tribal_status_was_not_disputed: The parties did not dispute that the judgment-debtor was a member of a Scheduled Tribe.
predicates.parties_knew_sanction_was_needed: The parties knew that the property could not be sold without the competent authority’s sanction.

members.legal_issue: An executing court's failure to decide an objection under Order 21 Rule 23(2) does not bar the judgment-debtor from raising the objection after sale.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor objected to execution, including on the basis that money sufficient to satisfy the decree was already deposited.
The executing court did not decide those objections under Order 21 Rule 23(2) before ordering the sale.
The judgment-debtor later challenged the sale.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 23(2) requires the executing court to consider objections to execution and make an order. An order made on those objections may be appealable, but omission to consider them is not. Section 47 addresses questions relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of a decree; Order 21 Rule 90 addresses material irregularity or fraud in the publicity or conduct of a sale, subject to proof of substantial injury.
members.conclusion: The objections remained open to be raised after the sale under Section 47 or Order 21 Rule 90; the executing court's omission to decide them was not itself appealable.

rule.if: decree_execution and judgment_debtor_objected_to_execution and court_failed_to_decide_objection and sale_challenged_afterward

predicates.decree_execution: The proceeding is an execution of a decree.
predicates.judgment_debtor_objected_to_execution: The judgment-debtor raised an objection to execution.
predicates.court_failed_to_decide_objection: The executing court did not consider and decide the objection as part of the execution proceeding.
predicates.sale_challenged_afterward: The judgment-debtor challenged the sale after it took place.

members.legal_issue: Order 21 Rule 90(3) does not bar a judgment-debtor from challenging pre-sale defects where the court failed to give the notice required for settlement of the sale proclamation.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor was not given notice before the proclamation was to be settled.
The executing court did not draw up a proper sale proclamation.
The judgment-debtor challenged the sale after it occurred.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 90(3) precludes grounds that an applicant could have raised on or before the date the proclamation was drawn up. The Court explained that the rule presupposes notice and an opportunity to act; it does not penalize a judgment-debtor who was denied the mandatory notice under Order 21 Rule 54(1-A). Under Section 47, pre-sale defects relating to execution may be raised; under Order 21 Rule 90, post-sale material irregularities or fraud in publicity or conduct require proof of substantial injury.
members.conclusion: The judgment-debtor was not precluded by Rule 90(3) from raising the defects after the sale; the sale defects could be considered under Section 47 or Order 21 Rule 90 as appropriate.

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: The proceeding challenges a sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.judgment_debtor_not_notified_before_proc: The judgment-debtor was not notified before the sale proclamation was to be settled.
predicates.pre_sale_defect_challenged_after_sale: The judgment-debtor raises after the sale a defect that arose before the sale.

members.legal_issue: The possession-based limitation rule requiring prior possession by the plaintiff does not govern a possession claim brought solely by succession where the plaintiffs were never in possession under that title.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed the property as heirs, but neither had possessed it in that capacity.
One plaintiff had possessed part of the property for a time under a transfer from the adopted son, not under the succession title asserted in the suit.
members.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908, applies where the plaintiff was initially in possession and was dispossessed by the defendant or someone through whom the defendant claims, or where the plaintiff discontinued possession. Possession under a different title does not establish the possession required for a claim brought under succession.
members.conclusion: Article 142 did not apply to the suit.

predicates.possession_suit: The plaintiffs brought a suit to recover possession of property.
predicates.plaintiffs_never_possessed_under_claimed: The plaintiffs had never possessed the property under the title on which they brought the suit.

members.legal_issue: The special limitation rule for a tenant dispossessed from a tenancy holding does not govern a possession suit brought on the basis of a reversionary title that arose after the life interest ended.
material_facts: The claimant had earlier held the property as a tenant under a gift to the claimant’s mother and was dispossessed while that tenancy interest existed.
The claimant brought the suit after the widow’s death on the basis of a reversionary title, rather than as a tenant seeking recovery for the earlier dispossession.
The earlier dispossession was not the basis of the reversionary possession claim; that title arose on the widow’s death.
members.legal_principle: Section 104(1) and Article 1 of the Second Schedule to the C.P. Tenancy Act applied to a possession suit brought by a person claiming to be a tenant who had been dispossessed or excluded from possession. The claimant’s suit was instead based on a new title as reversioner arising after the widow’s death. The claimant’s earlier tenancy right could be extinguished under those provisions, but that did not make them applicable to the later reversionary claim.
members.conclusion: Section 104(1) and Article 1 of the Second Schedule to the C.P. Tenancy Act did not apply to the suit; limitation for the suit was governed by the Limitation Act, 1908.

rule.if: suit_for_possession and claim_based_on_reversionary_title and claim_arose_after_life_interest_ended and not suit_based_on_tenant_dispossession

predicates.suit_for_possession: The claimant seeks possession of property through a court proceeding.
predicates.claim_based_on_reversionary_title: The claimant bases the possession claim on a right to inherit after a life interest ends.
predicates.claim_arose_after_life_interest_ended: The claimant’s asserted reversionary right arose only when the life interest ended.
predicates.suit_based_on_tenant_dispossession: The claimant seeks possession in the capacity of a tenant on the ground of an earlier dispossession from the tenancy holding.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for challenging a customary alienation of ancestral property does not govern a suit for possession based on inheritance where the plaintiffs’ title arises on the termination of a life interest.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession as heirs after the death of the holder of a life interest.
An earlier final decree had declared that the gift would not affect the reversionary rights arising after the life-interest holder’s death.
The plaintiffs’ claim was based on inherited title, rather than a fresh challenge to an alienation as contrary to custom.
members.legal_principle: Entry 2(b) of the Schedule to the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 applies to a suit for possession of ancestral immovable property alienated where the plaintiff asserts that the alienation is not binding under custom. It did not apply to a claim based on title already declared in an earlier suit and inheritance on the termination of a life interest.
members.conclusion: The three-year limitation provision for a suit challenging an alienation of ancestral property under custom did not apply.

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_inheritance: The claimants brought a civil suit seeking possession on the basis of inherited title.
predicates.claim_arises_when_life_interest_ends: The claimants’ entitlement arose when a limited life interest ended.
predicates.suit_challenges_alienation_as_customaril: The claimants sought possession on the ground that an alienation of ancestral property was invalid under custom.

members.legal_issue: The limitation rule requiring proof of dispossession by the defendant does not bar a title-based possession suit when the defendant did not dispossess the claimant.
material_facts: The suit sought ejectment and recovery of possession on the basis of title.
In relation to part of the land, the claimant's mother had possession after a mortgage was redeemed.
The government later took possession of that land and, when the attachment was vacated, delivered possession to the defendant rather than the claimant.
The court found that the defendant had not dispossessed the claimant.
members.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Limitation Act did not apply because the suit was against a person not entitled to possession, and the defendant had not dispossessed the claimant. The court treated the claimant's right to sue for possession as arising when possession was delivered to the defendant instead of the claimant.
members.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act because the defendant had not dispossessed the claimant and the suit was against a person not entitled to possession.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The claimant brought a suit to recover possession on the basis of title.
predicates.defendant_did_not_dispossess_claimant: The defendant did not remove the claimant from possession.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for a suit based on dispossession does not apply when the plaintiff's claim is that the defendants' possession became unlawful, rather than that the plaintiff was dispossessed in the relevant sense.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration of title and possession, and also claimed mesne profits.
The plaint, read as a whole, alleged that the defendants' possession became unlawful from a certain date and that the plaintiffs consequently became entitled to possession.

The plaint referred to orders under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as giving rise to a cause of action, not as establishing dispossession in the sense relevant to the limitation article.
members.legal_principle: Article 3 of Schedule III of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885, prescribes a two-year limitation period for a suit to recover possession of land claimed by a landlord or raiyat, running from the date of dispossession. It did not apply because the plaint alleged that the defendants' possession became unlawful, rather than that the plaintiffs had been dispossessed in the sense used by that article.
members.conclusion: Article 3 of Schedule III of the Bihar Tenancy Act did not apply, so the suit was not barred by that article.

predicates.land_possession_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking possession of land.
predicates.plaintiff_claims_defendant_possession_be: The plaintiff alleged that the defendant's possession became unlawful from a particular point and that this entitled the plaintiff to seek possession.
predicates.plaintiff_alleges_relevant_dispossession: The plaintiff alleged that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiff in the sense relevant to a limitation rule for possession claims.

members.legal_issue: A title-and-possession suit is barred where neither the claimant nor the claimant’s predecessor was in possession within the applicable twelve-year period before the suit.
material_facts: The claimant acquired the asserted interest after the later auction purchaser had obtained possession.
Neither the claimant nor the claimant’s predecessor had obtained possession within twelve years before the suit.
The claimant sought a declaration of title and an injunction or, alternatively, possession.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the twelve-year limitation period to the claim for title and possession, finding that neither the claimant nor the predecessor had been in possession during that period. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because neither the claimant nor the predecessor in title had been in possession within twelve years before it was filed.

predicates.title_possession_suit: A party brought a suit seeking a declaration of title and relief concerning possession of land.
predicates.neither_claimant_nor_predecessor_in_poss: Neither the claimant nor the claimant’s predecessor was in possession during the applicable period before the suit was filed.

members.legal_issue: A suit seeking possession after alleged dispossession is barred under the applicable possession limitation rule when the plaintiffs fail to establish possession within the relevant preceding period.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sued for a declaration of title and possession, alleging that the defendants had dispossessed them of the land.
The High Court found no evidence that the plaintiffs had been in possession of the land within the twelve years preceding the suit.
