The plaintiffs’ counsel could identify no evidence on the record establishing possession within that period.
members.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908 applied to a suit for possession following alleged dispossession, and the plaintiffs had to establish that they had been in possession within twelve years before instituting the suit.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to hold that the suit was barred under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

predicates.possession_suit_after_alleged_dispossess: The plaintiffs brought a suit seeking possession after alleging that they had been dispossessed.
predicates.evidence_of_possession_within_relevant_p: Evidence established that the plaintiffs had possessed the land during the relevant period preceding the suit.

members.legal_issue: A person already occupying property as a tenant cannot use part performance to resist eviction unless the requirements for that protection are established, including a change in the character of possession and performance or willingness to perform the contract.
material_facts: The occupant entered possession as a tenant before the alleged agreement to sell was made.
A civil court found that an agreement to sell existed but dismissed the occupant’s suit for specific performance and found that the occupant had not disowned the character of tenant.

The occupant did not prove that the parties had changed the basis of possession from tenancy to possession under the agreement, or that an independent act in furtherance of the agreement had occurred.
The subsequent purchaser was found to have purchased for consideration without notice of the agreement or any part performance.
The eviction proceeding was based on the landlord-tenant relationship.
members.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires possession taken or continued in part performance, an act in furtherance of the contract where the transferee was already in possession, and performance or willingness to perform the transferee’s obligations; the protection is unavailable against a transferee for consideration without notice. A person already in possession must show something beyond mere retention of possession to establish part performance. A final dismissal of the specific-performance suit on merits is inconsistent with the claimant having performed or being willing to perform the contract. The Court relied on G.H.C. Ariff v. Jadunath Majumdar Bahadur, Bhagwandas Parsadilal v. Surajmal, Dakshinamurthi Mudaliar v. Dhanakoti Ammal, A.M.A. Sultan v. Seydu Zohra Beevi, Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai, and Shrimant Shamrao Suryavanshi v. Pralhad Bhairoba Suryavanshi; the last case does not make limitation alone a bar where the other requirements are met. Section 91 of the Indian Trust Act was also discussed in connection with the rule concerning a subsequent purchaser with notice.
members.conclusion: The occupant could not rely on part performance to resist eviction, and the eviction order was maintained. A bar of limitation alone would not defeat the defence if all other requirements for part-performance protection were satisfied.

rule.if: rent_eviction_case and agreement_to_sell_found and tenant_possession_preceded_contract and no_independent_act_in_furtherance and specific_performance_claim_rejected and transferee_without_notice

predicates.rent_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction of an occupant on the basis of a landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.agreement_to_sell_found: A court found that an agreement to sell the property in favour of the occupant existed.
predicates.tenant_possession_preceded_contract: The occupant was already in possession as a tenant before the alleged sale contract was made.
predicates.no_independent_act_in_furtherance: The occupant did not establish an act beyond retaining possession that showed possession had continued under the sale contract rather than the earlier tenancy.
predicates.specific_performance_claim_rejected: A court rejected the occupant’s claim for specific performance of the sale contract.
predicates.transferee_without_notice: A subsequent purchaser for consideration acquired the property without notice of the contract or its part performance.
predicates.part_performance_defence_unavailable: The occupant cannot use part performance to resist the eviction claim.

members.legal_issue: A transferee already in possession under a mortgage cannot rely on continued possession and acts not unequivocally referable to a concluded written sale contract to obtain protection under the doctrine of part performance.
material_facts: The mortgagee was already in possession under a subsisting mortgage with possession before the alleged sale contract.
The parties disputed whether the proposed sale was conditional or absolute, and the mortgagee relied on an unregistered sale deed as the written contract.
Most of the payment for stamps and registration expenses preceded the alleged written contract, and the remaining payment was not established as an act in furtherance of it.

The mortgagee did not establish other independent acts unequivocally referable to the sale contract and did not perform, or show willingness to perform, his obligations, including paying creditors or the remaining consideration.
members.legal_principle: Section 53A requires a written contract signed by the transferor, with ascertainable transfer terms, possession taken or continued in part performance, an act in furtherance of the contract, and performance or willingness to perform by the transferee. Acts relied on must have a real nexus with, and be unequivocally referable to, the pre-existing contract; preliminary acts and mere retention of possession that is independently justified do not suffice. A payment may support the claim when considered with other acts, but is not automatically part performance. The Court applied Nathulal v. Phool Chand, considered Steadman v. Steadman and Maddison v. Alderson, and relied on the distinction between first entering possession and retaining prior possession reflected in cases including Jahangir Begum v. Gulam Ali Ahmed and Kukali v. Basantilal.
members.conclusion: The mortgagee was not entitled to protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, and the mortgagors’ redemption suit was restored.

rule.if: redemption_proceeding and transferee_claims_part_performance and claimant_previously_possessed_property and continued_possession_independently_justified and no_independent_act_unequivocally_linked_to_contract and relied_on_acts_preceded_or_were_ambiguous and transferee_failed_to_perform_or_show_willingness

predicates.redemption_proceeding: The dispute is a proceeding seeking redemption of a mortgage over the property.
predicates.transferee_claims_part_performance: A transferee relies on part performance to resist the transferor’s claim concerning the property.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_property: The person claiming part-performance protection was in possession before the alleged transfer contract.
predicates.continued_possession_independently_justi: The claimant’s continued possession was supported by an existing legal relationship independent of the alleged transfer contract.
predicates.no_independent_act_unequivocally_linked_: The claimant did not establish an independent act that unequivocally connected the claimant’s conduct to the alleged contract.
predicates.relied_on_acts_preceded_or_were_ambiguou: The acts relied on occurred before the alleged contract or could not be unequivocally attributed to it.
predicates.transferee_failed_to_perform_or_show_wil: The transferee did not perform, or demonstrate willingness to perform, the transferee’s obligations under the contract.

members.legal_issue: A proposed transferee cannot protect possession of immovable property by part performance unless a written contract states terms from which the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty.
material_facts: The respondents claimed that an oral agreement had been made to sell one co-owner’s half share and that part of the price had been paid.

The co-owner’s letters acknowledged an agreement to sell and demanded payment of the balance, but did not set out essential terms, including when the sale deed was to be executed and who would pay registration charges.
The occupant had originally entered the property permissively, and possession had not been given pursuant to a written agreement containing the terms of the proposed transfer.
members.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act requires a contract to transfer immovable property for consideration, in writing and signed by the transferor or someone on the transferor’s behalf, with terms ascertainable with reasonable certainty; it also requires possession in part performance, an act in furtherance, and performance or willingness to perform by the transferee. The written contract must precede possession claimed under it. The Court relied on Nathulal v. Phool Chand (1969) 3 SCC 120 and Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai (1982) 1 SCC 237 for these requirements.
members.conclusion: The letters were not a written agreement to sell satisfying the requirements for protection by part performance. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the owners’ suit for possession and mesne profits was decreed.

predicates.part_performance_possession_claim: The proceeding includes a claim by a proposed transferee to protect possession of immovable property on the basis of part performance.
predicates.writings_only_acknowledge_oral_sale: The available writings merely acknowledge an oral sale agreement rather than recording its terms as a written contract.
predicates.essential_transfer_terms_absent_from_wri: The writings do not state essential terms needed to ascertain the proposed transfer with reasonable certainty.
predicates.possession_not_given_under_written_contr: The proposed transferee was not put in possession pursuant to a written contract containing the terms of the proposed transfer.

members.legal_issue: A person cannot protect possession under the doctrine of part performance without satisfying its requirements for a written contract, ascertainable transfer terms, possession in part performance, and willingness to perform.
material_facts: The person initially defended a possession suit on the ground that he was a tenant and later sought to add a defense based on an alleged agreement of sale.
The application to amend the defense was made after the tenancy proceedings had ended and was rejected as belated and mala fide.
There was no written contract of sale signed by the owner; a letter from the owner's brother referred to an alleged oral agreement.
The letter did not set out terms sufficient to ascertain the transfer with reasonable certainty.
The person obtained possession under a power of attorney as an agent, and the evidence did not show that the character of his possession changed.
He continued at intervals to pay the owner the agreed annual sum, a course of conduct inconsistent with possession as a prospective purchaser.
members.legal_principle: Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act requires a written contract signed by or on behalf of the transferor, terms from which the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty, possession taken or continued in part performance of that contract, an act in furtherance where applicable, and willingness by the transferee to perform. A letter that is only written evidence of an oral sale agreement is not the written contract itself. No earlier case is relied on.
members.conclusion: The person was not entitled to protect his possession under section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act.

rule.if: possession_defense_proceeding and (late_new_sale_defense or no_signed_written_sale_contract or uncertain_sale_terms or possession_not_under_sale_contract or conduct_inconsistent_with_purchaser_status)

predicates.possession_defense_proceeding: A person facing a claim for possession relies on an alleged sale agreement as a defense to remaining in possession.
predicates.late_new_sale_defense: The person sought to introduce the sale-agreement defense only after pursuing a different defense through separate proceedings.
predicates.no_signed_written_sale_contract: There was no written sale contract signed by the owner or on the owner's behalf.
predicates.uncertain_sale_terms: The written material did not state terms from which the proposed transfer could be ascertained with reasonable certainty.
predicates.possession_not_under_sale_contract: The person obtained possession under an agency arrangement, and the evidence did not show that possession later changed character under a sale agreement.
predicates.conduct_inconsistent_with_purchaser_stat: The person continued to make payments to the owner on terms inconsistent with possession as a purchaser.

members.legal_issue: A person who entered possession under a sale agreement cannot establish title by adverse possession while relying on that agreement as the basis for remaining in possession.
material_facts: The appellant entered possession under an agreement of sale and relied on that agreement to claim a right to retain possession.
The appellant also pleaded that he had acquired title by adverse possession.

He did not disclaim the agreement and establish that he had openly asserted hostile possession to the knowledge of the transferor or successor in title, with acquiescence throughout the required period.
members.legal_principle: A person who entered possession lawfully under an agreement must disclaim the contractual basis of possession and plead and prove an independent, hostile assertion of title to the knowledge of the owner or successor, together with acquiescence for the full prescriptive period. A claim under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, implicitly admits that possession began lawfully under the agreement and continued on that basis.
members.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea was unavailable because it was inconsistent with the appellant’s reliance on the agreement as the basis of his possession.

rule.if: possession_suit and possession_began_under_agreement and (claimant_relies_on_agreement or not hostile_possession_proved)

predicates.possession_suit: A person seeking possession brought a suit against the occupant.
predicates.possession_began_under_agreement: The occupant entered possession pursuant to an agreement to transfer the property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_agreement: The occupant relies on the agreement as the basis for a right to remain in possession.
predicates.hostile_possession_proved: The occupant disclaimed the agreement and proved an openly hostile claim of title known to the owner or successor, with acquiescence for the full prescriptive period.

members.legal_issue: A claim to retain possession under part performance of an agreement and a claim of adverse possession are inconsistent where the possessor relies on lawful entry under the agreement without proving a later hostile assertion of ownership.
material_facts: The defendant relied on an alleged agreement to sale as the basis for lawful possession and also claimed title by adverse possession.
The alleged sale agreement was not proved, and the lower courts found that possession had instead been delivered for cultivation.
There was no evidence that the defendant later asserted hostile ownership against the plaintiff.
members.legal_principle: A plea of adverse possession is inconsistent with retaining possession under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act where the possessor accepts lawful entry under an agreement and continued possession under it; adverse possession may be available only if hostile animus after entry is asserted and proved. The Court relied on Mohan Lal v. Mirza Abdul Gaffar, (1996) 1 SCC 639.
members.conclusion: The adverse-possession plea was unavailable on the basis of the asserted lawful entry under the agreement unless a later hostile assertion of possession as owner was established.

rule.if: part_performance_defense and adverse_possession_claim and lawful_entry_under_agreement and not later_hostile_assertion_proved

predicates.part_performance_defense: A person relies on part performance of an agreement as a basis for retaining possession of property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim: The person also claims title to the property by adverse possession.
predicates.lawful_entry_under_agreement: The person asserts that possession began lawfully under the agreement.
predicates.later_hostile_assertion_proved: The person proves a later assertion of hostile ownership after entering possession.

members.legal_issue: A custom governing inheritance must be proved unless repeated judicial recognition has made it entitled to judicial notice, and the alleged custom preferring collaterals over a sister in succession to non-ancestral property had not reached that status.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a sister's claim to her brother's non-ancestral property against a collateral relative.
The collateral relied on paragraph 24 of Rattigan's Digest for the asserted custom excluding sisters in favour of collaterals.
The reported decisions were divided on whether that custom existed, and decisions in the preceding ten years uniformly rejected the view in the Digest.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 48 and 57(1) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, custom may be proved, but proof is unnecessary where courts can take judicial notice of it. A custom becomes entitled to judicial notice when it has been repeatedly brought to the courts' attention and recognised as part of the law. The Court relied on Raja Rama Rao v. Raja of Pittapur for that threshold, and on Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh and Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero for the ordinary burden on the party asserting a custom. It also observed that Rattigan's Digest, though highly authoritative, did not establish judicial recognition in the face of conflicting decisions.
members.conclusion: The alleged custom could not be judicially noticed on the authority of the Digest alone and required proof in the case; customs, whether described as general or otherwise, ordinarily require proof unless repeated recognition by courts entitles them to judicial notice.

rule.if: inheritance_custom_dispute and non_ancestral_property and conflicting_court_decisions and not repeated_court_recognition

predicates.inheritance_custom_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property under an asserted customary rule of inheritance.
predicates.non_ancestral_property: The disputed property is not ancestral property of the deceased owner.
predicates.conflicting_court_decisions: Earlier courts have reached conflicting conclusions about whether the asserted custom exists.
predicates.repeated_court_recognition: Courts have repeatedly recognised the asserted custom as a rule of law.

members.legal_issue: A party claiming succession under a custom that permits a Gurbhai to succeed without appointment must prove that institution-specific custom with adequate evidence.
material_facts: The claimant pleaded that a Gurbhai could succeed to the Dera's headship without appointment by the Bhekh or fraternity.
The evidence consisted of witness statements describing a general practice and referring to examples without sufficient particulars.
The evidence did not establish whether the fraternity had recognized, appointed, or confirmed the successors in the examples cited.
The claimant had not been appointed by the Bhekh or fraternity.
members.legal_principle: A party asserting a usage or custom as the basis for succession to a religious office must establish it affirmatively by proper legal evidence. The Court applied the principle stated in Rattigan's Digest of Customary Law that each Punjab religious institution is regulated by its own custom and practice, and referred to Jiwan Das v. Hira Das, A.I.R. 1937 Lah. 311, and Sital Das v. Sant Ram, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 606.
members.conclusion: The claimant did not establish the alleged custom that a Gurbhai could succeed without appointment by the Bhekh or fraternity.

rule.if: religious_headship_succession_claim and institution_specific_custom_is_asserted and evidence_lacks_particulars and evidence_does_not_show_whether_fraternity_confirmed_precedent_successors

predicates.religious_headship_succession_claim: A claimant seeks succession to the headship of a religious institution.
predicates.institution_specific_custom_is_asserted: The claimant asserts a custom of the institution as the basis for succession.
predicates.evidence_lacks_particulars: The evidence describing the alleged custom or its examples lacks sufficient particulars.
predicates.evidence_does_not_show_whether_fraternit: The evidence does not establish whether the fraternity recognized, appointed, or confirmed the alleged precedent successors.
predicates.asserted_institutional_custom_is_not_pro: The evidence is insufficient to establish the asserted custom of the institution.

members.legal_issue: A party asserting a custom that differs from Hindu law must prove the custom before it governs succession.
material_facts: The parties were Hindus in Punjab and the claim concerned succession.
The claimant relied on a customary rule said to differ from Hindu law.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872 makes Hindu law the initial rule for Hindus, subject to an applicable custom. The burden to establish a custom rests on the party asserting it, as stated in Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh, approved in Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero and followed in Ujagar Singh v. Mst. Jeo.
members.conclusion: Hindu law applies in the first instance, and a party asserting a different custom must prove both that the custom applies and what its terms are. The proof required may be less for a general, well-recognised custom than for a special custom.

predicates.punjab_inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns inheritance among parties governed by the law applicable in Punjab.
predicates.custom_claimed_to_displace_personal_law: A party relies on a customary rule that differs from the otherwise applicable personal law.

members.legal_issue: A sister may establish a local custom entitling her to inherit her brother's non-ancestral property ahead of collaterals through relevant instances of such succession, while entries that concern only ancestral property do not prove a contrary rule for non-ancestral property.
material_facts: The parties belonged to the same agriculturist Jat sub-caste and village, and the property was not ancestral.
The sister relied on settlement records showing sisters or sisters' sons succeeding to property in the village despite the presence of collaterals.

The collateral relied on Riwaji-i-am entries that did not show that their answers concerned non-ancestral property; the recorded instances did not establish exclusion of a sister from non-ancestral property in the presence of collaterals.
The High Court accepted the sister's evidence, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disagree.
members.legal_principle: The party relying on a custom must prove it. Riwaji-i-am entries are ordinarily treated as referring to succession to ancestral property unless the entry or its context shows otherwise. The Court relied on the rule stated in Mst. Hurmate v. Hoshiaru concerning the scope of such entries, and assessed the local settlement records as evidence of the custom asserted for non-ancestral property.
members.conclusion: The sister proved a custom entitling her to succeed in preference to the collateral relatives.

rule.if: inheritance_custom_dispute and non_ancestral_property and local_sister_succession_instances and contrary_entries_not_shown_to_cover_non_ancestral_property

predicates.inheritance_custom_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property under asserted customary rules of inheritance.
predicates.non_ancestral_property: The disputed property is not ancestral property of the deceased owner.
predicates.local_sister_succession_instances: Records from the relevant community or locality show sisters or their descendants succeeding to property despite the presence of collaterals.
predicates.contrary_entries_not_shown_to_cover_non_: Entries relied on to exclude sisters are not shown by their wording or context to address succession to non-ancestral property.

members.legal_issue: Under the customary law governing the community, a daughter is preferred to collaterals in succession to non-ancestral property.
material_facts: The dispute concerned property inherited by a widow from her husband, part of which was found to be non-ancestral.

The parties relied on a customary-law compilation stating that a daughter is preferred to collaterals in respect of her father's acquired property, and on a settlement record stating generally that daughters did not succeed under any circumstances.
The settlement record did not distinguish ancestral from non-ancestral property, and the Court found no clear indication that the question or answer covered non-ancestral property.
The oral evidence was insufficient to establish a custom preferring collaterals to daughters for non-ancestral property.
members.legal_principle: Under paragraph 23 of Rattigan's Digest of Customary Law, daughters are preferred to collaterals in succession to acquired property. Under section 35 of the Evidence Act, entries in a Riwaj-i-am are relevant and ordinarily carry a presumption of correctness; that presumption is weak where the entry adversely affects females who had no opportunity to appear, as explained in Mt. Subhani v. Nawab. A general question and answer in a Riwaj-i-am ordinarily relates to ancestral property unless there is a clear indication otherwise. The Court approved Mt. Hurmate v. Hoshiaru and disapproved Mohinder Singh v. Kher Singh; earlier decisions relying on the contrary interpretation of the entry did not establish the custom.
members.conclusion: The daughter is preferred to collaterals in succession to the non-ancestral property; the settlement-record entry did not establish a contrary custom for that property.

rule.if: customary_succession_dispute and property_is_non_ancestral and settlement_question_is_general and no_clear_indication_of_non_ancestral_property and no_independent_proof_of_collateral_preference

predicates.customary_succession_dispute: The case concerns succession under a community's customary law.
predicates.property_is_non_ancestral: The property in dispute was not ancestral property.
predicates.settlement_question_is_general: The recorded customary-law question and answer did not distinguish between ancestral and non-ancestral property.
predicates.no_clear_indication_of_non_ancestral_pro: The recorded question and answer did not clearly show that they addressed non-ancestral property.
predicates.no_independent_proof_of_collateral_prefe: Evidence apart from the general settlement entry did not establish that collaterals were preferred to daughters for non-ancestral property.

members.legal_issue: When neither party establishes a custom governing succession, the parties' personal law supplies the rule of decision even if the claimant pleaded custom, and under the applicable Hindu law a sister inherits ahead of collaterals.
material_facts: The sister pleaded a customary basis for her claim, but the Court held that her claim could also succeed under the parties' personal law if her custom were not established.
The collateral's alleged custom preferring collaterals was not proved.
The parties were Sikhs to whom Hindu law applied, and the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, made a sister an heir ahead of collaterals.
The collateral did not dispute that the sister would take under Hindu law if that law applied.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, 1872, makes applicable custom the first rule of decision in succession matters and, where no applicable custom is established, the parties' personal law. The Court relied on Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh, whose approach was approved in Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero, and on Mst. Fatima Bibi v. Shah Nawaz for allowing a claimant who pleaded custom to rely on personal law when custom was not established. Under the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, a sister was entitled ahead of collaterals.
members.conclusion: Even if the sister had not proved her custom, she was entitled to succeed under the parties' Hindu personal law because the collateral had not proved a custom defeating that entitlement.

rule.if: succession_dispute and hindu_personal_law_applies and sister_claims_against_collateral and opponent_custom_not_proved

predicates.succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns who inherits property from a deceased person.
predicates.hindu_personal_law_applies: The parties are governed by Hindu personal law for succession.
predicates.sister_claims_against_collateral: A sister claims the deceased person's property against a collateral relative.
predicates.opponent_custom_not_proved: The opposing party has not proved a custom that would displace the personal-law succession rule.

members.legal_issue: Where a custom excluding sisters and their sons from non-ancestral property is not established, succession to that property is governed by personal law, under which the sister takes in preference to the collateral.
material_facts: The deceased's sister and the son of another sister claimed the estate in preference to the deceased's fourth-degree collateral.
The relevant customary answer stated that sisters or their sons did not succeed, but it applied to ancestral property.
The courts found the property non-ancestral and found no evidence establishing a custom excluding sisters and their sons from non-ancestral property.
The courts below applied personal law in allowing the claim.
members.legal_principle: Customary answers of the kind recorded in the Riwaj-i-am apply to ancestral property; no custom excluding sisters from non-ancestral property was established here. Paragraph 24 of Rattigan's Digest, which states that sisters are excluded from inheritance to non-ancestral property, is too widely stated. The Court relied on Ujagar Singh v. Mst. Jeo, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 781, and Waryam Singh v. Smt. Sukhi, Civil Appeal No. 452 of 1961, decided April 23, 1963. In the absence of an applicable proved custom, personal law governed and preferred the sister to the collateral.
members.conclusion: The courts below correctly applied personal law, and the sister and her sister's son were entitled to succeed in preference to the collateral.

predicates.inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns competing claims to inherit a deceased person's property.
predicates.property_is_non_ancestral: The property at issue is non-ancestral.
predicates.customary_exclusion_not_proved: No applicable custom excluding the sister from succession to the non-ancestral property is established.

members.legal_issue: The Part II acquisition procedure applies to land acquired for a public purpose when compensation is paid wholly or partly from public funds, even if a private company participates in the project.
material_facts: The state-owned corporation was the nodal agency for the project and was to pay the entire compensation for the acquired land.
A private company participated in implementing the project through a joint venture with the state-owned corporation.
The acquisition was undertaken for the State’s public infrastructure project, rather than as an acquisition funded entirely by a private company for that company alone.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 6 permit acquisition for a public purpose or for a company. Under the second proviso to Section 6, compensation for a public-purpose acquisition must be paid wholly or partly from public revenues or an applicable public fund; Explanation 2 treats compensation paid from a corporation owned or controlled by the State as paid from public revenues. Part VII, including Sections 39 to 41, applies where land is acquired for a company and the cost is borne entirely by that company. The Court relied on Pandit Jhandulal v. State of Punjab, R.L. Arora v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Pratibha Nema v. State of Madhya Pradesh and Devinder Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The acquisition could proceed under Part II; the procedure for acquisition for a company under Part VII was not required.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_public_purpose: The land is acquired for a purpose serving the public rather than solely for a private company’s benefit.
predicates.compensation_is_paid_wholly_or_partly_fr: The compensation is paid wholly or partly from public revenues or by a government-owned or government-controlled corporation.

members.legal_issue: The company-acquisition procedure applies when the company bears the entire acquisition cost, while an acquisition primarily for a company may proceed as a public-purpose acquisition if acquisition costs are paid wholly or partly from public funds.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a company, and the company was to pay the entire compensation.
The government did not claim that any part of the compensation would be paid from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6(1), 39 and Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, distinguish company acquisitions from public-purpose acquisitions for which compensation is paid wholly or partly from public funds. The Court relied on Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab for the proposition that a company-related acquisition with public funding may proceed as a public-purpose acquisition without the Part VII procedure.
members.conclusion: Because the company was to pay the entire compensation, the company-acquisition procedure applied and its conditions had to be satisfied.

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government acquired land for the benefit or use of a company.
predicates.company_pays_entire_compensation: The company was to bear all compensation for the acquired land, with no contribution from public funds.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition for a company need not proceed under the statutory provisions governing company acquisitions when the State contributes toward the acquisition cost.
material_facts: The acquisition benefited a company.
The acquisition was made at public expense, and the State contributed toward its cost.
The pleadings did not permit the challengers to contend that the State had made no contribution.
members.legal_principle: Where the State contributes toward the cost of acquisition, it is not necessary to proceed under Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court relied on Smt. Somavanti v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: It was not necessary to conduct the acquisition under Part VII of the Act.

predicates.appeal_challenging_land_acquisition: A party appealed a decision in a proceeding challenging a land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_benefits_company: The acquisition was for the benefit of a company.
predicates.state_contributed_to_acquisition_cost: The State contributed toward the cost of acquiring the land.

members.legal_issue: The procedure for acquisition for a company under the company-acquisition provisions is unnecessary when public funds bear part of the acquisition cost, but applies when the company bears the entire cost.
material_facts: The land was acquired for the benefit of a cooperative society that qualified as a company under the acquisition statute.
The government housing scheme provided for public funds to contribute to the cost of the land and structures through subsidies and loans.
The society or its members were to provide the remaining contribution.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 6 and 39–41 of the Land Acquisition Act, read with Part VII, an acquisition for a company alone requires compliance with the company-acquisition procedure. An acquisition for a public purpose may be made where the cost is borne wholly or partly from public funds; an acquisition for a company for a public purpose is therefore outside that procedure when public funds contribute to its cost. The Court relied on Babu Barkaya Thakur v. State of Bombay concerning the distinction between public-purpose acquisitions and acquisitions for companies.
members.conclusion: Because public funds were to bear part of the compensation cost, the acquisition was not for the company alone and compliance with the company-acquisition procedure was unnecessary.

predicates.acquisition_for_company: The land was acquired for the benefit of a company or an entity treated as a company for acquisition purposes.
predicates.public_funds_cover_part_of_cost: Public funds were to bear some part of the cost of acquiring the land.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition sought by a non-government company and funded by that company must follow the statutory procedure for company acquisitions; a later nominal contribution by the State does not convert it into an acquisition for a public purpose under the ordinary procedure.
material_facts: The company sought acquisition of land for its own manufacturing project and was not a Government company.
The agreement required the company to pay the compensation and deposit sums demanded for the acquisition.
The State’s nominal contribution was made after the landowners had filed their court challenges, and the agreement did not provide for a State contribution.
The acquisition declaration described the purpose as public, while the acquisition was undertaken at the company’s request.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(e) and 3(f), the second proviso to Section 6, and Parts II and VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the source of the acquisition cost distinguishes the two routes: an acquisition for a company funded entirely by the company is subject to Part VII, while a public contribution may support the Part II route. A declaration must identify the acquisition as being either for a public purpose or for a company, not both. The Court relied on Pratibha Nema v. State of M.P., Somawanti v. State of Punjab, Shyam Behari v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Srinivasa Cooperative House Building Society Ltd. v. Madam Gurumurthy Sastry.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was governed by the company-acquisition procedure, and the State could not rely on its belated nominal contribution to treat it as an acquisition under the ordinary public-purpose procedure.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landowners challenged a compulsory land acquisition in court.
predicates.acquisition_requested_by_non_government_: A company that was not a Government company asked the State to acquire land for its own project.
predicates.company_bears_acquisition_cost: The agreement placed the acquisition compensation and related deposits on the company.
predicates.state_contribution_not_part_of_original_: The State’s nominal contribution was not part of the arrangement when the agreement was made and was made only after the acquisition was challenged.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of land for an integrated public infrastructure project implemented with private-sector participation can be for a public purpose even when a private company benefits from the project.
material_facts: The State adopted a policy to develop an integrated business, tourism and infrastructure project intended to promote the State’s economic and social development.
A state-owned corporation acted as the project’s nodal agency, and the project was to be implemented through a joint venture with a private company.
The project was presented as generating employment, revenues and wider economic opportunities, and the state-owned corporation was to pay the compensation for the acquired land.
members.legal_principle: The inclusive definition of “public purpose” in Section 3(f), read with Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is broad and can encompass a project that benefits the public even if private interests also benefit. Public ownership or direct public use of every part of a project is not essential. The Court relied, among other authorities, on Somawanti v. State of Punjab, State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy, Pratibha Nema v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organisation, Berman v. Parker and Kelo v. City of New London.
members.conclusion: The acquisition served a public purpose; private-sector participation and benefit to the private company did not make the acquisition invalid.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and state_instrumentality_leads_project and project_serves_wider_public_interests and private_sector_participates

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges the compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.state_instrumentality_leads_project: A government instrumentality leads or coordinates the project for which the land is acquired.
predicates.project_serves_wider_public_interests: The project is intended to produce benefits for the public beyond the interests of a particular private party.
predicates.private_sector_participates: A private company participates in or benefits from implementation of the project.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition for an integrated public infrastructure project implemented through a private concessionaire is for a public purpose rather than an acquisition for a company when the project assets do not vest permanently in the concessionaire.
material_facts: The State conceived an integrated project comprising an expressway and developed land parcels intended to support industrial, commercial, residential, institutional and recreational development.
The project was conceived before the concessionaire existed, and a transparent tender process selected the concessionaire to implement it on a build-operate-transfer basis.
The acquired land and project assets were to revert to the public acquiring body or the State after the relevant operating or lease periods; the concessionaire did not receive permanent ownership.
The concession agreement provided for payment related to acquisition costs, but the funds passed through the development authority, which made the compensation payments.
The expressway, interchanges and developed land parcels were found to be complementary parts of one planned development project serving the public.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3(f) of the Land Acquisition Act, an acquisition serving a public purpose may be undertaken under Part II even where a private concessionaire implements the project. Sections 39–41 and Part VII apply to acquisitions for companies in the circumstances specified there, including the contemplated transfer of acquired land to the company; a build-operate-transfer arrangement in which the public body retains or ultimately receives the assets is not, merely because a company implements the project or contributes funds, an acquisition for that company. The Court relied on State of Karnataka v. All India Manufacturers Organization, Sooraram Pratap Reddy v. District Collector, Ranga Reddy District, Pratibha Nema v. State of M.P. and Naihati Municipality v. Chinmoyee Mukherjee; it distinguished Devinder Singh v. State of Punjab and also discussed Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, Somavanti v. State of Punjab and Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was for a public purpose, was not an acquisition for the private company, and was not a colourable exercise of power; the procedure applicable to acquisitions for companies under Part VII did not apply.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_appeal and integrated_public_infrastructure_project and private_party_implements_project and (assets_revert_to_public_body or project_conceived_independently_of_concessionaire)

predicates.acquisition_challenge_appeal: The case is an appeal challenging an acquisition of land for a public project.
predicates.integrated_public_infrastructure_project: The acquiring public body planned connected infrastructure and development components as parts of a single project serving public needs.
predicates.private_party_implements_project: The public body selected a private party to implement or operate the project rather than acquiring the land solely for that party's own undertaking.
predicates.assets_revert_to_public_body: The project assets or acquired land are to return to the public acquiring body or the State rather than vest permanently in the private implementer.
predicates.project_conceived_independently_of_conce: The public project was conceived before the selected private implementer existed or was selected.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition under a supplementary scheme that advances a public town-expansion and industrial-development scheme is for an authorized public purpose even when land is allotted to a private industrial concern for development.
material_facts: The original scheme sought industrial development and relief of congestion by encouraging movement from crowded areas.
The supplementary scheme acquired additional land because the area provided under the original scheme was inadequate for the industrial concern's requirements.
The Trust retained general supervision and control, and the concern was to develop the land subject to town-planning controls.
members.legal_principle: Sections 24(h) and 32 of the United Provinces Town Improvement Act, 1908, permit a town-expansion scheme that provides for industrial development and residence for employees and others. A supplementary scheme that effectuates the public purpose of the original scheme is not invalid merely because land is to be allotted to a private concern for development under the Trust's control. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this issue.
members.conclusion: The original and supplementary schemes were one composite scheme serving industrial development and relief of congestion; the acquisition was not a device to secure private gain and was for the purposes of the Act.

rule.if: challenge_to_acquisition_scheme and supplementary_scheme_advances_original_public_plan and trust_retains_development_control and not acquisition solely_for_private_gain

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_scheme: The proceeding challenged the validity of an acquisition made under a supplementary scheme.
predicates.supplementary_scheme_advances_original_p: The supplementary scheme provided additional land to further the public objectives of an existing development scheme.
predicates.trust_retains_development_control: The public body retained general supervision and control over development of the land.
predicates.acquisition solely_for_private_gain: The land was acquired solely to transfer it to a private concern for that concern's private gain.
predicates.acquisition_serves_authorized_public_pur: The acquisition serves an authorized public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree concerning possession and a lease does not bar a later suit on title when the parties did not compromise the title issue.
material_facts: An earlier suit sought a declaration that the property was wakf property and sought possession.
The parties compromised the earlier suit on the lessee’s continued occupation, rent, and eventual surrender of possession.
Neither the compromise nor the decree determined or compromised title to the property.
members.legal_principle: A consent or compromise decree is not, strictly, a decision that has been heard and finally decided for Section 11 CPC, but it may create an estoppel by conduct according to its terms. Pulavarthi Venkata Subba Rao v. Valluri Jagannadha Rao and Sunderabai v. Devaji Shankar Deshpande support that distinction. Order 23 Rule 3A CPC bars a suit challenging a compromise decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful; it does not bar a later suit that raises an issue the compromise did not resolve.
members.conclusion: The compromise decree did not bar the later suit on title by res judicata or estoppel by conduct; the provision barring a suit to challenge an unlawful compromise decree did not apply.

rule.if: civil_suit_after_compromise_decree and prior_decree_was_based_on_compromise and compromise_resolved_only_possession_or_lease and later_suit_raises_title

predicates.civil_suit_after_compromise_decree: A civil suit concerning property was brought after an earlier suit ended in a compromise decree.
predicates.prior_decree_was_based_on_compromise: The earlier decree recorded the parties’ compromise rather than an adjudication after contest.
predicates.compromise_resolved_only_possession_or_l: The compromise addressed possession or leasing arrangements but did not resolve ownership or title.
predicates.later_suit_raises_title: The later suit asks the court to determine title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A consent decree does not operate as res judicata on a matter that the court did not adjudicate.
material_facts: An earlier suit sought recognition of a right to exhibit films under an agreement.
The earlier suit ended in a compromise decree recording the parties’ agreement; the court did not adjudicate whether the agreement created a lease.
A later suit raised the nature of the rights created by the agreement.
members.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a matter operates as res judicata only if it has been adjudicated by the court. A consent decree is a record of a contract between the parties to which the court’s seal is added, not an adjudication of the matter in contest.
members.conclusion: The consent decree did not operate as res judicata on whether the agreement created a lease.

predicates.later_civil_suit_contests_prior_matter: A party brings a later civil suit that contests a matter raised in an earlier suit.
predicates.earlier_suit_ended_by_consent_decree: The earlier suit ended in a decree recording the parties’ compromise.
predicates.prior_matter_not_adjudicated_by_court: The court did not adjudicate the matter in contest in the earlier suit.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree does not create res judicata on an issue that the court did not decide.
material_facts: The debtors had previously sought scaling down in the original suit, but the suit ended in a compromise decree.
The court accepted the parties' agreement and did not decide whether the debtors qualified for scaling down.
The debtors later raised the issue in an application under the amended law.
members.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, res judicata requires a matter to have been heard and finally decided by a court; constructive res judicata likewise rests on a prior judicial decision. A compromise decree records the parties' agreement rather than a decision by the court. The court also recognized that the amended law conferred new rights to seek scaling down, subject to the terms of that law.
members.conclusion: The compromise decree did not operate as statutory or constructive res judicata and did not prevent the debtors from raising the issue again.

predicates.later_debt_scaling_proceeding: A later proceeding seeks debt scaling after an earlier decree was made.
predicates.earlier_compromise_decree: The earlier decree embodied an agreement accepted by the court.
predicates.earlier_judicial_determination_of_the_is: The court in the earlier proceeding actually decided the issue later raised.

members.legal_issue: An earlier order requiring an authority to hear an exemption claim and decide it on its merits does not bind the parties on substantive issues that the earlier court did not determine.
material_facts: In earlier proceedings, the court directed the Trust to give the owners a full opportunity to be heard and then decide their exemption claim on its merits.
The earlier court did not decide the disputed substantive questions concerning the owners’ entitlement to exemption.
The Trust later heard and rejected the owners’ application, and the owners relied on the earlier order in challenging that decision.
members.legal_principle: An order directing a hearing and a decision on the merits does not constitute a considered decision on substantive issues that were left open. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The earlier order did not determine or bind the parties on the substantive issues raised in the later proceedings.

predicates.exemption_challenge_proceeding: A landowner challenges the rejection of a request for exemption from acquisition.
predicates.prior_order_directed_hearing_only: An earlier order required the authority to hear the claimant and decide the claim on its merits.
predicates.no_substantive_issue_decided: The earlier court did not decide the substantive entitlement now disputed.

members.legal_issue: An earlier order that expressly leaves the merits undecided does not establish a precedent on the merits of the same disputed issue.
material_facts: The applicants relied on an earlier appellate order that had allowed construction subject to specified restrictions.
That order expressly stated that it expressed no opinion on the parties’ contentions or the questions decided by the High Court and addressed the disposition of the earlier parties’ proceedings.
The applicants invoked that order as support for their own claims.
members.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Shoriar Baharam Irani & Ors. v. Pune Cantonment Board & Ors., Civil Appeal No. 2184 of 1987, order dated 23 February 1990, because that order expressly disclaimed any opinion on the merits or the questions decided by the High Court.
members.conclusion: The earlier order was not a precedent on the disputed questions and did not support the applicants’ claims.

predicates.building_restriction_dispute: The proceeding concerns the merits of a dispute over building restrictions.
predicates.earlier_order_expressly_reserved_merits: An earlier order expressly stated that it did not decide the merits of the relevant contentions or issues.
predicates.earlier_order_limited_to_its_parties: The earlier order disposed of the proceedings of the parties before it without determining the issue for other cases.

members.legal_issue: A consent order expressly reserved from precedential use, or made without argument or consideration of the point later raised, does not bind a later court as precedent on that point.
material_facts: The earlier court directed rehabilitation by constructing stalls after counsel for the parties requested a direction and undertook to comply.
The earlier court expressly stated that its direction was not to be treated as a precedent.
The earlier order did not address the statutory provisions governing removal of public-way encroachments or decide whether an alternative site had to be provided.
The High Court relied on that order in directing relief for another pavement occupant.
members.legal_principle: Only the ratio decidendi of a case is binding; statements outside the ratio are obiter dicta. A consent order does not adjudicate the parties’ rights or lay down a principle. A decision made without argument or consideration of a point is not authority on that point, and a decision given in ignorance of a relevant statute may be per incuriam. The Court referred to Salmond on Jurisprudence, Gerard v. Worth of Paris Ltd. and Lancaster Motor Co. (London) Ltd. v. Bremith Ltd.
members.conclusion: The earlier consent order was not a binding precedent on whether an alternative site had to be provided, and the High Court was not bound to follow it.

predicates.later_court_is_asked_to_follow_prior_ord: A court in a later proceeding is asked to treat an earlier judicial order as controlling authority.
predicates.prior_order_was_by_consent_and_disclaime: The earlier order was made by consent and expressly stated not to be treated as a precedent.
predicates.relevant_legal_point_was_not_argued_or_c: The earlier court did not hear argument on or consider the legal point for which the order is later cited.

members.legal_issue: Observations in an earlier decision about acquisition steps are not binding precedent on an issue that the earlier case did not decide.
material_facts: The earlier case concerned when the period following a landowner’s notice began to run, including whether it began only after the owner supplied requested information.
The earlier case did not require the Court to decide what steps an authority had to take to commence acquisition after receiving a notice seeking release of the land.
The observations in that decision linking acquisition steps to steps contemplated by the relevant acquisition provision were not necessary to resolve the earlier case.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 141 of the Constitution, the binding part of a decision is its ratio decidendi: the principle applied to the material facts to decide the issue before the Court. Observations on an issue not requiring decision are obiter and do not become binding merely because they appear in a judgment. The Court relied on Quinn v. Leathem, 1901 AC 495; State of Orissa v. Sudhansu Sekhar Misra, (1968) 2 SCR 154; Additional District Magistrate, Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla, (1976) 2 SCC 521; Union of India v. Dhanwanti Devi, (1996) 6 SCC 44; Director of Settlements, A.P. v. M.R. Apparao, (2002) 4 SCC 638; and Shin-Etsu Chemical Co. Ltd. v. Aksh Optifibre Ltd., (2005) 7 SCC 234.
members.conclusion: The earlier observations about what constitutes steps for acquisition after service of a release notice were not part of the ratio decidendi and did not bind the Court in deciding that issue.

predicates.precedent_interpretation_case: The court is deciding whether observations in an earlier judicial decision bind it on a legal issue.
predicates.earlier_case_did_not_require_deciding_th: The issue now before the court was not necessary to resolve the earlier case.
predicates.earlier_observations_were_not_necessary_: The earlier court’s observations on that issue did not form a necessary basis for its result.

members.legal_issue: A tenant does not use residential premises for a different purpose merely by taking paying guests into a spare room while continuing to reside there with family and using the premises residentially.
material_facts: The premises were let for residential use.
The tenant continued to reside there with family members.
The tenant took one or two paying guests at a time into a spare room and charged an amount that included food.
The tenant did not carry on a business in the premises, which continued to be used for residential purposes by the tenant, family, and guests.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(h) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act provides a ground for eviction where premises are used for a purpose different from the purpose for which they were let. On these facts, taking paying guests while continuing residential occupation did not change the purpose of use.
members.conclusion: The premises continued to be used for a residential purpose, so the eviction decree on the different-purpose ground could not stand.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_for_different_use and premises_let_for_residential_use and tenant_and_family_continued_residing and paying_guests_stayed_in_spare_room and no_business_carried_on

predicates.eviction_proceeding_for_different_use: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant used the premises for a purpose different from the letting purpose.
predicates.premises_let_for_residential_use: The premises were let to the tenant for residential use.
predicates.tenant_and_family_continued_residing: The tenant continued to live in the premises with family members.
predicates.paying_guests_stayed_in_spare_room: The tenant accommodated paying guests in a spare room while continuing to occupy the premises.
predicates.no_business_carried_on: The tenant did not conduct a business in the premises.

members.legal_issue: A temporary secondary commercial activity carried on alongside the business for which premises were leased does not amount to an actionable change of user when it does not prejudice the landlord’s interest.
material_facts: The premises were leased for a cycle and rickshaw repair business.
The tenant continued the repair business while also selling televisions for about seven months, then stopped selling them because the business was not viable.
The lease did not expressly prohibit the tenant from conducting any business other than cycle or rickshaw repairs.
The tenant had not obtained the landlord’s consent to start selling televisions.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the premises had been put to a different use; the eviction order was challenged by the tenant.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, restricts a tenant’s use of leased premises to protect the landlord’s interests. It is akin to Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which prohibits use for a purpose other than that for which the property was leased. The concept of injury to the premises underlying Section 108(o) informs the statutory eviction ground: ordinarily, a small change in use is not actionable if the landlord’s interest is not prejudiced. Applying Mohan Lal v. Jai Bhagwan, the Court held that the temporary additional business here did not amount to a change of user; Des Raj v. Sham Lal, concerning premises used exclusively as a godown rather than as a shop, did not govern the case. The Court also referred to U Po Naing v. Burma Oil Co. and decisions of the Kerala and Bombay High Courts concerning whether a different trade injures the leased property.
members.conclusion: The temporary sale of televisions alongside the continuing repair business did not constitute a change of user that entitled the landlord to eviction. The appeal was allowed, and the eviction order was set aside.

rule.if: tenant_appeal_challenges_eviction_for_change_of_use and premises_leased_for_commercial_repair and original_repair_business_continued and secondary_business_was_temporary and landlord_interest_was_not_prejudiced

predicates.tenant_appeal_challenges_eviction_for_ch: The tenant appealed an eviction order founded on an alleged change in the use of the premises.
predicates.premises_leased_for_commercial_repair: The premises were leased for a commercial repair business.
predicates.original_repair_business_continued: The tenant continued the repair business for which the premises were leased.
predicates.secondary_business_was_temporary: The tenant carried on an additional business only temporarily alongside the original business.
predicates.landlord_interest_was_not_prejudiced: The additional business did not prejudice the landlord’s interest in the leased premises.
predicates.eviction_not_warranted_for_change_of_use: Eviction is not warranted on the ground of change of user.

members.legal_issue: Occasional use of space in commercially let premises as a resting place for the tenant, servants, or a guard does not amount to diversion of the premises to residential use when the commercial business continues and the space is not used as residential accommodation.
material_facts: The premises were let for the non-residential purpose of running a clocks and watches business, which the tenant continued to operate.
The tenant and servants used the additional space only casually as a resting place, including to accommodate a guard watching the shop’s valuables.
The additional space was not used as residential accommodation.
members.legal_principle: The court distinguished incidental, occasional use of part of commercially let premises as a resting place from using the premises for a different, residential purpose. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case in support of this principle.
members.conclusion: The occasional use did not divert the premises from commercial to residential use. The eviction decree was set aside.

rule.if: tenant_appeals_eviction_for_change_of_use and premises_let_for_business and business_continues and occasional_resting_use and no_residential_accommodation

predicates.tenant_appeals_eviction_for_change_of_us: A tenant appeals an eviction decision based on alleged use of the premises for a purpose different from the one for which they were let.
predicates.premises_let_for_business: The premises were let for a business purpose.
predicates.business_continues: The tenant continues to conduct the let business at the premises.
predicates.occasional_resting_use: The tenant, servants, or a guard use some space only occasionally as a resting place.
predicates.no_residential_accommodation: The space is not used as residential accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s incidental residential use of part of premises while continuing the small trade for which they were let does not constitute use for a different purpose where it is not a substantial change in the mode of enjoyment.
material_facts: The tenant continued to work as a cobbler in the shop while cooking and sleeping in its rear portion on working days.
The tenant went home on days when the shop was closed.
The tenant’s wife had become mentally ill, and he brought her to the premises while he worked and cared for her there.
The landlord’s predecessor knew of the residential use and had provided a sink to facilitate it.
The tenant did not stop the trade and convert the premises into a residence or a substantially different business.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(b) concerns use of a building for a purpose other than that for which it was leased. In this context, a different purpose requires a substantial change in the mode of enjoyment, not minor variation or incidental residential use alongside a continuing small trade. The provision, as welfare legislation intended to protect tenants from unreasonable eviction, is interpreted in its social setting and with a proportionate assessment of the use.
members.conclusion: The residential use was incidental to the continuing trade and did not amount to use for a different purpose under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949; the statutory ground for eviction was not made out.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_kept_trading and tenant_used_part_for_incidental_residence and landlord_knew_of_residential_use and not tenant_substantially_changed_use

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control legislation on the basis of the tenant’s use of the premises.
predicates.tenant_kept_trading: The tenant continued the trade carried on in the premises.
predicates.tenant_used_part_for_incidental_residenc: The tenant used part of the premises for residential needs while continuing the trade.
predicates.landlord_knew_of_residential_use: The landlord or the landlord’s predecessor knew that the tenant used the premises residentially.
predicates.tenant_substantially_changed_use: The tenant stopped the original trade or otherwise substantially changed the premises’ mode of use.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s use of commercial premises for an additional or different trade does not constitute use for a purpose other than that for which the premises were let when the basic purpose remains trade and the letting contains no covenant restricting the tenant to a particular trade.
material_facts: The premises were let for the purpose of carrying on a trade, and there was no lease deed or covenant prohibiting the tenant from carrying on another trade.
The tenant continued selling shoes and also began selling ready-made garments.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the additional trade was a change of purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 10(2)(ii)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, change of use must be assessed in light of the terms of the letting, any restrictive covenant, and the nature of the tenancy. Section 21 of the Act and Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act inform the inquiry. A change that makes the use alien to the purpose for which the premises were let may justify eviction, but a variation in the commodities sold does not do so where the basic activity remains trade and there is no covenant restricting other trades. The Court applied M.K. Palaniappa Chettiar v. A. Pennuswami Pillai, Mohan Lal v. Jai Bhagwan, Gurdial Batra v. Raj Kumar Jain, and Dashrath Baburao Sangale v. Kashimath Bhaskar Data; it distinguished M. Arul Jothi v. Lajja Bal because that case involved an express negative covenant, and also distinguished Ram Gopal v. Jai Narain because it concerned a change from commercial use to manufacturing.
members.conclusion: The tenant’s additional trade did not amount to use of the premises for a purpose other than that for which they were let, so eviction on this ground was not justified.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and commercial_premises_leased_for_trade and no_covenant_limiting_trade and tenant_used_premises_for_another_trade and tenant_continued_original_trade

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on the ground of change of use.
predicates.commercial_premises_leased_for_trade: The premises were let for the purpose of carrying on a trade.
predicates.no_covenant_limiting_trade: The letting contained no covenant restricting the tenant to a particular trade.
predicates.tenant_used_premises_for_another_trade: The tenant used the premises to carry on a trade in addition to or different from the trade initially carried on there.
predicates.tenant_continued_original_trade: The tenant continued the original trade while carrying on the additional or different trade.
predicates.change_of_user_eviction_unavailable: The tenant’s use does not justify eviction for change of purpose.

members.legal_issue: Changing the business conducted in premises leased for business purposes does not constitute a change of user warranting eviction when the new business is suitable for the premises and causes no damage, impairment, or nuisance.
material_facts: The tenant leased a shop under a rent note specifying an English liquor business.
After the liquor licence was not renewed, the tenant discontinued that business and began selling general merchandise in the shop.
The shop continued to be used for business, and the new business could conveniently be carried on there without impairing the shop’s utility, damaging it, or creating a nuisance.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had changed the use of the shop.
The tenant tendered the rent arrears at the first hearing; the issue decided on appeal was the alleged change of user.
members.legal_principle: Under section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, a tenant may be evicted for using premises for a purpose other than that for which they were leased. Whether a different business amounts to a different purpose must be assessed in light of the rent legislation’s purpose and the circumstances, including whether the new use impairs the premises or creates a nuisance. The rule that only allied businesses can avoid being a change of user, stated by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Sikander Lal v. Amrit Lal, must be read with reservation. Maharaj Kishan Kesar v. Milkha Singh treated an allied business as not constituting a change of user. In interpreting legislation, the meaning of an expression is to be found in the felt necessities of the time; the Court referred to Duport Steels Ltd. v. Sirs on the judicial role in interpreting legislation.
members.conclusion: The change from a liquor business to general merchandise did not constitute a change of user attracting the statutory eviction ground. The appeal was allowed and the eviction order was set aside.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and premises_leased_for_business and tenant_used_premises_for_different_business and new_business_suited_to_premises and no_impairment_or_damage and no_nuisance

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.premises_leased_for_business: The premises were leased for the purpose of carrying on a business.
predicates.tenant_used_premises_for_different_busin: The tenant conducted a business different from the one specified when the premises were leased.
predicates.new_business_suited_to_premises: The different business could conveniently be carried on in the premises.
predicates.no_impairment_or_damage: The different business did not impair the utility of or damage the premises.
predicates.no_nuisance: The tenant’s different business created no nuisance.
predicates.different_business_not_change_of_user_gr: The different business does not establish a change-of-user ground for eviction.

members.legal_issue: A categorical admission in a pleading cannot be wholly withdrawn by amending the pleading.
material_facts: The defendants repeatedly stated in an affidavit and written statement that their predecessor had separated from the family and relinquished his interest in the disputed property, and that they had no interest in it.
About twenty-five years after the written statement, the defendants sought to amend it to resile from those admissions.
The defendants had also commenced a separate suit challenging the alleged relinquishment.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a categorical admission in a pleading cannot be withdrawn by amendment, although it may be explained or clarified. Judicial admissions, admissible under Section 58 of the Evidence Act, stand on a higher footing than evidentiary admissions and can themselves found the rights of the parties. The Court relied on Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam and Gautam Sarup v. Leela Jetly, and overruled Panchdeo Narain Srivastava v. Km. Jyoti Sahay to the extent it held that an admission could be withdrawn. Modi Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co. also supports refusing an amendment that displaces the opposing party from an admission.
members.conclusion: The application to amend the written statement so as to wholly withdraw the admissions was rejected; the decision allowing that amendment was modified.

predicates.amendment_application_in_pending_suit: A party applied to amend its pleading in a pending suit.
predicates.categorical_pleading_admission: The party made a clear admission of fact in its pleading.
predicates.amendment_wholly_retracts_admission: The proposed amendment would wholly resile from, rather than explain or clarify, the admission.

members.legal_issue: An amendment to a written statement cannot withdraw an admission when doing so would displace the opposing party’s case and cause irretrievable prejudice.
material_facts: In a partition suit, the defendants’ original written statement admitted that seven listed properties were joint family properties and that the plaintiff had a share in them.
After the plaintiff sought appointment of a receiver for the admitted properties, a defendant sought to amend the written statement to withdraw the admission as to five of those properties.
Allowing the amendment would remove the basis for the plaintiff’s claim to a share in those properties, despite the possibility of a preliminary decree on the admitted position.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an amendment to a written statement cannot withdraw an admission in favour of the plaintiff if the withdrawal would displace the plaintiff’s case and cause irretrievable prejudice. Order XV Rule 1 supported the conclusion that, where the parties were not at issue on the admitted properties, the plaintiff could have sought judgment on that basis. Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co. governs; Akshaya Restaurant v. P. Anjanappa was contrary to that binding three-judge decision to the extent that it permitted such a prejudicial withdrawal and was treated as per incuriam. Basavan Jaggu Dhobi v. Sukhnandan Ramdas Chaudhary was distinguishable because the alternative plea there did not displace an admission in the plaintiff’s favour.
members.conclusion: The amendment seeking to withdraw the admission as to the five properties was not permissible, and the High Court’s order allowing that amendment was set aside.

rule.if: partition_suit and defense_admitted_claimant_share and amendment_withdraws_admission and withdrawal_would_displace_claim and withdrawal_would_irretrievably_prejudice_claimant

predicates.partition_suit: The claimant brought a civil action seeking division of jointly held property.
predicates.defense_admitted_claimant_share: The defending party’s written statement admitted that the claimant had a share in specified property.
predicates.amendment_withdraws_admission: The defending party sought to change its written statement to retract an earlier admission.
predicates.withdrawal_would_displace_claim: Retracting the admission would remove the basis of the claimant’s case concerning the property.
predicates.withdrawal_would_irretrievably_prejudice: The claimant would lose a benefit accrued from the admission, including the ability to obtain judgment on the admitted position.

members.legal_issue: A party may not amend a written statement to withdraw a categorical admission and thereby displace the opposing party’s case when the admission remains attributable to that party.
material_facts: The respondent first filed a written statement accepting the appellant’s case in its entirety, including his claim to a share under the will.
The respondent later sought to replace or amend that statement to deny the claim and the will.
The respondent’s challenge that she had not engaged the advocate or signed the first written statement was rejected after an inquiry found that she had engaged the advocate and filed the statement.
The proposed amendment would have repudiated the earlier admission, rather than merely explaining or clarifying it.
Other defendants’ dispute of the will did not alter the fact that the respondent sought to resile from her own admission.
members.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendments are considered liberally but the court must exercise its discretion judiciously. A categorical admission in a pleading is a judicial admission, admissible against its maker and capable of dispensing with proof under Section 58 of the Evidence Act; admissions may also have consequences under Order VIII Rule 5 and Order XII Rule 6 of the Code. A party cannot amend a pleading to withdraw such an admission so as to displace the opposing party’s case. An admission may, where its nature permits, be explained or clarified, and alternative pleas may be taken if they are not mutually destructive. The Court relied on Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co., Heeralal v. Kalyan Mal, Sangramsinh P. Gaekwad v. Shantadevi P. Gaekwad, Union of India v. Pramod Gupta, State of Haryana v. M.P. Mohla, and Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam. Heeralal treated Akshaya Restaurant v. P. Anjanappa as per incuriam to the extent it conflicted with the rule in Modi Spinning; the Court distinguished cases concerning explanation of an admission or amendments that did not erase it.
