members.conclusion: The amendment allowing the respondent to resile from her categorical admission could not stand. The appeal was allowed and the impugned judgment was set aside.

rule.if: written_statement_amendment_case and categorical_admission and proposed_amendment_erases_admission and admission_authorship_challenge_rejected

predicates.written_statement_amendment_case: A party seeks to amend a written statement already filed in the proceeding.
predicates.categorical_admission: The party’s written statement unequivocally accepts the opposing party’s case on the matter in dispute.
predicates.proposed_amendment_erases_admission: The proposed amendment repudiates the admission and would displace the opposing party’s case rather than merely explain or clarify the admission.
predicates.admission_authorship_challenge_rejected: The party’s claim that the admission was not made by or attributable to that party is rejected.

members.legal_issue: A plaint amendment that replaces the original case, withdraws a clear admission, and adversely affects the opposing party is not permissible.
material_facts: The plaintiff originally sought recovery of money on the basis that the sale deed had become void, relying on the obligation to restore an advantage received under a void agreement or contract.

The proposed amendment recast the plaintiff’s position to assert the sale deed as valid and to seek relief based on the defendants’ alleged unauthorized occupation of the building, including mandatory possession and injunctions.
The amendment was sought about four years after the suit was instituted and would introduce a materially different case while removing the original admission.
The trial court allowed the amendment, but the High Court set that order aside; the plaintiff appealed.
members.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 CPC gives courts discretion to allow amendments necessary to determine the real controversy, subject to just terms; after trial has commenced, its proviso also requires a finding that despite due diligence the matter could not have been raised earlier. The court must assess whether the amendment is imperative for effective adjudication, bona fide, likely to cause prejudice that cannot adequately be compensated, whether refusal would cause injustice or multiplicity of litigation, whether it fundamentally changes the nature and character of the case, and, as a general rule, whether a fresh suit on the amended claim would be time-barred. A plaint amendment that materially substitutes the cause of action or nature of the claim is treated more restrictively than an amendment to a written statement; a clear admission in a plaint cannot be displaced where doing so would prejudice the opposing party. The court relied, among other authorities, on Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Hnaung, AIR 1922 PC 249; Cropper v. Smith (1884) 29 Ch D 700; Usha Balashaheb Swami v. Kiran Appaso Swami, (2007) 5 SCC 602; Heeralal v. Kalyan Mal, (1998) 1 SCC 278; Gautam Sarup v. Leela Jetley, (2008) 7 SCC 85; Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ladha Ram & Co., (1976) 4 SCC 320; Ganesh Trading Co. v. Moji Ram, (1978) 2 SCC 91; Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar, (1974) 2 SCC 393; and B.K. Narayana Pillai v. Parameshwaram Pillai, (2000) 1 SCC 712.
members.conclusion: The amendment was properly refused. The appeal was dismissed with costs.

rule.if: plaint_amendment_appeal and amendment_changes_nature_of_claim and amendment_withdraws_clear_admission and amendment_adversely_affects_opponent

predicates.plaint_amendment_appeal: A party challenged on appeal a decision allowing an amendment to its plaint.
predicates.amendment_changes_nature_of_claim: The proposed amendment replaced the original basis and nature of the plaintiff’s claim with a materially different case and relief.
predicates.amendment_withdraws_clear_admission: The plaintiff sought to remove a clear admission made in the original plaint about the legal effect of the transaction.
predicates.amendment_adversely_affects_opponent: The proposed change would adversely affect the opposing parties’ rights by requiring them to meet the materially different case.

members.legal_issue: A litigant who abandons a position to obtain a procedural benefit cannot later take the inconsistent position after receiving that benefit.
material_facts: The licensee initially sought a declaration that its licence was irrevocable.
After the suit was returned on a jurisdictional ground, the licensee represented that it would delete that declaration and the supporting pleadings.
The suit was revived and proceeded after that representation, and the licensee later again asserted that the licence was irrevocable.
members.legal_principle: The doctrine of election and the rule against approbating and reprobating are facets of estoppel. A litigant who unequivocally chooses a position, communicates it, and obtains a benefit on that basis may be held to that choice. The Court relied on Benjamin Scarf v. Alfred George Jardine (1881–82) 7 Appeal Cases 345; Tinkler v. Hilder (1849) 4 Exch 187; Clough v. London and North Western Rail Co. [(1861–73) All ER, Reprint, 646]; Harrison v. Wells [1966 (3) All ER 524]; Kok Hoong v. Leong Cheong Kweng Mines Ltd. [1964 Appeal Cases 993]; Dwijendra Narain Roy v. Joges Chandra De [AIR 1924 Cal 600]; C. Beepathumma v. V.S. Kadambolithaya [1964 (5) SCR 836]; and M/s New Bihar Biri Leaves Co. v. State of Bihar [(1981) 1 SCC 537].
members.conclusion: The licensee could not revive its abandoned claim that the licence was irrevocable after obtaining the benefit of proceeding on the contrary position.

rule.if: civil_litigation_proceeding and litigant_communicated_clear_election and court_granted_benefit_on_that_basis and later_inconsistent_position

predicates.civil_litigation_proceeding: The dispute involves a litigant taking positions in court proceedings.
predicates.litigant_communicated_clear_election: The litigant clearly communicated a choice between inconsistent positions to the court or the opposing side.
predicates.court_granted_benefit_on_that_basis: The court allowed the proceeding or granted relief after relying on the litigant’s communicated choice.
predicates.later_inconsistent_position: The litigant later advanced a position inconsistent with the one on which the benefit was obtained.

members.legal_issue: A party may not withdraw a deliberate concession in litigation when the opposing party relied on it to its detriment and the party's later position is inconsistent with that concession.
material_facts: At the compensation reference, the government conceded that the owner was entitled to compensation based on the market value of the land on the declaration date.
Relying on the concession, the owner did not challenge the acquisition or take steps to recover the land.

The government later argued in its appeal that compensation could not be awarded because there had been no separate preliminary notice; it had remained in adverse possession of the land for more than twelve years.
members.legal_principle: A litigant cannot take inconsistent positions to the detriment of its opponent, withdraw a concession on which the opponent relied, or approbate and reprobate. The Court relied on Rama Charan Chakrabarty v. Nimai Mondal, 15 C.L.J. 58, Bigelow on Estoppel, 6th ed., p. 783, and Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd ed., vol. 15, art. 340.
members.conclusion: The government could not resile from its deliberate election and concession, and the appeal had to be considered on the footing that the owner was entitled to compensation based on the market value on the declaration date.

predicates.compensation_appeal_after_concession: An acquiring authority appealed a compensation ruling after making a concession on the compensation basis before the lower court.
predicates.authority_deliberately_conceded_compensa: The authority deliberately accepted a particular basis for calculating the owner's compensation.
predicates.owner_relied_to_detriment: The owner relied on the concession by foregoing a challenge or remedy to the owner's detriment.
predicates.authority_later_took_inconsistent_positi: The authority later advanced a position inconsistent with its concession.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline to interfere under its special-leave jurisdiction when the High Court's decision is eminently just, even if the High Court may have exceeded its revisional powers.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave against a High Court decision made in revision.
The Supreme Court considered the High Court's decision eminently just.
The Supreme Court found it unnecessary to decide whether the High Court could correct the lower appellate court's interpretation in revision.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary power, and the Court may decline to interfere where the decision under appeal is eminently just, even assuming that the lower court may have lacked the revisional power in question.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party brings an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave against a High Court decision.
predicates.high_court_decision_is_eminently_just: The Supreme Court considers the High Court's decision eminently just.
predicates.special_leave_interference_is_declined: The Supreme Court declines to interfere with the High Court's decision.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline discretionary appellate relief despite identifying legal errors when the circumstances do not warrant interference.
material_facts: The Supreme Court identified errors in the Reference Court's valuation and in the High Court's review.
The amount in dispute in each appeal was small compared with the likely cost of further litigation.
The acquiring authorities had deposited part of the awarded compensation, which the claimants had presumably withdrawn.
Remitting the matters for reconsideration would require both sides to incur substantial further litigation costs.
members.legal_principle: The Court may refuse discretionary relief even where an order is legally wrong. It relied on Article 136 of the Constitution and S.D.S. Shipping (P) Ltd. v. Jay Container Services Co. (P) Ltd. (2003) 9 SCC 439, as well as High Court of Judicature at Bombay v. Brij Mohan Gupta (2003) 2 SCC 390, N.K. Prasada v. Government of India (2004) 6 SCC 299, Inder Parkash Gupta v. State of J&K (2004) 6 SCC 786, and Board of Control for Cricket in India v. Netaji Cricket Club (2005) 4 SCC 741. The Court also noted its power under Article 142 to make appropriate orders to do complete justice.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere in its discretionary jurisdiction and dismissed the appeals despite its findings of error.

rule.if: supreme_court_discretionary_appeal and lower_court_error_found and amount_at_stake_small and further_litigation_costs_disproportionate

predicates.supreme_court_discretionary_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court invoking its discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.lower_court_error_found: The Supreme Court identifies an error in the decision under appeal.
predicates.amount_at_stake_small: The financial amount at stake is small in relation to the proceedings.
predicates.further_litigation_costs_disproportionat: Further litigation would impose costs disproportionate to the amount at stake.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court retains its discretionary power in an appeal after granting special leave and may decline to interfere despite identifying an error in the decision below.
material_facts: The appeal was being heard after special leave had been granted.
The plaintiff knew of the alleged trespass but did not promptly object or seek relief while the two rooms were being constructed.
The plaintiff delayed giving notice and filing suit, and the rooms had remained for many years.
The Court identified errors in the High Court’s treatment of the second appeal but found the circumstances did not warrant disturbing its decree.
members.legal_principle: The discretionary power under Article 136 continues after special leave is granted. It is exercised sparingly, generally where exceptional circumstances and substantial and grave injustice justify intervention; the Court may declare the law yet decline to interfere or mould relief according to the justice of the case. The Court relied on Pritam Singh v. The State, Hem Raj v. State of Ajmer, M/s Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Their Workmen, and Municipal Board, Pratapgarh v. Mahendra Singh Chawla.
members.conclusion: The Court retained its discretion under Article 136 after granting special leave and declined to interfere with the decree, notwithstanding its determination that the High Court had erred.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and known_trespass and no_prompt_objection and prolonged_delay and longstanding_structures

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal heard after special leave has been granted.
predicates.known_trespass: The claimant knew that another person had entered onto the disputed land.
predicates.no_prompt_objection: The claimant did not promptly object or seek relief while the construction was underway.
predicates.prolonged_delay: The claimant waited a substantial time before taking formal steps to challenge the occupation.
predicates.longstanding_structures: The structures had remained on the disputed land for many years.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline to interfere with a lower court’s erroneous procedural dismissal of an application when the circumstances do not warrant appellate intervention.
material_facts: The decree for specific performance had become final.
The balance consideration was deposited while a second appeal was pending.
No steps had been taken to bring the alleged default in timely payment to the High Court’s attention.
The decree-holder had been in possession of the land for a long time, and execution was midway.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its discretionary power under Article 136 of the Constitution, concluding that the circumstances did not call for interference despite the High Court’s error in dismissing the application on procedural grounds. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136, dismissed the appeal without costs, and allowed the application to lie in quietus where it had been filed.

rule.if: appeal_to_supreme_court_against_procedural_dismissal and decree_for_specific_performance_final and payment_made_during_further_appeal and alleged_default_not_brought_to_appellate_court and decree_holder_in_long_possession and execution_underway

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_against_procedur: A party appeals to the Supreme Court after a lower court has dismissed an application on procedural grounds.
predicates.decree_for_specific_performance_final: The decree granting specific performance has become final.
predicates.payment_made_during_further_appeal: The balance consideration was paid while a further appeal was pending.
predicates.alleged_default_not_brought_to_appellate: No steps were taken to bring the alleged payment default to the attention of the court hearing the further appeal.
predicates.decree_holder_in_long_possession: The decree-holder had been in possession of the property for a long time.
predicates.execution_underway: Execution of the decree had already begun and was midway.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court will not disturb a refusal to amend a pleading where the application was rejected for laches and the circumstances do not warrant appellate interference.
material_facts: The defendants applied in the High Court to amend their written statement to include additional land in the claim for repartition.
The High Court disallowed the application on the ground of laches.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with that decision at that stage.
members.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure was invoked for the amendment application. The Court declined appellate interference with the High Court’s laches-based refusal in the circumstances and at that stage of the case.
members.conclusion: The refusal to permit the amendment was left undisturbed.

predicates.appeal_challenging_refusal_to_amend_plea: A party appealed against a court’s refusal to allow an amendment to its pleading.
predicates.amendment_application_rejected_for_lache: The court rejected the amendment application because it had been made with undue delay.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_warrant_interferenc: The appellate court found no sufficient reason in the case circumstances to disturb the refusal.

members.legal_issue: An appeal may be considered as one by special leave despite an unreasoned certificate where the questions involved warrant consideration.
material_facts: The High Court granted a certificate to appeal that disclosed no reasons.
The respondents objected that the certificate should be cancelled.
The Court considered the questions raised in the appeal to warrant consideration and heard it as one by special leave.
members.legal_principle: Although the certificate was defective because it gave no reasons, the Court could hear the matter as an appeal by special leave when the questions involved warranted consideration.
members.conclusion: The Court treated the appeal as one by special leave and considered it despite the certificate’s lack of reasons.

predicates.appeal_presented_under_high_court_certif: The proceeding was presented as an appeal under a certificate granted by a High Court.
predicates.certificate_gives_no_reasons: The certificate contained no reasons for granting it.
predicates.questions_warrant_consideration: The questions raised in the appeal warranted consideration by the Court.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may consider whether to exercise its special appellate power even when an appeal is not properly certified under the discretionary certificate route.
material_facts: After holding that the certificate was invalid, the Court considered whether the case was fit for the exercise of its special powers.
One ground raised a legal question about convicting persons for unlawful-assembly offences on the basis of mere presence in the assembly.
members.legal_principle: Article 136(1) gives the Supreme Court a discretion to grant special leave to appeal. The invalidity of a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) does not prevent the Court from considering whether to exercise that separate discretion.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the matter under the certificate route but proceeded to consider the case under its special appellate power and found the legal ground concerning mere presence sufficient to do so.

predicates.appeal_certificate_is_invalid: The proceeding does not have a valid certificate for an appeal through the discretionary certificate route.
predicates.special_appeal_power_is_invoked: A party asks the Supreme Court to use its separate discretionary power to review the case.
predicates.case_raises_substantial_legal_error: The case raises a significant legal question about whether the lower court applied the law correctly.

members.legal_issue: Deemed vesting without actual taking of possession does not preserve land-ceiling proceedings after repeal becomes operative.
material_facts: The land had been treated as vested in the government after action under the statutory vesting and possession provisions.
A notice had called on the appellant to hand over possession, but the record contained no indication that the government or an authorized person had actually taken possession.
The government’s counsel accepted that actual possession had not been taken; the High Court had dismissed the petition on the basis of deemed vesting.
The repeal had become operative in the state while the proceedings concerning the land remained unresolved.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2 and 3(1)(a) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, the saving for land vested under Section 10(3) of the principal Act applies only where possession has also been taken by the government, an authorized person, or the competent authority. Mere vesting by operation of law is insufficient; proceedings do not survive repeal where possession was not taken. This accords with Ritesh Tewari v. State of Uttar Pradesh and the authorities it relies on: Pt. Madan Swaroop Shrotiya Public Charitable Trust v. State of U.P., Ghasitey Lal Sahu v. Competent Authority, Mukarram Ali Khan v. State of U.P., and Sulochana Chandrakant Galande v. Pune Municipal Transport.
members.conclusion: The proceedings concerning the land stood abated, and the appeal was allowed to that extent.

rule.if: land_ceiling_proceeding and repeal_operated and deemed_vesting and not actual_possession_taken

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The matter concerns proceedings to regulate land under a land-ceiling regime.
predicates.repeal_operated: The repeal of the land-ceiling regime became operative in the relevant state.
predicates.deemed_vesting: The land was treated as vested in the government by operation of law.
predicates.actual_possession_taken: The government, an authorized person, or a competent authority actually took possession of the land.

members.legal_issue: Where the landholder retains actual possession when repeal of the land-ceiling scheme takes effect, the government cannot rely on statutory vesting or a later transfer receipt to continue possession proceedings.
material_facts: The state adopted the repeal legislation after the land-ceiling proceedings had begun.
The Principal Secretary stated that actual possession had not been taken under the land-ceiling statute before the repeal took effect.
The landholder had not surrendered possession, and there was no proof of a lawful takeover before repeal.
A possession receipt recording transfer to a development authority was executed after repeal without notice to the landholder.
The High Court had relegated the landholder to a civil suit concerning the land.
members.legal_principle: The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999 applies where actual possession was not taken before the repeal became effective. Applying State of U.P. v. Hari Ram (2013) 4 SCC 280 and its interpretation of Sections 10(3) to 10(6) of the 1976 Act, the Court held that de jure vesting alone does not establish that the government obtained actual possession. A later administrative transfer cannot cure the absence of actual possession before repeal.
members.conclusion: The landholder was entitled to the benefit of the repeal. The government could not retain the land on the basis of statutory vesting or the later possession receipt, and the notice and subsequent proceedings were quashed.

predicates.appeal_challenges_land_ceiling_possessio: The proceeding is an appeal challenging government action to take or retain land under a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.repeal_applies_to_state: The state is subject to the repeal of the land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.actual_possession_not_taken_before_repea: The government had not obtained actual possession of the land before the repeal took effect.
predicates.later_transfer_receipt_is_only_proof_of_: The only later record of possession is an administrative receipt transferring the land to another public authority, rather than proof of possession obtained from the landholder before repeal.
predicates.land_ceiling_proceedings_are_quashed: The notice and subsequent proceedings to take or retain the land under the repealed scheme are set aside.

members.legal_issue: A pending proceeding challenging an order declaring land surplus abates after the repeal takes effect when the State has not taken possession of the land.
material_facts: An authority declared land surplus, and the challenge to that order remained pending in appeals before the Court.
The repeal had taken effect in the State before the Court decided the appeals.
The record did not indicate that the State had taken possession of the surplus land; the appellant maintained that possession remained with it, and the State filed no reply on possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999 provides that proceedings relating to an order under the principal Act that are pending when the Repeal Act commences abate. Its proviso excludes specified proceedings relating to Sections 11, 12, 13 and 14 of the principal Act to the extent they concern land whose possession has been taken by the State or an authorized person. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The proceedings abated because the record did not indicate that the State had taken possession of the surplus land.

rule.if: pending_challenge_to_surplus_order and repeal_in_force and not state_possession_taken

predicates.pending_challenge_to_surplus_order: A challenge to an order declaring land surplus remained pending before a court or other authority.
predicates.repeal_in_force: The repeal of the law governing the surplus-land order had taken effect in the relevant state.
predicates.state_possession_taken: The State or a person authorized by it had taken possession of the land.
predicates.proceeding_abates: The pending proceeding ends by abatement.

members.legal_issue: Proceedings under a repealed land-ceiling regime abate if the State had not taken possession of the land when the repeal took effect.
material_facts: The land had been declared surplus under the former land-ceiling regime.
The authorities had issued notices directing the tenure holders to surrender possession, but the record did not show that the State had taken actual physical possession.
The former regime was repealed, and the Court addressed the effect of repeal on proceedings where possession had not been taken.
members.legal_principle: Applying the repeal legislation and relying on Pt. Madan Swaroop Shrotiya Public Charitable Trust v. State of U.P., Ghasitey Lal Sahu v. Competent Authority, Mukarram Ali Khan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Smt. Sulochana Chandrakant Galande v. Pune Municipal Transport, the Court held that pending proceedings abate upon repeal where the State has not taken possession.
members.conclusion: All proceedings pending under the former regime abated automatically upon repeal if possession of the land had not been taken by the State.

predicates.pending_land_ceiling_proceeding: A proceeding concerning land ceiling remains pending when the former land-ceiling regime is repealed.
predicates.repeal_takes_effect: The repeal of the former land-ceiling regime takes effect.
predicates.state_has_not_taken_possession: The State has not taken possession of the land before the repeal takes effect.

members.legal_issue: Land not identified in the statutory excess-land proceedings and not lawfully taken into possession before repeal does not vest in the State, and its holder is entitled to retain it.
material_facts: The land at issue was omitted from the draft and final statements and from the published notices declaring excess land; those notices identified different plots.

The State relied on a handwritten corrigendum and a panchnama to claim that possession of the omitted land had been taken, but the corrigendum had not been given effect to and the record did not establish that possession had been taken.
There was no evidence that the holders voluntarily surrendered the land, were asked to deliver possession of it, or were forcibly dispossessed before repeal.
members.legal_principle: Sections 8 and 9 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 require the land to be identified through the draft and final statement process. Under Sections 10(1), 10(3), 10(5), and 10(6), deemed vesting alone does not establish de facto possession: possession must be voluntarily surrendered, delivered peacefully following notice, or taken by force after refusal or failure to comply with notice. The notice requirements in Sections 10(5) and 10(6) are mandatory. If none of those forms of possession is established before repeal, Section 4 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999 preserves the holder’s claim to the land. The Court applied State of U.P. v. Hari Ram, (2013) 4 SCC 280.
members.conclusion: The land did not vest in the State, and the holders were entitled to retain possession of it under the saving provision of the Repeal Act.

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_repeal_case: The dispute concerns a holder’s claim to land following repeal of a statutory land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.land_omitted_from_statutory_proceedings: The land claimed by the holder was not identified in the statutory proceedings that determined and notified the excess land.
predicates.lawful_possession_established_before_rep: The State established that the holder voluntarily surrendered the land, delivered it after notice, or was dispossessed after failing to comply with notice before repeal.

members.legal_issue: A donor’s reservation of lifetime use and income from immovable property does not invalidate a gift where the donor executes a registered and properly attested instrument transferring absolute ownership and the donee accepts the gift.
material_facts: The donor executed a registered gift deed attested by two witnesses in favour of the donee.
The courts below found that the donee accepted the gift, and that finding was not challenged.
The deed transferred absolute title to the donee but reserved to the donor the right to use the property and receive its income during her lifetime.
The donor’s challenges alleging fraud, misrepresentation and undue influence had been rejected by the courts below.
The appeal’s relevant contention was that the donor’s retention of use, income and possession made the gift invalid.
members.legal_principle: Sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 require a voluntary gift of existing property, acceptance during the donor’s lifetime while capable of giving, and, for immovable property, a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses; they do not require delivery of possession. Section 129 no longer saves Hindu or Buddhist rules from Chapter VII, and Section 6 permits transfer of property except as specified, with its personal-enjoyment restriction not applying merely because the donor reserves lifetime use. The Court agreed with K. Balakrishnan v. K. Kamalam, (2004) 1 SCC 581, that ownership may be gifted while possession and enjoyment are retained by the donor. Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranjivandas Maganlal Thakker, (1997) 2 SCC 255, was distinguished because the gift there was conditional, had not been accepted, and did not transfer absolute ownership. The Court also relied on the interpretation of Section 123 in Lallu Singh v. Gur Narain, AIR 1922 All. 467, and approved the relevant approach in Revappa v. Madhava Rao, AIR 1960 Mysore 97, and Tirath Singh v. Manmohan Singh, AIR 1981 Punjab and Haryana 174.
members.conclusion: The gift was valid notwithstanding the donor’s reservation of lifetime use and income and the absence of a transfer of possession; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: gift_validity_appeal and immovable_property_gift and registered_donor_signed_attested_instrument and donee_accepted_during_donor_lifetime and absolute_title_transferred and donor_reserved_lifetime_use and not possession_delivered

predicates.gift_validity_appeal: A party appealed from a decision concerning the validity of a gift of property.
predicates.immovable_property_gift: The disputed gift concerned immovable property.
predicates.registered_donor_signed_attested_instrum: The donor executed a registered instrument transferring the property and the instrument was attested by at least two witnesses.
predicates.donee_accepted_during_donor_lifetime: The donee accepted the gift while the donor was alive and capable of giving.
predicates.absolute_title_transferred: The instrument transferred absolute ownership of the property to the donee.
predicates.donor_reserved_lifetime_use: The donor reserved the right to use the property or receive its income during the donor’s lifetime.
predicates.possession_delivered: Possession of the gifted property was transferred to the donee.

members.legal_issue: A donor's retention of possession or enjoyment during the donor's lifetime does not, by itself, invalidate an otherwise completed gift.
material_facts: The Court considered the principle in a case involving a registered gift of immovable property that was accepted by the donee although the donor reserved possession and the right to receive rent during her lifetime.
The Court distinguished that situation from the deed before it, which was conditional and stated to take effect after the donor's death.
members.legal_principle: Sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 require a gift to satisfy the statutory conditions for a gift and prescribe how a gift of immovable property is effected. Relying on Reninkuntla Rajamma v. K. Sarwanamma, (2014) 9 SCC 445, the Court held that ownership may be gifted without transferring possession, provided the gift is accepted during the donor's lifetime and the other requirements are met.
members.conclusion: Retention of possession or enjoyment alone does not prevent a valid gift, provided the legal requirements for a gift are satisfied.

rule.if: civil_appeal_about_a_purported_gift and donor_reserved_lifetime_enjoyment and gift_accepted_during_donor_lifetime and gift_formalities_satisfied

predicates.civil_appeal_about_a_purported_gift: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning whether a document styled as a gift deed transferred property as a gift.
predicates.donor_reserved_lifetime_enjoyment: The donor retained possession or the right to enjoy the property during the donor's lifetime.
predicates.gift_accepted_during_donor_lifetime: The donee accepted the gift while the donor was alive and capable of making the gift.
predicates.gift_formalities_satisfied: The gift satisfies the applicable requirements for its execution and completion.
predicates.retained_enjoyment_alone_does_not_invali: A donor's retention of possession or enjoyment, by itself, does not invalidate a gift.

members.legal_issue: A conditional gift of immovable property does not become complete where acceptance is unproved and the donor retains possession and enjoyment during life, and the donor may cancel it before death while it remains incomplete.
material_facts: The donor executed a registered deed describing the transfer as conditional and limiting the donee’s rights until the donor’s death.
The deed reserved to the donor possession of the property and the right to let rooms and collect their rents during the donor’s lifetime.
The deed contained no recital of acceptance, and there was no evidence proving acceptance by the donee.
The donor executed a cancellation deed before death, stating that possession had not been handed over and that the conditional gift was cancelled.
After the cancellation, the donor executed a will in favour of the appellant and another beneficiary.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, a gift requires acceptance by or on behalf of the donee during the donor’s lifetime and, as the court explained, execution of the registered gift deed, acceptance, and delivery of the property together complete the gift. The court read the deed as a whole, harmonising its clauses to give effect to the parties’ manifested intention. Because acceptance was unproved and the donor retained possession and enjoyment under a conditional, limited transfer, the gift had not become complete and could be cancelled before the donor’s death. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The gift did not become complete during the donor’s lifetime and was ineffective and inoperative; it was duly cancelled. The appeal was allowed and the suit claiming title under the gift was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_from_title_decree and donee_acceptance_not_proved and donor_retained_lifetime_possession_and_enjoyment and gift_rights_limited_until_donor_death and donor_executed_cancellation_before_death

predicates.appeal_from_title_decree: A party appealed a decree in a suit seeking a declaration of title based on a disputed gift.
predicates.donee_acceptance_not_proved: The donee’s acceptance of the gift was not established by the deed or other evidence.
predicates.donor_retained_lifetime_possession_and_e: The donor retained possession and the right to enjoy the property during the donor’s lifetime.
predicates.gift_rights_limited_until_donor_death: The gift deed limited the donee’s rights until the donor’s death.
predicates.donor_executed_cancellation_before_death: The donor executed a deed cancelling the gift before the donor died.

members.legal_issue: A purported gift conditioned to take effect only after the donor's death is not a completed gift during the donor's lifetime, and the donor may cancel it while it remains incomplete.
material_facts: The deed stated that the gift would take effect after the appellant and her husband's deaths.
The deed was also conditional on the respondent looking after the appellant and her husband.
The appellant cancelled the deed, and the Court found that no completed gift had been made.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a gift is a transfer of existing property without consideration, accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Under Section 123, a gift of immovable property must be made by a registered, signed and attested instrument. A conditional gift becomes complete only when the conditions in the deed are complied with. The Court relied on Naramadaben Maganlal Thakker v. Pranivandas Maganlal Thakker, (1997) 2 SCC 255, concerning completion of a gift, and distinguished the valid gift in Reninkuntla Rajamma v. K. Sarwanamma, (2014) 9 SCC 445, where acceptance occurred during the donor's lifetime.
members.conclusion: There was no completed gift, and the appellant was entitled to cancel the deed.

predicates.civil_appeal_about_a_purported_gift: The proceeding is a civil appeal concerning whether a document styled as a gift deed transferred property as a gift.
predicates.deed_conditioned_to_take_effect_after_do: The deed provides that the purported gift will take effect only after the donor's death.
predicates.donor_may_cancel_incomplete_gift: The donor may cancel a purported gift that did not become complete during the donor's lifetime.

members.legal_issue: A claimed oral gift under Mohammedan law is not established unless the required elements of the gift, including delivery of possession, are proved.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that his father had orally gifted him a house occupied by tenants.
The claimant did not show how possession was delivered to him, that he collected rent, paid property-related taxes, or took steps to have the property recorded in his name.
The alleged will said to accompany the oral gift was found fabricated by the trial court.
The purchaser, by contrast, produced evidence of possession and acts of ownership, including proceedings against tenants and a change in municipal records.
members.legal_principle: A valid oral gift under Mohammedan law requires the donor’s intention to gift, the donee’s acceptance, and the donee’s taking possession; constructive possession may suffice in appropriate circumstances. The Court relied on Abdul Rahim v. Sk. Abdul Zabar (2009) 6 SCC 160.
members.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish the essential requirements of the oral gift, particularly delivery of possession, and the lower courts erred in accepting the gift claim.

predicates.property_claim_based_on_mohammedan_oral_: A claimant bases a claim to property on an oral gift said to have been made under Mohammedan law.
predicates.not_possession_delivered_or_constructive: The claimant does not establish that possession was delivered, directly or constructively, to the donee.

members.legal_issue: A gift of immovable property under Muhammadan law is incomplete unless the donor declares the gift, the donee accepts it, and possession is delivered actually or constructively to the donee.
material_facts: The alleged donor's written instrument described him as the owner in possession and did not support the claim that an earlier oral gift had been made.
The alleged donee was not shown to have lived at the property with the donor and the evidence indicated that she lived elsewhere with her husband.
No rent receipts showed that she collected rent from tenants; receipts showed the donor continued to issue them after the instrument was executed.
The property had not been mutated in her favour, and she did not possess the title deeds.
The evidence therefore did not establish either actual possession or constructive possession by the alleged donee.
members.legal_principle: Under Muhammadan law, a valid gift requires declaration by the donor, express or implied acceptance by the donee, and delivery of possession actually or constructively. Sections 149, 150 and 152 of Mulla's Principles of Mahomedan Law describe these requirements, including the need for an overt act showing transfer of possession where donor and donee reside together. Valia Peedikakkandi Katheessa Umma v. Pathakkalan Narayanath Kunhamu recognizes the importance of actual or constructive possession. Possession may be shown by control over the property, as described in section 394 of Tyabji's Muslim Law. Mahboob Sahab v. Syed Ismail and Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid also state the essential requirements of a valid gift.
members.conclusion: The alleged gift was not complete because the alleged donee had not proved actual or constructive possession. The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's judgment and dismissed the appeal, leaving the suit dismissed.

predicates.suit_concerns_validity_of_muhammadan_gif: The proceeding concerns whether an alleged gift under Muhammadan law is valid.
predicates.donee_proved_actual_or_constructive_poss: The alleged donee established actual possession or constructive control of the gifted property.

members.legal_issue: An apparently absolute testamentary gift is limited to a life interest when that construction reconciles it with the will’s provisions giving the property to others after the first beneficiary’s death.
material_facts: The will described the widow as owner of the property during her lifetime.
It also provided that two other beneficiaries would take the property after her death.
The will prohibited the widow from transferring the property by will to other heirs and separately stated that she could not sell or mortgage it during her lifetime.
members.legal_principle: A court should, so far as legally possible, give effect to every disposition in a will and harmonize its provisions. Where a gift appears absolute but a successive gift is made to take effect on the first beneficiary’s death, the first interest may be construed as a life interest to give effect to both dispositions. If repugnant provisions cannot be reconciled, the later provision may prevail. The Court relied on Ramchandra Shenoy v. Mrs. Hilda Brite.
members.conclusion: Read as a whole, the will gave the widow a life estate, not an absolute estate.

rule.if: will_construction_dispute and apparently_absolute_gift and successive_gift_after_first_beneficiary_death and restrictions_support_limited_interest

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The court must determine the extent of an interest created by a will.
predicates.apparently_absolute_gift: The will uses language that, read alone, appears to give the first beneficiary an absolute interest.
predicates.successive_gift_after_first_beneficiary_: The will gives the same property to another beneficiary after the first beneficiary dies.
predicates.restrictions_support_limited_interest: Other terms of the will restrict the first beneficiary’s dealings with the property.

members.legal_issue: A bequest to a first beneficiary is limited to a life interest when the will gives later beneficiaries an absolute interest after the first beneficiary’s lifetime and that construction gives effect to both dispositions.
material_facts: The will provided that the testatrix’s eldest daughter would enjoy the movable property after the testatrix’s death and that, after the daughter’s lifetime, her male children would enjoy it permanently and with absolute rights.
The will used similar language elsewhere to create interests limited to a beneficiary’s lifetime, including one instance without an express prohibition on alienation.

The parties agreed that the will intended to confer an absolute and permanent interest on the daughter’s male children; construing the daughter’s interest as absolute would prevent that gift from taking effect.

The dispute arose in a suit for partition and separate possession, in which the competing claims depended on whether a court-sale purchaser acquired the daughter’s entire interest or only her life interest.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 69, 72 and 73 of the Indian Succession Act, 1865, a will is read as a whole, reasonable meaning should be given to every part, and the same words ordinarily carry the same meaning throughout. Section 82 presumes that a bequest conveys the testator’s whole interest unless the will shows a restricted interest. Section 84 and its illustrations distinguish words that make later beneficiaries direct objects of an independent gift from words that merely describe the first taker’s interest; illustration (c) supports successive interests where the gift to the later beneficiaries follows the first taker’s death. A cardinal principle of will construction is to give effect, as far as legally possible, to every disposition and to avoid a construction that makes a later gift ineffective. The court noted that each will must be construed on its own terms and in the setting of its clauses, and found the cited authorities unhelpful as precedents for that task.
members.conclusion: The daughter received only a life interest, and the absolute remainder was conferred on her male children. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.will_construction_case: The dispute concerns the construction of a will that disposes of property through successive interests.
predicates.later_beneficiaries_are_direct_gift_reci: The will gives later beneficiaries an independent interest in the property, rather than merely describing the extent of the first beneficiary’s interest.
predicates.later_gift_takes_effect_after_first_take: The will provides that the later beneficiaries’ interest takes effect after the first beneficiary’s lifetime.
predicates.life_interest_preserves_both_disposition: Treating the first beneficiary’s interest as lasting only for that beneficiary’s life allows both the first gift and the later gift to take effect.

members.legal_issue: The description of a spouse as the owner of property in a will may confer only a life estate when the will as a whole shows that the testator intended the property to pass absolutely to another beneficiary after the spouse’s death.
material_facts: The testator’s will described his wife as owner of his entire estate after his death and gave her proprietary powers, but did not expressly give her the power to make transfers of all kinds.

The will expressly gave the later beneficiary the power to make transfers of all kinds after the wife’s death, and provided that the beneficiary would take absolutely if the wife died before the testator.
The testator described the beneficiary as his heir, directed that the beneficiary serve the wife, and provided that future property would pass to them on the same stated conditions.
The will recited the testator’s concern that his brother and nephew might trouble his wife and the beneficiary, and the testator did not intend his property to pass to those relatives.
The wife later made a gift and a will concerning some of the property in favour of the appellant.
members.legal_principle: A will must be construed by ascertaining intention from its words, read as a whole and in light of the circumstances, the testator’s position and family relationships; effect should, where legally possible, be given to every disposition and expression, and apparently conflicting provisions should be reconciled where possible. The word “malik” ordinarily describes an owner with full proprietary rights, including alienation, but context and surrounding circumstances may show that full rights were not intended. The Court relied on Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal; Venkata Narasimha v. Parthasarathy; Gnanambal Ammal v. T. Raju Ayyar; Raj Bajrang Bahadur Singh v. Thakurain Bakhtraj Kuer; Pearey Lal v. Rameshwar Das; Ramachandra Shenoy v. Mrs. Hilda Brite; Sasiman Chowdhurain v. Shib Narayan Chowdhury; Musammat Surajmani v. Rabi Nath Ojha; Krishna Biharilal v. Gulabchand; and Dhyan Singh v. Jugal Kishore.
members.conclusion: The will gave the wife only a life estate and gave the later beneficiary an absolute estate after her death. The wife’s gift and will in favour of the appellant therefore failed, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: will_construction_proceeding and will_gives_spouse_property_after_testator_death and will_names_later_beneficiary_after_spouse and will_gives_later_beneficiary_transfer_power_but_not_spouse and will_shows_intent_to_keep_property_from_testators_heirs

predicates.will_construction_proceeding: A court was asked to determine the effect of a testamentary instrument.
predicates.will_gives_spouse_property_after_testato: The testator’s will gives the spouse property to enjoy after the testator’s death.
predicates.will_names_later_beneficiary_after_spous: The will provides that another beneficiary is to take the property after the spouse’s death.
predicates.will_gives_later_beneficiary_transfer_po: The will expressly gives the later beneficiary power to transfer the property but does not expressly give that power to the spouse.
predicates.will_shows_intent_to_keep_property_from_: The will indicates that the testator wanted to prevent the testator’s own relatives from inheriting the property.

members.legal_issue: Irreconcilable gifts in a will are governed by the later clause, so a later direction that property pass to others on the beneficiary’s death limits the beneficiary’s interest to a life interest.
material_facts: The will first described the daughter as owner of the remaining property, but later provided that the testator’s brothers would inherit that property on her death.
The daughter’s claim to ownership arose under the same will.
members.legal_principle: Section 88 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 provides that where two clauses of gifts in a will are irreconcilable, the last clause prevails because it represents the testator’s latest intention.
members.conclusion: Read as a whole, the will conferred only a life interest on the daughter; the later clause prevailed over the inconsistent earlier description of her as owner.

predicates.testamentary_property_dispute: The dispute concerns the interest created in property by a will.
predicates.will_clauses_conflict: The will contains clauses that cannot be reconciled as to the beneficiary’s interest in the same property.
predicates.later_clause_redirects_property_on_benef: A later clause directs that the property pass to others when the beneficiary dies.

members.legal_issue: A will grants a life estate rather than an absolute estate when its provisions, read as a whole, show that the testator intended successive enjoyment by the beneficiary’s heirs and restricted alienation as a central feature of the disposition.
material_facts: The will described the initial beneficiary as an absolute owner but prohibited him and his heirs from transferring the properties.
It stated that the beneficiary’s heirs and successors were to enjoy the properties generation after generation and that the properties would return to the larger estate if that line became extinct.
The will was intended to provide for the beneficiary and his heirs and to prevent disputes between them.
members.legal_principle: The testator’s intention must be gathered from the will as a whole, without treating isolated expressions as decisive or disregarding provisions as redundant. Expressions such as “malik kamil” and “naslan bad naslan” ordinarily indicate full proprietary rights, but restrictions that are central to and consistent with the will may displace that implication. A restraint on alienation is repugnant where an absolute estate was intended, but may help show that only a limited estate was intended. The Court applied these principles to the will and referred to no earlier case on this issue.
members.conclusion: The initial beneficiary received only a life interest, not an absolute estate.

rule.if: will_construction_dispute and absolute_owner_language and heirs_generation_benefit and (transfer_restriction or reversion_on_line_extinction)

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The dispute requires the court to determine the nature of an interest created by a will.
predicates.absolute_owner_language: The will uses language describing the beneficiary as an absolute owner.
predicates.heirs_generation_benefit: The will shows that the testator intended successive generations of the beneficiary’s heirs to benefit.
predicates.transfer_restriction: The will restricts the beneficiary’s ability to transfer the property.
predicates.reversion_on_line_extinction: The will provides for the property to return to another estate if the beneficiary’s line becomes extinct.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary grant that limits a beneficiary to enjoyment during life of income from property confers a life estate when the will as a whole confirms that limited intention.
material_facts: The will gave property to each widow and stated that she could enjoy the income as owner during her lifetime.
For one widow's property, the will expressly limited her enjoyment to the income.
The will directed that an adopted son would become entitled to the properties after the widows' deaths.
Elsewhere, the will used different and more explicit language when making an absolute bequest.
members.legal_principle: A will must be construed as a whole, considering surrounding circumstances and contrasting its clauses to ascertain the testator's intention. The words describing enjoyment as owner do not confer an absolute estate when the clause limits enjoyment to income during the beneficiary's lifetime; the remainder provision and contrasting language used for an absolute bequest reinforce that limitation. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this construction.
members.conclusion: The bequests of the relevant properties to the widows conferred life estates, not absolute estates.

rule.if: will_construction_proceeding and lifetime_income_limited and (remainder_after_beneficiary_life or absolute_bequest_contrasted)

predicates.will_construction_proceeding: The dispute requires a court to determine the nature of an interest created by a will.
predicates.lifetime_income_limited: The will limits the beneficiary's enjoyment to income from the property during the beneficiary's lifetime.
predicates.remainder_after_beneficiary_life: The will provides that another person becomes entitled to the property after the beneficiary's death.
predicates.absolute_bequest_contrasted: The will uses materially different, explicit language to give an absolute estate elsewhere.

members.legal_issue: An earlier testamentary disposition of property remained effective when a later clause referred to the property in a different adoption contingency.
material_facts: The testator's will gave a daughter a life interest in the disputed property and provided that the property would pass after her death to another daughter and her children, subject to a payment to the life tenant's child.
A later clause stated that the life tenant would enjoy the property as described earlier, but did not repeat the remainder disposition.
The widow adopted a son of one of the testator's nephews, and the will contained no express alteration of the earlier disposition of the disputed property for that contingency.

The will made family provisions in its earlier paragraphs and specified modifications for the different adoption contingencies; it did not indicate that the earlier family provisions were cancelled when a nephew's son was adopted.

The trial court accepted the interpretation that the earlier remainder disposition applied, while the appellate court held that the later clause alone governed and allowed the adopted son's claim as heir.
members.legal_principle: A will must be construed as a whole to ascertain the testator's intention primarily from its language, with surrounding circumstances used as an aid to understanding that language; a court must give effect to the intention expressed and may not add to the testamentary dispositions. Under Venkata Narasimha v. Parthasarthy, the court may consider the testator's circumstances and relationships in construing the document. A presumption against intestacy may be used only where the context or surrounding circumstances justify it and there is genuine ambiguity; it does not permit plain words to be given an unnatural meaning, as stated in Re Edwards; Jones v. Jones. The court concluded that it was unnecessary to rely on that presumption here.
members.conclusion: The earlier disposition remained operative under the adoption contingency that occurred, so the property passed to the designated daughter and her children after the life tenant's death, subject to the stated payment. The appeal was allowed and the trial court's decree was restored.

rule.if: testamentary_construction_appeal and earlier_family_bequest_covers_property and later_clause_refers_to_only_part_of_bequest and no_express_change_to_remainder and will_scheme_applies_family_gifts_across_contingencies and different_adoption_contingency_occurred

predicates.testamentary_construction_appeal: A party appealed a judgment that construed a testamentary document disposing of property.
predicates.earlier_family_bequest_covers_property: The testator earlier disposed of the property by granting a life interest and designating who would take afterward.
predicates.later_clause_refers_to_only_part_of_bequ: A later clause refers to the earlier life interest without repeating the disposition of the remaining interest.
predicates.no_express_change_to_remainder: The testator made no express alteration to the earlier disposition of the remaining interest for the relevant contingency.
predicates.will_scheme_applies_family_gifts_across_: The testamentary document's structure shows that family gifts made earlier were intended to apply across the different contingencies it describes.
predicates.different_adoption_contingency_occurred: The adoption contingency that occurred differed from the one associated with the original principal disposition.

members.legal_issue: A will’s earlier disposition of property after a life interest remains effective under a later adoption contingency when the will, read as a whole, shows that the contingency provisions modify only specified gifts and do not revoke that disposition.
material_facts: The will gave a daughter a life interest in a village and provided that after her death the property would pass to another daughter and her children, subject to a payment to the life tenant’s daughter.

A later paragraph provided that the village would be enjoyed by the life tenant as stated in the earlier paragraph, but did not repeat the earlier paragraph’s disposition of the property after the life interest.
The will addressed alternative adoption contingencies and made specific changes to certain gifts while leaving the earlier disposition of the village unaltered.
The widow adopted a son of the testator’s nephew, and after the life tenant died, the adopted son claimed the village on the basis that the will left the remainder undisposed of.
members.legal_principle: The primary aim in construing a will is to ascertain the testator’s intention from the language of the document read as a whole. Surrounding circumstances and the testator’s family position may assist in interpreting the language, but a court may not add to the dispositions once the will is construed. A presumption against intestacy may assist only where there is undoubted ambiguity; it cannot displace the plain meaning of words. The Court applied the principles stated in Venkatanarasimha v. Parthasarathy (41 I.A. 51) and Re Edward; Jones v. Jones ([1906] 1 Ch. 570).
members.conclusion: The earlier paragraph applied despite the adoption of a nephew’s son. The village passed to the designated daughter after the life tenant’s death, subject to the stated payment, and the claim that it passed to the adopted son as heir was rejected.

rule.if: will_construction_dispute and integrated_contingency_scheme and earlier_clause_disposes_remainder and later_clause_repeats_only_life_interest and earlier_disposition_is_not_modified

predicates.earlier_remainder_beneficiary_takes_afte: The person designated by the earlier clause takes the property after the life tenant’s interest ends.

members.legal_issue: An amendment creating assessment liability does not authorize demands for periods before the amendment took effect when the amendment is not retrospective.
material_facts: The demands included periods both before and after the amendments that brought qualifying leased government land within the assessment scheme.
The amendments had no retrospective effect, and the State’s defence to the challenge relied on those amendments.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the amendments to Sections 2(j) and 12 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act had no retrospective effect. Therefore, they could not support demands for assessment for periods before they came into force.
members.conclusion: Demands for periods before the amendments took effect were quashed; the amendments did not authorize retrospective assessment.

predicates.demand_covers_pre_amendment_period: The demand seeks assessment for a period before the relevant amendment took effect.
predicates.liability_depends_on_nonretrospective_am: The asserted liability arises from an amendment that does not apply retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: An amendment imposing assessment liability cannot support demands for periods before the amendment took effect when the liability claim rests on that amendment.
material_facts: The demands included periods before and after the 1974 amendment took effect.
The State’s defence to the company’s challenge rested on the amendments made in 1974.
The amendments had no retrospective effect.
members.legal_principle: The amendments made by Act 28 of 1974 to the definition of owner and the scope of the Act had no retrospective effect. They could not support an assessment demand for a period before they came into force.
members.conclusion: Demands for periods before the amendment took effect were quashed.

predicates.assessment_demand_challenge: A party challenges a demand for assessment imposed on land.

predicates.demand_period_precedes_amendment: The demand covers a period before the amendment took effect.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment affecting contributions does not authorize recovery of contributions for a period before a non-retrospective takeover notification took effect.
material_facts: The takeover notification was issued after the period for which the State demanded contributions.
The notification did not operate retrospectively.
The State demanded contributions for periods preceding the notification.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6 of the Aided Schools Act, the amendments to sections 52 and 59 of the Punjab Municipal Act operated upon a qualifying resolution or takeover. Because the takeover notification was not retrospective, those amendments could not support a contribution demand for the earlier period.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the relevant statutory provisions were valid, the State could not demand contributions for the period before the notification took effect.

predicates.challenge_to_contribution_demand: A party challenges a government demand for contributions connected with schools taken over by the government.
predicates.demand_covers_pre_notification_period: The demand includes contributions for a period before the takeover notification took effect.
predicates.takeover_notification_not_retroactive: The notification taking over management does not operate retrospectively.

members.legal_issue: A municipal authority may amend a finalized assessment list after the relevant assessment year has begun and apply the amended assessment to that year when the governing scheme permits later amendments and the property was eligible but mistakenly omitted.
material_facts: A building was completed and occupied before the assessment year for which it was to be assessed.
The building was omitted from the assessment list for that year, although it ought to have been included.
After the list had been finalized, the municipal authority notified the owner of a proposed amendment, considered the owner’s objection, and added the building to the list for that year.
members.legal_principle: Sections 66 and 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, read together, permit an assessment list to be amended after finalization: section 66 makes the list subject to amendments duly made thereafter, and section 67 authorizes amendment at any time on the grounds specified there. The meaning of “at any time” depends on context. The Court considered Central Bank of India Ltd. v. Hartford Fire Insurance Co. Ltd., AIR 1965 SC 1288, and Ex parte Norris, In re Salder, 17 Q.B.D. 728, in addressing that contextual interpretation.
members.conclusion: The municipal authority was entitled to amend the assessment list after it had been finalized and to assess the building for the year to which the list applied; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.municipal_tax_assessment_challenge: An owner challenged a municipal authority’s addition of property to an assessment list for property taxation.
predicates.property_ought_to_be_listed: The property met the requirements for inclusion in the assessment list for the relevant taxation year.
predicates.property_omitted_through_mistake: The property was left out of the assessment list through a mistake.
predicates.amendment_made_after_list_finalization: The municipal authority amended the assessment list after it had been finalized.
predicates.later_amendment_authorized_without_deadl: The governing scheme allowed the municipal authority to amend the list later without requiring the amendment to occur before the assessment year began.
predicates.affected_owner_given_notice_and_hearing: The municipal authority notified the affected owner of the proposed amendment and allowed the owner to object and be heard.
predicates.later_amendment_can_support_tax_for_asse: A later amendment may support taxing the property for the assessment year covered by the list.

members.legal_issue: A municipal authority may amend a finalized property-tax assessment list after the year for which it was in force to include property that escaped assessment, with the amendment operating on the list for the year to which that list applied.
material_facts: A building was assessed to property tax for several years on the basis of rent received, but rent from a portion of its basement was alleged to have been omitted from the assessment lists.
After those lists had been finalized and the relevant years had passed, the municipal authority gave notice that it intended to amend the lists to include the omitted rent.
The High Court held that amendments could operate only prospectively, and the municipal authority appealed.
members.legal_principle: Sections 66 and 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 must be read together: the tax in an authenticated list applies to the ensuing year subject to amendments duly made afterward, and the words “at any time” permit amendment after finalization and after the list’s operative year has expired. An amendment to a list operates for the year for which that list was in force, rather than only for the year following the amendment. The power is subject to reasonableness. Section 68A, added later, expressly limits the effective date of amendments for property already included but erroneously valued or assessed; its different wording and scope support the wider operation of amendments under section 67 for property omitted altogether. Punjab National Bank v. New Delhi Municipal Committee supports amendment after finalization, while Municipal Corporation of City of Hubli v. Subha Rao Hanumanatha Rao Prayag is inapplicable because it concerned a different statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The municipal authority had power to amend the finalized lists, even after the relevant years had expired, and the amendments could correct the lists for the years to which they originally applied. That power is subject to the requirement that it be exercised within a reasonable time; the reasonableness of the timing was not at issue.

members.legal_issue: A newly enacted reassessment power does not apply retrospectively to reopen an estate-duty assessment completed before it took effect absent express or necessarily implied retroactive intent.
material_facts: The estate-duty assessment was completed before the new reassessment provision came into force.
After that provision came into force, the revenue authority issued a notice seeking to reopen the completed assessment because property was said to have escaped duty.

The former provision chiefly authorized rectification of mistakes, while the new provision addressed property escaping assessment; the Court found their powers materially different despite some overlap concerning omitted property.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 56–65 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, as amended by the Estate Duty (Amendment) Act, 1958, the former section 62 concerned rectification of mistakes, whereas the substituted section 59 concerned property escaping assessment and conferred a materially different power. Section 59 was analogous to section 34 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 and section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Retrospective operation must be expressly stated or necessarily implied; absent that, later legislation does not interfere with vested rights, and a completed assessment cannot be reopened unless the statute permits it. The Court relied on Controller of Estate Duty, West Bengal v. Smt. Ila Das and Others, [1981] 132 I.T.R. 720.
members.conclusion: The new reassessment provision was not retrospective, and reopening the completed assessment under it was unlawful.

predicates.estate_duty_reassessment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an attempt by a revenue authority to reassess estate duty.
predicates.assessment_completed_before_new_power_ef: The revenue authority completed the assessment before the new reassessment power took effect.
predicates.new_power_materially_differs_from_prior_: The new reassessment power addressed a materially different situation from the earlier power to correct assessment mistakes.
predicates.retroactive_intent_expressed_or_necessar: The legislation expressly stated, or necessarily implied, that the new power applied retrospectively.
predicates.reopening_of_completed_assessment_is_unl: The revenue authority may not reopen the completed assessment under the new power.

members.legal_issue: An amendment allowing reassessment on the basis of a court order cannot revive an assessment that had already become time-barred before the amendment took effect.
material_facts: The tax authority sought to reassess income arising from interest on compensation, relying on a court award made in land-acquisition proceedings.
The limitation period for the relevant assessment years had expired before the amendment adding court orders under other laws as a basis for reassessment took effect.
The amendment did not expressly provide that it would apply retrospectively.
members.legal_principle: Sections 149 and 150(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, read with section 150(2), do not permit a limitation period that had already expired to be revived by an amendment that is not expressly retrospective. Limitation provisions require strict construction and protect finality. The Court relied on S.S. Gadgil v. Lal and Co. (1964) 53 ITR 231, which held that an amendment cannot authorize proceedings that were already time-barred before it came into force absent express provision or clear implication.
members.conclusion: The amended provision operated prospectively and did not authorize reopening assessments that had become final because of limitation before the amendment took effect.

predicates.tax_reassessment_proceeding: The revenue authority sought to reopen a tax assessment.
predicates.amended_court_order_basis_invoked: The revenue authority relied on a court order as a basis for reopening the assessment under an amended reassessment provision.
predicates.assessment_time_barred_before_amendment: The time allowed to reassess the relevant income had expired before the amendment took effect.

members.legal_issue: A sentence for attempted murder may be reduced to the period already served while compensation is ordered for a victim who suffered serious injuries and trauma.
material_facts: The offender had been in custody for more than three years when the sentence was reconsidered.
The assault arose during a dispute over reeds and a wordy altercation.
The victim suffered grievous head injuries, was deeply comatose, underwent urgent surgery and experienced treatment-related trauma.
The offender had offered compensation, but the victim had refused that offer.
members.legal_principle: The court must exercise sentencing discretion by considering the gravity of the offence, the motive, the nature of the offence and all attendant circumstances. Section 357(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits an order for compensation. The Court relied on Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh for compensation and on State of M.P. v. Bablu Natt, Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra and Soman v. State of Kerala for sentencing discretion.
members.conclusion: The custodial sentence was reduced to the period already served, and the offender was ordered to pay compensation to the victim, with a further custodial sentence to apply in default of payment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_attempted_murder: The matter is an appeal challenging a sentence for attempted murder.
predicates.offender_has_served_substantial_custody: The offender has already served a substantial period in custody.
predicates.assault_arose_from_dispute_and_altercati: The assault arose from a dispute followed by a wordy altercation.
predicates.victim_sustained_grievous_injuries_and_t: The victim suffered grievous injuries and trauma, including serious consequences requiring treatment.

members.legal_issue: A court may reduce a sentence for bodily-injury offences and order compensation when the circumstances justify that sentencing outcome.
material_facts: The appellant’s convictions for bodily-injury offences were upheld, including an offence involving a fracture.
He had faced a prolonged trial and appeal, had no criminal antecedents, and had already served part of his sentence.
He offered to compensate the victims and was able to pay; the court considered the injuries and the victims’ losses.
members.legal_principle: Section 357 of the CrPC empowers a court to award compensation to victims, including in addition to other sentences. The amount and use of that power depend on the circumstances, including the nature of the offence and injury, the victim’s claim and needs, and the offender’s ability to pay. The Court relied on Hansa v. State of Punjab, Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh, Manish Jalan v. State of Karnataka, and Rachpal Singh v. State of Punjab, and referred to the Law Commission’s 42nd Report.
members.conclusion: The Court reduced the custodial sentence for the offence involving the fracture to the period already served and ordered compensation for the victims, with the original sentence to revive if the required deposit was not made.

rule.if: appeal_from_bodily_injury_conviction and prolonged_proceedings and no_prior_criminal_record and part_of_sentence_already_served and offender_offered_compensation_and_could_pay

predicates.appeal_from_bodily_injury_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by a person convicted of an offence causing bodily injury.
predicates.prolonged_proceedings: The offender experienced a prolonged trial or appellate process.
predicates.no_prior_criminal_record: The offender had no prior criminal history.
predicates.part_of_sentence_already_served: The offender had already served part of the custodial sentence.
predicates.offender_offered_compensation_and_could_: The offender offered compensation and the court found the offender able to pay it.

members.legal_issue: A court may limit imprisonment to the custody already undergone and order compensation for victims or their families when the circumstances make compensation an appropriate response to the offence.
material_facts: The victims and the accused were near relations, and a family property dispute led to the incident.
The deceased victim's widow and children suffered an irreparable loss, and the Court considered that imprisonment alone would not benefit them.
The appellants were in a position to pay compensation and had already served more than two years in custody before being released on bail.
The Court directed that compensation be paid to the widow and children and provided for recovery and revival of the trial-court sentence if it was not paid.
members.legal_principle: Section 357(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits compensation to be ordered in addition to other sentences. In deciding whether and how much compensation is appropriate, the court should consider the nature of the crime, the injury suffered, the justness of the claim, the offender's capacity to pay, and other relevant circumstances. The Court referred to Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh (1988 (4) SCC 551), Dr. Jacob George v. State (1994 (3) SCC 430), and Balraj v. State of U.P. (1994 (4) SCC 29).
members.conclusion: The Court limited the appellants' imprisonment to the period already undergone and ordered each appellant to pay compensation to the deceased victim's widow and children, with the trial-court sentence to revive if the compensation was not paid.

rule.if: criminal_sentencing_appeal and victim_family_suffered_serious_loss and offender_has_capacity_to_pay and imprisonment_alone_will_not_benefit_victims and compensation_is_just_in_the_circumstances

predicates.criminal_sentencing_appeal: The accused appealed the sentence imposed in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.victim_family_suffered_serious_loss: The victim's family suffered serious loss as a result of the offence.
predicates.offender_has_capacity_to_pay: The offender was in a position to pay compensation.
predicates.imprisonment_alone_will_not_benefit_vict: The court considered that imprisonment alone would not benefit the victims or their family.
