The Court relied on its decisions in Jaigobind Singh v. Lachmi Narain Ram and Soli Pestonji Majoo v. Gangadhar Khemka, and on State Bank of Mysore v. G.P. Thulasi Bai.
members.conclusion: The mortgage-specific provision applies to interest in a mortgage suit; the general provision governing interest in money decrees does not apply.

predicates.mortgage_recovery_proceeding: A creditor brought a proceeding to recover a debt on the basis of a mortgage.
predicates.interest_after_filing_is_at_issue: The court had to determine interest accruing after the proceeding was filed.

members.legal_issue: Arrears of interest subject to a statutory ceiling are calculated up to the date of the decree, not the date of suit or the date fixed for redemption.
material_facts: The trial court passed its decree on 27 March 1952 and awarded the maximum arrears permitted by the governing law.
The High Court later fixed 19 March 1959 as the date for payment of the redemption money and treated interest up to that date as arrears.
The Supreme Court held that the appellate decree took effect from the date of the trial court decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Mysore Money Lenders Act, 1939 directs the court to limit arrears of interest when passing a decree, so the relevant cutoff is the decree date. An appellate decree takes effect from the date of the original court decree. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The capped arrears of interest were to be calculated only up to the date of the trial court decree; the High Court erred in extending them to the date fixed for redemption.

predicates.mortgage_recovery_suit: The proceeding seeks recovery of a debt secured by a mortgage.
predicates.arrears_subject_to_statutory_ceiling: The governing lending law limits the amount that may be decreed as arrears of interest.
predicates.decree_passed: The court has passed a decree in the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: The statutory limit on arrears of interest applies to interest accrued up to the date of the trial court’s decree, and an appellate decree takes effect from that decree’s date.
material_facts: The trial court entered a decree, and the High Court later fixed a date for payment of the redemption money.
The High Court treated the capped arrears of interest as extending to the later redemption-payment date.
The Supreme Court held that the arrears were to be calculated only up to the trial court’s decree and that the appellate decree took effect from the date of the trial court’s decree.
members.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Mysore Money Lenders Act, 1939 directs the court not to decree arrears of interest above the principal of the original loan. Because the court gives effect to that direction when passing its decree, the limit applies to interest payable up to that date. An appellate decree takes effect from the date of the original court’s decree. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: Arrears subject to the statutory limit are calculated up to the date of the trial court’s decree, not the date of suit, the later redemption date, or the date the appellate court issues its decree.

predicates.money_lending_suit_involves_capped_inter: A court is deciding a money-lending claim that seeks arrears of interest subject to a statutory ceiling.
predicates.appellate_court_changes_decree: An appellate court later varies or replaces the trial court’s decree.

members.legal_issue: A consent decree allowing occupants to remain temporarily after they became liable to eviction does not create a new tenancy when its terms grant only a concession in return for mesne profits.
material_facts: The occupants were liable to immediate eviction after the lease ended.
The consent decree allowed them to remain in possession for five years as a concession and required payment of mesne profits at a substantially higher rate than the original rent.
The decree required the mesne profits to be paid within a shorter period than the period of continued possession and allowed possession to be demanded immediately upon default.
The occupants argued in an execution proceeding that the consent decree created a tenancy protected by later rent-control legislation.
members.legal_principle: The terms of the consent decree must show an intention to create a landlord-and-tenant relationship; temporary continued possession in return for mesne profits is not enough. The court distinguished Gurupadappa, Shivlingappa Itgi v. Sayad Akbar Sayad Budan Kadri, where the consent decree expressly recognized the occupant as a monthly tenant. The court considered the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, but identified no particular provision of that Act as the basis for its conclusion.
members.conclusion: The consent decree did not create a tenancy, and the occupants were not protected from eviction on that basis.

rule.if: execution_challenge and occupants_were_liable_to_eviction and decree_granted_temporary_possession and decree_required_mesne_profits

predicates.execution_challenge: Occupants argued in an execution proceeding that a consent decree protected them from eviction.
predicates.occupants_were_liable_to_eviction: The occupants were liable to be evicted when the prior lease ended.
predicates.decree_granted_temporary_possession: The decree allowed the occupants to remain in possession temporarily as a concession rather than recognizing an ongoing tenancy.
predicates.decree_required_mesne_profits: The decree required the occupants to pay mesne profits for the period of temporary possession.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree resolving an eviction suit created a licence rather than a lease where its terms and context showed no intention to establish a landlord-and-tenant relationship.
material_facts: The property owner had brought an action to evict the occupant, and the parties then entered into a compromise decree allowing the occupant to remain for a specified period.
The decree described payments for continued occupation as rent and required a deposit to be adjusted against the final period of occupation.
If the occupant failed to pay for three consecutive months, the owner could execute the existing decree to evict the occupant before the specified period ended.
The compromise was reached after the owner had lost at trial and during the appeal.
members.legal_principle: The decisive test for distinguishing a lease from a licence is the parties’ intention, determined from the substance of the agreement and all relevant circumstances. Exclusive possession is not conclusive; an interest in the property may indicate a lease, while circumstances showing that the parties did not intend a legal landlord-and-tenant relationship may indicate a licence. The use of the word “rent” or payment for occupation is not decisive because rent may also describe payment by a licensee. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapur, M. N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, State of Punjab v. British India Corporation Ltd., Issac v. Hotel De Paris, and approved Sumatibai Waman Kirlikar v. A. B. Shirgaonkar.
members.conclusion: The compromise decree created a licence, not a lease, because the parties did not intend to create a landlord-and-tenant relationship.

predicates.eviction_suit_resolved_by_compromise_dec: The property owner initiated proceedings to recover the property, and the parties resolved those proceedings by a compromise decree.
predicates.continued_occupation_permitted: The compromise decree allowed the occupant to remain in the property for a period after the settlement.
predicates.existing_decree_executable_to_evict_on_p: The decree allowed the owner to use that same decree to evict the occupant if the occupant defaulted on payments for continued occupation.
predicates.prior_eviction_action_indicates_no_new_t: The owner had sought to evict the occupant before the compromise, and the circumstances of that action indicated no intention to create a new tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree that arranges temporary occupation pending eviction does not create a new lease, and therefore does not require registration on that basis.
material_facts: The compromise admitted the landlord’s claim for ejectment and repeatedly provided that the landlord could execute the decree if the tenants did not vacate as agreed.
The tenants could remain in a specified portion for a defined period before vacating it.
The compromise also provided for mesne profits and permitted certain alterations and improvements associated with the period before vacating.
The terms and overall tenor of the compromise indicated an arrangement for vacating the premises rather than an intention to create a new landlord-tenant relationship.
members.legal_principle: The dominant intention of the document, determined from its terms and overall tenor, governs its construction. An arrangement allowing temporary occupation before vacating, where the document preserves enforcement of the eviction decree and does not intend to create a new lease, does not require registration as a lease. The Court relied on Girdharilal v. Hukam Singh and considered the distinction in Konchada Ramamurthy Subudhi v. Gopinath Naik.
members.conclusion: The compromise did not create a new lease; registration of the decree was therefore not required on that ground.

predicates.consent_eviction_decree: The eviction decree records an agreement between the landlord and tenant.
predicates.temporary_occupation_pending_vacatur: The agreement allows the tenant to occupy some or all of the premises temporarily before vacating them.
predicates.decree_preserves_enforcement_intent: The agreement’s terms and overall tenor preserve enforcement of the eviction decree rather than indicate an intention to create a new tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree that provides for an underlease only upon a future payment does not itself create a present lease requiring registration as a lease, and may be exempt from registration as a court decree.
material_facts: A compromise decree provided that one set of parties would hold disputed land as tenants under another set of parties, with revised royalty obligations.
The arrangement was conditional on payment of a sum to the original lessor within a specified period; until payment, the parties could not execute the decree or take possession of the disputed land.
The decree also provided for execution of further lease documents, or for the compromise document itself to operate on the stated terms if those further documents were not executed.
The appeal challenged the use of the compromise decree in a claim for royalties and cesses on the ground that the decree was unregistered.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(7) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, includes an agreement to lease within the term “lease,” but, as explained in Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Midnapur Zamindari Co., an agreement for a lease must effect an actual demise and create a present and immediate interest in land. The conditional arrangement therefore did not fall within section 17(1)(d). It was nevertheless within section 17(1)(b) and exempt as a court decree under section 17(2)(vi).
members.conclusion: The contingent arrangement was not a lease under section 17(1)(d), because it did not create a present and immediate interest in the land. Although it fell within section 17(1)(b), it was exempt from registration under section 17(2)(vi), so the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_contests_registration_of_compromi: A party in an appeal challenged the use of a compromise decree on the ground that it was unregistered.
predicates.decree_records_immovable_property_arrang: The compromise decree records an arrangement concerning rights in immovable property.
predicates.proposed_underlease_depends_on_future_pa: The decree makes the proposed underlease effective only if a party makes a required payment within a stipulated period.
predicates.possession_or_enforcement_is_barred_unti: The decree prevents possession or enforcement of the arrangement until the required payment is made.

members.legal_issue: A defendant may challenge an ex parte decree by first appeal, including on the grounds that the material in the ex parte proceedings did not entitle the plaintiff to a decree or that the suit should not have proceeded ex parte.
material_facts: The defendant challenged the ex parte decree by filing a first appeal.
The High Court found adequate grounds to set aside the decree, including defects in the service process and in the order authorizing substituted service.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 96(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, as explained in Bhanu Kumar Jain v Archana Kumar and followed in Rabindra Singh v Financial Commissioner, Cooperation, Punjab and Mahesh Yadav v Rajeshwar Singh, an appeal against an ex parte decree may be based on the contention that the material brought on record in the ex parte proceedings does not entitle the plaintiff to a decree, or that the suit should not have been posted for ex parte hearing. A defendant may pursue an appeal and an application to set aside the decree for non-appearance simultaneously; filing the latter does not remove the right of appeal. The judgment also states that, after dismissal of an appeal arising from the application to set aside the decree, the same contention cannot be raised in a first appeal.
members.conclusion: A first appeal was an available remedy, and the defendant established adequate grounds in that appeal to set aside the ex parte decree.

predicates.defendant_challenges_ex_parte_decree_by_: The defendant challenges a decree made in the defendant’s absence by filing a first appeal.
predicates.ex_parte_material_does_not_entitle_plain: The material placed before the court in the defendant’s absence does not entitle the plaintiff to the decree granted.
predicates.suit_should_not_have_proceeded_ex_parte: The suit should not have been heard in the defendant’s absence.

members.legal_issue: Dismissal on the merits of an application to set aside an ex parte decree does not bar a regular appeal challenging the decree on its merits.
material_facts: The defendants’ application to set aside the ex parte decree was dismissed on its merits.
The defendants subsequently filed a regular appeal challenging the ex parte decree itself.
members.legal_principle: Order IX Rule 13 CPC concerns whether summons were duly served or whether sufficient cause prevented the defendant from appearing; Section 96(2) CPC permits an appeal from an original ex parte decree and allows the appellate court to examine the decree on its merits. The statutory right of appeal cannot be curtailed without express statutory language or necessary implication. Under Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar, dismissal of an Order IX Rule 13 application does not prevent a first appeal on the merits, although the appellant cannot use that appeal to relitigate the grounds concerning the ex parte hearing addressed by that application. The Court also referred to Deepal Girishbhai Soni v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. and Chandravathi P.K. v. C.K. Saji on the statutory nature of appeal rights.
members.conclusion: The regular appeal under Section 96(2) CPC is not barred merely because the application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC was dismissed on its merits.

predicates.appeal_against_ex_parte_decree: The litigant filed a regular appeal challenging a decree entered in the litigant’s absence.
predicates.set_aside_application_dismissed_on_merit: The court dismissed on its merits the litigant’s application seeking to set aside that decree.
predicates.regular_appeal_not_barred: The regular appeal remains available and is not barred by dismissal of the set-aside application.

members.legal_issue: A defendant may pursue an appeal against an ex parte decree and an application to set it aside concurrently, and dismissal of the setting-aside application does not by itself extinguish the appeal on the merits.
material_facts: A preliminary decree was passed in the defendants’ absence.
The defendants applied under Order 9 Rule 13 to set aside the decree; that application and an appeal from its dismissal were rejected.
A first appeal against the decree was also pursued.
members.legal_principle: Section 96(2) confers a statutory right of appeal against an ex parte decree, and that right cannot be curtailed absent an express or necessarily implied statutory bar. The Explanation to Order 9 Rule 13 bars a setting-aside application when an appeal against the ex parte decree has been dismissed; it does not establish the converse. The Explanation is to be strictly construed, as held in Rani Choudhury v. Lt.-Col. Suraj Jit Choudhury, P. Kiran Kumar v. A.S. Khadar and Shyam Sundar Sarma v. Pannalal Jaiswal.
members.conclusion: The remedies of an appeal under Section 96(2) and an application under Order 9 Rule 13 may be pursued simultaneously. Dismissal of the Order 9 Rule 13 application does not, by itself, bar the first appeal on the merits. If the appeal against the ex parte decree is dismissed, however, the decree merges with the appellate order and the Explanation to Order 9 Rule 13 bars a subsequent application under that rule.

rule.if: ex_parte_decree and defendant_seeks_appeal_and_setting_aside and not appeal_against_decree_dismissed

predicates.ex_parte_decree: A court has passed a decree against a defendant in that defendant’s absence.
predicates.defendant_seeks_appeal_and_setting_aside: The defendant pursues both an appeal against the decree and an application to have it set aside.
predicates.appeal_against_decree_dismissed: The appeal against the ex parte decree has been dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A first appeal against an ex parte decree may examine whether the record supports the decree and whether the suit was maintainable or the court had jurisdiction, even if an application to set aside the decree was dismissed.
material_facts: The defendants pursued proceedings to set aside the decree, which were unsuccessful.

The High Court allowed the first appeal on procedural grounds, and the Supreme Court held that the defendants could nevertheless argue the merits of the plaintiff’s case using the material on the record.
The Supreme Court did not decide the merits and remitted the appeal for the High Court to consider them.
members.legal_principle: Section 96(2) provides a statutory appeal against an ex parte decree. Under Section 105, an appellant may also challenge an interlocutory order in the appeal, subject to the statutory conditions. A merits appeal is distinct from an application under Order 9 Rule 13: the appeal examines whether the decree is supported by the record and is otherwise legally sustainable, while the setting-aside application may address sufficient cause for absence. The statutory appeal cannot be curtailed without an express or necessarily implied bar; the Court relied on Deepal Girishbhai Soni v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. and Chandravathi P.K. v. C.K. Saji.
members.conclusion: In the first appeal, the defendants may contend that the material on the record does not support the decree, that the suit was otherwise not maintainable, or that the trial court lacked jurisdiction. The High Court must consider those merits contentions on the existing record, but the Supreme Court expressed no view on their outcome.

rule.if: appeal_against_ex_parte_decree and (record_insufficient_to_support_decree or suit_not_maintainable or trial_court_lacked_jurisdiction)

predicates.appeal_against_ex_parte_decree: The defendant brings a first appeal against a decree passed in the defendant’s absence.
predicates.record_insufficient_to_support_decree: The material available in the suit record is said to be insufficient to justify the decree.
predicates.suit_not_maintainable: The defendant contends that the suit could not legally be maintained.
predicates.trial_court_lacked_jurisdiction: The defendant contends that the court that passed the decree lacked jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional amendment that takes away or abridges fundamental rights is subject to the prohibition against such laws and cannot validly do so.
material_facts: The petitions challenged land-reform laws on the ground that they infringed fundamental rights.
A later constitutional amendment altered the definition of protected land and placed the challenged laws in a constitutional schedule that insulated them from rights-based challenge.
Earlier decisions had upheld Parliament’s power to amend fundamental rights.
members.legal_principle: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making a law that takes away or abridges fundamental rights, and an amendment made through Article 368 is subject to that prohibition. Article 368 prescribes the amending procedure; it does not displace the protection in Part III. The Court rejected the reasoning in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India, [1952] SCR 89, and the contrary conclusion in Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1965] 1 SCR 933. The Court relied on the constitutional scheme protecting fundamental rights and referred to A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha, and Ujjam Bai v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The Court held that an amendment taking away or abridging fundamental rights is a law within the meaning of Article 13(2) and is void to that extent; Parliament has no power to make such an amendment. The Court overruled the contrary holding in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and rejected the contrary view in Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: A party challenged a constitutional amendment in a proceeding concerning the protection of fundamental rights.
predicates.amendment_reduces_fundamental_rights: The amendment took away or abridged rights protected as fundamental rights.

members.legal_issue: Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to take away or abridge fundamental rights.
material_facts: The amendments under challenge altered protections for property and protected land-reform legislation from challenges based on fundamental rights.
The Court reconsidered earlier decisions that had recognized Parliament’s power to amend Part III.
members.legal_principle: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making law that takes away or abridges rights in Part III. The Court held that this prohibition applies to constitutional amendments and overruled the contrary view in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan. The Court also recognized that the Constitution itself provides for specified modifications or suspensions of rights in particular circumstances, including under Articles 33, 34 and 35.
members.conclusion: Parliament has no power to amend Part III so as to take away or abridge fundamental rights.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether Parliament may change the Constitution by amendment.
predicates.amendment_changes_part_three: The proposed amendment changes provisions protecting fundamental rights.
predicates.amendment_reduces_fundamental_rights: The amendment takes away or diminishes a fundamental right.

members.legal_issue: Parliament’s constitutional amendment power extends to changing or making fundamental-rights provisions inapplicable in particular cases, and the prohibition on ordinary laws abridging those rights does not invalidate an amendment made through that power.
material_facts: The amendment changed provisions in the fundamental-rights part of the Constitution and protected specified state agrarian laws from challenges based on fundamental rights.
The petitioners argued that the amendment abridged fundamental rights and was therefore invalid under the constitutional prohibition on such laws.
The Court held that the amendment power applied to all constitutional provisions and that the challenged measure was made in exercise of constituent, rather than ordinary legislative, power.
members.legal_principle: The majority held that Article 368 authorises amendment of all provisions of the Constitution, including Part III, and that the term “law” in Article 13(2) means rules made in the exercise of ordinary legislative power, not constitutional amendments made in the exercise of constituent power. The Court followed Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and referred to A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras and In re The Delhi Laws Act, 1912. Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar reserved their opinions on the Article 13 issue.
members.conclusion: The amendment power includes the power to modify fundamental rights, including making them inapplicable in specified cases, and the prohibition on laws abridging fundamental rights does not apply to constitutional amendments made under that power.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a constitutional amendment.
predicates.amendment_made_through_constitutional_am: The challenged measure was enacted through the Constitution’s prescribed amendment process.
predicates.amendment_changes_fundamental_rights: The amendment modifies fundamental-rights provisions or makes them inapplicable in particular cases.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on laws abridging fundamental rights does not apply to amendments made through the constitutional constituent power.
material_facts: The amendment inserted provisions that protected certain land-related laws from challenges based on fundamental rights.
The petitioners argued that the amendment abridged rights guaranteed by the Constitution.
The constitutional amendment provision authorized Parliament to amend the Constitution without an express exception for fundamental-rights provisions.
members.legal_principle: Articles 12, 13(2) and 368 must be read harmoniously. In Article 13(2), “law” means rules or regulations made through ordinary legislative power, not constitutional amendments made through constituent power. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The prohibition on laws abridging fundamental rights did not invalidate the constitutional amendment.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenge: A proceeding challenges a constitutional amendment as inconsistent with guaranteed fundamental rights.
predicates.amendment_was_made_through_constituent_p: The legislature acted under the constitutional process for amending the Constitution rather than its ordinary lawmaking power.
predicates.challenged_measure_was_a_constitutional_: The challenged measure changed the text or operation of the Constitution through the prescribed amendment process.

members.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a statutory appeal from an arbitrator acts as a court when the appeal is directed to the High Court and is governed by its ordinary procedure.
material_facts: The compensation dispute was referred to an arbitrator, whose award was appealed to the High Court under the governing statute.
The statute provided for an appeal to the High Court, and neither the statute nor its rules prescribed a special procedure for that appeal.
The High Court determined the appeal under its ordinary rules of practice and procedure.
members.legal_principle: When legislation directs an appeal to an established court without prescribing a special procedure, the court’s ordinary procedure and incidents of appeal apply. The Court relied on National Telephone Co., Ltd. v. Postmaster-General and National Sewing Thread Co., Ltd. v. James Chadwick and Bros. Ltd.; it also referred to Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. P. N. Sharma and Secretary of State for India in Council v. Chelikani Rama Rao. It rejected the contrary view in Hanskumar Kishanchand v. Union of India, distinguishing the issue there concerning whether the decision was a judgment, decree or final order from whether the High Court acted as a court.
members.conclusion: The High Court acted as a court, not as a persona designata, and its determination was within the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction to review by special leave.

predicates.appeal_from_arbitrator_award: A party appealed a decision made by an arbitrator.
predicates.appeal_directed_to_high_court: The governing scheme directed the appeal to the High Court itself.
predicates.ordinary_high_court_procedure_applies: No special procedure was prescribed, so the High Court determined the appeal under its ordinary procedure.

members.legal_issue: An appeal from an arbitrator’s award under the governing compensation scheme is heard as an appellate proceeding, not as an application to set aside the award.
material_facts: The compensation dispute had been referred to an arbitrator under a statutory scheme that provided an appeal to the High Court.
The Government appealed the arbitrator’s award to the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, the High Court acts as an appellate court when hearing an appeal from an arbitrator’s award; it does not act as a court hearing an application to set aside the award. The Court relied on Collector of Varanasi v. Gauri Shankar Misra.
members.conclusion: The High Court heard the appeal as an appellate court, rather than as a court deciding an application to set aside an award.

predicates.statutory_compensation_award_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the High Court from an arbitrator’s award of compensation.

members.legal_issue: A decision of a High Court on an appeal from a statutory arbitrator’s award remains an arbitral award and is not appealable as an ordinary court judgment, decree, or order.
material_facts: The dispute concerned compensation for property requisitioned by the Government, and the amount was referred by statute to an arbitrator because the parties had not agreed on compensation.
The arbitrator made an award, and a party appealed that award to the High Court under the same statutory scheme.

The statute described the arbitrator’s decision as an award and provided an appeal to the High Court; the proceedings originated as arbitration rather than as a civil suit heard by the High Court in its ordinary jurisdiction.
The High Court modified the award, and both parties obtained certificates to appeal further under the ordinary civil procedure provisions.
members.legal_principle: A decision made by a court in its ordinary civil jurisdiction is generally appealable under the Code of Civil Procedure, but an adjudication of an arbitrator that receives the court’s imprimatur is final, subject to the applicable statutory provisions. The same distinction applies to statutory arbitration: a reference to a court as a court ordinarily attracts its usual procedures and appeal rights, whereas a reference to it as an arbitrator or designated authority produces an award. An appeal from an award continues the original arbitration proceedings and does not change their character. The Court applied the principles in Rangoon Botatoung Company v. The Collector, Rangoon; The Special Officer, Salsette Building Sites v. Dossabhai Bezonji; The Special Officer, Salsette Building Sites v. Dassabhai Bozanji Motiwala; Manavikraman Tirumalpad v. The Collector of the Nilgiris; Secretary of State for India in Council v. Hindusthan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd.; and Kollegal Silk Filatures Ltd. v. Province of Madras. It distinguished National Telephone Company Ltd. v. Postmaster-General, where the reference was to a tribunal as a court. The relevant statutory framework included sections 19(1)(b), 19(1)(f), and 19(1)(g) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, and sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s decision was an award, not a judgment, decree, or order appealable under the ordinary civil procedure provisions or the relevant Letters Patent. Both appeals were incompetent and were dismissed.

predicates.statutory_appeal_from_arbitrator_award: A party brought a statutory appeal to a High Court from an arbitrator’s award.
predicates.compensation_referred_to_arbitrator: A statute assigned the determination of compensation to an arbitrator because the parties did not agree on the amount.
predicates.arbitrator_decision_designated_as_award: The governing statutory scheme described the arbitrator’s decision as an award.

members.legal_issue: A decision of a High Court on a statutory appeal from an arbitrator’s award remains an arbitral decision and is not appealable as an ordinary court judgment, decree, or order.
material_facts: A statutory reference was made to an arbitrator to determine compensation for requisitioned property after the parties could not agree on the amount.
The High Court heard an appeal from the arbitrator’s award and varied the compensation.
Both sides sought to appeal the High Court’s decision to the Supreme Court under ordinary civil appellate provisions and the applicable Letters Patent.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 19(1)(b), 19(1)(f), and 19(1)(g) of the Defence of India Act, the compensation dispute was referred to an arbitrator and the statutory appeal from the award remained part of the arbitration proceedings. Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, reflects that statutory arbitrations generally stand on the footing of arbitrations by agreement. Whether a decision is appealable under sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure or the Letters Patent depends on whether the court acted in its ordinary civil jurisdiction or as a designated arbitral authority. The Court relied on Rangoon Botatoung Company v. The Collector, Rangoon; The Special Officer, Salsette Building Sites v. Dossabhai Bezonji; The Special Officer, Salsette Building Sites v. Dossabhai Basenji Motiwala; Manavikraman Tirumalpad v. The Collector of the Nilgris; Secretary of State for India in Council v. Hindusthan Co-operative Insurance Society Limited; National Telephone Company Limited v. Postmaster General; Secretary of State for India v. Chelikani Rama Rao; and Kollegal Silk Filatures Ltd. v. Province of Madras.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s decision was an award made in the course of the statutory arbitration, not a judgment, decree, or order appealable under the ordinary civil appellate provisions or the Letters Patent. Both appeals were therefore incompetent.

predicates.statutory_arbitration_proceeding: A statute refers a dispute to an arbitrator for determination.
predicates.appeal_from_arbitrator_award: A party brings the statutorily provided appeal against the arbitrator’s award before a High Court.
predicates.appellate_stage_continues_same_proceedin: The High Court hears the appeal as a further stage of the original arbitral proceeding rather than as a newly instituted ordinary civil case.

members.legal_issue: Leave to appeal under an inherited jurisdiction limited to appeals from judgments in civil cases cannot be granted against a High Court decision that is an arbitral award rather than a judgment.
material_facts: The parties sought to rely on a power said to have passed from the Privy Council to the Federal Court and then to the Supreme Court to grant leave to appeal.
The challenged High Court decision arose from an appeal against an arbitrator’s award and was held not to be a judgment, decree, or order of the High Court.
The asserted power to grant leave was limited to a proposed appeal against a judgment of a High Court in a civil case.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3(a)(ii) of the Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948, the Federal Court’s power to grant leave applied only where the proposed appeal was against a judgment; section 2(b) defined the relevant judgment as a judgment, decree, or order of a High Court in a civil case. The Court held that Article 135 of the Constitution did not enlarge that power to cover an arbitral award that was not such a judgment.
members.conclusion: The asserted inherited jurisdiction did not permit leave to appeal because the challenged decision was an award, not a qualifying judgment. No order granting leave could have been made under that power.

predicates.special_leave_sought: A party sought special leave to appeal under a jurisdiction asserted to have been inherited from an earlier appellate court.
predicates.impugned_decision_was_arbitral_award: The challenged decision was an arbitral award rather than a judgment, decree, or order of a High Court in a civil case.
predicates.inherited_leave_power_limited_to_civil_j: The asserted inherited power permitted leave only for an appeal from a High Court judgment in a civil case.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court cannot use inherited special-leave jurisdiction to entertain an appeal from a High Court decision that is an arbitral award rather than a judgment, decree, or order in a civil case.
material_facts: The proposed appeals challenged the High Court’s decision in an appeal from an arbitrator’s award.
The appellants argued that the Supreme Court could grant leave under jurisdiction inherited from the former Federal Court even if ordinary appellate routes were unavailable.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(a)(ii) of the Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948, empowered the Federal Court to grant leave only for a proposed appeal against a judgment, and section 2(b) defined that term as a judgment, decree, or order of a High Court in a civil case. The Court held that the asserted power had not passed to it under Article 135 of the Constitution in relation to a decision that did not meet that requirement.
members.conclusion: The Court could not grant special leave through the asserted inherited jurisdiction because the challenged decision was an award, not a judgment, decree, or order within the relevant jurisdictional requirement. The appeals were dismissed as incompetent.

predicates.special_leave_sought_under_inherited_jur: A party asks the Supreme Court to grant special leave by relying on jurisdiction inherited from a former court.
predicates.proposed_appeal_is_from_statutory_arbitr: The proposed appeal challenges a High Court decision made in an appeal from a statutory arbitrator’s award.
predicates.challenged_decision_is_an_award_not_a_co: The challenged decision is an arbitral award rather than a judgment, decree, or order made by the High Court in its ordinary civil jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A memorandum accompanying a deposit of title deeds requires registration when the parties intend it to embody their bargain and create the mortgage.
material_facts: The bank relied on an unregistered printed form signed in connection with the deposit of title deeds.
The form was incomplete because unnecessary printed terms had not been struck out.
The form described itself as recording terms already agreed upon.
members.legal_principle: Under section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, a document that embodies the bargain creating a mortgage by deposit of title deeds must be registered. Where the parties do not intend the document to embody their bargain, the mortgage arises by implication from the deposit with the requisite intention, and a merely evidential memorandum need not be registered. The Court applied Rachpal Maharaj v. Bhagwandas Daruka, Pranjivandas Mehta v. Chan Ma Phee, Shaw v. Foster, and Subramonian v. Lutchman.
members.conclusion: A document intended to embody the mortgage bargain requires registration; this document was not intended to do so and was only evidential.

predicates.mortgage_by_title_deposit: The parties deposited title deeds with a creditor intending to create security over the property.
predicates.written_bargain_intended: The parties intended their written document itself to embody the bargain creating the security.

members.legal_issue: A memorandum that records a completed equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds, rather than itself creating the security, does not require registration.
material_facts: The money was advanced and the hundies were executed in the morning.
That afternoon, the borrower brought the title deeds to the creditor; the deeds were examined and approved, and a list of them was made.
The letter stated that the deeds had been delivered and deposited to create security and that the borrower would execute a formal mortgage when called upon.
The majority construed the evidence as showing that the equitable mortgage had been completed by the deposit of the deeds before the letter was given.
members.legal_principle: Under the Registration Act, a document requires registration when it is an operative instrument that creates or declares an interest in property; a memorandum that merely records a transaction already completed does not. The document must be read in its context, and its wording cannot be altered to make it operative. The majority relied on United Bank of India v. Lakharam Sonaram and referred to Hari Sankar Paul v. Kedar Nath Saha; it rejected any broad reading of Kedarnath Dutt v. Shamlall Khettry that would require registration for a document that does not, properly construed, disclose the creation of a mortgage.
members.conclusion: The letter did not require registration and was admissible as evidence. The appeal was dismissed, leaving the mortgage decree in place.

rule.if: mortgage_decree_appeal and memorandum_records_title_deed_deposit and (deposit_completed_before_memorandum or memorandum_not_operative)

predicates.mortgage_decree_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a decree based on a mortgage.
predicates.memorandum_records_title_deed_deposit: A document records the deposit of title deeds as security for a debt.
predicates.deposit_completed_before_memorandum: The title deeds were deposited and the security was created before the memorandum was given.
predicates.memorandum_not_operative: The memorandum recites an earlier deposit or transaction rather than itself creating the security.

members.legal_issue: A memorandum concerning a mortgage created by depositing title deeds requires registration only if the parties intended it to embody and operate as their agreement creating the security.
material_facts: The debtor deposited title deeds with the creditor as security for amounts already due and amounts that might become due from their business dealings.
After the deposit, the debtor signed and delivered a memorandum stating that the deeds had been deposited with intent to create an equitable mortgage.

The courts found that the parties had already agreed orally on the security and that the memorandum merely recorded the completed transaction; it was not intended to form the basis of their rights and liabilities.
members.legal_principle: Under section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a mortgage may arise when title deeds are delivered with the requisite intention to create security. Ordinarily, the contract is implied by law from the deposit and intention. If the parties instead reduce their bargain to an operative written agreement, that document creates an interest in immovable property and requires registration under section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908; section 59 addresses registration of other forms of mortgage. If the document merely records a transaction already concluded and is evidential rather than operative, it does not require registration. The timing of the memorandum is not decisive. Obla Sundarachariar v. Narayana Ayyar illustrates an evidential memorandum that did not require registration; Hari Sankar Paul v. Kedar Nath Saha illustrates an operative written agreement that did.
members.conclusion: The memorandum did not require registration and was admissible in evidence to prove creation of the charge. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: title_deed_security_dispute and bargain_completed_on_deposit and not memorandum_as_operating_agreement

predicates.title_deed_security_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a memorandum connected with security created by depositing title deeds must be registered.
predicates.bargain_completed_on_deposit: The debtor deposited title deeds with the creditor with the requisite intention to secure the debt, and the security bargain was already concluded at that time.
predicates.memorandum_as_operating_agreement: The debtor and creditor intended the memorandum itself to embody their agreement and operate as the instrument creating the security.

members.legal_issue: A preliminary authorization for depositing title deeds requires registration only if it forms an integral part of the written bargain creating security over immovable property.
material_facts: The authorization permitted a representative to deposit title deeds to secure advances, but did not state the principal amount borrowed or to be borrowed, the interest rate, or the details of the deeds to be deposited.
The court found that the authorization was not intended to form an integral part of the transaction and did not itself create an interest in the property.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, a mortgage by deposit of title deeds is created when title deeds are delivered with intent to create security. Ordinarily, the law implies the mortgage contract from the deposit and intent. If the parties reduce their bargain about the security to writing, that written bargain is the sole evidence of its terms and requires registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act if it creates an interest in immovable property; Section 59 does not otherwise require a registered instrument for this form of mortgage. The distinction between a written bargain and a memorandum that merely records or evidences a transaction is supported by Kedarnath Dutt v. Shamloll Khettry, Pranjivandas Mehta v. Chan Ma Phee, Shaw v. Foster, Obla Sundarachariar v. Narayana Ayyar, and Rachpal Mahraj v. Bhagwandas Daruka.
members.conclusion: The authorization was merely evidential and did not require registration.

rule.if: appeal_from_denial_of_mortgage_decree and preliminary_authorization_for_title_deposit and authorization_omits_loan_amount and authorization_omits_interest_rate and authorization_omits_deed_details

predicates.appeal_from_denial_of_mortgage_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from the denial of a mortgage decree.
predicates.preliminary_authorization_for_title_depo: A written authorization permits another person to deposit title deeds as security for advances.
predicates.authorization_omits_loan_amount: The authorization does not state the amount borrowed or to be borrowed.
predicates.authorization_omits_interest_rate: The authorization does not state the interest rate for the loan.
predicates.authorization_omits_deed_details: The authorization does not identify the title deeds to be deposited.

members.legal_issue: A payment to acquire a long-term right to extract minerals still embedded in land is capital expenditure rather than revenue expenditure.
material_facts: The assessee claimed a deduction for the balance of the amount paid under a lease of mining areas for twenty years.
The areas had previously been worked, and mica pillars had been exposed, but the mica remained embedded in the land and further mining operations were needed to extract it.
A separate amount paid for mica scrap already lying on the surface was allowed as revenue expenditure by the Tribunal; the disputed lease payment related to the right to extract the remaining mica.
members.legal_principle: Under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, expenditure for acquiring an enduring right over land to win minerals embedded in it is capital expenditure; the need for mining operations to extract the minerals distinguishes it from acquiring surface minerals as stock-in-trade. The Court followed Pingle Industries Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and applied the fact-specific approach discussed in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. and Abdul Kayoom v. Commissioner of Income-tax. It also referred to Golden Horse Shoe (New) Ltd. v. Thurgood, Mohanlal Hargovind v. C.I.T., and M.A. Jabbar v. Commissioner of Income-tax in distinguishing minerals already obtained or lying on the surface.
members.conclusion: The disputed lease expenditure was capital expenditure and was not allowable as revenue expenditure.

rule.if: income_tax_deduction_claim and mining_lease_acquired and long_term_right_to_extract and mineral_embedded_in_land and extraction_operations_required

predicates.income_tax_deduction_claim: A taxpayer claimed that an expense incurred in its business was deductible in computing income.
predicates.mining_lease_acquired: The taxpayer obtained a lease conferring rights to work a mineral deposit.
predicates.long_term_right_to_extract: The lease conferred a right to extract minerals over an extended period.
predicates.mineral_embedded_in_land: The minerals covered by the disputed payment remained embedded in the land rather than already being obtained and lying on the surface.
predicates.extraction_operations_required: The taxpayer had to perform mining operations to extract the minerals.

members.legal_issue: A fee paid for a prospecting licence to search for minerals and initiate a mining business is capital expenditure rather than revenue expenditure.
material_facts: The assessee claimed a deduction for a fee paid to obtain a prospecting licence.
The fee was payable per acre and did not depend on the quantity of minerals obtained.
The licence permitted investigation and search for minerals, which had to be won and extracted from the earth; the authorities found that the payment was to initiate mining operations.
The licence was for one year, but the Court held that this duration did not make the payment revenue expenditure.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, does not allow a prospecting fee as revenue expenditure where its object is to initiate the business of extracting minerals from the earth. A fee unrelated to the quantity of minerals obtained and paid for the right to investigate, search for, and find minerals is not a payment to acquire stock-in-trade; the short duration of the licence does not alter its character. The Court applied its capital-versus-revenue analysis, including the principles discussed in Pingle Industries Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax.
members.conclusion: The prospecting licence fee was capital expenditure and was not allowable as revenue expenditure.

rule.if: income_tax_deduction_claim and prospecting_license_obtained and license_for_mineral_search and minerals_require_extraction_from_earth and fee_independent_of_mineral_quantity

predicates.income_tax_deduction_claim: A taxpayer claimed that an expense incurred in its business was deductible in computing income.
predicates.prospecting_license_obtained: The taxpayer obtained a licence to prospect for minerals.
predicates.license_for_mineral_search: The licence permitted investigation and search to locate minerals for a proposed extraction business.
predicates.minerals_require_extraction_from_earth: The minerals sought under the licence had to be won and extracted from the earth.
predicates.fee_independent_of_mineral_quantity: The fee was payable without reference to the quantity of minerals obtained.

members.legal_issue: Payments made for a long-term right to extract stones from quarries are capital expenditure rather than deductible revenue expenditure when the right secures a source of raw material from land.
material_facts: The assessee carried on a business of extracting, dressing and selling flagstones.
Under a twelve-year contract, the assessee obtained the exclusive right to extract stones from quarries in six villages, without a limit on the quantity it could extract.
The stones had to be extracted methodically and skilfully from the quarries before they could be dressed and sold.
The contract required annual payments even if no stones were extracted or could be extracted; part of the total obligation was paid in advance and the balance in monthly instalments.
The assessee also had a contract with the Government for quarry rights, but its terms were not produced; the parties and courts treated it as similar in nature to the principal contract.
The assessee claimed the payments as business expenditure, and the tax authorities treated them as capital expenditure.
members.legal_principle: Under section 12(2)(xv) of the Hyderabad Income-tax Act, corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, expenditure is capital if its object is to acquire an asset or enduring advantage for the business, and revenue if it is incurred to run the business or obtain its stock-in-trade. The object of the expenditure, rather than whether payment is made periodically or in a lump sum, determines its character. The Court applied the principles approved in Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and the enduring-benefit test in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd.; it distinguished the raw-material arrangements in Mohanlal Hargovind v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Benarsidas Jagannath, and relied on the distinction between raw material and a right to win material from land reflected in Alianza Co. v. Bell and Stow Bardolph Gravel Co. Ltd. v. Poole.
members.conclusion: The payments acquired a long-term right to win stones and a capital asset of enduring benefit; they were capital expenditure and were not deductible as business expenditure. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: income_tax_deduction_appeal and long_term_quarry_right and exclusive_extraction_right and unrestricted_quantity_right and extraction_requires_winning_material_from_land and fixed_obligation_paid_in_installments and payments_due_even_without_extraction

predicates.income_tax_deduction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning whether expenditure claimed in computing business income is deductible.
predicates.long_term_quarry_right: The business obtained a right to extract material from quarries for a long, fixed term.
predicates.exclusive_extraction_right: The contract gave the business the exclusive right to extract material from the specified quarries.
predicates.unrestricted_quantity_right: The contract did not limit the quantity of material the business could extract.
predicates.extraction_requires_winning_material_fro: The material was part of a quarry and had to be extracted from the land before it could be used or sold.
predicates.fixed_obligation_paid_in_installments: The business undertook a fixed payment obligation for the right, with the total amount divided into instalments.
predicates.payments_due_even_without_extraction: The business had to make the payments even when no material was extracted or available for extraction.

members.legal_issue: Expenditure incurred to remove an obstruction to an existing mining business is revenue expenditure when it does not acquire a capital asset.
material_facts: The business operator held a mining lease covering the land beneath a railway area and had the right to extract minerals from the leased land.
Railway tracks, a station, yards and buildings obstructed mining operations in part of the leased area.
After failing to remove the railway occupation through litigation, the operator agreed with the relevant authorities and other parties to share the cost of relocating the railway establishment.
The operator paid its share of the relocation cost to remove the obstruction and enable mining in the leased area; it acquired no new mineral right or capital asset through the payment.
After relocation, the operator mined the previously obstructed area and supplied the extracted gypsum to a customer.
members.legal_principle: Under section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and the corresponding principle in section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, the character of expenditure depends on the nature of the business, the purpose and commercial effect of the expenditure, and the nature of the right or advantage obtained. Where a business already has the right to operate, expenditure incurred in the course of business to remove a restriction, obstruction or disability is on revenue account if it does not acquire a capital asset, even if it benefits the business. The enduring-benefit test is not conclusive. The Court applied and affirmed the approach in Empire Jute Company v. Commissioner of Income Tax and relied on Gotan Lime Syndicate v. Commissioner of Income Tax, M.A. Jabbar v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Carron Company. It referred to Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax and K.T.M.T.M. Abdul Kayoom v. Commissioner of Income Tax for the fact-specific nature of the inquiry, explained the test in British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. v. Atherton, and distinguished R.B. Seth Moolchand Suganchand v. Commissioner of Income Tax because that case concerned obtaining rights to initiate mining activity rather than removing an obstruction to an existing business.
members.conclusion: The relocation payment was revenue expenditure and deductible. The appeal was allowed, the High Court's order was set aside, and the Tribunal's order allowing the deduction was restored.

rule.if: tax_deduction_dispute and existing_mining_right and expenditure_in_course_of_business and railway_obstruction and payment_removed_obstruction and no_new_capital_asset

predicates.tax_deduction_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether expenditure incurred in a business is deductible in computing taxable income.
predicates.existing_mining_right: The business operator already held the right to mine the land where operations were obstructed.
predicates.expenditure_in_course_of_business: The business operator incurred the expenditure while carrying on its existing business.
predicates.railway_obstruction: Railway infrastructure on the leased land obstructed the business operator's mining operations.
predicates.payment_removed_obstruction: The business operator paid toward relocating the railway infrastructure so it could carry on mining operations in the obstructed area.
predicates.no_new_capital_asset: The payment did not give the business operator a new right to minerals or any other capital asset.

members.legal_issue: Expenditure to restore a temporarily suspended operating unit of an existing business is revenue expenditure when it creates no new asset or enduring business advantage.
material_facts: The assessee carried on coal-mining through a network of collieries, and the business continued while one colliery was temporarily unable to operate because it had been requisitioned for military use.
The assessee incurred expenditure to renovate the buildings, recondition the machinery and remove accumulated debris to resume mining operations after the colliery was returned.
No new asset was brought into existence and no enduring advantage for the business was acquired.
The colliery had been treated as an asset of the continuing business during its occupation, and expenditure incurred for it during that period had been allowed as business expenditure.
members.legal_principle: Whether expenditure is capital or revenue is determined by applying relevant tests in light of the particular facts. Under the tests referred to in Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. v. C.I.T., restoration of an existing business unit after a temporary suspension, without creating a new asset or acquiring an enduring business advantage, is revenue expenditure when incurred as part of the profit-earning process.
members.conclusion: The expenditure was revenue in character and not capital expenditure.

rule.if: business_income_deduction_claim and business_operates_through_multiple_units and one_unit_temporarily_suspended and restoration_work_resumes_existing_operations and no_new_asset_created and no_enduring_business_advantage_acquired

predicates.business_income_deduction_claim: A taxpayer claims a deduction for expenditure in computing income from a business.
predicates.business_operates_through_multiple_units: The business is carried on through multiple operating units.
predicates.one_unit_temporarily_suspended: One operating unit's activity was temporarily suspended while the business continued through other units.
predicates.restoration_work_resumes_existing_operat: The expenditure was incurred to restore an existing unit so that its established operations could resume.
predicates.no_new_asset_created: The restoration work brought no new asset into existence.
predicates.no_enduring_business_advantage_acquired: The expenditure acquired no enduring advantage for the business.

members.legal_issue: A law that neither transfers ownership of land to the state nor vests in the state the owner’s right to recover rent or compensation does not violate Article 31(1) as applied in this case.
material_facts: The Act regulated occupation of land and allowed the state to collect penal charges from occupiers.
It did not transfer ownership of covered land to the state or a state-controlled corporation.
It did not vest in the state the owner’s or occupier’s right to recover rent or compensation for use and occupation of the land.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that Article 31(1) was not violated because the Act did not transfer ownership of land to the state or vest in the state the owner’s or occupier’s right to recover rent or compensation. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Act did not violate Article 31(1) of the Constitution as it then stood.

predicates.article_31_1_challenge: The proceeding claims that a law violates the constitutional protection against deprivation of property.
predicates.no_transfer_of_land_ownership: The law does not transfer ownership of the affected land to the state or a state-controlled body.
predicates.no_state_vesting_of_recovery_right: The law does not vest in the state the owner’s or occupier’s right to recover rent or compensation for use of the land.

members.legal_issue: A law that does not transfer the right to possession of private land to the state or its instrumentalities is not a measure of requisition requiring compensation under Article 31(2), and the absence of presidential assent does not invalidate it on that ground.
material_facts: The Act provided for regulation of occupation and possible eviction from land.
It did not transfer the right to possession of covered land to the state, its agents, or its instrumentalities.
The challenge asserted that the Act amounted to requisition without compensation and was invalid for want of presidential assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 31(2) was not attracted because the Act did not transfer the right to possession of private land to the state, its agents, or its instrumentalities. Consequently, the asserted requirement of presidential assent under Article 31(5) did not arise. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The Act did not amount to requisition, did not violate Article 31(2), and was not invalid for want of presidential assent under Article 31(5).

predicates.article_31_2_or_assent_challenge: The proceeding claims that a law requisitions private property without compensation or is invalid for want of required presidential assent.
predicates.no_transfer_of_possession_to_state: The law does not transfer the right to possess private land to the state, its agents, or its instrumentalities.

members.legal_issue: Presidential assent to a state law on a concurrent subject overrides only those conflicting central laws whose repugnancy was included in the proposal placed before the President for consideration.
material_facts: The state repeatedly extended the duration of its rent-control law and obtained presidential assent to the extension legislation.
The proposals seeking assent identified repugnancy with specified central laws concerning property transfers and small-cause courts.
The proposals did not identify repugnancy with the central public-premises eviction law.
The High Court examined the correspondence concerning the proposals for assent.
members.legal_principle: Article 254(1) gives precedence to a repugnant parliamentary law, subject to Article 254(2). Under Article 254(2), reservation for consideration and assent require the President's attention to be directed to the relevant repugnancy and the reasons for the state law. The assent is limited to the proposal made by the state; where the proposal is confined to specified central laws, it does not extend to other laws. Gram Panchayat of Village Jamalpur v. Malwinder Singh and P.N. Krishan Lal v. Government of Kerala support this approach. Examining the proposal to identify the scope of assent does not amount to reviewing the validity of the President's decision; Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar and Bharat Sevashram Sangh v. State of Gujarat recognise that the assent itself is not justiciable.
members.conclusion: The assent did not make the state rent-control law prevail over the central public-premises eviction law, because the proposal for assent did not seek assent in respect of repugnancy with that law.

predicates.concurrent_law_conflict_case: The proceeding concerns conflicting state and central laws on a concurrent subject.
predicates.state_seeks_presidential_assent: The state submits a proposal seeking presidential assent to its law.
predicates.proposal_identifies_specific_conflicting: The state proposal identifies the central laws whose conflict with the state law is submitted for consideration.
predicates.competing_central_law_not_identified_in_: The central law in dispute is not identified in the proposal seeking assent.

members.legal_issue: Presidential assent supports a State law's precedence over conflicting parliamentary law when the assent request identifies the parliamentary law in question and the asserted conflict.
material_facts: The State's request for assent identified the parliamentary land acquisition law and stated that the revived State laws might conflict with it.
The request described the State's purpose in seeking assent and the relevant differences between the laws.
The President assented to the State enactment after it was placed for consideration.
members.legal_principle: Article 254(2) requires the State law to be reserved for presidential consideration and to receive assent so that it may prevail over a particular conflicting parliamentary law. Judicial examination is limited to whether assent was sought in relation to an identified parliamentary law, rather than as general assent against all parliamentary laws; it does not decide whether the assent was rightly or wrongly granted. The Court relied on Kaiser-I-Hind Pvt. Ltd. v. National Textile Corporation (Maharashtra North) Ltd.
members.conclusion: The assent process complied with the constitutional requirement, and the Court found no basis to intervene on this ground.

rule.if: presidential_assent_review_case and assent_request_identifies_conflicting_law and assent_request_discloses_asserted_conflict and presidential_assent_received

predicates.presidential_assent_review_case: The proceeding concerns whether assent allows a State law to prevail over a conflicting parliamentary law.
predicates.assent_request_identifies_conflicting_la: The State's request for assent identifies the parliamentary law against which the State law is intended to prevail.
predicates.assent_request_discloses_asserted_confli: The State's request explains that the State law is, or may be, in conflict with the identified parliamentary law.
predicates.presidential_assent_received: The State law received presidential assent after being placed for consideration.

members.legal_issue: A State law that has received the required presidential assent cannot be invalidated solely because it remains repugnant to parliamentary legislation.
material_facts: The State enactment addressed a concurrent subject and conflicted in some respects with the parliamentary law.
The State enactment was reserved for and received presidential assent in relation to that parliamentary law.
The challenge argued that the State enactment remained invalid because its provisions were still repugnant.
members.legal_principle: Article 254(2) permits a State law on a concurrent subject to prevail in that State over an inconsistent earlier parliamentary law when the State law is reserved for and receives presidential assent. The purpose of the provision is to allow the State law to operate notwithstanding the conflict; the Court described the repugnancy in such circumstances as having been constitutionalized and relied on Pt. Rishikesh v. Salma Begum.
members.conclusion: Once the constitutional assent requirement was met, the remaining repugnancy was not a ground to invalidate the State enactment.

rule.if: state_law_repugnancy_challenge_case and concurrent_subject_law and repugnancy_exists and presidential_assent_received_for_conflict

predicates.state_law_repugnancy_challenge_case: The proceeding challenges whether a State law may operate despite a conflict with parliamentary legislation.
predicates.concurrent_subject_law: The State law addresses a subject on which both the State and Parliament may legislate.
predicates.repugnancy_exists: The State law contains a provision that conflicts with a provision of parliamentary legislation on the same subject.
predicates.presidential_assent_received_for_conflic: The State law was reserved for and received presidential assent in relation to the conflicting parliamentary law.

members.legal_issue: A state law providing for custody, management, or disposal of evacuee property is not invalid for lack of legislative competence or repugnancy when it is within the relevant legislative field and operates as additional, non-conflicting legislation with presidential assent.
material_facts: The State Legislature enacted the repealing and distribution legislation, which provided for vesting qualifying trust property in the Custodian.
The legislation received the President’s assent.
The Court found that the provision was additional legislation on evacuee property and was not repugnant to the central evacuee-property law.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Entries 41 and 27 of the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule and Article 254(2) of the Constitution. It held that the provision was additional legislation concerning evacuee property, did not conflict with the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and had received the President’s assent.
members.conclusion: The provision was within the State Legislature’s competence and was not invalid on the ground of repugnancy.

predicates.state_legislature_enacted_evacuee_proper: A State Legislature enacted a law providing for custody, management, or disposal of property belonging to evacuees.
predicates.presidential_assent_given: The President assented to the State law.
predicates.provision_adds_to_existing_law_without_c: The provision supplies an additional means of dealing with evacuee property and does not conflict with the existing central law on that subject.

members.legal_issue: An extra-judicial confession that lacks plausibility and credibility is insufficient to establish guilt.
material_facts: Three accused were alleged to have confessed to witnesses who had no particular relationship or connection with them.

The alleged confessions were improbable in light of the secretive manner in which the crimes were said to have been committed and the accused’s alleged choice to confess to those witnesses rather than surrender directly to the police.
The confession evidence did not inspire confidence.
members.legal_principle: An extra-judicial confession is, by its nature, a weak piece of evidence; its weight depends on whether the evidence of the confession is plausible and inspires confidence. No earlier case or statutory provision is cited for this principle.
members.conclusion: The alleged extra-judicial confessions were improbable, lacked credibility, and could not support a finding of guilt.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the prosecution seeks to establish the accused’s guilt.
predicates.prosecution_relies_on_extra_judicial_con: The prosecution relies on an alleged confession made by an accused to a person outside a formal judicial proceeding.
predicates.confession_lacks_credibility: The circumstances of the alleged confession make it implausible or otherwise fail to inspire confidence.

members.legal_issue: An alleged extra-judicial confession is not reliable where its circumstances are doubtful, it is made after a long interval, and a supporting witness denies it.
material_facts: The alleged confession was said to have been made years after the killing, when the accused was apprehended in another matter and produced before a village head.
The accused allegedly said he was wanted in a murder case and asked not to be handed over to police before allegedly confessing.
One of the two witnesses to the alleged confession denied in cross-examination that the accused had made it.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed the confession on the reliability of its proof and the circumstances in which it was allegedly made. It applied the evidentiary principles identified under Sections 3 and 14 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The alleged confession could not be relied on and had to be left out of consideration.

rule.if: criminal_case_relies_on_circumstantial_evidence and alleged_extra_judicial_confession and confession_made_after_long_interval and supporting_witness_denies_confession and circumstances_of_statement_are_doubtful

predicates.criminal_case_relies_on_circumstantial_e: The prosecution relies on circumstantial evidence to prove the accused’s guilt.
predicates.alleged_extra_judicial_confession: A witness claims that the accused confessed outside court.
predicates.confession_made_after_long_interval: The alleged confession was made a substantial time after the event under investigation.
predicates.supporting_witness_denies_confession: At least one witness who was said to have heard the confession denies that it was made.
predicates.circumstances_of_statement_are_doubtful: The setting and circumstances in which the statement was allegedly made undermine confidence in its reliability.

members.legal_issue: An uncorroborated extrajudicial confession made to a person without demonstrated influence or status may carry very little evidentiary weight.
material_facts: The accused allegedly confessed to an acquaintance, saying he had done so because the police were pursuing him and he wished to avoid harassment.
The recipient had no demonstrated influence with the police or status to protect the accused, and there was no other evidence corroborating the confession.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated an extrajudicial confession as weak evidence in the circumstances, particularly where the recipient had no demonstrated ability to protect the accused and there was no corroboration. The judgment cites no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The confession was a very weak piece of evidence and was hardly of any consequence.

rule.if: circumstantial_murder_appeal and confession_made_outside_court and recipient_lacks_demonstrated_influence and confession_lacks_corroboration

predicates.circumstantial_murder_appeal: The accused appealed a murder conviction resting on circumstantial evidence.
predicates.confession_made_outside_court: The accused allegedly confessed to a person outside court.
predicates.recipient_lacks_demonstrated_influence: The person who received the confession had no demonstrated influence with the police or status to protect the accused.
predicates.confession_lacks_corroboration: No other evidence corroborated the alleged confession.

members.legal_issue: An alleged extra-judicial confession should not be relied on when its words are not adequately reproduced and the circumstances undermine its voluntariness and truthfulness.
material_facts: A witness attributed a confession to the accused but did not reproduce its exact words or words as nearly as possible.
The witness said the statement was made after the witness and accused had consumed liquor.
The trial court and High Court did not rely on the confession.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the alleged confession as unreliable because its words were not adequately stated and the circumstances gave reason to doubt that it was voluntary and truthful.
members.conclusion: The alleged extra-judicial confession was excluded from consideration as a basis for guilt.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial or an appeal from a criminal trial.
predicates.alleged_extra_judicial_confession: A witness attributes an out-of-court confession to the accused.
predicates.confession_words_not_reproduced: The witness does not state the confession's exact words or words as nearly as possible.
predicates.circumstances_undermine_voluntariness_or: The circumstances of the alleged statement give reason to doubt that it was voluntary and truthful.
predicates.confession_not_relied_on: The alleged confession is not relied on to establish guilt.

members.legal_issue: A co-accused’s confession is not safe corroboration of an approver when it lacks assurance of independence or was obtained without adequate safeguards before its recording.
material_facts: Two co-accused had made confessions and later retracted them; the confessions were relied on to corroborate the approver.
One co-accused was brought to the magistrate together with the approver, and the record did not establish that their accounts were independent or made without prior opportunity for concert.

For the other co-accused, the magistrate did not establish that he had been warned that he was not bound to confess and that a confession could be used against him, or that he had been given adequate time to reflect on whether to confess.
The confessions could not be tested by cross-examination.
members.legal_principle: Under section 30 of the Evidence Act, a confession by a co-accused jointly tried for the same offence may be taken into consideration, but it is not proof and is weaker than evidence tested by cross-examination. A confession may lend assurance to other evidence, but one accomplice’s confession should not ordinarily be used to corroborate another without independent evidence implicating the accused; apparent agreement between confessions is less weighty where independence is not established. A person produced for confession must be free from possible police influence, given time to reflect, and told that confession is not compulsory and may be used against him. The Court relied on Bhuboni Sahu v. The King, Kashmira Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Sarwan Singh v. The State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: Neither co-accused confession could safely be relied on to corroborate the approver.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.co_accused_confessions_offered_as_corrob: The prosecution relied on confessions by co-accused to corroborate an accomplice’s testimony against the accused.
predicates.co_accused_confessions_lacked_independen: The record did not establish that the confessions were independently made, or showed that a confession was recorded without adequate warning and time for reflection.
