members.legal_issue: A co-accused’s confession that creates strong suspicion against an accused police officer is not, without independent evidence, a safe basis for conviction.
material_facts: The police officers were charged with conspiring to conceal evidence and screen the actual offenders through a dishonest investigation.
The only evidence implicating those officers was the confessional statements of co-accused.
The confessions created strong suspicion about the officers’ connections with the gangs and possible assistance, but there was no independent evidence of their alleged participation.
members.legal_principle: Although a confession under Section 15 of the TADA Act may be substantive evidence against a co-accused if admissible, voluntary and believable, the court held that the evidence in this case did not safely support conviction of the police officers without independent evidence. Its discussion of Section 30 of the Evidence Act and the views in Nalini recognized the need for caution in relying on a confession against another accused.
members.conclusion: The court did not consider it safe to convict the police officers solely on the co-accused confessions and affirmed their acquittals.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging acquittals.
predicates.accused_is_charged_with_conspiracy: The accused was charged with participating in a conspiracy.
predicates.only_evidence_against_accused_is_coaccus: The only evidence implicating the accused consisted of confessions made by co-accused.
predicates.confession_creates_suspicion_without_ind: The confessions raised suspicion but lacked independent evidentiary support for the accused’s alleged participation.

members.legal_issue: An occupant whose authority to occupy public premises has expired and who remains after receiving the required eviction notice is in unauthorised occupation and may be evicted under the public-premises procedure.
material_facts: The lease expired and was not extended.
The occupant remained in the premises after the lease expired and did not vacate after agreeing to seek time to do so.
The Estate Officer issued the required notice and ordered eviction, and the occupant had no acceptable defence to continued occupation.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(g) of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 defines unauthorised occupation; Sections 4 and 5 provide for notice and an eviction order. The Court held that the expired lease had not been extended and that the required notice had been given.
members.conclusion: The occupant was in unauthorised occupation after the lease expired, and the eviction order was justified.

rule.if: appeal_from_public_premises_eviction_order and occupancy_authority_expired and occupant_remained and required_notice_given

predicates.appeal_from_public_premises_eviction_ord: The proceeding is an appeal concerning an eviction order made under a public-premises procedure.
predicates.occupancy_authority_expired: The occupant’s authority to occupy the premises had expired without extension.
predicates.occupant_remained: The occupant remained in the premises after that authority expired.
predicates.required_notice_given: The eviction authority gave the notice required before ordering eviction.

members.legal_issue: A licensee’s continued occupation of a public building after the licence expires or is terminated constitutes unauthorised occupation for the purpose of statutory eviction proceedings.
material_facts: A public corporation owned the building and had allowed the occupant to use it under a licence.
After the occupant defaulted on licence fees, the licence was terminated, but the occupant remained in the building.
An Estate Officer issued notice and ordered eviction under the public-buildings eviction legislation.
The occupant brought a civil suit seeking to prevent eviction under that order.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(f) covers both occupation without authority from the outset and continued occupation after authority expires or is determined. Its words “whether by way of lease or any other mode of transfer” include a licence. Reading the provision to exclude licensees would defeat the purpose of the speedy statutory remedy. The Court relied on the distinction between lease and licence under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, and on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, B.M. Lall v. M/s. Dunlop Rubber Co. (India) Ltd., Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, Khalil Ahmed Bashir Ahmed v. Tufelhussein Samasbhai Sarangpurwala, Ashoka Marketing Ltd. v. Punjab National Bank, M/s. Jain Ink Manufacturing Company v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, and Jiwan Dass v. Life Insurance Corporation of India. The Court also noted the materially similar definition in Section 2(g) of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. Under Sections 3–5 of the Kerala Act, an Estate Officer may conduct eviction proceedings and order eviction; Section 10 provides an appeal, and Section 15 bars a suit challenging the eviction order.
members.conclusion: The continued occupation of a public building by a licensee after the licence expires or is determined is unauthorised occupation under Section 2(f) of the Kerala Public Buildings (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1968. The Estate Officer had jurisdiction to order eviction, and the statutory bar on suits challenging the order applied.

rule.if: public_building_occupation and occupation_under_license and license_authority_ended and statutory_public_building_eviction_proceeding

predicates.public_building_occupation: A person remained in a building that belonged to or was held by a public authority covered by the applicable eviction scheme.
predicates.occupation_under_license: The public authority had permitted the person to occupy the building under a licence.
predicates.license_authority_ended: The licence expired or was terminated while the person remained in the building.
predicates.statutory_public_building_eviction_proce: An eviction officer proceeded under a statutory scheme for eviction from public buildings.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who remains in public premises after the authority under which the tenant entered has expired or been terminated is in unauthorised occupation.
material_facts: The occupants had entered the premises as tenants under leases.
The tenancies later expired or were terminated, but the occupants continued to occupy the premises.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(g) defines unauthorised occupation to include continued occupation after the authority under which a person was allowed to occupy has expired or been determined. The words covering a grant or any other mode of transfer are broad enough to include a lease under the Transfer of Property Act. The Court distinguished Brigadier K.K. Verma v. Union of India, which concerned an earlier enactment without this express definition, and referred to Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The continued occupation after expiry or determination of the tenancy falls within unauthorised occupation under the public-premises eviction regime.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_case and occupant_entered_as_tenant and tenancy_authority_expired_or_terminated and occupant_remained

predicates.public_premises_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns occupation of premises covered by a public-premises eviction regime.
predicates.occupant_entered_as_tenant: The occupant initially took possession under a tenancy or lease.
predicates.tenancy_authority_expired_or_terminated: The authority created by the tenancy later expired or was brought to an end.
predicates.occupant_remained: The occupant continued to possess the premises after that authority ended.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who entered premises before they became public premises may become an unauthorised occupant when the tenancy is validly determined and the tenant continues to occupy them.
material_facts: The occupant had been inducted as a tenant by the prior private owner before the premises were acquired by a public corporation.
After acquiring the premises, the corporation gave a notice determining the tenancy; the validity of that notice was not challenged for deciding this issue.
The occupant continued to occupy the premises after the tenancy was determined and after the public-premises eviction law came into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(2)(g) of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 concerns occupation, a continuing state, and expressly includes continued occupation after the authority to occupy has expired or been determined. A tenant's original lawful entry does not prevent later occupation from being unauthorised once the tenancy is determined. Raj Kumar Devendra Singh v. State of Punjab was distinguished because the Punjab statute focused on entry into possession, unlike section 2(2)(g); the court also relied on the notice determining the tenancy under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.
members.conclusion: The occupant was in unauthorised occupation, and the Estate Officer could proceed under the public-premises eviction law.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_proceeding and occupant_entered_under_tenancy_before_public_ownership and tenancy_validly_determined and occupant_continued_occupying

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction through a special process for premises belonging to a public body.
predicates.occupant_entered_under_tenancy_before_pu: The occupant first took possession lawfully as a tenant before the premises became publicly owned.
predicates.tenancy_validly_determined: The landlord validly ended the occupant's authority to remain under the tenancy.
predicates.occupant_continued_occupying: The occupant remained in the premises after that authority ended.

members.legal_issue: An authority using a statutory summary process to evict an occupant from public premises must comply with the prescribed notice and opportunity-to-show-cause procedure before eviction.
material_facts: The occupants were in possession of the premises when the authority took possession, demolished their factory, and removed machinery and other goods.
The authority relied on a notice said to terminate the lease, but neither side produced it and its contents could not be established.
The other notice described in the record concerned payment of damages and an opportunity to show cause about those damages, not the proposed eviction.
The authority did not establish that the occupants had been given an opportunity to show cause against eviction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958 require the prescribed notice procedure, including notice of the grounds for proposed eviction and an opportunity to show cause, before eviction under the Act. The authority bears the burden of satisfying the Court that it acted in accordance with the law. Denying the opportunity to answer the proposed eviction also contravenes natural justice. The Court relied on no earlier case for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The prescribed eviction procedure was not shown to have been followed, so the eviction was unlawful; the petition was allowed and the premises and seized goods were ordered restored.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_case and occupant_evicted and eviction_notice_compliance_unproven and no_opportunity_to_answer_eviction

predicates.public_premises_eviction_case: An authority pursued a statutory summary process to evict an occupant from premises treated as public premises.
predicates.occupant_evicted: The authority took possession of premises occupied by a person and removed that person's property.
predicates.eviction_notice_compliance_unproven: The authority did not establish that it had followed the required notice procedure for the proposed eviction.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_answer_eviction: The occupant was not given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed eviction.

members.legal_issue: A local authority exercising a summary-eviction power must hear affected occupants and give reasons for its decision.
material_facts: The occupants faced summary eviction after the final scheme allocated their lands for public purposes.
Whether the occupants remained entitled to occupy the lands had to be determined by interpreting the final scheme.
The local authority exercised the power, and the governing rule did not expressly exclude a hearing.
members.legal_principle: Natural justice applies to the quasi-judicial decision whether occupants remain entitled to occupy land under a final scheme. The requirement of a hearing and a reasoned order is read into the summary-eviction procedure. The Court agreed with the High Court’s construction of section 54 and Rule 27; it also described the safeguards of hearing and reasons as features of quasi-judicial power, consistent with its discussion of Organo Chemical Industries v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The power is quasi-judicial and must be exercised after hearing the occupants and issuing a reasoned speaking order.

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns summary eviction of occupants from land they are alleged to have no continuing right to occupy.
predicates.occupant_entitlement_depends_on_scheme_i: The decision-maker must interpret the applicable scheme to determine whether the occupants are entitled to remain.
predicates.occupants_face_adverse_eviction_decision: The decision-maker is considering an order that would remove the occupants from the land.

members.legal_issue: A mining lease grant or renewal requires a fresh environmental clearance, and an earlier clearance cannot by itself authorize the later grant or renewal.
material_facts: The earlier leases had expired, and the State was required to grant fresh mining leases.
Some operators relied on environmental clearances issued under the 1994 notification, while others relied on clearances under the 2006 notification.
The Court found that the 1994 clearances had a five-year validity and that a clearance was required when a lease was renewed.
The Court found that the 2006 clearances could remain valid for the estimated project life, subject to a maximum of thirty years, but a fresh lease still required a fresh clearance.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the Environment Impact Assessment Notification of 27 January 1994 and paragraph 9 of the Environment Impact Assessment Notification of 14 September 2006. It relied on M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (2004) 12 SCC 118, which held that a mining operation requires environmental clearance and that a 1994 clearance is valid for five years, and Common Cause v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 499, which reaffirmed that renewal after 27 January 1994 requires clearance. The Court also relied on Ambica Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, (1987) 1 SCC 213, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P., 1989 Supp (1) SCC 504, and State of M.P. v. Krishnadas Tikaram, 1995 Supp (1) SCC 587, on compliance with statutory requirements at renewal. Under the 2006 notification, a mining-project clearance lasts for the estimated project life up to thirty years; that does not dispense with a fresh clearance for a fresh lease.
members.conclusion: Fresh environmental clearances were required for fresh mining leases. A valid clearance under the 2006 notification did not need to be set aside merely because of its validity period, but a new clearance was required upon a fresh lease. The 1994 clearances did not remove the need for a fresh clearance at renewal and had expired by the relevant time.

predicates.mining_project_requires_fresh_lease_or_r: A mining project is proceeding under a fresh lease or a renewed lease.
predicates.prior_clearance_relates_to_earlier_lease: The environmental clearance relied on was issued for an earlier lease or an earlier grant.

members.legal_issue: Environmental clearance is required when a mining lease is renewed after the environmental-clearance notification takes effect, even if the original lease predates the notification.
material_facts: Some mining leases had been granted before the notification requiring environmental clearance, while others were granted afterward.
Renewal of many leases came up for consideration after the notification, but the required environmental impact assessment clearance had not been obtained.
The notification required clearance before mining operations could be undertaken, and the court found that the renewal was a fresh grant.
members.legal_principle: The notification dated 27 January 1994, issued under Sections 3(1) and 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, requires clearance for covered mining projects before operations commence. A renewal is a fresh grant and must comply with the law then in force. The court relied on Ambica Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P., and State of M.P. v. Krishnadas Tikaram; it distinguished Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, which did not decide the application of the notification at the renewal stage.
members.conclusion: The environmental-clearance notification applies to renewals considered after it took effect, and mining operations cannot commence without the required clearance.

predicates.mining_lease_renewal_is_considered: An authority is considering renewal of a mining lease.
predicates.clearance_requirement_is_in_force: A requirement for environmental clearance applies to the mining project when renewal is considered.
predicates.environmental_clearance_is_absent: The required environmental clearance has not been obtained.

members.legal_issue: Mining operations requiring environmental clearance cannot lawfully proceed without prior clearance, and an approved or modified mining plan does not replace that requirement or make a later clearance retrospective.
material_facts: The mining operations included new projects, renewals, expansions, and production exceeding environmental-clearance limits.
Some lessees relied on approved or modified mining plans, administrative circulars, or the possibility of later clearance to justify operations without prior environmental clearance.
Environmental clearances had been granted for some operations after the relevant mining had already occurred.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the Environment Impact Assessment Notifications of 27 January 1994 and 14 September 2006, Sections 3(1) and 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and Rule 5(3)(d) of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986. It relied on M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, holding that the notifications are mandatory, apply to renewal, and are not displaced by approval of a mining plan or by circulars. For the 1994 notification, a pre-existing project could continue without clearance only within the stated exemption, including the required pre-notification pollution-control consent and no disqualifying expansion; the production benchmark for assessing expansion was 1993–94. Under the 2006 notification, covered leases of five hectares or more required clearance.
members.conclusion: Environmental clearance was required for new projects, relevant expansions and modernizations, and renewals; for covered projects, a clearance takes effect no earlier than its grant and cannot retrospectively authorize earlier mining.

rule.if: mining_operations and (new_mining_project or lease_renewal or expansion_increases_pollution or covered_large_lease) and not prior_environmental_clearance

predicates.mining_operations: A lease holder undertakes operations to extract minerals.
predicates.new_mining_project: The mineral extraction is part of a newly commenced mining project.
predicates.lease_renewal: The lease holder seeks or operates under a renewal of the mining lease.
predicates.expansion_increases_pollution: An expansion or modernization is expected to increase the project’s pollution load.
predicates.covered_large_lease: The mining project falls within the category for which the applicable environmental framework requires clearance based on the lease’s size.
predicates.prior_environmental_clearance: The project received environmental clearance before undertaking the operations in question.

members.legal_issue: An administrative circular cannot extend the environmental-clearance deadline so as to authorize mining undertaken without the clearance required by the statutory notification.
material_facts: Mining activity had been undertaken without the environmental clearance required by the 1994 notification.
A ministry circular extended the opportunity for defaulting units to seek clearance after commencing activity.
The court found that the circular did not purport to legalize mining without compliance and, in any event, could not alter the statutory notification.
members.legal_principle: The 1994 notification, issued under Sections 3(1) and 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, is mandatory. A statutory notification cannot be modified by an administrative circular, and the clearance requirement must be satisfied before covered mining commences.
members.conclusion: The circular does not apply to mining activity and cannot authorize commencement or continuation of mining without the required clearance.

predicates.mining_began_without_required_clearance: Mining activity began without a clearance required by an applicable environmental rule.
predicates.administrative_circular_is_relied_on_to_: An administrative circular is relied on as authority to cure the failure to obtain that clearance.

members.legal_issue: A direction to grant fresh mining leases does not permit the State to satisfy that direction by renewing expired leases.
material_facts: A prior final judgment held that the leases had expired and directed the State to decide how to grant mining leases in the future.
The State granted second renewals rather than granting fresh leases.
The prior judgment had been made with the existing second-renewal applications and related payments in view.
members.legal_principle: The meaning of a judicial direction is determined in its context. Here, the declaration and directions in Goa Foundation v. Union of India, (2014) 6 SCC 738, required fresh grants and did not authorize renewals of expired leases. Although renewal may in some contexts amount to a fresh grant, a direction to grant a fresh lease is not a direction to renew an expired lease. The Court also distinguished the interim direction in Common Cause v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 499. The State’s grant of leases must comply with the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and constitutional requirements.
members.conclusion: The State was required to grant fresh leases, not second renewals; the second renewals were contrary to the prior judgment and were quashed.

rule.if: challenge_to_second_renewal and leases_expired and prior_judgment_required_fresh_grants and state_granted_renewals

predicates.challenge_to_second_renewal: A proceeding challenges the validity of second renewals of mining leases.
predicates.leases_expired: The mining leases had expired before the State made its later decisions.
predicates.prior_judgment_required_fresh_grants: A prior final judgment directed the State to make fresh grants rather than continue the expired leases by renewal.
predicates.state_granted_renewals: The State granted renewals of the expired leases instead of making fresh grants.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot direct execution of second-renewal leases where a prior final judgment requires the State to grant fresh mining leases.
material_facts: A High Court directed the State to execute leases for some applicants and to decide other second-renewal applications.
The High Court relied in part on applicants’ timely applications, approved mining plans, payments, and promissory estoppel.
A prior final judgment of the Supreme Court required fresh mining leases rather than second renewals.
members.legal_principle: The prior decision in Goa Foundation v. Union of India, (2014) 6 SCC 738, required fresh mining leases and did not authorize second renewals. A lower court’s directions cannot contradict that binding determination. The Court accordingly set aside the decision in Lithoferro v. State of Goa, MANU/MH/1292/2014, and rejected its interpretation of the earlier judgment.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment and directions were set aside because they proceeded on an erroneous understanding of the prior Supreme Court judgment.

predicates.appeal_challenges_renewal_direction: An appeal challenges a court order concerning renewal of mining leases.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_required_fresh_gran: A prior final judgment required fresh grants rather than renewals of expired leases.
predicates.lower_court_ordered_second_renewals: The lower court directed the State to execute or decide second-renewal leases.

members.legal_issue: A law that was void for want of legislative competence when enacted cannot qualify as an existing law protected from constitutional challenge.
material_facts: The challenged acquisition law was enacted before the Constitution commenced.
The law did not satisfy the compensation condition that limited the legislature's power to authorize compulsory acquisition.
The law was not certified under the constitutional procedure that could protect certain pre-commencement laws despite non-compliance with that condition.
members.legal_principle: Under section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, providing for compensation was a condition on legislative power, and a law made without satisfying that condition was a nullity. Article 366(10) defines an existing law as one made by a legislature or other body having power to make it. Articles 31(5) and 31(6), read together, do not save a law that was void when made; unlike clause (5), clause (6) expressly provides a route for certification of certain laws that did not comply with section 299(2). The court referred to H. P. Khandalwal v. State of U.P., Assistant Collector, Thana Prant v. Jamnadas Gokuldas Patel, and State of West Bengal v. Bon Behari Mondal.
members.conclusion: The law was void from its inception and was not an existing law protected by Article 31(5)(a).

predicates.pre_constitution_acquisition_law_challen: The case challenges a law concerning compulsory acquisition that was enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.law_lacked_power_condition_when_enacted: The legislature enacted the law without satisfying a condition on its power to authorize compulsory acquisition.
predicates.no_constitutional_certification: The law did not receive the certification available under the constitutional procedure for certain pre-commencement laws.

members.legal_issue: Constitutional protection for laws concerning acquisition of estates does not revive a pre-constitutional law that was void from its inception.
material_facts: The challenged law was void from its inception because it failed to satisfy the pre-constitutional condition on legislative power.
The law therefore had no legal existence when the Constitution commenced.
The State relied on the constitutional protection for laws concerning acquisition of estates or rights in estates.
members.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects laws within its scope from specified challenges based on rights under Articles 14, 19 and 31, but does not revive laws that were void when enacted. The court distinguished Dhiruba Devisingh Gohil v. State of Bombay and State of U.P. v. H. H. Maharaja Brijendra Singh, which concerned the distinct protection in Article 31-B. Article 31-B is not governed by Article 31-A and is not merely illustrative of laws that would otherwise fall within Article 31-A.
members.conclusion: Article 31-A did not save the law because it had no legal existence when the Constitution commenced.

predicates.pre_constitution_acquisition_law_challen: The case challenges a law concerning compulsory acquisition that was enacted before the Constitution commenced.
predicates.law_was_void_when_enacted: The law was void at the time it was enacted because the legislature lacked power to enact it in that form.
predicates.law_had_no_legal_existence_at_constituti: The law had no legal existence when the Constitution commenced.

members.legal_issue: A post-constitutional law that deprives a person of property without the compensation required when the law was enacted is invalid and cannot be revived by a later constitutional amendment removing the restriction.
material_facts: The challenged transfer law was enacted after the Constitution came into force and declared specified transfers void, depriving transferees of rights they would otherwise acquire.
The law did not provide for compensation for that deprivation.
A later constitutional amendment changed the constitutional rule governing compulsory acquisition, but was not retrospective.
members.legal_principle: The constitutionality of a law is judged by the Constitution as it stood when the law was enacted, subject to a retrospective constitutional amendment. Under Articles 13(2) and 31(2), as they stood at enactment, the law contravened the constitutional protection against uncompensated deprivation of property. The Fourth Amendment was not retrospective and could not validate the law through the doctrine of eclipse, which applies to pre-constitutional laws under Article 13(1), not post-constitutional laws under Article 13(2). The Court relied on State of West Bengal v. Sabodh Gopal Bose, Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P., Karam Singh v. Nihal Khan, Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. State of Bombay, Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay, Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay, Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The transfer law was unconstitutional and of no force or effect; the later constitutional amendment did not revive it.

predicates.constitutional_challenge: A person challenged the validity of a law in a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.post_constitution_law: The challenged law was enacted after the Constitution came into force.
predicates.deprives_property_without_required_compe: The law deprived a person of property without providing the compensation required by the constitutional rule in force when the law was enacted.
predicates.later_amendment_removes_constitutional_b: A later constitutional amendment removed the constitutional restriction that the law had contravened, without retrospectively validating the law.

members.legal_issue: A post-Constitution law made in violation of fundamental rights is void from its inception and cannot be treated as operative law.
material_facts: An earlier amendment had removed the right to seek eviction of a tenant from a non-residential building for the landlord’s own use.
The Supreme Court had held that the amendment’s distinction between residential and non-residential premises violated Article 14 and struck it down.
members.legal_principle: Article 13(2) makes a post-Constitution law that contravenes fundamental rights void to the extent of the contravention. Such a law is a nullity from its inception, rather than a valid law that later ceases to operate. The Court relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Harbilas Rai Bansal v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The amendment was void from its inception and could not be relied on as part of the law later extended to the territory.

predicates.constitutional_validity_issue: A proceeding considers whether a law is constitutionally valid.
predicates.post_constitutional_law: The challenged law was enacted after the Constitution came into force.
predicates.fundamental_rights_infringement: The challenged law takes away or abridges a fundamental right.

members.legal_issue: A validating law that depends on deeming acquisitions under an unconstitutional earlier law cannot validate those acquisitions.
material_facts: The later law deemed certain land taken before it came into force to have been acquired under the earlier acquisition law.
Its compensation, award, and other ancillary provisions relied on the earlier law, and its central deeming provision was the basis for treating the acquisitions as valid.
The earlier acquisition law was unconstitutional and had no legal existence.
members.legal_principle: A legislature cannot make an acquisition valid by deeming it to have been made under a constitutionally invalid law. Where a later law's core deeming provision depends on that earlier law, the later law's ancillary provisions fall with it and cannot be enforced.
members.conclusion: The later law was invalid because its deemed acquisitions and ancillary provisions depended on the unconstitutional earlier law; the legislature could not validate acquisitions made under that law.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_validating_l: A party challenged the validity of a law intended to validate earlier land acquisitions.
predicates.underlying_acquisition_law_invalid: The earlier law under which the acquisitions are deemed to have occurred was held unconstitutional.
predicates.later_law_depends_on_underlying_law: The later law's central deeming provision and its ancillary acquisition or compensation provisions depend on the earlier law.

members.legal_issue: A prospective extension of another law cannot validate a demand that was invalid when made.
material_facts: The State relied on legislation extending a different reclamation law to the affected area to support the demands.
That extension operated prospectively, while the demands had already been made and were invalid when made.
members.legal_principle: The Madhya Pradesh Reclamation of Lands (Extension to Bhopal) Act, 1957 operated prospectively, not retrospectively. It therefore could not supply a legal basis after the fact for demands that were invalid when issued. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The extension could not sustain the demands because it operated prospectively and did not validate demands that were invalid when made.

predicates.appeal_relies_on_later_extension_of_anot: An appeal relies on legislation that later extended a different legal regime to the relevant area.
predicates.extension_operates_prospectively: The extending legislation applies only from its commencement and does not operate retrospectively.
predicates.demand_invalid_when_made: The demand lacked a valid legal basis at the time it was issued.

members.legal_issue: The statutory rule deeming a previously assessed Hindu undivided family to continue applies to a partial partition of property even when the family members remain unchanged.
material_facts: The family had previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
It claimed that some properties had been partitioned while the same members continued to hold the remaining family properties as an undivided family.
The claimed partition was not recognized under the statutory requirements because the properties capable of physical division were not physically divided.
members.legal_principle: Section 171(1), read with the provisions governing claims of total or partial partition and Explanation (b), applies to partial partitions as to property as well as to partitions as to persons. Parliament expressly extended the statutory scheme beyond Section 25A of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, which had not applied to partial partitions. The principle in Appovier v. Rama Subba Aiyan recognizes that property subject to a partial partition may be held by members as tenants-in-common while other family property remains undivided; Section 171 nevertheless supplies a tax-law rule deeming the family to continue until the required finding is recorded. The earlier interpretation in Sir Sunder Singh Majithia v. Commissioner of Income-tax concerned the former statutory scheme.
members.conclusion: The continuation rule applies to a partial partition of property even though the family remains undivided as to its other property and its membership does not change.

rule.if: tax_assessment_partition_claim and previously_assessed_family and partial_property_separation and family_membership_unchanged

predicates.tax_assessment_partition_claim: A family previously assessed as undivided asserts a partition during an income-tax assessment.
predicates.previously_assessed_family: The family has previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.partial_property_separation: The family members claim to have separated some property while retaining other property jointly.
predicates.family_membership_unchanged: The same members remain in the family after the claimed separation of property.

members.legal_issue: Income from property subject to a claimed partial partition remains includible in the Hindu undivided family's income unless the required statutory finding of partition is recorded.
material_facts: The family claimed that its properties had been partially partitioned under Hindu law and that income from them thereafter belonged to individual members.
The tax authority rejected the claim because the properties capable of physical division had not been physically divided, and no statutory finding recognizing the partial partition was recorded.
The High Court nevertheless held that the income from those properties should be excluded from the family's income; the Revenue challenged that ruling.
members.legal_principle: Section 171(1) deems a family previously assessed as undivided to continue as such except to the extent a finding of partition is given under that section. Under Sections 171(2) and (3), the assessing officer must inquire into the claim and record a finding; the assessment consequences of a qualifying finding are addressed in Sections 171(4) and (5). The definition in the Explanation requires physical division where property admits of it. Section 10(2) does not displace that statutory scheme. The rule differs from the former Section 25A scheme, which did not cover partial partitions. Nor does the analogy to an alienation in favour of a stranger apply where the family seeks to treat its own property as partitioned without satisfying the statutory conditions; A. Kannan Chetty v. Commissioner of Income-tax distinguished an alienation from a family transaction in which the family retains the property and its income.
members.conclusion: The income from the properties remained includible in the family's total income because no finding recognizing the partial partition had been recorded under Section 171.

rule.if: tax_assessment_partition_claim and family_previously_assessed_as_undivided and partition_finding_not_recorded and income_from_claimed_partition_property

predicates.tax_assessment_partition_claim: A family previously assessed as undivided claims a partition in an income-tax assessment.
predicates.family_previously_assessed_as_undivided: The family was previously assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.partition_finding_not_recorded: No statutory finding recognizing the claimed partition has been recorded after inquiry.
predicates.income_from_claimed_partition_property: The income being assessed comes from property that the family claims to have partitioned.

members.legal_issue: Income from property claimed to have been partially partitioned remains included in the total income of a previously assessed Hindu undivided family until an income-tax finding recognizes the partition.
material_facts: The family claimed that the eighteen properties had been partially partitioned under Hindu law and that their income thereafter belonged to the individual members.
The claim did not result in a finding recognizing the partial partition under section 171.
The family had previously been assessed as an undivided family.
members.legal_principle: Under section 171(1), a Hindu family previously assessed as undivided is deemed to continue as such for the purposes of the Act except to the extent that a finding of partition is recorded under that section. The provision applies to partial partitions as well as total partitions, as reflected in section 171 and its Explanation. Until such a finding is recorded, the family is deemed to own the property and receive its income, even if a partition has occurred under Hindu law. The Court rejected reliance on decisions under section 25A of the 1922 Act, which had been construed as not applying to partial partitions, and distinguished A. Kannan Chetty v. Commissioner of Income-tax, which concerned an alienation that removed property and income from the family’s hands.
members.conclusion: The income from the properties had to be included in the family’s total income because no finding recognizing the partial partition had been recorded.

predicates.income_tax_assessment_of_previously_undi: An income-tax assessment concerned a family that had previously been assessed as undivided.
predicates.property_claimed_as_partially_partitione: A family member claimed that particular family property had been partially partitioned.
predicates.official_partition_finding: The tax authority recorded a finding recognizing the claimed partition for tax purposes.

members.legal_issue: A Hindu undivided family previously assessed as undivided continues to be treated as such for tax purposes when a partition is claimed but no order apportioning tax liability on the basis of that partition has been made.
material_facts: The family had previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
The appellant claimed that the family had partitioned and that tea estates had fallen to his share.
No order apportioning tax liability on the basis of the claimed partition had been made.
The appellant challenged assessments made in respect of agricultural income from the tea estates.
members.legal_principle: Rule 23 of the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Rules, 1939 provides that a Hindu family hitherto assessed as undivided or joint is deemed to continue in that status for the purposes of the Act unless an order apportioning tax liability on the basis of partition is made. The Court held that the language of the rule is clear and applies even where the assessment in question is not merely a recovery of tax under an earlier assessment.
members.conclusion: The family was to be treated as continuing to be a Hindu undivided family for the purposes of the Act because no order apportioning liability on the basis of the alleged partition had been passed.

rule.if: tax_assessment_challenge and prior_joint_assessment and partition_claimed and not apportionment_order_passed

predicates.tax_assessment_challenge: The proceeding challenges an assessment of tax on income attributed to a family previously assessed as undivided or joint.
predicates.prior_joint_assessment: The taxing authority had previously assessed the family as undivided or joint.
predicates.partition_claimed: A member of the family claimed that the family had partitioned.
predicates.apportionment_order_passed: The taxing authority made an order apportioning tax liability on the basis of the claimed partition.
predicates.family_treated_as_joint_for_tax_purposes: The family is treated as continuing to be undivided or joint for tax purposes.

members.legal_issue: A later civil partition decree does not require income-tax authorities to recognize a partition that they previously rejected for tax purposes when the family was assessed as undivided and the tax-law appeal was not pursued by reference.
material_facts: A claim of partition under Section 25A was rejected, and the family was assessed as undivided.
A civil court passed a preliminary partition decree after the tax partition claim had been rejected.
The appeal against the tax decision was dismissed, and no reference challenging the Tribunal’s decision was sought.
members.legal_principle: Section 25A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 provided that a family assessed as undivided continued to be deemed an undivided Hindu family for purposes of the Act if no order accepting partition had been passed. The Court held that the later civil decree did not bind the income-tax authorities, particularly when no reference under the Act had been sought from the Tribunal’s decision. No earlier judicial case was cited for this holding.
members.conclusion: The income-tax authorities were not bound by the later preliminary partition decree, and the family continued to be treated as undivided for purposes of the tax proceedings.

rule.if: tax_partition_proceeding and partition_claim_rejected and family_assessed_as_undivided and later_civil_partition_decree and no_tax_reference_sought

predicates.tax_partition_proceeding: The matter concerns a tax proceeding in which a family’s claim that it had partitioned was considered.
predicates.partition_claim_rejected: The tax authority rejected the family’s claim that it had partitioned.
predicates.family_assessed_as_undivided: The family was assessed for tax as an undivided family.
predicates.later_civil_partition_decree: A civil court issued a partition decree after the tax authority had rejected the partition claim.
predicates.no_tax_reference_sought: The affected party did not seek a reference challenging the tax tribunal’s decision.

members.legal_issue: A matter should be remanded for a fresh trial when errors in handling pleadings and title evidence have left material questions of title and property identification unresolved.
material_facts: The trial court refused the proposed amendment and excluded the certified copy of the old lease without first giving the claimant an opportunity to establish the relevant foundation.
The appellate court did not properly assess the claimant’s documentary evidence and placed undue reliance on City Survey records.
Whether the disputed property fell within the lease and whether it could be identified required further consideration and potentially a commission.
members.legal_principle: A fresh trial is appropriate where errors in procedure and evaluation of evidence have prevented a satisfactory determination of the real dispute and material questions remain unresolved. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this disposition in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The judgments and decrees below were set aside and the suit was remanded for a fresh trial and disposal, with the specified opportunities to amend the pleading, address the lease evidence, and identify the property.

predicates.appeal_from_dismissal_of_property_suit: The proceeding is an appeal from the dismissal of a suit concerning property.
predicates.material_title_questions_unresolved: Material questions about title or the identity of the property remain undecided.
predicates.procedural_errors_prevented_satisfactory: Errors in handling pleadings or evidence prevented a satisfactory adjudication of the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A property dispute must be remanded for fresh determination when inadequate investigation and an incomplete record leave material questions of title and possession unresolved.
material_facts: The appeal arose from a suit concerning title to and possession of disputed property.

The record included old documents, but the sale deed's referenced plan and mortgage were not produced, relevant agreements were missing, and the relationship between the claimed property and land for which compensation had been paid was unresolved.
The courts below had not adequately investigated or assessed the central factual disputes, including the extent and location of the property.
The Supreme Court considered that a local investigation by a commissioner could assist if a party applied for one.
members.legal_principle: Where the record and the courts' inquiry do not adequately resolve the real factual controversy, the matter may be remanded for fresh determination. The remand was confined to title and possession; the parties could provide relevant evidence and seek a commissioner, and could seek only amendments strictly necessary to clarify those issues without changing the nature of the case. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this direction.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the case was remanded to the trial court to decide title and possession afresh, with further evidence and any requested commissioner investigation confined to those issues.

predicates.appeal_from_property_title_and_possessio: An appeal arose from a suit in which title to and possession of property were disputed.
predicates.material_title_or_possession_questions_u: Material questions about the parties' title or possession remained unresolved.
predicates.record_or_inquiry_inadequate: The evidence or investigation below was insufficient to resolve those material questions.
predicates.case_remanded_for_fresh_determination_of: The case is sent back for a fresh decision on title and possession.

members.legal_issue: A suit may be remanded for retrial where the evidence leaves material factual questions unresolved and the parties seek and accept a retrial.
material_facts: The plaintiff requested that the suit be remanded for retrial after the appellate court set aside the ex parte decree.
The defendant opposing the plaintiff's claim supported the request for remand and conceded that the suit should be retried.
The existing evidence raised questions about the third defendant's possession before the earlier decree, requiring further evidence and consideration of other issues.
members.legal_principle: In the circumstances, including the plaintiff's request, the opposing defendant's concession, and the further factual issues requiring evidence, the interests of justice supported remanding the suit for retrial. No earlier cases or specific statutory provisions are relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The appellate judgments were set aside and the suit was remanded to the trial court for retrial and disposal in accordance with law.

rule.if: appeal_from_suit_disposition and material_factual_issues_require_further_evidence and plaintiff_requests_retrial_remand and opposing_party_concedes_retrial_remand

predicates.appeal_from_suit_disposition: A party appeals from a court's disposition of a civil suit.
predicates.material_factual_issues_require_further_: The existing pleadings and evidence leave material factual issues that require further evidence and consideration.
predicates.plaintiff_requests_retrial_remand: The plaintiff asks that the suit be sent back for a new trial.
predicates.opposing_party_concedes_retrial_remand: The opposing party agrees that the suit should be sent back for a new trial.

members.legal_issue: For an execution proceeding involving a final, unconditional partition decree, limitation begins when the decree is enforceable, not when it is later engrossed on stamp paper.
material_facts: A final partition decree determined the parties’ shares and left no substantive matter for later adjudication.
The court directed the decree-holders to provide stamp paper, but they did not do so within the time allowed.
Providing the stamp paper was within the decree-holders’ control, and the execution application was filed more than twelve years after the decree was passed.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 runs from when a decree becomes enforceable. Enforceability is distinct from executability: where a final decree has determined the rights and the court has not postponed enforcement or made it conditional on an external event, a later ministerial step controlled by the decree-holder does not suspend limitation. The Court applied Yeswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Watch and Ramchand Kothari and W.B. Essential Commodities Supply Corporation v. Swadesh Agro Farming and Storage Pvt. Ltd.; it distinguished Shankar Balwant Lokhande v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande because that case concerned a preliminary decree without a final decree, and relied on Biswapati Dev v. Kennsington Stores and Kishori Mohan Pal v. Pravash Chandra Mondal for the literal meaning of enforceability.
members.conclusion: The decree was enforceable from the date it was passed, and the later failure to provide stamp paper did not postpone the commencement of limitation. The execution application was therefore time-barred.

rule.if: decree_execution_proceeding and final_partition_decree_passed and rights_fully_determined and enforcement_not_postponed_by_court and decree_holder_controlled_stamp_filing

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: The decree-holder sought to enforce a civil court decree through an execution proceeding.
predicates.final_partition_decree_passed: The court passed a final decree determining the division of property.
predicates.rights_fully_determined: The decree settled the parties’ rights without leaving a substantive matter for later adjudication.
predicates.enforcement_not_postponed_by_court: The court did not make enforcement conditional on a later event or expressly postpone it.
predicates.decree_holder_controlled_stamp_filing: The decree-holder could provide the stamp paper required for formal preparation of the decree but failed or delayed in doing so.

members.legal_issue: For a final partition decree that has determined the parties’ rights and is not contingent on a further event, the execution limitation period begins when the decree is pronounced, even if the decree-holder has not yet supplied stamp paper needed to engross it.
material_facts: A final partition decree determining the parties’ shares was pronounced after the commissioner’s report was accepted.
The decree-holder was notified to provide stamp paper but did not do so; providing it was within the decree-holder’s control.
The decree contained no condition requiring a further event or adjudication before it could be enforced.
The decree-holder’s legal representatives filed an execution application more than twelve years after the decree was pronounced.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963, starts the twelve-year period when a decree becomes enforceable. ‘Enforceable’ is to be given its literal meaning; enforceability is distinct from executability. A decree that finally determines rights and is not conditional is enforceable when pronounced, even if a ministerial step such as supplying stamp paper remains. A decree-holder cannot suspend limitation through failure to perform an act within their control. This applies the approach in Yeswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, W.B. Essential Commodities Supply Corporation v. Swadesh Agro Farming & Storage Pvt. Ltd., Biswapati Dey v. Kennsington Stores, and Subhash Ganpatrao Buty v. Maroti Krishnaji Dorlikar. Shankar Balwant Lokhande v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande concerned a different situation in which no final decree had been passed and does not govern this case.
members.conclusion: The decree became enforceable when pronounced, and the execution application filed more than twelve years later was barred by limitation.

rule.if: decree_execution_limitation_case and final_partition_decree_pronounced and rights_fully_determined and no_contingent_event_or_further_adjudication and stamp_paper_within_decree_holder_control and application_after_limitation_period

predicates.decree_execution_limitation_case: The proceeding sought execution of a decree, and the court had to decide whether the application was within time.
predicates.final_partition_decree_pronounced: The court pronounced a final decree partitioning property.
predicates.rights_fully_determined: The decree conclusively determined the parties’ rights without leaving those rights for later adjudication.
predicates.no_contingent_event_or_further_adjudicat: The decree did not make enforcement dependent on an external event or a further determination by the court.
predicates.stamp_paper_within_decree_holder_control: The decree-holder was responsible for supplying the stamp paper needed to engross the decree and could do so without awaiting an external event.
predicates.application_after_limitation_period: The execution application was filed after the applicable limitation period had elapsed.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for executing a final partition decree runs from the date the decree is passed, not the later date on which it is engrossed on stamp paper, unless the court has specifically postponed its enforceability.
material_facts: A final decree in a partition suit fixed the parties’ rights on 7 August 1981.
The decree holders supplied stamp papers on 25 May 1982, and the decree was engrossed thereafter; the court had not directed them to supply stamp papers.
The execution application was filed on 21 March 1994.
The lower courts treated the date of engrossment as the start of limitation.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 starts limitation when a decree becomes enforceable. Under Order 20 Rule 6A of the Code of Civil Procedure, a decree is generally enforceable from the pronouncement of judgment. In a partition suit, when the decree finally determines the parties’ rights, supplying stamp paper and engrossing the decree are ministerial acts; delay in those acts, which are within a party’s control, does not suspend limitation. Enforceability is postponed only where the court leaves an issue for later adjudication or specifically makes enforceability contingent on a later event. Sections 2(14), 2(15), 3, 33, 35, 40(b) and 42, and Article 45 of Schedule I of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 establish the fiscal treatment of partition decrees and the consequences of insufficient stamping; they do not suspend limitation under Article 136. The Court applied Hameed Joharan v. Abdul Salam, Renu Devi v. Mahendra Singh, and Yeshwant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari; it treated the relevant observations in Shankar Balwant Lokhande v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande as obiter and the partition illustration in W.B. Essential Commodities Supply Corporation v. Swadesh Agro Farming & Storage as not an exposition of law. It also relied on Hindustan Steel Ltd. v. Dilip Construction Co. for the revenue-raising purpose of stamp legislation.
members.conclusion: The decree became enforceable when it was passed, and later engrossment related back to that date. The execution application was time-barred; the impugned judgment was set aside and the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: partition_decree_execution and final_rights_fixed and not judicial_postponement and execution_outside_limitation_from_decree

predicates.partition_decree_execution: A party seeks execution of a final decree made in a partition proceeding.
predicates.final_rights_fixed: The court has finally determined the parties’ rights, leaving no matter for later adjudication.
predicates.judicial_postponement: The court has specifically made the decree’s enforceability contingent on a later event or postponed it to a later time.
predicates.execution_outside_limitation_from_decree: The execution application was filed after the applicable limitation period, counted from the date the decree was passed.

members.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on acting upon an unstamped partition decree does not suspend limitation for executing the decree.
material_facts: The final partition decree had been passed, but the decree-holders had not supplied the stamp paper needed to engross it.
The decree-holders argued that the restriction on acting upon an unstamped instrument prevented the decree from being enforceable until it was engrossed.
The stamp-paper requirement was a formal step, and the decree-holders controlled whether and when to complete it.
members.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 governs the commencement of limitation for execution, while Sections 2(15) and 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 address partition instruments and the admissibility or use of unstamped instruments. The Court held that the Stamp Act’s restriction does not govern when limitation begins under Article 136 or override its mandate. It disapproved Bholanath Karmakar v. Madanmohan Karmakar, which had treated engrossment as postponing limitation, and distinguished Shankar Balwant Lokhande as a case in which no final decree had been passed.
members.conclusion: The Stamp Act restriction did not suspend limitation; the period ran from when the final decree became enforceable, notwithstanding that it had not yet been engrossed on stamp paper.

rule.if: decree_execution_proceeding and final_partition_decree_passed and decree_not_yet_engrossed and stamp_formality_restricts_use_of_decree and decree_holder_controls_stamp_filing

predicates.decree_execution_proceeding: The decree-holder sought to enforce a civil court decree through an execution proceeding.
predicates.final_partition_decree_passed: The court passed a final decree determining the division of property.
predicates.decree_not_yet_engrossed: The final decree had not yet been formally engrossed on stamp paper.
predicates.stamp_formality_restricts_use_of_decree: A stamp-related requirement restricted the decree’s admission or use until the required formality was completed.
predicates.decree_holder_controls_stamp_filing: The decree-holder could provide the stamp paper required for formal preparation of the decree but failed or delayed in doing so.

members.legal_issue: The stamp-law restrictions on receiving or acting upon an unstamped instrument do not suspend the limitation period for execution of a final partition decree.
material_facts: The final partition decree had been pronounced and had crystallised the parties’ rights.
The decree-holder had not supplied stamp paper needed to engross the decree, although doing so was within the decree-holder’s control.
The execution application was filed more than twelve years after the decree was pronounced.
The decree-holder argued that the stamp-law restrictions prevented the decree from being enforceable until it was engrossed on stamp paper.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(15) and 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, address the status and use of an instrument that is not duly stamped; they do not govern when limitation for execution begins. Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963, operates in a distinct sphere, and the stamp-law restrictions do not suspend its limitation period. The Court rejected the contrary view in Bholanath Karmakar v. Madanmohan Karmakar. It distinguished Shankar Balwant Lokhande v. Chandrakant Shankar Lokhande, which involved the absence of a final decree, and relied on the distinction between enforceability and executability explained in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The stamp-law provisions do not suspend limitation; the execution application was barred because the limitation period ran from the date the decree became enforceable.

rule.if: decree_execution_limitation_case and final_partition_decree_pronounced and unstamped_decree_or_pending_stamp_formality and stamp_formality_within_decree_holder_control and application_after_limitation_period

predicates.decree_execution_limitation_case: The proceeding sought execution of a decree, and the court had to decide whether the application was within time.
predicates.final_partition_decree_pronounced: The court pronounced a final decree partitioning property.
predicates.unstamped_decree_or_pending_stamp_formal: The decree had not been engrossed on stamp paper or a stamp-related step needed for engrossment remained outstanding.
predicates.stamp_formality_within_decree_holder_con: The decree-holder could complete the outstanding stamp-related step without an external event or action by another person.
predicates.application_after_limitation_period: The execution application was filed after the applicable limitation period had elapsed.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent higher offer alone does not justify refusing confirmation once the court is satisfied that the sale price is adequate.
material_facts: A later offeror proposed a higher price after the commissioners had accepted the original offer.
Another higher offer was made before confirmation, with a complaint that inadequate publicity had prevented a timely offer.
The Court held that the sale process in this case did not establish an adequate price because publicity and public participation had been inadequate.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that once the court concludes that the price offered is adequate, no subsequent higher offer is a valid ground for refusing confirmation of the sale or offer already received. It relied on S. Soundarajan v. M/s. Roshan & Co., AIR 1951 Mad 986, while also applying the court’s duty to assess adequacy before confirmation.
members.conclusion: A higher subsequent offer cannot by itself justify refusing confirmation if the court has already concluded that the offered price is adequate; that condition was not met in this case.

predicates.company_property_sale_in_liquidation: A company’s property is being sold as part of its liquidation.
predicates.court_finds_price_adequate: The court has concluded that the offered price is adequate having regard to the property’s market value.
predicates.subsequent_higher_offer_made: A person makes a higher offer after the offer under consideration has been received or accepted.

members.legal_issue: A confirmed auction sale conducted fairly at an adequate price is not ordinarily reopened merely because a higher offer is made later.
material_facts: The company court confirmed the sale after a competitive process that included an open bid, further advertisement, and no offer exceeding the accepted bid during that process.
The accepted price was found to be fair in light of valuation material and the competitive sale process.
No illegality, irregularity, fraud, or collusion in the auction was established.
A later higher offer was made after confirmation of the sale.
members.legal_principle: Under Valji Khimji & Co. v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Ltd., a later higher offer does not ordinarily justify setting aside a confirmed sale after an adequately publicized auction, though a grossly inadequate sale price may support an inference of fraud or collusion. Vedica Procon Private Limited v. Balleshwar Greens P. Ltd. approved the principle in Navalkha and Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das that a company court may accept or reject a bid before confirmation, but once satisfied that the price is adequate, a subsequent higher offer is not a ground to refuse confirmation.
members.conclusion: The confirmed sale was not set aside, and the appeals challenging it were dismissed; the later higher offer did not by itself justify disturbing the sale.

rule.if: confirmed_auction_sale_appeal and sale_was_fairly_publicized and competitive_sale_was_fair and accepted_price_was_adequate and no_sale_misconduct_established and later_higher_offer_only

predicates.confirmed_auction_sale_appeal: A party challenges an order confirming an auction sale.
predicates.sale_was_fairly_publicized: The sale was advertised in a manner that gave eligible bidders a fair opportunity to participate.
predicates.competitive_sale_was_fair: The auction or bidding process was conducted competitively and fairly.
predicates.accepted_price_was_adequate: The court found the accepted price adequate in light of the sale process and relevant valuation material.
predicates.no_sale_misconduct_established: No fraud, collusion, illegality, or material irregularity in the sale was established.
predicates.later_higher_offer_only: A higher offer was made after confirmation, without other established grounds that undermine the sale.

members.legal_issue: A completed public-auction sale cannot be set aside solely because nonparticipants later offer more or property values subsequently rise, absent concrete proof of a defect that vitiated the auction or made the sale price wholly inadequate.
material_facts: The property was sold through a public auction conducted after the prescribed procedure, with 45 participants.
The successful bidder’s offer substantially exceeded the announced expected price, and the sale was confirmed by the competent authority after a report from the Assistant Commissioner.
The full consideration was paid, a sale deed was executed, and possession was delivered.
The challengers had not participated in the auction; one later offered a higher price but did not deposit the money, and the other made a later offer.
No court or authority found the auction illegal or irregular, and no concrete material established fraud, collusion, or that the property had been sold at a throwaway price.
The High Court ordered a re-auction more than two decades after the sale, relying on later offers and an inference about the property’s value.
members.legal_principle: A public-auction sale to the highest bidder, once confirmed and completed, should not be disturbed on the basis of subsequent offers by nonparticipants. There must be concrete material establishing a vitiating ground, such as fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality, or a throwaway price. The Court relied on the locus and writ-jurisdiction principles in Jasbhai Motibhai Desai v. Roshan Kumar, Haji Bashir Ahmed (1976) 1 SCC 671, and on the cautions against non-genuine public-interest litigation in State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) 3 SCC 402. It acknowledged the general principles concerning obtaining the best price in public sales discussed in Navalkha and Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das (1969) 3 SCC 537, Divya Manufacturing Company (P) Ltd. v. Union Bank of India (2000) 6 SCC 69, Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd. (1995) 4 SCC 595, and Union Bank of India v. Official Liquidator (2000) 5 SCC 274, but held that they did not assist the challengers on these facts.
members.conclusion: The direction for a re-auction was set aside because later offers and an unsupported inference of undervaluation did not justify disturbing the completed sale; concrete proof of fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality, or a throwaway sale price was absent.

rule.if: completed_public_auction_challenge and auction_followed_required_process and sale_confirmed_and_completed and challenger_did_not_participate and no_proven_vitiating_defect and challenge_relies_on_later_offer_or_price_inference

predicates.completed_public_auction_challenge: The proceeding challenges a sale completed through a public auction.
predicates.auction_followed_required_process: The authority conducted the auction after following the applicable procedure.
predicates.sale_confirmed_and_completed: The competent authority confirmed the sale and the purchaser completed payment and obtained a sale deed or possession.
predicates.challenger_did_not_participate: The person challenging the sale did not participate in the auction or submit a bid.
predicates.no_proven_vitiating_defect: The record does not concretely establish fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality, or a throwaway sale price.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_later_offer_or_price: The challenge relies on a later offer or an unsupported inference that the property was worth more than the auction price.

members.legal_issue: A court sale of a company’s assets cannot be reopened solely because a higher offer is made later or a subsequent event increases the asset’s value, where the accepted sale was not challenged for fraud, irregularity, or inadequacy when it was approved.
material_facts: The highest bid for the land was accepted after the stakeholders had been heard, and no stakeholder objected at that time that the sale was fraudulent or irregular or that the price was inadequate.
The successful bidder paid the full sale consideration, and the official liquidator arranged for possession to be handed over.
After the sale was accepted, a regulatory change increased the development potential and value of the land, and the unsuccessful bidder offered substantially more than the accepted bid.
The unsuccessful bidder did not initially challenge the sale on grounds of fraud, irregularity, or inadequacy.
members.legal_principle: Under Navalkha & Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das, the company court must satisfy itself that the price is adequate when considering confirmation, but once it has concluded that the price is adequate, a subsequent higher offer is not a valid ground for refusing confirmation. Valji Khimji & Company v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Limited reinforces that objections after confirmation are ordinarily limited to grounds such as fraud. Divya Manufacturing Company departed from Navalkha to the extent it permitted reopening on a higher offer alone; FCS Software Solutions involved material irregularities in the sale, while Shradhha Aromatics turned on peculiar facts and Manoj I. Naik involved rejection of the highest offer by the company court itself. Those decisions do not establish a general rule permitting reopening whenever a higher offer is later received.
members.conclusion: The later increase in the land’s value and the unsuccessful bidder’s higher offer did not justify recalling the accepted sale; the High Court was not justified in setting it aside.

rule.if: company_liquidation_sale and accepted_highest_bid and stakeholders_heard and no_initial_objection_to_price_or_sale and (later_higher_offer or post_sale_value_increase) and not sale_fraud and not sale_irregularity

predicates.company_liquidation_sale: A court is reviewing a sale of assets conducted in the course of a company’s liquidation.
predicates.accepted_highest_bid: The court accepted the highest bid for the asset.
predicates.stakeholders_heard: The stakeholders entitled to an interest in the sale proceeds were heard before the bid was accepted.
predicates.no_initial_objection_to_price_or_sale: No objection was made when the bid was accepted that the price was inadequate or that the sale was fraudulent or irregular.
predicates.later_higher_offer: A higher offer was made after the court accepted the bid.
predicates.post_sale_value_increase: An event after the bid was accepted increased the asset’s value or development potential.
predicates.sale_fraud: Fraud affected the conduct or approval of the sale.
predicates.sale_irregularity: An irregularity affected the conduct or approval of the sale.
predicates.sale_recall_unjustified: The accepted sale should not be recalled on the stated grounds.

members.legal_issue: An authority cannot set aside an execution sale under its pre-confirmation power after the sale has been confirmed.
material_facts: The recovery authority confirmed the auction sale, issued a sale certificate, and executed a sale deed in favour of the purchaser.
The deputy registrar later set aside the confirmed sale, relying on alleged undervaluation of the property.
The purchaser challenged that decision, and the Supreme Court found that the sale had become final upon confirmation.
members.legal_principle: Rule 38(6)(a) permits the Recovery Officer, for recorded reasons, to set aside a sale in the circumstances specified there, but that power must be exercised before an order confirming the sale. Rule 38(7) makes the sale certificate conclusive evidence of the sale. The court distinguished J. Rajiv Subramaniyan v. Pandiyas, concerning a different statutory scheme, and Vasu P. Shetty v. Hotel Vandana Palace; neither assisted a debtor who failed to pursue the remedy provided by Rule 38.
members.conclusion: The confirmed sale could not be set aside under the authority’s power to set aside a sale before confirmation; the orders setting it aside were quashed.

predicates.execution_auction_proceeding: A creditor pursued recovery by auctioning immovable property through an execution process.
predicates.sale_confirmed: The competent recovery authority confirmed the sale and issued the sale documents to the purchaser.
predicates.authority_attempts_to_set_aside_sale_aft: An authority later tried to undo the sale by exercising a power that applies before confirmation.

members.legal_issue: A court should not set aside an unchallenged rejection of a fraud objection after the execution sale has been confirmed and a sale certificate has been issued.
material_facts: The judgment debtors did not promptly challenge the executing court’s order rejecting their fraud objection.
The property was sold in execution, the sale was confirmed, and a sale certificate was issued and registered before the judgment debtors challenged the earlier order.
The appellate court later set aside the earlier order rejecting the objection.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXI Rules 92 and 94 of the Code of Civil Procedure, when the relevant applications to set aside an execution sale are disallowed, the sale is confirmed and becomes absolute, and a sale certificate is then issued. The Court treated the sale’s confirmation and issuance of the certificate as final in the circumstances of this case.
members.conclusion: The appellate court could not properly set aside the earlier order after the sale had been confirmed and the sale certificate issued; its decision setting aside that order could not be sustained.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The dispute arises in proceedings to enforce a court decree.
predicates.fraud_objection_order_left_unchallenged: The party alleging fraud did not challenge the order rejecting that objection before the execution sale was completed.
predicates.execution_sale_confirmed_and_certificate: The court confirmed the execution sale and issued a certificate to the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: A draft arbitration clause for disputes under a future concession agreement does not govern a tender-stage dispute between parties who are not the parties to that concession agreement.
material_facts: The draft arbitration clause applied to disputes connected with the concession agreement between the authority and the concessionaire.
The dispute concerned the bidding process and the withdrawal of the letter of award, before any concession agreement was executed.
The proposed concessionaire was to be a special-purpose entity, while the arbitration was invoked against the consortium members.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle concerning the scope and incorporation of arbitration clauses discussed in M.R. Engineers and Contractors Pvt. Ltd. v. Som Datt Builders Ltd. (2009) 7 SCC 696. The clause must govern the particular dispute and the parties to it; a clause directed to disputes under a future contract between different parties does not extend to a tender-stage dispute between bidders and the authority.
members.conclusion: Even assuming that the arbitration clause had otherwise been incorporated, it was inapt to cover this dispute because it concerned a future concession agreement and different contracting parties.

predicates.arbitration_jurisdiction_challenge: A party challenges whether an arbitration clause governs the dispute.
predicates.arbitration_clause_limited_to_future_con: The clause applies to disputes arising under or connected with a proposed future contract.
predicates.tender_bid_dispute: The dispute arises from the tender process before the proposed contract is executed.
