predicates.dispute_parties_differ_from_future_contr: The parties to the dispute are not the same as the parties identified for the proposed future contract.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator appointed under one of two independent agreements lacks authority to decide disputes arising under the other agreement unless those disputes fall within the arbitration submission.
material_facts: The parties entered into separate lease and dealership agreements, each with its own arbitration clause and designated appointing authority.
The respondent invoked the dealership agreement’s arbitration clause, and an arbitrator was appointed under that clause.
The arbitrator nevertheless decided disputes about the lease, including the lease rent and lease period.
The appellant objected that the respondent’s requested change to the lease rent was outside the arbitration proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 34(2)(a)(iv) and 34(2)(a)(v) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, an award may be set aside to the extent it decides matters beyond the submission, and the tribunal’s composition or procedure must accord with the applicable agreement. An arbitral tribunal is a creature of contract and must act within the authority conferred by the agreement under which it is constituted. The Court relied on Rahul Yadav v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. for the independence of lease and dealership agreements.
members.conclusion: The arbitrator appointed under the dealership agreement had no authority to decide disputes under the separate lease agreement. The award changing the lease rent and lease period dealt with matters beyond the submission to arbitration and was set aside to that extent.

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party seeks judicial review of an arbitral award.
predicates.agreements_have_separate_arbitration_ter: The parties made distinct agreements that provide for separate arbitration arrangements.
predicates.arbitrator_appointed_under_one_agreement: The arbitrator was appointed under the arbitration arrangement in one of the agreements.
predicates.award_decides_dispute_under_other_agreem: The arbitrator decided a dispute arising under the other agreement.

members.legal_issue: An arbitration clause does not cover a dispute arising from a separate agreement to which the clause does not apply.
material_facts: The applicant sought arbitration concerning an alleged agreement to sell the estates that predated the lease deed.
The parties had not included an arbitration agreement in the alleged sale agreement.
The arbitration clause in the lease deed covered disputes relating to or touching upon that deed.
members.legal_principle: An arbitration agreement must be between the parties to the dispute and must relate to or apply to the dispute or its subject matter. The Court relied on Yogi Agarwal v. Inspiration Clothes & U, (2009) 1 SCC 372, which stated this principle in considering sections 7 and 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
members.conclusion: The applicant could not seek arbitration of disputes concerning the alleged sale agreement under the arbitration clause in the lease deed.

predicates.application_for_arbitrator_appointment: A party has applied for the appointment of an arbitrator.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_separate_agreement: The dispute arises from an agreement distinct from the instrument containing the arbitration clause.
predicates.arbitration_agreement_does_not_cover_tha: The arbitration agreement does not apply to the separate agreement or the dispute arising from it.

members.legal_issue: A dispute may be referred to arbitration despite one named party to the suit not being a party to the arbitration agreement when the other material parties are bound by it and the non-signatory has no relevant right in the dispute.
material_facts: The plaintiffs were parties to the arbitration agreement or claimed through a person who was a party to it, and the relevant defendants were also parties or claimed through parties.
One defendant was not a party to either deed containing an arbitration clause.
On the plaintiffs’ own case, that defendant had inherited no right or share in the partnership or the scheduled property.
The suit dispute concerned benefits arising from the retirement deed and partnership deed, and the trial court found that referring it would not require bifurcation of the cause of action or parties.
members.legal_principle: Applying Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to the facts, the Court endorsed the trial court’s view that a non-signatory defendant’s presence did not prevent referral where the plaintiffs and the other material parties were parties to the arbitration agreement personally or through those from whom they claimed, the non-signatory had inherited no relevant right, and referral would not bifurcate the cause of action or parties. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.
members.conclusion: The presence of the one defendant who was not party to the arbitration agreement did not prevent referral of the dispute between the parties to arbitration.

rule.if: court_referral_application and dispute_arises_from_arbitration_agreement and material_parties_bound and non_signatory_lacks_relevant_right and no_bifurcation_needed

predicates.court_referral_application: A party asks a court to refer a civil dispute to arbitration.
predicates.dispute_arises_from_arbitration_agreemen: The dispute concerns rights or benefits arising from deeds containing an arbitration agreement.
predicates.material_parties_bound: The parties with relevant rights in the dispute are parties to the arbitration agreement or claim through someone who is a party.
predicates.non_signatory_lacks_relevant_right: A named party who did not agree to arbitration has no inherited or other relevant right in the dispute.
predicates.no_bifurcation_needed: Referring the dispute does not require separating the cause of action or the parties for adjudication.

members.legal_issue: A dispute may be referred to arbitration between the parties to the arbitration agreement even when another person interested in the subject matter is not a party, if that person’s share is not in dispute.
material_facts: The arbitration agreement was made by the disputing parties with knowledge that another person held an interest in the forest.
The person was not a party to the arbitration agreement or the application seeking reference.
The extent of that person’s share was undisputed, so the arbitrator could determine the dispute between the parties while leaving that share out of the award.
members.legal_principle: Under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, a court should give effect to the forum chosen by the parties even if an interested non-party cannot participate, where that person’s share is not in dispute and the arbitrator can leave it out of the award. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The absence of the interested person did not prevent reference of the dispute between the parties to arbitration.

predicates.arbitration_reference_application: A party applied to have an arbitration agreement filed and the dispute referred to arbitration.
predicates.parties_chose_arbitration_with_knowledge: The disputing parties agreed to arbitration knowing that another person had an interest in the subject matter, but did not include that person in their agreement.
predicates.nonparty_share_undisputed: The extent of the non-party’s share in the subject matter was not disputed.

members.legal_issue: A person who is not bound by the arbitration agreement invoked for a dispute cannot be made a party to the arbitration under that agreement.
material_facts: The borrower and developer entered into a construction agreement containing an arbitration clause; the lender was not a party to that agreement.
The borrower invoked that clause to arbitrate claims arising from the developer’s alleged failure to complete the apartment.
The borrower also had a separate loan agreement with the lender containing an arbitration clause, but the developer was not a party to the loan agreement and the borrower did not invoke that clause.
The alleged tripartite agreement did not contain an arbitration clause.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 require an arbitration agreement applicable to the dispute between the parties to be referred. The Court relied on Jagdish Chander v. Ramesh Chander, 2007 (5) SCC 719, Yogi Agarwal v. Inspiration Clothes & U, 2009 (1) SCC 372, and S.N. Prasad v. Monnet Finance Ltd., (2011) 1 SCC 320. An arbitration clause in a separate contract does not permit a party to be joined in an arbitration concerning another contract, and a non-party impleaded in a section 11 proceeding must be deleted or expressly excluded from the arbitration.
members.conclusion: The lender could not be included in the arbitration based on the construction agreement. The appointment remained effective for disputes between the borrower and developer, and the court should exclude a non-party to the invoked arbitration agreement or make clear that the arbitration is limited to parties bound by it.

predicates.section_eleven_appointment_proceeding: A party sought appointment of an arbitrator through a court proceeding of this kind.
predicates.invoked_agreement_binds_claimant_and_dis: The claimant and the party against whom the underlying dispute was raised entered into the agreement containing the invoked arbitration clause.
predicates.proposed_arbitration_party_not_bound_by_: The additional party sought to be included in the arbitration did not enter into, or otherwise become bound by, the agreement containing the invoked arbitration clause.

members.legal_issue: A change in the amount of a tax or in the local law under which it is claimed does not necessarily make it a different tax for the purpose of continuing a pre-constitutional tax on Union property.
material_facts: The railway property had been liable to municipal taxes before the Constitution under the law then applicable.
After the area became part of a different State, the municipality claimed taxes under that State's municipal law.
The amount of tax had varied, but the claimed tax remained of the same nature and type and concerned the same property.
members.legal_principle: Article 285(2) concerns continuation of the same tax on Union property. The Court relied on Governor General of India in Council v. Corporation of Calcutta and Union of India through General Manager E.I. Railway v. Municipal Board, Lucknow, and distinguished The Town Municipal Committee, Amravati v. Ramchandra Vasudev Chimote, which concerned the imposition of new taxes. A change in amounts or a changed statutory reference does not make the tax different when its nature, type, and subject property remain the same.
members.conclusion: The variation in tax amounts and the change in the municipal law under which the tax was claimed did not, by themselves, make it a different tax.

predicates.continuation_claim_for_union_property: A local authority sought to continue a tax on property owned by the Union that had been liable to tax before the Constitution.
predicates.same_tax_type_and_property_before_and_af: The pre- and post-constitutional claims concerned the same type of tax and the same property.
predicates.tax_amount_changed: The amount claimed after the Constitution differed from the amount previously charged.
predicates.governing_local_law_changed: The local law relied on for the later claim differed from the law applicable to the earlier claim.

members.legal_issue: Changes to the amount of a continuing tax or to the local law under which it is claimed do not, by themselves, make it a different tax for the purpose of the constitutional continuation rule.
material_facts: The municipality had taxed railway property before the Constitution under the municipal law then applicable.
The claim concerned the same kind of municipal taxes on the same railway property after the Constitution.
The amount of tax had varied, and the municipality later relied on a different municipal law after that law was extended to the area.
members.legal_principle: Article 285(2) permits continuation of the tax to which Union property was liable or treated as liable immediately before the Constitution, so long as that tax continues to be levied in the State. The tax remains the same where its nature, type and the property taxed remain the same; variation in amount or a change in the municipal law relied on does not alone alter its identity. The Court relied on Governor-General of India in Council v. Corporation of Calcutta and Union of India through General Manager E.I. Railway v. Municipal Board, Lucknow, and distinguished Town Municipal Committee, Amravati v. Ramchandra Vasudeo Chimote, which concerned Article 277 and new taxes.
members.conclusion: The variation in amounts and the change in the applicable municipal law did not make the tax different from the tax previously levied.

predicates.municipal_claim_seeks_continuation_of_ta: A local authority claims to continue a tax that was levied on the property before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.same_kind_of_tax_on_same_property: The nature and type of tax, and the property on which it is levied, remain the same.
predicates.only_amount_or_local_law_changed: The differences relied on are a change in the amount payable or a change in the local law under which the tax is claimed.

members.legal_issue: A person who knowingly improves property without the true owner's consent cannot require the owner to pay for those improvements.
material_facts: The father possessed and improved property belonging to his daughters after their mother's death.
He knew, according to the position ultimately established, that the property belonged to the daughters, but dealt with it as he chose.
The improvements were not made with the consent of the co-heir whose share was claimed.
The father and those claiming through him sought to make the co-heir bear a proportionate share of the improvement costs.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a person who knowingly lacks title and spends money improving property cannot charge the true owner for improvements made without that owner's consent. The claim under section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act and reliance on acquiescence did not assist the improver; Ramsden v. Dyson was distinguished.
members.conclusion: The co-heir was not liable to pay any part of the alleged improvement costs.

predicates.property_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns possession of property claimed by its true owner.
predicates.improver_knew_lacked_title: The person who made the improvements knew that they had no title to the property.
predicates.improvements_made_without_owner_consent: The improvements were made without the consent of the person entitled to the property.

members.legal_issue: A deliberate trespasser who improves land while knowing that they have no right to occupy it is not entitled to compensation for trees planted on the land merely because they intended to improve it.
material_facts: The claimant’s possession began after an application to register the land had been rejected.
The claimant made the improvements after that rejection, knowing that ownership of the land was disputed and that the government claimed it.
The claimant had no bona fide claim of title and entered or remained on the land without permission.
The claimant argued that a bona fide intention to improve the land entitled a trespasser to compensation.
The claim concerned the value of trees planted on the land after the claimant was evicted.
members.legal_principle: Section 5 of the Travancore Land Conservancy Act, 1916 prohibited occupation of government land without permission, and section 6 made contravention punishable. The maxim quicquid plantatur solo, solo cedit does not apply in India, but that does not give a wrongful trespasser a right to trees planted on another’s land. The court applied Vallabdas Narainji v. Development Officer, Bandra, A.I.R. 1929 P.C. 163, which did not establish that a mere deliberate trespasser is entitled to compensation. The court also reasoned that a trespasser’s position cannot be better than that of a lawful tenant who has lost possession and cannot claim compensation for improvements.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled under general law to compensation for the trees; an intention to improve the land does not turn a deliberate, wrongful trespass into a compensable one.

rule.if: appeal_from_improvements_compensation_claim and deliberate_unauthorised_occupation and knowledge_of_lack_of_right and trees_planted_by_occupier

predicates.appeal_from_improvements_compensation_cl: A person appeals a decision on a claim for compensation for improvements made to land.
predicates.deliberate_unauthorised_occupation: The claimant deliberately occupied land without permission.
predicates.knowledge_of_lack_of_right: When occupying or improving the land, the claimant knew they had no right or title to do so.
predicates.trees_planted_by_occupier: The claimant planted the trees for which compensation is sought.

members.legal_issue: A person in unlawful possession of assigned land is not entitled to compensation for improvements made to it.
material_facts: The appellant made improvements to the land after entering possession under the agreement.
The required permission for alienation had been refused, the agreement was void, and the Court held that the appellant’s possession was unlawful.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the appellant’s unlawful possession as insufficient to give him a right to compensation for improvements made to the assigned land.
members.conclusion: The appellant was not entitled to compensation for improvements made to the land.

predicates.improvements_made_to_land: The possessor made improvements to land while occupying it.
predicates.possession_without_authorized_transfer: The possessor occupied the land without an authorized transfer.

members.legal_issue: An occupant’s expenditure on repairs or reconstruction does not create proprietary ownership when the occupant knew the true state of title.
material_facts: The defendant argued that he had spent money on repairs and reconstruction after the title document was issued.
The Court found that the defendant had not established that he spent money on that work.
The Court added that even if he had spent money, expenditure with knowledge of the actual state of ownership would not confer a proprietary interest.
members.legal_principle: Expenditure on repairs or reconstruction, even if proved, does not itself confer a proprietary interest where it is made with knowledge of the true state of ownership.
members.conclusion: The defendant acquired no proprietary interest through the alleged expenditure, which was not proved in any event.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The parties disputed ownership of property occupied by one of them.
predicates.occupant_spent_money_on_repairs_or_recon: The occupant spent money repairing or reconstructing the property.
predicates.occupant_knew_true_ownership: The occupant knew who owned the property when the expenditure was made.

members.legal_issue: An occupant’s expenditure on repairs or reconstruction does not by itself confer a proprietary interest in property when the occupant knows the actual state of title.
material_facts: The defendant alleged that he had spent money on repairs and reconstruction after the title document was issued in the plaintiffs’ names.
The Court found that the defendant had not established that he spent money on the work.
The Court added that even if the defendant had spent money with knowledge of the actual state of affairs, that expenditure would not confer a proprietary interest.
members.legal_principle: Expenditure on repairs or reconstruction, even if made with knowledge of the actual state of title, does not in law confer a proprietary interest in the property.
members.conclusion: The alleged repair and reconstruction expenditure did not give the defendant any proprietary interest in the property.

predicates.property_title_is_disputed: The parties disputed who owned the property.
predicates.occupant_spends_on_repairs_or_reconstruc: A person occupying the property spends money on repairs or reconstruction while knowing the actual state of title.

members.legal_issue: A claim for past rent cannot succeed when the alleged tenancy and its terms have not been established.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed past rent on the basis that the defendant was a tenant.
The High Court was not satisfied that the tenancy or its terms had been established and rejected the claim for past rent.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with that rejection.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to interfere with the High Court's rejection of past rent because the alleged tenancy and its terms had not been established. The High Court had also observed that, under the relevant U.P. control-of-rent legislation and the preceding Ordinance, letting premises required permission from the competent authority and a tenancy without that permission would be invalid; the Supreme Court did not separately elaborate on that statutory point.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the claim for past rent was upheld.

predicates.past_rent_claim_in_ejectment_suit: A claimant sought past rent in a proceeding also seeking ejectment.
predicates.alleged_tenancy_and_its_terms_not_establ: The claimant failed to establish the alleged tenancy and the terms on which rent was said to be due.

members.legal_issue: A claim for past rent cannot be sustained when the alleged tenancy and its terms are unproved and the required permission for letting was absent.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought past rent on the basis of an alleged tenancy.
The courts did not accept the plaintiff’s account of the tenancy or establish its terms.

The High Court found that the relevant law required permission from the District Magistrate or another appropriate authority before premises could be let, and that the alleged tenancy would have been invalid even if proved.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s rejection of the claim for past rent.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to interfere with the rejection of past rent where the alleged tenancy and its terms had not been established. It noted the applicable U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, and the preceding ordinance, which required permission from the District Magistrate or another appropriate authority before premises could be let.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the claim for past rent was left undisturbed.

predicates.past_rent_claim_in_ejectment_suit: A claimant sought past rent in a suit also seeking to recover possession of property.
predicates.tenancy_terms_unproved: The claimant did not establish the alleged tenancy and its terms.
predicates.required_letting_permission_absent: The permission required for letting the premises was not obtained.

members.legal_issue: Solatium cannot be denied or differentiated solely because land was acquired under a different enactment when the government could apply the general land-acquisition provisions to that acquisition.
material_facts: The claimant sought solatium for land acquired under a state enactment.
That enactment empowered the government to apply provisions of the general land-acquisition law to the acquired land.
The Court relied on its recent decision holding that there was no justification for discriminating in solatium between acquisitions under different enactments.
The respondent did not controvert that position.
members.legal_principle: Under section 4(3) of the Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, the government was empowered to apply provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to acquired land. Relying on State of Kerala v. T.M. Peter, the Court held that there was no justification for discrimination in solatium between acquisitions under different enactments, particularly where such application was authorized.
members.conclusion: The Court directed payment of solatium on the compensation awarded by the High Court and otherwise confirmed the decree.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: An appeal concerns compensation for land acquired under a statutory acquisition framework.
predicates.solatium_claimed: The claimant seeks solatium in addition to compensation.
predicates.acquisition_framework_allows_general_lan: The framework for the acquisition permits the government to apply general land-acquisition provisions to the acquired land.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsory acquisition cannot differ for equally situated owners merely because the land is acquired for a different public purpose, by a different authority, or under a different acquisition law.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a housing accommodation scheme under the improvement legislation, although the government could acquire land for the same purpose under the general acquisition law.

Under the improvement legislation, market value was limited to the use to which the land was being put, excluding potential value for another use, and the owner did not receive the additional amount ordinarily payable for compulsory acquisition.
The Court found that these disadvantages substantially outweighed the minor advantages under the improvement legislation.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable legislative classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia rationally related to a lawful legislative object. For compulsory acquisition, the purpose of acquisition, the identity of the acquiring authority, or the acquisition law ordinarily does not justify different compensation because those features do not warrant different treatment of the owner's individual right. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Govt., P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Madras, and Balammal v. State of Madras.
members.conclusion: The provisions producing the different compensation treatment violated Article 14; the appeal was dismissed, leaving the award set aside and the matter remitted for compensation to be determined according to law.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: An owner challenged the legal validity of compensation treatment in a compulsory land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.land_could_be_acquired_under_either_regi: The government could acquire land for the relevant purpose under either of two available acquisition regimes.
predicates.equally_situated_owners_receive_differen: Owners in materially equivalent circumstances receive different compensation treatment.
predicates.compensation_difference_is_based_on_publ: The difference in compensation follows from the public purpose, acquiring authority, or acquisition law rather than a relevant difference in the owners' circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A statutory solatium entitlement cannot be denied merely because the local enactment governing an acquisition does not provide for it.
material_facts: The respondents argued that the local land development and planning enactment did not contemplate solatium for the acquired land.
The Court relied on earlier decisions holding that deprivation of solatium under that enactment violated Article 14 and that its exclusion provision was invalid.
members.legal_principle: The solatium provided by Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act is mandatory. Monoranjan Routh v. State of West Bengal and Ramendranath v. State of West Bengal held that deprivation of solatium under the local enactment violated Article 14 and that the exclusion provision was invalid.
members.conclusion: The argument that the local enactment excluded solatium was rejected, and solatium remained payable.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.local_law_excludes_solatium: The local law governing the acquisition does not provide for, or purports to exclude, solatium.
predicates.exclusion_deprives_owner_of_statutory_so: Applying the local-law exclusion would deprive the owner of statutory solatium.
predicates.solatium_remains_payable: The owner remains entitled to solatium notwithstanding the local-law exclusion.

members.legal_issue: The exclusion of solatium and interest from compensation for compulsory acquisition under a highway-acquisition scheme violates equal protection when the exclusion distinguishes owners only by the public purpose or statute under which their land is acquired.
material_facts: The landowners’ property was compulsorily acquired for highway development under a special statutory scheme that did not provide solatium.
Landowners whose property was compulsorily acquired for other public purposes could receive solatium and interest under the general acquisition law.
The 1997 amendment’s stated aim was to expedite land acquisition and highway construction, and the court found that awarding solatium and interest did not impede that aim.
Solatium and interest had been available for highway acquisitions before the amendment and became available again under the later compensation framework.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not permit different compensation treatment for similarly situated owners merely because their land was acquired for a different public purpose or under a different acquisition statute, absent a rational basis for the distinction. Solatium compensates for the compulsory nature of acquisition and is part of compensation. The court relied on P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector for Land Acquisition (1965) 1 SCR 614, Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao (1973) 1 SCC 500, Balammal v. State of Madras (1969) 1 SCR 90, State of Kerala v. T.M. Peter (1980) 3 SCC 554, and Sunder v. Union of India (2001) 7 SCC 211.
members.conclusion: The exclusion of solatium and interest was unconstitutional to that extent. The relevant provisions governing solatium and interest under the general acquisition law apply to acquisitions under the highway-acquisition scheme, and the exclusionary provision was declared unconstitutional to that extent.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_a: A party challenges the constitutionality of the compensation treatment for compulsory acquisition.
predicates.owners_are_similarly_situated: The compared property owners are similarly situated with respect to the compulsory acquisition of their land.
predicates.compensation_difference_is_based_only_on: The owners receive different compensation treatment solely because their land was acquired for a different public purpose or under a different statute.
predicates.distinction_lacks_rational_relation_to_l: The different treatment has no rational relation to the object the legislation seeks to achieve.

members.legal_issue: Compulsory deprivation of private property by the State without legal authority or due process requires compensation.
material_facts: The State took the owner’s land for construction of a public road without initiating acquisition proceedings or following another legally prescribed process.
The State admitted that it had used the land and had not initiated acquisition proceedings for it.
The owner had received no compensation for the taking.
members.legal_principle: Article 31, applicable when the land was taken, protected property from deprivation without due process and just and fair compensation. After the Forty-Fourth Amendment, the right to property remained a constitutional right under Article 300A and a human right; deprivation must be authorized by law, and an obligation to compensate can be inferred from Article 300A. The Court relied on The State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose, Tukaram Kana Joshi v. M.I.D.C., K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, N. Padmamma v. S. Ramakrishna Reddy, Delhi Airtech Services Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P., and Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The taking without legal sanction or due process violated the owner’s right to property, and the State was directed to pay compensation.

rule.if: state_compulsory_taking_case and state_took_private_property and no_legal_process_followed and no_compensation_paid

predicates.state_compulsory_taking_case: The proceeding concerns the State’s compulsory taking of private property.
predicates.state_took_private_property: The State took or used a person’s private property for a public purpose.
predicates.no_legal_process_followed: The State did not follow a legally authorized process to take the property.
predicates.no_compensation_paid: The owner received no compensation for the taking.

members.legal_issue: The State may not take or retain a person's property without authority of law and must use a legally prescribed process to acquire it.
material_facts: The owners' predecessors held title to the land, and the State authorities took physical possession in 1964.
The initial acquisition proceedings lapsed, and a later acquisition attempt also lapsed without completion.
The State did not claim title and conceded the owners' right, title, and interest in the land.
The authorities nevertheless retained and transferred possession without completing acquisition or paying compensation.
members.legal_principle: Article 300-A permits deprivation of property only by authority of law and through a procedure prescribed by statute; executive action alone cannot deprive a person of property. The Court relied on Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat. It also recognized the right to property as a human right, relying on Lachhman Dass v. Jagat Ram, Amarjit Singh v. State of Punjab, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar, and Delhi Airtech Services v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The State's possession without a lawful acquisition process was impermissible, and the owners were entitled to lawful acquisition and compensation.

predicates.property_deprivation_claim: A person seeks relief because the State has taken or retained that person's property.
predicates.state_possession_without_law: State authorities took possession without completing a legally authorized process.
predicates.owner_title_conceded: The State accepted that the affected person held title to the property.

members.legal_issue: A statutory power to take steps to secure possession of acquired property does not authorize the government to evict occupants by force without using a procedure recognized by law.
material_facts: The State acquired the hotel undertaking and was empowered to take steps it considered necessary to secure possession.
The occupants remained in premises within the hotel undertaking.
The State removed them with police assistance without first obtaining possession through a procedure recognized by law.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(8) of the Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1980, authorizes steps necessary to secure possession but does not authorize the use of force to evict occupants. Under Bishan Das v. State of Punjab and State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh, the State cannot take possession otherwise than in due course of law; legal steps require action under a relevant law rather than executive self-help.
members.conclusion: The possession-securing power did not authorize eviction by force; the State had to obtain possession in due course of law.

rule.if: government_possession_dispute and property_vested_in_government and occupants_remain_in_possession and government_uses_force_without_lawful_possession_process

predicates.government_possession_dispute: The proceeding challenges government action to obtain possession of property occupied by others.
predicates.property_vested_in_government: The property or undertaking has vested in the government.
predicates.occupants_remain_in_possession: People continue to occupy the property when the government seeks possession.
predicates.government_uses_force_without_lawful_pos: The government uses force to remove occupants without first following a procedure recognized by law to obtain possession.

members.legal_issue: A claim that property is required for a public purpose does not permit the government to evict occupants by force without following due process of law.
material_facts: The State argued that the premises were required for a public purpose and that this justified forceful eviction.
The hotel was a commercial venture used by paying guests and was described as serving an affluent section of society rather than the general public.
The occupants were removed by force without a lawful possession process.
members.legal_principle: Applying Bishan Das v. State of Punjab and State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh, the Court held that even an asserted public purpose cannot justify executive eviction by force absent specific legal authority. The acquisition's stated object of providing better boarding and lodging facilities did not make this commercial hotel operation a public purpose that could excuse bypassing due process.
members.conclusion: The public-interest argument did not justify forceful eviction; possession had to be obtained in accordance with law.

rule.if: government_eviction_dispute and occupants_are_in_possession and government_relies_on_public_interest and government_uses_force_without_lawful_possession_process

predicates.government_eviction_dispute: The proceeding challenges government action to remove occupants from property.
predicates.occupants_are_in_possession: The people the government seeks to remove are in possession of the property.
predicates.government_relies_on_public_interest: The government asserts that the property is needed for a public purpose or public interest.
predicates.government_uses_force_without_lawful_pos: The government uses force to remove occupants without following a procedure recognized by law to obtain possession.

members.legal_issue: A statutory authority must follow the procedure prescribed for a transfer of agricultural land for industrial use, and a superior executive authority cannot dictate the outcome of an individual matter assigned by statute to that authority.
material_facts: The original purchaser acquired agricultural land for an industrial project but later informed the Collector that it no longer wished to establish an industry and wanted to sell the land.
The Collector did not conduct the statutory inquiry or take the steps prescribed when a purchaser failed to use the land for the permitted purpose.
The Revenue Minister directed that the sale be permitted as a special case despite departmental advice that the land should be resumed under the statute.
The State Government directed the Collector to permit a direct transfer to a second industrial purchaser, and the Collector issued the permission accordingly.
members.legal_principle: Sections 89 and 89A of the Tenancy Act restrict transfers of agricultural land and create a limited exception for bona fide industrial use. Section 89A assigns the relevant inquiry and action on failure to the Collector, with a specified process for vesting and subsequent disposal; Section 126 permits general control, not directions in individual matters assigned to the Collector. A statutory power prescribed to be exercised in a particular manner must be exercised in that manner and not another: Taylor v. Taylor; Nazir Ahmed v. King Emperor; Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh; State of U.P. v. Singhara Singh; Chandra Kishore Jha v. Mahavir Prasad; Dhananjaya Reddy v. State of Karnataka; Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power Ltd. An appellate authority cannot convert itself into the primary statutory authority: State of Punjab v. Hari Kishan. External dictation to an authority required to act independently is impermissible: Anirudhsinhji Karansinhji Jadeja v. State of Gujarat.
members.conclusion: The Government’s direction and the Collector’s consequent permission were arbitrary and contrary to the statutory scheme; the direct sale was invalid and inoperative.

predicates.statutory_land_transfer_challenge: A court proceeding challenges an administrative decision concerning agricultural land transferred for industrial use.
predicates.statute_assigns_individual_decision_to_d: The governing law assigns the relevant individual inquiry and decision to a particular statutory officer.
predicates.higher_authority_directs_individual_outc: A superior executive authority directs the statutory officer to reach a particular result in an individual matter.
predicates.prescribed_statutory_process_is_bypassed: The decision-makers do not follow the inquiry and procedure prescribed by law for the proposed transfer.

members.legal_issue: A government direction to a statutory development authority is binding only when it is authorized and directed toward carrying out the authority's statutory purposes.
material_facts: A communication issued on behalf of the government, based on a note from the Chief Minister, directed the authority to reconvey the land.
The direction relied on a High Court judgment that was set aside in this appeal.
The authority disputed the direction because reconveyance was contrary to the governing legislation and the purposes of the development scheme.
The Court found no showing that the Chief Minister was authorized to issue the direction and stated that a government order must conform to Article 166 of the Constitution.
members.legal_principle: Section 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976, permits government directions only when they are necessary or expedient for carrying out the Act's purposes; the authority is not bound by directions contrary to the Act. A government order must also conform to Article 166 of the Constitution. The Court additionally relied on the principle in Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Gordhandas Bhanji and Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner that the validity of a public order is assessed objectively by the order and its stated grounds.
members.conclusion: The direction to reconvey the land was not binding because it was unauthorized and contrary to the statutory purposes of the authority.

rule.if: statutory_authority_direction_dispute and direction_orders_return_of_acquired_land and direction_not_authorized and direction_conflicts_with_statutory_purpose

predicates.statutory_authority_direction_dispute: The dispute concerns a government direction to a statutory authority.
predicates.direction_orders_return_of_acquired_land: The direction tells the authority to return land acquired for its statutory development work.
predicates.direction_not_authorized: The person or body issuing the direction lacked authority to issue it in the required manner.
predicates.direction_conflicts_with_statutory_purpo: The direction would obstruct rather than carry out the purposes for which the authority was established.

members.legal_issue: A government direction to a statutory development authority cannot require action contrary to the governing statute or the purpose of the development scheme.
material_facts: The government ordered the conversion of an area reserved for a public park and approved its allotment to a private trust.
The authority implemented those directions rather than independently deciding whether the statutory conditions for changing the scheme were met.
The proposed action conflicted with the statutory purpose of orderly development and preservation of public open space.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15(3) and 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 do not confer unrestricted power on the government to direct the authority. Directions must be reasonably necessary or expedient to carry out the Act’s purposes and cannot displace the specific power and conditions in Section 19(4). General powers cannot validate action that the statute does not permit. The authority must exercise its own statutory responsibilities rather than abdicate them to the government.
members.conclusion: The government’s directions were beyond the permissible scope of its powers, and the resulting action was invalid.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_statutory_authority_ac: A person or group brought a writ challenge to action taken by a statutory authority following a government direction.
predicates.government_directed_action_contrary_to_s: The government directed action inconsistent with the purpose of the governing statute or scheme.
predicates.authority_implemented_direction_without_: The statutory authority implemented the direction without independently making the decision entrusted to it by law.

members.legal_issue: Disposal of land vested in a statutory development authority must be undertaken by that authority under the governing rules, and the State cannot independently allot the land or take over the authority’s disposal function.
material_facts: The lands had vested in the development authority and were developed lands within its scheme.
The State directed allotments and relied on a general policy concerning State land, although the development authority’s rules governed disposal of the lands.
The rules assigned disposal of authority land to the development authority, subject to the prescribed procedure and, where required, the State’s prior approval.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 58, 72 and 73 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, and Rules 3–5 and 19–20 of the 1975 Rules, disposal of authority land lies with the development authority, subject to the rules and any required State approval. The State’s supervision and policy-direction powers do not permit it to usurp the authority’s statutory function or interfere with its day-to-day work. The Court relied on Bangalore Development Authority v. R. Hanumaiah, Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Gordhandas Bhanji, and Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner.
members.conclusion: The development authority alone could undertake disposal of the authority land in accordance with the applicable rules; the State could not independently allot it or usurp the authority’s function.

predicates.public_interest_land_allotment_challenge: A public-interest proceeding challenges the allotment of land governed by a statutory land-disposal scheme.
predicates.land_vested_in_development_authority: The land had vested in a statutory development authority responsible for its disposal.
predicates.state_directed_disposal: The State directed or undertook disposal of land whose disposal function belonged to the development authority.

members.legal_issue: A government authority cannot transfer public sites held by a development authority or require that authority to acquire its own road land and compensate former claimants without legal authority.
material_facts: The development authority sanctioned the layout subject to roads, civic amenity sites, parks, and utility connections vesting in it without compensation.
The civic amenity sites and road land formed part of the land granted to the association and were included in the sanctioned layout.
The government later directed that vacant civic amenity sites be handed to the claimants and that the development authority acquire the land used for a road and pay compensation to them.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(5) of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 permits the authority to require transfer of layout roads and open spaces without compensation. Section 38-A restricts disposition of areas reserved for parks, playgrounds, and civic amenities, and Section 65 does not authorize government directions contrary to the Act's purposes. The Court relied on Bangalore Medical Trust v. B.S. Muddappa and Bangalore Development Authority v. R. Hanumaiah.
members.conclusion: The directions to transfer the civic amenity sites and to acquire the road land and pay compensation were without authority of law and were set aside.

predicates.development_authority_sanctioned_layout: A development authority sanctioned a layout containing roads and public amenity areas.
predicates.public_sites_and_roads_vested_in_authori: The layout conditions provided for the roads and public amenity areas to vest in the development authority without compensation.
predicates.government_order_directed_transfer_or_ac: A government order directed that those areas be transferred to claimants or that the authority acquire road land and compensate them.

members.legal_issue: Joint family property does not lose its character merely because one coparcener remains, while a widow of a deceased coparcener continues to have a right of maintenance from it.
material_facts: The property was ancestral joint family property held by two brothers.
After one brother died, the surviving brother was the sole coparcener.
The deceased brother’s widow remained alive and had a right to maintenance from the property.
members.legal_principle: A joint family may consist of a single male member and widows of deceased male members; a temporary reduction of the coparcenary to one person does not convert joint family property into that person’s separate property. The rights of family members, including a widow’s right to maintenance, remain relevant. The Court followed Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Mysore and applied Attorney General of Ceylon v. A.R. Arunachalam Chettiar.
members.conclusion: The property retained its character as joint family property in the hands of the sole surviving coparcener.

rule.if: joint_family_property_character_dispute and (only_one_coparcener_remains and widow_of_deceased_coparcener_is_alive and widow_has_maintenance_right)

predicates.joint_family_property_character_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property retains its joint family character when only one coparcener remains.
predicates.only_one_coparcener_remains: One member of the family remains as the sole coparcener holding the property.
predicates.widow_of_deceased_coparcener_is_alive: The widow of a deceased coparcener remains alive.
predicates.widow_has_maintenance_right: The widow has a right to maintenance from the family property.
predicates.property_retains_joint_family_character: The property continues to be joint family property despite being held by a sole coparcener.

members.legal_issue: Joint family property does not cease to belong to the family merely because, after a member's death, the family is represented by a sole coparcener.
material_facts: After the common ancestor died, his son was the sole coparcener.
The property continued to be treated as joint family property, and the ancestor's widow remained in the family.
members.legal_principle: In Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Mysore, Bangalore, this Court held that joint family property does not cease to belong to the family merely because a sole coparcener represents it; the family may include a widow and other females born into it.
members.conclusion: The joint family continued after the ancestor's death, with his son as the sole coparcener, and the property continued to belong to the family.

predicates.joint_family_property: Property belonged to a joint family before a member died.
predicates.sole_coparcener_remained: After that death, one coparcener alone represented the family.

members.legal_issue: Joint family property retains its character when the coparcenary is temporarily reduced to one member while the joint family continues.
material_facts: The properties were ancestral property jointly held by two brothers.
After one brother died, the surviving brother became the sole surviving coparcener.
The deceased brother’s widow remained alive and had a right to maintenance from the joint family property.
members.legal_principle: A Hindu joint family may continue to exist despite having only one male coparcener, and its property does not become that coparcener’s separate property merely for that reason. The Court relied on Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Mysore and Attorney General of Ceylon v. A. R. Arunachalam Chettiar.
members.conclusion: The property did not cease to be joint family property merely because only one coparcener remained.

predicates.joint_family_property: The property was held as property of a joint Hindu family.
predicates.coparcenary_reduced_to_one: The death of a family member left only one male coparcener.
predicates.widow_maintenance_right_continues: A widow of a deceased family member remained in the family and had a maintenance right against the property.

members.legal_issue: Property that was joint-family property before partition retains its joint-family character when allotted to a sole coparcener who has a wife and daughters but no son.
material_facts: The assets in question had belonged to a Hindu Undivided Family before partition among the assessee, his father, and his brothers.
The assessee received his share of those assets on partition.
At the relevant time, the assessee had a wife and two minor daughters and no son or other male coparcener.
The assessee sought wealth-tax assessment of the assets as belonging to a Hindu Undivided Family, rather than to him individually.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act makes a Hindu Undivided Family an assessable entity, and section 5(1)(ii) refers to a member’s interest in coparcenary property. The Court distinguished property that was separate property before receipt from property already impressed with the character of joint-family property. Under Hindu law, the latter does not lose that character merely because partition leaves one coparcener; the rights of existing and future family members, including a son who may be born or adopted and female members’ rights to maintenance, are relevant. Attorney General of Ceylon v. A.R. Arunachalam Chettiar and Gowali Buddanna’s case support that principle. The distinction from Kalyanji Vithaldas and the treatment of Gomedalli Lakshminarayan and A.P. Swamy Gomedalli explain why property originating as joint-family property is treated differently from separate property. T.S. Srinivasan v. Commissioner of Income Tax did not decide this issue.
members.conclusion: The partition did not convert the assets into the assessee’s individual property; they remained property of the Hindu Undivided Family of the assessee, his wife, and his daughters, and the Tribunal was right to determine his status as a Hindu Undivided Family.

rule.if: wealth_tax_assessment and property_was_joint_family_property_before_partition and coparcener_received_property_on_partition and recipient_has_wife_or_daughters and recipient_has_no_son

predicates.wealth_tax_assessment: The proceeding determines the status in which property is assessed to wealth tax.
predicates.property_was_joint_family_property_befor: The property belonged to a Hindu joint family before partition.
predicates.coparcener_received_property_on_partitio: A coparcener received the property as his share on partition.
predicates.recipient_has_wife_or_daughters: The recipient has a wife or daughters who are members of his family.
predicates.recipient_has_no_son: The recipient has no son at the relevant time.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s eviction suit requiring prior permission is not validly instituted if the Commissioner cancels the District Magistrate’s permission before the suit is filed.
material_facts: The District Magistrate initially refused permission to sue, and the Commissioner later granted it on revision.
The court considered the effect of a Commissioner cancelling permission before a landlord institutes an eviction suit.
members.legal_principle: Under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, permission is subject to an order made by the Commissioner under section 3(3); section 3(4) makes the Commissioner’s order final subject to an order of the State Government under section 7(F). The court agreed with Munshi Lal v. Shambhu Nath Ramkishan to this extent and held that Bashi Ram v. Mantri Lal was incorrect insofar as it said a Commissioner’s later cancellation could not make the suit infructuous.
members.conclusion: If the Commissioner cancels the District Magistrate’s permission before the suit is instituted, no effective permission remains and the suit is treated as filed without valid permission.

predicates.eviction_suit_requiring_permission: A landlord filed an eviction suit for which permission had to be obtained before filing.
predicates.commissioner_canceled_permission_before_: The Commissioner cancelled the permission before the landlord filed the suit.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s eviction suit requiring prior permission is not validly instituted if the State Government revokes the permission before the suit is filed.
material_facts: The tenant moved the State Government to revoke the Commissioner’s permission before the landlord filed the eviction suit.
The State Government’s actual revocation order was made only after the suit had been filed and a decree had been passed.
The court stated that a revocation before institution would leave no valid permission to sue.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(1) and 3(4), read with section 7(F) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, make the Commissioner’s order subject to the State Government’s order. A revocation before institution therefore leaves no effective permission for the suit.
members.conclusion: If the State Government revokes the permission before the suit is instituted, there is no valid permission to sue.

predicates.eviction_suit_requiring_permission: A landlord filed an eviction suit for which permission had to be obtained before filing.
predicates.state_government_revoked_permission_befo: The State Government revoked the permission before the landlord filed the suit.

members.legal_issue: A State Government revocation of permission after a validly instituted eviction suit does not make the suit unmaintainable or the resulting decree unenforceable.
material_facts: The Commissioner granted permission to institute the eviction suit after the District Magistrate had refused it.
The landlord filed the suit after the Commissioner granted permission.
The tenant had applied to the State Government for revocation before the suit was filed, but the State Government revoked permission only after the trial court had passed a decree.
The appellate court set aside the decree on the basis of the State Government’s revocation, but the High Court restored it.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3(1), 3(4), and 7(F) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 contain no provision making a suit validly instituted after the required permission cease to be maintainable because of a later State Government order. Section 14 concerns specified decrees passed before the Act commenced and does not invalidate a decree in a suit validly instituted under the Act. A court will not infer that a competent court’s decree has become unenforceable unless legislation does so expressly or by necessary implication. The court upheld Bashi Ram v. Mantri Lal on the effect of a State Government revocation after institution, while rejecting its contrary holding about a Commissioner’s cancellation; it also referred to Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand concerning the breadth of the State Government’s power.
members.conclusion: Once an eviction suit is validly instituted, the State Government’s power to revoke the permission is exhausted; a later revocation does not end the suit’s maintainability or invalidate the decree.

predicates.eviction_suit_validly_filed_after_permis: A landlord filed an eviction suit after obtaining the permission required to institute it.
predicates.state_government_revoked_permission_afte: The State Government revoked the permission after the landlord had filed the suit.

members.legal_issue: A suit for eviction validly instituted after the required permission has been obtained remains maintainable when the State Government later revokes that permission.
material_facts: The landlord obtained permission from the District Magistrate to sue for eviction, and the tenant’s revision to the Commissioner was dismissed.
The landlord filed the eviction suit before the State Government decided the tenant’s further revision.
After the suit was filed, the State Government set aside the Commissioner’s order and revoked the permission to sue.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3(1)–(4) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, institution of a suit outside the specified grounds required the District Magistrate’s permission, which was expressly subject to revision by the Commissioner, but section 3(1) did not make institution subject to a later order under section 7-F. Section 7-F permits revision before the suit is instituted and does not invalidate a suit already filed; absent statutory language making a decree inexecutable or reopening proceedings, a validly instituted suit must take its course. Bhagwan Das v. Paras Nath was followed; Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand and Bansi Ram v. Mantri Lal were considered.
members.conclusion: The later revocation did not make the suit incompetent; the suit, validly instituted after the required permission, remained maintainable.

predicates.eviction_suit_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.required_permission_obtained: The landlord obtained the permission required to institute the eviction suit, including the relevant review by the intermediate authority.
predicates.suit_filed_before_state_revision_decisio: The landlord filed the suit before the State Government decided the further revision concerning permission.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made after the specified date but before the commencement of a later law expressly invalidating certain transfers is not void merely because of the earlier transfer-restriction law, which treated the transferor as continuing to own the property for ceiling purposes.
material_facts: The disputed transfers were made after 16 August 1971 but before the Rajasthan Urban Property Ceiling Act, 1972 came into force.
The earlier transfer-restriction legislation provided that, despite a transfer, the property would be deemed to remain owned by the transferor; it did not declare the transfer void.
The earlier legislation was repealed in 1978.
The later ceiling legislation expressly made transfers after its commencement null and void.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Rajasthan Urban Property (Restrictions of Transfers) Act, 1973 deemed the transferor to remain the owner for purposes of preventing evasion of the contemplated ceiling law; it did not invalidate the transfer. The 1973 Act was repealed by the Rajasthan Urban Property (Restrictions of Transfers) Repeal Act, 1978. Section 5 of the Rajasthan Urban Property Ceiling Act, 1972 invalidated transfers made after that Act commenced, but the transfers at issue preceded its commencement. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The disputed transfers were not void under the earlier transfer-restriction legislation.

rule.if: challenge_to_transfer_validity and transfer_after_restriction_cutoff and transfer_before_absolute_transfer_ban and restriction_law_repealed

predicates.challenge_to_transfer_validity: A party challenged the validity of a transfer of urban property.
predicates.transfer_after_restriction_cutoff: The property was transferred after the date from which an earlier law applied a special ownership rule to transfers.
predicates.transfer_before_absolute_transfer_ban: The property was transferred before a later law began expressly invalidating transfers made after its commencement.
predicates.restriction_law_repealed: The earlier law imposing the special ownership rule was later repealed.

members.legal_issue: A later ceiling-law provision deeming specified transfers to defeat the law does not apply to an earlier bona fide transfer where the earlier ceiling regime governs the reopened case.
material_facts: The land was transferred by gift in 1963, before the period covered by the later law’s deeming provision.
The reopened case was decided under the earlier tenancy-law ceiling provisions, and the repeal of those provisions was not retrospective.
The Court found no evidence that the gift was actuated by extraneous consideration and treated it as bona fide.
members.legal_principle: Section 40 of the Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973 repealed the relevant chapter of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 without retrospective effect. Section 6 of the 1973 Act applies its deeming rule to transfers made within the period specified there; it does not capture a transfer made before that period. The Court also noted that bona fide transfers not actuated by extraneous consideration are exempt from that rule. No earlier case was relied on.
members.conclusion: The later ceiling-law provision did not affect the transfer, which was a bona fide transfer made before the provision’s specified period.

rule.if: land_ceiling_proceeding and case_governed_by_earlier_ceiling_regime and transfer_predates_later_law_trigger_period and transfer_is_bona_fide

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: An authority determined whether land was available for resumption in a ceiling case.
predicates.case_governed_by_earlier_ceiling_regime: The reopened case was decided under the ceiling rules that applied before the later law took effect.
predicates.transfer_predates_later_law_trigger_peri: The transfer occurred before the period to which the later law’s transfer-deeming rule applies.
predicates.transfer_is_bona_fide: The transfer was genuine and was not shown to have been made for an extraneous or evasive purpose.

members.legal_issue: A later-enacted restriction on transfers does not make a transfer that occurred before the restriction took effect unlawful under that restriction when the restriction is not retrospective.
material_facts: The tenancy surrender and settlement took place in 1938.
Section 46, which restricted transfers by raiyats belonging to Scheduled Tribes, was introduced by an amendment that came into force in 1948.
The Court noted that Section 46 had no retrospective effect and that the transfer had not been shown to contravene another provision in force when it occurred.
members.legal_principle: Section 46 of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, was introduced by the 1947 amendment with effect from 5 January 1948 and was not retrospective. In Jai Mangal Oraon v. Mira Nayak, the Court likewise recognized that the restriction did not apply to a surrender made before it came into force. The Court found no established contravention of another provision applicable to the transfer in this case.
members.conclusion: The 1938 transfer could not be treated as contravening Section 46, which was not in force when the transfer occurred.

predicates.restoration_proceeding_based_on_a_transf: A restoration proceeding relied on a legal restriction on transfers as a basis for challenging the transfer.
predicates.transfer_predated_the_restriction: The transfer occurred before the transfer restriction took effect.
predicates.the_restriction_has_no_retroactive_effec: The transfer restriction was not made applicable to transfers that occurred before it took effect.

members.legal_issue: A transfer made before a later-enacted ceiling law does not become inconsistent with the earlier ceiling law expressly identified in the validation provision merely because it may affect the later law.
material_facts: The transactions in question took place in 1965, and possession was delivered at that time.
The validation applications were made within the extended period for applying.
The validation provision referred to inconsistency with the ceiling law enacted in 1961, while the law said to have been defeated came into force later.
The Collector cancelled validation certificates on the basis that the transactions defeated the later ceiling law.
members.legal_principle: Section 50-B(1) and (2) of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, governs validation of specified transfers; the reference to inconsistency with the ceiling law of 1961 is specific and cannot be read, through Section 18 of the Andhra Pradesh General Clauses Act, as referring instead to a later ceiling law. The Court agreed with the High Court’s interpretation and its conclusion that a transaction predating the later law could not have been made to defeat that law.
members.conclusion: The later ceiling law could not be substituted for the specific earlier law identified in the validation provision. The transactions could not have been made to defeat a law that came into force after they occurred, and the cancellation of the certificates was not justified on that ground.

predicates.validation_certificate_cancellation_revi: A reviewing authority is considering whether to cancel a certificate validating a land transfer.
predicates.transfer_preceded_later_ceiling_law: The land transfer occurred before the ceiling law relied on as having been defeated came into force.
predicates.validation_test_identifies_earlier_ceili: The governing validation test expressly identifies an earlier ceiling law as the law with which the transfer must be consistent.

members.legal_issue: An enhanced compensation valuation that has become final cannot be reopened through execution objections merely because it was reached on an incorrect principle.
material_facts: A court enhanced the compensation valuation for the acquired land.
The appellant allowed that enhanced valuation to become final.
The execution objection concerned the additional statutory benefits, while the appellant accepted the enhanced valuation as binding.
members.legal_principle: A final determination of the compensation valuation is binding and cannot be reopened in execution merely to correct an error in the exercise of jurisdiction; this is distinct from a jurisdictional nullity, which may be challenged in execution under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The appellant was bound by the final enhanced valuation, although the additional benefits awarded without jurisdiction could be challenged in execution.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is seeking to enforce or resist enforcement of a decree in execution.
predicates.compensation_valuation_final: The enhanced compensation valuation has become final.
predicates.challenge_seeks_to_reopen_valuation_only: The execution objection seeks to revisit the valuation because of an alleged error rather than because the court lacked jurisdiction to make it.

members.legal_issue: A previously challenged original compensation award that has become final cannot be reopened, although a later enhancement found to be unlawful may be set aside.
material_facts: The original award had been challenged in an earlier petition for special leave, which was dismissed.
A later award enhanced the compensation.
The Court found the enhanced award impermissible, while treating the original award as final.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the dismissal of the earlier challenge as rendering the original award final and res judicata, while separately holding that the later enhancement was impermissible.
members.conclusion: The original award remained final and could not be reopened; the Court set aside only the unlawful enhancement.

predicates.appeal_against_compensation_award: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a compensation award.
predicates.earlier_challenge_to_original_award_dism: An earlier challenge to the original award was dismissed.
predicates.later_enhancement_found_unlawful: The court finds that a subsequent enhancement of the award was unlawful.

members.legal_issue: A final writ direction granting additional equitable compensation cannot be reopened in later land-acquisition reference or appellate proceedings between the same parties or their privies when it has been acted upon and was not challenged.
material_facts: A final writ order directed payment of equitable interest from the date possession was taken, in addition to statutory compensation and interest.
The direction applied to the affected landowners, was acted upon, and was reflected in the Land Acquisition Officer’s award.
The State did not challenge the writ direction or the award granting the additional interest.
The later reference and appeal concerned compensation for the acquired land, and the High Court displaced the additional interest despite the prior final direction.
members.legal_principle: The rule of res judicata, including cause-of-action and issue estoppel, applies between proceedings and at later stages of the same proceedings, including writ proceedings under Article 226. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure embodies the rule’s purpose of conclusively settling issues and preventing renewed litigation. The Court relied on Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board, Swamy Atmananda v. Sri Ramakrishna Tapovanam, Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh v. State of Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh Road Transport Corporation v. Balwant Singh, Bhanu Kumar Jain v. Archana Kumar, Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, Prahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh, Y.B. Patil, and Ishwardas v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Sections 18 and 54 of the Land Acquisition Act concern reference and appellate proceedings, but did not authorize reopening the final direction in these proceedings.
members.conclusion: The prior direction and the award granting the additional interest had attained finality and could not be reopened; the Reference Court and the High Court in its appellate jurisdiction could not revisit that question.

rule.if: land_acquisition_reference_or_appeal and prior_final_writ_order and same_compensation_issue and prior_order_implemented and no_challenge_to_prior_order

predicates.land_acquisition_reference_or_appeal: The proceeding is a reference or appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.prior_final_writ_order: A court previously made a final writ order concerning the compensation now in dispute.
predicates.same_compensation_issue: The later proceeding concerns the same compensation issue determined by the earlier order.
predicates.prior_order_implemented: The party bound by the earlier order acted in accordance with it.
predicates.no_challenge_to_prior_order: The party bound by the earlier order did not challenge it through an available procedure.

members.legal_issue: A grant expressed to be of a named village does not by itself create a presumption that the land constitutes an estate when some lands within the village were separately granted.
material_facts: The grant confirmed by the principal title deed was expressed to be of a named village.
Other lands within the village were covered by minor inam grants, but the evidence did not establish when those grants were made.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Explanation (1) to section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, and approved Varadaraja-Swamivari Temple v. Krishnappa. It rejected the presumption reasoning in Janakiramaraju v. Appalaswami and disapproved Narayanaswami Nayadu v. Subramaniyan. It concluded that the Explanation created no presumption either way.
members.conclusion: The legislature created no presumption either that the land was, or that it was not, an estate. A named-village grant can fall within the Explanation where the excluded minor inams had been granted before the grant of the rest of the village as a named village; the named-village description alone does not establish that fact.

predicates.inam_estate_classification_case: A court is deciding whether land covered by an inam grant constitutes an estate.
predicates.grant_expressed_as_named_village: The grant described the subject of the inam as a village by name.

members.legal_issue: A grant covering less than an entire village qualifies as an estate only when the grant is expressly of the named village and the excluded lands satisfy the statutory conditions for exclusion.
material_facts: The original grant was unavailable, and the claim that the land formed part of an estate rested on incomplete entries in an inam register.

The entries indicated that most of the village area had been granted to one holder and a smaller area to another under separate personal grants; they did not establish that the main grant covered the whole village.

The evidence did not satisfactorily establish that the grant was expressed as a grant of the named village or that the excluded area had previously been granted on a qualifying tenure or reserved for communal purposes.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, an inam village means a whole village granted in inam, not merely a substantial part of a village. Explanation 1 permits a grant expressed to be of a named village to qualify despite excluded lands only if those lands fall within the stated categories. The claimant bears the burden of establishing estate status. The Court relied on Janakirama Sastri v. Jagani Gopalam for the construction of “any inam village.” The judges differed on whether “other tenure” should be limited by ejusdem generis to tenures like service tenure or could include personal inams; the evidence did not establish the necessary prior exclusion either way.
members.conclusion: The grant was not proved to be a grant of a whole village or a grant of a named village with qualifying excluded lands; the land therefore was not an estate under the Act.

rule.if: inam_estate_classification_case and grant_did_not_cover_entire_village and (not grant_expressed_as_named_village or not excluded_lands_proven_previously_granted_or_reserved)

predicates.inam_estate_classification_case: The proceeding requires the court to decide whether land qualifies as an estate under the applicable land-tenure definition.
predicates.grant_did_not_cover_entire_village: The evidence shows that the grant covered less than the entire area of the village.
predicates.grant_expressed_as_named_village: The grant expressly describes itself as a grant of the named village, rather than a grant of a specified area within it.
predicates.excluded_lands_proven_previously_granted: The evidence establishes that lands excluded from the grant had already been granted on a qualifying tenure or had been reserved for communal purposes.
predicates.land_is_not_an_estate: The land does not qualify as an estate under the applicable definition.

members.legal_issue: Lands do not constitute an estate under the applicable definition when the original grant was not of the entire village and the Government did not confirm or recognize it as such.
material_facts: The original grant concerned certain lands, and the original grant document was not available.
During enfranchisement, only the cultivated area was confirmed; waste, banjar and other uncultivated lands were excluded.
The Zamindar dealt with the excluded waste and banjar lands as its own, including granting jeroyiti pattas, and its title to the tank was recognized.
The documentary evidence supported the finding that the grant was not of the entire village.
