members.legal_principle: Under section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, as applied by the Court, the relevant category required a grant of the whole village and confirmation or recognition of that grant by the Government. Because the evidence established a grant of less than the entire village and confirmation of only part of the area, the lands did not meet that definition; accordingly, the Madras Estates Rent Reduction Act, 1947, which had been applied on the basis that the lands were an estate, did not apply. The Court relied on the documentary evidence and the parties’ dealings with the excluded lands; it cited no earlier case as authority for this issue.
members.conclusion: The lands were not an estate within section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, and the Madras Estates Rent Reduction Act, 1947 did not apply to them.

rule.if: estate_status_dispute and grant_not_of_entire_village and confirmation_limited_to_part_of_area and (excluded_waste_treated_as_separate_property or zamindar_title_to_excluded_land_recognized)

predicates.estate_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether granted lands qualify as an estate for application of rent-reduction legislation.
predicates.grant_not_of_entire_village: The evidence shows that the original grant did not include the entire village.
predicates.confirmation_limited_to_part_of_area: The government confirmation or recognition covered only part of the village area.
predicates.excluded_waste_treated_as_separate_prope: The excluded waste or uncultivated lands were dealt with separately from the granted lands.
predicates.zamindar_title_to_excluded_land_recogniz: The evidence recognized the zamindar’s ownership of lands excluded from the grant.

members.legal_issue: A grant expressed to be of a named inam village is treated as a grant of an estate unless the party challenging that treatment proves the relevant exception concerning minor inams.
material_facts: The register described the grant as an agraharam of a named village and recorded its extent in local measures.
A minor inam existed, but there was no evidence establishing when it had been granted or whether it had been carved out of the original grant.
The party contending that the village was not an estate did not discharge its burden of proof.
An earlier judgment, which had the original grant before it, had held the village to be an estate; the village had also been notified as an estate under the abolition legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 3(2)(d), Explanation (1), proof that an inam grant was expressed to be of a named village raises a presumption that the granted area is an estate, including despite certain lands having been granted earlier or reserved for communal purposes. The burden falls on the party asserting that the grant falls outside the definition to establish the relevant exception, including by showing that minor inams not comprised in the grant were created contemporaneously with or after the village grant by the original grantor. Explanation (1-A), inserted by Act XXXV of 1956, confirms that an inam village, hamlet, or khandriga remains an estate even if confirmed or recognised on different dates, under different title deeds, or in favour of different persons. The Court relied on Aluru Kondayya v. Singaraju Rama Rao, approving Nelluru Sundararama Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Korukonda Bhattam Appalacharyulu, Janakiramaraju v. Appalaswami, and Sri Varadarajaswamivari Temple v. Sri Krishnappa Govinda.
members.conclusion: The village was an estate within the meaning of Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act; the party disputing that status failed to rebut the statutory presumption.

predicates.named_village_inam_grant: The grant was expressed to be an inam grant of a named village.
predicates.challenger_proved_minor_inam_exception: The party disputing estate status proved that the relevant minor inams were created contemporaneously with or after the village grant by the original grantor.
predicates.village_treated_as_estate: The village is treated as an estate.

members.legal_issue: An inam grant expressed to be of a named village gives rise to a presumption that the area forming its subject matter is an estate, even when the grant excludes some lands in that village.
material_facts: The dispute concerned tenants’ claimed permanent occupancy rights in lands associated with an inam village and the shrotriemdars’ claim that the tenants lacked those rights.
The original grant deed was unavailable, but the records and descriptions treated the shrotriem as a grant associated with the named village.
Separate minor inams existed, but the evidence did not show that they had been created by the grantor contemporaneously with or after the village grant.
The case arose under the amended definition of an estate, including the 1945 Explanation, which applied retrospectively from the 1936 amendment.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(2)(d), Explanation 1, of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, as added by Act 2 of 1945 and applicable from the 1936 amendment, creates a rebuttable presumption when an inam grant is expressed to be of a named village. The non-obstante clause means that the presumption does not depend on proof that excluded lands had previously been granted on service or other tenure or reserved for communal purposes. The party alleging that the grant falls outside the definition must prove that case, including, where relevant, that minor inams not included in the grant were created by the grantor contemporaneously with or after the village grant. The court relied on the interpretation in Janakiramaraju v. Appalaswami, Nelluru Sundarama Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Korukonda Bhattam Appalacharyulu, Sri Varadarajaswamivari Temple v. Sri Krishnappa Govinda, and Mantravadi Bhavanarayana v. Merugu Venkatadu; it explained District Board of Tanjore v. M. K. Noor Mohammad Rowther and rejected the contrary approach preferred in Varada Bhavanarayana Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: Once the grant was shown to be expressed as a grant of a named village, the presumption that its subject matter was an estate arose without proof that excluded lands had previously been granted on other tenures or reserved for communal purposes. The party contending that the grant fell outside the definition had to prove that case; the shrotriemdars’ suit therefore failed.

rule.if: occupancy_rights_dispute_in_inam_village and named_village_grant and post_amendment_proceeding and not proven_facts_excluding_estate_status

predicates.occupancy_rights_dispute_in_inam_village: A dispute concerns occupancy rights claimed in land associated with an inam village.
predicates.named_village_grant: The inam grant is expressed to be of a village identified by name.
predicates.post_amendment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the amended legal definition governing whether an inam village is an estate.
predicates.proven_facts_excluding_estate_status: The party opposing estate status proves facts that take the grant outside the statutory definition, rather than relying only on the existence of excluded lands of the kinds specified in the explanation.

members.legal_issue: A failure to pay disputed dues does not amount to wilful disobedience in contempt proceedings when the order did not decide the liability and the person acted on a bona fide understanding of the order.
material_facts: The respondent disputed that any amount remained payable, relying on the parties’ arrangements and the petitioner’s alleged continued use of a trademark.
The High Court had left the parties to pursue the disputed accounts and liability in execution proceedings, and the order alleged to have been breached did not determine the amount payable.
The respondent maintained a bona fide understanding that no dues were outstanding.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Sections 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, contempt requires wilful disobedience proved beyond reasonable doubt. Ram Kishan v. Tarun Bajaj (2014) holds that bona fide conduct and genuine interpretive uncertainty do not establish wilfulness, and that where two interpretations are possible and conduct is not contumacious, contempt is not maintainable. R.N. Dey v. Bhagyabati Pramanik (2000) holds that contempt should not be used instead of an available execution remedy. Jhareswar Prasad Paul v. Tarak Nath Ganguly (2002) holds that a contempt court cannot decide matters not determined by the order allegedly breached and should leave ambiguous or undecided matters to the appropriate court.
members.conclusion: The Court found no intentional violation or wilful disobedience on the dues allegation and left the parties to pursue their claims in execution proceedings or other proceedings permitted by law; it did not decide the underlying liability.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and dues_liability_not_decided_in_order and execution_forum_left_claim_open and bona_fide_understanding_no_dues

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A court is considering an allegation of civil contempt for disobedience of its order.
predicates.dues_liability_not_decided_in_order: The order said to have been breached did not determine whether dues were payable or their amount.
predicates.execution_forum_left_claim_open: A court left the parties to pursue their disputed payment claims in execution proceedings or another lawful proceeding.
predicates.bona_fide_understanding_no_dues: The person relied on a bona fide understanding that no dues were outstanding.

members.legal_issue: Alleged damage to property does not warrant contempt action when the evidence does not establish permanent damage or intentional disobedience and the dispute is factually complex.
material_facts: The allegation of damage relied on photographs showing debris at the premises.
The respondent produced photographs showing the condition of the premises when vacated and relied on its entitlement to remove certain fixtures.
The water park became functional within two to three months, and any minor repairs were not shown to be intentional disobedience.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Sections 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, contempt requires wilful disobedience proved beyond reasonable doubt. Ram Kishan v. Tarun Bajaj (2014) excludes negligent, inadvertent, or otherwise non-wilful conduct from contempt. R.N. Dey v. Bhagyabati Pramanik (2000) cautions against using contempt instead of an available remedy for enforcement or resolution of a disputed claim.
members.conclusion: The Court found that the damage allegation did not warrant contempt action and left the property-condition claim open to be pursued in execution proceedings or another proceeding permitted by law.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and property_damage_allegation and evidence_does_not_establish_permanent_damage and damage_dispute_is_factually_complex

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A court is considering an allegation of civil contempt for disobedience of its order.
predicates.property_damage_allegation: A person alleges that property was damaged while another person was vacating it.
predicates.evidence_does_not_establish_permanent_da: The evidence, including the condition of the property afterward, does not establish permanent damage to its structure.
predicates.damage_dispute_is_factually_complex: Resolving the property-condition claim requires determination of disputed facts beyond the contempt allegation.

members.legal_issue: A contempt finding cannot be made where the order’s scope admits competing reasonable interpretations and the alleged contemners adopted a reasonable interpretation that leaves doubt about disobedience.
material_facts: The interim order directed maintenance of the status quo regarding possession for members of the association who were before the High Court in the underlying writ petition, and a later order barred implementation of vesting orders affecting those members.

The applicants had become association members after the underlying writ petition was filed; the applicants argued that the orders covered them, while the officers understood them to cover only members who had been before the High Court.

The officers proceeded with vesting and possession measures, but the Court found that the order’s wording left a persistent doubt about whether the applicants were covered and that the officers’ interpretation could not be treated as wholly unwarranted.
members.legal_principle: Because contempt is quasi-criminal, competing reasonable interpretations of an order may create doubt that must benefit the alleged contemner. The Court relied on Re Bramblevale, (1969) 3 All ER 1062; The Aligarh Municipal Board v. Ekka Tonga Mazdoor Union, (1970) 3 SCC 98; and V.G. Nigam v. Kedar Nath Gupta, (1992) 4 SCC 697. It also noted Murray & Co. v. Ashok Kumar Newatia, (2000) 2 SCC 367, regarding cautious use of contempt jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The alleged breach was not established beyond reasonable doubt, so the contempt petition failed and was dismissed.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A party initiated a proceeding alleging disobedience of a court order.
predicates.order_scope_admits_competing_readings: The wording of the court order reasonably supports more than one interpretation of who or what it covers.
predicates.alleged_contemners_adopted_reasonable_re: The persons accused of disobedience acted on an interpretation of the order that was not wholly unwarranted.

members.legal_issue: Failure to comply with a consent order does not amount to contempt when no clear undertaking to the court was given.
material_facts: A consent order appointed a receiver to take charge of and run a business, directed the appellant not to interfere with the receiver, and required the appellant to provide cooperation the receiver might require.

The order did not expressly direct the appellant to hand over possession, and no application, affidavit, or undertaking incorporated into the order stated that the appellant had undertaken to hand over possession.
The appellant was convicted of contempt for failing to hand over possession to the receiver.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, a consent order or compromise decree is distinct from an undertaking to the court. A breach of a consent order ordinarily concerns the parties, and may be addressed through enforcement or execution under the Code of Civil Procedure, rather than contempt. The court may not infer an undertaking that is absent from the record. The principle that an undertaking must be carefully construed is supported by Bhatnagar & Co. Ltd. v. Union of India; the purposes of contempt proceedings and the need for care in exercising contempt powers are discussed in Aligarh Municipal Board v. Ekka Tanga Mazdoor Union.
members.conclusion: The failure to comply with the consent order did not amount to contempt in the absence of a clear undertaking to the court; the contempt conviction and sentence were set aside.

predicates.contempt_appeal: A party appealed a finding that the party had committed contempt.
predicates.consent_order_not_complied_with: A party failed to comply with an order made by the court with the parties’ consent.
predicates.no_clear_undertaking: The alleged contemnor did not clearly undertake to the court, in a filed application or affidavit or in an oral statement incorporated into the court’s order, to perform the act said to have been breached.

members.legal_issue: Failure to deliver possession cannot be treated as breach of an undertaking for contempt when no undertaking was given.
material_facts: The firm obtained time to vacate after representing that it would file the usual undertaking.
No undertaking, written or otherwise, was given to the Court.
The applicants sought contempt proceedings based on the failure to deliver possession.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, as explained in Babu Ram Gupta v. Sudhir Bhasin, wilful breach of an undertaking may constitute contempt where the undertaking is expressly given, in writing or orally and recorded by the court; a court cannot assume an implied undertaking where none is on the record.
members.conclusion: The firm could not be found guilty of violating an undertaking because no undertaking had been given, though the Court separately ensured compliance with its order.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: An application seeks to hold a person in contempt for failure to comply with a court-related obligation.
predicates.undertaking_not_given: The person did not expressly give an undertaking to the court, whether in writing or orally.

members.legal_issue: Substantial delay in seeking revision does not by itself require the Supreme Court to disturb the revisional authority’s discretionary decision to entertain the proceeding when no statutory time limit applies.
material_facts: The State sought revision many years after the challenged order, although proceedings concerning the property had occurred in the interim and the interests of purchasers had intervened.
The Court considered that the State’s authorities appeared grossly negligent in protecting the asserted public interest.
The Custodian-General exercised the view that the revision should nevertheless be entertained.
The appeal challenged that exercise of discretion.
members.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 authorises revision at any time and prescribes no limitation period. The revisional power is judicial, and delay, particularly where other persons’ titles have intervened, may bear on whether the authority should exercise its discretion. The Supreme Court declined to interfere under Article 136 of the Constitution with the authority’s discretionary decision on that matter.
members.conclusion: Whether to entertain a substantially delayed revision was within the Custodian-General’s discretion, and the Supreme Court would not interfere with that decision in the appeal.

predicates.appeal_from_revision_decision: The proceeding before the Supreme Court challenges a decision made by a revisional authority.
predicates.revision_power_has_no_time_limit: The law granting revision power sets no time limit for its exercise.
predicates.authority_entertained_revision_despite_s: The revisional authority chose to hear a revision brought after a substantial delay.

members.legal_issue: A delay in seeking revision does not by itself prevent the Government from exercising revisional authority when the governing law prescribes no limitation period; the Government determines whether the delay is reasonable.
material_facts: The Government’s revisional order followed an application concerning an order made many years earlier.
The governing Act specified no period of limitation for an application for revision.
The Government considered that there were strong reasons to interfere despite the lapse of time.
members.legal_principle: The Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, specified no limitation period for an application for revision. In the absence of such a period, the Government would normally act only if moved within a reasonable time, and what is reasonable in a particular case is for the Government to consider.
members.conclusion: The age of the earlier order did not prevent the Government’s action from being treated as an exercise of quasi-judicial revisional power; the Government determines what is a reasonable time in the circumstances.

predicates.revision_proceeding: The matter is an application asking the Government to exercise revisional authority over an earlier order.
predicates.no_statutory_revision_deadline: The governing law sets no limitation period for seeking revision.
predicates.government_considers_delay_reasonable: The Government considers the circumstances and finds a sufficient basis to act despite the delay.

members.legal_issue: A challenge that a writ petition should have been dismissed for delay cannot succeed in the appeal where the delay ground was not raised in that appeal and the lower courts accepted the explanation for the delay.
material_facts: The appellants argued that one writ petition should have been dismissed for delay.
The lower courts accepted the explanation for the delay and decided the petition on its merits.
The appellants did not raise the delay ground in the special leave petition in that matter.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to accept the delay argument in light of the lower courts’ treatment of the explanation and the failure to raise the ground in the appeal. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The argument that the writ petition should have been dismissed for delay was rejected.

predicates.acquisition_appeal: A party appealed a decision in proceedings challenging compulsory acquisition.
predicates.lower_courts_accepted_delay_explanation: The lower courts accepted the explanation offered for the time taken to file the challenge.
predicates.delay_ground_not_raised_in_appeal: The appellant did not raise the delay ground in the appeal before the Supreme Court.

members.legal_issue: A delay-based challenge does not by itself require reversal of a High Court’s discretionary decision to entertain a writ petition.
material_facts: A company and a shop-keeper filed a writ petition nearly two years after later administrative proceedings concerning the assessments.

The High Court considered the procedural history, including conflicting indications about the proper remedy and further steps taken before the petition was filed, and chose to entertain it despite the delay.
The Supreme Court considered the corporation’s challenge to that exercise of discretion.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the decision whether to entertain the writ petition despite delay as a matter of the High Court’s discretion and declined to interfere with that exercise on delay alone. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: Although the delay was substantial and the High Court’s reasons might be inadequate, the Supreme Court would not set aside the High Court’s discretionary decision on delay alone.

predicates.appeal_challenges_discretionary_writ_rel: An appeal challenges a High Court’s discretionary decision to entertain a writ petition.
predicates.high_court_entertained_delayed_petition: The High Court entertained a petition despite delay in filing it.
predicates.procedural_history_provided_a_basis_for_: The High Court considered procedural events that could explain or mitigate the delay.
predicates.writ_relief_is_not_set_aside_for_delay_a: The discretionary writ relief is not reversed solely because the petition was delayed.

members.legal_issue: A landlord's suit to recover property after a lawful lease by a prior manager was governed by the limitation rule for recovery from a tenant, not the rule for recovery after an unauthorised transfer by a manager.
material_facts: The temple manager had authority to grant the year-to-year lease in the ordinary course of management, and the lease bound the temple.
The lease continued after the manager left office and remained effective until terminated by notice.
The suit was brought by the landlord to recover possession from the tenant after termination of the tenancy.
The suit was instituted within the time allowed for a landlord's recovery action against a tenant.
members.legal_principle: Article 134-B of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, concerns an illegal or unauthorised transfer by a previous manager and does not apply where a lawful transfer remains effective after the manager leaves office. A suit by a landlord to recover possession from a tenant is governed by Article 139; the Court held that the suit was timely because it followed termination of the tenancy and was filed within the applicable period. The Court also considered section 28 and Article 144 in addressing the claim that title had been extinguished by adverse possession.
members.conclusion: The rule concerning recovery after an unauthorised transfer by a previous manager did not apply; the landlord's suit was governed by the limitation rule for recovery from a tenant and was timely.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_recovery_suit and prior_manager_made_lawful_lease and lease_remained_effective_after_manager_left and tenancy_terminated_before_suit and suit_filed_within_applicable_recovery_period

predicates.landlord_tenant_recovery_suit: The proceeding is a landlord's suit to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.prior_manager_made_lawful_lease: A previous manager made a lease that was within the manager's authority and bound the property owner.
predicates.lease_remained_effective_after_manager_l: The lease remained in force after the manager left office.
predicates.tenancy_terminated_before_suit: The tenancy ended before the landlord filed the recovery suit.
predicates.suit_filed_within_applicable_recovery_pe: The landlord filed the suit within the time allowed for recovery after the tenancy ended.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for a landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant under rent-control protections is governed by the specific provisions for possession suits, rather than the residual limitation provision.
material_facts: The landlord sued to recover possession from a tenant, alleging permanent alterations and acts of waste and damage that were grounds for eviction under the rent-control statute.
The trial court found the eviction grounds established and decreed possession.
The appellate court dismissed the suit as time-barred under the residual three-year limitation provision; the High Court set that decision aside.
The appeals challenged only the applicable limitation period and the accrual of the cause of action.
The possession suit was filed within twelve years of the relevant trigger for limitation.
members.legal_principle: The limitation statute is not inherently inapplicable to possession suits under rent-control legislation. The provisions protecting tenants from eviction and allowing eviction on specified grounds must be read harmoniously. Under the limitation statute, the provision for a landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant applies when the tenancy is determined; alternatively, the provision for possession following forfeiture or breach may apply. Either provision displaces the residual provision. The Court applied Haji Suleman Haji Ayub Bhiwandiwala v. Narayan Sadashiv Ogale on the coexistence and harmonious construction of the rent-control provisions, and considered Dhanpal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, Pradesh Kumar Bajpai v. Binod Behari Sarkar, and Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar on eviction under rent legislation and determination of tenancy.
members.conclusion: The limitation statute applied, but the suit fell under either the provision governing a landlord’s suit against a tenant after determination of the tenancy or the provision governing possession after forfeiture or breach of condition. The applicable period was twelve years, not three years, and the suit was not time-barred.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_possession_suit and rent_control_eviction_protection_applies and statutory_eviction_ground_established and suit_filed_within_applicable_twelve_year_period

predicates.landlord_tenant_possession_suit: A landlord brought a suit to recover possession of property from a tenant.
predicates.rent_control_eviction_protection_applies: The tenant’s protection against eviction was governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_established: The court found that the tenant had committed conduct that constituted a statutory ground for eviction.
predicates.suit_filed_within_applicable_twelve_year: The landlord brought the possession suit within twelve years of the relevant event from which the applicable limitation period ran.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant after a fixed-term tenancy ends is governed by the limitation rule for recovery from a tenant, and an unproved termination notice cannot start limitation earlier than the proved determination of the tenancy.
material_facts: The defendant entered into a fixed-term lease that expired by efflux of time.
The plaintiffs later sued for possession, alleging that the defendant had been their tenant and had not returned the leased land after the lease ended.
The defendant relied on an earlier termination notice as the starting point for limitation, but that notice was not produced or proved in the possession suit by primary or secondary evidence.
The suit was filed within twelve years of the lease’s expiry, and forfeiture before expiry was not proved.
members.legal_principle: Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the Limitation Act distinguish a title-based possession suit, a forfeiture-based suit, and a landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant. Where the landlord sues to recover from a tenant after determination of the tenancy, the specific rule in Article 67 applies and time runs from determination of the tenancy. Sections 62 and 64 of the Evidence Act require a document to be proved by primary evidence unless a basis for secondary evidence exists. Section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act addresses determination of leases. The Court relied on Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, Badrilal v. Municipal Corporation of Indore, R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P., Sevoke Properties Ltd. v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd., Bisheshar Nath v. Kundan, Sheo Dulare Lal Sah v. Anant Ram, Sidram Lachmaya v. Mallaya Lingaya Chilaka, and MEC India Pvt. Ltd. v. Lt. Col. Inder Maira.
members.conclusion: The suit was governed by Article 67 of the Limitation Act and was within time because it was filed within twelve years of the tenancy’s determination by expiry of the lease; the unproved notice did not establish an earlier starting date.

rule.if: landlord_suit_to_recover_from_tenant and lease_expired_by_fixed_term and not earlier_termination_proved and suit_filed_within_limitation_from_expiry

predicates.landlord_suit_to_recover_from_tenant: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking possession from a person who entered possession as a tenant.
predicates.lease_expired_by_fixed_term: The tenancy ended when its agreed fixed term expired.
predicates.earlier_termination_proved: Evidence in the possession proceeding establishes that the tenancy was determined before the fixed term expired.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_from_expiry: The possession suit was filed within the applicable limitation period measured from expiry of the fixed term.

members.legal_issue: The limitation period for a landlord’s application for possession begins when the tenancy is terminated, not when the tenant’s underlying breach occurs.
material_facts: The tenant defaulted on rent, with the last default occurring more than two years before the possession application.
The landlord served written notice terminating the tenancy on the ground of default, and the tenancy was properly terminated.
The landlord applied for possession within two years after the tenancy was terminated.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 14(1) and 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the tenant’s breach alone does not terminate the tenancy or give the landlord the right to apply for possession. The right to apply accrues when the tenancy is terminated by the required notice, and the right to obtain possession is then deemed to have accrued for limitation purposes, although possession still requires an order. The Court relied on Raja Ram Mahadev Paranjype v. Aba Maruti Mali and approved Ramachandra Anant v. Janardan; it overruled Chimanbai Rama v. Ganpat Jagannath. The legislative history also supported termination as the starting point.
members.conclusion: The application was within the limitation period because it was filed within two years of the tenancy’s termination; the appeal was allowed and the orders granting possession were restored.

predicates.possession_application: A landlord applied to the competent authority for an order granting possession of land held by a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_terminated_by_notice: The landlord gave the required notice following a tenant’s breach, and the tenancy was terminated.
predicates.application_within_two_years_of_terminat: The landlord filed the possession application within two years after the tenancy was terminated.

members.legal_issue: A separate suit cannot be used to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful, even when the claimant was not a party to the compromise but claims through a party to it.
material_facts: The claimant was not a party to the compromise decree but claimed an interest in the property through a sale by a party to the pending partition litigation.
The claimant filed a separate suit seeking a declaration that the compromise decree was illegal and had been obtained by fraud and misrepresentation.
The separate suit was brought before a court other than the court that recorded the compromise and passed the decree.
members.legal_principle: Order 23 Rule 3A CPC bars a suit to set aside a decree on the ground that the compromise on which it is based was unlawful. Under the proviso to Order 23 Rule 3 CPC, the court that recorded the compromise decides a dispute about its validity. Order 43 Rule 1A(2) CPC permits a party who contested whether the compromise should have been recorded to raise that issue in an appeal against the decree; Section 96(3) CPC does not bar such an appeal when the factum of compromise is disputed. The principles in Pushpa Devi Bhagat (Dead) Through LR Sadhna Rai (Smt) v. Rajinder Singh and Others and R. Rajanna v. S.R. Venkataswamy and Others confirm that a separate suit is not available to challenge the compromise decree. A claimant may separately pursue protection of rights claimed through a party, but may not thereby question the decree itself.
members.conclusion: The separate suit was barred. A challenge to the lawfulness of the compromise had to be examined by the court that recorded it; the claimant could not use a separate suit to invalidate the decree, although a suit to protect any independent property rights could be examined on its own merits.

predicates.separate_suit_seeks_to_set_aside_comprom: A claimant brings a separate suit seeking to set aside a decree made on a compromise.
predicates.challenge_alleges_compromise_was_unlawfu: The claimant bases the challenge on the assertion that the compromise was unlawful, invalid, or improperly obtained.
predicates.claimant_claims_through_compromise_party: The claimant asserts an interest derived from a person who was a party to the compromise proceeding.

members.legal_issue: An independent suit whose substance is to invalidate a compromise decree because the compromise was unlawful is barred, even if the plaint frames the requested reliefs as declarations or other forms of relief.
material_facts: A compromise decree had been passed in an earlier suit concerning the property and the plaintiff later brought an independent suit seeking declarations and other reliefs relating to the property and the decree.
The reliefs sought in the later suit could be granted only if the compromise decree were set aside.
The plaintiff had also applied to the court that recorded the compromise to challenge the decree.
members.legal_principle: Order XXIII Rule 3A CPC bars a suit to set aside a decree on the ground that the underlying compromise was unlawful; under the Explanation to Order XXIII Rule 3, a void or voidable compromise is not lawful. The challenge must be made before the court that recorded the compromise. The Court relied on R. Janakiammal v. S.K. Kumarasamy, Banwari Lal v. Chando Devi, Pushpa Devi Bhagat v. Rajinder Singh, R. Rajanna v. S.R. Venkataswamy and Triloki Nath Singh v. Anirudh Singh. It also applied the principle against using clever drafting to disguise a barred claim, relying on T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal and Ram Singh v. Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, among other cases.
members.conclusion: The independent suit was barred, and the trial court was justified in rejecting the plaint. The reliefs could not avoid the bar merely because they were framed as declarations or other claims.

predicates.independent_suit_challenges_compromise_d: A plaintiff brings a separate suit seeking relief that challenges a decree made on the basis of a compromise.
predicates.compromise_lawfulness_is_challenged: The plaintiff's claim rests on the contention that the compromise underlying the decree was unlawful.
predicates.requested_reliefs_require_decree_to_be_s: The requested reliefs could not be granted unless the compromise decree were set aside.
predicates.plaint_uses_indirect_reliefs_to_obtain_s: The plaint frames its requests as other kinds of relief but seeks, in substance, the same result as setting aside the compromise decree.

members.legal_issue: A separate suit cannot be used to set aside a consent decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful, including because consent was allegedly obtained by fraud or misrepresentation.
material_facts: The suit sought to declare a compromise decree invalid, sham, collusive, and unenforceable.
The plaintiffs alleged that they signed the compromise after being told it would merely protect family property from bank claims and would not affect their rights.
The allegations therefore challenged the compromise as voidable for want of free consent.
The challenge was brought in a separate suit rather than before the court that recorded the compromise.
members.legal_principle: Order XXIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including its proviso and Explanation, requires the court recording a compromise to decide a dispute about its lawfulness; an agreement void or voidable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 is not lawful for this purpose. Sections 10, 14 and 19 of the Contract Act address valid agreements, free consent and voidability. Order XXIII Rule 3A bars a separate suit to set aside a decree on the ground that its compromise was unlawful. Banwari Lal v. Chando Devi, Pushpa Devi Bhagat v. Rajinder Singh, R. Rajanna v. S.R. Venkataswamy, and Triloki Nath Singh v. Anirudh Singh establish that the challenge must be made to the court that recorded the compromise.
members.conclusion: The separate suit was barred. A party seeking to challenge the lawfulness of a compromise must raise the issue before the court that recorded it.

rule.if: separate_suit_challenging_consent_decree and challenge_claims_compromise_was_unlawful and (challenge_alleges_fraud_or_misrepresentation or challenge_alleges_other_invalid_consent)

predicates.separate_suit_challenging_consent_decree: A party to a consent decree brought a separate suit seeking to set it aside.
predicates.challenge_claims_compromise_was_unlawful: The separate suit alleged that the compromise underlying the decree was unlawful.
predicates.challenge_alleges_fraud_or_misrepresenta: The party alleged that fraud or misrepresentation caused them to agree to the compromise.
predicates.challenge_alleges_other_invalid_consent: The party alleged another defect that made consent to the compromise invalid.

members.legal_issue: A tenant may be evicted for continuously failing to use rented premises for their established purpose without reasonable cause, even where the rent note requires rent to be paid during periods of non-use.
material_facts: The premises were let for the purpose of a tobacco business, as shown by the firm in whose name they were taken and by the tenant’s and counsel’s admissions.
The tenant shifted the business elsewhere and had stopped using the premises for several years before the suit.
Municipal and excise records supported the evidence of non-use.
The rent note required rent to be paid even if the premises were not used or were kept closed.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(k) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947 permits eviction where premises have not been used for the purpose for which they were let for a continuous period of six months immediately preceding the suit without reasonable cause. The Act’s preamble reflects a purpose of controlling eviction amid scarcity of accommodation; a rent stipulation about payment during non-use does not permit a tenant to contract out of the Act’s protections and obligations.
members.conclusion: The tenant was liable to eviction on the ground of non-use, and the landlord’s suit was decreed.

rule.if: eviction_suit_for_nonuse and letting_purpose_established and continuous_nonuse_without_reasonable_cause and (tenant_stopped_the_established_use or premises_kept_unused)

predicates.eviction_suit_for_nonuse: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding on the ground that the tenant had not used the premises for the legally relevant period.
predicates.letting_purpose_established: Evidence established the purpose for which the tenant took the premises.
predicates.continuous_nonuse_without_reasonable_cau: The tenant continuously failed to use the premises for the established purpose, without reasonable cause, for the legally relevant period.
predicates.tenant_stopped_the_established_use: The tenant stopped carrying on the business or other activity for which the premises had been let.
predicates.premises_kept_unused: The tenant left the premises unused or closed for a prolonged period.

members.legal_issue: For eviction based on cessation of occupation, occupation requires actual use of the premises for the purpose for which they were let, and proof of continuous non-use for the statutory period shifts the burden to the tenant to establish reasonable cause.
material_facts: The premises were leased for use as an office and godown.
The premises were found closed, with rusted shutters and gates, overgrown grounds, dusty and unusable furniture, and no electricity supply.
A notice on the premises stated that operations had been suspended from October 2001.
The tenant did not produce relevant attendance, wage, stock, electricity-payment, or business-transaction records to establish continued use or reasonable cause for non-use.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(1) and 11(4)(v) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, occupation means actual possession or use for the purpose for which the premises were let, not merely legal possession or keeping articles under lock and key. The landlord bears the initial burden of producing tangible evidence of continuous non-occupation for six months; the burden then shifts to the tenant to prove reasonable cause. The Court relied on Ram Dass v. Davinder, Mathai Antony v. Abraham, Kurian Thomas v. Sreedharan Menon, Paulina Joseph v. Idukki District Wholesale Co-operative Consumer Stores Ltd., and Simon v. Rappai.
members.conclusion: The landlord proved continuous cessation of occupation for more than six months, and the tenant failed to establish occupation or reasonable cause; eviction was therefore warranted.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_petition: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on the basis of non-occupation.
predicates.landlord_proved_continuous_nonuse_for_st: The landlord produces tangible evidence that the tenant did not actually use the premises for their letting purpose throughout the required continuous period.
predicates.tenant_proved_occupation_or_reasonable_c: The tenant produces evidence establishing actual use of the premises or a reasonable cause for not using them.

members.legal_issue: A lease permitting continued occupation for an indefinite period is not perpetual unless its terms clearly make the leasehold interest heritable.
material_facts: The lease was made to allow construction of a residential building and specified an initial fixed term.
It allowed the lessee to remain in possession after that term while paying the agreed rent, which the lessor could not increase.
The lease allowed the lessee or heirs to remove the building in specified circumstances and allowed transfer of the building, but did not clearly make the leasehold interest heritable.
members.legal_principle: A lease must be construed as a whole to determine whether the parties intended a permanent interest. An indefinite term ordinarily lasts for the lessee’s lifetime unless the lease clearly shows an intention to make the interest hereditary; transferability alone does not make it heritable. The Court relied on Sivayogeswara Cotton Press v. Panchaksharappa, which approved the approach in Bavasaheb v. West Patent Company, and distinguished that case because the lease there expressly bound the parties’ heirs and successors. It also discussed Abdul Rahim v. Sarafalli and Lekhraj Roy v. Kunhya Singh.
members.conclusion: The lease lasted for the initial fixed term and, if the lessee remained in possession afterwards, for the lessee’s lifetime; it did not create a perpetual or hereditary interest.

rule.if: civil_appeal_on_leasehold_land_claims and building_lease and continued_occupation_at_fixed_rent and no_clear_hereditary_grant and transferability_without_hereditary_terms

predicates.civil_appeal_on_leasehold_land_claims: The proceeding is a civil appeal involving the duration of a leasehold interest in land.
predicates.building_lease: The parties made the lease for the purpose of constructing a building.
predicates.continued_occupation_at_fixed_rent: The lease allowed the lessee to remain in possession indefinitely after its initial term while paying an unchanged rent.
predicates.no_clear_hereditary_grant: The lease did not clearly provide that the leasehold interest would pass to the lessee’s heirs as a continuing interest.
predicates.transferability_without_hereditary_terms: The lease allowed a transfer of the building or leasehold interest but did not state that the interest was hereditary.

members.legal_issue: A building-purpose lease for an indefinite period after an initial fixed term, construed as a whole, may create a permanent tenancy rather than a tenancy at will or a tenancy limited to the lessee’s lifetime.
material_facts: The lease was for agricultural land to be used for a factory and other buildings, and it authorized the lessee to erect and alter substantial structures.
The lease set an initial twenty-year term, after which the lessee could continue in possession for as long as desired by paying the stipulated rent.
The lessor agreed not to require the lessee to give up possession while the lessee wished to retain the land and observed the lease terms.
The lease was expressed to bind the parties’ heirs, successors, and assigns, and the lessee could sublet or re-let the land.
The lessee could surrender the lease after the initial term, but the lessor had no corresponding right to terminate it at will.
The lower courts decreed ejectment, and the High Court treated the post-term tenancy as one for an indefinite period rather than a permanent tenancy.
members.legal_principle: The nature of a tenancy must be determined by construing the lease as a whole and identifying the parties’ intention. A lease of land for building purposes without a fixed period raises a presumption of a permanent tenancy; the presumption is supported where the lease is heritable and assignable and the lessor has no right to terminate possession. The lessee’s right to surrender does not by itself rebut that presumption. The Court applied the principles in Navalram v. Javerilal, Promada Nath Roy v. Srigobind Chowdhry, Forbes v. Hanuman Bhagat, Commissioner of Income-tax v. Maharajadhiraj Kumar Visheshwar Singh, Janaki Nath Roy v. Dina Nath Kundu, and Baboo Lekhraj Roy v. Kunhya Singh, and distinguished Babasaheb v. West Patent Co., Ltd. No statutory provision was relied on.
members.conclusion: The lease created a permanent tenancy, so the ejectment decree was set aside and the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: appeal_against_ejectment_decree and building_purpose_lease and indefinite_continuation_after_initial_term and lessor_cannot_end_possession_at_will and lease_binds_successors and lease_allows_assignment

predicates.appeal_against_ejectment_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree ordering the lessee or a successor to surrender possession.
predicates.building_purpose_lease: The land was leased for building purposes, and the lease authorized the construction of substantial buildings or structures.
predicates.indefinite_continuation_after_initial_te: After an initial fixed term, the lessee could continue in possession for as long as desired under the lease terms.
predicates.lessor_cannot_end_possession_at_will: The lessor agreed not to require the lessee to give up possession while the lessee wished to remain and complied with the lease.
predicates.lease_binds_successors: The lease states that its terms bind the parties’ heirs or successors.
predicates.lease_allows_assignment: The lease permits the lessee to transfer the leasehold interest or sublet the land.

members.legal_issue: A lease that does not grant a permanent interest in its terms does not become a permanent lease merely because the lessee and successors remain in possession for a long time at the same rent.
material_facts: The lease granted the village for a fixed annual payment but specified no duration.
Its terms required annual payment in installments and did not state that the lease was permanent or that the payment could never be varied.
The appellants’ ancestor and successors remained in possession for more than a century at the same rent.
members.legal_principle: The instrument must be read according to its plain terms; prolonged possession and payment of an unchanged rent do not make an otherwise non-permanent lease permanent. The court relied on the terms of the lease and rejected the claimed inference from long possession.
members.conclusion: The lease did not grant a permanent lease, and the duration of possession at the same rent did not change its terms.

rule.if: lease_right_dispute_in_possession_suit and lease_sets_fixed_annual_payment and lease_specifies_no_duration and not lease_expressly_grants_permanent_interest and long_possession_at_same_rent

predicates.lease_right_dispute_in_possession_suit: The parties dispute in a possession suit whether a lease grants a permanent interest.
predicates.lease_sets_fixed_annual_payment: The lease requires payment of a fixed amount annually.
predicates.lease_specifies_no_duration: The lease states no duration for the grant.
predicates.lease_expressly_grants_permanent_interes: The lease expressly grants a permanent interest.
predicates.long_possession_at_same_rent: The lessee or successors remain in possession for a long period while paying the same rent.

members.legal_issue: A company-funded land acquisition under Part VII is permitted for construction of a work useful to the public only when the work itself is directly useful to the public and the public is entitled to use it directly.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a company to construct a factory manufacturing textile machinery parts, and the company was to pay the entire compensation.
The Government considered the factory’s products useful to the public.

The agreement gave access to and use of the land or works to people as necessary to transact business with the company, but did not give the public a right to use the work directly for its own benefit.
members.legal_principle: Under ss. 39, 40(1)(b), 41(5) and 42 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, where the company bears the acquisition cost, the provisions governing acquisition for a company apply. Sections 40(1)(b) and 41(5) must be read together: the work itself must be directly useful to the public, and the agreement must provide for the public’s direct use of the work. The usefulness of a company’s products and access for those doing business with it are insufficient. The Court relied on Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, including its examples of works of public utility, and distinguished Ezra v. Secretary of State.
members.conclusion: The factory’s products being useful to the public, and business users having access to the factory, did not satisfy the statutory requirements. The acquisition notification was invalid and the proceedings resulting from it were quashed.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_for_company and company_pays_entire_acquisition_cost and work_is_not_directly_usable_by_public and public_access_is_only_for_business_with_company

predicates.acquisition_challenge_for_company: A person challenges, in an appeal or other proceeding, a compulsory land acquisition made for a company.
predicates.company_pays_entire_acquisition_cost: The company bears the whole cost of acquiring the land.
predicates.work_is_not_directly_usable_by_public: The work to be constructed is not itself available for direct use by the public for its own benefit.
predicates.public_access_is_only_for_business_with_: The agreement permits members of the public to access or use the work only as needed to transact business with the company.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of land for a company under the company-acquisition procedure is permissible for a work only when the work itself is directly useful to the public and the agreement secures public use of the work, rather than merely access for business with the company.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a company to construct a textile machinery parts factory, and the company was to pay the entire compensation.
The factory’s products were said to be useful to the public, but the factory itself was not available for direct public use.
The agreement provided only for access to and use of the land or works as necessary for the public to transact business with the company.
members.legal_principle: Sections 40(1)(b) and 41, read together and in the context of sections 39 and 42 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, require the work itself to be directly useful to the public and the agreement to provide for public use of that work as such. The Court relied on Baba Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay for the restricted purposes permitted for company acquisitions, and distinguished the public-funded acquisition in Pandit Jhandu Lal v. State of Punjab. The public usefulness of a company’s product alone is insufficient.
members.conclusion: The factory’s useful products and the public’s limited business access did not satisfy the statutory requirements; the acquisition notification and resulting proceedings were quashed.

rule.if: company_land_acquisition and company_pays_entire_compensation and work_not_directly_usable_by_public and public_access_only_for_business

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government acquired land for a company through a compulsory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.company_pays_entire_compensation: The company was to bear the entire compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.work_not_directly_usable_by_public: The work constructed on the acquired land was not itself available for direct use by the public.
predicates.public_access_only_for_business: The agreement allowed members of the public to access or use the work only as needed to transact business with the company.

members.legal_issue: A compulsory acquisition for a company’s building or work is constitutionally permissible only when that building or work serves the public purpose of the company’s industry or work.
material_facts: The amended law allowed acquisition for a building or work for a company engaged, or taking steps to engage, in an industry or work for a public purpose.
The challenge argued that the company’s industry alone needed to serve a public purpose, even if the acquired land would be used for a building or work unrelated to that purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 31(2) and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, compulsory acquisition must be for a public purpose and restrictions on holding property must be reasonable. A court may consider statutory setting and circumstances to control an otherwise broad literal reading; where two constructions are possible, it should prefer the constitutionally consistent one. The Court relied on The Mysore State Electricity Board v. The Bangalore Woollen, Cotton and Silk Mills Ltd. and Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar. The construction also governs the consequential amendment to section 41, including its requirement for an agreement specifying the time and conditions for construction or execution.
members.conclusion: The provision is to be read as requiring the building or work itself to serve the public purpose of the company’s industry or work; so construed, it does not violate the constitutional protections for property or the right to hold property. The related amendments governing the required agreement are also valid.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_company_land: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of land for a company.
predicates.company_industry_serves_public_purpose: The company is engaged, or is taking steps to engage, in an industry or work that serves a public purpose.
predicates.building_or_work_serves_that_public_purp: The building or work for which the land is acquired serves the public purpose of the company’s industry or work.

members.legal_issue: For acquisition for a company engaged in a public-purpose industry, the required public purpose is assessed by whether the building or work serves the public purpose of the company, with regard to the nature and benefits of its industry, rather than by requiring a public purpose in the general sense.
material_facts: The company manufactured sodium silicate, plaster of Paris and other goods that were widely used and had previously been imported on a large scale.
The company's production saved foreign exchange and benefited the public.
The company sought adjoining land to expand production and provide space for underground storage tanks.
members.legal_principle: Section 40(1)(aa) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended, requires that the building or work serve the public purpose of the company; the words “public purpose” take their colour from the nature of the industry, its products, and the benefit they provide. The Court applied R. L. Arora v. State of U.P. (the second Arora case), approved the approach in P. Girdharan Prasad Missair v. State of Bihar and Chhotubhai Babarbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat, and also referred to the second Arora case’s treatment of production serving the general public.
members.conclusion: The acquisition served the public purpose of the company because the proposed expansion supported an industry whose products benefited the public and saved foreign exchange.

predicates.land_acquisition_for_company: The land was acquired for construction or work for a company.
predicates.company_industry_benefited_public: The company's industry or work produced benefits for the public, considering its products and their economic or practical effects.
predicates.acquired_work_supported_company_industry: The building or work for which the land was acquired supported the company's industry or work.

members.legal_issue: A land lease permitting construction of houses or other uses is not within a rent-protection definition limited to land let principally for business or trade unless that principal commercial purpose is established.
material_facts: The land was leased separately, with permission to construct houses or to use the land in any manner.
The lease did not establish that the land was let principally for business or trade, even though buildings were later constructed and some were rented out.
In an execution proceeding, the occupants challenged the consent decree for possession as contrary to the rent restriction law.
members.legal_principle: Under section 4(2)(b) of the Bombay Rent Restriction Act, 1939, separately let land falls within the definition of premises only when it is let principally for business or trade. A lease merely permitting construction of houses, or other use of the land, does not itself establish that principal purpose. The court did not rely on any earlier case for this issue.
members.conclusion: The land was not within the statutory definition of premises, so the rent restriction law did not apply and the consent decree was not invalid on that ground.

predicates.execution_challenge: Occupants challenged a decree for possession in an execution proceeding on the ground that rent protection applied.
predicates.separately_leased_land: The lessor leased land separately rather than leasing a building or part of a building.
predicates.lease_not_principally_commercial: The lease permitted construction of houses or other uses but did not establish that the land was to be used principally for business or trade.

members.legal_issue: The rent-control provisions governing premises let for specified purposes do not apply when land is leased for construction of buildings of any description rather than for one of those specified purposes.
material_facts: The lease covered land and allowed the lessees to construct buildings of every description, without restricting construction to residential, educational, business, trade, or storage purposes.
The lease permitted construction loans from prospective tenants as an exception to restrictions on mortgaging, charging, or assigning the land or buildings.
The appellant argued that the loan provision showed the lease was for constructing residential buildings; the court found that it addressed a contingency and did not define the lease’s purpose.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Part II applies only to premises let for residence, education, business, trade, or storage. The purpose of the lease, not the lessee’s future choice about what to build, determines whether the premises were let for one of those purposes. Permission to take construction loans for residential buildings under section 18(3), when included as an exception to a covenant restricting encumbrances, does not establish that the land was let for residential construction. The court explained Mrs. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy v. Khemchand Gorumal & Ors. [1962] 3 S.C.R. 921, where land let for putting up structures for residence fell within section 6(1).
members.conclusion: Part II of the Act, including section 18(1), did not apply because the land was not let for one of the purposes specified in section 6(1).

rule.if: lease_scope_dispute and premises_are_land and lease_allows_buildings_of_any_description and lease_is_not_limited_to_specified_uses

predicates.lease_scope_dispute: The dispute concerns whether rent-control provisions apply to premises under a lease.
predicates.premises_are_land: The leased premises consist of land.
predicates.lease_allows_buildings_of_any_descriptio: The lease allows the lessee to construct buildings without restricting their description or type.
predicates.lease_is_not_limited_to_specified_uses: The lease does not limit the purpose of construction to residence, education, business, trade, or storage.

members.legal_issue: Rent-control protection for leased premises does not extend to a lease of vacant land merely because the tenant constructed structures on it.
material_facts: The lease was of a vacant site for use as a petrol outlet.
The lease allowed the tenant to construct accessory structures, and the showroom shed mentioned in the lease belonged to the tenant.
The landlord’s claim and notices described the premises as vacant land, and the landlord sought possession after removal of the tenant’s structures.
members.legal_principle: The Pondicherry Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1969 regulates the letting of buildings and defines a building to include a building or hut let separately for residential or non-residential purposes, along with specified appurtenances. A lease of vacant land on which the tenant may construct accessory structures is not, on these facts, a lease of a building under that definition.
members.conclusion: The lease was of vacant land rather than a building covered by the applicable rent-control statute, so the tenant could not claim statutory tenant protection under that statute.

rule.if: rent_control_protection_claim and lease_was_of_vacant_land and tenant_constructed_accessory_structures and structures_were_not_leased_from_landlord

predicates.rent_control_protection_claim: A tenant claims protection from eviction under a law regulating the letting of buildings.
predicates.lease_was_of_vacant_land: The property leased was vacant land rather than a building let by the landlord.
predicates.tenant_constructed_accessory_structures: The tenant constructed structures on the land for use connected with the leased activity.
predicates.structures_were_not_leased_from_landlord: The structures were not buildings belonging to the landlord that formed part of the premises let.

members.legal_issue: A tenancy confined to land does not constitute accommodation where tenant-built structures never became the landlord’s property.
material_facts: The land was originally let to a tenant who built a verandah and a room on it.
The original tenant did not return possession of the land and structures to the landlord, but transferred them to the appellant.
The courts found that the structures never became the landlord’s property and that the appellant’s tenancy from the landlord was for the land alone.
The landlord’s successors filed an ejectment suit without obtaining permission from the District Magistrate.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(a) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, accommodation means residential or non-residential accommodation in a building or part of a building. Section 3 requires the District Magistrate’s permission for a suit to evict a tenant from accommodation. Where the tenancy is only of land and tenant-built structures never became the landlord’s property, the tenancy is not of accommodation for these purposes. Section 108(h) of the Transfer of Property Act permits a lessee to remove constructions made by the lessee while still in possession. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The land alone did not fall within the statutory definition of accommodation, so permission from the District Magistrate was not required before filing the ejectment suit.

predicates.ejectment_suit: A landlord or successor sought to recover possession of rented property through an ejectment suit.
predicates.tenancy_was_only_for_land: The tenant’s tenancy from the landlord covered land alone, rather than a building or part of a building.
predicates.tenant_built_structures_never_became_lan: The tenant-built structures did not become the landlord’s property before the tenant transferred possession of the land and structures.

members.legal_issue: A prior mortgagee who purchases the mortgaged property in execution and thereby acquires the equity of redemption has priority over a later-mortgage purchaser in the competing rights to redeem.
material_facts: The owner created an earlier mortgage and later mortgages over the same property.
The earlier mortgagee sued without joining the later mortgagees, and there was no finding that their omission was designed to prejudice them.
The earlier mortgagee purchased the property in execution of the earlier mortgage decree and later transferred his interest.
A later mortgagee subsequently obtained an execution-sale purchase subject to the earlier mortgage, and the competing purchasers asserted rights to redeem.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the mortgage principle that a later mortgagee may redeem an earlier mortgage, but an earlier mortgagee who purchases the property in execution acquires the mortgagor’s equity of redemption and has the superior, last right of redemption against later mortgagees. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The purchaser under the earlier mortgage acquired the equity of redemption and had the preferential right to redeem the later mortgages over the purchaser under the later mortgages.

rule.if: competing_mortgage_redemption_case and prior_mortgagee_execution_purchase and prior_buyer_acquired_redemption_equity and junior_purchase_subject_to_prior_mortgage

predicates.competing_mortgage_redemption_case: The dispute concerns competing purchasers under execution sales on successive mortgages who each claim a right to redeem.
predicates.prior_mortgagee_execution_purchase: The holder of the earlier mortgage purchased the mortgaged property in execution of that mortgage decree.
predicates.prior_buyer_acquired_redemption_equity: The earlier-mortgage purchaser acquired the mortgagor’s equity of redemption through the execution purchase.
predicates.junior_purchase_subject_to_prior_mortgag: A purchaser under a later mortgage obtained the property subject to the earlier mortgage.

members.legal_issue: A transferee of the interest acquired by a prior mortgagee at an execution sale is entitled to possession when that prior mortgagee has the preferential right to redeem the later mortgages.
material_facts: The earlier mortgagee purchased the property in execution and later transferred his interest.
The transferees claimed possession of the property against persons occupying it under the earlier mortgagee.
The court upheld the earlier mortgagee’s preferential right to redeem the later mortgages.
members.legal_principle: The court held that, once the earlier mortgagee’s preferential redemption right was established, the transferees of that mortgagee’s interest were entitled to possession. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited.
members.conclusion: The transferees of the earlier mortgagee’s interest were entitled to possession of the property.

predicates.possession_claim_by_prior_mortgagee_tran: A transferee of an earlier mortgagee’s interest claims possession of the mortgaged property.
predicates.prior_mortgagee_preferential_redemption_: The earlier mortgagee has been found to have the preferential right to redeem the later mortgages.
predicates.prior_mortgagee_interest_transferred: The earlier mortgagee transferred the interest acquired through the execution purchase to another person.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagor’s right of redemption may be extinguished as against a mortgagee when that mortgagee purchases the mortgaged property and thereby acquires the equity of redemption.
material_facts: The property had been mortgaged to two mortgagees, one of whom later purchased the property from the mortgagor under a sale deed.
The claimant sought redemption as alternative relief in a suit whose principal relief challenged the mortgage and sale documents.
The High Court treated the suit as a simple redemption action and ordered payment of the mortgage amount and delivery of possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 recognizes the right of redemption, subject to its proviso permitting extinction by an act of the parties or a court decree. The Court relied on Shivdev Singh v. Sucha Singh (2000) 4 SCC 326 concerning the statutory nature of the right of redemption and explained that the later purchase of the property by a mortgagee merged that mortgagee’s mortgage interest with the purchase.
members.conclusion: The sale to the mortgagee was an act of the parties by which the right of redemption was extinguished as against that purchaser; the High Court was not right to decree redemption in the manner it did.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: A party seeks to redeem property subject to a mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_purchases_mortgaged_property_f: A mortgagee later purchases the mortgaged property from the mortgagor.

members.legal_issue: The mortgagor’s right to redeem the secured property is extinguished upon registration of the completed sale in favour of the purchaser.
material_facts: The bank was permitted by the tribunal to proceed with the sale after the guarantors failed to satisfy the conditions for interim protection.
The successful bidder paid the sale consideration, and the sale was registered in the purchaser’s favour.
The challenge seeking to set aside the sale was pursued after registration.
members.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, preserves the right of redemption until it is extinguished by an act of the parties; the right survives a contract for sale until completion of the sale by a registered instrument. Mathew Varghese v. M. Amritha Kumar (2014) 5 SCC 610 applied that principle to secured assets under the SARFAESI Act. Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam (1977) 3 SCC 247 states the underlying rule, and Dwarika Prasad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 5 SCC 491 and Shakeena v. Bank of India (2019) SCC OnLine SC 1059 support extinction of the redemption right upon registration of the sale certificate.
members.conclusion: The mortgagor’s right of redemption had been extinguished upon registration of the sale, and the later challenge could not restore that right or invalidate the sale.

predicates.mortgage_sale_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a sale of mortgaged property conducted by a secured creditor.
predicates.secured_property_sale_registered: The completed sale of the secured property has been registered in favour of the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: A court may appoint a sole arbitrator to resolve the parties' disputes when the agreed arbitral tribunal has not been constituted and the parties agree to the court making the appointment.
material_facts: The parties had each nominated an arbitrator under their agreement, but those arbitrators had not nominated a presiding arbitrator despite the passage of more than a year.
The application seeking appointment of a third arbitrator was pending, and the parties agreed that the Supreme Court could appoint either a presiding arbitrator or a sole arbitrator.
The Supreme Court appointed a former Chief Justice of India as sole arbitrator to decide disputes arising from the parties' agreement and power of attorney.
members.legal_principle: The court acted after the agreed appointment procedure had failed to constitute the tribunal and both parties agreed that the court could appoint a sole or presiding arbitrator. The appointment was made in the context of the parties' arbitration agreement and the pending request for appointment under Section 11(4)(b) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
members.conclusion: The court appointed a sole arbitrator to decide the parties' disputes and revoked the parties' earlier nominations of arbitrators.

predicates.arbitration_dispute: The parties have a dispute that they agreed to resolve by arbitration.
predicates.agreed_tribunal_not_constituted: The parties' agreed appointment procedure has failed to constitute the arbitral tribunal.
predicates.parties_agree_to_court_appointment: Both parties agree that the court may appoint an arbitrator to resolve the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A court may appoint the arbitrator nominated by a party where the arbitration agreement provides for a sole arbitrator and the other party does not respond or object to the nomination.
material_facts: The arbitration clause provided for a sole arbitrator to be mutually agreed by the parties and for appointment through a court if they disagreed.
The petitioner invoked the arbitration clause, proposed a sole arbitrator, and sought the respondent's concurrence.
The respondent did not reply to the appointment notice and did not appear to oppose the appointment petition.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the Court may make the appointment where the agreed appointment process has not resulted in an appointment. In this case, the sole-arbitrator clause, the proposed nomination, and the respondent's failure to respond or object supported appointment of the proposed arbitrator.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the petition and appointed the sole arbitrator proposed by the petitioner.

rule.if: arbitrator_appointment_proceeding and sole_arbitrator_clause_exists and party_proposed_sole_arbitrator and other_party_did_not_respond_or_object

predicates.arbitrator_appointment_proceeding: A proceeding seeks court appointment of an arbitrator under an arbitration agreement.
predicates.sole_arbitrator_clause_exists: The parties agreed that their dispute would be decided by a sole arbitrator.
predicates.party_proposed_sole_arbitrator: A party invoked the arbitration agreement and proposed a person to serve as sole arbitrator.
predicates.other_party_did_not_respond_or_object: The other party neither responded to the appointment request nor objected to the proposed arbitrator.

members.legal_issue: A substitute arbitrator may be appointed when a named arbitrator’s mandate terminates in a court-referred arbitration, unless the parties’ agreement expressly or by necessary implication bars substitution.
material_facts: While a suit was pending, the parties agreed in consent terms to refer unresolved disputes to a named retired judge for arbitration.
The court recorded the consent terms, disposed of the suit, and referred the unresolved disputes to the named arbitrator.
The arbitrator resigned, and the agreement contained no express or implied prohibition on appointing a substitute or indication that only the named arbitrator could decide the disputes.
The party seeking a replacement applied to the same High Court that had recorded the consent terms and appointed the original arbitrator; that court appointed a substitute arbitrator.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 15(1) and (2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, when an arbitrator’s mandate terminates, a substitute is to be appointed according to the rules applicable to the original appointment; those rules include the parties’ arbitration agreement. Read liberally and purposively to promote effective arbitration, Section 15(2) permits substitution unless the agreement expressly or by necessary implication prohibits it. Sections 15(3) and (4), concerning continuation of proceedings and preservation of prior rulings after replacement, support that construction. Section 89 CPC provides for court referral to arbitration by agreement in a pending suit; a consent order is more than a contract because it carries the command of a judge. The Court relied on Yashwith Constructions (P) Ltd. v. Simplex Concrete Piles India Ltd., SBP and Company v. Patel Engineering Ltd., ACC Ltd. v. Global Cements Ltd., Parbhat General Agencies v. Union of India, C.F. Angadi v. Y.S. Hirannayya, and P. Anand Gajapati Raju v. P.V.G. Raju.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly appointed a substitute arbitrator. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: court_referred_arbitration and arbitrator_mandate_terminated and agreement_does_not_bar_substitution and original_appointment_made_by_court and substitute_sought_from_original_court

predicates.court_referred_arbitration: A court handling a suit referred unresolved disputes to arbitration after the parties agreed to that method of resolution.
predicates.arbitrator_mandate_terminated: The arbitrator appointed to decide the referred disputes withdrew, died, or otherwise ceased to hold the mandate.
