In that situation, the procedure under Order XXI Rule 90 for material irregularity does not apply.
members.conclusion: The procedure for setting aside a sale on the ground of material irregularity does not apply when the sale is treated as a nullity for breach of a mandatory sale requirement.

predicates.execution_auction: A property is sold at auction in proceedings to enforce a decree.
predicates.sale_set_aside_as_nullity: The executing court sets aside the auction sale on the basis that it was void.
predicates.mandatory_sale_requirement_not_met: The required act under a mandatory condition for an auction sale was not completed.

members.legal_issue: A District Magistrate identified by an eviction statute as the official responsible for granting permission is not a persona designata when the authority attaches to the office and the statutory scheme permits other officers to exercise that authority.
material_facts: The eviction statute assigned the permission function to the District Magistrate and defined that term to include an officer authorized to perform the District Magistrate’s functions.
The relevant Additional District Magistrate held a public office and had been appointed with powers under other laws, including the eviction statute.
The challenge asserted that the District Magistrate was a persona designata and that only the District Magistrate or an officer specifically authorized by that official could act.
members.legal_principle: A persona designata is a person selected as an individual, rather than as the holder of an office or a member of a class. The Court applied that distinction, referring to Parthasaradhi Naidu v. Koteswara Rao, and held that an official named by virtue of office is not a persona designata where the statute permits other officers to exercise the office’s powers. Kedar Nath v. Mool Chand was disapproved.
members.conclusion: The District Magistrate was not a persona designata; the authority was attached to the office, and the statutory scheme allowed other officers to exercise it.

predicates.tenant_eviction_permission_case: A landlord sought permission to bring a suit to evict a tenant where such permission was required.
predicates.authority_attached_to_public_office: The relevant function was assigned to an official by virtue of holding a public office, rather than to that person in an individual capacity.
predicates.statutory_scheme_allows_other_officers_t: The governing scheme allowed other officers to perform the officeholder’s functions.

members.legal_issue: A District Judge exercising statutory functions is not a persona designata when the statute permits those functions to be exercised by other judges or courts.
material_facts: The sale proceeding was heard by a District Judge exercising functions under the statutory scheme.
The statute provided that those functions could also be exercised by a judge of a city civil court, the High Court in specified circumstances, or an additional District Judge.
members.legal_principle: Section 32(11) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, provided for the functions of a District Judge under the section to be exercised by specified other judicial officers or courts. That allocation shows that the authority is attached to a judicial office or court and not to a particular person designated individually; no earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Act did not confer jurisdiction on the District Judge as a persona designata.

predicates.statutory_judicial_proceeding: The matter was a statutory proceeding assigned to a District Judge in a judicial capacity.
predicates.statutory_function_transferable_among_ju: The governing scheme allowed the same function to be exercised by other judges or courts.

members.legal_issue: The party who propounds a disputed document bears the burden of proving its execution, rather than requiring the opposing party to prove forgery.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought specific performance on the basis of an agreement that the alleged seller denied executing.
The plaintiff relied on his own evidence and that of the scribe and one attesting witness.

The trial court identified circumstances casting doubt on the agreement, including old stamp papers, the relationship of witnesses to the plaintiff, non-delivery of possession and title deeds as recited, and the failure to examine one attesting witness.
The first appellate court placed the burden on the defendants to prove that the agreement was forged or concocted.
members.legal_principle: A party who propounds a document must prove it when its execution is denied; the opposing party is not required to prove the negative or establish forgery. The Court applied that burden to the evidence as a whole and treated the cumulative circumstances identified by the trial court as undermining the evidence offered to prove execution.
members.conclusion: The burden remained on the plaintiff, as the party propounding the agreement, to prove its execution. The first appellate court erred by requiring the defendants to prove the negative, and the circumstances considered together created sufficient doubt to dislodge the plaintiff's evidence.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and claimant_propounded_agreement and alleged_signatory_denied_execution and supporting_evidence_weakened_by_cumulative_circumstances

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.claimant_propounded_agreement: The claimant relies on an agreement as the basis for the relief sought.
predicates.alleged_signatory_denied_execution: The person alleged to have executed the agreement denied doing so.
predicates.supporting_evidence_weakened_by_cumulati: The evidence offered to prove execution is undermined by multiple circumstances concerning the document, witnesses, possession, or related conduct.

members.legal_issue: The party who relies on a disputed document must prove its execution; the opposing party need not prove that it was forged.
material_facts: The brother relied on the disputed agreement to support his claim.
The sister denied the agreement and alleged that it was forged or that she had signed blank stamp papers under undue influence.
The brother did not examine the agreement’s attesting witnesses or its scribe to prove its execution.
members.legal_principle: The party who propounds a disputed document must prove its execution, rather than requiring the party denying it to prove forgery. The Court relied on Thiruvengada Pillai v. Navaneethammal. Where fraud, misrepresentation, or undue influence is alleged, the burden generally rests on the alleging party, subject to the shift where a fiduciary or dominant party is required to establish good faith and fair dealing, as described in Krishna Mohan Kul v. Pratima Maity.
members.conclusion: The burden rested on the brother, as the party relying on the agreement, to prove its execution; the trial court had wrongly shifted that burden to the sister.

predicates.civil_case_relying_on_disputed_document: A party in a civil case relies on a document whose execution is disputed.
predicates.execution_denied: The opposing party denies having executed the document.

members.legal_issue: For a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement that fixes a date for performance, limitation runs from the fixed date, as extended by an agreed extension, and is not postponed by delivery of possession, pending permission, or a later allegation of avoidance.
material_facts: The written agreement fixed a date for execution of the sale deed, and the sellers later sought extensions to obtain the lessor’s permission; the last requested extension expired on 1 February 1977.
The buyer had received possession when the agreement was made, and the permission remained unobtained.
The buyer alleged that the sellers began avoiding the buyer after August 1991 and that the cause of action was continuing, but filed suit in April 1994.
The plaint did not give particulars of any alleged oral extension of time.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, a suit for specific performance must be filed within three years from the date fixed for performance; where no date is fixed, time runs from when the claimant has notice that performance is refused. Delivery of possession does not alter the limitation rule, and failure to obtain permission does not by itself postpone the cause of action. The judgment does not rely on an earlier decision in its reasoning.
members.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation because it was filed more than three years after the final date fixed for performance; possession, the unobtained permission, and the later allegation of avoidance did not defer or renew the limitation period.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and performance_date_fixed and final_extension_expired and filing_followed_expired_limitation_window and buyer_received_possession and permission_remained_unobtained and later_avoidance_alleged and later_extension_lacked_particulars

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.performance_date_fixed: The agreement fixed a date for performance.
predicates.final_extension_expired: The last extension sought for performance expired.
predicates.filing_followed_expired_limitation_windo: The claimant filed suit after the applicable limitation period had elapsed from the final performance date.
predicates.buyer_received_possession: The seller delivered possession to the buyer when the agreement was made.
predicates.permission_remained_unobtained: Permission needed for the transaction remained unobtained.
predicates.later_avoidance_alleged: The claimant alleged that the seller later avoided the claimant.
predicates.later_extension_lacked_particulars: The claimant alleged a further oral extension without stating when it was given or how long it lasted.

members.legal_issue: When a contract fixes a date for performance, the limitation period for a specific-performance claim begins on that date even if time is not of the essence.
material_facts: The parties’ sale agreement fixed May 28, 1989, as the date for performance.
The purchasers argued that time was not of the essence and that there was an oral agreement to perform after the seller obtained required permissions.
The application to add a specific-performance claim was filed on November 5, 1992.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 and the first part of Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provide that a specific-performance claim must be brought within three years from the date fixed for performance. Whether time is of the essence does not affect that rule. Chand Rani (dead) by LRs. v. Kamal Rani (dead) by LRs. explains the distinction between time being of the essence and the limitation period running from a fixed date; K. Raheja Construction Ltd. v. Alliances Ministries and Tarlok Singh v. Vijay Kumar Sabharwal apply the fixed-date rule. Ramzan v. Hussaini explains that a date may be fixed by reference to an event that makes it ascertainable.
members.conclusion: Because the agreement fixed a date for performance, limitation began to run from that date under the first part of Article 54; whether time was of the essence was not material to that computation. The specific-performance claim therefore had to be brought within three years of the fixed date, absent an agreed extension.

rule.if: specific_performance_limitation_claim and performance_date_fixed and not performance_deadline_extended

predicates.specific_performance_limitation_claim: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.performance_date_fixed: The parties fixed a date for performance, either directly or by reference to an event that makes the date ascertainable.
predicates.performance_deadline_extended: The parties agreed to extend the fixed performance deadline.

members.legal_issue: A signatory to a will may qualify as an attesting witness without being labelled as one when the evidence establishes the required witnessing and signing.
material_facts: The will bore the signatures of three people beneath the testatrix’s thumb-mark, although it did not describe them as attesting witnesses.
A signatory testified that he and the other signatories saw the testatrix place her thumb-mark on the will and signed it in her presence.
members.legal_principle: Under section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1975, an attesting witness signs in the executant’s presence after seeing execution or receiving the executant’s personal acknowledgment of it. Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act requires an available attesting witness to be called to prove execution of a document required by law to be attested. The label given to a signatory is not decisive; the evidence must establish the acts constituting attestation.
members.conclusion: The signatory’s evidence established that he was an attesting witness, and the objection that no attesting witness had proved execution failed.

predicates.will_probate_proceeding: A party sought probate of a will whose execution had to be proved.
predicates.signatory_saw_execution: A signatory saw the testator execute the will or received the testator’s personal acknowledgment of its execution.
predicates.signatory_signed_in_executant_presence: The signatory signed the will while the testator was present.

members.legal_issue: A will is duly attested when the statutory requirements for the testator’s signature or acknowledgment and each attesting witness’s signature are met, even if the witnesses do not attest simultaneously.
material_facts: The testator signed the disputed will in the presence of both attesting witnesses, and each witness signed it in the testator’s presence.
The witnesses’ evidence supported that sequence, although they did not necessarily sign at the same time.
members.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires the testator to sign or acknowledge the will before each attesting witness and each witness to attest it in the testator’s presence; it does not require simultaneous attestation. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one attesting witness must be called to prove execution when available and capable of giving evidence. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma and the propositions set out in Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.
members.conclusion: The will was not invalid merely because the attesting witnesses did not sign simultaneously; the evidence supported due attestation.

predicates.will_attestation_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a will was duly attested.
predicates.testator_signed_or_acknowledged_before_e: The testator signed the will before each attesting witness or personally acknowledged the testator’s signature to each witness.
predicates.each_witness_signed_in_testators_presenc: Each attesting witness signed the will while the testator was present.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s future interest under a will vests when the will takes effect if the beneficiary is identified with certainty and the gift is not conditional on surviving the prior life tenant.
material_facts: The will identified the daughter and her heirs as the absolute beneficiaries of the entire estate after the widow’s lifetime.
The daughter was alive when the testator died but died before the widow, and none of her children survived her.
The plaintiff was the daughter’s husband and sole heir, and he claimed through her vested interest.
members.legal_principle: The law leans in favour of vesting, and a gift of future enjoyment vests when the will takes effect where the beneficiary and the property are identified with certainty and vesting is not made conditional on surviving the prior life tenant. The court relied on the principle stated in Jarman on Wills and distinguished a contingent expectancy under Hindu law from a present vested right to future enjoyment.
members.conclusion: The daughter obtained a vested interest in the estate on the testator’s death, and that interest passed to her husband on her death.

rule.if: hindu_will_dispute and later_beneficiary_certain and gift_covers_entire_estate and gift_not_conditional_on_survival

predicates.hindu_will_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an interest created by a Hindu testator’s will vested in a later beneficiary.
predicates.later_beneficiary_certain: The will identifies the later beneficiary with certainty.
predicates.gift_covers_entire_estate: The will gives the later beneficiary the entire estate after the prior life tenant’s interest ends.
predicates.gift_not_conditional_on_survival: The will does not make the later beneficiary’s gift conditional on surviving the prior life tenant.

members.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s absolute interest under a bequest following a life estate vests at the testator’s death when the will does not indicate a contrary intention.
material_facts: The will gave the testator’s sons life interests and provided that male heirs of the sons would thereafter take the property absolutely.
The beneficiary’s possession was postponed until after the life interest ended.
The beneficiary was alive when the testator died.
members.legal_principle: Section 119 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 provides that, unless a contrary intention appears, a legatee’s right to receive a bequest at the proper time becomes vested on the testator’s death even when possession is postponed. Illustration (iii) to Section 119 addresses a fund bequeathed to one person for life and thereafter to another. Sections 19 and 21 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 distinguish vested rights from contingent interests.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary’s absolute interest vested on the testator’s death, notwithstanding the postponement of possession until the end of the life estate.

predicates.bequest_postpones_possession: The will postpones the beneficiary’s possession of the bequeathed property.
predicates.bequest_grants_absolute_remainder: The will gives the beneficiary an absolute interest after a prior life interest ends.
predicates.no_contrary_intention_appears: The will does not show an intention that the beneficiary’s interest remain unvested until possession becomes available.

members.legal_issue: A remainder bequeathed after a life interest to the testator’s legal heirs vests at the testator’s death in the person who is then the sole legal heir, absent a contrary intention.
material_facts: The will gave the house to the testator’s wife for life and stated that after her death it would go to the testator’s legal heirs.
The son was the testator’s only legal heir when the testator died; the daughters became legal heirs under later succession law.
The will’s provision for the wife’s prior life interest did not indicate that vesting of the remainder was postponed.
members.legal_principle: Section 119 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, including Illustration (iii), provides that a remainder ordinarily vests when the testator dies even if possession follows a prior life interest. The exception to Section 111 did not apply because the class was described by reference to the testator, not a specified individual other than the testator. Section 120 did not apply because the wife’s death was not a specified uncertain event. The Court relied on Chilanakuri Pullappa v. Guruka Bayanna, AIR 1962 AP 54, and P. Somasundaram v. K. Rajammal, AIR 1976 Mad 295, on Section 119; it distinguished N. Krishnammal v. R. Ekambram, (1979) 3 SCC 273, as involving a contingent bequest.
members.conclusion: The remainder vested in the son at the testator’s death and was not postponed until the wife’s death; the daughters did not take a share in the remainder under the will.

rule.if: will_construction_dispute and life_interest_precedes_remainder and remainder_given_to_testator_legal_heirs and sole_legal_heir_exists_at_testator_death

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The dispute requires the court to construe a will.
predicates.life_interest_precedes_remainder: The will gives one person a life interest before the remainder is to pass.
predicates.remainder_given_to_testator_legal_heirs: The will gives the remainder to the testator’s legal heirs.
predicates.sole_legal_heir_exists_at_testator_death: One person is the testator’s only legal heir when the testator dies.

members.legal_issue: Any defendant in a suit for specific performance may contest whether the plaintiff has met the requirement of readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an agreement to sell.
The plaintiff had not initially pleaded readiness and willingness, but later added that plea by amendment.
The defendants were subsequent purchasers of the property and sought to contend that the plaintiff and her legal representatives had not been ready and willing to perform the agreement.
The lower courts declined to permit that contention, relying on the rule that the plea was available only to the vendor or the vendor’s legal representatives.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act bars specific performance where the plaintiff fails to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness to perform the essential terms of the contract, except where performance was prevented or waived by the defendant. The obligation is on the court to withhold specific performance if the requirement is not met; any defendant may raise the issue. This accords with Ardeshir H. Mama v. Flora Sassoon and Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Palaniswami Nadar, and the contrary limitation stated in Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh was erroneous. Lakhi Ram v. Trikha Ram had doubted that limitation but was decided on another point.
members.conclusion: The contention was available to the subsequent-purchaser defendants, and the court had to determine whether the plaintiff had averred and proved performance or continuous readiness and willingness. The decision limiting the plea to the vendor was erroneous. The appeal was allowed, the judgments below were set aside, and the suit was remanded for that determination.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant seeks a decree compelling performance of a contract.
predicates.defendant_contests_plaintiff_readiness: A defendant disputes that the claimant performed or was ready and willing to perform the claimant’s contractual obligations.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser who is a defendant in a specific performance suit may raise the plaintiff’s failure to establish readiness and willingness, but the requirement is met where the plaintiff pleaded readiness and willingness and the defendants did not specifically deny it.
material_facts: The subsequent purchaser was a defendant in the specific performance suit.
The plaintiff pleaded that she had been and remained ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement.
The defendants did not specifically deny the readiness-and-willingness allegation, and the court found the pleading sufficient.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(a), (b), and (c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 prevents specific performance where the plaintiff fails to meet the statutory requirements, including pleading and proving performance or continuous readiness and willingness. A subsequent purchaser may raise that objection, as recognized in Ram Awadh v. Achhaibar Dubey; the Court also referred to Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh concerning the plaintiff’s readiness-and-willingness obligation and a subsequent purchaser’s ability to defend the purchase.
members.conclusion: The subsequent purchaser could raise the readiness-and-willingness issue, but the plaintiff had sufficiently pleaded that requirement, so the objection did not defeat the claim for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and subsequent_purchaser_is_defendant and plaintiff_pleaded_readiness and defendants_did_not_specifically_deny_readiness

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A party brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_is_defendant: A person who acquired the property after the agreement to sell was joined as a defendant in the enforcement suit.
predicates.plaintiff_pleaded_readiness: The plaintiff alleged that she was ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement.
predicates.defendants_did_not_specifically_deny_rea: The defendants did not specifically deny the plaintiff’s allegation of readiness and willingness.

members.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser may rely on the plaintiff’s failure to establish continuous readiness and willingness in a suit for specific performance when the property was conveyed to the purchaser before the suit was filed.
material_facts: The vendor unequivocally resiled from taking a step toward completing the sale, but the plaintiff took no action for about one year and eleven months before issuing a notice offering the balance consideration.
The property was conveyed to two subsequent purchasers before the plaintiff filed the specific-performance suit.
The plaintiff had not received a conveyance after a decree for specific performance.
members.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires the plaintiff to aver and prove performance or continuous readiness and willingness, and obliges the court to deny specific performance if that requirement is unmet. In Ram Awadh (dead) by LRs v. Achhaibar Dubey, a three-Judge Bench held that any defendant may raise this failure and overruled Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh. M.M.S. Investments, Madurai v. V. Veerappan was distinguishable because the purchasers there acquired the property after a decree and a conveyance to the plaintiff; here, the subsequent conveyances preceded the suit.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff was not ready and willing throughout to perform the agreement, and the subsequent purchasers could rely on that failure; the suit was therefore barred from succeeding on that basis.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and subsequent_purchaser_defendant and conveyances_preceded_suit and vendor_unequivocally_repudiated and plaintiff_inactive_after_repudiation

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_defendant: A defendant acquired the property through a conveyance from an earlier purchaser.
predicates.conveyances_preceded_suit: The conveyances to the subsequent purchasers occurred before the plaintiff filed the suit.
predicates.vendor_unequivocally_repudiated: The vendor clearly refused to take a step required to advance completion of the agreed sale.
predicates.plaintiff_inactive_after_repudiation: The plaintiff took no meaningful step toward completing the sale for a substantial period after the vendor’s clear refusal.
predicates.plaintiff_not_entitled_to_specific_perfo: The plaintiff cannot obtain specific performance because continuous readiness and willingness to perform was not established.

members.legal_issue: Interest on a refund of amounts deposited for a housing unit is payable at the rate adopted by the Court, with a later starting date where the unit has been transferred.
material_facts: The consumers in these appeals sought refunds of amounts deposited with the developer.
The State Commission had awarded interest at fifteen per cent per annum from the respective deposit dates until repayment.
The Court considered the interest rate adopted in earlier appeals concerning the same project and reduced the rate to nine per cent.
The Court directed that, where a flat had been transferred, interest would run from the later of expiry of three years from the agreement or the transfer date.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the interest rate used in the earlier consent dispositions concerning the same project, including DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. v. Himanshu Arora and DLF Homes Panchkula (P.) Ltd. v. Sushila Devi. For a transferred flat, the Court applied the later of expiry of the three-year period from the agreement or the transfer date as the starting point.
members.conclusion: The refund was to carry interest at nine per cent from the respective deposit dates until refund, except that for a transferred flat interest was payable from the later of expiry of three years from the agreement or the date of transfer.

predicates.refund_claim_consumer_proceeding: A consumer brings a consumer-forum claim seeking refund of payments made for a housing unit.
predicates.deposits_made_for_housing_unit: The consumer made deposits towards the housing unit.
predicates.refund_ordered: The adjudicating body directs repayment of the deposited amounts.
predicates.applicable_start_date: The starting point is the dates of deposit, or, if the unit was transferred, the later of expiry of the agreed three-year period and the transfer date.

members.legal_issue: Interest on a refund for delayed delivery of a housing unit runs on each deposit from the date it was made until the refund.
material_facts: The purchasers had deposited amounts for apartments in a housing project that had not made substantial progress after the promised delivery period.
Some purchasers sought refunds, and the parties agreed that refund cases would carry interest at 9% on deposits from their respective deposit dates until refund.
members.legal_principle: The Court adopted the parties’ agreed framework, applying the approach in Himanshu Arora, where the Court confirmed interest at 9% while modifying the period to conform to the State Commission’s order. No statutory provision was identified as the basis for this agreed calculation.
members.conclusion: In refund cases, interest at 9% is payable on each deposit from the date of deposit until the date of refund.

predicates.is_consumer_housing_refund_case: A purchaser pursued a consumer proceeding seeking a refund for a housing unit.
predicates.purchaser_sought_refund: The purchaser asked to recover money paid for the housing unit rather than take possession.
predicates.deposits_were_made: The purchaser made one or more payments toward the housing unit.
predicates.parties_agreed_to_refund_interest_framew: The parties accepted an interest-based framework for calculating the refund award.

members.legal_issue: A building-plan application for residential use cannot be rejected on the basis of a proposed development plan that has not been brought into force.
material_facts: The owners’ land had been permitted for non-agricultural use and was being used for residential purposes within a residential area.
A building-plan application was filed while the existing comprehensive development plan remained in force.
The planning authority rejected the application because the land fell within a valley zone identified in a proposed revised plan.
The proposed revised plan had not been approved or brought into force; the State was still considering objections to it.
members.legal_principle: The right to property includes the right to construct, although legislation may regulate that right. A restriction on construction must have a clear basis in law; an anticipated or proposed change cannot take away the right before it becomes effective. Ecological considerations do not permit a court or authority to substitute a proposed planning rule for the law in force. The Court relied on the principles in Director of Public Works v. Ho Po Sang, Howrah Municipal Corporation v. Ganges Rope Co. Ltd., and Kuldeep Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi; it also noted that planning legislation governs ecological aspects.
members.conclusion: The proposed revised plan could not provide a lawful basis for rejecting the application. The rejection and the Division Bench judgment upholding it were set aside, and the authority was directed to consider the application under the law in force.

rule.if: building_plan_appeal and residential_use_permitted and existing_plan_in_force and proposed_revision_unapproved and rejection_based_on_proposed_revision

predicates.building_plan_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the rejection of an application for approval of building plans.
predicates.residential_use_permitted: The landowners were permitted to use the land for non-agricultural residential purposes.
predicates.existing_plan_in_force: An existing development plan remained legally in force when the application was considered.
predicates.proposed_revision_unapproved: A proposed revised development plan had not been approved or brought into force.
predicates.rejection_based_on_proposed_revision: The planning authority rejected the application because of a restriction identified in the proposed revision.

members.legal_issue: A development application cannot be rejected solely because revision of the development plan is contemplated when no draft revised plan or other concrete planning material exists.
material_facts: The sanctioned plan placed the land in a residential zone.
The landowner submitted a development plan for a hotel.
The Municipal Commissioner rejected the application solely because the land might be earmarked for recreation during a contemplated revision of the development plan.
No draft revised plan existed when the application was rejected.
members.legal_principle: Sections 45 and 46 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 require regard to relevant development plans and proposals published or sanctioned under the Act, but do not prevent consideration of other relevant material. A rejection must be supported by concrete material; a merely contemplated plan revision is insufficient. The Court distinguished Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, where a draft revised plan existed as relevant material.
members.conclusion: The ground for rejecting the application was untenable, and the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal.

rule.if: development_permission_appeal and application_for_development_submitted and refusal_based_only_on_future_plan_revision and no_existing_draft_plan and no_concrete_planning_material

predicates.development_permission_appeal: An applicant appealed the refusal of permission to develop land.
predicates.application_for_development_submitted: A landowner submitted a plan seeking permission to develop land.
predicates.refusal_based_only_on_future_plan_revisi: The planning authority relied solely on a possible future revision of its development plan to refuse permission.
predicates.no_existing_draft_plan: No draft revised development plan existed when the planning authority refused permission.
predicates.no_concrete_planning_material: The planning authority had no concrete planning material supporting its refusal.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot prevent residential construction by relying on an earlier open-space designation when an unchallenged approved development plan designates the land for residential use.
material_facts: The land had earlier been earmarked as open space adjoining a school.
An approved development plan later designated the land as residential, and the land was allotted and used as a residential plot.
The public-interest writ petitioner did not challenge the approved plan or its change in land use.
The High Court nevertheless treated the earlier open-space designation as preventing construction.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 19(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, the approved development plan showing the land as residential became final because it was not challenged. The High Court could not ignore that plan and rely on an earlier open-space designation to prevent construction; no earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The appeals were allowed, the High Court judgment was set aside, and the writ petition was dismissed.

rule.if: public_interest_writ_challenging_construction and approved_plan_designates_residential and earlier_open_space_designation_changed and plan_change_unchallenged

predicates.public_interest_writ_challenging_constru: A person brought a public-interest writ petition seeking to prevent construction on the land.
predicates.approved_plan_designates_residential: An approved development plan designated the land for residential use.
predicates.earlier_open_space_designation_changed: The land had previously been designated as open space, but that designation was changed to residential use in the approved plan.
predicates.plan_change_unchallenged: The petitioner did not challenge the approved plan or its change in land use.

members.legal_issue: Open spaces reserved in an approved subdivision layout cannot be used for construction merely because a later, broader development plan shows the area as residential.
material_facts: A layout subdividing a large allotted area was submitted by the allottee’s architect and approved by the municipal authority.
The approved layout identified two sub-plots as open spaces or gardens, while the other plots were used for construction.
A later development plan for the larger scheme showed the area containing the two sub-plots as residential but did not show the internal subdivisions or the open spaces in the approved layout.
The allottee sought to build on the two sub-plots, asserting that the earlier layout was temporary and that open-space requirements were met elsewhere in the larger scheme.
The High Court prohibited construction on the two sub-plots, and the allottee challenged that decision on appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Regulation 39 of the Development Control Rules, 1967, layouts or subdivisions of qualifying holdings had to reserve a specified portion for recreational space. Sections 302 and 302-A of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, required statutory approval for layouts dividing land into plots. The 1991 Development Control Regulations also required open spaces in relevant layouts or subdivisions. A broad development plan indicating general land use does not override open spaces reserved in an approved internal layout, and the governing scheme did not recognize a temporary layout. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The appeals were dismissed. The two sub-plots must remain open spaces and cannot be used for construction; the later development plan does not displace their status under the approved layout.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_open_space_protection and approved_subdivision_layout and sites_marked_as_open_space and later_broad_plan_shows_residential_use and other_plots_used_under_layout

predicates.appeal_challenges_open_space_protection: A party appealed a decision protecting open spaces identified in an approved layout.
predicates.approved_subdivision_layout: A competent authority approved a layout subdividing a larger holding into plots.
predicates.sites_marked_as_open_space: The approved layout identified particular plots as open space or garden.
predicates.later_broad_plan_shows_residential_use: A later plan for a larger area showed the relevant area as residential without depicting the internal layout details.
predicates.other_plots_used_under_layout: Other plots in the approved layout were used for construction while the designated open-space plots remained open.

members.legal_issue: When a defendant alleged to be a trespasser claims tenancy in agricultural land and the tenancy issue belongs to an exclusive special forum, the civil court must obtain that forum’s decision before resolving the possession claim.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession on the basis that the defendant was a trespasser.
The defendant claimed to have been lawfully inducted as a tenant by the landowner.
The tenancy question was assigned to the Mamlatdar, and the civil court was barred from deciding it.
The suit had been instituted in a court that was competent when the suit was filed, before the change in law took effect.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 58(2) of the Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act reserve tenancy questions to the Mamlatdar and bar civil courts from deciding them. Following the procedure described in Bhimaji Shankar Kulkami v. Dundappa Vithappa Udapudi and Dhondi Tukaram v. Hari Dadu, the civil court should not dismiss a suit merely because the issue has become reserved to the special forum after filing; it should obtain the special forum’s decision and then proceed accordingly.
members.conclusion: The tenancy issue should be referred to the Mamlatdar. If the defendant is found to be a tenant, the civil court may have to dismiss the possession suit; if the tenancy claim is rejected, the civil court may consider granting possession.

predicates.pending_possession_suit_against_alleged_: A civil suit seeking possession from a defendant alleged to be a trespasser was pending.
predicates.defendant_claims_tenancy: The defendant asserted that the defendant held the land as a tenant.
predicates.tenancy_question_reserved_to_special_for: The governing law assigns the disputed tenancy question exclusively to a special forum.

members.legal_issue: A civil court must refer a disputed tenant-status issue to the tenancy authority when a defendant raises a tenancy claim in a suit to recover agricultural land, and must stay the suit pending that determination.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking possession of agricultural land on redemption of a transaction alleged to be a mortgage.
The defendants asserted that the transaction was a lease and that they were protected tenants.
Whether a defendant was a tenant was an issue that arose in the suit.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 29, 70(b), and 85 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the Mamlatdar has exclusive authority to decide whether a person is a tenant, protected tenant, or permanent tenant, while the civil court may hear a landowner’s suit to recover possession from a trespasser or mortgagee. If the defendant raises a tenancy claim and the issue arises, the civil court must refer it to the Mamlatdar rather than decide it or dismiss the suit outright. Section 85A, introduced while this litigation was pending in the second appeal, provides machinery for that reference. Dhondi Tukaram v. Hari Dadu was approved as correctly stating the law before section 85A; Mudugere Rangaiah v. M. Rangaiah was distinguished, and the Court expressed no view on its correctness.
members.conclusion: The civil court could entertain the possession suit but could not decide the disputed tenant-status issue. It had to refer that issue to the Mamlatdar and stay the suit pending the Mamlatdar’s decision, then dispose of the suit in light of that decision.

predicates.civil_suit_to_recover_agricultural_land: A landowner brings a civil suit seeking possession of agricultural land.
predicates.defendant_claims_tenant: A defendant claims to hold the land as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_status_is_in_dispute: The parties dispute whether the defendant has tenant status.

members.legal_issue: An appeal filed without the decree is defective, but where the decree had not been drawn up and the defect passed unnoticed until admission, the appellate court may allow the appellant to obtain and file the decree rather than dismiss the appeal.
material_facts: The appellants applied for certified copies of both the judgment and decree before the decree had been drawn up, but were supplied only the judgment and costs memo.
They filed the appeal without a copy of the decree, believing the documents supplied would suffice.
The trial court had not prepared the decree, and the appellate court’s office did not identify the defect before the appeal was admitted.
After the objection was raised, the appellate court allowed time to obtain and file the decree; the decree was subsequently filed.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires an appeal to be accompanied by a copy of the decree and the appellate court cannot dispense with that requirement; an appeal presented without the decree is incomplete and defective. Sections 33 and Order XX, rules 3, 4(2), 6 and 7 place the task of preparing and signing the decree on the court and its office. Where a decree has not been drawn when the appeal is presented and a copy has been sought, the court may direct that the decree be prepared and allow the appeal to proceed once the copy is filed, particularly when court-office failures contributed to the defect. A litigant need not remind the court to perform its duty to draw up the decree. The court relied on Rodger v. Comptoir d'Escompte de Paris for the principle that courts must ensure their acts do not injure litigants.
members.conclusion: The appellate court correctly allowed time for the decree to be drawn up and filed instead of dismissing the appeal. The decree-copy requirement is mandatory, but the appropriate response to defective presentation depends on the circumstances; where the decree was not yet drawn and the appeal passed admission through oversight, the hearing could be adjourned to permit the defect to be cured.

rule.if: civil_appeal_against_decree and decree_not_drawn_when_appeal_presented and appellant_applied_for_decree_copy and court_offices_failed_to_prepare_or_detect_defect and appeal_passed_admission_stage

predicates.civil_appeal_against_decree: A party brought a civil appeal challenging a decree.
predicates.decree_not_drawn_when_appeal_presented: The court had not prepared the decree when the appellant presented the appeal.
predicates.appellant_applied_for_decree_copy: The appellant applied for a certified copy of the decree but did not receive it because it had not been prepared.
predicates.court_offices_failed_to_prepare_or_detec: The trial court’s office failed to prepare the decree, and the appellate court’s office failed to identify the missing copy at the initial stage.
predicates.appeal_passed_admission_stage: The appeal proceeded through admission before the missing decree copy was addressed.
predicates.missing_decree_copy_should_be_cured_with: The appellate court should permit the missing decree copy to be obtained and filed rather than dismiss the appeal in these circumstances.

members.legal_issue: An appeal may be maintained without a copy of the decree when the appellant could not file one because the court failed to draw up the formal decree.
material_facts: A trial court varied the shares in an existing partition decree but did not prepare a formal decree recording the variation.
The appealing party could not file a copy of the decree and, despite obtaining time and applying to the trial court to prepare one, the trial court refused.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure ordinarily requires a copy of the decree to accompany the memorandum of appeal. Under Jagat Dhish Bhargava v. Jawahar Lal Bhargava, (1961) 2 SCR 918, the requirement is generally mandatory, but exceptional circumstances may permit an appeal without the copy. A party should not lose the right of appeal when the court’s failure to prepare the decree made filing a copy impossible.
members.conclusion: The appeal was maintainable despite the absence of a copy of the decree because the defect was not the appellant’s fault and resulted from the trial court’s failure to prepare the decree.

predicates.appeal_from_share_variation_order: A party appealed an order varying shares previously specified in a decree.
predicates.formal_decree_not_prepared: The court that made the order did not prepare a formal decree recording it.
predicates.appellant_could_not_obtain_copy_despite_: The appellant tried to obtain the formal decree but could not do so because the court did not prepare it.

members.legal_issue: A court must hear the appellant’s counsel before disposing of an application seeking additional evidence in a criminal appeal.
material_facts: During the criminal appeal, the appellant applied to recall a witness for further cross-examination and to have other witnesses examined or summoned.
The application was disposed of without giving the appellant’s counsel an opportunity to be heard in support of it.
The High Court judge dealt with the application after deciding the appeal.
members.legal_principle: A party seeking relief through an application in a criminal appeal must be afforded a reasonable opportunity to be heard in support of that application. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: Disposing of the application without hearing the appellant’s counsel was wrong and unjust, and the appellant had a right to a reasonable opportunity to be heard; the Court did not decide the merits of the request for additional evidence.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal.
predicates.application_seeks_additional_evidence: A party applies to recall or summon witnesses to obtain additional evidence.
predicates.application_disposed_without_counsel_hea: The court disposes of that application without hearing the applicant’s counsel.

members.legal_issue: A court must give an accused a reasonable opportunity to be heard before disposing of an application seeking relief in a criminal appeal.
material_facts: The accused filed an application seeking further examination of witnesses and other relief in the High Court.
The application was not listed or heard in court and was disposed of in the judge’s chambers without hearing the accused’s counsel.
members.legal_principle: The court applied the requirement of a reasonable opportunity to be heard when disposing of an application under section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The application should have been disposed of after hearing the accused’s counsel; disposing of it without that opportunity was wrong and unjust, and the accused had a just grievance about the procedure.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused pursued a criminal appeal from a conviction.
predicates.application_disposed_without_hearing: The court disposed of the accused’s application without hearing the accused or counsel in court.
predicates.application_disposal_was_unjust: The court disposed of the application unjustly by denying the accused a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

members.legal_issue: Execution of a mortgage decree for money secured by an estate cannot proceed after the entire mortgaged estate vests in the State, even where certain lands are settled back with the former proprietor as raiyat.
material_facts: The mortgage decree covered an estate, including Bakasht lands and other lands.
The entire estate covered by the notification vested in the State under the land-reform law.
Certain lands, including the Bakasht lands, were deemed settled by the State with the former proprietor, who held them as a raiyat.
The decree-holders sought to execute the mortgage decree against the Bakasht lands after vesting and had applied to have their compensation determined under the Act.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 3, 4 and 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the notified estate first vests in the State free of encumbrances; the later deemed settlement of raiyat rights in specified lands does not mean those lands never vested. Section 4(d) bars suits and proceedings for recovery of money secured by a mortgage of an estate and includes execution proceedings. The creditor’s remedy is the claim procedure under Chapter IV, including section 14; section 24(5) addresses payment of compensation to a mortgage creditor. The Court relied on Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank Ltd., Krishna Prasad v. Gauri Kumari Devi, and Raj Kishore v. Ram Pratap, and rejected the contrary majority view in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh v. Ram Saroop Singh.
members.conclusion: The mortgage decree could not be executed against the Bakasht lands. The decree-holders’ remedy was to pursue their claim through the Act’s compensation procedure.

rule.if: mortgage_execution_proceeding and debt_secured_by_estate_mortgage and entire_mortgaged_estate_vested and some_lands_settled_back_to_former_owner

predicates.mortgage_execution_proceeding: A decree-holder sought to recover a mortgage debt through execution proceedings.
predicates.debt_secured_by_estate_mortgage: Payment of the debt was secured by a mortgage of an estate.
predicates.entire_mortgaged_estate_vested: The whole estate covered by the mortgage vested in the State.
predicates.some_lands_settled_back_to_former_owner: The State settled certain lands with the former proprietor to be held under a new raiyat right.
predicates.execution_cannot_proceed: The mortgage decree cannot be enforced through execution against the lands in the vested estate.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee cannot enforce a mortgage decree by selling a new tenure right created for the mortgagor after the mortgaged proprietary interest has vested in the state.
material_facts: A simple mortgage secured a decree against the mortgagor’s proprietary interests in several villages.
While execution of the decree was pending, legislation vested the proprietary interests in the state.
The legislation created new tenure rights in certain lands for the former intermediary because of his cultivatory possession.
The mortgagee sought to sell those new tenure rights in execution of the mortgage decree.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 6(a)(i) and 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the proprietary interests in the relevant lands vested in the state, and the tenure rights subsequently conferred on the intermediary were new rights, not a continuation of the mortgaged rights. Section 6(h), read with section 73 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, directs the mortgagee to pursue the compensation for acquired mortgaged property; the new tenure rights are not compensation or substituted security. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The new tenure rights could not be sold in execution of the mortgage decree. For the lands that vested in the state, the mortgagee could pursue the compensation payable for the acquisition, rather than sell the new tenure rights.

predicates.mortgage_decree_execution: A mortgagee is seeking to enforce a mortgage decree through execution proceedings.
predicates.mortgaged_proprietary_interest_vested_in: The proprietary interest that was mortgaged vested in the state.
predicates.new_tenure_right_created_after_vesting: After the vesting, the state conferred a new tenure right on the former holder because of that holder’s possession or cultivation of the land.
predicates.new_tenure_right_not_liable_to_mortgage_: The newly created tenure right cannot be sold to enforce the mortgage decree.

members.legal_issue: A supervisory court cannot disturb a final eviction decree on the basis of a subsequent event that occurred while the challenge to the decree was pending.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an eviction order from the statutory appellate authority on the ground that the premises were bona fide required to start a business.
The tenant challenged that order in a writ petition, during which the landlord died.
The tenant asked the High Court to take the landlord’s death into account and set aside the eviction order.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, a High Court cannot interfere with a final eviction decree of the statutory appellate authority on the basis of a subsequent event. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court could not interfere with the final eviction decree in supervisory jurisdiction by taking account of the landlord’s subsequent death; the Supreme Court found no error warranting interference and dismissed the appeal.

predicates.supervisory_challenge_to_eviction_decree: A tenant challenged an eviction order in a supervisory proceeding.
predicates.final_appellate_eviction_order: A statutory appellate authority issued an eviction order that was final under the governing scheme and treated as a decree.
predicates.subsequent_event_during_challenge: An event occurring after the eviction order took place while the supervisory challenge was pending.
predicates.supervisory_court_cannot_disturb_decree_: The supervisory court cannot disturb the final eviction decree on the basis of the subsequent event.

members.legal_issue: Later events do not defeat a final eviction order when the governing transitional scheme bars reconsideration of the established need and the events do not materially alter that need.
material_facts: The landlord had obtained a final eviction order based on a need to occupy the premises after retirement.

An agreement to sell part of the property to a family member of the tenant stated that the landlord’s need continued; the sale was not completed, and the purchaser did not proceed to execute the sale deed.
The court considered the effects of restrictions on transfer and increased building costs, and found that the landlord’s need had not been met or shown to be capable of being met otherwise.
The alleged agreements to sell the premises to other purchasers were not proved to have been acted upon or given effect.
The court found that the later events had not materially altered the position so as to defeat the final order.
members.legal_principle: Courts may ordinarily take cautious account of later events to mould relief, subject to fairness to both sides: Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor & General Traders and Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad. But a concluded eviction matter cannot be reopened where finality has attached, and section 43(2)(rr) specifically bars a fresh inquiry into the ground once the qualifying permission has become final. The court relied on Syed Asadullah Kazmi and approved the approach in Bansilal Sahu; it also noted that, on the facts, the later events did not materially alter the landlord’s need.
members.conclusion: The subsequent events did not defeat the landlord’s need or justify disturbing the final eviction order, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.transitional_eviction_proceeding: The landlord pursued eviction through a procedure for carrying forward a permission obtained under an earlier rent-control regime.
predicates.eviction_order_final: The order for eviction had become final in the relevant proceedings.
predicates.later_sale_agreements_uncompleted: Agreements made after the original eviction proceedings did not result in a completed sale of the premises relied on to defeat eviction.

members.legal_issue: In a statutory recovery auction where the prescribed certificate effects the transfer of property, the sale takes place when the certificate is issued rather than when the auction is held.
material_facts: The taxpayer’s property was auctioned to recover unpaid statutory dues, and the purchaser paid the full purchase price shortly after the auction.
Objections delayed the issue of the sale certificate until after the auction and payment.
The applicable recovery procedure provided for confirmation of the sale and made the certificate a valid transfer of the property.
The taxpayer relied on the general civil-procedure rule that can deem a purchaser’s title to relate back to the auction, but the recovery procedure was inconsistent with applying that rule.
members.legal_principle: Sections 279 and 286 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and rule 281 of the Rules provide for recovery and auction of property, while rule 285-M makes the certificate a valid transfer. Section 341 applies the Code of Civil Procedure only insofar as it is consistent with the Act; therefore section 65 of the Code does not apply where it would conflict with the certificate-based transfer procedure. The sale date consequently determines whether section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, applies.
members.conclusion: The sale took place when the certificate was issued, because the certificate itself effected the transfer and the recovery procedure excluded the general relation-back rule. Accordingly, the sale was not treated as having occurred before the capital-gains provision became effective.

rule.if: tax_timing_dispute_over_recovery_sale and recovery_auction_proceeding and certificate_effects_transfer and recovery_process_displaces_general_relation_back_rule

predicates.tax_timing_dispute_over_recovery_sale: The proceeding concerns when a property sale in a recovery process occurred for tax purposes.
predicates.recovery_auction_proceeding: A public authority auctioned property to recover a debt through a prescribed recovery process.

predicates.recovery_process_displaces_general_relat: The recovery process did not permit the general procedural rule that would date the transfer back to the auction.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser at a statutory auction acquires title upon confirmation of the sale when the full purchase price has been paid, even if the sale certificate is issued later.
material_facts: The property was sold by public auction, and the purchaser paid the full purchase price before the bid was approved.
The bid was approved on October 3, 1956, and the sale certificate was issued later, recording the date of confirmation.
The tenant was told to pay rent to the purchaser from the date of confirmation and treated the purchaser as landlord from that date.
members.legal_principle: Under Rules 90 and 92 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, title under the statutory auction process passes when the full price has been paid and the sale is confirmed; issuance of the certificate thereafter is not essential to the transfer. The fiction in Section 65 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which dates title from the auction, does not apply because the Rules contain no such provision. Bombay Salt and Chemical Industries v. L. J. Johnson did not decide when title passes where the price had been paid and the sale confirmed. The Court agreed generally with the observations in Roshanlal Goswami v. Gobind Ram and referred to Jaimal Singh v. Smt. Gini Devi.
members.conclusion: Title passed to the purchaser on confirmation of the sale, so the purchaser could claim rent from that date and maintain the eviction proceedings.

predicates.statutory_auction_title_dispute: The dispute concerns when a purchaser acquired title through an official auction sale governed by a statutory sale process.
predicates.full_purchase_price_paid: The purchaser paid the full purchase price for the property.
predicates.sale_confirmed: The competent authority approved or confirmed the auction sale.

members.legal_issue: A tenant whose commercial tenancy continues only under statutory protection after the lease ends cannot bequeath the right to occupy the premises to a legatee who does not meet the statutory qualification for succession.
material_facts: The premises had been let for business, and the tenant continued to have a right to occupy them only under statutory protection after the contractual tenancy ended.
Before her death, the tenant bequeathed the tenancy right to the claimant.
The claimant was not a member of the tenant’s family carrying on business with her in the premises at the time of her death.
The landlord sought possession, and the claimant relied on the will to assert a right to remain in the premises.
members.legal_principle: Under section 5(11)(c)(ii) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the right to a protected tenancy in premises let for business, trade or storage devolves only on a qualifying member of the tenant’s family, subject to the stated conditions; the provision does not authorize a testamentary bequest to another person. Section 15(1) prohibits a tenant, absent a contract to the contrary, from assigning or transferring the tenant’s interest, and the Court approved Dr. Anant Triamback Sabnis v. Vasant Pratap Pandit, which treated a bequest as within that prohibition. Gian Devi v. Jeevan Kumar concerned intestate succession and a different statute that did not restrict succession to commercial tenancies, so it did not support the legatee’s claim; Jaspal Singh v. The Additional District Judge, Bulandshahr was also referred to in considering restrictions on transferring tenancy rights. The Court left open the wider question whether a statutory tenancy personal to a tenant can ever be bequeathed.
members.conclusion: The bequest did not make the claimant a tenant because he did not satisfy the statutory qualification; the landlord was not required to treat him as a tenant, and the petition was dismissed.

rule.if: commercial_tenancy_after_lease_termination and tenant_bequeathed_occupancy_right and legatee_not_qualifying_family_member and landlord_seeks_possession

predicates.commercial_tenancy_after_lease_terminati: The tenant occupied premises let for business, trade, or storage under statutory protection after the contractual tenancy ended.
predicates.tenant_bequeathed_occupancy_right: The tenant purported to leave the right to occupy the premises to another person by will.
predicates.legatee_not_qualifying_family_member: The legatee was not a member of the tenant’s family carrying on the relevant business, trade, or storage with the tenant in the premises at the tenant’s death and continuing it afterward.
predicates.landlord_seeks_possession: The landlord sought possession from the person claiming the tenancy under the will.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming tenancy rights solely as a legatee is not an heir who succeeds to a residential tenancy under the statutory succession provision.
material_facts: In both appeals, the claimant relied on a will purporting to bequeath the deceased tenant’s tenancy rights and did not claim to qualify as a family member who had resided with the tenant at death.
In the disputed premises, family members or other occupants had been residing with the deceased tenants at the time of their deaths.
The claimants brought eviction suits on the basis of the bequests, and the High Courts rejected those claims.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 5(11)(c)(i) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a family member residing with the tenant at death has priority to be treated as tenant; only in the absence of such a member may an heir be selected, with the court deciding in default of agreement. The statutory scheme and the words providing for court selection concern heirs succeeding under ordinary succession, not testamentary legatees, whose inclusion could defeat the statutory priority and render the court-selection provision ineffective. The meaning of “heir” depends on the scheme and purpose of the legislation, as recognized in Jaspal Singh v. District Judge. The Court followed Bhavarlal L. Shah v. Kanaiyalal N. Intawala, which approved Anant T. Sabnis (Dr) v. Vasant Pratap Pandit. The Court also rejected the contention that this interpretation impermissibly discriminates between family members claiming under a will and those claiming by intestate succession.
members.conclusion: The word “heir” in the residential-tenancy succession provision does not include a legatee; a claimant cannot obtain tenant status under that provision solely by taking under a will.

predicates.residential_tenancy_succession_case: The dispute concerns who succeeds to a deceased tenant’s rights in premises let for residence.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_will: The claimant bases the claim to the deceased tenant’s tenancy rights on a testamentary gift.
predicates.claimant_qualifies_as_resident_family_me: The claimant is a member of the tenant’s family who resided with the tenant when the tenant died.

members.legal_issue: Failure to give a landholder a fair opportunity to be heard on an objection to compulsory acquisition invalidates the acquisition.
material_facts: The landholder filed an objection to the proposed acquisition.
The notices allegedly issued to the landholder and his wife did not bear their signatures acknowledging receipt, and the authorities offered no explanation for this.
The record showed a signature attributed to the landholder at the hearing, but the Court found it did not match his signatures on court documents; the authorities could not explain the discrepancy.
The acquisition officer proceeded on the assumption that notice had been delivered and did not provide the landholder an opportunity to be heard.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires the Collector to give an objector an opportunity to be heard, consider the objections, make further inquiry, and report recommendations to the appropriate government. The hearing embodies natural justice and must be fair; the recommendations must reflect objective consideration of the objections and brief reasons. Munshi Singh v. Union of India described the hearing and reporting duties; State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh emphasized the need for a hearing before compulsory deprivation of property; and Shyam Nandan Prasad v. State of Bihar held compliance with Section 5A to be essential to valid acquisition. The Court also relied on Union of India v. Mukesh Hans, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, Anand Singh v. State of U.P., and Radhy Shyam v. State of U.P.
members.conclusion: The landholder was not given the required opportunity of hearing. The acquisition of his land was illegal and was quashed.

members.legal_issue: Failure to provide a mandatory personal hearing invalidates the acquisition order, and later approval or confirmation cannot cure that defect.
material_facts: The landowners submitted written objections to the compulsory acquisition.
The Commissioner gave no personal hearing despite the applicable mandatory hearing requirement.
The Standing Committee approved the acquisition order and the State Government later confirmed it.
members.legal_principle: Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, made the personal hearing mandatory. The Court treated the failure as noncompliance with a statutory requirement, not merely a failure of natural justice. An order invalid at inception cannot be made valid by subsequent approval or confirmation. Welfare schemes must also be implemented according to the law governing them; their beneficial purpose does not excuse noncompliance.
members.conclusion: The acquisition order and the State Government's confirmation were invalid; their approval and confirmation did not cure the original defect.

members.legal_issue: A rent-control requirement for prior permission to terminate a tenancy by a landlord does not apply when the tenant chooses to surrender the tenancy.
material_facts: The landlords applied for permission to terminate the tenancy under the applicable rent-control order.
The tenant then agreed to surrender the tenancy rights and undertook to vacate the premises by an agreed date.
The Rent Controller filed the proceedings after the parties submitted their compromise.
members.legal_principle: Clause 13 of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 restricts the landlord’s right to determine a tenancy and requires permission when the landlord seeks to terminate it. It does not restrict a tenant from surrendering the lease. Sections 106 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 recognize termination by either lessor or lessee and the ending of a lease by surrender.
members.conclusion: Prior permission was not required because the tenancy was terminated by the tenant’s surrender, not by the landlord’s determination of the tenancy.

predicates.rent_control_permission_proceeding: A landlord sought permission in a proceeding to terminate a tenant’s lease under a rent-control restriction.
predicates.tenant_agreed_to_surrender: The tenant agreed to end the tenancy by surrendering the tenancy rights.

members.legal_issue: An owner may take possession of premises after the tenant vacates them without first obtaining permission from the rent-control authority.
material_facts: The tenant vacated the premises and surrendered possession to the owner.
The owner took possession and moved into the premises.
The owner informed the authorities that the premises had been vacated and that he was occupying them.
members.legal_principle: Section 7 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 provides for notification of a vacancy and permits the District Magistrate to regulate a landlord’s letting of vacant premises, but it does not bar the landlord from taking possession after the tenant has vacated.
members.conclusion: The owner’s occupation was not unlawful; the rent-control provision did not prevent a landlord from taking possession after a tenant vacated.

predicates.tenant_vacated: The tenant ceased occupying the premises and vacated them.
predicates.owner_took_possession: The owner accepted possession of the premises after the tenant vacated.
predicates.owner_occupied_premises: The owner moved into and actually occupied the premises.

members.legal_issue: A recorded occupant who is distinct from a tenant of sir and is in actual possession or enjoyment of the land takes adhivasi status in preference to that tenant.
material_facts: The dispute concerned land held by the landholder as sir and a claim to recover possession from a tenant of sir.
The court considered how the statutory scheme treated a tenant of sir when another person was recorded as occupant of the land and was in actual possession or enjoyment.
The court interpreted the provisions in light of the legislation’s object of removing intermediaries and establishing a direct relationship between the State and the tiller of the soil.
members.legal_principle: Sections 20(a)(i) and 20(a)(ii) confer adhivasi status on qualifying tenants of sir and sub-tenants, subject to the exception in section 20(b)(i), which gives priority to a qualifying recorded occupant. Section 21(1)(h) may deem an occupant within section 20(b)(i) an asami if its conditions are met. The expression “occupant” means a person holding the land in possession or actual enjoyment, as explained in Amba Prasad v. Abdul Noor Khan and affirmed in Nath Singh v. Board of Revenue. The interpretation is consistent with Kumari Radha Kishori v. Joint Director of Consolidation and the Act’s purpose of removing intermediaries; where statutory language permits competing interpretations, the interpretation advancing that purpose is preferred.
members.conclusion: A distinct person recorded as occupant in the relevant land records, and actually possessing or enjoying the land, obtains adhivasi status in preference to a tenant of sir who is not in possession; the tenant’s claim under the tenant category does not displace that occupant’s priority.

predicates.land_possession_recovery_proceeding: A proceeding concerns recovery of possession of land under a land-tenure system.
predicates.sir_tenant_claims_adhivasi: A person who held the land as a tenant of sir claims adhivasi status.
predicates.distinct_person_recorded_as_occupant: The relevant land record identifies someone other than the tenant as the occupant of the land.
predicates.distinct_person_in_actual_possession: The person identified as occupant was in actual possession or enjoyment of the land.
predicates.distinct_recorded_occupant_has_adhivasi_: The distinct recorded occupant obtains adhivasi status in preference to the tenant of sir.

members.legal_issue: A tenant of sir who is not displaced by a distinct recorded occupant becomes an adhivasi under the tenant category and is not deemed an asami merely because the landholder is disabled.
material_facts: The landholder had held the disputed land as sir and had become its bhumidhar.
The defendants were tenants of sir and were recorded as tenants of sir in the relevant land records.
No one else was shown as the occupant of the disputed land in those records.
The landholder was a disabled person, and sought possession on the theory that the defendants were asamis.
The lower courts dismissed the possession suits, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.
members.legal_principle: Sections 20(a)(i) and 20(b)(i), read together, give adhivasi status to a tenant of sir when no distinct person is recorded as occupant, while section 21(1)(h)’s occupant limb applies to an occupant contemplated by section 20(b)(i), not to the tenant who obtains status under section 20(a)(i). The interpretation follows the statutory structure and the Act’s purpose of removing intermediaries. Amba Prasad v. Abdul Noor Khan, Nath Singh v. Board of Revenue, and Kumari Radha Kishori v. Joint Director of Consolidation support the meaning and priority of an occupant in actual possession or enjoyment.
members.conclusion: Because no distinct occupant was shown, the defendants became adhivasis under section 20(a)(i); section 21(1)(h) did not apply to make them asamis, and the suits for possession were rightly dismissed.
