members.legal_issue: A written proposed tenancy agreement submitted with an application for a limited residential tenancy does not require registration, and no separate lease after permission is required.
material_facts: A proposed written agreement was submitted with the application for permission to create the limited tenancy.
The Controller granted permission for the agreed residential letting and fixed period.
No separate registered lease was executed after permission was granted.
members.legal_principle: The Court approved the Delhi High Court’s answer in Vijay Kumar Bajaj v. Inder Sain Minocha that an agreement submitted with an application is a proposed agreement which takes effect on grant of permission and does not require registration. It relied on the longstanding Delhi High Court view, including Kasturi Lal v. Shiv Charan Das Mathur, that the permission is itself authority and no further lease is necessary. Under Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari, a High Court’s settled interpretation of a local statute should normally be followed where changing it would create uncertainty and unsettle transactions.
members.conclusion: The proposed agreement took effect after permission was granted and did not require registration; the permission itself sufficed without a further lease.

predicates.limited_residential_tenancy_case: The proceeding concerns permission to create a limited tenancy for residential use.
predicates.written_proposed_agreement_submitted: The parties submitted a written proposed tenancy agreement with the application for permission.
predicates.controller_granted_permission: The Controller granted permission for the limited tenancy.

members.legal_issue: Permission for a limited tenancy is not invalid merely because the parties did not execute a separate written lease after the permission was granted.
material_facts: The parties made and signed statements before the Rent Controller setting out the proposed limited residential tenancy and its terms, and a draft lease was submitted.
The Rent Controller granted permission on the basis of the application and the parties’ statements.
The tenant argued that no separate written lease had been executed after permission was granted.
The Delhi High Court had consistently treated the statutory procedure as a complete code and had held that no separate post-permission agreement was required.
members.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, was treated as a complete code by the established interpretation of the Delhi High Court. The Court adhered to that settled interpretation of a local statute to avoid uncertainty and disruption of transactions made in reliance on it. It relied on Kasturi Lal v. Shiv Charan Das Mathur, Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari, and its decision in Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna.
members.conclusion: The signed statements and the material before the Rent Controller sufficiently complied with the requirement; the absence of a separate written lease did not invalidate the permission or defeat the possession proceeding.

predicates.limited_tenancy_possession_execution: The proceeding seeks possession under a tenancy granted for a limited period with the Rent Controller’s permission.
predicates.signed_controller_statements_set_out_ter: The parties signed statements before the Controller that set out the terms of the proposed tenancy.
predicates.local_high_court_interpretation_long_set: The local High Court had consistently applied an interpretation under which the permission procedure did not require a separate written lease after permission was granted.

members.legal_issue: Omitting the public purpose from a requisition order does not invalidate the order when the purpose is established by other evidence.
material_facts: The initial orders requisitioned premises without stating the purpose.
Later orders and affidavits on behalf of the government stated that the premises were requisitioned to house people without accommodation.
Evidence described an acute housing shortage and the public problems associated with homelessness.
members.legal_principle: A requisition order need not itself state the purpose if the facts establishing that purpose are shown to the court in another way. The Court applied the underlying principle of Biswabhusan Naik v. The State of Orissa.
members.conclusion: The omission of the purpose from the initial orders was not fatal because the public purpose was established through other evidence.

predicates.challenge_to_requisition_order: A person challenges a government order requisitioning property.
predicates.order_omits_its_purpose: The requisition order does not state the purpose for which the property is taken.
predicates.public_purpose_established_by_other_evid: Evidence outside the order establishes that the requisition serves a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A requisition must serve a public purpose, but the purpose need not be stated in the requisition order if the State can establish it to the court.
material_facts: The requisition order did not state the public purpose for which the flat was requisitioned.

The State placed no material before the court showing the public purpose for the requisition, and the relevant assertion that the allottee was neither a government servant nor a homeless person was not denied.
members.legal_principle: A requisition must be for a public purpose, but the purpose need not be recited in the order if the necessary facts establishing it are proved to the court's satisfaction. The Court relied on State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji & Anr. and section 6(4)(a) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948.
members.conclusion: Omitting the public purpose from the order did not by itself invalidate it, but the State had to establish the purpose by other means; on the material before the court, it had not done so.

predicates.requisition_order_challenged: A person with an interest in property challenged an order requisitioning that property.

predicates.state_fails_to_establish_public_purpose: The State has not shown that the requisition was made for a public purpose.

members.legal_issue: A landlord who has retired before receiving a demand to vacate authority-allotted residential accommodation may still qualify for the special right to recover possession if the statutory conditions are met.
material_facts: The landlord had occupied residential accommodation allotted by the government and owned a residential property in the territory.
The government required him to vacate the allotted accommodation because he owned that property, but he had retired before receiving the demand.
He sought possession of the property let to the tenant under the special recovery procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 14A(1) speaks of a landlord who is a person occupying residential premises allotted by the Central Government or a local authority and required to vacate them because of ownership of residential accommodation; it does not limit the right to serving government employees. The word “person” must be given its plain meaning where the statutory wording is precise and unambiguous. The Court referred to Nihal Chand v. Kalyan Chand Jain, [1978] 2 SCR 183, while explaining the issue of retirement.
members.conclusion: Retirement before the demand to vacate did not disqualify the landlord from the benefit of section 14A.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s right to seek immediate possession accrues when an ownership-based order requiring the landlord to vacate government accommodation is served, and retirement before filing the eviction application does not defeat that accrued right.
material_facts: The landlord occupied residential accommodation allotted by the government and owned a residential house in the relevant territory.

Before retiring, the landlord was served with a general order requiring him to vacate the allotted accommodation, or otherwise incur an enhanced licence-fee obligation, because he owned a house there.
The landlord retired before filing an eviction application under the newly introduced immediate-possession procedure.
The High Court held that retirement before the eviction application made the special procedure unavailable; the Supreme Court considered the appeal from that ruling.
members.legal_principle: Under section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a landlord in occupation of government-allotted residential accommodation who is required by a general or special order to vacate, or otherwise incur an obligation, on the ground that the landlord owns residential accommodation in the territory acquires the right to recover immediate possession on or from the date of that order. Section 25B provided the speedy procedure for pursuing that right; its later availability did not change when the cause of action accrued. The court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The landlord could invoke the immediate-possession provision notwithstanding his retirement before filing, because the ownership-based order had been served before his retirement and the right accrued on service of that order. The appeal was allowed, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the Rent Controller’s eviction order was restored.

members.legal_issue: A plaint seeking specific performance over immovable property must describe the property sufficiently for it to be identified, and the trial court must require an adequate description where the plaint does not do so.
material_facts: The suit concerned part of a larger revenue plot, but the sub-plot numbers used in the parties’ title documents did not appear in the revenue records or survey map.
The property could not be identified merely by the stated sub-plot numbers or boundaries.
The plaint contained no map of the suit property, and the trial court nevertheless decreed the suit.
members.legal_principle: Order 7 Rule 3 CPC requires a plaint concerning immovable property to describe it sufficiently to identify it and, where identification is possible by boundaries or numbers in survey or settlement records, to specify them. This enables a proper decree under Order 20 Rule 3 CPC. No earlier cases are relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs should have filed a map of the property, and the trial court should have noticed the omission and required one before proceeding with the suit.

rule.if: suit_concerns_immovable_property and property_not_identifiable_from_boundaries_or_survey_records and plaint_lacks_identifying_map and trial_court_decreed_suit

predicates.suit_concerns_immovable_property: The proceeding seeks relief concerning a particular item of immovable property.
predicates.property_not_identifiable_from_boundarie: The property cannot be identified from its stated boundaries or numbers in the applicable survey or settlement records.
predicates.plaint_lacks_identifying_map: The plaintiff did not include a map sufficient to identify the property in the plaint.
predicates.trial_court_decreed_suit: The trial court entered a decree despite the inadequate property description.

members.legal_issue: A plaintiff seeking possession must identify the property claimed sufficiently for the court to determine what was purchased and for possession to be delivered under any decree.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought relief concerning land claimed under a deed of sale.
The deed, later documents and a plan contained descriptions of boundaries, lanes and neighbouring properties that did not readily correspond.
The plaintiffs relied on a sketch to establish the location and identity of the land.
members.legal_principle: A plaintiff seeking recovery of possession must establish the cause of action concerning the property and identify it sufficiently for the court to determine the subject of the claim and for the executing court to deliver possession. The court applied this requirement to the deed and identification evidence in the case.
members.conclusion: The property had to be adequately identifiable, and the plaintiffs had to show that the property described in their deed corresponded with the property identified by the other evidence.

predicates.possession_claim: A plaintiff seeks recovery of possession of property.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_title_document: The plaintiff relies on a document to establish what property was acquired.
predicates.identification_evidence_does_not_readily: The descriptions in the title document and the other evidence relied on to locate the property do not readily correspond.

members.legal_issue: A compromise adjusting a claim in a suit or appeal must be in writing and signed by the parties, even when the settlement is reached during a court hearing and recorded in the proceedings.
material_facts: During the hearing of an appeal, one side offered to pay a sum on a future date in full and final settlement, and the other side accepted the offer in a statement before the court.
The statements formed part of the court proceedings, but the compromise terms were not reduced to writing and signed by the parties.
Before the payment date, the accepting party resiled from the proposed compromise.
The court had to decide whether the appeal could be disposed of on the basis of that compromise.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as amended, an adjustment by lawful agreement or compromise requires a completed agreement in writing and signed by the parties, including when the compromise is made during a suit or appeal hearing. The amendment was intended to prevent false or frivolous pleas of oral compromise that could delay proceedings. The agreement must be capable of being embodied in a decree. The contrary view in Manohar Lal v. Surjan Singh was overruled. The rule’s Explanation excludes agreements that are void or voidable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, from being lawful compromises.
members.conclusion: The compromise could not be given effect to as an adjustment under Order XXIII Rule 3 because it was not in writing and signed by the parties. The appeal had to be heard and decided on its merits.

predicates.suit_or_appeal_adjustment_proceeding: The court is deciding whether a claim in a suit or appeal has been adjusted.
predicates.claimed_agreement_adjustment: A party relies on an agreement or compromise as having adjusted the claim.
predicates.written_signed_terms: The terms of the agreement or compromise were reduced to writing and signed by the parties.
predicates.claimed_agreement_adjustment_cannot_be_r: The court cannot record the claimed agreement as an adjustment and must decide the proceeding on its merits.

members.legal_issue: A compromise decree may comply with the requirement for a written, signed compromise even when the court records separate agreements at different stages and later decrees the suits after all parties have settled.
material_facts: The relevant parties filed written applications setting out their respective agreements and supported them with affidavits affirming the facts.
The court first recorded the separate agreements while disputes with other parties remained unresolved, and later passed a decree after the remaining parties had settled their differences.
Each agreement was signed by the parties to that agreement; the appellants had already signed their own agreements and submitted affidavits supporting them.
The court recorded statements from the assignee who signed the final agreement and from representatives of the other heirs.
members.legal_principle: Order XXIII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the court to be satisfied that the suit has been adjusted by a lawful written agreement signed by the parties, to record that agreement, and to pass a decree in accordance with it. Satisfaction may be presumed unless the contrary is shown. The staged recording of agreements is permissible where the settlement of all parties is completed before the final decree. Ajad Singh v. Chatra was distinguishable because there was no proceeding under Order XXIII Rule 3 and the compromise was not recorded through the procedure required by that rule.
members.conclusion: The procedure complied with Order XXIII Rule 3; the court was not required to record the appellants’ statements again or to obtain their signatures on the other parties’ separate agreement.

rule.if: compromise_decree_proceeding and written_agreements_signed_by_relevant_parties and supporting_affidavits_on_record and all_parties_settled_before_final_decree

predicates.compromise_decree_proceeding: The court is asked to record a settlement and dispose of pending suits by compromise decree.
predicates.written_agreements_signed_by_relevant_pa: The parties to each separate settlement signed that written agreement.
predicates.supporting_affidavits_on_record: The applicants filed affidavits affirming the facts and supporting the compromise applications.
predicates.all_parties_settled_before_final_decree: The court passed the final decree only after the remaining parties to the suits had settled their disputes.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee who defaults on rent for which the mortgagee is liable and thereby contributes to a rent sale cannot extinguish the mortgagor’s right of redemption by purchasing the property at that sale, even when the mortgagor also defaulted.
material_facts: The mortgage terms made the mortgagees liable for part of the rent of the consolidated holding, and the mortgagees defaulted on that liability; the mortgagor also defaulted on the rent for which he was liable.
The defaults led to a rent decree and an execution sale of the mortgaged property.
The first appellate court found that the auction purchasers had purchased for the benefit of the contesting mortgagees.
The mortgagees argued that the sale extinguished the right of redemption because the mortgagor’s default would have led to the sale even if the mortgagees had paid their share.
members.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act requires a qualified owner who gains an advantage by availing himself of that position, in derogation of the rights of others interested in the property, to hold the advantage for their benefit, subject to repayment of their proper share of expenses and indemnity for proper liabilities. A mortgagee’s contribution to bringing about a sale through failure to pay rent for which the mortgagee is liable is directly connected to the mortgagee’s position. The mortgagor’s concurrent default does not negate that contribution. The rule applies even where the mortgagee’s rent liability is less than the major portion of the rent; the Court left open the case of a liability so small that the property would not ordinarily be sold for it. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The mortgagees gained an advantage by using their position as mortgagees to acquire the property at the execution sale. Under section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act, they must hold that advantage for the benefit of the persons interested in the property, and the mortgagor’s right of redemption remains available. The appeal was allowed and the preliminary decree for redemption was restored.

rule.if: redemption_suit and mortgagee_owed_rent_for_property and mortgagee_default_contributed_to_sale and mortgagee_or_beneficiary_acquired_property_at_sale

predicates.redemption_suit: The proceeding sought redemption of mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_owed_rent_for_property: The mortgagee was responsible for paying rent for the property, in whole or in part.
predicates.mortgagee_default_contributed_to_sale: The mortgagee failed to pay rent for which the mortgagee was responsible, and that failure helped bring about the execution sale.
predicates.mortgagee_or_beneficiary_acquired_proper: The mortgagee, or a purchaser acting for the mortgagee’s benefit, acquired the property at the execution sale.
predicates.mortgagor_retains_right_to_redeem: The mortgagor’s right to redeem the property remains available.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee’s purchase of mortgaged property at a rent sale does not benefit the mortgagor when the mortgagee’s trifling rent default was not an effective cause of the sale and the mortgagor’s default alone caused it.
material_facts: The mortgaged land formed part of larger holdings, and the mortgagee and mortgagors had agreed to pay specified portions of the rent of those holdings.
The mortgagors repeatedly failed to pay their substantial share of the rent.
The mortgagee paid almost all of the rent it had agreed to pay, leaving only a trifling balance unpaid.
The mortgagee purchased the lands at rent and certificate sales following the rent arrears.
There was no evidence that the mortgagee left the trifling balances unpaid in bad faith or to bring about a sale and purchase by the mortgagee.
members.legal_principle: Under section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, a qualified owner who gains an advantage by availing himself of that position, in derogation of others’ rights, must hold the advantage for their benefit. Illustration (c) applies where a mortgagee deliberately allows revenue to fall into arrears so that the land is sold and the mortgagee can purchase it. In Basmat Devi v. Chamru Sao, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1707, the mortgagee’s substantial default contributed to the sale, so the purchase benefited the mortgagor. Here, the mortgagee’s trifling default was not a real contributory cause, there was no shown improper purpose, and the mortgagors’ default was the effective cause of the sale; the required advantage gained by availing oneself of the mortgagee’s position was therefore absent.
members.conclusion: Section 90 and Illustration (c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 did not apply. The mortgagee’s purchases did not enure for the mortgagors’ benefit, and the sales extinguished the right of redemption.

rule.if: redemption_claim and mortgagee_purchase_at_rent_sale and mortgagor_default_effective_cause and mortgagee_default_trifling and not mortgagee_default_sale_motive

predicates.redemption_claim: The claimant sought redemption of property that had been mortgaged.
predicates.mortgagee_purchase_at_rent_sale: The mortgagee purchased the mortgaged property at a sale following unpaid rent.
predicates.mortgagor_default_effective_cause: The mortgagor failed to pay rent, and that failure was the effective cause of the sale.
predicates.mortgagee_default_trifling: The mortgagee left unpaid only a trifling part of the rent it had agreed to pay.
predicates.mortgagee_default_sale_motive: The mortgagee left rent unpaid in order to bring about a sale and purchase of the property.

members.legal_issue: A transaction in which a husband provides the purchase money for property registered in his wife's name is not benami unless the evidence, assessed as a whole, establishes that he intended the wife to hold title only nominally.
material_facts: The property was conveyed in the wife's name, and the Court assessed the case on the assumption that the husband provided the purchase money.
The wife’s power of attorney stated that she had decided to purchase the property; her husband witnessed it and she was described as her father’s daughter rather than as his wife.
The wife was recorded as owner, possessed the property, paid taxes and participated in its construction; the husband had no evident need to conceal assets or avoid liability.

The husband made his wife the nominee under his life insurance policy, and the children later sought mutation in their names as heirs; the son objected but did not pursue the matter after mutation was allowed.
One daughter gave evidence supporting the mother’s ownership; the son’s wife did not testify, and the only other defence witness was born long after the purchase and lacked personal knowledge of it.
members.legal_principle: The person alleging a benami transaction bears the serious burden of proving it; the person named as purchaser begins with the presumption that the apparent state of affairs is real. Intention is central and must be inferred from the totality of the evidence, including the source of purchase money, possession and nature of the property, motive, parties’ relationship, custody of title deeds and subsequent conduct. The source of funds is important but is not conclusive by itself. The Court relied on Jaydayal Poddar v. Mst. Bibi Hazira, (1974) 1 SCC 3; Thakur Bhim Singh v. Thakur Kan Singh, (1980) 3 SCC 72; Valliammal v. Subramaniam, (2004) 7 SCC 233; Kanakarathanammal v. V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271; and Tulsi v. Chandrika Prasad, (2006) 8 SCC 322, including its principle on drawing an adverse inference where a party who could give material evidence does not testify.
members.conclusion: The evidence showed that the husband intended the property to benefit his wife, not that she was a benamidar. The burden of proving a benami transaction rested on those alleging it, and they did not discharge it. The judgment reversing the trial court was set aside and the trial court’s decree was restored.

rule.if: benami_title_dispute and purchaser_named_as_owner and (owner_exercised_ownership or transaction_documents_support_owner_intent) and no_compelling_evidence_of_nominal_ownership

predicates.benami_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns an allegation that a person named as purchaser holds property only for another person.
predicates.purchaser_named_as_owner: The conveyance identifies the person whose ownership is disputed as the purchaser or owner.
predicates.owner_exercised_ownership: The named owner possessed, managed, or dealt with the property as an owner after purchase.
predicates.transaction_documents_support_owner_inte: Documents or circumstances connected with the purchase indicate that the named owner was intended to benefit from it.
predicates.no_compelling_evidence_of_nominal_owners: The party alleging nominal ownership did not produce compelling evidence that the named owner was intended to hold title only for another.

members.legal_issue: The rule that an immovable-property gift may not become a wife’s stridhan under Dayabhaga law does not prohibit a husband from gifting money for a purchase in her name and does not establish that the purchase was benami.
material_facts: The property was purchased in the wife’s name, and the Court proceeded on the assumption that the husband provided the purchase money.
The High Court relied on Dayabhaga law to reason that the husband could not have gifted the property to his wife.
The Court distinguished a gift of purchase money from a gift of the immovable property itself and held the asserted limitation on stridhan irrelevant to whether the transaction was benami.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that Dayabhaga law’s treatment of an immovable-property gift as not becoming the wife’s stridhan concerns inheritance and succession, not whether a transaction is benami; the money used to buy property may be gifted to the wife. It relied on Kanakarathanammal v. V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271, and K.K. Das, Receiver v. Sm. Amina Khatun Bibi, AIR 1940 Cal 356, and noted the Transfer of Property Act’s treatment of restrictions on transfer.
members.conclusion: The Dayabhaga-based reasoning did not support the finding that the transaction was benami; a husband could gift the money used to purchase property for his wife, and that issue did not determine the nature of the transaction.

rule.if: benami_title_dispute and property_purchased_in_wifes_name and husband_provided_purchase_money and dayabhaga_stridhan_rule_invoked

predicates.benami_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property registered in one person’s name is held benami for another.
predicates.property_purchased_in_wifes_name: The property was purchased and registered in the wife’s name.
predicates.husband_provided_purchase_money: The husband supplied the money used to purchase the property.
predicates.dayabhaga_stridhan_rule_invoked: A party relies on the rule that an immovable-property gift does not become the wife’s stridhan under Dayabhaga law.

members.legal_issue: A notice proposing to alter a municipal assessment must disclose the actual reason for the proposed alteration and identify the assessment error sufficiently to allow the affected person to answer it.
material_facts: The notice proposed increasing the annual value of the premises and used a printed formula stating that the premises had been under-assessed by mistake, fraud, or misrepresentation.

The notice’s details said that two rooms had been erected and that the premises were being used as bank premises, but did not say that the rooms had been omitted from the earlier valuation or explain how that omission caused an under-assessment.
Misrepresentation was not a statutory ground for altering the assessment, and no misrepresentation by the assessee was alleged.
members.legal_principle: Section 67(1) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 permits alteration of an assessment for erroneous valuation or assessment through fraud, accident, or mistake, subject to notice to affected persons. The notice must communicate the reason for the proposed alteration so that the assessee has a reasonable opportunity to answer it. This follows from natural justice and the strict construction required for a taxation provision, particularly where the committee is judge in its own cause. The notice requirement is a condition precedent to a valid alteration. The Court referred to Cholisgaon Borough Municipality v. Multanchand Fulchand Sancheti and Kaviraj Khazan Chand v. New Delhi Municipal Committee.
members.conclusion: The notice did not satisfy the statutory requirements because it failed to identify the actual reason for the proposed alteration; the enhancement was therefore invalid, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.municipal_assessment_amendment_notice: A municipal body gives notice proposing to amend an existing property assessment.
predicates.notice_does_not_identify_actual_reason: The notice gives alternative or formulaic grounds without identifying which actual error is said to justify the proposed amendment.
predicates.notice_does_not_explain_assessment_error: The notice does not explain how the stated circumstances caused the existing assessment to be erroneous.

members.legal_issue: A notice proposing amendment of a municipal assessment must state sufficiently specific grounds to allow the affected person a reasonable opportunity to object.
material_facts: The notice said the property had been wrongly omitted from the assessment list or had been assessed too low due to mistake, fraud, or intention, without identifying which ground applied.
The notice did not identify material supporting the proposed revision.
The property owner objected to the proposed amendment.
members.legal_principle: Section 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 authorizes further amendments on specified grounds and requires notice to affected persons, at least one month to object, and an opportunity to be heard. The notice is not an empty formality: it must give enough particulars of the grounds for amendment to enable an effective objection. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The notice was vague, did not comply with the statutory requirements, and did not provide a reasonable opportunity to object; the resulting amendment could not stand.

predicates.municipal_assessment_amendment_proceedin: A public authority initiated a proceeding to amend an assessment of property.
predicates.affected_person_received_notice: The person affected by the proposed assessment amendment received a notice about it.
predicates.notice_did_not_identify_specific_ground: The notice did not specify which ground for amending the assessment applied.
predicates.notice_did_not_disclose_basis_for_propos: The notice did not identify material supporting the proposed change to the assessment.
predicates.proposed_assessment_amendment_is_invalid: The proposed assessment amendment is invalid.

members.legal_issue: A court may permit correction of a deficient court-fee appeal even where the opposing party claims that doing so would impair a limitation defence.
material_facts: The respondents appealed from a decree but initially paid insufficient court fees.
After an objection, they amended the relief sought, and the High Court later allowed them to delete that amendment and gave them time to pay the required fees.
The claimants argued that allowing the correction deprived them of a limitation defence.

The decree as drawn was declaratory and did not direct delivery of possession, and the Supreme Court found no violation of recognised legal principles or gross injustice in the High Court’s exercise of discretion.
members.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the court discretion to allow correction of a court-fee deficiency, and the limitation plea may be ignored when that discretion is exercised. The exercise should not be disturbed absent a violation of recognised principles of law or gross injustice. The judgment refers generally to decisions of high authority but names no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The preliminary objection failed; the High Court acted within its discretion in permitting the appeal to be corrected and the required court fees to be paid.

rule.if: appeal_from_decree and court_fee_deficient and correction_permitted and no_gross_injustice

predicates.appeal_from_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree.
predicates.court_fee_deficient: The appellant initially pays less than the required court fee.
predicates.correction_permitted: The court permits the appellant to correct the appeal or its requested relief and to pay the required fee.
predicates.no_gross_injustice: The circumstances disclose no gross injustice and no violation of recognised legal principles in allowing the correction.
predicates.court_may_permit_fee_deficiency_to_be_cu: The court may allow the appellant to cure the deficient court fee.

members.legal_issue: A defective appeal filed before a statutory bar on that class of appeals takes effect remains pending from its original filing when the court permits the court-fee deficiency to be cured and the deficiency is later made good.
material_facts: A special appeal from a single judge’s judgment in appellate jurisdiction was presented before the law abolishing that class of appeals took effect.
The memorandum was deficient in court-fee when presented. The court allowed the deficiency to be made good, and the appellant paid it after the abolition law had taken effect.
The memorandum was not rejected; after the deficiency was paid, it was accepted and registered.
The abolition law barred the relevant class of appeals but preserved appeals that were pending immediately before the law took effect.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 41, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an appeal is instituted by presenting a memorandum of appeal. Section 149 of the Code permits the court, in its discretion, to allow a deficient court-fee to be paid later; upon payment, the document has the same force and effect as if the fee had been paid initially. Section 149 must be read harmoniously with section 4 of the Court Fees Act, as a proviso permitting the deficiency to be cured, so the appeal is treated as pending from its original presentation. This applies the pending-appeal exception in section 3(2) of the U.P. High Court (Abolition of Letters Patent Appeals) Act, 1962, notwithstanding its general bar in section 3(1). The reasoning is supported by Gavarnga Sahu v. Botokrishna Patro, Faizullah v. Mauladad, Wajid Ali v. Isar Bano, and Nagendra Nath v. Suresh.
members.conclusion: The appeal was pending from the date it was originally presented and was preserved by the exception for pending appeals. The statutory bar did not apply, and the appeal was to be heard.

rule.if: special_appeal_covered_by_new_bar and memorandum_presented_before_bar_took_effect and court_fee_deficient_at_presentation and court_allowed_time_to_cure and fee_deficiency_later_cured and appeal_not_rejected

predicates.special_appeal_covered_by_new_bar: The proceeding was a special appeal of a kind that a newly effective legal bar would otherwise prohibit.
predicates.memorandum_presented_before_bar_took_eff: The appellant presented the appeal memorandum before the new bar took effect.
predicates.court_fee_deficient_at_presentation: The fee paid with the memorandum was less than the required fee when it was presented.
predicates.court_allowed_time_to_cure: The court allowed the appellant time to make good the fee deficiency.
predicates.fee_deficiency_later_cured: The appellant later paid the deficiency as permitted by the court.
predicates.appeal_not_rejected: The court did not reject the appeal memorandum before the deficiency was cured.

members.legal_issue: A mineral-concession rule made under parliamentary authority for regulation and development does not violate the constitutional guarantee of free trade merely because it restricts private extraction.
material_facts: The challenged rule was made under authority delegated by a parliamentary enactment expressly directed to regulating mines and developing minerals in the public interest.
The rule restricted private leases for quarrying black granite, while providing for extraction by the State or a State-owned corporation.
The rule was notified as a statutory rule pursuant to the delegated authority.
members.legal_principle: Article 301 addresses restrictions that directly and immediately impede the free flow or movement of trade; regulatory measures that facilitate or regulate trade are outside its scope. Article 302 permits Parliament to impose restrictions in the public interest. A statutory rule made under delegated authority is to be treated as law for this purpose. The Court relied on Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam, The Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, and State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya.
members.conclusion: The Act and rules properly made under it were outside the restrictions prohibited by Article 301, and the public-interest authority in Article 302 also answered the challenge based on Article 301; the asserted constitutional challenge failed.

predicates.constitutional_trade_restriction_challen: The proceeding challenges a restriction on mineral activity as inconsistent with constitutional freedom of trade.
predicates.rule_made_under_parliamentary_regulatory: The rule was made under authority conferred by a parliamentary enactment directed to regulating the relevant economic activity.
predicates.rule_is_regulatory_measure: The rule forms part of a regulatory scheme for the activity rather than being an unrelated impediment to trade.
predicates.rule_properly_made: The rule was made within the authority delegated to the rule-maker.

members.legal_issue: A royalty on quarrying does not violate the constitutional freedom of movement of trade where movement of goods between States is not a direct consequence of the quarrying activity.
material_facts: The challenged levy applied to quarrying minor minerals.
The Court found that quarrying itself did not involve movement of goods between States and that any later removal of minerals outside the State was not a direct consequence of quarrying.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that quarrying does not itself involve inter-State movement and that any later movement of minerals outside the State is not a direct consequence of the quarrying activity.
members.conclusion: The levy did not violate the constitutional freedom of trade and movement between States.

predicates.minor_mineral_royalty_rule_challenge: The case challenges a royalty imposed on the extraction of minor minerals.
predicates.quarrying_does_not_itself_move_goods_bet: The quarrying activity does not itself involve movement of the extracted goods from one State to another.
predicates.later_outbound_movement_is_not_a_direct_: Any later transport of minerals outside the State is not a direct consequence of the quarrying activity.

members.legal_issue: An appeal challenging an order made by consent is not maintainable where the order records the parties’ consent and the asserted grounds do not establish a basis to invalidate that consent.
material_facts: The writ petition was disposed of on terms recorded by the court as a compromise agreed to by counsel for both parties.
The appellants did not appeal that order at the time and later filed a writ appeal challenging it.

The allegation that the compromise had not been authorized or that the recorded consent was false was not made until late in the proceedings, and the court found no sufficient basis for disturbing the order.
members.legal_principle: The court upheld the objection based on Section 96(3) CPC, which bars an appeal from a decree passed with the consent of the parties, and found no established ground on the facts to undo the recorded consent. It also applied the principle in State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak that statements in a judgment recording what occurred in court cannot be contradicted on appeal.
members.conclusion: The High Court correctly upheld the preliminary objection to the maintainability of the appeal against the consent order.

predicates.appeal_challenges_consent_order: A party brings an appeal challenging an order that was made on the basis of recorded consent.
predicates.consent_recorded_by_court: The order records that the parties agreed to the disposition through their representatives.
predicates.no_proven_basis_to_set_consent_aside: The appellant does not establish that the recorded consent should be invalidated.

members.legal_issue: An appeal under the ordinary civil appeal procedure is not maintainable against a consent decree.
material_facts: A civil court disposed of the landlords’ possession suit as settled and passed a decree on the parties’ recorded statements.
A defendant challenged the consent decree by filing an appeal rather than pursuing her application before the court that recorded the compromise.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 96(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, no appeal lies from a decree passed with the parties’ consent. Order 43 Rule 1(m) was deleted, and Order 23 Rule 3A bars an independent suit to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful. The court that recorded the compromise may decide, under the proviso to Order 23 Rule 3, whether a valid compromise existed. The Court allowed the jurisdictional objection to be raised for the first time on appeal, relying on Shanti Devi v. Bimla Devi, Zahoor v. State of U.P., and Hiralal v. Kasturi Devi.
members.conclusion: The appeal against the consent decree was not maintainable; a party seeking to avoid such a decree must approach the court that recorded the compromise and establish that there was no valid compromise.

predicates.appeal_against_consent_decree: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decree that was passed with the parties’ consent.
predicates.challenge_brought_by_appeal: The party seeks to set aside the consent decree by appeal rather than by applying to the court that recorded the compromise.

members.legal_issue: An appeal concerning an order awarding compensation for land acquisition attracts ad valorem court fees, and the order need not have the force of a decree.
material_facts: The Special Deputy Collector appealed the arbitrator’s compensation award to the High Court.
The applicable court-fee law provided that the fee on an appeal against an order relating to acquisition compensation was computed by comparing the amount awarded with the amount claimed.
The appellant’s cross-objection sought compensation beyond the amount awarded.
members.legal_principle: Section 7(1) of the Bombay Court-fee Act, 1959, was a computation provision, not a charging provision, and its comparison of the amount awarded with the amount claimed indicated an ad valorem fee under Schedule I rather than a fixed fee under Schedule II. The Court applied Anandalal Chakrabarti, which construed the corresponding provision of the Court-fee Act, 1870, and held that no requirement that the order have the force of a decree should be added to the statutory text.
members.conclusion: The compensation appeal attracted ad valorem court fees under the applicable fee schedule; the court-fee provision did not require the order under appeal to have the force of a decree.

predicates.appeal_concerns_compensation_award: A party appealed a decision determining compensation for acquired property.
predicates.compensation_claim_differs_from_award: The compensation claimed differs from the amount awarded.

members.legal_issue: An appeal challenging a statutory arbitrator's compensation award for property requisitioned for a public purpose attracts ad valorem court fee rather than the fixed fee under the residuary provision.
material_facts: The owners appealed under section 11 of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 against an arbitrator's award determining compensation for requisitioned property.
The owners claimed a higher amount of compensation than the amount awarded and disputed the difference in the appeal.
The property was held by the Government for a public purpose.
members.legal_principle: Section 51 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955 provides that the fee on a memorandum of appeal against an order relating to compensation under an enactment for acquisition of property for public purposes is computed on the difference between the amount awarded and the amount claimed. Read with Article 1 of Schedule I, it requires ad valorem court fee. Article 3(iii)(A)(1)(a) of Schedule II, the residuary fixed-fee provision, is not attracted. The Court applied its conclusions on the broad meaning of acquisition and on a statutory arbitrator's award being an order, relying particularly on Sahadu Gangaram Bhagade v. Special Deputy Collector.
members.conclusion: Court fee is payable ad valorem on the difference between the compensation awarded and the amount claimed; the residuary fixed-fee provision does not apply.

rule.if: compensation_award_appeal and property_taken_for_public_purpose and appeal_seeks_difference_between_award_and_claim and award_formally_expresses_decision and award_binds_parties

predicates.compensation_award_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an award that determines compensation for property taken or held by the government.
predicates.property_taken_for_public_purpose: The property is taken or held for a public purpose.
predicates.appeal_seeks_difference_between_award_an: The appellant seeks compensation beyond the amount awarded and disputes the difference between the two amounts.
predicates.award_formally_expresses_decision: The authority's award formally states its decision.
predicates.award_binds_parties: The award binds the parties to the compensation proceeding.

members.legal_issue: An execution-sale purchaser of the shares of some coparceners is entitled only to the interests actually sold and cannot obtain the share of a coparcener whose interest was not sold.
material_facts: At the time of the execution sale, the shares of four coparceners were put up for sale.
Another son had been born before the sale but was not a party to the suit or execution proceedings, and his share was not sold.
The four sons’ shares, initially described as four-fifths, amounted to two-thirds after the additional son’s birth.
members.legal_principle: An execution-sale purchaser acquires the interests of the judgment-debtors that were actually put up for sale; an interest that was not sold does not pass to the purchaser. No earlier case was relied on for this determination.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to a two-thirds share, not a four-fifths share, and could not claim the additional son’s share.

predicates.partition_suit_by_execution_sale_purchas: A purchaser at an execution sale sought partition and possession of joint family property.
predicates.only_some_coparceners_interests_sold: The execution sale included the interests of only some of the coparceners.
predicates.another_coparcener_excluded_from_sale: A coparcener’s interest was not included in the sale because that coparcener was not a party to the proceedings.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser of an undivided interest in joint family property at an execution sale cannot recover a share of the family’s income or obtain possession before a partition makes a specific allotment to the purchaser.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired an undivided interest in joint family property at an execution sale.
The purchaser sued the other family members for a share of the income or profits from the properties from the date of purchase.
No specific portion of the property had been allotted to the purchaser by partition.
members.legal_principle: An execution purchaser of an undivided coparcenary interest acquires no title to a defined portion of the property and is not entitled to joint possession from the date of purchase. The purchaser must work out the acquired rights through a partition suit, with possession beginning when a specific allotment is made.
members.conclusion: The purchaser could not recover a share of the income or profits from the date of purchase; the purchaser had to pursue partition, and the right to possession would begin when a specific allotment was made.

predicates.execution_purchase_case: A purchaser acquired an interest in joint family property through an execution sale.
predicates.purchased_interest_undivided: The interest acquired was undivided and did not identify a specific portion of the property.
predicates.no_specific_allotment: A partition had not made a specific allotment of property to the purchaser.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court should not disturb a discretionary reduction of interest applicable after a suit is filed when the circumstances support leaving that reduction in place.
material_facts: The High Court reduced the interest rate from the filing of the suit, exercising its discretion over interest for the period while the suit was pending.
The mortgages had been made many years before the suit was filed, and the creditor would receive interest substantially exceeding the principal amount of the loans.
The Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s reduction, although the High Court had not stated its reasons.
members.legal_principle: The court may exercise discretion over interest for the period while a suit is pending. The Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with that exercise of discretion in the circumstances, including the substantial delay before suit and the substantial interest the creditor would receive. No earlier case was cited for this point.
members.conclusion: The reduction of interest for the period after the suit was filed was left undisturbed.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_pendente_lite_interest and lower_court_exercised_interest_discretion and suit_filed_long_after_loan and expected_interest_substantially_exceeds_principal

predicates.appeal_challenging_pendente_lite_interes: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the interest set for the period while a suit was pending.
predicates.lower_court_exercised_interest_discretio: The lower court exercised its discretion in setting interest for the period after the suit was filed.
predicates.suit_filed_long_after_loan: The suit was filed long after the loan was made.
predicates.expected_interest_substantially_exceeds_: The creditor would receive interest substantially exceeding the principal amount of the loan.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to increase an interest rate reduced by the lower court where the reduction is reasonable in the circumstances of the case.
material_facts: The State appealed against the lower court's reduction of the interest rate sought from the mining lessees.
The litigation had continued for a long time and multiple commercial transactions had taken place.
Commercial and bank interest rates had changed substantially, and bank rates had for some time been below the rate awarded by the lower court.
The lower court considered the higher rate excessive and its reduced rate reasonable in the circumstances.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court declined discretionary interference with the lower court's assessment, taking account of the prolonged litigation, intervening commercial transactions and changes in interest rates. The Court expressly confined its decision to the facts and parties before it and stated that it did not override Rule 64A of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the lower court's reduced rate in the exercise of its discretionary appellate jurisdiction, while making clear that this case-specific concession was not a precedent for overriding the governing rule.

rule.if: appeal_seeks_higher_interest_rate and prolonged_litigation and commercial_interest_rates_changed and lower_court_reduced_rate_reasonably

predicates.appeal_seeks_higher_interest_rate: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to restore a higher interest rate that the lower court reduced.
predicates.prolonged_litigation: The dispute has continued for a long period before the appellate decision.
predicates.commercial_interest_rates_changed: Commercial or bank interest rates changed substantially during the period of the dispute.
predicates.lower_court_reduced_rate_reasonably: The lower court reduced the rate after finding the higher rate excessive in the circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot refer a complaint for investigation against a public servant accused of a protected corruption offence without the required prior sanction.
material_facts: The complaint alleged that public officials had abused their official positions in connection with land-conversion proceedings.
The complaint was referred for investigation under the Code of Criminal Procedure before any sanction had been obtained.
members.legal_principle: Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act bars a court from taking cognizance of the specified offences against a public servant without prior sanction. Applying the broad meaning of cognizance, the court held that a judicial referral for investigation under Section 156(3) also requires sanction. It relied on Anil Kumar v. M.K. Aiyappa, which directly held that sanction is required before such a referral, and on Manharibhai Muljibhai Kakadia v. Shaileshbhai Mohanbhai Patel, which explained that cognizance includes taking authoritative notice of allegations through application of judicial mind. It also referred to Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the principles in State of U.P. v. Paras Nath Singh and Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh.
members.conclusion: A court cannot direct investigation under Section 156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure against a public servant for an offence covered by Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act in the absence of valid prior sanction.

predicates.magistrate_refers_complaint_for_investig: A magistrate refers a complaint for investigation before taking cognizance of the alleged offence.
predicates.public_servant_is_accused_of_protected_c: The complaint accuses a public servant of an offence for which the law requires prior sanction before the court may take cognizance.
predicates.valid_prior_sanction_obtained: The authority competent to grant sanction has given valid prior approval for the prosecution.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot refer a private complaint for investigation into alleged corruption offences by a public servant without the required prior sanction, even at the pre-cognizance stage.
material_facts: A private complaint alleged that a public servant had acted in concert with other officers in issuing an order concerning valuable land and asserted offences under corruption and general criminal laws.
The complainants sought investigation by police under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.
No valid sanction under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act had been produced.
members.legal_principle: Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act bars a court from taking cognizance of the specified offences against a public servant without previous sanction. That bar applies to a referral for investigation under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. as well as at a later stage. Section 19(3), which limits reversal of a finding, sentence or order for a sanction defect absent a failure of justice, does not make prior sanction directory. The Court relied on State of Uttar Pradesh v. Paras Nath Singh, Subramanium Swamy v. Manmohan Singh, and General Officer, Commanding v. CBI.
members.conclusion: The required prior sanction is mandatory, and the court could not refer the complaint for investigation without it; the High Court's decision quashing the referral and complaint was upheld.

rule.if: private_complaint_proceeding and public_servant_accused and corruption_offence_alleged and official_duty_alleged and prior_sanction_absent and pre_cognizance_investigation_sought

predicates.private_complaint_proceeding: A complainant brings a private criminal complaint before a court.
predicates.public_servant_accused: The complaint accuses a person who holds public office.
predicates.corruption_offence_alleged: The complaint alleges an offence of the kind for which prior governmental authorization is required before prosecution.
predicates.official_duty_alleged: The alleged conduct is said to have occurred in the discharge of the accused person's official duties.
predicates.prior_sanction_absent: No valid prior authorization to proceed against the accused person has been produced.
predicates.pre_cognizance_investigation_sought: The complainant asks the court to refer the matter for police investigation before the court takes cognizance.

members.legal_issue: A court deciding anticipatory bail in a case alleging an offence under special legislation protecting Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes must confine its assessment to whether the complaint prima facie discloses the offence and must not conduct a critical analysis of the evidence.
material_facts: The accused sought anticipatory bail in a case that included an accusation under the special legislation.
The Court considered the complaint’s specific allegations of caste-based abuse and assault in deciding whether the statutory bar applied.
members.legal_principle: Sections 18 of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 operate together to bar anticipatory bail where an offence under the special legislation is prima facie disclosed. In considering the application, the court’s scope to appreciate evidence and other material is limited; the Court relied on no earlier Supreme Court case for this proposition and stated that contrary High Court decisions cited by counsel could not be treated as precedent against the statutory bar.
members.conclusion: The court’s inquiry is limited: it must verify whether the complaint prima facie makes out an offence and must not critically analyze the evidence or undertake an elaborate discussion of it.

predicates.anticipatory_bail_proceeding: An accused sought release before arrest in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.protected_offence_accusation: The criminal accusation included an offence under legislation protecting Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes.

members.legal_issue: In a complaint case involving an offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the magistrate must apply a preliminary threshold and must not meticulously assess the evidence as if conducting a trial.
material_facts: The complaint alleged offences exclusively triable by the Court of Session.
At the preliminary inquiry, the complainant and witnesses stated that the accused had shot the complainant and caused the fatal shooting of another person.
The magistrate rejected the allegations after extensively assessing the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 200, 202, 203 and 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the magistrate must determine on a cursory perusal whether sufficient ground exists to proceed, not weigh evidence as at trial. For an offence exclusively triable by the Court of Session, prima facie evidence is sufficient to issue process and commit the case; Sections 209 and 227 provide for commitment and for discharge by the Sessions Judge where sufficient ground to proceed is absent. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh.
members.conclusion: There was prima facie evidence against the accused that required consideration by the Court of Session; the magistrate erred by dismissing the complaint against him after a meticulous appraisal of the evidence.

predicates.complaint_case_exclusively_sessions: The proceeding began with a complaint alleging an offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session.
predicates.preliminary_evidence_supports_accusation: The material gathered in the preliminary inquiry provides prima facie support for the accusation against the person concerned.
predicates.magistrate_meticulously_weighed_evidence: The magistrate assessed the preliminary evidence in detail as though deciding the case at trial.

members.legal_issue: A tenant claiming a statutory right of pre-emption must retain the qualifying tenancy through the decree, and cannot succeed after the tenancy has ended and the tenant has been dispossessed.
material_facts: The claimant had been a tenant-at-will of the land under its former owner when the land was sold.
The purchasers obtained a decree for the claimant's eviction, and the claimant was dispossessed before filing the pre-emption suit.
The claimant's tenancy had ended before the pre-emption suit was instituted.
members.legal_principle: Under s. 15(1)(a) Fourthly of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, the right vests in a tenant who holds the land under tenancy of the vendor. The settled rule is that a pre-emptor must retain the qualification to pre-empt through the decree. The Court relied on Hans Nath v. Ragho Prasad Singh, Thakur Madho Singh v. Lt. James R. R. Skinner, Faiz Mohammad v. Fajar Ali Khan, Surjit Singh v. Gurnam Singh, and Ramji Lal v. State of Punjab, which it approved; it overruled Kashmiri Lal v. Chuhar Ram and Sohan Singh v. Udho Ram. The statutory right attaches to the land, and a tenant whose tenancy has ended no longer meets the requirement of holding the land as a tenant.
members.conclusion: The claimant could not obtain possession by pre-emption because he no longer held the land as a tenant and had lost his qualifying status before the decree; the suit was dismissed.

rule.if: preemption_suit and claimant_tenant_at_sale and (tenancy_ended_before_suit or tenancy_ended_during_suit_before_decree)

predicates.preemption_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking possession by pre-emption.
predicates.claimant_tenant_at_sale: The claimant held the land as a tenant under the seller when the land was sold.
predicates.tenancy_ended_before_suit: The claimant's tenancy ended before the pre-emption suit was filed.
predicates.tenancy_ended_during_suit_before_decree: The claimant's tenancy ended while the pre-emption suit was pending and before the decree was made.
predicates.claimant_cannot_succeed_in_preemption: The claimant cannot obtain possession by pre-emption.

members.legal_issue: A tenant claiming a right of pre-emption must retain the qualifying status of tenant until the pre-emption decree, and an eviction order passed before that decree ends the tenancy even if physical dispossession has not occurred.
material_facts: The claimants were tenants of the land when its owner sold it to the purchasers.
An eviction order was passed against the claimants after the sale but before the trial court decreed the pre-emption suit.
The claimants had obtained an injunction against dispossession, but it did not prevent an eviction order from being obtained.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 15(1)(a), Fourthly, of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, a tenant claiming pre-emption must hold the land as a tenant. The general rule of pre-emption requires the claimant to retain the right until the date of the decree. Applying Bhagwan Dass (dead) by L.Rs. v. Chet Ram, the Court held that an eviction order determines the tenancy; actual dispossession is not necessary. The Court declined to distinguish that decision or refer the matter to a larger bench.
members.conclusion: The claimants were no longer tenants when the pre-emption decree was passed and could not obtain a decree for pre-emption.

predicates.tenant_based_preemption_case: The proceeding is a claim for pre-emption based on the claimant's status as a tenant of the property sold.
predicates.claimant_was_tenant_at_sale: The claimant held the property as a tenant when it was sold.
predicates.valid_ejectment_order_before_preemption_: A competent authority entered an effective order for the claimant's eviction after the sale and before the pre-emption decree.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may construe a decree in light of applicable law to determine whether an act complies with it, without thereby varying the decree.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether a deposit made on the first day the court reopened complied with the compromise decree.
The decree required a court deposit by a specified deadline and provided for dismissal on default.
The lower courts treated the deposit as compliance with the decree, and the High Court affirmed their decision.
members.legal_principle: An executing court must execute a decree as it stands and may not modify or vary its terms. It may, however, construe the decree in light of applicable law; if that construction establishes that the act performed complied with the decree, enforcing the decree on that basis is not a variation. The Court applied this principle to the legal rule permitting an act required in court to be done at the first practicable opportunity when court closure prevents performance on the deadline.
members.conclusion: The executing court did not vary the decree by treating the deposit as compliant; it was entitled to construe and execute the decree as it stood in light of applicable law.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and decree_requires_court_deposit and court_closed_on_deadline and deposit_made_first_practicable_day

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party asks an executing court to enforce a decree.
predicates.decree_requires_court_deposit: The decree requires a party to make a payment by depositing it in court.
predicates.court_closed_on_deadline: The court is closed on the deadline for making the required deposit.
predicates.deposit_made_first_practicable_day: The party deposits the payment on the first day the court is available to receive it after the closure.

members.legal_issue: An executing court may interpret a decree but may not alter its operative terms by treating a liability preserved in the decree as discharged.
material_facts: The decree separately stated the reduced amount payable by some debtors and the unreduced amount payable by the claimant.
The claimant asked the executing court to record full satisfaction based on payments amounting to the reduced debt rather than the amount stated as his liability.
The High Court, acting as the executing court, accepted the request and directed that full satisfaction be recorded.
members.legal_principle: In a proceeding under section 47 and Order XXI, rule 2, of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court must give effect to the decree as passed. It may interpret the decree, but it cannot use interpretation to make a new decree for the parties or contradict clear terms fixing a debtor’s liability.
members.conclusion: The executing court could not treat the decree as satisfied contrary to its terms; the order allowing full satisfaction was set aside.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The court was dealing with a request concerning enforcement or satisfaction of an existing decree.
predicates.decree_expressly_sets_claimants_liabilit: The decree clearly stated the amount for which the claimant remained liable.
predicates.claimant_seeks_satisfaction_on_less_than: The claimant sought full satisfaction based on payment of less than the amount stated as his liability in the decree.

members.legal_issue: A sale may be held not binding on a claimant when the claimant challenged the alienations in the pleadings and the sale was unsupported by consideration.
material_facts: The plaint challenged the alienations generally, sought relief concerning the scheduled lands, and included the lands covered by the sale.
The purchaser was a minor, the seller acted as her guardian, and the purchaser had no property of her own.
The High Court found the sale to be without consideration and not genuine.
members.legal_principle: A pleading that challenges alienations generally and seeks relief concerning the scheduled properties can encompass a sale even if the sale is not specifically identified in the paragraph relied on by the opposing party, where the relevant properties are included in the schedule. The Court upheld the finding that this sale was without consideration and not genuine.
members.conclusion: The sale was not binding on the claimant.

rule.if: partition_suit_with_cross_objection and plaint_challenges_alienations and disputed_property_in_schedule and sale_without_consideration

predicates.partition_suit_with_cross_objection: The proceeding is a partition suit in which a cross-objection challenges the treatment of a property sale.
predicates.plaint_challenges_alienations: The claimant’s pleadings challenge the family’s alienations and seek relief concerning them.
predicates.disputed_property_in_schedule: The property covered by the sale is included in the property schedule to the pleadings.
predicates.sale_without_consideration: The sale was found to be unsupported by consideration and not genuine.

members.legal_issue: A sale of family property to a minor is not binding on a claimant to the family property when the sale is found to be without consideration and not genuine.
material_facts: The buyer was a minor when the sale was made.
The seller acted as the minor’s guardian, and the minor had no property of her own.
The High Court found the sale to be without consideration and not genuine.
members.legal_principle: The Court affirmed the finding that the sale was not genuine and was without consideration, given the circumstances that the buyer was a minor, the seller acted as her guardian, and she had no property of her own. No statute or earlier case was cited for this determination.
members.conclusion: The sale was not binding on the plaintiff.

rule.if: property_partition_appeal and family_property_sale and buyer_was_minor and seller_acted_as_buyer_guardian and sale_without_consideration and sale_not_genuine

predicates.property_partition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a dispute over partition of family property.
predicates.family_property_sale: A sale of property claimed as family property is challenged by a claimant to that property.
predicates.buyer_was_minor: The buyer was a minor when the sale was made.
predicates.seller_acted_as_buyer_guardian: The person who made the sale acted as guardian for the minor buyer.
predicates.sale_without_consideration: The sale was made without consideration.
predicates.sale_not_genuine: The sale was not a genuine transaction.

members.legal_issue: A representative suit may proceed where the persons represented share a common interest or grievance, even if they have separate causes of action.
material_facts: The suit was brought on behalf of low-income allottees in the same colony who had received allotments under the same housing scheme and materially identical lease terms.
The challenged demands rested on the same basis for all the represented allottees, and the plaintiff's plea was available to them.
The authority argued that separate demands gave rise to separate causes of action and required separate suits.
The trial court permitted the representative suit, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
members.legal_principle: Order I, Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, serves the public interest by avoiding multiplicity of litigation. Its essential requirement is sameness of interest, shown by a common interest or a common grievance; the court should assess whether there is sufficient community of interest to justify the procedure. In Kodia Goundar v. Velandi Goundar, ILR 1955 Madras 339, the Full Bench emphasized sameness of interest and an interpretation that advances the rule's purpose. The Explanation to Order I, Rule 8, added by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976, clarifies that represented persons need not have the same cause of action.
members.conclusion: The suit was maintainable as a representative suit because the allottees had a sufficient common interest and grievance; their separate causes of action did not make the procedure unavailable.

rule.if: representative_suit and same_scheme_and_material_facts and common_basis_for_challenge and (common_interest or common_grievance)

predicates.representative_suit: One or more persons brought a suit on behalf of a larger group of persons.
predicates.same_scheme_and_material_facts: The represented persons' relevant circumstances arose under the same scheme and shared materially common facts.
predicates.common_basis_for_challenge: The challenged conduct rested on a basis applicable to the represented persons, and the representative's plea was available to them.
predicates.common_interest: The represented persons shared an interest in the matter the suit sought to resolve.
predicates.common_grievance: The represented persons shared a grievance that the suit sought to redress.

members.legal_issue: A consumer complaint may proceed in a representative capacity only where its pleadings and requested reliefs establish that the numerous consumers represented have the same interest.
material_facts: The complainants sought to represent purchasers of about 1,134 apartments, although none of the purchasers in one of the three blocks had joined and the complaint did not plead that block’s completion timeline.
The complaint did not specifically plead how purchasers in the other two blocks shared the same interest.
The period of delay could differ between purchasers, and purchasers differed in whether they accepted offered compensation, accepted it under protest, or refused it.
The requested delay compensation depended on the circumstances of each purchaser; some purchasers had also pursued separate grievances.
members.legal_principle: Section 35(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 requires numerous consumers to have the same interest; Section 38(11) applies Order I Rule 8 CPC. Under the Explanation to Order I Rule 8, sameness of interest is distinct from sameness of cause of action: a shared cause of action alone does not establish shared interest. The pleadings and reliefs must be considered. Chairman, Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. T.N. Ganapathy was distinguishable because the challenged demand there was uniform and the decision was limited to a particular group of allottees. Rameshwar Prasad Shrivastava, Anjum Hussain and Vikrant Singh Malik were also considered in explaining the requirements for representative consumer complaints.
members.conclusion: The permission to file the complaint in a representative capacity for all purchasers should not have been granted. The complaint is to be treated as a joint complaint by the complainants, not as a representative complaint for all purchasers.

predicates.consumer_representative_case: One or more consumers seek to pursue a complaint on behalf of, or for the benefit of, numerous other consumers.
predicates.pleadings_establish_shared_interest: The complaint’s pleadings and requested reliefs establish that the consumers represented share an interest in the matter.

members.legal_issue: An application to set aside an execution sale and the required deposit made within the extended limitation period are sufficient despite the shorter period stated for the deposit in the execution procedure rule.
material_facts: A property was sold in execution of a money decree.

The judgment-debtor made an initial deposit and an application to set aside the sale, then made a further application and deposited the balance; the full decretal amount and 5% of the purchase price were deposited within sixty days of the sale.
The auction-purchaser objected that the deposit had not been completed within thirty days.
The lower courts held the sale liable to be set aside, and the Supreme Court dismissed the challenge to that decision.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rules 89 and 92(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, read literally, required both the application and deposit within thirty days. Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963, as amended by Act 104 of 1976, provides sixty days for an application to set aside an execution sale, including an application under Rule 89 or Rule 90. The provisions should receive a harmonious construction; Rule 92(2) is inconsistent with Article 127 and requires legislative amendment. The Court approved the approach in Thangammal & Ors. v. K. Dhanalakshmi & Anr., AIR 1981 Mad. 254.
members.conclusion: The application and required deposit made within sixty days of the sale were within the limitation period under Article 127, so the sale was liable to be set aside; the special leave petition was dismissed.

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside_proceeding: A party sought to set aside a sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.application_within_applicable_limitation: The application to set aside the execution sale was made within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.full_required_deposit_within_applicable_: The party completed the deposit required to seek setting aside of the sale within the applicable limitation period.

members.legal_issue: The time limit for depositing the required amounts when seeking to set aside an execution sale is the same as the time limit for filing the application, rather than a separate 30-day limit.
material_facts: Property was sold in execution of a decree.
An application to set aside the sale and the required deposit were made on the 59th day after the sale.
The executing court dismissed the application because the deposit was made after 30 days; the appellate court set aside the sale, and the High Court upheld that decision.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for an application to set aside an execution sale upon deposit but prescribes no time limit for either the application or the deposit. Article 127 of the Limitation Act prescribes the application period, extended from 30 to 60 days, while Order XXI Rule 92(2) provides that the court must set aside the sale when the application is allowed and the deposit is made within 30 days. Rule 92(2) removes the court’s discretion in that circumstance; it does not prohibit a later deposit within the application period. This reading gives effect to the legislative purpose of the extension without adding words to the statute. The court rejected the contrary interpretation in P.K. Unni v. Nirmala Industries and distinguished its conclusion from the harmonising approach in Basavantappa v.
