Gangadhar Narayan Dharwadkar; it also applied the general statutory interpretation principles discussed in P.K. Unni.
members.conclusion: The 30-day period does not impose a deadline for making the deposit. An application and deposit may be made within the 60-day application period; if the deposit is made after the first 30 days but within that period, the court has discretion whether to grant the application. The appeal was dismissed.

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside_application: A person seeks to have a sale conducted in execution of a decree set aside.
predicates.initial_deposit_window_elapsed: The required deposit is made after the period in which the court is required to set aside the sale if the application is allowed.
predicates.application_and_deposit_within_applicabl: The application and required deposit are made within the period allowed for filing the application.

members.legal_issue: A Division Bench hearing a Letters Patent appeal from a judgment in a first appeal may review both factual and legal issues.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the possession suit, and a single judge dismissed the plaintiffs’ first appeal.
The Division Bench allowed the Letters Patent appeal, reconsidered the evidence, and set aside the earlier judgments.
The appellants argued that the Division Bench should not have disturbed the concurrent findings of the lower courts.
members.legal_principle: Under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent, a Division Bench hearing an appeal from a single judge’s decision in a first appeal has the same power as that first appellate court over questions of fact and law; its power is not confined to the scope of Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Court relied on Asha Devi v. Dukhi Sao, AIR 1974 SC 2048; (1974) 2 SCC 492.
members.conclusion: The Division Bench had the same power as a first appellate court to decide questions of fact and law, and was not limited to questions of law.

predicates.letters_patent_appeal_from_first_appeal: The proceeding is a Letters Patent appeal from a judgment given in a first appeal.
predicates.single_judge_decided_as_first_appellate_: A single judge decided the matter while exercising first-appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.division_bench_may_review_questions_of_f: The Division Bench may review questions of both fact and law.

members.legal_issue: A bench hearing an intra-court appeal may reconsider a single judge’s findings when resolving a mixed question of law and fact involving the construction of documents.
material_facts: A temple sued for title to agricultural land, possession, and mesne profits, and the trial court dismissed the suit.
The single judge, hearing an appeal from the trial court, construed two documents as showing that a grant was personal to the temple’s priest and upheld the dismissal.
In an intra-court appeal, a later bench reconsidered the documents alongside the surrounding circumstances and concluded that the grant was intended for the temple.
The challenge to that reconsideration argued that the later bench could not disturb the single judge’s factual finding.
members.legal_principle: An intra-court appeal is ordinarily an appeal in which the later bench acts as a court correcting the High Court’s own order and exercises the same jurisdiction as the single bench. It differs from an appeal against a subordinate court’s order, in which the High Court acts as a court of error. The construction of documents that presents a mixed question of law and fact falls within the later bench’s powers.
members.conclusion: The later bench was empowered to reconsider the documents, and it committed no error by reaching a different conclusion about the intended recipient of the grant.

predicates.intra_court_appeal: A bench of the same court hears an appeal from an order made by that court’s single judge.
predicates.document_construction_is_mixed_question_: The issue before the later bench requires construing documents in a way that involves both law and fact.

members.legal_issue: A claim that land was wrongly treated as agricultural land cannot be resolved when it was not raised before the lower authorities and the record does not establish the factual basis for the claim.
material_facts: A landholder asserted that homestead urban land not connected with agriculture had been included as agricultural land in a draft statement.
The claim had not been raised before the High Court or the authorities under the land-reform law.
The counter-affidavit denied that the landholder had homestead or non-agricultural land in the area, and the record did not permit the Court to make a finding on the claim.
members.legal_principle: Where a factual claim was not raised before the lower authorities and the record does not establish the facts needed to decide it, the Court may decline to make a factual determination.
members.conclusion: The Court could not record a finding on the land-classification claim and expressed no opinion on it.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The dispute arises in a proceeding to determine surplus land under a land-ceiling regime.
predicates.claim_not_raised_below: The landholder did not raise the factual claim before the lower authorities or the reviewing court below.
predicates.record_does_not_establish_claim: The evidence in the record does not establish the facts needed to resolve the claim.

members.legal_issue: A claim of discriminatory land allotment is not established when the alleged comparator and the details of the different allotment are not specifically pleaded, and the claim was not shown to have been raised before the deciding judge.
material_facts: The appellant alleged generally that similarly situated institutions had received land allotments, but did not identify the comparator or provide details of its allotment in the writ petition.
The appellant did not substantiate its assertion that discriminatory treatment had been raised before the Single Judge, and it did not seek review of that judge’s decision.
A different educational society had received a four-acre allotment before the challenged policy decision, but no four-acre allotment after that decision was shown.
members.legal_principle: A judge’s record must be accepted as correct. Where a party says an argument was raised but not addressed, it may seek review; an unsupported assertion in an appeal does not establish that the argument was made. A discrimination claim must identify the allegedly comparable treatment with sufficient specificity to permit a response.
members.conclusion: The High Court committed no error in rejecting the claim, and the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The party appealed after a court dismissed its petition challenging an administrative decision.
predicates.discrimination_claim_lacks_comparator_de: The party alleged unequal treatment but did not specify the comparator and the relevant details of that comparator’s treatment.
predicates.claim_not_shown_raised_before_deciding_j: The party did not substantiate that it had raised the discrimination argument before the judge who first decided the petition.
predicates.no_review_sought: The party did not ask the first-instance judge to review the decision for failing to address the alleged argument.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator appointed by a court cannot award relief beyond the claim specified in the court’s reference without a further order of reference.
material_facts: The claimant’s application and plaint sought Rs. 68,582 for additional transport costs and Rs. 25,000 for road construction, for a total claim of Rs. 93,582.
The court referred the matters claimed in the plaint to the arbitrator.
Before the arbitrator, the claimant advanced an additional Rs. 68,582 for transport, beyond the transport claim specified in the plaint and reference.
The arbitrator rejected the road-construction claim but awarded Rs. 1,16,570 for transport.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 20(1) and 20(4) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, when an agreement is filed in court and the court makes an order of reference, the arbitrator’s authority is limited to the relief referred. If the claim is specified in the plaint and the reference is confined to that claim, the arbitrator cannot enlarge the reference or entertain a fresh claim without a further court order. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The arbitrator exceeded the scope of the reference by allowing the additional transport claim. The award could not exceed the specified transport claim of Rs. 68,582.

predicates.court_referred_arbitration: The dispute was referred to an arbitrator by a court order.
predicates.claim_amount_specified: The claimant specified a monetary limit for the claim in the pleading incorporated into the reference.
predicates.additional_claim_outside_reference: The claimant advanced before the arbitrator an additional claim that was not included in the specified claim referred by the court.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator acting under the Arbitration Act, 1940 cannot grant interim relief beyond the reference or the powers conferred by the arbitration agreement.
material_facts: During the arbitration, the arbitrator permitted one party to resume and complete construction, although no specific agreement conferred interim-measure powers on the arbitrator.
The direction affected matters central to the parties’ disputes and was not made with the other party’s consent.
The arbitrator had declined the parties’ request for an interim award on title and had not yet received their claims and counterclaims.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 41(b) and the Second Schedule to the Arbitration Act, 1940, interim injunctions and related measures may be sought from a court in relation to arbitration proceedings; the proviso does not empower an arbitrator unless such power has been conferred. An arbitrator is a tribunal of limited jurisdiction, confined to the agreement and reference, and consent cannot confer jurisdiction that does not exist. The Court relied on The United Commercial Bank Ltd. v. Their Workmen, Hakam Singh v. M/s Gammon (India) Ltd., Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das, and the jurisdictional-nullity principles in Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan and the other cases cited. It contrasted Section 17 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which expressly confers limited interim-measure powers.
members.conclusion: The interim direction was without jurisdiction and was a nullity; it could not provide a basis for sustaining the later award.

rule.if: award_challenge_proceeding and arbitrator_issued_interim_direction and direction_exceeded_reference and no_agreement_authorized_interim_measures

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A party challenged an arbitral award in a proceeding seeking judicial review of the award.
predicates.arbitrator_issued_interim_direction: An arbitrator directed a party to take action while the arbitration was pending.
predicates.direction_exceeded_reference: The direction went beyond the disputes referred to the arbitrator or the subject matter the arbitrator could decide under the agreement.
predicates.no_agreement_authorized_interim_measures: The parties had not agreed to confer on the arbitrator the power used to make the interim direction.

members.legal_issue: A High Court may set aside an acquittal in a private revision and order a retrial only where the acquittal suffers from manifest illegality, a gross miscarriage of justice, or a comparable glaring defect; it may not do so merely by reweighing the evidence.
material_facts: A Sessions Court acquitted the accused after finding the prosecution evidence unsatisfactory and the identity of the assailant doubtful.
A private party sought revision of the acquittal.
The High Court reconsidered the evidence and the Sessions Court’s findings in detail, reached different inferences, set aside the acquittal, and ordered a retrial.
The High Court identified no qualifying defect in the acquittal; apart from a legal error concerning the treatment of defence witnesses’ prior statements, it found no defect of procedure or law.
members.legal_principle: Under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, interference with an acquittal in revision requires manifest illegality or a gross miscarriage of justice, or a defect analogous to a glaring procedural defect, such as lack of jurisdiction, exclusion of admissible material evidence, consideration of inadmissible evidence, or overlooking evidence. The examples are not exhaustive, but ordinary reassessment of evidence, a wrong view of law, or a misapprehension of evidence does not suffice. The Court applied D. Stephens v. Nosibolla, Logendranath Jha v. Shri Polailal Biswas, and K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh.
members.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its revisional jurisdiction by reweighing the evidence as if hearing an appeal. The order for retrial was revoked and the acquittal restored.

rule.if: private_revision_against_acquittal and high_court_reweighed_evidence_de_novo and not manifest_illegality_or_gross_miscarriage and not analogous_glaring_defect

predicates.private_revision_against_acquittal: A private party sought revision of a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.high_court_reweighed_evidence_de_novo: The High Court reconsidered the evidence and reached its own inferences instead of identifying a qualifying defect in the acquittal.
predicates.manifest_illegality_or_gross_miscarriage: The acquittal contains a manifest illegality or results in a gross miscarriage of justice.
predicates.analogous_glaring_defect: The acquittal contains a glaring defect comparable to a serious procedural defect, such as lack of jurisdiction or mishandling material evidence.

members.legal_issue: A High Court may set aside an acquittal in revision when the acquittal rests on compounding an offence that cannot legally be compounded.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after the complainant said he did not wish to proceed and the court treated the offences as compounded.
One of the charged offences was not compoundable, with or without court permission.
members.legal_principle: Under section 345(7) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, an offence may be compounded only as provided by that section. An acquittal based on compounding that is invalid in law may be set aside in revision, as held in K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 412.
members.conclusion: The High Court rightly set aside the acquittal and directed the trial to proceed.

predicates.criminal_revision_of_acquittal: A reviewing court considers a criminal revision against a trial court's acquittal.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_compounding: The trial court acquitted the accused because it treated the offence or offences as compounded.
predicates.at_least_one_offence_not_legally_compoun: At least one offence underlying the acquittal could not legally be compounded.

members.legal_issue: A substantive term of imprisonment is not mandatory for an offence arising from cheque dishonour, and a fine-only sentence may be imposed.
material_facts: The respondent was convicted of cheque dishonour.
The Magistrate imposed a fine payable as compensation without a substantive jail sentence, taking account of money already deposited.
The complainant challenged the sentencing orders, and the proceedings had continued for about fourteen years.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a jail sentence is not mandatory and the sentencing court may impose a fine alone. The Court described the offence as almost in the nature of a civil wrong given criminal overtones, whose gravity is not to be equated with offences under the Indian Penal Code or other criminal offences. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: A substantive jail sentence was not required; imposing a fine alone was within the Magistrate’s discretion. The Court did not disturb that approach, while separately ordering additional compensation with simple imprisonment in default of payment.

predicates.cheque_dishonour_prosecution: A person was prosecuted and convicted for dishonouring a cheque.
predicates.appeal_over_sentence: An appeal concerns the sentence imposed in a cheque-dishonour prosecution.
predicates.fine_only_imposed: The sentencing court imposed a fine without imposing a substantive term of imprisonment.

members.legal_issue: A custodial sentence for a cheque-dishonour offence may be replaced with a fine where the circumstances make a fine an adequate response, while imprisonment may remain as the consequence of default in payment.
material_facts: The conviction concerned a cheque issued to repay part of an advance in a proposed house sale, rather than an out-and-out commercial transaction.
The complainant’s case was that the accused was in financial distress when the proposed sale was arranged.
A substantial period had passed since the transaction, during which the parties’ social and economic circumstances could have changed.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered the circumstances of the transaction, the passage of time, and the proposition in Kaushalya Devi Massand v. Roopkishore Khore, (2011) 4 SCC 593, that the gravity of a complaint under the Negotiable Instruments Act is not equivalent to that of offences under the Indian Penal Code or other criminal offences. It concluded that an enhanced fine would meet the ends of justice, with imprisonment reserved for default.
members.conclusion: The Court restored the conviction but replaced the immediate term of imprisonment and original fine with an enhanced fine, payable within the specified period, with imprisonment in default; part of the fine was ordered as compensation.

rule.if: cheque_dishonour_conviction and transaction_not_commercial and accused_financial_distress and substantial_time_has_passed

predicates.cheque_dishonour_conviction: The accused stands convicted in a prosecution involving a dishonoured cheque.
predicates.transaction_not_commercial: The cheque arose from a transaction that was not an out-and-out commercial transaction.
predicates.accused_financial_distress: The circumstances included the accused being in financial distress in connection with the underlying transaction.
predicates.substantial_time_has_passed: A substantial period passed between the underlying transaction and the sentencing decision.

members.legal_issue: A company incorporated as a separate legal person does not become the property of the Union merely because the Union owns all its shares, so the Union’s constitutional tax immunity does not protect the company’s property.
material_facts: The appellant was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, and its shares were wholly owned by the Union.
The company was assessed in respect of land that it used, although the land itself was owned by the Central Government.
members.legal_principle: Article 285 exempts the property of the Union from State taxation, but does not make a company’s property Union property merely because the Union holds its shares. The Court relied on Western Coalfields Limited v. Special Area Development Authority, Korba, Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, and Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar, which recognize the separate legal personality of an incorporated company and distinguish company property from shareholder property. The Court also referred to New Delhi Municipal Council v. State of Punjab for the absolute character of Article 285’s protection, but held it inapplicable where the property being assessed was not the Union’s property.
members.conclusion: Article 285 did not apply to the company’s property or prevent assessment against it; the company remained a legal entity distinct from the Union.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_immunity_claim and incorporated_company and government_owns_company_shares and company_has_separate_legal_personality

predicates.constitutional_tax_immunity_claim: A party in a tax dispute claims that constitutional immunity for Union property prevents the assessment.
predicates.incorporated_company: The entity whose property or liability is at issue was incorporated as a company.
predicates.government_owns_company_shares: The Union owns all or some of the company’s shares.
predicates.company_has_separate_legal_personality: The company exists as a legal person distinct from its shareholders.

members.legal_issue: Property owned by a separately incorporated company is not exempt from property tax merely because the government owns all of the company’s shares.
material_facts: The companies were incorporated under the Companies Act and owned the lands and buildings at issue.
The government had subscribed the companies’ entire share capital.
The companies claimed exemption on the ground that their property was government property.
members.legal_principle: Article 285(1) of the Constitution and the exemptions in section 127A(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 and section 136 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 concern property of the Union, not property owned by a separate corporate person whose shares the Union owns. The Court relied on Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, Heavy Engineering Mazdoor Union v. State of Bihar, Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation v. Income-tax Officer, and Tamlin v. Hansaford.
members.conclusion: The companies’ property was not exempt as property of the Union merely because the government owned all their shares.

rule.if: tax_demand_appeal and company_owns_taxed_property and government_owns_all_shares and company_has_separate_legal_personality

predicates.tax_demand_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a property-tax demand.
predicates.company_owns_taxed_property: The taxed land or buildings are owned by a company.
predicates.government_owns_all_shares: The government owns the company’s entire share capital.
predicates.company_has_separate_legal_personality: The company is incorporated as a legal person distinct from its shareholders.

members.legal_issue: A transferee landlord may recover pre-transfer rent as rent and rely on that arrearage in seeking eviction when the right to recover the arrears was assigned to the transferee.
material_facts: The predecessor landlord’s communication to the tenants stated that the property and arrears of rent were transferred to the new landlord and directed the tenants to pay the arrears to him.
The new landlord’s notice likewise claimed the pre-transfer rent arrears, and the tenants did not comply.
The tenants had not disputed in their pleadings that the predecessor assigned the right to recover the arrears.
The first appellate court found that the transferee was entitled to recover the pre-transfer arrears, and the Supreme Court inferred an assignment from the communications and that finding.
Including the assigned arrears, the tenants were in default for longer than the period required for eviction under the applicable rent law.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the transferee is ordinarily not entitled to pre-transfer rent arrears unless the right to recover them is assigned. If assigned, the arrears retain their character as rent and can support eviction under the applicable rent law. The Court relied on Satti Krishna Reddy v. Nallamilli Venkata Reddy, which rejected the contrary view in Smt. Daya Debi v. Chapla Debi; it also relied on Girdharilal v. Hukam Singh and N.M. Engineer v. Narendera Singh Virdi. It noted Ramchander Narsey & Co. v. Wamanrao Shenoy and held the single-judge view in Vinayak Mahadeo Nirgum v. Savannas Sanitarium Bandekar inconsistent with the applicable principles. Under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, default exceeding six months on the date the suit is filed permits eviction on that ground.
members.conclusion: Because the right to recover the pre-transfer arrears had been assigned, the transferee could recover them as rent and seek eviction on the ground of default; the tenants’ arrears exceeded the statutory threshold, so the eviction order stood.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and arrears_assigned_to_transferee and assigned_rent_remains_unpaid and arrears_exceed_applicable_eviction_threshold

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction under rent-control law on the ground of non-payment of rent.
predicates.arrears_assigned_to_transferee: The predecessor landlord transferred to the new landlord the right to recover rent arrears that accrued before the transfer.
predicates.assigned_rent_remains_unpaid: The tenant did not pay the assigned rent arrears after the transferee sought payment.
predicates.arrears_exceed_applicable_eviction_thres: The unpaid rent arrears exceed the period of default required to support eviction under the applicable rent law.

members.legal_issue: A transferee may recover rent arrears that accrued before the transfer where a contract to the contrary is embodied in the compromise between the parties.
material_facts: The claim included arrears of rent that accrued before the transfer.
The compromise petition, incorporated into the compromise decree, contained an express arrangement contrary to the ordinary rule against a transferee recovering pre-transfer arrears.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the proviso to Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act, holding that a transferee is ordinarily not entitled to rent arrears due before the transfer unless there is a contract to the contrary. It found such a contract in the compromise petition incorporated into the decree. No earlier cases were cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The transferee was entitled to the pre-transfer arrears under the express arrangement in the compromise.

predicates.rent_claim_after_property_transfer: The proceeding seeks rent after an interest in the property has been transferred.
predicates.arrears_accrued_before_transfer: Some of the rent sought became due before the transfer.
predicates.express_contrary_contract_in_compromise: The parties expressly agreed in a compromise, incorporated into a court decree, that the transferee could recover the earlier arrears.

members.legal_issue: A statutory tenant whose contractual tenancy has ended may grant a valid licence while remaining in possession under statutory protection and before an eviction decree is passed.
material_facts: The original tenant's contractual tenancy had been terminated, but he remained in possession under the protection of rent-control law.
Before his death, he granted two occupants a licence to use part of the premises.
No eviction decree had been passed against him when he granted the licence.
members.legal_principle: A statutory tenant who continues in occupation under rent-control protection and against whom no eviction decree has been passed can create a licence. The Court relied on Chandavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram.
members.conclusion: The licence was legally valid notwithstanding the termination of the contractual tenancy.

rule.if: license_creation_dispute and statutory_tenant_remained_in_possession and no_eviction_decree and license_granted

predicates.license_creation_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a person who granted permission to occupy premises created a valid licence.
predicates.statutory_tenant_remained_in_possession: A tenant whose contractual tenancy had ended continued in possession under statutory protection.
predicates.no_eviction_decree: No decree for eviction had been passed against the tenant when permission to occupy was granted.
predicates.license_granted: The tenant gave another person permission to occupy premises under a licence arrangement.

members.legal_issue: A tenant protected by rent-control legislation may grant a licence before an eviction decree, and a licensee in actual occupation on the statutory date may become a deemed tenant despite a contrary contract or a restriction on transferring the tenancy interest.
material_facts: The subordinate appellate court found that the obstructionist had continuously occupied the premises as a licensee from before the statutory date and was in occupation on that date.
The tenant’s eviction decree was passed after the statutory date, so the tenant’s protected tenancy had not ended when the licence was created or on the statutory date.
The licence was created before the statutory date, and the tenant’s original tenancy terms did not specifically authorize the creation of a licence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15A(1) and 14(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, read together, protect a licensee who was in actual occupation on the statutory date and provide for the licensee to become the landlord’s tenant when the licensor’s tenant interest ends. Section 15(1) restricts later grants of licences, and section 13(1)(e) provides a ground for eviction for unlawful grants after the relevant amendment; those provisions do not defeat the protection for qualifying pre-date licensees. Under sections 52 and 53 of the Indian Easements Act, a licence is a personal privilege, not an interest in property, and its creation is not a transfer of the tenancy interest under section 108(j) of the Transfer of Property Act. A statutorily protected tenant remains in the position of a contractual tenant until an eviction decree is passed and may create a licence before then. The Court relied on Waman Shrinivas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co., V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, and B.M. Lall v. Dunlop Rubber & Co.; it distinguished Ludhichem Agencies v. Ahmed R.V. Peer Mohamed because the licence there was created after the tenant’s interest had ended. It rejected the restrictive construction adopted by the Bombay High Court Full Bench in Ratanlal Chandiprasad Jalan v. Raniram Darkhan. In construing the overriding words of section 15A, the Court also relied on The South India Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Secretary, Board of Revenue, Aswini Kumar Ghosh v. Arabinda Bose, Dominion of India v. Shribai A. Irani, Nokes v. Doncaster Amalgamated Collieries, Heydon’s case, and Becks v. Smith.
members.conclusion: The licensee was entitled to be treated as a tenant under the Act; a tenant protected by statute could grant a licence before an eviction decree, whether or not the tenancy agreement expressly permitted it.

rule.if: rent_control_licensee_protection_claim and licence_created_before_statutory_cutoff and licensee_in_actual_occupation_on_cutoff and licensor_still_tenant_when_licence_created

predicates.rent_control_licensee_protection_claim: A person seeks tenant protection under rent-control law on the basis of occupation as a licensee.
predicates.licence_created_before_statutory_cutoff: The tenant granted the licence before the statutory cutoff for protection of existing licensees.
predicates.licensee_in_actual_occupation_on_cutoff: The licensee was in actual occupation of the premises on the statutory cutoff date.
predicates.licensor_still_tenant_when_licence_creat: The person granting the licence remained a protected tenant and had not yet been evicted by decree when the licence was created.

members.legal_issue: A person invoking public interest jurisdiction must act bona fide and not as a proxy for private or other oblique interests.
material_facts: The applicant brought a challenge to a land lease in the name of public interest, but the Court found material connecting him and the person representing him with a competitor of the lessee.

The applicant’s disclosed financial resources did not explain the substantial litigation expenses, and the claimed donations and the role of an associated society raised questions about the funding of the litigation.
The Court found that the applicant had been set up by others and was a name lender, but nevertheless examined the evidence concerning the land’s status.
members.legal_principle: Public interest standing is available to bona fide litigants, not to persons acting for personal gain, private profit, political motivation, or other oblique considerations. Courts must guard against misuse of public interest litigation by proxies and busybodies. The Court relied on S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary, Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware v. State of Maharashtra, State of Maharashtra v. Prabhu, Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation v. GAR Re-Rolling Mills, and Dr. B.K. Subbarao v. K. Parasaran.
members.conclusion: The application was mala fide and was dismissed with costs for abuse of the process of law.

predicates.public_interest_litigation: A person brings a proceeding asking the court to act in the public interest.
predicates.applicant_is_proxy_for_private_interest: The applicant acts on behalf of another person or interest rather than pursuing the stated public cause independently.
predicates.litigation_funding_is_inconsistent_with_: The costs of pursuing the proceeding substantially exceed the applicant’s disclosed financial means, and the source of support does not credibly explain that gap.
predicates.applicant_has_links_to_private_beneficia: The applicant or the person acting for the applicant has links to a private party that would benefit from the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A petition invoking fundamental-rights jurisdiction in the public interest must be refused when it is a cloak for personal enmity rather than a genuine effort to protect society.
material_facts: A letter alleging environmental harm was treated as a petition invoking the Court’s fundamental-rights jurisdiction on behalf of the public.
The record disclosed a long history of rivalry and animosity between the petitioner and the industrial proprietor.
The allegations were not supported by any complaint from another person or authority, and scrutiny disclosed no fundamental-rights violation.
members.legal_principle: Article 32 is a safeguard for enforcing fundamental rights, including the right to quality of life under Article 21, and may be invoked on behalf of society by a person genuinely interested in its protection. The Court must exercise caution to prevent misuse; a petition that is a cloak for an old grudge or enmity should be refused and its misuse discouraged. The Court referred to Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India for the importance of satisfactory verification of allegations.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the petition was not genuinely founded on public interest, amounted to an abuse of its process, and should be dismissed.

predicates.public_interest_fundamental_rights_petit: A person asks the court to exercise its fundamental-rights jurisdiction in a proceeding presented as being for the public interest.
predicates.personal_grudge_motive: The petitioner’s resort to the court is a cloak for advancing a personal grudge or enmity.
predicates.genuine_societal_interest: The petitioner is genuinely interested in protecting society or the community.

members.legal_issue: A petition invoking public interest jurisdiction must be brought bona fide to address a genuine public wrong, rather than to advance personal, political, publicity-seeking, or other oblique interests.
material_facts: The petitioner described himself as a spokesperson for a political party, and the challenged allotments concerned a company represented by a person active in electoral politics.
The pleadings contained political allegations, and the respondents disputed the petitioner's bona fides.
The Supreme Court did not determine whether the petition was in fact motivated by an improper purpose; it remitted the matter without expressing an opinion on the merits.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing public interest litigation and locus standi stated in The Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary, Kazi Lhendup Dorji v. Central Bureau of Investigation, Ramjas Foundation v. Union of India, K.R. Srinivas v. R.M. Premchand, State of Maharashtra v. Prabhu, Andhra Pradesh State Financial Corporation v. GAR Re-Rolling Mills, Dr. B.K. Subbarao v. K. Parasaran, S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, State of H.P. v. A Parent of a Student of Medical College, Simla, Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of West Bengal, Dr. B. Singh v. Union of India, and Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware v. State of Maharashtra. A public interest proceeding is for enforcing a public or general interest affecting the rights or liabilities of the public or a class of the community. The court should assess the applicant's credentials, the prima facie correctness and specificity of the information, and its gravity and seriousness, while preventing abuse of its process; relaxation of locus standi does not authorize busybodies or persons acting for personal gain, political motivation, or another oblique consideration to litigate as public interest petitioners.
members.conclusion: Courts must scrutinize the credentials and bona fides of a public interest petitioner and the reliability and seriousness of the information presented; a vexatious petition brought for an oblique purpose should be rejected at the threshold. In an exceptional case, a court may pursue a matter of greater public interest without the petitioner, including by appointing an amicus curiae.

predicates.public_interest_proceeding: A person brings a court proceeding claiming to act in the public interest.
predicates.petitioner_has_oblique_motive: The petitioner acts to advance a personal, political, publicity-seeking, or other improper interest rather than a genuine public interest.
predicates.petition_lacks_genuine_public_interest: The proceeding does not seek to address a genuine public wrong or injury affecting the public or a class of the community.

members.legal_issue: A simple repeal of a law that made a second marriage void does not retrospectively validate that marriage or undo its prior legal consequences.
material_facts: The marriage was contracted while a regional law prohibited a person with a living spouse from contracting another marriage and made such a marriage void.
That law was later repealed without an expressed intention to undo the prior operation of the law or liabilities incurred under it.
The dispute concerned inheritance to property left by a party to the second marriage.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(b) and (c) of the Kerala Interpretation and General Clauses Act provides that, absent a different intention, repeal does not affect an enactment's previous operation or liabilities incurred under it. The later enactment effected a simple repeal and expressed no contrary intention; the earlier marriage's void status was therefore not undone.
members.conclusion: The repeal did not validate the marriage, which remained void under the law in force when it was contracted.

rule.if: inheritance_dispute and second_marriage_contracted_during_prior_spouse_lifetime and law_at_marriage_made_second_marriage_void and later_repeal_was_simple and not repeal_expressed_contrary_intention

predicates.inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to inherit property following a person's death.
predicates.second_marriage_contracted_during_prior_: A person contracted another marriage while a prior spouse was living.
predicates.law_at_marriage_made_second_marriage_voi: The law in force when the later marriage was contracted made that marriage void in those circumstances.
predicates.later_repeal_was_simple: The law that made the marriage void was later repealed without replacing that repeal with a new rule governing the prior marriage.
predicates.repeal_expressed_contrary_intention: The repealing enactment stated an intention to undo the earlier law's operation or the consequences of acts under it.
predicates.second_marriage_remains_void: The later marriage continues to be treated as void.

members.legal_issue: The later repeal of a prohibition does not validate a transaction that was void when made under that prohibition.
material_facts: The exchange occurred while the regulation's transfer prohibition was in force.
The exchange was invalid under that prohibition.
The prohibition was repealed later.
members.legal_principle: The court held that repeal of sections 27 and 28 by the Santal Tenancy (Supplementary Provisions) Act, 1949, could not render a transaction that was invalid and void when made into a valid and binding transaction.
members.conclusion: The later repeal did not make the previously invalid exchange valid or binding.

predicates.transfer_prohibition_in_force_when_trans: A legal prohibition on the transfer was in force when the transaction occurred.
predicates.transaction_void_under_prohibition: The transaction was void under the prohibition when it occurred.
predicates.prohibition_later_repealed: The prohibition was repealed after the transaction occurred.

members.legal_issue: A further revision under the general civil procedure code is unavailable after the revision route provided by a rent-control statute has been used and the statute makes the matter final subject to that route.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought under a rent-control statute that provided an appeal and a designated revision from the appellate authority’s decision.
The appellate authority was a subordinate judge, so the statutory revision lay to the district court.
After the district court dismissed the statutory revision, the landlord sought a further revision in the High Court under the general civil procedure code.
The High Court entertained that further revision, set aside the decisions below, and ordered eviction.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 18(5) and 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, a decision is final and cannot be called in question except through the revision provided by section 20. Read together, those provisions exclude a second revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure after the designated statutory revision has been decided. The statutory scheme provides its own tier of courts and requires finality; it does not contemplate two revisions. The Court relied on Kydd v. Watch Committee of City of Liverpool, South Asia Industries Private Ltd. v. S.B. Sarup Singh and Others, and Vishesh Kumar v. Shanti Prasad; distinguished Maung Ba Thaw and Another—Insolvents v. Ma Pin; approved Kurien v. Chacko; and overruled Ouseph Vareed v. Mary.
members.conclusion: The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure; its judgment and order were set aside.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A party brought an eviction proceeding under a statute governing rent-controlled premises.
predicates.statute_limits_challenge_to_designated_r: The governing statute makes the decision final subject to a specified revision and does not provide for a further revision after that route.
predicates.designated_revision_already_decided: The party pursued the specified revision, and the reviewing court decided it.
predicates.further_challenge_sought_under_general_c: After the specified revision was decided, a party sought another revision under the general civil procedure code.

members.legal_issue: A further revision under the general civil procedure law does not lie against a district court’s revision order in the rent-control procedure where the governing statutory scheme makes the appellate decision challengeable only through the statutory revision.
material_facts: The proceedings concerned claims for eviction under a rent-control statute that provided for an initial decision, an appeal, and, in specified cases, revision by the District Court.
The District Court exercised that statutory revisional jurisdiction, after which the High Court entertained further revisions under the general civil procedure law.

The rent-control statute made the appellate decision final and not challengeable in any court except as provided by its revision provision; the revisional authority could examine legality, regularity, or propriety and could remand a case.
A different state’s rent-control statute had materially different provisions, and a prior decision allowing a further revision under that statute was also considered.
members.legal_principle: Sections 18(5), 20(1), and 20A of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, read together, make the statutory revision the permitted means of challenging the appellate decision and exclude a second revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the District Court’s revisional order. The breadth of the statutory revisional power, the power to remand, and the scheme’s provision of trial, appeal, and revision support that construction. Aundal Ammal v. Sadasivan Pillai is reaffirmed; Vishesh Kumar v. Shanti Prasad supports construing the scheme to advance its purpose and avoid defeating the legislative allocation of revisional jurisdiction. Shyamaraju Hegde v. G. Venkatesha Bhatt concerns materially different Karnataka provisions and creates no conflict.
members.conclusion: A further revision to the High Court under the general civil procedure law was unavailable against the District Court’s revisional order under the Kerala rent-control statute. The High Court’s orders in the appeals were set aside and the District Court’s revisional orders restored. The decision allowing further revision under the materially different Karnataka statute did not conflict with this result, and the earlier ruling on the Kerala statute was reaffirmed.

predicates.rent_control_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a dispute governed by a statutory rent-control process.
predicates.district_court_exercised_statutory_revis: A District Court reviewed an order through the revision procedure provided by the rent-control process.
predicates.appellate_decision_final_except_through_: The governing scheme makes the appellate decision final and permits it to be challenged only through the specified statutory revision.
predicates.statutory_revision_includes_review_of_le: The statutory revisional authority may examine the legality, regularity, or propriety of the order under review.

members.legal_issue: Surviving appellants may continue an appeal on the basis that the deceased appellant's right survived to them alone only when that basis is established.
material_facts: An appellant died while the appeal was pending, and no application to substitute his legal representatives was made within the prescribed time.
The appellants were given an opportunity to provide evidence that they and the deceased formed a joint Hindu family, but their affidavits did not assert that fact.
The application to substitute the deceased appellant's sons described them as his heirs and legal representatives.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXII, Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an action may continue against or by the surviving parties when the right to sue survives to them alone. Where that condition is not established and a party dies during an appeal, Order XXII, Rules 3 and 11 govern abatement and the need to bring legal representatives on the record within the prescribed time.
members.conclusion: The joint-family relationship was not proved, so the surviving appellants could not continue the appeal on the basis that the right to appeal survived to them alone under Order XXII, Rule 2.

rule.if: appeal_pending and appellant_died and substitution_not_timely and joint_family_not_proved

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal was pending when one of its appellants died.
predicates.appellant_died: A party to the appeal died during its pendency.
predicates.substitution_not_timely: The deceased party's legal representatives were not brought on the record within the prescribed time.
predicates.joint_family_not_proved: The surviving parties did not establish that they and the deceased party formed a joint family such that the right survived to them alone.
predicates.survivors_cannot_continue_on_survival_of: The surviving parties cannot continue the appeal on the basis that the right survived to them alone.

members.legal_issue: Surviving co-defendants with an independent interest may prosecute an appeal from a joint decree resting on a ground common to them, even if another appellant dies during the appeal.
material_facts: The landlord obtained an eviction decree against several defendants who were in possession of the premises, on the common ground of personal requirement.
The defendants appealed jointly, and two co-defendants remained alive after the tenant died during the appeal.
The allegation that the tenant had sublet the premises was not pursued, and the eviction decree did not rest on subletting.
members.legal_principle: Order XLI rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits any one of multiple defendants to appeal from the whole decree when it rests on a ground common to them, and permits the appellate court to vary or reverse the decree in favour of all. Because the decree was joint and indivisible, dismissing the appeal could also risk inconsistent decrees. The Court did not need to decide whether the deceased tenant’s heirs had a surviving interest. The High Court’s reliance on Anand Nivas Private Ltd. v. Anandji Kalvanji Pedhi did not remove the surviving co-defendants’ independent right to appeal.
members.conclusion: The appeal could not be dismissed merely because the tenant died or his heirs lacked a surviving cause of action. The surviving co-defendants had a substantial interest in prosecuting it, and the appellate courts should have heard the appeal on its merits.

predicates.appeal_from_joint_decree: The proceeding is an appeal by defendants from a decree made against them jointly.
predicates.decree_based_on_common_ground: The decree rests on a ground common to the defendants appealing together.
predicates.surviving_coappellants_have_substantial_: One or more appellants remain alive and have a substantial interest in challenging the decree.

members.legal_issue: An authority that lacks jurisdiction cannot initiate a valid assessment by notice, and another authority cannot rely on the resulting return after the proceeding is set aside for want of jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Sub-Divisional Officer issued the notice requiring a return and received the assessee’s return in response.
The Sub-Divisional Officer found that the assessee’s gross agricultural income exceeded the limit for that officer’s jurisdiction.
The assessment proceeding was set aside as unauthorized, and the governing scheme provided no procedure for transferring the proceeding to the Collector.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(6), 14 and 15(3) of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, the power to issue the special notice belonged to an assessing authority authorized to assess the income. Where assessment proceedings begun on a return made in response to an invalid notice are set aside for want of jurisdiction, the entire proceeding is vacated, and another authority cannot rely on that return. The Act and Rules provided no procedure for transferring such proceedings from the Sub-Divisional Officer to the Collector. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Sub-Divisional Officer’s notice was unauthorized and was treated as quashed; the proceeding was vacated, and the Collector could not make an assessment based on the return filed in response to that notice.

rule.if: is_tax_assessment_proceeding and notice_issued_by_unauthorized_officer and return_filed_in_response_to_that_notice and assessment_set_aside_for_lack_of_jurisdiction

predicates.is_tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding is one to assess tax.
predicates.notice_issued_by_unauthorized_officer: The notice requiring a return was issued by an officer who lacked authority to assess the income concerned.
predicates.return_filed_in_response_to_that_notice: The assessee filed the return in response to that officer’s notice.
predicates.assessment_set_aside_for_lack_of_jurisdi: The assessment proceeding was set aside because the assessing officer lacked jurisdiction.
predicates.another_authority_cannot_assess_on_that_: A different authority cannot base an assessment on the return filed in response to the unauthorized notice.

members.legal_issue: A general notice to file a return does not permit an authority to begin a fresh assessment using a return filed with another authority in response to an invalid special notice.
material_facts: The Court assumed that a general notice had been issued by the Collector.
The assessee filed the return in response to a special notice issued by the Sub-Divisional Officer, not to the Collector.
The special notice and proceeding were unauthorized because the Sub-Divisional Officer lacked jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Sections 15(1) and 15(3) of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, provide distinct routes for requiring a return. A general notice does not make a return filed with another authority in response to an unauthorized special notice a return to the Collector; the Collector must issue the required notice before commencing assessment. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The Collector could not rely on the assumed general notice to begin fresh assessment proceedings on a return that had not been made to the Collector in response to that notice.

predicates.is_fresh_tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding is a fresh attempt to assess tax.
predicates.general_return_notice_was_issued: A general notice requiring returns was issued by the authority proposing to assess.
predicates.return_was_filed_with_another_authority_: The return was filed with a different authority in response to a special notice that was invalid.
predicates.general_notice_cannot_support_assessment: The general notice cannot support an assessment based on that return.

members.legal_issue: A statutory requirement to pay land-acquisition compensation in instalments is unreasonable and violates equality guarantees when the owner needs compensation in place of the land taken.
material_facts: The scheme required compensation above a small threshold to be paid in equal annual instalments rather than as a lump sum.
The Court considered that an owner would need compensation promptly to establish a new residence, acquire other agricultural land, or otherwise re-establish themselves.
The instalment requirement could be severed without invalidating the rest of the scheme.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits statutory provisions that are arbitrary or unreasonable. The Court held that delaying compensation through instalments was wholly unreasonable because an owner needs compensation in place of the land to re-establish themselves. The provision was severable, so only the instalment requirement was struck down.
members.conclusion: The provision requiring payment of compensation in instalments was unconstitutional under Article 14 and was severed; compensation had to be paid in a lump sum.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compensation: A constitutional challenge concerns the method by which compensation for acquired land is paid.
predicates.compensation_is_paid_in_installments: The law requires compensation to be paid in multiple payments over time rather than in a lump sum.
predicates.owner_needs_prompt_substitute_compensati: The owner needs the compensation promptly to obtain a substitute residence, land, or other means of re-establishing themselves.

members.legal_issue: Requiring compensation for acquired land to be paid in instalments rather than promptly in a lump sum is unreasonable under the equality guarantee.
material_facts: The scheme required compensation above a specified threshold to be paid in equal annual instalments instead of in a lump sum.
The owner or another interested person could need the compensation promptly to obtain a new residence, agricultural land, or another means of re-establishing themselves.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 invalidates a provision that is unreasonable in its effect on landowners. A person whose land is taken may need compensation forthwith to re-establish themselves, making compulsory deferred payment by instalments unreasonable.
members.conclusion: The requirement to pay compensation in instalments was unconstitutional; the compensation had to be payable in a lump sum.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: A party challenges a rule governing payment for land taken through compulsory acquisition.
predicates.compensation_is_paid_in_instalments: The acquisition regime requires the compensation to be paid in separate instalments rather than in a lump sum.
predicates.landowner_needs_compensation_to_reestabl: The landowner may need the compensation promptly to obtain a new residence, land, or another means of re-establishing themselves.

members.legal_issue: A special acquisition scheme applies to acquisition proceedings for its stated purpose that began under the general acquisition law before the special scheme commenced, provided no award had been made before the special scheme applied.
material_facts: The special scheme expressly applied to earlier proceedings for its stated welfare purpose where no award had been made before the special scheme commenced.
The Court noted that the earlier judgment striking down the special scheme had not been stayed and that proceedings might have been revived and completed in the meantime.
The Court clarified that the special scheme would have no effect in cases where awards had already been made.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the transitional provision governing pending acquisition proceedings, read with the provision making the special scheme the exclusive means of acquisition for the specified purpose. It clarified that the transitional provision could not affect cases in which awards had already been made.
members.conclusion: The special scheme applied to qualifying pending proceedings, but did not affect cases in which an award had already been made.

predicates.acquisition_proceeding_for_covered_welfa: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land for a welfare purpose covered by the special scheme.
predicates.proceeding_started_before_special_scheme: The acquisition proceeding began under the general acquisition process before the special scheme commenced.
predicates.no_award_made_before_special_scheme_appl: No award had been made in the proceeding before the special scheme applied to it.

members.legal_issue: A special acquisition regime may apply to earlier proceedings commenced under the general acquisition law for the specified welfare purpose if no award had been made before the special regime took effect, but it does not undo an award already made.
material_facts: Proceedings had been started under the general acquisition law to acquire land for the welfare scheme before the special acquisition law commenced.
The special law provided for its application to such pending proceedings, subject to publication of a notice that the land was required for the specified purpose.
The Court noted that some earlier proceedings might have been completed and awards made before its decision, and clarified that the special law would have no effect in those cases.
members.legal_principle: The application of a new acquisition regime to pending proceedings is not unreasonable where the former regime ceases to govern acquisitions for the specified purpose and the new regime requires its own notice. The special law’s pending-case provision does not affect cases in which an award has already been made.
members.conclusion: Applying the special law to pending proceedings in which no award had been made was not unreasonable, but the law did not affect cases in which an award had already been made.

predicates.pending_acquisition_proceeding_for_a_spe: An acquisition proceeding for a specified welfare purpose remains pending when a new acquisition regime takes effect.
predicates.proceeding_started_under_an_earlier_acqu: The pending proceeding began under an acquisition regime that preceded the new one.
predicates.no_award_was_made_before_the_new_regime_: No award had been made in the proceeding before the new regime was applied.
predicates.required_new_notice_is_published: The acquiring authority publishes the notice required to bring the land within the new regime.

members.legal_issue: A business conducted by a member of a Hindu joint family is not joint family property merely because its proprietor is a family member or manager.
material_facts: The business was started by one family member after he took over a pre-existing business and its assets in his own right.
The other family members had little income and the family lacked sufficient funds to contribute to the business when it began.
The courts below found no evidence that joint family property or funds assisted the business or that the business was treated as a family business.
Documents and correspondence generally described the person who started the business as its proprietor.
members.legal_principle: Hindu law creates no presumption that a business standing in a family member’s name is a joint family business, even if that member manages the family. The party asserting joint family character must establish assistance from joint family property or funds, or blending of the business earnings with the joint family estate; whether such assistance or treatment occurred is a question of fact. The Court relied on Bhuru Mal v. Jagannath, AIR 1943 PC 40; Pearey Lai v. Nanak Chand, AIR 1948 PC 108; and Chattanatha Karayalar v. Ramachandra Iyer, AIR 1955 SC 799.
members.conclusion: The business was the separate business of its proprietor, not a joint family business, and the claim to partition its assets was rejected.

predicates.business_claimed_as_joint_family_propert: A party claims that a business conducted by a family member belongs to the joint family.
predicates.no_joint_family_funds_assisted_business: Joint family property or funds did not assist in starting or carrying on the business.
predicates.business_earnings_not_blended_with_famil: The business earnings were not blended with the joint family estate.

members.legal_issue: A business started by a father is not presumed to be a joint-family business merely because he is the father or manager of the family.
material_facts: The appellant’s father started a new business involving a government contract for felling and transporting timber.
The Tribunal found that the business was a new venture but treated the father’s status as a basis for presuming that the business belonged to the joint family.
The Tribunal did not assess the evidence bearing on whether the father entered the contract for himself or on behalf of the family.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, there is no presumption that a business standing in the name of a family member is joint-family business, even if that member is the manager or father. The father’s debts from a newly started trade may bind his sons under the doctrine of pious obligation, unlike a manager’s debts absent necessity, but that does not make the trade itself a joint-family concern. The Court referred to Ram Nath v. Chiranji Lal, Chhotey Lal v. Dalip Narain Singh, and Hayat Ali Shah v. Nem Chand for the distinction concerning debts. Sections 7(d) and 9(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, make the relevant disqualification depend on the contract being entered into by or on behalf of a joint family, subject to the stated separate-business exception.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal applied an erroneous presumption; the father’s position did not, by itself, establish that the business or contract was a joint-family concern.

predicates.family_business_ownership_dispute: A dispute concerns whether a business or contract belongs to a joint family.
predicates.business_started_by_family_father: The father of family members started the business or venture under consideration.

members.legal_issue: The required inquiry and procedural safeguards for acquisition of land for a company must be completed before a declaration of acquisition is made.
material_facts: The acquisition was pursued for a society treated as a company under the acquisition law.
The High Court found that the Collector's Rule 4 inquiry report had not been forwarded to the Land Acquisition Committee and that the required consultation and consideration had not occurred.
The High Court also found that landowners had not been given a proper opportunity to contest relevant aspects of the company's case.
members.legal_principle: Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 requires inquiry into the company's efforts to find suitable land and negotiate a reasonable price, the suitability and extent of the land, its prospective use, and, where relevant, agricultural considerations. The Collector must give the company a reasonable opportunity to make representations and afford landowners a sufficient opportunity to contest relevant matters. The Government must consult the Committee and consider the required reports, and no declaration may be made before the agreement under Section 41 is executed. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Patel Chaturbhai Narsibhai, State of Gujarat v. Ambalal Haiderbhai, and General Government Servants Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. Wahab Uddin.
members.conclusion: The Rule 4 requirements are mandatory, including the Collector's inquiry and report, consultation with the Committee, consideration of the required reports, and execution of the agreement before a declaration is made.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns State acquisition of land.
predicates.acquisition_sought_for_company: The land is sought through acquisition for a company or an entity treated as a company for acquisition purposes.
predicates.declaration_proposed: The Government is considering making the formal declaration that the land is needed for the proposed purpose.

members.legal_issue: The prescribed inquiry and related safeguards for acquisition for a company are mandatory and must be completed before the acquisition declaration, although the inquiry need not precede the initial acquisition notification.
material_facts: The land was agricultural land.
The acquisition was for a company and was governed by the company-acquisition procedure.
The State did not comply with the required inquiry and related steps before making the declaration.
The applicable procedure required consideration of the Collector’s report, consultation with the committee, and execution of the agreement before the declaration.
members.legal_principle: Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, made under Section 55 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is mandatory. Under Rule 4, the Collector must inquire into the specified matters, including the suitability and extent of the land, efforts to obtain it by negotiation, and whether alternative sites can avoid acquiring good agricultural land; the company must have a reasonable opportunity to participate. Before a declaration, the Government must consider the inquiry report and consult the committee, and the company must execute the agreement under Section 41. The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Patel Chaturbhai Narsibhai, General Government Servants Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. Wahab Uddin, M/s Fomento Resorts and Hotels Ltd. v. Gustavo Ranato Da Cruz Pinto, and Abdul Husein Tayabali v. State of Gujarat. It held that Rule 4 need not be complied with before the initial notification, but its requirements must be met before the declaration.
members.conclusion: The failure to comply with the mandatory company-acquisition procedure made the acquisition invalid; the required inquiry need not, however, precede the initial notification.

predicates.company_acquisition_challenge: Landowners challenged an acquisition made at a company’s request.
predicates.required_company_inquiry_omitted: The authorities failed to carry out the required inquiry into the company’s land needs, alternatives, negotiation efforts, or other prescribed matters.
predicates.declaration_made_without_required_predec: The authorities made the acquisition declaration without completing the required report consideration, committee consultation, or agreement steps.

members.legal_issue: A claim that some accused were not identified is not a basis for excluding them where the first information report names them and eyewitnesses repeat those identifications in court.
material_facts: The first information report named all the accused as participants in the attack.
The eyewitnesses identified the accused in their trial testimony, and the Supreme Court found their accounts cogent and reliable.
The defence argued that some accused had not been named, but the record did not support that contention.
members.legal_principle: The identification of accused persons in the first information report and reliable repetition of those identifications in court may defeat a claim that particular accused were not named. The Court applied this principle to the evidence in the record and cited no earlier case by name.
members.conclusion: The Court rejected the claim that some accused should be acquitted because their names were absent from the first information report or the trial testimony.

rule.if: criminal_group_attack_case and accused_were_named_in_initial_report and eyewitnesses_identified_them_in_court and identifications_were_reliable

predicates.criminal_group_attack_case: The criminal proceeding concerns the identity of accused persons alleged to have participated in a group attack.
predicates.accused_were_named_in_initial_report: The accused persons were named in the initial report of the occurrence.
predicates.eyewitnesses_identified_them_in_court: Eyewitnesses identified the accused persons in their testimony at trial.
predicates.identifications_were_reliable: The identifications were found cogent and reliable.

members.legal_issue: Failure to state an accused’s proper name in the first information report does not invalidate identification when the report describes the person and witnesses who know the person identify them.
material_facts: The first information report described the alleged shooter by his relationship to another accused and by distinctive physical characteristics rather than by his proper name.
The eyewitnesses knew the person and identified him in court.
The courts found no reason for the witnesses to falsely implicate him.
members.legal_principle: Identification may be accepted where the report sufficiently describes the person and witnesses familiar with that person identify them; omission of the proper name alone does not require rejection of the evidence.
members.conclusion: The absence of the accused’s proper name from the first information report did not justify rejecting the eyewitness identifications.

rule.if: criminal_trial and accused_not_named_properly_in_initial_report and accused_described_in_report and known_witnesses_identify_accused

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial for an alleged offence.
predicates.accused_not_named_properly_in_initial_re: The accused’s proper name was omitted from the initial report.
predicates.accused_described_in_report: The initial report described the accused by other identifying details.
predicates.known_witnesses_identify_accused: Witnesses who knew the accused identified that person as involved in the occurrence.

members.legal_issue: A sale deed is not inadmissible merely because its vendor, vendee, or attesting witness was not examined, although the transaction may still be rejected as sham or mala fide on other grounds.
material_facts: A lower court rejected sale deeds because neither a party to the transactions nor an attesting witness testified to prove them.
The Supreme Court held that the earlier authority relied on for that requirement had been overruled by a Constitution Bench.
The Supreme Court separately found that the transactions could be rejected on the evidence of collusion and lack of bona fides.
members.legal_principle: Cement Corporation of India v. Purya overruled A.P. State Road Transport Corporation, Hyderabad v. P. Venkaiah. A certified copy of a sale transaction may be accepted without examining the parties, but State of Haryana v. Ram Singh confirms that the transaction itself may still be rejected as mala fide or sham when that challenge is before the court.
members.conclusion: The sale deeds could not be excluded solely for want of testimony from a vendor, vendee, or attesting witness; that did not prevent their rejection on independent grounds.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding concerns the valuation of land compulsorily acquired for compensation.
predicates.sale_deed_documentary_evidence_present: Documentary evidence of a sale transaction has been produced for valuation.
predicates.transaction_parties_not_examined: The vendor, vendee, and any attesting witness to the transaction have not testified.

members.legal_issue: A transfer supported by a sale deed is not a sham merely because the purchaser may not have acted in good faith.
material_facts: The plaintiff alleged that the purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser and that the sale was intended to complicate the dispute.
The amended pleading did not allege that the sale deed was a sham transaction.
The sale deed was executed in favour of the purchaser, and the Court distinguished a sham transaction, which conveys no title, from a transaction in which the purchaser’s good faith is disputed.
members.legal_principle: A sham transaction and a sale that is not bona fide are different: a sham transaction conveys no title, whereas a non-bona-fide purchaser may still acquire title. The Court considered the distinction between a sham transaction and the bona-fide-purchaser question arising under Section 19(1)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in characterising the sale as a sham transaction; the sale deed conveyed title, and the alleged absence of bona fides was a distinct issue.

predicates.sale_deed_executed: A sale deed was executed in favour of the purchaser.
predicates.sham_transaction_not_pleaded: The claimant did not plead that the transaction was a sham.
predicates.only_purchaser_good_faith_disputed: The dispute concerned the purchaser’s good faith rather than whether the parties intended any sale at all.

members.legal_issue: A caretaker or agent who holds property on behalf of its owner has no independent possessory right to maintain an injunction suit against that owner.
material_facts: The claimant had established title to the property through the pleadings and documents, including records of the proceedings in which the property was acquired.
The opposing occupant did not claim title and failed to prove the alleged family arrangement under which he said he was entitled to occupy the property.
The property had been entrusted to the occupant to look after it while the owner was away, and the occupant was acting as a caretaker.
The occupant sued for an injunction against the title-holder.
members.legal_principle: A caretaker, agent or servant holds property on behalf of the principal and acquires no independent right or interest in it, regardless of the length of the occupation. Such an occupant cannot maintain a suit against the principal on the basis of that possession. The Court relied on Puran Singh v. The State of Punjab (1975) 4 SCC 518 and Mahabir Prasad Jain v. Ganga Singh (1999) 8 SCC 274, and applied the principles in Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu (2004) 1 SCC 769 and Southern Roadways Ltd. v. S.M. Krishnan (1989) 4 SCC 603.
members.conclusion: The caretaker's injunction suit against the true owner was not maintainable, and the caretaker was required to hand over possession on demand.

predicates.caretaker_or_agent_occupation: The occupant entered or remained in the property as a caretaker or agent holding it on behalf of another person.
predicates.owner_has_established_title: The person seeking possession established title to the property.
predicates.injunction_suit_against_owner: The occupant brought an injunction suit against the person who established title.

members.legal_issue: A watchman or caretaker who occupies property only on behalf of its owner does not acquire an independent right to the property through continued occupation and cannot resist the owner’s demand for possession on that basis.
material_facts: The property was owned by the society and had been dedicated for a community purpose.
The occupant’s father was employed by the society as a watchman and was permitted to live on the premises in that capacity.
After his father’s death, the occupant continued to serve as a watchman and remained in the premises with the society’s permission.
The occupant claimed adverse possession, but the Court found that the claim was not proved and that documents such as ration cards and house-tax receipts did not establish it.
members.legal_principle: A watchman, caretaker, servant or agent holding property for the principal acquires no right or interest in it merely through long occupation and must hand over possession when required. Courts should not protect such occupation against the lawful owner. The Court relied on Alagi Alamelu Achi v. Ponniah Mudaliar, AIR 1962 Madras 149, and the principles stated in Maria Margarida Sequeria Fernandes v. Erasmo Jack de Sequeria, (2012) 3 SCALE 550. It also noted that injunctions ordinarily depend on a prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury.
members.conclusion: The occupant had no independent right or interest in the property, including by adverse possession, and was not entitled to an injunction protecting his occupation against the owner. The appeals were dismissed and he was directed to vacate and hand over possession.

rule.if: civil_property_possession_dispute and owner_title_established and occupant_entered_as_watchman_or_caretaker and not independent_right_to_occupy_proved

predicates.civil_property_possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns a civil claim to possession of property.
predicates.owner_title_established: The person seeking possession has established legal title to the property.
predicates.occupant_entered_as_watchman_or_caretake: The occupant entered or remained on the property to look after it on behalf of its owner.
predicates.independent_right_to_occupy_proved: The occupant has proved a legal basis for occupation independent of the watchman or caretaker role.

members.legal_issue: Courts in civil proceedings must actively pursue the truth and use available procedural powers to obtain relevant evidence needed for a just decision.
material_facts: The dispute concerned competing accounts of ownership, possession and the basis on which the occupant entered and remained in the property.
The Court found that the lower courts had failed to properly assess the pleadings and documents relevant to those matters.
The Code of Civil Procedure provides courts with powers concerning discovery, interrogatories, production of documents, summonses and proof by affidavit.
members.legal_principle: Truth is the foundation of justice, and courts have a duty to seek it through an active but legally bounded role in proceedings. Section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides powers for discovery and production of evidence. The Court relied on Mohanlal Shamji Soni v. Union of India, 1991 Supp (1) SCC 271, Ritesh Tewari v.
