members.legal_principle: A preliminary administrative step that does not finally determine rights or obligations ordinarily does not furnish a basis for a writ petition; where the decision-making process remains tentative and a party has been invited to respond, the party should be heard before challenging the eventual decision. The Court referred to the proposed hearing under Rule 26(1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, but relied on no earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was premature and should not have been allowed to proceed against the interdepartmental communication.

rule.if: writ_petition_challenges_preliminary_administrative_step and internal_communication_is_not_final and no_final_government_decision and show_cause_process_is_pending

predicates.writ_petition_challenges_preliminary_adm: A party has brought a writ petition challenging an administrative step taken before the relevant government decision is final.
predicates.internal_communication_is_not_final: The challenged communication is an internal administrative communication that does not itself finally determine the party's rights or obligations.
predicates.no_final_government_decision: The government has not made a final decision on the proposed action.
predicates.show_cause_process_is_pending: The government has issued a notice inviting the affected party to respond before deciding whether to take the proposed action.

members.legal_issue: A writ petition challenging a preliminary notification proposing an area’s inclusion within a local authority’s limits is premature when no final notification has been issued and the proposal has not affected the petitioners’ rights.
material_facts: The State issued a notification proposing to include certain areas within the limits of a town panchayat.
Residents alleged that their objections to the proposal had not been considered and filed a writ petition under Article 226.
No final notification including the areas had been issued when the appeal was heard.
The preliminary notification had not affected the petitioners’ rights.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a challenge to a preliminary notification proposing inclusion of areas within a town panchayat is premature where no final notification has been issued and the proposal has not affected the petitioners’ rights. The notification was issued under Section 349 read with Section 4 of the Karnataka Municipalities Act, 1964. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The writ petition was premature and ought not to have been entertained; a decision on the preliminary notification was unnecessary. The High Court’s judgment was modified accordingly.

predicates.writ_petition_challenges_proposed_area_i: The petitioners filed a writ petition challenging a notification proposing to include areas within a local authority’s limits.
predicates.no_final_inclusion_notification_issued: No final notification including the proposed areas had been issued.
predicates.proposal_has_not_affected_petitioners_ri: The preliminary proposal had not affected the petitioners’ rights.

members.legal_issue: Municipal house and water taxes paid by a lessor are deductible from the annual value of property as annual charges that are not capital charges to which the property is subject.
material_facts: The dispute arose in an income-tax assessment concerning income from property.
House tax and water tax were imposed by a municipality on the annual value of buildings or land.
The owner paid the taxes as lessor because the property was let.
The municipal law made sums due for these taxes a first charge on the property.
The relevant municipal tax provisions were substantially similar to those considered in an earlier Supreme Court decision.
members.legal_principle: Section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 permits deduction from annual value of annual charges that are not capital charges to which the property is subject. The Court applied this provision, read with section 9(1) and (2), to municipal taxes imposed under sections 128 and 149 of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, noting the first charge created by section 177. It followed New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay ([1950] S.C.R. 553).
members.conclusion: The house tax and water tax were deductible from the bona fide annual value of the property; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: property_income_tax_assessment and municipal_taxes_based_on_annual_value and lessor_liable_for_taxes and taxes_are_noncapital_charges_on_property

predicates.property_income_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns the assessment of income from property for income-tax purposes.
predicates.municipal_taxes_based_on_annual_value: A municipality imposes taxes on property by reference to its annual value.
predicates.lessor_liable_for_taxes: The owner pays the taxes because the property is let and the owner is liable for them as lessor.
predicates.taxes_are_noncapital_charges_on_property: The taxes are recurring, non-capital charges to which the property is subject.

members.legal_issue: Municipal property tax and urban immoveable property tax imposed as recurring annual liabilities secured on property are deductible in computing income from that property as annual charges that are not capital charges.
material_facts: The assessee derived income from property and claimed deductions for municipal property tax and urban immoveable property tax paid during the relevant year.
The taxes were levied annually on the annual value of the property, with the annual liability payable in half-yearly instalments.
The governing enactments made the property a statutory security for payment of the taxes.
The High Court answered against deduction, and the assessee appealed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, an annual charge means a charge securing an annual liability, while a capital charge means a charge securing a liability of a capital nature. A recurring annual liability does not cease to be annual because it is payable in instalments or varies in amount. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. Mahomedbhoy Rowji for the meaning of annual charge, while rejecting its conclusion on deductibility; it approved Gappumal Kanhaiya Lal v. Commissioner of Income-tax. It also relied on Moss Empires Ltd. v. Inland Revenue Commissioners and Cunard’s Trustees v. Inland Revenue Commissioners for the principle that variability or contingency does not prevent a payment from being annual. The statutory provisions creating the municipal tax and its property charge were sections 143, 146, 154, 156, 167, 197 and 212 of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888; the urban tax and its property security arose under sections 22 and 24(2)(b) of the Bombay Finance Act, 1932. Bijoy Singh Dudhuria v. Commissioner of Income-tax was discussed as background to the amendment adding the annual-charge deduction. The separate allowance for land revenue under section 9(1)(v) did not exclude taxes that otherwise fell within section 9(1)(iv).
members.conclusion: Both taxes qualify as annual charges that are not capital charges, and their amounts are deductible in computing income from property under section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act.

rule.if: property_income_tax_computation and tax_is_an_annual_property_levy and property_secures_payment_of_tax and not tax_secures_a_capital_liability

predicates.property_income_tax_computation: The assessment concerns income derived from property and the computation of that income for tax purposes.
predicates.tax_is_an_annual_property_levy: The tax is imposed recurrently on the annual value of the property, even if payable in instalments.
predicates.property_secures_payment_of_tax: The law makes the property security for payment of the tax.
predicates.tax_secures_a_capital_liability: The tax charge secures discharge of a liability of a capital nature.
predicates.annual_property_tax_is_deductible: The annual property tax is deductible in computing income from the property.

members.legal_issue: Statutory interim maintenance allowances paid while compensation for the loss of a property interest is being determined are income rather than capital receipts when they are distinct from the compensation.
material_facts: Payments called interim maintenance allowances were made under a regulation after the Jagir’s income began to be collected by the government and before the commutation terms were determined.
The allowances were recurring and measured by reference to current Jagir income, while the separate commutation sum was calculated by reference to annual revenue.
The regulations treated the allowances as ending when the terms of commutation were determined and distinguished them from the commutation sum.
The allowances compensated for the loss of income during the interim period, rather than for the loss of the Jagir itself.
members.legal_principle: Under the Income-tax Act, 1922, the character of the receipts is determined from the regulations creating them. Sections 10, 11 and 14 of the Hyderabad (Abolition of Jagirs) Regulation, 1358F, and sections 3, 4 and 7(2) of the Hyderabad Jagirs (Commutation) Regulation, 1359F, distinguish recurring interim allowances from the capital commutation sum. The Court applied Commissioner of Income-tax v. Shaw Wallace & Co. (recurrence and regularity as characteristics of income) and approved the analysis in Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Butterley & Co. Ltd., under which statutory interim payments may be sui generis income-compensation, arising from the statute rather than from property, investment or the right to compensation.
members.conclusion: Interim maintenance allowances that do not form part of the commutation amount are income and liable to tax.

rule.if: income_tax_classification_proceeding and statutory_interim_allowance and recurring_payment and allowance_compensates_interim_income_loss and not part_of_commutation

predicates.income_tax_classification_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a receipt is taxable as income.
predicates.statutory_interim_allowance: A statute creates a payment described as an interim maintenance allowance pending determination of compensation.
predicates.recurring_payment: The payment is made regularly or recurs over an interim period.
predicates.allowance_compensates_interim_income_los: The payment compensates the recipient for income lost during the interim period.
predicates.part_of_commutation: The payment forms part of the separate sum paid to compensate for the loss of the underlying property interest.

members.legal_issue: Interim payments made after an income-producing estate is taken, but before final compensation is determined, are capital receipts when they compensate for the loss of the income-producing asset rather than for the loss of interest on compensation.
material_facts: An estate vested in the government, depriving its former holders of the income-producing asset.
The former holders received recurring interim payments before the compensation for the estate was finally determined.

The amount of the interim payments was calculated by reference to the income the former holders would have received had they continued to own the estate, rather than by reference to estimated compensation.
The former holders were not entitled to the final compensation until it was determined, and the interim payments were not fixed as interest on that compensation.
members.legal_principle: The character of a receipt depends on its substance, not the label given to it or the method used to calculate it. Section 3(e) treated the former holders as entitled only to compensation for the taking of their estates; sections 50(2) and 50(8) did not make the interim payments interest or exclude their character as compensation for recurring loss caused by taking an income-producing asset. Because final compensation became payable only after determination under section 39, and the interim payments were based on lost income rather than estimated compensation, they were not payments for being kept out of money already due. The Court relied on Dr. Sham Lal v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Punjab, for the distinction between interest and compensation; Senairam Doongarmall v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Assam, and Simpson v. Executors of Bonner Maurice, for the principle that the quality and substance of a payment determine its character. It distinguished Raja Rameshwara Rao v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Hyderabad, and Chandroji Rao v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madhya Pradesh, and disapproved Kumara Rajah of Venkatagiri v. Income-tax Officer.
members.conclusion: The interim payments compensated the former holders for the loss of their income-producing asset and were capital receipts, not taxable revenue receipts.

rule.if: income_tax_receipt_classification and income_producing_asset_taken and interim_payment_based_on_lost_income and final_compensation_not_yet_determined and not interim_payment_based_on_estimated_compensation

predicates.income_tax_receipt_classification: The proceeding requires a determination of whether a receipt is taxable income.
predicates.income_producing_asset_taken: The government took an asset that had produced income for its former holders.
predicates.interim_payment_based_on_lost_income: The government calculated recurring interim payments by reference to income the former holders lost when the asset was taken.
predicates.final_compensation_not_yet_determined: The former holders received the interim payments before their entitlement to final compensation had been determined.
predicates.interim_payment_based_on_estimated_compe: The government calculated the interim payments by reference to an estimate of the final compensation.
predicates.receipt_is_capital_not_taxable: The receipt is a capital receipt and is not taxable as revenue income.

members.legal_issue: A court should not replace the statutory insolvency resolution mechanism with a parallel court-supervised process for resolving a corporate debtor's affairs.
material_facts: The parties proposed that the Court appoint an independent committee to assess the developers' ability to complete the projects and to supervise a resolution outside the statutory process.
The statutory process assigns resolution decisions to insolvency professionals and the committee of creditors and requires specialized financial determinations.
The Court had decided to recommence the corporate insolvency resolution process under the statutory framework.
members.legal_principle: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, establishes a market-driven process that assigns responsibility to the resolution professional and committee of creditors and gives primacy to their commercial decisions. The Court held that its power to do complete justice should not be used to supplant those statutory mechanisms with a court-directed process.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to appoint a committee to oversee a resolution outside the statutory process and required the resolution to follow the statutory insolvency framework.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_proceeding: A corporate debtor is undergoing a corporate insolvency resolution proceeding.
predicates.statutory_expert_resolution_mechanism_ex: A statutory process assigns the resolution work and relevant decisions to designated insolvency professionals and creditor representatives.
predicates.parallel_court_supervised_process_propos: A party proposes that a court create and supervise a separate resolution process outside the statutory mechanism.

members.legal_issue: During a corporate insolvency resolution process, a court should not order an interim preferential distribution to one class of creditors at the expense of other creditors and the collective resolution process.
material_facts: Money deposited during the proceedings was held by the Court while the corporate insolvency resolution process was pending.
Some home buyers sought refunds and requested that the deposited money be distributed to them on a pro-rata basis.
Most of the home buyers sought possession rather than refunds, and secured creditors had claims against the corporate debtor's assets.
The Court considered that distributing the money to the refund-seeking group would prefer that group and could prejudice other creditors and a composite resolution plan.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, during the corporate insolvency resolution process, a preferential payment to a particular class of financial creditors would be impermissible and could cause injustice to other creditors. The process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, requires a composite approach to the corporate debtor's financial situation. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The Court refused to direct a pro-rata interim disbursement to the home buyers seeking refunds and directed that the deposited money remain invested pending directions in the insolvency process.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_process_pending: A corporate insolvency resolution process remains pending.
predicates.creditor_group_seeks_interim_distributio: A group of creditors asks for money held in connection with the debtor to be distributed before the resolution process is complete.
predicates.distribution_would_prefer_that_group_ove: The proposed distribution would give one creditor group an advantage over other creditors or prejudice a collective resolution.

members.legal_issue: A court-ordered stay affecting proceedings under a composite land-acquisition notification suspends the limitation period for declarations concerning the lands covered by that notification, even for owners who did not obtain a separate stay.
material_facts: The lands were covered by composite notifications issued for a single planned development scheme.
Courts had stayed the authorities from issuing declarations under those notifications in proceedings brought by other landowners.
The declarations concerning the appellants’ lands were issued after the stays ceased to operate.
The notifications fell within the period for which the statutory scheme allowed the stay period to be excluded when computing the time limit.
members.legal_principle: Under the first proviso to Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, read with Explanation 1, the period during which a court stays action or proceedings pursuant to a Section 4 notification is excluded from the applicable time limit. The Court applied the broad construction of “any” in Explanation 1 adopted by the Delhi High Court Full Bench in B.R. Gupta-I, and relied on Abhey Ram (Dead by LRs) v. Union of India, which treated a stay concerning a composite notification as inhibiting further action concerning other lands covered by it. The rationale is that a stay affecting an integrated acquisition scheme can prevent the authorities from proceeding with declarations for the scheme as a whole.
members.conclusion: The period during which the stays operated had to be excluded in computing the time limit, so the declarations were not invalid as time-barred merely because the appellants had no separate stay order.

rule.if: is_land_acquisition_challenge and composite_acquisition_notification and related_landowner_stay_order and declaration_issued_after_stay_lifted

predicates.is_land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges an acquisition of land under a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.composite_acquisition_notification: The government issued a notification covering multiple parcels as part of an integrated acquisition scheme.
predicates.related_landowner_stay_order: A court stayed the authorities from taking further action under the notification in a proceeding brought by another landowner whose land was covered by it.
predicates.declaration_issued_after_stay_lifted: The authorities issued the declaration after the relevant court-ordered restraint had ceased to operate.

members.legal_issue: A stay restraining further steps in a land-acquisition proceeding may extend the time for a declaration for landowners who did not personally obtain the stay when the restraint inhibited the authority from proceeding with a common acquisition.
material_facts: A common acquisition notice covered land in multiple villages and belonging to multiple owners.
Some landowners obtained court orders restraining further acquisition steps, including publication of the declaration.
The declaration was published beyond the ordinary statutory period, and the appellants had not personally obtained a stay.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to Section 6(1) and Explanation II to the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, time during which action or proceedings are stayed is excluded when computing the period for publication of a declaration. The Court applied the broad meaning of an inhibitive stay discussed in Yusufbhai Noormohmed Nendoliya v. State of Gujarat, Hansraj Jain v. State of Maharashtra, Sangappa Gurulingappa Sajjan v. State of Karnataka, Gandhi Grah Nirman Sahkari Samiti Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, G. Narayanaswamy Reddy v. Government of Karnataka, and Roshnara Begum v. Union of India, and upheld the Full Bench’s approach in Balak Ram Gupta v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The period during which the related stay orders inhibited further proceedings was excluded for the appellants as well; the declaration concerning their land was not time-barred.

predicates.land_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land by a public authority.
predicates.common_acquisition_notice: One acquisition notice covers land belonging to multiple owners or situated in multiple areas.
predicates.related_court_order_barred_further_steps: A court order in a related challenge restrained the authority from taking further steps in the acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A transferee pendente lite of property involved in a partition can exercise the transferor’s rights, including seeking an equitable partition.
material_facts: The purchasers acquired interests in fields from parties to the partition proceedings while those proceedings were pending.
The purchasers were in possession of the fields and had acquired title to them.
The transfer of their interests and their claims to the fields were undisputed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, a transferee pendente lite is bound by the proceedings concerning the transferred interest and is a representative-in-interest of the transferor. A transferee from a party to a partition can exercise the transferor’s rights, including the right to seek an equitable partition. The Court also relied on Rule 10 of Order XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure in recognizing a transferee’s participation rights. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The transferees could seek an equitable partition just as their transferors could.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns partition of property.
predicates.interest_transferred_during_proceeding: A party transferred an interest in the property to another person while the partition proceeding was pending.
predicates.transferor_could_seek_equitable_partitio: The transferor could ask for the property to be divided equitably.

members.legal_issue: In a partition referred to a revenue authority, an undisputed transferee pendente lite may seek an equitable allotment, and the authority may consider the transferee’s interest without referring the matter back to the civil court.
material_facts: The partition of land assessed to government revenue was being carried out by a Collector under a civil court decree.
The purchasers had acquired and possessed fields from parties to the partition proceedings during their pendency.
The transfers and the purchasers’ rights were undisputed, but the Collector allotted the purchasers’ fields to another share without considering their request for an equitable allotment.
The other parties did not object to the partition made by the Collector.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a revenue-assessed estate to be partitioned in accordance with the decree and the law relating to partition or separate possession. The Court held that this permits the Collector, where there is no dispute about a transfer or devolution of interest, to take the affected interests into account and make an equitable allotment. This construction avoids unnecessary referral to the civil court and does not violate the decree or exceed the Collector’s authority. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act also makes the transferee pendente lite bound by the proceedings while recognizing the transferee as representative-in-interest. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The purchasers had standing to request an equitable allotment, and the Collector could consider their undisputed interests and make an equitable partition without violating the decree or referring the matter back to the civil court. The existing partition was set aside and the matter remanded for a fresh equitable partition.

predicates.revenue_authority_partition_proceeding: A civil court decree for partition is being implemented by a revenue authority.
predicates.undisputed_transfer_to_transferee: A party transferred an interest in the property during the proceeding, and the transfer and the transferee’s interest are not disputed.
predicates.transferee_seeks_equitable_allotment: The transferee asks the authority to take the acquired interest into account in dividing the property equitably.

members.legal_issue: A general reference to a tenure-holder’s personal law applies the law in force when succession opens, including later amendments to that law.
material_facts: The dispute concerned succession to land held by a tenure-holder after his widow died.
The governing revenue provision stated that a tenure-holder’s interest passed on death subject to the holder’s personal law.
The widow died after the Hindu Succession Act had come into force.
members.legal_principle: Section 151 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954 referred generally to the holder’s personal law. A general reference to the law governing a subject incorporates that law as it stands when it is applied, including subsequent amendments; this differs from specific incorporation of another statute as it stood at adoption. The Court relied on this principle in approving Smt. Indubai v. Vyankati Vithoba Sawadha, Kumari Ramlali v. Mst. Bhagunti Bai, and Tare C.J.’s view in Nahar Hirasingh v. Mst. Dukalhin. The Court found it unnecessary to decide whether Section 151 fell within the exception in Section 4(2) of the Hindu Succession Act because Section 151 itself made personal law applicable.
members.conclusion: The reference to personal law included the Hindu Succession Act as in force when the widow died and succession opened; the Court did not decide whether the revenue provision was otherwise saved as a law governing devolution of tenancy rights.

rule.if: tenure_holder_inheritance_dispute and personal_law_reference and general_reference_to_subject_law and amended_law_in_force_when_succession_opens

predicates.tenure_holder_inheritance_dispute: The proceeding concerns inheritance to an interest held by a tenure-holder.
predicates.personal_law_reference: The governing rule makes devolution of the tenure-holder’s interest subject to that holder’s personal law.
predicates.general_reference_to_subject_law: The governing rule refers generally to the law on a subject rather than specifically incorporating a particular statute as it stood at adoption.
predicates.amended_law_in_force_when_succession_ope: The later or amended personal law was in force when the succession opened.

members.legal_issue: A statutory direction that a tenure-holder’s interest devolves subject to personal law applies the personal law in force when succession opens, rather than fixing that law as of the enactment of the direction.
material_facts: The deceased held an interest as a tenure-holder, and the governing land-revenue provision directed that the interest pass subject to the holder’s personal law on death.
The deceased died after the Hindu Succession Act had come into force, and the parties disputed whether succession was governed by that Act or by the earlier Mitakshara law.
The Supreme Court found it unnecessary to decide whether the land-revenue provision was itself a law for the devolution of tenancy rights within the saving clause of the Hindu Succession Act.
members.legal_principle: A general reference to the law governing a subject adopts that law as it stands when applied, including later amendments, unlike a specific incorporation fixed at the time of adoption. The Court relied on Sutherland’s Statutory Construction and Corpus Juris Secundum for this principle. It applied that principle to Section 151 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, whose words ‘on his death’ indicated that personal law as amended up to the date of death governed. The Court did not decide whether Section 151 fell within the saving clause in Section 4(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; it held that Section 151 itself referred the matter to personal law.
members.conclusion: The reference to personal law included the Hindu Succession Act in force when the deceased died and succession opened; the reference was not limited to Hindu law as it stood when the land-revenue code was enacted.

rule.if: inheritance_dispute and tenure_holder_interest and personal_law_referred_to_generally and succession_opened_after_later_law

predicates.inheritance_dispute: The parties disputed who inherited an interest after its holder died.
predicates.tenure_holder_interest: The deceased held the disputed land interest directly from the State as a tenure-holder.
predicates.personal_law_referred_to_generally: The governing land-holding rule referred generally to the holder’s personal law without fixing it to a named enactment or date.
predicates.succession_opened_after_later_law: The deceased died after a later body of succession law had come into force.
predicates.personal_law_in_force_at_succession_appl: The personal law in force when succession opened governs the inheritance.

members.legal_issue: Construction that materially changes the form or structure of rented accommodation is a material alteration even if it does not damage the premises or diminish their value.
material_facts: The tenant lowered the shop floor by excavating earth and installing a new floor.

The tenant correspondingly lowered the front door and cut away the plinthband on which it rested, lowered the staircase and added new steps, and lowered the exterior platform to match the new floor level.
The tenant made these changes without the landlord’s permission; the lower courts found them to be material alterations.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(1)(c) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, requires a fact-specific assessment of material alteration. In its ordinary meaning, material alterations are important changes that materially or substantially change the front or structure of the premises. Wates v. Rowland and Another and Blackmore v. Dimmer provide assistance in identifying structural alterations; Hyman v. Rose concerned a different question about a lease covenant and waste and did not govern this issue.
members.conclusion: The changes altered the form and structure of the accommodation and were material alterations, regardless of whether they caused damage or diminished its value. The landlord was therefore entitled to maintain the eviction suit without prior administrative permission.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding to evict a tenant that is ordinarily subject to prior administrative permission.
predicates.tenant_made_unapproved_construction: The tenant made or permitted construction without the landlord’s written permission.
predicates.construction_changed_form_or_structure: The construction materially changed the form or structure of the rented accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s construction materially alters an accommodation only when it makes a substantial change to the building’s character, form, or structure.
material_facts: The tenant placed a six-foot partition in a hall without a foundation and without reaching the ceiling; it could be removed without damage and served to divide the hall for convenient use.
The disputed tin shed stood on adjoining open land, was made with temporary materials, and could be removed without damage; an existing shed had merely been extended.
The lower appellate court found that these constructions did not substantially change the accommodation, but the High Court treated them as material alterations.
members.legal_principle: The expression “materially altered” means a substantial change in the character, form, or structure of a building without destroying its identity. The court considers the nature and character of the construction and the extent of the change, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation was let. Minor alterations for convenient use do not qualify when the building’s form and structure remain unaffected. The Court relied on the dictionary meanings of “alter” and “materially,” Babu Manmohan Das Shah v. Bishun Das, S.B. Mathur v. K.P. Gupta, Dr. J.G. Gupta v. Bodh Mal, Sita Ram Sharan v. Johri Mal, and Baldev Das v. Ram Khilawan.
members.conclusion: Neither the partition nor the tin shed materially altered the accommodation, so the statutory ground for eviction was not established.

rule.if: eviction_claim_based_on_tenant_construction and tenant_made_unauthorized_construction and (construction_is_temporary_and_removable and not substantial_change_to_building)

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_tenant_construct: The landlord seeks eviction on the basis of construction made or permitted by the tenant.
predicates.tenant_made_unauthorized_construction: The tenant made or permitted construction without the landlord’s consent.
predicates.construction_is_temporary_and_removable: The construction is temporary and can be removed without damage to the building.
predicates.substantial_change_to_building: The construction substantially changes the building’s character, form, or structure.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who fails to prove an alleged prior payment and accepts conditional permission to remove forest produce cannot recover the amount paid to obtain that permission.
material_facts: The claimant alleged that he had already paid the proprietor the balance due under the forest contract, but did not testify to the payment and produced no material establishing that he had the funds to make it.
The claimant's agent testified to a cash payment, but the evidence did not establish that the proprietor received it; the claimant's correspondence did not mention the alleged prior payment.

After the forest vested in the State, the State permitted removal of the trees on condition that the claimant pay a specified amount. The claimant accepted the condition, paid the amount, and removed the timber without protest.
members.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the alleged prior payment was proved on the evidence and found it was not. It further held that, after vesting, the State's offer under section 6(2) to permit removal on payment of a stated amount did not ratify the earlier contract; a claimant who accepted that condition, paid, and removed the timber could not seek a refund.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not entitled to a refund of the amount paid to the State; the conditional permission was not a ratification of the earlier contract.

predicates.forest_contract_refund_claim: The proceeding includes a claim to recover money paid in connection with removal of forest produce under a disputed forest contract.
predicates.alleged_prior_payment_not_proved: The claimant's alleged earlier payment to the proprietor is not established by the evidence.
predicates.conditional_removal_permission_accepted_: After the State acquired the forest rights, the claimant accepted permission to remove the produce on a payment condition and paid the required amount.

members.legal_issue: A claimant cannot obtain relief for the value of trees transferred under accepted, unchallenged felling-permission conditions where the trees were admitted to be reserved trees.
material_facts: The claimants sought the value of trees transported to a government depot after permission to fell the trees had been granted subject to conditions.
The permission required specified reserved trees to be transferred to the government depot.
The claimants did not challenge the conditions attached to the permission.
A claimant witness admitted that the trees in question were reserved trees.
The High Court granted relief without examining the effect of the admission or adequately addressing the absence of a challenge to the conditions.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a decision must be assessed in light of the material facts and that precedent cannot be applied without considering factual context. The Karnataka Preservation of Trees Act, 1976 was cited as governing the permission, but the Court did not decide a separate question of statutory ownership. It relied on the admitted reserved-tree status and the unchallenged conditions of the permission in finding the High Court's judgment unsustainable.
members.conclusion: The High Court judgment was unsustainable and was set aside; the appeal was allowed.

rule.if: appeal_from_relief_granting_judgment and conditional_tree_felling_permission_accepted and permit_conditions_not_challenged and reserved_tree_status_admitted and claim_seeks_value_of_transferred_trees

predicates.appeal_from_relief_granting_judgment: A party appeals from a judgment that granted the opposing claimant relief.
predicates.conditional_tree_felling_permission_acce: The claimant accepted permission to fell trees that was granted subject to conditions.
predicates.permit_conditions_not_challenged: The claimant did not challenge the conditions attached to the permission.
predicates.reserved_tree_status_admitted: A claimant or witness admitted that the trees covered by the claim were reserved trees.
predicates.claim_seeks_value_of_transferred_trees: The claimant seeks payment for trees that were transferred to a government depot under the permission.

members.legal_issue: The statutory ground for eviction based on unauthorized transfer or subletting applies to non-residential premises.
material_facts: The landlord brought an ejectment suit concerning premises used for non-residential purposes.
The suit sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had transferred or sublet the premises without the landlord’s written consent.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 applies to any premises defined by that Act and does not distinguish between residential and non-residential premises. The Court relied on the wording of that provision and its relationship to clauses (b) to (e) and Section 14 of the Act.
members.conclusion: The eviction ground applies to premises covered by the tenancy legislation whether they are residential or non-residential.

rule.if: tenancy_eviction_proceeding and premises_governed_by_tenancy_law and nonresidential_premises and eviction_sought_for_unauthorized_transfer_or_subletting

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.premises_governed_by_tenancy_law: The premises are governed by the applicable tenancy law.
predicates.nonresidential_premises: The premises are used for a non-residential purpose.
predicates.eviction_sought_for_unauthorized_transfe: The landlord sought eviction on the basis that the tenant transferred, assigned, or sublet the premises without the required consent.

members.legal_issue: The ground for eviction based on a tenant securing alternative accommodation applies to both residential and non-residential premises.
material_facts: The tenant used the rented premises as a clinic, rather than as a residence.
The tenant had built another, large house and let portions of it to a government department.
The relevant provision referred to a “house,” which the governing order defined to include residential and non-residential buildings.
An explanation addressed a limited situation involving a tenant who owned a residential house constructed on specified kinds of sites; the main provision itself was left unchanged.
members.legal_principle: Under clause 13(3)(v) of the C.P. & Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, “house” includes a residential or non-residential building. The provision covers two situations—securing alternative accommodation and leaving the area for a continuous period of four months without reasonably needing the house—and does not distinguish between residential and non-residential premises. The explanation creates a limited legal fiction for specified cases involving ownership of a residential house; it clarifies what counts as securing alternative accommodation in those cases but does not displace the wider main provision. The court also rejected reliance on other States’ rent laws, observing that legislative policy differs.
members.conclusion: The ground applies to non-residential as well as residential premises; the explanation does not exclude non-residential premises from its scope.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and rented_premises_used_for_nonresidential_purpose and tenant_secured_other_accommodation and main_ground_covers_two_situations and explanation_covers_only_limited_residential_class

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought permission to end a tenancy under a rent-control eviction procedure.
predicates.rented_premises_used_for_nonresidential_: The tenant used the rented premises for a purpose other than residence.
predicates.tenant_secured_other_accommodation: The tenant obtained other accommodation apart from the rented premises.
predicates.main_ground_covers_two_situations: The governing ground covered both obtaining other accommodation and leaving the area without reasonably needing the rented premises.
predicates.explanation_covers_only_limited_resident: An explanation to the governing ground addressed only a limited class of cases involving ownership of a residential house.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser that is factually a continuation of the former consumer may be held liable for that consumer’s outstanding electricity charges.
material_facts: A company purchased the assets of a former consumer in an auction and sought electricity supply for the premises.
The former consumer had outstanding electricity charges.
The evidence showed substantial overlap between the companies’ promoters and directors, and the Court found that factually there was no new entity.
members.legal_principle: The general rule that a distinct third-party purchaser does not inherit the former consumer’s contractual electricity debt does not prevent liability where the Court finds that the purchaser is not in fact a new entity. The Court relied on the factual overlap in promoters and directors in reaching that finding; the judgment does not establish that common management alone invariably transfers a separate company’s debt.
members.conclusion: The Court held the purchaser liable for the former consumer’s outstanding arrears because, on the facts, it was not a new entity.

predicates.auction_purchaser_seeks_supply_for_premi: A person who acquired premises or assets at an auction seeks electricity supply for them.
predicates.prior_consumer_left_unpaid_electricity_c: The former consumer used electricity and left charges for that use unpaid.
predicates.purchaser_is_factually_a_continuation_of: The facts show that the purchaser is not a genuinely new entity but is a continuation of the former consumer.

members.legal_issue: An auction purchaser may be required to pay a previous owner's unpaid electricity dues where the sale terms disclose and allocate those dues to the purchaser and the applicable supply conditions require clearance before electricity is supplied.
material_facts: The former owner failed to pay electricity charges, and a secured creditor auctioned the unit to recover its debt.

The auction notice described the sale as being on an as-is, without-recourse basis, disclosed outstanding local-government dues including electricity bills, and stated that the purchaser would bear statutory dues and that the authorised officer would not be responsible for electricity dues.
The sale deed's indemnity covered specified losses arising from defects in title and did not extend to electricity arrears.
The auction purchaser sought a new electricity connection to operate the unit. The electricity distributor refused supply because of the former owner's unpaid electricity dues.
The applicable supply conditions allowed the distributor to refuse a new or existing connection until dues were cleared.

The lower courts had quashed the demand, relying on decisions in which the sale terms did not specifically address electricity dues or the applicable rules did not require a fresh-connection applicant to clear them.
members.legal_principle: Electricity dues imposed under the Electricity Act, 2003 and the terms and conditions of supply have a statutory character and are not merely contractual; Section 56 of that Act is in pari materia with Section 24 of the Electricity Act, 1910. Hyderabad Vanaspathi Ltd. v. A.P. State Electricity Board supports the statutory character of such dues. Under Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Paramount Polymers (P) Ltd. and Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited v. DVS Steels and Alloys Private Limited, a supplier may require outstanding dues to be cleared where the applicable terms so provide, and a clearance condition is not per se arbitrary or unreasonable. Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board, Haryana State Electricity Board v. Hanuman Rice Mills, Special Officer, Commerce, NESCO v. Raghunath Paper Mills, and Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Limited v. Gopal Agarwal involved materially different circumstances, including the absence of specific sale-term disclosure or rules requiring clearance for a fresh connection. Where the auction terms specifically disclose electricity dues and allocate statutory dues to the purchaser, and the supply conditions cover the connection sought, the purchaser may be required to clear the arrears.
members.conclusion: The distributor was entitled to demand payment of the former owner's electricity arrears from the auction purchaser. The appeal was allowed and the orders quashing the demand were set aside.

rule.if: auction_purchaser_seeks_electricity_supply and prior_owner_left_electricity_arrears and sale_notice_discloses_electricity_dues and sale_terms_allocate_statutory_dues_to_purchaser and sale_is_as_is_without_recourse and supply_terms_require_clearance_for_the_connection_sought

predicates.auction_purchaser_seeks_electricity_supp: An auction purchaser sought electricity supply to use the purchased property.
predicates.prior_owner_left_electricity_arrears: The previous owner left unpaid charges for electricity supplied to the property.
predicates.sale_notice_discloses_electricity_dues: The auction notice disclosed that electricity dues were outstanding.
predicates.sale_terms_allocate_statutory_dues_to_pu: The sale terms stated that the purchaser would bear statutory dues relating to the property.
predicates.sale_is_as_is_without_recourse: The property was offered for sale on an as-is basis without recourse.
predicates.supply_terms_require_clearance_for_the_c: The applicable supply conditions required outstanding dues to be cleared before the type of connection sought could be supplied.

members.legal_issue: A court may add a party despite the plaintiff’s choice of defendants only when that person is necessary or proper for effective and complete adjudication of the questions in the suit.
material_facts: The plaintiff objected to adding the lessee as a defendant, arguing that he was dominus litis and claimed no relief against it.
The lessee sought to be joined, asserting that it had evidence about the alleged unauthorised constructions and an interest in the premises.
members.legal_principle: Order I, Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 gives the court discretion to add parties at any stage. A necessary party is one without whom no effective order can be made; a proper party is one whose presence is needed for a complete and final decision on the questions involved. A person’s relevant evidence or interest in the correct resolution of a question alone is insufficient: the person must have a direct or legal interest such that the result may affect their legal rights. The Court relied on Razia Begum v. Anwar Begum, [1959] SCR 1111, and referred to Amon v. Raphael Tuck & Sons Ltd., (1956) 1 All E.R. 273, and Dollfus Mieg et Compagnie S.A. v. Bank of England, (1950) 2 All E.R. 611.
members.conclusion: A plaintiff’s status as dominus litis does not prevent the court from adding a defendant, but the court may add only a necessary or proper party whose presence meets the requirements for effective and complete adjudication.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit in which the court is considering whether to add a person as a party.
predicates.party_needed_for_effective_order_or_comp: The person’s presence is necessary to make an effective order or to reach a complete and final decision on the questions in the suit.

members.legal_issue: A person claiming relief under a separate transaction may be added as a defendant only if that person ought to have been joined or has a direct legal interest making their presence necessary for complete adjudication of the suit.
material_facts: The pending suit concerned the validity of an earlier transfer of controlling shares in companies, and a claim to possession of a tea estate through one of those companies.
The applicant sought specific performance of a later agreement for sale of the tea estate, in a separate suit.
The applicant had no direct legal interest in the validity of the earlier share-transfer agreement that was the subject of the pending suit.
The two suits were being tried together.
members.legal_principle: Under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a person may be added if they ought to have been joined or their presence is necessary to enable the court to effectually and completely adjudicate and settle the questions in the suit. A direct legal interest, rather than an indirect or commercial interest, is required; preventing multiplicity of proceedings is not by itself the object of the rule. The court relied on Moser v. Marsden, Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum, and Ramesh Hirachand Kundanmal v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay.
members.conclusion: The applicant was not entitled to be added as a defendant. The order allowing impleadment was set aside and the order refusing it was restored.

predicates.party_addition_application_in_pending_su: A person applied to be added as a party to a pending suit.
predicates.applicant_lacks_direct_legal_interest: The applicant had no direct legal interest in the issues to be decided in the pending suit.
predicates.applicant_seeks_relief_on_separate_cause: The applicant sought relief based on a separate cause of action rather than an issue in the pending suit.

members.legal_issue: A composite letting of land and a building is governed as a letting of a building when the parties intended the land and building to go together, and the lease cannot be divided without a clear contrary intention.
material_facts: The original lease included vacant land, a well, and the lessor-owned structure as one letting.
The lease required the lessee to remove the structures he had put up but to return the lessor-owned structure without damage.
The structure was of substantial size, was used in connection with the lessee’s business, and was treated in the lease documents as a material part of the property.
The surrounding circumstances supported the inference that the lessor intended to let the land and structure together; the lease did not clearly express an intention to separate them.
members.legal_principle: In a composite lease, the court should consider whether the parties intended the land and building to go together and whether the lessor could have intended to let the land without the building; the dominant-purpose test is not invariably helpful. Section 2(2) includes land let along with a building, and a joint letting should not be split in the absence of a clear intention in the deed. The Court drew assistance from Sultan Bros. P. Ltd. v. C.I.T. on inseparable letting, considered Larsen & Toubro and the other composite-leasing authorities, and distinguished the extreme proposition that any building on leased land automatically brings the whole lease within rent control, as well as the reliance placed on Irani v. Chidambaram Chettiar and Salay Mohd. Sait v. J.M.S. Charity.
members.conclusion: The letting was a composite lease of land and building within the scope of the Rent Control Act, and it could not be dissected into separate land and building leases in the absence of a clear contrary intention.

rule.if: composite_lease_classification_case and land_and_building_leased_together and parties_intended_joint_enjoyment and not clear_intention_to_separate

predicates.composite_lease_classification_case: The proceeding required classification of a letting that included both land and a building.
predicates.land_and_building_leased_together: The lessor included both land and a building in the same letting.
predicates.parties_intended_joint_enjoyment: The lease terms and surrounding circumstances showed that the parties intended the land and building to go together.
predicates.clear_intention_to_separate: The lease clearly expressed an intention to separate the building letting from the land letting.

members.legal_issue: A lease of a building and land is not divisible into separate leases when its terms and the property do not identify a distinct, separately demised area of land.
material_facts: The deed referred jointly to the building and land as the demised premises and provided for a single lease term, renewal, termination, and surrender.
It stated an aggregate monthly rent, although the rent was apportioned between land and building, and required a consolidated advance.
The deed did not provide for separate termination or renewal of the building lease and the land lease.
The deed did not define or delineate an area that could be treated as a separate lease of vacant land.
The deed permitted construction, subletting, and a possible sale option, but the Court regarded these as provisions addressing contingencies during the lease rather than creating separate leases.
members.legal_principle: The lease must be construed as a whole in light of its terms and the nature of the property. Separate rents, permissions to build or sublet, and a purchase option do not by themselves establish separate leases where the deed otherwise treats the property as one demise and does not specify a distinct area for a separate land lease. Under the Act's definitions, a composite lease of a building with appurtenant land does not confer the rights in sections 3 or 9.
members.conclusion: The deed created one indivisible composite lease of the building and its appurtenant land, not two separate leases.

rule.if: tenant_seeks_statutory_protection_in_ejectment and deed_covers_building_and_land and deed_treats_premises_as_one_demise and no_separately_defined_land_area

predicates.tenant_seeks_statutory_protection_in_eje: A tenant facing an ejectment suit claims statutory protection based on the lease.
predicates.deed_covers_building_and_land: The lease deed covers both a building and land.
predicates.deed_treats_premises_as_one_demise: The deed provides for the building and land to be held under a single lease arrangement, including common term and termination provisions.
predicates.no_separately_defined_land_area: The deed does not identify and delineate an area of land as the subject of a distinct lease.

members.legal_issue: Demolishing a building does not terminate a tenancy when the land forming part of the leased property continues to exist, particularly when the demolition is by the tenant or a person claiming under the tenant.
material_facts: The tenancy concerned a building on land, and the case did not proceed on the basis that the land was excluded from the tenancy.
The occupants demolished the building, but the land beneath it continued to exist.
The demolition was by the occupants claiming through the tenants, not by the landlord or an act of nature.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 describe a lease as a transfer of an interest in immovable property and a right to enjoy that property. Relying on Raja Dhruv Dev Chand v. Raja Harmohinder Singh and the cited authorities, the Court held that destruction of a building alone does not end a lease of the building and its site when the land remains; the doctrine of frustration applicable to contracts does not determine such a lease.
members.conclusion: The tenancy did not end merely because the building was demolished; the land remained part of the subject matter of the lease.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and leased_property_included_land and land_survived and building_demolished_by_tenant_or_successor

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking eviction from premises held under a tenancy.
predicates.leased_property_included_land: The tenancy covered a building together with the land on which it stood.
predicates.land_survived: The land forming part of the leased property continued to exist after the building was destroyed.
predicates.building_demolished_by_tenant_or_success: The tenant or a person claiming through the tenant demolished the building.

members.legal_issue: The destruction of a leased building does not determine the tenancy when the lease includes the land beneath the building and that land continues to exist.
material_facts: The appellant had rented a godown standing on part of a plot and had continuously paid rent and used the godown.
The respondent acquired the ownership interests in the plot, while the appellant’s leasehold interest was not acquired by the respondent.
The godown was demolished or collapsed, but the land beneath it remained.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 105, 108 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers an interest in immovable property, and destruction of a building alone does not determine a lease when the land forming part of the subject matter continues to exist. Section 108(B)(e) gives the lessee an option to treat a lease as void in the specified circumstances; it does not make the lease automatically terminate. A lease of a building standing on land ordinarily comprises both the building and its site. The Court followed T. Lakshmipathi & Ors. v. R. Nithyananda Reddy & Ors., relying also on Section 5 of the Act and Raja Dhruv Dev Chand v. Raja Harmohinder Singh, and on the understanding of a building’s site in D.G. Gose & Co. (Agents) (P) Ltd. v. State of Kerala and Corporation of the City of Victoria v. Bishop of Vancouver Island. It overruled Vannattankandy Ibrayi v. Kunhabdulla Hajee to the extent it held that complete destruction of a building extinguished the tenancy in these circumstances.
members.conclusion: The tenancy was not determined by the demolition or destruction of the godown. The ruling that the tenancy had lapsed was set aside.

rule.if: ordinary_property_lease and leased_structure_stood_on_land and structure_destroyed and land_site_remains

predicates.ordinary_property_lease: The dispute concerns a lease of immovable property governed by ordinary property-lease law rather than a special rent-law regime.
predicates.leased_structure_stood_on_land: The tenant leased a building or structure standing on land as the subject matter of the lease.
predicates.structure_destroyed: The leased building or structure was destroyed or demolished.
predicates.land_site_remains: The land on which the leased building or structure stood continues to exist.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional petition cannot enforce a right that a competent court has already negatived by adjudication.
material_facts: A competent court appointed another person as guardian and rejected the petitioner's application.
The petitioner appealed, but the appeal was dismissed, and the order became final.
The petitioner later sought under Article 32 to enforce the guardianship right that had been rejected in those proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Relief under Article 32 for enforcement of a right requires proof of the right and its infringement. Where adjudication by a competent court has negatived the claimed right, Article 32 cannot be used to enforce it notwithstanding that adjudication. The Court relied on Article 32 and cited no earlier cases on this issue.
members.conclusion: The Article 32 petition could not be entertained to enforce a right already negatived by the adjudication of a competent court.

predicates.constitutional_enforcement_petition: A person brings a constitutional petition seeking enforcement of an alleged right.
predicates.claimed_right_was_adjudicated_by_compete: A competent court previously adjudicated the claimed right.
predicates.adjudication_negatived_claimed_right: The previous adjudication rejected the claimed right.
predicates.constitutional_petition_cannot_enforce_n: A constitutional petition cannot enforce a right that a competent court has already rejected.

members.legal_issue: A constitutional petition cannot be used to circumvent the rejection of an application for special leave to appeal.
material_facts: The petitioner sought special leave to appeal against the order dismissing his appeal, and the application was rejected.
The petitioner then sought relief under Article 32 concerning the same guardianship dispute.
members.legal_principle: An order rejecting an application for special leave under Article 136 cannot be circumvented by an application for a writ under Article 32. The Court relied on Articles 136 and 32 and cited no earlier cases on this issue.
members.conclusion: The rejection of the special-leave application could not be circumvented by filing a petition under Article 32.

predicates.constitutional_enforcement_petition: A person brings a constitutional petition seeking relief in a dispute.
predicates.special_leave_application_was_rejected: An application for special leave to appeal concerning the dispute was rejected.
predicates.petition_seeks_to_reopen_same_dispute: The constitutional petition seeks to reopen the dispute addressed by the special-leave application.
predicates.constitutional_petition_cannot_circumven: A constitutional petition cannot be used to circumvent the rejection of an application for special leave to appeal.

members.legal_issue: A government’s grant of general relief to a class of persons before an election, and political statements promoting or explaining that relief, do not establish a corrupt practice where the relief is not a gratification and the government actors are not shown to have acted as the candidate’s agents.
material_facts: A state government enacted an ordinance exempting certain small agricultural holdings from land revenue after the issue had been debated and advocated by different political parties.
The relief applied to a large number of agriculturists and was granted by the government through the ordinance, not by the political party supporting the candidate.
The chief minister announced the relief and a party member circulated a pamphlet supporting the party’s electoral position on the issue.
The evidence did not establish that the chief minister or the pamphlet’s author acted as the candidate’s agent.
members.legal_principle: Section 123(1)(A) concerns a candidate’s or agent’s gift, offer, or promise of gratification to induce electoral support. General relief granted by the government through an ordinance was not such gratification, and the government’s political alignment with the candidate’s party did not make the government the candidate’s agent. The chief minister’s announcement and the party member’s pamphlet did not establish agency. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The charge of corrupt practice under section 123(1)(A) was not established.

rule.if: election_petition_challenging_election and government_enacts_general_public_relief and relief_is_not_candidate_gratification and (government_not_candidate_agent and public_speakers_not_candidate_agents)

predicates.election_petition_challenging_election: A petitioner seeks to set aside an election by alleging a corrupt practice.
predicates.government_enacts_general_public_relief: The government grants relief to a class of people through a general governmental measure.
predicates.relief_is_not_candidate_gratification: The relief is granted as a governmental measure rather than as a gift, offer, or promise of gratification by or for the candidate.
predicates.government_not_candidate_agent: The evidence does not show that the government acted as the candidate’s agent in granting the relief.
predicates.public_speakers_not_candidate_agents: The evidence does not show that the officials or political speakers who announced or promoted the relief acted as the candidate’s agents.

members.legal_issue: A government’s announcement of increased employee allowances to meet an employment demand does not establish a corrupt practice where the government’s action is not shown to be gratification provided by or through the candidate or to have been undertaken by the candidate’s agent.
material_facts: Government employees had given notice that they would strike shortly before the election, and their cooperation was necessary for the election to proceed.
The government considered the employees’ demand for increased allowances legitimate and announced an increase effective at a later date.
The chief minister announced the increase at election meetings.
The evidence did not establish that the government or the chief minister acted as the candidate’s agent.
members.legal_principle: Section 123(1)(A) concerns a candidate’s or agent’s gift, offer, or promise of gratification to induce electoral support. The allowance increase, announced to meet what the government regarded as a legitimate employee demand, was not a gift, offer, or promise of gratification within that provision; nor was the government or chief minister shown to be the candidate’s agent. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The charge of corrupt practice under section 123(1)(A) was not established.

rule.if: election_petition_challenging_election and government_increases_employee_benefits and employees_threaten_work_stoppage and government_responds_to_employee_demand and government_not_candidate_agent

predicates.election_petition_challenging_election: A petitioner seeks to set aside an election by alleging a corrupt practice.
predicates.government_increases_employee_benefits: The government announces an increase in benefits for its employees.
predicates.employees_threaten_work_stoppage: Employees threaten to stop work shortly before the election.
predicates.government_responds_to_employee_demand: The government announces the benefit increase in response to a demand it considers legitimate.
predicates.government_not_candidate_agent: The evidence does not show that the government acted as the candidate’s agent in deciding or announcing the increase.

members.legal_issue: A sale agreement signed only by the vendor may be a valid and enforceable contract when the vendor’s signature is genuine and the purchaser accepts the agreement.
material_facts: The vendor’s signature on the written agreement was found genuine on the basis of expert and witness evidence, and the reviewing court found no reason to disturb that factual finding.
The vendor signed and delivered the agreement to the purchaser, and four witnesses witnessed it.
The vendor acknowledged receipt of an initial payment on the agreement and later endorsed receipt of a further payment on it.
The purchaser accepted and acted on the agreement, and the evidence showed that the parties had concluded a contract.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 10 of the Contract Act, an agreement meeting the requirements for a contract is valid; the court found no applicable requirement that this sale agreement be written, signed by both parties, witnessed, or registered. A sale agreement is bilateral in its promises, but need not be signed by both parties: it may be oral, made through communications, or evidenced by a vendor-signed document delivered to and accepted by the purchaser. The court rejected the contrary views in S. M. Gopal Chetty v. Raman, AIR 1998 Madras 169, and Md. Mohar Ali v. Md. Mamud Ali, AIR 1998 Gauhati 92; it also explained that the latter decision incorrectly described a sale agreement as unilateral, referring to Calamari and Perillo, The Law of Contracts, 4th ed., paragraph 2-10(a).
members.conclusion: The agreement was valid and enforceable even though only the vendor signed it.

rule.if: purchaser_specific_performance_claim and vendor_signed_agreement and vendor_delivered_agreement and purchaser_accepted_agreement

predicates.purchaser_specific_performance_claim: A purchaser sought to enforce a sale agreement through a claim for specific performance.
predicates.vendor_signed_agreement: The vendor signed the sale agreement, and the signature was established as genuine.
predicates.vendor_delivered_agreement: The vendor delivered the signed agreement to the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_accepted_agreement: The purchaser accepted and acted on the delivered agreement.

members.legal_issue: The absence of the buyer’s signature on a sale agreement does not by itself invalidate the agreement when the seller signed it and the connected transaction evidence supports the agreement.
material_facts: The sale agreement was signed by the alleged seller and stated the property and consideration for the proposed sale.
A connected receipt evidenced payment of earnest money, bore the seller’s signature, and also bore the buyer’s signature.
The agreement and receipt formed part of the same transaction.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the absence of the buyer’s signature does not ipso facto nullify an agreement where the seller’s signed document records the agreement to sell for consideration and a connected receipt evidences payment and receipt of earnest money. The Court treated the agreement and receipt as parts of the same transaction.
members.conclusion: The absence of the buyer’s signature on the sale agreement did not invalidate the agreement.

predicates.civil_dispute_over_sale_agreement: The proceeding concerns the validity or enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.seller_signed_agreement_recording_sale_t: The seller signed a document recording the proposed sale and its terms.
predicates.connected_receipt_supports_transaction: A receipt connected with the agreement supports the transaction, including payment or receipt of earnest money.

members.legal_issue: Failure to establish that the purchaser was put in possession of part of the property does not defeat specific performance when the agreement is enforceable and the purchaser has satisfied the other requirements for relief.
material_facts: The purchaser claimed to have been put in possession of part of the property, but that claim was not accepted by the trial court.
The court upheld the finding that the agreement was valid and enforceable and that the purchaser had satisfied the other requirements for specific performance.
members.legal_principle: The court applied Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 and held that, where the agreement is enforceable and the purchaser has satisfactorily established the other requirements for specific performance, failure to prove delivery of possession does not defeat the claim. The court cited no earlier case for this point.
members.conclusion: The failure to establish part performance by delivery of possession did not prevent the decree for specific performance.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_possession_not_established and enforceable_sale_agreement and purchaser_satisfied_other_specific_performance_requirements

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_possession_not_established: The purchaser’s claim to have been put in possession of part of the property was not established.
predicates.enforceable_sale_agreement: The evidence established an enforceable sale agreement between the vendor and purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_satisfied_other_specific_perfo: The purchaser established the other requirements for obtaining specific performance, including performance and readiness and willingness to perform the purchaser’s obligations.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser is not disentitled to specific performance merely because additional property was discussed or requested when the relief sought in the suit is confined to the property covered by the written agreement and the evidence does not establish that the purchaser acted without clean hands.
material_facts: The parties corresponded about draft sale deeds and an alleged additional area that was not part of the written agreement.
The lower courts found that the plaintiff sought relief only for the property covered by the written agreement.
The plaintiff had paid more than half of the consideration, and the defendant avoided executing the sale deed.
The Court found no evidence supporting the allegation that the plaintiff came to court without clean hands.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirements of Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 and affirmed the trial court's exercise of discretion after finding that the plaintiff performed or was ready and willing to perform the agreement, the defendant avoided completion, and the relief was confined to the agreed property. The Court found no evidentiary basis for the unclean-hands allegation and relied on the lower courts' findings that the plaintiff did not claim property outside the agreement.
members.conclusion: The allegations about additional property and unclean hands did not defeat the plaintiff's claim, and the decree for specific performance was properly granted.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaintiff_claimed_only_agreed_property and no_evidence_of_unclean_hands and seller_avoided_completion_after_substantial_payment

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell.
predicates.plaintiff_claimed_only_agreed_property: The plaintiff limited the requested relief to property covered by the agreement, even though additional property had been discussed or requested.
predicates.no_evidence_of_unclean_hands: The evidence did not support the allegation that the plaintiff acted without clean hands in seeking relief.
predicates.seller_avoided_completion_after_substant: The seller accepted a substantial part of the consideration and then avoided completing the sale.

members.legal_issue: A second criminal complaint on the same facts is not absolutely barred, but may be entertained only in exceptional circumstances.
material_facts: A first complaint concerning allegedly forged documents and trespass was investigated, and the police concluded that the dispute was civil and that the complainant had executed the acknowledgment.
The Magistrate accepted the police disposal report, and the complainant’s protest petition and complaint were closed; that order was not challenged.
The complainant later filed another complaint on the same allegations, and the High Court set aside the resulting process on the ground that the second complaint was barred.
The Supreme Court held that the second complaint was not completely barred and remitted the matter for the Magistrate to consider afresh whether there was sufficient ground to take cognizance.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 203 and 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, dismissal of a prior complaint does not create an absolute bar to a second complaint on the same facts, though exceptional circumstances are required for its entertainment. Such circumstances include an incomplete record, a misunderstanding of the complaint, a previous order that was manifestly absurd or unjust, or new facts that could not with reasonable diligence have been produced earlier. If the earlier complaint was dismissed without reasons, the Magistrate may take cognizance if sufficient ground for proceeding exists. The Court relied on Pramatha Nath Taluqdar v. Saroj Ranjan Sarkar and Bindeshwari Prasad Singh v. Kali Singh.
members.conclusion: There is no statutory bar to a second complaint on the same facts, but it may be entertained only in exceptional circumstances. The High Court’s order was set aside, and the Magistrate was directed to consider afresh whether the alleged offences warranted cognizance.

rule.if: second_complaint_proceeding and same_allegations_as_prior_complaint and prior_complaint_disposed and (prior_record_incomplete or prior_order_misunderstood_complaint or prior_order_manifestly_absurd_or_unjust or new_facts_unavailable_with_diligence or (prior_dismissal_without_reasons and sufficient_ground_to_proceed))

predicates.second_complaint_proceeding: A complainant initiated a later criminal complaint after an earlier complaint concerning the matter had been disposed of.
predicates.same_allegations_as_prior_complaint: The later complaint alleged substantially the same facts as the earlier complaint.
predicates.prior_complaint_disposed: A court disposed of the earlier complaint.
predicates.prior_record_incomplete: The earlier decision was made on an incomplete record.
predicates.prior_order_misunderstood_complaint: The earlier decision resulted from a misunderstanding of the nature of the complaint.
predicates.prior_order_manifestly_absurd_or_unjust: The earlier decision was manifestly absurd or unjust.
predicates.new_facts_unavailable_with_diligence: The complainant later produced new facts that could not, with reasonable diligence, have been produced in the earlier proceedings.
predicates.prior_dismissal_without_reasons: The earlier complaint was dismissed without reasons being assigned.
predicates.sufficient_ground_to_proceed: The material before the court provided sufficient ground to proceed on the later complaint.
predicates.second_complaint_may_be_entertained: The court may entertain the later complaint.

members.legal_issue: A second protest petition treated as a complaint may be entertained in exceptional circumstances when the earlier petition was not decided on its merits and the later petition supplies the material needed for consideration.
material_facts: The first protest petition was filed before the police submitted its final report, was not pursued, and was not acted on by the court.
