predicates.purpose_recognized_by_muslim_law: The property was dedicated for a purpose recognized by Muslim law as pious, religious, or charitable.

members.legal_issue: A secured creditor may realise its security outside a company’s winding up without leave of the winding-up court, and a sale made without the court’s intervention is not void merely because leave was not obtained.
material_facts: The company was in winding up and its debenture trustees held security over its assets.
The trustees’ receiver, acting under the security, sold company assets after the winding-up order without seeking leave of the winding-up court or using the court’s process.
The sale was challenged as void under the provision governing sales made without the court’s leave during winding up.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 171, 229 and 232(1) of the Indian Companies Act, a secured creditor remains outside the winding up when realising its security without the court’s intervention, although leave is required to bring or pursue legal proceedings against the company. The words concerning a sale in section 232(1), read alongside attachment, distress and execution, refer to court-mediated sales. The court applied the contextual construction principle expressed in noscitur a sociis and Angus Robertson v. George Day, and the presumption against implied alteration of law, supported by Murugian v. Jainudeen, National Assistance Board v. Wilkinson and Vasudeva Mudaliar v. Srinivasa Pillai. It also relied on Food Controller v. Cork and The Governor-General in Council v. Shiromani Sugar Mills Ltd. for the secured creditor’s position outside the winding up, and considered Kayastha Trading and Banking Corporation Ltd. v. Sat Narain Singh and Baldeo Narain Singh v. The United India Bank Ltd. in explaining the purpose of the amendment.
members.conclusion: The sale was valid and binding; the statutory reference to a sale made without leave applies to sales through the intervention of the court, not a secured creditor’s sale outside the winding up.

predicates.company_in_winding_up: The company whose assets are involved is being wound up.
predicates.secured_creditor_realizes_security: A creditor holding security over the company’s property acts to realise that security.
predicates.sale_without_court_intervention: The secured creditor sells the property outside the winding-up court’s process.

members.legal_issue: A bona fide sale of secured assets outside a company’s winding up cannot be set aside for inadequate publicity or undervalue in the absence of fraud or recklessness.
material_facts: The receiver advertised the intended sale, but the High Court found that the publicity was inadequate.
The courts below found that the accepted offer was the best price available in the circumstances.
The receiver’s bona fides were not challenged, and no fraud or recklessness in making the sale was alleged.
The sale was challenged in proceedings seeking to set it aside.
members.legal_principle: The court accepted the conclusion that, where a secured creditor realises its security outside the winding up and there is no allegation of want of bona fides, recklessness or fraud, the sale is not avoided merely because of inadequate notice or undervalue. The court relied on the concurrent findings that the sale was bona fide and obtained the best price available, and on the secured creditor’s right to realise its security outside the winding up as explained in Food Controller v. Cork.
members.conclusion: The sale could not be avoided on the grounds of inadequate publicity or undervalue in the circumstances of the case.

rule.if: proceeding_seeks_to_set_aside_secured_sale and secured_sale_outside_winding_up and bona_fide_sale and best_price_available and no_fraud_or_recklessness_alleged

predicates.proceeding_seeks_to_set_aside_secured_sa: A proceeding seeks to set aside a sale made by a secured creditor.
predicates.secured_sale_outside_winding_up: The secured creditor sells the property outside the company’s winding-up process.
predicates.bona_fide_sale: The sale was made bona fide.
predicates.best_price_available: The accepted offer was found to be the best price available in the circumstances.
predicates.no_fraud_or_recklessness_alleged: No fraud or recklessness in making the sale was alleged.

members.legal_issue: A former wife who neither establishes nor claims a continuing right to reside in the tenanted premises cannot continue an appeal against the eviction claim after divorce.
material_facts: The wife’s marriage to the tenant was dissolved by mutual-consent divorce while the matter was pending.
She did not place the divorce terms before the Court and did not claim that they gave her a right to reside in the tenanted premises as maintenance.
She sought to continue the appeal against the landlord’s eviction claim.
members.legal_principle: The right of an occupying spouse to defend tenancy rights as part of a residence-based maintenance right ends when the marriage ends, unless the divorce terms or a maintenance provision preserve a right to reside in the tenanted premises. The Court applied its construction of Section 18 and Section 3(b) of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, and Sections 25 and 27 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, together with the principle that a divorced wife’s position depends on the provision made for her residence.
members.conclusion: Because the former wife did not establish or claim a right to residence in the premises under the divorce settlement or a maintenance obligation, she could not prosecute the appeal or defend against the eviction claim. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: eviction_appeal and marriage_ended_by_divorce and not residence_right_claimed_or_established

predicates.eviction_appeal: A person seeks to continue an appeal challenging an eviction claim against the tenant of residential premises.
predicates.marriage_ended_by_divorce: The marriage between the appellant and the tenant has been terminated by divorce.
predicates.residence_right_claimed_or_established: The former spouse claims or establishes that the divorce terms or a maintenance arrangement provide a right to reside in the tenanted premises.

members.legal_issue: A divorced spouse who claims a right to occupy a rented home through a former spouse is not entitled to be added as a party to the landlord’s eviction suit when the former tenant is contesting the suit and the divorce arrangements make no provision for the spouse’s residence in the home.
material_facts: The suit was brought by the landlady to evict the recorded tenant on grounds including unauthorised subletting.

The appellant was divorced from the recorded tenant. The divorce order, made by mutual consent, provided maintenance for the minor children only and made no provision for the appellant’s residence in the tenanted premises.
The recorded tenant was alive, had filed a written statement, and was contesting the eviction suit.
The appellant had no contractual tenancy with the landlady and claimed her right to remain in the premises through her former husband and her role as custodian of their children.
The landlady’s letter described the appellant’s occupation as unauthorised and illegal pending completion of formalities; the Court held that it did not recognize her as a subtenant.
members.legal_principle: Order 1 Rule 10(2) CPC permits addition only of a necessary party, without whom no effective order can be made, or a proper party whose presence is needed for complete and final adjudication. Under B.P. Achala Anand v. S. Appi Reddy, a divorced spouse’s right to residence in a tenanted matrimonial home depends on the divorce arrangements, including whether residence was provided for; the spouse’s rights cannot exceed those of the tenant. The Court also applied the distinction between necessary and proper parties stated in Balvant N. Viswamitra v. Yadav Sadashiv Mule and relied on Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum regarding the discretionary exercise of the joinder power. Sections 3(b), 18 and 23 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 define and address maintenance, including residence; Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 concerns permanent alimony and maintenance. The Court found that the divorce order provided maintenance for the children only and did not provide residence for the appellant.
members.conclusion: The appellant was neither a necessary nor a proper party under Order 1 Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the courts below correctly rejected her application to be added as a defendant.

rule.if: eviction_suit and proposed_party_is_divorced_former_spouse and divorce_order_provides_support_only_for_children and tenant_is_alive_and_contesting and (no_contractual_tenancy_with_landlord and claims_occupation_through_former_spouse)

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of the recorded tenant.
predicates.proposed_party_is_divorced_former_spouse: The person seeking to join the proceeding was divorced from the recorded tenant.
predicates.divorce_order_provides_support_only_for_: The divorce arrangements provided support for the children but did not provide the former spouse residence in the rented home.
predicates.tenant_is_alive_and_contesting: The recorded tenant was alive and actively contesting the eviction proceeding.
predicates.no_contractual_tenancy_with_landlord: The person seeking to join was not a party to a tenancy agreement with the landlord.
predicates.claims_occupation_through_former_spouse: The person seeking to join based the claimed right to occupy the home on the former spouse’s tenancy.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who has possessed a flat without paying rent remains liable for the unpaid balance with simple interest where payment was withheld during litigation.
material_facts: The respondents had possessed the flats since 1984 without paying rent.
The balance demanded by the authority remained unpaid while the writ petition and appeal were pending.
The authority sought interest at a higher rate from the date possession was delivered.
members.legal_principle: The Court considered that the respondents had enjoyed possession without paying rent and had not paid the balance amount. Taking all the circumstances into account, it ordered simple interest at a reduced rate; no statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this direction.
members.conclusion: The respondents were directed to pay the balance with simple interest at 6% per annum from the date they obtained possession until payment.

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dispute: A party appealed in a dispute over the cost of housing units decided in writ proceedings.
predicates.possession_without_rent: The purchasers possessed the housing units without paying rent.
predicates.balance_unpaid_during_litigation: The purchasers had not paid the demanded balance while the dispute was being litigated.

members.legal_issue: A tenant who obtains an interim stay and ultimately loses the substantive proceeding remains liable for appropriate interest on rent withheld during the stay.
material_facts: The tenants obtained court orders staying payment of the enhanced rent.
The tenants’ substantive challenges were dismissed.
The High Court imposed interest at 18% per annum for the period during which payment was stayed.
The Supreme Court held that interest was payable for that period but reduced the rate to 15% per annum, considering the higher rate excessive.
members.legal_principle: A stay order does not confer an additional substantive right, and when the proceeding ends, the court should restore the parties, so far as possible, to the position they would have occupied without the interim order. Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. v. Church of South India Trust Association and Kanoria Chemicals and Industries Ltd. v. U.P. State Electricity Board support liability for payment and interest on amounts withheld under a stay that is followed by dismissal; Kashyap Zip Industries v. Union of India likewise supports interest during the stay period. The rate must be just and not punitive.
members.conclusion: The tenants were liable to pay appropriate interest on the rent withheld during the stay, at 15% per annum rather than 18%.

predicates.court_stay_obtained: The tenant obtained an interim court order staying payment of rent.
predicates.rent_withheld_during_stay: The tenant withheld rent while the interim stay was in force.
predicates.substantive_challenge_dismissed: The court ultimately dismissed the tenant’s substantive challenge.

members.legal_issue: Identification evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction when the occurrence took place in darkness and the alleged source of light is not reliably established.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses said they identified the assailants by a lantern, but the lantern's presence at the scene was open to grave doubt.
The night was dark, and the trial court had accepted that identification was not possible without light.
The accused were familiar with the deceased, yet the prosecution alleged that they mistook him for their intended target.
The State appealed after the High Court acquitted the accused.
members.legal_principle: Identification depends on the circumstances permitting a witness to see the assailant. Where the alleged light source is doubtful and identification otherwise was not possible, the identification evidence may not establish guilt. The court also considered the inconsistency between the claim that witnesses identified the accused by lantern light and the claim that the accused could not identify a person familiar to them. Motive need not be proved by the prosecution, but when a particular motive is alleged, it is relevant to consider whether the pattern of the crime fits that motive. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on.
members.conclusion: The High Court was right to find that the witnesses could not have identified the assailants and to acquit the accused; the State's appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: state_appeal_from_acquittal and occurrence_in_darkness and identification_required_light and lantern_presence_doubtful

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The State appealed a judgment acquitting the accused.
predicates.occurrence_in_darkness: The alleged offence occurred in darkness.
predicates.identification_required_light: The prosecution witnesses' identification of the assailants depended on a source of light.
predicates.lantern_presence_doubtful: The claimed lantern at the scene was not reliably established.

members.legal_issue: Identification evidence is unreliable when the occurrence took place in darkness and the record provides no basis for identifying the assailants.
material_facts: The evidence indicated that the occurrence took place at about 8 p.m., when it would have been dark.
No witness established that a light was burning at the place of the occurrence or that the assailants were identified by their voices.
members.legal_principle: Where the circumstances of an occurrence leave no evidentiary basis for identifying the assailants, the prosecution identification evidence cannot safely establish who committed the offence. The Court relied on the circumstances of the case and cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this point.
members.conclusion: The witnesses’ identification of the appellants was not reliable, and the possibility of mistaken identification could not be excluded.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.occurrence_in_darkness: The occurrence took place in conditions of darkness.
predicates.no_identification_basis: No witness provides a basis, such as adequate lighting or recognition by voice, for identifying the assailants.

members.legal_issue: A public authority cannot create an ad hoc allotment quota outside its declared scheme and allocation policy without lawful authority.
material_facts: The housing scheme brochure prescribed how flats were to be allotted and identified the categories for which reservations were made.
The central government sought to place the applicants in an out-of-turn quota as hard cases, although that category was not authorized for them by the scheme or the stated policy.
The housing authority was a public body subject to the constitutional requirement of equality.
members.legal_principle: A public authority must act within its lawful framework and comply with the standards and procedures by which it has professed to act. Article 14 of the Constitution precludes arbitrary departures from a declared public scheme. The Court relied on Vitarelli v. Seaton, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, and Harjit Singh v. State of Punjab.
members.conclusion: The purported decision to create or apply an unauthorized quota was without jurisdiction and a nullity.

rule.if: public_scheme_allotment_dispute and scheme_defined_allocation_categories and officials_created_an_extra_quota and public_authority_was_bound_by_equal_treatment

predicates.public_scheme_allotment_dispute: The proceeding concerned the allocation of benefits under a public housing scheme.
predicates.scheme_defined_allocation_categories: The published scheme specified the categories and method governing allocation.
predicates.officials_created_an_extra_quota: Officials sought to allocate benefits through a category not provided for by the scheme or the governing policy.
predicates.public_authority_was_bound_by_equal_trea: The authority making or implementing the allocation was a public body required to treat applicants consistently and fairly.

members.legal_issue: A planning authority may not use a general resolution or offence-compounding power to create a blanket scheme for regularizing unauthorized construction without statutory authority.
material_facts: A municipal council passed a resolution proposing common regularization of unauthorized constructions in its area upon payment of penalties.
The state government did not approve the resolution.

The builders had constructed a multi-storey building under a permission that authorized repairs, and they had not applied for permission to retain the unauthorized construction under the statutory notice procedure.
The council was a statutory planning authority whose powers were limited to those conferred by law.
members.legal_principle: Sections 44, 52, 53 and 143 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 provide for development permission, penalties for unauthorized development, notices and applications for retention, and compounding of offences. Section 189 of the Maharashtra Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats and Industrial Townships Act, 1965 does not give the council a general power to regularize unauthorized construction. A statutory authority must act within the powers conferred on it; the power to compound offences is not a general power to regularize construction.
members.conclusion: The council lacked authority to regularize unauthorized construction through the general resolution; the resolution could not confer a right to regularization on the builders.

predicates.proceeding_challenges_blanket_regulariza: The proceeding challenges a public authority's general decision to regularize unauthorized development.
predicates.public_authority_is_statutorily_limited: The public authority exercises powers conferred on it by statute.
predicates.resolution_covers_unauthorized_developme: The public authority adopted a general resolution covering development carried out without the required permission or contrary to permission.
predicates.compounding_power_is_invoked_as_regulari: The public authority relies on its power to compound offences as authority to regularize development generally.
predicates.public_authority_lacks_blanket_regulariz: The public authority has no power to regularize unauthorized development through a blanket scheme unless the law confers that power.

members.legal_issue: Administrative guidelines that lack statutory force do not, by themselves, create an enforceable legal right to an allotment.
material_facts: The applicants relied on an administrative communication concerning consideration of their cases under an out-of-turn quota.
The communication did not identify a statutory basis for that quota, and the governing scheme did not provide the applicants with that allotment entitlement.
The applicants sought to enforce the communication as a basis for obtaining flats.
members.legal_principle: Guidelines are advisory in character and do not, by themselves, confer legal rights; judicial intervention may be warranted where a departure is arbitrary, discriminatory, or defeats a basic public purpose. The Court relied on Narendra Kumar Maheshwari v. Union of India, Maharao Sahib Shri Bhim Singhji v. Union of India, J.R. Raghupathy v. State of A.P., and Uttam Parkash Bansal v. L.I.C. of India. It also distinguished Union of India v. K.P. Joseph, which concerned an executive order within the issuing authority’s jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: The communication and administrative guidance did not confer an enforceable right to allotment.

predicates.public_scheme_allotment_dispute: The proceeding concerned a claim to an allotment under a public scheme.
predicates.claimed_right_rests_on_administrative_gu: The applicants relied on administrative guidance as the basis for their claimed allotment entitlement.
predicates.guidance_lacked_statutory_force: The guidance was not backed by a statutory rule conferring the claimed entitlement.

members.legal_issue: Administrative guidelines governing government pleaders do not, without more, create an enforceable right to control the allocation of government cases.
material_facts: The government pleader relied on state rules concerning government pleaders and their work.
The court characterized those rules as administrative prescriptions serving as guidelines and found that they did not contradict the government’s power to appoint more than one government pleader.
The dispute concerned the internal allocation of work among government pleaders.
members.legal_principle: The Bihar rules concerning government pleaders were administrative guidelines, not a source of legal rights. They neither conferred exclusive control over cases nor displaced the government’s authority under section 2(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order 27 rules 4 and 8B(c), to appoint multiple pleaders and allocate work.
members.conclusion: The state’s administrative rules did not establish an enforceable right to control the allocation of cases, and the allocation of work was an internal arrangement.

predicates.government_pleader_case_allocation_dispu: The proceeding concerns a government pleader’s challenge to the government’s allocation of its cases.
predicates.applicable_rules_are_administrative_guid: The rules governing the pleader are administrative prescriptions intended to serve as guidelines.
predicates.rules_do_not_grant_exclusive_control: The applicable rules do not give one government pleader exclusive control over the government’s cases.

members.legal_issue: Legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel cannot make an unlawful and unauthorized allotment direction enforceable.
material_facts: The applicants relied on the central government communication as the basis for an expectation that they would receive flats.
The communication proposed an exception to the governing scheme despite lacking lawful authority.
The applicants identified no regular and consistent practice supporting the claimed expectation.
members.legal_principle: Legitimate expectation may arise from a valid representation or a regular, consistent, predictable, and certain practice, but it cannot be founded on an illegal or unauthorized order. Even a legitimate expectation does not invariably entitle a person to the expected benefit. The Court relied on Ram Pravesh Singh v. State of Bihar.
members.conclusion: The doctrines of legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel could not be used to enforce the purported allotment direction.

predicates.allotment_claim_relies_on_expected_admin: The applicants claimed an allotment on the basis of a benefit they expected the administration to provide.
predicates.expectation_is_based_on_an_unlawful_dire: The expected benefit arose from an administrative direction made without lawful authority.
predicates.no_established_practice_supports_expecta: The applicants did not rely on a regular and consistent administrative practice supporting the expected benefit.

members.legal_issue: An allottee has no enforceable vested right to possession of land where the proposed allotment would contravene legal restrictions or harm the public interest, and legitimate expectation or estoppel cannot compel an unlawful allotment.
material_facts: The administration included land in an industrial development scheme despite an existing forest reservation and restrictions on construction around an air-force base.
Applicants paid part or all of the price for plots, and some received lease deeds or formal possession, but the legal restrictions prevented the intended industrial use of some land.
The administration made a mistake in preparing the scheme, while the court found no material establishing mala fides.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(3) of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, and Rules 4, 6 and 10 of the Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973, do not create a vested right to use land contrary to other legal restrictions. Public interest prevails over promissory estoppel and legitimate expectation when fulfilment of a promise would breach the law. The Court relied on M/s Jit Ram Shiv Kumar v. State of Haryana, distinguishing Union of India v. Indo-Afgan Agencies Ltd. and Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. v. State of U.P., and referred to M. Ramanatha Pillai v. State of Kerala and State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. It also applied the principles that public welfare is paramount and that the law does not compel the impossible, while recognizing the duty of administrative fairness to provide appropriate redress for losses caused by official error.
members.conclusion: The applicants could not compel delivery of the original plots or rely on vested rights, promissory estoppel, or legitimate expectation to require allotments contrary to law and public interest. The administration remained responsible for fair administrative redress, but monetary compensation was not ordered because it would also harm the public interest.

predicates.industrial_plot_allotment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns an allotment of land for industrial use.
predicates.proposed_land_legally_restricted: The proposed land is subject to a legal restriction that prevents the intended use.
predicates.proposed_use_harms_public_interest: Giving effect to the proposed allotment would harm the public interest.

members.legal_issue: A transfer of possession and tenancy rights to another entity through a court-sanctioned amalgamation can attract the ground for eviction based on transfer without the landlord’s written consent, regardless of the transfer’s voluntariness or its purpose.
material_facts: The original tenant’s undertaking in India was amalgamated with an Indian company under a scheme sanctioned by a court.
The scheme transferred the original tenant’s leases and tenancy rights to the Indian company, which thereafter occupied the premises and carried on business there.
The original tenant ceased to exist as a separate corporate entity from the effective date of the amalgamation.
The landlord had not given written consent to the transfer.
The foreign-exchange direction required a reduction in the original tenant’s equity capital but did not require amalgamation; the companies chose that method of restructuring.
members.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act covers subletting, assignment, or otherwise parting with possession without the landlord’s written consent. Whether the transfer was voluntary, involuntary, or undertaken to comply with law is irrelevant. The Court relied on M/s. Parasram Harnand Rao v. M/s. Shanti Prasad Narinder Kumar Jain, M/s. General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd. v. M.A. Khader, and Cox & Kings Ltd. v. Chander Malhotra. It also considered sections 391 and 394 of the Companies Act, 1956, and section 29 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973, and distinguished Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Shyam Co-operative Housing Society, which concerned a transfer provided for by statute.
members.conclusion: The transfer brought the case within the statutory ground for eviction, and the eviction order was upheld.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_transferred_possession_to_another_entity and transferee_occupied_premises and no_written_landlord_consent

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.tenant_transferred_possession_to_another: The tenant transferred possession of the rented premises to another entity.
predicates.transferee_occupied_premises: The recipient entity took possession of and occupied the premises.
predicates.no_written_landlord_consent: The landlord had not given written consent to the transfer of possession.

members.legal_issue: A tenant’s transfer of its tenancy interest and possession to another company through a tenant-initiated amalgamation sanctioned by a court constitutes an actionable transfer under rent-control law when the landlord has not consented in writing.
material_facts: The original company held the tenancy under a written rental agreement that prohibited subletting without the landlord’s written consent.
The original company petitioned for an amalgamation with another company, and the court sanctioned a scheme transferring its property and tenancy rights to the other company.
The original company later ceased to exist, and the transferee company occupied the premises.
The landlord had not given written consent to the transfer.
The landlord sought eviction, and the tenant companies appealed the eviction order.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(ii)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 permits eviction where a tenant transfers its right under the lease or sublets without the landlord’s written consent; the Act contains no exception for a transfer under a court-sanctioned amalgamation. Sections 391 and 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 enable a court-sanctioned scheme to transfer a company’s rights and liabilities, but the transfer here followed a petition by the transferor company and was not involuntary. The court relied on Sabhayanidhi Virudhunagar Ltd. v. A.S.R. Subrahamanya Nadar for the effect of a sanctioned scheme, Parasaram Harnand Rao v. Shanti Prasad Narinder Kumar Jain for the breadth of provisions covering transfers of possession, and Venkatarama Iyer v. Renters Ltd.; it held Devarajulu Naidu v. Ethirajavalli Thyaramma inapplicable.
members.conclusion: The amalgamation resulted in a transfer of the original tenant’s interest in the premises to the transferee company, without the landlord’s written consent, and the transferee was liable to eviction. The court’s sanction of the scheme did not make the transfer involuntary or exempt it from rent-control law.

members.legal_issue: A selection committee may consider service reports prepared late where the applicable service rules preserve their validity, and an officer should not lose consideration because the responsible reporting authority failed to prepare reports on time.
material_facts: Some annual service reports had been prepared after the deadline that applied under an earlier version of the service rules.
Later amendments removed the deadline, and the rules subsequently in force preserved matters duly done under the earlier rules.
The Selection Committee considered the reports in assessing the candidates.
members.legal_principle: The Karnataka Civil Services (Performance Reports) Rules, 1994, as amended in 1999, removed the relevant time limit retrospectively; the 2000 Rules preserved matters done under the earlier rules. An officer should not suffer because the authority responsible for preparing or reviewing a report failed to do so within time.
members.conclusion: The reports were not required to be ignored, and considering them did not constitute a statutory breach.

predicates.promotion_selection_proceeding: The proceeding concerns selection for promotion to a public service.
predicates.service_rules_preserve_late_reports: The applicable service rules preserve the validity of reports prepared late under the governing framework.
predicates.candidate_not_responsible_for_reporting_: The delay in preparing the reports resulted from the reporting or reviewing authority rather than the candidate.

members.legal_issue: A selection committee may obtain and consider a special service report when ordinary annual reports are unavailable, and the candidate should not be penalized for the reporting authority’s failure to prepare those reports.
material_facts: Annual reports for some years were unavailable because the reporting or reviewing authorities had not prepared them.
A special report was obtained for a candidate whose ordinary reports were missing.
The Selection Committee considered that special report in assessing the candidate.
members.legal_principle: Rule 11-A of the Karnataka Civil Services (Performance Reports) (Amendment) Rules, 1996 permitted the appointing authority to direct preparation of reports for periods for which reports were unavailable. The Court also recognized that special reports may be obtained in administrative practice so that an officer does not suffer from an authority’s failure to complete reporting.
members.conclusion: Obtaining and considering the special report was a permissible administrative practice and was not arbitrary or discriminatory.

predicates.promotion_selection_proceeding: The proceeding concerns selection for promotion to a public service.
predicates.annual_reports_unavailable: Ordinary annual service reports are missing for one or more relevant periods.
predicates.special_report_obtained_for_missing_peri: The authority obtains a special report addressing a period for which an ordinary report is unavailable.
predicates.candidate_not_responsible_for_missing_re: The missing reports resulted from the reporting or reviewing authority rather than the candidate.

members.legal_issue: A state authority that fails to decide a mining-lease application within the prescribed period cannot later grant that application when the applicable rules treat the failure as a refusal.
material_facts: An applicant sought a mining lease, and the application remained undisposed of beyond the period applicable to pending applications.
The state authority later granted the lease after that period had expired.
The central revisional authority set the grant aside on the basis that the application had been deemed refused.
members.legal_principle: Reading rules 28(1-A) and 57(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 together, the deemed refusal operates for the purposes of the rules generally, not merely to permit an application for review. The state authority therefore loses power to deal with the application after the prescribed period. Dey Gupta & Company v. State of Bihar was referred to, but its contrary view that the authority retained power to decide after the period was not accepted.
members.conclusion: The failure to decide within the prescribed period amounted to refusal for the purposes of the rules, and the state authority was incompetent to grant the lease after the period expired.

rule.if: mining_lease_application and decision_deadline_expired and application_undisposed and applicable_rules_treat_failure_as_refusal

predicates.mining_lease_application: An applicant sought a mining lease from a state authority.
predicates.decision_deadline_expired: The time allowed for the state authority to decide the application passed.
predicates.application_undisposed: The state authority had not decided the application by the end of the allowed period.
predicates.applicable_rules_treat_failure_as_refusa: The applicable rules treated failure to decide within the allowed period as a refusal for the purposes of those rules.

members.legal_issue: A government representation that an application remains pending cannot prevent application of a mandatory statutory rule that deems the application refused after the decision period expires.
material_facts: In court proceedings, a government advocate represented that the applicant's lease application was still pending and that the state government would decide it on the merits.
The application had remained undecided beyond the period prescribed by the applicable rules.
The state government later granted the lease, and the High Court relied on the representation in concluding that the state could not contend that the application had been refused.
members.legal_principle: Rules 28(1-A) and 57(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 are statutory rules that bind the government and cannot be waived by it. A representation by a government advocate cannot alter their requirements or confer authority inconsistent with them.
members.conclusion: The representation could not change the legal effect of the rules or confer power on the state government to act contrary to them; there can be no estoppel against a statute.

predicates.mining_lease_application: An applicant sought a mining lease from a state authority.
predicates.mandatory_rule_governs_application: A mandatory rule governed how or when the state authority could decide the application.
predicates.government_represented_application_as_pe: A government representative told a court that the application remained pending.

members.legal_issue: A decree entered against an original defendant after the defendant’s interest has devolved is not executable against the successor who was not made a party to the suit.
material_facts: The State acquired the relevant division while the suit was pending.
The suit was decreed against the original defendant after that acquisition, without the State being added as a party.
The decree-holder later sought to execute the decree against the State.
The plaintiff had not sought leave to continue the suit against the State.
members.legal_principle: Order XXII Rule 10 CPC permits a suit to be continued against a person upon whom an interest devolves during the suit, with leave of the court; the plaintiff who seeks to continue against that person normally must apply for leave. Section 47 CPC places execution questions before the executing court. Sections 50 and 52 concern execution against legal representatives in specified circumstances and do not authorize execution against a successor who was not brought on record after devolution during the suit. The Court distinguished State of Orissa v. Klockner and Company, which addressed successor-in-interest status but not this execution issue, and Bhagwan Dass Chopra v. United Bank of India, which concerned proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act. It relied on Dhurandhar Prasad Singh v. Jai Prakash University for the requirement of leave under Order XXII Rule 10, and distinguished Rai Charan Mandal v. Biswanath Mandal and Mahanth Harihar Gir v. Karu Lal on their facts.
members.conclusion: Shah J. held that the decree was not binding on, and could not be executed against, the State, and allowed the appeal. The concluding order in the supplied text records a difference of opinion and directs that the matter be placed before a larger Bench.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and interest_devolved_during_pending_suit and decree_entered_after_devolution and successor_not_made_party and plaintiff_did_not_seek_leave

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder sought to enforce a decree against a successor to an original defendant.
predicates.interest_devolved_during_pending_suit: The original defendant’s interest passed to a successor while the suit was pending.
predicates.decree_entered_after_devolution: The court entered the decree after the interest had passed to the successor.
predicates.successor_not_made_party: The successor was not added as a party to the suit before the decree was entered.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_seek_leave: The plaintiff did not seek the court’s permission to continue the suit against the successor.
predicates.decree_not_executable_against_successor: The decree cannot be enforced against the successor.

members.legal_issue: Execution of a decree cannot proceed against a person who was named in the suit but against whom the operative decree granted no relief.
material_facts: A minor was impleaded as a defendant in the specific-performance suit, but the decree expressly granted relief against the other defendants only and stated that no relief was sought against him.
Execution was sought against the minor, who claimed an interest in the property and had a separate suit concerning that claim pending.
The High Court held that execution could not be pursued against him because there was no decree against him, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal challenging that result.
members.legal_principle: Execution must remain within the terms of the decree and cannot impose liability on a person against whom the decree grants no relief. The rule that a court cannot go behind or beyond the decree, applied in construing decrees as discussed in Topanmal Chhotamal v. Kundomal Gangaram, supports this result.
members.conclusion: Execution cannot proceed against the person who was not made subject to the decree; his claim to an interest in the property depends on the outcome of his pending suit.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party sought to enforce a court decree against a person.
predicates.person_named_as_defendant: The person was named as a defendant in the proceeding that resulted in the decree.
predicates.operative_decree_grants_no_relief_agains: The operative decree granted no relief against that person.

members.legal_issue: A de facto guardian who is not the minor’s legal guardian cannot bind the minor’s immovable property through a settlement, and describing the transaction as a family arrangement does not validate it.
material_facts: A minor heir’s elder brother executed a deed distributing estate property on the minor’s behalf.
The brother was not the minor’s legal guardian and had no authority to transfer the minor’s interest in immovable property.
The deed was defended as a family settlement and was found by the trial court to be beneficial to the minor.
The deed was held void, not only as to the minor but as to all parties to it.
members.legal_principle: Under Mahomedan law, a de facto guardian has no power to convey to another an interest in a minor’s immovable property that the transferee can enforce against the minor; whether the transaction benefits the minor is immaterial. A void transaction cannot be made valid merely by describing it as a family arrangement. The Court relied on Imambandi v. Mutsaddi (1918) 45 I.A. 73 and rejected the contrary reasoning in Mahomed Keramutullah Miah v. Keramatulla, A.I.R. 1919 Cal. 218, and Ameer Hassan v. Md. Ejaz Hussain, A.I.R. 1929 Oudh 134.
members.conclusion: The deed could not bind the minor, and its invalidity meant it was void as to all parties, including those who were legally competent.

predicates.minor_heir_property_settlement_dispute: The dispute concerns a settlement of estate property that purports to affect a minor heir’s interest.
predicates.minor_interest_in_immovable_property_tra: The settlement purports to transfer or distribute the minor’s interest in immovable property.
predicates.representative_not_legal_guardian: The person acting for the minor is not the minor’s legal guardian.

members.legal_issue: A purported guardian who is not legally recognized as a guardian cannot validly alienate a minor’s separate property merely by managing the minor’s affairs.
material_facts: A minor inherited a share of property from her father, and the property was not joint family property.
The minor’s sister, who was not a guardian within the statutory definition, purported to act as the minor’s guardian and sold the minor’s share to a purchaser.
The purchaser took possession under the sale, and the minor’s later purchaser claimed the minor’s share under a subsequent sale deed.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(b), 6 and 11 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, a sister who is not a legally recognized guardian cannot deal with a minor’s property merely as a de facto guardian or manager; Section 11 prohibits such a disposition, which is void ab initio. Section 8 provides for a natural guardian’s powers and for dispositions in contravention of its requirements to be voidable, but that regime does not validate a de facto manager’s disposition under Section 11. The Court relied on Kondamudi Sriramulu v. Myneni Pundarikakshayya, which described a de facto guardian as a de facto manager, and Ganayya v. Radhabai, which applied Section 11’s prohibition. It distinguished Sri Narayan Bal v. Sridhar Sutar because that case concerned an undivided interest in joint family property, and noted that the pre-Act rule in Hunooman Persaud Pandey’s case did not survive the statutory prohibition.
members.conclusion: The sister’s sale of the minor’s share was void, and the first purchaser acquired no interest in it. The sale was prohibited irrespective of whether it was for legal necessity; the ruling on joint-family property was unnecessary because the property was not joint family property.

predicates.transferor_managed_minor_estate: The transferor had taken on the management of the minor’s estate and purported to transfer the minor’s property.

members.legal_issue: An abettor’s liability for instigating an offence is not extinguished merely because the person instigated is acquitted, but liability for abetment on the basis that the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment requires proof of that connection.
material_facts: The appellant was found to have instigated a co-accused to set fire to a hut.
The co-accused was acquitted of setting fire to the hut, and the courts found that he had not done so.
Although the hut was set on fire by someone, there was no finding that the person who set it on fire participated in the incident with the appellant or acted at his instigation.
The High Court’s finding that the appellant had instigated the co-accused was maintained.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 107 and 108 of the Indian Penal Code, abetment may occur through instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid, and the abetted act need not be committed for abetment by instigation or conspiracy to be complete. Section 109 applies when the act is committed in consequence of the abetment; section 115 provides punishment for abetting an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life when that offence is not committed in consequence of the abetment. The Court relied on Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. The King Emperor and Faguna Kanta Nath v. The State of Assam, and distinguished Gallu Sah v. The State of Bihar, where the findings supported that a member of the unlawful assembly had acted in consequence of the appellant’s instigation. Where the alleged abetment is intentional aid, acquittal of the alleged principal may defeat the charge if the underlying offence is not established.
members.conclusion: The conviction for abetment on the basis that the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment could not stand because the required causal connection was not established. The appellant remained guilty of abetting the offence by instigation even though the instigated person did not commit it, so the conviction was altered to abetment of an uncompleted offence and the sentence was reduced.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_abettor_convicti: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a conviction for abetting an offence.
predicates.appellant_instigated_another_to_commit_o: The appellant instigated another person to commit the offence.
predicates.instigated_person_did_not_commit_offence: The person who was instigated did not commit the offence.
predicates.another_person_committed_act_without_fin: Another person committed the relevant act, but the courts made no finding that this person acted in consequence of the appellant’s instigation.

members.legal_issue: A person may be convicted of abetting an offence even when the alleged principal offender is acquitted, if the evidence establishes that the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment.
material_facts: The trial court found that the accused ordered another member of an unlawful assembly to set fire to a hut and that the hut was set on fire in consequence of that abetment.
The appellate court acquitted the person accused of setting the fire because the evidence did not satisfactorily establish that he was the person who did so.
The appellate court nevertheless found that the hut had been set on fire by a member of the unlawful assembly and that the accused had given the order to set it on fire.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 107 and 108 of the Indian Penal Code, abetment includes instigating another to do an act, and an abettor is a person who abets the commission of an offence. Under section 109, where the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor is punishable as provided for the offence; its explanation treats an act as committed in consequence of abetment when it follows the instigation, conspiracy, or aid constituting the abetment. The general proposition in Raja Khan v. Emperor, AIR 1920 Cal. 834, that failure to establish the principal offence precludes abetment liability does not apply where evidence satisfactorily establishes that the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment; Umadasi Dasi v. Emperor, (1924) ILR 52 Cal. 112, recognized that exception.
members.conclusion: The conviction for abetting the offence was legally sound because the findings established that the offence was committed in consequence of the accused’s instigation, notwithstanding the alleged principal offender’s acquittal.

rule.if: abetment_conviction_appeal and alleged_principal_acquitted and accused_instigated_offence and offence_committed and offence_followed_instigation

predicates.abetment_conviction_appeal: The proceeding challenges a conviction for abetting an offence.
predicates.alleged_principal_acquitted: The person alleged to have personally committed the offence was acquitted.
predicates.accused_instigated_offence: The accused instigated another person to commit the offence.
predicates.offence_committed: The evidence establishes that the offence was in fact committed.
predicates.offence_followed_instigation: The evidence establishes that the offence was committed in consequence of the accused’s instigation.

members.legal_issue: For a tenant eviction suit, the first hearing is the date fixed for the court to consider the dispute, rather than the date fixed for filing a written statement or the date on which the court actually takes up the hearing.
material_facts: The eviction suit was heard by a Court of Small Causes, whose summons were for final disposal of the suit.
The governing explanation defined the first hearing by reference to the first date for a step or proceeding mentioned in the summons.
The dispute concerned whether the relevant date was the date fixed for hearing or the date on which the court actually applied its mind or settled issues.
members.legal_principle: Section 20(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, read with Explanation (a) added by the 1976 amendment, makes the first hearing the first date for a step or proceeding mentioned in the summons. In light of Order 5, Rules 5 and 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, summons in a Small Causes Court suit are for final disposal. Siraj Ahmad Siddiqui v. Prem Nath Kapoor held that the date is when the court proposes to apply its mind to the points in controversy and frame issues if necessary, not the date for filing a written statement. Advaita Anand v. Judge Small Causes Court followed that interpretation and overruled Srinath Aggarwal to the extent it treated the written-statement date as the relevant step. The earlier decisions in Ved Prakash Wadhwa v. Vishwa Mohan and Sham Lal v. Atme Nand Jain Sabha were also discussed; the pre-amendment interpretation in Ved Prakash Wadhwa did not displace the post-amendment decisions.
members.conclusion: The first hearing is the date fixed for the purpose of the court considering the points in controversy and, if necessary, framing issues. The date fixed for filing a written statement is not the first hearing, and the relevant date is not postponed merely because the court does not actually hear the matter on that date.

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking eviction of a tenant and the tenant's opportunity to avoid eviction by making the required payment.
predicates.small_causes_summons_for_final_disposal: The summons in the tenant eviction suit fixes a date for final disposal of the suit.

members.legal_issue: The first hearing for tendering rent arrears in a rent-control eviction proceeding is the date when the court applies its mind to the case, not merely the returnable date stated in the summons.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction on the ground of rent default.

On the returnable date, the tenant appeared and sought time to file a written statement; the matter was adjourned without the Rent Controller assessing the application costs or taking up the hearing of the case.
On the next date, the tenant filed a written statement and tendered the arrears, interest, and costs assessed by the Rent Controller.
The Rent Controller treated the returnable date as the first hearing and ordered eviction; the appellate authority held the later tender valid, but the High Court restored the eviction order.
members.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the tenant must tender the rent arrears, interest, and assessed application costs by the first hearing. Because the Act is beneficial legislation intended to protect tenants, “first hearing” means the date when the court applies its mind to the case, not the returnable date. The Court followed Ved Prakash v. Vishwa Mohan, which interpreted a pari materia provision, and approved Mangat Rai v. Ved Prakash, Shah Ambalal Chhotalal v. Shah Babal Das Dayabhai, and Khanderao Malkarjun Dhotre v. Anandrao Laxmanrao Mashalkar. The Court also relied on the procedural significance of preliminary examination and settlement of issues reflected in Orders 10, 14, and 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.conclusion: The returnable date was not the first hearing. The tenant's tender on the later date, when the application costs were assessed, was valid; the eviction order was set aside and the application for eviction dismissed.

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and appearance_was_only_for_appearance and hearing_had_not_started and costs_not_assessed_on_return_date and tender_made_when_costs_were_assessed

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord initiated a rent-control proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant for rent default.
predicates.appearance_was_only_for_appearance: On the summons return date, the tenant appeared and sought time to file a written response, and the court adjourned the matter.
predicates.hearing_had_not_started: The court had not yet taken up the case for hearing or applied its mind to it.
predicates.costs_not_assessed_on_return_date: The court had not assessed the application costs on the summons return date.
predicates.tender_made_when_costs_were_assessed: The tenant tendered the rent arrears, interest, and costs on a later date when the court assessed those costs.

members.legal_issue: Allowing review of a decree vacates and supersedes the original decree.
material_facts: A court allowed an application to review an original decree and then issued a new decree changing the compensation awarded.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the established rule that allowing review vacates the original decree and the decree subsequently passed on review supersedes it. It relied on Nibaran Chandra Sikdar v. Abdul Hakim, Kanhaiya Lal v. Baldev Prasad, Brijbaso Lal v. Salig Ram, and Pyari Mohan Kundu v. Kalu Khan; the review application had been made under Order 47, Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code.
members.conclusion: The decree passed on review was a new decree that superseded the original decree, whether it modified, reversed, or confirmed it.

predicates.a_review_proceeding_was_decided: A court considered an application to review a decree.
predicates.review_application_was_allowed: The court granted the application to review the decree.

members.legal_issue: Granting review supersedes the original decree, and an appeal cannot be maintained against the superseded decree in its entirety.
material_facts: The suit for specific performance was dismissed in its entirety.
The trial court later granted review because the original judgment had not decided whether the earnest money should be refunded or forfeited, and restored the suit for that limited purpose.
The respondents appealed against the original dismissal decree in its entirety after the review had been granted.
The original decree did not survive the order granting review.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XLVII Rules 1, 4 and 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure, granting review displaces the original decree and permits the court to rehear the case or make directions for rehearing. An appeal under Section 96 must be maintainable when filed; it cannot be filed in anticipation of a decree that may later become appealable. The Court relied on Sushil Kumar Sen v. State of Bihar, Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbaiah Choudhury, and Gour Krishna Sarkar v. Nilmadhab Saha. It distinguished Hameed Joharan v. Abdul Salem and Ratansingh v. Vijaysingh, and held that the appeal could concern only the part of the decree not reopened by review.
members.conclusion: The High Court was not correct in holding that the appeal against the original decree in its entirety was maintainable.

rule.if: civil_decree_appeal and review_granted and original_decree_superseded and appeal_challenges_entire_original_decree

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: A party brought an appeal from a civil decree.
predicates.review_granted: The court granted review of the decree and reopened some part of the case.
predicates.original_decree_superseded: The grant of review displaced the original decree.
predicates.appeal_challenges_entire_original_decree: The appellant challenged the original decree in its entirety, including matters reopened by review.
predicates.appeal_not_maintainable: The appeal against the superseded decree in its entirety cannot be maintained.

members.legal_issue: A pre-emptor who does not exercise the right of pre-emption when it first arises on a transfer cannot claim that right against a later transfer of the same property.
material_facts: The property had been transferred in earlier transactions, including a transfer made after the relevant pre-emption law came into force.
The plaintiff did not challenge the post-commencement transfer.
The plaintiff later sued to enforce pre-emption rights in relation to a subsequent transfer of the same property; the plaintiff’s eligibility to claim pre-emption was otherwise undisputed.
The High Court held the later suit timely, while the trial court and first appellate court had held it barred.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3, 6, 8, 9 and 21 of the Rajasthan Pre-Emption Act, 1966, read with Article 97 of the Limitation Act, 1963, govern the right, its exercise and limitation. A pre-emption right is a weak, secondary right of substitution, not a right to the property itself, and must be superior to the vendee’s right when exercised. Under Section 9, failure to exercise the right in relation to a transaction results in its loss; that loss is attributable both to the transaction and to the pre-emptor, so the right does not arise again for that person on a later sale of the same property. The Court relied on Barasat Eye Hospital v. Kaustabh Mondal and Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh for the nature of the right as substitution; on Indira Bai v. Nand Kishore for the principle that a pre-emptor may give up the right and that it does not pass to anyone; and on the consistent approach in Ghanshyam v. Chand Bihari, Rukmani Devi v. Prabhu Narayan and Prahlad Kumar v. Kishan Chand. The Court distinguished Kutina Bibi v. Baikuntha Chandra Dutta on its facts.
members.conclusion: The right of pre-emption was exercisable only on the first occasion when it arose. By not exercising it against the earlier post-commencement transfer, the plaintiff waived the right and could not enforce it against the later transfer. The suit was barred, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the trial court and first appellate court orders were upheld.

rule.if: preemption_enforcement_suit and earlier_qualifying_transfer and earlier_transfer_not_challenged and later_transfer_of_same_property

predicates.preemption_enforcement_suit: A plaintiff brings a suit seeking to enforce a right of pre-emption.
predicates.earlier_qualifying_transfer: The same property was transferred earlier after the pre-emption right had become legally available to the plaintiff.
predicates.earlier_transfer_not_challenged: The plaintiff did not seek to enforce the pre-emption right in relation to that earlier transfer.
predicates.later_transfer_of_same_property: A later transfer of the same property is the transaction against which the plaintiff seeks pre-emption.
predicates.subsequent_preemption_claim_barred: The plaintiff cannot enforce the pre-emption right against the later transfer.

members.legal_issue: A claimed right of pre-emption is unavailable where the claimant, despite liberty to pursue the claim, does not exercise it and later deals with the disputed property.
material_facts: The co-owner claimed a right of pre-emption under the applicable succession law.
After a court proceeding concerning redemption of the mortgage, the co-owner had liberty to pursue any rights in the property according to law.
The co-owner did not pursue the claim within the period contemplated by the court’s decision and later sold the property.
The parties’ conduct also included allowing the property to face a bank sale rather than taking steps to preserve their claimed interests.
members.legal_principle: Applying the conduct-based and equitable reasoning in the judgment to the claimed right under Portuguese law, the Court held that the co-owners’ failure to pursue the right after being given liberty to do so, together with their subsequent conduct, meant that no right of pre-emption remained available.
members.conclusion: The Court held that the co-owners had no available right of pre-emption in the circumstances.

rule.if: property_dispute_involving_claimed_preemption and claimant_given_liberty_to_pursue_right and claimant_did_not_pursue_right and claimant_later_dealt_with_property

predicates.property_dispute_involving_claimed_preem: The proceeding concerns a disputed property over which a person claims a right of pre-emption.
predicates.claimant_given_liberty_to_pursue_right: A court or other proceeding leaves the claimant at liberty to pursue the claimed property right according to law.
predicates.claimant_did_not_pursue_right: The claimant takes no timely step to pursue the claimed right after that liberty is given.
predicates.claimant_later_dealt_with_property: The claimant later sells or otherwise deals with the disputed property.

members.legal_issue: A tenant of qualifying land acquires occupancy-tenant status when the landlord’s disability existed when the lease was granted but had ended by the commencement of the governing code.
material_facts: The land was ryotwari land leased for cultivation to a tenant by the Court of Wards while managing the landlord’s estate.
The landlord was a minor when the lease was granted but had attained majority before the code commenced.
After the estate was released from the Court of Wards, the landlord terminated the tenancy and sued for possession and mesne profits.
The tenant held land of the kind described in the provision conferring occupancy-tenant status.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 185(1) and 185(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, a tenant holding land of the specified kind acquires occupancy-tenant status, except where the tenant holds the land from a disabled Bhumiswami. Read with sections 168(2) and 168(5), the relevant question is whether the Bhumiswami belonged to a disabled class when the Code commenced, not whether the landlord was disabled when the earlier lease was made. The Court relied on Rao Nihalkaran v. Ramgopal, [1966] 3 S.C.R. 427.
members.conclusion: The landlord’s earlier minority did not attract the exception because the landlord was not disabled when the code commenced. The tenant acquired occupancy-tenant status at that time; the appeal was allowed and the possession suit was dismissed.

predicates.occupancy_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a tenant acquired statutory occupancy-tenant status in land.
predicates.tenant_held_qualifying_land_at_commencem: The tenant held land that qualified for statutory conversion to occupancy-tenant status when the governing code commenced.
predicates.landlord_disabled_at_commencement: The landlord belonged to a legally disabled class when the governing code commenced.

members.legal_issue: A person inducted as a tenant of inam land may acquire occupancy-tenant status even if the tenancy was terminated before the revenue code commenced, provided the person continued to hold the land at commencement.
material_facts: The landholder terminated the tenancy on the ground that he wanted the land for personal cultivation and sued for ejectment.
The tenant continued to hold the land when the revenue code came into force.
The tenant claimed occupancy-tenant rights under the code while the ejectment suit was pending.
members.legal_principle: Under section 185(1)(ii)(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, the expression “tenant” is read in context and in light of the protective purpose of the Madhya Bharat Muafi and Inam Tenants and Sub-tenants Protection Act, 1954. The definition in section 2(y) does not determine the status of a person at the code’s commencement. Sections 3 and 4 of the 1954 Act protected a person inducted as a tenant who continued to hold the land even after the contractual relationship had ended. The parallel treatment of ryotwari sub-lessees under section 185(1)(ii)(b), read with the Madhya Bharat Ryotwari Sub-Lessee Protection Act, 1955, supports the same construction for inam-land tenants.
members.conclusion: The tenant acquired occupancy-tenant rights under the code notwithstanding the earlier termination of the tenancy.

rule.if: occupancy_status_claim and inam_land_tenancy and tenancy_terminated_before_code and continued_to_hold_land

predicates.occupancy_status_claim: The person claimed the statutory status of an occupancy tenant.
predicates.inam_land_tenancy: The person had been inducted into inam land in a tenant category covered by the statutory protection.
predicates.tenancy_terminated_before_code: The tenancy relationship had ended before the revenue code commenced.
predicates.continued_to_hold_land: The person remained in possession of the land when the revenue code commenced.

members.legal_issue: An objection to an arbitral award is not time-barred when the prescribed notice that the award has been filed in court was not served.
material_facts: A party sued to have the award made a rule of court.
The opposing party challenged the award in its written statement.
There was no proof that the opposing party had been served with notice that the award had been filed in court.
members.legal_principle: Article 158 of the Limitation Act, 1908, allows 30 days to apply to set aside an award or have it remitted, running from service of notice of the filing of the award. Without proof of service of that notice, the time period does not bar the objection.
members.conclusion: The objection to the award could not be rejected as time-barred.

predicates.award_objection_proceeding: A party to an arbitration challenges the award in a court proceeding to have it set aside or remitted.
predicates.notice_of_award_filing_not_served: The party challenging the award was not served with notice that the award had been filed in court.
predicates.award_objection_is_timely: The objection to the award is not barred by the applicable time limit.

members.legal_issue: A reference application is not barred solely because it was filed more than six weeks after receipt of a notice of the award when the notice was not accompanied by a copy of the award.
material_facts: The applicant was absent when the award was made and received a notice of the award from the Collector.
The notice was not accompanied by a copy of the award; the applicant obtained a certified copy through an advocate and then applied for a reference.
The State produced no evidence that a copy of the award had been sent with the notice.
The Reference Court and the High Court treated the application as late without considering the absence of the copy.
members.legal_principle: Sections 12(2) and 18(1) and (2)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require notice of the award to enable an interested person to exercise the right to seek a reference effectively; a copy of the award should accompany the notice. The limitation principles in Harish Chandra Raj Singh v. Land Acquisition Officer, AIR 1961 SC 1500, State of Punjab v. Qaisar Jehan Begum, AIR 1963 SC 1604, and Bhagwan Das v. State of Uttar Pradesh, (2010) 3 SCC 545, recognize the importance of knowledge of the essential contents of the award.
members.conclusion: The application was not barred on the basis relied on by the lower courts, which erred in rejecting the reference as time-barred.

rule.if: compensation_reference_application and notice_received and notice_lacked_award_copy and application_filed_after_notice_based_limit

predicates.compensation_reference_application: An interested person applied to have a land-acquisition compensation dispute referred for determination.
predicates.notice_received: The interested person received notice that the award had been made.
predicates.notice_lacked_award_copy: The notice delivered to the interested person did not include a copy of the award.
predicates.application_filed_after_notice_based_lim: The interested person filed the reference application after the period ordinarily measured from receipt of the notice.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator's reliance on personal knowledge, without informing the parties of that knowledge and giving them an opportunity to respond, vitiates the award when the reference does not specifically authorize that method of decision.
material_facts: The arbitrators decided the dispute primarily on the basis of their personal knowledge.
The agreement permitted the arbitrators to decide in whatever manner they thought fit but did not specifically authorize reliance on personal knowledge.
The parties were not informed of the nature of the arbitrators' personal knowledge or given an opportunity to correct any misconception or wrong assumption.
members.legal_principle: Arbitration proceedings are quasi-judicial and must comply with natural justice. A general term allowing arbitrators to decide in whatever manner they think fit does not authorize them to decide on personal knowledge. Parties may include terms in a reference unless prohibited by law, and the ordinary implied requirement that arbitrators decide according to law may be displaced only by specific provision. Arbitrators must disclose the nature of personal knowledge relied on and allow the parties an opportunity to respond. The Court referred to Chandris v. Isbrandtsen Moller Co. Inc., [1951] K.B. 240, on the ordinary implied term that arbitrators decide according to the ordinary law.
members.conclusion: The arbitrators committed legal misconduct, and the award was vitiated.

predicates.arbitration_proceeding: The dispute was referred to arbitrators for a decision.
predicates.arbitrators_relied_on_personal_knowledge: The arbitrators based their decision on knowledge they personally possessed about the dispute.
predicates.parties_not_informed_and_given_opportuni: The arbitrators did not disclose the nature of that personal knowledge to the parties and give them an opportunity to respond to it.
predicates.award_is_vitiated: The award is invalid because the arbitrators committed legal misconduct.

members.legal_issue: An arbitrator commits legal misconduct by receiving and considering evidence from one party in the absence of the other party, without giving the absent party an opportunity to answer it, and the misconduct vitiates the award regardless of proof of prejudice.
material_facts: The parties referred their pending civil dispute to a sole arbitrator and agreed to abide by the award.
The arbitrator separately examined each side and obtained a statement from one party containing factual assertions beyond that party’s pleadings.
The arbitrator considered that statement and a settlement document when making the award.
The other party received no notice of the separate examination and had no opportunity to cross-examine, respond to the evidence, or present evidence to meet it.
members.legal_principle: The principles of natural justice require both sides to be heard in each other’s presence and prohibit one side from using material to influence the decision-maker that the other side does not know of and cannot meet. This applies to arbitration as well as court proceedings. The Court relied on Harvey v. Shelton (1844) 7 Beav. 455, Ganesh Narayan Singh v. Malida Koer (1911) 13 Cal. L.J. 399, Walker v. Frobisher (1801) 6 Ves. 70, and Haigh v. Haigh (1861) 31 L.J. Ch. 420; the arbitration was referred under section 21 of the Indian Arbitration Act.
members.conclusion: The arbitrator was guilty of legal misconduct, which was sufficient to vitiate the award even without proof that the misconduct caused prejudice.

rule.if: arbitration_proceeding and award_made and arbitrator_received_one_sided_evidence and other_party_lacked_opportunity_to_answer

predicates.arbitration_proceeding: The dispute was referred to an arbitrator for decision.
predicates.award_made: The arbitrator issued an award resolving the referred dispute.
predicates.arbitrator_received_one_sided_evidence: The arbitrator received evidence from one party outside the presence of the other party.
predicates.other_party_lacked_opportunity_to_answer: The absent party had no opportunity to know of and respond to the evidence before the decision was made.

members.legal_issue: A mortgage deed stating that the property becomes an absolute transfer if the debt is not repaid within a fixed period is construed as making the mortgagee the owner when that condition is met, if the stipulation is enforced.
material_facts: The deed secured a loan against a shop and required repayment within 15 years for redemption.

The deed stated that after the 15-year period the shop would be deemed an absolute transfer, and used the words “Mala Kalam,” which the Court understood in context to mean that the mortgagor would have no further say.
The debt was not repaid within the stipulated period.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed the deed’s words in their context: a term that left the mortgagor no scope to assert any further say over the property meant that the mortgagor lost title and the mortgagee became its absolute owner. This construction addressed the effect of the term if it prevailed; the Court separately held that the term was unenforceable as a clog on the equity of redemption.
members.conclusion: If the deed’s terms were enforced, the mortgagee would become the absolute owner of the shop after the stipulated period expired without repayment.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_dispute: A party seeks to redeem property given as security for a debt.
predicates.deed_provides_absolute_transfer_after_no: The deed states that the secured property will become an absolute transfer if the debt is not repaid within a fixed period.
predicates.debt_unpaid_when_fixed_period_expired: The borrower or the borrower's successor did not repay the debt before the fixed period expired.

members.legal_issue: A mortgage term stating that the property becomes an absolute transfer if the debt is not repaid within the specified period makes the mortgagee the absolute owner under the instrument if that term is enforceable.
material_facts: The deed required repayment within a specified period and stated that after that period the shop would be an absolute transfer, leaving the mortgagor no further say.
Neither the mortgagor nor the mortgagor’s heir repaid the debt within the specified period.
members.legal_principle: The deed must be read as a whole and in context. The phrase indicating that the mortgagor would have no further say in the property after the specified period meant that the mortgagor would lose title and the mortgagee would become its absolute owner, if the deed’s terms prevailed.
members.conclusion: On the deed’s terms, non-payment within the specified period would extinguish the mortgagor’s title and make the mortgagee the absolute owner.

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: A claimant seeks redemption of property held by a mortgagee.
predicates.instrument_makes_property_absolute_trans: The mortgage instrument states that the property will become an absolute transfer to the mortgagee if the debt is not repaid by the stated deadline.
predicates.debt_unpaid_at_deadline: The mortgagor and any successor do not repay the debt by the stated deadline.

members.legal_issue: The construction-based exemption from rent-control legislation applies to buildings completed before the legislation came into force as well as to buildings completed afterward.
material_facts: The building was found to have been constructed in 1968, before the 1972 Act came into force.
The eviction suit was instituted in 1977, less than ten years after the building’s construction was completed.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, provides that the Act does not apply to a building during the ten years after completion of its construction. In Om Prakash Gupta v. Dig Vijdendrapal Gupta, the Court held that this applies regardless of whether the building was constructed before or after the Act commenced. Ratan Lal Shinghal v. Smt. Murti Devi did not establish that the Act applied to all pre-commencement buildings regardless of their construction date.
members.conclusion: The ten-year exemption applied to the building, notwithstanding that it had been constructed before the Act came into force.

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord instituted a suit seeking eviction of a tenant from a building.
