predicates.building_within_construction_exemption_w: The suit was instituted before ten years had elapsed from completion of the building’s construction.

members.legal_issue: The initial period of non-application of the rent-control law applies to buildings completed before the law came into force.
material_facts: The shop was completed before the rent-control law commenced.
The eviction proceeding was brought while the shop was still within the initial period following its completion.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(2) states without ambiguity that the law does not apply to a building during the ten years from completion and does not limit that rule to buildings completed after commencement. The court applied the rule that legislative intent is primarily found in the enacted words and that clear words should not be supplemented by adding words. It rejected the contrary view in Rattan Lal Shinghal v. Smt. Murti Devi and followed the contrary interpretation in Ram Saroop Rai v. Lilavati.
members.conclusion: The law did not apply to the shop during the initial ten-year period, even though it had been completed before the law commenced.

predicates.rent_regulation_applicability_dispute: A party to a building-related proceeding disputed whether rent regulation applied to the building.
predicates.building_within_initial_exemption_period: The building had not yet completed the initial period following completion of its construction.

members.legal_issue: The statutory allocation of criminal cases between a local village tribunal and ordinary criminal courts was not discriminatory merely because the two forums followed different procedures.
material_facts: The statute gave the village tribunal jurisdiction over specified offences, subject to other provisions of the statute.
A case cognizable by the village tribunal could not ordinarily be taken cognizance of by another court unless an authorized judicial officer ordered otherwise.
Other provisions allowed cases to be transferred to the village tribunal, withdrawn from it, or removed from its jurisdiction in specified circumstances.
The village tribunal was not bound to follow the ordinary rules of evidence and procedure.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 14, the challenged scheme was not discriminatory because, read as a whole, it did not leave a complainant free to choose between the village tribunal and an ordinary criminal court. Section 62, which made the tribunal’s jurisdiction concurrent, was subject to the rest of the Act, including section 68, which generally reserved cognizance of tribunal cases to that tribunal unless an authorized order provided otherwise. Sections 69, 70 and 73 provided for transfer, withdrawal, and intervention in cases of miscarriage or apprehended miscarriage of justice; these provisions explained the reference to concurrent jurisdiction. The different procedure under section 60 therefore did not create the asserted choice of forums.
members.conclusion: The statutory scheme was not discriminatory and did not infringe the constitutional guarantee of equality.

predicates.case_cognizable_by_village_tribunal: The proceeding concerned an offence assigned by law to a village tribunal for trial.
predicates.ordinary_court_cognizance_requires_autho: The law generally prevented an ordinary court from taking cognizance of a case assigned to the village tribunal unless an authorized judicial officer ordered otherwise.
predicates.exceptional_transfer_or_withdrawal_is_pr: The law allowed an authorized judicial officer to transfer a case, withdraw it from the village tribunal, or intervene when justice might miscarry.

members.legal_issue: The statutory arrangement assigning cases to local village courts, while permitting transfer to ordinary courts in specified circumstances, does not discriminate between persons in violation of the constitutional equality guarantee.
material_facts: The village court had jurisdiction over specified offences concurrently with ordinary criminal courts, but another provision barred ordinary courts from taking cognizance of cases assigned to the village court unless an authorized order directed otherwise.
The Act permitted cases to be transferred to or withdrawn from the village court in specified circumstances.
The village court followed a procedure that was not bound by the ordinary rules of evidence or procedure.
members.legal_principle: The Court read sections 62 and 68 together, with sections 69, 70 and 73, and held that the reference to concurrent jurisdiction did not allow a party to choose between the village court and ordinary criminal court. The scheme assigned cases to the village court subject to specified transfer, withdrawal and jurisdiction-cancellation powers. The Court rejected the challenge under Article 14 of the Constitution. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The challenged provisions were not discriminatory because cases within the village court’s jurisdiction were to be tried there unless an authorized order provided otherwise.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_forum_alloca: A person challenges the allocation of cases between a local adjudicatory body and ordinary courts as unequal.
predicates.ordinary_court_cognizance_requires_an_au: The governing scheme prevents ordinary courts from taking cognizance of cases assigned to the local body unless an authorized decision permits it.
predicates.transfers_or_withdrawals_are_limited_to_: The governing scheme allows cases to be transferred or withdrawn only in specified circumstances.

members.legal_issue: A supported criminal conviction may be maintained while a short custodial sentence is replaced with a fine when imprisonment would serve no useful purpose.
material_facts: Prosecution witnesses identified the accused as a participant in removing the crops.
The Court considered that accused’s conviction to be rightly made.
The sentence was a short period of imprisonment, and the Court found no useful purpose would be served by sending the accused to jail for that period.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the conviction as supported by the evidence but exercised its appellate power to modify the sentence because it considered that the short custodial term would serve no useful purpose. No specific earlier case or statutory sentencing provision was cited for this sentencing modification.
members.conclusion: The conviction was maintained, but the sentence was reduced to a fine, with imprisonment in default as directed by the village tribunal.

rule.if: appeal_against_criminal_conviction and evidence_supports_conviction and custodial_sentence_is_short and imprisonment_would_serve_no_useful_purpose

predicates.appeal_against_criminal_conviction: The proceeding was an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.evidence_supports_conviction: The evidence identified the accused as a participant in the offence.
predicates.custodial_sentence_is_short: The sentence imposed was a short term of imprisonment.
predicates.imprisonment_would_serve_no_useful_purpo: The Court considered that serving the short custodial term would serve no useful purpose.

members.legal_issue: A brief custodial sentence may be replaced with a fine when imprisonment would serve no useful purpose.
material_facts: The appellant whose conviction was upheld had received a short term of imprisonment.
The Court considered that sending him to jail for that short period would serve no useful purpose.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its sentencing discretion, concluding that imprisonment for the brief term would serve no useful purpose and substituting a fine. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The custodial sentence was reduced to a fine, with imprisonment in default as directed by the local court.

predicates.appeal_includes_sentence_challenge: An appeal places the sentence imposed on a convicted person before the reviewing court.
predicates.custodial_sentence_is_brief: The custodial sentence imposed is brief.
predicates.imprisonment_would_serve_no_useful_purpo: The reviewing court concludes that serving the brief custodial sentence would serve no useful purpose.

members.legal_issue: An advocate’s failure to account to clients for money received on their behalf, when coupled with a false claim of payment, establishes professional misconduct where the asserted evidence of payment is found unreliable.
material_facts: The advocate received and cashed a court cheque issued for money to which his clients were entitled.
The advocate did not dispute receiving the money on the clients’ behalf.
After the clients demanded the money, the advocate asserted that he had already paid it and that a receipt had been returned among the case papers.
The High Court found the witness said to support the payment defence to be an impersonator or, alternatively, wholly unworthy of belief.
The High Court found that the advocate had not paid the money to his clients.
members.legal_principle: A practitioner’s duty to a client includes properly accounting for money received on the client’s behalf. The High Court’s factual findings on whether payment was made and whether a witness was credible were not open to reappraisal by the Supreme Court in the absence of an exceptional ground for interference. The Court held that the witness’s asserted admission could not support the payment defence because the High Court had found the testimony devoid of truth.
members.conclusion: The finding that the advocate failed to pay the money to his clients and was guilty of professional misconduct was upheld.

rule.if: professional_misconduct_appeal and practitioner_received_client_money and clients_entitled_to_money and money_not_paid_to_clients and payment_witness_found_unreliable

predicates.professional_misconduct_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a finding of professional misconduct.
predicates.practitioner_received_client_money: The practitioner received money on behalf of clients in the course of professional work.
predicates.clients_entitled_to_money: The clients were entitled to receive the money held by the practitioner.
predicates.money_not_paid_to_clients: The practitioner did not pay the money to the clients despite their demand.
predicates.payment_witness_found_unreliable: The fact-finding court rejected as untruthful or unreliable the witness testimony offered to show that payment had been made.

members.legal_issue: An advocate’s failure to apply or account for client money entrusted for a specific purpose constitutes professional misconduct when established by reliable evidence.
material_facts: A client entrusted the advocate with money to complete a property purchase and discharge an outstanding mortgage.
The mortgage was not discharged, and the advocate did not account for the entrusted money.
The disciplinary tribunal and the High Court found that the advocate had not repaid the money he claimed to have given to an intermediary.
The Supreme Court found that a large body of reliable oral and documentary evidence supported the misconduct finding.
members.legal_principle: An advocate must apply entrusted client money to the purpose for which it was given and account for it. The Court applied the Bar Councils Act and considered the findings of the Bar Council Tribunal and the High Court; it also referred to In the matter of an Advocate, Case No. XVI of 1942, and In re D. A. Shanmugasundaraswami, Misc. Case No. X of 1948, in discussing disciplinary action following High Court proceedings.
members.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court’s order removing the advocate from its roll was upheld.

rule.if: professional_discipline_appeal and client_money_entrusted_for_specific_purpose and money_not_applied_to_that_purpose and money_not_accounted_for and reliable_evidence_supports_misconduct

predicates.professional_discipline_appeal: An advocate appealed a disciplinary decision concerning professional misconduct.
predicates.client_money_entrusted_for_specific_purp: A client entrusted money to an advocate for a specified purpose in carrying out the client’s matter.
predicates.money_not_applied_to_that_purpose: The advocate did not use the entrusted money for the purpose for which the client provided it.
predicates.money_not_accounted_for: The advocate did not account for the entrusted money to the client.
predicates.reliable_evidence_supports_misconduct: The disciplinary record contains reliable evidence supporting the finding that the advocate committed misconduct.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the validity of a rule need not be decided when the rule is repealed during the appeal and the requested relief is confined to that rule.
material_facts: The appellants sought to have the forest rule declared invalid and sought a permit as relief.
The challenged rule was deleted while the appeal was pending.
The appellants did not seek permission to amend their petition after the deletion.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the validity question had become academic because the challenged rule had been deleted during the appeal and the appellants had not amended their requested relief. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this point.
members.conclusion: The Court treated the challenge to the rule’s validity as academic and did not decide its merits.

predicates.appeal_challenging_a_rule: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the validity of a rule.
predicates.challenged_rule_repealed_during_appeal: The rule challenged in the appeal was repealed while the appeal was pending.
predicates.requested_relief_limited_to_challenged_r: The requested relief remained confined to the challenged rule after its repeal.

members.legal_issue: A challenge to the absence of an appeal in the original recovery law requires no further constitutional ruling once an appeal provision has been enacted during the case.
material_facts: The original law provided no appeal from the relevant administrative order.
During the case, an amendment added an appeal provision.
The Court consequently did not make a final pronouncement on whether the original absence of an appeal made the law constitutionally unreasonable.
members.legal_principle: The Court expressed doubt that the absence of an appeal might constitute procedural unreasonableness, but did not decide that issue because an amendment supplied an appeal against the administrative order before judgment.
members.conclusion: The question did not survive for further consideration after the amendment provided an appeal, and the Court made no final ruling on the original appeal provision’s constitutionality.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_no_appeal: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a recovery process that originally provided no appeal.
predicates.appeal_added_before_final_decision: An appeal provision was added to the recovery process before the court made its final decision.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser may satisfy the requirement to relinquish claims to the unperformable part of a contract and compensation at a late stage of litigation, including by an amended prayer and an unequivocal statement in court.
material_facts: The purchasers sought to amend their requested relief to limit it to the seller’s share.
Their amended request did not seek performance of the other owner’s share or compensation for its non-performance.
Their counsel stated that they relinquished any claim for damages and would not press their cross-objection.
The amendment and statement were made after the litigation had reached the appellate stage.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(3)(ii) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires relinquishment of claims to performance of the remaining part and compensation for the defendant’s default, but does not impose a time limit for doing so. Rachakonda Narayana v. Ponthala Parvathamma and Surjit Kaur v. Naurata Singh recognize that an application to relinquish claims may be made at the appellate stage. Kalyanpur Lime Works Ltd. v. State of Bihar holds that relinquishment may be made at any stage of the litigation. The court must read the amendment as a whole, and an unequivocal statement in court may establish relinquishment.
members.conclusion: The relinquishment could be made at that stage and did not have to be specifically pleaded in prescribed words. The amended request, read as a whole, and the statement in court sufficiently established relinquishment.

predicates.partial_specific_performance_proceeding: A party seeks specific performance limited to the part of an agreement that the other party can perform.
predicates.purchaser_limits_requested_relief_to_per: The purchaser amends or states the requested relief to cover only the performable part.
predicates.purchaser_abandons_remaining_performance: The purchaser gives up the claim to performance of the part that cannot be performed.
predicates.purchaser_disclaims_compensation: The purchaser expressly or by necessary implication gives up compensation for the default.

members.legal_issue: A claimant may relinquish claims to further performance during litigation to satisfy the condition for seeking performance of the remaining part of a contract.
material_facts: The contract covered a longer lease period, but a substantial part of that period had already passed.
During the litigation, the company sought relief for the remaining period and stated that it relinquished claims to further performance and to compensation for the earlier period.
The company confirmed in argument that it insisted on no further performance and claimed no compensation for the period before performance could be given.
members.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act permits relief for the performable part of a contract subject to its conditions, including relinquishment of claims to further performance and compensation for the unperformed part. The Court relied on Waryam Singh v. Gopi Chand for the principle that relinquishment of the claim to further performance may be made at any stage of litigation.
members.conclusion: The relinquishment was sufficient, and it could be made at any stage of the litigation. The company could therefore seek relief under section 15 of the Specific Relief Act, subject to the Court’s decision on what relief to grant.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brings a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.substantial_part_of_contract_already_ela: A substantial part of the contract’s performance period has passed before relief is considered.
predicates.claimant_relinquished_claim_to_further_p: During the litigation, the claimant gives up claims to further performance beyond the part for which relief is sought.

members.legal_issue: A claim that acquired land comprised areas protected by a government exclusion policy cannot be resolved in the proceeding when the existence of those areas is a disputed question of fact.
material_facts: The government had a policy of excluding recorded village settlements, contiguous houses, and certain hamlets from acquisition.
The parties disputed whether the particular acquired lands contained areas covered by that policy.
The Court found that the disputed factual existence of those areas could not be determined in the proceeding.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the existence and location of the alleged settlements and hamlets as a disputed factual issue that could not be resolved in these proceedings; it also noted that the High Court had not accepted the claim.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to decide the exclusion claim because it depended on disputed facts about the existence of the protected areas.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.exemption_claim_depends_on_disputed_site: The claimed exclusion from acquisition depends on whether particular protected settlements or hamlets existed on the acquired land, and the parties dispute that fact.

members.legal_issue: Whether acquired land qualifies as protected abadi land under a government policy is a disputed factual matter that cannot be conclusively determined on the record of this proceeding.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that their lands had existing residential or industrial construction and were covered by a policy against acquiring abadi land.

The evidence about the nature, extent and timing of the construction was disputed; the record included a civil-court finding in one case, a pending further appeal, and conflicting inspection material.
The State was not a party to the civil-court proceedings, and the evidence did not establish whether the lands were village-site lands or whether the construction existed at the relevant time.
The appellants accepted that the Court need not decide the abadi issue if they could pursue a suitable alternative remedy.
members.legal_principle: A court deciding a writ challenge cannot determine a claimed exemption where material factual questions remain disputed, including the character and timing of construction and whether a government policy covers it. A prior civil-court finding does not bind a State that was not a party to that proceeding. The Court left the matter for the State authorities to assess, including whether abadi existed at the relevant time, was legally permissible, continued to exist, and came within a policy then in force. The judgment discusses the proposed representation under Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act as the route for that consideration.
members.conclusion: The Court made no finding that the lands were protected abadi land or immune from acquisition; it left the question open for consideration by the State authorities on the appellants’ representations.

predicates.land_acquisition_writ: The proceeding is a writ challenge to a land acquisition.
predicates.abadi_status_disputed: The parties dispute whether the acquired land had qualifying residential settlement or construction at the relevant time.
predicates.abadi_policy_coverage_unresolved: The record does not establish whether a policy against acquiring such land applied to the land.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court that has disposed of an appeal cannot use a later clarification application to make a substantive order that changes the relief granted.
material_facts: The appellate court had disposed of the appeals brought by the purchaser and the bank against the order setting aside the sale.
The debtor later applied for clarification in those disposed appeals.

The appellate court issued further directions about disbursing the funds and paying additional interest, and those directions operated to the debtor’s benefit despite his failure to challenge the relevant order.
members.legal_principle: Once an appeal has been finally disposed of, the appellate court is functus officio and cannot use a clarification application to pass a new substantive order. The court applied that principle to the orders made after disposal of the appeals; no earlier case was relied on for this point.
members.conclusion: The appellate court could not make those substantive orders in the guise of clarification after disposing of the appeals; the clarification orders were set aside.

predicates.appellate_proceeding_disposed: An appellate court had finally disposed of the appeal.
predicates.later_clarification_application: A party applied for clarification after the appeal had been disposed of.
predicates.clarification_order_changes_substantive_: The court’s later order introduced or changed substantive relief rather than clarifying the existing decision.

members.legal_issue: A court permitting withdrawal of an appeal ordinarily cannot grant further relief after the appeal has ended without hearing the merits.
material_facts: The applicants withdrew their appeal against the refusal of interim injunction.
The appellate court permitted withdrawal without hearing the parties on the merits or giving reasons for further relief.
The appellate court nevertheless directed the parties to maintain status quo temporarily.
members.legal_principle: Ordinarily, a court allowing an appeal to be withdrawn cannot grant a further relief. Once the appeal was withdrawn, the court became functus officio; the Court relied on G.E. Power Controls India v. S. Lakshmipathy.
members.conclusion: The appellate court had no jurisdiction to grant the further status quo relief after permitting withdrawal of the appeal.

rule.if: appeal_from_interlocutory_order and appeal_withdrawn and no_merits_hearing and further_relief_granted

predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_order: A party brought an appeal from an interlocutory order.
predicates.appeal_withdrawn: The appellate court permitted the party to withdraw the appeal.
predicates.no_merits_hearing: The appellate court did not hear the parties on the merits of the appeal.
predicates.further_relief_granted: The appellate court granted relief beyond permitting withdrawal of the appeal.

members.legal_issue: Becoming an occupant of forest land does not, without the required survey settlement or concession, give the former holder a right to cut and remove trees from that land.
material_facts: The former holders’ jagirs were abolished, and they became occupants of forest lands under the abolition law.
The villages containing the forest lands had not been surveyed or settled.
The former holders claimed a right, as occupants, to cut and remove trees, including reserved species.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3 and 5(1)(b) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 extinguished jagir rights except as expressly preserved and conferred occupancy rights in the land. Under section 40 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, the government’s rights to trees are deemed conceded to occupants in the circumstances specified for surveyed and settled villages or land occupied after settlement; no such concession follows where the required survey settlement has not occurred. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The former holders acquired occupancy rights in the forest lands, but those rights did not include a right to cut and remove the trees. Because the villages had not been surveyed and settled, the government’s rights to the trees could not be deemed conceded to the occupants.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order_recognizing_tree_cutting_rights and former_holder_became_land_occupant and land_is_forest_land and village_not_surveyed_or_settled

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order_recognizing_tree_: The proceeding is an appeal from an order allowing a writ petition that recognized a claimed right to cut and remove trees.
predicates.former_holder_became_land_occupant: A person who formerly held rights under an abolished tenure became an occupant of land under the applicable transition law.
predicates.land_is_forest_land: The land at issue is forest land bearing trees.
predicates.village_not_surveyed_or_settled: The village containing the land had not undergone the survey settlement required for a deemed concession of tree rights.

members.legal_issue: A person who becomes an occupant by operation of law does not thereby receive factual permission to occupy land for purposes of a rule deeming permission to include a concession of tree rights.
material_facts: The appellants claimed occupant status under the provision governing the consequences of jagir abolition.
They argued that this status amounted to permission to occupy the land and therefore included a concession of rights to the trees.
The court found that the asserted permission was a legal consequence of occupant status, not factual permission to occupy.
members.legal_principle: The court interpreted paragraph 3 of section 40 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, which provides for tree rights to accompany permission to occupy land in specified circumstances. It held that this means factual permission to occupy, not the legal status of occupant conferred under section 5(1)(b) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953.
members.conclusion: The permission-based argument did not establish the appellants' tree rights; permission for this purpose means factual permission and not the conferral of occupant status by law.

predicates.tree_rights_dispute_based_on_permission_: The proceeding concerns a claim that permission to occupy land carries rights to trees on it.
predicates.occupancy_status_conferred_by_operation_: The claimant's occupant status arose by operation of law rather than from a factual grant of permission.
predicates.no_factual_permission_to_occupy: No factual permission to occupy the land was granted.
predicates.occupancy_status_alone_does_not_confer_t: Occupant status alone does not count as permission that confers tree rights.

members.legal_issue: The additional-accommodation eviction provision applies only when the landlord and tenant occupy different portions of the same building, not separate buildings owned by the landlord.
material_facts: The landlord occupied one building for his residence and business and sought additional business space.
The tenant occupied an adjoining building that the landlord had acquired separately and that had previously been owned by another person.

The buildings were separated by a single wall and were under common ownership, but the tenant’s building could be sold and transferred without affecting the landlord’s possession and enjoyment of his building.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(3)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 permits a landlord occupying only part of a building to seek possession of another portion of that same building for additional residential or business accommodation. It requires oneness of the building, not merely common ownership. Section 2(iii), defining “building,” does not permit separate adjoining buildings in different occupation to be treated as one integrated building for this purpose. Whether adjoining premises are parts of one building may be assessed by whether one can be sold and its purchaser placed in possession without affecting the landlord’s possession and enjoyment of the other; a common wall does not determine the issue. The Court referred to Balaganesan Metals v. M.N. Shanmugham Chetty, JT 1987 (2) SC 247, M. Ramaswamy Naidu v. P. Venkateswarlu, Vol. II (1961) 1 A.W.R. 400, and Balaiah v. Lachaiah, AIR 1965 AP 435.
members.conclusion: The landlord could not obtain eviction under the additional-accommodation provision because the tenant occupied a separate building, not another portion of the building occupied by the landlord. The appeal was allowed and the dismissal of the eviction petition was restored.

predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_case: A landlord seeks a tenant’s eviction to obtain additional residential or business accommodation.
predicates.landlord_and_tenant_occupy_different_bui: The landlord occupies one building while the tenant occupies a separate building, rather than another portion of the landlord’s building.
predicates.tenant_building_independently_transferab: The tenant’s building can be sold and its purchaser placed in possession without affecting the landlord’s possession and enjoyment of the other building.
predicates.additional_accommodation_eviction_not_au: The landlord cannot obtain eviction on the ground of needing additional accommodation.

members.legal_issue: A deeming rule for a landlord’s residential requirement applies only when the tenant’s accommodation and the landlord-occupied remainder form parts of one unit of accommodation, not merely because they are in the same structure.
material_facts: The ground floor had two separate tenements: the tenant occupied one and the landlord occupied the other for residential purposes.
The lower authorities treated the ground floor as a building to which the deeming rule applied, without deciding whether the two tenements together formed a single unit of accommodation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 21(1)(a) and Explanation (iv) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the phrase referring to a building of which the tenanted building is a part requires a single unit of accommodation. Because the Explanation creates a conclusive presumption favouring the landlord in tenant-protective legislation, it must be construed strictly against the landlord. The Court approved the construction in Chunnoo Lal v. Additional District Judge, Allahabad.
members.conclusion: The deeming rule applies only when the accommodation under tenancy and the accommodation occupied by the landlord together constitute one unit; separate and independent units do not qualify. The matter was remanded for the lower court to apply that construction.

predicates.residential_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of rented accommodation for residential use.
predicates.tenant_occupies_part_of_single_unit: The tenant occupies part of one unit of accommodation, rather than an independent unit in a larger structure.
predicates.landlord_resides_in_remainder: The landlord occupies the remaining part of that same unit for residential purposes.

members.legal_issue: The statutory requirement to exhaust revenue appeals before bringing a civil suit does not bar a title suit between private parties.
material_facts: The parties had jointly purchased the property and later asserted competing rights to it.

A revenue appeal concerning the property was dismissed, and the party who brought it did not pursue a further revision before filing a civil suit seeking a declaration of title and a perpetual injunction.
The civil suit was between private parties and sought determination of rights in the property.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act bars a suit against the Government concerning an act or omission of a Revenue Officer unless the plaintiff first exhausts the appeals available within the prescribed period; it does not bar a suit between private parties. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not expressly or by necessary implication exclude civil jurisdiction over a suit based on title. Section 37 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code concerns land vesting in or belonging to the State and does not govern inter se claims of private parties. Mutation entries facilitate revenue collection and may evidence enjoyment, but do not create title, which must be established independently of those entries.
members.conclusion: The civil suit between the private parties was maintainable, notwithstanding that the further revenue remedy had not been pursued.

predicates.civil_suit_between_private_parties: The proceeding is a civil suit brought by one private party against another, rather than a suit against the Government.
predicates.seeks_determination_of_property_title: The plaintiff asks the civil court to determine title or other rights in property.

members.legal_issue: The requirement to exhaust revenue appeals does not bar a civil suit when the complained-of administrative act was not an appealable decision or order.
material_facts: The complained-of act was the Collector’s administrative authorization for a subordinate official to make a nominal bid.
No appeal was provided against that authorization as an administrative act, and no other appealable decision was identified.
The suit challenged the purported sale as void.
members.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act requires a claimant to pursue available appeals before suing the government. Its application requires an act or omission giving rise to the claim, an appeal provided by law against that act or omission, and failure to use that remedy. Section 203 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code permits appeals from decisions or orders of revenue officers, but the administrative authorization at issue was not an appealable decision or order.
members.conclusion: Section 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act did not bar the suit.

predicates.suit_against_public_authority: A civil suit seeks relief against a public authority based on an act of a revenue official.
predicates.complained_of_act_is_not_appealable: The act complained of is not a decision or order for which an appeal is provided.
predicates.no_available_appeal_was_omitted: The claimant did not fail to pursue an appeal that was available against the complained-of act.
predicates.appeal_exhaustion_bar_does_not_apply: The requirement to exhaust revenue appeals does not bar the civil suit.

members.legal_issue: A certificate permitting an appeal must state adequate reasons, including the question of public or private importance to be determined, but a defective certificate need not be vacated when the appeal has no merit.
material_facts: The matter was an appeal brought under a certificate granted by the High Court.
The certificate did not set out the question of public or private importance that was to be determined in the appeal.
The Court found no merit in the appeal.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution, a High Court certificate must be supported by adequate reasons and must state the question of public or private importance that, in the High Court's opinion, falls to be determined in the appeal. The Court found it unnecessary to vacate the certificate in this case because the appeal lacked merit.
members.conclusion: The certificate was defective because it lacked adequate reasons identifying the question of importance, but the Court did not vacate it because the appeal had no merit.

predicates.certified_appeal: The matter was an appeal brought under a certificate granted by a lower court.
predicates.certificate_omits_importance_question: The certificate did not state the question of public or private importance to be determined in the appeal.
predicates.appeal_lacks_merit: The Supreme Court concluded that the appeal had no merit.

members.legal_issue: A defective certificate for appeal does not require dismissal solely on that ground when the appeal raises a substantial question of law of general public importance.
material_facts: The appeal reached the Supreme Court on a High Court certificate that merely stated that the case was fit for appeal and did not specify the applicable constitutional category or the question to be determined.
The appeal raised a substantial question of law of general public importance.
members.legal_principle: A certificate of fitness must give adequate reasons and identify the substantial question of law or matter of importance to be determined; a certificate that does not do so is defective. The Court nevertheless declined to dismiss this appeal solely on that basis because it raised a substantial question of law of general public importance and special leave could have been granted. It relied on Article 133 of the Constitution as it then stood, Sohanlal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, [1971] 1 SCC 275, Railway Board v. Observer Publications (P) Ltd., [1972] 3 SCR 865, Nund & Samont Co. P. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, [1970] 78 ITR 268, and India Machinery Stores P. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, [1970] 78 ITR 50.
members.conclusion: The preliminary objection was overruled, and the appeal was not dismissed solely because the certificate was defective.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_on_high_court_ce: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court brought on a certificate granted by a High Court.
predicates.certificate_defective: The certificate does not state adequate reasons or identify the question or matter that warrants appeal.
predicates.substantial_general_public_law_question: The appeal raises a substantial question of law of general public importance.

members.legal_issue: A conclusive statutory declaration that a listed religious institution is of a particular faith does not violate constitutional rights where a claimant may still seek adjudication of a claim to the physical property as private property or as property of another institution.
material_facts: A shrine was listed in the statute and declared to be a religious institution of the specified faith.
A claimant alleged that the shrine was instead associated with another religious order and challenged the conclusive effect of the declaration.

The State and the religious management body accepted that claims could be made to the listed property, including the building, as private property or as property of another institution, and that such claims could be adjudicated by the tribunal.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(4) of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, read consistently with the interpretation permitting claims to the physical property, was not unconstitutional under Articles 19(1)(f) and 26. A provision should be construed, where possible, to sustain its constitutionality; the Court also relied on the presumption of constitutionality and the principle of stare decisis for a long-standing construction of a local statute. It referred to the decisions in Mahant Davinder Singh v. Shromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari, and Brownsea Haven Properties v. Poole Corporation, and to the earlier tribunal interpretation concerning Gurdwara Rupar.
members.conclusion: The conclusive effect of the declaration did not violate the claimant’s rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 26 because a claim to the property remained open for adjudication.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_pr: A claimant brings a constitutional challenge to a law’s classification of a religious institution.
predicates.institution_listed_and_declared_by_law: The institution is listed under the law and declared to belong to the specified religious category.
predicates.claimant_can_seek_adjudication_of_physic: The claimant is permitted to ask the designated adjudicator to determine whether the physical property belongs privately or to another institution.

members.legal_issue: A conclusive declaration that a shrine is a Sikh place of worship does not prevent a claimant from asserting that the physical property listed in connection with the shrine belongs to a non-Sikh religious institution.
material_facts: The shrine was included in a statutory schedule and a notification declared it to be a Sikh place of worship.
The claimant was identified as being in possession of property listed in connection with the shrine and sought to claim that the property belonged to an Udasi institution.
The respondents accepted that a claim could be made concerning the listed property, including the property described as the shrine itself.
Earlier interpretations of the statutory scheme permitted claims to the physical property while distinguishing such claims from a claim to the shrine as a religious institution.
members.legal_principle: Khanna J. relied on the presumption of constitutional validity, the longstanding construction of the local enactment, and the interpretations in the Sikh Gurdwara Tribunal’s order concerning Gurdwara Rupar and Mahant Davinder Singh v. Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. He also referred to Raj Narain Pandey v. Sant Prasad Tewari on adhering to a settled interpretation of a local statute.
members.conclusion: In Khanna J.’s concurring opinion, the statutory declaration did not bar a claim that the listed physical property, including the shrine building, belonged to an Udasi institution; on that construction, the provision did not violate the claimant’s rights.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_conclusive_s: A party challenges the constitutionality of a conclusive declaration about a shrine’s religious status.
predicates.claimant_asserts_property_belongs_to_dif: The claimant asserts that the physical property listed in connection with the shrine belongs to a different religious institution.
predicates.property_claim_remains_adjudicable: The statutory process permits the tribunal to adjudicate the claimant’s property claim despite the declaration.

members.legal_issue: Whether a shrine associated with a charitable institution was a public temple under the statutory definition when the evidence did not establish that the Hindu community or a section of it used the shrine as of right for religious worship.
material_facts: The institution's grants were principally recorded as supporting its head or the distribution of food and alms to fakirs, sadhus, and travellers; the grants did not establish that the shrine was endowed for public worship.
The shrine was constructed after the original grants, and part of the institution's income was spent on worship and related expenses.
Witnesses for the appellants said they sought the head's permission to enter and described not seeing members of the public worship there; the Supreme Court accepted their evidence.
The Board's witness asserted that the shrine was public, but the Court considered his testimony unreliable, and no member of the Hindu public testified that worship there was a matter of right.
Visitors attended and participated in festivals, but the Court held that such attendance did not by itself establish a right of access.

The High Court had relied on the shrine's physical features and entries in the inam registers; the Supreme Court considered those entries in their full context and concluded that they did not establish a public temple.
members.legal_principle: Section 9(12) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 required a place to be used for public religious worship and to be dedicated to, for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it for religious worship. Public attendance alone does not prove use as of right, since visitors may be admitted to a private shrine. The presumption that temples are public in parts of the Madras Presidency is rebuttable and was weak for a shrine near the Presidency's boundary; see Mundancheri Koman v. Achuthan Nair. Inam register entries have substantial evidentiary value, especially where original grants are unavailable, but must be assessed in their full context rather than by accepting individual entries at face value; see Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal. The statutory challenge proceeded under section 84(2).
members.conclusion: The shrine was not a temple within the statutory definition because the Hindu community, or any section of it, was not shown to use it as of right for religious worship. The appeal was allowed, the Board's order was set aside, and the District Judge's order was restored.

rule.if: statutory_temple_classification_appeal and private_access_control_evidence and (no_evidence_of_public_rightful_worship or public_attendance_without_proof_of_right)

predicates.statutory_temple_classification_appeal: An appeal challenged a determination that a shrine or religious institution fell within a statutory definition of a public temple.
predicates.private_access_control_evidence: People who entered the shrine sought the institution head's permission, and witnesses reported no observed public worship there.
predicates.no_evidence_of_public_rightful_worship: No member of the relevant religious community testified that the community or a section of it had a right to worship at the shrine.
predicates.public_attendance_without_proof_of_right: Visitors attended the shrine or its festivals, but the evidence did not establish that they attended or worshipped there as of right.

members.legal_issue: Whether the evidence established that a temple associated with a Hindu community was dedicated to or used as of right by the general Hindu community, rather than being a denominational temple for that community.
material_facts: The temple was founded by families belonging to one Hindu community, and its trustees had always belonged to that community.
The temple’s landed properties had been endowed by members of that community, with no reliable evidence of immovable-property endowments by outsiders.
Witnesses from outside the community did not claim a right to worship; their offerings were voluntary and produced little income.
Members of the community alone were allowed to participate in the more important ceremonies.
Other Hindus were not prevented from worshipping, but the evidence did not establish that their use was as of right.

The High Court treated references to the temple’s general body and evidence of outside worship and offerings as supporting public dedication, but the Supreme Court found those inferences unsupported by the evidence.
members.legal_principle: Under section 6(17) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, a temple includes a place dedicated to, for the benefit of, or used as of right by the Hindu community or any section of it. Free admission of the public does not by itself justify an inference of dedication to the public; the evidentiary value of public use depends on circumstances supporting the inference that the use was as of right. The Court relied on Bihar State Board Religious Trust, Patna v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das, [1971] 3 SCR 680, 689.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not establish that the general Hindu community used the temple as of right or that it was dedicated to that community. The temple was a denominational or sectional temple belonging to the relevant Hindu community, and the trial court’s decision was restored.

rule.if: civil_appeal_on_temple_status and temple_founded_and_managed_by_one_hindu_section and temple_properties_endowed_by_that_section and outsiders_did_not_claim_a_right_to_worship and important_rites_limited_to_that_section

predicates.civil_appeal_on_temple_status: The proceeding was a civil appeal concerning whether a temple was public or belonged to a Hindu section.
predicates.temple_founded_and_managed_by_one_hindu_: Families of one Hindu section founded the temple, and members of that section managed it as trustees.
predicates.temple_properties_endowed_by_that_sectio: Members of that Hindu section endowed the temple’s landed properties, and no reliable evidence showed outsiders endowed immovable property.
predicates.outsiders_did_not_claim_a_right_to_worsh: Witnesses from outside the section did not claim a right to worship, and their offerings were voluntary and small.
predicates.important_rites_limited_to_that_section: Members of the section were allowed to participate in the more important ceremonies.

members.legal_issue: The allegations did not prima facie establish the essential ingredients of the charged offences.
material_facts: The parties had entered into development agreements and a later memorandum permitting the developer company to sell some of the landowner’s share to facilitate repayment of the landowner’s loan.

The landowner alleged that the developer company sold four flats beyond its authorized share; the developer company maintained that additional sales were agreed as an adjustment for payments made toward the loan.
The developer company initiated arbitration after the landowner revoked the power of attorney, and the landowner later filed the criminal complaint while the contractual dispute was ongoing.
The parties disputed the authority to sell the flats, and the landowner withdrew the claim concerning the four allegedly excess flats from arbitration to pursue it in civil proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 405 and 406 IPC require dishonest misappropriation, conversion, use, or disposal of entrusted property; cheating under Section 415, punishable under Section 420, requires dishonest or fraudulent intention. Section 419 concerns cheating by personation. Applying these requirements, the Court held that dishonest or fraudulent intention was not prima facie established. It relied on Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar, which holds that dishonest or fraudulent intention must exist when the promise or inducement is made for a breach of contract to amount to cheating; it also considered the principles in Priti Saraf v. State of NCT of Delhi and Sri Krishna Agencies v. State of Andhra Pradesh that civil or arbitral proceedings alone do not bar criminal proceedings.
members.conclusion: The allegations and circumstances did not make out a cogent prima facie case of criminal breach of trust or cheating, and the charged offences were not shown to have the necessary criminal intent.

rule.if: criminal_charge_proceeding and (contractual_property_dispute and disputed_authority_to_sell) and no_dishonest_intent_at_inception

predicates.criminal_charge_proceeding: A person is facing criminal proceedings alleging offences arising from the disputed transaction.
predicates.contractual_property_dispute: The parties’ disagreement concerns rights and obligations under an agreement dealing with property.
predicates.disputed_authority_to_sell: The parties dispute whether one side had authority to sell the property in question.
predicates.no_dishonest_intent_at_inception: The circumstances do not show that the accused had dishonest or fraudulent intent when the relevant promise or transaction began.

members.legal_issue: A complaint alleging a disputed sale arrangement and payment, without allegations supporting the criminal elements of the charged offences, does not disclose a prima facie criminal case.
material_facts: The complaint alleged an oral agreement to transfer a plot for an agreed price and payments toward that price.
It alleged that the sellers later denied receiving the payments and refused to transfer the plot.
The complaint placed the agreement in July 2002 but alleged that payments began in July 2000, making the account self-contradictory.
The complaint and recorded witness statements contained no allegations supporting criminal intent to deceive or other facts constituting the offences for which cognizance was taken.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that the material had to disclose allegations constituting the offences charged. It concluded that the allegations did not support the guilty intention or intention to deceive needed for the alleged cheating and did not otherwise disclose the charged offences under Sections 406, 419, 420 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code.
members.conclusion: The allegations, even if accepted as true, disclosed a civil dispute over a sale and did not make out a prima facie case for the charged criminal offences.

predicates.complaint_concerns_sale_dispute: The complainant alleged an agreement to sell property and payments toward its price, followed by refusal to complete the transfer.
predicates.complaint_lacks_facts_supporting_crimina: The complainant's allegations and witness statements did not state facts supporting the criminal elements of the offences charged.
predicates.complaint_account_is_self_contradictory: The complainant alleged that payments began before the date on which the alleged sale agreement was made.

members.legal_issue: Adverse possession against a Hindu widow during her lifetime did not defeat the reversioners’ right to claim property after her death.
material_facts: The daughter possessed the property under the widow’s gift deed.
The gift deed was not permitted under the Hindu law then in force.
The daughter relied on adverse possession against the widow, while the other daughter claimed as a reversioner after the widow’s death.
members.legal_principle: Where a Hindu widow alienated property without legal necessity, the reversioners were not required to bring a declaratory suit during her lifetime; they could wait until her death and sue the alienee for possession, treating the alienation as a nullity. The Court relied on Radha Rani v. Hanuman Prasad, AIR 1966 SC 216.
members.conclusion: Even if the donee’s possession was adverse to the widow, that possession did not give the donee title against the reversioners or prevent them from claiming the property after the widow’s death.

predicates.reversionary_property_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to property by a person asserting a reversionary interest.
predicates.possession_under_unpermitted_widow_trans: The possessor holds property under a transfer made by a widow that was not permitted under the governing Hindu law.
predicates.adverse_possession_claimed_only_against_: The possessor relies on adverse possession against the widow who made the transfer, rather than against the reversioner.
predicates.reversioner_claims_after_widow_death: The reversioner asserts the claim to the property after the widow’s death.

members.legal_issue: Full ownership acquired by a Hindu female over property in her possession at the commencement of the succession statute is not defeated by a subsequent adoption to her deceased husband.
material_facts: The widow inherited property from her deceased husband and possessed it when the succession statute came into force.
After the statute came into force, the widow adopted a son and later settled part of the property on her daughter.
The adopted son challenged the settlement, arguing that the adoption related back to the husband’s death and made the widow unable to transfer the property.
members.legal_principle: Under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property possessed by a Hindu female when the Act commenced is held by her as full owner, not as a limited owner. Section 4(1)(a) makes Hindu law texts, rules, and interpretations cease to have effect on matters for which the Act provides. Accordingly, the Hindu law fiction that adoption relates back to the adoptive father’s death cannot restrict the ownership conferred by section 14(1). The Court approved Yamunabai v. Ram Maharaj Shreedhar Maharaj, AIR 1960 Bom. 463; it referred to Shrinivas Krishnarao Kango v. Narayan Devji Kango, [1955] 1 SCR 1, and Krishnamurthi Vasudeorao Deshpande v. Dhruwaraj, [1962] 2 SCR 813, on the relation-back doctrine, and to Sukhram v. Gauri Shankar, [1968] 1 SCR 476, and S. S. Munna Lal v. S. S. Rajkumar, [1962] 3 Supp. SCR 418, on the effect of the Act on Hindu law rules.
members.conclusion: The subsequent adoption did not defeat the widow’s full ownership or invalidate her settlement; the appeal was allowed and the trial court’s decree was restored.

predicates.female_possessed_property_at_statutory_c: A Hindu female possessed the property when the succession statute came into force.
predicates.adoption_occurred_after_commencement: The female adopted a child after the succession statute came into force.
predicates.female_transferred_property_after_adopti: The female transferred the property after making the adoption.
predicates.adopted_child_challenged_transfer: The adopted child challenged the female’s transfer on the basis that the adoption related back to an earlier death.

members.legal_issue: Courts should make reasoned findings on deliberate dereliction and may direct disciplinary action against responsible officials, including officials who have retired.
material_facts: The doctor recorded no injuries or cause of death despite other evidence recording injuries, and the investigating officer failed to account for the viscera and omitted the doctor’s explanation from the record.
The Court found that the officials’ conduct involved deliberate dereliction, irresponsible performance, and a designedly defective investigation prejudicial to the prosecution.
Earlier directions to take action against the officials had not been implemented.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the duties of fair investigation and fair trial and on the public interest in the administration of justice, referring to State of Punjab v. Ram Singh, Ex-Constable (1992) 4 SCC 54, Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar (1995) 6 SCC 31, Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat (2006) 3 SCC 374, National Human Rights Commission v. State of Gujarat (2009) 6 SCC 767, and section 2 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. It held that courts should record reasoned findings on deliberate dereliction, designedly defective investigation, and breaches of professional or investigative duties, and may direct disciplinary or other lawful action even where the official has retired.
members.conclusion: The Court directed the appropriate authorities to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the doctor and investigating officer, whether or not they remained in service, and held that courts should record specific, reasoned findings about such misconduct and may direct appropriate action.

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which the conduct of officials involved in the investigation or evidence is considered.
predicates.court_finds_deliberate_official_derelict: The court makes a reasoned finding that an official deliberately failed to perform a duty or acted in serious breach of professional obligations.
predicates.dereliction_impairs_fair_investigation: The official’s conduct compromises or prejudices the proper investigation or trial.

members.legal_issue: A serious investigative lapse may warrant a court-directed disciplinary inquiry against the investigating officer, including when the officer has retired.
material_facts: The investigating officer failed to obtain serological reports for recovered articles, a lapse the court described as serious.
The court directed the state police chief to take disciplinary action against the officer, whether he remained in service or had retired.

For a retired officer, the court directed that action concerning pension be taken under the applicable service rules, and that any limitation bar in those rules not prevent the inquiry directed by the court.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on its assessment that the failure to obtain the serological reports was a serious investigative lapse. It also drew on the principles in Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal and the authorities discussed there concerning the court’s responsibility to address defective investigation and ensure proper administration of justice. The judgment directs pension-related action in accordance with the applicable service rules.
members.conclusion: The police chief was directed to take disciplinary action against the investigating officer, including appropriate pension-related action if the officer had retired; a limitation bar in the applicable rules was not to prevent the court-directed inquiry.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding was a criminal case in which the court assessed the conduct of the investigation.
predicates.investigating_officer_committed_serious_: The investigating officer committed an investigative omission that the court regarded as serious.
predicates.court_directed_disciplinary_action: The court ordered the competent authority to take disciplinary action concerning the investigating officer.

members.legal_issue: A person under twenty-one years of age is not eligible for the statutory probation benefit when convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for life, even if the offence also permits a lesser term of imprisonment.
material_facts: The appellant was assumed to have been under twenty-one years of age when convicted.
The appellant was convicted of voluntarily causing grievous hurt as a member of an unlawful assembly.
The offence was punishable with imprisonment for life or, alternatively, imprisonment for a term of up to ten years.
The sentence for the principal offence was reduced to three years, after which the appellant sought the benefit of probation.
members.legal_principle: Section 6(1) of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 applies to an offender under twenty-one only when the offence is punishable with imprisonment but not with imprisonment for life. An alternative lesser term does not remove an offence from the category of offences punishable with life imprisonment; construing the provision otherwise would make the words excluding life imprisonment ineffective. The Court followed Som Nath Puri v. State of Rajasthan, which applied the same construction to section 4 of the Act.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not claim the probation benefit because the offence was punishable with imprisonment for life; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.probation_eligibility_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a convicted person is eligible for release on probation.
predicates.offender_under_twenty_one: The convicted person was under twenty-one years of age at the relevant time.
predicates.offense_punishable_with_life: The offence of conviction carries imprisonment for life as an available punishment.
predicates.probation_benefit_unavailable: The convicted person is not eligible for the statutory probation benefit.

members.legal_issue: The special protection against imprisonment for a person under twenty-one does not apply when the offence of which that person is found guilty is punishable with imprisonment for life.
material_facts: The accused was under twenty-one years of age.
He was found guilty under Section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code, an offence punishable with imprisonment for life.
The accused sought the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, and argued that the offence should instead be treated under Section 304 Part II to make that protection available.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 applies to a person under twenty-one found guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment but not with imprisonment for life. The Court held that the offence of conviction was punishable with imprisonment for life and that the conviction could not be changed to attract Section 6. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act did not apply because the offence of which the accused was found guilty was punishable with imprisonment for life; the sentence was maintained.

predicates.sentencing_or_probation_issue: The proceeding concerns whether a young offender may receive special probation protection at sentencing.
predicates.offender_under_twenty_one: The offender was younger than twenty-one when found guilty.
predicates.offence_punishable_with_life_imprisonmen: The offence of which the offender was found guilty is punishable with imprisonment for life.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who represents that interest will not be claimed for a period in order to obtain a stay may not later claim interest for that period.
material_facts: The claimants asked the Reference Court to stay proceedings and represented that they would not claim interest on any enhanced compensation during the stay.
The acquiring authority did not object to the stay on those terms, and the Court stayed the proceedings accordingly.
The High Court nevertheless allowed interest for the period covered by the stay.
members.legal_principle: Interest under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is discretionary as to whether it is awarded, although the prescribed rate is mandatory when interest is awarded. The Court held that statutory rights may be waived by agreement or conduct where public interest is not involved, and applied the principle that a party may not take advantage of its own representation. It relied on Raghubans Narain Singh v. Uttar Pradesh Government, State of Assam v. Jitendra Kumar Senapati, Krishna Bahadur v. Purna Theatre, Superintendent of Taxes, Dhubri v. Onkarmal Nathmal Trust, and the principle actus curiae neminem gravabit.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing interest for the period of the stay; the claimants could not claim interest for that period after obtaining the stay on their representation.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.claimant_requested_stay: The claimant asked the court to stay the compensation proceedings.
predicates.claimant_waived_interest_during_stay: The claimant represented that interest would not be claimed for the period of the stay, and the stay was granted on that basis.

members.legal_issue: A claimant who expressly gives up interest for a period to obtain a stay of proceedings may not claim interest for that period.
material_facts: The claimants sought and obtained a stay of the reference proceedings after representing that they would not claim interest on enhanced compensation for the period of the stay.
The acquiring authority had no objection to the stay on those stated terms.
The High Court nevertheless allowed interest for the stay period on the ground that the statutory interest provisions could not be waived.
members.legal_principle: The right to interest may be waived, including by conduct, where a party expressly represents that it will not claim interest in order to obtain a benefit, and no public interest prevents waiver. A party cannot take advantage of its own representation to obtain the stay and then claim contrary to it. The Court relied on sections 28 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, Raghubans Narain Singh v. Uttar Pradesh Government, State of Assam v. Jitendra Kumar Senapati, Krishna Bahadur v. Purna Theatre, Vijay Cotton & Oil Mills Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, Sushil Kumar v. Rakesh Kumar, and Laxminarayan R. Bhattad v. State of Maharashtra.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in awarding interest for the period covered by the claimants’ representation. The claimants were not entitled to interest for that period.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation following acquisition of land.
predicates.claimant_expressly_waived_interest_for_s: The claimant represented that interest would not be claimed for a specified period in seeking a stay.
predicates.stay_granted_on_that_basis: The proceedings were stayed on the terms of the claimant’s representation.

members.legal_issue: A court should not direct payment of all acquisition compensation to one claimant while the competing claimants' entitlement remains unresolved in pending proceedings.
material_facts: Competing parties asserted interests in the acquired land, and their inter se claims were pending in separate proceedings.
The High Court directed payment of the entire compensation to one claimant's family entity despite those pending disputes and without an application by that entity for the direction.
The governing statute preserved the liability of a recipient to pay compensation to the person legally entitled to it.
members.legal_principle: Under the third proviso to Section 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a person who receives compensation remains liable to pay it to the person lawfully entitled. Competing title claims must be determined in the appropriate proceedings; receipt of compensation does not finally determine entitlement.
members.conclusion: The direction to pay the entire compensation to the family entity was unjustified and was set aside. The entitlement to compensation remained for determination in the pending proceedings, and a recipient found not to be entitled would have to repay the compensation with any interest determined under restitution principles.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.competing_entitlement_claims_pending: Different claimants assert entitlement to the acquired land or its compensation, and their dispute remains pending.
predicates.compensation_directed_to_one_claimant_be: A court directs payment of the compensation to one claimant before deciding the competing claims.

members.legal_issue: Compensation deposited during a pending dispute over entitlement cannot be ordered paid entirely to one claimant without a proper basis for resolving or protecting the competing interests.
material_facts: Inter se disputes over ownership and entitlement to the compensation were pending in proceedings before the High Court.
The High Court directed payment of the entire compensation to a family entity through its representative despite those pending disputes and without an application by that entity for the direction.
The acquiring authority had deposited compensation, and one claimant had already withdrawn amounts awarded earlier.
members.legal_principle: A person who receives compensation remains liable to pay it to the person lawfully entitled. The Court applied the restitution principle and considered the third proviso to section 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
members.conclusion: The direction authorizing the family entity to collect the entire compensation was unjustified and was set aside. Any recipient remained liable to pay the compensation to the person ultimately found lawfully entitled to it, with restitution as appropriate.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_dispute: The proceeding concerns payment of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.competing_entitlement_claims_pending: Competing claims to ownership or entitlement remain pending for determination.
predicates.entire_deposit_awarded_to_one_claimant_w: The court directs the whole deposited amount to one claimant without resolving or adequately protecting the competing claims.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may invoke its constitutional power to set aside procedural orders and remit a case to secure complete justice in exceptional circumstances involving mishandled proceedings and substantial public funds.
material_facts: The acquiring authority did not challenge certain orders concerning amendment and additional evidence.
The case involved a large amount of public money and a history of mishandled proceedings and conflicting court orders.
The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had not properly considered material legal and evidentiary issues.
members.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to make orders necessary to do complete justice between the parties. The Court relied on Deb Narayan Shyam v. State of West Bengal as an example of invoking that power where the state's handling of proceedings had created an anomalous situation.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to set aside the relevant orders and judgments and remit the matters for fresh consideration.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and proceedings_mishandled and substantial_public_funds_involved and existing_orders_prevent_complete_justice

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court on appeal.
predicates.proceedings_mishandled: The proceedings were mishandled, resulting in material procedural or adjudicative errors.
predicates.substantial_public_funds_involved: The dispute involves a substantial amount of public money.
predicates.existing_orders_prevent_complete_justice: The existing orders prevent a fair and complete determination of the dispute.

members.legal_issue: A court may invoke its constitutional power to do complete justice to set aside consequential procedural orders in exceptional circumstances involving substantial public funds and mishandled litigation.
material_facts: The acquiring authority did not challenge orders allowing amendments and additional evidence.
The litigation had been mishandled by the State and different courts had made inconsistent orders.
A large amount of public money was involved.
members.legal_principle: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to make orders necessary to do complete justice in the case before it. The Court relied on Deb Narayan Shyam v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: The Court invoked its power under Article 142 to set aside the procedural orders and remit the matters for fresh consideration.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and public_funds_substantially_involved and (state_litigation_mishandled or inconsistent_court_orders)

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.public_funds_substantially_involved: The challenged outcome concerns a substantial amount of public money.
predicates.state_litigation_mishandled: The State’s handling of the litigation contributed to the anomalous procedural situation.
predicates.inconsistent_court_orders: Different courts made inconsistent orders in the course of the litigation.

members.legal_issue: Payment or tender of the estimated compensation before taking possession is a mandatory precondition to taking possession under the urgency procedure.
material_facts: The State took possession under the urgency procedure and maintained that the statutory requirements had been met.
The record indicated that only part of the compensation had been paid, while the balance remained unpaid.
The Court considered the statutory requirement to tender a portion of estimated compensation before taking possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 17(3A), read with Section 17(3B), makes tender of the required portion of estimated compensation a mandatory precondition to taking possession, subject to the specified payment impediments in Section 31(2). The word “shall” and the phrase “Before taking possession” prescribe a required sequence. Under Taylor v. Taylor and the authorities applying it, including Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor, Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v. State of Vindhya Pradesh, State of U.P. v. Singhara Singh, Babu Verghese v. Bar Council of Kerala, and Hussein Ghadially v. State of Gujarat, a statutory procedure must be followed as prescribed.
members.conclusion: The Collector must tender the statutorily required portion of the estimated compensation to the persons entitled before taking possession, unless a specified statutory impediment prevents payment.

predicates.urgency_acquisition: The proceeding is an acquisition in which the State invokes an urgent procedure to take land for a public purpose.
predicates.possession_taken: The State has taken possession of the land from its owner.

members.legal_issue: Payment of the prescribed advance compensation is a condition precedent to taking possession and vesting land under the emergency acquisition procedure.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the emergency procedure and possession was taken before an award was made.
The landowners were not paid the prescribed portion of the estimated compensation before possession was taken.
The beneficiary said it had deposited funds with State authorities, but the landowners had not received the advance compensation before possession.
members.legal_principle: Justice Ganguly relied on Sections 17(1), 17(2), 17(3A), and 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and Article 300A of the Constitution. He applied strict construction of expropriatory legislation, reading the emergency-acquisition provisions as a composite scheme, and relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, R.C. Cooper v. Union of India, Gujarat Electricity Board v. Girdharlal Motilal, Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation v. Darius Shapur Chenai, and Bharat Petroleum Corporation v. Maddula Ratnavalli. He rejected the contrary observation in Satendra Prasad Jain as unnecessary to that case and, alternatively, contrary to the statute. Justice Kumar relied on the absence of an express statutory consequence for default, the vesting scheme, and Satendra Prasad Jain and Tika Ram v. State of U.P. for the view that default does not invalidate the acquisition.
members.conclusion: Justice Asok Kumar Ganguly held that the advance-payment requirement is mandatory and a condition precedent to valid possession and vesting; without compliance, taking possession is illegal and vesting does not occur.
