Justice Swatanter Kumar held that non-compliance does not invalidate the acquisition or undo vesting, although the payment obligation remains. The judges differed, and the matter was referred to a larger Bench; neither position was resolved by a binding majority ruling.

predicates.emergency_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked an emergency procedure.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land.
predicates.advance_compensation_received_before_pos: The landowners received the prescribed advance compensation before possession was taken.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court should not overturn the execution courts’ rejection of a tenancy objection or direct transfer of trust property when the tenancy plea has no factual basis.
material_facts: The execution court rejected the respondents’ objection, and the trust obtained possession of the land through execution.
The District Judge dismissed the appeal from the execution court’s orders.
The High Court accepted that the scheme could be executed as a decree but directed referral of a tenancy issue and ordered the trust to hand possession to the claimant.
The tenancy claim lacked material particulars, and the earlier tenancy-authority proceedings had not determined the claimant’s tenancy status.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that revisional interference was unwarranted in the circumstances because the tenancy plea had no supporting factual basis. The pleading principles in Order VI Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as discussed in Ram Sarup Gupta v. Bishun Narain Inter College (1987) 2 SCC 555, and the requirement of particulars reflected in M/s Nilesh Construction Company v. M/s Gangubai, AIR 1982 Bombay 491, supported that conclusion. The Court also relied on Pandu Dhondi Yerudkar v. Ananda Krishna Patil, 1947 (76) BLR 368, concerning the particulars needed for a tenancy plea.
members.conclusion: The High Court ought not to have interfered in revision without a factual basis for the tenancy plea. Its directions referring the issue and requiring transfer of possession were set aside.

predicates.revision_proceeding_from_execution: A revisional court is reviewing orders made in execution proceedings.
predicates.lower_courts_rejected_tenancy_objection: The execution court rejected the tenancy objection and the appellate court left that rejection undisturbed.
predicates.tenancy_claim_lacks_factual_basis: The party claiming tenancy provides no material facts supporting how the tenancy arose or what its terms were.
predicates.revisional_interference_unwarranted: The revisional court should not interfere with the execution courts’ orders on the unsupported tenancy claim.

members.legal_issue: A revisional court should not set aside a reasoned refusal of leave to defend when the tenant has raised no triable issue.
material_facts: The trial court considered the parties’ pleadings, affidavits, and supporting documents and refused leave after finding the tenant’s defences false, frivolous, and legally unsustainable.
The High Court allowed the tenant’s revision on the view that the pleadings raised a triable issue.
The Supreme Court concluded that the tenant’s title denial was barred by estoppel and that no triable issue had been raised.
members.legal_principle: In the exercise of revisional jurisdiction, interference was unwarranted with the trial court’s well-considered and reasoned refusal of leave where the tenant’s defence did not raise a triable issue under Section 14 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982.
members.conclusion: The High Court ought not to have interfered with the trial court’s reasoned order; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and restored the trial court’s order.

predicates.revision_from_refusal_of_leave_to_defend: The proceeding is a revision challenging a trial court’s refusal to grant leave to defend an eviction claim.
predicates.trial_court_gave_reasoned_assessment: The trial court considered the pleadings, affidavits, and supporting material and explained its decision.
predicates.tenant_raised_no_triable_issue: The tenant’s disclosed facts do not present a genuine issue capable of affecting the landlord’s entitlement to eviction.

members.legal_issue: A technical challenge to publication of a scheme fails when the government’s published sanction is conclusive evidence that the scheme was duly framed and sanctioned.
material_facts: A petitioner alleged that the scheme’s notice had not been published in the required manner.
The petitioner knew of the scheme and had submitted objections and representations.
The government published a notification sanctioning the scheme, and the governing law made that publication conclusive evidence that the scheme had been duly framed and sanctioned.
members.legal_principle: The provision governing publication of a government sanction makes that publication conclusive evidence that the scheme was duly framed and sanctioned. In this case, the petitioner’s awareness of the scheme and participation by objection further supported rejecting a delayed technical challenge to publication.
members.conclusion: The publication challenge was rejected as lacking merit.

rule.if: scheme_publication_challenge and government_sanction_notification_published and sanction_publication_is_conclusive and challenger_knew_of_scheme_and_objected

predicates.scheme_publication_challenge: A person challenges whether the required notice or publication for an improvement scheme was properly made.
predicates.government_sanction_notification_publish: The government published a notification sanctioning the scheme.
predicates.sanction_publication_is_conclusive: The governing law makes publication of the sanction conclusive evidence that the scheme was duly framed and sanctioned.
predicates.challenger_knew_of_scheme_and_objected: The challenger knew of the scheme and submitted objections or representations about it.

members.legal_issue: A statutory provision making publication conclusive evidence that a scheme was duly framed and sanctioned does not prevent a challenge based on the authority’s complete lack of jurisdiction to frame the scheme.
material_facts: The scheme was published after it had been considered and approved by the State Government.
The scheme concerned an area that was outside the statutory definition of a damaged area, so the authorities lacked jurisdiction to frame it.
The affected property owner challenged the scheme and the resulting acquisition proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 5(4) of the Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951 makes publication conclusive evidence that a scheme has been duly framed and sanctioned only in relation to the formalities under sections 3, 4 and 5. It does not cure or foreclose a challenge where the authorities had no jurisdiction because the scheme was not for a statutorily eligible area.
members.conclusion: The publication clause did not bar the challenge because its conclusive effect concerned compliance with procedural formalities, not the existence of jurisdiction; the acquisition proceedings were quashed.

predicates.challenge_to_published_development_schem: An affected person challenges a published development scheme and action taken under it.
predicates.scheme_area_outside_authorized_scope: The scheme concerns an area for which the authorities had no statutory authority to frame a scheme.

members.legal_issue: A civil appeal cannot proceed without a necessary party who was included in the appeal below when the appellants knew of that party’s participation and sought to add the party only belatedly without due diligence.
material_facts: After the original plaintiff died during the appeal in the High Court, the plaintiff’s legal representatives, including another son, were brought on record, and that son was represented by counsel.
The appellants knew that the son had been made a party but did not include him in their appeal to the Supreme Court.
The appellants offered no good reason for omitting him and sought to add him only after the appeal came before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: A necessary party must be joined in an appeal. An appellant who knew of the party’s participation below cannot rely on an unclear judgment to excuse the omission, and a belated request to add the party may be refused where the appellant did not act with due diligence. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The late application to add the omitted party was refused, and the appeal was dismissed as not properly instituted.

rule.if: civil_appeal and omitted_person_was_party_in_appeal_below and omitted_person_was_necessary_party and appellants_knew_of_participation and late_joinder_request_lacked_due_diligence

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal.
predicates.omitted_person_was_party_in_appeal_below: The person omitted from the current appeal had been made a party to the appeal below.
predicates.omitted_person_was_necessary_party: The court treated the omitted person as necessary to the appeal.

members.legal_issue: A civil appeal cannot proceed without a person who was added as a party in an earlier appeal when the appellants knew of that joinder, omitted the person from later appeals, and sought joinder only belatedly.
material_facts: After a party to the suit died during the first appeal, some of that party’s legal representatives applied to continue the appeal.

The opposing party objected that the deceased party’s estate would not be fully represented unless another legal representative was joined; the first appellate court accepted an application to join that person as a respondent.
The appeal was dismissed, and the appellants omitted the joined person from both their second appeal and their appeal to the Supreme Court, although they knew of the earlier joinder.
The appellants sought to add the person only after the appeal reached the Supreme Court. They also contended that the person had no interest in the premises.
members.legal_principle: A party who was joined in an earlier appeal cannot be omitted from a later appeal to the advantage of appellants who knew of that joinder. A belated request to add the person may be refused where the appellants were not duly diligent, and a claim that the absent person has no interest cannot be decided in that person’s absence. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The late application to add the omitted party was refused, the contention about that person’s interest was not considered in the person’s absence, and the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: The scope of property conveyed by a sale in execution of a money decree is determined by what the court intended to sell, assessed from the evidence, and does not extend to underlying permanent tenancy rights when only the structures were intended to be sold.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a sale in execution of a money decree and the rights conveyed by that sale.

The execution application and attached schedule described the structures standing on the land as the property to be attached and sold; a later application stated that the attached property consisted of the structures.
The landowner’s permanent tenancy rights were the subject of pending litigation when the sale took place, and a court had held that the permanent tenancy could not be terminated by eviction.
The sale purchaser was also the decree-holder, and the structures were purchased for a comparatively small sum.
members.legal_principle: Under Pettachi Chettiar v. Sangili Veera Pandia, in a sale in execution of a money decree the relevant questions are what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser understood was bought; these are questions of fact or mixed law and fact determined from the evidence in the particular case. Here, the execution documents, the pending dispute over the permanent tenancy, the ruling that the tenant could not be evicted, and the sale price showed that the sale was of the structures alone, not the underlying site or tenancy rights.
members.conclusion: The execution sale conveyed the structures, meaning their materials, but did not convey the land beneath or appurtenant to them or the permanent tenancy rights in that land. The appeal was dismissed and the decree in the landowner’s favour was upheld.

rule.if: execution_sale_case and execution_documents_described_structures and execution_application_identified_structures_as_attached_property and (tenancy_rights_were_in_pending_litigation or permanent_tenancy_could_not_be_terminated_by_eviction)

predicates.execution_sale_excludes_underlying_perma: The execution sale does not convey the permanent tenancy rights in the land beneath or appurtenant to the structures.

members.legal_issue: The scope of a certificate issued after a sale in execution of a money decree depends on the right, title, and interest actually intended to be sold, and the sale of structures alone does not convey the land or tenancy rights beneath or appurtenant to them.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the scope of a sale in execution of a money decree and the certificate issued to the purchaser.
The execution schedule described the structures standing on the land, and the decree holder later described the attached property as consisting of those structures.
When the sale took place, the occupant’s rights in the land were the subject of pending litigation.
In related litigation, a court had found the occupant’s tenancy to be permanent and had rejected a request to evict her.
The decree holder purchased the property for a price the Supreme Court considered paltry in light of the rights claimed to have been sold.
members.legal_principle: In a sale in execution of a money decree, the court determines from the evidence what right, title, and interest was actually intended to be sold. A court’s or purchaser’s misapprehension cannot alter the sale’s true legal effect. The judgment addresses the certificate under Order XXI Rule 94 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and follows Pettachi Chettiar v. Sangili Veera Pandia, L.R. 14 I.A. 84 at 85, which frames the inquiry as what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser understood was bought, determined on the evidence in the particular case.
members.conclusion: The sale covered only the materials of the structures; it did not convey the site or the permanent tenancy rights in the land underneath or appurtenant to the structures. The appeal was dismissed, leaving the High Court’s decree in place.

members.legal_issue: In a suit for permanent injunction, lawful possession should be decided without adjudicating title when title is not framed as an issue and is not genuinely disputed.
material_facts: The suit sought permanent injunction against an attempted encroachment.

The defendants claimed ownership and possession of a different property, acknowledged that other properties lay between it and the suit property, and did not genuinely dispute the plaintiffs’ title to the suit property.
Municipal records, registered conveyances, tax records, and commissioners’ reports supported the plaintiffs’ possession.
The lower courts dismissed the suit after treating the plaintiffs’ failure to establish title as a reason they had not established lawful possession.
members.legal_principle: Where the relief sought is permanent injunction and title is neither an issue framed for decision nor genuinely disputed, the court should decide the claim by assessing possession and interference rather than unnecessarily adjudicating title. The court relied on the documentary and commissioner evidence in the record; no earlier case was cited for this specific principle.
members.conclusion: The plaintiffs had sufficiently established lawful possession, and the dismissals based on the lower courts’ erroneous focus on title were unsustainable; the appeal was allowed and the dismissals were set aside.

rule.if: permanent_injunction_suit and title_not_genuinely_disputed and possession_supported_by_evidence and interference_attempted

predicates.permanent_injunction_suit: The claimant brought a civil suit seeking protection of possession by permanent injunction.
predicates.title_not_genuinely_disputed: The opposing party did not genuinely claim title to the property in dispute or pursue a genuine challenge to the claimant’s title.
predicates.possession_supported_by_evidence: Records or other evidence supported the claimant’s possession of the disputed property.
predicates.interference_attempted: The opposing party attempted to interfere with the claimant’s possession.

members.legal_issue: A permanent injunction may be granted on established possession without determining title where the suit seeks only protection of possession and the circumstances establish that the defendant is not in possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a permanent injunction to protect possession and did not seek a declaration of title.
The plaintiff’s possession was found established and was supported by the defendant’s admission.
The defendant had previously brought a claim for declaration and recovery of possession of the same property, and that claim and the ensuing appeal were dismissed.
The plaintiff’s plaint did not set out a title dispute requiring a declaration.
members.legal_principle: Possession is good against all but the true owner, and even a person in established possession may obtain an injunction. The Court relied on Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander and the principle affirmed in Parry v. Clissold. A bare injunction suit may be decided on possession where the pleadings and circumstances do not require adjudication of title; the Court distinguished Nagar Palika, Jind v. Jagat Singh, Advocate, where title and possession were denied and the title document was not produced.
members.conclusion: The injunction suit was maintainable and could be decreed on the basis of the plaintiff’s admitted and established possession without deciding the validity of the plaintiff’s title documents.

rule.if: proceeding_is_bare_possession_injunction and plaintiff_possession_is_established and defendant_admitted_plaintiff_possession and defendant_prior_claim_to_possession_failed

predicates.proceeding_is_bare_possession_injunction: The plaintiff brought a proceeding seeking to restrain interference with possession rather than seeking a declaration of title.
predicates.plaintiff_possession_is_established: The evidence in the proceeding established that the plaintiff was in possession of the property.
predicates.defendant_admitted_plaintiff_possession: The defendant’s own evidence or statements acknowledged the plaintiff’s possession.

members.legal_issue: A statement of objects and reasons may assist when an enactment's purpose is disputed or uncertain, but it cannot override clear operative statutory language.
material_facts: The parties disputed the purpose and effect of the state enactment concerning mineral rights.
The enactment's operative provisions expressly addressed acquisition of proprietary mineral rights and did not mention leasehold or licence rights.
members.legal_principle: A statement of objects and reasons is not part of the statute and may be relevant when the object or purpose is disputed or uncertain. It cannot override the effect that follows from explicit and unmistakable operative language, which is the best evidence of legislative intention.
members.conclusion: The enactment's effect had to be determined from its substantive provisions; its statement of objects and reasons could not override their clear language.

predicates.statutory_interpretation_case: A court must determine the meaning or effect of an enactment.
predicates.operative_language_is_unambiguous: The enactment's operative provisions express their effect clearly and unmistakably.

members.legal_issue: A statement of objects and reasons may explain the background and mischief of legislation but may not determine the meaning and effect of its substantive provisions.
material_facts: The amendment introducing the special recovery ground followed a government policy requiring employees who owned homes at their place of posting to vacate government accommodation or pay market rent.
The Court referred to the statement of objects and reasons accompanying the amendment to understand the background and purpose of the legislation.
members.legal_principle: In interpreting legislation, a statement of objects and reasons accompanying a bill cannot determine the true meaning or effect of the enacted substantive provisions, but may be considered to understand the background, antecedent state of affairs, surrounding circumstances, and the evil the legislation sought to remedy.
members.conclusion: The statement of objects and reasons could be used to understand the background, surrounding circumstances, and mischief addressed, but not to determine the true meaning and effect of the substantive statutory provisions.

predicates.statutory_interpretation_proceeding: The court must interpret the meaning or effect of enacted statutory provisions.
predicates.legislative_statement_of_objects_and_rea: The court considers a statement of objects and reasons accompanying the bill that became the legislation.

members.legal_issue: The market value for compensation in an acquisition under a local improvement law is determined as of the local notice that serves the same purpose as the general preliminary acquisition notice, under the compensation procedure in force when the acquisition proceedings began.
material_facts: The acquisition proceeded under a local improvement law that applied the general acquisition law except where the local law provided otherwise.
The local law's preliminary notification was published in 1965, before a later declaration under that law.
The general acquisition law's compensation procedure had been amended in 1927 to use the date of its preliminary notification, rather than the date of its later declaration, as the valuation date.
The High Court used the date of the later local declaration, following an earlier ruling that applied the unamended procedure.
members.legal_principle: Section 23 of the City of Mysore Improvement Act applied the Land Acquisition Act's procedure, as it stood when acquisition proceedings began, except where the local Act expressly deviated from it. Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, as amended in 1927, made the general preliminary-notification date the valuation date; under section 6 of the Mysore General Clauses Act, only proceedings commenced before repeal would remain governed by the former procedure. The local preliminary notification served the same purpose as a notification under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, so its date governed valuation. The Court followed Land Acquisition Officer, City Improvement Trust Board v. H. Narayanaiah and overruled Venkatamma v. Special Land Acquisition Officer.
members.conclusion: The valuation date was the date of the local preliminary notification, which served the same purpose as the general preliminary notification. The High Court's judgment was set aside and the case remanded for determination of market value on that basis.

rule.if: compensation_valuation_appeal and acquisition_under_local_improvement_law and local_law_adopts_general_acquisition_procedure and not local_law_expressly_preserves_old_valuation_rule and current_general_procedure_uses_preliminary_notice and local_preliminary_notice_has_same_purpose

predicates.compensation_valuation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the date used to value property for compensation in a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_under_local_improvement_law: The property was acquired under a local law providing for an improvement scheme.
predicates.local_law_adopts_general_acquisition_pro: The local law directs that acquisition follow the general acquisition procedure except where the local law provides otherwise.
predicates.local_law_expressly_preserves_old_valuat: The local law expressly retains a valuation rule that has been replaced in the general acquisition procedure.
predicates.current_general_procedure_uses_prelimina: When the acquisition proceedings began, the general procedure used the date of its preliminary notice to determine market value.
predicates.local_preliminary_notice_has_same_purpos: The preliminary notice under the local law served the same purpose as the preliminary notice under the general procedure.

members.legal_issue: The market value in a land acquisition under a special improvement law that adopts the general acquisition procedure is determined as of the date of the special law’s preliminary notification when it serves the same function as the general law’s preliminary notification.
material_facts: The special law provided for an initial notification concerning a completed improvement scheme and a later declaration that the land was required for a public purpose.
The special law treated the later declaration as equivalent to the general acquisition law’s final declaration.
The special law contained no separate principle for determining compensation, and its general-procedure clause applied the general acquisition law so far as applicable.

The High Court used the later declaration date to determine market value, relying in part on an earlier decision interpreting a different improvement law enacted before the general acquisition law was amended.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 27 and 16 of the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945, the special notification procedure replaces the general preliminary-notification procedure where their objects and functions are identical. Section 27(2) equates the special law’s later declaration with a declaration under section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; section 23(1) of that Act therefore supplies the market-value date, and the special initial notification corresponds to the notification under section 4(1). The words “so far as they are applicable” do not mean “only if specifically mentioned”; provisions not expressly or necessarily excluded remain applicable. Equity cannot supplant the statutory scheme, and delay between notifications does not alter the interpretation of the provisions governing the valuation date. Venkatamma v. Special Land Acquisition Officer was distinguishable because it interpreted a law enacted in 1903 against the acquisition law as it then stood; M. Manicklal v. State of Mysore was approved.
members.conclusion: The market value must be determined as of the special law’s initial notification, which serves the function of the general acquisition law’s preliminary notification. The appeals were allowed and the matters remanded for fresh determination on that basis.

rule.if: scheme_based_land_acquisition and special_initial_notice_serves_preliminary_function and later_notice_equated_to_final_declaration and no_separate_compensation_principle

predicates.scheme_based_land_acquisition: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land under a law providing for an improvement scheme.
predicates.special_initial_notice_serves_preliminar: The special law’s initial notice performs the same preliminary function as the general acquisition procedure’s preliminary notice.
predicates.later_notice_equated_to_final_declaratio: The special law treats a later notice or declaration as equivalent to the general acquisition procedure’s final declaration.
predicates.no_separate_compensation_principle: The special law does not prescribe a distinct principle for determining compensation.

members.legal_issue: Interim protection from dispossession pending an appeal may be granted subject to conditions securing payment of arrears and ongoing rent and an undertaking to give up possession if the appeal fails.
material_facts: The tenants sought protection from dispossession while their appeal was pending.
The Court required the tenants to deposit the arrears and to make timely deposits of rent during the appeal.
The tenants’ counsel undertook that they would deliver possession if the appeal was dismissed.

The Court allowed the landlord to withdraw deposited rent without prejudice to the appeal, and provided that the stay would end if the tenants failed to deposit the arrears or made two consecutive defaults in monthly rent deposits.
members.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion to grant interim protection from dispossession subject to conditions requiring payment of arrears and ongoing rent and an undertaking to deliver possession if the appeal failed; no earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this interim order.
members.conclusion: A stay of dispossession was granted pending disposal of the appeal, subject to the stated deposit conditions and undertaking.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal concerning the tenants’ eviction remained pending before the court.
predicates.tenants_seek_stay_of_dispossession: The tenants asked the court to protect them from being dispossessed while the appeal was pending.
predicates.tenants_required_to_pay_arrears_and_ongo: The court required the tenants to deposit arrears and make ongoing rent payments as conditions of interim protection.
predicates.tenants_undertake_to_surrender_possessio: The tenants’ counsel undertook that the tenants would give up possession if the appeal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: A court hearing an appeal in a contested building-possession suit may make an order for deposit of rent during the appeal.
material_facts: The landlord’s suit sought recovery of possession of a building, and the tenant contested the claim for eviction.
During the appeal, the Subordinate Judge ordered the tenant to deposit rent under section 11A.
The tenant argued that an order under section 11A could be made only by the trial court.
members.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 permits an order for deposit of rent in a contested suit for possession of a building. Since an appeal is a continuation of the suit, the landlord may obtain the benefit of such an order in the appellate court as well as in the trial court. No earlier cases are relied on for this principle.
members.conclusion: An order under section 11A may be made at any stage of the litigation, including in appeal, because an appeal is a continuation of the suit.

predicates.contested_building_possession_suit: A tenant contests a landlord’s suit seeking possession of a building.
predicates.matter_in_appeal: The building-possession suit is being considered by an appellate court.
predicates.landlord_seeks_rent_deposit_order: The landlord seeks an order requiring the tenant to deposit rent while the litigation is pending.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may overrule an earlier constitutional decision that it concludes was wrong, while limiting the effect of its new rule to the future to preserve settled transactions.
material_facts: An earlier Supreme Court decision had upheld Parliament’s power to amend fundamental rights, and a later decision had followed that position.
The challenged constitutional amendment and subsequent land-reform measures had been relied on in numerous transactions and had substantially altered agrarian arrangements.
The Court concluded that the earlier rule was wrong but considered retrospective invalidation likely to cause serious disruption.
members.legal_principle: The Court adopted prospective overruling for constitutional matters, relying on Articles 32, 141 and 142 and on Great Northern Railway v. Sunburst Oil & Refining Co., Chicot County Drainage District v. Baxter State Bank, Griffin v. Illinois, Wolf v. Colorado, Mapp v. Ohio and Linkletter v. Walker. It held that the Supreme Court may restrict the retrospective operation of a newly declared rule in accordance with the justice of the case, and that the doctrine is available in matters arising under the Constitution and only to the Supreme Court.
members.conclusion: The Court overruled the earlier decision but applied its new rule prospectively, leaving the earlier amendments and transactions based on them unaffected.

predicates.constitutional_case: The proceeding raises an issue arising under the Constitution.
predicates.supreme_court_replaces_earlier_rule: The Supreme Court replaces a rule stated in its earlier decision with a new rule.
predicates.retrospective_effect_would_disrupt_settl: Applying the new rule to past events would unsettle transactions or arrangements made in reliance on the earlier rule.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may limit the retrospective effect of a new constitutional ruling to preserve transactions and arrangements made in reliance on earlier decisions.
material_facts: The Court departed from earlier decisions that had permitted amendments affecting fundamental rights.
For many years, legislatures had enacted land-reform laws on the basis of those earlier decisions, and those laws had substantially changed landholding and created new titles.
The Court considered that applying its new ruling retrospectively would unsettle those arrangements and create serious disruption.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on Articles 32, 141 and 142 to recognize its authority to declare law prospectively and mould relief to do complete justice. It drew on Great Northern Railway v. Sunburst Oil & Refining Co., Chicot County Drainage District v. Baxter State Bank and Linkletter v. Walker. It stated that prospective overruling may be used only in matters arising under the Constitution, only by the Supreme Court, and with the extent of retrospective operation left to the Court’s discretion according to justice in the case.
members.conclusion: The Court applied prospective overruling, so its new rule did not invalidate the challenged amendment or other earlier amendments affecting fundamental rights.

predicates.supreme_court_constitutional_case: The Supreme Court is deciding a case arising under the Constitution.
predicates.supreme_court_changes_constitutional_pre: The Supreme Court replaces an earlier constitutional rule with a new one.
predicates.prior_precedent_underpinned_widespread_r: Legislatures or others substantially relied on the earlier rule in making laws or arranging their affairs.
predicates.retroactive_change_would_disrupt_establi: Applying the new rule to the past would unsettle established transactions or create serious disruption.

members.legal_issue: Appreciation in land from which agricultural income is derived is not converted into a capital asset or taxable capital gain by attributing to the land the non-agricultural portion of the income from manufactured tea.
material_facts: The companies owned tea-estate land on which they grew tea, and the land yielded green tea leaves.
The income from selling tea after it was grown and manufactured was integrated income, apportioned between an agricultural component and a manufacturing component.
The companies sold their estates, and the dispute concerned the surplus associated with land and reserves created by revaluing estate assets.
The revenue argued that the portion of tea-sale income treated as non-agricultural made a corresponding proportion of the land a capital asset.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(4A)(iii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 excludes land from which agricultural income is derived from the definition of capital asset; section 2(6A)(c) addresses liquidation distributions attributable to accumulated profits. Rule 24 apportions the integrated income from tea grown and manufactured by the seller: the agricultural component is derived from the land, while the non-agricultural component is attributable to manufacturing. The court relied on Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd. v. State of Kerala and Anglo-American Direct Tea Trading Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax for the treatment of tea income, and First Income-tax Officer, Salem v. Short Brothers (P.) Ltd. for the treatment of appreciation in agricultural land on liquidation.
members.conclusion: The revenue’s proposed proportionate treatment of the land was rejected. The land yielded agricultural income and was excluded from the definition of capital asset, so appreciation in its value did not constitute a capital gain or become a dividend on liquidation; the court upheld the High Court’s treatment of the land and revaluation items.

predicates.liquidation_distribution_tax_case: The dispute arose in a tax assessment concerning a distribution made on a company’s liquidation.
predicates.land_yields_agricultural_income: The company used land to grow crops, and the land yielded agricultural income through those crops.
predicates.nonagricultural_tea_income_arises_from_m: The non-agricultural component of the company’s income from selling tea arose from manufacturing the tea leaves rather than from the land.

members.legal_issue: A liquidation distribution attributable to capital appreciation from transferring land that produces agricultural income is not a dividend to the extent that the appreciation is neither commercial profit nor a taxable capital gain.
material_facts: The company sold assets that included land from which agricultural income was derived.
The liquidators distributed proceeds from the asset sales to shareholders.
The disputed amount was claimed to represent appreciation in the value of the agricultural land rather than accumulated business profits or taxable capital gains.
The tax authority sought to treat the whole distribution as dividends without determining whether any part represented that appreciation.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(6-A)(c) and 12 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, treat a distribution as a dividend only to the extent attributable to accumulated profits. The Explanation to section 2(6-A) includes capital gains outside its specified excluded periods in accumulated profits. Under section 12-B and the definition of capital asset in section 2(4-A), however, land from which agricultural income is derived is not a capital asset, so gain from its transfer is not a taxable capital gain. Accumulated profits are profits as understood in commercial practice; realization of an appreciated capital value is not itself commercial profit unless it falls within taxable capital gains. Bacha F. Guzdar concerned whether a shareholder’s dividend from profits earned through agricultural income was exempt under section 4(3)(viii); it did not determine whether a receipt was a dividend in the first place.
members.conclusion: The appreciation in the value of the agricultural land was not accumulated profit and was not a dividend; the whole distribution could not be treated as a dividend without determining whether part represented that appreciation. The rule in Bacha F. Guzdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax did not apply because the claim was that the receipt was not taxable as a dividend, not that dividend income was exempt as agricultural income.

rule.if: liquidation_distribution and agricultural_income_land_transferred and distribution_includes_land_appreciation and appreciation_not_commercial_profit_or_taxable_capital_gain

predicates.liquidation_distribution: A company in liquidation distributed assets or money to its shareholders.
predicates.agricultural_income_land_transferred: The company transferred land from which agricultural income was derived.
predicates.distribution_includes_land_appreciation: The shareholder distribution included an amount attributable to appreciation in the value of that land.
predicates.appreciation_not_commercial_profit_or_ta: The appreciation was neither treated as commercial profit nor within the category of gains chargeable as capital gains.

members.legal_issue: A remand order that sets aside a ceiling determination solely because proceedings were initiated against a deceased person does not bar later contentions on the merits under res judicata when the remand order made no finding on those merits.
material_facts: An earlier ceiling determination was set aside because the tenure-holder had died before notice was issued to her.
The matter was remanded for fresh disposal after notices were issued to the heirs.
The remand order made no findings on the merits of the State’s contentions.
The later decisions were challenged on the ground that the earlier remand order barred those contentions.
members.legal_principle: Res judicata does not bar an issue that was not decided in the earlier proceeding. The earlier order set aside the determination as a nullity because it had been made against a dead person and remanded the matter without deciding the merits.
members.conclusion: The earlier remand order did not bar the State’s contentions on the merits, and the High Court was wrong to dismiss the writ petition on res judicata grounds.

predicates.challenge_to_post_remand_ceiling_decisio: A party challenges a decision made after a matter was remanded for fresh determination of a land-ceiling matter.
predicates.earlier_remand_set_aside_order_as_nullit: The earlier remand set aside an order because the proceeding had been taken against a person who had died.
predicates.earlier_remand_made_no_merits_finding: The earlier remand order made no finding on the merits of the parties’ contentions.
predicates.later_contentions_not_barred_by_res_judi: Contentions not decided in the earlier proceeding are not barred by res judicata.

members.legal_issue: A party cannot rely on an earlier eviction decree as an existing decree unaffected by the landlord’s death when that decree was set aside and the matter remanded before the later proceedings.
material_facts: A trial court had passed a partial eviction decree during the original landlord’s lifetime.
The High Court later set aside that decree and remanded the matter for a fresh decision, including consideration of the substituted heirs’ requirement.
The appellants argued that the earlier decree could not be disturbed after the landlord’s death.
members.legal_principle: The court distinguished the asserted exception discussed in Phul Rani & Ors. v. Naubat Rai Ahluwalia, noting that no final opinion had been expressed there on the question. In this case, the prior decree had been set aside and the matter remanded, leaving no existing decree to which the exception could apply.
members.conclusion: The argument was rejected because the earlier decree had been set aside and the matter remanded, so no decree remained in existence to attract the asserted exception. The court expressed no final opinion on whether an extant decree passed before a landlord’s death could be disturbed on that death.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal_or_revision: The proceeding is an appeal or revision arising from a rent-control eviction claim.
predicates.landlord_dies_during_proceedings: The landlord dies while the appellate or revisional proceedings are ongoing.
predicates.earlier_eviction_decree_was_set_aside_an: An earlier eviction decree was set aside and the matter was remanded before the later proceedings.

members.legal_issue: The custodian cannot be required to evict occupants and deliver vacant possession of property leased or allotted by the custodian unless a permitted ground for eviction exists.
material_facts: The mortgagee’s interest in the mortgaged property vested in the custodian after the mortgagee was declared an evacuee.
The custodian took possession and let or allotted the property to occupants.
The custodian refused the mortgagor’s requests to remove those occupants and give him vacant possession.
The case did not establish a ground for eviction under rent-control law or a breach of the occupants’ lease or allotment conditions.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 gives that Act overriding effect, so ordinary rights under the Transfer of Property Act do not override the statutory scheme. Sections 8, 10 and 12 of the Administration Act give the custodian control over evacuee property, while rule 14 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 limits eviction of occupants under leases or allotments granted by the custodian to permitted rent-control grounds, breaches of the lease or allotment, and the further grounds specified by that rule. The custodian is not subject to the control of the competent officer under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951.
members.conclusion: The custodian could not be required to deliver vacant possession by evicting occupants except on a ground permitted by the applicable rules governing the custodian’s leases and allotments.

predicates.evacuee_property_under_custodian_control: The property or an interest in it has vested in the authority administering evacuee property.
predicates.occupants_hold_custodian_leases_or_allot: The custodian has let or allotted the property to occupants.
predicates.permitted_eviction_ground: A ground permitted by the rules governing the custodian’s leases or allotments for evicting the occupants exists.

members.legal_issue: A custodian administering evacuee property cannot require an alleged unauthorized occupant to account for or pay rents and profits through a summary order when the governing law provides no such power.
material_facts: The property owners had migrated to Pakistan, and the properties in India were treated as evacuee property vested in the Custodian.
The appellants possessed the properties under exchanges that were not confirmed; the Custodian set aside the earlier confirmations and treated their possession as unauthorized.
The Custodian ordered the appellants to surrender possession and to account for rents and profits they had received.
The appellants challenged the Custodian’s authority to order the accounting; the issue pressed before the Court was limited to that authority.
members.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, including its general management power and enumerated powers, did not authorize the Custodian to determine and summarily recover rents and profits from an unauthorized occupant. Rule 10(1) authorized recovery of possession, and Rule 10(2) concerned certain tenants or licensees, but neither authorized the summary determination or recovery of rents and profits at issue. Such a claim had to be pursued through the ordinary remedy of a suit. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Custodian had no power under the Act to order the appellants to account for rents and profits without using the ordinary legal remedy of a suit. The Court quashed the part of the order requiring payment of rents and profits, while leaving both sides free to pursue any claims available to them by law.

rule.if: evacuee_property_custodian_proceeding and occupant_alleged_unauthorized and order_requires_rent_accounting and summary_accounting_power_not_granted

predicates.evacuee_property_custodian_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a custodian administering property treated as evacuee property.
predicates.occupant_alleged_unauthorized: The custodian treats a person in possession of the property as lacking lawful authority to possess it.
predicates.order_requires_rent_accounting: The custodian orders the occupant to account for rents or profits received from the property.
predicates.summary_accounting_power_not_granted: The governing law does not grant the custodian power to determine and summarily recover rents and profits from the occupant.
predicates.custodian_cannot_order_summary_rent_acco: The custodian cannot require the occupant to account for rents and profits by summary order.

members.legal_issue: A competent officer cannot order the custodian to deliver vacant possession of mortgaged property without the custodian’s agreement.
material_facts: The mortgagor sought to pay the mortgage debt and obtain vacant possession of the property.
The custodian had placed tenants or allottees in the property and did not agree to deliver vacant possession.
The mortgagor’s mortgage claim was dealt with by a competent officer under the separation scheme.
members.legal_principle: Sections 7, 8 and 10 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 provide for claims concerning composite property and empower the competent officer to separate interests, including by paying the mortgage debt, redeeming the property, selling it or partitioning it. Section 10 makes those powers subject to rules. Rule 11B(b) of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Rules permits redemption or partition where the custodian and claimant agree, and otherwise provides for sale to satisfy the mortgage debt. The Separation Act does not make the custodian subject to the competent officer’s control or empower that officer to cancel the custodian’s leases or allotments. Rule 14 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 independently restricts eviction of occupants. The Court noted the hardship of this result and referred to The All India Film Corporation Ltd. v. Raja Gyan Nath, [1970] 2 S.C.R. 581.
members.conclusion: Without an agreement between the custodian and the mortgagor, the competent officer could not order redemption with vacant possession or direct the custodian to remove the occupants; at most, the officer could direct symbolic possession.

predicates.separation_proceeding_involving_mortgage: A proceeding to separate interests concerns property subject to a mortgage and containing both evacuee and non-evacuee interests.
predicates.custodian_has_placed_occupants_in_proper: The custodian has let or allotted the property to occupants.
predicates.custodian_agrees_to_vacant_possession: The custodian has agreed to deliver the property free of its occupants.

members.legal_issue: After accepting full payment of the mortgage debt, the competent officer must direct symbolic possession but cannot direct vacant possession without the custodian’s agreement.
material_facts: The mortgagor paid the full mortgage debt after the sale order was made, and the competent officer accepted it.
The custodian had placed occupants in the property and had not agreed to deliver vacant possession.
The mortgagor sought possession of the property after the mortgage debt had been satisfied.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to section 10 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 requires the competent officer to accept a mortgagor’s tender in full satisfaction of the mortgage debt. Section 10 makes the competent officer’s powers subject to the rules, and rule 11B(b) of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Rules prevents redemption with vacant possession in the absence of the custodian’s agreement. The competent officer cannot use section 10 to cancel or vary leases or allotments granted by the custodian; rule 14 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 restricts the custodian’s power to evict occupants. The resulting direction may therefore be limited to symbolic possession.
members.conclusion: The mortgage was discharged and the competent officer was bound to direct symbolic possession to the mortgagor, but could not order the custodian to give vacant possession.

rule.if: separation_proceeding_involving_mortgaged_composite_property and full_debt_paid_and_accepted and custodian_has_placed_occupants_in_property and not custodian_agrees_to_vacant_possession

predicates.separation_proceeding_involving_mortgage: A proceeding to separate interests concerns property subject to a mortgage and containing both evacuee and non-evacuee interests.

predicates.custodian_has_placed_occupants_in_proper: The custodian has let or allotted the property to occupants.
predicates.custodian_agrees_to_vacant_possession: The custodian has agreed to deliver the property free of its occupants.

members.legal_issue: A demand for property or valuable security as consideration for a proposed marriage falls within the statutory prohibition on demanding dowry, even when made during marriage negotiations before the marriage takes place.
material_facts: Marriage negotiations took place and included demands for property, jewellery, cash, and money for a car as consideration for the proposed marriage.
The proposed marriage did not take place after the parties failed to agree on the demands.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 2 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, the definition of dowry includes property or valuable security given or agreed to be given as consideration for marriage, and Section 4 penalizes the demand itself. The definition applies to demands made before, at, or after marriage, including in negotiations for a proposed marriage. The Court adopted a purposive reading of the Act, relying on L.V. Jadhav v. Shankar Rao Abasaheb Pawar, Reserve Bank of India v. Peerless General Finance and Investment Co., N.K. Jain v. C.K. Shah, and the purposive-interpretation approach in Seaford Court Estates Ltd. v. Asher.
members.conclusion: A demand made before, at, or after a marriage is covered if it is made as consideration for the marriage; the prohibition includes demands made in relation to a proposed marriage.

rule.if: dowry_demand_prosecution and (demand_made_during_marriage_negotiations or demand_made_at_or_after_marriage) and demand_as_consideration_for_marriage

predicates.dowry_demand_prosecution: The proceeding concerns an allegation that a person demanded property or valuable security in connection with a marriage.
predicates.demand_made_during_marriage_negotiations: A person made the demand while the parties were negotiating a proposed marriage.
predicates.demand_made_at_or_after_marriage: A person made the demand at or after the marriage.
predicates.demand_as_consideration_for_marriage: The demanded property or valuable security was sought as consideration for the marriage.

members.legal_issue: A demand for property or valuable security constitutes a dowry demand when it has a connection with the marriage, regardless of the reason for making the demand.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the husband sought money from his father-in-law to establish a business.
The principal witness’s account of a demand for money was not included in his earlier statement to the investigating officer.
The court found that even if the alleged business-related demand had been made, the evidence did not establish that it had the required connection with the marriage.
members.legal_principle: In Appasaheb v. State of Maharashtra, (2007) 1 SCC 721, the Court observed that a demand for money for financial stringency, urgent domestic expenses, or purchasing manure would not normally be understood as a dowry demand. Bachni Devi v. State of Maharashtra, (2011) 4 SCC 427, clarified that Appasaheb did not lay down a rule of universal application: a demand for property or valuable security, directly or indirectly connected with the marriage, is a dowry demand, and the reason for the demand is immaterial.
members.conclusion: A demand for property or valuable security is a demand for dowry if it has a nexus with the marriage; the reason for the demand is immaterial. On the evidence in this case, the alleged business-related demand was not reliably established as a dowry demand.

predicates.dowry_related_criminal_case: The proceeding concerns an allegation that a demand for property or valuable security amounted to dowry.
predicates.demand_for_property_or_valuable_security: A person sought property or valuable security from another person.
predicates.demand_has_nexus_with_marriage: The demand was connected, directly or indirectly, with the marriage.

members.legal_issue: The maximum penalty for an under-stamped instrument is discretionary and cannot be imposed mechanically or justified solely by an intention to evade stamp duty.
material_facts: The trustees executed a deed transferring property to beneficiaries, describing it as a deed of assent, although an earlier resolution contemplated a deed of transfer.
The deed was treated as a gift deed and had been stamped for only a small amount compared with the duty assessed as payable.
The Collector imposed the maximum penalty, reasoning that the document’s nature had not been disclosed with an intention to evade duty; the High Court relied on substantially the same reason.
Neither the Collector nor the High Court identified dishonest or contumacious conduct or gave any further reason supporting the maximum penalty.
members.legal_principle: Section 40(1)(b) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 makes a penalty up to ten times the proper duty or deficient portion discretionary through the words “if he thinks fit”; the maximum is not automatic and discretion must be exercised rationally and fairly. Read with Sections 33, 35, 38 and 39, the statutory scheme does not contemplate that the maximum penalty must ultimately be realised in every case. The Collector should consider relevant circumstances, including conduct and intent; mere evasion does not by itself justify the maximum, while fraud, deceit or undue enrichment may be relevant to its extent. A penalty is generally deterrent, not retributive. The Court relied on Gangtappa v. Fakkirappa, 2019 (3) SCC 788, on the statutory discretion to reduce or refund penalty, and Peteti Subba Rao v. Anumala S. Narendra, 2002 (10) SCC 427, which stated that the maximum is for very extreme situations and is not to be imposed as a matter of course.
members.conclusion: The maximum penalty was not justified on the reasons given. The Court reduced it from ten times to five times the deficient duty and partly allowed the appeals.

rule.if: stamp_penalty_appeal and under_stamped_instrument and maximum_penalty_imposed and evasion_intent_was_only_reason and no_dishonest_or_contumacious_conduct_found

predicates.stamp_penalty_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the maximum penalty imposed for an under-stamped instrument.
predicates.under_stamped_instrument: The authority found that the instrument was chargeable with duty and had not been sufficiently stamped.
predicates.maximum_penalty_imposed: The authority imposed the highest penalty available for the deficient duty.
predicates.evasion_intent_was_only_reason: The authority relied only on an intention to evade duty as its reason for imposing the maximum penalty.
predicates.no_dishonest_or_contumacious_conduct_fou: The authority did not find that the person responsible for the instrument acted dishonestly or contumaciously.

members.legal_issue: A penalty for deficient stamp duty is subject to a statutory maximum and is not automatically fixed at that maximum.
material_facts: The revenue officer determined that additional stamp duty was due on the instrument and imposed a penalty equal to ten times the deficiency.

The Supreme Court explained that, when the Collector adjudicates an instrument sent after impounding, the maximum penalty is not mandatory and the Collector must consider the relevant factors in fixing the penalty.
members.legal_principle: Section 40 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, provides for the Collector to require payment of proper or deficient duty together with a penalty not exceeding ten times the proper duty or the deficient portion. The stated maximum is a ceiling, and the Collector must consider all relevant factors in deciding the appropriate penalty. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: The penalty amount is for the Collector to determine in light of the relevant factors; ten times the proper duty or deficient portion is an upper limit, not an automatic penalty.

predicates.collector_adjudicates_stamp_deficiency_a: The Collector determines the stamp-duty deficiency on an instrument sent after it was impounded.
predicates.collector_considers_penalty: The Collector considers whether and how much penalty to impose in that adjudication.
predicates.penalty_is_discretionary_and_subject_to_: The Collector must determine the appropriate penalty in light of relevant factors, within the applicable maximum.

members.legal_issue: Tribal customary succession rules should not be declared unconstitutional in the abstract without examination of the particular custom and its effects.
material_facts: The petitions challenged succession rules affecting tribal communities whose customary practices and views about inheritance differed from those under generally applicable personal laws.
The State reported that tribal representatives opposed changing the rules because of concerns about alienation of tribal land and community disruption.
The court considered that imposing other communities’ personal-law principles on tribal communities through judicial action would disregard those differences.
members.legal_principle: Constitutional equality does not require every community to have uniform succession rules, and differences in succession treatment do not invariably violate Article 14. Courts should exercise restraint in applying other communities’ personal laws to tribal customs or creating a uniform succession scheme through judicial action. The court agreed with the approach in the opinion of K. Ramaswamy, J., while emphasizing that particular cases must be assessed on their facts.
members.conclusion: The court declined to declare tribal customs offending Articles 14, 15 and 21, stating that each case must be examined on its full facts.

predicates.tribal_customary_succession_case: The proceeding challenges succession practices followed by a tribal community.
predicates.community_customs_materially_differ: The community follows inheritance customs that differ from those applied to other communities.
predicates.effects_of_the_particular_custom_are_not: The court does not have a full examination of the particular custom and its effects in the case before it.

members.legal_issue: A blanket declaration that customary rules excluding tribal women from inheritance are unconstitutional is unwarranted where tribal succession customs vary and the relevant custom has not been established on case-specific evidence.
material_facts: The petitions challenged customary exclusions from inheritance across tribal communities and regions.
The evidence described differing succession practices among tribes, including differences in whether daughters or widows could inherit.
The Court found that the validity, certainty, antiquity, and operation of a custom could not be determined for every tribe without acceptable material concerning that tribe.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 13(3)(a), a custom having the force of law is subject to fundamental rights, but a claimed custom must be established by clear and unambiguous evidence as to its antiquity and certainty. Ramalaxmi Ammal v. Shivanadha Perumal Sheroyar and Abdul Hussain Khan v. Bibi Sona Dero are relied on for the requirements of proving custom; Sant Ram v. Labh Singh is relied on for the proposition that custom is subject to Part III of the Constitution.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to declare generally that tribal customs excluding women from inheritance violate the Constitution and stated that each case must be decided on its own facts.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_tribal_cu: A constitutional writ proceeding challenges customary rules governing tribal inheritance.
predicates.customs_vary_across_tribes: The succession practices of the relevant tribal communities differ from one another.
predicates.tribe_specific_custom_evidence_is_inadeq: The record does not adequately establish the relevant community's custom and its legal characteristics.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition for a company is invalid if the mandatory preliminary inquiry and reporting requirements for company acquisitions are not followed.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a registered co-operative housing society, which was a company for purposes of the Act.
The Collector did not conduct or report the inquiry required by Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963.
The report that was submitted was under section 5A, not Rule 4, and did not address the claimant’s objections or the matters required by Rule 4.
members.legal_principle: For an acquisition for a company, Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act applies. Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, requires an inquiry and report on the specified matters, followed by the prescribed consideration and consultation. The rule is mandatory, and compliance must precede the section 4 notification as well as the section 6 declaration. Non-compliance makes the section 6 notification invalid. The provisions relied on were sections 4, 5A, 6, 3(e), and 41 of the Act and Rules 3 and 4 of the 1963 Rules; no earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The notification under section 6 was invalid for non-compliance with Rule 4.

predicates.company_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns acquisition of land for a company.
predicates.acquisition_for_company: The government sought to acquire land for the use or benefit of a company.
predicates.required_company_acquisition_inquiry_com: The Collector completed and reported the required inquiry into the matters relevant to an acquisition for a company.

members.legal_issue: An acquisition for the benefit of a company is invalid when the compensation is payable only from the company's own funds and the required company-acquisition procedure has not been followed.
material_facts: The land was being acquired for the benefit of the transport corporation, although the stated purpose was public.
The corporation was a company and not a local authority.
The entire compensation was to be paid by the corporation from funds belonging to it, and no part was to come from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority.
The procedures in Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, had not been followed.
members.legal_principle: The proviso to section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permits a declaration where compensation is to be paid by a company or wholly or partly from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority. Although payment by the company satisfied that proviso, the acquisition for the company's benefit was invalid because Part VII had not been complied with. Funds transferred to a separate corporation become its own funds and do not remain public revenues merely because their source was public.
members.conclusion: The acquisition was invalid, and the Court allowed the appeals and decreed the suits.

predicates.land_acquisition_for_company: The land was acquired for the benefit of a company.
predicates.compensation_payable_only_from_company_o: The company alone was to pay the compensation from funds it held as its own property.
predicates.no_compensation_from_public_or_local_fun: No part of the compensation was to come from public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority.
predicates.company_acquisition_procedure_not_follow: The required procedure for acquiring land for a company was not followed.

members.legal_issue: A lease clause allowing specified materials to remain after expiry transfers only manufactured building materials left beyond the permitted period, not machinery, equipment, or plant.
material_facts: The lease allowed the lessee to keep bricks, boilers, engines, trucks, kilns, railway and tram lines, and other materials on the premises for three months after expiry.
A separate clause addressed early termination for breach and required removal of boilers, engines, trucks, kilns, railway and tram lines, and other materials.
The lease expired in the ordinary way, and bricks and other manufactured materials remained on the premises beyond the permitted period.
The lessee’s boilers, engines, trucks, kilns, railway and tram lines, and similar plant were distinct from building materials such as bricks and tiles.
members.legal_principle: The lease must be construed as a whole. The early-termination clause applied when the lessor terminated for breach and did not govern expiry by efflux of time. The clause governing ordinary expiry made building materials left in contravention of its removal period the lessor’s property; “other materials” in that context referred to building materials, not machinery, tools, or plant.
members.conclusion: The lessor acquired only the building materials, such as bricks, tiles, and similar articles manufactured on the premises. The lessee was allowed time from the decree to remove the boilers, engines, trucks, kilns, railway and tram lines, and similar items.

predicates.lease_expiry_dispute: The dispute concerns ownership or removal of items left on leased premises when the lease ends.
predicates.lease_expired_by_efflux_of_time: The lease ended through the ordinary expiry of its term rather than early termination for breach.
predicates.manufactured_building_materials_left_bey: The lessee left building materials manufactured on the premises beyond the period allowed for their removal.

members.legal_issue: A lease clause providing for temporary retention of manufactured items after expiry transfers only leftover building materials to the lessor, not machinery or plant.
material_facts: The lease allowed the lessee to keep manufactured items on the premises temporarily after expiry and provided that items left contrary to that condition became the lessor’s property.
Read as a whole, the lease distinguished building materials manufactured on the premises from machinery, tools, and plant.
Building materials remained on the premises after the permitted period; machinery and plant also remained there.
members.legal_principle: The Court construed the lease as a whole, distinguishing its clause governing expiry in the ordinary course from the clause governing early termination for breach. In the ordinary-expiry clause, “other materials” referred to manufactured building materials, not machinery, tools, or plant.
members.conclusion: Only building materials such as bricks, tiles, and similar articles became the lessor’s property. The lessee was given time to remove the boilers, engines, trucks, kilns, railway and tram lines, and other plant.

rule.if: lease_expiry_dispute and lease_allows_temporary_retention and lease_distinguishes_building_materials_from_plant and building_materials_left_after_deadline

predicates.lease_expiry_dispute: The dispute concerns the consequences of a lease expiring in the ordinary course.
predicates.lease_allows_temporary_retention: The lease permits the lessee to retain items on the premises for a limited time after expiry.
predicates.lease_distinguishes_building_materials_f: The lease, read as a whole, treats manufactured building materials separately from machinery, tools, or plant.
predicates.building_materials_left_after_deadline: The lessee leaves manufactured building materials on the premises after the permitted retention period.

members.legal_issue: A lessor established to own materials left on leased premises may obtain an injunction restraining their removal or disposal even if the lessor is not in possession of them.
material_facts: The lessor sought an injunction to prevent the lessees from removing or disposing of the materials left on the premises.
The court found that the building materials left beyond the permitted period had become the lessor’s property.
The lessees argued that the lessor could not obtain an injunction without seeking a declaration of title and possession over the materials.
members.legal_principle: Where the claimant’s title to the property is established, there is no legal objection to an injunction restraining its removal or disposal. Ratnasabhapathi Pillai v. Ramaswami Aiyar, Bhramar Lal Banduri v. Nanda Lal Chowdhuri, and Valia Tamburatti v. Parvati were considered inapplicable to the circumstances.
members.conclusion: The injunction could be granted because the lessor’s ownership of the materials had been established; there was no legal objection to the relief sought.

predicates.property_injunction_dispute: The dispute concerns a request to restrain removal or disposal of property.
predicates.claimant_ownership_established: The claimant has established ownership of the property at issue.
predicates.removal_or_disposal_is_sought_to_be_rest: The claimant seeks to prevent another person from removing or disposing of the property.

members.legal_issue: An owner may obtain an injunction preventing removal of property even when the owner is not in possession of it.
material_facts: The lease terms made the remaining building materials the lessor’s property.
The former lessee could remove or dispose of those materials, and the lessor sought an injunction to prevent that conduct.
The lessor was not in possession of the materials.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that, once ownership of the materials had been established, there was no legal objection to an injunction restraining their removal. It distinguished Rathnasabhapathi Pillai v. Ramaswami Aiyer, Bhramar Lal Banduri v. Nanda Lal Chowdhuri, and Valia Thamburatti v. Parvati as inapplicable.
members.conclusion: The lessor was entitled to an injunction restraining removal or disposal of the materials that had become its property, despite not being in possession.

rule.if: injunction_dispute and claimant_owns_property and another_party_may_remove_property and claimant_not_in_possession
