predicates.another_party_may_remove_property: The other party may remove or dispose of the property.
predicates.claimant_not_in_possession: The claimant is not in possession of the property.

members.legal_issue: When an arbitral tribunal is already hearing the dispute in the matters before the Court, the arbitrability issue may be left to that tribunal, subject to remedies against the award.
material_facts: In the principal appeal and one special-leave petition, the arbitral tribunal was hearing the dispute.
In another special-leave petition, an award had been made and the tribunal had rejected its jurisdictional objection.
The Court applied its conclusions on the tribunal’s primary jurisdiction and the court’s post-award review.
members.legal_principle: Sections 16 and 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act empower the tribunal to rule on its jurisdiction and preserve the court’s post-award review. The Court applied the principles of competence-competence and limited judicial intervention established in this judgment.
members.conclusion: The Court left arbitrability for the tribunal to decide in the matters where proceedings were ongoing. Where an award had already been made, the objecting party could pursue a challenge under Section 34. The parties remained free to challenge an award in accordance with law.

predicates.arbitration_dispute_case: The court is considering an arbitrability objection in a dispute referred to arbitration.
predicates.tribunal_is_already_hearing_dispute: The arbitral tribunal has been constituted and is already hearing the dispute.

members.legal_issue: When a preliminary decree is under appeal and further proceedings remain before the trial court, either the trial court or the appellate court may refer all matters in dispute to arbitration.
material_facts: A preliminary decree had been made and appeals against it were pending before the appellate court.
Proceedings subsequent to the preliminary decree, including steps toward a final decree, remained before the trial court.
The disputes in the appeals and the further trial-court proceedings were connected, and the parties jointly sought one reference covering all matters in dispute.
members.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940, when a preliminary decree is under appeal, some matters in dispute are before the appellate court and subsequent proceedings remain before the trial court. Because those matters may be closely connected and effective arbitration may require one reference, either court may refer all matters in dispute. The trial court had jurisdiction here because post-decree proceedings were pending before it.
members.conclusion: Either court could make a reference covering all matters in dispute; because post-decree proceedings were pending before the trial court, that court was competent to make the reference in this case.

rule.if: partition_suit_with_preliminary_decree_appeal and trial_court_proceedings_remain and appellate_matters_remain_pending and all_interested_parties_agree

predicates.partition_suit_with_preliminary_decree_a: The proceeding is a partition suit in which an appeal has been brought against a preliminary decree.
predicates.trial_court_proceedings_remain: Further proceedings under the preliminary decree remain pending before the trial court.
predicates.appellate_matters_remain_pending: Matters in dispute under the preliminary decree remain pending before the appellate court.
predicates.all_interested_parties_agree: Every party interested in the suit agrees to refer the matters in dispute to arbitration.

members.legal_issue: The special eviction procedure applies on the same principle to qualifying proceedings based on personal need and to proceedings under the separate landlord-occupation category.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought under the personal-need ground and the special procedure.
The tenants argued that the separate landlord-occupation category justified a special procedure, but the personal-need ground did not.
The Court held that the distinction between the two categories did not warrant different treatment for purposes of the special procedure.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14(1)(e), 14A, and 25A–25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, form part of a special scheme for specified landlord eviction claims. The Court relied on Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal and Kewal Singh v. Lajwanti in rejecting the proposed distinction between the categories.
members.conclusion: There was no difference in principle or law between the two categories that would prevent the special procedure from applying to the personal-need ground.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_special_rent_p: The landlord brings an eviction proceeding under the statutory special procedure.
predicates.claim_falls_within_personal_need_or_land: The eviction claim is based on either a qualifying personal housing need or a qualifying landlord-occupation circumstance.

members.legal_issue: The two special landlord-need grounds for eviction are governed by the same principle of law despite applying in different situations.
material_facts: The eviction order under review rested on bona fide requirement under one of the special landlord-need grounds.
The Court considered that the two grounds concern eviction in different situations.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that sections 14(1)(e) and 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, do not differ in principle or law, notwithstanding that they address different eviction situations. It relied on Ravi Dutt Sharma v. Ratan Lal Bhargava, [1984] 2 SCR 614.
members.conclusion: There is no difference in principle or law between the two special landlord-need grounds, although they apply to different situations.

predicates.eviction_case_under_either_of_two_specia: The landlord seeks eviction under one of two special grounds that apply in different situations.

members.legal_issue: A tax liability deductible from compensation affects the compensation right’s market value when deduction remains possible, but is not separately deducted from net wealth.
material_facts: The estate had vested in the State, and compensation was payable to the assessee under the land-reform scheme.
Agricultural income tax was due from the assessee and was deductible from the compensation under the scheme if it had not already been deducted before issue of the compensation bond.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 7 and 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, asset valuation and deduction of debts operate at different stages, but section 7(1) requires valuation by reference to market value and relevant hazards. A liability deductible from compensation is a factor a willing purchaser would consider. The Court followed Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bihar, Patna v. Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh, Civil Appeal Nos. 1238 to 1240 (NT) of 1973.
members.conclusion: The agricultural income tax arrears were not to be deducted separately from net wealth. If they had not already been deducted, the possibility and hazard of their deduction had to be considered in valuing the compensation right.

rule.if: wealth_tax_valuation_case and compensation_right_is_an_asset and tax_liability_is_deductible_from_compensation and deduction_not_already_made

predicates.wealth_tax_valuation_case: The proceeding concerns valuation of a taxpayer’s wealth for wealth tax purposes.
predicates.compensation_right_is_an_asset: The taxpayer holds a right to receive compensation that is included among the assets being valued.
predicates.tax_liability_is_deductible_from_compens: A tax liability of the taxpayer may be deducted from the compensation payable.
predicates.deduction_not_already_made: The possible deduction has not already been made from the compensation before its valuation.

members.legal_issue: A potential liability deductible from compensation must be considered when estimating the open-market value of the right to receive that compensation, even if the liability itself is not deductible from net wealth as a debt.
material_facts: The assessee held a right to compensation after the estate vested in the State.
Agricultural income-tax arrears remained outstanding and could be deducted from the compensation under the applicable land-reform law.
The possibility and amount of that deduction had not been finally determined or fully reflected in the compensation amount.
The wealth-tax authorities valued the compensation right without accounting for the potential deduction.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, net wealth is computed by first valuing assets and then deducting eligible debts; section 7(1) requires an asset other than cash to be valued at the price it would fetch in the open market. A factor that would deter a willing purchaser or reduce the price must be considered at the valuation stage, even when the related debt is excluded from deduction at the separate net-wealth stage. Section 4(c) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, permitted specified arrears to be recovered by deduction from compensation. The Court also referred to Pandit Lakshmi Kant Jha v. Commissioner of Wealth-tax, Bihar and Orissa for the proposition that the right to receive compensation is an asset; it found Standard Mills Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Wealth-tax and Commissioner of Wealth-tax v. Purshottam N. Amersey not relevant to the issue.
members.conclusion: The possibility of deducting the agricultural income-tax dues was a factor that had to be considered in estimating the compensation right’s open-market value. The extent of its effect was a matter of quantification. The appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: wealth_tax_assessment and compensation_right_valued and deduction_hazard_exists and hazard_not_already_resolved

predicates.wealth_tax_assessment: The proceeding concerns the computation of a person’s net wealth for wealth-tax purposes.
predicates.compensation_right_valued: The value being assessed includes a right to receive compensation.
predicates.deduction_hazard_exists: A liability may lawfully be recovered by deducting it from the compensation.
predicates.hazard_not_already_resolved: The liability has not been finally determined or already reflected in the compensation value.

members.legal_issue: A police statement recorded during investigation of a separate cross-case is inadmissible in the prosecution case, and a prior statement relied on to contradict a witness must first be put to that witness.
material_facts: The investigating officer referred to statements made during investigation of a separate cross-case.
Those statements were used to suggest that prosecution witnesses had not explained how the opposing-side injuries occurred.
The statements had not first been put to the relevant witness in the present case.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in holding that the statement made during investigation of the cross-case was inadmissible in the present case. It also required that the statement be put to the witness before the investigating officer's evidence could be used to contradict that witness.
members.conclusion: The statement recorded during investigation of the cross-case was inadmissible in this case; in any event, it could not be used without first putting it to the witness.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which evidence is being assessed.
predicates.statement_recorded_in_separate_case_inve: The statement was recorded by police while investigating a separate case arising from the same incident.
predicates.statement_not_put_to_witness: The statement was not put to the witness whose account it is said to contradict.
predicates.statement_offered_as_evidence_from_separ: The statement is offered as evidence in a different case from the investigation in which it was recorded.

members.legal_issue: A statement recorded from a person under police investigation is not admissible under the rule for evidence from a prior proceeding when it was not given as testimony in such a proceeding.
material_facts: The injured person's statement to the Investigating Officer was recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The trial court relied on that statement under Section 33 of the Evidence Act, but the High Court held it inadmissible on that basis, and the Supreme Court agreed.
members.legal_principle: Section 33 of the Evidence Act did not make the police statement admissible; the Court affirmed that the Section 161 statement could not be admitted under that provision.
members.conclusion: The injured person's statement under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not admissible under Section 33 of the Evidence Act.

rule.if: criminal_trial and police_investigation_statement and not testimony_in_prior_proceeding

predicates.criminal_trial: The statement was offered in a criminal trial.
predicates.police_investigation_statement: The person made the statement during a police investigation.
predicates.testimony_in_prior_proceeding: The statement was given as testimony in a prior proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A consumer forum may hear an eligible consumer’s complaint about a real-estate project even when a remedy is available under real-estate regulation law.
material_facts: The apartment purchasers brought complaints before the consumer commission, seeking refunds because the project had not been completed on time.
The project was registered under the real-estate regulatory law after the purchasers had entered into their agreements.
The developer argued that the regulatory authorities had exclusive jurisdiction and that the consumer commission could not entertain the complaints.
members.legal_principle: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, Sections 3 and 12(4), preserve additional consumer remedies and prevent transfer of an admitted complaint to another forum. Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Sections 18, 71, 79, 88 and 89 do not displace those remedies: Section 79 bars civil courts, not consumer fora, and Sections 18 and 88 preserve other remedies. The Court relied on Secretary, Thirumurugan Cooperative Agricultural Credit Society v. M. Lalitha; National Seeds Corporation Ltd. v. M. Madhusudhan Reddy; Virender Jain v. Alaknanda Cooperative Group Housing Society Ltd.; Emaar MGF Ltd. v. Aftab Singh; Malay Kumar Ganguli v. Dr. Sukumar Mukherjee; and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The regulatory law did not bar the consumer commission from entertaining the complaints; the remedies available under consumer law remained available alongside the regulatory remedy.

predicates.consumer_complaint: An allottee files a complaint in a consumer forum about a service connected with a real-estate purchase.
predicates.eligible_consumer: The complainant qualifies as a consumer in relation to the transaction.
predicates.real_estate_regulatory_remedy_available: A regulatory law provides the allottee with a remedy concerning the same real-estate dispute.
predicates.consumer_forum_jurisdiction_not_barred: The consumer forum is not barred from hearing the complaint merely because the regulatory remedy is available.

members.legal_issue: The consumer forum may order a refund with interest under the Consumer Protection Act even when real-estate remedies are also available under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act.
material_facts: The consumer brought the complaint before the consumer forum and sought only a refund with interest.
The developer argued that choosing the consumer forum meant the real-estate statute's remedies did not apply.
The consumer forum ordered the developer to return the money with interest for its failure to deliver possession as agreed.
members.legal_principle: Section 14 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 authorizes an order returning the price or charges paid when a complaint about services is proved; Section 2(g) includes contractual shortcomings in the definition of deficiency. Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 makes its remedies available without prejudice to other remedies, and Sections 79 and 88 do not bar a consumer-forum complaint. The Court applied Imperia Structures Ltd. v. Anil Patni and IREO Grace Realtech (P) Ltd. v. Abhishek Khanna, and relied on Pioneer Urban Land Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India for the concurrent-remedies principle.
members.conclusion: The consumer forum had jurisdiction to order a refund with interest, and the remedies under the two statutes operate concurrently rather than excluding or contradicting one another.

predicates.consumer_forum_proceeding: The consumer brings a complaint before a consumer forum about a developer's service.
predicates.consumer_chooses_refund: The consumer seeks return of the money paid rather than, or as an alternative to, possession.
predicates.developer_fails_to_deliver_as_agreed: The developer does not deliver the apartment in accordance with the agreed terms.

members.legal_issue: A developer’s failure to deliver possession by the agreed deadline, without substantiated events excusing the delay, supports a finding of deficient service.
material_facts: The agreed period for completing construction had expired, but the project remained incomplete.
The developer acknowledged delay and relied on matters including labour shortages, delays in obtaining approvals, and demonetisation to explain it.
The consumer commission found that the developer had not provided evidence establishing force majeure events, and the Supreme Court upheld the findings of delay and deficiency.
members.legal_principle: The Court upheld the consumer commission’s determination of deficiency in service in light of the expired contractual completion period, the admitted delay, the absence of proof substantiating force majeure, and the agreement’s provisions concerning delay and failure to deliver possession, including Clauses 11.4 and 41.
members.conclusion: The consumer commission’s findings that the developer delayed completion and was deficient in service were correct and did not warrant interference.

rule.if: appeal_against_consumer_order and contractual_completion_deadline_expired and possession_not_delivered and developer_failed_to_substantiate_excusing_events

predicates.appeal_against_consumer_order: A developer appeals from a consumer-forum order concerning delayed possession of an apartment.
predicates.contractual_completion_deadline_expired: The completion or possession deadline specified in the agreement has passed.
predicates.possession_not_delivered: The developer has not delivered possession of the apartment by the agreed deadline.
predicates.developer_failed_to_substantiate_excusin: The developer relied on events to excuse the delay but did not substantiate that those events caused or excused the failure to deliver on time.
predicates.delay_and_deficiency_finding_upheld: The finding that the developer delayed delivery and provided deficient service is upheld.

members.legal_issue: A finding that a rehabilitation developer caused prolonged delay may be upheld where the record supports the finding and the developer has not adequately explained its failure to progress the project.
material_facts: The developer agreed to complete the project within a specified period but made little progress for years and completed only two rehabilitation buildings.
The developer did not earnestly pursue approval of further plans and failed to produce the required resident agreements despite repeated opportunities and commitments.
Restrictions affected only part of the land, and other circumstances relied on by the developer did not explain its failure to develop the remaining area.
The authority and the High Court both found the developer responsible for the delay, and the Supreme Court reviewed the record and found that conclusion was not perverse.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated responsibility for delay as a factual finding supported by the record and reviewed it for perversity. No earlier case was cited for this issue; the Court considered the development agreements, authority communications, planning history, and the limits of the asserted impediments.
members.conclusion: The developer was responsible for the delay, and the authority and High Court were justified in so finding.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_delay_finding and rehabilitation_developer_failed_to_progress_project and asserted_obstacles_do_not_explain_delay and record_supports_delay_finding

predicates.appeal_challenging_delay_finding: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a finding that a rehabilitation developer caused delay.
predicates.rehabilitation_developer_failed_to_progr: The developer failed to make substantial progress on the rehabilitation project over a prolonged period.
predicates.asserted_obstacles_do_not_explain_delay: The obstacles relied on by the developer do not adequately account for the failure to progress the project.
predicates.record_supports_delay_finding: The documentary and procedural record supports the finding that the developer caused the delay.

members.legal_issue: The removal of an express debt-payment power from one provision does not eliminate the custodian’s power to pay evacuee debts when that power remains under the custodian’s general administration authority.
material_facts: An amendment removed the custodian’s express power to pay evacuee debts from one clause.
The custodian’s power to administer evacuee property and discharge evacuees’ obligations remained under other provisions.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 10(1) and 10(2)(n) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, the power to administer evacuee property includes the power to discharge obligations and pay debts the custodian considers binding. Raja Bhanupratap Singh v. Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property, U.P. was followed; it held that deleting the power from section 10(2)(m) did not affect the power arising under section 10(2)(n) read with section 10(1).
members.conclusion: The amendment did not impair the custodian’s power to pay evacuee debts, so it was unnecessary to decide whether the amendment was invalid.

predicates.claim_against_evacuee_debtor: A creditor seeks payment of a debt owed by a person whose property is administered as evacuee property.
predicates.custodian_debt_administration_proceeding: The matter concerns the custodian’s administration of an evacuee debtor’s obligations.
predicates.custodian_retains_general_administration: The custodian continues to have authority to administer the debtor’s property.
predicates.custodian_can_discharge_evacuee_obligati: The custodian’s continuing authority includes discharging obligations binding on the debtor.

members.legal_issue: Removing an express power to pay an evacuee’s debts does not eliminate an independent power to pay a person found entitled to money from the administered estate.
material_facts: The Act originally expressly authorized expenditure for debts due by an evacuee, and a rule provided a procedure for registering claims.
An amendment deleted the express reference to payment of evacuee debts, and the rule providing the claim-registration procedure was later deleted.
The claimant sought payment under the separate provision permitting payment to any other person whom the custodian considered entitled.
The tribunals rejected the claim for lack of power without deciding its merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(1) states the custodian’s general powers and duties, while section 10(2)(n) permits payment to any other person considered entitled. The specific clauses are illustrative and not mutually exclusive. The deletion from section 10(2)(m) of the express reference to evacuee debts and the deletion of Rule 22 did not restrict the separate authority under section 10(1) and section 10(2)(n). No earlier cases are relied upon in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The deletion of the express debt-payment language and the claim-registration rule did not remove the custodian’s independent power under section 10(1) and section 10(2)(n) to consider and pay qualifying claims.

predicates.claim_for_payment_from_administered_prop: A claimant asks the administrator of property held for an absent owner to pay a monetary claim from that property.
predicates.express_debt_payment_authority_removed: An express authorization for the administrator to pay the absent owner’s debts has been removed.
predicates.independent_authority_to_pay_entitled_pe: A separate continuing authorization allows the administrator to pay a person whom the administrator considers entitled to money from the administered funds.

members.legal_issue: Acquisition of evacuee property does not violate a decree-holder’s right to acquire, hold, or dispose of property when the decree-holder has no proprietary interest in the acquired property.
material_facts: The appellant held decrees against evacuees but had no interest in the building that was acquired.
The building vested absolutely in the Central Government, free from encumbrances, after a notification was issued.
The appellant could no longer proceed against the building in execution of the decrees.
members.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 extinguished the evacuees’ interests in property acquired by notification and vested that property in the Central Government free from encumbrances. Because the appellant had no interest in the building, the acquisition did not interfere with his right under Article 19(1)(f) to acquire, hold, and dispose of property; the Court therefore did not need to consider whether section 12 was saved by Article 19(5).
members.conclusion: Section 12 did not interfere with the appellant’s property in the decrees, and the appellant could not rely on Article 19(1)(f) to challenge the acquisition of the building.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law or action that transfers property to the government.
predicates.decree_against_evacuee: The challenger holds a decree against a debtor whose property is treated as evacuee property.
predicates.acquired_asset_vested_in_government: The asset was transferred to and vested in the government through the acquisition process.
predicates.decree_holder_has_no_proprietary_interes: The decree-holder has a claim against the debtor but no ownership or other proprietary interest in the acquired asset.

members.legal_issue: A later acquisition of evacuee property does not extinguish the rights of a person who was not an evacuee.
material_facts: The respondents contended that a notification under the later compensation and rehabilitation legislation had acquired the houses.
The petitioners had not been declared evacuees, and their interests had not vested in the custodian through the earlier declaration.
members.legal_principle: Section 12(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, extinguishes an evacuee’s right, title and interest in property specified in a notification; it does not extinguish the rights of a person who is not an evacuee.
members.conclusion: The later notification did not extinguish the petitioners’ rights because the statutory extinguishment applied only to the rights of an evacuee.

predicates.claimant_challenges_extinguishment_under: A claimant contests the asserted extinguishment of property rights through a later acquisition process.
predicates.claimant_has_property_interest: The claimant is entitled to an interest in the property said to have been acquired.
predicates.claimant_was_not_declared_evacuee: The claimant was not declared to be an evacuee.

members.legal_issue: A creditor whose execution against acquired evacuee property is barred may ask the custodian to consider payment from funds held when the property vested, if the creditor establishes that the property belonged to the debtor and satisfies the custodian’s requirements.
material_facts: The appellant could not proceed against the building or its income after the building vested in the Central Government.
The appellant alleged that release deeds in favour of the judgment-debtors’ wives were fictitious and fraudulent and that the property therefore belonged to the judgment-debtors.
The Court directed the trial court to decide the release-deed issue and observed that, if the appellant succeeded, he could approach the custodian concerning any money held on the date of vesting.
The custodian’s decision whether to pay remained subject to the applicable requirements and the custodian’s judgment.
members.legal_principle: Sections 10(1) and 10(2)(n) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 permit the custodian to consider paying a debt from funds under the custodian’s control. Under Raja Bhanupratap Singh v. Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property, U.P., a civil decree does not itself determine entitlement to payment; the custodian determines whether the claimant is entitled. The Court directed the trial court to decide whether the release deeds were fictitious and fraudulent and held that a favourable finding would permit the appellant to approach the custodian, not guarantee payment.
members.conclusion: The appellant could not proceed against the building or its income after vesting, but if the trial court found in his favour on the release deeds, he could ask the custodian to make such orders as the custodian considered appropriate concerning money held at vesting.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenging_transfer_as_fraudulent and creditor_claim_against_evacuee_debtor and property_vested_in_government and funds_held_by_custodian_at_vesting and trial_finds_property_belonged_to_debtor

predicates.civil_suit_challenging_transfer_as_fraud: A creditor brings a civil suit alleging that a transfer of the debtor’s property was fictitious or intended to defeat creditors.
predicates.creditor_claim_against_evacuee_debtor: The claimant seeks satisfaction of a debt owed by a person whose property is administered as evacuee property.
predicates.property_vested_in_government: The property at issue vested in the government through acquisition.
predicates.funds_held_by_custodian_at_vesting: The custodian held money associated with the property when it vested in the government.
predicates.trial_finds_property_belonged_to_debtor: The trial court determines that the disputed property belonged to the debtor rather than to the transferee.

members.legal_issue: A custodian administering property held for an evacuee may consider and pay a creditor’s claim from the administered funds when the claimant is found entitled and payment serves the administration of the property.
material_facts: The claimant held money decrees against a debtor whose property had vested in the custodian.
Execution against the property was unavailable while it remained vested in the custodian.
The claimant applied for payment from the administered estate, but the application was rejected on the ground that the custodian lacked power to grant relief.
The tribunals had not decided whether the claim was genuine, whether the claimant was entitled to payment, or whether payment should be made for the purposes of administration.
members.legal_principle: Section 10(1) gives the custodian general powers to secure, administer, preserve, and manage evacuee property and to discharge duties under the Act. Section 10(2)(n) permits payment from funds in the custodian’s possession to the evacuee, a family member, or any other person whom the custodian considers entitled. Administration includes discharging obligations binding on the evacuee, not merely collecting and managing assets. The clauses of section 10(2) illustrate, and are not mutually exclusive limits on, the general powers in section 10(1). No earlier cases are relied upon in the judgment.
members.conclusion: The custodian had power, coupled with a duty to exercise that power, to consider the claim and to pay it if the custodian was satisfied that the claimant was entitled and payment served the statutory purposes of administration. The rejection orders were set aside and the matter remanded for that determination.

predicates.claim_for_payment_from_administered_prop: A claimant asks the administrator of property held for an absent owner to pay a monetary claim from that property.
predicates.property_held_for_evacuee: The property whose funds are sought is held by an administrator for an evacuee.
predicates.claimant_found_entitled: The administrator determines that the claimant is entitled to receive the claimed money.
predicates.payment_serves_property_administration: The administrator determines that paying the claim serves the administration or management of the property or the discharge of the administrator’s duties.

members.legal_issue: Claims to exclude property from evacuee-property status cannot be newly entertained after the applicable outer limit, and pending stale claims are subject to dismissal, while finally adjudicated claims are not reopened on that basis.
material_facts: The governing provision required a claim to be made within thirty days of the relevant notification or demand but allowed delayed applications for sufficient recorded reasons.
The Court held that the extension could not permit a claim beyond twelve years from the property’s vesting in the Custodian.
The claimant’s predecessor applied within twelve years, and no limitation objection had been raised against that claim before the Court considered the issue.
The Court directed that new applications not be entertained, that pending applications entertained after twelve years be dismissed, and that claims already finally decided not be reopened.
members.legal_principle: Section 8(2) made the stated filing period mandatory, subject to the Custodian’s power to allow delay for sufficient reasons recorded. That power did not authorize unlimited delay; the Court treated twelve years as the outer limit by reference to Section 28 and Article 142 of the Jammu and Kashmir Limitation Act. The Court held that the direction applied to pending, unadjudicated claims and did not reopen claims already finally adjudicated.
members.conclusion: The Court established the twelve-year outer limit and its prospective and pending-case consequences, but declined to reject this claimant’s claim as time-barred because it had been filed within that limit and limitation had not previously been raised.

predicates.claim_to_exclude_property_from_protected: A person seeks to have property removed from the statutory administrator’s protected estate on the ground that it is not properly included in that estate or that the person’s interest was not affected.
predicates.new_claim_after_outer_limit: The person first seeks to bring the claim after the outer limit recognized by the Court has elapsed.
predicates.pending_claim_after_outer_limit: The claim was entertained after that outer limit and remains undecided.

members.legal_issue: The later transition provision does not revive stale or barred claims or reopen claims conclusively rejected in earlier litigation.
material_facts: The Court considered claims concerning acquisitions that had been completed or challenged many years earlier, sometimes through multiple rounds of litigation.
Some claimants had previously lost challenges, obtained compensation, or failed to raise possession-related arguments in earlier proceedings.
The Court considered the risk that long delay could make material evidence unavailable and that later claims might contradict prior final findings, including findings based on possession memoranda.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the doctrines of delay and laches, res judicata, and constructive res judicata. It relied on Mahavir v. Union of India, Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. M. Meiyappan, Jasveer Singh v. State of U.P., Rabindranath Bose v. Union of India, and Dharappa v. Bijapur Co-operative Milk Producers Societies Union. It also applied section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, preserved by section 114 of the 2013 Act, to conclude that repeal did not undo accrued rights or existing proceedings absent a different intention.
members.conclusion: The transition provision does not revive dead, stale, or barred claims, undo final judgments, or permit a claim to be raised again when it was or should have been raised in earlier litigation.

predicates.transition_lapse_claim: A claimant invokes a later transition rule to seek lapse of an earlier land acquisition.
predicates.claim_stale_or_barred: The claim was brought after a substantial unexplained delay or had already become barred or non-existent.
predicates.prior_final_adjudication: An earlier court decision finally rejected the claim, or the claimant could and should have raised it in that proceeding.

members.legal_issue: Land allotted to a displaced person as compensation for land granted for gallantry does not qualify for the exemption from surplus-area computation applicable to the original gallantry-grant land.
material_facts: The original land granted to the landholder for gallantry was situated in territory he left after partition.

The land in which he was later assessed for surplus area was allotted in India under the displaced-person rehabilitation scheme, as compensation for his loss, rather than being the original gallantry-grant land.
The surplus land was allotted to other persons, who paid compensation to the landholder and took possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 51A, inserted with retrospective effect, exempts the land granted for gallantry, subject to its stated conditions; it does not extend the exemption to different land transferred as compensation for that land. Sections 7 and 8 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 provide for determining and paying compensation, including through transfer of property from the compensation pool, which does not make that property the same as the displaced person’s original land. The Court applied Sailen Krishna Majumdar v. Malik Labhu Masih, 1989 Supp. (1) SCC 302, which rejected extension of the gallantry-land exemption to replacement land granted under the rehabilitation legislation. It distinguished Gurbachan Singh v. Puran Singh, AIR 1961 SC 1263, and also referred to Piarey Lal v. Hori Lal, AIR 1977 SC 1226.
members.conclusion: The rehabilitation land was different from the original gallantry-grant land and was not exempt from surplus-area computation under section 51A of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955. The judgment setting aside the surplus declaration on that basis was set aside.

predicates.surplus_area_determination: A proceeding determined whether land held by a person exceeded the permissible area.
predicates.original_gallantry_land_abandoned: The person left the original land granted for gallantry and no longer held that specific land.
predicates.replacement_land_received_as_rehabilitat: The land being assessed was transferred to the person as compensation or rehabilitation property, rather than being the original gallantry-grant land.

members.legal_issue: Land allotted as compensation for gallantry-grant land lost after partition does not acquire the exemption attached to the original granted land merely because it compensates for that loss.
material_facts: The original gallantry-grant land was in territory left behind after partition.
The family migrated to India, where the government allotted different land as compensation for the land left behind.
The respondent possessed part of the compensation land as a tenant and obtained permission to purchase it under the tenancy law.
The appellant sought possession of the compensation land, asserting that it inherited the original land’s gallantry exemption.
The Court was shown no provision in the displaced-persons compensation legislation that transferred the exemption to replacement land.
members.legal_principle: Section 19DD of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, exempts qualifying gallantry-grant land, but the Court found no basis for extending that exemption to different land allotted as compensation. The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, contained no provision shown to transfer the exemption to compensation land. Section 18 was therefore not displaced on that basis. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The compensation land was not exempt from the tenant-purchase provisions on the ground that it replaced the original gallantry-grant land; the respondent’s purchase right therefore prevailed.

predicates.tenant_purchase_dispute: The proceeding concerns a tenant’s claimed right to purchase land.

predicates.land_sought_is_not_the_original_gallantr: The land sought to be purchased is different land from the original gallantry grant.
predicates.compensation_scheme_does_not_transfer_th: The compensation arrangement contains no term transferring the original land’s exemption to replacement land.

members.legal_issue: A concurrent finding on the non-ancestral character of property is not reopened on appeal where the issue was conceded below and the admitted facts cannot be separated from the legal conclusion.
material_facts: The lower courts had concurrently found that the property was non-ancestral.
The appellant’s counsel had conceded that point in the courts below.
The finding involved a mixed question of law and fact, and the admitted facts were not shown to be separable from the legal conclusion.
Earlier judgments between the parties or their predecessors had also determined that the property was non-ancestral.
members.legal_principle: The court treated the character of the property as a mixed question of law and fact that could not be reconsidered on the basis proposed once the relevant point had been conceded and the admitted facts could not be disentangled from the legal conclusion. It also observed that the earlier judgments determining the property’s character were res judicata.
members.conclusion: The court did not allow the appellant to reopen the finding and accepted that the property was non-ancestral.

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.finding_was_concurrent: The courts below had reached the same finding on the issue.
predicates.issue_was_mixed_law_and_fact: The issue depended on both facts and the legal conclusion drawn from them, and those elements could not be separated on the record presented.
predicates.appellant_conceded_issue_below: The appellant’s counsel accepted the issue in the courts below.
predicates.prior_judgments_determined_the_issue: Earlier judgments involving the parties or their predecessors had already determined the same issue.

members.legal_issue: An appeal confined to allocation of shares does not permit reopening concurrent findings on the existence of the joint family and its joint ownership of property.
material_facts: The appeal notice confined scrutiny to allocation of shares in properties found to be joint family properties.
The lower courts had concurrently found that a joint family existed and that the relevant properties were jointly held.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated the terms limiting the appeal's scope as confining review to allocation of shares and excluding reconsideration of the concurrent findings on joint family status and joint ownership.
members.conclusion: The concurrent findings on the existence of the joint family and the joint holding of property could not be reopened in the appeal.

predicates.appeal_scope_limited_to_share_allocation: The appeal is confined to determining the allocation of shares.
predicates.concurrent_findings_establish_joint_fami: The lower courts made concurrent findings that a joint family existed and that the property was jointly held.

members.legal_issue: A priest who holds temple land only to manage the deity’s property does not acquire Bhumiswami status merely because the land is associated with religious service.
material_facts: The land in dispute was temple land, and the priest’s role under the applicable historical arrangements was to manage the property and perform religious duties.
The priest could cultivate the land or have it cultivated for the temple’s upkeep, but did not hold it as an ordinary tenant or landholder with ownership rights.
The priest was not within the classes of landholders whose rights were protected as Bhumiswamis under the applicable land legislation.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 158(1)(b) of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 2007 and the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, specified classes of landholders could become Bhumiswamis; a priest holding land only to manage temple property does not fall within those classes. Section 57’s protection of existing rights does not create a proprietary right where none existed. Pancham Singh v. Ramkishandas Guru Ramdas held that a priest managing such land was not a tenant in cultivation or ordinary tenant; this Court approved that view in Mst. Kanchaniya v. Shiv Ram. M. Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das also supports the principle that performing worship does not by itself confer independent rights in religious property.
members.conclusion: A priest who manages temple land on behalf of the deity is not a Bhumiswami on that basis and has no ownership right in the temple land.

predicates.temple_land_belongs_to_deity: The land is held for a temple and belongs to the deity rather than to its priest.
predicates.priest_holds_land_only_for_management: The priest holds or manages the land on behalf of the deity to maintain the temple and perform its religious functions.
predicates.priest_is_not_an_ordinary_landholder: The priest does not hold the land in an ordinary tenant or other landholder capacity that carries the relevant land rights.

members.legal_issue: A person who performs worship and manages temple property with the shebait’s permission does not thereby acquire the office of shebait.
material_facts: The successive holders of the estate appointed priests and arranged for worship at the temple.
A priest acknowledged that he lived in the temple with permission and held the deity’s ornaments on behalf of the estate holder, undertaking to return them on demand.
The priest’s descendants and their widows performed worship and took part in temple management, but the evidence did not show that they had asserted shebaitship before the widow’s will.
The widow’s performance of temple duties and payments to temple officers were consistent with her acting for the shebait.
members.legal_principle: The character of a person’s role in temple management is determined from the documentary evidence and the parties’ acts. Performing worship or exercising control under the shebait’s permission does not, without evidence of an independent claim to the office, establish shebaitship. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The estate holder and his successor were the shebaits; the widow was only a pujari and did not acquire shebaitship through her performance of worship or management of the property.

predicates.temple_management_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over who holds the shebaitship of a temple.
predicates.worshipper_performed_duties_under_shebai: The worshipper performed worship or managed temple affairs under the authority or permission of the shebait.
predicates.records_show_shebait_retained_management: Documents or other evidence show that the shebait retained responsibility for temple management and treated the worshipper as acting on his behalf.
predicates.worshipper_is_only_pujari: The worshipper holds the role of pujari rather than the office of shebait.

members.legal_issue: A municipal demolition decision based on a substantial breach of building limits and rejecting an alternative method of compliance should remain undisturbed when no jurisdictional or legal defect is established.
material_facts: The housing society constructed substantially beyond the permissible floor space index, with excess construction exceeding 24,000 square feet.
A demolition order was made, challenged unsuccessfully in court, and had attained finality.
The society later proposed vertical demolition as an alternative to demolishing the upper floors.
The municipal commissioner had the alternative proposal examined by architects and engineers and rejected it with detailed reasons.
The demolition order had been substantially carried out, and the court found no lack of jurisdiction, violation of law or rules, or mala fides in the municipal action.
The court considered unlawful construction contrary to the public interest and hazardous to the safety of occupants and residents.
members.legal_principle: Building rules and limits are made in the larger public interest and must be obeyed; unlawful construction can endanger occupants and residents and should be dealt with firmly. A municipal decision is not to be disturbed where it was made within jurisdiction and is not contrary to law or rules or tainted by mala fides. The court relied on the finality of the earlier demolition order and the society’s failure to establish a basis for intervention. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The court found no justification to interfere with the municipal decision or the High Court’s order and dismissed the petition.

rule.if: judicial_challenge_to_municipal_demolition and substantial_building_limit_violation and prior_demolition_order_final and alternative_compliance_proposal_examined_and_rejected and no_jurisdictional_or_legal_defect

predicates.no_jurisdictional_or_legal_defect: The municipal decision was not shown to be outside the authority’s jurisdiction or contrary to law or rules.

members.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that premises are required for demolition and reconstruction should stand when no material illegality is shown as a basis for disturbing them.
material_facts: The rent-control authorities concurrently found that the premises were required for demolition and reconstruction.
The High Court upheld those findings, and no illegality warranting their reversal was identified before the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court declined to interfere with concurrent findings of the rent-control authorities and the High Court when no material illegality had been shown.
members.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the premises were required for demolition and reconstruction was not disturbed.

predicates.concurrent_finding_of_reconstruction_req: The rent-control authorities reached the same finding that the premises were required for demolition and reconstruction.
predicates.no_material_illegality_shown: The challenging party identified no material illegality warranting reversal of the concurrent finding.

members.legal_issue: An appellate court must give an appellant an opportunity to make good a court-fee deficiency before dismissing an insufficiently stamped memorandum of appeal.
material_facts: The appellate court found that the fee paid on the memorandum of appeal was insufficient.
The appellate court dismissed the memorandum without first allowing the appellant time to pay the deficiency.
members.legal_principle: Sections 107(2) and 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with the procedure under Order VII applicable to suits, require an opportunity to make good a fee deficiency. Section 149 permits the court, in its discretion, to allow payment at any stage, after which the document has the same force and effect as if the fee had been paid initially. The court also relied on fairness of procedure.
members.conclusion: The dismissal was inappropriate because the appellant should have been given an opportunity to pay the deficient court fee within a time fixed by the court; dismissal could follow if the appellant failed to comply.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party filed an appeal from a decision in a civil suit.
predicates.court_found_fee_deficient: The appellate court determined that the fee paid on the appeal document was insufficient.
predicates.court_dismissed_without_allowing_payment: The appellate court dismissed the appeal document without first allowing the appellant time to pay the deficiency.

members.legal_issue: When a second-appeal memorandum fails to state a substantial question of law precisely, the High Court should ordinarily give the appellant an opportunity to correct the deficiency unless the appellant was previously alerted and persisted in the default.
material_facts: The appellant's memorandum of second appeal did not precisely state the substantial question of law relied upon.
The High Court did not previously bring the defect to the appellant's attention.
The High Court dismissed the appeal without giving the appellant an opportunity to frame the question.
members.legal_principle: Section 100(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the memorandum of second appeal to state precisely the substantial question of law involved. The Court held that, where the High Court notices a failure to comply, an opportunity to frame the question should ordinarily be afforded unless the deficiency was previously brought to the appellant's attention and the appellant persisted in the default.
members.conclusion: The High Court should ordinarily have afforded an opportunity to state the question; the appeal was remitted for fresh consideration.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to a High Court from an appellate decree of a subordinate court.
predicates.memorandum_omits_precise_substantial_que: The appellant's memorandum does not precisely state the substantial question of law proposed for the appeal.
predicates.deficiency_not_previously_notified: The court or its registry has not previously alerted the appellant to the defect.

members.legal_issue: A deed that only undertakes not to alienate property does not create a charge unless it clearly obligates payment of the debt out of that property.
material_facts: The debtor executed a deed of security over identified property to obtain the lifting of an attachment before judgment of money payable to him.
The deed referred to the amount of the security and an existing prior mortgage, and stated that if a decree were passed the debtor would not alienate the property until the decree was discharged.
The deed contained no clear recital obligating payment of the decreed amount out of the identified property.
members.legal_principle: A charge is an obligation to make payment out of specified property. The Court construed the deed according to its substance and held that a promise not to alienate property if a decree were passed did not, without a clear obligation to pay out of that property, create a charge. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: The deed created no charge over the property and was only an undertaking not to alienate it.

predicates.security_deed_given_to_lift_prejudgment_: A debtor gave a deed concerning property in order to obtain the lifting of an attachment before judgment.
predicates.deed_only_promises_nonalienation: The deed states that the debtor will not alienate the property until the debt is discharged.
predicates.no_clear_payment_obligation_from_propert: The deed does not clearly require payment of the debt out of the identified property.

members.legal_issue: A deed creates a charge on specified property only when it shows an intention to make that property liable for payment of the debt.
material_facts: The father had given a personal guarantee for the overdraft debt of a bank managed by his son.

A deed distributing the father’s properties among family members stated that the son would pay any amount due under the guarantee and that the son and the property allotted to him would be answerable if the father had to pay.
The deed was intended to arrange responsibility for the debt among family members; it did not show an intention to secure the bank’s debt against the property.
The father retained rights to income from some of the properties, and his wife was permitted to occupy certain houses and use their income.
members.legal_principle: A charge requires an intention, disclosed by the deed, to make specified property or a fund liable for the debt; no particular form of words is necessary. A direction allocating responsibility for a debt among family members may create an indemnity arrangement without creating a charge for the creditor. The Court relied on Akalla Suryanarayana Rao v. Dwarapudi Basivireddi, which treated a similar covenant as an indemnity rather than a charge.
members.conclusion: The deed did not create a charge in favour of the creditor bank over the property allotted to the son.

predicates.charge_claim_in_civil_proceeding: A creditor in a civil proceeding seeks to enforce an alleged charge against property under a deed.
predicates.deed_allocates_debt_responsibility_withi: The deed allocates responsibility for a debt among family members and identifies property from which one family member is to satisfy that responsibility.
predicates.deed_shows_intent_to_secure_creditor_aga: The deed shows an intention to make specified property liable to the creditor for payment of the debt.

members.legal_issue: The special statutory rules of succession do not govern property after the death of a qualifying family legatee who received only a life interest under a will.
material_facts: The disputed properties included property governed by special statutory rules of succession.
The legatee was a younger son within the class of persons referred to in the statutory scheme.
Under the will, the legatee received only a life interest, followed by interests intended for others.
members.legal_principle: Sections 11, 13, 13-A and 14 of the Oudh Estates Act, 1869, permit a taluqdar to dispose of property and prescribe special succession consequences for qualifying transfers or bequests. Section 14 applies where the qualifying legatee becomes entitled to the property as an absolute owner; it does not displace a will that gives the legatee only a life interest followed by later interests. Section 12’s application of the rule against perpetuities indicates that future estates and limitations are not prohibited if they do not transgress that rule. The Court also considered section 22(5) in rejecting the claimant’s asserted statutory entitlement.
members.conclusion: The special statutory rules of succession did not apply on the legatee’s death; succession to the property followed the interests created by the will, and the next person entitled under it could take.

predicates.taluqdari_property_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns succession to property subject to a special statutory succession scheme.
predicates.qualifying_family_legatee: The person who received the property under the will belongs to a family class covered by the special succession scheme.
predicates.will_grants_only_life_interest: The will gives the legatee only a life interest and creates a later interest in another person.

members.legal_issue: The statutory rules governing intestate succession do not apply when succession opened before those rules came into force.
material_facts: The last male holder of the disputed properties died in 1936–37, before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
A stepmother claimed that she inherited the properties under the Act, although the respondents had obtained a decree recognizing their claim as heirs.
members.legal_principle: Under section 8, the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolves according to the Act; the words “dying intestate” and “shall devolve,” read in the context of section 6, which expressly concerns a male Hindu who dies after the Act’s commencement, show that section 8 is not retrospective. No earlier cases are relied on.
members.conclusion: Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is not retrospective, and does not apply where the male Hindu died and succession opened before the Act came into force.

predicates.inheritance_claim_under_new_succession_l: A person claims inheritance under a statutory succession law that came into force after the relevant death.
predicates.succession_opened_before_law_commencemen: The person whose estate is claimed died, and succession to the estate opened, before that law came into force.

members.legal_issue: A person lawfully cultivating agricultural land under a lease granted by a life-estate holder with authority to manage the land is a deemed tenant and may acquire ownership under a statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
material_facts: The landholder held a life estate and was authorized to manage the estate after attaining majority.
The settlement deed contained no specific restriction preventing the landholder from leasing the land.
The landholder leased the agricultural land to the cultivators, who lawfully cultivated it and did not fall within any of the statutory exceptions to deemed tenancy.
members.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 deems a person lawfully cultivating another's land to be a tenant unless the person falls within an enumerated exception. Sections 32 and 32G provide for the tenant's statutory purchase and determination of price. Following Dahyalal v. Rasul Mohammed Abdul Rahim, a person lawfully cultivating land under authority derived from someone other than the owner may qualify; the exclusion of a mortgagee in possession does not necessarily exclude a cultivator inducted by that mortgagee. Prabhu v. Ramdeo and section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act support the possibility that statutory tenancy protections may attach to a person inducted by a mortgagee in possession.
members.conclusion: The cultivators were deemed tenants under section 4 and were eligible to acquire ownership under the statutory purchase scheme.

rule.if: statutory_tenant_purchase_proceeding and land_belonged_to_another and cultivator_lawfully_cultivated_land and cultivator_not_in_excluded_category and life_estate_holder_authorized_to_manage and life_estate_holder_leased_land

predicates.statutory_tenant_purchase_proceeding: A proceeding concerned whether an agricultural cultivator qualified for ownership through a statutory tenant-purchase scheme.
predicates.land_belonged_to_another: The agricultural land belonged to someone other than the person cultivating it.
predicates.cultivator_lawfully_cultivated_land: The person cultivated the land under lawful authority.
predicates.cultivator_not_in_excluded_category: The cultivator was not a family member, qualifying servant or labourer, or mortgagee in possession within the statutory exceptions.
predicates.life_estate_holder_authorized_to_manage: A person holding a life estate had authority to manage the land.
predicates.life_estate_holder_leased_land: The life-estate holder granted the cultivator a lease of the land.

members.legal_issue: A person who lawfully cultivates agricultural land under authority derived from a mortgagee may qualify as a deemed tenant even without authority derived directly from the owner.
material_facts: The land belonged to the owners and was in the possession of a mortgagee.
The mortgagee inducted the cultivator as a tenant, and the cultivator was lawfully cultivating the land on the relevant date.
The cultivator did not fall within any of the categories excluded from deemed tenancy.
The owners obtained possession through execution of an award without an order under the statutory tenancy procedure.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(18) and 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, a person lawfully cultivating land belonging to another is deemed a tenant if the land is not cultivated personally by its owner and the person is not within the exceptions in section 4(a), (b), or (c). The statute does not require the cultivator's authority to derive directly from the owner. Its protective purpose would be unduly restricted by importing that requirement. Although under the ordinary rule of the Transfer of Property Act a tenant inducted by a mortgagee in possession ordinarily loses that right when the mortgage ends, that rule does not govern the statutory status conferred on a person lawfully cultivating agricultural land.
members.conclusion: The cultivator qualified as a deemed tenant and was entitled to the protection of the tenancy statute, notwithstanding that his authority to cultivate derived from the mortgagee rather than directly from the owners.

members.legal_issue: A grant of village land and specified water does not convey ownership of a river’s flowing water where the grant does not expressly include the river or its flow.
material_facts: The grant conveyed the village with rights described as including “water,” trees, grass, wood, stones, and hidden treasures, but did not refer to a river or to flowing water.
The river flowed through only part of the granted village and continued beyond it, where other riparian owners had land.
The appellant claimed compensation for the military authorities’ diversion of the river water on the basis that the grant gave the village sharers title to that flowing water.
members.legal_principle: The court considered section 37 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code and section 8 of the Transfer of Property Act, but held that neither displaced the grant’s wording. It applied the principle that a grant referring to “water” without referring to a river conveys water in ponds or wells and, by necessary implication, excludes flowing river water, as consistently held in Annapurnabai Gopal v. Government of Bombay. It also relied on Lyon v. Fishmongers’ Company for the principle that title to a river bed does not carry exclusive ownership of its running water. A grant of flowing water must be made in terms, particularly where the river continues beyond the granted land and other riparian owners could be prejudiced.
members.conclusion: The grant conveyed only water in ponds or wells, not the river’s flowing water. Ownership of the river bed did not itself give the appellant ownership of the water flowing over it, so the appellant could not recover compensation on the asserted title to the flowing water.

predicates.appeal_challenges_denial_of_water_compen: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the denial of compensation claimed on the basis of ownership of flowing water.
predicates.grant_mentions_water_but_not_river_or_fl: The grant refers to water but does not expressly include the river or its flowing water.
predicates.river_continues_beyond_granted_land: The river flows beyond the granted land, where other riparian owners may have rights.

members.legal_issue: A grant of a village referring to water, but not expressly granting the river, does not convey the river’s flowing water merely because the grant includes the riverbed.
material_facts: The claimant’s title derived from a historic grant of a village that included the term “water” but did not expressly mention the river or its flowing water.
The river passed through only part of the village and continued beyond its boundaries.
The claimant sought compensation on the basis that the grant gave him title to the river’s flowing water.
members.legal_principle: The grant must be construed according to its language and the established use of the term “water” in such grants; that term refers to water in ponds or wells and, by implication, excludes flowing river water. A grant of the riverbed does not necessarily carry exclusive ownership of the flowing water. The Court relied on Annapurnabai Gopal v. Government of Bombay (1931) 47 Bom. L.R. 839 and Lyon v. Fish-Mongers’ Company [1876] 1 App. Cas. 662. The arguments based on s. 37(1) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879 and s. 8 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 did not change the construction of the grant.
members.conclusion: The grant conveyed static water in ponds or wells, not the river’s flowing water; ownership of the riverbed did not by itself confer ownership of the flowing water.

predicates.grant_uses_general_water_term: The grant refers generally to water.
predicates.grant_does_not_expressly_include_river: The grant does not expressly identify the river or its flowing water as part of what was granted.

members.legal_issue: A delegated authority to regulate mineral concessions may include a prohibition on private leases for a particular mineral when the prohibition serves conservation and prudent exploitation.
material_facts: Black granite was classified as a minor mineral, and the State had authority to make rules regulating concessions for minor minerals.
The rule barred leases to private persons for quarrying black granite but allowed the State or a wholly State-owned corporation to quarry it.
The State gave reasons concerning unsystematic mining, mineral wastage, inadequate worker safety, and the failure of many lessees to establish effective processing industries.
members.legal_principle: The purpose of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, including section 15 read with sections 4A, 17 and 18, is the conservation and prudent, discriminating exploitation of minerals for the community’s benefit. In context, “regulation” can include prohibition; its meaning depends on the statute’s purpose and the subject regulated. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, Attorney General for Ontario v. Attorney General for the Dominion, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Hindustan Aluminium Corporation, G. K. Krishnan v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Commonwealth of Australia v. Bank of New South Wales.
members.conclusion: The prohibition was within the delegated rule-making power and was a bona fide measure for conservation and prudent exploitation, not a misuse of that power to advance the State’s self-interest.

predicates.mineral_concession_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a rule governing concessions to extract a mineral.
predicates.state_authorized_to_regulate_minor_miner: The State had authority to regulate concessions for the category of mineral involved.
predicates.private_extraction_banned_for_conservati: The rule barred private extraction of the mineral for reasons directed to conserving it or ensuring its prudent exploitation.
predicates.public_extraction_remained_available: The rule allowed the State or a State-owned entity to extract the mineral.

members.legal_issue: A delegated rule may reserve the exclusive right to quarry a minor mineral to the State and prohibit private quarrying where that measure is within the State’s regulatory authority and serves a public-interest purpose.
material_facts: A committee reported extensive environmental and structural damage caused by haphazard, unscientific and unauthorized private sand quarrying.
The committee recommended prohibiting private quarrying, and the State decided to undertake sand quarrying exclusively.
members.legal_principle: Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 empowers the State to make rules regulating quarry leases for minor minerals. The regulatory power can extend to prohibiting private exploitation and reserving exploitation to the State in an appropriate case. State of Tamil Nadu v. Hind Stone and Gem Granites v. State of Tamil Nadu recognize that power.
members.conclusion: The provision vesting the exclusive right to quarry sand in the State was valid.

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_mining_rule: The proceeding challenges a rule made under delegated authority to regulate mining or quarrying.
predicates.expert_committee_found_environmental_har: An expert committee found that private quarrying caused environmental or related public harm.
predicates.state_adopted_exclusive_quarrying_policy: The State adopted a policy of undertaking quarrying exclusively to address that harm and serve the public interest.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser of specified assets sold by a secured financial corporation is not liable for the former owner's excise dues merely because it acquired those assets, where it did not acquire the entire business as an ongoing concern and the governing law creates no first charge for those dues.
material_facts: A borrower defaulted on its loans, and the financial corporation took possession of the mortgaged industrial property and sold the land, building, plant and machinery by public auction.
The purchaser acquired the specified assets, but did not acquire the entire business as an ongoing concern.
Excise duties and penalties had been assessed against the former owner for its manufacturing activity.
The financial corporation's security interest over the assets predated the demand for excise dues, and the excise department sought payment from the purchaser.
The purchaser appealed a judgment upholding the demand against it.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 29 and 46-B of the State Financial Corporations Act, a financial corporation enforcing its security has priority over unsecured government dues. Rule 230(2) of the Central Excise Rules authorises detention of specified goods and property but does not create a charge over them; Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguishes a charge from detention. The common-law priority of Crown debts, as explained in Dena Bank v. Bhikhabhai Prabhudas Parekh & Co., applies to unsecured creditors and does not defeat a prior secured interest. Shreyash Papers held that excise law created no charge in the circumstances considered. SICOM Ltd. distinguished Macson Marbles and clarified that liability may attach to a purchaser of an entire business as an ongoing concern, but not merely to a purchaser of specified assets. The later proviso to Section 11 of the Central Excise Act did not apply to this case.
members.conclusion: The purchaser was not liable for the former owner's excise dues under the statutory framework, and the secured financial corporation had priority over those dues. The demand against the purchaser was quashed.

predicates.secured_lender_sold_collateral: A secured lender took possession of collateral following the borrower's default and sold it.
predicates.buyer_acquired_specified_assets: The purchaser acquired specified property and equipment rather than the former owner's entire business.
predicates.buyer_acquired_ongoing_business: The purchaser acquired the former owner's entire business as an ongoing concern.
predicates.former_owner_owed_excise_dues: The former owner incurred excise dues through its business activity.
predicates.no_tax_first_charge: The governing law did not give the tax authority a first charge over the assets for the former owner's dues.

members.legal_issue: A sale term requiring the purchaser to bear statutory liabilities arising out of property does not make the purchaser responsible for the former owner's excise dues arising from its manufacturing activity.
material_facts: The public auction notice and the sale instruments stated that the assets were free from encumbrances and that the purchaser would bear statutory liabilities arising out of the land, building or plant and machinery.
The excise dues arose from the former owner's manufacture of excisable goods, rather than from the land, building or machinery themselves.
The excise department demanded those dues from the purchaser, and the purchaser appealed a judgment that treated the sale terms as making it liable.
members.legal_principle: The contractual language must be applied according to its stated connection to the property: liabilities arising out of land, buildings or machinery include property-related dues, but do not include excise dues incurred through manufacturing goods using those assets. The distinction is between liabilities attached to or arising from the property and liabilities arising from the former owner's business activity.
members.conclusion: The sale terms covered statutory liabilities arising from the purchased properties, not excise dues arising from the former owner's manufacturing activity; the purchaser was not liable for those dues under the terms.

rule.if: appeal_against_demand_to_asset_buyer and sale_terms_assign_property_arising_liabilities_to_buyer and excise_dues_arose_from_former_owner_manufacturing and not excise_dues_arose_from_purchased_property

predicates.appeal_against_demand_to_asset_buyer: The purchaser of assets appealed a decision upholding a tax authority's demand that it pay the former owner's dues.
predicates.sale_terms_assign_property_arising_liabi: The sale terms required the purchaser to bear statutory liabilities arising out of the purchased property.
predicates.excise_dues_arose_from_former_owner_manu: The former owner's excise dues arose from its manufacture of excisable goods.
predicates.excise_dues_arose_from_purchased_propert: The excise dues arose from the land, building or equipment as property, rather than from the former owner's manufacturing activity.

members.legal_issue: An appellate determination of comparative hardship must consider the applicable hardship rule, and failure to do so may require the prior order to be set aside and the matter remanded for reconsideration.
material_facts: The appellate court did not consider Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 when addressing comparative hardship.
The High Court confirmed the appellate court’s order.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and remanded the appeal for reconsideration of comparative hardship under Rule 16(2).
members.legal_principle: Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 had to be considered in assessing comparative hardship. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The order was set aside and the matter remanded for the appellate court to reconsider comparative hardship in light of Rule 16(2). The appellate court could consider the earlier agreement, the tenant’s offer to return his own shop to the landlord, and the equities of the case, and the parties could submit additional evidence by affidavit.

predicates.landlord_ejectment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in an ejectment suit brought by a landlord.
predicates.applicable_hardship_rule_not_considered: The appellate court did not consider the applicable rule when assessing comparative hardship.
predicates.prior_order_set_aside_and_matter_remande: The prior order is set aside and the matter is remanded for reconsideration of comparative hardship.

members.legal_issue: A retrospective change making comparative hardship relevant requires orders that omitted that assessment to be set aside and the matter remanded, while leaving an independent finding of bona fide need undisturbed.
material_facts: A landlord sought release of a rented shop for a bona fide need, and the authority found that need established but rejected release after weighing comparative hardship against the landlord.

On appeal, the appellate court did not consider comparative hardship because a Full Bench had held the relevant rule requiring that assessment invalid; it allowed release based on the bona fide need finding.
A later retrospective amendment required comparative hardship to be considered and validated the relevant rules.
members.legal_principle: Section 21 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, as retrospectively amended by U.P.
