Act No. 28 of 1976, required comparative hardship to be considered; the amendment also retrospectively validated Rule 16. The Full Bench decision in Chandra Kumar Shah v. District Judge had treated Rule 16(2) as ultra vires, which explained why the appellate court had omitted the comparison, but the retrospective amendment displaced that basis for the orders. Accordingly, the court remanded for the required comparative-hardship assessment without reopening the distinct finding of bona fide need.
members.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the High Court and appellate court orders were set aside, and the matter was remanded for consideration of comparative hardship under the amended law. The finding that the landlord bona fide required the shop was not to be disturbed.

rule.if: release_proceeding_on_appeal and retrospective_hardship_requirement and appellate_decision_omitted_comparison and bona_fide_need_already_found

predicates.release_proceeding_on_appeal: A dispute over release of rented premises was before a court on appeal.
predicates.retrospective_hardship_requirement: A later retrospective legal change required comparative hardship to be considered and validated the rules governing that assessment.
predicates.appellate_decision_omitted_comparison: The appellate court decided the release dispute without weighing the comparative hardship of the landlord and tenant.
predicates.bona_fide_need_already_found: An earlier decision had found that the landlord bona fide required the premises.

members.legal_issue: Failure to comply with an eviction-related court order constitutes civil contempt when the court’s time extension was based on the parties’ agreement and no undertaking was given.
material_facts: The court extended the tenant’s time to vacate, recording terms agreed to by both parties; the tenant did not file the undertaking mentioned in the order.
The tenant did not vacate by the extended deadline, but the court found that the extension was based on the parties’ agreement rather than on a representation by the tenant that he would vacate.
members.legal_principle: A clear and deliberate breach of an undertaking to the court to vacate premises may constitute civil contempt. Even without an undertaking, a litigant may be liable if the court was induced to act on the litigant’s representation and that representation was false or made without an intention to act on it. Here, however, the extension was granted on the parties’ agreement, not on the tenant’s representation.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not liable for civil contempt for the alleged breach of the order.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and eviction_time_extension_recorded_by_court and no_undertaking_given and extension_based_on_parties_agreement

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A party seeks to establish civil contempt based on an alleged breach of a court order.
predicates.eviction_time_extension_recorded_by_cour: The court records an extension of time for a tenant to vacate premises subject to an eviction order.
predicates.no_undertaking_given: The tenant does not give the undertaking contemplated by the court’s order.
predicates.extension_based_on_parties_agreement: The court grants the extension on terms agreed by the parties, rather than in reliance on a representation by the tenant.

members.legal_issue: Failure to file an undertaking required in connection with an extension of time to vacate does not by itself establish civil contempt when the person vacates within the original deadline.
material_facts: The order granted additional time to vacate subject to payment of outstanding dues and filing an undertaking within two weeks.
The respondent vacated the premises before the deadline in the order and did not file the undertaking.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 129 of the Constitution and Sections 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, civil contempt requires wilful disobedience. Ram Kishan v. Tarun Bajaj (2014) explains that the disobedience must be deliberate and established beyond reasonable doubt; a failure that does not amount to wilful disobedience does not justify contempt action.
members.conclusion: The failure to file the undertaking was not a basis for initiating contempt action because the undertaking was required only if the respondent wished to avail of the additional time, which the respondent did not need.

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A court is considering an allegation of civil contempt for disobedience of its order.
predicates.undertaking_conditioned_on_extra_time: The order requires an undertaking only as a condition for using additional time to comply.
predicates.vacated_before_original_deadline: The person vacated the premises before the deadline that applied without the additional time.

members.legal_issue: The factum of a customary adoption is established by evidence showing a clear adoption intention and the adopter’s subsequent acknowledgment and treatment of the adoptee as a son.
material_facts: A formal deed recited the adoption and the adopter’s intention to treat the adoptee as his son.
The adopter made public declarations of the adoption and treated the adoptee as his adopted son, who enjoyed the rights of a son.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted the concurrent findings on factum based on the adoption deed and the adopter’s subsequent conduct; it applied no separate statutory provision or earlier case to this issue.
members.conclusion: The evidence was ample to sustain the finding that the adoption had in fact occurred.

rule.if: adoption_validity_challenge and formal_deed_records_adoption and adopter_publicly_acknowledged_adoption and adopter_treated_adoptee_as_son

predicates.adoption_validity_challenge: A civil proceeding challenges whether an adoption occurred or is valid.
predicates.formal_deed_records_adoption: The adopter executed a formal deed recording the adoption.
predicates.adopter_publicly_acknowledged_adoption: The adopter publicly declared that the adoptee had been adopted.
predicates.adopter_treated_adoptee_as_son: The adopter treated the adoptee as his son.

members.legal_issue: A customary adoption under the relevant local custom requires both a declaration of adoption and general treatment of the appointed heir as a son.
material_facts: The adopter was a sonless Jat and declared the claimant adopted before the village panchayat, distributed jaggery, and executed a deed of adoption.
The adopter lived with the claimant for only a short period, then left him and cancelled the deed within a few months.
There was no evidence that the adopter treated the claimant generally as his son; instead, the adopter repudiated the earlier declaration and association.
The adopter died several years after the purported adoption.
members.legal_principle: The customary law recorded for Jats of the relevant district requires both a declaration of adoption and general treatment of the appointed heir as a son. A declaration or deed alone, without precedent or subsequent treatment as a son, is insufficient. The Court relied on the Ludhiana District rewaj-i-am and the general customary-law discussion in paragraph 35 of Rattigan’s Digest of Customary Law, and referred to Gurbachna v. Bujha (1911) 46 Punjab Record 151, Baj Singh v. Partap Singh (1923) 77 I.C. 473, Chhajju v. Mehr Singh (1930) 31 P.L.R. 997, Chanan Singh v. Buta Singh, A.I.R. 1935 Lah. 83, and Kishan Singh v. Taru, A.I.R. 1949 East Punjab 342.
members.conclusion: The claimant was not validly adopted because the declaration and deed were not accompanied by general treatment as a son; the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: customary_adoption_dispute and declaration_of_adoption_made and not general_treatment_as_son

predicates.customary_adoption_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an adoption made under local custom was valid.
predicates.declaration_of_adoption_made: The alleged adopter declared that the person was adopted or appointed as his heir.
predicates.general_treatment_as_son: The alleged adopter generally treated the appointed heir as his son, either before or after the declaration.

members.legal_issue: Relief sought against private defendants cannot be severed from a barred claim against the Crown when the relief depends on the government’s orders concerning the land.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought relief against family members on the basis that the government lacked authority to alter the earlier order recognizing the plaintiff as sole Saranjamdar.
The family members held their respective portions under government orders, and the plaintiff wanted the government bound by the decree sought against them.
The plaintiff refused to remove the government or the claims against it from the suit.
members.legal_principle: A claim against private defendants is not severable from a barred claim against the Crown where the claims are interdependent and the requested decree is intended to bind the Crown. The court relied on Basalingappagouda v. The Secretary of State for India, 28 Bom. L.R. 651, and Basangauda v. The Secretary of State, 32 Bom. L.R. 1370.
members.conclusion: The claims against the private defendants could not be separated from the claim against the government, so the suit could not proceed by granting relief against the private defendants alone.

predicates.civil_suit: A person brought a claim for determination in a civil court.
predicates.private_relief_depends_on_government_ord: The claimant sought relief against private persons on the basis that government orders concerning the subject matter were invalid or ineffective.
predicates.government_retained_for_binding_effect: The claimant kept the government in the suit so that the requested decree would bind it.
predicates.private_relief_cannot_be_severed_from_ba: The relief against the private persons cannot be considered or granted independently of the barred claim against the government.

members.legal_issue: Claims against private defendants cannot be separated from a barred claim against the government when the claimed private rights depend on the government’s orders.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s claims against the other family branches depended on the assertion that the government’s later order was invalid and the earlier order remained operative.
The other branches held their respective portions on the basis of the government’s orders.
The plaintiff retained the government as a party, and the requested relief against the other branches was connected to the relief sought against the government.
members.legal_principle: Where the rights claimed against private defendants cannot be divorced from the claim against the Crown, the court cannot consider the private claims separately to avoid the jurisdictional bar. If the government’s claim is ignored, its orders remain unchallenged, and parties holding their properties under those orders cannot be displaced through the remaining claim. Basalingappagouda v. Secretary of State and Basangauda v. Secretary of State support this approach.
members.conclusion: The plaintiff could not obtain the relief claimed against the other defendants by severing those claims from the claim against the government.

predicates.civil_suit: A person brought a civil suit seeking relief against the government and private defendants.
predicates.claims_against_private_parties_depend_on: The plaintiff’s claimed rights against the private defendants depended on the asserted invalidity or effect of government orders.
predicates.government_retained_as_party: The plaintiff kept the government in the suit rather than proceeding only against the private defendants.

members.legal_issue: A prior assessment of income in the hands of one person does not prevent the tax authority from assessing the person who is legally liable for that income under the applicable income-tax law.
material_facts: Two individuals jointly purchased land and shared the compensation received when it was acquired.
The tax authority had previously assessed each individual's share of the compensation in that individual's own hands for other assessment years.
The tax authority later proposed to assess the joint activity as an association of persons for the same income, and the respondent challenged its authority to do so.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 2(31) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, tax is charged on the person legally liable for the income; those provisions give the assessing officer no option to tax either an association of persons or its members individually. The contrast with Section 3 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, which expressly allowed that choice, supports this construction. Section 183 of the 1961 Act also shows that Parliament expressly provided a choice where it intended one. The decisions in Mahendra Kumar Agarwal v. Income Tax Officer, Rodamal Lalchand v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Choudry Brothers v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Punjab Cloth Stores v. Commissioner of Income Tax were consistent with this view. The contrary decisions in Commissioner of Income Tax v. Blue Mountain Engineering Corporation and Commissioner of Income Tax v. Pure Nichitpur Colliery Company were not followed. Ramanlal Madanlal v. Commissioner of Income Tax recognized the distinction between the two Acts in the context of an unregistered firm. Commissioner of Income Tax v. Kanpur Coal Syndicate and Commissioner of Income Tax v. Murlidhar Jhawar and Purna Ginning and Pressing Factory were decided under the 1922 Act and did not determine the issue under the different language of the 1961 Act.
members.conclusion: The prior assessments in the individuals’ hands did not bar assessment of the association of persons if it was the person legally liable for the income. The appeal was allowed and the High Court’s judgment was set aside; the Court expressed no opinion on the respondent’s other objections.

predicates.tax_assessment_proceeding: A tax authority initiated or pursued a proceeding to assess income for tax.
predicates.income_legally_belongs_to_assessee: The income was legally taxable to the person whom the authority sought to assess.
predicates.same_income_assessed_to_other_person: The same income had previously been assessed in the hands of a different person.

members.legal_issue: A transitional provision allowing the successor tax law’s procedures to be used to reassess escaped income does not apply that law’s new substantive personal liability to tax years governed by the prior law.
material_facts: Assessments for earlier tax years were reopened after the successor tax law came into force because income had escaped assessment.
The reassessments were made using the successor law’s procedure for reopening assessments.
The recovery orders relied on a new provision that imposed personal liability on family members, a liability not imposed by the law governing the earlier tax years.
members.legal_principle: Section 297(2)(d)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, read with Sections 147 and 148, permits the successor law’s provisions to apply when escaped income from an earlier year is reassessed. The words “all the provisions of this Act shall apply accordingly” refer to the machinery for assessment and do not incorporate substantive provisions creating new rights or liabilities. The substantive law governing liability remains the law applicable to the relevant tax year; Section 171(6) is substantive because it creates personal liability.
members.conclusion: The transitional provision made the successor law’s assessment machinery applicable to the reopened assessments, but did not import its new substantive personal-liability provision; the prior law governed that liability.

predicates.reassessment_of_earlier_year_escaped_inc: The proceeding reassesses income alleged to have escaped assessment for a tax year that occurred before the successor law applied.
predicates.reassessment_under_successor_law_procedu: The reassessment proceeds under the successor law’s procedures for reopening assessments.
predicates.asserted_member_liability_is_substantive: The recovery sought would impose on family members a personal tax liability that did not exist under the law governing the relevant tax year.

members.legal_issue: The duty to consider a borrower’s representation and communicate reasons for rejecting it is mandatory.
material_facts: After receiving a demand notice, the borrower sent the creditor a representation proposing rescheduling of the loan.
The creditor did not send a written response stating reasons for rejecting the representation.
members.legal_principle: Section 13(3A) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, read with Rule 3A of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, requires consideration and a reasoned communication when a representation is rejected. The imperative language and the provision’s purpose of giving the creditor a pause to reconsider make the duty mandatory. The Court relied on Mardia Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India, Transcore v. Union of India, Keshavlal Khemchand & Sons (P) Ltd. v. Union of India, and the principles of statutory construction discussed in State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya and other cited decisions.
members.conclusion: The creditor must actively consider a borrower’s representation or objection and, if it rejects it as unacceptable or untenable, communicate its reasons within the prescribed time; this requirement is mandatory.

predicates.secured_creditor_receives_borrower_repre: A borrower makes a representation or objection after a secured creditor sends a demand notice.
predicates.secured_creditor_rejects_representation: The secured creditor decides not to accept the borrower’s representation.
predicates.secured_creditor_finds_representation_un: The secured creditor concludes that the borrower’s representation is untenable.

members.legal_issue: A secured creditor must consider and communicate reasons for rejecting a borrower’s response to an enforcement notice only when the borrower has made such a response.
material_facts: The borrower had defaulted on a loan secured by mortgaged property, and the bank served a notice demanding payment before taking enforcement measures.
The borrower claimed it sent a representation the day after receiving the notice, but the bank denied receiving it and said a letter it did receive referred to telephone discussions, not the notice.

The borrower did not file a rejoinder denying the bank’s account until after the Court had noted that the bank’s denial remained unrebutted; the record did not establish that a response to the notice had been received.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 13(2) and Section 13(3-A) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, and the principles stated in Mardia Chemicals Ltd. v. Union of India, when a borrower responds to a notice under Section 13(2) with an objection or relevant facts, the secured creditor must consider the response with due application of mind and communicate reasons for rejecting it. Communication of those reasons is for the borrower’s information and does not itself confer a right to apply to the Debt Recovery Tribunal at that stage. The duty depends on a response having been made; the Court found that fact was not established here.
members.conclusion: The borrower did not establish that it had submitted a representation requiring the bank’s consideration, so no failure by the bank to consider or respond to such a representation was shown and no relief was warranted on that ground.

predicates.secured_enforcement_challenge: The proceeding challenges a secured creditor’s enforcement action following a payment default.
predicates.borrower_defaulted: The borrower failed to make required repayments on the secured credit.
predicates.no_response_to_notice_established: The borrower did not establish that it sent a response to the enforcement notice.

members.legal_issue: A court in whose territory a cheque is presented for collection, or another component of the cheque-dishonour offence occurs, may have territorial jurisdiction to try the complaint even when the drawee bank is elsewhere.
material_facts: The complainant, who resided and maintained his bank account in Bhiwani, presented the cheque for collection through his bank there.
The cheque was returned unpaid to the complainant through his bank in Bhiwani, and the complaint stated that dishonour occurred there.
The complainant sent the demand notice from Bhiwani and received the drawer’s reply there.
The cheque was drawn on a bank in Guwahati, outside Bhiwani.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 177, 178(d) and 179 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an offence involving acts in different local areas may be tried in a court having jurisdiction over any such area. In K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan, the Court held that the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act comprises drawing the cheque, presenting it, its return unpaid, giving written demand notice, and failure to pay within the prescribed period, and that a court where a component occurs may have jurisdiction. Ishar Alloy Steels Ltd. v. Jayaswals Neco Ltd. concerned the statutory time for presenting a cheque to the drawer’s bank, not territorial jurisdiction, and does not displace K. Bhaskaran. Harman Electronics Pvt. Ltd. v. National Panasonic India Pvt. Ltd. establishes that sending a notice from a place alone does not confer jurisdiction; communication of the notice and subsequent non-payment are relevant.
members.conclusion: The Bhiwani court had territorial jurisdiction to try the complaint. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the refusal to interfere under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

rule.if: cheque_dishonour_complaint and (cheque_drawn_in_forum or cheque_presented_in_forum or cheque_returned_unpaid_in_forum or demand_notice_communicated_in_forum_and_nonpayment_followed or drawer_resides_in_forum or payee_resides_in_forum)

predicates.cheque_dishonour_complaint: A complainant brought a criminal complaint alleging that a cheque was dishonoured and the drawer failed to pay after demand.
predicates.cheque_drawn_in_forum: The cheque was drawn within the territory of the court whose jurisdiction is in issue.
predicates.cheque_presented_in_forum: The cheque was presented for collection within the territory of the court whose jurisdiction is in issue.
predicates.cheque_returned_unpaid_in_forum: The cheque was returned unpaid within the territory of the court whose jurisdiction is in issue.
predicates.demand_notice_communicated_in_forum_and_: The written demand was communicated within the territory of the court, and the drawer thereafter failed to pay within the required period.
predicates.drawer_resides_in_forum: The drawer resided within the territory of the court whose jurisdiction is in issue.
predicates.payee_resides_in_forum: The payee resided within the territory of the court whose jurisdiction is in issue.
predicates.forum_court_has_territorial_jurisdiction: The court in the relevant territory is competent to try the complaint.

members.legal_issue: Territorial jurisdiction over a dishonoured-cheque complaint may lie in any area where a constituent act of the offence occurred.
material_facts: The appellant filed a complaint concerning a dishonoured cheque.

The High Court’s factual account treated the cheque as having been presented for encashment in Delhi, but held that Delhi courts lacked jurisdiction and directed the complaint to be returned for filing elsewhere.
The Supreme Court decided the appeal on the factual position stated by the High Court.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the offence is completed by the combination of drawing the cheque, presenting it to a bank, its return unpaid, giving written demand notice, and failure to pay within the prescribed time. Under Sections 177 and 178(d) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, where an offence consists of acts in different local areas, a court in any area where one of those acts occurred may try it. K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan permits the complainant to choose any such court. Harman Electronics Private Limited v. National Panasonic India Private Limited does not displace that principle; sending a notice from a place alone does not confer jurisdiction, whereas the court where the cheque was presented may have jurisdiction. Ishar Alloy Steels Ltd. v. Jayaswal Neco Ltd. does not displace the jurisdiction recognized by K. Bhaskaran. The Court also relied on Nishant Aggarwal v. Kailash Kumar Sharma and FIL Industries Limited v. Imtiyaz Ahmed Bhat.
members.conclusion: On the factual position recorded by the High Court, the courts in the area where the cheque was presented had territorial jurisdiction, and the High Court’s contrary order was set aside.

rule.if: dishonoured_cheque_complaint and (cheque_drawn_in_area or cheque_presented_in_area or cheque_returned_unpaid_in_area or demand_notice_given_in_area or drawer_failed_to_pay_in_area)

predicates.dishonoured_cheque_complaint: A complainant files a complaint concerning a cheque that was returned unpaid.
predicates.cheque_drawn_in_area: The drawer draws the cheque in the area.
predicates.cheque_presented_in_area: The complainant presents the cheque to a bank in the area.
predicates.cheque_returned_unpaid_in_area: The bank returns the cheque unpaid in the area.
predicates.demand_notice_given_in_area: The complainant gives the drawer a written demand notice in the area.
predicates.drawer_failed_to_pay_in_area: The drawer fails to pay the demanded amount in the area after receiving the notice.
predicates.court_in_area_has_territorial_jurisdicti: A court with territorial jurisdiction over the area may try the complaint.

members.legal_issue: A landlord required to leave government accommodation cannot use the summary eviction procedure when the landlord already occupies another part of the same building that can be separately enjoyed as a dwelling.
material_facts: The landlord, a government servant, was required to vacate government accommodation and sought summary eviction of the tenant from the first floor of his house.
The landlord occupied the ground floor of that house.
The first and ground floors had common facilities and a common passage, but the first floor had a staircase providing access without going through the ground floor.
The landlord’s mother had previously occupied the ground-floor portion separately, and after her death that portion had been let to a tenant who occupied it separately.
The Court found that the occupied portion could be separately enjoyed for dwelling purposes, even though it could not be independently locked up.
members.legal_principle: Sections 24A, 24B and 24C of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 provide an urgency procedure for a landlord required to leave government accommodation. Section 24B(1) and its proviso must be read in light of that purpose. A dwelling house is a building used, constructed or adapted principally for human habitation and may include a separately occupied part of a house. Whether parts form one dwelling or separate dwellings depends on their cumulative circumstances, including situation, entrance, municipal number, construction, intercommunication, completeness and independence; no single factor is decisive. The portion must be capable of separate enjoyment, but independent locking is not essential. The Court relied on Busching Schmitz Private Ltd. v. P.T. Menghani, Jai Singh Jairam Tyagi v. Mamanchand Ratilal Agarwal, and the workable factors discussed in S.S. Makhijani v. V.K. Jotwani; it distinguished Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal and referred to Narain Khamman v. Parduman Kumar Jain.
members.conclusion: The landlord was not entitled to use the summary urgency procedure because the portion he occupied was a separate dwelling capable of being separately enjoyed. The appeal was dismissed, without preventing the landlord from seeking eviction through other available legal proceedings or arranging to separate the units.

predicates.summary_urgency_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks eviction through a special summary procedure based on an urgent need for residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_required_to_leave_government_ho: The landlord was required to vacate government-provided housing.
predicates.landlord_occupies_another_part_of_same_b: The landlord occupies a portion of the same building from which the tenant is sought to be evicted.
predicates.occupied_part_separately_enjoyable_as_dw: The portion occupied by the landlord can be used and enjoyed separately as a dwelling, assessed from the relevant circumstances together.
predicates.summary_urgency_eviction_unavailable: The landlord cannot obtain eviction through the special summary urgency procedure.

members.legal_issue: A landlord cannot use the special recovery ground when another dwelling owned by the landlord or specified close family members is available for the landlord's residence or the landlord has already moved into it, even if that dwelling is unsuitable.
material_facts: When the landlord filed the eviction application, the landlord was residing in other premises belonging to the landlord.
Those premises were separate from the premises let to the tenant.
The Rent Controller considered the parties' respective needs and held that the landlord's occupied premises were not reasonably suitable residential accommodation.

The Court held that the landlord's existing owned premises prevented use of the special recovery ground and that any claim based on their unsuitability had to proceed under the ordinary bona fide-requirement ground.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14A(1) and 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, provide distinct grounds. Section 14A(1), read with its proviso, does not allow a landlord with another owned dwelling available for residence, or already occupied by the landlord, to use the special ground to recover another let dwelling. The special ground is meant to address the need to vacate allotted housing, not to enable a landlord to choose between owned dwellings or profit from the order requiring vacation. Where the owned dwelling is not reasonably suitable, the landlord must rely on section 14(1)(e). Section 25C supports that distinction by modifying restrictions applicable to the specified landlord category when proceeding under the ordinary ground.
members.conclusion: The eviction application under section 14A(1) was not maintainable because the landlord had moved into another owned dwelling; the application was dismissed. If the other owned dwelling is unsuitable, the landlord must proceed under section 14(1)(e).

rule.if: special_recovery_proceeding and landlord_owns_another_dwelling and (another_dwelling_available_for_residence or landlord_moved_into_another_dwelling)

predicates.special_recovery_proceeding: The landlord seeks possession through the special statutory procedure for a person required to vacate residential accommodation allotted by a public authority.
predicates.landlord_owns_another_dwelling: The landlord, or the landlord's wife or dependent child, owns another dwelling.
predicates.another_dwelling_available_for_residence: The other owned dwelling is available to the landlord for residential accommodation.
predicates.landlord_moved_into_another_dwelling: The landlord has already moved into the other owned dwelling.

members.legal_issue: Mining operations assessed as unsuitable for continuation, or falling within designated closure classes, must be discontinued.
material_facts: The petitions concerned limestone quarrying and the Court had received reports from a court-appointed committee and a government working group.
The Court accepted the reports’ assessments that some quarries were unsuitable for continued mining and directed their closure.

The Court also directed closure of other quarries assigned to a designated closure class, subject to specified exceptions, and closed quarries in a sensitive area despite their placement in an intermediate class.
members.legal_principle: The Court accepted the findings and reasons in the Bhargav Committee and Working Group reports. It relied on those assessments to distinguish quarries suitable for continued operation from those that should be closed; no earlier cases were cited for this determination.
members.conclusion: The Court directed that the quarries it identified as unsuitable or within the applicable closure classes be closed.

predicates.mining_writ_proceeding: A court considered a public-interest proceeding concerning the operation of mines or quarries.
predicates.joint_reports_find_mining_unsuitable: Inspection reports assessing the mine concluded that it was unsuitable for continued operation.
predicates.mine_falls_in_closure_class_without_revi: The mine was assigned to a class designated for closure and was not among the cases reserved for further review.
predicates.mine_is_in_sensitive_area_requiring_clos: The mine was situated in an area for which the court directed closure even though its general classification would otherwise permit further consideration.

members.legal_issue: Mining operations at quarries assessed as unsuitable because of serious environmental or safety concerns must cease, and the associated mining rights cannot continue.
material_facts: The court-appointed committee identified quarries with serious safety deficiencies and hazards, and the government working group classified certain quarries as unsuitable for further mining.
The court accepted those assessments for the quarries directed to close, including the quarries in the specified block and the other quarries classified as unsuitable, subject to stated exceptions.
Some affected leases were still subsisting, and some proceedings or stay orders sought to continue mining.
members.legal_principle: In a constitutional environmental writ proceeding, the court may act on expert assessments to protect a healthy environment and ecological balance, even where closure causes economic hardship. The judgment refers to Articles 32 and 48A of the Constitution in its subject matter; it cites no earlier cases for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The specified unsuitable quarries were ordered closed; relevant stay orders were dissolved, subsisting leases were terminated, and pending proceedings seeking continuation of those leases were dismissed.

predicates.environmental_mining_writ: The proceeding seeks judicial intervention concerning the environmental or safety effects of mining.
predicates.expert_assessment_finds_mining_unsuitabl: An expert assessment finds that continued mining at the site is unsuitable because of its environmental effects or serious safety concerns.

members.legal_issue: A mine assessed as suitable for continued operation and located outside an urban area may operate subject to compliance with applicable mining and safety requirements.
material_facts: The Bhargav Committee and Working Group both assessed the relevant class of quarries as suitable for continued mining.
The Court permitted the quarries in that class that were outside the urban limits to operate subject to applicable mining, safety, and other regulatory requirements.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the concordant suitability assessments in the Bhargav Committee and Working Group reports and conditioned continued operation on compliance with the Mines Act 1952, the Metalliferous Mines Regulations 1961, and other relevant statutes, rules, and regulations. No earlier cases were cited.
members.conclusion: The Court allowed the identified suitable quarries outside the urban area to operate, subject to compliance with applicable requirements.

predicates.mining_writ_proceeding: A court considered a public-interest proceeding concerning the operation of mines or quarries.
predicates.reports_assess_mine_suitable: The relevant inspection assessments concluded that the mine was suitable for continued operation.
predicates.mine_is_outside_urban_area: The mine was located outside the relevant urban limits.

members.legal_issue: Mining may continue at quarries assessed as suitable when they are outside the relevant urban limits, subject to applicable mining and safety requirements.
material_facts: The court-appointed committee and the government working group both classified a group of quarries as suitable for continued mining.
The quarries at issue were outside the city limits.
The court noted that continued operations remained subject to applicable statutes, rules, and regulations.
members.legal_principle: The court relied on the assessments of the appointed committee and working group, and made continued operation conditional on compliance with the Mines Act, 1952, the Metalliferous Mines Regulations, 1961, and other relevant statutes, rules, and regulations. No earlier cases are cited for this ruling.
members.conclusion: The suitable quarries outside the city limits were permitted to operate subject to compliance with the applicable mining, safety, and other legal requirements.

predicates.environmental_mining_writ: The proceeding seeks judicial intervention concerning the environmental or safety effects of mining.
predicates.expert_assessment_finds_mining_suitable: Expert assessments find that mining at the site is suitable for continuation.
predicates.site_outside_urban_limits: The mining site is outside the relevant urban limits.

members.legal_issue: A registered instrument styled as a release may transfer property rights when its terms and circumstances establish an intention to transfer those rights for valuable consideration.
material_facts: The instrument was registered and was styled a release deed concerning kanom rights.
The transferee paid consideration to the transferor.
The operative wording stated that the transferor’s rights, liabilities, and claims under the earlier instruments were surrendered to the transferee.
The instrument disclosed an intention to transfer the transferor’s kanom rights, and its operative words were capable of passing title.
members.legal_principle: A deed’s substance and operative terms, rather than its title alone or the stamp used, determine whether it transfers rights. The Court distinguished Mt. Oodey Koowur v. Mt. Ladoo, 13 Moo Ind App 585 (PC), where a bare admission without consideration did not convey a subsequently acquired title, and the release or relinquishment cases Jadu Nath Poddar v. Rup Lal Poddar, ILR 33 Cal 967, Dharam Chand v. Mauji Sahu, 16 Cal LJ 436, Narak Lall v. Magoo Lall, and Mathuramohan Saha v. Ram Kumar Saha. Those authorities did not establish that a document styled a release can never convey property. The Court relied on Hemendra Nath Mukerji v. Kumar Nath Roy, 12 Cal WN 478, in which a registered deed styled a disclaimer was construed as a transfer, and held that a release deed for valuable consideration may operate as a conveyance if it clearly manifests an intention to transfer.
members.conclusion: The release deed operated as an assignment of the kanom rights.

rule.if: property_rights_dispute and registered_instrument and valuable_consideration_paid and instrument_discloses_transfer_intent and operative_words_capable_of_passing_title

predicates.property_rights_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an instrument transferred rights in property.
predicates.valuable_consideration_paid: The transferee paid valuable consideration for the transfer.
predicates.instrument_discloses_transfer_intent: The instrument’s terms and circumstances show that the parties intended to transfer the transferor’s rights to the transferee.
predicates.operative_words_capable_of_passing_title: The operative wording is capable of transferring the rights in question.

members.legal_issue: An instrument described as a release deed can transfer ownership to a recipient who had no prior interest in the property if its operative words sufficiently express an intention to transfer title.
material_facts: The recipients had no interest in the properties before execution of the deed.
The deed described the transferor as owner and its operative words conveyed the properties and associated rights to the recipients.
The deed was intended to transfer ownership, rather than merely enlarge an existing limited interest.
members.legal_principle: The legal effect of an instrument depends on its operative words and intended effect, not merely on its description as a release deed. A release can transfer title to a person who previously had no interest if its words are sufficiently broad. Hutchi Gowder v. Bheema Gowder and S. P. Chinnathambiar v. V. R. P. Chinnathambiar were distinguished: neither established that a document styled as a release could never transfer title to a person without a prior interest.
members.conclusion: The deed transferred ownership to recipients who had no prior interest in the properties.

rule.if: instrument_styled_as_release and recipient_had_no_prior_interest and operative_words_sufficiently_convey_title and intention_to_transfer_ownership

predicates.instrument_styled_as_release: The instrument was described as a release deed.
predicates.recipient_had_no_prior_interest: The recipient had no interest in the property before the instrument was executed.
predicates.operative_words_sufficiently_convey_titl: The instrument’s operative words were broad enough to convey ownership to the recipient.
predicates.intention_to_transfer_ownership: The instrument was intended to transfer ownership rather than merely enlarge an existing interest.

members.legal_issue: An interim stay of an order terminating a rehabilitation proceeding does not revive the proceeding that the order had already terminated.
material_facts: The rehabilitation board had concluded that the company should be wound up, and the appellate authority had dismissed the company’s challenge.
A court later stayed the operation of those orders while a challenge was pending.
The orders had not been quashed or set aside when the stay was granted.
members.legal_principle: Under Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. v. Church of South India Trust Association, staying the operation of an order does not wipe it out or restore the position that existed before it; quashing an order may do so. Accordingly, the stay did not revive the proceeding already disposed of by the board and appellate authority.
members.conclusion: The interim stay did not revive the terminated rehabilitation reference or make it pending again.

predicates.rehabilitation_proceeding_case: The proceeding concerns a company’s rehabilitation reference before the relevant board or appellate authority.
predicates.underlying_reference_already_terminated: The relevant authority had already disposed of the reference before the later stay was granted.
predicates.interim_stay_only: A court stayed the operation of the termination order without quashing it or remanding the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A stay of an appellate order dismissing an appeal does not revive the disposed appeal or make the underlying proceeding pending.
material_facts: The industrial company’s proceedings before the relevant statutory bodies had ended, and its appeal against the decision recommending winding up had been dismissed.
A court later stayed the operation of the dismissal order but did not quash it.
A winding-up proceeding against the company was being considered.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, the bar applies only when one of the specified proceedings is pending. A stay of an order suspends its operation but does not erase it; unlike quashing, it does not restore the position that existed before the order. Quashing may restore a disposed appeal, but a stay alone does not.
members.conclusion: The stay did not revive the dismissed appeal, so no proceeding was pending before the statutory bodies and the winding-up proceeding could continue.

rule.if: winding_up_proceeding and industrial_company_appeal_dismissed and dismissal_order_only_stayed and not statutory_proceeding_pending

predicates.winding_up_proceeding: A proceeding seeking the winding up of an industrial company is before a court.
predicates.industrial_company_appeal_dismissed: An appeal by an industrial company was disposed of by dismissal.
predicates.dismissal_order_only_stayed: A court stayed the operation of the dismissal order without quashing it.
predicates.statutory_proceeding_pending: A proceeding concerning the industrial company remains pending before the relevant statutory body.

members.legal_issue: The ordinary-residence condition for succession to a tenancy applies to heirs of a tenant remaining in possession after termination, not to heirs of a contractual tenant.
material_facts: The deceased held a contractual tenancy when she died.
The claimant was found to be the deceased tenant’s daughter and heir; that finding was not challenged.
The trial court had also found that the claimant was not ordinarily residing with the deceased, but the appellate court’s decision did not depend on that question.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(h) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, as amended in 1965, the words concerning the death of a person continuing in possession after termination refer to that person alone. The ordinary-residence condition therefore limits succession by heirs of a statutory tenant, not succession to a contractual tenancy, which is inheritable by the tenant’s heirs absent a provision to the contrary. The Court considered the Statement of Objects and Reasons as background to the amendment and relied on Anand Nivas (P) Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi only to interpret Section 2(h), noting that its principle on inheritance of statutory tenancy had been overruled by Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar.
members.conclusion: The claimant inherited the contractual tenancy as the deceased tenant’s heir, irrespective of whether she was ordinarily residing with the deceased at the time of death; the appeal was dismissed.

predicates.tenancy_inheritance_dispute: A dispute over inheritance of a tenancy arose in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.deceased_had_subsisting_contractual_tena: The deceased tenant held a subsisting contractual tenancy when they died.
predicates.claimant_was_deceased_tenant_heir: The claimant was found to be an heir of the deceased tenant.

members.legal_issue: The statutory tenant definition includes qualifying heirs but excludes subtenants and their heirs.
material_facts: The statutory definition separately included heirs of tenants in specified protected categories and expressly excluded subtenants and their heirs.
The companies' buildings were operated by dealers or other third parties, and the companies sought the protections available to tenants.
members.legal_principle: Section 2(4)(ii)(c) includes heirs of persons described in Section 2(4)(i), Section 2(4)(ii)(a), or Section 2(4)(ii)(b), while expressly excluding subtenants and their heirs. The court read that express exclusion to apply to rights under the Act, including the rights under Sections 3 and 9.
members.conclusion: Heirs of tenants within the specified protected categories may receive the Act's benefits, but subtenants and their heirs are excluded from those benefits, including the right to seek purchase of the land and compensation under the Act.

predicates.claimant_seeks_statutory_tenant_protecti: A claimant seeks benefits available to a tenant under the statutory scheme.
predicates.claimant_is_heir_of_covered_tenant: The claimant is an heir of a tenant within one of the protected statutory categories.
predicates.claimant_is_subtenant_or_subtenant_heir: The claimant is a subtenant or an heir of a subtenant.

members.legal_issue: An assessee who has claimed depreciation on a depreciable asset cannot elect its historical fair market value as the cost of acquisition when computing capital gains on its transfer.
material_facts: The assessee had owned the properties since before the relevant historical valuation date and sold some of them during the year in question.
Depreciation had been claimed and allowed on the properties in earlier years.
In computing capital gains, the assessee elected to use the properties’ fair market value on the historical valuation date instead of their written-down value.
The dispute concerned assets acquired directly by the assessee, not through one of the modes specified for the special rules governing transferred assets.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 48 and 50 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, where depreciation has been obtained on an asset, the adjusted written-down value is taken as its cost of acquisition. Section 55(2), which provides an option to use historical fair market value, applies for the purposes of Sections 48 and 49 but does not displace the special method in Section 50. Section 55(1)(a) explains the adjustment to written-down value. The Court agreed with Rajnagar Vaktapur Ginning, Pressing and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1975) 99 ITR 264, CIT v. Upper Doab Sugar Mills (1979) 116 ITR 240, Prime Product Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT (1979) 116 ITR 473, India Jute Co. Ltd. v. CIT (1982) 136 ITR 597, and the impugned Kerala High Court decision, and rejected the contrary approach in Goculdas Dossa and Co. v. J.P. Shah (1995) 211 ITR 706.
members.conclusion: The assessee could not substitute the historical fair market value for the cost of acquisition. For depreciable assets on which depreciation had been allowed, the cost of acquisition had to be determined under Section 50 read with Section 48, and the appeal on this issue was dismissed.

rule.if: income_tax_capital_gains_proceeding and asset_transferred and asset_depreciable and depreciation_allowed and asset_owned_before_valuation_date and historical_value_elected

predicates.income_tax_capital_gains_proceeding: The proceeding concerns computation of capital gains for income-tax purposes.
predicates.asset_transferred: The assessee transferred the asset during the relevant period.
predicates.asset_depreciable: The transferred asset was of a kind on which depreciation could be claimed.
predicates.depreciation_allowed: Depreciation had been claimed and allowed on the asset before its transfer.
predicates.asset_owned_before_valuation_date: The assessee had owned the asset before the date for which historical fair market value could be elected.
predicates.historical_value_elected: The assessee elected to use the asset's historical fair market value instead of its written-down value as the cost of acquisition.

members.legal_issue: A difference between the fair market value of a transferred asset and its declared consideration, without understatement of the consideration actually received, does not permit the fair market value to be substituted as the consideration for computing capital gains.
material_facts: The asset was sold for the same price for which it had been purchased.
The revenue authorities found that the sale was an honest and bona fide transaction and that the consideration received was correctly disclosed.
The proposed assessment relied on the fair market value being substantially higher than the declared sale price.
members.legal_principle: The provision must be construed in light of its purpose and statutory context, rather than by a literal reading that produces absurd or unjust results. The Court read a requirement of understatement into the provision, relying on its purpose of reaching concealed consideration, its marginal note and placement, and contemporaneous administrative circulars. The mover’s speech may be used to identify the mischief and purpose of legislation. Circulars issued under section 119 bind the revenue authorities even if they depart from the correct statutory interpretation. Relevant authorities include Luke v. Revenue Commissioner, Heydon’s Case, In re May Fair Property Company, Eastman Photographic Material Company v. Comptroller-General of Patents, Bushel v. Hammond, Bengal Immunity Company Ltd. v. State of Bihar, Navnitlal C. Jhaveri v. R.K. Sen, and Ellerman Lines Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax.
members.conclusion: The statutory fair-market-value substitution could be used only where the consideration had been understated; it did not apply to an honest transaction in which the consideration received was correctly disclosed.

rule.if: capital_gains_transfer_case and market_value_gap_exceeds_tolerance and consideration_correctly_disclosed and bona_fide_transaction

predicates.capital_gains_transfer_case: The proceeding concerns the computation of capital gains on a transfer of a capital asset.
predicates.market_value_gap_exceeds_tolerance: The asset’s fair market value exceeds the consideration declared for the transfer by more than the permitted margin.
predicates.consideration_correctly_disclosed: The transferor disclosed the full consideration actually received for the transfer.
predicates.bona_fide_transaction: The transfer was an honest transaction without concealment or suppression of consideration.

members.legal_issue: A law creating a state monopoly is protected against a challenge based on the right to carry on a trade, while incidental effects on other fundamental rights do not invalidate the monopoly provision.
material_facts: The challenged law restricted the purchase and transport of the commodity to the State, its authorised officers, or agents for the relevant area.
The law was intended to create a state monopoly in the trade.
The challenge relied on fundamental rights concerning property and the carrying on of trade.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(6)(ii), as amended, permits laws relating to the State carrying on a trade, business, industry or service to the complete or partial exclusion of citizens; such a monopoly is presumed reasonable and in the interests of the general public for purposes of Article 19(1)(g). Only provisions integral and essential to creating the monopoly receive that protection. Other provisions must satisfy the ordinary constitutional tests, and a direct effect on another right under Article 19(1) must be assessed under the corresponding clause. The Court relied on the direct-versus-indirect-effect approach in A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, Ram Singh v. State of Delhi, Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India and State of Bombay v. R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala; it also referred to Saghir Ahmed v. State of U.P., Parbhani Transport Co-operative Society Ltd. v. Regional Transport Authority, Dosa Satyanarayanamurty v. Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation and H. C. Narayanappa v. State of Mysore on state monopolies.
members.conclusion: The creation of a state monopoly is permitted by the latter part of Article 19(6), and the monopoly provision cannot be invalidated under the right to carry on a trade merely because it restricts citizens from that trade. An indirect or incidental effect on another fundamental right does not invalidate the monopoly provision, although provisions that are not essential to the monopoly must be assessed separately.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_monopo: A person challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a state monopoly.
predicates.state_is_the_monopolist: The law provides for the State itself to carry on the monopolised trade or business.
predicates.challenged_provision_is_integral_to_crea: The challenged provision is essential to creating the state monopoly, rather than merely incidental to its operation.

members.legal_issue: A prohibition on others conducting the same business is protected as an essential feature of a State monopoly and does not, on that account, infringe the freedoms to conduct business or to hold property.
material_facts: The legislation gave the State a monopoly to hold cattle fairs.
It prohibited individuals and local authorities from holding cattle fairs, a restriction directly necessary to make that monopoly effective.
The legislation did not extend the monopoly to every trade or occupation involving cattle.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 19(6), the basic and essential provisions necessary to create a State monopoly are protected against a challenge under Article 19(1)(g). Other provisions that are merely subsidiary or incidental must satisfy the ordinary test under Article 19(6). Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa, [1963] Supp. 2 SCR 691, was followed. The Court also held that the presumption of reasonableness of a State-monopoly statute may assist against a claim under Article 19(1)(f); State of Bihar v. Rameshwar Pratap Narain Singh, [1962] 2 SCR 382, and M. V. P. Ramunni Kurup v. Panchayat Board, Badagara, AIR 1954 Mad 754, were referred to but held not to determine the question.
members.conclusion: The essential prohibition on others holding cattle fairs was not open to challenge as an unreasonable restriction on the freedoms to carry on business or to hold property.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_busine: A party challenged a law creating a State monopoly on the basis of constitutional freedoms relating to business or property.
predicates.prohibition_is_essential_to_create_monop: The challenged prohibition prevented others from conducting the same business and was basic and necessary to establish the State monopoly.

members.legal_issue: An incidental price-control provision in a state-monopoly law is valid when its restrictions are reasonable and in the interests of the general public.
material_facts: The law required the State Government to fix the purchase price after consulting an advisory committee.
The price-fixing provision was not essential to the operation of the monopoly.
The price was fixed in consultation with the committee, and the petitioner neither established that it was unfair nor produced evidence that it was unreasonable.
The material before the Court indicated that the price compared favourably with prices in previous years and was intended to provide growers a fair return.
members.legal_principle: A provision that is not essential or integral to creating a state monopoly is not protected merely by Article 19(6)(ii); its validity must be tested under the first part of Article 19(6) as to the right to carry on a trade and under Article 19(5) as to the right to property. The Court held that the price-fixing restriction satisfied those tests because it was intended to protect growers from hardship and there was no showing that the price was unfair or unreasonable. The constitutional framework applied was Articles 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), 19(5) and 19(6).
members.conclusion: The price-fixing restrictions were reasonable and in the interests of the general public, and the provision was valid.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_incidental_price_control and price_control_not_essential_to_monopoly and price_fixed_after_advisory_consultation and price_not_shown_unfair_or_unreasonable

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_incidental_p: A person challenged a price-control provision included in a law creating a state monopoly.
predicates.price_control_not_essential_to_monopoly: The price-control provision is incidental rather than essential to creating the monopoly.
predicates.price_fixed_after_advisory_consultation: The State fixed the price after consulting an advisory body.
predicates.price_not_shown_unfair_or_unreasonable: The challenger did not establish that the fixed price was unfair or unreasonable.

members.legal_issue: A law creating a State monopoly in trade may impose restrictions that are presumed reasonable and in the interest of the general public.
material_facts: The law placed trade in specified forest produce under a State monopoly.
The challengers argued that the annulment of their contracts and restrictions on their trading rights were unreasonable or arbitrary.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(6)(ii) permits laws relating to State monopolies, and a law governing such trading activity is presumed reasonable and in the interest of the general public. The Court relied on Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa, [1963] 2 Supp. SCR 691.
members.conclusion: The restrictions were to be presumed reasonable and in the interest of the general public; the State could create a partial or complete monopoly in trade.

predicates.state_monopoly_restriction_challenge: The proceeding challenges restrictions imposed in connection with a State monopoly in trade.
predicates.law_places_trade_under_state_monopoly: The law places the relevant trade under a partial or complete State monopoly.

members.legal_issue: The State may use agents to operate a state monopoly if they conduct the trade strictly on the State's behalf and for its benefit.
material_facts: The law authorised the Government, authorised government officers, and agents for the relevant areas to purchase or transport the commodity.
The Court construed the officers and agents contemplated by the law as acting for the Government and for its benefit.
The Court accepted that using agents could be appropriate where operating the trade through government departments or employees would be inexpedient.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(6)(ii) permits the State to conduct a monopoly through its departments, officers, or agents, but any agent must act for the State and its benefit, within the strict and narrow sense of agency. Whether an arrangement is genuine agency depends on its substance, including the agreement and the circumstances in which it was made. The Court upheld the relevant statutory provisions on the construction that they contemplated only agency consistent with those limits.
members.conclusion: The statutory authorisation for government officers and agents to operate the monopoly was valid, provided the agents act strictly on behalf of the State and not for themselves.

predicates.state_monopoly_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the operation of a trade that the State has made a monopoly.
predicates.state_trade_requires_operational_assista: The State's operation of the trade requires assistance from officers or other persons.
predicates.proposed_agents_act_strictly_for_state: The persons assisting the State conduct the trade on its behalf and for its benefit, rather than for themselves.

members.legal_issue: A State carrying on a monopoly trade cannot use private contractors or agents to conduct that trade for their own benefit rather than on the State’s behalf.
material_facts: The legislation established a State monopoly in specified forest produce.
The challengers contended that the law did not bar future contracts like their existing collection contracts.
The Court stated that State parties or agents employed in the trade must work on behalf of the State and not for themselves.
members.legal_principle: When the State conducts trade, it may act through its officers or agents, but agents must carry on the trade on behalf of the State rather than for themselves. The Court relied on Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa, [1963] 2 Supp. SCR 691.
members.conclusion: It would be impermissible for the State to enter into future contracts of the kind in which private parties conduct the monopoly trade for their own benefit.

predicates.state_monopoly_trade: The State conducts or is entitled to conduct the relevant trade under a monopoly.
predicates.proposed_private_contracts_allow_agents_: Proposed contracts would allow private parties or agents to conduct the monopoly trade for their own benefit rather than on the State’s behalf.

members.legal_issue: A rule governing state-monopoly agency appointments is invalid if it leaves the terms of the agency agreement to an officer's discretion instead of prescribing them by rules.
material_facts: The rule required an appointed agent to execute an agreement in whatever form the Government directed.
The rules prescribed an application form but did not prescribe the form or principal terms of the agency agreement.
The rule therefore left the terms to be set on an ad hoc basis by the officer concerned.
members.legal_principle: Under the rule-making authority in section 18, the principal terms and conditions of an agency used to operate the monopoly must be prescribed by rules. Leaving those terms to the ad hoc choice of an officer exceeds the State Government's competence. The Court accordingly held Rule 7(5) invalid.
members.conclusion: The rule was invalid because the terms and conditions of the agency agreement had to be prescribed by rules and could not be left to an officer's discretion.

predicates.state_monopoly_agent_appointment_proceed: The proceeding concerns a rule for appointing agents to operate a state monopoly.
predicates.agreement_terms_left_to_officer_discreti: The rule leaves the terms of the agent's agreement to the discretion of a government officer.
predicates.principal_terms_not_prescribed_by_rules: The rules do not prescribe the principal terms and conditions of the agency agreement.

members.legal_issue: A rule that gives an official unguided discretion to specify taxable classes of machinery, without an effective appeal, is invalid for excessive delegation.
material_facts: The rules empowered the Commissioner, with the Corporation's approval, to specify classes of machinery to be treated as part of land or buildings for valuation.
The rules provided no principle to guide which machinery classes could be specified.
The Commissioner was the only decision-maker on the specification, and no right of appeal against the specification was provided.
members.legal_principle: The legislature may not delegate a power without providing guiding principles for its exercise. The Court held that the power to specify machinery classes depended on the Commissioner's arbitrary choice and that the absence of a right of appeal reinforced the defect. The judgment does not rely on an earlier case for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: Rule 7(3) was invalid because the legislature had excessively delegated power.

rule.if: property_tax_assessment_proceeding and official_can_select_taxable_machinery_classes and no_guiding_standard and no_appeal_from_selection

predicates.property_tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding challenges rules used to determine the property subject to municipal taxation.
predicates.official_can_select_taxable_machinery_cl: An official has power to decide which classes of machinery are treated as taxable property.
predicates.no_guiding_standard: The rule supplies no principle or standard to guide the official's selection of machinery classes.
predicates.no_appeal_from_selection: The affected person has no right of appeal against the official's selection.

members.legal_issue: A usufructuary mortgagee who is not entitled to take all property receipts in lieu of interest and remains entitled to interest when the property produces no receipts must render accounts of the property.
material_facts: The mortgagee took possession of the mortgaged property.
The mortgage terms entitled the mortgagee to a fixed monthly sum in lieu of interest, rather than all receipts from the property.
The mortgagors remained liable for interest when the property was vacant or the mortgagee could not collect rents.
The mortgagee could increase rents or replace a tenant, but could appropriate only the fixed monthly sum toward interest, not the entire increased rent.
members.legal_principle: Sections 76 and 77 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguish between a mortgagee in possession who must account for the property's administration and the specified mortgage arrangement to which section 77 applies. The terms of the mortgage govern that classification; where the mortgagee's entitlement is not confined to the property's receipts and does not extend to all increased rents, section 77 does not apply and the duty to account under section 76 applies.
members.conclusion: The mortgage did not fall within the category described in section 77 of the Transfer of Property Act; section 76 applied, and the mortgagee was liable to account for the administration of the property.

predicates.usufructuary_mortgage_accounting_case: The proceeding concerns accounting for a property held by a mortgagee under a usufructuary mortgage.
predicates.mortgagee_took_possession: The mortgagee took possession of the mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_was_not_entitled_to_all_proper: The mortgage terms limited the sums the mortgagee could take toward interest instead of giving the mortgagee all receipts from the property.
predicates.interest_remained_payable_without_proper: The mortgagor remained liable for interest during periods when the property produced no receipts or the mortgagee could not collect rent.

members.legal_issue: A mortgagee in possession need not render accounts where the parties contracted that the entire receipts from the mortgaged property would be taken in lieu of interest, even though the mortgagee had a separate personal obligation to pay a specified amount to the mortgagor.
material_facts: The suit sought redemption and an accounting of the income received from the mortgaged property.
The deed authorized the mortgagee to take the entire income from the land and appropriate it towards interest; the mortgagor agreed not to claim the produce or any increase in it.
The mortgagee’s obligation to pay a specified amount to the mortgagor was unconditional and personal, and did not depend on the receipts or yield from the land.
The deed stated an interest rate, which the Court found was used to estimate the amount of income to be appropriated and did not contradict the parties’ clearly expressed agreement.
The Court considered that the same result followed whether the mortgage was usufructuary or anomalous.
members.legal_principle: Sections 76(g) and 76(h) of the Transfer of Property Act ordinarily require a mortgagee in possession to keep and render accounts and to apply net receipts in reduction of interest and, where appropriate, principal. Section 77 provides an exception where the parties contract that receipts from the mortgaged property are taken in lieu of interest or interest and a defined portion of principal. A specified interest rate does not by itself defeat that exception if the deed, properly construed, provides that the entire receipts are taken in lieu of interest. The Court relied on Pandit Bachchu Lal v. Chaudhri Syed Mohammad Mah, (1933) 37 C.W.N. 457. It also stated that, if the mortgage was anomalous, the contractual terms under section 98 led to the same result.
members.conclusion: The mortgagee was not liable to render accounts to the mortgagor.

predicates.mortgage_accounting_dispute_in_redemptio: A suit for redemption disputes whether the mortgagee must account for receipts from the mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_in_possession: The mortgagee took possession of the mortgaged property or received its income as mortgagee.
predicates.contract_assigns_entire_property_receipt: The parties agreed that the entire receipts from the mortgaged property would be taken in lieu of interest.
predicates.mortgagor_payment_is_personal_and_indepe: The mortgagee separately undertook to pay the mortgagor a specified amount regardless of the property’s receipts or yield.

members.legal_issue: The Usurious Loans Act does not apply to a suit solely for accounts and a surplus where the reliefs constituting redemption have already been obtained and the relevant security was created before the Act came into force in the area.
material_facts: The mortgagors' transferee deposited money under section 83 of the Transfer of Property Act, and the mortgagee accepted it, delivered possession of the property and the relevant documents, and received payment.

The later suit sought accounts of the mortgagee's administration and payment of any surplus; it did not seek delivery of the mortgage deed or other documents, possession, or retransfer of the property.
The security was created in 1933, when the Usurious Loans Act did not apply in the area; the Act was applied there later.

The High Court applied the Usurious Loans Act to grant additional relief, and the Supreme Court held that the suit did not qualify under the Act's categories for redemption or enforcement of an agreement in respect of a loan.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(3)(b) and (c) of the Usurious Loans Act, the relevant suit must be one for enforcement of an agreement in respect of a loan or for redemption of a security, and the relevant agreement must have been made or security given after commencement of the Act. Under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, a suit for redemption enforces the right to obtain the mortgage documents, possession where applicable, and retransfer or extinguishment of the mortgagee's interest. A suit solely for accounts and a surplus is not thereby a redemption suit or a suit to enforce an agreement. Section 3(3) of the Usurious Loans Act addresses the form of a suit and does not remove section 2(3)'s timing requirements. Under sections 3(13) and 5(3) of the General Clauses Act, commencement is when the Act comes into force in the relevant area, not merely when it comes into operation elsewhere. The Court relied on Gajambal Ramalingam v. Rukn-ul-Mulk Syed Abdul Wajid and Re Hayes on the area's status, and rejected the contrary interpretation in Vaishnu Dass v. Thaker Dass.
members.conclusion: The Usurious Loans Act did not apply to the suit, and the mortgagors were not entitled to relief under it.

rule.if: mortgage_accounting_suit and suit_seeks_only_accounts_and_surplus and redemption_reliefs_already_obtained and security_predates_local_applicability

predicates.mortgage_accounting_suit: The proceeding is a suit by a mortgagor seeking accounts of a mortgagee's administration of mortgaged property.
predicates.suit_seeks_only_accounts_and_surplus: The suit seeks accounts and any resulting surplus, rather than relief enforcing redemption or an agreement in respect of a loan.
predicates.redemption_reliefs_already_obtained: Before the suit, the mortgagee accepted a deposit and delivered the relevant documents and possession, so the mortgagor had already obtained the reliefs constituting redemption.
predicates.security_predates_local_applicability: The security was created before the relevant law became applicable in the area where the property was situated.

members.legal_issue: The Usurious Loans Act does not provide relief in a mortgagor’s redemption suit where the security was given before that Act commenced.
material_facts: The representatives sought redemption of mortgages created in 1896 and 1897.
The Usurious Loans Act, 1918, applied to specified kinds of suits, including redemption of security given after the Act commenced.
The securities in issue were given before the Act commenced.
members.legal_principle: Under section 2(3) of the Usurious Loans Act, clauses (a) and (b) do not apply to a mortgagor’s suit for redemption, and clause (c) covers redemption only where the security was given after the Act commenced. The court cited no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The legal representatives could not claim the benefit of the Usurious Loans Act in the redemption suit.

predicates.redemption_proceeding: A mortgagor or the mortgagor’s representative brings a proceeding to redeem secured property.
predicates.security_predates_usury_law: The security being redeemed was created before the relevant usury-law protections commenced.

members.legal_issue: Dismissal for default of an application seeking to reopen a decree does not constitute a review that starts a fresh limitation period for execution.
material_facts: A judgment-debtor applied to reopen a preliminary mortgage decree, but the application was dismissed for default without the court considering whether the decree should be reopened.
The application to restore the reopening proceeding was also dismissed.
The decree-holder later applied to execute the final decree.
members.legal_principle: Under Article 182, clause 3, of the Limitation Act, 1908, a fresh starting point requires that the court undertake to review the relevant decree or order and decide the review. Even assuming an application under section 36 of the Bengal Money-lenders Act could be treated as an application for review, dismissal for default without consideration of the merits is not a review. The Court relied on no earlier cases.
members.conclusion: The dismissal for default was not a review of the decree under Article 182, clause 3, of the Limitation Act, 1908, and did not provide a fresh starting point for limitation; the execution application was time-barred.

rule.if: execution_application and reopening_proceeding and reopening_dismissed_for_default and court_did_not_consider_reopening_merits

predicates.execution_application: A decree-holder applied to execute a decree.
predicates.reopening_proceeding: A judgment-debtor applied to have a decree reopened.
predicates.reopening_dismissed_for_default: The court dismissed the application to reopen the decree because of default.
predicates.court_did_not_consider_reopening_merits: The court did not consider whether the decree should be reopened.

members.legal_issue: A later execution application is not a continuation or revival of an earlier application that was finally dismissed because the decree-holder failed to take a required step.
material_facts: The earlier execution application was dismissed after the decree-holder failed to pay the process fee required for a warrant of possession.
The earlier application was not left pending.
The decree-holder later filed another application seeking possession.
members.legal_principle: A later execution application may be treated as a continuation or revival only where the earlier application remains pending or was dismissed through no fault of the decree-holder, and the applications are substantially similar in scope and character. A properly and finally disposed-of application cannot be revived by a later application. The Court relied on Vadlamannati Bala Tripura Sundaramma v. Abdul Khader.
members.conclusion: The later application was not a continuation or revival of the earlier application.

predicates.execution_limitation_case: A decree-holder applies to execute a decree and limitation is disputed.
predicates.prior_application_finally_dismissed_for_: An earlier execution application was finally dismissed because the decree-holder failed to take a required procedural step.
predicates.prior_application_not_pending: The earlier execution application was no longer pending when the later application was filed.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser claiming through a party to a pending property-title suit is not a necessary or proper party when the dispute can be fully adjudicated between the existing parties and the purchaser has no independent ground to contest the title on which the suit is based.
material_facts: The suit sought a declaration of ownership founded on a registered will.
An earlier decree, which had become final, had adjudicated a claim based on the same will after one of the testator’s daughters was made a party.
While the later suit was pending, the defendants sold the disputed property to the proposed parties.
The purchasers claimed through heirs of the daughter who had been a party to the earlier suit, and their asserted title did not give them a ground to challenge the will.
