members.legal_principle: Under Order 1, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a necessary party is one whose presence is indispensable to effective and complete adjudication; a proper party is one whose presence is needed for effective and complete adjudication of the dispute. The court applied those tests to the purchasers’ derivative claim and the final earlier adjudication of the will. It held that New Redbank Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. Kumkum Mittal and Ramesh H. Kundanmal v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay did not apply to these facts.
members.conclusion: The purchasers were neither necessary nor proper parties, and the application to implead them was dismissed.

predicates.property_title_declaration_suit: The proceeding seeks a determination of title to property.
predicates.purchaser_claims_through_party_to_suit: The proposed party claims an interest derived from a person who is already a party to the proceeding.
predicates.existing_parties_can_fully_litigate_disp: The dispute can be effectively and completely adjudicated between the parties already before the court.
predicates.purchaser_has_no_independent_ground_to_c: The proposed party’s asserted interest supplies no independent ground to contest the title basis relied on in the proceeding.
predicates.purchaser_not_necessary_or_proper_party: The proposed party is neither necessary nor proper for adjudication of the proceeding.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser whose rights are subject to a pending partition suit need not bring a separate suit to cancel the transfer before being bound by the partition decree.
material_facts: The sale occurred during the pending partition suit and was subject to the suit’s outcome.
The seller lacked authority to transfer the other co-heirs’ shares.
The preliminary decree later determined the seller’s share, and the purchasers’ rights were addressed in the final-decree proceedings.
members.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act binds a pendente lite transferee to the result of the litigation and avoids multiplicity of proceedings. K.N. Aswathnarayana Setty v. State of Karnataka supports the principle that the transferee is bound by the decree as if a party and cannot use the transfer to defeat the court’s jurisdiction.
members.conclusion: A separate suit to cancel the sale deed was not necessary; the purchasers were bound by the partition decree, and the deed operated only within the seller’s share.

predicates.transfer_during_pending_litigation: A party transferred the disputed property before the partition proceeding was finally disposed of.
predicates.transferor_lacked_authority_over_other_s: The transferor had no authority to convey the interests of the other co-owners.
predicates.partition_decree_determined_rights: The partition court determined the rights in the property by decree.

members.legal_issue: The government must give existing licensed traders preference in allotting premises in a newly established market when the new market requires them to shift their trade there.
material_facts: The traders had conducted business for many years in existing market areas.
The government established new market townships, and traders needed to conduct their agricultural-produce business at the new markets.
The government proposed allotting plots and buildings through open auction without giving existing traders any preference.
The government acknowledged that sufficient space was available to accommodate the existing traders.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(1) and 3(2) of the Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, the government may create a new mandi and transfer its land or buildings by auction, allotment, or otherwise. Rule 3, made under Section 3(2) and Section 25(a), permits sale by public auction or allotment. Section 4 restricts use or occupation of buildings and sites without the administrator's written permission, leaving traders dependent on authorized allotments. The Court affirmed the principle in M/s Prem Chand Trilok Chand v. State of Haryana that the government has an inherent obligation to provide sufficient accommodation for licensed dealers when it regulates the place of sale, and rejected Chand Ram Ram Chand v. State of Punjab insofar as it treated an opportunity to compete as sufficient. Equal competition was not enough because existing traders already had the same opportunity as the public without a special provision.
members.conclusion: The existing licensed traders must receive preference in the allotment of buildings or plots in the new markets; merely allowing them to compete in an open auction does not discharge the government's obligation.

predicates.new_market_allotment_dispute: The dispute concerns allotment of premises in a newly established market.
predicates.existing_licensed_traders_must_shift_tra: Existing licensed traders must conduct their relevant market trade at the new market.
predicates.open_auction_only_offers_equal_competiti: The government proposes only an open auction in which existing traders compete on the same terms as other bidders.
predicates.sufficient_space_is_available: The government has sufficient premises available to accommodate the existing traders.

members.legal_issue: Preference for existing licensed traders in a newly established market does not require free allotment or allotment below the reserved price, and any preferential price must not be unreasonable.
material_facts: The government was allotting land and buildings in newly established markets to traders who had to conduct their agricultural-produce business there.
The government contended that allotment could be through open auction and sought to earn revenue.
The Court considered the government's statutory powers to allot or transfer land and buildings and the existing traders' need for premises in the new markets.
members.legal_principle: Section 3(2) of the Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, and Rule 3, made under Section 3(2) and Section 25(a), allow transfer by allotment as well as public auction. The government may set an allotment price having regard to market price, but its broad discretion must account for the handicaps faced by existing traders and may not be exercised to their detriment. The Court clarified that the preference required by M/s Prem Chand Trilok Chand v. State of Haryana does not mean free allotment or a price below the reserved price; a higher price is permissible if it is not unreasonable.
members.conclusion: The government need not allot premises free of charge or below the reserved price; it may set a price above the reserved price for preferential allotment, provided the price is not unreasonable.

predicates.new_market_allotment_dispute: The dispute concerns allotment of premises in a newly established market.
predicates.existing_licensed_traders_are_entitled_t: Existing licensed traders are entitled to preferential consideration because the new market requires them to shift their trade there.
predicates.government_sets_a_reasonable_allotment_p: The government sets a price for allotment that is not unreasonable.

members.legal_issue: The property was ancestral where settlement records and the surrounding circumstances showed that it descended from a common ancestor and remained held according to ancestral shares.
material_facts: Settlement records showed that the common ancestor had seven sons and that the descendants of each branch held land in shares recorded as portions of the family holding.
The records described the relevant holdings as ancestral shares, with subdivisions corresponding to the number of descendants in each branch.
The records stated that the common ancestor’s descendants held the land and divided the village common land according to ancestral shares.
No acquisition by purchase or introduction of strangers into the holdings, or sale of ancestral land, was suggested.
The village history did not show that the scale of ancestral holdings in the relevant branch had been disturbed.
members.legal_principle: Entries in settlement records carry a presumption of truth. Where those entries describe branch holdings as ancestral shares, and the evidence discloses no intervening acquisition or other explanation for the pattern of holdings, the court may infer that the land descended from the common ancestor. No provision or earlier case was relied on for this determination.
members.conclusion: The land was ancestral property that had descended to the owner from the common ancestor.

rule.if: inheritance_property_dispute and settlement_records_show_branch_shares and records_identify_shares_as_ancestral and no_intervening_acquisitions

predicates.inheritance_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to property based on inheritance from an owner.
predicates.settlement_records_show_branch_shares: Settlement records show land held by descendants in shares corresponding to their family branches.
predicates.records_identify_shares_as_ancestral: The settlement records describe the branch holdings or their division as based on ancestral shares.
predicates.no_intervening_acquisitions: No evidence or allegation indicates that intervening purchases, sales, or other events explain the holdings instead of descent from the common ancestor.

members.legal_issue: Land may be ancestral when its possession is recorded in the hands of a remote direct ancestor, even though possession by the immediate common ancestor is not recorded, if the land’s history indicates no acquisition other than inheritance.
material_facts: Revenue records traced some of the disputed land to the possession of a remote direct ancestor.
The claimants traced their descent through the family line from that ancestor.
Although the immediate common ancestor’s possession was not shown in the revenue records, the history of the land gave no indication that it had been acquired other than by inheritance.
members.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, ancestral character depends on descent from a lineal ancestor through whom the claimants also claim; proof that the immediate common ancestor possessed the land is not indispensable where possession by a more remote direct ancestor is shown and the land’s history indicates acquisition only by inheritance. The Court distinguished the principle in Attar Singh v. Thakar Singh (1908) and approved Haveldar Mihan Singh v. Piara Singh (1946) and Gurdev Singh v. Dasa(u)ndhi (AIR 1948 EP 22). No statutory provision was relied on.
members.conclusion: The land traced to the remote direct ancestor was ancestral, and the lower appellate court was right to treat that portion as ancestral.

predicates.civil_appeal_concerning_ancestral_charac: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which the ancestral character of land is disputed.
predicates.land_possession_recorded_for_remote_dire: Revenue records show that a remote direct ancestor possessed the land.
predicates.claimants_trace_descent_through_that_anc: The claimants trace their descent through the family line from the ancestor whose possession is recorded.
predicates.land_history_indicates_acquisition_only_: The history of the land gives no indication that it was acquired by a means other than inheritance.
predicates.land_is_ancestral: The land is treated as ancestral.

members.legal_issue: Administrative rules governing the allocation of government land do not create a vested right to receive a lease, but an applicant is entitled to fair and non-arbitrary consideration of the application.
material_facts: The appellant applied for a government land lease and challenged the grant of the plot to another applicant under administrative rules governing land settlement.
The High Court dismissed the writ application on the ground that the rules were administrative and their non-compliance could not support a writ.
members.legal_principle: An administrative order generally confers no justiciable right, but that general rule has exceptions; administrative orders may confer rights and impose duties. As recognised in Union of India v. K.P. Joseph, the nature and effect of the particular administrative order must be considered. An applicant has no vested right to a lease of government land, but is entitled to fair, non-arbitrary disposal of the application.
members.conclusion: The rules did not give the appellant a vested right to obtain the lease, but he had a right to have his application dealt with fairly and not arbitrarily.

predicates.government_land_lease_application: A person applied to the government for a lease of land.
predicates.allocation_governed_by_administrative_ru: Administrative rules governed the process for allocating the land.
predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: The matter came before the court in an appeal from the dismissal of a writ application challenging the allocation.

members.legal_issue: The requirement that an administrator allot a site after receiving an application and deposit gives an applicant a right to consideration, not an automatic right to allotment.
material_facts: The applicants submitted applications with the required earnest money.
There were more applicants than available sites, and the administration used a draw to select applicants.
The applicants argued that the rule's use of the word “shall” required the administrator to allot them sites.
members.legal_principle: Rule 8(3) of the Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973, was read in context and in light of the rule's purpose. The Court held that treating “shall” as mandatory would require allotment to every applicant and defeat a workable process for considering competing applications. The meaning of “shall” depends on context, purpose, and the consequences of the competing interpretations.
members.conclusion: The applicants were entitled only to have their applications considered; submission and acceptance of an application did not create a right to a site.

rule.if: appeal_claims_automatic_site_allotment and application_submitted_with_earnest_money and applications_exceeded_available_sites and allotment_requires_comparison_of_applicants

predicates.appeal_claims_automatic_site_allotment: An appeal asserts that submitting an application requires the administrator to allot a site automatically.
predicates.application_submitted_with_earnest_money: An applicant submitted an application accompanied by the required earnest money.
predicates.applications_exceeded_available_sites: The number of applicants exceeded the number of sites available.
predicates.allotment_requires_comparison_of_applica: The administrator must consider competing applications and select among applicants when sites are insufficient.

members.legal_issue: The State cannot acquire title to a citizen’s property by relying on adverse possession when its possession began with an unlawful taking.
material_facts: The State had remained in possession of the land since taking it for road construction without legal sanction.
The State argued that its long possession had converted its title into adverse possession.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that a welfare State cannot invoke adverse possession to grab a citizen’s property after taking it without legal sanction. It referred to State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar and the principle discussed in Tukaram Kana Joshi v. M.I.D.C. that the State must use a lawful procedure to acquire or requisition property.
members.conclusion: The State could not rely on adverse possession to perfect title over the citizen’s land.

predicates.government_adverse_possession_claim: The government claims that its possession has given it title by adverse possession.
predicates.government_possession_began_with_unlawfu: The government’s possession began when it took a citizen’s property without legal sanction.

members.legal_issue: A government department, public undertaking, or police authority may not use adverse possession to perfect title to a citizen’s property.
material_facts: A state authority, acting through a senior police official, sued to obtain ownership of privately claimed land on the basis of adverse possession.
The private owners disputed the authority’s alleged long possession and maintained that the land had been occupied by force only recently.
Revenue records showed the property in the private owners’ names, and the lower courts rejected the state authority’s claim.
The state authority continued to challenge the adverse rulings, including by filing the special leave petition.
members.legal_principle: The Court treated protection of citizens’ property as a central responsibility of the State and held that state instrumentalities should not use adverse possession to take citizens’ property. It relied on the discussion of adverse possession in P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma and Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan, including the latter’s criticism of the doctrine’s harsh effects. The Court urged Parliament to reconsider or amend the law; it did not abolish adverse possession generally.
members.conclusion: The special leave petition was dismissed, and the Court stated that government departments, public undertakings, and especially police departments should not be permitted to perfect title to citizens’ land or buildings by adverse possession.

predicates.government_entity_property_claim: A government department, public undertaking, or police authority claims a right to property.
predicates.adverse_possession_title_claim: The government entity seeks to obtain title by asserting adverse possession.
predicates.private_owner_claimant_opposed: A private citizen claims ownership of the property against the government entity.

members.legal_issue: Evidence of statements made immediately after an occurrence may be admitted as part of the same transaction when the surrounding circumstances connect the statements to that occurrence.
material_facts: Two witnesses arrived at the scene immediately after the incident.
They found the deceased and an injured person there and heard accounts of the incident from people present.
Their evidence corroborated the eyewitness accounts and the allegations in the first information report.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act admits facts forming part of the same transaction. The court treated the witnesses’ immediate arrival and receipt of accounts at the scene as connecting their evidence to the occurrence.
members.conclusion: The evidence of the two witnesses recounting what they heard immediately after the occurrence was admissible under the same-transaction rule and corroborated the prosecution evidence.

predicates.criminal_trial_appeal: The proceeding was a criminal trial or an appeal arising from one.
predicates.witness_arrived_immediately_after_occurr: A witness reached the scene shortly after the incident.
predicates.witness_heard_account_at_scene: The witness heard an account of the incident from a person present at the scene.
predicates.circumstances_connected_account_to_occur: The timing and setting connected the account to the incident rather than to a later, separate event.

members.legal_issue: A victim's identification of an assailant made substantially contemporaneously with an attack or immediately thereafter may be admitted as part of the same transaction.
material_facts: A witness heard a shot, went to the scene, and saw the injured person lying on the ground.
When the witness asked him what had happened, the injured person said that the assailant had shot him.
The witness did not see the shooting, but the statement was made immediately after the event, without an interval sufficient to allow fabrication.
members.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Evidence Act makes a statement relevant as part of the same transaction when it is substantially contemporaneous with the event or made immediately thereafter, with sufficient proximity to exclude an opportunity for fabrication. The Court applied Gentela Vijayavardhan Rao v. State of A.P. and Rattan Singh v. State of H.P.
members.conclusion: The injured person's statement to the witness was admissible under Section 6 of the Evidence Act as part of the same transaction.

rule.if: criminal_trial and statement_related_to_event and statement_made_immediately_after_event and no_interval_allowed_fabrication

predicates.criminal_trial: The statement was offered in a criminal trial.
predicates.statement_related_to_event: The statement described the event that was in issue.
predicates.statement_made_immediately_after_event: The statement was made substantially contemporaneously with the event or immediately thereafter.
predicates.no_interval_allowed_fabrication: There was no interval sufficient to allow the statement to be fabricated.

members.legal_issue: An agricultural sublease that specifies annual rent but no duration is not treated as a five-year lease merely because the tenant could lawfully sublet for up to five years.
material_facts: The sublease reserved annual rent but stated no term.
The tenant’s authority to sublet was limited to a maximum period of five years.
No conduct of the parties showed that they intended the sublease to last five years.
The lessees did not contend that the sublease was permanent, which would have made it invalid in their case.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle stated in Janaki Nath Roy v. Dina Nath Kundu that an indefinite lease of this kind is either permanent or from year to year, with no intermediate interpretation. It referred to Surendra Kumar Sen Chaudhury v. Chandratara Nath for the use of the parties’ conduct where lease terms are ambiguous, and distinguished Mohd. Sher Khan v. Special Manager, Court of Wards, which did not establish that an unspecified term should be treated as five years.
members.conclusion: The sublease was from year to year, not for a fixed term of five years.

rule.if: agricultural_sublease and annual_rent_reserved and duration_omitted and no_conduct_supports_five_year_term and permanent_term_not_claimed

predicates.agricultural_sublease: The parties made a sublease of agricultural land.
predicates.annual_rent_reserved: The sublease reserved rent payable annually.
predicates.duration_omitted: The sublease did not state how long it would last.
predicates.no_conduct_supports_five_year_term: The parties’ conduct did not show that they intended the sublease to last five years.
predicates.permanent_term_not_claimed: The tenant did not claim that the sublease was permanent.

members.legal_issue: The terms of an unregistered agricultural lease cannot establish a fixed duration where the governing registration requirements apply, and the lease is treated as running from year to year.
material_facts: The lease concerned agricultural land and was not registered.
The applicable notifications extended Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 to the relevant territory, while Section 117 of that Act had not been extended there.
The stated lease term was relied on to argue that the tenancy had ended, but the lease terms could not be considered to determine its duration.
members.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, read with Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, prevent the terms of an unregistered instrument from being used to establish the duration of a lease requiring registration. Although Section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act generally excludes agricultural leases from Chapter V, it had not been extended to the relevant territory; Section 107 therefore applied to agricultural leases there. In the absence of an admissible instrument establishing a different term, Section 106 treated the lease as running from year to year. Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons was distinguished because it concerned a non-agricultural lease governed by rent-control legislation.
members.conclusion: The lease terms were inadmissible to determine the lease’s duration, and the agricultural lease was deemed to run from year to year under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

predicates.agricultural_lease_duration_dispute: The parties dispute the duration of a lease of agricultural land.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The document recording the lease was not registered.
predicates.applicable_law_requires_registration_for: The law applicable to the dispute requires leases of the relevant duration to be made by a registered instrument.
predicates.agricultural_leases_are_not_exempt_from_: The governing law in the relevant territory does not exempt agricultural leases from the registration requirement.

members.legal_issue: Criminal liability for alleged dishonest retention of property cannot be established beyond reasonable doubt where the accused’s title or agency status depends on unresolved civil disputes over ownership of the property.
material_facts: The accused was convicted under Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for allegedly retaining land and its profits that he was said to hold as trustee and agent for the complainant.
The accused claimed that he had bought the land for charitable use, while the complainant claimed that he held it for her as a benamidar.

The nature of the accused’s relationship to the property was difficult to determine from the evidence, and the property had been transferred to a trust that would be a necessary party to a civil title dispute.
The complainant still had an available civil remedy to establish her rights to the property and seek its return.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirement that criminal liability be established beyond reasonable doubt. Although the charge was under Section 409 of the Indian Penal Code, the Court did not decide whether criminal breach of trust can be committed in respect of immovable property, nor did it set out the elements of that offence. It held on the circumstances before it that the essentially civil dispute over title had to be resolved before criminal liability could be satisfactorily adjudicated. No earlier cases were relied on.
members.conclusion: The Court dismissed the appeal against the acquittal, holding that criminal liability could not be fastened beyond reasonable doubt before the complainant’s rights and title to the property were properly established in a civil suit.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed a judgment acquitting a person who had previously been convicted.

predicates.ownership_evidence_inconclusive: The evidence did not establish whether the accused held the disputed property for another or owned it in the accused’s own right.
predicates.civil_title_remedy_available: The person claiming the property could pursue a civil proceeding to establish title and seek its return.

members.legal_issue: Criminal liability for breach of trust cannot be established beyond reasonable doubt when the accused’s ownership of the disputed property is unresolved and the complainant’s rights first require determination in a civil suit.
material_facts: The accused had a long and intimate association with the complainant’s family and was implicitly trusted by the complainant.
The parties had numerous transactions involving properties that stood in the accused’s name but were alleged to be held for the complainant as benami property.
The accused did not relinquish the disputed property to the complainant and claimed that he had bought it for the use of his disciples and dedicated it to charitable purposes.
By the time of the complaint, the disputed property stood transferred to a trust, which would be a necessary party to a civil dispute over title.
The evidence did not establish whether the accused’s claim to the property was honest or a camouflage for cheating.
The prosecution appeal challenged the High Court’s judgment of acquittal.
members.legal_principle: For the charge under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code, criminal liability could not be fastened beyond reasonable doubt on this record while ownership and the complainant’s rights in the property remained unresolved. The Court held that the essentially civil dispute had to be decided first; it did not decide whether criminal breach of trust can be committed in respect of immovable property entrusted to an agent.
members.conclusion: The complainant’s rights and title to the disputed property had to be established in a civil suit before criminal liability could be satisfactorily adjudicated. Criminal liability was not established beyond reasonable doubt, and the appeal against the acquittal was dismissed.

members.legal_issue: High Courts must exercise restraint and circumspection when granting far-reaching ad interim relief under their writ jurisdiction, particularly where the relief affects public interests and effectively grants the main relief sought.
material_facts: A large quantity of seized goods, alleged to be essential commodities and worth a substantial amount, was the subject of pending prosecution and confiscation proceedings.
In an appeal from an interlocutory order in a writ proceeding, the High Court directed release of the goods before the State had an opportunity to file a return.
The release was conditioned on security that was negligible in comparison with the value of the goods, and the order effectively granted the principal relief sought.
members.legal_principle: The powers under Article 226 are extensive, but their use requires self-restraint, prudence, discretion and circumspection. Courts should consider not only whether a prima facie case exists, but also the balance of convenience, irreparable injury and public interest, and should be especially cautious with ex parte interim orders that have far-reaching effects or effectively grant the main relief. The Court relied on Siliguri Municipality v. Amalendu Das, Titaghur Paper Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, Union of India v. Oswal Woollen Mills Ltd., Assistant Collector of Central Excise v. Dunlop India Ltd., Union of India v. Jain Shudh Vanaspati Ltd., Samarias Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. S. Samuel, and State of Rajasthan v. Swaika Properties.
members.conclusion: The ad interim order directing release of the goods was illegal and invalid; the order refusing release was restored, and recovery of the goods was directed.

rule.if: interim_writ_proceeding and seized_valuable_goods and release_order_before_public_authority_response and (main_relief_effectively_granted or security_inadequate) and public_interest_at_stake

members.legal_issue: Interim relief in a public interest proceeding must be granted only after applying the relevant injunction safeguards and balancing the consequences for all affected interests.
material_facts: The High Court passed interim directions in a public interest challenge to amended development regulations before the writ petition had been finally heard.
Interested mill owners and other affected parties had intervened, but their affidavits had not yet been filed and they had not been given a full opportunity to respond.
The challenged directions could affect workers, financial institutions, mill owners and third-party purchasers, and delay had allowed transactions and investments to advance.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the injunction factors and exceptional-circumstances test in Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das and Andhra Bank v. Official Liquidator; the public interest litigation principles in Dr. B. Singh v. Union of India and Dattaraj Nathuji Thaware v. State of Maharashtra; and the principles on exceptional interim relief, terms and undertakings, and delay defeating equity in Deoraj v. State of Maharashtra, Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd., Guruvayoor Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan, Chairman & MD BPL Ltd. v. S.P. Gururaja, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, and R & M Trust v. Koramangala Residents Vigilance Group.
members.conclusion: The Court held that an interim order, particularly in a public interest proceeding, requires consideration of a prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable injury, along with the applicable public interest litigation principles. An order affecting a person should normally not be made without a hearing; ex parte relief is exceptional. The court must also weigh the possibility that refusing relief would defeat the petition against the losses and hardships that granting it may cause.

predicates.interim_relief_in_public_interest_procee: A party seeks interim relief in a proceeding brought in the public interest.

predicates.affected_person_not_heard: A person whose interests would be affected has not yet had an opportunity to be heard.
predicates.relief_may_have_irreversible_effect: Granting or withholding interim relief may effectively determine the practical outcome or cause harm that cannot readily be undone.

members.legal_issue: An advance payment of rent received in excess of the statutory limit may be applied to later rent arrears without a further request by the tenant when no agreement makes such a request a condition of adjustment.
material_facts: The tenant paid two months’ rent in advance when the tenancy began, although the landlord could lawfully receive no more than one month’s rent in advance.

The advance was understood to be available for set-off against rent whenever necessary or required; there was no agreement requiring the tenant to request adjustment, and no other debt between the parties.
The landlord sought eviction for non-payment of rent for two months, and the advance was sufficient to cover those arrears.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 prohibited a landlord from receiving more than one month’s rent in advance, and section 11(1)(d) permitted eviction for failure to pay two months’ rent. In applying those provisions, the Court relied on Mohd. Salimuddin v. Misri Lal, which allowed an advance made in violation of section 3 to be adjusted against subsequently accruing rent. The Court distinguished Budhwanti v. Gulab Chand Prasad, where eviction was sustained on bona fide requirement, and did not decide the general correctness of the Patna High Court’s broader observation in Gulab Chand Prasad v. Budhwanti.
members.conclusion: The advance could be appropriated towards the rent arrears without a further request by the tenant, so the tenant was not in default for two months and was not liable to eviction on that ground.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_for_rent_default and landlord_received_excess_advance_rent and advance_available_for_setoff and not tenant_request_required_by_agreement and advance_covers_rent_arrears

predicates.rent_control_eviction_for_rent_default: A landlord seeks eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the ground that the tenant failed to pay rent.
predicates.landlord_received_excess_advance_rent: The landlord received rent in advance beyond the amount the law permits.
predicates.advance_available_for_setoff: The parties’ arrangement made the advance available to be set off against rent when necessary or required.
predicates.tenant_request_required_by_agreement: The parties agreed that adjustment could occur only if the tenant requested it.
predicates.advance_covers_rent_arrears: The advance is sufficient to cover the rent arrears relied on for eviction.

members.legal_issue: A tenant is not in default for claimed rent arrears when the landlord holds an excess advance that is immediately payable to the tenant and exceeds the arrears.
material_facts: The lease required a large advance, part of which was to be adjusted against rent and the balance repaid at the end of the lease.
The landlord continued to hold the balance of the advance when seeking eviction for alleged unpaid rent.
The amount held by the landlord exceeded the rent arrears claimed.
members.legal_principle: Under section 7(2)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, a landlord may not receive or stipulate for an advance exceeding one month's rent; section 7(2)(b) requires an excess sum to be refunded or, at the tenant's option, adjusted; and section 7(3) makes a contrary stipulation null and void. The excess held by the landlord therefore became payable to the tenant immediately. The Court applied the reasoning in Mohd. Salimuddin v. Misri Lal & Anr., [1986] 1 SCR 622, and M/s. Sarwan Kumar Onkar Nath v. Subhas Kumar Agarwalla, [1987] 4 SCC 546, that a tenant is not in default where a prohibited advance held by the landlord is available to meet the claimed rent arrears.
members.conclusion: The excess advance was payable to the tenant immediately because the stipulation postponing its repayment was null and void. The tenant could not be treated as a defaulter for the claimed smaller amount, so eviction on that ground could not be sustained.

members.legal_issue: The doctrine of in pari delicto does not prevent a tenant from relying on an unlawfully received advance payment of rent to seek adjustment against rent arrears.
material_facts: The landlord received two months’ rent in advance even though the law prohibited receiving more than one month’s rent in advance.
The tenant relied on the advance as a credit against the later rent arrears in an eviction proceeding based on non-payment.
The payment was rent in advance, not excess rent paid over a long period under an agreement to enhance rent unlawfully.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 prohibited the landlord from receiving more than one month’s rent in advance. Following Mohd. Salimuddin v. Misri Lal, the Court held that the doctrine of in pari delicto did not prevent adjustment of an advance made in violation of that prohibition. It distinguished Budhwanti v. Gulab Chand Prasad, which did not decide the default or adjustment question, and declined to decide the broader issue concerning excess rent paid over a long period under an illegal rent-enhancement agreement discussed in Gulab Chand Prasad v. Budhwanti.
members.conclusion: The tenant could rely on the statutory prohibition and claim adjustment of the advance; the doctrine of in pari delicto did not bar that claim.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_for_rent_default and landlord_received_prohibited_advance_rent and tenant_seeks_adjustment_of_advance and advance_was_rent_not_prolonged_illegal_enhancement

predicates.rent_control_eviction_for_rent_default: A landlord seeks eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the ground that the tenant failed to pay rent.

predicates.tenant_seeks_adjustment_of_advance: The tenant seeks to credit the advance against rent arrears.

members.legal_issue: A tenant compelled to make a prohibited advance to secure a tenancy may apply that advance to rent accruing later when the agreement provides for adjustment, and is not in pari delicto with the landlord.
material_facts: The tenant advanced Rs. 2,000 under an agreement providing that the amount would be adjusted against rent accruing later.
The advance was sufficient to cover the landlord’s claim for rent arrears.
The landlord required the advance as a condition of granting the tenancy amid an acute housing shortage, leaving the tenant to yield to the demand or go without a roof.
The landlord brought an eviction suit alleging rent arrears.
members.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act prohibited the advance payment at issue. The doctrine of pari delicto does not bar relief where a statute is intended to protect one class from another’s exploitation and the protected party was compelled to submit; the doctrine applies where both parties freely join in violating the law for mutual gain and neither is a victim of exploitation. The Court relied on V.S. Rahi v. Smt. Ram Chambeli, which referred to the oppression exception, Smith v. Cuff, and Cheshire and Fifoot’s Law of Contract.
members.conclusion: The tenant was not in arrears of rent. The advance could be adjusted against the rent, so the eviction suit was dismissed and the lower appellate court’s judgment was restored.

members.legal_issue: Parliament may impose service tax on the service of making a venue available for temporary use for a function, and that levy is not a tax on land merely because the service involves immovable property.
material_facts: Venue owners allowed clients to occupy premises temporarily for official, social, or business functions for consideration.
The statutory definition of the taxable service covered services provided in relation to venue use, including facilities and catering.
The challenge argued that the levy was in substance a tax on land, a matter assigned to the States.
members.legal_principle: Under Articles 246 and the Seventh Schedule, Parliament may legislate under the residuary Entry 97 of List I where no entry in Lists II or III covers the tax. A tax on land under Entry 49 of List II must be directly on land; a tax on an activity or income connected with land is not for that reason a tax on land, as explained in India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu. The service-tax power was recognised in Laghu Udyog Bharati v. Union of India. The nature of a levy is determined by its substance, and incidental overlap with another legislative field does not invalidate it; the distinct aspects of a transaction may be taxed separately, as recognised in Federation of Hotel and Restaurant v. Union of India and the aspect-theory cases. The broad phrases “in relation to” and “including” encompass connected services and facilities, consistently with Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India and Regional Director, Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Highland Coffee Works.
members.conclusion: The levy on venue-related services was within Parliament’s legislative competence and was not a tax on land. Making premises available temporarily for a function is a service, and associated facilities may also fall within the taxable service.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_service_tax: A provider or representative challenged the constitutional validity of a service tax on venue-related activities.
predicates.venue_use_for_functions: A venue owner allowed clients temporary use of immovable property for official, social, or business functions.
predicates.tax_imposed_on_service_activity: The levy applied to charges for services associated with making a venue available, rather than to the mere existence or ownership of land.

members.legal_issue: The temporary provision of premises for a specified function may itself constitute a taxable service even when the provider supplies no additional facilities or services.
material_facts: A clarification stated that service tax applied when open land or ground was let for an official, social, or business function, even without accompanying or incidental services.
The statutory definition covered services in relation to use of a venue in any manner.
The Court held that making premises available temporarily for a function could itself be a service.
members.legal_principle: The statutory language covering services in relation to venue use “in any manner” is broad enough to include temporary provision of premises itself. The expansive meaning of “in relation to” was explained in Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, and the word “include” ordinarily enlarges rather than restricts a statutory definition, as explained in Regional Director, Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Highland Coffee Works.
members.conclusion: Temporary provision of premises for an official, social, or business function may be a taxable service even without additional facilities or services.

predicates.service_tax_scope_dispute: A dispute concerned whether venue-related conduct fell within a service-tax definition.
predicates.premises_temporarily_provided_for_functi: A provider let premises to a client temporarily for an official, social, or business function.
predicates.no_additional_services_provided: The provider supplied no accompanying or incidental facilities or services beyond making the premises available.

members.legal_issue: Rules made under a repealed mining statute and continued by a replacement statute are valid under the replacement statute when they conform to it.
material_facts: The 1956 rules were made under the 1948 mining statute and did not provide compensation for some reductions in lease terms.
The 1957 statute repealed the 1948 statute and deemed rules made or purportedly made under the earlier statute to have been made under the replacement statute.
The dissent found the 1956 rules to conform to the 1957 statute.
members.legal_principle: The dissent applied section 29 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, which deemed the earlier rules to have been made under the 1957 Act, and assessed their validity by reference to that Act. It also addressed section 7(2)(b) of the 1948 Act and referred to Bharat Kala Mandir v. Municipal Committee, Dhamangaon, in considering whether the rules purported to have been made under the earlier Act.
members.conclusion: The dissent held that the 1956 rules were valid under the 1957 statute despite their possible original invalidity for failing to provide compensation under the earlier statute. The majority did not decide the issue.

rule.if: challenge_to_continued_mining_rules and rules_made_under_repealed_mining_law and replacement_law_deemed_rules_reenacted and rules_conformed_to_replacement_law

predicates.challenge_to_continued_mining_rules: A party challenged the validity of mining rules continued after replacement of the statute under which they were made.

predicates.replacement_law_deemed_rules_reenacted: The replacement statute treated the earlier rules as having been made under the replacement statute.
predicates.rules_conformed_to_replacement_law: The rules’ requirements were consistent with the replacement statute.

members.legal_issue: Rules made or purportedly made under an earlier mining statute can continue under a later mining statute when they concern matters provided for by the later statute and are not inconsistent with it.
material_facts: The 1956 Rules were made or purportedly made under the 1948 Act.
The later 1957 Act provided for the relevant subject matter and included a provision continuing qualifying earlier rules.
The appellant argued that any invalidity under the 1948 Act prevented the Rules from continuing under the 1957 Act.
members.legal_principle: Section 29 of the 1957 Act deems rules made or purportedly made under the 1948 Act, concerning matters provided for in the 1957 Act and not inconsistent with it, to have been made under the 1957 Act and to continue until superseded. Applying Abdul Majid v. P.R. Nayak, the court treated the later Act as having been in force when the earlier rules were made for purposes of their legal status under the later Act.
members.conclusion: Even if the Rules were inconsistent with the 1948 Act, they could continue under the 1957 Act because they were deemed to have been made under it, subject to its terms.

members.legal_issue: A holder's vacant and partly built plots must be aggregated when determining the applicable ceiling, and the holder may choose which area to retain within that ceiling.
material_facts: The Court considered how to compute the ceiling where a holder had several plots, some entirely vacant and others partly built and partly vacant.
The plots could be in different places, and the Act provided the holder an option to select the area to retain.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 6 govern the ceiling and the holder's selection of land to retain. The Court held that all relevant plots, whether wholly vacant or partly built and partly vacant, must be totalled before applying the ceiling and the selection option.
members.conclusion: The competent authority must total the holder's relevant land across the plots, apply the applicable ceiling, and allow the holder to select the area to retain so long as it does not exceed that ceiling.

predicates.holder_has_multiple_relevant_plots: The holder possesses more than one relevant plot, whether vacant or partly built and partly vacant.

members.legal_issue: Where a holder has vacant land in urban agglomerations belonging to different ceiling categories, the ceiling must be determined using the statutory category-based formula.
material_facts: The Court addressed the computation of a holder's vacant land situated in urban agglomerations belonging to two or more categories.
The Act prescribed different ceiling limits for different categories of urban agglomeration.
members.legal_principle: Section 4(1)(a) to (d) prescribes the category-based ceiling limits and the formula applicable where vacant land is held in two or more categories of urban agglomeration.
members.conclusion: The competent authority must determine the ceiling in accordance with the formula prescribed for holdings in multiple categories.

predicates.vacant_land_in_multiple_ceiling_categori: The holder has vacant land in urban agglomerations assigned to more than one ceiling category.

members.legal_issue: A binding compensation award made by a competent non-court authority is an order for purposes of determining court fees, even if it is not a civil court order or is not executable.
material_facts: A competent arbitrator determined the compensation payable for acquired property and issued a formal award binding on the parties.
The governing acquisition law required the competent authority to pay the compensation awarded.
The arbitrator was not a civil court, and the award was not shown to be executable.
members.legal_principle: The applicable court-fee provision used the undefined term “order,” so the Court applied its ordinary meaning: a formal expression of a decision by a competent authority that binds the parties. The statutory requirement to pay the compensation supported the award’s effect; neither the absence of a civil-court order nor the question of execution was determinative.
members.conclusion: The award was an order for purposes of the court-fee provision; its non-executability and lack of the force of a decree did not prevent that characterization.

members.legal_issue: A binding award determining compensation made by a statutory authority is an order relating to compensation, even if it is not an order of a civil court.
material_facts: A statutory arbitrator determined the compensation payable for the requisitioned property.
The award formally expressed the arbitrator's decision and bound the parties.
The owners appealed against the award under the applicable statutory appeal provision.
members.legal_principle: Section 51 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955 refers to an order relating to compensation under an enactment concerning acquisition for public purposes. Under section 3 of that Act, definitions apply unless the context otherwise requires; section 3(iv) refers to meanings in the Code of Civil Procedure where applicable, and section 2(14) of that Code defines an order as the formal expression of a civil court's decision. In the context of section 51, however, the order need not be made by a civil court and may be made by a statutory authority. The Court relied on Sahadu Gangaram Bhagade v. Special Deputy Collector, which treated an arbitrator's award as a formal, binding decision, and approved the reasoning in In re Ananda Lal Chakrabutty and C.B.G. Trust v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The arbitrator's award is an order relating to compensation within the meaning of the court-fee provision.

members.legal_issue: Whether payment of part of the agreed sale price was established despite evidence that differed from the pleaded account.
material_facts: The purchasers pleaded that they paid part of the sale price when the deed was registered, but their witnesses testified that payment occurred earlier at a residence.
The sale deed recited that part of the price had been paid, but there was no separate receipt or endorsement by the registering officer confirming payment.
The first appellate court considered the oral and documentary evidence, including the failure to call two alleged witnesses to the payment, and found that no part of the price had been paid.
The High Court affirmed that factual finding, and the purchasers challenged it in a civil appeal by special leave.
members.legal_principle: A party cannot rely on evidence contrary to its pleadings; where the evidence departs from the pleaded case, the contrary evidence cannot establish that case. A factual finding reached after consideration of the evidence and affirmed by the High Court is not to be disturbed in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution without a valid ground for interference.
members.conclusion: The finding that the purchasers had not proved payment of any part of the sale price did not warrant interference.

predicates.civil_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal by special leave challenging a factual finding.
predicates.evidence_contradicts_pleadings: The evidence about when or how payment occurred differs from the account pleaded by the party asserting payment.
predicates.fact_finding_considers_the_record: The lower appellate court assessed the oral and documentary evidence before finding whether payment was proved.
predicates.no_valid_ground_to_interfere: No valid basis is shown for disturbing the lower appellate court's factual finding.
predicates.part_payment_not_established: The party asserting payment has not proved that any part of the price was paid.

members.legal_issue: Whether the sellers’ claim that the buyer paid only part of the recorded advance was sufficient to establish that the sale agreement had been cancelled.
material_facts: The written memorandum, signed by both sides, expressly recorded that the sellers had received the full advance.

The sellers later claimed that only part of the recorded advance had been paid and that the balance was due within three days, but there was no contemporaneous written reservation or acknowledgment of an unpaid balance.
The buyer and the document’s writer testified that the full advance had been paid; the court found their account more consistent with the circumstances than the sellers’ account.
The buyer promptly brought a suit for specific performance and deposited the remaining purchase price in court.
members.legal_principle: An express recital in a written agreement that payment was received is significant evidence of payment. In the circumstances, the burden lay heavily on the sellers to prove that the recital was false, and the evidence and broad probabilities did not support their account.
members.conclusion: The sellers’ account that only part of the advance had been paid was untrue; the recorded advance was treated as paid, so the agreement was not cancelled on that ground.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and written_agreement_recites_advance_received and sellers_claimed_less_was_paid and no_contemporaneous_written_reservation_of_unpaid_balance and buyer_promptly_deposited_remaining_price

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The buyer brought a proceeding seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.written_agreement_recites_advance_receiv: The signed sale memorandum stated that the sellers had received the recorded advance payment.
predicates.sellers_claimed_less_was_paid: The sellers later claimed that the buyer had paid less than the amount recorded as received.
predicates.no_contemporaneous_written_reservation_o: When the sellers delivered the memorandum, they made no written record that part of the advance remained unpaid.
predicates.buyer_promptly_deposited_remaining_price: The buyer promptly deposited the remaining purchase price in court.

members.legal_issue: Whether a vendor may repudiate a sale and convey the property to another purchaser when title has not passed and the agreed consideration remains unpaid.
material_facts: The vendor retained the registration receipt and possession because the sale price had not been paid.
The purchasers did not tender the full price before the vendor repudiated the sale.
The vendor repudiated the sale and subsequently conveyed the property to another purchaser, to whom possession was delivered.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, payment of the entire price is not ordinarily a condition precedent to a completed sale; if title has passed, the vendor's remedy for unpaid price is generally to sue for it and the vendor may have a charge under Section 55(4)(b). But the parties' intention determines whether title passed. Where the parties intended title to pass only upon payment and exchange of equivalents, the transaction remains uncompleted until that exchange, and the vendor may repudiate for non-payment. Bishundeo Narain Rai v. Anmol Devi and Kaliaperumal v. Rajagopal support these principles; the judgment also relies on the Patna High Court decisions recognizing ta khubzul badlain.
members.conclusion: The vendor was justified in repudiating the sale for non-payment, and the subsequent sale was valid.

rule.if: title_not_passed_to_purchaser and consideration_unpaid and no_full_price_tender_before_repudiation and vendor_repudiated_before_resale and vendor_conveyed_to_later_purchaser

predicates.title_not_passed_to_purchaser: The purchaser did not acquire title under the earlier deed because the parties intended transfer to await payment and exchange.
predicates.consideration_unpaid: The agreed price remained unpaid when the vendor repudiated the transaction.
predicates.no_full_price_tender_before_repudiation: The purchaser did not offer the entire agreed price before the vendor repudiated the transaction.
predicates.vendor_repudiated_before_resale: The vendor repudiated the earlier transaction before conveying the property again.
predicates.vendor_conveyed_to_later_purchaser: The vendor subsequently transferred the property to another purchaser.
predicates.repudiation_and_later_sale_valid: The vendor's repudiation and subsequent conveyance are legally effective.

members.legal_issue: Whether a purchaser may obtain specific performance after the vendor lawfully repudiates a sale that was conditional on payment of the full price.
material_facts: The purchasers sought delivery of the registration receipt or original deed upon payment of the asserted remaining balance.
The courts found that the purchasers had not proved payment of any part of the price and had not tendered the full price before the vendor repudiated the sale.
The vendor repudiated the sale before the purchasers established that title had passed.
members.legal_principle: Where the parties intended that title would pass only after payment of the full sale price and the exchange of equivalents, the registered deed remains an agreement to be performed until that exchange. A purchaser who fails to tender the full price before lawful repudiation cannot claim performance on the basis of an offer to pay only part of the price. The principle follows from Sections 8 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and the rules on intention and exchange of equivalents explained in Bishundeo Narain Rai v. Anmol Devi and Kaliaperumal v. Rajagopal.
members.conclusion: The purchasers were not entitled to claim performance of the sale.

rule.if: suit_for_specific_performance and title_not_passed_to_purchaser and no_full_price_tender_before_repudiation and vendor_lawfully_repudiated

predicates.suit_for_specific_performance: The proceeding seeks to compel completion of a sale transaction.
predicates.title_not_passed_to_purchaser: The purchaser did not acquire title because the parties intended transfer to await the required exchange.
predicates.no_full_price_tender_before_repudiation: The purchaser did not tender the full agreed price before the vendor repudiated the transaction.
predicates.vendor_lawfully_repudiated: The vendor repudiated the transaction when the agreed conditions for transfer had not been fulfilled.
predicates.specific_performance_unavailable: The purchaser is not entitled to compel performance of the sale.

members.legal_issue: A devise to a person described in a will as an adopted child is not dependent on proof of adoption when that description identifies the devisee and the devise was motivated by affection and services.
material_facts: The will described the beneficiary as the testator's adopted son and heir.
The will also recorded that the beneficiary lived with and rendered services to the testator and another family member.
The beneficiary had served them during illness and was affectionately attached to them.
The courts found that affection and the services rendered, rather than the legal relationship of adoption, motivated the devise.
members.legal_principle: A will is construed in light of its language and surrounding circumstances. Where the reference to adoption describes the devisee as understood by the testator, but affection and services motivate the testamentary disposition, failure to establish the adoption does not defeat the devise. The court referred to Ranganathan Chattiar v. Periskaruppan in connection with treating the relationship description as distinct from the motive for the will.
members.conclusion: The devise was not defeated by the failure to prove the adoption because the relationship was used as a description of the beneficiary, not as the reason for the devise.

rule.if: will_dispute and devisee_described_as_adopted_child and affection_or_services_motivated_devising and adoption_not_proved

predicates.will_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a testamentary disposition remains effective despite a challenge to the beneficiary's stated relationship to the testator.
predicates.devisee_described_as_adopted_child: The will described the beneficiary as the testator's adopted child.
predicates.affection_or_services_motivated_devising: The testator's affection for the beneficiary or the beneficiary's services motivated the devise.
predicates.adoption_not_proved: The asserted adoption was not established by the evidence.

members.legal_issue: A testamentary gift to a person described as an adopted son remains effective despite the adoption being invalid when the will and surrounding circumstances show that the person was designated to take personally rather than because of a valid legal status.
material_facts: The purported second adoption was invalid, and the will repeatedly described the intended beneficiary as the testator’s adopted son.
The will expressly excluded the first adopted son and his heirs from the testator’s property.
The testator had recently faced a challenge to the second adoption, but the compromise ending that litigation left the adoption’s validity unresolved.
The will made the beneficiary’s enjoyment depend in part on his conduct, indicating the testator’s concern with his character as well as his status.
The beneficiary remained in possession and enjoyment of the property for more than fourteen years after the testator and his wife died, without a claim by the excluded family members.
members.legal_principle: Whether a gift to someone described by a legal status depends on that status or is instead made to that person as a designated individual depends on the wording of the instrument and the surrounding circumstances. The distinction between language that merely describes the recipient and language that states the reason or motive for the gift is drawn from those considerations. The Court relied on Nidhoomoni Debya v. Saroda Pershad Mookerjee (1876) L.R. 3 I.A. 253 and Fanindra Deb Raikat v. Rajeswar Das (1884) L.R. 12 I.A. 72.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary was intended to take as a designated person, notwithstanding the invalid adoption, and the will effectively conveyed the residue of the testator’s property to him.

rule.if: succession_suit_challenges_will and invalid_adoption and will_excludes_other_claimants and adoption_challenge_left_unresolved and beneficiary_possessed_property_unchallenged

predicates.succession_suit_challenges_will: A succession proceeding challenges a will as ineffective because the beneficiary’s purported legal status is invalid.
predicates.invalid_adoption: The purported adoption through which the beneficiary was described in the will is found to be invalid.
predicates.will_excludes_other_claimants: The will expressly excludes other potential claimants from the property.
predicates.adoption_challenge_left_unresolved: A prior dispute raised the validity of the purported adoption but ended without determining that question.
predicates.beneficiary_possessed_property_unchallen: The beneficiary possessed and enjoyed the property for a substantial period without a competing claim from the excluded persons.

members.legal_issue: A life tenant who receives property under a will may not defeat the testator's valid direction that the property pass to a named beneficiary after the life tenancy ends.
material_facts: One will gave the property to a woman for her lifetime and directed that it pass to the beneficiary after her death.
The woman later made a will devising that property to the same beneficiary.
Her disposition was consistent with the prior testator's direction.
members.legal_principle: A valid testamentary direction giving property to a life tenant and directing its subsequent devolution to a beneficiary remains effective independently of the life tenant's later will. The life tenant's later devise, to the extent consistent with that direction, merely carries out the original testator's behest.
members.conclusion: The beneficiary's right under the first will remained effective; the later will did no more than carry out that direction.

rule.if: will_dispute and property_given_to_life_tenant and first_testator_directed_remainder_to_beneficiary and later_will_names_same_beneficiary

predicates.will_dispute: The dispute concerns the effect of successive wills on the same property.
predicates.property_given_to_life_tenant: An earlier will gave the property to a person for that person's lifetime.
predicates.first_testator_directed_remainder_to_ben: The earlier will directed that the property pass to a beneficiary after the life tenancy ended.
predicates.later_will_names_same_beneficiary: The life tenant's later will named the beneficiary designated by the earlier will.

members.legal_issue: A donee from a life tenant cannot retain the property against the beneficiaries entitled to it after the life estate ends.
material_facts: The will gave the widow only a life estate and gave the property thereafter to other beneficiaries.
The widow gifted the property to a religious institution during her lifetime.
The widow later died, ending her life estate.
The institution claimed through the widow, and the beneficiary under the will sought possession.
members.legal_principle: A transferee cannot obtain a greater title than the transferor had. A gift by a life tenant cannot survive the termination of that life interest so as to defeat the remainder beneficiaries’ right to possession under the will.
members.conclusion: The gift could not prevent the beneficiaries under the will from recovering possession after the widow’s life estate ended.

rule.if: possession_claim_under_will and transferor_had_life_interest and transferee_claims_through_life_tenant and life_interest_has_ended

predicates.possession_claim_under_will: A beneficiary seeks possession on the basis of a valid testamentary gift of the property.
predicates.transferor_had_life_interest: The person who transferred the property held only a life interest under the will.
predicates.transferee_claims_through_life_tenant: The person resisting possession received the property from the life tenant.
predicates.life_interest_has_ended: The life tenant has died or the life interest has otherwise ended.

members.legal_issue: Reversal of a preliminary mortgage decree removes the foundation for a final decree previously passed under it.
material_facts: The Court considered the situation in which a final decree for sale had been passed while an appeal from the preliminary decree was pending and the appellate court later reversed the preliminary decree.
members.legal_principle: Under Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure, a final mortgage decree depends on the preliminary decree. The Court relied on the principle in Talebali v. Abdul Aziz that setting aside the preliminary decree removes the basis for the final decree; it distinguished cases where the preliminary decree is affirmed or varied.
members.conclusion: The final decree falls with the reversed preliminary decree, and the executing court must refuse to execute it when the reversal is brought to its notice, even if more than three years have passed since the appellate decree.

rule.if: mortgage_sale_proceeding and appeal_from_preliminary_decree and final_decree_passed_before_appeal_decided and appellate_court_reversed_preliminary_decree

predicates.mortgage_sale_proceeding: The proceeding seeks sale of property mortgaged as security for a debt.
predicates.appeal_from_preliminary_decree: A party appealed from the preliminary decree in the mortgage proceeding.
predicates.final_decree_passed_before_appeal_decide: The court passed a final decree while the appeal from the preliminary decree was still pending.
predicates.appellate_court_reversed_preliminary_dec: The appellate court set aside the preliminary decree.

members.legal_issue: A final decree and an auction sale founded on a preliminary mortgage decree do not remain effective when an appellate preliminary decree substitutes that decree and the mortgagor fulfils the substituted terms.
material_facts: A trial court passed a preliminary mortgage decree that allowed payment by instalments and permitted a final decree for sale if the mortgagors defaulted.
While an appeal from that preliminary decree was pending, the trial court passed a final decree for sale and the property was sold in execution of it.
The parties later agreed to, and the appellate court passed, a substituted preliminary decree that fixed the amount payable; the mortgagor paid the amount and the decree was recorded as satisfied.
The judgment debtor challenged the execution and sale under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 2(2) and its Explanation to the Code of Civil Procedure, a preliminary decree requires further proceedings before the suit is completely disposed of, while a final decree completely disposes of it. In a mortgage suit governed by Order 34, the final decree for sale must accord with the operative preliminary decree. An appellate decree may redefine the parties’ obligations, and rights arising from the displaced decree cannot be retained while those obligations are replaced. Questions concerning execution, discharge or satisfaction are determined under Section 47 by the executing court. The Court distinguished the protection of a stranger auction purchaser discussed in Janak Raj v. Gurdial Singh, [1967] 2 SCR 77, and considered Hukumchand v. Bansilal, [1967] 3 SCR 695, and Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai, [1982] 2 SCR 186.
members.conclusion: The substituted appellate preliminary decree displaced the original preliminary decree. Because the mortgagor fulfilled the substituted decree, there was no basis to maintain the application for sale; the auction sale and its confirmation became non-est, and the judgment debtor’s objection was sustainable.

rule.if: mortgage_suit_execution_objection and appellate_preliminary_decree_substituted and sale_executed_under_old_final_decree and mortgagor_fulfilled_substituted_terms

predicates.mortgage_suit_execution_objection: A judgment debtor raises an objection in execution of a decree arising from a mortgage suit.
predicates.appellate_preliminary_decree_substituted: An appellate court replaces the preliminary decree with a substituted preliminary decree.
predicates.sale_executed_under_old_final_decree: The property is sold under a final decree founded on the preliminary decree that was replaced.
predicates.mortgagor_fulfilled_substituted_terms: The mortgagor fulfils the payment obligations imposed by the substituted preliminary decree.
predicates.auction_sale_is_non_est: The auction sale and its confirmation have no continuing legal effect.

members.legal_issue: The enactment of a later succession law does not retrospectively enlarge an owner’s power to alienate ancestral property or nullify an earlier declaratory decree limiting the alienation.
material_facts: An owner had alienated ancestral property, and a declaratory decree obtained before the later succession law took effect provided that the alienation would not bind the estate beyond the owner’s lifetime.
The owner died after the succession law took effect.
The respondents argued that the succession law had made the owner a full owner and eliminated the basis for the earlier decree; they had not appealed the existing decree granting the sons a share.
members.legal_principle: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not retrospectively enlarge the power of a holder of ancestral land or nullify a decree passed before its enactment. The Court also relied on the fact that the respondents had not appealed the decree granting the sons a share. No earlier cases were cited on this issue.
members.conclusion: The preliminary objection seeking dismissal of the suit in its entirety was rejected. The succession law did not retrospectively enlarge the owner’s power over the ancestral property or nullify the earlier decree, and the respondents could not challenge the unappealed award to the sons.

rule.if: appeal_from_possession_decree and prior_declaratory_decree_limited_alienation_to_owner_lifetime and succession_law_took_effect_after_decree and respondents_did_not_appeal_existing_award

predicates.appeal_from_possession_decree: The case is an appeal concerning a decree for possession of property.
predicates.prior_declaratory_decree_limited_alienat: A court had declared that an alienation would not bind the owner’s estate beyond the owner’s lifetime.
predicates.succession_law_took_effect_after_decree: A succession law took effect after the declaratory decree was made.
predicates.respondents_did_not_appeal_existing_awar: The respondents did not appeal the existing award of a share to other claimants.

members.legal_issue: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not retrospectively enlarge the alienor’s power over ancestral property or nullify a declaratory decree made before the Act came into force.
material_facts: The ancestor had alienated ancestral property and a declaratory decree had been made concerning that alienation before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The respondents argued that the Act made the ancestor a full owner and left his sons without a subsisting reversionary interest despite the earlier decree.
members.legal_principle: Nothing in the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 operates retrospectively to enlarge the power of a holder of ancestral land or to nullify a declaratory decree passed before the Act came into force.
members.conclusion: The Act did not retrospectively enlarge the ancestor’s power over the ancestral property or nullify the earlier declaratory decree.

predicates.appeal_in_property_dispute: An appeal concerned rights to property.
predicates.ancestral_property_was_alienated_before_: An ancestor alienated ancestral property before the relevant succession law came into force.
predicates.declaratory_decree_preceded_succession_l: A declaratory decree concerning the alienation was made before the relevant succession law came into force.
predicates.retrospective_effect_is_claimed: A party claimed that the later succession law retrospectively changed the effect of the prior alienation or decree.

members.legal_issue: A decree-holder's purchase of property at an execution sale without express court permission may be set aside when the applicable procedure retains that safeguard and an affected person applies.
material_facts: A decree-holder purchased property at a court sale without obtaining the executing court's express permission.
Before the sale was confirmed, the judgment-debtor applied to set it aside on that ground.
The local amendment that had removed the permission requirement and the remedy for an unauthorised purchase was inconsistent with the procedure governing the proceedings.
The executing court set aside the sale, and the District Judge affirmed that decision.
members.legal_principle: Order 21 Rule 72(1) of the Code requires a decree-holder to obtain the court's express permission to bid for or purchase property sold in execution. Under Order 21 Rule 72(3), the court may set aside a purchase made without permission on an application by the judgment-debtor or another person whose interests are affected. Section 97(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976 caused the inconsistent local deletion of these safeguards to cease to operate. No earlier judicial decisions were relied on.
members.conclusion: The sale was properly set aside, and the order affirming that result was restored.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and decree_holder_bought_without_permission and affected_person_applied_to_set_aside and local_procedure_inconsistent_with_uniform_code

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A party sought review of the result of a sale conducted by a court to enforce a decree.
predicates.decree_holder_bought_without_permission: The decree-holder purchased the property at the execution sale without express permission from the executing court.
predicates.affected_person_applied_to_set_aside: The judgment-debtor or another person whose interests were affected applied to set aside the sale.
predicates.local_procedure_inconsistent_with_unifor: A local procedural amendment had removed the general safeguards against a decree-holder's unauthorised purchase.

members.legal_issue: A decree-holder's purchase of property at an execution sale without the court's express permission is not automatically void, although the court may set it aside on an affected person's application.
material_facts: The Court considered the construction of the rule governing a decree-holder's purchase at an execution sale.
The purchasers in this case were mortgagees, not decree-holders, and had no decree on their mortgage.
members.legal_principle: Order XXI, rule 72, prohibits a decree-holder from bidding for or purchasing property in execution of that decree without express court permission. It permits a set-off when the decree-holder purchases with permission, and gives the court discretion to set aside a purchase made without permission on an affected person's application. The Court relied on Rai Radha Krishna v. Bisheshar Sahai in treating the provision as directory.
members.conclusion: The restriction on a decree-holder purchasing without permission is directory; if the decree-holder purchases without permission, the court may set aside the sale on an application by the judgment-debtor or another person whose interests are affected.

rule.if: execution_auction_case and decree_holder_bought_execution_property and not express_permission_obtained and affected_person_applied

predicates.execution_auction_case: The property was sold in proceedings to enforce a decree.
predicates.decree_holder_bought_execution_property: The holder of the decree being enforced purchased the property at the execution sale.
