predicates.express_permission_obtained: The decree-holder obtained the court's express permission to bid for or purchase the property.
predicates.affected_person_applied: The judgment-debtor or another person whose interests were affected applied to set aside the sale.

members.legal_issue: A family's ceiling holding is determined by its membership on the appointed day and does not fluctuate with later changes in membership, except where the statutory scheme provides for redetermination.
material_facts: The ceiling proceedings concerned a family holding agricultural land under the applicable ceiling legislation.
Three children were born into the family after the appointed day.
The Revenue Tribunal did not count those children when fixing the family's ceiling area.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(4), 3 and 4 establish the appointed day and provide for the ceiling to be imposed and determined by reference to that day; sections 8 and 9 regulate transfers and acquisitions on or after that day. Section 12 provides for reassessment in specified circumstances, but not merely because family membership later changes. The Court relied on State v. Dinkarrao Narayanrao Deshmukh (1969) 72 Bom. L.R. 237, Murari Rao S. Gube Patil v. State, Spl. C.A. No. 767 of 1968, and Spl. C.A. No. 229 of 1968, and held the contrary view in Civil Application No. 1578 of 1969 to be incorrect.
members.conclusion: The Tribunal correctly excluded the children born after the appointed day when determining the family's ceiling area.

predicates.ceiling_determination_proceeding: The proceeding determines the ceiling holding of a person or family under an agricultural land ceiling scheme.
predicates.family_membership_changed_after_referenc: The number of family members changed after the day used to determine the ceiling holding.
predicates.no_statutory_redetermination_event: No specified event requiring the ceiling holding to be reassessed occurred.
predicates.ceiling_area_remains_based_on_reference_: The ceiling area remains based on the family's membership on the reference day.

members.legal_issue: A later change in the composition of a family does not alter the ceiling applicable to it when the ceiling is determined by reference to its composition on the notified date.
material_facts: On the notified date, the landholder’s family included his wife and children, two of whom were minors.
Those two children attained majority after the notified date.
The landholder relied on the children’s later majority and the subsequent gifts to argue that the family’s landholding did not exceed its ceiling.
members.legal_principle: Sections 82 and 83 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964 determine the ceiling by reference to the notified date, and section 85 requires surrender of land exceeding that ceiling. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. Philomina for the rule that the ceiling and surrender obligation are determined by the position on the notified date.
members.conclusion: The notified date is the relevant date for fixing the ceiling, and subsequent changes in the composition of the family are irrelevant to that determination.

predicates.ceiling_surrender_proceeding: A proceeding concerns whether a landholder must surrender land exceeding an applicable land ceiling.
predicates.family_composition_changed_after_cutoff: The composition of the landholder’s family changed after the date used to determine the applicable ceiling.
predicates.ceiling_is_fixed_by_family_composition_o: The applicable ceiling is determined using the family’s composition on the date used to determine the ceiling.

members.legal_issue: The validity under Hindu law of a perpetual dedication primarily for worship at the tomb of an ordinary deceased person.
material_facts: The settlement permanently dedicated properties to services connected with the deceased person's tomb, including daily worship and annual ceremonies.
The deed's other stated purposes were part of the tomb-related services or dependent on a surplus after their expenses.
There was no evidence that the community concerned had a widely recognized practice of making such endowments; the pleadings asserted that tomb ceremonies were not usual in that community.
members.legal_principle: A perpetual dedication can escape the rule against perpetuity only if it is for a religious or charitable purpose recognized by Hindu law. Where religious merit is relied on without public benefit, the purpose must have a Shastric basis; a later practice may also qualify if it has wide recognition among a substantial class. The Court approved Kunhamutty v. Thondikkodan Ahmad Musaliar, A. Draviasundaram Pillai v. N. Subramania Pillai, and Veluswami Goundan v. Dandapani, which rejected perpetual endowments for tomb worship. It distinguished M. K. A. Ramanathan Chettiar v. Vada Levvai Marakayar, concerning Muslims, and Board of Commissioners for Hindu Religious Endowments v. Pidugu Narasimham, concerning public worship of installed images and a sovereign grant. It also referred to Fatma Bibi v. Advocate-General of Bombay, Dwarakanath Bysack v. Burroda Persaud Bysack, Rupa Jagashet v. Krishnaji, and Parthasarthy Pillai v. Thiruvengada Pillai in discussing Hindu religious purposes and religious merit.
members.conclusion: A perpetual dedication primarily for worship at the tomb was invalid under Hindu law, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: perpetual_endowment_validity_dispute and tomb_worship_is_dominant_purpose and no_shastric_basis_is_shown and no_widely_recognized_practice_is_shown

predicates.perpetual_endowment_validity_dispute: The proceeding concerns the validity of a perpetual dedication of property for a religious or charitable purpose.
predicates.tomb_worship_is_dominant_purpose: The endowed property is primarily devoted to worship of or at the tomb of a deceased person.
predicates.no_shastric_basis_is_shown: No basis in Hindu sacred texts is shown for treating the purpose as one that produces religious merit.
predicates.no_widely_recognized_practice_is_shown: No widely recognized practice among a substantial class is shown to support the purpose as religious.

members.legal_issue: A perpetual dedication to worship at the tomb of an ordinary ancestor is not a valid religious or charitable purpose under Hindu law unless a qualifying religious practice is established.
material_facts: The deed dedicated property for charities and directed that part of the income from property allotted to a matam be spent on puja at a tomb containing the remains of the settlors’ ancestors.
The tomb was not shown to be a shrine associated with a saint or other person whose worship had become a recognized public religious practice.
The person relying on the tomb worship did not plead or prove a community practice of building tombs over ancestors’ remains and performing puja there.
members.legal_principle: The validity of a religious purpose for a perpetual dedication is determined according to Hindu law and Hindu notions, not English law concerning tombs. A claimed purpose grounded in religious merit must have a Shastric basis, or, if based on a later religious practice, must be shown to have wide recognition among a substantial class. The person asserting such a community practice bears the burden of proving it. An ordinary ancestor’s tomb is not recognized as religious merely because worship is performed there, although the rule may differ for saints or other shrines of recognized public worship, and for certain memorials following cremation. The Court relied on Saraswathi Ammal v. Rajagopal Ammal, Kunhamutty v. Thondikkodan Ahmad Musaliar, A. Drainasundaram Pillai v. N. Subramania Pillai, Veluswami Gounder v. Dandapani, Sri Ramanasramam v. Commissioner for Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Board of Commissioners for Hindu Religious Endowments v. Pidugu Narasimham, Ratnavelu Mudaliar v. Commissioner for H.R. & C.E., and Ramaswami v. Board of Commissioners. The dispute arose in a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure concerning charitable trusts.
members.conclusion: The provision for puja at the ancestors’ tomb was invalid as a religious or charitable purpose.

rule.if: charitable_trust_appeal and ancestral_tomb_worship_dedication and ordinary_person_tomb and not community_religious_practice_proved

predicates.charitable_trust_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the validity or administration of a charitable trust.
predicates.ancestral_tomb_worship_dedication: A person has dedicated property to support worship at the tomb of an ancestor.
predicates.ordinary_person_tomb: The tomb is of an ordinary person and is not shown to be a shrine of a saint or another figure of recognized public worship.
predicates.community_religious_practice_proved: The person relying on the dedication has proved that the relevant community widely recognizes the tomb worship as a religious practice.

members.legal_issue: Failure to send a phenolphthalein handwash sample for chemical examination does not, by itself, invalidate trap evidence where recovery and the accused’s handling of the gratification are established by direct evidence.
material_facts: A trap was conducted using currency treated with phenolphthalein powder.
The accused accepted the currency and put it in a desk drawer, from which the currency was recovered and identified.
The accused’s handwash solution turned pink, but the collected solution was not sent for chemical examination.
The court found no evidence that investigators shook hands with or caught the accused’s hands, and relied on direct evidence of the recovery.
members.legal_principle: The phenolphthalein test and chemical examination of its solution are not statutory requirements for proving a trap. The test is used for the satisfaction of officials, and its absence is not fatal where direct evidence proves recovery and the relevant conduct. The court applied State of U.P. v. Zakaullah (1998) 1 SCC 557.
members.conclusion: The absence of chemical examination of the handwash sample did not undermine the prosecution case or make the conviction unsafe.

rule.if: corruption_trap_case and handwash_sample_not_chemically_examined and direct_evidence_proves_gratification_recovery and no_evidence_of_transfer_from_investigator

predicates.corruption_trap_case: The proceeding concerns a trap conducted to prove a public-servant corruption offence.
predicates.handwash_sample_not_chemically_examined: The handwash solution collected during the trap is not sent for chemical examination.
predicates.direct_evidence_proves_gratification_rec: Witnesses or other direct evidence establish the recovery of the treated gratification from the accused’s custody.
predicates.no_evidence_of_transfer_from_investigato: There is no evidence that contact with an investigator transferred the test substance to the accused.

members.legal_issue: Failure to send the solution used in a phenolphthalein test for chemical examination does not, by itself, impair the proof of a trap.
material_facts: The public servant was intercepted with the marked currency after the alleged payment.
A phenolphthalein test produced a positive result.
The solution collected after washing the public servant's fingers was not sent to a chemical examiner.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that phenolphthalein solution is used to satisfy the investigating officer that the public servant handled the bribe money, and that no statutory direction requiring the collected solution to be sent to a chemical examiner was identified.
members.conclusion: The failure to send the solution for chemical examination did not impair the reliability of the trap evidence.

rule.if: bribery_trap_case and positive_handling_test and marked_currency_recovered_from_accused and test_solution_not_chemically_examined

predicates.bribery_trap_case: The prosecution alleges that a public servant accepted a bribe in a planned trap.
predicates.positive_handling_test: A test used to detect contact with treated currency produces a positive result.
predicates.marked_currency_recovered_from_accused: The marked currency used in the trap is recovered from the accused.
predicates.test_solution_not_chemically_examined: The solution collected during the handling test is not sent for chemical examination.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may determine the statutory limits and jurisdiction of a tribunal even when it cannot decide the merits of the inter-state water dispute assigned to that tribunal.
material_facts: The appeals challenged the tribunal’s refusal to entertain interim-relief applications on the ground that the applications were outside its jurisdiction.
The appellants asked the Supreme Court to determine the tribunal’s authority, not to decide the merits of the water dispute pending before it.
members.legal_principle: The judiciary authoritatively interprets statutes and determines the jurisdictional boundaries of statutory bodies. The Court relied on Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Company v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. and Kehar Singh v. Union of India, and referred to Tamil Nadu Cauvery Neerppasana Vilaiporulgal Vivasayigal Nala Urimal Padhugappu Sangam v. Union of India.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court had jurisdiction and an obligation to determine the scope and limits of the tribunal’s authority under its governing statute.

predicates.appeal_from_tribunal_jurisdiction_order: A party appealed an order in which a statutory tribunal declined to act because it considered itself outside its authority.
predicates.challenge_concerns_tribunal_authority_no: The challenge asks whether the tribunal’s governing law gives it the authority at issue, rather than asking the court to decide the underlying inter-state water dispute.

members.legal_issue: The Supreme Court cannot decide the merits of an inter-state water dispute that has been referred to a tribunal under the statutory scheme.
material_facts: The dispute concerning the use, distribution, and control of the waters of an inter-state river had been referred to a tribunal and remained pending there.
The appellants sought interim relief from the tribunal, while these appeals challenged the tribunal’s refusal to entertain their applications.
members.legal_principle: Article 262 of the Constitution permits Parliament to exclude the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts over inter-state water disputes. Section 11 of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956, excludes court jurisdiction over water disputes that may be referred to a tribunal under the Act.
members.conclusion: The Supreme Court had no jurisdiction to decide the merits of the water dispute pending before the tribunal.

predicates.inter_state_water_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a dispute over the use, distribution, or control of the waters of an inter-state river or river valley.
predicates.supreme_court_asked_to_decide_referred_d: A party asks the Supreme Court to decide the merits of a water dispute that has been referred to a tribunal.

members.legal_issue: A court cannot resolve a disputed agricultural-land exemption without considering the relevant material and making a factual finding on the land’s character.
material_facts: The debtors disputed the secured creditor’s enforcement of the security, asserting that the land was agricultural.
The debt tribunal rejected that assertion, while the appellate tribunal found the land to be agricultural.
The High Court dismissed challenges to the appellate tribunal’s decision but did not discuss the parties’ material or make a specific finding on whether the land was agricultural.
The Supreme Court therefore could not determine the land’s agricultural character on the record before it.
members.legal_principle: Whether land is agricultural must be decided on the totality of the facts and circumstances, including its nature and character, its use, and the purpose and intent of the parties when the security interest was created. Where the reviewing court has not addressed the material bearing on that factual question or made a specific finding, the matter should be reconsidered on remand.
members.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside, and the proceedings were remitted to it for fresh consideration of the evidence and a determination of whether the land was agricultural.

predicates.appeal_from_review_court_decision: A party appeals a reviewing court’s decision concerning enforcement of a security interest over land.
predicates.agricultural_status_contested: The parties dispute whether the land is agricultural in character.
predicates.reviewing_court_omitted_evidence_analysi: The reviewing court does not address the material bearing on the land’s character or make a specific factual finding about it.

members.legal_issue: A factual determination about agricultural character must be reconsidered when the reviewing court relies on land-use potentialities without addressing the taxing authorities' finding on intended use or explaining why that finding lacks evidentiary support.
material_facts: The taxing authorities and Tribunal found that the land had never been used and was not intended to be used for agriculture.
The High Court relied on the land's agricultural potentialities and its revenue classification.
The High Court did not find that the taxing authorities' finding on intended use rested on no evidence and gave no reasons for rejecting that finding.
members.legal_principle: The character of land is a question of fact to be determined from all relevant evidence under the correct test: agricultural connection and user, not mere potentiality. A reviewing court cannot resolve that question by relying on inconclusive potentialities while leaving an adverse factual finding unaddressed. The Tribunal must reconsider the evidence consistently with section 2(e)(i) of the Wealth Tax Act and the principle in Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy.
members.conclusion: The High Court's judgment was set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for a fresh factual determination under the correct legal test, with both sides given an opportunity to adduce further evidence.

predicates.appeal_from_high_court_factual_determina: The matter is an appeal challenging a High Court's resolution of a factual question about land's agricultural character.
predicates.taxing_authority_found_no_agricultural_u: The taxing authorities found that the land was neither used nor intended to be used for agriculture.
predicates.high_court_relied_on_potentiality: The High Court relied on the land's capability or potential for agricultural use.
predicates.high_court_did_not_explain_rejection_of_: The High Court neither found that the taxing authorities' finding lacked evidentiary support nor explained why it rejected that finding.
predicates.set_aside_and_remand_for_fresh_factual_d: The High Court's decision is set aside and the factual question is remitted for a fresh determination.

members.legal_issue: Requisitioning vacant premises to house genuinely homeless people serves a public purpose, and government may reasonably select beneficiaries under a general allocation policy.
material_facts: The government requisitioned premises amid an acute housing shortage, in part associated with an influx of refugees.
The government had used first informants to identify suppressed vacancies and allotted some such premises to informants who genuinely needed accommodation.
The allocation policy was intended both to house homeless people and to encourage disclosure of vacancies; no fraud, invidious discrimination, nepotism, bribery, or corruption was alleged.
The shortage required selection among many homeless applicants, and the government considered practical and public-policy factors in choosing an allocation scheme.
members.legal_principle: A public purpose is fulfilled when requisitioned accommodation is allotted to a person who is in fact homeless. Government has wide discretion to implement the statutory policy and may choose among reasonable allocation schemes; courts do not substitute a different scheme merely because it may seem preferable. A particular allotment may be challenged on grounds such as fraud, invidious discrimination, nepotism, bribery, or corruption.
members.conclusion: Housing a person without accommodation was a public purpose, and the challenged requisition and allotment orders were not ultra vires on the ground that the beneficiary was a first informant or that another allocation method might have been preferable.

rule.if: challenge_to_requisition_or_allotment and accommodation_allocated_to_a_genuinely_homeless_person and allocation_uses_informant_status and selection_follows_a_reasonable_general_policy and no_improper_selection_is_shown

predicates.challenge_to_requisition_or_allotment: A person challenges a government requisition or the allocation of requisitioned accommodation.
predicates.accommodation_allocated_to_a_genuinely_h: The recipient of the accommodation in fact has no housing accommodation.
predicates.allocation_uses_informant_status: The allocation scheme considers whether a person identified a previously undisclosed vacancy.
predicates.selection_follows_a_reasonable_general_p: The government selects recipients on broad principles and through a reasonable policy suited to the circumstances.
predicates.no_improper_selection_is_shown: The challenger does not establish fraud, invidious discrimination, nepotism, bribery, corruption, or comparable improper selection.

members.legal_issue: Premises made vacant by a court-ordered eviction for the landlord’s occupation may be requisitioned for a public purpose and allotted to a homeless person.
material_facts: The landlords obtained possession through execution of an eviction decree, which included their bona fide requirement to occupy the room.
The former occupant applied to the accommodation authority for requisition and allotment, stating that he had no other accommodation.
The government requisitioned the room for the public purpose of housing a homeless person and allotted it to the former occupant.
The Requisition Act was enacted after the Rent Act and did not exclude premises made vacant by an eviction on the ground of the landlord’s requirement.
members.legal_principle: Sections 6(1) and 6(4) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 permit requisition of premises that become vacant upon a tenant’s eviction, for a public purpose. Under The State of Bombay v. Bhanji Munji, requisitioning premises to house a homeless person serves a public purpose. Sections 13 and 17 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 do not prevent such requisition: the Acts address different matters, the later Requisition Act contains no exception for this kind of eviction, and non-occupation required by the requisition law may be for reasonable cause under the Rent Act.
members.conclusion: The requisition and allotment were not invalid merely because the room became vacant after an eviction decree based on the landlords’ need to occupy it; there was no conflict between the relevant provisions of the two Acts.

rule.if: requisition_challenge and vacancy_followed_court_ordered_eviction and eviction_included_landlord_occupation_need and government_requisitioned_for_public_housing and allottee_was_homeless

predicates.requisition_challenge: A party challenged a government requisition and the related allotment.
predicates.vacancy_followed_court_ordered_eviction: The premises became vacant after a court-ordered eviction.
predicates.eviction_included_landlord_occupation_ne: The grounds for the eviction included the landlord’s need to occupy the premises.
predicates.government_requisitioned_for_public_hous: The government requisitioned the premises to provide housing as a public purpose.
predicates.allottee_was_homeless: The person to whom the premises were allotted had no other accommodation.
predicates.requisition_and_allotment_are_not_invali: The eviction ground and subsequent allotment do not, by themselves, invalidate the requisition or allotment.

members.legal_issue: A Magistrate may direct further investigation after a police report has been filed and cognizance has been taken, until the trial commences, including after process has issued and the accused has appeared.
material_facts: The police filed a charge-sheet, the Magistrate took cognizance and issued summons, and the accused appeared.
The accused applied for further investigation after cognizance had been taken.
The investigation and inquiry had not reached commencement of trial, which occurs when the relevant charges are framed or, in a summons case, when the accused is asked to plead or state a defence.
members.legal_principle: Sections 156(1), 156(3), 173(8), and 2(h) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, read with Article 21, permit the Magistrate to ensure a fair and proper investigation through further investigation until trial begins. Sections 190, 200, 202, and 204 form part of the procedural scheme. The Court relied on Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P., State of Bihar v. J.A.C. Saldhana, Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police, Ram Lal Narang v. State (Delhi Administration), Union Public Service Commission v. S. Papaiah, Hasanbhai Valibhai Qureshi v. State of Gujarat, Hemant Dhasmana v. CBI, Samaj Parivartan Samudaya v. State of Karnataka, Vinay Tyagi v. Irshad Ali, and Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab. It rejected the contrary approach in Devarapalli Lakshminarayana Reddy and overruled, to the extent inconsistent, Amrutbhai Shambubhai Patel, Athul Rao, Bikash Ranjan Rout, Randhir Singh Rana, and Reeta Nag.
members.conclusion: The Magistrate retains power to direct further investigation after a police report and cognizance, including after process has issued and the accused has appeared, up to commencement of trial. The power may be exercised suo motu or on an application, but does not extend to ordering a fresh or de novo investigation.

rule.if: criminal_case_on_police_report and post_report_proceeding and before_trial_commences and further_evidence_needed_for_fair_investigation

predicates.criminal_case_on_police_report: The criminal proceeding began with a police investigation and report to a Magistrate.
predicates.post_report_proceeding: The police report has been filed and the proceeding has continued before the Magistrate.
predicates.before_trial_commences: The relevant trial has not begun, including because charges have not been framed where charges are required.
predicates.further_evidence_needed_for_fair_investi: The circumstances indicate that collecting additional evidence is needed to achieve a fair and proper investigation.

members.legal_issue: A magistrate may refer a complaint for police investigation before taking cognizance, where the allegations disclose a cognizable offence and investigation is an appropriate course.
material_facts: A social worker filed a complaint alleging that land had been purchased from a person who was already dead, and the complaint named several people, including public officials.
The magistrate heard the complainant’s counsel and considered the complaint and its supporting documents before directing the police to investigate and report.
The magistrate directed investigation before issuing process or otherwise taking cognizance of the alleged offence.
The accused sought to quash the proceedings, and the High Court declined to do so.
members.legal_principle: Under Sections 156(3) and 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an empowered magistrate may direct investigation before taking cognizance. If the magistrate takes cognizance and proceeds under Chapter XV, the magistrate cannot return to the pre-cognizance stage to use Section 156(3). A magistrate may choose police investigation where the complaint alleges a cognizable offence and referral would be conducive to justice, including by avoiding a judicial inquiry into a matter primarily for police investigation. The Court relied on CREF Finance Ltd. v. Shree Shanthi Homes (P) Ltd., Devarapalli Lakshminarayana Reddy v. V. Narayana Reddy, and Tula Ram v. Kishore Singh. Sections 200 and 190 and the procedures in Chapter XV govern the alternative course where the magistrate takes cognizance.
members.conclusion: The magistrate acted within his power in directing a pre-cognizance police investigation, and the High Court was right to refuse to quash that direction; the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: challenge_to_pre_cognizance_investigation_order and empowered_magistrate and before_cognizance and cognizable_offence_alleged and investigation_conducive_to_justice

predicates.challenge_to_pre_cognizance_investigatio: The proceeding challenges a magistrate’s direction for police investigation made before deciding whether to take cognizance.
predicates.empowered_magistrate: The magistrate who made the direction was empowered to act on the complaint.
predicates.before_cognizance: The magistrate directed investigation before taking cognizance or beginning the post-cognizance complaint procedure.
predicates.cognizable_offence_alleged: The complaint alleged facts disclosing a cognizable offence.
predicates.investigation_conducive_to_justice: The magistrate considered police investigation an appropriate course, including because it could advance justice or avoid a judicial inquiry into a matter primarily for police investigation.

members.legal_issue: A High Court cannot use its inherent criminal jurisdiction to entertain a second revision application by the same party after that party’s revision has been rejected.
material_facts: The respondent challenged the Magistrate’s order withdrawing attachment by filing a revision before the Sessions Court.
After the Sessions Court dismissed that revision, the respondent sought the same relief from the High Court under its inherent jurisdiction.
members.legal_principle: Section 397(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure bars a second revision application by the same party. Section 482 cannot be used to exercise powers expressly barred by the Code. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment for this principle.
members.conclusion: The High Court erred in entertaining the respondent’s second revision application, and its order was set aside.

rule.if: criminal_revision_proceeding and same_applicant_previously_sought_revision and prior_revision_rejected and inherent_jurisdiction_invoked

predicates.criminal_revision_proceeding: The proceeding sought review of an order made in a criminal matter.
predicates.same_applicant_previously_sought_revisio: The person seeking inherent relief had already applied for revision of the challenged order.
predicates.prior_revision_rejected: The earlier revision application was rejected by the revisional court.
predicates.inherent_jurisdiction_invoked: The person then asked the High Court to use its inherent jurisdiction to obtain relief from the same order.

members.legal_issue: A High Court may decline to interfere in revision even when grounds for exercising revisional jurisdiction exist, where the circumstances, including an unsuccessful earlier attempt to obtain the same relief, do not warrant interference.
material_facts: An award requiring delivery of a house was previously presented to the court, and an application to make it a rule of court was dismissed.
After the award was later filed again by arbitrators, an application was made to have it made a rule of court; the trial court ruled against the applicants.
The High Court treated the challenge as a revision and declined to interfere, noting that the earlier application had failed and that the later attempt sought the same relief after a long interval.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court had exercised its discretion consistently with settled principles.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, revisional jurisdiction is discretionary, and the High Court need not interfere merely because the statutory conditions for exercising that jurisdiction are met. Relevant considerations include the character of the order, the availability of another remedy, the general equities, and whether the order caused a substantial failure of justice. The Court relied on Major S.S. Khanna v. Brig. F.J. Dillon.
members.conclusion: The High Court was justified in refusing revisional interference, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: revision_challenge and prior_application_for_same_relief_rejected and later_proceeding_seeks_same_relief and substantial_delay

predicates.revision_challenge: The proceeding is a challenge asking a court to exercise its discretionary revisional jurisdiction.
predicates.prior_application_for_same_relief_reject: An earlier application seeking the same substantive relief was rejected.
predicates.later_proceeding_seeks_same_relief: A later proceeding seeks to obtain that substantive relief again through a different procedural route.
predicates.substantial_delay: The later attempt to obtain the relief occurs after a substantial interval.

members.legal_issue: An agreement to construct a unit for a purchaser before construction is complete constitutes a works contract, and the transfer of goods involved in that construction is taxable.
material_facts: The developer entered into agreements with prospective purchasers before construction was complete.
Under the agreements, the developer undertook to construct units for purchasers in return for consideration payable in instalments.
The agreements provided for purchasers to acquire units and an undivided interest in the land.
The tax authorities assessed tax on the transfer of property in goods involved in the construction.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(1)(v-i), 2(1)(k)(viii) and 5B of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, a works contract broadly includes any agreement for construction for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration; it is not limited to the conventional meaning of work performed for another. Tax under section 5B applies to the taxable turnover of property in goods transferred in executing such a contract. The Karnataka Ownership Flats Act does not determine whether an agreement is a works contract for this purpose.
members.conclusion: Construction undertaken for purchasers under agreements made before completion is a works contract, and tax is payable on the turnover of goods transferred in its execution. An agreement made after the unit is already constructed does not constitute a works contract.

rule.if: sales_tax_assessment_appeal and agreement_precedes_completion and construction_for_purchaser and consideration_for_construction and goods_transferred_in_construction

predicates.sales_tax_assessment_appeal: The proceeding concerns an appeal from a sales tax assessment relating to construction activity.
predicates.agreement_precedes_completion: The construction agreement was made before the unit was fully constructed.
predicates.construction_for_purchaser: The developer undertook under the agreement to construct the unit for a purchaser.
predicates.consideration_for_construction: The purchaser agreed to provide cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration for the construction.
predicates.goods_transferred_in_construction: Property in goods was transferred in the course of carrying out the construction.

members.legal_issue: A developer’s construction of a flat under an agreement made with a purchaser before completion is a works contract to the extent of construction performed after that agreement.
material_facts: Developers entered into agreements with intended flat purchasers while construction was incomplete, and the agreements provided for construction and eventual transfer of the flats with an interest in the land.
The purchasers paid or were required to pay consideration, and goods used in construction were incorporated into the buildings and transferred to purchasers.
In the leading dispute, a developer also had a development agreement with a landowner under which the project was divided between them.
members.legal_principle: Article 366(29-A)(b), read with Entry 54 of List II, treats the transfer of property in goods involved in a works contract as a deemed sale, including goods incorporated into immovable property. Building contracts are works contracts, and a contract may combine construction with transfer of immovable property without losing its character as a works contract. The Court approved K. Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka; it relied on Builders’ Association of India v. Union of India, Gannon Dunkerley (II), State of U.P. v. P.N.C. Construction Co. Ltd., and State of A.P. v. Kone Elevators. The taxable construction activity begins when the developer contracts with the purchaser; goods incorporated before that point are not deemed sold to a purchaser who was not yet party to a construction contract.
members.conclusion: The construction activity is a works contract from the stage at which the developer enters into an agreement with the flat purchaser. The value addition to goods transferred after that agreement may be taxed. Construction completed before any purchaser agreement is not taxable on the basis of a later sale of the completed building.

predicates.construction_tax_appeal: The proceeding concerns a challenge to sales tax on goods used in constructing a building or flat.
predicates.developer_purchaser_agreement_before_com: The developer and purchaser agreed to the construction of the flat while construction was incomplete.
predicates.valuable_construction_consideration: The developer was entitled to valuable consideration for the construction undertaken for the purchaser.
predicates.construction_goods_transferred_to_purcha: Goods used in the construction were incorporated into the building and transferred to the purchaser in the completed property.

members.legal_issue: An occupant who remains in premises after revocation of a licence remains liable for compensation for their use and occupation.
material_facts: The occupant continued to use the premises after the limited-period licence expired.
The licensors were willing to accept money for use and occupation as compensation, without prejudice to their position that the licence had ended.
members.legal_principle: The judgment applies section 62(c) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, under which a limited-period licence is deemed revoked when the period expires, and explains that post-revocation occupation may give rise to compensation or damages for use and occupation. The judgment relies on no earlier cases for this principle.
members.conclusion: Continued occupation after revocation remains compensable, and payment or acceptance of compensation does not undo the revocation or restore the licence.

predicates.license_revoked: The permission to occupy the premises ended by expiry, withdrawal, or revocation.
predicates.occupant_continued_using_premises: The occupant continued to use or occupy the premises after the permission ended.

members.legal_issue: Licensees who continue to occupy premises must pay compensation for their use and occupation to the owners entitled to receive it.
material_facts: The occupants had paid compensation for the initial licence period and deposited an additional sum with the original tenant.
They did not claim to have paid further compensation for their continued occupation.
The tenant's heirs disclaimed any interest in the premises, and the owners remained entitled to the compensation.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed payment of compensation for use and occupation to the owners because the occupants continued in possession and the former tenant's heirs claimed no interest in the premises.
members.conclusion: The occupants were liable to pay compensation to the owners for their use and occupation, with the amounts already paid credited against their liability and further payments made as directed by the Court.

predicates.occupants_remained_in_possession: The licensees continued to occupy the premises after the initial licence period.
predicates.owners_entitled_to_compensation: The owners were entitled to receive compensation for the occupants' use and occupation.
predicates.prior_payments_made_to_former_tenant: The occupants had paid an amount to the former tenant for the initial period of occupation.

members.legal_issue: The statutory preservation and settlement of a building applies to a person who lawfully held it, not merely to whoever physically possessed it when the estate vested.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a building within an estate subject to statutory vesting and settlement.

The respondents had held the building and its site as tenants, while the appellants claimed the benefit of settlement based on their physical possession after entering the site and demolishing the respondents’ buildings.
members.legal_principle: Sections 4, 6 and 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act distinguish the estate’s vesting in the State from the subsequent deemed settlement of specified buildings and lands. In context, “held” denotes possession by legal title, not bare possession. The Court relied on Rana Sheo Ambar Singh v. Allahabad Bank Ltd. concerning vesting, Shivashankar Prasad Shah v. Vaikunth Nath Singh concerning similar vesting provisions, K.K. Handique v. The Member, Board of Agricultural Income Tax, Assam on the meaning of “holds,” and Eramma v. Verrupanna on the meaning of “possessed.” It accepted the interpretation in Pheku Chamar v. Harish Chandra.
members.conclusion: The word “held” in Section 9 means lawfully held; mere physical possession, including possession by a trespasser, is insufficient to obtain the statutory benefit.

rule.if: building_settlement_proceeding and building_within_vested_estate and person_physically_possessed_building and not person_had_legal_title_to_hold_building

predicates.building_settlement_proceeding: The dispute arose in a proceeding about who was entitled to a building affected by estate vesting and statutory settlement.
predicates.building_within_vested_estate: The building was situated within an estate that vested in the State.
predicates.person_physically_possessed_building: The person claiming the benefit was physically possessing the building at the relevant time.
predicates.person_had_legal_title_to_hold_building: The person claiming the benefit had a legal title to hold the building.

members.legal_issue: The statutory term for a building being held at the time of vesting requires lawful holding, not mere physical possession.
material_facts: The statutory scheme provided for estate vesting and deemed settlement of specified buildings with the persons who held them.
The appellants were physically occupying the site and a cow-shed at vesting after unlawfully entering the site and demolishing the respondents’ residential buildings.
The respondents claimed that they had lawfully held the buildings and site before their temporary departure.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 6 and 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, read in the context of the Act’s scheme and language, “held” in section 9 means lawfully held. This construction accords with justice and reason and with the use of “held” alongside “belonging.” The Court approved Pheku Chamar v. Harish Chandra, disapproved Bharat v. Ch. Khazan Singh, and applied the interpretive approaches in K.K. Handique v. Member, Board of Agricultural Income-tax, Assam and Eramma v. Verrupanna.
members.conclusion: The term “held” means lawfully held; mere physical possession by a trespasser does not qualify for deemed settlement.

predicates.land_reform_building_settlement_case: The dispute concerns whether a person’s holding of a building qualifies for settlement under a land-reform scheme.
predicates.claimant_had_legal_title_to_building: The claimant had legal title to the building.
predicates.claimant_lawfully_held_building: The claimant held the building lawfully.

members.legal_issue: A temporary absence from a building does not end the lawful holder’s possession where the holder did not voluntarily abandon it, and an unlawful occupier does not gain rights by demolishing the building and replacing it with another structure.
material_facts: The respondents’ family had held the site and residential buildings for many years as tenants.
The respondents left temporarily during communal disturbances for safety and returned when conditions improved; they had not voluntarily abandoned the buildings.
During their absence, the appellants occupied the site, demolished the residential buildings and built a cowshed there.
The Court found that the new structure was a substitution for the demolished buildings and that the respondents were the owners of the building when vesting occurred.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 9, the persons lawfully holding a building at vesting retain the benefit of its deemed settlement. Temporary absence for safety is not abandonment where possession was not voluntarily given up. An unlawful trespasser’s demolition and replacement construction does not enhance the trespasser’s rights; on the facts, the replacement structure was treated as a substitution for the former building.
members.conclusion: The respondents remained the lawful holders and owners of the building at vesting and were entitled to recover both the site and the replacement building; the appellants’ trespass and construction gave them no rights.

rule.if: recovery_proceeding_after_statutory_vesting and claimant_lawfully_held_building and claimant_absence_was_temporary and claimant_did_not_abandon_building and opposing_party_entered_unlawfully and opposing_party_replaced_demolished_building

predicates.recovery_proceeding_after_statutory_vest: The claimant sought recovery of a site and building after a statutory vesting event.
predicates.claimant_lawfully_held_building: The claimant lawfully held the building before the disputed occupation.
predicates.claimant_absence_was_temporary: The claimant left the building temporarily for safety and later returned.
predicates.claimant_did_not_abandon_building: The claimant did not voluntarily give up possession of the building.
predicates.opposing_party_entered_unlawfully: The opposing party entered and occupied the site without a lawful right to do so.
predicates.opposing_party_replaced_demolished_build: The opposing party demolished the claimant’s building and erected a replacement structure on the site.

members.legal_issue: A lawful holder who temporarily leaves a building without abandoning it may recover the building and site after a trespasser demolishes the building and replaces it with a structure that is merely a substitute.
material_facts: The respondents’ family had obtained the site from the appellants’ ancestors and built residential buildings on it.
The respondents temporarily left the village for safety during communal disturbances and returned when conditions improved.
The appellants unlawfully entered the site, demolished the respondents’ buildings and erected a cow-shed in their place.
The Court was not satisfied that the cow-shed was worth more than the demolished buildings and treated the new structure as a substitute for them.
The appellants refused to return possession, and the respondents’ possession claim was pending when vesting occurred.
members.legal_principle: A temporary departure for safety does not, without more, amount to abandonment. The trespassers’ demolition and replacement construction did not enhance their rights under the Transfer of Property Act. On the facts and equitable considerations, the respondents remained owners of the substituted building and were entitled to recover it. The Court left open the broader question whether a landowner may recover land together with a building erected on it by a stranger.
members.conclusion: The respondents had not abandoned their buildings; they were entitled to recover the site and the replacement building, which they owned and lawfully held at the time of vesting.

rule.if: property_possession_dispute and lawful_occupants_temporarily_left and not occupants_abandoned_building and trespasser_demolished_building and trespasser_erected_substitute_structure and substitute_not_shown_more_valuable

predicates.property_possession_dispute: The case concerns a claim to possession of a building and its site.
predicates.lawful_occupants_temporarily_left: The lawful occupants temporarily left the building for safety.
predicates.occupants_abandoned_building: The lawful occupants voluntarily gave up their building.
predicates.trespasser_demolished_building: A trespasser unlawfully demolished the lawful occupants’ building.
predicates.trespasser_erected_substitute_structure: The trespasser erected a replacement structure on the site.
predicates.substitute_not_shown_more_valuable: The replacement structure was not shown to be more valuable than the demolished building.

members.legal_issue: A family’s tax liability that accrued while it was joint remains enforceable against its members after a later partition.
material_facts: The family business and its income belonged to the joint family during the relevant accounting years.
The tax liability arose no later than the close of those accounting years, before the claimed partition.
No order recording partition was made under section 25A(1), although a claim of partition had been brought to the tax officer’s attention.
The assessments were made on the family as an undivided family.
members.legal_principle: Under section 25A of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922, tax liability arises from the income and accrues no later than the close of the accounting year; later quantification does not postpone that liability, as explained in Wallace Brothers & Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax. Where liability arose while the family was joint, a later partition does not displace the family tax liability. Under section 25A(3), without an order recording partition the family is deemed to continue as undivided for the Act. If partition is recorded under section 25A(1), section 25A(2) apportions liability but its proviso preserves the members’ joint and several liability for tax assessed on the family income. The Court also relied on Sardar Bahadur Sir Sunder Singh Majithia v. Commissioner of Income-tax in describing the section’s operation.
members.conclusion: The family was properly assessed as undivided in the absence of an order recording partition; even if such an order had been made, the members would remain jointly and severally liable for the tax assessed on the family income.

predicates.family_tax_liability: A tax liability is assessed on income received by a family as a family.
predicates.liability_accrued_during_joint_status: The tax liability arose while the family still existed as a joint family.
predicates.family_tax_debt_remains_enforceable_agai: The family tax debt remains enforceable against family members despite a later partition.

members.legal_issue: A member’s share in family property and the income from that share may be reached to satisfy tax dues assessed against a family that continues to be treated as undivided for tax purposes.
material_facts: The family’s partition claim was rejected, and it continued to be treated as undivided for the tax proceedings.
The member challenged attachment of funds in a bank account operated by a receiver appointed in the partition suit.
The Court found that the member was bound by the assessments against the family and that his share in the family property or income from it was liable for the tax dues.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 25A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, the family continued to be deemed undivided for purposes of the Act because no order accepting partition had been passed. The Court accordingly held that the member was bound by the assessments and that his share or its income was liable for the family’s tax dues. No earlier judicial case was cited.
members.conclusion: The member was bound by the family assessments, and his share in the family property or the income from it was liable for the tax dues.

rule.if: tax_recovery_challenge and family_assessed_as_undivided and partition_claim_rejected and member_has_family_share_or_income

predicates.tax_recovery_challenge: The matter concerns a challenge to recovery of tax assessed against a family.
predicates.family_assessed_as_undivided: The family was assessed for tax as an undivided family.
predicates.partition_claim_rejected: The tax authority rejected the family’s claim that it had partitioned.
predicates.member_has_family_share_or_income: The member received or had a share in family property or income from that property.

members.legal_issue: A sanad issued on the basis of an allotment does not preserve title after the underlying allotment is set aside.
material_facts: The appellant received a sanad after a managing officer allotted land to him.
A settlement authority later cancelled the allotment, and the appellant challenged that cancellation.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied its decision in Shri Mithoo Shahani v. Union of India, [1964] 7 S.C.R. 103, that title founded on an allotment order cannot continue after that order is set aside.
members.conclusion: The appellant’s title based on the sanad fell when the allotment order was set aside.

predicates.allotment_cancellation_appeal: The proceeding challenges a decision cancelling an allotment.
predicates.sanad_based_on_allotment: An official issued a sanad to the claimant on the basis of the allotment.
predicates.underlying_allotment_set_aside: A competent authority set aside the allotment on which the sanad depended.

members.legal_issue: A grant and title derived from an allotment do not survive when the underlying allotment is set aside, absent an express provision preserving them.
material_facts: Sanads were issued to the later allottees on the basis of their allotment of the land.
The allotment underlying those sanads was set aside, and the later allottees’ title depended on that allotment continuing in force.
No provision in the Act or its rules was identified as preserving the grant after the allotment was set aside; the sanad’s stated resumption condition was not fulfilled.
members.legal_principle: Under section 20 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 and rule 91(8), a sanad can be issued only on the basis of a valid allotment. When that allotment is set aside, the grant based on it also falls unless an express provision preserves the grant. The court approved Balwant Kaur v. Chief Settlement Commissioner (Lands), I.L.R. [1964] Punjab 36, and distinguished Partumal v. Managing Officer, Jaipur, I.L.R. 11 Rajasthan 1121.
members.conclusion: The sanads and the title obtained under them could not survive the setting aside of the allotment on which they were based.

predicates.grant_based_on_allotment: An authority issued a grant or title to a person on the basis of an allotment.
predicates.underlying_allotment_set_aside: An authority set aside the allotment on which the grant or title depended.
predicates.no_express_survival_provision: No express legal provision preserves the grant or title after the underlying allotment is set aside.

members.legal_issue: A stranger to a genuine sale deed cannot dispute the payment or adequacy of its consideration when the challenge concerns only consideration.
material_facts: The defendant challenging the sale deed was not a party to the transaction between the vendor and the purchaser and had no personal knowledge of its terms or payment.
The vendor admitted the claim based on the sale deed, did not challenge it, and testified that he executed the deed and received the consideration.
The lower courts found the registered sale deed genuine, and the challenge at issue concerned whether the full consideration had been paid.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle in Lal Achal Ram v. Raja Kazim Hussain Khan that a stranger to a genuine sale deed cannot dispute payment or adequacy of consideration, while distinguishing a deed alleged to be fictitious or collusive. The vendor, as executant, could have disputed consideration, but admitted the sale and its consideration.
members.conclusion: The defendant could not invalidate the sale deed merely by disputing the payment or adequacy of consideration.

rule.if: civil_suit and challenger_is_stranger_to_transfer and deed_was_intended_to_transfer_title and challenge_is_only_about_consideration

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute was heard as a civil suit.
predicates.challenger_is_stranger_to_transfer: The defendant challenging the transaction was not a party to it.
predicates.deed_was_intended_to_transfer_title: The deed was intended by its parties to effect a genuine transfer of title.
predicates.challenge_is_only_about_consideration: The challenge concerned whether the consideration was paid or was adequate, rather than whether the deed was fictitious or collusive.

members.legal_issue: A third party who has not established a legal interest in a sale cannot challenge whether consideration passed under the sale deed.
material_facts: The defendant challenged the sale deed on the ground that consideration had not passed.
The defendant’s asserted status as an adopted daughter and heir was not proved.
The defendant was therefore a third party to the sale deed.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that a third party cannot question the passing of consideration under a sale deed, relying on Pandit Ramjilal Tiwari v. Vijai Kumar, 1970 MPLJ 50, and noting the consistent views in Mt. Akli v. Mt. Daho, AIR 1928 Patna 44, and Maroti Bansi Teli v. Radhabai, AIR 1945 Nagpur 60.
members.conclusion: The defendant could not challenge the passing of consideration under the sale deed.

predicates.sale_deed_consideration_challenged: A person disputes whether consideration passed under a sale deed.
predicates.challenger_is_not_party_or_representativ: The person challenging consideration was neither a party to the sale nor a representative of a party.
predicates.challenger_has_not_established_legal_int: The challenger did not establish an independent legal interest in the property that would entitle them to contest the sale.

members.legal_issue: A sale of immovable property may pass title even if the whole purchase price has not been paid, provided the parties intended to transfer ownership and the price was paid or promised.
material_facts: The vendor executed and registered a sale deed conveying the property to the purchaser.
The deed recited a total price, part of which the purchaser allegedly had not paid.
The vendor admitted executing the deed and receiving the full consideration, and the deed and surrounding evidence showed an intention to transfer ownership.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act defines a sale as a transfer of ownership for a price paid, promised, or part-paid and part-promised; payment of the whole price at execution is not essential to completion of the sale. The intention to transfer ownership is assessed from the deed, conduct, and evidence. Section 55(4)(b) gives the seller a charge on the property for unpaid purchase money and interest. The Court referred to Gyatri Prasad v. Board of Revenue, Sukaloo v. Punau, Goode v. Burton, Webb v. Macpherson, Venkataperumal Naidu v. Rathnasabhapathi Chettiar, Shobhalal Shyamlal Kunni v. Sidhelal Halkelal Bania, and Basalingaya Revanshiddappa v. Chinnaya Karibasappa.
members.conclusion: The sale was not invalid merely because part of the purchase price might remain unpaid; title passed to the purchaser, subject to the vendor’s statutory charge for any unpaid purchase money.

rule.if: civil_suit_involving_title_to_immovable_property and deed_was_executed_and_registered and parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership and price_was_paid_or_promised

predicates.civil_suit_involving_title_to_immovable_: The civil suit concerned title to immovable property.
predicates.deed_was_executed_and_registered: The parties executed and registered an instrument of transfer.
predicates.parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership: The parties intended the instrument to transfer ownership, rather than merely to create a future contract or a sham transaction.
predicates.price_was_paid_or_promised: The agreed price was paid, promised, or partly paid and partly promised.

members.legal_issue: Non-payment of some or all of the price does not invalidate a completed sale where the parties intended to transfer ownership for a price paid or promised.
material_facts: The plaintiffs admitted executing and registering the sale deed and sought its cancellation on the ground that most of the consideration represented by cheques had not been paid.
The deed recited that the full consideration had been paid and that possession had been transferred.
The plaint sought cancellation of the deed rather than merely recovery of the alleged unpaid balance.
members.legal_principle: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines a sale as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised, or part paid and part promised. Actual payment of the whole price at execution is not essential to completion of a sale. Once the deed is executed and registered with an intention to transfer ownership, non-payment of part of the price does not undo the transfer or justify cancellation. The Court relied on Vidyadhar v. Manikrao.
members.conclusion: Even assuming the alleged non-payment was true, it did not entitle the plaintiffs to cancel the sale deed; they could pursue other remedies to recover the unpaid consideration.

rule.if: suit_seeks_cancellation_of_sale and conveyance_executed_and_registered and parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership and price_was_paid_or_promised and price_allegedly_remains_unpaid

predicates.suit_seeks_cancellation_of_sale: The plaintiff brings a suit seeking cancellation of a conveyance of property.
predicates.conveyance_executed_and_registered: The parties executed and registered a document conveying the property.
predicates.parties_intended_to_transfer_ownership: The parties intended the conveyance to transfer ownership to the purchaser.
predicates.price_was_paid_or_promised: The transfer was made for a price paid, promised, or partly paid and partly promised.
predicates.price_allegedly_remains_unpaid: The plaintiff alleges that some or all of the agreed price was not paid.
predicates.nonpayment_does_not_invalidate_sale: The alleged non-payment does not invalidate the completed sale or entitle the plaintiff to cancel it.

members.legal_issue: A scheme should permit an application to the court for alteration, modification, or addition to its provisions.
material_facts: The scheme did not provide for an application to the District Judge to address matters arising under the scheme.
Counsel agreed that such a provision should be included.
The Court directed that a provision allowing applications to alter, modify, or add to the scheme be inserted.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the practice of providing a mechanism for applications concerning a scheme and referred to Sevak Kirpashankar Daji v. Gopalrao Manohar, 15 Bom. L.R. 13 (P.C.).
members.conclusion: The Court directed that a clause be added allowing the scheme to be altered, modified, or added to on application to the District Judge.

predicates.management_scheme_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a court-settled scheme for managing a religious endowment.
predicates.scheme_lacks_application_clause: The scheme contains no provision for applying to the court to alter, modify, or add to its terms.

members.legal_issue: A court may make only modifications needed for the proper working of an approved scheme; a substantial change to the scheme or an essential term requires fresh approval at a meeting.
material_facts: The general meeting had approved a scheme based on partial revival of the company's spinning operation.
The appellate court accepted additional undertakings from a developer who was not a member, creditor, or other person identified as entitled to participate in approval under the statutory procedure.
Those undertakings materially changed the scheme, including the proposed use and transfer of the mill land and obligations concerning industrial activity.
The changed scheme had not been placed before a further meeting for approval by the requisite majority.
members.legal_principle: Section 392 of the Companies Act, 1956, permits modifications necessary for the proper working of an arrangement but does not authorise substantial changes to the arrangement or its essential terms. Such changes require approval at a meeting under Section 391. Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd. (1997) 1 SCC 579 requires compliance with the statutory meeting and approval procedure before a scheme can be sanctioned.
members.conclusion: The material modifications required fresh approval at a meeting under Section 391; the appellate court could not approve them as mere modifications for proper working under Section 392. The matter was remitted for a meeting and fresh consideration by the Company Court.

predicates.scheme_proceeding: A proceeding was conducted to consider or approve a proposed arrangement for a company.
predicates.court_approved_scheme_materially_changes: The court-approved arrangement materially differed from the terms approved at the meeting.
predicates.fresh_meeting_approval_absent: The changed arrangement had not been submitted to a further meeting for approval by the requisite majority.

members.legal_issue: A court considering interim relief must determine that the case warrants the relief rather than routinely granting it and leaving the opposing party to seek its discharge.
material_facts: The company repeatedly sought court orders that gave it time or permission to proceed while it remained in default of payment obligations to the public authority.
The Court observed that interim orders had sometimes been granted mechanically and that applications to vacate them had resulted only in repeated adjournments.
The Court stated that such orders could cause harm to the opposing party and to the public interest.
members.legal_principle: The power to grant interim injunctions or stays requires judicial consideration of whether the case warrants the relief before the order is made. The Court stated that the court’s obligation cannot be displaced by directing the opposing party to seek vacation of an order granted mechanically.
members.conclusion: Before granting an interim injunction or stay, a court must satisfy itself that the case calls for that order; it should not shift the burden to the opposing party to apply to vacate a routinely granted order.

predicates.interim_relief_application: A party asks a court for an interim injunction, stay, or comparable temporary order.
predicates.proposed_order_could_harm_opposing_party: The proposed temporary order may cause harm to the opposing party or affect the public interest.

members.legal_issue: Courts deciding interim relief should assess practical justice and the parties’ competing risks rather than automatically refusing to decide matters that overlap with the merits of the suit.
material_facts: The interim dispute concerned possession of the same properties whose possession was at issue in the suit.
The suit had not been finally decided, and the interim dispute had reached the Supreme Court.
members.legal_principle: The Court stated that the practical realities of delay make strict neutrality or automatic refusal to decide an interim matter impracticable. It directed courts to weigh the consequences for both parties, consider partial relief, and exercise judicial discipline when interim findings overlap with issues for trial.
members.conclusion: Courts should decide interim matters when necessary, while considering whether relief can rest on issues distinct from the main suit, whether partial relief would suffice, and the consequences to each party if relief is granted or refused; interim relief amounting to a pre-trial decree should be avoided where possible.

predicates.interim_relief_proceeding: A court is deciding an application for relief before the main proceeding has been finally determined.
predicates.interim_issues_overlap_with_trial: The issues relevant to interim relief are connected with issues that will be decided at trial.
predicates.immediate_relief_is_needed: The circumstances call for a decision on relief before the main proceeding is finally determined.

members.legal_issue: Courts should not invalidate economic policy choices unless they clearly violate law or the Constitution or are shockingly arbitrary.
material_facts: The government adopted de-licensing as part of its economic policy after committee recommendations and consideration of the industry’s development.
The challengers disputed the policy and the process by which it was adopted, but no violation of law was shown in the notification or press note.
The lower court had relied on suspicions and conjectures about illegality and unfairness.
members.legal_principle: Courts ordinarily defer to executive and legislative choices in economic and fiscal matters, and do not assess their relative wisdom. Judicial intervention is limited to clear statutory or constitutional violation, or arbitrariness so extreme as to be shockingly arbitrary. The Court relied on Balco Employees’ Union v. Union of India, Premium Granites v. State of Tamil Nadu, M.P. Oil Extraction v. State of M.P., Ugar Sugar Works Ltd. v. Delhi Administration, Bhavesh D. Parish v. Union of India, Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal, Prag Ice & Oil Mills v. Union of India, Sitaram Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Union of India, India Cement Ltd. v. Union of India, and Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass. It also stated that legitimate expectation does not restrict an authority’s choice where it is empowered to decide policy.
members.conclusion: The economic policy was not open to invalidation on the grounds advanced, and the notification and press note were valid.

predicates.economic_policy_challenge: A party asked a court to invalidate a government choice concerning economic or regulatory policy.
predicates.no_clear_legal_or_constitutional_conflic: The record did not show a clear conflict between the policy and a legal or constitutional requirement.
predicates.policy_not_shockingly_arbitrary: The policy was not shown to be shockingly arbitrary.

members.legal_issue: A court may invalidate legislation only when its conflict with the Constitution is clear, and should uphold a reasonable constitutional interpretation, particularly for economic or tax measures.
material_facts: The High Court had invalidated the deposit condition as arbitrary and beyond the object of the Stamp Act.
The Supreme Court considered the challenged amendment an economic measure intended to prevent evasion and secure prompt revenue collection.
The Court found no clear constitutional violation and emphasized that invalidating legislation is a grave step.
members.legal_principle: The Court relied on the presumption of constitutionality and the requirement of a clear constitutional transgression, as stated in Charanjit Lal Chowdhury v. Union of India, M.H. Quareshi v. State of Bihar, State of Bihar v. Bihar Distillery Ltd., Union of India v. Elphinstone Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., and Kedarnath v. State of Bihar. It endorsed Thayer’s doctrine of judicial restraint, relied on R.K. Garg v. Union of India for greater latitude in reviewing economic legislation, and stated that a court should prefer a constitutional interpretation where one is reasonably available.
members.conclusion: The amendment could not be invalidated on the grounds advanced; the Court applied a presumption of constitutionality and upheld the legislation.

predicates.legislation_is_challenged_as_unconstitut: A party asks a court to invalidate legislation on constitutional grounds.
predicates.economic_or_tax_measure: The challenged legislation regulates an economic or tax matter.
predicates.no_clear_constitutional_conflict: The legislation’s conflict with the Constitution has not been established clearly and beyond reasonable doubt.

members.legal_issue: A village is unsettled on the date of resumption when no valid rent-rate settlement had been made applicable by that date, even if later rates are given retrospective effect.
material_facts: The rent-rate settlement made before resumption was quashed for failure to follow the prescribed procedure.
Replacement rent rates were fixed after resumption and were made retrospectively applicable from an earlier date.
The compensation authority used the replacement rates to treat the village as settled on the date of resumption.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 2(n) and 6(3)(a)(i) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, a village is settled for compensation purposes when rent rates determined in settlement operations have been made applicable. A settlement quashed for procedural invalidity leaves no valid determination. Section 86 of the Jaipur State Grants Land Tenures Act, 1947 permits rent to be payable from an earlier date, but retrospective rent realization is distinct from the prior effectuation of a valid settlement. No earlier judicial cases are relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: The quashed settlement left no valid determination of rent rates, and the later rates did not make the village settled on the date of resumption. The village had to be treated as unsettled.

predicates.compensation_claim_on_resumption: A party sought compensation for property or rights taken on resumption.
predicates.valid_rent_rates_effective_before_resump: Valid rent rates from a settlement had been made applicable before the resumption took effect.

members.legal_issue: Compensation for an unsettled village must be determined by reference to actual rental income rather than rates from a later settlement.
material_facts: The village was unsettled on the date of resumption because no valid rent-rate settlement had taken effect by then.
The compensation authority calculated compensation using rates fixed after resumption.
The governing compensation scheme provided a method based on actual rental income for an unsettled village.
members.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952 provides for compensation for an unsettled village to be assessed on actual rental income during the specified agricultural years. For a settled village, section 6(3)(a)(i), read with section 2(n), uses the applicable settlement rent rates. No earlier judicial cases are relied on for this holding.
members.conclusion: Compensation had to be redetermined treating the village as unsettled and using actual rental income under section 7 of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952.

predicates.resumption_compensation_proceeding: A proceeding determines compensation payable because property or rights were resumed.
predicates.village_unsettled_at_resumption: No valid rent-rate settlement had been made applicable to the village by the time of resumption.

members.legal_issue: An agent who acquires property for a principal while acting in a fiduciary capacity holds it for the principal, and the prohibition on benami claims does not bar the principal’s claim to title and possession in those circumstances.
material_facts: The purchaser acted as the claimant’s agent and power-of-attorney holder in managing the claimant’s properties.
The purchase and improvement expenses were met from the claimant’s funds.
The purchaser acquired the property for the claimant’s benefit but held the sale certificate in his own name without the claimant’s knowledge or consent.
The claimant sought declaration of title and recovery of possession.
members.legal_principle: Section 88 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, requires a person acting in a fiduciary capacity to hold a benefit obtained in that capacity for the person whose interests the fiduciary was bound to protect. Section 4(3)(b) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act excludes property held by a trustee or other person in a fiduciary capacity for another from the prohibition in Section 4. Section 7 of that Act did not repeal Section 88 of the Trusts Act. No earlier cases are cited.
members.conclusion: The agent held the property in trust for the claimant; the benami prohibition did not prevent the claimant from obtaining declaration of title and possession.

rule.if: civil_property_claim and agent_acted_in_fiduciary_capacity and property_acquired_for_principal and principal_funds_used_for_acquisition

predicates.civil_property_claim: A claimant brought a civil claim seeking rights to property held in another person’s name.
predicates.agent_acted_in_fiduciary_capacity: The person who acquired the property was acting as an agent or in another fiduciary capacity for the claimant.
predicates.property_acquired_for_principal: The property was acquired for the benefit of the person whose interests the acquirer was bound to protect.
predicates.principal_funds_used_for_acquisition: The acquisition was funded by the person for whose benefit the property was acquired.

members.legal_issue: The prohibition on asserting rights in property held in another person’s name does not bar a claim where the named holder held the property in a fiduciary capacity for the claimants’ benefit.
material_facts: The property had been occupied by a deceased family member as a tenant, and the family members’ tenancy interests would ordinarily have devolved on her legal heirs.
The property was transferred into one heir’s name because the public authority required transfer to a single individual, not because the other heirs had abandoned their interests.
The other family members continued to evince an interest in the property and contributed, along with their father, to the purchase consideration.
The family members were closely related, and the claimants continued in possession of the property.
The suit to establish co-ownership was filed after the legislation took effect, although the sale deed had been executed earlier.
members.legal_principle: Sections 2(a) and 4(1), (2) and (3)(b) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 apply to a post-enactment suit concerning property transferred before enactment, subject to the statutory exception for property held by a trustee or another person in a fiduciary capacity for another’s benefit. A fiduciary relationship connotes trust and confidence on one side and good faith on the other, and may extend beyond technical trustee relationships; its existence is determined from the factual context. The Court relied on Central Board of Secondary Education v. Adiya Bandopadhyay (2011) 8 SCC 497 for the meaning of fiduciary relationship. The High Court had also referred to Section 45 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, but the Supreme Court affirmed the result on the fiduciary exception.
members.conclusion: The transaction fell within the fiduciary-capacity exception, so the suit was not barred by the prohibition on recovering property held benami.

predicates.ownership_claim_against_named_holder: A claimant brings a suit asserting an ownership right in property held in another person’s name.
predicates.property_held_for_claimants_benefit: The property was held for the benefit of the claimant or claimants.
