predicates.named_holder_in_fiduciary_capacity: The person named as holder occupied a position of trust and confidence toward the claimant or claimants in relation to the property.

members.legal_issue: A suit by a licensor to recover possession from a gratuitous licensee is within the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court when the property is within its territorial jurisdiction and no other applicable law excludes the suit.
material_facts: The occupants were permitted to use a bedroom without paying consideration and to share the hall and kitchen as common amenities.
After the permission was revoked, the occupants did not vacate, and the property owners sued to recover possession.
The suit concerned immovable property within the Small Causes Court’s territorial jurisdiction.
The Small Causes Court found the occupants to be gratuitous licensees and ordered eviction.
members.legal_principle: Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, as amended in 1976, gives the Small Causes Court jurisdiction over suits between licensors and licensees concerning recovery of possession of immovable property, irrespective of the subject matter’s value. Section 41(2) excludes matters to which specified or other applicable laws apply. The term “licensee” is not defined in the PSCC Act and is used in its wider, ordinary sense, consistent with the definition of licence in Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, which does not require payment of consideration. It is not confined to the narrower, consideration-based meaning in Section 5(4A) of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947; suits governed by that Act fall within the Section 41(2) exclusion. In Mansukhlal Dhanraj Jain v. Eknath Vithal Ogale, the Court identified the relevant jurisdictional conditions as a suit between licensor and licensee (or landlord and tenant) relating to recovery of possession of property in Greater Bombay (or recovery of fees or rent). The Court also applied the ordinary-meaning approach to statutory interpretation and relied on State of Punjab v. Brig. Sukhjit Singh for the principle that payment of a licence fee is not essential to a licence.
members.conclusion: The term “licensee” in Section 41(1) of the PSCC Act includes a gratuitous licensee. The Small Causes Court may entertain and try a licensor’s suit for possession against such a licensee, subject to the exclusion in Section 41(2); the appeals were dismissed.

rule.if: is_suit_by_property_grantor_against_permitted_occupant and suit_seeks_recovery_of_immovable_property_possession and property_within_small_causes_territory and occupant_is_gratuitous_licensee and not special_rent_regime_applies

predicates.is_suit_by_property_grantor_against_perm: A person who granted another permission to use property brings a suit against that occupant.
predicates.suit_seeks_recovery_of_immovable_propert: The suit seeks recovery of possession of immovable property.
predicates.property_within_small_causes_territory: The property is within the territorial jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court.
predicates.occupant_is_gratuitous_licensee: The occupant uses the property with the grantor’s permission and pays no consideration for that permission.
predicates.special_rent_regime_applies: The suit is governed by a special rent-control regime that displaces this court’s jurisdiction.

members.legal_issue: A suit by a person claiming to be a licensee against an alleged licensor for an injunction protecting possession from threatened unlawful dispossession relates to recovery of possession and falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the designated small causes court when the property is within its territorial area.
material_facts: In both suits, the plaintiffs alleged that they occupied the premises under licences granted by the defendants and paid or were liable to pay consideration for those licences.
The plaintiffs sought injunctions to prevent the defendants from dispossessing them or interfering with their possession without due process of law.
The premises were immovable property within the relevant territorial area.
The court considered jurisdiction on the plaint allegations, taking them to be true, rather than deciding the parties’ competing claims on the merits.
members.legal_principle: Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, gives the Small Causes Court exclusive jurisdiction over suits between licensor and licensee relating to recovery of possession of immovable property within the specified area. The words “relating to” are broad and encompass an injunction suit seeking to prevent a licensor from forcibly recovering possession. The substance of the relief and the plaint allegations govern; a declaration of licensee status need not be separately sought. Section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act uses materially similar language. The Court relied on Renusagar Power Co. v. General Electric Co. for the broad meaning of “relating to,” Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for the breadth of related expressions, and Babulal Bhuramal v. Nandram Shivram and Natraj Studios v. Navrang Studios on suits concerning possession and exclusive jurisdiction. It also approved the same approach in Ambalal v. Narmada, Ramkishore v. Vijaybahadursingh, and Dattatreya Krishna v. Jairam Ganesh. A pure possessory suit of the kind contemplated by Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, stands on a different footing because the claimant need not establish a licensor-licensee relationship or title.
members.conclusion: The suits related to recovery of possession and could be entertained only by the Small Causes Court, not the City Civil Court. The appeals were dismissed, with the plaints to be returned for presentation to the proper court.

rule.if: licensee_injunction_suit and license_relationship_pleaded and property_within_forum_area and threatened_unlawful_dispossession

predicates.licensee_injunction_suit: A person claiming to occupy property as a licensee sues the alleged licensor for an injunction protecting possession.
predicates.license_relationship_pleaded: The claimant pleads a licensor-licensee relationship between the parties.
predicates.property_within_forum_area: The property is within the territorial area assigned to the specialized small causes court.
predicates.threatened_unlawful_dispossession: The claimant alleges that the licensor threatens to dispossess the claimant without following lawful process.

members.legal_issue: A tax on machinery cannot be imposed as a tax on land or buildings when the legislature's taxing authority extends only to land and buildings.
material_facts: The taxation rules treated specified plant and machinery situated in or on land or buildings as part of the property for fixing rateable value.
The resulting property tax included machinery, even though the machinery was located in or on the building for use in operating the factory.
The relevant legislative taxing authority extended to taxes on land and buildings.
members.legal_principle: Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution authorises taxes on land and buildings, not on machinery merely because it is situated in or on a building. In re The Central Provinces and Berar Act No. XIV of 1938, [1939] F.C.R. 18, and Diamond Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, [1961] 3 S.C.R. 242, were considered on the limits of construing legislative entries: they are read broadly, but not beyond the reasonable meaning of their words. Ralla Ram v. Province of East Punjab, [1948] F.C.R. 207, was also considered in relation to legislative competence and taxation.
members.conclusion: Rule 7(2), insofar as it authorised taxation of plant and machinery as part of land or buildings, was beyond the legislative competence of the State.

predicates.property_tax_assessment_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a municipal property-tax assessment.
predicates.machinery_included_in_property_tax: The assessment treats machinery situated in or on a property as part of the taxable property.
predicates.taxing_power_limited_to_land_and_buildin: The relevant taxing authority extends to land and buildings but not to machinery merely because it is situated there.

members.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot impose a cess on entry into factory premises by treating those premises as a local area within the State’s legislative authority over local-area taxes.
material_facts: A state law authorised a cess on sugarcane entering an area specified by notification.
The notification imposed the cess on sugarcane entering areas comprising factories that crossed a specified quantity threshold.
The area relevant to the levy was factory premises, not an area administered by a municipality, panchayat, or other local body.
members.legal_principle: Entry 52 of List II concerns taxes on the entry of goods into a local area, which, when within a State, means an area administered by a local body; factory premises are not such a local area. The Court followed Diamond Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Jaora Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. v. State of M.P., which held that a levy on entry into factory premises did not fall within Entry 52 and that no other State or Concurrent List entry supported the law.
members.conclusion: The state law was beyond the State Legislature’s competence and could not be saved by construing “an area” to mean a local area.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_taxing_law and state_levy_on_entry and levy_area_is_factory_premises and area_not_administered_by_local_body

predicates.challenge_to_state_taxing_law: The proceeding challenges the validity of a state law imposing a tax or cess.
predicates.state_levy_on_entry: The state measure imposes a levy when goods enter an area.
predicates.levy_area_is_factory_premises: The area to which the levy applies consists of factory premises.
predicates.area_not_administered_by_local_body: The area is not administered by a municipality, panchayat, or another local body.

members.legal_issue: A court may summon a person who is not already an accused during trial only when evidence before it provides a substantially stronger basis than a mere prima facie case.
material_facts: The complainant applied during the trial to add persons who had not been charge-sheeted as accused.
The trial court considered the evidence recorded in court and dismissed the application; the High Court reversed that decision.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence recorded at trial did not provide the required strong and cogent basis for summoning the proposed accused.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court may act on material brought before it during the trial, including examination-in-chief not yet tested by cross-examination, but the required satisfaction is stronger than that for framing a charge and falls short of satisfaction that the evidence would lead to conviction. The power must be exercised sparingly, not casually. The Court relied on Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab (2014) 3 SCC 92 and Brijendra Singh v. State of Rajasthan (2017) 7 SCC 706.
members.conclusion: The power to add a person as an accused during trial is discretionary and extraordinary and may be exercised only on strong and cogent evidence; the evidence here did not meet that threshold.

predicates.proceeding_is_trial_request_to_add_non_a: A court is considering during an ongoing criminal trial whether to add a person who is not already an accused.
predicates.trial_evidence_is_strong_and_cogent: Evidence brought before the court during trial strongly and cogently indicates the proposed person's involvement, beyond mere probability or a prima facie case.

members.legal_issue: The threshold for summoning a person who is not already an accused to stand trial with the accused on the basis of evidence recorded during trial is higher than a prima facie case but lower than satisfaction that the evidence would establish guilt if unrebutted.
material_facts: During the trial, the prosecution sought to summon additional persons on the basis of the complainant’s testimony.
The complainant attributed specific roles to the proposed additional accused and said they were present during and participated in the attack.
members.legal_principle: Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits a court to proceed against a person who is not already an accused if the evidence indicates that the person committed an offence for which they could be tried with the accused. Under Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab, including its discussion of Vikas v. State of Rajasthan, this discretionary and extraordinary power must be exercised sparingly on strong and cogent evidence. The evidence need not establish guilt to the point that it would result in conviction if unrebutted, and the court must not form an opinion on guilt when applying this threshold.
members.conclusion: The power to summon an additional accused requires strong and cogent evidence, more than mere probability of complicity or the prima facie standard used at the framing-of-charge stage, but does not require satisfaction that the evidence would lead to conviction if unrebutted.

predicates.additional_accused_application_during_tr: The prosecution applied during a criminal trial to have a person not already charged proceed to trial with the accused.
predicates.witness_attributed_specific_roles: A witness gave testimony attributing specific roles in the alleged offence to the proposed additional accused.
predicates.additional_person_may_be_summoned_on_str: A proposed additional accused may be summoned when the evidence is strong and cogent, exceeds the prima facie standard used at the framing-of-charge stage, and does not have to establish that conviction would follow if it went unrebutted.

members.legal_issue: A trust with continuing, substantial secular or family benefits alongside charitable or religious purposes is not held exclusively for charitable or religious purposes.
material_facts: The deeds combined specified charitable or religious expenditure with substantial provisions for family maintenance and other family benefits.
The family provisions remained operative, and the appellants did not claim that the beneficiaries had been exhausted.
The governing statute applied notwithstanding contrary laws or instruments and provided an exemption only for property held exclusively for charitable or religious purposes.
members.legal_principle: Sections 3, 4, and 5 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 provided for the Act’s overriding effect and the vesting of intermediaries’ estates and rights, while section 6(1)(i) allowed retention only where the relevant holding was exclusively for charitable or religious purposes. The word “exclusively” restricts the exemption to holdings solely within those purposes, and the exemption cannot be enlarged beyond the statutory words. The meanings of charitable and religious purpose are set by sections 2(c) and 2(n), respectively.
members.conclusion: The wakfs did not qualify for the exemption because their operative purposes included substantial secular and family purposes as well as charitable or religious purposes; the appeals were dismissed.

predicates.claim_under_retention_exemption: The proceeding involved a claim to retain property under an exemption from a property-vesting law.
predicates.charitable_or_religious_purposes_present: The trust or endowment provided for at least one charitable or religious purpose.
predicates.continuing_substantial_family_or_secular: The trust or endowment also provided substantial benefits for family members or other secular purposes.
predicates.family_or_secular_purposes_not_inoperati: The family or secular provisions remained operative rather than having ended or become inoperative.

members.legal_issue: A trust remains within the scope of the provision governing public charitable or religious trusts when it provides benefits to the founder’s family as well as devoting a substantial portion of its income to public charitable or religious purposes.
material_facts: The deed dedicated the property to religious purposes, maintenance of the settlor’s relations and descendants, and the poor and meritorious.
The deed required an annual sum to be spent on mosques and religious schools and on helping the poor and needy, and provided for further charitable contributions if funds permitted.
The deed also provided for the maintenance of the settlor’s family and descendants.
members.legal_principle: Under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, whether a trust falls within its scope depends on whether it was created substantially for a public charitable or religious purpose. Family benefits do not take a trust outside the section where a substantial portion of its income is devoted to public charitable or religious purposes. The Court relied on S. Massirat Hossain v. Hossain Ahmad Chowdhury and Vaidya Nath Aiyyar v. Swaminatha Ayyar.
members.conclusion: The trust was created substantially for a public charitable or religious purpose and fell within the scope of section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, notwithstanding its provisions benefiting the settlor’s family.

predicates.trust_created_by_dedication: A settlor permanently dedicated property to be held and administered as a trust.
predicates.substantial_income_for_public_charity_or: The trust deed directed a substantial portion of the trust income to public charitable or religious purposes.
predicates.family_benefits_also_provided: The trust deed also provided benefits for the settlor’s family or descendants.

members.legal_issue: A trustee is assessable at the maximum rate when the beneficiaries’ shares in the trust property are indeterminate on the relevant assessment dates.
material_facts: On the relevant valuation dates, the settlor and his wife were alive and entitled to maintenance from the trust property and to reside in part of it.
The settlor’s sons had rights to maintenance and education from the trust property.
The trust deed also provided for the children’s benefit, and the beneficiaries’ interests were not confined to fixed, ascertainable shares on the relevant dates.
members.legal_principle: Under Section 21(4) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, as it stood at the relevant time, a trustee is assessed at the maximum rate where the shares of the beneficiaries are indeterminate. Rights to maintenance, education, or residence from trust property may make those shares indeterminate.
members.conclusion: Because the beneficiaries’ shares were indeterminate on the relevant dates, the trustee had to be assessed under Section 21(4) as it then stood, at the maximum rate.

predicates.trust_asset_wealth_tax_assessment: The proceeding is an assessment of wealth tax on assets held in trust.
predicates.trustee_holds_under_written_trust: A trustee holds the assets under a written trust instrument.
predicates.beneficiary_shares_indeterminate: The beneficiaries’ shares in the trust property cannot be determined on the relevant assessment dates, including because beneficiaries have rights to support or residence from the property.

members.legal_issue: Income received by a wakf manager is taxable at the maximum rate when the beneficiaries’ individual shares are indeterminate.
material_facts: The wakf deed directed the manager to use income for maintenance of family members, religious ceremonies, charitable purposes, and other expenses, and to invest any surplus in income-producing property.
The deed specified no individual shares in the income; beneficiaries had a right to maintenance according to their requirements, with allocation left to the manager’s discretion.
The income was assessed through the wakf’s manager, and the dispute concerned whether the first proviso to section 41(1) applied.
members.legal_principle: Under section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, income received by a trustee on behalf of beneficiaries is generally assessed as it would be in the beneficiaries’ hands. The first proviso requires assessment at the maximum rate where the beneficiaries’ individual shares are indeterminate or unknown. Shares are indeterminate where a deed grants only a right to maintenance according to requirements and leaves allocation to the manager’s discretion; the fact that beneficiaries can be identified does not establish specified shares.
members.conclusion: The beneficiaries’ individual shares were indeterminate under the deed, so the income was assessable at the maximum rate under the first proviso to section 41(1).

rule.if: trust_income_tax_assessment and deed_grants_only_maintenance_rights and manager_controls_allocation and deed_specifies_no_individual_shares

predicates.trust_income_tax_assessment: An income-tax assessment concerns income received by a manager under a trust arrangement on behalf of beneficiaries.
predicates.deed_grants_only_maintenance_rights: The deed gives beneficiaries a right to maintenance according to their requirements rather than a defined share of income.
predicates.manager_controls_allocation: The deed leaves the allocation of income among beneficiaries to the manager’s discretion.
predicates.deed_specifies_no_individual_shares: The deed does not expressly or by necessary implication specify each beneficiary’s share of income.

members.legal_issue: A licensee whose licence derived from a tenant does not obtain statutory tenant status when the tenant’s interest and the licence have ended before the qualifying date.
material_facts: The petitioners claimed statutory protection as licensees under an agreement with the tenant.
The tenant’s contractual tenancy ended after notice, and her statutory tenancy ended when the ejectment decree was passed, both before the qualifying date.
The petitioners’ licence depended on the tenant’s interest in the premises and had ended with that interest.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 5(4A), 14(2) and 15A(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a licensee must be in occupation under a subsisting licence on the qualifying date to claim the statutory benefit. A licence granted by a tenant ordinarily ends when the tenant’s interest ends; section 14(2) operates from the loss of the licensee’s status and may then make the erstwhile licensee a tenant of the landlord on the terms of the licence. Madhusudan A. Mahale v. P.M. Gidh was held inapplicable.
members.conclusion: The petitioners were not licensees under a subsisting agreement on the qualifying date and were not entitled to become tenants of the landlord under the statutory protection claimed.

rule.if: licensee_protection_claim and licence_granted_by_tenant and licensor_tenancy_ended_before_qualifying_date and licence_ended_with_licensor_tenancy

predicates.licensee_protection_claim: The occupant claimed statutory protection on the basis of being a licensee.
predicates.licence_granted_by_tenant: The occupant’s licence was granted by a person who held the premises as a tenant.
predicates.licensor_tenancy_ended_before_qualifying: The licensor’s tenancy ended before the date on which the occupant had to qualify for statutory protection.
predicates.licence_ended_with_licensor_tenancy: The occupant’s licence ended when the licensor’s tenancy and interest in the premises ended.

members.legal_issue: A licensee whose licence was no longer subsisting at the statutory qualifying date did not acquire deemed tenancy or rent-law protection under the statutory provisions for qualifying licensees.
material_facts: The occupant’s leave-and-licence agreement had been terminated years before the statutory qualifying date.
The occupant was not in occupation under a subsisting licence on that qualifying date.
The occupant’s earlier suit asserting tenant status had been dismissed, and the finding that the occupant was a licensee operated as res judicata.
members.legal_principle: Sections 5(4A) and 15A of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 require that a licensee be in occupation under a subsisting licence on the statutory qualifying date for the legal fiction of tenancy to apply. A qualifying licensee in premises of a cooperative housing society is deemed to be a tenant and may invoke the Act, including the forum provisions in section 28; a person whose licence was already terminated does not qualify. The Court also relied on section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for the binding effect of the earlier determination that the occupant was a licensee, not a tenant.
members.conclusion: The occupant did not acquire deemed-tenant status under section 15A and was not protected by the Rent Act.

predicates.licensee_protection_proceeding: An occupant claims statutory protection on the basis of having occupied premises as a licensee.
predicates.licence_ended_before_qualifying_date: The occupant’s licence had ended before the date on which the statute requires qualifying occupation.
predicates.no_subsisting_licence_at_qualifying_date: The occupant was not in occupation under a continuing licence on the statutory qualifying date.

members.legal_issue: A lease deed granting a fixed initial term and providing for rent enhancement in connection with renewals does not permit enhancement during the initial term when the renewal provisions operate only at its end.
material_facts: The deed granted a fixed initial lease term at a stated annual rent, in consideration of a premium.
The renewal covenant provided for new leases at the end of the term granted and at the end of successive renewal terms.
A separate covenant made rent subject to enhancement on a renewal.
The lessor’s successor increased the rent and demanded arrears during the initial term.
The lessee sought a declaration that the rent could not be enhanced during that term.
members.legal_principle: A deed must be construed from its language read as a whole, ordinarily applying the literal rule unless it produces an absurd result. The construction should give effect to all clauses rather than render any nugatory. Sections 90–94 of the Indian Evidence Act give statutory recognition to the primary rule of construction, subject to the exceptions in Sections 95–98. Where uncertainty in a grant cannot be resolved, ambiguous words may be disregarded so that clear operative terms prevail; where two reasonable constructions remain, the construction favouring the grantee over the grantor is preferred. The Court relied on Monypenny v. Monypenny, Re Meredith, ex parte Chick, Radha Sunder Dutta v. Mohd. Jahadur Rahim, Sahebzada Mohd. Kamgar Shah v. Jagdish Chandra Rao Dhabel Deo, Smt. Bina Das Gupta v. Sachindra Mohan Das Gupta, Glynn v. Margetson & Co., and Raja Rajendra Chand v. Mst. Sukhi. It did not apply a special rule construing grants in favour of the sovereign, particularly where the grant was for valuable consideration.
members.conclusion: The enhancement clause could operate only upon the grant of a fresh lease after expiry of the initial term, so rent could not be enhanced during the initial lease. The appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: lease_deed_interpretation_case and fixed_initial_lease_term and renewal_starts_at_end_of_term and enhancement_is_tied_to_renewal and whole_deed_supports_end_of_term_trigger

predicates.lease_deed_interpretation_case: The proceeding concerns the interpretation of a deed granting a lease.
predicates.fixed_initial_lease_term: The deed states a fixed term for the initial lease.
predicates.renewal_starts_at_end_of_term: The deed provides that renewal is to take place at the end of the term already granted.
predicates.enhancement_is_tied_to_renewal: The deed connects rent enhancement to the grant of a renewal lease.
predicates.whole_deed_supports_end_of_term_trigger: The operative grant and the deed’s other terms support reading the renewal provisions as taking effect only when the initial term ends.

members.legal_issue: Rent cannot be enhanced during a fixed contractual lease term when the lease does not authorize an increase during that term.
material_facts: A lessee’s lease ran for a fixed three-year term at a stated rent.
The lease provided for renewal for a further term at rent determined by the government, but did not authorize an increase during the initial three-year term.
The authority sought to apply the enhanced rent before that initial term expired.
members.legal_principle: The terms of the lease controlled during its fixed initial term. The provision allowing renewal at rent determined by the government applied to the renewal term, not to an increase during the initial term.
members.conclusion: The enhanced rent was not valid during the initial three-year term but was valid from the start of the renewal term; the lessee was entitled to pay the contractual rent during the initial term.

predicates.government_lease_rent_proceeding: The proceeding concerns rent charged under a government lease.
predicates.fixed_term_lease: The lease sets a fixed period during which the tenancy continues on stated terms.
predicates.rent_increase_not_authorized_during_fixe: The lease does not authorize the lessor to increase rent during the fixed term.

members.legal_issue: A stepchild is not included among the children who inherit first from a female Hindu who dies intestate, and cannot share in that category simultaneously with her own child.
material_facts: A woman died intestate leaving property that had devolved to her from her husband.
She was survived by her son from that husband and by the son of her husband’s other wife, who claimed a share alongside her son.
The lower courts held that the woman’s own son was entitled to the property.
members.legal_principle: Under sections 15(1)(a) and 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, heirs in an earlier entry take before heirs in a later entry, and heirs within the same entry take simultaneously. “Sons” in section 15(1)(a) includes sons born to the woman by the same or different husbands, illegitimate sons deemed related to their mother under section 3(j), adopted sons, and the children of predeceased sons; it does not include step-sons. The Court reasoned that this accords with the prior Hindu law rule giving a woman’s own son precedence over a step-son, and that a departure from that rule would have required express language. It approved Mallappa Fakirappa Sanna Nagashetti v. Shivappa, Rama Ananda Patil v. Appa Bhima Redekar, Gumam Singh v. Smt. Ass Kaur, and Smt. Kishori Bala Mondal v. Tribhanga Mondal, and overruled Ram Katori v. Prakash Wati.
members.conclusion: The word “sons” in section 15(1)(a) does not include a step-son. A step-son is an heir of the husband under section 15(1)(b), and does not share with the deceased woman’s own children under section 15(1)(a). The son of the deceased woman was therefore entitled to the property in this case.

predicates.female_intestate_succession_case: A female Hindu died without a will and the dispute concerns succession to her estate.
predicates.claimant_is_spouse_child_from_other_unio: A claimant is the child of the deceased woman’s spouse from another union, rather than a child of the deceased woman.
predicates.deceased_has_qualifying_child: The deceased woman was survived by a child, including a child of a predeceased child, who qualifies in the first category of heirs.
predicates.stepchild_not_first_entry_heir: The stepchild is not treated as a first-category child heir who takes alongside the deceased woman’s own qualifying children.

members.legal_issue: A daughter of a predeceased son is not entitled to inherit a Hindu woman’s stridhana under the Mitakshara order of succession when she is not included among the heirs specified in that order.
material_facts: The suit property was found to be the deceased woman’s stridhana, and that finding was not open to challenge in the appeals.
The property was not shulka, and the woman had married in an approved form.
The competing claimants included daughters in the line of a predeceased son; the dispute was whether they could inherit despite not being included in the stated order of succession.
The High Court had held that the plaintiff was the nearest heir and exclusively entitled to the property.
members.legal_principle: Under Yajnyawalcya’s text as explained by Vijnyaneswara in the Mitakshara, and as reflected in paragraph 147 of Mulla’s Principles of Hindu Law, stridhana other than shulka devolves in the specified order, which includes a son and a son’s son but not a son’s daughter. The Court accepted Colebrooke’s translation of the Mitakshara, noting that it accords with other translations and the interpretation in Bhimacharya Bin Venkappacharya v. Ramcharya Bin Bhimacharya. It rejected reliance on Kumar Raghava Surendra Sahi v. Babui Lachmi Kuer and Bai Kesserbai v. Hunsraj Morarji as not deciding this question, and held that the masculine term “son’s son” does not include a daughter, particularly given the distinct ordering of a daughter’s daughter and a daughter’s son.
members.conclusion: The order of succession is exhaustive and does not include a son’s daughter after a son’s son; the daughters’ claim therefore fails, and the appeals are dismissed.

rule.if: stridhana_inheritance_dispute and property_is_not_shulka and applicable_order_ends_descendant_classes_at_sons_son and claimant_is_a_sons_daughter

predicates.stridhana_inheritance_dispute: The dispute concerns succession to a Hindu woman’s stridhana.
predicates.property_is_not_shulka: The property being inherited is not shulka.
predicates.applicable_order_ends_descendant_classes: The applicable order of succession lists a son and a son’s son but does not list a son’s daughter.
predicates.claimant_is_a_sons_daughter: The claimant is a daughter of the deceased woman’s son.
predicates.sons_daughter_is_not_entitled_to_inherit: A son’s daughter is not entitled to inherit under the applicable order of succession.

members.legal_issue: The Constitution does not require auction as the exclusive method for allocating every natural resource, and choosing another method is not unconstitutional solely because an auction was not held.
material_facts: The challenged allocations occurred in a context of coal and power shortages and the Government stated that private participation and investment needed to be encouraged.
The Government explained that competitive bidding was considered but not pursued, including because of concerns about delay, increased input costs and objections from State Governments.

The Court separately found defects in the allocation process, but concluded that the decision not to adopt competitive bidding was not, by itself, so arbitrary or unreasonable as to warrant judicial interference.
members.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 39(b) do not prescribe auction as the exclusive method for distributing natural resources; the method must be assessed in light of the facts, circumstances and policy objective, and the Court may review its legality and constitutionality without choosing an economic policy for the Executive. The Court relied on Natural Resources Allocation, In re, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, including its discussion of Article 39(b), and on Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir, Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal, Haji T.M. Hassan Rawther v. Kerala Financial Corporation, M.P. Oil Extraction v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal and Villianur Iyarkkai Padukappu Maiyam v. Union of India. It also considered Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, whose auction observation was confined to spectrum.
members.conclusion: Auction is not a constitutional requirement for the allocation of all natural resources. The Government’s decision not to pursue competitive bidding in the circumstances described was not, on that ground alone, arbitrary or unreasonable.

predicates.public_interest_challenge_to_natural_res: The proceeding challenges the public allocation of a natural resource.
predicates.government_selected_a_nonauction_method: The government chose to distribute or allocate the resource without an auction.
predicates.a_rational_policy_reason_supported_that_: The government relied on a policy objective or practical circumstances that rationally supported its choice of method.

members.legal_issue: The Constitution does not require every allocation of a natural resource to be made by auction, although a decision to use another method remains subject to judicial review.
material_facts: The State’s policy contemplated granting mining leases without competitive bidding, and the dispute concerned the allocation of a natural resource other than spectrum.
The Court considered that the mining activity principally served private commercial profit and lacked an evident social or welfare purpose.
The Court did not finally adjudicate whether the State’s decision not to auction fresh leases was arbitrary, and did not quash that decision on this ground.
members.legal_principle: Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, (2012) 10 SCC 1, held that auction is not the only constitutionally permissible method for allocating natural resources and that Article 14 does not prescribe a single economic policy. It also held that non-auction methods remain reviewable for arbitrariness and fairness, particularly where scarce resources are allocated to private commercial interests without a social or welfare purpose. The Court discussed Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, (2012) 3 SCC 1, Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary, (2014) 9 SCC 516, and M/s Ajar Enterprises Private Limited v. Satyanarayan Somani, 2017 (10) SCALE 346. Article 39(b) is relevant to whether distribution serves the common good. The Court also noted the State’s authority to choose a lawful method under the MMDR Act and its rules.
members.conclusion: The State was not under a constitutional obligation to grant fresh mining leases by auction. Auction is generally preferable for commercial allocation of natural resources, but it is not constitutionally mandatory in every case; the State’s choice remains reviewable under Article 14. The Court did not finally decide whether the State’s non-auction policy was arbitrary.

predicates.natural_resource_allocation_review: A proceeding examines a public authority’s choice of method for allocating a natural resource.
predicates.resource_is_not_spectrum: The resource being allocated is not spectrum.

members.legal_issue: Machinery embedded in land is immovable property when the circumstances show it was permanently affixed for the continuing use of an industrial plant.
material_facts: The machinery was embedded in the land to form a fertilizer plant and was used in manufacturing fertilizer.

The nature and arrangement of the machinery, and its description in the conveyance schedule, showed that it was installed permanently to operate the factory rather than to be dismantled and sold as machinery or scrap.
members.legal_principle: Whether machinery embedded in land is movable or immovable depends on the facts and circumstances, particularly the intention behind its attachment and the purpose for which it was installed. The Court agreed with the High Court’s reliance on Reynolds v. Ashby & Son (1904 AC 466) and Official Liquidator v. Sri Krishna Deo (AIR 1959 All. 247). Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise, Hyderabad (1998 1 SCC 400) did not control because the machinery there was attached for operational efficiency and could be removed for sale, unlike the permanently installed plant here.
members.conclusion: The machinery was immovable property.

predicates.stamp_duty_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the assessment of stamp duty on a conveyance.
predicates.machinery_embedded_in_land: The machinery was fixed or embedded in land.
predicates.permanent_industrial_use_intended: The circumstances show that the machinery was installed to remain in place for the continuing operation of an industrial plant.

members.legal_issue: A conveyance transfers permanently installed plant and machinery when the agreement, conveyance and surrounding circumstances show that the transaction conveyed the industrial business as a going concern together with that property.
material_facts: The sale agreement provided for transfer of the fertilizer business as a going concern and included the land, buildings, plant and machinery for a single slump price.
The conveyance referred to transferring the fertilizer factory and its business as a going concern, and included a schedule plan depicting the factory machinery.
The machinery was not dismantled and separately delivered apart from the land.
The purchaser’s materials submitted to the income-tax authority included the plant and machinery as part of the property being transferred.
members.legal_principle: The parties’ intention as to what was conveyed must be determined from the conveyance read with the agreement pursuant to which it was executed and the surrounding circumstances. A court may consider prior agreements when determining that intention. Himalaya House Co. Ltd., Bombay v. Chief Controlling Revenue Authority (1972 1 SCC 726) does not establish an absolute bar on considering prior agreements; whether earlier terms are incorporated depends on the facts and the parties’ intention. Under the Stamp Act, the value of property conveyed is relevant to the stamp duty payable.
members.conclusion: The conveyance transferred the vendor’s title to the fertilizer business, including the plant and machinery, and their value could be included in determining stamp duty.

rule.if: stamp_duty_appeal and transaction_is_business_as_going_concern and agreement_includes_plant_and_machinery and conveyance_and_surrounding_evidence_show_transfer

predicates.stamp_duty_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning the assessment of stamp duty on a conveyance.
predicates.transaction_is_business_as_going_concern: The transaction provides for transfer of an operating business as a going concern.
predicates.agreement_includes_plant_and_machinery: The agreement for the transaction includes the plant and machinery among the property to be transferred.
predicates.conveyance_and_surrounding_evidence_show: The conveyance and relevant surrounding evidence indicate that the plant and machinery were included in the transfer.

members.legal_issue: The evidence concerning an alleged conspiracy to obtain compensation for leased government land did not provide sufficient ground to frame charges.
material_facts: The acquired land was Khasmahal land belonging to the Government, and the accused claiming compensation held a lessee’s interest in it.
A letter from that accused referred to the land as government land, and government records and witnesses indicated that its government status was known to the authorities.
The acquisition proceedings and estimates identified the interest being acquired as the Raiyyati or lessee’s interest.

The prosecution relied on the speed of the acquisition and the accused’s knowledge of the compensation estimate as evidence of concerted criminal conduct; the Court considered the sequence of official estimates and approvals and found those circumstances explainable.
The Court found no legal evidence of a meeting of minds between the accused.
members.legal_principle: Under section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the judge assesses the total effect of the prosecution material and may discharge where the material does not provide sufficient ground to proceed. The Court applied the principles in State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh, K. P. Raghavan v. M. H. Abbas, and Almohan Das v. State of West Bengal.
members.conclusion: There was no sufficient ground to try the accused, and the discharge was upheld.

rule.if: special_judge_pretrial_case and alleged_conspiracy_to_obtain_compensation and government_land_status_disclosed and acquisition_identified_lessee_interest and no_evidence_of_meeting_of_minds and prosecution_circumstances_explainable

predicates.special_judge_pretrial_case: A Special Judge is deciding before trial whether the prosecution material warrants proceeding against the accused.
predicates.alleged_conspiracy_to_obtain_compensatio: The prosecution alleges that accused persons conspired to obtain compensation through the acquisition of land.
predicates.government_land_status_disclosed: The person claiming compensation disclosed, or the available records and evidence showed, that the land belonged to the Government.
predicates.acquisition_identified_lessee_interest: The acquisition material identified the interest being acquired as the claimant’s lessee or equivalent limited interest.
predicates.no_evidence_of_meeting_of_minds: The prosecution material contains no legal evidence that the accused agreed or acted together in a conspiracy.
predicates.prosecution_circumstances_explainable: The circumstances relied on by the prosecution, including the pace of the proceedings or knowledge of an estimate, have an explanation consistent with the absence of criminal conduct.

members.legal_issue: The prosecution materials in this case did not provide sufficient ground to try the accused for the alleged conspiracy to obtain compensation by concealing the government’s interest in the land.
material_facts: The accused who held the lease wrote that the land was government land and did not represent it as private property.
Government records and witnesses indicated that the land was government land and that the accused held a lessee’s interest.
The land acquisition officer’s report identified the government’s interest and the accused’s status in relation to the land.
The compensation estimate was submitted to and sanctioned by the government before the accused referred to the amount in a letter.
The acquisition concerned the lessee’s interest, and the amount was accepted as representing the market value of that interest.
The record contained no legal evidence of a meeting of minds between the accused.
The rapid completion of the acquisition proceedings was explained by the acquiring agency’s urgency and the steps taken to obtain prior approval.
members.legal_principle: Applying Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and the principles stated in State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh, the judge may consider the broad probabilities, total effect of the materials and basic infirmities, but must not conduct a roving inquiry or weigh evidence as at trial. Materials that leave only suspicion, rather than grave and unexplained suspicion, may support discharge where two views are equally possible.
members.conclusion: The Court agreed that there was no sufficient ground to try the accused and affirmed the discharge.

rule.if: criminal_case_challenging_discharge and alleged_conspiracy_to_obtain_compensation and government_interest_not_concealed and compensation_estimate_previously_sanctioned and compensation_reflected_lessee_interest and no_evidence_of_meeting_of_minds and rapid_proceedings_explained

predicates.criminal_case_challenging_discharge: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the prosecution challenges an order discharging the accused before trial.
predicates.alleged_conspiracy_to_obtain_compensatio: The prosecution alleges that the accused conspired to obtain compensation through a land acquisition.
predicates.government_interest_not_concealed: The accused disclosed the government’s interest in the land, and records or witnesses also identified that interest.
predicates.compensation_estimate_previously_sanctio: The compensation estimate had been submitted to and approved by the government before the accused referred to the amount.
predicates.compensation_reflected_lessee_interest: The compensation was calculated for the accused’s leasehold or other outstanding private interest, rather than the government’s proprietary interest.
predicates.no_evidence_of_meeting_of_minds: The prosecution materials contain no legal evidence that the accused reached an agreement to carry out the alleged conspiracy.
predicates.rapid_proceedings_explained: The speed of the proceedings is explained by the acquiring agency’s urgency and the administrative steps taken before the award.

members.legal_issue: When the Government already owns the proprietary interest in land, acquisition of another person’s interest does not require acquisition or compensation for the Government’s own interest.
material_facts: The land was Khasmahal land whose proprietary interest belonged to the Government.
The person claiming compensation held a lessee’s or Raiyyati interest, and the acquisition was of that interest.
The acquisition estimate and award concerned the lessee’s interest rather than the Government’s proprietary interest.
members.legal_principle: The Court applied Collector of Bombay v. Nusserwanji Rattanji Mistri and The Special Land Acquisition Officer, Hosanagar v. K. S. Ramachandra Rao: the Government cannot acquire what it already owns, though the value of its interest may be relevant to determining compensation for the outstanding interests being acquired.
members.conclusion: Only the lessee’s interest was acquired; the Government’s proprietary interest was not itself subject to acquisition or compensation.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition of an interest in land.
predicates.government_owns_proprietary_interest: The Government already holds the proprietary interest in the land.
predicates.only_outstanding_lessee_interest_acquire: The acquisition is confined to a lessee’s or other outstanding private interest in the land.

members.legal_issue: When the government already owns an interest in land being acquired, that interest is outside the acquisition, and only the outstanding interests need to be acquired.
material_facts: The land was government land subject to a lease, and the accused held the lessee’s interest.
The acquisition and compensation estimate concerned the lessee’s interest, while the government retained the proprietary interest.
members.legal_principle: In Collector of Bombay v. Nusserwanji Rattanji Mistri, the Court held that a government interest in land is outside the acquisition because the government cannot acquire what it already owns, although the interest’s nature and value may be relevant to determining compensation for the interests outstanding in claimants. The Special Land Acquisition Officer, Hosanagar v. K.S. Ramachandra Rao likewise recognizes that the acquisition officer values the rights of the claimants in the acquired land. These principles apply to acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act.
members.conclusion: The government’s proprietary interest did not itself have to be acquired or compensated; the acquisition could concern only the outstanding lessee’s interest.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the acquisition of land for public use.
predicates.government_already_owns_an_interest: The government already holds an interest in the land being acquired.
predicates.only_outstanding_private_interest_is_sou: The acquisition seeks to obtain the interest in the land that remains outstanding in a private claimant.

members.legal_issue: Authorities must protect adults who marry across caste or religious lines from harassment, threats and violence, and must take action against those responsible.
material_facts: The petition alleged that relatives opposed the woman’s inter-caste marriage and threatened the couple and their relatives.
The petition also alleged assaults, intimidation, detention of a relative, and interference with the husband’s family property.
The Court noted that reports of threats, harassment and violence against adults who marry outside their caste were occurring in several parts of the country.
members.legal_principle: The Court held that threats, harassment and violence against adults who voluntarily enter inter-caste or inter-religious marriages are wholly illegal. It stated that relatives who disapprove may end social relations but may not threaten, commit or instigate violence. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited as the basis for this general direction.
members.conclusion: The Court directed police and administrative authorities throughout the country to ensure that adult couples who marry across caste or religious lines are not harassed, threatened or subjected to violence, and to institute criminal proceedings and take stern action against those responsible in accordance with law.

predicates.adult_intergroup_couple: Two adults entered a marriage across caste or religious lines.
predicates.threats_or_harassment_or_violence: A person threatened, harassed or committed violence against the couple because of their marriage.

members.legal_issue: Authorities must institute criminal proceedings in accordance with law against persons alleged to have committed unlawful acts against a couple and their relatives in reaction to the couple’s inter-caste marriage.
material_facts: The petition alleged that the woman’s brothers assaulted and threatened members of her husband’s family, took possession of property, and caused relatives to be arrested through a false kidnapping report.
The Court directed that criminal proceedings be instituted against the brothers and others involved in the alleged acts.
members.legal_principle: The Court directed criminal proceedings on the basis of the allegations set out in the petition, while requiring that proceedings be conducted in accordance with law. No particular statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this direction.
members.conclusion: The Court directed the concerned authorities to institute criminal proceedings forthwith against the woman’s brothers and others involved, in accordance with law.

predicates.court_proceeding_on_alleged_retaliation: A court is considering a matter in which alleged unlawful conduct is said to have been retaliation for a couple’s marriage.
predicates.alleged_unlawful_acts_against_couple_or_: The petition alleges that persons assaulted, threatened, unlawfully confined or dispossessed the couple or their relatives.

members.legal_issue: The statutory procedure for suits concerning public trusts does not displace a trustee’s ordinary right to sue in the name of an idol to recover trust property.
material_facts: The suit was brought in the name of the temple’s idol, represented by a trustee, to recover property said to belong to the temple.
The property was allegedly held adversely to the trust after the occupants’ permission to reside there had ended.
members.legal_principle: Sections 50 to 52 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act create and regulate an additional statutory right to sue; they do not extinguish the ordinary right of a manager, trustee, or shebait to sue in the usual way on behalf of an idol. The Court rejected the contrary implication drawn from section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure and distinguished Bishwanath v. Shri Thakur Radhaballabhji, [1967] 2 S.C.R. 618, because it addressed section 92 rather than the wider scheme of section 50.
members.conclusion: The statutory procedure in section 50 supplements rather than defeats the ordinary right of a manager, trustee, or shebait to bring a suit in the name of an idol to recover trust property.

predicates.public_trust_property_recovery_proceedin: The proceeding concerns recovery of property belonging to a public trust from a person holding it adversely.
predicates.trustee_sues_for_idol: A trustee brings the recovery suit in the name of the idol on whose behalf the trust property is held.

members.legal_issue: A suit brought on behalf of an idol to establish its title to property and recover possession from an unlawful possessor falls outside the scope of the restrictions governing public religious or charitable trust suits.
material_facts: The suit was brought on behalf of the idol seeking a declaration of its title to property and possession from the purchaser under an alienation made by the temple manager.
The courts below found that the alienation was not for the idol’s benefit and that its consideration was inadequate.
members.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies only where the trust is created for public charitable or religious purposes, there is a breach of trust or a need for the court’s direction in administering it, and the relief sought is one of those enumerated in the section. A suit by an idol to declare its title and recover possession from a person in possession under a void alienation enforces the idol’s private right and seeks relief not enumerated in section 92. The Court relied on Abdur Rahim v. Barkat Ali and Mahant Pragdasji Guru Bhagwandasji v. Patel Ishwarlalbhai Narsibhai, and referred to Mukhda Mannudas Bairagi v. Chagan Kisan Bhawasar, Darshan Lal v. Shibji Maharaj Birajman, and Madhavrao Anandrao Raste v. Shri Omkareshvar Ghat.
members.conclusion: The suit was outside the scope of section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure and was not barred by that section.

predicates.idol_property_recovery_suit: A proceeding is brought on behalf of an idol to recover property claimed as belonging to it.
predicates.seeks_title_declaration_and_possession: The proceeding seeks a declaration of the idol’s title and possession of the property from its possessor.

members.legal_issue: A payment described as premium under a lease is a capital receipt when, in substance, it is the price for transferring the right to enjoy the property, even if paid in instalments, rather than payment for its continuing use.
material_facts: The lessor leased tea estates and their buildings and machinery for a fixed term, transferring a substantive interest in the estates and the right to use them.
The lease separately specified a total premium for the transfer and annual rent for use of the estates; the premium was payable partly at execution and partly in instalments.
The parties were experienced businesspeople and used the terms “premium” and “rent” to describe distinct payments.
The amount of annual rent was substantial, and the instalment schedule for the premium could have accommodated the lessee.
The default clause and the inconclusive comparison of profits before and after the lease did not establish that the premium was disguised rent.
members.legal_principle: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 distinguishes the price paid for transferring a right to enjoy property, called premium, from rent rendered periodically for that enjoyment. The substance of the transaction controls; nomenclature is not conclusive, though it may help establish the parties’ intention. Premium may be paid in one sum or by instalments; the test is whether it is consideration for the tenant being let into possession. The Court applied Raja Bahadur Kamakshya Narain Singh of Ramgarh v. Commissioner of Income-tax, which treated payment for acquiring the lessee’s general right as capital; Member for the Board of Agriculture Income-tax, Assam v. Sindhurani Chaudhurani, which identified salami as consideration for being let into possession; and Chintamani Saran Nath Sah Deo v. Commissioner of Income-tax, which applied that principle to a grant of a right to a capital asset. The lease’s default clause and inconclusive financial comparisons did not displace the substance indicated by its main terms and the separate premium and rent.
members.conclusion: The premium instalment was a capital receipt, not a revenue receipt, and the appeal was dismissed.

rule.if: income_tax_lease_receipt_classification and substantive_interest_transferred and payment_is_price_for_possession and separate_periodic_rent_for_continued_use and premium_paid_in_installments and no_evidence_of_disguised_rent

predicates.income_tax_lease_receipt_classification: The dispute concerns whether a payment received under a lease is a capital or revenue receipt for income-tax purposes.
predicates.substantive_interest_transferred: The lessor transferred a substantive interest in the property and gave the lessee a right to enjoy it for a term.
predicates.payment_is_price_for_possession: The payment was consideration for the lessee being let into possession, rather than payment for the continuing enjoyment of the property.
predicates.separate_periodic_rent_for_continued_use: The lease separately required periodic rent for the lessee’s continuing use of the property.
predicates.premium_paid_in_installments: The payment described as premium was payable partly at execution and partly in instalments.
predicates.no_evidence_of_disguised_rent: The evidence did not establish that the amount described as premium was, in substance, rent.

members.legal_issue: A non-recurring lump-sum premium paid in connection with a lease is a capital receipt rather than a revenue receipt where the circumstances do not establish that it represents rent.
material_facts: The lessees paid a one-time lump sum toward construction of the premises, without a provision to adjust it against rent or repay it.
The lease separately fixed monthly rent, which was to begin after the lease was made.
The lessees took possession after construction was complete.
The tax authorities did not establish facts showing that the payment was revenue in character or that the stipulated rent was unreasonably low.
members.legal_principle: Whether a premium or salami is capital or revenue depends on the facts and circumstances of the case. Prima facie, premium or salami is not income, and the income-tax authorities must show facts that make it a revenue receipt. Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguishes a single premium from recurring rent. The Court applied the principles in Member for the Board of Agricultural Income-tax v. Sindhurani Chaudhurani, and relied on Henriksen v. Grafton Hotel Ltd. and Commissioner of Income-tax, Bihar & Orissa v. Visweshwar Singh, which discussed Commissioner of Income-tax, Bengal v. Shaw Wallace & Company.
members.conclusion: The lump sum had the characteristics of a capital payment and was not a revenue receipt.

rule.if: income_tax_receipt_classification_case and lump_sum_nonrecurring and rent_stipulated_separately and rent_begins_after_lease_grant and possession_follows_completion and not tax_authorities_proved_revenue_character

predicates.income_tax_receipt_classification_case: A court is deciding the character of a receipt for income-tax purposes.
predicates.lump_sum_nonrecurring: The payer made a single payment that was not recurring.
predicates.rent_stipulated_separately: The parties fixed rent separately from the disputed payment.
predicates.rent_begins_after_lease_grant: The agreed rent was payable from a time after the lease was granted.
predicates.possession_follows_completion: The lessee took possession after the leased premises had been completed.
predicates.tax_authorities_proved_revenue_character: The tax authorities established facts showing that the payment was revenue in character.

members.legal_issue: A landlord's prolonged failure to object to a tenant's changed use of premises, followed by raising that change for the first time in an eviction proceeding, supports acceptance of the non-residential use.
material_facts: The premises had been used in part for commercial activity since 1973.
The landlords did not object to that use for seven years.
The landlords first relied on the changed use as a ground for eviction in 1980.
The tenant maintained that mixed use was the basis of the tenancy.
members.legal_principle: The Court inferred acceptance of the non-residential use from the landlords' failure to object for seven years and their raising the matter for the first time when seeking eviction. No earlier case was cited for this conclusion.
members.conclusion: In the circumstances, the landlords had accepted use of the premises for purposes other than residential use, so the changed use did not sustain the eviction petition.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and premises_used_for_nonresidential_purposes and landlord_made_no_objection_for_years and change_first_raised_in_eviction

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from premises whose use was disputed.
predicates.premises_used_for_nonresidential_purpose: The tenant used the premises, at least in part, for purposes other than residential use.
predicates.landlord_made_no_objection_for_years: The landlord knew of the non-residential use and did not object to it over a prolonged period.
predicates.change_first_raised_in_eviction: The landlord first relied on the changed use as a ground when seeking eviction.

members.legal_issue: A landlord’s conduct and the surrounding evidence may establish that a tenant’s construction was made with implied consent, or that the landlord gave up the objection to it.
material_facts: The predecessor landlord omitted the balcony from two notices sent before the eviction suit, despite its presence at the premises.
He testified that he had not objected after the tenants said they would remove the balcony when they vacated.
He paid for a window that provided light and air to the balcony.
The later purchasers continued the pending eviction suit.
members.legal_principle: The court inferred implied consent from the landlord’s conduct and the surrounding evidence. It also observed, relying on Dawsons Bank Ltd. v. Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha, that waiver is an agreement to release or not assert a right, but stated that it was unnecessary to discuss waiver further once the evidence did not establish construction without consent.
members.conclusion: The evidence did not support a finding that the tenants had constructed the balcony without the landlord’s express or implied consent; the circumstances supported implied consent or, alternatively, waiver of the objection.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant on the ground of an unauthorized construction.
predicates.landlord_omitted_construction_from_notic: The landlord sent pre-suit notices while the construction was present but did not identify it as an objection or ground for eviction.
predicates.landlord_accepted_tenant_removal_assuran: The landlord refrained from objecting after the tenant said the construction would be removed when the tenant left.
predicates.landlord_paid_for_feature_serving_constr: The landlord paid for a feature that supplied light or air to the construction.

members.legal_issue: An allegation of inaccurate statements in an application for special leave does not justify rejecting the application when the statements are not shown to be deliberate falsehoods and the issue described was the issue considered below.
material_facts: The respondent objected to special leave, alleging that the appellant had made inaccurate and misleading statements about whether the validity of the deposits had been raised before the Rent Controller and the appellate authority.
The High Court stated that the validity of the deposits was the only point considered by the courts below.
The court found no basis to regard the appellant's statements as deliberate falsehoods of the kind involved in the cited cases.
members.legal_principle: Hari Narain v. Badri Das and Rajabhai Abdul Rehman Munshi v. Vasudev Dhanjibhai Mody concerned gross misstatements in which an applicant had deliberately made false statements or pleas. The court distinguished those cases because the alleged inaccuracies here did not establish deliberate falsehood, and the deposit issue had been considered below.
members.conclusion: The objection to the grant of special leave was rejected.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and material_inaccuracy_alleged and issue_was_considered_below and not deliberate_false_statement_established

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party seeks special leave to appeal from a lower-court decision.
predicates.material_inaccuracy_alleged: The opposing party alleges that the applicant misstated material facts about the proceedings below.
predicates.issue_was_considered_below: The lower courts considered the issue to which the alleged inaccuracy relates.
predicates.deliberate_false_statement_established: The record establishes that the applicant deliberately made a false statement or plea.

members.legal_issue: An inaccurate valuation statement in an application for special leave does not require cancellation of leave when the inaccuracy resulted from an error in the lower court’s judgment, was not deliberately misleading, and was immaterial to the legal issues.
material_facts: The special leave application repeated a valuation stated in the certified copy of the High Court judgment.
The valuation in that judgment was later corrected, with both sides agreeing that the original figure was an error.
The appellant should have been more careful, but the Court found no deliberate attempt to mislead it.
The issues in the appeal concerned the legal applicability of the tenancy legislation, so the valuation was not of much consequence.
members.legal_principle: An applicant for special leave must take care not to make inaccurate, untrue, or misleading statements on material matters. Special leave may be cancelled where a deliberate false statement on a material matter or valuation misleads the Court. The Court referred to Hari Narain v. Badri Das, Sita Bai v. Sonu Vanji Wani, and S. R. Shetty v. Phirozeshah Nusserwanji Golabawalla, but held that the circumstances here did not warrant cancellation.
members.conclusion: The Court declined to cancel the special leave granted.

rule.if: special_leave_application and valuation_error_in_lower_court_judgment and not deliberate_misrepresentation and valuation_immaterial_to_legal_issues

predicates.special_leave_application: A party sought special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.valuation_error_in_lower_court_judgment: The valuation stated in the application came from an erroneous figure in the lower court’s judgment.
predicates.deliberate_misrepresentation: The applicant deliberately made a false statement to mislead the Court.
predicates.valuation_immaterial_to_legal_issues: The valuation did not materially affect the legal issues the Court had to decide.

members.legal_issue: A contractual disclaimer of compensation for inaccurate auction particulars does not bar repudiation and recovery of payment when the available subject matter is substantially reduced after the auction.
material_facts: The auction notice stated that announced quantities were not guaranteed and excluded claims for compensation or other relief if the quantities proved incorrect.
The auction particulars included a substantial number of marked and numbered trees in an area later declared reserved, where cutting was prohibited.
The purchaser refused to accept the coupes after finding that the available timber was substantially less than the auction particulars indicated.
members.legal_principle: A disclaimer directed to compensation for incorrect quantity particulars does not remove the right to repudiate a contract where there is a substantial variance between the subject matter represented at auction and what is actually available. The Court relied on the terms of the sale notice and the principle that a substantial alteration of the foundation of the contract permits repudiation and recovery of the payment; no earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this holding.
members.conclusion: The disclaimer barred a claim for damages or compensation based on inaccurate particulars, but did not prevent the purchaser from repudiating the contract and recovering the payment made when the substantial reduction altered the foundation of the contract.

predicates.auction_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns a contract made through an auction for the right to extract goods or produce.
predicates.quantity_disclaimer_present: The auction terms stated that announced quantity particulars were not guaranteed and excluded compensation claims if they proved inaccurate.
predicates.substantial_post_auction_reduction: After the auction, a substantial part of the goods or produce represented as available became unavailable for extraction.
predicates.buyer_may_reject_contract_and_recover_pa: The buyer may repudiate the contract and recover the payment made toward the purchase price.

members.legal_issue: A purchaser who repudiates the contract after a substantial reduction in the auctioned subject matter is entitled to protection against coercive recovery of unpaid instalments.
material_facts: The purchaser refused to sign the boundary certificate after finding a substantial reduction in the timber available for extraction.
The authorities demanded the remaining instalments and initiated steps to recover them as land revenue.
The authorities later issued a notice proposing termination of the contract and resale of the coupes at the purchaser's risk.
The Supreme Court restored the trial court decree, including its permanent injunction, while modifying only the amount of the refund.
members.legal_principle: The Court restored the trial court decree after holding that the purchaser could repudiate the contract because the substantial reduction altered its foundation; the decree's injunction against recovery of the remaining instalments therefore remained effective.
members.conclusion: The permanent injunction against coercive recovery of the remaining instalments was left in force.

predicates.auction_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns a contract made through an auction for the right to extract goods or produce.
predicates.buyer_entitled_to_reject_contract: The buyer is entitled to repudiate the auction contract because a substantial reduction altered its foundation.
predicates.unpaid_installments_demanded: The seller demanded unpaid instalments after the buyer rejected the contract.
predicates.coercive_recovery_of_unpaid_installments: The seller may not coercively recover the unpaid instalments from the buyer.

members.legal_issue: A qualified rule disregarding certain post-cutoff land transfers to prevent evasion of a land ceiling is a reasonable restriction on property rights.
material_facts: The ceiling law directed the authority to disregard certain transfers made after a specified statutory date if, without the transfer, the land would have been declared surplus.
The law preserved exceptions for transfers made in good faith for adequate consideration under an irrevocable instrument and not for the benefit of the transferor or family members.
The Court found that invalidating transfers made after the cutoff served the purpose of preserving surplus land for redistribution and was not a blanket prohibition.
members.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) was subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6). The legislature could adopt measures ancillary to a land-ceiling policy to prevent transactions defeating that policy; Section 5(6) was upheld as a qualified, purpose-related restriction.
members.conclusion: The Court held the transfer rule fair and valid, and not violative of the property-right restriction in Article 19(1)(f).

predicates.land_ceiling_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges a restriction operating as part of a land-ceiling law.
predicates.post_cutoff_transfers_could_reduce_surpl: Transfers made after a specified cutoff could leave less land available as surplus.
predicates.transfer_rule_is_qualified_and_purpose_r: The rule disregards only specified transfers and is directed at preventing evasion of the ceiling policy.

members.legal_issue: A temporary restriction on transfers of land above an agricultural ceiling, pending determination and possession of the surplus, is a reasonable measure to implement the ceiling scheme.
material_facts: The legislation restricted a raiyat whose holding exceeded the ceiling from transferring or partitioning land while the surplus remained undetermined and unpossessed.
The restriction allowed transfers with written permission from the responsible officer.
The Court found that transfers could otherwise frustrate implementation of the ceiling scheme.
members.legal_principle: Sections 14U and 14P were ancillary to the agricultural ceiling scheme and necessary to prevent transfers from defeating it. The right to acquire, hold and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f) was subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6).
members.conclusion: The transfer restriction was not an absolute bar and was a reasonable ancillary measure.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_cei: A person brings a constitutional challenge to a law imposing a ceiling on agricultural holdings.
predicates.holding_exceeds_the_ceiling: A raiyat holds more agricultural land than the applicable ceiling permits.
predicates.transfer_restriction_is_limited_until_su: The restriction lasts only until the surplus land is identified and taken into State possession.
predicates.permission_is_available: The law allows a responsible official to authorize a transfer.

members.legal_issue: An allowance of additional land to a landholder on account of adult sons does not, without deprivation of women’s property or unequal treatment of women as landholders, establish unconstitutional sex discrimination.
material_facts: The law allowed a landholder additional permissible area on account of adult sons but not adult daughters.
The additional area remained the landholder’s property; the adult son acquired no property right under that allowance.
The law did not take a daughter’s property while retaining a son’s property, or deny a daughter a share given to a son.
members.legal_principle: Articles 14 and 15 do not invalidate a land-ceiling scheme on this ground where it does not discriminate between male and female landholders or take women’s property. The Court held that Section 5(3) did not confer property on an adult son or withdraw property from an adult daughter.
members.conclusion: The Court found no tangible sex discrimination in the additional-area rule and rejected the challenge.

rule.if: sex_discrimination_challenge_to_land_ceiling_law and adult_son_based_allowance and no_child_acquires_property_from_allowance and women_property_is_not_taken

predicates.sex_discrimination_challenge_to_land_cei: The proceeding alleges sex discrimination in a land-ceiling scheme.
predicates.adult_son_based_allowance: The scheme allows a landholder additional permissible area because of adult sons.
predicates.no_child_acquires_property_from_allowanc: Neither the adult son nor another child acquires property merely because of the allowance.
predicates.women_property_is_not_taken: The scheme does not take a woman’s property while retaining comparable property belonging to a man.

members.legal_issue: Excluding an adult unmarried daughter from the statutory definition of a landholder’s family does not, by itself, establish unconstitutional discrimination between women and men.
material_facts: The statutory definition included minor daughters but excluded adult daughters, including adult unmarried daughters, from a landholder’s family.
The holder argued that this distinction discriminated against adult unmarried daughters compared with adult unmarried sons.

The provision did not take property from a daughter or give property to a son; the scheme allowed a holder with a propertyless adult son to retain additional land, without giving the son a right to that land.
members.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require the Court to extend an additional land-retention allowance to a holder because an adult unmarried daughter exists where the legislation does not take her property or confer property on a comparable son.
